The jury ultimately ruled in favor of the will, stating that it was valid and that Black was of sound mind at that time. The trial court upheld this verdict, leading to further judicial review of the proceedings.	The plaintiffs, Brace and Cullimore, contended that their father, William Black, was not of sound mind and memory when he executed the will, thus rendering it invalid. They sought to demonstrate that his alleged insanity influenced the distribution of his estate in an unjust manner, particularly against the interests of his daughters. Their claims were supported by eyewitness accounts that were intended to establish their father's mental incompetence at the time he made the will.	The defendants, represented by John W. Black and others, argued that William Black had sufficient testamentary capacity when he executed the will, and they maintained that his decisions regarding property distribution were valid. They asserted that the plaintiffs were unable to testify about their father's mental state due to their vested interest as potential heirs, and they contended that any alleged prejudices he held against family members did not negate his understanding of property ownership and family relationships.

John G. McHatton was appointed as the collector of Schuyler County, Illinois, for the year 1839 and entered into an official bond for the faithful performance of his duties. Under the existing law, he was required to pay all collected taxes to the State Treasury by March 1, 1840. However, on February 18, 1841, a special Act of the Legislature allowed him an extension until April 1, 1841, to settle his debts with the State and county. Subsequently, the State initiated legal proceedings against McHatton and the sureties on his bond to recover the taxes due for 1839. The sureties argued that since the extension of time was granted without their consent, they should be discharged from all liability on the bond. The court had to consider whether this plea was valid under the law.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, sought a judgment against John G. McHatton and his sureties for the amount of taxes owed for the year 1839. They contended that McHatton violated his duties as the tax collector by failing to pay the collected taxes by the required deadline, and thus, the sureties should be liable under the bond.	The defendants, represented by McHatton and his sureties, argued that the special Act of February 18, 1841, which extended the payment deadline, was passed without their consent. They claimed that this extension materially altered the original contract's terms, effectively discharging them from their obligations under the bond as it suspended the State's right to pursue claims against them until after the new deadline.

In 1858, a legal case commenced in the DeKalb circuit court involving Charles O. Boynton as one of the sureties in an injunction bond. The bond was executed at the request of Hiram E. Whitney to restrain the enforcement of judgments obtained by Albert G. Robb against Whitney. The sheriff of DeKalb County, William Phelps, had previously levied these judgments on Whitney's property. An injunction was granted upon the execution of the bond, but was later dismissed in 1857, leading to a lawsuit against Boynton to recover on the bond. By the time the case reached the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1869, George L. Wood, who had acquired the judgments, had passed away, prompting the inclusion of his administrator and administratrix in the action. The jury ruled against Boynton, awarding damages to the plaintiffs. The case examined whether Whitney's actions to dismiss the injunction without Boynton’s consent released Boynton from his obligations as a surety.	The plaintiffs, represented by George L. Wood’s administrator, argued that Boynton, as a surety on the injunction bond, was liable for the debt and damages resulting from the dismissal of the injunction. They contended that their stipulation with Whitney did not violate the agreement to the detriment of Boynton because there was no collusion or fraud established. They claimed a total award based on the bond amount and incurred damages.	Boynton's main argument was that the stipulation made between Whitney and Wood, which led to the dismissal of the injunction, was a material alteration that released him from responsibility as a surety since he had not consented to it. He cited various legal precedents to support his assertion that such actions without a surety's consent could discharge their liabilities. Furthermore, Boynton claimed the plaintiffs had a sufficient levy on Whitney's property, which they failed to utilize, thereby breaching their obligations that could have benefited him.

In the case "William H. Barclay v. Lafayette H. Smith," which took place in Chicago, Illinois, the court addressed the question of whether a certificate of membership in the Board of Trade of the city could be considered property liable for the debts of its holder. The case was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 10, 1883. William H. Barclay was appealing to assert that his membership, which had a significant initiation fee of $5,000 and market value of around $4,000, should be subject to legal claim for debt satisfaction. The Court analyzed the corporation's charter, noting that membership did not provide any income or dividends and was not freely transferable since transfers required board approval. The nature of the membership was described as a privilege rather than property, and thus not subject to execution by creditors.	The plaintiff, William H. Barclay, claimed that his membership in the Chicago Board of Trade should be considered property that could be subjected to his debts through legal proceedings. He sought to recover the value of this membership through the court, arguing that the right to transact business and benefits from membership should be available to satisfy his financial obligations.	The defendant, Lafayette H. Smith, argued that a certificate of membership in the Chicago Board of Trade is not property in the legal sense and therefore cannot be seized or sold under court process for the payment of debts. The defense maintained that membership restrictions and corporate by-laws prevent the transferral of the certificate without board approval, thereby reinforcing the position that the membership is merely a privilege rather than an asset subject to creditor claims.

The case of Sardis S. Lawrence, use, etc. v. Darius Johnson et al. took place in September 1872 in Illinois. The plaintiff, Sardis S. Lawrence, was bringing an action against Darius Johnson and other defendants on a promissory note executed by them. These defendants claimed they were acting as sureties for another party, William Cleary, and asserted that the note's holder, Lucius Winston, had extended the payment deadline without their consent, which they argued relieved them of their obligations under the note. Lawrence, on the other hand, asserted that Winston was not the rightful holder of the note and thus had no authority to extend its payment terms. The case was decided by a judge in the Circuit Court of Livingston County, presided over by Honorable L. E. Payson, where a trial by the court was conducted without a jury. The court ruled in favor of the defendants, prompting Lawrence to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, Sardis S. Lawrence, contended that Lucius Winston did not hold the promissory note and, therefore, had no legal right to extend its payment deadline. Lawrence sought to hold the defendants accountable for their obligations under the note, asserting that their claims of release from liability were without merit.	The defendants argued that they signed the promissory note solely as sureties for William Cleary and claimed that the agent, Lucius Winston, extended the payment time without their consent, which they believed discharged them from their obligations. They contended that Winston's actions were unauthorized and that they should not be held liable for the note under those circumstances.

In September 1883, in DeWitt County, Illinois, John Warner loaned DeLand $2700, secured by a chattel mortgage on mules, with DeLand's daughter, Emma L. Magill, and W. H. Wheeler as sureties. After a financial settlement in November 1883, DeLand owed Magill $16,000 and transferred the mules to her, which were still subject to Warner's mortgage. In January 1884, the DeWitt County National Bank won a judgment against DeLand and executed the sale of the mules, which resulted in the bank offering Warner a settlement which he declined. Warner then sought to reclaim the mules through a writ of replevin. Following an injunction from the bank, Magill filed her own replevin against the sheriff for the mules. Eventually, Magill recovered a judgment in June 1884 for $3955.50 against the sheriff. The bank's attempts to assert its rights to the mortgage were complicated by Magill's claims. After multiple legal proceedings, the court decided to subrogate the bank to Warner’s rights under the mortgage, requiring Magill to pay the bank an amount associated with the mortgage within thirty days, ultimately affirming the decree of the Appellate Court.	Emma L. Magill, the plaintiff, contended that she rightfully owned the mules that were secured under Warner's mortgage and sought to recover from the sheriff through replevin. Following her successful recovery against the sheriff, she argued that the DeWitt County National Bank's claim to the proceeds was invalid, as she had settled her claim with the sheriff and held rightful ownership over the mules.	The DeWitt County National Bank, as the defendant, argued that it should be subrogated to Warner's rights under the mortgage after paying the owed amount into court. The bank maintained that since it had satisfied the debt owed to Warner, it was entitled to the security of the chattel mortgage and the proceeds derived from the sale of the mules, even though Warner wrested the mules via replevin proceedings.

In January 1874, a legal case took place in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning Thomas C. Reeves and Carrie M. Webster. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Tazewell County, where Carrie M. Webster, a married woman, initiated an action of replevin against Thomas C. Reeves, the county sheriff. The dispute arose from a purchase Carrie made on November 15, 1871, where she acquired a lot and its contents, including billiard tables, from John Brownlee. Despite the deed of sale transferring ownership, the defendant presented evidence of an execution against Carrie’s husband, Oliver D. Webster, which included a levy on the billiard tables. The key legal issue revolved around whether Carrie could establish her ownership of the property and the source of payment, as common law presumed that the husband owned all property in the wife's possession when living together. The court ruled that while Carrie showed she purchased the property, she failed to prove that the payment came from her separate and independent funds, which was necessary under the pertinent statutory provisions of the time.	Carrie M. Webster claimed ownership of the lot and billiard tables, arguing that she had purchased these items independently from her husband and paid for them with her own funds. She sought replevin to recover the property, asserting that she should be protected under the act of 1861 that allowed married women to hold separate property from their husbands.	Thomas C. Reeves contended that the judgment in favor of Carrie Webster was unsupported by evidence. He argued that as her husband possessed the property and was subject to creditor claims, the presumption of property ownership under common law prevented her from successfully claiming the items against the creditors of her husband. Furthermore, Reeves maintained that the plaintiff failed to establish that the purchase was made with money or property acquired independently from her husband.

The case 'Duncan, Sherman & Co. v. Nathaniel Niles' took place in Belleville, Illinois, with the events occurring around August 1, 1860, when Nathaniel Niles, the County Judge of St. Clair County, executed a promissory note promising payment of $10,000 to John F. Anderson & Co. The note stated that the county of St. Clair would repay this sum on or before August 1, 1861, without any discounts, and with interest at a rate of ten percent per annum. The plaintiffs, Duncan, Sherman & Co., received this note through endorsement on the same date it was created. However, a legal action was raised against Niles by the plaintiffs due to the non-payment of the note, leading to a demurrer being filed. The focal issue was whether Niles had the authority from the county to bind them in such an agreement, and whether he could be personally liable on the promissory note given that the contract was intended to benefit the county, not him personally. The court evaluated various precedents and the nature of the contractual representations made by Niles.	The plaintiffs asserted that Nathaniel Niles, as County Judge, was liable for the $10,000 promissory note despite the fact that he lacked authority to bind the county in this agreement. They claimed that the absence of explicit wording to hold Niles personally accountable did not absolve him from liability since he was the one who executed the agreement.	The defendant, Nathaniel Niles, contended that he had no authority from the county to enter into the promissory agreement. He argued that the note was void, as it did not contain any clear language indicating a personal obligation on his part, and maintained that any liability for the note fell upon the county, not himself.

John B. Boudreau v. Aglean Boudreau, Administratrix, etc. is a legal dispute that emerged in September 1867, in Kankakee County, Illinois. The case revolves around the ownership of two bay mares claimed by Aglean Boudreau, the administratrix of Emilien Boudreau’s estate, who alleged that her deceased husband had received these mares as a gift from his father, John B. Boudreau. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court following a jury trial, where the jury had initially sided with Aglean Boudreau, ruling that the mares were a gift. However, the evidence presented during the trial was disputed, particularly the testimony of Flora Beterneau, who suggested that the defendant had given the horses to his deceased son. In contrast, credible evidence from Louis Boudreau, Emilien's brother, indicated the horses were still owned by John B. Boudreau prior to Emilien's death. John B. Boudreau sought to overturn the jury's verdict, claiming that the evidence did not support the gift assertion, prompting the appeal.	Aglean Boudreau, as the administratrix, argued that the two bay mares were given to her deceased husband, Emilien Boudreau, as a gift from his father, John B. Boudreau. The primary legal request was for the court to recognize this purported gift and thus allow her to reclaim possession of the mares, which she asserted were rightfully part of her late husband's estate.	John B. Boudreau contested the claim, asserting that the supposed gift of the mares had not been proven with the requisite evidence. He maintained that the witnesses who could confirm the actual ownership and circumstances surrounding the mares refuted Aglean Boudreau's claims. He requested a new trial, arguing that the jury's decision was significantly against the weight of the evidence presented, which established that he retained ownership of the mares and had not given them as a gift.

The case of Abel C. Benedict et al. v. James Miner took place in January 1871 in Morgan County, Illinois. The dispute centered around a promissory note totaling $1,700, dated March 3, 1868, which was originally set to be paid in May but had been altered to draw interest from April 1. The payee, James Miner, was attempting to enforce the note against defendants Abel C. Benedict and Theodore E. Curtis. While Benedict was aware of the alteration, Curtis was not informed of it. After the change, Curtis made a payment of $1,000 towards the note but only learned about the mortgage executed by Benedict, which was meant to indemnify him, months later. The case was brought to trial, which was held without a jury, and the court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, granting Miner a judgment of $876.84, despite the contested details of the note's alteration.	James Miner, the plaintiff, claimed that the defendants had an obligation to fulfill the terms of the altered promissory note that drew interest from April instead of May. He argued that despite the alteration—made without Curtis's knowledge—Curtis's subsequent payment and the mortgage from Benedict should validate the enforceability of the note. Miner sought to recover the amount owed on the note after them deducting the prior payment.	The defendants, particularly Curtis, contended that the alteration of the promissory note voided his obligation to pay because he was not informed of the change. Curtis argued that his payment of $1,000 did not constitute a ratification of the altered note as he made the payment without knowledge of the change and was unaware of the mortgage intended to protect him from loss related to the note. Therefore, they claimed the judgment should favor the defendants.

The case "Ezekiel Morrison v. Armanella R. Brown" took place in September 1876, involving a dispute over a lien on a piece of real estate in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals in the case are the plaintiff, Ezekiel Morrison, and the defendant, Armanella R. Brown. The situation arose when Mrs. Brown, as a feme sole, sold a property (lot 6, in block 4 of Brainard & Evans’ addition) to Mrs. Elizabeth Martin for $2,500 on February 10, 1872. Mrs. Martin paid a third of the price upfront, leaving an outstanding balance of $1,666.66, which she secured through two promissory notes and a trust deed executed to Mrs. Brown via a trustee, William Post. The deeds were recorded on February 18, 1872. Subsequently, on May 10, 1873, Mrs. Martin sold the property to Michael Flynn without disclosing Mrs. Brown's lien, receiving $3,700. Flynn claimed he was unaware of any liens. Later, Ezekiel Morrison purchased Flynn's promissory notes and the deed of trust in August 1873, also without knowledge of Mrs. Brown’s claim. Mrs. Brown then sought a court decree to recognize her lien as superior to subsequent claims, leading to the current litigation seeking reversal of that decree.	Ezekiel Morrison, the appellant, argued that the previous court's recognition of Mrs. Brown’s lien was erroneous as it was based on a deed of trust executed solely by a married woman, which lacked validity as a conveyance. He contended that he had purchased the notes without any notice of Mrs. Brown's claim, implying that subsequent purchasers should not be held accountable for undisclosed liens.	Armanella R. Brown, the appellee, maintained that despite the deed of trust being invalid as a conveyance due to her not having her husband’s consent, it still served as a declaration preserving her vendor’s lien. She argued that her lien should be upheld since her deed was recorded, providing constructive notice to any subsequent purchasers, thereby protecting her equitable rights.

In 1874, the case "Mary E. Heald v. Charles A. Wright et al." was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court following prior proceedings in the Superior Court of Cook County. The case transpires around an intricate land transaction that began on June 16, 1857, when H.M. Heald sold a tract of land to J. Augustus Wright for $3,700, receiving $600 cash and three promissory notes of $700 each, secured by a mortgage. The transaction included an agreement allowing Heald to repurchase the land within a year. By June 16, 1858, Wright expressed his intention to resell the property back to Heald under the terms stipulating that Heald would pay back the amount owed. However, the parties involved tangled in subsequent transactions, with Heald’s son, Dwight S. Heald, assuming responsibilities to pay off the debt in connection with the land, but without making any payments. Wright passed away intestate in 1862, leaving behind minor heirs and no administration was undertaken for his estate. The case centers on Mary E. Heald's claim regarding her right to redeem the property after receiving it via her son’s will, amidst arguments related to the nature of the deed and Wright's failure to declare forfeiture.	Mary E. Heald, as the plaintiff, sought a decree recognizing the deed from her husband to Wright as a mortgage instead of a sale, allowing her to redeem the property by paying the amount owed without any encumbrances by Wright or his heirs. Her main arguments hinged on asserting her rights following her son’s demise and claiming that Wright held the title merely as security for the original payment.	The defense, represented by the heirs of J. Augustus Wright, contended that Wright acquired a clear title to the land and that Heald had forfeited any rights through laches, having waited until property values had increased before trying to assert rights to the land. They insisted there was no basis for Mary E. Heald to claim redemption, given the circumstances surrounding Wright's estate and the timeline of transactions.

In the case of **James B. Close v. John R. Stuyvesant**, which took place in Illinois, the legal dispute arose from a contract exchange made on July 22, 1887. The plaintiff, John R. Stuyvesant, and the defendant, James B. Close, agreed that Stuyvesant would exchange his 4,320-acre ranch in Osborne County, Kansas, for Close's properties in Chicago, which were encumbered by mortgages. The agreement was clear, yet Stuyvesant claimed that Close refused to fulfill his part of the contract. The court had to assess the legitimacy of the property titles involved. Stuyvesant believed he held a valid title to the acreage, while Close contended that certain parts of the land ownership were either unpatented or fraudulently acquired under pre-emption and homestead laws. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, with Justice Bailey delivering the opinion on May 10, 1890.	The plaintiff, John R. Stuyvesant, argues that he is entitled to a decree for the specific performance of the exchange agreement whereby he would swap his Osborne County ranch for Close's properties in Chicago. Stuyvesant claimed that he was ready to fulfill his obligations under the contract but faced refusal from Close to proceed with the exchange. He maintained that his titles to the ranch were valid and sought enforcement of the contract.	The defendant, James B. Close, contended that he should not be compelled to enter the contract due to significant doubts regarding the legitimacy of Stuyvesant’s title. Specifically, he alleged that the lands in question were acquired through fraud, as the settlers who claimed them allegedly made entries merely to benefit Stuyvesant. Close argued that the entries made under the pre-emption and homestead laws were void, and thus, he requested that the court not enforce the contract until Stuyvesant could provide acceptable security against the potential failure of the title.

In 1868, in Titusville, Pennsylvania, John G. Brown and his associates were engaged in shipping and dealing in crude petroleum oil. Their business dealings intersected with Albert A. Pierce and his associates, who were also dealers in oil and interested in a pipe line at Titusville. The defendants purchased oil from the plaintiffs, buying 25 cars of oil at a rate of $4 per barrel on October 30 and 6 additional cars at $3.30 per barrel on November 12, with cash on delivery stipulated as the payment method. After the oil was loaded into their cars by a pipe company, it was inspected and accepted by the defendants’ agent. However, when the plaintiffs received a draft for payment, it was protested, leading to a complicated settlement that included an accepted draft and a bill of sale for a pipe line owned by the defendants. Disputes arose regarding the quality of the oil, which the defendants claimed was not of prime quality and contained water and sediment. Consequently, the plaintiffs sued on three bills of exchange for the payment of the oil. The issue was tried without a jury in the Superior Court of Cook County.	The plaintiffs argued that they fulfilled their contractual obligation by providing oil that was inspected and accepted by the defendants' agent. They claimed that the bills of exchange were valid and had not been paid despite being drawn in connection with the oil sale. The plaintiffs sought recovery of the face value of the three bills of exchange along with accrued interest.	The defendants contended that the oil provided by the plaintiffs was not of the quality they had represented. They claimed that before accepting the drafts, they had not had the opportunity to adequately inspect the oil, which they asserted was largely contaminated with water and sediment. They also introduced claims related to the use and hire of their cars by the plaintiffs as part of their defense.

The case of Jo Robinson et al. v. John Moore was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1860. The dispute arose from a judgment rendered in the Circuit Court of Saline County, Illinois. The appellants, Jo Robinson and others, challenged the judgment on the grounds that it was rendered in Harrisburg, arguing that the legal county seat of Saline County was Raleigh. The primary issue was whether Harrisburg or Raleigh served as the true legal county seat. However, the court found that the record did not provide clear evidence regarding the location of the court proceedings or the county seat itself. The court concluded that such a question regarding the location of the county seat could not be settled collaterally and needed to be addressed in a direct proceeding instead.	The plaintiffs, Jo Robinson et al., claimed that the judgment should be invalidated because it was rendered in Harrisburg rather than Raleigh, which they asserted was the official county seat of Saline County. They sought to have the court recognize Raleigh as the legal county seat to support their case.	The defendant, John Moore, contended that the plaintiffs' arguments were unfounded, as there was no clear evidence in the record to support their claim about the county seat's location. He argued that regardless of any claims about Harrisburg being void, the plaintiffs had participated in the case by filing a plea and defending the action, which negated their position.

Hart H. Harris et al. v. George M. Pullman et al. was adjudicated in September 1876 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case involved two plaintiffs, John S. Harris and Charles H. Wheeler, who were residents of Wisconsin, and several defendants, including George M. Pullman, David A. Gage, and Franklin Parmelee, who were based in Illinois, along with non-resident defendants James E. Lyon and Charles H. Moore. The plaintiffs sought a ruling that the defendants were trustees of specific mining properties in Colorado, and they requested the defendants to account for the earnings from these properties, vacate possession, and refrain from interfering with the properties or pursuing judgments obtained against them in Colorado. The crux of the dispute centered around ownership and possession of various mining claims, especially to fiscal receipts and profits derived from these claims. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants wrongfully possessed the property through invalid judgments, while the defendants asserted that they rightfully owned the property based on legal deeds executed during sheriff sales resulting from those judgments.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants were holding certain mining properties in Colorado as trustees and sought a legal declaration to that effect. They requested an accounting of all profits and receipts from the properties, demanded the return of possession, and sought to enjoin the defendants from entering these properties or pursuing any claims against them in other courts.	The defendants contended that they were the rightful owners of the mining properties based on valid legal transactions, including sheriff's sales resulting from judgments against the plaintiffs. They claimed that the plaintiffs' assertions were unfounded and denied any obligation to return possession of the properties as well as any fiduciary responsibilities.

The case "The Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company v. The People ex rel., etc" arose in Springfield, Illinois, where the plaintiff sought a mandamus to compel the Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company to make certain improvements to Salome Avenue. This legal proceeding stemmed from an ordinance passed on March 5, 1869, granting the Pana, Springfield & Northwestern Railroad Company the right of way, contingent upon them ensuring the street would remain passable for teams and carriages. The ordinance also mandated adequate crossings for pedestrians and proper drainage for the street. The railway company later acquired the rights to this track. By August 8, 1887, the city passed an ordinance requiring the construction of a sewer along Salome Avenue, which was deemed necessary for the drainage and usability of the street. The plaintiff argued that the railway company failed to comply with this ordinance despite being properly notified. The court had to assess whether the requested improvements were necessary for the street’s drainage and use, given the railway's assertions that the area was adequately drained and passable.	The plaintiffs argued that the Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company was legally obligated to construct a sewer along Salome Avenue, as mandated by a city ordinance passed in 1887. They claimed this sewer was essential for adequate drainage and the safe passage of teams and carriages. The plaintiffs contended that the railway company's refusal to comply with the ordinance warranted a peremptory mandamus to enforce the construction of the sewer.	The defendants, representing the Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company, contended that the requested sewer was not necessary for the drainage or travel along Salome Avenue. They argued that a natural ravine already served the drainage needs and claimed that the company had inherited any obligations only after substantial time had passed since those obligations were originally imposed. Furthermore, they asserted that the passage of time had barred the plaintiffs' claims under the doctrine of laches and the statute of limitations, requesting dismissal of the case.

In 1875, in the Piatt Circuit Court, Illinois, the case of John M. Skidmore v. Annabel Bricker arose from a prior incident involving a riot. Annabel Bricker (the appellee) brought an action against John M. Skidmore (the appellant) alleging malicious prosecution and unlawful imprisonment. The prosecution stemmed from a complaint made by Skidmore, who acted on his knowledge of the facts rather than on hearsay. The case proceeded to trial, where the jury ruled in favor of Bricker, awarding damages of $770. Following the verdict, Skidmore filed a motion for a new trial, which was denied, prompting him to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. During the appeal, several key legal issues were addressed, including the admissibility of character evidence, the prosecutor's reliance on legal advice, and the appropriateness of admitting the record of acquittal evidence into court.	Annabel Bricker claimed that John M. Skidmore maliciously prosecuted her, leading to her wrongful imprisonment. She argued that Skidmore lacked probable cause for his actions and that he acted with malice. In her lawsuit, she sought damages for the emotional and physical distress caused by the prosecution and imprisonment.	John M. Skidmore contended that he acted on the advice of a respectable attorney, who assured him he had probable cause to proceed with the prosecution against Bricker. He claimed that since the prosecution was based on his own knowledge of the events, he did not act maliciously. Furthermore, he argued that evidence regarding Bricker's character and the record of her acquittal should not have been admitted during the trial.

Ezra M. Prince v. Sarah P. Dulin et al. took place in McLean County, Illinois. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision rendered on November 23, 1889, following an evaluation that began at the May term of 1888. The case revolves around a replevin action, where Ezra M. Prince filed against Sarah P. Dulin and others. The parties involved were engaged in a dispute concerning a chattel mortgage and a $500 note intended to secure contract performance. The court found that the defendants, Dulin et al., had failed to comply with their part of the agreement, leading to complications regarding the mortgage and associated damages. A stipulation was later filed to reinstate the case in the county court, enabling a summary hearing of the evidence to determine the damages. A judgment in favor of Prince amounting to $20 was made following the trial.	The plaintiff, Ezra M. Prince, claimed that the defendants had failed to fulfill their contractual obligations, which had caused him damages. He requested the court to allow the consideration of all costs and expenses incurred due to this breach. Prince sought to hold the property covered by the chattel mortgage or the financial equivalent necessary to cover his incurred costs.	The defendants, represented by Tipton & Beaver, contested the claim and the basis for the appeal, arguing that the proceedings did not constitute a suit suitable for appeal. They sought to dismiss the appeal based on this argument, claiming that the legal action brought against them lacked validity.

M. M. Thompson et al. v. J. F. Duff is a case stemming from a replevin action initiated in the Circuit Court of Jackson County, Illinois, which culminated in a decision rendered on June 12, 1886. The key individuals involved included the plaintiffs, M. M. Thompson, Lipe, and Wm. O. Woods, and the defendant, J. F. Duff. The dispute revolved around the ownership of a steam engine, boiler, sawmill, and related tools. The central issue arose from a contract between the Mansfield Machine Works of Ohio and J. A. Woods, Wm. C. Woods, and James H. Vaughn, specifying sale terms that remained unfulfilled, notably the failure of Woods and Vaughn to make the required cash payment or provide necessary security. The plaintiffs argued they had acquired interests in the property through subsequent transactions with Woods, despite dubious payment claims. Duff, the defendant, countered that he had purchased the property legitimately from the agent of the Machine Works and had made payments as agreed. The jury's task was to determine the validity of the transactions and claims asserting ownership amidst conflicting testimonies.	The plaintiffs, Thompson and Lipe, claimed ownership of the property based on alleged purchases from Wm. O. Woods and Wm. C. Woods. They argued that they had either been defrauded or misled regarding the legitimate title to the property. They sought recovery of the steam engine, boiler, sawmill, and tools, asserting that their transactions were valid and asserting rights based on their claimed investments.	The defendant, J. F. Duff, contended that he held legitimate ownership of the disputed property, having acquired it from the agent of the Mansfield Machine Works per a recognized contract, with payments made by him. He argued that the plaintiffs’ claims derived from fraudulent transactions and that they should not benefit from alleged sales that were not conducted in good faith. Duff's defense highlighted that the plaintiffs were aware of the original vendor's rights and obligations that undermined their ownership claims.

On October 19, 1884, Joseph Corder died intestate in Coles County, Illinois. The only heirs of Joseph were his two brothers, William B. Corder and James B. Corder. William filed a lawsuit to partition approximately five hundred acres of land owned by Joseph at the time of his death. James was named as the defendant in this case. While James admitted most of the allegations in the bill, he countered with a cross-bill claiming that a specific farm known as the "Pierce farm," totaling one hundred and forty acres, belonged to Joseph's estate. James alleged that William had purchased this land with funds provided by Joseph, thus asserting that William held the title in trust. William denied these claims and contended that Joseph had no interest in the Pierce farm. The court dismissed James's cross-bill after a thorough examination of the extensive evidence presented by both parties. The evidence indicated that William purchased and controlled the land as his own for several years without Joseph asserting ownership or providing credible evidence of financial involvement.	James B. Corder, the plaintiff, claimed ownership of the Pierce farm, arguing that it was part of Joseph Corder's estate. He alleged that William B. Corder acquired the property using Joseph's money and thus held title only as a trustee for Joseph. James requested a partition of this land between himself and William.	William B. Corder, the defendant, denied James's allegations, asserting that the Pierce farm was purchased legitimately in his name, and that Joseph did not provide any funds for the purchase. William maintained that he had leased the farm and operated it as his own for years after acquiring it, contesting the validity of James's claims regarding a resulting trust.

Edward H. James and James L. James, the appellants, pursued a legal action against Alexander Dunlap, the appellee, in a case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1840. The event in question centered around an incident that occurred on November 29, 1838, in Morgan County, Illinois. The plaintiffs alleged that Dunlap, serving as the county sheriff, unlawfully seized their mules and horses, which were their property, taking them out of their possession. Dunlap countered that he had acted within his duties as sheriff, having seized the animals under attachments issued against the plaintiffs' goods and chattels just a day prior to the seizure. The plaintiffs contended that Dunlap was not the sheriff at the time the attachments were issued and, therefore, his actions were unlawful. This legal dispute centered around the interpretation of whether Dunlap was indeed acting as sheriff when he seized the animals and whether the plaintiffs' defense against this claim was valid. The case presented key questions regarding authority and legal procedural requirements for sheriff actions in property seizure cases.	The plaintiffs claimed that Alexander Dunlap unlawfully took their mules and horses out of their possession on November 29, 1838. They argued that Dunlap was not the sheriff of Morgan County at the time the attachments were issued on November 28, 1838, and therefore lacked the legal authority to confiscate their property. They sought the return of their animals and damages for the unlawful replevin.	The defendant, Alexander Dunlap, contended that he acted within his legal capacity as the sheriff of Morgan County when he seized the plaintiffs' property based on valid attachments issued against them. He demurred to the plaintiffs' plea, arguing that the issue of whether he was sheriff when the attachments were issued was immaterial to the case, as he was undoubtedly the sheriff at the time of the property seizure on November 29, 1838.

The case "City of Lake View v. H. Tate" was brought to the Illinois Appellate Court on April 17, 1889, following a previous trial in the Criminal Court of Cook County. The city of Lake View, located along Lake Michigan, had enacted an ordinance limiting the speed of trains in one railroad district to ten miles per hour. The engineer H. Tate, employed by the Chicago & Evanston Railway Co., was charged with violating this ordinance by running a train through the city at a prohibited speed. The Criminal Court found Tate not guilty, leading the City of Lake View to appeal the decision. The ordinance in question aimed to differentiate between two competing railroads that traversed Lake View, essentially regulating only the operations of the Chicago & Evanston Railway and allowing the Chicago and North-Western Railway to operate without restrictions. This created discrimination against the Chicago & Evanston Railway. The court needed to determine whether the ordinance was a just and reasonable exercise of the city's regulatory power.	The City of Lake View contended that H. Tate violated the municipal ordinance by operating his train in excess of the speed limit set for the East Railroad District. The city argued that the ordinance was a valid exercise of its police powers to ensure public safety within its jurisdiction.	H. Tate, representing the Chicago & Evanston Railway, argued that the city’s ordinance was unreasonable and discriminatory. He noted that the ordinance only restricted one railroad while permitting its competitor to operate unrestricted, thereby creating an unfair advantage and violating principles of equal treatment under the law. Tate asserted that the ordinance failed to justify such differential treatment and should be deemed invalid.

In the year 1872, Andrew Anderson faced a legal challenge from the People of the State of Illinois, with proceedings held in the Circuit Court of Ford County. The indictment against Anderson was for selling liquor without a legal license, which was a violation of Illinois state law. Under the relevant statute, individuals without a license to operate a grocery were prohibited from selling vinous, spirituous, or mixed liquors, especially in quantities less than a gallon. The case centered around whether the indictment properly stated that Anderson sold the liquor for his gain or on his premises. The court found that the specific averments about selling for gain or benefit, and about selling on his premises, were not necessary within the context of statutory interpretation. Chief Justice Lawrence delivered the court's opinion, affirming the conviction, stating that the language of the statute was clear and did not require extensive discussion.	The plaintiff, represented by Mr. M. D. Brown, argued that Andrew Anderson had violated the statute by selling liquor without a license. The claims were based on the statutory provision that prohibits the sale of liquors for personal gain or benefit without the requisite license. The plaintiff sought a conviction of Anderson for this illicit sale under the established law.	The defendant, Andrew Anderson, contended that the indictment was insufficient as it did not allege he sold the liquor for his gain or that such sales occurred on his premises. He argued that these specifications were necessary for a valid indictment. The defense aimed to have the charges dismissed based on this technicality regarding the interpretation of the statute.

In the case of Francis Honner v. The Illinois Central Railroad Company, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, during May 1854, the plaintiff, Francis Honner, was an employee of the railroad company. The court case arose from an incident involving a turntable used to maneuver locomotives and cars. It was claimed that while Honner was operating the turntable along with his fellow workers, an iron bar attached to the turntable malfunctioned and struck him, resulting in injury. Honner alleged that the defendants, through their agents and servants, negligently constructed and managed the turntable and its components, leading to the accident. Legal precedents had not favored similar actions historically, as such claims generally revolved around whether an employer could be held liable for the negligent acts of one servant towards another when both were engaged in their employment duties.	The plaintiff, Francis Honner, argued that he was injured due to the careless construction and management of the turntable, which he claimed was the responsibility of the defendants. He sought compensation for his injuries, asserting that the defendants should be liable due to negligence in ensuring safe working conditions for their employees.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company's defense centered on the principle that an employer is not liable for the negligent acts of one servant towards another when both are engaged in the same business. They contended that the plaintiff's injury may have been partially due to his own carelessness and pointed out that liability for such injuries should not extend to the employer without clear evidence of wrongdoing or knowledge of defects on their part.

In September 1868, the case of George A. Seaverns et al. v. Joseph W. Tribby was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over the sale of a quantity of broom corn, specifically seventy-seven tons and five hundred forty-two pounds, which the plaintiff, George A. Seaverns, claimed he had sold to the defendant, Joseph W. Tribby, at a price of $140 per ton. The corn was delivered as per the contract, and the plaintiff sought to recover a balance he alleged was still owed after deducting payments made by the defendants. During the trial, the court provided specific jury instructions regarding how to determine the amount owed based on the evidence presented. The defendants contended that the total amount for the corn had already been paid and objected to the jury instructions, arguing they assumed a debt still existed and were misleading. The case went to appeal after the trial court rendered a judgment in favor of the plaintiff, but the instructions and evidentiary issues raised by the defense prompted a need for reconsideration.	The plaintiffs’ main arguments centered around their assertion that they sold a specified amount of broom corn to the defendants, which was delivered and accepted according to the contract terms. They claimed there was a remaining balance due after accounting for previous payments made. The plaintiffs requested that the court ensure the jury was instructed to consider only the correct evidence and calculate the remaining balance owed based on the full sale amount minus any credits.	The defendants insisted that the entire amount due for the broom corn had already been settled. They argued that the jury instructions were erroneous, as they assumed an outstanding balance when they believed that no such debt existed. Furthermore, they pointed out that the instructions did not adequately allow for all credits concerning a note against the plaintiff, which contributed to their objection to the proceedings.

The case "The St. Louis and Sandoval Coal and Mining Company v. The Sandoval Coal and Mining Company" involves a dispute over possession of a coal mine located in Sandoval, Marion County, Illinois. The action of ejectment was initiated by the St. Louis and Sandoval Coal and Mining Company, which claimed title in fee to the property. The plaintiff was incorporated in December 1877, with a capital stock of $50,000, specifically for coal mining operations in the area. Due to financial difficulties, a receiver was appointed via a complaint filed by creditors, leading to the dissolution of the corporation and the sale of its assets. The original sale of the property was contested on the grounds that the court lacked proper jurisdiction over the company. The proceedings went through various legal challenges, culminating in an appeal from the plaintiff after the lower court found in favor of the defendant. The crucial issue revolved around whether the court had acquired proper jurisdiction to validate the receiver's sales, with past precedents influencing the ruling on jurisdictional authority and potential errors in earlier judgments.	The plaintiff argued that they maintained ownership of the coal mine property since its incorporation, claiming that the sale executed by the receiver was invalid due to a lack of jurisdiction in the preceding court case. They sought a judgment to recover the possession of the mine, based on their legal ownership, and contended that the actions taken under the alleged invalid decree were null and void.	The defendant contended that the plaintiff was not a legally recognized corporation at the time the ejectment action was initiated, claiming that they rightfully purchased the property from the receiver appointed by the court. The defendant argued that the original court had jurisdiction over the matter, and thus, any resulting decree—including the appointment of the receiver and the subsequent sale—was valid. They requested the court to affirm the judgment rendered in favor of the defendant in the lower court.

The case of Philip Clark v. Bayless Lake was tried in December 1835 in the Sangamon Circuit Court, Illinois. The dispute arose when the plaintiff, Philip Clark, accused defendant Bayless Lake of erecting a dam across the navigable Sangamon River, which had been designated as a public highway by state law. Clark claimed that due to the dam, he was unable to navigate the river while transporting a boat load of corn, resulting in the loss of both his boat and its contents. The plaintiff intended to reach lower markets in Natchez or New Orleans but was impeded by the dam. During the trial, evidence was presented from which the plaintiff argued that he had ample water to navigate the river were it not for the obstruction caused by the defendant's dam. However, the defendant queried whether another dam downstream could have posed the same obstruction, leading to Clark's inability to reach his destination, which the court allowed despite objections from the plaintiff's counsel. Ultimately, the case revolved around whether the Circuit Court made an error in admitting this testimony during the trial.	Philip Clark claimed that the defendant, by constructing a dam across the Sangamon River, obstructed his navigational rights on a public highway, leading to the loss of his boat and cargo. He argued that the obstruction caused significant economic damage as his corn was worth considerably more in the market than where it was stranded. Clark sought compensation for the value of the lost corn and boat due to the alleged negligence of the defendant in erecting the dam in a navigable waterway.	The defendant, Bayless Lake, argued against the plaintiff's claims by questioning the relevance of the testimony regarding other dams in the river. Lake's key argument revolved around the assertion that if Clark could have passed over his dam, he would have been met with further obstacles downstream, which would have likewise prevented him from reaching his market destinations. The defendant contended that this evidence was crucial in understanding the complete circumstances surrounding the navigation issues faced by the plaintiff.

The case of Harvey S. Hayden et al. v. A. J. Hoxie et al. took place in Wisconsin during the winter of 1885-1886, involving the sale of lumber. The plaintiffs, Hayden and associates, purchased lumber from the defendants, Hoxie and Hellor, at a rate of $10 per thousand feet. There was a lack of a clear agreement regarding inspection prior to loading, although there had been discussions that implied the quality of the lumber shipped would be acceptable. An issue arose over the quality of the lumber delivered, as the plaintiffs received lumber that included varying grades, specifically common grade and mill culls. During the proceedings, disputes occurred regarding the admissibility of memoranda that documented the inspection and grading of the lumber, leading to confusion over the quantity and quality of the lumber in question. The trial court ruled the memoranda inadmissible, which the defendants contested, asserting that their witness could accurately testify based on those records. The trial primarily hinged not on the quantity of lumber received but on its quality and whether the defendants had fulfilled their contractual obligations regarding that quality.	The plaintiffs contended that the lumber provided by the defendants did not meet the quality standards implied during negotiations. They sought to hold the defendants accountable for the inferior quality of lumber, arguing that the lumber was not as described and that they should only be required to pay for the value of the lesser quality delivered. Their primary legal request involved a balance owed for the lumber that they deemed unacceptable based on the terms of the sale.	The defendants argued that they had fulfilled their contractual obligations by delivering the agreed-upon quantity of lumber. They maintained that the quality of the lumber was as per agreement, and any discrepancies were not disclosed at the time of sale, as their agent had not intended to rely on the inspection conducted by the appellees. They contested the trial court's refusal to allow their memoranda into evidence, asserting that this prevented a fair assessment of the lumber's quality, and requested that the judgment be reversed.

William Byars was prosecuted by the City of Mt. Vernon, Illinois, in June 1875, for selling intoxicating liquors without a legal license, in violation of a city ordinance. The events leading to the prosecution began on March 2, 1874, when city marshal Samuel D. Cooper filed a complaint against Byars, claiming he sold intoxicating liquors without possessing a license to operate a grocery store. After the police magistrate denied Byars’ motion to quash the complaint, he was found guilty in a trial and fined $200. Byars appealed the decision, arguing the complaint was insufficient and that he may have held a license. The circuit court upheld the original decision, prompting him to continue his legal battle.	The City of Mt. Vernon claimed that Byars sold intoxicating liquors in the city without a proper license, violating city ordinance No. 37. The city provided evidence, including the ordinance itself, which explicitly prohibited unlicensed sales of intoxicating liquors and established penalties for violating its provisions. The plaintiff sought to enforce the ordinance and collect fines imposed for each violation recorded against Byars.	Byars contended that the complaint against him was insufficient as it was based merely on hearsay ("information and belief") and did not definitively show he lacked a grocery license. He also argued that the complaint did not specify the penalty amount on summons and claimed procedural errors, such as insufficiently established evidence of his alleged violations. Byars requested to quash the complaint and sought to contest the judgment against him.

The case of Edward Prince v. The City of Quincy was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court on January 29, 1883. The dispute originated over a contract in which Edward Prince, the plaintiff, claimed that the city of Quincy failed to pay him for water services rendered under a special contract. This contract was agreed to by the city council, obligating Prince to supply water for a period of thirty years at specified prices. However, the city of Quincy raised a significant constitutional defense, asserting that at the time the contract was made, it was already indebted beyond the constitutional limit of five percent of its taxable property value. Therefore, the city contended that it could not incur any additional debt, including for ordinary expenses like the contract with Prince. The court referenced previous judgments, emphasizing that once a city is deemed indebted beyond the constitutional limit, it is powerless to create further debts.	Edward Prince argued that he had fulfilled his contractual obligations to provide water to the city of Quincy and sought compensation for the services rendered. He contended that the city's existing indebtedness should not invalidate the contractual relationship established between himself and the city.	The city of Quincy defended against Prince's claims by asserting that it was already indebted beyond constitutional limits, thereby rendering any contract for additional debts, including Prince's claims for unpaid water services, unenforceable. The city argued that this constitutional provision applies universally, regardless of the purpose of the debt, including necessary current expenses.

On August 7, 1857, in Rockford, Illinois, Edward N. Mitchell and Reuben P. Layton, bankers, agreed to loan $200 to John B. Young, who needed a surety for the loan. Young proposed Richard Montague as the surety, and the bankers consented. However, Montague had no interest in the loan, which was for Young's benefit. Young signed the note and obtained Montague's signature without informing him about the nature of the agreement. As the note became due, Young requested extensions from the bankers without Montague's knowledge or consent, paying small fees for extensions. In Feb 1859, based on the signed note, the bankers entered a judgment against Montague for $220, including costs, leading to an execution that threatened to levy Montague's property. Montague filed a bill of complaint on April 5, 1858, seeking to have the judgment set aside and an injunction against execution due to improper procedures regarding the judgments and lack of consent.	Montague argued that he was merely a surety and that the extensions granted to Young without his knowledge discharged him from liability on the note. He claimed that he was wrongfully subjected to a judgment that was entered without his consent or notice. Montague sought the court's intervention to set aside the judgment against him and to grant a perpetual injunction against the collection of the judgment.	The defendants, including Young and the bankers, contended that Montague was aware of the loan arrangements and that he had previously been a partner with Young in the lumber business. They argued that the note was understood to be for the joint benefit of both Montague and Young, and denied that extensions of the loan constituted an agreement that discharged Montague from his obligations. They maintained that the entry of judgment was lawful and contested Montague's claims for an injunction.

In 1857, Nelson Mason sold a property in Sterling, Whiteside County, Illinois, to Allen Schenck, who later transferred an interest to his partner, B.G. Wheeler. Mason's legal title was fraudulently conveyed to John A. Bross, who intended to return it to Mason in his will. After Bross's death, a court proceeding to settle debts of Wheeler & Co. led to Mason regaining legal title, allegedly through a deceptive scheme to evade creditors. The plaintiffs, claiming equitable ownership, filed a bill against Mason and Robert Cochran, seeking a legal conveyance of the property. A lower court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to an appeal by Mason and Cochran against the court's decision. The Supreme Court of Illinois evaluated the original transaction, the validity of the decrees involved, and ultimately affirmed the lower court's judgment based on the established facts and procedural integrity.	The plaintiffs argued that they were the equitable owners of the real estate in question and sought specific performance of the contract for the sale and conveyance of the property from Mason. They asserted that the previous judgments established their rightful claim and that Mason's attempts to contest the sale and title were invalid. They emphasized that due process had been followed in the prior decrees, which allowed for the sale of the property to them.	Mason and Cochran contended that the decrees under which the plaintiffs claimed title were flawed, mainly arguing that the initial sale did not legally include their interests. They raised objections to the validity of the previous court proceedings and asserted that there had been no proper hearing or evidence presented against them. Mason also claimed that he had not been fully compensated for the property, aiming to uphold his rights against the equitable judgments.

In the Matter of the Conservatorship of Henry P. Hall took place in Illinois, with the legal proceedings culminating in a court decision on February 25, 1886. The case involved A. L. Barnett, who served as the conservator for Henry P. Hall, a person deemed insane. Barnett was appointed in 1863, but his management of Hall’s affairs was marked by a lack of organization and negligence. His first financial report was submitted in 1876, revealing no proper accounting of receipts or expenditures for the thirteen years of his conservatorship. Initially, he reported a balance of $26.55; however, subsequent audits revealed discrepancies amounting to a balance of $1,055.50. Following his removal in February 1884 due to mismanagement, Barnett sought to contest the court's findings, leading to multiple appeals through the circuit court. Eventually, the circuit court determined that Barnett owed a reduced balance of $612.28 to his successor based on further evaluations of his financial practices, which were then challenged once again on appeal.	The plaintiff, representing the interests of Henry P. Hall, claimed that A. L. Barnett, the conservator, had mismanaged Hall's finances, failed to maintain proper accounts, and thus owed restitution based on inaccurate financial reports. They asserted that Barnett's negligence and failure to fulfill statutory requirements necessitated the court's intervention to determine the correct balance to be transferred to the new conservator.	A. L. Barnett, the defendant, contended that the court erred in disallowing specific credits he claimed for his services during the conservatorship. He challenged the court's decision to limit his compensation from $390 to $25 per annum from 1876 onward. Barnett argued that the expenses incurred in contesting the earlier county court order were legitimate and should be compensated. Moreover, he asserted that he should not be held responsible for the alleged mismanagement, claiming he acted without intentional wrongdoing.

Abijah Hull brought an action of trespass against defendants Abner Blaisdell, a constable, and John C. Smith, a justice of the peace, for unlawfully seizing his property. This incident occurred on July 2, 1832, in St. Clair County, Illinois, when Smith issued an attachment for a debt owed by Hull that exceeded the $30 limit allowed by law. The attachment called for seizing property, specifically two hundred bushels of lime and other items belonging to Hull, which Blaisdell executed. The key individuals involved in this case were Abijah Hull (the plaintiff), Abner Blaisdell (the constable), and John C. Smith (the justice of the peace). Hull argued that the attachment was illegal and that both Blaisdell and Smith were liable for the trespass, as they acted outside their legal authority.	Hull claimed that Blaisdell and Smith unlawfully seized his property without proper legal authority, as the attachment issued by Smith was for an amount exceeding the allowed limit of $30. He argued that this action constituted a trespass, and he sought damages for the unlawful taking of his goods. Hull's main legal requests included a reversal of the judgment from the lower court and an award for the costs of the case due to the defendants' improper actions.	The defendants, Blaisdell and Smith, pleaded the general issue, asserting that their actions were lawful under the circumstances presented. They contended that the attachment was valid and justified, despite the amount exceeding the statutory limit. Their defense relied on the claim that there was no material variance between the evidence presented and the declaration filed by Hull. They requested that the court uphold the judgment in their favor from the earlier trial.

The case of "The St. Louis and Southeastern Railway Co. v. Henry Britz" took place in April 1874 in French Village, Illinois. The plaintiff, Henry Britz, was employed as a laborer on a construction train operated by the defendant, The St. Louis and Southeastern Railway Co. During his work, Britz was tasked with shoveling gravel, which necessitated riding on the train while it operated. On the evening of April 3, 1873, while Britz was aboard the train, it collided with a stationary passenger train. As a result of this collision, Britz was either thrown from the car or jumped off to avoid further injury, leading to the injuries he subsequently claimed in court. The jury ruled in favor of Britz, determining that he suffered due to the negligence of the railway company, and awarded him $250 in damages.	The plaintiff, Henry Britz, claimed that his injuries resulted from the negligence of The St. Louis and Southeastern Railway Co. He argued that the railway company failed to provide proper brakes for the train cars, which contributed to the accident. Britz sought damages for his injuries, asserting that if the brakes had been in working order, the accident could have been avoided.	The defendant, The St. Louis and Southeastern Railway Co., countered that Britz's injuries were not due to negligence on their part but were instead the result of his own carelessness. They argued that the engineer and other crew members were competent and that Britz, as a fellow servant, assumed the risks associated with his work, including any defective machinery. The company insisted that it had exercised due diligence in selecting its employees and maintaining its equipment.

In the case of Joseph Ator and William Stubblefield v. John Rix and William Rix, which took place in McLean County, Illinois, the legal dispute arose in November 1886. The central figures were the plaintiffs, Joseph Ator and William Stubblefield, who were acting in their professional capacities as landlord and bailiff, respectively. They filed a replevin action to recover crops that had been levied against by Stubblefield under a distress warrant. However, it was established that this distress proceeding was wrongful because the rent was not due at the time and the tenants had not attempted to remove the property. The plaintiffs succeeded in getting a judgment for nominal damages of one cent and costs.  Despite the initial ruling, an appeal followed, focusing on the issue of rightful possession at the commencement of the replevin suit. The court highlighted that while Stubblefield had a lien on the crops, which had accrued rent and remained unpaid at the time of the judgment, the original taking of the crops was deemed wrongful. Thus, the court had to determine if the defendants (the tenants, John and William Rix) were entitled to a return of the property based on the asserted lien of the landlord.	The plaintiffs argued that their actions were justified as Stubblefield had a landlord's lien on the crops for unpaid rent. They sought to affirm their right to retain possession of the crops in question. The primary argument was that the lien, although not yet pursued to possession at the time of the court's judgment, should warrant the return of the property to the landlord, given that the rent had accrued and remained unpaid.	The defendants contended that the original distress proceeding was wrongful and asserted that they were entitled to return of their crops, as the initial wrongful taking did not justify the landlord's claim over the crops. They maintained that the landlord's lien did not provide a basis for possession if obtained wrongfully. The Rixes argued that since the crops had been improperly seized, they should be restored to them despite any liens that may have arisen subsequently.

In 1876, in DeWitt County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose regarding the will of Paschal Mills, who had recently passed away. The will, purportedly his last testament, was initially admitted to probate by the county court. Edwin Wild, named as the executor in the will, was involved in the proceedings to prove its validity. However, upon appeal to the circuit court, the decision of the county court was reversed, and the probate of the will was denied. This prompted Edwin Wild to file a bill in equity to establish the will. The case presented the critical question of whether a court of chancery had jurisdiction to adjudicate such matters given existing statutory provisions that clearly designated county courts as the exclusive venue for probating wills. The court examined the constitution and relevant statutes, ultimately determining that the jurisdiction for such cases was firmly ensconced in the county court, reinforcing its authority in probate matters.	Edwin Wild contended that the circuit court's refusal to admit the will to probate was erroneous and argued that the court of chancery should have jurisdiction to hear his case. He sought a judgment that would validate the will, asserting his rights and duties as the executor.	The defendants argued that the probate of a will is a matter exclusively confined to county courts, citing multiple statutory provisions that support this assertion. They contended that Edwin Wild had adequate legal remedies within the county court system and that he could not invoke the jurisdiction of the court of chancery after having exercised his rights in the circuit court.

On May 1, 1881, a contract was formed between Preston, Kean & Co. and Gilbert A. Colby for the lease and eventual purchase of a property in Cook County, Illinois, which housed smelting works. Colby agreed to rent the property for $100 a month and purchase it for $15,000 under specific payment terms. After defaulting on payments and rental obligations, Colby arranged to convey the property back to Preston, Kean & Co. while executing a deed of trust to secure the purchase money and other debts. This deed, which involved John Farson as trustee, created a lien against the property. Charles J. Gorham was involved as he had a prior judgment against Colby for $8,500 which became a lien on the property when Colby purchased it. Gorham later purchased the premises through a sheriff's sale. The case arose from a foreclosure action initiated by Farson, representing the interests of Preston, Kean & Co., against Gorham's claim of ownership.	The plaintiff, John Farson (as trustee), claimed the lien created by the deed of trust against Colby took precedence over Gorham's later interest. Farson sought to foreclose on the property, asserting that Gorham's claim was subordinate to the existing liens. The plaintiff argued that Gorham's prior judgment and subsequent purchase were subject to the deed of trust and sought to enforce the sale of the property to satisfy the outstanding debts secured by the lien.	Gorham contended that his interest in the property—acquired through a sheriff's sale following his judgment—should take precedence over the lien created by the deed of trust. He argued that changes in the nature of the debt and associated agreements amounted to a waiver of the original lien's enforcement against him. Gorham challenged the legality of the proceedings during the pendency of an appeal regarding the property’s possession, maintaining he was entitled to possession and the beneficial rights acquired through his purchase.

In April 1864, the case of George M. Mixell and Phares Mixell v. John Lutz was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. This legal dispute originated from a property transaction that took place on September 21, 1852, when Phares Mixell purchased land and placed the deed in the name of his minor son, George P. Mixell. The plaintiff, John Lutz, claimed that this conveyance was fraudulent and intended to delay or hinder Phares Mixell's creditors, as he had subsequently secured a judgment against Phares Mixell in September 1861 for $525, for which execution returned with no property found. Lutz argued that Phares Mixell was still indebted to him and that the deed should be set aside, allowing the land to become subject to Phares’s debts. The Mixells contended that Phares did not owe Lutz at the time of the deed and that there was no intent to defraud any creditors. The case involved testimony from both parents of George, why the property should not be deemed fraudulent, and intricate questions regarding the admissibility of evidence in relation to the interests of the witnesses.	John Lutz claimed that Phares Mixell had fraudulently conveyed property to his minor son to avoid paying his debts, insisting that the deed should be set aside. He sought to have the land made subject to his judgment against Phares Mixell, asserting that Phares had become indebted to him through loans and services provided. Lutz requested the court to nullify the deed, arguing that it was executed with the intent to defraud creditors.	The Mixells denied all allegations of fraud and contended that Phares Mixell did not owe any debts to Lutz when the deed was executed. They argued that the property was purchased with funds that did not come from Lutz, and therefore, the conveyance was legitimate and not intended to obstruct creditors. Furthermore, they challenged the admissibility of evidence concerning testimony from Phares and his wife, claiming it was improperly included and adversely impacted their case.

In July 1859, a dispute arose in Decatur, Illinois, involving the Great Western Railroad Company of 1859 (plaintiff) and Jesse W. Hanks (defendant). The case revolved around a contract for the sale of wood, for which the plaintiff claimed he had an agreement with L. M. Mason, Hanks's agent, to deliver wood to the railroad. Both E. D. Walton and W. F. Walton witnessed a conversation where Mason agreed to take wood at $2.50 per cord, with payment to be made when the railroad was financially able. The plaintiff alleged he delivered approximately 135 to 140 cords of wood as per the agreement. However, Mason later testified that he never agreed to purchase the wood and only allowed the plaintiff to stack it along the railroad's path with the understanding that the railroad would take it when they needed it. Some of the wood was destroyed by fire, complicating the case. Ultimately, the plaintiff sought recovery for the delivered wood, while the defendant maintained that there was no binding agreement to purchase.	The plaintiff claimed that a contract existed between him and Mason, the defendant's agent, for the sale of wood at $2.50 a cord. He argued that he delivered the wood according to this contract and that the defendant was now financially able to pay for it. The plaintiff requested full payment for the wood delivered, amounting to $337.50.	The defendant contended that Mason never actually purchased the wood from the plaintiff, arguing that there was no obligation to pay because the plaintiff delivered the wood without a formal agreement to confirm the purchase. The defendant maintained that Mason had only allowed the wood to be stacked along the line without committing to take or pay for it until they needed it, which had not occurred.

In January 1871, the case of Richard C. Keily vs. The Board of Supervisors of Sangamon County was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal dispute revolved around Keily, the acting treasurer of Sangamon County, who was part of a committee appointed to raise funds for the purchase of the old State House in Springfield. The Board of Supervisors allocated a total of $300,000 for this purchase, appointing a committee to negotiate bonds to raise this amount. The committee successfully raised $200,000 by negotiating county bonds, which were paid directly into the State treasury, bypassing the county treasurer's office entirely. Keily claimed that he was entitled to retain a 3% commission on these funds, arguing that his role as treasurer warranted this compensation. The case was decided based on an agreed statement of facts without a jury and involved interpretation of various statutory provisions concerning treasurers' commissions in Illinois.	The plaintiff, Richard C. Keily, argued that he was entitled to a 3% commission on the $200,000 raised by the committee as well as on additional commissions for taxes collected as the county treasurer. Keily referenced previous case law that supported his claims regarding the entitlement to these commissions based on his role in receiving and managing funds for county purposes.	The defendant, The Board of Supervisors of Sangamon County, contended that Keily was not entitled to commissions for the funds raised, as they had never passed through his office and were not revenue obtained from ordinary sources. They argued that the law did not specifically require those funds to be paid to the county treasurer, nor did it grant him authority or entitlement to commissions for money that did not originate from his responsibilities as treasurer.

The case involves George Van Blaricum, who was indicted, tried, and convicted of larceny during the February term of 1855 in the Recorder’s Court of the city of Chicago, Illinois. Following his conviction, he was sentenced to four years in prison. During the trial, certain jurors had expressed opinions regarding the guilt of Van Blaricum. Specifically, four jurors, including Alonzo A. Smith, Jacob H. Kingsley, and Lewis Doyle, admitted to having formed and expressed opinions about the case. Despite this, these jurors were accepted by Van Blaricum's defense. However, the court unilaterally ordered these jurors to stand aside without an official challenge from the prosecution. This decision prompted Van Blaricum's counsel to take exception, arguing that the defendant had the right to trial by a juror he accepted, regardless of any expressed opinion. The case ultimately revolves around the legality of the court's action in dismissing a juror who had not been challenged or rejected by either party prior to the court's intervention.	Van Blaricum argues that the court erred by dismissing a juror who had been accepted by the defense, thus depriving him of his right to be tried by a jury of his choice. He contends that the juror, having stated his opinion, should have been allowed to serve unless properly challenged by the prosecution. Van Blaricum's primary legal request is for a new trial, asserting that the premature removal of the juror compromised his right to a fair trial by a jury of his peers.	The People, as the prosecution, did not actively challenge the jurors in question. Their defense centers on the court's role in ensuring the jurors’ impartiality. The prosecution likely argued that the court acted within its discretion to maintain the integrity of the jury, suggesting that allowing a juror with a formed opinion to serve could undermine the trial's fairness. The prosecution appears to have requested that the court's decision to remove the juror be upheld.

In the case of James M. Helm v. Helen G. Boyd, decided on March 27, 1888, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the central dispute involves the ownership of a one-seventh interest in a tract of land located in Wabash County, Illinois. The parties include the plaintiff Helen G. Boyd (formerly Helen G. Helm), who inherited the property after her mother's death in 1874, and her brother, James M. Helm, the defendant. On January 10, 1882, Helen conveyed her interest to their father, John J. Helm, for what was claimed to be a loan of $1000, while believing that the deed was a mere security for that loan and not a complete sale. Three years later, in January 1885, John J. Helm transferred that same interest to his son, James, also for $1000. Helen argued that her father promised her that the land would return to her and that she never agreed to the deed as a sale.
