He contended that he presented evidence, including enlistment certificates, to establish that these men were credited to the town, thus justifying the payment claimed.	The defendants, John Tribby, contested the validity of the enlistment certificates introduced by the plaintiff, arguing that the evidence was improper and should not have been admitted in court. They maintained that the plaintiff failed to provide adequate proof that the enlisted men were credited to the town of Lynn in time to prevent the draft, which was essential for fulfilling the contractual agreement.

On March 23, 1855, in Peoria County, Illinois, Joseph Blanchard filed a petition in the Peoria Circuit Court against Frederick B. Gunn, Samuel Gates, and Sylvester S. Philley to enforce a mechanic's lien for the amount of $964.51 related to lots owned by Gunn and Gates. Blanchard claimed that he furnished lumber for a building project on the lots beginning in July 1854 but had not been paid after delivery. After Gunn and Gates' financial failure and assignment of assets to Philley for creditor benefit, the case later introduced Allen Hunter and others as defendants who claimed to have interests in the lots. The court proceedings involved disputes over the admission of evidence, legitimacy of the lien, and whether Blanchard's material had actually been used in the construction. In November 1856, a jury found for Blanchard, awarding him $632.19 after determining the amount due for the lumber supplied. The case featured extensive legal arguments regarding the lien on materials, proper application of payments, and testimony regarding interests.	The plaintiff, Joseph Blanchard, argued that he was owed payment for lumber provided under a contract with partners Gunn and Gates, used in constructing buildings on specific lots. Blanchard sought enforcement of a mechanic's lien, claiming that his materials entitled him to the lien regardless of the actual usage in construction, and he requested a decree for the amount due plus costs.	The defendants, including Allen Hunter et al., denied the validity of the lien and claimed ignorance of Blanchard's contract with Gunn and Gates. They contended that Blanchard must prove the lumber he supplied was specifically used in the buildings and argued that payments made should be fully accounted, asserting that the proper steps were not followed to establish the lien. They sought a dismissal of the claims and protection against any financial liability connected to the disputed amounts.

In 1883, in McLean County, Illinois, the legal case "William Rix et al. v. William Stubblefield et al." unfolded. The appellants, William Rix and his associates, initiated a replevin action to recover oats that had been distrained by the appellees, William Stubblefield and others. The case was argued upon the same evidence as a preceding case, where the court had previously determined the property in question was subject to a distress warrant. The trial was overseen by Judge O. T. Reeves, and the proceedings involved legal representations from William E. Hughes for the appellants and Thomas and Harry V. Tipton for the appellees. Ultimately, the case revolved around a dispute over the ownership and recovery of the distrained oats.	The plaintiffs, William Rix et al., claimed that they had the right to recover the distrained oats that were wrongfully taken by the defendants. They sought a judgment allowing them to reclaim their property and argued that the previous decision regarding the property was incorrectly applied.	The defendants, William Stubblefield et al., contended that the oats were rightfully distrained according to the law. They maintained that the evidence presented justified the distress warrant and asserted that the trial court's previous ruling on the matter should be upheld.

In 1888, The Phœnix Insurance Company and Catherine Van Allen et al. were involved in a legal dispute stemming from a fire that destroyed a barn covered by an insurance policy valued at $2,200. The policy was issued to the Van Allens, who claimed they were misled by an insurance adjuster regarding the validity of their policy. After the fire, the adjuster informed the Van Allens that due to a mortgage placed on the property after the issuance of the policy, and that other ownership details were incorrectly stated, the policy was essentially worthless. Following this, the adjuster offered a settlement of $100 for the loss, which was accepted by the Van Allens, despite their later claims that they did not understand they were surrendering their policy. They received the payment and signed a receipt acknowledging full settlement and cancellation of the policy. However, the plaintiffs later sued to recover the value of the insurance policy, alleging fraud in the settlement process.	The plaintiffs, Catherine Van Allen and her family, contended that the settlement with the insurance adjuster was obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation and coercion. They argued that they did not realize they were relinquishing their insurance policy and sought to recover the full value of the policy for the loss of their barn, maintaining that the adjuster's conduct misled them regarding the implications of the settlement.	The Phœnix Insurance Company defended itself by asserting that the settlement made with the Van Allens was valid and should not be disturbed, as it was entered into freely and with full understanding of the circumstances. They pointed out that the Van Allens had acknowledged the settlement in writing and that any claims of misunderstanding were unsubstantiated. The insurance company highlighted the existence of the mortgage, which they argued rendered the insurance invalid and justified the settlement agreement.

In December 1839, in Peoria County, Illinois, Charles Ballance was involved in a legal dispute originally filed before a justice of peace by Lewis Bigelow regarding money owed. Following Bigelow's death, William Frisby and George T. Metcalf, as administrators of Bigelow’s estate, continued the suit against Ballance. The matter centered on claims related to an arbitration award where Bigelow and another party, Isaac Underhill, had contested certain financial obligations with Ballance. The arbitrators had determined a payment of $150 for services rendered in relation to the arbitration, which Ballance disputed. The case was later moved to the Circuit Court, where evidence was presented, including a receipt from an arbitrator, Dan Stone, which Ballance objected to but was ultimately admitted as evidence. The court concluded that the admission of the receipt was correct, and since Ballance did not challenge the administrators' standing at trial, the court proceeded with the judgment.	The plaintiffs, represented by Frisby and Metcalf, claimed that they were owed $150 based on an arbitration award involving Ballance. They sought to prove that the payment was made to Dan Stone for his services during the arbitration process and that Frisby and Metcalf had the right to continue the legal action as administrators of Bigelow’s estate.	Ballance, the defendant, argued against the admission of the receipt as evidence and contended that the court should not have accepted it without Dan Stone testifying in person. He claimed that the plaintiffs were required to prove several elements: the legitimacy of the payment specified in the receipt, that Stone participated in the arbitration, and that the plaintiffs were indeed the lawful administrators of Bigelow's estate. Ballance requested that the verdict be overturned.

In the case of Benjamin P. Miller v. William E. Johnson, which occurred in Carroll County, Illinois, in September 1875, the conflict arose from a slander claim. William E. Johnson, the plaintiff, accused Benjamin P. Miller, the defendant, of publicly asserting that Johnson had stolen corn and oats from him, thereby branding him a thief. The case was initially heard in the Circuit Court, where a jury found in favor of Johnson and awarded him $1,000 in damages. Miller, believing the verdict to be unjust, appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court. Chief Justice Scott delivered the opinion of the court, reviewing evidence that the allegedly slanderous statements were made in the presence of Johnson's family, which constituted proof of publication under slander law. The court also considered the implications of the words spoken and the context in which they were uttered, emphasizing that the defendant's angry state did not justify the slanderous accusation. The court held that the reputation of an individual deserves protection, and special consideration was given to Johnson's previously good character and the lack of any provocation from him that could have incited Miller's anger.	The plaintiff, William E. Johnson, claimed that defendant Benjamin P. Miller slandered him by accusing him of theft, specifically of stealing corn and oats. Johnson argued that the statements were made publicly in the presence of family members, which amounted to actionable slander. He sought legal redress for the damage to his reputation and requested a verdict that would hold Miller accountable for the defamatory remarks, resulting in the jury awarding him damages.	The defendant, Benjamin P. Miller, denied the accusations and claimed that he did not intend to accuse Johnson of theft with the words he used. Miller attempted to argue that his statements were misunderstood and that he was in a state of anger at the time they were made, suggesting this emotional state should mitigate his liability. However, he did not provide evidence that Johnson had provoked this anger, which is necessary to lessen the severity of damages in slander cases.

George Byrne filed a case against Byron W. S. Clark, which was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court on April 3, 1889. The case originated in Cook County's Superior Court, presided over by Judge Elliott Anthony. The legal matter involved a declaration in assumpsit with both special and common counts. However, the records presented to the appellate court lacked necessary documentary evidence, including exhibits or copies of instruments that were essential to understanding the details of the case. These omissions and procedural issues raised concerns about the completeness of the appeals process and whether the judgment issued in the lower court could be fairly evaluated. The appellate court highlighted that it is bound by authenticated documents and cannot consider evidence that is not properly incorporated into the bill of exceptions. The absence of these critical pieces of evidence led to the difficulty in assessing the testimony and overall relevance in the case.	The plaintiff, George Byrne, claimed entitlement to relief based on a declaration in assumpsit, implying an obligation for payment. His main argument was that the evidence and documents demonstrating the validity of his claim were relevant, but were not adequately presented in the lower court proceedings. He likely sought to reverse the judgment of the Superior Court and obtain a favorable ruling based on the merits of his case.	The defendant, Byron W. S. Clark, contested the adequacy of the plaintiff's case, emphasizing the absence of documentation necessary for the appellate court to properly review the case. His defense focused on the procedural deficiencies in the plaintiff's appeal, particularly the failure to attach necessary evidence and the reliance on a stipulation to include materials not formally part of the court record. The defendant sought affirmation of the lower court's judgment based on these grounds.

The case "The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company v. The City of Quincy" took place in Quincy, Illinois, with the court's decision rendered on February 14, 1890. The dispute arose from the city of Quincy filing a bill in chancery against the railway company seeking an injunction to prevent the railroad from placing obstructions along Broadway and Spring streets, specifically in the areas extending west of Front Street. These streets are significant thoroughfares that provide access to the Mississippi River and have historically been utilized for public transportation. The city claimed that the company's actions threatened to block public access to these streets, as well as the river and its landing sites. The railroad company countered by asserting its rights under a deed from the Northern Cross Railroad Company, which it claimed entitled it to facilitate construction and improve the streets for its operations. The railroad contended that its construction activities would not hinder public access, arguing that the infrastructure upgrades were essential for its operational feasibility. The Circuit Court of Adams County examined the claims, the historical usage of these streets, and the legal framework established by the deed before issuing a decree based on its findings.	The city of Quincy, as the plaintiff, argued that the defendant's planned construction and potential obstructions would violate the public's right to freely use Broadway and Spring streets. The city sought an injunction to prevent the railroad from depositing materials or constructing any barriers that would prevent the public from traversing these streets to access the adjoining Mississippi River and other public utilities. The plaintiff maintained that the railroad could not override public rights in city streets without proper authorization, contending that the actions of the railroad posed an imminent threat to public access and safety.	The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, as the defendant, argued against the injunction, asserting that its operations were based on an established deed that granted it rights to grade and improve parts of Broadway and Spring streets. The railroad claimed that it needed to lay down tracks and construct embankments essential for operational integrity. It maintained that its actions would not obstruct public use but would instead allow vehicles and pedestrians to continue accessing the streets as they had before. The defendant insisted that its right to use the streets for railway purposes was clear and lawful, and any perceived obstruction was unfounded.

The case "The People ex rel. Abraham Brokaw v. Commissioners of Highways" was decided on September 21, 1888, by the Illinois Appellate Court. It arose in McLean County, Illinois, involving the parties Abraham Brokaw as the relator and the local highway commissioners as the defendants. The background of the case centers on a public highway that had been open and in use for over twenty years. A fence, characterized as an obstruction, was constructed across this highway, allegedly with the permission of the highway commissioners. Despite being notified in writing by Brokaw to remove the obstruction, the commissioners failed to act. Brokaw sought a writ of mandamus to compel the commissioners to remove the fence and restore the highway to public use, as it was their duty to keep the roads free of obstructions.	The plaintiff, Abraham Brokaw, claimed that the commissioners of highways had neglected their duty by allowing a fence to obstruct a public highway. He argued that his remedy for the obstruction was inadequate and that the commissioners should be compelled to remove the obstruction through a writ of mandamus. He maintained that the highway had been used for many years, and the obstruction not only violated public rights but also endangered public safety.	The defendants, the commissioners of highways, contended that Brokaw's remedy through mandamus was inappropriate. They argued that there were existing statutory remedies available to him, such as fines and the abatement of nuisances by the sheriff. They emphasized that the issues concerning obstruction could also be addressed through legal prosecution rather than through mandamus. Therefore, they requested the court to sustain the demurrer to Brokaw's petition and dismiss the case.

Cornelia Austin, serving as the administratrix, appealed a decision made in April 1862 by the County Court of Grundy, Illinois. The case involved a judgment that had been entered by confession four terms prior to the appeal. The appeal was brought against Lewis P. Lott, the appellee. The dispute centered around whether the administratrix could successfully motion to set aside the earlier judgment. The court found that the motion to set aside was filed too late, and the affidavit supporting the motion was not properly included in the record as it had not been preserved through a bill of exceptions, a procedural requirement established by Illinois law over the prior two decades. This procedural context shaped the nature of the appeal brought forth by Austin.	The plaintiff, Cornelia Austin, claimed that the prior judgment entered by confession should be set aside. She argued that there were valid reasons to do so and sought to have the court rule in her favor by overturning the judgment made against her.	The defendant, Lewis P. Lott, contended that the motion to set aside the judgment was untimely as it was filed too late and that the affidavit supporting this motion was not part of the court record as it was not preserved properly. Lott argued that because of these procedural issues, the appeal lacked merit, and that the original judgment should be affirmed.

In April 1864, the case of Allen Howes v. Joshua N. Austin was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. The action originated from a check drawn by Allen Howes in favor of Lyman S. Knox, which was later endorsed to Joshua N. Austin. The dispute arose when Austin attempted to collect on the check after it was presented at the Marine Bank, which refused payment, citing the bank's inadequate funds. The case proceeded from a lower court in Chicago, where Howes had failed to respond to specific counts laid out in Austin's declaration, resulting in a judgment in favor of Howes for those counts due to Austin's default. Despite this judgment, the trial continued based on the common counts of the declaration related to the same check. The central issues were whether the check was payable in depreciated Illinois currency and whether Austin's delay in presenting the check had caused him any loss. The case involved several witnesses, including bank personnel, and dealt with the complexities of obtaining payment within the legal definitions of currency at that time.	Joshua N. Austin claimed that he was entitled to recover the full amount of the check ($874) after it was presented for payment, which was refused by the bank. He argued that the check should be honored in "lawful money of the United States" and that the refusal to pay was unjust. Austin maintained that the defendant, Howes, was liable for the amount of the check plus interest, even considering the bank's insolvency and its ability to pay with current money.	Allen Howes defended against Austin's claims by arguing that he was not liable because the check was presented significantly after its issue date, an act that he contended resulted in no damages to the plaintiff. He asserted that since the bank was insolvent when the check was presented, he should not be held responsible for the payment, and he requested dismissal of Austin's claim based on laches, arguing that any delay in presentment had benefited Austin.

On July 16, 1873, in Jacksonville, Illinois, Benjamin F. Bergen mortgaged two lots to William Richardson for $1,000 due on June 16, 1874. Bergen later sold the lots to Thomas O’Brien, who assumed the mortgage. In June 1874, O’Brien faced two judgments from Hichols & Brennan for $284.60 and from Hockenhull, King & Elliott for $500. By October 24, 1874, after Richardson prepared foreclosure papers, O’Brien transferred his equity of redemption to Richardson via quitclaim deed, in satisfaction of the mortgage. Concurrently, Bergen made a quitclaim deed to Richardson, and two days later, the $1,000 note was surrendered, releasing the mortgage. However, after the mortgage cancellation, executions were issued on the two judgments and levied against the property. Richardson then filed a bill to enjoin the property sale and foreclose the mortgage. The circuit court denied his request, leading Richardson to appeal. The critical issue was whether the mortgage had merged with the fee when Richardson accepted the deed from O’Brien.	Richardson claimed that accepting the quitclaim deed from O’Brien did not extinguish his original mortgage lien. He argued that the intent was not to merge the two interests but to preserve his claim against the property, especially since the mortgage was the first lien and exceeded the property’s value. He sought to maintain the enforceability of his mortgage and prevent the property from being sold due to junior judgments against O'Brien, asserting that his rights should be recognized by the court.	The defendants contended that when Richardson accepted the quitclaim deed, his mortgage was merged into the fee, thus ceasing to be a lien on the property. They argued that this merger negated Richardson’s claim to the property, allowing the execution of the judgments against O’Brien to proceed. They maintained that the judgment lien was superior once the mortgage was canceled, leaving Richardson without grounds for preventing the property sale.

Matthew T. Wright, the testator, was the owner of certain lands in Clay County, Illinois. On May 15, 1871, he executed a will that bequeathed all his real estate and appurtenances in Clay County to his sister, Elizabeth Minshall. Prior to executing the will, he had contracted to sell the lands, which led to the issuance of a bond for a deed. At the time of his death, the purchaser's notes for the land were still unpaid. After Wright's passing, the collateral heirs-at-law, including Minshall, sought a pro rata distribution of approximately $1,175, the funds generated from the sale of the real estate, which were reported to the probate court. However, the probate court ruled that the entire amount should be awarded to Elizabeth Minshall. This decision was affirmed by the circuit court, prompting the heirs-at-law, excluding Minshall, to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. They argued that the proceeds should not solely belong to Minshall since they were derived from property subject to a sales contract prior to the will's execution.	The heirs-at-law contended that the proceeds from the sale of the real estate should not exclusively be allocated to Elizabeth Minshall. They claimed it was incorrect to distribute the entire amount solely to her, arguing for a pro rata share among all collateral heirs based on their familial rights to the estate.	Elizabeth Minshall, as the sole devisee under the will, defended the probate court's decision by asserting that the testator’s intention was clear: she was entitled to the proceeds from the real estate that had been devised to her. While she acknowledged the contract of sale, she argued that it would not affect the legal title and the rightful share of the proceeds belonging to her as outlined in the will.

On November 16, 1883, in Collinsville, Illinois, Charles H. Pabst, a merchant, executed a chattel mortgage to John H. Yager, giving him security on Pabst's stock of dry goods valued at not less than $5,000. The mortgage was intended to cover two promissory notes that Pabst owed to Horeph Johnson and Isaac Cook, totaling $3,300. The mortgage stipulated that Pabst could sell goods as part of his business, and it was recorded on November 17, 1873. On December 28, 1883, Pabst assigned his goods to Yager for the benefit of creditors, and Yager subsequently sold the goods for $13,600. However, the mortgagee demanded possession of the goods, leading Yager to file a lawsuit on February 5, 1884, to clarify the legality of the mortgage. The case centered on whether the mortgage was valid, given that it permitted the mortgagor to maintain possession and operate his business, which could undermine the rights of creditors.	The plaintiff, John Mersinger, claimed that the chattel mortgage issued by Pabst to Yager was void as it allowed Pabst to sell goods in violation of statutory regulations. Mersinger argued that the mortgage was essentially fraudulent, as it undermined the rights of creditors and third parties, and sought the return of the goods based on the invalidity of the mortgage.	The defendant, John H. Yager, contended that the mortgage was valid under the agreement made with Pabst and that as Pabst's assignee, he had the right to sell the goods. Yager claimed that his actions were in good faith and that he fulfilled the terms of the mortgage by taking possession of the goods following Pabst's assignment for creditors. He requested that the court uphold the validity of the mortgage.

John B. Camden and others initiated a legal case against Kenneth McKoy and Jacob Johnson in Illinois during December 1842. The dispute centered around a promissory note dated January 26, 1838, where John C. Gray was the maker, and McKoy and Johnson endorsed the note, purportedly as securities for Gray. When the case went to court, the plaintiffs produced a promissory note indicating a promise to pay $480, but the circumstances surrounding McKoy's and Johnson's endorsement were unclear. There was no definitive evidence showing whether they endorsed the note when it was executed or at a later date, nor was their connection to the original consideration established. The court dismissed the plaintiffs' attempt to introduce the note into evidence, stating the endorsement did not confirm their liability as joint and several makers of the note alongside Gray. The plaintiffs subsequently faced a judgment of nonsuit, meaning they could not recover any amount and were responsible for court costs.	The plaintiffs argued that McKoy and Johnson were liable as joint and several makers of the promissory note because they endorsed it as securities for Gray's payment. They maintained that the endorsement was legitimate and sought to recover the sum owed based on the promissory note.	McKoy and Johnson contended that the plaintiffs could not prove they had endorsed the note at the time it was executed or that they had any awareness of the transaction. Their defense was centered on the assertion that there was no sufficient evidence to establish their liability as makers of the note, as their endorsement lacked connection to the original consideration.

In 1867, in Chicago, Illinois, James L. Stark, a practicing lawyer, was involved in a legal case against Francis E. Corey and another party regarding a financial transaction. The plaintiffs, Corey and Dwight, were a firm that had previously lent money to a business entity called E. W. Robinson & Company, which consisted of E. W. Robinson and Stark. Robinson, the managing partner of the firm, had a history of borrowing checks to meet business financial obligations. On one occasion, he requested a $400 check from the plaintiffs, promising to return the money shortly after collecting some lime debts. However, he failed to repay the loan as promised, leading the plaintiffs to initiate legal proceedings against Stark, as he was served with the legal notice. In court, Stark argued against the loan's validity based on procedural and evidential grounds, claiming that the court had admitted improper evidence.	The plaintiffs argued that Stark, as a partner in the firm E. W. Robinson & Company, was personally liable for the $400 loan made to the partnership, regardless of how the borrowed funds were used. They presented evidence that the loan was made on behalf of the firm with an expectation of repayment. The court was urged to affirm their claim based on the established partnership agreement and previous practices within the firm.	Stark contended that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that the funds were borrowed for legitimate firm business and argued that the admissibility of certain evidence presented in court was improper. He challenged the validity of the loan on the basis that the check given to Robinson did not have his cognizance and that the partnership articles prohibited mingling personal and partnership funds.

In January 1870, the case of Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Sylvester J. Fears took place in Greene County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Sylvester J. Fears, sought damages from the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company following an accident involving his wagon and a passing train. According to the events, Fears approached a railroad crossing with his wagon and team. While thirty yards away, he saw the smoke of the locomotive and knew a train was coming. Despite this knowledge, he did not stop his horses until he reached the track, resulting in a collision with the train. The collision overturned his wagon and caused him injuries. Initially, a jury ruled in favor of Fears, leading to a judgment against the railroad company, which prompted the railroad to appeal the decision on the grounds of contributory negligence.	The plaintiff, Sylvester J. Fears, claimed that the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company was negligent in their operations, specifically alleging that the company failed to provide adequate warning of the approaching train, as the bell or whistle was not sounded. He sought damages for the injuries he sustained and for the destruction of his property as a result of this alleged negligence.	The defendant, Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, argued that the accident was caused by the plaintiff's own gross negligence. They contended that Fears was fully aware of the approaching train, as he saw the smoke and could have stopped before reaching the track. The railway’s counsel maintained that it was the plaintiff's reckless decision to attempt to cross the tracks that led to the collision, thereby absolving the railroad of liability.

In 1869, Parker B. Mason filed a lawsuit against Thomas McNamara and others in the Superior Court of Chicago. The summons was not served ten days prior to the term's opening. Consequently, the plaintiff's declaration was not filed until October 22, after which a default for lack of a plea was entered against the defendant. Following the default, the defendant filed a motion to set it aside, citing a substantial defense and issues in finding the declaration. His attorney, Edward Eoby, submitted affidavits indicating diligent attempts to locate the declaration, which were ultimately unsuccessful. The motions were denied, leading to an appeal based on the argument that due process was not afforded due to the mishandling of court documents.	The plaintiff, Parker B. Mason, contended that the default judgment should stand as the defendant failed to respond timely to the complaint. Mason's attorneys argued that it was within the court's discretion to deny the request to set aside the default, emphasizing that the procedural rules regarding the declaration were followed correctly.	The defendant, Thomas McNamara, asserted that he had a legitimate and substantial defense to the action but was unable to respond adequately due to the unavailability of the filed declaration, which he believed had been lost or deliberately withheld. McNamara’s attorney argued that the default should be set aside as justice required it, highlighting the lapses in diligence by the court personnel that obstructed McNamara's ability to plead.

The case "Board of Education, etc., v. Frank Helston" unfolded in Montgomery County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment on February 14, 1890. The central figures in this legal dispute were Frank Helston, a 14-year-old pupil, and the Board of Education of District No. 1. Helston was suspended from school on November 9, 1888, after he refused to disclose the name of another pupil whom he believed had defaced the school building with obscene writing. Despite multiple requests from school authorities, including the superintendent and school committee, Helston remained defiant and insisted he would not provide the information, which culminated in his suspension. The Board subsequently upheld this suspension, asserting it was justified due to his gross disobedience. Following his controversial suspension, Helston sought legal intervention through a petition for a writ of mandamus, aiming to compel the Board to reinstate him and restore his privileges as a student. The case revolved around issues of student conduct, authority of school boards, and the right to education within public schools.	Frank Helston, as the plaintiff, contended that his suspension was illegal and sought reinstatement to the school. He argued that he was wrongfully denied his right to education as guaranteed by the state, claiming that the Board’s actions constituted an unjustified exclusion from a public institution funded by taxpayer money. Helston sought not only the restoration of his school privileges but also the legal acknowledgment of his right to attend school without undue punishment.	The Board of Education defended its actions by asserting that Helston's refusal to provide the name of a fellow pupil, coupled with his disobedience and disrespectful conduct towards the Board, justified his suspension. The Board maintained that disciplinary measures were necessary to uphold order and propriety within the school environment. They argued that the ability to enforce school rules—including requiring students to report misconduct—was within their discretion and essential for maintaining a safe and respectful learning environment. The Board requested the dismissal of Helston’s petition for reinstatement.

The case of "James H. Eames v. Thomas Hennessy" took place in Chicago, Illinois, with a court case filed during the June term of 1857 in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas. The plaintiff, Thomas Hennessy, initiated an action of assumpsit against the defendant, James H. Eames, based on a draft or check amounting to $109.20 that Eames had drawn in Hennessy's favor upon Huntington & Co. Hennessy claimed that after presenting the draft for payment, it was refused, leading to the current legal action. Hennessy's declaration included both special counts detailing the draft and common counts for money claimed to be due. Eames responded with several defenses, including a plea of no consideration and the assertion that Hennessy had no right to claim the fees for which the check was issued. In October 1857, the court rejected Eames's motion for a continuance predicated on the absence of a witness essential to his defense. The court subsequently found in favor of Hennessy, awarding him $127.72 in damages and court costs, prompting Eames to appeal the ruling.	The plaintiff, Thomas Hennessy, argued that Eames had issued a check for payment of fees related to services Hennessy had performed as a constable, specifically for taking care of a vessel during an attachment. Hennessy claimed that he had incurred reasonable expenses for these services and that Eames's refusal to pay constituted a breach of contract. Hennessy’s legal request was for the enforcement of the payment per the check issued by Eames.	The defendant, James Eames, contended that the check was issued without good or valuable consideration, asserting that the fees claimed by Hennessy were illegal and not warranted by law. Eames produced evidence that no proper services had been rendered by Hennessy justifying the charges. He argued that the court should dismiss the claims based on the failure of consideration for the check, demanding that the judgment be overturned.

William A. Boley v. Bernard Barutio took place in Pekin, Illinois, with a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 23, 1887. The case arose from an assumpsit action for the use and occupation of the south half of an ice-house built jointly by Boley and Barutio in 1874, where both parties owned an undivided half. In 1875, a partition was established, allowing Boley to occupy the north half and Barutio the south half. After years of shared use, Barutio began occupying the entire building, including the south half, without compensating Boley. In 1883, Barutio was notified that he would be charged rent for the use of the south half. The case progressed through the circuit court of Tazewell County, where a jury ruled in favor of Barutio, and this judgment was later affirmed by the Appellate Court.	Boley claimed that Barutio had unlawfully occupied the south half of the ice-house and failed to pay rent for its use. He argued that even in a co-tenancy situation, an agreement to compensate for the use of the property can be implied based on the conduct of the parties. Boley requested payment for the reasonable value of the occupying use of the south half for the years in question.	Barutio contended that his occupation of the ice-house did not entitle Boley to claim rent, asserting that as co-tenants, neither party could make a claim for rent simply based on occupancy. He argued that without a formal agreement to pay rent, Boley's claim should not be upheld and sought to have the judgment against him dismissed.

In 1884, a legal dispute arose in Lawrence County, Illinois, involving the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company as the appellant and John W. McCleave, the county treasurer, as the appellee. The railway company sought a court injunction against taxes levied against its property, alleging that the board of supervisors exceeded its authority by imposing taxes beyond the limits set by law for county purposes. The company claimed that certain taxes levied for town purposes were being improperly categorized as county taxes and thus unconstitutional under section 8, article 9 of the Illinois constitution, which limits county tax rates. During the hearing, the circuit court dissolved the temporary injunction and ultimately dismissed the case, ordering the railway company to pay McCleave $60 in attorney's fees. This judgment triggered an appeal, leading to the case being reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court, where the nature and legality of the tax levies were scrutinized.	The plaintiff, Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company, argued that the taxes imposed were in excess of the legal limits and characterized those levied for town purposes as unconstitutional county taxes. The railway company sought to have the court enjoin the collection of these taxes, asserting that the board of supervisors had overstepped its authority in levying amounts above what was permitted by the constitution for county taxes.	The defendant, John W. McCleave, contended that the taxes in question were properly levied as municipal taxes by the relevant town authorities and fell within legal bounds. McCleave argued that the taxes were essential for corporate purposes and that the board of supervisors acted within its jurisdiction, asserting that the claim of exceeding tax limits was unfounded according to both state law and constitutional provisions.

In the case of Charles S. Mosely et al. v. Kate E. Schoonhoven, decided on February 9, 1883, the Illinois Appellate Court reviewed a mortgage foreclosure dispute originating from Kane County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Charles S. Mosely and others (the plaintiffs in error), were embroiled in legal proceedings concerning a mortgage held by the defendant, Kate E. Schoonhoven (the defendant in error). A foreclosure decree had been issued, leading to the sale of the mortgaged premises. However, the sale amount was less than what was required to satisfy the decree, including accrued interests and costs. When the master's report was submitted, a decree for the deficiency amounting to $626.70 was entered against Mosely. It was argued that the amount awarded was erroneous, as only $274 was actually due. The case included legal complexities regarding the correct application of deficiencies in foreclosure cases and the roles of involved parties, including the rights of subsequent mortgagees. Notably, the adult plaintiffs could not leverage the infancy defense of their co-plaintiff during the proceedings.	The plaintiffs contended that the decree for the deficiency was too high — specifically, they argued that only $274 was owed at the time of the decree's issuance, rather than the judgment of $626.70. They sought to correct this perceived error, emphasizing the need for equitable treatment regarding the costs imposed by the court and the proper adjudication of the rights of involved parties, including the assertion that certain parties should have been included in the proceedings.	The defendant's key argument was that the decree for foreclosure was appropriately issued and that the claimed deficiency, despite being excessive, could be mitigated by remitting the overage in the appellate court. The defense maintained that the original decree was valid, and the admitted remittance of the excess amount addressed the error related to the deficiency judgment. They requested the court affirm the foreclosure decree and the corrected deficiency amount of $274, while also asserting that costs should be divided equally due to the prior error before the remittitur.

The case "William A. Howard, Plaintiff in Error, v. Henry Babcock, Defendant in Error" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1859. It originated in Fulton Circuit Court, where a dispute arose between William A. Howard and Henry Babcock over the sale and delivery of two mares. The events began in May 1857, when Babcock offered to let Howard have the mares and wagon as part of the payment for a farm being sold to him. An agreement was reached where Howard would purchase the mares for $300, with the understanding that he could use them for a few weeks before they would be formally transferred. During this period, one of the mares died while in Babcock’s possession. Howard claimed the death resulted from Babcock’s negligence. Babcock countered that the mare's death was due to disease or accident despite his proper care. The case featured various legal arguments surrounding the definitions of possession and neglect, ultimately leading to a jury trial to resolve the dispute.	Howard argued that the mare died due to Babcock's negligence while in his care and that he expected to receive compensation for its value, which he estimated to be between $130 and $150. He sought to enforce the agreed price related to the transaction, emphasizing that the absence of proper care by Babcock led to the mare's death, thereby justifying his claim.	Babcock contended that he was not negligent and that the mare had died from an illness or an accident beyond his control. He asserted that he had taken reasonable care of the mare while it was in his possession and challenged Howard’s claim regarding the agreed price, emphasizing that the award made for the mare was vague and not enforceable due to its uncertainty.

The case "The City of Springfield v. Ninian W. Edwards" originated in the year 1877 and was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case was initiated after a citizen and taxpayer of Springfield, Ninian W. Edwards, filed a bill in chancery to prevent the municipal authorities of Springfield from incurring new debts and levying taxes in a manner that violated the city’s charter and the Illinois state constitution. The court determined that since the adoption of the constitution, the city's debt had consistently exceeded legal limits, with significant annual indebtedness recorded. For instance, in 1871, the city incurred debts amounting to $4,171.89, which steadily increased over the following years. Edwards argued that the debts and taxes imposed by the city went against the constitutional provisions that restrict municipal indebtedness to no more than five percent of the taxable property value. The court found sufficient evidence to support Edwards' claims regarding the mismanagement of city funds and prohibited the city from continuing these practices.	The plaintiff, Ninian W. Edwards, claimed that the municipal authorities of Springfield were acting illegally by incurring debts beyond the limits set by the state constitution and city charter. Edwards requested a court injunction to prevent the city from incurring any further debt exceeding five percent of the valuation of taxable property as per the last assessment.	The defendant, represented by city officials, contended that liabilities and appropriations made within the limits of expected revenue were not considered debts under the constitutional limitation. They argued for legal allowances for short-term borrowing against anticipated revenues, claiming no violation occurred as the debts were to manage operational costs and services that were expected to be funded through future revenues.

In September 1870, the case of Frederick Sulzer v. Lydia Yott took place in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Frederick Sulzer (the appellant) and Lydia Yott (the appellee). The case arose from a breach of promise to marry, with Yott claiming that Sulzer had engaged to marry her but later refused to fulfill his promise. Yott filed an action of assumpsit in the circuit court, seeking damages for the breach of that promise. During the trial, Yott testified positively about the engagement, which was corroborated by a witness, Mrs. Campbell. Sulzer, on the other hand, denied the existence of any such engagement. The jury, after considering the evidence, reached a verdict in favor of Yott, awarding her $2,039.58. Following a remittance directed by the court, the total judgment against Sulzer was set at $1,500 plus costs. Sulzer's appeal primarily argued that the evidence presented did not support the jury's verdict.	Lydia Yott claimed that Frederick Sulzer had made a binding promise to marry her and subsequently breached that promise. She sought damages for the emotional and social distress caused by this breach, asserting her position was corroborated by testimony from a disinterested witness. Yott maintained that the evidence provided was sufficient to validate her claims and implied that she was entitled to a fair compensation for Sulzer's actions.	Frederick Sulzer's main defense was that he never entered into a promise to marry Lydia Yott, completely denying the existence of such an engagement. Additionally, he attempted to introduce testimony from his father, claiming that Yott had released him from the engagement, a claim Yott and her sister-in-law contradicted. Sulzer argued that the evidence against him did not sufficiently support the jury's verdict and sought a reversal of the judgment based on these grounds, including a motion for a new trial that was ultimately denied by the circuit court.

In November 1854, Isham Blankenship and Joseph Cutrell were involved in a legal dispute over a contract related to improvements made on public land in Illinois. The events leading to the case began when Cutrell declared in assumpsit, claiming that Blankenship was obligated to pay him for improvements made on land that Blankenship had purchased from the government. The two men met on a road, where Cutrell inquired about Blankenship's plans for the land. Blankenship suggested he could give Cutrell and his son each twenty acres, but Cutrell rejected this idea, stating it would hinder his agricultural efforts. Blankenship affirmed that he would be fair regarding compensation. The lack of concrete evidence regarding a binding contract led to the question of whether an enforceable agreement existed for payment of the improvement costs. Legal principles surrounding the enforceability of promises regarding public land improvements were referenced, revealing the complexities of such agreements under Illinois law during that period.	Isham Blankenship argued that there was no binding contract to pay Joseph Cutrell for improvements made to the land prior to its purchase by Blankenship. He asserted that any agreement to pay was insufficiently defined and lacked a express promise from him to compensate Cutrell. Blankenship contended that Cutrell’s claims exceeded moral obligations and failed to meet legal standards for enforceable contracts.	Joseph Cutrell maintained that Blankenship had made promises that implied a duty to compensate him for the improvements he made to the land. Cutrell argued that Blankenship's words and actions during their conversation suggested an understanding that compensation would be forthcoming. He sought to establish that there indeed existed an implied agreement based on Cutrell's work on the property, despite Blankenship's rejection of the land transfer offer.

The case of John King v. C. H. Edwards et al. arose from a lease agreement dated November 11, 1887, between John King (the lessor) and C. H. Edwards and Henry C. Young (the lessees) for a tract of coal land in Peoria County, Illinois. The lease stipulated that the lessees were to pay five cents per ton in rent for coal mined from the land, with payments due on January 1 and July 1 of each year. By April 14, 1888, King declared a forfeiture of the lease, alleging that the lessees had failed to mine coal or pay royalties as required. The case was brought before a justice of the peace and subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court, where it was tried without a jury. The primary dispute revolved around the interpretation of the lease terms regarding when the lessees were obligated to commence mining operations. The lessees had begun to excavate a small hole shortly after signing the lease but had not constructed any machinery or extracted any coal from the premises. Instead, they worked on a subterranean route from adjacent land, which they claimed was a more practical approach. The trial judge found in favor of the lessees, leading to King's appeal.	John King, the plaintiff, claimed that the defendants failed to fulfill their obligations under the lease by not mining any coal or paying the required royalties since the lease's inception. He alleged that the lessees were bound to commence mining operations within a specific timeframe and sought a judgment to declare the lease forfeited and to recover possession of the land.	The defendants (C. H. Edwards and H. C. Young) contended that the lease did not impose a specific obligation to begin mining operations by a fixed date. Their argument hinged on the interpretation that the lease allowed them to open the mine at any point on the premises and that they were using reasonable diligence to commence mining through a subterranean approach from nearby land. They maintained that there was no legal basis for forfeiture, as they had demonstrated a genuine intention to mine coal.

The case of Laban Agney v. John Strohecker took place in Stephenson County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment on December 11, 1886. The dispute arose after Laban Agney purchased a parcel of land from Samuel Diffinbaugh while John Strohecker was already in possession of the land under a verbal rental agreement with Diffinbaugh. The terms stipulated that Strohecker would pay one-third of the grain produced on the farm, without obligations for delivery, except for necessary feed. Agney contested these terms, claiming Strohecker was responsible for additional payments concerning hay and potatoes. On October 20, 1884, when Agney sought to collect what he perceived as due rent, conflict ensued. With a distress warrant issued by the local deputy sheriff, Agney laid claim to the grain divided from the harvest. However, the proceedings were deemed irregular, as they did not conform to legal standards for distress actions. The jury found for Strohecker, concluding that he had already satisfied his rent obligations through the grain delivered and enjoyed by Agney, leading to the case being presented in court.	Laban Agney, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to recover rent payments due under the lease terms with John Strohecker for the land in question. He insisted that Strohecker failed to deliver the full amounts owed and sought a legal resolution through the distress warrant process, aiming to compel Strohecker to pay what he believed was rightfully due.	Defendant John Strohecker countered the claims by asserting that he had already satisfied his rent obligations by delivering the agreed-upon portions of the grain to Agney. He maintained that the distress process employed by Agney was both irregular and illegal. Strohecker contended that he was not liable for any further rent payments due to the fulfillment of the terms of his rental agreement with Diffinbaugh, and thus he requested the case be dismissed in favor of his claims of satisfaction of the obligations.

The case "The Matthiessen & Hegeler Zinc Company v. The City of La Salle" was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court on August 13, 1886. It arose from a controversy involving the rights to mine coal beneath city streets and alleys in La Salle, Illinois. The Matthiessen & Hegeler Zinc Company, through a legal filing, claimed ownership of the coal underlying its property and sought to secure access across the public streets for mining purposes. The original incorporation of the city was said to occur after a plat for the area had been recorded, which the plaintiff argued meant the streets and alleys were dedicated to the city for public use and could not be mined without permission. The company asserted that a contract the city had made with other individuals to mine coal was invalid and posed a threat to their own mining operations, potentially leading to legal actions against them. Thus, the plaintiff requested an injunction to prevent the city and its contractors from mining the coal beneath the streets, which would interfere with its ability to access and extract the coal from its lots.	The Matthiessen & Hegeler Zinc Company contended that it held rights to the coal beneath its property and sought an injunction to prevent the city of La Salle and its contractors from mining coal under the streets and alleys without authorization. The plaintiff argued that the city did not have the right to sell or remove coal beneath these public ways, as their incorporation occurred after the street platting. The company claimed these actions could lead to multiple lawsuits against them, which would cause irreparable harm.	The City of La Salle admitted to making a contract granting mining rights to other individuals. However, it argued that the contract was ultra vires (beyond its powers) and thus invalid. The city maintained that they held the rights to the streets and alleys as public highways, emphasizing that the purposes of the streets as thoroughfares must be preserved, and the plaintiff's actions in mining underneath these rights could threaten their integrity. The city requested the court dismiss the plaintiff's claims based on these contentions.

In the case of *Commissioners of Highways of Town of Oran v. John A. Hoblit*, which occurred in 1886 in Illinois, the main issue revolved around the validity of a petition by the Commissioners of Highways to lay out and establish a new highway. The petition was intended to create a road starting near the southwest corner of section 6 in township 20 north, range 1 west, ultimately running across land owned by John A. Hoblit to reach section 31 in township 21. The petitioners, the Commissioners, had a legal obligation under the Road and Bridge Law of 1883 to provide proper notice of the meeting where this proposal would be discussed. However, the notice issued was found to be insufficient as it failed to clearly inform the public about the time and specific place of the meeting. The notice only vaguely referred to "Beason," a small village, without detailed information about the exact venue, which led to challenges regarding the procedural validity of the actions taken by the Commissioners. Additionally, there were no records showing that any damages incurred by Hoblit were agreed upon or assessed as required by the law. The circuit court ultimately quashed the Commissioners' decision, leading to the appeal by the Commissioners and a review of the case by the Illinois Appellate Court.	The plaintiff, John A. Hoblit, contended that the Commissioners of Highways did not comply with the jurisdictional requirements set by the Road and Bridge Law, specifically the necessity of proper notice for meetings regarding road establishment. He argued that the lack of detailed notification invalidated their authority to act and that the commissioners failed to demonstrate they had legally assessed or agreed upon any damages for the taking of his land. Consequently, he sought to have the commissioners' order quashed, highlighting that the legal process had not been followed correctly.	The defendants, the Commissioners of Highways, argued that their proceedings to establish the highway were lawful and that the notice they provided was sufficient. They claimed that the meeting was duly noticed and took place in accordance with legal requirements. In response to the challenges raised by Hoblit, they filed a motion to quash the court's judgment based on alleged procedural defects in how the case was handled. However, they faced a significant hurdle regarding the clarity and adequacy of the notice issued as well as the legitimacy of the claims about damage assessments.

The case of Jesse Hanley v. James P. Erskine was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1857. The dispute originated from a prior judgment issued in May 1855, where Erskine had commenced an action of ejectment against Hanley over a portion of land, leading to a recovery of nineteen-twentieths of that land by Erskine at the March 1857 term. Following this, Erskine filed for mesne profits against Hanley, claiming $300 for use and occupation of the property as of May 15, 1857. During the trial presided over by Judge Walker, evidence was presented that included testimonies regarding tenants of the land and their interactions with Hanley. The key point of contention was whether statements made by McGuire, a tenant claiming to be Hanley’s, could be used against Hanley in court. Hanley objected to this evidence, which the court ultimately allowed, leading to the trial's outcome that found in favor of Erskine, awarding him $181.50 in damages.	Erskine claimed that as a result of winning the ejectment case against Hanley, he was entitled to recover mesne profits for the use and occupation of the land. He argued that Hanley had not only lost the right to continue occupancy but also owed a debt for the time he had used the premises. Erskine sought to establish that McGuire was a tenant under Hanley and that his admissions regarding tenancy should weigh against Hanley.	Hanley defended against Erskine's claims by asserting that the admissions made by McGuire regarding his tenancy were inadmissible as evidence since they were not made in Hanley's presence and lacked the necessary privity of relationship. Hanley contended that the court's allowance of these statements was improper and therefore requested a reversal of the judgment based on the alleged incompetence of the evidence presented.

John M. Clevenger v. John Dunaway was a legal dispute decided in January 1877 in Illinois, involving Clevenger (the plaintiff) and Dunaway (the defendant). The case arose from a rental agreement where Clevenger rented out 135 acres of land to Dunaway in 1873, requiring payment in the form of 15 bushels of corn per acre to be delivered at Mahomet. After the rental period ended on March 1, 1874, Clevenger claimed that Dunaway failed to deliver all the corn and that some of what was delivered was unsound. In response, Dunaway asserted that he met the contractual obligations. The disagreement escalated when Clevenger issued a distress warrant, claiming unpaid rent and seizing sixty-four of Dunaway's hogs through constable Weller. Dunaway contested this action, revealing that a prior judgment had already determined that no rent was due to Clevenger. Ultimately, the court found in favor of Dunaway, awarding him $200 in damages after a jury trial, during which evidence was presented that supported Dunaway's claim regarding the distress warrant and the rent payments.	Clevenger's main argument was that Dunaway had failed to pay the rent agreed upon in their lease, justifying his issuance of a distress warrant to seize Dunaway's property. He contended that there was a legitimate claim for unpaid rent, and sought to reverse the judgment from the lower court that ruled against him.	Dunaway's defense was centered on the assertion that he had previously complied with the rental agreement and that a court had already adjudicated the issue, finding that no rent was due from him to Clevenger. He argued that the subsequent distress warrant issued by Clevenger constituted a form of trespass, effectively disregarding the prior judgment, and sought damages for the wrongful seizure of his hogs.

Henry H. Gage filed an action of ejectment against William C. Goudy regarding certain city lots located in Chicago, Illinois. The case was tried in the Superior Court of Cook County and was overseen by Judge Sidney Smith. Both parties waived their right to a jury trial, allowing the case to be decided by the court alone. On May 16, 1889, the court rendered a judgment in favor of Goudy. Gage later appealed the decision, claiming errors had been made in the judgment and court proceedings. However, the records indicated that there were no exceptions taken to the judgment, nor was there a motion for a new trial or any objections noted in the findings of the trial court.	Gage's main arguments centered around alleging errors made by the Superior Court in the handling of the case. He claimed that the court erred in entering judgment against him, finding him guilty, not allowing a judgment that he “go thence without day,” and made improper findings of facts and conclusions of law. He sought to have the court's decision reversed and the judgment entered in his favor.	Goudy, representing himself, contended that the judgment entered by the Superior Court was correct and should be upheld. He did not formally submit a written defense but relied on the absence of objections and the legal standing of the court's finding. Goudy’s position was that the procedural irregularities claimed by Gage could not be considered by the higher court due to the lack of documented exceptions or motions on record.

The case "Town of Whitfield v. William Horrocks" unfolded over several years in the vicinity of Whitfield, Illinois. It involved key individuals, primarily William Horrocks and the commissioners of highways of the Town, who aimed to address the obstruction of a public road. Historical context indicates that a traveled track had existed across the land since 1840, and in 1866, the commissioners surveyed and officially mapped the road. Following several ownership changes, including the conveyance of land between Horrocks and his son George, the road remained open for public use until 1880. At that time, William Horrocks obstructed the road by constructing a fence, leading to legal action from the town. Horrocks was fined for this obstruction, and the town subsequently sought an injunction to prevent him from interfering with the highway's use. The claim was primarily based on the argument that the road had been dedicated to the public, and the obstruction constituted a violation of that dedication.	The Town of Whitfield claimed that the road in question had been dedicated to public use as early as 1866, with acceptance of that dedication by the town and continued public use over the years. They sought an injunction to prevent William Horrocks from further obstructing the highway, arguing that the obstruction presented irreparable harm to the public and was compounded by Horrocks' financial irresponsibility. The town aimed for the injunction to be made permanent, effectively reaffirming the established status of the road as a public highway.	William Horrocks contested the allegations brought forth by the Town of Whitfield, arguing that he did not own the land in question in 1866, thus disputing the claims of dedication. He denied ownership and asserted that he had the right to alter the road's configuration as he saw fit. Moreover, upon the court's final hearings, the defense sought to have the injunction dismissed, arguing that there was no legally established highway and that the bill should be dismissed regarding Frances Horrocks, who had also been implicated.

The case "The Chicago and North Western Railway Company v. Charles Dement" was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. The dispute arose in Lee County, Illinois, concerning a cow owned by Charles Dement, which was allegedly killed by a passing train belonging to the Chicago and North Western Railway Company. The cow was discovered lying on her back in a railway ditch, about two to three feet from the track. It was noted that the animal was bloated and had blood oozing from her nose but showed no visible external injuries. The jury concluded that the cow's death was due to the train's passing, despite the lack of physical evidence of injury. The court deliberated on whether the jury's finding was supported by the evidence, and acknowledged the unusual circumstances, ultimately deciding not to overturn the verdict.	The plaintiff, Charles Dement, claimed that his cow was killed by a train owned by the Chicago and North Western Railway Company. He sought to recover the value of the cow, asserting that the circumstantial evidence—such as the position of the cow when found and the absence of any other plausible explanation for its death—strongly suggested that the train was responsible for the fatal injury.	The defendant, the Chicago and North Western Railway Company, argued that there was insufficient evidence to support the claim that their train killed the cow. They pointed out the absence of external injuries on the animal as a significant factor. The defendant also contended that the jury instructions were flawed because they did not require proof that the railway had been in operation for six months leading up to the incident, although they acknowledged that the road had been operational for a longer period.

In January 1865, the case of Henry McKoy et al. v. Gerard B. Allen was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following an incident that occurred in Christian County, Illinois. The action originated as a forcible entry and detainer case, initiated by Gerard B. Allen against Henry McKoy and Eli Jacobs. Allen had previously secured a judgment against McKoy and Jacobs before a justice of the peace. Dissatisfied with the judgment, McKoy and Jacobs filed an appeal to the Circuit Court. However, Allen moved to dismiss the appeal, citing the insufficiency of the bond filed by McKoy and Jacobs. The Circuit Court agreed and dismissed the appeal, leading to McKoy and Jacobs challenging this decision in the Supreme Court. The crux of the appeal rested on whether the defects in the bond, which failed to conform to statutory requirements—particularly the absence of a clause for the payment of rents—could be overlooked because the defendant had appeared in court.	The plaintiffs, Henry McKoy and Eli Jacobs, contended that the Circuit Court should have considered their case based on the merits despite the alleged deficiencies in the appeal bond. They argued that the presence of the defendant (Allen) in court constituted a waiver of any objections to the bond’s form. Additionally, they maintained that their bond should be deemed sufficient under Illinois law and that technical objections should not preclude them from having their case heard.	The defendant, Gerard B. Allen, argued that the appeal bond submitted by McKoy and Jacobs was fundamentally flawed and did not comply with statutory requirements. He highlighted that the bond lacked essential particulars, such as the description of the type of action and a provision for the payment of rents due during the appeal. Allen maintained that because the Circuit Court had no original jurisdiction over forcible entry and detainer actions and detected substantial defects in the bond without a motion for amendment from the plaintiffs, the court correctly dismissed the appeal.

The case "Almon B. Ives v. Walter Vanscoyoc" arose in McLean County, Illinois, where a partnership dispute unfolded surrounding a grain elevator owned jointly by Ives and Vanscoyoc. In May 1872, the partners attempted a settlement over mutual debts, with Ives claiming that he became the sole owner of the elevator property and that Vanscoyoc owed him $563.98 after the settlement. However, Vanscoyoc disputed this, asserting that he still owned half of the elevator and was entitled to profits, claiming Ives owed him money instead. A writ of execution was issued against Vanscoyoc, leading to the sheriff levying the garnishment on Ives. Ives obtained a temporary injunction to prevent the sale of the property, claiming sole ownership. A jury later found that Ives owed Vanscoyoc $419.61 at the time of the writ's service. The case revolved around the unresolved issues of partnership debts and property ownership.	Almon B. Ives argued that he had settled all partnership accounts and became the sole owner of the grain elevator. He requested the court to recognize this settlement and prevent the sheriff's sale of the property that would satisfy Vanscoyoc's judgment against him. He asserted that he was not indebted to Vanscoyoc and sought a judgment to uphold the terms of their alleged settlement.	Walter Vanscoyoc contended that there was no final settlement between the partners and claimed that he still held an interest in the elevator. He argued that Ives was largely indebted to him instead and requested that the court recognize his ongoing ownership rights and the debts owed to him from Ives.

On November 13, 1883, P. S. McKenzie, a constable, received an execution for $82.15 against C. C. Biggs. In response, Biggs provided McKenzie with a schedule of his personal property on December 22, 1883. On January 22, 1884, McKenzie appraised Biggs' property, which was valued at $400.75, excluding a gold watch that Biggs claimed had been stolen. On the same day that the appraisal was returned with no property found, another execution was issued against Biggs, at which point McKenzie levied upon Biggs' property. Biggs claimed exemption from the levy due to his previous schedule presented for the first execution, but he did not provide a new schedule for the subsequent execution, nor did he inform McKenzie of the new execution's issuance until after the levy occurred. The court case originated in the county court of Franklin County, Illinois, and Biggs sought to recover twice the value of the property sold in the execution.	C. C. Biggs argued that the property levied and sold by P. S. McKenzie was exempt from execution because he had previously submitted a sworn schedule of his personal property. Biggs contended that he was not required to submit a new schedule for a second execution, as he believed the original schedule should suffice. He sought recovery of twice the value of the property that was wrongfully sold.	P. S. McKenzie defended his actions by asserting that Biggs was required by law to submit a new sworn schedule of his property for each execution. McKenzie claimed that Biggs failed to meet this legal obligation and that therefore, the property in question was not exempt from levy. He maintained that as a result of Biggs' failure to comply with the statutory requirements, he was justified in seizing and selling the property.

The case "Rufus W. Robbins et al. v. Clinton H. Moore et al." arose in Illinois, with the plaintiff, Rufus W. Robbins, filing a bill to foreclose a mortgage on land he believed he acquired legitimate title to through a series of transactions involving Thomas J. Bunn. The original mortgage was taken by Bunn from his father, Lewis Bunn, who lost his claim against Mitchell and Moore, other land purchasers who contested Bunn’s title. Through a series of appeals, it was eventually determined that the patents should revert to Moore and Mitchell. Robbins claimed he purchased the land from Bunn after securing assurances from Mitchell that he had no claim on the property. However, when Robbins sought foreclosure, Moore and Warner intervened, alleging Robbins' title was fraudulently obtained. The case spanned over several years beginning with Robbins’ mortgage filing in 1866, with critical developments occurring from the 1850s through the late 1870s, amidst various claims and counterclaims as different parties sought to assert their rights to the disputed lands.	The plaintiff, Rufus W. Robbins, argued that he had acquired rightful ownership of the land in question through a legitimate series of transactions, including a mortgage agreement. He claimed that Mitchell had disclaimed any interest in the property at the time of his purchase, thus making his acquisition valid. Robbins requested the court to enforce his mortgage and establish his title over the land against Moore and Warner, who contested the validity of his claim.	The defendants, Clinton H. Moore and Vespasian Warner, countered Robbins’ claims by asserting that Mitchell had a valid claim to the land which had not been duly acknowledged or processed in the original mortgage foreclosure proceedings. They argued that Robbins’ title was based on a fraudulent representation by Mitchell and requested the court to annul the deeds and patents through which Robbins claimed ownership and establish their own legal title to the disputed land.

William M. Stetham (Appellant) filed a legal case against John Shoultz (Appellee) in 1855, in the St. Clair Circuit Court, Illinois. The suit arose from a debt claim related to a sealed note, where Shoultz and other co-defendants were involved. At the March term of 1855, the defendants presented a demurrer against the plaintiff's declaration, which was overruled by the court. Subsequently, the defendants entered a plea of non est factum and raised several defenses regarding the failure of consideration. Stetham sought a continuance citing the absence of a key witness, claiming he could prove his defense of part failure of consideration. The court granted the continuance, but on August 1855, after waiving the jury, the trial was held, resulting in a judgment against the defendants. Stetham later moved to set aside this judgment, alleging he had been ill and unable to attend the trial, and that his co-defendants were only sureties on the note, unaware of the defense. The court overruled his motion, leading Stetham to appeal to a higher court.	Stetham's main argument was that his co-defendants did not understand his defense for the sealed note, as they were merely sureties. He also claimed that his illness prevented him from attending the trial, which hindered his ability to present a complete defense. Stetham requested that the judgment against him be set aside and for a new trial to fairly present his defense.	The defendant, representing Shoultz and co-defendants, argued that the plaintiff failed to show diligence in preparing for his defense and that his sickness did not justify the lack of representation. They contended that Stetham could have compelled the attendance of his witnesses and did not demonstrate any reasonable efforts to gather evidence or testimony, thus requesting the court to uphold the judgment against the defendants.

Isaac Cook filed a bill in chancery against Joseph Stout, Mary E. Stout, James Cotton, and Henry G. Cotton, originally in the Circuit Court of LaSalle County, seeking to set aside a sheriff's deed to certain premises held by Henry G. Cotton. After the court granted this request, it appointed a special master to examine the damage, or "waste," that had occurred on the property. The case underwent a change of venue to the Superior Court of Chicago for final hearings. During the proceedings, issues arose regarding the evidentiary value of depositions that were lost or destroyed. These depositions had contained testimony from key witnesses. Despite attempts to re-establish the evidence from these depositions, challenges regarding the admissibility of testimonies led to a complex legal discussion. The Superior Court ultimately rendered a decree in favor of Cook for $2,706.47, but the defendant appealed the decision, which brought the case before the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868.	The plaintiff, Isaac Cook, claimed that the sheriff's deed to the premises should be set aside. He sought to prove instances of waste committed on the property and requested that damages for such acts be accounted for, leading to the decree in his favor.	The defendants, led by Joseph Stout and others, contended that the basis for the decree was unjustified, primarily because key evidence was derived from lost depositions which were not admissible under the circumstances. They argued that the re-examination of witnesses could not adequately replace the original testimonies and sought to suppress the secondary evidence presented by the plaintiff’s side.

In October 1851, Henry Loop & Sons purchased a one-fourth interest in the mills of Saxton and took possession of the entire mill, either through themselves or tenants. The lawsuit arose over a specific installment of rent under a lease agreement between Henry L. Crosby and Robinson & Co. Crosby had tendered an assignment of the specified portion of the rent to Loop & Sons, which they refused to accept. This case builds on a previous decision where it was established that the drawing of an order for a rent payment did not constitute an assignment of the rent, thus preventing Loop & Sons from pursuing an action in their own name. The court examined whether new facts presented in this instance would alter the previous legal conclusions. The judgment ultimately affirmed that Loop & Sons were not obligated to accept the rent assignment, as it required mutual consent and was not part of the original contract. Additionally, the sole right to instigate proceedings for rent recovery rested with Crosby.	The plaintiff, Henry L. Crosby, argued that Loop & Sons improperly refused to accept the formal assignment of rent and claimed that they were liable for the amount specified in the order, as it was drawn upon past consideration. Crosby maintained that as the landlord, he had the exclusive right to collect rent from the lessees (Robinson & Co.), and their possession of the property, with or without his consent, did not absolve them from their rental obligations.	The defendants, Henry Loop & Sons, contended that they were not bound to accept the assignment as it required both parties' consent and was not stipulated in the original lease agreement. They argued that despite having exclusive possession of the premises, that arrangement did not alter the contractual obligations to Crosby, and they were not liable for the rent owed by Robinson & Co. since that was a separate landlord-tenant relationship.

The case "The City of Cairo v. Leonard Everett" took place in Illinois, culminating in a court decision on June 16, 1883. The key individuals involved were Leonard Everett, the plaintiff, and the City of Cairo, the defendant. The dispute began when Everett obtained a judgment against the city on July 1, 1878, for $1,200 and costs following a lawsuit in the circuit court of Alexander County. The city appealed the judgment, but the Appellate Court for the Fourth District upheld it in February 1879. Despite the judgment being affirmed, the city failed to pay Everett, prompting him to file a petition for a writ of mandamus on October 6, 1882.
