Essentially, Wittmer sought the court's enforcement of the debt obligation against Ellison, challenging the defense's basis for claiming non-liability.	John Ellison, the defendant, maintained that he was acting solely as a surety for Blakeman and that the subsequent extension of the payment deadline was null and void without his consent. Ellison's defense emphasized that the agreement to extend the time for payment was made without acknowledging his role and therefore could not be enforced against him. He argued that the remedy for such a situation lies within a court of equity rather than a court of law, and by doing so, Ellison sought to have the debt claim dismissed.

The case Edwin D. Tucker v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in 1885 in Kankakee County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Edward D. Tucker, was indicted for bigamy by a grand jury during the April term of the circuit court. After being arrested, tried, and initially convicted, his judgment was reversed by the Illinois Supreme Court, which remanded the case for a new trial. The venue was changed from Kankakee to Livingston County upon the defendant's request, and a second trial was conducted in the circuit court of Livingston County, where Tucker was again convicted. During the trial, questions arose regarding the jurisdiction of the Livingston court due to the condition of the transcript from Kankakee. The indictment charged Tucker with marrying Mary B. Markham while still married to Mary I. Bennett, as well as legal issues surrounding the validity of the marriage license and evidence presented at trial.	The plaintiff's main argument centered on the claim that Tucker was rightfully convicted of bigamy for marrying Mary B. Markham while still married to Mary I. Bennett. They maintained that the evidence presented, including the certified marriage license and correspondence between Tucker and his first wife, supported the prosecution's case. Additionally, they contended that the court proceedings were held correctly and that the evidence met legal standards set for proving marriage in bigamy cases.	Tucker's defense argued that the Livingston County circuit court did not have jurisdiction due to defects in the transcript certified from Kankakee County. They also claimed that the divorce decree obtained in Utah voided the initial marriage to Mary I. Bennett, thus making the subsequent marriage valid. Furthermore, they raised objections regarding the admissibility of evidence used against him, claiming violations of his rights to confront witnesses in a criminal prosecution.

In December 1843, in the jurisdiction of Illinois, a legal case arose involving The People of the State of Illinois, represented by James M. Duncan, the late Clerk of the Supreme Court, against John B. Roper, the late Sheriff of Clinton County. The context of the case pertained to the failure of Sheriff Roper to return a fee-bill within the stipulated ninety-day period following its issuance. The court examined whether this failure constituted a liability for Roper to pay the fee-bill amount. The proceedings included representation from attorneys Wm. Brown and H. B. McClure for the relator, and L. Trumbull for the defendant, Roper.	The plaintiff, James M. Duncan, claimed that Sheriff Roper's negligence in returning the fee-bill within the required ninety days rendered him liable for the payment of that fee. The legal request emphasized holding the sheriff accountable for his inaction according to the established legal obligations governing public officers' duties.	The defendant, John B. Roper, likely argued against the implications of liability, potentially questioning the enforceability of the fee-bill or asserting that he had followed proper procedures within his duties as sheriff. However, the specific defenses outlined in the case details were minimal and not elaborated upon.

In 1874 in Illinois, the case of Stewart Neil v. Don Alonzo Cummings arose from a transaction related to a patent for a harrowing machine known as "Niel’s Patent Cylindrical Harrow." In 1867, Stewart Neil appointed Joshua Matthews as his agent to sell rights to the patent. Matthews sold the rights to Cummings for four counties, receiving three promissory notes secured by a mortgage on Cummings' real estate. These notes were made out to Matthews, who acted on behalf of Neil. Later, Neil claimed to be the assignee of the notes and mortgage and attempted to foreclose on Cummings’ mortgage, but withdrew his suit when it seemed unfavorable. Subsequently, Cummings filed a suit seeking to cancel the mortgage and the notes, alleging they were obtained through fraud and lacked consideration. Neil countered with a cross-bill for foreclosure. The court ultimately ruled against Neil, noting Matthews’ fraudulent practices in misrepresenting the value of the territory sold and concluded that Cummings's claims were justified.	Cummings, the plaintiff, claimed that the notes and mortgage were procured through fraud by Neil’s agent, Matthews. He sought a decree to cancel the mortgage as it clouded his title to the land and requested that the notes associated with the fraudulent transaction be surrendered for cancellation, asserting they were acquired under false pretenses and without any legitimate consideration.	Neil, the defendant, contended that he should be regarded as an innocent assignee of the notes and mortgage, claiming his position should not be affected by Matthews' actions. His defense relied on the argument that he acted in good faith and should not be held liable for any alleged fraud committed by his agent during the sale of the patent rights to Cummings.

The case of Sterling P. Rounds v. George C. Smith et al. was adjudicated in April 1866 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a series of transactions involving checks drawn by the defendant, Sterling P. Rounds, on the Western Marine and Fire Insurance Company bank. On September 30, 1864, Rounds had his bookkeeper, W. W. Wheeler, certify checks worth $5,306.70 and $306.70, which were delivered to the plaintiffs (bankers) as payment for promissory notes held by them for collection. Upon receiving the checks, the plaintiffs stamped the notes as "paid" and sent the amounts to the original note holders, L. Johnson & Co. However, the Western Marine and Fire Insurance Company closed before the plaintiffs could present the checks for payment, causing them to become worthless. The parties argued about the nature of these checks, whether they constituted cash payment or merely a promise to pay, as well as the responsibilities regarding their presentation and the resulting financial liabilities.	The plaintiff claimed that they accepted the certified checks from Rounds as cash in full payment of the promissory notes. They argued that Rounds was still liable for the amounts after the checks were presented for payment, despite the bank's subsequent closure, asserting that the checks should have been presented promptly, which was the plaintiffs' responsibility.	The defendant, Rounds, contended that by certifying the checks as good, the funds were effectively transferred to the plaintiffs, absolving him of further liability. He argued that the plaintiffs negligently held onto the checks without presenting them for payment in a timely manner, leading to their loss in value. Rounds maintained that their failure to act swiftly released him from liability for the amounts on the checks.

Jonas Conger, the plaintiff, entered into a deed in which he granted the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company the right of way across his property in Bureau County, Illinois, in 1854. The grant included the condition that the railroad company must construct a fence along the right of way within a reasonable timeframe. Despite accepting the deed and taking possession of the land to construct the railroad, the company failed to build the required fence. Due to this omission, Conger faced damages, primarily through cattle trespassing on his property. In response to his claims, the rail company filed a demurrer against Conger's declaration, which was upheld by the Bureau Circuit Court. Conger brought the case to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking to challenge the circuit court's decision.	Conger argued that the railroad’s failure to erect a fence as stipulated in the deed constituted a breach of duty, which led to his damages from cattle trespassing on his land. He sought to maintain an action on the case to recover those damages, contending that, by accepting the deed, the railroad company impliedly assumed the responsibility to fulfill the conditions outlined, including the construction of the fence.	The railroad company contended that it did not formally enter into a covenant to build the fence, citing that it did not sign the deed. They asserted that since they did not execute the deed, they could not be held liable for failing to construct the fence. As a result, they argued that Conger's action on the case should be dismissed due to lack of a formal agreement.

In the case of Jo Robinson v. Wilson K. Brown et al., the legal proceedings took place in Saline County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1876. The original dispute originated from a judgment rendered in August 1859 against John S. Eubanks, William G. Sloan, Moses P. McGehee, and Jo Robinson. A scire facias action was initiated by Wilson K. Brown to revive this earlier judgment. All defendants except Eubanks were served, and the court addressed the pleas raised by Sloan and Robinson, including bankruptcy and claims of no debt and partial payment. Eventually, the court found itself reviewing these matters after Robinson appealed the decision. The trial was marked by irregularities, particularly regarding unanswered pleas. The court concluded that the defendants had waived their right to contest these issues by not demanding responses during trial. The court confirmed the judgment against Robinson and McGehee for the remaining balance owed, dismissing objections by the defendants regarding various aspects of the proceedings, including procedural errors with the judgment’s form and handling of levies on real estate.	The plaintiff, Wilson K. Brown, claimed that Jo Robinson and Moses P. McGehee owed the remaining amount from a previous judgment totaling $67.82, after accounting for a payment of $270. Brown sought to revive the judgment through scire facias, asserting that the court should uphold the original judgment despite the procedural challenges raised by the defendants related to bankruptcy and various pleas.	The defenses presented by Robinson and McGehee included arguments of bankruptcy for Sloan and claims of no debt and partial payment regarding the original sum. They contended that the court erred in proceeding to judgment without fully addressing the remaining pleas and raised objections to the procedures followed during the trial, including the handling of the former judgment as evidence and the alleged improper revival of the judgment.

The case "Chicago and Alton Railroad Company v. William Pratt" took place on January 22, 1884, near the city of Alton, Illinois. The key individuals involved were William Pratt, the plaintiff and a brakeman employed by Chicago and Alton Railroad Company (the defendant). The incident occurred shortly after midnight when Pratt fell from a train car as he was performing his duties. He was ascending a ladder on top of the train cars when one of the ladder rungs gave way, leading to his severe injuries, including the loss of a leg. The lawsuit alleges that the defendant was negligent in maintaining safe working conditions, particularly regarding the condition of the ladder used by the brakemen. The position of the train cars is crucial to the case, as evidence indicated that if Pratt fell from a cattle car, he would have no valid claim, since that car was reportedly in proper condition. Discrepancies in testimonies, particularly concerning the arrangement of the train cars, highlighted the complexity of the case.	The plaintiff, William Pratt, claimed that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was negligent in allowing the ladder on the train cars to become unsafe, leading to his injury. He sought damages for the injuries sustained while performing his duties as a brakeman, arguing that the company failed to maintain the ladders in a secure condition. The suit contained multiple counts of negligence describing the circumstances of the accident and emphasizing the company's responsibility to provide safe working conditions.	The defendant, Chicago and Alton Railroad Company, argued that the preponderance of evidence confirmed Pratt fell from a stock car, which was in good condition, thus negating any claim of negligence on their part. They contended that they had exercised reasonable care by inspecting all cars before operation and that no known defects existed. The defense emphasized the burden on Pratt to prove negligence and maintained that they could not be held responsible for unseen defects that weren't reported during inspection.

The case of Sarah Alwood et al. v. Henry Mansfield et al. was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1876. The key individuals involved were plaintiffs Sarah Alwood and others, and defendant Henry Mansfield and others. The plaintiffs filed a bill in the Mason Circuit Court, which later had its venue moved to Tazewell County, Illinois. On March 2, 1874, the appellants (defendants) entered into an injunction bond, which was subsequently dissolved on February 17, 1875, leading to the dismissal of the underlying bill without an assessment of damages. Following this, the appellees (plaintiffs) initiated a debt action on the bond. The appellants filed a demurrer against this declaration, which was overruled by the court, resulting in damages being assessed at $100 in favor of the appellees. This judgment against the defendants was met with an appeal, raising questions about the applicability of the relevant statutory acts to the case at hand.	The plaintiffs, Sarah Alwood et al., argued that they were entitled to damages based on the defendants' failure to maintain the injunction after it was dissolved. They claimed that since they had not been able to assess damages at the time of the dissolution, they were still entitled to recover damages via their action on the injunction bond. They contended that changes in law (specifically the act of 1874) should allow them to pursue damages even if the dissolution occurred before this act was effective.	The defendants, Henry Mansfield et al., contended that the plaintiffs could not recover damages on the bond because they failed to have damages assessed at the time the injunction was dissolved, per the previous law from 1861. They argued that the assessment of damages was a requisite part of the contract and that the 1874 act did not retroactively apply to bonds executed prior to its effective date. Their position was that the act should not alter the obligations set forth in the original bond executed under the earlier statute.

Green W. Bruce initiated a legal dispute against Miers F. Truett, which was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1843. This case stems from a previous trial in June 1841, where a jury rendered a verdict in favor of Bruce for $452. Following this, Truett sought a new trial, citing an affidavit claiming he could present testimony from a witness, O. Ellers, who purportedly had proof that a charge of $300 in Bruce's account had already been settled. However, Ellers had disappeared prior to the trial but was later located in Delaware. Truett’s affidavit indicated he did not know Ellers' whereabouts until after the verdict. The court noted several issues with this application, especially regarding the necessity of all previous testimonies to assess its merits properly. Ultimately, the court found that the affidavit did not merit a new trial, as the evidence would likely have been cumulative to what was already presented during the initial trial.	Bruce argued that the existing evidence presented during the trial was adequate to support the jury's verdict. He contended that Truett's motion for a new trial was based on insufficient grounds, as the testimony from the absent witness, Ellers, would only serve to reinforce the claims already supported by evidence. Bruce sought to uphold the original jury's decision and the judgment rendered in his favor.	Truett’s defense rested on the argument that he could provide crucial new evidence through the deposition of O. Ellers, which would demonstrate that the $300 in Bruce's account was paid off, thus disputing part of the judgment against him. He maintained that he had made diligent efforts to locate Ellers but was only able to do so after the trial’s conclusion, claiming this constituted grounds for a new trial. Truett’s motion was grounded on the assertion that this new information could substantially change the case outcome.

On January 15, 1875, William H. Gather executed a note for $500 in favor of William P. Brinton, due three years later with interest. This note, along with another for $1,000 to a different individual, was secured by a trust deed on real estate. In the summer or fall of 1882, Brinton endorsed the note in blank and delivered it to Warren F. Pitney for negotiation. Pitney subsequently sold it to Herman Einhaus for its face value, minus a small amount in unpaid interest. In October 1883, Einhaus filed a bill in equity to foreclose the trust deed, naming Gather, his wife, and Brinton as defendants. The court later ruled that Gather had paid off the $500 note before it was transferred to Einhaus, and the assignment to Einhaus was unauthorized. The court dismissed Einhaus's original bill, barring him from enforcing the payment of the note. Subsequently, Einhaus sought legal recourse against Brinton, arguing that Brinton's prior assignment of the note was inaccurate since the note was allegedly paid off, making it worthless. The case was decided without a jury, resulting in a finding for Einhaus and an award of damages.	Einhaus claimed that Brinton, through the assignment of the $500 note, warranted that the note was unpaid, and he alleged that the transfer was invalid since the note had already been paid by Gather. Einhaus sought damages based on these assertions, arguing that the representation made by Brinton constituted a breach of warranty, rendering the assignment ineffective, and ultimately aimed to recover the costs associated with pursuing the note.	Brinton contended that when he transferred the note, it was indeed unpaid, and he claimed that the assignment was meant for Pitney, not Einhaus. He further asserted that the prior court ruling established the payment of the note by Gather, which meant Einhaus had no valid claim against him. Brinton argued that Einhaus’s suit lacked merit because he had received value for the assignment in good faith before knowing of any potential fault regarding the note’s actual status.

The case "Eugene L. Johnson et al. v. William Pollock" took place in January 1871 before the Illinois Supreme Court. It emerged from a dispute over land ownership in Schuyler County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Eugene L. Johnson and other plaintiffs, who were asserting a claim to a certain tract of land, and William Pollock, the defendant, who was in possession of the land. The conflict arose when the plaintiffs entered a written contract with Pollock, who was already in possession, to transfer the patent title of the land in exchange for a stipulated sum. The plaintiffs believed they held the legal title to the land due to a prior deed, but the court found that the contract did not establish a vendor-vendee relationship as the plaintiffs never had the ability to convey the patent title. Pollock's possession was deemed independent, and he was unwilling to pay for less than the full patent title that he had contracted for. The case hinged on contract interpretation and the potential injustices of ejectment given Pollock's readiness to fulfill the contract upon receipt of a valid title.	The plaintiffs, led by Eugene L. Johnson, argued that they were entitled to reclaim the land held by Pollock due to a contract agreement that required Pollock to pay for the patent title. They contended that Pollock had acknowledged their title through this agreement and that he should be compelled to pay for the land under the contract terms.	William Pollock, the defendant, claimed that he should not be obligated to pay for the land without receiving the actual patent title as stipulated in their contract. He argued that his possession was obtained independently of the plaintiffs and that they never performed their contractual obligation to convey the patent title. Pollock also pointed out that he had always been willing to pay as soon as the plaintiffs could provide the necessary title.

The case "Lake Shore & Michigan Southern R. R. Co. v. Harriet Hunt, Adm’r, etc." involves an incident that occurred on November 18, 1880, near South Englewood, Illinois. Louis P. McBride, who was the conductor of a freight train, was involved in a fatal accident while it was dark and cold outside. McBride and his brakeman were tasked with transporting the freight train with a caboose attached, and they ended up stopping on the main track due to other trains ahead of them. Despite knowing that other trains were expected, they failed to follow company rules which required them to post warning signals to prevent an accident. Instead, McBride and the brakeman chose to lie down and sleep in the caboose. An incoming freight train, unaware of McBride’s train on the track due to the lack of signals, collided with the caboose, resulting in McBride's death. Subsequently, the administrators of his estate filed a lawsuit against the railroad company, claiming negligence on their part.	The plaintiffs, represented by Harriet Hunt as administrator for Louis P. McBride's estate, claimed that the railroad company was negligent in its operations, resulting in McBride's death. They argued that his death should be compensated due to the damages suffered by his next of kin. The plaintiffs maintained that the railroad company failed to manage its trains appropriately and did not take adequate safety precautions, leading to the fatal accident.	The defendant, Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railroad Company, countered that McBride's death was a direct result of his own negligence. They argued that McBride, being an experienced conductor, was well aware of the company's safety rules regarding warning signals. The defense maintained that the conductor's decision to sleep in an unprotected caboose without placing any signals amounted to gross negligence and that such actions absolved the company from liability for the incident.

In the case of Eliza C. Heslop v. Zachariah W. Gatton, Executor, the events unfolded in Cass County, Illinois, where Helen Clendenin passed away on May 9, 1872, leaving behind a will that only addressed her personal property. The will bequeathed a legacy of $1,000 to her sister, Catharine P. Schooley, and made nominal bequests of $1 each to her two daughters, including Eliza C. Heslop. The executor of the estate, Zachariah W. Gatton, filed a bill in equity seeking to interpret the will and compel the sale of real estate to cover the legacy, based on the assertion that the personal estate was insufficient for its payment. Heslop contested this decision, appealing the ruling that directed the sale of the real estate to satisfy the legacy to Schooley. The primary legal question centered on whether the real estate could be subject to pay the legacy, given that the will did not explicitly state any charge on the real estate for such payments.	Eliza C. Heslop, as the appellant, contended that the real estate should not be subjected to the payment of her deceased mother's legacy to Catharine P. Schooley. She argued that the will did not express an intention to charge the real estate for the legacy, as it did not include any provisions for distributing the real property. Heslop claimed that the law dictates legacies should be satisfied from personal estate unless explicitly stated otherwise by the testator.	Zachariah W. Gatton, the executor, defended the decision to sell the real estate by asserting that the testatrix intended for the legacy to be paid from the proceeds of the real estate. He argued that while the will lacked direct language to that effect, the situation surrounding the personal estate's insufficiency and the state's property implied such an intention, necessitating the sale of the real estate to fulfill the legacy obligation to Schooley.

In June 1868, the Illinois Central Railroad Company was involved in a legal case against Jacob Frazier, originating in Marion County, Illinois. The dispute arose after a fire escaped from the railroad's engine, spreading to Frazier's meadow and causing damage to his hay, rails, and hedges. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, where the plaintiff, Frazier, claimed damages due to negligence on the part of the railroad company. The primary focus was on whether the railroad company had acted negligently by allowing grass and weeds to grow on its right of way, which purportedly contributed to the fire. The court's deliberation referenced prior decisions that established the baseline responsibilities of railroad companies regarding the maintenance of their property in similar scenarios.	Jacob Frazier, the plaintiff, argued that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent in maintaining its right of way, which led to the fire damaging his property. He sought monetary compensation for the losses incurred due to the destruction of hay, rails, and hedges, asserting that the railroad should have taken necessary precautions to prevent such an incident.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company, represented by Mr. George W. Wall, contended that it did not have a higher duty to maintain its right of way than any adjoining landowners. Their defense was built on citing previous legal cases that indicated that the mere presence of grass and weeds was not sufficient to establish negligence. They requested the court to reverse the initial judgment against them, arguing that the evidence did not substantiate the claims of negligence.

The legal case of Henry H. Porter, Impl’d, etc., v. William H. Clark took place in 1887 in Cook County, Illinois. In this dispute, Henry H. Porter appealed a decision regarding a vendor’s lien against property he purchased from William H. Clark. The central issue revolved around whether Clark's previous possession of the property and the way he handled his vendor's lien had any bearing on his claims against Porter. Clark had entered into a rental agreement after transferring the deed to Parker, which led to questions about the rights Clark retained concerning the property. The case involved various pieces of evidence, including letters and a notice of lien filed in the recorder’s office. Ultimately, it was determined that Clark's possession of the property at the time of the sale served as constructive notice to Porter regarding Clark's rights, hinting that any misunderstanding regarding the lien was insufficient to negate Clark’s claims.	Henry H. Porter argued that he had a legitimate claim to the property without any encumbrances from a vendor's lien. He contended that the notice of lien filed by Clark was ineffective as constructive notice and that there was insufficient evidence supporting Clark's argument for waiver of the lien. Porter sought to have the court uphold his rights to the property free from Clark's claims.	William H. Clark defended his position by asserting that he maintained a vendor's lien on the property due to the incomplete payment for the purchase. He argued that Porter's awareness of his possession of the land constituted constructive notice of all rights. Clark claimed that his actions did not amount to a waiver of his lien and highlighted that the rental payments were misinterpreted, supporting his case for maintaining the vendor's lien on the property.

In early 1857, William Evans entered into a contract with the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company, in which he agreed to deliver 1,500 cords of wood at a rate of $2.50 per cord. The contract stipulated that 80% of the payment would be made monthly, as the wood was delivered, with the remaining 20% due within 30 days after the completion of the contract, which was set for May 1, 1857. Throughout January and February 1857, Evans delivered approximately 495 cords of wood to the railroad. However, he did not complete the total quantity by the deadline established in the contract. Despite this, the railroad company received and utilized the delivered wood. Evans filed a lawsuit seeking to recover the retained 20% of the payment for the wood delivered, asserting that the company had defaulted on its obligations. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, which examined the contractual relationship and the parties' actions regarding the contract terms.	The plaintiff, William Evans, claimed that he was entitled to the recovery of the 20% payment for the wood he had delivered, arguing that the defendant had not fulfilled its contractual obligations. He asserted that the company had engaged with the wood he delivered, thereby acknowledging the contract, and contended that he should not bear the consequences of the incomplete delivery as the defendant's actions had implied acceptance of the contract terms.	The defendant, Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company, contended that they had made payments for 80% of the wood delivered and had not received the full quantity as agreed upon in the contract. They argued that since Evans did not complete his delivery of all 1,500 cords of wood, he was not entitled to the remaining 20% payment. Additionally, the defendant claimed that the retention of the 20% was a protective measure against potential damages due to Evans's non-compliance with the contract.

Thomas S. Ridgway and another individual (collectively referred to as the plaintiffs) filed a suit against Job Smith (the defendant) in the Gallatin Circuit Court, Illinois, in November 1854. The plaintiffs sought a writ of attachment against Smith's estate, alleging that he owed them $1,350 and was about to remove his property from the state, which would harm their interests. The attachment was served on a flatboat carrying a load of corn owned by Smith. In response, Smith filed a plea in abatement, denying the claim that he was planning to remove his property in a way that would injure the plaintiffs. A jury trial resulted in a verdict for Smith. The court did not accept the plaintiffs' proposed jury instruction, which would have required a finding for the plaintiffs unless there was evidence that Smith was not about to remove his property, but instead accepted Smith's instruction to find for him if the jury believed he was not removing property to harm the plaintiffs. The evidence indicated that Smith intended to sell his goods in New Orleans and return with the proceeds, which could potentially help him pay his debts. The court ultimately quashed the attachment and ruled against the plaintiffs for costs.	The plaintiffs, Ridgway and his associate, claimed that the defendant, Job Smith, was indebted to them in the amount of $1,350 and was planning to remove his assets from Illinois, which would adversely affect their ability to recover the debt. They requested the court to grant a writ of attachment against Smith's property to secure their claim.	The defendant, Job Smith, argued against the allegations made by the plaintiffs. He filed a plea in abatement to contest the claim that he was about to remove his property from the state in a manner that would harm the plaintiffs. Smith maintained that his intended removal of the flatboat and cargo was for the purpose of sale, which would not necessarily be to the plaintiffs' detriment and could be essential for him to settle his debts.

In September 1874, the case of Charles H. Weaver et al. v. William A. Poyer was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from a judgment rendered in the Superior Court of Cook County. The case arose after Weaver obtained an injunction to prevent Poyer from collecting a judgment that had been previously awarded against him. Weaver executed an injunction bond with Hiram H. Marsh as his surety. However, the injunction was later dissolved, and the bill was dismissed. After this dissolution, Weaver attempted to obtain another injunction for the same judgment, which was still pending at that time. The court had to determine whether the existence of the new injunction affected the enforceability of the bond related to the first injunction.	The plaintiff, William A. Poyer, claimed that the bond executed by Weaver and Marsh obligated them to cover the amount of the original judgment, including any awarded damages, after the first injunction was dissolved. Poyer argued that once the initial injunction was lifted, he had the right to enforce the bond for debt upon the amount owed, as the bond terms clearly stipulated.	The defendants, Charles H. Weaver and Hiram H. Marsh, contended that the existence of the second injunction, which was still pending, interrupted any proceeding concerning the bond related to the first injunction. They claimed that since another injunction was obtained for the same judgment, it should serve as a defense against the suit pertaining to the bond given in the first case, arguing that the two actions were interconnected.

In 1871, in Illinois, Charles R. Richardson, as the assignee of Thomas Meighan, initiated a legal action against Andrew Schirtz and Henry Hershberger regarding a promissory note for the sum of $50.55. The case arose after the defendants had signed the note, allegedly under false pretenses. At a public sale conducted by Meighan, Schirtz purchased hedge plants totaling $5.50. The clerk present at the sale indicated to the defendants that the note reflected this amount, misrepresenting it as $5.55 (including a stamp cost). The defendants, who were unable to read English, signed the note without understanding that it was for a far greater amount, $50.55. This deception claimed by the defendants not only pertained to the consideration of the note but also represented fraud and circumvention in its execution. After an initial unfavorable ruling in the circuit court, the case was then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Charles R. Richardson, contended that the defendants executed the promissory note under fraudulent misrepresentation. He argued that the note should be deemed invalid due to the defendants not being aware of its true value, as they were misled by the clerk regarding the amount. The plaintiff sought to recover the sum stated in the note, claiming that the circumstances indicated fraud, which voided the note in the hands of a bona fide assignee before maturity, in line with established legal precedent.	The defendants, Andrew Schirtz and Henry Hershberger, argued that they were victims of fraud regarding the execution of the promissory note. They maintained that they signed the document under the belief that it was for a much smaller amount due to the clerk's misrepresentation. Moreover, they emphasized their inability to read or understand English, underscoring their vulnerability to deception. Therefore, they requested that the court uphold the ruling of the lower court, asserting that the note should be considered void and unenforceable.

In January 1872, the case of Louis Zeigler v. W. J. & J. H. Cox was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Circuit Court of McLean County, presided over by Judge Thomas F. Tipton. The primary issue involved a writ of attachment filed by the plaintiff, Louis Zeigler, against the defendants, W. J. and J. H. Cox. The plaintiff accused the defendants of fraudulent conveyance and concealment of property within the two years preceding the affidavit's filing, actions taken to hinder and delay creditors. The affidavit used by Zeigler was challenged by the defendants for its alleged insufficiency, particularly arguing that it did not specify that the fraudulent acts were to the detriment of Zeigler specifically as the attaching creditor. The Supreme Court's review focused on the validity of the affidavit and whether it sufficiently substantiated the plaintiff's claims of fraudulent activity impacting creditors' rights.	The plaintiff, Louis Zeigler, claimed that the defendants had engaged in fraudulent conveyance and concealment of their property, violating provisions under the act of 1865. He sought a writ of attachment to reclaim damages incurred due to these fraudulent actions, arguing that their conduct hindered and delayed creditors, which included him as the attaching creditor.	The defendants, W. J. and J. H. Cox, contended that the affidavit on which the writ of attachment was based was deficient. They specifically argued that it failed to explicitly state that the fraudulent acts harmed Zeigler as the particular attaching creditor. They requested the court to uphold the lower court’s decision to quash the writ due to the alleged insufficiencies in the affidavit.

In June 1872, the case of John P. Phillips v. Rebecca Quick was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated after Phillips, the plaintiff, brought an action against Quick in a police magistrate's court seeking recovery of a $300 judgment on a note. The case took place in Centralia, Illinois. On March 10, 1871, during the initially scheduled trial, Quick filed a motion to dismiss the case, arguing the police magistrate lacked jurisdiction, but the motion was denied, resulting in judgment against her for $285. Quick appealed to the circuit court, which confirmed the magistrate's judgment and increased the amount to $300.90, adding damages and costs. Quick continued to contest the court's jurisdiction, based on a city charter that purportedly extended the jurisdiction limit. However, under state law, at that time, police magistrates could only adjudicate matters involving up to $100 unless explicitly provided by law. The constitution of 1870 mandated uniform jurisdiction for these officers. The court needed to determine whether the charter provision exceeded constitutional authority.	Phillips argued that the police magistrate had jurisdiction to enforce the judgment on the note for $300 as allowed by the law. He insisted that the appeal to the circuit court, which validated the magistrate's judgment, was correct and that the judgment should therefore stand in his favor.	Quick's defense centered on claiming that the police magistrate exceeded jurisdiction, as the amount in question exceeded the legal limit of $100 established by the state's constitution. She contended that the city charter’s provisions were invalid under the larger state legal framework, which dictated uniform jurisdiction for police magistrates. Quick requested dismissal of the case based on a lack of jurisdiction.

Alpheus Badger brought a legal action against The Batavia Paper Manufacturing Company in September 1873, regarding the alleged conversion of a 25-foot-long rotary boiler valued at approximately 10,000 pounds. This case took place in Batavia, Kane County, Illinois. The Chicago Fibre and Paper Company originally acquired this boiler on September 1, 1859, from the Eagle Works Manufacturing Company, securing the payment through a chattel mortgage. The boiler was installed on their premises, which later became a point of contention when the company went bankrupt, and the premises, including the boiler, were sold to the Batavia Paper Manufacturing Company. The relevant deed expressly excluded the boiler from the sale, acknowledging the chattel mortgage had been assigned to Badger. When Badger attempted to reclaim the boiler after the mortgage was due, he was allegedly prevented from doing so by the defendants, arguing that he must pay incurred expenses first. An initial court decision sided with the defendants, leading to Badger's appeal based on claims that the defendants improperly barred his attempts to reclaim the boiler and that the jury instructions were misleading.	Badger claimed that he was wrongfully denied access to the boiler he had the right to reclaim based on the chattel mortgage. He argued that the defendants had converted his property by forbidding its removal and contended that the absence of a formal demand should not negate his right to reclaim the boiler under the circumstances. Badger sought a favorable judgment for the conversion of the boiler, which he asserted was still his property according to the chattel mortgage.	The Batavia Paper Manufacturing Company refuted Badger’s claims, asserting that there was no unlawful conversion as they had made arrangements that allowed the boiler to remain without incurring storage costs. They argued that a formal demand for the boiler was necessary before any claim of conversion could be upheld. Additionally, they contended that as the boiler was considered a fixture, it became part of the real estate during the sale, which should defeat Badger’s claims.

The case of Jane Kelley et al. v. Titus W. Vigas et al. was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on September 27, 1884. The dispute centers around the estate of Titus W. Vigas, who had passed away, leaving behind a will that specified how his property should be divided among his heirs. Key individuals involved in this case include Jane Kelley, the daughter of the deceased, her husband Milton F. Kelley, and the grandchildren of Titus W. Vigas, namely William, Titus, Hattie, and Josephine Vigas. The will provided a life estate to Vigas's widow, who has since died, and stipulated a monetary bequest to Jane Kelley and specific property to her deceased brother’s widow, Sarah L. Vigas. The central issue arose as Jane and her husband challenged a circuit court decree that interpreted the will to allocate the estate primarily to her deceased brother's heirs, limiting Jane’s share to one-fifth. The plaintiffs contested this interpretation, leading to the appeal in this higher court to determine the correct division of the "remainder" of the estate as prescribed in the will. The court examined whether the estate should be divided per stirpes (by branch of the family) or per capita (equally among all members), as ambiguity existed in the will regarding the use of the terms in question.	The plaintiffs, Jane Kelley and her husband, claimed that the distribution of the estate as decreed by the circuit court was incorrect. They argued that, according to the will, Jane Kelley was entitled to a larger share of the estate, asserting that the heirs of Titus W. Vigas should inherit the remainder of the estate per stirpes. They sought to reverse the circuit court's decree and to have the estate equitably divided as per their interpretation of the will and statutory laws governing inheritance.	The defendants, representing the heirs of James Vigas (Titus W. Vigas's deceased son), contended that the circuit court's interpretation was proper, arguing that the terms in the will indicated that the estate should be divided equally among the heirs at law. They maintained that since James Vigas had no surviving issue, the estate should primarily benefit his heirs, thus limiting Jane Kelley's entitlement to one-fifth of the estate.

The case "The Norwich Fire Insurance Company v. George Boomer" was decided in September 1869 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, involving a policy of insurance issued by Norwich Fire Insurance Company to George Boomer. The insurance policy, dated April 3, 1867, covered a frame packing and slaughter house owned by Boyington, Cash & Wilder. The policy insured against fire loss for a year with a maximum coverage of $4,000. Following a fire that partially destroyed the property, Boomer sought to recover a total of $2,757.56 based on his insurance claim. The plaintiff's case hinged on the assertion that he had an insurable interest in the property insured. However, the insurance company asserted defenses related to the validity of the policy, claiming Boomer failed to disclose the nature of his interest as a mortgage hold on the property, which they contended voided the policy. The court held a trial resulting in a verdict favoring Boomer, leading to the insurance company appealing the decision.	George Boomer, the plaintiff, claimed that he suffered a loss due to fire damage to the property covered by the insurance policy. He argued that he sustained an insurable interest in the property and that the company was liable for the loss as specified under the terms of the insurance policy. Boomer's legal requests included the recovery of the aflorementioned amount based on the verdict in his favor from the trial court.	The defendant, Norwich Fire Insurance Company, presented multiple defenses, arguing that Boomer failed to disclose the nature of his interest in the property, which they claimed rendered the policy void. They contended that his omission constituted a material misrepresentation. Additionally, they argued that the premises became vacant for more than twenty days, violating the policy conditions, which would void the coverage. Furthermore, they claimed that other insurances were taken out by the mortgagors without the written consent of the insurance company, which they argued also invalidated the policy.

The case of Spencer & Gardner v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in September 1873, in Will County, Illinois. It involved key individuals including landowners Spencer and Gardner, and the collector representing the People of the State of Illinois. The case arose from an application by the collector for judgment against the lands owned by Spencer and Gardner due to delinquent taxes for the year 1871. The landowners contended that the assessment of their property was excessively high and not compliant with constitutional requirements, as they argued that their property was assessed at a value significantly higher than adjacent properties of equal value. Additionally, they claimed that not all properties in the jurisdiction had been assessed, which they believed constituted an unfair taxation practice. The landowners' objections were initially raised before the circuit court after an earlier ruling in the county court, where the court did not allow the objections to be proved based on the grounds that the defendants had failed to present them to the designated boards for review.	The plaintiffs, represented by Spencer and Gardner, claimed that the property assessment was unconstitutional due to disproportionate valuation, arguing that their property was assessed several times higher than neighboring properties. They requested the court to reject the tax judgment based on these alleged violations of uniformity in taxation as specified in the state constitution.	The defense, representing the People of the State of Illinois, argued that the objections raised by the landowners were invalid because the law does not allow for a court to revise assessments made by an assessor if those assessments were done honestly. They contended that the plaintiffs should have brought their complaints to the proper review boards before challenging the judgment in court, which they did not, thereby waiving their right to contest the assessment.

The case "Zephaniah B. Job et al. v. Albert Tebbetts" was adjudicated in December 1848 in Madison County, Illinois, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The appellants, Zephaniah B. Job and others, were involved in a dispute regarding land ownership against the appellee, Albert Tebbetts. The case arose after Job claimed title to a parcel of land through an Auditor’s deed resulting from a tax sale in 1832. The Circuit Court had previously ruled in favor of Tebbetts, leading Job to appeal the decision. The appeal centered around the admissibility of certain evidentiary documents, including the Auditor’s deed and other related tax documents. Key legal questions addressed included the sufficiency of certificates attached to deeds, the compliance of tax sale procedures, and the validity of documents submitted as evidence.	Job argued that he possessed a valid title to the land through the Auditor's deed from the tax sale of 1832, which was prima facie evidence of the sale's regularity and legality. He requested that the court recognize his title and set aside the Circuit Court's decision, which had favored Tebbetts. The plaintiff contended that procedural errors were made in admitting evidence related to the land's taxation history, which prevented a fair evaluation of his claim.	Tebbetts contended that the Auditor’s deed was insufficient due to non-compliance with legal requisites related to the property's tax listing. He asserted that the court erred in excluding the deposition of the current Auditor, which aimed to show that the land was not properly assessed for taxes. Tebbetts maintained that without this proof, Job's claim could not stand. He requested that the court uphold the lower court's ruling, arguing that the required evidence to challenge the validity of the tax sale was not adequately presented.

In the case of Edgar L. Butler v. William Randall, the dispute was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court and centered around claims for unpaid labor and an alleged indebtedness. The case originated in the Warren Circuit Court, where Butler, the plaintiff, sought to recover $171.14 for work performed for Randall, the defendant, during the period from November 8, 1878, to February 7, 1880. The relationship involved Butler acting in the capacity of an employee for Randall, who paid Butler a monthly salary of $50. However, during the proceedings, Randall filed a counterclaim or set-off demanding a substantial amount of $51,917.39, claiming Butler owed him due to expenses and mishandled funds incurred during Butler's employment. The matter was referred to three referees to address the issues of law and fact. Eventually, the referees determined that Butler was indeed indebted to Randall by an amount of $6,625.10, based on an assessment of funds received and expenditures detailed during the course of their employment relationship. The court later ruled against Butler when he sought to dismiss his action, ultimately siding with the conclusions of the referees’ report.	The plaintiff, Edgar L. Butler, claimed a total of $171.14 was owed to him for his labor while employed by William Randall. His main arguments hinged on the assertion that he had fulfilled his duties and thus deserved compensation for the work performed during the period in question.	The defendant, William Randall, countered Butler's claims by submitting a set-off that claimed an amount significantly greater than what Butler sought. Randall argued that Butler was accountable for a total of $51,917.39, asserting that Butler had mishandled funds during their employment relationship and owed him a balance of $6,625.10 based on a thorough analysis of their financial transactions.

John Harnit filed a trespass action against William Thompson, Henry H. Atwood, and Bentley in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1868. The case originated in Champaign County, where Harnit owned land and had previously sold it to one Allaback, who built a house on the property under a purchase contract. After Allaback's death, during which he had not completed payment for the land, Harnit regained possession as Allaback's widow and family abandoned the property. Despite Harnit's absence, the defendants removed the house from the land without his consent, prompting the legal action. The lower court's trial involved instructions given to the jury regarding the widow's possession of the house, which were contested by Harnit's legal counsel for being misleading and irrelevant to the case.	Harnit argued that the jury instructions given to the defendants were irrelevant and misled the jury into thinking that the widow of Allaback had rightful possession, thereby denying Harnit his claims for damages due to the removal of the house. He contended that he was entitled to recover damages as he had possession of the property through his tenant, and he sought the reversal of the lower court's judgment on these grounds.	The defendants claimed that the instructions provided to the jury regarding the widow's rights to possess the house were valid. They asserted that according to the laws regarding equitable title, the contract of sale gave the widow rights that affected Harnit’s claims. Their request was for the court to affirm these instructions and uphold the jury's verdict.

This case, 'Charles F. Foskett v. John Wolf,' was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on April 25, 1886. It involves Charles F. Foskett, who served as the executor of the estate of E. J. French, deceased, since March 10, 1880. Prior to August 17, 1880, several claims against the estate worth thousands of dollars had been probated and allowed in the County Court of Richland County. Foskett paid thirty cents on the dollar for these claims, and one of the claims, amounting to $560.45, was approved, prompting a payment of $164.52 to the appellant, John Wolf. Later, Foskett paid Wolf the remaining $395.93, believing that all debts had been presented and sufficient assets were available. However, additional claims were later allowed, leading Foskett to determine that the estate was insolvent, with only seventy cents of the dollar allocated to the seventh class claims. Foskett seeks to recover the thirty percent he erroneously overpaid Wolf, arguing it was a mistake. The estate had not been formally settled, nor had the insolvency been established in court.",	Foskett claims that he mistakenly overpaid John Wolf, believing the estate was solvent and all debts settled. He seeks to recover the thirty percent, citing that the payment was made in error without court approval or a proper accounting of the estate's liabilities. Foskett argues that he should be reimbursed for an amount he believes Wolf should not have retained since the estate is now recognized as insolvent.",	John Wolf argues that he was legally entitled to receive the full amount paid by Foskett as it was due to him. He contends that Foskett has not suffered any individual loss since the payments made were from the estate's funds and not Foskett's personal money. Wolf asserts that without a court order establishing the insolvency of the estate and the pro-rata distribution to creditors, there is no legal basis for Foskett's claim to recover the overpayment.",

James M. Campbell initiated a legal action against Horace S. Head in the Circuit Court of McDonough County, Illinois, concerning the wrongful detention of a horse named Nephi, valued at $100. The case originated in 1850 when Campbell filed a plaint and affidavit in replevin, claiming rightful ownership and subsequent wrongful detention of the horse by Head. The affidavit stated that the horse had not been taken for any tax, assessment, or fine under Illinois law. Head's response included a motion to quash the writ, deeming the affidavit defective due to its failure to explicitly state that the horse had not been distrained for taxes or assessments. The Circuit Court sustained Head's motion, quashing the writ, which led Campbell to seek permission to amend his affidavit. This request was denied. The court then proceeded to assess damages, ruling that damages could be determined by the court rather than a jury, which Campbell also contested. The case culminated in an appeal brought by Campbell to the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1851.	Campbell claimed he was the lawful owner and entitled to possess the horse Nephi, which Head was allegedly wrongfully detaining. He requested a return of the horse and asserted that the affidavit supporting his claim was sufficient as it stated that the horse had not been taken for any tax, assessment, or fine under state law. Campbell's application to amend the affidavit after the court's decision was denied, prompting his appeal.	Head argued that Campbell's affidavit was defective because it did not adequately prove that the horse had not been distrained for taxes or assessments according to Illinois law. He maintained that, under the law, the court had the authority to quash the writ and that the damages should be assessed without a jury since the verdict had favored him. Head contended that the refusal to allow an amended affidavit was appropriate given the procedural errors and that the matter should be resolved without further trial.

In the case of George Hosmer et al. v. Marcus Teller, which took place in 1888 in Cook County, Illinois, the plaintiffs, George Hosmer and others, initiated legal action against the defendant, Marcus Teller, under an attachment claim. They alleged that Teller had fraudulently conveyed or assigned his assets within the two years preceding the filing of their affidavit, with the intention of hindering and delaying his creditors. During the trial, the jury was instructed to find in favor of the defendant after the plaintiffs rested their case. The court evaluated the evidence provided by the plaintiffs and concluded that, while some actions by the defendant might raise suspicion, there was insufficient evidence to substantiate a claim of fraud that would justify a verdict against Teller.	The plaintiffs claimed that Marcus Teller engaged in fraudulent activity by conveying or assigning his effects to evade his creditors. They sought to establish that such actions were intended to hinder and delay them from recovering debts owed. Their primary legal request was for the court to uphold their attachment and rule against the defendant based on these claims of fraud.	The defendant, Marcus Teller, countered the allegations of fraud, asserting that the claims made by the plaintiffs were unfounded. He argued that the evidence presented did not support a legitimate claim of fraudulent conveyance and emphasized that the actions noted by the plaintiffs did not warrant a verdict in their favor. Teller sought to have the court uphold the jury's instruction to find for him based on the lack of sufficient evidence of fraud.

The case "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Henry L. Rucker, Judge of the Cook County Court" took place in Chicago, Illinois, in June 1853. The Illinois Central Railroad Company, having been incorporated in February 1851, sought to construct a railroad extending from La Salle to Chicago, which included portions that encroached upon land owned by the Chicago Hydraulic Company. This work involved land along the shores of Lake Michigan and was subject to state and city regulations. The Illinois Central Railroad Company had applied to the county judge for the appointment of appraisers to assess damages resulting from their construction, which the judge denied. The railroad company contended that the judge had overstepped his bounds by refusing to appoint appraisers, claiming the legal right to locate their road as granted in their charter. The situation involved multiple parties, including landowners whose property would be impacted and whose interests had to be assessed. The railroad company claimed it had obtained the necessary permissions but faced opposition on grounds including the timing of the road's location and the legality of their actions concerning the lake's waters.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company (plaintiff) argued that it had the legal right, per its charter, to construct the railroad over the disputed lands with city assent. They asserted that the county judge's refusal to appoint appraisers for damage assessment was inappropriate. The company contended that failure to meet the initial deadline for the road's location did not constitute forfeiture of their rights, especially since city assent was required and only granted after the deadline had passed. They sought a writ of mandamus compelling the judge to appoint appraisers.	Henry L. Rucker, the county judge (defendant), defended his refusal to appoint appraisers by asserting that the railroad company did not have the right to locate its road over the waters of Lake Michigan. He outlined several objections, including that the company’s failure to locate the road within the lawful timeline imposed a forfeiture of rights and emphasized the hazardous implications for navigation and property interests of the hydraulic company. Furthermore, he argued that allowing the railroad to proceed would interfere with rights already granted to the hydraulic company.

William S. Frink and Elias S. Peabody were involved in a legal dispute against Sarah E. Peabody, stemming from a promissory note executed on February 7, 1877. The note, totaling $3,673.14, was executed by Henry Tanner as the principal, with Frink and Peabody serving as sureties. Following a series of assignments, the note led to a judgment against all three parties in September 1877 for an increased amount. Execution efforts, however, faced challenges over the years, including unsuccessful attempts to satisfy the judgment through the sale of Tanner's personal property. The case centered on a later transfer of property interests related to Peabody, whose interests were sold in quit claim deeds. The dispute escalated to court when Sarah E. Peabody filed a bill in chancery, asserting rights over the property in question and challenging the enforceability of the judgment obtained against her late co-surety, Tanner. The court examined the equity involved, specifically what obligations Frink had regarding the payment of the judgment and shared responsibilities as a surety.	Sarah E. Peabody argued that the judgment obtained against her and her co-sureties had been improperly assigned and that it was inequitable to allow enforcement against her property. She claimed that since Frink had effectively made a payment on the judgment, he could not pursue further claims against her. Additionally, she sought a declaration that her property was free from the judgment's lien.	Frink and Morrison contended that the judgment was still valid and that Frink's payment did not negate the credit owed by his co-surety. They argued that the assignment of the judgment to Morrison was legitimate and that they were entitled to enforce it, thereby seeking payment from Peabody for her portion of the judgment obligation.

William J. Davis v. John A. Hamlin is a case that dates back to November 20, 1883, in Chicago, Illinois. John A. Hamlin had been the lessee and manager of the Grand Opera House for over a decade. After the Chicago fire in 1871, he rebuilt the theater and secured a significant lease with William Borden, the property owner. Hamlin had invested over $75,000 into its construction and was generating substantial profit from its operations. As the manager, he employed William J. Davis, who was responsible for coordinating performances and managing business matters. When Hamlin's lease was approaching expiration, he sought to renew it. However, during this time, Davis secretly negotiated with Borden to acquire the lease for himself at a significantly higher rental amount than Hamlin was willing to pay. Despite Davis's assurances to Hamlin that he was not pursuing the lease, he acted contrary to this and ultimately procured the lease for his own benefit. This led Hamlin to file a bill in equity against Davis, claiming that Davis was acting as a trustee for him in the lease matter and had betrayed his fiduciary duty.	John A. Hamlin's primary claim was that William J. Davis, as his agent and employee, had breached his fiduciary duty by acquiring the renewal lease of the Grand Opera House for himself rather than for Hamlin’s benefit. Hamlin argued that he had a reasonable expectation of renewing the lease and held a vested interest that Davis had undermined by securing the lease for his own profit. He sought a declaration from the court that Davis was a trustee for him in this matter, claiming that any benefits obtained from the lease should rightfully belong to Hamlin.	William J. Davis contended that he did not have a formal fiduciary duty regarding the lease renewal since he was not expressly charged with that responsibility by Hamlin. He claimed that his employment was restricted to managing the business of the theater and that Hamlin had no legal claim or interest in the property after the expiration of his lease. Davis maintained that his actions in negotiating the lease were therefore permissible and did not constitute a breach of trust or fiduciary duty to Hamlin.

This case, "Henry H. Gage v. Jacob Mayer," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 15, 1886. The context of the case involves a tax deed issued to Henry H. Gage on March 26, 1880, concerning several lots in Lake Township, Cook County, which had been sold due to non-payment of taxes on August 27, 1877. Jacob Mayer, as the plaintiff, filed a bill in the Cook County Circuit Court seeking to invalidate this tax deed. The central issue revolved around the validity of the tax deed, specifically whether proper notice was served to all parties in possession of the land in accordance with the Illinois statutes. An affidavit claimed service of notice on W. H. Rice and Jacob Mayer but failed to confirm that I. Mayer, another person named on the tax assessment, received the notice. The court had to determine if service to one party sufficed for another with a similar name, ultimately deciding that both I. Mayer and J. Mayer were not legally interchangeable without clear evidence to the contrary.	Jacob Mayer argued that the tax deed issued to Gage was invalid because it did not comply with the mandatory requirements outlined in the Illinois Revenue Act for proper service of notice. Mayer claimed that the affidavit did not demonstrate that notice was served on I. Mayer, who was listed as the record owner, rendering the tax deed null and void. The primary legal request was to have the tax deed set aside to remove it as a cloud on his title to the property.	Henry H. Gage contended that he properly acquired the tax deed, citing that service to J. Mayer (assuming it referred to I. Mayer) should suffice, given the doctrine of idem sonans (the idea that similar-sounding names can be considered identical in legal context). Gage also filed a cross-bill claiming ownership of the property under four different legal titles, arguing that his claims were legitimate and should not be dismissed. He maintained that even if the court found issues with the specific tax deed in question, his other titles remained valid.

The case "City of Ottawa v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. John D. Caton et al." was heard in September 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It arose from a legislative act passed on March 7, 1867, which authorized the construction of two pivot bridges over the Illinois & Michigan Canal in Ottawa, LaSalle County. Commissioners were appointed to oversee the project, and a tax of $12,000 was raised for the bridges' construction. After the completion of the bridges, the city authorities neglected their duty to maintain and operate them, leading to citizen concerns about public safety and increased risks in the canal navigation. Citizens and property owners, representing their interest, petitioned for a writ of mandamus in the Circuit Court of LaSalle County to compel the city to take responsibility for the bridges. The city council, however, challenged the petition, claiming discretionary power over the bridges and alleging that the legislative act was unconstitutional.	The plaintiffs, represented by John D. Caton and others, asserted that the City of Ottawa had a statutory duty to maintain, repair, and operate the newly constructed bridges as mandated by the legislative act. They sought a writ of mandamus to compel the city to fulfill these obligations, arguing that the city's inaction endangered public safety and contradicted the interests of local property owners and businesses.	The City of Ottawa, through its attorney, argued that the legislative act was unconstitutional, claiming that it improperly authorized the appointment of commissioners to levy taxes. They contended that the city had discretion regarding the maintenance of the bridges and that the plaintiffs had adequate legal remedies available to address any grievances they might have against the city.

In 1871, in Iroquois County, Illinois, the case "Samuel B. Walton et al. v. J. D. Develing et al." arose involving the town's election regarding a proposition to subscribe $30,000 to the capital stock of a railroad company. Samuel B. Walton and others, the plaintiffs, obtained a writ of injunction to prevent the election on grounds that there had already been a previous vote against a $50,000 subscription. The town's clerk posted notices for the election based on a petition from ten legal voters. Despite the injunction, the election was held, leading to a contempt charge against the election officials for disobeying the court’s order. The case was escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court to determine if the lower court had jurisdiction over the matter and whether the defendants' actions constituted contempt.	The plaintiffs argued that the election should not proceed because a previous election on the same issue had been held, thus claiming a violation of legal and procedural rights. They sought to have the injunction enforced, claiming that the actions of the election officials were unlawful and in contempt of court.	The defendants contended that the writ of injunction was void since the election was conducted in accordance with the law, which permitted the solicitation of a vote for subscribing to the stock. They argued that the court had no authority to restrict the lawful election process and maintained that they complied with their legal duties. The defendants requested the court to dismiss the injunction and reverse any contempt fines imposed on them.

In 1881, J. V. Farwell & Co. initiated a case against Clarence V. Shove in the Mercer County Circuit Court, Illinois, by obtaining a writ of attachment for Shove's estate. The issuance of the writ was based on an affidavit claiming that Shove had fraudulently conveyed and concealed his assets within the two years preceding the affidavit to hinder his creditors. Farwell & Co. alleged that Shove's actions were intended to obstruct their ability to collect debts owed by him. Shove responded with a plea challenging the allegations in the affidavit. The case was tried without a jury, and the trial court ruled in favor of Shove. The decision was subsequently appealed, and the Appellate Court for the Second District affirmed the trial court's judgment. The case eventually reached the Illinois Supreme Court for further review.	J. V. Farwell & Co. claimed that Clarence V. Shove had engaged in fraudulent activities that hindered their ability to collect debts. They argued that Shove had intentionally concealed or disposed of his assets, violating the rights of creditors. The plaintiff sought to reverse the judgment of the lower courts and enforce their claims for the recovery of amounts owed.	Clarence V. Shove contested the allegations made by Farwell & Co., asserting that the claims were unsubstantiated. He filed a plea in abatement to counter the accusations of fraud, maintaining that he had not engaged in any fraudulent conveyance or concealment of assets. Shove's legal stance focused on challenging the evidential basis for the plaintiffs' claims and requested the court to uphold the lower court's judgment in his favor.

In 1867, in Massac County, Illinois, Albert P. Mingia was indicted for the murder of John T. Collier. The indictment presented by the grand jury at the November term resulted in multiple continuances of the trial, with the final setting scheduled for May 1869. During the trial, a juror accepted by Mingia was dismissed after the State’s attorney questioned his name. Despite various motions by Mingia's counsel, including a motion to dismiss the prosecution, the jury ultimately rendered a guilty verdict, sentencing him to twenty years in prison. Mingia’s legal team later sought a new trial, arguing that the verdict was contrary to law and evidence, including claims of newly discovered evidence and improper jury instructions. These motions were denied by the court, leading to a writ of error filed by Mingia, claiming multiple errors in the trial process.	Albert P. Mingia, the plaintiff in error, argued that the trial was flawed due to various procedural issues. He claimed that a juror was improperly discharged, the prosecution should have been dismissed, and that the guilty verdict was against the evidence. Additionally, he sought a new trial based on alleged newly discovered evidence that could prove his innocence and errors in jury instructions that he contended impacted the fairness of the trial.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by the Attorney General, contended that the trial was conducted fairly according to the law. They defended the dismissal of the juror by asserting it was within the court’s rights, arguing that the claims for a new trial lacked adequate evidence or grounds. The State also maintained that there was no error in the court's previous rulings, including the denial of the motion to dismiss the case or arrest judgment, asserting that the laws governing the trial were appropriately applied.

In June 1851, the case titled "Samuel P. Bailey, et al., Appellants, v. J. E. Hardy, Appellee" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The origins of the case trace back to an action brought by J.E. Hardy before a justice of the peace, followed by an appeal to the Circuit Court of Tazewell County. Samuel P. Bailey, representing the appellants, sought a continuance for a trial due to the absence of a key witness. In his affidavit, Bailey claimed he could only prove that a note central to the case was owned by Clement Turner, who acquired it through a series of assignments starting with Benjamin Prettyman. On the denied application for a continuance, the Circuit Court judge proceeded to try the case without a jury in September 1850, ultimately ruling in favor of Hardy. This judgment led to an appeal by Bailey, challenging the court's refusal to continue the trial on the grounds of absent witness testimony.	The plaintiff, J.E. Hardy, argued that despite the note's previous ownership by Clement Turner, this did not negate his rights as the current holder of the note. In seeking a judgment, he relied on the assertion that the procedural rules allowed him to continue without the absent witness, asserting that the ownership of the note had not been effectively transferred back to the original payee.	The defendants, represented by Samuel P. Bailey, maintained that the absent witness’s testimony was critical. They claimed that proof of the note's ownership by Clement Turner, established through various assignments, was essential to their defense. Bailey argued that the court erred in denying the continuance as it did not allow for adequate preparation for trial, insisting that without this testimony, they could not safely proceed.

The case "The Marine Bank of Chicago v. The Auditor of State" took place in December 1852, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The Marine Bank of Chicago, a financial institution, filed a petition for a writ of mandamus against the Auditor of State, seeking a share of the two mill tax promulgated for the purpose of addressing the State's debts. The Bank had deposited public stocks with the Auditor as required by the general banking law. These stocks served to secure the redemption of the bank's circulating notes and were supposed to remain under strict controls to ensure their integrity and availability for fulfilling financial obligations. When the bank sought to participate in the distribution of the tax, the Auditor rejected its claim, asserting that while the stocks were deposited, they were not entitled to share in the tax distribution. The court was tasked with adjudicating whether the bank could claim a distributive share of the tax given this context.	The Marine Bank of Chicago argued that the public stocks it deposited should entitle it to a share of the two mill tax under the Illinois constitution intended for servicing the State debt. It contended that since the value of the securities exceeded the outstanding notes issued by the Auditor, it had a right to participate in the fund and receive payments related to its equity in the deposited stocks.	The Auditor of State maintained that according to the general banking law, while the Illinois stocks were deposited, they did not qualify for distribution in the two mill tax. The Auditor had the authority to allow banks to withdraw stocks after they provided sufficient substitute securities, but the bank had failed to comply accurately with the conditions set for presenting claims against the deposited stocks.

In January 1867, in the city of Cairo, Illinois, a legal action was initiated by the firm Gaff, Cochran & Co., comprising Thomas Gaff, James W. Gaff, and George W. Cochran, against Joel S. Byington. The dispute arose from a promissory note executed on June 23, 1865, for $2,500, which was part of the purchase price for the steamboat "Ella," sold to the firm of Musson & Culley. Byington had guaranteed this note. The plaintiffs contended that the sale of the vessel was valid and that Byington was liable for the debt as per his guaranty. The defendant, Byington, claimed that the original agreement was abandoned when the plaintiffs sold the boat solely to Rodney Culley without his knowledge or consent, thereby discharging him from liability. The case involved testimonies regarding the delivery of the boat and the contractual obligations between the parties involved.	The plaintiffs argued that the boat was legally sold and delivered to Musson & Culley, and that the contract was never abandoned. They contended that Byington, as a guarantor, remained liable for the debt represented by the note. They sought judgment against Byington for the amount owed under the guaranty, asserting that the requirements for a valid sale and transfer of the vessel were met and that they acted appropriately under the terms of the agreement.	Byington’s primary defense was that the plaintiffs had abandoned the original sales contract by transferring the boat only to Culley without his consent, thus discharging him from his guarantor obligations. He asserted that the transfer was fraudulent and not in accordance with the original agreement, which specified that the boat was to be sold to both Musson and Culley. Byington claimed that his liability as a guarantor was thus nullified, as the conditions upon which he guaranteed the note had fundamentally changed without his agreement.

Abraham Bernstein filed a legal case against E. R. Walker in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose from a dispute over certain furniture that Bernstein claimed was converted by Walker. The action took place in Cook County, Illinois, and the final court opinion was filed on January 18, 1888. Bernstein initially sought a remedy through replevin but recovered only a small portion of the goods. Subsequently, a count in trover was filed, and the issues were presented before a jury.
