Nancy Myers claimed that the state’s construction of the Copperas Creek dam caused severe flooding on her lands, rendering them almost worthless. She sought compensation for the damages, initially estimating the loss at $1,680 and later providing various assessments from other witnesses that ranged up to $5,760. Myers contended that her claims were valid and not barred by the statute of limitations as they were filed within two years after the cause of action began.	The State of Illinois contended that Myers's claims were not substantiated by evidence of significant damages. The Attorney General's office argued that the claim was barred by the statute of limitations and presented a general denial regarding the effects of the dam construction on Myers's property. Witnesses for the state testified that the damages to her land were minimal or nonexistent and that some of the land was already swampy before the dam's construction.

On March 10, 1845, P. S. Loughborough, who resided in Kentucky and owned extensive land in Illinois, sold a specific tract to Lawrence Young, the defendant. Young did not record this deed until December 31, 1855. Loughborough passed away in 1852, leaving his property to his mother, Elizabeth Loughborough. In 1855, Elizabeth sold all her remaining Illinois lands, including the tract in question, to a group including Gamble and Crawford through a quit claim deed. Jesse Bayles, who obtained rights to this land through an intermediate conveyance from Gamble and his associates, filed a bill against Young seeking to annul Young's deed, claiming it cast an unjust cloud on his title. Bayles was already in possession of the tract and argued for his rights based on this possession. The court ultimately ruled in favor of Young, finding that Bayles’ claims were not valid as proper notice of Young's prior conveyance was established before gambling and his co-grantees conveyed their title.	Jesse Bayles claimed that Lawrence Young's deed, recorded after Bayles’ acquisition, represented an unjust cloud on his title to the disputed land. Bayles sought the cancellation of Young’s deed, arguing that he held rightful possession of the property and that Young’s claims to it were void due to the lack of proper recording prior to Bayles acquiring his interest.	Lawrence Young contended that he had a valid deed to the property, recorded legally before any transaction involving Bayles. He argued that Bayles and his co-grantees were fully aware of the earlier conveyance from P. S. Loughborough to him, which nullified Bayles' position as an innocent purchaser. Young maintained that the information about the prior sale was readily accessible and that the court should dismiss Bayles’ claims based on this knowledge.

In June 1876, the case of Daniel F. Harrah v. John Conley et al. was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court, following proceedings that took place in the Circuit Court of Jasper County. The case originated from a petition filed by Daniel F. Harrah in December 1873, seeking the appointment of a commission of surveyors to permanently locate a disputed section corner of land. The defendants, represented by John Conley and others, responded by denying that the section corner was in dispute, asserting it had already been duly established. Despite the defendants' answer, the Circuit Court, upon Harrah's motion, defaulted the defendants and appointed three surveyors to survey the corner. The surveyors ultimately confirmed its previously established location without making any changes. The court then ruled against Harrah, ordering him to pay the costs of the proceedings. Harrah found this judgment erroneous, leading to the appeal which focused on technical legal questions regarding the default of the defendants despite their filed answer.	Daniel F. Harrah, the plaintiff, contended that the court's decision to appoint surveyors to establish the disputed section corner was justified. He sought to secure control over the corner in question, alleging that its location was uncertain and had not been properly surveyed. Harrah challenged the subsequent judgment that required him to pay all costs of the proceedings, arguing that the defendants' presence and answer should have been considered before defaulting them.	The defendants, led by John Conley, argued that there was no valid dispute regarding the section corner, maintaining that it had been properly established prior to the petition. Their key argument centered on the assertion that the Circuit Court erred by defaulting them despite their posted answer which denied any dispute. They requested that the judgment against Harrah should stand, asserting that the answer provided sufficient grounds for the court not to take a default action.

In 1876, in Illinois, Amos Atkins initiated a legal action against Thomas Byrnes regarding a replevin bond. The case arose when Atkins sought to reclaim possession of certain mules that Byrnes possessed under a distress warrant for unpaid rent owed by a third party, William A. Skeen. The replevin action was initially brought against Byrnes, and following that, a suit on the replevin bond was brought forward by Lewis W. Moore, the sheriff, for the use of William Cool. The central issue of the case revolved around whether the sheriff could bring a suit on the bond for someone who was not a party to the original replevin suit. There was also contention regarding the admissibility of evidence related to the value of the mules and any liens on them, particularly as it pertained to testimony provided by William Cool regarding Byrnes' agency role and the ownership interests in the mules. The legal proceedings were overseen by Hon. William H. Snyder at the Circuit Court of Madison County.	Amos Atkins, the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to recover the full value of the mules under the replevin bond, arguing that his rights as a chattel mortgage holder permitted him to sell the mules and thus seek compensation. He contended that he had the right to the property despite the existing distress warrant held by Cool, and he sought a handling of the bond that recognized his legal interest in the property.	Lewis W. Moore, representing the defendant's interests, argued that the suit could only be maintained for the use of the defendant in the original replevin suit and not for another party who had no direct connection to the case. Moreover, he emphasized that the court had correctly excluded evidence pertaining to the lien on the mules, as it was not relevant to Atkins, who allegedly had no direct ownership interest in the mules at the hearing.

The case titled "The United States Life Insurance Company v. Elizabeth Kielgast, Administratrix" took place in New York City and involved the insurance policy of Otto Wilhelm Kielgast, who died on January 17, 1885. The plaintiff, Elizabeth Kielgast, acting as administratrix of her late husband’s estate, sought to recover the amount of the life insurance policy issued by The United States Life Insurance Company, dated July 22, 1884. A condition of the policy stated that if the insured died by self-destruction within three years, the contract would be void. The insurance company contended that Kielgast's death was a result of self-destruction. During the trial, evidence from a Coroner's inquest was disputed, focusing on whether it was admissible to prove the circumstances surrounding the death. The court ruled against the insurance company's request to include the Coroner's inquest verdict, leading to a trial verdict in favor of the plaintiff, granting her $85,597.50 plus costs.	The plaintiff’s main arguments included that she had complied with all requirements of the insurance policy concerning proof of death. She presented various documents to the insurance company, including a sworn statement and testimonies from relatives about her husband's death. The plaintiff sought the insurance amount claiming that her husband's death should not be classified as self-destruction due to underlying mental health issues, specifically temporary insanity at the time of death.	The defendant claimed the insurance policy was void because the insured died by self-destruction, thus not fulfilling the terms of the policy. They argued that the Coroner's verdict, which found the death was due to a self-inflicted gunshot wound while the insured was temporarily insane, should be admissible to support their case. Furthermore, they maintained that the plaintiff's submissions regarding the death, particularly her testimony at the inquest, were not sufficient and should discredit her claims.

The case of Charles Simpson et al. v. George Kincaid took place in 1890, specifically on February 4, in Effingham County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Charles Simpson and others, were sellers who filed a lawsuit against the defendant, George Kincaid, seeking damages for his alleged breach of a contract regarding the purchase of a stallion. The claim arose after Kincaid did not complete the purchase as agreed. During the trial, evidence was presented that Kincaid asserted false representations were made by the plaintiffs concerning the horse's identity. Kincaid testified that he had been misled about the horse being the one he intended to buy, leading to a conflict in testimonies, as Simpson and other witnesses contradicted Kincaid’s assertions. The trial judge instructed the jury on how to evaluate the defense of false representation presented by Kincaid, emphasizing that if the plaintiffs knowingly made false claims, the defendant was not obligated to complete the sale. The jury sided with Kincaid, resulting in a judgment against the plaintiffs for costs, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs claimed that Kincaid breached the contractual agreement to purchase the stallion, positing that they had fulfilled their obligations as sellers. They argued that Kincaid's assertion of false representations was invalid, and insisted that the contract was valid and enforceable, thereby entitling them to recover damages for non-performance.	The defendant, Kincaid, argued that he was induced into the purchase by false representations made by the plaintiffs regarding the identity of the stallion. He maintained that if the plaintiffs intentionally misled him about the horse he thought he was buying, he should not be held accountable for failing to complete the sale. Kincaid requested that the court instruct the jury to consider these claims of misrepresentation when deliberating on the case.

On September 15, 1856, F. Parmelee & Co., a partnership based in Chicago, borrowed $50,000 from Daniel Lawrence, a lender from Medford, Massachusetts. To secure the loan, they conveyed certain real estate in Chicago to Lawrence. The arrangement included a deed that referred to their obligations under a lease and a purchase contract and included a covenant for quiet enjoyment. The partners agreed to repay the amount in five annual installments with 10% interest. They paid interest up to April 1861 but ceased any principal repayments thereafter. On August 4, 1864, three partners filed a bill in chancery against Lawrence, misrepresenting the nature of their transaction as a purchase while omitting the fact that they had previously conveyed the property to him. They sought an injunction against Lawrence, claiming he was unable to convey a perfect title and was threatening to collect the debt and evict them. Lawrence countered with a cross-bill, clarifying the transaction as a loan secured by a mortgage and asked for repayment or the sale of the premises. After various legal maneuvers, including one partner settling and claiming a release from obligations, the case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for final judgment, focusing on the interpretation of the release and obligations among the partners.	The plaintiffs, Parmelee & Co., argued that they were entitled to a discharge from all covenants related to the debt owed Lawrence following a settlement between one partner and Lawrence, which they claimed satisfied their obligations. They sought reformation of their covenants and the reconveyance of the property held by Lawrence, asserting that the release provided to Bigelow served to extinguish their liabilities to Lawrence.	Lawrence maintained that the transaction was a loan secured by a mortgage and that the release given to Bigelow did not absolve the remaining partners of their obligations. He argued that the release was executed under the influence of fraudulent representations by Bigelow and emphasized that maintaining his rights against the other partners was a pivotal aspect of the agreement. Lawrence sought a decree for repayment of the debt or a sale of the premises.

In 1871, in Kane County, Illinois, Henry P. Pierce, who was elected as the county clerk in December 1861, filed a petition for a writ of mandamus against the Board of Supervisors of Kane County. Pierce served as clerk until December 1869 and claimed to have attended probate court sessions for 1459 days. After serving, he submitted a bill for compensation to the board in March 1870, which the board subsequently refused to process. The circuit court of Kane County initially granted an alternative writ but sustained the county’s demurrer, leading to an appeal from Pierce. The main issue under contention was whether the county board was obligated to compensate him for this service under the relevant statutes, which provided details about fees and allowances for county clerks. There was a particular focus on whether a per diem allowance was mandatory for clerks attending probate court.	Henry P. Pierce, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to a per diem allowance for the days he attended probate court as county clerk. He based his claim on the statute that states while clerks cannot charge fees for county work, they may receive reasonable compensation, including a per diem for court attendance. He contended that the Board of Supervisors was obliged to audit and compensate him for the services provided.	The Board of Supervisors of Kane County countered that they were not legally required to grant Pierce a per diem allowance for attending probate court. They claimed that the statute allowed for discretion in providing such compensation and that the board's decision not to pay was acceptable given that Pierce already received fees for the probate services rendered. Hence, they argued that no writ of mandamus should compel them to allow any specific amount.

The case "The People, for the use of Stark County v. Ammon Moon et al." arose in December 1841 and was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The key figures involved included Ammon Moon, the treasurer of Putnam County, and the county commissioners of Stark County. The plaintiff, representing Stark County, claimed that Moon refused to pay $1,600.45, which was part of the internal improvement fund allocated to Stark County according to the law. The funds were initially received by Moon from the Fund Commissioners of Illinois, but he did not distribute the allocated funds to Stark County upon their request. The plaintiffs contended that Moon, as treasurer, was obligated to comply with this demand, and his failure to do so constituted a breach of duty. The circumstances of the case included Moon's appointment as an agent to collect these funds for Putnam County and the legal argument over whether he failed in his official duties as treasurer.	The plaintiff claimed that Ammon Moon, as the treasurer of Putnam County, received $9,870 from the Illinois Fund Commissioners for purposes defined by the internal improvement law but failed to pay $1,600.45 to Stark County as required by the statute. The plaintiffs requested recovery of this amount along with interest, arguing that Moon's refusal to pay constituted a failure to perform his legal duties, and sought to hold him and his sureties accountable for this breach.	The defendants argued that Moon performed all legal duties required of him as treasurer and that he did not actually receive the funds in his official capacity as treasurer but rather as an agent for Putnam County. They contended that the funds were allocated for specific purposes and that Moon's receipt of them did not establish a liability for his sureties under the bond. The defendants maintained that since Moon's actions were outside the scope of official duties, they should not be held financially liable.

The case titled "The Joliet and Northern Indiana Railroad Company, Appellant, v. Robert Jones, Appellee" took place in 1858 in Will County, Illinois. The dispute arose when Robert Jones, the plaintiff, accused the Joliet and Northern Indiana Railroad Company (then known as the Oswego and Indiana Plank Road Company) of failing to fulfill a contractual obligation to construct a fence along the south side of a railroad after acquiring a right of way from Jones. This contract was established in 1853 when Jones sold his land to the railroad company, with the express condition that the company would build a fence to protect his sheep from entering the railroad tracks. After the railroad began operations, some of Jones's sheep escaped onto the tracks and were killed by passing trains. The plaintiff sought damages of $500, claiming negligence on the part of the railroad company for not building the fence. The case was tried at the May term of 1857, resulting in a jury verdict in favor of Jones for $231.50.	Robert Jones claimed that the Joliet and Northern Indiana Railroad Company breached their contract by failing to build the required fence, leading to the death and injury of his sheep. He argued that the company’s neglect directly contributed to his damages and sought compensation for the loss of his livestock, which he attributed to the railroad's failure to fulfill its obligations outlined in their agreement.	The Joliet and Northern Indiana Railroad Company contended that Robert Jones failed to show that the railroad was the same entity as the original plank road company that received the deed. They argued that there was no evidence proving the identity of the two companies and that Jones had a responsibility to exercise ordinary care to prevent his sheep from entering the tracks. The defendant maintained that any negligence on their part in failing to fulfill the fencing obligation did not absolve Jones of his own responsibility in managing his sheep.

In September 1868, the case of Leverett S. Chittenden v. John Evans was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following a series of legal proceedings that began in a justice of the peace court. The appellant, Leverett S. Chittenden, sought to recover a colt from the appellee, John Evans. The initial judgment in the justice court favored Evans, prompting Chittenden to appeal to the Circuit Court of Kendall County, which subsequently transferred the trial to DuPage County due to a change of venue. Despite the change, the outcome remained the same, with the jury finding in favor of Evans again. Chittenden then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking a reversal of the decision on several grounds, including alleged errors regarding the jury's verdict and instructions during the trial. The case raised issues related to the formality of the verdict and the handling of jury instructions, reflecting broader practices in Illinois courts regarding verdicts and jury guidance.	Chittenden claimed ownership of the colt and argued that the lower courts erred in changing the jury's verdict and refusing certain jury instructions he had requested. He contended that the jury's decision was not supported by sufficient evidence and sought a reversal of the judgments rendered against him.	John Evans contended that the jury's verdict was correct and that the changes made by the clerk to formalize the verdict were proper under the law. He maintained that the judge's refusal to provide certain instructions was justified, as those instructions were misleading and argumentative. Evans argued that the evidence presented in the case supported the jury’s finding and that multiple juries had consistently ruled in his favor.

In September 1868, in Kane County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between William C. Wilder and Lydia A. House regarding a property occupancy issue. A tenant named Eich had been renting a house and allowed Mrs. House to occupy certain rooms. They lived there together for several months until Eich surrendered his possession to Wilder, who became the new tenant. After a few weeks, while Mrs. House was temporarily absent, Wilder forcibly entered the room she occupied, disposed of her furniture, and used physical violence to prevent her from returning. This incident led Mrs. House to seek refuge with a neighbor. In response to these actions, she filed a lawsuit against Wilder for trespass upon her person and property, resulting in a jury verdict in her favor for $256.	Mrs. House claimed that Wilder unlawfully trespassed on her property and used physical force against her. She argued that even if Eich had improperly allowed her to occupy the premises, Wilder had no legal right to resort to force to regain possession. Her primary legal request was for compensation for damages sustained due to the trespassing actions.	Wilder contended that Mrs. House was unlawfully occupying the property since Eich had surrendered his tenancy to him. He argued that he was justified in taking possession of the property. Additionally, he raised concerns regarding certain jury instructions given during the trial, asserting that they assumed disputed facts not supported by evidence.

The case, "The City of Chicago v. James Turner," was decided in September 1875 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It involved a dispute between the City of Chicago and James Turner, who owned a slaughterhouse and was engaged in the business of slaughtering. The conflict arose when the City Council made an ordinance granting John Beid & Co. the exclusive right to conduct all slaughtering within Chicago, effectively monopolizing the business. This ordinance required the city to prevent any other slaughtering, leading city servants to disrupt Turner’s business by driving away his customers and causing significant harm. Turner claimed damages resulting from these actions, arguing that the ordinance was outside the city's legal powers, thus making the city liable for the acts of its servants.	Turner, the plaintiff, contended that the city’s ordinance was unlawful and constituted an abuse of power. He argued that despite the ordinance being invalid, the city should still be held accountable for the damages incurred due to city agents enforcing it. Turner sought damages for the disruption and financial loss caused by the city's actions that violated the rights of other slaughterhouse operators.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant, maintained that the actions taken to enforce the ordinance were not liable because the ordinance was ultra vires, meaning it was outside the lawful powers granted to the city. The city argued that since the ordinance did not pertain to any valid regulatory authority but instead created a monopoly, it could not be held responsible for the consequences of attempting to enforce it. The city asserted that there was no legal basis for liability because the ordinance allowed for no proper exercise of municipal powers.

In December 1846, in the Illinois Supreme Court, John A. Young (plaintiff) appealed a decision from the Schuyler Circuit Court against Samuel Mason and John Mason (defendants) regarding an appeal bond. The bond stipulated that if the Masons did not prosecute their appeal effectively and failed to pay the judgment rendered by the Circuit Court, they would be liable. The appeal was initially taken by the Masons, but they did not follow through, leading to a default judgment against them in the Circuit Court, which affirmed a prior judgment and awarded Young additional damages and costs. In the subsequent trial, the Circuit Court found in favor of Young, awarding him six cents in damages despite the debt being significantly higher. Young claimed the damages should amount to $89.92, and he sought a new trial after the court ruled in his favor with nominal damages. The court found that the bond, while non-compliant in some respects with statutory language, was still enforceable to some extent.	Young’s main arguments were centered on the alleged breaches of the appeal bond by the Masons, specifically that they failed to prosecute their appeal effectively and did not pay the affirmed judgment causing him damages. He requested the court to award a new trial on the grounds that the damages assessed were inadequate and did not reflect the actual debt owed.	The Masons argued against Young's claims on the basis of non esl factum, contending that the appeal bond was not a valid basis for his lawsuit due to informalities in its drafting. They maintained that the bond did not meet the necessary statutory requirements and hence should not be enforceable.

The case of Trustees of Schools v. Lemuel Southard et al. arose from a dispute concerning a promissory note executed on April 1, 1872, by W. W. Luttrell, with Southard and Fahnestock as sureties. The plaintiffs, the Trustees of Schools, filed a lawsuit against the defendants to collect the owed amount on the note after it became due. The defendants interposed a general issue plea and a special plea by Fahnestock, who argued he acted as a surety and provided notice to the school treasurer, requesting that the plaintiffs sue Luttrell. Fahnestock asserted that the plaintiffs failed to take action within a reasonable timeframe, thereby discharging his liability. Southard presented a similar argument. The plaintiffs demurred to the special pleas, which was overruled. They elected to proceed, resulting in a trial without a jury, where the court ruled in favor of the defendants, leading to costs being adjudged against the plaintiffs. Significant legal principles discussed included the sufficiency of notice given to the treasurer and the nature of suretyship obligations.	The plaintiffs, Trustees of Schools, claimed that the defendants, as sureties, were liable for the amount due on the promissory note. They argued that the failure of Fahnestock to notify the Trustees of the need to collect the debt was inadequate, as the notice should have been directed to the Trustees themselves, asserting that both defendants remained liable despite Fahnestock's plea to be released from the obligation due to the alleged failure to sue.	The defendants, represented by Fahnestock and Southard, contended that the notice given by Fahnestock to the treasurer constituted sufficient grounds for their discharge from liability on the grounds of prolonged inaction by the plaintiffs. They argued that under statute, the plaintiffs were required to act on the note within a reasonable time and that the lack of action after the notice meant they could not claim the debt from the defendants. They also challenged the plaintiffs' demurrer and sought affirmation of their release from obligations.

Andrew Neatherly v. The People of the State of Illinois is a legal case that took place in 1887 in Fayette County, Illinois. The case arose when Andrew Neatherly was charged with assault and battery before a Justice of the Peace. Neatherly was found guilty and fined $10, along with costs. Unsatisfied with the judgment, he appealed to the County Court. However, the County Court dismissed his appeal, claiming it lacked jurisdiction, as such appeals should have been directed to the Circuit Court instead. This led Neatherly to bring his case to the Illinois Appellate Court, where the primary issue debated was whether the appeal to the County Court was valid. The court examined relevant statutes, including the Criminal Code and a legislative act from 1877 that established concurrent jurisdiction between the County and Circuit Courts for appeals from Justices of the Peace. The court aimed to determine the appropriateness of the County Court's dismissal of Neatherly's appeal based on the jurisdictional claims made by both parties.	Andrew Neatherly, the plaintiff, argued that his appeal to the County Court from the Justice of the Peace's ruling was valid under the statutory provisions that conferred concurrent jurisdiction on the County Court. He contended that the action of the County Court in dismissing his appeal was improper and based on a misinterpretation of the relevant laws. Neatherly sought to reverse the County Court's decision and to have his appeal heard and determined on its merits.	The defendant, represented by The People of the State of Illinois, claimed that the County Court did not have jurisdiction over criminal appeal cases originating from Justices of the Peace and that Neatherly's appeal should have been directed to the Circuit Court. They argued that the legislation in question did not apply to criminal cases and insisted that the County Court's dismissal of the appeal was correct based on existing statutes regarding jurisdiction.

In January 1859, in Adams County, Illinois, Harrison Dills initiated an action of ejectment against Silas B. Hubbard to recover possession of the southwest quarter of section seventeen in township two north, range five west. The case arose after a trial in which Hubbard was granted a verdict of not guilty. Dills's petition for a new trial was denied, leading him to appeal the court's judgment. The central issue revolved around the admissibility of a tax deed that Dills attempted to introduce as evidence to support his claim of possession. The court ruled that the deed's admission was improperly limited and did not allow Dills to fully present his case regarding his claimed possession of adjoining tracts of land. The majority opinion noted the relationship between the actual occupancy of a part of a tract and the claim of an entire tract, leading to a foundational discussion of adverse possession in the context of the case.	Dills argued that his prior possession and the introduction of the tax deed should have been sufficient to establish his claim to the entire tract of land, not merely the portion he occupied. He contended that his intentions and actions in improving the land supported his claim against any trespassers and that he was entitled to protect his overall possession based on the concept of adverse possession.	Hubbard's defense lay in the rejection of Dills's evidence, asserting that the tax deed did not adequately prove Dills's title to the entire property. Hubbard maintained that the trial court's decision to limit the interpretation of Dills's deed was appropriate and upheld the validity of his own claim to the land.

In December 1872, Matthew Hansen entered into a lease agreement with John Hoffman for a storeroom located in a hotel building at the corner of two streets in Bloomington, Illinois. The lease was set for one year with monthly rental payments in advance, allowing Hansen the option to extend it with a 60-day notice each year. Hansen was responsible for installing counters and shelving in the storeroom, which Hoffman would buy from him at a reasonable price after the first year. Hansen took possession of the storeroom and conducted a retail dry goods business, making the agreed-upon improvements. In July 1873, Hoffman sold the hotel building and the premises to the defendants, Anton Meyer and others, while Hansen continued to occupy the space. After the first year, Hansen sued the new owners, seeking compensation for the counters and shelving. The case was tried without a jury, and the court ruled in favor of the defendants. Hansen's appeal followed, challenging the applicability of the lease's covenant to the new owners.	Matthew Hansen claimed that as the lessee, he had a right to seek damages from the defendants, the assignees of the lessor's reversion, for their failure to fulfill the covenant of the lease that required compensation for the fixtures he installed. He argued that the lease's provisions should bind the new owners since they occurred within his lawful occupation of the premises.	The defendants contended that the lease explicitly did not extend the contractual obligations to assigns, as it only bound the lessor, his heirs, executors, and administrators. They argued that since the covenant regarding the counters and shelving related to an item not in existence at the time the lease was made and lacked clear wording extending obligations to assigns, they were not liable. Furthermore, they stated that a relevant statute did not apply to this case as it was enacted after the lease's execution.

In 1887, in Cook County, Illinois, Edward F. Dunne obtained a judgment against several defendants, including Horace B. Claflin, for $2,500 in an action of assumpsit. The case originated on March 1, 1884, when the defendants, represented by counsel, filed a plea of non-assumpsit. The trial, held on January 20, 1887, concluded with a judgment for the plaintiff after a jury waiver by both parties. However, it was revealed that Horace B. Claflin had died on November 14, 1885, before the judgment was rendered. On May 22, 1888, John Claflin, as executor of Horace B. Claflin's estate, filed a motion to vacate the judgment, asserting that it was invalid due to Claflin's death. Other defendants joined in the motion. The Superior Court denied their requests, leading to an appeal affirmed by the Appellate Court. The core legal issue revolved around whether the judgment rendered against Claflin posthumously was void or voidable and the jurisdiction of the court in such cases.	The plaintiff, Edward F. Dunne, defended the legitimacy of the judgment he secured against the defendants, asserting that the court had jurisdiction when the case commenced and that the subsequent death of Horace B. Claflin did not invalidate the judgment rendered against him. Dunne argued that the judgment was not void because the court had already acquired jurisdiction over Claflin during his lifetime and that this situation should be rectified through proper legal channels rather than directly disputing the judgment.	The defendants contended that the judgment against Horace B. Claflin was invalid because it was rendered after his death, which deprived the court of jurisdiction. They claimed that since the defeat occurred posthumously and without notice of death to the court, the judgment was void. They requested the judgment be vacated, asserting that errors made in the trial court constituted sufficient grounds for reversal.

In 1884, a legal case called "Peter Saup et al. v. J. S. Morgan & Co." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following events that unfolded primarily in Alexander County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, J. S. Morgan, S. E. Peabody, and J. C. Rogers, were involved in a dispute concerning taxes levied on the capital stock of the Cairo and Vincennes Railroad Company. The plaintiffs claimed ownership of the railroad's rolling stock, which was at risk of seizure for unpaid taxes by county collectors. A series of legal developments led to the appointment of receivers for the railroad in March 1874, who sought to raise funds to cover taxes and improvements. These receivers ultimately borrowed $80,027.85 from the plaintiffs, securing the loan with a mortgage on the rolling stock. A foreclosure of the mortgage occurred in April 1876, with the plaintiffs purchasing the stock. However, the State Board of Equalization had assessed the railroad's capital stock and levied taxes against it, which were recorded in the various counties through which the railroad operated. These tax warrants were subsequently returned uncollected, raising questions regarding the lien on the rolling stock and the legality of tax collection attempts by state collectors. The circuit court granted a permanent injunction against the tax collectors' actions, which was appealed by the People.	The plaintiffs argued that the tax levied on the capital stock of the Cairo and Vincennes Railroad Company was a personal tax and that the lien on their rolling stock had lapsed upon the return of the tax warrants to the county clerks. They contended that because they purchased the rolling stock free from any valid tax lien, the collectors' attempts to seize it for taxes were unlawful. They requested a perpetual injunction to prevent the collectors from selling their property to satisfy what they claimed were extinguished tax liabilities.	The defendants, representing the interests of the county tax collectors, contended that the subsequent warrants issued for the collection of past taxes would reinstate the lien on the rolling stock. They argued that the plaintiffs acquired the rolling stock subject to any existing tax obligations. The defendants sought to uphold the validity of the tax collection efforts and requested the court to reverse the lower court’s decision granting the injunction to the plaintiffs.

The case "Rollin P. Blanchard, Adm’x, v. The Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company" was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court and decided on April 11, 1888. The plaintiff, Rollin P. Blanchard, acting as the administrator for a deceased individual (intestate), brought the case against the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company following a fatal accident involving the railroad. The location of the events was Cook County, Illinois. The nature of the dispute revolved around the claim that the plaintiff's intestate had suffered injuries or death due to the negligence of the railway company. Previously, the court had ruled that the evidence did not support claims of negligence substantial enough to constitute wanton misconduct. In subsequent proceedings, the plaintiff sought to introduce an additional count maintaining the same cause of action, which the defendant responded to with a plea of the statute of limitations. However, the court previously adjudged the intestate a trespasser and held that the plaintiff needed to prove gross negligence by the railroad. In the end, it was concluded that no sufficient evidence was presented to support the necessary degree of negligence.	The plaintiff claimed that the defendant was liable for the death of the plaintiff’s intestate due to the negligence of the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company. The key arguments included the assertion that the additional count filed in the case merely restated the existing cause of action rather than constituting a new cause. The plaintiff requested that the jury assess the circumstances surrounding the accident and the actions of the deceased to determine if ordinary care was exercised and to ascertain whether the defendant's actions amounted to gross negligence or willful misconduct.	The defendant contended that the statute of limitations barred the additional count, asserting that the plaintiff's claims were time-barred. Furthermore, they maintained that the evidence was insufficient to demonstrate any level of negligence that would meet the legal threshold for gross negligence or willful misconduct necessary to impose liability. Therefore, the defendant requested the jury to rule in favor of the railway company based on the absence of sufficient evidence of negligence.

Frank J. Bowman and Ida M. Bowman were involved in a legal case heard by the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision rendered on December 14, 1887. The couple was allegedly married on June 27, 1886, but the nature of their union was contested, as the marriage was claimed to be a common law marriage rather than a ceremonial one. Ida, the plaintiff, filed for divorce on grounds of adultery, with allegations that Frank committed adultery in Washington and St. Louis. The case raised significant legal questions surrounding the validity of common law marriages in Illinois, particularly whether such marriages could be dissolved through legal means. Frank's arguments hinged on the assertion that common law marriages were not recognized under Illinois divorce statutes, claiming also that the evidence for their marriage was insufficient and asserting jurisdictional issues based on domicile. The court had to consider affidavits from both parties relating their history together, Frank's previous marriage, and issues of residency.	Ida M. Bowman claimed that she was lawfully married to Frank on June 27, 1886. She sought alimony pendente lite and suit money in conjunction with her divorce filing based on allegations of Frank committing adultery. She maintained that their common law marriage was valid and presented evidence to support her assertion, including affidavits detailing their relationship and Frank's promises of marriage.	Frank J. Bowman refuted the claims of a valid marriage, arguing that a common law marriage did not meet the legal requirements for divorce in Illinois. He contended that there was insufficient evidence to prove a marriage occurred and suggested that Ida had lost her legal residential status in Illinois upon marriage, insinuating there was a jurisdictional issue regarding where the divorce case should be filed.

The case, "The Curran Mutual Aid and Building Association v. Christopher Murphy," took place in Illinois and was decided on February 17, 1886. The dispute arose when Christopher Murphy, a stockholder in the Curran Mutual Aid and Building Association, sought to recover funds he had contributed as part of his investment—specifically, payments made for thirty shares of stock. Following the association's by-laws, Murphy gave notice of his intent to withdraw from the organization. The case was tried without a jury, as agreed by both parties, and was overseen by Judge Richard Prendergast. The trial focused on whether Murphy had met the requisite conditions to reclaim his investment after withdrawing from the association.	Christopher Murphy claimed that he was entitled to recover his investment in the amount of $535.20, which he had paid for thirty shares of stock in the Curran Mutual Aid and Building Association. He argued that his withdrawal from the association was conducted in accordance with the by-laws, thereby justifying his claim for the return of the funds.	The Curran Mutual Aid and Building Association, as the defendant, maintained that the conditions for Murphy's withdrawal might not have been adequately satisfied. They contested the legitimacy of his claim and sought to uphold the terms detailing stockholder withdrawals, which may have included additional requirements that Murphy did not fulfill.

In 1868, in the city of Aurora, Illinois, the case of Daniel L. Reeder et al. v. Erastus S. Purdy et ux. arose after an incident involving a trespass, assault, and battery. The plaintiffs, Erastus Purdy and his wife, filed the lawsuit against the defendants, Daniel L. Reeder, Albert Barker, and Dennis Baker. The conflict stemmed from the defendants allegedly using force to enter the Purdy's property and committing an unlawful assault on Mrs. Purdy in the absence of her husband. This case had previously been addressed in the courts, with earlier trial results being reported in 41 Ill. 219. The trial concluded with a jury awarding the plaintiffs damages of six hundred dollars, reinforcing the idea that malicious acts, like assault and battery, warrant justification for increased damages in court. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for further evaluation, as the defendants sought to reverse the earlier decision that found them liable for the assault and battery committed against Mrs. Purdy.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants unlawfully entered their property and assaulted Mrs. Purdy, resulting in damages. They sought vindictive damages on the grounds that the assault was malicious and unjustified. The plaintiffs argued that the jury's verdict for six hundred dollars was appropriate and reflected the seriousness of the defendants' wrongful actions.	The defendants argued that their entry onto the property was justified due to their ownership claims and that they only used necessary force. They challenged the previous court's rulings and the instructions concerning exemplary damages. The defendants contended that the plaintiffs were not entitled to vindictive damages, claiming that the assault had not resulted in significant harm to Mrs. Purdy.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois v. Henry A. Organ et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1861. This legal action originated in the Wayne Circuit Court, where the plaintiffs, representing the interests of the school district, sued Organ, who was the collector of Wayne County for 1859, and his sureties over a bond concerning the collection of school funds.  The bond was initially presented signed and sealed in a blank state, without an inserted penalty amount, leading to questions about its validity. Following discussions among the court members, the bond was accepted with a penalty of forty thousand dollars being inserted later at Organ's request, but crucially, this was done without the presence or consent of his sureties. The details of the bond were brought into question when the sureties denied its execution, arguing that they had not consented to the filling of the blank. The case was later moved to Clay County for trial, where it was determined whether the modifications to the bond post-signature were binding on all parties involved.	The plaintiffs claimed that the bond executed by Organ and his sureties was valid, asserting a right to recover funds due to the school district totaling $85. They argued that the bond was proper as it was presented for approval, and they sought to hold Organ and his sureties liable for the non-payment of school funds owed from the collection of taxes.	The defendants contended that the bond was invalid due to the alteration made after its execution, which occurred without the knowledge or consent of the sureties. They argued that filling in the penalty amount after the sureties had signed rendered the bond void as to them. The defendants maintained that they should not be held accountable since they did not approve or ratify the changes made to the bond, leading to their request for dismissal of the claim against them.

Alvira Robinson filed a petition in the Illinois Court of Claims for damages related to land possession under a contract for deed from Washington E. Cook, deceased. This case originated from the construction of a dam by the State of Illinois across the Illinois River near Copperas Creek in October 1877. The construction of the dam raised the water level by six and a half feet, resulting in the flooding of Robinson's lands, which made them nearly worthless. Robinson claimed damages amounting to $675. The case arose as a legal challenge concerning the timing of the claim, as state law requires that any claims against the state for property damage must be filed within two years of the event causing the damage. Robinson filed her claim on October 30, 1879, more than two years after the dam's construction on October 21, 1877, leading to questions of whether her claim was still valid.	Alvira Robinson claimed that the construction of the dam caused significant damage to her land, rendering it almost worthless due to water saturation. She sought financial compensation of $675 for these damages, asserting her right to claim against the state due to the public purpose behind the dam's construction.	The State of Illinois, represented by the Attorney General, argued against Robinson's claim by invoking the statute of limitations. They argued that the claim should have been filed within two years following the dam's construction, according to the statute of 1847. Since Robinson's claim was filed after this period, the defense contended that her case was barred and therefore should be rejected.

In August 1851, in Canton, Illinois, a man named Holden was examined on a charge of larceny before the town's president, who enforced a requirement for Holden to provide $300 in security for his future appearance in circuit court or else be jailed. Holden failed to meet this requirement and was subsequently committed to jail. In October of the same year, he acknowledged a recognizance with Joel Solomon acting as surety, which enabled his release in exchange for the same $300 promise. However, in November, an indictment for larceny was issued against Holden, and as a result, the recognizance was forfeited, leading to a scire facias being issued against Solomon. A judgment was entered against Solomon for the forfeited amount. The case hinged on the legality of the president's actions in demanding bail, as he possessed no judicial authority to do so, rendering the recognizance and subsequent commitment, as well as the judgment against Solomon, invalid.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, claimed that the recognizance entered into by Solomon was enforceable, despite the president of Canton having no judicial power. The state requested that the forfeiture of the recognizance be upheld, seeking to collect the $300 from Solomon based on the bond's conditions.	Solomon, the appellant, argued that the actions taken by the town president were illegal due to his lack of judicial authority, thus invalidating the recognizance. Solomon contended that since the president had no jurisdiction over the matter, the recognizance taken to secure Holden's release was without binding force and should not be enforced. He sought a reversal of the judgment against him.

The case, "Frederick Schmidt et al. v. The Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company," was decided in April 1866, in the state of Illinois. The plaintiffs, Frederick Schmidt and August Binzo, were involved in the tannery business located in Chicago. They entered into an insurance policy with the Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company on September 16, 1864, which insured their property against fire damage. The policy stipulated that there should be no fire in the building except for one under a kettle securely embedded in masonry and made safe against accidents. In March 1865, their tannery was destroyed by fire, which occurred approximately eight hours after the last fire in one of the two stoves present in the building. The insurance company contended that the presence of the stoves constituted a breach of warranty, thereby voiding the insurance. The case raised critical questions about the interpretation of the insurance policy, particularly regarding the nature of the fire-related provisions and whether the risk had increased due to the stoves.	The plaintiffs argued that the language in the insurance policy regarding fire was not a warranty prohibiting any fire usage other than that explicitly stated, but rather a confirmation of the property's condition at the time of issuance. They claimed that there was no violation of the policy because, at the time the fire occurred, there had been no active fire in the stoves for a significant duration. They sought compensation for the loss suffered due to the fire that destroyed their insured property.	The defendant, Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company, contended that the policy contained a warranty that no fire should occur in the building, except under specified conditions, and that the existence of the stoves constituted a breach of this warranty, thus voiding the policy. They also referenced another provision in the policy stating that any increase of risk would nullify the insurance coverage. The defendant argued that the presence of the stoves increased the risk of fire and led to the loss, which they used to deny liability.

The case of Village of Marseilles v. George Howland took place in La Salle County, Illinois in the late 1800s, specifically with a decision rendered on December 18, 1889. The dispute arose from procedural issues related to the filing of a bill of exceptions in an earlier trial. Mr. Bird Bickford represented the appellant, the Village of Marseilles, while the appellee, George Howland, was represented by the law firm of Brewer & Straws. The original case was overseen by Judge Dorrance Dibell. The core of the issue was whether the time for presenting a bill of exceptions could be extended by agreement after the initial deadline had already passed.	The Village of Marseilles argued that the trial judge had the authority to extend the deadline for signing the bill of exceptions. They claimed that even though the original time for presentation expired, the trial judge later extended that time, which should allow for the bill to be submitted. Therefore, they contended that the bill of exceptions should be considered valid.	George Howland contended that the trial court lost jurisdiction over the matter once the bill of exceptions was not presented in the time frame stipulated by the judge. He claimed that without the consent of both parties, any extensions granted by the judge were void, as the judge lacked the authority to modify the timeline outside of specified conditions. The defendant requested that the motion to strike the bill of exceptions from the record be upheld as legally justified.

In the case "The People, for use of John Dolan, v. Henry S. Herr et al.," decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1876, the background involves an action of debt against Henry S. Herr, a justice of the peace, and his sureties for failing to pay over money he collected during his official capacity. The bond in question was executed on April 5, 1866, shortly after Herr was elected. The action was initiated to recover funds that Herr had collected on a judgment rendered on December 21, 1867. However, the claim was made more than five years after Herr's term ended in April 1870. The court needed to determine the validity of the plaintiffs' action based on the time elapsed since the bond's enforcement was extinguished per statutory provisions.	The plaintiff, representing John Dolan, argued that Herr's failure to pay over the money collected rendered him liable under the official bond. The plaintiffs contended that the bond should still be valid as they believed the law allowed recovery. They sought recovery of the funds collected by Herr, claiming that the bond's stipulations were applicable despite the expiration of Herr's term.	The defendants, led by Herr and his sureties, asserted that the bond was no longer in force after five years from the end of Herr's term, based on the relevant statute. They maintained that the plaintiffs could not initiate this action as it was brought well beyond the allowable period. The defendants argued that the nature of the statute indicated the bond was void and could not support any legal claim, effectively barring the plaintiffs from receiving the money through this lawsuit.

In 1886, Ann Stillman filed a lawsuit against Raymond Palis in St. Clair County, Illinois, concerning a dispute over the division line between their adjoining properties. Initially, Stillman pursued a forcible detainer action and a trespass claim against Palis, both of which were decided in her favor by a Justice of the Peace. After the trespass case was resolved in her favor again in the Circuit Court, Stillman dismissed her appeal for the detainer case, leaving the earlier Justice of the Peace ruling intact. The core issue of the current case stemmed from an alleged agreement between the parties regarding the possession of the property and the effects of the dismissed appeal. During the court proceedings, Palis’s attorney from the earlier case testified, asserting the terms and implications of past judgments and agreements, which Stillman contested. The testimony was deemed improperly admitted, as it relied on parol evidence rather than official records, and lacked clear authorization from Stillman to bind her to the agreement discussed. The trial ultimately raised significant questions regarding the admission of evidence and the legal interpretations involved in property disputes between the adjacent landowners.	Ann Stillman claimed that she was entitled to retain possession of the property based on the earlier favorable rulings from the Justice of the Peace and the Circuit Court. She also argued that the dismissal of her appeal left the previous judgment intact, thereby supporting her position. Stillman’s legal team contended that the testimony provided by Palis’s attorney regarding agreements made after the appeal was dismissed should not have been considered valid evidence.	Raymond Palis defended his position by asserting that the dismissal of Stillman's appeal effectively upheld the judgment from the Justice of the Peace, giving him rightful possession of the property. He argued that the attorney’s testimony concerning the earlier cases and the expectations of both parties post-dismissal reinforced his claim. Palis maintained that Stillman’s attorney could not challenge the attorney’s statements, which indicated an agreement to return possession of the property.

Jehu Scott, the appellant, brought a case against John Cromwell, the appellee, in the Illinois Supreme Court in July 1820. The dispute originated from the lower court, where Cromwell, as the defendant, demurred to Scott's declaration, citing informalities. The court affirmed this demurrer but permitted Scott to amend the declaration. Following this, Cromwell requested a continuance to respond appropriately to the amended declaration. However, the court denied Cromwell’s motion for a continuance, which led Scott to appeal the decision, seeking to reverse the court’s ruling regarding the denial of the continuance. This case underscores the procedural intricacies of court rules regarding amendments to declarations and the entitlement to continuances.	The plaintiff, Jehu Scott, argued that the lower court's decision to deny the requested continuance following his amendment to the declaration was erroneous. Scott contended that the amendments were merely formal, and the defendant was not entitled to a continuance based on those changes. He requested the Supreme Court to affirm the lower court's ruling, reinforcing the established legal principles regarding formal amendments.	John Cromwell, the defendant, maintained that he should have been granted a continuance to prepare his defense in light of Scott’s amendments to the declaration. He argued that such amendments, although formal, warranted a continuance to ensure a fair trial. Cromwell's primary defense centered on the assertion that the court's refusal to grant a continuance was a procedural error that impeded his ability to respond adequately to the amended claims.

In September 1875, the legal case of Thomas S. Dobbins et al. v. Henry O. Higgins et al. was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from a contract dispute in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Thomas S. Dobbins and others, claimed that the defendants, Henry O. Higgins and others, failed to fulfill their contractual obligation to make timely payments for work completed on a railroad grading project. According to the contract terms, the plaintiffs expected payment at the end of each month for the labor performed. However, the defendants did not pay for the work done in October 1872, despite being notified that further failures to pay would lead to a contract abandonment. The plaintiffs eventually abandoned the project due to the lack of funds caused by non-payment and sought damages for the unpaid work. The dispute involved issues concerning the measure of damages and the legality of withholding payments to cover expenses related to subcontractors.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants breached the contract by failing to make payments for the work completed in October 1872. They requested compensation for unpaid work at the contract price and sought damages due to the forced abandonment of the project because of the defendants' non-payment. The plaintiffs maintained that they had the right to abandon the contract following the defendants' failure to pay and that the proper measure of damages was for the work done according to the contract terms.	The defendants contended that they had the right to withhold payments citing an alleged agreement to pay subcontractors. They further argued that the plaintiffs had abandoned the claim concerning specific items and that the plaintiffs had authorized certain payments to subcontractors. The defendants also claimed that the plaintiffs' evidence was insufficient and that the issues had been adequately covered by agreement and stipulation.

The case "C. M. Henderson & Co. v. D. Schaas et al." involves a legal dispute that began in 1888 in Helena, Montana. The plaintiff, C. M. Henderson & Co., a firm based in Chicago, was owed $541 by the defendant, D. Schaas, a retail merchant in Helena, which was due around June 1, 1888. After Schaas's stock was destroyed by fire on June 6, 1888, he made a voluntary assignment for the benefit of his creditors to an individual named Kleinschmidt. In response, Henderson & Co. initiated an attachment suit against Schaas, and insurance companies were served as garnishees since they owed amounts related to Schaas's policies. The insurance companies admitted owing $483.33 and $161.11 but argued the voluntary assignment of Schaas should preclude payment to Henderson & Co. After several legal proceedings, including a trial without a jury, the court ruled in favor of Schaas’s assignee, leading to an appeal by Henderson & Co.	The plaintiffs, C. M. Henderson & Co., claimed that the assignment made by Schaas was invalid against their interests as creditors in Illinois. They sought to collect the debts owed by the insurance companies based on attachment proceedings, arguing that their right to the funds was superior, notwithstanding Schaas's assignment. They contended that presenting their claim to the assignee and receiving a dividend did not validate or confirm the assignment.	The defendant, represented by the insurance companies and Schaas's assignee, argued that the voluntary assignment in Montana was valid and should be honored. They contended that because Henderson & Co. had presented their claim to the assignee and received a dividend, they had effectively assented to the assignment, thus being estopped from disputing its validity. They requested the court to deny Henderson & Co.'s claims based on this premise.

In 1877, the legal dispute "James Mix et al. v. William F. Singleton et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after an appeal from the Circuit Court of Kankakee County where Judge Nathaniel J. Pillsbury presided. The case arose from a previous injunction suit in which Mix and others (the plaintiffs) had prevailed, resulting in the dissolution of the injunction against Singleton and others (the defendants). The case involved a $6,000 appeal bond conditioned on the defendants’ obligation to pay any damages resulting from wrongfully filing the injunction if their appeal was unsuccessful. The plaintiffs claimed damages not only from previous legal costs but also accused the defendants of causing substantial financial loss due to the injunction that prevented them from utilizing their mill-dam and water-power property. The situation posed significant financial implications for the plaintiffs, who reported considerable losses during the appeals process.	The plaintiffs, Mix et al., claimed multiple breaches of the appeal bond by the defendants. They argued that they were owed $5,000 for the damages incurred from the wrongful suing of the injunction, which restricted their access to a valuable mill-dam and water-power resource, resulting in lost income and property damage. Additionally, they sought compensation of $500 for expenses related to defending against the injunction suit, $100 for preparation costs for the Supreme Court brief, and unfulfilled obligations concerning the plaintiffs' judgment costs from the appeal.	The defendants contested the claims by asserting that the bond did not obligate them to cover losses incurred by the plaintiffs due to the injunction being in force during the appeal. They argued that the phrasing of the bond specified that they would only be responsible for damages that occurred before the bond was established, limiting their liability significantly. Moreover, they framed their request around the argument that the plaintiffs' claims exceeded the terms of the bond, thus contesting the legitimacy of the alleged damages and the breaches claimed.

On March 23, 1866, in Hancock County, Illinois, David C. Smart was confined in jail under an indictment for larceny. James J. Smart, the plaintiff in error, arranged for the release of David by placing $800 in the hands of William L. Simons, a deputy sheriff, intending that the money would be returned upon David's appearance at the next court term. The agreement under which the money was deposited stipulated that if David failed to appear, the money would be forfeited to the people. However, when James later attempted to retrieve the money by offering a bond that he had signed with three others, the sheriff refused to return it unless David was present to sign as well. The court found against James, leading him to file a writ of error, claiming that the sheriff unlawfully received the money. The case hinged on whether the sheriff had the legal authority to accept the money for bail, as the plaintiff asserted that the acceptance of such a deposit was unauthorized.	James J. Smart contended that the sheriff illegally retained the $800 he had submitted for David C. Smart's release, arguing that the sheriff was not authorized by law to accept money in lieu of proper bail. He maintained that the acceptance of the deposit was illegal and that he had the right to recover the funds.	William C. Cason, the sheriff, defended by asserting that the arrangement and acceptance of the money were unauthorized and in violation of the law, which requires a mandatory recognizance signed by the accused for bail to be lawful. He argued that since the plaintiff was complicit in the illegal discharge of the prisoner, he could not recover the money, as it would make him a participant in a misdemeanor.

The case "Peoria and Oquawka Railroad Company v. John Elting" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1856. The dispute arose in Peoria, Illinois, involving the Peoria and Oquawka Railroad Company as the plaintiff and John Elting as the defendant. The legal action concerned Elting's refusal to fulfill his financial obligations under a subscription agreement for stock in the railroad company, where he had pledged to purchase ten shares totaling $1,000. The plaintiff contended that Elting had made a valid agreement to contribute to the capital of the railroad company, which was incorporated under laws enacted by the Illinois legislature in February 1849 and amended in February 1851, before his subscription on February 4, 1850. Elting paid a small percentage initially but subsequently failed to pay the full amount after subsequent assessments were made by the company's board. The core of the case revolved around the validity of the subscription agreement and whether changes in the railroad company's charter nullified Elting's obligations.	The plaintiff, Peoria and Oquawka Railroad Company, argued that the subscription agreement signed by Elting was enforceable despite any alleged inconsistencies regarding the timing of the laws and amendments related to their corporate charter. The plaintiff contended that subsequent amendatory acts did not alter the essence of the original subscription, and as such, Elting's obligations to pay for his shares remained intact. They sought to recover the unpaid balances under the subscription agreement based on the legal principle that a stock subscription can be enforced even with subsequent amendments to the corporate charter.	John Elting, the defendant, raised several objections in his demurrer regarding the validity of the plaintiff's claims. He argued that the declaration was inconsistent in stating that certain laws took effect prior to his subscription, leading to confusion regarding the terms of his obligation. Elting claimed that the plaintiff did not properly show the amount of stock subscribed, failed to provide adequate notice for payment requests, and that the changes in the company's charter fundamentally altered the terms of his subscription. He maintained that these issues invalidated his obligation to pay for the stock and that his only remedy should lie in chancery.

The case "The Mutual Mill Insurance Company v. Clarence Gordon, use, etc." was decided on June 20, 1887, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It involved a dispute over an insurance policy issued by the Mutual Mill Insurance Company for a milling property owned by James Gordon and later assigned to his son, Clarence Gordon. The property in question was part of the Union Mills in Sparta, Randolph County, Illinois. Prior to the events leading to the lawsuit, James Gordon, along with co-owners Barker and Roseborough, had taken a joint loan of $37,000 secured by a mortgage on their property. Following financial difficulties, they partitioned the property, orally agreeing that Gordon would be responsible for only $17,000 of the mortgage, while his partners would take on the remainder. On October 1, 1884, Gordon applied for a $2,000 insurance policy on the mill machinery, declaring the property's value at $25,000 and the incumbrance at $17,000. After the property's destruction by fire on May 17, 1885, an insurance claim was made, which led to litigation regarding the validity of Gordon's statements in the insurance application. The case proceeded through several court levels, including a circuit court and subsequently an appellate court, before reaching the supreme court.	The plaintiff, The Mutual Mill Insurance Company, argued that the insurance policy was void due to misrepresentations made by James Gordon in the application. Specifically, they contended that Gordon falsely represented both the cash value of the property and the amount of the incumbrance. The plaintiff sought to have the court declare that the policy was invalid and that they were not liable to pay any insurance claim resulting from the fire.	The defendant, Clarence Gordon, contended that the statements made in the application were not false representations but reflected the agreement between the parties regarding the mortgage. He argued that since the mortgage had been partitioned and his responsibility was limited to $17,000, it was justifiable for him to declare that as the incumbrance. The defense maintained that the insurance company was aware of the property’s true condition and thus should honor the policy.

The case "Ira C. Woodward et al. v. Illinois Central Railroad Company" was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court, with a decision rendered on July 11, 1889. The incident occurred in October 1885, at a railroad station in Chicago, where the Illinois Central Railroad received a shipment of 125 barrels of "Gold Dust" meal. The railroad company delivered all but 35 barrels of this shipment. The plaintiffs, Ira C. Woodward and associates, were notified by the railroad on two occasions to remove the remaining barrels or they would be sent to storage. By November 11, 1885, the last notice was issued, indicating that the barrels would be moved the next day. In December, individuals who had ordered part of the remaining meal attempted to collect it but were informed that it had not arrived due to the clerk forgetting about it. It wasn't until January 12, 1886, that one of the appellants discovered the meal had been sent to a storehouse, which was subsequently burned, leading to the destruction of the meal. The court noted that the railroad company was negligent in failing to notify the order holders about the storage location of the meal, thus raising questions of contributory negligence between both parties.	The plaintiffs, Woodward and his associates, claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad was responsible for the value of the 35 barrels of meal lost in the fire due to the railroad's negligence. They argued that the railroad failed in its duty to inform the order holders that the meal had been placed in storage, which directly resulted in the destruction of the goods. The plaintiffs sought compensation for their losses due to this negligence.	The Illinois Central Railroad defended itself by asserting that any negligence in handling the barrels was not the proximate cause of the loss. They argued that the plaintiffs were also negligent in not keeping track of their shipment and in failing to communicate effectively with the railroad company. Moreover, the defendant maintained that the issue of negligence was shared between both parties, as the plaintiffs did not provide sufficient details to locate their goods, and thus requested that the court uphold the lower court's judgment in their favor.

In the case of The People, for use of Thomas McKee v. Daniel Abbott et al., filed on November 20, 1882, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the main individuals involved included Thomas McKee, the administrator of the estate of the deceased Kate H. Lee, her husband Henry R. Lee, Daniel Abbott, and Louisa McCall, executors of the estate of Catharine Dwire. The dispute arose following Kate H. Lee’s death on December 21, 1876. At that time, she left no children and her husband inherited her personal property, valued at around $14,000. Henry R. Lee had paid all debts and funeral expenses of his wife before entering a contract with her mother, Catharine Dwire, to divide Kate’s estate. Following this division, Dwire ended up with certain promissory notes that Thomas McKee, as the administrator, later claimed as part of the estate's assets. After the circuit court ordered the notes be delivered to McKee, this decision was reversed by the Appellate Court, leading to an appeal to the Supreme Court to determine the rightful ownership of the notes.	The plaintiff, Thomas McKee, argued that as the administrator of Kate H. Lee’s estate, he was entitled to the possession of certain promissory notes that were a part of the deceased's estate. He sought a court order compelling the defendant executors, Abbott and McCall, to surrender the notes which he argued were rightfully owed to the estate under Section 80 of Chapter 3 of the Illinois Revised Statutes.	The defendants contended that Henry R. Lee, the sole heir to Kate H. Lee’s estate, had already settled all debts and had effective possession of the estate’s assets. They argued that McKee's role as administrator was unnecessary since there were no debts to pay or claims to settle, and thus there was no legal basis for compelling them to surrender the promissory notes to him.

John D. Hawkins filed a legal case against Warren Taber and others in June 1868, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered on the partition of a property and an account of rents and profits associated with it. The key individual involved, James M. Taber, who was a defendant and a co-tenant of the property, reportedly received rents amounting to $455. A decree was initially rendered against him to account for these rents. However, during subsequent court sessions, including a March term in 1868, affidavits were submitted which led to a modification of the original decree regarding the payment of rents by James M. Taber. The court found that the evidence concerning Taber’s liability for rents was conflicting and ruled that the decree should not be disturbed despite irregularities in the procedure, as the parties had consented to the manner in which evidence was presented.	The plaintiff, John D. Hawkins, claimed that James M. Taber had received rents from the property without appropriately accounting for them to his co-tenants. Hawkins sought a decree for partition of the property and an accurate account of the rents collected, requesting that Taber reimburse the amount received.	The defendants, particularly Warren Taber, argued against the decree that required him to account for the rents received from the property. They contended that the court lacked the jurisdiction to render a judgment for the rents and that the evidence against Taber was insufficient due to its conflicting nature. Additionally, they asserted that the motions made in the court followed an irregular procedure.

In September 1871, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of William R. Page et al. v. The City of Chicago arose as an appeal from a judgment made by the Superior Court concerning a special assessment for improvements to Milwaukee Avenue. The case involved key individuals such as William R. Page, who represented the property owners challenging the assessment, and the City of Chicago's legal representatives. The City had passed an ordinance to improve a specific section of Milwaukee Avenue by constructing curb walls and paving it with wooden blocks. However, some property owners did not pay the assessment, prompting the city collector to seek a judgment against them. A point of contention was that the ordinance's validity was questioned based on previous case law, specifically the decision in Foss v. City of Chicago, which had set a precedent regarding the government's discretion in similar municipal improvements.	The plaintiffs argued that the ordinance under which the special assessment was made was void, citing the Foss case as a precedent. They contended that the ordinance conferred too much discretion to the board of public works to determine the necessity and execution of the improvements, thereby leading to potential abuse of power. The plaintiffs sought a reversal of the judgment made against them and a reconsideration of the assessment.	The City of Chicago contended that the ordinance was valid and distinguishable from those ruled void in prior cases. They maintained that the ordinance did not place discretion in the hands of the board since it clearly stated the conditions under which the curb walls should be constructed. Additionally, the City argued that there was no evidence that the adjacent horse railway was exempt from the assessment, indicating that it should also bear its share of the costs related to the street improvement.

The case "David B. Watt v. Eliab B. Kirby" took place in December 1853 in Illinois. The plaintiff, Eliab B. Kirby, filed an action of debt against D. B. Watt, the surviving partner of D. Watt & Son, a flouring mill business. The dispute arose over the delivery of wheat to the mill, which Kirby claimed was delivered by Palmer. The legal arguments involved whether the wheat was delivered before or after the formation of the partnership between D. Watt and his son. The plaintiff's evidence suggested that Kirby had a prior arrangement with D. Watt for purchasing wheat, and thus he sought to recover the value of the wheat delivered. The defendant countered by claiming the statute of limitations and arguing that any obligation to pay for the wheat had not been established due to insufficient evidence regarding the delivery.	Kirby claimed that he was entitled to recover the value of wheat delivered to the mill, asserting that the partnership had an obligation to account for the delivery. He argued that even if the wheat was initially contracted with D. Watt before the partnership, the surviving partner is bound to account for it as long as it benefited the partnership and that it had not been proven that the wheat was paid for.	D. B. Watt contended that the wheat was delivered before the partnership was formed and thus the claim should not extend to him as a partner.
