He also argued that Kirby had to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the wheat was delivered to the partnership specifically, and that the statute of limitations should bar the claim as the time frame exceeded the required five-year limit.

On December 31, 1881, Fort Dearborn Lodge No. 214, I. O. O. F. filed a trespass action in the Superior Court of Cook County against Albert Klein and others, claiming illegal entry onto their property. Over time, the case saw several amendments, eventually focusing solely on the defendant Klein. The appellant claimed they had authority to build a partition wall on the premises, asserting ownership of the property. In response, the plaintiffs contended they were lawful tenants at the time of the alleged trespass. The case went to trial, where the jury favored the plaintiffs, awarding them $500. This verdict was appealed, leading to an examination of the legal definitions surrounding possession and ownership relevant to the trespass claim. The appellate court's certification of the case resulted in significant legal analysis regarding the sufficiency of the plea and the concept of seizin.	The plaintiffs, Fort Dearborn Lodge No. 214, contended that they were in lawful possession of the premises as tenants of the defendant, Albert Klein, when the trespass occurred. They argued that Klein's actions were unauthorized, resulting in damages worth $500, for which they sought compensation.	The defendant, Albert Klein, maintained that he, as the owner of the property, had the right to make a peaceable entry to conduct necessary construction, and hence claimed that the action of trespass was unfounded. He pleaded a lack of wrongdoing, asserting that his actions did not constitute a trespass due to his ownership and right to access the property.

In the case titled "The Trustees of the Illinois and Michigan Canal, appellants, vs. Elizabeth Dewes and others, appellees," the events unfolded in Chicago, Illinois, around the mid-19th century. The Illinois Legislature had enacted a guidance for the construction of a canal basin at the confluence of the north and south branches of the Chicago River. The legislation included provisions for the appropriation of specific blocks of land—namely, Block 14 owned by Dewes and others, to be exchanged for Block 7, which belonged to the canal. Following these legislative directives, the trustees of the canal were required to manage these properties accordingly. However, in 1845, the trustees refused to proceed with the necessary appropriation and opted to sell Block 7 instead. In September 1848, Dewes and others filed a lawsuit against the trustees claiming ownership of Block 14 and seeking an injunction against the sale of Block 7, insisting on the exchange mandated by the legislative acts. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, prompting the trustees to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, led by Elizabeth Dewes, contended that they were the rightful owners of Block 14 and were ready to comply with the legislative requirements to exchange it for Block 7. They claimed that the trustees failed to honor the legislative provisions that mandated the appraisal and exchange of the properties and sought a court order to enjoin the trustees from selling Block 7. Essentially, the plaintiffs requested a court intervention to enforce the previous legislative acts and compel the trustees to proceed with the exchange.	The trustees of the canal argued that there was no binding contract or obligation to enforce the exchange of Block 7 for Block 14. They maintained that the plaintiffs lacked a legal or equitable interest in Block 7, as there had been no formal agreement to proceed with such an exchange as outlined in the legislative acts. The trustees asserted that they were under no legal compulsion to act on the plaintiffs' claims, which were deemed contingent upon future actions that had not occurred. They requested that the court reverse the lower court’s decree, arguing that the matter fell solely within the state's jurisdiction.

In the case of Junius Mulvey v. Daniel H. Carpenter et al., heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875, the dispute arose over property rights following a foreclosure-related sale. The key individuals involved were Junius Mulvey, the appellant and judgment creditor, Daniel H. Carpenter, a complainant, and Amos F. Tompkins, who was allegedly liable for the mortgage. The events began with a foreclosure sale involving a property that Tompkins had obtained through a prior judgment in a separate case (Monroe v. Tompkins). After the foreclosure, Mulvey attempted to redeem the property from the sale under the impression that the sale had been lawful. However, there were significant concerns regarding the validity of the foreclosure judgment concerning Tompkins's jurisdiction. The court found that the original decree did not properly confer jurisdiction over Tompkins at the time of the execution, meaning the subsequent sale and any redemptions were void. This led to legal challenges regarding ownership and the rightful claims over the land.	Junius Mulvey, as the plaintiff, claimed that his redemption of the property was valid and that he held rightful title to it based on the judgment he had against Tompkins. He argued that the sale resulting from the execution should be upheld and that he subsequently acquired a legitimate claim to the property after successfully bidding for it at auction.	The defendants, represented by Carpenter and Tompkins, contended that the execution under which Mulvey redeemed the property was void. They maintained that the court had lost jurisdiction over Tompkins when it awarded the execution for the balance due on the original decree, and consequently, any sale following that execution was null and barred any claims by Mulvey to the property.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois v. The Commissioners of the Wild Cat Special Drainage District" took place in 1889 in Champaign County, Illinois. The context of the case involved the validity of the organization of the Wild Cat Special Drainage District, initiated through a legal petition process. The Illinois Agricultural Company and B. J. Gifford, who owned a significant portion of the land involved, submitted a petition conforming to legal requirements for the establishment of this drainage district. Notably, the court found the petitioners' actions valid, noting that necessary notice was provided and the court ultimately declared the district organized and appointed commissioners. However, the proceedings faced opposition through replications arguing that the petition lacked signatures from the required number of landowners, questioned the legal ownership of land by the Illinois Agricultural Company, and contested the necessity of a combined drainage system. The Circuit Court sustained the defenses against these claims, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court.	The plaintiffs contended that the petition used to establish the drainage district did not meet statutory requirements concerning the number of landowners needed to sign. They argued that the Illinois Agricultural Company was not a legal landowner and that many of the petitioners were not actual landowners. Additionally, they claimed that the lands did not require a combined drainage system as asserted by the petitioners. Ultimately, their request was for the court to invalidate the formation of the drainage district.	The defendants argued that the petition for the drainage district was properly signed and complied with statutory requirements. They maintained that though the Illinois Agricultural Company's legal status was contested, it still possessed the necessary control over the lands in question. Furthermore, they asserted that the County Court had jurisdiction over the matter, and since appropriate procedures were observed, the court's findings should be binding on all potential objectors. They sought to have the appeals dismissed and the initial judgment upheld.

On October 9, 1871, in Chicago, a devastating explosion occurred in a warehouse operated by the Chicago & North Western Railway Company. The plaintiffs, A. J. Wright and others, owned a valuable building situated 30 feet away from the defendant's warehouse, which was an old one-story frame structure used for storing freight. The defendant had unlawfully stored large quantities of highly flammable materials such as crude petroleum and gasoline in this warehouse. A fire in the defendant's building led to an explosion that sent burning debris onto the plaintiffs' property, resulting in severe damage and the destruction of their belongings. The legal case stemmed from the plaintiffs' assertion that the defendant's negligence and the unlawful storage of hazardous materials were directly responsible for their losses. The case had previously been appealed due to errors in excluding crucial evidence, and it was retried focusing on several counts in the plaintiffs' declaration, including allegations of negligence and violation of city ordinances concerning the storage of petroleum.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant's negligence in storing dangerous quantities of petroleum and other flammable liquids caused the explosion that destroyed their property. They argued that the defendant violated city ordinances regarding the safe storage of hazardous materials. They sought damages for the loss incurred due to the defendant's improper practices.	The defendant argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiffs was insufficient to prove that the explosion originated from their warehouse. They contended that the explosion's cause was not clearly established, and claimed that the fire was an unexpected event beyond their control. Additionally, they invoked the legal principle of res judicata, asserting that prior judgments should bar the plaintiffs from re-litigating the same evidence and claims.

In September 1836, Daniel G. Whitney was appointed as the administrator for the estate of Nathaniel Pease, deceased, in Adams County, Illinois, with a bond secured by John Wood and other sureties. In May 1847, Whitney submitted his administrative account, revealing he owed $5,870.14 to Nathaniel Pease, Jr., an heir. Despite a court order to pay this sum, Whitney failed to do so, leading Pease to sue Wood as a surety. Wood was found liable for $6,248.39 in damages and costs, a judgment he settled in August 1848. Whitney was also appointed guardian for Pease Jr., and when it was determined he was liable for $8,158.80 as guardian, further complications arose regarding debts owed by Whitney as both administrator and guardian, particularly concerning retained funds. After Whitney's default, Wood initiated a suit for contribution against the heirs of another surety, Samuel Alexander, asserting that they should contribute to the amount he paid as surety. The heirs contested this claim, asserting fraudulent behavior by Wood. The case raised questions about liability and fraudulent intent in the context of administrative bonds and guardianship.	Wood, the plaintiff, seeks contribution from the heirs of Samuel Alexander, whom he acted as a surety alongside. He claims the heirs should pay a portion of the amount he settled on a judgment held against him due to Whitney’s failure to fulfill his obligations as administrator. Wood argues that since he has settled the judgment in favor of Pease Jr., the other sureties, particularly Alexander's heirs, are liable for their share of the financial responsibility.	The heirs of Alexander defend against Wood's claims by asserting that the payments made by Wood were due to fraudulent circumstances, suggesting that he allowed a judgment to be entered against him to compel them to contribute unjustly. They argue that Whitney fraudulently mismanaged funds as both administrator and guardian, leading to unjust liabilities placed upon sureties. Furthermore, they contest the validity of the previous probate court orders and claim that Wood's actions were complicit in this fraudulent behavior, preventing them from being held liable for any payments owed to him.

On May 24, 1854, Charles Casselberry signed a lease with William Forquer for land located in St. Clair County, Illinois, for three years at an annual rent of $150, to be paid semi-annually. Following the lease agreement, on June 3, 1857, Susannah Forquer filed two legal actions for $75 each as payment for rent due from March 1, 1856, to December 25, 1856, and from December 25, 1856, to March 1, 1857. After securing judgments against Casselberry for these amounts, he appealed. Subsequently, Forquer brought forth additional suits for further payments that had also become due. The cases were presented for trial together in September 1859. At trial, the lease and related documentation were introduced as evidence, including a decree that had ordered the sale of the leased property, which was later overturned by the Supreme Court in January 1859. The court ultimately decided to dismiss Casselberry's appeals based on the principle that a plaintiff may not initiate separate actions for multiple overdue payments under a single lease agreement.	Susannah Forquer, as the plaintiff, argued that Charles Casselberry owed multiple payments under their lease and sought recovery of those amounts through legal action. She maintained that each missed payment could be individually litigated, having initially brought separate lawsuits for the sums due. Her legal request was thus aimed at recovering the rental payments consistently owed, totaling $75 for each period of rental as outlined in her actions.	Charles Casselberry contended that the legal actions brought against him were improperly segregated, violating established legal principles that require multiple overdue lease payments to be consolidated into a single lawsuit. He asserted that since an entire debt was owed at the time, the plaintiff should not have split the claims into separate cases. Additionally, he argued that there were jurisdictional issues with the leasehold interest and the legitimacy of the sales related to it.

In the case of Michael Keeley v. Lawrence O’Brien, Administrator, the incident took place in September 1872 in Cook County, Illinois. The action was initiated by Lawrence O’Brien, the administrator of the estate of Daniel O’Brien, who had passed away. The plaintiff claimed a debt owed for services rendered by the deceased, leading to a trial in the Superior Court of Cook County. During the trial, a jury found in favor of the plaintiff, resulting in a judgment for $450 against the defendant, Michael Keeley. After the verdict, Keeley filed a motion for a new trial, alleging that he and his counsel were not present during the trial and were surprised by the proceedings. Two conflicting affidavits were presented: one from Keeley’s attorney’s clerk claiming miscommunication about the trial schedule, and one from the plaintiff’s attorney denying any promises regarding notice of the trial. The court had to assess these claims while considering whether any partnership existed between O’Brien and his brother concerning their work for Keeley, which could impact the validity of the debt claim. Ultimately, the court found no substantial evidence to support Keeley’s defenses or claims of surprise.	The plaintiff, Lawrence O’Brien, claimed that he was entitled to recover $450 owed to the estate of Daniel O’Brien for services rendered before his death. O’Brien contended that no valid defenses were established by Keeley regarding the debt and that the case was appropriately prosecuted by the administrator.	Michael Keeley argued that he was misled about the trial schedule, resulting in his absence during the proceedings. He claimed that he had settled the owed amount with Daniel O’Brien's brother and pointed to potential misunderstandings regarding their employment relationship. Keeley sought a new trial on grounds of surprise and lack of notice.

Atwood T. Hobson filed a legal action against Emporium Real Estate and Manufacturing Company in the Circuit Court of Pulaski County, Illinois, during the April Term of 1861. The case arose from a foreign attachment, which is a legal procedure allowing a plaintiff to secure a debt owed by a defendant in a jurisdiction where the defendant does not reside. Hobson filed an affidavit claiming an indebtedness of $173.86 and issued a notice for an attachment based on that amount. However, a default judgment was rendered against Emporium for $429.91 and costs, which was significantly higher than the original claim. The plaintiff’s case hinged on this attachment process, with no personal service or appearance by the defendant noted in the court records. Upon examination of the proceedings and the amounts involved, the Supreme Court of Illinois identified serious procedural errors leading to the appeal by the defendant.	The plaintiff, Atwood T. Hobson, argued that the attachment was valid based on the affidavit claiming $173.86. He sought to recover this amount in damages along with additional costs. Hobson's main argument rested on the validity of the foreign attachment process initiated against Emporium Real Estate and Manufacturing Company.	The defendant, Emporium Real Estate and Manufacturing Company, contended that the judgment amount of $429.91 was erroneous since it exceeded the sum claimed in the plaintiff's affidavit and notice. The company maintained that the procedure used to secure the judgment lacked proper grounds, as there was no personal service or appearance, and thus the larger judgment was not legally justified.

In Chicago, on July 3, 1872, Charles C. P. Holden and Thomas H. Armstrong executed a party wall agreement concerning their adjacent properties, where Holden owned lot twelve and Armstrong owned lot eleven. The agreement allowed Holden to build a wall on the line between the two lots, specifying that both parties would share maintenance costs and that Armstrong would pay Holden for half the wall's cost when he used it. The wall was completed on March 1, 1873. Later, Holden executed deeds of trust, eventually leading to Emeretta A. Gibson purchasing lot twelve on May 17, 1876, after foreclosure. When Kedzie, owning lot eleven, intended to use the party wall, he filed a bill in December 1883 to determine who was entitled to the compensation for the wall. The court initially ruled in favor of Gibson, leading Holden to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, Charles C. P. Holden, argued that he was entitled to compensation for half the cost of the party wall based on the original agreement with Armstrong. Holden maintained that the right to compensation was personal to him and should not have passed to Gibson, the current owner of lot twelve. He sought to have the court reverse the previous ruling that awarded the compensation to Gibson.	Emeretta A. Gibson, the defendant, contended that the right to compensation for the party wall had transferred with the title of the land to her upon purchasing the property. She argued that the covenant in question was binding and that she was entitled to the amount paid into court by Kedzie for the use of the wall, as it was part of the agreement that benefited her property.

This case, Floyd K. Whittemore v. David S. Fisher, Admr., was filed in the Illinois Supreme Court and decided on March 31, 1890. The dispute arose from financial difficulties faced by the plaintiff, David S. Fisher, who dealt with jewelry and musical instruments in Springfield, Illinois. By February 26, 1883, Fisher owed nearly $15,000 to the State National Bank, where Whittemore served as cashier, and about $3,300 to the Farmers’ National Bank. After a judgment was entered against Fisher, he sought Whittemore's assistance to prevent foreclosure on his stock. Whittemore agreed to help by purchasing the judgment against Fisher and accepting a satchel of goods as collateral. Following this arrangement, Fisher continued to operate the business under Whittemore's financial backing. Over time, the business relationship deteriorated, leading Whittemore to replevy the goods from Fisher, asserting ownership as a result of the transactions that took place. Fisher contended the sale was merely a mortgage. This culminated in a legal battle where Fisher sought the return of his goods and accounting for transactions, while Whittemore argued for the legitimacy of his possession and financial claims.	Fisher, the plaintiff, argued that the transaction with Whittemore was not a true sale but rather a mortgage meant to secure advances against his debts. He claimed wrongful replevin of his goods, sought damages, requested a return of his personal property, and demanded an accounting of the financial transactions. Fisher's claims included a request for a receiver to manage the business until the matter was resolved.	Whittemore, the defendant, contended that the transfer of goods and real estate was an absolute sale, not a mortgage. He argued that he was entitled to possession of the goods as a result of the replevin suit, maintaining that the arrangement allowed Fisher to act as his agent in running the business. Whittemore insisted that the management and use of the goods by Fisher were permitted under the terms of their agreement and that all payments made to creditors were to secure his advances.

Parker C. Pusey v. Philo W. Peck was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1873. The case arose in McLean County, Illinois, and involved a dispute over a promissory note. The plaintiff, Philo W. Peck, brought an action of assumpsit (a legal term for a type of lawsuit for a breach of contract) against Parker C. Pusey. At the heart of the case was a note that Peck claimed was due from Pusey. The defendant, Pusey, contended that the note had been initially issued under specific conditions tied to a partial settlement with a third party named Thomas. Pusey claimed that there was a verbal agreement that the note would be kept by Thomas until a full settlement occurred and that any potential credits due to Pusey from Thomas should be endorsed on the note. Pusey also argued that Peck's son acquired the note with knowledge of this agreement. The Circuit Court of McLean County, presided over by Hon. Thomas F. Tipton, sustained a demurrer to Pusey’s special pleas—essentially dismissing the defenses raised regarding the interpretation of the contract. The case ultimately went to trial on the general issue.	The plaintiff, Philo W. Peck, claimed that Parker C. Pusey owed him $777.43 based on the promissory note. Peck's position was that the note was valid and due, and he sought recovery of the amount stated in the note, asserting that the defenses raised by the defendant were invalid and unsupported by evidence of an actual agreement altering the terms of the written contract.	The defendant, Parker C. Pusey, presented two special pleas. He argued that the promissory note was executed under a verbal promise made by Thomas, the payee, that the note would be retained until a full settlement was reached. Pusey also claimed that Thomas owed him a larger sum than what was stipulated in the note and sought a set-off based on those alleged debts. However, the special pleas did not adequately demonstrate how the claimed indebtedness arose, leading to their rejection by the court.

In the case of George P. Bay v. Simeon B. Williams, which reached the Illinois Supreme Court on November 17, 1884, the dispute centers around a real estate transaction that took place in the vicinity of Chicago. In March 1873, Mrs. Camelia J. Williams sold 40 acres of land to Newman & Sissons for $12,000, which was secured by a trust deed. George P. Bay later purchased this land from Newman & Sissons for $24,000, with a specific clause in the warranty deed stating he would pay the mortgage debt owed to Mrs. Williams. However, after several years, Bay sought to be released from this obligation and approached Sissons, who granted him a release for a small payment. Nonetheless, Newman would not release him from the debt, ultimately declaring bankruptcy. In November 1879, Mrs. Williams began foreclosure proceedings due to the unpaid mortgage, and in May 1881, she obtained a decree of foreclosure. The land was sold, but Bay was left with an unpaid balance that the court concluded he was personally liable for. Despite an appeal, the court’s ruling that Bay assumed the mortgage debt and was therefore responsible for the deficiency was upheld.	Mrs. Williams claims that George P. Bay, by assuming the mortgage obligation in the deed when he purchased the land, is personally liable for the unpaid balance of the mortgage. She argues that the release obtained from Sissons does not absolve Bay of his responsibility towards her, as the mortgagee. Therefore, she seeks enforcement of her rights and the issuance of a legal execution for the unpaid balance resulting from the foreclosure.	George P. Bay contends that the evidence does not support that he consented to or accepted the obligation to pay the mortgage debt since he believed he had been released from it by Sissons. He argues that the court erred in finding him liable for the debt secured by the mortgage due to an alleged lack of consideration and the assertion that a release from the mortgagor (Sissons) should absolve him of any responsibility to the mortgagee (Mrs. Williams). Therefore, he requests the court to overturn the previous decree against him.

In September 1867, in LaSalle County, Illinois, Revillo Hubbard and his business partner Shagreen, joint owners of a patent right, sold the patent for the State of Pennsylvania to Frederick W. Jasinski. They received $1,000 in cash and Jasinski's notes for $1,800, secured by a mortgage on his farm. After investing considerable effort and resources, Jasinski returned from Pennsylvania, feeling deceived about the patent's worth. He had a conversation with Shagreen, who agreed to cancel the notes and mortgage in exchange for Jasinski paying an additional $400. Following this agreement, Shagreen executed a release of interest in the mortgaged property. Jasinski later sold the land to Arneson. When Hubbard attempted to foreclose the mortgage without involving Jasinski, Jasinski initiated a suit against Hubbard to prevent the foreclosure and demand that Hubbard satisfy the mortgage. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Jasinski, prompting Hubbard to appeal this decision.	Revillo Hubbard, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to foreclose the mortgage on the property despite Jasinski's claims. Hubbard asserted that there was a complete remedy available at law for Jasinski, namely the ability to assert payment of the mortgage as a defense against Arneson. He contended that Jasinski's actions did not properly involve Hubbard, and therefore, the Circuit Court's ruling in favor of Jasinski was unwarranted.	Frederick W. Jasinski, the defendant, countered that he was misled regarding the worth of the patent he purchased and that the binding agreement made with Shagreen, which involved the pay-off of the mortgage, should affect Hubbard as a partner. Jasinski maintained that Hubbard was informed about the settlement and that the mortgage should be canceled as Jasinski had settled his debt. He requested that the court prevent Hubbard's foreclosure actions and officially cancel the mortgage.

Rockwell King filed a legal case against The City of Chicago in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision rendered on September 27, 1884. The background of the case revolves around the fiscal practices of the city council pertaining to the annual appropriation bill. The city of Chicago is organized under general law for the incorporation of cities, requiring that the city council pass the annual appropriation bill within the first quarter of each fiscal year (January 1 to January 1). On March 31, 1884, the city council adopted the appropriation bill, which included funding for three policemen at a salary of $1,000 each. However, the mayor vetoed this amount, asserting that only two policemen were necessary and that $945 each was sufficient. At a subsequent council meeting on April 7, 1884, the council reconsidered the matter and passed a reduced appropriation for two policemen at the lower salary, which was then approved by the mayor. King claimed that this appropriation was illegal as it exceeded what was allowed outside the designated period for appropriations and requested an injunction to prevent the city from incurring expenses based on this appropriation. The lower court sustained a demurrer (a response that objects to the legal sufficiency of a complaint) and dismissed the bill, leading to King’s appeal.	The plaintiff, Rockwell King, argued that the amended appropriation for two policemen, made by the city council after the first quarter of the fiscal year, was illegal. He contended that the city council's actions violated the general laws regulating the timing of appropriation bills, which requires that they be passed within the first quarter of the fiscal year. King sought an injunction to prevent the city and its officers from incurring any expenses or entering into contracts based on this purportedly illegal appropriation.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant, contended that the appropriation was legal, asserting that while the original appropriation was passed at the end of the fiscal quarter, the subsequent actions taken by the city council to modify and reduce this appropriation were valid within the legal framework. They argued that the law allows for redetermination of appropriations, and the council’s approval of reduced funding constituted adherence to the original appropriation, thus not violating any laws regarding fiscal year appropriations.

In September 1875, Reason C. Kile filed a case against The Town of Yellowhead in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a dispute over the obstruction of a public highway located in Kankakee County, Illinois. The central issue involved determining the proper description and proof of the highway claimed to be obstructed by Kile. The highway was described using specific land descriptions based on the township, section, and range. Kile appealed a judgment from a lower court that convicted him for obstructing the road, arguing that there was a variance in the description of the highway. He claimed that the documentation presented did not accurately describe the road, but the court found that despite different wordings, the descriptions sufficiently identified the same road. Kile also contended that the highway record was void because the commissioners of highways did not act on the petition within the legally required timeframe. However, the court identified an estoppel since Kile had accepted $75 in damages for land use, which inhibited him from claiming the proceedings were invalid.	The plaintiff, Reason C. Kile, claimed that the established highway was improperly described and contended that a variance existed between the complaint and the evidence. He argued that the highway record was void due to a lack of timely action by the commissioners and that he could not be held liable for obstruction because the road had not been properly established.	The Town of Yellowhead, as the defendant, argued that there was no significant variance between the allegations in Kile's complaint and the evidence presented. They maintained that the description of the road was sufficiently adequate for identification, and the court should notice the meaning of the initials used in land descriptions. The defendant also contended that Kile’s acceptance of damages for the road’s establishment served as an estoppel, preventing him from claiming the proceedings were void.

The case "Samuel Marshall v. John Gridley" took place in Peoria, Illinois in 1867. The suit arose from a contractual dispute where John Gridley (the plaintiff) claimed Samuel Marshall (the defendant) failed to deliver between ninety to one hundred hogs as per their agreement made on August 21, 1865. The contract stipulated that the hogs were to be delivered on January 1, 1866, at a price of eight dollars per hundred pounds, with a deposit of $100 made by Gridley. Gridley also had the option to take a carload of hogs the previous December. Although Marshall claimed he was prepared to fulfill his part of the contract on the agreed date, Gridley refused to accept the hogs, leading to the lawsuit for damages due to breach of contract. The trial concluded with a jury verdict favoring Gridley, who was awarded damages of $200. Marshall appealed the decision, contesting various errors in the trial court’s proceedings regarding the admissibility of evidence and the instructions given to the jury.	John Gridley, the plaintiff, argued that Samuel Marshall breached their contract by not delivering the hogs as agreed. He claimed that he was ready to take the hogs but that Marshall failed to fulfill his contractual obligations. Gridley sought damages of $200 for the breach of contract, asserting that he had made the necessary payment and was entitled to receive the hogs as stipulated in their agreement.	Samuel Marshall claimed he was ready and willing to deliver the hogs but argued that Gridley refused to accept them when they were to be delivered. He provided several pleas asserting that the delivery was contingent on Gridley paying the previously agreed price, which was demanded but not paid. Marshall also indicated that he was entitled to the $100 payment made by Gridley since he was prepared to meet the contract terms, countering Gridley’s claims for damages.

John P. Zipp initiated a legal suit against Uhland Hain No. 16 and Concordia Hain No. 15, related to a dispute concerning the renting of stands at a picnic event. The case commenced before a justice of the peace and was later appealed to the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, where the presiding judge was Hon. Rollin' S. Williamson. The case was heard on February 16, 1889. During the proceedings, the court allowed an amendment to add a co-plaintiff, affirming compliance with the practice act and precedent set in McDowell v. Town. Central to the case was the legality of the contract for renting stands, which the defendant claimed was void due to the picnic being held on a Sunday. However, the court found that there was insufficient evidence to prove the picnic occurred in Illinois, where such Sunday laws would be applicable, suggesting it may have taken place in an adjoining state where the law may not be the same. The jury's verdict was upheld, emphasizing the finality of their decision given the conflicting evidence.	The plaintiff, John P. Zipp, argued that the defendants were required to honor the contract for the renting of stands at the picnic. He contended that the claim of the contract being void due to the event occurring on a Sunday was invalid, primarily due to a lack of evidence demonstrating that the picnic took place in Illinois, where relevant Sunday laws would apply. He sought enforcement of the contract and relief from the defendants' refusal to comply.	The defendants, Uhland Hain No. 16 and Concordia Hain No. 15, contended that the contract for renting stands was void as the picnic was held on a Sunday, referencing local laws governing such events. They argued that the circuit court should recognize the alleged illegality of the contract and dismiss the plaintiff's claims based on this grounds. They sought a judgment favorable to them, reinforcing their position against the validity of the contract.

In September 1875, the case of A. Green Courson v. Geo. Browning et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, having originated in the Superior Court of Cook County. The case involved A. Green Courson as the plaintiff and Geo. Browning and others as defendants. Central to the proceedings was an appeal bond that was purportedly insufficient because it did not include the names of all plaintiffs and defendants in its caption. The plaintiff provided as grounds that the bond lacked the necessary judicial approval; however, the court emphasized that an objection to such bonding should be raised at the earliest opportunity, which the defendants had failed to do. The appeal concerned the validity of legal judgments made during the trial and whether procedural errors occurred due to four judges being present at the trial instead of a single presiding judge. The court meticulously reviewed the objections raised about the bond's legality and the presence of multiple judges, ultimately determining that they were not valid reasons to uphold the judgment from the lower court.	The plaintiff, A. Green Courson, argued that the appeal bond was void due to improper approval procedures and the failure to include all necessary parties in the caption. They contended that the lower court's decision was based on an invalid bond and that the multiplicity of judges presiding in the trial represented a significant procedural error, warranting a reversal of the judgment.	The defendants, represented by Geo. Browning et al., contended that the objections to the appeal bond were raised too late and that the bond met all legal requirements, asserting that the presumption was in favor of its validity. They argued that since the bond functioned as expected, and they had raised no objections during the initial trial, any claims against it should not stand. Additionally, they contended that the presence of multiple judges did not inherently invalidate the trial process.

In 1840, Thomas Morgan and Powell engaged in a bet regarding the outcome of the presidential election in Kentucky, specifically if General Harrison would receive a majority of over three thousand votes. The bet stipulated that if Harrison received the majority, Morgan would pay Powell $50; conversely, if he received less, Powell would pay Morgan the same amount. Samuel Pettit, as Morgan's surety, was obligated to pay Powell if Morgan lost the wager. After Harrison won by more than three thousand votes, Pettit paid Powell the $50 and subsequently filed a lawsuit against Morgan to recover the amount. The case, which began as an action of assumpsit before a justice of the peace, was appealed to the Scott Circuit Court, where the jury found in favor of Pettit, leading Morgan to appeal. The court instructed the jury that the wager was valid under common law and not affected by Illinois statutory law since it pertained to an election outside the state. Morgan challenged this instruction, leading to further appellate considerations.	Samuel Pettit, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to recover the $50 he paid to Powell as a result of the wager made between Morgan and Powell regarding the presidential election. He maintained that the bet did not violate any local laws pertaining to wagers on elections, as it concerned an election outside Illinois, thus making his claim recoverable under common law.	Thomas Morgan, the defendant, contended that the trial court erred by refusing his proposed jury instructions and instead giving instructions favorable to Pettit. He argued that the wager should be deemed illegal under Illinois law, which prohibits bets on elections held within the state, and maintained that this legal principle should extend to transitory bets made by residents regarding elections in other states.

The case "First National Bank of Chicago v. Pettit & Smith" involves events that took place in June 1865 in Chicago, Illinois. George M. Allen entered into an arrangement with the First National Bank to facilitate payments for a cargo of corn amounting to between $8,000 and $9,000. The agreement stipulated that the bank would pay Allen's checks up to this amount, secured by the bill of lading for the corn. However, on June 15, 1865, after the bank had already paid over $10,000 against Allen's checks, Pettit and Smith presented a check from Allen for $998.86, which the bank refused to honor due to the overdrawn account. The bank had also paid a previous check for $5,936.74 unrelated to the corn purchase. Allen had attempted to deposit a check for $5,798.88 to keep his account from being overdrawn, but that check was subsequently dishonored. The core issue arose because Pettit and Smith claimed entitlement to payment for the check drawn against their corn sale to Allen, while the bank argued it had no obligation to pay checks drawn after the credit limit was exceeded. The initial trial ruled in favor of Pettit and Smith, prompting the bank to appeal.	The plaintiffs, Pettit and Smith, claimed that First National Bank was obligated to honor a check drawn by George M. Allen in their favor for a corn sale, arguing that the bank had agreed to ensure payments for checks related to the cargo of corn. They sought to recover the amount of the check after the bank refused payment, asserting that their transaction and Allen’s arrangement with the bank created a rightful expectation for payment.	The First National Bank contended that it was not liable to pay any of Allen's checks once his account was overdrawn. The bank argued that their agreement to advance funds was solely backed by the corn purchase and that Allen's credit arrangement did not obligate them to pay checks drawn after the limit was exceeded. Furthermore, the bank highlighted there was no direct relationship or promise to Pettit and Smith regarding payment of Allen's check.

In 1841, in Winnebago County, Illinois, Francis Burnap, acting as the administrator of the estate of John Miller, deceased, faced legal challenges from William P. Dennis. Burnap sought to sell a quantity of bricks belonging to the estate for the benefit of its creditors. However, Dennis allegedly threatened individuals interested in purchasing the bricks, stating he would prosecute anyone who attempted to remove or touch them. These threats occurred during a public auction and other negotiations, significantly deterring potential buyers. Burnap claimed that because of Dennis's actions, he could not proceed with the sale, resulting in the bricks being damaged and losing their value. Burnap filed a special action against Dennis in the Winnebago Circuit Court, presenting three counts in his declaration that detailed the threats to potential buyers, which allegedly thwarted the sales process.	The plaintiff, Francis Burnap, argued that William P. Dennis maliciously interfered with his sale of bricks intended for the estate of John Miller. He claimed that Dennis's threats dissuaded potential buyers, causing his inability to sell the bricks, which subsequently decayed and lost value. Burnap sought damages for the loss incurred due to Dennis's intimidating actions that were said to be without any reasonable cause.	Dennis defended against Burnap's claims by arguing that the plaintiff's declaration was insufficient and failed to demonstrate that specific efforts to sell the bricks had been made. He contended that Burnap did not fulfill his legal duties as an administrator, which would require proper public sale procedures and did not adequately show how Dennis's threats caused any actual damage.

The case "Hernando A. Fuller and Andrew De Graff v. Joseph E. Langford, Grice W. Thurlby, Samuel H. McPherran, Andrew McPherran, and William Irvin" was adjudicated in April 1863 in Illinois. The plaintiffs, Fuller and De Graff, faced a legal challenge initiated by the defendants through writs of foreign attachment issued from the Circuit Court of Stephenson County. These writs were directed to the sheriff of Livingston County and were levied upon property belonging to Fuller. However, there was a lack of personal service on either of the defendants, and no writ had been issued within Stephenson County prior to the motion to quash the writ. The circuit court later amended the writ but again failed to serve the defendants personally. The plaintiffs secured a default judgment after claiming non-appearance by the defendants, leading to the sale of the attached property. The defendants contested this judgment, arguing that the court did not possess jurisdiction due to the absence of proper service or proper writs being issued in Stephenson County—the location where the suit was initiated.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had a right to initiate a writ of foreign attachment to secure a judgment against the defendants due to outstanding debts. They argued that despite the lack of personal service, the property belonging to Fuller was rightfully attached as per the legal procedure, and they sought damages assessed by a jury.	The defendants contended that the Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction over them due to the absence of personal service and the failure to issue a writ within the county of origin (Stephenson County) before proceeding with the default judgment. They argued that without proper jurisdiction, any judgments rendered were void and requested to quash the original writs and reverse the judgments.

The case "Lyman Sanderson v. The Town of La Salle" took place in Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 15, 1886. Lyman Sanderson, the appellant, was involved in a dispute concerning a personal judgment awarded to the Town of La Salle for the amount of $95.96, which was claimed to be due for unpaid property taxes on a lot assessed in Sanderson's name. This lot had been forfeited to the state due to non-payment of taxes. The action was brought against Sanderson in the La Salle County court under the 230th section of the Revenue Act, which allows towns to sue for taxes owed on forfeited property. Sanderson appealed the county court decision, challenging the validity of the tax proceedings and the authority of the attorneys who represented the Town of La Salle. Key issues included whether the proper notice of the proceedings was published and whether the attorneys had the necessary authorization to initiate the suit, but the court concluded that these objections did not provide valid grounds for reversal.	The plaintiff, the Town of La Salle, argued that they were entitled to recover the unpaid taxes due on a forfeited property owned by Lyman Sanderson. They claimed that the action of debt was properly instituted under the relevant section of the Revenue Act, asserting that irregularities or omissions in tax proceedings did not negate their right to recover taxes legitimately owed. They requested enforcement of the judgment requiring Sanderson to pay the tax amount.	Lyman Sanderson's defense centered on the claim that the Town of La Salle's attorneys lacked proper authority to initiate the lawsuit, as their representation was not shown to be authorized by a town vote. Additionally, he argued that the county court's record did not demonstrate compliance with statutory notice requirements regarding delinquent property. Sanderson contended that these flaws undermined the judgment against him and sought a reversal of the county court's decision.

Chauncey A. Lake filed a legal complaint on July 16, 1881, in the Circuit Court of Kankakee County, Illinois, against Milner Brown and other parties. The case arose from a deed of trust executed by Lake on July 3, 1872, which secured a loan of $2,000 from Brown, payable over five years with interest. The trust deed allowed for the sale of the property in case of default. A property sale occurred under this deed on October 9, 1877, where Brown purchased the property for $2,160. Lake subsequently claimed he was entitled to redeem the property, citing usury as a basis for his appeal and arguing that the sale was flawed because Burr, the substituted trustee, had no right to sell the property. During the proceedings, Lake alleged that Brown had accepted payments towards his debt, thus waiving the sale. The case further escalated when Brown conveyed the land to Thomas Dailey on August 19, 1881, prompting Lake to petition courts regarding this transaction as well. The agreements made between Lake and Brown also stipulated that failure to pay certain sums of money would allow Brown to retain previously paid amounts. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court following an appellate court ruling that favored the defendants.	Lake's primary claims included that the sale of the property under the trust deed was invalid due to alleged usury, claiming Brown had accepted payments from him that should invalidate the sale. He contended that the substitution of Burr as trustee was improper and baseless, and he sought to have the sales and conveyances set aside, reclaim ownership of the premises, and account for the rents and profits.	Brown's defenses revolved around the legality of the trustee's appointment and the sale under the deed. Brown argued that the appointment of Burr as trustee adhered to the provisions of the deed, which allowed for a successor in case the original trustee declined to act. He maintained that Lake had effectively waived his rights by not objecting to the trustee's actions at the time and by entering into agreements that confirmed Brown's right to retain the amounts paid by Lake following the sale.

In the case of Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Nathan S. Purvines, which took place in September 1868 in Murrayville, Illinois, Nathan S. Purvines, the appellee, delivered a car load of hogs to the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company for transportation to Chicago. The dispute arose when the railroad company allegedly failed to deliver the hogs to the consignees at Chicago as per the shipping agreement. The plaintiff contended that he had directed the freight agent to ship the hogs to himself in Chicago. In contrast, the railroad company argued that Purvines had left the responsibility of shipping to Wesley Wyatt, who claimed that he purchased the hogs from Purvines and instructed the freight agent to ship them to Strahan & Co. The case went to trial, where a jury initially found in favor of Purvines, awarding him $475 in damages. The railroad company appealed the decision, claiming that the verdict was not supported by the evidence, as E. M. Wyatt testified to having purchased the hogs directly from Purvines.	Nathan S. Purvines, the plaintiff, argued that he had intended for the hogs to be shipped directly to him in Chicago and that he had not sold them to E. M. Wyatt. He maintained that Wyatt's claims regarding the sale were false and insisted that he provided explicit instructions to the freight agent for the shipment. Purvines sought to recover the value of the hogs due to the railroad's failure to deliver them as agreed.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company defended its actions by asserting that Purvines had given operational control to Wesley Wyatt, who claimed he was authorized to sell the hogs. According to the railroad company, Wyatt directed them to ship the hogs under his name after negotiating their purchase. The defense argued that the evidence overwhelmingly indicated that Purvines had indeed sold the hogs to E. M. Wyatt, and they sought to overturn the initial jury verdict that ruled in favor of Purvines.

John E. Sutherland v. Adeline B. Sutherland is a legal case that arose in September 1873 and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centers around the estate of John E. Sutherland, who passed away intestate, leaving behind substantial real and personal property. At the time of his death, he was survived by his widow, Adeline B. Sutherland, but he had no children or descendants. Prior to their marriage in 1862, John and Adeline entered into a written contract intended to bar Adeline’s dower rights by granting her specific real estate for her lifetime in lieu of those rights. After John’s death, a legal battle ensued over the distribution of his estate, with his nephews and nieces contesting Adeline’s claims. The Circuit Court of Cook County ruled that the contract did not prevent Adeline from claiming a share of the estate as his heir, prompting an appeal from John’s relatives, who sought to overturn that decision.	The plaintiffs, John E. Sutherland’s nephews and nieces, argue that the ante-nuptial contract executed by John and Adeline barred Adeline from claiming any inheritance at all from John's estate. They sought reversal of the previous court ruling and requested judicial confirmation that the contract fulfilled its purpose to disallow any inheritance claims by Adeline.	Adeline B. Sutherland, the widow, contends that the written contract she signed does not deny her rights as an heir of John E. Sutherland. She asserts that the contract only addressed her dower rights and did not affect her entitlements as an heir at law. Therefore, she maintains her claim to one-half of the real estate and all of the personal property left by her husband after his debts were settled.

In June 1867, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of August Werner v. Frederick Ropiequet, stemming from an event that took place in St. Clair County, Illinois, on October 20, 1866. The main individuals involved were August Werner, the plaintiff, and Frederick Ropiequet, the defendant. The dispute arose over a replevin action for the recovery of personal property that the defendant was alleged to have taken and detained. The defendant, Ropiequet, submitted a fourth plea defending his actions by asserting that he was acting as sheriff when he executed a landlord's warrant issued by James C. Hasselton against Henry Strieker, the tenant who owed rent. The plea indicated that at the time of the distress, the property in question belonged to Strieker, not Werner, and claimed that this distress was lawful as it was under the authority of the warrant issued against Strieker for overdue rent.	The plaintiff, August Werner, contended that the distress conducted by Frederick Ropiequet was unlawful because it was executed after the expiration of the lease agreement and more than six months after the rent had become due. Werner argued that the landlord's warrant was null and void as a result of these reasons. He sought the return of his property that had been wrongfully seized by the defendant.	Frederick Ropiequet defended his actions by stating that he was executing a landlord’s warrant as the sheriff, which gave him the authority to distress Henry Strieker's property for overdue rent. He asserted that the goods he seized were indeed the property of Strieker and that his actions were lawful under the warrant, as it was properly issued while he was performing his duties as bailiff for the landlord.

Solomon Andrews was indicted in September 1871 in Cook County, Illinois, specifically in the recorder's court of Chicago, for receiving stolen goods, which included overcoats and shirts belonging to Morse, Loomis & Co. Following a plea of not guilty, Andrews faced two trials; the first jury was deadlocked, but he was convicted in the second trial, resulting in a two-year penitentiary sentence. The basis for the prosecution's case was the testimony of Clark, a clerk who admitted to stealing and selling the goods to Andrews at a fraction of their value. The defense sought to present evidence showing that purchasing second-hand clothing at a reduced price was common practice in that trade, which would counteract the presumption of guilty knowledge; however, this evidence was not permitted in the trial. Andrews's character was defended by multiple witnesses, while others from the police contradicted this. The court acknowledged conflicts in the evidence presented and concluded that the exclusion of defense evidence was erroneous, prompting a decision to remand the case for a new trial.	The plaintiff, representing the State of Illinois, argued that Andrews knowingly received stolen goods, as evidenced by the significantly reduced prices he paid for them. They relied heavily on the testimony of Clark, asserting that Andrews's purchase demonstrated guilty knowledge.	The defendant, Solomon Andrews, contended that he had no guilty knowledge regarding the stolen goods, claiming that the practice of buying second-hand clothing at reduced prices was standard in the industry. He argued that the exclusion of evidence about this industry standard prevented a fair trial, thus warranting a reversal of the conviction. Andrews also challenged the credibility and reliability of the prosecution's evidence, pointing out inconsistencies and conflicts in testimony.

In May 1836, the defendants, including Joshua Dryden, Charles A. Warfield, and others, formed the 'Baltimore and Western Land Association' in Baltimore, Maryland, with a capital of $20,000, aimed at buying and selling lands in Illinois. Warfield served as their agent, purchasing land on behalf of the association using the company's funds. By March 11, 1840, Warfield conveyed the disputed lands to Dryden and others in trust for the company, a transaction recorded in December 1840. In July 1840, plaintiff John T. Martin filed an attachment against Warfield, asserting a debt which led to a judgment in his favor. He subsequently bought the lands under execution in late 1841. On September 6, 1841, the defendants filed a bill against Martin and Warfield, claiming that Martin had notice of Warfield's agency and the company's interest in the lands at the time of the attachment, seeking to have Martin's claims dismissed. The case revolves around whether Martin acted with knowledge of the defendants’ interest at the time of his attachment and subsequent purchase.",	Martin contended that he was unaware of the defendants' claim to the lands when he filed his attachment. He appealed the lower court's decision, asserting that he had no notice of the defendants' interests when he levied the attachment and later purchased the lands at sheriff's sale. He argued the court erred in finding he had notice of the defendants' interest and in discharging his lien.",	The defendants claimed that Martin had full knowledge of Warfield’s agency and the partnership's interest in the lands prior to the attachment, thus arguing that Martin's claim was invalid. They contended that any proceedings by Martin were ineffective due to this prior notice and sought to have his claims dismissed, asserting that all liens arising from his actions should be nullified.",

The case "Benjamin Scholes et al. v. Abraham Ackerland et al." revolves around the non-delivery of goods that were shipped from Cincinnati to Peoria via St. Louis. The incident occurred in 1850 when a shipment, comprising six boxes of goods, was entrusted to the steamer Movastar for transport. The plaintiffs, who operated the steamer, provided a bill of lading but claimed that part of the shipment was not delivered upon reaching Peoria. The goods were reported to have been properly packed and shipped, supported by testimonies stating the boxes appeared to be in good order when originally sent. However, upon delivery at Peoria, it was observed that one box was partially open, some items were damaged, and others were missing. The case was initially heard in the Peoria Circuit Court where the jury ruled in favor of the defendants, leading to an appeal by the plaintiffs. The court ultimately examined the evidence, which included various witness testimonies regarding the condition of the goods and the responsibilities of the carrier.	The plaintiffs contended that they had fulfilled their obligations as carriers by ensuring the boxes were packed properly and shipped with the appropriate documentation. They argued that the defendants, as recipients of the shipment, failed to receive the goods in good order, which entitled them to a claim for the lost and damaged items. Their legal requests included seeking damages for the value of the goods that were either missing or damaged upon delivery in Peoria.	The defendants argued that they were not liable for the missing or damaged goods, asserting that they had received the boxes in poor condition due to mishandling that likely occurred before the goods reached their custody. They presented testimonies from crew members of the steamer, who claimed there was no evidence of disturbances or losses during the transport. Their request was for the court to uphold the jury's verdict in their favor, thereby dismissing the plaintiffs' claims against them.

Green C. Patterson, the administrator of the estate of William McClintock, appealed the decision made by the Circuit Court of St. Clair County regarding claims made by Nancy Collar. The case originated on May 3, 1886, when Collar filed a claim for sixteen years of service rendered to McClintock, initially requesting $240 per year. In an amended claim filed on April 30, 1887, she sought $312.50 per year and an additional amount of $5,000 as acknowledged in McClintock's will. Collar had resided with McClintock's family for about sixteen years and was treated as a member of the household, assisting with domestic responsibilities, especially during her aunt's ill health. A jury initially granted Collar $2,250, but this was later increased to $5,000 in a subsequent trial. Following a judgment favoring Collar, Patterson appealed. The central legal question revolved around whether services rendered in familial relationships imply a contract for compensation.	Nancy Collar, the plaintiff, argued that she provided valuable services to the McClintock family during her long-term residence with them and sought payment for these services. Her main contention was based on the implicit acknowledgment by McClintock of a monetary obligation represented in his conversations and a will testament specifying $5,000 due to her for her services. She asserted that her role in the household justified her legal right to claim compensation.	Green C. Patterson, the defendant and administrator of McClintock's estate, contended that there was no express or implied contract obligating the estate to pay Collar for her services. Patterson argued that the familial relationship between Collar and McClintock created a presumption that services were rendered without the expectation of payment. He further claimed that expressions of kindness made by McClintock did not constitute a legally binding obligation and that the statute of limitations barred Collar's claims.

The case involves "The President, Directors, and Company of the State Bank of Illinois" against "The People of the State of Illinois" and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1843. The dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, concerning the bank's taxation status. The State Bank owned substantial real estate that was assessed for taxation for the year 1840. When the state sought to sell the bank's lands to satisfy tax debts, the bank challenged this action, claiming its lands were exempt from taxation based on its charter. The charter, enacted in 1835, specified that the bank would pay a fixed percentage of its capital stock to the state treasury "in lieu of all taxes and impositions whatever." The lower court ruled against the bank, asserting that it was not exempt, prompting the bank to appeal that decision, questioning the accuracy of the ruling regarding its tax-exempt status.	The plaintiffs, representing the State Bank of Illinois, argued that their lands should be exempt from taxation as stated in their charter. They contended that the 1835 statute explicitly grants the bank immunity from all taxes and that this exemption constitutes a binding contract with the state. They requested the court to reverse the lower court's judgment that allowed for the sale of the bank’s property to satisfy tax debts.	The defendants, representing the People of the State of Illinois, argued that the bank's exemption from taxation was not absolute and that the state retained the right to levy taxes. They contended that the interpretation of the charter's language did not exempt the bank from all forms of taxation. They aimed to uphold the lower court's judgment and allow the sale of the bank's lands for tax purposes.

The case of Winne v. Hammond took place during the April Term of 1864 at the Illinois Supreme Court. It arose from the Circuit Court of Cook County. The key parties involved were the appellant, Winne, and the appellee, Hammond. The case concerned an appeal made by Winne, in which a motion was entered to compel Hammond to join in error regarding the appeal. The central issue was that there had not been thirty days between the time of making the appeal and the beginning of the current term of the Supreme Court. The court had to consider whether the appellant could require the appellee to join in error at that term even though the appellant could not have been compelled to file his record at that time, according to the statute (Rev. Stat. 1845, 420, § 48).	The plaintiff, Winne, claimed that despite the requirement of a thirty-day interval before filing an appeal, he was in a position to file the record voluntarily. He moved for a rule upon Hammond to join in error at this term, arguing that his position did not relieve Hammond of this obligation.	The defendant, Hammond, contended that since the thirty-day period had not elapsed between the appeal and the start of the current term, it was inappropriate for Winne to compel him to join in error. Hammond argued that the rights of the parties should be reciprocal and that Winne could not impose this requirement on him if Winne himself was not bound to file the record at that term.

The case "Rose Keegan and John Keegan, Imp’d, etc. v. Hannah Kinnare, Administratrix, etc." was decided on April 26, 1887, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated from the Superior Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Kirk Hawes. The plaintiffs, Rose Keegan and John Keegan, filed an action of debt on a bond against the defendant, Hannah Kinnare, who was acting as administratrix. The case involved a jury verdict that assessed the plaintiffs' debt at $3,000, with damages of $1,840 determined by the jury. After a motion for a new trial, the plaintiffs remitted a portion of the damages, leading to a court judgment requiring the defendant to pay $1,760, along with interest and costs, as the conditions for discharging the debt. Although there were formal defects in the judgment, the core elements were upheld as correct and substantial, ultimately leading to the court's affirmation of the judgment.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were owed a total of $3,000 and sought damages assessed by a jury at $1,840. After a motion for a new trial and a remittitur of $80, the plaintiffs requested the court to enter judgment for the amount of $1,760 plus interest and costs, asserting that this payment would satisfy the debt in question.	The defendant, Hannah Kinnare, argued against the order and the formal judgment entered by the court, claiming that the language used did not accurately reflect the jury's findings or protect her from being required to pay more than was due. Nonetheless, the main defense focused on contesting the procedural formality of the judgment rather than denying the underlying debt itself.

In September 1870, Wilhelmina Von Kettler and her husband John H. Von Kettler filed a lawsuit against Madison Y. Johnson in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, claiming false imprisonment. Wilhelmina had been appointed administratrix of her late husband's estate and was alleged to have failed to comply with a county court order to pay a creditor, Julius K. Graves. After failing to meet the court's payment deadline, an attachment was issued, resulting in the arrest of both Wilhelmina and John by the sheriff. They were held in county jail until the judgment was satisfied on May 3, 1870. The couple contested this imprisonment, asserting the legality of the arrest was questionable and that they were wrongfully imprisoned without proper justification.	The Von Kettlers argued that Madison Y. Johnson, as an attorney for the creditor, committed trespass through wrongful imprisonment of Wilhelmina. They sought damages for the alleged unlawful arrest and confinement, claiming that Johnson's actions were not justified under the law, particularly because proper legal procedure regarding the attachment was not adhered to.	Madison Y. Johnson defended his actions by asserting that he acted under the orders of the county court and that the court had the necessary jurisdiction to issue the attachment for non-compliance with the payment order. He contended that the circumstances warranted the arrest, as Wilhelmina did not pay the judgment as ordered by the court.

In 1866, in Will County, Illinois, Seth W. Hardin and his colleague Wakeman brought separate actions of ejectment against James Kirk for the same tract of land. Each plaintiff filed independently with different attorneys, yet the case was treated as a single suit. The court required the plaintiffs to choose which declaration they would pursue, ultimately proceeding in favor of Hardin. An issue arose regarding the admissibility of a deed relevant to the case, and after examining the evidence, the lower court ruled in favor of the defendant, Kirk. The central legal questions involved whether the court erred in requiring the election of the plaintiff and in excluding a deed from evidence due to inadequate acknowledgment.	The plaintiffs, Hardin and Wakeman, argued for the right to recover the entirety of the disputed land. They claimed that the separate filings were sufficient to support their individual interests, and they challenged the lower court's requirement to elect a single declaration. Furthermore, they asserted that the deed which was excluded should have been admissible to establish their titles to the land.	The defendant, James Kirk, contended that the plaintiffs were improperly attempting to consolidate their separate claims without consent. He argued that the court rightfully required the election between declarations and that the evidence presented by the plaintiffs did not establish a valid claim to the property, specifically highlighting the failure of Wakeman to articulate any recoverable interest. Kirk also maintained that the deed's inadequacies justified its exclusion.

The case of Charles S. Newell v. School Directors of District No. 1 took place in Illinois, adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873. The dispute arose from orders issued by the school directors, which required payment from the school treasury for articles that the directors had not provided, despite these articles being lawful purchases. The situation escalated when Newell made a demand for the payment of these orders after they were due. However, the school treasurer, informed by the directors, refused to process the payment. The directors maintained that they lacked the authority to issue such orders without stating their purpose, leading to the claim that the orders were invalid. The legal question revolved around whether the orders were negotiable and if Newell, as an assignee, could claim the amount due.	The plaintiff, Charles S. Newell, argued that the orders issued by the school directors were negotiable instruments akin to promissory notes. He contended that after proper endorsement and transfer, he acquired the right to collect without any further defenses being applicable. Newell sought a judgment favoring his claim, contending that the school treasurer’s refusal to pay constituted a breach of the school directors' obligations under the law.	The defendants, the school directors, argued that the orders they issued were invalid as they did not adhere to the statutory requirements. They maintained that the directors lacked the power to create debt without explicit authority, particularly when the purpose for the orders was not stated. The directors contended that the orders were not negotiable and that Newell, as an assignee, held no better rights than the original payee due to this invalidity.

The case "Josiah Wright v. John Armstrong" took place in 1826 in Madison County, Illinois. The dispute arose when John Armstrong filed a writ of replevin against Josiah Wright for the wrongful taking of a horse. The key individuals involved included Josiah Wright, the defendant, and John Armstrong, the plaintiff, who claimed ownership of the horse based on his wife’s prior ownership. The argument centered around the horse allegedly straying from the wife’s possession prior to their marriage and not being in her possession for over five years before the suit was filed. The defendant, Josiah Wright, argued that he had obtained the horse through a series of sales from another individual, Philip Creamer, claiming no unlawful taking occurred. The jury initially found in favor of Armstrong, but Wright challenged this in a higher court, citing a lack of proven unlawful taking.	John Armstrong asserted that the horse in question was the property of his wife before their marriage and that Wright unlawfully took the horse from her possession. Armstrong argued that the horse had strayed from his wife for more than five years prior to the suit's initiation, and as such, pursued the replevin action to recover the horse, as he believed Wright had no right to retain it.	Josiah Wright contended that he did not unlawfully take the horse and that no tortious action had taken place on his part. He presented evidence that the horse had passed through several owners and argued that there had been no actual taking from Armstrong’s possession. Moreover, he highlighted that the horse had strayed from Armstrong's wife for an extended period, which weakened the basis of Armstrong's claim.

In 1887, in Cook County, Illinois, Martin J. Ryan and Michael J. Ryan (the plaintiffs) entered into a written contract with Omar H. Allen (the defendant) concerning the sale of property that was part of Allen's inherited estate from his stepmother, Elizabeth H. S. Allen. The contract stipulated that Allen would convey a specific portion of land to the Ryans in fee simple, free of any encumbrances, for the price of $450. Following Elizabeth's death, the property passed to Allen and his adopted sister through a will and codicil that outlined specific conditions regarding the inheritance. The Ryans took possession of the property but refused to pay the agreed sum, arguing that Allen only held a life estate and could not convey clear title. Allen then filed a bill for specific performance in the Superior Court to enforce the contract.	The plaintiffs, Ryan and Ryan, claimed that Omar H. Allen did not possess a clear title to the property due to the nature of the inheritance, arguing that he only had a life estate based on the will and codicil left by his stepmother, Elizabeth. They therefore sought a declaration that the contract was void and requested the court to deny Allen's bill for specific performance.	Omar H. Allen contended that he had a fee simple interest in the property due to the legal interpretation of the will and codicil, asserting that all conditions for transferring estate title were met. He argued that even though his father had the right to sell the estate, he never exercised that right. Allen requested the court to enforce the specific performance of the contract, insisting that he was able to convey the property as per the agreement with the Ryans.

In April 1866, the case of William T. Hughes v. Henry Atkins et al. was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Chicago, where Hughes was acting as a receiver for the Sherman House hotel. Atkins & Co. (the plaintiffs) initiated an action of assumpsit against Hughes, seeking payment for goods that were sold and delivered at Hughes's order. The central issue was whether Hughes was the actual purchaser of the goods or merely a guarantor for Roberts, the former proprietor of the hotel. The court instructed the jury to consider whether credit was extended to Hughes personally or to Roberts. Ultimately, the jury concluded that the goods were sold on Hughes's personal credit, leading to the assessment of liability.	The plaintiffs, Atkins & Co., argued that they sold goods to Hughes based on his personal promise to pay. They contended that the credit was extended to him, making him liable for the payment. They sought the court's recognition of Hughes's obligation to pay for the goods delivered.	Hughes's defense focused on the argument that he was not the actual purchaser of the goods but rather acted as a guarantor for Roberts. He contended that since the goods were sold to Roberts, he should not be held liable, even though he had agreed to assume responsibility for the payment.

The legal case "Ephraim Palmer et al. v. William O’Donnell" took place in La Salle County, Illinois, with the decision filed on August 20, 1884. The primary individuals involved were Ephraim Palmer and David Terry, the appellants, and William O’Donnell, the appellee. The dispute arose when the appellants, serving as commissioners of highways, dug a tile drain to address a flooding issue caused by a wet weather pond located on the property of John Dobbins, another appellant. This pond, approximately three-fourths of an acre in size, had no drainage before the appellants' intervention and discharged water onto the lands of appellee Palmer. The new tile drain redirected the water to the same culvert that had historically discharged water onto Palmer's land. Palmer claimed that this change increased flooding on his property, resulting in damage. However, testimony indicated that the flow of water was not significantly altered by the construction of the drain, as it emptied at the same point as before and actually improved the condition of the road. The court's analysis focused on the rights of landowners regarding drainage and the legal authority of highway commissioners to manage flooding issues.	The plaintiff, Ephraim Palmer, claimed that the defendants' construction of a tile drain altered the natural flow of water, causing flooding and damage to his land. He argued that the change had negatively affected his property, which had previously experienced lesser water flow. He sought damages for the alleged harm caused by the defendants' actions.	The defendants contended that they acted under their legal authority as highway commissioners and that the tile drain they constructed did not increase the flow of water onto Palmer's land in any material way. They asserted that the drainage system was necessary for maintaining the road and that the historical drainage patterns were preserved by their actions. They maintained that Palmer suffered no actual damage due to the changes made and requested the court to reverse the judgment rendered in favor of the plaintiff.

Samuel T. Brush contested the election of William A. Lemma to the office of mayor of Carbondale, Illinois. This legal proceeding began in January 1874 in the county court of Jackson County after Lemma was declared elected by the city council. Brush, an elector in the city, filed a verified written statement detailing the grounds for contesting the election and served a summons to Lemma for the February term. Lemma responded with a motion to dismiss, arguing that the county court lacked jurisdiction and that Brush, as a voter, had no legal right to contest the mayoral election. The county court granted Lemma's motion, leading Brush to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court for a review of the dismissal.	Brush argued that the county court had the jurisdiction to contest the election of any mayor under the relevant statutes. Specifically, he cited an 1872 act that allowed elections for local offices to be contested. Brush contended that the laws provided him the right to challenge the election results and sought a reversal of the county court's dismissal.
