Lemma's defense hinged on two main points: first, that the county court did not have jurisdiction over mayoral election contests, as mayors do not fall within the same classification as other officers mentioned in the statutes; and second, that Brush, as a voter, was not legally entitled to contest the election results for the office of mayor. He argued effectively that the statutes cited by Brush did not apply to the mayoral election conducted under a specific charter for Carbondale.

In 1873, in Bloomington, Illinois, John E. Thomas (the appellant) entered into an agreement with Thomas Coultas and his wife, Mrs. Coultas (the appellees), to exchange a house and lot for a farm owned by Thomas. The deal involved additional terms where Mrs. Coultas was to provide a half section of land in Kansas, and the appellees agreed to pay off a mortgage of $2,500 on the farm and give Thomas $700. After the deal, it was revealed that Thomas only owned five-sixths of the farm, which had additional judgments against it amounting to about $1,300, unbeknownst to the appellees. Their complaint alleged fraud due to Thomas misrepresenting the ownership and encumbrances on the property. Following legal proceedings, the jury determined that the appellees were unaware of the outstanding title at the time of the agreement. The case moved through the courts when Mrs. Coultas, with her husband, filed a bill to rescind the contract because of these fraudulent misrepresentations.	The plaintiffs, John E. Thomas and Mrs. Coultas, asserted that Thomas misrepresented the farm's title, claiming it was free from other encumbrances except the disclosed mortgage. They argued that they were deceived into the agreement, as Thomas concealed crucial details about the farm's ownership and encumbrances. They requested the court to rescind the contract and restore the property exchanged.	Thomas Coultas contended that the couple was aware of the existing liens and that the conditions of the agreement allowed them to assume these liabilities. He argued that the appellees had not proven any fraud occurred, and thus he should not be held accountable for reparation or rescission of the agreement. He also maintained that the plaintiffs failed to convey the Kansas properties, which should limit their ability to rescind the contract.

In the case of Board of Supervisors of Madison Co. v. The People, the proceedings took place in Madison County, Illinois, with the Circuit Court presided over by Judge William H. Snyder. The legal dispute arose when the commissioners of highways for the township of Wood River sought a mandamus to compel the Board of Supervisors to appropriate $2,500 for the construction of a bridge over Wood River. The commissioners had previously filed a petition for the appropriation on September 2, 1882, and although the board approved $1,000, it did not meet the requested amount, prompting the commissioners to take legal action. The case was contested on grounds including the sufficiency of the town's financial provision for half of the bridge's construction cost, necessary before the county board was obliged to respond. The Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of the commissioners, awarding the writ of mandamus, but this decision came under scrutiny in the appellate court.	The plaintiffs, representing The People (the commissioners of highways), argued that the Board of Supervisors was legally obligated to appropriate funds for the bridge as per the statute. They maintained that their request for the full appropriation necessary for the bridge was justified due to financial limitations on the township, which could not unilaterally fund the entire project without external assistance.	The Board of Supervisors, the defendants, contended that the plaintiffs did not meet the statutory prerequisites for obtaining the funds, specifically that the town had not raised or appropriated one-half of the necessary funds for the bridge. They asserted that without evidence of the town's financial readiness, they could not legally be compelled to make the appropriation, thereby contesting the validity of the mandamus.

In July 1883, the Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company filed a petition in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, seeking to condemn a triangular plot of land owned by the Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company, located on the west side of the North Branch of the Chicago River and on the north side of Kinzie Street in Chicago. The land was needed for the construction of a railroad bridge. The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company, asserting that the land was already devoted to a public use, opposed the petition, claiming it had no right to take the property. The trial took place from April 9 to April 15, 1884, culminating in a court ruling that assessed damages to the defendant at $28,000. The defendant subsequently appealed the ruling. The key individuals in this case were representatives from both railway companies, with Mr. B. C. Cook and Mr. Melville W. Fuller representing the appellant (Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company) and Mr. E. Walker representing the appellee (Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company).	The plaintiff, Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company, argued that it had the statutory right to condemn the land for constructing a bridge necessary for its railroad operations. They contended that the taking of the property was justified under the Eminent Domain Act and that the court had the jurisdiction to rule on the petition, as the property was not devoted to a public use that would conflict with their intended railroad purposes.	The defendant, Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company, presented several arguments against the plaintiff's claims, asserting that the land was already used for a public purpose, which prohibited its condemnation. They argued that the plaintiff lacked the authority to acquire the property for the proposed use and that the construction of a bridge would result in significant damages to their adjacent properties and operations. Furthermore, they claimed that the trial court erred by denying their motion to require a detailed plan of the proposed structure, which was essential for accurately addressing their concerns regarding damages.

In the case of George Edmanson v. A. H. Andrews & Co., the legal proceedings occurred in Cook County, Illinois, with the final judgment delivered on January 22, 1890. The case involved George Edmanson, the plaintiff, and A. H. Andrews & Co., the defendant. The matter came before the Illinois Appellate Court after Edmanson appealed a previous ruling from the Superior Court, presided over by Judge John P. Altgbld. During the trial, a witness testified regarding a conversation he had with an individual he believed was Edmanson in the office of the defendant. The court faced several objections related to the leading nature of questions asked during the testimony. The appellate court was tasked with reviewing whether there were legal errors in the trial's proceedings. The primary legal issue centered on the admissibility of certain witness identifications and testimonies regarding identity.	The plaintiff, George Edmanson, argued that the trial court erred in allowing leading questions during the witness's testimony, which he claimed could have influenced the jury's decision. Edmanson sought to challenge the validity of the identification made by the witness in court and contended that the proceedings did not uphold appropriate legal standards necessary for fair adjudication, ultimately requesting a reversal of the lower court’s ruling.	The defendant, A. H. Andrews & Co., claimed that the objections raised by Edmanson's counsel were insufficient to demonstrate any legal error and that the witness's testimony was competent. They argued that the identification presented was prima facie evidence and maintained that the trial was conducted properly, supporting their stance that the judgment should be upheld.

In the case of Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railway Company v. James Brisbane, which took place on June 1, 1886, Brisbane attempted to board a train from Hew Lenox to Joliet. The ticket office was closed at the time, and he could not buy a ticket. The train, known as the 10:44 train, left the station shortly after he boarded without a ticket. When the conductor requested the fare of 29 cents, Brisbane argued that he should only pay the 19 cents fare and refused to pay more. Following a brief dispute, the conductor stopped the train approximately a quarter-mile from the Hew Lenox depot and ejected Brisbane. He then walked the remaining distance to Joliet, during which his asthma was aggravated and he suffered health issues for a few days afterward. Brisbane subsequently filed a lawsuit against the railway company for damages following his ejection from the train, resulting in a jury verdict and judgment in his favor for $150.	Brisbane claimed damages against the railway company for the wrongful ejection from the train, arguing that the conductor's actions caused him unnecessary embarrassment and physical harm. His legal request included compensation for his pain and suffering, along with punitive damages based on the treatment he received during the incident.	The railway company contended that they had the right to eject any passenger who refused to pay the fare, asserting that Brisbane should be held accountable for not purchasing a ticket when given the opportunity. They also argued that no unreasonable force was used during the ejection and that any health issues incurred by Brisbane as a result of his walk to Joliet were too remote to be considered causally connected to the incident.

In September 1870, Eri L. Waterman filed a case against John D. Caton in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose in LaSalle County, where a judgment had been entered by confession upon a warrant of attorney. The central issue of the case was a claimed variance between the note referenced in the warrant of attorney and the actual note on which the judgment was based. The court highlighted that the judgment was entered during term time, affecting how the necessary documents related to the judgment were to be treated as part of the official court record. According to precedent cases, when judgments are entered during vacation, relevant documents do not require a bill of exceptions to be included in the record, but this rule differs when entered during term time. Since no bill of exceptions was filed in this case, the relevant documents were absent from the record, leading the court to conclude that the alleged variance could not be established.	The plaintiff, Eri L. Waterman, claimed that there was a substantive difference between the note that was supposed to be referenced by the warrant of attorney and the note upon which the judgment was executed. Waterman sought to have the judgment overturned due to this alleged discrepancy.	John D. Caton, the defendant, argued that the judgment was valid as entered, asserting that the required documents became part of the record by statute and did not need to be included through a bill of exceptions. Caton's defense relied on procedural rules regarding judgments entered in term time versus vacation.

Benjamin F. Edwards et al. v. John B. Helm was a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December of 1842. The dispute originated from a mortgage executed on May 29, 1837, to secure a debt owed by Edwards to Helm, who was both a creditor and a surety for Edwards. The mortgage was part of a larger complex financial arrangement involving a note of $6,000 owed to N. A. Ware, and a subsequent debt of $7,000 owed by Edwards to Helm. Following default by Edwards, Helm sought a strict foreclosure on the mortgage. The other key parties involved were Craig and Warner, who claimed a judgment lien against Edwards and sought to protect their interests after purchasing property that had been sold under execution. The case took place against the backdrop of legal practices in 19th-century Illinois regarding mortgages and creditor rights.	The plaintiffs, represented by Helm, argued for strict foreclosure of the mortgage to satisfy the debt of $7,000 owed by Edwards. They contended that the conditions of the mortgage allowed Helm to secure his loan as well as function as a surety, thereby expecting to recover the due amount through foreclosure.	The defendants, Craig and Warner, contended that they had purchased property through legal execution to satisfy a judgment against Edwards and were willing to relinquish their claim to the land if Helm agreed to allow the foreclosure under specific conditions. They argued that forcing them to redeem the mortgage would unjustly compel them to pay again for the land sold, which had already been acquired for less than its purported value.

William D. Messinger filed a case against Harlan P. Tracy in the Illinois Appellate Court on November 23, 1887. The case arose from a dispute involving promissory notes, where Messinger claimed that the notes in question were accommodation papers. This controversy centered around the interpretation and validity of these notes, with conflicting evidence presented regarding their nature. The case was heard in Cook County, Illinois, before Judge Richard Pbehdeegast. Key individuals involved included the plaintiff, William D. Messinger, and the defendant, Harlan P. Tracy, along with their respective legal representatives, Mr. J. A. Sleeper for Messinger and Messrs. Flower, Remy & Holstein for Tracy.	The plaintiff, William D. Messinger, argued that the promissory notes in dispute were accommodation papers and sought to enforce their payment. He aimed to prove that the notes were binding despite any conflicting evidence and requested the court to validate his claim.	The defendant, Harlan P. Tracy, countered Messinger's claims with arguments undermining the validity of the promissory notes. Tracy's defense likely included contesting the characterization of the notes as accommodation papers and questioned their enforceability based on the surrounding circumstances and evidence.

In January 1875, in LaSalle County, Illinois, a series of judgments were rendered against Donald HacKay amounting to $13,181.95. Executions for these judgments were issued to Sheriff A. C. McIntire, who subsequently levied on HacKay’s stock of goods and sold them for $7,142.07. Following this sale, the plaintiffs, Jeremiah R. Lawrence and George B. Murray, partners operating as J. B. Lawrence & Co., initiated a lawsuit against HacKay to recover a debt of $108.07 through a judgment obtained from a justice of the peace. After the execution of this judgment yielded no property, the plaintiffs filed a transcript of the judgment with the circuit court, seeking to have their claims satisfied from the proceeds of HacKay’s earlier sale. However, they alleged that no part of the proceeds was distributed to them, and the sheriff wrongfully returned their execution unsatisfied. The case became a matter of determining the distribution of the sale proceeds among concurrent judgments.	The plaintiffs contended that their judgment, filed during the same term of court as the previous judgments against HacKay, merited a pro-rata share of the distribution of sale proceeds from the sale of HacKay's goods. They argued that the statute entitled them to participate in the proceeds, as their execution was delivered to the sheriff prior to the sale of the goods.	The defendant, Sheriff A. C. McIntire, claimed that the statutory provision cited by the plaintiffs applied solely to the sale of real estate and did not extend to personal property. He argued that judgments are not liens on personal property, and executions become liens based on their order of delivery, with priority given to earlier executions. The sheriff maintained that he rightfully distributed the entire proceeds to the holders of the prior judgments.

The case "Ætna Life Insurance Company et al. v. James R. Paul" took place in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision rendered on August 3, 1887. The key individuals involved included James R. Paul as the plaintiff and Ætna Life Insurance Company as the defendant. The action was initiated by Paul to recover damages due to an alleged libel that he claimed was published by the defendants. The libel was purportedly aimed at damaging Paul’s reputation for honesty and integrity. The trial led to issues surrounding the admission of evidence regarding Paul's character, with the court initially allowing witnesses to testify to Paul's good character before any rebuttal or related evidence was introduced. The jury ultimately found for Paul and awarded him damages of $4,810. However, the case was appealed by the defendants, challenging the trial court's ruling on the evidence and procedures followed during the trial.	The plaintiff, James R. Paul, claimed that the defendants published a libel that harmed his reputation for honesty and integrity. He aimed to demonstrate through witness testimony that he had a good reputation prior to the alleged defamatory statements and sought monetary damages amounting to $4,810 for the harm he suffered as a result of the defendants' actions.	The defendants, represented by Ætna Life Insurance Company, contended that the trial court erred in allowing evidence of the plaintiff's character to be introduced prematurely in the trial. They asserted that this prejudicial admission of character testimony before any relevant challenges were made adversely affected their defense. The defendants' argument focused on procedural errors, claiming that the plaintiff's good character was improperly established without any prior attack on that character.

The case of "The Jacksonville Railway Company v. The City of Jacksonville" took place in 1885 in Jacksonville, Illinois. The appeal arose from the Morgan County Circuit Court, which confirmed an assessment made by the city against the Jacksonville Railway Company's road-bed and franchise for its share of the costs associated with constructing a brick pavement on East State Street. The total estimated cost for the improvement was $17,569.31, with $915.43 to be borne by the city and $1920 allocated to the railway company. Following an appeal, a jury reduced the railway's assessment to $1062, which was later slightly further adjusted to $1040.76. The railway company alleged that the ordinance under which the assessment was made was invalid due to defects regarding the specification of construction materials. The court reviewed the legitimacy of the ordinance, asserting that it indeed met statutory requirements.	The Jacksonville Railway Company argued that the ordinance allowing the city to assess costs for the pavement was invalid as it failed to specify the materials required for the pavement's foundation, which should have been clearly defined in accordance with statutory requirements. The plaintiff claimed that the city's assessment was thus unenforceable and requested that the judgment confirming the assessment be reversed.	The City of Jacksonville defended the validity of the ordinance, arguing that it provided adequate details regarding the pavement's construction, specifically mentioning the use of sand and cinders. They contended that the ordinance was not ambiguous or invalid and maintained that the city's right to levy the special assessment was legitimate even if they had exceeded their constitutional debt limit without incurring additional debt. The city sought to uphold the court's judgment confirming the assessment.

The case “The Kankakee & Seneca Railroad Company et al. v. Frank Horan” originates from Grundy County, Illinois, in 1881. The Kankakee & Seneca Railroad Company was organized in February 1881 to construct a railroad across land owned by Frank Horan’s family. Following the construction of this railroad, Horan claimed that the railroad embankments diverted water from natural flows, resulting in significant flooding and crop damage to his land over the years 1881, 1882, and 1883. Horan was a tenant of the land, which comprised three eighty-acre tracts, through which the railroad was constructed. The railroad’s construction was claimed to have obstructed drainage from local sloughs, causing excessive water accumulation on Horan’s property and leading to loss of crops. The case was previously appealed and remanded for a new trial due to procedural issues. The trial included testimonies about the adequacy of the railroad's drainage and the causation of the alleged damages.	Frank Horan, as the appellee, argued that the Kankakee & Seneca Railroad Company (and indirectly the Cincinnati, Indianapolis, St. Louis & Chicago Railroad Company) was responsible for the flooding of his land due to improperly constructed embankments and insufficient drainage. Horan claimed damages amounting to $700, asserting that the railroad's construction diverted water flow from adjacent sloughs onto his farmland, resulting in significant crop loss across three years. He sought compensation based on the resultant agricultural losses from the floods caused by the defendants' actions.	The appellants, The Kankakee & Seneca Railroad Company and the Cincinnati Company, defended themselves by asserting that they were not liable for the flooding. They argued that the drainage provided by the railroad was sufficient and that Horan’s damages were not caused by their construction. They further contended that external factors, such as prior ditches leading into the Parker slough and extraordinary flooding events, were responsible for the damage, which should be considered acts of God beyond their control. The appellants claimed that the evidence presented did not conclusively link their operations to the alleged damages experienced by Horan.

The case "The Belleville Savings Bank v. James A. Bornman et al." took place in 1888 in Belleville, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Conrad Bornman, the president of the Belleville Nail Mill Company, Edward Abend, a bank director, and representatives of the Belleville Savings Bank. In July 1874, Bornman endorsed a draft for $10,000 from the Belleville Nail Mill Company to the bank, but stipulated that Abend also needed to endorse it as a co-guarantor, of which the bank was notified before acceptance. Abend did not sign the draft; instead, he executed a separate guaranty. The mill company eventually did not pay the draft, leading the bank to present a claim against Bornman's estate following his death. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after the lower courts ruled against the bank's claim.	The Belleville Savings Bank argued that it was entitled to recover against Bornman's estate based on the draft he endorsed. The bank maintained that although Abend did not co-sign the draft, the prior draft from March 14, 1874, which Bornman guaranteed, still rendered him liable. The bank claimed that it should have been allowed to recover based on the existing guarantees despite the renewal.	The defense, representing Bornman's estate, contended that Bornman's endorsement was conditional upon Abend also signing the draft, which did not occur. Therefore, Bornman had no liability as the condition was not satisfied. They argued that the acceptance of the new draft did not extinguish Bornman's obligation since this acceptance was never intended as payment for the original draft.

In 1850, Robert Roney left for California, leaving personal property valued at about $100 with his mother in Scott County, Illinois. Before leaving, Roney arranged with Joel Bruce, who was to marry his mother, to buy certain land for him. After arriving in California, Roney communicated with Bruce, who claimed to have purchased the land and subsequently requested more funds from Roney. Although Roney sent money, he alleged that Bruce appropriated some of his personal property. There was a dispute over the land deed, as it was taken in Bruce's name. Roney filed a bill in chancery seeking the enforcement of a resulting trust, asserting that he had paid for the land in part while Bruce claimed ownership. The central question of the case focused on whether the money used to purchase the land was indeed Roney's, thereby establishing a trust. Testimony was provided to support each party's claims, ultimately leading to a master’s report that indicated financial exchanges between both parties.	Roney claimed that Bruce had agreed to purchase the land on his behalf and that he had sent money for this purpose. He alleged that Bruce misappropriated personal property left behind, owed him for labor, and utilized Roney’s funds for the land purchase. Roney requested an accounting of the transactions, a decree compelling Bruce to convey the land to him, and sought relief regarding any encumbrances.	Bruce denied any arrangement with Roney regarding the purchase of the land, asserting that he solely bought the land for himself. He contended that he had paid for the property entirely from his own funds, and counter-claimed that Roney owed him money for various expenses. Bruce argued against Roney's claims of trust, stating that Roney’s contributions were minimal and not sufficient for a resulting trust claim.

In the case of The American Fire Insurance Company v. The Brighton Cotton Manufacturing Company, the events unfolded in Illinois, culminating in a judgment delivered by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 16, 1888. The plaintiff, The American Fire Insurance Company, issued an insurance policy covering a four-story brick cotton mill owned by the defendant, The Brighton Cotton Manufacturing Company. The mill was leased to third parties who operated it until it was destroyed by fire on July 16, 1885. Before the fire, many of the mill's employees were temporarily laid off, although a number remained on-site, performing necessary duties and preparations for restarting operations, which were anticipated shortly after the fire. The insurance policy included specific conditions regarding vacancy and operation of the manufacturing establishment. Central to the case was the determination of whether the mill was considered "vacant and unoccupied" at the time of the fire and whether it had "ceased to be operated," as stipulated in the insurance contract.	The plaintiff claimed that the insurance policy was still valid and should cover the loss incurred due to the fire. Their main arguments focused on demonstrating that the conditions requiring the mill to be occupied and operational were met, arguing that the presence of employees and preparations for resuming operations indicated that the mill was neither vacant nor had it ceased to be operated in the contractual sense.	The defendant contended that the insurance policy had become void due to breaches of its terms, specifically claiming that the mill had become vacant and unoccupied and that it had ceased to operate. They argued that the temporary suspension of work due to a lack of cotton supply constituted a violation of the operational clause, which they claimed rendered the insurance ineffective at the time of the fire.

Morris Neustadt and the City of La Salle filed a case against the Illinois Central Railroad Company in 1863 in Illinois. The central issue was whether the city had the authority to impose municipal taxes on the railroad company's property located within the city limits. The Illinois Central Railroad was incorporated by an act of the General Assembly on February 10, 1851, which specified that the company’s property would be exempt from all taxation until sold or conveyed. This act served as a contract between the state and the railroad company, protecting the company from local taxation. The case arose after the local authorities attempted to levy a tax, prompting the railroad company to defend its position based on the exemptions outlined in its incorporation. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the railroad, confirming that no city could impose such taxes due to the existing exemption.	The plaintiffs, Morris Neustadt and the City of La Salle, claimed that the city had the authority to tax the Illinois Central Railroad Company for municipal purposes under the act that incorporated the city. They argued that changes in the law or circumstances might allow for taxing the property of the railroad, thus challenging the exemption claimed by the railroad company.	The defendant, Illinois Central Railroad Company, contended that the 1851 incorporation act provided them with undeniable tax exemptions for their property located within La Salle. They argued that this act constituted a binding contract that could not be altered without mutual consent and explicitly exempted them from municipal taxation. They requested confirmation from the court that they were not liable to pay any local taxes.

The case "Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company v. Daniel Diehl" took place in September 1869, in Whiteside County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Daniel Diehl, the plaintiff, and the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company, the defendant. The dispute arose when Diehl sought compensation for two colts that were allegedly killed by the railway company's operations. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, with Mr. Justice Lawrence delivering the opinion. The jury was instructed to find for the plaintiff if specific evidence was presented, but the court later found that an essential fact—namely that the railway line had been open for six months—was not proved. Because of this lack of evidence, the court determined that the earlier judgment favoring the plaintiff was not warranted.	The plaintiff, Daniel Diehl, claimed that the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company was negligent in its operations, resulting in the death of his two colts. He sought damages for the value of the killed livestock, arguing that the railway company should be held responsible for their actions that led to the incident.	The defendant, Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company, contended that the court's instructions to the jury were flawed because they omitted an essential fact: the railway had been in operation for at least six months at the time of the incident. They argued that this critical detail was not substantiated by the evidence presented, and therefore, they should not be held liable for the damages claimed by the plaintiff.

Nathaniel Swingley brought a suit against John Haynes in Ogle County, Illinois on May 17, 1857. The case arose after a judgment was rendered against Haynes for $98.34 in a justice court when he failed to appear. The summons served by Constable Upton Swingley was delivered to Haynes' residence, but the defendant was absent. On the date of the trial, May 23, 1857, the justice ruled in favor of Swingley due to Haynes' absence. Following this, Haynes appealed the judgment to the Ogle County Circuit Court, contending that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction and that the service of summons was inadequate. At the October 1857 term, the Circuit Court agreed with Haynes and dismissed the suit, charging Swingley with costs. Subsequently, both parties filed a stipulation for the case to be heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, waiving the requirement for a writ of error. The plaintiff argued that the Circuit Court erred in dismissing the suit and requested the decision to be overturned.	Swingley claims that the Circuit Court erred in their decision to dismiss the case. He asserts that, according to Illinois law, the court had jurisdiction to hear the appeal despite any perceived deficiencies in the summons. He argues that the dismissal was premature, asserting that evidence should have been heard to determine if the justice of the peace had jurisdiction over the matter.	Haynes contends that the lower court lacked jurisdiction and argues that the service of summons was inadequate. Haynes maintains that the dismissal was justified on these grounds and requests that the judgment from the lower court be upheld, thereby absolving him from the charges and associated costs.

In the early part of 1859, a legal case was filed in Coles County, Illinois involving John S. Dill and other plaintiffs against the Wabash Valley Railroad Company. The plaintiffs contended that they had subscribed to stock in the railroad company with the understanding that the funds would be used specifically for constructing the railroad in Edgar County. After subscribing, the plaintiffs alleged that the railroad company failed to fulfill this agreement by not locating the railroad in Edgar County and, instead, misusing the funds in other locations. As a result of their dissatisfaction, Dill and his co-plaintiffs sought a court injunction to prevent the railroad from collecting stock payments from them. The argument was grounded in their claim that the railroad's actions violated the terms stipulated in the subscription agreement and that the company had since become insolvent. The case culminated in a legal challenge in the Illinois Supreme Court questioning whether the plaintiffs could successfully enjoin the railroad from collecting the subscribed amounts due to alleged misapplication of funds and the company’s insolvency.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Wabash Valley Railroad Company was in violation of the subscription agreement by failing to use the funds exclusively for the construction of the railroad in Edgar County. They argued that their subscription demands were conditional upon the company's adherence to this agreement and sought legal remedy to prevent the railroad from enforcing the collection of stock amounts, citing the company's insolvency and misuse of funds.	The Wabash Valley Railroad Company, through its attorneys, filed a general demurrer, arguing that the injunction should not be granted because the subscription agreement did not explicitly state that the funds must be used in Edgar County. It contended that any conditions not clearly outlined in the written contract could not serve as a legal defense. Furthermore, they asserted that the company's insolvency could not justify halting the collection of stock subscriptions, emphasizing the necessity of collecting funds to satisfy creditors.

Jonas Weatherford, the appellant, was involved in a legal dispute with Josephus Cunningham, the appellee, regarding a land transaction in Illinois in January 1859. Weatherford had a contract with Lewis Massie to sell 100 acres of land for $1,700. Before the final deed was executed, Weatherford sold half of the land to Cunningham for $850. As part of their agreement, Cunningham was to pay Massie an additional $180 for the choice of halves of the land. The parties agreed that Weatherford would execute deeds to both Cunningham and Massie, reflecting their respective payments. Weatherford's deed to Cunningham was for $1,030, of which Cunningham paid $940 but refused to pay the remaining $90. Consequently, Weatherford sought judgment for the unpaid amount in a justice court and won, but Cunningham appealed, resulting in judgment being reversed in favor of Cunningham in the circuit court. Weatherford then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court to have the case reviewed.	Weatherford claimed that Cunningham owed him a total of $1,030 for half of the land, which Cunningham had initially agreed to pay. He emphasized that Cunningham only paid $940 and refused to remit the remaining $90. Weatherford sought judgment for the unpaid balance, along with the associated costs incurred in the previous judgments.	Cunningham argued that the payment made to Weatherford was sufficient, and he contended that he had fulfilled his duties as per the agreement. He claimed that the circuit court's reversal of the justice's ruling was justified. Cunningham sought to maintain this judgment in his favor and to dismiss Weatherford's claims for the additional payment.

The legal case "City of East St. Louis v. M. Millard" took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, with the judgment being filed on April 18, 1884. The case stemmed from a bill in chancery filed by the complainant, who had previously secured a judgment of $3,000 against the defendant in 1881. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant had failed to satisfy this judgment, despite having sufficient revenue and funds available to do so. Key individuals involved included John M. Sullivan, the city treasurer, who allegedly had control over $7,000 that could be used to pay the judgment, and L. J. Cauty, the city clerk, who also held a considerable amount of city funds. The complaint alleged that there had been gross mismanagement of the city's finances, including the payment of illegal claims. The plaintiff sought various injunctions to prevent the city from making these payments and to compel the city officials to account for the funds available for settling the debt. The case revolved around the legal implications of the city officers' handling of funds and the demand for fulfilling the judgment.	The plaintiff argued that the City of East St. Louis had failed to pay a judgment of $3,000 won in 1881, despite having sufficient funds readily available. The plaintiff's main legal requests included seeking an injunction against the city from paying illegal claims, ensuring that city officers would not draw warrants unless there were funds to support them, and compelling a proper accounting of city funds to confirm amounts available for satisfying the judgment.	The defendant contended that the plaintiff had adequate remedies available at law, particularly through a writ of mandamus, to enforce payment of the judgment. The defendant maintained that the allegations of fraud within the complaint were too vague and lacked specificity, thus contending that the case should not fall under the jurisdiction of a court of chancery.

The case "Charles A. Dupee et al. v. Charles P. Swigert, Auditor" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on April 5, 1889. The dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, where Charles A. Dupee and others sought a permit to organize a bank under an Act concerning corporations with banking powers approved on June 16, 1887. The State Auditor, Charles P. Swigert, refused their application, claiming two main reasons: first, that the Act did not apply to cities with populations exceeding ten thousand, and second, that a provision regarding shareholder liability was unconstitutional. The court examined these claims and determined that the Act intended to allow bank organization across the state, regardless of population size. It concluded that the auditor's reasoning for denying the permit was insufficient and that the prohibition against organizing banks in larger cities was in fact unconstitutional.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to a permit to organize a bank in Chicago, as authorized by the Illinois banking law of 1887. They argued that the law allowed for the formation of banks without restriction based on city population size, as the Act was designed to apply broadly across Illinois. The plaintiffs sought a writ of mandamus to compel the auditor to issue the permit they requested.	The defendant, represented by the Auditor, contended that the Illinois banking law did not permit the organization of banks in cities with populations greater than ten thousand, and thus he was justified in denying the permit. Additionally, the auditor argued that the provision requiring shareholders to be jointly liable for bank debts was unconstitutional, claiming it imposed illegal restrictions on the organization of the bank.

On October 1, 1870, Andrew Bauch mortgaged specific land in Macoupin County, Illinois, to O. B. Heaton to secure a loan. Later, in February 1877, Bauch borrowed $4,772 from Prentiss D. Cheney, securing this debt with two mortgages on the same land. In August 1878, a court decreed the foreclosure of Heaton’s mortgage, and the land was sold to Heaton’s estate executors in November 1878. The same month, Chenney was made a party to the foreclosure suit. Bauch failed to redeem the land after the sale, and Cheney subsequently acquired the certificate of purchase. In May 1877, Yaneil obtained a judgment against Bauch and assigned it to James W. Patton in August 1879. Patton issued an execution against the mortgaged land, also redeeming the land from the Heaton foreclosure sale. On May 23, 1877, Henry J. Smith claimed to have purchased the Cheney mortgages. In May 1880, he sought to foreclose those mortgages and redeem from Heaton’s sale. Patton contested this, asserting ownership of the land through his redemption and purchase. The case hinged on whether Smith was a necessary party to the prior foreclosure and if he had a legitimate claim to the mortgages.	James W. Patton claimed that he rightfully owned the land following his redemption from the Heaton foreclosure sale and subsequent purchase at the sheriff's sale. He argued that Henry J. Smith, having not been included as a necessary party to the Heaton foreclosure suit, lacked the standing to redeem the property as he could not establish ownership of the Cheney notes and mortgages due to a missing recorded assignment.	Henry J. Smith contended that he was entitled to redeem the property based on his ownership of the Cheney notes and mortgages. He claimed to have acquired them before the Heaton foreclosure that excluded him from being a necessary party. Smith argued that Patton’s rights did not extend to blocking his ability to redeem since he was not aware of Smith's interest during the foreclosure proceedings.

In December 1842, the case "William F. Bradshaw v. Peter McKinney" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a dispute involving a promissory note and a guaranty. The case was brought by William F. Bradshaw, the plaintiff, against Peter McKinney, the defendant. The proceedings were conducted at the September term of 1841, presided over by Hon. Thomas C. Browne. The circuit court awarded judgment in favor of Bradshaw, awarding him damages amounting to $139.80, as well as the costs of the suit. However, this judgment became the subject of an appeal as the defendant raised issues related to the procedural handling of the case, specifically concerning the lack of resolution on a demurrer to one of the counts in the declaration and the consideration of the defendant's pleas.	The plaintiff, William F. Bradshaw, claimed that Peter McKinney had defaulted on a promissory note and sought damages for this breach. He requested the court to uphold the judgment rendered by the circuit court, which had already awarded him damages and costs associated with the suit.	The defendant, Peter McKinney, countered the plaintiff's claims by arguing procedural errors in the preceding court’s judgment. Specifically, he asserted that it was erroneous for the court to render judgment without addressing the outstanding demurrer to one count of the declaration and without examining the issues posed by his first and second pleas, which were essential for a fair assessment of the case.

In 1870, Francis M. Griffin engaged in a legal dispute with the City of Chicago concerning a special assessment warrant. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, which reviewed an appeal made by Griffin regarding a judgment rendered against his property. The application for judgment was based on a special assessment published in the city related to property taxes or liens. A notice was published for ten consecutive days beginning January 18, 1869, but it did not specify that the days were "exclusive of Sundays and holidays" as Griffin contended was necessary for validation. The court examined the certificate of publication and determined that the language used was sufficient for the court to ascertain relevant dates. The presiding judge for this matter was Joseph E. Gary in the Superior Court of Chicago. Griffin, represented by attorney Edward Roby, challenged the lower court's judgment, while the City of Chicago defended its position through attorney M. F. Ttjlby.	Griffin's primary argument revolved around the validity of the certificate of publication, asserting that it should have stated the assessment was published "exclusive of Sundays and holidays." He contended that the failure to include this language rendered the judgment invalid. Additionally, he called witnesses that he later attempted to impeach, asserting that their previous statements contradicted their courtroom testimony. Griffin's legal request was essentially to overturn the judgment against his property.	The City of Chicago, in defense, maintained that the certificate of publication was sufficient as stated in the appeal to clearly ascertain relevant dates. They argued that the absence of language regarding Sundays and holidays did not invalidate the judgment. Furthermore, the City contested Griffin’s efforts to impeach his witness due to the principle that a party cannot discredit a witness they called themselves. Their request was for the court to affirm the validity of the lower court's ruling and dismiss Griffin's appeal.

In 1878, John H. Dougherty and Herald Catlett entered into a written agreement for the sale of certain lands in Vermilion County, Illinois. As part of the contract, Dougherty paid a sum of money upfront and agreed to make additional payments, while Catlett promised to convey the land to Dougherty upon completion of the payments. Dougherty took possession of the land but later sold half of it to a third party, McCabe, with Catlett's assistance. In October 1881, Dougherty and Catlett made a verbal agreement in which Dougherty agreed to surrender his remaining interest in the land to Catlett for $3,500, which Dougherty subsequently did. Catlett later sold this remaining interest to a third party for $4,000. When Dougherty did not receive payment from Catlett for the $3,500, he sued Catlett to recover the amount owed. The central legal issue revolved around the application of the Statute of Frauds, which requires certain contracts concerning land to be in writing to be enforceable.	Dougherty claimed that the verbal agreement constituted a binding contract for the sale and surrender of his remaining interest in the land, and he requested the court to hold Catlett liable for the agreed payment of $3,500. He argued that his actions in surrendering possession under the verbal agreement should be sufficient performance to take the case out of the provisions of the Statute of Frauds, asserting that he was entitled to recover the amount due.	Catlett defended against Dougherty’s claims by citing the Statute of Frauds, arguing that the verbal agreement was unenforceable because it was not in writing. He contended that the partial performance alleged by Dougherty was insufficient to remove the case from the purview of the statute, as the required legal formalities for such contracts had not been satisfied. Therefore, he asserted that he could not be held liable for the payment claimed by Dougherty.

In September 1865, Thomas H. O’Neal filed a legal action in Chicago against The Wabash Avenue Baptist Church and others regarding a parcel of land. The case stems from a contract made on June 18, 1852, between O’Neal and Stephen Bronson Jr., who agreed to sell the property to O’Neal for $722.37, with the condition that O’Neal would pay taxes on the property. The contract specified that failure to meet payment deadlines could result in forfeiture of the agreement. O’Neal failed to make the final payment by the due date of June 18, 1855, and Bronson subsequently conveyed the property to Sherman P. Tracy on August 29, 1855, notifying O’Neal of this transfer. O’Neal claimed that Bronson had extended the payment period after this transfer. However, the court noted that after Bronson transferred the title to Tracy, he no longer had the ability to alter the contract with O’Neal, leading to the legal status of the land being questioned.	O’Neal argued that he had a rightful claim to the property based on his contract with Bronson, asserting that the extension of time for payment was valid and that Bronson could not declare a forfeiture after the conveyance to Tracy. O’Neal sought to reverse the judgment favoring the defendants and reclaim legal title to the property.	The defendants contended that the title to the property was legally transferred to Tracy before O’Neal's subsequent deed in February 1865. They argued that Bronson’s transfer marked a clear forfeiture of O’Neal’s contract, as he failed to meet the payment deadlines, and thus the contract was no longer valid. Additionally, they maintained that Bronson had no power to extend the contract or waive its consequences after parting with the title.

In 1875, Joseph Morley filed a legal action against The Town of Metamora in Illinois. The case arose from the official bond of a supervisor who was elected twice, first in April 1872 and re-elected in April 1873. At the end of his first term, the supervisor reported having a specific amount of money in his possession, which was approved by the relevant town officers. Upon being re-elected, he provided a new bond but failed to pay over the reported amount to his successor upon demand. The dispute centers around whether the sureties on the first or the second bond are liable for the default, as the supervisor himself was the person responsible for both terms. The court needed to determine the liability for the default and whether the sureties should be held accountable for the funds reported but not transferred.	Joseph Morley, as the plaintiff, argues that the sureties on the supervisor's second bond are responsible for the amount he reported having at the end of his first term. He asserts that this obligation is ongoing as the supervisor continued in office and that the report made was approved, thus creating an assumption of the funds' existence in his hands.	The Town of Metamora contends that any default occurred during the first year of the supervisor’s term, making the sureties on the first bond liable for the funds. They argue that since the reported default occurred during the first term, the obligations should not fall on the second bond’s sureties, as those bonds were separate and pertained only to his subsequent term.

In December 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, Michael Hellmuth filed a lawsuit against Charles Katschke after sustaining injuries from being struck by a barrel. The barrel fell from a platform in a cooper shop where Hellmuth was working. It was alleged that the barrel was improperly placed on the platform by Katschke's foreman. During the incident, Hellmuth was exercising proper care when the barrel fell, resulting in significant injury. The evidence presented indicated that the foreman had placed the barrel carelessly, and the jury determined that the foreman was acting in his capacity as a superior, thus not considered a fellow servant of Hellmuth. The court affirmed the jurors' judgment, suggesting that they had reasonable grounds for their decision based on the evidence provided regarding the circumstances of the accident.	Michael Hellmuth claimed that Charles Katschke was negligent in the placement of the barrel that fell on him. He asserted that the foreman, acting on Katschke's behalf, failed in his duty to ensure a safe working environment, resulting in Hellmuth's injuries. Hellmuth sought damages amounting to $1,500 for the injuries sustained from the incident.	Charles Katschke’s defense argued that the barrel's placement was not negligent and sought to introduce evidence suggesting that another fellow servant, Toms, admitted responsibility for the barrel falling. They contended that this declaration should be considered admissible under the res gestae doctrine. Additionally, Katschke's defense maintained that Hellmuth's injuries did not arise from any wrongdoing on the part of the foreman, as he was merely a fellow-servant, not a superior.

In the case of Edmund S. Holbrook v. Mary M. Gouveneur, the dispute arises from an action of ejectment related to a tract of land in Will County, Illinois. The case involves multiple parties, initially starting with Seth W. Hardin against Peter Bickey, but later transitioning to Holbrook as the plaintiff against Gouveneur as the newly substituted defendant. The action was brought on February 24, 1866, with Bickey initially served with a declaration regarding land ownership but later withdrawing his plea. Gouveneur then entered the case to defend as to the portion of the land referred to in the declaration. Over the years, multiple trials occurred, with judgments favoring the defendant, Gouveneur, after he established claims of color of title and tax payments over an extended period while the land was vacant. The plaintiff, Holbrook, maintained his ownership claim, arguing that the evidence was insufficient to establish Gouveneur’s possession under color of title. However, significant admissions by both parties, the legal understanding of possession, and the court's consideration led to a remanding order and eventually a trial that upheld Gouveneur's right to the property based on the evidence presented.	The plaintiff, Edmund S. Holbrook, argued that he had established a prima facie title to the land in question and contended that the defendant, Gouveneur, had not adequately proven his claims of possession under color of title or payment of taxes during the relevant period. Holbrook sought to reverse the trial court's judgment in favor of Gouveneur, claiming the evidence did not support the conclusion that Gouveneur was in possession of the land when the suit was initiated.	In defense, Mary M. Gouveneur argued that he had established color of title and that he had paid taxes on the land for seven consecutive years while it was vacant. Moreover, Gouveneur admitted to being in possession of the land at the commencement of the action, and he asserted that the plaintiff's failure to prove his claims about possession negated Holbrook’s argument. Gouveneur sought to uphold the trial court's judgment, citing admissions made by the plaintiff that supported his claims.

On October 6, 1884, Abraham Brokaw filed a petition in the Circuit Court of McLean County, Illinois, against the Commissioners of Highways. He sought a writ of mandamus to compel the commissioners to repair a road that included reconstructing two bridges over the Little Kickapoo Creek in Bloomington Township. The circuit court initially ruled in Brokaw's favor, ordering the repairs and funding to be secured through taxation. However, this decision was appealed to the Appellate Court, which reversed the circuit court's ruling. The case then progressed to the Illinois Supreme Court for further appeal. The commissioners argued that the repairs requested were not ordinary maintenance and that they lacked the funds necessary to construct the bridges, as they had already levied the permissible taxes and exhausted their financial resources. They contended that the decision to build the bridges fell within their discretionary powers as public officers.	Brokaw claimed that the commissioners had a legal obligation to repair the road and construct the essential bridges. He argued that the absence of these bridges impacted public access and that the public highway required urgent attention. The plaintiff requested the court to compel the commissioners to execute the necessary repairs and secure funding through taxation, presenting the argument that there was a clear legal necessity for the work to be performed.	The defendants, the Commissioners of Highways, argued that the request for repairs was outside the scope of their ordinary duties and that they had exercised their discretion in determining the necessity of such repairs. They stated that they had already exhausted their financial resources and were not legally bound to construct new bridges without additional funding. The commissioners emphasized that the decision to proceed with the repairs and funding was discretionary and not something that could be imposed on them by mandamus.

The case "Aaron Hoig et al. v. Joel S. Thrap et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1876. It originated from the Circuit Court of Warren County, where a petition for leave to file a bill of review was submitted by the plaintiffs, Aaron Hoig and others. The key issue arose when the plaintiffs claimed there was a mistake concerning the death of one of them, which erroneously suggested he was deceased and led to the appointment of a supposed legal representative. Additionally, they argued that newly discovered evidence warranted the reconsideration of the case. The circuit court, presided over by Judge Arthur A. Smith, refused their request, prompting the plaintiffs to bring a writ of error to the Supreme Court, seeking recourse.	The plaintiffs contended that the circuit court erred in refusing them leave to file a bill of review based on two key grounds: firstly, that a mistake in the record suggested that one of the complainants was dead, when in fact, he was still alive; secondly, that newly discovered evidence could impact the outcome of their case, justifying a review of the previous decree.	The defendants, represented by Messrs. Stewart & Phelps, defended the circuit court's decision, arguing that the court appropriately exercised its discretion in denying the petition for a bill of review. They noted that the decree the plaintiffs sought to review had already been reversed at the present term on appeal, rendering the filing of the bill of review moot and unnecessary for further discussion.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois, for use, etc., v. Silas Brumback et al." took place in 1887 in Milford, Iroquois County, Illinois. The key individuals involved are the plaintiff, Matilda J. Baird, and the defendants Silas Brumback and Morgan Hix, along with others. The case arose from a liquor bond that the defendants executed, permitting them to sell intoxicating liquors. The plaintiff alleged that the defendants sold liquor to her husband, William Bail'd, which led him to become a habitual drunkard. On April 24, 1882, while intoxicated from alcohol supplied by the defendants, Bail'd wandered onto the tracks of the Chicago & Eastern Illinois Railroad and was struck and killed by a train. Matilda J. Baird claimed damages of $3,000 for loss of support due to her husband's death, which she attributed to the defendants' actions. The initial trial resulted in a verdict for the defendants, and an appeal was subsequently made, citing errors in the trial's instructions and evidence handling.	Matilda J. Baird claimed that the defendants' sale of intoxicating liquor to her husband led to his habitual drunkenness and subsequent death after being hit by a train. She sought to hold the defendants liable under the liquor bond, arguing that their actions were the direct cause of her husband's demise, and requested damages of $3,000 for the financial support she lost as a result.	The defendants, Silas Brumback and Morgan Hix, maintained a plea of "nil debit," denying any liability. They argued that the jury instructions provided during the trial were misleading and errant. The defendants contended that Baird’s death was not solely due to their actions but was also related to the intoxicated state leading to the train incident. They sought to uphold the verdict rendered by the lower court.

The case, "The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. Henry Booth v. Charles E. Lippincott, Auditor," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1872. It centered around a dispute regarding the salary of circuit judges elected under the new Illinois constitution of 1870. The key individuals involved were Henry Booth, the relator and a newly elected circuit judge in Cook County, and Charles E. Lippincott, the Auditor of Public Accounts. Booth claimed he was entitled to a judicial salary of $3,000 per annum, as stipulated in the new constitution, while Lippincott refused to issue his warrant for more than $1,000 per annum, the amount determined by the previous constitution of 1848. The case raised questions about the effective date of salary provisions in the new constitution and whether Booth's salary should be paid directly by the state treasury or if other compensatory provisions applied.	The plaintiff, Henry Booth, argued that under the new Illinois constitution, specifically section 25 of article 6, circuit judges were entitled to salaries of $3,000 annually. He claimed that Lippincott's refusal to authorize payment beyond $1,000 was incorrect and sought a court order (mandamus) to compel the auditor to issue a payment warrant for the full amount he believed he was owed.	The defendant, Charles E. Lippincott, maintained that according to section 21 of the schedule of the new constitution, the judges of Cook County were to receive a salary based on the established law at the time of the new constitution's adoption, which limited their pay to $1,000 per annum. He argued that the two constitutional provisions did not conflict, and therefore, the salary of $3,000 could not be claimed until the legislature provided a new rate for the county's compensation.

The case "Andrew T. Thompson et al. v. The Board of Trustees of Township Sixteen North, Range Three West of the Third Principal Meridian" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1863. The case arose in Sangamon County, Illinois, involving Andrew T. Thompson, the township treasurer, and his sureties. They were defendants in an action of debt initiated by the Board of Trustees regarding a bond for $4,000. It was admitted that Thompson had $608.85 in school funds on April 7, 1860, which were stolen from an iron safe in his store in Mechanicksburgh. Thompson claimed he acted with due care in securing the funds, which were allegedly safe before the theft. The main legal question was whether Thompson and his sureties were liable for the stolen funds, given they asserted their obligation was only to exercise ordinary care. The court had to interpret the statutory requirements for a township treasurer regarding the safekeeping of public funds and the implications of the executed bond.	The plaintiffs, the Board of Trustees, claimed that Thompson and the sureties were liable on the bond for failing to safely keep the school funds entrusted to them. They argued that the treasurer's duties included an absolute obligation to safeguard the funds, and the contract's language supported this requirement. The plaintiffs maintained that the treasurer’s negligence or inability to avoid the theft did not absolve him of responsibility, as he was an insurer of the public funds.	The key defense from Thompson and his sureties focused on the argument that their obligation under the bond was limited to exercising reasonable care rather than an absolute duty to keep funds safe. They contended that they should not be held liable for an unforeseen theft that occurred despite their reasonable efforts to secure the funds. They sought the court's ruling to dismiss the claim against them based on this interpretation of their liabilities under the bond.

In June 1870, Philo Morehouse contracted W. H. H. Miller to construct a double dwelling-house for $20,900 in Cook County, Illinois. The contract stipulated that payment would be made as work progressed based on the architect's certification, with 15% withheld until completion as security for the owner. The construction drew materials from sub-contractors, specifically Thomas Moulding, Harlan for bricks amounting to $1,442, and Kelly, Wood & Co. for lumber costing $555.85. These sub-contractors sought to establish a mechanic's lien for the amounts owed after they provided written notice of their claims. As disputes arose regarding payments made after notice was served, the case was consolidated in court for resolution. The completion cost of the building ultimately exceeded $30,000, predominantly due to additional work requested by Morehouse.	The plaintiffs, Moulding and Harlan, along with Kelly, Wood & Co., claimed that they were owed for materials supplied for Morehouse's construction project and sought to enforce a mechanic's lien under the Illinois statute after notifying Morehouse of their claims. They argued that payments made by Morehouse to Miller post-notification disregarded their legal rights, and they requested their proportionate share of the owed payments.	Morehouse contended that he had the right to decide how to allocate the remaining payments owed to Miller and that he could use these funds to pay other workers or suppliers who would help complete the project. He argued that the payments made to Miller were justified and that his actions did not infringe on the rights of the sub-contractors.

The case, "The County of Lawrence v. Ed. Schmaulhausen et al.," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 8, 1887. It arose from an election held on November 2, 1886, in Lawrence County, Illinois, where residents voted on whether to issue $50,000 in bonds to construct a new courthouse. After the election, a canvassing board mistakenly counted votes from the town of Petty, which did not submit the required poll returns or certificates as mandated by state election laws. The board counted 17 votes in favor and 307 votes against the bond issue from Petty. As a result, the canvassing board declared that there was a majority against the bond issuance, despite the county-wide results showing a majority in favor when only valid returns were considered. Electors from the county contested this decision, arguing that the board acted improperly by including the unverified votes from Petty. The case hinged on whether the circuit court could amend the results of the canvass instead of just reviewing the board's decision.	The plaintiff, represented by a group of electors, contended that the canvassing board unlawfully included votes from the town of Petty due to the absence of mandatory certification and proper documentation. They argued that this counting resulted in a false declaration of vote outcomes and requested the court to exclude these invalid votes from the total count, correct the abstract of votes, and declare the correct result of the election showing a valid majority in favor of issuing the bonds.	The defendants, including the county clerk and justices of the peace, acknowledged the election took place and that returns were made, but disputed the plaintiffs' claims about the validity of the returns from Petty. They contended that valid returns were indeed submitted from Petty and that any irregularities in the documentation were minor and did not invalidate the election results. The defendant's position was that the canvassing board acted within its authority and discovered that the overall majority was against the bond issuance.

On April 23, 1883, the City Council of Springfield passed an ordinance to improve certain streets by paving them. The costs would be covered by special taxation on property owners whose land abutted the streets, based on the property frontage. The Council appointed three commissioners to estimate the improvement costs, which they reported on May 7, 1883. A petition was filed in the county court, initiating an assessment process for the improvement costs, which the court confirmed after hearing objections from property owners. The plaintiffs, led by Zimri A. Enos, appealed the confirmation, raising concerns about the legality of the tax assessments on the grounds that the process failed to comply with statutory requirements under the Illinois Revised Statutes. The case ultimately reached the Illinois Supreme Court, which reviewed numerous objections about the tax's validity, including the process of special taxation, the nature of local improvements, and the overall assessment methodology.	The plaintiffs argued that the special tax levied on their properties was illegal because it did not conform to the procedural requirements stipulated by law regarding special assessments. They claimed issues with how the assessment was conducted, specifically contesting the basis for tax calculations and arguing that the city had excessive discretion in determining how costs could be assigned among property owners.	The City of Springfield's defense maintained that the ordinance for the street improvements was valid and that the assessment process followed legal guidelines. They argued that special taxation based on property frontage was an accepted practice and within the city's authority. The city contended that objections raised by the plaintiffs were either improperly filed or without merit, thus justifying the confirmed assessment.

The case "The Burlington Lumber Company v. Fred Willetts, Collector" was decided on November 13, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The Burlington Lumber Company, a corporation organized in Iowa, operated a lumber manufacturing business, purchasing logs from Wisconsin and Minnesota, transporting them via the Mississippi River to Burlington, Iowa. In 1884, the company rafted logs near the Chippewa River and left some in New Boston harbor, Illinois, for safekeeping until they were needed for milling. The company leased shore privileges for this storage and employed E. L. Willits to oversee the logs. When the logs were assessed for taxes in 1885 by Mercer County, the Burlington Lumber Company sought to enjoin the tax collection, claiming the logs were in transit and not subject to taxation under state law. The case revolves around whether the logs were in transit or had acquired a taxable situs as they were stored at New Boston for an indefinite period, raising significant legal questions about property taxation in transit and the implications of the company’s activities within the state.	The Burlington Lumber Company contended that the logs should not be taxed because they were in transit between states and thus exempt under the state’s revenue laws. They argued that the logs were stored at New Boston for safekeeping during winter and did not constitute a taxable location under state jurisdiction, insisting that the collection of taxes on these logs was unlawful.	Fred Willetts, the collector, argued that the logs were not in transit at the time of assessment and that they were in a leased location managed by the company’s employee for an extended period, indicating that the property had a taxable situs. He maintained that the logs were sufficiently located in New Boston for taxation purposes, as the company had engaged in business operations there by leasing land and employing individuals to supervise the logs.

The case "Franklin MacVeagh et al. v. Bailey & Hanford" was decided on March 10, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The parties involved included the plaintiffs, Franklin MacVeagh & Co., a Chicago-based company, and the defendants, Bailey & Hanford, who were indebted to the plaintiffs and had executed judgment notes. The debt amounted to $1,084.84, with the final note maturing on November 17, 1886. Following a judgment entered by confession on November 20, 1886, a deputy sheriff named Leonard Kennedy was tasked to levy execution against the defendants. However, the defendants argued against levying on their personal goods, insisting that there was sufficient real estate available to satisfy the debt. Despite this, Kennedy proceeded with the levy on the stock of goods in their store, leading to the closure of the establishment. The levy was implemented in haste, which sparked legal disputes regarding the refusal to levy on the identified real estate owned by the defendants. Subsequent legal proceedings confirmed the plaintiffs' intent to hold the defendants accountable for damages incurred due to this improper levy.	Franklin MacVeagh & Co. claimed that the defendants, Bailey & Hanford, were liable for damages resulting from the deputy sheriff's refusal to levy on their real estate instead of their personal goods. They argued that the hasty action of seizing inventory led to the closure of their store, damaging their business and credit. The plaintiffs requested compensation for physical damages to the goods and the financial impact of losing business during the store's closure.	The defendants contended that they were not liable for damages as the execution was conducted following the instructions given to the deputy sheriff. They maintained that any failure to properly notify the plaintiffs of the levy was not grounds for liability since there was no malicious intent. Moreover, they argued that the plaintiffs should have provided a legal description of the real estate for the sheriff to levy upon, and that their responsibility in this matter was not met.

Henry M. Stow filed a lawsuit against his tenant, Edgar M. Gregory, in December 1846, in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose when Stow issued a distress warrant against Gregory for unpaid rent, which was levied upon Gregory's property. A trial conducted by a justice of the peace found that Gregory had a set-off greater than the alleged amount due, resulting in a jury verdict in favor of him for $31. Stow appealed this judgment to the Circuit Court. During the Circuit Court trial, a key point of contention was the exclusion of a witness, Wesencroft, who served the distress warrant and was deemed incompetent by the court. The jury ultimately returned a verdict for Gregory, increasing the awarded amount to $75. Following this, Stow moved for a new trial, which the court denied.	Stow argued that the trial court erred by excluding Wesencroft from testifying as he was a necessary witness to establish the amount of rent due. Stow contended that the exclusion of this relevant testimony compromised the fairness of the trial and requested that the judgment be reversed and a new trial granted to correctly establish the owed rent.	Gregory claimed that the testimony of Wesencroft was not relevant and that the court acted correctly in declaring him incompetent as a witness. He maintained that he had already effectively proven a set-off that outweighed any claims for rent and that the jury's verdict in his favor was justified. Gregory requested the court uphold the jury's decision and deny Stow's appeal for a new trial.

The case revolves around Jonathan Richards and others (plaintiffs) who filed an action of assumpsit against the Michigan Southern and Northern Indiana Railroad Company (defendant) in the Illinois Supreme Court. The events took place in August 1856, involving the shipment of a box of goods from Toledo, Ohio to Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiffs delivered the box of goods, valued at $185, to the defendant for transport. Upon reaching Chicago on the evening of August 12, 1856, the box was unloaded into the defendant's warehouse at noon on August 13. A notice regarding the arrival of the box was posted to the plaintiffs but was only received by them at 10 A.M. on August 14. Later that same evening, a fire broke out near the warehouse, which engulfed the building and ultimately destroyed the goods. The fire was determined not to be caused by any negligence on the part of the defendant. The case was tried without a jury, leading to a judgment in favor of the defendant, which the plaintiffs subsequently appealed.	The plaintiffs' claims asserted that the defendant, as a common carrier, failed to uphold its duty to safely transport and deliver the box of goods to them in Chicago. They argued that the defendant's notice did not absolve it of liability, and they sought compensation for the value of the goods lost in the fire, claiming that the defendant retained responsibility until they were officially notified and given the opportunity to retrieve their property.	The defendant contended that its liability as a common carrier ended once the goods were safely unloaded into its warehouse. They argued that the notice provided to the plaintiffs was adequate, and they had no legal obligation to maintain the goods any longer than the notice permitted. The defendant further asserted that there was no negligence involved in the handling of the goods or the subsequent fire, thus negating any liability for the loss.

Edward Roby filed a case against The City of Chicago in September 1868, stemming from a dispute regarding property taxes assessed on certain lots. Roby had purchased fractions of lots at city tax sales in 1865 and 1866 and sought to have these fractions individually listed and assessed for the payment of taxes. However, the City refused Roby's request, maintaining that the purchaser at a tax sale does not become the owner until the redemption period ends and a deed is obtained. Roby argued that because the city had acknowledged these fractions as distinct and had accepted payment from him, he should be allowed to list and pay taxes on them separately. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, presided over by Justice Lawbence, which considered the fairness of the city's refusal to allow Roby to list these portions individually for tax purposes.	Edward Roby's main argument was that he should be allowed to have the fractions of the lots he purchased at tax sales listed and assessed separately for tax purposes. He claimed that it was unjust for the City of Chicago to sell him these fractions and then refuse to acknowledge his right to pay taxes on them individually. Roby sought the court's intervention to ensure that he could protect his interest in these properties by enabling the separate assessment and listing of the purchased lots.	The City of Chicago contended that Roby, as a purchaser at a tax sale, only had a lien on the properties until the redemption period was over and a deed was issued. Hence, they argued that he had no right to request the separate assessment of the fractions he bought. The city maintained that allowing such a request would undermine the legal framework governing tax sales and assessments.

In 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, the plaintiffs, Leopold Schlesinger and David Mayer, filed an action against James B. Keifer and his wife. The case revolved around a claim under Section 15 of Chapter 68 of the Illinois Revised Statutes, which pertains to liability for family expenses. The plaintiffs alleged that they provided ladies’ and children’s apparel to the defendants, claiming the goods were purchased as family expenses. However, the key issue in the case was whether the defendants constituted a family at the time of the purchase. Evidence indicated that the defendants had not lived together for several months before the purchases occurred, and the plaintiffs were unaware of their separation. The court found that, without a family unit existing, the husband was not liable for the expenses incurred through his wife's purchases. The judgment examined the historical context of the law, concluding that family expenses could only be charged if a family, in fact, existed.	The plaintiffs, Schlesinger and Mayer, argued that they were entitled to recover the costs of the apparel sold to Mrs. Keifer under the premise of family expenses. They invoked Section 15 of Chapter 68, asserting that the expenses were the legal responsibility of both husband and wife, and consequently, Mr. Keifer should be jointly liable for the debts incurred by his wife, regardless of their living situation.	James B. Keifer's defense hinged on the argument that he could not be held liable for the purchases because he and his wife were not living together as a family at the time the goods were bought. The absence of a family unit meant that no liability existed under the relevant statute for family expenses, and thus the plaintiffs' claims were invalid.
