The defense contended that the goods were not acquired for family use, as evidenced by the couple's separation.

In the case of M. Millard v. County of Richland, the proceedings dated back to February 3, 1877, when M. Millard entered into a contractual agreement with the County of Richland in Illinois. The contract mandated Millard to serve as legal counsel for the county in defense of lawsuits aimed at forcing the county to issue bonds to the Grayville and Mattoon Railroad Company. In return, Millard was to receive a retainer fee of $500 and a contingent fee of seven and a half percent of the amount of bonds, contingent upon the county not being required to issue them. A mandamus suit was ongoing at the time of the contract. In February 1877, the court issued a judgment against the county, compelling them to issue the bonds. Subsequently, on February 28, 1877, the county board of supervisors decided not to appeal this decision, contrary to Millard's recommendations. Instead, the board opted to allow the issuance of the bonds, effectively preventing Millard from fulfilling his contractual obligations. The case was initially determined in the circuit court, which ruled in favor of the defendant, leading to the appeal in question.	Millard asserted that the county's failure to appeal the mandamus ruling obstructed him from carrying out his responsibilities as outlined in their contract. He argued that he was fully prepared to perform his duties and claimed the right to the contingent fee because his inability to act was due solely to the county board's decision not to appeal. Millard sought compensation based on the contention that he was entitled to his fee regardless of the outcome, mirroring the scenario had he fulfilled his contractual obligations.	The County of Richland contended that Millard was not entitled to recover any fees because he failed to adequately fulfill the contract terms, claiming he did not prevent the issuance of the bonds. They argued the contract was unenforceable as it contravened public policy. Additionally, the county asserted that Millard had abandoned his contractual duties, as they had opted not to pursue an appeal based on a collective resolution rather than his actions.

In the case of Isaac M. Brown v. J. C. Duncan, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 31, 1890, the dispute arose over the possession of certain lands located in Sangamon County, Illinois. The case originated in a partition proceeding from February 1885, where costs were assessed and allocated among the involved parties, including Isaac M. Brown. A writ of execution was subsequently issued to enforce the payment of these costs. After this execution was carried out, the property was sold in a sheriff's sale, and the ownership transferred to John E. Everhart, who later conveyed the property to Brown. The case escalated when Duncan, the defendant, challenged Brown’s claim to the land based on the legitimacy of the execution process. The appellate court considered objections regarding the execution's validity, including whether proper separations were made for individual liabilities, and whether the execution sufficiently identified the underlying judgment.	Isaac M. Brown, the plaintiff, argued that he obtained a legitimate title to the lands in question through a sheriff's sale authorized by the execution issued for costs in the partition proceeding. He maintained that the previous decree allowed for such execution and that the subsequent purchase by Everhart and conveyance to him entered him as a rightful owner.	J. C. Duncan, the defendant, contended that the execution was void for several reasons: it did not specify the amount due from each party, it improperly combined liabilities, and it failed to follow procedural requisites, such as indicating the judgment upon which it was based. Duncan argued that these failings invalidated the sale of the property and did not confer legitimate title to Brown.

In 1874, the case of Mary A. Riggin et al. v. James Love et al. was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a property dispute in Madison County, Illinois. The dispute revolved around the interpretation of a deed concerning real estate originally granted to Eliza McGilton for her lifetime, with its subsequent ownership transitioning to her husband, Andrew McGilton, upon her death. Andrew died intestate before Eliza, and she later passed away, leaving behind only one heir, Mary A. Riggin, the appellant. The appellees argued that, based on a life estate granted to Eliza McGilton and subsequent provisions in the deed regarding inheritance, the interest belonged to them as they claimed an undivided one-half interest. Riggin contended that the deed conveyed a fee simple estate to Eliza, entitling her to the entire property. The legal discussions centered on the interpretation of the habendum clause and the nature of the estate conveyed in the deed, with both sides interpreting the terms of the deed differently to assert their claims.	The plaintiffs, represented by Mary A. Riggin, argued that the deed from Erastus and Julia A. Wheeler to Eliza McGilton granted her a fee simple estate in the property. They maintained that the granting clause in the deed did not limit Eliza’s interest and that the habendum clause should not contradict the original grant. Riggin requested that the court recognize her entitlement to the entire property following her mother Eliza's death, disputing the interpretation that only a life estate was conveyed.	The defendants, represented by James Love and others, contended that the deed granted Eliza McGilton only a life estate with a remainder interest going to her husband, Andrew McGilton, and subsequently to his heirs. They argued that since Andrew died before Eliza, the property should rightfully pass to them, as they asserted an undivided one-half interest based on the provisions outlined in the deed. They sought to uphold the Circuit Court’s ruling that recognized their claim over the property.

The case "Susannah Forquer et al. v. George Forquer et al." took place in the St. Clair Circuit Court in Illinois during March 1856, after the death of William Forquer on October 8, 1855. William had devised all his estate to his widow, Susannah Forquer, for her lifetime, while also designating certain legacies for his twelve children. Susannah executed a deed on October 31, 1855, conveying 92½ acres of property to her children in joint tenancy, retaining a clause regarding rent from a tenant, C. Casselbury. The complaint arose from allegations of errors in the deed's descriptions and sought correction and partition of the land or the sale of the property under the Circuit Court’s direction. A decree was issued for an absolute sale without acknowledging the existing lease, prompting Susannah to appeal, claiming this was in error as it did not honor her reserved rights.	Susannah Forquer, the plaintiff, argued that the decree ordering the absolute sale of the property was erroneous. She intended the sale to be subject to the existing lease held by C. Casselbury, which generated rental income that she claimed. The correction of the deed's descriptions and the proper partition of the land were central to her requests, emphasizing that her rights to rent should be explicitly reserved in any sale proceedings.	The defendants, George Forquer and others, contended that the original decree was valid and did not require amendments. They argued that since Susannah did not formally contest the sale order through her appearance or direct objections, the court was justified in issuing the absolute sale decree. They maintained that the sale should stand as executed without consideration for Susannah’s claimed reservations of rent.

The case "Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company v. Jacob Zeigler" was decided on October 1, 1883, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It arose in DeWitt County, Illinois, involving the plaintiff, Jacob Zeigler, and the defendant, Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company. Zeigler, an adjoining landowner, sought to recover double the value of a fence he constructed to protect his land from the railroad, following the company's alleged failure to build the required fence after the line opened to use. This claim was based on a statute that mandated railroad companies to construct fences within a specific timeframe and allowed landowners to build such fences themselves if the company failed or refused to do so, with penalties for non-compliance. The litigation centered on whether Zeigler had built the fence in compliance with the law—specifically, on the appropriate side of the right of way.	Jacob Zeigler claimed that the Wabash Railway failed to construct the necessary fences along its right of way, legally entitling him to build the fence himself and to seek double compensation from the railroad for its value. He asserted that his actions were compliant with the statutory requirements allowing for such recovery and that the railroad neglected its duty, which justified his claim for damages.	The Wabash Railway contended that the fence constructed by Zeigler was built two feet inside the right of way, which they argued violated statutory requirements. They maintained that the law stipulates the fence should be built on the side of the railroad, not encroaching into the right of way. Thus, they argued that Zeigler did not meet the legal criteria for recovering the double value of the fence, stating that such a penalty could not be recovered due to his improper building position.

In 1880, Daniel Pierce, a resident of Courtland in DeKalb County, Illinois, was the target of tax collection efforts by Alexander C. Sivwright, the collector for the town of Sycamore. Pierce had properly assessed and paid taxes on his personal property, including credits, to the collector of Courtland where he resided. Despite not engaging in business as a banker, broker, or stock jobber in Sycamore at any time during 1880, the board of review in Sycamore mistakenly extended a tax assessment against him for credits unrelated to his business, totaling $61,000, which led to a warrant for collection issued to Sivwright. To prevent the unlawful tax collection, Pierce filed a bill in the De Kalb Circuit Court seeking an injunction against Sivwright’s actions, resulting in a temporary and subsequently a perpetual injunction being granted in his favor.	Daniel Pierce contended that the town of Sycamore had no legal authority to assess personal property taxes against him since he was a permanent resident of Courtland and had already paid taxes there. He argued that the tax imposed by Sycamore was illegal and sought an injunction to prevent the collection of the erroneously assessed tax, emphasizing that he had never been assessed individually for personal property in Sycamore during 1880.	Alexander C. Sivwright, the collector, argued that the assessment made by the board of review was valid and that it should not be annulled simply based on Pierce's residency status. He contended that issues surrounding the assessment's legitimacy could not solely be addressed through equitable relief without proving special circumstances, implying that the collection process was rightly followed according to the law.

In April 1862, in LaSalle County, Illinois, Edward Sweeney was charged with the offense of obstructing a public road. The case arose when Sweeney was found guilty of continuing to obstruct a highway by keeping a fence that rendered the road inconvenient and dangerous to pass. The indictment included three counts against him, alleging various aspects of the obstruction. Sweeney's defense involved a motion to quash the indictment, which was denied by the trial court, leading to his convictions by a jury. However, legal arguments were presented regarding the nature of the offense and the validity of the indictment, particularly whether an indictment for continuing an obstruction could be sustained without evidence that Sweeney had been ordered to remove the obstruction before his prosecution.	Sweeney's main argument was centered on the legality of the indictment against him for continuing to obstruct a public road without having received a prior order to remove the obstruction. He contended that the law required such notice before any indictment could be valid and that the indictment was, therefore, fatally defective as it did not allege any order for removal.	The prosecution, representing "The People," maintained that Sweeney was guilty of the offense as charged. They argued that there was adequate basis for the indictment and that the jury's verdict should stand. However, they faced challenges regarding the procedural aspects of the indictment, particularly in showing that proper legal procedures were followed in defining the offense.

William Jones v. Barney Nellis was a legal case heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1866. The case revolved around a seven-thirty government bond worth $500 that Jones claimed was stolen from his safe on January 5, 1866. The bond was stolen by an individual named Joslyn, who was later convicted for larceny. Joslyn sold the stolen bond to Barney Nellis, the defendant, for the full value, and Nellis purchased it in good faith without knowledge that it had been stolen. The bond, being payable to bearer, meant that its title passed merely by delivery, similar to currency. After Jones attempted to reclaim the bond post-theft, Nellis refused to return it, leading to Jones filing an action of trover to recover its value. The trial court found in favor of Nellis, prompting Jones to appeal the decision.	Jones claimed that he was the rightful owner of the $500 bond, asserting that the theft of the bond by Joslyn entitled him to recover its value. He argued that despite Nellis' good faith purchase, the bond was still stolen property and should be returned to him. Jones's legal request included the recovery of the bond's value through the action of trover, emphasizing the principle that theft does not transfer ownership.	Nellis defended himself by stating that he was a bona fide purchaser who acquired the bond without any knowledge of it being stolen. He argued that under common law, the holder of negotiable instruments obtains a perfect title if they acquire it in good faith and in the usual course of trade. Nellis contended that his rights to retain the bond could not be overridden by Jones’s claim to ownership, as the law allows for innocent purchasers to keep property acquired under such circumstances.

The case of John C. Gore v. Chauncey Smith took place in Illinois, with the declaration filed on October 1, 1827. The action revolved around a debt related to a penal bond. The court proceedings were marked by irregularities, particularly regarding a judgment entered by default due to the defendant's absence. The record indicated that the defendant, Chauncey Smith, was called three times and did not appear. However, the court found that proper protocol had not been followed, as the declaration had not been filed 10 days prior to the term of the court, a requirement stated under the practice act. This led to complications regarding the defendant's ability to make a defense, suggesting that the entries in the record might have resulted from a clerical error. Ultimately, the case was referred back to the Franklin Circuit Court for further action.	The plaintiff, John C. Gore, claimed a debt against the defendant, asserting the validity of the penal bond. Gore sought a judgment to be affirmed against Smith based on the default judgment that had initially been entered.	The defendant, Chauncey Smith, contested the judgment by default, arguing that there had been a procedural error in entering the judgment without complying with established timelines for filing and service of the declaration. Smith maintained that he had not waived his right to contest the entry of default and therefore should be entitled to present a defense.

In January 1885, the case of Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Ry. Co. v. Rollin P. Blanchard was filed in Cook County, Illinois. The incident leading to the case involved the death of John W. Biordan, a 16-year-old worker employed by the Chicago and Northwestern Railroad Company. On the day of the accident, Biordan was walking home for dinner. He left the freight house where he worked and traversed multiple railway tracks, ultimately walking along the main track of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad. He was struck and killed by a westbound engine while on the track, approximately two feet east of Halsted Street. The day was windy, and though he was familiar with the area, he failed to look or listen for approaching trains. His actions and the circumstances were heavily scrutinized during the trial, particularly regarding his awareness of the dangers present on the railway tracks. The court noted that determinations had to be made about whether Biordan had exercised ordinary care and whether he had a right to be on the tracks where he was killed.	The plaintiff, Rollin P. Blanchard, the administrator of Biordan's estate, claimed that his death resulted from the negligence of the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company. He argued that the company failed to ensure proper safety measures, such as sounding bells or whistles, to alert individuals near the tracks. Blanchard sought damages for the wrongful death of Biordan, alleging that the defendant's employees acted negligently in their operations.	The defendant, Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company, contended that Biordan was trespassing on the railway track and was therefore required to exercise a heightened degree of care for his safety. The company claimed that their employees had acted prudently, maintaining that the engine was traveling at a slow speed of about five miles per hour and that the bell was ringing while the engine was in motion. Testimonies suggested they were unaware of Biordan's presence on the tracks. The defendant requested that the case be dismissed, asserting that the evidence did not support the plaintiff's claims of negligence.

In January 1868, a legal case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court involving Pulaski Scovil as the plaintiff and James P. Kelsey as the defendant. The case originated in Mason County, Illinois. Kelsey had purchased a piece of land at a tax sale and later sold it to a married woman, Mrs. Connell, without her husband’s consent. Mrs. Connell subsequently conveyed the property to Scovil. After the land was redeemed, Kelsey received the redemption money from the county clerk but refused to pay it to Scovil. Kelsey argued that the right to the redemption money was tied to the certificate of purchase, which he believed could only be transferred through its assignment, asserting that his deed only conveyed a contingent interest. The court examined whether the conveyances made by Kelsey and Mrs. Connell were valid and led to a conclusion about the right to the redemption money.	The plaintiff, Pulaski Scovil, claimed that he had acquired rights to the redemption money through the conveyance from Mrs. Connell. He argued that Kelsey, as the seller, was obligated to pay this money to him, asserting that a valid transfer of interest in the land occurred through the deed given by Mrs. Connell, despite the lack of her husband's signature.	The defendant, James P. Kelsey, contended that the redemption money right was linked to the certificate of purchase, which he had not assigned to Scovil. He maintained that the deed from Mrs. Connell only conveyed an equitable interest and did not grant Scovil any rights to the redemption money. Kelsey argued that the transfer was legally insufficient because Mrs. Connell, being married, required her husband to be joined in the deed for it to be valid.

Edmund D. Taylor v. Churchill Coffing and John H. Costing is a legal dispute originating from a partnership agreement among Taylor, Churchill Coffing, and Isaac D. Harmon in December 1847 for commercial operations in Peru, Illinois. The partnership initially involved contributions of $5,000 from Taylor and $10,000 from Coffing, with Harmon later withdrawing from the business in 1850. The remaining partners, Taylor and Coffing, continued operations until April 27, 1852, when they executed agreements regarding their interest in the firm. A significant aspect of the case revolves around the financial transactions, particularly the amount withdrawn by Coffing totaling $18,340, and the subsequent £mortgage that secured this debt. The firm dealt with various properties and debts, complicating their financial relationship. Ultimately, these funds were inadequately accounted for during the partnership’s dissolution, leading to the legal action initiated by Coffing against Taylor in the Circuit Court of La Salle County on April 3, 1856. The issue at hand was the appropriate accounting of the partnership's profits and losses and determination of the amounts owed between the parties.	The plaintiff, Churchill Coffing, asserts that during their partnership, he withdrew substantial sums from the partnership accounts and that due accounting for these transactions remains unresolved. Coffing seeks a settlement reflecting the funds withdrawn during the partnership and asserts that Taylor has not equitably accounted for the rents and profits collected, hence requesting Taylor to reimburse the surplus amounts due upon settlement. Coffing also seeks a formal release of Taylor's interest in the partnership properties.	Edmund D. Taylor acknowledges the partnership and the contributions made by both Coffing and himself but disputes the full extent of Coffing's claims. Taylor argues that he should be credited for his investments and any counterbalances incurred during their dealings, alleging that if an account is to be taken, Coffing should be responsible for debts attributed to him, including a claim for $13,340 which he believes should offset Coffing's demands. Taylor contends that any accounting should consider his contributions and corresponding withdrawals to achieve an equitable settlement.

On December 11, 1886, the Illinois Appellate Court examined a replevin case involving the parties James K. Eagle and George E. Letourneau (appellants) against Moses Rohrheimer (appellee). The dispute originated from a situation in Kankakee County where Sheriff Letourneau had levied personal property, specifically a horse, buggy, cutter, and harness, based on an execution issued from a judgment against James H. Craddock for $1,510 in favor of Eagle. The contention arose as the property in question was claimed to be under the ownership of Craddock, who had previously given Rohrheimer a chattel mortgage to secure a debt that matured in January 1884. Craddock executed a bill of sale to Rohrheimer post-mortgage but continued to use the horse without a significant change in possession. During the trial, the jury initially ruled in favor of Rohrheimer, but issues regarding the ownership of the horse and the lack of evidence supporting a legitimate change of possession were central to the appeal.	The plaintiffs, Eagle and Letourneau, argued that the sheriff's seizure of the property was justified as it belonged to Craddock, with whom there was a valid execution for debts owed. They maintained that the ownership transfer through the chattel mortgage and subsequent bill of sale was not effectively communicated to third parties, as Craddock retained possession and control over the property, indicating no change in ownership.	Rohrheimer contended that he had rightful ownership of the property based on the chattel mortgage agreement and the executed bill of sale. He claimed that despite Craddock's continued possession, the legal ownership had already transferred to him with the valid sale, and any use by Craddock constituted a loan rather than a claim of ownership. Rohrheimer requested the court to uphold the jury's verdict in his favor, asserting he had the legal right to the property.

In this legal case, "The Chicago and North Western R R. Company v. Charles L. Williams," which took place in April 1867 in Illinois, the central issue involved a shipment of iron. Charles L. Williams (the plaintiff) filed a lawsuit against The Chicago and North Western Railroad Company (the defendant), claiming that 2,269 pounds of iron he delivered to them for transportation from Chicago to Harvard was lost while in their possession. According to the testimony, the iron was transferred to the defendant's cars from the Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne and Chicago Railroad Company, and it was unaccounted for when checked out at the defendant's depot. The case was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court, and substantial evidence was presented from employees of both the plaintiff and the defendant concerning the handling and delivery of the iron. The court sought to determine whether sufficient evidence supported the jury’s verdict against the claims made by the defendant regarding their responsibility for the loss.	The plaintiff, Charles L. Williams, argued that he delivered iron to The Chicago and North Western Railroad Company for transport and that the company was responsible for its loss. He requested compensation for the value of the lost iron, contending that the evidence clearly demonstrated that the iron was transferred to the defendant's custody and subsequently went missing.	The defendant, The Chicago and North Western Railroad Company, contended that the iron was never properly placed in their cars for transport, asserting that there was no record of the iron being received into their possession. They argued that the iron could have been stolen or misplaced after it was supposedly placed on their cars, thereby denying liability for the loss.

Alvah D. Drew v. Leonard W. Beall is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871. The case stems from a property exchange that involved a fraudulent transaction. Beall, the plaintiff, owned a house and lot in Dixon, Illinois, which he sold to Drew, the defendant, in exchange for eighty acres of land in Mason County, Missouri, along with $800. Beall alleged that Drew made fraudulent representations about the quality and value of the Missouri land during the transaction. The trial took place in the Circuit Court of Lee County under Judge William W. Heaton. The plaintiff's claims were based on the assertion that the property exchanged did not match the representations made by the defendant regarding its condition and value.	Beall claimed that Drew engaged in deceit and fraud regarding the Missouri land, which led to his agreement to sell his property for less than its actual value. He sought damages for the alleged fraudulent misrepresentation that induced him to enter into the exchange.	Drew’s defense rested on challenging the admissibility of certain evidence and the handling of the trial court's instructions, contending that the plaintiff did not adequately prove the alleged fraud. He also argued that the court improperly refused to allow cross-examination regarding certain testimony and rejected evidence that he believed would demonstrate the actual value of the house and lot that Beall exchanged.

The case 'Samuel Lair v. Alfred S. Mayfield' was heard in January 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from Macoupin County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Samuel Lair, initiated an action of ejectment against the defendant, Alfred S. Mayfield, claiming ownership of a property based on a deed executed in 1831 by the county commissioners. This deed was issued to a group of individuals, including Lair, who were described as the 'Trustees of the Carlinville School Union', intended for the benefit of the inhabitants of Carlinville and its vicinity. Lair's argument stemmed from being the sole surviving grantee of the deed. The defendant, Mayfield, countered Lair's claims by presenting evidence of color of title and demonstrating that he had consistently paid taxes on the disputed lot from 1857 to 1860 while the property remained vacant. The conflict arose over the assertion that the land was designated as school property, which the plaintiff argued exempted it from taxation and the statute of limitations. The court ultimately noted the insufficiency of evidence to support the claim that the property was indeed school land, affirming that additional record details were lacking to establish this claim.	Samuel Lair claimed ownership of the lot based on the 1831 deed, asserting that as the sole surviving trustee of the Carlinville School Union, he had rightful title to the property. He contended that the land was school property and thereby not subject to taxation. Thus, he argued that the statute of limitations should not apply, seeking a legal affirmation of his ownership.	Alfred S. Mayfield's defense hinged on proving color of title and the payment of property taxes for several years, thereby establishing a form of ownership. He argued that the land was indeed vacant and unoccupied, countering Lair’s claims by suggesting that the evidence presented was inadequate to prove that the property should be considered as exempt school land. Mayfield requested that the court recognize his evidence as sufficient to uphold his claim to the property.

John J. Heath filed a bill in equity against George W. Hyde in the Circuit Court of Will County, Illinois, in September 1874, seeking to remove a purported cloud from his title to a lot in Joliet. Heath claimed to be the owner and in possession of the lot, arguing that Hyde had acquired a tax deed on August 14, 1867, through an invalid tax sale, which clouded Heath's title. Heath asserted that there had never been a valid judgment against the lot prior to the sale, nor the required legal processes followed at the time of the transaction. Hyde, in his defense, denied Heath's ownership of the premises and maintained that the tax deed was valid and thus did not represent a cloud on the title. Neither party provided evidence regarding the validity of the title or the tax deed, leading the court to rely solely on the allegations in Heath's bill and Hyde's denial. Ultimately, the court highlighted that while Heath made assertions against the validity of the tax title, the burden of proof rested with him to validate his claims.	John J. Heath, the plaintiff, argued that he was the rightful owner of the lot in question and that a tax deed held by George W. Hyde was obtained through an invalid sale, constituting a cloud on his title. Heath claimed there were no valid legal proceedings against the property prior to the supposed tax sale and that the deed had no legal standing. He requested the court to acknowledge this lack of validity and remove the cloud from his title.	George W. Hyde, the defendant, responded by denying Heath's ownership claims and asserting that the tax deed was both regular and valid. Hyde claimed that the deed did not represent a cloud on Heath's title and maintained that Heath had not provided sufficient proof to substantiate his allegations against the validity of the tax title.

During the year 1867, in Iroquois County, Illinois, a legal case arose involving George S. Wright and others (the plaintiffs) against Achsah Dunning (the defendant). The case was initiated when Achsah Dunning, as the widow of Eben Dunning, sought recovery and assignment of her homestead rights to certain lands owned by her late husband, asserting that the property had been her home at the time of his death. While the ownership and occupancy of the land were not contested, the plaintiffs contended that Achsah had no homestead rights due to prior court findings which had established her dower rights. A partition proceeding was conducted in which Achsah was a party, during which the court initially confirmed her entitlement to dower but later determined that partition could not be made. Consequently, a yearly allowance was awarded to Achsah in lieu of dower. Following the sale of the land, Achsah vacated the premises and did not claim her homestead rights until after her departure, which became a point of contention in the court proceedings.	The plaintiffs argued that Achsah Dunning was barred from claiming homestead rights due to the previous Circuit Court decree that established her dower rights. They asserted that she had abandoned her claim to the homestead prior to the filing of the current suit, as evidenced by her actions and declarations that she did not intend to return to the property after it was sold. The plaintiffs requested that the court recognize the finality of the previous judgment regarding her dower and deny her claim to any homestead rights.	Achsah Dunning contended that her rights to a homestead were not adequately addressed during the prior partition proceedings since she was never given the opportunity to assert them. She argued that her status as the widow of Eben Dunning entitled her to claim homestead rights despite the previous findings regarding her dower. Achsah sought to recover her homestead rights from the plaintiffs, believing that her claims were valid regardless of the earlier court rulings.

In the case of James W. Burt v. Polly Quisenberry et al., the events unfolded in the late 19th century, specifically when the deeds pertinent to the case were executed on July 9, 1881. The lawsuit arose in Illinois, concerning the estate of William Burt, who died on July 21, 1883, at the age of 83. He had executed a deed that conveyed significant portions of his land to his youngest son, James W. Burt. The plaintiffs, Polly Quisenberry and Elizabeth Quisenberry, along with other siblings, contended that their father lacked the mental capacity to execute such deeds due to his advanced age and health issues, including partial blindness and poor hearing. They claimed that James W. Burt exerted undue influence over their father, which led to the execution of the deeds that favored him. The case was pursued in the Logan Circuit Court in Illinois, where the plaintiffs sought to annul the deeds and partition the remaining estate. The court proceedings involved extensive testimony and examination of evidence regarding William Burt's mental state, the nature of his relationships with his children, and the legitimacy of the deeds executed prior to his death.	The plaintiffs claimed that William Burt was incapable of executing the deeds due to a lack of mental capacity, as he was physically and mentally impaired at the time the deeds were signed. They argued that influencing his will, James W. Burt, along with John H. Burt, had manipulated their father into executing the deeds. The plaintiffs sought to have the deeds declared void, contending that they represented a cloud on the title of the property. They requested a partition of the lands among the heirs, alleging that their father acted under undue influence.	The defendants, represented by James W. Burt, disputed the claims made by the plaintiffs. They argued that William Burt was of sound mind and fully understood his actions when he executed the deeds. The defendants contended that the allegations of undue influence were unfounded, asserting that any influence exerted by James W. Burt stemmed from affection and was not wrongful. They claimed that the given properties were valid gifts and that the arrangements made were in accordance with William Burt's intentions, as evidenced by subsequent actions and documentation, including William Burt's will.

In December 1855, the case of Samuel Warner et al. v. Gustavus Manski was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a legal dispute in Morgan County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included Samuel Warner and others as the plaintiffs and Gustavus Manski as the defendant. The case arose during a trial in which the plaintiff examined a witness. During cross-examination, the defendant attempted to discredit the witness by posing a leading question that had not been previously addressed by the plaintiff. The court, however, prohibited the witness from responding to this question. The plaintiffs contended that this refusal constituted an error, as they believed it affected the credibility of the witness and the overall outcome of the case. The case was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court to determine if the lower court's decision was justified.	The plaintiffs argued that the trial court erred by not allowing a key question to be answered during cross-examination of a witness they had examined in chief. They believed that this question was crucial for assessing the witness's credibility and claimed that the court’s refusal impacted the trial's fairness and outcome. They sought the court's intervention to rectify this purported error, ultimately hoping for a favorable judgment.	The defendant, Gustavus Manski, contended that the trial court acted correctly in disallowing the question posed during cross-examination, as this question was possibly irrelevant and impertinent concerning the witness's credibility. The defense maintained that without knowledge of what the question entailed, it was impossible for the Supreme Court to determine whether there was any error in the lower court's decision. Therefore, they sought affirmation of the circuit court's ruling.

In December 1833, during a term of the Illinois Supreme Court, a legal case was brought forth involving John Mitcheltree as the appellant and Matthew Sparks as the appellee. The case originated in Schuyler County, Illinois. During the proceeding, the Court reversed the previous judgment due to a default. However, an issue arose regarding the accuracy of the records; instead of the correct name, "Matthew Sparks," "Nathan Sparks" had been erroneously recorded multiple times throughout the documentation. This mistake was identified when Mitcheltree's attorney, Ford, brought a motion to amend the record to reflect the correct name. The Court examined the records and confirmed the error, ultimately granting the motion to amend the records by replacing "Nathan" with "Matthew" wherever necessary.	John Mitcheltree, the appellant, claimed that there was a clerical error in the court records that required correction. He requested the Court to amend the record to accurately reflect the appellee's name, asserting that the name "Nathan Sparks" should be corrected to "Matthew Sparks" to ensure the proper identity of the parties involved.	Matthew Sparks, as the appellee, did not present a substantive defense against Mitcheltree's motion for correction. The primary issue at hand was the typographical error in the court records rather than a contentious legal argument against the claims made by the plaintiff.

In January 1869, a case arose in Macon County, Illinois, involving Thomas Weaver (the appellant) and John Crocker (the appellee) regarding a dispute over payments relating to a real estate transaction. Michael Weaver purchased a half section of land from a seller named Powers, with an agreement to pay $1,080 secured by a mortgage on the property. Thomas Weaver later bought half of Michael's land and assumed responsibility for half of both existing mortgages. A key contention in this case was a $640 payment that Thomas was allegedly to cover as part of his agreement for selecting the preferred quarter of the land. Following a foreclosure of the Powers mortgage, Crocker redeemed the property, claiming a right to the $640 based on an alleged agreement. Testimonies presented conflicting accounts between Weaver and Crocker regarding the existence of this agreement and the payment of the $640. Ultimately, the circuit court sided with Thomas Weaver and awarded him $462 in damages, leading to an appeal by Crocker.	Thomas Weaver claimed that he was not liable for the $640 payment to John Crocker, arguing that he never agreed to pay that amount as part of their arrangement related to the land sales. Weaver maintained that he fulfilled his financial obligations related to the property and denied any recognition of Crocker’s claims regarding the disputed payment. He sought to uphold the circuit court's judgment in his favor for the damages awarded.	John Crocker argued that he had a valid agreement with Thomas Weaver regarding the $640 payment pertinent to the choice of land quarters. He corroborated his claims with testimony from his son about a settlement and calculations involving the disputed amount. Crocker claimed that the payment was rightfully owed to him and that the circuit court’s initial judgment was erroneous.

In the case of Samuel Simons v. Asa D. Waldron et al., decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873, the dispute arose from an appeal bond related to a prior case against Waldron involving the tug boat "E.P. Dorr." This original case was affirmed by the court in 1871, but the bond was lost in a fire at the Chicago courthouse. Samuel Simons, as an appellant, contested his obligation on the bond by pleading "non est factum," asserting he did not execute it. The trial was held to determine this issue, resulting in a verdict against Simons, as the primary obligor of the bond, Joseph Moffitt, had not been served with process. The court ruled that evidentiary admissions were favorable towards Simons and noted that the discrepancies in names were not significant since he had not raised them properly in his defense. The jury's resolution of conflicting evidence was upheld, and thus the case was meticulously examined without finding grounds for reversal.	The plaintiffs, Asa D. Waldron and others, claimed that Samuel Simons was liable on an appeal bond executed in the earlier case. They argued that despite the original bond's destruction, there was sufficient evidence, including Simons' acknowledgments, to establish his obligation. They sought a judgment against Simons for the amount due under the bond, which was $1,260.50.	Samuel Simons, the defendant, contended that he had not signed the bond in question and thus should not be held liable. He claimed a variance in the names used in the writ and declaration, which he argued was a fatal error. Additionally, he suggested that his acknowledgments referred to different bonds signed under the direction of another party, potentially undermining the plaintiffs' claims regarding his liability on the bond.

On February 20, 1858, a financial assignment was made by Wisner & Taylor to John A. Marshall for the benefit of their creditors in Knox County, Illinois. Wisner & Taylor owed debts to Sheppard & Reeves, secured by a mortgage held by Wilson G. Hunt & Co. Morse K. Taylor served as surety for this debt. To protect Taylor's contingent liability, Wisner & Taylor issued him a note, which they designated as a preferred debt in the assignment. The parties involved, including Titsworth, agreed that the assignment's proceeds would first settle the Sheppard & Reeves mortgage. However, on December 1, 1858, Morse K. Taylor improperly assigned his note to Sarah E. Currier and notified Titsworth and Marshall not to pay the assigned funds toward the mortgage. Titsworth, believing the payment should still go to Sheppard & Reeves, refused to send the funds to Currier. This led to a legal dispute wherein Currier filed a bill in chancery to compel payment, while Hunt & Co. also sought their rights through a cross-bill. After substantial delay, an agreement to pay Hunt & Co. was reached, but they sought interest on the funds, which the court only partially granted. The primary issue concerning the denial of interest, particularly from the time of the cross-bill, became the focus of the appeal.	The plaintiffs, represented by Sarah E. Currier and others, argued that Titsworth should have paid the funds he received to satisfy the Sheppard & Reeves mortgage. They asserted that his refusal to pay, based on Morse K. Taylor's later claim, was improper and unjustified. Currier sought the payment of the funds and argued for interest on the amount as Titsworth had wrongfully retained it since April 1858, complicating the matter with competing claims.	The defendant, Titsworth, argued that he was justified in withholding the payment from Sheppard & Reeves due to Morse K. Taylor's instruction not to pay and the complications introduced by Currier's claim to the note. He contended that the interests of all parties at stake complicated the situation and that he should not be liable for interest due to the contested nature of the claims against the funds.

The case, titled "North Presbyterian Church of Chicago v. Otto Jevne, Peter Almini and Charles Daegling," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1863. The lawsuit took place in Chicago, where the plaintiffs, Jevne and Almini, along with Daegling, sought to enforce mechanic's liens on the church property owned by the North Presbyterian Church. They claimed a combined amount of $150 and additional sums for work done on the church's edifice, totaling $888.97. The defendants, represented by various individuals including Wesley Hunger, argued that due to other financial arrangements and mortgages associated with the property, the claims of the workmen should be adjusted accordingly. The church had borrowed $12,000 secured by a mortgage on the lots to fund the construction of the church, which was integral to the dispute over the rightful claims to the property and the distribution of sale proceeds. The trial concluded with a decree in favor of the contractors, mandating that the church pay the claimed amounts, thus generating further legal complications concerning property liens and sales.	The plaintiffs asserted that they had performed labor and provided materials for the construction of the church edifice, for which they were owed compensation. They requested the court to declare a mechanic's lien on the church property and the lots, thereby allowing their claims to be satisfied through the sale of the property.	The defendants acknowledged the debts but contended that the overall financial structure around the church property complicated the claims. They argued that the values contributed towards the building should influence the distribution of proceeds from any sale, emphasizing the necessity of properly accounting for prior mortgages and liens involved.

On August 30, 1859, William Hoskins filed a bill in chancery against Hervey Litchfield and his wife, Elizabeth Litchfield, in the Circuit Court of Bureau County, Illinois, to foreclose a mortgage they had executed on December 10, 1857. The mortgage did not explicitly include a release of the defendants' homestead rights. After the defendants failed to respond, the court granted a foreclosure decree and subsequently confirmed the sale of the mortgaged property, which Hoskins purchased.  On February 12, 1861, roughly a year later, the Litchfields filed a motion to set aside the decree and sale, claiming the property was their homestead, valued at less than $1,000, and that they had not legally relinquished their homestead rights. The Circuit Court eventually granted their motion, set aside the foreclosure decree, and ordered that the property be restored to its previous state as if no proceedings had occurred. This decision prompted Hoskins to file for a writ of error, seeking to contest the Circuit Court's ruling.	William Hoskins, the plaintiff, argued that the Circuit Court erred in setting aside the foreclosure decree. He contended that the sale was legitimate and pursued according to law, asserting no mistakes or fraud invalidated the sale. Hoskins emphasized that the Litchfields' delay in claiming their homestead rights constituted a waiver of those rights, and he maintained that the defendants had not provided justifiable grounds for their late claim. He sought to reinstate the original foreclosure decree and the sale of the property.	The Litchfields argued that their homestead rights were inappropriately disregarded in the foreclosure proceedings because the mortgage did not contain an express relinquishment of those rights. They contended that the law protected their homestead by preventing foreclosure without such a waiver. Furthermore, they maintained that the Circuit Court acted correctly in its decision to set aside the foreclosure due to the absence of a proper claim or acknowledgment of homestead rights during the initial proceedings. They requested the court to affirm their standing and restore their rights to the property.

John T. Lester faced legal issues stemming from a previous lawsuit involving Berkowitz, arising in Cook County, Illinois, where Lester & Co. acted as stock brokers. Between March 1 and April 10, 1884, Berkowitz engaged in buying and selling stocks through Lester & Co. Later, Berkowitz filed a motion to compel the inspection of Lester's business books to aid in preparing for trial. An order was issued requiring the defendants to produce these books, but they failed to comply, leading the court to hold Lester in contempt and impose a fine of $200. The case then progressed to the Illinois Supreme Court on appeal, focusing on the legal validity of the lower court's order and the contempt ruling.	The plaintiff, Berkowitz, claimed that he needed to inspect the defendants' books and accounts to prepare for trial effectively. He argued that the information contained within those books was pertinent to his case, as it would provide evidence relevant to the transactions he engaged in with Lester & Co.	The defendant, John T. Lester, contended that the court had overstepped its authority by ordering the impounding of his business books for inspection. He asserted that the order violated his constitutional rights against unreasonable searches and seizures and argued that compliance was not warranted because the books did not contain evidence necessary for Berkowitz’s claims.

In November 1851, the case "James McFarlan et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois" was tried in the Hardin Circuit Court, Illinois. The key individuals involved included James McFarlan, Charles C. Guard, Benjamin Spriggs, and the justices Peter Holland and Thomas Converse who accepted the recognizance. The case arose from a penal bond executed in connection with a manslaughter charge against Benjamin Spriggs, who had been accused of being an accessory to the manslaughter of Thomas Coleman. Spriggs, along with McFarlan and Guard, bound themselves to appear before the Hardin Circuit Court and abide by its decisions. When the case was called, Spriggs failed to appear, prompting the court to issue a scire facias—a legal order—against him and the co-cognizors. The plaintiffs claimed that the recognizance was valid despite a demurrer filed by Guard and McFarlan challenging various aspects of the recognizance and the scire facias. The court found in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to a judgment against the defendants.	The plaintiffs argued that the scire facias was valid and properly issued based on a recognizance executed according to the law. They claimed that despite the demurrer raised by Guard and McFarlan, the recognizance taken before the two justices of the peace was legally binding. They stated that the allegations concerning the recognizance being void due to jurisdiction issues or procedural defects were insufficient, and they effectively requested the court to affirm the validity of the recognizance and hold the defendants accountable for the default of Spriggs.	The defendants, Guard and McFarlan, contended that the scire facias was defective due to several reasons. They argued that the recognizance was not effectively returned into court, lacked necessary certifications from the justices, and contained blanks. Furthermore, they claimed it was erroneous to issue a judgment against them while not all cognizors had been properly summoned. They filed a demurrer challenging the sufficiency of the allegations in the scire facias and requested the court to dismiss the scire facias.

George Lickmon, acting as the executor in a legal matter, brought a case against Nathan Harding in September 1872. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the underlying issue rooted in a deed acknowledgment that took place in Warren County. The central question revolved around whether a formally executed deed acknowledgment, taken by a magistrate, should hold more weight than the claim of the grantor (Nathan Harding) that it was false and forged. The circuit court had previously ruled in favor of the acknowledged deed. This case touches on public policy matters regarding the security of land titles and the credibility of official acknowledgments when no fraud or collusion is present.	The plaintiff, George Lickmon, argued that the acknowledgment of the deed executed before a magistrate should be considered valid and should prevail against the unsupported claims of Nathan Harding that the acknowledgment was false. Lickmon sought to confirm the legitimacy of the deed and maintain the security of legal titles to land, emphasizing the importance of officials' certifications.	Nathan Harding, the defendant, contended that the acknowledgment of the deed was false and forged, insisting that his testimony should invalidate the deed. He aimed to prove the deceit surrounding the execution in order to contest the validity of the title.

The case of Frederick Bartlett et al. v. The Board of Education of Freeport School District took place in September 1871 in the state of Illinois. The key individuals involved included Esrom Mayer, who was elected treasurer of the Freeport School District on June 11, 1869, and was required to give a bond amounting to $20,000. Mayer executed this bond with the signatures of Frederick Bartlett and others as sureties. After completing his term, Mayer failed to transfer the funds he held to his successor, resulting in a lawsuit for $7,351.36 against him and his sureties by the board of education. A jury trial in the Stephenson circuit court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to an appeal by the defendants regarding procedural matters associated with the bond’s approval and its enforceability.	The plaintiffs, representing the Board of Education of Freeport, claimed that the bond provided by Mayer was valid and had been accepted by the board, making Mayer and his sureties liable for the funds he failed to turn over at the end of his term. They argued that the failure to formally approve the bond in the records did not nullify its validity, as it was accepted and acted upon by all parties involved. They sought to recover the amount due from the treasurer's bond, asserting their claim was supported by statutory provisions.	The defendants, including Mayer's sureties, contended that the bond was invalid because it had not been formally approved by the board. They claimed that the board did not fix the penalty amount prior to execution and had not acted properly in accepting the bond. Additionally, they argued that the bond was effectively altered after signing without their consent, thereby voiding its legitimacy as a security instrument under the law. They requested the court to dismiss the claims based on these defenses.

Hugh Garrity was indicted along with Charles Weed for assaulting Benjamin G. Buchanan in Illinois, with the intent to commit robbery. The incident occurred in the evening hours when street lights were still burning, making the area public and visible. Buchanan was carrying some kindling wood and personal items, which were not of substantial value. During the encounter, Garrity initially did not participate in the fight but encouraged Weed, who engaged in a physical altercation with Buchanan. After a trial, Garrity was found guilty and sentenced to six years in the penitentiary. However, he sought to overturn the verdict, arguing that there was a lack of evidence supporting the jury's finding of intent to rob, highlighting that the circumstances did not sustain such a conclusion.	The plaintiff argued that there was no sufficient evidence indicating that Garrity had an intent to commit robbery during the assault on Buchanan. He contended that while the act of assault was clear, it was not accompanied by any evidence or facts suggesting the purpose of robbery. Garrity's legal request included a motion for a new trial based on the argument that the conviction was unsupported by the necessary legal proof of intent.	The defense maintained that the evidence presented did not support a conviction for assault with intent to rob, asserting that the prosecution had failed to prove that Garrity intended to take anything from Buchanan. They pointed out that there was no real opportunity for robbery given the public setting and the lack of provocation. The defense's request was for the court to reverse the conviction on the grounds of insufficient evidence.

The case "William Shaeffer et al. plaintiffs in error v. Harriet Weed et al. defendants in error" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1846. The dispute arose after William Weed's death, who had commissioned the plaintiffs to furnish materials and perform work on a house. Following Weed's death, the project remained unfinished. His widow, Harriet, and his only son, William, were the primary parties involved alongside Sidney Cave, who initially administered the estate, and later John Grillison, who took over after Cave's death. Seven months after Weed's death, the plaintiffs filed a petition under the mechanics' lien law to secure payment for their services, identifying the widow and son as parties in the case. The administrator of the estate contended that the estate was insolvent, the widow had a right to her dower, and the petition was filed too late. The court ruled against the plaintiffs after they insisted on pursuing their petitional arguments, leading the judgment in favor of the administrator.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to payment for the labor and materials they provided to complete the construction of a house commissioned by William Weed. They contended that the mechanics' lien should be enforced against the property, despite the claims from the estate that the petition was filed too late and raised issues regarding the widow's dower rights.	The defendant, represented by the estate's administrator, argued that the estate was insolvent and that the widow had a lawful claim to her dower in the property. They further defended that the plaintiffs had failed to file their lien petition within the six-month timeframe specified by the law, thus invalidating their claim.

The case "Aaron Cariker v. William L. Anderson" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1862. The matter arose from a legal action by attachment initiated by William L. Anderson against Robert J. Hayes, with Aaron Cariker named as the garnishee. The original attachment writ was served to Cariker on May 6, 1857. Subsequently, in March 1858, a judgment by default was rendered against Hayes for $265.25, and Cariker's default was also entered. A "scire facias" was issued in December 1858, directing Cariker to respond to the court. However, at the March 1859 term, a final judgment was entered against Cariker, ordering him to pay the amount due, along with associated costs. Throughout the proceedings, various procedural irregularities were noted, including the failure to issue a conditional judgment against Cariker, lack of proper notice, and difficulties in service returns.	The plaintiff, William L. Anderson, contended that Aaron Cariker, as the garnishee, failed to comply with the necessary legal requirements set forth in the attachment statutes. Anderson argued that the court's proceedings were valid, seeking the collection of a judgment amounting to $265.25. He requested enforcement of the judgment against Cariker based on the existing defaults and a scire facias.	Aaron Cariker's defense hinged on significant procedural errors throughout the attachment process. He argued that there was no conditional judgment entered against him and cited errors in service returns, insufficient notice of the lawsuit, and absence of a proper writ of scire facias. Cariker contended that the court lacked jurisdiction to enter a final judgment against him due to these failures.

In early February 1854, Cyrus Bentley, the plaintiff, leased two buildings located at 19 and 21 Dearborn Street, Chicago, to John McCardel. The lease was for a term of ten years and three months, with an annual rent of $2,000 payable quarterly. Due to financial difficulties, McCardel was unable to continue his obligations under the lease, resulting in a court-appointed receiver, Ezekiel Hooper, who sold McCardel's leasehold interest to Robert Law on August 15, 1855. Law later assigned part of his interest to Hooper and subsequently transferred the lease to Joseph H. Martin, reserving certain rights. Martin occupied the leased premises until November 1857 when he fell behind on rent payments owed to Bentley. After issuing distress warrants for unpaid rent, Bentley reached a compromise with Martin's associate, William Lili, resulting in the release of claims against Martin as long as certain notes were paid. The case progressed through various legal actions, ultimately leading to Bentley suing Law for one-half of the reserved rent value from November 1857 to May 1858. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Bentley, leading to the appeal by Law to the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1860.	Cyrus Bentley claims that he is entitled to recover proportionate annual rent from Robert Law for the reserved portions of the leased properties, which amounted to one-half of the total value during specific months when Martin failed to pay rent. He argues that he is owed damages resulting from Law's non-compliance with terms stipulated in the lease and assignments.	Robert Law contends that the Circuit Court erred in its ruling that Bentley was entitled to recover damages. Law argues that the ruling was unjust and that the lower court's decision to award damages based on the lease and assignments lacked appropriate legal foundation. He challenges the claim, asserting that any obligations related to unpaid rent should not fall on him due to various legal proceedings surrounding the lease.

In the case of Mathias Rickart v. The People of the State of Illinois, the proceedings took place around September 1875, in DuPage County, Illinois. Mathias Rickart, the defendant, was previously licensed to operate a dram shop but lost this license by July 1, 1874. Subsequently, he became involved with the “Wheaton Co-Partnership Company No. One,” a newly formed association that claimed to promote temperance and community goodwill. Despite this claim, the association set up a bar in the same premises where Rickart had previously operated his saloon and began selling intoxicating liquors without a valid license. Rickart effectively continued to manage the bar under the guise of being the “treasurer” of the association. Witnesses testified that Rickart was selling alcohol in smaller quantities and that the operation was merely a means to circumvent the licensing laws. Ultimately, the prosecution initiated action against Rickart based on these allegations under the "Dram Shops" Act, which mandates licensing for the sale of intoxicating liquors.	The plaintiff, representing the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Rickart unlawfully sold intoxicating liquors without a license by utilizing a deceptive arrangement through the Wheaton Co-Partnership Company. They contended that the association’s setup was merely a guise to evade legal restrictions, as Rickart maintained complete control over the liquor sales and operations. The plaintiff's primary legal request was for the enforcement of penalties against Rickart for the violation of the Dram Shops Act, asserting that he resorted to a "shift" or "device" in conducting his business.	In defense, Rickart’s legal team argued that the formation of the Wheaton Co-Partnership Company placed the ownership of the bar’s inventory in the hands of the association, thus alleviating him from direct responsibility for selling liquor without a license. They contended that the arrangement allowed individuals to purchase tickets to claim their share of drinks, effectively portraying the setup as permissible communal ownership. However, the court found this argument unpersuasive, as it was deemed a thinly veiled attempt to circumvent the law.

In January 1873, the legal case of William S. Linn v. William Sigsbee was held in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from an agreement made on October 18, 1868, involving two practicing physicians, William S. Linn and William Sigsbee, concerning the sale of a house and lot in the town of Chili, Hancock County, Illinois, for a total of $2,000. The agreement included a clause wherein Linn agreed not to establish a medical practice within six miles of his residence after selling his practice to Sigsbee. Sigsbee claimed that after fulfilling his obligation by paying the agreed amount, Linn violated this agreement by resuming his medical practice within the restricted area, leading to losses for Sigsbee. The case was initially tried in the Circuit Court of Hancock County, where Sigsbee was awarded $450 for damages, but Linn appealed the decision, asserting that the testimony regarding damages was improperly admitted.	The plaintiff, William Sigsbee, argued that William S. Linn breached their agreement by resuming his medical practice within the restricted area, which caused him significant damages amounting to $2,000. He sought compensation based on the assertion that the breach of contract directly resulted in financial loss to him as a practicing physician in the same locality.	The defendant, William S. Linn, contended that the admissions of testimony regarding damages from the plaintiff’s expert witnesses were inappropriate, as their opinions did not qualify as expert evidence according to legal standards. He argued that the plaintiffs should prove damages through relevant facts rather than opinions, and maintained that the agreement's restriction was unreasonable or lacked legal consideration.

Frank F. Cole v. Davison Dalziel is a legal case that took place in 1881 in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Davison Dalziel, had entered into an agreement with the defendant, Frank F. Cole, whereby Dalziel borrowed $242 from Cole and pledged a $500 promissory note as collateral for the loan. This pledge permitted Cole to sell the note, with or without notice, to recover the owed amount. On July 20, 1881, after the loan became due, Cole sold the pledged note for $200 to a third party, Whalen, reportedly without sufficient notice to Dalziel. Dalziel claimed that this sale constituted a wrongful conversion of the note. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court after Dalziel obtained a judgment of $293 against Cole in the lower court. The trial focused on whether Cole had the right to sell the note under the agreed terms and whether adequate notice was given prior to the sale.	The plaintiff, Davison Dalziel, argued that the defendant, Frank F. Cole, wrongfully converted the $500 promissory note by selling it without providing sufficient notice. Dalziel sought compensation for the value of the note and claimed damages due to this alleged conversion, which he asserted was unlawful since the sale occurred without complying with the necessary notification protocols.	The defendant, Frank F. Cole, contended that he acted within his rights under the agreement, which explicitly allowed him to sell the pledged note at any time, without notice. Cole argued that the sale was executed lawfully and that the proceeds were justly applied toward the debt owed by Dalziel. He maintained that, in any case, the amount Dalziel owed exceeded the value of the sold note, suggesting that Dalziel was only entitled to nominal damages if any wrongful conversion was found.

In 1866, Margaret Johnson, who later married Martin, owned several lots in Chicago and conveyed six lots to William Bayland to secure a debt owed by her father. After her father's death, Bayland obtained a judgment against Margaret for $2800 due to the debt. Margaret verbally agreed with her brother-in-law, John F. Temple, to sell these lots and others to raise money to satisfy the judgment. In 1869, Temple found a potential buyer, Mulvy, but negotiations fell through due to encumbrances on some lots. Temple then proposed selling joint lots with Margaret's mother, which was approved. However, the specifics of the agreement between Margaret and Temple became a point of contention, with differing accounts regarding their understanding of the arrangement. In March 1867, Temple and his mother-in-law sold seven lots, eventually generating $3000, which wasn’t applied to the judgment until February 1868. Temple claimed rights to additional lots as part of the agreement, while Margaret later sold other lots to James B. Johnson and another party, raising further disputes over ownership and compensation. The court initially agreed to partition the lots but dismissed Temple's cross-bill, prompting his appeal for the court to recognize his claims.	H. Frederick Temple argued that he and Margaret Johnson's mother agreed that they were to receive a portion of the fourteen lots sold for the judgment payment. He claimed he was entitled to one-half of the unsold lots and funds from earlier sales, asserting that the agreement had been established and validated by their verbal arrangement. Temple contended that the lack of a formal written contract did not invalidate their agreement, arguing for a specific performance based on the claim that they had provided funds to pay the judgment.	James B. Johnson and Margaret Johnson defended against Temple’s claims by asserting that no concrete agreement had been made. They maintained that even if an understanding existed, it was not documented as required by the Statute of Frauds. Johnson argued that Temple did not take possession or make improvements on the property, rendering the alleged agreement unenforceable. They further contended that any claims to conveyance of the lots were inequitable given that Temple had already received substantial financial benefits from previous transactions.

In 1887, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving George Kronenberger and Charles C. Fricke concerning the sale of real property. Fricke, the plaintiff, had initially approached the defendant, Kronenberger, seeking commissions for the sale of a property to a buyer named Howe. Fricke claimed that he had been employed by Kronenberger to find a purchaser. However, evidence suggested that Fricke was already acting as an agent for Howe while simultaneously negotiating the sale for Kronenberger. After several months of searching for property for Howe, Fricke alerted him to the availability of Kronenberger's real estate, leading to a subsequent purchase by Howe. During the trial, the jury ruled in favor of Fricke, awarding him $190 in commissions. This prompted Kronenberger to appeal the decision, asserting that Fricke's dual agency status (acting for both him and the purchaser) was not disclosed.	Fricke's main argument was that he was entitled to commissions for successfully bringing a buyer, Howe, to Kronenberger’s property. He contended that he acted within the scope of his employment and should be compensated for his efforts in facilitating the sale.	Kronenberger's defense rested on the assertion that Fricke acted primarily as the agent for Howe without disclosing this relationship. He argued that since Fricke failed to reveal his dual agency, he could not rightfully demand commissions for the sale as it constituted a breach of trust and a conflict of interest.

In 1873, a legal proceeding was initiated by William B. Gilkerson before a justice of the peace in Ford County, Illinois, under the Drainage Act of 1871. The case involved a petition for the construction of a drain on the lands of both Gilkerson and Harriet B. Scott. After a hearing, the justice instructed the local highway commissioners to lay out and construct the drain. The commissioners submitted a report indicating that the project could be completed at a cost below the expected benefits to the affected lands. A jury assessed the damages and benefits, declaring benefits of $40 to Gilkerson’s land and $150 to Scott’s land, with no damages recorded for either party. Following a series of legal maneuvers, including an appeal to the county court by Scott which resulted in a dismissal, Gilkerson subsequently appealed to the circuit court. The circuit court upheld the decision against Gilkerson's request for a de novo hearing and ruled in favor of Scott, leading Gilkerson to seek further review from the Illinois Supreme Court.	Gilkerson argued that the circuit court erred in not providing a trial de novo when he appealed from the county court's decision. He contended that irregularities existed in the jury's proceedings, including the inclusion of a new juror during the confirmation of the assessment, which he claimed undermined the fairness of the assessment process. He sought to reverse the judgment of the circuit court, aiming to have the assessment of benefits and damages amended.	Scott’s defense centered on the assertion that the circuit court was correct in its ruling and that the legal process followed prior to the confirmation of the assessment was valid. Scott contended that the original jury’s assessment was flawed by the improper introduction of a new juror and that the entirety of the costs had been misassessed to her property without a fair share being allocated to Gilkerson’s land.

The case "Ohio & Mississippi Ry. Co. v. John J. O’Donnell" took place in Sangamon County, Illinois, with a decision rendered on November 18, 1887. The case arose when John J. O'Donnell brought an action against the Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company, which was accused of negligence in the operation of its train. Specifically, O'Donnell claimed that the railway company’s train ran over and killed his cow. The incident involved the train allegedly traveling backward on a curve within city limits at a speed that violated local ordinances. O'Donnell secured a verdict in the lower court, recovering $55 in damages. The central issue in the appeal revolved around whether the negligence on the part of the railway was adequately proven. The appellate court found sufficient evidence to support the jury's conclusion that the railway was indeed negligent under the circumstances presented.	John J. O'Donnell, the plaintiff, claimed that the Ohio & Mississippi Railway Co. was negligent in their operations, leading to the death of his cow. He argued that the train was running backward at a forbidden speed within city limits, thereby violating local ordinances. O'Donnell requested damages for the loss of his livestock, ultimately winning a judgment of $55 in the lower court.	The defendant, Ohio & Mississippi Railway Co., contended that their operation of the train did not constitute negligence. They maintained that the evidence presented did not sufficiently establish that their actions were careless or led to the cow's death. The railway company's counsel requested a dismissal of the charges on the grounds that adequate proof of negligence was lacking, arguing that the jury's findings were unsupported by the evidence.

John Doe, ex dem. Murray McConnel, initiated an ejectment action in the Morgan Circuit Court, Illinois, to reclaim possession of the west half of the southwest quarter of section number 32 in Morgan County. The case dates back to the October 1838 term when the Hon. Jesse B. Thomas allowed McConnel to amend his declaration, adding demises from Henry H. Haynie and Seth Pratt. The defendant, Isaac Johnson, countered these claims with an affidavit stating that neither Pratt nor Haynie had any valid interest in the land, asserting they had conveyed the property to others before McConnel’s claim. The trial faced numerous procedural challenges, including denied continuances and the admissibility of various deeds presented by both parties. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of Johnson, leading McConnel to pursue an appeal based on claimed trial errors regarding excluded evidence and the rejection of a continuance request.	McConnel claimed ownership of the land based on a sheriff's deed, arguing that Johnson's conveyance from Pratt was fraudulent and intended to evade creditors. He sought to present evidence through witness testimony to establish the illegitimacy of Johnson's claim and emphasized that the titles held by Pratt and Haynie were improperly asserted in the action, necessitating their inclusion as demises.	Johnson defended the suit by asserting that he possessed legal title through a valid deed from Pratt and contested the legitimacy of McConnel's claims, which depended on imperfect titles. He posited that the court erred by not allowing his full defenses, and he argued that the testimony and deeds presented by McConnel were irrelevant since both parties relied on the same source for title. Johnson maintained that the verdict should reflect his rightful ownership based on the evidence presented.

The case "Charles Hanson, John Grayam and James K. Edsall v. Jacob Armstrong" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1859. It originated in the Lee County Circuit Court when Jacob Armstrong initiated a declaration in ejectment against the plaintiffs, which included Hanson, Grayam, and Edsall, concerning specific premises. The trial occurred in November 1858, where Armstrong provided evidence that established his connection to the property's prior possessors, starting from Gilbraith to Manchan, Herrick, Hanson, and finally to Grayam. At the time of the trial, Grayam was confirmed to be in exclusive possession of the property in question. The plaintiffs attempted to introduce a copy of a deed from Hanson to Edsall to bolster their claims, but the court allowed this despite objections regarding the lack of a proper foundation for its admission. The jury subsequently ruled in favor of Armstrong, leading the plaintiffs to file for a new trial, which was denied.	The plaintiffs contended that Armstrong did not hold a valid legal title to the property and contested the admission of the deed copy that was introduced as evidence. They maintained that their possession or ownership rights to the premises should supersede Armstrong’s claims. Their legal request was primarily for a new trial based on alleged errors in the proceedings, particularly regarding the evidentiary rulings made by the court.	Armstrong argued that he had a legitimate claim to the premises based on a clear chain of title and possession that could be traced back through multiple previous owners, ultimately to the time Armstrong asserted control over the property. Armstrong claimed that the admission of the deed was justifiable and criticized the plaintiffs' failure to establish their own legal title to refute his ownership. He requested that the original judgment in his favor be upheld, asserting that the plaintiffs lacked the necessary evidence to justify their claims.

In June 1859, John R. Snyder, who was indebted to Calvin Griswold for $1,791, executed three deeds for tracts of land in LaSalle County, Illinois, Iowa, and Minnesota. The transaction was made under the pretense of an absolute sale but was accompanied by a written agreement stipulating that Griswold would convey the land back to Snyder upon the payment due by January 1, 1860.
