The case involved claims from Thomas B. Ellis, who asserted rights based on previous transactions concerning the mill and property, including allegations of fraud against the complainants. After considerable testimony and procedural complexities, the original court's decision led to appeals, focusing on the enforceability of the mortgage and the competing claims of the involved parties.	The plaintiffs, led by Austin Sumner, claimed a foreclosure of a mortgage supposedly executed by Waugh and Ellis to Sisson, which they had acquired through assignment. They argued that their interests were valid and should be prioritized over any competing claims, particularly those arising from Thomas B. Ellis, who alleged prior rights to the mortgage due to ongoing legal proceedings at the time of the assignment. The plaintiffs contended that they were entitled to enforce their rights through foreclosure due to the legitimacy of their mortgage interest.	The defendants, including Waugh and Ellis, countered that the plaintiffs were not entitled to foreclosure due to several factors, most notably the prior agreements made by Waugh and Ellis with Sisson. They argued that the plaintiffs took the mortgage assignment subject to pre-existing equities held by Thomas B. Ellis, including the pending lawsuit regarding the specific performance of contracts related to the same properties. Moreover, they maintained that the assignment of the mortgage was influenced by fraudulent conduct and denied knowledge of any defects when they assumed ownership.

The case of Daniel P. Smith, Exr. v. P. S. McLaughlin et al. took place in June 1875 in Illinois, involving the estate of John M. Bennett, who had passed away. The plaintiffs, P. S. McLaughlin and J. H. Maxwell, were practicing physicians who performed a post-mortem examination on Bennett's body at the request of the coroner. Following their examination, they submitted a claim for payment to Bennett's estate in the probate court, where they were awarded $50. However, the case was appealed to the circuit court, which upheld the original judgment for the same amount. The matter was further escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the legal questions revolved around whether the fees for the physicians' services constituted a legitimate claim against the deceased's estate, given that such services had not been previously codified into law. The court examined the nature of the claims made by the physicians and the statutory framework that governed the payment of fees for such examinations.	The plaintiffs claimed compensation for the post-mortem examination services they rendered as a part of a coroner's inquest. They argued that their professional services were necessary and thus warranted payment from John M. Bennett’s estate, asserting that the probate court rightfully awarded them compensation and that this decision should be upheld.	The defendant, representing the estate of John M. Bennett, contended that there was no statutory basis for allowing the physicians' claim for payment. They argued that fees for post-mortem examinations had not been defined by law and asserted that such services were not debts incurred by the deceased during his lifetime. It was claimed that the costs should not be charged to the estate as these examinations served public interests rather than benefiting the estate directly.

In June 1870, the case of William Reeves et al. v. Ann Reeves was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose after the death of John Reeves, who had been married to Ann Reeves. The major point of contention was Ann's right to dower, which is a legal provision that grants a widow a share of her deceased husband's estate. The defendants contested Ann's claim by arguing that her marriage to John Reeves was invalid because she was still married to another man, Teasdale, at the time of her marriage to John. Evidence was presented showing that Teasdale was already married to another woman when he purportedly married Ann in 1857, making their marriage void. Contrarily, the court found sufficient counter-evidence indicating that Teasdale's marriage was itself invalid, thus validating Ann's marriage to John. The court also addressed procedural issues, including the improper lien placed on the dower and questions regarding the adjudication of mesne profits from the property, which had not been correctly assigned in the original ruling.	Ann Reeves, the plaintiff, claimed her legal right to dower following the death of her husband, John Reeves. Her primary argument was that her subsequent marriage to John was valid since her previous marriage to Teasdale was void. She requested a decree stating her rights to the dower, inclusive of a fair determination of any liens against the property and the payment of mesne profits by the party in possession.	The defendants argued against Ann's claim to dower, asserting that her marriage to John Reeves was invalid due to her existing marital status with Teasdale, who was alive at the time of her marriage to John. They maintained that this previous marriage rendered Ann's claim legally untenable. Additionally, they challenged the legal proceedings concerning the lien on the property and the assignment of responsibilities regarding mesne profits.

Gustavus Skelley, the plaintiff, was a sub-mail contractor who entrusted $30 to Solomon Kahn, the defendant, for delivery to Mr. Sartain, the principal contractor. The incident occurred in Logan County, Illinois, around April 1854. Kahn, the postmaster at Postville, was approached by a boy working for Sartain, who claimed he was authorized to collect the money. Skelley informed Kahn that he had not yet collected the funds but would do so shortly. Eventually, Skelley provided the money to Kahn before the boy's next mail trip. Kahn handed the money to the boy during that trip and later informed Skelley, who did not object, indicating that he found the arrangement acceptable. However, after the boy absconded with the money, Skelley demanded restitution from Kahn, who refused. Consequently, Skelley filed a lawsuit against Kahn. The case was originally decided in favor of Kahn, leading to Skelley’s appeal.	Skelley claimed that Kahn was negligent in handing over the money to the boy without adequate verification of his authority. He argued that Kahn's failure to exercise proper care constituted gross negligence and sought to hold Kahn liable for the amount lost due to the boy's actions.	Kahn defended himself by arguing that he acted within the bounds of his duty as a bailee, suggesting that he reasonably entrusted the money to the boy based on the facts presented at the time. He contended that there was no gross negligence on his part and requested the court to uphold the lower court's decision, which found him not liable for the loss.

Michael O’Conner v. John Mullen is a legal case that originated in the Sangamon County Circuit Court in March 1846, where a capias was issued against O’Conner for debt related to a bond for the conveyance of land. Mullen, the plaintiff, claimed $500 in debt and $300 in damages. Following a default judgment against O’Conner, the court awarded Mullen $200 in damages but did not initially enter a judgment for the debt owed. This omission prompted Mullen to seek an amendment, which occurred in August 1849, allowing the judgment to be amended to specify the $500 debt, which was to be satisfied by the payment of the assessed damages. The defendant objected to this amendment, arguing that it should not have been allowed without his notification, raising questions about the authority of the Circuit Court to amend judgments post-term and emphasizing the necessity of notice to the opposing party. The case ultimately highlights issues of procedural correctness in debt judgments and the importance of notice in legal proceedings.	Mullen's primary argument asserts that the original judgment was flawed as it awarded only damages instead of addressing the debt for which the action was initiated. He contends that the judgment should have specified both the debt and the damages. After the amendment, Mullen seeks to have O’Conner pay the $500 debt, discharging it with the previously assessed damages.	O’Conner argues that the amendment to the judgment was improper and that he did not receive notice prior to the amendment, which he claims violates due process. He maintains that the original judgment, which did not include a determination of the debt, was correct in its rendering. O’Conner contends that allowing the amendment without notice undermines the finality of judgments and poses a risk of affecting his rights without appropriate legal safeguards.

In September 1873, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the case of John M. Bryant et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois. The dispute arose from a judgment rendered in the county court of Cook County concerning delinquent taxes owed on certain lands. The county court ruled against the landowners, requiring them to pay the delinquent taxes before allowing any appeal. The landowners, represented by attorney Mr. Edward Roby, sought to challenge this judgment, filing a writ of error and requesting an order to allow an appeal and an injunction to prevent the sale of their lands to satisfy the tax judgment. The court found that the landowners had not complied with the statutory requirement to deposit the tax amount owed, which was a prerequisite for their request for a supersedeas (a court order to suspend the enforcement of a judgment). Additionally, it was stated that the Supreme Court lacked jurisdiction to grant an original injunction without an appropriate bill being filed.	The plaintiffs, John M. Bryant and others, claimed that the county court wrongly rendered a judgment against their lands for delinquent taxes without allowing them an appeal. They argued that they should be permitted to file an appeal without making the requisite tax payment in advance and requested an injunction to prevent the sale of their properties until the appeal could be heard.	The State of Illinois defended the judgment by asserting that granting a supersedeas was not a constitutional right and that the legislature had set conditions that required the deposit of the tax judgment amount in order for an appeal to be permitted. Furthermore, the State contended that the Supreme Court had no jurisdiction to grant an injunction in this matter since it was a proceeding under statutory law rather than a case in equity.

The case "Ludwig Hofferbert et ux. v. Edward Klinkhardt" was adjudicated in January 1871 in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a decision from the Circuit Court of St. Clair County. The case originated from a mortgage foreclosure action initiated by Edward Klinkhardt against Ludwig Hofferbert and his wife. The foreclosure proceedings began in 1868 when Klinkhardt filed a bill in chancery to recover the amount due on the mortgage. A decree was issued in favor of Klinkhardt by the Circuit Court, which prompted the Hofferberts to seek a reversal of this decree based on procedural errors. The key individuals involved included Ludwig Hofferbert and his wife as plaintiffs in error, and Edward Klinkhardt as the defendant in error. The case centered on the technicalities of the decree's wording and its implications regarding both defendants being named.	The plaintiff, Ludwig Hofferbert, claimed that the decree issued by the Circuit Court was erroneous due to the use of the singular term "defendant" instead of the plural "defendants," despite both Hofferberts being duly served and present before the court. They argued that this singular reference created uncertainty about who the decree was directed against, thereby rendering it void. The plaintiffs sought to have the decree reversed on the grounds of this alleged clerical mistake.	The defendant, Edward Klinkhardt, contended that the decree was valid despite the clerical error concerning the wording. Klinkhardt argued that the overall context of the decree made clear the intention of the court, which was to address both defendants uniformly. He maintained that the omission of the letter "s" was a minor clerical mistake and should not undermine the substantive validity of the decree. Klinkhardt sought affirmation of the lower court's decree and argued that technical objections like these do not warrant a reversal.

In 1883, Horace H. Thomas negotiated four promissory notes, each valued at $2,500, made by H. L. Culver to Culver, Page, Hoyne & Company. Each note was set to mature six months after its respective date, which was between August 13 and August 28 of that year. The company indorsed its name twice on each note. Following this, the notes were transferred to the Commercial National Bank, which provided a guaranty for their payment. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court after Thomas, as the indorsee of the notes, filed an action against Culver, Page, Hoyne & Company as the guarantor. Throughout the trial, evidence was presented, primarily concerning the authority of the company to issue a guaranty due to the double indorsement on the notes. However, no clear authority was shown, leading to a judgment against the defendant solely as a guarantor.	The plaintiff, Horace H. Thomas, argued that Culver, Page, Hoyne & Company was liable for the payment of the four promissory notes based on their double indorsement and the subsequent guaranty written by the Commercial National Bank. He sought enforcement of the guaranty for the payment owed under the notes, asserting that the company's endorsement constituted a valid guarantee of payment.	The defendant, Culver, Page, Hoyne & Company, defended against the claims by asserting that the endorsements did not create a binding guaranty. They contended that the mere act of placing their name twice on the notes was insufficient to enable the holder to write a guaranty over one or both signatures. Thus, they maintained that their liability was limited to that of an indorser and challenged the interpretation of the guaranty implied by the endorsements.

Porter S. West v. James S. Carter is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 15, 1889. The conflict originated in Cook County, Illinois, when West claimed to have won a horse race organized by the Chicago Driving Park Association, which offered a $300 purse for “gentlemen’s roadsters.” West and three others entered their horses, each paying a $15 entrance fee, which contributed to the total purse. West emerged victorious; however, the association disputed the claim, leading West to obtain a judgment of $180 from a justice of the peace. The association subsequently appealed, with James S. Carter acting as security on the appeal bond. The circuit court later dismissed the appeal for lack of prosecution. When West sought to enforce the judgment against the bond, Carter contended that the underlying contract was a gambling contract, making the judgment void under Illinois law. The case went through several courts, including the Superior Court and the Appellate Court, and centered on issues of the legality of the original contract and whether Carter, as a surety, had standing to challenge the judgment.	West's primary argument was that the judgment rendered by the justice of the peace was valid and that he fairly won the prize based on the rules set by the Chicago Driving Park Association. He insisted that the entry fees were applicable to a legitimate competition and denied that the underlying transaction was a gambling contract. He sought enforcement of the judgment against Carter and a declaration that Carter’s claims were without merit.	Carter's defense was rooted in the claim that the judgment was based on a gambling contract, which is deemed absolutely void under sections 131 and 135 of the Illinois Criminal Code. Carter argued that he, as a surety on the appeal bond, had the right to seek relief from the judgment due to its illegal basis. He sought a court order to declare the judgment void, to cancel the appeal bond, and to enjoin West from further pursuing claims based on that judgment.

This case, titled Henry A. Treadwell v. John McEwen et al., was reviewed by the Illinois Appellate Court and decided on May 27, 1887. The dispute originated in Kane County, Illinois, involving Henry A. Treadwell as the appellant and John McEwen, the appellee, along with other defendants. The legal contention arose when John M. Treadwell, Henry's father, transferred a farm of 149 acres to his son, Henry, shortly after incurring debts. The plaintiff, John McEwen, claimed this conveyance was fraudulent, made to evade creditor judgments of $651.62 and $522.49 against John M. Treadwell from earlier disputes regarding an estate's executor bond. Evidence indicated that John M. Treadwell intended to defraud creditors by transferring his assets to his son, who was then young and financially incapable of making such purchases without coercive influence from his father. The court examined several aspects, including the surrounding circumstances and the intent behind the conveyance, ultimately finding sufficient evidence of fraud.	The plaintiff, John McEwen, asserted that the transfer of the property from John M. Treadwell to his son, Henry, was fraudulent and intended to evade creditors. He sought to have the court set aside the conveyance, declaring it void, and to allow the sale of the land to satisfy the existing judgments against John M. Treadwell.	The defendant, Henry A. Treadwell, contested the allegations of fraud, arguing that the conveyance was legitimate and that he had merely assumed his father's debts, which was a fair and legal transaction. He positioned his claim on the pretext that he had not participated in any fraudulent activities and maintained that there was insufficient evidence to prove any intent to defraud creditors.

In the case of David Blalock v. Stephen A. Randall, which took place in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875, the legal dispute stemmed from an incident involving an accusation of forgery. David Blalock, the defendant, claimed that Randall, the plaintiff, fraudulently obtained his signature on a promissory note purportedly worth $360 through deceitful means. The events leading to the trial began on May 8, 1871, when Blalock swore before Justice of the Peace George Goodman that Randall had committed forgery. Following this, a warrant was issued for Randall's arrest, and on May 18, he was taken before the justice. After being required to post bail for his appearance at a later circuit court term, Randall was imprisoned when he failed to do so. He subsequently sued Blalock for trespass, alleging assault and unlawful imprisonment, as well as for malicious prosecution. The case unfolded with complicated legal arguments regarding the justifications for the arrest and the proper handling of evidence in court.	Stephen A. Randall, the plaintiff, contended that David Blalock unlawfully arrested and imprisoned him based on unfounded allegations of forgery. Randall's claims were directed towards asserting that Blalock acted with malice and without probable cause, ultimately seeking damages for the wrongful actions against him. He aimed for legal redress, emphasizing the unlawful nature of the arrest and imprisonment based on a complaint he argued was unjustified.	David Blalock, in his defense, asserted that the actions taken against Randall, including the issuance of a warrant for his arrest and subsequent imprisonment, were lawful, founded on a valid complaint made before a competent authority. Blalock argued that there were reasonable grounds to suspect Randall of forgery, and he asserted that his actions were justified under the legal process. He emphasized that trespass claims cannot stand when done under legally issued processes and cited the absence of malice or lack of probable cause.

In December 1830, the case of Timothy Brinkley v. Reuben Going was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The matter arose in Gallatin County, Illinois. The central issue revolved around the legal standing of the payee and holder of a negotiable note that had an assignment to a third person. The dispute questioned whether the original payee could initiate legal action to enforce the note without having to reassign it. The court previously dealt with a similar case, Brinkley v. Going, where it was decided that the payee could maintain a suit in his own name. Chief Justice Wilson, presiding over this case, noted that it was analogous to the prior decision and aligned with established legal principles.	Timothy Brinkley, the appellant, argued that as the payee and holder of the negotiable note, he had the right to file a lawsuit in his own name despite the assignment. Brinkley sought affirmation of the court's interpretation that such legal actions could be maintained without reassignment, thereby asserting his entitlement to enforce the payment of the note.	Reuben Going, the appellee, did not present a substantial defense against the claim of Brinkley related to the standing to sue. The focus was primarily on the legal interpretation of the rights associated with collectible notes, which Brinkley had in his possession. Given the precedent set in the analogous case, the defenses were not explicitly articulated or contested.

The case "George C. Barnes v. George Simmons" took place in April 1862 in Illinois. The dispute arose from a suit regarding a note, where Barnes (the appellant) was being sued by Simmons (the appellee) for an amount of $429.66. The trial involved testimonies and evidence related to a loan that Barnes claimed to have taken from Simmons. Barnes testified about his inability to access the borrowed funds, which he believed were held in a bank he accused of being insolvent. Simmons offered evidence, including bank records, to support his claim that the loan was valid and enforceable. The court found that the bank records he submitted were crucial to the case, but Barnes objected to their admissibility. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Simmons, which led Barnes to seek an appeal based on the decision made at trial.	The plaintiff, George Simmons, claimed that George C. Barnes owed him $429.66 as per a note signed by Barnes. Simmons presented evidence of the transaction, supported by bank records, indicating that he had made loans to Barnes, and asserted that Barnes had not fulfilled his obligations to repay the loan. He requested the court to uphold the jury's verdict in his favor and affirm the judgment against Barnes.	The defendant, George C. Barnes, argued that the evidence presented by Simmons, particularly the bank records, should not have been admissible since they were not made with the parties' knowledge or consent and were hearsay. Barnes contested the validity of the loan and maintained that he had tried to access the funds that were allegedly inaccessible due to the bank's insolvency. He requested that the court set aside the jury's verdict and grant a new trial based on these claims.

The case "E. P. Reed & Co. v. F. C. Pinney & Co." was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on April 21, 1890. It took place in Cook County, Illinois, involving the appellant, E. P. Reed & Co., and the appellees, F. C. Pinney & Co. The case centered around a replevin action in which E. P. Reed & Co. sought to recover goods that had previously been sold on credit. They contended that the sale had been induced by fraudulent misrepresentations made by Pinney regarding his financial condition. During the trial, the court's instructions to the jury were pivotal. The plaintiffs argued that based on the defendants’ misleading statements, they were justified in claiming the goods back. The trial court provided specific guidance on how to judge the legitimacy of the plaintiffs’ claims, which would ultimately have significant implications for the legal standards governing fraud in the context of sales. The central issue revolved around whether the plaintiffs needed to demonstrate the defendant's intent to deceive in addition to proving that false statements were made about financial capability.	E. P. Reed & Co. claimed that they were misled by false representations from F. C. Pinney regarding his financial condition at the time of the sale. They argued that had they known the truth about Pinney’s financial status, they would not have entered the sale agreement and, therefore, should be entitled to reclaim the goods on the grounds of fraud. The plaintiffs sought to prove that the defendants intended to deceive them in order to obtain goods on credit.	F. C. Pinney & Co. contended that the plaintiffs had failed to demonstrate that any fraudulent misrepresentations were made and that they had not acted with any intent to deceive. They argued that for the plaintiffs to succeed, they must prove, through a preponderance of evidence, that false representations were knowingly made. The defendants asserted that the burden of proof lay with the plaintiffs to show both the existence of the fraud and the defendants' intent.

The case of Harvey G. Coursey v. Mary S. Coursey was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871. The conflict arose in Kankakee County, Illinois, between Harvey G. Coursey (the defendant) and Mary S. Coursey (the plaintiff), who were married. Mary sought a divorce on the grounds of extreme and repeated cruelty experienced during their marriage. The court examined testimonies describing incidents where Harvey exhibited drunkenness and violent behavior, which included physical intimidation, threats, and actual physical abuse towards Mary. Over the past two years, Mary testified that she had endured multiple instances of harm, including being thrown out of the house and being kept outside in the snow. The jury found these claims credible, leading to Mary’s request for a divorce based on such behavior. Harvey, meanwhile, acknowledged he had sometimes misused his wife during his drunken episodes but denied repeated instances of cruelty.	Mary S. Coursey argued that her husband, Harvey G. Coursey, had committed extreme and repeated cruelty, which justified her request for a divorce. She claimed that his drunkenness was part of a pattern of abusive behavior, creating a reasonable fear of bodily harm and making it impossible for her to fulfill her marital duties. Mary's legal request was for a legal decree to dissolve their marriage due to the unhealthy and abusive environment she had been subjected to.	Harvey G. Coursey contended that the accusations against him were exaggerated and that any acts of cruelty were either unproven or provoked by Mary’s own conduct. He asserted that if his violent actions were a result of his wife's misconduct, those acts could not be grounds for divorce. Additionally, he emphasized that the jury instructions related to the necessity of proving his drunkenness in conjunction with threats were in error and sought a dismissal of the claims against him.

The case involves the People of the State of Illinois ex rel. Lorenzo Bull, who filed for a writ of mandamus against Orlin H. Miner, the Auditor of Public Accounts, in January 1868. This legal action took place in Quincy, Illinois. The primary issue arose when the Merchants and Banners' National Bank of Quincy, represented by Lorenzo Bull as a shareholder, sought a court directive to compel the state auditor to issue a refund for taxes the bank had paid in 1865. The taxes were assessed on the shareholders’ respective shares, and the payments were made under protest. Bull argued that although taxes were due, the way in which they were assessed was illegal under established laws. The case referenced precedents, notably the ruling in Bradley v. The People, which dealt with similar tax assessments on banks, suggesting that the tax liability was based on a contractual agreement that could not be easily altered.	The plaintiff, Lorenzo Bull, contended that the taxes levied on the shareholders of the bank were illegally assessed. He sought a mandate from the court to compel the Auditor to issue a warrant to refund the taxes paid under protest. Bull argued that, per the precedent set in Bradley v. The People, the assessments were not in accordance with the legal guidelines, claiming that the taxes represented an inequitable and unlawful financial obligation.	The defendant, Orlin H. Miner, argued that the taxes paid were legally assessed and that any technical irregularities in the assessment process did not negate the fundamental tax liability. He asserted that the property on which taxes were levied was legally taxable, and thus, the bank could not recover taxes that were voluntarily paid. Miner maintained that since the taxpayers were aware of their obligations and chose to pay, they could not later claim reimbursement based simply on a technicality in the assessment method used.

The case of "The People ex rel. C. D. F. Smith v. The Common Council of the City of Aurora et al." took place in September 1875 in Illinois, involving the cities of Elgin and Aurora. C. D. F. Smith, acting as relator, initiated proceedings against the common councils of both cities seeking a mandamus. This action was prompted by the failure to hold an election for the position of judge for the Courts of Common Pleas of Elgin and Aurora on the scheduled date, the fourth Monday of February 1875. The act of February 16, 1859, had established a system for electing a single judge for both courts, and Smith argued it was imperative for a new election to take place since none occurred as required by law. The legal debate centered around the interpretation of subsequent legislative changes, specifically the act of July 1, 1874, which continued the existence of these courts under a new naming convention. The question was whether the new act altered the requirement that judges be elected from both cities.	The plaintiff, C. D. F. Smith, claimed that the common councils of Elgin and Aurora were legally required to hold an election for the position of the judge for their respective courts, as stipulated in the earlier act of 1859. He requested a peremptory mandamus, compelling the councils to conduct an election in accordance with the law, asserting that the absence of an election constituted a violation of this legal requirement.	The defendants, represented by attorneys for the common councils of Aurora and Elgin, argued that the act of July 1, 1874, modified the process of electing judges, focusing on the interpretation that it established these courts under new jurisdictional names and redefined how judges should be elected. They contended that the new legislation allowed for a different approach to the election process, implying that a judge could be elected by a single city rather than requiring votes from both Elgin and Aurora.

In June 1875, the case John C. Clymore v. Abram D. Williams was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The action originated in the Circuit Court of Johnson County, where Abram D. Williams initiated a suit against John C. Clymore on the basis of assumpsit, which is a legal term for a promise or agreement that is not yet fulfilled. The suit included an attachment, which is a legal mechanism that allows a plaintiff to seize a defendant's property to secure a judgment. The core issue involved the court's jurisdiction due to the lack of personal service on Clymore, meaning he had not been properly notified of the lawsuit, nor had he appeared in court. The court found that awarding a general execution against Clymore's property was improper under these circumstances. Furthermore, the execution against specific lands was contested because the required legal steps, including a signed levy under the attachment writ, had not been followed, leading to confusion regarding the status of any property involved.	Abram D. Williams claimed damages from John C. Clymore due to an alleged breach of an agreement, seeking a legal recovery of the amount owed. He argued that the attachment was necessary to secure his claim against Clymore's property, asserting that, despite the lack of personal service, he was entitled to an execution against Clymore’s assets to fulfill the debt.	John C. Clymore defended against Williams' claims by highlighting procedural errors in the lawsuit. He asserted that the lack of personal service and the absence of a proper levy on property meant that the court did not have jurisdiction over the case. Clymore contended that without these legal prerequisites being met, any execution awarded against him was invalid.

The case of "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. William R. Phelps" took place in Carbondale, Illinois, in November 1862. The plaintiff, William R. Phelps, initiated a legal action against the Illinois Central Railroad Company seeking compensation for the value of his horse, which was killed by a passenger train while the train was in motion. Phelps claimed that the train ran over his horse, which had run onto the track after the train had begun moving from the station where it had stopped to take on wood. Initial rulings had been in favor of Phelps at lower courts, including a judgment from a justice of the peace and a subsequent appeal in the Circuit Court, leading to a judgment that also favored Phelps. Following these rulings, the railroad company appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, contesting the liability for the horse's death and the circumstances surrounding the incident.	Phelps claimed that the railroad company was negligent in its operation, specifically for failing to ring the bell or sound the whistle as required at road crossings. He argued that this negligence directly contributed to the accident, resulting in the loss of his horse. Phelps sought damages for the value of his horse based on the assertion that the company failed to fulfill its legal duty, thus warranting compensation for the injury incurred.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that it could not be held liable for negligence due to the specific circumstances of the accident, such as the location where the incident occurred, which was not a designated crossing where fencing was required. The company argued that the engineer was not negligent and had acted appropriately while the horse was on the track. They also highlighted that there was insufficient evidence linking the failure to ring the bell or sound the whistle to the horse's death, as the injury did not occur at a crossing. Given these points, the company requested that the court reverse the lower court's judgments in favor of Phelps.

James Painter (Appellant) sued Jacob Baker (Appellee) in 1854 following an incident involving Painter's horse being killed. The events took place on a field that both Baker and another individual, Mr. Moore, were cultivating separately. They were responsible for maintaining the fence around the field. In the spring of 1854, a cow owned by Baker breached a poor section of this fence, allowing Painter's horses to enter the field. Although Painter's horses were initially removed, they returned and were pursued by Baker's dog, leading to one of the horses being killed while attempting to escape over the fence. Witnesses testified on the sequence of events, some stating that Baker had commanded his dog to chase the horses. The primary issue centered around whether to classify the case as trespass or a case of consequential harm and the adequacy of jurisdiction held by the justice of the peace.	Painter claimed that Baker was responsible for the death of his horse due to negligence in maintaining the fence. He sought damages amounting to $95, asserting that Baker's actions directly led to the injury and death of his horse.	Baker contended that the proper form of remedy should be classified as a case and not as trespass, indicating that the injury resulted from consequential actions rather than immediate hostility. He argued that the circuit court had correctly identified the nature of the action, thus requesting dismissal of Painter's claims.

In 1850, in Jefferson County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between James Woods (the plaintiff) and David Dial (the defendant). Woods had an agreement with Dial regarding a trade valued at forty dollars for improvements made on Congress land. This agreement was verbal (parol) and lacked detail, omitting specifics like the nature of trade goods, timing, or place of delivery. Woods brought a lawsuit against Dial to recover the forty dollars after Dial vacated the premises in the spring. The initial case was heard by a jury in the Circuit Court of Jefferson County, where Woods won a judgment for the full amount and costs. Dial appealed the decision, resulting in this case being brought before the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, James Woods, claimed that he was entitled to recover the sum of forty dollars based on the verbal agreement made with David Dial. Woods argued that a proper demand for the trade value should not have been required before bringing the lawsuit and that he had fulfilled his obligation by initiating the claim. He sought a judgment in his favor for the amount specified in the original agreement.	The defendant, David Dial, contested the lawsuit by asserting that Woods had not made a proper demand for the trade owed to him prior to litigation, which was necessary for such a contract. Dial argued that without a specific demand, Woods had no grounds to recover the claimed amount. Dial requested the court to acknowledge this lack of demand and to uphold the motion for a new trial on these grounds.

Clara H. Bangs and her husband, Isaac W. Bangs, were involved in a legal dispute with John J. Brown and other heirs over the partition of a tract of land formerly belonging to John Brown. The case was initiated in 1885 in Illinois. John Brown had conveyed the property to his wife, Sarah Brown, prior to his death in 1854. When Sarah died in 1881, the property was to be divided among their heirs. Clara H. Bangs, who lived on the property with her mother, claimed entitlement to rental payments and additional compensation for caring for Sarah. The crux of the case revolved around the validity of the deed from John to Sarah, which was contested by John J. Brown, alleging it was void. The court found that all heirs had accepted the deed's validity during Sarah's lifetime, impacting the rights to the estate and rents.	The plaintiffs, consisting of the heirs of Sarah Brown, argued for a partition of the property and claimed rents from Clara H. Bangs, as they sought to adjust her interests for the income generated from the property since Sarah’s death. Clara H. Bangs countered, requesting compensation for boarding and taking care of her mother, asserting this should be charged against the inheritance due to other heirs.	The defendants, Clara H. Bangs and her husband, contested the legitimacy of the deed transferring the property from John to Sarah, claiming it was void at law. They sought to hold John J. Brown accountable for rents collected from lot 7, asserting that the income from it belonged to all heirs. Furthermore, they argued for the right to be compensated for the caregiving services provided to Sarah Brown during her final years.

In September 1868, Benjamin Hartley filed a legal action against his brother, Zenas Hartley, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a circuit court in Woodford County, presided over by Judge S. L. Richmond. The case was an action of assumpsit, which means it was a claim for breach of a contract, where Benjamin sought to recover a judgment amounting to $25. The proceedings at the higher court examined the validity and evidence surrounding the original judgment that favored Benjamin. The Chief Justice, Mr. Breese, noted that the case was minor and suggested it should not have escalated to this level; however, he affirmed that the evidence supported the original verdict and no errors were found in the court instructions. The court indicated that they would not interfere with the lower court's ruling.	Benjamin Hartley claimed that he was owed $25 due to a breach of contract by Zenas Hartley. He sought to have the decision of the lower court upheld in his favor, as he had already obtained a judgment against his brother for the specified amount. Benjamin's appeal was based on the assertion that the original verdict was justified and supported by proper evidence.	Zenas Hartley, through his attorney John Clark, did not present specific defenses detailed in the case summary but likely aimed to contest the validity of the original judgment and the implied assertion that he owed the plaintiff. His request would have been for the higher court to overturn the lower court's ruling for lack of substantial evidence.

Edwin E. Kendall v. Samuel A. Brown is a legal case decided in September 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The background of the case involves Samuel A. Brown, who sought treatment for a fractured leg from Edwin E. Kendall, a physician and surgeon. Brown was treated for approximately 29 to 30 days, during which Kendall visited daily except for one or two days. Brown claimed that due to Kendall's unskillful and careless treatment, his leg became shortened by one and a half inches, resulting in significant pain and loss of function. The case revolves around the quality of medical care provided, with a marked conflict in evidence regarding whether Kendall's treatment caused the leg's shortening. The trial court had ruled in favor of Brown, awarding him $1,375.17 in damages. Kendall appealed this verdict, resulting in a legal examination of the professional standards of care expected from a surgeon and the circumstances under which he could be found liable.	The plaintiff, Samuel A. Brown, claimed that Edwin E. Kendall provided unskillful treatment for a fractured leg, which resulted in his leg becoming significantly shortened, causing him pain and a loss of function. Brown's primary legal argument was that Kendall's negligent care directly led to these damages, and he sought compensation for the injury sustained due to this alleged medical malpractice.	The defendant, Edwin E. Kendall, argued that he should not be held liable for Brown's injuries as the shortening of the leg was not necessarily due to his treatment but could have resulted from the natural progression of the injury or the conditions surrounding it. Kendall contended that he adhered to the standards of medical care expected of a surgeon, and any extension of the limb required could not have been safely applied before the bony union started to take place. He requested the court to recognize that the circumstances of the case precluded his liability for the injury claimed.

The case of The Supreme Council of Royal Templars of Temperance v. Amanda A. Curd took place in Charleston, Illinois, with the decision rendered on September 27, 1884. Daniel Curd applied for membership in the Supreme Council of Royal Templars of Temperance on November 26, 1881, committing to uphold a pledge of total abstinence and comply with the organization's regulations. Upon approval, he received a beneficiary certificate naming Amanda A. Curd as the beneficiary. On June 26, 1882, charges were levied against him for violating his pledge by being intoxicated. However, before the charges could be addressed, Curd died on July 5, 1882. The trial in question debated whether the evidence of his alcohol consumption, which breached his pledge, could be used to deny Amanda Curd's claim to the beneficiary fund. The circuit court did not allow such evidence, leading to an appeal regarding whether this exclusion affected the outcome of the case.	Amanda A. Curd, as the plaintiff, argued that she was entitled to the beneficiary funds promised in the certificate issued to her deceased husband, Daniel Curd. She contended that despite the claims of his alcohol use, her husband had not been formally tried or expelled for any infractions, and thus she should recover the amount stipulated in the certificate.	The defendant, the Supreme Council of Royal Templars of Temperance, argued that Daniel Curd's violation of his pledge of total abstinence amounted to a forfeiture of his rights under the beneficiary certificate. They asserted that the conditions of the certificate clearly indicated that any such violation, regardless of formal charges or conviction, disqualified Amanda A. Curd from receiving the specified death benefits.

The case of David L. Hough v. John Hastings took place in La Salle County, Illinois, and culminated in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1857. The underlying dispute arose from Hough's action of ejectment, wherein he aimed to recover a specific piece of land (the southwestern quarter of Section 15, Township 33 North, Range 1 East of the 3rd Principal Meridian) that he claimed in fee simple. The complaint was filed during the November term of the La Salle Circuit Court in 1856. The defendant, Hastings, responded by pleading the general issue. The case proceeded to trial without a jury by mutual agreement and was overseen by Judge Hollister. During the trial, Hough presented evidence including a judgment record from a county court related to taxes from 1851. However, the judgment was found to have procedural deficiencies, particularly regarding the administration of oaths by the town collector and the lack of an official meeting between key town officials—essentially depriving Hough of the legal rights associated with contesting the tax assessment. Testimony revealed that the necessary notifications and meetings for tax assessments had not occurred, which played a crucial role in the circuit court's findings.	David L. Hough, the plaintiff, argued that the tax judgment record and subsequent actions taken to collect the taxes on the disputed land were invalid due to non-compliance with the relevant statutes. Specifically, he contended that the oath taken by the town collector was improperly administered before the county clerk, rather than before the county treasurer or a justice of the peace as mandated. Furthermore, Hough claimed he had not been given the right to a hearing with the assessors and other officials empowered to review the tax assessment, which he argued rendered him unlawfully deprived of his property rights.	John Hastings, the defendant, maintained that the procedural steps taken regarding the tax assessment and collection were valid. He argued that Hough had not met his burden of proving that the necessary procedural law had not been complied with, insisting that the tax-related documents presented were sufficient to establish Hastings' rightful claim to the property. Hastings sought to reinforce his defense by providing evidence showing that he had paid the taxes on the land in question for the year 1856 and argued against Hough's claims of improper procedural conduct.

Nathaniel Buckmaster and Evans initiated legal actions against Zephaniah B. Job in Madison County, Illinois, in December 1853. The plaintiffs sought to recover a statutory penalty for the alleged unauthorized cutting of trees on a tract of land, as well as to reclaim cord-wood made from those trees through an action of replevin. During the proceedings, the plaintiffs needed to establish their title to the land on which the trees were cut. They provided evidence of a chain of title that included deeds executed by Joseph Bartlett, Rufus Easton, and John Finley, with the oldest deed dated September 12, 1814. The court, however, excluded certain deeds and copies of deeds from being presented as evidence, concluding that the acknowledgment of one crucial deed did not conform to the statutory requirements. As a result, the jury found in favor of the defendant, Job, and the initial judgments were rendered against Buckmaster and Evans.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to recover damages for the unauthorized cutting of trees on their land and the restitution of the cord-wood derived from those trees. They sought to prove their ownership of the land through a series of recorded deeds and requested the court permit the introduction of certain deed copies as evidence to support their claims.	The defendant contended that the plaintiffs failed to provide valid evidence of their title to the land as the critical deed’s acknowledgment did not meet statutory requirements. Job argued that the plaintiffs could not adequately prove the authenticity of their claimed ownership necessary for the court to rule in their favor, and he requested the court to exclude the evidence presented by the plaintiffs.

In November 1849, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of James Marshall (plaintiff in error) vs. Nathan Adams, for the use of John M. Ogleby (defendant in error). The action involved a debt dispute related to five sealed promissory notes executed by John W. Roach and James Marshall, which were to be paid to Nathan Adams, who was serving as guardian for the minor heirs of James Blair, deceased. The initial trial took place during the August term of 1848, where the jury found in favor of Adams, awarding him $550.92. Marshall contended that the notes were paid off by Roach prior to the transfer of interest to Adams. During the trial, the court admitted certain evidence and testimonies that Marshall argued were inappropriate, including the admission of the administrator of Roach, which he claimed could not bind him. The jury’s decision led to Marshall seeking to reverse the judgment based on the grounds that evidentiary procedures were incorrectly followed and that the admissions of the co-defendant (the administrator) should not have been permitted as binding evidence against him.	James Marshall claimed that the promissory notes in question had been paid by John W. Roach during his lifetime and therefore should not be enforceable by Nathan Adams. He sought to have the previous judgment against him overturned on the basis of improper evidence being admitted at trial, specifically the claims made by the administrator of Roach and the lack of proper substantive evidence that the notes belonged to Adams in his representative capacity as guardian.	Nathan Adams contended that the notes were validly executed and not paid off by Roach before his death. He argued that the evidence presented, including the testimonies and probate records, substantiated his claim to collect the debt based on the written agreements. Adams maintained that the legal framework allowed for the admissions of an administrator to bind the estate and that the notes themselves were rightfully his as guardian.

The case "Gurdon Hewitt et al. v. Charles Dement et al." took place in September 1870, in Illinois, specifically in Ogle and Stephenson counties. The key individuals involved are Gurdon Hewitt, the lender, and Charles Dement, the borrower. The dispute arose from a loan transaction whereby Hewitt loaned $5,000 to Dement, secured by a trust deed on certain real estate. The plaintiffs filed a bill in equity seeking to restrain the sale of the property, alleging that the sale was set to occur for more than what was legally or equitably due to Hewitt. They claimed that the loan involved usurious practices, and thus a deduction should be made concerning the interest owed. After being heard in the circuit court, the issue was moved to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the plaintiffs contended errors in the previous court's findings, particularly regarding the determination of usury and the pertinent account details between the parties.	The plaintiffs, led by Gurdon Hewitt, argued that the loan transaction was usurious and sought to restrain the impending sale of the real estate serving as collateral. They requested that an accounting take place to properly ascertain the amount owed, emphasizing that the original amount stipulated was not fully disbursed and should be adjusted to account for any usury present in the loan agreement.	Charles Dement, the defendant, contended that the court erred in its findings related to usury, asserting that all transactions were proper and within legal bounds. The defense challenged the allowance of amendments to the plaintiffs' bill, arguing they prejudiced the case and claimed no usury existed in their agreement, as the financial arrangements had been appropriately structured.

The case "George Hunt, Attorney General, et al. v. Vimeria Fowler et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 17, 1887. It originated in the Circuit Court of LaSalle County, presided over by Judge Dobkance Dibell. The case involved a legal dispute concerning the estate of Esther S. Chapman, who had passed away, leaving behind both real and personal property. At the heart of the contention was the residuary clause in Chapman's will and a subsequent codicil she executed on April 5, 1885. The codicil directed that the residue of her estate be distributed among "the worthy poor of the city of La Salle," but plaintiffs argued that there were no established mechanisms in the city for such distribution, rendering the clause ineffective. The heirs-at-law of Chapman sought to have the court declare the estate to be intestate due to the ambiguity in the will's provisions regarding charitable trust. The Attorney General and the executors of the will contested this claim, maintaining that the will was valid and enforceable. The lower court found in favor of the plaintiffs, declaring the clause void due to vagueness. This judgment was then appealed by the Attorney General, executors, and some legatees.	The plaintiffs, heirs-at-law of Esther S. Chapman, claimed that the residuary clause from the codicil was incapable of execution due to the uncertainty regarding its beneficiaries. They argued that since there was no existing structure or entities in La Salle to distribute funds to the designated group, the clause was void and should not be followed. They sought court recognition that the estate should be treated as intestate property and distributed among them as heirs.	The defendants, including the Attorney General and the estate's executors, contended that the residuary clause was valid and enforceable. They argued that the language of the will, while possibly vague, did not invalidate the entirety of the estate's distribution plan. They maintained that the court had the authority to appoint a trustee to carry out the charitable distribution effectively, and even if the initial clause was found invalid, the remaining estate could still be distributed according to the will's terms.

On October 5, 1870, Walter Treleaven borrowed $6,000 from Edward Morrell, executing a promissory note and a deed of trust on certain real estate owned by his wife, Jane Treleaven, as security for the loan. The note was later acquired by Charles H. Morrell, who died after obtaining the note. The note remained unpaid at maturity, leading the trustee to sell the property to Alexander J. D. Dixon and Fitz Eugene Dixon, the executors of Charles H. Morrell’s estate. Jane Treleaven subsequently filed a bill against Alexander J. D. Dixon to set aside this sale, claiming that the loan's repayment term was extended through a contract between her husband and Morrell, which she contended was without her consent, thus extinguishing the trust deed as security. The court was tasked with determining the credibility of the evidence presented, particularly regarding the potential incompetence of Walter Treleaven as a witness, due to the nature of the case involving the estate of a deceased creditor.	Jane Treleaven's primary argument was that the sale of her property by the trustee should be invalidated because it was based on a promissory note whose repayment term had been extended through an agreement between her husband and Morrell, made without her consent. She maintained that this extension released the deed of trust, which should accordingly render the sale void.	Alexander J. D. Dixon contended that the sale of the property was valid, arguing that Jane Treleaven had no legal basis to set aside the sale since the only evidence supporting her claim came from her husband, who he argued was an incompetent witness due to the circumstances of defending as the executor of a deceased individual. Dixon emphasized that the lack of admissible evidence supporting Treleaven's claims warranted dismissal of the case.

Chester Carpenter filed an appeal against John Ambroson in April 1858, following a judgment rendered against him by a justice of the peace in McHenry County, Illinois. The case originated from a financial dispute in which Ambroson claimed that Carpenter owed him money related to various transactions that took place in the spring of 1852. Carpenter had sold Ambroson a yoke of steers for $28, provided hay valued at $6, and Ambroson had also performed prairie breaking for Carpenter, amounting to $10.63. A note for $48 was held by Ambroson as an agent for Carpenter's brother, Daniel Carpenter, who had traveled to California. There was a disagreement about how the payments for the steers and additional services should be applied to the debt and interest owed. The jury ultimately found in favor of Ambroson, awarding him $52.02, which Carpenter contested in his appeal.	The plaintiff, John Ambroson, claimed that Chester Carpenter owed him money resulting from the sale of cattle and other services rendered. He asserted that there was an agreement to apply the proceeds from the transactions toward the outstanding debt that Carpenter had with Daniel Carpenter, which was represented by the note held by Ambroson. Ambroson sought to have the court uphold the jury's decision and enforce the claim for payment against Carpenter.	Chester Carpenter contended that the court made errors in excluding crucial evidence regarding previous arrangements and conversations about the debt settlement. He argued that the jury's finding was not supported by evidence, as he believed that the amounts owed should not have been applied in the manner that Ambroson claimed. Carpenter sought a new trial on these grounds, believing the verdict was unwarranted.

This case, "Lionel W. Richardson v. William H. Gregory," was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court and decided on November 15, 1888. The partnership between Richardson and Gregory was formed on June 23, 1870, for manufacturing and selling plows under a patent that Richardson had applied for. Though the patent was not yet issued, both partners agreed that Gregory would provide up to $10,000 in capital, to be repaid with interest, while profits would be distributed with Richardson receiving nine-sixteenths and Gregory seven-sixteenths. The partnership required equal sharing of expenses and stipulated that financial settlements would occur twice a year. However, by January 1873, the firm ceased active operations, later issuing a license to a third party, Thompson. By 1876, the partnership had effectively abandoned plow manufacturing. The crux of the dispute arose from Richardson's claims that Gregory failed to account for funds belonging to the partnership. Gregory asserted that the firm was dissolved by mutual consent after a settlement in May 1878, which Richardson disputed. The court had to determine whether the partnership had indeed dissolved and if the claims were barred by the statute of limitations.	Richardson, the appellant, claimed that the partnership with Gregory had not been dissolved and sought an accounting for funds he alleged Gregory refused to disclose. He argued that he was entitled to his fair share of the partnership assets and profits that had not been settled. Richardson contended that mistakes were made during previous settlements and sought judicial intervention to rectify these purported errors.	Gregory, the appellee, acknowledged the existence of the partnership but contended that it was officially dissolved following a comprehensive settlement in May 1878, where all assets were divided and the business ceased. He invoked the statute of limitations as a defense, maintaining that more than five years had lapsed since the dissolution before Richardson filed his claim, which barred him from seeking relief.

Henry H. Carr, the Plaintiff in Error, and William Waugh, the Defendant in Error, were involved in a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1862. The conflict arose in Putnam County, Illinois, where Waugh, as a judgment creditor of James S. Simpson, initiated garnishment proceedings against Carr. The garnishee process was based on a lease agreement between Carr and Simpson, in which Carr was to pay Simpson $4 per acre for land rented to raise crops. The lease covered approximately 19.75 acres. However, it became evident that Simpson had assigned the lease to A. H. Turner on the same day it was executed. The case included testimonies about the lease and its assignment, including discussions about whether Carr understood the assignment and its implications. The lower court found Carr indebted to Simpson and ruled against him, leading to Carr appealing the decision to the higher court.	The plaintiff's primary argument was that the garnishee (Carr) was indebted to the judgment debtor (Simpson) based on the lease agreement. Waugh claimed that despite the lease assignment to Turner, Carr still owed money as stipulated in the lease. Waugh maintained that the court should enforce the garnishee process and require Carr to pay the determined amount of $78.66 to satisfy Simpson's debt.	Carr contended that the assignment of the lease to Turner conveyed an equitable interest that protected him from the garnishee process initiated by Waugh. Carr argued that he was not informed of the assignment at the time of the garnishment, and therefore, was not liable to pay the rent directly to Waugh. He also raised several procedural complaints regarding the lower court's handling of the case, including the denial of his motions for discharge and new trial, claiming the judgment against him was improper and invalid.

The case of Watson Trowbridge et al. v. John Seaman took place in the Circuit Court of Adams County, Illinois, in June 1858. The plaintiffs, Watson Trowbridge and others, were involved in a legal dispute with the defendant, John Seaman, concerning several promissory notes. These notes, made on June 1, 1857, were each for $500, payable in currency with interest. The notes were due on different dates between October 1857 and February 1858 and had been assigned to Seaman by a third party, John B. Bennett. The plaintiffs did not appear in court when summoned more than ten days prior to the June term and default judgment was entered against them, leading to the clerk assessing damages amounting to $2,762.50. The appellants challenged the court’s authority to have the clerk assess damages instead of a jury.	The plaintiff, John Seaman, claimed damages based on several promissory notes that Trowbridge and others had issued to John B. Bennett, which were later assigned to him. Seaman argued that the notes were legally binding obligations for payment in currency, which had considerable value at the time they were due.	The defendants, Trowbridge and others, contended that the assessment of damages by the clerk was improper, asserting that damages should have been determined by a jury. They challenged the manner in which the judgment by default was rendered and the damages were assessed following their non-appearance in court.

In June 1886, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Lyman Everingham et al. v. Edward A. Lord emerged from a dispute concerning a sale of corn made by sample. The key individuals involved were plaintiff Lyman Everingham and defendant Edward A. Lord, both members of the Chicago Board of Trade. The plaintiffs alleged that the corn, sold under the express warranty that the bulk would equal the sample, did not meet this standard upon delivery. The sale was conducted with the corn shipped to Cessna Station, Pennsylvania, where the controversy over whether the corn matched the quality of the sample arose. The plaintiffs claimed that there was confusion regarding a customary requirement on the Board of Trade that corn sold by sample must be inspected and rejected within 24 hours if found faulty; failure to do so would indicate acceptance of the corn as-is. The trial court's ruling on this custom and the warranty's nature became the focal point of the case.	The plaintiffs argued that their warranty claimed by the seller distinctly assured that the bulk of the corn would equate to the sample shown. They contended the court improperly dismissed evidence of customary practices related to sales by sample and erroneously instructed the jury that such custom could not negate an express warranty. The plaintiffs sought damages for the breach of warranty regarding the quality of the corn.	The defendant maintained that a customary practice existed on the Chicago Board of Trade mandating inspection and rejection of corn within 24 hours post-sale. The defendant argued that, upon failure to do this, the plaintiffs accepted the corn and could not later claim a breach of warranty. They requested that the court allow the introduction of the custom as evidence that would affirm the validity of their defense and negate the breach claims made by the plaintiffs.

In the case of Chicago, St. Louis & Pittsburg Ry. Co. v. Welsh, which occurred in Chicago on July 28, 1886, the plaintiff, a seven-year-old girl, suffered a serious injury while playing near the defendant's freight cars. These cars were located at the end of a side-track that terminated close to May Street, with no safety barriers to prevent cars from rolling onto the street. At the time of the incident, the plaintiff was playing on the sidewalk with a friend when employees of the railway company drove additional freight cars onto the side-track. This caused a collision that resulted in one of the cars rolling off the track and running over the plaintiff, leading to severe injuries that necessitated the amputation of her leg. During the trial, a jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding her $5,000 in damages. The defendant presented evidence suggesting she was not on the street but rather playing further away on their property, but the jury's determination favored the plaintiff's account. The court deemed the jury's finding justified based on the evidence presented, considering the plaintiff's young age and her family's circumstances, which limited their ability to supervise her.	The plaintiff claimed that the railway company was negligent in allowing freight cars to be operated in a manner that jeopardized the safety of children playing near the tracks. She sought damages for her personal injuries, specifically highlighting that the lack of barriers and the reckless operation of the train cars directly led to her severe injury, requiring amputation.	The defendant contended that the plaintiff exhibited contributory negligence by playing on or near the railway's right of way, suggesting she was at a considerable distance from the street and engaged in potentially dangerous behavior, such as collecting coal pieces. The defense argued that the circumstances of the incident were misconstrued and that the plaintiff's actions contributed to her injury.

The case, "The Franklin Savings Bank v. Julia S. Taylor," was decided on January 21, 1890, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute involved property located in Chicago, Illinois, that once belonged to Frank C. Taylor and his wife, Maria L. Taylor. On June 13, 1871, the Taylors conveyed their property to Ira Scott in trust, which established terms for managing the property. Frank C. Taylor later took out a mortgage for property improvements, but this mortgage was subsequently released. After a fire destroyed the original trust deed records, the Taylors petitioned the court to restore the trust deed in 1873, which was granted. Julia S. Taylor, wife of George Taylor, took possession of a portion of the property (sub-lot 3) in April 1873, and the Taylors subdivided the main lot a few months later. The Franklin Savings Bank became involved after the Taylors executed mortgages on their sub-lots. Subsequent petitioning for mechanic’s liens by various contractors, including Henry Gilsdorff and F. and E. Bauman, complicated matters, particularly as Julia S. Taylor was not made a party in these proceedings. Ultimately, the Franklin Savings Bank acquired a certificate of purchase after the foreclosure of the mortgages but faced legal challenges regarding the validity of that purchase, leading Julia S. Taylor to seek the removal of a cloud on her title due to the bank's claims.	Julia S. Taylor, the plaintiff, argues that she holds rightful ownership of sub-lot 3, which she claims was improperly encumbered by deeds executed without her consent in relation to the Franklin Savings Bank’s claims. She contends that she was not a party to the mechanic’s lien proceedings and never authorized her husband to represent her in these legal matters. Therefore, she requests the court to set aside the sale of sub-lot 3 and declare the bank's claims void, asserting that the sale created a cloud on her title.	The Franklin Savings Bank, as the defendant, contends that the mechanics' liens established by Gilsdorff and Baumans were valid and that Julia S. Taylor was bound by the actions of her husband, George Taylor, who acted as her representative in these proceedings. The bank argues that the mortgage agreements and subsequent foreclosure were legally sound and that they acquired rights through the appropriate legal channels. Their request is to uphold the validity of their claims over the property and maintain the sale as executed.

On July 31, 1869, in Chicago, Illinois, Emma Gilbert delivered a package to the American Merchants’ Union Express Company, intending to send it to herself in New York. The package was enclosed in a standard money envelope and was supposed to contain $1000. After being transported, the package reached New York on August 2, 1869. When Gilbert later retrieved the package on August 28, it was discovered to be open at one end, containing only newspaper slips cut into the shape of banknotes, rather than the expected money. During the trial, evidence emerged linking the paper used in the package to a specific batch from the Illinois Central Railroad Company's office, where it had been prepared. The trial resulted in a verdict for Gilbert, prompting the express company to appeal on grounds including improper evidence handling and inadequate support for the verdict.	Emma Gilbert claimed that the American Merchants’ Union Express Company lost her package containing $1000, which she had delivered for transport. She argued that the company, as a common carrier, failed in its duty to safeguard the contents of the package and should be held liable for the alleged loss. Gilbert sought restitution for the claimed amount.	The American Merchants’ Union Express Company contended that the evidence presented did not clearly support Gilbert's claim. They argued that certain portions of witness testimony should have been excluded, as it was deemed irrelevant and prejudicial to their case. The company maintained that there was insufficient proof that they were responsible for any loss, asserting that any potential tampering or mishandling occurred outside their control.

In September 1872, the case of William M. Kelgour v. John Wood was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a dispute over property possession in Whiteside County, Illinois. The plaintiff, William M. Kelgour, sought to recover possession of land from the defendant, John Wood, through an ejectment action. The central issue in this case revolved around property titles derived from the same source. Kelgour introduced evidence of a deed from Bressler, the common source of title, and a subsequent chain of deeds regarding past ownerships and litigations against Brink and others, which led to his claim on the property. In contrast, the defendant, John Wood, presented a mortgage deed from Bressler on the same property, along with foreclosure proceedings that resulted in a sale to a third party and a subsequent chain of title to himself. The court had to investigate whether the foreclosure decree was valid despite the absence of other interested parties not being named in the proceedings. The crux of the argument lay in the assertion that since subsequent purchasers were not made parties to the foreclosure, the foreclosure decree was void.	The plaintiff, William M. Kelgour, claimed that the foreclosure ruling was invalid because it excluded previous title holders, specifically Myers, and a judgment creditor who were not parties to the foreclosure, infringing on their rights. Kelgour argued that without the proper parties being included in the foreclosure proceedings, the decree could not genuinely affect the property, thereby asserting his legal entitlement to the land and requesting the court to recognize the invalidity of the foreclosure proceedings.	John Wood, the defendant, countered by asserting that the foreclosure proceedings were valid and legally sound, detailing that he acquired legal title through the foreclosure process in which all necessary parties had been included. Wood argued that the foreclosure did not void the rights of subsequent purchasers, maintaining that Kelgour, not being a party in the prior proceedings, had lost his chance to contest the ownership via ejectment. He requested the court to uphold his possession rights as the lawful titleholder of the property.

The case "Samuel Biggs et al. v. William A. Clapp et al." was adjudicated in September 1874, in the Illinois Supreme Court, focusing on a dispute involving construction contracts. The key individuals included the plaintiffs, Samuel Biggs and others, who were subcontractors, and the defendants, William A. Clapp and others, who were the property owners. The case arose after Clapp contracted with J.B. Smith & Son to construct a building for $13,300, with payments tied to construction milestones. Biggs and his associates supplied cut stone for the project, which resulted in a balance of $1,675 owed to them by Smith and Son. After Clapp made substantial payments to Smith and Son, the latter abandoned the project, forcing Clapp to spend an additional $5,500 to complete it. This led to Biggs filing a mechanic's lien against Clapp for unpaid dues. The jury ruled against Biggs, prompting an appeal focusing on the court's jury instructions related to the mechanic's lien law and the misinterpretation of the original contract.	The plaintiffs claimed that under the Illinois mechanic's lien statute, they were entitled to recover for the value of the materials they supplied, arguing that they should receive payment irrespective of the contract's original price, especially after the abandonment by the original contractor. They contended that their rights as subcontractors were disregarded when the jury was instructed that no payment exceeding the original contract amount was necessary.	The defendants maintained that they were not liable for additional payments exceeding the original contract amount following the abandonment by the primary contractor. They argued that the mechanic's lien law was properly interpreted, emphasizing that they had already paid a substantial sum and were not obligated to pay more than the original contract price for the building’s completion.

Phineas Oakes was involved in a legal dispute with Tiffany Ward and others in an action of debt based on a judgment previously obtained in the State of Ohio. The case took place in Gallatin, Illinois, with the trial occurring in May 1857. The defendants in error initiated the lawsuit against Oakes and a deceased individual named Cyrus Thayer, whose estate was implicated in the case. Oakes claimed that he should not be held liable because Thayer had died in New York prior to the lawsuit's commencement. The court had only served Oakes with process. The trial included testimonies regarding Thayer’s death and the circumstances surrounding it. Despite Oakes’ argument, the court ruled in favor of the defendants, awarding them damages of $1,568.99. However, the judgment was later challenged due to it being for more damages than originally claimed.	The plaintiff, Phineas Oakes, contended that he could not be sued alone for the debt as the co-defendant, Cyrus Thayer, was deceased at the time of the suit. Oakes attempted to present a plea in abatement, stating that since Thayer was dead, the suit should not proceed against him without the inclusion of Thayer's estate. Oakes argued that the evidence provided was insufficient to hold him liable for the damages claimed.	The defendants, Tiffany Ward et al., challenged Oakes’ plea in abatement, asserting that the case should proceed despite Thayer's death. They maintained that the judgment against Oakes was valid and provided the court with evidence of the debt owed based on the original judgment obtained in Ohio. They sought enforcement of that judgment and the awarded damages.

Samuel C. Orr v. E. M. Ward is a legal dispute that took place in 1873 in Illinois. The case involved Samuel C. Orr, the plaintiff, who was employed as a traveling salesman for the firm of Cleveland, Johnson & Company, represented by E. M. Ward, the defendant. Under a work contract agreed upon at the beginning of 1873, Orr was to be compensated a total of $4,500 over two years and was required to devote his entire attention to the company’s business. His employment continued until June 11, 1873, when the firm declared bankruptcy, leading to his discharge. Orr subsequently filed a suit seeking damages for being laid off, arguing that his employer should have retained him for a longer period based on the contract's terms. The defense claimed that the contract did not stipulate a specific duration of employment and that Orr had breached the contract by engaging in side activities unrelated to the firm. The court proceedings focused on interpreting the contract and whether Orr had met the terms before claiming damages.	Orr argued that he was entitled to damages due to being discharged prematurely from his employment with the firm, asserting that the defendant had an obligation to retain him for the duration of the contract. He contended that the contract should be construed to ensure job security for the agreed employment term and sought compensation for the loss of income during what he claimed to be an unjust termination.	The defendant argued that the contract did not specify a duration of employment, meaning there was no obligation to retain Orr for a specific period. The defense maintained that the firm could not be liable for damages related to employment cessation, especially since Orr had failed to fulfill his part of the contract by engaging in external business activities during his tenure, which justified the termination.

In the case of Samuel Dolton v. George H. Erb et al., the events trace back to 1851 when George H. Erb purchased a tract of land through Cockle, who was acting as the attorney for Jacquemart, the landowner. Erb paid the contract price but did not receive a deed for the land. After Jacquemart's death, Erb initiated legal action against the unknown heirs of Jacquemart in 1858, claiming he had paid for the land. The McDonough Circuit Court ruled in favor of Erb, and a deed was issued to him. He subsequently sold parts of the land to Walters and Crawford.
