In January 1867, Samuel Dolton, who claimed to be a purchaser from Jacquemart's heirs, filed a bill of review against Erb, Walters, and Crawford. Dolton's actions were based on alleged errors in the original decree, particularly the claim that the power of attorney was revoked due to Jacquemart's death before the sale. The case was heard based on the pleadings and evidence submitted, ultimately leading to the dismissal of Dolton's bill.	Samuel Dolton, as the plaintiff, claimed that the original sale made by Cockle on behalf of Jacquemart was invalid due to Jacquemart's death. He alleged that the power of attorney was revoked at that time and requested the court to review the original decree that favored Erb. Dolton aimed to assert his claim over the property he purchased from the heirs of Jacquemart, seeking to overturn the prior ruling that had granted Erb legal title to the land.	The defendants, including Erb, Walters, and Crawford, argued that they rightfully possessed the land under color of title and had maintained adverse possession for over seven years, including paying taxes on the property. They contended that Dolton's bill of review was filed too late, as nearly nine years had passed since the original decree and that the court should uphold their title based on these established facts.

On November 21, 1874, in Carlinville, Illinois, Herman Schaper purchased property from his mother, Caroline Schaper, and brother, Christian Schaper. The property included land and personal belongings that were originally owned by Herman's father, Christopher Schaper, who had passed away. In exchange for the property, Herman issued promissory notes totaling $8247. He executed a deed of trust on the real estate and a chattel mortgage on personal property to secure these debts. The deed of trust included Maria Schaper, Herman's wife, who purportedly relinquished her homestead rights. Maria later claimed that the execution of these documents was fraudulent and that she was unaware of what she was signing, leading to a lawsuit against Herman, Caroline, and Christian. The case explored the nature of the relationships and the intentions behind the transactions, revealing that there had been growing tensions between Maria and Caroline, which culminated in Maria feeling alienated and oppressed. Ultimately, the court had to evaluate conflicting testimonies regarding Maria's understanding of the documents she signed and whether fraud had indeed taken place.	Maria Schaper, the plaintiff, contended that the deeds and promissory notes executed by Herman were fraudulent. She alleged that Caroline and Herman intended to defraud her of her rights in the property and that her signatures were obtained through deception. Maria requested the court to cancel all the instruments executed during this transaction, aiming to restore her rights to the property as they existed prior to the transaction.	The defendants, Caroline and Herman Schaper, argued that Maria was fully aware of the contents of the documents she signed and did so of her own volition. They contended that Maria was informed and understood the implications of the deed of trust and the related transactions. The defense maintained that there was no fraudulent intent in the execution of the deed and asserted that they acted in a legitimate manner throughout the process.

The case "Joliet Iron and Steel Company v. Scioto Fire Brick Company" took place in September 1876 in Illinois. The dispute arose from an action of assumpsit based on a promissory note valued at $3,953. The Joliet Iron and Steel Company, as the plaintiff, claimed that the defendant, Scioto Fire Brick Company, had defaulted on this note. The defendant asserted that the plaintiff had previously sold a number of valuable railroad bonds that were placed as collateral for the note, which led to significant financial damages for the defendant. The plaintiff countered that they had given public notice about the auction of those bonds and ultimately sold them for $1,800. The defendant responded to the plaintiff's claims by demurring, leading to a judgment in favor of the plaintiff by the lower court. Dissatisfied, the defendant appealed the decision, prompting the case to reach the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Joliet Iron and Steel Company, argued that they rightfully sold the railroad bonds secured as collateral to satisfy the default on the promissory note. They maintained that proper public notice was provided and that the bonds were auctioned off, even though they did not fetch their full value. The plaintiff requested the court to uphold the lower court's judgment in their favor.	The defendant, Scioto Fire Brick Company, contended that the plaintiff acted improperly by selling the bonds without a special power allowing for the liquidation of the pledged collateral. They argued that the sale did not adhere to the legal requirements for handling pledged securities and claimed that they suffered substantial losses as a result. The defendant requested that the court reverse the lower court's decision.

Joseph R. G. Poole filed an appeal against Oliver C. Vanlandingham in December 1822 in Gallatin, Illinois, contesting a decision made in a debt action involving a promissory note. The case revolved around various pleas presented by both parties regarding the existence of consideration for the debt in question. Poole claimed that Vanlandingham owed him money based on a note, while Vanlandingham, in turn, raised multiple defenses, including that the note was executed without good consideration. The court had sustained a demurrer against five of the pleas raised by Vanlandingham, which led Poole to seek a reversal of that decision in the Illinois Supreme Court.	Poole's main argument was that Vanlandingham was liable for the debt stated in the promissory note. He challenged the defendant's pleas of lack of consideration and failure of consideration, asserting that the claims were insufficient and did not warrant dismissal of the action. Ultimately, Poole sought to have the lower court's judgment against him reversed and to proceed with his claims.	Vanlandingham's primary defenses included the pleas of "nil debet," stating that he did not owe the debt, and claims of lack of good consideration for the promissory note. He argued that the plaintiff had not met the burden of proof regarding the existence of consideration and that the allegations made in support of his defenses were adequate under state law. The defendant requested to sustain these defenses, asserting that the case against him should not proceed without proper substantiation of the debt.

In November 1850, in Edwards County, Illinois, William S. Burkett initiated a legal action against John Bond, claiming negligence in an incident involving a mare owned by Burkett. The animal had strayed into Bond's cornfield, and during an attempt to drive her out, Bond reportedly frightened the mare in such a way that she jumped over a fence, sustaining a broken thigh in the process. Witnesses testified that Bond had expressed a wish for the mare to break her neck while handling her roughly. The value of the mare was estimated by witnesses to be between forty and forty-five dollars. Burkett alleged that Bond's actions were negligent, leading to the mare's injury. The case was presented to a jury at the Edwards Circuit Court, which returned a verdict for the defendant, Bond. Burkett's subsequent motion for a new trial was denied, prompting him to appeal based on the admission of testimony deemed improper and the refusal of the court to give specific jury instructions.	The plaintiff, William S. Burkett, claimed that John Bond acted negligently and carelessly by improperly driving a trespassing mare out of his field, which resulted in the mare's injury and subsequent death. Burkett sought to recover damages for the mare's value and argued that the trial court erred in allowing certain testimony and in refusing to grant a new trial. He contended that the evidence presented was misleading and that Bond's actions were not those of a prudent individual.	The defendant, John Bond, argued that he acted within the bounds of reasonable behavior when attempting to drive the mare out of his cornfield. He contended that the mare was known to be "breechy," or prone to jumping fences, and that a prudent person might have acted in the same manner in such circumstances. Bond maintained that the trial court properly admitted evidence regarding the mare's character and that any errors alleged by Burkett did not warrant a new trial. His defense was based on the assertion that he was not negligent in his actions.

In the case of Mary J. Thompson et al. v. Charles H. Weeks, which took place in 1889 in New Lenox, Will County, Illinois, the plaintiff, Charles H. Weeks, initiated legal proceedings against the defendants, Mary J. Thompson and her husband, over a dispute regarding the excavation of sand and loam from their farm. The initial agreement, executed on October 6, 1886, granted Weeks the exclusive right to remove these materials for a term of three years. However, the contract specified that excavations should be limited to a certain area for the convenience of all parties involved and emphasized that changes to the area required consent from the Thompsons. Despite this, Weeks sought permission to excavate at a new point marked “C,” which he claimed was more suitable and profitable. The Thompsons denied this request, asserting that the contract did not permit excavation at that location without their consent. Eventually, Weeks commenced excavating at point “C” without approval, leading to a confrontation wherein the Thompsons attempted to stop the operations, prompting Weeks to seek an injunction from the court to prevent the Thompsons from interfering.	In his claims, Weeks argued that the Thompsons were interfering with his right to excavate the sand and loam as per their contract. He sought a legal injunction to restrain the Thompsons from preventing him and his workers from excavating at point “C” on their farm. Weeks claimed that such interference was causing him irreparable harm and asserted that he was entitled to excavate at that location under the terms of their agreement.	The Thompsons countered by asserting that Weeks did not have the right to excavate at point “C” without their explicit consent, as the contract clearly reserved the right to approve any changes in the excavation locations. They argued that Weeks's actions constituted unauthorized trespass and emphasized that a legal remedy was available to Weeks if he felt entitled to damages, thus contending that equity did not have jurisdiction in this matter.

Marianna Sontag v. Rosina Schmisseur et al. is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875. The case originated in St. Clair County, Illinois. It involved Marianna Sontag, the widow of a deceased man who owned real estate. Marianna claimed her rights as a widow under the homestead acts of 1851 and 1857, asserting that she deserved to retain the homestead worth $1000 in addition to her dower rights against her husband's heirs. The court below rejected her claim, leading her to appeal the decision. The primary legal question was whether a widow, who is the mother of the deceased’s heirs and lives in the deceased's homestead, is entitled to an additional claim on the homestead property against the heirs when the deceased left no debts.	The plaintiff, Marianna Sontag, argued that under the homestead acts of 1851 and 1857, she was entitled to a homestead worth $1000, in addition to her dower rights. She contended that the law should allow her to claim a homestead free from the heirs’ claims, as she was the widow of the deceased owner of the real estate and had no debts.	The defendants, Rosina Schmisseur et al., contended that the widow does not have the right to claim a homestead against the heirs in a partition proceeding. They argued that the statutes only exempt the homestead from forced sales or voluntary alienations involving the husband, and they asserted that the legislative intent did not include provisions for the widow to hold a homestead against the heirs.

In September 1872, Parker T. Putnam filed a lawsuit in the Illinois Supreme Court against John Traeger and his sureties, following an incident involving a constable's official bond. The case was initially heard in the Circuit Court of Peoria County, presided over by Judge Sabin D. Puterbaugh. The core of the dispute revolved around the alleged neglect of the constable to levy an execution that had been placed in his hands. Putnam claimed that the officer had failed to act upon an execution and thus caused the loss of a debt. However, during the trial, no actual execution was presented as evidence, nor was there an attempt to prove the contents of a potentially lost execution. The court scrutinized the statutory duties of the constable under sections of the Illinois Revised Statutes, emphasizing that the plaintiff bore the burden of proof to produce a valid execution to establish any liability on the part of the constable. The court concluded that without evidence of the execution or its validity, no neglect of official duty could be established.	Parker T. Putnam contended that John Traeger, as the constable, failed to properly levy an execution on property belonging to the defendant, resulting in the loss of a debt. He argued that there was a statutory responsibility for the constable to endorse and return the execution within specified timeframes, and his failure to do so warranted liability under the terms of the official bond.	John Traeger defended against Putnam's claims by asserting that the plaintiff had not produced the actual execution or demonstrated its contents due to its alleged loss. As a result, Traeger argued that without proof of a valid execution, he could not be held liable for any neglect or failure to act. Therefore, he contested that there was no breach of duty and requested that the court dismiss the claims against him.

In December 1852, the case of Elizabeth Shillinger v. George Jacob Shillinger was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated when George Jacob Shillinger filed for divorce in the circuit court of Morgan County, alleging that his wife, Elizabeth, had willfully abandoned him for over two years without reasonable cause. They married in Philadelphia in 1843 and lived together until 1848 when they agreed that she would stay in Philadelphia while he moved to Illinois to find a home for them. After settling in Cass County in October 1848, George informed Elizabeth of his location and requested her to join him, sending her money for her expenses. However, Elizabeth refused to move, stating she would never live with him again. Their separation continued, leading George to seek a divorce in 1852. The court proceedings involved a special master who took evidence and recommended that the divorce be granted based on his findings. However, Elizabeth challenged the divorce decree, leading to this appeal.	George Jacob Shillinger claimed that Elizabeth had abandoned him without justifiable cause for over two years, asserting that he had consistently invited her to come and live with him in Illinois. He argued that their separation was not due to any fault of his own and was seeking a divorce based on her refusal to reunite and her rejection of financial support offered to facilitate her move.	Elizabeth Shillinger contested the divorce, arguing that she did not unreasonably abandon her husband. She contended that their agreement allowed her to remain in Philadelphia until George sent for her. Additionally, she claimed that substantial evidence was lacking regarding her alleged refusal to move to Illinois, emphasizing that she had not been given a legitimate opportunity to join him.

In December 1842, the legal case Asa Holdridge v. Lewis Bailey was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a transaction dating back to February 1836, when Lewis Bailey (the plaintiff) claimed that Asa Holdridge (the defendant) executed a bond promising to convey a tract of land to him. The bond stipulated that if Bailey paid Holdridge $250 by February 1, 1838, Holdridge would transfer the property. Bailey argued that he paid the full purchase price, but Holdridge refused to convey the land. The bond, crucial to the case, was not presented as evidence in court, leading to a dispute over the bond's execution and the alleged payment. During the proceedings, Holdridge acknowledged signing a bond but could not recall its exact terms or confirm that it was correctly represented in Bailey's bill. The court ultimately decided that the bond needed to be properly submitted as evidence for a decree.	Bailey asserted that he fulfilled the conditions outlined in the bond by paying the agreed sum and therefore requested the court to compel Holdridge to convey the land in question to him. He maintained that the bond was a valid contract, which Holdridge had failed to honor.	Holdridge contended that he was unsure about the terms of the bond as recited by Bailey. He denied that payment had been adequately proven and argued that the bond was not sufficiently presented to the court, as it was not included in the record. He maintained that without the bond being produced, Bailey was not entitled to a decree for specific performance of the contract.

In September 1872, the Illinois Supreme Court was involved in the case of Western Union Railroad Company v. Wesley Fulton, stemming from a railroad crossing incident in Carroll County, Illinois. Wesley Fulton, the plaintiff, claimed that he suffered personal injuries and damage to his property due to the negligent operation of a train by the agents of the Western Union Railroad Company, the defendant. Fulton argued that the railroad failed to adhere to the requirements of an 1849 act mandating that trains must ring a bell or sound a whistle before reaching a public road crossing. The case was presided over by Judge W. W. Heaton, and the jury ruled in favor of Fulton, awarding him $500 in damages. The decision was based upon the jury's findings regarding negligence from both parties, and the applicability of the 1849 act to all railroads, including those chartered after its enactment.	Wesley Fulton claimed that the Western Union Railroad Company was negligent in the management of their train, leading to an accident at a public road crossing. He argued that the company failed to ring a bell or sound a whistle as required by the 1849 legislation, which he contended applied to all railroad companies in the state. Fulton sought damages for the injuries inflicted upon him and the damages to his property, asserting that the negligence on the part of the railroad led to the unfortunate incident.	The Western Union Railroad Company defended itself by arguing that the 1849 act regarding signaling at crossings did not apply to companies chartered after that date and sought to have the verdict overturned on these grounds. The defendant also claimed that Fulton was negligent, suggesting that he did not act in a reasonable manner in attempting to cross in front of the approaching train, which could limit their liability. Furthermore, they contended that the jury instructions provided were sufficient and that the damages awarded to the plaintiff were not excessive.

In December 1844, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case of John Anderson and Rodolph W. Paddleford against Edward B. Talcott. This action of replevin originated from the Kane Circuit Court, initiated by the plaintiffs who claimed that Talcott wrongfully seized their stock of goods. Talcott, acting as a deputy marshal for the United States, defended his actions by asserting that he seized the goods under a fieri facias associated with a debt owed by Cyrus K. Anderson. The plaintiffs contested the claim of belonging, arguing that the goods were their property and not the property of C. K. Anderson, who was a partner of Paddleford. The jury trial resulted in a verdict favoring the defendant, which prompted the plaintiffs to request a new trial, citing errors related to the admission of evidence and the jury's verdict being against the weight of the evidence.	The plaintiffs, John Anderson and Rodolph W. Paddleford, claimed ownership of the goods unlawfully seized by Edward B. Talcott. They requested the court to overturn the jury's verdict, arguing that the evidence supported their claim to the property. They maintained that the defendant’s justifications for taking the goods were insufficient and that the court had incorrectly allowed improper testimony to be admitted during the trial.	Edward B. Talcott defended against the replevin action by asserting that he seized the goods in accordance with a fieri facias issued on behalf of a judgment creditor, thereby claiming that the goods belonged to Cyrus K. Anderson and could be lawfully seized. Talcott contended that the plaintiffs failed to prove their ownership and effectively did not demonstrate any right to the property. He requested confirmation of the jury's verdict in his favor and sought to uphold the judgment based on the evidence presented during the trial.

In January 1875, the case of Ezekiel H. Palmer v. Thomas Gardiner et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following a series of legal proceedings originating in the DeWitt Circuit Court. The primary parties involved included Ezekiel H. Palmer (the appellant), who had signed a promissory note as surety for I. N. Mitchell, the principal borrower. The payee of the note, A. Mitchell, resided in Ohio, and after legal actions in Ohio, the note's validity was challenged by Palmer, arguing he was not the principal but merely a surety. The case escalated when the payee passed away, leading to the appeal regarding judgments obtained against Palmer. The specific contention by Palmer included claims of excessive land levies pertaining to judgments executed against him. The circuit court found against Palmer, dismissing his bill to enjoin the collection of the judgments. Palmer later appealed this dismissal, which led to a lengthy evaluation of procedural correctness and merits, including discussions on the legality of note ownership, the insufficiency of defenses presented, and the handling of appeals and judgments by the court.	Palmer argued that he was merely a surety on the promissory note and not the principal debtor. He sought to enjoin the collection of the judgments, claiming they were based on a defective legal standing since they originated from a note that was claimed to be invalid at the time of the suit. Additionally, he asserted that the execution on his land, approximately 1200 acres, was excessive. He requested that the court analyze the legitimacy and excessiveness of these levies.	The defendants, including Gardiner (the sheriff) and Gunn (executor of A. Mitchell's estate), argued that Palmer was indeed the principal debtor on the note and thus liable. They maintained that the judgments were valid and binding, and that Palmer failed to follow proper legal protocol in his appeal process. They contended that the issue of excessive levy was not a matter for equitable relief, and asserted that the courts traditionally do not intervene in such financial matters if the appropriate statutory remedies were not pursued.

In 1888, Robert T. Miller, the relator, along with other landowners, organized the Kaskaskia Drainage District in Champaign County, Illinois, under the Drainage Act of 1885. Miller owned eighty acres within this district, which had established and maintained a drainage system that was operational and satisfactory. However, other landowners in the Kaskaskia District sought to create another drainage district within its boundaries. Miller argued that these actions by the defendants, who were claiming to be drainage commissioners of this new district, were unlawful and that their organization was void. Miller initiated a quo warranto proceeding in the circuit court of Champaign County to contest the legality of this new drainage district formation. The circuit court sustained the defendants' demurrer, prompting Miller to appeal this decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Robert T. Miller, claimed that the formation of a new drainage district within the established boundaries of the Kaskaskia Drainage District was illegal. He sought a ruling to affirm the legality of the Kaskaskia Drainage District, asserting that the defendants, acting as drainage commissioners of the new district, were unlawfully exercising their powers.	The defendants contended that the establishment of a new drainage district was permissible under the provisions of the Drainage Act of 1885. They argued that the law allowed not only main districts but also sub-districts to be formed by the landowners within existing drainage districts, thus defending their actions as lawful.

The case of The Elgin Hydraulic Company v. The City of Elgin took place in September 1874, in Elgin, Illinois. The Elgin Hydraulic Company, whose stockholders owned a water power facility, brought an action against the City of Elgin seeking damages for costs incurred in removing debris (dirt, gravel, and refuse) from a raceway designed to transport water from a mill-dam to various mills and factories owned by the company's stockholders. The debris had accumulated as a result of a sewer constructed by the city, which discharged waste into the raceway. During trial proceedings, the jury was instructed by the court to find in favor of the defendant (the City of Elgin) after the plaintiff presented its evidence. This prompted the plaintiff to appeal the decision, arguing that they had a legitimate claim for damages despite not owning the raceway itself because they were tasked with its maintenance and restoration.	The Elgin Hydraulic Company contended that, as a corporation established for the purpose of maintaining the raceway leading to their mills, they had the right to sue for monetary damages. They argued that the city’s construction of the sewer, which led to the deposit of harmful debris in the raceway, obstructed water flow and caused financial detriment, requiring the company to expend $170 to remove the debris. The plaintiff maintained that the expenditure was a direct result of the city’s actions, and the company should be compensated for their incurred costs.	The City of Elgin asserted that the Elgin Hydraulic Company did not have a legal right to claim damages as the raceway was not owned by the company; therefore, they had no property interest in the raceway. The city argued that the company acted merely as an agent for repair, lacking the standing to file a lawsuit. Additionally, the defendant highlighted that any damages incurred were the responsibility of individual mill owners, and allowing the company to sue could lead to multiple lawsuits for the same injury.

In October 1850, Sylvester Emmons filed an ejectment action against Otho Bishop in the Adams Circuit Court, Illinois. The case was brought to trial on October 17, 1850, and the court rendered a judgment in favor of Bishop on the same day. Emmons did not successfully contest this judgment during the term that ended on October 30, 1850. Subsequently, on September 30, 1851, Emmons paid all accrued costs and filed a petition for a new trial, seeking to have the judgment vacated. The next court term commenced on October 21, 1851, where Emmons moved to have the judgment vacated, but the motion was denied due to a failure to apply for a new trial within the statutory timeframe. The court confirmed that the one-year period for filing a motion for a new trial began on the date of the original judgment, effectively making Emmons's motion untimely. The court emphasized the necessity for the motion to be made during the active term in which the judgment was issued.	Sylvester Emmons argued that he was entitled to a new trial based on the statutory provisions governing ejectment actions. He contended that he had paid all costs and damages associated with the prior judgment in favor of Otho Bishop, and he requested the court to vacate the earlier judgment and grant a new trial, asserting that the necessary legal conditions were met.	Otho Bishop maintained that the application for a new trial filed by Emmons was not timely according to statutory requirements. Bishop argued that the law stipulates that a motion must be made within one year of the judgment and that a mere petition to the court clerk did not suffice to fulfill the legal criteria for such a request. The defendant contended that since Emmons failed to act within the specified timeframe, the court lacked the authority to entertain the motion.

In the case "John Thomason v. John W. Clark," which originated in 1889 in White County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose regarding the collection of a balance owed on a joint promissory note. The note, executed by Hargrave, Thomason, and Stewart on January 4, 1881, for $153, was due one year later and bore interest at eight percent. Interest payments were made in full until January 4, 1886. A crucial development occurred on June 3, 1887, when Stewart paid a portion of the amount owed on the note and obtained an indorsement from Clark, expressing that the payment was "in full" for his part. This payment became a point of contention as both Thomason and Stewart were sureties on the note, combined with the knowledge that Hargrave, the principal, was insolvent. Disputes emerged regarding the interpretation of the indorsement and the implications of an alleged agreement among the sureties about prorating their payments and releasing each other from further liability. The case moved from a justice court to the Circuit Court, where the judgment favored the plaintiff, resulting in the defendant's appeal.	The plaintiff, John W. Clark, argued that a balance remained due on the promissory note that Thomason, as one of the sureties, was liable to pay. Clark contended that the indorsement made by Stewart did not constitute a release for Thomason. He maintained that an agreement existed where the sureties would pay half the amount due, and each would be freed from further liability upon payment. He sought to recover the unpaid balance from Thomason as part of this obligation.	The defendant, John Thomason, denied that he owed any further payments based on the indorsement signed by Stewart, which he interpreted as a release from liability. Thomason's defense centered on the assertion that the payment recorded on the note absolved him of additional responsibility, arguing that the Circuit Court incorrectly interpreted the legal implications of the indorsement and the context of the agreements among the co-sureties. He contended that the admission of certain conversations as evidence was erroneous and that prior claims of defense were overlooked.

Joseph Lovenguth brought a legal action against the City of Bloomington in the circuit court of McLean County in Illinois in January 1874. The case arose after Lovenguth's eighteen-year-old son, Emil, suffered an injury while passing over a sidewalk in the city. Emil was working at the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company and was on his way back to his boarding house when he stepped on a loose board on a defective sidewalk, which caused him to fall and fracture his ankle. Emil was familiar with the condition of the sidewalk, which he knew to be unsafe, yet chose to use it instead of an alternative, safer sidewalk available to him. Testimony presented during the trial indicated that Emil was in a hurry and may have been reckless, as he attempted to navigate the defective area rapidly. Ultimately, the jury’s verdict favored the city, indicating that Emil's own negligence contributed to his injury rather than any failure on the city's part to maintain the sidewalk.	The plaintiff, Joseph Lovenguth, claimed that the City of Bloomington was negligent for failing to maintain safe sidewalks, leading to his son’s injury. Lovenguth argued that the city should be held accountable for the damages incurred due to the hazardous conditions of the sidewalk. He sought a new trial after the jury found in favor of the city, asserting that the court had erred in its instructions to the jury and in refusing certain instructions he had proposed.	The City of Bloomington defended itself by arguing that Emil Lovenguth was aware of the sidewalk’s poor condition and chose to use it recklessly rather than taking a safer route. The city maintained that Emil’s actions, which included hurrying and attempting to jump over hazardous areas, were the primary cause of his accident. They contended that the plaintiff's claims were unfounded given that a safe alternative was available and that the verdict reflected the jury's correct assessment of the evidence presented.

In September 1867, in Chicago, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Alice B. Smith and Bartholomew Brown. Brown filed a lawsuit against Smith for goods sold and delivered, claiming she owed him a total of $862.60. During the proceedings, Brown presented evidence from a disinterested witness who testified that he had repeatedly presented the account to Smith and left it with her for review. Smith did not challenge the account at the time and allegedly promised payment on multiple occasions. In her defense, Smith contended that she had not received all the goods listed in the bill and claimed that her actual debt was only $585.65. After considering the testimony from both sides, the court ultimately favored Brown's claim and ruled in his favor for the entire amount he sought.	The plaintiff, Bartholomew Brown, contended that Alice B. Smith was liable for the full amount of $862.60 for goods that were sold and delivered to her. He presented evidence indicating that he had made multiple attempts to collect the debt, including presenting the account for her examination without objections from her side. He sought the total amount claimed based on his belief that Smith's promises to pay and lack of challenge to the account validated his claim.	The defendant, Alice B. Smith, argued that not all the items for which she was being charged had been delivered. She acknowledged owing some amount but insisted that it was only $585.65, rather than the full amount claimed by Brown. Smith’s defense relied on her assertion that the billing was inaccurate due to undelivered goods.

In the case of *Henry H. Gage v. Christian C. Busse et al.*, the legal dispute unfolded in Chicago, Illinois, around the year 1885. The case originated when Henry H. Gage, the appellee, initiated an equity bill against Christian C. Busse, the appellant, in an attempt to annul specific tax sales that Gage alleged were inappropriately levied by the city of Chicago. The initial proceedigs were influenced by a prior ruling from this court in 1882, which had previously favored Gage but was overturned due to erroneous terms related to the relief granted. Following the reversal, a second decree was made by the Superior Court, which was upheld by the Appellate Court, prompting Busse to appeal again. Central to the dispute was the issue of redemption from tax sales and whether the taxes included were valid. Specifically, the court had to examine the terms on which Gage could redeem the property and whether the prior county court judgments on tax sales were conclusive.	Henry H. Gage contended that the decrees to which he was subjected were flawed because they required payment based on illegally levied taxes. Gage sought to reverse the earlier tax sales and requested a fair redemption payment corresponding with the legitimate amount of taxes owed, exclusive of the illegal charges. He argued that the statutory right for redemption must be adhered to, which entails paying only the legal taxes plus the appropriate interest as outlined by the law.	Christian C. Busse defended against Gage's claims by asserting that the decree conformed to a prior opinion issued by the court regarding the necessary terms of redemption. He argued that the judgment in the county court should be considered conclusive and not subject to collateral attack, emphasizing that Gage's appeal should fail because the proper terms for redemption had not been violated, and all legal taxes included in the judgment were rightfully assessed.

E. C. Benefield v. James Albert took place in Lawrence County, Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court on April 22, 1890. The case involved an action of ejectment initiated by James Albert against E. C. Benefield to recover ownership of specific land tracts known as the Harrison land, totaling 608 acres. The land had historical ties dating back to a confirmation to William Henry Harrison from the governor of a territory in the early 19th century. Albert argued that he had established adequate title through evidence of prior possession by the heirs of John Cleves Symmes Harrison, the original party connected to the land. However, the plaintiff's attempt to present a deed related to this transfer was excluded by the court. The defense, on the other hand, contested claims related to tax deeds purporting to legitimize Albert's ownership. The court examined prior possession claims and legal documentation regarding the property’s title, alongside the defenses raised by Benefield regarding the validity of tax sales and procedural concerns in the partition process involving minor heirs. Ultimately, the remnant legal questions revolved around principles of ownership transfer and possession rights.	James Albert, the plaintiff, claimed that he had sufficient legal ground to recover the four locations of land using prior possession as evidence of ownership. He aimed to establish his entitlement through a chain of title linked to the heirs of John Cleves Symmes Harrison. Albert also sought to counter the defendant's title claims by introducing evidence of adherence to legal standards in property ownership, specifically surrounding partition proceedings that deemed his claims valid.	E. C. Benefield, the defendant, contended that the partition decree claiming ownership was void due to the failure to serve process on minor heirs involved. He relied heavily on a tax title, asserting that the sale claims accompanying the tax deeds were invalid due to improper notice of redemption timelines. Benefield maintained that procedural flaws fundamentally undermined the validity of the plaintiff's ownership claims, and sought dismissal of the ejectment action based on these arguments.

In the case of Sylvester Paddock v. Catharine Robinson, which took place in 1872, both parties were situated in Illinois. The action was a breach of promise of marriage, with Paddock (the plaintiff) claiming Robinson (the defendant) had promised to marry him. In the trial, the court allowed Paddock to present evidence of promises made during a time when both he and Robinson were already married to other individuals, a fact known to both parties. This situation raised significant ethical and legal questions regarding the validity of such promises made under conditions that were deemed to violate marital duties. The chief justice, Lawrence, emphasized that a contract formed under such immoral circumstances should not be recognized by the court due to its inherent conflict with societal norms and legal principles. Ultimately, the court found no precedent validating the enforcement of a promise made under these conditions and reversed the initial judgment.	Sylvester Paddock claimed that Catharine Robinson made a promise of marriage to him, entitling him to legal recourse due to her breach of that promise. He sought to establish that the promise was valid despite both parties being aware of their existing marriages, seeking compensation for the emotional and relational damages caused by her refusal to fulfill her promise.	Catharine Robinson argued that the promises of marriage she allegedly made to Paddock should not be considered valid because both parties were married at the time the promises were made. She contended that the nature of the promise was immoral and lacked legal standing. Robinson’s defense maintained that the plaintiff’s assertion should be dismissed as the contract was fundamentally flawed, and no legal obligation could arise from such an inherently corrupt agreement.

In April 1866, a trespass action was initiated by Elias H. Morse against George W. Iman in Henry County, Illinois, after Iman allegedly removed three loads of hay from land that Morse claimed as his own. The conflict arose over the usage rights of a tract of land that had been fenced and shared by Morse and a third party named Larson. Both Morse and Larson had an informal agreement regarding the use of the land, with each occupying designated portions (Morse the north half and Larson the south half) without a formal division. Larson granted Iman permission to cut grass from the land, but it was unclear which section was specified. The situation led to a disagreement over property rights and the legality of the hay removal. The case was initially tried before a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment for the plaintiff, Morse, which was appealed by Iman to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Elias H. Morse, claimed ownership of the hay that George W. Iman had cut from the land he occupied. Morse argued that his actual possession of the property entitled him to recover damages for the removal of his property, asserting that only the true owner of the land could grant permission to harvest resources from it. He requested the court to affirm the initial judgment in his favor.	The defendant, George W. Iman, contended that he acted under a license granted by Larson, who was a co-occupant of the land. Iman argued that the informal agreement between Morse and Larson did not legally restrict him from cutting the grass, as Larson had given him permission. He requested the court to uphold the judgment received in the lower court and dismiss Morse's claims.

In June 1874, in Cairo, Illinois, a case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court involving Anthony Hall, who was struck by a train operated by the Illinois Central Railroad Company. At the time of the incident, Hall was walking along the railroad tracks on Levee Street, which ran through the city. The railroad had two tracks in the area that were frequently used. An ordinance in place limited the maximum speed of trains within the city limits to six miles per hour, but there was conflicting testimony regarding the actual speed of the trains at the time of the accident. Hall, accompanied by three neighbors, attempted to avoid one train by stepping onto the other track where he was subsequently struck. Although warning bells were sounded, Hall and his companions did not notice the approaching trains until only a few yards away, partly due to wind conditions that obscured the sounds. The court noted that Hall could have avoided the accident by exercising more caution, as there were safer paths available.	Anthony Hall, the plaintiff, claimed damages for injuries sustained after being struck by a moving train on the railroad tracks. He argued that the railroad company was negligent, specifically alleging that the trains were being operated at an unlawful speed and failed to provide adequate safety measures for pedestrians.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company defended against the claims by arguing that Hall's own negligence contributed to the accident. They asserted that the trains were not exceeding the legal speed limit and highlighted that Hall could have used safer paths instead of walking directly on the tracks. The company contended that they gave appropriate warnings and did not act with recklessness.

The case "Consolidated Coal Company of St. Louis v. Mary Ann Schmisseur" arose in St. Clair County, Illinois, with the decision rendered on February 4, 1890. The central individuals involved were Mary Ann Schmisseur, the landowner, and the Consolidated Coal Company, which operated a coal mine. In March 1873, Schmisseur leased portions of her land to an entity called the Schuremans, allowing them to mine coal for thirty-five years while retaining ownership of the underlying coal. The lease granted the Schuremans access to eleven acres for mining operations. However, after some years, the Schuremans sold their interest to the Consolidated Coal Company, which began to mine coal from adjacent lands (owned by Ward and Krelich) through shafts and pits that penetrated Schmisseur's property. This led to allegations that the company was unlawfully using her land to facilitate the transportation of extern from other land, effectively causing irreparable harm to Schmisseur and taking undue advantage of her property rights. Schmisseur sought an injunction to prevent this unauthorized use, asserting that it conflicted with the terms of the original lease. The Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of Schmisseur, issuing a decree to enjoin the company's actions concerning the usage of her land.	Mary Ann Schmisseur claimed that the Consolidated Coal Company was unlawfully transporting coal mined from other lands through her property, which was contrary to the terms of the lease. She asserted that such actions caused her irreparable harm and violated the agreement's intent, as it was not envisioned that the land leased would be used for mining outside coal reserves under her land. She sought an injunction to restrain the company from this unauthorized use to protect her rights and prevent further damage.	The Consolidated Coal Company argued against the injunction by contending that there was no demonstrable irreparable harm suffered by Schmisseur, as the lease allowed for a thirty-five-year term to extract the coal. They claimed that the extraction of coal did not necessarily require completion before this term’s expiration and implied that their practices did not violate the lease's terms. They maintained that using the shaft for other coal was a legitimate business practice and that there was no grounds to restrict their mining operations under the current legal framework.

In 1869, Christian Fiedler passed away, leaving behind a widow, Wilhelmina Gueck, and their children. After his death, Wilhelmina was appointed as the administratrix of his estate and subsequently built a house on a piece of property in Calhoun County, Illinois, using funds from the estate, amounting to approximately $82,200. In 1871, she remarried Frederick Gueck, and in 1872, the house was constructed by Morris Fisher, who served as both a carpenter and insurance agent for the German Insurance Company. Fisher approached Wilhelmina regarding insuring the house, leading to discussions with Frederick Gueck. On October 14, 1872, Fred Gueck informed Fisher that Wilhelmina wanted to insure the house for $1,400, but the application was incorrectly prepared and not disclosed to Gueck or Wilhelmina. The insurance policy remained active through renewals until the house burned down in October 1886. When claims were submitted, the adjuster refused to pay, citing that the title of the property belonged to Fiedler's estate and not to Frederick Gueck. The case sought to rectify the insurance policy and enforce payment despite the mistakes made in identifying the property owners.	The plaintiffs, Wilhelmina Gueck and her family, argued that there was a mistake in the insurance application and policies regarding the ownership of the insured property. They sought to correct the insurance policy to accurately reflect the rightful owners and enforce the collection of the insurance proceeds following the total loss of the house due to fire.	The defendant, German Insurance Company, contended that the policy was issued in the wrong name and asserted that there was no intention of fraud involved. They maintained that the absence of proper title representation voided the claim and insisted that the errors in the policy were not the company's responsibility. The company requested that the court not enforce the payment of the insurance claim due to these discrepancies.

In September 1873, in Chicago, Illinois, a legal case arose between James Shanley and William Wells. Shanley, the plaintiff, filed an action of trespass for assault, battery, and false imprisonment against Wells, who was acting as a policeman at the time of the incident. The case centered around an arrest made by Wells, who claimed that Shanley was a vagrant as defined by a city ordinance. The court described the events leading to the arrest, noting that Shanley was apprehended without a warrant and had several hundred dollars on him at the time, indicating he was not vagrant. The defense argued that Wells acted in accordance with his duties as a police officer but was challenged on the grounds of whether the necessary elements for a vagrancy arrest were met under the law. The court reviewed various aspects, including the definition and conditions of vagrancy, the authority of police in making arrests, and the admissibility of evidence.	James Shanley claimed that he was wrongfully assaulted and imprisoned by William Wells, who arrested him under the claim of vagrancy without proper authority. He asserted that he was not indeed a vagrant, as he had visible means of support and was engaged in legitimate business activities at the time of his arrest. Shanley sought damages for the harm he suffered due to the unlawful actions of the defendant.	William Wells contended that his actions were justified under the city’s vagrancy ordinance, which allowed for the arrest of individuals deemed to lack visible means of support. He argued that he acted without malice and in good faith based on his understanding of Shanley's conduct. Wells requested the court to acknowledge his probable cause for the arrest, stressing that he was simply performing his duties as a policeman.

In September 1867, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Henry A. Mix v. Melville Beach et al., stemming from a dispute over a real estate transaction in Lee County, Illinois. The case began in January 1861 when the defendants filed a bill against Mix and Josiah B. Williams. The original land in question was purchased by Mix from Williams in 1855. Mix subsequently sold the land to Jacob W. Thayer, who then transferred it to John E. Pearl. Pearl owed Mix $615 and a contractual agreement was established so that Mix would convey the land to Pearl upon payment. This arrangement included a clause indicating that failure to fulfill this agreement would result in a complete forfeiture of the contract. Melville Beach acquired the property from Thayer's successor, Johnston, and took possession of the land, making improvements valued at $800, without having paid the final amount defined in the contract. After Mundane dealings and the refusal of Mix to convey the title, Beach filed for specific performance to compel Mix to uphold the contract. The case was ultimately focused on the legal obligations of the parties involved and whether Mix had the right to declare a forfeiture.	The plaintiffs, led by Melville Beach, argued that Henry A. Mix failed to fulfill his part of the agreement by not conveying the title to the property after receiving partial payment. They sought specific performance of the contract, demanding that the court enforce the agreement and compel Mix to provide the deed to them, based on the claim that they had upheld their obligations under the contract.	Mix contended that the contract was forfeited due to non-payment of the final installment by Beach or his predecessors. He argued that since he had not received the complete payment, he was not obligated to convey the title. Mix further claimed that the legal principle of mutuality rendered the agreement unenforceable against him, as he was not in a position to fulfill his obligation to convey the property without having secured a valid title from Williams.

In the case of Zephemiah Dowden v. Jesse F. Wilson, which occurred in Ford County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose surrounding a patent that was held by Jesse F. Wilson. The case reached the Illinois Appellate Court and was decided on February 7, 1883. The legal action was initiated after a prior suit involving the same parties had been previously reversed by the Illinois Supreme Court. The matter focused on the validity and worthlessness of the patented invention that Wilson had claimed. The plaintiffs aimed to prove that the invention was defective, and a significant aspect of the court's evaluation involved the admissibility and credibility of the evidence presented, particularly concerning expert opinions from individuals who had not directly observed the invention in operation. The case also explored the obligations of each party regarding the patent's validity and the nature of agreements related to it.	The plaintiff, Zephemiah Dowden, contended that the patent held by Jesse F. Wilson was worthless and sought to nullify any agreements associated with the patent, including notes and a mortgage tied to this invention. Dowden aimed to demonstrate that the invention had been inadequately tested and that expert testimonies presented were from individuals who lacked firsthand experience or evidence to substantiate their claims.	Jesse F. Wilson's defense hinged on maintaining the validity of the patent, arguing that the evidence presented by the plaintiff did not convincingly demonstrate the purported worthlessness of the invention. Wilson contended that the testimonies provided, including expert opinions, failed to substantiate the claims of defectiveness. He requested that the court affirm the earlier ruling in his favor, asserting that the plaintiff’s arguments were insufficient to invalidate the patent rights.

Jacob Weaver initiated a legal action against Walter H. Penny in the Illinois Appellate Court, which resolved on December 4, 1885. The case stemmed from a promissory note given by Weaver to Penny for the purchase of approximately two hundred sheep. The location of the case was Henderson County, Illinois. The dispute arose when Weaver claimed that the sheep sold to him were warranted to be sound and free from disease, but in reality, many of the sheep were diseased and died. Moreover, he contended that the disease spread to his herd of short-horn cattle, causing further fatalities among the cattle. Weaver sought damages due to this breach of warranty, and the case included discussions about the appropriateness of recoupment for those damages.	The plaintiff, Jacob Weaver, argued that Walter H. Penny breached the warranty of soundness regarding the sheep sold to him. He claimed damages not only for the dead sheep but also for the loss of several of his cattle that were infected by the disease from the sheep. Weaver’s primary request was for a set-off against the amount due on the promissory note, arguing that the damages he suffered exceeded the unpaid principal and interest on that note.	Walter H. Penny, the defendant, maintained that he was not liable for the alleged damages because, at the time of sale, he was unaware of any disease affecting the sheep, nor did he have any notice that the sheep would be placed among cattle. Penny argued that damages resulting from the breach of warranty did not reasonably arise from the sale, and he emphasized that the jury should limit any recoupment Weaver sought to the amount owed on the note.

The case "F. O. Cunningham et al. v. Patrick Thornton" took place in Peoria County, Illinois, with the final decision dated May 28, 1888. The dispute centers around competing claims to a parcel of land involving multiple parties. Alvah Moffit and his wife conveyed land to John Thornton on May 24, 1867, with a warranty deed that was recorded on the same day. In subsequent years, John Thornton executed a trust deed on this property to secure a loan from Patrick Thornton and later rectified the deed due to a misdescription of the land. Cunningham and other appellants later acquired trust deeds and mortgages on the same land, essentially claiming liens through John Thornton. The legal issue arose over the priority of these liens, specifically regarding the construction and sufficiency of the land descriptions in the deeds and when, if at all, the appellants were chargeable with notice of the appellee's trust deed.	The plaintiff, Patrick Thornton, claimed that his trust deed had priority over the various trust deeds and mortgages held by Cunningham and others. He argued that the appellants were chargeable with constructive notice of his trust deed due to its recording despite the misdescription of the land in question. Additionally, he maintained that the descriptions in both his trust deed and the original deed from Moffit were sufficient to establish his claim to the property.	The defendants, represented by F. O. Cunningham and associates, argued that the descriptions in the trust deeds and mortgages they acquired were legally valid and took precedence. They contended that they had no actual knowledge of the appellee's trust deed at the time of their transactions, and thus could not be held responsible for noticing it. They insisted that their rights should be enforceable and that the court was incorrect in granting priority to the appellee's claims, given the questionable legality of the descriptions in the deeds involved.

The case "The State of Illinois v. The Illinois Central Railroad Company" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1861. It arose from an action of debt initiated by the State of Illinois against the Illinois Central Railroad Company for unpaid taxes for the year 1857. This case was particularly concerned with the assessment and valuation of the railroad company's property for taxation purposes. At the heart of the dispute was whether the railroad company was liable to pay taxes exceeding two percent of their gross receipts, according to the stipulations in their charter. Following a series of events that included negotiations and the filing of an assessment list by the railroad company in August 1857, it was determined that they had already paid a total of $145,645.32 into the State treasury, yet there remained a contention over what amount was still owed based on the assessment made by the State Auditor. Evidence was presented regarding the true value of the railroad’s property, with testimonies given by railroad professionals. Ultimately, the court focused on the agreed-upon issues of taxing liability and property valuation under the laws existing at the time. The case took place at a time when legal interpretations of tax law and property valuation methodologies were being scrutinized.	The State of Illinois claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company owed taxes for 1857 that exceeded two percent of its gross receipts. The state maintained that the company was obligated to pay these taxes as assessed under state law. It also sought to clarify whether the valuation placed upon the company's property by the State Auditor was correctly executed and consistent with legal standards for taxation.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company defended against the claims by arguing that they had already overpaid their taxes for the taxable year in question. They contended that the assessment placed on their property was excessive and not reflective of its actual market value. The company sought a recalibration of the assessed value to align with the true taxable worth of their assets for the year that would adequately support their position that all due taxes had been satisfied.

In February 1854, Harvey B. Lucas and William B. Driver entered into an agreement in Illinois where Driver was to haul railroad ties for Lucas using two teams for a duration of six months at a rate of seven cents per tie. Lucas was responsible for providing all necessary ties during this period, commencing when his saw-mill became operational. The saw-mill began operations on May 18, and Driver started hauling ties. However, the saw-mill could not produce enough ties to support both Driver's and Lucas's own teams, based on the agreement. A month later, on June 18, the parties reached a settlement where Driver received a payment of $64.08 as full compensation for all demands up to that date. Afterward, Driver continued to fulfill his duties, hauling an additional 663 ties until Lucas refused to provide more ties and ultimately discharged him. Evidence indicated that Driver had incurred additional costs, such as constructing a makeshift shelter at the mill. The jury ruled in favor of Driver, awarding him $86.41 for the breach of contract by Lucas.	The plaintiff, Lucas, contended that the settlement receipt received by Driver effectively covered all demands, including damages for the contract breach. Lucas argued that since they had settled previously, no further obligation to furnish ties remained. He sought to overturn the jury's verdict in favor of Driver, asserting the ruling was erroneous based on the prior settlement.	The defendant, Driver, maintained that Lucas violated the contract by failing to supply the agreed-upon ties for the entirety of the six-month term after their settlement. Driver argued that the receipt did not negate his claim for damages incurred after the settlement, as the contract obligations remained intact. He requested compensation for lost wages resulting from Lucas's refusal to supply ties.

The case "William F. Bryan v. Sylvanus Whitford et al." was decided in September 1872 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated in the Peoria circuit court, where the appellees, referred to as original contractors, brought a suit against the appellant, William F. Bryan, and a co-defendant named Gilbert. The plaintiffs sought to enforce a mechanic's lien on a property and building based on labor and materials they provided in the spring of 1871. The work performed involved making alterations in the internal arrangements of a room and installing new features, such as windows and flooring, in a building that had previously been completed and occupied in the prior year. A key issue of the case was whether such alterations constituted grounds for a mechanic’s lien under the relevant statutes. The court examined statutes from 1845 and 1869 that defined the scope and rights concerning liens for labor and materials, ultimately concluding that the claims made by the plaintiffs did not qualify for a lien, as the work done was not classified as erecting or repairing under the law.	The plaintiff, Sylvanus Whitford and associates, claimed that they were entitled to a mechanic's lien on the property for labor and materials provided during alterations made to an already completed building. They argued that under the Illinois statutes, particularly those amended in 1869, their work fell within the definitions that warrant a lien because it involved updates and improvements to the property, thus seeking compensation for what they believed was owed to them for their services.	The defendant, William F. Bryan, contended that the plaintiffs were not entitled to a mechanic's lien based on the work performed. He relied on the interpretation of relevant Illinois statutes that dictated the limits of lien applicability, arguing that the work done did not constitute "erecting or repairing" a building but rather minor alterations to an already completed structure. Therefore, he sought dismissal of the plaintiffs' claims on the basis that the statutory requirements for a lien were not met in this case.

In January 1863, the case of James Ellis v. Robert Southwell was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal dispute originated from a foreclosure action initiated by Robert Southwell, who filed a bill in the Scott Circuit Court in October 1860 to foreclose a mortgage on a parcel of land. This mortgage, amounting to $1,000, was executed by Southwell to secure a debt. The foreclosure action included not only Ellis but also subsequent mortgagees, Weinhagen & Hornbostle, W. W. Chapman, and Thomas Ellis, as co-defendants. Following various proceedings, including the dismissal of a related cross-bill, default judgments were entered against James Ellis and his wife. The court subsequently decreed the payment of Southwell’s claim, as well as that of Weinhagen & Hornbostle. A sale of the mortgaged property took place, generating proceeds that were insufficient to cover all mortgage debts, leading to questions regarding the distribution of any remaining funds.	James Ellis, the plaintiff in error, contended that the court erred in its decree regarding the foreclosure and the payment of claims. Ellis argued that the court’s decision favored Thomas Ellis and Weinhagen & Hornbostle without establishing their claims adequately, as there was no evidence presented to support their cross-bills. Ellis sought to contest the application of the mortgage proceeds and challenged the validity of the decrees rendered against him.	Robert Southwell, the defendant in error, defended the validity of the foreclosure and the decrees against Ellis, asserting that the prior mortgage and subsequent claims were established and recognized throughout the process. Southwell maintained that there was no necessity for further proofs given the admissions of the parties involved. He sought the enforcement of his decree for the foreclosure and the application of the proceeds from the sale of the mortgaged property according to the established liens.

In 1873, the case of James Kelly et al. v. John Donlin et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a dispute over property inheritance after the deaths of John Donlin, senior, and his widow, Mary Donlin. The plaintiffs, John Donlin and Catharine J. Crouse, heirs of John Donlin, claimed that they possessed a rightful interest in a property located in Cook County, Illinois. They argued that the death of their father and later their mother entitled them to undivided shares of the estate. Conversely, the defendants, James Kelly and David Mergentheim, claimed title to the property through a series of conveyances stemming from an administrator’s sale, which was later deemed invalid by the court due to lack of proper notice to the heirs. The case further hinged on the Statute of Limitations, as the defendants asserted that they had maintained possession of the property for seven years, thereby acquiring rights through adverse possession. However, the plaintiffs contended that an injunction from a previous lawsuit had prevented them from asserting their claims. The court ultimately deemed the plaintiffs' claims valid regarding John Donlin’s interest but ruled against Catharine Crouse, stating that she had no valid claim.	The plaintiffs asserted that they were the rightful heirs to the property in question, entitling them to recover an undivided five-twelfths interest following the intestate succession from their deceased parents. John Donlin argued that the possession and inheritance from his father should be recognized legally, while Catharine contended that the previous decree concerning her brother's interest should not affect her claim since she had not alleged lack of jurisdiction in time. They requested the court to rule in their favor for partition and rightful ownership of their inherited shares.	The defendants claimed that they had a valid title to the property gained through a series of conveyances, including a deed from an administrator's sale that had been deemed invalid due to lack of notice to the heirs. They relied on the Statute of Limitations, asserting that since they had possessed the property and paid taxes on it for seven years, the heirs' claims were barred. Furthermore, the defendants argued that the equitable injunction from a prior lawsuit prevented the plaintiffs from asserting their claims during the statutory period, contending that this should affirm their right to retain the property.

In September 1871, in Galva, Illinois, an ejectment action was initiated by John L. Finley and others (plaintiffs) against William H. McConnell and others (defendants) in the Henry Circuit Court. The central issue was the recovery of a house and lot that was previously owned by John Youngberg, who had conveyed it to C. C. Bemis in trust for his creditors due to significant debts. This conveyance did not release Youngberg's homestead right. Bemis later transferred the property to Finley, who acted for the creditors, while Youngberg subsequently sold the property to Clark M. Carr, who then passed it to Olof Johnson and eventually to the defendants, McConnell and others. The court trial was conducted without jury intervention, where the plaintiffs claimed rightful ownership based on the series of deeds. The defendants contended that the initial transfer from Youngberg was void due to the homestead exemptions that prevented removal of possession until the homestead was abandoned, which, they asserted, was not properly accounted for in the transfers.	The plaintiffs argued that they were rightful owners of the property based on the chain of title originating from Youngberg's initial conveyance to Bemis, who then transferred it to them. They claimed that the deed was legitimate and justified under the debts Youngberg owed to his principal creditors, despite the subsequent sales and possession issues raised by the defense. The plaintiffs sought to recover possession of the property and affirm their legal title against the defendants.	The defendants asserted that the conveyances were invalid due to Youngberg's homestead rights not being released in the deeds. They argued that the absence of a homestead release meant that the transfer to Bemis could not fully vest title, as Youngberg retained occupancy rights until abandoning the homestead. The defendants requested that the court recognize their claim to the property based on this defense and declared the plaintiffs' ownership void.

The case "Matthew Laflin et al. v. The City of Chicago" took place in September 1868 in Chicago, Illinois. It arose from matters concerning a special assessment imposed for the opening of a street. The plaintiff, Matthew Laflin and others, appealed a judgment from the Superior Court of Chicago regarding this reassessment after a previous assessment was deemed void due to irregularities. The legal dispute involved the interpretation of the 36th section of chapter 7 of the revised charter of 1863 pertaining to special assessments. The Supreme Court of Illinois was tasked with evaluating whether a new assessment could be made despite the void status of the original one, and whether the costs of the failed initial assessment and its interest could be included in the new judgment.	The plaintiffs contended that the original assessment used to collect funds for the street opening was void due to irregularities and consequently argued that the reassessment should not impose costs from the previous assessment. They sought a judgment that would exclude these costs and the associated interest when determining their liability under the new assessment.	The defendant, represented by the City of Chicago, argued that the charter permitted a new special assessment despite the irregularities of the original assessment. They maintained that since the charter explicitly allowed for reassessments in cases where the city failed to collect all or part of an assessment, they had the authority to pursue this re-evaluation. The city sought to retain the costs from the original assessment and interest in the new judgment.

Carrie Culver brought a legal action against The City of Streator in Illinois, stemming from an incident that occurred on May 10, 1887. The city had an ordinance prohibiting unmuzzled dogs from running at large, which allowed city officials to destroy such dogs. While the city enforced this ordinance, a city officer, as part of his duties, accidentally injured Culver. She alleged that due to the negligence and carelessness of the city's employees while they were executing their duty, she was shot and sustained significant injuries, resulting in medical expenses amounting to $1,000 and claiming damages of $25,000. The case was reviewed by the Illinois Appellate Court after the Circuit Court sustained a general demurrer filed by the defendant city, which ultimately led to a judgment against Culver for costs.	Culver's main argument was that the City of Streator was liable for the injury she suffered due to the negligence of its officers while enforcing an ordinance regarding the destruction of unmuzzled dogs. She contended that this negligence caused her significant bodily harm, pain, and substantial medical expenses.	The City of Streator argued that it could not be held liable for the actions of its officers when those actions were performed in the enforcement of an ordinance aimed at public welfare. The city asserted that municipal corporations are not responsible for injuries incurred by individuals in the course of executing such ordinances, as these actions serve the interests of public safety and order.

In 1868, in Chicago, Illinois, Edward McDonald was indicted for arson by the Recorder’s Court, charged with setting fire to his own house in an attempt to defraud the Western Insurance Company of Buffalo. The indictment was presented during the court's October term of 1867, and McDonald was tried in March 1868. He pleaded not guilty, claiming that the prosecution must prove the existence of a legal insurance policy and that the act constituted a fraud upon the insurance company. McDonald was convicted and sentenced to five years in prison. His counsel argued that the name under which he was tried differed slightly from the name in the indictment, a claim deemed a minor technicality by the court, and that the evidence did not sufficiently prove the existence of a valid insurance policy. The court maintained that the intent to defraud is central to the crime of arson, regardless of the validity of the insurance policy. The jury ultimately found him guilty, leading to the appeal for a new trial being denied.	The plaintiff, Edward McDonald, contended that he did not burn his house with the intention of defrauding the insurance company. He argued that the prosecution failed to prove the existence of a valid insurance policy and that the evidence for the charge of arson was therefore insufficient. He requested the court to reverse the conviction on these grounds and grant a new trial.	The defendant, represented by the State, asserted that McDonald was rightfully convicted of arson as he intentionally set fire to his property with the aim of defrauding the Western Insurance Company. They argued that the intention to commit fraud was clear, regardless of the validity of the insurance policy McDonald believed he held. The State maintained that the indictment sufficiently established the elements of arson as defined in the criminal code and sought affirmance of the conviction.

In 1860, in Salem, Marion County, Illinois, Benjamin F. Anderson filed a legal suit against William White concerning a property transaction. Anderson had purchased a lot from White on November 11, 1858, with a total price of $700, partially financed by two promissory notes secured by a mortgage on the property. White initiated a suit when Anderson failed to pay one of the notes due on November 11, 1859, resulting in a judgment against him. Subsequently, in April 1860, White and Anderson entered into a new agreement wherein White agreed to satisfy the previous judgment and release Anderson from the mortgage in exchange for a horse valued at $100 and additional payments. Despite some payments being made, Anderson contended that White repudiated the agreement by ordering the sheriff to levy on his property. Anderson sought an injunction to prevent the sale of his property, which led to further court proceedings.	Anderson claimed that White had agreed to rescind the original contract provided Anderson fulfilled certain conditions, including returning the horse and paying a portion of the rent. He asserted that he had indeed performed his part (paid the costs of the previous suit and tendered the property deed to White), yet White refused to accept the deed and continued actions against him for the enforcement of the original judgment. Anderson requested that the court enjoin White from selling his property, enforce the specific performance of the new agreement, and return the note and mortgage based on the completion of his obligations.	White denied the claims made by Anderson, asserting that the new contract required Anderson to fulfill conditions promptly and had not been satisfied. He claimed that Anderson's delay constituted a breach and justified his actions to pursue the original judgment. White contended that the agreement had not been properly executed by Anderson, as he did not submit the deed and pay all required amounts within the agreed timeframe. He requested the court to dismiss Anderson's claims and allow him to proceed with executing the judgment.

Ogden Monell filed a case against Christian Scherrick and the administrator of Christian W. Scherrick's estate in the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1870. The case arose in Newton, Jasper County, where Monell alleged that Christian W. Scherrick conveyed real estate (two lots and a house valued at $1300) to his son, Christian Scherrick, to defraud creditors. Monell claimed that the conveyance was made with the intention of hindering and delaying the collection of debts owed by the elder Scherrick, as the latter was insolvent at the time of the transfer. The proof revealed that Christian W. Scherrick continued to occupy the property and treat it as his own until his death nearly two years later, while claiming he intended to keep the property out of reach of his creditors. The only defense against the claim of fraud was that Christian W. Scherrick received a nominal payment of $300 from his son for the property, which was considerably less than its value. The initial court dismissed Monell's bill, leading him to appeal the decision.	Ogden Monell claimed that the transfer of real estate from Christian W. Scherrick to his son was fraudulent. He argued that the conveyance was made with the intent to defraud creditors, especially given the lack of sufficient consideration (only $300 for property worth $1300) and the continued occupation and claim to the property by the grantor after the transfer. Monell sought to have the conveyance set aside to reclaim the property to satisfy the debts owed to him.	The defendants argued that the evidence presented by Monell did not clearly demonstrate that the conveyance was fraudulent. They contended that the payment of $300 indicated a legitimate transaction, despite the property's value and the circumstances surrounding the conveyance. The defendants maintained that the claim of fraudulent intent was not sufficiently established and requested that the court uphold the dismissal of Monell's claims.

John M. Bunn and others (plaintiffs) filed a replevin case against Thomas Gardiner (defendant) in the Illinois Appellate Court on December 4, 1885. The case originated from a dispute over a stock of goods valued at $2,500 that the plaintiffs claimed possession of under a chattel mortgage and an order for delivery from J. R. Turner & Son, dated August 22, 1884.
