The defendant, Gardiner, contended that he had taken possession of the goods as the sheriff under a writ of fi. fa. from the Circuit Court of DeWitt County, which was in favor of Mack, Stadler & Co., for a debt owed by the mortgagors. Additionally, Gardiner presented a second defense based on another writ issued by the County Court of Peoria County for a smaller amount owed to M. Pettingill & Co. The court heard the case without a jury, leading to various pleadings and responses. The plaintiffs argued that the judgments underlying the writs were invalid, as they were entered in vacation without proper affidavits proving the authority of the attorney involved. Ultimately, the issues were found in favor of the defendant, and a judgment was rendered for costs and the return of the goods.	The plaintiffs, Bunn et al., argued that the defendant's possession of the goods was unlawful due to the invalidity of the judgments supporting the writs under which Gardiner seized the goods. They contended that the judgments were improperly entered by the clerk without the requisite proof of the power of attorney, lacking necessary affidavits. Thus, they requested the return of the goods and claimed that their rights to the property were superior due to the chattel mortgage.	Thomas Gardiner defended his possession of the goods by stating that he acted within his rights as sheriff under valid writs of execution. He argued that the plaintiffs acquired no property interest in the goods prior to his seizure, having only acted as general creditors. Gardiner claimed the writs were prima facie sufficient to justify his actions and that the plaintiffs failed to prove any facts that would render the writs void.

Stephen H. Pitkin filed an action of ejectment against John S. Yaw in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1851 to reclaim possession of two lots located in Farmington, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute over tax title, with the plaintiff alleging ownership title dated June 1, 1850. During the trial, Pitkin presented evidence from a mixture of court decisions and tax documents, including a judgment from the Fulton Circuit Court rendered in March 1847 regarding taxes owed for eight town lots, which included the two lots in question. The judgment amount was ninety-nine cents for the year 1844. Several key pieces of evidence were presented by Pitkin: the precept related to the judgment and a sheriff's deed. However, the precept was excluded by the court due to a significant variance in the stated judgment amounts, and both deeds submitted were rejected due to procedural and substantive flaws. The defendant, Yaw, was ultimately favored by the court, leading to a ruling against Pitkin.	The plaintiff, Stephen H. Pitkin, asserted that he had legal title to the two lots based on a tax deed. He attempted to introduce evidence including a judgment from the Fulton Circuit Court and sheriff's deeds to establish his ownership and reclaim possession of the properties. Pitkin requested the court to recognize the validity of his tax title and ultimately grant him possession of the lots.	John S. Yaw, as the defendant, argued against Pitkin’s claims, emphasizing that the precept and deeds presented by the plaintiff were improperly executed and contained significant variances from the judgments they purported to reflect. Yaw contended that Pitkin had failed to show valid title at the time specified in the declaration, and therefore he maintained that the court should rule in his favor based on the deficiencies in Pitkin’s evidence and assertion.

The case "Elgin Lumber Company v. Solomon Langman and George Utman" originated in Elgin, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on June 9, 1887. The dispute arose when the Elgin Lumber Company filed a bill to enforce a lien for materials they had supplied to George Utman for constructing a house on a lot he owned. The house was destroyed by fire before its completion. The Elgin Lumber Company sought a decree asserting that their lien as material suppliers was superior to a mortgage lien held by Solomon Langman, who had provided a loan for the purchase of the lot on which the house was built. An insurance policy intended to cover the construction was issued, with the loss payable to Langman. The court held funds related to the insurance payment pending its final ruling, with the case addressing the priority of liens related to the destroyed property and the distribution of the insurance proceeds.	The Elgin Lumber Company claimed that their lien for materials furnished was superior to Solomon Langman’s mortgage lien regarding the insurance proceeds from the fire. They argued that the timing of the agreements indicated their lien was prior, and they sought a decree directing that the mortgage lien be deemed secondary in regard to the insurance money, which was set to be disbursed to Langman.	Solomon Langman argued that his mortgage held precedence over the Elgin Lumber Company’s lien due to its earlier recording date. He contended that the circumstances did not infringe upon the rights of the lumber company, as he had procured the insurance policy and paid the premium, thereby securing his mortgage interest. Langman asserted that the insurance money represented compensation for his secured loan and should rightfully go to him.

In 1850, in Peoria, Illinois, an action of ejectment was initiated by John Spellman and others against Alfred G. Curtenius regarding the possession of lot number four in block fifty-one of Bigelow and Underhill’s Addition to Peoria. The case arose after Curtenius presented evidence of a land certificate showing the entry of the land by John L. Bogardus in 1837, which traced a chain of title from Bogardus to Curtenius. The defendants, tenants of Charles Ballance, claimed a competing title based on a 1845 tax sale of the property due to unpaid taxes from 1843. They provided a Circuit Court judgment and a tax deed to establish their ownership. However, the Court excluded this deed from the jury’s consideration. The appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court focused on whether the judgment and evidence presented adequately supported the plaintiff’s claims and if the challenges posed by the defendants were valid.	The plaintiffs argued that they were the rightful owners of the lot based on a valid chain of title traced back to the original entry of the land. They contended that the application of the defendants’ presented tax title was improperly excluded from the jury’s consideration and that the defendants had not provided sufficient proof to defeat the established title. The plaintiffs requested judgment to reclaim possession of the property.	The defendants contended that the tax deed they presented constituted valid proof of ownership as it was based on a judgment for unpaid taxes. They argued that the exclusion of their tax deed from the jury fundamentally undermined their defense. The defendants sought to establish that a valid tax title existed for the property, thus challenging the plaintiff's claims of ownership based on the tax sale and adherence to statutory requirements in tax proceedings.

The case of Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company v. Emanuel Fowler took place in Shelby County, Illinois, with the final judgment rendered in January 1877 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict arose when Fowler, the plaintiff, sought damages after his steer was killed by a train operated by the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company. The specific incident occurred under circumstances where it was lawful for livestock to roam freely in the county. The railroad company had not erected a fence along the section of track where the animal was struck, which led to questions about liability and contributory negligence. The case was presided over by Hon. Horatio M. Yandeveer in the Circuit Court before it advanced to the Supreme Court for appeal.	Emanuel Fowler claimed that the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company was liable for the death of his steer due to their failure to fence the railroad track. He argued that since it was legal for livestock to run at large in the area, the company’s negligence in maintaining a proper barrier constituted a breach of duty. Fowler requested compensation for the loss of his property, asserting that the railroad's actions directly resulted in the fatality of his steer.	The Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company, represented by Mr. J. G. Essick, contended that contributory negligence could be invoked since it was lawful for stock to run at large. However, they predominantly focused on the argument that they were not liable due to the legal status of the livestock's presence in the area. The defense maintained that the responsibility did not lie with the railroad company since it was operating under the prevailing local laws regarding livestock.

In September 1871, a legal case was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court involving Joshua L. Marsh and others as plaintiffs against the City of Chicago. The case originated from a special assessment dispute and was appealed from the Superior Court of Cook County. The city collector had applied for a judgment to enforce the collection of special assessments; however, this was brought into question due to the new constitution that had been adopted. The significant argument revolved around whether the city collector had the authority to seek such judgment, given the updated constitutional provisions. Additionally, there were issues regarding the adequacy of notices that were published preceding the judgment application. Specifically, it was noted that the certificates of publication were defective because they did not state the date of the last publication, which contravened legal requirements, undermining the legitimacy of the application.	The plaintiffs claimed that the city collector of Chicago was unauthorized to apply for a judgment regarding the special assessments due to changes in the law following the adoption of the new constitution. They argued that any judgment based on such an unauthorized application should be reversed. They also pointed out the defects in the certificate of publication of the notices, asserting that the failure to include critical dates rendered the application for judgment invalid.	The defendant, the City of Chicago, maintained that the application for judgment was proper and that the collector had acted within his rights. They might have argued against the legitimacy of the plaintiffs' claims regarding the constitutionality of the judgment and the notice's sufficiency. However, the case notes primarily highlight the legality concerning the authority of the city collector and the procedural validity of the notice.

Gustave Koch filed a slander case against Mary Heideman in the Illinois Appellate Court arising from a sermon delivered by Koch, who was the minister at St. Paul’s German Church in Elgin, Illinois, on March 26, 1882. During the sermon, he read a statement in German, which translated to “She has been laying on the lounge with a male boarder,” referring to Heideman, who was married and the wife of a boarding house operator. Koch's words suggested an implication of adultery, though he argued he did not directly accuse her of that behavior. Heideman's claims rested on the interpretation of these words and their impact on her reputation. The case proceeded to a jury trial, where Heideman received a verdict in her favor amounting to $500. Koch then appealed the decision, arguing that the words spoken were not actionable as slander under the relevant legal provisions since they did not directly charge her with adultery.	Heideman claimed that Koch's statements during the sermon were damaging and implied an accusation of adultery, resulting in public disgrace. She requested compensation for slander based on these assertions and sought a jury trial, arguing that Koch's words clearly conveyed inappropriate implications that had harmed her reputation.	Koch defended himself by arguing that his statements did not directly accuse Heideman of adultery and that the words spoken were not actionable at common law. He contended the translations did not amount to a public charge of fornication or adultery and asserted that despite the jury's verdict, the evidence did not support the claim of slanderous intent necessary to uphold the judgment against him.

In the year 1850, Martin T. Kurtz and Vines Davis formed a copartnership to operate a steam flouring mill located in Madison County, Illinois. John Loyd later joined the partnership by investing $7,000, which was used to settle prior debts. Over time, the firm accumulated debts totaling $18,000. Tragically, both Davis and Loyd died in an accident, leaving Kurtz unable to satisfy the remaining debts or continue operations without incurring losses. Consequently, Kurtz filed a bill seeking the sale of the firm’s property to distribute the proceeds among creditors. The court ordered the sale of the partnership's assets. After the sale, the court found that Guy Morrison, a creditor with a secured debt through a deed of trust on Loyd's separate property, could only be partially satisfied from the real estate before sharing in the general distribution with other creditors. Morrison appealed this decision, contending that he should be treated equally with other creditors regarding his claim from the proceeds of the sale.	Guy Morrison argued that as a creditor of the partnership, he was entitled to a distributive share of the sale proceeds alongside other creditors. He claimed that the estate was insolvent, and it would be unjust to prioritize the payment from Loyd’s separate estate over the claims of general creditors. Morrison sought a ruling that would grant him equal treatment in the distribution of the funds generated from the sale of the partnership assets.	The defendants, represented by Martin T. Kurtz among others, maintained that Morrison’s debt was secured by a deed of trust on separate real estate owned by Loyd. They contended that he should first seek payment from that secured estate before being considered alongside the other creditors of the partnership. The defendants' argument relied on principles of equity, asserting that the partnership's assets should be exhausted before resorting to individual partner’s separate properties, to ensure fair treatment of all creditors.

In September 1873, the case of Hollida & Ball v. William H. Hunt was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose in Mercer County, Illinois, where William H. Hunt, the plaintiff, initiated an action of assumpsit against Hollida & Ball, the defendants, based on a promissory note originally given by the defendants to Charles T. Davison, which was subsequently assigned to Hunt. The specific legal issue at stake involved the constitutionality of a state law enacted on March 25, 1869, aimed at regulating the sale of patent rights and preventing associated frauds. The law required individuals to submit affidavits and documentation to county clerks before selling patent rights, and imposed penalties for non-compliance. Hunt challenged this law, asserting that it infringed on the exclusive jurisdiction granted to Congress over patent rights and negatively impacted patentees and their assignees. The court provided a detailed examination of the state law's provisions and their implications on federally granted rights before arriving at a decision regarding the case.	The plaintiff, William H. Hunt, argued that the Illinois law regulating the sale of patent rights was unconstitutional as it encroached upon the authority of Congress to regulate patent rights at the federal level. Hunt requested that the court affirm the impropriety of the state law, asserting that it could not limit the rights granted under the U.S. Constitution and that it contained provisions that discriminated against the transaction of patent rights.	Hollida & Ball, the defendants in this case, contended that the state law was a valid exercise of the state's legislative powers. They argued that it could impose certain reasonable requirements regarding the sale of patent rights. The defendants also claimed that the specific provisions of the law did not infringe upon the fundamental rights granted by federal law, asserting that some regulation of sales would not violate the Constitution.

The case "Eliphalet W. Blatchford et al. v. N. B. Boyden, for use, etc." revolves around events that transpired in Cook County, Illinois, on April 6-7, 1883. The plaintiff, N. B. Boyden, the coroner of Cook County, filed a replevin action for the recovery of goods seized by the sheriff under two executions against Charles S. Munson. These executions were issued for debts owed to John L. Barnum, Ralph Arthur, and Robert E. Jenkins. The defendants, Eliphalet W. Blatchford, Caleb F. Gates, and Nathaniel H. Blatchford, replevied the goods (furniture and fixtures of the Massasoit House) after a replevin bond was posted. The defendants argued that the property belonged to them based on a chattel mortgage from 1881 and attempted to mitigate damages by stating that the merits of their case were unresolved in a prior replevin suit, which was later dismissed. The circuit court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $2,543.50. This judgment was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court, leading the defendants to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs’ case was built on the assertion that the replevin bond was valid despite the defendants claiming it was incorrectly described. They contended that the sheriff was the proper party to be made a defendant in a replevin suit, and since the property was held under execution, the sheriff had the right to recover damages resulting from the wrongful taking of the goods. They sought enforcement of the replevin bond, arguing that the actions of the defendants did not conform to the legal requirements, primarily that the plaintiffs lacked claims to the replevied goods.	The defendants argued that the bond was improperly recited and that they had legal ownership of the property under a chattel mortgage dated April 4, 1881. They contended that no trial had occurred concerning the merits of the replevin suit and that the suit was dismissed before the claims could be adjudicated. Additionally, they claimed a superior lien over the goods, suggesting that the transactions made surrounding the mortgage were valid and thus exempt from the executions held by the sheriff.

The case "Terre Haute & Indianapolis Railroad Co. v. Andrew J. Bowles et al." took place in Hagerstown, Illinois, and was decided on April 6, 1885, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The plaintiff, Andrew J. Bowles, claimed damages after a cow was killed by a train belonging to the defendant, Terre Haute & Indianapolis Railroad Company. At the time of the incident, Hagerstown was an unincorporated village with significant shipping activity for stock and grain, featuring a depot and platform north of the railroad’s main track, with related infrastructure located to the south. The key issue was whether the railroad company was required to maintain a fence around its depot due to the presence of a stock pen and other operational necessities. The circuit court ruled initially in favor of the plaintiff based on statutory interpretation, but the case brought forth questions about the necessity of fencing for public convenience and safety regarding access to the depot.	The plaintiff argued that the railroad company was liable for the death of his cow, asserting that under Illinois statute (Section 48, Chapter 114), the railroad was obligated to maintain a fence around the grounds near the station, particularly because of the significant public activity in the area. Bowles contended that the lack of a fence contributed to the accident and that the railroad should therefore compensate him for the loss of his livestock.	The defendant argued that they were not obligated to fence the depot area based on the interpretation of the aforementioned statute, highlighting that such a requirement would hinder public access to the depot, which is essential for freight and passenger services. They referenced a prior court decision which established that depots and stations should be accessible to accommodate public needs. Consequently, the railroad requested the court to reverse the initial ruling that found them liable for the damages.

The case of George A. Lowry v. John Craig Hately originated in March 1889 in Cook County, Illinois. George A. Lowry filed a lawsuit against John Craig Hately alleging false arrest and malicious prosecution due to the issuance of a contempt of court order under which Lowry was taken into custody. Lowry had been released from custody on a writ of habeas corpus. The case's focal point was an affidavit submitted by Hately, which stated that Lowry possessed a valuable gold watch and chain, as well as approximately $10,000 in money, thus justifying the order for Lowry’s arrest. Lowry argued that the information provided in the affidavit was incorrect and that the arrest lacked probable cause. The case hinged on whether Hately had acted with malice and without probable cause when seeking the order for arrest.	Lowry's main arguments were centered around his claim of false arrest, asserting that Hately maliciously pursued legal action against him without sufficient grounds. He contended that the affidavit used to justify his arrest was based on erroneous beliefs about his possessions, and he sought damages for the alleged false arrest and malicious prosecution.	Hately defended his actions by arguing that he had probable cause based on the circumstances presented to him at the time of the affidavit. He maintained that a belief, if founded on substantial evidence, qualifies as probable cause. Hately contended that he acted under the assumption that Lowry's possessions were indeed as described, and thus, he did not act with malice. He sought the court to dismiss Lowry's claims as he believed the process followed was lawful.

In the case of James M. Aortson et al. v. Edward H. Ridgway and Daniel G. Anderson, the events unfolded in Mount Vernon, Jefferson County, Illinois, during the early to mid-1840s. The case originated from two judgments against the defendants, Edward H. Ridgway and Daniel G. Anderson, one by Burk, McKee & Co. in April 1842 for approximately $300 and another by Eiggs & Co. in September 1842 for around $1,000. Various executions were issued against the defendants' real estate, leading to the sale of lots 59 and 61 to the plaintiffs under questionable circumstances. The sales were conducted without public notice and with the express consent of the defendants, who had waived notice. Over time, the plaintiffs acquired these properties at sheriff's sales to satisfy their judgments, only to discover that the same properties were also sold under a later execution for a prior judgment by Burk, McKee & Co., which they were unaware of due to the defendants' failure to inform them. The plaintiffs filed their bill in equity in May 1851, claiming the sales were fraudulent and seeking restitution or the setting aside of the sales.	The plaintiffs, represented by James M. Aortson, argued that the sales of lots 59 and 61 should be annulled due to constructive fraud by the defendants. They contended that the defendants, particularly Eidgway who served as clerk of the court, failed to disclose the existing prior judgment which had a lien on the property, effectively misleading them during the purchase. The plaintiffs sought a decree for the actual amount due with interest, claiming that they had lost their investment due to the defendants' lack of transparency and good faith in the transactions.	The defendants, Ridgway and Anderson (the latter represented posthumously by his administrator), maintained that the sales were conducted with the plaintiffs’ full knowledge and consent. They argued that the plaintiffs had waived their rights to notice regarding the sales and that the executed prices were fair and reflective of the properties' actual values. They contended that the plaintiffs were responsible for their awareness of the existing liens and should have been vigilant regarding the titles to the properties they purchased.

The case, "David A. Barry et al. v. Alexander E. Guild, Jr.," was decided on May 28, 1888, by the Illinois Appellate Court in Du Page County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a foreclosure action initiated by Alexander E. Guild, Jr. against David A. Barry and others involving a trust deed mortgage that Barry secured for unpaid purchase money. The facts detailed that Barry had purchased land from John Atkinson, who previously acquired the property through a series of deeds. However, there were complications regarding the title, specifically a twenty-acre tract of land that was conveyed earlier to another party, Charles Fitzsimmons, creating a potential title failure. The court examined several historical conveyances and title claims, noting that Barry had sought legal recourse to challenge Guild's foreclosure efforts. The major dispute centered on whether the title defects could be used by Barry as a defense against the foreclosure.	The plaintiff, Alexander E. Guild, claimed the right to foreclose the mortgage given by Barry for the non-payment of $4,000, arguing that the mortgage was valid despite any alleged title defects. Guild maintained that any issues with the title did not impact his right to pursue foreclosure, as they were not directly relevant to the promises Barry made in the mortgage agreement.	The defendants, led by Barry, claimed that the title to twenty acres of the land had failed due to prior conveyances to Fitzsimmons, which they asserted excused their obligation to fulfill the mortgage terms. They sought a deduction from the mortgage debt proportional to the value of the land for which they no longer had clear title, arguing they were unaware of these title defects when they engaged in the transaction.

On August 31, 1871, in Lee County, Illinois, George Probst filed a bill in equity against Elias B. Stiles and his wife, Sybil C. Stiles, concerning a mortgage on certain lands. Probst claimed that the mortgage, alleged to have been lost, needed to be established and foreclosed. The dispute originated from a loan of $4,800 made by Probst to Elias B. Stiles on November 24, 1860. To secure this loan, Elias executed a mortgage on January 6, 1862, which included Sybil as a joint grantor but was not executed by her at that time. Evidence suggested that Stiles became financially troubled and was retaining possession of the mortgage until it could be executed by his wife. The mortgage was recorded on December 1, 1863. By July 21, 1871, Sybil executed the mortgage, which was then acknowledged in proper form. The Stiles denied the allegations and provided a set-off defense, leading to a court case where the mortgage was eventually established against both defendants. The case was taken to the Illinois Supreme Court on appeal.	The plaintiff, George Probst, argued that the mortgage on the land, although initially incomplete due to the lack of Sybil's signature, was intended to be finalized with her acknowledgment. He sought to have the mortgage established and foreclosed against the Stiles, claiming that as the creditor, he was entitled to enforce the mortgage once it was duly executed and acknowledged by Sybil.	The defendants contended that the mortgage was not valid as a result of Sybil not executing it at the time of the initial delivery in 1862. They argued that the delivery of the mortgage was null without her acknowledgment and that no valid relinquishment of her dower had occurred. Additionally, they claimed that the mortgage could not have been re-delivered after its execution by the husband, making the decree barring her dower erroneous.

James Mix filed a case against The Lafayette, Bloomington and Mississippi Railway Company in January 1873 concerning a side track installation along Holmes Street in Paxton, Illinois. Mix owned multiple lots in the vicinity, and the railway company sought to condemn a right of way to construct the side track, which would run near Mix's lots but not directly on them. Concerns arose regarding potential damages to Mix’s properties due to the proximity of the side track and the interruptions caused by rail traffic. The case revolved around evidence and arguments concerning the extent of damages attributable to the construction and operation of the railway track. The trial judge had to address whether certain ordinances of Paxton relevant to the railway's construction could be included in the evidence, as well as Mix's claims regarding potential damages to his lots.	The plaintiff, James Mix, argued that the construction of the railway's side track would result in significant damages to his properties. He sought to prove that the placement of the side track would adversely affect the usability of his lots and harm their value, leading to a request for compensation for the damages incurred by this construction. Mix claimed that the court erred in excluding evidence related to damages to adjacent lots he owned collectively.	The defendant, The Lafayette, Bloomington and Mississippi Railway Company, contended that the construction of the side track was legally justified and adhered to local ordinances. They argued that the damages claimed by Mix were exaggerated and that the assessment should only consider specific lots mentioned in the petition. The railway company also contested the inclusion of evidence about potential damages from their operations, claiming that certain losses were not compensable under state law.

Thomas B. Boyd initiated a legal action against John Dullaghan, which was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court and concluded on June 14, 1889. The dispute arose from Boyd's services as a real estate broker related to the exchange of Dullaghan's hotel and opera house property located in Portage, Wisconsin. In late 1885, Dullaghan entrusted Boyd with the property for sale or exchange. Boyd actively marketed the property and facilitated contact with O’Brien, a Chicago businessman who had goods to sell. Dullaghan and O’Brien negotiated an exchange, facilitated by Boyd, but the arrangement fell through when O’Brien refused to fulfill the contract. Unbeknownst to Boyd, Dullaghan and O’Brien later agreed on a different transaction in January 1887. The Circuit Court initially ruled against Boyd by striking his evidence and directing the jury to favor Dullaghan, citing that Boyd had not disclosed acting as an agent for both parties, thus failing to earn his commission.	Boyd claimed he was entitled to a commission for acting as a broker during negotiations for the exchange of Dullaghan's property with O’Brien. He argued that he had fulfilled his obligations by introducing the two parties and negotiating the exchange. Boyd sought payment of his commission based on the agreed terms between himself and Dullaghan for the sale or exchange of the property.	Dullaghan contended that Boyd acted as a secret agent for O’Brien without informing Dullaghan, which constituted a breach of fiduciary duty. Dullaghan maintained that he was not liable to pay any commission since he was unknowing of Boyd's dual role. The defense asserted that under agency law, Boyd could not recover commissions due to his undisclosed representation of both sides in the transaction.

In 1855, the case of Brewer Woods v. James W. Gilson took place in Macoupin County, Illinois. The dispute arose when Brewer Woods (the plaintiff) filed a replevin action against James W. Gilson (the defendant), who was acting as a deputy sheriff. The defendant had seized Woods' property under an execution related to a judgment against a third party, Watts and Arbuckle, in favor of Dorothy Jones. Woods contested the seizure, arguing that the property was not subject to the execution and that Gilson was not legitimately acting as a deputy sheriff at that time. The case revolved around the legal issues surrounding property rights, execution processes, and the interests of involved parties, especially concerning how the property came under execution and whether Gilson's role as a deputy sheriff disqualified him from executing the writ. After various arguments and trials, the court examined the legitimacy of the execution and the relationship between the parties involved.	Brewer Woods argued that the property in question was not subject to the execution filed by Dorothy Jones and claimed that James W. Gilson was not legally able to act as a deputy sheriff in this matter. Furthermore, Woods contended that Gilson had a conflict of interest as he had served as a surety for Watts in an appeal bond related to the original judgment. Woods sought to reclaim the property seized by Gilson, emphasizing that the levy made on the property was improper.	James W. Gilson defended his actions by stating that he was executing a valid judgment against Watts and Arbuckle, which he had been assigned as a deputy sheriff. He argued that Woods' claims about the property being exempt from the execution were unfounded. Gilson contended that he did not have a direct legal interest in the execution process that would disqualify him from carrying out the writ. He sought dismissal of Woods' claims and upheld the execution of the property.

On September 1, 1873, in Chicago, Illinois, Alfred Guest filed a lawsuit against William H. Reynolds in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Cook County Circuit Court and centered around an alleged obstruction of light and air to Guest's residence at 73 South Sangamon Street, caused by a high board fence erected by Reynolds on his adjacent property. Guest argued that this fence hindered the use of his windows and rendered his home dark, unwholesome, and uncomfortable for habitation. The plaintiff contended that the obstruction was intentional, seeking damages for the injury caused to him and his family’s enjoyment of their home. The declaration contained two counts: one focused on the obstruction of light and the second on the annoyance caused by the construction of the fence. The defendants pleaded not guilty, stating that they had the right to erect the fence as it was on their property. The jury initially ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him $500 after reducing the amount from $838.	The plaintiff, Alfred Guest, claimed that the fence erected by William H. Reynolds obstructed the light and air entering his home, violating his right to enjoy his property. Guest argued that this action was done willfully and maliciously, leading to discomfort and making his residence uninhabitable. He sought damages for the nuisance and the interference with his family's use and enjoyment of their dwelling.	William H. Reynolds defended against the claims by asserting that he had the legal right to construct the fence on his own property. The defendant argued that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate any prescriptive right to the light and air that was claimed to have been obstructed by the fence. Reynolds maintained that the law allows property owners to use their property as they see fit, so long as it does not involve offensive materials, which was not the case here.

John Walker v. Reuben M. Pritchard et al. is a legal case that took place in DeKalb County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment on June 17, 1887, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centers around the estate of Reuben Pritchard, who, before his death, devised certain properties via his will. Elotia Pritchard, his widow, was granted a life estate in a tract of land (168 acres) along with various personal belongings, while also having powers to sell the property. The plaintiffs, represented by John Walker, argued that Elotia Pritchard's interests included more than just a life estate, particularly in a 154-acre tract that Pritchard had purchased but was titled to Elotia. With Elotia's death, disputes arose about the true ownership and rights to the properties, particularly the 154-acre tract and the proceeds from the sales of personal property. Elotia's sons from a previous marriage, Reuben M. and Ethan A., were entangled in these rights alongside Walker, creating a convoluted situation of ownership claims.	The plaintiffs claimed entitlement to a conveyance of the 154-acre tract of land in Ogle County along with financial sums derived from the sale of other property. They contended that while Reuben Pritchard bought the land, the deed was made to Elotia Pritchard and her heirs, thereby suggesting that the plaintiffs had a rightful claim to the property and proceeds as part of their inheritance from Reuben’s estate.	The defendants argued that Elotia Pritchard owned the land and the title was solely hers, independent of any claim from the plaintiffs. They denied that Elotia was granted only a life estate by Reuben’s will, asserting instead that she had the fee simple title to the 168 acres. Moreover, they contested the identification of any funds as proceeds from the sales of the properties purportedly bequeathed by Reuben Pritchard.

In 1868, in the Circuit Court of McLean County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Warner H. Wortman and Henrietta C. Price regarding the ownership of approximately seventy hogs. The hogs were seized under an execution against Mrs. Price's husband, who had reportedly engaged in a trade business with the capital provided by his wife, derived from her inheritance and the sale of property. Mrs. Price testified that she had received $2,960 from her husband's father and sold land for $800, which her husband used to manage a grain and stock trade. The court heard testimony from Mr. Price's business partner, who confirmed the partnership but stated that he was unaware of Mrs. Price's involvement. The partnership ended before the seizure occurred. The central issue was whether the husband's use of his wife's funds in business exempted the property from claims by creditors. The case did not involve a jury and was submitted directly to the court for a decision.	The plaintiff, Henrietta C. Price, claimed ownership of the hogs levied under a judgment against her husband. She argued that her husband was merely her agent operating a business on her behalf, as permitted under the married woman's act of 1861, which allows husbands to manage their wives' separate property. Her claim rested on the assertion that the funds used for the business came from her own finances, thereby making the resulting property hers and not subject to her husband's liabilities.	The defendant, Warner H. Wortman, contended that Mrs. Price’s arrangement with her husband was more akin to a loan than a legitimate agency relationship. He argued that the law does not allow a wife to engage in trade through her husband while insulating her property from his debts. The defense maintained that the lack of a formal agreement between husband and wife regarding compensation and profit-sharing rendered the claim invalid since it concealed the transaction from potential creditors, who would have rightful claims on the husband's business assets.

In 1836, John Dedman, the appellant, initiated an appeal against Rouanta Barber, the appellee, following a judgment that Barber had received against Dedman for $50 and costs. The judgment was issued by a justice of the peace in Hancock County, Illinois. During the April term of the Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Richard M. Young, Dedman faced a motion to dismiss his appeal due to the inadequacy of the appeal bond he submitted. The bond mistakenly indicated an appeal from the Circuit Court to the Supreme Court, failing to reference the judgment from the justice of the peace. However, Dedman sought permission to file a proper bond that aligned with requirements stipulated in the relevant legislative provisions. The court denied his request and dismissed the appeal, which prompted Dedman to subsequently appeal this decision to the Illinois Supreme Court. The Supreme Court, in its analysis, recognized that the legislation governing such proceedings aimed to simplify legal processes and ensure fair trials, ruling in favor of Dedman's right to submit a valid bond.	The plaintiff, John Dedman, contended that the Circuit Court erred by dismissing his appeal based on an inadequate bond. He argued that the failure of the bond should not prejudice him as the law permitted a party to rectify such a mistake by filing a proper bond within a reasonable timeframe. He maintained that he had complied with all requirements prior to the bond being deemed insufficient and requested that the Court allow him to file a new bond.	The defendant, Rouanta Barber, did not provide detailed defenses in the given account, but the motion to dismiss focused on the assertion that Dedman's appeal lacked a sufficient bond as required by law. The defense seemingly supported the circuit court's dismissal of the appeal due to the bond's inadequacy.

In 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving John L. Swanson and others against Canute R. Matson. The case began when a man named Bodelson, who was in jail under a capias ad satisfaciendum issued from the Circuit Court at the suit of a party named Carlson, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. The circuit court judge ordered that the writ be issued, and that bail be taken for Bodelson’s appearance. However, after multiple postponements, the bail was forfeited due to Bodelson's failure to appear in court. This case was brought forward to recover the amount that was supposed to be collected as a result of the capias ad satisfaciendum that was not executed. The crux of the matter revolved around the validity of the bail and the bond associated with it, questioning their legality under existing statutes and common law.	The plaintiffs, represented by Messrs. Condee & Rose, claimed that they were entitled to recover the amount that should have been collected under the capias ad satisfaciendum after Bodelson's bail was forfeited. They argued that the bond issued for bail, which was taken under improper court orders, should be enforceable in order to recover the damages incurred. However, they failed to specify the underlying judgment against Bodelson, which was critical for establishing their claims.	The defendants, represented by Messrs. A. C. and F. W. Story, contended that the bond was void because there was no legal basis for taking bail from a prisoner in custody under final civil process, as dictated by the statute regarding insolvents. They argued that the court's order to take bail was inherently invalid and that no legal remedy could arise from such an invalid bond. Therefore, they requested the court to dismiss the claims against them due to the lack of a legitimate cause of action.

The case "The Union Hide and Leather Company v. Benjamin Shoenmann et al." took place in September 1868 in Chicago, Illinois. The primary individuals involved were the Union Hide and Leather Company (the plaintiff) and Benjamin Shoenmann along with other defendants (the appellants). The case revolved around a sale of 447 dry hides, which the defendants acquired under an alleged special contract. Following the sale, a dispute arose regarding the quality of the hides and whether there had been a warranty concerning that quality. The case was tried without a jury in the Superior Court of Chicago, presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gaby. The court found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding them $120.95, leading to the defendants appealing the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court based on conflicting evidence over the warranty.	The Union Hide and Leather Company claimed that the defendants failed to adhere to the terms of a special contract for the sale of hides. They argued that there was an implied warranty regarding the quality of the hides sold. The plaintiff’s legal request was for the court to uphold the judgment made in the lower court that was in their favor, confirming the verdict and enforcing the payment for the hides sold.	The defendants, represented by Messrs. Gookins & Roberts, contended that the finding of the lower court was against the evidence. They maintained that the selection of the hides was made by the defendants without influence from the plaintiffs, suggesting that any undesirable qualities of the hides were the defendants' misfortune rather than the plaintiffs' fault. The defense sought to overturn the lower court’s judgment and asserted that the evidence did not support the claims made by the plaintiff.

In December 1826, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Ladd and Taylor v. Ninian Edwards concerning an error filed against the court's earlier judgment. The case involved three joint and several obligors, with the issue revolving around the discontinuation of proceedings against one defendant who had not been served with process, but had appeared by attorney. This situation arose when Ladd and Taylor, as plaintiffs, sought to obtain a judgment against the two other defendants after one of them appeared but had not been served. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court to address the alleged error in proceeding to judgment without including the third defendant, raising concerns based on established statutory practices in Illinois regarding the treatment of defendants in similar cases.	Ladd and Taylor contended that the court erred by proceeding to judgment against the two defendants while neglecting to include the third defendant who had appeared through an attorney but had not been served. They argued that this constituted a discontinuous proceeding that could not be cured under the relevant statute. They sought to have the judgment reversed and the case remanded to allow them to proceed appropriately against all defendants.	Ninian Edwards, as the defendant, maintained that the court's actions were justifiable based on existing precedents and the nature of the appearing defendant's status. The defense asserted that the appearance by attorney, without proper process, did not necessitate further action against that defendant and that the plaintiffs’ appeal failed to adhere to fundamental legal principles regarding judgments against joint obligors.

In September 1871, the case of Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company v. Henry B. Head took place in Woodford County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff, Henry B. Head, and the defendant, Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company. The incident occurred when Head, who was working on a bridge adjacent to the railway tracks, called for his eleven-year-old son to lead their horse across the tracks. Despite being aware of an approaching train, the horse became frightened and escaped from the boy, resulting in the horse being struck and killed by the train. The incident raised questions of negligence on the part of both the railway company and the plaintiff.	Henry B. Head claimed that the railway company was negligent in failing to provide adequate warning measures, such as ringing a bell or sounding a whistle at the crossing, which was a farm crossing. He argued that this negligence directly led to the death of his horse and sought compensation for its value.	The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company contended that they were not liable for negligence, as the evidence demonstrated that the plaintiff's actions were extremely reckless. The defendant pointed out that the plaintiff had ordered his son to lead the horse across the tracks despite knowing an approaching train was nearby. The company argued that the crossing was a farm crossing, which did not legally require them to ring a bell or sound a whistle, and thus, they bore no responsibility for the incident.

James W. English, the appellant, filed a legal claim against Murray McConnel, the appellee, in the Illinois Supreme Court around January 1860. The case originated from a contract dated March 5, 1851, between McConnel and George Vail, authorized by Abram Melick. Under this contract, McConnel was to prosecute a claim for Vail and share any recoveries from the action. English entered an agreement with McConnel to assist in this prosecution, but his involvement was strictly limited to resolving one suit against Moore and Munn, which resulted in no recoveries and was ultimately dismissed in August 1854. Following this, McConnel successfully brought another suit, without any aid from English, in 1855, recovering damages for Vail. Throughout the proceedings, English remained uninvolved in the successful suit and did not assert any claim to the fees collected until 1859, which led to the current legal dispute where he sought compensation from McConnel for the suit he failed to prosecute. The trial concluded with the court’s judgment in McConnel's favor.	English argued that he should receive compensation for his efforts under the agreement pertaining to the suit he initiated on behalf of Vail. He emphasized that he had fulfilled his obligations per their contract, and thus claimed a share of the amounts McConnel was able to recover in their agreement with Vail.	McConnel contended that English was not entitled to any compensation as the suit English had prosecuted was unsuccessful, and the contract strictly provided English with the privilege to commence and conduct only one suit. He maintained that he had executed his duty by successfully bringing the case to resolution independently and that English rendered no assistance in the subsequent successful prosecution.

In January 1874, the case of Joseph L. Keedy v. Nancy E. Howe et al. took place in Illinois, specifically starting in the Moultrie Circuit Court and later transferred to Shelby County. The case revolved around a lawsuit brought by Nancy E. Howe and others against Joseph L. Keedy, alleging that he was liable for selling intoxicating liquor to Howe's husband, which contributed to the husband's intoxication and subsequent health issues. The plaintiffs claimed that Keedy's employees sold liquor to Howe’s husband despite Keedy's alleged orders not to do so. The primary legal consideration was whether Keedy could be held liable for the actions of his clerks, especially in light of his instructions against selling liquor to intoxicated individuals. The case referenced prior rulings and established the doctrine of "respondeat superior," which holds an employer liable for the actions of employees conducted within the scope of their employment, regardless of the employer's personal involvement or knowledge.	The plaintiffs argued that Keedy should be held liable for the sale of intoxicating liquor to Nancy E. Howe's husband, which they claimed resulted in harm. They sought recovery for actual damages, suggesting that the sale of liquor aggravated the husband's alcoholism, leading to significant personal and financial losses for the widow and her children.	Joseph L. Keedy contended that he should not be held accountable for the actions of his clerks, insisting that he had explicitly ordered them not to sell liquor to Howe's husband. He argued that the court's refusal to give a jury instruction on this point was erroneous and would unfairly hold him liable for acts done without his knowledge or consent. Keedy maintained that, under civil law principles, he could only be liable for his own actions, not those of his employees acting contrary to his explicit instructions.

The case "Amherst Hayes et al. v. Maria B. Hayes et al." was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The dispute arises from the estate of Rev. Harvey H. Hayes, who died on July 20, 1867, in Rock Island, Illinois. He was survived by his widow, Maria B. Hayes, but had no children, parents, or descendants. After his death, Maria took out letters of administration on his estate. The plaintiffs, claiming to be the heirs of Dr. Hayes, contest the distribution of his personal estate, arguing that he was domiciled in Iowa at the time of his death, which would affect distribution laws. The plaintiffs assert that the widow's award of $1,832 granted by the appraisers should be set aside, and that the remaining estate should be distributed according to Iowa law. The key issue in the case is the determination of Dr. Hayes' domicile, whether it was Illinois or Iowa at the time of his death. The Circuit Court of Rock Island found that Dr. Hayes was domiciled in Illinois, which prompted the plaintiffs to seek a reversal of that decree.	The plaintiffs contend that Rev. Harvey H. Hayes was domiciled in Iowa at the time of his death, contrary to the Circuit Court's finding. They argue that because he was a resident of Iowa, the distribution of his estate should be governed by Iowa law rather than Illinois law. They seek to invalidate the widow's award and request that the remaining estate be distributed in accordance with Iowa's intestacy laws.	The defendants, led by Maria B. Hayes, maintain that the Circuit Court correctly determined that Dr. Hayes was domiciled in Illinois at the time of his death. They argue that despite his travels, his true, fixed, and permanent home was Rock Island, Illinois, where he owned significant property and had no intention to abandon it. The defendants request that the court affirm the lower court's decision regarding the domicile and the rightful distribution of the estate.

The case of Henry C. Childs v. Laflin, Butler & Co. took place in September 1870 in Chicago, Illinois. The dispute arose from a promissory note given by defendant Henry C. Childs to the plaintiffs, Laflin, Butler & Co. The note, dated October 15, 1868, indicated that Childs promised to pay $1178.31 eighteen months after the date at the office of the plaintiffs. When the case reached the Superior Court of Chicago, the trial was held without a jury, and the court found in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $1198 in damages. Childs appealed the decision, arguing that there was a variance between the note described in the declaration and the one actually produced during the trial. The central issue was the description of the place of payment, which Childs contended was incorrectly stated in the declaration, as it implied the payment was to be made at a specific office location in Cook County, while evidence showed the plaintiffs had offices in other locations as well.	The plaintiffs, Laflin, Butler & Co., claimed that Childs had executed a valid promissory note promising to pay them a specified sum of money, as described in their declaration. They argued that the note should be upheld based on the evidence presented, despite the defense's claim of a variance regarding the place of payment.	The defendant, Henry C. Childs, contended that there was a fatal variance between the promissory note as described in the declaration and the note presented in court. Childs asserted that the declaration's claim that the note was payable specifically at the plaintiffs' office in Cook County mischaracterized the instrument, as it also referenced their office in another county, leading to ambiguity regarding the proper place of payment.

On December 2, 1858, in La Salle County, Illinois, Claudius B. King, facing debts amounting to $3,524.44 to creditors Hunt, Osborne, and Bacon, borrowed $3,500 from William H. W. Cushman to settle these debts. As security, King provided Cushman with several notes and mortgages, including one from his brother, Hervey King. To further protect these securities, King executed a deed of trust to Samuel B. Gridley. On October 16, 1858, Joseph O. Glover purchased town lots in Ottawa from a sheriff's execution sale on a judgment against Claudius and Hervey King, with the sale occurring two days before the scheduled date. Cushman later acquired Glover's title to these lots for $800 under the belief that it would secure his interests. Claudius B. King challenged on appeal a decree from the Circuit Court that established monetary obligations and transferred the ownership of the mortgage from Claudius to Glover and subsequently to Cushman due to the irregularity of the sale.	Claudius B. King argued that the decree order to pay Cushman $3,500 (minus $300 already paid) was unjust, particularly the clause divesting him of the mortgage title. He contended that Cushman's acquisition of Glover's title was as a trustee for King’s benefit and asserted that both parties were aware of the irregularities regarding the sale. King requested the court to compel Cushman to relinquish the securities upon payment of the debt.	William H. W. Cushman contended that his acquisition of the Hunt, Bacon, and Osborn notes and mortgages entitled him to their proceeds, regardless of the amount exceeding what he loaned to Claudius. He argued that the securities secured by the mortgages were unaffected by usury claims related to King’s debt and positioned that he rightfully transferred the mortgage with legitimate and enforceable rights.

Jacob Gibbons brought a legal action against Peter Bressler in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871, following a series of events rooted in a disputed sale of land in Whiteside County, Illinois. Gibbons claimed that his title to certain lands was clouded due to Bressler purchasing the property at a sheriff's sale after a judgment was obtained against Gibbons in a prior attachment suit. Gibbons asserted that the judgment was procured through fraudulent means, alleging that there was no actual debt owed to Bressler at the time of the suit. The appeal originated from a bill in equity seeking to invalidate the sale, which Gibbons argued resulted from Bressler’s fraudulent actions, including irregularities in the legal proceedings and the inadequacy of the sale price. The circuit court had previously dismissed Gibbons's bill, leading to the appeal. The case revolved around the legitimacy of the attachments against Gibbons's property and the validity of the debt that initiated them.	The plaintiff, Gibbons, argued that the sheriff's sale of his lands was fraudulent due to the absence of any indebtedness to Bressler when the attachment suit began. Gibbons contended that the judgment was obtained under false pretenses and that there were irregularities in the court proceedings. He sought to have the sale set aside and to clear the alleged cloud on his title due to Bressler's actions.	The defendant, Bressler, denied all allegations of fraud and maintained that he had a valid claim against Gibbons based on a written instrument indicating a debt. Bressler argued that the court had obtained jurisdiction through proper processes and that any irregularities in the proceeding did not invalidate the judgment. He asserted that the sale was conducted fairly, and the price paid was sufficient, thus defending the legitimacy of his ownership.

In the case of "The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company v. Samuel Warner," the events unfolded on August 20, 1875, involving Samuel Warner, a freight conductor employed by the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company. The incident occurred early in the morning while Warner was attempting to uncouple a moving freight car. As he climbed a ladder on the car's side, he expected to grasp a handle and rest his foot on a step located at the end of the car. However, both the handle and step were absent. Consequently, Warner lost his grip and fell onto the tracks, leading to severe injuries, including the need for amputation of his arm after it was struck by a passing train. The case delved into the issue of negligence, particularly the company’s failure to provide necessary safety equipment, which Warner claimed resulted in his injuries. The legal proceedings began at the Circuit Court of Cook County, were reversed for a new trial by the Illinois Supreme Court in 1884, and eventually led to an appeal after the Circuit Court ruled in favor of Warner again.	Samuel Warner, the plaintiff, argued that the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company was negligent for failing to provide a handle and step on the freight car, which were essential for safely uncoupling the cars. He requested damages for the injuries sustained as a result of this negligence, asserting that his injury was primarily due to the railroad's lack of proper safety equipment and that this negligence was gross compared to any minor negligence he might have exhibited during the incident.	The defendant, the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company, contended that Warner was partially negligent, as he should have checked for safety features like the handle and step before acting. They argued that they were not obligated to furnish the very best safety appliances and that the freight cars, in their condition, did not present unreasonable danger. They asserted that since Warner had the responsibility to exercise ordinary care, his negligence should bar recovery.

In the case of "James Mix, impleaded, etc., et al. v. Peyton R. Chandler et al.", the legal proceedings occurred during the May Term of 1865 in the Superior Court of Chicago, Illinois. The central parties involved included the plaintiffs—Peyton E. Chandler, Samuel L. Keith, and Thomas Snell—and the defendants, including James Mix and others. The plaintiffs initiated an action of assumpsit (a legal term for a type of contract action) against the defendants. The case was brought forth amidst the backdrop of the post-Civil War era, highlighting the legal complexities of economic agreements at that time. As the trial progressed, a demurrer raised by the defendants was heard, and damages were assessed against them by a jury. Following this, one of the defendants attempted to overturn the verdict based on procedural claims, which led to the appellate review by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs contended that the demurrer filed by the defendants should not impede the court's judgment against them. They maintained that the procedural rules were appropriately followed, asserting that a formal joinder in demurrer was unnecessary. The plaintiffs sought to have the judgment in their favor upheld and to recover damages as assessed by the jury.	The defendants argued that the judgment should be reversed because it was rendered without a proper joinder in demurrer, claiming that this was a necessary procedural element. They also contended the trial violated established rules of practice from the Superior Court, emphasizing a supposed lack of adequate notice regarding the arguments made on the demurrer, which they believed warranted a reconsideration of the case.

Reuben R. Rees passed away on December 7, 1880, in Jackson County, Illinois, leaving behind a widow, Sarah L. Rees, and twelve children from two marriages. His will, made on November 26, 1880, named Sarah as the executrix and detailed specific bequests, including land designated for his daughter, Dora L. Rees. However, discrepancies arose regarding the description of land bequeathed and the identification of some heirs, particularly concerning a clause that referred to "the four boys" among his sons. This led Leo H. Rees, Ephraim L. Rees, Mary E. Striger, and Ellen Kilmer to file suit in February 1881, claiming their father's will was invalid due to his lack of mental capacity and undue influence from his wife, as well as unclear land descriptions. The Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, agreeing to set aside the will. The case was later appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court on March 26, 1885, to determine the validity of the will based on the contested clauses.	The plaintiffs argued that at the time of the will's creation, Reuben R. Rees was not of sound mind and was unduly influenced by his wife, Sarah L. Rees. They challenged the validity of the fifth clause of the will, asserting that the land description given for Dora L. Rees was insufficiently precise and that the phrase "the four boys" was ambiguous and could not legitimately indicate which of the seven sons was meant. Their request was for the court to set aside the will, redistribute the estate equally among all children and grandchildren, and revoke the letters testamentary issued to Sarah.	The defendants, including Sarah L. Rees and other younger children, argued that the will was valid and that the descriptions provided were clear enough to determine ownership and beneficial heirs. They contended that the claim of ambiguity was unfounded, asserting that the words "the four boys" referred clearly to the four minor sons living with the testator at the time of his death. They sought to have the court uphold the will as written and dismiss the plaintiffs' claims.

The case "Chicago & Alton R. R. Co. v. John Stites" took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, culminating in a judgment rendered on January 8, 1887. The plaintiff, John Stites, was employed as a yard switchman for the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company. He claimed that he sustained injuries due to the defendant's negligence—specifically, the alleged failure to maintain a railroad switch in a safe condition. The incident occurred while Stites was riding on an engine that derailed as it transitioned onto a side track via the defective switch. Stites argued that this negligence caused him to either be thrown from the engine or forced to jump to avoid injury, resulting in significant harm. During the appeal, the defendant contended that the switch was properly maintained and in good working order prior to the accident. They cited the presence of repair crews and the fact that the switch had been inspected shortly before the incident. The core of the case hinged on whether the defendant had indeed acted negligently regarding the condition of the switch.	John Stites, the plaintiff, claimed that he suffered injuries due to the negligence of the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company. He argued that the company allowed a crucial switch to remain in a defective state, leading to the derailing of the engine he was operating. His primary legal request was for damages amounting to $3,550 for the injuries sustained during the incident, which he attributed directly to the company’s failure to maintain safe working conditions.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, the defendant, argued that the evidence did not support the plaintiff’s claims of negligence. They maintained that the railroad switch was functional and had been inspected regularly by qualified personnel. The defendant contended that the switch was in good repair shortly before the accident and asserted that the occurrence was not due to any negligence on their part. They sought to have the judgment rendered in favor of the plaintiff overturned, asserting that there was no proof that they were aware of any defect before the incident.

The case "Huntington W. Jackson, Receiver, v. Oliver H. Horton, Receiver, et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court and revolves around legal disputes over a property involving multiple parties. The case began when Huntington W. Jackson, appointed as the receiver for the Third National Bank of Chicago, filed a lawsuit against Oliver H. Horton, who was the receiver of the German Savings Bank of Chicago, and several other individuals. The original bill was filed on March 13, 1884, and subsequently an amended bill followed. Jackson claimed that Horton had executed a deed conveying 70 acres of land to Luther K. Tucker instead of the intended 60 acres; he argued that 10 acres of the land in question should rightfully belong to Jackson and others, as they had equitable interests in that land. A series of negotiations and court orders regarding the parties’ interests in the land ensued, culminating in a legal battle over the rightful ownership of the 10 acres. The court of origin dismissed the case for lack of equity, prompting an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Huntington W. Jackson, as the receiver of the Third National Bank, claimed that Horton unlawfully conveyed 10 acres of land to Tucker, which belong to him and others based on equitable ownership. He sought the reformation of the deed to ensure the conveyance only applied to 60 acres, requested that Horton transfer the 10 acres to him and asked for a partition of the land to resolve ownership disputes.	The defendant, Oliver H. Horton, argued that he had acted within his legal powers as a receiver and that any prior agreements or settlements had been properly executed. Horton claimed that Jackson and others should have been aware of the complexities regarding the land title and that the issue of equitable ownership had been settled previously. He contended that the sale of the property had been done in good faith and claimed that no further obligations existed on his part concerning the 10 acres.

In the case of Mary J. Hall et al. v. William H. Davis, the events unfolded between 1856 and 1867 in Jackson County, Illinois. The case began when William H. Davis filed a petition for partition of approximately 700 acres of land belonging to the estate of Samuel B. Hall, who had passed away. Mary J. Hall and James H. Hall were named as the defendants. A summons was issued on July 10, 1856, but only Mary J. Hall was served, while James H. was not found. A notice of the court proceedings was published in a local newspaper. Subsequently, the court defaulted the defendants and ordered a partition and sale of the land. Over the next few years, various hearings took place, leading to a judgment of partition where Davis acquired ownership of three-fifths of the land as he had purchased interests from other heirs. Mary J. Hall, being a minor at the time of the original proceedings, later sought to reinstate the case, claiming her rights had not been protected. Her motions were ultimately denied in the lower court, prompting her to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The main argument presented by Mary J. Hall in her appeal was that she was a minor during the original proceedings and was never properly notified of the suit concerning her inheritances. She claimed that her rights were not represented due to the oversight of her deceased sibling, Juliet W. Hall, whose shares were not accounted for in the partition. Mary J. Hall sought the reversal of the previous decree of partition, a vacating of all proceedings against her, and a trial to properly address her and her mother's respective claims to the property.	William H. Davis contended that the court had proper jurisdiction over the case, asserting that the service of summons was valid even though there was ambiguity regarding the counties involved. He also maintained that Mary J. Hall, being a minor at the time, had no standing to contest the previous decree as her legal representation was not established during the initial proceedings. Davis argued that all necessary parties were appropriately notified and that the partition had been conducted lawfully.

In April 1864, Solomon Baker purchased a colt from Barton when it was only a few days old. Baker took the colt home and cared for it until it strayed away in July 1865. In October of the same year, Baker and his son found the colt at the home of Charles Robinson, approximately four miles away, and took it back to their possession. In June 1866, Robinson arrived at Baker's residence claiming ownership of the colt. A dispute ensued regarding its ownership, leading to Robinson taking the colt under the condition that he would return it if his family could not identify it as theirs. However, he never returned it. Baker then initiated a writ of replevin against Robinson, resulting in an initial jury verdict in Baker's favor, but this was appealed to the circuit court, where the jury found for Robinson instead. Baker subsequently took the case to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Baker argued that he was the rightful owner of the colt, having purchased it from Barton and maintained possession until it was taken by Robinson. He contended that Robinson had no valid claim to the animal, as the conditions under which Robinson took possession had not been met, namely failing to return the colt after his family's examination did not confirm ownership.	Robinson claimed ownership of the colt, asserting that he had acquired it from Baker under the stipulation that it would be returned if not identified as his by his family. He maintained that since he had possession, he held the superior claim at that point. Robinson argued that the jury's verdict supported his claim and that the lower court had appropriately handled the instructions given to the jury during the trial.

On May 23, 1840, Robert B. McDowell, the guardian of minors Elizabeth and Julia Ann Bates, resigned his guardianship in the Probate Court in Galena, Illinois. The court accepted the resignation and appointed Thomas Drum as their new guardian. Subsequently, a dispute arose regarding the legality of Drum's appointment and the sale of real estate belonging to the wards. The primary contention was whether the court had the jurisdiction to order the sale of said property, given that Drum claimed he had no personal property of his wards to manage. The estate in question involved the north half of lot five and the south half of lot six in block twenty-nine of Galena. The plaintiffs initiated legal proceedings to reclaim their property, arguing undue dispossession by the defendants, who had acquired it through a sale conducted under Drum's guardianship. The case ultimately moved to the Illinois Supreme Court for appellate review.	The plaintiffs, Alexander Young and Elizabeth Young, claimed ownership of an undivided half of the property based on a U.S. patent granted to Elizabeth and Julia Ann Bates, heirs of Nehemiah Bates. They argued they were unlawfully dispossessed, seeking restitution of their property rights and challenging the legitimacy of the sale conducted by Drum, the guardian.	The defendants, John Lorain and others, contended that the Circuit Court had jurisdiction to sell the property and asserted the validity of the sale conducted by Drum. They maintained that the Probate Court had the authority to appoint Drum as guardian and that all procedural requirements for the sale had been met, including the proper notices and petitions. They argued that the plaintiffs could not claim ownership after the sale, irrespective of subsequent patent issuance.

In the case of Ruckman v. Allwood, heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1867, the dispute arose from legal proceedings initiated in the Circuit Court of Peoria County, Illinois. The case progressed following the appearance of Mr. H. M. Wead, who filed a plea of release of errors on behalf of the defendants (Allwood et al.). This prompted a trial in the lower court, which resulted in a jury verdict that was certified back to the Supreme Court for review. The defendants later sought to withdraw the plea by Wead, claiming he had not been authorized to represent them. They presented several affidavits attempting to contest Wead's authority. However, the court noted that the defendants had been duly served and had not objected to Wead's representation until the motion was filed, thereby waiving their right to question his authority.	Ruckman, as the plaintiff, primarily contended that the defendants’ attempts to withdraw their plea of release of errors came too late because they had been properly brought into court and were presumed to have approved Wead's actions. The plaintiff argued that any objections to the authority of the attorney should be deemed waived due to their delay in raising them.	The defendants argued that they had not authorized Mr. H. M. Wead to appear as their attorney or to file the plea of release of errors, contesting the validity of the legal proceedings based on this alleged lack of authority. They further claimed that the case should be dismissed because the non-resident plaintiff failed to file a bond for costs before initiating the writ of error.

William Brown filed a case against Cyrus Strait and his associates in Wayne County, Illinois, after recovering a judgment against them in a lower court. The background of the case involves a debt owed to Brown by Collins, who was indebted to him for forty dollars. Collins had sold a mill to Strait and Crews and had verbally promised to settle his debt to Brown with the funds from this sale. However, after Brown’s demand for payment, Strait and Crews refused to honor this commitment. The circuit court ruled in favor of Strait and Crews, which led Brown to take the case to the Illinois Supreme Court by way of a writ of error, challenging the lower court's decision against him.	Brown argued that he was a third-party beneficiary to the verbal contract between Collins and the defendants. He maintained that since Collins had promised to use the proceeds from the sale of the mill to pay his debt, he had a valid claim for breach of contract. Brown sought to have the previous judgment reversed, asserting his right to enforce the agreement despite not being present at the contract's formation.	Strait and Crews contended that the agreement did not obligate them to pay Brown since he was not a party to the contract between them and Collins. They claimed that any promise made regarding paying Brown was not enforceable and that they had already fulfilled their obligations under their agreement with Collins. Consequently, they filed for the judgment to be upheld, requesting that Brown's appeal be dismissed and that he pay the costs incurred.

On March 20, 1850, in Will County, Illinois, John W. Day purchased a right of way from Taylor, covering a tract of land that included a public highway known as the Chicago road. Taylor had held a bond from Daggett for multiple tracts of land, including a forty-acre area and a thirty-five-acre tract, and the sale included rights for access to the DesPlaines River. After Taylor's death, his estate sold the property to Matthewson, who conveyed it to Fitzpatrick. McCann later bought the property from Fitzpatrick. In 1868, McCann obstructed Day's access to the river by fencing off the right of way that Day had been using, which was critical for his land as it lacked a water source. Day filed a complaint seeking an injunction against McCann to prevent her from obstructing his right of way, asserting that he legally obtained the right and had been using it continuously. The court ultimately ruled in favor of Day, emphasizing that he had established his right to the easement despite the lack of a recorded deed.	Day's primary argument was that he had legally acquired a right of way across the land from Taylor, which was critical for accessing the DesPlaines River. He claimed that even though the deed was unrecorded, his continuous use of the right of way, which was fenced on both sides, constituted sufficient notice to any subsequent purchasers, including McCann, of his property rights. Day requested that the court issue a perpetual injunction against McCann to stop her from obstructing this right of way.	McCann's defense focused on challenging Day's claim to the easement, arguing that he did not have a recorded right of way at the time of her purchase, and therefore, she was unaware of any such claims. The defense contended that Fitzpatrick, from whom McCann purchased the property, had no obligation to recognize Day's unrecorded right. McCann maintained that her ownership rights to the property should prevail.

George W.
