The case went to the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision rendered on September 28, 1882. James W. Goodman, the defendant, argued that he acquired possession of the real estate under a valid administrative deed following a court decree to settle debts of a deceased property owner, Isaiah Cheek, who had died intestate in 1870. Goodman had been in possession of the property for seven years, paying all legal taxes. The court looked into the legitimacy of Goodman’s title and his good faith in acquiring it. The court determined that Goodman’s claim to the property was lawful and that any issues raised by the plaintiffs were unsupported due to their neglect in pursuing their rights sooner. The majority opinion emphasized the principle that possession acts as notice and that the statute of limitations barred the plaintiffs' claims.	The plaintiffs, George B. Conner and others, argued that they were wrongfully deprived of their property due to a fraudulent transaction related to the partition sale. They sought to have the decree set aside, claiming they were unaware of the alleged fraud until shortly before filing their bill, which they believed exempted them from the statute of limitations.	The defendant, James W. Goodman, contended that he purchased the property in good faith under a valid administrative deed and had maintained possession for over seven years, continuously paying taxes. He argued that the plaintiffs had not learned of their claims until too late due to their own neglect. Goodman asserted that the statute of limitations barred the plaintiffs' claims and that their lack of action did not grant them immunity.

In 1870, John F. Pritchard filed a lawsuit against George Keefer in Sangamon County, Illinois, seeking compensation for the value of his dog, which was shot and killed by a city marshal's agent, John Bell. Bell had been instructed by Keefer to shoot dogs that were running at large without muzzles due to a proclamation from the city's mayor concerning a potential rabies outbreak. While attempting to follow this directive, Bell accidentally shot Pritchard's dog, which was in the enclosed backyard of Pritchard's home, where the gate was closed and the dog was not running at large. Pritchard argued that his dog, valued at fifty dollars, had not violated any ordinance, as it was in an enclosed area. The case was initially decided in favor of Keefer in the circuit court, prompting Pritchard to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Pritchard's main argument revolved around the assertion that his dog was not at large and was improperly killed under the circumstances. He contended that Keefer, as the city marshal, was responsible for the actions of his agent and should be held liable for the wrongful killing of his dog, which he valued at fifty dollars. Accordingly, he sought damages for the loss of his property.	Keefer defended against the claims by asserting that he had been acting under lawful authority granted by the mayor's proclamation and the city ordinance, which permitted the destruction of dogs running at large without muzzles. He argued that Bell did not intend to kill Pritchard's dog and that Pritchard's dog was indeed at large as per the stated ordinance. Keefer maintained that he could not be liable for Bell's actions, as he had given no direct orders to kill the dog and had simply tasked Bell to carry out the ordinance.

The case, "The Michigan Southern and Northern Indiana Railroad Company, Appellant, v. Justin Day, Junior, Appellee," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1858. The dispute originated when Justin Day hired the Michigan Southern and Northern Indiana Railroad Company (the defendant) to transport a box containing goods valued at $3,000 from Adrian, Michigan, to Chicago, Illinois. Day alleged that the company failed to deliver the goods in a timely manner, as per the contracted agreement. The box was shipped on October 29, arriving in Chicago on November 3, but was not delivered until November 15, which Day deemed unreasonable. The plaintiff claimed that the delivery took an unwarranted twelve days and sought damages. The trial ended with a jury verdict favoring Day, awarding him $820. The railroad company then appealed, focusing on various alleged errors during the trial.	The plaintiff, Justin Day, claimed that the Michigan Southern and Northern Indiana Railroad Company breached their contract by failing to deliver his goods in a reasonable time. He argued that the agreement explicitly required the delivery of the box within three days of receipt, yet there was a significant delay, negatively impacting him. Day sought damages of $3,000 for the failure to fulfill the delivery terms as contracted, alleging that the defendant was liable as a common carrier for the breach of duty.	The defendant, Michigan Southern and Northern Indiana Railroad Company, contended that they did not cause any unreasonable delays in delivery. They argued that upon arriving in Chicago, the goods were delivered to a freight agent in adherence to standard practices. The company maintained that their responsibility ended when the goods reached their destination and that any subsequent directions given by Day's agent were not in line with the original contract. They sought to have the judgment against them overturned, claiming that proper delivery had occurred and that they were not liable for any delays after the goods had reached Chicago.

In the late 19th century, specifically on May 11, 1888, a legal case unfolded in East St. Louis, Illinois, involving Anton Kiefer, serving as the administrator of his deceased son, John Kiefer. Kiefer brought suit against The Consolidated Ice Machine Company and the Heim's Brewing Company following the tragic death of his son, who died due to an accident involving an iron tank that fell while he was working on the roof of the brewery's engine house. The ice machine company was responsible for erecting a refrigerator plant at the brewing company’s direction. The tank's support system, constructed of timber and hog chains, was deemed inadequate. The plaintiff alleged that both companies operated negligently by failing to provide a safe working environment and directing the deceased to dangerous areas without proper warnings. The case hinged on proving negligence regarding the structural support that ultimately failed, leading to the fatal incident.	The plaintiff, Anton Kiefer, claimed that both The Consolidated Ice Machine Company and Heim's Brewing Company were negligent in allowing unsafe working conditions. He argued that the defendants failed to ensure the tank was adequately supported and did not inform the deceased of the dangers present, thereby leading to his death. Kiefer sought damages for the wrongful death of his son, emphasizing the defendants' roles in recklessly contributing to the hazardous environment that resulted in the tragedy.	The defendants contended that they should not be held liable as they had employed competent mechanics and used suitable materials for the construction. They claimed that the failure of the support system was due to a hidden defect in the weld of the swivel, which was not discoverable by ordinary inspection. Additionally, they argued that the deceased had been warned against going on the roof until the tank was emptied and that his actions contributed to his own demise, thus asserting a degree of negligence on the part of the deceased.

Frederick Remann, Jr. Exr. v. John H. Buckmaster et al. arose in June 1877 in Illinois. The case involved a dispute over the foreclosure of a mortgage originally made by John H. Buckmaster to Frederick Remann, who had since died. The mortgage, executed on May 6, 1872, was duly acknowledged and recorded. The key individuals included Frederick Remann's estate, represented by his executor, and John H. Buckmaster, who was involved in a cross-bill with Richard H. Gray, the administrator of the estate of Joseph Hall. The controversy began when Gray filed a cross-bill after Buckmaster, who had sold land to Hall, claimed the right to foreclose on Remann's mortgage. Buckmaster had also taken back promissory notes for the purchase price of the land from Hall, which were secured by a prior mortgage. The legal proceedings examined whether the Hall mortgage held a prior lien over Remann’s mortgage, considering Buckmaster's actions and knowledge about the unpaid notes covered by Hall’s mortgage.	The plaintiff, represented by Remann's estate, claimed that they had a proper legal interest in foreclosing the mortgage against Buckmaster. They argued that they were not adequately informed about the prior mortgage held by Hall, which limited their rights. The plaintiff sought enforcement of the Remann mortgage and requested that the court recognize their claim as a primary lien over the property in question.	The defendant, Buckmaster, contended that the Hall mortgage was prior to the Remann mortgage and had not been properly satisfied when Remann took the second mortgage on the property. Buckmaster argued that he had informed Remann about the outstanding obligations connected to the Hall mortgage before executing the second mortgage. He maintained that Remann's claims should be dismissed as he held both constructive and actual notice regarding the original mortgage and its terms.

In 1874, in Kankakee County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving William B. Fonville and other plaintiffs against defendants James Monroe and another party. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court and stemmed from issues related to the process of legal notice and representation in the initial court proceedings. The plaintiffs claimed that a variance existed between the writ and the declaration concerning the name of a plaintiff, Charles D. Reed, who was included in the summons but not in the declaration. This discrepancy led to the defendants arguing that this was a procedural error preventing a proper judgment against them. The court addressed this variance and other procedural matters such as appearances and service of process, indicating that no timely objection was raised in the lower court regarding these issues.	The plaintiffs contended that the variance in naming Charles D. Reed did not invalidate the judgment as no objections were made in the lower court regarding his inclusion. They argued that since Reed was a plaintiff, the judgment in his favor, along with the other plaintiffs, was appropriate and should stand. They sought to uphold the judgment rendered in their favor from the lower court.	The defendants, primarily represented by appellant Dunham, argued that he was not served with process, claiming this rendered any judgment against him invalid. However, they had previously filed a demurrer and a general issue which were ruled on by the court. The defendants also claimed that the removal of their plea from the record constituted an error but were informed that their subsequent extension for filing a plea indicated a full appearance, thus legitimizing the judgment against them.

The case of William R. Milligan v. Andrew J. O’Conor et al. involves a replevin action that originated in 1884 in La Salle County, Illinois. The core issue arose from financial difficulties faced by the Eliel Brewing Company, which was significantly indebted, totaling around $125,000. Following several judgments against the company in May 1884, a receiver was appointed to manage its property. In September 1884, an agreement was made between the brewing company and its principal creditors which included relinquishing rights to the property to newly appointed trustees, who would manage the business for the benefit of creditors. The appointed trustees assumed control of the brewing company's assets and undertook substantial repairs and expansions at a cost of about $46,000. In December 1884, the sheriff, representing creditors who had judgments against the brewing company, executed a levy on the property still in the hands of the trustees. The creditors, specifically the Streator National Bank and James J. Vernon, did not participate in or agree to the earlier arrangement and contested the validity of the trustees' control over the property's assets, arguing that the conveyance to the trustees was invalid as it potentially delayed and hindered their ability to recover debts owed.	The plaintiff, William R. Milligan (the sheriff), claims the right to reclaim certain personal property, including horses and wagons, that are in possession of the trustees. He argues that the conveyance of the property to the trustees was invalid with respect to the non-consenting creditors, namely the Streator National Bank and Vernon. Milligan asserts that the trustee's management and the subsequent arrangement violated state laws regarding voluntary assignments, which should protect the rights of all creditors.	The defendants, represented by trustees Andrew J. O’Conor et al., argue that they legitimately acquired the brewing company's assets under an agreement aimed at protecting the interests of creditors. They contend that the arrangement was lawful and should be upheld, as the primary creditors had relinquished their claims voluntarily. They maintain that the recipe and management model implemented prioritized the creditors’ eventual interests, and they request the court to dismiss Milligan's claims based on the validity of the initial agreement and the abandonment of claims by other creditors.

The case "The City of Chicago v. Daniel O'Hara" was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871. The litigation arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving Daniel O'Hara, the clerk of the criminal court of Cook County, seeking to compel the City of Chicago to pay certain fees owed to him. The legal framework was shaped by an act from 1853 establishing the recorder's court in Chicago, which stipulated that fees of the sheriff and clerk in cases where they could not be collected from defendants should be paid from the city treasury. A new constitution broadened the jurisdiction of the court to encompass the entire county, which led to the City of Chicago contesting its responsibility to cover these fees. The city argued that now that the court operated on a county level, the fees should be the county’s responsibility. However, the court clarified that no general statute mandated counties to pay such fees and highlighted that Cook County was not included in specific legislation that allocated liability for fees to counties. The ruling underscored the clerk's right to claim the fees from the city under existing laws until legislative changes were made.	Daniel O'Hara, as the clerk of the criminal court, claimed that he had a legal right to collect fees for his services from the City of Chicago, as established by earlier statutory provisions. He argued that the city was obligated to pay these fees despite the court's transition to a county jurisdiction, citing the lack of a general statute requiring counties to assume responsibility for such payments.	The City of Chicago contended that, following the constitutional changes, the fees should now be covered by Cook County instead of the city. The city argued that since the jurisdiction expanded to the county level, it was unreasonable to hold Chicago responsible for fees that should be borne by the county. They insisted that the clerk should pursue payment from the county, as the current legal framework did not impose a duty on the city.

In January 1865, the case titled "George Fishback v. Hannah A. Lane et al." was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from the Macoupin Circuit Court. The case involves George Fishback, who purchased a homestead from Davis, who had previously transferred the property to a trustee, Freeman, for the benefit of several creditors after Lane, the judgment creditor, obtained a judgment against Davis. Lane then attempted to levy execution on the homestead based on the prior judgment. In response, Fishback filed a bill in chancery seeking to prevent Lane from enforcing the execution. The Circuit Court dismissed Fishback's bill, prompting Fishback to appeal the decision. The case raises questions about the validity of the homestead right in relation to prior judgments and the potential obligations of all parties involved.	George Fishback contended that his purchase of the homestead exempted him from Lane’s prior judgment lien because he had taken possession of the property. He requested the court to prevent Lane and the sheriff from levying execution on the homestead, arguing that the lack of a statutory waiver in the deed did not invalidate his claim to ownership and possession.	The defendants, led by Hannah A. Lane, argued that Fishback's claim to the homestead was still subject to Lane's prior judgment. They maintained that, regardless of possession, the homestead rights did not protect Fishback from the execution on the property connected to the earlier judgment against Davis, and requested that the initial dismissal of Fishback's injunction bill be upheld.

In 1869, in St. Clair County, Illinois, William Nichols borrowed $2,450 from William B. Bradsby, for which he executed a promissory note due fifteen months later. Alongside this note, Nichols conveyed a warranty deed for a tract of land to Bradsby, intending it to serve as collateral for the loan. Bradsby, however, claimed the transfer was an outright sale and denied the existence of any adhesive promissory note or debt after the conveyance. After the fifteen months lapsed without Nichols repurchasing the land, Bradsby sold the property to Schaefer. Nichols, who remained in possession pending a settlement, later received $400 from Bradsby, which they hoped would cover the amount of sale surplus over Bradsby's debt. Confusion ensued over the bond and note exchanged after the sale; both parties claimed the documents were misplaced. Nichols subsequently filed a lawsuit seeking the excess from the sale price concluded by Bradsby’s deal with Schaefer, which led to a jury’s verdict favoring Nichols, awarding him $498.94.	William Nichols claimed that the warranty deed he executed was only meant to secure his debt to Bradsby, and that he was entitled to a surplus from the sale of the land. He filed suit to recover the excess money generated from the sale to Schaefer beyond what he owed Bradsby, asserting that Bradsby's later payment did not constitute a full settlement of all claims.	William B. Bradsby contended that the deed was an outright sale, denying any original debt post-conveyance. He argued that Nichols had no valid claims since they had settled their accounts after the sale, asserting that the bond was merely a promise to re-convey the land under different terms. Bradsby maintained that the stated payment was not a recognition of any prior agreement or obligation.

Jacob Vogel filed a legal case against Sylvanus Shurtliff et al., stemming from a mortgage dispute that was initially considered by the Illinois Appellate Court in May 1886 and subsequently remanded in November 1886. The case revolves around real estate transactions involving Thomas B. Adkisson, who had mortgaged two lots (lot five and a reversionary interest in lot four) to secure a loan of $158.27. Following the mortgage, Adkisson sold lot five to Andrew Ilutehin and his reversionary interest in lot four to O. H. Moore. The legal question is regarding the liability of these properties for the mortgage debt post-sale. The court found that contributions for this debt should be made among those involved based on the grantees' understanding of the deed terms and the resulting financial obligations from the sale of the properties. The case was heard again after specified directions were provided, focusing on the financial contributions and liens that might arise from these transfers regarding the original mortgage debt.	Jacob Vogel, representing his interests, argues that the transactions conducted by Thomas B. Adkisson and the implications of the deeds should determine the respective financial responsibilities concerning the mortgage debt. Vogel's claims are directed toward establishing that both Ilutehin and Moore are liable for their corresponding shares of the debt based on the agreements made at the time of the transfers and seek a decree that recognizes these obligations.	The defendants, including Shurtliff and the other relevant grantees, respond by asserting that the terms of the deed modified the usual rule regarding liability for the mortgage. They argue that the deed specifically outlined and limited their obligations and that the interpretation of these terms should absolve them from a disproportionate share of the mortgage debt, claiming that this structure was understood and agreed upon at the time of the property transactions.

Henry Abrahams initiated a legal action against Herman Weiller in September 1877 in Cook County, Illinois. The case revolved around a dispute involving five barrels of whisky, which Abrahams claimed were rightfully his but had been unlawfully appropriated by Weiller. The whisky had been shipped to a storage facility run by Schmed & Labes in Chicago and was meant for Abrahams. A former soliciting agent for Abrahams, by the name of Ike Ruble, took the whisky from the storage, sold it to Weiller, and kept the money for himself. Ruble's former agency, which only allowed him to solicit orders, had been revoked prior to this transaction. The court trial was conducted without a jury, and the judge ruled in favor of Abrahams for the value of the whisky, leading Weiller to appeal the judgment on two grounds: questioning the evidential support for the ruling and requesting a new trial due to newly discovered evidence.	The plaintiff, Henry Abrahams, argued that he was the rightful owner of the five barrels of whisky that had been taken and sold without authorization. He contended that Ruble, who executed the sale to Weiller, did not have the authority to sell the goods or collect payment because his previous agency had been revoked. Abrahams requested the court to affirm the judgment in his favor, asserting his property rights and seeking recovery of the whisky's value.	Herman Weiller, the defendant, sought to overturn the lower court's judgment by claiming that the evidence presented did not support the ruling. Additionally, Weiller argued for a new trial on the basis of newly discovered evidence, asserting that this evidence could potentially alter the outcome of the case. He contended that there was apparent authority for Ruble’s actions, which should make the sale binding upon Abrahams. Weiller sought to invalidate the court's decision and have the case retried.

In 1887, Richard H. Fiddick, a dry goods merchant, entered into a lease agreement with Lena Schmohl, who was constructing a new building in Galena, Illinois. The lease, set for five years at an annual rental of $1,200, required the lessor to provide a functional elevator for Fiddick’s use between the first and third floors. After Fiddick took possession of the building in early April 1887, he encountered issues when the Schmohls, including John G. Schmohl, attempted to charge him for operating costs related to the elevator. Fiddick claimed that it was the Schmohls’ responsibility under the lease to maintain and operate the elevator without imposing these costs. The dispute escalated when the Schmohls cut off the water supply to the elevator after Fiddick refused to pay the disputed charges. To avoid business disruptions, Fiddick paid the charges under protest. The main contention revolved around the interpretation of the lease’s terms regarding the operations of the elevator, particularly a clause stating that the lessor would provide an elevator in “successful operation.” Fiddick argued that both parties had an understanding that the Schmohls would cover the elevator's operational costs, while the Schmohls denied any obligation to maintain it. This led to Fiddick filing a bill to construe the lease and seek reimbursement for the costs he had incurred.	Richard H. Fiddick argued that the lease agreement implied Lena Schmohl was required to maintain and operate the elevator at her own expense throughout the term of the lease. He contended that the decisions made by John G. Schmohl during the lease negotiations led him to believe that he would not be responsible for the additional operating costs. Fiddick sought a legal construction of the lease to affirm this understanding and requested repayment for the amounts he had paid under protest for the elevator's operation.	The Schmohls claimed that the lease explicitly stated their obligations and that Fiddick's interpretations were not supported by its terms. They argued that Fiddick should be bound by the written terms of the lease without considering prior negotiations. The Schmohls contended that their verbal assurances did not constitute a binding obligation and that the parol evidence rule prevented alteration of the lease's written terms. They sought a reversal of the Circuit Court's decree that found in favor of Fiddick.

George H. Forbes, the administrator of the estate of Delilah Deeds, brought a legal suit against Lillie Williams, claiming compensation owed following Deeds' death in Pleasant Valley, Illinois, in October 1875. Deeds had acknowledged a debt of $2,500 to her niece Lillie for personal services performed over a long period. The court case initially emerged in the county court but was appealed to the circuit court after being rejected. The primary evidence consisted of a written note that Lillie claimed was a formal acknowledgment of debt in exchange for services rendered, although those supporting the claim had only indicated the services without any detailed labor description. The case involved another claimant, Mary J. Williams, who similarly contested into the matter, with both claims drafted by the same individual. Ultimately, the court reviewed the claim's validity, focusing on the considered evidence indicating no actual compensation expectation for the services provided.	The plaintiff, George H. Forbes, argued that Deeds' written acknowledgment of a $2,500 debt due to Lillie Williams for personal services constituted a legitimate claim for payment from the estate. He requested the court to recognize the note as a binding obligation of the estate to ensure Lillie's rightful compensation for the services purportedly rendered.	The defendant, Lillie Williams, contended that the note represented a legitimate obligation of the deceased, asserting that the services performed indeed warranted compensation. Lillie argued that there was a clear intent for the debt to be recognized despite the absence of formal agreements on labor expectations, maintaining that the acknowledgment was valid and binding upon the estate.

The case involves Thomas Rogers as the plaintiff and John Holden as the defendant, with proceedings taking place in Adams County, Illinois. The events began in October 1850, when the parties appeared before a justice of the peace to address a dispute regarding a lease executed by Nathan Ward to Rogers. They agreed to submit their disagreement to the arbitration of three individuals. An award was subsequently made in favor of Holden, granting him $15 and costs. Rogers appealed this judgment to the Circuit Court of Adams County, questioning the jurisdiction and the validity of the award that served as the basis of the judgment. The Circuit Court dismissed Rogers' appeal, asserting that no appeal could be taken from a judgment based on an arbitrator's award. The ruling cited a previous case, Van Winkle v. Beck, to support this stance. However, Rogers challenged the dismissal on the grounds that the award might be invalid and sought the right to appeal.	Rogers argues that the judgment made by the justice of the peace was incorrect and that he should be allowed to appeal it. He contends that the statutory provisions permit appeals from such judgments, especially when the basis of the judgment—the arbitrator's award—could potentially be invalid. He claims that the dismissal of his appeal by the Circuit Court was erroneous and seeks to have the case reviewed in order to explore the merits of the award.	Holden contends that the Circuit Court was correct in dismissing Rogers' appeal, arguing that the parties voluntarily chose arbitration as their method of resolving disputes and must abide by the award made. He supports his position with the precedent set by Van Winkle v. Beck, maintaining that appeals are not permissible when the judgment is derived from an award of arbitrators. Holden requests that the court affirm the dismissal of the appeal and uphold the original judgment in his favor.

In the case of Emily A. Green et al. v. The City of Springfield, which took place in Sangamon County, Illinois, the history of the case revolves around the city’s imposition of a special tax for the paving of certain streets and alleys. Initially, the issues surrounding the tax were brought before the County Court of Sangamon County, where objections to the tax were made but ultimately overruled. A previous judgment had confirmed a prior tax levy, which was later reversed by the Illinois Supreme Court, leading to the reinstatement of proceedings in the County Court. The city had enacted an ordinance to levy a special tax on property abutting the streets to be paved, but the plaintiffs argued that the ordinance was unconstitutional and the tax improperly applied, as it did not meet the requirements of “contiguous property” as defined by the Constitution. The case had seen multiple hearings, reflecting disputes about the legality of the tax levy and the process by which it was assessed, culminating in a further appeal by the plaintiffs after their objections had been overruled once more.	The plaintiffs, represented by Emily A. Green and others, alleged that the ordinance under which the special tax was levied was unconstitutional, claiming it did not properly assess tax on “contiguous property.” They also contended that the procedure for levying the special tax was not legally sound, asserting the city failed to follow proper statutory requirements and that the tax imposed on their properties was excessive.	The City of Springfield defended itself by arguing that the ordinance was valid and in line with previous court decisions. They maintained that the tax was appropriately assessed based on the properties' frontages abutting the improvements, as established under Illinois law. The City contended that the objections raised by the plaintiffs had been previously addressed and were therefore not valid, asserting their right to levy taxes in this manner as supported by existing precedent.

The case "Maria L. Kinney et al. v. Jacob Knoebel" was heard in June 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Circuit Court of St. Clair County. The dispute arose after the heirs of William O. Kinney filed an ejectment action against Jacob Knoebel, who had acquired property through a sheriff’s sale following several judgments against Kinney prior to his death. The defendant, Knoebel, provided documentation of multiple judgments and sheriff returns indicating legitimate purchases at various times in 1857 and 1859, culminating in a sheriff's deed executed to Adolphus Berchelmann. The plaintiffs contended that Knoebel purchased the property for himself, despite the documentation stating otherwise. The court allowed amendments to the sheriff's return without notifying the plaintiffs, which they argued was improper. The jury ruled in favor of the defendant, leading to the plaintiffs' appeal.	The plaintiffs, heirs of William O. Kinney, argued that the court erred in allowing amendments to the sheriff's return and in excluding their evidence intended to show that Knoebel purchased the property for himself, thus challenging the validity of the sale. They claimed that discrepancies between the sheriff’s sale documentation undermined Knoebel's title.	The defendant, Jacob Knoebel, defended his title to the property by asserting the validity of the judgments and sheriff's deeds. He contended that the amendments to the sheriff’s return were permissible and that the discrepancies raised were immaterial to the validity of the title acquired through the sheriff's sale. Knoebel maintained that regardless of the claims made by the plaintiffs about his intent in the purchase, the sheriff’s sale and related documents were legally sound.

In the case of Miner N. Knowlton v. George L. Warner, Executor, a dispute arose regarding a breach of covenant related to two deeds that conveyed land from Knowlton to Anna Hanbury. The events took place in Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a trial after Hanbury's death, during which her executor, George L. Warner, was substituted as the plaintiff. The central issue was the non-payment of certain taxes and interest that had become a lien on the property prior to the conveyance. A trial resulted in a verdict favoring the plaintiff for $128.56 due to breaches asserted regarding the covenant against encumbrances and taxes. Specific attention was given to non-payment of taxes on the land and the accrued interest of $307.55 on a deed of trust, which were both paid by Hanbury. The plaintiff's evidence included a prior court decree that established Knowlton's liability for the interest amount in controversy, addressing the overlapping legal matters that had previously been adjudicated.	The plaintiff, represented by George L. Warner as the executor of Anna Hanbury's estate, claimed damages for breach of covenant due to Knowlton's failure to pay specific taxes and interest on a deed of trust related to the properties conveyed. The plaintiff argued that Knowlton was liable for the unpaid amount of $307.55 in accrued interest and sought a judgment for this sum, relying on a prior court decree that established Knowlton's liability for these amounts.	The defendant, Miner N. Knowlton, contended that the interpretation of the deeds did not impose liability for the interest that had accrued prior to the conveyance. He may have argued that the decision not to issue a personal decree against him in the previous little case diminished the current claim’s validity. Knowlton's defense rested on the interpretation of contractual covenants within the deeds, seeking to refute the claims made based on prior adjudications and the understanding of his obligations under the covenants described.

In the spring of 1862, John Parker's house was destroyed by fire, prompting him to store his household furniture with a man named Fergus. When Fergus needed the storage space, Parker moved his furniture to the building of Joseph H. Tiffany, who operated an auction and commission house on Dearborn Street in Chicago. Parker didn’t take a receipt for the furniture but maintained a list of items. Tiffany sold a portion of the furniture with Parker's permission and sent some to Alexander's auction store to sell without explicit authority from Parker. Despite Tiffany selling some items and making some payments to Parker, there were disagreements over the amounts owed and the condition of the remaining items. Ultimately, Tiffany acknowledged his debt to Parker on multiple occasions but failed to settle it. Parker’s claim before the court arose from Tiffany’s alleged failure to account for the furniture and the sums owed after acknowledging Parker’s ownership. The jury initially awarded Parker $511.49, leading to Tiffany’s appeal based on claims that the evidence did not support the verdict.	John Parker claimed that Joseph H. Tiffany was liable for the value of his furniture that was stored and subsequently sold without proper authority. He argued that Tiffany had recognized his ownership of the items and failed to account for their sale, claiming damages consistent with the loss of his property. Parker sought recovery for the total value of the goods, asserting that Tiffany's actions constituted a breach of their agreement and led to financial losses.	Joseph H. Tiffany contended that he did not unlawfully convert Parker’s furniture for personal gain and outlined that any sales made were conducted with Parker's knowledge. He argued that the evidence did not sufficiently prove that he had sold or converted the entire amount of Parker’s goods. Tiffany claimed damages were improperly assessed by the jury and requested the court to overturn the jury’s decision, asserting that he had also incurred storage fees that offset any amount owed to Parker.

In 1866, the legal case Narcisse Rivard et al. v. Hiram Walker was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following actions that began in 1851. The case originated in Sangamon County, Illinois, when John T. Sinclair executed a deed of real estate to his children from a previous marriage to protect their property from being squandered by his then-wife due to domestic difficulties. After a divorce, Sinclair sought to set aside the deed as he claimed his initial motive no longer existed. His children, as the grantees of the deed, were made defendants. The Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of Sinclair, stating there had been no delivery of the deed. However, the evidence suggested that the deed had indeed been delivered to a magistrate for recording. The dispute centered on whether the act of recording the deed constituted a valid delivery to the children. The court needed to determine if Sinclair could reclaim the title and invalidate the deed after his intentions became moot.	The plaintiffs, the children of John T. Sinclair, argued that the deed had been validly delivered and recorded, effectively transferring ownership of the property to them. They maintained that Sinclair intended to protect their interests, and therefore, the court’s initial decree to set aside the deed was unjust. They sought a reversal of the Circuit Court's decision, asserting their rightful ownership of the property.	Sinclair, the defendant, contended that the deed had not been delivered, which would render it ineffective, asserting that his intention changed after obtaining a divorce. He argued that since his original motive for executing the deed no longer existed, the deed should be annulled. He requested that the court uphold the Circuit Court's decree to set aside the deed, thereby transferring the property back to him.

The case of Frederick Mapes v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in 1873, in Winnebago County, Illinois. Frederick Mapes was indicted for selling intoxicating liquor to Bissel Rice, a person alleged to be in the habit of getting intoxicated. The indictment claimed that Mapes unlawfully sold intoxicating liquors to Rice, which was contrary to state statutes. During the trial in the circuit court, the prosecution presented evidence that established Rice's habitual intoxication, including testimonies from several witnesses who had seen him under the influence of alcohol frequently. The jury found Mapes guilty, and the court subsequently rendered judgment based on the verdict. Numerous technical objections and errors were raised by Mapes, including challenges to the court's jurisdiction and the drawing of jurors, but they were ultimately dismissed by the court as trivial.	The plaintiff, representing the state, argued that Frederick Mapes violated the law by selling intoxicating liquor to Bissel Rice, who was known to frequently become intoxicated. The prosecution contended that it was sufficient for the state to prove that Rice was a person in the habit of drinking excessively, thus justifying the indictment and the conviction, regardless of whether Mapes had personal knowledge of Rice's drinking habits. The plaintiff sought a conviction based on the evidence presented.	Frederick Mapes, through his attorneys, challenged the indictment on several grounds, primarily arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction over the case as it should have been tried in county court due to the nature of the charges. Mapes also raised numerous technical objections regarding the jury selection process and claimed that the indictment was flawed because it did not allege that he knew Rice was in the habit of getting intoxicated. His defense requested that the charges be dismissed based on these claims.

In April 1862, the case of Thomas Lewis, Administrator of William Dougherty, deceased, v. Oliver Lindley et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The origins lie in a judgment rendered in December 1837 against Oliver Lindley and Irvin B. Doolittle for $3,441.41 in favor of William Dougherty. Following Dougherty's death in 1839, Thomas Lewis was appointed as his administrator, and an execution to enforce the judgment was issued on July 8, 1843. This execution, however, contained clerical errors, including discrepancies in the amount owed and the proper recital of the judgment creditor. The controversy revolved around land sold under this erroneous execution, which was levied against Oliver Lindley's property. The case also involved claims related to the subsequent conveyance of the land, with various parties asserting their interests.	The plaintiff, Thomas Lewis, claimed that the execution issued against Oliver Lindley erroneously misstated the amount of the judgment and failed to correctly identify the judgment creditor due to Dougherty’s death. The plaintiff sought to amend the execution to reflect the accurate judgment amount and to include appropriate recitals regarding the deceased creditor.	The defendants, represented by W. W. Heaton, contended that the execution errors were substantial and that correcting them would unfairly affect parties claiming interest in the property. They resisted the proposed amendments to the execution.

In 1871, in the village of Winnetka, Illinois, property owners led by Joseph Sherlock filed a lawsuit against the Village of Winnetka and its council members, including Artemus Carter, Timothy Wright, Barnum Blake, and others. The complaint stemmed from actions taken by the council, which had authorized the purchase of land and the construction of buildings purportedly for an educational institution, the Winnetka Academy. The plaintiffs alleged that the council's actions were not in the village's interest, as a majority of the council members were also trustees of the academy, resulting in a conflict of interest. They claimed that the council engaged in fraudulent activities by selling bonds, purchasing land and buildings for private gain rather than for corporate educational purposes, and ultimately appropriating village property for private enterprise. The council's actions included leasing the property to the academy at a nominal rate, allowing the academy to operate for private benefit while raising taxes to pay for the bonds, which led to the lawsuit seeking injunctions to prevent tax collection for these bonds.	The plaintiffs contended that the Village of Winnetka's council acted unlawfully by using public funds and resources for personal gain, and that the bonds issued for the land purchase were invalid due to the conflict of interest, as several council members were also trustees of the Winnetka Academy. They sought an injunction against the execution of tax warrants related to these bonds, claiming that the council's actions breached the trust placed in them as public officials and constituted fraud against the taxpayers.	The defendants argued that the council acted within its charter's bounds and that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate any actionable fraud or malfeasance. They contended that the transactions were legitimate and that raising taxes to sustain the bonds was within their authority. The defendants also alleged that the complaint's claims were multifarious, suggesting that the issues raised were distinct and improperly combined in a single lawsuit, which should warrant dismissal of the case.

In 1872, Alonzo A. Wheelock was elected as the sheriff of Scott County, Illinois. Upon his election, the county board convened on December 5, 1872, to establish his compensation, determining it to be the fees and emoluments of the sheriff's office after deducting necessary expenses, with a maximum cap of $1,500 as per state constitutional guidelines. Following this, an order was issued on June 4, 1873, which sought to clarify this arrangement, indicating that the sheriff would be entitled to an additional amount for expenses, contingent on the remaining office fees after compensation. During Wheelock's tenure, claims were made against him regarding two breaches: he allegedly failed to remit excess funds totaling $1,500 from the office's earnings to the county treasury. Legal actions ensued from the county against Wheelock and his sureties on his official bond, leading to multiple legal pleadings about the interpretation of compensation and allowances due to constitutional restrictions on changes during an official's term.	The plaintiffs argued that Wheelock, as sheriff, failed to pay into the county treasury all earnings received from the office beyond his fixed compensation. They claimed that he unlawfully converted those earnings for his personal use, leading to significant financial losses for Scott County. The plaintiffs sought the enforcement of the bond against Wheelock and his sureties for the full amount of damages, citing breaches of duty and legal obligations per the orders established by the county board.	The defendants contended that the actions taken by the county board regarding Wheelock's compensation and allowances were legally binding and constituted a full defense against the claims made. They asserted that the original order set the sheriff's compensation and any subsequent orders attempting to alter that compensation were void as per state constitutional provisions. Moreover, they argued that after deducting all legitimate expenses, the actual compensation received was well within legal limits and did not warrant the claimed sums from the county.

In April 1865, the case of Frederick Severin v. The People of the State of Illinois was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court concerning events that transpired on August 1, 1864, in DeKalb County, Illinois. Frederick Severin was accused of assaulting Richard Long with a large piece of wood, intending to cause bodily injury. Long's complaint led to a warrant for Severin's arrest, and he was tried before a justice of the peace, Justice Mayo, where he was found guilty and fined eighteen dollars. Severin sought to challenge this verdict in a higher court, arguing that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction due to the nature of the charges being indictable offenses. The case highlights the issues surrounding the jurisdiction of justices of the peace for different classifications of assault and battery.	Frederick Severin, the plaintiff in error, claimed that the justice of the peace did not have jurisdiction over the charges presented because they involved a serious offense described as assault with a deadly weapon. Severin contended that since his complaint was categorically for an indictable offense, only a higher court should have the authority to adjudicate the matter. He sought to have the judgment against him reversed and the proceedings quashed based on this lack of jurisdiction.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by the state's attorney, countered that the justice of the peace had indeed possessed jurisdiction over the charge of assault and battery, which is intrinsically included in any claim of assault with a deadly weapon. They maintained that despite how the complaint was framed, the jurisdiction for assault and battery was upheld, as it is a lesser included offense. The state sought to affirm the conviction and the fine imposed by the justice of the peace.

On December 17, 1884, in Earlville, Illinois, Byron Mosher, acting on behalf of Harriet Mosher, delivered certain hogs to George McDonald. As payment, McDonald issued a check for $54 on the "Exchange Bank" of Earlville. The central issue in the case revolves around whether the check was presented for payment in a timely manner. Mosher claimed he could not present the check on December 18 due to severe winter weather, stating that it was unfeasible to travel the two miles to the bank. While he reported the conditions hindered his ability to go to town, other witnesses contended that the roads were manageable, as they managed outdoor work that day. The bank had failed by December 19, and since Mosher did not present the check on the 18th, it became a matter of whether he exercised proper diligence in doing so. The La Salle County Court initially ruled in favor of Mosher, upholding the claim for the amount of the check.	The plaintiff, George McDonald, contended that Mosher did not present the check for payment within the necessary timeframe after its receipt. He argued that under Illinois law, checks must be presented by the next business day to ensure the drawer's liability, and failing to do so obviates any responsibility on his part due to the bank's subsequent insolvency. McDonald requested a ruling that would enforce this principle and negate Mosher's claim for payment.	The defendant, Byron Mosher, maintained that the extreme weather on December 18 made it unsafe and impractical for him to travel to present the check. He argued that the conditions constituted a valid excuse for his delay in presenting the check and that he took reasonable steps given the circumstances. Mosher requested the court to uphold his claim for payment based on these grounds.

In September 1867, John R. Allen sold furniture from a hotel he was occupying in Kankakee, Illinois, to Chauncey M. Payne, which included the unexpired portion of his lease. After the sale, a dispute arose regarding the delivery of the purchased furniture, with Payne claiming he did not receive all items. Allen contended that he delivered all the furniture and asserted that Payne owed him for services rendered by himself and his family after Payne took possession of the hotel, as well as for money collected during the county fair, which was to be shared. The matter was presented to a jury, which ultimately ruled in favor of Payne. The case involved contradictory testimonies from both parties, and the evidence was notably unclear, leaving it to the jury to determine the credibility of each party's claims.	Payne's main argument was that he did not receive all the furniture he had purchased from Allen as part of their verbal agreement. He sought a judgment acknowledging the incomplete delivery and likely aimed to recover damages related to this claim.	Allen contended that he delivered all the furniture he sold to Payne. Additionally, he claimed that Payne owed him not only for the services provided by his family after the transition of possession but also for a share of the profits from the county fair, which were part of their initial agreement.

In 1883, the case of Henrietta Lang v. William W. Clemens was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a disputed title to property that originated in a partition action dating back to April 1852, when Patrick and Sarah Lang initiated proceedings for assignment of dower against the heirs of a deceased individual named Aikman. Henrietta Lang, the only daughter and heir of Patrick and Sarah Lang, claimed her mother’s interest in the property after Sarah’s death. However, during the initial proceedings, Sarah's name was omitted from the court decree, and her interest was awarded to her husband, Patrick Lang. This decree, although erroneous, remained unchallenged for decades and led to a sale of the property under execution due to debts against Patrick. Henrietta sought to remove what she claimed was a cloud on her title, arguing that the original court decrees were invalid due to the omission of her mother’s name.	Henrietta Lang contended that the original partition decree was invalid as it omitted her mother, Sarah Lang, and claimed that this error constituted a cloud on her title to the property. She argued that the decrees should be set aside on the grounds of fraud and that she was entitled to her rightful share of the inheritance.	William W. Clemens, the appellee, defended against Henrietta's claims by asserting that the original court decrees were valid and binding, regardless of their erroneous nature. He argued that no appeal or writ of error had been sought to contest the decree, and as such, it had the same force and effect as any judgment. The defendant maintained that the lawful distribution of the property had been established for over thirty years, providing stability and interest to third parties who relied on the title.

In the case of Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company v. Thomas Pratt et al., the events took place in November 1880 when hogs were shipped by the plaintiffs (consignors) from Catlin, Illinois, to the Union Stock Yards in Chicago. The shipment was made via the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company. Due to an error in the way bill prepared by the Wabash agent, the names of the consignees were omitted, which subsequently led to confusion upon arrival at the stockyards. The stock remained unclaimed until the following Wednesday, as the consignees were unaware of the arrival. The plaintiffs claimed that the delay caused depreciation in the market value of the hogs. They argued that it was the carrier's responsibility to either deliver the stock directly to the consignees or notify them of its arrival, while the defendants maintained their position as common carriers, asserting that their duty ended once the stock was delivered and unloaded at the stockyards.	The plaintiffs claimed damages resulting from the depreciation in value of their hogs due to the defendants' negligence in failing to deliver the stock to the consignees or notify them of its arrival. They argued that the defendants' omission in the way bill was negligent and that such negligence led to their financial losses.	The defendants contended that they were not obligated to deliver the stock to the consignees or notify them of its arrival. They asserted that their responsibilities as common carriers ceased upon unloading the stock at its destination. Furthermore, the defendants argued that any damages incurred were the result of the plaintiffs’ failure to demand the delivery of their stock within a reasonable time, thus relieving the defendants of liability.

In January 1869, the case of William R. Huey v. Billings Grinnell, Administrator, etc., was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in Clinton County, Illinois, where William R. Huey claimed ownership of a specific piece of land—the northeast quarter of section 22—which he believed he had purchased from his brother, James Huey. After this purchase, another party, Simeon L. Barce, claimed to have acquired the same land from the Illinois Central Railroad, leading to a conflict. To resolve this, Huey and Barce allegedly reached a written agreement—now lost—where they established terms for dividing the land and compensating each other based on who had a rightful claim. The agreement included provisions for payment and improvements made by Huey. After Barce died in 1866, Huey presented a claim against Barce’s estate to cover the costs of improvements made to the land. In 1867, the defendants, who were Barce’s estate administrators, acquired a deed for the land from the railroad and later refused to convey the west half to Huey, citing a lack of authority. They contended that Huey had waived his claims by pursuing compensation through Barce's estate.	Huey argued that he was entitled to specific performance of the agreement with Barce, seeking conveyance of the west half of the land. He claimed to have made valuable improvements and posited that the agreement justified his entitlement. Huey also sought compensation for the enhancements he had made and insisted that the administrators had a duty to abide by the agreement despite Barce's death.	The defendants, led by administrator Billings Grinnell, contended that Huey's pursuit of a claim against Barce's estate constituted an abandonment of the original agreement regarding the land. They asserted that Huey was not entitled to the west half of the land or compensation for the improvements, arguing that his actions demonstrated a waiver of his rights under the agreement. The estate admitted to Barce's purchase of the land but emphasized that a proper division was recognized and executed posthumously.

The case, "People of Illinois ex rel. Commissioners of Highways v. Board of Supervisors," took place in Illinois, with significant events occurring in 1883 and culminating in a court decision in 1887. The dispute arose from a petition presented by the Highway Commissioners of St. Mary’s to the county's Board of Supervisors, requesting financial assistance for rebuilding a bridge over Crooked Creek, which had been destroyed during high water in February 1883. The bridge was considered essential for the local community and the most important roadway in the township. The Highway Commissioners estimated the cost for construction at $4,590, with an additional $700 needed for approaches. They sought a contribution of half the total cost from the county, as required by the newly enacted Road and Bridge Act of 1883. However, during several meetings, the County Board postponed taking action and ultimately refused the requested aid. This led to a legal proceeding by mandamus, wherein the commissioners sought to compel the county to fulfill its financial obligation under the law. The case was eventually tried in the Hancock Circuit Court.	The plaintiff, represented by the Highway Commissioners of St. Mary’s, claimed that the immediate construction of the new bridge was necessary for the public's interest and that the County Board was obligated to provide financial assistance as stipulated in the Road and Bridge Act of 1883. The commissioners argued that the emergency caused by the destruction of the bridge warranted the county's contribution, even though the bridge's destruction occurred before the act was enacted. They requested a writ of mandamus to compel the County Board to allocate half of the construction costs.	The defendants, the Board of Supervisors, contended that the emergency which led to the bridge's destruction did not apply under the new law, as it occurred before the act went into effect. They argued that the law should not apply retrospectively and thus refused to grant aid for the bridge. The County Board maintained that the town had not sufficiently established its financial preparedness to contribute half of the construction costs, which they deemed necessary for the County's obligation.

In the case of William Shennefield et al. v. Albert Dutton, the events transpired in Altamont, Illinois, upon the dissolution of the partnership Dutton, Shennefield & Co. on January 1, 1874. The key individuals involved were Albert Dutton and former partners William Shennefield and Jerry Oliver. Following the dissolution, Dutton entered into an agreement with Shennefield and Oliver, wherein he sold them his half of the firm's stock and they agreed to assume the firm's debts. A central issue arose regarding a $1,000 note to Stover that Dutton claimed was a firm debt that Shennefield and Oliver were responsible for under the agreement, but which they contended was a personal debt of Dutton. Dutton's claims included having paid this note and seeking repayment from his former partners. The dispute unfolded in the Illinois Supreme Court after Dutton won a judgment in the lower court, leading Shennefield and Oliver to appeal. The case involved conflicting testimonies about the nature of the note and the responsibilities outlined in the written agreement governing the dissolution of their partnership.	The plaintiff, Albert Dutton, argued that the $1,000 note was a debt of the partnership that Shennefield and Oliver were required to pay. He contended that since he had paid this note, he was entitled to reimbursement plus interest and costs. Dutton's claims were based on the assertion that the agreement they entered into upon dissolution clearly assigned the responsibility for all firm debts to his former partners, including the disputed note.	Shennefield and Oliver defended against the claims by asserting that the note was not a partnership debt but rather a private obligation of Dutton, claiming that Dutton was the primary debtor and that they were merely sureties. They also argued that Dutton had an outstanding debt to the firm, which should be considered as a set-off against any claims he might have. Their position was supported by testimony that denied the existence of an agreement obligating them to pay the contested note.

Albert P. Oakes v. James A. Williams was a legal case that took place in Massac County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment delivered on June 16, 1883, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from an action of ejectment, where both parties claimed titles to the property deriving from a common source, MeBean. The appellee, James A. Williams, claimed title through two judgments against MeBean, one being from the circuit court of Massac County and another from a U.S. Circuit Court. Both judgments were prior to the one claimed by the appellant, Oakes, who held title through a judgment from the county court similar to the appellee's claims. The legal dispute centered on the validity of the titles given the overlapping judgments and a pending appeal of one of the judgments at the time of execution and sale. The court considered arguments over irregularities in the execution process and whether the appeal affected the validity of the actions taken against the property before its resolution.	The plaintiff, Albert P. Oakes, sought to establish his ownership over the property based on a judgment he obtained against MeBean, which was executed prior to the deeds derived by the defendant, James A. Williams. Oakes argued the illicit nature of the defendant's title due to the appeal pending at the time of the judgment execution, claiming that any actions taken during that period were void and that he had rightful title through his valid prior judgment.	The defendant, James A. Williams, contended that his titles were established through valid executions and subsequent sheriff's deeds, therefore qualifying him for possessory rights over the property in dispute. Williams argued that while some irregularities existed in the execution process, they did not void the transfers and, since the appellant failed to challenge the irregularities in a timely manner, he had no recourse to question the validity of the proceedings.

In the case of Selden F. White et al. v. Joseph Weaver, the legal proceedings arose from an action of assumpsit concerning a promissory note dated October 31, 1856. The plaintiffs, Selden F. White and his brothers, alleged that Joseph Weaver provided a written guarantee for the payment of a promissory note made by Samuel Stanley. The note was valued at $340.10 and was payable five months post date. The case originated in Warren Circuit Court and was later moved to Peoria County. Despite the note's existence and Weaver's signature, the controversy centered on whether Weaver's signature constituted a guarantee or an assignment of the note. The trial was conducted without a jury, and the court found in favor of the defendant, Joseph Weaver. The plaintiffs' subsequent motion for a new trial was denied, prompting their appeal. The core issue was whether Weaver had signed as a guarantor before the note's delivery or as an indorser afterward, with implications for his liability.	The plaintiffs contended that Joseph Weaver had guaranteed the payment of the promissory note made by Samuel Stanley and that this guarantee was made before the note's delivery to them. They argued that the absence of evidence proving that Weaver signed the note as a mere indorser meant he was liable as a guarantor. The plaintiffs sought a ruling to reverse the lower court's judgment and enforce Weaver's obligation to pay the amount due on the promissory note.	Joseph Weaver's primary defense was that he did not execute a guarantee for the payment of the promissory note. He contended that his signature was placed on the note after its delivery, making him merely an indorser rather than a guarantor. Weaver asserted that the plaintiffs had not proven that he had agreed to guarantee the payment of the note, and therefore, he claimed he held no responsibility for the debt outlined in the note. He requested the court to uphold the lower court's ruling that favored him.

The case, "The People ex rel. Thomas F. Witherow v. D. James Leary," took place in Chicago, Illinois, with the decision issued by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1876. The proceedings were initiated by the Bar Association of the City of Chicago, with Thomas F. Witherow representing the case as relator against D. James Leary, an attorney charged with unprofessional conduct. The complaint against Leary involved his submission of a false affidavit in a divorce case where he represented Annie Powers, the defendant. This had occurred during court proceedings in December 1872 while Mrs. Powers was confined after giving birth. Leary sought a court order for alimony on her behalf, supporting his motion with the disputed affidavit, which he purportedly fabricated. Upon investigation, it was established that neither Mrs. Powers nor the notary public, William E. Cowper, had signed or sworn to the affidavit as claimed by Leary. Evidence, including testimonies, demonstrated that Leary created the affidavit himself, later substituting his name with that of Mrs. Powers. The court found Leary's actions to be deceitful and damaging to the integrity of the legal profession.	The plaintiff, represented by Thomas F. Witherow, claimed that D. James Leary had engaged in unprofessional conduct by submitting a knowingly false affidavit in court to receive financial support for his client, Mrs. Powers. The plaintiff sought to have Leary's name stricken from the roll of attorneys due to this misconduct, stressing the seriousness of his actions in undermining the honor of the legal profession.	D. James Leary defended against the allegations by providing affidavits in support of his actions, attempting to justify the circumstances under which he had filed the affidavit for Mrs. Powers. He claimed that the affidavit was legitimate and presented evidence to support his defense. However, his arguments were ultimately undermined by the corroborating testimonies from Mrs. Powers and the notary, who denied his claims about the affidavit's validity.

In the case of Catharine Stunz et al. v. Maria Stunz, filed on September 23, 1887, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed a dispute regarding the partition of real estate after the death of Carl Stunz on March 8, 1885. He left behind a will stipulating that his widow, Maria Stunz, was entitled to a one-third interest in the net income from the real estate during her lifetime and the right to live in the homestead until she remarried. The plaintiffs, Catharine, Louisa, and Mina Stunz—his children from a previous marriage—were named as defendants. The will designated them as the residuary legatees. Following the death of another child, a son who left Maria as the only heir, Maria filed for partition, asserting her rights under the will and seeking a partition of the property to reflect their respective interests. The case escalated through the courts, where the initial findings ruled in favor of Maria, granting her claims regarding her interests, including an allowance for a homestead valued at $1,000. Subsequent evaluations found the property to be worth $5,125, with various reports and decrees leading to the ordering of a sale of the property, amidst concerns of misrepresentation and failure of a guardian ad litem to adequately represent the interests of the minor heirs.	Maria Stunz, the plaintiff, claimed a one-tenth interest in the property as a tenant in common, alongside the defendants, who received three-tenths each. She further asserted her rights to a $1,000 homestead interest and a remaining balance of $1,203.70 from a widow's award. Ultimately, she sought a partition of the property and the fulfillment of her financial claims, requesting the court to uphold her designated rights as stipulated in her husband’s will.	The defendants, Catharine, Louisa, and Mina Stunz, contended that the court improperly recognized Maria's homestead and other claims due to inconsistencies between the provisions of the will and statutory entitlements. They argued that the appointed guardian ad litem failed to represent their interests effectively, leading to a biased judicial process. They believed the valuation of the property was manipulated, resulting in an unfair distribution of assets that did not account for their entitled rights under the law.

In January 1877, the case of William B. Phillips et al. v. Charles D. Webster et al. was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Circuit Court of Champaign County. The dispute arose from a promissory note executed by the Indianapolis, Bloomington and Western Railway Company, where the plaintiffs (Phillips and others) sought to hold the defendants (Webster and others) liable as assignors of the note. The plaintiffs alleged that the railway company was insolvent when the note matured, rendering a suit against the company futile. To support their case, they presented evidence of unsatisfied executions from previous lawsuits against the railway company. In response, the defendants argued that evidence they provided—such as property deeds and the company’s possessions—demonstrated that the railway had assets. However, the plaintiffs countered with evidence of a mortgage and involvement of a receiver, appointed by the DeWitt Circuit Court, which indicated the company’s insolvency. The legal proceedings primarily revolved around the admissibility of evidence relating to the insolvency and the appointment of the receiver.	The plaintiffs argued that the railway company was insolvent at the time the promissory note matured, which justified their action against the defendants (the assignors). They requested recovery based on the premise that a legal suit against the railway company would have been ineffective due to its insolvency, evidenced by the returns of unsatisfied executions in other cases.	The defendants contended that they provided sufficient evidence of the railway company's assets and contended that the evidence of insolvency presented by the plaintiffs was inadequate. They disputed the admission of the evidence related to the appointment of the receiver, arguing that it lacked the necessary formalities and relevance to their case, claiming there was no need for the plaintiffs to avoid direct legal action against the railway company.

On July 3, 1871, John F. Lander executed a promissory note for $5,000 to the Rockford Insurance Company, with a ten percent annual interest rate, due in five years. This note was secured by a trust deed on real estate, which permitted the trustee, R. P. Lane, to sell the property if payments were not made. Although the first two semi-annual interest payments were timely, the third payment, due January 3, 1873, wasn't made until March 13, 1873. Payments resumed sporadically until January 3, 1883. After Lander's death in 1874, his son Franklin became the inheritor of the property. On September 28, 1885, Julian P. Jones, the administrator of Robert M. Brantingham's estate, sought to foreclose the trust deed in the Winnebago Circuit Court. The court dismissed Jones' case, ruling that the right to foreclose was barred by the ten-year limitation statute, as more than a decade had passed since the initial default. The court concluded that the limitation statute applied because the interest payment was overdue by more than thirty days.	The plaintiff, Julian P. Jones, contended that he had the right to foreclose on the trust deed due to John F. Lander's failure to make timely payments on the promissory note. He argued that the provisions of the Limitation Act of 1872 did not apply retroactively to the instruments executed before its enactment, and thus he maintained his right to seek foreclosure despite the court's earlier ruling.	Franklin C. Lander, the defendant, argued that the claims made by the plaintiff were barred by the Limitation Act of 1872, which limited the duration for enforcing such actions to ten years after the default. He contended that the plaintiff waited too long, and thus the court's dismissal of the foreclosure attempt was justified under the applicable statutory framework.

In March 1883, Amelia T. Robinson brought a personal injury lawsuit against the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company in the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident occurred while Robinson and her husband were traveling in a buggy and attempted to cross a railroad track at a public road crossing. At that moment, a special train operated by the defendant collided with their buggy, resulting in severe and permanent injuries to Robinson. The plaintiff alleged that the railroad company was negligent due to several factors: failing to ring a bell or sound a whistle as required at public crossings; allowing obstructions such as weeds and earth banks to prevent a clear view of oncoming trains; and operating a "wild train" (a train without a schedule) at an unusually high speed. The case went through the Appellate Court and was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for further review.	Amelia T. Robinson claimed that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was negligent, leading to her injuries. She argued that the railroad failed to give adequate warning by not ringing the bell or sounding the whistle as required by law at public crossings. Additionally, she contended that the presence of obstructions near the crossing prevented her from seeing the approaching train and that the train was operating at an unsafe speed. Robinson sought damages for her injuries caused by this negligence.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company's defense centered around the assertion that any injuries to Robinson were not due to willful intent or gross negligence by their employees. They argued that the instructions provided to the jury could mislead them by introducing issues not supported by the pleadings or evidence. The defendant maintained that the trial court's errors in jury instructions could have affected the outcome and requested that the judgment be reversed.

On August 16, 1859, David C. Cushman and his wife, Eliza, executed a mortgage on a property in Sterling, Illinois, securing a $100 note due in two years. After David's death, the mortgage went unpaid, leading his administratrix to obtain a foreclosure decree in May 1865. However, this decree was never executed and was later assigned to Sarah T. Roberts to settle estate debts. On June 12, 1877, Eliza, now a widow, mortgaged six lots for $890.92 to James D. Bingham. After Eliza's death, in November 1879, Sarah filed a bill to enforce the foreclosure decree against the Cushman heirs and Bingham. Meanwhile, Bingham’s executor also attempted to foreclose but did not involve Sarah Roberts. The Circuit Court found that the original decree’s lien was lost due to the lack of execution within a year and dismissed Sarah's claims based on the Statute of Limitations. She appealed the dismissal.	Sarah T. Roberts, the plaintiff's administratrix, argued that the original foreclosure decree remained valid and should be enforced against the Cushman heirs. She contended that the debt and mortgage were still valid, as the statute's limitations had not extinguished them, and sought to carry the foreclosure decree into effect.	The defendant, John Lawrence, contended that the lien from the original decree was lost as no execution was performed within the required timeframe. They asserted that both the original note and the mortgage were barred by the Statute of Limitations, claiming that this invalidated Roberts’ right to foreclose on the mortgage.

The case of Ambrose Fox v. William Turtle took place in Chicago, Illinois, in the late 19th century, specifically around September 1870. It involved a dispute over the title to a piece of land, specifically lot 16 in block 1, Carpenter’s addition to the city. The action was initiated by William Turtle against Ambrose Fox, who was claiming ownership through two tax deeds. The first deed was a sheriff's sale conducted by John Gray for non-payment of state and county taxes in 1857, while the second involved a tax sale by the city of Chicago for delinquent city taxes in 1858. The primary issue before the court revolved around the validity of these tax titles. The plaintiff's claim was challenged based on several legal objections, particularly the lack of specificity regarding the types of taxes collected and the proper certification of publications related to the tax sales.	The plaintiff, William Turtle, argued that he had valid titles to the property based on two separate tax sales conducted for non-payment of taxes. He claimed that the tax deeds he possessed from both the sheriff of Cook County and the city of Chicago conferred him legal ownership of the lot in question. Turtle sought to recover possession of the property through an action of ejectment, asserting that the deeds were legally actionable and that he was entitled to the property.	Ambrose Fox, the defendant, contended that the titles claimed by Turtle were defective and invalid. Fox's primary arguments focused on the inadequacies of the sheriff's report regarding delinquent taxes, which failed to separate state from county taxes. Additionally, he pointed out that the publication certificate regarding the collector's notice for the city tax sale was insufficient, as it was not properly signed by the publisher. Fox requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims due to these defects in the tax titles.

In the case of Cornelia Martin v. Wilson H. Stubbings, the events took place in Chicago, Illinois, involving significant parties including Cornelia Martin, the widow of Heal K. Martin, and Wilson H. Stubbings, a business partner. The case emerged from a financial dispute related to a life insurance policy and a partnership agreement. The partnership began on April 16, 1883, between Heal K. Martin and Stubbings, focusing on painting and supply sales. By January 1, 1886, an accounting revealed Martin had overdrawn $3,411.66 from partnership profits, leading Stubbings to consider dissolving their partnership. However, after discussions, Martin proposed to provide a promissory note for the outstanding debt, secured by assigning his life insurance policy (issued in June 1883) as collateral. Cornelia Martin co-signed this note and assignment. Following Heal K. Martin's death on July 27, 1886, a dispute arose regarding the entitlement to $5,000 from the insurance policy, with Stubbings claiming a lien for the debt and Cornelia asserting her right as the beneficiary. Stubbings had filed an interpleader to resolve the conflict, leading to the present case.	Cornelia Martin contended that there was no valid consideration for the promissory note or the assignment of the insurance policy to Stubbings and argued the assignment was against public policy and the statute governing the insurance association.
