The court proceedings involved disputes over the items seized, the legitimacy of Mitchell's actions as a constable, and whether he had proved a valid judgment to support his actions.	Jacob Schemerhorn's main argument was that he had a right to recover property specified in a chattel mortgage executed by Schnell and Finley. He contended that the furniture, fixtures, and stock were rightfully his based on this mortgage. Additionally, he argued that A. K. Mitchell, as the defendant, wrongfully seized property that belonged to him, thereby necessitating the legal action to reclaim it.	A. K. Mitchell defended his actions by asserting that he was a constable who acted under a valid execution against Schnell, which gave him the right to seize the property as Schnell's. He invoked defenses of non cepit and non detinet (denying the seizure of property), as well as claiming ownership of the items seized. Furthermore, he argued that any property not covered by the mortgage was rightfully his due to the legal execution and that the mortgage itself had been invalidated by Schnell's actions of selling the goods.

In the case of Isaac P. Coates v. David Preston et al., decided on November 20, 1882, by the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute arose from a check drawn by Schuyler S. Gardner on the banking firm of Preston, Kean & Co., where he was a member of another firm, Colby, Gardner & Co. The check, for $2,190, was made payable to Gardner’s own order and was indorsed to Coates, the plaintiff. The defendants contended that Gardner’s firm owed them more than the amount of the check and that Gardner did not have sufficient funds deposited with them to justify payment of the full amount. The bank thus refused to honor the check. Coates claimed ownership of the check, while the defendants sought to set off Gardner’s firm’s indebtedness against Coates’ claim. The case faced multiple proceedings, including a demurrer from Coates that was overruled, leading to the defendants’ judgment being affirmed by the Appellate Court.	Isaac P. Coates, as the plaintiff, argued that he was the bona fide holder of the check drawn on the defendants and claimed that the bank was obligated to pay the amount specified. He asserted that he had paid value for the check and was entitled to recover the full amount, irrespective of Gardner’s relationship with the bank and his firm’s indebtedness to them.	The defendants, represented by the banking firm, contended that Gardner, the maker of the check, did not have sufficient funds on deposit to cover the check's amount at the time of its presentation. They argued that any debts owed by Gardner's firm to them should be offset against the claim made by Coates, emphasizing that debts must be mutual in nature to qualify for set-off, which they believed was not the case here.

In September 1867, Milton Parker filed a lawsuit against Charles Follensbee and Samuel M. Standish in the Superior Court of Chicago, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute over a bail bond related to an alleged breach of a contract made by Standish to construct a building for Parker. The contract specified that Standish would build a two-story structure for a total fee of $3,500, with payments made as work progressed. However, Parker claimed that Standish fraudulently induced him to provide $4,100 under the pretense of escalating material costs but abandoned the project, failing to complete the construction. Parker contended that the materials and labor provided by Standish amounted to only $1,900, resulting in significant financial loss for him. The crux of the legal battle centered on the validity of the affidavit used to secure Standish's bail, which Follensbee, as Standish's security, argued failed to meet the constitutional requirements related to presumption of fraud.	Milton Parker claimed that Samuel M. Standish had fraudulently induced him to advance payments for a construction project under the guise of a written contract. He alleged that Standish did not apply the funds as promised and abandoned the project, resulting in his financial loss. Parker sought to hold Follensbee, the surety on Standish's bail bond, liable for the debt incurred due to Standish’s alleged fraudulent actions, contending that the affidavit supporting the bail was sufficient, and requested that it be upheld.	Charles Follensbee defended against Parker's claims by asserting that the affidavit which initiated the capias ad respondendum against Standish was insufficient. He argued that it did not meet the constitutional requirements, as it failed to provide clear facts or circumstances raising a strong presumption of fraud by Standish. Follensbee claimed that, on these grounds, he was discharged from any liability related to the bond and requested that the court dismiss the case.

The case, John Barker et al. v. The International Bank of Chicago, took place in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision handed down in September 1875. At the center of the dispute was a deed of trust executed on January 16, 1868, by Henry H. Walker, who made a $25,000 promissory note to his own order and subsequently delivered it to Samuel J. Walker as part of a financial arrangement involving Greenebaum & Foreman, who advanced a loan of $14,000 secured by the note. Henry H. Walker subsequently sold the property to James M. Walker for $103,000. Samuel J. Walker had debts to S. Sturges’ Sons, which were partially settled when he sold the property to James M. Walker, and a portion of the sale was meant to cover the outstanding $25,000 note secured by the deed of trust. The International Bank of Chicago later became involved when they advanced funds against the deed of trust, and the legality of the bank's right to foreclose on the deed of trust for the amount due became the crux of the case, as the defendants argued that the bank could not pursue the lien against James M. Walker as he was a grantee of the conveyed property.	The International Bank of Chicago, as the plaintiff, claimed the right to foreclose the deed of trust securing a $25,000 outstanding note owed by Henry H. Walker, which had been adequately documented and secured against the property. The bank asserted that they legally acquired the note after Walker conveyed the land and that the debt was valid and enforceable against the property, despite the dispute raised by the grantees. Their request was for the court to uphold their right to collect the debt by selling the property under the terms of the deed of trust.	The defendants, including John Barker and other parties related to Samuel J. Walker, argued that the International Bank of Chicago could not enforce the lien against them as they were grantees after Henry H. Walker had conveyed the property. They contended that since there was an indicated understanding that the $25,000 deed of trust would not encumber the property post-sale and should be treated as an accommodation, they should be exempt from the bank's foreclosure proceedings. They sought to have the foreclosure denied, asserting that the original conditions of the property sale negated the bank's claims.

The case "The Western Union Telegraph Company v. Herman Lieb et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875. The key parties involved included the Western Union Telegraph Company, a foreign corporation established under New York law, and Herman Lieb, the county clerk of Cook County, along with H. B. Miller, the county tax collector. The dispute arose when the Board of Equalization assessed the capital stock and franchise of the Western Union Telegraph Company for taxation, amounting to $1,168,394 for the tax year 1873. The Western Union Telegraph Company sought to enjoin the collection of this tax on the grounds that there was no legal authority under Illinois law for such an assessment of a foreign corporation's capital stock. The Circuit Court of Cook County initially sustained a demurrer against the company’s bill and dismissed it, prompting the company's appeal to the state supreme court.	The Western Union Telegraph Company, the plaintiff, contended that the assessment of its capital stock and franchise for taxation was unauthorized under Illinois law. It argued that the "Act for the assessment of property and for the levy and collection of taxes" only permitted the taxation of capital stock for corporations created under Illinois law, not for foreign corporations. Consequently, the company requested that the court issue an injunction to prevent the extension and collection of these taxes.	Herman Lieb and H. B. Miller, representing the defendants, argued that the Illinois legislature had the authority to impose taxation on foreign corporations operating within the state. They maintained that such taxation was a necessary condition for these corporations to exercise their franchises and privileges in Illinois. They contended that the assessment was valid under existing state law and therefore opposed the company's requests for an injunction.

John A. Wakefield, the plaintiff in error, brought a legal action against Robert Goudy, the defendant in error, which was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1841. The case arose from a judgment rendered by the Morgan County Circuit Court in favor of Wakefield for $906 and costs without a jury trial in November 1839. The core of the dispute centered around the jurisdiction of the Morgan County Circuit Court to hear the case, particularly because the legal process initiated in Morgan County was directed to a sheriff in Jo Daviess County. Goudy challenged the court's jurisdiction, requesting the dismissal of the case on the grounds that the declaration filed did not adequately establish that the Morgan County Circuit Court had jurisdiction over the matter, specifically not indicating that the cause of action arose in Morgan County or that Wakefield was a resident of that county. The defendant's motion to dismiss was denied, allowing the plaintiff to amend the declaration to address the jurisdiction issue. However, the Supreme Court ultimately found error in allowing the amendment post-denial of the motion, which led to the reversal of judgment.	Wakefield's primary argument was that the Morgan County Circuit Court had the jurisdiction to hear his case against Goudy, which was an action of assumpsit. He contended that the lower court's judgment in his favor, rendered without a jury, should be upheld, and he sought to maintain his awarded damages and costs despite the challenge to the court's jurisdiction by Goudy.	Goudy's defense rested on the assertion that the Morgan County Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction because the original declaration did not fulfill the necessary legal requirements. He maintained that the plaintiff failed to present sufficient averments to prove that the cause of action was appropriately situated within Morgan County, and he requested that the court dismiss the case outright based on this jurisdictional deficiency.

The case of Jefferson Wall v. Lewis S. Goodenough took place in La Salle County, Illinois, during the March term of 1855. Jefferson Wall, the appellant, had leased premises to a tenant named Penfield, who had occupied the property for approximately six months before abandoning it. On the same day Penfield left, Goodenough moved his family into the unoccupied house without any evidence indicating that he entered through collusion with Penfield or as Wall's tenant. Wall had some belongings left in the house by Penfield, which remained at the property post-abandonment. The legal question revolved around Wall's right to reclaim possession of the premises, leading to the jury finding Goodenough guilty of withholding possession.	Jefferson Wall, the plaintiff, claimed that Lewis S. Goodenough wrongfully withheld possession of the premises after his tenant vacated. Wall's main arguments centered around his assertion of property rights stemming from the lease with Penfield, arguing that the continued possession of the premises, including belongings left behind, entitled him to reclaim the property from Goodenough.	Lewis S. Goodenough, the defendant, contended that he entered the property legally as there was no one in possession at the time of his entry. He argued that there was a lack of collusion with Penfield or any formal eviction process that would grant Wall the basis for reclaiming possession of the premises. Goodenough maintained that Wall's claims were unfounded and sought dismissal of the action against him.

In 1872, the case of Deborah Evans et al. v. Ithamer H. Aldrich et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute involved a mistake in a deed concerning a 40-acre plot of land initially owned by John L. Allison. After Allison's death, his brother Francis had conveyed the land to Deborah under conditions meant to help her during her widowhood, after it was sold at a sheriff’s auction for a fraction of its value. A significant error occurred when Deborah executed a deed intended to convey the same land to Francis, but it mistakenly described a different tract. Following the error, Francis sold parts of the land to various complainants, who then developed and occupied the land in good faith, believing they had valid title. When Deborah realized the mistake years later, she filed an action of ejectment, prompting the complainants to seek reform of the deed. The court found no fraud involved and affirmed that the deed could be corrected in accordance with the parties' original intent.	The plaintiffs (Aldrich, Williams, and King) argued for the rectification of the deed executed by Deborah Evans to Frances Allison, citing an accidental error in its description. They maintained that they purchased their interests in good faith and were in rightful possession based on the belief that they had been properly conveyed the title. They requested the court to reform the deed to align with the original intent of the parties.	The defendants, represented by Deborah Evans and her husband, contended that at the time she executed the deed, she was unaware of which land was being described and did not know of the prior conveyance to her. They argued that she had been misinformed regarding the deed's implications and maintained that the process lacked fraudulent intent. Their main request revolved around contesting the validity of the deed's description and possibly denying the claims of the plaintiffs.

John Groff filed a legal action against Nicholas Ankenbrandt in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the final judgment rendered on June 12, 1886. The case originated from an incident where an embankment on Ankenbrandt's land obstructed the flow of surface water. This obstruction caused water to accumulate on Groff's adjacent property, rendering approximately twenty acres wet and unsuitable for cultivation. The case was brought to the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge C. C. Boggs. The factual basis revolved around the claim that Ankenbrandt was responsible for maintaining the nuisance, despite not initially constructing the embankment. The legal discussion focused on whether Ankenbrandt could be held liable for the ongoing nuisance without prior notice to remove the embankment.	Groff claimed that the embankment, which Ankenbrandt maintained, obstructed natural water flow and led to flooding on Groff’s property. He argued that this situation was a private nuisance that caused significant damage to his land, making it unfit for cultivation. Groff sought damages from Ankenbrandt for the negative impact on his property and contended that Ankenbrandt should be held liable for allowing the embankment to remain.	Ankenbrandt asserted that he was not responsible for the creation of the embankment and argued he could not be held liable for merely maintaining it as he found it. His defense emphasized the legal principle that a property owner cannot be held liable for a nuisance unless they had prior notice to abate it or committed an affirmative act that worsened the situation. Ankenbrandt maintained that Groff did not provide notice to remove the nuisance, which was crucial for liability in such cases.

The case "Thomas J. Robinson et al. v. William H. Appleton et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 26, 1888, following an appeal from the Appellate Court for the Second District. The underlying dispute arose from a contract executed on December 1, 1866, in Rock Island County, Illinois. James E. Cooley, possessing certain tracts of land, entered into an agreement with David B. Sears to sell his right, title, and interest in exchange for $30,000, to be paid in installments. Cooley provided Sears a bond for deed, stipulating that upon receiving full payment, he would convey the land through a quitclaim deed. Sears paid the initial sum and part of the notes but defaulted on the last payments. Cooley passed away in 1882, and after probate proceedings, his executors (plaintiffs) sought specific performance of the contract, claiming that Sears failed to honor his part, causing them to initiate a lawsuit for the recovery of the unpaid balance and to enforce their lien on the property. The case highlights the complexities relating to vendor’s liens and the effects of contracts for the sale of land.	The plaintiffs, as executors of James E. Cooley's will, claimed that David B. Sears had defaulted on the contract for the sale of land and failed to pay the remaining balance of the purchase price. They sought specific performance of the contract, requesting the court to declare their claim a first lien upon the property. They demanded a sale of the land to satisfy the unpaid purchase money and requested that other defendants, claiming rights to the property under Sears, be enjoined from putting forth their claims against the plaintiffs' rights.	The defendants, including Thomas J. Robinson and others, argued that James E. Cooley had no title to sell, claiming their rights to the property arose independently of Cooley's ownership. They contended that no vendor’s lien existed since they asserted they took no obligation for the payment. The defendants sought to have the case dismissed, challenging the legitimacy of the plaintiffs' claims and the order for a sale by the court.

The case of Christian Belslay v. Edward C. Engel took place in 1883 in Illinois, concerning the interpretation of the will of Joseph Belslay. The primary individuals involved were Christian Belslay, the plaintiff, and Edward C. Engel, the defendant. The central issue revolved around the interpretation of specific clauses in the will concerning the estate granted to Joseph Belslay's granddaughter, Catharine Belslay. Joseph Belslay's will contained a sixth clause that explicitly granted Catharine the right to use and occupy the specified lands for the duration of her natural life, suggesting that she would only receive a life estate. However, the thirteenth clause introduced ambiguity about the nature of the estate by stating that if any grandchildren died without issue, their share would be divided among the remaining grandchildren, creating confusion regarding whether Catharine was entitled to a fee simple or merely a life estate. The case ultimately aimed to clarify the testator's intentions and whether the language used in the will allowed for the application of the rule in Shelly’s case, which might grant greater rights to the devisees than intended.	The plaintiff, Christian Belslay, argued that the will's clauses did not confer a fee simple estate to Catharine Belslay. His position was that the sixth clause provided her only with a life estate in the specified lands, a view supported by the thirteenth clause which expressed that no fee simple title would vest in the grandchildren. He requested clarification from the court that would uphold the testator's intent, confirming that Catharine's rights were limited to the use and enjoyment of the property during her lifetime.	The defendant, Edward C. Engel, contended that the will's language could be interpreted to grant a more substantial interest than merely a life estate. He argued that despite the express language regarding a life estate, the ambiguity in the thirteenth clause suggested the possibility of a greater estate involving a fee simple title. Engel sought the court's interpretation to recognize these broader rights as appropriated by the will's language.

In April 1878, in Verona, Grundy County, Illinois, merchants Samuel Ward and William Scott Pierce, who were engaged in livestock and lumber trading, wanted to transition their business to Wm. Young & Co. They provided a financial statement indicating assets of $36,629 and liabilities of $14,200, leaving a purported surplus of $22,429. However, this statement was found to be intentionally misleading, as it falsely claimed ownership of land and other assets. Wm. Young & Co. advanced $1,000 to Ward & Pierce based on this statement. Subsequently, Ward & Pierce transferred significant property and assets to their relatives without disclosing this to Wm. Young & Co., while still drawing funds from them. In September 1878, Wm. Young & Co. initiated legal action after realizing the potential fraud, seeking to protect their interests against the fraudulent transfers and recover amounts owed.	The plaintiff, Wm. Young & Co., argued that the financial statement provided by Ward & Pierce was fraudulent and intended to deceive them into advancing funds. They sought legal relief through a creditors' bill to establish the fraudulent nature of the conveyances made by Ward to his relatives and to reclaim their financial losses stemming from these deceptive transactions.	The defendants, including Samuel Ward and his relatives, claimed that their transactions were legitimate and intended to settle debts. They argued that any assignments and conveyances made were made in good faith, asserting that there was no fraudulent intent towards Wm. Young & Co. Additionally, they contended that the plaintiffs had no grounds to challenge the validity of the transfers, as they had no standing to assert claims against the conveyed properties.

In February 1864, John Gates sold a farm to George Hackethal for $10,000, with a payment schedule that included initial payments and deferred amounts secured by a deed of trust. However, when the first payment was due, Hackethal was unable to pay due to financial difficulties relating to funds he expected from Germany. Consequently, Gates and Hackethal reached an agreement to postpone the sale under the deed of trust, with Hackethal issuing a new note for $5,600. Over the years, payments were made and disputes arose regarding the application of these payments. In December 1866, Hackethal made a payment of $4,750, which he claimed was meant to settle two notes of $2,000 each. Gates asserted he retained $1,200 from this payment as a premium on gold, leading to a contention that this retention was usurious and not backed by valid consideration. The case revolved around the nature of the agreements made in light of the payments and whether the agreed-upon terms constituted valid contracts. The Illinois Supreme Court was tasked with determining the validity of these agreements and the application of the payments made.	The plaintiffs, John Gates and others, claim that Hackethal failed to adhere to the terms of the original sale and agreed payment schedule by not making timely payments. They argue that the $1,200 retained was a premium claimed justified under the circumstances. Gates contends that the new note issued was improperly treated as an extension of the previous debt without proper consideration, thereby asserting that the agreements constituted usury.	The defendant, George Hackethal, contends that the payment arrangement was agreed upon with his sons, and the application of the $4,750 was legitimate according to this understanding. He argues that Gates had no right to retain the $1,200 for gold premium, stating it was an unjust charge lacking valid contractual basis. Hackethal insists that the new note was meant to protect him against the depreciation of treasury notes, pushing back against the claim of usury.

In the case of "William Beeler v. Stephen C. Webb," a legal action was initiated when Stephen C. Webb accused William H. Burns and William Beeler of enticing away his wife, resulting in her elopement with Burns. The events unfolded shortly after Webb and his wife married on August 31, 1882. Just a few weeks later, on September 17, 1882, Burns reportedly persuaded Mrs. Webb to leave her husband, during which time they were away together for about a week, presumably engaging in an illicit relationship. Upon her return, Mrs. Webb resumed living with Webb. The plaintiff, Webb, claimed that Beeler, as Mrs. Webb's father, conspired and assisted Burns in this elopement. During the court proceedings, Burns was defaulted, and a general plea was made by Beeler. Following a trial, the jury rendered a verdict against both defendants. Beeler appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court after the Appellate Court affirmed the judgment against him. The court addressed various points of contention, including the admissibility of evidence, allegations of excessive damages, and whether the aforementioned testimony impacted Beeler’s case.	The plaintiff, Stephen C. Webb, claimed that the defendants, William H. Burns and William Beeler, conspired to entice his wife to elope with Burns, thereby infringing upon his marital rights. He sought damages for the emotional distress and disruption caused by this alleged conspiracy. Webb argued that Beeler, as the father of Mrs. Webb, had played a role in facilitating and encouraging the elopement, and thus he was liable for the actions of Burns.	The defendants asserted various defenses, including a challenge to the admissibility of certain evidence presented against them, specifically relating to Burns' declarations before a conspiracy was proven. They contended that these statements should not be used against Beeler. Furthermore, they argued that the trial court wrongly excluded evidence that might demonstrate Webb's failures in their own marriage, which they believed could mitigate the damages claimed by Webb. Lastly, they claimed that any damages awarded were excessive.

The case of "The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company v. August Hintz" was filed in Illinois and heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, culminating in a decision on March 29, 1890. The dispute originated in October 1888 when Hintz recovered a judgment of $5,000 against the Chicago and Northwestern Railway in the Cook County Superior Court. Following that verdict, the railway company appealed the judgment to the Appellate Court for the First District, which was set to be heard in March 1889. During this process, the railway sought extensions to file its legal briefs, with stipulations made between the attorneys regarding deadlines. Eventually, the railway's briefs were filed late, prompting Hintz’s counsel to request that the court affirm the original judgment due to this failure. The Appellate Court ultimately held that the agreement between the attorneys to stipulate the timing of the filings could be enforced, despite the railway's later attempt to withdraw from the agreement. The record showed that the stipulation was validly made and acted upon, leading the court to side with Hintz.	The plaintiff, August Hintz, argued that the Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company failed to adhere to the stipulation regarding the timely filing of their briefs, which he asserted entitled him to a judgment affirmance. Hintz maintained that the original judgment of $5,000 should be upheld because the railway breached its agreement with his counsel.	The defendant, Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company, contended that the affirmation of the judgment was unjust and sought to withdraw from the stipulation made concerning the filing of its briefs. The railway claimed that the stipulation was not properly enforced due to a lack of clear grounds for requiring compliance and that it should be allowed to argue the case on its merits after its briefs were filed.

In 1865, Charles D. Arter, a merchant in Cairo, Illinois, engaged in the sale of gunpowder and shot, which led to suspicion from Joel S. Byington, the defendant. Byington believed the items were intended for the Confederate States during the Civil War. While the goods were being loaded into a skiff at night, Byington seized them and attempted to arrest the loaders, who managed to escape. Subsequently, Byington confronted Arter, threatening to close his store and report him to the United States Marshal unless Arter paid him $1,000. To avoid exposure and potential legal troubles, Arter complied and paid the sum. Arter later filed a lawsuit to recover the money he had paid. The Circuit Court ruled in Arter's favor with a verdict for the amount claimed. Byington appealed the decision, arguing that Arter should not have been allowed to recover the money due to the illegal nature of their dealings.	Arter claimed that Byington’s demand for $1,000 constituted a bribe and that he had been coerced into paying it to avoid being reported for engaging in illicit trade during the Civil War. He sought the return of the $1,000, asserting his entitlement because the payment was made under duress.	Byington argued that if Arter was engaged in illegal activity by selling military goods to the enemy, then the law should not permit Arter to recover the payment. He contended that the principles of law prevent recovery in cases involving immoral or illegal acts, known by the maxim "ex turpi causa, non oritur actio." Byington requested the court to instruct the jury that if Arter acted with knowledge of the illicit nature of his commerce and paid to prevent exposure, he could not claim the money back.

Charles H. Weaver filed a bill in equity against William A. Poyer and Timothy M. Bradley in 1872 in Cook County, Illinois. Weaver, a commission merchant, was sued by Poyer for $1,446.50 due to the destruction of consigned goods in a fire. Weaver claimed he was not served properly with the court summons and had no knowledge of the lawsuit until after a judgment was issued against him. On May 16, 1872, the Superior Court rendered a default judgment in favor of Poyer, which led to an execution being placed in the hands of sheriff Timothy M. Bradley for collection. Weaver sought to have the judgment enjoined and declared void, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction. The court initially issued a temporary injunction, but this was later dissolved after the defendants presented their motion. Weaver appealed the dissolution, asserting that he was entitled to a final decision regarding the judgment.	Weaver claimed that he was never served with the court summons related to the judgment against him and thus lacked proper notice of the case. He argued that the judgment was rendered without jurisdiction and was therefore invalid. Additionally, he sought an injunction to prevent Poyer from enforcing the judgment while seeking to have the judgment declared void, asserting he had a valid defense based on the circumstances surrounding the destruction of the goods in question.	The defendants contended that the dissolution of the temporary injunction was justified and that the judgment rendered against Weaver was valid. They argued that Weaver had no grounds for the injunction since he was notified about the lawsuit through a return of service by reading. The defendants sought to have the appeal dismissed, claiming that Weaver's appeal was not valid as he had previously moved for the bill's dismissal if the court found no equity.

John Byler et al. v. John Asher took place in January 1868 in Adams County, Illinois. The case involved a legal dispute over the rights of John Asher, who alleged that the election judges, John Byler and Charles F. Talcott, refused to accept his vote during an election held on November 6, 1866. Asher, a white man who had lived in the precinct for many years and was personally known to the judges, applied to vote but was denied because his name was not listed on the voter registration roll. The judges claimed he had left the state to avoid military service and was therefore not entitled to vote. In his defense, Asher provided an affidavit claiming his residency and eligibility but did not provide the additional proof required by law, specifically the affidavit of a registered voter and householder. The Adams Circuit Court initially ruled in Asher's favor, awarding him $5 in damages. Byler and Talcott appealed this decision, leading to the case reaching the Illinois Supreme Court, where the judges examined the requirements for voting and the evidence surrounding the refusal.	The plaintiff, John Asher, argued that he was wrongfully denied the right to vote despite his long-standing residency and the personal knowledge of the election judges regarding his eligibility. He claimed that his affidavit was sufficient proof of his right to vote, and he sought damages for the refusal of his vote. Asher contended that the judges acted improperly by requiring additional verification that was not mandated by law.	The defendants, John Byler and Charles F. Talcott, asserted that they acted within their legal rights by refusing to accept Asher's vote since he was not registered as a voter. They maintained that his affidavit alone did not meet the statutory requirements, which required both his affidavit and corroboration from a registered householder in the district. The defendants contended that evidence presented to mitigate damages should not be admissible as a defense and argued that their refusal, while based on statutory grounds, was not improper.

In 1884, the legal dispute of John Tomlinson et al. v. Emanuel Earnshaw took place in Cook County, Illinois, presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gary. The case arose from a contract in which the plaintiffs, John Tomlinson and others, sought to recover payment for the sale of Aux Sable sandstone that was contracted to be of first quality. Following a trial, a verdict was reached, but issues arose regarding the amendment of the ad damnum (the claim for damages) after the verdict and the presence of iron spots in the sandstone. The defendant, Emanuel Earnshaw, contested the quality of the stone delivered, asserting that all such stone contained defects, which was a central point during the trial. After the Appellate Court reversed and remanded the case, directing the Superior Court to enter judgment in favor of the plaintiffs for the remaining amount due, the Superior Court had to revisit whether it properly admitted evidence related to the stone's quality. The key legal discussions focused on procedural matters about amendments and the admissibility of evidence relevant to the qualities of the sandstone supplied.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to recover the full amount due under the contract for the sale of first quality Aux Sable sandstone. They argued that the amendment to the ad damnum was justifiable and that the evidence presented in court demonstrated the contractual nature of their claim, thereby reinforcing their demand for payment.	The defendant contended that the Superior Court erred in allowing an amendment to increase the ad damnum post-verdict. He argued that the Appellate Court's direction to enter judgment based on an improper remittitur was unwarranted and claimed that the evidence regarding the iron spots in the stone was not admissible as it pertained to material defects that were common to all stone of the contracted quality.

In the case of Seth Austin, administrator of Elijah Austin, vs. The People of the State of Illinois for the use of Haney Burr, the legal proceedings took place in 1845 at the Edgar Circuit Court. The suit arose from a debt action on a guardian's bond with a penalty amount of $600. Seth Austin, as the administrator, became the defendant in this case. The plaintiffs, representing Haney Burr and others, initially won a jury verdict, which assessed damages at $636.47. Following remissions of part of the damages by the plaintiffs, the judgment was rendered for the total debt of $600. The defendant raised defenses of non est factum (not my deed) and nil debet (no debt exists). The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court upon an appeal from the Circuit Court’s judgment, with the findings from previous cases influencing the decision.	The plaintiff, Haney Burr et al., claimed that Austin, as administrator of the guardian's bond, was liable for a debt that arose from the bond's penalty. They successfully argued that the jury found the defendant guilty of the debt, leading to the award of damages. The plaintiff’s legal request was for the court to uphold the jury’s findings and enforce the judgment rendered by the Circuit Court, which included recovering the assessed damages plus costs.	The defendant, Seth Austin, argued through his legal counsel that the jury's verdict was insufficient to support the judgment rendered, as it did not properly articulate the amount of the debt alongside the damages. His defenses included non est factum, asserting that he did not ratify the bond, and nil debet, denying the existence of any debt owed under the circumstances. Austin’s request was for the court to overturn the judgment of the Circuit Court based on these defenses.

John Jones sued John Warner in January 1876, in the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a deed of conveyance for a 40-acre tract of land in Jasper County, Missouri. The deed, executed on February 27, 1861, included several covenants; notably, it stated that Warner was well seized of the land and had the right to convey it free of any encumbrances. Jones claimed breaches of those covenants, arguing that Warner was neither well seized of the land nor had the right to convey it. The lower court had ruled in favor of Warner, asserting Jones had been evicted from the land due to a prior title held by Elizabeth Eose, who had obtained a decree confirming her ownership. Warner's defense relied on the assertion that the covenants Jones relied upon were valid at the time of the deed's execution. The court found that Jones's arguments about the validity of the subsequent decree were convoluted; it noted that the Missouri decree did not establish a claim against Warner. The complexities of the evidence and the failure of Jones to adequately prove his claim led to confusion during the trial. The court ultimately stated that the covenants in question were not breached as Jones had failed to provide sufficient evidence to prove any wrongdoing by Warner.	Jones argued that Warner had breached the covenants in the deed by claiming that he was not well seized of the land and did not have the right to convey it. He asserted that he had been evicted from the property as a result of a decree favoring a third party, Elizabeth Eose, and sought remediation for those breaches, looking to recover ownership rights of the land based on the covenants included in the deed.	Warner maintained that the covenants in the deed were valid and had not been breached since he owned the land at the time of sale to Jones. He contended that any failure to enforce property rights on Jones's part was due to his own negligence, particularly regarding the failure to record the deed, which allowed for the confusion surrounding title validity. Warner also introduced evidence suggesting that Jones had misrepresented the nature of other transactions pertaining to the land.

In the case of Samuel Ritchie v. Village of Warrensburg, the legal proceedings initiated in Warrensburg, Illinois, revolve around a violation of a local ordinance. The case was first brought before a justice of the peace, where Ritchie was fined $3 for the alleged infraction. Dissatisfied with this ruling, Ritchie appealed to the County Court of Macon County. During the jury trial at the County Court, Ritchie was again found guilty of the ordinance violation, leading to the same fine being imposed. Subsequently, Ritchie appealed the decision, bringing the case to the Illinois Appellate Court on November 23, 1889. Central to the appeal was the argument that the case should be dismissed due to the absence of a complaint or warrant on file, a claim the court found unsubstantiated. There were procedural challenges regarding the admission of the ordinance as evidence, but the court ruled that sufficient proof existed for the jury's verdict of guilt to stand.	The plaintiff, Samuel Ritchie, contended that the case should be dismissed because there was no proper complaint or warrant filed in the proceedings against him. He argued that this lack of documentation rendered the case invalid and that the trial court erred in refusing to dismiss it. Ritchie sought to have the conviction overturned based on these procedural deficiencies.	The Village of Warrensburg, as the defendant, maintained that the trial was conducted properly and that adequate evidence supported the jury's verdict. They argued that the absence of the original complaint or warrant did not undermine the validity of the proceedings, as the trial court had sufficient basis to allow the ordinance into evidence. The defense requested that the appellate court uphold the jury's conviction and affirm the imposition of the fine.

On April 20, 1872, in Illinois, Krone purchased an interest in a stock of goods (drugs and merchandise) from Christopher Wineberg, conveying eighty acres of land in Iowa valued at $5 per acre as part of the transaction. The stock was estimated to be worth between $200 to $600. Subsequently, on April 29, 1872, two creditors of Wineberg obtained judgments against him and executed them, leading to confiscation of the goods by Constable Johnson. The plaintiffs sought an injunction to prevent the sale of these goods, arguing that Krone's purchase was fraudulent, designed to hinder Wineberg's creditors. The circuit court granted a temporary injunction and appointed a receiver to manage the goods. After selling the perishable items, the receiver divided the proceeds between contesting claimants. Appellants argued they should be prioritized for repayment based on being bona fide creditors of Krone, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court to reverse the circuit court's decision.	The plaintiffs claimed that Krone's purchase of goods from Wineberg was fraudulent and made with the intent to delay payments to Wineberg’s creditors. They requested that the court enjoin the sale of the stock and appropriate the proceeds specifically to satisfy the claims of Wineberg’s creditors before paying any claims of Krone’s creditors.	The defendants, represented by Krone and supported by the sale's legitimacy, argued that Krone's purchase was made in good faith and for adequate consideration. They maintained that the stock of goods and the subsequent business should prioritize the payment of debts incurred after the purchase. They requested the court uphold the circuit court's division of funds, asserting that their rights as bona fide creditors should not be compromised.

Leander B. Reynolds, as the administrator of S. Hubbell Reynolds' estate, was involved in a legal case against the People of the State of Illinois that culminated in September 1870. The background of the case begins with S. Hubbell Reynolds’ death on January 29, 1869, after which Leander was appointed as the administrator of the estate on March 11, 1869. The estate was valued at $80,000, and the only heirs were Leander and Elizabeth B. Benton. By the time of the case, Leander had collected between $15,000 and $20,000, but he had only distributed $720 to Elizabeth, who was in financial need. Elizabeth sought a partial distribution by filing a citation in county court, which ordered Leander to pay her $1,000, contingent upon her executing a refunding bond. Leander appealed this order, claiming it was prohibited under the statute that prevents actions against administrators within the first year of their appointment. He was met with affirmations from both the county court and the circuit court, necessitating his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Elizabeth B. Benton, contended that she was entitled to a portion of her inheritance from the estate. Her main argument was founded on her urgent financial need and the assertion that the estate had sufficient assets to meet her claims. Elizabeth sought a court order to compel Leander to make a partial distribution of $1,000 from the estate, arguing that the law permitted such an order within the first year after administration, especially since the estate had no substantial debts.	Leander B. Reynolds, as the defendant, asserted several defenses against the order for partial distribution. Firstly, he claimed that the court lacked jurisdiction to compel distribution within the first year after the issuance of letters of administration, as per statutory restrictions. He argued that the county court's order was unauthorized and improperly classified, asserting that the proceeding should not have been initiated in the name of the people. He also contended that the nature of the action was inappropriately framed as a demand for a debt rather than a rightful claim to an inheritance.

Russell Crossett v. Sallie G. Owens et al. is a legal case that took place in Marion County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 13, 1884. The dispute arose over the existence of a road claimed to pass through a field owned by the defendants, Owens and others. The plaintiff, Russell Crossett, was a road commissioner who sought to remove fences obstructing what he argued was a legally established public road. The defendants contended that no such road had been legally laid out and that their actions to fence off the area were justified. The conflict centered on whether a road was established by commissioners appointed under Illinois law in 1842 and 1847, and whether the procedural requirements for the road's establishment and maintenance had been followed, particularly the necessity for the commissioners to take an oath before undertaking their duties.	The plaintiff, Russell Crossett, claimed that a public road had been established by user and formal action by county commissioners. He argued that it was his duty as a road commissioner to remove obstructions and maintain the road for public access. Crossett sought an injunction to prevent the defendants from interfering with his duties related to the accused road.	The defendants, Sallie G. Owens et al., countered by asserting that no legally established road existed at the location in question. They maintained that the evidence presented by the plaintiff did not meet the necessary legal requirements to prove the road's existence, specifically regarding the proper documentation of the commissioners' actions and their oath-taking. The defendants sought to uphold their right to fence their property and requested the dismissal of the plaintiff's claims.

On December 2, 1847, in Madison County, Illinois, Peter Lott and Joseph Arters filed a chancery bill regarding a marriage agreement involving Fitzroy Sommerville (also known as John Vyvian Fitzroy Sommerville) and Mary Turnbull Milburn, who were to be married on April 22, 1841. The marriage was based on Fitzroy's representations of being a wealthy heir to Admiral Sir John Fitzroy Sommerville, leading Mary to agree to marry him. Following this, an agreement was made to assign various properties in trust for Mary in the event of Fitzroy's death, but Fitzroy died on August 28, 1847, after having divorced Mary for misconduct. The plaintiffs claimed that the marriage was entered into under false pretenses. Mary sought enforcement of the agreement after their marriage ended. The complexity increased with disputes over property and claims of divorce impacting the enforceability of the initial agreement.	The plaintiffs, who include Mary and her supporters, argue that the marriage agreement should be enforced despite the divorce, asserting that the divorce should not negate her rights to the property as initially outlined in the agreement. They contend that Fitzroy’s misrepresentations induced Mary into the marriage and that she retains a legitimate claim to trust benefits established by the marriage contract. The plaintiffs request the court's intervention to compel the defendants to honor the agreement and convey the properties as intended.	The defendants, including those representing Fitzroy’s estate, argue that the divorce nullified any claims Mary had arising from the marriage agreement, labeling her as guilty of misconduct. They argue that the divorce extinguished all rights related to dower and jointure, denying claims for any property or provisions stemming from the now-void marriage contract. They assert that the agreement had no validity after Mary’s alleged departure from the marriage vows and maintain that the plaintiffs lack standing as they were not part of the original marriage agreement.

In the case of Mary T. Owens et al. v. Guy Stapp, Receiver, etc., which took place in Warren County, Illinois, a series of transactions involving loans from the First Rational Bank of Monmouth were disputed between the plaintiffs, Mary T. and James F. Owens, and the bank's receiver, Guy Stapp. The background dates back to May 21, 1880, when James F. Owens borrowed $2,400 from the bank, requiring his wife, Mary T., to co-sign a mortgage on their property as security. Over the years, additional loans were taken, including a $280 loan that matured in 1883. By early 1884, pressures mounted on Owens to renew and consolidate his debts. In February 1884, an agreement was made to take out a new loan of $3,500 to pay off old debts, under the assurance that previous notes and mortgages would be canceled. However, during this process, bank president B. T. O. Hubbard sold some of the original notes to third parties without the plaintiffs' knowledge, complicating the transactions. The bank eventually closed in April 1884 due to Hubbard's fraudulent actions, and Stapp was appointed receiver. The plaintiffs filed for relief against the bank's actions, including the cancellation of certain notes and acknowledgment of their claims against the bank's assets.	The plaintiffs claimed that the bank, through its cashier Hubbard's wrongful actions, had failed to fulfill their agreement and sought relief in the form of the cancellation of the $280 note and overdrafts totaling $512.04, as well as a decree against the bank for amounts in excess of $3,500. They requested the surrender of an unsold $1,000 note and sought general relief based on the circumstances surrounding the bank's operations and their reliance on the bank's management.	Guy Stapp, as receiver for the bank, denied the allegations made by the plaintiffs and asserted a claim for the $1,000 note as collateral for the $280 loan and OW...

William C. Goudy v. The City of Lake View is a case adjudicated by the Illinois Appellate Court, with the final judgment filed on May 29, 1889. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, where the City of Lake View condemned part of Goudy’s property for the expansion of a public highway. The highway encroached upon the east line of Goudy's lot, reducing its size by fifty feet and altering its immediate access from the adjacent Lincoln Park. Goudy had maintained a private entrance from his lot to the park, with the consent of the Lincoln Park commissioners, for approximately seventeen years. Although there was no dispute regarding the compensation for the land actually taken, Goudy contested the jury's verdict which claimed that the remaining property sustained no damage due to the highway construction. The evidence presented comprised conflicting opinions from real estate experts and property owners, but ultimately, the jury deemed that the remainder of Goudy's lot suffered no financial detriment due to the city's actions.	Goudy's main claims revolved around the assertion that the remainder of his property was significantly damaged by the city's condemnation of the lot for public use. He argued that the jury’s decision did not adequately reflect the evidence concerning the impact of the highway improvement on the value of his property. Goudy sought a reassessment of damages to account for this perceived loss and challenged the jury's conclusion that the remaining lot was unaffected.	The City of Lake View defended its actions by asserting that the jury's verdict was well-supported by evidence, particularly the substantial opinions of experts indicating no damage to the remaining property. The city also countered Goudy's claims regarding the revocability of the private entrance permitted by the park commissioners, contending that the law did not support Goudy's arguments about the limitations on this permission. The city requested for the court to affirm the jury's verdict regarding the compensation for the land taken and dismiss Goudy's claims of additional damages.

In December 1853, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with a legal action involving David Crouch (the Appellant) and John Hall (the Appellee) concerning a promissory note made on September 16, 1837. The note was due on October 20, 1838, executed while Crouch and his co-maker resided in Kentucky. The note was assigned to McCoy on September 22, 1841, and later assigned to Hall on May 10, 1851, in Illinois. Hall claimed against Crouch under the note, leading to a demurrer by Crouch on multiple counts presented by Hall. The court upheld a demurrer concerning the first two counts while rejecting the third count, which claimed the note was made without consideration. Under Illinois law, an assignor can only be held liable under specific circumstances, including having made efforts to collect from the makers. The court noted that since the note was overdue and Crouch was not physically present in Illinois when it matured, the liability did not apply under the statute governing assignments in Illinois.	John Hall, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to judgment on the promissory note assigned to him. He claimed that the note was valid and enforceable despite being executed in Kentucky, asserting that the lack of payment qualified him for recovery under the assignment. Hall maintained that the failure to sue the makers earlier was justified as pursuing them would have been futile.	David Crouch contended that Hall’s action was not legally substantiated because the note lacked consideration and was overdue at the time of assignment. He argued that since the makers had not been shown to be collectible and were not residents of Illinois, the claims against him were invalid under the applicable laws of Illinois. Crouch challenged the sufficiency of Hall’s allegations regarding why prior legal proceedings against the makers would have been unavailing.

In 1844, in Jersey County, Illinois, a legal case arose involving the estate of Elisha Madden, who had passed away. The case was brought by Thomas Madden against Abram Cooper, relating to the sale of real estate from Elisha's estate to cover debts. The Circuit Court, presided by Judge Samuel D. Lockwood, had ordered the sale of a 160-acre tract of land after determining that the estate's personal assets were insufficient to meet outstanding debts. The administrator of the estate, John M. Davis, submitted a petition to the court outlining the financial situation of the estate, noting personal property amounting to $310.87 and debts totaling approximately $703.30. The court's jurisdiction was contested, particularly the adequacy of the notice of the sale, which was published for three weeks in a local newspaper. Despite objections regarding the notice and other procedural irregularities, the court eventually affirmed its decision to allow the sale of the land.	The plaintiff, Thomas Madden, challenged the authority of the Circuit Court to order the sale of the real estate, claiming that the notice provided for the sale was insufficient and that the court lacked jurisdiction over the matter. Thomas argued that the notice did not specify the exact day of the term when the application for the sale would be presented, which he believed was contrary to the statutory requirements. He sought to reverse the Circuit Court's judgment regarding the order to sell the estate's real property.	The defendant, Abram Cooper, represented by attorneys L. & L. Davis, contended that the notice of the application complied with statutory requirements, having been published for three consecutive weeks prior to the hearing, thus granting the court jurisdiction. Furthermore, Cooper argued that any objections to the procedural aspects of the sale should not invalidate the sale after a significant lapse of time since the proceedings took place. He maintained that the evidence presented was sufficient for the court to justify the order for sale due to the estate's clear deficiency in personal assets.

The case "Knickerbocker Life Insurance Company v. Edward Barker" originated in September 1870, in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, Edward Barker, initiated an action of debt against the Knickerbocker Life Insurance Company to recover a sum based on a judgment that had been rendered against the company in Milwaukee County, Wisconsin. The court overseeing the case was the Illinois Supreme Court. At the heart of the dispute was the defendant's response to the debt claim, where they pleaded "nil debet" (which means "no debt") and "nul tiel record" (meaning "no such record"). The dispute escalated to a higher court after the plaintiff successfully demurred to the defendants' plea. The case ultimately addressed whether the plea of nil debet was a sufficient defense in this context.	The plaintiff, Edward Barker, claimed that he had a valid judgment against the Knickerbocker Life Insurance Company from Wisconsin and sought to enforce this judgment in Illinois. Barker's main legal argument was that the defendants' pleas (nil debet and nul tiel record) were insufficient to deny the obligation to pay the debt.	The Knickerbocker Life Insurance Company, as the defendant, argued that the plea of nil debet was a valid defense against the action brought by the plaintiff. They contended that there was no debt owed based on the circumstances surrounding the original judgment from Wisconsin. The defendants sought to have the court reverse the prior judgment that sustained the plaintiff's demurrer against their plea.

The case "The Chicago and Great Eastern Railway Company v. John S. Vosburgh" was adjudicated in September 1867 in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, John S. Vosburgh, initiated an action of assumpsit against the Chicago and Great Eastern Railway Company to recover payment for work and labor performed, specifically in the construction of an embankment, as well as for materials provided in connection with such work. The matter was tried before a jury in the Superior Court of Chicago, resulting in a verdict favoring Vosburgh for the amount of $5,639.42. The railway company appealed the trial court's ruling, asserting that errors were made in sustaining objections to their evidence, excluding certain testimonies, and contended that the verdict did not align with the law and evidence presented. During the trial, they argued that a witness's estimation of the work's value was improperly excluded and that the verdict was unexpectedly high due to unanticipated costs and changes made after the original contract was established.	John S. Vosburgh claimed compensation for the work done in constructing the embankment, asserting that the contract he entered into stipulated the agreed-upon payment for the services rendered. He argued that the railway company was bound by their understanding of who would supply necessary materials, particularly the earth required for the embankment, and that any changes requiring him to source materials from farther locations warranted additional compensation. Vosburgh maintained that the jury's finding was supported by credible evidence and aligned with the terms of their agreement.	The Chicago and Great Eastern Railway Company contended that there were errors in the trial, specifically that the court improperly excluded pertinent testimony that could demonstrate the work's fair value was less than what Vosburgh claimed. They also argued the verdict was contrary to the evidence and requested a new trial, claiming surprise at the trial due to unexpected additional claims for labor costs, which had not been adequately disclosed prior to the proceedings. The railway company's defense relied on the idea that the contract's terms allowed for no additional compensation beyond what was originally agreed.

Frank H. Follansbee filed a lawsuit against Gustavus P. Adams in September 1877, concerning a contract for the sale of 60,000 bushels of wheat. The contract, made on June 8, 1874, allowed for delivery at any time during July 1874. However, on June 11, 1874, Follansbee became insolvent and informed Adams of his inability to deliver the wheat. He requested a settlement based on the current market price. Subsequently, a settlement was reached, determining that Adams owed Follansbee $2,043.75. The case was tried in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, before a judge without a jury. The court examined whether the contract was rescinded before the delivery date, ultimately finding in favor of Adams.	Follansbee argued that he had a valid contract for the sale of wheat and that Adams failed to perform by not accepting and paying for the wheat. He sought damages for this failure, asserting that Adams had an obligation to fulfill the original terms of the contract despite his insolvency.	Adams contended that Follansbee's insolvency was a significant factor that allowed him to rescind the contract. Adams argued that Follansbee's declaration of inability to deliver the wheat constituted a rescission of the contract before the delivery date and that the settlement reached was valid and binding.

In September 1868, the case "Hiram A. Pool, for the use of Cyrus Niles, v. Elijah Marshall" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over a piece of land purchased by Hiram A. Pool and Elijah Marshall from a common grantor, Baker, which was encumbered by a mortgage. Pool retained some of his purchase money to pay off the mortgage and, in turn, claimed that he should be able to recover a portion of the amount paid from Marshall, under the assertion that they both purchased land subjected to the same mortgage. The trial took place in Woodford County, before Judge S. L. Richmond, where a jury ruled in favor of Marshall. Pool sought to reverse this decision by appealing to the Supreme Court.	Pool, representing the interest of Cyrus Niles, claimed that since he paid the entire mortgage on the property, he should be entitled to recover from Marshall the proportion of the mortgage debt attributable to Marshall's land. Pool argued that he acted as an agent in this transaction and that the payment made to discharge the mortgage was aimed at benefiting both parties involved in the land purchase.	Elijah Marshall's defense contended that Pool was not the true party responsible for paying the mortgage as the funds used came from Baker, the common grantor, not from Pool's own finances. They maintained that Pool could not recover the payment since he only acted as an intermediary with Baker's money, thus invalidating Pool's claim to any reimbursement from Marshall regarding the mortgage.

In September 1868, in Chicago, Illinois, the case of James W. Scoville et al. v. Maria E. Hilliard et al. arose concerning the partition of a lot of ground. The plaintiffs, Scoville and others, filed a petition under the Illinois Revised Statutes, seeking to partition a lot that they claimed to have an undivided interest in, which was subject to a life estate held by Elizabeth Snowhook. The matter was originally addressed in the Superior Court of Chicago, where the petition was dismissed on the grounds that the plaintiff's claims did not conform to legal requirements necessary for a partition action. The core legal question was whether a remainder-man or reversioner could maintain a partition suit against another owner of an undivided interest when a life estate still existed. The court examined the relevant statutes, analyzed the ownership interests involved, and noted that life tenants must also be considered in these proceedings. The plaintiffs appealed the dismissal to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking clarity on their rights concerning the property.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had a right to partition the property based on their ownership of an undivided interest, despite the presence of a life estate. They argued that the statutory language allowed individuals with a remainder interest to pursue partition without needing to demonstrate current possession of the property. Their legal request was for the court to recognize their right to partition, asserting that allowing such an action would not negatively affect the life tenant's interests.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs were not entitled to maintain the partition action because they lacked possession of the premises. They argued that the statute required a showing of possession for any party seeking partition, positing that the plaintiffs' claim was invalid unless possession could be demonstrated. The defense maintained that allowing the plaintiffs to proceed would contravene existing legal provisions and disrupt the rights of the life tenant.

In 1880, the Sarah A. Reno and Eugenia M. Little, along with their husbands, sold a portion of their land in Chicago to the Pittsburg, Fort Wayne & Chicago Railroad Company. The sale included a stipulation that the railroad would restore switch connections to the coal yard operated by Reno & Little. After the railroad laid new tracks, it initially maintained the switch connections. However, in August 1881, the railroad conveyed part of the property to the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, which removed the switch tracks and refused to restore them. This disruption severely impacted the business of Reno & Little, who relied on the aforementioned switch connections for transporting coal without incurring switching charges. Following failed attempts to restore the connections, the plaintiffs filed a lawsuit seeking damages for the breach of the covenant by the railroad company. The case was tried in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the jury ultimately awarding the plaintiffs $85,000 after determining the railroad had indeed breached their contractual obligation.	The plaintiffs, Sarah A. Reno and Eugenia M. Little, along with their husbands, claimed that the Pittsburg, Fort Wayne & Chicago Railroad Company breached the covenant contained in their contract regarding the restoration and continuation of the switch connections to their coal yard. The plaintiffs sought damages for the loss of business and depreciation of property value resulting from the defendant’s actions.	The defendant argued that they had fulfilled their obligations under the covenant by re-establishing switch connections after laying new tracks. They contended that subsequent removal of the connections by the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company was beyond their control and thus not a breach of the original contract. Furthermore, they claimed that the plaintiffs' damages should not be recoverable in a single action since the interests of the various parties were separate.

In September 1875, the case of George Webster et al. v. Flavel K. Granger et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a sale involving goods, specifically flax seed, that were sold and delivered from the plaintiffs, George Webster and others, to the defendants, Flavel K. Granger and others. The transaction took place in Cook County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs shipped 134 sacks of flax seed to their commission merchants, Foss & Co. in Chicago. The sale occurred on October 7, 1871, when the defendants purchased the goods by sample for $1.55 per bushel and received a delivery ticket. Unfortunately, the goods were destroyed in a fire the same day, leading to contention over the ownership and risk of loss connected to the sale. The defendants claimed they were entitled to inspect the goods and argued that the title did not pass to them until they had a reasonable opportunity to do so.	The plaintiffs asserted that the delivery ticket given to the defendants represented a complete transfer of ownership of the flax seed. They contended that upon receipt of the delivery ticket, the defendants had all necessary indicia of ownership and assumed all risks associated with the goods, including their loss in the fire. The plaintiffs sought to enforce payment for the agreed price despite the destruction of the goods.	The defendants argued that a proper title transfer had not occurred as they had not yet had a reasonable opportunity to examine the goods, which they asserted should occur within a designated timeframe. They maintained that merely having a delivery ticket was insufficient to establish that they bore the risk of loss from the fire, emphasizing the need to inspect the goods before taking ownership.

In 1872, Frederick W. Newhall entered into a contract with John Woolacott to design and construct a brick structure, with Woolacott responsible for all materials and labor. Woolacott subcontracted the brickwork to Louis Reinhardt, who failed to complete the contract and abandoned the project, forcing Woolacott to finish the work at his own expense. After accounting for payments made to Reinhardt and the costs incurred by Woolacott to complete the project, a sum of $399.52 remained, which both Woolacott and Reinhardt claimed. Additionally, other defendants, who had provided labor or materials to Reinhardt, also laid claim to this fund, asserting lien rights under Illinois' Mechanic's Lien Law. To resolve these conflicting claims and avoid multiple lawsuits against him, Newhall filed a bill in equity to enjoin the defendants from pursuing their claims and to have the court determine who was entitled to the disputed funds.	Newhall claimed that he was merely a stakeholder holding the remaining sum of $399.52 and sought judicial intervention to resolve the conflicting claims of Woolacott, Reinhardt, and other defendants. He argued for a bill of interpleader, requesting the court to determine the rightful claimant to the funds and enjoin all parties from initiating further claims against him, thus protecting his property from the pressure of multiple lawsuits.	Woolacott and Reinhardt contended their right to claim the remaining funds based on their respective contracts. Additionally, the other defendants argued they were entitled to liens under the Mechanic's Lien Law due to the labor and materials they provided under Reinhardt's subcontract. They asserted that their claims should be recognized and enforced against the funds held by Newhall, alleging that they were justified in seeking compensation for their contributions.

On April 20, 1835, a group of individuals in New York City, including Charles Butler and Edward A. Hicoll, entered into a joint venture with Kinzie & Pearson in Chicago to invest in western lands. Each party contributed $5,000, amounting to $50,000, for the purchase of real estate. Kinzie & Pearson were to manage these investments, sell the properties, and reinvest the earnings while charging no management fees. The venture had a set termination date of July 1, 1841, with all profits split equally between the investors and Kinzie & Pearson. However, as the property values declined, the venture faced substantial losses, prompting the contract's cancellation and transferring remaining assets to William Bard as a trustee on July 1, 1841. Subsequent property transfers and partitions occurred over several years, leading Frances B. Nicoll, representing her deceased husband, to petition for her dower rights regarding the property. The lower court dismissed her petition, prompting her appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868.	Frances B. Nicoll claimed entitlement to her dower rights in the disputed property, contending that the trust arrangement had transformed personal interests into equitable estate rights. She argued that her deceased husband had a legitimate claim to ownership in the property conveyed to the trustee, and thus she should be able to recover her legal dower rights.	Richard Mason defended against the petition by arguing that the title to the property had not shifted from its original character as personalty, and that the conveyed deed did not reflect an intent to grant any ownership that would provide Nicoll with dower rights. The defense maintained that no valid agreements or actions by the parties had occurred to modify the property’s original status or to substantiate Nicoll's claims after such a significant lapse of time.

In the case of Christian Obrock v. Louisa Obrock, the legal proceedings took place in Adams County, Illinois, with a decision rendered on November 23, 1889. The case arose from a petition filed by Louisa Obrock, seeking separate maintenance from her husband, Christian Obrock, under statutory provisions. The couple, who both had children from previous marriages, faced ongoing conflicts primarily instigated by Christian's children, particularly his two older daughters, aged twenty-five and twenty-two. These conflicts reportedly placed a strain on Louisa’s position in the household, leading to accusations from Christian and his daughters about her habits and ability to maintain the home. Christian allegedly made comments indicating a desire for Louisa to leave their home, which compounded the tensions. Upon hearing the evidence provided by both parties, the court determined that Louisa had justified reasons to live apart from Christian without fault on her part.	Louisa Obrock claimed that her living situation with Christian was intolerable due to the hostile environment created primarily by his children. She argued that Christian's behavior and the ongoing conflicts made it impossible for her to maintain her dignity and self-respect as his wife. As part of her legal request, she sought a decree for separate maintenance, along with specific financial allowances for her support during the period of separation.	Christian Obrock contested Louisa's claims, arguing that the evidence did not support her assertion of living apart due to her husband's faults. He indicated that most of the marital conflict arose from the behavior of Louisa and that he had made efforts to maintain family unity. Christian also sought to challenge the financial allowances set by the court, disputing the amount decreed for Louisa’s maintenance and alleging that her charges against him were exaggerated.

The case "The Keokuk Packet Company v. John Henry" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1869. The incident occurred on June 1, 1867, when John Henry, accompanied by his daughter, boarded the steamer Bob Boy, operated by the Keokuk Packet Company, at the City of Alton. After the boat docked, Henry attempted to escort his daughter safely to the cabin. However, without warning, the boat began to back away from the landing while Henry was still on board. Due to the boat's racing with another vessel and the lack of proper notification that it would depart, Henry was not afforded enough time or means to safely leave the boat. In desperation, he was forced to jump from the boat to the shore to avoid being taken away, resulting in a significant injury—specifically, a dislocated ankle and fractured bones in his leg. He subsequently filed a lawsuit claiming negligence against the boat's operators for failing to give him appropriate time and facilities to disembark safely.	John Henry claimed that the Keokuk Packet Company was negligent in its operation of the Bob Boy by failing to provide sufficient time for passengers to disembark after docking. He argued that the boat's captain did not blow the whistle or provide any indication before departing, which caused him to take an unsafe leap off the boat, resulting in severe injuries. The plaintiff sought damages due to the alleged recklessness of the boat's crew and the violation of safety regulations by racing another vessel.	The Keokuk Packet Company defended itself by arguing that it had no legal obligation to warn Henry or provide him with a safe way to disembark since he had not notified them that he intended to leave the boat. They claimed that Henry was a passenger and thus the company had fulfilled its duty by ensuring he was safely on board. Furthermore, the company contended that Henry’s own negligence contributed to his injuries, asserting that the risks he took in jumping from the vessel should preclude him from recovering damages.

James T. Hair Company v. Willis C. Thorne is a legal case that took place in 1888 in Cook County, Illinois. The case revolves around a dispute regarding legal services rendered by the James T. Hair Company to Willis C. Thorne. At the time the services were provided, W. J. Ennison was in partnership with Thorne in the legal business. The case emerged when Thorne, as the appellant, appealed a judgment that favored the Hair Company, the appellee, for the value of the legal services. During the trial, the question arose whether Ennison should have been a co-plaintiff, but it was determined that the contract was solely between Thorne and the Hair Company. The services were performed outside the State of Illinois while both parties had their business in Chicago. There was no clear evidence presented regarding the terms of the partnership or how the compensation was to be divided, leading to the conclusion that Thorne alone was entitled to receive compensation for the services rendered.	The plaintiff, James T. Hair Company, claimed compensation for legal services they provided to the defendant, Willis C. Thorne. They argued that despite the existence of a partnership between Thorne and Ennison, the contract for services was made solely with Thorne, and the services were performed entirely by them. The plaintiff sought to recover fees that they believed were owed for the legal work conducted.	The defendant, Willis C. Thorne, argued that W. J. Ennison should have been included as a co-plaintiff in the case since he was a partner when the services were rendered. Thorne contended that the lack of evidence regarding the terms of the partnership raised questions about whether he was entitled to compensation solely on his own. The defendant requested that the court overturn the judgment based on these claims.

The case "John Rudesill et al. v. County Court of Jefferson County" occurred in Jefferson County, Illinois, and involved an action of debt concerning an official bond executed by William D. Watson, a justice of the peace. Watson was elected on April 5, 1870, and filed an official bond that was accepted. Following the release of the original surety, Isaac Garrison, on June 21, 1871, Watson submitted a new bond with John Rudesill and others as sureties on June 22, 1871. After fulfilling his official duties and collecting a judgment in 1873, Watson failed to pay the sum, prompting Rudesill and co-plaintiffs to seek recovery.
