The key point of contention was whether a subsequent alteration made to the bond by the county clerk—without the sureties' knowledge—rendered the bond void. The defendants claimed the alteration was material and relieved them of liability, while the plaintiffs argued correct compliance with statutory requirements.	The plaintiffs, John Rudesill et al., claimed that the bond executed by the sureties was valid and enforceable. They argued that the bond continued to indemnify against Watson's official misconduct, as the bond was executed in line with statutory requirements, and the clerk’s alteration of the bond did not materially affect the sureties' liabilities. They sought to collect the amount due from Watson, asserting that the sureties were liable under the bond.	The defendant, represented by the sureties who were appellants in the case, contended that the clerk's alteration in the bond was a material change that invalidated their obligations as sureties. Their argument was based on the assertion that the alteration increased their liability without their consent. Thus, they requested that the court dismiss the plaintiffs' claims based on this alleged defect in the bond.

Martin O. Walker v. Frederick R. Wilson is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1869. The case originated from a lease agreement between the plaintiff, Frederick R. Wilson, and the defendants, Martin O. Walker and his partners. Wilson, the lessor, claimed that the lessees—Walker and his partners—were wilfully holding over the leased property after the lease expired on May 1, 1868. The lessees occupied the property from September 1865 until they held over until July 6, 1868. During this period, Wilson sought to recover double rent under the statute, asserting that the defendants had not paid their share of the taxes as outlined in the lease agreement. After a trial in the Superior Court of Chicago, the court found in favor of Wilson, leading Walker to appeal the decision. The issue of whether a parol license granted to the lessees to remain in possession after the lease's expiration could be revoked was also central to the case.	The plaintiff, Frederick R. Wilson, argued that the defendants wilfully held over the leased property after the expiration of their lease, thereby entitling him to double rent under Illinois law. He claimed that Walker and his partners continuously occupied the property without paying the requisite taxes or rent from May 1, 1868, to July 6, 1868. Wilson sought recovery of the unpaid rent and taxes, reflecting the terms of the lease.	The defendant, Martin O. Walker, contested the claims by stating that a parol license had been granted to them to remain in possession of the property after the lease expired. Walker argued that this license should have allowed them to keep possession without incurring liability for double rent. Additionally, he contended that the lease did not specify a requirement for double rent, and therefore, the court should not grant Wilson's request.

The case "Robert E. Jenkins v. William E. Merriweather" arose from events that began on July 24, 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, when Merriweather obtained a judgment against Samuel J. Walker for $19,645.33. Subsequently, an execution was issued on September 11, 1874, which was returned on February 16, 1875, noting “no property found.” An alias execution was issued on July 1, 1881, and returned on September 14, 1881, indicating it was “in no part satisfied.” On July 23, 1881, the sheriff levied upon numerous properties owned by Walker in compliance with the execution. Following this, a venditioni exponas was issued, and Merriweather’s judgment was assigned to William C. Eitchie. The sheriff sold the land for $21,000 and, after deducting fees, satisfied Merriweather’s judgment only partially. Jenkins became involved after Walker was declared bankrupt on April 26, 1878, transferring Walker's property rights to Jenkins as his assignee. In 1883, Jenkins filed a motion to quash the venditioni exponas, which was denied by the Superior Court, leading to an appeal that affirmed the lower court's judgment.	Robert E. Jenkins, the plaintiff, argued that the execution sale should be set aside based on legal principles governing such sales. Jenkins sought to quash the venditioni exponas that permitted the sale of Walker's property, claiming that the sale was improper and should not stand. He contended that there were sufficient grounds to challenge the sale’s legality and that the court had the authority to invalidate it based on procedural irregularities.	William E. Merriweather, the defendant, maintained that the sale and the subsequent deed were valid and could not be set aside merely by motion. He argued that the title to the property had vested and that any challenge to the sale must be made in equity, not by motion in this context. Merriweather emphasized that after the property was sold and a deed was executed, the court lacked jurisdiction to overturn that action without a full equitable proceeding to address the interests of all affected parties.

In April 1850, Edmund S. Holbrook, along with co-signers Ebenezer Higgins and William Paul, executed a bond as township treasurer to the trustees of schools in La Salle County, Illinois, in the penal sum of $2,000. The bond stipulated that Holbrook would faithfully perform his duties and transfer all funds to his successor. In April 1856, David L. Hough was appointed as Holbrook's successor and demanded the $2,000 from Holbrook, who refused to pay. The case escalated into a legal action initiated by the trustees against Holbrook and Higgins for nonpayment. The trial revealed disagreements regarding the succession of the treasurer and the validity of Holbrook’s bond. The defendants argued that Hough was not Holbrook’s official successor and raised multiple defenses related to the issuance and conditions of the bond. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, presided over by Chief Justice Caton.	The plaintiffs, represented by the trustees of schools, claimed that Holbrook had failed to deliver the $2,000 he held as township treasurer upon the appointment of Hough as his successor. They argued that Holbrook had notice of Hough's appointment and that he neglected his duties by refusing to pay the demanded funds. The plaintiffs sought a judgment for the amount owed, claiming Holbrook was liable under the bond he had executed.	The defendants, Holbrook and Higgins, contended that Holbrook had not officially been removed from office before Hough was appointed, claiming there was no vacancy. They asserted that Holbrook had been re-appointed and thus could not be held accountable under the claim that he neglected to remit the funds. They also challenged the approval of Hough's bond, which was necessary for his valid appointment, and claimed Holbrook had not received the moneys owed as alleged.

The case involves The Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railway Company and E. W. Felton, Admr., filed on June 16, 1888, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The events transpired on the night of March 19, 1881, when a train operated by the railway company started its journey from Bureau Junction to Chicago amidst a severe storm with heavy winds and snow, disrupting regular train schedules. Arriving at Ottawa in the early hours of March 20, some passengers, including Luke H. Goodrich, boarded the train. As the train traveled towards Morris, it had to switch tracks due to a snow-plow obstructing the south track. The train then moved onto the north track. Approximately a mile west of Minooka, the train encountered a snow bank, halting its progress. Witnesses testified that Goodrich and fellow passengers mistook an approaching snow-plow on the south track as a potential collision threat after hearing an alarm whistle from the train's engine. Panic ensued, leading Goodrich and another passenger to jump from the train onto a track, where they were subsequently struck by the fast-moving snow-plow, resulting in Goodrich sustaining injuries that led to his death two days later.	The plaintiff, represented by E.W. Felton as administrator for the deceased, claimed that the railway company exhibited negligence by failing to manage their locomotive and snow-plow safely. They alleged that the actions of the railway's employees, specifically the sounding of alarm signals that misled passengers into believing they were in danger, directly led to Goodrich abandoning the train and subsequently being fatally injured. The plaintiff sought damages for the wrongful death resulting from this negligence.	The railway company contended that they were not negligent, asserting that the alarm signal used was appropriate under the circumstances. They argued that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate that any negligence contributed to Goodrich’s injury. The defense claimed that the evidence did not support the assertion that the signal was improperly given or that it caused Goodrich to act recklessly by leaving the train. They insisted that Goodrich's injuries were the result of an inevitable accident rather than the railway's negligence.

William F. Jenks initiated legal action against David H. Vandolah in the Illinois Appellate Court concerning a contract for digging a well. The events unfolded in McLean County, Illinois, with the court session held on September 21, 1888. Jenks and a joint contractor, Parks, had an agreement with Vandolah to dig a well at a specified rate per foot. However, Jenks filed the suit solely in his name, which became contested during the trial. Upon presentation of evidence, it was revealed that the suit should have appropriately named both Jenks and Parks as plaintiffs. Jenks then sought to amend the declaration to include Parks, but the court granted this amendment conditionally, requiring Jenks to cover two-thirds of the accrued costs, which he claimed he could not afford. The court's insistence on this condition ultimately led to Jenks declining to proceed, compelling the jury to rule in favor of Vandolah.	Jenks claimed that he had a joint contract with Parks for the services rendered in digging the well and argued that the trial court's refusal to allow the amendment to include Parks as a joint plaintiff was unjust. He requested the court to reconsider the amendment conditions and to permit him to proceed with the case.	Vandolah's defense rested on the fact that the original contract was between himself and both Jenks and Parks, and since the suit was filed only in Jenks' name, he moved for a jury verdict in his favor. Vandolah argued that the conditions placed on amending the declaration by the court were reasonable and that Jenks' failure to comply justified the verdict.

The case of **Alexander McArthur v. Isaac Artz** took place in **1889** in **Mercer County, Illinois**. The central issue arose when Isaac Artz was prosecuted for keeping the peace and disorderly conduct before a justice of the peace. Following his conviction and requirement to give bond and pay costs, Artz appealed to the Circuit Court. The Circuit Court clerk subsequently refused to docket the case until the required fees were paid, which led Artz's attorneys to seek a court order ensuring the case could proceed without this pre-condition. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Artz, prompting the clerk to appeal this decision. The legal discourse revolved around whether a defendant in a criminal case could be asked to pay a docket fee in advance of their trial. The Appellate Court upheld the Circuit Court's ruling, affirming that costs in criminal cases should not be advanced before trial, especially when the defendant had not yet been convicted.	Alexander McArthur, representing the state as the appellant, argued that the clerk was within his rights to request the payment of docket fees before the Circuit Court would docket Artz's appeal. He contended this was standard procedure and necessary for the orderly processing of cases.	Isaac Artz contended that requiring him to pay docket fees in advance of his trial was unlawful, arguing that in criminal proceedings, he could not be compelled to pay fees unless he was convicted. Artz emphasized that costs in criminal cases should be borne by the county treasury if he was acquitted, and therefore he should not have to advance costs prior to his trial.

The case of Herman Classen v. John Cuddigan took place in 1886 in Iroquois County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a rental agreement where John Cuddigan rented approximately eighty acres of land from Herman Classen to plant corn. According to their agreement, Cuddigan was to pay Classen one-third of the corn produced. After the harvest, Cuddigan only delivered about 343 bushels of corn, leading Classen to claim he was owed significantly more. There was conflicting evidence regarding the yield from the land; Classen's position was that the land could have produced around twenty bushels per acre, which would equal an excess of 190 bushels compared to what was delivered. In contrast, Cuddigan and his witnesses claimed the land was too wet and did not yield sufficient corn. The case initially ruled in Classen's favor, but after appeal, the County Court ruled for Cuddigan. Classen subsequently appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court.	Herman Classen, the plaintiff, argued that John Cuddigan failed to fulfill the rental agreement by delivering insufficient corn. Classen claimed that the land was capable of producing a higher yield, and thus he was owed more than what Cuddigan delivered. He sought to have the County Court's decision overturned and to receive the due compensation for the corn he believed he was entitled to based on their agreement.	John Cuddigan, the defendant, contended that he had fulfilled his obligations under the rental agreement by delivering all the corn produced, claiming that the wet conditions of the land affected the yield. He argued that the evidence presented by Classen regarding the potential yield was not credible and highlighted the jury's finding in his favor as justification for his position. Furthermore, Cuddigan opposed Classen's motion for a new trial based on newly discovered evidence, asserting that this evidence was merely cumulative and insufficient for a retrial.

The case "Board of Education v. Smith Hoag" took place in Kane County, Illinois, and culminated in a court decision on December 9, 1887. The dispute arose from a contract for the sale of flooring and lumber provided by Smith Hoag to the Locust Street School in early 1881. Although a previous ruling had determined the Board of Education was liable to pay for the materials, the issue at hand was the manner of payment and the time it took for the Board to fulfill its financial obligation. The jury had previously awarded Hoag $8148.37 in damages, but the Board appealed the decision, particularly contesting the judgment's enforcement regarding an unreasonable delay in payment, interest rates applied to the overdue balance, and specifics of the payment method prescribed in the judgment form. The case was re-evaluated after being remanded from an earlier appeal in the May term of 1886, with the legal considerations centering around interest laws related to delayed payments and the statutory obligations of school boards.	Smith Hoag, the plaintiff, argued that the Board of Education failed to pay for lumber and flooring supplied in a timely manner, leading to a claim for damages including interest due to unreasonable and vexatious delays in payment. He sought to enforce the jury's decision and recover the full amount invoiced along with applicable interest based on the statutory guidelines governing financial obligations of school boards.	The Board of Education contended that the trial court's judgment form was contrary to law and challenged the inclusion of interest on the grounds that it should not be enforced against funds that they had no ability to control. They argued that the language in the judgment could not compel them to pay from township funds not appropriated for such debt, thereby seeking to have the judgment overturned due to these legal discrepancies.

In 1862, in DeKalb County, Illinois, Samuel F. Hopkins initiated legal action against Joseph E. Glidden and other directors of School District No. 7. The case revolved around an instrument promising payment of eighty dollars, plus interest, by the district's treasurer. This instrument was signed by the directors, but the defendants contended that it lacked clarity regarding its purpose, was a time obligation rather than a demand for payment, and was not properly signed. During the trial in the DeKalb Circuit Court, the plaintiff sought to admit this instrument as evidence, which the court allowed despite the defendants' objections. The jury ruled in favor of the plaintiff, leading the defendants to seek a reversal of this judgment, arguing that the order was invalid and did not meet legal requirements set forth by state law regarding the operation of school district funds.	The plaintiff, Samuel F. Hopkins, claimed that the written instrument constituted a valid obligation of the school district directors, which was admitted into evidence against the defendants' objections. Hopkins argued that although the order might not have followed all statutory requirements, the defendants’ acknowledgment of past interest payments implied validation of the order.	The defendants contended that the financial order was void on its face, lacking necessary information about its purpose and not being signed in compliance with the law. They maintained that the order was improperly executed by one director on behalf of others, which violated their statutory responsibilities. They requested that the court overturn the lower court's ruling that admitted the evidence and ultimately resulted in the judgment in favor of the plaintiff.

On November 18, 1871, Andrew Warren (the appellant) and James E. Tyler et al. (the appellees) were involved in a legal dispute in Cook County, Illinois. Warren was found indebted to the appellees in the sum of $7,831.28. To settle this debt, the appellees accepted certain lands located in Wisconsin from Marcus Warren, Andrew's brother, on December 11, 1871, despite the lands being worth significantly less than the debt owed. The appellees were misled into this settlement by Warren's false representations, where he claimed to have lost everything and was unable to pay his debts. Upon discovering the fraud, the appellees sought to rescind the contract and recover the total debt, bringing the case to court. The dispute centered on the issues of fraud, the timing of the rescission of the contract, and the recovery of interest on the original debt.	The plaintiffs (Tyler et al.) argued that they were fraudulently induced by Warren’s false claims to accept the lands as a settlement for the debt. They contended that the contract was voidable due to these fraudulent representations and asserted their right to recover the full amount of the debt without deductions for the lands’ actual value. They also claimed that the lawsuit was timely, as they had only recently discovered the true nature of Warren's deceit.	The defendant (Warren) contended that the jury's finding was excessive and that the plaintiffs should not have been allowed to recover an amount exceeding the actual value of the lands taken as payment. Additionally, he argued that the 18-month delay before the lawsuit was filed was too lengthy, suggesting that the plaintiffs had ample time to discover the fraud. He also claimed that the interest rate of seven percent applied to the case was not valid since it was out of alignment with the statutory interest regulations.

The case of James W. Converse et al. v. Ann Rankin et al. originated in Cook County, Illinois, and was decided on January 25, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case involved a dispute over property title clouded by a tax deed issued to the defendant, James W. Converse, based on a tax sale. Ann Rankin, the original complainant, claimed that she had attempted in good faith to redeem her property by depositing an amount with the county clerk that she believed sufficient for the redemption process. She was issued a certificate of redemption but was later informed that the amount was insufficient. Despite efforts to ascertain the exact amount needed, difficulties arose when her agent tried to reach the defendant Reed (the purchaser at the tax sale), who initially expressed willingness to provide information but failed to do so. After the issuance of the tax deed, Rankin and her co-complainants sought to have the cloud removed from their title, arguing they had fulfilled all obligations regarding the property’s redemption prior to the deed being issued.	The plaintiff, Ann Rankin, claimed that her attempts to redeem the property from tax sale were genuine, as she had complied with all legal requirements up to that point, including paying the clerk the amount she was advised to. She argued that any mistake in the redemption amount was minor and occurred without her fault. The plaintiffs sought relief from the court to remove the cloud on their property title caused by the tax deed, contingent upon paying the deficiency amount claimed by the defendants.	The defendants, Converse and Reed, contended that the plaintiffs did not meet the legal requirements for a valid redemption because the amount paid was insufficient. They argued that the plaintiffs' failures and alleged lack of diligence in pursuing the necessary payments constituted a legal barrier to their claims. The defendants requested that the court deny the plaintiffs' claim to relief from the tax deed, maintaining that the tax deed was valid as issued and that the plaintiffs should bear the consequences of their purported errors.

Jedediah Jack, the plaintiff in error, was involved in a legal matter that arose in November 1857 in Illinois. The case concerns a recognizance—a type of bond taken to secure the appearance of an individual named Lane in response to a criminal charge. Jack entered into a joint and several bond for this purpose, alongside others. Following Lane's failure to appear, a forfeiture of the recognizance was declared, leading to the issuance of a capias and scire facias against Jack. In his defense, Jack claimed that he was an attorney and counselor at law at the time of signing the recognizance, arguing this should exempt him from his obligations under the bond. However, the court sustained a demurrer against his plea, meaning they rejected his defense. The trial took place in the Massac Circuit Court, and the case ultimately involved interpretations of statutory provisions regarding who may serve as special bail in Illinois law, particularly as it relates to attorneys.	The primary argument made by Jedediah Jack was based on his status as a licensed attorney and counselor at law. He contended that this status exempted him from providing surety in the recognizance he had signed, claiming that he should not be held liable due to what he considered a statutory disability. Jack requested the court to validate this argument and rule in his favor against the forfeiture of the bond.	The defendants, represented by J.S. Robinson, maintained that the statute regarding special bail was applicable even in this context and that Jack's argument concerning his professional status did not exempt him from liability. They argued that the recognizance was valid regardless of Jack’s plea about his profession. The defendants sought to affirm the findings of the lower court that Jack remained liable for the bond’s obligations despite his claims of professional privilege.

Philander Woodworth brought a case against the administrators of Enoch Paine, who had passed away. The legal proceedings took place in December 1830, in Illinois. Woodworth had previously obtained a judgment against Paine in 1822 for $1,056.61 and sought to revive this judgment. The defendants, Greenup and Conway, filed a plea citing outstanding claims against Paine's estate that exceeded the total assets available for distribution, including funeral and administrative expenses. However, they failed to specify the nature and timing of these claims. The court overruled Woodworth's demurrer to the defendants' plea, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. Central to the case was the interpretation of the 1823 statute concerning the distribution of deceased estates, which was argued to treat all claims equally. The court examined whether this statute could retroactively affect judgments made prior to its enactment and the rights of creditors against the assets of an intestate estate in insolvency situations.	Woodworth contended that his judgment should be prioritized over other claims against Paine's estate, arguing that the 1823 statute did not diminish the rights of judgment creditors like himself. He sought to have the judgment revived and enforced, asserting that he was entitled to a preference in the distribution of the deceased's assets in light of his existing judgment.	The defendants maintained that the assets left by Paine were insufficient to cover all claims, claiming that the total claims against the estate far exceeded the available assets. They argued that Woodworth had already received some payment on his claim and did not hold a preferential right over the remaining assets. Their plea cited the necessity to treat all claims equally per the 1823 statute, which should apply to the distribution of Paine's estate.

Mechanics’ Savings Institution on St. Louis, Mo. v. James Givens et al. is a legal case heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1876. The case originated in the Jefferson County Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Tazewell B. Tanner. The context involves multiple writs of attachment against James Givens, with judgments rendered in favor of several defendants at the February term of the Jefferson County Circuit Court in 1875. All writs were aimed at the same property, and the Mechanics’ Savings Institution issued its attachment only two days before the same court term, which became a point of contention. The institution contended its right to share in the sales proceeds from the attached property along with other creditors, arguing that its writ was returnable to the same court term where other judgments were made. However, its initial motion to share in proceeds was overruled, leading to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The Mechanics' Savings Institution argued that under the statutory framework, all judgments in attachment against the same defendant that are returnable at the same term should share pro rata in the proceeds of the property attached. Although its writ was issued shortly before the term, the plaintiff believed it should still be entitled to participate in the distribution of proceeds from the property alongside other creditors whose judgments were made at the same term.	James Givens and the other defendants contended that the attachment filed by the Mechanics’ Savings Institution was invalid due to procedural issues, specifically the timing of the attachment's return. They argued that since the writ was not filed in compliance with the statutory requirements, the Institution had no right to claim proceeds from the attached property that was subject to the previously granted attachments and judgments.

In the case of George F. Forney v. John M. Thompson, decided on January 22, 1884, the dispute involved a sale transaction concerning a machine. The case arose from Ford County, Illinois, where George F. Forney, the plaintiff, alleged that John M. Thompson, the defendant, breached a warranty related to the machine sold to him. The key individuals involved in the case were Forney and Thompson, with their respective attorneys representing them in court. The trial court proceedings focused on whether the sale was absolute or conditional and whether there was any breach of warranty in the transaction. The jury's instructions during the trial were numerous and contradictory, leading to confusion regarding the proper legal standards applicable to the case.	George F. Forney argued that John M. Thompson had breached an implied warranty concerning the machine sold. He emphasized that the representations made during the sale constituted a warranty, and he sought damages for the alleged breach. Forney contended that the jury's verdict did not adequately reflect the damages he suffered due to Thompson's failure to fulfill the terms of the sale.	John M. Thompson defended against Forney's claims by asserting that there was no warranty attached to the sale of the machine. He argued that the statements made at the time of sale did not amount to a formal warranty and claimed that the jury's findings were not supported by sufficient evidence. Thompson maintained that he was not liable for the damages asserted by Forney and requested that the court affirm the jury's verdict or dismiss the claims against him.

In 1866, James L. Gillmore sought to purchase a mower from Burke, an agent of the defendants, Joseph K. Russell et al. Burke initially offered a "Russell mower" for $130, but after negotiations failed, Faulk, a third-party, intervened. Faulk agreed to buy the mower, mow a meadow, and then sell it to Gillmore for $125 after an offset of debts owed by Burke. After a year of use, the sickles on the mower broke, prompting Gillmore to seek assistance from Burke, who contacted the defendants’ general agent for replacement. However, after replacement sickles also broke, Gillmore became dissatisfied and left the mower in front of Burke's office. Subsequently, Gillmore filed a lawsuit seeking a refund for the purchase price of the mower, claiming a breach of warranty and failure to deliver a suitable machine.	Gillmore, as the plaintiff, argued that the mower was not functioning properly due to faulty parts, claiming a breach of warranty based on the understanding that the machine was suitable for purchase. He sought to recover the $125 he had paid for the mower, asserting that the defendants were responsible for the defects that rendered the mower unusable.	The defendants contended that Gillmore did not directly purchase the mower from them but from Faulk, and therefore there was no privity of contract between Gillmore and the defendants. They argued that Gillmore's claims were improperly framed under a general action of indebitatus assumpsit instead of a specific contract breach. Furthermore, they maintained that the issues with the mower were due to improper usage rather than defects in the machine itself. Consequently, they requested the court to dismiss Gillmore's claims.

The case "James H. Kennedy v. John H. Hall" took place in June 1873, in the Washington Circuit Court, Illinois. The key individuals involved were James H. Kennedy, who was one of the defendants, and John H. Hall, who was representing the plaintiff as the surviving partner of the firm Donaldson & Hall. The dispute arose from a promissory note dated June 2, 1858, which was produced by the firm Walker, Kennedy & Co. The note was for $67.80 and was signed by Washington Walker and Burrell and James Kennedy. The plaintiff, John H. Hall, brought the action of assumpsit against Kennedy and the other partners, claiming that they were liable for the amount stated in the note. During the trial, Kennedy filed a plea of non-assumpsit, asserting that he was not a partner in the firm and, thus, not liable for the note. The court ultimately instructed the jury that the burden of proof rested on Kennedy to demonstrate his non-partnership, which he contested.	The plaintiff, John H. Hall, argued that James H. Kennedy and his co-defendants, as partners in Walker, Kennedy & Co., were jointly liable for the payment of the promissory note. Hall contended that the partnership’s existence and mutual liability were established by the terms of the note. His legal request was a judgment ordering the defendants to fulfill their obligation under the note, thereby enforcing the payment to the firm of Donaldson & Hall.	The defendant, James H. Kennedy, challenged the claim by asserting a plea of non-assumpsit, which placed the existence of the partnership into question. He claimed that it was the plaintiff's burden to prove not only that he was a partner but also that he was liable as a joint maker of the promissory note. Kennedy argued that the trial court erred in shifting the burden of proof onto him, requiring him to demonstrate his non-partnership instead of the plaintiff demonstrating the existence of the partnership and subsequent liability.

In 1877, in Peoria, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Lorinda D. Smith and the children of John McClay Smith from his former marriage, Arthur McClay Smith et al. Lorinda D. Smith sought to foreclose a mortgage on real estate. She claimed that the mortgage was executed by John H. Morse and his wife to her, before her marriage, securing an indebtedness of $700. The plaintiffs contended that they, as John McClay Smith's heirs, were wrongfully deprived of the funds that rightfully belonged to their late mother. They alleged that their mother had lent the same $700 to John H. Morse, and John McClay Smith created a mortgage in his own name to secure those funds. After their mother’s death, John McClay Smith married Lorinda D. Smith, who allegedly compelled him to create a new mortgage to conceal the original transaction, effectively defrauding the plaintiffs of their inheritance. The case involved complex testimony regarding the ownership and legitimacy of the mortgage in question, with the circuit court initially ruling in favor of Lorinda D. Smith.	The plaintiffs claimed they were the rightful heirs to the $700 provided by their mother to John H. Morse, which was supposedly secured by a mortgage made in their father John McClay Smith's name. They argued that Lorinda D. Smith received the second mortgage to cover up a transfer of their inheritance and held the mortgage as a trustee for them. They sought a decree affirming their ownership of the funds and declaring the mortgage invalid since its consideration stemmed from money that rightfully belonged to them.	Lorinda D. Smith firmly contested the claims of the plaintiffs, asserting that the money for the mortgage was indeed hers, and she was the rightful owner as per the original agreement and transactions that occurred prior to her marriage to John McClay Smith. The defense maintained that there was no fraudulent intent in the creation of the mortgage and challenged the legitimacy of the plaintiffs' claims regarding the ownership of the funds.

The case "Ex parte George W. Thatcher" took place in December 1845 in Hancock County, Illinois, involving George W. Thatcher, the Clerk of the County Commissioners' Court. Following the submission of a claim for payment from the county treasury, Thatcher was ordered to enter this claim into the court records. After refusing to comply with this order, he was summoned to show cause for his refusal. When he failed to satisfy the court regarding his conduct, an order for his removal from office was issued. Thatcher appealed this order and provided the required bond, which paused the removal action. Amidst this, the court appointed George Edmonds as Thatcher's successor, prompting Thatcher to refuse to turn over the office's books and records. Consequently, an order for his commitment to jail for fifteen days was issued due to his contempt in not complying with the court's orders. The Sheriff, Backenstos, arrested him based on this commitment order. However, the facts presented in the court indicated significant procedural issues surrounding the removal and subsequent contempt ruling, leading to a profound examination of jurisdictional authority and the legality of the actions taken against Thatcher.	The plaintiff in this case is George W. Thatcher, who claims that the order for his removal from office was improper given that he had appealed the removal order, which should have put a hold on any such action. He argues that the County Commissioners' Court exceeded its authority by appointing a successor while he was appealing the removal, thereby making the contempt ruling for his non-compliance with the turnover of office materials invalid.	The defendant, represented indirectly through the actions of the County Commissioners' Court and their appointed clerk, George Edmonds, argues that Thatcher’s refusal to comply with court orders justified his contempt charge. They maintain that the court had the authority to appoint a new clerk, especially given Thatcher’s refusal to perform his duties, which they viewed as a violation of the court’s order.

The case of Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Amira Nelson took place in 1870, involving the Illinois Central Railroad and a passenger, Amira Nelson. On March 27, 1870, Nelson purchased a first-class ticket for a passenger journey from Ashley to Centralia and boarded a freight train, which is not typically permitted. Upon boarding, the conductor discovered that she had the wrong type of ticket and subsequently required her to disembark the train. The railroad had established regulations stating that individuals wishing to ride on freight trains must obtain specific tickets for that service, a regulation that Nelson contended was unreasonable. The main legal question revolved around the railroad's authority to enforce such regulations and the obligations it had towards passengers in terms of where they could board and disembark the freight train. The company maintained that it was within their rights to impose rules regarding ticket types and where passengers could be allowed on and off freight trains, especially if customary practices were followed.	Amira Nelson argued that her first-class ticket entitled her to travel on any train, including freight trains, and that the railroad's requirement for a special ticket violated this right. She sought recovery for injuries claimed to result from her wrongful ejection from the freight train.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company asserted that their requirement for specific tickets for freight train travel was reasonable and lawful. They argued that since passenger trains have different modes of operation and that the law does not require them to accommodate passengers on freight trains, they had the right to enforce their ticketing policies. The defense also contended that Nelson should have been removed from the train at an appropriate station, which they defined based on customary practices.

The case "Daniel Wann et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois, for the use of John Birk" took place in September 1870, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Daniel Wann and others, were wards under the guardianship of an appointed guardian who had leased their lands and failed to provide a required special bond to secure the proceeds from the lease for the benefit of the wards. The guardian had not accounted for the money received from the leasing of the land, resulting in the wards not receiving the funds they were entitled to as minors. The plaintiffs brought a suit against the sureties of the guardian's general bond to recover the lost rents. The circuit court found for the plaintiffs, rendering a judgment against the defendants for $8000. The defendants subsequently prosecuted a writ of error, disputing the court's ruling concerning the liability of the sureties under the guardian’s bond statutes.	The plaintiffs claimed that the sureties on the guardian's general bond should be held liable for the proceeds received by the guardian from the leasing of their lands, despite the guardian’s failure to execute a required special bond. They argued that the guardian's actions and the subsequent mishandling of the funds constituted a breach of the bond conditions, justifying their suit to recover the money owed to them.	The defendants contended that the special bond's requirement indicated that the liability for the proceeds from leased land was not covered by the general bond. They argued that the legislative intent in requiring the special bond implied the sureties on the general bond should not be liable for amounts related to the lease. They asserted that the plaintiffs had to follow specific legal requirements, such as settling with the probate court, before being able to maintain a suit on the bond.

In the case of The Andes Insurance Company v. Elias Shipman, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875, the central issue revolved around a fire that destroyed property insured under a policy issued by the Andes Insurance Company to Elias Shipman. The event occurred in Bloomington, Illinois, in the early hours of October 2, 1872. Shipman, the plaintiff, had secured an insurance policy on his distillery and related machinery worth $10,000. At the time of the fire, the policy stipulated that a watchman needed to be present on the premises, but there were contentions regarding the actual compliance with this stipulation. A jury trial in the McLean County Circuit Court concluded with a verdict in favor of Shipman for $10,825. Disputes arose over whether the absence of a watchman in specific buildings constituted a breach of contract, and whether Shipman misrepresented facts when obtaining the policy. Additionally, the court faced challenges regarding the admissibility of certain evidence from the defendant. Ultimately, the jury affirmed that while a watchman was present on the premises, the specifics of the watchman's position related to the insured property were vital to the case's outcome.	Elias Shipman claimed damages from The Andes Insurance Company for the destruction of his property by fire, arguing that he had complied with all conditions of the insurance policy, including maintaining a watchman on the premises during the time of repairs. He sought recovery of the insured amount, asserting that the property's value far exceeded the policy amount. Shipman maintained that the exclusions of evidence by the court regarding the property’s prior litigation were inappropriate and that the insurance company was liable despite the contractual clauses they emphasized as breaches.	The Andes Insurance Company contended that Shipman failed to comply with the insurance policy's requirement of having a watchman present specifically on the insured properties at the time of the fire. They argued that Shipman made misrepresentations when he obtained the insurance policy and insisted that the court incorrectly excluded evidence regarding the property's history related to litigation. Furthermore, they pointed to a contractual clause requiring a record of the watchman’s activities, which they claimed Shipman did not fulfill, as a basis for denying the insurance claim.

Juliet Pease, represented by her next friend Albert Morgan, initiated a legal action against Charles Hubbard, a constable, in December 1864 in Bureau County, Illinois. The case arose because Hubbard negligently allowed Kent, who had been arrested under a bastardy warrant filed by Pease, to escape. This case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after the Circuit Court sustained Hubbard’s demurrer against Pease's declaration. The central issue in this case was whether Hubbard, as an officer, could be held liable for the escape of the prisoner, which negatively impacted Pease, the mother of the illegitimate child. The court's decision was influenced by previous rulings that identified bastardy proceedings as civil matters, aimed at ensuring the father’s responsibility for supporting his child. The court ultimately examined the implications of Hubbard's negligence on Pease's legal rights and obligations regarding the care of her child.	Juliet Pease claimed that Charles Hubbard, by his negligence in allowing Kent to escape, was directly responsible for the financial burden she faced in supporting her illegitimate child. She argued that as the plaintiff in a bastardy proceeding, she had the right to seek damages from the constable for his failure to fulfill his duties, which resulted in her being left liable for the support of the child.	Charles Hubbard contended that he should not be held liable for the escape of Kent under the bastardy warrant. He maintained that the prosecution under the bastardy act was civil in nature, and thus, the legal responsibilities of officers in such matters did not extend to personal liability for escapes resulting from their actions or omissions.

On October 4th, 1835, in Edwardsville, Illinois, a legal case arose involving plaintiffs William G. Pinckard, David Pembroke, B. F. Long, Nathan C. D. Taylor, and Henry Long against the People of the State of Illinois. The plaintiffs were subject to a judgment related to a bond or recognisance, requiring their appearance to testify but they failed to appear on the set date. Consequently, their default was recorded, and a final judgment was rendered against them for the penalty stipulated in the recognisance, along with associated costs. The judgment was handed down during the November special term of the Madison Circuit Court in 1834 by Judge Theophilus W. Smith. Pinckard and his co-plaintiffs disputed the judgment and sought to overturn it, claiming that the appropriate legal process had not been followed concerning defaults on the recognisance.	The plaintiffs argued that the final judgment against them was irregular because, according to legal standards, a "scire facias" should have been issued instead of entering a final judgment immediately due to their failure to appear. They contended that the court should not have rendered a final judgment without affording them a proper opportunity to show cause for their non-appearance. Their primary legal request was to reverse the final judgment and remand the case for further proceedings based on procedural grounds.	The defendant, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, did not provide specific defenses in the case description. However, they maintained the validity of the judgment rendered against the plaintiffs due to their non-appearance. The absence of detailed arguments from the defendant implies a reliance on the initial court proceedings that resulted in the judgment.

The legal case "Andrew J. Thomas v. Thomas O. Rutledge et al. Trustees, etc." took place in January 1873, in LeRoy, McLean County, Illinois. The key individuals involved include Andrew J. Thomas, the plaintiff and pastor of the Cumberland Presbyterian Church, and Thomas O. Rutledge along with other trustees of the church. The case revolved around the construction of a church building, which cost approximately $3,600. The contractors refused to relinquish the completed building until they were paid, prompting Thomas to take personal responsibility for the outstanding amount. He claimed he paid $300 more than what he was reimbursed. The trial occurred without a jury, and the evidence presented was conflicting regarding whether the entire sum owed was collected and returned to Thomas. Ultimately, the circuit court found in favor of the defendants, leading Thomas to appeal the decision.	Andrew J. Thomas claimed that as pastor, he was unjustly left responsible for costs associated with the church building that he believes he shouldn't have to bear. His main argument was that he had paid a total of $300 more than what he had received back, asserting the trustees owed him for these excess payments. He requested the court to hold the trustees accountable for these funds.	The defendants, represented by Thomas O. Rutledge and other trustees, argued that admissions of certain congregation members could not be used as evidence against them since they were not parties in the case. They maintained that the building committee's admissions could not bind the trustees, as the committee served a limited purpose and did not have the authority to alter the trustees’ obligations. They requested that the court uphold the circuit court's decision, as they believed the trustee's actions were valid and justified.

In June 1874, Edward S. Wilson filed a lawsuit against David Miller in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a promissory note dated June 18, 1868, in the amount of $100, which was originally made by Miller to T. W. Barbour and subsequently endorsed to Wilson. The dispute centered on whether the note was valid, as Miller claimed it was obtained through fraud. During the trial, Miller testified that he never signed the note; rather, he had been approached by an individual who asked him to sign his name and address in a book, promising to send him a fork in return for his trouble. This individual never returned, and Miller denied ever agreeing to sign a note or purchase anything. Despite conflicting testimonies, the jury found in favor of David Miller, leading to the rejection of Wilson's motion for a new trial.	Edward S. Wilson, as the appellant, contended that the court should reverse the jury's verdict in favor of David Miller, asserting that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence. Wilson sought to recover the amount owed on the promissory note, claiming it was valid despite Miller's assertions.	David Miller, the appellee, defended against Wilson's claim by asserting that the execution of the promissory note was obtained through fraudulent means. Miller provided uncontradicted testimony that he did not actually sign the note and that he had merely provided his name for an unrelated purpose. He maintained that a promise made by Wilson about leaving the note with another individual was incorrect, and that the jury was justified in believing his account.

The case, titled "The People of the State of Illinois v. Madison y. Johnson et al.," was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1853. The background of the case stems from a judgment obtained by the State against an individual named Snyder. The state attempted to enforce this judgment through a garnishment process against Johnson, who was believed to hold funds for Snyder. Initially, a circuit court had dismissed the garnishment process. However, the State argued that it was entitled to garnishment, asserting that Johnson, as the garnishee, was holding funds owed to Snyder. Johnson contended that he had received a power of attorney from Snyder to collect money from another party, Bradley, and was directed to withhold a specific amount to satisfy a debt while forwarding the remainder to Snyder's half-brother in St. Louis. The legal question was whether the funds were rightfully attached and whether Johnson was chargeable for the money he held.	The State of Illinois claimed that it had the same rights as other judgment creditors and was entitled to garnishment of funds that Johnson held, which were expected to belong to Snyder. The State contended that the garnishee process was appropriate and that Johnson should be charged for the amount he was holding, as the garnishee's statement about the funds did not sufficiently prove that they were not owed to Snyder.	Johnson, the garnishee, argued that he was not indebted to Snyder and claimed that the money he received was intended for Snyder’s half-brother, not for Snyder himself. He maintained that he acted on the legal authority granted by Snyder and claimed he should not be charged as the funds were ostensibly designated for another individual, without clear title or acceptance for the funds from Snyder’s brother.

Samuel Davis and Mary Ann Davis were married on January 27, 1853, in Montgomery County, Illinois. Following their marriage, Mary Ann alleged that Samuel subjected her to extreme cruelty for over two years, including physical abuse and infidelity. Due to this abusive environment, she left their residence in March 1862. After filing for divorce, default was entered against Samuel at the September 1862 term of the Montgomery Circuit Court, as he failed to respond to the proceedings. The court appointed Joseph T. Eccles as a special master to take testimony regarding the case. The court found sufficient evidence to support Mary Ann's claims, leading to the decree of divorce along with decisions regarding alimony and custody of their two children.	Mary Ann Davis, the plaintiff, claimed that her husband, Samuel, had engaged in extreme and repeated cruelty, including physical abuse and adultery. She sought a divorce, alimony, and custody of their two children, citing her husband's violent behavior as the reason for her separation from him.	Samuel Davis, the defendant, challenged the validity of the divorce proceedings, claiming lack of jurisdiction and disputing the allegations of cruelty and infidelity. He argued that the charges against him were vague and not sufficiently substantiated. He requested that the default judgment be overturned and that he be allowed to present a defense against the claims made by Mary Ann.

On May 26, 1887, the County Court of Cook County, Illinois, appointed Mrs. G.B. Marsh as the guardian of Annie Barnes, a dependent girl, and ordered her commitment to the Illinois Industrial School for Girls in Chicago until she turns eighteen, unless otherwise discharged. On October 6, 1887, Annie's mother, Ida Barnes, motioned to amend the earlier commitment order, seeking to allow the court the power to vacate the previous orders regarding Annie's guardianship and commitment. The court granted this and set aside the original orders, replacing them with a commitment to a different school and appointing a new guardian. The Industrial School appealed the decision, claiming the amendment to the original order was made based on mere clerical error rather than judicial discretion. The case centers around the validity of the court’s ability to amend previous orders and whether sufficient evidence was provided to support such amendments.	The plaintiff, represented by the Illinois Industrial School, contended that the amended order issued on October 6, 1887, which set aside the original commitment and guardianship appointments, was improper. They argued that the court had no authority to substantially change its earlier decision regarding Annie's commitment. The plaintiff primarily requested that the appellate court reverse the amending order and uphold the original commitment and guardian appointment.	The defendant, represented by Ida Barnes, argued that the original order was amended due to an inadvertent mistake and that the court had the right to correct such errors. They maintained that the amendment was necessary to prevent unjust confinement and to allow for a more suitable guardianship arrangement. The defendant's defense hinged on the assertion that the previous orders did not accurately reflect the court’s intention or the facts at hand.

In the case of James M. Allen et al. v. John Hoffman, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, a former sheriff, John Hoffman, filed an action of debt against A. W. Kellogg for the use of the Excelsior Iron Works. The case centered around a replevin bond that Kellogg had executed, with James M. Allen acting as the surety. Allen was served with process but was absent during the trial, which led to a verdict in favor of Hoffman, resulting in a judgment against Allen for a substantial sum of $545.61 plus costs. After the judgment, Allen, through an attorney, sought to vacate the judgment and request a new trial, arguing that he had a valid defense that was not presented due to his absence and the misleading title under which the case appeared on the trial calendar. The defense was complicated by the fact that Allen's attorney failed to recognize the case on the calendar due to its misleading designation, which did not include Allen's name and was thought to pertain to a different matter. This misidentification, grounded in good faith, prevented both Allen and his attorney from attending the trial.	The plaintiff, John Hoffman, argued that a default judgment should be upheld against James M. Allen, as Allen failed to appear for the trial and had not provided valid reasons for his absence. Hoffman sought the enforcement of the judgment which included damages owed under the replevin bond and recovery of associated costs.	James M. Allen's principal defense was predicated on the claim that he had a meritorious argument regarding the damages awarded, which he could not present due to the mistaken identification of his case on the trial calendar. He contended that both he and his attorney had relied on the court's calendar, which misrepresented the name of the parties, thus leading to their absence and the resulting default judgment. Allen requested the court to vacate the judgment, asserting that the judgment was unjust due to his valid defense.

Richard P. Morgan et al. v. Louis M. Andrick is a legal case that was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1865. The case arose from a dispute between Richard P. Morgan and others (the plaintiffs) and Louis M. Andrick (the defendant) in the Superior Court of Chicago, Illinois. While the specific events leading to the case are not detailed, it is indicated that the current case is substantially similar to a previous case involving Morgan et al. against Roberts. This led to the court's consideration of the principles established in that earlier case when determining the resolution here.	The plaintiffs, Richard P. Morgan and others, likely asserted claims involving the reversal of a lower court’s decree that adversely affected them. They sought judicial relief by appealing the previous decision, arguing that the decree was unjust and should be overturned in light of similar precedents.	Louis M. Andrick, the defendant, presented his case in defense against the plaintiffs' claims. His legal representation worked to maintain the lower court's decree, arguing that it should stand. Specific defenses aren't provided, but they would typically focus on justifying the actions that led to the original ruling or establishing that the rule of law was correctly applied.

The case "The County of Montgomery v. Sanford Robinson" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1877. The case emerged from Montgomery County, Illinois, when Sanford Robinson sought compensation of $300 from the county. The basis of the claim was for expenses incurred in the pursuit and arrest of a horse thief named Barringer, who had stolen Robinson's horse and subsequently fled to North Carolina. After learning of Barringer’s arrest in North Carolina, Robinson obtained a requisition from the Illinois Governor to have Barringer returned. He appointed an agent, named White, to bring Barringer back, paying him $100 for the expenses related to this task. In June 1865, Montgomery County had passed an order offering a reward of $300 for the capture and conviction of horse thieves who had fled the county. The jury in the Montgomery Circuit Court found in favor of Robinson, leading to a motion for a new trial by the county due to claims concerning witness absence and the nature of the arrest, which were ultimately denied.	Sanford Robinson claimed that he should be awarded the $300 reward offered by Montgomery County for the successful pursuit and arrest of the horse thief who had stolen his horse. He argued that he had effectively engaged an agent, White, who acted on his behalf to apprehend the thief and return him for a trial, thus fulfilling the conditions stipulated in the county's reward order.	The County of Montgomery contested Robinson's claim, arguing that White acted independently and not as Robinson’s agent, and asserted that since the sheriff in North Carolina had detained Barringer, Robinson himself or an agent could not claim to have made an arrest. The county emphasized that Robinson did not technically apprehend the thief, urging that this should negate the validity of his claim for the reward.

On January 1, 1848, Edmund D. Taylor, Churchill Coffing, and Isaac D. Harmon formed a mercantile partnership in Peru, Illinois, under the name Harmon & Co. The partnership dissolved on September 30, 1850, when Harmon left, and Taylor and Coffing continued the business as Taylor & Coffing. According to their partnership agreement, their operations aimed to pay off debts owed by Harmon & Co. and reimburse the partners' capital. However, by May 17, 1851, it was revealed that Coffing owed Taylor and the business a significant debt of $18,340, which far exceeded their combined capital. To secure this debt, Coffing transferred property, including warehouses, to Taylor and Coffing, conditioned on his repayment within three years, with provisions allowing him to pay the debt by selling or mortgaging the properties. The partnership continued until April 27, 1852, when they formally dissolved, with Taylor agreeing to assume all debts and payments owed by Coffing in exchange for ownership of the partnership assets. Disputes arose over the interpretation of the dissolution agreement, particularly regarding the ownership of the indebted property and whether Coffing still had responsibilities connected to his debt after the dissolution.	Taylor claimed that following the dissolution of their partnership, he became the absolute owner of all properties and accounts related to Taylor & Coffing, including the debts owed to the firm by Coffing. He asserted that under the terms of their agreement, Coffing was obligated to repay the $13,340 that remained due after credits related to their operations. Taylor requested a judgment for this amount plus interest.	Coffing contended that the dissolution agreement protected him from any further liabilities regarding the debts associated with the partnership. He argued that by the terms of the dissolution, he should not be required to pay the debt represented by the indenture since it was understood that Taylor would assume all partnership debts. Coffing requested a dismissal of Taylor's claims asserting he owed nothing further.

The case of The Chicago Dredging and Dock Company v. Matthew McMahon took place in 1889 in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Matthew McMahon, was an employee working on a dredge operated by the Chicago Dredging and Dock Company. While carrying out his duties, he suffered a severe injury resulting in the loss of an arm. The jury determined that McMahon was exercising due care for his own safety when he was injured. The injury was attributed to commands given by a superior employee of the dredging company, who, despite having been warned of the inherent dangers, ordered McMahon to act in a way that led to his injury. This situation raised legal questions regarding employer liability for injuries caused by the negligence of fellow employees. The court's ruling revolved around the doctrine of negligence among fellow employees and the resulting responsibilities of the employer.	McMahon claimed that his injury was due to the negligence of a fellow employee, who, as a supervisor, provided an unsafe order that led to the accident. He argued that this negligence fell outside the general rule exempting employers from liability for injuries caused by fellow servants since the supervisor was exercising authority over his co-laborers when the order was given. The plaintiff sought damages for his injuries, claiming that the dredging company was responsible for the actions of its employees under these circumstances.	The Chicago Dredging and Dock Company contended that they were not liable for McMahon's injuries since the accident was caused by the negligence of a fellow employee, which is generally not the employer's responsibility under the law. They maintained that the company had taken necessary precautions by hiring competent workers and claimed that McMahon, being knowledgeable about the risks associated with his position, should share responsibility for his injury. The defense argued that the evidence did not demonstrate sufficient grounds for the verdict against them, particularly in light of the protections offered under the fellow servant rule.

In December 1846, the case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court concerning The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. Daniel S. Harris and others against Thomas C. Browne, a judge. The case originated from the Jo Daviess Circuit Court in 1842, where Daniel S. Harris and others were plaintiffs against John H. Rountree and others. During the trial, the plaintiffs voluntarily took a nonsuit, essentially withdrawing their case. Subsequently, the plaintiffs requested Judge Browne to sign and seal a bill of exceptions, which is a formal statement of the objections lodged during the trial, so they could appeal the court's prior rulings. However, Judge Browne refused to sign the bill of exceptions since the plaintiffs had already taken a voluntary nonsuit during the trial. This refusal prompted the plaintiffs to seek a peremptory writ of mandamus from the Illinois Supreme Court to compel Browne to sign the document.	The plaintiffs primarily argued that they were entitled to have the bill of exceptions signed and sealed by Judge Browne, which they believed was necessary for them to appeal the court's prior decisions. They contended that Judge Browne's refusal to sign the bill was unlawful and unjust, particularly since it prevented them from holding the judge accountable for any potential errors made during the trial. They sought the court’s intervention through a peremptory writ of mandamus to ensure compliance from the judge.	Judge Browne's defense centered on the assertion that since the plaintiffs voluntarily took a nonsuit during the trial, they effectively exited the court system and could not thereafter seek to file a bill of exceptions. He maintained that the law did not allow a party to take a nonsuit and still demand actions that would reserve their rights for appeal. Browne argued that allowing such an appeal would create an unfair advantage for plaintiffs who could withdraw their cases and still challenge court decisions without consequence.

In September 1874, the case of William S. Moss v. Louisa McCall et al. was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court after originating in the Peoria Circuit Court. The case involves a dispute among former partners from the firm Moss, Bradley & Co., established in 1853, which engaged in milling and distillery businesses. Key individuals in this case include William S. Moss, Louisa McCall (the administratrix of Tobias Bradley's estate), Perry Frazer, and James H. McCall. The partnership saw changes over the years, including Frazer joining in 1856 after purchasing a one-fourth interest. Conflicts arose regarding the interpretation of the partnership agreement, particularly concerning the charging and crediting of interest on individual partner accounts. The court's analysis focused on whether there was a subsequent agreement to alter the original terms concerning interest, which played a crucial role in the claims made by the plaintiffs, who sought to settle financial equity between themselves and Moss, leading to a decree against him claiming he owed over $82,000.	The plaintiffs, James H. McCall and Perry Frazer, argued that Moss was liable to pay for alleged mismanagement and that a proper accounting of partnership profits and losses required charging interest on individual accounts, as established through unwritten agreements among the partners. They requested a settlement of the outstanding financial equities due to the complex nature of their partnership dealings, relying on historical records and testimonies to support their claims.	Moss contended that no substantial evidence of an agreement to charge interest on individual accounts was proven and that the original partnership agreement did not include such provisions. He argued that the calculations presented in court were flawed and asserted the need for a detailed and clear accounting process, suggesting the complexity of partnership transactions warranted referral to a master to resolve these claims accurately.

Gabriel Gunderson v. Sigwald Peterson took place in September 1872 at the Illinois Supreme Court. The case concerns an incident that occurred in April 1871 when Gabriel Gunderson was serving as the second mate on the schooner Monitauk, owned by Sigwald Peterson. While performing his duties, Gunderson ascended the mainmast of the vessel, which was alleged to be defective—specifically, it was claimed to be split, twisted, and unsafe. During his ascent, the mast broke, causing Gunderson to fall onto the deck, resulting in significant injuries. He subsequently filed a lawsuit against Peterson, asserting that the injuries were due to the negligence of the defendant for allowing the unsafe mast to be used. A trial ensued, leading to a verdict in favor of Gunderson with a judgment of $450 awarded for his injuries.	Gunderson contended that Peterson was negligent by failing to maintain the safety of the mainmast on the Monitauk, which had been known to be twisted and defective. He argued that this negligence directly caused the mast to break while he was performing his duties, leading to his fall and subsequent injuries. Gunderson sought damages for the personal injuries incurred due to this alleged negligence.	Peterson's defense challenged the claims of negligence by demonstrating that the alleged defects in the mast were at least 12 feet away from the actual break point, which was sound and showed no signs of decay. The defense argued that the accident was not a result of any negligence but was rather an incident related to the service under conditions of strong winds, which led to the mast breaking. They requested the court to reverse the judgment in favor of the plaintiff.

John Crabtree and James B. Crawford were involved in a legal dispute in 1861 related to a transaction involving the purchase of two horses. On March 22, 1858, Crabtree purchased the horses from a man named Blackburn for $500, to be paid in lumber, with half the amount due by June and the rest by September of the same year. One of the horses was reported to be lame, and Blackburn had warranted that it would recover. After receiving possession of the horses, Crabtree let Rankin and Wiley take the lame horse, who issued a note to Blackburn for $250, with Crabtree simultaneously giving a note for the remaining half of the purchase price. However, claims arose that the horse had not recovered, raising issues of breach of warranty. The case was evaluated on the basis of whether Crabtree could defend against the enforcement of his note by claiming the warranty was breached. The court found that no objections were made when the notes were given, and thus Crabtree had waived any claims.	The plaintiff, James B. Crawford, as the assignee of the promissory note, argued that Crabtree was liable on a $250 note due to his agreement during the horse transaction. Crawford sought the enforcement of the note on the basis that Crabtree had fully entered into the agreement without objections regarding the condition of the horses or the warranty after the time of purchase.	The defendant, John Crabtree, contended that there was a breach of warranty regarding the horse's lameness. He argued that since the horse did not recover as warranted, he should be able to recoup damages from the amount owed on the note. Crabtree claimed that the circumstances surrounding the warranty created grounds for his defense against the payment of the promissory note.

In the spring of 1884, the Town of Houston's commissioners of highways levied a poll tax of $1.50 against John W. Sherrick for road purposes. Sherrick refused to pay the tax, leading the commissioners to file a suit against him in a justice of the peace court. The case was then appealed to the Circuit Court, where a jury trial resulted in a verdict that required Sherrick to pay the tax. Sherrick's defense centered on his claim that he was not an "able-bodied" man due to a wound he received during the Battle of Chickamauga, which had caused lasting damage to his leg. Seven medical experts testified that his injury prevented him from performing labor without risking his health, while others asserted he was indeed capable of such work. The court's jury was instructed that an "able-bodied" man was someone who could ordinarily perform the labor of able-bodied workers on public roads, which they interpreted to apply to Sherrick despite his injuries. Other technical objections raised by Sherrick regarding the tax's assessment process were deemed unsubstantial by the court.	The plaintiff, John W. Sherrick, contended that he was physically unable to perform road labor due to debilitating injuries sustained in battle. He requested exemption from the poll tax, arguing that the legal definition of "able-bodied" should not apply to him given his medical condition. Sherrick sought to prove that the tax was unjustly levied as he did not meet the criteria for those required to perform labor.	The Town of Houston argued that Sherrick was, in fact, an "able-bodied" man under the legal definition applicable to the case, as established by the jury instruction. They presented evidence that contradicted Sherrick's claims of incapacity, including testimonies of individuals who observed him working on his farm. Additionally, they asserted that any technical objections regarding the tax's assessment process were minor and properly overruled, affirming the legitimacy of the tax.

Richard J. Kehoe filed a legal action in May 1883 in the Illinois Circuit Court concerning his role as a trustee for certain personal property that was bequeathed to him by John W. Kehoe shortly before his death. The bequest was based on oral instructions, which specified that the funds should be utilized for procuring masses for the souls of John W. Kehoe and his deceased mother. The defendant parties, representing the legal interests of the deceased, challenged the validity of the trust. They argued that the trust was void because it was not entirely documented in writing and was granted for what they labeled as a superstitious purpose, according to English common law. The case centered on interpreting the statute of frauds as it related to trusts involving personal property and the judicial view of religious bequests, especially those deemed superstitious. The legal context included historical references to English statutes that declared such bequests invalid.	The plaintiff, Richard J. Kehoe, contended that the oral trust regarding the bequest should be honored, asserting that the statute of frauds does not apply to trusts of personal property. He sought judicial instruction on how to execute his responsibilities as a trustee, emphasizing that honoring the donor's wishes aligns with the principles of religious freedom and constitutional rights.	The defendants asserted that the trust was void for two main reasons: first, it was not entirely in writing, violating the statute of frauds; and second, it was established for a superstitious purpose, where the funds were intended to pay for masses, contravening common law principles. They argued that the traditional English legal stance on this matter should be adopted by the court.

In early 1865, in the town of Fox, Kendall County, Illinois, several taxpayers, including Wesley Misner and others, filed a bill to restrain the collection of a special town tax aimed at paying bounties to volunteers who would enlist and fill the town's quota of soldiers. Following a notice from the town clerk on January 23, 1865, a special meeting was held on February 3, where citizens voted to approve a tax for the stated purpose. The outcome was overwhelmingly in favor, with 58 votes for and only 4 against the tax. Subsequently, the board of auditors certified debts incurred for paying bounties and determined a 3% tax should be levied on all taxable property to cover the $7,900 owed. In September 1865, while J. Murray Bullard, the town collector, was set to collect this tax, the plaintiffs sought an injunction to halt the collection, claiming they were not liable for the draft and questioning the authority under which the tax was levied. The court eventually dissolved the injunction, leading to further legal action whereby the plaintiffs appealed the decision.	The plaintiffs argued that the tax was improperly levied since most of them were over 45 years old and therefore not subject to the draft. They also asserted that the town auditors lacked the authority to approve the tax for a purpose they contended was not a legitimate town purpose. Furthermore, they sought to establish that the law enabling the tax was unconstitutional and requested the court to enjoin its collection.	J. Murray Bullard, representing the defense, acknowledged the facts presented by the plaintiffs but countered that the funds collected from the tax were necessary to repay the loans advanced for the bounties. Bullard also communicated that the tax was duly authorized by law, which allowed for taxes to cover indebtedness due to bounties paid to volunteers. Furthermore, he sought to recover $100 for attorney fees incurred due to the plaintiffs' wrongful filing of the injunction.

Bartholomew Van Valkenburgh v. Lucien Peyton is a legal case originating from a lease dispute in La Salle, Illinois, in April 1838. Van Valkenburgh leased a farm from Peyton for a term concluding on September 1, 1838, with a lease agreement requiring him to pay fifty dollars upfront and conditions to maintain the property and not to sub-let without permission. After the lease term, Van Valkenburgh surrendered the property to Peyton but had previously sub-let portions of it, thus allowing others to cultivate crops, including a stack of oats. In the spring, Peyton, having threshed and sold these oats, faced a trespass suit initiated by Van Valkenburgh claiming ownership. The Circuit Court sided with Peyton, asserting that Van Valkenburgh's sub-letting violated the lease terms. Van Valkenburgh appealed this decision.	Van Valkenburgh argued that the oats, which he cultivated, belonged to him and that he had the right to remove them post-lease. He claimed that Peyton had no grounds to appropriate his property, contending that the lease lacked any forfeiture clause regarding violations. Thus, he sought damages for the property taken without his consent.	Peyton contended that Van Valkenburgh's violation of the lease provisions by sub-letting the premises entitled him to the oats, arguing that Van Valkenburgh forfeited his rights to the property. He asserted that because of this breach, he was justified in selling the oats to cover his losses.

In 1884, in Chicago, David Launder, a licensed pawnbroker, faced a legal challenge from the City of Chicago regarding the violation of section 1713 of the city’s municipal ordinances. This section mandated that licensed pawnbrokers report to the police superintendent daily on their business transactions, including detailed descriptions of all pledged items. Launder had been operating his business for eighteen years and had always complied with prior regulations. However, he refused to adhere to this new ordinance, arguing that it was unreasonable and would severely impact his business. The case began in the Criminal Court of Cook County, where Launder was found guilty and fined $10. This decision was upheld by the Appellate Court, prompting Launder to take the case to the Illinois Supreme Court for appeal.	The City of Chicago claimed that Launder violated section 1713 of the municipal code, which required him to report daily on his pawn transactions.
