The city argued that the ordinance was a lawful exercise of police power aimed at preventing crime and maintaining public order. The plaintiff sought affirmation of the lower court’s ruling and the enforcement of the ordinance against Launder.	Launder contended that the ordinance was unjust, unreasonable, and oppressive, arguing that it imposed excessive burdens on his business and did not provide fair authority for the city to enact such regulations. He maintained that the required disclosures would harm his business practices and that he had complied with other relevant ordinances, indicating that the strict reporting requirement was unnecessary. Launder's key argument was an assertion that the ordinance made him guilty of a penal offense without due cause.

The St. Louis, Alton & Chicago Railroad Company v. Joseph A. Dalby is a legal case that dates back to December 1857, and it took place in Illinois. The plaintiff, Joseph A. Dalby, and his wife attempted to travel from Elkhart to Lincoln on a train operated by the railroad company. The case arose when Dalby attempted to purchase a ticket but was informed by William Rankin, the station agent, that there were no tickets available. Rankin provided Dalby with a written statement as proof of his attempt to obtain a ticket, which Dalby later presented to the conductor. Upon boarding the train, the conductor demanded fare payment of four cents per mile, which Dalby refused, asserting that he had already offered the fare as per the ticket price of three cents. In response, the conductor and two brakemen attempted to forcibly remove Dalby from the train, leading to a violent confrontation. Witnesses testified that Dalby was assaulted during the removal process, resulting in significant injuries. The case focused on the liability of the railroad company for the actions of its employees and whether a corporation could be held liable for assault and battery committed by its agents.	Joseph A. Dalby asserted that the railroad company was liable for the assault and battery he experienced at the hands of its conductor and brakemen while he was a passenger on the train. He argued that he had attempted to purchase a ticket and was not at fault for not having it. Dalby contended that the company's actions and the way its agents behaved constituted a violation of his rights, and he sought damages for the injuries and suffering he endured as a result of the assault.	The St. Louis, Alton & Chicago Railroad Company defended against the claims by asserting the following arguments: they maintained that as a common carrier, they had the right to charge a higher fare for passengers who failed to produce tickets. The company claimed that Dalby refused to pay the fare and thereby warranted removal from the car, arguing the conductor was acting within his rights. Additionally, the railroad company argued that they were not responsible for any excess force used by their employees, interpreting such acts as personal rather than representative of the company.

In the case of Carlos A. Cook v. Elizabeth J. Norwood, the events took place in Chicago, Illinois, with the legal proceedings starting on July 19, 1881. The case revolved around a promissory note dated March 31, 1881, in the amount of $2500, issued by Carlos A. Cook. The initial payees were Lawrence & Martin, who allegedly assigned the note to the United States Distilling Company before maturity, which was then assigned to the plaintiff, Elizabeth J. Norwood. The defendant, Cook, claimed that the note was executed without consideration and merely as an accommodation for the payees, asserting that the United States Distilling Company was aware of this lack of consideration at the time of assignment. Additionally, Cook emphasized that Lawrence & Martin's insolvency and a subsequent compromise affected his liability on the note. Throughout the litigation, various procedural motions were made, including requests for continuances and challenges to the admissibility of evidence. The Superior Court's rulings, including the decision to strike a demurrer filed by the defendant, were ultimately upheld by the Illinois Supreme Court.	Elizabeth J. Norwood, the plaintiff, claimed that she was a legitimate holder of the promissory note, acquired before its maturity and for value. She contended that the execution and assignment of the note were valid, asserting that Cook's defenses against the assignment were not admissible due to her lack of notice regarding any potential defenses at the time of the note's assignment.	Carlos A. Cook, the defendant, argued that the promissory note was invalid due to a lack of consideration, asserting it was merely an accommodation for Lawrence & Martin. He claimed that the United States Distilling Company had notice of this fact at the time of the note's transfer and that the assignment occurred after the maturity of the note. Cook sought to demonstrate that he had been released from liability based on a compromise agreement between Lawrence & Martin and their creditors, which he contended should affect the enforcement of the note.

In April 1860, in Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving Ezekiel S. Smith and Henry A. Mix as plaintiffs and Elisha Doty as the defendant. The plaintiffs appealed from a decision of the Ogle Circuit Court which had sustained a demurrer to the defendant's pleas concerning a promissory note for four hundred dollars. The plaintiffs claimed that Doty failed to pay this note, which had been delivered to him as part of a larger transaction involving another promissory note from one Dan Higly, purportedly worth eight hundred dollars. The defendant's plea asserted that the note was void due to lack of consideration, alleging that the Higly note was fraudulently represented as valid and collectible by the plaintiffs. The circuit court found that the defendant's claims did not sufficiently demonstrate a failure of consideration, leading to the sustained demurrer. As a result, the plaintiffs were allowed to recover damages and costs. The ruling was contested by the defendant, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that the promissory note in question was valid, supported by adequate consideration. They contended that the defendant's claims regarding the lack of consideration were insufficient and that the pleas did not demonstrate a valid legal defense. The plaintiffs requested the court to rule in their favor, allowing for the collection of the owed amount plus costs.	The defendant's main argument claimed that the promissory note had been given without valid consideration, as the underlying note from Higly was misrepresented to be valid and collectible. The defense asserted that the lack of consideration for the Higly note nullified the legitimacy of the note against which this action was brought. The defendant requested to dismiss the case based on these assertions.

The case "Edmund S. Holbrook et al. v. The Trustees of Schools of Township 33 North, Range 1 East of Third Principal Meridian" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1862. The case arises from a legal dispute involving the search for a lost bond which was supposed to be maintained by the School Commissioner. The appellants, led by Edmund S. Holbrook, argued that adequate notice was given to produce the bond, which was not found in the appropriate office where it was expected to be kept. The key individuals involved were Holbrook and the officials of the school trustees. The court reviewed a previous judgment related to the admissibility of evidence regarding the bond's existence and the sufficiency of the search conducted to locate it.	The plaintiffs, represented by E. S. Holbrook, claimed that sufficient notice had been provided regarding the bond and that they were entitled to introduce secondary evidence regarding its contents. They argued that the failure to produce the bond was due to negligence or oversight by the School Commissioner.	The defendants, represented by Glover, Cook & Campbell, contended that the search for the missing bond was inadequate and not thorough enough to justify the introduction of secondary evidence. They argued that there should be demonstrable proof of a comprehensive search in the office, which had not been satisfactorily provided.

On April 7, 1883, in Madison County, Illinois, Horace Fairbanks and Company sold a pump and boiler to Henry Malloy for $388. The terms included a $200 payment within thirty days and the balance to be paid in one year with interest. Over time, the boiler and pump were exchanged for larger models, resulting in an additional $125 charge. Malloy made one payment of $200 but subsequently failed to pay the remaining $313. The parties had executed written contracts that specified Fairbanks retained title to the equipment until full payment was made, allowing them to reclaim the equipment upon default. Initially, Malloy claimed the equipment failed to perform as expected, testifying that the pumps could not effectively remove water from his coal mine. Fairbanks contended that any issues arose from Malloy's mishandling and that they had warned him to choose a more powerful pump. After trial by court without a jury, judgment was rendered in favor of Malloy, leading Fairbanks to appeal, alleging errors in the trial court's rulings.	The plaintiffs, Horace Fairbanks and Company, claimed they were entitled to reclaim the pump and boiler because Malloy had defaulted on payments under their contracts. They argued that the contracts expressly allowed them to retain title to the property until full payment was made and that upon Malloy's default, they were entitled to retrieve the property without returning previous payments.	The defendant, Henry Malloy, contended that the pumps and boiler were unfit for the purpose intended, asserting warranty claims for their performance in draining water from his coal mine. He argued that Fairbanks had made verbal warranties regarding the effectiveness of the equipment, thus asserting that Fairbanks should not have been allowed to reclaim the property without compensating him for the unfulfilled promises.

In May 1886, the case of James Todd v. City of Chicago was assessed by the Illinois Appellate Court. The incident that initiated this case occurred on July 23, 1831, when Mary Wells fell into an open excavation in front of a building owned by James Todd, who was in the process of erecting the structure at that time. The excavation was allowed beneath the sidewalk to facilitate the building's construction; however, it was improperly left without adequate protection, resulting in Wells' injury. The City of Chicago had given Todd a permit for the construction but the permit did not explicitly authorize the excavation work. After the incident, the city was held liable and paid damages to Wells, prompting it to seek recovery from Todd for the amount it had paid out, arguing that Todd's negligence in not ensuring the excavation was covered or guarded was the cause of the injury. The case highlighted the legal obligations of an owner when construction is in progress, particularly regarding the safety of public access around such works.	The City of Chicago, as the plaintiff, claimed that James Todd was responsible for the unsafe condition in front of his property, which led to Mary Wells' injury. The city argued that Todd, by allowing the excavation to remain uncovered, failed to protect the public from potential harm, thereby rendering him liable. The city sought to recover the amount it paid in damages to Wells, contending that the judgment it paid was based on Todd's negligence.	James Todd, the defendant, contended that he could not be held liable because the work was being performed by multiple contractors and he did not have full control over the construction site at the time of the accident. Todd argued that the contractors responsible for covering the excavation had not yet begun their work, and therefore he should not be held responsible for the accident. He claimed that the city was wrongly assigning liability to him, given the shared responsibilities among contractors.

In September 1867, the legal case of Mahlon B. Lloyd v. John Karnes took place in the Circuit Court of Henry County, Illinois. The dispute originated from a foreclosure action filed by John Karnes against Mahlon B. Lloyd and others, concerning a mortgage executed by Thomas F. Davenport and his wife to Francis Karnes in 1857. The mortgage secured three promissory notes of $2,000 each, due in 1859, 1860, and 1861. The mortgage covered three tracts of land in Henry County. The case became complicated when, in 1862, a prior mortgage on the same property, held by Joshua Harper, was foreclosed, leading to a sale where another party, Thomas Mellon, acquired the property. Amendments to the property claims followed, including quitclaim deeds and a judgment against Davenport. The appellant Lloyd asserted that he had successfully redeemed the property under a statutory right, claiming superior title denied to the mortgagee, Karnes. During the proceedings, both parties presented their relevant claims and defenses, with the court ultimately tasked with determining the superior right to the property.	John Karnes, as the plaintiff, argued that Mahlon B. Lloyd's redemption of the property was invalid, asserting that Lloyd should have settled the entirety of the first mortgage obligations before attempting to redeem the property. Karnes insisted that once he had the legal title, Lloyd could not claim superior rights as a judgment creditor. Furthermore, Karnes contended that because he had taken an unrecorded assignment of the certificate of purchase, his rights should be preserved, and Lloyd’s actions did not extinguish the second mortgage.	Mahlon B. Lloyd, as the defendant, maintained that his redemption of the property through execution and payment was legitimate and that he had complied with the statutes governing redemption. Lloyd argued that since he had settled the purchasing bid and obtained a sheriff’s deed, he held the paramount title to the premises, irrespective of the second mortgage held by Karnes. He contended that Karnes had neither recorded his claims nor properly exercised his rights, rendering Karnes's attempts to enforce the mortgage ineffective.

The case "Annie E. Nichols v. Homer E. Sargent" took place in Cook County, Illinois, and was decided on February 2, 1887. The proceedings were presided over by Honorable Judge Joseph E. Gary in the Superior Court. The case revolved around a legal dispute involving Annie E. Nichols as the plaintiff against Homer E. Sargent as the defendant. While the details of the specific incidents leading to the lawsuit are not provided in the summary, it is noted that the court carefully examined the record in the case to determine the appropriateness of the lower court's findings and rulings. The court expressed confidence that no errors were committed by the lower court, affirming the overall proceedings without the need for a detailed analysis of the evidence presented.	Annie E. Nichols, as the appellant, claimed that the court below made errors in its judgment regarding her case. She requested a review of the trial court's decisions, asserting that the findings were not substantiated by the evidence and challenging the legal principles applied in the case.	Homer E. Sargent, as the appellee, argued that the findings of the initial court were fully supported by the evidence presented. He maintained that the lower court did not err in its judgment or in the legal propositions that were submitted. Sargent sought to have the appellate court affirm the initial ruling without modification.

On May 1, 1865, William Evans entered into a partnership with Ralph Hanson and John M. Moore in a general produce and commission business in Chicago, operating under the firm name Hanson, Evans and Moore. The partnership agreement stipulated that the total capital would be $25,000, split evenly between the partners. Evans was responsible for employing his brother to manage the business, and there were strict rules regarding withdrawals from the partnership's earnings. Over time, it was found that the capital contributions were unequal, with Hanson and Moore contributing $10,850.34 and Evans contributing $10,235.08. As the partnership progressed, disputes arose regarding financial settlements after Evans decided to withdraw, leading him to draw a total of $12,295.19 from the firm. After his departure, Hanson and Moore liquidated the partnership's remaining assets and incurred various expenses for closing the business, which they sought to recover from Evans. The Superior Court of Chicago subsequently ruled that Evans owed payments to Hanson and Moore based on the overstated amounts he had received from the partnership upon dissolution.	Hanson and Moore claimed that Evans had overdrawn his share of the partnership assets upon withdrawing and sought a financial accounting to settle the partnership’s accounts. They argued that Evans owed them $1,683.27 after adjusting for various business expenses they incurred while closing the firm and other financial discrepancies related to the partnership's assets.	Evans contended that the court erred in attributing the $2,000 he paid to join the partnership to Hanson and Moore. He sought to have that sum recognized as his property rather than as an asset belonging to his partners. Additionally, he challenged the court's assessment of the partnership's financial obligations, claiming that other claimed expenses should not have been charged to him and requested the reversal of the lower court’s decree.

John H. Strong brought a legal action against George B. Leoffler in January 1877 in the Circuit Court of Champaign County, Illinois. The case centered on a dispute involving a promissory note. Strong alleged that Leoffler had defaulted on the payment of this note. Leoffler's defense revolved around the assertion that Strong had provided the note as part payment for several tax certificates that Strong had sold and assigned to him. Leoffler claimed that Strong made various express warranties regarding the condition and legitimacy of these tax certificates, contending that these warranties were false. The jury found that Leoffler's allegations of express warranty did not hold up under scrutiny. The court subsequently reviewed the evidence and determined that the implications of warranty in terms of the tax certificates were more limited than Leoffler suggested, which ultimately led to the legal conclusion of the case.	The main argument presented by John H. Strong, the plaintiff, was that George B. Leoffler had defaulted on the promissory note. Strong sought a judgment for the amount due under the note, along with interest. He claimed that the note was valid and enforceable and contested Leoffler's defenses regarding the tax certificates.	George B. Leoffler, the defendant, argued that the promissory note was linked to tax certificates that Strong had sold to him, for which Strong had allegedly made warranties. Leoffler contended that these warranties were false, particularly regarding the validity of the tax certificates and the assessments tied to them. He argued for dismissal of the claim on the grounds that Strong did not fulfill the implied responsibilities associated with the sale of these certificates.

In 1868, in Illinois, Arthur Dempsey, Jr., was indicted for the murder of Benjamin Rainey. Initially charged in Washington Circuit Court, the venue was moved to Randolph County, where his trial commenced in September 1867 but resulted in a hung jury. Dempsey was subsequently released on bail. In April 1868, a second trial was conducted, leading to a conviction and a death sentence for Dempsey. A key testimony in the trial came from Lewis W. Jackson, who claimed to have been hired by Dempsey to kill Rainey. Jackson stated that he shot Rainey while he was plowing in a field. During the proceedings, a juror sought validation from an unsworn bystander about Jackson’s statement regarding his travel through Georgetown, which led to controversy regarding the admissibility of unsworn evidence in capital cases. Dempsey's defense claimed that this unsworn testimony was improperly allowed, potentially influencing the jury’s decision and violating Dempsey’s rights to a fair trial. The court must address various claims and procedural issues related to the trial.	The plaintiff, Arthur Dempsey, Jr., asserted several errors in his trial, contending that the introduction of unsworn testimony from a juror regarding Lewis W. Jackson's statements was a violation of legal principles and unfairly prejudiced the jury against him. Dempsey claimed that he had been denied a fair trial, which is crucial given the gravity of a capital case. He argued that the trial court should have excluded the unsworn testimony, regardless of any lack of objection from him, as capital defendants retain all their rights in such matters. He also questioned the validity of being indicted for murder as an accessory before the fact rather than being solely held accountable as the principal.	The defense, representing the People of the State of Illinois, maintained that the evidence presented during the trial was sufficient to uphold the conviction. They argued that the unsworn testimony, although problematic, was not damaging enough to have influenced the jury's decision significantly. Additionally, the prosecution likely contended that the nature of Dempsey's actions qualified him to be indicted as a principal, as Illinois law permits this practice. The defense sought to uphold the jury’s verdict and argued against the claims raised by Dempsey regarding the trial procedures.

In June 1868, the case of Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Peter Carraher was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident took place near a railway in Alexander County, Illinois. Peter Carraher, the plaintiff, claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent by allowing an uncovered well to exist near their right of way. According to the evidence presented, Carraher rode his mule near the railroad tracks and the mule fell into the well, resulting in its death. The plaintiff argued that the company should be held responsible for the loss as they had a duty to ensure the safety of their right of way. However, evidence was presented that suggested the well it was unclear if the well was indeed on the railroad's property or if the company had any knowledge of it.	Peter Carraher alleged that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent for allowing an uncovered well to exist near their right of way, which led to the death of his mule. He argued that the railroad company had a duty to cover or secure such dangerous openings on their property to prevent harm to animals.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company countered that they could not be held liable for negligence because the well was not dug by them and was unknown to them. They argued that there was no statutory or common law requirement obligating them to cover wells or ensure safety against such hazards, especially since the well was situated beyond their immediate knowledge of the right of way.

Dudley Laycock filed a legal action against Severin Oleson in September 1871 in Livingston County, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute over the sale of a lot of corn, which Laycock, acting as the administrator of the estate of the deceased Hannah Laycock, claimed was sold to Oleson. The contention was that the plaintiff had the right to recover the value of the corn due to the sale made during the administration of the estate. The case initially began before a justice of the peace and was later tried in the circuit court, where the defendant argued that Laycock needed to prove he was the administrator of Hannah Laycock's estate to proceed with the claim. The trial court accepted this instruction, leading to a further appeal on the grounds that the description used (administrator) did not necessitate proof.	The plaintiff, Dudley Laycock, argued that as the appointed administrator for Hannah Laycock's estate, he had the legal right to sue for the price of the corn sold to Severin Oleson. He maintained that the references to him as administrator in the suit were merely descriptive and did not require him to prove his capacity to act as an administrator during the proceedings.	The defendant, Severin Oleson, contended that Laycock had not sufficiently proven his status as the administrator of Hannah Laycock's estate. Oleson's defense hinged on an instruction given to the jury that stipulated the necessity for the plaintiff to produce evidence of his administrator status to win the case, suggesting that without such proof, they should find in favor of the defendant.

William B. Miller and John T. Finch were involved in a legal dispute regarding a lease agreement for a farm in Henry County, Illinois. The lease was signed for one year, starting March 1, 1880, wherein Miller agreed to pay Finch $360 for renting eighty acres of farmland, which included twenty-two acres of pasture and fifty-eight acres cultivated in grain. The lease contained an option for Miller to extend the rental for two additional years for the same amount or to pay rent in the form of two-fifths of the grain harvested. Miller opted for the grain rent and delivered the agreed-upon amount for the year 1882. However, Finch claimed additional rent for the twenty-two acres that were not cultivated in grain, accusing Miller of underpayment based on the pasture land and building grounds not specified in their written lease. The case was appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court, where the legal interpretations of the lease terms were debated, particularly regarding the entitlement to the entire farm versus just the cultivated land.	Finch, as the plaintiff, claimed that Miller was liable for additional rent for the twenty-two acres of pasture land that were not included in the grain rent agreement. He sought to recover cash rent at the rate of $4.50 per acre for this land, arguing that the written lease did not adequately express that the entire farm was to be rented solely for the grain rent.	Miller, the defendant, contended that the lease agreement clearly stipulated that the entire eighty acres were rented under the grain rent arrangement for the second and third years. He argued that Finch’s claim for additional rent was not supported by the terms of the lease, which only included the rental for the grain produced. Miller requested that the initial demurrer to Finch's claim be sustained to dismiss it based on these arguments.

In September 1867, the case of William T. Shufeldt and George A. Shufeldt v. John Buckley, Jr. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a prior action of debt in New York, where Buckley had obtained a judgment against the Shufeldts in November 1856 for damages amounting to $97.82 and additional costs of $42.38. This Illinois case was initiated as an appeal from a Superior Court judgment in Chicago, which had favored Buckley. The crux of the case rested on the jurisdiction of the New York court that issued the original judgment. The Shufeldts' legal team, represented by Messrs. Haines, Story & King, challenged the validity of the New York court's decision based on jurisdictional concerns, particularly that it was a court of limited and inferior jurisdiction.	The plaintiffs, William T. Shufeldt and George A. Shufeldt, argued that the New York court lacked proper jurisdiction to issue the original judgment against them. They claimed that they were never served with legal process, had no representation authorized by an attorney, and were unaware of the proceedings that took place. Thus, they sought to have the prior judgment reversed and requested that the court acknowledge their lack of notice and the issues surrounding the jurisdiction of the earlier court.	John Buckley, Jr., the defendant, maintained that the original judgment from the New York court should stand. His defense centered on the assertion that the procedural requirements of the court were properly followed and that the Shufeldts had opportunities to contest the judgment. Buckley relied on the legal principle that once a judgment is issued by a court, it should be presumed valid unless proven otherwise by the opposing party.

In 1855, Peter Baty filed an application for pre-emption of land in Ford County, Illinois. He built a residence on the southwest quarter of section 17, township 23, range 9 east, and moved in shortly thereafter. By December 1856, his application for the pre-emption was approved, and he received a certificate of purchase. However, after Baty's initial application, Thomas C. W. Sale entered the same land and received a patent. This led to a dispute over who had the legal entry for the land, which was taken to the commissioner of the general land-office. The commissioner concluded that Baty’s entry was void for not renewing his application after the discontinuation of the land office at Danville, claiming Sale’s entry held preference. Following Baty's death, his heirs sought to contest the dismissal of their suit which aimed to cancel Sale’s patent and recover the land through an injunction against Sale's action of ejectment.	The plaintiffs, the heirs of Peter Baty, claimed that his original pre-emption rights were valid despite the subsequent entry by Sale. They argued that Baty had met all legal requirements for pre-emption under the applicable law and sought a reversal of the lower court's dismissal. They requested the court to cancel Sale's patent and grant them possession of the land based on their rights under the pre-emption act.	The defendant, Thomas C. W. Sale, maintained that he had a valid patent and that Baty's entry was irregular and void due to procedural issues raised by the commissioner of the general land-office. Sale's primary argument was that Baty had failed to renew his application as required by the regulations following the closure of the Danville office. Thus, he asserted that the entry made by him had rightful preference, and he requested the court to uphold the validity of his patent and dismiss the plaintiffs' claims.

In the case of E. S. Fowler v. S. H. Richardson, dated November 23, 1889, the legal proceedings took place in Sangamon County, Illinois. The plaintiff, E. S. Fowler, entered into a written contract with the defendant, S. H. Richardson, on May 10, 1888, for the painting of his house for a total of $100. Fowler advanced Richardson $70 to purchase the required materials, including linseed oil, mineral paint, and white lead. The contract stipulated that any leftover paint after the job was to be delivered to Fowler. When Richardson failed to deliver the paint and oil as agreed, Fowler initiated a replevin action, which was initially heard before a justice of the peace. The case was later appealed to the Circuit Court where Fowler sought to present evidence of an oral agreement that specified how the $70 was to be used. However, the court ruled that this oral evidence could not be admitted because it would vary the written contract. Consequently, the court instructed the jury to find in favor of the defendant, leading to the appeal.	E. S. Fowler claimed that he contracted with S. H. Richardson for the painting of his house, providing $70 for paint and materials. He argued that Richardson was obligated to deliver the remaining paint to his barn after completing the work, and since Richardson refused to do so, Fowler sought the return of the materials through a replevin action. He requested the court to admit evidence of an oral agreement to clarify the use of the advanced money and to assert his ownership of the materials.	S. H. Richardson contended that the written contract was clear and legally binding, stating that he was to receive $100 for the complete job, with the understanding that he controlled the materials until the work was finished. Richardson argued that allowing oral evidence would alter the terms of the written contract and that Fowler had no legal basis to claim possession of the materials once he had signed the agreement.

In the case of Samuel E. Barrett et al. v. Elijah S. Alexander, which was adjudicated in September 1869, the proceedings took place in Cook County, Illinois. This legal matter had previously been before the Illinois Supreme Court, as recorded in 46 Illinois 226, where initial facts were presented. Subsequently, the case was re-tried, with the involved parties now serving as witnesses. During this trial, both Barrett and Alexander provided conflicting testimonies, while other evidence remained similar to that of the first trial. The circuit court conducted the trial without a jury, ultimately ruling in favor of the plaintiff, Barrett. The justices asserted that, despite the complexity of the testimonies, the evidence was not overwhelmingly in favor of the defendant, and thus they upheld the ruling of the lower court.	The plaintiffs, Samuel E. Barrett and others, contended that the preponderance of evidence supported their claims against Elijah S. Alexander. They argued that their testimonies, although challenged, were credible enough to substantiate their position. The plaintiffs sought a verdict from the court that would affirm their claims and provide compensation or relief based on the evidence they presented.	The defendant, Elijah S. Alexander, disputed the plaintiffs' claims, emphasizing the inconsistencies in the testimonies provided. Alexander maintained that the evidence did not substantiate the plaintiffs’ position effectively and requested the court to dismiss the claims against him, asserting that the findings were not justified based on the presented evidence.

Sarah Jane Clark filed an ejectment action against Miles Thompson in the Randolph Circuit Court, Illinois, in 1868. The case revolves around the sale of land belonging to Cuthbert S. Crane, deceased. Sarah Jane Clark claimed to inherit the property, which descended to Crane's children upon his death, while Miles Thompson asserted his legal right to the property derived from a series of transactions involving Crane's heirs, specifically through his wife, Mrs. McConnell. The Circuit Court found in favor of Thompson, stating that the court had not acquired jurisdiction over the minor heirs of Crane as required by law. Clark appealed this judgment, arguing errors in the original trial regarding the jurisdiction over heirs and the legitimacy of Thompson’s claim to the property.	Sarah Jane Clark argued that the prior sale of the land was invalid because the court did not properly acquire jurisdiction over the minor heirs of Cuthbert S. Crane. She maintained that the proper notice and procedures were not followed as mandated by statute. Clark requested the reversal of the judgment that favored Thompson, asserting that the land belonged to her as an heir.	Miles Thompson contended that the Circuit Court had jurisdiction and that the legal processes followed were adequate under the law. He argued that the guardianship proceedings adequately represented the minor heirs and admitted that debts existed, thus allowing for the sale of the land. Thompson maintained that he possessed a valid title to the property, having acquired it through lawful transactions, including an estate by curtesy through his wife.

In December 1857, the case of Thomas Davis et al. v. Shapleigh, Day et al. was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court following a series of legal proceedings that began in 1854 in the Greene Circuit Court. Attachments were issued against a defendant named William Pankey due to allegations that he had departed the state intending to remove his assets. The attachments were levied on personal property possessed by Thomas Davis, Ransom Davis, and John B. Choquette. These individuals filed pleas of interpleader, claiming ownership of the levied property. The court later moved the venue to Morgan County. In March 1855, Thomas Davis, as a garnishee, filed a motion indicating that Pankey had died, arguing that the death of the defendant should dissolve the attachments against him. Despite the plea, the court ruled to continue the proceedings. Pankey’s administrator eventually confessed judgment in favor of the plaintiffs for monetary damages, but Davis and Ransom Davis sought to cancel their bonds related to the attachment due to Pankey's death. The case consisted of interpleader and attachment proceedings that raised significant questions regarding the application of an abatement law to such cases.	The plaintiffs argued that the death of William Pankey, the original defendant, did not abate the attachment proceedings against him. They contended that the abatement law, specifically the eighth section concerning the death of a single defendant, should allow the case to continue against Pankey's estate through his administrators. They sought to affirm their right to recover the damages and costs, as well as to proceed against the garnishees based on the attachments previously issued.	The defendants, represented by Thomas and Ransom Davis, maintained that the attachment and legal proceedings should be dissolved due to Pankey's death, asserting that his demise effectively nullified the attachments. They requested that the court cancel any bonds associated with the property previously attached, claiming that the property was released from the attachments following Pankey's death.

In December 1828, the legal case of Wm. C. Greenup and Clement C. Conway v. A. B. Brown took place in Randolph County, Illinois, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiffs sought to overturn a decree that dismissed their bill for equitable relief against a prior judgment obtained in the circuit court. This judgment had been granted against them in a personal capacity due to a devastavit—a legal term describing the waste of an estate by an executor or administrator. The plaintiffs aimed to review the fairness and correctness of the earlier judgment, asserting that they had met all defenses during the trial. The court, however, noted that there was no evidence of fraud or mistake and that the defendants had sought to establish their claims through appropriate trial procedures. The court focused on the legalities surrounding the executory sale of real estate and the timing of actions related to potential financial liability as defined by the laws of 1825.	The plaintiffs, Greenup and Conway, argued for the reversal of a decree that dismissed their equity bill concerning a previous judgment against them. They contended that the judgment had been regular and fair, but they sought additional relief from the equitable jurisdiction due to claims associated with a devastavit. They requested that the court re-examine the circumstances surrounding the execution against their real estate and argued that the sale should not proceed under the provisions of the act of 1825, which regulated the sale of real estate under execution.	The defendant, A. B. Brown, contended that the previous judgment against the plaintiffs was valid and had been obtained through a fair legal process. Brown maintained that all defenses presented during the trial were duly considered and resolved by the circuit court. Furthermore, he argued that the issues raised by the plaintiffs in their bill of equity were matters that should have been addressed within the legal trial rather than being suitable for equitable relief. The defendant requested the court to affirm the dismissal of the plaintiffs' bill due to a lack of equity.

The case of The Wight Fire Proofing Company v. Peter Poczekai took place in Chicago, Illinois, on October 31, 1889, within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident at the center of this case occurred on December 6, 1886, during construction at a building for the Phoenix Insurance Company. The plaintiff, Peter Poczekai, was employed by a masonry contractor, Busse & Sturtevant, and was working to lower scaffolding planks through an elevator shaft when he was injured. At the same time, employees of the defendant, Wight Fire Proofing Company, were working on the roof of the building, where one worker, Lynch, stepped on a loose iron girder. This loose girder fell as they were attempting to haul up timber with a rope and struck Poczekai, causing him injuries. The Superior Court of Cook County initially ruled in favor of Poczekai, awarding him $2,000 in damages, a decision reaffirmed by the Appellate Court for the First District. The case revolved around issues of negligence on the part of the defendant and whether their actions directly resulted in Poczekai’s injuries.	The plaintiff, Peter Poczekai, argued that the defendant’s negligence was the direct cause of his injuries. He claimed that the defendant's workers, knowing that the girder was loose and resting on slippery supports, acted recklessly by remaining in close proximity to the falling girder while attempting to haul up timber. Poczekai sought damages for the injuries inflicted upon him due to this alleged negligence.	The defendant, Wight Fire Proofing Company, contended that the evidence presented by the plaintiff did not sufficiently establish negligence on their part or directly link any actions of their employees to the accident. They argued there was a variance between the plaintiff's allegations and the evidence provided, suggesting the mishap was more accidental than due to negligence. Furthermore, the defendant requested the trial court direct a verdict in their favor, asserting that the plaintiff had failed to prove the necessary components of negligence.

William B. Smith et al. v. Diantha J. Hays is a legal case that took place in 1887 in Warren County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Diantha J. Hays, initiated an action against Smith & Dunbar, a druggist firm, after she suffered severe health consequences from consuming a poison, extract of belladonna, which was mistakenly sold to her instead of the harmless extract of dandelion that she had requested. The sale was conducted by a clerk, McLain, who was not a registered pharmacist. After consuming the poison, Hays experienced serious health issues, including near-death conditions, leading her to claim permanent damage to her health. The court heard arguments regarding the negligence of the druggist and McLain's lack of qualifications, alongside various objections made by the defendants about the trial's proceedings and jury instructions. The trial court ruled in favor of Hays, awarding her $800 in damages.	The plaintiff, Diantha J. Hays, claimed that the druggist firm negligently sold her a dangerous poison (extract of belladonna) instead of a harmless medicine (extract of dandelion). This mistake resulted in her serious injury, permanent health impairment, and inability to perform her regular work activities. Hays sought damages for her suffering and losses, contending that the druggists were liable for the mistake made by their employee, regardless of his lack of registration.	The defendants, Smith & Dunbar, argued against the verdict and judgment, claiming various procedural errors during the trial, particularly concerning witness examinations and jury instructions. They insisted they were not liable for the employee's negligence since he was acting without proper supervision as a registered pharmacist. They also argued that evidence about the nature of injuries and causation was insufficient to justify the damages awarded to Hays.

John P. Hudson and Sellers brought a legal action of replevin against Enoch Maze in Scottville, Illinois, in December 1842. This case stemmed from Hudson and Sellers' claim for certain store books of account that had been recently utilized by Samuel McFarlan, a merchant. The plaintiffs argued that McFarlan had assigned these books to them as security for a debt he owed them amounting to $610.84, after which they sought to enforce their right to these books. The defendant, Maze, contended that the books were not in the possession of McFarlan at the time of the assignment but rather had been placed under a deed of trust to another party, J.M. Palmer, who had no knowledge of the assignment to Hudson and Sellers. The court trial led to a verdict for the defendant, indicating that the plaintiffs had not sufficiently proven their claim or right to the possession of the books.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had a legal right to the possession of the store books of account owned by Samuel McFarlan through an assignment made to them, under which they were to select and collect the debts owed to McFarlan. They sought a replevin action to retrieve these books, alleging that the defendant wrongfully was in possession of property that belonged to them.	The defendant, Enoch Maze, contended that he lawfully held the store books as the agent of J.M. Palmer, who had a superior claim to them through a deed of trust executed by McFarlan. He argued that the plaintiffs had failed to establish that they had rightful possession and that their assignment did not equate to ownership of the books themselves. Furthermore, he asserted that the plaintiffs should have made a demand for the books before initiating the lawsuit.

The case of Edward C. Murray et al. v. Charles H. Beckwith took place in September 1868, in Chicago, Illinois. The appellants, Edward C. Murray and others, entered into a promissory note with the appellee, Charles H. Beckwith. The appellants claimed that prior to signing the note, they were deceived into believing that the tobacco they purchased from the payees was of equal value to the samples presented. The payees were said to have represented that the tobacco was of high quality and that they would not assign the note to a third party or would allow the appellants to set off damages from its value. Upon execution of the note, the payees allegedly fraudulently conveyed their financial distress to coerce the appellants, leading them to sign the note. Later, a trial concluded with a verdict against the appellants despite their claims of fraud in the procurement of the note, leading them to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Edward C. Murray et al., argue that the promissory note was obtained through fraud, specifically that the tobacco purchased was not as represented, leading to a loss equivalent to the value of the note. They contend that the payees had warranted the quality of the goods and that the false representations made to them induced the signing of the note. Moreover, they sought damages for the alleged breach of warranty and claimed that the assignment of the note was fraudulent as it barred their defense.	The defendant, Charles H. Beckwith, maintained that the allegations of fraud were unfounded and that the note was valid as is. He argued that the claims regarding the quality of the tobacco did not represent fraud in the execution of the note but rather pertained to the contract itself, which did not constitute a defense against the enforcement of the note. The defendant also requested the court to dismiss the claims made by the plaintiffs, asserting that the note remained collectible despite the plaintiffs' allegations.

In 1884, in Metropolis, Massac County, Illinois, the Metropolis and New Columbia Gravel Road Company initiated an ejectment action against Hamilton Shirk and Albert P. Oakes to recover the north half of block 120 in the city of Metropolis. The plaintiff's legal standing was supported by a previous judgment from the Circuit Court of Massac County against Charles McBean, which had been appealed. Despite that appeal, McGlanery & Co. sought an execution on this judgment in January 1878 and levied it on the disputed real estate. The property was sold at a sheriff's sale on April 13, 1878, to James A. Williams, who later assigned the certificate of purchase to the gravel road company. The defendants argued that they held title to the property based on a different judgment against McBean that had also resulted in a prior sale of the property in 1877. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the Gravel Road Company, issuing a judgment for recovery of the premises, leading the defendants to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff argued that they had valid title to the property based on a successful execution sale following a judgment that had not been adequately contested during the appeal process. They maintained that the execution was valid and that, pending the appeal, the issuance of the execution did not affect the lien of the original judgment. They requested confirmation of their title and recovery of the property in fee simple.	The defendants contended that the execution resulting in the sale of the property was void because it was initiated while the initial judgment was under appeal, which should have prevented any further action on it. They argued that the sale was illegitimate and asserted their title through previous ownership established by their own execution sale. Their request was to overturn the Circuit Court's ruling and confirm their ownership of the property.

William S. Brackett v. The People ex rel. F. D. Weiennett is a case that took place in Peoria, Illinois, with the final decision rendered on November 14, 1885. The case arose when William S. Brackett, the owner of a specific lot in Ballance’s addition to Peoria, objected to a special assessment for the improvement of Depot Street. The collector of Peoria County sought a judgment against Brackett's lot for the amount due in 1883. Brackett argued against this judgment by citing a previous court ruling at the May term of 1884, in which a similar application was denied. The crux of his objection lay in procedural errors; he contended that a clerk had failed to properly certify the assessment roll, making the collector's claim void. Evidence was presented regarding the ongoing nature of the special assessment and the validity of prior proceedings. Ultimately, the court ruled that the previous judgment did not bar the current application for judgment, asserting that the lien of the assessment continued and that the proper steps had since been followed.	The plaintiff, William S. Brackett, claimed that a previous court ruling from June 1884 denied the collector's earlier application for the same special assessment on his property, which he argued should similarly negate the current assessment. He maintained that due to procedural failures, including the clerk’s lack of certification, the collector had no standing to collect the dues and, therefore, requested that the court dismiss the application for judgment against his lot.	The defendant, represented by the collector of Peoria County, argued that the previous judgment did not prevent a new application for judgment once the errors had been rectified. They contended that the special assessment lien remained valid, and procedural corrections, including proper certification of records, rendered the objection moot. Thus, the collector sought the court's judgment affirming the validity of the special assessment against Brackett's lot.

The case 'The German Insurance Company of Freeport v. Charles F. Churchill' took place in Illinois, with a decision rendered on November 18, 1887. The key individuals involved include Charles F. Churchill, the plaintiff, and representatives of the German Insurance Company of Freeport, the defendant. The essential issue arose from a fire insurance policy taken out by Churchill on mortgaged property that was already in litigation due to foreclosure proceedings initiated by the Union National Bank of Chicago, which held the mortgage on the property. The property was originally owned by John B. Snyder, who, facing financial difficulties, mortgaged his property to Churchill. The Union National Bank was assigned the related note and mortgage. Litigation ensued when creditors of Snyder challenged the validity of the assignments. Churchill applied for the insurance policy while the foreclosure proceedings were ongoing. Despite the complexities and the fact that the insurance agent was aware of the property's encumbered status, the insurance policy was issued with specific clauses benefiting the mortgagee's interests. A subsequent foreclosure led to the property's purchase by J. C. Kerrick on behalf of the receivers, complicating the insurance situation. Notably, the policy included stringent provisions regarding assignments and conditions under which it could become void, yet the court found inconsistencies between these provisions and the mortgage clause meant to protect the mortgagee's interests.",	Charles F. Churchill, the plaintiff, argued that the German Insurance Company should honor the fire insurance policy despite the ongoing foreclosure proceedings. He maintained that the policy explicitly allowed for claims to be made by the mortgagee or its assigns, and that any changes in interest or ownership should not void the policy. Churchill contended that the insurance company was aware of the foreclosure situation when the policy was issued and that its actions (or lack thereof) after the foreclosure sale indicated that the company accepted the risks associated with the existing policy.",	The German Insurance Company contended that the insurance policy became void under its stringent conditions due to the change in ownership and the commencement of foreclosure proceedings. They argued that Churchill's insurance claim should not be honored because the policy explicitly stated that any litigation or change in ownership without consent would nullify the coverage. The company maintained that they had the right to refuse the claim based on these provisions, emphasizing that these conditions were meant to protect them from the increased hazards posed by the litigation.",

In September 1873, in Aurora, Illinois, George M. Hadden, the plaintiff, was a landlord of Dudley Randall, who fell into arrears on his rent. Hadden issued a distress warrant to reclaim the owed rent, giving it to an officer, Graves, for execution. However, before the warrant was executed, Oscar B. Knickerbocker and another party claimed to have purchased Randall's property to settle a pre-existing debt and had already taken possession of it. When the distress warrant was levied, the property was claimed by the defendants, resulting in Hadden filing a replevin action to recover it. A jury determined that the defendants were bona fide purchasers without prior notice of Randall's rent due to Hadden. The key legal question centered on whether Hadden retained a lien on the property after it was removed from the rental premises, which the court had to resolve in light of common law and statutory provisions.	Hadden argued that he had a right to reclaim the property based on his landlord's lien, asserting that the property should remain under his control regardless of its removal from the premises. He maintained that as the property owner, he was entitled to collect the outstanding rent through the distress warrant and that the defendants should have been aware of his claim when purchasing the property.	The defendants, Knickerbocker and his associate, contended that they were bona fide purchasers who had acquired the property legally in exchange for settling a pre-existing debt. They argued that the landlord's right to distrain for unpaid rent was terminated once the property was removed from the premises, and thus, they were entitled to retain possession of the property despite any prior debts owed to the landlord.

The case, "Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Co. v. William H. McLallen, Admr. etc.", took place in August 1873 in Illinois. The plaintiff, William H. McLallen, Administrator of the estate of conductor Briggs, initiated the legal action following the tragic death of Briggs during a train collision on the 5th of August. Briggs was in charge of an extra freight train when he received telegraphic orders to run fifteen minutes behind another freight train, No. 46. As he executed these orders, believing the passenger train (No. 10) would be behind schedule, he departed from Naperville but was subsequently struck by the passenger train, leading to his fatal injuries. The jury found that Briggs was not guilty of negligence that caused the accident, attributing the blame to the lack of adequate communication from the railroad's management regarding the train schedules. The case highlighted negligence not only on the part of the railroad company but also on the individuals involved in managing train communications.	McLallen claimed that his intestate, Briggs, was killed due to the negligence of the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad. He argued that the railroad failed to properly inform the conductor of passenger train No. 10 regarding the orders given to Briggs. McLallen sought damages for the loss of life and argued that the company’s failure to ensure safety led to the tragic accident.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad, maintained that Briggs acted negligently by failing to properly manage the situation and assumed the passenger train was behind schedule without sufficient evidence. They asserted that due to this negligence from Briggs, the company could not be held liable for the resulting accident. The railroad requested a dismissal of the claims based on this premise of contributory negligence.

The case "Matthew S. Scott v. William Maxwell" took place in McLean County, Illinois, with a court decision rendered on December 4, 1885. The dispute arose from a suit in assumpsit, where Matthew S. Scott, the plaintiff (appellee), claimed that William Maxwell, the defendant (appellant), owed him $3,000 based on an account statement relating to their business dealings. Maxwell, however, claimed that the balance due to him was actually $5,000. The dispute required a thorough examination of extensive accounts, spanning ten years and involving transactions totaling over $400,000. The significant issues included an alleged partnership related to a nursery and grader, along with Maxwell's involvement in managing various farms for Scott over the years. The case was referred to a referee who took testimony and reviewed the complex financial records. The referee ultimately concluded that Maxwell owed Scott $594.56. However, after exceptions were filed against this finding, the court modified the amount to $400 and approved the referee's compensation at $1,500 for his extensive work in the case.	Matthew S. Scott argued that an accurate accounting revealed that William Maxwell owed him a balance of $3,000. He sought the enforcement of this claim through legal remedy, asserting that the extensive financial dealings between them necessitated a formal resolution and that the evidence provided justified a finding in his favor.	William Maxwell contended that the balance due was in fact $5,000, thereby challenging Scott's assertions. His defense rested on the complexity of the accounts and the nature of their business relationship, disputing the accuracy of Scott's claims concerning their financial transactions and seeking a resolution that favored his position.

In the case "Nancy J. Turney, Admrx of the estate of J. Turney, deceased, Pltff in Error, v. A. B. Gates, Deft in Error," which was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1850, the dispute originated from a judgment rendered against John Turney in March 1842. Turney passed away in 1844, and in 1846, A. B. Gates sought to revive the judgment against Turney's administratrix, Nancy J. Turney, through a scire facias. The Jo Daviess Circuit Court ordered that the revived judgment execute against the assets of the deceased's estate. However, the plaintiff argued there had not been an execution issued within a year of the original judgment, which would cause the lien on Turney's land to be lost. As this order was deemed erroneous, the case led to an appeal before the state Supreme Court, which had to determine the appropriateness of the execution order that favored Gates against the administratrix instead of following proper procedural protocol regarding estate administration.	Nancy J. Turney, as the administratrix of John Turney's estate, contended that the judgment awarded against her was erroneous because there had been no execution issued on the original judgment within the required time frame. She argued that as a result of this failure, the lien on her deceased husband's property was lost, and therefore, the appropriate action should have been to revive the judgment against her as administratrix to be paid in the ordinary course of administration rather than executing against the deceased's assets.	A. B. Gates maintained that the judgment in his favor should be revived and executed against John Turney's estate despite the lapse in time for issuing an execution. Gates argued that the court's original order against the administratrix was valid and that he should be allowed to recover against the deceased's goods and assets to satisfy the debt owed to him. He based his position on the assumption that his rights as a judgment creditor warranted execution against the estate.

Selden Fish v. Charles Gilbert Wheeler is a case that was decided on April 3, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Rollin S. Williamson. The legal dispute arose when a judgment by default was entered against Charles Gilbert Wheeler, the defendant, without addressing an outstanding demurrer to the plaintiff's declaration. A demurrer is a formal response to a complaint, arguing that the complaint is insufficient to warrant a legal response. The procedure followed in this case raised questions about the appropriateness of issuing a default judgment while there remained an unresolved demurrer on the record. This situation highlighted procedural issues relating to defaults in court judgments, leading to the appeal by Selden Fish, the plaintiff.	Selden Fish, the plaintiff, claimed that a judgment by default had been entered against the defendant, Charles Gilbert Wheeler, without properly addressing a demurrer that was filed regarding the declaration. Fish contended that this procedural misstep was improper and unjust, as it did not allow for an adequate judicial examination of the merits of the case. The plaintiff sought to have the judgment reversed on the basis that it violated legal proceedings.	Charles Gilbert Wheeler, the defendant, argued against the default judgment by highlighting the existence of the pending demurrer which had not been resolved prior to the judgment being made. Wheeler's defense was rooted in procedural arguments, asserting that the judgment was invalid due to the failure to address the demurrer adequately. He sought to have the case remanded for proper judicial process to ensure that his arguments could be heard.

In the case of Benjamin F. Turner v. Bayard Wright et al., dated July 27, 1883, the dispute arises from a bond issued to Turner by road commissioners of the town of Evans, Marshall County, Illinois, on September 18, 1880. The bond, totaling $88.34, was conditioned upon the opening of a public road across Turner's property, with damages assessed at $111.66—a figure Turner deemed inadequate. The bond stipulated that if Turner did not appeal the damages and the road was opened within five years, the amount would become due. Despite Turner's objections, the road was opened for travel within the specified timeframe, allowing public use. Turner contended that the bond's conditions were met because the road had been open and actively used by the public for over a year, despite the existence of some obstruction. The key legal contention centered on whether Turner, as a road commissioner and landowner, could recover full damages. The court ultimately found that public policy did not prohibit him from entering the contract and that the road, while containing obstructions, was legally open for travel.	Turner claims that the bond obligates the appellees to pay him the amount due under its terms since he did not appeal the damage assessment and the public road was opened within the stipulated five-year period. He insists that the road’s actual public use satisfies the opening requirement of the bond, despite some obstructions along the route.	The appellees argue that, being a road commissioner, Turner should not have entered into a contract to receive damages related to the road opening, claiming public policy prohibits such contracts. They also contend that the road was not legally opened for travel due to the obstructions, which they assert violate the bond's conditions.

On May 5, 1842, in Boone County, Illinois, Solomon W. Bristol and McKnight initiated a lawsuit against Hiram Waterman over an unpaid promissory note before Justice Albert Neely. Waterman was served with the process but did not appear in court, leading to a default judgment on May 10 for $47.56 plus costs. Waterman subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court of Boone County. At the September 1842 term, Bristol and McKnight were allowed to file an additional account not previously presented in the justice's court. The case was tried afresh, resulting in a judgment in favor of Bristol and McKnight for $63.91 plus costs. Waterman appealed this decision, claiming that the allowance of the additional account constituted an error. The court ruled that the Circuit Court was entitled to allow amendments to ensure a fair trial and that the amendments did not exceed the original demand from the justice's court.	The plaintiffs, Bristol and McKnight, argued that the Circuit Court acted appropriately in allowing them to submit an additional account during the trial. They asserted that the amendments were necessary for a fair trial and that such amendments were within the discretionary powers of the Circuit Court as stipulated by Illinois statutes governing appeals from justices of the peace.	Waterman contended that the Circuit Court erred in allowing the plaintiffs to file an additional account not presented in the original proceedings before the justice of the peace. He argued that this decision was unjust and exceeded the original claim amount, thus alleging that his rights were compromised by the court's discretion to permit further accounts.

Lawrence Leonard, a roadsman and tracklayer, was employed by the Niantic Coal and Mining Company in September 1885. On September 17, 1885, while descending a 360-foot mine shaft in a cage with four others, the cage descended rapidly and crashed to the bottom, resulting in severe injuries to Leonard. Although the injuries included severe cuts and bruises, the primary damage was nerve-related, leading to permanent disability and requiring ongoing medical care. Leonard's account indicated a sudden increase in speed and a jarring impact upon reaching the bottom. His injuries were attributed to the combination of the fall and the jarring motion that caused damage to his vertebrae. He subsequently sued the company for negligence, claiming that the operator's incompetence and improper handling of the cage led to the accident. The jury initially ruled in Leonard's favor, awarding him $4,600, which the company contested.	Leonard claimed that the Niantic Coal and Mining Company was negligent in multiple respects: (1) the engineer improperly operated the cage, (2) the company contravened safety provisions by placing a prop on the cage, (3) the company employed an incompetent engineer, and (4) the company failed to assess the fitness of its employees adequately. He sought damages for the injuries sustained, asserting that these failures directly resulted in his life-altering injuries.	The Niantic Coal and Mining Company contended that Leonard and the engineer were fellow-servants, suggesting that any negligence of the engineer was not the company's responsibility. They argued that Leonard's own actions contributed to his injuries, particularly his decision to place a prop on the cage under the direction of the pit boss. The company maintained that the engineer was qualified for the position and that allegations of his incompetence were unfounded. Their request was to have the prior verdict overturned and the case dismissed.

In 1883, the case of Roscoe G. Jordan v. R. F. Davis et al. arose in Illinois concerning a dispute over a lease agreement for a property previously owned by Pearce. Jordan, the plaintiff, claimed a right to the premises through a lease from Pearce effective March 1, 1882, with an annual rent of $1650. On the other hand, Davis, the defendant, claimed that he also had a lease from Pearce, dated October 6, 1881, which purportedly allowed him to occupy the same property at a yearly rent of $1500. The conflict centered around whether the lease Davis claimed was valid and effectively delivered by Pearce. Evidence showed that while Davis and Pearce discussed leasing terms and signed a lease, the actual delivery was contingent upon obtaining a guaranty from Snyder, Davis’s father-in-law, which was never completed. Consequently, Pearce later chose to lease the property to Jordan instead. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of the defendants (Davis), which prompted Jordan to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, questioning the nature of the lease's delivery.	Jordan argued that the lease he held from Pearce was legally binding and entitled him to possess the property, as it was established after the previous negotiations with Davis fell through, particularly due to the failure to secure Snyder's guaranty. He requested that the court reverse the circuit court's decision and grant him possession of the property.	Davis defended his claim by asserting that the lease he held was valid because it had been executed and considered delivered. He contended that no conditions needed to be met for the delivery of the lease, arguing that even if there was an expectation for a guaranty from Snyder, it was irrelevant to the legality of the lease. Thus, he sought to have the decision of the lower court affirmed.

In 1874, in Indian Grove township, Illinois, Benjamin Walton, the plaintiff and owner of a grist and flour mill, was involved in a legal dispute with William Westwood, the local tax collector. Walton had been assessed taxes on grain valued over twelve thousand dollars, which he had bought and stored as an agent for other parties. He argued that these taxes were unauthorized, illegal, and a fraud against his rights, claiming the grain had already been taxed in the respective owners' towns where they lived. The case arose when Walton provided a list of his taxable property to the tax assessor, which included the grain he purchased for other owners. Westwood demanded payment for the taxes assessed on the grain, threatening distraint if Walton failed to comply. As the case proceeded through the circuit court, a key issue was the proper application of several sections of the Revenue Act of 1872 concerning the taxation of personal property held by agents. Walton sought an injunction to prevent the collection of these taxes.	Walton claimed that the taxes assessed on the grain were illegal because the property was listed and fully paid by the actual owners in their respective localities. He argued that, as the grain was not in transit and had been assessed legally elsewhere, it should not be taxed again in his possession. Walton requested the court to restrain the tax collector from collecting these taxes.	Westwood contended that Walton, as the agent, was liable for the taxes on the grain because it was in his possession on the assessment date, May 1. He argued that Walton's position as an agent did not exempt him from taxation under the Revenue Act. Westwood further asserted that Walton's claim that the owners had already paid taxes was not adequately supported by factual allegations and that the law required tax payments regardless of his agency status.

Henry Keech was involved in a legal case against The People concerning an indictment found by the grand jury of Peoria County on September 7, 1857. Keech was charged with building a fence across a public road located in the township that ran north and south. The fence obstructed the path at a specific location in the area. After entering a plea of "not guilty," Keech was tried in front of a judge and jury, who ultimately found him guilty. During the trial, evidence was presented regarding various road commission orders and appeals related to the road in question. It was established that previous dismissals of an appeal taken by Keech concerning the road were made properly; however, there were procedural issues about the authority of the supervisors to act after the dismissal of the appeal. The court upheld points about the proper notifications and allotments concerning road management between two towns related to the matter.	The plaintiff, The People, argued that Keech had unlawfully obstructed a public road and sought to impose fines as well as a court order to remove the obstruction. They asserted he had failed to comply with prior orders requiring the road opening and maintained that Keech's actions were unjustifiable under public law.	Keech's defense contended that the supervisors of highways had no legal authority to order the removal of his fence since there were no proper notices or allotments made regarding the road's management between the towns involved. The defense argued that the road was never officially declared open and thus, Keech should not be penalized for maintaining his fence in what they claimed was a lawful manner. They asked the court to overturn the verdict against him based on these procedural deficiencies.

Jacob D. Herkimer v. Nora Shea was a legal dispute that arose in 1886 in Mattoon, Illinois. The case involved Nora Shea, who was employed as a servant in the Herkimer household. After a week of service, Shea and another servant girl requested their wages and communicated their desire to leave abruptly, without giving prior notice. This request incited anger from Jacob Herkimer, who confronted Shea and accused her of lying about her wages. Following a heated exchange, he ordered her to leave the house and retrieved her belongings, which he carelessly dragged out into the street. The valuable items included a trunk and a hat, which were damaged during this process. Although initially, Shea left her items behind and sought Herkimer's permission to retrieve them later, he refused, saying she needed to leave immediately. Claims of her belongings being in perfect condition were undermined by the fact that damage occurred when Herkimer mishandled them. The case escalated through legal channels, with Shea seeking damages for the injury to her possessions.	Nora Shea claimed damages for the injury to her personal effects, which she argued were worth $16.40 when new but were significantly damaged due to Jacob Herkimer's actions. Shea contended that her belongings were left behind involuntarily and that she was entitled to compensation for their poor condition. She also suggested that Herkimer's aggressive behavior added to the distress and provocation of the situation, and she believed she deserved punitive damages for his misconduct.	Jacob Herkimer's defense centered on the claim that Shea's abrupt departure and her careless decision to leave her belongings behind denied him any obligation to treat her property with care. He asserted that Shea had given up her claim to her belongings when she chose to leave without notice. Furthermore, Herkimer argued that any damages incurred were not due to his gross negligence or malice, and he rejected the excessive claims made regarding the valuation of the damaged items, suggesting that the plaintiff's lawyer's inflammatory comments may have prejudiced the jury against him.

The case "R G. Parks v. N. Brown" was initiated in the early 1850s in LaSalle County, Illinois, and revolved around a promissory note made payable to Nathaniel Brown. The action began before a justice of the peace and was appealed to the Circuit Court, where it was tried by Judge Leland in May 1854. During the trial, the note was initially presented as evidence but was challenged due to its blank indorsement. The plaintiff’s attorney struck out the indorsement, allowing the note to be admitted as proof despite objections from the defendant. The core issue centered on whether a plaintiff could lawfully strike out a blank indorsement on a promissory note during the trial. The legal precedents and statutory provisions were referenced to support the plaintiff's right to proceed with the trial without the indorsement.	The plaintiff, R G. Parks, argued that he had the right to strike out the blank indorsement on the promissory note during the trial, and based on this action, sought to have the note admitted as evidence. He contended that the legal framework permitted such an adjustment to facilitate the suit, enabling him to pursue the claim without formal objections based on the indorsement status.	The defendant, N. Brown, maintained that the initial exclusion of the note from evidence was warranted due to the blank indorsement. Brown contended that the suit could not proceed without addressing this issue, which he believed represented a legal technicality that should prevent the plaintiff from successfully claiming the amount due under the note.

The case involves "The Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company" as plaintiffs and "The Marseilles Manufacturing Company" as defendants, presented to the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1844. The action began in the Madison Circuit Court in September 1842, concerning two insurance policies related to property damaged in a fire on April 19, 1842. The insured properties included a flouring mill and two saw mills located in Marseilles, La Salle County, Illinois, with a total insured value of $10,000. The Marseilles Manufacturing Company filed declarations against the insurance company for $12,000 in damages, later amended to include $10,000. Key arguments surrounded the legitimacy of the insurance claims, particularly focusing on whether the manufacturing company had a full title to the property in question and the implications of undisclosed mortgages and other liens on the insured property. Evidence was presented at the May 1843 trial, leading to a jury verdict favoring the Marseilles Manufacturing Company for $10,000. The outcome was contested by the Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company, resulting in further legal scrutiny and appeals concerning matters of interest, insurance representation, and definitions of ownership.	The Marseilles Manufacturing Company claimed damages for the loss of their insured property due to fire. They argued that they had made legitimate applications for insurance and owned the property in question. They asserted that the Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company refused to pay the insured amounts after the fire and that they duly notified the company of the loss within the required timeframe.	The Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company contended that the Marseilles Manufacturing Company lacked a full fee-simple title to the property and had concealed crucial information regarding existing debts and liens incurred before obtaining the insurance. They argued that alterations made to the insured buildings increased the risk of fire without notifying the insurers.
