The plaintiffs, Kerr and Bell, contended that the lower court made several errors: it improperly set aside the default judgment; it accepted the defendant’s affidavit that contradicted the sheriff’s return of service, which was in favor of the plaintiffs; and it allowed the setting aside of a judgment that had been lawfully obtained at a previous term. They argued that such actions undermined the integrity of the legal process and requested the court to reverse the lower court's decision.	In his defense, Whiteside argued that he was never properly summoned to the court and was unaware of any proceedings against him, as he claimed he had not been served with process. His affidavits asserted that the return of service documented by the sheriff was, in fact, false. The defendant sought to have the default judgment reversed because he believed the original ruling was based on incorrect information and emphasized that procedural errors by court officers should be rectifiable at a subsequent court term.

On July 2, 1885, John R. Benedict, the plaintiff, was injured while using a public sidewalk on the east side of West Street in Galesburg, Illinois. The sidewalk was under the control of the City of Galesburg, the defendant, which had allowed it to fall into a dilapidated and unsafe condition. Benedict was using due care but tripped on a loose board and subsequently sought damages, alleging negligence on the part of the city for failing to maintain the sidewalk. The case was initiated on December 31, 1885, and after a trial on February 12, 1886, the jury found in favor of Benedict, awarding him $1,250 in damages. The city appealed, leading to the appeals process discussed in the judgment.	The plaintiff, John R. Benedict, claimed that the City of Galesburg was negligent for allowing the sidewalk to become dangerous, resulting in his injuries when he tripped on a loose board. He sought compensation in the form of $5,000 for damages due to the city's failure to maintain a reasonably safe walkway.	The City of Galesburg contended that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence and argued that the trial court erred by refusing to appoint a commission of physicians to examine the plaintiff. The city also claimed that the plaintiff’s instructions regarding comparative negligence were improperly refused, asserting that if Benedict had been even slightly negligent, he could not recover unless the city's negligence was gross compared to his.

In the case "The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. Taylor G. Chase v. The County Court of Macoupin County," the events unfold in Macoupin County, Illinois, during the 1869-1870 period. Taylor G. Chase, the relator and holder of a court house bond issued by the county court, sought to compel the county court to invalidate an order that annulled a previously enacted tax to meet court house indebtedness, which he argued included his bond. The county court, from its October 1869 session, had ordered a tax levy to cover this indebtedness, which was duly recorded and collected. However, at the March 1870 term, the county court, responding to certain taxpayers' motions, declared the tax illegal and arrested its collection, declaring that there was no remaining indebtedness that warranted such a levy. Chase then petitioned for a writ of mandamus to restore the tax assessment, claiming he had a right to it as a bondholder and taxpayer. The county court defended its decision, asserting that the tax was unnecessary since the debt had been satisfied and that the other tax orders still in effect were adequate to meet the bond interest.	Taylor G. Chase, as the relator, argued that he was wronged by the county court's decision to annul the tax that was intended to pay the courthouse indebtedness, which included his bond. He requested the court to issue a mandamus to compel the county court to restore the tax order for collection, claiming that the annulment violated his rights as a taxpayer and bondholder, and insisted that the tax was legally necessary for the payment of his bond.	The county court defended its annulment of the tax by stating that the previous court house indebtedness had already been paid off, rendering the tax order unnecessary. Moreover, they argued that the existing tax provisions were sufficient to cover any interest payments on the bonds, and therefore, there was no injury to Chase. They claimed that Chase was estopped from contesting the annulment since he had already received a tax refund after the rescinded order. The court also highlighted its legal authority to rescind unnecessary tax orders for the public good.

The case "The Ætna Insurance Company, Plaintiff in Error, v. William Phelps, Defendant in Error" was heard in January 1862 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The central individuals involved were William Phelps, the plaintiff who filed the suit, and The Ætna Insurance Company, the defendant. The dispute arose from Phelps's claim against Ætna under a fire insurance policy after his property was destroyed by fire. Phelps alleged that the company had failed to pay him the insured amount of $2,500. The case included four special counts related to the policy, with the main argument focusing on the perceived deficiencies in the declaration made by the plaintiff. The insurance policy had a specific clause allowing Ætna the option to rebuild or replace the property instead of paying the insured amount, which became a point of contention when the defendant contested the sufficiency of Phelps's claims. The lower court had previously ruled in favor of Phelps by overruling the defendant's demurrer, leading to the assessment of damages by a jury summoned by the sheriff after the regular jury was discharged.	The plaintiff, William Phelps, claimed that The Ætna Insurance Company failed to compensate him for damages arising from a fire that destroyed his insured property. He argued that the insurance policy entitled him to a sum of $2,500, which he had not received. Phelps asserted that the declaration made upon the policy properly stated the legal effect and alleged the breach for non-payment, thus demanding fulfillment of the policy's obligations.	The Ætna Insurance Company, represented by its counsel, argued that the declaration made by Phelps was insufficient. They contended that the policy included a condition allowing the company to rebuild the property instead of making a cash payment. As such, they claimed it was unnecessary for Phelps's declaration to refute this option, as it was a condition subsequent, which meant that if they pursued rebuilding, it fell under their defense rather than Phelps's claim. They also raised concerns regarding the court's right to abruptly impanel a jury after the regular panel was discharged.

In September 1872, Peter McNab filed a case against Rebecca Bennett in Livingston County, Illinois, before the Illinois Supreme Court. McNab was allegedly subjected to a wrongful arrest facilitated by Bennett, who fraudulently accused him of a crime to obtain jurisdiction over him for civil proceedings. The plaintiff contended that Bennett manipulated the system, initiating a false complaint and securing a warrant, leading to McNab's arrest outside his home county. This was purportedly done to serve him with civil process in a different jurisdiction. After being arrested, McNab was released by a justice of the peace due to the malicious nature of the charge against him, but by then, a default judgment had been entered against him without proper service or knowledge of the civil suits. The case raised significant questions regarding jurisdiction, proper service of process, and the rights of the defendant against fraudulent actions.	McNab argued that Bennett acted fraudulently by inducing his wrongful arrest and that he had no knowledge of the civil suits until after a default judgment had been entered against him. He claimed that the jurisdiction was improperly established based on this deceitful arrest, and he requested that the default be vacated, allowing him to defend himself against the civil claims properly.	Bennett contended that McNab was sufficiently served in the county where the suit was filed, claiming that his arrest and transport constituted proper service. She argued that the process should not be dismissed on the basis of jurisdiction as the claims were brought following a legally executed warrant.

In 1858, Porteus B. Roberts (the appellant) initiated legal action against William H. Haskell (the appellee) regarding a promissory note originally made by M. Zanoni. The incident took place in Peoria, Illinois. Zanoni issued a note promising to pay $200 to Isaac Underhill, which was subsequently endorsed to Roberts, who later transferred it to Haskell. At the time the note became due, Zanoni was declared insolvent, rendering any legal action against him futile. The case included multiple counts regarding the ownership of the note and Zanoni's financial status. During the trial, evidence was presented by both parties, including testimony about Zanoni's insolvency and his ownership of property that was mortgaged. The court faced issues related to the admissibility of evidence and the instructions given to the jury concerning ownership and the consequences of insolvency. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of the plaintiff Roberts.	Roberts claimed that the note was valid and sought to recover the amount due due to Zanoni's insolvency, which made pursuing him legally fruitless. He argued that as a holder of the note, he was entitled to collect from Haskell as the indorsee. Roberts maintained that he had fulfilled his obligations under the noted endorsements and that Haskell should be financially liable for the amount owed given the circumstances of Zanoni's financial status.	Haskell contended that the plaintiff did not adequately prove that Zanoni was insolvent at the time of the note's maturity. He argued that if due diligence had been exercised, the debt could have been collected from Zanoni. Haskell asserted that the instructions given to the jury were flawed and prejudicial. He claimed the evidence concerning the property belonging to Zanoni was improperly admitted and that the court erred in refusing to allow certain jury instructions that would have bolstered his defense.

In 1875, a legal dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, between Francilia M. Hotchkiss and Alvin S. Wadhams. The case originated in a justice court, where Hotchkiss brought a suit against Wadhams. After a judgment was rendered in favor of Hotchkiss, Wadhams appealed to the Superior Court of Cook County. During the process, issues emerged regarding the amendment of the plaintiff's name and jurisdiction concerns. The justice of the peace amended the summons to reflect the true name of the parties involved, a change that was not objected to by Wadhams during the trial. The legal proceedings faced complications when the appeal documents were mistakenly filed in the circuit court, but these were later transferred properly to the Superior Court. The court addressed the procedural legitimacy of these actions and confirmed that Wadhams had the right to appeal to the chosen court, demonstrating the procedural nuances of amendments to legal documents and jurisdictional disputes.	Francilia M. Hotchkiss claimed that the justice of the peace correctly amended the summons to reflect the true names of the parties without needing a written request on record. She argued that the judgment rendered against her was valid, and she had the right to appeal the decision in the Superior Court.	Alvin S. Wadhams contended that jurisdiction was incorrectly established when the appeal documents were inadvertently filed in the circuit court. He argued that this filing mistake should have invalidated the proceedings, claiming that the Superior Court did not have the authority to hear the case due to this error.

In 1887, Porter S. West initiated legal action against James S. Carter regarding an appeal bond related to a judgment previously rendered by a Justice of the Peace in favor of West against the Chicago Driving Park Association. James S. Carter served as the surety for the appeal bond. The case was brought before the Circuit Court after the appeal was dismissed. During the proceedings, the defendant argued that the underlying judgment was based on a gaming transaction, specifically a wager on a horse race, and that it was issued by default without a trial on the merits. West challenged this defense but ultimately faced an unfavorable ruling from the court, which found in favor of the defendant on the gambling issue. The trial occurred on July 18, 1887, with both parties represented by legal counsel. The judgment ultimately led to the court ruling against West despite most other issues being in his favor.	West claimed that Carter, as the surety on the appeal bond, was liable for the default judgment issued against the Chicago Driving Park Association. He argued that the gambling defense raised by Carter was immaterial and did not negate his entitlement to damages as a result of the bond, requesting the court to grant him judgment for the debt and damages incurred.	Carter contended that the original judgment was void due to its foundation on a gambling transaction and argued that the judgment could not be enforced through the appeal bond. He asserted that the court's finding on the gambling issue invalidated West’s claims. Carter's key request was for the court to dismiss West's motion for a new trial on the gambling issue, maintaining that the default judgment could not confer rights when it was based on an illegal wager.

In the case of Matthew Faloon et al. v. R. S. McIntyre et al., the dispute centers around a real estate transaction in Bloomington, Illinois, in 1883. The plaintiff, Matthew Faloon, sought to invalidate a deed of trust executed by Joshua R. Fell (his father-in-law) in favor of R.S. McIntyre. The deed was intended to secure the property for Fell and his wife while providing for the collection of rents and maintaining the property. For the preceding 20 years, Faloon and his wife had cared for the elder Fells, who moved in with them before leaving for their own residence in 1881. Following their departure, Faloon charged Fell for services rendered, totaling $7,764, despite no prior agreement to do so. In 1882, Fell executed the questioned deed, which conveyed his property into trust to protect it from Faloon’s claims. In 1883, Flon obtained a promissory note from Fell for $2,500, leading him to attempt to claim the property to satisfy this supposed debt. The circuit court ultimately dismissed Faloon’s bill seeking to invalidate the deed, thus causing him to appeal.	The primary argument presented by Faloon was that the deed of trust executed by Fell to McIntyre should be set aside to facilitate the collection of a debt he believed to be owed to him by Fell for the care and services provided over the years. Faloon asserted that the deed was a voluntary conveyance made to hinder the collection of his judgment against Fell based on the promissory note, which he claimed was tied to their prior arrangement concerning board and care.	The defendants (McIntyre and others) countered Faloon's claims by arguing that the deed of trust was a legitimate and voluntary transfer meant to secure the financial support for the Fells. They contended that Faloon’s relationship with Fell did not establish obligations for payment regarding the services Faloon provided. Furthermore, they noted that Fell's mental state at the time he executed the covenant indicated substantial influence from Faloon, which undercut Faloon’s claims to legal enforceability regarding the supposed debt.

In 1881, Nathan A. Stone and Dora Appel, both of the Hebrew faith, entered into mutual promises of marriage, intending to celebrate their union according to the customs of their religion. They allegedly agreed upon a specific date for their marriage: September 25, 1881. However, as that date approached, Stone expressed his unwillingness to marry Appel on that day, claiming it fell within a holy period during which such ceremonies were prohibited by their church. Consequently, on September 27, 1881, Appel initiated legal action against Stone for damages due to an alleged breach of promise of marriage. The trial resulted in a jury verdict against Stone for $2,000. Stone appealed the decision, arguing that no specific marriage date was agreed upon, and that his refusal to marry on the September date was justified by religious customs. The case presented complex legal questions regarding the enforceability of oral contracts for marriage and the balancing of religious beliefs with contractual obligations.	Dora Appel claimed that Nathan A. Stone breached their mutual promise of marriage by refusing to marry her on the agreed date of September 25, 1881. She argued that their agreement constituted a binding contract, and that Stone's refusal to celebrate the marriage amounted to damages for which she sought compensation.	Nathan A. Stone defended himself by asserting that there was no agreed-upon date for the marriage; rather, it was left to him to determine the timing. He maintained that he could not marry Appel on September 25 due to the religious prohibitions against marriage during that holy season, and he indicated his willingness to marry her after the period of prohibition had ended. Stone argued that his refusal was not a breach of promise, as it was justified by their shared religious customs.

In December 1838, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case originating from the Edwards Circuit Court involving Joseph L. Wilson and Thomas S. Hinde as appellants against John C. Campbell, John Brown, and John Gardner as appellees. The case pertained to a covenant action based on a bond signed by Wilson and Hinde on March 21, 1836, in which they agreed to pay $520 to the appellees. A critical note indicating that Hinde was signing the bond as security for Wilson was included. The case was heard during the April term of 1838, where a judgment of $585 was rendered against Wilson and Hinde. The central issue was whether Hinde's plea, asserting he was only a surety and not primarily liable, could exempt him from the obligation of the bond. The court determined that despite Hinde's designation as a surety, he remained equally bound along with Wilson.	The appellees, John C. Campbell, John Brown, and John Gardner, claimed that Joseph L. Wilson and Thomas S. Hinde were jointly responsible for repaying the sum stipulated in the bond, which included a request for damages assessed at $585 resulting from this debt. They argued that the bond was a binding contract that required both appellants to fulfill their obligation, irrespective of Hinde's asserted role as a surety for Wilson.	The appellants, Wilson and Hinde, contended that Hinde’s role as a surety should exempt him from liability on the bond. Hinde specifically pointed out that the bond included a memorandum clarifying his status as security for Wilson. They requested the court to sustain their plea against the plaintiffs' claims, arguing that the plaintiffs were aware of Hinde's limited liability and had no grounds for the claim against him in this case.

On May 3, 1861, Thomas L. Rushmore and partners, doing business in New York, sent five certificates of deposit to The Marine Bank of Chicago for collection. These certificates, dated April 19, 1861, were made payable in Illinois currency and referred to current currency. The letter accompanying the certificates instructed the bank to hold the proceeds until June 1, 1861, before remitting by draft to New York, with an option to remit sooner if exchange rates were favorable. The bank duly collected the funds in depreciated Illinois currency, which was losing value during that period. On May 30, Rushmore instructed the bank not to remit, believing that exchange rates would improve. However, by June 1, the bank indicated that the community refused to accept Illinois bank notes at their stated value. The jury ultimately found in favor of the plaintiffs, assessing their damages at $375.62.	The plaintiffs contended that the Marine Bank acted merely as an agent to collect the certificates and, by crediting them with the proceeds turned into their general funds, established a debtor-creditor relationship. They argued they were entitled to recover the collected amount in the form of current funds as stipulated, not in depreciated currency.	The Marine Bank claimed it was simply acting under instructions as an agent for the plaintiffs, thus limiting its liability to the amount they collected in what was understood to be depreciated currency. The bank argued that, since they had tendered the same value collected back to the plaintiffs soon after the request, they were not in default. They maintained that no obligation existed for the plaintiffs to expect anything beyond what had been collected under the terms of the certificates.

Samuel Hawkins filed a suit in chancery against Philip Vineyard and Hoge in November 1852 at the Illinois Supreme Court. The issue arose after Vineyard obtained a judgment against Hawkins and subsequently executed a sale of a quarter section of land, containing 160 acres, after which Vineyard purchased the land for $160. Hawkins claimed ownership of 65 acres within that tract but had no title to the remaining acres. Within a year of the sale, Hawkins approached Hoge, the sheriff, to redeem his 65 acres, offering $65 plus ten percent interest since the sale date. However, Hoge refused to accept the payment or allow the redemption application. Hawkins later brought the amount to court and sought permission to redeem his 65 acres. The court faced the challenge of whether Hawkins could redeem only part of the sold land while leaving the rest of the sale intact.	Hawkins argued that he should be allowed to redeem the 65 acres of land he owned by paying a proportional share of the sale price, along with relevant interest. He contended that the refusal of the sheriff to accept his payment was unjust and that he should be permitted to regain his property.	The defendants maintained that since the land had been sold as a single tract, Hawkins could not redeem only the portion he owned without affecting the integrity of the entire sale. They asserted that allowing a partial redemption would create an inequitable situation whereby Hawkins would benefit from a credit on his judgment based on property he did not own, arguing it would be unfair to the creditor.

The case "The People, etc., ex rel. The Illinois Institution for the Education of the Deaf and Dumb v. Orlin H. Miner, Auditor of Public Accounts" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1868. The conflict arose when the Illinois Institution for the Education of the Deaf and Dumb, established by the Illinois General Assembly in 1839, claimed its entitlement to a portion of the interest accrued from the state's school, college, and seminary funds. According to the initial legislation, the Auditor of Public Accounts was required to allocate one-quarter percent of these funds to the institution annually. However, in 1867, the Auditor refused to issue the warrants necessary for this payment, citing the establishment and funding of the Normal University as the reason, contending that its appropriation of funds superseded the Institution’s claims. The case involves allegations that the Auditor's refusal was unwarranted and interpretations of previous legislative acts from 1839 to 1867 that defined funding distributions. An application for mandamus was made to compel the Auditor to fulfill the funding obligation to the Deaf and Dumb Institution.	The plaintiff, represented by the Illinois Institution for the Education of the Deaf and Dumb, claimed that the Auditor was obligated to provide one-quarter percent of the annual interest from the school, college, and seminary funds. They argued that the recent refusal to issue payment was not supported by any statute and that any prior appropriation to the Normal University did not nullify their right to the funds, especially since the 1867 act reaffirmed their entitlement. They requested a peremptory mandamus to compel the Auditor to issue the necessary warrants for the funding.	The defendant, Orlin H. Miner, the Auditor, admitted to the allegations but maintained that he was not liable to pay the funds to the Deaf and Dumb Institution. He argued that the establishment of the Normal University and the appropriation of interest necessary for its maintenance subordinated the Institution's claims. The Auditor contended that since the Normal University had declared the necessity for the total interest funds, he was uncertain as to which party was entitled to the payments, which justified his refusal to issue the warrants.

Frederick Aholtz v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in Macon County, Illinois, in 1887. The case stemmed from an indictment against Frederick Aholtz for forgery, specifically related to three counts concerning an injunction bond. Aholtz was accused of forging the name of George Stare on the bond, which he used in a legal matter against James H. Durfee and others. The court trial revealed that George Stare never signed the bond and did not authorize Aholtz to use his name. During the trial, the jury's decision to convict Aholtz was based largely on Stare’s testimony, which contradicted Aholtz's claims that he had authority to sign the bond. After Aholtz was found guilty on the third count, he was sentenced to one year in the penitentiary. Aholtz’s appeals centered around claims of insufficient evidence to prove his guilt, but the court found no error in relation to the trial proceedings.	The plaintiff, representing the People of Illinois, claimed that Aholtz committed forgery by signing George Stare's name to an injunction bond without authorization. The argument emphasized that Stare clearly stated he never executed or permitted anyone to sign the bond on his behalf, constituting a criminal act under forgery laws. The plaintiff sought a conviction for Aholtz based on the evidence that Aholtz’s actions directly violated legal statutes governing forgery.	Aholtz's defense centered on the assertion that he had received verbal permission from George Stare to use his name for the bond, which he claimed took place during a conversation at a specific location. Aholtz admitted that Stare had testified against him but contended that another witness, Darius Sipe, had indicated Stare had previously authorized Aholtz to sign on his behalf, albeit at a different time. The defense suggested that the jury misjudged the credibility of the witnesses and that there was reasonable doubt regarding Aholtz’s guilt based on the conflicting testimonies.

The case titled "The People ex rel. William B. Jones v. Timothy T. Beach" dates back to January 1875 and took place in Illinois, specifically in Logan County. The principal individuals involved are William B. Jones (the relator or plaintiff) and Timothy T. Beach (the appellee or defendant). The dispute arose when McGalliard, the then master in chancery of Logan County, resigned on October 8, 1872. William B. Jones was appointed to fill McGalliard's position the same day and served as the master until October 4, 1873. On that date, the court appointed Timothy Beach as the new master in chancery. Jones maintained that his appointment was for a full term of two years from his original appointment date, which he argued had not yet expired when Beach was appointed. Conversely, Beach contended that since the term legally expired on April 1, 1873, the circuit judge had the authority to appoint any suitable person after that date, making his own appointment valid. The case eventually ended in court, where Jones sought to be reinstated and remove Beach from the office, claiming that Beach's appointment was illegal and unauthorized.	The plaintiff, William B. Jones, argued that his appointment as master in chancery was for a full term of two years starting from October 8, 1872, and asserted that it had not yet expired when Timothy Beach was appointed. Jones claimed that he was therefore entitled to hold the office, labeling Beach an intruder who should be ousted. He sought legal relief to be reinstated in his position, highlighting the illegitimacy of Beach's appointment.	Timothy T. Beach, the defendant, contended that the term of office for masters in chancery, as defined by the relevant statute, expired on April 1, 1873. He argued that after this date, the circuit judge had the authority to appoint a successor, making his own appointment valid. Beach maintained that Jones held the position only as an officer de facto during the brief period following April 1, 1873, and that his appointment was fully legitimate under the established law.

The case titled "Thomas Bentley, plaintiff in error v. John Doe, ex dem. Miron K. Brownson, defendant in error" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1835. The legal dispute originated in the town of Naples, Illinois, where the plaintiff, Thomas Bentley, initiated an action of ejectment to recover certain lots of ground described in the declaration as lot numbers twenty-five and six in block nine. The case was submitted to the Circuit Court without a jury, where the court found the defendant guilty of trespass and ejectment regarding lot number five in block nine, a lot not mentioned in the plaintiff’s original claim. Bentley contended that the court's judgment erroneously concerned premises that were not part of the original declaration, thus raising questions about the legitimacy of the court's findings. Following this, the plaintiff appealed, leading to a higher court's review.	The plaintiff, Thomas Bentley, claimed that the Circuit Court's decision was erroneous because it focused on a lot not described in his original declaration. He argued that as the finding and judgment related to lot number five, which was outside the scope of the pleadings, the ruling was not valid. Bentley sought a reversal of the judgment from the Circuit Court and the awarding of costs incurred during the case.	The defendant, represented by Miron K. Brownson, did not provide a detailed defense in the case description. However, the defense likely relied on the findings of the Circuit Court that deemed them guilty of trespass regarding the lot in question. The key argument from the defense centered around the validity of the court's findings, which were ultimately challenged by the plaintiff’s claims about the precise description of the property in question.

In 1861, in Illinois, the case of Alexander Cruikshank vs. Robert Cogswell revolved around the ownership of a horse. The dispute arose from a replevin action, initiated by Cruikshank, to recover a horse that he claimed he had purchased from Wm. D. Briggs in May 1857 for $80. Although Cruikshank had possession of the horse for a time, it was taken by defendant Cogswell, who was acting as a constable and had a judgment creditor that supposedly allowed him to seize the horse. The case began with a trial in the La Salle County Court, where several testimonies were presented regarding the purchase and possession of the horse. After a trial and a verdict in favor of Cogswell, Cruikshank’s motion for a new trial was denied, prompting him to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The main issue at stake was whether the sale of the horse was legitimate and whether the delay in delivery constituted fraud or not.	Alexander Cruikshank argued that he had legally purchased the horse from Wm. D. Briggs, who had given Cruikshank possession to strengthen the legitimacy of the sale. He maintained that the sale was completed and paid for, asserting that as long as it occurred before any judgment creditor's lien could attach, Cogswell could not lawfully seize the horse. Cruikshank requested the court to reverse the lower court's ruling that favored Cogswell and to recognize his ownership.	Robert Cogswell contended that the defendant had the rights to seize the horse based on his judgment creditor's claim. He presented several claims of ownership, arguing that the horse did not belong to Cruikshank, but rather to Briggs or to the creditor in question. Cogswell maintained that proper legal procedures, including the potential for loss of possession and attachment, were on his side, thus requesting the court to uphold the lower court's decision.

In 1866, in La Salle, Illinois, an ejectment action was initiated by John Buck against John Conlogue concerning the recovery of lots 9 and 10 in block 94 of the city of La Salle. The case revolved around a deed executed on January 26, 1868, from George H. Buck (the deceased husband of Mrs. Morse) to John Buck, which was duly acknowledged but did not include a release of homestead rights. George H. Buck had actually occupied the property as a homestead before his death, and his widow, after his passing, continued to occupy the property with her minor child until she remarried and moved to Sterling, Illinois. After her removal, she rented out the property to a tenant, directing the rents toward her child's education. The core issue at trial was whether the widow's subsequent actions—particularly her move and abandonment of the property—had legally forfeited her homestead rights, which could affect the rights of her daughter.	The plaintiff, John Buck, claimed that he held rightful ownership of the property, arguing that the widow's abandonment of the homestead and subsequent marriage to Mr. Morse constituted a loss of her homestead rights. He requested that the court affirm his right to recover the property based on these claims and the legal precedent concerning the homestead exemption.	The defendant, John Conlogue, contended that Mrs. Morse had maintained her homestead rights despite the alterations in her living situation, asserting that her prior intentions and payment of rent to occupy the property served as a barrier against Buck's claims. He emphasized the legal framework allowing her to retain homestead rights unless a formal release was effected, thereby requesting the court to rule in favor of retaining the property.

Lavina Wallace filed a legal case against Jefferson J. White and others in LaSalle County, Illinois, in 1883, regarding a dispute over property and creditor claims. The case drew attention due to property transactions between Jefferson and his family members that allegedly aimed to defraud existing creditors. Jefferson J. White was found to have owned certain real estate which was conveyed, first to Jacob A. Dupee without any consideration, and subsequently from Dupee to Bertha White (wife of James White), again without consideration. This series of transactions occurred in the context of a partition proceeding initiated by Wallace, where she was entitled to recover sums from Jefferson J. White and James White for rents and profits. It was claimed that the transfers of property were done intentionally to hinder Wallace’s ability to collect her claim. Following a decree stating that Wallace was owed funds, an execution issued against Jefferson returned no property found, prompting Wallace to file the current bill in aid of that execution. Ultimately, the case revolved around the legality and implications of these voluntary property transfers in relation to Wallace's claims against Jefferson.	Lavina Wallace claimed that the transfer of property from Jefferson J. White to Jacob A. Dupee, and then from Dupee to Bertha White, was executed without any valid consideration, designed to obstruct her from collecting debts owed to her. She alleged that these transactions were fraudulent against her as a pre-existing creditor. Her main argument was that these conveyances, being voluntary and without consideration, should be deemed invalid, allowing her to pursue her claim for the debts owed.	The defendants, particularly Bertha White, contended that she was a good faith purchaser of the property for valuable consideration, asserting ownership and protection under the law against claims made by Wallace. However, Jefferson J. White and James White were defaulted and did not provide a substantive defense. Their lack of response effectively conceded to the claims made by Wallace regarding the fraudulent nature of the property transfers.

In September 1870, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Joshua Collins et al. v. James Waters, originating from Will County, Illinois. The central event took place on January 29, 1866, when Joshua Collins and his associate Jeremiah Collins were accused of assaulting James Waters. The dispute began with accusations that Waters had verbally threatened the Collins brothers several days prior. Subsequently, an altercation occurred where Waters claimed to have been kicked in the head by the defendants. At trial, the court allowed testimony from a physician who treated Waters, which included details of how the injury was allegedly inflicted. The defense argued that the injuries were sustained by Waters's fall on the icy ground and not due to any actions taken by them in self-defense. The appeal arose from objections against the evidentiary rulings and jury instructions deemed improper.	The plaintiffs, Joshua Collins and Jeremiah Collins, claimed that James Waters assaulted them and sought damages for the injuries sustained during the encounter. They argued that Waters had acted aggressively, threatening them before the incident and that their actions were justified in response to his threats. They requested compensation for actual damages as well as punitive damages for the pain and humiliation caused by Waters's actions.	The defendants, James Waters and his counsel, asserted their defense by pleading the general issue and claiming the injuries were inflicted in necessary self-defense. They contended that Waters had initiated the confrontation with provocative words and that they were justified in their actions to protect themselves. They requested that the jury be instructed to consider these factors and to evaluate whether their actions constituted a lawful self-defense response.

Otto Brauns, elected as a highway commissioner in Peoria, Illinois, on November 2, 1870, served alongside Thomas Honnihan and Peter Beed. In April 1871, he was elected treasurer of the highway commissioners. Brauns and Honnihan placed contracts for road repairs due to damages from heavy rains, undertaking work without sufficient funds in the treasury. By August 1872, the board had exhausted their revenue for the year, yet they continued to draw on anticipated future funds to let contracts for repairs. Brauns's claims arose from his expenditure on these projects, asserting that the town was liable to reimburse him as their auditors had recognized his expenses. The controversy focused on the limitations of the highway commissioners’ authority and the legality of their actions under the prevailing statutes, which mandated that funds for such expenditures must already exist or be duly levied.	The plaintiff, Otto Brauns, argued that he was entitled to payment for expenses incurred in repairing roads and bridges, as these had been recognized by the town auditors. He contended that although the funds were not available in the treasury, his expenditures were valid as responsibilities of the town could not be disputed based on an alleged lack of authority by the highway commissioners. Brauns requested compensation for the amounts he claimed to have advanced on behalf of the town for repair work.	The Town of Peoria asserted that the highway commissioners had spent all their available revenue unlawfully by contracting work without the authority to incur a debt beyond their means. The town maintained that Brauns's actions violated the statutory requirements that dictated how highway commissioners could conduct expenditures and manage funds. They argued that the contracts made by Brauns and Honnihan were invalid and that payment for such unauthorized work could not be demanded from the town.

In September 1868, in Grundy County, Illinois, Joshua Collins and others were indicted for assault and battery. The indictment did not specify the charge as aggravated assault or riot as defined under Illinois law. During the trial, three jurors disclosed that they had prior knowledge of the case and had formed fixed opinions based on this information, although they claimed they could remain impartial. The trial judge disallowed challenges to these jurors, stating that they believed they could render a fair verdict based solely on the evidence presented. This ruling was a significant point of contention for the defendants. Ultimately, the case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court, which reviewed the jury selection process and juror competency in light of the claims made regarding their biases. The Supreme Court determined these jurors were indeed disqualified and that the trial court had erred in allowing them to serve.	The plaintiffs, represented by the State, argued that Collins and the others engaged in behaviors constituting assault and battery, seeking to uphold the jury's verdict against the defendants. They contended that the jurors were sufficiently capable of overcoming their prior biases and rendering an impartial judgment based on the presented evidence.	The defendants claimed that the trial court had erred in not allowing challenges to jurors who had pre-formed opinions on the case. They argued that a fair trial requires jurors to be impartial and without preconceptions, highlighting the necessity for jurors to be unprejudiced to ensure a rightful judgment. Furthermore, they pointed out that the court had mistakenly assumed facts that should have been determined by the jury, thus compromising the integrity of the trial.

In January 1867, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the case of John Guedel, who had been indicted for the murder of Adam Zimmerman in Madison County. The indictment alleged that Guedel killed Zimmerman by striking him on the head with a gun. Guedel previously faced a similar charge in October 1864 but was acquitted after a jury trial, where the indictment described the killing as having been committed by shooting with gunpowder and leaden shot. In the present case, Guedel pleaded "autrefois acquit" (previously acquitted), asserting that the two indictments described the same offense. However, the prosecution countered that the circumstances of the two incidents were different, thus allowing for different indictments. The case centered on whether the evidence of a different manner of killing (beating vs. shooting) could support the new charge and whether Guedel could legitimately claim jeopardy from the first indictment. The court ultimately examined the distinctions between the two types of killings and their legal implications.	The plaintiff, the People of the State of Illinois, argued that despite Guedel's previous acquittal for murder by shooting, the current indictment charged him with a different mode of killing, namely, striking Zimmerman with a gun. They contended that the original indictment's method of killing was fundamentally different from the current allegations, and thus, the legal principle of jeopardy did not apply. They sought to uphold the conviction based on the new indictment.	Guedel's defense hinged on the argument that he could not be tried again for the same homicide for which he had already been acquitted, as both indictments pertained to the murder of the same victim. He claimed that the variance in how the murder was allegedly committed (shooting vs. striking) did not constitute a separate offense, thus prompting his plea of autrefois acquit.

On January 9, 1862, in Chicago, Illinois, William Wayman and Thomas Shergold executed a joint bond for $5,000 to John P. Crozier, with a stipulation to pay ten percent interest. To secure this payment, the Waymans provided a mortgage on real estate. Following a default on payments, Crozier obtained a judgment at law by confession, and on February 14, 1862, he initiated a suit in chancery against the Waymans and Isabella Cochrane to foreclose the mortgage. The summons for this suit was reportedly served on Jane Wayman by "William Wayman," who was acting as a deputy sheriff. The bill against the defendants was taken as confessed, and a final decree was issued, determining the amount owed, inclusive of interest at the rate of ten percent per annum, corresponding with the bond. The defendants appealed, arguing errors regarding the service of process and the interest calculation.	The plaintiffs, represented by Crozier, contended that the mortgage and bond conditions warranted the collection of ten percent interest annually as established in the bond. They asserted the validity of the service of summons and that the decree to foreclose the mortgage was justified based on the amount stated in the bond, including those interest terms.	The defendants claimed that the service of process on Jane Wayman was invalid since it was executed by her husband, thereby raising a procedural objection. They also argued that the bond had merged into the judgment, which should limit the interest to six percent per annum, not ten percent, hence contending that the foreclosure should reflect that lower interest rate on the judgment amount instead of the bond.

In 1889, in Franklin County, Illinois, the case of American Central Insurance Company v. Sophronia R. Brown arose regarding a dispute over an insurance policy. Sophronia R. Brown, the appellee, initiated the action against the American Central Insurance Company, the appellant, after a fire damaged her insured property. The insurance policy in question contained a clause stating it would be void if the title to the insured property was subject to litigation. Prior to purchasing the insurance, Brown's husband, E.J. Brown, had conveyed the property to Sophronia despite ongoing litigation involving the property. The litigation included a specific performance bill filed by the Polar Star Lodge against E.J. Brown and his wife, with a decree that had reversed on appeal prior to the issuance of the insurance policy. The insurance agent was aware of the ongoing litigation when the policy was issued. The case's complexity heightened due to the understanding of whether the title was still in litigation and whether the insurance company's objections were valid, especially regarding proof of loss documentation provided by the plaintiff after the fire.	Sophronia R. Brown claimed that the insurance company wrongfully denied her claim based on the assertion that the property’s title was involved in litigation. She argued that the appeal process had reversed the initial decree, and therefore, the title should not be considered as in litigation at the time of her insurance claim. Additionally, Brown maintained that the insurance company had waived its right to challenge the policy based on prior knowledge of the litigation status, and that her proof of loss met the policy requirements despite the company’s objections.	The American Central Insurance Company contended that the insurance policy was void due to the title of the property being involved in litigation at the time of the fire. They argued that the risk of litigation had not been adequately communicated, and therefore, they were not liable for the loss. Moreover, the company claimed that Brown failed to provide the necessary evidence of loss required by the policy, which was a condition for coverage.

The case "N. W. Benevolent and Mutual Aid Association v. John W. Prim" was decided on February 25, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose in Logan County, Illinois, where the plaintiff, N. W. Benevolent and Mutual Aid Association, initiated an action to collect an insurance claim of $83,000 upon the life of Laura L. Prim, the wife of the defendant, John W. Prim. The plaintiff filed the declaration on June 25, 1885. Shortly after, on June 29, 1885, the defendant entered their appearance. When the case was set for trial at the September 1885 term of the court, the defendant filed a motion for a continuance due to the unavailability of their primary counsel, who was engaged in another trial. They supported their motion with affidavits indicating the necessity of having their lead attorney present during the trial. However, both the initial motion for continuance and a subsequent request at the same term were denied by the court, which exercised its discretion to manage the case schedule.	The plaintiff argued that the insurance policy should be enforced, resulting in a payment of $83,000 due to the death of Laura L. Prim. They contended that the insurance contract was valid and enforceable, citing the defendant's failure to provide a timely defense and necessary witnesses who could substantiate their case.	The defendant claimed that they were not prepared for trial due to an unexpected overlap in counsel's legal commitments. They asserted both a lack of diligence in preparing their defense and an agreement with the plaintiff's attorney to take evidence before a stenographer, which had not been honored. Thus, the defendant requested a continuance to gather necessary testimony, arguing that the absence of witnesses would fundamentally harm their case.

The case of Alonzo L. Bushnell et al. v. Herman K. Wood was heard in January 1877 in Illinois, specifically in McLean County. The key individuals involved were the plaintiffs, Alonzo L. Bushnell and others, and the defendant, Herman K. Wood. The dispute centered around a chattel mortgage given by Mrs. D. K. Dodge to the plaintiffs, which covered certain property in question. This mortgage was properly executed, acknowledged, and recorded before an execution was issued against the property by the defendants. A key issue in the case was whether the mortgage was fraudulent as to other creditors, which prompted conflicting evidence. The court determined that this issue was suitable for jury consideration, and the jury ultimately found that the mortgage was not fraudulent. The property was in the possession of the defendants, and the court affirmed the jury's findings regarding the priority of the mortgage lien.	The plaintiffs, Alonzo L. Bushnell et al., claimed that the chattel mortgage executed by Mrs. D. K. Dodge was valid and held a priority position over any executions against the property by the defendants. They requested a legal determination confirming the authenticity and precedence of their mortgage, arguing that any claims of fraud against creditors should be evaluated by a jury.	The defendant, Herman K. Wood, contended that the chattel mortgage was fraudulent concerning creditors, questioning its validity and asserting that the property belonged to him under the execution he held. Wood's arguments leaned on the claim that the mortgage had not been executed in good faith, seeking to challenge the jury's finding and the legality of the plaintiffs' claims on the property.

On September 1870, in Iroquois County, Illinois, the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company was involved in a legal dispute with Frank Webster. The case arose from an incident where Webster claimed that his property, specifically a colt and some hogs, was killed or injured due to the railroad company's alleged negligence in failing to maintain proper fences and cattle guards along their tracks. Webster testified that he found a colt in a ditch alongside the railroad with a broken leg and hip, which was already dead at that point. He valued the colt at $70 and mentioned that he had four hogs that were injured as well, two of which died. The hogs were originally worth $10 each but significantly depreciated in value after the incident. Witnesses testified that the injury to the livestock occurred in an area devoid of nearby towns or established fencing, indicating a need for protective measures. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Webster, resulting in a verdict of $100 in damages.	Frank Webster, the plaintiff, argued that the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company was negligent in not constructing and maintaining necessary fences and cattle guards to protect livestock from wandering onto the railway tracks. He requested compensation for the value of his property that was killed or injured due to this neglect, specifically seeking $100 for the colt and hogs from the railway company's failure to provide adequate safety measures.	The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, as the defendant, contended that the evidence presented did not affirmatively prove that the injuries occurred within the jurisdiction of the court (Illinois), as required for this type of claim. They argued that because the plaintiff failed to demonstrate that the livestock injuries happened within the state, the claim could not stand. The defense sought a new trial based on these procedural objections and argued against the sufficiency of the evidence supporting the plaintiff's claims.

In 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, Nicholas Staaden was indicted for allegedly setting fire to a building he owned, which was used as a store and dwelling. The fire occurred on July 28, 1874, while the building was insured against loss by the Etna Insurance Company of Hartford, Connecticut. The indictment claimed that Staaden acted unlawfully and with malice, intending to injure the insurance company by destroying the insured property. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following a motion to quash the indictment, based on the legal requirement of properly alleging guilty intent and the nature of the injured party. Specifically, the court addressed whether the invalidity arose from not adequately demonstrating that the Etna Insurance Company was an incorporated entity.	The plaintiff, representing the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Nicholas Staaden intentionally set fire to his insured property with the objective to defraud the Etna Insurance Company. They emphasized the need for strict adherence to legal standards in indictments, asserting that showing the defendant's malice and intent to injure an insurer is critical in such cases.	Staaden’s defense contended that the indictment was fundamentally flawed because it failed to properly allege that the Etna Insurance Company was an incorporated entity. The defense argued that without establishing the company’s legal status, the prosecution could not validly claim that Staaden intended to injure a recognizable party. This lack of specificity in the indictment warranted its dismissal.

In 1867, in De Kalb County, Illinois, the case "Jambs S. Dwen, Executor, etc., et al. v. Thatcher Blake, Executor, etc." progressed through the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a series of transactions involving Thomas R. Green, who dealt in land warrants in Chicago, and his agent, Henry A. Mix, who operated in Ogle County. In 1849, Asa Talmadge sought to purchase land warrants to enter specific parcels of land and engaged Mix to facilitate the purchase. Talmadge acquired land warrants for 360 acres for $432.25, for which he executed notes secured by bonds for conveyances from Mix. However, a series of events unfolded, including the death of Green, modifications in land ownership among Green’s heirs, and Talmadge's unsuccessful attempts to pay off the notes. In 1858, after Talmadge's possessions were sold due to debts, Francis Burnap redeemed the lands and subsequently filed a bill in equity to redeem the lands, claiming the right to do so as Talmadge's purchaser. The legal title to the properties resided with Green’s heirs, who continuously disputed Talmadge’s claim, resulting in this court case.	The plaintiff, Jambs S. Dwen, argued that as the purchaser of Talmadge’s title, he had the right to redeem the lands from the mortgage due to the failure of proper ownership transfer and payment recognition by Green’s heirs. He sought to redeem the property by offering to pay the principal and interest on the original notes, requesting that the court account for the amount due and grant him legal relief.	The defendants, heirs of Thomas R. Green, denied the claims made by the plaintiff, asserting that Mix had sold the land warrants intending to benefit himself and Green exclusively, and not Talmadge. They contended that Talmadge had forfeited any rights concerning the lands due to nonpayment and argued that the original transaction should be regarded as an outright sale rather than a mortgage, denying any entitlement to redeem the lands.

In September 1874, the legal dispute arose in Mercer County, Illinois, between Conrad Littiech and Samuel Mitchell. The case centered around a road allegedly obstructed by Mitchell, which Littiech claimed was impacting his rights. The appeal was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court, where Chief Justice Walker highlighted various questions that had also emerged in a previous case. He pointed out that the lower court had allowed evidence regarding obstructions at locations unrelated to the claims made by Littiech. It was noted that Littiech had failed to object to certain evidence, leading to the presumption that he waived those objections. The court assessed that there was clear evidence that the road ran over Littiech's land, yet the testimony from Mitchell’s witnesses lacked clarity regarding its location. The court found that instructions given to the jury did not align with existing legal precedents, and evidence indicated that the road was heavily used until it was obstructed by Mitchell or others.	Littiech argued that the obstruction of the road by Mitchell violated his rights and sought legal redress. He contended that the road was essential for public use and should remain accessible. Littiech requested that the court overturn the verdict from the lower court, which he believed was erroneous in allowing inappropriate evidence that undermined his case.	Mitchell's defense centered on the claim that Littiech had not sufficiently proven the road's location or the legitimacy of his claim of obstruction. They argued that surrounding obstructions by other parties should be considered relevant in assessing the situation. Moreover, Mitchell maintained that the jury instructions provided were competent and that there was a lack of substantial evidence to support Littiech's assertions.

In 1848, Mary Jane Stewartson married William Stewartson in Shelby County, Illinois. At the time of marriage, Mary Jane brought $320, which William subsequently appropriated for his own use. Shortly thereafter, he used $40 of her money to purchase a forty-acre tract of land in her name. In April 1850, William abandoned Mary Jane, leaving her in possession of his dwelling and some personal property. Mary Jane sold some of this personal property and used the proceeds to buy another forty-acre tract of unimproved land in her own name. On May 1852, two years after the abandonment, Mary Jane filed for divorce, which was granted in November 1852, along with a yearly alimony of $50. The Shelby Circuit Court left the issues of property titles and alimony modifications for future consideration. In May 1853, an agreed case was presented to the court regarding the disposition of the lands and the modification of alimony, which resulted in a decree for Mary Jane to convey a tract of land to William and reducing her alimony to $30 per year, with William responsible for the costs.	Mary Jane Stewartson argued that she should retain full ownership of the land purchased with her money and sought to have her alimony maintained or increased, given her financial circumstances post-divorce. She contended that after her husband’s abandonment, she was left with limited resources and that a fair division of the property and adequate alimony were necessary for her support.	William Stewartson claimed that the tract of land acquired in Mary Jane’s name was purchased with funds he had provided and sought to have that land conveyed back to him. He also requested a reduction in the alimony from $50 to $30, arguing that it would be unfair given his own financial situation and the income generated by his farm.

George Winkler filed a bill in chancery against Christian Winkler and the commissioners of highways in Worth Township, Illinois, in February 1865. Winkler sought to enjoin the defendants from appropriating part of his land for a private road, which Christian Winkler had petitioned for without the plaintiff’s consent. The case arose from a series of events where Christian, who had previously sold the property occupied by George, claimed he should have access to a road crossing that land due to an agreement made during the sale. The bill of complaint alleged that the defendants failed to provide the required legal notice for the proceedings related to the road and requested that they be restrained from further actions until compensation was paid for the land affected by the road. The defendants admitted certain facts but denied any unlawful conduct. After proceedings and motions regarding the injunction, the court found that the bill must be dismissed since there was no equity in it and that the plaintiff had adequate legal remedies to address his grievances. The final decision came after a joint hearing on the pleadings without any proof being presented.	The plaintiff claimed that Christian Winkler's petition for a private road was filed without proper notice and sought to prevent the defendants from conducting any further proceedings regarding the road. He requested that the court stop Christian from accessing the land for the road, arguing that he should first pay for the land and any necessary fencing costs. The plaintiff asserted that his rights were being infringed without his consent.	The defendants, including Christian Winkler, argued that their actions were lawful and denied any oppression of the plaintiff. They acknowledged the petition and admitted their intent to lay out the road but claimed that there was no legal requirement for them to do so without notice. Christian contended that he had a prior agreement regarding the road during the sale of the land, which justified his request. They also sought to dissolve the injunction and assessed damages for any wrongful claims brought by the plaintiff.

The case "The Newark Fire Insurance Company v. Thomas J. Sammons et al." took place in Illinois, with the Illinois Supreme Court rendering its decision on May 19, 1884. The lawsuit arose from an insurance policy issued to Thomas J. Sammons and his associates by the Newark Fire Insurance Company on December 23, 1880. The policy was intended to cover losses by fire, but the insurance company claimed it had been canceled before a fire loss occurred. The insurance agents, Ryan & Co., who procured the policy, were allegedly notified of this cancellation, but the plaintiffs argued they had not been informed of such a cancellation. During the trial, conflicting evidence was presented regarding whether the cancellation notice was served, leading the jury to find against the insurance company. The Superior Court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, and this judgment was upheld when appealed to the Appellate Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Newark Fire Insurance Company was liable for the insurance policy issued on December 23, 1880, as it had not been lawfully canceled before their property was lost in a fire on January 28, 1881. They argued that the insurance company failed to provide them with proper notice of cancellation and asserted their entitlement to the insurance claim payout based on the terms of the policy.	The Newark Fire Insurance Company contended that the insurance policy was validly canceled before the fire loss, asserting that notice of cancellation was provided to Ryan & Co., claiming they acted as agents for the plaintiffs. The defendant requested that the court find in their favor, arguing that since the policy was canceled, they were not liable for any claims related to the fire loss.

In December 1831, in St. Clair County, Illinois, an action of debt was initiated by Thomas S. Locke against James Semple. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court after Semple was served with process, while another defendant was not mentioned. On the first day of the term, Locke obtained a rule requiring Semple to plead by the following day. Semple responded by filing pleas of "nul tiel record" (a term indicating no such record exists) and "payment." However, Semple did not appear on the day to plead, leading the court to enter a judgment by default against him for the debt claimed by Locke. Semple appealed this judgment, arguing that it was erroneous to enter a default judgment without addressing the pleas filed by him.	Locke's main argument revolved around his action of debt based on a record from a foreign state. He maintained that he had followed the proper legal protocols in seeking a judgment against Semple and had the right to obtain a default judgment due to Semple's failure to appear on the required day for pleading.	Semple's defense was that he had complied with the court's requirement to file pleas and therefore should not have been subjected to a default judgment. His argument cited that the plaintiff had no right to call him into court to plead, as his pleas had already been filed. Semple claimed that entering judgment by default was an error based on precedent.

In 1874, in Marshall County, Illinois, Mathew Heneberry initiated an ejectment action against Asa Whitman and others (the appellants) to reclaim a quarter section of land. The case moved to Peoria County for trial, where a jury eventually ruled in favor of Heneberry. To establish his title, Heneberry presented several key documents, including an exemplified copy of a patent from October 21, 1818, originally granted to Mica Clark, as well as a deed from Clark to Jehosophat Eldred dated March 29, 1818, although acknowledged in 1819. A significant piece of evidence was a deed from commissioner Chas. D. Hodges to Heneberry, derived from a partition decree of Pike County court concerning Eldred's heirs. Notably, all original documents burned in 1871, creating challenges in presenting the evidence. The court allowed the ancient deed to be admitted despite claims of improper foundation from the appellants, who argued that the deed’s validity was questionable since it was dated before the patent issuance. The court examined historical evidence surrounding the transaction, ultimately supporting the legitimacy of the documents and title claimed by Heneberry.	Mathew Heneberry, the plaintiff, argued that he had rightful ownership of the land based on the ancient deed from Mica Clark to Jehosophat Eldred, which had been in continuous possession and record for over fifty years. He contended that the evidence showed the deed was executed and delivered properly after the patent was issued, and he successfully established a lawful chain of title through the deceased's heirs. Heneberry sought to recover possession of the land based on both his own title and the prior ownership claims justified by the evidence presented at trial.	The appellants, led by Asa Whitman, contested Heneberry’s claims by asserting that the ancient deed should not have been admitted since it did not meet the legal requirements of authenticity necessary to be treated as evidence. They argued that the deed was effectively void because it was dated before the patent's issuance. Furthermore, they highlighted that the prior proceedings in the partition case may have been flawed, claiming the court made errors in admitting certain evidence, which they believed led to a wrongful judgment in favor of Heneberry.

In 1886, a legal dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, between Milo Covel and Edwin Benjamin, along with Litchfield, over patent rights related to improvements in machines for sharpening saws. The core issue revolved around contracts executed on May 17, 1886, which Covel claimed did not fully encompass the agreements made with Benjamin and Litchfield prior to the contract's execution. Covel argued these earlier negotiations included additional agreements regarding claims held against the firm of Halladay, Litchfield & Co. Although subsequent assignments of such claims were executed in November 1886, there was no new consideration for these assignments, and Covel contended they were part of the original agreement. The evidence presented was complex, involving numerous testimonies and contradictory statements. Ultimately, the lower court concluded that the written contracts from May 17, 1886, represented the complete agreement between the parties, dismissing Covel's claims that additional agreements existed.	Milo Covel claimed that the written contracts executed on May 17, 1886, did not encompass all agreements made with Edwin Benjamin and Litchfield. He argued that prior to signing the contracts, negotiations had established additional commitments, including the assignment of claims against Halladay, Litchfield & Co. Covel sought to enforce these claims as integral to the contract, requesting the court to recognize them in light of the earlier agreements.	Edwin Benjamin and Litchfield defended against Covel's claims by asserting that the written contracts represented the entirety of their agreements and that no additional commitments were made regarding claims against the partnership. They contended that once the contract was finalized, any prior negotiations were legally merged into that writing, making it inadmissible to introduce oral evidence to affect its terms. Their position sought dismissal of Covel’s claims on the grounds that the written document was comprehensive and binding.

The case "The Town of Lake View v. Frederick Letz et al." took place in Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. The Town of Lake View was incorporated in 1857, and by an act in February 1865, its board of trustees was granted various powers, including the authority to abate nuisances. In April 1866, the trustees passed an ordinance prohibiting the establishment of cemeteries within the town without their permission. Frederick Letz and other defendants planned to establish a cemetery within the town, prompting the Town of Lake View to bring this bill in chancery to prevent that action. The initial ruling by the Superior Court dismissed the Town's request to prevent the establishment of the cemetery, leading to this appeal.	The Town of Lake View claimed that the establishment of a cemetery would constitute a nuisance and infringe upon public health. They argued that their ordinance, which required permission for any cemetery openings, was within their duly granted powers to regulate nuisances and protect the community.	The defendants, led by Frederick Letz, contended that the Town's ordinance lacked legal standing and violated their rights. They argued that the proposed cemetery would not necessarily constitute a nuisance and that the issue must be resolved through a trial to determine whether the cemetery would indeed be detrimental. They highlighted that the ordinance could not preemptively ban the establishment of a cemetery without direct evidence of harm.

Charles M. Sherfy filed a case against James M. Graham in January 1874, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute involved an award from arbitrators regarding a financial disagreement. The central issue was about a deposit of $2,900 that Graham had made either individually or with a bank where he served as cashier. The arbitrators ruled in favor of Sherfy, awarding him $2,512.50, leading to Graham's appeal. The case examined if the arbitrators had exceeded their authority by considering matters not specifically included in the submission. Sherfy claimed that Graham owed him the amount, while Graham contended that the bank was liable, not he personally. This disagreement raised questions of jurisdiction over the funds and the role of the arbitrators in making their decision based on the submission's terms.	Sherfy's primary argument was that Graham was personally liable for the full amount of the deposit. He contended that the arbitrators had the appropriate jurisdiction to decide the matter based on the submission, despite Graham's claims that the bank owed Sherfy the funds. Sherfy sought to uphold the arbitrators' decision and collect the awarded amount.	Graham’s defense centered on the assertion that the funds had been deposited with the bank, which should be held accountable for the amount owed to Sherfy. He argued that the arbitrators exceeded their jurisdiction by ruling against him personally for funds that he claimed were obligations of the bank. Graham maintained that there was no evidence of fraud or misconduct by the arbitrators, simply a mistake in understanding the legal relationship regarding the deposits.

This case, titled Milton H. Swift et al. v. Levi Lee et al., took place in September 1872 in De Kalb, Illinois. The key individuals involved included the plaintiffs Milton H. Swift and others, and the defendants Levi Lee and others. The dispute arose over a conveyance of 240 acres of land from Lee to Webster, which the plaintiffs alleged was fraudulent and intended to hinder creditors, specifically in relation to a judgment held against Lee. The plaintiffs claimed they derived title from a judgment and execution against Lee in favor of Harris. The case ultimately progressed to the Illinois Supreme Court after the De Kalb Circuit Court dismissed the plaintiffs' bill for lack of equity. The plaintiffs challenged this dismissal, arguing issues regarding the sufficiency of legal descriptions in titles and the legitimacy of the original execution sales.	The plaintiffs, Swift and his party, argued that the conveyance from Lee to Webster should be set aside due to allegations of fraud, claiming it was made to defraud Lee's creditors. They sought to establish that the sale made under the judgment held by Harris was legitimate and that the attorney's appearance in the attachment suit should have been sufficient to confer jurisdiction over Lee, despite his attorney's assertion of limited representation.	The defendants, represented by Lee, contended that the plaintiffs lacked valid title to the land due to insufficient descriptions and questioned the jurisdiction of the original court proceedings. They argued that any purported appearance of Lee in the attachment case was invalid, and the legal descriptions in the sheriff's deeds were inadequate to support the plaintiffs' claims of title, thereby rendering the execution sales void.

In the case of **Samuel H. Crowl v. Francis C. Nagle et al.**, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the legal proceedings initiated in June 1872 aimed to enforce a mechanic's lien. The complainant in the case was Francis C. Nagle, with defendants including Clarissa Filkins, John L. Manning, Charles P. Marsh, and later Samuel H. Crowl. During the litigation, Crowl was added as a defendant after the petition was amended in November 1875. The legal issues arose from a trust deed executed by Clarissa Filkins in favor of Edwin Rogers on January 16, 1873, which secured a loan of $1,000. Rogers sold the property to Crowl after Filkins defaulted on the payment. Crowl contended that the enforcement of the mechanic's lien was initiated too late, as the claims against him came more than two years after the last payment for labor and materials was due, violating the statutory requirement to file within six months after the last payment became due. The case was appealed after the circuit court ruled in favor of the mechanic's lien, ordering the sale of Crowl’s interest in the property.	The plaintiff, Francis C. Nagle, claimed that a mechanic's lien was validly filed and sought to enforce it against all parties who had an interest in the property, including Crowl. Nagle contended that the original suit against the other defendants was initiated within the six-month statutory period after the last payment had become due and that Crowl’s subsequent addition as a party did not prejudice the enforceability of the lien against him.	The defendant, Samuel H. Crowl, argued that the attempt to enforce the mechanic's lien was invalid as he was not included in the suit within the six-month timeframe stipulated by the statute. He asserted that since he was not made a party until more than two years after the relevant contract, the lien should not apply to him. Crowl claimed that the proceedings initiated against him were prejudicial and that the statute required strict compliance to protect creditors' interests.

In 1834, in Gallatin County, Illinois, Alexander Swan contested a property levy executed in favor of Jesse Pearce and Lavina Sharp, who were seeking to recover goods they claimed belonged to them as executors of William Sharp's estate. An execution issued by a justice of the peace had authorized the constable to levy on Swan's personal property. Following the levy, Swan notified the constable that the levied property belonged to him, effectively forbidding its sale. This prompted a trial to determine the rightful ownership of the property. Initially, a jury found in favor of Pearce and Sharp; however, Swan appealed this decision to the Gallatin Circuit Court. During subsequent proceedings, in April 1835, the Circuit Court jury reversed the initial verdict, concluding that the property belonged to Swan and ordered its return to him, along with recovery of his legal costs. Pearce and Sharp subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, challenging the Circuit Court’s judgment.	Jesse Pearce and Lavina Sharp contended that Swan's notification to the constable was inadequate as it incorrectly referenced the execution in favor of John Pearce instead of themselves. They argued that the appeal bond had not been executed properly on the day of the trial, and claimed the judgment was confusing regarding whom it was rendered against.	Alexander Swan maintained that his notice to the constable was sufficient under the law and did not need to specify whose execution the levy was under. He argued that any objections to the notice should have been raised earlier and that Pearce and Sharp waived their rights to contest the irregularity of the appeal by appearing in the Circuit Court without objection. Swan further clarified that the judgment for costs was correctly applied in his favor.

In September 1872, the case of Archibald McCoy v. The People of the State of Illinois was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case stemmed from allegations of bastardy, as the complainant alleged that McCoy was the father of her child, born on August 15, 1871. She claimed that the child resulted from a single act of illicit intercourse with McCoy in late November 1870. The complainant asserted that this was the only instance of intercourse she had experienced with him or any other man. McCoy, the defendant, denied the allegations entirely and testified to the contrary. Furthermore, a witness for the defendant stated that he had engaged in sexual relations with the complainant frequently during October and November 1870, and that she had notified him of her pregnancy. Additional witnesses corroborated that they had seen the complainant engaged in sexual acts with another individual around the same time.
