The defendant, The Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company, contended that the plaintiff could not maintain the trespass action because the properties were occupied by his tenants at the time of the alleged trespass. They argued that, under legal principles, only the party in actual possession (the tenants) could bring a trespass action. Therefore, they requested the court to dismiss Halligan's claims based on the grounds that he lacked standing to sue as he did not possess the premises when the alleged trespass occurred.

In June 1851, in Peoria, Illinois, John Rankin (the plaintiff) filed an action of ejectment against Alfred G. Curtenius and others (the defendants) to recover possession of a specific lot discussed as covered by French Claim seventy. The trial involved various pieces of evidence presented by the plaintiff, including a patent from the United States dated December 11, 1849, which indicated that the claim was entered under the name of Louis Pensoneau by Augustine Laroche as the settler. Rankin's evidence also included a deed from Laroche to Louis Pensoneau and subsequent transfers to Rankin. The defendants contested Rankin’s ownership, presenting a report from the register of the Land Office that described the lot claimed by Louis Pensoneau. The court, at the instigation of the defendants, excluded all of the plaintiff’s evidence from the jury. Consequently, Rankin submitted to a nonsuit but later moved to have that nonsuit set aside, a motion the court denied. The case ultimately revolved around the validity of the patent and the right to the claim based on past ownership.	John Rankin argued that he had established ownership of the lot through valid evidence, including a federal patent, deeds from legal heirs of previous owners, and rightful claim to the property as per the laws governing land in Illinois. Rankin sought a reversal of the nonsuit and aimed to present his case in full to the jury to validate his claim legally.	The defendants contended that the court properly excluded the plaintiff's evidence, arguing that the patent was invalid because it was not issued to the real claimant or their legal representatives. They asserted that Louis Pensoneau was the sole claimant and that the patent issued did not confer rights to Rankin. Additionally, they maintained that the plaintiff voluntarily submitted to a nonsuit and thus could not challenge the court’s ruling on the evidence exclusion.

The case "Lucy M. Doolittle et al. v. Joshua C. Jenkins et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1870, originating from Whiteside County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Lucy M. Doolittle, the grantee of the property, and Joshua and Wilson Jenkins, the judgment creditors. The case stemmed from previous debts owed by Henry and Martin Bush, who conveyed real estate to Mrs. Doolittle in 1866. In consideration of this transfer, Mrs. Doolittle was to pay $1,000 to settle Bush’s debts, including the Jenkins' judgment. A mutual agreement was made where E.G.L. Allen would receive $1,500 from Mrs. Doolittle to pay these debts. However, Allen only partially settled the obligations and retained a portion of the money, without paying the Jenkins. Subsequently, the Jenkins filed a bill in chancery to subject the property to sale in satisfaction of their judgment, claiming a vendor's lien over the property. The court had to determine if such a lien existed and explore the trust created by the arrangement involving Allen.	The plaintiffs, Joshua and Wilson Jenkins, claimed that a vendor's lien existed on the property conveyed to Mrs. Doolittle, asserting their right to be subrogated to the rights of Henry and Martin Bush, the original property owners. They contended that this lien should enable them to collect on their previous judgment against Bush by selling the property in question.	The defendant, Mrs. Doolittle, contended that no vendor's lien existed because the grantor, Bush, believed that the judgment had been satisfied at the time of the conveyance. She argued that Allen, having received the money, was a trustee for the creditors and had failed to execute the trust by not settling the debts. Thus, she should not be held liable as a vendor under the intent of the transaction.

In June 1870, the case of Alexander Bissett v. John B. Bowman was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from an ejectment action initiated by Bissett in the St. Clair circuit court. The case centered on the recovery of lot five in block four of Illinoistown. Key individuals involved included Alexander Bissett, the plaintiff, and John B. Bowman, the defendant. The trial occurred in October 1869, resulting in a verdict favoring Bissett. Significant evidence included a series of deeds related to the lot, including a 1816 deed from Pensonneau to McKnight and Brady and a partition deed executed in 1821 that conveyed the lot to McKnight in severalty. Additionally, evidence was presented concerning the 1831-1832 proceedings involving Thomas McKnight, who was the administrator of John McKnight's estate. The defendant contested the introduction of certain evidence, arguing it was insufficient to identify the specific lot in question. Following a detailed examination of the evidence and objections, the court determined that the plaintiff failed to establish a clear title to the property through the administrator's sale.	The plaintiff, Alexander Bissett, argued that he possessed rightful title to lot five through a series of legal documents indicating ownership transferred from deceased parties to himself. Bissett sought to prove that the lot was sold under a proper administrator's sale and aimed to recover possession of the land based on this alleged title.	John B. Bowman, the defendant, contended that the evidence presented by Bissett was deficient in identifying the specific lot in question. He argued that the administrator's sale did not adequately describe the property sold and maintained that the reports of the administrator were not approved by the court, questioning their validity as proof of ownership.

In November 1856, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case of Ellender Masterson et al. v. Rufus D. Wiswould et ux. This case originated when the plaintiffs, heirs of Benjamin T. Masterson, filed a bill to quiet title on a parcel of land in Monroe County, Illinois. They claimed ownership by arguing that Sarah Wiswould is the sole surviving heir of Amelia Masterson, who acquired the land through a partition order in 1817. The plaintiffs alleged that a will left by Benjamin T. Masterson, who had died in 1853, devised the land to Ellender Masterson for her lifetime and to her children thereafter. They sought to cancel this will's claim to the land and requested that others be enjoined from asserting title against it. The case was heard at the September term of the Monroe Circuit Court, where the court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, enjoining the defendants from claiming any title to the land.	The plaintiffs argued that they are the rightful owners of the land in question, asserting that Sarah, as the sole heir of Amelia Masterson, has inherited the property. They contended that the title should not be recognized under Benjamin T. Masterson's will, which bequeathed the land to Ellender Masterson during her life, and sought a decree to cancel that will concerning the land. Their request included protections against any other claims to the property.	The defendants, who were in possession of the land, contended that there was insufficient legal proof to support the plaintiffs' claim, particularly regarding the existence and validity of the will cited. They argued that since the plaintiffs did not establish that their claims were derived from the will and provided only parol evidence of its existence, the decree against them lacked a solid basis. They requested that the decree be reversed and that they should not bear the costs since the burden of proof had not been met.

The case "The Grover & Baker Sewing Machine Company v. Aristarchus Bulkley" originated from a contract dispute that arose in August 1864, in Chicago, Illinois. The Grover & Baker Sewing Machine Company entered into a written agreement with Aristarchus Bulkley, appointing him as their agent for one year, effective from August 8, 1864, with a salary of one thousand dollars payable monthly. Initially stationed in St. Louis, Bulkley expressed dissatisfaction with his pay in April 1866 and notified the company he would quit his position. He argued for a higher wage based on his contributions, claiming he was underpaid in comparison to bookkeepers who had lesser responsibilities. In response, the company contended that due to a downturn in business, they could not accommodate his salary demands. Subsequently, Bulkley left his position on May 8, 1866, and later pursued legal action to claim unpaid wages. The trial court ruled in favor of Bulkley, but the Grover & Baker Sewing Machine Company appealed the verdict, arguing the contract's terms governed the payments due.	The Grover & Baker Sewing Machine Company claimed that the trial court incorrectly instructed the jury regarding the payment obligations under the original contract. They argued that Bulkley was only entitled to the specified salary of one thousand dollars per annum, plus a potential increase that was contingent upon the company's business performance, which had not materially improved. The company sought a reversal of the judgment that favored Bulkley, arguing that he had not adequately violated the terms that would entitled him to a higher salary.	Aristarchus Bulkley maintained that the company owed him payments that exceeded the original contract amount due to his prolonged service beyond the contract's expiration. He argued the disparity in pay compared to other employees was unjust and that he was deserving of higher wages based on his efforts and responsibilities. His claims included a detailed calculation demonstrating a balance owed to him by the company, asserting that he had consistently strived to manage the company’s interests effectively.

In 1863, in Momence, Illinois, James Mix entered into a written agreement to sell the north half of lot 4 in block 44 to Sarah Balduc for $50, promising to execute the deed upon her payment within three years. This transaction was conducted through an interpreter due to Balduc's inability to read or speak English. In 1861, Mix had initially agreed to sell the same lot to Balduc's husband, Alexander Deslauries, who improved and occupied the property until his death in 1862. After Mix's agreement in 1863, Balduc lived on the property but did not make an offer to pay until 1866, significantly after the stipulated three-year term. The court findings revealed a delay and inconsistency regarding the payment timeline as well as Balduc's competence in understanding the agreement. The court had to determine whether the agreement was enforceable and if Mix had waived the time requirement for payment due to recognizing Balduc's occupancy and tax payments.	Sarah Balduc, the plaintiff, claims that her right to compel the conveyance of the lot was valid despite her delay in payment, asserting that the agreement granted her four years for payment, which had not been effectively communicated by Mix. She argued that Mix's acknowledgment of her occupancy and payment of taxes constituted a waiver of the strict payment timelines outlined in the agreement, thus seeking specific performance to enforce the sale of the property.	James Mix, the defendant, contended that Balduc's delay in offering payment for over three years precluded her right to seek specific performance. He argued that she had not made a valid offer within the agreed timeframe and that the written agreement did not imply mutual obligation since Balduc had built structures on the property and made tax payments only after that period. Mix maintained that the writing clearly outlined a three-year limit for payment, which Balduc had exceeded without an excuse.

In 1874, in the city of Monmouth, Illinois, Vinton G. Harbaugh was implicated in an action brought by the City to recover a penalty for selling spirituous liquors in violation of local ordinances. The case began before a police magistrate, where Harbaugh was found guilty. He subsequently appealed to the circuit court, where a jury rendered a verdict against him, ordering him to pay a fine of $200. The Ordinance in question prohibited the sale of liquor within the city limits, with exceptions for medicinal and other non-beverage uses. Harbaugh's primary argument rested on the claim that the ordinance was beyond the authority granted to the city by its charter. Ultimately, the case was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court, which evaluated the legality of the ordinance and Harbaugh's assertions regarding its validity.	The plaintiff, the City of Monmouth, claimed that Harbaugh sold spirituous liquors in violation of the city's ordinance, which deemed such sales a nuisance. The City sought to enforce the ordinance and recover penalties from Harbaugh for his illegal sales, asserting that the city council had the authority to impose such regulations under its charter.	Harbaugh contended that the ordinance was ultra vires (beyond legal authority) and argued that it prohibited all sales of intoxicating liquors regardless of the exceptions for medicinal or mechanical purposes provided in the charter. He suggested that the ordinance should not apply to him as he maintained that he only sold liquor for purposes allowed by law.

The case "The Central City Horse Railway Company, etc. v. The Fort Clark Horse Railway Company" arose in Peoria, Illinois, with a timeline extending from 1867 to 1876. The Central City Horse Railway Company was incorporated following an 1867 act enabling horse railways' construction. After obtaining city council permission in 1869, they built and began operating a horse railway on Adams Street in December 1870, incurring expenses around $80,000. Subsequently, in 1872, the Fort Clark Horse Railway Company was formed, and the Peoria city council authorized it to construct a railway on several streets, but notably not on Adams Street, which was already occupied by the complainants. In 1874, the Fort Clark company sought a city ordinance to run its railroad on Adams Street, prompting the Central City company to file for an injunction to prevent what they believed would be irreparable harm to their franchise. Initially, an injunction was granted but was later dissolved; Central City appealed, leading to the Supreme Court of Illinois examining the rights of both companies regarding eminent domain and competition.	The Central City Horse Railway Company claimed that the Fort Clark Horse Railway’s attempt to operate on Adams Street violated their established rights and would undermine the value of their existing franchise. They argued that allowing a competing company to interfere in this manner compromised their operation and profitability, effectively destroying their investment in the railway. They requested an injunction to prevent the Fort Clark company from using their tracks and argued that only a complete transfer of rights could justify any such action.	The Fort Clark Horse Railway Company defended its position by asserting that current laws permitted them to seek the use of tracks through eminent domain and that they sought only a minor portion of the Central City Railway's operation. They contended that this action promoted public interest by potentially expanding transportation options within Peoria, despite Central City's claims of impending harm to their business.

In 1856 in Oregon, Ogle County, Illinois, an action of replevin was initiated by Jonathan H. Ransom and others against William Davis. The controversy arose when Davis, acting as the marshal of the northern district of Illinois, seized a stock of goods belonging to Edmund P. Sexton under an execution issued from the United States Court for the Northern District of Illinois. Sexton, who had executed a chattel mortgage for the goods to Ransom and the other plaintiffs, was in significant debt. The chattel mortgage allowed Sexton to retain possession of the goods while he sold them to pay off his debts, with a promise to pay the plaintiffs from the proceeds. However, the plaintiffs claimed ownership of the goods based on this mortgage. The case revolved around whether the mortgage was valid against creditors and if the plaintiffs held rightful ownership of the goods, particularly given that the mortgage terms may have hindered the collection of Sexton's debts. The plaintiffs produced evidence of the mortgage during the trial. A jury originally ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, resulting in a small damage award.	The plaintiffs, Ransom and others, claimed ownership of the goods based on the chattel mortgage executed by Sexton, which was presented as evidence. They argued that despite Sexton's retention of possession to sell the goods, they had a rightful claim to the property, as reflected in the mortgage's terms, which stipulated payments to them as preferred creditors. They sought a reversal of any ruling that denied their claim, arguing that the mortgage granted them a legal interest in the goods.	William Davis, as the defendant, defended his actions by asserting that he lawfully seized the goods under the execution issued by the circuit court as the marshal. He contended that the chattel mortgage was void because it did not comply with statutory requirements for mortgages to be valid against third parties. Davis argued that the mortgage effectively represented a delay against Sexton’s other creditors by allowing him to keep the goods and sell them despite his inability to pay his debts. His defense hinged on the legal flaws in the plaintiffs' claims regarding the mortgage.

In 1873, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of William H. Hoyt v. Jacob R. Shipherd et al. unfolded in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case emerged as an action of assumpsit, where the plaintiffs, Jacob E. Shipherd and Benjamin J. Sweet, sought to recover commissions for a real estate sale that they alleged they had executed on behalf of the defendant, William H. Hoyt. The plaintiffs claimed to have sold property for a price of $48,000, with specific payment terms laid out, but the sale was not brought to completion as the purchaser refused to proceed due to concerns regarding the title. During the trial, the jury ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $1,200. However, Hoyt challenged this ruling, claiming there were errors in allowing the jury to hear evidence regarding the contract and that the verdict was not supported by sufficient evidence.	The plaintiffs argued that they were duly authorized agents for Hoyt to sell the property and had negotiated a sale for $48,000, with terms that included a commission of two and a half percent. They sought to recover the commission of $1,200 after the sale fell through due to claims of a defective title, asserting that they had acted within their authority and that any issues with the title were not their responsibility.	Hoyt contended that the sale was unauthorized because the terms under which the plaintiffs attempted to sell the property exceeded the authority granted to them. He argued that the initial agreement required one-third of the payment to be made in cash, while the plaintiffs allowed a twenty-day grace period for this payment. Additionally, he claimed that he had not ratified the contract and emphasized that the plaintiffs were not entitled to commissions since no sale was effectively made, thus no benefit was gained by him.

John Turney, as the administrator of William Campbell's estate, and other plaintiffs brought forth a petition for a mechanic's lien in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1843. The case originated when William Campbell, who held a right of pre-emption on a tract of public land, hired contractors Crook and Saunders in October 1839 to construct a building known as Argyle Cottage. The work continued until August 1841. Plaintiffs asserted that Campbell owed them a balance of $306.75 after receiving a partial payment of $180. Subsequently, William Campbell transferred his interest to John W. Campbell while still maintaining the pre-emption right with the U.S. Government. The petition claimed that the materials and labor provided gave rise to a lien under Illinois law, specifically an act passed in 1839. The circuit court initially overruled a demurrer to the petition and later directed a jury to assess damages against Campbell’s administrators, resulting in a verdict in favor of the plaintiffs, which led to an appeal by the defendants.	The plaintiffs claimed they were entitled to a mechanic's lien for their labor and materials used in constructing a building for William Campbell. They argued that they fulfilled their contractual obligations but were owed an outstanding balance. Their legal request included seeking a lien on the property and initiating sale proceedings to recover the debt.	The defendants, including the administrators of William Campbell’s estate, contended that the petition should have been dismissed based on a lack of sufficient property description and the argument that no lien could attach because the land was still technically owned by the United States. They also claimed procedural errors during the judgment process, asserting that the court improperly ordered assessments and did not duly consider their demurrer.

Hiram H. Rosencrantz filed a legal case against William W. Mason in Macon County, Illinois, which was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1877. The dispute centered around three promissory notes: the first note, dated April 1, 1872, was for $368 payable one day after date, and accrued interest at a rate of ten percent per annum. The second note, dated May 5, 1870, was originally payable to Anderson Bradley, who assigned it to Rosencrantz, for the amount of $14, with similar interest conditions. The third note, dated April 2, 1872, was for $95, also accruing ten percent interest, due nine months later. The plaintiff brought an assumpsit (a legal action for breach of contract) against the defendant, seeking recovery on these notes. The defendant opposed these claims by bringing forth a general denial and a set-off. The case was heard without a jury, resulting in a judgment for the plaintiff after the court allowed credit for specific amounts, totaling $641.65 against the principal and accrued interest due.	The plaintiff, Hiram H. Rosencrantz, claimed that William W. Mason failed to pay the amounts due on three promissory notes. He sought a judicial confirmation of the total outstanding balance of $641.65, inclusive of principal and interest, asserting that the promissory notes were valid and enforceable.	William W. Mason, the defendant, claimed that he should be entitled to additional credits beyond those acknowledged by the court during the trial. He contended that the evidence presented, including discussions regarding the settlement of accounts and the circumstances surrounding the promissory notes, warranted a reassessment of the credits he should receive, thereby disputing the plaintiff's claims regarding the outstanding balance.

In the case of George W. Temple v. Ingar Freed, decided on August 26, 1886, in Champaign County, Illinois, the core issue revolved around the rights of a married woman regarding property exemptions under Illinois law. The case involved George W. Temple as the appellant and Ingar Freed as the appellee. The appellant contended that the appellee, a married woman living with her husband, was not entitled to claim her property as exempt from execution based on the traditional view that her husband serves as the head of the family. However, it was established that the appellee's husband had previously suffered from mental illness, significantly impairing his ability to support the family. At the time of the case, although he lived at home, he contributed little to the family's upkeep. The appellee actively managed the family's farm, handling various tasks and financial responsibilities, which led to the argument that she effectively became the head of the family. The court ultimately evaluated whether this circumstance would allow her to claim property exemptions typically reserved for family heads under Illinois law.	The plaintiff, George W. Temple, argued that Ingar Freed should not be recognized as the head of the family simply because she lived with her husband. He sought to establish that the husband retained the title of family head and, consequently, Freed should not have been entitled to property exemptions as outlined in Illinois law.	Ingar Freed, the defendant, argued that due to her husband's mental health issues, he was unable to fulfill the traditional role of the head of the family. She maintained that she had assumed full control of the family's financial and operational responsibilities, which qualified her to be considered the head of the family under the law, thereby justifying her claim for exemption from property execution.

The case of The Chicago and North-western Railway Company v. Albert T. Ames et al took place in April 1866 in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Albert T. Ames and Ambrose D. Turner, brought an action of assumpsit against the Chicago and North-western Railway Company, a common carrier, for failing to deliver their livestock—a shipment of sixty hogs and nineteen cattle—originally intrusted to the railway for transport from Belvidere, Boone County, to Chicago. Upon arrival at the Sherman yards in Chicago, the plaintiffs found that their livestock had been incorrectly delivered to a third-party, P.J. Garcelon, due to a clerical error where the railway company combined the shipments of both parties under one bill of charges. This resulted in the plaintiffs losing their cattle and hogs, worth a total of $1,860, plus interest. The court found negligence on the part of the railway’s clerk, and the plaintiffs sought compensation for their lost property.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Chicago and North-western Railway Company failed in their duty as common carriers by incorrectly combining the shipments and delivering their livestock to the wrong person. They argued that this negligence resulted in a loss of their property and unfairly deprived them of its value. The plaintiffs sought to recover damages for the value of the livestock, totaling $1,860, along with interest on this amount from the time of the loss.	The defendant, Chicago and North-western Railway Company, contended that the mistake leading to the loss of the plaintiffs' property was an error made by a clerk in the station agent’s office. They argued that the circumstances fell outside their control and, therefore, they should not be held liable for the loss of the livestock. The defense likely sought to minimize accountability or potentially contest the amount of damages claimed by the plaintiffs.

Thomas Renwick et al. v. Horace P. Hall et al. took place in DeKalb County, Illinois, around September 1876. The case involved the trustees of schools from two adjacent towns who attempted to establish a new school district by taking territory from existing districts in both towns. The appellants, who were the owners of real estate in the older districts and the new district, filed a bill in equity in the circuit court claiming that the establishment of this new district was irregular and illegal. They argued that no lawful new district had been formed and that the directors of this new district were planning to incur debts to build a new school, which could create an improper burden on their properties. They sought an injunction to prevent the directors and public officials from recognizing the new district's legal existence and from contracting any debts related to the construction of a schoolhouse. The circuit court dissolved the injunction and dismissed the complaint, prompting an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, represented by Thomas Renwick and others, argued that the establishment of the new school district was fraught with legal irregularities, asserting that it did not meet the criteria established by law for creating a valid school district. They claimed that the proposed contracting of debts for a new school would unfairly impose burdens on their properties. They requested an injunction against the recognition of the new district and to prohibit the directors from undertaking any financial commitments related to the construction of a new educational facility.	The defendants, represented by Horace P. Hall and others, contended that the challenges presented by the plaintiffs were merely technical and did not merit the intervention of a court of equity. They argued that any objections regarding the legality of the new district could be addressed through appropriate legal remedies, such as a quo warranto proceeding. They maintained that the plaintiffs had not presented sufficient grounds to establish that the court should have jurisdiction over the matter, suggesting that the legal existence of the new school district could be tested through other legal avenues.

The case of Ruth Campbell et al. v. George W. Campbell et al. took place in Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court on October 31, 1889. The central issue revolved around a will attributed to Joshua Neely, who had passed away. The plaintiffs, led by Euth Campbell and other heirs of Neely, sought to contest the validity of the will on the grounds of the testator's lack of testamentary capacity and undue influence exercised by Charles W. Enos and others. Enos, named as executor in the will, ultimately declined to act in that capacity and filed a disclaimer related to any interest in the estate. The plaintiffs argued that this nullified his position as a key party in the case. Key testimonies came from various witnesses related to the Neely family, revealing disagreements over Neely's mental competence at the time of the will's execution, as well as issues related to the admissibility of certain testimonies due to interests the witnesses had in the estate. The court faced errors regarding witness competence and jury instructions focused on testamentary capacity.	The plaintiffs contended that Joshua Neely lacked the requisite testamentary capacity to execute a valid will, which they argued was underscored by evidence of his mental deterioration. They further claimed that undue influence was exerted upon Neely, primarily by Charles W. Enos, leading him to create the contested will. This prompted them to seek the annulment of the will in favor of a fair distribution of the estate in line with state intestacy laws.	The defendants, including Charles W. Enos, argued that Neely was competent to make a will, citing that mere mental impairment did not equate to a lack of testamentary capacity. They maintained that Enos's disclaimer of interest in the estate justified his removal from the suit, thereby contesting the plaintiffs' views on Enos's influence. The defense also focused on the exclusion of the testimony from certain witnesses due to conflicting interests, contending that their exclusion was justified as they could gain if the will were set aside.

Edmond Campbell was involved in a legal dispute concerning surety on three promissory notes totaling $695, made by his son John F. Campbell, payable to Jefferson Vining and T. R. Vanmeter, dated October 6, 1851. Two notes for $297.50 each were due on July 1, 1852, and one note for $100 was due on December 25, 1851. Edmond made payments on the notes in the summer and fall of 1852 and the summer of 1853, but was unaware that they had already been paid by John to Vanmeter. The suit was initiated on March 26, 1859, after he failed to present his claim during the estate's adjustment period of Thomas Vanmeter, who had passed away. The primary legal issue was whether Edmond's claim was barred by the statute of limitations due to the delay in bringing the action after the notes were paid.	Edmond Campbell claimed that he was entitled to recover the amounts he had paid on the notes, arguing that he should be allowed to assert his claim against the defendant due to fraud or mistake in the non-disclosure of the payment by the principal debtor (his son). He contended that the statute of limitations should not bar his claim because he did not discover the essential facts regarding the payment until shortly before filing the case.	Jefferson Vining, the defendant, argued against the plaintiff's claims, asserting that the action was barred by the statute of limitations. Vining maintained that he had no knowledge of the payments made by John F. Campbell and that the plaintiff failed to inform himself of his rights concerning the notes. As a result, the defendant contended that fraud could not be asserted against the statute of limitations.

In 1857, in Quincy, Illinois, Robert S. Benneson and his company engaged in a settlement with William B. Thayer and his brother Sylvester Thayer, of the firm S. and W. B. Thayer. The plaintiff, represented by Corrill, brought an account against William B. Thayer amounting to $815.77 for labor and materials, along with another claim against S. and W. B. Thayer for $73.46. Acknowledging a mutual debt of $40.40 owed by Benneson to the Thayers, the amount owed was adjusted, reflected in a promissory note issued by S. and W. B. Thayer in payment of the remaining balance owed to Benneson & Co. This transaction followed their customary practice for settling accounts, which had previously involved the consolidation of debts between the firms. However, S. and W. B. Thayer later experienced financial difficulties, leading to a sale of the property upon which improvements funded by the plaintiffs were conducted. The plaintiffs subsequently sought enforcement of a mechanics' lien for their claim.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to enforce a mechanics' lien for the work and materials they provided to William B. Thayer. They claimed that the promissory note received in their settlement did not adequately settle their lien rights for the improvements made. They sought to hold the property where the improvements were made accountable for the payment of their outstanding claim.	The defendants contended that the promissory note issued was proper and constituted full payment for the claims brought by the plaintiffs. They argued that the settlement was made in accordance with their usual business practices and that the plaintiffs did not demand security beyond the note. Furthermore, they asserted that a mechanics' lien could not be maintained after the settlement was finalized.

The case, "The Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company v. Robert Hervey and Frances W. Hervey, et ux.", was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1864. The plaintiff, initially Frances W. Smith and later Robert Hervey through marriage, filed the action against the Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company in Chicago. The dispute arose over an insurance policy originally issued to Thomas B. Bishop. On October 22, 1859, Bishop sold the insured property to Frances W. Smith. The defendants (the insurance company) consented to an assignment of the policy and issued a renewal certificate, which stated the risk would continue for another year in exchange for a premium payment of $45. On August 19, 1860, the property was lost to fire, prompting Smith to submit a claim for the damages incurred. The trial resulted in a verdict for the plaintiff, which the defendants appealed, claiming that the action of assumpsit could not be maintained in Smith's name based on the policy issued to Bishop.	The plaintiff claimed that she was entitled to the insurance benefits because she had paid the premium for the renewal of the insurance policy and had a valid assignment from Bishop. The plaintiff argued that the defendants became obligated to cover the damages for the loss that occurred during the insurance term. She maintained that the insurance company had entered into a new contract with her upon accepting the premium for the renewal of the coverage and that this contract was legally binding, allowing her to pursue a claim in her own name.	The defendants contended that the original insurance policy issued to Bishop was the only valid contract, and thus, the plaintiff, as an assignee of the policy, could not bring suit in her own name. They argued that the policy, being a sealed instrument, was not assignable under common law principles. The defendants insisted that the renewal merely continued the risk associated with the original contract and did not constitute a new agreement with the plaintiff. Consequently, no valid contract existed between the insurance company and Frances W. Smith that would permit her to maintain the action.

In December 1853, the case of Edward Cummerford and his wife, Bridget Cummerford, against Daniel McAvoy was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident took place in Jacksonville, Illinois, where Bridget Cummerford was accused of theft. The case stemmed from a conversation wherein the defendant, McAvoy, allegedly slandered Bridget by asserting that she had stolen items from a store and a trunk belonging to Dennis Shields. The plaintiffs claimed that these statements were false, malicious, and damaging to Bridget's reputation. Witnesses were called, including James Gorman, who testified that McAvoy mentioned Bridget's alleged thefts, and Patrick Devine, who claimed he had heard about Bridget's actions but did not affirm that she committed theft. The defense introduced evidence suggesting that Bridget had indeed taken items without proper authority. The jury ultimately returned a verdict for the defendant, stating that McAvoy did not act with malice in repeating the accusations.	The Cummerfords claimed that McAvoy slandered Bridget by accusing her of theft in public. They argued that McAvoy's statements, made in the presence of James Gorman, were false and malicious, leading to damage to Bridget's character. The plaintiffs sought damages for the slanderous remarks and contended that McAvoy acted with malice.	McAvoy defended against the slander claims by pleading not guilty and contending that Bridget Cummerford had actually stolen items from both the store and Shields' trunk. He argued that he was merely repeating what he had heard from others, specifically Patrick Devine, and did not intend to defame Bridget. His defense asserted that he acted without malice, which would absolve him of liability.

The case "Samuel Grubb v. William B. Crane" took place in December 1841 in Sangamon County, Illinois. Samuel Grubb, as the defendant in an earlier case, was involved in a legal conflict concerning two tracts of land originally owned by William B. Crane, who sold the land to Grubb for $1,800, receiving promissory notes in return. Grubb paid the first note but failed to pay the full amount of the second. After recovering a judgment for the unpaid balance of $964.25, Crane sought to enforce the judgment through the sale of the land when Grubb possessed no other property to satisfy the debt. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of Crane, leading to Grubb’s filing of a bill of review to reverse that decree. The case progressed through various legal arguments regarding the execution of the judgment, the legitimacy of the court's procedures, and the rights of Crane as a vendor. The legitimacy of taking the bill pro confesso and other procedural nuances formed the basis of the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Samuel Grubb claimed he was wrongfully denied the opportunity to contest the original chancery proceeding in which William B. Crane was awarded a decree for the sale of the tracts. He argued that Crane was bound to execute a deed for the land after partial payment of the notes and insisted that the court had erred in allowing the bill to be taken pro confesso and in approving the commissioner’s sale.	William B. Crane defended the actions of the court, asserting that he had the right to choose among multiple legal remedies to satisfy his judgement and was not obligated to execute a deed for the lands to Grubb. Crane argued that the bill taken pro confesso was in accordance with court rules and that dismissal of the bill of review was appropriate because Grubb had not provided a sufficient defense to challenge the original decree.

In April 1862, in Whiteside County, Illinois, a legal case arose between Ferdinand B. Hubbard (Appellant) and Renselear M. Firman (Appellee). The dispute involved an award made by Solomon Hubbard concerning a real estate transaction. The underlying contract stipulated that Hubbard would pay Firman an additional amount on top of previous payments for a specific lot described in the contract. Following a trial, a jury found in favor of Firman, awarding him $1,600. Hubbard's legal representation subsequently filed motions for an arrest of judgment and for a new trial, both of which were denied by the court. Consequently, Hubbard appealed the court's decisions, arguing that the arbitrator failed to account for previous payments made on the land when arriving at the award amount.	The plaintiff, Renselear M. Firman, claimed that Ferdinand B. Hubbard was obligated to pay the amount determined by the arbitrator, Solomon Hubbard, for a specific parcel of land. Firman contended that the award was in strict accordance with the terms outlined in their agreement, and he requested that the court uphold the jury's verdict of $1,600.	The defendant, Ferdinand B. Hubbard, argued that the arbitrator had deviated from the terms of the submission by not considering prior payments made for the land. Additionally, Hubbard suggested that the evidence presented regarding the consideration named in the deed was vague, ultimately asserting that the award should not be upheld due to this lack of clarity. He requested that the judgment be reversed and the case be remanded for further proceedings.

The case "The International Bank of Chicago v. Joseph H. Bowen et al." was decided in September 1875 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the International Bank of Chicago as the plaintiff, Joseph H. Bowen, and others as defendants, including Ira Holmes and Fred. H. Pieper. The dispute arose from the refusal of the lower court to foreclose a deed of trust executed by Bowen to secure two promissory notes worth $5,000 each. Bowen had secured the notes through a deed of trust to a trustee, Henry M. Ketchum. The complications began following subsequent transactions involving Bowen and another individual, Benjamin F. Guyton, who also executed a deed of trust for his own promissory notes. The property was sold to Henry E. Pickett, who assumed the payments on both deeds of trust. Pickett later obtained a loan of $5,000 from the International Bank, pledging Bowen's notes as collateral. The crux of the issue was whether the Bowen notes had been paid or were still enforceable when the bank extended credit to Pickett. The defendants claimed the notes were paid, while the bank alleged they were misled into believing the notes were still valid liens. The court ultimately had to determine the effects of allegations relating to estoppel and the enforceability of the trust deed.	The International Bank of Chicago, as the plaintiff, claimed that it was misled into believing that the Bowen notes were unpaid and that the deed of trust remained in effect when it granted a $5,000 loan to Pickett. The bank sought to foreclose on the trust deed to secure its loan repayment and any additional outstanding debts owed by Pickett. The central argument was based on the assertion that the defendants' representations led the bank to extend credit under the incorrect belief that the underlying obligations were still valid.	The defendants argued that the Bowen notes had been paid before being pledged to the bank, which would extinguish the corresponding trust deed. They contended that as a result, the bank was not entitled to foreclose. The defendants highlighted that the bank had prior notice of the payment and the release of the trust deed, which undermined any claims of valid collateral. They maintained that the bank’s understanding was flawed due to its failure to consider the actual condition of the notes and the related releases.

Jonathan Booth filed an action of ejectment against John Cook in April 1858, located in Marshall County, Illinois. Booth sought to recover a specific parcel of land described as the east half of the north-west quarter of section twenty-six, in township thirty north, range two west of the third principal meridian. To establish his claim, Booth presented a certified copy of a deed from Joseph L. James and others to Cephas Mills, dated January 3, 1837. This deed was contested by Cook, who argued that Booth had not provided sufficient justification for the absence of the original document. In response, Booth submitted an affidavit stating that he had never possessed the original deed and did not know its whereabouts. The court overruled Cook's objection and admitted the copy of the deed. Booth further attempted to introduce a second deed from Cephas Mills to Joseph P. Martin, dated March 29, 1841, which was also challenged on grounds of lack of certification or official acknowledgment. Despite these challenges, the court permitted the second deed's admission. The only issues raised in the appeal were related to the admittance of these two deeds into evidence.	Booth's primary argument was that the certified copy of the deed from Joseph L. James and others was necessary to establish his claim to the land. He argued that because he had no access to the original deed, he detailed his lack of possession and knowledge of the original's whereabouts through an affidavit. Booth insisted that the court's admission of the copy into evidence was justified under the applicable statute regarding lost documents.	Cook contended that Booth's affidavit was insufficient to validate the admission of the copy of the deed, as it did not demonstrate that Booth had made reasonable efforts to locate or produce the original document. Cook argued that strict adherence to evidentiary standards was necessary to prevent fraud and ensure the integrity of property claims. Additionally, he challenged the validity of the acknowledgement of the second deed, as it lacked proper notarization.

In 1885, Henry H. Gage filed a case against John Williams in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, seeking to remove a tax deed held by Williams that he claimed was a cloud on his title to lot 15 in block 14 of Eavenswood, Cook County. Prior to this, Gage's agent had conducted an inspection of the property and found it unoccupied and unfenced, except for an old fence with an opening. Gage's agent took measures to secure the lot by placing bars in the opening and posting a notice indicating the property was for sale. Gage established a chain of title from the original owner, Goslee, who had owned the lot since 1869. The primary issue was whether Gage was in possession of the lot when filing the bill. The evidence was conflicting, but the court ultimately found that Gage sufficiently demonstrated possession, as well as ownership, and identified several grounds to challenge the validity of the tax deed, especially regarding an excessive judgment amount that invalidated it.	Gage claimed that he was in possession of the lot and sought to have the tax deed issued to Williams set aside as a cloud on his title. He argued that the deed was invalid due to an erroneous tax judgment amount that exceeded the property taxes owed and was improperly calculated. Additionally, Gage emphasized that his actions to secure the property, including placing bars and posting a sale notice, were indicative of his possession and ownership rights.	Williams contended that Gage had not demonstrated possession of the property at the time he filed the bill. He relied on the argument that, without showing possession, Gage could not invoke the court's equity jurisdiction to remove the cloud on his title. Williams did not address the specific objections raised against the validity of the tax deed.

In the case of Julius Stein et al. v. Leo Metzger et al., which took place in 1883 in Chicago, Illinois, the plaintiffs, fur dealers from New York, entered into a contract with defendants, cloak manufacturers based in Chicago. The defendants placed an order for specific quantities of fur goods that were to be delivered promptly, given the seasonal nature of the goods. The plaintiffs shipped several batches from November 12 to November 24, 1883, which were accepted by the defendants. However, shipments made after November 24 were rejected by the defendants, who returned the goods, citing a breach of contract by the plaintiffs for failing to deliver in a timely manner. The case was tried without a jury, leading to a judgment of $621.25 in favor of the plaintiffs, despite the defendants admitting they owed $256.50. The defendants appealed the decision, arguing that the rejected goods were rightly returned, and the judgment exceeded the evidence.	The plaintiffs argued that they fulfilled the contract by delivering the goods as agreed prior to November 24, 1883. They claimed the defendants had no right to refuse the subsequent shipments and sought to recover the full amount under an indebitatus count for goods sold and delivered, totaling $621.25.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs breached the contract by failing to deliver all goods as stipulated by the agreed timeline. They argued that since the goods were not delivered "at once" as required, they were entitled to return the goods shipped after November 24, 1883. Therefore, they requested a reversal of the judgment awarded to the plaintiffs.

In April 1867, the case of Frederick W. Storing v. Oliver W. Onley was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a distress for rent proceeding, which took place in Ogle County, Illinois, presided over by Judge William W. Heaton. Frederick W. Storing, the plaintiff, contended that a general judgment had been rendered in error, and execution was awarded based on the jury's finding. This situation prompted Storing's legal team, represented by Messrs. Leland & Blanchard, to appeal the judgment, claiming that the procedural error warranted reversal. The case also drew parallels to an earlier case, Alwood v. Mansfield, which addressed similar issues concerning judgment practice in the appellate court.	The plaintiff, Frederick W. Storing, argued that the general judgment rendered by the lower court was erroneous, as it was awarded based on the jury's finding in a distress for rent action. He sought a reversal of this judgment, contending it was improper and did not conform with statutory requirements.	The defendant, Oliver W. Onley, acknowledged the error in rendering a general judgment and therefore supported the reversal of the judgment. However, he requested that the Supreme Court enter a final order in the appellate court, similar to the resolution in a prior case, Alwood v. Mansfield, despite acknowledging potential complications with this approach.

In September 1875, the case of The Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific R. R. Co. v. Sarah A. Clayton was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from an incident involving Sarah A. Clayton, a passenger who intended to travel from Chicago to Utica. After her arrival in Chicago from the East, she discovered that her baggage had not arrived. In an effort to continue her journey, she surrendered the baggage check she obtained from the Fort Wayne road to the baggage-master of the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad, receiving a new check from them. This transaction was understood to entail that the defendant's agent would claim her baggage from the previous carrier and forward it to her destination. A key issue in the case was determining whether Clayton's baggage was actually received by the defendant. The evidence presented suggested that although the defendant's agent sent the check for the baggage to the Fort Wayne depot, it was not confirmed whether the baggage ever arrived at the defendant's station.	The plaintiff, Sarah A. Clayton, claimed that her baggage was lost while under the custody of the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad Company. She argued that the delivery of a baggage check constituted prima facie evidence that the baggage was received by the carrier and that the defendant had a legal obligation as an insurer to safeguard her baggage once in their possession.	The defendant, Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad Company, contended that they never actually received the baggage in question. They argued that the burden of proof lay with the plaintiff to demonstrate that her baggage was in the defendant's possession at the time of loss, implying that the evidence did not sufficiently establish their liability.

The case "Jacob Zuckermann et al. v. Wolf Solomon" was decided in September 1874 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Jacob Zuckermann and others (the appellants) against Wolf Solomon (the appellee). The conflict arose after the appellants confessed to a judgment under a power of attorney concerning a note given for the balance due on a previous transaction with the "First Bohemian Brick Manufacturing Co." This note was associated with the sale of a steam engine and machinery, which allegedly were not delivered in the agreed-upon condition. The appellants sought to vacate the judgment, claiming that there was a breach of warranty and the presence of usury in the note, aiming to set off damages from the manufacturing company against the amount due on the note. The court found that the warranty claim did not belong to the appellants, as the right of action rested solely with the manufacturing company, which could not assign the claim to them. The judgment in question had also been assigned to the appellee before maturity, further complicating the appellants' defense.	The plaintiffs, Jacob Zuckermann and others, argued that the judgment against them should be vacated due to alleged breaches of warranty relating to the steam engine and machinery, which were not fulfilled as agreed. They also argued that the note included an improper amount of usury. They sought to have the judgment set aside to claim damages against the warranty and adjust the note to reflect the excessive interest.	The defendant, Wolf Solomon, contended that the warranty, for which the plaintiffs sought to set off damages, was not enforceable by them because it belonged to the manufacturing company. He argued that since the note had been assigned to him before maturity without notice of any defense, the plaintiffs could not contest the judgment. The defense asserted that the right of action was solely with the corporation and thus could not be used by the appellants in this case.

In 1888, in Gallatin County, Illinois, the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company sought to condemn ten acres of land owned by Alanson Reed, outside its right of way. The railway company's intention was to appropriate the land for extracting sand, rock, gravel, and earth for maintaining and improving its railroad, which had been operational for a decade. The railway's charter was authorized under Illinois law in 1867, permitting it to condemn land beyond its right of way for the necessary materials. However, the railroad failed to prove that it had attempted to negotiate with Reed over compensation for the land. The case was subsequently submitted to a jury which determined the compensation for Reed. The defendant contended against the petition, except for acknowledging ownership of the land. Ultimately, the court found that the railway did not adequately demonstrate its right to condemn Reed's property due to a lack of evidence indicating good-faith negotiations.	The plaintiff, the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company, argued that it had the right to condemn Reed's land under its charter, which allowed for such actions when seeking materials necessary for maintaining the railroad. The railroad requested the court authorize the appropriation of Reed's land for this purpose, asserting that it was essential for the operation and improvement of their railway.	Alanson Reed, the defendant, denied the claims of the plaintiff and argued that the railway company had not shown any proof of being unable to negotiate compensation for his land. Reed contended that the condemnation petition lacked evidence of a failure to reach an agreement and was, therefore, insufficient to grant jurisdiction for such proceedings.

In 1890, in McLean County, Illinois, James P. Butler initiated a legal action against the County of McLean to claim rewards for capturing three horse thieves: Pearl Hosier, Benjamin Moore, and Silas Buckles. The case arose after the board of supervisors of McLean County raised the reward for capturing horse thieves from $50 to $100, as outlined in Section 15, Chapter 60 of the Revised Statutes. Under this regulation, Butler successfully apprehended the thieves; however, only two had stolen horses valued over $50, which was a requirement for claiming the full reward. While the court awarded Butler $100 each for the first two thieves, it denied his claim for the third thief, Buckles, arguing that the horse he stole was worth less than $50. This decision prompted Butler to appeal the ruling, questioning the interpretation of the statute regarding the reward's applicability based on the stolen horse's value.	James P. Butler argued that the County of McLean should honor the increased reward for all three captured thieves, regardless of the value of the stolen horse. He contended that the legal provision allowing for such rewards did not impose a value limit for specific types of stolen property, highlighting that the statutory language intended to provide protection to all horses stolen, regardless of their individual worth.	The County of McLean, represented by its attorneys, defended the ruling of the lower court, asserting that the statute explicitly stated a reward could only be given if the stolen property exceeded $50 in value. They emphasized that since one of the stolen horses was valued below this threshold, Butler was not entitled to the reward for that case, aligning with the Circuit Court's interpretation of the law.

The case "The Union Coal Company v. The City of La Salle" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 16, 1889. It arose in La Salle County, Illinois, where the Union Coal Company (the plaintiff) brought a trespass action against the City of La Salle (the defendant). The dispute centered around the mining of coal located under certain streets and alleys of the city. The facts established that La Salle is on land originally owned by the State of Illinois, which had been platted in 1838. The city claimed ownership of the coal underlying its streets, while the Union Coal Company had mined coal without the city's permission, resulting in the extraction of coal valued at $1,050. Both parties agreed to a set of facts for the trial, primarily focusing on the right of the city to sell the coal and the legality of the mining that had occurred. The court found the defendant guilty of trespassing and awarded damages to the plaintiff based on the mining done.	The Union Coal Company's main claim was centered on the recovery of damages for coal that the city allegedly mined without permission from beneath the city streets. They sought legal validation of the city's right to control and sell the coal located under its streets and alleys.	The City of La Salle contended that it did not have the authority to mine or sell the coal. They aimed to demonstrate that any rights the city had were limited to public use of the surface, and that the case of the Zinc Company v. The City of La Salle supported their claim against the plaintiff.

Ralph Lockwood v. Elisha L. Mills et al. is a legal case that took place in April 1864 in Marshall County, Illinois. The case emerged from a dispute over the ownership of 960 acres of land previously owned by Cephas Mills. Upon Mills's death, the plaintiffs, being his heirs, claimed the land as their rightful inheritance. The defendant, Ralph Lockwood, acquired a title to the land through a sale conducted by the estate's administrator, William B. Green, who was also a creditor in the estate. The plaintiffs challenged this sale, asserting that it involved fraud because Green acted in multiple roles (creditor, auctioneer, and purchaser) and sold the land at a price far below its actual market value. The case was initiated in the Circuit Court of Marshall County, where the plaintiffs presented a power of attorney authorizing the suit, despite one plaintiff, Allen Turner, not signing it. The court allowed the case to proceed, leading to a trial where the legitimacy of the title and the motives behind the administrator’s sale were scrutinized.	The plaintiffs argued that they, as the heirs of Cephas Mills, rightfully owned the land in question and that the sale conducted by the administrator was fraudulent. They contended that the administrator, acting in multiple conflicting roles, manipulated the sale process to acquire the land at an unfairly low price. Additionally, they supported their claim by demonstrating a clear family connection to the property and ensuring that the legal documentation, such as deeds and patents, substantiated their title.	The defendant, Lockwood, contended that the sale conducted by the administrator was legitimate and that he acquired the land lawfully. He argued that the plaintiffs' objections were unfounded, claiming that they failed to establish how the sale was fraudulent. Lockwood referenced his prior agreement with the administrator as part of their business arrangement, contending that the legal process was followed appropriately and that he did not engage in any deceitful practice regarding the transaction.

James Herrington filed a lawsuit against Charles C. Stevens in the Kane Circuit Court in May 1859. The case involved a financial dispute concerning the defendant's promise to pay the plaintiff $350 for his interest in a stock of goods co-owned with another individual, Karns. During the proceedings, Herrington initially received a judgment for $258, but after the defendant requested a new trial, the court allowed it, leading to an amended declaration. The defendant attempted to challenge aspects of the claim through demurrers and other defenses, but after multiple hearings and a series of legal maneuvers, including a default judgment and a re-assessment of damages, the court eventually assessed the damages at $384.56 in November 1860. The defendant appealed the judgment.	The plaintiff, James Herrington, claimed that Charles C. Stevens owed him $350 for his interest in a stock of goods, and he sought a judgment for that amount. After originally obtaining a lesser judgment, he amended his claim and requested further assessments of damages due to the defendant's failure to properly contest the action.	The defendant, Charles C. Stevens, argued against the validity of the plaintiff’s claims, including challenging the accuracy and admissibility of the declaration. He filed demurrers and attempted to introduce other contracts and defenses during the proceedings, although these were limited by the court's rulings and discretion regarding the legal process.

On August 27, 1868, Joseph Dayton executed a note for $3,500 to his mother, Mary E. Dayton, with a mortgaged piece of land as security. The mortgage described the land incorrectly, starting 38.25 feet west of the southwest corner of a lot in Charleston, Illinois, instead of the southeast corner. The mortgage was duly recorded in Coles County, Illinois. Joseph Dayton purchased the intended land in 1864 and occupied it for business until at least 1876. However, in 1876, The Citizens National Bank obtained a judgment against him for $2,213.30, which remained unpaid. Mary E. Dayton commenced a lawsuit in chancery, seeking correction of the mortgage and foreclosure. The Citizens National Bank denied knowledge of the mistake and claimed the mortgage was satisfied due to payment. The lower court found a mistake in the description and reformed the mortgage but also stated that the bank's judgment was a first lien on the property.	Mary E. Dayton sought reformation of the mortgage to correct the property description and foreclosure due to unpaid debts owed by Joseph Dayton. She argued that the incorrect mortgage description was due to mutual mistake and that the correct description should reflect the true intent of the parties involved.	The Citizens National Bank contended that they were unaware of any mistakes in the mortgage description and claimed that the mortgage had been satisfied through payment. They argued that their judgment constituted a valid first lien on the property and denied any obligation related to the correction of the mortgage.

In September 1873, in Illinois, James A. Reynolds (the appellant) was involved in a legal dispute with Palmer & Hopper (the appellees) concerning the sale of certain plows. The matter arose when Reynolds contested a jury verdict that favored Palmer & Hopper in a lawsuit aimed at recovering the value of thirty-three plows that they claimed had been sold and delivered to him. The jury's decision was upheld by the circuit court, leading Reynolds to appeal the judgment. The case presented two main issues: the admissibility of testimony regarding the plows charged to Reynolds without the introduction of the original account book, and whether the evidence supported the jury's verdict. The court found no objections to the testimony that might have prejudiced Reynolds. Given the conflicting evidence, the court reaffirmed that the jury, having directly assessed the witnesses, was in the best position to determine the outcome, concluding that there was insufficient basis to overturn their verdict.	James A. Reynolds, after being charged for thirty-three plows he allegedly purchased, claimed that not all of them were delivered. He argued that seven plows were unreceived, challenging the appellees on the grounds that he should not be held liable for the full amount due to this discrepancy. Reynolds sought to have the jury's verdict set aside, asserting that the evidence did not adequately support their finding that all plows were delivered.	Palmer & Hopper, through their testimony, maintained that they had indeed delivered the thirty-three plows to Reynolds. They argued against the objections raised by Reynolds regarding the admissibility of certain testimony, asserting that the evidence presented was appropriate and did not mislead the jury. Their defense rested on the assertion that the jury's findings were supported by the conflicting evidence, which they contended justified the original verdict.

On April 3, 1887, in Chicago, Illinois, Timothy Grady was involved in an incident that resulted in the death of Michael O’Brien, a police officer. Following an inquest by the coroner's jury, Grady was indicted for murder on April 27, 1887. He pleaded not guilty during his arraignment on May 2, 1887, and went to trial on July 18, 1887, where he was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to seventeen years in prison. Grady's defense raised concerns about procedural issues in his trial, claiming he was entitled to discharge under the criminal code due to delays in being tried. Specifically, he argued that he had been continuously held without trial and that the charges should have been dismissed because he was not released after a specified time. The trial court rejected his motion for discharge and affirmed his conviction, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Timothy Grady, as the plaintiff in error, asserted that his rights were violated because he was not granted a discharge under the Criminal Code for not being tried within a specific timeframe. He also claimed that his conviction should be reversed due to insufficient evidence supporting the verdict and due to newly discovered evidence that could potentially exonerate him.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by the State's Attorney, contended that the trial and conviction were lawful and valid. They argued that the court properly interpreted the statute concerning trial terms and had the authority to proceed with the trial despite the claims of delay. The prosecution maintained that there was sufficient evidence to support the jury's verdict, including eyewitness testimony that linked Grady to the shooting.

The case "Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railway Co. v. Mary H. Lewis" took place in July 1883 and stemmed from an incident occurring in March 1881. The incident took place near Prairie City, Iowa, when the railway company's cars derailed. Mary H. Lewis, a 29-year-old unmarried woman residing in Canton, Fulton County, Illinois, sustained severe injuries, rendering her unable to work as a housekeeper. She claimed the railway company was negligent for not maintaining their tracks, leading to her injuries. Following the accident, Lewis received a payment of $20 and signed a release, which she contended was obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation. The defendant, the railway company, asserted this release absolved them of further liability. The case proceeded through the legal system, ultimately reaching the Illinois Appellate Court.	The plaintiff, Mary H. Lewis, claimed that her injuries were a direct result of the railway company's negligence in maintaining the railway tracks. She sought damages for her permanent injuries, which included losing the use of her arm and the ability to work. Additionally, she argued that the release she signed was the result of fraud because she was misled into believing it was merely a receipt for her expenses due to the accident rather than a waiver of her right to sue for damages.	The defendant, Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railway Co., argued that the case should be dismissed based on the release signed by Lewis, which they claimed released them from any liability following the $20 payment made to her. They contended that the evidence did not sufficiently support Lewis's claim of fraud, asserting that she could have exercised greater caution by reading the release before signing it.

The case of "Margaret Phelps v. Jacob S. Phelps" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1874. It primarily revolves around the interpretation of an ante-nuptial agreement made between Margaret Phelps and her deceased husband, Michael Phelps. The agreement stipulated that the property of either spouse would remain separate and distinct, akin to being unmarried, and that upon the death of one party, their property would pass to their heirs free of claims from the survivor. Following Michael Phelps's death, Margaret sought her rights under Illinois' Statute of Wills, which grants specific property allowances to widows and their families for their support. The couple had a child together, who resided with Margaret at the time of the petition, alongside Michael's children from a previous marriage. The court's decision hinged on whether Margaret, by virtue of the ante-nuptial agreement, had forfeited her entitlement to this statutory support for both herself and their child. This issue was set against the backdrop of public policy and legislation aimed at protecting families left destitute after a spouse's death.	Margaret Phelps claimed that despite the ante-nuptial agreement, she was entitled to specific articles of property under the Statute of Wills for her support and that of her minor child. She argued that the agreement should not bar her from these statutory rights, which aimed to provide financial protection for widows and children, thereby ensuring their sustenance in the event of a spouse's death.	Jacob S. Phelps contended that the ante-nuptial agreement effectively severed all claims to property arising from the marriage, denying Margaret any right to her husband’s estate. His argument emphasized that the agreement was clear and legally binding, thus precluding any claim by Margaret for support based on statutory provisions, as it isolated individual property interests.

The case "Northern Transportation Company of Ohio v. Daily Sellick" took place in the fall of 1866 when Daily Sellick entrusted his carriage to the Northern Transportation Company for shipping from Ogdensburg to Chicago. The agreed shipping charge was ten dollars for immediate delivery, but if Sellick delayed until spring, the cost would be less. Sellick chose to delay the shipment, and the carriage arrived in Chicago around June 17, 1867. When he demanded his carriage upon arrival, he offered to pay the initially agreed freight of ten dollars, but the company insisted he pay twenty dollars plus one dollar for dockage, which he refused. As a result of the company's refusal to deliver the carriage unless he complied with this increased charge, the carriage remained in their possession until it was destroyed by fire in November of that year. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court, which was presided over by Chief Justice Breese and focused on the legal obligations and responsibilities surrounding the conversion of property.	Daily Sellick, the plaintiff, argued that the Northern Transportation Company wrongfully refused to deliver his carriage upon demand, despite his offer to pay the agreed-upon freight charge. He claimed this refusal constituted a conversion of his property, asserting that the company's demand for a higher fee was extortionate and unjustified. Sellick sought damages for the loss of the carriage, asserting that the company held responsibility for its destruction after their wrongful refusal to release it to him.	The Northern Transportation Company contended that there was no conversion of the carriage since Sellick had agreed to contact their agent about potential overcharges, which implied a temporary hold on the carriage. They maintained that the refusal to deliver was not absolute and was contingent upon Sellick’s inquiry about the shipping cost. The company’s argument hinged on the notion that Sellick's actions indicated a waiver of immediate possession, and they alleged that the plaintiff had not exhausted all avenues for resolving the payment dispute.

The case of J. Obermann Brewing Company v. William D. Adams et al. was decided on December 24, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case emerged from the Superior Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Elliott Anthony. The central figures in this legal dispute were the J. Obermann Brewing Company, the appellant, and William D. Adams along with others, the appellees. The legal proceedings appeared to rely heavily on the presence of a bill of exceptions, which is a formal record of the exceptions taken during a trial. However, during the appeal, it was revealed that no such bill was properly filed in the court, leaving the appellate court unable to examine certain arguments raised by the appellant. The absence of this critical document limited the ability of the court to address the claims made in the appeal, thus presenting an obstacle to the appellate process.	The J. Obermann Brewing Company, as the plaintiff, argued that errors had been made in the initial trial proceedings, relying on the existence of a bill of exceptions to substantiate their claims. They requested that the appellate court consider these errors and ultimately lead to a different judgment in their favor.	In response, the defendants, led by William D. Adams, maintained that the appeal should be dismissed due to the absence of a properly filed bill of exceptions, which is essential for reviewing trial errors. They argued that without this critical document, the appellate court lacked the authority to examine the claims made by the plaintiff.

In 1861, the case of "The Chicago, St. Charles and Mississippi Railroad Company, Appellant, v. Edwin C. Larned, Appellee" was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a legal service rendered to James H. Rees in a suit against Bennett and others, concerning a lost deed for approximately eight acres of land in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, including Rees, hired Edwin C. Larned to represent their interests in the Supreme Court after a lower court ruling. However, the Railroad Company, which stood to benefit from the outcome, had never formally retained Larned as their attorney. Testimonies revealed that although Rees had retained Larned, there was no evidence that the Railroad Company had explicitly communicated a desire for Larned's representation. Following a jury trial, Larned was initially awarded $1,000 for his services, but the Railroad Company subsequently appealed this judgment.	The plaintiff, Edwin C. Larned, claimed payment from the Chicago, St. Charles and Mississippi Railroad Company for legal services rendered on behalf of James H. Rees in a case that was argued in the Supreme Court. Larned argued that despite not being formally retained by the defendant, the company benefited from his work and should compensate him for those legal services.	The Chicago, St. Charles and Mississippi Railroad Company defended against Larned's claims by asserting that he was never formally employed or retained by the company to represent its interests. They argued that Larned's representation of Rees was separate and that the company had no legal obligation to pay for services that they did not request. The Railroad Company contended that allowing such a claim would set a dangerous precedent in which attorneys could claim payment based solely on indirect benefits received.

In 1885, in Flat Branch Township, Illinois, Sarah L. Wright claimed ownership of a tract of land but stated that her husband, James B. Wright, controlled and possessed it. A highway running through their land often became impassable due to accumulated surface water. There was an open ditch that was established by mutual consent for drainage purposes. The Commissioners of Highways, seeking to maintain the ditch, entered into a contract with James B. Wright to widen and deepen it, which they paid for in part. However, after the ditch was improved, James B. Wright constructed an embankment across it, jeopardizing its ability to drain water, thereby risking damage to the highways. The Commissioners sought an injunction to prevent the obstruction of the ditch, fearing it would cause irreparable harm. The defendants moved to dissolve the injunction, asserting there was no legal basis for the Commissioners' claims.	The Commissioners of Highways argued that they had a right to keep the ditch open for public benefit. They sought an injunction to prevent James B. Wright from filling or obstructing the ditch, claiming that such actions would lead to flooding and make the highways impassable. The Commissioners relied on the notion that there was a legal easement for public drainage purposes and requested the court to recognize their right to enforce this easement and protect public access.	The defendants, James B. Wright and Sarah L.
