Wright, contended that they had the right to fill the ditch on their property, as the filling would not obstruct the highway or violate any public easement. They argued that the claim for an injunction was not valid because it was based on a mere verbal license and that the Commissioners had no statutory authority to maintain the lawsuit. Furthermore, they implied that the right claimed by the Commissioners was not substantiated by any formal deed or legal easement.

In the case of Henry W. Newberry et al. v. Eliphalet W. Blatchford et al., decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on September 27, 1882, the dispute centers around the estate of Walter L. Newberry, who passed away in 1868, leaving a will that structured the distribution of his estate after the deaths of his widow and two daughters. The testator appointed trustees to manage the estate until the death of the last life tenant. After one daughter passed away, the surviving family members, claiming that the estate should now be distributed, petitioned the circuit court for immediate division, opposing the trustees who adhered to the will's terms. The circuit court initially ruled for immediate distribution, a decision that was later appealed by the trustees. The Illinois Supreme Court intervened, asserting that the period for distribution had not yet arrived as stipulated by the will, and remanded the case for compliance with this ruling. Following this, the original complainants amended their bill to include the Attorney General as a defendant, possibly to bolster their claims. Ultimately, the case returned to the Supreme Court for final adjudication regarding the procedural aspects and the interpretation of the will.	The plaintiffs, the heirs of Walter L. Newberry, argued that they were entitled to a division and distribution of the estate, claiming that the time for distribution had arrived following the death of the last daughter. They requested the court to construe the will and enforce the division of the estate based on their interpretation that it was ready for distribution at this time.	The defendants, including the trustees and now the Attorney General, contended that the distribution of the estate was not yet warranted under the terms of the will, as the widow was still alive and had a life interest in the estate. They sought to uphold the previous ruling by the court that the estate could not be divided until after the widow's death, asserting that any attempts to amend the bill after the Supreme Court's initial ruling were inappropriate and had no legal standing.

On April 26, 1832, in Morgan County, Illinois, a writ of attachment was issued against Peter D. Mordecai on behalf of Elisha Kellogg for $250. Samuel T. Matthews, the sheriff, executed the writ and attached a horse and other personal property belonging to Mordecai. To retain possession, Mordecai executed a bond with Jacob and Michael Crisman as sureties, pledging that the property would be available to satisfy any judgment against him. On June 22, 1833, Kellogg won a judgment against Mordecai, leading to an execution on July 12, 1833, which Matthews was unable to satisfy because the property could not be found. The Crismans were subsequently sued by Matthews for the bond's penalty. Throughout the proceedings, the Crismans argued that Matthews had not correctly levied the attachment. The case eventually reached the Illinois Supreme Court after various denials and pleas were filed, with the lower courts finding in favor of Matthews.	The plaintiffs, Jacob and Michael Crisman, contended that the sheriff had misrepresented the status of the attachment on Mordecai’s property and did not legally levy it. They argued that Matthews had not performed his duties as sheriff properly, which negated the terms of the bond they had signed. The Crismans sought to invalidate the bond and dismiss the claims against them based on these defenses.	The defendant, Samuel T. Matthews, maintained that the bond executed by the Crismans was valid and that the judgment obtained by Kellogg provided sufficient evidence to enforce the bond. Matthews argued that the Crismans, as sureties, were estopped from denying the existence of the underlying attachment, asserting that the judgment was conclusive and that he was not required to produce further evidence to prove the attachment’s execution.

William Clark brought a legal case against The People of the State of Illinois, which was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1863. The case appears to involve proceedings in the Recorder's Court of the City of Chicago. The details leading to the court case are not explicitly mentioned in the provided description, suggesting that the intricacies of the events may align closely with those from a preceding case, although specifics are not included. Key individuals involved include William Clark, as the plaintiff, and The People of the State of Illinois, representing the state, though details about specific actions, allegations, or events leading to the suit are not discussed.	The summary does not provide detailed claims made by William Clark; however, it can be inferred that Clark sought reversal of a prior judgment from the Recorder's Court. The context suggests he believed the earlier decision was flawed or unjust, leading him to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The defendant, represented by The People of the State of Illinois, did not present explicit defenses or arguments in the summary provided. It is indicated that the Illinois Supreme Court found no significant differences between this case and a preceding case, thus implying that the state's position may have relied on the findings of that earlier judgment.

In the case of Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Co. v. Joseph F. Wallace, the legal proceedings took place in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the final judgment issued on April 6, 1885. The dispute arose from an incident involving Joseph F. Wallace, an employee of the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company, during which he sustained injuries while working. The case stemmed from a lower court ruling made by Judge Wm. H. Snyder in the Circuit Court of St. Clair County. The key individuals involved included Joseph F. Wallace as the plaintiff, seeking damages for his injuries, and the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Co. as the defendant, responsible for the workplace conditions that allegedly led to his injury. The case presented a central question about the liability of the railway company for the actions of fellow employees.	Joseph F. Wallace claimed that the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Co. was liable for negligence leading to his injuries. He argued that the company failed to provide a safe working environment, thus exposing him to unnecessary risks while performing his duties. Wallace sought legal redress and compensation for his injuries, asserting that the company had a duty of care towards its employees.	The Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Co. contended that Joseph F. Wallace and the individual who caused his injuries, Needham, were fellow servants. Therefore, the railway company claimed it should not be held liable for Wallace's injuries based on the fellow servant rule, which states that employers are not responsible for the negligent acts of their employees when those acts occur between co-workers.

In the case of Barrett et al. v. Waters et al., which took place in Illinois, the appellants sought an injunction to prevent the imposition of certain taxes. The legal proceedings unfolded in the context of a dispute that led the appellants to voluntarily dismiss their bill after the defendants (appellees) had filed an answer to their charges. Following the dismissal of the bill, a suggestion of damages was made by the defendants, and the court heard evidence regarding these damages, resulting in an award of $25 as solicitors' fees against the appellants. This sequence of events prompted the appellants to appeal the court's decision, arguing that their voluntary dismissal indicated that the initial injunction had been improperly issued. The court had to determine whether proper legal protocols were followed during this process, including the timing of filings and the competence of the attorneys involved. The majority opinion, authored by Judge Conger, ultimately assessed that the circuit court acted within its rights and procedure during the course of these proceedings.	The plaintiffs, Barrett et al., argued that the defendants had effectively caused the dismissal of their bill by fulfilling all conditions necessary to dissolve the injunction. They contended that their voluntary dismissal should lead to a reversal of the judgment, asserting that it signified an acknowledgment of the improper issuance of the injunction.	The defendants, Waters et al., maintained that the dismissal of the plaintiffs’ bill was a clear acknowledgment that the injunction was wrongly issued. They argued that the circuit court had fulfilled its obligations appropriately and highlighted that the attorney for the defendants had acted as a master in chancery previously, yet was competent to appear as counsel after no longer holding that position.

In the case of Mary J. Illingworth v. Catharine Burley, the legal proceedings took place in Cook County, Illinois, and were decided on July 2, 1889. The key individuals involved include the plaintiff, Mary J. Illingworth, and the defendant, Catharine Burley. The action was initiated by Illingworth to recover rent for a house that her husband had rented starting around August 1, 1885. The house was occupied by both Illingworth and her husband until he passed away on August 22, 1886. Following her husband’s death, Illingworth continued to reside in the house for one additional month and did pay rent for that period. However, she refused to pay rent for the time her husband was alive, leading to the legal dispute. The trial court initially ruled that Illingworth was not liable for the unpaid rent, questioning whether the rent charged during her husband’s life could be considered a family expense.	Illingworth contended that the rent for the house was an essential household expense, aligned with the definition of family expenses as outlined in Section 15, Chapter 68 of the Illinois Revised Statutes. She argued that the cost of a home is as critical to a family’s existence as other family needs such as food and clothing. Thus, she claimed that her husband’s estate should be liable for the outstanding rent incurred during his lifetime.	The defendant, Catharine Burley, maintained that Illingworth should not be held liable for the rent during her husband's lifetime. The defense hinged on the interpretation of family expenses and whether rent should fall under this classification. Burley’s attorneys argued that the statute's stipulations did not explicitly include rent and thus supported the trial court’s conclusion that Illingworth was not responsible for the rent in question.

In December 1846, the case of John McCluskey v. John T. McNeely arose in Morgan County, Illinois, following a judgment rendered in the Morgan Circuit Court. The context involved a deputy sheriff, McCluskey, executing a judgment against McNeely, who was notified that his standing corn was claimed as exempt from execution under Illinois law. McCluskey levied an execution on eight acres of McNeely's corn and later sold it to a third party, Ray. However, prior to the sale, McNeely verbally communicated to McCluskey that he claimed the corn was exempt due to his limited assets and family obligations. The sheriff died before the sale, raising questions about the deputy's authority to proceed without the sheriff. The case was tried without a jury, and the court ruled in favor of McNeely, awarding him damages three times the corn's value, which prompted McCluskey to appeal the decision.	McCluskey, the plaintiff in error, argued that the deputy sheriff's authority to act ceased with the death of the sheriff, and therefore, any subsequent sale of the corn he levied upon was invalid. He claimed that McNeely's verbal notice regarding an exemption should have been in writing and timely submitted before the sale took place.	McNeely contended that the deputy sheriff retained the authority to act after the sheriff's death according to the law of 1825. He maintained that his property, including the corn, was exempt from execution since it constituted all he owned, and he had effectively communicated his claim for exemption before the sale. Furthermore, he argued that the notice of the exemption could be communicated verbally and did not necessarily require written confirmation, especially since he had not been properly notified by McCluskey beforehand.

In June 1875, in Greene County, Illinois, L. J. Thompson purchased certain properties—including growing wheat, corn, an undivided half of a Woods’ reaper, and a lot of stock hogs—from the execution debtor, William T. Wilhite. At the time of the purchase, no judgment had been rendered against Wilhite. However, the property was later levied upon by a constable as part of an execution against Wilhite. The controversy centered on whether Thompson's purchase and the delivery of property was sufficient to uphold his claim against subsequent creditors and purchasers who might not have been aware of the sale. While the wheat and corn had been adequately delivered, the court debated whether it was necessary for Thompson to take physical possession of the hogs at the time of the sale, which he did not, leading to legal complications. The case progressed through various trials, with previous verdicts favoring Thompson, but was ultimately appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court for further review.	Thompson argued that his purchase of the wheat and corn in good faith, along with the actions taken to hold possession before the harvest, entitled him to keep the property despite the execution. He claimed that there was sufficient delivery of the crops to pass title, arguing against the legality of the seizure which occurred when he had not yet harvested the crops.	Wilhite contended that the sale of the hogs was problematic due to the lack of delivery, making it vulnerable to creditor claims. He asserted that a transaction where personal property remains with the vendor is considered fraudulent against creditors, regardless of good faith. The defense emphasized that the instruction given to the jury regarding possession and delivery was flawed, as it assumed delivery of the hogs had occurred, which was the central point of contention.

In 1883, in Chicago, Illinois, Cornelius McGinnis entered into a contract with Edward P. De Wolf and John L. Agnew for the lease of his machine shops and foundry, known as the "Keystone Machine Works and Foundry." As part of this agreement, the defendants were to pay $2,000 in rent in the form of work delivered monthly, and also to build twelve "purifiers" as per McGinnis's orders, for which they would earn an additional 20% profit on the cost. However, after placing an order for the twelve purifiers in June, McGinnis encountered delays in their completion and subsequent disagreements over pricing. This lack of delivery prompted the defendants to terminate the lease. McGinnis then filed a lawsuit for breach of contract, seeking damages for unpaid rent, property damage, and the failure to deliver the purifiers. The plaintiff won a jury verdict of $1,462.50, which the Appellate Court later upheld. The defendants appealed, claiming errors related to evidence admission and the sufficiency of the declaration.	The plaintiff, Cornelius McGinnis, asserted that the defendants breached the lease contract by failing to deliver the ordered purifiers, as well as causing damage to the property during their possession. He primarily sought recovery for six months of unpaid rent, damages for property injuries, and damages stemming from the non-delivery of the twelve purifiers.	The defendants contended that the lower court improperly admitted evidence regarding the market for the purifiers, arguing that the plaintiff did not adequately outline specific prospective purchasers in his declarations. They maintained that without this information, the evidence which alleged lost profits on prospective sales should not have been allowed. Additionally, they argued against the sufficiency of the declaration in the context of their motion to arrest the judgment.

In 1874, in Chicago, Illinois, the case of John H. Dilcher et al. v. John H. Raap arose from an incident involving an affray between Raap (the plaintiff) and Dilcher (one of the defendants), a police officer. The confrontation occurred on the sidewalk in front of Raap's lager beer saloon. Following the affray, which saw Paap gaining the upper hand over Dilcher, Raap returned to his establishment. However, Dilcher and three other police officers later approached Raap and forcibly arrested him, even though no warrant was presented. Raap was taken to the police station, detained for about three hours, and subsequently released after posting bail, only to be discharged later by a justice of the peace. The case hinged on conflicting accounts of whether Dilcher or Raap was the aggressor in the initial altercation. The defendants argued that Raap was the aggressor and that they were acting in their official capacity to apprehend him after his escape. However, evidence suggested that the police officers may not have been acting in good faith, as they might have been assisting Dilcher in a personal matter rather than performing their official duties.	Raap claimed damages for assault, battery, and false imprisonment against Dilcher and the other police officers. He argued that he was not the aggressor during the affray and that the police officers acted unlawfully in arresting him without a warrant. Raap’s claims highlighted that the officers were thus liable for trespass due to their actions.	The defendants contended that Raap was the aggressor and had breached the peace, justifying Dilcher's initial attempt to arrest him. They claimed their actions were to assist Dilcher in re-apprehending a supposed escaped prisoner, believing they were supporting a lawful arrest. They argued they acted under the belief that they were fulfilling their duties as police officers and requested the court to find them not liable for trespass.

In December 1855, the case of Albon H. Hitchcock v. Benjamin E. Roney took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. Albon H. Hitchcock, the owner of real estate in Beardstown, Cass County, Illinois, sought to quash an execution related to a fine against Benjamin E. Roney. Roney had been convicted and sentenced in the Pike Circuit Court for an unspecified offense in March of 1855, resulting in an execution for $290.75 issued against him. This execution was received by the sheriff on May 9, 1855, and was subsequently levied on a lot owned by Hitchcock on May 25, 1855. The property was later sold to Lewis F. Saunders on June 23, 1855, for $319.45. Hitchcock filed a motion to quash the levy and sale, arguing that various legal irregularities rendered the execution void. The motion was heard at the November special term of the Pike Circuit Court, and despite Hitchcock's arguments, it was denied.	Hitchcock's main arguments included claims that the execution was illegal due to several unauthorized costs, that the Pike County court had no jurisdiction to issue the execution in Cass County, and that the levy by the sheriff was void. He contended that the judgment and resulting levy did not create valid liens against the property and that no certificate of levy was properly recorded.	The defense, representing the People in the case against Roney, argued that the execution and levy were valid based on the established lien created by the criminal code, which takes effect on the day of arrest or indictment. They contended that changes in venue did not affect the operation of the lien and asserted that as a stranger to the record, Hitchcock had no right to challenge the execution.

In 1852, in the Franklin Circuit Court, the case of Andrew J. Ice and others (Appellants) v. William A. McLain (Appellee) arose following a trespass claim regarding the seizure of property. The appellants, Andrew J. Ice, an acting justice of the peace, and Adams, an acting constable, were involved in an execution process against McLain, who was allegedly in possession of property belonging to Summers, the original defendant in the execution. Ice had issued a jury warrant to determine the right of property after being notified by Adams of McLain's claim over the levied property. McLain was aware of the trial's date and location but accused Adams of failing to provide the required written notice. A jury found against McLain, resulting in a judgment against him for costs. After a subsequent execution to collect these costs led to McLain’s property being levied and sold, he pursued legal action against Ice and Adams for trespass without valid title proof connecting him to the property in question.	McLain claimed that the execution against his property was invalid due to the constable's failure to provide written notice of the time and location of the trial of right of property. He argued that the judgment obtained by Ice as a justice of the peace lacked proper jurisdiction, as the statutory requirement for notice had not been met. McLain sought damages of $49 for the wrongful seizure and sale of his property.	Ice and Adams defended against McLain's claims by asserting that they properly followed statutory procedures in executing the judgment and claimed that the constable's responsibility for notifying involved parties regarding the trial resting solely with him. They emphasized that they had fulfilled their duties in accordance with the judicious process established and maintained that McLain's ownership of the property had not been established, thus defending the validity of their actions.

In the case of Margaret Ennis v. Lawrence M. Ennis, which took place in Cook County, Illinois in the early 1880s, the proceedings surround the administration of the estate of James Ennis, who had passed away, leaving behind a widow, Margaret Ennis, and several children from a previous marriage. The probate court had granted letters of administration to both Margaret Ennis and Lawrence M. Ennis, and subsequently assigned a “widow’s award” valued at $1960. However, a later decision by the probate court on June 3, 1881, apportioned this award, giving $750 to Margaret and her child, while $1210 was allocated to the seven minor heirs from James's former marriage. Margaret challenged this order, seeking a common law writ of certiorari to have the apportionment quashed. The court, however, ruled that the proper remedy for aggrieved parties in cases like this was an appeal to the circuit court, as the probate court had proper jurisdiction over such matters. With no substantial error found, the circuit and appellate courts upheld the decision to quash the writ, leading to the final judgment.	Margaret Ennis's main argument was that the probate court's order to apportion the widow's award was unjust. She sought to have this order quashed, alleging that the probate court had incorrectly divided the award between her and the surviving children of her deceased husband. Her legal request centered on the notion that the probate court had overstepped its jurisdiction, necessitating a judicial review by certiorari.	Lawrence M. Ennis, as the defendant, argued that the probate court acted within its general jurisdiction regarding estate administration and that the order to apportion the widow’s award was legitimate. He contended that a writ of certiorari was not appropriate since the statute provided an appeal mechanism for any aggrieved party in such cases. He requested that the court affirm the lower court’s decision to quash the petition for the writ of certiorari.

The case of John Lewis, David Lewis, and Ophelia Lewis vs. Simeon Mayo took place in January 1869 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the petitioners (the three Lewis children) and Simeon Mayo, the administrator of the estate of John Reelay, also known as Lewis. John Reelay, a colored man, was held as a slave in Virginia until he escaped to Chicago and changed his name. He died intestate approximately two years prior, leaving behind some property. The evidence presented showed that about twenty years previously, while still a slave, Reelay agreed to marry another slave with the consent of their masters. Following their marriage, they lived together for many years and had three children. However, the children's mother was sold shortly before the Civil War and lost to history. The petitioners sought to be recognized as legal heirs entitled to their father's estate, amidst claims regarding the validity of the marriage given the status of both parents as slaves at the time.	The plaintiffs, John Lewis, David Lewis, and Ophelia Lewis, argued that their parents' marriage, though occurring during slavery, should be recognized as valid. They requested the court to declare their marriage legal and identify them as the lawful heirs of their deceased father, John Reelay. Their argument relied on previous rulings affirming the legitimacy of slave marriages that occurred in the absence of statutes declaring them void, especially after emancipation.	The defendant, Simeon Mayo, contested the legitimacy of the marriage on the grounds that both parents were slaves at the time of the marriage. He argued that slaves were considered property and, therefore, unable to enter into valid contractual agreements, including marriage. The defendant's request was to dismiss the claim made by the plaintiffs based on the invalidity of their parents' marriage.

In 1883, Kimbro T. Barnett, the plaintiff and owner of a land adjacent to a public highway, initiated a legal action against the Board of Trade Telegraph Company for trespassing on his property. The defendant entered Barnett's land without permission to erect telegraph poles for a telegraph line. The case unfolded in Madison County, Illinois, where Barnett's allegations included the defendant's unauthorized use of his property, resulting in damages, including the cutting of his hedge and trees intended for gate posts. Barnett claimed that the telegraph poles were an inconvenience, hindering his ability to maintain his property. The Circuit Court initially found in favor of Barnett, assessing damages at $78, leading the defendant to appeal this decision in the Appellate Court for the Fourth District, which upheld the lower court's ruling. The case was then brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, which was asked to resolve questions regarding property rights and the authority of telegraph companies to use public highways without owner consent.	Kimbro T. Barnett, the plaintiff, argued that the Board of Trade Telegraph Company's actions constituted trespass as they entered his property without authorization, erected telegraph poles causing damage, and obstructed his use of the land. He claimed that the installation of telegraph poles represented a new burden on his property which had not been contemplated by the public easement granted for highway use and sought compensation for the damages inflicted on his property.	The defendant, Board of Trade Telegraph Company, contended that their activities were lawful as they had received written permission from the county board to erect telegraph poles along the public highway. They argued that their use of the highway did not impose a new burden on the property and thus suggested that Barnett had no claim for damages. The defendant maintained that the actions taken were necessary for the installation of their telegraph line, a service deemed essential under the powers granted to corporations by state statutes.

In April 1863, the case of *Hiram Fender et al. v. Elias B. Stiles* took place in Lee County, Illinois. The case originated from an action of debt initiated by Elias B. Stiles against three defendants: Hiram Fender, Harvey Wilson, and John Deeds. They were involved in a bond executed for a sum of $1,000, which concerned a wager related to a horse race between Fender and Edward Atkins. Stiles acted as the stake-holder, holding $872 ($436 from each party) meant for distribution based on the outcome of the race. A dispute arose when Stiles delivered the total sum to Fender, leading Atkins to sue Stiles for not receiving his rightful share. In the ensuing lawsuit, Atkins won a judgment against Stiles for $429. Stiles claimed he was not indemnified by Fender as stipulated in their agreement following Atkins' victory. The case proceeded through the Lee County Circuit Court, resulting in Stiles seeking $1,000 from the defendants to cover his incurred damages and costs as a result of Atkins' successful claim against him.	Stiles argued that Fender had failed to indemnify him against claims made by Atkins, as required by their bond. He claimed damages totaling $1,000, which included costs associated with the legal action initiated by Atkins. Stiles contended that even though he had been forced to pay Atkins due to the nature of the agreements and bonds among the parties, Fender and Wilson had neglected to uphold their obligation, thereby causing him financial harm.	Fender and Wilson contended that the court had erred in overruling their demurrer to the declaration, which they argued lacked sufficient basis in alleging important averments about the action related to the bond. They maintained that proper notice or an opportunity to defend themselves against Atkins' claims had not been established. Furthermore, they raised a procedural objection regarding the judgment entered against only two of the three defendants, as John Deeds had not been served or participated in the case.

In January 1871, George A. Kibbie brought a legal action against John H. Williams in the Illinois Supreme Court, following an ejectment action initiated in the Adams Circuit Court. The case revolved around the disputed ownership of a specific parcel of land located in Adams County. Kibbie claimed that he held title to the property through a direct link to the United States government, while Williams asserted he possessed color of title, having paid taxes and occupied the land from 1860 until 1870. Key individuals involved included George A. Kibbie as the plaintiff, representing himself through attorneys, and John H. Williams, the defendant, who represented himself pro se. The Circuit Court found in favor of Williams, leading Kibbie to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Kibbie, the plaintiff, argued that he had legal title to the land through a direct chain originating from the United States and claimed that Williams’ possession was unauthorized. He sought recovery of the property based on his legal ownership and requested that the court overturn the lower court's ruling in favor of Williams.	Williams, the defendant, contended that he had valid color of title supported by actual possession of the property for a specified duration, alongside payment of taxes. He asserted that his possession established legal rights under the limitations act of 1839, which he argued barred Kibbie's claims based on the statute of limitations concerning the life estate of a husband in a wife's property.

In the case of John W. Powell, Administrator, v. R. Wharton Ashlock, the legal proceedings occurred in 1886 in Greene County, Illinois. John W. Powell acted as the administrator of the estate of W.O. English, who had passed away. Powell brought a claim against Ashlock for money he had paid as a surety for the deceased's obligations. The complexities of the transactions involved made it challenging for Powell to present his case effectively, requiring a substantial amount of testimony and documentation to clarify the situation. After thorough examination of the records and arguments presented by both parties, the court found the claim against the estate to be valid and justifiable, deserving of payment.	The plaintiff, John W. Powell, claimed that he was owed $230.25 for money he paid acting as a surety for W.O. English's estate. He argued that the estate should be liable for these funds based on the transactions that had occurred and sought the court's ruling to affirm the validity of his claim and to ensure that the estate compensates him for the amount owed.	The defendant, R. Wharton Ashlock, likely contested the claim based on the validity and complexity of the transactions involved. While the specific arguments from Ashlock are not detailed in the judgment, his defense would revolve around challenging the necessity and the amount of the surety claim made against the estate of W.O. English, possibly questioning the evidentiary support presented by Powell.

In September 1875, a legal case titled "Levi C. Marsh v. William Green" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from Iroquois County, Illinois. The case involved a trust established by Robert and Frances M. Doyle for the benefit of Helen T. Green, aimed at securing a debt owed by Doyle. The trustee assigned to manage the trust, Mr. King, passed away before any default occurred in the payment of the owed amount. Subsequently, the Doyles conveyed the same property to Levi C. Marsh through a warranty deed, with Marsh agreeing to assume the payment obligation to Green. After default in the payment occurred, a bill was filed to appoint a new trustee to execute the trust and sell the property to raise the necessary funds. While initially, only Marsh was named as a defendant, the Doyles later appeared in court and waived formal service, allowing the case to proceed. Marsh contended that the Doyles were necessary parties to the case, prompting the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court after the lower court had appointed a new trustee.	The plaintiff, William Green, contended that a trustee should be appointed to manage the trust and sell the property to secure the payment of the owed debt. Green argued that since the trust had a specified purpose and a default in payment had occurred, appointing a trustee was imperative to execute the trust as intended by the Doyles' deed. Green maintained that the matters at hand were properly initiated despite Marsh's objections regarding the necessity of including the Doyles as defendants.	The defendant, Levi C. Marsh, argued that the Doyles should have been made parties to the suit because they originally held the interest in the property. Marsh contested the lower court’s ruling on the grounds that the appearance and waiver by the Doyles did not remedy the lack of their formal inclusion in the case. Furthermore, Marsh asserted that he should not be held accountable for the actions of a trustee that he claimed was improperly appointed without the necessary parties being included, which he believed was a procedural error that warranted reversal.

The case of Peoria & Pekin Union Ry. Co. v. Thomas O’Brien was decided on January 7, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose from the death of Edward Burk, who was working as a laborer and track repairer for the railway company in Peoria, Illinois. The accident occurred while Burk was picking out dirt from a railway crossing, and he was struck by a switch engine that was in plain sight. Evidence suggested that Burk was cautioned to look out for himself while working, yet he sustained injuries that led to his death. The plaintiff retrieved a suit against the railway, claiming that negligence on the part of the railway's servants was responsible for Burk’s death, despite him allegedly exercising reasonable care for his own safety during the incident.	The plaintiff, Thomas O’Brien, as administrator of Edward Burk’s estate, argued that the railway company was negligent in the operation of its switch engine and that this negligence directly caused Burk’s death. The plaintiff sought damages for the pecuniary injuries caused by Burk's death, asserting that he had been exercising ordinary care for his own safety at the time of the accident.	The defendant, Peoria & Pekin Union Ry. Co., contended that the jury was improperly instructed, leading to an erroneous verdict. They argued that the plaintiff's instructions failed to require the jury to consider Burk’s own care and caution during the incident, implying that his negligence should preclude recovery. The defense additionally claimed that there was insufficient evidence to suggest Burk was qualified to provide moral or intellectual training to his children, which was improperly considered in assessing damages.

In 1886, the Chicago-based firm Wilbur & Allin, specializing in crockery, filed for insolvency and made an assignment for the benefit of creditors. Subsequent negotiations led to a settlement agreement whereby the creditors accepted 50% repayment for their debts. To facilitate this, a new partnership was formed, with Benjamin C. Allin as the general partner and several individuals contributing as special partners, providing a collective capital of $10,500. This agreement stated that the special partners would not withdraw their capital until the company had settled its debts to these partners, and all creditors signed the agreement to halt further legal proceedings against Wilbur & Allin. However, this partnership also failed in October 1887. The case revolves around a promissory note, highlighting whether the parties acting as special partners had protected status under limited partnership law or if they were liable as general partners based on their failure to comply with statutory requirements for limited partnerships.	The Manhattan Brass Company, as the plaintiff, argued that the special partners involved in the limited partnership should be held liable as general partners due to non-compliance with the statutory requirements for limited partnerships. The plaintiff requested enforcement of the promissory note associated with the agreed settlement, asserting that these partners did not meet the legal criteria necessary to maintain their status as special partners.	The defendants, consisting of the special partners, contended that they had complied with the terms of the limited partnership agreement and that the contributions made were legitimate as per the statutes governing such partnerships. They argued that they intended to protect their limited partnership status and should not be liable as general partners. They sought to uphold the lower court's judgment which favored them, asserting their legal protection.

In December 1835, the case Asahel Hannum v. Elias Thompson was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal battle originated in Putnam County, where Elias Thompson filed an action for trespass against Asahel Hannum in the Circuit Court. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Thompson, awarding him one hundred dollars in damages. Dissatisfied with this judgment, Hannum appealed to the Supreme Court, contending that a procedural error occurred during the lower court proceedings. The key issue at hand was that the clerk of the Circuit Court had failed to affix the court's seal to the original summons, which Hannum’s counsel argued invalidated the summons and should lead to its quashing. The Supreme Court's examination focused primarily on this procedural flaw that could potentially affect the validity of the previous ruling.	Elias Thompson, the plaintiff, contended that he was wronged by Asahel Hannum's actions that constituted trespass. Thompson sought legal compensation for the damages incurred, amounting to one hundred dollars, which was awarded to him by the Circuit Court. He maintained that the court's ruling was justified based on the established claim of trespass against Hannum.	Asahel Hannum, the appellant, argued that the judgment rendered by the Circuit Court was flawed due to a significant procedural error; specifically, the original summons was issued without the necessary seal of the court. His counsel moved to quash the summons on these grounds, asserting that the lack of a seal rendered the summons invalid. Hannum sought to have the Circuit Court's judgment reversed due to this error, which he believed mandated a new consideration of the case.

In the legal case of James B. Hinde et al. v. The Wabash Navigation Company, which took place in November 1853 in Illinois, key individuals involved included plaintiffs James B. Hinde and Jacob Lesker, and the defendant, Wabash Navigation Company. The case arose from a dispute over timber and materials taken from the plaintiffs’ property, which were used by the Wabash Navigation Company during the construction of a dam and lock. The plaintiffs argued that the materials had been taken unlawfully without proper compensation. The court proceedings and arguments centered around whether the contractors, who were tasked with the construction work, operated under the authority of the navigation company and whether the plaintiffs had a right to seek damages for the timber taken from their property.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Wabash Navigation Company unlawfully took timber and material from their property in connection with the construction of a dam and lock. They argued that they were entitled to compensation for the losses incurred due to the unauthorized appropriation of their materials and sought legal recourse based on the charter provisions that allowed the company to take such materials while ensuring that the landowners could claim damages.	The defendant, Wabash Navigation Company, contended that the timber in question was taken by contractors, Samuel and Isaac Culbertson, who were working on behalf of the company. They argued that any claim for the taken materials should be directed against the contractors, rather than the company itself, as the contractors had acted outside the scope of their authorized duties. The defendant sought to limit their liability by distinguishing between damages assessed for actions taken by them versus those taken by the contractors.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. Edward E. Lawrence, v. The Board of Supervisors of Clark County" took place in January 1869, in Clark County, Illinois. Edward E. Lawrence, the relator, filed an appeal against the Board of Supervisors of Clark County. The core of the dispute was an alternative writ of mandamus that Lawrence sought to compel the Board to levy a tax to pay a county order he held. This order, issued to him for military services during the Civil War, amounted to $400. The Board had issued this order and it was signed by both the County Clerk and Treasurer. However, the court questioned whether the order was valid as it was drawn from the general revenue fund and not the specific "Bounty tax fund" which was established for military service remuneration. The court assessed that such orders do not confer a special status for the holder, and mandamus should not be used as a remedy for payment in this context. Instead, Lawrence should have pursued conventional legal remedies.	Edward E. Lawrence claimed the right to a mandamus to compel the Board of Supervisors to levy a tax for the payment of his military service order. He argued that the order he held, acknowledging his right to payment, entitled him to this extraordinary remedy. He contended that his position as a soldier merited the enforcement of payment of the $400 owed to him.	The Board of Supervisors contended that the writ of mandamus was not appropriate in this case, as there were existing legal remedies available. They maintained that orders drawn on the general revenue fund did not have priority and thus did not justify a mandamus action. They also argued that countless holders of similar orders could misuse the process if allowed to seek mandamus, leading to an unsustainable situation for county governance.

In 1885, in Cook County, Illinois, the case "Joseph C. Mackin v. The People of the State of Illinois" arose from an indictment against Joseph C. Mackin for perjury. The indictment stemmed from testimony Mackin provided to a grand jury investigating alleged election fraud during the November 4, 1884, election for local offices, including a senator position. The grand jury was tasked with discerning whether fake ballots had been used in the election. Mackin was accused of directing the printing of spurious ballots that imitated genuine tickets and lying about his involvement while under oath. The case gained attention due to its implications for electoral integrity and the judicial process, as the credibility of witnesses and testimony was central to the investigation. After a trial, Mackin was found guilty of perjury, which highlighted serious concerns regarding the conduct of elections and the accountability of individuals involved.	The plaintiff, represented by the State of Illinois, contended that Joseph C. Mackin provided willfully false testimony before the grand jury while investigating potential election fraud. The prosecution argued that Mackin's perjured statements concerning his engagement with the printing of fake ballots undermined the integrity of the election inquiry. The plaintiff sought a conviction for perjury, highlighting the material nature of Mackin's falsehoods that related directly to the criminal investigation at hand.	In his defense, Joseph C. Mackin argued against the validity of the grand jury’s indictment, asserting errors in the process of selecting the grand jury and questioning the materiality of the testimony that formed the basis of the perjury charges. He claimed that the trial court had erred in its instructions to the jury and asserted that the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that his testimony was false and relevant to a crime that had been committed, seeking to have the charges dismissed or the verdict overturned.

On September 15, 1856, Franklin Parmelee, Daniel A. Gage, Liberty Bigelow, and William S. Johnson, partners operating as F. Parmelee & Co. in Chicago, borrowed $50,000 from Daniel Lawrence of Medford, Massachusetts. To secure repayment in five annual installments with 10% interest, they conveyed certain real estate in Chicago to Lawrence, binding themselves to pay the obligations under a lease and a purchase contract. The deed included a covenant for quiet enjoyment. Concurrently, a contract was established stipulating that upon full payment, Lawrence would reconvey the property. They made interest payments at a higher rate until April 1861, when they stopped paying the principal amount. On August 4, 1864, Parmelee and two partners filed a chancery lawsuit against Lawrence, misrepresenting the transaction and claiming Lawrence could not provide a perfect title. Lawrence responded with a cross-bill revealing the true nature of the agreement, seeking repayment or the property's sale. The case continued with subsequent filings, including a supplemental bill claiming a release concerning one partner's payment to Lawrence, which Lawrence disputed as fraudulent. The Superior Court ruled against the plaintiffs, leading to an appeal.	The plaintiffs alleged that they were buyers of the property and claimed that Lawrence was unable to provide a clear title, thus warranting an injunction against Lawrence's attempts to collect debt or evict them. They further argued that a release agreement concerning one partner's payment should discharge all covenants against Lawrence for the remaining partners, asserting that this constituted a legal satisfaction of the debt.	Lawrence contended that the transaction constituted a loan secured by a mortgage, not a sale, and thus he was entitled to payment. He argued that the release obtained by Bigelow did not discharge his claims against the remaining co-obligors, emphasizing that it was induced by fraudulent behavior and should not serve to benefit the other partners.

In April 1865, the case Higgins v. Crosby took place before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case involved a dispute between Higgins, the plaintiff, and Crosby, the defendant. Central to the proceedings was a procedural issue concerning joinder in error, where the plaintiff's counsel argued that a rule requiring the defendant to join in error had expired, which, they claimed, warranted a default judgment and reversal for non-joinder. The defendant's counsel, however, contended that he was not aware of the rule being entered and expressed a willingness to join in error if given the opportunity. The court addressed the motion for default and ruled on the matter of joinder.	The plaintiff, Higgins, claimed that the defendant, Crosby, failed to join in error as required by the court rule. Consequently, Higgins sought a motion for default judgment due to this alleged non-compliance, thereby requesting a reversal of the previous decision based on Crosby's failure to adhere to procedural protocols.	The defendant, Crosby, countered the plaintiff's claims by asserting that he was not aware of the requirement to join in error and was therefore unprepared to do so immediately. He requested that the court allow him to join in error instanter, arguing that he should have the opportunity to correct the oversight.

Jonathan Gibbons was the administrator of Hiram Kimball, who had passed away. The case was initiated in the probate justice court of Morgan County, Illinois in the early 1840s concerning a lost note allegedly worth about $800. After the initial ruling favored Gibbons, the defendant, James Johnson, appealed, leading to a motion to change the venue to Scott County. During the trial, Johnson denied the execution of the note, while Gibbons stated the note was lost. After a jury trial, the judge instructed the jury that Gibbons had not provided sufficient evidence to warrant a judgment in his favor. The jury subsequently ruled in favor of Johnson, resulting in a series of assigned errors that Gibbons raised with the higher court, questioning the trial court's decisions regarding the appeal and jury instructions. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the legal framework governing appeals from the probate justice's rulings, the timing of exceptions taken by Gibbons, and the imposition of costs against the plaintiff.	Gibbons primarily argued that the appeal was valid under Illinois law, asserting that he had properly followed the legal procedures in seeking recourse for the lost note and that the trial court improperly instructed the jury regarding the sufficiency of evidence. He sought a reversal of the jury's verdict against him and a judgment in his favor for the amount claimed.	Johnson countered Gibbons's claims by denying the execution of the note and argued that the plaintiff had not presented adequate evidence to support his case. He also contended that the trial court's jury instructions were appropriate and upheld the ruling in his favor, seeking to maintain the judgment against Gibbons.

Martin Corley et al. were the plaintiffs in error in a case against Michael Kennedy, the defendant in error, which took place in Westfield township, Illinois. The events began with a petition for the establishment of a highway filed by three supervisors in October 1860. The petition was posted publicly on October 12, but the commissioners acted on it prematurely within 17 days instead of the mandated 20. A hearing was set for November 7, but the road was denied at that time. An appeal was filed on November 28, and after a subsequent order to establish the highway and assess damages, a Circuit Court was convened. However, the Circuit Court quashed the order of establishing the road and ruled in favor of the defendant, stating that procedural errors invalidated the commissioners' actions. Key individuals included Martin Corley, the highway commissioners, the town clerk, and the supervisors who oversaw the highway establishment.	The plaintiffs, represented by J. I. Taylor, contended that the actions of the supervisors in laying out the highway were valid and legal. They argued that the Circuit Court erred in quashing the orders and proceedings related to the highway. The plaintiffs requested the court to uphold the validity of the highway and argued that the legal notices and processes were properly followed.	The defendant, Michael Kennedy, represented by M. T. Peters and Gr. O. Ids, claimed that the highway's establishment was illegal and void due to multiple procedural violations. He argued insufficient notice was given prior to action on the petition, as the required 20 days had not elapsed. The defendant further contended that the commissioners failed to follow proper protocol regarding notice for meetings and damaged rights by acting prematurely and without the necessary formalities. Kennedy requested the annulment of the proceedings regarding the highway.

In 1866, a foreclosure proceeding took place in Chicago involving a mortgage held by Joseph Peacock, with Ellen Walter, among others, as defendants. A decree was issued, leading to the property being sold to Duncan McCollum for $6,000. McCollum died in 1867, leaving a document indicating his intent to sell the property to Solon Nickerson for a down payment and further payments. Ellen Walter claimed that she owned the equity of redemption in the property and alleged that McCollum had bought the property at her request, intended as a trust for her benefit. The case arose as she filed for a conveyance of the property after McCollum's death when his widow, Clarissa Klock, became a party to the suit. The lower court dismissed Walter’s bill, citing the statute of frauds, leading to an appeal.	Ellen Walter argued that McCollum purchased the property for her benefit, asserting an equitable interest because she believed he held the title in trust for her. She contended that at the time of the purchase, they had an understanding that he would hold the title as security for any future advances he made. Walter sought a court order to compel a conveyance of the property, claiming the right to it based on her financial contributions and the alleged trust agreement.	The defendants, represented by Klock and others, maintained that McCollum had taken the title in his own name and had executed a valid sale agreement to Nickerson. They argued that the statute of frauds applied, prohibiting the enforcement of any parol agreement related to the property. They contended there had been no fiduciary relationship or fraud, and that Barbara Klock had married McCollum after the contract was executed. Thus, Klock's heirs should retain their title without being liable for any implied trust.

In the case of John L. McCormick v. William L. Huse, the events unfolded in September 1872 in LaSalle County, Illinois. John L. McCormick, the plaintiff, claimed that the defendant, William L. Huse, committed several acts of trespass against his property. McCormick asserted he possessed a pontoon bridge and ferry across the Illinois River and had constructed a road for access. The defendant allegedly destroyed parts of the road and erected fences, obstructing travel to and from McCormick's bridge and ferry. The heart of the dispute revolved around an agreement with Theron D. Brewster, which was pivotal to the ownership rights over the land where the alleged trespasses occurred. Brewster had previously agreed to allow the Illinois River Bridge Company to use the land, but there were differing interpretations of the status of this agreement and the use of the road at the time of the alleged trespasses. The case was complicated by arguments about possession and the interpretation of written agreements.	McCormick claimed that Huse’s actions were illegal trespasses on his property, specifically disrupting the access to his ferry and bridge. He argued that he was in possession of the property under an agreement that granted him the right to use the road constructed over Brewster’s land, and he sought damages for the obstruction caused by Huse's actions.	Huse defended himself by claiming that the land was owned by Brewster and that he had the right to use it. He argued that the agreement allowing McCormick to use the road had expired, and therefore, McCormick had no rightful claim to the property at the time of the alleged trespasses. He contended that the road was no longer in use, and McCormick should not be entitled to recover damages.

In 1867, Charles W. Holder was elected as a director and subsequently appointed treasurer of the Lafayette, Bloomington and Mississippi Railway Company. During his tenure, which lasted until January 31, 1872, no official salary or compensation was established for his role as treasurer. Upon settling with the company, Holder was allowed a sum of $4,000 for his services and received a warrant from the company for that amount. However, this warrant was later contested, leading to a trial where the court determined the appropriateness of a financial claim made by Holder for his services as treasurer. The legal proceedings centered on whether Holder's work was outside the scope of his duties as a director and whether he was entitled to payment despite the absence of formal compensation arrangements. The court concluded that since no compensation was predetermined, Holder’s role as both a director and treasurer meant the services rendered were inherently part of his duties as an officer of the company, which led the court to rule against him.	Holder claimed that the services he provided as treasurer were extraordinary and should warrant compensation despite the absence of a fixed salary. He argued that there was an understanding that he would receive a fair remuneration for his services, thereby seeking to enforce the warrant for $4,000.	The railway company contended that since Holder was a director, the services he provided as treasurer did not qualify for additional compensation. They argued that the board of directors managed the company’s funds in a fiduciary capacity and that there had been no formal agreement for compensation established prior to the performance of his duties. They maintained that the lack of a predetermined salary meant that Holder could not claim payment for his services.

In 1855, George Crull and his wife initiated a legal action against Charles F. Keener, the executor of an estate, in the Scott Circuit Court, Illinois. The controversy arose over a claimed debt of $1,000 for services rendered by the wife to her father, who was the defendant's testator. The plaintiffs and defendant entered into a written stipulation regarding the circumstances of the case, agreeing on the key facts for the court to review. The case was filed in July 1855, but the defendant asserted that the claim was barred by the statute of limitations. Subsequently, the matter was escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court for a certificate decision regarding a question of law arising from the agreed facts. However, the Supreme Court determined that it lacked jurisdiction over the matter since no final decision had been made in the circuit court. Following this ruling, the defendant moved to strike the case from the circuit court's docket, a motion that was granted. The plaintiffs challenged this outcome, arguing that the circuit court had jurisdiction and should proceed to assess the case.	The plaintiffs, George Crull and his wife, contended that they were entitled to recover $1,000 for services that the wife provided to her father, the deceased individual represented by the defendant. They claimed that the statute of limitations did not bar their action and sought the circuit court’s ruling based on a stipulated set of facts. They argued that the procedural steps taken by the defendant to strike the case from the court were inappropriate given that both parties had already established jurisdiction by appearing in court and agreeing to the stipulation.	The defendant, Charles F. Keener, maintained that the plaintiffs' claim was barred by the statute of limitations. He argued that prevailing legal procedure mandates that, once an action is brought before the court, it must be decided within a specific timeframe, which he contended had not been adhered to in this case. Consequently, he sought to have the circuit court strike the cause from its docket, believing that the procedural missteps warranted such a dismissal.

In April 1858, a legal case was held in McHenry County, Illinois, known as Isaac Korsoski et al. v. Nathan H. Foster. The dispute arose from a clothing transaction and the payment details involving a note. Plaintiff Nathan H. Foster claimed against the defendants, Isaac Korsoski and his company, asserting that they owed him money based on a promissory note dated June 1, 1856, for $100. During the proceedings, the defendants contended that the amount was beyond the jurisdiction limits of a justice of the peace. The trial prior to the appeal had resulted in a judgment in favor of Foster, awarding him $99.60 plus costs of the suit, asserting that the justice had jurisdiction. The defendants sought an appeal, arguing against the jurisdiction of the justice and the validity of a credit given on the note for a rubber coat they sold to Foster.	The plaintiff, Nathan H. Foster, argued that the credit applied to the promissory note was valid and fair. He maintained that he was owed the amount indicated on the note and that the defendants were obligated to fulfill their debt to him. Foster requested the court to uphold the initial judgment in his favor, asserting that the note’s indorsement was a legitimate credit and that he was entitled to the amount awarded.	The defendants, Korsoski and his company, asserted that the justice of the peace did not have jurisdiction over the case, as the total amount involved exceeded the limits for such a court. They disputed the fairness of the credit applied towards the note, claiming that it was not a legitimate transaction. The defendants insisted that the judgment should be dismissed due to jurisdictional concerns and the irregularities of the credit on the note.

In the case of Edward McKinley v. James Braden, heard before the Illinois Supreme Court, the events unfolded in 1830 at the Madison Circuit Court, Illinois. The plaintiff, Edward McKinley, filed an action of trover and conversion against James Braden, the administrator of David Gregory, who was deceased. McKinley claimed ownership of a horse that belonged to Gregory. Following Gregory's death, the horse passed into the possession of Polly Gregory, David's widow, and later into Braden's custody. The plaintiff alleged that Braden wrongfully sold the horse and retained the proceeds for personal use. During the initial trial, Braden's demurrer against McKinley's declaration was overruled, and after various pleadings and trials, a verdict was initially rendered in favor of Braden. However, this verdict was later set aside due to the immateriality of the issue at hand, leading to a repleader by consent. In subsequent trials, Braden requested the jury instruction to ascertain McKinley’s status as administrator, which the court denied, instead focusing on whether McKinley had proven his possession of the horse and Braden's conversion of it. Ultimately, the court weighed procedural legality and the essential facts of possession and conversion in their resolution of the case.	The plaintiff, McKinley, claimed that as the administrator of David Gregory’s estate, he retained the right to the horse, which had been wrongfully converted by Braden. McKinley argued that it was unnecessary to prove his administrative status if he could establish that he had actual possession of the horse prior to the incident and demonstrate that Braden had converted it to his own use by selling it without authority.	The defendant, Braden, contended that McKinley needed to prove his status as the administrator of David Gregory’s estate and thereby establish his legal right to claim the horse. Braden argued that the jury should find in his favor unless they believed McKinley had definitively proven his administrative position or that he had previously possessed the horse.

In November 1823, in Gallatin, Illinois, Samuel L. White (the Plaintiff in Error) initiated a legal dispute against Thomas Thompson (the Defendant in Error). The case revolved around an action of trespass that was started by Thompson in the lower court. White claimed the pendency of a former suit involving the same cause of action as a defense against the current case. However, despite this defense being submitted, White proceeded to take a default judgment, leading to the impanelment of a jury that assessed damages. The legality of this action was contested as the defendant's plea remained unanswered at the time of judgment.	White asserted that his right to a fair legal process was violated when the court rendered a judgment by default while the defendant's plea was still pending. He argued that the existence of an ongoing prior suit regarding the same matter should have precluded the default judgment and demanded that the court acknowledge this oversight.	Thompson contended that the court erred in awarding a judgment by default without addressing his plea, which was filed prior to the judgment. He maintained that the proceedings were improper as they ignored the unresolved plea that challenged the legitimacy of the current action based on the prior case.

In December 1845, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of James Hill against John M. Ward. The conflict arose in Williamson County, Illinois, where Hill claimed that Ward’s construction of a mill dam led to backwater that flooded his land. This flooding rendered a ford on Hill's property inconvenient and resulted in damage to Hill's mill site. Hill had initiated preparations to build his own mill as early as June 1839, securing the necessary permits and patents for his land. Several witnesses testified that following the construction of Ward's mill dam, the water levels at Hill's mill site rose significantly, hindering its operation. Testimonies indicated that the current that once flowed freely had been obstructed, causing rising water levels below Hill’s mill that corresponded with the operation of Ward's mill. The defense countered this evidence by presenting testimonies asserting that there was no significant change in the water flow after Ward's dam was built.	James Hill claimed that the construction of John M. Ward's mill dam caused backwater that flooded his land, particularly affecting a ford and damaging his mill site. He argued that Ward's actions constituted a trespass on his property rights, warranting compensation for the damages he incurred due to the obstruction of the water flow. Hill sought a jury verdict to recover these damages.	John M. Ward defended against Hill's claims by asserting that the evidence did not support Hill's assertions of damage due to backwater from his mill dam. He emphasized that the state of the creek and the operation of Hill's mill were not adversely affected by his dam as claimed. The defense presented witness testimonies that contested Hill's narrative, suggesting that water flow had not changed significantly after Ward's dam was constructed.

In January 1862, the case of Michael Mullett, Appellant, against Dorothea Shrumph and William Shrumph, Administratrix and Administrator of the Estate of John E. Mullett, deceased, was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The origins of the case trace back to the Bond County Court, where the appellees sought payment for work performed by the deceased, John E. Mullett, on the Mississippi and Atlantic Railroad in 1854. The plaintiff's claim was built around testimony stating that John E. Mullett worked for 108 days without being compensated, and the work was acknowledged to be worth $2.15 per day. Despite an alleged agreement regarding payment, the defendant argued that the work was part of a partnership arrangement among the Mullett family members, which affected the obligations for remuneration. Testimonies were provided by both the plaintiffs and defendants regarding the alleged partnership and the conditions tied to the payment for work rendered. Ultimately, the case revolved around the interpretation of promises regarding payment and the constraints posed by the statute of limitations.	The plaintiff claimed that John E. Mullett provided substantial labor on the Mississippi and Atlantic Railroad for which he was never compensated. They asserted that the defendant had promised to settle the account as soon as he received payment for certain works, thus creating an express promise to pay. The plaintiffs requested compensation of $245, based on the work performed by the deceased.	The defendant argued that there was a partnership arrangement among Michael Mullett and John E. Mullett, which indicated that any payment obligation was shared and not solely on Michael Mullett's shoulders. He contended that his promise to pay was conditional and did not constitute a waiver of the statute of limitations unless it could be proved that he had received payment for the work completed.

John Gray et al. v. Minard L. Waterman is an 1866 trespass case originating from a dispute over a fence's location in relation to a public road in Grundy County, Illinois. The case arose after Minard L. Waterman, the plaintiff, accused defendants John Gray, Reuben Raymond, Christopher O. Massey, Charles Noble, Robert McFarland, and Thomas Gray of unlawfully tearing down his fence and damaging his crops. Initially, the trial took place in the Grundy Circuit Court but was later transferred to Kendall County. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Waterman, awarding him $883.12 in damages. The defendants argued their actions were justified since the removed fence was on a public highway, but this claim was met with scrutiny due to conflicting surveys regarding the road's exact location. The evidence presented included differing testimonies from surveyors and witnesses, complicating the case further, as the determination of whether the fence was indeed on public property was key to resolving the dispute.	The plaintiff, Minard L. Waterman, claimed that the defendants unlawfully removed his fence, which resulted in the destruction of crops on his property. He argued that the fence was not located on a public highway as claimed by the defendants and requested damages for the wrongful trespass and the loss of his crops, amounting to $883.12.	The defendants contended that their actions were justified since they believed the fence was on a public highway. They presented multiple pleas to back their claims, arguing that as part of the traveling public, they had the right to remove obstacles from the highway. Additionally, they sought to challenge the plaintiff's assertions of malice and the admissibility of certain pieces of evidence regarding the road's status.

In the case of Charles Dennehy v. The City of Chicago, the legal matter arose in 1887 in Cook County, Illinois. The appellant, Charles Dennehy, faced a conviction in the Criminal Court of Cook County for selling spirituous and vinous liquors in quantities of one gallon or more without a license from the city of Chicago. The ordinances in question mandated that no individual or corporation could sell these liquors in such quantities without first obtaining a license, along with a prescribed penalty for violations ranging from $50 to $200. The appellant contested the validity of the city ordinances, arguing that the city lacked the authority to impose such a license fee for wholesale liquor sales and that the licenses were imposed only for revenue and not for regulatory purposes. The case therefore primarily revolved around interpretations of city charters and the extent of municipal powers regarding liquor sales.	The plaintiff, the City of Chicago, argued that Dennehy was in violation of the city's ordinances requiring a license for selling liquors in certain quantities. The city asserted that it had the authority, under its charter, to regulate and impose fees on wholesale liquor sales to maintain public order and prevent the social issues associated with alcohol consumption. The legal requests centered on upholding the ordinances that mandated licensing for liquor sales to advance public health interests and economic regulation of liquor transactions.	Dennehy, the defendant, claimed that the ordinances enforcing licensing for liquor sales were invalid for two primary reasons: (1) the city purportedly lacked the charter power to impose a licensing fee on wholesale dealers and, (2) the requirement was claimed to be established solely for revenue generation rather than for genuine regulatory goals. He maintained that the legislative grants of authority did not extend to wholesale liquor operations and argued against the legal reasoning supporting the city's ordinances aimed at licensing liquor sales.

The case of Clarissa Miner v. Abraham Hess took place in January 1868 in Bushnell, Illinois. The key individuals involved include the plaintiff, Clarissa Miner, and the defendant, Abraham Hess. The dispute arose from a lease agreement executed on December 13, 1861, wherein Miner leased a property from Hess for three years at an annual rent of $125. The lease described the property as "Twenty-four feet of the south half of lot 4, block 33, Bushnell, Illinois." Miner sought to correct what she deemed a mistake in the description of the land, claiming that it should have referred to "Twenty-four feet off of the south side of lot 4." Although the defendant did not deny that the twenty-four feet were supposed to be from the south side of the lot, he argued that he only leased an undivided half of the premises and that it should be referred to as such in the lease. The property was utilized as a hardware store by the complainant. Testimonies were presented to support both parties' claims regarding the mistake in the lease description.	Clarissa Miner contended that the lease contained a mistake in the property's description, which sought to correct this discrepancy. She argued that the intended description should clarify that the lease was for "twenty-four feet off of the south side" instead of "the south half." Miner aimed to formalize this adjustment in the court to reflect what she believed was the true intention of the agreement.	Abraham Hess claimed that the lease as written was valid and contested Miner's assertion of a mistake. He argued that she had leased the undivided half of the twenty-four feet and insisted that any misunderstanding in the lease description was unfounded. Hess maintained that the evidence did not sufficiently support Miner's claims and highlighted that she had taken possession of the entire leased premises for three years without dispute regarding the rent.

In the case of Hiram Smith et al. v. George M. Hollenback et al., the dispute originated in Kendall County, Illinois, around the year 1866. The conflict involved a farm purchased by John Miller in the 1840s. Notably, John Miller executed a warranty deed to his son James Miller to settle debts, while a chattel mortgage was given to another son, Abraham Miller. Events leading to the legal issue included claims by eastern creditors against John and subsequent judgments entered against him without proper authority from James and Abraham. A sheriff’s deed transferred ownership of the farm to James and Abraham in the context of questionable claim settlements. After Abraham's death in 1852, James sold the farm to George Hollenback. Dispute arose when Getty Jane Smith, claiming as the widow of Abraham Miller, sought to assert her rights to a portion of the land, believing that the deeds were fraudulent and that she held equitable interests from earlier transactions. The case was brought to the Court of Common Pleas of Aurora and then to the Illinois Supreme Court on a writ of error after the Circuit Court dismissed the complaint, assessing the nature of the ownership and claims made.	The plaintiffs, represented by Getty Jane Smith, claimed an equitable title to land based on a combination of circumstances, including a sheriff's deed and an alleged parol division of land among John Miller's heirs. They argued that the deed from James to Hollenback was obtained fraudulently and asserted they had a right to reclaim the property. The plaintiffs requested the court to set aside the deed and restore their rights to the land.	The defendants, including George Hollenback, contended that the legal title had transferred to James Miller, and therefore, Getty Jane, having no legitimate claim or interest in the land, lacked standing to bring the complaint. They argued that the historical transactions and eventual conveyance were valid, and that the plaintiffs' claims were unsubstantiated due to the absence of any legitimate equitable interest stemming from improper title actions or debts.

The case of Thomas Vennum v. Thomas E. Thompson revolved around an action of replevin concerning a yoke of oxen. It took place in April 1865 in Illinois. The key individuals involved were Thomas E. Thompson, the plaintiff, and Thomas Vennum, the defendant. Thompson claimed ownership of the oxen, while Vennum challenged this claim based on an alleged purchase from a third party, Edmonds. The events unfolded after Edmonds, who had the oxen under a contractual agreement to purchase them, went to transport corn but claimed the oxen broke away and later could not be located. The case was brought to trial, where a jury found in favor of Thompson, leading Vennum to appeal the decision. The main issues at trial involved the admissibility of Edmonds' declarations regarding ownership and whether proper instructions were given to the jury.	Thomas E. Thompson argued that he was the rightful owner of the yoke of oxen and that Vennum wrongfully obtained possession of them through a breach of trust orchestrated by Edmonds. Thompson sought the return of the oxen, asserting that the declarations made by Edmonds about the ownership were admissible and supporting his claim of ownership against Vennum's allegations of a purchase.	Thomas Vennum contended that he legally purchased the oxen from Edmonds, who was in possession of the oxen as his bailee. Vennum claimed that Edmonds’ declarations regarding the sale occurred before Thompson's possession, and thus he had a legitimate ownership claim. He requested the court to overturn the trial verdict in favor of Thompson, asserting that the jury had been improperly instructed regarding the rules of evidence and property ownership.

Thomas S. Dickerson v. R. P. Derrickson is a legal case that occurred in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision rendered in April 1864. The dispute revolves around a written agreement by Thomas S. Dickerson, who guaranteed payment of $325 to R. P. Derrickson in the event that George Kimball, the original debtor, failed to pay. This agreement was made in May 1861 and included the assignment of a judgment against Kimball. Derrickson sued Dickerson in the Circuit Court, which ruled in favor of Derrickson. The case progressed through legal arguments at the Circuit Court level, focusing on whether there was adequate consideration to support the promise made by Dickerson and the implications of the nature of the guaranty involved.	R. P. Derrickson, as the plaintiff, claimed that Thomas S. Dickerson had provided a valid guaranty for the payment of $325, dependent on George Kimball's failure to pay.
