Derrickson argued that the assignment of the judgment against Kimball constituted sufficient consideration for Dickerson's promise, and thus he sought enforcement of the guaranty, asserting that he had not been notified of Kimball's payment.	Thomas S. Dickerson, the defendant, contended that his obligation to pay only arose if Kimball failed to make the payment, and argued that he should have been notified of Kimball's non-payment before being held liable. He claimed there were variances between the instrument described in court and what was presented as evidence, which he believed nullified his liability. Dickerson sought to overturn the judgment imposed by the Circuit Court.

In 1872 in Whiteside County, Illinois, George W. Fitch, the appellant, contested the validity of a quit-claim deed originally executed by Thomas K. Irwin to John Whalon concerning a ferry franchise. The case emerged from a series of transactions involving Alfred B. Campbell, who initially owned the franchise and had sold it to Irwin in January 1870. Following a legal issue that left Campbell liable for costs, his sureties, Smith & Scotchbrook, sought to secure themselves by negotiating with Alanson Campbell, Alfred's father. They aimed to arrange for the ferry's ownership, which Irwin believed would ensue from the arrangement. This led to a rescission of Campbell’s contract with Irwin upon the delivery of Irwin’s note, effectively establishing an equitable claim on the franchise by the sureties. Various legal interpretations arose, particularly regarding the legal versus equitable ownership of the ferry franchise, with Whalon claiming to be the owner after securing a deed from Irwin. The dispute centered on the legitimacy of the title transfers involved.	The plaintiff, George W. Fitch, argued that the quit-claim deed from Irwin to Whalon was null and void, asserting that Whalon’s claims to the ferry franchise were illegitimate. He sought a decree to recognize his equitable right to the franchise based on the rescission of the earlier contractual arrangements involving Irwin and Campbell. Fitch requested the court to prevent the clerk of Whiteside County from issuing a ferry license to the appellant (Whalon) under the challenged deed.	The defendant, Jared D. Conyne, countered that he possessed a valid legal title to the ferry franchise through his acquisition via Whalon. He argued that the title should prevail over any equitable claims made by Fitch. Conyne maintained that his ownership rights were firmly established through legitimate transactions and sought the court to affirm his rights to operate the ferry under the issued license.

In 1886, the case of Town of Aurora et al. v. Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad took place in Aurora, Illinois. The Town of Aurora, a municipal corporation, had collected $1,491.40 from the property of the railroad company (the appellee) through a special tax meant to pay for railroad bonds. The bonds, however, were declared void due to the statute under which they were issued being illegal. The Town had maintained the tax as a separate account, explicitly to cover these bonds, but intended to reallocate the funds for road and bridge purposes. The appellee, which owned substantial taxable property in Aurora, sought to restrain the Town from diverting the funds collected under this special tax, maintaining that the funds must either be used to pay the bonds or refunded. This case arose due to grievances over the usage and management of taxpayer funds in the context of municipal obligations and taxes applied in a non-typical manner.	The plaintiff, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad, argued that the $1,491.40 collected by the Town was a special fund raised for a specific purpose (payment on bonds) and constituted a trust fund. They requested the court to prevent the Town from reallocating the funds for road and bridge purposes, asserting that the money should either be applied to the purpose for which it was raised or refunded to them as the rightful contributors, given the lack of legitimacy of the bonds.	The Town of Aurora contended that the bonds were void and that the funds collected through the special assessment did not constitute a trust fund entitled to legal protection. They claimed that the money could not be recouped, citing that taxpayers had no right to recover the funds unless they were collected under duress. The Town also raised defenses based on the Statute of Limitations, arguing that the appellee's claims were barred because they waited too long to contest the fund's usage.

The case of Samuel Seeley v. William Peters, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1848, originated from Peoria County, Illinois. The dispute began when Peters, the plaintiff, initiated an action of trespass against Seeley, alleging that Seeley's hogs had entered his field and caused damage to his wheat. The case was originally heard by a justice of the peace and was appealed to the Circuit Court, where it was tried before a jury. During the trial, Peters presented evidence that Seeley's hogs had indeed damaged his crops. Seeley, in his defense, argued that the fence on the north side of Peters' field was inadequately constructed, allowing hogs to enter freely. He cited that the area adjacent to the fence was prairie land, unoccupied and unenclosed, and that a public road ran along the fence. The Circuit Court instructed the jury that the condition of Peters' fence did not matter in determining liability for damages. As a result, the jury ruled in favor of Peters, leading to an entry of judgment for him. The appeal questioned whether the common law regarding enclosures was applicable in Illinois, necessitating an interpretation of existing statutory laws related to fences and inclosure requirements.",	Plaintiff William Peters claimed that Samuel Seeley's hogs caused damage to his wheat crops by trespassing into his enclosure. Peters argued that Seeley's responsibility was clear under existing laws, which allow landowners to hold adjacent property owners liable for damages caused by their animals, regardless of the condition of the injured party's fence. He sought damages for the injury inflicted on his property by Seeley's livestock.",	Defendant Samuel Seeley contended that the inadequate condition of Peters' fence was a contributing factor to the trespass, claiming the fence was insufficient to keep his hogs out. Seeley argued the local custom permitted animals to run at large and emphasized that under common law, an owner of livestock was not obligated to keep them fenced in unless the adjacent property was adequately enclosed. He maintained that the context of the law did not impose a duty on him to fence against cattle from an adjacent unfenced prairie.",

Joseph Einstein filed an appeal against The City of Joliet in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1859. The case pertains to a legal dispute that took place in Joliet, Illinois. It is noted that the current case mirrors a previously adjudicated case, Brown v. The City of Joliet, indicating that similar legal questions were at stake. Details on the specific nature of the conflict are minimal, but the record suggests that the core issues had been previously addressed in this term of the court, rendering further discussion unnecessary. The case ultimately transitioned from the Circuit Court due to its similarity with past rulings.	Joseph Einstein, the appellant, sought to challenge the judgment made by the Circuit Court. His main argument likely revolved around disputing the legality of an action taken by The City of Joliet, similar to the claims presented in the prior case of Brown. Although specific claims and legal requests are not detailed, it can be inferred that Einstein was pursuing favorable legal recognition that would reverse or amend the earlier ruling.	The City of Joliet, as the appellee, did not provide detailed defenses in the available case summary. However, it can be assumed that their stance would involve justifying the judgment made by the Circuit Court and defending their actions in line with municipal regulations. Given the lack of specific defenses presented, their request would generally likely involve maintaining the Circuit Court's judgment in their favor.

On October 3, 1872, Pankratz Stayart filed a praecipe for a summons against the Garden City Insurance Company in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, alleging trespass on the case upon promises. The summon was duly issued and served, with a return date set for November 1, 1872. On November 7, when the company failed to appear, a default judgment was entered against them for damages amounting to $2,625. The company then sought to reverse this judgment, contending that there was no declaration on file at the time of the judgment entry. An amended record was later submitted, which included a declaration dated October 25, 1872, but lacking a file-mark. The plaintiff's attorney subsequently filed a motion to have the declaration marked as filed on that date. Evidence was presented from a party who had been tracking the case, affirming that no declaration was on file as of November 10, 1872. The court found the evidence indicating that the declaration was not properly filed to be convincing and thus ruled the prior judgment in error.	The plaintiff, Pankratz Stayart, claimed that the Garden City Insurance Company failed to appear in court, resulting in a default judgment against them amounting to $2,625. They sought to enforce this judgment based on the presumption that the necessary legal documents were filed appropriately at the time of the ruling.	The defendant, Garden City Insurance Company, argued that the judgment should be reversed as there was no declaration on file when the default judgment was entered. They contended that the motion to file a declaration nunc pro tunc was improperly granted, and presented evidence suggesting that no declaration existed in the court's records at the time of the judgment entry.

In March 1835, a legal dispute arose in Madison County, Illinois, involving Thomas R. Wilson as the plaintiff and John S. Greathouse as the defendant. The case was initially prosecuted before a justice of the peace but was subsequently removed to the Circuit Court. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant had not appeared on the return day of the summons due to an insufficient return by the constable regarding the service of the summons. The constable’s return stated that the summons was "Executed on the within defendant by his reading the within," without providing a specific date of service. The plaintiff sought to prove that the service was timely and valid. However, the Circuit Court reversed the justice of the peace's judgment against the defendant, leading to the plaintiff filing a writ of error to challenge the Circuit Court’s decision. The court analyzed the legal requirements for serving summons and found that the constable's return lacked essential information needed to confirm timely service, rendering the proceedings irregular and void.	The plaintiff argued that the constable's return was inadequate as it did not indicate when the service of process was made, making it impossible to ascertain if it complied with the law's requirement of being served at least three days before trial. The plaintiff requested that the court reverse the Circuit Court's decision to undermine the judgment entered by the justice of the peace.	The defendant contended that the service was invalid due to the insufficient return by the constable, which did not comply with the legal standard of clearly providing the date of service. The defendant requested that the Circuit Court's ruling be upheld, asserting that without proper service, any judgment rendered would be void.

In 1887, the case of William T. Burgess v. Alpheus C. Badger et al. was adjudicated in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, with Judge Henry M. Shepard presiding. The legal dispute arose over a partnership agreement related to prosecuting suits involving the estate of a bankrupt individual. The key individuals involved were William T. Burgess, the plaintiff, and Alpheus C. Badger along with other defendants. The case centered on the nature and extent of the agreements made concerning the partnership and an accounting for costs and expenses incurred during the proceedings. The plaintiff sought clarification and equitable relief related to these matters.	The plaintiff, William T. Burgess, asserted that there were issues regarding the partnership's agreements concerning the bankrupt estate's lawsuits. He requested an equitable proceeding to clarify the nature of these agreements and demanded an accounting of costs and expenses that were pertinent to the lawsuits in question.	The defendants, represented by attorneys John Woodbridge and Lyman & Jackson, contended that the plaintiff's claims lacked substantial evidence and legal grounding. They argued against the necessity of the requested accounting and sought to have the case dismissed, maintaining that the plaintiff had not established a valid basis for the claims he made.

The case "The Town of Bruce v. T. Lyle Dickey" was decided on March 27, 1886, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict arose in the context of legal representation regarding the validity of bonds issued by the town of Bruce, which were intended to aid the construction of the Ottawa, Oswego, and Fox River Valley railroad, amounting to approximately $400,000. T. Lyle Dickey, the plaintiff, was employed as an attorney to challenge the collection of taxes and enforce bonds that the town had issued. The litigation spiraled from earlier cases in which the bonds were ultimately declared invalid. The town's supervisor employed Dickey to represent Bruce in various lawsuits arising from the same issues. Over time, Dickey successfully argued cases that affected multiple towns and their bonds, leading to the dismissal of the lawsuits against Bruce based on his agreements with other municipalities. After extensive litigation lasting several years, Dickey claimed his fees for legal services rendered during this time. The town of Bruce contended that the supervisor did not have the authority to hire an attorney on its behalf and that Dickey's services were impermissible due to his dual role as a judge while representing legal disputes for compensation.	T. Lyle Dickey, the plaintiff, argued that he was rightfully employed by the supervisor of the town of Bruce to provide legal services in defending the town against multiple lawsuits arising from the bonds. He sought compensation for his professional legal services, arguing that the town had benefited from his efforts in the litigation that confirmed the invalidity of the bonds. Dickey requested a total of $2,000 for his services, asserting that the town was bound by the actions of its supervisor, who had engaged him for representation.	The town of Bruce, as the defendant, contended that the supervisor lacked the authority to hire counsel without express authorization from the town's electors. They argued that this unauthorized hiring rendered any contract void. Furthermore, they asserted that Dickey, having been elected as a Supreme Court judge, was prohibited by the Illinois Constitution from practicing law for compensation during his term, and thus, he should not be compensated for his services. They maintained that any fee agreement could not exceed $300 as stated by Dickey during his hiring negotiations.

Kelsey v. Snyder is a legal case decided on June 14, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute centers around Kelsey, the plaintiff, who claims equitable ownership of an undivided one-half interest in a silver mine known as the Milk Maid lode, located in Ouster County, Colorado. The legal title was held by Ira F. Benson, who had passed away before the case. Kelsey alleges that through fraud, she was induced to assign a part of her claim against Benson's estate to Fannie Snyder for $2,000 and to transfer ownership of her half interest in the mine to Snyder. Kelsey contends that she was already the rightful owner of the mine and that Snyder had no legitimate right to convey it. She is seeking a decree affirming her ownership and declaring the assignment of $2,000 fraudulent and void. The case involves complex issues of trust, ownership rights, and the legal implications of the communications Kelsey had with Benson before his death.	Kelsey argues that she was the equitable owner of half of the Milk Maid lode and claims that the assignment she made to Fannie Snyder was obtained through false representations and without consideration. She asserts that Snyder had no interest or right to the mine and requests a court decree confirming her full ownership of the one-half interest. Kelsey also seeks to have the assignment regarding the $2,000 claim against Benson's estate declared fraudulent and void.	Fannie Snyder, the defendant, contends that Kelsey’s claims are without merit and argues that the court should dismiss parts of Kelsey's amended bill as irrelevant. Snyder maintains that the assignment was legitimate and denies the allegations of fraud. The defendant requests the court to uphold the assignment and the ownership transfer, asserting that Kelsey does not have the legal standing to reclaim the interest in the mine.

In January 1875, in Morgan County, Illinois, Cyrus Fanning was involved in a legal proceeding against the First National Bank of Jacksonville concerning the garnishment of his bank deposit. Fanning had incurred a judgment against him from James W. Ash for the sum of $166.36. An execution issued for this judgment was returned as nulla bona, indicating no available assets were found to satisfy the debt. On May 19, 1873, a garnishee process was issued and served upon the bank, which revealed that Fanning had a deposit of $80.60. Following the garnishment, Fanning notified the bank in writing that he claimed the deposit as exempt from garnishment under state law, ordering the bank not to pay it to anyone without his instruction. The case hinged on whether the money in the bank was subject to garnishment. Fanning, described as the head of a family with only minimal household goods as his property, argued that the funds qualified for exemption under Illinois statutes citing $100 worth of property suitable to his condition. The circuit court initially ruled against the bank in favor of Ash for the garnished funds, prompting an appeal.	Cyrus Fanning, the plaintiff, claimed that the $80.60 he had deposited at the First National Bank was exempt from garnishment under Illinois law. He contended that, as the head of a family with no substantial property aside from a few exempt household goods, the deposit should not be reachable by the garnishee process. Fanning sought a reversal of the circuit court’s decision, maintaining that he properly claimed the exemption in accordance with the statute allowing debtors to select property amounting to $100 as exempt based on their living conditions.	The First National Bank of Jacksonville, the defendant, argued that despite Fanning's claims, the previously garnished funds were subject to the court's garnishee process due to the existing judgment against him by Ash. The bank maintained its position based on the garnishments outlined in state statutes and acted according to the process served to them, suggesting that they had a duty to comply with the court's instructions regarding the funds in question.

On August 29, 1883, in Cincinnati, Ohio, Charles E. Bronte and others executed a promissory note promising to pay George and John H. Leslie $3,000 six months later. This note was created as part of a transaction involving shares of a mining company in Mexico. The note was subsequently transferred to William Grant in Chicago, who later filed suit against Bronte and others when the note matured. Bronte and the other defendants claimed that they had received fraudulent representations regarding the stock's value, asserting that it was worthless. They successfully defended against Grant's lawsuit, resulting in a judgment in their favor over a year later. Subsequently, the Leslies filed a new lawsuit against the Bronte parties on the same note. In their defense, the Bronte parties raised the earlier judgment as a bar to the new action. The case proceeded without a jury, leading to a legal ruling on whether the Ohio judgment barred the Leslies' current suit.	The plaintiffs, George and John H. Leslie, claimed that the Bronte parties owed them money based on the promissory note executed in 1883. They sought to recover the amount due on the note despite the prior judgment in favor of the defendants, asserting their legal right as payees and owners of the note.	The defendants contended that the earlier judgment in Ohio, where the court ruled in their favor concerning the same note, should bar the current action by the payees. They argued that since the merits of the validity of the note had already been decided, the Leslies could not pursue further claims against them.

The case revolves around a dispute between the East St. Louis Connecting Railway Company (plaintiff) and the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company (defendant) regarding the loss of two flat cars loaded with coal. The incident occurred on December 16, 1883, when the plaintiff delivered these cars to the defendant as a common carrier to be transported to the East St. Louis Glucose Works. The defendant was supposed to safely carry the cars and return them to the plaintiff after unloading. However, the cars were lost as they were destroyed by fire while in the temporary custody of the Glucose Works, before they could be unloaded and returned. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant was negligent and failed in its duties as a common carrier, leading to the loss of the cars and resulting in damages of $600. The case was decided in the City Court of East St. Louis without a jury and, after finding for the plaintiff, the defendant appealed, arguing that it should not be held liable since the cars were only to be returned after unloading.	The plaintiff claims that the defendant, as a common carrier, failed to safeguard the two cars loaded with coal, which resulted in their destruction and the plaintiff's financial loss of $600. The plaintiff alleges that the defendant acted carelessly and negligently, thereby breaching the agreement to transport the cars safely and return them after unloading. The plaintiff seeks compensation for the damages incurred due to this negligence.	The defendant argues that it should not be held liable for the loss of the cars because they were in the possession of the Glucose Works at the time of the fire, and the terms of delivery stipulated that the cars would only be returned after unloading. The defendant contends that it had fulfilled its duty as a common carrier by delivering the cars as instructed. Furthermore, it challenges the sufficiency of the plaintiff's declaration, stating that it did not adequately detail the alleged negligence.

Andrew J. McNail v. David Ziegler is a legal case that was decided in June 1873 in the St. Clair County Circuit Court, Illinois. The case involved a dispute over the ownership of certain mules that McNail sought to reclaim through a replevin action against Ziegler. The central issue in this case arose from Ziegler's claim that the mules did not belong to him but were instead the separate property of his wife, Elizabeth Ziegler. During the trial, Elizabeth was allowed to testify about the execution of a bill of sale that McNail had reportedly signed over to her for the mules, as well as the manner of payment. The jury ultimately sided with the defendant, Ziegler, rendering a verdict in his favor. McNail subsequently sought a new trial, arguing that the admission of Elizabeth's testimony violated his rights, but the court denied his motion and upheld the jury's verdict.	McNail, the plaintiff, argued that the mules in question were his property and that he had not transferred ownership to Elizabeth Ziegler. He contended that the defendant's assertion that the property belonged to his wife was not valid. Consequently, McNail sought a ruling to regain possession of the mules, highlighting the supposed wrongful retention of his property by Ziegler.	Ziegler, the defendant, sought to establish that the mules were indeed the separate property of his wife, Elizabeth. He argued that a bill of sale had been executed by McNail, transferring ownership to her. Ziegler maintained that this bill of sale was irrefutable evidence of Elizabeth's title to the mules, thereby negating McNail's claim to replevin them.

In the case of William H. Goff v. The Toledo, St. Louis and Kansas City Railroad Company, which took place in Coles County, Illinois, a significant event unfolded in 1888. The plaintiff, William H. Goff, was involved in a railroad accident while assisting a wrecking crew sent by the defendant, a railroad corporation. Following a wreck on the tracks, the defendant dispatched an agent with machinery and ropes to clear the obstructions. It was alleged that the defendant negligently provided unsafe ropes, which ultimately led to Goff's injury. When the laborers struggled to pull a car involved in the wreck using one of the defective ropes, Goff was ordered by the agent to assist. While doing so, the rope broke, resulting in a severe injury—a broken leg for Goff. The case progressed to the Illinois Appellate Court after the Circuit Court had originally dismissed Goff’s claims based on a demurrer, prompting an appeal to determine if a valid cause of action was presented.	The plaintiff, William H. Goff, claimed that the defendant was negligent in providing unsafe and insufficient ropes for the wrecking operation. He argued that the defendant failed to uphold the duty of care by not ensuring the proper condition of the ropes and machinery used during the clearing of the wreck. Goff contended that he acted with due care while assisting the crew and claimed damages for the injuries sustained due to the defendant's negligence.	The defendant argued that there was no proper notice of the defective conditions of the ropes since neither count of the complaint alleged that the defendant was aware of the defect. They contended that the law does not make them an absolute insurer of the safety of the equipment, and maintained that they had exercised reasonable care in providing the tools. Furthermore, the defendant emphasized that any defects known to the master could only be claimed if it could be demonstrated that ordinary care would have revealed them.

In January 1859, the case of Frederick Schultz v. Joseph Lepage was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict arose when Joseph Lepage, the appellee, accused Frederick Schultz and an accomplice, Henry Solomon, of trespassing and converting his property by killing and taking three hogs without permission. The initial case was pursued before a justice of the peace, highlighting evidence where Schultz and Solomon were found responsible for the hogs' deaths and their conversion for personal use. Additional evidence indicated that Schultz's dogs had injured a sow belonging to Lepage, leading Schultz to offer $3 as compensation, which Lepage rejected. Schultz contested the basis of the claims around the sow and aimed to clarify the merits of the case regarding the hogs, maintaining that he was unaware of his dogs' actions that injured the sow. Following a jury verdict that awarded Lepage a total of $22 for his hogs, Schultz appealed the decision.	Joseph Lepage, the plaintiff, argued that Frederick Schultz and Henry Solomon unlawfully killed and converted his hogs for their own use. He presented evidence showing the trespass and the value of the animals, asserting a claim that included compensation for three hogs that had been slaughtered, totaling $22. Lepage sought to hold Schultz liable for the damages caused by his dogs to the sow, despite Schultz's tender of $3 for that damage being rejected.	Frederick Schultz, the appellant, contended that the suit was improperly based on claims regarding the sow, arguing that he was not culpable since he did not know or cause the injury to the animal. Schultz sought the court’s instruction to highlight that the case was strictly about the hogs and that if he was not aware of the dogs’ behavior leading to the sow's injury, he should not be held liable for its value. He objected to the inclusion of the sow in the damages being considered.

In November 1875, Booker Pickrel sold seventy acres of land in Wataga, Illinois, to G. V. Rose, the husband of Laura Rose, for $1,600. The purchase was partially paid with $800 in cash, and the remaining balance was to be paid in five annual installments of $160 plus interest, as per a written contract that stipulated time of payment was of the essence. Shortly after the contract execution, G. V. Rose died, and no estate administration was initiated. In early 1876, Laura Rose approached Pickrel to discuss rescinding the contract and seeking a refund of the purchase money. Rose claimed that they verbally agreed on terms that included allowing her to occupy the land without paying rent until she could pay the first note, with an offer of $500 for the rescission. Pickrel disputed this claim, stating he provided a written proposition that included terms for a rescission that did not mention waiving rent. Laura Rose occupied the land until late 1876, when she indicated she could not make payments. The case proceeded to trial, where the jury found in favor of Laura Rose, awarding her damages. The judgment was appealed by Pickrel.	Laura Rose primarily argues that a verbal agreement was made with Pickrel, allowing her to occupy the land rent-free until she could secure the funds to pay the note. She contends that since she could not meet the payment requirement, she is entitled to a rescission of the contract and a refund of a portion of the purchase price.	Booker Pickrel contests Laura Rose's claims by asserting that any verbal agreements are superseded by the written proposition he provided. He maintains that the terms of this written agreement must govern the situation, asserting that Rose accepted these terms by taking possession of the property. Pickrel emphasizes that he was not obligated to alter the written proposal or to refund any payments under the agreed terms.

In January 1875, the case of William W. Deatherage et al. v. Joseph R. Roach was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Morgan Circuit Court, where Joseph R. Roach initiated an action of assumpsit against William W. Deatherage and others based on a promissory note. The central issue of the appeal involved the defendant's motion to continue the cause, claiming that the plaintiff had not properly filed the declaration ten days before the term of court. The declaration had indeed been filed in a timely manner on October 27, 1874, but was later withdrawn by the plaintiff’s counsel for safekeeping. The withdrawal of the declaration was deemed a common but improper practice, and despite the technicality raised by the defendants, there was no evidence presented that they were prejudiced or prevented from making a defense. The court noted that the plaintiff had a valid claim for the amount stated in the promissory note and reaffirmed the importance of court process integrity.	The plaintiff, Joseph R. Roach, argued that he had a legitimate claim based on a promissory note owed to him by the defendants. His main request was for the court to uphold the validity of the declaration despite the technical irregularity of it being withdrawn after filing. Roach maintained that the declaration was filed within the appropriate timeframe and restored before any defense could have been made.	The defendants claimed that the plaintiff's withdrawal of the declaration constituted a failure to comply with procedural requirements, specifically the rule that declarations must be filed ten days before the term of court. They requested that the court dismiss the case or continue the cause based on this procedural defect. However, they did not assert any substantive defenses against the promissory note itself nor did they indicate any prejudice caused by the plaintiff's actions.

M. O. Walker brought a legal case against The City of Chicago in September 1871. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal from a judgment made in the Superior Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gary. The dispute arose from a special assessment warrant concerning public improvements in Chicago. The key issue revolved around whether the city’s ordinance, which purportedly transferred the responsibility for deciding the nature and extent of public improvements to the Board of Public Works, was lawful. The case referenced earlier decisions, notably the case of Foss v. City of Chicago, which had established precedents regarding the validity of such ordinances. The court was tasked with determining the legitimacy of the ordinance in light of statutory responsibilities assigned to the city’s common council.	The plaintiff, M. O. Walker, contended that the ordinance in question was invalid because it improperly delegated the authority for determining public improvements to the Board of Public Works rather than retaining that power exclusively with the common council as mandated by law. Walker sought a judgment that would recognize the ordinance as void and potentially halt any special assessments conducted under it.	The City of Chicago, represented by Mr. M. F. Tuley, likely argued for the validity of the ordinance and the actions taken under it. They may have asserted that the special assessment process was carried out in good faith and within the framework of their established legal powers. The defendant sought to defend the applicability of the ordinance and maintain the legitimacy of the assessment process based on it.

The case "The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company v. Willis Cauble" was decided in June 1877 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The issue arose in Jackson County, Illinois, when Willis Cauble, a sub-contractor working under H. E. Payson & Co., sought to establish a lien against the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company for materials he provided and labor he performed during the railroad's construction. The proceedings began when Cauble filed a petition to obtain a lien, alleging that he had furnished materials and completed labor in good faith. The circuit court initially sustained a demurrer against him but subsequently permitted amendments. However, Cauble only served the railroad company and failed to provide adequate notice regarding the residency of the company’s president and secretary, which was a statutory requirement for perfecting the lien. Ultimately, the railroad company was found liable by the circuit court, leading to the company's appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Willis Cauble, the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to a lien on the railroad property for the value of materials furnished and labor performed as a sub-contractor for the principal contractors, H. E. Payson & Co. He asserted that he followed the requisite legal procedures under the applicable statute to establish this lien. His main request was for the court to recognize and enforce his right to recover the amounts owed due to his contributions to the railroad's construction.	The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company, as the defendant, contended that Cauble's petition was defective because it did not sufficiently demonstrate that he had given proper notice as required by statute. Specifically, the company argued that the petition failed to show whether its president or secretary resided or could be found in the county, which would have allowed Cauble to file notice with the circuit court instead. The railroad company maintained that this lack of required notice meant that Cauble had no legal claim to perfect the lien against their property.

Arthur Christin filed his case against James Erwin in 1887, stemming from an incident at a street crossing in Cook County, Illinois, where a collision occurred between a buggy, in which Christin was riding, and a heavy wagon driven by Erwin's servant. Witness testimonies provided conflicting accounts of the events surrounding the accident, with three witnesses supporting Christin's claims and one favoring Erwin. The jury was tasked with determining the facts and negligence involved in the incident. The majority opinion noted that there was sufficient evidence to support a conclusion of negligence on the part of Erwin’s driver while indicating that Christin was exercising ordinary care during the incident. The court found that any potential error in jury instructions regarding comparative negligence did not affect the outcome of the case, as the essential requirements were covered adequately in other instructions. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of Christin and awarded him $2,500 in damages, which the court found to be reasonable and not excessive, leading to the affirmation of the lower court's decision.	Christin sought damages for personal injuries resulting from the collision, arguing that the negligence of Erwin's driver was the direct cause of the accident. He asserted that he and the driver of the buggy exercised ordinary care prior to the incident, thereby fulfilling his legal obligation to avoid contributory negligence. Christin requested compensation, claiming the amount awarded was justified based on the circumstances of the case.	Erwin contended that his driver was not negligent and that Christin may have shared in the responsibility for the accident, suggesting that the jury instruction on comparative negligence lacked clarity on the requirement for ordinary care. He also argued against the amount of damages awarded, alleging that it was excessive compared to the evidence presented. His counsel sought to have the jury's verdict reversed based on these points.

The case titled "The Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company, Appellant, v. William H. Taylor, Appellee" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1862. The case arose in Richland County, Illinois, when William H. Taylor initiated proceedings against the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company after his colt was allegedly killed by a train. Taylor claimed that the railroad was responsible for the injury. Testimony revealed that the incident occurred at a location that was not clearly identified as a public crossing, thus raising questions about the railroad's liability based on state statutes, which exempted railroads from fencing requirements at public crossings. The court had to evaluate the evidence presented regarding the location of the incident and whether proper proof was provided to establish that the injury occurred on the defendant’s railroad without public crossing defenses.	The plaintiff, William H. Taylor, claimed that his colt was killed by the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company’s train due to the company's negligence for not having a proper fence where a fence was necessary to keep livestock away from the tracks. Taylor requested compensation for the value of the colt, which he believed to be around $50.	The defendant, the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company, contended that there was no proof provided to establish that the injury occurred at a location where the company was required to maintain a fence as mandated by statute. They argued that the evidence failed to connect them to the incident, as there was no clear proof that the incident occurred on their railroad or that the plaintiff was the owner of the animal at the time of its death.

The case "The City of Chicago v. The People ex rel. Henry W. King et al." was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. It arose after the city of Chicago held an election on April 23, 1875, to decide whether to become incorporated under a law enacted by the General Assembly on April 10, 1872. The city council authorized the election without submitting the question of minority representation, which was required by the act. Voters were given insufficient notice regarding polling places and the details of the election. Despite these concerns, the election was held, and the council declared the adoption of the act. Subsequently, a quo warranto action was initiated by residents questioning the legitimacy of the incorporation based on irregularities during the election process, including allegations of changes to polling places and lack of adequate record-keeping. The case ultimately centered around whether the election was valid despite these procedural issues.	The plaintiff, on behalf of the People, claimed that the election held to incorporate Chicago was invalid due to several procedural failings. They argued that minority representation was not submitted for vote at the same time as the incorporation question, that the notice of the election was defective as it did not detail polling places, and that last-minute changes to polling locations also tainted the election’s validity. They requested that the court declare the city's incorporation void and that the city should explain its claim to the authority under the act of 1872.	The City of Chicago defended against the claims by asserting the validity of the election process. The city maintained that the act of 1872 inherently required the question of minority representation to be voted on simultaneously with incorporation, which occurred, as the act did not specify separate submission instructions. They argued that the notice sufficed in informing voters of the election without needing to explicitly state polling places and that changes to polling locations were customary and publicized before the election. They sought to have the court dismiss the claims made by the plaintiffs, upholding the election and the incorporation of the city.

In November 1864, the case of Spencer S. Ewbanks v. The President and Trustees of the Town of Ashley was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from an action brought by the town against Ewbanks for allegedly violating a local ordinance prohibiting residents from storing more than ten cords of wood within the town limits. The case originated before a justice of the peace in the town of Ashley, Illinois, where a writ was served on Ewbanks without an arrest. He contested this procedural aspect and was initially unsuccessful, leading to a trial that resulted in a judgment against him for a twenty-dollar penalty. Ewbanks subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court, where he again challenged the writ's validity but was denied. The trial continued without a jury, during which the town produced evidence of the ordinance and claimed Ewbanks had stored sixteen cords of wood, which they argued violated town regulations. However, Ewbanks insisted that the ordinance had not been violated since there was no evidence that his actions caused any nuisance to the townsfolk.	The plaintiff, represented by the President and Trustees of the Town of Ashley, asserted that Ewbanks violated a town ordinance intended to prevent wood storage beyond ten cords, which they argued constituted a nuisance if it could negatively impact the health or comfort of townspeople. They requested the imposition of a penalty based on Ewbanks' alleged infraction and sought enforcement of the ordinance and recovery of costs associated with the suit.	Ewbanks, the defendant, argued that the trial court erred in several ways, including the admission of a printed copy of the ordinance into evidence and the denial of his motion to quash the writ issued by the justice of the peace. He contended that there was insufficient evidence to demonstrate that storing wood violated the ordinance, as there was no proof that it constituted a nuisance or caused harm to the community. Ewbanks requested that the judgment against him be overturned due to these alleged errors.

In December 1843, the case of William Orr v. George Howard et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Adams County, Illinois, involving key individuals William Orr as the plaintiff and George Howard along with additional defendants. The dispute arose from a previous judgment in the lower court, which was reversed due to a default by the defendants after they were notified of the proceedings through a publication in a newspaper. The attorney for the defendants claimed ignorance of the case being taken to the supreme court months after the judgment had been reversed. The case hinged on whether the reversal should be set aside based on the alleged lack of proper knowledge and involvement of the legal representation for the defendants.	The plaintiff, William Orr, argued that the notice given to the defendants was sufficient as it complied with legal requirements for non-residents through publication in a newspaper printed at the seat of government. Orr contended that the case had been properly reversed due to the defendants' default and that there was no substantial reason to set aside the reversal of the judgment.	The defendants, represented by G. C. Dixon on behalf of I. N. Morris, argued for the setting aside of the default judgment based on an affidavit indicating their attorney was unaware that the case had been escalated to the supreme court until months later. Their defense centered on the claim that they did not receive appropriate notification regarding the appeal, which directly impacted their ability to respond and participate in the case.

The case "The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Co. v. Alfred C. Jones" occurred in St. Clair County, Illinois, and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1872. The dispute arose when Jones, the plaintiff, sought compensation for the death of his horse, which was allegedly killed by a train belonging to the defendant, the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company. The horse, valued at $100, had escaped from its enclosure and strayed onto the railway tracks, an area where the rail company was legally required to maintain a fence to prevent animals from accessing the tracks. The law in question was the 1867 statute aimed at preventing domestic animals from running at large, which the defendant argued nullified their fencing obligation. The court was tasked with determining whether this newer law implicitly repealed the older railroad fencing requirement.	The plaintiff, Alfred C. Jones, asserted that the railroad company was negligent for failing to fence its tracks, leading to the death of his horse. He argued that his horse was not "at large" in the legal sense since it had strayed without his knowledge or consent and had not broken out of its enclosure previously. He requested compensation for the horse's value, asserting that the railway company's negligence was the direct cause of the incident.	The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company contended that the 1867 law prohibiting domestic animals from running at large superseded the requirement for railroads to erect fences. They argued that since the horse was found on the tracks, it implied that the owner had permitted it to be at large, thereby relieving them of liability. The company maintained that their compliance with the newer law negated their obligation to fence their tracks against such occurrences.

L. A. Smith, representing John and M. P. Mitchell, initiated a garnishee proceeding against Patrick Finlen, who served as the County Clerk of La Salle County, Illinois. This case stemmed from a dispute over a sum of $52.99, which was held by Finlen as part of receiving money for redeeming land that had been sold due to tax delinquency. On June 19, 1885, this money was paid to Finlen for the redemption of a property located in Marseilles, Illinois. The underlying issue involved the assertion that L. A. Smith was the holder of the certificate of purchase for said property at the time of the garnishee process. The initial judgment favored Finlen in the local Circuit Court, leading to this appeal. The case primarily questioned whether Finlen, as County Clerk and an officer of the law, could be held liable as a garnishee for money received in the performance of his official duties.	The plaintiff contended that Finlen, as the garnishee, was liable for a specific amount of money he held, which was owed to Smith as the legal holder of the property redemption certificate. The plaintiff argued that the funds in question were subject to garnishment and that the court should direct Finlen to pay the stated amount to the rightful owner (Smith).	Finlen defended his position by asserting that as a County Clerk, he was not liable for garnishment of funds received for tax sale redemption. His argument was based on statutory provisions, emphasizing that he acted only as an agent of the law and that the money was not considered "in the custody of the law" as required for garnishment. Finlen requested the court uphold the decision in his favor and dismiss the garnishment claim.

In 1883, in Henderson County, Illinois, John H. Atkins initiated a legal proceeding under the act of March 25, 1869, aimed at establishing the permanent boundaries of his land. A commission of surveyors was appointed to survey the land, and their report was met with objections from the defendants, Thomas Huston and others. A jury trial was held, resulting in a verdict that favored the defendants, leading the court to dismiss Atkins' petition. Atkins filed a motion for a new trial, which was denied. Subsequently, the court set aside the initial commission's report and appointed a new commission for a fresh survey. The second commission's report faced objections from the defendants, and a second trial ensued, where the jury again ruled against Atkins. He appealed the decision to the Appellate Court, which upheld the ruling that dismissed his petition. The subsequent hearings primarily centered around the validity of using evidence from the first trial during the second trial, ultimately concluding with issues regarding procedural fairness.	Atkins claimed that the second survey conducted by the new commission did not consider the previous verdict's weight and believed that the introduction of evidence from the initial trial was erroneous. He argued for a re-evaluation based solely on the second commission's findings without any influence from the prior adjudication.	The defendants maintained that the lines reported by the second commission aligned closely with those from the first. They argued that since the first commission's findings had already been adjudicated by the first jury's verdict, Atkins was precluded from contesting the same issues again, supporting their position with evidence gathered from the prior trial's proceedings.

The case of August Krug v. Ann E. Ward took place in Clinton County, Illinois, around June 1875. The plaintiff, Ann E. Ward, charged the defendant, August Krug, with bastardy, asserting that he was the father of her unborn child. During the trial, Ward claimed to be an unmarried woman and pregnant, which led to Krug being summoned to court. The matter was settled without further litigation, with Krug issuing a promissory note for $300 to Ward. Two years later, Krug's wife, Emma Krug, filed an affidavit against Ward, alleging that she had committed perjury during the earlier trial by falsely claiming that Krug was the father of her child. A warrant was issued for Ward's arrest, which led to her being arrested by a constable on the instigation of Krug. After some delay, she was acquitted of the perjury charge. Ward then filed a lawsuit against Krug for malicious prosecution, false imprisonment, and slander, claiming damages for the wrongful actions taken against her, which included wrongful arrest and public defamation.	Ann E. Ward claimed that August Krug maliciously prosecuted her for perjury without reasonable cause, leading to her false imprisonment. She accused him of orchestrating her arrest to force her to relinquish the promissory note he gave her in the previous bastardy settlement. Ward sought damages for the distress and harm caused by Krug’s actions, presenting her case through multiple counts, including malicious prosecution and slander among others.	August Krug defended himself by pleading not guilty against the charges brought by Ward. He argued that his actions were justified and that his wife’s affidavit had legitimate grounds. However, the evidence presented against him indicated that the prosecution was pursued for personal motives rather than for justice, undermining his claim of justification. Krug's primary defense relied on questioning the validity of Ward's assertions concerning their prior relationship.

In December 1835, the case of Samuel Seward, for the use of George W. Chapman, against Abijah Wilson was decided in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated before a justice of the peace, where the plaintiff, Samuel Seward, was a non-resident, while the person for whom the suit was initiated, George W. Chapman, was a resident of the jurisdiction. The defendant, Abijah Wilson, objected to the suit's proceedings on grounds of the plaintiff's non-residency. A motion was presented to dismiss the case due to this non-residency, leading the Circuit Court to agree and dismiss the case, thus ruling in favor of the defendant for costs incurred. Samuel Seward sought to reverse this judgment, leading to this writ of error. The critical issue was whether the Circuit Court had erred in dismissing the suit based on the plaintiff's non-residential status.	The plaintiff, represented by Samuel Seward, claimed that the dismissal of the case was erroneous given that the suit was brought for the use of a resident, George W. Chapman. Seward argued that the Circuit Court's dismissal based on his non-residency was not justified and sought to reverse the judgment for recovery of costs.	The defendant, Abijah Wilson, contended that the non-residency of the plaintiff barred him from initiating the suit without a prior bond for costs, as mandated by statutes regulating actions before justices of the peace. Wilson maintained that the dismissal was appropriate and that the judgment favoring him for costs should stand.

In the case of Jeremiah Murphy v. William C. Holway, the lawsuit originated from a dispute regarding a board bill owed by Holway to Murphy. The incident took place in Cook County, Illinois, around 1888. Holway initially brought the case before a Justice of the Peace, which was eventually appealed to the Circuit Court. The plaintiff, William C. Holway, claimed he owed $206 for board services, while the defendant, Jeremiah Murphy, raised the defense of the Statute of Limitations, asserting that the claim was time-barred as the debt accrued over five years prior to the lawsuit. Holway countered this claim by alleging a new promise made by Murphy shortly before the suit was filed, which included Murphy acknowledging his debt but asking for the return of certain goods and chattels that Murphy had taken as security for the debt. The controversy centered around whether Holway's testimony constituted a valid new promise sufficient to overcome the Statute of Limitations. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of the plaintiff for $100 and costs, but this decision would later be challenged based on the conditions surrounding the alleged new promise.	The plaintiff, William C. Holway, argued that he was owed $206 for board services and claimed that a new promise made by the defendant, Jeremiah Murphy, shortly before the lawsuit revived the old debt and allowed him to pursue the claim despite the Statute of Limitations. Holway contended that during an encounter with Murphy, the defendant acknowledged the debt and expressed a desire for the return of his property taken by the plaintiff as security. Thus, he requested the court to uphold the jury's verdict in his favor.	The defendant, Jeremiah Murphy, contended that the claim was barred by the Statute of Limitations, as the debt had accrued over five years before Holway initiated legal action. Murphy asserted that any acknowledgment of the debt was conditional, as he requested the return of his property held by Holway in exchange for payment. He maintained that there was no valid new promise to revive the debt since the condition of returning the property was never fulfilled. Thus, he sought a reversal of the judgment rendered by the jury.

In the case of Daniel Maher v. The People, which occurred in Illinois in April 1860, the dispute arose from a fatal confrontation between Daniel Maher (the defendant) and James Maher (the deceased). Both men were neighbors and had come to the deceased's home, intoxicated, where they shared a meal. During their time together, a domestic altercation broke out involving the deceased's attempts to use a horsewhip on his family. Daniel intervened, leading to a physical scuffle where both men agreed to pause their fight until the following day. After leaving the premises, a confrontation occurred when the deceased pursued Daniel armed with a mop-handle, resulting in a violent exchange. The circumstances of the fight were disputed, particularly regarding who struck first, ultimately leading to the deceased's death. Daniel Maher faced an indictment for murder, and his defense argued that the killing was a case of justifiable homicide under the circumstances. However, multiple legal proceedings ensued, including motions to quash the indictment and to allow cross-examination of witnesses, which the courts rejected.	The plaintiff, representing the state, asserted that Daniel Maher committed murder by unjustifiably taking James Maher's life during their confrontation. They maintained that Maher had no legitimate claim to self-defense given the circumstances and that the court should provide proper instructions to the jury on the legal standards of justifiable homicide.	Daniel Maher's defense contended that he acted in self-defense against an imminent threat posed by James Maher, as there was a reasonable belief that he was in danger of significant bodily harm. They criticized the court for its refusal to grant a more favorable jury instruction regarding the nature of perceived threats and argued that the circumstances justified the actions taken by Maher in protecting himself.

The case "Village of Marseilles v. George Howland" originated in La Salle County, Illinois, wherein the proceedings were finalized on February 8, 1890. The central issue involved the Village of Marseilles, the appellant, being compelled to satisfy a judgment against it for $1,500 held by the appellee, George Howland. Howland initiated a mandamus action to enforce this payment from the village's treasury. The circuit court had previously ordered a writ of peremptory mandamus directing the Village to pay the specified amount to Howland. The appeal revolved around disagreements about the trial court's evidence evaluation and its decisions, especially focusing on the bill of exceptions that had been struck from the record, making it challenging to review the evidence presented during the lower court hearings. The court operated under the standard presumption that the lower court’s decisions were correct in the absence of evidence to the contrary.	George Howland, as the plaintiff, sought to compel the Village of Marseilles to pay a judgment of $1,500 that he held against the municipality. His claim was predicated on the assertion that the village had a legal obligation to satisfy the court's ruling in his favor, and thus he initiated mandamus proceedings to ensure that payment was made from the village's finances.	The Village of Marseilles, represented by Mr. Bird Bickford, contended against the plaintiffs' claims on the grounds that there were issues regarding the weight of evidence presented in the lower court and the implications of the bill of exceptions being stricken from the record. The appellant sought to reverse the circuit court's order, implying that the decision could have been incorrect due to the lack of evidence being reviewed effectively.

The case "James Wilhite et al. v. Zadock Pearce et al." took place in June 1868 in Crawford County, Illinois. The parties involved included Zadock A. Pearce and his wife Louisa Jane as the plaintiffs, and John M. Wilhite and others, heirs-at-law of Enoch Wilhite, as the defendants. The plaintiffs sought a partition of certain real estate, claiming that Enoch Wilhite died owning the property in question. The court served process to the defendants, although one defendant, I. P. Murphy, was served incorrectly. The adult defendants did not respond, leading to a default judgment. The court decreed that the land be sold, applying the proceeds to settle liens on the property. The defendants appealed the decree, arguing that evidence supporting the ruling was not preserved, that proper service was not completed for I. P. Murphy, and that no evidence was presented regarding the minor defendants. Numerous procedural errors were highlighted, particularly with respect to serving minors and appointing a guardian ad litem.	The plaintiffs claimed ownership of certain real estate belonging to Enoch Wilhite and sought a partition of that property. They requested that the court authorize the sale of the property and the application of the proceeds to settle existing debts, specifically a lien against the property. They argued that the adult defendants had defaulted, leading to a judgment in favor of the plaintiffs.	The defendants contended that the court's decree was based on irregularities, including improper service of process for I. P. Murphy and insufficient evidence being presented, particularly regarding the justification for partitioning the property. They argued that the decree against the minor defendants was erroneous due to a lack of proof, and that the process followed in appointing the master in chancery was inappropriate, as he had also acted as the attorney for the plaintiffs.

The case "Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railroad Co. v. Charles McMillan et al." took place in Cook County, Illinois, with notable events occurring from March 30, 1874, to September 1876. Charles McMillan filed a petition seeking a mechanic's lien against property owned by Gillespie, for debts owed for work and materials used in constructing a mill. Other defendants joined the proceedings and raised similar claims for mechanic’s liens. In response, the plaintiff, Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railroad Co., denied Gillespie's ownership of the property, claiming the mill was built with funds of the railroad company without their consent. They stated that Gillespie had executed a deed of trust recognizing the railroad's financial interest in the property. A bankruptcy petition against Gillespie was filed in January 1874, and he was subsequently declared bankrupt. The parties agreed to have the case heard without a jury, and the court ultimately ruled in favor of the defendants, allowing their liens and ordering the property sold to satisfy their claims.	The plaintiff contended that they had no obligation towards the mechanic's liens filed by McMillan and other defendants because Gillespie did not own the property in question. They argued that the mill was constructed using funds that belonged to the railroad, and they sought to establish that their financial interest was valid through a deed of trust. Furthermore, they asserted that the bankruptcy proceedings against Gillespie invalidated any claims by the defendants to the property.	The defendants, including McMillan, maintained that they were entitled to mechanic's liens for labor and materials provided for the construction of the mill. They claimed under the original petitions filed in court, asserting that their rights to a lien were valid and should be recognized by the court. They argued that the plaintiff lacked standing to contest the validity of their claims, as the plaintiff failed to demonstrate any ownership interest in the property.

Phineas Kimball, Jr. initiated legal proceedings against his tenant, Charles C. Riter, in Hancock County, Illinois, in 1861. Kimball sought to collect $100 in unpaid rent by leveraging a distress warrant on Riter's property. The local justice of the peace, John Bauer, presided over the case, where he ultimately ruled against Kimball, ordering him to pay court costs. Kimball then appealed this decision to the Circuit Court of Hancock County. However, Judge Sibley dismissed the appeal. The case revolves around whether the Circuit Court erred in not allowing the appeal to proceed, hinging on the interpretation of the ability to appeal decisions made by justices in landlord-tenant disputes.	Kimball contended that the justice of the peace's ruling constituted a final judgment subject to an appeal, despite the absence of explicit language in the statute allowing for such appeals. He argued that the finding should be treated as a judgment for all practical purposes, which subjects him to potential harm.	Riter maintained that the law did not permit an appeal from the justice's ruling, as the statutory language did not provide for it. He argued that the magistrate's decision and its characteristics did not warrant the classification as a judgment that could be appealed.

In the case of S. P. Hodgen et al. v. Wolrad Kief, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1872, the dispute arose from a business relationship that involved the buying and selling of grain. The individuals involved were plaintiffs S. P. Hodgen and Warner, who had a partnership engaged in this business from around 1860 until June 1869, when it was dissolved without any formal notice. Wolrad Kief, the defendant, had been selling grain to Hodgen & Warner. At the time of the partnership's dissolution, Kief owed the plaintiffs $123 for overpayment on prior grain sales. Misunderstandings ensued regarding the partnership's status, and in the fall of 1869, Kief believed he was still dealing with the partnership when he sold and delivered 741 bushels of barley to Warner, intending it to offset his debt to them. However, the barley was actually purchased by Martling & Warner, another partnership that formed later. In 1871, Hodgen contacted Kief to settle the $123 debt, which led to discussions about a promise to pay, further complicating the situation with conflicting testimonies regarding the nature of that promise.	The plaintiffs, Hodgen and Warner, claimed that Kief owed them $123 based on past transactions. They argued that Kief's promise to pay that amount should override any defense he claimed regarding the barley transactions, contending that it would hinder his ability to set off any alleged debts against them.	Kief contended that he was not liable for the $123 claim due to the promise made and his belief that Hodgen & Warner were still a partnership at the time of the barley sale. He maintained that the promise did not alter the existing obligations related to the grain transactions, and he should be able to set off the amount Hodgen & Warner owed him for the barley sold against the claimed $123 debt.

On April 19, 1858, in McLean County, Illinois, Alberry executed a mortgage on his land to Henry G. Ainsworth, which was already encumbered with a deed of trust that Alberry was obligated to pay off. The plaintiffs, Henry A. Ewing and others, had previously obtained a judgment against Alberry in January 1858 in Cook County. On May 28, 1859, they levied an execution on the property in question, filing a certificate of levy the same day. In 1860, Ainsworth foreclosed on the mortgage without including the plaintiffs in the proceedings and subsequently paid off the deed of trust, becoming the owner. By August 18, 1865, the sheriff of McLean County was set to sell the mortgaged property under a venditioni exponas originating from Cook County. Ainsworth filed a bill to prevent this sale, which led to Ewing and others filing a cross-bill seeking to redeem the property and request for an accounting of rents and profits. The court ultimately ruled against the plaintiffs, stating they had no grounds for redemption based on the expired liens and the actions taken by Ainsworth.	The plaintiffs asserted they had a right to redeem the property after the foreclosure despite not being included in the original proceeding. They sought an accounting of the rents and profits collected by Ainsworth during the foreclosure and the opportunity to pay the amount Ainsworth bid at the mortgage sale so they could reclaim their property.	Ainsworth contended that the plaintiffs had no legitimate right to redeem the property as the lien from their judgment had expired and their original claims were not valid since they had not been made parties to the foreclosure. He requested that the court uphold his right to keep possession of the property and invalidate the plaintiffs' attempts to exert a claim on it.

In 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, James D. Johnson and George P. Blair entered into a lease under seal with Charles D. Wilson for a dwelling. Following this arrangement, Johnson and Blair sought to recover rent from Wilson. They claimed they were misled into signing the lease due to false representations regarding the respectability and quality of the neighborhood. This dispute led to an action brought against Wilson, wherein significant evidence was presented by both sides concerning the claims of misrepresentation. The court, presided over by Judge John P. Altgeld, ultimately had to evaluate these claims and defenses to reach a factual conclusion regarding the lease's validity and the alleged misleading statements.	The plaintiffs, Johnson and Blair, claimed that they were induced to sign the lease due to false representations made by Wilson about the neighborhood's respectability and suitability. They sought to recover rent from Wilson, arguing that the misrepresentations were a significant factor influencing their decision to enter into the lease agreement.	Wilson, the defendant, contended that the claims of fraudulent inducement by Johnson and Blair could not be legally substantiated since they were attempting to show that they were misled concerning collateral matters outside the actual lease agreement. Their defense was based on the principle that fraudulent statements regarding a lease's external conditions do not constitute a valid defense in an action at law concerning a sealed instrument.

In 1874, in Kane County, Illinois, William Fredrick filed a lawsuit against George White concerning damage caused by White’s cattle to Fredrick’s corn crops. The case was initially heard by a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment in favor of Fredrick for fifty dollars. White appealed the judgment to the circuit court, where the same amount was awarded to Fredrick again. Throughout the proceedings, evidence was provided that demonstrated White had repeatedly allowed his cattle to roam freely, resulting in damage to Fredrick’s crops. This behavior was in direct violation of an act established on January 13, 1872, which took effect on July 1, 1872, that prohibited domestic animals from running at large. The jury found the evidence compelling and ruled in Fredrick's favor, thus the court accepted that just outcomes had been achieved based on the law and affirmed the judgment.	The plaintiff, William Fredrick, claimed that George White’s cattle had caused significant damage to his corn crops by being allowed to run at large. Fredrick argued that White’s actions were negligent and violated the law, making him liable for the damages. The plaintiff sought compensation for the loss amounting to fifty dollars, which he successfully obtained in both the initial and appeal hearings.	The defendant, George White, contended that the judgment for damages against him should be overturned. He likely argued the merits of his defense regarding the behavior of his cattle, potentially disputing the extent of the damages or claiming compliance with existing regulations. However, the details of specific defenses presented were not detailed in the court's opinion.

On February 5, 1870, in Pekin, Illinois, William Spurgin entered into an agreement with Louis Traub and his partner Herbig, who were brewers, regarding a debt of approximately $800 for a carload of malt. To secure this debt, the parties agreed that Traub and his wife, Maria Traub, would execute two notes for $800 each, secured by a mortgage on a homestead property owned by Maria. Subsequently, issues arose when Maria filed a bill in chancery to cancel the mortgage, claiming that it was fraudulently obtained through misrepresentations from her husband and the notary public who acknowledged her signature. She contended she was led to believe the mortgage was on the brewery property rather than her homestead, and that she had not been adequately informed of the mortgage's contents. The Circuit Court consolidated the two suits and ultimately decreed the foreclosure of an existing mortgage in favor of Spurgin and canceled his mortgage. Spurgin then appealed this decision.	William Spurgin, the plaintiff, claimed that he was owed a debt for malt sold to the defendants and that the mortgage on Maria Traub's property was rightfully executed to secure payment. He argued that the agreement was lawful and that he had acted in good faith in securing the mortgage, despite Maria's claims of misunderstanding and fraud.	Maria Traub challenged the validity of the mortgage, asserting that she was unable to read or understand English and had been misled by her husband and the notary public. She claimed that they represented the mortgage as securing the brewery property, which led her to wrongfully execute it under false pretenses. Therefore, she sought cancellation of the mortgage based on allegations of fraud and lack of understanding.

In July 1866, John J. Schwartz began constructing a four-story brick building in Chicago, Illinois. On the night of October 21, 1866, during a severe gale, the walls of the partially completed building collapsed, causing significant damage to the adjacent property owned by Thomas E. Gilmore, who suffered severe injuries from the incident and lost his wife and all his belongings. Gilmore ran a barber shop from his home, which was completely destroyed. He filed a lawsuit against Schwartz for negligence, claiming that the building plans were defective and that the construction was done hastily and carelessly. Schwartz contended that he had contracted an architect and a builder, Daegling, to oversee the construction, thus claiming he was not responsible for the wall's collapse. The court was tasked with determining liability based on Schwartz's level of control and whether he had taken adequate measures to secure the building, especially after being made aware of the potential danger.	The plaintiff, Thomas E. Gilmore, argued that Schwartz was negligent in overseeing the construction of his building, as the walls were built defectively and hastily. Gilmore claimed that Schwartz was aware of the walls leaning prior to the accident and failed to take necessary precautions. He sought damages for the severe injuries he incurred, the loss of his wife, and the destruction of his property resulting from the collapse of the building.	The defendant, John J. Schwartz, asserted that he had contracted with a professional builder and architect, which should absolve him from liability for any negligence occurring during the construction. Schwartz maintained that he was not responsible for the collapse of the walls, as he had entrusted the execution of the building to Daegling under the supervision of an architect. He argued that any carelessness or lack of skill on the part of the contractor should fall solely on him and not on Schwartz.

In 1889, the case of Emma A. Doyle v. Sylvester E. Brown took place in Cook County, Illinois. Emma A. Doyle, the plaintiff, initiated the action against Sylvester E. Brown and others, seeking legal remedies involving an injunction. As part of the proceedings, a demurrer was filed by the defendants in response to Doyle's bill, leading to the dissolution of the injunction previously granted. The case brought forth discussions on whether the dissolution provided grounds for assessing damages related to attorney fees incurred during the process. The legal discourse revolved around the procedures for injunctions and the implications of the demurrer, culminating in a scenario where the court found no sufficient basis for damages, thus impacting the evaluation of solicitor fees as related to the broader defense of the suit.	Emma A. Doyle argued that the dissolution of the injunction should allow her to recover damages for attorney services related to the case. She contended that the legal services were specifically tied to the needs arising from the injunction, warranting compensation. Doyle sought a final decree that would not only address the injunction but also grant her the relief necessary for the incurred legal expenses.	Sylvester E. Brown and the other defendants contended that the dissolution of the injunction on the basis of a demurrer did not substantiate a claim for damages associated with the plaintiff's solicitor fees. They maintained that attorney's fees were part of the general defense of the suit rather than directly tied to the injunction itself, thus opposing Doyle's claim for such compensation. The defendants did not file a brief, indicating a lack of engagement with the ongoing legal matter.

The case, The Pennsylvania Company and the Union Stock Yards & Transit Company v. Edwin H. Ellett, Administrator, was decided on January 22, 1890, by the Illinois Appellate Court. It stems from a tragic incident that occurred on February 14, 1887, in the town of Lake, Cook County, Illinois. William E. Walkup was crossing railroad tracks belonging to the Union Stock Yards and Transit Company when he was struck and killed by a freight train operated by the Pennsylvania Company. At the time, Walkup and other pedestrians were waiting for a freight train to pass on the third track before attempting to cross on Exchange Avenue, a well-trafficked area where thousands of people crossed daily. After the last car of the freight train passed, Walkup stepped onto the east track and was immediately hit by a backing train traveling at approximately seven miles per hour. The collision resulted in his death. A jury awarded $4,500 in damages to the plaintiff, the administrator of Walkup’s estate. The defendants argued procedural errors in the case, claiming a lack of proper legal allegations regarding their responsibility in the incident.	The plaintiff, Edwin H. Ellett, as administrator of William E. Walkup's estate, claimed damages for wrongful death resulting from the negligence of the Pennsylvania Company and the Union Stock Yards & Transit Company. The plaintiff argued that both companies failed to ensure the safety of individuals crossing the tracks by neglecting to erect safety gates and not adequately warning pedestrians of the approaching train. The evidence suggested that a regular train passed during high foot traffic without sufficient warnings from the crew. They sought compensation for the loss of life caused by the defendants' negligence.
