The defendants, Pennsylvania Company and Union Stock Yards & Transit Company, contended that the allegations against them were defective as the plaintiff failed to demonstrate a contractual relationship or consent for the use of the tracks where the accident occurred. They argued that the claim did not establish that their train was lawfully on the track at the time of the incident, implying it could have been there as a trespasser. The defense insisted that the evidence did not support the claim of negligence and maintained that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence, advocating for the judgment to be overturned.

In the case of Martin O. Walker et al. v. Hugh Martin, the events unfolded in March and April of 1866 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the appellants Martin O. Walker and Guy H. Cutting, and the appellee Hugh Martin. The legal conflict arose when Martin was charged with the larceny of coal allegedly owned by Walker and Cutting. Following a warrant issued on March 17, 1866, Martin was arrested on March 29 and detained for nine days, during which he sought a writ of habeas corpus from the Circuit Court of Cook County. He was discharged on April 7, 1866, without a trial on the merits of the larceny charge, leading him to file a malicious prosecution lawsuit against Walker and Cutting shortly thereafter. The case was moved to Will County for trial, where a jury initially awarded Martin $20,000 in damages, prompting the defendants' appeal based on claims the prosecution had not been legally terminated.	Hugh Martin claimed that he was maliciously prosecuted by Walker and Cutting without probable cause for the larceny of coal. He argued that the criminal charge was ended as he was acquitted by the Circuit Court after filing for habeas corpus. Martin sought compensatory damages for the wrongful prosecution and the emotional distress resulting from his detention.	Walker and Cutting contended that the lawsuit was prematurely filed since the criminal proceedings had not been concluded when Martin initiated his claim. They argued that the habeas corpus proceedings did not nullify the underlying charge or the requirement to appear in court. Moreover, they introduced evidence suggesting Martin had a poor character, implying that any damages awarded should be reconsidered in light of this character assessment.

In October 1842, John Lockridge filed a chancery bill in the Illinois Supreme Court against Peyton Foster, the administrator of George Foster's estate, along with other defendants. The case revolved around a land purchase made by Lockridge on December 19, 1836, for two hundred and forty acres and a stake in another tract, for a total of $2,400. Lockridge claimed he was led to believe by George Foster that he was acquiring a good title for the entire property, but later discovered that Foster had no title to four-elevenths of the most valuable fifty-eight-acre tract. Upon moving to Illinois in 1837 and realizing the defect in the title, he subsequently improved the property. After George Foster's death, his estate recovered a judgment against Lockridge for unpaid purchase money. Lockridge's bill sought either rescission of the contract due to misrepresentation or specific performance. The administrator admitted to the land sale but denied any fraud, asserting that only seven-elevenths of the mentioned acreage was sold. The court proceeded to hear evidence from both parties, leading to a decree that partially credited Lockridge's judgment for the value lost due to the failed title.	John Lockridge alleged that he was misled by George Foster regarding the title of the land he purchased, believing that he was acquiring full ownership. He claimed fraud, sought rescission of the contract, or alternatively, specific performance, arguing that he should not be held liable for the remaining balance on the notes because the property did not match the agreed conditions as he purchased it. Lockridge also sought an injunctive relief against the collection of the judgment obtained by the estate.	Peyton Foster, acting as administrator, defended against the claims by affirming familiarity with the sale but contended that no fraudulent assurances were made about the title. He argued that the intention had been to sell only a portion of the fifty-eight acres and indicated that the remaining land was not the most valuable. Foster contended that even if there was a defect in the title, it was only worth $120 and suggested that any remedy available to Lockridge should merely reduce the amount owed under the judgment rather than rescind the contract.

In the case of **Nelson Perin v. Augustus A. Parker**, which took place in **1888** in **Chicago, Illinois**, the plaintiff, **Augustus A. Parker**, was a commission merchant tasked by the defendant, **Nelson Perin**, to sell **50,000 bushels of corn** on the **Chicago Board of Trade**. The contract specified that **25,000 bushels** were to be delivered in **January** and the remainder in **May**. During the course of the sales, the price of corn began to rise significantly. Parker requested margins from Perin to cover potential losses, but Perin refused to supply these funds, stating he would only cover losses upon settlement of the differences. Parker continued to demand margins, but Perin remained steadfast in his refusal. As a result, Parker ultimately purchased corn himself to fulfill his obligations under the contracts. Perin claimed that Parker had violated his instructions by not buying the corn for January delivery, which was found to be a baseless claim. After trial, Parker was awarded a judgment for the amounts he had advanced on behalf of Perin. The case ultimately reached the Illinois Supreme Court after Perin appealed the judgment.	Augustus A. Parker claimed that he was entitled to recover for the money he advanced on behalf of Nelson Perin as well as for commissions earned during the execution of the sales contracts. Parker argued that when Perin employed him to sell corn, he implicitly agreed to provide the necessary margins to secure the transactions. Since Perin failed to fulfill his obligation to provide margins when requested, Parker contended that he incurred expenses and losses, which made Perin liable for the sums paid.	Nelson Perin contended that Augustus A. Parker did not establish a valid cause of action since the advances claimed were not made at his explicit request or under any enforceable agreement. Perin also argued that Parker acted outside his authority by purchasing corn to cover the contracts after Perin had refused to provide margins. Furthermore, Perin maintained that his refusal to pay was valid as he asserted that Parker had breached the duty by not buying the corn as initially ordered.

In March 1879, Arthur W. Windett was indebted to The Connecticut Mutual Life Insurance Company for $894,500, secured by mortgages on various real estate properties in Chicago. After Windett defaulted on payments, the company initiated foreclosure proceedings in the United States Circuit Court. Two suits were filed against Windett, leading to decrees in favor of the company that allowed for the foreclosure and eventual sale of the properties. By 1883, the company had received the master’s deeds for the properties after the completion of sales, as Windett did not redeem them. On June 17, 1885, Windett filed a suit in the Cook County Circuit Court aimed at redeeming the properties, alleging a prior agreement with the company to extend his payment terms and reduce the interest owed. Despite claiming the company acted in bad faith, the court dismissed his bill, stating he needed to present these claims during the initial Federal court proceedings rather than attempting to overturn the decree collaterally. The case raised legal issues regarding the jurisdiction and authority of state courts to review Federal court decrees.	Windett argued that there was an agreement to extend the payment period on his debt and reduce the interest rate from nine percent to six percent for five years, which the company allegedly violated. He contended that he was misled into not fully asserting his rights in the foreclosure cases due to assurances from the company regarding his right of redemption.	The defendant maintained that the decrees from the Federal court were final and binding, precluding Windett from contesting them in state court. They argued that even if an agreement existed, Windett failed to act on it in a timely manner during the Federal proceeding, and that the evidence presented by Windett was insufficient to overturn the strong presumption established by the foreclosure proceedings.

Charles Horn filed a legal case against Frederick Eckert in the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1872. The case emerged from a prior judgment in a lower circuit court in Madison County, presided over by Judge Joseph Gillespie. The details regarding the specific events that led to the dispute are not provided in the record. However, it is clear that Horn was dissatisfied with the outcome of his case and sought to contest the judgment in the higher court via a writ of error.	The main argument presented by Charles Horn was a challenge to the lower court’s decision, specifically focusing on the overruling of his motion to set aside the judgment and grant a new trial. Horn's legal request was for the Illinois Supreme Court to review the lower court's ruling.	Frederick Eckert's defense, presented through his attorney William H. Underwood, emphasized that there was no proper record of exceptions to review, as the motion to set aside the judgment lacked a bill of exceptions and supporting affidavits. Eckert maintained that the lower court’s judgment should stand as there was no apparent error in the record.

The case of George E. Welling v. Anthony Schiller took place in Illinois, with a decision rendered on September 18, 1888. The key parties involved were George E. Welling, the defendant, and Anthony Schiller, the plaintiff, who was the assignee of a promissory note originally issued to Albert Schenbeck by Welling. The dispute arose from a transaction dated March 13, 1886, when Schenbeck sold Welling fifty shares of stock in the Spitzer Patent Starch Company. Welling executed a promissory note worth $500 as part of that transaction, based on representations made by Schenbeck regarding the company's promising future and the value of the stock. However, Welling claimed that Schenbeck had fraudulently misrepresented the stock's value, leading to a failure of consideration as Schenbeck purportedly knew the shares were worthless. Welling's defenses revolved around this alleged fraud in the sale and the failure of consideration for the promissory note.	The plaintiff, Anthony Schiller, argued that he was entitled to enforce the promissory note executed by George E. Welling as it was assigned to him after maturity. The core of Schiller's claim was based on the assertion that Welling had validly executed the note in exchange for stock that was purchased under fraudulent pretenses. Schiller contended that the sale of the shares had been valid, and using the note was justified even if Welling later claimed there was a failure of consideration based on misrepresentations about the stock.	The defendant, George E. Welling, put forth two special pleas arguing that the promissory note was executed based on fraudulent representations made by Schenbeck regarding the stock's value and the operations of the Spitzer Patent Starch Company. Welling claimed that he was misled into believing the stock was worth something and would appreciate in value, whereas it was, in fact, worthless. Additionally, the second plea suggested that the assignment of the note to Schiller was made without consideration and lacked good faith. Welling sought to have the court dismiss the claim based on these arguments.

In December 1827, in Illinois, an action of debt was brought against Wm. C. Greenup and Clement C. Conway, who were administrators of an estate. Philander Woodworth was the defendant in this action. The case arose from a previous judgment against the plaintiffs as administrators, alleging that they had received goods and chattels equivalent to the judgment amount but had wasted them. The court rendered a default judgment against the plaintiffs, as they did not respond or contest the allegations regarding the assets. The court’s decision was based on the principle that in cases of default in actions of debt, the truth of the plaintiff's allegations is accepted, and no jury is needed unless specifically requested by the plaintiff.	The plaintiffs claimed that a jury should have been impaneled to determine the amount of assets they received and to confirm allegations of a devastavit (waste of estate assets). They sought to contest the default judgment, asserting that the method of recovery in actions of debt should allow for a jury inquiry to ascertain damages.	The defendant argued that the plaintiffs' default admitted the truth of the allegations in the declaration. It was contended that a jury inquiry is not necessary in cases of default in an action of debt, as the court traditionally awards the prescribed amount based on the allegations without requiring a jury.

In September 1873, in Kane County, Illinois, James Morgan and others brought a lawsuit against Riley W. Hoyt, seeking to enforce a conservator's bond held by Perry Hannah for William W. Merrill, an individual who had been declared insane. Perry Hannah was appointed as the conservator on August 22, 1865. In December of the same year, Morgan presented a claim against Merrill for $25, which was allowed by the county court. Hannah managed the estate, receiving $824.51 and paying out $926.09 without charging for his services. Upon Merrill's recovery, Hannah discharged his duties and returned the remaining property to him. The plaintiffs argued that Hannah failed to fulfill his duty to pay Merrill's debts, thereby justifying an action against his bond for the amount owed.	The plaintiffs claimed that Perry Hannah, as conservator, had a duty to pay the debts of William W. Merrill but failed to do so by not utilizing available property to satisfy these debts. They sought to hold Hannah and his sureties liable on his official bond for neglecting to properly pay the debt that was owed.	The defendants contended that Hannah fulfilled all the statutory duties required of a conservator, including adequately managing and returning Merrill's property upon his recovery. They argued that there was no legal obligation to pay debts unless there were sufficient funds available. Additionally, they claimed that the allowance of Morgan's claim in county court was not a proper legal proceeding and did not bind the conservator, as it was in effect a nullity and did not impose liability.

The case "Bridget Burns, Imp’d with The Lovingston Lumber Company and The Wiggins Ferry Company v. James A. Lane" was decided on June 7, 1887, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The key individuals involved include Bridget Burns, the defendant James A. Lane, her father John Burns, and the companies involved in the construction. In March 1881, Lane entered into a contract with John Burns to construct a house on a property that Bridget Burns was alleged to own. She contended that she did not have ownership of the property at the time the contract was made, nor did she authorize her father to act as her agent in this matter. The dispute centered around whether a mechanics' lien had been established for the construction work and if the work had been completed satisfactorily. The trial concluded with a jury's finding favoring Lane's claims regarding the lien and the payment due for his services.	The plaintiff, James A. Lane, claimed that he had entered into a valid contract with Bridget Burns' father to build a house on her property, asserting that Bridget had given her consent and that John Burns acted as her agent. He sought to enforce the mechanics' lien against the property for the balance owed on the contract, which included extra work he performed beyond the original agreement.	Bridget Burns denied having knowledge of the contract made by her father and any ownership of the property at the contract's inception. She argued that Lane had built the house without her consent and contended it was not constructed satisfactorily. Furthermore, she claimed to never have made any payments to Lane and that the work done had caused damages exceeding the amount he claimed.

The case of "The Coal Run Coal Company v. Patrick Finlen" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court and decided on May 9, 1888. The case originated in LaSalle County, Illinois. The Coal Run Coal Company, the plaintiff, brought a legal action against the county clerk, Patrick Finlen, seeking to enjoin the clerk from extending taxes on the assessed value of the company’s capital stock and franchise as set by the State Board of Equalization for the tax year 1883. The plaintiff contended that the taxation method employed violated the Illinois Constitution's rule of uniformity in taxation. Key arguments were presented regarding the classification of corporations and the varying methods of capital stock assessment directed by the state legislature. The case revolved around two main legal questions: whether the specific taxation section of the Revenue Act contradicts the Constitution and whether the State Board of Equalization acted improperly in their assessment process, thus infringing the established norm of uniformity in taxation.	The Coal Run Coal Company argued that the fourth division of section 3 of the Revenue Act, which governs the taxation of corporate capital stock, violates the constitutional requirement for uniformity in taxation. They maintained that differentiating assessment methods among various classes of corporations contravened the Illinois Constitution, which mandates uniform taxation methods. The plaintiff requested the court to invalidate the tax assessments made by the State Board of Equalization on the grounds of unconstitutional application of tax law.	In response, Patrick Finlen contended that the classification of corporations for tax purposes does not violate constitutional requirements. He argued that the legislature is entitled to create different methods for assessing the capital stock of various types of corporations, thus adhering to a uniform law applicable to each class. The defendant asserted that the assessment made by the State Board of Equalization was lawful, and the court lacks authority to interfere with the assessment process unless fraud is evident—an assertion stressed by the defendant due to the absence of such proof in this case.

In 1864, Albert M. Fellows, then residing in Logan County, Illinois, purchased a quarter section of land from William Grant and Harrison G. Wright for $125. The appellants had not paid taxes on the land for sixteen years and were uncertain if they had conveyed it along with other lands, as the records had been destroyed. Despite the uncertainty, Fellows believed he could clear up the title issues and attempted to remove the cloud over the title by commencing litigation against an occupant holding two tax titles for the land. After two years of legal proceedings, he successfully reclaimed the land. Following this, the appellants sought to rescind their deed, claiming that Fellows had made fraudulent representations about the existence and validity of tax titles at the time of the sale. The hearing involved conflicting testimonies, notably from an unbiased witness who corroborated Fellows' statements that did not claim ownership of the tax title but indicated a desire to resolve title questions. The court ultimately found no evidence of actual fraud in the appellants' arguments to rescind the contract, as they had not been influenced by any misrepresentation.	The plaintiffs, William Grant and Harrison G. Wright, asserted that they were entitled to rescind the deed due to fraudulent representations made by Fellows. They claimed that he misled them into believing their title was worthless and that they could only clear the title by selling to him. Their request was for the court to annul the transaction based on these alleged fraudulent statements.	Fellows defended himself against the claims by arguing that the allegations of fraud were unfounded. He maintained that he did not make any false statements regarding the ownership or value of the land, and any statements made about the tax titles were mere opinions on a legal issue. He contended that the agreement was a result of a mutual misunderstanding rather than deceit, and therefore, there was no basis for rescission.

In the case of Henry Willetts v. Oscar G. Wheeler et al., the legal proceedings took place in Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment filed on December 2, 1889. The case revolves around a loan transaction from 1875, in which the appellant, Henry Willetts, borrowed $3,614.74 from the appellees, Oscar G. Wheeler and others, and failed to repay the full amount. The case involves a series of promissory notes that constitute the only remaining evidence of this debt. The interest charged on the loan was reportedly in accordance with standard rates at the time.  During the proceedings, conflicting accounts made it challenging to ascertain the precise nature of the dealings, but it was acknowledged that Willetts had not repaid the full amount owed from the loan. The court had to examine the legal implications of usury, which is the practice of charging excessively high-interest rates. Ultimately, the appellees proposed to waive any amounts above the contested sum if it was determined that a usury defense was established, which influenced the court's decision.	The plaintiff, Henry Willetts, claimed that he owed money under certain promissory notes related to a loan obtained from Wheeler and others. He sought to recover the amount owed while arguing against the defense of usury presented by the defendants, who contended that the interest rates charged were improper. Willetts requested a judgment for the full amount of the notes, not acknowledging any usury issues.	The defendants, Oscar G. Wheeler et al., maintained that the loan involved an element of usury and offered to remit all amounts exceeding the principal sum of $3,614.74 if the court accepted their defense. They essentially argued that while there was a debt owed, the interest charged should be scrutinized for legality under usury laws, which may affect the amount recoverable. Their defense hinged significantly on the interpretation of interest rates and their legality.

In 1866, in Whiteside County, Illinois, Elmer Searle, identified as an insane person, had Henry R. Sampson appointed as his conservator by the county court. Sampson was authorized to sell certain lands held by Searle to pay off his debts. On August 18, 1866, Sampson sold the land to a buyer named Wilson, but failed to affix a scroll or seal to the deed. Wilson subsequently conveyed the land to James G. Galbraith, who then took possession. In October 1867, Searle initiated an ejectment action against Galbraith for the land, securing a judgment in his favor. However, that judgment was eventually set aside for a new trial. In the meantime, Searle filed a bill in the circuit court, hoping to enjoin the ejectment proceedings and compel Sampson to properly convey the land. The court found that Searle had been declared insane by a jury, but determined whether Searle could contest the validity of the conservatorship. It was established that despite his insanity, Searle's capacity to conduct business was not entirely hindered, as he had received benefits from the sale.	Elmer Searle argued that the proceedings leading to the sale of his land were invalid due to his appointment as a conservator and his mental state at the time. He sought to enjoin the ejectment proceedings initiated by Galbraith and requested that Sampson deliver a proper deed according to the initial decree that authorized the sale.	James G. Galbraith contended that the sale was valid despite the plaintiff's insanity, asserting that Searle had sufficient capacity to understand and benefit from the transaction. Galbraith emphasized that there was no actual fraud involved and that Searle had accepted proceeds from the sale, thereby estopping him from disputing its validity.

Solomon Sowards filed a legal action against Sarah Ann Sowards in the Marshall Circuit Court, Illinois, in September 1875 concerning a promissory note worth $285, dated December 26, 1868, which was due after twelve months with an interest rate of 10%. The dispute arose after a prior settlement in September 1872, where various suits between the parties were settled, including one regarding this note. The appellant, Solomon, indicated that Sarah Ann had agreed to dismiss all suits against him, including payments related to the note, which he claimed had already been settled. At the settlement, it was agreed that Sarah would pay Solomon a total of $1,800 for the conveyance of interest in a farm, but during the settlement, it was revealed that he could only convey three shares instead of four, leading to a complex exchange. Sarah Ann contended that the note's amount should be credited against another note she gave for $950. The case was characterized by conflicting testimonies regarding what was included in the settlement, complicating the understanding of the financial transactions and agreements made between the parties. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Sarah, leading to Solomon's appeal for a trial review.	The plaintiff, Sarah Ann Sowards, argued that the promissory note was to be credited against a larger note valued at $950 during a settlement that took place. She maintained that her testimony indicated there was an understanding that the note in question would be credited when the larger note was executed. Sarah sought recovery of the amount stated in the original promissory note after the settlement was not honored as agreed and contested Solomon's assertion that the note had been settled through payment.	The defendant, Solomon Sowards, contended that the note was paid off in a prior settlement and argued that the original agreement had included the note as part of the exchanges made during the settlement process. He claimed that since Sarah Ann had already compensated him with cash and notes totaling more than the originally agreed price for the farm shares, the note should not be in dispute. Solomon asserted that he had conveyed three shares in the estate and had sold further personal estate interests, which he claimed would justify the amounts charged, including the note in controversy.

Richard Pearce initiated legal action against Frederick Pearce in January 1873 in Clay County, Illinois. This case stemmed from an action of assumpsit, which is a legal term for a type of contract dispute regarding the recovery of a debt (in this case, a loan). The plaintiff's claim centered around money he alleged he had loaned to the defendant. In the trial, the plaintiff sought specific jury instructions that asserted the omission of Edward Pearce as a co-defendant should not affect the case’s standing. The defendant, however, raised the general issue and submitted a notice of set-off, which highlighted the absence of Edward Pearce as a co-defendant. The trial court favored the defendant's requests by instructing the jury that they must believe not only that the plaintiff lent the money but also that the defendant made an explicit promise to repay it. The jury returned a verdict in favor of the defendant, which led the plaintiff to file an appeal against this decision.	The plaintiff, Richard Pearce, argued that the trial court erred in denying his proposed jury instruction regarding the non-joinder of Edward Pearce, asserting that it should not impact the case. He contended that the requirement for the jury to believe in an express promise of repayment from the defendant was misplaced, as such proof should not be necessary to succeed in his claim for the loaned money.	Frederick Pearce's defense relied on two main arguments. First, he pointed out that the jury instructions wrongly required a finding of express promise for repayment, which he contended was not necessary. Second, he emphasized that the lack of Edward Pearce as a co-defendant should lead the jury to rule in his favor if they found that the loan was made jointly to him and Edward, rather than solely to him.

Andrew J. Roberts v. Parlin & Orendorff is a legal case that took place in 1876 in Mason County, Illinois. The case originated from an action brought by Parlin & Orendorff, partners, against Andrew J. Roberts, who was elected as constable for the town of Manito in April 1873. The plaintiffs alleged that Roberts failed to return an execution placed in his hands to enforce. The matter went before a justice of the peace and was later appealed to the Circuit Court, where a judgment was rendered in favor of the plaintiffs. The legal dispute centered around the validity of Roberts' bond and whether it met the statutory requirements under the act governing constables at that time. Specifically, the court examined whether the bond executed by Roberts was enforceable under the then-active law and its conforming to statutory requirements.	The plaintiff, Parlin & Orendorff, claimed that Andrew J. Roberts, in his capacity as constable, failed to properly execute an execution placed in his hands, and sought to recover damages for this failure. They argued that the bond executed by Roberts was legally required to ensure accountability in the performance of his duties. They sought a favorable judgement based on the established legal framework governing constables and their bonds.	The defendant, Roberts, contended that the bond executed was not enforceable, claiming it lacked the necessary elements to constitute a valid statutory or common law bond. He argued that the bond did not specify an obligee or a penalty amount, which he claimed were essential legal requirements for such instruments. Roberts maintained that the bond did not comply with the statutory changes in effect at the time it was executed and requested the court to reverse the judgment rendered against him.

The case "William E. Adams v. Robert V. Cutright" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1870. The dispute arose in Coles County, Illinois, where the plaintiff, William E. Adams, sued the defendant, Robert V. Cutright, who served as the county clerk. The case centered on the wrongful issuance of a marriage license for Adams' daughter, who was under the age of eighteen, in violation of legal requirements. Adams claimed that Cutright improperly granted the license without parental consent, and sought to recover a statutory penalty. The court was presented with several objections from the defendant regarding the legal standing and procedural validity of the suit, including the assertion that the case should have been brought in the name of the people, and the sufficiency of the declarations regarding the issuance of the marriage license.	The plaintiff, William E. Adams, argued that he was entitled to recover a statutory penalty of three hundred dollars for the county clerk's wrongful issuance of a marriage license to his underage daughter without his consent. He maintained that under the applicable statute, the father had the right to sue in his own name. Adams asserted that the court should uphold the validity of his declaration despite procedural challenges raised by the defendant.	The defendant, Robert V. Cutright, contended that the suit should be brought in the name of the people rather than the father. Cutright also argued that key elements necessary for liability were not properly averred in the declaration, including the requirement for publishing banns and for the father being capable of consent. Further, Cutright raised procedural objections concerning inconsistencies in the names used in the declaration. He suggested that the scope of the statute only applied to clerks of the county commissioners' court, and not the county court.

On May 8, 1834, Henry Rector, acting through his guardian Stephen Triggs, filed a bill in Chancery in the Alexander Circuit Court against Lydia Rector and others. The case revolves around the purchase of half of a specific land parcel by Elias Rector from Stephen Rector. Although the purchase price was unknown, the bill alleges that the full purchase money was paid. Stephen Rector was to convey the property to Elias after receiving a patent from the United States, but failed to do so before his death. Lydia, as administratrix of Stephen's estate, did not fulfill the obligations of the bond and subsequently sold the land to John Skiles, who obtained the patent. The plaintiff claimed that Lydia, alongside other defendants, conspired to defraud his deceased ancestor's estate by ignoring the existing bond and transferring the land. The case entails various parties, some of whom denied knowledge of the bond, while others indicated that bonds relevant to the land were indeed documented among Elias Rector's papers, suggesting Henry's rightful claim to the land.	Henry Rector claims that he is entitled to the land originally contracted between Elias and Stephen Rector, arguing that Stephen had executed a bond to convey the property, which he was unable to fulfill before his death. The plaintiff contends that the subsequent sale by Lydia Rector to John Skiles was done with notice of this bond and thus seeks a court order to compel Lydia and the other defendants to convey the land to him. He also requests general relief.	The defendants, primarily John Skiles and Lydia Rector, argue that they were unaware of the existence of any bond during the purchase of the property. Skiles contends that he purchased the land legally and in good faith without knowing about the alleged bond from Stephen to Elias Rector. The defense rests on the idea that since they acted as bona fide purchasers, they cannot be affected by claims related to the bond that they did not know existed at the time of purchase.

In 1833, in Madison County, Illinois, William Curtis was indicted for an assault with intent to kill Jacob C. Bruner. The incident occurred on August 31, 1833, when Curtis allegedly attacked Bruner with a stone and a brickbat, causing him serious harm. The case was presided over by Judge T. W. Smith at the Madison Circuit Court, where Curtis pleaded not guilty. The jury ultimately convicted him of assault and battery. Following the conviction, the court sentenced Curtis to a $20 fine, 20 days of imprisonment, and additional costs, and he was to be held until the fines and costs were paid. Curtis sought to quash the indictment before the trial, arguing that it was insufficient because it did not specify that his actions were felonious, which prompted his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	William Curtis, the plaintiff in error, argued that the indictment was flawed because it failed to specify that the assault was committed unlawfully and feloniously. He maintained that the indictment must charge the intent in clear terms and asserted that the jury found him guilty without sufficient evidence that he caused the injuries specifically as charged. He sought to have the indictment quashed and the subsequent judgment against him reversed.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by the Attorney General N. W. Edwards, contended that the indictment was sufficient for the charges brought against Curtis. The prosecution maintained that Curtis's actions constituted assault and battery, justifying the jury's verdict. They argued against Curtis's motions, asserting that he was rightly convicted based on the evidence presented during the trial.

In the case of Henry Abrahams v. A. M. Jones, the events transpired in Cook County, Illinois, with the final judgment rendered on July 16, 1886. The dispute revolved around a penal bond executed on June 15, 1881, wherein Thomas J. Martin and William H. Graham were plaintiffs in a replevin suit against multiple defendants, including the Traders Bank. Abrahams acted as a surety for the bond. The bond stipulated that Martin and Graham would return property, specifically fifty barrels of whiskey, to the defendants if so ordered by the circuit court. The court later ruled in favor of the Traders Bank, ordering the return of the whiskey, which Martin and Graham failed to comply with. Abrahams was therefore alleged to be liable under the bond for not fulfilling its conditions. The trial included assignments of breaches related to this failure, but the court found the allegations insufficient, leading to the defendant's contentions about the validity of the claim.	The plaintiff, Henry Abrahams, argued that the bond’s conditions were violated by Thomas J. Martin and William H. Graham when they failed to return the fifty barrels of whiskey as ordered by the court. The plaintiff claimed damages for the breach of the bond amounting to seven thousand dollars. Additionally, it was claimed that the Traders Bank incurred expenses in defending the replevin suit, which amounted to twenty-five hundred dollars, further asserting a cause of action against Martin, Graham, and Abrahams.	The defendant, Abrahams, contended that the claims against him were flawed and that the assignments of breach did not demonstrate a legal breach of the bond. He argued that both assignments presented by the plaintiff were materially defective, showing no cause of action against him as the surety. Abrahams moved for the arrest of judgment based on the insufficiency of the declarations made by the plaintiff and asserted that the defects in the claims were not cureable by the verdict rendered in the case.

In December 1889, the legal case "Israel P. Rumsey and Augustin C. Buell v. J. H. Nickerson, C. B. Kennedy, Intervenor" was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose from actions taken by J. H. Nickerson, who was a resident of Canton, Dakota. Nickerson engaged in the business of purchasing grain and stock, accumulating a debt of approximately $751.54 to the plaintiffs, Rumsey and Buell, by March 20, 1888. On that date, the plaintiffs commenced an attachment suit and seized a carload of flax seed that had been shipped by Nickerson to Chicago. Following a default judgment against Nickerson for $796.63, C. B. Kennedy intervened, claiming ownership of the flax seed based on an agreement with Nickerson that secured his loans for grain purchases. Kennedy's claim rested on two written contracts that established his lien over the grain. A trial without a jury favored Kennedy, leading the plaintiffs to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, Israel P. Rumsey and Augustin C. Buell, argued that their rights as creditors should prevail since they had levied an attachment against the flax seed owned by Nickerson. They contended that the flax seed was effectively Nickerson's property after a dishonored draft, which should have released any lien Kennedy claimed over it. Their requests centered on overturning the judgment favoring Kennedy, thereby asserting their right to the proceeds from the flax seed.	The defendant, C. B. Kennedy, argued that under the written agreements with Nickerson, he maintained a valid lien on the flax seed until his financial advances were repaid. Kennedy contended that the attachment by Rumsey and Buell was invalid because the flax seed legally belonged to him due to his prior agreements with Nickerson. He maintained that the positions taken by the plaintiffs were contrary to the established contracts, which required that any proceeds from the sale of the flax seed should go towards repaying the money advanced by him.

In April 1867, the case of Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company v. Samuel Wickery arose in Livingston County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Samuel Wickery, the plaintiff, and the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company, the defendant. The lawsuit originated when Wickery sought to recover damages for a cow that was killed on the railway company's property. Wickery claimed that the accident occurred at a location where the law mandated the railway to have a fence, which it had failed to construct despite the railway being operational for several years. The initial case was brought before a justice of the peace and, following an appeal, was moved to the Circuit Court. There, it was ruled in favor of Wickery, leading to a verdict that required the railway company to compensate him for the cow.	Samuel Wickery, the plaintiff, argued that the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company was negligent because it did not build a fence along a segment of its railway where such fencing was legally required. He claimed that this negligence led to the death of his cow and sought compensation for the value of the animal, insisting that the railway's failure to adhere to statutory fencing requirements was the direct cause of his loss.	The Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company contended that they were not liable for the cow's death. They sought to overturn the Circuit Court's judgment in favor of Wickery, arguing that the circumstances of the incident did not warrant their liability. The defense likely included assertions of compliance with the law or challenges to the factual basis of Wickery's claims, although specific arguments were not detailed in the summary.

In June 1873, in Illinois, the partnership between William P. Renfrow and Edwin Pearce was dissolved, with Renfrow appointed as the trustee of the firm's goods. His responsibility was to convert these goods into cash through retail sales to pay off any partnership debts. Instead, Renfrow engaged in questionable actions by exchanging partnership goods for land, subsequently conveying this property to his wife. This act was viewed as a fraudulent misuse of the partnership's assets, as Renfrow had been entrusted to liquidate the goods for the benefit of the creditors. Pearce filed a bill in chancery against Renfrow in the Circuit Court of Washington County, seeking to have the land sold to satisfy the partnership's debts. The case examined the implications of Renfrow's actions, especially his dealings with Dugger, who obtained a mortgage on the land. Notably, the court underscored that the land acquired inappropriately should be subject to the firm's debts due to the fraudulent actions surrounding its acquisition.	The plaintiff, Edwin Pearce, claimed that Renfrow had violated his fiduciary duty as a trustee by converting partnership goods into land instead of selling them for cash to pay off the partnership debts. Pearce sought the court's intervention to subject the acquired land to satisfy the collective debts owed by the partnership, arguing that Renfrow's actions constituted a fraudulent perversion of trust property.	The defendant, Renfrow, contended that his transaction with Dugger regarding the land was legitimate and should be upheld. He argued that any mortgage agreement with Dugger was entered into as a private transaction and not meant to defraud creditors. However, there was no substantial evidence to support his position as a bona fide purchaser for value without notice of the circumstances under which he acquired the land.

In the case of Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Ry. Co. v. Maria Peterson, the legal proceedings occurred following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Mason County, Illinois. The case was presided over by Judge C. Epleb, and the decision was filed on July 3, 1884. The key parties involved included the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company as the appellant and Maria Peterson as the appellee. The dispute revolves around a trial in which evidence was presented; however, the appellant's bill of exceptions was found to be defective. It lacked essential components such as the signature and seal of the presiding judge, and it terminated abruptly, failing to cover the necessary proceedings. As a result, the record could not be considered complete for reviewing errors that the appellant sought to assign.	The plaintiff, Maria Peterson, argued that the railway company had failed to meet legal standards in their conduct during the trial. They sought to have their claims validated through appropriate legal review, relying on the evidence presented in court which they believed supported their position against the railway company.	The defendant, Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Ry. Co., contended that the appeal was not valid due to the defective bill of exceptions that was presented. They argued this defect precluded any examination of errors claimed by the plaintiff, and therefore requested that the court affirm the circuit court's judgment.

In January 1875, in McLean County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose in the Illinois Supreme Court, involving plaintiffs Daniel O. Crist et al. and defendant Mary W. Wray. The case centered around a trespass action for the alleged taking and carrying away of a piano and an organ by Crist and his co-defendants. The case progressed through the Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Thomas F. Tipton. Wray initially claimed ownership of the piano and organ, which prompted Crist and others to respond with a plea. During the trial, after the plaintiff presented her evidence, the court permitted her to amend her declaration by dropping her claim regarding the piano. This amendment led one of the defendants to request a continuance, stating that he was unprepared to proceed. However, the court overruled this request, ultimately affecting the trial's proceedings. The trial encompassed conflicting testimonies regarding the ownership of the organ, and despite some controversies regarding evidence and jury instructions, the court found no significant basis for reversing the judgment.	Mary W. Wray, the plaintiff, argued that her property—specifically a piano and an organ—had been wrongfully taken and carried away by the defendants. She sought legal remedies for the trespass, initially claiming both the piano and the organ, but later amended her claim to focus solely on the organ. Wray's requests included the recovery of damages resulting from the alleged wrongful taking.	The defendants, including Daniel O. Crist, contended that the court had made errors during the trial, including its decision to sustain a demurrer to a plea and to deny a motion for a continuance based on Wray's amendment to her claims. They argued that the amendment rendered them less prepared for trial and sought a reversal of the judgment based on these alleged errors. The defendants also questioned the admissibility of certain evidence concerning the rental value of the organ, suggesting it misled the jury.

Elisha Essley applied for a loan of $2,000 on January 15, 1872, from John McKinney, agreeing to pay two percent interest in advance and ten percent at the end of the year. To secure this loan, he and his wife executed a trust deed on their real estate to Isaac M. Bassett as trustee. Essley paid the interest for several years but sold the land on February 8, 1878, to William Drury, who assumed the payment of the trust deed. The property changed hands multiple times, with each buyer (Drury, Bigelow, and Ballard) referenced in subsequent transactions. The case arose when Essley sought to redeem the property after it was advertised for sale, claiming the interest payment was usurious. The Illinois Appellate Court did not allow the usury defense, asserting that Essley had no right to interpose such a claim after making an appropriation to pay the debt and interest voluntarily. The case was before the court at the December term of 1884 and addressed the validity of the claim against those who acquired interests in the property in good faith.	The plaintiffs, led by Elisha Essley, primarily argue that the interest on the loan was usurious and that they should not be held to the terms of payment set by the trust deed. They sought the right to redeem the property after it had been advertised for sale and proposed to pay a sum deemed equitably binding by the court.	The defendants, led by John C. Sloan, contended that the claim of usury could not be interposed since the subsequent buyers of the property—Drury, Bigelow, and Ballard—had no knowledge of any usurious interest in the note or trust deed. They argued that Essley had made a voluntary appropriation of the property to satisfy his debt and insisted that the court's decree regarding the redemption terms was valid and that the plaintiffs had no right to adjust the interest paid.

The case "Granville S. Ingraham et al. v. Charles O. Whitmore et al." took place in Chicago, Illinois, surrounding events around October 6, 1871, leading up to the Great Chicago Fire that occurred shortly after. The plaintiffs, Granville S. Ingraham and his partners, operated as wholesale grocers known as Ingraham & Co., while the defendants, Charles O. Whitmore and Charles J. Whitmore, were partners transacting under the name Whitmore & Son, located in Boston. The matter arose when Ingraham & Co. was solicited for an order of sugar by a broker, J. H. Dunham & Co. During negotiations, an offer was made by Ingraham for 25 barrels of sugar. Dunham & Co. claimed to have sent an order to Ingraham & Co. for this sugar just before the devastating fire; however, Ingraham & Co. denied receiving it and claimed that there was no evidence that any sugar had been destroyed by the fire. Despite Dunham pressuring Ingraham & Co. to submit the matter to arbitration due to the unpaid claim, it was noted that Dunham lacked authority to bind the plaintiffs in such an agreement. The arbitration process was called into question as it lacked due representation for Ingraham & Co., leading to significant legal repercussions.	The plaintiffs contended that they were wrongfully held liable for the payment of sugar they never received. They claimed that there was an alleged oral agreement and reliance on an arbitration award made by a broker who lacked authority and failed to follow proper arbitration procedures. They sought legal relief that would absolve them of any financial responsibility for the sugar sale claimed by the defendants, arguing that the brokerage’s dealings were not binding to them.	The defendants maintained that an order was given to Ingraham & Co. for the sugar in question. They argued that the arbitration process, while contested, ultimately produced an award in their favor, assuming the legitimacy of the broker’s authority. The defense claimed that the arbitration conducted by the umpire constituted a valid method of resolving the matter, and denied any wrongdoing, insisting that Ingraham & Co. had a responsibility to honor the order and the resultant arbitration.

The case of Charles N. Munson, Collector, etc. v. John S. Miller was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. It stemmed from a dispute over a tax levied on property owned by John S. Miller in the town of Sterling, Illinois. The controversy began when, in April 1870, the local assessor asked Miller for a list of his taxable property. Miller complied, providing a complete account of his personal property and outstanding debts. However, the county clerk later assessed Miller’s personal property at a value of $5810 in 1871, claiming it had been omitted from the previous year's tax assessment. Consequently, a tax of $265.04 was levied against Miller. Miller, contesting this tax, filed a bill in equity in the Whiteside circuit court to enjoin (or stop) its collection, asserting that the assessment was improper. The case was heard without evidence presented, and the court initially ruled in favor of Miller.	Miller, the plaintiff, argued that the tax assessment on his property was illegal. He maintained that he had fully disclosed his personal property and debts to the assessor in 1870 and that any subsequent reassessment by the county clerk was unjust and not legally warranted. His legal request was for the court to permanently enjoin the tax levied against him, claiming that the assessment process had not been executed correctly.	Charles N. Munson, the defendant and tax collector, contended that the assessment was valid under the law. He argued that the county clerk had the authority to assess omitted properties from previous assessments and that there was no evidence to prove that the tax levied was illegal. Munson asserted that the plaintiff had not met the burden of proof to invalidate the tax assessment and requested that the court dismiss Miller's bill to enjoin the tax collection.

In September 1867, the legal dispute titled "William Drury v. Sabra Ann Sink; Courtney Drury v. Sabra Ann Sink; and Thomas Willitt v. Sabra Ann Sink" took place in Illinois. The case involved multiple plaintiffs—William Drury, Courtney Drury, and Thomas Willitt—against defendant Sabra Ann Sink. The precise nature of the claims and facts surrounding the case was paralleling a prior case, Finch v. Sink, which the Illinois Supreme Court had previously adjudicated. The appeals originated from the Circuit Court of Mercer County where the Honorable John S. Thompson presided. The court's decision concerned legal interpretations and factual circumstances related to the actions of Sink, which would be key to determining liability and any potential for damages.	The plaintiffs, William Drury, Courtney Drury, and Thomas Willitt, collectively claimed that Sabra Ann Sink was responsible for certain actions that warranted legal relief. Although the case specifics in terms of their direct allegations are not recorded in the summary, it is evident that the plaintiffs sought to overturn a prior unfavorable judgment, asserting their rights based on similar facts to those presented in Finch v. Sink.	The defendant, Sabra Ann Sink, presumably contended against the claims made by the plaintiffs. Her arguments likely included defenses outlined in the previous case, Finch v. Sink, asserting that the circumstances did not fulfill the criteria for liability or any claims for damages as claimed by the plaintiffs. The defense requested that the court uphold the previous judgment, maintaining that Sink was not at fault.

Adolph Mulheisen and William Lane were involved in a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1876. The dispute arose in Washington County, Illinois, regarding a sewing machine that was claimed to belong to John L. McNeil. Mulheisen, acting as a constable, had an execution ordering the seizure of McNeil's goods but had not levied or seen the machine in question. Instead, he was informed that the machine had been taken by Lane, who had a competing execution against McNeil. Mulheisen later contacted the plaintiff, another constable, to assert his claim to the machine, but when he demanded its return, Lane refused, wanting to consult the original creditor first. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him damages for the alleged value of the machine.	The plaintiff, claiming to be entitled to the possession of the sewing machine due to a prior execution, sought damages against Lane and Mulheisen for the value of the property. He argued that he had the right to claim the machine as his execution was older than the one Lane had, despite never having physically seized the machine. The plaintiff contended that the defendants wrongfully retained the property, leading to losses.	The defendants contended that the plaintiff had no legal standing to claim the sewing machine because he had never taken possession of it through a legal levy or seizure. They argued that without having physically seized the property, the plaintiff had no interest in it that would justify an action of trover. The defendants also pointed out that there was insufficient evidence to prove the machine belonged to McNeil, the execution debtor.

John Bull, the appellant, and Horace E. Griswold, the appellee, were involved in a legal dispute decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1858. The case originated from Winnebago County, where Griswold claimed that Bull committed trespass to his real estate by cutting and carrying away unthreshed wheat from his property. The events in question took place around the latter part of May or early June 1856, following a deed execution from Griswold to Bull. Upon trial at the June term of 1857, the jury ultimately found in favor of the appellee, awarding Griswold $760 in damages. This case raised important legal principles concerning the status of growing crops as personal property, the validity of verbal agreements regarding leases, and the nature of damages in cases of willful trespass. The court examined various jury instructions and witnesses' testimonies to determine the legality of the actions taken by both parties.	The plaintiff, Horace E. Griswold, claimed that the wheat was his personal property, asserting that Bull unlawfully cut and removed it from his land. Griswold contended that Bull’s statements implied ownership and that the removal of the wheat constituted a trespass. He sought damages not only for the actual value of the wheat taken but also asked for the jury to consider awarding smart money or punitive damages due to the willful nature of Bull's actions.	John Bull, the defendant, argued against the claims made by Griswold, suggesting that the cutting of the wheat was legal and asserting that any lease agreements made were valid. He contended that the wheat, once cut, should be valued at its condition at the time of the trespass, rather than its standing value. Additionally, he sought to introduce defenses regarding the procedural aspects of the deed’s delivery, attempting to assert that no valid lease existed based on the delivery timeline.

In the autumn of 1865, Uri Winchester and T. W. Grosvenor were operating the Garden City Brewery in Chicago, Illinois. The partnership was structured such that Winchester would provide the capital and materials, while Grosvenor managed the business operations. At the time, Grosvenor held around $2,500 in the business, which belonged to his wife, Mary Grosvenor, inherited from a deceased relative. During this period, Grosvenor sold the brewery’s assets to Sarah D. Winchester, with a total sale price of $3,231, for which he provided a receipt. The sale included some unpaid amounts, specifically $300, which was to be settled shortly, and $401.36, which was to remain outstanding until the conclusion of partnership accounting. Following the sale, there were additional beer barrels distributed that were to be accounted for separately, valued at $3.50 each but were excluded from the initial sale. Sarah Winchester pursued legal action to recover the value of these barrels, as well as the outstanding $300. A jury found in favor of Sarah, awarding her damages amounting to $1,100, which she reduced to $1,000, amidst disputes over the validity of the receipts and the amounts owed.	Sarah D. Winchester argued that she was entitled to recover the value of the ale barrels that had been delivered to customers, which remained unpaid and were not included in the original sale agreement. Additionally, she sought the outstanding amount of $401.36 from T. W. Grosvenor, which was purportedly agreed to be deferred until the partnership's accounts were settled.	Mary E. Grosvenor contended that the receipts issued indicated that amounts owed had been paid and denied the claim for the additional $401.36, asserting that the payment had been settled as part of the sale. Her defense emphasized the sufficiency of the written receipts, arguing that they represented clear and unambiguous evidence of the transaction terms that dismissed claims to recover additional amounts based on uncertain verbal assertions.

The case "William C. Bolvin et al. v. Albert G. Edwards et al." originated in December 1847 in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Albert G. Edwards, Rasin, and Cabanne, initiated a suit against W.C. and N. Bolvin in the Jo Daviess Circuit Court, claiming a breach of contract under the legal doctrine of "indebitatus assumpsit." The case faced procedural hurdles beginning with a lack of proper service, as the initial process issued was returned with "not found", prompting a summons to be sent to Peoria County where the defendants were eventually served. W.C. Bolvin initially filed a plea of "non assumpsit," meaning he denied the obligations of the claim. An agreement between attorneys resulted in the case being continued at the plaintiffs’ cost. Subsequently, W.C. Bolvin withdrew his plea, leading to a default judgment being entered against both defendants, with damages assessed at $1,630.74. This prompted the Boilvins to file a writ of error to reverse the judgment on jurisdictional grounds.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants owed them damages based on a breach of contract. They sought to recover $1,630.74 as the amount assessed by the jury in the default judgment entered against the defendants. The plaintiffs asserted that they properly followed judicial procedures to initiate the case and serve the defendants.	The defendants contended that the court lacked jurisdiction over the case since the declaration did not adequately specify the location of the action or the residency of the parties involved, as required by statute. W.C. Bolvin argued that withdrawing his plea negated any appearance that could confer jurisdiction over N. Bolvin, particularly since the initial process was improperly directed to Peoria County.

Thomas H. Smith and Belle W. Sullivan, as plaintiffs, initiated an ejectment action against Charlotte and Ferdinand Laatsch, the defendants, on April 17, 1884, in the Effingham Circuit Court, Illinois. The suit involved a dispute over the east half of the southwest quarter of section 29, township 7 north, range 4 east. The plaintiffs claimed title through their deceased father, Thomas H. Smith, while the defendants asserted their title from a series of deeds unrelated to the plaintiffs’ lineage. During the trial, both parties submitted affidavits regarding their claims. The plaintiffs introduced evidence linking their title back to their father through county court proceedings related to his estate, indicating that the sale conducted by the administrator of the estate was void due to lack of jurisdiction. The defendants, who did not provide any rebuttal evidence, argued that they held color of title and good faith possession with a clear chain of conveyances from their ancestor. The trial concluded with the court ruling in favor of the defendants, leading the plaintiffs to appeal the decision for reversal.	The plaintiffs argued that they were the rightful heirs of Thomas H. Smith, asserting their claim to the disputed land based on a valid chain of title from their deceased father. They filed an affidavit claiming they had a common source of title with the defendants, which they sought to prove through multiple pieces of documentation. The primary legal request was for the court to recognize their claim as heirs and reverse the judgment in favor of the defendants.	The defendants countered that they claimed title through a series of valid deeds and that they did not share the same source of title as the plaintiffs. They provided an affidavit denying the plaintiffs’ assertion of commonality and maintained that their possession and ownership were legitimate because they had held color of title and had paid taxes on the property for over seven years. Their legal request was for the court to uphold the initial judgment that favored them, asserting their right to retain possession of the property.

The case "The Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company v. August Dresel" took place in Chicago, Illinois, with the formal decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 19, 1884. The case arose when the Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company sought to condemn a portion of property owned and leased by August Dresel, which consisted of lots 2 through 15 in a specific block subdivision. Dresel had been using these lots collectively for an extensive flower-gardening business since 1870, holding lots 2 to 9 under a lease that would expire on July 1, 1885, while owning lots 10 to 15 outright. The railroad company had already acquired the fee simple of lots 2 to 5 from Dresel's landlord and aimed to take part of the leasehold interest in lots 2 to 5. The jury awarded Dresel $1,500 for damages resulting from the taking, leading to the legal arguments concerning evidence about lost profits and the basis for damages related to property value depreciation.	The plaintiff, the Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company, argued that the court erred in allowing evidence on potential profits from the property occupied by Dresel. They also challenged the jury's instructions related to loss of business due to the condemnation, contending that damages awarded to Dresel were excessive.	August Dresel, the defendant, contended that he was entitled to compensation for the depreciation of the entire property’s market value due to the taking of a portion of his leasehold. He argued that the court correctly ruled that while loss of business or profits was not recoverable, any reduction in the value of the property as a whole warranted financial compensation.

In 1872, Barnum Blake filed for divorce from Christine Blake in Cook County, Illinois, alleging that she committed adultery with Thomas M. Thompson. The couple had married in 1851 and had five children. After moving to Winnetka in 1867, their relationship soured, leading to allegations of infidelity. A jury trial decided that Christine was not guilty of the adultery charges, primarily based on circumstantial evidence provided by a private detective hired by Barnum. Christine filed a cross-bill accusing Barnum of extreme cruelty and adultery, which he denied, but failed to substantiate his claims. The jury's verdict favored Christine, leading Barnum to appeal the decision on multiple counts, including challenges to the jury's instructions and the court's ruling on newly discovered evidence.	Barnum Blake claimed that Christine Blake had engaged in adultery with Thomas M. Thompson, which he argued was sufficient grounds for divorce. He contended that the jury's verdict was contrary to the evidence presented, challenged the court's jury instructions, sought a new trial based on newly discovered evidence, and argued against the excessive solicitors' fees awarded to Christine's counsel.	Christine Blake denied having committed adultery and claimed that Barnum had subjected her to extreme cruelty. In her cross-bill, she maintained that Barnum was guilty of adultery himself and sought a divorce. The defense highlighted that no direct evidence of adulterous behavior was produced, and they emphasized the credibility issues surrounding the private detective's testimony and the hostile nature of Barnum's son’s testimonies.

In December 1846, the case of Levi Wilcoxon v. William Roby was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court after originating in the Circuit Court of Stephenson County. The dispute arose over a penal bond executed by Wilcoxon and Roby, wherein both parties mutually agreed to refrain from interfering with a tract of Government land to which they had both laid claims. The agreement stipulated that they would not engage in any interference until their respective claims could be settled and adjusted. Roby brought an action of debt against Wilcoxon, citing various breaches of the bond's conditions. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Roby, awarding him damages amounting to $400. However, the case record became convoluted due to several defective pleas and replications, making it difficult to ascertain the submitted issues. The court proceedings lacked argument or citation of authority, leading the appellee to admit errors in the Circuit Court's judgment.	The plaintiff, William Roby, claimed that Levi Wilcoxon breached the conditions of the penal bond by interfering with the Government land in question. Roby sought a judgment for the damages incurred as a result of this breach, which resulted in the Circuit Court awarding him $400 in damages.	Levi Wilcoxon, the defendant, contended that several aspects of the legal proceedings and the judgment rendered by the Circuit Court were defective and erroneous. He argued that an assessment of damages in an action of debt should not be determined without first establishing the underlying debt. Furthermore, he indicated that any errors in the jury's verdict could not be rectified post-verdict by the Circuit Court, which underscored the need for a new trial.

Jacob W. Vanmeter v. William McHard is a legal case that took place in April 1863 in Rock Island County, Illinois. The case arose when William McHard filed a writ of summons claiming against Jacob W. Vanmeter and a co-defendant, Caleb M. Clark, in a court proceeding. The sheriff's return indicated that the writ was served on C. M. Clark and S. W. Vanmeter, leading to the entry of a default judgment against both defendants in the Circuit Court. Vanmeter contested this judgment, claiming there was no proper service on him. Upon review, the court found discrepancies in the names indicated in the service documents, but ultimately decided that the service on J. W. Vanmeter was indeed valid based on the original writ which had been produced in court. The case was presided over by Judge John W. Drurt.	The plaintiff, William McHard, argued that the service of process was properly executed and sought to hold both defendants accountable through a default judgment. He maintained that both defendants, including Jacob W. Vanmeter, were adequately served according to the documentation provided and therefore were subject to the legal proceedings initiated against them.	Jacob W. Vanmeter contended that the default and final judgment entered against him were erroneous due to insufficient evidence of service upon him. He argued that the sheriff's return did not properly indicate that he had been served with the summons, claiming that the process was not valid without such evidence.

In 1886, James W. Sykes was a warehouseman operating a public warehouse in Cook County, Illinois. He was indicted by the grand jury for multiple offenses related to fraudulent activities involving warehouse receipts under a law regulating public warehouses. The indictment specified that Sykes had falsely claimed ownership of 4,500 bags of timothy seed stored in his warehouse, intending to deceive the Merchants’ Loan and Trust Company into granting him a loan of $15,500. Only three of the twenty-eight counts of the indictment were pursued during the trial, which led to a jury conviction and a two-year prison sentence. Sykes sought to reverse the judgment, arguing that there was a significant variance between the corporation's true name and that alleged in the indictment, thus claiming that the prosecution failed to prove his guilt adequately.	The plaintiff (the People of the State of Illinois) maintained that James W. Sykes acted fraudulently by issuing false warehouse receipts that misrepresented the existence and ownership of the timothy seed to defraud the Merchants’ Loan and Trust Company. The prosecution asserted that Sykes knew the representations were false and that this deception constituted a serious criminal offense under the specified regulations concerning public warehouses.	James W. Sykes contended that there was a material variance between the name of the corporation mentioned in the indictment (the Merchants’ Loan and Trust Company) and its actual name at the time of the alleged offense (the Merchants’ Savings, Loan and Trust Company). He argued this discrepancy rendered the indictment invalid, claiming that the prosecution had not met its burden of proof regarding the identity of the corporation defrauded.

In December 1837, Merritt Lyon filed an action of assumpsit against Nathan Barney in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in McLean County, Illinois, where Lyon alleged that Barney defaulted on a promissory note. On the same day that Barney filed his plea of non-assumpsit, Lyon secured a default judgment for debt and damages against Barney. However, the accuracy of the proceedings came into question as it was asserted that the judgment was rendered after the plea had been filed. This led to an appeal by Barney challenging the validity of the default judgment, arguing that it was entered erroneously since the plea was indeed filed prior to the judgment. The case hinged on the court's ability to establish the timeline of events based on the official record, which was found to confirm that the plea preceded the judgment.	Merritt Lyon claimed that Nathan Barney failed to fulfill his payment obligations under a promissory note, leading to financial damages. Lyon requested the court maintain the default judgment, asserting it was valid given Barney's failure to respond to the claim adequately.	Nathan Barney contested the validity of the default judgment, arguing that it was entered after his plea of non-assumpsit had been filed, which should have preempted any judgment by default. Barney requested the court to reverse the judgment and remand the case, contending that the judgment's form was erroneous, as it improperly combined a judgment for debt with damages.

On April 16, 1860, a partnership was formed between Cadwallader Bull of Buffalo, New York and Maher & Kelly, who operated in Chicago, Illinois, for a coal business. Under their partnership agreement, Bull was responsible for supplying coal, while Maher was to provide the necessary facilities, and Kelly would manage operations. Disputes arose concerning the payment and distribution of sales proceeds. On October 11, 1860, Bull filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership, claiming Maher & Kelly failed to pay the required proceeds from coal sales. A court injunction was placed on Maher & Kelly to prevent further sales. The Superior Court ruled in favor of Bull in March 1866, ordering Maher & Kelly to pay him over six thousand six hundred dollars due to non-compliance with the partnership agreement. Maher & Kelly appealed this verdict, leading to further court proceedings regarding the distribution of partnership assets and obligations.	The plaintiff, Maria Bull as the administratrix of Cadwallader Bull, claimed that Maher & Kelly did not pay over the proceeds of coal sales as stipulated in the partnership agreement, justifying a dissolution of the partnership. Bull sought an accounting of the partnership's financial dealings and requested an injunction against Maher & Kelly from collecting further sales proceeds without remitting the due amounts.	Maher & Kelly contended that they should not be liable for the claimed deficiencies in payments because Bull also failed to provide an adequate supply of coal necessary for the business operations. They argued that the inability to deliver coal affected their ability to fulfill sales contracts, and thus they sought damages for Bull's alleged breach of contract.

In the case of William L. Berry v. John P. Wilkinson and Elihu Wolcott, the legal proceedings took place in the Morgan Circuit Court during the October term of 1834, in Morgan County, Illinois. The plaintiff, William L. Berry, applied for a change of venue, arguing that he would not receive a fair trial due to prejudicial influences exerted by the defendants on the local populace. Berry's claim was based on an affidavit that expressed concerns about the potential bias of the jury pool in Morgan County. However, the Court denied this motion for a change of venue, stating that Berry failed to provide sufficient notice to the defendants regarding his application. The ruling was made under the discretion afforded to the judges, emphasizing that the notification period must be reasonable and considerate of the case's circumstances. The Court concluded that the notice given by Berry was inadequate, as he might have known about the alleged prejudice long before the term began, thereby affirming the initial decision of the lower court.	William L. Berry, as the plaintiff, claimed that he could not receive a fair trial in Morgan County due to the undue influence of the defendants over local jurors and prejudice against him. He sought a change of venue for the trial, supported by an affidavit that outlined his concerns about bias. Essentially, his main argument was predicated on the belief that the local community's prejudice against him would compromise the integrity of the trial.	The defendants, John P. Wilkinson and Elihu Wolcott, contended that Berry's request for a change of venue was unwarranted. They argued the notice provided for the application was insufficient and emphasized that the trial court had acted within its discretion in denying the motion. Moreover, they maintained that Berry's claims of prejudice lacked merit and were not backed by adequate evidence to necessitate a change in venue.

The case of Lawson A. Winslow v. A. F. Benedict was adjudicated in September 1873 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The background of the case involves a writ of attachment filed by Lawson A. Winslow, a medical professional, against a debtor named Daniel Kipp for the amount of thirty-five dollars, which represented medical services rendered. The claim was based on a judgment rendered against Kipp in a lower court. Simultaneously, a process of garnishment was initiated against A. F. Benedict, who was identified as a debtor of Kipp. Benedict acknowledged his indebtedness of twenty-five dollars and fifty cents as wages owed to Kipp for work performed as a journeyman painter. Kipp, however, claimed that twenty-five dollars of this sum was exempt from garnishment under the Illinois statute of 1872, which protects the wages of the head of a family residing with them. The justice of the peace upheld Kipp's exemption and ruled that only fifty cents should be garnished from Benedict. This resulted in an appeal by Winslow to the Court of Common Pleas of the City of Aurora, which upheld the original decision, leading to another appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Lawson A. Winslow, claimed that he was entitled to the entire garnished amount, less the exempt portion, citing that the garnishment process should not allow for the exemption of Kipp’s wages. Winslow sought to reverse the lower court's judgment, arguing that he was rightfully owed the amount for medical services rendered to Kipp.	The defendant, A. F. Benedict, maintained that the claim of exemption under the Illinois statute was valid. He acknowledged his debt to Kipp but contended that since Kipp was the head of a family residing with his family and his wages did not exceed the exempt threshold established by the law, the garnishment should only be for the amount exceeding the exempt twenty-five dollars. He requested that the judgment against him be upheld, reflecting that only fifty cents should be garnished.

In February 1862, Charles M. Vaughan executed a deed to his wife, Cecelia Vaughan, while enlisting in the United States Army, for the consideration of one dollar, intending for her to manage their real estate in case he did not return. Vaughan died in October 1862 from wounds sustained in battle, before he could return home. The deed remained among his papers, and Cecelia stated she didn't see it until after his death. She began receiving the rents from the property and authorized an agent to sell it. However, she did not complete the sale when it was proposed.
