The case centers around whether the deed was valid at law, given the argument that a husband could not convey land to his wife due to their legal status as one person. The proceedings took place in Kankakee County, Illinois, culminating in an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871.	The plaintiffs, represented by Robert T. Lincoln, argued that the deed executed by Vaughan to his wife was invalid at law and did not transfer title to her. They contended that there was no effective delivery of the deed since Cecelia Vaughan had not seen it prior to her husband's death and questioned the legal capacity of a husband to convey property rights to his wife.	Cecelia Vaughan, as the defendant, asserted that the deed was intended to provide for her and their children in case of Vaughan's death. She argued that, despite not having seen the deed until after his passing, the circumstances surrounding its execution and subsequent actions—receiving rents and attempting to sell the property—showed implied acceptance and delivery. Her counsel contended that equity should uphold the deed, despite its technical invalidity at law.

In January 1860, John White (Appellant) faced Thomas G. Watkins and John Murphy (Appellees) in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a scire facias proceeding initiated by the appellees to foreclose a mortgage held against property that White had purchased. The dispute centered on whether White had valid legal grounds to contest the mortgage due to claims of misrepresentation made during the property sale. White alleged that, based on the representations of ownership from Watkins and Murphy, he purchased the property for $4,160, paying $1,000 upfront and securing the remainder with notes and mortgages. He argued that later discoveries revealed that the appellees did not have a legitimate title to the property, which constituted a failure of consideration. The court examined the legal frameworks concerning defenses against foreclosure, highlighting that only defenses showing the mortgage was never a valid lien or had been released could be interposed. It concluded that even allegations of fraud were insufficient as a defense under the applicable statutes governing this type of foreclosure.	The plaintiff, John White, contended that the mortgage and associated notes were void due to fraudulent representations made by the defendants, Thomas G. Watkins and John Murphy, regarding the ownership of the property. White argued that he relied wholly on these representations when purchasing the property and requested the court to recognize these claims to annul the foreclosure of the mortgage.	The defendants maintained that the mortgage was valid and contested White's assertions of fraud, contending that the issues raised did not constitute legal defenses against the foreclosure. They argued that the court had already established legal precedent that fraud claims could not serve as a valid defense in a scire facias proceeding to foreclose a mortgage, thus supporting their position to uphold the mortgage.

In June 1872, a legal dispute arose in McLean County, Illinois, between the Illinois Central Railroad Company and Cobb, Christy & Co. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court and pertains to a series of ongoing legal issues between the same parties. The case involved the transportation of goods, specifically 17,000 bushels of corn that were shipped from Bloomington on April 6 by E. Fay & Co., agents for Cobb, Christy & Co. The plaintiff, Cobb, Christy & Co., owned the corn and sought to prove the entire shipment as one transaction, even though the shipment was documented across multiple bills of lading. The court deliberated on the admissibility of evidence related to the bills of lading and the nature of the plaintiff's claim regarding the delivery of goods within the expected time frame.	The plaintiff argued that they were improperly restricted to using only two bills of lading as evidence for their entire claim regarding non-delivery of the corn shipment. They asserted that as the owners of the goods, they should be allowed to present evidence of the entire shipment despite it being documented across several bills of lading. They requested the court to recognize the shipment as a single transaction.	The defendant, Illinois Central Railroad Company, contended that the case should be limited strictly to the evidence enumerated in the bills of lading, arguing that this limitation was necessary as the action was based on those documents. They maintained that only the specific bills outlined in the declaration should be admissible in the case, and requested the court to dismiss evidence related to other shipments not confined to the two bills mentioned.

In 1861, Harvey Rout initiated an ejectment action against Henry R. Gillespie in the Morgan Circuit Court of Illinois regarding a disputed piece of land. The case was marked by a series of continuations due to an agreement between the parties pending a decision in another related case involving Gillespie. As the case progressed, Gillespie maintained possession of the land. In April 1864, the court allowed Gillespie to retain possession temporarily while he pursued his rights in equity through a concurrent suit in chancery. This agreement stipulated that if Rout did not act for a year, he would waive his right to take possession. After a new trial was granted in September 1864, Rout contested this, asserting Gillespie's action violated their agreement. The lower court, however, set aside the order for a new trial, leading Gillespie to appeal the decision, arguing he was still entitled to a legal trial.	Rout claimed that Gillespie had no legal right to a new trial based on their prior agreement, which effectively barred him from executing that right. He argued that since the Supreme Court had ruled against Gillespie in the related case, judgment should be rendered in his favor without a trial, as per their mutual consent.	Gillespie contended that the court's actions to deny him a new trial were erroneous and unjust. He argued that all legal defenses should still apply and that the motions brought by Rout should not restrict him from pursuing a trial on the merits of the case, contending that costs had been paid, and claiming rightful possession.

On October 23, 1866, John M. Seward and William B. Herrick, equal owners of certain lands in Illinois, executed quit-claim deeds to effectuate a partition of the property. Herrick conveyed his interest in section 13 to Seward, while Seward conveyed his residual interests to Herrick. The partition was deemed fair and just, with Herrick's deed recorded on March 4, 1857, and Seward's deed recorded on January 28, 1862. Later, Herrick mortgaged his land for $20,000 and also had an outstanding judgment against him by Daniel L. Pettee, the defendant. Pettee's judgment led to an attempted sale of an undivided half of the lands allotted to Seward after a series of conveyances to Nesmith T. Manly (the plaintiff), who sought to enjoin the sale to quiet his title. The lower court dismissed Manly's bill.	The plaintiff, Nesmith T. Manly, argued that despite the unregistered deed from Herrick to Seward at the time of the judgment, the undivided half of the lands should not be subject to the judgment lien as there had been no actual notice of a partition. He contended that the partition should protect his right to the property and that he should not be disadvantaged by the non-registration of the deed. He requested that the court quiet his title against Pettee's claim on the property.	The defendant, Daniel L. Pettee, contended that his judgment lien was valid and took precedence over any claims by Manly or his predecessors, as the land in question remained recorded under Herrick's name post-partition. Pettee maintained that he was entitled to collect his judgment from the property that was still recognized as belonging to Herrick by the public records. He asserted that the partition did not provide adequate public notice to protect Manly's title claim due to the failure to register the deed.

In 1850, Abner B. Hall sold a 40-acre tract of land in Menard County, Illinois, to Johanna Pestel for $300, with a $100 down payment and the remainder secured by notes and a mortgage. By 1853, Hall assigned the mortgage to Thomas J. Primm. Following Pestel's death in 1856/57, Primm initiated foreclosure proceedings against her minor children, which led to a court-ordered sale of the property in 1859 to Primm for $212.30. Primm took possession of the property and claimed ownership through this sale. In 1881, Primm filed a bill in equity seeking a new deed for the land, alleging he had lost the original deed. The heirs of Johanna Pestel contested the legitimacy of the foreclosure, claiming they were not properly summoned, and sought to invalidate the proceedings via a cross-bill, which also requested an accounting for the rents they believed Primm had unjustly received since he took possession.	Primm argued that he had legally purchased the land in 1859 under a foreclosure decree, had occupied and maintained the property, and requested the court to issue a new deed because the original deed had been lost. He contended that he held a legitimate interest in the property through the prior court decree and that no substantial challenges had been made against the validity of that decree.	The heirs of Johanna Pestel denied any legal and valid service in the original foreclosure proceedings, thus arguing the sale to Primm was void. They sought to have the foreclosure decree set aside, the mortgage and notes declared invalid, and an accounting for the rents and profits received by Primm since 1860. They maintained that they were entitled to redeem the property based on alleged errors in the original proceedings.

In 1885, Rockford, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Rockford Insurance Company and Michael O’Connor regarding payment for services rendered. The case, denoted as Rockford Ins. Co. v. Michael O’Connor, was filed in the Illinois Appellate Court, where the court was led by Judge Amos Watts. Michael O’Connor, the appellee, claimed he acted as an agent for the Rockford Insurance Company and sought compensation for the services he provided. The lawsuit progressed through the legal system, ultimately eliciting a verdict that would be the subject of the appellate court's review. The court examined the facts and the amount claimed as due to O’Connor, determining whether the previous findings were adequately supported by evidence and aligned with legal standards.	Michael O’Connor, as the plaintiff, asserted that he was entitled to payment for his services as an agent of the Rockford Insurance Company. He argued that he had fulfilled his obligations under their agreement and that the company owed him for the work performed. O’Connor sought recovery of the payment he believed was due, emphasizing the need for the court to uphold his claim based on the factual evidence presented.	The Rockford Insurance Company, as the defendant, contested O’Connor's claims by arguing the validity of the alleged contract and the sufficiency of the services rendered. The defense maintained that there were discrepancies in the facts and sought to have the plaintiff's claims dismissed or reduced, questioning the basis of the compensation due. The defense likely aimed to demonstrate that the amount claimed was either unjustified or unsupported by the evidence presented during the trial.

In 1875, in Knox County, Illinois, Jonas Peterson filed a legal case against Jonas Berger and his wife, Guermina Berger, seeking to foreclose a mortgage on real estate. This mortgage was tied to an agreement executed between Peterson and Berger, where Berger sold a one-fourth interest in a patent related to musical instruments to Peterson for $1,000. The agreement stipulated that if Peterson failed to earn that amount through sales within three years, Berger would repay him upon reconveyance of the patent interest. Before filing the case, Peterson attempted to return the rights to the patent and requested the repayment of the $1,000, but Berger refused the reconveyance and payment. The circuit court found that Peterson was entitled to $1,000 plus interest, totaling $1,185, due to Berger's obligation to repay since Peterson had not made any income from the sales of the patent. Evidence indicated that Berger had impeded the sales, significantly affecting Peterson’s ability to recoup his investment.	The plaintiff, Jonas Peterson, asserted that he had complied with the conditions of the original agreement, as he did not earn the $1,000 from the patent sales due to restrictions placed by Berger. Peterson claimed that he made reasonable efforts to sell the patent rights, which were thwarted by Berger’s refusal to allow sales and his control over the patent, thus requesting the court to enforce repayment of the $1,000 plus interest as agreed upon in the original contract.	Jonas Berger argued that the transaction was a loan rather than a sale, and claimed that Peterson had failed to demonstrate adequate efforts to sell the patent rights. He contended that Peterson's inability to recoup his investment was a result of his own actions or lack thereof. Berger also claimed that he had offered to repay the $1,000 after the three-year period and that Peterson's refusal to reconvey the rights should prevent him from enforcing the contract.

In 1877, the case of The People ex rel. Louis C. Huck v. The Western Seaman’s Friend Society arose in Cook County, Illinois. The case involved a dispute regarding property taxes assessed against two lots owned by the Western Seaman’s Friend Society, which claimed to be an institution of purely public charity. The Society objected to the tax judgment, asserting that its properties were exempt from taxation under the state’s Revenue Act of 1872, which allows exemptions for charitable organizations. The case highlighted the Society's operations, indicating it provided lodging and boarding for sailors and laborers while supporting charitable activities. However, the Society was incorporated in Ohio, and the case questioned whether such a corporation could claim a tax exemption for property located in Illinois. The Illinois Supreme Court needed to determine if the Society's property qualified as tax-exempt and whether the tax assessment was valid under state law.	The plaintiff, represented by Louis C. Huck as the collector of Cook County, argued that the properties owned by the Western Seaman’s Friend Society were rightfully taxed. The plaintiff contended that the properties did not qualify for tax exemption under Illinois law, as the Society is a foreign corporation and its operations do not fit the definition of 'institutions of purely public charity' intended by the Revenue Act.	The defendant, the Western Seaman’s Friend Society, claimed that its properties were exempt from taxation because they were used for charitable purposes. It maintained that it operated as a public charity aimed at benefiting sailors and laborers and argued that it met the criteria of an institution of public charity as defined by the Revenue Act of 1872. The Society asserted that since it was engaged in charitable activities with all income being used to maintain the institution, the tax assessment against its properties should be overturned.

In December 1849, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case involving Furney Condrey, seeking to recover on a promissory note executed by John West for $139.75. The dispute originated from a transaction where Condrey sold a tract of land to West. This sale relied on an agreement with George Ellis B. George, who was to convey title to Condrey. Subsequently, West, with George's assent, took over Condrey's rights, resulting in a reformed agreement that substituted West as the purchaser. When West later claimed that the entire transaction was nullified due to George's purported lack of a clear title, Condrey brought suit to enforce the promissory note. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of West, leading Condrey to appeal the judgment. The central question was the validity of West's defense citing a failed consideration of the note.	The plaintiff, Furney Condrey, argued that he had executed a valid agreement with West and that West had assumed all risks associated with the underlying land deal with George. Condrey contended that the promissory note had sufficient consideration due to the transfer of equitable title, and thus West was obligated to honor the note despite any title issues with the land.	John West's defense rested on claims that the promissory note lacked valid consideration since the land was subject to existing encumbrances, which invalidated any claim he had on the property. West argued that the transfer of rights was ineffectual as it relied on an agreement with George, who had no clear title at the time of the sale. Consequently, he maintained that he should not have to honor the note under these circumstances.

In January 1883, in McLean County, Illinois, William Spillman was bound by recognizance to appear in court regarding an unspecified offense. The recognizance, amounting to $100, required Spillman to be present until the court issued a final order. Spillman was subsequently indicted, pleaded guilty, and received a fine of $50, which led to a temporary suspension of his commitment. In September 1883, the State sought to re-docket the case, leading to a judgment of forfeiture of the recognizance against Spillman's surety, Joseph Schicane. After Schicane failed to appear at a hearing, a default judgment was entered against him. He later filed a motion to set aside this judgment, claiming a lack of notice and asserting he had a meritorious defense. The court initially allowed an amendment to the judgment record, despite Schicane's objections. Schicane argued that the conditions under which he was held liable had been fulfilled by Spillman's previous submissions to the court, thus discharging him from further obligations.	The plaintiffs, representing the State, contended that Joseph Schicane was liable for the forfeiture of the recognizance because he had failed to ensure Spillman's court appearance after Spillman was indicted and sentenced. They argued that the judgment against Schicane should remain valid and that he had not demonstrated adequate diligence in defending against the allegations, which ultimately resulted in the forfeiture of the bond.	Joseph Schicane's primary defense was that he had fulfilled his obligations by ensuring Spillman's presence in court during the initial proceedings, where Spillman had submitted to the court's authority. He highlighted that the conditions of the recognizance became void once Spillman was convicted and fined, which negated any further liability. Schicane asserted he acted diligently, noting difficulties in communication and understanding the legal process due to his background, and contended that the judgment should be set aside as it unjustly penalized him under conditions that had already resolved.

The case "The Chicago Sectional Electric Underground Company v. The Congdon Brake Shoe Manufacturing Company" took place in Illinois, with the court's final judgment dated November 17, 1884. The appellant, the Chicago Sectional Electric Underground Company, was represented by attorneys Lynn Helm and George A. Hawley. The appellee, the Congdon Brake Shoe Manufacturing Company, was represented by attorney H. H. C. Miller. The dispute stemmed from a service of process issue where the appellant claimed that the summons was improperly served. Specifically, the summons was delivered to E. N. Koch, a company director, instead of the company's president, Louis Wahl, who the appellant claimed was present in Cook County at the time. The appellant filed a plea in abatement contending that service on Koch was insufficient since it should have been served on the president. However, the court ruled that service was adequate as per statutory requirements and ordered that the plea be stricken. After subsequent proceedings, the court entered a default judgment against the appellant for damages amounting to $2,018.	The plaintiff, Congdon Brake Shoe Manufacturing Company, argued that the service of process against the defendant was proper and in compliance with Illinois law. They maintained that even though the summons was served on a director instead of the president, it adequately met the statutory requirements for service, as the president's unavailability does not invalidate the service. The plaintiff requested that the court uphold the validity of the service and awarded them damages for non-compliance of the defendant.	The defendant, Chicago Sectional Electric Underground Company, contended that the service was improperly executed and that it was void because it was not served on the president of the company, who they asserted was within the jurisdiction and not absent. They argued that the plea in abatement should not have been stricken from the files as it raised a material issue regarding the sheriff's return and service of process. The defendant sought to have the court dismiss the case based on the alleged improper service and thereby avoid the judgment against them.

The case 'Henry M. Sherwood v. Samuel H. Kerfoot et al.' took place in Illinois and was decided on January 3, 1883. The key individuals involved were Henry M. Sherwood (the appellant) and Samuel H. Kerfoot along with his company (the appellees). Sherwood filed a bill of interpleader seeking to determine whether he or Kerfoot & Co. were entitled to commissions from the sale of a specific property. This case had been previously brought before the court, where a decision was made favoring Kerfoot & Co., but this was later reversed, indicating Sherwood’s right to the commissions. At the retrial, the evidence was examined again, including testimony from Walter Mattocks and a credible witness, Mr. Mason, who confirmed a commission-sharing agreement that favored both parties depending on who found a buyer. Ultimately, it was established that Sherwood independently located a buyer without utilizing any information from Kerfoot & Co., leading to the conclusion that denying Sherwood his earned commissions would violate principles of equity.	The plaintiff, Henry M. Sherwood, claimed he was entitled to the commissions from the sale of the property, asserting that he successfully found a buyer independent of any assistance from Kerfoot & Co. Sherwood argued that there was an agreement in place allowing him to share commissions if he found a buyer, and that he indeed fulfilled that role, thereby entitling him to the full commission amount.	The defendants, Samuel H. Kerfoot and his company, contended that Sherwood was not entitled to the commissions because they believed they had the exclusive right to find a buyer. They asserted that no formal arrangement was made with Sherwood to act as a broker, and therefore they should be granted the commissions for any potential sale.

In April 1867, in Tazewell County, Illinois, the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company was involved in a legal case with Martin Arnold concerning the accidental killing of Arnold’s livestock by the railway's trains. Arnold claimed that the railway's negligence in failing to sufficiently fence its tracks resulted in this incident. The plaintiff's arguments highlighted the need for compensation due to the lost livestock, arguing that the railway company's lack of proper fencing was a contributing factor to the incident. The case was tried in the Circuit Court of Tazewell County, presided over by Judge James Harriott, where a jury found in favor of Arnold, awarding him $441 for the damages caused. Following this, the railway company sought a writ of error to appeal the decision, asserting that the awarded compensation exceeded the proved value of the lost property.	Martin Arnold, the plaintiff, asserted that the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company was liable for the accidental death of his livestock due to the company’s failure to build a proper fence along its railroad. He sought compensatory damages based solely on the value of the animals killed, which amounted to $411. Arnold argued against the railway’s negligence and the necessity of adequate fencing to prevent such incidents.	The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, as the defendant, contended that the plaintiff was also partially responsible for the incident because he allowed his livestock to roam freely on the land where the trains operated. The company argued that the jury’s verdict awarding $441 exceeded the proven value of the livestock destroyed and was therefore unjustified. They requested that the court overturn the verdict based on this argument and the absence of intentional wrongdoing or malice related to the incident.

The case "Cleveland Co-operative Stove Company v. Thomas F. Wheeler" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 21, 1883. The dispute arose in Chicago, where Thomas F. Wheeler, a leather merchant, occupied the lower floor of a store at 203 Lake Street. The Cleveland Co-operative Stove Company operated above him on the entire floor. On November 30, 1882, a water-closet located in the appellant's upper floor overflowed, causing water damage to Wheeler's leather goods below. Wheeler claimed that the incident was a result of negligence on the part of the Cleveland Co-operative Stove Company in managing the water-closet. During the trial, Wheeler testified that the overflow caused damages estimated at $2,076.56. The jury ultimately found the defendant liable for the damage caused by the overflow.	Thomas F. Wheeler, the plaintiff, claimed that the Cleveland Co-operative Stove Company was negligent in its management of the water-closet, which led to significant water damage to his leather goods. He sought financial compensation for the losses incurred due to this negligence.	The Cleveland Co-operative Stove Company, the defendant, argued against the plaintiff's claims by asserting the inadmissibility of certain evidence. They contended that the plaintiff's ownership of the damaged goods was not clearly established and that the lease agreement presented by the plaintiff should not have been admitted as evidence. They maintained that they were not conclusively responsible for the overflow that caused the damage and objected to the handling of evidence related to the statements made by the defendant's porter.

In 1858, in Kane County, Illinois, Horace H. Goodrich sought damages against Crin D. Howell and Leland H. Angelí, co-partners who served as surgeons and physicians, alleging malpractice in the treatment of his son’s fractured arm, sustained when he was four years old. The initial action was taken by Howell & Angelí in August 1859 to recover $25 for their medical services, which Goodrich subsequently paid after protracted legal proceedings. In a later action brought by Goodrich for malpractice, he claimed that their treatment led to further complications. The case eventually reached the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal. The primary legal question was whether the earlier judgment by a justice of the peace, which ruled against Goodrich's malpractice claim, barred this later suit. Evidence presented indicated that Goodrich had indeed raised concerns over malpractice in the earlier case. However, the determination of no malpractice from that case rendered the present action moot, highlighting that claims involving malpractice could not be pursued in successive lawsuits for subsequent damages that might arise.	Goodrich argued that Howell and Angelí committed malpractice while treating his son's fractured arm, which he believed caused unnecessary complications and damages. He sought compensation for these damages, claiming in his lawsuit that the treatment provided was negligent, leading to further and ongoing injury to his son.	Howell & Angelí contended that the previous judgment by the justice of the peace, in which Goodrich was unable to prove malpractice, served as a barrier against his current claims. They maintained that the issues of malpractice had been conclusively determined in the past legal action and that Goodrich could not relitigate these matters. They argued that the nature of malpractice claims does not allow for successive lawsuits, emphasizing that any future damages claimed should have been included in the initial suit.

The case "Adelbert B. Kipp et al. v. Nicholas Massin" originated in September 1884 in Livingston County, Illinois, when the appellants, Adelbert B. Kipp and others, entered into a contract with the appellee, Nicholas Massin, to construct a dwelling house on Massin's farm, approximately six miles east of Minonk. According to the terms, Massin was responsible for performing all necessary excavations and providing construction materials, while Kipp and his associates were tasked with building the house within a specified timeframe. The total contract price was $1,451.17, with the expectation of completion by November 20, 1881. As the project progressed, delays occurred, which Kipp’s team attributed to Massin’s failure to provide timely access and necessary materials. On May 1, 1882, Massin forbade Kipp and his workers from continuing the work, citing unsatisfactory compliance with contract terms. Subsequently, Kipp filed a petition to enforce a mechanic’s lien in court, claiming substantial compliance with the contract and seeking payment for work completed. The case was heard in the Circuit Court, leading to various hearings and a master being appointed to review the evidence and report findings.	The plaintiffs, Kipp and his associates, argued that they had substantially fulfilled their obligations under the construction contract, despite some unfinished work due to being barred from completing the project. They claimed $1,564.53 for materials and labor, asserting that they were entitled to the contract price minus the cost of the remaining work, along with interest from May 1882, when they were prevented from proceeding. They sought to recover the full amount owed under the contract, claiming that any delays were attributable to Massin's actions.	The defendant, Nicholas Massin, contended that he had not breached the contract and that he was not liable for payment because the plaintiffs failed to meet the contract specifications regarding workmanship and materials. He argued that the timeline for completion had not been extended, denying any agreement to cover additional costs incurred due to changes made at his suggestion. Massin maintained that the plaintiffs were at fault for any unsatisfactory performance and sought to offset any potential claims against him with the alleged damages incurred.

William L. Hambleton v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. Levi Young is a legal case adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1867. The appeal arose from the Circuit Court of Pulaski County, where the Honorable John Olney presided. The proceedings were initiated as a quo warranto action, which is a legal challenge regarding the right to hold a public office. The Circuit Court issued a judgment of ouster against Hambleton due to his default in responding to a rule requiring him to plead. Though the defendant was notified of the intent to file this information, he was not formally served with a process that would bring him under the jurisdiction of the court. As a result, the court ruled on the case despite Hambleton being unaware of a pending lawsuit against him, leading to the argument that jurisdiction had not been properly established.	The plaintiff, represented by Levi Young and backed by the People of Illinois, claimed that Hambleton failed to respond to a rule to plead established by the court after leave was granted to file the information. The main argument revolved around the validity of the court's jurisdiction and the procedures followed, emphasizing that Hambleton defaulted without formal notification of a lawsuit against him.	The defendant, William L. Hambleton, contended that the court lacked jurisdiction to enter the rule requiring him to plead and subsequently render judgment against him. He argued that he was never formally served with the necessary legal writ under the seal of the court, nor was he given proper notice of the proceedings. Thus, Hambleton maintained that any judgment pronounced was invalid and should be reversed due to procedural errors.

In the spring of 1858, John Glenn, the appellee, moved into a house bordering two quarters of land located in the south half of section five, township 11, range one, east, in Warren County, Illinois. During his occupancy, he cultivated approximately five acres, with parts on each quarter section. By 1860, he expanded his cultivation to about fifteen acres, with some of it potentially on disputed land. Meanwhile, Jerome Hardisty, the appellant, moved onto the one hundred six acres in question in March 1859, breaking ground and living there ever since. He also extended his fencing to include part of the fifteen acres cultivated by Glenn. The conflict escalated into a legal dispute when Glenn filed a forcible entry and detainer complaint against Hardisty in December 1862, asserting he was unlawfully ejected from the southeast quarter of the section after having occupied it legally for an extended duration. Glenn presented leases from Scroggs & McFarland for the entire half section, claiming rightful ownership. Hardisty introduced a lease from Haydon for the land he occupied. The case, initially tried in a justice court and then appealed to the Circuit Court, focused on the interpretation of possession rights and the legitimacy of the leases presented.	John Glenn claimed that he was the rightful tenant of the south half of section five, having held legal possession for nine months before Hardisty's alleged unlawful entry. He sought to recover possession of the disputed land based on his leases and asserted that Hardisty's entry was forcible, violating the statute. Glenn's primary legal requests included recognizing his possession rights and restoring him to control over the southeast quarter of the section.	Jerome Hardisty contended that Glenn had not established rightful possession of the entirety of the land when he entered. Hardisty argued that his own lease provided him with legitimate claims to the 106 acres and that Glenn's possession was limited to the five acres he initially cultivated. He also claimed that any agreements regarding the division of fences were irrelevant to the matter at hand. Hardisty sought to have the judgment dismissing his claims reversed, asserting that the evidence did not support Glenn’s assertion of possession.

In September 1868, the case of Wheeler v. Kinzie was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The specifics of the case, including the exact nature of the conflict, were not detailed in the provided description. However, the case was noted to share its material features with a preceding case, suggesting similarities in circumstances or legal principles. The proceedings culminated in a decree that was initially upheld but eventually faced reversal by the court, which deemed it necessary to remand the cause for further consideration. The case reflects the legal disputes prevalent in the period, involving key individuals Wheeler and Kinzie, although further details regarding their roles and the core issues of the case are limited.	The plaintiff, Wheeler, argues for a reversal of a prior decree related to their legal issue with Kinzie. The specific claims brought forth by Wheeler are not elaborated upon in the provided information. However, it is indicated that the substantive elements of Wheeler's arguments align closely with those presented in the preceding case referenced in court.	The defendant, Kinzie, counters Wheeler's claims by defending the original decree that had been made earlier in the case. As with the plaintiff's claims, the defenses outlined by Kinzie are not detailed in the summary, yet it is implied that their arguments were insufficient to withstand the reversal mandated by the court, leading to the remand of the case for further evaluation.

The case "The Aultman and Taylor Company et al. v. Joseph T. Weir et al." was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on June 15, 1889. The dispute arose in Randolph County, Illinois, involving appellants The Aultman and Taylor Company and appellees Joseph T. Weir and William Weir. The appellants filed a bill in chancery to set aside alleged fraudulent conveyances and mortgages, claiming that certain lands and personal property should be subject to a debt owed to them by the Weirs. The case included a detailed examination of numerous facts, but the appellants did not provide a comprehensive abstract of the case, leading the court to review an extensive record of over 250 pages. Ultimately, the court found that the evidence did not substantiate the allegations of fraud, determining that the Circuit Court's dismissal of the bill was appropriate.	The plaintiffs, The Aultman and Taylor Company, claimed that Joseph T. Weir and William Weir had engaged in fraudulent conveyances and mortgages to evade a debt obligation. They sought to have certain lands and personal property set aside to satisfy the debt owed to them.	The defendants, Joseph T. Weir and William Weir, contended that the allegations of fraud were not supported by sufficient evidence. They argued that mere suspicion of wrongdoing was inadequate and highlighted the requirement of clear and cogent evidence to prove fraud in a court of law. The defendants requested the dismissal of the plaintiffs' claims.

The case "Toledo, St. Louis and Kansas City Railroad Co. v. Mark Cline" dates back to November 1, 1889, and was adjudicated by the Illinois Appellate Court. The incident occurred in Fayette County, Illinois, where Mark Cline, the plaintiff, was driving across a railroad track owned by the Toledo, St. Louis, and Kansas City Railroad Company when he was struck by a train. At the time of the accident, Cline was approximately 73 years old, familiar with the crossing, and did not expect a train from the east as a westbound train was due to arrive. Witnesses indicated that he looked toward the east and did not see the train while approaching the crossing, which he believed he had time to do safely. It was established that the train’s whistle was not sounded until it was within 150 to 200 yards of the crossing, contravening statutory obligations. The court had to evaluate whether Cline acted with ordinary care and contributed to his own injuries through negligence, alongside the railroad's failure to provide proper warning. The jury determined that Cline was not guilty of contributory negligence that would preclude recovery.	Mark Cline claimed he sustained personal injuries due to the railroad's negligence, specifically citing the failure to ring the bell or sound the whistle as required by statute, which lulled him into a false sense of security as he approached the crossing. He argued that he exercised ordinary care while expecting a train from the west and not from the east. Cline requested damages amounting to $1,295 for his injuries sustained.	The defendant, Toledo, St. Louis, and Kansas City Railroad Co., contended that Cline was guilty of contributory negligence because he should have seen the train approaching from the east, as it was in full view for a distance of a quarter-mile. They argued that Cline's expectations of a train from the west led him to neglect proper vigilance for trains coming from the east, and hence should bear responsibility for the accident. The Railroad's legal request included the dismissal of Cline's claim due to his alleged negligence.

In 1838, in Peoria County, Illinois, Enoch Cross filed an action for trespass de bonis asportatis against Thomas Bryant and John E. Smith. Cross claimed that the defendants, with Bryant as the sheriff and Smith as his deputy, unlawfully took possession of 80,000 feet of lumber valued at $2,000 belonging to him on April 9, 1838. The defendants justified their actions by stating that the lumber was owned by William Pierce and Simeon B. Johnson, who were subject to a writ of attachment related to a debt they owed to third parties. During the trial, both parties presented evidence regarding ownership of the lumber. Cross asserted that he had purchased the lumber two days prior and constituted Pierce as his agent for its handling. However, the court excluded key evidence related to the sale and a deed of assignment provided to establish Cross’s rightful ownership. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court on the basis that the lower court's decisions were erroneous.	Enoch Cross, the plaintiff, claimed ownership of the lumber taken by the defendants and argued that the circuit court improperly excluded evidence relating to the sale of the property as well as the deed of assignment that would prove his ownership. He sought the court's intervention to rectify these errors and to secure a ruling favoring his ownership of the lumber.	Thomas Bryant and John E. Smith, the defendants, contended that they acted within their authority as law enforcement when seizing the property due to a valid attachment concerning debts owed by Pierce and Johnson. They argued that the circuit court correctly excluded the evidence related to Cross’s claims of ownership, maintaining that the proper ownership of the lumber was not with Cross at the time of the taking.

In the case of Margaret Boyland v. William Boyland, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, Margaret Boyland and William Boyland were married in May 1833 and lived together as husband and wife until September 1, 1850, when Margaret allegedly deserted William without justification. William filed for divorce on November 11, 1852, claiming that Margaret had willfully absented herself for two years prior to the filing. The court issued a summons, which was served in a manner that left the summons at the dwelling of an individual named John McCawley rather than at the actual residence of Margaret. The service was deemed insufficient as it did not comply with the statutory requirements for personal service. Consequently, a default judgment was entered after Margaret failed to respond, leading to a decree that dissolved their marriage. However, the manner of service became the focal point of the error assigned and raised questions regarding the court's jurisdiction over the matter.	William Boyland, the plaintiff, argued that the decree dissolving the marriage was invalid due to improper service of notice to Margaret. He contended that the service of process did not meet the statutory requirements, as it was not served at Margaret's usual place of abode and did not provide proper notice to her regarding the lawsuit. William sought to have the decree reversed, asserting that the lack of adequate notice to Margaret rendered the court's jurisdiction over the case void.	Margaret Boyland, through her legal representation, maintained that the service of process was insufficient, which constituted a fundamental flaw that voided the court's jurisdiction. The defense emphasized that the notice was left at John McCawley's dwelling and not at Margaret's home, thereby failing to comply with the legal requirements for proper service. They argued that this defect could not be rectified simply by the decree referencing the service, as such compliance is critical for the court to have jurisdiction over a person in a case.

The case Elisha Ruckman et al. v. Sarah Alwood et al. took place in September 1873 in Illinois. It centers around a dispute involving a deed executed on February 26, 1856, between Andrew J. Alwood, the deceased, and his cousin, Elisha Ruckman. After Alwood's death in October 1856, his heirs sought to have the deed declared a mortgage rather than an outright transfer of property. Alwood was heavily in debt to Ruckman at the time of the deed and had faced significant hardship due to mob violence impacting his agricultural operations. The heirs argued that the deed was intended as security for a loan, while Ruckman claimed it was an absolute conveyance. The case unfolded through various legal proceedings, with the involvement of witnesses and evidence about the intentions behind the deed and the nature of the financial relationship between Ruckman and Alwood. The core of their argument was that the deed had been executed under conditions of duress and misrepresentation, and they sought to prove that it should be treated as a mortgage instead of an outright sale.	The plaintiffs, heirs of Andrew J. Alwood, contended that the deed granted to Elisha Ruckman was intended as a mortgage to secure a debt rather than an absolute transfer of property. They asserted that an indebtedness existed at the time of the deed amounting to approximately $1,400 and argued that Ruckman's claim of absolute ownership after Alwood's death was fraudulent. They sought a court order to declare the deed a mortgage and to allow the heirs to redeem the property upon payment of the alleged debt.	Elisha Ruckman denied the plaintiffs' claims, asserting that the deed was a legitimate, absolute transfer of ownership. He admitted to previously loaning money to Alwood but claimed to have settled all accounts, arguing that the transfer was for valuable consideration. Ruckman denied any understanding that the deed was intended to serve as security for a loan, stating that Alwood remained in possession of the property as a tenant after the deed was executed.

The case of "The Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company v. Mary Fell" originated in LaSalle County, Illinois, in August 1854. In this instance, Mary Fell sued the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company for trespass on personal property, specifically concerning the death of her cow, which was allegedly killed by the company's trains. The summons was served on August 22, 1854, to Rollin G. Parks, an agent of the railroad, as the company's president did not reside in the county. Without the company's knowledge of the suit, the justice of the peace ruled against the railroad on August 28, 1854, awarding Fell $64.16 for her claims and costs. The company sought a writ of certiorari to review the judgment, arguing that the justice lacked jurisdiction and that the summons was improperly served as Parks was not the appropriate agent to handle legal matters for the company.	Mary Fell argued that the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company should be held liable for the trespass caused by their trains, which resulted in the death of her cow. She sought damages for the value of the cow and the subsequent loss of milk. Additionally, she pointed out that the company was notified through an agent about the damages and the lawsuit, which underscored her claim against the company.	The Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company contested the jurisdiction of the justice of the peace, asserting that the summons was served upon an inadequate agent, meaning they were not properly notified of the legal proceedings. They argued that a trespass action related to the death of a cow could not be maintained against them. The railroad maintained that they did not receive adequate notice and thus were unable to defend themselves properly in the underlying suit. They requested the court to reverse the judgment against them and dismiss the case.

The case "Alexander Long et al. v. William P. Long et al." originated from a dispute involving the estate of William Long, who died intestate on July 4, 1877, leaving behind minimal real estate but a substantial amount of personal property. William P. Long, one of the grandchildren of the deceased, was involved in a legal argument over his entitlement to a share of the estate. Subsequently, in August 1877, William B. Long was appointed as the administrator of the estate. A series of hearings commenced, and in a county court, it was determined that William P. Long was entitled to a distribution of $5,240 from the estate. This decision was appealed to the circuit court. Meanwhile, in March 1881, other heirs filed a bill preventing William P. Long from claiming his share and requesting a release of all interests in the estate. This financial dispute was initially decided in favor of William P. Long but progressed to the circuit court of Lee County for further adjudication, where the bill against him was dismissed for lack of equity. The decree was upheld by the Appellate Court for the Second District, escalating to the Illinois Supreme Court for final review.	The plaintiffs, consisting of William P. Long's relatives, contended that a prior land transaction between William Long and his grandson represented an advancement that should exclude William P. Long from participating in the estate distribution. They claimed that this transaction was intended to satisfy his anticipated share in the estate in full, effectively requesting the court to compel William P. Long to execute a release of interests in the estate and seeking a perpetual injunction against him to prevent any claims.	William P. Long, the defendant, argued that the conveyance of the land was not an advancement but rather a legitimate transaction made under a separate arrangement. He rejected the notion that he accepted the land under the condition that it represented his full share of the estate. He insisted that the agreements regarding the land were clear and valid, and contended the plaintiff's claims lacked sufficient documentary and testimonial support to establish a binding contract necessitating a release from his claims on the estate.

In January 1866, the case of Illinois Central Railroad Co. v. Garish was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose involving the Illinois Central Railroad Company and an individual named Garish. The controversy pertained to the amendment of a court record transcript, with the plaintiff, Garish, seeking to modify the official documentation to include specific details that were not present in the original bill of exceptions. An attorney named Hr. O'Melveney represented the plaintiff in this legal matter. The underlying context of the case revolved around judicial procedures concerning the accuracy and integrity of court transcripts and the process by which amendments can be made when discrepancies arise. The court reviewed the submissions and motions made concerning the records presented.	The plaintiff, Garish, argued that the transcript of the record required amendments by removing certain interlined words from the bill of exceptions that were not part of the original documentation. Garish sought the court's permission to amend the record to ensure that the transcript accurately reflected the pertinent facts of the case. The legal request primarily involved the need for a correct and reliable transcript to be presented in the court.	The defendant contended that the court did not possess the authority to amend the transcript of the record, even if original papers were introduced. The argument emphasized the procedural constraints placed upon the court regarding the amendment of transcripts and highlighted that the proper course of action would necessitate a writ of certiorari to obtain a correct record, should discrepancies be apparent.

Joseph Leonard filed a legal action against W. T. Patton regarding a promissory note executed on June 4, 1877, for $7,054.56. This note was supposed to be paid to Leonard six months after its issuance. The case was heard in Illinois, and the trial took place before a jury. The defendant, Patton, presented several defenses, including claims of usury and tender. The jury found in favor of Patton, and Leonard subsequently appealed the judgment to the Appellate Court, which affirmed the original ruling. The core issue revolved around whether the terms of the note constituted usurious lending practices, which both parties presented evidence for during the trial. The court ultimately had to decide on matters such as the admissibility of the general issue withdrawal by Patton, the instructions given to the jury regarding usury, and the validity of any claims of compound interest.	Joseph Leonard claimed the right to recover the full amount of the promissory note from W. T. Patton, arguing that the note did not involve usury despite the defenses presented. He contended that the terms of the agreement were lawful and that any claims to the contrary were unfounded. Leonard requested that the court reverse the previous judgments against him and allow him to recover the amount due on the promissory note.	W. T. Patton's main defenses included the assertion of usury associated with the promissory note, contending that the note's terms involved an illicit charging of interest on interest. Patton emphasized that the plaintiff failed to prove any lawful agreement regarding compound interest and that he was entitled to a verdict based on his special pleas. He requested the court to uphold the previous judgments made by the trial court and the Appellate Court affirming his defenses.

Harry Huntington brought a case against James A. Chambers and others in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the opinion filed on November 21, 1884. The case originated from the Circuit Court of Coles County and was presided over by Judge C. B. Smith. Huntington's claim was based on an assumpsit declaration for goods and merchandise sold to him and his partner, John Fife. The plaintiff argued that they had received and owed for the goods purchased. During the court proceedings, the defendant, Chambers, primarily contended that Huntington was not a partner when the goods were bought. This dispute over partnership status was central, as it would determine Huntington's liability for the debts incurred. The court noted that the necessary defense regarding the partnership must be raised through a proper plea in abatement, which was not presented correctly by Huntington.	Harry Huntington, as the plaintiff, claimed that he and his partner, John Fife, purchased goods from the defendants, seeking a remedy for the debts owed. Huntington's legal arguments relied on the premise that the goods were indeed sold to him as a partner, and thus he should be held accountable for the payments due, as reflected in the assumpsit claim.	James A. Chambers and the other defendants countered Huntington’s claims by arguing that he was not a partner at the time of the purchase of the goods. They maintained that the partnership assertion required a specific plea that was not properly submitted by Huntington, thereby challenging his responsibility for the debt. The defendants also noted that any error by the court in refusing to allow an additional plea from Huntington was not valid since he did not register an exception at that time.

On August 26, 1884, in Madison County, Illinois, Cato Abbott and Henry Bobinson were each seized of an undivided half interest in a tract of land. Bobinson transferred his half interest to Abbott on the same day, with the deed recorded only on May 26, 1886. Abbott maintained possession of the land until it was sold to Christian Kahle for $1,800 on April 24, 1886. However, before this sale, Alkire & Co. had obtained a judgment against Bobinson, leading to a sheriff's sale of Bobinson's interest in the land to Charles N. Travous on August 24, 1885. Kahle later filed a bill in equity seeking to set aside this sale, claiming that Bobinson had no interest in the land at the time of the judgment and that if he did, it was subject to a valid equitable lien from Abbott due to partnership debts. The case involved accusations of a fraudulent alteration of the deed dates, as it was asserted that the deed from Bobinson to Abbott was dated February 26, 1884, but evidence suggested it was altered to appear older. After the Circuit Court ruled in favor of Kahle, the defendants, Alkire & Co. and Travous, appealed the decision.	The plaintiffs, represented by Christian Kahle, argued that Henry Bobinson had no interest in the land during the judgment period due to a prior conveyance to Abbott. They claimed the sheriff's sale should be set aside as it violated equitable rights regarding the transfer of partnership property. Furthermore, the amended bill asserted that any of Bobinson's remaining interest was subordinate to an equitable lien held by Abbott, stemming from financial contributions by Abbott to cover partnership debts.	The defendants countered that the deed from Bobinson to Abbott was falsified, asserting that it had been altered to misrepresent the execution date and that Bobinson's interest was subject to the existing judgment lien. They argued that Kahle was not a bona fide purchaser due to prior knowledge of these issues, and that the sheriff's sale to Travous should be upheld as legal and proper, offering protection under principles of good faith purchasing. They posited that the partnership did not constitute grounds for Kahle's claims and requested the court to dismiss the complaint.

Eleanor Fight v. Thomas Holt is a legal case decided in September 1875 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in LaSalle County, Illinois, involving Eleanor Fight, the widow of a deceased man, and Thomas Holt, who appears to be a grantee of the deceased's heirs. The case pertains to the ownership and partition of real estate seized by Eleanor's late husband. Specifically, the legal issue concerns whether the widow has the right to claim a homestead exemption against the heirs of her deceased husband. The court examined previous rulings, including Eggleston v. Eggleston and Sontag v. Schmisseur, which determined that homestead acts did not grant widows rights over the property against the heirs or their grantees. The court concluded that since the property could not be divided, it could be sold while considering the widow’s right to dower, which would be assigned according to statutory provisions.	Eleanor Fight, as the plaintiff, claimed a right to a homestead exemption from the real estate in question, arguing that her deceased husband’s property should not be partitioned in a way that disregards her rights as a widow. She asserted that the property should remain exempt from the claims of the heirs to protect her interest in it following her husband's death.	Thomas Holt, the defendant, countered that the rights established in previous cases clarify that the widow does not have a homestead claim against the property held by her husband at the time of his death, particularly against the heirs or purchasers from them. Holt argued that as a grantee from the heirs, he was entitled to the same rights as the heirs, emphasizing that the court's past decisions supported this stand.

In the case of Samuel C. Wiley, Impl’d, etc., v. James Stewart, which was decided on June 9, 1887, a legal dispute revolved around a promissory note for $800 signed by the firm of O. J. Wilson & Company, which was composed of Samuel C. Wiley and the Wilson brothers, O. J. Wilson and Wm. Wilson. The events leading to the lawsuit began in Earlville, Illinois, where Wm. Wilson acted as the general manager of the firm and had substantial authority over financial operations. The note, dated August 1, 1884, was executed when Wm. Wilson borrowed $800 from James Stewart, who had a deposit account at the local bank. Wm. Wilson withdrew the sum and loaned it to the firm, entering the transaction into both the bank's and the firm's books. Unfortunately, the bank failed in December 1884, and Wiley learned of the loan and the note only after the assignment of the bank's affairs to an assignee. The partnership of O. J. Wilson & Company was established based on a capital agreement of $1,500, with each member contributing $500, but the operations expanded to include a broader scope of business, including buying and selling agricultural implements.	The plaintiff, James Stewart, claimed that he was owed repayment on the promissory note signed by Wm. Wilson on behalf of the firm, asserting that the note was valid and enforceable against the firm O. J. Wilson & Company. Stewart argued that Wm. Wilson acted within the scope of his authority as general manager and had a mandate to borrow money on behalf of the firm, thus binding the firm to the note. He sought a judgment for the amount due plus interest.	Samuel C. Wiley, as the appellant, contended that Wm. Wilson did not have the authority to execute the promissory note in the firm's name or to borrow the money, as per their partnership agreement. Wiley claimed that the partnership agreement limited his liability to a maximum of $500 and that Wm. Wilson's actions were beyond the authority provided by the partnership. He requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claim on the grounds that he was not liable for the debt incurred without proper authority.

The case 'Joseph W. Helmer v. Edward H. Castle' was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 19, 1884. It originated in Cook County, Illinois, and focused on a dispute regarding property ownership. The key individuals involved were Joseph W. Helmer (the appellant) and Edward H. Castle (the appellee). The case revolved around the location of the north boundary line of premises conveyed by a deed from Philander Hickox to Martha J. Park. The land in question described a specific plot south of Lake Street in the city of Chicago. At the time the relevant deed was executed, the area was not within the city limits, and Lake Street was merely a common highway. The court had to determine whether the premises granted included those in the declaration or if they were owned wholly by the grantee of Martha J. Park, depending on whether the boundary was set at the south line or the center line of Lake Street. During trial, certain stipulations were established, including details of prior conveyance and boundaries of the property,",	The plaintiff, Joseph W. Helmer, argued that the property in question was included in the deed from Philander Hickox to Martha J. Park, asserting that the north boundary should be determined as the south line of Lake Street. He sought a judgment affirming his ownership rights to the land defined in the declaration, which was contested by the defendant's claim to the same area.",	The defendant, Edward H. Castle, contended that the ownership of the disputed property should extend to the center line of Lake Street, thereby arguing that the premises described in Helmer's declaration were not included in the original conveyance to Park. Castle maintained that the legally defined boundary aligned with the center of the street, asserting that the judgment for the plaintiff should be reversed.",

William Willard filed a lawsuit against the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company in the Illinois Appellate Court regarding an incident that occurred on a train in 1889. Willard had purchased a ticket to travel from East St. Louis to Springfield. While on the train, the conductor demanded to see his ticket shortly after departure. Despite searching his pockets, Willard could not find the ticket but assured the conductor that he had indeed purchased one and needed some time to locate it. However, the conductor forcibly removed Willard from the train at the next stop, Venice, in front of approximately fifty other passengers, leading to claims of emotional distress and humiliation. Willard sought damages amounting to $1,500 for what he believed was an unlawful ejection and assault by the railroad's staff.	The plaintiff, William Willard, contended that he was wrongfully ejected from the train despite having purchased a valid ticket. He argued that he should have been given reasonable time to find his ticket after the conductor's demand. Willard claimed that the conductor's actions constituted an unlawful assault and trespass, leading to significant emotional distress and public humiliation.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company defended its actions by stating that Willard failed to produce his ticket promptly and refused to comply with the conductor's request, thus forfeiting his right to remain on the train. The railroad argued that their conductor acted within lawful rights to enforce company rules, including ejecting passengers who could not demonstrate their ticket or pay their fare. The defendant requested the court to reverse the prior judgment in favor of Willard, asserting that the jury's decision did not align with the evidence presented.

In 1875, in Greene County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving William D. Gullett and James J. McClimans (the plaintiffs) against Charles E. Lippincott and several other individuals (the defendants). The plaintiffs, who were tax-payers and trustees of local schools, filed a bill in equity to prevent the Auditor from granting patents for certain school lands to the defendants and sought to annul the sale of these lands made by Caleb Worley, the superintendent of schools. They alleged that the sale was not authorized under the legislative act from January 17, 1835, since the defendants did not reside on the land or make any improvements prior to the Act's enactment. The defendants countered that they had the right to purchase the lands according to the 1835 Act and provided affidavits claiming their occupancy and ownership of improvements on the tracts. The circuit court heard the case and ultimately dismissed the plaintiffs' bill.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants illegally purchased school lands because they had not resided on or improved the lands before the passage of the 1835 Act. They claimed that the sale violated the provisions of that Act and sought to restrain the Auditor from issuing patents to the defendants. The plaintiffs requested the court to annul the sale of the school lands conducted by the superintendent.	The defendants contended that the sale of the lands complied with the 1835 Act, which allowed any person residing on or improving the land to apply for purchase, regardless of when the improvements were made. They argued that their affidavit of occupancy and the purchase of the lands at appraised values were legitimate under the statutory provisions.

The case of R. M. Blackman et al. v. Preston Brothers et al. was decided on October 5, 1887, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in Saline County, where Calvin S. Blackman, one of the plaintiffs, executed deeds on March 17, 1875, transferring his property to his children and wife as voluntary gifts. At the time of these conveyances, he was free from debt and did not intend to incur any liabilities. However, shortly thereafter, he entered into a mercantile business, incurring debts to the defendants, Preston Brothers. Despite having transferred ownership of the farm, Calvin S. continued to live there, pay taxes, and receive benefits as if he were the owner, which misled creditors into believing he owned the property. The deeds remained unrecorded in proper channels until August 6, 1881. The plaintiffs argued that the defendants were misled by Calvin’s ostensible ownership of the property when they extended credit, which should render the conveyances void under the law regarding fraudulent conveyances.	The plaintiffs argued that the conveyances made by Calvin S. Blackman to his family were fraudulent since they were not recorded and allowed Calvin to retain possession of the property. They claimed that this secrecy induced the defendants to extend credit to Calvin under the false impression that he owned the property, which violated the rights of subsequent creditors. The plaintiffs sought a court order to set aside the fraudulent conveyances and have the property subjected to payment of their judgments against Calvin S. Blackman.	The defendants contended that the conveyances were valid and made when Calvin S. was debt-free. They maintained that there was no intent to defraud creditors since the gifts were made to family members without anticipation of incurring debt. They argued that the plaintiffs failed to prove any fraudulent intent or misrepresentation on Calvin's part and requested that the court dismiss the case based on these assertions.

In April 1864, the case of Nathaniel Rising v. William N. Brainard was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Circuit Court of Winnebago County. The central issue involved a judgment entered by confession under a power of attorney for a promissory note, which had matured more than a year prior. The plaintiff, Nathaniel Rising, raised concerns that the judgment was improperly entered in vacation—that is, outside of the regular court sessions—without sufficient proof that the defendant, William N. Brainard, was alive or that the debt was justly due at the time the judgment was made. Rising sought a supersedeas, or legal stay, to challenge this judgment on the grounds that the requirements for such a judgment were not met. The court had previously established that when judgments are entered in vacation after a year and a day, there should be proof of the defendant's life and the validity of the debt to support the judgment. The case, therefore, revolved around procedural issues regarding the proper handling of confessions of judgment and the requisite evidence.	Nathaniel Rising, the plaintiff, argued that the judgment against him was invalid because it was entered in vacation without adequate proof that William N. Brainard was alive and that the debt was due. Rising claimed that despite the authority granted by the power of attorney, the procedural rules requiring proof were not followed, resulting in an improper judgment that needed to be overturned. He sought a supersedeas to halt enforcement of the judgment and requested the court to recognize the flaws in the process leading to the judgment entry.	William N. Brainard, the defendant, contended that the judgment entered by confession was valid due to the sufficient terms of the power of attorney that allowed for such a judgment. He argued that the court does not need to investigate the reasons behind the entry of the judgment if the power of attorney clearly grants authority for it. Brainard maintained that the plaintiff should have first sought redress in the lower court and that any failure to comply with procedural norms did not constitute grounds for equitable relief.

In the case of Richard S. Cole v. Benjamin Shetterly et al., dated September 21, 1883, the legal proceedings took place in Greene County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a mortgage executed on March 13, 1876, by Benjamin Shetterly and his wife Louisa to Richard S. Cole, intended to secure a note for $807.50 due on December 25, 1876, with a 10% interest rate. The mortgage was on property owned by Louisa, justifying its design to secure her indebtedness. A contentious point involved a clerical error in which the mortgage date was mistakenly recorded as 1873 instead of 1876. In 1881, Cole entered satisfaction of a previous mortgage he held against the Shetterlys, thinking it was the same mortgage due to the date error. However, after realizing the mistake in 1882, he notified all interested parties that the mortgage was still valid and not satisfied. The Shetterlys contested the claims, with Benjamin denying the allegations and asserting payment, while Louisa admitted to mortgage execution but claimed it was satisfied and charged that Cole had mishandled funds that rightfully belonged to her. The matter was brought to the court where proof was presented, leading to a decree that dismissed the case, prompting Cole to appeal.	Richard S. Cole argued that the Shetterlys were legally bound to repay the debt secured by the mortgage despite the mistaken satisfaction entry. He sought to foreclose the mortgage, asserting its validity based on the original note and the realization of his clerical error. Cole maintained that the mortgage was indeed executed in 1876 and that the Shetterlys had not adequately established their defenses against his claims.	The defendants, Benjamin and Louisa Shetterly, claimed that the mortgage had been satisfied and asserted that Cole had actually been paid. They argued that Cole had wrongfully applied funds owed to Louisa towards Benjamin's debts, challenging the validity of the mortgage claim. They insisted that the He had made no mistakes and that Cole's claims were baseless without proper evidence of outstanding debt.

Hugh W. Reynolds filed a case against Eli Wilson, the executor of the estate of a deceased individual, in 1854 in Peoria, Illinois. The dispute arose from the sale of two hundred acres of land owned by the deceased, which Wilson, as executor, was ordered by the court to sell in order to pay outstanding debts. The court's order specifically required Wilson to provide six weeks' notice of the sale through advertisement in a newspaper. However, Wilson only provided four weeks' notice, leading to objections from some of the heirs of the estate. After the sale, which Reynolds claimed to have conducted, the heirs filed exceptions, contesting the validity of the sale. The executor and Reynolds both filed motions for confirmation of the sale, but the court ruled to uphold the heirs' objections and denied the motions for confirmation, citing that the executor's noncompliance with the notice requirement rendered the sale invalid.	The plaintiff, Hugh W. Reynolds, argued that the executor's failure to comply with the statutory requirement for a six-week notice did not affect the validity of the sale. Reynolds sought confirmation of the sale, believing that despite the procedural misstep, the sale should be upheld.	The defendant, Eli Wilson (executor), contended that the sale conducted without adhering to the court's order regarding proper notice was invalid. Wilson argued that the executor must strictly follow the court's directives in property sales, which are aimed at ensuring compliance with legal standards and protecting heirs' rights.

T. S. Brockman, the appellant, entered into a partnership agreement with William Aulger, a wool carder, and Sidney Parker, who is mentioned but not detailed. The partnership involved Brockman providing a carding machine and covering operational expenses, while Aulger would operate the machine and manage sales, dividing carding revenues two-thirds to Brockman and one-third to Aulger. The partnership disputes arose over payments due to Brockman, amounting to $427.83, for his share of the carding revenues and a further $124.20 for additional goods sold. Despite multiple requests, Aulger failed to provide a complete accounting and only paid a partial sum of $606.43. After filing a bill for an accounting of the partnership transactions, a master was appointed, but his report did not properly account for all partnership transactions, leading to an inaccurate determination of debts owed. The case was subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the issues regarding the completeness of the accounting became central to the judgment.	The plaintiff, T. S. Brockman, argued that he was owed significant payments from his partnership with Aulger, including two-thirds of the earnings from the carding machine, totaling $1,494.72, and $40.66 from the sale of lard. Brockman's claims of $427.83 and $124.20 were based on the defendant's failure to provide an accurate account of their partnership transactions and refusal to pay the amounts due.	The defense from William Aulger contended that the master’s report indicated Brockman was in fact in debt to him, citing an amount owed of $269.00 after accounting. The defense focused on asserting that the accounting process conducted by the master was sufficient, and they disputed Brockman’s claims regarding the partnership revenues and expenses.

The case, "Charles F. Chickering et al. v. Julius Bastress et al.," arose in Cook County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs, Chickering & Sons, a piano manufacturing company based in New York, sought to reclaim possession of 17 pianos, valued at $6,000. The action took place in the Superior Court of Cook County on February 7, 1883, after Chickering & Sons entered into a contentious agreement with the Chicago-based firm Pelton, Pomeroy & Cross. Prior to the contested agreement, Pelton, Pomeroy & Cross had been experiencing financial difficulties and had borrowed significant sums from Bastress, who was unaware of the agreement's implications. The case centers around the nature of a contract executed on October 14, 1882, which was ostensibly for the consignment of pianos but was argued to be a disguised sale that aimed to preserve a lien on the goods for the plaintiffs. This contract was kept secret from Bastress, who later levied execution against Pelton, Pomeroy & Cross for debts incurred. The circuit court ruled initially in favor of the plaintiffs, but upon appeal, the Appellate Court reversed the decision, leading to a further judgment in favor of the defendants.	The plaintiffs, Chickering & Sons, claimed that the agreement with Pelton, Pomeroy & Cross was one of consignment that preserved their ownership of the pianos and enabled them to reclaim the goods upon demand. They asserted that the pianos were still their property and that the secretive nature of the agreement should invalidate any claims made by Bastress, who held an execution against Pelton, Pomeroy & Cross for a debt of $10,252.	The defendants, including Bastress and the sheriff, argued that the contract was not valid, asserting that it effectively covered a sale rather than a consignment. They maintained that the agreement was a fraudulent attempt to mislead creditors about the true ownership of the pianos. The defendants contended that Bastress, as an execution creditor, had priority over any secret lien held by Chickering & Sons, and thus the pianos could be seized to satisfy Pelton, Pomeroy & Cross's debts.

In the case "George E. Loar et al. v. Charles Heinz et al.", which took place in Morgan County, Illinois, the events unfolded over a period leading up to May 25, 1888, when the final judgment was made. The plaintiffs, including George E. Loar, brought an action against two county commissioners, Charles Heinz and another, claiming negligence regarding the repair of a bridge. The plaintiffs alleged that the commissioners allowed the use of unsuitable and defective timber, resulting in the bridge collapsing while they were driving five steers across it, causing injury to the animals. The bridge repairs were overseen by a contractor named Fletcher, considered experienced in bridge building. His assessment led to the use of pine timbers deemed sufficient for the bridge repairs, despite the availability of stronger oak alternatives. After the repairs, the bridge had been in service for about a year without prior complaints, until the incident occurred. During the trial, it was revealed that there was no evidence to suggest that the defendants acted willfully or in knowledge of using bad materials, and it was argued that what constituted suitable lumber was a matter of opinion and not clearly defined negligence.	The plaintiffs claimed that the county commissioners were negligent for permitting the use of defective timber in the bridge repair, which ultimately led to the collapse of the bridge and the injury of their cattle. They sought compensation for the damages incurred due to the incident, arguing that the commissioners failed to exercise reasonable care in the material selection and repair oversight.
