The defendants, commissioners Heinz and Kennedy, argued that the decision to use the specified timber was based on the recommendations of a qualified contractor, Fletcher, and that they had acted in good faith without malicious intent. They contended that the appropriate materials were a matter of expert opinion and demonstrated that the bridge had been used without incident prior to the accident. They also maintained that if they were liable, it would only involve a mistake in judgment rather than negligence.

In September 1876, in Lake County, Illinois, James H. Allen was indicted for assaulting a 17-year-old boy, Charles Davidson, with a pistol. The incident occurred when Allen was chasing Davidson's sheep off his property and Davidson retaliated by shooting Allen's dog. This led to a confrontation where Allen took the pistol from Davidson and struck him multiple times. The indictment against Allen was based on a statute which penalized individuals who committed assault with a deadly weapon without considerable provocation. The case involved legal arguments focused on the sufficiency of the indictment and whether Allen's actions could be justified as self-defense or justified by provocation from Davidson's actions.	The prosecution's main argument was that Allen unlawfully assaulted Davidson with a deadly weapon, specifically a pistol, intending to inflict harm without any substantial provocation. They contended that Allen's actions were not legally defensible, as he did not exercise reasonable self-defense in response to Davidson's initial act of shooting the dog.	Allen's defense claimed that the indictment was insufficient as it did not specify that the pistol was loaded or provide evidence that it was indeed a deadly weapon in the context of the conflict. Additionally, his defense argued that the jury's verdict was against the weight of the evidence, asserting that the encounter involved provocation from Davidson, given he shot the dog first, thus justifying Allen's response.

In 1882, in Cook County, Illinois, defendants Samuel I. Pope and Charles H. Batten employed Samuel E. Bullock as a general agent in their business of installing heating systems. Bullock was tasked with managing contracts, particularly one with the county for the installation of a steam heating apparatus. As part of his role, Bullock was involved in obtaining funds in advance of payments due from the county for this contract. The arrangement allowed Bullock to draw orders on the county for anticipated payments, which he subsequently negotiated. On December 30, 1882, Bullock borrowed money from plaintiff Elias Lowitz by producing a promissory note in the defendants' name, claiming he was authorized to act on their behalf, which the defendants denied. The case centers on whether Bullock had the authority to bind his employers to this financial action.	The plaintiff, Elias Lowitz, claimed that he loaned $1,475 to Bullock, who misrepresented himself as authorized to act on behalf of the defendants. He requested payment based on the promissory note Bullock executed, asserting that the defendants were bound by Bullock's actions as their agent, and he sought a judgment for the amount loaned plus costs.	The defendants contended that Bullock acted outside the scope of his authority in negotiating the loan and executing the note. They argued that they were not aware of any loan arrangements made by Bullock nor had they authorized him to borrow money on their behalf, which meant they should not be held liable for the amount claimed by the plaintiff.

On March 28, 1841, in Morgan County, Illinois, Murray McConnell (the appellant) entered into a financial agreement with William Hodson and others (the appellees), wherein Hodson executed three promissory notes totaling approximately $906, secured by a mortgage on real estate. These notes carried an interest rate of 12%. The case arose from complications surrounding additional promissory notes originally issued by Henry Saunderson that were secured against different real estate and pertained to the estate of Thomas Swain. The appellants sought to collect on these notes through foreclosure, believing that Hodson had transferred them to him as collateral for a debt. However, Hodson claimed he held these notes as a guardian for the minor heirs of Swain’s estate and argued that McConnell was aware of this at the time of the transfer. Following various legal proceedings and claims regarding ownership and authority over the notes, McConnell asserted his right to the payments while Hodson maintained that the transfer was void due to its nature as a misapplication of trust property. The case culminated in a decision that saw the Circuit Court's decree against McConnell.	Murray McConnell claimed that he was rightfully entitled to collect the money associated with the promissory notes transferred to him by William Hodson as collateral security for a debt owed to him. McConnell argued that he acted in good faith and without knowledge of any fiduciary obligations that Hodson might have had concerning the notes. He sought a court decree for payment on the notes, and, failing that, requested the foreclosure of the mortgage linked to the property.	William Hodson contended that he was acting in his capacity as guardian of the minor heirs of Thomas Swain when the notes were transferred to McConnell. He argued that the transfer to McConnell was illegal and void, asserting that McConnell was aware of this situation but failed to conduct due diligence regarding the ownership of the notes. Hodson sought an injunction against McConnell to prevent him from collecting on the notes, which he maintained belonged to the heirs of Swain.

In April 1859, the case of Joel H. Dix et al. v. The Mercantile Insurance Company was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiffs, consisting of Joel H. Dix, Horatio G. Sinclair, and George J. Harris, had taken out an insurance policy with the Mercantile Insurance Company in Chicago, covering their stock of groceries worth $2,000. The policy stipulated that the insurance would become void if there was any transfer or change of title in the insured property without the company’s consent. On February 12, 1857, Sinclair sold his interest in the groceries to Dix and Harris, effectively transferring ownership before a fire destroyed the stock on March 2, 1857. The plaintiffs filed a suit seeking compensation for their loss. However, the defendants claimed that since Sinclair no longer had an interest in the property at the time of the loss and because the policy was void due to the unauthorized transfer of interest, they were not liable for the damages.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to recover damages based on the insurance policy made on September 27, 1856, which covered their stock of groceries. They contended that they had complied with all terms stipulated in the policy and that the defendants had refused to pay the insurance claims following the fire. The plaintiffs sought compensation for the total amount insured under two policies, claiming a total loss of $5,000 from the fire damage.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs were not entitled to recover because at the time of the loss, Sinclair had already sold his interest in the goods to Dix and Harris, thus voiding the policy. They argued that the suit cannot be maintained since one of the plaintiffs had no legal interest in the insured property when the claim was made. The defense asserted that the policy specifically stated that any transfer or change of title without consent would void the insurance.

Dickenson B. Morehouse appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1857 after a verdict was reached in favor of William A. Phelps in a previous court regarding property disputes in Galena, Illinois. The case dates back to November 29, 1851, when Phelps sought to recover possession of half of two lots on Water Street. Morehouse, as the administrator of the estate of Robert P. Guyard, claimed an interest in the same lots. Phelps contended that he was the rightful legal representative of Guyard, given a previously attested purchase of the lots from Guyard. The legal proceedings involved various testimonies and documentation, including preemption certificates, claiming that Morehouse was not the rightful representative per the legislative definition of a 'legal representative' in the context of land grants. The case was previously argued under a different title as Phelps v. Smith. The court examined the term "legal representative," ultimately leading to a consideration of proper rights and ownership of the disputed lots.	The plaintiff, William A. Phelps, claimed that he was the legal representative of Robert P. Guyard, who had granted him rights to the disputed lots. He presented evidence including certificates from land commissioners affirming his legal right to the preemption of the lots in question, arguing that Morehouse, as the administrator, could not claim the rights to the property without valid proof of being the legal successor to Guyard’s interests.	The defendant, Dickenson B. Morehouse, contended that as the legal administrator of Robert P. Guyard's estate, he had the right to act on behalf of Guyard's interests in the disputed lots. He argued that he had previously established legitimate claims through the required legal processes, including obtaining preemption rights and entering records that were later accepted by the commission. Morehouse maintained that the intent and actions taken by him were fully consistent with legal expectations, arguing against Phelps's claims to sole representation.

The case of Hampton L. Story et al. v. Thomas Carter was decided on September 18, 1888, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose from a sale of lumber conducted by the appellee, Thomas Carter, to the appellants, Hampton L. Story and others. The lumber sale was initiated through a written order, and thereafter, a conversation occurred where the terms of inspection were discussed. A jury trial was held in the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Richard W. Clifford, resulting in a verdict against the appellants for $503.40 for the lumber. The case was appealed by Story, who argued that the trial court erred in allowing specific testimony related to the sale and in refusing certain jury instructions about the ownership of the lumber involved in the transaction.	The plaintiffs, Hampton L. Story and others, claimed that they were entitled to recover damages due to non-payment for the lumber sold to them by the defendant, Thomas Carter. They presented a written order as evidence of the sale, arguing that an agreement was formed and the conversation about inspection further clarified the terms of the transaction.	The defendant, Thomas Carter, defended himself by asserting that the conversation regarding the inspection was irrelevant to the written order and that additional evidence of ownership was unnecessary since a witness confirmed that the sale was made on behalf of the plaintiffs. He contended that the jury's verdict was based on sufficient evidence regarding the quality and value of the lumber and requested that the court uphold the jury’s decision without interference.

On October 6, 1886, in Illinois, Stephen L. Mershon and George Bancroft filed a suit against E. M. Hulse claiming unpaid debts. Mershon and Bancroft were judgment creditors seeking to recover $2,704.40 from Hulse after prior judgments returned unsatisfied. Hulse had been insolvent since September 9, 1886, when he engaged attorneys to prefer certain creditors through the use of judgment notes. These notes included generous attorney’s fees, totaling $1,258, which Hulse instructed his attorneys to prepare for the selected creditors. Even though the attorneys secured judgments based on these notes, the asset liquidation from Hulse's estate left no surplus to satisfy Mershon and Bancroft's claims. The case hinged on whether Hulse's inclusion of attorney fees constituted valid claims or fraudulent preferences. The trial court ultimately dismissed the plaintiffs' case for lack of equity.	The plaintiffs, Mershon and Bancroft, argued that Hulse's issuance of judgment notes containing additional attorney fees was an unlawful preferential treatment of certain creditors over others without equitable cause. They contended that the attorney fees should be considered gratuitous and hence fraudulent. They requested the court to rectify this by compelling a redress of Hulse's assets to satisfy their judgments.	The defendant, Hulse, contended that the actions taken were legitimate preferences allowable under insolvency laws. His attorneys argued that the issuance of the judgment notes was permissible, as the creditors’ acceptance of these notes was mutually agreed upon. They requested the court to uphold the validity of the attorney fees included in the judgment notes, asserting they were a lawful part of the agreement made with the creditors.

The case of *James Abrams v. Benjamin E. Taylor* was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1859. The dispute originated from a receipt dated March 20, 1852, indicating that Benjamin E. Taylor received 1,071 bushels of corn from James Abrams at a fixed price. Abrams initiated legal action for debt based on this receipt, claiming Taylor owed him money. Taylor defended himself by filing a plea that argued the claims were time-barred, as they did not occur within the five-year statute of limitations for such actions. Additionally, he countered Abrams' claims by asserting "nil debet," indicating he did not owe the alleged debt. The case was tried in 1858 without a jury, and substantial evidence was presented, including the receipt and a promissory note from Abrams to Taylor. Despite the evidence, the court initially found in favor of Abrams, leading to an appeal by Taylor.	James Abrams, the plaintiff, argued that the receipt he issued to Benjamin E. Taylor constituted a valid acknowledgment of debt for the corn provided. He claimed that there was an amount owed based on this receipt, along with associated damages, thereby seeking a judgment for the sum of $233.43 and additional damages.	Benjamin E. Taylor, the defendant, contended that the claims from Abrams were invalid because they had not accrued within the statutory period of five years. He also claimed "nil debet," asserting he did not owe any debt in connection with the receipt provided by Abrams. Taylor argued that the receipt itself did not conclusively prove indebtedness and requested the court to rule in his favor.

In 1868, the case of Louisa Plaster v. Jeptha Plaster was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The origins of the case date back to November 1854 when a divorce was granted to Louisa Plaster, the plaintiff, due to the desertion by Jeptha Plaster, the defendant. At that time, they had a three-year-old child whose custody was awarded to Louisa. As part of the divorce proceedings, Jeptha was deemed responsible for providing alimony, which amounted to one-fourth of his assets, totaling $1,000. However, in March 1866, Louisa sought to revisit the case, filing a petition for additional pay for the child’s support and education since the divorce. Subsequent legal proceedings included motions and a demurrer, which led to the case being effectively dismissed. This dismissal prompted Louisa to bring the case before the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing for the need for continued financial support from Jeptha for their child's upbringing.	Louisa Plaster claimed that Jeptha Plaster had a continued legal and natural obligation to support their child despite the custody being awarded to her. She argued for compensation for past support and future education expenses for the child, asserting that his neglect due to abandoning his family did not absolve him of his financial responsibilities toward their child.	Jeptha Plaster contended that the court’s prior decree awarding custody to Louisa effectively relieved him of any further obligation to support the child. He maintained that since Louisa was granted custody, she was responsible for the child's support, arguing that his lack of involvement should not impose financial penalties on him.

In the case of Lansing S. Wells v. Paris Mason et al., administrators, the events took place in Alton, Illinois, with significant proceedings occurring around 1834 to 1841. Lansing S. Wells entered into a lease agreement for a tract of land that included a distillery and buildings for a period of two years and six months, with rent payments structured to total $900. The plaintiffs, as administrators of the deceased intestate, argued that Wells breached the lease by failing to make timely rent payments. Wells contended that he was wrongfully ejected from the property by an individual named David Thorp, who claimed a superior title to the land. After multiple legal arguments and pleas presented by both sides, the case transitioned to the Madison circuit court in April 1841. A jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, rendering a verdict that included damages of $920.35. The case was complex, involving disputes over legal jurisdiction and questions of the plaintiffs' standing to claim the rent.	The plaintiffs claimed that Lansing S. Wells breached the lease agreement by failing to make several scheduled rent payments. They sought recovery of the amounts due and damages resulting from his breach, ultimately totaling $920.35. They argued that despite the defendant's claims, there was a clear obligation under the lease, and appropriate legal steps were taken to address the nonpayment.	Wells raised several defenses, including claims of prior eviction based on actions taken by David Thorp, who allegedly had superior title to the property. He argued that he was wrongfully ejected from the premises, which should legally nullify his obligation to pay rent. Additionally, Wells challenged the plaintiffs' legal standing to sue, suggesting that they did not adequately demonstrate the intestate's title at the time of the lease.

Michael Kelley, a coal miner employed in David Wilson's mine, sustained serious injuries when a heavy piece of rock fell from the roof as he was passing through an entry to reach his work area. The incident occurred in Vermilion County, Illinois, and Kelley's injury resulted from a known unsafe condition of the mine's roof, which had not been adequately supported despite prior knowledge of the danger. The pit boss, Henry, had noticed the hazardous condition earlier that day and failed to either remove the loose rock or warn other workers. The jury determined that Wilson was negligent in not providing a safer working environment and that Kelley had exercised due care by not noticing the specific danger of the loose rock.	The plaintiff, Michael Kelley, claimed that his injury resulted from the defendant's negligence in maintaining a safe workplace. He argued that the defendant was aware of the dangerous condition of the roof but failed to take appropriate measures to secure it or provide warnings. Kelley sought damages for his injuries, successfully obtaining a jury verdict in his favor amounting to $1,500.	David Wilson, the defendant, contended that he was not liable for Kelley's injuries. He argued that Kelley was aware of the general risks associated with working in the mine, which absolved him of responsibility. Wilson claimed that the evidence did not warrant a finding of negligence on his part, and he also challenged the jury instructions given during the trial, stating that they were improper and misleading regarding the standard of care expected of both parties.

John H. Cox initiated a legal action against William H. Reed and others in an Illinois court, following a complex chain of property transactions dating back to September 1, 1838, involving a lot in Mansfield, Ohio. The original deed with covenants of warranty was made by Joseph H. Reed to S. and J. Abernathy, but a subsequent judgment by the Farmers’ Bank of Mansfield resulted in a sheriff's sale of the lot in 1850 to James Weldon. Cox purchased the lot from Weldon in December 1850 and conveyed it to Harriet Pugh in February 1851, also with covenants of warranty. In 1855, the Lewis heirs, holding paramount title, successfully evicted Pugh, prompting Cox to face potential liability on his covenants. He ultimately settled Pugh's claims by paying over $1,100 and later sought damages from Reed's heirs for breach of warranty, leading to the trial that took place in 1859, with the court later granting a new trial due to arguments regarding the minors involved.	Cox's primary argument was that he suffered damages due to the breach of the warranty covenants by J. H. Reed's heirs. He asserted his right to recover these damages, given that he had already incurred substantial payments to Harriet Pugh and the Lewis heirs. His legal request was for the court to hold the defendants accountable and to award damages that reflected the financial loss he sustained due to the breach.	The defendants contested the authenticity of the deed executed by J. H. Reed, raising a plea of "non est factum," and also cited the statute of limitations in response to Cox's claims. They argued that since some co-defendants were minors not properly served or in court, this should affect the proceedings. The defense requested a ruling that would favor the assertion of their pleas and prevent Cox from obtaining a judgment against them.

In 1885, the case of The Covenant Mutual Benefit Association of Illinois v. Edward J. Sears et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose after the death of Edward J. Sears, who was a member of the Covenant Mutual Benefit Association. Following his untimely passing, his heirs, consisting of his father, mother, and two sisters, initiated a bill in chancery to recover $5,000 in benefits promised by the association as per a certificate of membership that Sears held. The association’s charter and by-laws stipulated that it aimed to provide financial aid to the widows, orphans, heirs, or devisees of deceased members. At the time of his death, Sears had complied with all membership conditions, including the payment of necessary fees. However, the primary contention arose because he died intestate, leaving no will, which led the association to deny the heirs' right to claim the benefit, stating that the benefits were meant for his devisees should he have left any, and only to heirs in their absence. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the complainants (the heirs), a decision that was affirmed by the Appellate Court, prompting the association to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to the $5,000 benefit stipulated in the membership certificate upon Sears' death. They argued that the deceased had fulfilled all conditions of the certificate and that the contract effectively provided for the payment of benefits to either devisees or heirs. They sought a decree affirming their right to the benefit money as legal heirs of Edward J. Sears.	The defendant, the Covenant Mutual Benefit Association, contended that the heirs had no rightful claim to the benefits since the certificate specifically mentioned payments to devisees, implying that the absence of such would disqualify heirs from receiving the funds. They further argued that the case should be dismissed on the basis that there were adequate legal remedies available, and they questioned the jurisdiction of the court, maintaining that the plaintiffs should have pursued their claims in a court of law, not equity.

On May 14, 1887, in Galesburg, Illinois, Mollie Bowes, the appellant, was involved in an altercation while operating a boarding house adjacent to another operator, Alice Sharp. This incident led to a complaint against Bowes under Sec. 21, Chap. 37 of the city's Revised Ordinances, for disturbing the public peace through disorderly conduct and assaulting individuals, including Mrs. Birdson and Sharp. Bowes was initially convicted by a justice of the peace and fined $3. She appealed to the Circuit Court of Knox County, where a jury trial resulted in a $50 fine against her. Bowes asserted that the jury's verdict was against the evidence's weight and alleged improper statements made by the city attorney during the trial that biased the jury against her. The evidence presented was conflicting, with testimonies from both sides, and the jury ultimately found sufficient grounds for Bowes's conviction.	Mollie Bowes, as the appellant, claimed that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence presented during the trial. She also argued that the city attorney made improper comments that were not substantiated by evidence, which adversely influenced the jury's judgment against her. Furthermore, she contended that the trial court excluded proper evidence from the jury's consideration.	The City of Galesburg, represented by the city attorney, maintained that the evidence supported the jury's decision, indicating that Bowes's conduct on the date in question was indeed disorderly and constituted a breach of peace. The defense argued that the comments made during the trial did not significantly affect the jury's decision as they reflected on the conduct of both parties involved in the conflict. They sought to uphold the jury's verdict by asserting that the overwhelming evidence warranted the decision rendered by the jury.

The case "Benjamin Huddle v. Robert Martin et al." was heard in June 1870 in Marion County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Robert Martin and Thompson Martin, doing business as Martin & Brother, sought to recover an alleged balance due from the defendant, Benjamin Huddle, for materials supplied to him to construct a fence around the courthouse square, pursuant to a contract Huddle had with the county. Initially, a justice of the peace ruled in favor of Huddle. However, upon appeal to the circuit court, the plaintiffs secured a judgment of $249.83 against Huddle. Huddle contested this decision, claiming errors during the trial, including being denied the right to open and conclude his case and that the jury received improper instructions regarding the impeachment of witness testimony. The case revolved around whether Huddle had indeed paid for the materials before the lawsuit commenced, which was an important point of contention.	The plaintiffs claimed that Huddle owed them $249.83 for materials supplied for the fence project. They argued that they had a valid contract and presented evidence of the alleged debt during the trial. They requested the court to uphold the judgment obtained in the circuit court, asserting that Huddle failed to provide clear proof of having paid the debt prior to the initiation of the lawsuit.	Huddle's primary defense was that he had paid the account in full before the suit was filed. He argued that he should have had the right to open and conclude his case before the jury, contending that the court's refusal to grant this right constituted an error. He also objected to the jury instructions that suggested a witness's testimony could be disregarded if successfully impeached, arguing that such a standard was erroneous without considering corroborating evidence.

In the case of Newton S. Gay v. Henry DeWerff, the events unfolded on June 3, 1882, in Madison County, Illinois. The case concerns a trespass and false imprisonment claim brought by Henry DeWerff against Newton S. Gay and two other defendants. DeWerff was accused of allowing his children (under the age of ten) to trespass on Gay's land, where there was growing wheat, after being explicitly forbidden. In response, Gay made an affidavit claiming DeWerff was guilty of advising and encouraging this trespass. A warrant was subsequently issued by a justice of the peace, leading to DeWerff's arrest. During the trial, Gay attempted to justify the actions by presenting the affidavit and warrant, arguing his actions were legally permissible under state statutes. However, the jury ruled in favor of DeWerff, awarding him damages. Gay's motion for a new trial was denied, prompting an appeal.	Henry DeWerff, the plaintiff, claimed that Newton S. Gay and the co-defendants had unlawfully trespassed on him and falsely imprisoned him. He argued that the actions of the defendants were without proper legal basis and sought damages for the distress caused by the arrest and subsequent detention, believing that Gay had acted maliciously and without proper justification.	Newton S. Gay, the defendant, contended that his actions were justified pursuant to a lawful affidavit which led to the warrant for DeWerff's arrest. Gay maintained that the justice had jurisdiction in the matter, and he sought to present the evidence of this justification during the trial. He claimed that the arrest was valid under the law, and thus, he could not be liable for trespass or false imprisonment. Gay's primary argument centered on the legality of the initial complaint, the issuance of the warrant, and the subsequent conviction of DeWerff.

Michael Keating and others brought a legal case against Charles H. Stebbins in 1887 in the Illinois Appellate Court. The suit arose from an open account for ice that Stebbins sold and delivered under a written contract to the plaintiffs. The trial was conducted without a jury, with the court governing the proceedings. The court found in favor of the plaintiff, Keating, and assessed damages at $589.74. The judgment was appealed, but the appeal focused on whether the evidence supported the court's finding without claiming specific legal errors. The court reviewed the evidence in the record and saw no reason to challenge the trial court's conclusions, as the evidence was presumed sufficient given that not all evidence was included in the bill of exceptions.	The plaintiffs, led by Michael Keating, claimed that they were entitled to recover damages based on an open account for ice sold and delivered by the plaintiff. They argued that the written contract between them and the defendant supported their claim, and they sought compensation for the amount due, assessed at $589.74.	The defendant, Charles H. Stebbins, did not put forth specific legal errors in his appeal. Instead, he maintained that the evidence presented at trial was insufficient to disturb the finding of the court below. His defense focused on the presumption that the trial court’s ruling was based on adequate evidence, given that not all evidence had been included in the bill of exceptions.

The legal case "The Union National Bank of Chicago v. Augustus Byram" originated in Cook County, Illinois, with the initial filing occurring on October 18, 1888. The Union National Bank, as the appellant, brought a suit against Nathan Corwith and Nathan Corwith Jr. involving an attachment of property, specifically ninety-one shares of stock in the Chicago Dock Company. After the sheriff delivered an attachment writ to the company’s secretary, Byram filed an interpleader arguing that the stock was not subject to attachment and sought to vacate the levy. The Union National Bank contested this assertion. The case attempted to address whether shares of stock in an incorporated company could be subjected to attachment as per Illinois law. After proceedings in the Superior Court and later the Appellate Court, the levy on the stock was quashed, awarding judgment to Byram for costs. The case ultimately made its way to the Illinois Supreme Court for further examination of the statutory interpretations regarding attachments and the nature of corporate stock.	The Union National Bank claimed that the shares of stock in the Chicago Dock Company were subject to attachment under Illinois law. The bank argued that the relevant statutes, which permitted attachment, included provisions for shares of stock, thus allowing the levying of attachments on such interests. The bank sought to uphold the attachment made by the sheriff and requested the reversal of the lower courts' judgments quashing the levy.	Augustus Byram contended that the stock in question was not liable to attachment under Illinois law. He filed an interpleader asserting ownership of the stock and argued that the Illinois statutes did not provide for the attachment of corporate stock. His motions to set aside the levy highlighted that the methods outlined for attaching physical property did not apply to shares of stock, thus seeking a judgment in his favor against the Union National Bank for costs.

Joseph Bohmann filed a lawsuit against the City of Chicago in 1884, following an alleged injury to his property pertaining to the elevation of Lincoln Avenue, which bordered his premises. The lawsuit was attempted to be resolved in the Illinois Appellate Court, where the case was heard in front of a jury. After Bohmann presented his evidence in support of his claims, the defendant's counsel sought to dismiss Bohmann's evidence and discharge the jury. The court granted the motion, despite Bohmann's objections and a request to introduce further testimony. Subsequently, the court found in favor of the defendant and issued a final judgment without Bohmann's consent. Bohmann contested this judgment, asserting that he was denied his constitutional right to a fair trial by jury, which could only be waived with mutual consent from both parties.	The plaintiff, Joseph Bohmann, claimed damages due to an injury to his premises caused by the City of Chicago raising the grade of Lincoln Avenue. Bohmann argued that the court's dismissal of his evidence and the discharge of the jury were improper actions, violating his constitutional right to a jury trial. He sought a reversal of the judgment rendered against him and the opportunity to continue his case, insisting that the proceedings should allow for his evidence to be fully considered.	The City of Chicago's defense hinged on the motion to exclude Bohmann’s evidence, asserting that the grounds for the claim were insufficient for a trial. The defense maintained that the court had acted appropriately by discharging the jury and granting the motion to exclude the plaintiff's evidence. The objective was to uphold the judgment rendered in favor of the defendant, asserting that the procedures followed aligned with legal standards.

Andrew Burton and others (plaintiffs) brought a legal action against Stephen Goodspeed and his associates (defendants) in Cook County, Illinois, in June 1872. The case, heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, arose from a contractual agreement involving the sale of 300 tons of hard coal, with a price set at $7.50 per ton. The plaintiffs allege that the defendants, represented by their authorized agent Benjamin Holbrook, failed to deliver the ordered coal. A contract was established where the plaintiffs would pay half in cash upfront, with the remaining balance paid as the coal was delivered. The contract stipulated various conditions, including that no additional storage charges would be assessed until May 1, 1873. On November 25, 1872, the plaintiffs made a special request for delivery, but the coal was not provided as agreed, leading them to seek compensation for the undelivered goods. The defendants contended that Holbrook’s authority to execute contracts on their behalf was limited according to a prior agreement they had with him.	The plaintiffs claimed that they entered into a valid contract for the purchase of 300 tons of coal from the defendants via their agent, Holbrook, who assured delivery under specific terms, including payment schedules. They argued that they fulfilled their payment obligations by paying $2,250 and alleged that the defendants failed to deliver 132 tons of the coal as stipulated. Consequently, the plaintiffs sought damages amounting to $1,452 due to the non-delivery of the coal.	The defendants contended that Holbrook lacked the authority to bind them to the coal sale contract beyond what was agreed in their own separate contract with him. They argued that Holbrook acted outside his authority when agreeing to the terms with the plaintiffs and sought to have the case dismissed based on these claims. Furthermore, they appealed the judgment by asserting that the court's ruling was contrary to the law and against the evidence presented.

The case "Therese LaFramboise v. Nathan S. Grow" took place in September 1870 in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, Therese LaFramboise, filed a bill in the Superior Court of Chicago seeking dower rights to certain premises formerly owned by her deceased husband, Joseph LaFramboise. Before the court could hear the case, Therese executed a release of her dower interest in the land to George E. Walker for valuable consideration. Subsequently, the defendant, Nathan S. Grow, filed a cross-bill against Therese, arguing that her release barred any claims she might have to the property. He stated that the property, once owned by Joseph LaFramboise, had been sold to Walker and Kinzie, who then conveyed it to Campbell, from whom Grow ultimately acquired his interest. Therese’s solicitor claimed that he was entitled to a share of the recovery due to a prior agreement with her. The litigation involved issues related to the validity of the release, the nature of dower rights, and the entitlement of the solicitor to recover fees. In a final hearing, the court dismissed the original bill and ruled in favor of the defendant, leading to the appeal.	Therese LaFramboise's primary claims included her entitlement to dower rights in the disputed property. She argued that her release of the dower interest to Walker might not be valid and that her attorney's contract for fees and costs should protect his interests in the event that her right was upheld. She sought to reverse the lower court's decree that dismissed her original bill.	Nathan S. Grow defended against Therese's claims by arguing that her prior release to Walker effectively barred her from pursuing the dower rights she claimed in the ongoing suit. He maintained that the release was obtained fairly and for valid consideration. Additionally, Grow contended that Therese's solicitor had no right or lien on the property for fees because the attorney-client agreement did not create any such interest in the dower right.

The case of Moses Robertson v. John Dodge took place in Warren County, Illinois, during the early 1860s, culminating with a decision in April 1862. The dispute arose from a contract regarding the construction of a partition fence between the adjoining farms of the plaintiff, Moses Robertson, and the defendant, John Dodge. According to the plaintiff, in March 1858, they entered into an agreement where Robertson would build a fence for which Dodge would be responsible for half the cost. Robertson constructed a fence comprising 106 rods of rails, valued at $30. However, complications surfaced regarding a subsequent arrangement for the fence to be made of posts and boards. Before the lawsuit ensued, Dodge had purchased Robertson's farm. He contended that part of this sale agreement included the transfer of any claims Robertson had against him regarding the fence's construction. The defendant claimed that he was released from any liabilities when Robertson sold the farm, yet this assertion became the focal point of the trial. The jury eventually rendered a verdict in favor of Dodge for $26.25 in costs owing to claims raised by Robertson.	Moses Robertson, the plaintiff, argued that John Dodge was liable for the agreed-upon payment for the construction of the partition fence. He maintained that despite any subsequent arrangements, there remained an obligation for Dodge to pay for the work completed. Robertson sought to recover the costs associated with the fence's construction, claiming Dodge had used the fence but had not paid for it.	John Dodge, the defendant, contended that any claims Robertson might have had regarding the fence were nullified when Robertson sold his farm to Bailey G. Robertson, effectively transferring the claim to Bailey. Dodge argued that he was released from financial responsibility when this agreement was made, asserting that he had settled the issue prior to the lawsuit's initiation. He requested the court to enforce this understanding and dismiss the claims made by Robertson.

Hiram Dingman v. The People of the State of Illinois involved an indictment against Hiram Dingman for operating a liquor-selling establishment within one mile of the University of Chicago, contrary to state statutes prohibiting such sales for non-mechanical or medicinal purposes. This case was presented to the Recorder’s Court of Chicago in September 1869. Dingman pleaded not guilty, but after a jury trial, he was found guilty. His motions for a new trial and for arrest of judgment were rejected. The court ordered Dingman to abate the nuisance created by his establishment and warned that failure to comply would result in his commitment. Dingman argued that his establishment was a public inn and that he had licenses allowing him to sell liquor, but the court disallowed this evidence. The legal conflict arose from the charter of the University of Chicago, which disallowed the sale of intoxicating liquors within a mile, and the city charter, which conferred the licensing power on the mayor and city council, leading to a potential contradiction in the law.	The plaintiff claimed that Dingman was operating a liquor-selling establishment in violation of the rule established by the University of Chicago's charter, asserting that such a business near the university was a public nuisance and should be subject to abatement under state law.	Dingman contended that he had proper licenses from both the city of Chicago and the federal government to operate as a public inn serving liquor. He argued that the prohibition in the university's charter did not hold since his establishment should be exempt from such constraints due to these licenses.

In the case of Eugene B. Mix et al. v. Harriet King, which was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872, the central issue revolves around Harriet King’s claim to her homestead rights against Eugene B. Mix and others. The events leading to the dispute began in 1858 when Harriet and her husband executed a deed of trust on their property to secure a debt. The deed did not release her homestead rights. In 1859, the property was sold to Russel C. Mix under the terms of the trust deed while Harriet continued to live there with her children after her husband abandoned her. In 1861, Mix recovered a judgment to evict the husband, which led to Harriet being forcibly dispossessed of the premises. Following this, she filed a bill in chancery to set aside the sale, asserting her rights to both the property and the rents from it. The lower court ruled in her favor but did not account for the rents owing to her. The case was subsequently appealed, and the Supreme Court needed to determine the extent of Harriet’s rights and equitable compensation regarding the unlawfully dispossessed homestead.	Harriet King, the plaintiff, claimed she was rightfully entitled to the use and profits arising from her homestead, which she had been forcibly removed from. She requested that the sale of her property be set aside and sought an accounting of the rents and profits collected by the defendants since her dispossession. Specifically, she argued that she should receive the full amount of rents proportional to her homestead interest, which was capped at $1,000, minus deductions for taxes and necessary repairs.	Eugene B. Mix and the other defendants contended that Harriet was not entitled to claim the entirety of the profits from the property since it had been sold under a trust deed. They argued that any claims to the rents or profits should only pertain to the period post the abandonment by her husband. They sought to affirm the legality of the previous judgment that allowed them possession of the premises and the derived benefits therefrom.

On March 12, 1853, the Town of Olney, Illinois, enacted an ordinance prohibiting the sale, barter, or disposal of any vinous, spirituous, or mixed liquors in quantities less than one barrel without obtaining a license. The plaintiffs, Alexander L. Byers and others, were fined $10 for violating this ordinance. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court, which examined the legality of the ordinance. The court considered previous cases that validated the powers of town corporations to legislate within their charter limits. The ordinance in question did not conflict with state laws, given that it extended the minimum sale quantity from one quart to one barrel, thereby regulating larger sales without contradicting existing regulations. The case was debated during the September term of 1853 at the Richland Circuit Court, with the judge ultimately favoring the town's authority to govern these sales under local law.	The plaintiffs argued that the ordinance imposed by the Town of Olney was illegal and unjust, leading to their unjust fine of $10. Their primary legal request was to challenge the validity of the ordinance under which they were penalized, asserting that it contravened state regulations regarding the sale of alcoholic beverages.	The defendants, represented by the Town of Olney, maintained that the ordinance was legitimate and within their rights as an incorporated town under state law. They argued that the ordinance was not contradictory to existing state laws and was, in fact, a necessary regulation that fell within their powers to legislate for the community's welfare.

Joseph Cornelius, Appellant, filed an appeal against Robert Wash, Appellee, following a legal dispute regarding attorney fees. The case originated around November 9, 1819, in Belleville, St. Clair County, Illinois, where Cornelius entered into an obligation to pay Wash for his legal services related to a suit concerning a black man's (George's) quest for freedom against Robert Whiteside and E. Bradshaw. The suit was eventually tried in the Randolph Circuit Court and was successful for George. However, Cornelius contested Wash's claim for payment, arguing that Wash did not fulfill his duties as the attorney for the case, as he was not present or involved during the critical moments of the proceedings. Instead, other lawyers, Peck and Carr, handled the case. Despite Cornelius' arguments, the Circuit Court ruled in favor of Wash for $59 in damages. Cornelius appealed this decision, leading to a reconsideration of the obligations involved in the attorney-client relationship.	Cornelius, the plaintiff, claimed that Wash was not entitled to the payment specified in their contract since he did not provide legal representation during the trial, as required. He argued that Wash's absence and the involvement of other attorneys negated any obligation for payment. Cornelius requested that the court instruct the jury to find in his favor based on Wash's failure to perform as stipulated in their agreement.	Wash, the defendant, maintained that while he did not personally appear in the trial, his contract was valid and entitled him to payment for legal services. He argued that the representation provided by Peck and Carr, while sufficient, did not absolve Cornelius's responsibility to pay for the services outlined in their agreement. Wash contended that the relationship between client and counsel required that the legal services contracted be fulfilled, even if another attorney represented the interests.

On January 27, 1837, Daniel A. Baldwin and his wife mortgaged certain properties in Chicago to Moses P. Hatch for $22,500. Due to financial difficulties, Baldwin sought help from the New York firm McNulty & Chapman to purchase the mortgage from Hatch. The firm provided Baldwin with funds in exchange for land and ownership stakes. However, various complex transactions and assignments of the mortgage took place over the years, eventually involving parties like Albert McNulty, Azor S. Marvin, and Ebenezer Thayer. After a series of legal disputes and claims of interests in the mortgage, Eunice Chapman, Baldwin’s representative, claimed ownership of the mortgage through a series of transactions from the 1830s onward, alleging that previous conveyances constituted a mortgage, not a sale. The case evolved over decades, with numerous individuals and entities involved, resulting in Eunice Chapman's legal claim against William B. Ogden and others regarding ownership of the mortgage and the properties.	Eunice Chapman, the complainant, argued that she was the lawful owner of the mortgage in question, alleging that it had been sold to her through a series of complex transactions, including a quit-claim deed from Baldwin. She claimed that the nature of previous transactions constituted mortgages rather than outright sales, asserting her right to redeem the properties held by the defendants and demanding an accounting for rent and profits derived from the premises.	The defendants, led by William B. Ogden, contended that the title to the properties had been properly transferred to them through legitimate sales. They argued that all transactions were conducted in good faith and that they were bona fide purchasers for value without notice of any alleged equities claimed by Chapman. Additionally, they cited the statute of frauds regarding trust claims and denied that the transactions behaved in a manner that supported the plaintiff’s position.

In January 1875, in Menard County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Aaron Hatfield and James W. Cheaney, who was the plaintiff in this case. The litigation stemmed from a suit brought by Cheaney against Hatfield and Thomas E. Clark concerning four promissory notes. The case was presided over by Judge Lyman Lacey in the Circuit Court of Menard County. Cheaney successfully recovered on the notes, prompting Hatfield to appeal the decision. The case ultimately centered around the validity of a plea made by Hatfield, which the court deemed insufficient as it did not adequately address all claims. A key issue also arose concerning the method by which a witness presented a computation of the amounts owed, which was criticized by the court as improper practice.	James W. Cheaney, the plaintiff, claimed that Aaron Hatfield and Thomas E. Clark owed him money based on four promissory notes. He argued that the defendants' plea was insufficient as it failed to provide a full answer to the allegations against them. He sought to have the court affirm the judgment in his favor, insisting that the amounts due on the notes were correctly calculated.	Aaron Hatfield, as the appellant, contended that the court below erred in accepting Cheaney's claims. He argued that the plea he submitted was misinterpreted and asserted that it should have been upheld. Hatfield claimed that the witness improperly provided a memorandum of calculations directly to the jury, which he believed compromised the trial's integrity. He requested a reversal of the lower court's judgment.

Adolph Krebaum v. Mansfield W. Cordell et al. was a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1872. The origin of the dispute took place in Mason County, Illinois, involving key individuals including Mansfield W. Cordell, his wife Delia B. Cordell, and George W. Cordell, a relation of the Cordells. The case arose when Mansfield and Delia Cordell filed a bill against George W. Cordell to compel him to convey a tract of land to Delia. During the pendency of the suit, Adolph Krebaum, who had obtained a conveyance of the land from George W. Cordell, was added as a defendant. The court found that a deed intended to convey the land from Mansfield to George was never delivered or accepted and was fraudulent. The land was deemed to have been purchased with Delia's money, making her the rightful owner. The case was litigated based on these principles of ownership and fraudulent claim.	The plaintiffs, Mansfield and Delia B. Cordell, claimed that the deed purportedly conveying the land to George W. Cordell was never valid since it was not delivered or accepted. They sought a decree to compel George to convey the land to Delia, arguing that she was the rightful owner as the property was purchased with her funds, and that her husband only acted as a trustee for her. They requested general relief to affirm Delia's rightful claim over the property.	Adolph Krebaum, as the defendant, raised several arguments against the plaintiffs' claims. He asserted that the circuit court should have dismissed the complaint against Delia and objected to certain testimony admitted during the trial. Krebaum contended that he should not be ordered to convey the land to Delia Cordell and that the court erred in not allowing his evidence. His primary defense rested on arguing the validity of his ownership claim through the conveyance from George W. Cordell.

In 1870, the legal case of *The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. Edward Hempstead et al. v. The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company* took place in Chicago, Illinois. Key individuals involved were Edward Hempstead, Calvin T. Wheeler, and representatives from the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company. The case arose when Hempstead and others applied for a peremptory mandamus to compel the railroad to accept all grain deliveries at their elevator located in Chicago. They sought the railroad's obligation to transport grain from points along their line without discrimination and to deliver it promptly. The defendants, the railroad company, contested this claim, asserting that they were not common carriers beyond their designated route and did not have the obligation to deliver goods to the relators' elevator, which was located beyond their terminal limits. The case revolved around the legal scope of a railroad company’s duty to receive and transport goods beyond its established route.	The plaintiffs claimed that as the owners and operators of the Illinois River Elevator, the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company had a legal obligation to accept and transport all grain delivered to their line and to deliver it to their elevator upon payment of the customary charges. They argued that the railroad company, as a common carrier, was required to deliver goods to the destinations specified by the consignors without unreasonable delay.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company contended that they were not common carriers to the extent claimed by the plaintiffs, maintaining that their obligation only extended along their own designated route. They also asserted that the plaintiffs' elevator was located beyond the terminus of their line, and that the tracks leading to the elevator belonged to other railroad companies, over which they had no authority or obligation. Furthermore, the defendants argued that requiring them to transport goods beyond their line would impose unjust burdens on their chartered rights.

The case, "The National Bank of Pontiac v. Solomon E. King et al.," was decided on June 13, 1884, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Livingston County, Illinois, involving several key individuals: the National Bank of Pontiac, Solomon E. King, Hugh M. Hamilton, Isaac Defenbaugh, and Franklin D. Sweetser. The background concerns a quarter section of land that Defenbaugh acquired from Sweetser in 1871, but he never made any payments for this land or the associated taxes. When Defenbaugh could no longer afford to maintain the property, he reconveyed it to Sweetser in 1875, satisfying his mortgage obligations without any monetary compensation. Subsequently, the National Bank obtained a judgment against Defenbaugh, which allowed them to levy the property, resulting in a sale. However, it was contended that the land was still subject to prior valid mortgages held by Hapgood, creating a complicated dispute regarding the bank’s claim to the property and the rightful ownership involving the complainants King and Hamilton.	The plaintiffs, King and Hamilton, argued that the National Bank was improperly trying to claim ownership of the land despite the existing prior liens and mortgages. They maintained that the bank did not acquire a legitimate title to the property through the sale as it appealed from Defenbaugh's equity of redemption, which was essentially worthless since he never paid for the land or the taxes. They claimed that the bank sought to unlawfully disregard the rights of the original lien holders and requested that the bank be required to pay the total amount owed on the mortgages and taxes before they could claim any rights to the property.	The National Bank contended that it held a valid judgment against Defenbaugh and thus claimed title to the quarter section of land through relative property laws. They asserted that the sale, which occurred through execution on the judgment, conferred legitimate ownership rights, despite the complexities regarding existing mortgages. The bank denied any wrongdoing or inequitable actions and sought to maintain its claim to the property without the obligation to discharge the existing liabilities associated with it.

In April 1864, in Lee County, Illinois, a legal case titled "Aaron L. Porter v. John Dement" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case centered around a replevin action concerning two horses. The plaintiff, Aaron L. Porter, claimed he held title to the horses based on a chattel mortgage from a third party named Glenn. Meanwhile, John Dement, acting as the sheriff of Lee County, had seized the horses while they were in Glenn’s possession under an execution against Glenn. The chattel mortgage that Porter claimed as his title was executed but never recorded. Subsequently, after the original mortgage was lost, Glenn created and certified a copy of the mortgage, which was then recorded in the county recorder’s office. However, this record did not comply with the state law requiring specific acknowledgments and proper recording processes. The court considered the merits of Porter's claims against the legal implications of the sheriff's execution and the validity of the chattel mortgage documentation.	The plaintiff, Aaron L. Porter, asserted that he had a valid title to the two horses due to a chattel mortgage executed to him by Glenn. He argued that despite the original mortgage being lost, the certified copy of the mortgage should protect his interest against any other claims, including those of the sheriff who had seized the horses.	The defendant, John Dement, contended that the chattel mortgage was invalid due to the lack of proper acknowledgment and recording as required by Illinois law. He argued that the recording of the copy of the mortgage was insufficient and that he had acted in good faith in levying upon the horses since the legal requirements to validate a chattel mortgage had not been met.

In 1870, in Peoria County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving a request for a writ of mandamus filed by James H. Rogers and Thomas Shaw against Thomas C. Hall and two other highway commissioners. The plaintiffs sought to compel the commissioners to take necessary legal steps to open a highway that had previously been laid out by a different board of commissioners. The petition detailed the procedural history surrounding the highway, including the legal voters' petition and damage assessments for landowners affected by the road. The defendants, Hall and his associates, raised several defenses, arguing, among other things, that the plaintiffs were not citizens of Radnor and that the highway was not legally established, as only two of the three commissioners acted in its layout. They also claimed that they should not open the road until legal notifications to landowners had been given and that sufficient time for such an opening had not yet elapsed. The Circuit Court sustained a demurrer by the relators against the defendants' return, leading to a writ of mandamus being issued in favor of the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to a writ of mandamus to compel the highway commissioners to perform their public duty of opening a previously designated highway, which had been laid out correctly. They asserted their standing as residents of Radnor township with a vested interest in the highway being opened for public use, and they contended that the respondents had failed to fulfill their legal obligations regarding the opening of the road after the procedural requirements were satisfied.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs lacked the legal standing to demand the highway's opening, asserting they were merely private citizens without special interests. They maintained that the highway itself was not legally established, citing procedural defects in its layout. Additionally, they claimed that openings could not occur until landowners were properly notified to remove fences, which had not happened, and that they had recently extended the timeline for this notification due to weather conditions, making immediate opening impractical.

In May 1972, in the town of Jefferson, Cook County, Illinois, Frederick Bœttcher was arrested by a group of local officials, including police captain Hugh H. Schweitzer and police magistrate Ingalls, for allegedly violating a town ordinance prohibiting the depositing of offensive materials on one's premises. This action was prompted by a complaint from Gray, the president of the board of trustees. Bœttcher was taken into custody around 2 a.m. on May 26 and was held in the town jail. He was presented for trial on May 29, where he was fined $50. Refusing to pay, he was recommitted to jail and remained there until he was released on a writ of habeas corpus on May 31. Bœttcher initiated a lawsuit against Schweitzer and others for trespass, assault, battery, and false imprisonment arising from his arrest and detention.	Bœttcher claimed that his arrest and subsequent imprisonment were unlawful as the town ordinance did not permit such actions. He argued that, according to the ordinance, the proper procedure for prosecution should have begun with a summons rather than an arrest warrant, as the ordinance only allowed for fines, not imprisonment. Bœttcher sought damages for the wrongful arrest and imprisonment, ultimately resulting in a jury verdict against the defendants for $2,000.	The defendants contended that they acted within their authority under the town's charter, which allowed for the issuance of a warrant based on a sworn complaint regarding an ordinance violation. They argued that the charter's language did provide grounds for their actions, and therefore the jury instruction given in Bœttcher's favor was incorrect. They sought to have the court reverse the judgment against them, maintaining that they were justified in their actions to uphold town ordinances.

In September 1873, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court involving William Payne as the plaintiff and Livingston Compton as the defendant. The case stemmed from an implied contract claim where Payne sought recovery for work and labor rendered. The trial concluded with a jury verdict in favor of the plaintiff. Compton's defense was based on a plea of non-assumpsit, but he subsequently appealed the decision. Evidence presented during the trial indicated that there was an existing special written contract under seal with Reuben H. Compton (presumably a relative or associate of Livingston). The court examined whether the work performed could support an implied contract or if it was solely bound by the special contract with the original parties.	The plaintiff, William Payne, argued that he was entitled to recover for work and labor performed under an implied undertaking, asserting that he had benefited the defendant through his services. Payne's legal request was to uphold the jury's verdict and the judgment of the lower court, which ruled in his favor.	The defendant, Livingston Compton, contended that the action was misconceived since the work was conducted under a specific written contract. Compton highlighted that recovery for such work must occur between the original contracting parties and stated that since the work was done under this special contract, individuals who benefited from it, such as himself, could not be held liable for the implied assumpsit.

In 1880, Arthur Birket, the plaintiff, filed a claim against the State of Illinois regarding damages to his lands caused by the construction of a lock and dam on the Illinois River at or near Copperas Creek, which was completed around October 21, 1877. The dam increased the water level of the river, leading to overflow and making Birket's lands unsuitable for agricultural use due to prolonged water saturation. This claim was officially submitted on April 16, 1880, and was based on the time of injury relating to the dam's completion. However, the case's procedural history includes a plea regarding the statute of limitations, as the claim was not filed within two years from when the injury occurred, and the Commission found that it arose when the dam was finished. The court carefully reviewed the evidence and testimonies but expressed no opinion on the extent of injury caused.	Arthur Birket argued that the construction of the dam raised the water level of the Illinois River, resulting in flooding that damaged his agricultural lands. He sought compensation for the loss in value and use of his property, claiming that the state was responsible for the effects of the dam.	The State of Illinois defended itself by arguing that Birket's claim was barred by the statute of limitations, as his petition was filed more than two years after the completion of the dam, which they asserted was when any potential cause of action arose. The state maintained that any claims for damages should have been filed within the stipulated time frame, and hence, they were not liable for the alleged damages.

In the case of George Hayden, Administrator, v. Martha Henderson, heard by the Illinois Appellate Court on November 20, 1886, the dispute centers around claims for services rendered to the deceased, Martha Henderson, by her daughter-in-law, Martha. The timeline of services extends from March 1, 1881, to April 1, 1884. Martha had been living with her mother-in-law since 1877 and provided both household support and care as the elder's health declined. The specific nature of their arrangement was unclear, as no express agreement regarding compensation was documented. Witnesses estimated the value of services rendered at rates between $2.50 and $5 per week. Initially, the court instructed the jury that they might infer a request for her services based on their acceptance, unless proven to be gratuitous. The defense argued that since the earlier services were rendered without payment, the same assumption should apply to later services unless explicitly stated otherwise. The court ultimately ruled in favor of the claimant for $400 after a Circuit Court trial, prompting the administrator, George Hayden, to seek a writ of error.	The plaintiff, George Hayden, contended that the services provided by Martha Henderson to his deceased mother, Martha, were either gratuitous or unacknowledged under the assumption they did not constitute a legal obligation. He claimed that prior services would create a presumption of continued gratuity unless the claimant could prove otherwise through an explicit contract or notice. The central argument was that no express agreement existed about compensating the latter services, which became relevant when evaluating the claimant's right to recover any payment.	The defendant, Martha Henderson, maintained that her relationship with the deceased was akin to that of a family member, typically where no compensation is expected for services rendered. She argued that the court's instructions were incorrect and erred by not properly addressing the implications of their family-like relationship in regard to compensation. The defense asserted that the burden of proof should fall upon the claimant to provide clear evidence of an intent to charge for her services, which did not materialize despite the potential prior gratuity.

In 1885, in Williamson County, Illinois, the case A. M. Askew et al. v. Leroy A. Goddard arose from a motion to modify a judgment previously entered against the plaintiffs, A. M. Askew and Mary Ann Askew, for the sum of $3,716.93. The judgment had been confessed on a promissory note for $3,540, which was due twelve months after its date. The plaintiffs had authorized their attorney, George W. Young, to confess judgment on their behalf. Issues arose when the confessed judgment included an attorney's fee and additional amounts not expressly due, leading the plaintiffs to challenge the legitimacy of the confession. During the court proceedings, it was revealed that the attorney exceeded his authority by confessing for more than the actual amounts owed. The circuit court’s ruling to uphold the judgment prompted the plaintiffs to file a writ of error, claiming the judgment was unfairly excessive and improperly constructed.	The plaintiffs argued that the attorney acted beyond his authority when confessing the judgment, including an attorney's fee that was not justified under the warrant given. They contended that the judgment was inequitable as it included excess amounts not legally due. The plaintiffs sought to modify the judgment to accurately reflect the amounts legitimately owed, excluding the improperly added attorney’s fee and excess principal and interest.	The defendant, Leroy A. Goddard, claimed that the plaintiffs had ratified the attorney's actions in confessing the judgment and could not challenge it after receiving excess proceeds from property sold under the judgment. The defense argued that the judgment was valid and argued against the plaintiffs’ motion for modification, asserting that the judgment had been satisfied by the sale of the property.

In 1850, Paschal Magee (the plaintiff) engaged in a transaction with J. C. D. Carmack (the defendant) in McDonough County, Illinois, where Magee paid Carmack a ten-dollar bill from the now-defunct Bank of St. Clair, which had been broken for over a decade. Magee later sought to recover this amount after discovering the bill had no value. The dispute escalated to a justice of the peace, where Carmack won, prompting Magee to appeal to the Circuit Court. During the April 1851 term, a jury again sided with Carmack. Magee's efforts to have the jury instructed on his right to return the worthless bill within a reasonable time were denied. The locations of the two parties were seven miles apart, complicating communication and the timely return of the bill. The case focuses on the validity of payment using a non-current banknote.	Magee argued that the ten-dollar bill he provided to Carmack was worthless due to the Bank of St. Clair being defunct and sought a return of his payment. He contended that he was entitled to recover the amount since the bill could not be considered valid currency due to its lack of value.	Carmack maintained that he was entitled to keep the ten-dollar bill as payment since he was unaware of the bank's failure at the time. He argued that even if the bill was from a broken bank, he should not be liable to return the amount unless Magee returned the bill within a reasonable timeframe after discovering it was worthless.

In 1864 and early 1865, George D. Lincoln, a grain buyer from Madison, Wisconsin, had been shipping his grain purchases to commission merchants J. Sherman Hall and Pope in Chicago. During this period, Hall and Pope experienced a significant loss of about $2,200 from a large sale of wheat for Lincoln. Dissatisfied with this outcome, Lincoln considered stopping his shipments. To retain Lincoln as a client, one of the merchants arranged a meeting with him in June 1865, during which it was allegedly agreed that Hall and Pope would compensate Lincoln with $1,000 for the loss if he continued shipping his grain to them. This agreement was primarily supported by Hooker, a clerk for Hall and Pope, who was a witness to the arrangement. Lincoln continued to ship his goods, expecting the compensation. However, when the season ended and the accounts were tallied, Hall and Pope refused to pay Lincoln the agreed sum, leading him to initiate legal action to recover the alleged amount owed.	Lincoln claims that Hall and Pope agreed to pay him $1,000 for losses incurred from their sale of his wheat, contingent upon his continued shipments. He argues that during their agreement, it was clearly stated that they would compensate him for his losses at the end of the season. Lincoln requests the court to enforce this agreement and order Hall and Pope to pay him the $1,000 he claims is owed.	Hall and Pope refute Lincoln's claims, arguing that the jury's verdict in his favor is unsupported by the evidence. They contend that certain letters written by Lincoln indicate that he had different expectations regarding the compensation, suggesting it was tied to speculative success in the grain market rather than a straightforward agreement. The defendants seek to have the court reverse the verdict based on their assertion that it lacks sufficient evidence to support Lincoln's claims.

Thomas F. Tomlin filed an action of ejectment against David W. Hilyard in January 1867, seeking to recover forty acres of land located in Mason County, Illinois. The land was originally part of an eighty-acre parcel purchased jointly by Hilyard and Thompson Tomlin on March 10, 1856. A judgment was rendered against both Hilyard and Thompson Tomlin on January 1, 1858, leading to the land being sold at a sheriff’s sale on March 16, 1858. Tomlin claimed title through this sale. However, Hilyard contended that before the judgment against him, he and Thompson Tomlin had agreed to a parol partition of the land whereby Hilyard received the southern forty acres, which was the subject of the dispute. Hilyard asserted that he had taken open and exclusive possession of his portion since spring 1857, establishing a homestead. The trial court heard the case without a jury and ultimately found in Hilyard's favor, drawing upon the evidence presented regarding the parol partition and subsequent possession.	Thomas F. Tomlin argued that he possessed legal title to the forty acres because he acquired the land through a sheriff's sale following a judgment against Hilyard and Thompson Tomlin. He sought to assert his right to the property based on this legal claim, challenging the validity of any prior arrangements regarding partition or possession made between Hilyard and Tomlin.	David W. Hilyard countered Tomlin's claims by asserting that a valid parol partition had been established prior to the judgment, which partition divided the eighty acres into two forty-acre portions — one for Hilyard and one for Thompson Tomlin. Hilyard maintained that he had continuously occupied the land in question as his homestead since the spring of 1857 and that the partition, although verbal, was evidenced by his long-standing, exclusive possession. Hilyard requested the court to affirm his rights to the land based on this partition.

In April 1862, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case of Nathaniel H. Hall v. Jonathan P. Burton. The dispute stems from an action of debt based on two promissory notes executed by Nathaniel H. Hall in Philadelphia, which were made payable to his own order and subsequently indorsed to Jonathan P. Burton. The case initially went to the Circuit Court, where Burton filed a suit against Hall, claiming he was due a specified amount based on the notes. The courtroom battle included challenges to the validity of these notes, specifically questioning whether they were legally binding as negotiable instruments without a proper payee. After a trial in August 1860, the court found in favor of Burton, awarding him $2,663.46 in debt and $805.69 in damages. Hall subsequently appealed the decision to the Supreme Court, raising issues about the legality of the notes in question.	Jonathan P. Burton, the plaintiff in error, argued that the promissory notes, although made payable to Hall's own order and indorsed by him, were valid and binding. He maintained that Hall’s endorsement effectively made him liable as both maker and indorser. Burton requested that the court affirm the judgment of the lower court, which had found in his favor and awarded him damages.	Nathaniel H. Hall, the defendant in error, contended that the notes were void and not enforceable as they lacked a proper payee. He asserted that the notes never became valid negotiable instruments under Illinois law, and thus, a legal action could not be maintained against him. Hall sought to reverse the lower court's decision, claiming that his indorsement did not provide the necessary legal effect to make the notes binding.

The case "Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company v. William Schaffer" took place in the Illinois Appellate Court on November 18, 1887. The dispute arose when the plaintiff, William Schaffer, sued the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company for damages resulting from a railroad bridge constructed over Harkness Branch, which obstructed the natural flow of water, leading to the flooding of Schaffer's land. The railroad bridge was alleged to have been negligently constructed, contributing to the overflow and damage to Schaffer's property. The original lawsuit stemmed from similar injuries occurring prior to October 1883, for which Schaffer had previously won a judgment against the railroad for $600, which was settled. The current case sought damages for the continuing impacts of the bridge's obstruction since that initial legal resolution.	Schaffer claimed that the railroad's bridge construction was negligent, leading to flooding on his property. He requested compensation for damages amounting to $500, asserting that the obstruction caused by the bridge had directly contributed to the overflow of his land and destruction of crops. Schaffer maintained that, despite his prior recovery from a similar issue, the damages claimed in this case were distinct and pertained to subsequent injuries since the last judgment.	The railroad company contended that Schaffer contributed to the flooding by constructing a levee on his land prior to the bridge's construction. Moreover, they argued that the overflow was due to an extraordinary storm, attempting to mitigate their liability. They insisted that they were not liable for the damages as they believed Schaffer had neglected to take preventative steps against flooding. Additionally, the railroad claimed that the previous judgment barred Schaffer from filing another action regarding the same adverse effects caused by the bridge's existence.

In 1850, the case of Hiram Brown, along with others, was brought against Matthew Throckmorton in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning an action of trespass. Throckmorton claimed damages for the value of certain rails he made from timber cut on a quarter section of land owned by the United States during the winter of 1844. In March or April of the following year, Hiram Brown took these rails. Brown had resided on the land since April 1843 and argued he had a pre-emption claim on the land. During the trial, the defendants attempted to submit evidence to support Brown's claim; however, the court rejected this evidence, which included certified copies from the land office and a purchase certificate that Brown obtained after the rails were cut.
