The court determined that the timber belonged to the United States and that Brown's right of pre-emption did not equate to ownership of the timber or the rails. The case closely referenced a prior decision (Wincher vs. Shrewsbury) that established similar legal principles. Ultimately, the jury initially found for Throckmorton, awarding him $12, which prompted Brown to appeal on the grounds of the excluded evidence.	Throckmorton, the plaintiff, claimed that he rightfully owned the rails made from timber he cut, asserting that the rails had value and that Brown's taking of the rails constituted a trespass. He sought compensation for the value of the rails, contending that the evidence he presented established his right to recover damages from Brown.	Brown, as the defendant, argued that he had a legal pre-emption claim on the land where the timber was cut, and sought to present evidence to support this claim. He contended that his occupancy and subsequent purchase of the land granted him rights that should negate Throckmorton’s claims. Brown's defense relied on the argument that preemption allowed him legal rights over the timber, although this evidence was ultimately excluded by the court.

The case, "The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. The South Park Commissioners, v. Erastus S. Williams," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1869. The dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving the South Park Commissioners, who sought a mandamus compelling Judge Erastus S. Williams of the Circuit Court to appoint three freeholders as park assessors. This request was in accordance with a statute from February 24, 1869, which mandated the appointment once the commissioners had determined the approximate amount needed for the condemnation of land designated for a park serving the towns of South Chicago, Hyde Park, and Lake. The judge had previously refused to act on the request, citing uncertainties regarding the law's validity and the necessity for the park commissioners to establish the compensation required for the land before proceeding.	The South Park Commissioners (plaintiffs) asserted that they were entitled to a writ of mandamus to compel the Circuit Court judge to appoint assessors as specified in the statutory framework. They argued that the law was valid and provided a necessary process for assessing the damages for property to be condemned for the park, and that they had complied with the statutory requirements for initiating the appointment.	Judge Erastus S. Williams (defendant) contended that he could not appoint the park assessors until the validity of the underlying act was confirmed and until the commissioners properly established the compensation amounts for the condemnation. He expressed doubts regarding the act's clarity and the procedures necessary for accurately determining the compensation.

In December 1850, the case "The People v. Henry M. Smith, et. al." was presented in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a dispute over a payment made by Henry M. Smith, the Collector of Pulaski County, for the collection of taxes for the year 1847. Smith paid $100 to Milton Carpenter, the then Treasurer of State, on January 12, 1848, and received a receipt. However, the receipt was not countersigned by the Auditor nor was a duplicate filed with the auditor, which was contrary to the requirements mandated by law at that time. Consequently, Smith was not credited with the payment in the auditor’s records. The court had to evaluate the validity of this payment and whether the collector was relieved of financial responsibility to the state due to this payment.	The plaintiff, represented by District Attorney D. B. Campbell, argued that the payment made by the Collector should be deemed invalid since the treasurer did not follow the required procedure of countersigning the receipt and filing a duplicate with the auditor. They sought to hold Smith responsible for the unpaid taxes.	The defendant, Henry M. Smith, represented by attorney A.G. Caldwell, contended that he had fulfilled his legal obligations by paying the revenue to the authorized treasurer. Smith maintained that the failure of the Treasurer to follow the reporting requirements should not prejudice his position, thus arguing he had discharged his liability to the State upon making the payment.

The case of Hector J. Humphrey et al. v. Orville H. Browning et al. took place in January 1868 in Illinois and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a bill filed in the Circuit Court of Hancock County by the appellees (Orville H. Browning and others) against the appellants (Hector J. Humphrey and others), who were seeking to establish a lien for attorney compensation related to real estate that was recovered in an action of ejectment. The core issue centered on whether an attorney can claim a lien on real estate recovered through their legal efforts. The court deliberated on the precedents and principles of attorney liens, ultimately stating that such a lien does not exist under the circumstances presented.	The plaintiffs asserted that they, as contractors who prosecuted the action of ejectment, were entitled to a lien on the real estate recovered as compensation for their legal services. They argued based on the nature of attorney-client relationships and precedents that established attorneys could have a lien on judgments to secure payment for their services.	The defendants contested the plaintiffs' claims, arguing that no lien exists for attorney compensation on the real estate recovered. They maintained that the precedents cited by the plaintiffs did not support their claim and highlighted that existing laws and past rulings did not confer the right to a lien on the property in question. They argued that any compensation due to attorneys must follow the usual contractual terms rather than impose an unusual secret lien on recovered properties.

The case "Garfield Manufacturing Co. et al. v. John H. McLean" took place in Illinois, with the final judgment issued on March 31, 1886. The incident occurred on May 6, 1884, in Chicago, where John H. McLean, the plaintiff, sustained personal injuries due to alleged negligence by the Garfield Manufacturing Company. The manufacturing company's building had openings along a public alley, and McLean, while trying to maneuver goods from a nearby saloon, fell into an unguarded area beside the building, leading to his injuries. During the trial, it was revealed that there was a conflict regarding McLean's state of sobriety at the time of the accident, as the defendants argued he was under the influence, which contributed to the incident. The lower court initially ruled in favor of McLean, awarding him $1,500 plus costs.	The plaintiff, McLean, argued that the Garfield Manufacturing Company was negligent for failing to provide adequate guards around the openings of their building, which directly caused his injuries. He contended that his accident was a result of the defendants’ lack of proper safety measures, and he sought compensation for the injuries he sustained due to this negligence.	The defendants, represented by the Garfield Manufacturing Company, claimed that the plaintiff was partly to blame for his injuries due to his own negligence, arguing that he was under the influence of alcohol at the time. They sought to demonstrate that any negligence on McLean's part was significant enough to bar his recovery and contended that the jury instructions given during the trial concerning comparative negligence were erroneous and misleading.

The case "The Litchfield Coal Company v. Mary A. Taylor" took place in January 1876 in Montgomery County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Mary A. Taylor, filed the suit as the widow of James Taylor, who died due to injuries sustained while working in a coal mine owned by the Litchfield Coal Company. The injury was allegedly caused by the company's willful disregard of safety regulations. Specifically, the company used uncovered cages to hoist miners and coal simultaneously, in violation of the miners’ safety provisions in the state statutes. During the trial, a jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding her $1,500 in damages. The defendant appealed the decision, contesting the jury's instructions and the validity of the claims based on the legal provisions pertaining to miners and safety regulations.	Mary A. Taylor claimed that the Litchfield Coal Company's actions led to the wrongful death of her husband. She argued that the company willfully violated safety regulations by hoisting coal and miners at the same time and using uncovered cages, which caused the fatal accident. Taylor requested damages for the loss of her husband, emphasizing the company's responsibility for adhering to safety laws designed to protect miners.	The Litchfield Coal Company contended that there was insufficient evidence to support the claims against them and argued that the instructions given to the jury were erroneous. They asserted that the plaintiff had not demonstrated that the company acted willfully and that negligence was not proven, suggesting that any potential fault lay with the deceased. They requested the court to reverse the judgment based on these grounds.

In 1872, in Chapin, Illinois, commission merchants W. P. Howard & Co. entered into an agreement with Edward P. Fox, who owned a public warehouse. Under this agreement, Howard & Co. would advance funds to Fox to purchase wheat, which Fox would then store in his warehouse until market conditions were favorable for sale. Fox was required to issue warehouse receipts for the wheat stored, which served as a security for advances made by Howard & Co. The transactions continued until January 20, 1873, when Fox issued a new warehouse receipt for wheat that was initially stored by a third party, Mr. Brownlow, who had assigned his policy of insurance to Howard & Co. Following a levy on the wheat by the Morgan County sheriff, William H. Broadwell, under an execution against Fox, the commission merchants sought legal action to reclaim the wheat on the basis that it was legally owned by them due to the warehouse receipts issued. The case revolved around whether the wheat was considered Fox's property at the time of the levy or if it belonged to Howard & Co., raising questions about the legal implications of warehouse receipts and property ownership.	The plaintiffs, W. P. Howard & Co., argued that they held valid warehouse receipts for the wheat, therefore claiming ownership of the grain stored in Fox’s warehouse. They contended that the wheat was acquired with their funds and intended for their benefit, regardless of the timing of the execution levied by the sheriff.	The defendant, Sheriff Broadwell, contended that the wheat remained the property of Edward P. Fox at the time of the levy, arguing that since Fox had initially purchased the wheat, title had not properly passed to Howard & Co. He claimed that without a physical delivery of the property as required by law, Howard & Co. could not assert ownership over the wheat against the execution.

On November 6, 1867, Warren H. Pease, the patentee of an improved well-tube, granted a power of attorney to J. D. Walker and A. B. Peterson to sell his patent rights. This power of attorney stipulated that the attorneys must account for half of the net proceeds from any sales and was irrevocable for two years. On January 21, 1868, Walker sold the patent rights for Ohio to Daniel A. Denison, receiving $50 and a sample filter in return. However, shortly before this sale, on November 21, 1867, Pease had assigned all his rights under the patent to Delos A. Danforth and Charles W. Seeley, making Walker's sale invalid as he lacked authority at the time. The assignment was recorded, and Pease had notified Walker of this transfer before the sale to Denison. Subsequently, Eunice E. Walker, the appellant, appealed the Circuit Court's decree that granted relief against the sale made by Walker to Denison, which was deemed unauthorized and without consideration.	Eunice E. Walker claimed that the deed conveying the house and land from Denison to her was void, as the agent (Walker) acted without authority due to Pease's prior sale of the patent rights. She requested the court to set aside the deed and reconvey the property to Denison and seek relief based on the lack of valid title from her husband’s actions.	The defendant, represented by Denison and his wife, argued that the sale conducted by Walker was valid because the power of attorney was irrevocable for two years, and thus, they contended that Denison had acquired legitimate rights to the property. They maintained that Walker’s authority remained intact until the power was revoked formally.

The legal case "Henry W. Kingsbury, an infant, by his next friend, v. Ambrose E. Burnside et al. and Mary K. Buckner and Simon B. Buckner v. Henry W. Kingsbury et al." was adjudicated in January 1871 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict arose in Cook County, Illinois, following the death of Julius J. B. Kingsbury in June 1856, who left two surviving children: Henry W. Kingsbury and Mary J. Buckner. In May 1861, Simon B. Buckner and his wife, without the knowledge of Henry W. Kingsbury, executed a deed transferring an undivided half of certain real estate to him. The deed was signed, sealed, and acknowledged in Louisville, Kentucky, and subsequently recorded in Chicago without Henry's consent. The key issue was whether the deed had been properly delivered and accepted. Although Henry became aware of the deed in July 1861, by then the deed was recorded without his possession or acknowledgment. Following the death of Henry W. Kingsbury in September 1862 while serving in the U.S. Army, questions arose about his estate and the nature of the title conveyed by the deed. The case initially involved a bill filed by the infant Henry W. Kingsbury seeking to remove a cloud on his title, while cross-bills were filed by the Buckners claiming an implied trust.	The plaintiff, represented by the next friend of Henry W. Kingsbury, argued that the deed executed by Simon and Mary Buckner was invalid as it lacked Henry's knowledge and acceptance. The claim focused on the contention that there was no legally operative deed because it was not properly delivered or accepted. The plaintiff sought a decree to remove the legal cloud over the title resulting from the recording of the deed.	The defendants, including the Buckners, contended that the deed effectively conveyed the property to Henry W. Kingsbury, asserting that his later verbal acknowledgment constituted acceptance, thus creating a resulting trust in favor of Mary K. Buckner. Their defense emphasized that the deed should be recognized and executed because Henry's subsequent actions and communications indicated he accepted the benefits and responsibilities associated with the property.

In the autumn of 1867, in Waukegan, Illinois, John Bishop, who had been engaged in the lumber trade, formed a partnership with F. W. Smith and a carpenter named Griffin to build houses while continuing his business. The firm operated under Smith's name, and it was Smith who primarily managed the enterprise. When John Georgeson, a carpenter, was hired to work for the partnership, he received payment for his work initially but grew concerned about receiving future compensation. His apprehensions led him to quit unless Smith could guarantee payment. After his cessation of work, Georgeson alleged that he was employed by the partnership and that Bishop was a partner with Smith and Griffin in the construction business. The case was initially held in Kane county court, where a jury ruled against the defendants. The defendants then appealed the decision, claiming errors in evidence admission, particularly concerning hearsay and the legal instructions given to the jury about partnership declarations.	John Georgeson, the appellee, claimed that he was part of a partnership that included John Bishop and F. W. Smith, asserting he was employed to work on buildings constructed by the firm. He sought compensation for work performed, relying on the argument that the partnership liable for payment. Georgeson maintained that the collective actions of Smith and Griffin established their partnership status which included Bishop.	John Bishop and F. W. Smith denied the existence of a partnership involving Bishop, asserting that Smith carried on business independently under his name. They contended that Georgeson’s claims were unsubstantiated and argued against his right to compensation from the partnership. Furthermore, they maintained that the admission of hearsay evidence had prejudiced the jury's decision against them.

Amanda S. Taylor filed a case against the Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company following an incident involving the loss of millinery goods shipped from Danville, Maine, to Chicago. The timeline of events traces back to September 20, 1871, when Taylor's husband, Robert Taylor, purchased tickets to travel to Sterling, Illinois, via the railway company. Upon arrival in Chicago, they sought to transfer their goods. Robert Taylor approached an employee at the railway's baggage department, who indicated that Edward Orb, a passenger agent, was responsible for the goods. Orb assured Taylor that he would send the goods to Sterling once they arrived. However, despite multiple checks by Orb, the goods were not picked up; they were left at a dock and ultimately destroyed in a fire on October 8-9, 1871. Throughout the proceedings, it became evident that Orb's role was strictly to solicit passenger business and he had no authority to handle freight, as he did so independently in a separate capacity as an expressman.	The plaintiff claimed that the defendant, as a common carrier, had a duty to watch for the arrival of her goods, obtain them, and ensure their transportation to Sterling. The complaint consisted of one count against the railway company as a common carrier and three special counts regarding the alleged failure to transport the goods, leading to their loss. The plaintiff sought compensation for the value of the lost goods, which were worth approximately $2,000.	The defendant argued that Orb, while being an agent of the company, did not have the authority to represent the railway in matters pertaining to freight or baggage transfer. The defense contended that Orb's role was limited to soliciting passengers and that he had no mandate to ensure the transport of goods. It was emphasized that the company was not bound by Orb's assurances since the act of transporting freight from another carrier was outside the company’s charter and business operations. Thus, the defendant sought dismissal of the plaintiff's claims based on Orb's lack of agency in this matter.

The case of *The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Joseph Pondrom* took place in Illinois in September 1869. The incident occurred on September 17, 1867, when Joseph Pondrom was a passenger on a train operated by the Chicago & Alton Railroad, traveling from Bloomington to Chicago. He had purchased a ticket for a first-class car and boarded the train around noon, arriving in Chicago at 9 PM. As the train approached Twelfth Street in Chicago, it stopped as usual, and Pondrom observed a freight train parked nearby. While sitting by the window, Pondrom claims that a sharp object seized his right arm as it rested on the window sill, pulling it out toward the window and fracturing it above his elbow. Another witness corroborated seeing Pondrom's arm in a vulnerable position but did not identify the object that caused the injury. The case revolved around whether the injury resulted from negligence on the part of the railroad company or contributory negligence by Pondrom.	Joseph Pondrom, the plaintiff, claimed that the railroad company was negligent by allowing freight cars to stand too close to the track, creating a dangerous condition for passengers. He argued that an iron instrument from the freight train struck his arm, causing the injury. Pondrom sought compensation for the injury, asserting that any negligence on his part was minimal compared to that of the railroad company.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company contended that Pondrom's arm was likely positioned outside of the train at the time of the injury, implying contributory negligence on his part. They argued that the allegation of a protruding object from the freight train was improbable. The defense maintained that if Pondrom's arm was outside, he should have been aware of the risks involved; thus, his actions contributed to his injury.

In the case of *Quintus Tibbs et al. v. Charles H. Allen*, the proceedings originated from a partition case that started in the Sangamon Circuit Court in Illinois around 1848. By 1859, after being off the docket for about a decade, the case was reinstated by Judge Rice. A commissioner was tasked with reporting on the sale of properties that were to be partitioned, which he had claimed to have advertised and sold. Several land parcels were sold at different times, but the process faced multiple complications, including changes in the parties involved due to marriages and deaths, many of whom were non-residents of Illinois. By 1860, objections were raised against the approval of the commissioner's report, leading to hearings and continued delays. The case highlighted the lack of notice to the involved parties, the questionable legality of the sales made based on the commissioner's reports, and the absence of proof verifying that proper notice had been issued for the sale. The proceedings lasted for years, with the commissioner failing to account for the funds received from sales effectively, resulting in further contention and the eventual reversal of prior court decisions.	The plaintiffs, Quintus Tibbs and others, alleged that the Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction to approve sales due to the failure to provide proper notice and that critical errors existed in the prior decrees. They claimed that the sales were not legally conducted according to statutory requirements and raised multiple objections concerning the changing interests of the parties involved. They sought to have the previous orders and confirmation of sales reversed, claiming the entire process was flawed and lacked legal standing.	The defendant, Charles H. Allen, argued that the court had the discretion to reinstate the case despite its prior removal from the docket. He maintained that the commissioner's report was valid and that the court's previous confirmation of the sales should be upheld. The defense contended that the legal requirements had been met and suggested that any objections should be dismissed on the grounds of procedural compliance.

In the case of John L. Marsh v. James O. Bennett, the legal proceedings took place in Peoria County, Illinois. The suit was initiated during the June term of 1858 when the plaintiff, John L. Marsh, filed a declaration based on a promissory note against the defendant, James O. Bennett. The note involved specific counts as well as common counts. Following the initial filings, the defendant demurred to the declaration, which the court sustained concerning the first special count but overruled for the others. Subsequently, the plaintiff submitted an amended declaration, prompting the defendant to file a plea asserting that both parties were co-owners of certain lands, and the note served as security for the payment of purchase money upon sale of those lands, which had not yet occurred. The case proceeded to trial in January of 1859, where a jury found in favor of Marsh, awarding him $1,927.36. The defendant's motion for a new trial was denied, leading to an appeal by Bennett.	The plaintiff, John L. Marsh, argued that he deserved payment on a promissory note executed by the defendant. Marsh's claims were founded on the assertion that the agreement underlying the note had been established, implying the existence of a valid consideration that warranted the payment. The plaintiff maintained that he was entitled to the amount specified in the verdict, rooted in the legal relationship between him and the defendant regarding the sale of the jointly owned lands.	The defendant, James O. Bennett, contended that the promissory note lacked consideration because it was tied to a joint ownership agreement of lands that had not yet been sold. He claimed that since the lands remained unsold and no transaction had been completed, there was insufficient basis for the payment demanded by Marsh. Thus, Bennett asserted that the court should reverse the lower court's decision based on this alleged failure of consideration regarding the note.

The case "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Isaac A. Arnold" took place around January 1868 in Illinois, specifically in DeWitt County. The central incident involved a cow owned by Isaac A. Arnold, the plaintiff, which was killed by a train belonging to the Illinois Central Railroad Company, the defendant. The cow had strayed onto a farm owned by Thomas Snell, which was accessible from the public highway due to an insufficient fence. From there, the cow entered onto the railway track through an open crossing where the railroad company had erected bars approximately one year prior to the incident. However, these bars had been down and neglected for three months before the cow was killed. The court noted that the railroad company was negligent for allowing the crossing to remain open without proper barriers, which constituted a violation of the statute that mandated the maintenance of sufficient fencing.	The plaintiff, Isaac A. Arnold, argued that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent in failing to maintain the bars at the crossing, which led to the death of his cow. Despite the cow accessing the farm through an insufficient fence, Arnold contended that under state law, cattle are allowed to roam freely unless private property is enclosed by a statutory fence. Arnold sought compensation for the loss of his cow as a result of the railroad company's negligence.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company, represented by Mr. C. H. Moore, claimed that the cow was a trespasser upon the property of Thomas Snell since it entered through an insufficient fence. The company argued that if Snell was responsible for the bars being down, it should limit Arnold's ability to recover damages. They maintained that the condition of the fence and the actions of the cow's owner impacted the case's outcome, suggesting that they should not be liable for the accident.

This case involves a legal proceeding by mandamus, initiated on June 4, 1871, by William Bonker and John Markle against the Commissioners of Highways of Yorktown, Henry County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Bonker and Markle, own farms adjacent to a public highway that runs east and west through the area. The highway had been established, opened, and continually traveled since 1855 but had been partially obstructed by fences erected by neighboring landowners, George and Sarah Lane. The conflict arose from the assertion that these fences encroached on the highway, obstructing public access. The defendants contended that the highway was never obstructed as alleged and argued that the route the plaintiffs claimed did not align with the highway as established and opened. Testimonies from both sides attempted to clarify the facts surrounding the highway's actual use versus its originally surveyed path.	The plaintiffs, Bonker and Markle, sought a writ of mandamus to compel the highway commissioners to open a roadway that was claimed to be obstructed by the defendants’ fences. They argued that the highway had been properly established and open to the public for many years, and requested that the commissioners remove the obstructions to restore public access.	The defendants claimed that the highway was not obstructed as alleged, defending the location of their fences as being within their property lines and not infringing on the highway. They argued that the highway had been established and open for over sixteen years, and any contention to the contrary was based on an improper understanding of the original survey and legal definitions of the highway’s limits. The defendants asserted that there was no statutory duty for the commissioners to remove obstructions in this case, particularly since the landowners had an honest claim to their property rights.

The case "City of East St. Louis v. Village of New Brighton" was decided on February 4, 1890, within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Appellate Court. The primary parties involved are the City of East St. Louis, a municipal corporation claiming jurisdiction over a designated territory, and the Village of New Brighton, along with its municipal officers, who were alleged to be unlawfully exercising municipal powers in that territory. The city contended that the Village of New Brighton had overstepped its jurisdiction by engaging in activities such as grading streets, constructing sidewalks, levying taxes, and collecting licenses within the boundaries of East St. Louis. The actions led the city to seek an injunction to prevent continued unlawful activities by the Village of New Brighton, claiming these actions were encroaching their rightful jurisdiction.	The City of East St. Louis, as the plaintiff, asserted that the Village of New Brighton and its officers were unlawfully exercising municipal functions within its territory. The city sought an injunction from the court to prevent the village from continuing these actions, arguing that the court had the jurisdiction to provide such relief and that a bill for injunction was the appropriate remedy for this case, rather than quo warranto.	The Village of New Brighton, as the defendant, raised a demurrer against the plaintiff's bill for an injunction, indicating that the allegations made by East St. Louis were not sufficient to support the claim. The defendant appeared to suggest that the matter at hand involved disputed facts which needed to be addressed through a full answer rather than through a demurrer, thereby challenging the jurisdictional claims and the appropriateness of an injunction.

William McMullen filed a case against Mary Gable concerning a piece of land that had been sold during a sheriff's auction due to a debt owed by Gable to a party named Morse. This legal dispute unfolded in January 1868 in Sangamon County, Illinois. The original judgment was made against Gable by a justice of the peace, and after the execution was issued and returned with no property found, the matter escalated to Circuit Court. The sheriff then levied upon the land in question and eventually sold it to Morse for $23.58. Following this, Morse transferred the certificate of purchase to McMullen. In December 1864, Gable sought to invalidate the sale, arguing that the land was more valuable than what it sold for and should have been sold in divisions to maximize its price. The case revealed disputes over the property's actual value and whether fraud occurred during the sale process. The court had to determine the legality of the sale and if the sheriff's actions warranted setting it aside, evaluating the evidence presented about the property's worth and the circumstances surrounding the sale.	The plaintiff, William McMullen, claimed that the sale of the land was fraudulent and invalid. He argued that had the land been divided into smaller parcels, it could have fetched a higher price than what it sold for at auction. McMullen contended that the sheriff acted improperly by not dividing the land into separate lots and demanded that the court set aside the sale based on alleged inadequacy in price and the potential for greater profit had proper procedures been followed.	Mary Gable, the defendant, along with Morse (the original debtor), denied any wrongdoing and asserted that the sale was legal and conducted properly. They maintained that the property, although potentially divided, did not have a confirmed higher value that would have justified the separation. Gable’s defense emphasized that the sheriff had properly notified her about the sale, and no efforts were taken to redeem the property before the sale was finalized. They argued that the stability of judicial sales should be upheld unless clear evidence of fraud or neglect by the sheriff was established.

In 1872, the case of Jackson M. Sheets, Impleaded, etc. v. The People of the State of Illinois was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court originating from the Edgar circuit court. The case focused on a writ of scire facias aimed at enforcing a forfeited recognizance involving John W. Sheets, the principal, and Jackson M. Sheets, the surety. The recognizance required that John W. Sheets appear in court at the next term and continue his attendance until legally discharged. The central issue was whether there was a variance between the terms of the recognizance as described in the writ and the documented evidence presented in court. Specifically, doubts arose regarding the binding language of the recognizance regarding the court appearance and discrepancies in the documented dates. The court scrutinized these claims, ultimately affirming that despite potential variances, the sense of obligation in the recognizance was clear and comprehensible, leading to the recognition of the attendance requirement as valid.	The plaintiff argued that there was a significant variance between the terms of the recognizance as stated in the scire facias and the actual evidence presented in court. They contended that the lack of specificity regarding where the principal was to appear constituted an inconsistency, which should invalidate the scire facias. Furthermore, the plaintiff raised questions about the legitimacy of the dates associated with the recognizance, asserting that the document's discrepancies presented sufficient grounds for challenge.	The defendant contended that there was no real variance or inconsistency between the writ and the recognizance since the latter clearly stated that the principal was obliged to appear and remain in attendance throughout the term. They argued that the alleged discrepancies in dates were merely clerical errors that did not affect the validity of the recognizance. Hence, the defendant maintained that the court’s judgment should uphold the recognizance due to its clear terms, affirming the original ruling of the Edgar circuit court.

Anton Mayer filed a lawsuit against Orpy E. Oldham and John M. Oldham concerning a mortgage foreclosure. The case took place in 1884 in Terre Haute, Indiana, and later in Clark County, Illinois. Mayer claimed that John Oldham had embezzled approximately $810 during his employment as a beer wagon driver. Subsequently, Oldham was arrested following a police inquiry directed by Mayer. To secure Oldham’s release, wife Orpy Oldham was pressured to sign a note for $904.50 and a mortgage on their property as settlement terms. The Oldhams testified that Mayer and his attorney threatened Orpy with her husband’s imprisonment if she did not comply. They maintained that her signature was coerced due to fear for John's fate. Conversely, Mayer and his attorney disputed these claims and denied making any threats. Ultimately, the Circuit Court dismissed Mayer's foreclosure bill, prompting his appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court.	Mayer asserted that he was entitled to the mortgage foreclosure on the grounds that Oldham had failed to repay the embezzled amount secured by the note. He sought to enforce the mortgage as a means to recover the money owed to him due to Oldham's misconduct.	The Oldhams countered Mayer's claims by arguing that the note and mortgage were signed under duress induced by the unlawful detention of John Oldham. They contended that Mayer’s actions constituted an abuse of criminal process, seeking to exploit the threat of legal action to settle a private debt rather than pursue legitimate criminal prosecution.

Charles W. Hunter filed a legal action against Samuel Gilham in the Madison circuit court, Illinois, in 1824. The case arose from two bail bonds that Gilham had executed to the sheriff of Madison County in previous cases where Hunter was the plaintiff. Gilham responded to Hunter's claims by demurring, asserting that the court should not recognize Hunter's standing in the matter. The court sustained Gilham's demurrer, leading Hunter to seek a writ of error to reverse the judgment. The relevant statute indicated that bail bonds should be in the name of the sheriff and that any action on such bonds should commence in the sheriff's name, not in Hunter's name.	Hunter argued that he was entitled to collect on the bail bonds issued by Gilham to the sheriff as he was the plaintiff in the underlying cases. He contended that the court improperly sustained Gilham's demurrer, which prevented him from proceeding with his claims against Gilham.	Gilham's defense rested on the notion that the proper party to the bail bonds was the sheriff, not Hunter. He pointed out that under the 1819 practice act, the bonds were to be enforced in the sheriff's name and highlighted that there was no authority for the sheriff to assign the bonds to Hunter.

The case of **The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Virginius E. Higgins et al.** took place in January 1871 in Illinois. The plaintiff, Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, entered into a bond with defendant Virginius E. Higgins, who was appointed as a freight agent at the Jacksonville station. The bond executed on July 18, 1868, required Higgins to properly manage and account for all money and goods he received in his capacity as freight agent. The Railroad Company alleged that Higgins failed to pay over sums that had come into his possession, notably claiming that he had received amounts due totaling $1,228.56 in December 1868 and $7,800.10 in January 1869. However, it was contended by Higgins that some of this money had been received by a subordinate, S. W. Neely, who was appointed by the Railroad Company and not by Higgins himself. This led to a dispute about the responsibilities arising from the bond and the accountability of Higgins for actions taken by his subordinates. Ultimately, the Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendant, leading the plaintiff to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff's principal claims rested on allegations that Higgins breached the bond by failing to pay over the sums he collected as a freight agent. They pointed out specific amounts that were purportedly unaccounted for, totaling sums due to the company. The plaintiff sought to hold Higgins liable for these amounts, asserting that he had not adequately performed his duties as outlined in the bond.	The defendant, Virginius E. Higgins, presented several defenses. He claimed to have complied with the bond's conditions by rendering an account and paying over all sums received, except for the amount of $1,121.17, which he asserted had been collected by Neely, a subordinate agent of the company. Higgins contended that Neely's actions fell outside his liability under the bond, which explicitly outlined the conditions of accountability for Higgins himself and not for any agent appointed by the plaintiff.

In 1869, in Chicago, Illinois, Leander Read filed an action of assumpsit against Mrs. Walker to recover payment for goods, wares, and merchandise that he alleged were sold and delivered at her request between March 1 and July 3, 1864. Mrs. Walker submitted a special demurrer to Read's declaration, arguing there was insufficient consideration for the promise to pay for the goods, lack of certainty regarding the timing of the transactions, and inadequacy in detailing the location for the claim. The trial court sustained the demurrer in favor of Mrs. Walker, which led to judgment being rendered against Read. Read subsequently appealed this decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking to reverse the lower court's judgment.	Leander Read claimed that he had sold and delivered goods to Mrs. Walker, for which she promised to pay. He argued that the declaration adequately stated the consideration for the contract, that the timing of the transactions was acceptable given the nature of the business, and that the venue was properly identified as Cook County, where Chicago is located. He sought to reverse the judgment against him and reinstated his claim for payment.	Mrs. Walker's defense relied on a special demurrer on three key points: first, that the declaration failed to show sufficient consideration for the alleged promise to pay; second, that the time frame given for the transaction was not sufficiently specific; and third, that the venue did not adequately detail the location of the alleged transactions. She requested that the lower court's judgment be upheld, thereby dismissing Read's claim.

The case "The Chicago Dock Company v. Juliette A. Kinzie" took place in Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. The key individuals involved are Juliette A. Kinzie, the plaintiff and widow of John H. Kinzie, and the defendants, the Chicago Dock Company represented by its owners. John H. Kinzie died in June 1865. The dispute centers around Juliette Kinzie's petition for an assignment of her dower interest in a property, lot thirty-five in Kinzie’s addition to the city of Chicago, which had been conveyed earlier by her late husband to William Jones in 1834. Due to a defective acknowledgment of the deed, Juliette Kinzie retained her dower right. After a series of transactions involving the property, including its transfer to Van H. Higgins and then to the Chicago Dock Company, the central question became whether Juliette's right of dower had been properly released when she executed a deed relinquishing her claim. The court focused on whether Higgins, as a purchaser in possession, had sufficient interest to receive the release, thus determining the validity of Juliette's claim to her dower rights.	Juliette Kinzie, the plaintiff, claims the right to an assignment of her dower in the property at hand. She argues that the acknowledgment of her prior conveyance to William Jones was inadequate, which should maintain her right to claim dower in the property despite the subsequent conveyances. Juliette contends that the deed executed by her to Ogden did not extinguish her dower right because at the time, Ogden was neither the lawful owner nor in privity with the existing title that could justifiably receive a release of her dower.	The Chicago Dock Company, as the defendant, contends that the release of Juliette's dower claim was valid as it had been executed to a party having an equitable interest in the property, namely Ogden. They argue that Ogden's involvement as a purchaser and his subsequent payments created a sufficient relationship to the title, allowing him to receive Juliette’s release. The defense also claims that any objections Juliette may raise concerning the validity of the verbal agreements made regarding property transactions cannot be asserted because they are extraneous to the agreement between Ogden and Higgins, asserting competence under the statute of frauds.

The case "St. Louis & Chicago Railway Company et al. v. D. A. Drennan" originated in Sangamon County, Illinois, with a judgment filed on November 18, 1887. The plaintiff, D. A. Drennan, claimed damages amounting to $4,760.44 for trespassing on his land by contractors of the St. Louis & Chicago Railway Company (the defendant). The railway company had contracted H. H. Cooley & Co., which was managed by Wing, the railway president. These contractors entered Drennan's property to construct a road, creating ditches and embankments without permission. It was revealed that the company had instructed the contractors to halt work on the land near Drennan's property due to a change in the road's planned route. Despite this, the work continued for about ten days. The case involved questions of liability regarding the actions of the contractors as agents of the railway company during the construction project. The key individuals involved included Drennan, Wing, and the contractors, highlighting the responsibilities of the railway in overseeing subcontractors.	D. A. Drennan claimed that the St. Louis & Chicago Railway Company and its contractors trespassed on his land, causing significant damages. He argued that the railway company was responsible for the actions of its contractors and should be held liable for the unauthorized entry and construction activities on his property. Drennan sought financial compensation for the damages incurred from these actions.	The St. Louis & Chicago Railway Company, represented by appellant Wing, contended that they were not directly liable for the trespassing acts of the contractors. They argued that it was not shown that they had given explicit instructions for the contractors to enter Drennan's land. The defendants asserted that the onus was on the plaintiff to prove a direct connection between the contractors' actions and the railway company’s directives, citing the lack of production of essential contracts and documents as a failure in the plaintiff's case.

George F. Work v. William E. Hall et al. is a legal case that took place in Chicago, Illinois, in the 1870s, specifically with proceedings beginning in July 1873 and culminating in a judgment in September 1875. The case involved George F. Work, who held a leasehold interest in certain lots in the city, and his partnership with Thomas Wilson to construct a business block valued at $30,000. Work and Wilson contracted with the petitioners, initially known as Hall & Frost, for materials such as doors, sash, and lumber needed for the building. The petitioners began supplying these materials until the project was completed on April 30, 1873, accumulating debts totaling $2,578.88. Disputes arose over payments when two notes were issued by Work and Wilson, which were not honored, and the petitioners sought to enforce their mechanic's lien claims against the property. The defendants, including Work, the Citizens' Bank, and other parties asserted defenses, claiming the notes accepted constituted full payment, thereby waiving the lien claims. The trial court proceedings grappled with the contractual obligations of the involved parties and the rights of lien holders against subsequent purchasers of the property.	The plaintiffs, Hall & Frost and W. E. Frost & Co., asserted that they had entered into contracts to supply materials for the building erected by Work and Wilson. They sought to enforce their mechanic's liens for the amounts due—to Hall & Frost for $1,037.42 and to W. E. Frost & Co. for $1,308.48—arguing that these liens should be prioritized and enforced against the property.	The defendants contended that the petitioners had accepted promissory notes as payment for their claims, thereby waiving any right to a mechanic's lien. They claimed that the last payment was due prior to the petitioners filing their liens, and that subsequent purchasers (like Edwin Walker) should not be liable for the debts associated with the property, asserting that the plaintiffs had no legal standing to enforce their claims after the lapse of time since the last payment.

In May 1873, at the way station of Chatten in Adams County, Illinois, an accident occurred involving a cow and a passenger train operated by The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company. The cow, which was unlawfully running at large by sufferance of its owner, William H. Barlow, found its way onto the railroad track at a public highway crossing. At approximately 9 PM, as the train approached, the engineer and fireman attempted to signal their approach with a whistle and bell. Despite their efforts to avoid injury, the cow was struck and killed by the train. The plaintiff, Barlow, filed a lawsuit against the railroad company for the cow's value, claiming negligence on the part of the railway in its operation. The central legal issue arose from a statute that made it unlawful for domestic animals to run at large, which had been in effect since the law's enactment, but there was no evidence that Barlow had complied with this statute in his locality.	The plaintiff, William H. Barlow, claimed that the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company acted negligently by failing to operate the train in a manner that would prevent the collision with his cow. Barlow contended that the train was running at an excessive speed and that the railway had a duty to ensure the safety of animals on or near the tracks. He sought compensation for the value of the cow that was killed in the accident.	The defendant, The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company, argued that the plaintiff was not entitled to recovery because the cow was unlawfully on the railway track, which, under the current statute, exempted the company from liability unless evidence was presented that its employees could have prevented the accident after discovering the cow in danger. They maintained that their conduct was not negligent, asserting that they had followed proper procedures to signal their approach and had taken necessary precautions to avoid an accident.

The case "Towner K. Webster, Receiver, v. Noble B. Judah, Assignee" was filed in the Illinois Appellate Court on September 19, 1888. The appellant, Towner K. Webster, appointed as receiver for the estate of Mershon & Bancroft (both citizens of Illinois), sought to recover approximately $2,500 from the New Haven Wire Company, a corporation based in Connecticut that became insolvent. The court appointed S. A. Galpin as the receiver for the New Haven Wire Company on September 6, 1887. After Galpin proved a claim against the estate of another insolvent firm, Sherman & Marsh, the County Court ordered that dividends from this claim be paid to Galpin. Webster filed a petition to direct Judah, the assignee for Sherman & Marsh's estate, to pay him any future dividends from his claim against the New Haven Wire Company. The County Court denied Webster's petitions, leading to this appeal where he argued for the right to garnishee Judah to recover funds from the dividends owed.	Towner K. Webster claimed that as a resident creditor with a lawful claim against the New Haven Wire Company, he was entitled to garnishee the assignee of Sherman & Marsh's estate to secure his dividends. He argued that the County Court improperly denied his petitions based on a prior non-final order and that resident creditors should be prioritized over foreign creditors in collecting debts within Illinois. Webster sought a reversal of the County Court's decision and permission to proceed with his legal claims.	Noble B. Judah defended against Webster's claims by asserting that the County Court's dismissal of Webster's petitions was justified due to prior orders regarding the payment of dividends to Galpin, which had already been executed. He contended that since Galpin had been given title to the dividends awarded, the court could not permit Webster’s garnishment against him. Judah maintained that the insolvency proceedings and established claims by foreign receivers should be respected to ensure proper creditor rights within their jurisdiction.

Prentiss D. Cheney, acting as guardian, entered a legal dispute against Harry W. Roodhouse regarding the estate of Peter Roodhouse, who died intestate on June 9, 1879, in Greene County, Illinois. He left behind a widow and two sons from different marriages as his sole heirs. After Peter's death, the widow, along with one son, Harry, handled the estate's administration and guardianship, which became contentious over time. In 1881, Harry was appointed guardian of his younger brother Benjamin. The controversy arose when Harry submitted his final report as guardian in January 1888, after a significant delay. The report faced criticism for inadequate formatting and incorrect calculations of interest and rents for the ward's land. The case deliberated on whether Harry's handling of the estate was negligent and whether he had fulfilled his responsibilities appropriately. The Circuit Court acknowledged some faults in Harry's management but ultimately determined that the rights of the ward had been adequately protected and the financial transactions accounted for properly.	Prentiss D. Cheney argued that Harry W. Roodhouse failed to correctly report and manage the ward's estate as guardian, asserting that the final report was improperly formatted and did not accurately present balances over the years. Cheney claimed that errors in interest calculations and low assessments of annual rent were detrimental to the ward's interests. He sought corrections to the financial accounting, including an increase in the reported rent and the collection of due interest.	Harry W. Roodhouse defended his actions by asserting that the guardian's report, while not in perfect form, sufficiently showcased the ward's financial interests and that the disputes over interest calculations stemmed from improper expectations of precision. He maintained that the annual rent reported was reasonable based on the evidence and denied any contractual obligation for higher rent. Roodhouse also pointed out that he should not be charged interest during the time the funds were held on court orders and that necessary improvements made to the land warranted reimbursement despite not having prior court approval.

Billings B. Cole, as the administrator, brought a case against William S. Duncan and others in 1871, in the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a mortgage foreclosure. The dispute arose in Champaign County, Illinois, where Duncan had executed a mortgage to secure a debt. After he declared bankruptcy under the federal bankruptcy law of 1868, Duncan pleaded his discharge in bankruptcy as a defense against the foreclosure. The central issue was whether the mortgagee's lien was affected by Duncan's bankruptcy and if the proper parties were included in the case.	The plaintiff, Cole, argued that the discharge in bankruptcy should not bar the foreclosure of the mortgage. He maintained that the provisions of the bankruptcy law did not include a provision that would allow Duncan to void the mortgage without the creditor’s consent. Cole sought to foreclose the mortgage on the grounds that the defendant’s bankruptcy should not interfere with his rightful claim to enforce the lien.	The defendant, Duncan, defended the foreclosure by arguing that his bankruptcy discharge protected him from the enforcement of the mortgage. He claimed that under the Bankruptcy Act, the mortgagee was required to have the lien adjudicated in the bankruptcy court, and since he had been discharged, any further claims against him should be dismissed. Duncan's defense hinged on the assertion that the plaintiff had failed to include the bankruptcy's assignee as a necessary party in the lawsuit.

In September 1868, in Chicago, Illinois, the case of *The Chicago Dock Company et al. v. Thomas H. Foster et al.* arose when plaintiffs Thomas H. Foster and Augustine Lee filed an action of replevin against defendants Moses and Godfrey Snydacker and the Chicago Dock Company. The plaintiffs sought the return of one hundred barrels of flour that they had allegedly sold to F. Smith & Co. However, the flour was deposited with the Chicago Dock Company by Smith & Co. as collateral for a loan from the Snydackers. The plaintiffs argued that the Snydackers, by receiving the flour and its warehouse receipt, did not possess any rightful claim to it since it was obtained under fraudulent circumstances. During the trial without a jury, the court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, finding that the plaintiffs were entitled to the flour. The defendants appealed, arguing that as bona fide purchasers and holders of a warehouse receipt, they held rightful ownership of the flour.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants illegally possessed their flour, which had been sold to F. Smith & Co. They argued that the flour was delivered under a sales contract which could be rescinded due to non-payment. They contended that since Smith & Co. had obtained the flour fraudulently, any interest claimed by the Snydackers or the Chicago Dock Company from possession was invalid. The plaintiffs sought the return of their property and maintained that the legal title remained with them due to the fraudulent circumstances under which the flour was possessed.	The defendants contended that they had lawfully received the flour and its warehouse receipt as part of a valid transaction. They argued that the warehouse receipt issued by the Chicago Dock Company conferred absolute title to the flour, making them bona fide purchasers. They insisted that any alleged fraud by Smith & Co. should not affect their ownership rights since they had no knowledge of the fraudulent acquisition of the flour. Therefore, they requested that the court reverse the judgment in favor of the plaintiffs and recognize their rightful ownership.

The case "Joseph M. Street, Plaintiff in Error, v. Solomon Blue, Defendant in Error" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1828. The litigation originated in Gallatin County, Illinois, involving Joseph M. Street as the plaintiff and Solomon Blue as the defendant. The case underwent considerable legal scrutiny, with a total of three jury trials having been conducted. The plaintiff sought a new trial after the jury had ruled in his favor on two occasions. The matter reached the Supreme Court when the circuit court refused to grant another new trial, prompting the plaintiff to appeal, challenging the discretion exercised by the lower court. The Illinois Supreme Court assessed whether the refusal to grant a new trial constituted an error.	Joseph M. Street, the plaintiff, contended that the circuit court's refusal to grant a new trial was erroneous. He argued that the matter warranted a further review and modification based on the previous jury verdicts favoring him. Street sought to overturn the circuit court's decision, which he believed impeded justice by denying him another opportunity for a trial based on the merits of his case.	Solomon Blue, the defendant, defended against the plaintiff's claims by maintaining that the circuit court acted within its discretion and that no valid grounds were presented for a new trial. The defendant argued that the case had been sufficiently litigated and decided by the jury twice, asserting that the appellate court should respect the jury's verdict and the lower court's ruling, thereby affirming the circuit court's decision.

In 1850, in Kendall County, Illinois, J. Young Scammon (the plaintiff) entered into a legal dispute with Earl Adams and others (the defendants) regarding the collection of a promissory note for $70 originally payable to Jacob Metzker. Scammon, as indicated in the proceedings, had received the note as an attorney for Barker & Best, who were the initial endorsees. After a judgment was rendered against Scammon in a lower court, he appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case revolved around the interpretation of a blank endorsement and the right of the defendant (Metzker) to receive funds from the note given the conditions of the endorsements and previous debts. The defendants presented evidence claiming that the first $35 of the note proceeds was to go to Barker & Best, with the rest entitled to Metzker. Testimony revealed that Metzker gave the note to Barker & Best in partial satisfaction of his debt. When Scammon attempted to collect on the note, the court had to consider the distribution of proceeds as agreed upon by the parties involved and whether the endorsements were sufficient for him to act as a rightful collector of the funds.	J. Young Scammon claimed that he had the legal right to collect the full amount of the promissory note based on the endorsements he received from Barker & Best. He argued that the blank endorsement did not impede his ability to collect, presenting the note as evidence of this right. Scammon also contended that objections regarding the endorsement's validity should have been raised in the lower court and could not be considered at this appellate stage.	The defendants, represented in part by Jacob Metzker, argued that the note was endorsed under an agreement that the first $35 of funds would satisfy Metzker’s debt to Barker & Best, with any remaining balance rightfully owed to Metzker himself. They asserted that since the endorsement was for collection only, Scammon could not claim the entire amount from Metzker. The defendants highlighted the importance of understanding the terms surrounding the endorsement and insisted that the court correctly allowed testimony to clarify these terms.

In the case of Jacob Kahn et al. v. Joseph A. Kohn et al., decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on March 10, 1890, the events unfolded in Wymore, Nebraska. The key individuals involved were A. M. Hayden, a debtor with stores in Wymore and Washington, Kansas, and creditors including Kolin Bros. and Bradley & Metcalf. Hayden owed substantial debts, including $2,400 to Kolin Bros. and $6,350 to Bradley & Metcalf. In an effort to manage his debts, Hayden, under the guidance of an attorney, mortgaged his stock of goods in both stores to these creditors and gave priority to certain debts through additional mortgages. However, Hayden still had many other debts that were not addressed by these arrangements. The appellants, who were other creditors of Hayden, attached the stock in Wymore, arguing that the mortgages were void under Nebraska law pertaining to assignments, particularly because they implied a preference of payments to certain creditors over others. The case deals with the legal interpretation of whether these mortgages were genuine and intended to pay legitimate debts or constituted a violation of the assignment statute. The court ultimately found that there was no evidence to support the claims that the mortgages were intended as preferences.	The appellants, Jacob Kahn and others, argued that the mortgages made by Hayden were void under the Nebraska statute on assignments. They contended that the mortgages created preferential treatment for certain creditors, thereby making them invalid in light of Hayden’s other debts. They sought a judgment against the appellees for trespass resulting from the attachment of the goods that were secured under the contested mortgages.	The appellees, Joseph A. Kohn and others, defended against the claims by asserting that the mortgages given to them were valid and intended to secure bona fide debts. They contended that the structure of the mortgages did not violate Nebraska's assignment laws and that there was no evidence suggesting that the mortgages were created with the intent to defraud other creditors or to establish preferences. They argued that since their mortgages secured real debts, the appellants were liable for the trespass claim associated with the goods they had attached.

The case titled "The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Adoniram J. Randolph" originated in the Logan Circuit Court and involves events that took place on September 21, 1868. Adoniram J. Randolph, the plaintiff, purchased a ticket in Lincoln, Illinois, intending to travel to Atlanta. He boarded a freight train that was in motion, unaware that it would not stop at his desired destination unless signaled. The conductor, who claimed he was not present while tickets were taken, later informed Randolph that the train would not make scheduled stops without prior signals. Randolph and another passenger were advised that they could leap off the train safely as it slowed down. While the other passenger declined to jump and continued to the next station unharmed, Randolph leaped off and suffered injuries. He later sued the railroad company for negligence and was awarded $1,200 in damages, prompting the railroad company's appeal based on several claims of error during the trial.	The plaintiff, Randolph, argued that he was injured due to the railroad's negligence in not properly notifying him that the freight train would not stop at Atlanta. He contended that he acted on the conductor's suggestion to jump from the train for safety when it slowed down. His main legal request was for compensation for the damages incurred as a result of his injuries sustained from the leap, claiming that he was misled regarding the train's stopping practices.	The defendant, Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, argued that Randolph was contributorily negligent for jumping from the train while it was in motion. They asserted that even if the conductor gave an opinion on the safety of jumping, it was Randolph's responsibility to exercise caution and judgment regarding his safety. The railroad claimed that they were not obligated to stop the freight train at every station and that Randolph should have confirmed whether the train would stop at Atlanta before boarding. Their request included a reversal of the jury's decision favoring Randolph.

The case "Jacob L. Wayne et al. v. M. Stern" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision rendered in September 1874. The dispute originated in a justice’s court in Chicago, where Jacob L. Wayne and others (the plaintiffs) initiated a replevin action against M. Stern (the defendant). The plaintiffs recovered a judgment in trover, leading the defendants to appeal to the Superior Court of Cook County in mid-November 1872. However, the appeal was dismissed by the court on December 4, 1872, due to the absence of an affidavit of merits, a requirement they deemed necessary under a statute from 1857. This statute, however, only applied under specific circumstances, primarily to contract actions, and there was no existing statute mandating such affidavits in cases like replevin or trover. The plaintiffs asserted that the general Practice Act, which was enacted in July 1872, made it clear that affidavits of merits were only required in contract actions when the defendant resided in the county. The Supreme Court ultimately found that the prior requirements were abrogated and that dismissing the appeal on this basis was an error.	The plaintiffs argued that the court's dismissal of their appeal due to the lack of an affidavit of merits was an error because there was no binding law requiring such an affidavit for actions in replevin or trover. They asserted that the general Practice Act of 1872 clarified that affidavits of merits were only necessary in contract-related cases and pointed out that the older Cook County statute did not apply to their situation. Therefore, they sought the reversal of the dismissal and the right to have their appeal heard.	The defendant contended that the appeal was correctly dismissed based on the allegation that the plaintiffs failed to file an affidavit of merits as a prerequisite for their right to trial in the Superior Court. They relied on the interpretation of the existing statutes that they believed supported the need for such an affidavit, emphasizing procedural compliance.

This case involves John J. Chenot as the appellant and Charles H. Lefevre as the appellee, heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1846. The proceedings originated in the Circuit Court of St. Clair County, where Lefevre initiated an action of debt against Chenot. The dispute revolved around several promissory notes issued in Phalsburg, France, dating from January 1, 1828, and May 16, 1830. These notes, amounting to twelve hundred francs and other sums, were allegedly executed by Chenot but made payable to Lefevre under different names, specifically “Mr. Hoffman Lefevre” and “Mr. Ch. Hoffman son.” The primary legal question arose over the applicability of the Statute of Limitations and whether Chenot, having resided outside Illinois for a significant duration, could dispute the claims based on the time limits set forth in the Illinois law and French law. Key issues included proof of identity regarding the payee on the notes and whether the defense of the statute could be invoked effectively given the defendant's absences from the state.	Lefevre, the plaintiff, asserted that Chenot was liable for the debts specified in the promissory notes. His primary arguments included that the notes were valid and enforceable and that Chenot, despite his long absence, had not effectively raised the Statute of Limitations as a defense. Lefevre aimed to recover the amounts due as stipulated in the notes, along with interest.	Chenot, the defendant, contended that the claims were barred by the Statute of Limitations because he had not resided in Illinois for the requisite sixteen years following the accrual of the cause of action. He argued that since the cause of action was established while he was out of the state, the legal claims were invalid. Furthermore, he claimed that the notes were void under French law as they were not properly stamped, and he sought dismissal of the case based on these legal grounds.

In 1888, in Chicago, Illinois, the case "The People ex rel. George R. Davis, Collector, v. The City of Chicago" arose when George R. Davis, the tax collector for Cook County, sought judgment against certain properties owned by the city for unpaid taxes and special assessments. The properties in question, known as the "Gage Farm," were acquired by the city of Chicago following the embezzlement of $507,703.56 from city funds by former treasurer David A. Gage in 1871. As part of the compensation for the missing funds, the city received these lands via a trust arrangement. However, the city contended that the properties were exempt from taxation, arguing they were public lands held for governmental purposes. The properties are located outside the corporate limits of Chicago, affecting their tax status. This led to legal disputes over whether the city should indeed be liable for property taxes on lands not being utilized for municipal purposes.	The plaintiff, represented by George R. Davis, claims that the properties in question are subject to taxation under Illinois law, asserting that all property must bear its fair share of tax burden unless explicitly exempted. The plaintiff maintains that the lands do not fall under any exemptions as outlined in state statutes, and thus, should be subjected to the same tax liabilities as private entities.	The defendant, the City of Chicago, argues that the lands represent public money and are held in its governmental capacity, thus should not be taxed. They assert that since the properties were received in trust to compensate for embezzled city funds, they are essential to recovering losses sustained by the city due to Gage’s actions. The city’s stance is that the properties serve public interests and should be exempt per constitutional provisions regarding public land.

In 1871, the case of Joseph Kuhner v. Anthony Griesbaum was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, originating in the Circuit Court of Clinton County. The dispute arose from claims by plaintiff Joseph Kuhner that the defendant Anthony Griesbaum had constructed an obstruction that led to the accumulation of water on Kuhner's land, causing damage. The properties in question were adjoining farms, with Kuhner's land located to the west of Griesbaum's. Evidence presented in court showed that water naturally flowed from Griesbaum's land towards Kuhner's due to the topography of the land, which included a pond on Kuhner’s property. Witness testimonies supported the claim that the water flowed westward, and the county surveyor's findings confirmed the inclination of the land. Despite this, Griesbaum argued that there was no legal obligation for him to drain the water accumulating on Kuhner's land. Kuhner's claims were initially supported by a jury's verdict that awarded him damages of $100, but this was contested by the defendant's appeal.	Joseph Kuhner claimed that Anthony Griesbaum's obstruction of water flow on his property resulted in significant damage. He argued that the natural drainage of water was impeded by Griesbaum's actions, which led to flooding on his land. Kuhner sought damages to compensate for the injuries to his property due to this obstruction.	Anthony Griesbaum contended that the water naturally flowed towards Kuhner's land and there was no legal requirement for him to manage the drainage. He pointed out that the responsibility to drain water lay with Kuhner, who could easily remove obstructions on his own property. Griesbaum argued that the jury's verdict was not supported by the evidence, and thus he requested a new trial based on these grounds.

In September 1876, the case of Arthur B. Meeker et al. v. The Chicago Cast Steel Company took place in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Chicago Cast Steel Company, filed a trover action against defendants Arthur B. Meeker and William L. Brown for the conversion of four hundred and eleven cast steel ingots. The case was tried before a jury, which found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding damages of $3,200. The defendants subsequently appealed the decision, challenging the sufficiency of evidence regarding the value of the ingots and the regularity of the corporate organization of the plaintiff. The appellate court addressed the admissibility of evidence concerning the value of the ingots and reaffirmed the presumption of the plaintiff's corporate existence based on previous legal standards.	The plaintiff, Chicago Cast Steel Company, argued that the defendants unlawfully converted their property, specifically the cast steel ingots, resulting in damages. They requested the court to affirm the jury's verdict and the damage award of $3,200, asserting that the evidence presented allowed the jury to justifiably determine the ingots' value despite the lack of direct proof of their market price.	The defendants, Arthur B. Meeker and William L. Brown, contended that there was insufficient legal evidence to support the jury's verdict regarding the value of the ingots. They argued that the court erroneously admitted evidence related to the conversion costs and argued against the legitimacy of the plaintiff's corporate formation, suggesting that questions about corporate existence could be raised collaterally.

The case "The Mobile and Ohio Railroad Company v. William Davis" took place in Columbia, Monroe County, Illinois, on June 15, 1886. William Davis, the plaintiff, was riding in his wagon pulled by two mules along a public highway from Columbia to Centerville when his team was struck by a passing train at a railway crossing. The impact caused Davis to be thrown from the wagon, resulting in severe bodily injuries. His wagon was rendered unusable, one mule was killed, and the other suffered a broken leg. Davis claimed he was exercising reasonable care to avoid an accident and argued that the accident was due to the negligence of the railroad's employees, who failed to ring a bell or blow a whistle at the required distance before the crossing. The Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of Davis, leading to an appeal by the railroad company arguing various points, including the applicability of a statute concerning railroad crossings in urban areas.	The plaintiff, William Davis, alleged that the Mobile and Ohio Railroad Company was negligent in failing to alert him of the approaching train at the crossing. He claimed the railroad's employees did not ring a bell or blow a whistle at least eighty rods before the crossing, as mandated by Illinois law. Davis sought damages for personal injuries, property damage, and loss of his mule due to the accident, maintaining that he was exercising ordinary care at the time of the incident.	The defendant, Mobile and Ohio Railroad Company, contended that the statutory requirement to ring a bell or blow a whistle did not apply to the road crossing within town limits. They also claimed that Davis was guilty of contributory negligence, arguing that he failed to look and listen for trains before attempting to cross the track. Furthermore, the railroad company argued that the trial court erred in not granting a new trial based on the improper conduct of Davis's attorney, who was seen socializing with one of the jurors during the trial.

The case of John W. Hedenberg v. Kiler K. Jones was decided in September 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict arose in Cook County, Illinois, stemming from a contract made on February 26, 1869, between Kiler K. Jones and two individuals named H. A. Jackson and W. H. Williams. After multiple assignments of the contract, John W. Hedenberg claimed rights to the contract through an assignment from Charles H. Adams on April 12, 1873. The original contract was destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire of October 9, 1871, but its essential terms were acknowledged. Hedenberg filed a bill on May 23, 1873, seeking specific performance to enforce the land sale contract. The defendant, Kiler K. Jones, countered that there had been an abandonment of the contract due to non-payment and lengthy delays, arguing that none of the previous assignees had sought to enforce it. The circuit court dismissed Hedenberg's bill, prompting the appeal and leading to considerations about laches, or unreasonable delay, in seeking to enforce the contract.	The plaintiff, John W. Hedenberg, sought judicial enforcement of a land sale contract, claiming he was an assignee of the contract through a valid chain of assignments. He argued that he should be granted specific performance despite the original contract's destruction, as its essential terms had been established. Hedenberg contended that his entitlement arose from his assignment, and he urged the court to compel Kiler K. Jones to convey the property as agreed.	Kiler K. Jones' primary defense involved asserting that the contract had been effectively abandoned due to substantial delays in its enforcement and a failure to perform its terms. He claimed that there was no serious effort from any assignee to fulfill the contract obligations for over four years, highlighting that the circumstances fundamentally changed, impacting his position as the seller. Jones argued that the plaintiff's claim was inequitable, noting that the previous assignees had never intended or been able to perform the contract, thereby justifying his decision to consider the agreement as forfeited.

Laura A. Dickson filed an action against The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875, seeking damages for a personal injury allegedly caused by the defendant's employees. The incident occurred in 1870, and Dickson initiated the lawsuit on July 6, 1874. The case was presided over by Judge Chauncey L. Higbee in the Circuit Court of Fulton County. The legal question at stake was whether the Limitation Act of 1872, which reduced the statute of limitations for personal injury claims from five years to two years, applied retroactively to actions that occurred prior to its enactment. The defendant argued that since the cause of action accrued more than two years before the suit was filed, the claim was barred by the new limitation period. The court below ruled in favor of the defendant, stating that the limitations of the newer act applied to the case.	Laura A. Dickson's main argument was that the Limitation Act of 1849, which allowed five years to initiate claims for personal injury, should apply to her case because her cause of action accrued before the Limitation Act of 1872 came into effect.
