She sought to overturn the ruling of the lower court, contending that the new act was not intended to retroactively affect rights and liabilities established under the previous law.	The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company contended that the Limitation Act of 1872, which limited the timeframe for filing personal injury claims to two years, should apply to this case since the action was initiated after the law had taken effect. They argued that the prior five-year limitation was effectively repealed and that Dickson's claim should thus be dismissed because it was filed more than two years following the incident.

The case of Town of Vinegar Hill v. John Busson took place in 1866 in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The Town of Vinegar Hill initiated a legal action against John Busson, claiming that he was obstructing a public road that the town asserted had been in use for over twenty years. The case began before a justice of the peace and was subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court, where the jury found in favor of Busson. The town sought to overturn this verdict by appealing to the Illinois Supreme Court, which reviewed the evidence presented regarding the road's public use and the legal requirements for its designation as a public highway. The Supreme Court focused on the conflicting evidence surrounding the road's usage and legal status, ultimately deferring to the jury's decision.	The Town of Vinegar Hill claimed that John Busson had obstructed a public highway that had been in continuous use for over two decades and was recognized as a public road by a survey conducted under town authority. They argued that the obstruction infringed upon public rights, and they sought a judicial decree to remove the obstruction and affirm the road's status as a public highway.	John Busson contended that the jury had incorrectly been instructed regarding the criteria necessary to establish the road as a public highway. He maintained that the plaintiff had failed to prove that the road in question was the same as the one surveyed and used for twenty years. Additionally, Busson argued that even if there were insufficiencies in the instructions given to the jury, other instructions clarified the law sufficiently, thereby rendering the type of confusion alleged by the plaintiff moot.

In November 1866, the case "Milton Dickie et al. v. James H. Carter" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal regarding the validity of a will. The case originated in the probate court of Alexander County, Illinois, where James H. Carter sought to have a document recognized as the last will and testament of Elizabeth Burnett, who had recently passed away. The probate court refused to admit the document for probate, citing concerns about its proper execution and the testatrix's mental competency. Carter appealed this decision, and the matter was subsequently tried in the Circuit Court, where a jury found in favor of establishing the will. The plaintiff, Milton Dickie and others who contested the will, argued that the instrument was not validly executed in compliance with statutory requirements and that Elizabeth Burnett was not of sound mind when the will was made. The jury's verdict led to further legal arguments about the instructions provided during the trial and allegations of improper influence related to Carter's involvement with Burnett at the time the will was created.	The plaintiffs in error, including Milton Dickie, contended that the document presented as Burnett's will did not meet the statutory requirements necessary for a valid will in Illinois. Their main arguments included claims that the will lacked proper execution, as it was not sufficiently witnessed, and they asserted that Burnett was not of sound mind and memory during the time of its creation. They further alleged that the will was unfairly influenced by Carter, who stood to gain under its terms.	The defendant, James H. Carter, maintained that the will was valid and had been properly executed according to the legal standards at the time. He argued that the evidence presented established the execution of the will and the testatrix's mental competency when it was made. Carter contended that the plaintiffs had the burden of proof to show that the will was the result of fraud or undue influence, which they failed to do. He sought to uphold the jury's verdict affirming the will's validity and contested the instructions given during the trial as being overly favorable to the plaintiffs.

Charles Chiniquy brought a legal challenge against the People, represented by Charles P. Swigert, the county collector, regarding the collection of delinquent taxes on lands and lots for the year 1873 in Kankakee County, Illinois. The case was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. Chiniquy and other objectors contested the judgment rendered by the county court, which overruled their objections and upheld the tax assessments. They argued that irregularities existed in the tax collection process, including concerns about the adequacy of notifications and the completeness of the collector’s reports. The court had to examine whether the published notice sufficiently indicated the years for which taxes were due and if the collection adhered to the requirements set forth by statute. Justice Walker provided the court’s opinion, addressing numerous procedural questions and ultimately affirming the lower court's decision to enforce the tax collection.	The plaintiff, Charles Chiniquy, contended that the process of tax collection was flawed due to several irregularities, including the collector's failure to provide adequate notice regarding delinquent taxes, the lack of proper affidavits required by law, and questions regarding the assessment of the land in question. Chiniquy sought to have the judgment against his property overturned on these grounds, arguing that the overall substantial justice of the tax collection was not met.	The defendant, represented by Charles P. Swigert, maintained that the collector’s notice met statutory requirements and that the objections raised by Chiniquy did not affect the substantial justice of the tax itself. They argued that any procedural omissions were remedied by legislative provisions and that the burden to show any injustice in the assessment fell on Chiniquy. The defense asserted that the assessments, as indicated in the collector’s return, were valid and that the court had the authority to enforce the tax collection.

In 1889, in Cock County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Matthias Schmidt and William M. Hughes concerning a claim of malicious prosecution. Schmidt, the plaintiff, alleged that Hughes caused his wrongful arrest on charges of larceny. After the arrest, Schmidt faced challenges in obtaining steady employment as a plasterer and bricklayer due to the stigma of the criminal charge. Schmidt's legal team argued that he should be permitted to present evidence of damages incurred after initiating the lawsuit. The court's examination revealed that there was sufficient evidence to support Schmidt's claims regarding the emotional and economic harm caused by the arrest. The case was presided over by Judge A. H. Waterman and later appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court.	Matthias Schmidt claimed that William M. Hughes maliciously prosecuted him by initiating false larceny charges that led to his arrest. He asserted that this prosecution caused him significant damages, including loss of employment opportunities and emotional distress. Schmidt sought compensation for the damages he suffered as a result of the arrest, highlighting the ongoing impact even after the lawsuit was filed.	William M. Hughes defended himself by contending that he had probable cause to believe that Schmidt was guilty of the theft based on information he received from witnesses. Hughes argued that his actions were justified given the circumstances surrounding the allegations and maintained that even if he had a personal vendetta against Schmidt, it did not negate the existence of probable cause for his actions. He requested the court to dismiss Schmidt's claims on the grounds that the accusations were made in good faith based on credible evidence.

Edwin Taylor Chapman and Annie Chapman were involved in a divorce case filed in Cook County, Illinois. The proceedings began when Annie filed for divorce on August 23, 1886, alleging that Edwin committed adultery. The trial took place in January 1888, and the court had to determine whether Annie was entitled to a divorce based on Edwin's alleged misconduct and her residency status in Illinois. The jury ultimately sided with Annie based on the evidence presented. A significant aspect of the case was the denial of Edwin's request to introduce letters written by Annie, which the court found irrelevant. The court also dismissed claims of newly discovered evidence regarding Annie's employment as an actress, asserting that there was no diligence shown in obtaining this evidence prior to the trial. The decision of the jury was deemed satisfactory as long as no procedural errors were made, leading to the court affirming their judgment.	Annie Chapman, the plaintiff, claimed that her husband, Edwin Taylor Chapman, had committed adultery, which was the grounds for her request for a divorce. She argued that she was a resident of the state at the time of filing the divorce suit and presented evidence supporting her claims against Edwin. Furthermore, she contested the relevance of evidence that Edwin sought to introduce regarding her character and employment.	Edwin Taylor Chapman, the defendant, contested the divorce on the basis that he did not commit adultery. He sought to introduce letters from Annie to aid his defense, arguing that they showed her potential consent to his behavior, but the court found this defense not sufficiently relevant and refused to admit the letters. Edwin also claimed that there was newly discovered evidence concerning Annie's engagements as an actress, which he believed would support his case, but the court determined this was not disclosed due to a lack of diligence.

In 1847, in Madison, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Margaret B. Lane and James P. Erskine regarding a mortgage foreclosure. Lane was a partner in a business with Hunt and Ridgely under the name Hunt, Ridgely & Co. This firm incurred debts to Erskine & Eichelberger, leading to its dissolution. Subsequently, Hunt and Lane formed a new partnership, John F. Hunt & Co., which assumed the previous firm's liabilities. After further dissolution, Lane agreed to discharge all liabilities and mortgaged property to Hunt as indemnity. A judgment was later rendered against Lane, Hunt, and Ridgely, prompting Erskine & Eichelberger to pursue foreclosure on the mortgaged property. During the proceedings, Lane passed away, leading to a dispute over whether the heirs were properly included in the case. Lane's wife claimed ownership of the mortgaged premises, which was contested. The court faced jurisdictional questions regarding Lane's heirs' necessity in the proceedings.	The plaintiffs, led by Erskine, claimed that they were entitled to foreclose the mortgage on property owned by Lane. They argued that Lane had assumed responsibility for the partnership's debts and that they had filed the necessary legal actions to enforce their judgment. They sought a decree to enforce the foreclosure despite Lane's death, asserting the validity of the mortgage and the debt owed.	The defendants contended that the mortgaged property belonged solely to Mrs. Lane at the time of the mortgage's execution, thus challenging the right of the plaintiffs to foreclose. They argued that Lane's death necessitated the involvement of his heirs in the proceedings, as he was the mortgagor, making their presence essential for a valid decree of foreclosure. They sought to have the case dismissed or to introduce the necessary parties to the suit.

In 1888, in Clay County, Illinois, the case of Henry Kluthe et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois arose when the appellants were charged with unlawfully and intentionally breaking and defacing a fence owned by Lewis Feith. The key individuals involved in this case included the appellants Henry Kluthe and others, as well as Lewis Feith. The charges stemmed from an incident where it was alleged that Kluthe and another individual named Avns either kicked or pulled on the fence, which was part of a property dispute likely related to claims about a nearby highway. Following their trial in the County Court of Clay, they were found guilty and fined. Dissatisfied with the outcome, the appellants appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court, contending that the evidence did not sufficiently support the charges against them.	The plaintiffs, representing the State of Illinois, claimed that the defendants (Henry Kluthe et al.) had engaged in malicious mischief by breaking and defacing the fence owned by Lewis Feith. They sought to establish the defendants' liability for the alleged vandalism, arguing that their actions constituted unlawful behavior that warranted penalties.	The defendants argued that the evidence presented in court was insufficient to support the charges of breaking and defacing the fence. They pointed out that while the testimony indicated that one of them was seen kicking the fence and the other was pulling on the wire, there was no direct evidence linking their actions to the actual damage. They contended that the evidence merely suggested a possible motivation for the fence being broken, without conclusively proving their involvement.

The case "The State of Illinois v. James M. Allen; Same v. Charles Atkinson" was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. It originated from the County Court of Henry County, where the county treasurer sought judgments against properties of the appellees for unpaid taxes from 1865. The appellees (Allen and Atkinson) objected to the tax judgments, claiming that the board of supervisors improperly equalized property assessments by making specific dollar adjustments per acre rather than assessing the property values uniformly based on a percentage. They argued that these changes resulted in an unequal burden across property values in towns including Loraine, Yorktown, and Phoenix. After their objections were overruled in the County Court, the case was appealed to the Circuit Court, which sustained their objections and refused to render judgments. The state then appealed to the Supreme Court of Illinois, which addressed the legality of the assessment equalizations and tax levies made by the town authorities, examining the restrictions on the powers of local government regarding property tax assessments.	The State of Illinois, as the appellant, claimed that the county treasurer's applications for judgment against the properties for delinquent taxes were valid. They argued that the actions of the board of supervisors in equalizing assessments were within lawful bounds and that the adjustments made—adding or deducting per acre—were legitimate. The state sought to reverse the Circuit Court's judgment that upheld the appellees' objections and to enforce the tax judgments against the properties in question.	The defendants, James M. Allen and Charles Atkinson, contended that the equalization methods used by the board of supervisors were unauthorized and rendered the entire assessment void. They argued that changes made to the assessment values violated the law, as they did not conform to statutory requirements for equalization based on proportional valuation. The defendants maintained that the tax levies imposed by town authorities were either improperly extended or exceeded the authority granted by law, thus rendering the actions invalid.

The legal case, "The Cheltenham Stone and Gravel Company v. The Gates Iron Works," took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered on November 9, 1887. The dispute arose from a transaction initiated on March 19, 1885, where the Gates Iron Works, a corporation, purchased goods from the Cheltenham Stone and Gravel Company amounting to $3,490.97. During the course of dealings, the defendant made payments totaling $2,795, leaving a balance of about $1,200 due by August. The president of the Cheltenham Stone and Gravel Company sought payment on multiple occasions but was unsuccessful. Eventually, the defendant provided a promissory note worth $1,000, issued by the insolvent Cheltenham Improvement Company. The plaintiff accepted this note and credited it against the defendant's account. After the note defaulted and the plaintiff could not collect on it, the Cheltenham Stone and Gravel Company charged the amount back to the Gates Iron Works along with an undisputed balance of $145.97. The trial focused on whether the note should be considered an absolute payment of the indebtedness owed by the defendant.	The plaintiff, Cheltenham Stone and Gravel Company, claimed that despite receiving a promissory note from the Cheltenham Improvement Company as partial payment, it did not constitute an absolute discharge of the defendant’s debt. They argued that the payment was conditional—only valid if the note was honored at maturity. As the note was not paid and the company was unable to collect it, the plaintiff sought to recover the outstanding balance, totaling $1,145.97, including the earlier undisputed amount of $145.97.	The defendant, Gates Iron Works, contended that the promissory note provided was meant to serve as an absolute payment of the debt owed to the plaintiff. They argued that the acceptance of the note discharged their liability, asserting that the subsequent recording of the note on the account justified their claim that the debt was satisfied. They disputed the plaintiff's interpretation of the agreement regarding the conditions under which the payment was accepted.

In 1868, a legal dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving land ownership claims between Joseph W. Rucker and Sarah Dooley, among others. The case's roots trace back to a sheriff's sale in 1838, where land was sold under a judgment favoring a creditor, with the certificate of purchase eventually assigned to H. L. Rucker, Joseph's brother. It was alleged that this certificate was assigned to Joseph W. Rucker in 1855, but he did not pursue a deed for the land until January 6, 1868. Meanwhile, the land had been continuously transferred among numerous purchasers, culminating in John Dooley purchasing the property in 1859, and eventually selling part of it to Weston, Davis, and Hambleton in November 1867. They took possession of the land with Dooley's consent. However, shortly after the deed was recorded by Rucker, it created doubt regarding the Dooley family's title. Dooley's family actively held possession, and Rucker's intent to establish ownership led to a suit to quiet the title, claiming Rucker's deed was a cloud on their title. The Illinois Supreme Court was asked to reverse a decision made by the Superior Court of Chicago, which had declared Rucker's deed void and fraudulent.	Joseph W. Rucker, the plaintiff, claimed that the sheriff's deed he received for the land should establish his legal title against Sarah Dooley and her co-defendants. He argued that he had the right to a deed based on the historical certificate of purchase, maintaining that there is no defined time limit in law for obtaining such a deed, even after extensive delays, and sought to set aside the court's decision that invalidated his title.	Sarah Dooley and the other defendants contended that the sheriff's deed held by Rucker was invalid due to the significant lapse of time since the original certificate was issued, which prevented enforcement of such a stale claim. They argued that the law protects the rights of subsequent bona fide purchasers who acted without knowledge of Rucker's claim and that Rucker's deed created an unwarranted cloud on their rightful ownership of the property.

On March 27, 1865, the Town of Olney, Illinois, enacted an ordinance mandating that anyone operating as a substitute broker or recruiting agent must pay a fee of $600 to the town's treasurer. This payment was necessary to obtain a license for a three-month period, with heavy penalties outlined for those engaging in the business without a license—fines up to $100 and potential imprisonment for 100 days for each infraction. Harvey and Boyd, engaged in this business, paid the fee under protest, asserting they would pursue legal action to recover the payment. They received a receipt from the treasurer, and subsequently, a license was issued. The plaintiffs contended that the ordinance was beyond the town's power, rendering their payment made under threat of prosecution rather than voluntarily. The court had to determine whether their payment was compulsory and whether the town’s defenses were valid.	The plaintiffs, Harvey and Boyd, argued that their payment of $600 was made under duress due to threats of prosecution for engaging in lawful business without a proper license under an invalid ordinance. They seek to recover the amount paid, asserting that their payment was not voluntary, as it was made to avoid the immediate risk of fines and imprisonment.	The defendants, represented by the Town of Olney, contended that since the ordinance was void, the payment must be viewed as voluntary and not recoverable. They argued that the payment made to the treasurer could not render the corporation liable, as the ordinance was ineffectively enacted. They also claimed that the plaintiffs voluntarily chose to pay and that the town had the authority to enact the ordinance.

In September 1873, the case of Richard Cole v. Calvin M. Favorite was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. Richard Cole stored 1,190 barrels with Favorite & Son in Chicago under an agreement that the barrels would be insured against fire losses until September 1, 1865. Cole was to pay for storage and any insurance costs. After Cole requested a receipt for the barrels for loan purposes, Favorite provided a receipt stating the barrels would be held until the specified date, which was crucial to the case later on. On October 19, 1865, the warehouse caught fire, destroying the barrels. Subsequently, Cole and Favorite agreed to pursue claims against the insurance companies for the lost property. However, the case against the insurers failed because the receipt given to Cole indicated that the insurance agreement was only valid until September 1, 1865. Despite Favorite fulfilling his obligation to insure the goods, the loss was attributed to the agreed expiration of the insurance contract. The court found that since there was no further agreement to insure after the cutoff date, Cole could not hold Favorite liable for the lost barrels.	Richard Cole, the plaintiff, claimed that Calvin M. Favorite breached their contract by failing to insure the 1,190 barrels he had stored. Cole asserted that Favorite was supposed to have the barrels insured in responsible insurance companies, and since they were destroyed in a fire, he sought damages for their value, arguing that Favorite's negligence in not renewing the insurance made him liable for the loss.	Calvin M. Favorite, the defendant, contended that he fulfilled his contractual obligation by obtaining insurance for the barrels until the agreed expiration date. After the barrels were destroyed, he acted in good faith to recover damages from the insurance companies on Cole's behalf. Favorite argued that the agreement to insure did not extend beyond September 1, 1865, and emphasized that any failure to recover from the insurers was not due to his negligence but rather the receipt's stipulation indicating the insurance coverage had ended before the fire.

Eber C. Preble filed a legal case against Crayton H. Conger and others in September 1872 regarding a dispute over a chattel mortgage and property transactions. The events mainly took place in Chicago, Illinois. Preble had purchased property from Morton B. Hull that was subject to existing debts, including a chattel mortgage to Jacob B. Shepherd & Co. for $7,500. Preble sought a written agreement from Conger, Walworth & Co., who had acted as guarantors for a contract related to hotel construction, indicating that once all debts were satisfied, the mortgage would be released. An indebtedness of around $7,000 was established, secured by the mortgage given to Conger, Walworth & Co. However, after Preble’s purchase, Conger claimed that the mortgage was still valid against Preble, asserting that the indebtedness was ongoing. Preble attempted to argue that Conger was estopped from enforcing the mortgage against him based on their prior assurances, leading to this litigation.	Preble's main argument revolved around the assertion that Conger and his firm led him to believe they would release the mortgage upon the completion of the hotel project. He requested the court to enjoin Conger, Walworth & Co. from proceeding against the mortgaged property and to declare that the mortgage should not be enforceable against him due to the claimed assurances made prior to his purchase of the property.	Conger, Walworth & Co. defended their position by arguing that Preble had misinterpreted any assurances given about the mortgage. They contended that they had a legitimate claim under the mortgage, which was based on substantial indebtedness associated with the hotel contract. Additionally, they stated that Preble was fully aware of the risks and liabilities associated with his purchase and could not rely on verbal statements to counteract the legal written agreements that were executed.

Albert Hurzfield and others filed a case against David Cohen in the Illinois Appellate Court on April 7, 1886. The court action took place in Illinois and involved various individuals led by the appellants, Hurzfield et al. The case was assigned docket number No. 47-2317 and reported in volume 18 of the Illinois Appellate Court Reports, on page 651. The oral arguments and written submissions were presented by attorneys representing both parties, with the appellants being represented by Messrs. Flower, Remy & Gregory and Mr. Fred. L. Brooks, while Mr. Cohen was represented by Messrs. Byam, Wein-SOHENK & GrIESBURG. After reviewing the case, the court found no merit in the claims raised by Hurzfield and his associates against Cohen.	The plaintiffs, Albert Hurzfield and others, contended that David Cohen had failed to meet certain obligations or legal standards. They sought relief or damages but did not provide detailed specifics in the summary. Their main legal argument hinged on perceived errors or omissions in Cohen's actions that they believed warranted a favorable judgment in their favor.	David Cohen, the defendant, countered the claims made by Hurzfield et al. by arguing that the record provided no support for the points raised by the appellants. He maintained that the plaintiffs' allegations lacked substantiation and requested that the court affirm the decision of the lower court, indicating that no valid claims were put forth against him.

Henry McNeil owned a tract of land in Ogle County, Illinois, and sought to secure a loan to pay off judgments against his property. In this context, he engaged Richard McGoon, who agreed to provide the loan but needed to acquire the property after it was sold at a sheriff's sale due to these judgments. McGoon purchased the land but, due to a lack of formal documentation – he neither received a certificate of purchase nor executed a bond to re-convey the property back to McNeil upon repayment – the arrangement remained somewhat informal (verbal). Subsequently, McNeil attempted to change the loan to Jacob Reigard by having McGoon convey the land to Reigard, who along with McNeil had an understanding that the transaction was more of a security for a loan than a traditional purchase. After Reigard collected rents on the property but refused to return it to McNeil upon repayment, McNeil filed a suit in equity seeking to have the transaction declared a mortgage, allowing him to redeem the property and account for the rents collected. The case moved through legal proceedings, with the Circuit Court ultimately ruling on the nature of the transaction.	The plaintiff, Henry McNeil, claimed that the conveyance from McGoon to Reigard was essentially a mortgage, rather than a true sale of property. He argued that the original agreement between him and McGoon was intended to secure a loan with the property as collateral. McNeil sought to have the court declare the sheriff’s deed a mortgage, allowing for his redemption rights and requesting an accounting of rents that Reigard collected from the property.	Jacob Reigard, the defendant, contended that he owned the land outright and denied that the transaction constituted a mortgage. He argued that the absence of formal written agreements (bond and certificate of purchase) meant that the transaction was legitimate and completed. Reigard claimed to have acquired the property free of McNeil’s claims and that he was under no obligation to reconvey the land, asserting his ownership rights.

The case "Frank O. Miller et al. v. The Robinson Bank et al." took place in Crawford County, Illinois, with the decision issued on February 4, 1890. The key individuals involved include Frank O. Miller and John S. Emmons, the partners running a mill, and The Robinson Bank, claiming debts from the partnership. The origin of the case traces back to the formation of a partnership by Miller, Emmons, and a predecessor, Newton, for operating a mill and selling grain. The partnership incurred significant debts, mainly to the Robinson Bank, totaling approximately $21,585.23, to which both Miller and Emmons paid amounts of $1,800 each towards. The disputes largely centered around the individual mortgages secured by Emmons and Miller to their individual creditors for debts incurred separately, which the bank contended were void concerning the firm debts. The court also dealt with multiple cross-bills initiated by the various mortgagees and creditors regarding the partnerships' assets and the validity of the mortgages against the claims of the bank.	The Robinson Bank claimed that the mortgages executed by Emmons and Miller were invalid as they were taken out for individual debts without the knowledge or consent of the other partners, specifically Newton. The bank argued that the debts they held should take precedence and sought to have the mortgages canceled, asserting that the partnership property should first be used to satisfy the firm's debts before addressing individual obligations.	The defendants, including Emmons and Miller, contended that the mortgages were legitimate as they secured bona fide debts that should be honored. They argued that the partnership primarily dealt with individual debts, and their mortgages should maintain their validity. They also submitted various cross-bills to foreclose their respective mortgages, asserting that the bank's claims should not diminish their secured interests in the property.

The case of John B. Miller v. Thomas L. Price took place in Clinton County, Illinois, in November 1866. The central issue involved a dispute over possession of specific lands claimed by both parties, each asserting title through Elisha Duncan. On July 7, 1859, Duncan executed a deed of trust to Nathaniel Holmes regarding the property. Due to irregularities, Duncan subsequently created another deed of trust dated July 11, 1859. Following these transactions, a deed of release was issued by Holmes to Duncan on July 14, 1859, which intended to release the first deed of trust. However, the records indicated some inconsistencies regarding the dates and the operations of these deeds. The plaintiff, Miller, argued that the release applied to the earlier deed, thus justifying his claim to the land. Conversely, Price claimed an unchallenged title resulting from a sale by Holmes under the later deed of trust. Ultimately, the court examined the records to determine their integrity and came to a conclusion about the rightful owner of the property.	John B. Miller contended that his title to the land was valid as it stemmed from an appropriate release by Holmes of a previous deed of trust. He argued that the subsequent deed of trust created confusion but that the release intended to clear the title to the property he received from Duncan. Miller requested the court to recognize his title and grant him possession of the land based on the deed of release.	Thomas L. Price defended his claim to the property by asserting that his title derived from a legitimate sale under the deed of trust dated July 11, 1859, which he maintained was still in effect because the release document referenced an earlier deed that had been altered in the recording process. Price contended that the judicial interpretation of the deed of release favored his claim, and he requested the court to affirm his rightful ownership of the property.

On March 10, 1869, the Illinois legislature passed an act to incorporate the Danville, Olney and Ohio River Railroad Company, granting it the authority to construct a railroad from Danville through Olney to the Ohio River. On October 11, 1881, the Olney city council passed an ordinance permitting the railroad to lay tracks along Camp Avenue, under specific conditions aimed at protecting the public's rights to the street. The plaintiff, Mary Wharf, owned two residential lots adjacent to Camp Avenue and claimed that the construction and operation of the railroad diminished her property's value due to disturbances from passing trains, obstructed views, and changes in street grade, impacting access to her property. Consequently, she sued the city of Olney for damages, asserting that the city was liable for the depreciation of her property value stemming from the railroad's operation.	Mary Wharf contended that the city of Olney was liable for the damages her property sustained due to the construction and operation of the railroad. She argued that the noise and disturbance from the trains, as well as obstructed views from her residential lots, constituted a significant depreciation in property value. The primary legal request was for the court to award her damages corresponding to the decline in property value caused by the railroad.	The City of Olney argued that it granted the right of way for the railroad's construction lawfully and took necessary precautions required by the ordinance to protect the interests of abutting property owners. The city contended that it had no negligence in granting the right to the railroad and that any damages incurred should be sought from the railroad company rather than the city itself. It maintained that the operation of the railroad constituted a legitimate use of the street and that the city was not liable for any resulting property damage.

On November 11, 1886, Owen W. Thomas passed away, leaving behind a widow, Sarah Thomas, and several children, including Abraham E. Thomas, Hannah E. Galbraith, Esther E. Wilkinson, Mary J. Wilkinson, and Hannah E. Witt. After his death, his will, executed on March 18, 1886, was not admitted to probate due to his subsequent marriage, and his estate was treated as intestate. Esther F. Wilkinson and her siblings brought a bill for partitioning Owen's real estate, claiming that some heirs had received advancements that ought to be deducted from their shares. The case was referred to a master who reported on the distributions among the heirs, suggesting that the widow receive dower and the rest be divided equally among the heirs, minus the amounts claimed as advancements. This report faced exceptions, which were first overruled but ultimately addressed by the court, leading to a decree for dower and an equal division of the remaining estate among the six heirs.	The plaintiffs, Esther F. Wilkinson, Mary J. Wilkinson, and Anna E. Witt, argued that five heirs had previously received advancements against their inheritance from Owen W. Thomas, which should be deducted from their shares during the estate's partition. They sought a formal partition of the real estate, asserting their rights in the distribution process based on the alleged advancements.	The defendants, including the widow Sarah Thomas and other heirs, contended that the claims of advancements made by the plaintiffs were unsubstantiated as there was no written evidence indicating that the gifts were meant as advancements. They argued that previous conveyances were gifts and not legally recognized advancements under the law since they lacked proper documentation as required by the statute.

The case "Moses Casler et al. v. Asahel B. Byers" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on October 31, 1889. The dispute originated from a mortgage foreclosure initiated by Asahel B. Byers against Moses Casler and his wife, Catherine M. Casler. The mortgage was executed on April 8, 1876, to B. L. Divine for 120 acres of land in DeKalb County, Illinois. It was intended to secure a promissory note of $3,350 due five years after its execution. After Divine's death, the note was assigned to Byers, who sought to foreclose the mortgage when the Caslers failed to meet their obligations. Initially, the case was heard in the DeKalb circuit court and, upon the Caslers' request, was transferred to Winnebago County. The circuit court ruled against the Caslers, leading to an appeal. Throughout the proceedings, the validity of the mortgage, including waivers of homestead rights by the Caslers and amounts owed, were contested by the plaintiffs. The circuit court confirmed a decree for foreclosure, asserting that enough legal grounds were established to justify the mortgage and the associated debts.	The plaintiffs, Moses and Catherine Casler, argued primarily that the mortgage should be invalidated as it didn't properly show a waiver of their homestead rights on the contested land in township 41. They contended that the mortgage described land in one township while the land existed in another, claiming they should be allowed to redeem the property by paying the actual debt owed, regardless of previous agreements made. Additionally, they challenged the amount claimed due on the mortgage, believing it to be inflated beyond what was owed.	Asahel B. Byers, the defendant, maintained that the mortgage was valid and clearly indicated a waiver of homestead rights through its original wording and subsequent acknowledgments. Byers argued that Moses Casler's conduct and statements during the dealings with B. L. Divine estopped him from contesting the amount owed, as he had previously acknowledged a debt of $4,500. Furthermore, Byers asserted that Catherine M. Casler, as a party to the mortgage, had also waived her rights and therefore could not claim a right of redemption for an amount less than what was owed.

The case "Toledo, Wabash & Western Railway Company v. Arthur Harmon" took place in January 1868 in Morgan County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Arthur Harmon, was involved in an incident where he was injured after his horse team panicked due to the sudden release of steam from a train's locomotive, which occurred as he was crossing the railway track. The steam was let off by the engineer of the railway company, and Harmon claimed that it was done wantonly and maliciously. This case followed an initial trial where a jury ruled in favor of Harmon, awarding him $500 in damages. The railway company appealed the decision, leading to further court proceedings.	The plaintiff, Arthur Harmon, contended that the railway company was liable for his injuries due to the reckless actions of its engineer, who released steam from the locomotive with the intent to frighten his horses, leading to their panic and subsequent injuries. He argued that the engineer acted negligently and should be held responsible for the harm caused, seeking damages for the injuries incurred.	The defendant, Toledo, Wabash & Western Railway Company, argued that the actions of the engineer were outside the scope of his employment and that Harmon may have contributed to the accident through his own negligence. They maintained that the engineer's actions were not authorized by the company and thus the company should not be held liable for the incident. Additional defenses included assertions about the nature of the engineer's actions being standard or necessary for operating the steam engine.

In 1861, Frances Morgan filed a case against John M. Clayton regarding a property dispute in Chicago, Illinois. The conflict involved the equity of redemption of a property originally mortgaged to George W. Lay, Sen. in December 1856. Horatio N. Heald, the initial owner, failed to pay interest on the mortgage and defaulted on other obligations. Lay, Jr., the son of the mortgagee, proposed buying the property via a trustee sale, which occurred in May 1861. He then conveyed the title to Clayton through a quit-claim deed in 1863. Morgan sought to redeem the property, arguing that Clayton's claim to the title was invalid due to his prior knowledge of existing equity interests. The case was adjudicated in Cook County, with the trial presided by Judge Erastus S. Williams. The legal discussions revolved around whether Clayton was a bona fide purchaser without notice of prior equities and if Lay had duly executed the trust when selling the property.	Frances Morgan claimed that Clayton lacked a legitimate title to the property because it was sold without proper authority and that he had constructive notice of existing equity interests. She requested the court to grant her the right to redeem the property, asserting that Clayton’s defenses were unfounded as he acted as a trustee in violation of the trust obligations.	John M. Clayton argued that he was a bona fide purchaser who had no notice of prior claims at the time of purchase. He maintained that the sale conducted by Lay, Jr. was valid and that he had adhered to the terms of the trust. Clayton contended that the delay in Morgan's objections implied acquiescence to his claim and requested that the court dismiss Morgan's claims regarding the redemption of the property.

In the case of Lake Erie and Western Railway Company v. Alphonso A. Oakes, which took place in 1882, the dispute arose regarding damaged goods during transportation. The key individuals involved included Alphonso A. Oakes (the plaintiff) and representatives from the Lake Erie and Western Railway Company (the defendant). The transportation of goods began in Cincinnati and was destined for Bloomington, where the plaintiff alleged the goods had arrived damaged. The car transporting these goods first came onto the defendant's railway in Lima, Ohio. The plaintiff claimed that the goods were in good condition when delivered to the initial carrier, but insufficient evidence was presented about their condition upon shipping. The court focused on the burden of proof concerning whether the defendant was responsible for the damage incurred while the goods were in their custody.	The plaintiff, Alphonso A. Oakes, argued that the Lake Erie and Western Railway Company was responsible for the damage to his goods while they were in transit. He sought compensation by providing evidence that the goods were in good condition prior to shipment. The main legal request was for the damages incurred during the carriage of the goods under the defendant’s supervision.	The Lake Erie and Western Railway Company contended that the plaintiff failed to provide sufficient evidence proving the goods were damaged while they were in the defendant's possession. They highlighted that there was no shipping bill or receipt demonstrating the condition of the goods at the time they were taken into the defendant's care. The defendant also asserted that the burden of proof rested on the plaintiff to establish that the damage occurred during their handling.

The case "David Honeyman, Impleaded, etc. v. Samuel Jarvis, Guardian, etc." took place in Mercer County, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. The primary parties involved were the plaintiff, David Honeyman, and the defendant, Samuel Jarvis, who served as a guardian. The dispute centered around a promissory note for which Honeyman was the original payee and Jarvis was one of the makers. Jarvis denied the validity of the note, arguing that it lacked consideration, meaning there was no underlying obligation or benefit. He submitted several special pleas, claiming that he was not indebted to Honeyman at the time of the note's issuance and that his promise was merely a "naked promise" without consideration. The court below sustained a general demurrer (a ruling that the plea was insufficient to support a legal defense), which led to Jarvis appealing the decision. The primary legal question addressed was whether the pleas submitted by Jarvis adequately met the standards required under Illinois law regarding failure of consideration and the requirements of pleading.	The plaintiff, David Honeyman, claimed that the promissory note was valid and enforceable, asserting that Jarvis had a legal obligation to repay the sum specified in the note. Honeyman's legal requests likely included seeking a judgment for the amount due under the promissory note, along with any applicable interest and costs. His position was founded on the premise that Jarvis, as a maker of the note, had undertaken a binding obligation that he was now failing to fulfill.	Samuel Jarvis, the defendant, contended that the promissory note was invalid due to the lack of consideration, a fundamental element required for the enforceability of contracts. He argued that the note was executed without any good or valuable consideration, and that he was not indebted to Honeyman at the time of signing. Jarvis's defense included multiple pleas, which he maintained were sufficient to establish his argument that the note was essentially void due to the absence of any supporting consideration for the agreement.

The case, titled E. F. Angel et al. v. The Plume and Atwood Manufacturing Company, was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. It originated in Cook County, where the Superior Court handled the action of assumpsit brought by the Plume and Atwood Manufacturing Company against E. F. Angel, H. Waterman, and W. P. Davis. The dispute arose from an account, and during the trial, the court exercised its discretion to take up and dispose of the case out of order from the docket, based on a rule that allowed for expedited trials in certain situations where it was believed the defense was raised merely to cause delay. The rule mandated that if the plaintiff provided a notice and affidavit supporting the urgency of the case, they could seek a trial ahead of others on the docket. However, the defendants did not comply with this rule, which later led to legal debates about whether the court had the authority to bypass the statutory order of trials as determined by the Practice Act of 1872.",	The Plume and Atwood Manufacturing Company claimed that they were entitled to a judgment as a result of the defendants' alleged failure to comply with court rules regarding the timely filing of defenses. They argued that the defendants had not provided an affidavit of merits to justify their defense, which was necessary for a timely trial on the case. Essentially, the plaintiff contended that the procedural rules should allow them to obtain a judgment by default due to the defendants' lack of diligence in contesting the claim.",	The defendants, represented by Mr. Henry Y. Freeman, contended that the court acted incorrectly in taking the case out of order on the docket, arguing that there were good and sufficient reasons to support the trial being expedited. They asserted that the rule applied by the court was valid only if the defendant had failed to file an adequate affidavit. They maintained that since no affidavit was filed regarding the merits of their defense, the procedure followed by the court should be upheld.",

The case of Snell, Taylor & Co. v. William H. Pells was decided on January 29, 1885, in the Illinois Supreme Court. Snell, Taylor & Co. had contracted with the Lafayette, Bloomington and Mississippi Railroad Company to construct a railroad and had the authority to locate depots along the route, excluding McLean County. William H. Pells, a director of the railroad company, owned property near Pellsville and wanted a depot located there. To facilitate this, local property owners promised financial support to Pells in exchange for the depot's construction. After Pells approached Snell, Taylor & Co. to build the depot and infrastructure at Pellsville, they initially refused without payment. Consequently, Pells claimed he could raise the necessary funds, and they entered an agreement that led to the creation of a promissory note. Subsequently, Pells collected proceeds from this note but did not pay Snell, Taylor & Co. for their services after they had constructed the depot. Snell, Taylor & Co. then filed a lawsuit against Pells for the money received.	Snell, Taylor & Co. claimed that Pells, as their agent, received approximately $3,400 for the construction of the depot and associated work, which he failed to transfer to them. They argued that the contract to construct the depot was legally binding. The plaintiffs requested that the court confirm their right to recover this money from Pells, as he had not paid them despite their demands.	Pells defended himself by arguing that the contract for the depot’s location was void as it was against public policy. His position was reinforced by his claim that, as a director of the railroad, any financial arrangements he made to secure construction fees created a potential conflict of interest. He contended that he could not be compelled to pay the money received due to the alleged illegality of the contract, asserting he was estopped from making payments arising from a transaction that could be seen as a bribe.

In the case of Thomas Ross v. Susan Ross, which took place in Kane County, Illinois in 1873, the couple's troubled marriage comes to light after a period of escalating conflict. Married in New York in 1841, they relocated to Illinois three years later, where they had three children. Over time, Thomas Ross began to exhibit increasingly abusive behavior towards Susan, including unjust accusations, public humiliation, and ultimately, physical threats. In June 1872, after years of mistreatment, Susan left their home due to Thomas's actions and the atmosphere he fostered. Following her departure, Susan initiated a legal action seeking separate maintenance based on the act of March 5, 1867, which allowed married women living apart from their husbands, without fault, to seek support in equity. The case questions whether Susan’s situation affords her rights under common law and the 1867 statute.	Susan Ross claims that Thomas Ross's improper treatment and abandonment necessitated her separation and that she is entitled to financial support. She argues that his actions elevated her living situation to a cause for claiming maintenance under the law. Thus, she requests a decree that obligates Thomas to provide her with $130 for maintenance covering a specified time frame and subsequent weekly support of $5, along with coverage for her legal fees.	Thomas Ross contests Susan's claims by asserting that her departure was voluntary, and thus he is not liable for her maintenance. He maintains that the allegations of his misconduct do not justify her separation without her own fault. Furthermore, he questions the grounds upon which Susan seeks relief under the act of 1867, intending to prove that she did not meet the prerequisites for claiming spousal support.

In 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, Charles Earll was indicted for the murder of Rosetta Jackson, whose death was attributed to a criminal abortion. Earll was found guilty of manslaughter by a jury and sentenced to one year in prison. Following the trial, Earll appealed the verdict, claiming various errors, including that the jury was not properly constituted and that he should have been acquitted rather than convicted of a lesser charge. Evidence presented included testimonies implicating Earll in performing the abortion, among other details of his interactions with the deceased shortly before her death. The conviction and trial process followed Illinois law as it related to manslaughter and the requirements for jury instructions.	The plaintiff, in error, argued that the court erred in several aspects of the trial, particularly in the handling of juror selection, and maintained that by law, he could not be convicted of manslaughter if he was indicted for murder. The plaintiff claimed that all evidence used against him was insufficient to warrant the manslaughter conviction and sought to have the original verdict overturned.	The defendant, representing the People, contended that the jury was within their rights to find the plaintiff guilty of manslaughter, as legal precedents allow for a conviction of a lesser offense from a greater charge, particularly if evidence supports such a lesser charge. The defense further argued that the trial was conducted fairly, with proper jury instructions, and that any objections raised by the plaintiff to the conduct of the trial were either without merit or had been waived due to inaction.

In the case of George D. Corwine v. Benjamin S. Talbot, which took place in Logan County, Illinois, a dispute arose concerning the sale of an agency for the Security Live Stock Insurance Company. The transaction occurred shortly before the company failed within thirty days post-sale. The plaintiff, George D. Corwine, paid $400 for this agency, and subsequently, he claimed to have sustained damages amounting to $300 due to alleged deceit by the defendant, Benjamin S. Talbot. The plaintiff asserted that Talbot made false representations regarding the financial stability and business prospects of the Security company. It was acknowledged that some of the statements made by Talbot were indeed untrue; however, he contended that he was unaware of their falsehood and that the plaintiff had not relied on them. Prior to the sale, Talbot had received warnings from agents of other companies about the company’s impending suspension, but claimed he later sought reassurance from the company's vice-president, who assured him of the company’s sound financial position. This representation was called into question during the trial, leading to disputes over the admissibility of evidence concerning this conversation.	The plaintiff, George D. Corwine, argued that the defendant, Benjamin S. Talbot, engaged in deceitful conduct by making false representations about the Security Live Stock Insurance Company's solvency and future prospects. Corwine maintained that he relied on these representations when he purchased the agency and sustained financial damages as a result. He sought compensation for his damages, estimating them at $300.	The defendant, Benjamin S. Talbot, contended that he did not know the statements he made about the company's financial status were false and that the plaintiff had not relied on those assertions. Talbot argued that he received assurances from the vice-president of the company regarding its stability and that this information was communicated to the plaintiff. He maintained that there was no fraudulent intent on his part since he believed the representations he made were accurate at the time of the sale.

Albert Standart, the plaintiff, was employed as a fireman on a switch engine operated by the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railway Company in Chicago. The incident occurred about a week after he began working there. Prior to the accident, another engine collided with a freight car, causing it to partially overturn, creating an obstruction on the track Standart was approaching. He did not see this obstruction until his engine collided with it, prompting him to jump from the engine to avoid further injury, which resulted in a severe ankle sprain. Standart brought an action against the railway company, claiming negligence in failing to keep the track clear and in not providing a proper connection between the engine and the tender. The case presented two main counts of negligence: one related to the obstruction on the track and the other concerning the absence of an apron covering the gap between the engine and the tender. At trial, the jury found the railway company guilty and awarded Standart $500 in damages.	Standart's claims centered around the negligence of the railway company. He argued that the company failed to keep the tracks free from obstructions and did not maintain proper safety measures—specifically, the omission of an apron that should have connected the engine and its tender. Standart sought damages for the personal injuries he sustained as a result of the company's negligence during his employment.	The railway company's defense was based on the argument that Standart had full knowledge of the existing defects in the engine and the absence of the apron and continued his employment despite this knowledge. They contended that under legal precedent, an employee cannot recover damages for injuries suffered from defective machinery if they are aware of the defect and choose to continue working. Additionally, the railway company argued against the jury instruction which suggested they had a higher standard of care than what was legally required, asserting that they were only obligated to exercise reasonable care.

The case "Mary J. Boies, adm’x of William H. Boies, dec’d, v. Adam K. Henney" took place in the Henry Circuit Court, Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1863. The legal dispute arose from an action of replevin, where Mary J. Boies, representing her deceased husband William H. Boies, sought to reclaim a quantity of broom corn brush that had been seized by the defendant, Adam K. Henney. The controversy centered around the ownership of this property, which the defendant claimed was rightfully attached due to financial obligations of George Farr, a third party. The plaintiff argued that the property belonged to her late husband, while the defendant presented multiple defenses, asserting that the broom corn was either George Farr's property or belonged to others associated with him. Notably, the case involved complex transactions and allegations of fraud concerning the assignment of a lease related to the broom corn, as well as the existing debt to Oloff Johnson, who had a judgment against Farr. The jury found in favor of the defendant, leading to an appeal to the higher court, where issues of intent and fraud in property assignments were thoroughly examined.	The plaintiff, Mary J. Boies, contended that she was the rightful owner of the broom corn brush, which had been wrongfully seized by Henney. She argued that the assignments and lease agreements made by Farr were fraudulent and aimed at delaying or hindering the collection of debts owed to Johnson, thus affecting her claim to the property.	The defendant, Adam K. Henney, defended against the claims by asserting that the broom corn belonged to George Farr and was seized legally due to outstanding judgments against Farr. Henney argued that the assignments of the lease and property were made with fraudulent intent to evade creditors, particularly Johnson, thus rendering any claims by Boies invalid. His case emphasized the fraudulent nature of the transactions that led to the lease's assignment.

Edward Swanston initiated a legal case against Lewis E. Ijams, the county treasurer of McLean County, Illinois, in January 1872. The dispute arose over a drainage tax that Swanston claimed was illegally assessed against him. The case was processed in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a trial that took place without a jury, presided over by Judge Thomas F. Tipton in the Circuit Court of McLean County. Swanston contended that he paid the tax under duress; however, the circumstances indicated that his land was at risk of being sold due to a void judgment. Swanston did not contest the judgment at the time but chose to pay the tax to avoid potential loss of his property. The court had to determine whether the payment was indeed made under duress and if Swanston was entitled to recover the taxes paid.	Swanston's main argument was that the drainage tax was illegally assessed, and he sought to recover the amount he paid to the county treasurer, claiming that the payment was made under duress. He argued that the threat of losing his land under a void judgment constituted sufficient pressure to classify the payment as involuntary.	Ijams, through his counsel, contended that Swanston's payment was made voluntarily, as there was no actual threat to either his person or property, and that Swanston had the opportunity to challenge the judgment before paying the tax. The defense maintained that since the plaintiff’s property was liable to a judgment that passed no title, he could have resisted it and thus was not entitled to a refund of the tax.

In September 1876, the case of Louisa Johnson et al. v. Bernhard Berlizheimer was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute involved a promissory note originally made payable to the firm Lazarus Silverman & Co. The core issue revolved around whether the plaintiff, represented by Louisa Johnson, had the right to claim judgment on this note, given that it was argued that the note had not been properly assigned to them. The note's indorsement was signed by Lazarus Silverman, who identified himself as the "successor to Lazarus Silverman & Co." However, it was unclear from the record how he obtained this status or whether he was the sole survivor of the firm. There was a procedural concern about whether the court had jurisdiction to confess judgment in favor of the plaintiff based on the indorsement of a possibly deceased firm's note. Despite these concerns, the court presumed the regularity of the previous court's actions, suggesting that some evidence must have been presented to justify the judgment.	The plaintiffs claimed that the judgment should be confessed in favor of Louisa Johnson, asserting that the indorsement by Lazarus Silverman effectively transferred the legal title of the promissory note to them. They argued that, as the sole survivor of the partnership or successor to the firm, Silverman had the authority to assign the note and thus the court should uphold the judgment conferring the debt owed to the firm to the assignee.	The defendant, Bernhard Berlizheimer, countered the plaintiffs' claims by arguing that the note had not been properly assigned to them, and therefore, there was no lawful basis for the judgment in their favor. The defendant pointed out the lack of clarity regarding Lazarus Silverman's status as the successor to the firm and raised questions about the jurisdiction of the court in accepting the judgment based on the contested indorsement. They requested that the court dismiss the judgment due to insufficient evidence of proper assignment and authority.

In December 1819, the case of Amos Chipps v. Thomas Yancey was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a judgment rendered in the State of Kentucky, which became the basis for Chipps's action of debt against Yancey. The key individuals involved were Amos Chipps, the appellant, and Thomas Yancey, the appellee. Chipps sought to enforce a judgment against Yancey that had been made in another state. Yancey responded by pleading "nil debet," asserting that he did not owe the debt. However, this plea was challenged by a demurrer from Chipps, leading to an appeal after the lower court sustained Chipps's demurrer against Yancey's plea. The legal debate centered around the validity of the plea of nil debet in the context of an action of debt on a judgment obtained in another state.	The plaintiff, Amos Chipps, argued that the plea of nil debet was not a valid defense in an action to recover a judgment rendered in another state. He requested that the court affirm the lower court's decision to sustain his demurrer, effectively allowing him to proceed with his claim against Yancey for the owed debt based on the earlier judgment.	The defendant, Thomas Yancey, contended that his plea of nil debet was a valid defense against Chipps's claim. He sought to have the appellate court reverse the lower court's ruling that sustained the plaintiff's demurrer, arguing that he did not owe the debt in question, which was based on the judgment from Kentucky.

On December 16, 1887, the Grant Wire & Spring Company, an Illinois corporation, declared insolvency and ceased operations. In response, a creditor named Joseph G. Bemis filed a request on December 17 for the appointment of a receiver and for the dissolution of the company, claiming outstanding debts and seeking legal action to protect creditors' interests. The company’s president and secretary were served with summons and injunctions to prevent interference with the company’s assets. The appellant creditors, including Charles H. Talcott, engaged legal counsel to establish priority over other creditors. A creditors' meeting on December 31 resulted in the company confessing judgments in favor of the appellants, who believed they had secured a first lien against the company's assets. Another creditor group, Naylor & Co., intervened in the case, arguing that the prior confessions of judgment were made under the understanding that all creditors would benefit equally. The court ultimately denied the appellants’ claim to preferential treatment and mandated a pro rata distribution of the remaining assets among all creditors, leading to subsequent appeals.	The plaintiffs, represented by Talcott and other creditors, argued that their confessions of judgment should grant them a preferential claim over the corporation's assets. They contended that the judgments were executed with the assurance that they would enter a creditors' bill for the benefit of all, allowing them to secure priority against other creditors. They sought recognition of their claims as a first lien in equity, which was denied by the lower court.	The defendant (Grant Wire & Spring Company) contended that the confessions of judgment were made in a context of equity—as they were conditional upon ensuring that all creditors would benefit from the creditor's bill. They argued for impartiality in asset distribution, asserting that appellants were not entitled to preferential treatment because no superior equity or obligations distinguished them from other creditors. The defendant requested the court to uphold the collective rights of all creditors and to distribute assets pro rata.

In September 1871, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Rudolph E. Schultz v. John Hay arose involving a dispute over labor and materials related to the construction of a house. The key individuals involved included Rudolph E. Schultz, who was the subcontractor, and John Hay, the owner of the property. Schultz had performed work and provided materials in the construction of Hay's house as part of a contractual arrangement with a contractor named Hayman. However, Hayman abandoned the work after receiving full payment for the tasks completed before Schultz gave any notice regarding his claims for labor and materials according to the Mechanics’ Lien Law. The court needed to determine whether Schultz was entitled to claim a lien on the property for the work he had performed under Hayman's contract.	The plaintiff, Rudolph E. Schultz, claimed that he was entitled to recover payment for the labor and materials he provided while working as a subcontractor on John Hay's house. Schultz argued that he should have a right to a mechanics' lien on the property for the value of his services, which he believed was appropriate despite the contractor abandoning the project.	The defendant, John Hay, contended that he had fully compensated the original contractor, Hayman, for the work completed before any notice of Schultz’s claim was made. The defense was based on the interpretation of the Mechanics’ Lien Law, asserting that Schultz could not claim a lien until proper notice was provided to the property owner. Furthermore, since the contractor had abandoned the project and no funds were owed to him at the time notice was given, Hay argued that Schultz's claims were invalid.

In the case of Enoch H. Raymond v. Miranda M. Raymond, the legal proceedings took place in La Salle County, Illinois, with the circuit court overseen by Judge George W. Stipp. The case dates back to July 27, 1883, and involves a divorce suit initiated by Miranda M. Raymond, the plaintiff, against her husband, Enoch H. Raymond, the defendant, on grounds of adultery. The case had previously been appealed concerning the original court's decree regarding alimony. During the ongoing appeal for alimony adjustments, the plaintiff sought further financial assistance to cover solicitor’s fees and maintenance costs. The court initially ordered the defendant to pay $250 for solicitor fees and an additional $10 per month for maintenance. However, the appellate court later reviewed the case considering the financial capabilities of the defendant and the existing property disposition. After assessing the merits, the court ultimately sought to modify the initial alimony decree granted to the plaintiff.	Miranda M. Raymond, the plaintiff, argued for the continuation of alimony payments and sought additional funds to cover solicitor’s fees and maintenance while the divorce appeal was pending. She claimed that the economic circumstances necessitated a higher allowance to adequately cover her legal expenses and support during this time of ongoing litigation.	Enoch H. Raymond, the defendant, contested the amount of alimony and solicitor’s fees granted to the plaintiff, arguing that the initial allowance of $250 was excessive. He pointed out that only $125 would have been reasonable given his financial situation and the previous allowances made to the plaintiff. He maintained that any costs beyond that amount should come from the plaintiff's allowance.

In December 1822, the case of Augustus Collins and Anson Collins v. John Waggoner was decided in Illinois. The conflict stemmed from an action of trespass initiated by Waggoner, who alleged that the Collins brothers, acting through a constable, unlawfully entered his property and seized his personal belongings. The Collins claimed to be justified by a prior judgment against Waggoner for which they obtained an execution allowing a seizure of his goods. They argued that their actions were lawful based on this execution. Waggoner contested the legality of this repossession by asserting that the execution lacked a necessary endorsement regarding payment methods, as required by the Illinois statute. Furthermore, he contended that he had made attempts to settle the execution by offering the full amount owed, but the constable refused his payment. This legal dispute became complex with challenges related to procedural correctness and statutory requirements regarding replevy and trespassing.	The plaintiffs, Augustus and Anson Collins, claimed that their actions in entering Waggoner's property were legally justified based on a judgment they had previously obtained against him. They contended that the execution issued from that judgment permitted them to take and carry away Waggoner's goods without committing trespass. They argued that their conduct was warranted because they had acted upon an execution directed to a constable by the court.	John Waggoner, the defendant, contended that the Collins brothers' case was improperly constructed since the execution they relied upon lacked the required endorsement. He argued that since the action arose before May 1, 1821, he had the right to replevy the debt for three years, and he had made offers to settle the execution that were unlawfully rejected by the constable. Waggoner asserted that by not allowing him to pay or replevy, the actions taken by the Collins and the constable constituted a trespass.

The case "The Sangamon and Morgan Railroad Company, Plaintiffs in Error, v. The County of Morgan and the Town of Jacksonville, Defendants in Error" arose in December 1852 in Illinois, specifically involving a railroad that extended from Naples to Springfield. The railroad spanned fifty-five miles, with twenty-seven miles running through Morgan County and two miles through the corporate limits of Jacksonville. The railroad was assessed for taxation in Morgan County and Jacksonville, with claims made by these entities against the railroad for state and local taxes. The value of the railroad for taxation purposes was stated to be $125,000, with the rolling stock valued at $51,250, but the railroad was assessed only $25,000 for tax purposes. The primary issue was whether these taxes were rightly assessed, particularly given the railroad's principal business office and operational management were located outside Morgan County. The Circuit Court had ruled in favor of the county's claim for taxes, prompting the railroad company to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The Sangamon and Morgan Railroad argued that the taxes levied by the County of Morgan and the Town of Jacksonville were improperly assessed. They contended that as a corporation, their property and income were primarily situated in Sangamon County, where their main office and agents resided. They maintained that taxation for the railroad's property in Morgan County was not justified because the valuations failed to correspond directly to the specific segments of track situated within that county as per legal requirements.	The County of Morgan and the Town of Jacksonville maintained that they had the authority to levy taxes on the property, including the rolling stock of the railroad, as it passed through their jurisdictions. They argued that the railroad was a part of their local infrastructure and thus subject to local taxation. They contended that the manner in which the property was assessed was valid, claiming that both capital and operational properties were correctly taxed according to statutes applicable to county and municipal revenues.

In the case of Benjamin S. Prettyman v. James G. Goodrich et al., initiated in January 1860, the dispute arose over a trust deed affecting lands in Tazewell and Mason counties, Illinois. The main individuals involved were Benjamin S. Prettyman, the plaintiff, and James G. Goodrich, among others, as defendants. Prettyman claimed to be a bona fide purchaser of certain lands conveyed to him by Trent, who had previously granted a trust deed to the defendants. Prettyman contended that the trust deed was invalid because an attorney, Samuel W. Fuller, had allegedly inserted additional land descriptions into the deed post-acknowledgment without Trent's knowledge or consent, constituting fraud and clouding Prettyman's title. The case was presided over by Judge Harriott in the Tazewell Circuit Court.	Prettyman asserted that he was a legitimate purchaser of lands and that the trust deed, granted by Trent to the defendants, was fraudulent. He claimed that the additional descriptions of land inserted by Fuller, without Trent's consent, violated his rights. Prettyman requested the court to declare the trust deed null and void, thereby clearing the title to the lands he purchased.	The defendants contended that the alterations made to the trust deed were with Trent's consent, thereby rendering the deed valid. They argued that Trent later took the modified deed to the recorder’s office and recorded it, indicating his acceptance of the changes. Furthermore, they asserted that any alterations did not affect Trent's title since he had approved the amendments.

In 1846, David Humphreys and Henry Matthews entered into a joint venture to purchase and sell 3,682 bushels of wheat. The wheat was transported to Oswego, New York, where Matthews was to grind it into flour and produce 736 barrels for their mutual profit. According to their agreement, Matthews would sell the flour, incurring no storage charges, and provide an account of the sales to Humphreys, who was entitled to half of the profits. By July 23, 1847, Humphreys received a letter from Matthews reporting on the sales made in Troy and Boston. The sales occurred in May 1847, with flour's average price in Troy being approximately $8 per barrel and around $8.25 per barrel in Boston. After accounting for expenses not exceeding $800, Matthews allegedly failed to pay Humphreys his entitled share, resulting in a claimed debt of $453.54. Subsequently, Humphreys sought an attachment against Matthews in the Cook Circuit Court, asserting that Matthews was not an Illinois resident. However, the court dismissed the attachment due to insufficient affidavit details, prompting Humphreys to appeal the decision.	David Humphreys contends that he is owed $453.54 by Henry Matthews due to non-payment for his share of profits from a joint venture involving the sale of flour. He argues that the attachment obtained against Matthews was justified under the attachment act and that the affidavit provided was adequate in terms of detailing the debt and Matthews's residency outside Illinois. Humphreys seeks the reversal of the Circuit Court’s dismissal of the attachment.	Henry Matthews, as the defendant, argued against the sufficiency of the affidavit that initiated the attachment. He maintained that the affidavit did not adequately demonstrate the basis for the attachment, leading to the Circuit Court's ruling dismissing the proceeding. Matthews likely requested the court to uphold the dismissal, asserting that the legal requirements for the attachment had not been met.

The case revolves around a legal dispute between The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company and The Springfield and Northwestern Railroad Company, taking place in January 1873 in Petersburg, Menard County, Illinois. The Springfield and Northwestern Railroad sought to condemn a portion of the right of way occupied by the Chicago and Alton Railroad as it planned to construct its tracks. The proposed construction would require the appellee’s road to cross underneath the existing tracks of the appellants, significantly altering the support of the latter's railroad. The Chicago and Alton Railroad was already in operation on elevated embankments. The initial trial resulted in a jury finding minimal damages of five cents to the appellants. However, the trial included controversial testimonies regarding the anticipated construction support and who would be responsible for maintenance, which the appellants argued undermined the integrity of the verdict. The appellants contended that several pieces of evidence were improperly admitted. The case subsequently reached the Illinois Supreme Court for an appeal.	The Springfield and Northwestern Railroad asserted its right to condemn a portion of the Chicago and Alton Railroad's right of way, claiming that the construction would not result in significant damages to the latter. They sought condemnation and minimal compensation, relying on the testimonies of their contractor and other witnesses who insisted that the proposed construction would not cause harm to the Chicago and Alton's operations.
