The Chicago and Alton Railroad challenged the assessments of damages, arguing that the testimonies presented by the plaintiff's witnesses were improper and should not influence the jury's verdict. They asserted that the expectation of maintaining the support for their tracks was not legally binding on the plaintiff, and therefore any claims of minimal impact were unfounded. The defense sought a real assessment of damages that would account for the true cost of keeping their tracks secure in light of the proposed construction.

In September 1868, the case Hope Insurance Company v. Thomas Lonergan took place in Illinois, specifically in the Superior Court of Chicago, presided over by Chief Justice Joseph E. Gaby. The key individuals involved included the Hope Insurance Company as the plaintiff and Thomas Lonergan as the defendant. The dispute arose from an incident where a steam boiler located 22 feet away from a mill exploded, resulting in a fire that destroyed the mill. The crux of the case revolved around whether the damage to the mill was primarily caused by the explosion or by the ensuing fire. The appellate court had to review the conflicting testimonies regarding the condition of the mill immediately after the explosion, including whether the walls were still standing or had fallen. The judges noted the evidence was contradictory and the lower court’s finding relied heavily on credibility determinations made regarding witness accounts.	The Hope Insurance Company argued that the damages incurred to the mill were exclusively due to the fire that followed the boiler explosion, which they asserted was covered under their insurance policy. They sought compensation for the full value of the damage, claiming that the fire resulted in a complete loss, justifying their request under the insurance contract's stipulations.	Thomas Lonergan contested the plaintiff’s claims by asserting that the explosion, rather than the fire, was the primary cause of the damage to the mill. He pointed out that the terms of the insurance policy stated that the company would not be liable for losses resulting from an explosion unless fire ensued. Consequently, he maintained that the findings of the lower court did not support the plaintiff's evidence regarding how the damage occurred.

The case of Archibald C. Wadsworth v. Mary M. Connell et al. took place in 1882, in Illinois, concerning the estate of Joseph O. Connell who died in 1867. Joseph Connell's will indicated the distribution of his estate, which primarily consisted of real estate, appointing Wadsworth as the executor and naming him as the guardian for Connell's children. Wadsworth was tasked with managing the estate, selling properties, and ensuring the welfare and education of the children. As executor, Wadsworth sold the properties and invested the proceeds. However, he incurred losses on loans made to two families, the Seiberts and the Dunlaps. After filing for a final settlement and facing objections regarding commissions and the losses, the lower court initially upheld some objections against him. An appeal followed, leading to the finding that Wadsworth, despite not formally qualifying as guardian, acted in that capacity and was liable for the funds loaned without authority. The case focused on his dual role as executor and testamentary guardian, investigating the legality of his actions in light of Illinois law regarding guardianship and executor duties.",	The plaintiffs, represented by Connell's widow and children, argued that Wadsworth mismanaged the estate funds. They contended that he improperly loaned a significant portion of the estate to the Seiberts and Dunlaps, resulting in financial losses for the estate. The plaintiffs sought accountability for these losses and objected to Wadsworth's claims of commission from the estate, demanding he repay the lost amounts.",	Wadsworth, the defendant, maintained that he acted within the terms of the will as executor and denied liability for the funds loaned, arguing that he should not be personally accountable for the losses incurred. He contended that the prior court orders regarding his reported accounts and the objections raised precluded further litigation on the same matters, asserting that he had not formally qualified as guardian and therefore should not be held to those legal standards.",

George Eichlor v. Stephen N. Holroyd is a legal case that dates back to January 16, 1885, heard in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in DeKalb County, Illinois, where the key individuals involved were George Eichlor (the appellant) and Stephen N. Holroyd (the appellee). Holroyd sold his equity of redemption for a 120-acre piece of land to one Grabbe, who was to assume existing incumbrances and pay $800 in total—$500 of which was paid upfront. The conditions dictated that the remaining $300 was to be secured before the deed was delivered. Eichlor was given the deed with instructions to release it to Grabbe upon receiving the balance; should this not be paid, the deed was to be returned. However, Grabbe managed to acquire the deed from Eichlor without paying the outstanding amount. In 1878, Holroyd commenced a legal action against Grabbe for the owed $300 but obtained no recovery. The land was subsequently sold due to unpaid mortgages, prompting Holroyd to sue Eichlor in 1880 for the $300, claiming wrongful delivery of the deed to Grabbe. The overall action hinged on the premise that since the condition of payment was not met, no valid title should have been transferred to Grabbe.	The plaintiff, Stephen N. Holroyd, argued that Eichlor wrongfully delivered the deed to Grabbe without ensuring the payment of the $300 balance, leading to a loss of his title through the insolvency of Grabbe. Holroyd’s claim focused on the wrongful act of delivering the deed under conditional terms that were not fulfilled. He sought to recover the unpaid $300 from Eichlor resulting from this alleged negligence or misstep in handling the deed delivery.	The defendant, George Eichlor, contended that Holroyd ratified the delivery of the deed by successfully obtaining a judgment against Grabbe for the $300 owed. Eichlor argued that by choosing to pursue a claim against Grabbe rather than repudiating the delivery of the deed, Holroyd effectively discharged Eichlor from any liability related to the initial conditions of the sale. Eichlor's defense was based on the principles of agency and ratification, claiming that Holroyd's subsequent actions indicated his acceptance of the situation created by the deed's improper delivery.

The legal case "Charles C. Stephens v. Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1867. The case arose from events primarily occurring around the mid-19th century concerning insurance claims. Charles C. Stephens purchased property, including a mill, from the firm Banks, Bell & Co., who had previously taken a mortgage on it from Gaylord, Son & Co. The property was insured for $5,000 by the Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company, with the policy expiring in November 1865. In May 1861, Gaylord, Son & Co. began foreclosure proceedings against Banks, Bell & Co. and Stephens. A decree was issued in June 1862 allowing for the sale of the property, which took place in August 1862, while retaining the right for two years for redemption post-sale as per a written agreement. The mill was destroyed by fire on October 10, 1863. The key issue in the case was whether Stephens retained enough interest in the property to claim insurance following the fire, given the prior foreclosure and sale actions.	The plaintiff, Charles C. Stephens, argued that he held an insurable interest in the property at the time of the fire due to his right of redemption despite the foreclosure. He sought to recover the full value of the insurance policy from Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company, claiming that his interest as a mortgagor remained intact until the expiration of his right to redeem.	The defendant, Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company, contended that Stephens had lost his insurable interest in the property due to the foreclosure and subsequent sale. They argued that the legal title passed to the purchasers at the foreclosure auction, meaning that Stephens was not entitled to receive any compensation for the loss incurred from the fire.

In 1883, within Jackson County, Illinois, the School Directors employed Scott Crews to teach a district school for five months at a rate of $30 per month. A formal written contract was established. Crews taught for one month and nine days before the schoolhouse was destroyed by fire, which interrupted the schooling. Crews expressed his willingness to continue teaching and requested the Directors to provide another classroom, but they failed to do so. After teaching his scheduled classes, Crews received payment for the time he taught but later filed a lawsuit seeking compensation for the entire contract period, arguing that the Directors’ failure to provide alternative accommodations prevented him from fulfilling the contract. The case raised important questions regarding the obligations of school Directors and the implications of a teaching contract disrupted by unforeseen circumstances.	The plaintiff, Scott Crews, claimed that he was entitled to the full payment for the five-month teaching contract despite not finishing the term, as the disruption was due to the fault of the School Directors, who did not provide an alternative teaching location after the schoolhouse burned down. He argued that he had a valid contract and was ready and willing to fulfill his teaching duties, and asserted that proving he could not find alternative employment was not necessary for his claim.	The School Directors contended that Crews was partially responsible for the fire due to negligence, as per a clause in their contract requiring him to use his best efforts to preserve the schoolhouse. They argued that because of this, he should not be entitled to recover the full amount of the contract. They also insinuated that Crews had an obligation to find alternative employment during his unfulfilled contract period, which he allegedly did not fulfill.

In the case of Isaac Cook v. Joseph Stout et al., the legal proceedings took place in 1868, originally filed in the Circuit Court of LaSalle County and later moved to the Superior Court of Chicago. The case arose from a dispute regarding a sheriff’s deed for certain premises, which the plaintiff, Isaac Cook, sought to have set aside. Cook's claim established that the deed to respondent Henry G. Cotton was invalid based on alleged waste committed on the premises. The Superior Court ultimately ruled in favor of Cook, granting him a decree for $2,706.47. The court appointed a special master to gather testimony regarding the alleged waste, but complications arose when key depositions were mislaid or destroyed, leading to a complex evidentiary battle. The case was further complicated by issues regarding the admissibility of secondary evidence to detail the contents of the lost depositions. The court ultimately decided that the decree issued against the defendant needed to be reversed due to the reliance on that secondary evidence.	Isaac Cook, the plaintiff, claimed that the sheriff's deed to the premises held by Henry G. Cotton was invalid and sought to have it set aside. He presented arguments alleging that significant waste had been committed on the premises, leading to his financial loss. Cook requested the court to decree a sum for the damages resulting from the waste.	The defendants, including Joseph Stout and others, argued against the evidence presented, particularly focusing on the validity of the secondary evidence provided regarding the lost depositions. They contended that since the original witnesses were still living, it was inappropriate to use secondary evidence of prior testimonies. The defendants aimed to suppress these depositions and defend their position by asserting that the evidence brought forth by the plaintiff was insufficient to support the decree against them.

In 1890, in Chicago, Illinois, plaintiffs James Maxwell and Henry B. Maxwell filed a case against defendant Henry Koeritz regarding a mechanics' lien dispute. The situation arose from a petition submitted by Koeritz, who claimed a lien for the price of bricks he supplied for a building constructed on lots within David B. Lee’s subdivision. The building stood on a combination of five lots, but there was uncertainty about the specific lots it occupied. The plaintiffs argued that since Koeritz had not filed the appropriate statement or account of his demand with the Circuit Court clerk, he could not enforce the lien as a subcontractor under the relevant Illinois statutes. The case examined the interpretation of the word "creditor" in the statute, considering whether it could apply to subcontractors like Koeritz or was limited to original contractors.	The plaintiffs contended that Henry Koeritz, as a subcontractor, failed to file a proper claim for his lien within the timeframe stipulated by Illinois law. They emphasized that the statutory definition of "creditor" did not include subcontractors and, therefore, Koeritz was not entitled to relief under the mechanics' lien law. They requested the court to dismiss Koeritz's petition to enforce the lien.	The defendant, Henry Koeritz, argued that he was entitled to enforce the lien despite not having filed a statement with the Circuit Court clerk, asserting that the statute's provisions were ambiguous regarding the applicability to subcontractors. He challenged the interpretation of the word "creditor" and maintained that he acted within his rights as a party involved in the contracting process. Koeritz sought the reinstatement of his lien against the properties in question.

In June 1874, a legal dispute arose in Mt. Vernon, Illinois, involving James D. Johnson et al. (plaintiffs) and James M. Pace, serving as a garnishee, related to a debt owed by George H. Woodward, a high school principal. Johnson, Taylor & Co., as attaching creditors, initiated a suit against Woodward, ultimately resulting in a garnishment action against Pace, who was the secretary of the board of education. On June 13 and June 25, 1874, Pace drew funds from the town treasurer, purportedly owed to Woodward, totaling $184, for which Woodward had previously issued an order to pay Oliver Holmes. The dispute revolved around whether the funds in Pace's possession belonged to Woodward or were rightfully owed to Holmes. The case escalated through judicial levels, concluding with a circuit court ruling that found the money rightfully belonged to Holmes, discharging Pace as garnishee and prompting Johnson, Taylor & Co. to appeal the decision.",	The plaintiffs, Johnson, Taylor & Co., claimed that the funds held by Pace should rightfully be considered part of Woodward's assets, which they contended could be subjected to their garnishment efforts. They argued for the court to reverse the prior ruling that discharged Pace as garnishee, asserting that the money was owed to Woodward and should be accessible to settle his debts.",	James M. Pace, as the garnishee, argued that the funds in his possession were not owed to Woodward but rather to Oliver Holmes, based on written orders from Woodward designating the payment to Holmes. Pace maintained that he acted as Holmes' agent, and that the garnishment process should not apply to him regarding these funds, as Woodward had already appropriated them to Holmes, prior to being garnished.",

In November 1855, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case involving Samuel Kirkham and others (Plaintiffs in Error) against Susan Justice and others (Defendants in Error). The dispute originated from a sheriff's deed related to land ownership issues following a sale conducted due to an execution in favor of William and Redman Lasswell against Samuel Kirkham. The plaintiffs contended they had the legal and equitable title to the land based on the sheriff’s deed but faced challenges regarding the assignment of the certificate of purchase, which was conducted before 1841 when the law allowed such assignments. Attempts to notify the heirs of Redman Lasswell and John M. Ham were complicated due to their unknown residences, leading to them being served as "not found." The case illuminated procedural shortcomings in how parties were identified and brought into the suit, as the plaintiffs were unable to properly handle the inclusion of unknown parties in accordance with statutory requirements. The lower court’s decree was ultimately found deficient, lacking jurisdiction over certain defendants.	The plaintiffs claimed legal ownership of the disputed land based on the sheriff’s deed obtained from the execution against Samuel Kirkham. They argued that although the deed was executed after the law permitted assignments, the prior certificate of purchase and the complexities surrounding the assignments should allow them to establish their title. Their main legal request was for the court to enforce the execution of a deed by the defendants to officially transfer the land to them.	The defendants contended that the bill filed by the plaintiffs was too uncertain and failed to comply with the statutory requirements for including unknown parties in a chancery suit. They argued that the lower court lacked jurisdiction because proper procedures were not followed in naming and serving all relevant parties, particularly the unknown heirs of the relevant deceased individuals.

The case "The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company v. The People ex rel. John L. Black, Collector" was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court and decided on January 25, 1887. The legal battle arose in Clay County, Illinois, after the county collector sought judgment for delinquent road taxes owed by the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company. The railway company contested the application, claiming that the county clerk lacked the authority to extend the tax against them for certain districts, as the county board had not properly authorized these extensions. During previous meetings in September and December 1885, the board of supervisors had made motions regarding the tax extensions, but the railway argued these were done without the necessary legal procedure. The central issues revolved around the classification and assessment of taxes as separate entities under different legal provisions and whether procedural irregularities in tax record-keeping invalidated the taxation.	The plaintiff contended that the county clerk unlawfully extended the road tax against the railway company without proper authorization from the county board. They argued that the tax was improperly assessed and extended against the entirety of the railroad property without adequate distribution among the road districts, thereby violating established statutory provisions. The railway company requested that the court overturn the county court's judgment and dismiss the tax claims.	The defendant, represented by the county collector, argued that the objections raised by the railway company were legally unfounded. They maintained that the actions of the county clerk, including the amendment of tax records, conformed to statutory requirements and that the railway's claims regarding improper assessment and extension lacked factual basis. The collector requested the court to uphold the county court's judgment and enforce the collection of the overdue taxes against the railway's entire track in Clay County.

The case of Benjamin F. Freeman v. James T. Hartman et ux. took place in September 1867 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered around a deed executed by Henrietta Hartman, who transferred her undivided interest in a farm to her brother, Benjamin F. Freeman, just three days prior to her marriage to James T. Hartman. The transfer was made for $200, despite the value of her interest being estimated between $800 and $900 at the time. This legal action was initiated by James and Henrietta Hartman, who sought to rescind the deed, claiming that it was executed under fraudulent circumstances, specifically arguing that it violated the marital rights of James Hartman. They contended that Benjamin exploited the trust placed in him by Henrietta, as he acted in a role akin to a guardian or caretaker over her affairs. The couple insisted that Benjamin paid an inadequate sum and that the transaction was meant to circumvent James's rights as Henrietta's future husband. The court examined evidence, including testimonies regarding family dynamics and the nature of the conveyance, ultimately deciding on the validity of the claims and the alleged fraud.	The plaintiffs, James T. Hartman and Henrietta Hartman, argued that the deed executed by Henrietta to her brother Benjamin was void due to constructive fraud. They claimed that the transfer was made without the knowledge of Henrietta’s intended husband, James, just days before their marriage. They asserted that the transaction was in derogation of James's marital rights and expectations, as it circumvented his consent and was done for an inadequate price, clearly designed to provide Benjamin with an unfair advantage.	The defendant, Benjamin F. Freeman, contended that the deed should be valid as it involved a monetary exchange, and he argued that the legal standards applicable to conveyances did not inherently render the deed fraudulent merely due to the timing. He claimed that the price paid represented a legitimate transaction considering supposed debts owed by Henrietta for board and clothing. Furthermore, Benjamin asserted that the marital rights of James Hartman were not violated based on the married woman’s law in effect during that period.

The case, "The People ex rel. George W. Chatterton v. The Secretary of State et al.," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1871. The matter arose in Illinois, involving George W. Chatterton, who had a contract to supply 2,000 reams of printing paper to the State. The Secretary of State had solicited bids for the paper, and after the bidding process, the contract was awarded to Chatterton. He delivered 1,000 reams of the paper, which the State accepted and used. However, a dispute arose when the Secretary of State refused to accept the remaining paper, and the auditor declined to issue a payment warrant, allegedly due to intentions of fraud in the bidding process and violations of statutory requirements regarding the award of contracts. Chatterton filed a petition for a writ of mandamus to compel payment for the delivered paper and to enforce the contract for the remaining paper.	Chatterton argued that the Secretary of State wrongfully refused to accept the remaining 1,000 reams of printing paper and that he was entitled to payment for the 1,000 reams already delivered. He maintained that he complied with the contract terms and challenged the allegations of fraud or statutory violations in the contract award process, insisting that no such misconduct occurred.	The Secretary of State and other respondents contended that the contract was invalid due to alleged fraud, claims that it had not been awarded according to statutory requirements, and the assertion that other bidders had proposed lower prices. They argued that the Secretary's decision to postpone the award and conduct it privately, without the auditor and treasurer present, rendered the contract non-binding on the State.

In September 1868, in Chicago, Illinois, the case of Abraham F. Croskey et al. v. Francis E. Corey et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The proceeding was initiated to enforce a mechanic’s lien claimed by the defendants, who were owed for lumber sold to Croskey used for improving a lot. The petition alleged that Croskey was the owner of the premises, and he, along with his business partner Shufeldt, had bought lumber worth $2,099.49 to enhance the lot. Croskey and Shufeldt acknowledged ownership and the purchase of the lumber but argued that it was intended for their firm rather than the specific lot in contention. Upon the submission of their legal arguments, the initial ruling determined the existence of a lien in favor of the defendants, ordering the sale of the premises to recover the outstanding payment for the lumber. However, the defendants’ claims included that there was no sufficient evidence presented to substantiate the lien, leading to critical arguments about the purpose behind the lumber purchase and the implications of a promissory note issued by Croskey & Co.	The plaintiffs, Francis E. Corey et al., asserted that the lumber sold to Croskey was specifically intended for the improvement of the lot in question, thereby creating a valid mechanic’s lien. They sought to enforce this lien through the court, claiming a total outstanding amount of $2,099.49 due for the lumber, and requested a sale of the property to satisfy the debt owed.	The defendants, Abraham F. Croskey and Shufeldt, contended that while they acknowledged ownership and the lumber purchase, it was not intended for the specific improvements on the contested lot, thereby nullifying the lien. They argued that the promissory note issued in payment constituted a full settlement of the debt, erasing any claims to a mechanic’s lien, and requested the court to dismiss the lien based on these assertions.

The case of The Kankakee Coal Company et al. v. Crane Brothers Manufacturing Co. took place in Kankakee County, Illinois, culminating in a court decision on December 8, 1888. The main individuals involved were representatives from The Kankakee Coal Company (plaintiffs) and Crane Brothers Manufacturing Company (defendants). The dispute arose when Crane Brothers sought to enforce a mechanic’s lien against Kankakee Coal Company for a horizontal link motion engine that had been supplied for hoisting purposes in the coal mine owned by the latter. The contract stipulated that the coal company would reimburse Crane Brothers a total of $2,200 in installments for the engine. After the engine was delivered and installed, Kankakee Coal Company failed to pay, prompting Crane Brothers to file a petition seeking foreclosure of the lien. During the court proceedings, several objections were raised by Kankakee Coal Company concerning the sufficiency of the petition and various technical issues, but the court ultimately found the petition sufficient and upheld the lien.	The Kankakee Coal Company, represented by Crane Brothers Manufacturing Co., claimed that the coal company failed to fulfill the payment terms for the hoisting engine as agreed in the contract. Crane Brothers sought to enforce a mechanic's lien on the coal company's lands to recover the total due amount, which included the purchase price of the engine and accrued interest, amounting to $2,803.09. They argued that the petition sufficiently detailed the terms of the contract and the intended location of the engine’s use.	The Kankakee Coal Company raised several defenses against the enforcement of the mechanic’s lien. They argued that the petition was insufficient as it did not clearly state the specific tract of land for the engine's placement. Additionally, they contended that the contract failed to specify a delivery time for the engine, claiming this omission rendered the lien invalid. They also sought to introduce evidence regarding the original contract but were denied, and they argued that certain notes related to the payment for the engine were not produced during the trial.

In the case of Thomas Gardiner, Sheriff, v. John W. Bunn & Company, the legal proceedings took place in 1887 in Illinois. The case was under the jurisdiction of the Illinois Appellate Court and involved a dispute regarding a Sheriff's execution of goods. Initially, the case was brought before the court during the November Term of 1885, leading to a judgment reversal by the appellate court and a remand for a second trial. The core issue stemmed from the execution proceedings related to a levy on goods, which the court later assessed based on the prior laws addressed in the earlier case. The primary legal discussion revolved around whether the Sheriff's possession of the goods was originally defective and whether third parties could contest the Sheriff's rights due to this defect. Ultimately, it was determined that the Sheriff's possession was lawfully perfected before the rights of third parties attached, thus upholding the validity of his actions.	The plaintiff, Thomas Gardiner, Sheriff, claimed that the execution of the levy on the goods was valid and should be upheld despite any initial defects in his possession. He argued that subsequent legal actions perfected his possession before any third-party rights were established, requesting the court to affirm the validity of the levy and the accompanying judgment from the circuit court.	The defendants, John W. Bunn & Company, contended that the Sheriff’s initial possession of the goods was defective and therefore invalid. They sought to challenge the ruling regarding the execution by asserting that their rights were infringed upon due to this defect. They requested the court to reconsider the previous findings and potentially overturn the enforcement of the levy.

In September 1872, in Iroquois County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between A. H. Spray and Richard Ammerman over a dog owned by Spray. The two parties lived on adjoining farms, where a partition fence was insufficient to prevent cattle from crossing into each other’s properties. Ammerman’s cattle had a habit of trespassing onto Spray's land, which led to ongoing conflicts between them. A weekend agreement was initially made to replace the inadequate brush fence with a more secure plank fence; however, Ammerman failed to remove the remaining portion of the brush fence as promised. On the day the incident occurred, Spray’s daughter directed their dog to chase Ammerman’s cattle back onto Ammerman’s property. After the dog returned to Spray’s vicinity and laid down, Ammerman shot and killed the dog, claiming he acted to protect his cattle. Spray sought damages for the dog’s death, and the case was appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court after the circuit court ruled in Ammerman's favor.	Spray claimed that Ammerman unlawfully killed his dog while it was merely fulfilling its role in driving cattle that were trespassing back onto Ammerman's property. Spray argued that the dog posed no immediate threat, as it did not bite or harass Ammerman's cattle; instead, it was engaged in actions prompted by Spray's daughter. Consequently, he sought damages for the unlawful killing of his dog, arguing that Ammerman's failure to maintain the fence contributed to the problem.	Ammerman contended that he had the right to protect his property and cattle from the dog, which he characterized as a nuisance due to its repeated trespassing activities. He argued that the instructions provided to the jury at trial were appropriate, asserting that he acted within his rights to safeguard his property. He claimed that without proper instructions regarding the nature of the dog’s behavior, the jury was misled regarding the fact that the dog could be deemed a nuisance. He requested the court to uphold the jury’s decision in his favor.

In 1873, Bridget McCarty, while living in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, fell ill and, fearing for her life, sought to execute a will. During this time, Patrick Kearnan, who had been providing labor and services to McCarty, reminded her of his contributions and implied that a compensation was due. McCarty agreed to give Kearnan twenty acres of her 240-acre property as remuneration for his labor. She executed a deed granting this land to him during the visit of a justice of the peace and a priest who were called to authenticate her will. After recovering from her illness, McCarty sought to set aside the deed, arguing that it was obtained through fraud and that she lacked the mental capacity to execute it. The case escalated through the legal system until it reached the Illinois Supreme Court.	McCarty claimed that the deed transferring twenty acres to Kearnan was obtained under duress and without a valid legal consideration. She contended that she did not knowingly or willingly execute the deed, asserting that she had been mentally unfit due to her illness. McCarty argued that the transaction should be viewed as a "donatio mortis causa," which would be revocable, similar to a will. She sought to have the deed declared void.	Kearnan contended that the deed was valid and executed with McCarty's full understanding and intent. He argued that she acknowledged his claim for compensation for his services and voluntarily agreed to the conveyance of land. Kearnan maintained that he provided valuable labor and that the deed was not a gift but a binding contract. He suggested that McCarty's claims of mental incapacity were not substantiated and that the circumstances of the transaction clearly indicated her ability to execute legal documents.

In the case of Seth Wadhams et al. v. Lucy C. Flagler Gay, decided in September 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court, the legal dispute arose over the ownership and rights to certain lands devised in the will of Augustus Garrett. The key individuals involved included Seth Wadhams, Christian S. Engles, Augusta M. Engles, Calvin Day, and Charles D. Flagler, a party central to the property interests outlined in the succession. The facts stemmed from a previous decree in a partition suit that declared Charles D. Flagler only held a life estate in the lands with his children inheriting the remainder in fee. However, following a bill of review, it was determined that Flagler was entitled to the full fee simple estate. This led to various agreements and deeds made between the parties, which later caused confusion over the rightful ownership among Wadhams, the Engles, and Day, who acquired their titles based on these transactions. The court was tasked with interpreting these events to ascertain the legitimacy of the property claims in light of prior judicial decisions.	The plaintiffs, Seth Wadhams and the Engles, claimed that their titles to the lands were valid and needed to be protected despite the earlier decree stating that Charles D. Flagler held only a life estate. They argued that their acquisition was made in good faith, relying on the enforceability of the decree from the bill of review granting Flagler a fee simple estate. They sought a declaration affirming their ownership and securing their rights against attempts by Charles Flagler's heirs to reclaim the lands.	The defendant, Lucy C. Flagler Gay, argued that the initial partition decree accurately established Charles D. Flagler's interest as a life estate with the remainder to his children. She claimed that subsequent transfers and deeds made by Charles did not validly convey a fee simple estate due to the existing decree and that her rights as an heir should supersede the claims of the plaintiffs as they were premised on an erroneous decree.

The case titled "Daniel S. Witter et al. v. Israel McNiel" was adjudicated in December 1842 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a contract concerning the construction of a stone steam mill by McNiel for Witter & Mellen. McNiel was to provide materials and complete the building for a total payment of $100, with the defendants pledging to pay $100 upon a sufficient quantity of rock being present and additional payments as work progressed. Upon disagreement concerning the fulfillment of contractual obligations, McNiel filed a lawsuit against Witter & Mellen in the Hancock Circuit Court. The defendants contended that they had performed all obligations under the contract and that McNiel had failed to fulfill his commitments. The case involved various pleas, including claims of non-execution of the contract and complete payment for work and materials. The trial included the presentation of the written agreement, which ultimately turned out to be signed in the names of Witter & Mellen. The jury trial resulted in a verdict favoring McNiel.	The plaintiff, Israel McNiel, argued that Witter & Mellen failed to meet their contractual obligations concerning the construction of the steam mill, leading him to seek judgment for payments due under the contract. McNiel asserted that he had adequately performed his end of the agreement and was owed compensation according to the terms set out in the contract.	The defendants, Witter & Mellen, presented multiple defenses. They claimed non-execution of the contract under a plea of "non est factum," contending that the contract was not validly executed by both parties. They also claimed to have fulfilled all contractual obligations but accused McNiel of failing to perform his responsibilities. Additionally, they asserted that all payments due had been made, seeking to establish that they owed no further compensation to McNiel.

Gertrude Stempel held a lien for an annuity on certain lands and filed a bill to enforce that lien. This legal action took place in 1889 in St. Clair County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Theodore Hummert, and defendants Mittendorff and Sauter, owned the lands that were the subject of the lawsuit. The defendants answered the original bill and filed a cross-bill against Mrs. Stempel and Hummert, asserting that the annuity owed to Mrs. Stempel had already been paid and that the remaining payments should be divided proportionately among the landowners based on the value of their respective portions of the land. They requested the court to appraise the land values and determine the amounts owed accordingly. Mrs. Stempel contended that her lien should apply to all the lands rather than being divided. Hummert defaulted in responding to the cross-bill, leading to a decree against him. The court appointed commissioners to appraise the land, subsequently determining the values of the portions owned by each defendant and assigning specific annual payments of the annuity they were each responsible for. The case ultimately included complex issues of lien enforcement and the equitable distribution of annuity liability.	The plaintiff, Gertrude Stempel, claimed that her lien on the properties should remain intact as a whole rather than being divided among the landowners. She insisted that the defendants continue to be liable for the annuity payments as outlined in her original bill. After the cross-bill was filed, she contested the notion that the lien's burden could be shared and insisted on the complete preservation of her rights under the lien for the full amount of the annuity.	The defendants, including Theodore Hummert, argued that the annuity owed to Mrs. Stempel had already been satisfied prior to the filing of the cross-bill and contended that any future payments should be prorated based on the value of each individual's share of the land. They sought the court to appraise the properties to ascertain the value owned by each and to direct how much each party should contribute toward the annuity in accordance with the land valuations they provided.

In 1872, in Kane County, Illinois, the legal dispute arose between Norman C. Thompson (plaintiff) and Chauncey H. White (defendant) involving an attachment proceeding. The case was complex, originating before a justice of the peace, with an initial judgment against a garnishee, Isaac B. Garrison, who was identified as having property belonging to the defendant. Thompson obtained this judgment but Garrison did not appeal through regular channels. Instead, he sought to remove the case to the circuit court via a writ of certiorari, claiming the justice's judgment was improperly rendered. In the circuit court, Thompson moved to quash Garrison's petition and dismiss the appeal on two grounds: that a standard appeal could have been filed and that the petition did not adequately justify the circuit court's jurisdiction. The bill of exceptions indicated that although Thompson made a motion to quash, it was unclear if the circuit court acted upon it or if any exceptions were taken to its ruling. The jury ultimately decided that the note at the center of the dispute did not belong to Garrison, which was a key factor in the judgment delivered.	The plaintiff, Norman C. Thompson, argued that the appeal taken by Chauncey H. White (garnishee) was improperly filed as it should have followed regular appeal procedures. He claimed that White's petition for certiorari was defective and filed a motion to quash it in the circuit court. Essentially, Thompson requested that the court uphold the original judgment made by the justice of the peace against White, thus affirming his claim.	The defendant, Chauncey H. White, contended that the note in question did not belong to Isaac B. Garrison, the individual from whom Thompson sought to recover property via garnishment. White's legal representation argued that the jury’s determination supported his position and maintained that the procedural objections raised by Thompson regarding the appeal process were without merit, as no proper action had been shown on the court's part regarding the preliminary motion to quash.

In the case of John Calhoun v. Bela C. Webster and Virgil Hickox, the events transpired in Sangamon, Illinois, with significant occurrences dating back to November 6, 1839. The legal dispute arose when a summons was issued against the defendants, Webster and Hickox, which was returnable at the next scheduled court term. The summons was served on November 7, 1839, and by the November term of court, a judgment was rendered by default against the defendants. The central issue of the case revolved around whether the judgment was regular, considering the timing of the summons and its subsequent service. The court recognized that when more than one term intervenes between the issuance and the return of the original process, such a writ is deemed a nullity. Consequently, the court found the process invalid and deemed the default judgment irregular.	The plaintiff, John Calhoun, claimed that the summons served on the defendants was valid under Illinois law. He argued that the defendants were aware of the court's schedule as the term dates are prescribed by law. Additionally, Calhoun contended that any additional wording regarding the return date within the summons should be disregarded as surplusage, thereby affirming the court's authority to proceed with a default judgment against the defendants.	The defendants, Bela C. Webster and Virgil Hickox, argued that the summons was improperly issued because it was made returnable too late in relation to when it was served. They maintained that the judgment by default rendered against them was invalid due to the irregularities regarding the summons. The defendants requested the court to reverse the default judgment on the basis that the original process was void.

In September 1875, the case "George H. Ward et al. v. Marvin A. Lawrence et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from a transaction in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Lawrence, Hartman & Quinn, were real estate agents seeking to recover commissions for a sale of land, which they attempted to facilitate involving defendants George H. Ward, B. F. Ray, and W. J. Faulkner. On August 27, 1872, during a meeting in Chicago, a written contract was drawn to sell 55 acres of land to Albert Price at $400 per acre. However, it was acknowledged that Faulkner lacked the written authority to bind Ward and Ray to this contract. Although they were willing to sell, the description of the land was disputed—Price insisted on a description that included land south of the Illinois and Michigan Canal, whereas Ward and Ray intended to sell it as lying to the center of the canal, leaving discrepancies of two to three acres. Consequently, the sale fell through and the defendants sold the land to another party, incurring commissions to a different agent. The case revolved around whether the plaintiffs were entitled to commissions despite the lack of effective authority from the sellers.	The plaintiffs claimed they were entitled to commissions for the sale of the land, arguing they had facilitated the agreement and had obtained a written contract from the purchaser. They asserted that even without written authority from the defendants, if the purchaser was willing to abide by the contract, the commission should still be earned.	The defendants contended that the written contract was not binding due to Faulkner's lack of authority. They highlighted that there was never an official agreement since the consent on the specific land description was ambiguous. Ray specifically stated he did not authorize any sale under the terms presented, and both defendants intended to sell the land only as it was conveyed to them (to the center of the canal).

In December 1843, in the Henderson circuit court of Illinois, Joseph Duncan, Stephen S. Phelps, and Alexis Phelps initiated a legal action against George A. Charles over a series of debt obligations. The dispute arose from three sealed notes totaling $138.75 due in one, two, and three years after their dates, respectively. The plaintiffs claimed these amounts, asserting that the notes were constituted as binding legal obligations. The defendant Charles countered by denying liability through multiple pleas, particularly arguing a total failure of consideration based on the assertion that the plaintiffs had not provided a good and sufficient warranty deed for a property involved in the transaction, which was to take place in Oquawka. Upon examination, the circuit court initially favored Charles, leading to the plaintiffs appealing the decision, asserting that the circuit court had made errors in assessing the validity of the defendant’s pleas.	The plaintiffs’ primary arguments revolved around their rights to recover on the three promissory notes executed by the defendant. They contended that the notes represented binding agreements, and therefore, the failure to pay constituted a breach. The plaintiffs sought recovery of the owed amounts and claimed that the defendant's defenses, particularly about the claimed failure of consideration, were unfounded given that they had fulfilled their obligations under the contract.	The defendant, George A. Charles, presented several defenses, chiefly arguing total failure of consideration. He claimed that the debts represented by the notes were void because the plaintiffs had not delivered a warranty deed for the property as stipulated in the terms of the sale agreement. He contended that the plaintiffs' failure to tender a deed meant they could not enforce the notes, and therefore, he should not be held liable. Furthermore, he emphasized that his default on payments should not result in any recovery by the plaintiffs due to their noncompliance with the contractual obligations.

In the case of Wilder et al. v. House, which was decided in April 1867, the events unfolded in Illinois. The central individuals involved were the plaintiffs, Wilder and others, and the defendant, House. The dispute arose from procedural issues concerning a bill of exceptions that the plaintiffs sought to have included in the record. The plaintiffs argued that the filing of this document was timely, while the defendant contested its validity, claiming it was filed later than the court's specified deadline. The defendant filed a motion to strike the bill of exceptions from the record, alleging that it was improperly filed in October 1866 instead of within the designated ten days after March 17, 1866. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, which had to consider the legitimacy of the filings and the inability to amend the record as requested by the defendant.	The plaintiffs claimed that the bill of exceptions had been properly signed and filed in accordance with the court's rules. They contended that any irregularity related to the bill's timing should be rectified by the lower court rather than by the Supreme Court. They sought to maintain the integrity of the bill of exceptions as part of the record.	The defendant argued that the bill of exceptions was not filed within the time frame mandated by the lower court, and thus should be struck from the record. They supported their motion with an affidavit from the clerk of the Circuit Court, highlighting that procedural errors in filing the document disqualified it from consideration by the Supreme Court.

In March 1832, Bird M. Simpson appealed a judgment against him that was issued by a justice of the peace in Marion County, Illinois. The case arose when Moses M. Rawlings initiated an action for the collection of a debt amounting to $110.47 as stated in a promissory note, which had an endorsement showing a credit of $10.50, resulting in a remaining balance of $99.97. The justice ruled in favor of Rawlings for the full amount owed along with interest, effective from August 11, 1831. Simpson contested this judgment, claiming that the justice lacked jurisdiction due to the initial note sum exceeding $100, despite the credits. The case was taken to the Circuit Court, where the justice’s decision was upheld, prompting Simpson to seek further review by the Illinois Supreme Court.	Bird M. Simpson contended that the justice of the peace did not have jurisdiction over the case since the original amount on the promissory note exceeded $100, even after credits were applied. He argued that this lack of jurisdiction invalidated the lower court’s judgment, and therefore sought to have the ruling reversed on these grounds.	Moses M. Rawlings, the defendant, maintained that the justice had correctly adjudicated the case based on the provisions of the law at the time. He argued that the endorsement of credits on the note did not diminish the original debt amount and thus did not affect the jurisdiction of the justice. Rawlings sought to have the judgment affirmed by the Circuit Court following the appeal.

In January 1860, the Great Western Railroad Company of 1859 was responsible for maintaining a railroad line in Macon, Illinois. The company established operations but failed to erect and maintain proper fencing along its tracks, particularly after more than six months of usage. On several occasions, livestock belonging to Guy Helm, the plaintiff, wandered onto the tracks and were subsequently killed by trains operated by the company. Helm filed a claim under tort law, arguing that the railroad's negligence in failing to comply with statutory fencing requirements led to the loss of his animals, including horses, cows, sheep, and hogs, amounting to $100 in damages. The case was brought before the Macon Circuit Court during its November term in 1861.	Helm contended that the Great Western Railroad breached its legal duty to erect and maintain adequate fencing to prevent animals from accessing the tracks, except at designated crossings. He argued that the defendants' negligence directly caused the death of his livestock. Helm sought monetary damages for the loss of his animals, asserting that the company should be held liable due to its failure to comply with the statutory fencing requirements.	The Great Western Railroad Company argued that Helm's declaration did not effectively negate the possibility that the animals might have been killed at a properly fenced farm crossing, which would absolve them of liability. They claimed that if the fencing was maintained as required, any intrusion by the animals would be a defense against the allegations. Furthermore, the company contended that the relevant objections regarding the declaration should have been raised earlier in the process and were thus not valid at this stage.

John Meister filed a case against Nicholas Lang in the Illinois Appellate Court concerning damages resulting from water overflow from Lang's building gutters. The event took place after a series of rainstorms, during which water from Lang's poorly maintained gutters dripped onto Meister's adjacent brick building, allegedly causing damage to its walls. The case was presided over by Judge George W. Hebdman in the Logan County Circuit Court, where two juries had previously ruled against Meister's claims. The plaintiff argued that the defendant was negligent in maintaining the gutters, while the defendant contended that the gutter system was sufficient for normal rain conditions typical to the area.	Meister's main argument revolved around the assertion that Nicholas Lang failed to maintain his building's gutters, leading to water damage on Meister's property. He sought damages for the repairs necessitated by this alleged negligence, claiming that Lang's lack of adequate gutter maintenance directly caused the harm to his brick building.	Nicholas Lang defended against the claims by asserting that the gutter system on his property was adequate to handle the normal rainfall expected for the region. He argued that the law does not require a building owner to maintain a gutter system that would prevent water overflow during extraordinary weather events, which are not typically anticipated. Furthermore, Lang contested the definition of "ordinary rain" and the jury's instructions related to it, maintaining that the jury's verdicts finding in his favor were justified and supported by the evidence.

James Q. Brown v. Thomas W. Berry is a legal case that took place in 1864, with the judgment rendered in January 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Piatt County, Illinois, after an action of assumpsit was initiated, originally brought in the Macon County Circuit Court. The key individuals involved were James Q. Brown (the plaintiff) and Thomas W. Berry (the defendant). On August 16, 1864, Berry purchased a farm and its personal property from Brown for $20,000, with specified payment terms, including $8,000 cash upfront and additional payments due on specified future dates. The agreement also required Brown to deliver the farm and associated goods, excluding specific household items and three horses. Berry alleged that he paid according to the contract but that Brown failed to deliver the items, leading Berry to seek damages in court. The case's trial resulted in a jury verdict favoring Berry, awarding him $402.50 and costs. Brown's subsequent motion for a new trial was denied, prompting his appeal to the Supreme Court.	Berry argued that he had fulfilled his payment obligations for the farm and personal property as stipulated in their contract, but Brown failed to deliver the items. Berry sought damages for this breach of contract, emphasizing that the non-delivery constituted a failure to adhere to their agreement.	Brown contended the court made errors during the trial, specifically regarding the recalling of a witness and the admissibility of certain evidence under a videlicet. He argued that these procedural issues and a claim of variance between the evidence presented and the assertions made in the counts could justify a reversal of the jury's decision. Brown requested that the court overturn the judgment in favor of Berry.

In December 1847, the case of Philemon B. Selby v. Richard A. Hutchinson was resolved in the Illinois Supreme Court. Selby appealed after a jury verdict ruled in favor of Hutchinson, the administrator of the estate of Charles Teed, at the Knox County Circuit Court during the November term of 1846. The trial determined that Selby owed Hutchinson $462.50, stemming from a contract related to the construction of a flouring mill where Teed was the primary worker. Disputes involved Teed and Selby's obligations under their agreement, which included conditions on furnishing materials and performing work. Key issues included allegations that Selby had defaulted on providing necessary materials, which led to a resolution of the contract by Teed's administrator. Testimonies revealed that while Teed made some progress, Selby's delays in furnishing materials were significant, but the court ultimately found that both parties bore some responsibility for the delays.	The plaintiff, Richard A. Hutchinson, claimed that as the administrator of Charles Teed's estate, he had fulfilled all conditions required under the contract, but Selby’s failure to provide materials resulted in delays that warranted the rescission of the contract. Hutchinson sought compensation for the work done by Teed on the mill, arguing that the delays constituted significant default by Selby, allowing for a legal recovery of the value of labor performed.	Selby maintained that any delays were minor and did not amount to a total breach of the contract that would allow for rescission. He claimed that the court should have recognized mutual delays on both sides and asserted that the jury's verdict was against the law and evidence. Selby further contended that he never received full compensation for costs and argued there were misjoinders in the counts presented, as well as procedural errors in the original trial.

Mary Larned brought a legal action against Francis Tiernan in the Illinois Supreme Court, which was filed on May 19, 1884. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, wherein Larned alleged that her husband, Elliot P. Larned, lost $2,000 while playing cards and subsequently paid this amount to the defendant, Tiernan. The core of the dispute was based on a clause in the amended Criminal Code of 1874, which allowed individuals to recover money lost in gambling. The court below had sustained a demurrer to Larned’s declaration, leading to a judgment in favor of the defendant. Larned then took further legal action, claiming that the statute in question was constitutional and seeking to overturn the lower court’s decision.	The plaintiff, Mary Larned, claimed that under the last clause of section 132 of the Illinois Criminal Code, she was entitled to recover treble the amount lost due to gambling, which amounted to $6,000 ($2,000 lost multiplied by three). She argued that the court’s dismissal of her claim was erroneous, emphasizing that the statute provided a valid civil remedy for recovering losses incurred from gambling and was therefore constitutional.	The defendant, Francis Tiernan, contended that the clause from the Criminal Code did not align with the constitutional provision requiring laws to express a single subject within their titles. Tiernan argued that the statute improperly mixed civil and criminal provisions, which could render it unconstitutional. He maintained that the lower court's judgment, which favored him, was correct and should be upheld.

In the case of Eric L. Hedstrom et al. v. Digory W. Baker et al., filed in the Illinois Appellate Court on June 27, 1883, the dispute arose between two coal wholesale dealers over an account for coal sold and delivered. The plaintiffs, Hedstrom & Co., were seeking to recover a balance of $1,027.37 from the defendants, Baker Bros. The litigation stemmed from allegations that the plaintiffs breached special oral contracts made with the defendants in 1880. Specifically, it was claimed that plaintiffs failed to supply the defendants with specific quantities of coal as per the agreed terms. The deliveries were supposed to occur at reduced prices during the coal season of 1880. The trial court allowed the defendants to argue that they were entitled to recoup damages for the alleged breach, leading to contradictory testimony regarding the existence of the contracts and the terms agreed upon.	The plaintiffs contended that they had delivered the coal stated in the account and sought to recover the full amount owed for these transactions. They claimed that the only disputed issue was the quality of one cargo delivery and maintained that the defendants had failed to fulfill their payment obligations for previous deliveries of the coal.	The defendants claimed that the plaintiffs breached their agreements to supply coal at previously established rates. They argued that due to the alleged breach of contract by the plaintiffs, they sustained damages, which they sought to recoup. They positioned that, without the plaintiffs fulfilling their contractual obligations, they were entitled to deduct those damages from any amount owed.

The case of The Ottawa Glass Company v. H. A. McCaleb took place in LaSalle County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1876. The Ottawa Glass Company, the plaintiff, was assessed for various taxes on its capital stock and franchise against what they considered an oppressive valuation by the county and state taxing authorities. The county board initially assessed their capital stock at $50,690, which was later reduced to $37,257 by the State Board of Equalization. Despite this reduction, the company was still impacted by a tax based on the assessed value of their capital stock, which they claimed was significantly overstated. The plaintiff filed a bill in chancery seeking to restrain the extension of these taxes, arguing that the company should not be taxed on shares that they believed had little market value and that belonged to their shareholders. The assessment of property and valuation for tax purposes involved a complex process and assertions regarding the legality and fairness of the taxation methods employed by state officials.	The Ottawa Glass Company claimed that the valuation of their capital stock and franchise for taxation was unauthorized and oppressive. They argued that the shares held no market value and that the taxation should solely apply to the tangible personal property and real estate owned by the company, which had been fairly valued at $46,000. They sought to restrain the county clerk from extending taxes based on the assessed value of the capital stock, declaring that such a tax was applied to property that rightfully belonged to the shareholders rather than the company itself.	H. A. McCaleb, the county clerk, defended the valuation and assessment practices used by the county and state boards. The defense asserted that the legislature had the right to tax corporate capital stock rather than individual shares, and the method applied was legally sound. They contended that the assessment reflected the full cash value of the capital stock and franchise and was necessary to ensure that both the company and its shareholders contributed their fair share of taxes. The defense argued that there were no errors, fraud, or illegitimacies in the assessment process that warranted judicial intervention and that the plaintiff’s claims were unfounded.

The case 'Anderson Walton v. Thomas E. Burton et al.' took place in Coles County, Illinois, in the context of a legal dispute surrounding a mortgage. Thomas E. Burton, residing in Ohio, and Elias Burton, his brother living in Illinois, were at the center of the case. In 1872, Elias borrowed money from Thomas and promised to secure the debt with a mortgage on his property, which included two lots in Charleston, Illinois. On September 17, 1872, Elias executed and recorded a mortgage intended for Thomas but due to an error by the draughtsman, the pertinent property was not correctly described. After recording, Elias obtained the mortgage from the recorder's office and lost it before formally transferring it to Thomas. Despite this, Thomas confirmed via letter his awareness of the mortgage and requested Elias to hold onto it until he could retrieve it in person. As a result of a subsequent mortgage issued to Anderson Walton in 1875, which similarly misdescribed the property, a legal battle ensued regarding whose mortgage held priority. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court after Walton sought to reverse the Appellate Court's decision affirming the rights of Thomas E. Burton regarding the corrected mortgage's enforceability and priority, resulting in this final ruling in June 1883.",	Thomas E. Burton, as the plaintiff, claimed the validity of his mortgage executed by Elias Burton, asserting that it was properly recorded and that the loss of the physical document should not negate its enforceability. He argued that the subsequent request for Elias to hold the mortgage until Thomas' arrival constituted acceptance and that the equity in the property should be forfeited to him due to the priority of his recorded mortgage over Walton's later claim.",	Anderson Walton, as the defendant, contended that the original mortgage to Thomas was never validly delivered, asserting that the necessary formalities for delivery were not met. Walton's arguments focused on the claim that he was unaware of Thomas's existing mortgage when he secured his own mortgage, and he sought to establish the validity and priority of his claims to the property based on this lack of knowledge.",

In the case of Jo Robinson v. Gillison Maghee, the events took place in Saline County, Illinois, culminating in a court decision in June 1877. The litigation stemmed from a foreclosure matter involving a mortgage. Jo Robinson, the plaintiff, filed a bill in chancery against Gillison Maghee, the defendant, to enforce the mortgage and seek foreclosure on the property in question. The case had a prior decree for foreclosure and sale issued on September 1, 1860, but the details surrounding the case’s progression appeared unclear. The defendant claimed that the case had been dismissed from the docket in August 1864 and that the plaintiff sought to reinstate it years later without providing proper notice. The court examined the records and determined that the decree of foreclosure had not been regularly dismissed, thus leading to an examination of the subsequent proceedings.	Jo Robinson, the plaintiff, asserted that she was entitled to foreclosure of the mortgage held against the property owned by Gillison Maghee. Robinson maintained that the previous proceedings leading to the decree had been properly executed, and that the court should approve the report of the special commissioner who sold the property. The plaintiff's main argument revolved around the legitimacy of the prior decree and her right to enforce the sale without the need for additional notice to the defendant.	Gillison Maghee, the defendant, contended that the foreclosure case had been dismissed years prior to the current proceedings and that any reinstatement of the case without notice would constitute an error. Maghee's defense rested on the assertion that after the alleged dismissal of the case, there could be no valid decree allowing for the sale of the property. He argued that the decree confirming the sale should not be upheld due to procedural irregularities associated with how and when the case was reinstated.

In December 1886, a legal case was filed in Cook County, Illinois, involving two defendants, Zeno Schirmeier and Johanna Mueller, against the plaintiff, Elizabeth Baecker. The case arose from allegations of malicious prosecution, where Baecker claimed that the defendants had wrongfully obtained warrants for her arrest based on accusations of violating a Chicago city ordinance. The first two counts related to the defendants’ actions before two different justices of the peace, George Kersten and Max Eberliardt, alleging that these actions were taken without probable cause and led to Baecker's arrest and imprisonment. The defendants did not initially appear in court, resulting in a default judgment. A jury later assessed damages at $250. After the damages had been assessed, the defendants appeared and filed a motion to dismiss judgment based on alleged misjoinder of counts, a claim that was ultimately overruled. The plaintiff amended her declaration by removing certain counts and the court upheld the remaining counts against the defendants. Ultimately, the court ruled in favor of the plaintiff and awarded her damages.	Elizabeth Baecker, the plaintiff, argued that Zeno Schirmeier and Johanna Mueller maliciously prosecuted her by obtaining arrest warrants without probable cause. She sought damages for the wrongful actions taken against her, which included her arrest and imprisonment based on false allegations regarding violation of a city ordinance. The plaintiff's claims were organized into multiple counts, focusing primarily on the malicious actions of the defendants that led to her wrongful prosecution.	The defendants, Zeno Schirmeier and Johanna Mueller, contended that there was a misjoinder of counts in the plaintiff’s declaration and motioned to set aside the verdict based on this argument. They requested the court to reconsider the default judgment and permit them to file a plea of not guilty. However, their motions to dismiss the judgment and to set aside the verdict were denied by the court, which maintained that the plaintiff had sufficiently amended her declaration and that no prejudice had occurred against the defendants.

In January 1859, in Illinois, Charles E. Quackenbush was involved in a legal dispute concerning a mechanics' lien action regarding a piece of land he owned. The case arose when the defendants sought to enforce a mechanics' lien against a parcel of land described as approximately three acres located in the southeast corner of the southwest quarter of the northwest quarter of section 22 in township 15 north, range 10 west of the third Principal Meridian. Quackenbush had been in possession of this land, holding a title bond from previous owner William B. Warren. During the proceedings, Quackenbush was defaulted at the appearance term, and the court issued decrees that directed the property to be sold. Quackenbush later objected to the validity of the sale on the grounds that the property description in the decrees was too vague and not legally sufficient. Nevertheless, the court overruled his objections, stating that the description was adequate given the extrinsic evidence available to locate the property.	Quackenbush claimed that the descriptions of the property in the mechanics' lien petitions and decrees were legally insufficient, arguing that they did not provide a clear and definite description of the premises to be sold. He sought to have the sale vacated on the basis that the lack of clarity in the property description would render any future deed invalid, thus infringing upon his rights to the property.	The defendants maintained that the descriptions provided in the legal documents were sufficient for the purpose of establishing a mechanics’ lien on the property. They argued that the property could be accurately located through existing circumstances and extrinsic evidence, asserting that Quackenbush's objections were unfounded. They sought to uphold the court's decrees and proceed with the sale of the property as previously ordered.

In September 1867, in Kankakee County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose in the case of John B. Boudreau v. Aglean Boudreau, Administratrix, et al. The case centered on a claim made by Aglean Boudreau, the widow and administratrix of Emilien Boudreau, who sought to recover two bay mares from John B. Boudreau, the deceased’s father. Aglean asserted that the horses were a gift from John to his son, Emilien, prior to his death. This claim was primarily supported by the testimony of a witness, Flora Beterneau, who recounted that John had stated he had given his son a team of horses. However, other witnesses, particularly Emilien's brothers, provided contrary evidence, suggesting no gift had occurred. The case was initially decided by a jury that ruled in favor of Aglean, leading John to file a motion for a new trial, claiming the verdict was against the weight of the evidence. This case was ultimately brought to the Illinois Supreme Court for review.	The plaintiff, Aglean Boudreau, claimed that two bay mares were gifted to her deceased husband, Emilien Boudreau, by his father, John B. Boudreau. She asserted that this asserted gift entitled her as the administratrix to reclaim the horses. The request was for the court to uphold the jury’s decision in her favor, which had initially found in her favor based on the claim of the gift.	The defendant, John B. Boudreau, argued that the jury's verdict was against the clear weight of evidence and sought a new trial. He contended that the evidence did not sufficiently support the allegation of a gift, highlighting the testimony from individuals who disputed Aglean's claim. He maintained that, under legal principles governing gifts, reasonable proof was lacking to substantiate the claim made by the plaintiff.

In the case of John E. Brooks et al. v. Azariah Sanders, the legal proceedings took place in Illinois, with the final decision rendered on January 19, 1884. The controversy began when Azariah Sanders obtained a judgment against Simpson W. Miller and Matilda Miller for $3,160 on March 12, 1879. Following an unsatisfied execution, Sanders executed a second alias on April 27, 1880, and the sheriff, John E. Brooks, was empowered to carry out a redemption of Miller's property on April 28, 1880, by paying $2,235 to the sheriff and securing a certificate of redemption. Subsequently, Sanders assigned his judgment to Healy & Stoddard for $2,300, transferring rights to collect the judgment and any sums related. On August 19, 1880, the sheriff sold the property to Healy & Stoddard for $5,793.85. Following these events, Sanders claimed he was entitled to a refund from the sheriff for the amount he had paid during the redemption process. The circuit court originally ruled in favor of Sanders, which was upheld by the Appellate Court, prompting the sheriff to bring the matter to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Azariah Sanders, argued that the sheriff should refund him the amount he paid to redeem the property from the previous sale. He contended that, based on the assignment of judgment to Healy & Stoddard, the sheriff became liable to compensate him for the redemption costs incurred after the sale of the property to the assignee. Sanders sought recovery of the $2,235 he had paid during the redemption as part of his claim against the sheriff's official bond.	The defendant, represented by the sheriff, contended that Sanders had no cause of action. According to the defendant's legal arguments, after redeeming the property, a judgment creditor only has a right to the proceeds of a future sale, not control over the redemption money itself. The sheriff maintained that he acted correctly according to the statutory framework regarding redemption and execution and that any claims Sanders had were invalid due to the nature of the assignment of the judgment, which transferred all rights to Healy & Stoddard.

The case of *The Jacksonville Southeastern Railway Company v. Claus F. Carlsen* was decided on November 30, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose in Cass County, Illinois, when the plaintiff, Claus F. Carlsen, sought damages after his cow and several hogs were killed by a train operated by the defendant, the Jacksonville Southeastern Railway Company. The incident occurred at a public highway crossing where the plaintiff claimed that the train's crew failed to exercise proper vigilance to prevent the collision. According to the plaintiff's assertion, the statutory signals required to notify road users of the approaching train were not given in the appropriate manner or at the proper distance, leading to the death of the cow. Witnesses contradicted the railroad crew's claim that they had signaled adequately, stating that they heard no alerts prior to the accident. The case did not involve a jury; instead, the court ruled directly on matters of fact, focusing on the potential negligence of the railroad company in both signaling and vigilant observation prior to the crossing.	The plaintiff's main argument centered on the claim that the Jacksonville Southeastern Railway Company was negligent in failing to provide the necessary statutory signals before reaching the highway crossing. Carlsen contended that the actions of the train's crew could have prevented the collision had they maintained a proper lookout for cattle on the track. He sought damages for the loss of his cow and hogs, emphasizing that the incidents were a direct result of the defendant's negligence.	The defendant, the Jacksonville Southeastern Railway Company, claimed that proper signals were given as mandated by law and asserted that the train crew had indeed seen several cattle prior to the collision, including the cow that was ultimately struck. They argued that the highway was lower than the railroad track and that the necessary precautions were taken to ensure the safety of both the train and any potential obstructions on the track. The defense maintained that they were not liable for the damages claimed by the plaintiff given that they had adhered to statutory requirements.

The case "Seth W. Hardin et al. v. James Kirk" took place in Will County, Illinois, and reached a resolution in September 1868. It involved two plaintiffs, Seth W. Hardin and Wakeman, who each brought separate actions of ejectment against the defendant, James Kirk, for the same tract of land. The two declarations were filed independently but were treated as one case in court. During the trial, the court, upon the defendant's request, required the plaintiffs to select one declaration to proceed with. The plaintiffs chose to move forward with Hardin's declaration. The court found in favor of the defendant, ruling that the plaintiffs had not established their right to recover the land due to complications involving a chain of title and the priority of deeds. One of the key issues was whether the court erred in requiring the plaintiffs to elect which declaration to pursue, which was linked to the ownership claims of the land by the previous owners and how the acknowledgments in the deed were handled.	The plaintiffs claimed wrongful ejection from the property and requested legal recognition of their ownership rights. They filed separate declarations for the same land, hoping to obtain a ruling that would grant them the right to the disputed property. The specific arguments revolved around the legitimacy of their claims to the land, citing outdated and improperly recorded deeds by previous owners that affected their titles.	The defendant, James Kirk, argued that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a legitimate claim to the property due to prior ownership disputes and issues with deed acknowledgment. He claimed that the acknowledgment for one of the key deeds was improperly documented, making it inadmissible in court. Moreover, he contended that the plaintiffs' separate actions could not be easily consolidated without consent, which had not been granted.

The case "Mart Q. Staley, Administratrix of the estate of Saunderson D. Staley, v. Charles E. Dodge and Ada Pearson, Administrators of the estate of George T. Pearson" took place in Sangamon County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1869. The case stemmed from a dispute involving attorney Mart Q. Staley, who was hired by the administrators of George T. Pearson's estate to collect debts owed to the estate. During his tenure, Staley collected funds and claimed the right to retain a portion of these for his legal fees. However, the administrators, Dodge and Pearson, contested this, leading to a lawsuit for the recovery of the collected funds. Staley argued that a settlement was reached with Ada Pearson regarding his fees, while Dodge disputed this claim, stating that Staley was obliged to look to the estate for his payment.
