The court examined the relationship between Staley and the administrators, focusing on whether Staley had disclosed all pertinent information about the estate's financial affairs.	The plaintiff, represented by Charles E. Dodge and Ada Pearson, asserted that Staley, as their attorney, was not entitled to retain the collected funds as fees without proper disclosure of his agreement to look to the estate for payment. They claimed that Staley's actions constituted an unfair advantage, leading them to seek recovery of the funds he retained improperly.	The defendant, Mart Q. Staley, contended that he had reached a settlement with Ada Pearson, wherein she agreed to pay him a sum in exchange for his services. He argued that this settlement was valid and that he was entitled to the funds he had collected. Staley maintained that he had communicated with Ada regarding his fees and that any settlement reached was legitimate.

The case "The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company v. Lycurgus K. Avery" originates from an incident on December 16, 1879, in Quincy, Illinois. Lycurgus K. Avery, an employee of the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company, was working in the railroad yard when he attempted to uncouple a freight car belonging to the Keokuk, St. Louis and Northwestern Railroad Company. Avery alleged that the car's coupling apparatus was defective, which had been known to be in a dangerous condition prior to the accident. As Avery operated the car, his right thumb was caught and crushed due to the malfunction of the coupling mechanism. Avery had significant experience in railroad operations, having worked for over 18 years, including the last five years at the defendant's yard as a switchman and foreman. The case revolved around whether the defendant had a legal duty to keep the car safe for handling, as it was operated by its employees. Following a trial in the Circuit Court of Adams County and an appeal to the Appellate Court, Avery's claims were upheld, leading to the defendant's appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Lycurgus K. Avery claimed that the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company was negligent in allowing the damaged way car to be in operation within its yard, posing a danger to its employees. He argued that the company had a duty to either maintain the safety of the car or ensure its owner repaired it. Avery sought damages for the injury he sustained as a result of this negligence, emphasizing that the company failed to provide safe equipment, which directly resulted in his injury while performing his work duties.	The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company contended that it was not responsible for maintaining the freight car belonging to another company, asserting that the master-servant relationship does not hold them liable for the negligence of a fellow employee in a different line of duty. The defendant argued that Avery had assumed the risks associated with his employment and that he was partly responsible for his injury due to his own lack of care when handling the defective equipment. They requested a judgment in their favor, asserting that Avery's injury resulted from his own negligence rather than a failure of the defendant to act.

Lillie Williams initiated a lawsuit against George H. Forbes, the administrator of Delilah Deeds' estate, in the county court of Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The case revolves around a document dated October 25, 1875, in which Delilah Deeds acknowledged a debt of $2,500 to her niece Lillie Williams for personal services rendered. Following a trial in the county court, the ruling favored the defendant, leading Williams to appeal to the circuit court. There, a jury awarded her $3,708.75, but the defendant subsequently appealed to the Appellate Court for the Second District. This court reversed the circuit court's decision, declaring that the note was a gift with no legal consideration supporting it. The Appellate Court found the facts differently from the circuit court, determining that the note represented a mere testamentary bequest and therefore could not constitute a valid claim. Williams appealed again, bringing the matter to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Lillie Williams argued that the written acknowledgment of debt from Delilah Deeds entitled her to recover the amount owed for her services. She contended that the circuit court's jury ruling validated her claim and that the Appellate Court erred by reinterpreting the facts to conclude the note lacked consideration. Williams sought to have the Appellate Court's ruling overturned in favor of her original judgment.	George H. Forbes contended that the note cited by Williams was not enforceable as it represented a gift, lacking any legal consideration. He argued that Delilah Deeds intended the note as a testamentary arrangement rather than as a binding obligation. Forbes maintained that the Appellate Court correctly identified the absence of consideration, thereby justifying the reversal of the circuit court's judgment.

In April 1859, the case of Anna B. Foote v. William E. Foote was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following a divorce decree issued by the Circuit Court that awarded Anna B. Foote a modest alimony and granted her custody of their two young boys, aged six and two. The marriage encountered severe discord marked by William E. Foote's displays of unrestrained anger and violence, leading Anna to seek separation. The court found Anna to be the “meritorious cause” for the divorce, and despite no counterclaims from William, significant financial disclosures during the trial revealed his substantial income as a proprietor of a thriving printing establishment in Bloomington. Anna, described as being in delicate health and unable to work much, was financially supported by her husband with a restoration of her initial property and interim financial assistance since her departure from their home. The court highlighted the necessity to ensure proper support for both Anna and the children, implying that William, despite his financial capabilities, had been neglectful towards his children.	Anna B. Foote argued that the alimony amount awarded by the Circuit Court was inadequate for her and her children's needs. She claimed that her necessary annual expenses amounted to approximately $1,200 to $1,400, based on testimonies presented during the trial. Hence, she sought a modification of the court's ruling to ensure a fair and sufficient alimony that would cover her living costs and support for their children.	William E. Foote did not contest the divorce allegations of cruelty nor attempted to counterclaim against Anna. While acknowledging the need for alimony, his defense centered around the claim that his property was of a perishable nature and he expressed concern that alimony demands might overly deplete his resources. He argued for a minimal and fair amount of support, emphasizing his financial limitations and potential impact on his business and assets.

Elisha C. Ware v. Thomas M. Jordan took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the court's decision rendered on March 28, 1888. The case arose from a promissory note executed by Elisha C. Ware, the defendant, to Thomas M. Jordan, the plaintiff, for $250. This note, dated December 16, 1879, was intended to be payable by October 1880, with an interest rate of eight percent. The lawsuit stemmed from transactions that occurred in late 1876, where Jordan, a commission merchant involved in trading on the Board of Trade of Chicago, managed wheat purchases and sales on behalf of Ware. These initial wheat transactions resulted in a profit for Ware, which he paid to Jordan; however, subsequent sales led to significant losses due to rising wheat prices and insufficient margins provided by Ware. A final accounting of these losses was rendered, totaling between $1,500 and $1,600. When Ware failed to pay for the losses he incurred, he issued the promissory note in question as a form of settlement. The court had to determine whether the note was valid or if it arose from illegal gambling activities, as claimed by the defendant. After evaluating the evidence and testimonies, the jury ruled in favor of the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, Thomas M. Jordan, claimed that Elisha C. Ware executed a promissory note for $250 to settle an outstanding debt related to trading losses on wheat transactions. Jordan argued that the note was issued in good faith and sought legal enforcement of it in court. He maintained that the transactions were legitimate and not gambling-related, asserting his right to recover the amount stated in the promissory note, along with interest.	Elisha C. Ware contended that the promissory note was intended as a settlement for losses incurred in gambling transactions rather than legitimate trading. He argued that there was an implied understanding that the transactions would be settled based on price differences without actual delivery of the commodities. Ware's defense aimed to demonstrate that the note should be invalidated on the grounds that it originated from illegal activities on the Board of Trade.

In the case of the City of East St. Louis v. East St. Louis Gaslight & Coke Co., which was decided on June 12, 1886, the dispute arose in East St. Louis, Illinois. The city had entered into a contract with the East St. Louis Gaslight & Coke Company on October 3, 1874, to light its streets with gas for a period of thirty years. According to the contract, the gas company was responsible for extending its gas mains, erecting lampposts, and providing gas for street lamps that needed to be lit from sunset to sunrise, with a stipulated payment of $32.20 per lamp annually. The gas company fulfilled these obligations, having installed 303 lamps by late 1878. However, an issue arose when the city, having accrued an indebtedness exceeding 5% of the assessed value of taxable property, notified the gas company on May 15, 1877, that it did not acknowledge any liability under the existing contract and would not recognize any claims unless a new agreement was reached. This disaffirmance led to the legal action initiated by the gas company to recover payments allegedly due for gas supplied after this notification.	The plaintiff, East St. Louis Gaslight & Coke Co., argued that the city had entered into a valid contract to provide gas lighting for the streets, which included specific obligations regarding the installation and maintenance of street lamps. They claimed that the city owed them $2,658.83 for gas services rendered for the months of September, October, and November 1878. The plaintiff maintained that they had complied with the terms outlined in the initial contract and had properly executed their obligations.	The defendant, the City of East St. Louis, contended that the contract was voidable and had been disaffirmed prior to the plaintiff's claims for payment. The city asserted that it notified the gas company in writing that it did not recognize any liability under the contract due to financial constraints, having exceeded its legal borrowing limits. Consequently, the city argued there was no legal foundation for any payment claims from the gas company after the notice of disaffirmance had been issued.

Edmund S. Holbrook initiated an action of ejectment in April 1865 against Mathias L. Cook for the recovery of a lot of land in Joliet, Illinois. Ellen Fellows, being the landlord of Cook, was allowed to defend the case. During the trial, Holbrook presented several pieces of evidence, including a patent for the land issued to James B. Campbell, a decree from the District Court declaring Campbell a bankrupt, documents indicating the appointment of an assignee, and a subsequent deed transferring the property to Holbrook. These documents were presented without objection from the defendant. In response, the defendant sought to introduce a tax deed issued by the Mayor of Joliet from April 27, 1859, disputing Holbrook's claim. Holbrook's objection to this deed centered on the lack of proof that the former owner had been properly notified about the tax sale, as mandated by the Illinois Constitution. The court needed to determine whether the admission of the tax deed was valid without such notice being properly proved.	Holbrook argued that he had rightful ownership of the property backed by a patent, a bankruptcy decree, and a legal transfer deed, all of which were admitted in evidence without objection. He asserted that the defendant's tax deed should be inadmissible due to the failure to notify the former owner, as required by law, thereby invalidating the defendant's claim to the property.	The defendant contended that the tax deed was valid and should be admissible in evidence against Holbrook's claims. The defendant's argument rested on the presentation of the tax deed itself, despite Holbrook's objections regarding the lack of proper notice of the tax sale to the former owner.

The case of Boynton v. Champlin was adjudicated in April 1867 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The proceedings took place in Illinois, following the reversal of a prior judgment by the court below. Key individuals involved included the plaintiff, Boynton, and the defendant, Champlin. After the court's earlier decision, the defendant filed a petition for rehearing, claiming a diminution of the record and submitted affidavits to support this argument. The court addressed whether it could entertain the defendant’s claims regarding the alleged incomplete record, asserting that the defendant should have raised the issue of record completeness before joining in error. The ruling emphasized that by joining in error, Champlin admitted the record was complete and that his subsequent objections could not be considered.	The plaintiff, Boynton, likely argued for the enforcement of the initial decision made by the court below, indicating that the record was complete and sufficient to uphold the court’s ruling. Boynton’s legal requests would have included maintaining the court’s previous judgment and rejecting the defendant's claims regarding record diminution.	The defendant, Champlin, contended that there had been a diminution of the record which impacted the fairness of the prior ruling. He argued that this issue should be considered and sought a rehearing to explore this claim further. Champlin’s request included a reexamination of the court’s earlier judgment based on the alleged incompleteness of the record.

The case "Matthew Johnson v. Anna C. Johnson" was decided on May 9, 1888, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved in the case were Matthew Johnson, the husband, and Anna C. Johnson, the wife. The couple was married in January 1881 and lived together until August 13, 1885, when Anna left Matthew, citing his abusive and cruel behavior as the primary reason for their separation. Anna filed for separate maintenance, claiming that she left without fault on her part, and alleged specific acts of cruelty and abuse committed by her husband. Matthew denied the allegations of cruelty and accused Anna of being abusive toward him. He claimed that she was responsible for their marital issues, asserting that her violent temperament contributed to their separation. After hearing conflicting testimonies from both parties and their witnesses, the court found in favor of Anna, granting her $80 per month in alimony, additional solicitor's fees, and expenses related to the appeal. Matthew subsequently appealed the decision to the Appellate Court, which affirmed the circuit court's ruling.	Anna C. Johnson, the plaintiff, claimed that she had good cause for living separately from her husband due to his abusive behavior, which included acts of cruelty and personal violence against her. She argued that she was living apart without fault on her part and sought separate maintenance from her husband, requesting a monthly alimony of $80 and reimbursement for her solicitor's fees due to the legal contest she faced in filing the complaint.	Matthew Johnson, the defendant, denied all allegations of cruelty and asserted that Anna was the one exhibiting violent behavior. He contended that she was not living separately without fault, suggesting that her temperament and abusive actions were detrimental to their marriage. Matthew also challenged the court's decision to grant Anna alimony and requested a reconsideration of the solicitor's fees awarded to her, arguing they were excessive.

In the case of **The Public Grain and Stock Exchange vs. The Western Union Telegraph Company and Board of Trade**, filed in 1883 in Illinois, the complainant sought to prevent the defendant telegraph companies from removing three “tickers” and two Morse instruments from their place of business. The telegraph companies had installed these instruments to provide real-time market quotations for grain and other merchandise to the Public Grain and Stock Exchange. They argued that their business included a “Commercial News Dispatch Department,” through which they gathered market data and shared it with various subscribers. However, they planned to withdraw the services due to pressure from the Board of Trade, which wanted to restrict information flow to what they deemed legitimate entities, accusing the complainant of running a “bucket shop” that facilitated gambling on future prices. The complaint hinged on whether the telegraph companies could withhold market information, alleging a public obligation to provide such services indiscriminately as a public utility.	The plaintiff claimed that the telegraph companies were under a legal obligation to provide them with market quotations as part of their public service duties. They argued that withholding these quotations would unfairly limit their business operations, as the market information was crucial for trading decisions. The plaintiff requested an injunction to stop the telegraph companies from removing their ticker and Morse devices and to compel them to continue supplying real-time market data.	The defendants contended that their business of supplying market data was a private venture and that they had the discretion to determine who received their services. They argued that complying with the Board of Trade's demand not to include the complainant was justified and necessary to maintain their relationships with the board. They also claimed the plaintiff was involved in a disreputable business, which should not be supported by judicial intervention.

The case "Drover’s National Bank of Union Stock Yards v. M. J. O’Hare" took place in January 1886 in Illinois. The dispute arose from a transaction involving the plaintiff, M. J. O'Hare, who owned a lot of steers. On April 10, 1884, he shipped these steers to Bensley Bros., commission merchants in Chicago, for sale on his behalf. The sale of the steers was completed on April 11, 1884, yielding proceeds of $1,053.16. O'Hare instructed Bensley Bros. to send these proceeds to him via the Henry Bank in Mineral Point, Wisconsin. Bensley Bros. deposited the funds into the Drover’s National Bank, indicating it was for the use of O'Hare on the depositing ticket. However, on April 11, 1884, the Henry Bank failed. Subsequently, on April 12, 1884, Drover’s National Bank transferred the funds to the Northwestern National Bank without acknowledging the trust or that the money was for the plaintiff's benefit. This transfer led to the funds being used to settle a debt owed by the Henry Bank to the Northwestern National Bank, prompting O'Hare to bring action against the Drover’s National Bank to recover his funds, which he claimed were wrongfully appropriated.	The plaintiff, M. J. O'Hare, claimed that the Drover’s National Bank wrongfully transferred funds that belonged to him, which had been deposited for transmission to the Henry Bank. He argued that the transfer occurred without any indication that the funds were held in trust for his benefit. O'Hare’s legal request was for the return of the proceeds totaling $1,129.50, which he argued were rightfully his and should not have been appropriated by the defendant bank.	The Drover’s National Bank contended that it was not liable to O'Hare because it transferred the funds to the Northwestern National Bank in good faith, believing it had fulfilled its obligation by doing so. The bank argued that it had not been made aware that the proceeds were intended for anyone other than the Henry Bank itself and claimed that this transfer had discharged it from any further responsibility to O'Hare.

In February 1855, the Illinois legislature chartered a railway company to construct a railway from Mount Vernon to Ashley. By November of that year, the company was organized and elected a board of directors. In 1856, the citizens of Jefferson County voted to allow the use of swamp and overflowed lands for the railway construction. These lands were then conveyed to Joel Pace, who held them in trust. In October 1858, the railway company entered into a contract with partners Yan Duzen, Smith & Co. for the construction of the railway, with a deadline set for March 1860. The contract included financial compensation and land in exchange for construction services. However, by July 1859, Yan Duzen, Smith & Co. abandoned the project after expending only $60,000 of the funds. They also left the state, remaining insolvent. Following this abandonment, the Jefferson County residents voted to allocate an additional $100,000 for the railway. The county court and Pace filed a bill in the Circuit Court to cancel the prior transactions, restore original stockholders' rights, and authorize a new board of directors. The Circuit Court agreed to the request, prompting an appeal.	The plaintiffs, including the county and Pace, argued for the rescission of the contract with Yan Duzen, Smith & Co. due to their failure to perform on the construction of the railway. They requested the reinstatement of the original stockholders and the re-establishment of their rights and franchise to elect a new board of directors and complete the railway.	The defendants, represented by Yan Duzen, Smith & Co., argued against the rescission and the resulting loss of rights and interests for Seymour, the trustee of the bondholders. They maintained that the bondholders had legal and equitable rights that were not being adequately represented in the proceedings and that the plaintiffs could not cancel their rights without due process.

The case "Isaac C. Brown et al. v. Isaiah Thomas" involves a lease agreement initiated on January 1, 1882, in Logan County, Illinois, between Isaac C. Brown and his son-in-law, David B. Yale, for farming purposes. Under the terms of the lease, Yale was to pay Brown one-half of the corn and other crops produced on the land. Prior to leasing the land, Yale sought credit from Isaiah Thomas and received goods totaling $435. After the corn was harvested, it was placed in Brown's cribs, but no division between Brown and Yale had occurred. Yale later executed a bill of sale to Thomas for the corn, with an understanding that payment would cover his debt to Thomas. However, Thomas's acquisition of the corn was contested when Brown attempted to enforce a chattel mortgage against it, resulting in a replevin action filed by Thomas against Brown and Caruthers, who were attempting to sell the corn. The dispute hinged on whether Brown had given Thomas assurances that he would be paid from the crop, which Brown denied.	The plaintiff, Isaiah Thomas, claims he had an agreement with David B. Yale to furnish provisions in return for being paid out of Yale's corn crop. He argues that there was an understanding that the crop would pay off Yale's debt for the goods provided. Thomas maintains that Brown is estopped from denying his right to the corn since he supplied the provisions under the belief that he would be compensated from the crop, leading to his entitlement as a secured creditor under that arrangement.	The defendant, Isaac C. Brown, contends that there was no formal agreement that the crop would serve as payment for Thomas's goods. He asserts that Thomas does not have a lien on the corn and could not claim possession of it since Brown had a chattel mortgage over the crop. Brown argues that he provided financial support to Yale during the farming process and that any assurances he gave Thomas should not constitute an estoppel, since he was not responsible for guaranteeing Yale’s debts from the crop.

In November 1874, the Circuit Court of DeWitt County, Illinois, appointed George B. Wright as the receiver for the Indianapolis, Bloomington and Western Railway Company, due to its involvement in a legal case. Shortly after, Jesse M. Richards, the plaintiff, initiated legal actions against the railway company without court permission and obtained judgments from a justice of the peace, Hess. He then attempted to collect these debts through garnishee proceedings against individuals possessing funds owed to the railway company. The receiver informed the court of these actions, prompting the court to issue an injunction against further proceedings. Although the injunction was not directly served to Richards, he was made aware of it and continued to pursue his claims, leading to contempt proceedings against him. The court found Richards guilty of contempt, resulting in ten days of imprisonment and a fine, which was later reduced to fifty dollars after he agreed to withdraw his garnishee actions.	Richards argued that the appointment of the receiver was void and claimed that he did not commit contempt as there was no actual interference with the receiver’s possession. He sought the reversal of the circuit court’s contempt ruling, insisting that his actions were lawful and that he aimed to collect debts owed to him through lawful means.	The defendant, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, maintained that the receiver’s appointment was valid and that Richards’ actions constituted interference with the court's authority. They contended that any attempts to collect debts without the court’s permission after a receiver’s appointment would directly obstruct the court's function, amounting to contempt.

In 1876, a legal battle emerged in Woodford County, Illinois, involving the parties Nannie E. Oldham and others (the appellants) against Adam Peleger (the appellee). The case revolved around a dispute over lands that the appellants claimed as heirs of Samuel L. Chorn, who had been absent and unheard from for over seven years, indicating he was presumed dead. In 1856, Chorn had acquired the lands in question through a deed from William Patten, who subsequently secured the transaction with a mortgage. After Chorn defaulted on payments, Patten initiated foreclosure proceedings. However, no personal notice was given to Chorn, raising questions about the validity of the foreclosure. Despite attempts to notify him through publication, the legitimacy of that notice was contested. The lands were eventually sold following a court decree, with Patten obtaining ownership. He later sold the property to other parties before it was ultimately acquired by Peleger, who maintained possession. The appellants contended that the foreclosure decree was void due to the lack of proper notice to Chorn and thus, the master’s deed obtained by Patten should not convey any title. Their claim primarily rested on the argument that the court had jurisdiction issues, which would nullify the decrees made in prior court proceedings.	The plaintiffs argued that the foreclosure of the mortgage held by Patten was invalid because Samuel L. Chorn did not receive proper notice or service regarding the foreclosure proceedings. They contended that, as heirs to Chorn's estate, they were entitled to regain possession of the lands based on the belief that the master’s deed to Patten was void. Their legal requests included an overturning of the previous court judgments and a restoration of their rights to the disputed property.	The defendant, Peleger, maintained that the judgments rendered in favor of the foreclosure were valid and that the title to the property had legally transferred through the appropriate channels. He argued that as Chorn had abandoned the country, the absence of personal notice was irrelevant if the court had valid jurisdiction. The defendant’s request was to dismiss the appeal by confirming the validity of the master’s deed and affirming his ownership and possession of the land.

The case "The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Patrick Keefe" took place in 1868 in Sangamon County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Patrick Keefe, was a laborer employed by the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, working on a construction train. During his duties, which involved unloading railroad iron, the engineer of the train started moving it without providing the necessary preliminary whistle signal, as mandated by the train's operational rules. This action led to Keefe being injured while performing his tasks on the train. Following the incident, Keefe filed for damages, claiming that the engineer's negligence caused his injury. A trial was held, and the initial judgment favored Keefe, prompting the railroad company to appeal the decision.	Patrick Keefe asserted that he was injured due to the negligence of the train's engineer, who failed to follow operational protocols by not signaling before moving the train. He contended that this negligence directly resulted in his injuries while he was working under the conductor's orders, and he sought damages for the injuries sustained during his employment.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company argued that under the established legal principle, one employee cannot recover damages from their employer for injuries caused by a co-employee's negligence if the employer exercised due diligence in hiring. They claimed that Keefe and the engineer were fellow servants, both working under the conductor’s authority, and thus should be subject to the same legal protections that preclude recovery in such instances. The railroad company sought a reversal of the judgment in favor of Keefe.

Richard Nash, the Plaintiff in Error, and James Nash, the Defendant in Error, were involved in a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1854. The dispute arises from an obligation concerning a monetary debt. The case's origins can be traced back to a partnership involving a flatboat loaded with pork transported to Vicksburgh, Mississippi, for which Richard Nash was promised $750 by James Nash in a written agreement dated March 25. The agreement indicated that the payment was to be made to Richard Nash or his order. Following the filing of the debt action, James Nash challenged the legal sufficiency of the claims through a demurrer, arguing that the declaration was insufficient due to the details contained in the specialty. The circuit court sustained James Nash's demurrer and ruled in his favor, leading Richard Nash to appeal the decision to the supreme court, where the nature of the contractual obligation and its enforceability became pivotal issues.	Richard Nash, the plaintiff, argued that the written obligation signed by James Nash constituted a valid promise to pay a sum of $750, which was clearly stipulated and not contingent upon any conditions. It was contended that the court erred in accepting the demurrer, as the declaration included viable counts that supported his claims for debt. Nash's legal request sought reversal of the lower court's decision and enforcement of the payment as outlined in the agreement.	James Nash, the defendant, contended that the language and conditions in the agreement rendered the plaintiff's claims insufficient. Through his demurrer, he maintained that the details of consideration muddied the obligation's nature and that the declaration did not adequately assert a viable claim for payment under the specified terms. He sought to uphold the circuit court's judgment affirming the demurrer as well as the dismissal of the plaintiff's claims.

In the case of Silas Shirley v. John Welty, the legal proceedings unfolded in Winnebago County, Illinois, with the initial judgment rendered in 1855. The plaintiff, Silas Shirley, filed a claim against the defendant, John Welty, over a promissory note for $120, which was due in May 1852. On the due date, Welty was unable to pay, resulting in an agreement between the two parties whereby Welty would cover any interest Shirley had to pay on a loan borrowed from Dean at a high interest rate to settle debts with Puller & Anyon. The agreed-upon interest for Welty's note was set at twenty percent per annum. The case progressed through the county court where a jury ultimately ruled in favor of Welty, granting him a verdict of $2.63. Shirley's subsequent request for a new trial was denied, prompting his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The primary focus of the appeal concerned the legality of the interest rate specified in their agreement, which raised questions about usury laws in Illinois.	The plaintiff, Silas Shirley, argued that the agreement allowed him to charge the defendant, John Welty, twenty percent interest on the unpaid note due to a mutual decision to extend the payment period. He claimed that since he had incurred a debt at the same interest rate for a loan he utilized to settle obligations to Puller & Anyon, Welty should be liable for that same interest rate. Shirley sought a judgment that included the specified interest amount he believed he was owed under the terms of their agreement.	The defendant, John Welty, contended that the agreement was usurious and thus invalid under Illinois law, which stipulated a maximum interest rate of six percent on loans. He introduced evidence of payments made towards the note, arguing that the higher interest rate for the extended payment term constituted an evasion of statutory provisions against usury. Welty maintained that the court accurately rejected the plaintiff's instructions to the jury concerning the calculation of potentially recoverable interest, asserting the agreement was legally untenable.

In the case of Weber v. Mueller, decided on October 27, 1886, in Illinois, the plaintiff, Weber, initiated a legal action against the defendant, Mueller, based on a claim related to goods sold and money lent. The case was presented in the Illinois Appellate Court, where Judge Joseph E. Gary presided over the proceedings. The core of the plaintiff's claim revolved around an account for goods sold and delivered, alongside an assertion that monetary advances had been made to the defendant. During the trial, conflicting evidence was presented, leading to a jury decision favoring the defendant. The plaintiff contended that the jury's verdict was against the evidence's preponderance, indicating that they believed they had a stronger case. However, the court found no sufficient basis to reverse the jury's decision and affirmed the ruling in favor of the defendant.	The plaintiff, Weber, claimed that he had provided goods to the defendant, Mueller, and had also lent him money, which remained unpaid. Weber argued that he was entitled to compensation for these transactions. He sought a judgment from the court that would require the defendant to fulfill his financial obligations.	The defendant, Mueller, defended himself by asserting that he had already made payments related to the plaintiff's claims. His primary argument centered on the claim that Weber was not entitled to further compensation, as he believed the debt had been settled. Mueller effectively challenged the evidentiary support for Weber's claims, leading to the establishment of a jury verdict in his favor.

The case "Austin et al. v. Bainter" was adjudicated during the January Term of 1866 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The events leading up to the case occurred on March 15, 1862, in Hancock County, Illinois. The central issue arose from a decree rendered by the Circuit Court of Hancock County, which the plaintiffs (Austin et al.) sought to challenge by filing a writ of error. The plaintiffs argued that errors existed in the decree; however, the defendant, Bainter, contended that those errors were released prior to the filing of the writ, thus no longer subject to appeal. The case involved complex legal matters regarding the nature of error releases and the consent of the parties involved, requiring examination of whether the errors persisted and how they could be contested. The discussion also raised procedural questions about the trial of factual issues related to the plea of release of errors, specifically whether such issues could be resolved in the Supreme Court or should be remitted to the lower court for jury determination.	The plaintiffs claimed that errors existed in the decree rendered by the Circuit Court that warranted a reversal. They argued against the defense's assertion of a release of errors, raising legal objections to the sufficiency and nature of the defendant's pleas. The plaintiffs sought to have the Supreme Court evaluate those errors and reverse the prior decree.	The defendant, Bainter, countered the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that all alleged errors, except for one specific point, had been previously released by the plaintiffs themselves on March 15, 1862. Bainter maintained that the decree challenged was entered by consent and that the plaintiffs had benefited from this agreement, effectively negating the basis for their current claims of error. Bainter requested that the Supreme Court affirm the decree of the lower court based on these defenses.

In the case of Henry Reinbach v. William and Philip Walter, which took place in Franklin, Morgan County, Illinois, the dispute arose over ownership of two lots. The judgment was rendered in January 1862, with the court proceedings taking place shortly before that date. The plaintiff, Henry Reinbach, had been involved in a financial judgment that led to the sale of the properties in question under a fieri facias decree. The appellees, William and Philip Walter, initiated the ejectment process to reclaim the lots. During the trial, it was established that Reinbach had possessed the properties and claimed them as his homestead. However, the court found that the relevant possession status at the time of the lien attachment was not adequately demonstrated, thereby denying Reinbach’s claims to a homestead exemption. The court confirmed the proceedings through the admission of evidence including the process of the judgment, the sheriff's sale, and the evidence of ownership and occupancy presented by Reinbach.	Henry Reinbach argued that he was the owner of the premises at the time of the levy and sale, claiming that these were his homestead properties occupied by his family. He contended that the stable and horse lot should be exempt from the execution under the homestead exemption laws. Reinbach maintained that these properties were essential for his family's domestic purposes, and thus he sought to overturn the judgment against him.	The defendants, William and Philip Walter, contended that Reinbach failed to prove that the premises were part of his homestead at the time the lien attached, despite being his homestead during the sheriff’s sale. They produced documentation demonstrating the validity of their judgment and the execution process leading to the sheriff's sale. The defense maintained that Reinbach was not in possession at the correct time and challenged his claims to a homestead exemption for the specific properties involved in the case.

On December 1, 1847, the case of Orrin Sherman et al. v. Henry Gassett et al. took place before the Illinois Supreme Court in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a mortgage executed on September 1, 1842, to secure the payment of three promissory notes worth $7,000. These notes were issued by Sherman & Pitkin to Gassett & Co., a Boston-based company, with interest set at ten percent per annum. The plaintiffs, who were residents of Massachusetts, initiated a scire facias to foreclose the mortgage. In response, Sherman & Pitkin, the defendants, presented pleas claiming that the agreement was usurious under Massachusetts law and argued part payment. The court sustained a demurrer to these pleas, and the plaintiffs were awarded a judgment for the amount due, leading Sherman & Pitkin to appeal, asserting the court erred in dismissing their defenses.	The plaintiffs claimed that the mortgage executed by the defendants was valid and enforceable under Illinois law. They argued that the pleas of usury presented by the defendants were not sufficient to invalidate the mortgage and that the interest stipulated was legal within Illinois. Hence, they sought a judgment in their favor to have the mortgaged premises sold to satisfy the debt owed.	The defendants contended that the mortgage should be invalidated on grounds of usury, as the interest rate agreed upon exceeded the maximum allowed in Massachusetts, where they alleged the notes were executed. They argued that the usury laws of Massachusetts should apply to this case, and thus, they requested the court to recognize the illegality of the contract under those laws.

The case "Barbara A. Green v. George V. Dietrich" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 14, 1885. It revolved around a dispute over a piece of land involving key individuals: George V. Dietrich (the plaintiff), and Barbara A. Green and her daughter Florence Green (the defendants). The dispute originated from a contract made on November 2, 1864, between Stephen B. Allen and Alfred Thurman for the sale of property. Following Thurman's death, Barbara A. Green, as his widow, and Florence, his heir, inherited the premises. The plaintiff, Dietrich, contended that he had acquired the title to the property through various mesne conveyances and sought specific performance of the contract, asserting that Thurman held the property in trust for Allen. The case involved clarification of the title and rights concerning the property, which were complicated by prior transactions and the absence of clear title at the time of the original contract.	George V. Dietrich argued that he was entitled to the specific performance of a contract made between Stephen B. Allen and Alfred Thurman regarding the sale of a property, claiming that wherever Thurman held title, it was held in trust for Allen. He requested that the court compel the defendants to transfer any titles or interests they held to him, asserting that the contract entitled him to such relief. Dietrich maintained that the defendants failed to fulfill their contractual obligations.	Barbara A. Green contended that her late husband, Alfred Thurman, had acquired true ownership of the property independently and had not held it in trust for Dietrich or Stephen B. Allen. She argued that the plaintiff lacked standing to demand a transfer of title, since he had failed to prove a valid agreement or claim of ownership that extended to her or her late husband. Green maintained that her possession of the land, strengthened by her agreements post-Thurman's death, rendered Dietrich's claims invalid.

In July 1880, individuals in Winnebago County, Illinois, sought to establish the Manufacturers and Merchants’ Mutual Insurance Company to provide fire insurance. They notified the Auditor and filed necessary documents for compliance. On July 7, the Attorney General confirmed that their proposals conformed to legal requirements, allowing the firm to begin soliciting insurance. William Gent, a factory owner, was approached by company promoters, who persuaded him to insure $1,000 of machinery, resulting in a $150 premium note and a $30 draft for an assessment on the premium. On February 5, 1881, while the corporators attempted to finalize their organization, Gent's factory was destroyed by fire, and he promptly reported the loss. However, the company subsequently asserted that no contract had been validly formed, citing its incomplete organization at the time of Gent's agreement. After Gent won a judgment in the Winnebago Circuit Court, the Appellate Court reversed this decision, leading Gent to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	William Gent argued that his execution of the premium note and draft, alongside the company's retention and usage of these documents, constituted a binding insurance contract. He maintained that the company, upon its eventual formal organization, should be estopped from denying the validity of the agreement made prior to its complete establishment. Gent contended this was justified under the spirit of insurance statutes, claiming he had fulfilled all requirements necessary for valid coverage.	The Manufacturers and Merchants’ Mutual Insurance Company contended that it could not be bound by any contracts made before its official organization was completed. The company argued that until it filed the required documentation with the county clerk, it lacked the legal capacity to enter into contracts. Moreover, they maintained that Gent's agreements were mere propositions for insurance and did not constitute binding commitments.

Job Smith, the plaintiff, was involved in a legal dispute with William Douglass, the defendant, in Gallatin, Illinois, in November 1854. The case originated when Douglass sued Smith before a justice of the peace in February 1853 for a debt of $5 related to the sale of corn. Douglass had agreed to act as a guarantor for Smith, who did not pay the witness Tally for the corn sold. After an arbitration process initiated by both parties, where each presented their statements, the arbitrators ruled that Douglass was not liable for the amount paid by Tally. Dissatisfied with this decision, Smith appealed the matter to the circuit court, leading to further examination of the arbitration process and its validity.	The plaintiff, Job Smith, argued that the arbitration decision made by the arbitrators was not valid due to the lack of evidence regarding the arbitration process when the matter was brought before the court. Smith's main claim was that Douglass should be held accountable for the payment to Tally, despite the arbitrators ruling otherwise. He sought to have the circuit court reverse the arbitration decision and find in his favor regarding the debt.	The defendant, William Douglass, maintained that the arbitration was a legitimate and binding resolution of the dispute between himself and Smith. Douglass argued that the verbal submission to arbitration was valid under the law, and the decision reached by the arbitrators was final and should be respected by the court. He sought to have the circuit court uphold the arbitration award, asserting that the issue had been adequately settled through arbitration.

In September 1875, the case of John W. Lowell et al. v. Margaret J. Wren was decided in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from Cook County, Illinois, involving the plaintiff John W. Lowell and others, and the defendant Margaret J. Wren. The dispute arose over a deed of trust executed allegedly by Wren to secure notes made out to Lowell and Dalton. Wren claimed that she never authorized the execution of the notes or the deed, stating that her husband, John Wren, had conspired with Lowell and Dalton to defraud her. Wren testified that she was illiterate, was not aware of what she was signing when her husband brought her a paper, and was misled into thinking it was merely a formality. She asserted that no one explained the document to her or confirmed her understanding before she made her mark. The court found substantial corroborating testimony from disinterested witnesses supporting her claims. The evidence presented undermined the legitimacy of the deed of trust, leading to a court decree in her favor.	The plaintiff, Margaret J. Wren, claimed that she never executed or recognized the deed of trust and that her husband conspired with Lowell and Dalton to defraud her by falsely procuring her signature. She requested the court to enjoin a sale purportedly authorized by the deed of trust, arguing that the deed was obtained through fraudulent means without her knowledge or consent.	The defendants, including John W. Lowell and Dalton, contended that the deed of trust was valid and acknowledged by Wren. They argued that Wren had signed the document knowingly, and they claimed corroborating testimony from their witness, Albin, who purported to have taken her acknowledgment. However, they failed to provide convincing evidence that Wren was aware of the document's implications when she marked the paper.

In June 1841, Valentine Briegel and Adam Briegel acquired a piece of land in Monroe County, Illinois, from John A. Frank and his wife. Valentine was supposed to hold an undivided one-third interest in the property, while Adam was to hold two-thirds. However, due to a mistake in the deed, the conveyance was made jointly without specifying their respective shares. In February 1843, Valentine conveyed his interest to Adam, describing it as one-third. Later, a dispute arose regarding the rightful ownership and the correction of the deed. Valentine asserted that he was entitled to an additional one-sixth of the land. The case was taken to the Illinois Supreme Court, where it was determined that the original communication and intent when purchasing the land indicated Valentine was to have only one-third. The court examined the roles of the involved parties and addressed whether the original grantor needed to be included in the proceedings to correct the deed.	Valentine Briegel, the plaintiff, claimed that the deed from John A. Frank mistakenly conveyed the land to him and Adam jointly, rather than reflecting their intended shares. He sought a correction of the deed to clarify ownership, remove the cloud on his title, and requested general equitable relief.	The defendant, John Moeller, contended that the intent behind the purchase was accurately represented in the conveyance. He argued that there was no claim to additional land beyond the one-third interest that Valentine had conveyed to Adam. Additionally, he raised the issue that the other grantor, Frank, was not a necessary party to the proceeding seeking to correct the deed.

In June 1854, in Kane County, Illinois, John C. Dill was driving a horse and buggy along a public highway that intersected with a railroad owned by The Galena and Chicago Union Railroad Company. Dill was crossing the railroad tracks with reasonable care when a locomotive, operated by the railroad company's crew, approached without warning. The railroad was required by law to ring a bell or blow a whistle at least eighty rods before reaching the crossing. However, the train did not slow down or provide any warning, resulting in a collision that severely injured Dill and destroyed his buggy. Following the incident, Dill sought compensation for his injuries, medical expenses, and damages to the buggy. The case was initially tried in the Kane Circuit Court but was transferred to the Cook Circuit Court for trial. A jury found in favor of Dill, awarding him $15,500, which was later reduced by the judge following a remittitur.	John C. Dill claimed that The Galena and Chicago Union Railroad Company was negligent for failing to ring a bell or blow a whistle as required by law before approaching the crossing. He argued that this negligence, along with the train's excessive speed, led to the collision and his resulting injuries. Dill requested damages for his medical expenses, loss of the buggy, and pain and suffering, totaling $20,000.	The Galena and Chicago Union Railroad Company contested Dill's claims, arguing that the admission of certain evidence during the trial was improper and asserting errors in jury instructions provided by the court. They maintained that the alleged failure to ring the bell or sound the whistle could not be deemed negligence without proof that it caused the injury. The railroad company also contended that a legislative act exempted them from the requirement to ring the bell at the crossing, asserting that this act was constitutional and should protect them from liability.

Julia Jarrot, the plaintiff in error, brought a legal action against Joshua Vaughn, the defendant in error, in the Madison Circuit Court in October 1844. The case revolved around the cutting of timber trees on the plaintiff's land, which allegedly occurred between October 10, 1839, and the date of the lawsuit. The plaintiff claimed recovery of penalties imposed by statute for these alleged trespasses. The court proceedings were delayed until the October term of 1845, during which the plaintiff amended her declaration after the court found the original declaration insufficient. The plaintiff presented evidence of ownership, including a patent and a deed that traced the title to the land back to the deceased husband, Nicholas Jarrot. However, the defendant admitted that the timber was cut, leading to a jury trial. The defendant contended, through his attorney, that the word "owner" in the relevant statute implied a fee simple interest in the land, and argued that the will of Nicholas Jarrot did not grant the plaintiff such title. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of the defendant.	Julia Jarrot argued that she was entitled to recover penalties for the alleged cutting of timber on her land, claiming ownership based on her late husband's will. She maintained that the statute allowed her to bring this action as the owner of the land or as the executor of her late husband’s estate. The plaintiff asserted that her legal standing as an executrix allowed her to hold title sufficient for the claims pursued in court.	Joshua Vaughn's defense rested on the interpretation of the term "owner" as requiring a fee simple interest, which the defendant contended the plaintiff did not possess. He claimed that the will of Nicholas Jarrot only granted Julia a life estate in the property, which was insufficient for her to maintain an action under the statute. The defense requested the court to instruct the jury along these lines, emphasizing that the plaintiff's claims lacked a legal basis due to her limited interest in the property.

In the case of Benjamin F. Allen v. William Hickling, filed on October 26, 1882, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the dispute arose from a financial transaction that took place on September 10, 1874. The transaction involved Hickling (the plaintiff) purchasing a promissory note for $8,000 from Allen (the defendant), which was secured by bonds purportedly issued by the Des Moines Gas Company. These bonds were meant to serve as collateral for the payment of the note. Hickling alleged that he had been induced to purchase the note and pay the money based on false representations made by Allen regarding the value of the bonds. On December 6, 1875, Allen was discharged from bankruptcy, which he claimed protected him from liability in this case. Hickling countered that the debt owed to him was exempt from the discharge because it was incurred through Allen’s fraudulent actions. The trial included evidence from both parties concerning the adequacy and validity of the bonds and whether Allen had committed intentional fraud.	Hickling claimed that Allen had committed fraud by making false representations about the value and reliability of the bonds used as collateral. He maintained that these misrepresentations led him to purchase the promissory note and ultimately suffer financial loss. Hickling sought to recover the sum he paid Allen, arguing that due to the alleged fraudulent conduct, the bankruptcy discharge did not apply.	Allen defended against Hickling’s claims by asserting that he did not engage in intentional fraud and that the discharge from bankruptcy absolved him of liability for the debts incurred before the bankruptcy declaration. He requested that the court instruct the jury that the discharge should serve as a complete defense unless they found evidence of his knowing participation in fraudulent representations regarding the bonds.

In 1889, in the State of Illinois, the case of A. W. Lawwill et al. v. Margaret R. Lawwill arose following the death of William H. Lawwill, who had taken out a life insurance policy with the Masonic Benevolent Association, naming his “legal heirs” as beneficiaries. At the time of his death, William left behind a wife, Margaret R. Lawwill, and several siblings, but no children or descendants. Both the widow and the siblings made claims to the insurance proceeds upon his death. The Masonic Benevolent Association opted for an interpleader action to determine the rightful heirs to the policy benefits. The trial court ruled in favor of Margaret, declaring her the sole beneficiary entitled to the insurance amount. This decision was contested by William’s brothers, sisters, and the descendants of a deceased brother, who claimed that the insurance money should be divided among all of them as legal heirs, as defined by Illinois intestacy laws.	The plaintiffs argued that they were the legal heirs of William H. Lawwill according to Illinois statute, which they claimed entitled them to a share of the life insurance proceeds. They contended that the term “legal heirs” in the insurance policy referred to all of William's surviving relatives, and that since he died intestate, the proceeds should be divided equally among his heirs, which included his siblings and their descendants.	Margaret R. Lawwill, the defendant, contended that as the widow of William H. Lawwill, she was entitled to the full amount of the insurance proceeds under the laws concerning intestate succession, which recognized her as the sole heir in the absence of children. She argued that the insurance policy was similar to other forms of property that she would inherit entirely as a preference over collateral relatives, reinforcing her claim to the benefits.

In August 1859, Abijah Whetstone and John Thomas, both from Adams County, Illinois, entered into an arbitration agreement to resolve various disputes between them stemming from their partnership in the buying and selling of livestock. They agreed to submit these disputes to three arbitrators: Elihu Ward, Wm. M. Dexter, and Hiram Elliston. The arbitrators conducted hearings and published their award on September 6, 1859, determining that Whetstone owed Thomas $2,528.81, which could be settled either in cash or through two promissory notes. However, Thomas alleged that Whetstone failed to pay or execute the required notes as stipulated in the award, leading to the legal action of debt on the award that unfolded in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1861. The case revolved around the validity of the arbitration award and whether it properly addressed the disputes presented.	Whetstone claimed that the arbitrators had made a valid award regarding the amount he owed Thomas, asserting that he was willing to make payment as per the award. He argued that Thomas did not fulfill his part by not accepting the promissory notes and thus should be held liable for the amount awarded, alongside seeking the costs of the arbitration proceedings.	Thomas contended that the award was void because the arbitrators did not decide on all matters of dispute submitted to them. He argued that the arbitration was supposed to resolve various significant financial matters—a final settlement of their partnership affairs, including debts owed by and to the partnership—which the arbitrators failed to address adequately. Thomas requested the court to recognize this alleged insufficiency in the arbitrators' judgment and rule in his favor.

The case "Lincoln Avenue and Niles Centre Gravel Road Company v. Philip Daum" was decided in September 1875 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving the Lincoln Avenue and Niles Centre Gravel Road Company, a corporation that had constructed a toll road under a legislative act from 1859 allowing for the construction and operation of such roads. The central issue was whether a traveler who utilized the road but turned off before reaching a toll gate was obligated to pay the toll. The court examined the provisions of the charter, which specified that tolls could only be collected at designated gates. The traveler, Philip Daum, claimed he was not liable for tolls because he left the road before reaching a gate, while the road company contended that he should pay for the distance traveled based on the tolling system stipulated in their charter. The court ultimately evaluated the purpose of toll gates and the implications for toll collection along the road.	The Lincoln Avenue and Niles Centre Gravel Road Company, as the plaintiff, argued that tolls should be collected from every traveler who passes through a toll gate and that regardless of whether someone exits the road before reaching a toll gate, they still should be accountable for payment based on the distance traveled on the road. They sought the enforcement of the toll payment as established by their charter.	Philip Daum, the defendant, contended that he should not be required to pay tolls since he did not pass through a toll gate while traveling on the road. He maintained that his departure from the road occurred in good faith and not for the purpose of evading toll fees, arguing against the necessity of toll payment when the journey did not conclude at a toll gate.

The case "Samuel Coffman v. William Young et al." took place in 1886, specifically decided on July 7, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The key individuals involved were Samuel Coffman (the defendant) and William Young along with his co-partners (the plaintiffs). The case arose from a series of transactions carried out on the Board of Trade of Chicago, where Coffman, led by an agent named Mcllhaney, engaged the plaintiffs, who were commission merchants, to execute trades for him. These dealings, which took place from November 1882 to July 1883, amounted to approximately $371,000, with Coffman initially providing margins for trades and experiencing some profit. However, losses accumulated over the course of these transactions, leading to a claimed indebtedness of $15,497.47 owed by Coffman to the plaintiffs. A jury ruled in favor of the plaintiffs for this amount plus interest, culminating in a total judgment of $16,892.26. The trial's focus included whether these transactions constituted lawful trades or gambling contracts, dictated by the intentions of the parties involved.	The plaintiffs claimed they were owed $15,497.47 as a result of losses incurred while managing trades on Coffman's behalf. They argued that despite some initial profits, the ongoing dealings led to significant losses which they covered, justifying their claim for the total judgment amount. They sought recovery of this debt as well as interest on the amount claimed, asserting that their transactions were legitimate and not mere gambling.	The defendant, Coffman, contended that the transactions were gambling activities disguised as legitimate trades. He claimed that both parties intended to settle purely on market price differences without actual buying or selling of commodities. This assertion was backed by conflicting testimony, particularly from Mcllhaney. Coffman requested the court to instruct the jury on the illegality of their dealings, pointing to the criminal code that defines such contracts as void. He argued that without proof of real transactions, he should not be held liable for the debt claimed by the plaintiffs.

The case "The County of Cook v. Henry Harms" took place in 1883 in Chicago, Illinois. The conflict arose from a contract established on October 6, 1875, wherein Henry Harms agreed to supply materials and labor for the construction of the foundation of a new courthouse. This contract was predicated on plans approved by the Cook County Board, which subsequently rescinded its approval in January 1876 and adopted new plans. Despite these changes, Harms continued to supply materials and perform work on the foundation as directed by the architect. The county contested this, which led Harms to seek compensation for the value of materials and labor from the circuit court. The case progressed through various levels of the legal system, culminating in an appeal concerning the instructions given to the jury and evidence admitted during the trial.	The plaintiff, Henry Harms, argued that the Cook County Board's material changes to the courthouse plans constituted a breach of the original contract, thereby relieving him from its terms. He claimed entitlement to compensation for the labor and materials he provided following the new direction and plans, asserting that the changes were substantial enough to represent a new job, and not merely alterations of the original contract. He sought payment based on the actual value of the completed work rather than the initial contractual terms.	The defendant, Cook County, contended that the changes made to the courthouse plans were permissible under the original contract terms, which allowed for alterations to be made without invalidating the contract. They argued that Harms was bound to the contract, and any payment for extra work should adhere to the evaluation rendered by the architect. The county asserted that Harms, through his conduct, might be estopped from claiming the original contract was rescinded, due to his continued performance under the new plans.

In 1823, Shadrach Bond and Pierre Menard entered into a promissory note with Josiah T. Betts, the administrator of an estate, promising to pay them $19.25. The transaction was framed with Bond and Menard listed as agents for Warren Brown, yet the essence of the agreement maintained that the promise to pay was made directly to Bond and Menard. When a legal dispute arose regarding the enforceability of the note, the case proceeded to the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1826. The primary issue at hand was whether the title "agents for Warren Brown" affected the core enforceability of the promissory note. A majority opinion written by Justice Smith expounded on the legal principles surrounding the case and analyzed the nature of the agents' roles in the transaction, ultimately determining that the description was surplusage and did not impact the plaintiffs' rights to collect under the note.	The plaintiffs, Shadrach Bond and Pierre Menard, contended that they had the right to enforce the note against Josiah T. Betts, despite the note referencing them as "agents for Warren Brown." They argued that this phrasing was merely descriptive and did not invalidate their right to receive payment. Their primary legal request was for the court to recognize the validity of the promissory note and allow them to recover the owed amount.	The defendant, Josiah T. Betts, argued that the use of the term "agents for Warren Brown" in the note implied that the payment obligation was not directly to Bond and Menard but rather to Warren Brown as they were acting on his behalf. Betts contended that this description invalidated the direct promise to pay Bond and Menard, which, according to him, should preclude the enforcement of the note as it was presented.

In the case of "Maggie O'Malley v. Chicago City Railway Company," the events took place in Cook County, Illinois, leading to a court decision on July 2, 1889. The key individuals involved were Maggie O'Malley, the appellant, who claimed to have sustained personal injuries due to the negligence of the Chicago City Railway Company, the appellee. O'Malley's assertion was that the electric railway company was responsible for her injuries, which prompted her to seek a legal remedy. In the initial trial, O'Malley achieved a verdict against the Railway Company based solely on her unsupported testimony, which stood in contrast to the accounts provided by two disinterested witnesses. Despite winning the verdict, she was awarded only $100 in damages. Believing this amount was insufficient for her injuries, O'Malley sought a new trial based on inadequate damages. However, her position was challenged regarding her actual entitlement to recover any damages at all, establishing the foundation for the appeal and subsequent court ruling.	Maggie O'Malley, the plaintiff, claimed that she sustained personal injuries due to the negligence of the Chicago City Railway Company. Her main arguments revolved around the assertion of the injury's causation by the defendant's actions and the inadequacy of the damages awarded by the jury. O'Malley sought a new trial on the grounds that the compensation of $100 was insufficient to address her claims of personal injury, despite the conflicting testimonies.	The Chicago City Railway Company, as the defendant, contended that the plaintiff’s claims were unsupported and conflicted with the testimonies of two disinterested witnesses. They argued against the necessity of a new trial essentially positing that O'Malley was not entitled to recover damages in the first place. The Railway Company's stance was that the verdict awarded to the plaintiff was already more than she deserved, and therefore any adjustments or demands for a new trial were unwarranted.

In December 1851, the case of David Newsom against Thomas M. Luster and others took place in Illinois, specifically in Sangamon County. The dispute centered around a property title issue related to a tract of land that was the subject of a trespass action. The plaintiff, David Newsom, sought to establish his title to the land by introducing a certified copy of a deed from John Huston to Vincent A. Bogue. The original deed was claimed to be lost, and the affidavit stating this was provided by David Spear, the agent for the plaintiffs. Spear claimed he never had the deed, which had been recorded over twenty years prior, and asserted that Bogue, the presumed holder of the original deed, was unavailable. The plaintiffs also attempted to submit another deed from Bogue to McCandless and Emerson, although this deed was not acknowledged and involved issues regarding the absence of a subscribing witness. The trial court admitted both deeds into evidence despite the defendant's objections, triggering a series of legal arguments over the admittance of these documents.	The plaintiff, David Newsom, claimed that he was entitled to use a certified copy of the deed from Huston to Bogue as evidence of title, arguing that the affidavit from David Spear sufficiently demonstrated that the original was not in his possession or power. The plaintiffs also asserted that the execution of the deed from Bogue to McCandless and Emerson could be proven by establishing the handwriting of Bogue, despite the absence of a subscribing witness.	The defendants, led by Thomas M. Luster, provided several defenses: they asserted a general denial, invoked the statute of limitations, and raised the defense of liberum tenementum. They specifically contended that the trial court erred in admitting both deeds into evidence, arguing that the affidavit of David Spear was insufficient to demonstrate that the original deed was lost or not in the power of the plaintiffs. Furthermore, the defendants claimed that proper proof of the subscribing witness's handwriting was not provided for the second deed, thus rendering it inadmissible.

In the case of Alfred Osborn v. John V. Farwell, the events occurred in Chicago. The dispute arose over a lease agreement dated August 12, 1873, between John V. Farwell, the owner of the Arcade Building, and a tenant named Darling. The lease allowed Darling to occupy the fifth floor for a duration that extended until September 20, 1876. As part of the lease arrangement, Farwell accepted payment in the form of certain lands in Dunklin County, Missouri, valued at $5700. An important clause in the lease stipulated that if the US government required Darling to vacate before the lease term ended, he would be entitled to a proportionate rent allowance for the abridged occupancy. Following Darling's assignment of the lease to Alfred Osborn, Osborn occupied the premises until July 1874, when he was instructed by the US government to vacate. This led to Osborn seeking the proportionate rent allowance as per the lease terms. The main point of contention in court revolved around whether Farwell was required to compensate Osborn in cash or had the option to pay in land as specified in the lease.	Alfred Osborn, as the plaintiff, contended that he was entitled to a proportionate allowance of rent due to the abridgement of his occupancy by the US government. He argued that the specific language of the lease mandated a cash payment rather than a payment in land, asserting that the punctuation and structure of the lease clearly indicated that only the second contingency allowed for such payment in land, whereas the first implies a cash payment.	John V. Farwell, the defendant, maintained that he was within his rights to pay Osborn in the lands located in Dunklin County, Missouri, regardless of the reason for the abridged occupancy. Farwell argued that the lease's wording encompassed both contingencies, meaning that whether the premises were vacated due to government demands or destruction by fire, he could opt to compensate in land as stipulated in the lease.

In 1886, in Ottawa, Illinois, Henry F. Bennett entered into a contract with John W. Teetzel to sink a well that would provide adequate water for Bennett's livestock. Bennett promised to pay $86 with a stipulation that payment was contingent on the well consistently yielding ten barrels of water per day. The parties disputed the outcome of the well and payments related to its construction. After the well was considered faulty by Bennett, he expressed a need for immediate water and asked Teetzel to return and fix the well. Teetzel arrived in January 1887, prepared to make repairs; however, Bennett allegedly refused to allow him to proceed, leading to misunderstandings about the contract's fulfillment. Bennett later demanded the return of the sewer pipe used in the well's construction and refused to fix the situation further. The relationship deteriorated, prompting the legal action regarding the original contract for payment and repairs.	Bennett (the plaintiff) argued that Teetzel failed to fulfill his contractual obligation to ensure the well functioned properly. He claimed that the well did not provide the necessary water and that Teetzel had been given the opportunity to fix this issue but refused. Bennett was seeking to enforce the contract and recover the payment due, asserting damages stemming from incomplete work on the well.	Teetzel (the defendant) contended that he offered to remedy the issues with the well but was denied access by Bennett, who claimed everything was satisfactory as it was. Teetzel argued that any failure in the well's water supply was due to Bennett's decisions, including his installation of a pump that was inadequately deep. He sought to have the court dismiss the claims against him, supporting that he did not owe Bennett any duty or payment due to his lack of cooperation.

The case "William M. Ross, and John H. Ross, Appellants, v. Adam G. Innis, Appellee" took place in Chicago, Illinois, with the decision being rendered in April 1861. Adam G. Innis was employed as a cashier by Ross & Co., a mercantile partnership founded by William M. and John H. Ross. The controversy arose when Innis allegedly embezzled $166, leading the Rosses to file a criminal complaint, claiming that he converted company funds without permission. The events leading to the arrest began in December 1859, after William M. Ross traveled to New York and received information about suspected embezzlement. Innis, who had previously been regarded as a reputable employee, was arrested but later discharged following an examination by a magistrate. The lawsuit that followed was for malicious prosecution, where Innis asserted that his arrest was without probable cause and made with malice. The case was tried twice; initially, Innis was awarded $5,000, but after a motion for a new trial, he received a verdict of $3,000.	Adam G. Innis claimed that the Rosses had falsely accused him of embezzlement, alleging that they caused him to be arrested without probable cause and with malicious intent. He argued that he had taken the money as wages he believed he was entitled to, having acted in good faith. Innis sought damages for the harm caused by the wrongful accusation and sought a jury verdict in his favor.	The Rosses defended against Innis's claims by emphasizing that they acted on the advice of legal counsel after reviewing the facts surrounding the alleged embezzlement. They contended that they had probable cause to believe that Innis had committed embezzlement based on the circumstances presented to them, including his alleged efforts to take funds without authority. Their defense was also centered on the argument that any action they took was justified based on the professional guidance they received.

In April 1865, in Woodford County, Illinois, Sarah Sevier initiated legal proceedings resulting in a decree that placed a tract of land, owned by Harriet Gr. Magguire (wife of Samuel L. Magguire), under obligation to pay a judgment owed to Sevier by Samuel L. Magguire. This prior decree was rendered by default and did not account for homestead rights, subsequently ordering the sale of Harriet's land to satisfy not only Sevier’s judgment but also a separate judgment from Edgerly, who had not been involved in the case. Samuel and Harriet Magguire filed a bill to annul this earlier decree, citing apparent errors and asserting that the land was their homestead. They contested the payment to Edgerly, arguing it was unnecessary as Edgerly was not a party seeking relief. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case, acknowledging an error regarding Edgerly’s judgment and deciding that the decree should not be completely invalidated but modified to respect the homestead rights of Harriet and their children.	Sarah Sevier contended that the land owned by Harriet Gr. Magguire should be subject to payment for the judgment owed by Samuel L. Magguire. She argued that the initial decree was valid and sought to enforce the sale of the land to satisfy her claims. Moreover, the decree did not take into consideration that the property was the homestead, which she believed was a significant oversight.	Samuel L. Magguire and Harriet Gr. Magguire asserted that the previous decree should be set aside due to errors over Edgerly’s judgment, which was improperly included as a basis for the land’s sale. They argued that the property had always served as their homestead and therefore should be exempt from seizure. Their request sought to enjoin the sale of the land, emphasizing the need to correct the decree rather than void it.

In 1883, the case of Charles Humpeler v. Cynthia Hickman, Adm’x took place in Fayette County, Illinois. The dispute arose over two promissory notes, each for $350, that Humpeler issued to Montgomery Hickman, who was the payee before his death. The notes were due between 1876 and 1877 and bore 10% annual interest. Following Hickman's death, his estate, represented by administratrix Cynthia Hickman, filed a lawsuit against Humpeler to recover the amounts due on these notes. During the proceedings, Humpeler claimed he had paid the amounts owed to Hickman before his death.
