The evidence presented indicated that the notes were part of the purchase price for land Humpeler bought from Hickman for $1,200, and Hickman had delivered a warranty deed to him without retaining security for the notes, raising questions about the validity of the claim for payment.	The plaintiff, Cynthia Hickman as administratrix of Montgomery Hickman's estate, claimed that Humpeler owed the full amounts due on the two promissory notes, asserting that their possession by the estate was prima facie evidence that they had not been paid. The plaintiff requested the court to recognize the unpaid status of the promissory notes and to compel Humpeler to pay the amounts owed with applicable interest.	Humpeler contested the claims, arguing that the amounts due on the promissory notes had been paid back to Hickman before his death. He contended that evidence, including a warranty deed and the arrangements made regarding the purchase of land, demonstrated that the debts were settled. Humpeler requested the court to dismiss the case and recognize that the notes had been paid, overriding the presumption established by the estate.

The case "John C. Jones et al. v. John W. Neely" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1876. The underlying dispute originated in Randolph County, Illinois, involving plaintiffs John C. Jones and others against defendant John W. Neely, along with an execution creditor, Bilderback. The plaintiffs claimed that a judgment against them obtained by Bilderback was fraudulent, as they were neither served with process nor aware that there was any legal action pending. They contended that the judgment significantly exceeded any valid debt owed and that they had no opportunity to defend themselves. The Court examined the legitimacy of the judgment, particularly considering the lack of service and the absence of the plaintiffs at the proceedings, concluding that an equitable resolution was warranted due to a grave jurisdictional flaw in how the initial judgment was obtained. The court stated that the defendant, Neely, was complicit in the alleged fraud and had no protection as an "innocent purchaser," ultimately finding the judgment void.	The plaintiffs argued that the judgment against them was fraudulent and invalid, as they were not served with process, did not appear in court, and had no knowledge of the lawsuit. They requested equitable relief from this judgment, asserting that it was unjust and disproportionately high relative to any actual debt owed. They sought to have the judgment nullified in light of these facts.	The defendant contended that the sale of the judgment was legitimate, arguing that the plaintiffs had notice of the proceedings and were thus bound by the judgment obtained against them. They claimed that the plaintiffs' failure to appear or respond did not invalidate the judgment and asserted that the court should uphold its original ruling without granting the requested equitable relief.

On July 20, 1886, David H. Keyes contracted with George Lehman & Sons Company and Clark & Findlay to perform construction work on a property with a 50-foot frontage on Wabash Avenue in Chicago, Illinois. Under this agreement, Clark & Findlay were to carry out carpenter work for a building on the southern 16 feet of the property, while George Lehman & Sons were responsible for the masonry on another building on the northern 16 feet. Keyes agreed to convey the respective portions of the land to both contractors. Subsequently, on August 20, 1886, to secure a $6,500 loan for construction purposes, the title of the property was transferred to Hibbert J. Lehman, son of George Lehman, at the suggestion of the loan lender, E. S. Dreyer & Company. Hibbert did not pay for the property, but the loan was utilized for construction on the center 16 feet, which was to be built by George Lehman & Sons. By July 1, 1887, additional payments were due for labor performed, leading to a $300 promissory note issued by the company to Clark & Findlay. A mechanic’s lien was filed to enforce payment, resulting in an appeal from the company and others after a Circuit Court decree favored the lien holders.	The plaintiffs, Arthur R. Clark and Johnson S. Findlay, claimed they were owed $300 plus interest for additional labor and materials provided for the center house construction. They filed for a mechanic's lien against the property, asserting their right to secure payment for the work done, as stipulated in the contracts with George Lehman & Sons. Their argument relied on the establishment of a resulting trust, implying that Hibbert J. Lehman held the title in trust for the benefit of the company, and the plaintiffs were entitled to recover their due payments.	The defendants, including George Lehman & Sons Company and Hibbert J. Lehman, contended that Hibbert was the absolute owner of the property and denied the trust claim. They argued that the plaintiffs failed to prove that the labor and materials corresponding to the $300 note were actually used on the building. They maintained that since there was no dishonesty in their dealings regarding payments and property ownership, the plaintiffs' claims for the mechanic's lien were unfounded and should be dismissed.

Hardin Myers filed a case against A. H. Antrim in the Moultrie County Court during the August term of 1883. The proceedings revolved around a bill of exceptions that was signed and filed by the trial judge within the prescribed thirty-day period. However, issues arose when it was later discovered that the bill was not properly under the court's seal, and it failed to document exceptions taken by the appellant during the trial. Myers then sought to amend this record in light of the missing details. The case was taken up by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 4, 1883. However, upon review, the court found that the attempt to amend the bill of exceptions was not substantiated with the necessary legal evidence or proper procedure. The court indicated that an amendment must be done with due process and that the absence of facts justifying the amendment rendered the judge's action in signing a new bill of exceptions improper.	The plaintiff, Hardin Myers, contended that the original bill of exceptions was incomplete and sought to have it amended. He argued that the lack of documented exceptions deprived him of his rights in challenging the trial court's decisions and sought judicial intervention to formally rectify the record to accurately reflect the trial proceedings.	A. H. Antrim, the defendant, opposed the plaintiff's request to amend the bill of exceptions, arguing that the original bill had already become part of the court’s records and could not be changed without proper procedure. The defendant maintained that any amendment must be supported by evidence heard at the trial and performed with due legal process.

In June 1871, in Sparta, Randolph County, Illinois, a legal case arose between Henry Gardner (the plaintiff) and Henry A. Witbord (the defendant) regarding a promissory note. Gardner had brought an action of assumpsit against Witbord, claiming he was owed $300 based on this note. The Common Pleas Court of Sparta issued a writ directed to the city marshal and other law enforcement officials to summon Witbord to appear before the court. However, the defendant filed a motion to quash the writ, arguing several procedural errors, including improper direction beyond the court's jurisdiction and lack of proper venue. The court initially sustained this motion, resulting in a judgment favoring Witbord that prompted Gardner to appeal the decision.	Henry Gardner's primary claim was based on a promissory note issued by Witbord, which he argued entitled him to collect $300. Gardner contended that the writ was valid and that proper service had been completed, requesting that the court enforce the writ and hold Witbord accountable to appear in court.	Henry A. Witbord's defense rested on the assertion that the writ issued against him was improperly directed and flawed. He claimed it exceeded the jurisdiction of the court, as it directed the summons to the city marshal as well as all other officials outside the specified jurisdiction. Witbord argued that the writ was invalid and that the motion to quash it was justified, ultimately seeking dismissal of the case against him.

In 1872, Richard Edwards entered into a legal dispute with H. Hartt and others in Cook County, Illinois, regarding the exchange of goods, specifically printing presses and a safe. The case arose from indebitatus assumpsit, where Hartt & Co. claimed that Edwards owed them for goods sold and delivered, which included the trade of printing presses. The agreement between Edwards and Hartt involved Edwards exchanging a printing press for a smaller one and a safe valued at $300. The trial was agreed to be heard by the court without a jury. The main evidence presented was that Hartt claimed no cash payment or safe had ever been provided by Edwards in their transaction. While the court found in favor of the plaintiffs (Hartt & Co.) for damages of $599.15, the specifics of their claim regarding the safe became contentious. There was a lack of clarity in testimony about the agreement and whether Edwards had made a formal demand for the safe, leading to an examination of whether the finding was supported by evidence.	The plaintiffs, Hartt & Co., argued that Edwards had failed to fulfill his part of the contract by not paying either in cash or providing the safe worth $300 as agreed upon in their exchange of printing presses. They claimed the total owed was $599.15 for the value of goods sold and demanded a judgment for that amount.	Edwards contended that the safe, valued at $300, had been made available to him and that he was entitled to take possession of it. He argued that no specific demand for the safe had been established before bringing the lawsuit, meaning he could not be held in default. His testimony aligned with the assertion that he had agreed to provide a safe worth $800 rather than a cash payment, and he maintained that the plaintiffs had not properly requested the delivery of the safe before initiating legal action.

The case of Victor Atwood v. Cyrus L. Buck, decided on January 22, 1885, took place in Illinois, specifically concerning lands in Warren County. The dispute originated from a bill filed by William Buck against Cyrus L. Buck for the partition of certain lands that were said to belong to their deceased father, Murray Buck, who died intestate in March 1855. Following William Buck's bankruptcy, Victor Atwood was substituted as the complainant. Most heirs conveyed their interests in the land to defendant Cyrus L. Buck, leading to a focus on William Buck’s claim. In the circuit court, it was determined that Victor Atwood was entitled to one share of the land, leading to a partition that allocated a portion to him while designating the remainder, along with an easement, to Cyrus L. Buck. The core issue was whether the commissioners had the authority to create an easement on property allocated to the complainant. The defendant contested the court's decision and claimed that the will of Murray Buck, which supposedly left all property to Cyrus, was valid, disputing the claim that Murray had died intestate.	Victor Atwood, as the assignee of William Buck, claimed entitlement to a share of the land inherited from their father, Murray Buck. He argued that the commissioners did not have the authority to grant easements over his allocated share of the land. Atwood sought to reverse the circuit court’s allotment of property and the creation of easements, asserting his legal right to a partition of the estate without such encumbrances.	Cyrus L. Buck contended that the will of Murray Buck was valid and effective, arguing that it had been duly admitted to probate in Illinois and passed the title of the land to him. He asserted that since the will was contested in Vermont but ultimately recognized in Illinois, the circuit court's decree to grant Atwood any share was erroneous. Furthermore, he aimed to confirm that the will's legitimacy concluded the matter, negating Atwood’s claims.

On April 6, 1857, in Chicago, Illinois, a partnership consisting of Asher Rossiter, John D. Pahlman, George O. Smith, and John E. Smith, operating under the name Rossiter, Pahlman & Smiths, executed two promissory notes for the total amount of $510.75 in favor of Riley M. Graves. After the partnership's general assignment for the benefit of creditors on October 5, 1857, and Rossiter's death on February 25, 1858, Graves sought to recover the amount owed through legal proceedings. A judgment was awarded to Graves in the Circuit Court of Cook County against the surviving partners, but payment was not made. Graves later filed a claim against Rossiter's estate, which was deemed insolvent. The County Court allowed the claim, prompting Pahlman, the executor, to appeal based on jurisdictional grounds, arguing that joint debts should first be addressed from the partnership's assets before seeking payment from Rossiter's separate estate.	Graves, the plaintiff, argued that he had a valid claim against the estate of the deceased partner, Rossiter, based on the promissory notes. He requested the court to allow his claim for payment from Rossiter's estate, contending that he was entitled to receive payment despite the partnership's insolvency, as his claim had been acknowledged by the County Court.	Pahlman, the executor for Rossiter's estate, contended that Graves, as a joint creditor, was required to seek payment from the partnership's assets first before claiming from Rossiter's individual estate. He argued that the County Court lacked jurisdiction to rule on this matter, and therefore, the claim should not have been allowed, as the joint creditors should be paid from joint assets before touching individual estates.

The case "Thomas Bradshaw v. John Newman" originated in the Madison Circuit Court and was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1825. The conflict arose over a sealed note dated October 31, 1818, which was executed in the then-territory of Missouri. The plaintiff, Thomas Bradshaw, claimed a right arising from this note, while the defendant, John Newman, presented three pleas as defenses. Newman's first plea questioned the legality of the note, arguing that it was based on the sale of an improvement on public land in Arkansas, which may not be valid. The second plea asserted that the consideration for the note had entirely failed, while the third contended that Bradshaw possessed the improvement without proper purchase or lease from Newman, thereby implying a failure of consideration. The lower court sustained these pleas, leading to a judgment in favor of Newman, prompting Bradshaw to seek a reversal of this decision from the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Thomas Bradshaw, contended that the note was valid and enforceable even though it was for an improvement on public land in Arkansas. He argued that the laws governing the contract should be those of Missouri, where it was made, and insisted that the defendant's pleas did not adequately challenge the note's validity or utility. Bradshaw requested that the court reverse the previous ruling and reinstate his claim for the amount due under the note.	The defendant, John Newman, presented three primary defenses. His first claim asserted that the consideration for the note was unlawful as it involved a sale related to an improvement on public land, which may not be allowed. His second argument indicated that the consideration for the note had completely failed, implying no obligation to pay. Lastly, Newman's third plea stated that Bradshaw was unlawfully in possession of the improvement without any agreement to purchase or lease from him, arguing that this also indicated a failure of consideration.

In the 1860s, the legal case of Francis Keys v. Oakley V. Test took place in Illinois, specifically originating in Pike County and later moving to Adams County. The dispute arose over a parcel of land previously owned by Nimrod B. McPherson, who sold the property in a parol agreement to his father, Benjamin McPherson, for $800 around 1854. After taking possession and improving the land, Benjamin sold it to James Hummer, who then sold it to Oakley Y. Test for $1,000. Test made further improvements and claimed ownership of the land. However, after these transactions, Nimrod purportedly conveyed the property to Charles W. Troy, who then transferred it to Francis Keys. Test, claiming to be the rightful owner, sought legal remedy against both Keys and Troy, alleging they acted fraudulently regarding the land's ownership.	Oakley Y. Test, the plaintiff, argued that he was the legitimate owner of the property based on a prior parol sale from Nimrod B. McPherson to his father, Benjamin. He contended that this sale was valid due to valuable consideration and significant improvements made to the property, and he sought for the court to compel Keys to convey the property to him. Test also requested that the court issue an injunction to prevent Keys and Troy from pursuing claims to the land, as he believed their transactions were fraudulent and void against his claim.	Francis Keys, the defendant, denied all allegations concerning the validity of the alleged sale between Nimrod and Benjamin, asserting that it was unenforceable under the statute of frauds, which requires certain agreements to be in writing. Keys maintained that he was a bona fide purchaser who acquired the property without knowledge of any prior claims to it, claiming a legitimate interest based on a deed he received from Troy.

In early 1871, a legal dispute arose in Alton, Illinois, between John Smith and his wife (plaintiffs) and Wise, Stigleman & Co. (defendants) regarding unpaid rent for leased premises. The plaintiffs initially brought several actions before a local justice of the peace for monthly rent, winning judgments in their favor. However, upon the defendants' appeal to the City Court, the cases were consolidated and tried by a jury. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of the defendants. The plaintiffs requested a reversal of this judgment through a writ of error, citing various issues during the initial trial, including jury deliberations involving an inadmissible paper purportedly containing Mrs. Smith's testimony. This raised legal questions about the nature of eviction and the right to collect rent when a tenant is negatively impacted by the landlord's actions on the leased property.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants were liable for unpaid rent for the premises they leased. They contended that a paper handed to the jury, which represented Mrs. Smith's potential testimony, was improperly considered during deliberations, infringing upon their legal rights. The plaintiffs sought redress for this perceived judicial error and aimed to overturn the jury's verdict favoring the defendants.	The defendants countered that the plaintiffs effectively evicted them from part of the leased premises without consent, which legally entitled them to cease rent payments. They emphasized that the law states that any actions taken by a landlord that infringe on a tenant's enjoyment of the property can be classified as eviction. The defendants argued that the jury's instructions appropriately reflected legal standards and properly affirmed their right to withhold rent.

On November 9, 1882, Augustus W. Cowan was declared elected as the county treasurer of Livingston County, Illinois. John Zimmerman, the defeated candidate, sought to contest the election results. On December 9, 1882, within thirty days of the election declaration, Zimmerman filed a petition in the county court to formalize this contest, in accordance with section 113 of chapter 46 of the Revised Statutes of 1874. However, Cowan responded with a plea in bar, arguing that Zimmerman's filing was late since it occurred after business hours, specifically after 6:00 PM. The court agreed with Cowan's plea, stating that the thirty-day period outlined by the statute ended at 6:00 PM on December 9. The initial ruling favored Cowan, dismissing Zimmerman's petition as untimely. The interpretation of the statute focused on whether the entire day was available for filing, despite the clerk's office hours.	Zimmerman contended that he filed his contest petition within the statutory deadline, arguing that the law allowed for the full day, meaning December 9 should extend until midnight. He asserted that his filing was compliant with the requirement to contest the election within thirty days of the declared results. Additionally, he claimed that the absence of immediate docketing or issuing summons did not nullify his right to contest the election.	Cowan's primary defense was that Zimmerman did not file his petition within the required timeframe, as it was submitted after the official business hours of the clerk’s office. He contended that the law restricts actions to be completed during the specified office hours of 8 AM to 6 PM, implying that any actions taken outside these hours were invalid. Cowan requested dismissal of Zimmerman's petition based on this interpretation of the statute.

The case of Asahel Gage v. John T. Davis took place in Chicago, Illinois, and was filed on June 15, 1889. It originated from a dispute over two tax deeds issued after a tax sale. The first deed was issued to Henry H. Gage in 1873, but the notice informing of the sale was deemed insufficient as it did not clarify whether the property was sold for taxes or special assessments. This defect led the court to set aside the deed. The second tax deed, issued in 1879, followed a tax sale from 1876, but the notice provided was also found inadequate, as it inaccurately stated the date for redemption, which fell on a Sunday—thereby extending the redemption period to the following day. As a result, the court deemed both tax deeds invalid, confirming that the purchaser's compliance with statutory requirements was essential for a valid tax title. The case was presided over by Judge Henry M. Shepard in the Superior Court of Cook County, and the final decree of the court affirmed the setting aside of the tax deeds.	Asahel Gage, the plaintiff, sought to set aside the two tax deeds that he believed were improperly issued. He argued that the notices associated with both deeds failed to meet legal standards, specifically lacking in detail about whether the properties were sold for taxes or special assessments, and providing erroneous information regarding the redemption dates. His legal request was to have these deeds nullified based on these insufficiencies.	John T. Davis, the defendant and holder of the tax deeds, contended that the notices provided were adequate and had adhered to the requirements set forth by law. He argued against the plaintiff's claims regarding the notices' validity, asserting that they met the necessary legal thresholds. However, he did not present any cross-errors in response to the plaintiff's claims, which limited his ability to challenge the court's findings regarding the deeds' validity.

The case "Christopher Sleuter et al. v. Augustus Wallbaum" took place in September 1867 in Chicago, Illinois. Augustus Wallbaum initiated the action of assumpsit against defendants Christopher Sleuter and Christopher Tegtmeeger, alleging a breach of contract for the delivery of one million bricks that was supposed to occur during the 1866 season. Wallbaum claimed that the contract was formed in June of that year. The Superior Court of Chicago conducted a trial, after which the jury found in favor of Wallbaum, awarding him $1,000. The defendants subsequently sought a new trial, arguing that the evidence did not sufficiently establish the existence of a contract and that the court had provided erroneous jury instructions regarding how to measure damages. The court refused their motion for a new trial, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiff, Augustus Wallbaum, claimed that there was a valid contract for the sale and delivery of one million bricks at $8.50 per thousand. He argued that he demanded the delivery of the bricks and that the defendants refused, causing him a financial loss. Wallbaum requested damages based on the difference between the contract price and the market value of the bricks at the time of the refused delivery, along with interest.	The defendants, Sleuter and Tegtmeeger, contested the existence of the contract, asserting that the evidence did not demonstrate that a valid agreement was formed. They also argued that the court provided misleading instructions on how to measure damages, which they claimed led to an erroneous verdict. They requested that the appellate court reverse the trial court's decision and grant a new trial based on these grounds.

The legal case of August Thebus v. Mary Smiley was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 13, 1884. The case arose in Belleville, Illinois, where August Thebus, a depositor, sought to hold Mary Smiley, a stockholder of the People’s Bank, accountable under the bank’s charter. The charter stipulated that stockholders are individually liable for debts incurred by the corporation amounting to the stock they hold when there is a default. The court needed to determine the applicability of this liability in instances where the stockholder also had debts owed to them by the bank. Specifically, they addressed three main questions: whether a stockholder can set off corporate debts against personal liabilities, the implications of judgment against a stockholder and subsequent transfers of stock, and the priority rights of creditors suing stockholders. The court examined precedents, statutory language, and principles of equitable liability to reach its decisions.	The plaintiff, August Thebus, argued that as a creditor of the corporation, he was entitled to enforce individual liability against stockholder Mary Smiley. He maintained that the indebtedness of the bank to the stockholder could not be used to set off the liabilities owed to him as a creditor. Thebus sought essentially to hold Smiley responsible for her financial obligations as a stockholder in relation to the debts of the corporation.	The defendant, Mary Smiley, contended that she should be allowed to set off the bank's indebtedness to her against any liability she would owe as a stockholder. Additionally, she argued for clarity regarding the treatment of successive stockholders and their liabilities, advocating for a position that would limit her personal responsibility for corporate debts once she had taken the necessary steps to settle her dues.

Meshach Pike filed a legal case against Daniel O. Crist and others in January 1872, in McLean County, Illinois. The dispute originated from two promissory notes issued by Ralph and Rebecca Bennett to Pike, secured by mortgages on their land. The first note, dated January 19, 1868, was for $2039.94, and the second note, dated January 16, 1869, was for $854.23. Both notes were characterized by an interest rate of ten percent, which would escalate to twenty percent if not paid at maturity. The central issue revolved around the claims of usurious interest embedded in these notes, which resulted from earlier transactions between Pike and the Bennetts. Evidence suggested that usurious interest amounting to $180.40 was included in the first note, and $347.96 in the second. Pike had justified his interest structure, believing the rates would not violate Illinois statutes against usury. The case further complicated when Crist, as the grantee of the Bennetts, contested the validity of the mortgages, asserting he should not bear the usurious debt.	The plaintiff, Meshach Pike, contended that the notes were legitimate debts despite the claimed usury. He argued that the interest rates were legally acceptable and represented liquidated damages for late payment. Pike sought to enforce the payment of the principal sums and the specified interest rates from the Bennetts and, subsequently, from Crist, asserting that the mortgages secured these debts.	Daniel O. Crist, the defendant, argued against the validity of the mortgages due to the usurious interest attached to them. He contended that the interest rates stated were not in good faith and merely disguised a usurious transaction. Crist claimed the right to contest the mortgages as a matter of principle based on the warranty deed's clause, which excluded any usurious and illegal interest, thus opposing Pike's claim.

The case of Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Co. v. Abel Byam took place in January 1870 in Whiteside County, Illinois. The incident involved William Crosby, who was killed while attempting to cross a railroad track that had dangerous conditions. On the day of the accident, Crosby was familiar with the crossing, which had a diagonal approach that often caused wagons to get stuck. As he crossed the track with a team and wagon, a train, running slightly behind schedule, approached. Witnesses noted that the train's whistle was sounded from a distance of ninety rods, and the bell was rung continuously as required by law. Despite these warnings, Crosby did not heed the approaching train until he was on the tracks, at which point he attempted to prompt his horses to speed up but was struck and killed by the train. The case was argued based on the negligence of both parties, particularly questioning whether the railroad’s employees properly signaled their approach and whether Crosby exercised appropriate caution.	The plaintiff, Abel Byam, claimed that the railroad company's negligence resulted in William Crosby's death, specifically alleging that the company failed to provide a safe crossing and did not adequately signal the approach of the train. Byam sought compensation for the wrongful death, arguing that the company should have taken more precautions to prevent such an accident, especially considering the challenging conditions of the crossing.	The defendant, Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Co., countered by asserting that the deceased was grossly negligent. They argued that William Crosby disregarded obvious dangers, failed to look for the approaching train, and was aware of the crossing’s hazardous nature. The company's representatives claimed that all proper signals were given, and that they took every reasonable measure to avoid the accident. They requested that the court dismiss the claims based on the deceased's responsible conduct in the situation.

George Wells, along with John Ryan and Isaac W. Swan, contested a legal issue against The People of the State of New York, which was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. The central matter revolved around whether Wells was a resident of Illinois on May 2, 1864. Originating from Medina, New York, Wells moved to De Kalb County, Illinois in 1859, where he purchased a farm. He did not fully occupy the farm until the spring of 1861 when he began living there permanently. Even though his wife remained in New York, Wells lived, managed, and cultivated the farm until he sold it in August 1864. His voting records indicated a shift of residency, as he voted in Illinois during this period. A key factor was the timing of an attachment issued against his property, claiming he was a non-resident. The trial court ruled that he was indeed a non-resident, but the evidence presented indicated otherwise, showing Wells' intent to make Illinois his permanent home.	The plaintiff contended that Wells was not a resident of Illinois by the time the attachment was sought, arguing that he continued to maintain his residence in New York due to his wife's presence there. The legal claim hinged on the interpretation of residency under Illinois attachment law and the implications of Wells’ living situation, voting, and expressed intentions regarding his farm in Illinois.	The defendants argued that Wells had established residency in Illinois through his continuous occupation and cultivation of the farm, as well as his declaration of intent to make Illinois his permanent home. They maintained that despite his wife residing in New York, Wells' actions and intentions demonstrated that he was an Illinois resident at the time of the attachment, rendering the attachment illegal.

The case "Chicago Safe and Lock Company v. Michael Cremen" took place in 1888, with the appeal filed on September 19. The primary individuals involved included the Chicago Safe and Lock Company as the appellant (plaintiff) and Michael Cremen as the appellee (defendant). The appellant corporation manufactured fireproof safes and filed a lawsuit against Cremen to recover the agreed price for a safe sold under a contract. The plaintiff presented the contract and evidence indicating that they delivered a safe that met the contractual specifications. In contrast, the defendant claimed the safe was useless due to a defect; specifically, he faced difficulty in opening the outer door without assistance. The plaintiff argued this issue stemmed from the defendant's improper use rather than a manufacturing defect. The court delivered instructions to the jury that were challenged by the plaintiff, leading to a dispute regarding the instructions given concerning the contract's terms and the alleged defects.	The Chicago Safe and Lock Company argued that they fulfilled their contractual obligations by delivering a safe as described in the contract. They contended that any issues relating to the safe's function were due to the defendant's failure to properly close an inner door, rather than any defect in the safe's construction. The plaintiff sought to recover the agreed price for the safe, asserting that the defendant did not provide adequate evidence of a defect that would warrant non-payment.	Michael Cremen defended against the plaintiff's claims by asserting that the safe was defective at the time of delivery, rendering it useless for its intended purpose. He argued that he promptly informed the plaintiff of the defect after discovering the issue, which he believed rescinded the contract. His defense was built upon the premise that the plaintiff was not entitled to recover the contract price due to the alleged failure to deliver a functional product.

In the year 1822, William Thompson, the appellant, filed a legal action against George Armstrong, the appellee, regarding a promissory note executed by one Colston 0. Wallis in Kentucky on August 30, 1814. This note was for the payment of a specified sum of money, which could be discharged in pork, and was due on January 1, 1817. Thompson received the assignment of the note from Armstrong on March 2, 1815. However, the declaration did not specify where the assignment took place. On June 1, 1818, Thompson initiated a lawsuit in the Muhlenburgh circuit court against the maker of the note, ultimately leading to the maker's insolvency. The circuit court subsequently sustained a demurrer to Thompson's declaration for failure to show due diligence in recovering the debt, prompting Thompson to appeal the ruling.	Thompson argued that Armstrong, as the assignor of the promissory note, should be held liable for its payment. He contended that he had used due diligence to collect the amount due by pursuing the maker of the note and claimed that the maker's insolvency excused further attempts at recovery. Thompson's legal request included reversing the lower court's judgment and allowing him to proceed with his claim.	Armstrong's defense relied on the assertion that due diligence had not been exercised by Thompson in pursuing the note's payment. He argued that a lawsuit filed years after the note was due could not be considered due diligence. Additionally, he challenged the assignment of the note, claiming it was not properly assignable as there were no averments regarding its assignment.

The legal case of Mary M. Chambers et al. v. John R. Jones took place in June 1874 in White County, Illinois. The dispute centers around the real estate left by Aaron West, who died owning several tracts of land. His heirs, including Mary M. and Sarah E. West, sought to nullify a sale conducted under a circuit court decree for partitioning the estate, arguing that the sale was invalid due to jurisdictional issues. The sale was authorized by a court decree that allowed the land to be sold as it was deemed impractical to partition without causing harm to the parties' rights. The sale was conducted by an agent of the commissioner, who was not authorized to oversee the sale personally. The defender, Jones, purchased the property but the heirs contended that proper legal procedures regarding their interests had not been observed. As minors at the time, the heirs argued that no proper service was made upon them, leading to the conclusion that the original court’s actions were without jurisdiction. This prompted them to seek legal relief to set aside the sale and return the property to its rightful heirs.	The plaintiffs, heirs of Aaron West, claimed that the sale of the land was null and void due to the court lacking jurisdiction over them as minors, since proper service of process was not conducted. They sought to set aside the sale and requested a court order to reclaim the land, alongside an account of the rents and profits generated from the property during the time Jones had possessed it.	The defendant, John R. Jones, argued that he lawfully purchased the land under the judicial sale and that the principle of "caveat emptor" (let the buyer beware) should apply. He contended that any irregularities during the sale process did not negate his rights as a purchaser, and he opposed the plaintiffs’ request for the return of the property without refunding the purchase price and compensations for improvements and taxes paid on the property.

The case of Lewis W. Pitcher v. The Board of Trade of the City of Chicago took place in 1886, when Lewis W. Pitcher was expelled from the Board of Trade in Chicago. Following his expulsion on May 13, 1886, Pitcher filed for a preliminary injunction in the Circuit Court of Cook County on June 8, seeking to restrict the Board from preventing him access to the exchange hall and conducting his business as he had previously. After a trial involving sworn testimonies and documents, the Circuit Court ruled to dissolve the injunction and dismissed Pitcher's bill due to a lack of equity, a decision that was upheld by the Appellate Court before being appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court. Pitcher argued that the Board could not delegate the power of expulsion to its board of directors; however, the Board's charter allowed for such delegation. Additionally, Pitcher raised issues about the impartiality of the directors and the validity of the trial proceedings, but these claims were determined to be without merit.	Pitcher's main arguments centered around the assertion that his expulsion from the Board of Trade was illegal because it was carried out by the board of directors rather than the entire membership. He claimed that the rules defining expulsion were not duly followed and that he was denied a fair trial by an impartial tribunal. He sought the court's intervention to restore his membership and grant him continued access to the exchange hall where he had conducted business.	The Board of Trade's defenses emphasized that the expulsion was validly executed under the powers granted to the board of directors by the corporation's charter, which allowed for the adoption of rules regarding member expulsion. They argued that the expulsion process followed was in accordance with the established rules and that Pitcher had agreed to abide by them upon joining. The Board maintained that the proceedings were regular and justified, asserting that the merits of Pitcher's expulsion could not be reexamined by the court.

In 1886, a special assessment was levied by Danforth Drainage District No. 3 in Iroquois County, Illinois. The county collector, Charles E. Barber, sought to collect this assessment against the lands owned by Charlotte E. Chapman and others in the district. The owners filed objections in the county court, which resulted in a $400 rebate from the amount assessed against their lands. This prompted the collector to appeal the judgment. Prior to the drainage district's organization, the landowners had constructed ditches on their properties, which were later used by the district. Although the drainage commissioners recognized an agreement was made to credit Chapman $400 for the ditches, they argued they lacked the authority to grant this adjustment after the assessment roll was filed. This case focused on the proper procedure and legal limitations regarding the assessment and credits for previous work performed by landowners.	The plaintiff, Charles E. Barber as County Collector, claimed that the county court erred in granting a $400 rebate to the landowners, arguing that the drainage commissioners had no authority to make any adjustments once the assessment roll was filed with the town clerk. The plaintiff maintained that all matters regarding the assessment should be resolved through the statutory appeal process rather than through the county court.	The defendants, represented by Charlotte E. Chapman and others, contended that they deserved the credit for the ditches they had previously constructed and used by the drainage district. They argued that a meeting among the drainage commissioners resulted in an agreement to allow the credit, which should therefore stand despite the collector's appeal. They maintained that they followed the proper procedures in requesting a reduction based on the prior construction.

In 1890, a legal case was filed in the Illinois Appellate Court concerning life insurance coverage. The case arose from the death of John B. Keach, who had an insurance policy issued by Penn Mutual Life Insurance Company. Keach had consistently paid premiums, but allegedly failed to pay the premium due on May 5, 1888, shortly before his death on July 27, 1888. The plaintiff, Anna C. Keach, the beneficiary of the policy, asserted that the premium payment was waived and postponed by the company's general agent, B. P. Hinman, who managed the company's activities in Illinois from his Chicago office. The court examined correspondence between Hinman and the Keaches, which indicated that the agent was actively engaged in discussing payment methods and had previously accepted notes in lieu of cash for premium payments. The primary dispute focused on whether the non-payment of the May premium was waived due to the agent’s dealings and correspondence. The court concluded that the company was estopped from asserting a forfeiture, based on the established course of dealing with the insured.	The plaintiff, Anna C. Keach, argued that while her husband did not pay the premium due on May 5, 1888, the payment was waived by the defendant's agent, B. P. Hinman, who failed to send the required note for signature in time. She contended that Hinman’s communications established an understanding that premium payments could be postponed and that the belief created by the company’s previous conduct should prevent them from claiming forfeiture for non-payment.	The defendant, Penn Mutual Life Insurance Company, contended that the policy clearly stipulated the non-payment of premiums would result in forfeiture. They argued that the absence of the requisite cash payment was a breach of conditions under the contract, and they were not liable for the policy amount due to this breach. The company maintained that Hinman lacked authority to waive the payment terms stated in the policy.

In September 1876, in Peoria, Illinois, a legal case titled "George W. McLain v. Susan Farden" arose concerning a trespass action. The plaintiff, Susan Farden, sought damages for the alleged killing of her grey mare, valued at $150, by the defendant, George W. McLain. The case was heard in the Peoria Circuit Court, where a jury trial concluded with a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, awarding her the full amount sought. The defendant, McLain, denied the allegations and appealed the verdict, arguing that the jury's decision was contrary to the evidence presented. The court's examination revealed insufficient proof directly implicating McLain in the act of killing the mare. However, circumstantial evidence indicated that his behavior following the incident—including instructing others to remain silent and burying the horse in secrecy—was suspicious. The mare had been trespassing on McLain's property, creating an antagonistic relationship that served as potential motive for his actions. Ultimately, the jury's decision was upheld by the court.	Susan Farden, the plaintiff, claimed that George W. McLain had unlawfully killed her grey mare and sought damages amounting to $150. Her arguments relied heavily on circumstantial evidence suggesting that McLain's actions after the mare's death implied guilt, particularly the secretive manner in which the mare was buried and the lack of transparency in McLain’s interactions with her regarding the incident.	George W. McLain, the defendant, contended that the verdict was unsupported by direct evidence proving that he killed the mare. His defense centered on the assertion that circumstantial evidence was insufficient to hold him liable. McLain and his son denied any wrongdoing and attempted to discredit the plaintiff's primary witness while requesting a new trial based on these arguments.

Jonathan Hullinger filed a legal action against Edwin A. Worrell, the sheriff of Whiteside County, in September 1876. Hullinger’s case arose from an incident involving Gardner Barker, who had previously been indicted for assaulting Hullinger with a deadly weapon. Hullinger claimed that the sheriff negligently allowed Barker to escape from custody, subsequently leading to further threats and assaults by Barker against Hullinger. Hullinger was forced to incur expenses related to having Barker bound over to keep the peace due to these threats. The initial legal action included two counts against the sheriff: the first argued that allowing Barker to escape caused Hullinger subsequent damages due to further assault, and the second alleged that the sheriff not only permitted the escape but incited Barker to commit more assaults against Hullinger. However, the Circuit Court of Whiteside County sustained a demurrer to the declaration, prompting Hullinger to appeal the decision.	Hullinger's primary arguments against Worrell were based on claims of negligence, asserting that the sheriff's actions directly resulted in Barker's escape and subsequent threats and assault against him. He sought damages for the expenses incurred while securing Barker's peace bond and claimed that the sheriff had a duty to prevent the escape of an indicted prisoner, which he failed to uphold.	Worrell's defense revolved around the assertion that allowing Barker to escape did not cause any legal injury to Hullinger. The sheriff contended that Hullinger, not being a party to the original criminal proceedings, could not seek damages based on the escape of Barker. Furthermore, it was claimed that the subsequent assault was not a natural outcome of the escape, so Hullinger's claims did not warrant a legal cause of action.

In September 1877, the case of Albert S. Race v. Charles W. Weston was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over a contract involving a real estate transaction in Chicago, Illinois. Albert S. Race (the appellant) sought specific performance of a contract claiming that Charles W. Weston (the appellee) was to convey certain lots in exchange for a leasehold estate of twenty-five years in another property, which was facilitated by Race's brother, Richard T. Race, acting as his agent. Weston admitted to signing an agreement to convey the property but argued that it was done under the condition that the contract would only be delivered if he was satisfied with the property's truthfulness after investigation. After conducting such investigation, Weston concluded that the representations made about the property were false and refused to proceed with the contract. The court had to determine whether to grant Race's request for specific performance, which would require clear evidence of an enforceable agreement and the absence of fraud or misrepresentation.	Albert S. Race claimed that there was a valid contract for the exchange of properties and sought specific performance, asserting that Weston was obligated to fulfill the terms of the agreement. He argued that the material representations made by his agent regarding the dimensions and value of the property were relied upon when signing the contract. Race sought the court's intervention to compel Weston to convey the property as initially agreed.	Charles W. Weston contended that the claimed contract was never finalized and was contingent upon his satisfaction with the property's state, which he determined to be unsatisfactory after further investigation. He highlighted that the dimensions and values provided by Richard T. Race were false and material, thus constituting misrepresentation that invalidated the basis of the agreement. Weston requested the court to deny Race's request for specific performance, arguing it was not enforceable due to these misrepresentations.

In September 1868, Richard Ammerman filed a legal case against Robert Teeter in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a dispute over a small account. The key individuals involved were Ammerman, the appellant, and Teeter, the appellee. The conflict arose when Ammerman claimed that Teeter owed him a few dollars for services rendered, while Teeter maintained he had no outstanding debt beyond the seven dollars he had tendered before the lawsuit commenced. The case initially went to a justice of the peace, where Teeter claimed a judgment of nine dollars. However, during the appeal in the circuit court, a jury ruled in favor of Teeter. Ammerman subsequently brought the case to the Illinois Supreme Court, challenging the circuit court's jury verdict on the grounds that the evidence did not support the jury's decision and questioned the jury instructions provided during the trial.	The plaintiff, Richard Ammerman, argued that Robert Teeter owed him a greater sum than the seven dollars paid prior to the lawsuit. Ammerman claimed that the evidence of payment provided by Teeter did not account for other debts owed to him, asserting that the total amount due exceeded the payments Teeter had claimed. Ammerman requested a reversal of the jury's verdict from the circuit court, contending that it was not supported by the evidence presented during the trial.	Robert Teeter, the defendant, maintained that he had already paid off his debt to Ammerman and argued that the amount he owed did not exceed the seven dollars tendered. Teeter's defense was supported by evidence that he had provided certain materials and had been paid for services, which he claimed squared his accounts with Ammerman. He sought to uphold the jury's verdict from the circuit court that found in his favor, arguing that the evidence indeed supported the conclusion that he had settled his obligations.

On August 19, 1872, William J. Tewksbury and Hugh Maher engaged the services of Harmon Spruance and Josiah W. Preston, partners in a commission house located in Chicago, to purchase 25,000 bushels of wheat on their behalf. Following the purchase, the wheat was sold, leading to a financial loss of $7,700 for Tewksbury and Maher. The plaintiffs filed a lawsuit seeking recovery for this loss, claiming that the wheat was not purchased as directed. The defense argued that the plaintiffs had authorized the type of purchase made, which involved acquiring 10,000 bushels of cash wheat and the remaining 15,000 through settlement of a prior contract with another party. The courts had to determine if the manner of purchase adhered to the original order given by Tewksbury, considering conflicting testimonies from both parties regarding the agreement's terms. The trial presented a factual dispute about the legitimacy of the purchase method and the responsibilities of agents in executing their duties.	The plaintiffs claimed that the commission merchants did not fulfill their order to buy 25,000 bushels of cash wheat. They argued that by not acting within the scope of their authority and selling wheat previously owned without notifying them, the merchants incurred a significant financial loss. They sought compensation for the $7,700 loss experienced due to this alleged breach of duty.	The defendants contended that the manner in which the wheat was obtained was authorized by the plaintiffs. They maintained that Tewksbury had given them permission to purchase wheat in settlement, which they argued complied with the terms of the order. The defendants asserted that they had acted within their authority and the wheat sold to the plaintiffs was in fact, held ready for delivery, dismissing the claims of improper sale.

In September 1875, Alfred Covington filed a legal case against The City of East St. Louis in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered around an ordinance passed by the City Council on May 5, 1875, which declared that a tract of land known as "Illinois City" would be annexed to East St. Louis. Covington, a resident and business owner within the territory marked for annexation, sought to prevent the enforcement of this ordinance, arguing that it exceeded the city council's authority. He raised two main objections: first, that the section of the city charter allowing the annexation was nullified by the adoption of the Illinois constitution of 1870; and second, that it conflicted with a 1872 state law governing the annexation and exclusion of territories. The case examined whether Illinois City constituted a valid part of East St. Louis under current laws.	Alfred Covington contended that the annexation of Illinois City by The City of East St. Louis was invalid. He argued that the governing city charter provision permitting such annexation was rendered obsolete by the new constitution of 1870 and that the ordinance contravened the state law established in 1872 regarding municipal boundaries. Covington sought an injunction to prevent the city and its officers from enforcing the annexation ordinance.	The City of East St. Louis, represented by their attorneys, maintained that the annexation was lawful under the provisions of their city charter. They argued that the city council had the authority to declare territories as part of the city, and the constitutional changes did not repeal prior city charters or local laws unless there was an explicit contradiction. They claimed that the ordinance complied with both the city charter and relevant state statutes and should therefore be upheld.

In the case of "John D. Pahlman, Ex’r of A. Rossiter, dec’d, Henry L. Rucker and James Campbell, Guardians of Minor Heirs of A. Rossiter, and Martha A. Rossiter, Widow, Plaintiffs in Error, v. Horatio G. Shumway, Miller & Davis, John B. King, E. Blackman, Adm’r, and H. H. Magie, Survivor of High & Magie, H. Stevens, Adm’r of F. M. Kerwin, Defendants in Error," the central events unfolded in Chicago, Illinois. The case arose following a deed of trust executed on March 12, 1857, by Asher Rossiter and his wife to Shumway, securing a debt that involved eight notes, each worth $2,000, which were due within a year. In 1859, after a default on the payments, Shumway sold the property at a public auction for $30,000, using the proceeds to satisfy the debts while holding the remaining surplus subject to judicial direction. Following the sale, various parties, including the estate of Rossiter, claimed the surplus funds. The estate's executor, Pahlman, along with Rucker and Campbell, sought to clarify these claims and the rightful distribution of the surplus, which led to the litigation regarding their roles and rights to the funds held by Shumway.	The plaintiffs argued that the surplus from the sale of the land should be distributed among the creditors as per the Statute of Wills, asserting that the prior judgments against Rossiter did not attach as liens on the surplus after the sale. They contended that since Shumway did not enforce the liens through a levy and sale, the surplus rightfully belonged to the executor of Rossiter's estate for distribution among general creditors.	The defendants contended that they held valid liens against the property based on prior judgments against Rossiter, which should entitle them to priority over the surplus. They maintained that the trust deed's sale, conducted without addressing these liens, did not extinguish their rights, and that they were entitled to be paid from the surplus before any distribution to the estate or other claimants.

In the legal case of **William A. Christy v. Richard W. Stafford**, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the action originated when Bichard W. Stafford filed a case against Christy, Walker & Co. in March 1885. The dispute revolved around a contract dated November 15, 1883, involving the sale of pickles, where Stafford agreed to sell 3,000 barrels of various types of pickles at specified prices, with cash on delivery and delivery terms that included shipping. Stafford claimed that he was ready and willing to deliver the pickles within the agreed period, from the contract date until January 1, 1885, but the defendants refused to accept or pay for them. Following the initial trial, which favored Stafford, the case was appealed but the judgment for Stafford was affirmed by the Appellate Court. Ultimately, the case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for further review regarding the sufficiency of the evidence and adherence to legal standards.	The plaintiff, Bichard W. Stafford, asserted that he fulfilled his obligations under the contract to deliver the pickles but that the defendants (Christy, Walker & Co.) refused to accept the goods and failed to make payment. He sought a judgment to recover the amount owed, which amounted to $1,523 plus court costs.	The defendant, William A. Christy, maintained a plea of the general issue but did not present substantive defenses directly challenging the facts of the case. Instead, he focused on procedural aspects and argued that the decision of the Appellate Court was based on unsound reasoning. The defendant sought to have the judgment reversed but could not demonstrate any errors that warranted such action.

The case "The University of Chicago v. The People ex rel. William C. Seipp" took place in 1886 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the University of Chicago as the appellant and William C. Seipp representing the People as the appellee. The dispute arose from the county court's judgment approving the sale of university real estate to cover two special assessments imposed by the city of Chicago for the improvement of adjacent streets. The University claimed that its properties were exempt from taxation or assessments according to its charter from 1857, which stated that its property was free from such financial obligations. However, the court's decision would ultimately hinge on the constitutionality of this exemption claim.	The University of Chicago argued that its real estate was exempt from all taxation and assessment by virtue of Section 10 of its charter enacted in 1857. They contended that any attempts by the city to levy assessments for local improvements contradict the charter’s provisions. The university sought to have the court overturn the county court's judgment that favored the special assessments.	The People, represented by William C. Seipp, contended that the provision in the university's charter attempting to exempt its property from assessments for local improvements was unconstitutional and void under the Illinois Constitution of 1848. They cited precedence from the case "City of Chicago v. Baptist Theological Union," asserting that similar charter provisions had been deemed unconstitutional. The defense maintained that such exemptions could not be applied to assessments meant for public improvements, advocating for the enforcement of the county court's judgment.

In the case of William B. Ogden v. Gustave Stock, which dates back to April 1864, the dispute took place in Illinois, focusing on a dwelling house removed from a property owned by Ogden. Ogden was the fee owner of the lot since 1856. He had signed a contract with a man named Schuster to sell the lot, but Schuster failed to make full payments, only having paid one installment by the time the lawsuit began. Schuster and Stock constructed a house on the lot while Schuster was in possession. After Schuster sold his half of the house to Stock in January 1861, Stock removed the house in June of that same year without Ogden's consent. Ogden demanded the return of the house, but Stock refused, prompting Ogden to file a replevin action for its recovery. At trial, the court ruled against Ogden, stating that Stock had the right to remove the house as it was not considered a fixture of the property. Ultimately, the court had to consider whether Schuster had the right to treat the house separately given his default on the payments.	Ogden argued that the house, being built on his owned land, was legally his property despite having been erected by Schuster and Stock. He maintained that Schuster, by defaulting on payments, had forfeited any rights to the property. Ogden contended that the house was a fixture permanently attached to the land and thus could not be removed. Therefore, he sought a judgment to recover the house in replevin asserting his legal ownership as the vendor of the land.	The defense, represented by Stock, asserted that Schuster had the legal right to erect the house and to permit Stock to occupy and remove it. They argued Ogden had not legally declared the purchase agreement forfeited or demanded possession of the lot, thus granting Schuster the right to lease the lot. The defense also claimed that since the house was not permanently affixed to the lot and built with the intent to be removable, Stock should not be liable for its removal.

In 1888, in Greene County, Illinois, Adam Chapman, as the administrator of the estate of his deceased aunt, Hannah Chapman, presented a claim against her estate. He sought compensation for the board and personal nursing services he provided to her during a severe illness caused by phlegmonous erysipelas, a highly contagious disease. This illness required extensive care over several months, during which Ms. Chapman lived with Adam's family and was treated almost like a family member. Despite Ms. Chapman having some wealth—about $82,000 in loans secured by promissory notes at the time of her death—there was no firm agreement regarding payment for Adam's services until near the end of her life when she expressed her intent to compensate him. Evidence suggested that Hannah believed she could never repay Adam fully but intended to give him all her possessions. The jury found in favor of Adam, awarding him $700. The case revolved around the necessity and unusual nature of the care provided, leading to questions of whether payment was warranted, especially considering the lack of explicit arrangements made prior to her illness.	Adam Chapman claimed that he was entitled to compensation for the extraordinary nursing and board services he rendered to his aunt during her prolonged illness. He argued that there was an implicit understanding of payment for these services, supported by Hannah's statements indicating her intention to compensate him for his care. He requested the court uphold the jury's verdict and award the amount claimed against the estate, emphasizing the meritorious nature of his service and the expectation of compensation by both parties.	The defendant, William B. Barnes, contested the claims by arguing that there was no formal contract or agreement for payment between Adam and Hannah Chapman prior to her illness. He asserted that the services rendered were familial and not rendered with the expectation of compensation. The defense challenged the admissibility of certain evidence and jury instructions regarding the case, arguing they were flawed and misleading. Ultimately, they requested that the court reverse the jury's decision and dismiss the claim.

The case of John Buck v. John Conlogue took place in La Salle, Illinois, with proceedings that initiated in June 1866. The plaintiff, John Buck, sought to recover ownership of lots 9 and 10 in block 94 of La Salle after a dispute arose involving the homestead rights associated with the property. At the center of the matter was a deed dated January 26, 1868, where George H. Buck (the deceased husband of the defendant's widow, Mrs. Morse) conveyed the property to the plaintiff. Importantly, while George in life had occupied the property as a homestead, he did not release his homestead rights in the deed. After George's death, Mrs. Morse and their minor child continued to occupy the property until she remarried and moved to Sterling, leaving the premises leased to a tenant and claiming that she intended to return. The appeal arose after a trial without a jury found in favor of the plaintiff, asserting that the homestead claim was lost due to the mother's actions. The court had to determine both the status of the homestead claim and the rights of the heirs to the property.	The plaintiff, John Buck, claimed that George H. Buck's widow and child lost their homestead rights to the property after Mrs. Morse married and moved away from La Salle. He asserted that their abandonment of the property meant they could not invoke their homestead rights as a defense in his attempt to reclaim the property. The crux of Buck's argument was based on the legal premise that by moving and acquiring a new home, Mrs. Morse forfeited her and her daughter's rights to the original homestead, thereby legitimizing his claim to the land.	The defendant, John Conlogue, argued that Mrs. Morse and her daughter retained the right to the homestead despite her relocation, as the initial deed did not effectively strip them of this right. He contended that her earlier intention to return to La Salle demonstrated that the homestead claim had not been abandoned. The defense cited case law establishing the need for a clear and definite abandonment of homestead rights, which they believed had not occurred since Mrs. Morse reportedly intended to return to the property.

Nelson B. Beers filed a case against Elbridge Williams in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the case being heard at the November term of the Cass Circuit Court in 1853. The legal matter arose from a promissory note for a steam boiler and fire-place that Beers manufactured and sold to Williams. Williams paid $300 in cash and executed a note for the remaining balance. However, he claimed that the boiler and fire-place were defective and not fit for their intended purpose of operating machinery at a grist and saw mill in Virginia, Cass County, Illinois. This defect led to the explosion of the boiler during operation, rendering it valueless. As a result, Williams asserted that the consideration for the promissory note had failed, leading to Beers' legal action to recover the amount owed.	The plaintiff, Nelson B. Beers, argued that the defectiveness of the steam boiler and fire-place did not absolve Williams of his obligation to pay the promissory note. Beers contended that the implied and express warranties regarding the quality and functionality of the product should not render the note unenforceable. Beers requested the court to uphold the validity of the promissory note and enforce payment from Williams.	Elbridge Williams, the defendant, claimed that the promissory note was given in consideration of a steam boiler and fire-place that were explicitly warranted to be fit for their intended use. He argued that the explosion of the defective boiler resulted in a total failure of consideration for the note, rendering it unenforceable. Williams requested the court to sustain his defense, asserting that the manufacturer has an implied responsibility to provide products made with sound materials and workmanship, which Beers failed to deliver.

In 1885, a legal case unfolded involving Charles L. Rutledge and the Drainage Commissioners District No. 6 in McLean County, Illinois. The case arose out of a bill filed by Rutledge to prevent the drainage commissioners from constructing a ditch across his property. The drainage district had previously been organized under the act of 1879, and the commissioners provided a plat of the proposed work, which inaccurately depicted the line of the intended ditch. During a jury trial to assess the damages caused by the construction, evidence revealed that the line on the plat did not accurately match the line surveyed by the commissioners, leading to concerns about substantial variation and potential greater harm to Rutledge's land. An amended plat was later filed, reflecting the ditch's alignment with an existing old ditch. Rutledge filed his bill to restrain the work, arguing that the variation from the original plat constituted an illegal appropriation of his property without due compensation being determined. The circuit court dismissed Rutledge's bill, prompting him to appeal.	Rutledge claimed that the drainage commissioners' attempt to construct the ditch varied significantly from the line specified in the original plat, arguing that such a deviation constituted an illegal appropriation of his property for public use without just compensation, as mandated by the Illinois Constitution. He sought a perpetual injunction to prevent the construction of the ditch as proposed, asserting that he was entitled to relief based on these grounds.	The drainage commissioners defended their actions by stating that they had attempted to comply with legal requirements regarding the construction of public works and that the new line was not necessarily more injurious than the line indicated in the original plat. They argued that no irreparable harm was being done to Rutledge’s property and contended that the injunction sought should be denied based on the absence of substantial injury.

The case "Washington Parkinson v. Alexander F. Trousdale" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court during the July term of 1842, following an earlier judgment made in the Madison Circuit Court in September 1841. The plaintiff, Washington Parkinson, was previously ordered to pay the defendant, Alexander F. Trousdale, $1000 in damages due to an action for slander. After this judgment, Parkinson filed a chancery bill to obtain an injunction that would prevent the collection of those damages while he had ongoing claims against Trousdale for slander, false imprisonment, and malicious prosecution. Parkinson asserted that he faced the danger of losing potential damages owed to him unless these could be set off against Trousdale's claim, especially alleging Trousdale's insolvency. Trousdale admitted the prior judgment and the existence of lawsuits against him but denied any wrongdoing and claimed that his assets exceeded his debts. He also mentioned that he had assigned half of the damages to a third party before the filing of the bill. The court eventually dissolved the injunction and dismissed Parkinson's bill, leading him to appeal the decision.	Parkinson argued that the court should prevent Trousdale from collecting the $1000 judgment until he was able to adjudicate his claims for slander and false imprisonment against Trousdale. He sought to have any damages awarded to him in these cases set off against the judgment he owed. Additionally, Parkinson alleged that Trousdale's insolvency posed a significant risk of him losing the potential damages unless they were set off.	Trousdale countered by admitting the previous judgment but denied any wrongdoing related to the slander or any of the claims made against him. He asserted that he was not insolvent and that his assets outweighed his debts. Moreover, he argued that he had already assigned half of the damages to a third party before the case arose, thereby complicating Parkinson's claims.

The case "City of Chicago v. Patrick Farrell" took place in 1888 in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, Patrick Farrell, brought a lawsuit against the City of Chicago following a personal injury incident that occurred due to the city's alleged neglect. Farrell suffered significant injuries, including the amputation of his leg, after falling from a sidewalk on Archer Avenue that lacked a guard or rail near a bridge over Ogden Slip. The absence of this safety feature at the time of his fall was central to his claim. During the trial, evidence presented showed that the city may have had constructive notice of the missing guardrail due to its absence for a considerable time before the accident. The case was tried before a jury, which ultimately ruled in favor of Farrell, leading to an appeal from the city regarding the judgment.	Patrick Farrell argued that the City of Chicago was negligent in failing to maintain a safe sidewalk by not having a guard or rail at the location where he fell. He sought damages for the personal injuries resulting from this negligence, including medical expenses and compensation for pain and suffering. Farrell contended that the city had constructive notice of the hazardous condition due to the guard's prolonged absence.	The City of Chicago, represented by Clarence A. Knight and John W. Green, argued against the claims by asserting that the evidence did not conclusively demonstrate negligence. They claimed that the instructions given to the jury, which were refused by the court, did not adequately present a valid basis for a verdict in favor of the city. The defense aimed to show that the city was not liable for the injuries incurred as there was insufficient proof of direct negligence.

In 1877, a legal case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court involving William Adam and George M. Arnold. The case stemmed from actions taken in the Circuit Court of Will County, where William Adam filed a petition to declare certain prior judgments, which had been entered by confession during court vacation, null and void. These judgments had been authorized by the parties involved and properly entered by the clerk, leading to executions issued and money collected by the sheriff. Adam had subsequently obtained a judgment against the same party and sought to gain a preference over other creditors by challenging the validity of the earlier entries. The court had previously denied Adam's petition, leading him to appeal the decision. The court's opinion emphasized that there were no sufficient grounds to deem the judgments invalid, stating that objections related to the nature of the instrument and timing of the judgments were insufficient.	William Adam claimed that the judgments entered against the debtor party were null and void. He argued that the entries did not comply with proper legal standards and requested that the court declare these judgments invalid so he could receive payment to satisfy his own execution against the same debtor.	George M. Arnold, representing the appellee, defended the validity of the judgments. He contended that the objections raised by Adam did not warrant nullification, including arguments about the nature of the instrument and timing of its execution. Arnold asserted that only the debtor could contest the judgments, and that Adam, as a stranger to the initial proceedings, had no standing to challenge them.

On October 22, 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, Cyrus F. Cook and Hyman L. Seixas, operating as the firm Cook & Seixas, sold a bill of boots and shoes to Adolph Kahn for a total of $459.60. The plaintiffs claimed this amount as owed for the goods delivered. Kahn, however, pleaded non assumpsit, indicating that he was not responsible for the payment. During the trial, it was established that the only disputed issue was whether the debt was due at the time the lawsuit commenced. The plaintiffs asserted that all prior transactions between them and Kahn were cash sales, while Kahn countered that he had been purchasing goods on a thirty-day credit basis. The jury ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, assessing damages at the claimed amount. However, the plaintiff's instructions given to the jury were questioned, particularly regarding the assumption that goods sold without stated payment terms were to be paid for in cash. This led to the appeal where it was argued that the sale should have been interpreted under the credit arrangement established in previous dealings.	The plaintiffs' main argument revolved around the assertion that Kahn was indebted to them for the full amount of $459.60 for the boots and shoes delivered on October 22, 1884. They sought a judgment for this amount, maintaining that previous sales had been handled on cash terms and that the current claim was valid as the debt existed at the time of the lawsuit's initiation.	Kahn's defense was predicated on the claim that the debt for the boots and shoes was not due when the lawsuit was filed, as he had a longstanding arrangement with the plaintiffs to pay on a thirty-day credit basis. He argued that because the suit was initiated only six days post-purchase, it was premised on a debt that was not yet due, thereby rendering the plaintiffs unable to recover in court without proof of a matured obligation. Kahn requested the jury be instructed that they must find for him if the evidence did not show a matured debt.

The case of *William Jones et al. v. John P. King et al.* took place in September 1877 in Will County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, William Jones and Francis Kiernan, were involved in a bill in equity to set aside a deed executed on January 29, 1873. This deed involved the conveyance of certain lots in Joliet from Jones to Kiernan, which the plaintiffs claimed was fraudulent. The plaintiffs sought to have the property subjected to sale to satisfy a judgment they had obtained against Jones on January 23, 1875. In the circuit court, the defendants denied any fraudulent intent and argued the conveyance was made in good faith for consideration. A decree was issued by the circuit court in favor of the plaintiffs, which prompted the defendants to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs argued that the conveyance from Jones to Kiernan was fraudulent and aimed at avoiding debts, particularly a judgment they held against Jones. They contended that the conveyance was colorable, lacking genuine intent and consideration since the property was vastly undervalued compared to its actual worth. They requested that the court set aside the deed and allow the property to be sold to satisfy their judgment.	The defendants claimed that the conveyance was legitimate and executed in good faith for valuable consideration. They denied any intent to defraud and pointed out that evidence presented by the plaintiffs was flawed. They argued that the plaintiffs, not being creditors at the time of conveyance, had no grounds to contest the validity of the deed.

The case "The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company v. The People of the State of Illinois" arose from a legal dispute in April 1882 during a session of the Ford County Circuit Court in Illinois. The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company (the appellant) sought to transfer its case to the United States Circuit Court for the Southern District of Illinois.
