This motion was denied by the court, and no proper bill of exceptions was filed at that time. Subsequently, the court sustained the appellant's demurrer (a formal objection) and awarded judgment for costs against the plaintiff (the People of the State of Illinois). An appeal was made by the Wabash Railway Company, which led to a reversal of the circuit court's judgment by the Illinois Supreme Court. In December of the same year, the appellant attempted to introduce a bill of exceptions regarding the previous ruling, but the court was hesitant to accept it due to procedural issues and the timing of its filing. Ultimately, the court concluded that the bill of exceptions presented was too late and decided to strike it from the record.	The plaintiff, The People of the State of Illinois, argued that the Wabash Railway Company's attempted filing of a bill of exceptions concerning the transfer of its case to federal court was invalid because it was submitted after the relevant court term had ended. The plaintiff contended that without a timely and properly filed bill of exceptions, the rulings of the lower court should stand.	The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company (the appellant) maintained that the rulings regarding the transfer of the case to federal court should be part of the official record. They sought to have a bill of exceptions signed and included, claiming that their request for transfer was improperly denied, and that their rights were not preserved due to procedural discrepancies. They contended that the prevailing practice allowed for certain exceptions to be recognized despite the timing.

In December 1856, the case of Eli Dennis v. James Hopper was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over ownership of a parcel of land, with Eli Dennis claiming title based on a series of deeds. The plaintiff presented evidence that a patent for the contested land had been issued by the United States to one Coiu’tney, who subsequently transferred ownership to a third party, Hubbard, via a deed dated August 12, 1820. This deed, although recorded in the proper county in 1852, faced issues of admissibility due to objections from the defendant, Hopper, regarding the lack of proof of its execution. The court upheld these objections, leading to a trial centered on the proper legal interpretation of the relevant statutes concerning the acknowledgment of deeds executed outside of Illinois. It was determined that the law required further proof of execution beyond provided certifications, ultimately culminating in a judgment favoring the defendant.	Eli Dennis contended that he held rightful ownership of the land in question through a legitimate chain of deeds originating from a patent issued by the United States. He sought to admit a certified copy of a deed from Hubbard to confirm his title, which had been recorded in 1852. Dennis argued that the acknowledgment of the deed conformed to the laws of Rhode Island at the time of its execution and therefore should be deemed valid and admissible evidence.	James Hopper argued against the admissibility of the deed presented by Dennis, claiming that it lacked adequate proof of execution. He maintained that the statutory requirements necessitated more than just a certificate of conformity and that the deed could not be considered competent evidence without further proof. Hopper requested that the court reject the evidence and rule in his favor, ultimately affirming his ownership claim.

In 1869, Isaac Means entered into an agreement involving the purchase of five thousand bushels of corn from Marvin A. Lawrence and others (appellees). The contract was made on July 26, amidst conditions that suggested a potential rise in the market price due to an anticipated small crop. Means intended to capitalize on market fluctuations rather than actually taking physical possession of the corn. Throughout the year, he did not pay any margin, indicating he was primarily interested in market advantages rather than the corn itself. By December 31, 1869, the market price would determine his financial outcome. A letter from Means to the sellers revealed that he was prepared to settle at the contract's conclusion, but would not pay any amounts in advance. The case arose from a breach of this contract, leading to the plaintiffs seeking damages. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court following a verdict for the plaintiff from the Superior Court of Cook County.	The plaintiffs, Marvin A. Lawrence and others, argued that there was a valid contract with Means for the sale of corn, which he breached by failing to accept delivery and not providing any required margin. They contended that the agreement was enforceable and sought damages resulting from the breach, asserting that the preponderance of evidence supported their claims.	Isaac Means (the appellant) argued that no enforceable contract existed, primarily contending that he had not intended to take possession of any corn but was looking to profit from market fluctuations instead. He claimed the plaintiffs’ failure to actually possess the corn at the time of the agreement rendered the contract unenforceable. Means requested that the court reverse the previous judgment in favor of the plaintiffs based on this interpretation of the contract's validity.

In the case of Hosea B. Throop et al. v. Reuben R. Sherwood, the legal proceedings took place in the McHenry Circuit Court, Illinois, in August 1847. Reuben R. Sherwood (the appellee) was involved in a contractual dispute with Hosea B. Throop, Thomas, Macomber, and Brink (the appellants) regarding the construction of a bridge over Fox River. The appellants, appointed as a committee by local citizens, contracted Sherwood to build the bridge for a total of $790, with specific payment terms. Sherwood completed the bridge by November 1846; a settlement identified $256 due immediately and an additional $200 due one year later. The appellants signed notes to pay Sherwood, contingent upon his providing a bond to guarantee the bridge’s structural integrity for three years. However, Throop refused to accept the bond presented by Sherwood, claiming it didn't satisfy the necessary conditions, leading to the lawsuit. The case centers on the terms of the original contract and whether all parties were bound by it.	The plaintiff, Reuben R. Sherwood, claimed compensation for the construction of the bridge, asserting that all appellants, including Brink, had accepted the completed work and were jointly responsible for payment based on an account stated. He argued that the contractual arrangements had been satisfied on his part and that he was entitled to recover the overdue amounts legally owed to him. Sherwood contended that regardless of the written contract, an accounting had been established, obligating the appellants to pay reflected sums.	The defendants argued against the claims on several grounds. They contended that Brink should not be held liable since he did not sign the initial contract and that the work was performed under a written contract which required a special declaration for recovery. They claimed that without an acceptance from all appellants, particularly Throop and Brink, Sherwood could not claim under the common counts of his lawsuit. Furthermore, they sought a new trial, asserting that the court failed to adequately consider whether all requirements for liability were met, especially regarding the original contract terms and acceptance of work.

In 1853, Joseph McClellan filed a legal action of ejectment against Philo Kellogg in Peoria County, Illinois, concerning a specific tract of land: the west half of the southwest quarter of Section 36, Township 10 North, Range 5 East. McClellan asserted ownership based on a deed from William B. Tucker, recorded shortly after Tucker's entry of the land in 1836. The case progressed to trial in May 1854, where the court heard evidence from both parties. McClellan presented his prior ownership documentation, while Kellogg provided a chain of title tracing back to a patent from the United States through various assignments. Kellogg's defense rested on the argument that he had possessed the land for several years, including evidence of paying taxes on the property, whereas McClellan claimed that Kellogg had not established legal ownership or adverse possession.	McClellan claimed rightful ownership of the land based on his recorded deed from Tucker. He argued that Kellogg could not demonstrate continuous and exclusive possession of the property necessary to assert any legal claim against him. McClellan sought judicial recognition of his title, aiming to be reinstated as the rightful possessor of the land.	Kellogg contended that he had a legitimate claim to the land through a deed from a previous assignee of Tucker. He argued that he had possessed the land, even if only a part of it, and had made improvements while paying taxes on it. Kellogg asserted that McClellan's claims were insufficient to negate his established presence and that the defendant had the right to claim title via adverse possession.

In the case of John Wood et al. v. William Price, which was decided in January 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute arose from a series of bills of exchange dated May 1, 1861. The plaintiffs, John Wood and others, contended that the bills did not accurately specify the kind of payment required—specifically, they argued that the bills should have been payable in bank notes from Illinois banks, rather than merely in "current funds" or "currency." They sought an injunction to prevent an action based on the bills and requested that the bills be amended to reflect the correct terms of the agreement regarding payment. However, the Circuit Court of Adams County, presided by Judge Joseph Sibley, rejected their plea for an injunction and dismissed the case, placing the costs on the complainants. The case's basis lay in equity and the assertion of a fundamental mistake in the terms of the bills.	The plaintiffs claimed that there was an error in the drafting of the bills of exchange that led to them being payable in the ambiguous terms of "current funds" and "currency" instead of the intended specific bank notes. They requested the court to issue an injunction to prevent further action based on these bills and sought a reformation of the bills to reflect their true intended agreement.	The defendant, William Price, argued that the terms used in the bills were deliberately chosen and thus reflected the true intention of the parties involved. He asserted that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate any specific factual mistake that would justify reformation of the contracts as per their claims. The defendant contended that the court should uphold the written terms of the bills as the definitive evidence of the agreement, without entertaining parol evidence or prior negotiations that might suggest a different intent.

In September 1877, in Illinois, the legal case "Burton Godfrey v. Albert Brown" involves a dispute over the ownership of a quantity of standing corn in a field. The key individuals in the case are Burton Godfrey, the plaintiff, and Albert Brown, the defendant, who took action as a constable. The defendant levied the corn under an execution enforcing a judgment against George Brown. The plaintiff, Albert Brown, claimed the corn belonged to him, while the defendant contended that it rightfully belonged to George Brown. The controversy centered around the determination of the ownership of the corn, which was initially decided by two juries, favoring the plaintiff. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the circumstances surrounding the levy and possession of the corn, eventually siding with the findings of the juries that the corn was indeed owned by the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, Albert Brown, asserted ownership of the corn standing in the field and initiated an action of replevin against the defendant, Burton Godfrey, to recover his property. He argued that despite the defendant's claim of lawful possession due to the levy, the evidence overwhelmingly supported his ownership of the corn. Thus, he sought a judgment affirming his title and the return of his property.	The defendant, Burton Godfrey, justified the taking of the corn by claiming he acted as a constable under an execution against George Brown, arguing that the corn was the property of George Brown, not the plaintiff. He contended that the levy was permissible as he notified the plaintiff of the action taken. His defense was based on the assertion that he had legitimate possession due to the property being in the field, even if actual physical removal was impractical.

The case, titled "The Commercial Union Assurance Company v. J. Young Scammon," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 21, 1890. It involved a dispute over an insurance policy issued by Commercial Union Assurance Company to J. Young Scammon for a four-story brick building in Chicago, which was mortgaged to the United States Mortgage Company. The case arose after the building was destroyed by fire, and the insurer had paid a claim related to the same property under a policy issued to Babcock, a subsequent owner. The initial ruling was against Scammon, who appealed. The Appellate Court reversed this ruling, but upon further appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, the judgment was affirmed after establishing that equity courts do not have jurisdiction to review law court decisions if those courts had appropriate jurisdiction and the party had adequate legal remedies available. The case involved various legal arguments and defenses regarding the validity of the insurance policy and the handling of the claims.	Scammon, as the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to recover under the insurance policy after the loss of his property due to fire. He argued that the previous judgment against him, which benefited the defendant, was invalid due to issues regarding the sale and the title of the property, and he sought to have the judgment enforced, asserting that he was indeed entitled to the insurance payout based on the terms of the policy.	The defendant, Commercial Union Assurance Company, presented several defenses, including the argument that the property was conveyed under a mortgage, resulting in a change of title that nullified the insurance coverage. They also contested the sufficiency of the proof of loss provided by Scammon and argued that another policy issued to Babcock invalidated Scammon's claim.

The legal case of Canal Boat “Col. Mulligan” v. John H. Buck took place in September 1870 in LaSalle County, Illinois. The key individuals involved include the plaintiff, John H. Buck, who provided supplies to the canal boat “Col. Mulligan,” and the defendant, the canal boat itself. Buck initiated a proceeding through attachment to claim a sum of $103.64 for supplies alleged to have been furnished at the request of the boat's master over nine months prior to the affidavit's filing on November 10, 1865. The affidavit asserted that the canal boat was navigating Illinois waters at that time but failed to explicitly state that the boat was engaged in navigation when the supplies were provided. The defendant contended that the affidavit did not sufficiently establish jurisdiction, and a motion to dismiss the case was presented but initially overruled by the court, leading to a subsequent appeal questioning the jurisdictional adequacy of the affidavit.	The plaintiff, John H. Buck, claimed that he provided necessary supplies and materials to the canal boat “Col. Mulligan” at the request of its master. He sought a writ of attachment to secure his claim and emphasized that the value of the supplies amounted to $103.64. Buck argued that the supplies were essential for the fitting and equipping of the boat and that he deserved remuneration for his services as a tradesman.	The defense revolved around questioning the sufficiency of the plaintiff's affidavit, which the defendant argued did not adequately establish jurisdiction. Specifically, it failed to demonstrate that the canal boat was navigating the waters of Illinois when the supplies were provided. The defendant's motion to dismiss the case was grounded in the claim that the affidavit did not clearly meet the requirements mandated by the act of 1857, rendering the court unable to take jurisdiction over the matter.

In September 1877, a legal case titled "Frank A. Bowen v. The Wilcox & Gibbs Sewing Machine Company" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, located in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, The Wilcox & Gibbs Sewing Machine Company, charged the defendant, Frank A. Bowen, with a default on a promissory note amounting to one hundred and fifty dollars. The court proceedings highlighted an issue concerning an affidavit of merits submitted by Bowen, which claimed he had a valid defense against the plaintiff's allegations. However, the court struck the defendant's pleas from the files on the grounds of an alleged improper title in the affidavit. This prompted Bowen to appeal the decision, arguing that the technicalities of the title of the affidavit should not have resulted in the dismissal of his case. The Supreme Court of Illinois found that the title of the affidavit was indeed legally sufficient and ruled that the trial court's objections to it were erroneous. Consequently, the court reversed the lower court's judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings.	The plaintiff, The Wilcox & Gibbs Sewing Machine Company, claimed that Frank A. Bowen had failed to honor a promissory note worth one hundred and fifty dollars. They sought payment of the amount owed as per the terms specified in the engagement. They presented their case under the principles of assumpsit, aiming to recover the debt stated in the promissory note.	Frank A. Bowen, the defendant, contended that he had a valid defense against the claims made by the plaintiff. He asserted his belief, supported by an affidavit of merits, that the plaintiff had no legitimate demand as founded on the promissory note. Bowen maintained that the affidavit, despite the objections regarding its title, should be considered valid and sufficient to support his defense against the plaintiff's allegations.

The case "The Cincinnati, La Fayette & Chicago Railroad Co. v. The Danville & Vincennes Railway Co." arose in 1871 in Iroquois County, Illinois. A group of individuals, numbering twenty-five, formed a corporation under the general railroad law of 1849 to construct a railroad line connecting Cincinnati, Ohio to Chicago, Illinois. They subscribed to stock, elected a board of directors, filed articles of association, and obtained a certificate from the Secretary of State, effectively establishing the appellant corporation. By May 1, 1872, their railroad was operational. In November 1872, the appellee was organized under the same general railroad act to construct a similar line and initiated condemnation proceedings for land in Iroquois County without notifying the appellant, which was already in possession of the right of way. The appellant claimed the appellee's actions were fraudulent, aiming to usurp its right of way without proper procedure or compensation. The appellee neglected to reference the appellant in their petition to the county court, raising concerns of intentionally concealing information to execute a scheme for unjust possession.	The plaintiff, The Cincinnati, La Fayette & Chicago Railroad Co., claimed that the Danville & Vincennes Railway Co. engaged in fraudulent proceedings to condemn their established right of way without notice. They sought an injunction to prevent the appellee from taking possession, arguing that they were a de facto corporation and had rightful ownership of the right of way since they had operated the railroad publicly and notoriously.	The defendant, The Danville & Vincennes Railway Co., contended that the appellant was not lawfully organized and, therefore, lacked standing to claim rights in the proceedings. They asserted that irregularities in the appellant's formation meant it had no valid claim to the right of way and that their petition to the county court did not require appellant's involvement or notice.

In December 1833, in Hamilton County, Illinois, Reuben Clark was indicted alongside three others for the crime of arson. The case was tried during the March term of the Hamilton Circuit Court before Judge Thomas C. Browne. Clark’s defense attorney, Walter B. Scates, argued for a change of venue based on an affidavit claiming that local prejudice against Clark would prevent a fair trial. However, the court denied this motion. Following this, Clark's team attempted to quash the indictment, which was also denied. The jury ultimately returned a verdict of guilty, which led to Clark being sentenced to three weeks in jail, a fine of $360, public whipping, and court costs. Clark subsequently appealed, claiming errors in the court's refusal to grant a change of venue and to quash the indictment, arguing that the indictment was defective because it did not include the value of the property allegedly involved in the arson.	Reuben Clark, the plaintiff in error, claimed that he could not receive a fair trial in Hamilton County due to local prejudice. He requested a change of venue, asserting that his rights to an impartial trial were violated. Additionally, he argued that the indictment was flawed because it failed to specify the value of the property alleged to have been burned, a requirement under the relevant statute that affects the judgment regarding the fines applicable.	The People of the State of Illinois, the defendants in error, defended the decision of the trial court noting that changing the venue for just one of several jointly indicted defendants could complicate proceedings. They argued that the court was correct in denying the change of venue request and in upholding the indictment. The prosecution also pointed out that while the indictment may have had imperfections, the jury had still found sufficient evidence for a conviction, asserting the validity of the original judgment under current statute.

In the case of John W. Taylor v. William Adams, filed on January 25, 1886, in Will County, Illinois, John W. Taylor had mortgaged certain premises to Edmund Wilcox in 1862 to secure purchase money notes. After Wilcox assigned the notes to Clement, and the mortgage was foreclosed, William Adams purchased the property at a master’s sale and subsequently obtained a deed. Although Taylor and his wife conveyed the equity of redemption to her father on two occasions, they continued to occupy the mortgaged premises. Adams, claiming rightful title from the foreclosure, initiated an action of ejectment against Taylor, asserting his right to evict him from the property. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after Taylor disputed the possession claim, arguing that it belonged to his wife.	The plaintiff, William Adams, argued that he had obtained rightful title to the premises through foreclosure proceedings and claimed that Taylor's continued possession was illegitimate. Adams contended that under established legal principles governing foreclosures and ejectments, Taylor, as a mortgagor, did not possess valid title or the right to remain on the property after the foreclosure had occurred.	John W. Taylor, the defendant, claimed that his wife held a superior title to the property due to previous conveyances and thus contested the legality of the foreclosure. He argued that he was not in possession of the property at the time the suit was filed, alleging that any possession held was under the auspices of his wife. Taylor also raised objections regarding the admissibility of the foreclosure record.

The case involves Catharine Oehm, who contracted to provide masquerade costumes for a ball scheduled for December 25, 1868, in South Bend, Indiana. On December 24, Oehm purchased a passenger ticket from Chicago to South Bend and checked two trunks as personal luggage, paying an extra fee for their weight. Upon arrival in South Bend, one trunk containing the costumes was not delivered in time for the event, leading Oehm to lose the benefits of her contract. The trunk was later returned to her in Chicago, with its contents intact. This situation prompted Oehm to file a lawsuit against the Michigan Southern & Northern Indiana Railroad Company seeking damages for the lost profits due to the late delivery.	Catharine Oehm argued that the railroad company failed to deliver her trunk containing masquerade costumes in a timely manner, resulting in lost profits from her contractual obligations. She sought $500 in damages, asserting that the company had a responsibility to deliver her personal baggage on time.	The Michigan Southern & Northern Indiana Railroad Company contended that they were not liable for the non-delivery of the costumes because the plaintiff failed to inform their personnel of the trunks' contents. They argued that the shipment was merely personal baggage and that they had no knowledge of any commercial value or urgency attached to the contents. Therefore, the company claimed that they were released from liability as common carriers since they were not notified of the specific nature or importance of the items being transported.

John W. Ferguson initiated a legal action for ejectment against Jesse Miles in the Peoria Circuit Court in Illinois, seeking possession of the southwest quarter of section 20 in township 9 north of range 8 east. The case began when Ferguson filed a declaration at the October 1845 term and obtained a rule for the defendant to plead within twenty days. By the May term of 1846, the court allowed Miles to file a plea of not guilty prior to any default judgment. By October 1846, the case proceeded to trial before a jury. Ferguson presented evidence including a prior judgment in his favor, sheriff's sales, deeds, and a lease between Miles and a third party, George Morton. Ferguson argued that Miles was unlawfully in possession as Morton's tenant. However, Miles countered with evidence regarding the validity of titles and possession rights. The jury ultimately delivered a verdict of not guilty for the defendant, leading Ferguson to appeal based on several alleged errors in the court's instructions and evidentiary rulings.	Ferguson's main arguments were that he had established ownership of the disputed property through a prior judgment, execution, and sheriff's deed that conveyed the title to him. He asserted that Miles was in possession of the property as a tenant of Morton, the judgment debtor, and sought to recover possession based on this claim. Ferguson contended that he met the legal requirements to assert his title in the action of ejectment.	Miles's defense hinged on questioning the validity of Ferguson's claims regarding the deed and the ownership of the property. He argued that the prior deed from Morton was valid and that Ferguson failed to demonstrate that Morton had the actual possession of the property at the relevant time. Miles maintained that the court's exclusion of certain evidentiary documents was appropriate and that Ferguson had not proven his entitlement to recover the property under the legal standards governing ejectment.

Edward Coles, the plaintiff in error, was involved in a legal dispute with the County of Madison, the defendant in error, in June 1826. The case originated from an action of debt brought by the county commissioners of Madison County, seeking to impose a $2,000 penalty on Coles for bringing ten enslaved individuals into the county and freeing them without the legally required bond, as mandated by a legislative act from 1819. After pleading the statute of limitations, Coles’ plea was overruled, and he went to trial, resulting in a verdict against him in September 1821. However, judgment wasn't passed until September 1825, during which time the Illinois legislature enacted a new law releasing penalties from the 1819 act. Coles attempted to use this new law as a defense to renew his motion for a new trial, but the court rejected his plea. The primary legal question was whether the legislature had the authority to release a penalty for actions that had already occurred before a judgment was rendered.	The plaintiff, County of Madison, argued that Coles was liable for the penalty as he violated the act of 1819 by liberating enslaved individuals without providing the necessary bond. They sought to enforce this penalty and argued that the statute of limitations did not apply, as the case was still active.	Coles contended that the Illinois legislature's 1825 act releasing penalties under the 1819 law invalidated the basis for the County's claims against him. He argued that it represented a successful defense against the penalty despite the prior verdict. His legal request was that the court should recognize the 1825 law's effect in nullifying the previous claims against him, and he sought relief from the judgment.

Richard Cole v. Henry Cole is a legal case that occurred in the spring of 1875 in Bridgeport, Chicago. The key individuals involved are Richard Cole, the appellant (plaintiff), and Henry Cole, the appellee (defendant), who is Richard's cousin. Richard owned several small lots purchased for approximately $200-$250 each. During that time, both Henry Cole and William Cole, their elderly uncle, were employed by Richard in his cooper shop, where William had been boarding with Richard. Richard proposed a deal to Henry: if Henry would board their uncle for four years, he would transfer ownership of one of the lots to him. Henry accepted the offer, and after two years, Richard offered a second proposal to buy and improve an old barn on the lot, which Henry agreed to, again under the condition of boarding William for three and a half years and transferring a small building to Richard. Henry fulfilled his obligations, boarding William for a total of seven and a half years, taking possession of the newly constructed house, and managing expenses such as taxes and insurance. The central issue arose as Richard claimed the lot was to be shared with William as tenants in common, while Henry argued it was to be solely his. The lack of written agreements complicated matters, and Richard later sought to appeal a decision from the Superior Court of Cook County that had ordered specific performance on the agreement.	Richard Cole, the appellant, claimed that the initial agreement regarding the lot was intended to convey the property to both himself and William Cole. He asserted that under the circumstances and evidence presented, it was unreasonable for Henry to claim sole entitlement to the property, particularly given that William had contributed nothing to its purchase or upkeep.	Henry Cole maintained that the agreement was meant to transfer sole ownership of the lot to him. He argued that he had fully performed his obligations by boarding William for the required duration and presented testimony supporting his version of the agreement. Henry emphasized the lack of any written documentation and sought reversal of the Superior Court’s decree.

Polly Hopper initiated a legal case against Zadock Ferguson, the surviving administrator of her deceased husband, Joshua Hopper, in Illinois in January 1860. The case arose from a previous decree in a divorce case between Polly and Cavil Hopper, which stated that if Cavil received a certain allowance from Joshua's estate, Polly would be entitled to receive one-third of that allowance. After Cavil Hopper was awarded an allowance of $600 from Joshua Hopper’s estate, the administrator, knowing of the previous decree, paid the full amount to Cavil instead of retaining the amount owed to Polly. Consequently, Polly sought to recover the $200 she was entitled to under the decree, but the County Court refused her petition. The Circuit Court affirmed this decision, prompting Polly to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Polly Hopper claimed that she was entitled to $200 from the allowance paid to Cavil Hopper by Joshua Hopper's estate, in accordance with the prior decree. She argued that the administrator was bound by this decree and that her proportion of the allowance should have been paid to her. Polly sought a legal order for the payment of this amount plus interest from the date specified.	Zadock Ferguson, the surviving administrator, contended that he was not a party to the prior chancery suit and was not legally obligated to follow the decree. He argued that the decree only created a contractual obligation between Polly and Cavil and did not impose any duty on him as the administrator. Consequently, since he legally discharged the estate’s obligations by paying the full allowance to Cavil, he asserted that Polly's claim had no legal basis and urged the court to deny her appeal.

The case of Hamilton C. Daniels et al. v. Daniel B. Heartrunft et al. took place in DuPage County, Illinois, in September 1870. The central figures in this legal matter were Daniel B. Heartrunft and others (the plaintiffs) who filed a suit in chancery against Hamilton C. Daniels and Allen C. Yundt (the defendants). The dispute centered around a promissory note worth $3,080 that Yundt deposited with Daniels on April 30, 1864, as part of a conditional agreement concerning the payment of expenses related to the illness and subsequent death of Mrs. Heartrunft, the mother of the complainants. Before her death, accusations were made against Yundt regarding complicity in procuring an abortion for Mrs. Heartrunft, which led to the deposit of the note as security for Yundt’s return to settle related expenses. Different versions of the agreement emerged from the testimonies of Yundt, Daniels, and Becker, particularly regarding the note’s intended purpose. The court determined that the evidence provided in the testimonies did not adequately support the claims made regarding the trust, and the credibility of witness statements was a significant factor in the proceedings.	The plaintiffs, represented by Daniel B. Heartrunft, argued that the promissory note deposited by Yundt was intended to create a trust in favor of the complainants so that funds could be used for their support and to cover funeral expenses for Mrs. Heartrunft. They asserted that Yundt was obligated to use the deposited funds for the plaintiffs' maintenance following the death. Therefore, the plaintiffs sought a decree compelling the execution of this alleged trust and the release of the funds for their benefit.	The defendants, Hamilton C. Daniels and Allen C. Yundt, contended that the promissory note was deposited solely as a security for Yundt's return from Chicago and to cover the medical and funeral expenses of Mrs. Heartrunft if needed. They explicitly denied any intent for the note to serve as a means of support for the complainants. Yundt also highlighted that if the expenses were paid, he would be entitled to reclaim the note, indicating that there was never an agreement to use the funds for the benefit of the plaintiffs.

In September 1875, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case of Conrad Ross v. Eliza Ross, which originated from the Peoria circuit court. Eliza Ross filed for a divorce from Conrad Ross in March 1871, citing habitual drunkenness and extreme cruelty as grounds for her claim. The divorce was granted during the same term after the defendant’s failure to dispute the allegations. Following the divorce, Conrad Ross challenged provisions regarding alimony and child custody included in the decree. The court ruled that Eliza would have custody of their four children and receive substantial personal and real estate as alimony. The total property value claimed by Eliza encompassed approximately $5,000, consisting of personal property and real estate in Peoria. However, records of the court proceedings are unclear regarding Conrad’s debts and other financial obligations.	Eliza Ross’s claims were centered on obtaining a divorce due to her husband's habitual drunkenness and cruel behavior. She requested alimony that included all of Conrad's personal and real property, along with custody of their four children. The initial decree granted her these demands, allowing her to retain the majority of Conrad's assets.	Conrad Ross contested the alimony awarded to Eliza, arguing that the court had excessively allocated his property to her, which disregarded precedent on reasonable alimony limits. He contended that the decree wrongfully required Eliza to pay his debts and questioned the decision that vested fee ownership of real estate solely to her rather than structuring it as an annual allowance or life estate.

William Ross filed a bill in Chancery in 1847 to challenge the sale of certain tracts of land and town lots that had been sold under an execution favoring defendants Edward Mead and Adriance against James Davis. The sale raised concerns for Ross, who claimed the right to redeem the property since he was a grantee of the defendant in execution. The Circuit Court dismissed Ross's request to set aside the sale, allowing Mead to retain the purchased interest and appointed Commissioners to partition the lands. Upon their determination that the land could not be divided, the court ordered the land to be sold and denied Ross the opportunity to redeem. Ross's subsequent appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court resulted in the case being examined based on two main errors claimed: 1) the lots were purportedly sold en masse rather than separately, and 2) Ross should have been allowed to redeem the property once the partition report indicated non-divisibility.	Ross contended that the sale of the town lots was improper as they were sold en masse rather than as individual parcels, which he argued compromised the value of the properties. He claimed he should have been given the chance to redeem his interest in the property, particularly after the Commission's report confirmed the land could not be divided.	The defendants argued that the properties were sold in separate parcels and that there was no evidence of a fraudulent or prejudicial sale. They maintained that Ross's right to redeem had expired by the time he attempted to redeem, as he had not acted within the legal timeframe after the sale. Consequently, they requested the court to affirm the Circuit Court’s decision dismissing Ross's claims.

The case "Jacob Scheik et al. v. Trustees of Schools" was heard on December 9, 1887, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose following an action taken against the sureties of the School Treasurer's bond. Jacob Scheik and others (the plaintiffs) contested certain financial claims made by the treasurer, Philip Reitz, who had control over school funds. After initially experiencing a reversal of a lower court's judgment by the appellate court, the case was appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court ruled that there was indeed liability on the part of the sureties, prompting a reevaluation of specific claims raised by the appellants against the judgment. The appeal centered on improper amounts included in the judgment against the sureties, questioning charges for commissions and credits for certain financial transactions.	The plaintiffs, Jacob Scheik and others, argued that certain amounts included in the judgment against the sureties were improper. Specifically, they contested a claim of $185.20 for commissions, a $72.50 credit for a McGlashan note, and $616.10 for excess loans. They sought reconsideration of these financial items in the context of the judgment rendered against the defendants.	The defendants, the sureties on the School Treasurer's bond, contended that the amounts charged, particularly the commissions and the failure to credit certain transactions, were unjustified. They argued that the commission claim was an afterthought made just before Reitz relinquished his responsibilities, and they requested that the contested amounts be excluded from the judgment against them.

In May 1886, Anna Welsh, a seven-year-old girl, was injured while playing on the sidewalk of May Street in Illinois. At the time, she and a playmate were engaging in play when a switch-engine operated by the Chicago, St. Louis and Pittsburgh Railroad Company pushed a loaded coal car, causing it to derail and roll onto the sidewalk. The accident resulted in severe injuries to Anna, leading to the amputation of her leg, while her companion was killed instantly. Anna's next friend, Mary Welsh, initiated a lawsuit against the railroad company, claiming negligence. During the trial, the Superior Court ruled in Anna’s favor, awarding her damages. This ruling was subsequently upheld by the Appellate Court, prompting the railroad company to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, represented by her next friend Mary Welsh, argued that the railroad company was negligent in its operation of the switch-engine, which led to the accident that caused her severe injuries. Anna maintained that she was too young at the time to take any precaution for her safety and asserted that her mother had done nothing negligent that would have endangered her. Consequently, the plaintiff sought compensation for the personal injuries sustained.	The Chicago, St. Louis and Pittsburgh Railroad Company defended itself by arguing that the instructions given to the jury were erroneous as they did not sufficiently address the issue of comparative negligence, asserting that the jury should have been made aware of Anna's negligence relative to her injuries. The defendant claimed that the trial court modified their instructions in a way that prejudiced their defense without proper legal justification and therefore requested a reversal of the previous judgments.

C. Aultman & Co. v. R. F. Osborne is a legal case decided on November 23, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose from a transaction involving a separator that C. Aultman & Co. sold to R. F. Osborne, who had executed a promissory note as payment under a warranty concerning the separator's working qualities. After purchasing the separator, Osborne claimed that it did not work as guaranteed, leading to his defense based on the alleged failure of this warranty. Additionally, he sought to offset the amount owed with the value of a second-hand machine that he had traded in as part payment. The case was presided over by Judge James A. Creighton in the Circuit Court of Christian County, which ruled in favor of Osborne and awarded him a verdict of $75.	C. Aultman & Co., the plaintiff, argued that R. F. Osborne was liable for the full payment of the promissory note executed for the separator sold. They claimed that the warranty regarding the separator's working qualities was valid and that Osborne's arguments of failure of warranty were unfounded. Therefore, the plaintiff sought to recover the amount due on the note.	R. F. Osborne, the defendant, contended that the separator did not perform as warranted, citing a failure of warranty as a defense against the plaintiff's claim for payment. Additionally, he filed a plea of set-off, arguing that the value of a second-hand machine he had provided as part of the payment should be deducted from the amount owed under the note. Consequently, he sought to limit his liability based on these arguments.

In the case of John Friberg et al. v. James H. Donovan, the events unfolded in the context of a legal dispute surrounding a promissory note executed in the 1870s. James H. Donovan was involved as a surety for the firm Beisecker & Johnson on a promissory note to Samuel A. Barry. Following a judgment against the firm, which resulted in no service to one of the principal debtors, Beisecker, Barry successfully obtained a judgment against Johnson and Donovan. Johnson appealed this judgment, which the Supreme Court affirmed. Subsequently, Donovan paid the judgment against him to avoid execution against his property. He then filed a bill against John Friberg and Otto Johnson (the sureties on the appeal bond) to be subrogated to Barry's rights. The case was complicated further when Otto Johnson died during the proceedings, necessitating the substitution of his administrator and heirs. The ruling focused on whether Donovan was correctly identified as a surety and the liabilities stemming from the appeal bond.	The plaintiffs, led by James H. Donovan, claimed equitable subrogation to the rights of the original judgment creditor, Samuel A. Barry, after having paid off the judgment against himself and the primary debtor, Johnson. They argued that as Donovan had acted as a surety and subsequently satisfied the judgment, he was entitled to pursue compensation from Friberg and the deceased Johnson’s estate under the appeal bond.	The defendants, John Friberg and the representatives of Otto Johnson, argued that Donovan had not sufficiently alleged his status as a surety and that the original complaint lacked necessary specificity. They claimed further that the insolvency of Johnson made them unnecessary parties to the litigation. Their position was that the legal framework did not support Donovan’s claims against them regarding the appeal bond, and that the case should be dismissed on those grounds.

The case of "The People ex rel. McCracken v. Clovis Soucy" was adjudicated in 1887 in Cahokia, Illinois. The lawsuit arose when Nicholas McCracken, representing the state, accused Clovis Soucy of unlawfully usurping the position of supervisor in Cahokia. The initial ruling in the circuit court to oust Soucy was overturned by the Appellate Court. On re-trial, the circuit court again found against Soucy, who appealed. The core of the dispute centered on the counting of three ballots that were improperly received through the back door of a polling place rather than the designated front window, allegedly due to intimidation tactics employed by McCracken or his supporters. The Appellate Court maintained that the essential facts had not changed since previous hearings and cited that no valid claim of usurpation could be established against Soucy. The Supreme Court of Illinois was tasked with determining the factual disputes and the legality of McCracken's election, particularly focusing on the process and legality of how the votes were cast and counted.	The plaintiff, Nicholas McCracken, argued that Soucy had unlawfully taken the office of supervisor by usurpation, focusing on the handling and legitimacy of the three contested ballots. McCracken sought to establish that these ballots were cast by unqualified voters and requested a judgment to remove Soucy from his position, claiming the election process had been compromised.	Clovis Soucy contended that he had not usurped the office and that the ballots in question were valid. He argued that the circumstances of their casting were due to interference and intimidation from McCracken’s supporters, which prevented qualified voters from casting their votes properly at the designated location. Soucy requested the court to affirm the previous findings that supported his election as legitimate.

In January 1875, the case of Lewis W. Ross v. Chicago, Burlington and Quincy R. R. Co. et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a dispute over a strip of land in Lewistown, Fulton County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Lewis W. Ross, had initiated an action of ejectment against the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company, seeking to recover possession of a right of way over his land that the railroad company had occupied. In response to Ross's action, the railroad company filed a bill in chancery to enjoin these proceedings and demanded specific performance of an earlier agreement in which Ross had pledged to convey the right of way in exchange for consideration. A key aspect of the dispute was the validity of the Peoria and Hannibal Railroad Company's charter, which transferred rights to the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company. The case centered on the legal existence of Peoria and Hannibal Railroad Company based on claims that its charter was invalid, along with whether Ross had valid grounds to rescind his agreement to provide the right of way.	The plaintiff, Lewis W. Ross, argued that the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company lacked the legal right to occupy the land due to alleged irregularities in its charter, claiming to recover possession of the strip of land in question. Additionally, he sought damages for alleged trespass and harm due to the construction of the railway on his property.	The defendants, represented by the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company, contended that Ross, as a stockholder and former director of the Peoria and Hannibal Railroad Company, was bound by his prior commitments and the acceptance of amendments made to the charter. They argued that Ross's objections were superseded by his actions as a director and that he had a duty to notify them of any intention to rescind his agreement before construction took place. Moreover, they claimed that Ross had effectively waived his rights by dismissing previous suits against the company in exchange for benefits.

The case involves Denison F. Holmes as the plaintiff and Nicholas N. Shaver as the defendant, heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. The dispute arose from a chancery bill filed by Holmes to restrain Shaver from pursuing legal action to recover amounts from two promissory notes that Holmes executed in favor of Shaver. The background dates back to 1850 when Henry Smith executed a mortgage on certain land to the trustees of schools. The trustees initiated a foreclosure, leading to a judicial sale, at which Holmes purchased the property. Subsequently, Shaver, having acquired judgments against Smith, redeemed the property from the sheriff and arranged with Holmes to accept promissory notes instead of cash for the purchase price. Holmes later claimed that other parties had initiated legal proceedings that could invalidate the judgments and the sale, arguing this affected the consideration for his notes to Shaver.	Denison F. Holmes contended that the promissory notes executed to Nicholas N. Shaver should not be enforceable since other lien claimants had initiated a lawsuit to invalidate the earlier judgments and judicial sale, suggesting that his agreement lacked consideration. Holmes sought to have the court prevent Shaver from proceeding to collect on the notes, claiming potential inequity in the situation should the prior claims succeed.	Nicholas N. Shaver argued that the terms of the agreement and the execution of the notes were legitimate and that Holmes received what he contracted for during the purchase of the property. Shaver maintained that in the absence of fraud, the court could not relieve Holmes of his obligations under the notes, emphasizing the principle of "caveat emptor" which disallows a purchaser from seeking relief based on the failure of title post-judicial sale.

The case of "Town of Charleston v. William E. McCrory" took place in January 1865 in Charleston, Illinois. The action was initiated by William E. McCrory, who served as the town clerk, claiming that he was owed $61.20 for filing 612 lists of personal property submitted by residents of the town for taxation. The plaintiff argued that this filing was in accordance with an act passed by the Illinois General Assembly in 1853 regarding the assessment of property and collection of taxes. Initially, McCrory won a judgment in a justice court, but this decision was appealed to the Circuit Court where it was reversed in favor of him, thus leading to the plaintiff (the Town of Charleston) pursuing a writ of error to contest this judgment.	The Town of Charleston, as the plaintiff, argued that McCrory's claim for compensation was invalid because the law required property tax lists to be submitted to the county clerk, not the town clerk. Sections of the 1853 act governing taxation did not authorize the town clerk to receive or file the lists, and therefore, the town had no legal obligation to compensate McCrory for his actions in relation to the filing.	McCrory, the defendant in this case, contended that he was entitled to compensation for his role in filing the lists of taxable personal property. He claimed that he had performed a service in accordance with the laws of the state. His defense was likely predicated on the assertion that the lists should have been managed appropriately and that any duty imposed on him should warrant payment, despite the legal argument of authority over the filing process.

Henderson E. Massey filed a case against The Farmers’ National Bank of Virginia concerning a promissory note allegedly executed by him alongside his son, Henry C. Massey, and son-in-law, George W. Laurie. The case took place in the Circuit Court of Sangamon County, Illinois, with the final decision made on March 30, 1885. Initially, the bank sued all three individuals, but the court dismissed the case against Henry C. Massey and Laurie, focusing solely on Henderson E. Massey's responsibility. The bank claimed that the note was for money borrowed by Henry C. Massey, while Henderson denied having executed the note. The case had previously reached the Illinois Supreme Court in 1882, where a judgment was reversed due to improper evidence rulings. Upon retrial, the original judgment against Henderson for $6,439.56 was affirmed, and the case centered around the admissibility of evidence regarding the execution of the note and related transactions.	The Farmers’ National Bank claimed that Henderson E. Massey was liable for the debt stemming from the promissory note executed in connection with a loan made to Henry C. Massey. The bank sought to establish the authenticity of the note and Henderson's obligation to repay the amount owed, despite Henderson's denial of signing the note.	Henderson E. Massey argued that he did not execute the promissory note in question and challenged the admissibility of certain evidence presented by the bank, particularly regarding the questioning of witnesses and the existence of the note itself. He contended that the lower courts made errors in admitting evidence that should have been suppressed and sought to have the earlier judgment reversed.

The case of Samuel C. Wiley v. William Deering et al. was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 16, 1889. It involved a suit by Samuel C. Wiley, a member of the partnership O. J. Wilson & Co., against William Deering for unpaid amounts related to a promissory note executed by the firm. The partnership was specifically formed for operating a blacksmith and repair shop, with capital limited to $500, and its activities were poorly managed as O. J. Wilson and Wiley were preoccupied with other businesses. The firm’s operations included dealing in agricultural implements, a matter that arose when William Wilson, the son of O. J. Wilson, acted as the de facto manager. Despite objections from Wiley and O. J. Wilson, William Wilson facilitated sales and signed notes in the firm’s name, leading to his eventual financial ruin and disappearance. This situation culminated in the suit after a note, prepared by the bank's clerk and signed in the firm name, remained unpaid at maturity, prompting backend claims by Deering for the said debt.	The plaintiff, Samuel C. Wiley, alleged that William Wilson had the authority to bind the partnership for the debt incurred from selling agricultural implements. He contended that the firm, as represented, was responsible for all contracts executed under its name. The request was for payment based on the promissory note signed by the firm's agent, which had not been settled by maturity.	The defendant, Samuel C. Wiley, countered by asserting that William Wilson lacked the necessary authority to bind the partnership for the agricultural transactions due to their internal agreement, which confined the firm’s operations strictly to a commission basis for handling implements. They argued that the relationship and authority amongst partners were not made known to the party suing, and thus, the secret understanding among partners should absolve them from the obligation arising from the note.

The case of *St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad Company v. David Winter* was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1868. The key individuals involved were the St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad Company as the plaintiff and David Winter as the defendant. The case originated from the Circuit Court of Morgan County, presided over by Judge D. M. Woodson. The circumstances of the case mirrored those of a previously decided case, indicating that similar legal questions were at stake. The case focused on a dispute between the railroad company and Winter, although specific details of the events leading to the litigation are not outlined in the provided case description.	The plaintiff, St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad Company, contended that it had a valid claim against David Winter concerning issues similar to another case previously adjudicated. They sought legal redress or a ruling that would affirm their position regarding the matters at hand.	The defendant, David Winter, likely presented arguments in opposition to the plaintiff's claims, although the specific defenses are not detailed in the description. The defense would generally involve rebuttals to the plaintiff's allegations and possibly raises counterclaims or challenges to the jurisdiction or appropriateness of the complaint based on the similarities to the preceding case.

On January 1, 1876, in Illinois, the legal case "Jerome B. Massey v. William S. Hardin" arose from a dispute concerning a chattel mortgage agreement. The plaintiff, Jerome B. Massey, sought to recover two promissory notes of $956.25 and $5.25, along with an account for $22.30, all owed by the defendant, William S. Hardin. The mortgage was executed by Hardin on May 9, 1874, to secure the payment of the principal note. A sale of the mortgaged property, including livestock and equipment, took place at Massey’s request, with Hardin acquiring the items to continue the mortgage arrangement. Discrepancies emerged regarding ownership of the property and whether the mortgage debt was satisfied. After a jury trial, a verdict favored Hardin with an award of $203.25, leading Massey to appeal by claiming the verdict was inconsistent with the evidence presented.	Jerome B. Massey claimed that he was owed payment on the notes and the account for services rendered, arguing that the sale of the mortgaged property did not legally extinguish the debt. He contended that although Hardin purchased the property, it was merely a pretext to maintain ownership and did not resolve the mortgage obligation.	William S. Hardin defended against the claims by asserting that the property sale satisfied the debt according to the chattel mortgage terms. He pleaded non-assumpsit, payment, accord and satisfaction, and set-off, expressing that he was not liable for the amounts Massey claimed, as the sale completed the obligation under the mortgage.

On June 23, 1882, in Joliet, Illinois, Michael Meaghan was injured while walking on a sidewalk maintained by the City of Joliet. The plaintiff alleged that the city allowed the sidewalk to remain in a dangerous condition, with broken and loose planks. As Meaghan passed over the sidewalk, he stumbled on a loose plank, resulting in significant injuries to his right knee. He filed a lawsuit claiming damages due to the city's negligence in keeping the sidewalk safe. The case involved three counts of negligence against the city, asserting that the municipality had control and knowledge of the defective sidewalk prior to the incident. The City of Joliet denied these claims, leading to a trial where the jury found in favor of Meaghan, awarding him $400 in damages. The city appealed the decision, arguing that the verdict was contrary to the evidence and the law.	The plaintiff, Michael Meaghan, argued that the City of Joliet was negligent in its duty to maintain the sidewalk safely. He claimed that the city had control over the sidewalk and was aware of its hazardous condition due to loose planks. Meaghan requested damages for the injuries sustained from tripping over the loose plank while walking on the sidewalk, asserting that he was exercising ordinary care at the time of the incident.	The City of Joliet contended that it should not be held liable for the injuries sustained by Meaghan. The defense asserted that the municipality had exercised reasonable diligence in maintaining the sidewalk and argued that there was no evidence of actual or constructive notice of the dangerous condition. They claimed that the sidewalk had been well-constructed and that any loose boards were promptly addressed. The city requested the court to overturn the verdict based on the alleged insufficiency of evidence to support the plaintiff's claims.

The case of "The Fort Clark Horse Railway Company v. James F. Anderson" took place in Peoria, Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 20, 1883. The Fort Clark Horse Railway Company (the plaintiff) operated a street railroad, running multiple cars frequently along specific streets in the city. The defendant, James F. Anderson, a house-mover, threatened to move a large house along the railway's track, which would temporarily hinder the operation of the railway for several days. The plaintiff filed for an injunction to prevent Anderson from moving the house lengthwise on the track, claiming that while the interruption would be short-term and cause limited financial damage, it posed a continuous threat to their business operations and the public's access to transportation. The circuit court dismissed the plaintiff's request, stating that adequate legal remedies existed for the alleged harm, which prompted the plaintiff to appeal to the Appellate Court and subsequently the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff's main arguments centered around the need for an injunction to prevent the defendant from obstructing their railway operations by moving a house along the track. They argued that while individual interruptions might be temporary, the defendant's potential for future hindrances could cause irreparable harm to their franchise and inconvenience to thousands of passengers. The plaintiff sought not just a temporary stop to the specific act but a perpetual injunction against any similar future actions during operational hours.	The defendant contended that the plaintiff had a complete legal remedy available should any actual damages arise from their actions. He argued that the moving of the house was a rare occurrence and not likely to repeat in the future, meaning the potential harm was not sufficiently severe to warrant equitable relief. The defendant claimed he merely exercised a right to use public streets for his business, and any interruption would be temporary, for which the plaintiff could seek damages in court rather than through an injunction.

On August 12, 1887, J. H. Randolph filed a bill in chancery against Drew Inman seeking to settle a partnership dispute. The case took place in DeWitt County, Illinois. Randolph claimed that a partnership existed between him and Inman, which was formed on March 1, 1878, and dissolved on March 4, 1879. Randolph contended that although more than five years had elapsed since the dissolution, Inman had promised to settle outstanding partnership matters within that timeframe. Inman's response asserted that the partnership had been dissolved in 1879 and that any claims Randolph had were barred by the statute of limitations. The court's findings concluded that the partnership was officially dissolved on March 4, 1879, and supported Inman’s defense regarding the statute of limitations. However, it was acknowledged that there were unresolved matters that Inman had been attempting to address, leading to an evaluation of whether the delay in filing the bill was justified and should prevent relief.	Randolph argued that he sought an accounting and settlement of the partnership's affairs, believing that unresolved business existed between him and Inman despite the time elapsed since the partnership's dissolution. He maintained that Inman had acknowledged these unsettled matters and had promised to resolve them within five years prior to filing the bill.	Inman’s principal defense was that the partnership had ceased operations since March 4, 1879, and that Randolph's claims were barred by the statute of limitations, as they exceeded the five-year period following the dissolution. Additionally, Inman argued that he had not been in a partnership with Randolph since that date, and that sufficient time had elapsed without any valid claims being raised that would necessitate a legal accounting.

The case of The Cairo And Vincennes Railroad Company v. James Fackney took place in 1875 and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in the Lawrence Circuit Court, where James Fackney, the defendant in error, brought an action of assumpsit against the Cairo and Vincennes Railroad Company. The lawsuit was over a claim for goods sold and delivered to the railroad, which included supplies necessary for operating the railroad and for the sustenance of its employees. Fackney claimed a statutory lien on the railroad's property, arguing that specific supplies and labor were provided under a contractual agreement. He maintained that he had taken over various certificates from the railroad that owed money to employees and had received powers of attorney to collect the debts owed for labor on the construction of the road. The circuit court ruled in Fackney's favor, leading the Railroad Company to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, James Fackney, claimed that he was entitled to a lien on all the property of the Cairo and Vincennes Railroad Company due to the goods and supplies he provided. Fackney argued that he had advanced money to settle debts for supplies and labor on behalf of the railroad based on an agreement and insisted that the statute provided him a right to a lien due to the nature of the services rendered.	The defendant, Cairo and Vincennes Railroad Company, contended that the lien Fackney sought was not assignable under the statute as it applied only to materials used and labor performed in connection with the railroad’s operations. The company argued that Fackney was essentially loaning money to be used for paying their debts rather than supplying goods or services directly related to the construction or operation of the railroad, and therefore no lien could be established. They requested that the lien declared by the lower court be deemed erroneous.

Balthaser Schneider passed away in 1884, leaving behind a will that included a legacy of $1,000 to Catharine Kundert. Rudolph Graffenreid was appointed as the executor of Schneider's estate. In January 1885, Graffenreid transferred a certificate of deposit, valued at $1,800 and due three years later, to Kundert and received $800 in cash in return, along with her receipt for the legacy amount. However, the bank associated with the certificate failed shortly thereafter. Kundert initiated a lawsuit against Graffenreid (later against his estate) to recover the $800 she paid. The court had previously ruled that the transfer of the certificate was void, indicating Graffenreid acted without legal authority as executor, and thus Kundert had no valid claim against Schneider’s estate. The key figures involved were Susannah V. Graffenreid (as executrix of Rudolph Graffenreid’s estate) and Catharine Kundert. The case took place in Madison County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on June 15, 1889.	The plaintiff, Catharine Kundert, claimed that she was entitled to recover the $800 paid to Graffenreid on the basis that he assured her it would be safe. She argued that because Graffenreid acted outside the authority given to him as an executor, she should be allowed to reclaim the funds, despite the prior court ruling concerning the nullity of the transfer of the certificate.	Rudolph Graffenreid (now represented by his estate) argued that the transaction was valid at the time and contested Kundert's claim on the grounds that she had already accepted the certificate. The defense maintained that the earlier judgment absolved Graffenreid of liability for the funds Kundert sought to reclaim, asserting that the agreement did not bind Schneider’s estate.

The case "Strong et al. v. Allen" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. It arose in Illinois, following the filing of a writ of error. The central issue in the case was the failure to file the transcript of the record within the specific timeline required by the court's rules. The plaintiff, represented by Strong and others, challenged the defendant Allen, who sought to have the court dismiss the case due to this omission. The court encountered the motion to dismiss presented by the defendant after the second day of the term when it became evident that the necessary documentation had not been provided in time. The court took into consideration the procedural aspects surrounding the writ of error and the evidence relating to filing obligations under Rule 75 of their regulations.	The plaintiffs contended that the omission to file the transcript within the first two days was not sufficient grounds to dismiss the writ of error. They implied that procedural errors should not impede the judicial process, reinforcing the principle that a failure to meet timelines should not automatically detract from the merits of the case.	The defendant's main argument rested on the assertion that the plaintiffs' failure to submit the transcript of the record in a timely manner warranted dismissal of the writ of error. The defense sought to have the case dismissed, arguing that adherence to procedural rules is crucial for maintaining proper legal proceedings.

Clarissa Filkins filed a legal case against Harry Byrne in January 1874 in Cook County, Illinois. The case was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court, presided over by Judge Henry Booth in the Circuit Court. The central issue revolved around procedural matters regarding the service of process and the requirement for an affidavit of merits in pleadings. The plaintiff, Filkins, had taken action against the defendant, Byrne, claiming relief based upon contractual obligations. The court assessed whether the defect in process service could be raised as an argument after the defendant had entered an appearance and pled the general issue, which traditionally waives such objections. Notably, the court referenced prior legal precedents and statutory requirements that necessitated an affidavit in cases concerning money.	Filkins argued that the defendant's plea was invalid due to failures in adherence to the legal requirements of the service process and the absence of the necessary affidavit of merits accompanying the plea. She contended that these defects warranted the court's intervention, seeking to have the defendant's plea struck from the record based on these procedural issues.	Byrne countered the claims by asserting that by appearing and pleading in bar, he waived any defects related to the service of process. He argued that the court did not err in proceeding with the case despite these objections, noting that the plaintiff's assertion regarding the striking of his plea was unfounded, as he believed his actions conformed to the law governing court practices in Illinois.

Nicholas Spannagle initiated a legal case against the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company regarding personal injuries he sustained while attempting to board a train at the Mitchell station. This incident occurred in St. Clair County, Illinois, in 1889. Spannagle claimed he was injured due to the train's failure to remain at the depot platform long enough for passengers to board. Evidence presented revealed that the station was equipped with a waiting room for passengers and an agent was present at the depot. Spannagle had previously purchased a round-trip ticket but did not indicate his intention to board this specific train, nor did he utilize the facilities provided at the station to wait for it. On the day of the incident, he was located at a saloon approximately 200-300 feet away and, upon hearing the train, rushed to the depot only to attempt boarding while the train was in motion, resulting in his injury. The court found that he had not established a contractual relationship as a passenger and acted with gross negligence in his attempt to board.	Spannagle's main argument was that he suffered injuries because the train did not stop long enough at the depot for him to board safely. He sought damages for his injuries, claiming that he had purchased a round-trip ticket and expected to board the train without difficulty. He contended that the railroad company had a duty to allow adequate time for passengers to board.	The railroad company contended that no duty was owed to Spannagle since he had not made known his intention to board the train, nor did he use the designated facilities to wait. They argued that merely purchasing a ticket did not establish a carrier-passenger relationship for this specific train since Spannagle did not give notice to the company of his intention to board. They characterized his attempt to board a moving train as gross negligence and asserted that the plaintiff's actions negated any claims for damages.

Elsa Bannerman, the plaintiff, and her husband were traveling on a Chicago & Northwestern Railway train in 1884, heading from Evanston, Illinois, to Crystal Falls, Michigan. The couple presented a special 1,000-mile commutation ticket issued to “Mr. E. Bannerman.” The train conductor refused to accept the ticket for Elsa's fare since it was designated for a male and demanded that she either pay her fare or leave the train. Mr. Bannerman declined to pay for her fare, leading to Elsa being expelled from the train at Waukegan, Illinois. During the incident, no excessive force was used, and there were no claims of physical injury. The couple claimed they understood the ticket's non-transferable nature and conditions. The case focused on the validity of the ticket and whether the conductor acted appropriately under the circumstances.	The plaintiff, Elsa Bannerman, claimed that her expulsion from the train was wrongful. She argued that the conductor should have honored the ticket despite it being issued to "Mr. E. Bannerman," as her husband indicated that it was meant for her. She sought damages for the indignity and distress caused by the expulsion.	The defendant, Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company, argued that the conductor acted within his rights in refusing to accept the non-transferable ticket under the given circumstances. They maintained that the ticket, being specifically issued to a male, justified the conductor's actions, and the expulsion was necessary since neither the plaintiff nor her husband offered to pay the fare. They requested that the court dismiss the plaintiff's claims based on these grounds.

On September 10, 1873, Meredith Cooper executed a note for $2,000, payable to Abraham McNeill and Samuel T. Henry after twelve months, with a ten percent interest rate, secured by a deed of trust. Cooper and McNeill had been partners in a live stock business, where they borrowed money, resulting in liabilities to a bank. At the time of the note, the firm owed the bank $72.69, which Cooper covered, along with a prior note totaling $1,149.10, partially paid by McNeill. The lawsuit arose when Cooper sought an accounting of their partnership, contending that the $2,000 note was meant to indemnify McNeill for what Cooper owed him and any future liabilities. Subsequently, the note was assigned to a third party, Yocum, who sought to foreclose the deed of trust. The court’s master found that Cooper owed McNeill $687.09 as of January 12, 1876, and added interest, leading to a foreclosure judgment favoring Yocum for $1,193.79. Cooper appealed, contesting certain disputed amounts.	Meredith Cooper claimed that the original accounting by the master failed to consider certain payments he made that should reduce his indebtedness. Specifically, he argued he should have been credited for a loan payment of $300 and denied the charge of a check for $182.32 that was unrelated to the partnership. He also objected to the high interest rate of ten percent being applied to his outstanding balance, advocating for a lower standard rate of six percent as more equitable.	Abraham McNeill contended that Cooper’s obligations were accurately represented in the master's report, asserting he had no liability for the contested payments. McNeill argued that the interest rate applied was justified based on the agreement tied to the original note of $2,000, claiming this interest should be upheld as Cooper had a duty to settle their accounts fairly after a lengthy delay.

In the case of William P. Corbin v. The People of the State of Illinois, the incident took place in Moultrie County, Illinois, around May 6, 1888. William P. Corbin was charged with the murder of Charles T. Harris. After a trial at the April term of 1888, the jury found Corbin guilty of murder, sentencing him to fifteen years in prison. Prior to the trial, Corbin requested a continuance, citing the absence of key witnesses whose testimonies were crucial to his defense. He claimed that witnesses had been subpoenaed but failed to appear, and provided affidavits from others, including a critical witness residing in Indiana, who was unable to leave home due to family illness. Corbin maintained that there was a conflict in witness accounts regarding who was the initial assailant in the altercation that led to Harris’s death, suggesting he was attacked first.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, contended that Corbin was guilty of murder, arguing that he was the assailant in the incident that resulted in Harris's death. The state sought a conviction based on evidence presented during the trial, which indicated Corbin acted without justification.	Corbin's defense centered on the argument that he was not the aggressor in the fatal altercation. He maintained that he had exercised diligence to procure the attendance of his witnesses, who would corroborate his account that Harris had attacked him first, throwing bricks and firing shots at him before he responded. Corbin's legal team requested a continuance of the trial due to the absence of critical witnesses, asserting their testimonies were essential for a fair trial.

In the case of Virgil A. Bogue v. Chester K. Williams, which was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868, the dispute centered around land ownership and possession rights dating back to the early 1840s. Chester K. Williams, the defendant, had purchased the land in question from Horatio Wales in October 1840. Following this, Williams maintained possession of the property until he was dispossessed by a writ of possession during a legal ejectment process. The facts revealed that while Kellogg had entered the land under a preemption agreement, he had also recognized Bogue’s rights and had sought financial assistance from him to secure the land from the government, which required a payment of $25.
