The key issue arose when a judgment was rendered against Kellogg and others in March 1841, followed by a sheriff's sale that eventually led to the land being conveyed to Williams. The court had to examine whether Bogue's claims to the property had any valid legal standing, especially considering the judgment lien that attached once Kellogg entered the land. Ultimately, the case revolved around the complex interplay of property rights, notice to creditors, and equitable interests, as Bogue attempted to assert his claim despite not being in possession of the land at the time of the judgment lien.	Virgil A. Bogue, the plaintiff, claimed that he had an equitable interest in the land based on his financial contribution to the purchase under Kellogg’s preemption. Bogue contended that he had the right to the land since he had made payments to Kellogg and had an agreement for the conveyance of the land from Kellogg. He argued that when the sheriff's sale occurred, his equities should have been protected by his prior financial arrangement, despite his lack of physical possession.	Chester K. Williams, the defendant, argued that he had purchased the land legally and held the rightful title based on a sheriff's deed following a judgment against Kellogg. He maintained that Bogue’s claims were invalid since Bogue was not in possession of the land and that the judgment lien had attached at the moment of Kellogg’s entry. Williams contended that Bogue lacked any recorded interest or credible notice to legally challenge the sale, emphasizing that the chain of ownership was properly executed through the sheriff's sale.

On February 21, 1883, a fatal accident occurred involving a hand car operated by section workers of the Chicago & Eastern Illinois Railroad near Wellington, Illinois. Barbara McKnight, along with several section men including James McDonald and Thomas Connors, was traveling on the hand car when it collided with a construction train that was backing without adequate warning signals. The construction train, guided by road master James Sevan, had a small red light that was reportedly insufficient for visibility in the dark. McKnight and McDonald were killed instantly in the collision. The plaintiff, Thomas McKnight as administrator, brought this suit asserting wrongful death, accusing the railroad of negligence in operating the train recklessly and without sufficient signaling. Key individuals included the railroad section men, the road master, and the plaintiff representing the deceased. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court, where it was determined that the deceased was not trespassing but was riding with permission, thus complicating the liability issues surrounding the accident.	The plaintiff claimed that the railroad company acted negligently by operating the construction train recklessly while backing without any significant light, which led to the collision and wrongful death of Barbara McKnight. The plaintiff requested damages for the injuries sustained and emphasized that at the time of the incident, the deceased was exercising due care while traveling on the hand car.	The defendant contended that the deceased was effectively a trespasser and was partly or wholly responsible for the accident due to her own negligence. They argued that she was aware that trains could approach at any moment and failed to take necessary precautions after seeing the train's light, which indicated an oncoming train. The defense claimed that the railroad's statutory obligations regarding signaling were irrelevant because the injury occurred on the railroad track and not at a crossing, hence should not constitute grounds for recovery.

In January 1862, in the state of Illinois, Henry McHenry (the plaintiff) entered a legal dispute against Elizabeth Yokum and Jesse Yokum, the administrators of the estate of the deceased Mathias Yokum (the defendants). The case arose from a note made out for $1,485.40, which Mathias Yokum signed, promising to pay Henry McHenry this amount with interest, as consideration for a piece of land conveyed to him by McHenry under a full warranty deed. Subsequently, it was revealed that a widow, Mrs. Penny, had a dower interest in the land, which had been recognized by a court and assigned a value of $350, with an annual worth of $120. The defendants argued that the existence of Mrs. Penny's dower right constituted a partial failure of consideration for the note, as Mathias Yokum did not receive the full value of what he paid for the land. The case progressed from the probate court, where McHenry was initially awarded judgment, to the Circuit Court, where the defendants maintained their claims regarding the offset against the note due to the dower interest.	Henry McHenry argued that the note was valid and should be paid in full despite the claims regarding the dower interest. He insisted that the court was mistaken in allowing the defendants to use the dower interest as a basis to reduce the amount owed. McHenry contended that it would be impossible to compute the exact financial impact of the dower claim on the value of the note and sought the court's affirmation of his original judgment amount.	Elizabeth and Jesse Yokum defended the claim by asserting that the dower interest represented a significant reduction in the value of the land sold to Mathias Yokum and, consequently, the consideration for the note. They argued that since Mathias Yokum did not receive the full value for the land due to the dower, the obligation to pay the note should be diminished accordingly. They requested that the court consider this offset in their decision regarding the enforcement of the note.

In 1874, a legal case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, involving Thomas Bates and defendants Owen Ball et al. The case stemmed from an action of trover regarding the alleged conversion of a promissory note belonging to Bates. Bates accused the defendants of inducing him to assign the note to John McVey, a co-defendant, while he was under arrest. He claimed that his assignment was made under duress, executed while he faced arrest through a capias ad respondendum, without any consideration, thus coercing him into the agreement to regain his freedom. The defendants denied these claims, asserting that Bates was not arrested under the capias but under a different procedure unrelated to the transaction in question. The circuit court tried the case, and a jury found the defendants not guilty, leading to further review by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Thomas Bates, claimed that his assignment of the promissory note to John McVey was forced under duress while he was being unlawfully detained by the defendants. He argued that the assignment occurred without any legitimate consideration and was done solely to secure his release from wrongful arrest. Bates sought the return of the note and compensation for its alleged conversion.	The defendants contended that Bates was not arrested under the capias as he claimed; rather, he was arrested under a bail piece, unrelated to the issues at hand. They presented evidence stating that Bates was coherent during the transaction and that the assignment was not procured through fraud or duress. The defendants also asserted that any drunkenness Bates experienced did not impair his ability to contract, arguing that he had sufficient mental faculties when the assignment occurred.

On November 12, 1863, William Brownfield and several heirs of John Brownfield filed a bill in chancery in the Champaign Circuit Court against Thomas and Milton Brownfield to contest the validity of John Brownfield's last will, executed before his death on July 6, 1863. The plaintiffs claimed the will was procured through fraud and undue influence exerted by Thomas, the youngest son of the deceased, who received the majority of John’s estate. They argued that John Brownfield, in his last illness, was not competent to execute the will and had expressed the desire to destroy it, requesting Thomas to burn it, which he failed to do. The defendants, Thomas and Milton, admitted the will's existence but denied any wrongdoing, contending that the will was duly executed and reflected the testator's rightful intentions. A jury trial found in favor of the defendants, leading to a bill dismissal by the court. The plaintiffs subsequently sought to reverse the decree, asserting errors in the trial's management, specifically concerning the admissibility of certain evidence and the jury's instructions.	The plaintiffs contended that the will was invalid due to fraud and undue influence from Thomas Brownfield. They alleged that Thomas prevented the testator from destroying the will during his illness and that John Brownfield lacked the mental capacity to create a valid will at that time. They sought a decree to nullify the will and distribute the estate according to intestate succession laws.	The defense maintained that the will was legally executed and that John Brownfield was fully competent in making testamentary decisions. Thomas denied the accusations of fraud or undue influence, arguing that his father had entrusted him with the will before his illness. They asserted that the plaintiffs failed to present sufficient evidence to prove their claims and that the jury's verdict supported the validity of the will, which they believed should stand.

M. M. Thompson et al. v. J. F. Duff is a legal case that took place in 1885 in Jackson County, Illinois. The case reached the Illinois Appellate Court and involved a dispute between the appellants, M. M. Thompson and others, and the appellee, J. F. Duff. The main judicial figure in the case was Judge O. A. Habiceb, who presided over the Circuit Court. The case revolved around certain alleged errors in the initial court proceedings, particularly concerning the evidence and jury instructions. The appellants contended that the verdict rendered was against the evidence presented, which they believed warranted a different judgment. They also raised concerns about the refusal of the trial court to provide what they considered proper instructions to the jury. However, the procedural requirements regarding the submission of a bill of exceptions were not met, as the bill in question was neither signed nor sealed by the presiding judge, making it invalid for review. Therefore, the higher court was unable to evaluate the claims regarding errors in the original ruling.	The plaintiffs, M. M. Thompson and others, argued that the trial court's verdict was against the evidence presented in the initial proceedings. They requested that the appellate court review the case on these grounds, as well as challenge the court’s refusal to give proper jury instructions that they argued were pertinent to their case.	The defendant, J. F. Duff, contended that the appeal should not be considered since the bill of exceptions, which the plaintiffs relied upon to support their claims, was not in compliance with legal requirements. The defendant requested the court to dismiss the appeal on procedural grounds, asserting that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate any reversible errors in the trial court's judgment.

This case, "Clarissa A. Klock et al. v. Ellen Walter," took place in Illinois and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873. The conflict arose from a transaction involving the sale of property affected by mortgages. Clarissa A. Klock, the plaintiff, had a complicated arrangement involving a property that was encumbered by both a senior mortgage, held by the city, and a junior mortgage, held by a third party, Peacock. Initially, her associate, McCollum, was to assist in paying off the mortgages and bid on the property during a master sale for $6,000, under the agreement that she would ultimately repay him once she sold the property at a profit. Despite difficulties in raising the required funds, Klock maintained primary responsibility for covering all costs associated with the transaction, including paying Peacock’s mortgage. McCollum’s role was to hold the legal title until Klock could reimburse him, establishing a trust in her favor. When Klock's agent attempted to finalize the purchase, there was a shortfall in covering the total costs, which Klock's agent covered personally but charged back to Klock. Ultimately, Klock demonstrated that she had paid all costs and established a clear equity in the property, which formed the basis of her claims against the heirs of McCollum, who now sought to assert title to the property.	The plaintiff, Clarissa A. Klock, argued that the arrangement regarding the property constituted a mortgage rather than an outright sale, asserting that she had paid the full amount necessary to cover the purchase price and both mortgages. Klock maintained that McCollum never contributed any funds of his own for the property and that all payments made were ultimately her responsibility. Therefore, she requested that the court enforce the equitable interest she had in the property, given that she had paid the purchase money and that McCollum had disclaimed any claim to it.	The defendant's (the heirs of McCollum) main argument centered on the assertion that McCollum was the legal owner of the property following the master sale, thus having a rightful claim to the title. They contended that Klock did not have the standing to seek a conveyance of the property as McCollum's heirs were entitled to inherit his interests, regardless of the agreements made between Klock and McCollum.

In the case of Stephen W. Rawson v. Meckie L. Rawson, filed on September 29, 1886, in Cook County, Illinois, the parties were married on March 1, 1886. The couple lived together until June 23, 1886, when they separated. Meckie Rawson (the plaintiff) claimed that she was living apart from her husband without fault. She sought a decree for separate maintenance and requested solicitors' fees and suit money to proceed with her case. Stephen Rawson (the defendant) responded by denying her allegations and asserting that the separation was due to her misconduct. The court had to address issues surrounding her financial needs and the grounds for her lawsuit, leading to extensive testimonies and evidence presented during the hearings. The defendant aimed to prove that the plaintiff had sufficient separate property, rendering her requests unnecessary and that she had engaged in adultery, which further complicated the case.	Meckie Rawson claimed that she was entitled to a separate maintenance decree as she was living apart from her husband due to no fault of her own. She sought financial assistance from her husband to cover legal costs for prosecuting the case, arguing that she lacked sufficient funds to do so independently.	Stephen Rawson denied the claims made by his wife, asserting that she was responsible for the separation due to her own gross misconduct, including allegations of adultery. He argued that she possessed enough personal assets to support her legal endeavors, and therefore, requests for solicitors' fees and temporary alimony should be denied.

In 1874, in Bureau County, Illinois, a legal case arose between Andrew Gosse and Cyprian Jones regarding an alleged parol contract for the sale of a piece of land. The plaintiff, Gosse, claimed that Jones had agreed to sell him a lot, while Jones was not inclined to recognize this agreement. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, where Mr. Justice Breese delivered the opinion. The court stated that, under the laws governing such transactions, proof of the contract must be clear and satisfactory. Throughout the proceedings, it was highlighted that the evidence for the existence of the alleged contract was vague and uncertain. Key facts included the prolonged use of the lot by Jones without payment of rent or taxes, suggesting no formal agreement existed. Discrepancies arose regarding the alleged payment for the lot, with conflicting testimonies about whether the exchange involved butcher’s meat. The court examined the evidence presented and concluded that it did not support the existence of a valid sale between the parties.	The plaintiff, Andrew Gosse, claimed that Cyprian Jones had entered into a parol contract for the sale of a lot of land. Gosse sought court intervention to compel the specific performance of this alleged agreement, arguing that he had relied upon the terms and that a sale had been made. His legal request was to have the court enforce the specific performance of the land sale contract.	The defendant, Cyprian Jones, provided a robust defense against the claims, asserting that there was no evidence of a valid contract for the sale of the lot. Jones argued that he had not received payment for the land and that the prolonged non-payment of taxes by Gosse further suggested no sale took place. He emphasized that the law's requirement for clear proof of such contracts was not met and invoked the Statute of Frauds to protect his ownership interest in the property.

The case "Thomas L. Morgan et al. v. Henry D. Corlies" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1876. It originated from the Circuit Court of Champaign County. The key individuals involved were Thomas L. Morgan and others as plaintiffs, and Henry D. Corlies as the defendant. The legal dispute arose concerning a partnership and an unresolved account between the parties. The court proceedings underwent several changes in judges and jurisdiction, leading to various decisions about whether certain pleas and orders were appropriate. A notable decree from March 1874 acknowledged the existence of a partnership and ordered a reference to a master in chancery to state the account. In a subsequent ruling, the court declared certain conveyances fraudulent and set them aside, ultimately finding that Thomas L. Morgan owed Henry D. Corlies $3,900, which was to be paid within ninety days.	The plaintiffs, led by Thomas L. Morgan, claimed that there was an unsettled partnership account with Henry D. Corlies. They sought a decree to confirm the existence of the partnership and to resolve the financial matters at hand, including the determination of the amounts owed.	The defendant, Henry D. Corlies, argued against the proceedings citing various errors, including the validity of having a judge from another circuit preside over the trial and objecting to a plea concerning another pending suit. He contended that certain evidence, such as depositions, should not have been admitted but failed to object during the trial, thus weakening his position.

The case "The Howe Machine Company v. John B. Willie" took place in June 1877 in St. Clair County, Illinois, focusing on a dispute between John B. Willie (the plaintiff) and The Howe Machine Company (the defendant). Willie purchased a sewing machine intended for his niece who resided in St. Louis. Although the agreement was structured as a lease, the actual transaction was an installment sale. The plaintiff argued that the company sent the wrong machine, which was also defective and failed to function properly despite multiple repairs. After being repeatedly assured by the company's agents that a replacement machine would be provided, the plaintiff ceased payments when no replacement was offered. The defendant then replevied the machine, claiming a breach of contract due to non-payment. The situation led the plaintiff to seek rescission of the contract and recovery of payments made.	The plaintiff, John B. Willie, claimed that The Howe Machine Company breached their agreement by sending a defective sewing machine instead of the one promised. He argued that the repeated assurances from the company's agents to replace the faulty machine created an obligation that the company failed to fulfill. As a result of the unsatisfactory performance of the machine and the defendant's failure to provide a replacement, he sought to rescind the contract and recover the payments he had made for the machine.	The Howe Machine Company contended that Willie breached the contract by stopping payments on the machine. They asserted that the contract, as understood by the parties, allowed for replevining the machine due to non-payment. The company argued that since the machine was sent as agreed and that repairs had been attempted, the claims made by the plaintiff regarding the company's obligations were unfounded.

The case, "The Peoria and Rock Island Railway Company v. George McClenahan," took place in September 1874 in Illinois. The plaintiff, George McClenahan, initiated legal action after a cow and her calf were killed on the railway track of the Peoria and Rock Island Railway Company. The case began before a justice of the peace, where McClenahan sought to recover damages for the loss of his animals. The dispute was then escalated to the Circuit Court of Stark County. The court's decision exceeded McClenahan's initial claim of $50, awarding him $56.50 instead. A significant point of contention was whether the railway company had a duty to keep excavations near the track free from water and ice, which allegedly prevented the cow's escape, leading to its death. The court ultimately identified two legal errors in the judgment rendered at the circuit court.	McClenahan's main argument centered on the assertion that the Peoria and Rock Island Railway Company was liable for the death of his cow and calf due to their negligence. He argued that the railway company's excavations filled with water and froze, creating a barrier that prevented the cow from escaping the track when the train approached, thus causing her death. He sought damages reflecting the value of the cow and calf killed.	The Peoria and Rock Island Railway Company contended that they were not legally required to maintain the excavations along their track in a condition free of water or ice. The railway company's defense argued that holding them accountable for the cow's death due to conditions they could not reasonably control was unjust and not backed by legal precedent. Therefore, they called for a reversal of the judgment based on errors identified in the circuit court's decision.

In September 1867, in the city of Chicago, Illinois, William Linton initiated a legal case for the benefit of Benjamin F. Quimby against the City of Chicago. This case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County, where it was presided over by Judge E. S. Williams. The primary issue under consideration was the city's liability concerning the process of garnishment. The court examined this question in light of a prior case, Merwin v. The City of Chicago, and reached a decision regarding the city's obligations in such financial matters.	The plaintiff, William Linton, argued that the City of Chicago was liable for garnishment, seeking recognition of this liability in the legal proceedings for the benefit of Benjamin F. Quimby. Essentially, Linton's claims revolved around the assertion that the city should be held responsible according to the garnishment process in favor of Quimby.	The City of Chicago, represented by attorney S. A. Irwin, contended that it should not be held liable for the garnishment process as argued by the plaintiff. The defendant's core assertion centered on the principle established in the earlier case of Merwin v. The City of Chicago, which supported their stance of non-liability.

The legal case of "Lamping Bros. v. William Payne" took place in September 1874 in Rock Island County, Illinois. The case arose when Lamping Bros. (the plaintiffs) initiated a replevin action against William Payne (the defendant), who was serving as the county sheriff at the time. The dispute centered around certain goods that were allegedly in the possession of Payne, which the plaintiffs claimed were theirs. Payne contended that, as sheriff, he had taken possession of these goods based on two valid executions issued by the circuit court, related to debts owed by one Michael J. Murphy. The plaintiffs questioned the validity of Payne's actions and the claims he made regarding the ownership of the goods, leading to legal proceedings that prompted a thorough examination of the execution process and rights to property in this context.	Lamping Bros. argued that the goods in question were rightfully theirs and that Payne's actions as the sheriff were unjustified. They contended that the execution upon which Payne acted was void and therefore could not support his possession of the goods. The plaintiffs sought the return of their property and challenged the legitimacy of the defense presented by Payne, aiming for a judgment that affirmed their ownership rights.	William Payne defended himself by asserting that the goods were not owned by Lamping Bros. but rather belonged to Michael J. Murphy at the time he levied them as sheriff. He stated that the executions issued by the court were valid and were properly followed in seizing the goods as part of his official duties. Payne's key argument was that, since the plaintiffs confessed by a general demurrer that the goods were not theirs, the action could not be maintained, regardless of any specific claims about the executions or the ownership rights involved.

In September 1872, Edmund D. Taylor leased a property in Chicago to John W. Bailey for his wholesale tea business. Prior to this, Taylor owned a double building that was destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. The building was rebuilt and included a shared water system. On March 28, 1873, a water pipe burst in the building's second story due to freezing, resulting in damage to Bailey's tea stock. As per the lease, Bailey was responsible for maintaining the premises and had access to a mechanism for turning off the water to prevent such occurrences. Despite this, Bailey pursued legal action seeking recovery for the damages. A jury trial in Cook County resulted in a judgment favoring Bailey for $1,471.75. Taylor appealed, contesting the ruling based on lease terms and the alleged negligence of the tenant.	Bailey argued that Taylor, as the landlord, was responsible for the damages caused by the leakage from the burst water pipe. He claimed negligence on Taylor's part for failing to ensure the water system was adequately maintained and safe. Bailey sought compensation for the cost of the damaged tea stock, which he attributed to the landlord's oversight.	Taylor contended that the damages were a direct result of Bailey's own negligence. He pointed out that Bailey had access to a mechanism for shutting off the water and was obligated by the lease to maintain the property in good condition. Furthermore, the lease specifically exempted Taylor from responsibility for any damages incurred due to leakage, including from the pipes located in areas retained under Bailey's control. Taylor argued that the lease's provisions clearly indicated that he should not be held liable for the damages suffered by Bailey.

In 1889, in the village of Oakland, Illinois, S. G. Cash, who served as the village constable, was involved in an incident where he arrested William F. Gwinn for allegedly violating a village ordinance. Gwinn was accused of being intoxicated and disturbing the peace. However, instead of properly detaining him for trial, Cash allegedly assaulted and beat Gwinn unnecessarily and brutally while effecting the arrest. The case was brought against Cash and his sureties on his official bond, claiming damages resulting from his actions. The Circuit Court of Coles County heard the case, where it was argued that Cash's assault was not justifiable in the execution of his duties as a constable, leading to a verdict in favor of Gwinn for $275. The case raised fundamental issues around the legal responsibilities of law enforcement officers and the liabilities their sureties face regarding their illegal acts.	The plaintiff, William F. Gwinn, argued that S. G. Cash had assaulted him unnecessarily and brutally during his arrest for a village ordinance violation. Gwinn claimed that this act was not in the course of Cash's official duties, thus entitling him to damages from Cash and his sureties on his official bond.	The defendant, S. G. Cash, provided several defenses, including a plea of "non, est factum," which questioned the validity of the claims against him. He also denied the assault, arguing that he used only necessary force while arresting Gwinn, who was found intoxicated and causing a disturbance. Cash contended that due to the circumstances of the late hour, it was necessary to detain Gwinn for a time in the village prison to prevent further disturbance.

In April 1859, a legal case titled "Charles McDonnell, Appellant, v. William Harter, for the use, etc., Appellee" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from an action of assumpsit concerning a monetary demand where the plaintiff, Charles McDonnell, claimed that the defendant, William Harter, owed him a certain amount of money. During the proceedings, a plea of the general issue was filed by the defendant, indicating that he had a valid defense against McDonnell’s claims, except for $458. Despite this plea being on record, the court proceeded to enter a default judgment in favor of McDonnell, assessing damages without properly addressing the lexicon of the plea. This led to an appeal from the Cook County Court of Common Pleas, questioning the appropriateness of the judgment given the unresolved plea. The core legal issue revolved around the effect of the general issue plea on the court's actions.	Charles McDonnell's primary argument was that he was entitled to judgment due to the defendant's default. He claimed damages for the monetary demand he asserted was owed to him, which the court initially supported by entering a default judgment in his favor without adequately addressing the existing plea of general issue.	William Harter's defense centered on the plea of the general issue, asserting that he had a legitimate defense to McDonnell's claims aside from a part of the demand. He contended that the court improperly assessed damages while the plea remained on file, which should have barred the action until resolved by a jury or agreement by the parties.

On April 16, 1860, Cadwallader Bull, the now-deceased partner whose administratrix is Maria Bull, entered into a partnership with Hugh Maher and Kelly in the coal business in Chicago, Illinois. According to their partnership agreement, Bull was responsible for supplying coal from Buffalo, Maher was to provide the coal yard and carts, and Kelly was to oversee daily operations. Any expenses would be shared equally, except Bull would pay the bookkeeper's salary. In October 1860, Bull filed a lawsuit seeking dissolution of the partnership, claiming Maher and Kelly failed to transfer sales proceeds as agreed. The Superior Court granted a temporary injunction against Maher and Kelly, prohibiting further sales or collections. By March 1866, the court ordered Maher and Kelly to pay Bull $6,676.11, which led them to appeal the decision due to an alleged failure on Bull’s part to provide coal.	Maria Bull, as the administratrix of Cadwallader Bull's estate, claims that Hugh Maher and Kelly violated the partnership agreement by not transferring the proceeds from coal sales. She seeks the dissolution of the partnership, an accounting of the sales, and recovery of the amount owed based on the terms of their agreement.	Maher and Kelly argue that they should not be held accountable for the amounts owed to Bull due to his failure to supply enough coal for their operations. They also contend that any financial shortfalls result from factors beyond their control, including debts related to sales made to irresponsible parties. Moreover, they seek damages for what they claim is Bull's breach of contract.

On January 5, 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, Herman C. Degener and Louis Degener executed and delivered two promissory notes to Michael Brulebach, one for $1,000 and the other for $800, both bearing 10% interest. The notes were later assigned to Simon Reid and others (the plaintiffs). In November 1874, the plaintiffs filed a lawsuit against the Degener brothers and obtained a judgment amounting to $1,990. However, a subsequent court order set aside this judgment except for $628.69, allowing the defendants to plead regarding this balance. The defendants raised multiple defenses, including the general issue and the claim of infancy by Louis Degener, who stated he was 21 years old at the time the notes were issued. The court allowed the case to go to trial, resulting in a verdict for the defendants. The plaintiffs appealed this decision, seeking to overturn the judgment rendered against them, particularly regarding the issue of Louis's infancy and the binding nature of the contract.	The plaintiffs, Simon Reid et al., argued that the promissory notes were valid and that the defendants owed the stated amounts. They maintained that Louis Degener's plea of infancy should not discharge the valid contract, citing previous legal precedents. The plaintiffs requested that the court reinstate the original judgment of $1,990 plus costs.	The defendants, Herman C. and Louis Degener, contended that Louis raised an applicable defense of infancy, thus invalidating his obligation on the notes. They argued that the judgments should not apply to Louis due to his age at the time of the agreement. Furthermore, they asserted that any agreement to transfer Louis's obligation to a third party (Forlin) lacked consideration and therefore was not binding on them.

Charles L. Anderson filed a creditor's bill in the Illinois Supreme Court on November 14, 1885, to enforce a judgment against Mary H. Hawhe. The underlying judgment was rendered on December 18, 1882, in favor of John and Johanna Anderson, in the Circuit Court of Cook County, amounting to $1,617. The case against Hawhe arose from an attachment action, but crucially, she claimed she was never personally served, did not appear in court, and never authorized anyone to represent her. Her representation during the initial trial came from attorney J. W. Waughop, who admitted to acting without her authorization. The attorney’s actions were alleged to confer no jurisdiction since there was no valid service of process on Hawhe. The court needed to determine whether a creditor's bill could be based on a judgment deemed void due to lack of jurisdiction over the defendant.	The plaintiff, Charles L. Anderson, contended that a valid judgment existed and that the creditor's bill could be enacted to enforce the owed amount. He sought to argue that Hawhe's absence from the court did not invalidate the legitimacy of the previous judgment, maintaining that the attorney's appearance substantiated the court's jurisdiction.	Mary H. Hawhe's defense was predicated on the assertion that the Circuit Court had no jurisdiction over her person, as there was no proper service of process. She established through testimony that the attorney Waughop acted without her consent or authority, rendering any previous appearances void. As such, she contested the validity of the judgment against her, claiming it was void and thus could not form the basis for Anderson's creditor's bill.

In December 1836, the case of James W. Crain v. David Bailey and others took place in Tazewell County, Illinois. The defendants were individuals who acted as sureties for Crain, who had been the executor of the estate of Lewis F. Crain, deceased. The Probate Court of Tazewell County revoked the letters testamentary granted to Crain, prompting him to appeal the decision to the Circuit Court. However, the appeal bond filed by Crain was incorrectly made payable to the defendants rather than to the People of the State of Illinois, violating the statutory requirements for appeal bonds in such cases. During the May 1836 term of the Tazewell Circuit Court, the defendants moved to dismiss the appeal based on this issue. Crain requested either to amend the bond or to file a new one to comply with the statute, but the court denied his motions and dismissed the appeal entirely, leading to his exceptions and an appeal to a higher court.	Crain argued that the Circuit Court erred in refusing to allow him to amend the appeal bond or file a new one. His main legal request was to overturn the dismissal of his appeal and to allow him the opportunity to correct the deficiencies in the bond to comply with statutory requirements. He contended that the statute did not explicitly prohibit the amendment or re-filing of the bond.	The defendants contended that the appeal bond was invalid, as it was improperly made payable to them instead of to the People of the State of Illinois, as required by statute. They argued that the Circuit Court had the authority to dismiss the appeal to ensure compliance with legal standards regarding bonds in probate appeals. Furthermore, because the statute did not allow for the amendment of the bond once it was deemed insufficient, they maintained that the court acted correctly in dismissing Crain's appeal.

The case "Edwin Lee Brown et al. v. City of Chicago" originated from an appeal concerning the opening or extension of Franklin Street in Chicago. The events leading to this legal action occurred during the March term of 1871 at the Superior Court of Cook County. Edwin Lee Brown and others challenged the authority of the city's collector to apply for a judgment regarding special assessments. They argued that the new constitution had abrogated the collector's power. Additionally, the court proceedings faced scrutiny due to procedural issues, particularly the inadequacy of the certificate of publication that was supposed to inform residents about the meeting of commissioners for making the assessment. The failure to mention the date of the last newspaper containing the notice was identified as a significant error that warranted the reversal of the judgment.	The plaintiffs, Edwin Lee Brown and others, argued that the City of Chicago’s collector had no authority to apply for a judgment on the special assessments due to changes instituted by the new constitution. They also contended that the protocols for notifying the public about assessment-related meetings were not properly followed, particularly highlighting that the notice did not include crucial information about its publication date, which they claimed invalidated the actions taken.	The City of Chicago's defense centered on maintaining the legality of the collector's actions and the validity of the assessments being challenged. The city likely asserted that the procedures followed were consistent with existing laws and that notice was appropriately provided, thus arguing that any procedural deficiencies should not nullify the judgment related to the street assessment.

In June 1877, the legal case of Daniel Dowty v. J. W. Holtz was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Effingham County, presided over by Judge James C. Allen. The case revolved around a promissory note issued by J. W. Holtz (the defendant) to Daniel Dowty (the plaintiff). Dowty initiated the action through a formal summons to claim the amount owed under the promissory note. The dispute concerned the validity of an attorney’s fee of ten dollars that had been included in the judgment against Holtz.	Daniel Dowty claimed that he was entitled to recover the full amount specified in the promissory note along with interest. He argued that the terms of the power of attorney attached to the note provided for an attorney's fee only in cases where judgment was confessed, which did not apply to this situation since he pursued a lawsuit instead.	J. W. Holtz contended that the additional attorney's fee authorized by the power of attorney could not be included in the judgment since the plaintiff initiated a suit rather than confessing judgment. He argued for a revision of the amount awarded to Dowty, asserting that the verdict should not exceed the principal and interest of the note itself.

The case of Albert W. Rudd v. Thomas Williams took place in April 1867 in Livingston County, Illinois. The main individuals involved were Thomas Williams (the plaintiff) and Albert W. Rudd (the defendant). The dispute arose from an obstruction of water flow in the Vermilion River, which the plaintiff claimed adversely affected his mill operations. Williams asserted that he had been using the river's water for his saw and grist mill for thirty years until Rudd increased the height of his dam downstream. This raised the water level back onto Williams’ mill wheel, disrupting its operation. Williams claimed a prescriptive right to the water usage and filed for damages due to Rudd's actions. A jury sided with Williams, awarding him $335 in damages. Rudd then sought to reverse this verdict through a writ of error, alleging that the evidence did not support the claim of a prescriptive right and that the issue rested more on mutual rights to use the river without harming each other.	The plaintiff, Thomas Williams, contended that he had a prescriptive right to use the water of the Vermilion River for his saw and grist mill, which he claimed to have operated for thirty years. He argued that the defendant's actions in repairing and raising his downstream dam caused damage by obstructing the natural flow of water to his mill, resulting in financial loss. Williams requested damages in the amount of $335 for the obstruction and interference with his mill operations.	The defendant, Albert W. Rudd, argued that the plaintiff failed to establish a prescriptive right to the water flow, as the evidence revealed that Williams' mill had been constructed within the last decade, undermining Williams’ claims of historical usage. Rudd maintained that both parties had equal rights to build dams and mills on the river and asserted that Williams’ claim was improperly based on a notion of prescription, which was not supported by sufficient proof in the trial. Rudd requested the judgment against him to be reversed.

In December 1845, the case of Alonzo Cook et al. v. John H. Foster, for the use of Nathan F. Corbin was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated with Foster bringing an action for trespass against Cook and others after Cook entered and enclosed a field that belonged to the United States, building a house and continuing to possess the land. After the land was purchased by Foster from the government, Cook, along with the other defendants, removed the house and other structures, prompting Foster to sue for damages. The jury ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding Foster $45. The defendants appealed the decision, contesting the basis of the plaintiff's standing to bring the action, given that Foster did not have actual possession of the land at the time of the alleged trespass.	The plaintiff, John H. Foster, claimed that he was entitled to maintain the action of trespass because he had purchased the land from the United States government and argued that Cook's entry and subsequent removal of property constituted a wrongful act. Foster contended that he had the rightful ownership of the land, even though he did not have physical possession at that moment, asserting that according to legal principles, ownership follows possession, and therefore he could recover damages for the trespass.	The defendants, led by Alonzo Cook, argued that Foster could not maintain the trespass action because he was not in actual possession of the property at the time of the alleged violations. They contended that Cook had been in possession of the land, and thus, as the "squatter," he should not be liable to Foster, who was claiming based on mere ownership without possession. The defendants requested a new trial after the jury's verdict was rendered against them, insisting that their possession negated the plaintiff's claims.

The case of Samuel Nicholson v. The People, etc. transpired in Lewiston, Illinois, with the court's final decision issued on May 25, 1888. The case arose from allegations against Samuel Nicholson, who was accused of operating a dram-shop—a bar or tavern—where he sold intoxicating liquor in violation of the state’s dram-shop act. Specifically, he was charged with two counts: the first being that he sold alcohol to intoxicated persons and habitual drunkards, thereby sustaining a common nuisance; and the second involving the sale of intoxicating liquors in less than one gallon and to minors without the necessary written order from a guardian. During the trial, evidence was presented, including testimonies that Nicholson had sold beer to a minor, leading to a guilty verdict on that charge. However, Nicholson contended that the allegations did not constitute distinct offenses, arguing that only a single offense of maintaining a common nuisance was present. The Illinois Appellate Court examined the evidence offered, the jury instructions, and various legal interpretations before arriving at its conclusion.	The plaintiff, represented by The People, argued that Samuel Nicholson was guilty of maintaining a common nuisance by selling intoxicating liquors unlawfully in his establishment. The primary claims included: selling alcohol to minors without obtaining the required written orders and permitting intoxicated individuals to purchase alcohol, which violated specific provisions of the dram-shop act. The plaintiff requested that Nicholson be held accountable for operating a dram-shop that constituted a public nuisance, leading to fines and the potential closure of the business.	In defense, Samuel Nicholson pointed out that the evidence presented did not conclusively show that he knowingly managed a location from which unlawful alcohol sales occurred, especially if those sales occurred without his knowledge or permission. He highlighted the distinction between the act of selling alcohol and the charge of maintaining a nuisance, arguing that the sale must involve his intentional involvement to warrant a conviction. Nicholson sought to have his case dismissed based on these arguments, asserting that the jury's instructions were improper.

The legal case "Andrew B. McConnell et al. v. The People, for use of David Purvines" took place in 1877 in Illinois, during a time when debt enforcement and property sales were often litigated. The key individuals involved included Andrew B. McConnell, the sheriff of Sangamon County, and David Purvines, the plaintiff who had sold his chattel property under a mortgage. Purvines had granted a chattel mortgage to John Champion on September 16, 1872. After the condition of the mortgage was broken, a sheriff's execution in favor of M. A. Cartwright was issued against Purvines. McConnell sold Purvines' property under both the execution and the mortgage. This led to a dispute over the remaining balance collected from the sale after satisfying claims. The case originally came before the court previously, and in this appeal, the evidence showed that Purvines assented to the appropriation of the proceeds from the sale, which became the central focus in determining the legality of the sheriff’s actions.	David Purvines claimed that he was entitled to a balance after the sale of his mortgaged property under sheriff's execution. Purvines argued that the sheriff improperly handled the sale and did not account for the surplus that should have benefited him after satisfying the mortgage owed to John Champion. Essentially, he sought relief under the official bond of Sheriff McConnell.	Sheriff Andrew B. McConnell defended himself by stating that as an agent of the mortgagee, he had the right to sell the property to satisfy the mortgage debt first. He argued that any surplus from the sale was correctly applied to the execution against Purvines. Furthermore, he asserted that the regularity of the sale under the mortgage could not be questioned, and that Purvines was equitably estopped from claiming any money as he had previously assented to the sale and the application of proceeds.

On July 27, 1883, E. Hess Malting Co. and Nathaniel H. Warren engaged in a transaction at the Chicago Board of Trade, where Warren (representing the appellees) sold 5,000 bushels of "Mo. 2 barley" to Hess (representing the appellant) at a price of 76 cents per bushel. The barley was to be delivered in September 1883, with payment due upon delivery. At the time of the contract, the Board of Trade had established rules defining the quality for "Mo. 2 barley," which included specifications regarding brightness and cleanliness. However, on September 1, 1883, a new definition was adopted that omitted certain quality descriptors. On September 13, 1883, Warren tendered warehouse receipts for the barley, which Hess refused to accept, claiming it did not meet the original quality standards set by the rules in force when the contract was made. The case revolves around whether the contract could be interpreted under the original rules or the new rules established after the contract was signed.	The plaintiff, E. Hess Malting Co., argues that they are not obligated to accept the barley because it did not meet the specific quality requirements defined by the original rules of the Board of Trade in place at the time the contract was executed. They seek a judgment confirming that the barley tendered does not fulfill the contractual obligations and, consequently, that they are not liable for the purchase price.	The defendants, Nathaniel H. Warren et al., contend that the barley tendered met the standards defined by the new rule in effect at the time of delivery. They argue that Hess could not assume that the rules were immutable and that they had no right to rely on the old standard after the change was publicly announced. Their request is for the court to uphold the validity of the delivery based on the new grading standards.

In the fall of 1870, Perry G. Law purchased 106 acres in Coles County, Illinois, for $2,230, financed partly through a $1,000 loan from the Eastern Illinois Loan Company. His wife, Keziah Law, later received the land in a conveyance dated August 1877, intended as a life estate with the remainder going to their children. In July 1878, Edward Y. McQuown, the plaintiff, obtained a judgment against Law for $537.87 for unpaid notes, but was unable to collect due to Law's lack of assets. As the land was about to be sold to satisfy the debt to the loan company, McQuown filed a bill in November 1881 to set aside the earlier conveyance to the Laws, arguing it was fraudulent and without valuable consideration. The trial court dismissed his bill, and during the proceedings, Law testified that he had borrowed money from Keziah which justified the conveyance as being for an honest debt. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, culminating in a final judgment in December 1884.	McQuown's primary contention was that the conveyance of the land from Perry G. Law to his wife and children was intended to defraud creditors and meet Law's personal obligations. He sought to set aside the conveyance in order to access the proceeds from the sale of the property to satisfy his judgment against Law. He argued that the deed lacked valuable consideration and was, therefore, invalid, aiming to demonstrate that the transfer was made to evade creditors.	In response, Perry G. Law and Keziah Law contended that the conveyance was made as payment for a legitimate debt Law owed to his wife. They argued that the debt was a sufficient consideration for the conveyance, asserting it was made bona fide and not intended to defraud creditors. They maintained that the conveyance was protective of the actual debt Law had incurred and that their actions were legitimate in light of Law's financial circumstances at the time of the transfer.

Charles P. Coggeshall v. Richard R. Mates was a legal case that took place in Illinois, with the decision issued by the Illinois Appellate Court on June 27, 1883. The case arose from a dispute initiated by Richard R. Mates against Charles P. Coggeshall. Initially brought before a justice of the peace, it was later appealed to the circuit court. The plaintiff, Mates, sought compensation for work performed as a carpenter and builder, claiming that he had fulfilled several contracts with the defendant. The central point of contention was a specific contract where Mates was to complete the construction of a building for Coggeshall for a total of $340. Evidence suggested that while Mates began the work, he ultimately abandoned the project without completing a substantial portion of it, which led to the disagreement over payment. The circuit court trial resulted in a jury judgment awarding Mates $140 plus costs. The core of the dispute revolved around whether Mates had the right to recover payment for the incomplete work and whether Coggeshall had accepted the work done, which he denied.	The plaintiff, Richard R. Mates, argued that he was owed payment for work completed under a contract with the defendant, Charles P. Coggeshall. He contended that multiple special contracts existed between the parties, primarily disputing payment related to the unfinished building project. Mates requested the jury to find in his favor for the work he had performed, despite his abandonment of a portion of it, claiming that any acceptance of the work by Coggeshall warranted compensation.	Charles P. Coggeshall, the defendant, contended that Mates did not complete the contractual work as agreed and abandoned the project without fault on his part. Coggeshall's defense included a request to instruct the jury that Mates could not recover any payment due to his failure to fulfill the contract terms. Additionally, he argued that there was no evidence to suggest that he accepted or used Mates's work, which would have allowed Mates to recover based on the value of the work rather than the contract price.

In the case of Hartman Markoe v. Mary Wakeman et al., filed on December 6, 1870, in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, the dispute centers around ownership of land near Chicago. Hartman Markoe claimed to own an undivided half of an eighty-acre tract, specifically the east half of the southeast quarter of section 27, township 38, range 14. This land was initially entered in 1835 by Herman Bond. In December 1835, Bond sold his certificate of purchase to Edward Shepard and Hartman Markoe, leading to the issuance of a patent to both as tenants in common in 1839. However, Shepard sold the east half of the quarter section to Maurice Wakeman in September 1836. The heirs of Wakeman, after his death, were named as defendants. The case arose over the claim made by Markoe, who, along with his successors, argued for ownership of the undivided half following alleged partition arrangements made years earlier. The court reviewed the validity of these claims through historical documents and testimonies, detailing transactions and relationships among the parties involved, particularly focusing on Markoe and Shepard’s dealings.	Hartman Markoe, the plaintiff, argued that he retained ownership of an undivided half of the east half of the quarter section through a series of transactions and sought a legal partition of the land. He contended that a partition had been agreed upon between himself and Shepard, and even though he had not claimed the title to the east half for over thirty-four years, his historical rights should affirm his ownership.	The defendants, heirs and successors of Maurice Wakeman, contended that they held full and clear title to the east half of the quarter, substantiated by a warranty deed from Shepard in 1836 and continuous payment of taxes on the property. They argued that Markoe had not asserted any interest in the east half for decades and that a valid partition occurred, divesting Markoe of any claims to the east half, thereby reinforcing their ownership.

On August 28, 1878, Walter L. Pease owned lot 28 in block 9 of the Fort Dearborn addition to Chicago, Illinois. He filed a voluntary petition in bankruptcy, mistakenly listing lot 9 in block 28 instead of the correct lot. Pease was subsequently adjudicated a bankrupt, and Albert T. Lewis was appointed as his assignee. In accordance with the Bankrupt Act, a deed of assignment was issued to Lewis. Following this, Lewis petitioned the court to sell the assets, including the incorrectly described lot, which was then advertised and sold at public auction. Stephen L. Inslee purchased the property for five dollars, and the transaction was approved by the district court. However, the reported sale information contained a description of a non-existent lot. After Pease's bankruptcy discharge, various subsequent transactions clouded the title, with Ritchie claiming interest through subsequent deeds that derived from prior invalid claims. This case arose out of efforts to resolve the conflicting claims regarding property ownership and the legitimacy of the transactions concerning the deed in question.	The plaintiffs, led by Pease, argued that the assignee's deed to Inslee should be reformed to accurately reflect Pease's rightful ownership of lot 28, block 9, as the original deed described non-existent property. They requested that the court set aside the deeds from those claiming title after the erroneous sale and sought a declaration affirming that the assignee’s deed had duly transferred title to Pease.	The defendants contended that the deed from the assignee did not convey any valid title due to the incorrect property description in the initial bankruptcy documents. They argued that since the property described in the deed never existed, the deed was ineffective in transferring ownership. The defendants also maintained that the state court lacked authority to rectify errors made by a federal court regarding bankruptcy proceedings.

Jasper J. Peddicord and others were bankers located in Decatur, Illinois. The case dates back to February 1, 1866, when Charles E. Connard, a dealer in stock and produce, opened a deposit account with Peddicord and associates. Connard frequently overdrew his account, at times exceeding $17,000, and was permitted to do so by the bankers. The process involved charging interest on the overdrawn sums, and although both parties had an understanding that the interest would be around 10% per annum, the plaintiffs charged more than this agreed rate. The dispute arose when they calculated the total interest charged, which amounted to $2,981.40, as exceeding this legal limit. The case was subsequently tried without a jury, focusing on claims of usury, which led to a court judgment for the outstanding balance, reducing it to $1,886.95 after deducting the usurious interest. The court had to address whether the transactions and settlements made constituted a usurious agreement and its implications on later payments made by Connard.	The plaintiffs argued that the bank had a right to charge interest on the overdrawn amounts, suggesting that their methods of calculating interest were standard banking practices. They maintained that while the total interest charged exceeded the statutory limits, this did not constitute usury because there was no explicit agreement to that effect when the overdrafts occurred. As such, they initially sought to recover the amounts due under the contractual agreements formed through the course of the banking relationship.	Connard contended that the bank's interest charges exceeded the legally permitted rates, constituting usury. He asserted that he did not explicitly agree to such high interest rates when he overdrawn his account. He also argued that since excess interest was charged without his knowledge or consent, he should not be held accountable for these charges. Connard’s defense included claims that previous settlements made with the bank should foreclose any additional claims for usurious interest.

On June 1, 1833, Richard H. McGill executed a mortgage to Nathaniel A. Ware for a loan of $2500 at an interest rate of 12% per annum, payable in advance for a term of five years. This transaction took place in Illinois. McGill later sold the equity of redemption, which was assigned to Manning. Ware subsequently filed a bill to foreclose the mortgage, naming both McGill and Manning as defendants. In response, McGill and Manning admitted the facts but argued that the contract was usurious. They contended that deducting a year's interest from the principal amount at the time of the loan constituted usury, which is a legal violation. The case hinged upon interpreting the legality of the mortgage interest terms as they related to the state statute regulating interest. The court noted that while the transaction had elements that could suggest usurious practices, the advancement of interest was part of established bank practices that had differing legal interpretations historically. The case spanned a period of legal review and involved assessing the intentions behind the contract and whether they satisfied the lawful maximum interest rates.	The plaintiffs, McGill and Manning, claimed that the loan contract with Ware was usurious, as the interest for one year was deducted from the principal at the outset of the loan. They contended that this arrangement violated the Illinois statute that prohibits reserving interest beyond the legally permissible rate and sought a forfeiture of threefold the amount of the usurious interest according to the law.	The defendant, Ware, argued that the loan agreement was legally valid and fell within the allowable interest rates set by Illinois law. He maintained that taking interest in advance was consistent with banking practices and did not constitute usury under the prevailing legal framework. Therefore, he contended that the foreclosure proceedings should proceed as the terms of the mortgage were lawful.

The case of "Mississippi Valley and Western Ry. Co. use, etc. v. The United States Express Company" originated in the state of Illinois in January 1876. The context involved the Mississippi Valley and Western Railway Company, which had mortgaged its property and income to trustees to secure certain indebtedness. A dispute arose concerning whether the railway’s earnings, generated after the mortgage execution but before any foreclosure or possession by the trustees, could be claimed by other creditors. This situation emerged when John Meyer & Co. initiated legal action through a garnishment process against the railway company, with the United States Express Company named as the garnishee. The case escalated through various legal proceedings, eventually reaching the Illinois Supreme Court, which had to interpret the terms of the mortgage and the rights of the involved parties.	The plaintiff, John Meyer & Co., argued that the earnings of the railway company were subject to garnishment and could be accessed by other creditors despite the existing mortgage. They maintained that since the railway company operated the road and produced income until the mortgage trustees took possession, those earnings should be available to satisfy their debt.	The defendants, represented by the Mississippi Valley and Western Railway Company's trustees, contended that the mortgage provisions prevented other creditors from claiming the income earned from the railroad until the trustees took possession due to a default. They asserted that while the company maintained possession and continued to operate, the earnings belonged to the railway and were protected by the terms of the mortgage.

The case of Alexander McArthur v. Isaac Artz was decided on December 13, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. It revolved around a criminal prosecution for misdemeanor initiated by the people against Isaac Artz in Mercer County. Artz was convicted on one count and was ordered to pay costs on another but appealed the judgments to the Circuit Court. The clerk of the Circuit Court refused to docket the appeals without upfront payment of clerks' fees, leading Artz to seek a court order compelling the clerk to docket the cases without requiring advance fees. The court had to determine whether Artz was liable for the payment of those fees in advance when appealing a misdemeanor conviction. The case raised significant questions about the right of defendants to appeal without financial impediments, especially in light of Constitutional provisions aimed at ensuring access to justice without the necessity of payment upfront.	The plaintiff, represented by the clerk of the Circuit Court, argued that Artz should be required to pay the clerk’s fees in advance for docketing the appeals, asserting that the standard practice in legal proceedings necessitates the payment for services rendered by court officials.	Isaac Artz contended that the Constitution and relevant legislative enactments exempted him from paying the clerks' fees in advance. He argued that requiring such payment would obstruct his right to a fair trial and appeal, undermining the foundational principle that justice must be freely accessible without financial barriers.

The case "The Springfield Fire and Marine Insurance Company v. Sarah Newman" was tried in the Illinois Appellate Court with the decision rendered on June 15, 1889. The key individuals involved included the plaintiff, The Springfield Fire and Marine Insurance Company, and the defendant, Sarah Newman. The suit originated from a claim made by the plaintiff to recover losses due to a fire that destroyed property insured under a policy issued by the company. The case was presided over by Judge Robert W. McCartney in the Circuit Court of Pulaski County, where a jury ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding $900 in damages. Following this verdict, the defendant appealed the decision, which gave rise to the discussions surrounding the bill of exceptions presented by the appellant.	The plaintiff, The Springfield Fire and Marine Insurance Company, claimed they were entitled to recover the amount of loss attributable to the fire as stipulated in the insurance policy. They sought a judgment from the court for the damages assessed by the jury, which amounted to $900, along with the costs of the suit, arguing that the appeal did not warrant a re-examination of the case due to insufficient documentation from the defendant.	The defendant, Sarah Newman, challenged the ruling, indicating that there were errors in the trial that merited a reversal of the jury's verdict. However, the defense's bill of exceptions was deemed fundamentally flawed, lacking essential documentation such as the insurance policy, instructions from the trial court, and evidence critical to the error claims. The defendant's appeal, therefore, could not be substantiated due to these omissions.

In January 1873, the case of Nancy L. Beacroft et al. v. Phebe B. Strawn, administratrix, was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The context involves a prior judgment in the Morgan circuit court whereby Jacob Strawn obtained a ruling against Aquilla and George Beacroft for $577.09, which remained unpaid despite several executions. George Beacroft died intestate in 1865, leaving behind his parents and siblings as heirs. Nancy L. Beacroft, the mother of George, possessed a life estate in certain lands that had been conveyed to her through a trust arrangement to benefit her and her children. After George's death, his share of this life estate was unlawfully subject to Jacob Strawn's debt due to judgments against him. The case hinged on whether Nancy L. Beacroft owned a fee simple absolute or merely a life estate, with the legal debate focused on the implications of specific terms used in the deed relating to her children’s inheritance rights.	The plaintiffs argued that Nancy L. Beacroft held a fee simple absolute over the land conveyed to her, thus claiming that her interests were not subject to Jacob Strawn's judgment against George. They contended that any encumbrance on George's share of the estate was not applicable as she maintained ownership free from external debts, highlighting the misunderstanding of the language used in the conveyance.	The defendant maintained that Nancy L. Beacroft only possessed a life estate and that her children were entitled to the remainder as purchasers. This position argued that the language in the deed indicated that George's interest, and by extension that of any deceased siblings, remained liable for their respective debts, affirming that the interest was indeed subject to sale for the purpose of settling the judgment owed.

In the case of Edward S. McDonald v. The People of the State of Illinois, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the defendants, including Edward S. McDonald, Nicholas Schneider, William J. McGarigle, and Frederick Faber, were charged with conspiracy to defraud Cook County by means of false pretenses, specifically relating to repairs at the Normal School. The indictment included multiple counts, with some focusing on general conspiracy while others specified the Normal School repairs. McDonald and McGarigle were tried together and found guilty by a jury, which sentenced them to three years in prison. Dissatisfied with the trial's conduct, McDonald sought a writ of error, asserting that the trial was not fair and that several procedural errors, including the admission of improper evidence and incorrect jury instructions, contributed to the conviction. The trial court’s handling of the bill of particulars and instructions to the jury were particularly contested, leading McDonald to argue that he did not receive a fair trial as guaranteed by state law.	The plaintiff, the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that McDonald and his co-defendants entered into a conspiracy to obtain money from Cook County through false pretenses. The plaintiff asserted that sufficient evidence was presented to establish guilt regarding the fraudulent claims submitted for work purportedly done at the Normal School. They sought to maintain the conviction and the sentence imposed by the lower court, arguing that the defendants had engaged in criminal activity that warranted punishment.	The defendant, Edward S. McDonald, argued that his trial was marred by several significant errors, asserting that he did not receive a fair and impartial trial. His defense included claims of improper evidence admission, as the prosecution introduced evidence unrelated to the specific charges outlined in the bill of particulars. Additionally, McDonald contested the jury instructions given by the court, which failed to adequately instruct the jury on the specific conspiracy charge they were required to consider. His legal team requested the reversal of the conviction based on these procedural shortcomings, citing the defendant's entitlement to a fair trial under state law.

Robert Moir, along with his co-defendants, faced a trespass lawsuit filed by Manassah Hopkins in 1855 in Henderson Circuit Court, Illinois. Hopkins, who had been working with his team for the Moirs, fell ill and left his team under the care of his brother, William Hopkins. While sick, the Moirs needed a team to haul lumber and directed William to either hire one or use Hopkins' team. William took the team without consent from Hopkins, leading to an accident where one horse fell off a steep hill and was killed, valued at $115. The jury found Robert Moir liable for the incident, resulting in damages awarded to Hopkins while finding the other defendants not guilty. Moir's motions for a new trial and to contest the jury’s instructions on liability were overruled.	Manassah Hopkins, the plaintiff, claimed that his horse, worth $115, was killed due to the unauthorized use of his team by the Moirs. He argued that Robert Moir directed his brother to take the team without Hopkins' consent, thus committing a trespass. Hopkins sought compensation for the loss of his horse, asserting that the Moirs, as the defendants, were liable for damages arising from their instructions to take the horse.	Robert Moir, the defendant, argued against the jury instructions given to the jury that suggested he was liable for the trespass committed by his agent. He claimed that there was a misunderstanding regarding the authorization for using Hopkins' team and contended that he had expected his agent to seek permission. Moir requested a new trial on the grounds that the jury's instructions misapplied the law of agency and liability.

August H. Scharf was accused of being the father of a child born to Florence Whitmore, an unmarried woman. The legal proceedings began in July 1886, following the birth of the child on September 20, 1886, who unfortunately died on January 6, 1887. The case was initially tried by a jury in the County Court and resulted in a verdict against Scharf, which was upheld by the Circuit Court upon appeal. Throughout the trial, the evidence presented was contested, with the appellant arguing for a lack of supporting evidence for the verdict, as well as mistakes in the admission of evidence, jury instructions, and the calculation of damages. The jury’s role in determining the credibility of witnesses and the weight of the evidence was emphasized, as they observed the demeanor of witnesses firsthand. Ultimately, despite the appellant's claims that the trial was flawed, the court found that the juries' conclusions were warranted based on the conflicting evidence presented.	The plaintiff, Florence Whitmore, contended that Scharf was the father of her illegitimate child. She sought a verdict affirming this claim and financial support for the child's upbringing, which was set at $50, reflecting necessary expenses following childbirth and the child's short life span. The legal request was legitimized through testimonies and evidence that supported the intimate relationship between the parties.	Scharf’s key arguments centered on the assertion that the evidence did not sufficiently prove his paternity and that there were procedural errors in how the case was handled. He contested the admissibility of certain evidence that he believed was irrelevant and argued that the jury had been improperly instructed. Additionally, he claimed that the amount determined for damages was excessive, given the child's brief life and the circumstances around it.

The case, titled "The President and Directors of the State Bank of Illinois, Plaintiffs in Error, v. Hazle Moreland, Defendant in Error," originated in the Gallatin Circuit Court in Illinois. It was decided in December 1828 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved are the President and Directors of the State Bank of Illinois (plaintiffs) and Hazle Moreland (defendant). The proceedings began with a scire facias action, which is a writ requiring the performance of a specific act, related to a mortgage executed to the bank that was duly recorded. The defendant, Hazle Moreland, responded by demurring to the scire facias, arguing that the mortgage does not contain a binding promise for payment, and therefore the bank could not enforce it without referring to a promissory note outside the mortgage itself. The Gallatin Circuit Court upheld the demurrer in favor of Moreland, prompting the bank to bring the case before the Illinois Supreme Court by way of writ of error.	The plaintiffs, the State Bank of Illinois, argued that the circuit court erred in sustaining the demurrer to the scire facias. They contended that as per Illinois law, specifically the act concerning judgments and executions from 1825, they were entitled to sue via scire facias for the foreclosure of the mortgage securing the money lent to Moreland. They sought to reverse the circuit court's decision and to recover the owed amounts through the enforcement of the mortgage.	The defendant, Hazle Moreland, maintained that the mortgage did not contain an absolute promise to pay the borrowed money, which constituted a valid basis for the demurrer. By arguing that the plaintiffs needed to refer to an external promissory note to enforce the mortgage, Moreland asserted that the circuit court properly upheld the demurrer and denied the plaintiffs' right to proceed with the scire facias.

In the case of Susan E. Bice v. Owen H. Hall, the legal matter took place in Sangamon County, Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 12, 1887. The case revolves around the validity of the last will and testament of Benjamin L. Hall, Sr., who had passed away. The executor presented a will for probate that was attested by two subscribing witnesses who claimed they saw Hall sign the document and believed him to be of sound mind at that time. However, one heir challenged the validity of this will in circuit court, resulting in a ruling that the paper was not Hall's valid will. Susan E. Bice, identified as one of the devisees in the will, appealed this decision to the Supreme Court. The central issue on appeal dealt with the testimony regarding the testator's mental state and the sufficiency of the witnesses' affidavits. The court needed to determine whether the statutory requirements for testamentary capacity had been met and if the evidence presented was adequate for validating the will.	Susan E. Bice, the plaintiff and one of the beneficiaries named in the contested will, argues that the circuit court erred in its decision to invalidate the will. She contends that the subscribing witnesses sufficiently attested to Benjamin L. Hall's testamentary capacity and that their testimony met the legal requirements for admitting the will to probate. Bice seeks a reversal of the circuit court's decision, requesting that the Supreme Court affirm the probate of Hall's last will and testament, allowing her to inherit the designated property.	The defendant, Owen H. Hall, asserts that the will should not be admitted to probate based on the insufficient testimony of the subscribing witnesses, particularly their inability to conclusively affirm that Benjamin L. Hall was of sound mind at the time of signing the will. The defense emphasizes that the law requires clear statements regarding the testator’s mental capacity, and since the witness’s testimony left doubt about Hall's mental state, the will should be deemed invalid. Consequently, the defendant requests that the Supreme Court uphold the circuit court's ruling that rejected the will.

Alexander Whitehall filed an appeal against William Smith following a malicious prosecution case that took place in the Iroquois Circuit Court of Illinois. The incident originated when Smith, on February 27, 1856, accused Whitehall and another individual of stealing multiple items, including cattle and farming equipment. Smith, without probable cause, went before Justice of the Peace Samuel M. Ayres, swearing to the alleged theft and actively procuring a warrant for Whitehall's arrest. Subsequently, Whitehall was arrested and imprisoned until he was discharged by Ayres, who acquitted him of the charges against him. Whitehall sought damages of $5,000, claiming that Smith's actions were malicious and baseless. During the trial, the defendant presented a plea of not guilty along with a special notice suggesting that the case had been settled. However, the trial court struck this notice from the record after the jury was empaneled, which led to a jury verdict awarding Whitehall $200 in damages. Smith’s motion for a new trial was denied, prompting him to appeal the decision.	Whitehall’s claims focused on malicious prosecution, alleging that Smith had falsely accused him of theft without any basis, leading to his wrongful arrest and imprisonment.
