He argued that Smith's actions were motivated by malice and sought compensation for the damages he incurred as a result of the accusations.	Smith’s defenses included a general plea of not guilty and a claim of settlement, suggesting that the allegations made by him were resolved prior to the trial, hence negating liability. He contended that the trial court erred in striking his notice of settlement after the jury was impaneled, asserting that the notice presented a legitimate defense that should have remained.

In 1843, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, the case of Herman R. Carstens et al. v. Ephraim Little et al. involved a dispute over a promissory note. The plaintiffs, Carstens and others, sued the defendants, Little and others, as endorsers of the note. The original note was executed by Stewart & Brown to the plaintiffs, who then endorsed it to the defendants, who later re-endorsed it back to the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs claimed three main points: the insolvency of the note's makers at its maturity, their absence from the state at that time, and the due diligence exhibited by the plaintiffs when they initiated suit against the makers as soon as they returned to the state, eventually obtaining a judgment and execution which disclosed a "nulla bona" return. However, the defendants denied the validity of the plaintiffs' claims through a general demurrer. The initial court affirmed the demurrer in favor of the defendants, leading to costs against the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs contended that they were entitled to recover against the defendants as endorsers of the promissory note. They argued that the note's makers were insolvent and absent when the note matured and that they had diligently pursued legal action against the makers, which resulted in a judgment against them.	The defendants asserted their denial of liability through a general demurrer, claiming that the plaintiffs could not maintain a cause of action against them as subsequent endorsers. They referenced existing legal precedents indicating that a prior endorser cannot successfully sue a subsequent endorser without special circumstances, which they argued were absent in this case.

In 1850, Jacob Trout, the plaintiff, appointed J.G. Bowman as his agent to rent out a farm. Westley B. Emmons, the defendant, leased the farm from Bowman, paying rent for several years. However, a dispute regarding the rent for the dry year of 1854 arose, leading to disagreements between Emmons and Bowman. Despite the conflict, Emmons continued to occupy the farm and pay rent until 1857. On February 2, 1857, Trout filed a lawsuit against Emmons for the unpaid rent of 1854. During this time, Trout and Emmons reached an agreement to submit their rent dispute to arbitration, appointing referees to decide on the matter. The arbitration concluded that Emmons owed nothing to Trout, indicating that the rent for 1854 was already paid. In June 1860, without Emmons' knowledge, the Wabash Circuit Court awarded Trout a judgment for $374 for the unpaid rent. Emmons, unaware of this judgment, attempted to defend himself when he found out, and subsequently sought an injunction against Trout, arguing that the judgment was unjust and that his agent did not have the authority to settle the dispute via arbitration.	Trout claimed that his agent did not have the authority to submit the rent dispute to arbitration without explicit consent. He acknowledged the rental agreement but contended that Emmons ceased to pay rent due to crop failures and did not inform Trout about any arbitration. Trout sought to have the court enforce the judgment obtained in June 1860 against Emmons for $374.	Emmons contended that he had reached an agreement with Trout's agent to settle his rent disputes through arbitration, which concluded that he owed no rent for 1854. He argued that the judgment awarded to Trout was invalid since he was unaware of the court session where the judgment was rendered. Emmons claimed that the lack of a response to Trout's injunction request should have allowed for a reconsideration, emphasizing that Trout's agent did not possess the necessary authority to bind him to an arbitration agreement.

The case "David S. Curtis v. Martha Jane Marrs" took place in January 1863 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a bill of exchange drawn by David S. Curtis, which was due for payment to Bart Whalon. The legal proceedings began when the Edgar Circuit Court rendered a judgment against Curtis in a case concerning the bill. The plaintiff, Curtis, declared two counts: one for a common account stated and another based on the bill of exchange asserting that it was payable to Bartholomew Whalon. The defendant, Marrs, objected during the trial to the introduction of the bill of exchange as evidence, claiming a variance since the bill was not noted to be in favor of Bartholomew Whalon. The court had to decide on the admissibility of this evidence and the competency of the witness provided by Curtis, who was Bartholomew Whalon himself. The trial concluded with Marrs being found liable; however, Marrs contested the ruling, citing errors in evidence admission and witness competence as grounds for appeal.	The plaintiff, David S. Curtis, asserted that the court erred in its admission of the bill of exchange as evidence, claiming that the naming discrepancy between "Bart Whalon" and "Bartholomew Whalon" constituted a variance. He argued that this variance undermined the validity of his claim. Furthermore, Curtis maintained that the court wrongly allowed Bartholomew Whalon to testify since he was an interested witness and should have been disqualified. Curtis sought to reverse the lower court's judgment and allow amendments to his declaration.	The defendant, Martha Jane Marrs, contended that the lower court had made multiple errors, including admitting the bill of exchange which she argued was inconsistent with the declaration. She insisted that "Bart" and "Bartholomew" are not interchangeable names without explicit averment and thus should not have been presumed the same. Additionally, she highlighted that Bartholomew Whalon, as an indorser, should not have been permitted to testify since his interests were directly tied to the outcome of the case. The defense sought to uphold the lower court's judgment against Curtis.

In 1836, a disputed property ownership case emerged involving Daniel McNary and Elizur Southworth in Montgomery County, Illinois. The case traces back to a failed deed by Harris to convey property to Blair due to not naming a grantee. Blair took possession and later conveyed it to O’Connell, who mortgaged the property to Watson with a right to sell. In 1863, Watson transferred the property to Crawford in a private sale. The situation became complicated when Watson eventually sold to McNary, who paid $310 for the property, while Southworth acquired it from O’Connell for only $100 in 1865. Amidst these transactions, McNary obtained a quitclaim deed from Harris while Southworth sought to redeem the mortgage against the property. The litigation focused on determining who held rightful ownership and whether McNary was a bona fide purchaser. The Illinois Supreme Court assessed the equities between the parties and the nature of the purchases, emphasizing McNary's good faith and the circumstances of each party’s claim.	Southworth claimed ownership of the property derived from his purchase from O’Connell. He filed a bill to redeem from the mortgage and sought an accounting for rents and profits, asserting that McNary's acquisition of the quitclaim deed from Harris constituted a fraud upon his rights.	McNary defended his ownership by asserting that he was a bona fide purchaser who had no knowledge of any alleged irregularities or claims on the property when he bought it. He argued that he purchased the property in good faith, for a fair price, and his acquisition was justified by the rightful expectation of obtaining legal title, further supporting his position by obtaining a subsequent deed from Harris.

In the case of Stephen Paddon et al. v. The People’s Insurance Company, which was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, the events took place in the early 1880s, specifically culminating in a decision on June 16, 1883. The key individuals involved were Stephen Paddon and his associates, who constituted the plaintiffs, and the People’s Insurance Company, the defendant. The case revolved around claims made by the plaintiffs against the insurance company regarding alleged insurance contracts. The plaintiffs claimed that they had both written and verbal contracts of insurance with the company, under which they had incurred a loss, specifically due to fire damage. On the initial trial, the jury favored the plaintiffs, awarding them damages consistent with the amounts specified in the contracts. However, the defendant appealed this decision, leading to a reversal by the Appellate Court. During a second trial, the court found in favor of the defendant, determining that the contracts had not been proved to exist before the loss occurred, leading to further appeals by the plaintiffs up to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Stephen Paddon et al., argued that they entered into contracts with the People’s Insurance Company, both written and verbal, prior to a fire that caused their losses. They contended that all necessary formalities were fulfilled, including the submission of proofs of loss, which established their eligibility for recovery based on the insurance agreements.	The People’s Insurance Company contended that there was no binding contract that existed prior to the loss. They maintained that the contractual agreements claimed by the plaintiffs were not proven to have been made before the property was destroyed by fire. The defense requested that the court uphold the trial court's decision, which found in favor of the defendant due to the failure of the plaintiffs to establish the existence of the alleged contracts.

In 1886, in Jasper County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between William Deimel and George Obert regarding the removal of a division fence between their properties. Deimel, the plaintiff, claimed that Obert had unlawfully removed their shared fence without providing the required one-year written notice to inform him of his intentions. Following the removal of the fence, domestic animals entered Deimel's crops, causing significant damage. To mitigate these damages, Deimel rebuilt the fence at his own expense. The case details the contrasting testimonies regarding whether notice was served properly. While a constable testified that he read a notice to Deimel, others claimed it was handed to him. The jury sided with Deimel, finding that the notice was not properly served as required by state law. Obert's actions were deemed unlawful, leading to Deimel seeking recompense for both the damages to his crops and the costs incurred to rebuild the fence.	William Deimel asserted that he suffered damages due to George Obert's illegal removal of their shared division fence without the proper one-year written notice. Deimel argued that the removal led to domestic animals invading his property and damaging his crops. He sought compensation for the destruction of his crops as well as the costs incurred for rebuilding the division fence to protect his remaining crops.	George Obert contended that he had provided the necessary notice of his intention to remove the fence, though the case details revealed conflicts about whether he had delivered a copy of the notice to Deimel. Obert argued that his actions complied with the legal requirements, asserting that he should not be held liable for any consequent damages to Deimel's crops or the costs associated with rebuilding the fence.

The case, Timothy Rogers et al. v. George W. Ward and others, took place in January 1860 in Illinois. The plaintiffs, including Timothy Rogers and David V. N. Radcliff, filed multiple petitions for mechanics’ liens against various defendants, including George W. Ward and Albert H. Pierce. The situation arose from disputes regarding construction contracts and the completion of work associated with those contracts. In all petitions, the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the work required under their contracts was to be completed within a two-year timeframe. This omission was deemed crucial by the Illinois Supreme Court, which had previously ruled that such a deficiency is fatal to the petitions for mechanics’ liens.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to mechanics’ liens for work done under contracts with the defendants. They argued that the defendants were obligated to pay for the completed work and requested that the court grant liens to secure their claims.	The defendants, including George W. Ward and Albert H. Pierce, contended that the petitions were insufficient because they did not establish that the work was to be completed within two years, as required by law. They argued that the absence of this crucial detail invalidated the plaintiffs' claims for mechanics’ liens and sought that the court dismiss the petitions.

Alice P. Prescott filed a legal case against William Maxwell in 1868 in Cook County, Illinois. The conflict arose from a construction project involving a mechanic's lien petition by Maxwell, a sub-contractor who took over plumbing work after the original contractors, Clancy & Walsh, had been fully paid for their work. The original contract with Clancy & Walsh was made on June 9, 1864, for $3,100, which included a provision for the owner to retain 10% as security. Prescott had made full payments by September 26, 1864, but the work was not complete. Maxwell entered into a contract on October 26, 1864, to complete the plumbing for $239. After Prescott refused to pay Maxwell, he filed for a mechanic’s lien. A jury ruled in favor of Maxwell, awarding him $286 including interest. Prescott appealed, claiming the verdict was based on erroneous jury instructions regarding the nature of the payments and the responsibilities of the parties involved.	Prescott's main argument centered on the assertion that Maxwell was not entitled to payment for the work performed based on the original contract terms. Prescott contended that she had fully paid the original contractors before Maxwell undertook the plumbing work, thereby discharging her obligation to pay for further work thereafter. She requested reversal of the jury's verdict, asserting that a prior payment prohibited any subsequent claims against her for services rendered after that payment.	Maxwell's defense claimed that he was owed for the plumbing work done after the original contractors were paid, stating that he believed there was still money due. He argued that the jury's instructions were correct, especially regarding the implied obligation of Prescott to inform him about any prior payments made to the original contractors. Maxwell maintained that he relied on Prescott's agreements when undertaking the work and that he deserved compensation for his services.

Martin O. Walker filed a lawsuit against Hugh Martin, which has been presented in the Illinois Supreme Court multiple times by September 1871. The case stemmed from a dispute that resulted in three separate jury trials, each returning different verdict amounts. In the first trial, the jury awarded $20,000, increasing to $25,000 in the second. However, both judgments were reversed due to excessive damages. The third trial resulted in a reduced verdict of $6,000; to prevent a retrial, there was a remittitur for $1,000, leading to a final court judgment of $5,000. The circuit court proceedings were presided over by Judge Josiah McRoberts in Will County. The nature of the underlying issue between the parties is not detailed, but the case revolved around conflicting evidence that was ultimately decided by the jury.	The plaintiff, Martin O. Walker, sought to appeal the previous verdicts which had been reversed due to excessive damages. Walker aimed to solidify the jury's latest decision of $5,000 and contested the previous judgments, asserting that the evidence in the case warranted the damages awarded. Walker’s primary argument was that the jury's decision on damages should be upheld given that the grounds for reversal had been addressed.	The defendant, Hugh Martin, presumably contended that the jury's verdict from the third trial was excessive, yet he did not pursue further claims. His defense emphasized the sufficiency of the evidence provided during the trials and supported the lower court's decision which reduced the damages to $5,000, suggesting that the legal grounds for excessive claims were no longer relevant.

In September 1877, in Iroquois County, Illinois, Mary Vogel initiated a trespass action against William Henries and his wife, Anna Henries. The case arose from an incident where Vogel, along with her daughter and others, broke into the Henries’ house, leading to a confrontation. During this confrontation, it was alleged that William Henries assaulted Vogel, reportedly striking her on the head with a hammer or hatchet. Although there were claims of provocation, it was unclear if Vogel sustained serious or permanent injuries. The venue was changed from Livingston County to Iroquois County for trial purposes. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of Vogel, awarding her $1700 in damages. The Henries appealed the decision, claiming errors in the trial process and arguing that the damages were excessive.	The plaintiff, Mary Vogel, claimed damages for assault and battery, asserting that William Henries had struck her during a confrontation arising from her alleged trespass on his property. She argued that the injury caused by the hatchet was severe enough to warrant significant compensation. Vogel's legal request included the enforcement of the jury's verdict, which awarded her $1700 for her suffering and the alleged harm caused by the defendants.	The defendants, William and Anna Henries, maintained their innocence, claiming that the allegations of assault and battery were exaggerated. They argued that the verdict was not backed by evidence and contended that their actions were provoked by Vogel's unlawful entry into their residence. Additionally, they challenged the integrity of the trial proceedings, stating that improper remarks made by Vogel's attorney during jury selection could have biased the jury against them. They sought to have the judgment reversed on these grounds.

The case “The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway Company v. Herman Krueger” took place in May 1888 within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved include Herman Krueger, the plaintiff, an employee of the railroad company, and the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway Company, the defendant. Krueger was working in the yard of the railway company, engaged in washing passenger cars. On the day of the incident, while transitioning from track No. 1 (where he had just finished washing a car) to track No. 2 (to continue washing another car), Krueger was struck by a car that rolled down track No. 2 with no one at the controls, causing him injury. The plaintiff alleged negligence on the part of the railway company, asserting that proper warnings were not provided about the approach of the moving car. The legal issues at hand revolved around whether the defendant acted negligently and whether Krueger exercised due care.	Krueger claimed that the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway Company was negligent in allowing a car to move on track No. 2 without any operator or warning signs, which led to his injury. He argued that he was performing his job duties when the incident occurred and sought damages for the personal injury he sustained because of the alleged negligence from the defendant.	The railway company contested the claims by arguing that Krueger may have acted carelessly by positioning himself in a dangerous area next to track No. 2 while he was not required to go there. They claimed that if he was negligent and had placed himself in harm’s way, he could not recover damages, regardless of any negligence attributable to the company. The defense also highlighted that the refusal to give certain jury instructions was justified due to the presence of evidence supporting Krueger’s actions.

John Magloughlin and others filed a lawsuit against Albert B. Clark in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision rendered on January 22, 1890. The case originated in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose over a deed of trust, in which the plaintiffs sought to foreclose after a series of financial transactions related to a loan secured by the deed. The plaintiffs, having a superior claim, alleged that Clark, as the assignee of the principal notes, acquired rights that affected the deed's validity. Central to this case were questions about the sufficiency of evidence regarding attorney's fees in foreclosure and the mere ownership transfer of the debt impacting the security, as the debt and mortgage are inherently linked. The court analyzed whether a purchase made by the holder of a junior incumbrance affected the rights and claims defined by the original trust deed, examining legal precedents concerning the priority of debt satisfaction and the attorney's fees allowable in such actions.	The plaintiffs argued that the evidence supported the allowance of the $100 attorney's fee specified in the trust deed in the case of foreclosure. They contended that the legal and customary fees associated with such foreclosure actions substantiated their claim. Furthermore, they claimed that any transactions pertaining to the assignment of part of the debt should not negate their rights over the security established by the deed.	The defendant, Albert B. Clark, contended that the purchase of overdue interest notes and certificates relating to the property secured by the deed invalidated the plaintiffs' claims, suggesting that such actions removed the security from the deed's purview. His argument centered on the notion that the acquisition affected the rights to enforce the deed and should be considered a separate repayment obligation, thereby impacting the original agreement's security.

In 1868, in Mercer County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Cyrus Low and William Pardee regarding the sale of a corn planter. The case was initially heard by a justice of the peace and later appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court. The central issue was that Pardee sold a corn planter to Low under the condition that if Low was dissatisfied with the machine, he would return it without payment. Pardee claimed that Low failed to return the planter, thus entitling him to recover $28.75, the price of the planter. During the trial, evidence was presented indicating that Pardee, through an agent, waived the requirement for Low to return the planter and preferred that it remain in Low's possession. This crucial piece of evidence was overlooked, which led to the jury being instructed improperly. Following this, the Supreme Court intervened, stating that the judgment given to Pardee was contrary to the evidence presented.	Cyrus Low, the plaintiff, argued that he was not liable to pay for the corn planter based on the agreement that permitted him to return it if dissatisfied. He contended that since he was willing to return it, he should not owe the purchase price. Low’s primary legal request was for the reversal of the judgment against him for the amount claimed by Pardee.	William Pardee, the defendant, maintained that Low had breached the contract by retaining the corn planter without returning it within a reasonable time. Pardee argued that he was entitled to recover the full price of the planter because Low did not fulfill the terms of their original agreement. His defense focused on the assertion that Low's retention of the planter constituted acceptance and obligation to pay for it.

In 1884, a divorce decree was issued in Vermilion County, Illinois, allowing Melvina Oliver alimony of $400 per year, payable in quarterly installments, along with her solicitors’ fees of $57. This alimony and fee were made a lien on Bushrod Oliver's land, with provisions for execution if payments were not made. After several installments remained unpaid, the sheriff sold the land under execution, with Melvina Oliver purchasing it. In December 1885, Corydon H. Campbell, the plaintiff, redeemed this land and subsequently purchased it through executorial sales for unpaid alimony installments assigned to him by Oliver. Samuel W. Leonard, as the conservator of Bushrod Oliver, filed to redeem the land from Campbell, seeking to have the deed declared void and to have the land returned. The court had to determine the validity of the sale made to Campbell regarding the lien created by the divorce decree.	The plaintiff, Corydon H. Campbell, claimed that he validly purchased the land following the issuance of several executions due to unpaid alimony installments. He argued that his redemption of the property should establish his ownership and that the sale was executed in accordance with the law. Campbell sought to maintain his ownership against the claims made by Leonard, asserting that the prior proceedings were adequate to secure his right to the property.	The defendant, Samuel W. Leonard, contended that the sale of the land to Campbell was improper because it failed to maintain the existing lien for subsequent unpaid installments of alimony. He argued that the sale needed to be made subject to these outstanding liabilities, and since it wasn’t, the sale was voidable. Leonard requested that the court declare the deed issued to Campbell void, emphasizing that Campbell could not benefit from a sale that did not comply with statutory regulations concerning alimony liens.

In June 1871, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case of James A. Piggott et ux. v. Asa Snell, originating from a chancery suit in Jersey County, Illinois. The case involved Asa Snell seeking to foreclose a mortgage executed by James A. Piggott and his wife, Susan J. Piggott, on certain premises. The court of first instance ruled in favor of Snell, entering a default judgment against the Piggott defendants due to their failure to contest the matter. However, the Piggott family contested the judgment, claiming issues with how the legal summons was served, particularly concerning Susan's notification. They argued that the service was invalid since it was delivered to James alone, without confirming that a copy was left at Susan's usual place of abode, which was required under the law. The Supreme Court found that the prevailing statute necessitated direct service on Susan, especially when her property rights were at stake. Consequently, it was determined that the earlier ruling lacked jurisdiction for Susan, prompting the reversal of the decree.	The plaintiff, Asa Snell, claimed that he was entitled to enforce the mortgage against the Piggott defendants due to their default on payments. He argued that the legal process served against them was sufficient as it followed traditional norms, particularly asserting that a summons served on the husband constituted valid service for both him and his wife, thereby justifying the foreclosure of the property.	The defendants, James A. and Susan J. Piggott, contended that the service of the summons against Susan was inadequate and legally insufficient. They maintained that service must be made directly to the defendant in order to confer jurisdiction, particularly when the legal action affected Susan’s property rights. They argued that the traditional view that service on the husband also serves the wife was outdated due to legislative changes and reforms on married women's property rights.

In April 1865, the case of Benjamin S. Prettyman and Samuel P. Bailey v. John Barnard was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a mortgage foreclosure dispute in Tazewell County, Illinois. The dispute originated when Barnard sought to foreclose on a mortgage executed by Abraham Brown and his wife, which had been assigned to him by Bailey. The background detailed significant debts owed by Brown to Bailey, consisting of multiple promissory notes and a total of $16,400. Barnard claimed that he had received assignments for the collateral securing Bailey's debts. However, Bailey contested Barnard's interest in the notes and asserted various defenses regarding payments made, credit claims, and the validity of the mortgage assignment. Bailey also conducted a cross-bill alleging wrongful actions by Barnard. After several court proceedings, including hearings and modifications of previous decrees, the case was ripe for appeal due to contested facts concerning the assignments and payments involved.	The plaintiffs, represented by Bailey, argued that Barnard had no valid claim over the collateral as the Kellogg notes and other securities were submitted as collateral but not paid. They requested the court to set off specific amounts against the $6,000 note owed to Barnard, as well as for an accounting of the payments received by Barnard. The plaintiffs also sought a rehearing based on several alleged mistakes made by the lower court regarding service of process, the treatment of their exceptions to Barnard's answers, and Barnard's refusal to account for certain notes belonging to a third party, Nathan P. Walton.	The defendant, John Barnard, denied the claims made by Bailey. He contended that the Kellogg notes were only received as collateral and had not been paid, asserting that Bailey had no right to offset those amounts against the $6,000 note. Barnard insisted that all contractual obligations were fulfilled as per their agreements and that Bailey had received several payments that were to be credited to his obligations. Barnard sought to have the court affirm the previous decrees, asserting no errors were made in the previous proceedings.

In December 1838, the case of Thomas Elliot v. William Sneed was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal dispute arose after Hugh Ronalds, who had initially won a judgment against Thomas Elliot through a justice of the peace in Clay County, had the judgment satisfied by Wickersham, the judge, who owed money to Elliot. Subsequently, Ronalds sought to enforce his judgment against Elliot via a mandamus, prompting Wickersham to issue an execution against Elliot. Wickersham's constable, Nathaniel Duff, collected the money from Elliot on this execution. Complications ensued when Wickersham then issued an attachment against Ronalds, which was acted upon by Sneed, another constable and surety for Wickersham. Meanwhile, Elliot ordered Sneed to pay $25 to Peter Green, which Sneed complied with. When Ronalds reversed the initial judgment against himself via certiorari, he successfully sued Duff for the money collected from Elliot, who, in turn, demanded the returned payment from Sneed. Ultimately, Sneed sued Elliot to recover the amount he paid to Green, claiming he had to return the money collected. The facts of the case indicate a complex interaction among multiple parties resulting from the execution of a judgment and subsequent reversals in the court.	Sneed, the plaintiff, claimed he was owed the money he paid to Peter Green on behalf of Elliot. He argued that due to the reversal of the judgment against Ronalds, which affected the validity of the funds collected from Elliot, he was entitled to recover from Elliot for the payment he made under the order issued. Sneed essentially sought restitution for money he had disbursed due to the legal entanglements arising from the reversals of the judgments.	Elliot, the defendant, contended that Sneed had mistakenly identified him as a party liable for the funds paid to Green. Elliot argued that the liability for the payment rested with Wickersham, who had originally collected the funds and subsequently paid them to Green on Elliot's order. He asserted that the chain of judgments and payments ultimately did not create further liability on his part, indicating that Sneed’s recourse should be against Wickersham rather than him.

In 1865, a legal dispute arose in Edwards County, Illinois, involving Catharine Fahs, William T. Shelby, and Adaline Darling. The plaintiff, Catharine Fahs, along with her co-plaintiff, sought to challenge a judgment previously obtained by her and her husband against the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company. They aimed to restrain the collection of a $4,000 judgment through an injunction pertaining to a bond executed by the railroad's trustees and their sureties. The case was transferred to St. Clair County's circuit court, where the injunction was ultimately dissolved and the bill dismissed. The plaintiffs contended that they were wronged due to an unresolved breach tied to the unpaid judgment. The defendant argued that the underlying judgment had been reversed by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1860, hence negating any claims for the bond in question. The case revolves around the issues of proper jurisdiction, notice, and the legality behind the plaintiffs' claims.	The plaintiffs claimed that the dissolution of the injunction in St. Clair County was erroneous. They argued that the judgment they were trying to enjoin remained unpaid and that various deceptive practices, including inadequate notice of proceedings, prevented them from adequately defending their rights. They sought to have the bond enforced, asserting that since the underlying judgment was not properly acknowledged, the defendants remained liable.	The defendants maintained that the judgment the plaintiffs sought to enjoin had been reversed by the Illinois Supreme Court, thus negating the grounds for the injunction and subsequent claims on the bond. They asserted that the plaintiffs had been adequately notified of the proceedings, and any agreements made concerning the litigation did not impact the court's jurisdiction or the validity of the judgment. The defendants requested a dismissal of the case, emphasizing that the dispute should not be entertained given the previous judgment reversal.

In 1839, in the Municipal Court of the city of Chicago, an action of assumpsit was initiated by plaintiffs William Jones, Henry B. Clark, and Byram King against defendant Cornelius C. Van Horn. The process was served in Will County. The plaintiffs filed a declaration that included counts for goods sold and delivered, along with common money counts, but it lacked any assertion that the plaintiffs resided in Cook County or that the contract was specifically made payable there. A judgment was rendered by default against Van Horn. The case revolved around jurisdictional issues, particularly whether the Municipal Court could send process to another county without the necessary averments regarding residency and the location of the cause of action.	The plaintiffs argued that the Municipal Court had the jurisdiction to serve process to other counties, based on a law that supposedly curbed errors related to jurisdictional claims. They maintained that the original declaration regarding the contract and the defendants' residency was adequate under the municipal statutes.	Van Horn contended that the Municipal Court lacked jurisdiction over him because the declaration failed to state that he resided in Cook County or that the cause of action accrued there. He asserted that the process issued by the Municipal Court was invalid per the requirements that must be fulfilled to establish jurisdiction in such cases.

In 1873, in Erie, Pennsylvania, the plaintiff Jerome F. Downing, a prominent insurance company manager, became involved in a mining investment opportunity presented by defendant J.H.L. Tuck and his associate Lucien P. Sanger. Tuck claimed to possess a deed from a property owner named Scribner for a two-thirds interest in specific mineral lodes located in the West Mountain Mining District of Utah Territory, which he represented as rich in copper, gold, and silver. He asserted that Scribner’s asking price for his remaining interest was $40,000, emphasizing the mines' potential profitability. Downing, trusting Tuck's assertions and accompanied by others, formed a company to purchase a share of these mining interests. After conducting a committee-led examination of the mines, which Tuck facilitated, they were assured of the mines' value. Downing purchased an undivided twelfth interest for $5,000, financing it with a promissory note by Tuck. However, after attempts to mine the land, Downing discovered the mines were worthless, leading him to claim that Tuck’s earlier representations were fraudulent and designed to mislead him.	The plaintiff, Jerome F. Downing, claimed that Tuck fraudulently misrepresented the value and productivity of the mining interests. He contended that Tuck’s statements about the worth of the mines and the existence of his obligations were false and made with the intent to deceive. Downing sought the cancellation of a $5,000 note given to Tuck, arguing he was induced to enter the contract based on these misrepresentations, and sought an injunction against the note's enforcement.	The defendant, J.H.L. Tuck, denied all allegations of fraud, claiming that all representations made were truthful and supported by the findings of the committee established to investigate the mines. Tuck contended that Downing, an experienced businessman, acted on his judgment and the committee's examination of the mines rather than solely on Tuck’s assertions. He maintained that he had not made any fraudulent claims and argued that Downing's reliance on his statements constituted a forgone conclusion, absolving Tuck of responsibility for any misrepresentation regarding the mines' value.

On September 2, 1855, Peter Ferbrache died intestate in Stark County, Illinois, leaving behind a widow, Elizabeth Ferbrache, and several children. Following his death, a partition of his estate was conducted, and Elizabeth was assigned a certain sixty acres of land as her dower. Shortly thereafter, she purchased the reversion of the same land, receiving a deed, and continued to occupy it until she transferred ownership to her son, Daniel D. Ferbrache, via a warranty deed in November 1856. Daniel, who initially lived on the property with Elizabeth, later moved to Lawn Ridge, leaving Elizabeth in possession of the land. Daniel died around 1865 or 1866, leaving minor children as his heirs. The deed from Elizabeth to Daniel was recorded after his death by the estate administrator. In 1874, Elizabeth executed another warranty deed, this time transferring the land to her son, Peter A. Ferbrache, under the condition that he support her for life. Subsequently, Peter A. filed a lawsuit against the heirs of Daniel D. Ferbrache, seeking to remove Elizabeth's deed to Daniel as a cloud on his title. The case hinged on allegations of a rescission of the deed between Elizabeth and Daniel, which the heirs contested. The lower court ruled in favor of Peter A., prompting the heirs to seek a writ of error.	The plaintiffs, heirs of Daniel D. Ferbrache, argued that there was a valid rescission of Daniel's purchase from their mother, Elizabeth, as evidenced by Daniel's intent to relinquish the land for Elizabeth's lifetime occupancy. They contended that Elizabeth's deed to Peter A. was fraudulent and sought to have it declared void. Essentially, they aimed to establish their rightful claim to the property as heirs of Daniel and requested the court to recognize Daniel's ownership of the land.	The defendant, Peter A. Ferbrache, countered the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that the contract to rescind Daniel's deed was invalid. He maintained that the ownership transfer to him via Elizabeth's deed was legitimate and legally binding. He contended that claims of a verbal agreement or agreement based on parol evidence did not satisfy the Statute of Frauds, which mandates all contracts for land transfers to be in writing.

In October 1864, a legal suit was initiated in the Richland Circuit Court of Illinois by Henry Green and his wife, Elizabeth M. Green, against Allen B. Daniel. The case centers around a property dispute concerning lots 13 and 14 in Lilly’s addition to the town of Olney, which belonged to Ashael L. Powers, who died in 1843. Elizabeth, as Powers' widow, claimed dower rights and half-ownership in these properties. The legal proceedings revealed a complex history of ownership: Powers had left no descendants but his widow, who later married Henry Green. The defendant, Daniel, argued that he acquired the property through a chain of ownership from Powers to George L. Butler and then to John E.T. Wilson, who possessed a title from the court. Elizabeth's claim was complicated by her death before the trial, leading to the revival of the case in the names of her children. Ultimately, the crux of the case became who held the legal title to the property, with the court determining that equitable jurisdiction was lacking since no grounds for equity were presented beyond the simple title dispute.	The plaintiffs, Henry Green and Elizabeth M. Green, initially claimed dower rights to one-half of the property left by Ashael L. Powers, as well as partition rights to the property itself. After Elizabeth’s death, her heirs continued the suit, seeking to assert their title against Allen B. Daniel, who claimed to own the property based on a series of title transfers.	The defendant, Allen B. Daniel, contended that he held lawful title to the property derived from a series of transactions starting with the purchase from Ashael L. Powers by George L. Butler, followed by transfer to Wilson. Daniel also disputed Elizabeth Green's status as a widow, which impacted her dower claim. He argued that the court lacked jurisdiction to decide the case since it was a straightforward legal title issue that should be handled in a court of law, not equity.

In the case of *Alexander H. Irvin v. The County of Alexander*, which took place in June 1872, the plaintiff, Alexander H. Irvin, was serving as the sheriff of Alexander County, Illinois, from December 1, 1871. During his tenure, he transported four individuals to the insane hospital in Jacksonville, a journey that spanned 572 miles round trip, requiring three days to complete. For this duty, Irvin took along an assistant to help transport two of the individuals. He incurred expenses amounting to $318.22, which included $119.87 for himself and his assistant, and $118.35 for the insane individuals’ transportation. Irvin had already received $340.90 from the county as reimbursement for these services and expenses. The central legal question was whether he was entitled to any additional compensation beyond what the county had already paid. This matter was submitted to the Illinois Supreme Court following a lower court ruling in favor of the county.	The plaintiff, Alexander H. Irvin, argued that he was entitled to additional compensation for the expenses incurred while transporting individuals to the insane hospital. He claimed that the fees and allowances set forth in the statute did not fully cover the expenses of the transport, including necessary travel costs. Irvin requested the court to reverse the lower court's judgment, asserting that his actual outlays should be reimbursed as part of his official duties as sheriff.	The County of Alexander contended that the statutes, specifically sections 12 and 13 of chapter 50, Gross’ Statutes, clearly stipulated the compensation framework for the sheriff’s services. The county argued that the set compensation of four cents per mile and fixed daily allowances for travel adequately covered the expenses incurred in the transportation of insane individuals. Therefore, they maintained that Irvin was not entitled to any additional reimbursement beyond what was already paid.

The case titled "The People ex rel. William C. Seip v. The Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, with the final decision rendered on January 25, 1886. The case arose from tax disputes involving the assessment of property owned by the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company (the defendant) in Cook County, Illinois. In 1883, the county collector sought a judgment for unpaid taxes from 1882. The railroad company raised objections against the judgment concerning certain properties it had listed under the classification of "railroad track." The controversy centered on whether these lots, which the railroad claimed were held for right of way, could be categorized as "railroad track" for the purposes of taxation. The railroad operated tracks south of certain street intersections and had acquired land necessary for future expansion, awaiting condemnation proceedings for additional land. Disputes arose regarding the assessment jurisdiction—whether the local assessors or the State Board of Equalization should evaluate the railroad's properties. The trial judge's rulings on these assessments were contested through appeals by both parties.	The plaintiff, represented by the county collector, argued that the properties under contention should not be classified as "railroad track" because they were not actively in use for railroad purposes at the time of assessment. They contended that only properties with actual tracks laid and used by the railroad should be recognized as such, and therefore, the collector sought a judgment for taxes assessed on these properties.	The defendant, the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company, maintained that the properties in question should be classified as "railroad track" since they were "held for right of way" and had been acquired in good faith for future railroad use, despite the lack of continuous tracks at the time of assessment. They argued that the statute did not require the property to be in active use for railroad purposes but only to be legitimately acquired for such use, and therefore, the local assessor had no authority to assess these properties.

The case "The St. Louis National Stock Yards v. The Wiggins Ferry Company" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on September 27, 1884. The dispute arose over the construction of a railway track across land owned by the Wiggins Ferry Company, which is located near East St. Louis, Illinois. The plaintiff, the St. Louis National Stock Yards, claimed that a superintendent for the ferry company had verbally permitted them to construct a connecting railway track on the company’s land in exchange for enabling future manufacturing developments nearby. The plaintiff spent about $12,000 constructing a 3,150-foot track, part of which was built on the ferry company’s land. However, after initially agreeing to grant permission and allowing the construction, the ferry company later sought to revoke this permission and took legal action to reclaim possession of the land, which resulted in a forcible detainer suit. After losing in the lower courts, the plaintiff sought injunction relief and specific performance for the right of way.	The St. Louis National Stock Yards contended that they had a valid agreement, based on the verbal license granted by the superintendent of the Wiggins Ferry Company, to construct the railway track. They sought to enjoin the ferry company from reclaiming the land upon which the track was built and requested specific performance to compel the ferry company to convey the right of way for the track. The plaintiff asserted that they relied on the ferry company’s permission, which justified their significant investment in constructing the track.	The Wiggins Ferry Company argued that the arrangement made with the superintendent was merely a parol license to build on their land, not a formal contract. They maintained that a verbal commitment for a right of way did not constitute a binding agreement because it was not in writing, thereby falling under the Statute of Frauds. The defendant claimed that they had the right to revoke the license and reassert possession of the land, as no equitable estoppel applied given that no fraud or deception was practiced during the construction.

The case "David Chalmers, Plaintiff in Error, v. Thomas C. Moore, Defendant in Error" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1859. It involved a promissory note that fell due on March 23, 1858. The plaintiff, David Chalmers, was the indorser of the note, while Thomas C. Moore was the second indorsee who initiated the legal action as the assignee. After the note's due date, a series of legal actions were taken against the makers of the note, but multiple executions returned with no property found. The plaintiff alleged due diligence in attempting to collect the debt, while the defendant argued there was a lack of diligence in prosecuting the claim. Complications arose regarding the timings of summons and the handling of the executions. Ultimately, it was determined that proper procedures had not been followed to establish due diligence in recovering the owed amount, leading to the case being reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Thomas C. Moore, claimed that he had exercised due diligence in attempting to recover the amount owed from the indorsers of a promissory note. He sought recovery on the basis of this diligence, arguing that legal actions against the makers of the note had been properly instituted and pursued according to the requirements of law.	The defendant, David Chalmers, contended that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate adequate diligence in pursuing the debt. He pointed out that the initial suit against the makers was not commenced until three months after the note became due, and that proper execution of writs had not been followed. The defendant requested the court dismiss the claims due to the plaintiff’s failure to meet the legal standards of diligence.

Hiram C. McMurphy passed away on October 13, 1867, after drafting a will that specified that half of his personal estate's income should go to his wife, Hannah A. McMurphy, for her lifetime, with the remainder going to his collateral relatives after her death. The other half of the estate was bequeathed to various other individuals. Hannah renounced the will and claimed entitlement to the entire estate, which led to a legal dispute. The probate court initially ruled that she was only entitled to one-third of the estate, prompting her to appeal. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court to examine the legal extent of the widow’s claims against her husband's will, especially in the absence of lineal descendants.	Hannah A. McMurphy, the widow, contended that her renunciation of her husband's will entitled her to the entire personal estate, as there were no children or descendants to consider. She argued that the act of renouncing the will effectively converted her husband’s estate into an intestate estate, thus allowing her to receive a full share.	The executors of Hiram C. McMurphy's estate, S. S. Boyles and W. F. Coolbaugh, contended that the widow's claim was unfounded. They argued that the will should remain effective despite her renunciation, and thus, under Illinois law, she was only entitled to one-third of the personal estate remaining after debts were settled, in addition to specific property awards, rather than the entire estate.

In the case of John Schweyer v. F. Oberkoetter, the incident took place in 1885 in Chicago and McLean County, Illinois. John Schweyer, a liquor dealer, issued a due bill for $175 to Jeremiah Welch, allowing Welch to redeem it for whisky or wine. Welch later assigned this due bill to F. Oberkoetter, agreeing to act as a surety for the note. Schweyer was sued in the Circuit Court of McLean County as a joint maker along with Welch when they both failed to appear in court, leading to a default judgment against them. Upon Schweyer’s later appearance, he filed various pleas, including a general issue and claims that he was not jointly liable with Welch and that there had been a failure of consideration. The court sustained demurrers to some of his pleas, and a jury ultimately found in favor of Oberkoetter. After further motions and disputes regarding the court's jurisdiction and the nature of the assignment, the judgment was affirmed.	The plaintiff, F. Oberkoetter, claimed that he was entitled to recover the $175 amount as stipulated in the due bill issued by Schweyer, asserting that both Schweyer and Welch were jointly responsible as makers of the note. Oberkoetter argued that despite the assignment and legal intricacies, Schweyer was liable for the debt after demand and refusal for payment in accordance with the terms of the due bill.	John Schweyer, the defendant, contended that he was not jointly liable with Jeremiah Welch and argued a failure of consideration regarding the due bill as well as the claim that Welch was not licensed to deal in intoxicating liquors. He also attempted to contest the court’s jurisdiction over him, stating that he had not been properly served in McLean County, which he believed was grounds for dismissal of the case against him.

In April 1858, the case of John Nash v. Marks Monheimer took place in Bureau County, Illinois. The dispute originated from a wager of $25, where Nash claimed he could make a particular horse rack a distance of half a mile in one and a half minutes. The trial began before a justice of the peace and was appealed to the Bureau County Circuit Court, where the plaintiff (Nash) initially won. During the trial, it was established that the horse was racked within the corporate limits of the town of Princeton, where a local ordinance prohibited fast riding or driving. The trial confirmed that Nash's horse did not meet the stipulated performance, only racking the required distance in one minute and thirty-four seconds. The parties did not set a specific location for the trial prior to the wager, and Monheimer, present during the horse's trial, raised no objections to the location. As a result of the trial’s findings, Nash's claims would ultimately be scrutinized based on the legality of the wager.	John Nash, the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to recover the $25 wagered against Marks Monheimer due to an agreement made regarding the speed of his horse. He contended that the act of racking the horse was executed in accordance with their agreement, despite the failure to achieve the prescribed speed within the specified time.	Marks Monheimer, the defendant, argued that the wager was invalid because it violated local laws prohibiting fast riding within the town’s limits. He contended that the contract was connected to an illegal act under local ordinance, making it unenforceable in court. Monheimer cited that both parties were complicit in breaching this ordinance, thus nullifying any obligation Nash believed he had to collect the wager.

In September 1875, the case of Elizabeth Haas et al. v. The Chicago Building Society was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a dispute over property in Chicago. The key individuals involved were Elizabeth Haas and her husband, Valentine Haas, who were defendants in the case, and the Chicago Building Society, the plaintiff. The plaintiffs contended that they were entitled to sell property secured by a trust deed in order to recover a debt owed to them by Mrs. Haas. The case arose after the defendants claimed that a significant portion of this debt included usury and compound interest, and they also argued that some of the claimed debt was not actually received. A stipulation was submitted by Mrs. Haas's attorney, agreeing to a specific sum owed and establishing that they would pay it to avoid further claims from the society. The trial court dismissed the Haas's bill, ruling in favor of the Chicago Building Society and ordering the property to be sold, prompting the Haases to appeal the decision.	The Chicago Building Society claimed that the Haases owed them a debt of $24,785.56 based on a trust deed securing funds loaned to Mrs. Haas. They sought to sell the property in question to satisfy this debt, which they claimed had accrued due to interest and fees that the Haases disputed as being excessive or unreceivable.	Elizabeth and Valentine Haas argued against the validity of the debt, claiming it consisted of usurious amounts and unreceived funds. They maintained that the stipulation filed by their attorney should not be held against them, claiming that the interest terms and additional fees constituted unfair practices. Furthermore, the defendants aimed to challenge the decree's provision for a ten percent interest rate, stating it exceeded the statutory limit.

The case "The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company v. Stephen Green" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1873. It originated in the Circuit Court of Morgan County, where Stephen Green, the plaintiff, filed an action against the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company. The central issue revolved around a hedge fence that Green had planted on his property, which was located adjacent to the railway's right of way. The railway company took measures to trim the hedge under the assumption that it obstructed their operations, claiming a right to maintain the right of way following earlier established rules about such obstructions. The dispute presented a question concerning whether there was an implied contract for the railway company to have purchased the hedge after they took action regarding it. The evidence showed that there was no explicit purchase agreement, and the trimming was done with Green's consent but did not amount to ownership transfer of the hedge.	Stephen Green contended that the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company had effectively purchased the hedge on his property by actively engaging in its trimming. He sought compensation for the value of the hedge as if it were sold under a contract and claimed that the company's actions implied a purchase agreement.	The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company defended itself by arguing that there was no express contract proving the purchase of the hedge. They maintained that any act taken to trim the hedge was necessary to avoid obstruction of their right of way and did not equate to ownership of the hedge. The company requested that the court not hold them liable for compensating Green for the hedge's value, as no valid contract existed.

On May 11, 1843, a recognizance was filed in the clerk’s office of the Madison Circuit Court in Illinois involving William Shattuck, G. W. Richardson, and Francis Van Amberg. The recognizance was a bond of $300, ensuring that Van Amberg, who had been found guilty of passing counterfeit money on May 6, 1843, would appear in court on the fourth Monday of May and not depart without permission. Van Amberg failed to appear, leading the court to declare the recognizance forfeited and initiate a scire facias against Shattuck and Richardson, who also did not appear. A default judgment was rendered against them, resulting in the plaintiffs, The People of the State of Illinois, being awarded the amount of the recognizance plus costs. The defendants then sought to reverse this judgment through a writ of error, raising the issue of whether the bond could be considered a valid recognizance under the law.	The plaintiff, The People of the State of Illinois, argued that the recognizance executed by the defendants was valid and binding, asserting that the defendants failed to fulfill the conditions stated in the bond by not ensuring Van Amberg's appearance in court. They requested that the judgment of forfeiture be upheld and that the court enforce the payment of the $300 penalty as agreed in the recognizance.	The defendants contended that the bond should not be considered a valid recognizance due to technical deficiencies, including assertions about the procedures followed by the justices of the peace who approved the bond and the absence of proper documentation pertaining to the bond's authority. They argued that the conditions required by law for the bond to be valid were not fulfilled. Their defense sought to have the judgment against them reversed, claiming that the bond was not executed properly.

John A. Cavanaugh filed a lawsuit in the Livingston Circuit Court in Illinois on January 8, 1887, seeking to foreclose a junior mortgage on a parcel of land comprising forty acres. The series of transactions began in 1876 when the original mortgagor, O'Donnell, executed a senior mortgage to secure a debt of $600 owed to Thurston Macomber. This primary mortgage was later transferred to Watkins and then to David McWilliams, the current owner of the land. In 1878, O'Donnell took out a junior mortgage with a promissory note for $135.41 to Ellen Carey, which was transferred to Cavanaugh in 1879 as part of a transaction for $10. The case primarily revolves around ownership and transfer of the junior mortgage and the accompanying note. McWilliams contended that he had purchased the mortgage and note from Cavanaugh, asserting that the transaction was valid, even though there were conflicting claims regarding the assignment's validity.	John A. Cavanaugh's primary argument was that he was entitled to foreclose on the junior mortgage he obtained from Ellen Carey. He sought judicial affirmation of his claim that McWilliams did not rightfully own the mortgage and that therefore, he could proceed with the foreclosure to recover the amounts owed under the promissory note.	David McWilliams argued that he was the rightful owner of the promissory note and junior mortgage, which he claims were sold to him by Cavanaugh for $40. He contended that there was an agreement regarding this sale, and that he had attempted to formalize the assignment but found it informal and unsatisfactory. McWilliams maintained that he was prepared to fulfill the financial obligation and had tendered payment to Cavanaugh, which he believed validated his defense.

In the case of Bliss, Williams & Co. v. William Perryman, which took place in White County, Illinois, the plaintiffs, Bliss, Williams & Co., initially sued the defendant, William Perryman, over a bond of $28 that Perryman executed while he was still a minor. The bond was related to the purchase of a windmill and stipulated conditions regarding payment and potential future purchase issues. During the trial, Perryman successfully claimed infancy as a defense, demonstrating that he was under 21 at the time of signing. The plaintiffs attempted to establish a new claim based on Perryman's alleged promise to pay $18 in lieu of the bond after he reached adulthood, but they failed to provide disinterested testimony to support this assertion. The plaintiffs sought to have Perryman swear to this promise, but the court ruled that the proposed testimony was inadmissible, as it would introduce a different cause of action than was originally brought. This issue was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal from a lower court's judgment in favor of Perryman, who had been awarded costs.	The plaintiffs, Bliss, Williams & Co., argued that Perryman made an actionable promise to pay $18 after reaching the age of majority as a substitute for the original $28 bond. They sought to have him sworn to affirm this promise, believing that his acknowledgment would support their claim for payment. They maintained that the court should allow this testimony as evidence.	The defendant, William Perryman, contended that he could not be held liable for the bond he signed while a minor, citing infancy as a valid defense. He argued that the plaintiffs' attempt to prove a new parol agreement was flawed, as it sought to establish a cause of action that was distinct from the original contract. Perryman emphasized that the plaintiffs should have initiated their action based on the subsequent promise rather than on the bond.

In 1889, in Monroe County, Illinois, F. W. Brickey initiated an ejectment action against Frank English and others concerning a parcel of land. Brickey claimed ownership through a tax deed pertaining to the property, specifically a tract described as “Part of survey No. 743, claim No. 93, containing 31 acres.” During the proceedings, defendants Hardy and Demint, as English's landlords, filed a plea of not guilty. English did not appear, resulting in a default against him. The trial was conducted without a jury, leading to a judgment favoring the defendants. Brickey presented a tax deed as evidence of ownership; however, the court found the deed's description to be too vague, rendering it void for uncertainty. Additionally, flaws in the affidavit for notice of the tax sale were identified, severely undermining Brickey’s claim. Following the trial, the plaintiffs sought a writ of error due to the judgment rendered.	F. W. Brickey claimed ownership of the disputed land based on a tax deed, which he argued entitles him to possession. He presented various documents to support his claim, including the tax sale certificate and an affidavit stating that he complied with legal notification requirements necessary for acquiring the deed. Brickey's main legal request was for the court to issue a deed transferring title of the land to him.	The defendants, led by Frank English, contended that Brickey’s tax deed was invalid due to the ambiguous description of the property that left the land’s specific location indeterminate. They argued that the proceedings under the tax deed were void because the required affidavit lacked essential details about the service of notice to land occupants, which failed to satisfy legal standards. Thus, they requested the court to affirm the prior judgment in their favor.

On November 6, 1866, a significant election for the office of sheriff took place in Morgan County, Illinois, which involved Milton Mayfield and Sylvester L. Moore as opposing candidates. Following a canvass of the votes, Moore was declared the winner and received a commission to serve in the role from November 17, 1866, until January 13, 1868. Shortly after the election, Mayfield contested the results, claiming that illegal votes had been cast for Moore. The dispute was brought before justices of the peace, which ruled in favor of Mayfield, declaring him the rightful sheriff. Moore appealed this decision to the circuit court, which upheld the ruling. Moore later sought a review from the Illinois Supreme Court, which dismissed his appeal. After trial proceedings confirmed Mayfield’s right to the office, he was duly commissioned and subsequently filed a suit against Moore to recover the fees Moore had collected during his time in office. During the trial, objections arose about the admissibility of evidence regarding fees received by Moore prior to the circuit court's decision, leading to a pivotal ruling on the matter.	Mayfield claimed that he was entitled to the fees and emoluments received by Moore during the latter's time as sheriff, asserting that since he (Mayfield) was the rightful officeholder based on the election results, all fees earned during Moore's assumption of the office rightfully belonged to him. He argued that the principle of law supports that an individual who holds legal title to a public office is entitled to the fees generated from it, regardless of when the official determination of rights was made.	Moore contended that he should only be liable for the fees he collected after the circuit court's ruling declared Mayfield as the rightful sheriff. His defense was based on the assertion that once he surrendered the office upon the judicial determination, his responsibility to account for previous fees should be limited to those earned during the official duties performed only after that ruling.

Frank Dalby, representing George W. Whitehead, initiated a replevin suit against J. M. Campbell and others in Edwards County, Illinois, culminating in a court decision on January 4, 1888. The case arose from a dispute over the wrongful detention of property, including a printing press and related equipment used by Whitehead for newspaper publishing and job work. The trial involved a demurrer to the amended declaration, which was partially sustained and partially overruled. Whitehead opted NOT to pursue certain damages after the court’s rulings and chose instead to stand by his amended declaration. The circuit court ultimately dismissed the case due to the plaintiff’s failure to prosecute the remaining claims, leading to a judgment against Whitehead for court costs. Whitehead appealed this judgment, focusing on the allowed areas of recovery for damages resulting from the alleged wrongful detention of his property.	The plaintiff claimed entitlement to damages from the wrongful detention of property, specifically for the value of its use during that period, attorney's fees related to defense against the replevin suit, and losses resulting from depreciation of the property. The plaintiff also sought to recover for vindictive and punitive damages, asserting harm to good will in his business due to the actions of the defendants.	The defendants contended that the claims for vindictive and punitive damages were not recoverable under the terms of the replevin bond. They argued that the plaintiff failed to plead specific damages appropriately and that only actual damages directly associated with the wrongful detention were eligible for recovery. They maintained that claims related to business good will should be considered irrelevant under the action.

John Stanley filed a legal proceeding against the People of the State of Illinois in 1874, stemming from a charge of bastardy. The case took place in the Iroquois County court, where it was initiated under the act of 1872. It was not until the October term of 1874 that the trial was held, resulting in a judgment against Stanley. Unsatisfied with the outcome, he appealed the case to the circuit court as provided by the act of 1874. However, the circuit court dismissed the appeal on a motion, prompting Stanley to raise this dismissal as an assignable error in his pursuit of justice.	John Stanley's primary argument centered on his statutory right to appeal the judgment rendered against him in the county court for the bastardy charge. He contended that the circuit court improperly dismissed his appeal, thereby infringing upon his legal rights and denying him the opportunity for a trial de novo.	The People of the State of Illinois defended the dismissal of the appeal, arguing that the circuit court’s ruling was correct. They maintained that due legal procedures justified the dismissal and sought to uphold the initial judgment against Stanley.

Lawrence S. Beardsley v. John W. Gosling was a legal case adjudicated in September 1877 by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a dispute in Cook County, Illinois. The case involved a lawsuit initiated by John W. Gosling against Lawrence S. Beardsley on the grounds of assumpsit concerning a draft. The complaint was filed in the Superior Court, which recorded an affidavit stating the amount owed. Beardsley responded to the complaint by filing a general issue along with an affidavit of merits, but the affidavit was challenged on a technicality related to its caption. The court ultimately struck the defendant’s plea and affidavit from the files, leading to an appeal by Beardsley.	The plaintiff, John W. Gosling, claimed that the defendant Lawrence S. Beardsley owed him money as evidenced by a draft. In his declaration, he included both special and common counts, supported by an affidavit of the amount owed. The essence of his claim was rooted in asserting the legitimacy of the debt represented by the draft.	The defendant, Lawrence S. Beardsley, contended that the objections raised against his affidavit of merits were overly technical and did not warrant the striking of his plea and affidavit from the files. He argued that the affidavit conformed to the statutory requirements and should be recognized as valid despite any concerns regarding its caption. His request was to have his plea reinstated and the initial judgment against him reversed.

Edward C. Rice filed a lawsuit against the St. Louis and Southeastern Railway Company in June 1873 to recover $13,950 for services rendered as a civil engineer. Rice had been employed by the company from early 1869 until June 1, 1873, with an annual salary of $4,000. However, he had only received one year of pay and, upon resigning, settled with the company's president by accepting $15,000 in consolidated bonds as payment. These bonds were believed to be worth eighty-five cents on the dollar at the time of the settlement. Once the company's insolvency became apparent, the bonds lost significant value, prompting Rice to sue for his unpaid wages. The trial did not reveal any clear conflicts in evidence, focusing instead on whether Rice was induced to accept the bonds through fraudulent statements made by the company president regarding the financial condition of the railway and the value of the bonds.	Rice claims that he was misled into accepting the bonds due to fraudulent representations by the company's president, specifically regarding the company's financial health and the bonds' value. He asserts that, had he known the true state of affairs, he would not have agreed to the settlement and is therefore entitled to recover his wages in full.	The railway company argues that no fraud occurred, as the company had indeed made payments for operating expenses and interest. They maintain that the statements made by the president were opinions and not fraudulent misrepresentations, as there was no evidence he knowingly provided false information. The company contends that Rice voluntarily accepted the bonds and, if he incurred a loss, it is solely due to market fluctuations after the agreement.

In the case of Charles J. Wheeler v. John D. Randall, which took place in September 1868 in Illinois, the plaintiff, John D. Randall, filed a lawsuit against the defendant, Charles J. Wheeler. The case stemmed from allegations of deceit involving the sale of a flock of sheep. Randall claimed that Wheeler had made false and fraudulent representations regarding the condition of the sheep, asserting they were healthy when in fact they had a contagious disease known as "scab." The trial occurred in the Court of Common Pleas in Aurora, Illinois, where the presiding judge was Richard G. Montony. Ultimately, Wheeler appealed a judgment against him that had favored Randall. The core of the legal discussions revolved around the necessity of proving Wheeler's knowledge of the falsehood of his representations in order to constitute fraud.	Randall argued that Wheeler engaged in fraudulent behavior by knowingly misrepresenting the health of the sheep sold to him. He sought damages based on the premise that these misrepresentations had caused him financial loss. Specifically, Randall requested vindictive damages in addition to actual damages, claiming that Wheeler's actions in selling diseased sheep warranted punitive compensation due to their potential impact on the broader sheep population.	Wheeler's defense centered on the assertion that mere falsity of representations was not enough to establish liability for fraud; it was essential to demonstrate that he knew the representations were false at the time of sale. Furthermore, Wheeler contended that the trial court had made errors in jury instructions that improperly suggested punitive damages could be awarded not strictly based on fraud but also for the act of selling diseased sheep, which was legal. He sought to have the judgment against him overturned, arguing that the jury had been misled regarding the criteria for awarding damages.

The case, August C. Swarth et al. v. The People ex rel. Paxton, took place in Chicago, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 15, 1884. The appellants, led by August C. Swarth, were in the business of selling intoxicating liquors at a retail establishment on 385 and 387 N. Clark Street. Their license, issued on June 29, 1883, authorized them to operate until April 1, 1884. This license was granted under an ordinance passed by the city, despite the new High License Law (enacted June 15, 1883) which mandated a higher fee of at least $500 for such licenses, effective July 1, 1883. The Attorney General sought to oust Swarth and his associates, arguing that their license was invalid due to various procedural issues, including that the license was issued without the required petition from local voters and was not compliant with the new law. The Superior Court of Cook County had originally decided against the appellants, claiming they were unlawfully exercising a franchise.	The plaintiffs, represented by the Attorney General, claimed that the license issued to Swarth and his associates was invalid. They argued that the issuance did not comply with the High License Law, asserting that the license was granted without the necessary petition from voters and that the signatures of the mayor and clerk were improperly affixed. The plaintiffs sought to establish that the appellants were engaging in unauthorized retail of intoxicating liquors and requested the court to reverse the lower court's judgment and issue an ouster.	The defendants (Swarth and associates) contended that their license was valid and should be upheld. They argued that the issuance by the city was lawful, noting that no application in writing was necessary under city authority, and that the mayor was authorized by city council ordinances to issue licenses. They maintained that the license's validity was not affected by the procedural concerns raised and that the changes to the municipal year did not retroactively invalidate their license. They also claimed that previous licenses do not hinder the issuance of a new one, and thus requested the court to dismiss the information against them.

In the case of Siegel, Cooper & Co. v. The Chicago Trust and Savings Bank, which took place in Chicago, Illinois, the background revolves around a promissory note dated March 5, 1887, in which Siegel, Cooper & Co. promised to pay $300 to D. Dalziel for the privilege of advertising on the North Chicago City Railway Co. streetcars for three months, starting May 15, 1887. The note was later endorsed to the Chicago Trust and Savings Bank (the appellee). Before the advertising privilege commenced, Dalziel lost the right to the advertisement, leading to the contention about whether the note was negotiable despite this failure of consideration. The case was brought by appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court after the Appellate Court affirmed the lower court's judgment in favor of the plaintiff. The core legal question was about the negotiability of the note when the payment depended on the future execution of a contract.	The plaintiff, Chicago Trust and Savings Bank, argued that the promissory note was negotiable and thus enforceable even though the payee (Dalziel) had failed to perform the obligation of providing advertising services. They claimed that the note’s face value and the specific payment date made it valid despite the potential lack of consideration at the time of endorsement. They sought to enforce the payment of the $300 against Siegel, Cooper & Co. based on the terms of the promissory note.	The defendants, Siegel, Cooper & Co., contended that the promissory note was not negotiable due to the failure of consideration, given that Dalziel forfeited the right to the advertising prior to the execution of the agreement.
