They argued that the condition for the payment depended on Dalziel's performance, which did not occur. They maintained that the bank could not recover the amount stated in the note as they should be aware of the failure of consideration on the part of Dalziel.

In 1884, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of National Furnace Company v. Keystone Manufacturing Company. The Keystone Manufacturing Company, a corporation based in Sterling, Illinois, initiated the lawsuit against the National Furnace Company, located in Depere, Wisconsin. The crux of the case revolved around a contract under which the National Furnace Company was supposed to supply Keystone with approximately seven hundred tons of "Lake Superior charcoal iron" for the upcoming business season, from July 9, 1879, to July 1, 1880. A.B. Meeker & Co., based in Chicago, acted as the sole agents for the National Furnace Company to sell its entire product. Issues were raised regarding whether Meeker & Co. had the authority to involve William M. Cox & Co. to fulfill the contract. The plaintiff argued that a valid contract existed, while the defendant contended that Meeker & Co. did not have the authority to bind the furnace company for future delivery of iron.	The Keystone Manufacturing Company claimed that it had a binding contract with the National Furnace Company, wherein the latter was obligated to supply all the pig iron required for its manufacturing needs during the specified season at a price of $22.35 per ton. The plaintiff argued that sufficient evidence proved the contract's existence and validity and sought damages for the defendant's alleged breach.	The National Furnace Company asserted that A.B. Meeker & Co. lacked the authority to authorize contract obligations on behalf of the furnace company, arguing that their commission agreement only allowed for the sale of existing products and not future deliveries. They contended that the contract lacked mutuality and certainty, asserting that it was void as it did not impose a binding obligation on the plaintiff to purchase any fixed quantity of iron.

The case "People’s Gaslight and Coke Co. v. Chicago Gaslight and Coke Co." was decided on January 6, 1887, in the State of Illinois. The parties involved were two gas companies: the People’s Gaslight and Coke Company (the appellant) and the Chicago Gaslight and Coke Company (the appellee). The conflict originated from a contract made in April 1862 wherein both companies agreed to refrain from laying gas mains or supplying gas in certain parts of Chicago—specifically, the north and south divisions for the appellant and the west division for the appellee. The appellant had previously laid pipes and established infrastructure in the city, acquiring rights and permissions from the legislature and local government. The contract was intended to prevent competition between the two companies in designated areas, benefitting both by allowing efficient service and investment in their respective operations. However, the issue arose when the appellee sought to breach this contract by attempting to extend its service into the appellant's territory, inciting the appellant to seek judicial enforcement of the agreement to avoid what they claimed would result in significant financial losses.	The People’s Gaslight and Coke Company argued that the Chicago Gaslight and Coke Company was threatening to breach their agreement not to compete in designated territories. They claimed that the enforcement of this contract was essential to protect their investments and that the damages associated with a breach would be difficult to quantify in a legal sense. The plaintiff requested specific performance of the contract, seeking a court order to restrain the appellee from laying any new gas mains or supplying gas within their agreed-upon territory.	The Chicago Gaslight and Coke Company contended that their previous agreement with the plaintiff constituted an illegal restraint of trade and was therefore void. They argued that such contracts, especially when they limit competition across significant areas, are against public policy. Furthermore, they claimed that the contract unjustly benefited one party over another and inhibited the market's natural competitive nature. They sought to have the court dismiss the plaintiff's claims and allow them the ability to expand their operations unimpeded.

In 1875, in Madison County, Illinois, John T. Fahnestock, on behalf of Gersham P. Gilham, initiated a legal action regarding a replevin bond. This case stemmed from a prior action where Gilham sought to reclaim approximately 1200 rails constituting a fence on his property, asserting ownership and the right to possess these goods. Initially, the replevin action was conducted before a justice of the peace, but after an amendment to the affidavit, some specifics regarding the property were altered. When the case was brought to the circuit court, the court ruled the bond inadmissible, claiming that the justice did not have jurisdiction over the replevin action. The jury subsequently ruled against Fahnestock. This appeal questioned whether Gilham, after seeking the court’s process and losing, could later contest the jurisdiction upon which the bond was based.	The plaintiff, John T. Fahnestock, contended that the replevin bond was valid and should be enforceable. He argued that even if the initial action lacked jurisdiction, it did not negate the obligation established under the bond. He sought to recover against the defendants based on the stipulations of the bond for the goods in question.	The defendants contended that the replevin bond was void as the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction when the bond was executed. They argued that the bond was intended solely for the protection of the constable involved in executing the writ and thus should not be enforceable. They maintained that claiming jurisdiction in the initial action, only to later challenge it, rendered any obligation under the bond invalid.

On December 20, 1877, George C. Lord filed a bill in equity against Henry Durand and others in the Cook County Circuit Court to quiet title to the Adams street property, which was the west half of the east half of lot 7, block 117, school section addition to Chicago. The defendant, William O. Heacock, had previously conveyed this property to Andrew Garrison for $3,000 in 1858; however, after obtaining a judgment against Heacock in 1860, the plaintiffs filed a creditors' bill claiming that the conveyance was fraudulent. In 1863, the court set aside certain fraudulent deeds but did not disturb the deed to the Adams street property. Following various legal proceedings and even a significant event, the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, the case was extensively delayed. After considerable litigation, including a decree in August 1875 that declared the deed from Heacock to Garrison as fraudulent, Lord subsequently acquired the property as a bona fide purchaser. By 1877, conflicting claims emerged between Durand and Lord, leading to this case where Durand sought to assert their claim over the disputed property continuously from claims and decrees stemming from previous court rulings.	The plaintiffs, Henry C. Durand and others, argued that the deed transferring the Adams street property from Heacock to Garrison was fraudulent and made without consideration to hinder creditors. They requested that the court recognize their prior judgment against Heacock, thus entitling them to the property in question. The plaintiffs sought to establish that under the current legal circumstances involving previous court rulings, their rights took precedence over the defendant's claim to the property.	The defendant, George C. Lord, contended that he was a bona fide purchaser without notice of the plaintiffs' claims regarding the history of the title. He argued that the ongoing litigation had been substantially abandoned by the plaintiffs, who failed to act diligently to preserve their claims in a timely manner. Lord maintained that the previous judgments and decrees did not affect his rights as a subsequent purchaser and that the plaintiffs' earlier claims had been waived due to lack of action, asserting this as grounds to maintain ownership of the property.

The case "O. L. Baskin v. R. Y. Benjamin" originated on October 20, 1882, in Turner Junction, Illinois, involving key individuals O. L. Baskin (the appellant) and R. Y. Benjamin (the appellee). Baskin, along with his associates, was engaged in preparing a history of DuPage County. Benjamin allegedly entered into a contract, promising to pay Baskin $70 for including a lithograph portrait of himself in the history. However, at the time of signing, Benjamin claimed he did not agree to the contract but rather signed a blank note to provide a sample of his handwriting at the request of an agent, John M. Rouk. The case was initially heard by a justice of the peace and later appealed to the circuit court, where a jury ruled in favor of Benjamin. Baskin moved for a new trial, which was denied, prompting the appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court. The trial introduced testimonies regarding inaccuracies and omissions in the history, which the court later deemed improper evidence. The court expressed that such evidence could mislead the jury and distract from the core issue.	The plaintiff, O. L. Baskin, argued that R. Y. Benjamin entered into a valid contract agreeing to pay $70 for the inclusion of his portrait in a history book. Baskin sought enforcement of this contract and recovery of the owed payment upon the completion of the history.	The defendant, R. Y. Benjamin, defended against Baskin's claims by asserting the contract's invalidity, stating he never authorized the signing of the contract and only provided a handwriting sample. He also raised a defense of the failure of consideration, arguing that the work was not done as promised and claimed inaccuracies in the history that should nullify any obligation under the contract.

In September 1871, in Grundy County, Illinois, the case "Solyman Bell v. Allen F. Mallory" arose from allegations of malicious prosecution. The plaintiff, Solyman Bell, claimed that the defendant, Allen F. Mallory, falsely accused him, along with two others, of committing a riot. Mallory alleged that Bell and the others had trespassed on his property, used violent language, and threatened him with a pistol while attempting to take a colt owned by Mallory. As a result of these accusations, Mallory secured an arrest warrant for Bell, compelling him to appear in court. Ultimately, there was no indictment against Bell, and he was released. In his lawsuit, Bell sought damages for the harm caused by the false charges, originally seeking $10,000, and a jury awarded him $1,830 in damages, which was later reduced by the court to $600 upon a motion for a new trial.	The plaintiff, Solyman Bell, claimed that defendant Allen F. Mallory maliciously and without cause accused him of participating in a riot. He argued that Mallory falsely swore to these charges, which led to his wrongful arrest and court appearance. Bell sought compensation for the damages incurred due to the malicious prosecution, initially demanding $10,000, which represented the losses and legal troubles he faced because of the baseless accusations made by Mallory.	The defendant, Allen F. Mallory, contended that he had probable cause for his accusations against Bell, as the actions taken by Bell and his companions constituted a riot as defined by law. Mallory argued that the evidence presented demonstrated that the group acted unlawfully by attempting to take the colt by force. He maintained that Bell was a significant participant in the unlawful acts and sought to have the judgment against him reversed.

In September 1873, the case "The Columbus, Chicago and Indiana Central Railway Company v. William B. Skidmore" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County. The case originated when William B. Skidmore sued the Columbus, Chicago and Indiana Central Railway Company over two promissory notes initially executed by the Chicago and Cincinnati Railroad Company. These notes were endorsed to Skidmore by Thomas Munroe. The plaintiff contended that after a series of consolidations, the original note makers became part of the railway company now being sued. The court's attention was drawn to the certificates from the Secretary of State regarding the articles of consolidation, which the defendants challenged as competent evidence. However, the court affirmed that these certified copies were indeed valid and could be used as evidence in court. The central legal question revolved around the capacity of the consolidated company to be sued under the new name they had assumed after the consolidation.	The plaintiff, William B. Skidmore, asserted that he was owed the amount from two promissory notes that had been endorsed to him. He argued that the defendant railway company, being a consolidation of previous entities, was legally obligated to honor these notes. He requested the court to declare the defendant liable for the debts incurred by the former companies that had merged into the current railway entity.	The Columbus, Chicago and Indiana Central Railway Company defended itself by arguing the general issue and disputing the competency of the certificates of the Secretary of State as evidence to prove the consolidation of the companies. The defendant sought to reverse the circuit court's judgment in favor of the plaintiff, questioning whether the new consolidated company could be held liable under the name by which it was sued.

On February 23, 1865, a co-partnership was formed between Charles H. Rosenstiel, William S. Gray, and Henderson to manufacture and sell woolen goods in Stephenson County, Illinois. Following the sale of Henderson's interest to David H. Sunderland, the firm continued as C. H. Rosenstiel & Company, with Rosenstiel, Gray, and Sunderland as partners. This partnership lasted until March 4, 1873, when Rosenstiel sold his one-third interest in the firm to George Thompson and Charles D. Blanchard. Subsequently, on June 14, 1873, Gray and Sunderland sold a one-third interest to William W. Robey. A dispute arose regarding the accounting of partnership profits and losses, leading Gray, Sunderland, and Robey to file a bill against Rosenstiel for an accounting of all partnership affairs since its inception. The Appellate Court upheld the Circuit Court's decree after a master's report determined amounts owed among the partners, including Rosenstiel owing $4,332.84. Rosenstiel raised several exceptions to this report, which were ultimately dismissed by the court.	The plaintiffs, Gray, Sunderland, and Robey, sought a thorough accounting of the partnership's financial dealings from its inception to the sale of Rosenstiel's interest. They argued that Rosenstiel owed specific amounts to each of them based on partnership profits and financial contributions. The bill aimed to clarify the division of assets and liabilities after the partnership's dissolution.	Rosenstiel contended against the findings of the master's report, arguing that the accounting methodology was flawed and that it did not consider the partnership’s assets. He claimed that he had been debited for payments made on behalf of the firm which should not have been his personal liability. Rosenstiel also asserted that Robey was not a valid partner at the time his liabilities were assessed and requested that the court not enforce the payment to Robey.

The case, titled "The Dueber Watch Case Manufacturing Company v. Peter Lapp et al.," was adjudicated in the Illinois Appellate Court in February 1890. The conflict arose in Cook County, Illinois, wherein the Dueber Watch Case Manufacturing Company (plaintiff) sought to recover payments for goods sold to the defendants, Peter Lapp et al. The defendants filed a notice of set-off, contesting the amount owed by claiming discounts or rebates based on an alleged agreement with the plaintiff concerning the sale of watch cases. During the trial, the evidence presented indicated a longstanding business relationship with a specific understanding regarding discounts if prices were reduced for retail trade. The jury found in favor of the defendants, determining that the evidence supported their claims of set-off. The plaintiff subsequently moved for a new trial, arguing surprise due to the defendants’ testimony and the existence of newly discovered evidence, which the court found insufficient. It concluded that the plaintiff had prior notice of the defendants' claims and failed to substantiate their surprise adequately.	The plaintiff claimed the right to recover for goods sold to the defendants and asserted that the trial court erred in ruling against them. They argued that they were taken by surprise by the defendants’ evidence about an old agreement which they claimed was negated by a new contract. Furthermore, the plaintiff sought a new trial on the grounds of newly discovered evidence that could demonstrate the defendants were not entitled to the set-off.	The defendants contended that their claim of set-off was based on a long-established agreement concerning discounts on previously purchased goods. They maintained that the plaintiff was not surprised by their claims, having been informed in advance through the notice of set-off. The defendants argued that the plaintiff’s request for a new trial was unwarranted, as the evidence presented was sufficiently compelling to support their case without any errors of law by the trial court.

In September 1869, in Peoria County, Illinois, Lewis Garrison and Benjamin Garrison were involved in a legal dispute with Duncan McGregor arising from a horse race betting incident. The case originated when McGregor sought to recover $200, which he lost on the race, from the Garrison siblings. The amount had been placed in the hands of a stakeholder, identified as Camp, who distributed the winnings following the race results—$100 to Lewis Garrison and $50 each to Benjamin and Jeremiah Garrison. McGregor appealed after obtaining a judgment in his favor in the circuit court for the full $200, arguing that he should not have to pursue each Garrison individually for the portions they received.	The plaintiff, Duncan McGregor, claimed that he was entitled to recover the total amount lost due to the horse race betting. He argued that the Garrison brothers were liable for the entire sum because they were the parties with whom he made the bet, regardless of how the winnings were distributed afterward.	The Garrison brothers contended that McGregor should not be able to recover the full amount from them, as they had not all jointly participated in the bet and the winnings were not claimed collectively. They argued that McGregor should sue each Garrison individually for the portions each received from the stakeholder. Additionally, they maintained that any arrangement they had for the distribution of winnings did not affect McGregor's rights to recover.

In 1862, in Marion County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between James A. Davenport and John V. Davenport (Plaintiffs in Error) and Martha D. Haynie, along with her minor son William D. Haynie (Defendants in Error). The case centers around a property that, prior to 1853, was owned by Abner F. Haynie, who had entered into a partnership with James Marshall for running a drug store. When the partnership dissolved, Marshall continued to possess the property without transferring it to Haynie, despite the latter's legal claim. Haynie passed away in 1853 without securing the property's conveyance, leaving Martha D. Haynie and her son as the rightful claimants. They filed a bill in chancery to reclaim the property, asserting that Marshall had unlawfully occupied it and rented it to the Davenports. The court documents revealed accusations against Marshall for wasteful alterations to the property and failure to pay rents owed since Abner's death, amounting to over $200. Various arguments ensued regarding the rightful ownership and rental agreements made during the partnership.	The plaintiffs, Martha D. Haynie and William D. Haynie, claimed that they were entitled to the property's conveyance and demanded an account of the rents, damages for waste, and that the court prevent further harm to their estate. They argued that James Marshall had possessed and rented the property unlawfully and had neglected to convey it after Abner Haynie complied with all court directives regarding the sale.	The defendants, including James Marshall and the Davenports, argued that they had rented the premises in good faith, believing that they had the right to do so. They contended that the rental agreements were valid and asserted that the alterations made to the property did not constitute waste. Furthermore, they indicated that the liability for rent should be limited to the respective periods each tenant occupied the property and that they had not acted fraudulently in their dealings.

Spoor Mackey filed a legal case against Edward McCaffrey in the Illinois Appellate Court, with a decision date of August 3, 1887. The case stemmed from prior proceedings where Mackey recovered a judgment in the Superior Court of Cook County on November 11, 1886, for damages amounting to $1,044.55. Following this judgment, a writ of execution was issued, allowing the Sheriff to levy on McCaffrey's stock of goods, which were ultimately sold for $607.64 on November 23, 1886. The plaintiff's recovery was subsequently challenged by Cary, Ogden & Parker, who claimed to have had their own judgment against McCaffrey from a Justice’s court dated October 1, 1886, for the amount of $303. They filed a petition to have the Sheriff pay them a portion of the proceeds from Mackey’s execution sale, claiming a priority lien based on their earlier judgment. However, the court noted issues with the validity of their execution and petition.	Mackey's primary argument was that his judgment and the execution were valid and rightful in levying on the defendant's goods, thereby entitling him to the proceeds from the sale of those goods. He contended that the claims made by Cary, Ogden & Parker were insufficient and lacked the proper validating facts necessary to supersede his claim regarding the priority of the lien.	The defendant McCaffrey did not explicitly defend against the original judgment but rather became a part of the dispute when the Cary, Ogden & Parker petitioned the court. Their claim hinged on asserting a priority for their earlier judgment; however, they struggled to demonstrate that they possessed a valid execution or a confirmed lien against McCaffrey's property that would justify a claim against the proceeds generated from Mackey's execution sale.

In the case of Nathan P. Herrington et al. v. George McCollum, the events unfolded in Peoria County, Illinois, during the 1860s, culminating in a judgment by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The dispute originated from a series of promissory notes secured by a trust deed. Plaintiffs Nathan P. Herrington and others argued that under an agreement with A. B. Moore, two of the notes were to be prioritized for payment over a third note retained by Moore. Over the course of legal proceedings, it was claimed that the notes were transferred in line with this agreement. The case had a history of earlier hearings, dismissed bills, and subsequent reinstatements, which added complexity regarding notice to involved parties. As new evidence was introduced, including claims of property sales during litigation, the rights of subsequent purchasers John P. Havighorst and John H. Kramer came into question. Their claims of bona fide purchase without notice of the original lien became central to the court's decision.	The plaintiffs contended that they had a prior claim on the property based on an agreement related to the notes secured by the trust deed. They asserted that subsequent purchasers had notice of their rights, even if only constructive, and sought a decree for the sale of the property to settle the unpaid claims under the trust deed.	The defendants, including the subsequent purchasers Havighorst and Kramer, argued that they had purchased the property in good faith for valuable consideration without actual or constructive notice of the plaintiffs' claims. They maintained that the original dismissal of the case meant that they were unaffected by any claims made during the litigation and contended that the plaintiffs had failed to diligently pursue their rights, thus waiving any possible claim.

In the case of Elias Merwin v. The City of Chicago, which took place in September 1867 in Cook County, Illinois, the plaintiff, Elias Merwin, initiated a suit in attachment against a third party, Samuel Nicolson. The City of Chicago was summoned as a garnishee during this judicial proceeding. Prior to providing any response, the city was discharged from the garnishee process on July 20, 1867, at the direction of the court, which ruled that municipal corporations are not liable to the process of garnishment regardless of the nature of their debts. This decision stemmed from a concern for public policy, as allowing garnishment against such corporations could impede their governmental functions and public service responsibilities. This ruling was based on precedents, including The City of Chicago v. Hasley, confirming that municipal corporations should not be drawn into private debt collection matters, thereby protecting their operations and the public good. Merwin subsequently appealed the court's decision.	The plaintiff, Elias Merwin, asserted that the City of Chicago should be held liable to the process of garnishment to facilitate the collection of debts owed to him by Samuel Nicolson. He argued that the city’s financial obligations should be addressed through legal proceedings like any private entity, urging the court to require the city to respond to the garnishment summons.	The City of Chicago, represented by its counsel, argued against the liability for garnishment, citing the principle that municipal corporations are not subject to such processes due to public policy considerations. They contended that allowing garnishment would undermine the city's ability to fulfill its governmental duties and could lead to extensive litigation, distracting from its primary functions. The city requested to be discharged from the garnishee status without needing to provide an answer.

John R. Steele was indicted for forgery by the Recorder’s Court in Chicago during the October Term of 1866. He was accused of attempting to pass a forged check drawn by H. M. Thompson & Co. on September 25, 1866, for the amount of $990, supposedly in favor of William E. Hudson or bearer. Following his arraignment, Steele pleaded not guilty and sought a continuance to present testimony from a material witness, John Lynch, who resided in Philadelphia. Despite his efforts to secure Lynch's attendance through letters and telegrams, Steele was unable to do so, leading the court to deny his request for continuance. The trial proceeded, resulting in Steele's conviction, with the jury imposing a 13-year sentence to the penitentiary for his crimes. Steele's lawyer argued that there were glaring flaws in the prosecution's case and highlighted the importance of witness testimony in establishing his defense. However, the court found no merit in Steele's claims for an extension of time and concluded that the evidence against him was substantial.	The plaintiff, John R. Steele, contended that the check he attempted to pass was received in payment of a prior debt and was represented to him as genuine. He asserted that his defense relied on the testimony of key witnesses, particularly John Lynch, who could affirm the legitimacy of the check. Steele argued that the absence of vital witnesses impaired his ability to prepare a sufficient defense against the charges.	The defense emphasized that Steele did not knowingly possess a forged document and was merely acting under the belief that the check was genuine. They highlighted Steele's efforts to procure witness testimony to support his claims and sought to establish reasonable doubt regarding his intent and knowledge of the forgery. The defense contended that the evidence presented by the prosecution was insufficient to convict Steele.

In January 1869, in Marion County, Illinois, a legal case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court involving Wilson Campbell as the plaintiff and Nathan D. Beck as the defendant. The case arose when the defendant, who was serving as the county clerk, issued a marriage license for the marriage of a minor daughter belonging to the plaintiff without obtaining the necessary consent from the parent or guardian. The license originally authorized the marriage of Ephraim Boaz and Zenia Beck, but it was later altered by a justice of the peace to permit Ephraim Bolds to marry Zenia Beck instead. The deputy clerk confirmed that he issued the license, but was unaware of the alterations made. The case presented the central question of whether the clerk could be held liable for the penalty specified in the marriage laws for issuing a license that was later altered in a way that led to a marriage taking place—the marriage ultimately did not occur by virtue of the license as it was initially issued. The evidence was put forth to examine the roles and responsibilities of the involved parties with respect to the stipulations of the marriage statute.	The plaintiff, Wilson Campbell, asserted that Nathan D. Beck should be held liable for the penalty associated with the issuance of a marriage license to his minor daughter without proper consent. Campbell contended that the alteration of the license and subsequent unauthorized marriage resulted in a violation of the law meant to protect parents or guardians from such actions. He sought a judgment that would impose the statutory penalty upon the defendant for his actions as the county clerk.	Nathan D. Beck, the defendant, argued that he could not be held liable for the statutory penalty because the marriage did not occur as authorized by the original license. He claimed that the license issued did not grant approval for the marriage between the minor daughter and Ephraim Bolds, as there was a fundamental discrepancy in the names presented. Additionally, Beck maintained that the responsibility lay not with him but with the justice of the peace who altered the license, thus absolving him of any wrongdoing or liability in connection with the matter.

The case "Ann Beers v. Leonard Myers, Administrator" took place in Vermilion County, Illinois, with the final judgment issued on May 25, 1888. The key individuals involved were Ann Beers, the appellant, and Leonard Myers, the administrator of the estate of Joseph L. Shepherd, the deceased guardian of Ann Beers. The background of the case revolves around a claim made by Ann Beers against the estate of Joseph Shepherd for $2,371.80, which she alleged was received by him as her guardian. Joseph Shepherd had been appointed guardian of Ann and her sisters on June 24, 1862, after stating in his petition that they were entitled to property from the estate of their deceased mother. Despite having received funds from this inheritance dating from 1857 to 1860, Shepherd never reported his actions as a guardian nor made any official accounting. After Shepherd's death in 1886, Ann Beers waited nearly thirteen years after reaching the age of majority before pursuing her claim, raising the question of whether the claim was barred by the statute of limitations.	Ann Beers argued that the funds her guardian received constituted a direct trust, and therefore, her claim should not be barred by the statute of limitations. She contended that Shepherd’s failure to account for the money constituted a breach of duty as her guardian and sought compensation from the estate for the funds mismanaged or lost by him. Her primary legal request was for the full amount of her claim against the estate, with the assertion that she had the right to recover the funds as her guardian's action, or lack thereof, had created a fiduciary obligation.	Leonard Myers, representing the estate of Joseph L. Shepherd, contended that Beers' claim was barred by the statute of limitations because it was filed only after a considerable delay after Beers reached adulthood. The administrator argued that during her father's life, Beers had not pursued the claim, indicating a lack of legal obligation for Shepherd to account for the lost funds. Myers maintained that the character of the funds did not constitute a direct trust as claimed by Beers, thus supporting the application of the statute of limitations.

In 1883, Sarah A. Greenman filed a case against her former husband, William R. Greenman, and their sons, Bradley D. Greenman and George H. Greenman, in the Knox Circuit Court of Illinois. The case emerged after Sarah claimed a right to their homestead property and sought to contest fraudulent conveyances made by her husband to their sons while they temporarily relocated to Michigan. Sarah alleged that William had forged deeds transferring ownership of the property to their sons without consideration, thereby obstructing her right to collect alimony following their divorce. The circuit court ruled in favor of Sarah, granting her a homestead claim, half of the property rents, and the right to have the property sold to satisfy her judgment. The case was subsequently appealed, leading to judicial scrutiny of the alleged fraudulent actions.	Sarah A. Greenman argued that she had equitable rights to the homestead property due to her prior occupancy and that the conveyances her husband executed to their sons were fraudulent and intended to defraud her of her rightful alimony. She sought validation of her homestead claim, the resignation of fraudulent deeds, and restitution in the form of the property's rental income to satisfy her judgment.	The defendants, William R. Greenman and his sons, contended that the conveyances were legitimate transactions backed by legal title and alleged that Sarah's claims were barred by statutes of limitation. They argued that the formal ownership of the property had legally passed to Bradley D. Greenman, and therefore, Sarah had no claim to either the property or its rents.

Henry Mansfield, Administrator of the estate of Joseph I. Moore, brought this case against Andrew Hoagland in the Illinois Supreme Court. The events trace back to the assignment of a judgment on the land of Joseph I. Moore, which had been sold under execution. In 1859, a court ruled in favor of Joshua J. Moore, stating that an innocent purchaser, in this case Andrew Hoagland, could retain the property. He claimed that the assignment he received was valid and not fraudulent. After further hearings and the introduction of additional evidence in 1869, the Court was required to determine whether the assignment of the judgment and certificate of purchase from Joseph C. Hoagland to Andrew Hoagland was fraudulent. The court conducted a retrial to assess the validity of the assignment and the evidence surrounding its execution.	The plaintiff, Henry Mansfield, argued that the assignment from Joseph C. Hoagland to Andrew Hoagland was fraudulent and should be set aside. He maintained that the real intent behind the assignment was misleading and that the heirs or administrator of Joseph I. Moore should not have to bear the consequences of perceived fraudulent transactions.	Andrew Hoagland defended his position by asserting that the assignment was made in good faith and for valuable consideration. He denied the allegations of fraud and argued that he was an innocent purchaser who had no knowledge of any wrongdoing. His main request was that the court recognize the validity of the assignment and uphold his rights to the property.

In the case of Brown v. Keller, decided in April 1864, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed issues arising from a previous judgment that had been reversed in April 1863 due to non-joinder in error. The legal proceedings took place in Illinois, and the defendant’s attorney, Mr. Redfield, moved for the court to set aside the reversal. The motion was based on the argument that the required legal notice (scire facias) had not been served ten days prior to the term in which the judgment was reversed. The court noted that no notice had been given for this application, and there was no valid reason for the delay in bringing the matter before the court. As a result, the court found the application fundamentally flawed. Furthermore, the court emphasized the seriousness of attorneys’ pledges regarding the sufficiency of documents presented to justify such orders, citing that procuring an order under inaccurate circumstances was a serious misconduct that would lead to the court taking action. Ultimately, the court ruled to set aside the earlier judgment of reversal for non-joinder.	The plaintiffs, represented by Mr. Redfield, contended that the prior judgment of reversal was invalid because the required notice (scire facias) had not been appropriately served before the reversal. They argued that the court should rectify this oversight to restore the previous ruling.	The defendant’s defense focused on the procedural aspects of the case, asserting that the application to set aside the reversal was lacking due to the absence of notice and a reasonable explanation for the delay in the appeal process. They contended that the procedural failures constituted a fatal flaw in the claims against them.

In April 1849, Israel B. Holmes (the appellant), then a minor, entered a land purchase at the land office in Dixon, Illinois, using a warrant he earned through his own labor. Appellant had previously worked for a man named Smith, who agreed that the wages earned would be used to purchase a land warrant which would allow them to acquire land together, with each receiving half. However, when the appellant entered the land, it was done independently and in his own name, with his father's (the appellee) agreement. A dispute arose over the ownership of the land after the appellee, John H. Holmes, claimed that the appellant was holding the legal title as a trustee for him based on a verbal agreement. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following a decree favoring the appellee in a lower court.	The plaintiff, John H. Holmes, argued that he was entitled to a half interest in the land entered by his son, Israel B. Holmes, based on an alleged verbal agreement prior to the entry that the land would be entered in the son's name, but upon reaching majority, he would convey half to his father. The plaintiff sought a legal conveyance of the land title from the appellant.	The defendant, Israel B. Holmes, contended that the land warrant and the title of the land belonged solely to him as he had earned the warrant through his own work and entered the land in his own name. He argued that the father had no ownership claim since there was no evidence of any agreement that resulted in a trust, and furthermore, there was no payment made by the father towards the purchase price as required to establish any claim.

The case "The Continental Life Insurance Company v. Catharine Thoena, Adm’x" was decided on January 4, 1888, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute originated in East St. Louis, where George Thoena, the insured, had taken out a life insurance policy with Continental Life Insurance Company on May 15, 1883. Following Thoena’s death on February 10, 1885, his representative, Catharine Thoena, sought to claim the death benefit of $1,500 under the policy. The insurance company contested the claim, arguing that Thoena had made false statements in the insurance application regarding his occupation and lifestyle, specifically that he had misrepresented his profession as a "general merchant" when he was actually a saloon keeper, and had falsely claimed to use stimulants moderately without excess. Evidence showed that the insurance agent was aware of Thoena's true occupation and habits at the time of the application. The jury ruled in favor of Thoena, leading to an appeal by the insurance company against this verdict.	Catharine Thoena, as the plaintiff, argued that her late husband had fulfilled all obligations under the insurance policy by paying the premiums required up until his death. She contended that the insurance application’s alleged misstatements regarding occupation and use of stimulants were not made with an intention to deceive, and thus should not void the policy. The plaintiff sought the payment of the life insurance benefit amounting to $1,500.	The defendant, Continental Life Insurance Company, claimed that George Thoena misrepresented his occupation and habits, stating he was a "general merchant" instead of a saloon keeper and provided false assurances about his moderate use of alcohol and avoidance of tobacco and narcotics. They asserted that these misrepresentations constituted breaches of warranty that invalidated the insurance contract, allowing them to deny the claim. The defendant also argued that the jury should not have admitted certain evidence presented by the plaintiff.

The case "St. Patrick’s Catholic Church of Sterling v. John Daly" was decided on January 25, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Sterling, Illinois, involving St. Patrick’s Catholic Church and John Daly, the church's priest at the time. The case traces back to conflicting claims regarding property ownership and financial transactions between the church and Daly. Daly had advanced money for the purchase and improvement of certain church lots. The primary contention was whether Daly, who held legal title to the lots, had purchased them for the church and if he was to be held accountable for the church's financial activities. The case had previously been reviewed by the court, which led to a reference to a master in chancery to account for the financial dealings. The court found issues regarding the ownership of lots and the responsibility of the priest for funds raised through pew rents and collections, which were deemed to belong to him for his support, rather than the church itself. Ultimately, it was concluded that certain lots belonged to the church, yet others did not, affecting financial obligations between the parties.	St. Patrick’s Catholic Church argued that it had a rightful claim to the properties in question. It sought a decree to establish that Daly was holding the titles to the lots in trust for the church. The church contended that the funds used regarding the properties were church assets and that Daly should be accountable for specific collections and pew rents, which they believed should contribute to the church's financial well-being.	John Daly defended against the church’s claims by asserting that he had purchased the lots with his own funds and was thus entitled to retain the title. He contended that, according to church laws and customs, he was not accountable for the pew rents or penny collections. In his cross-bill, he claimed the right to an accounting for the money he had advanced for the church, seeking recognition of this advancement as a debt owed to him, secured by a lien on the properties.

In the case of James Bozarth et al. v. William Largent, which took place in Tazewell County, Illinois, the event surrounding the legal dispute began with the ownership of certain lands by Louisa Bozarth. Louisa was the sole owner of the property, having inherited it from her father, and she was married to Asa Bozarth on August 19, 1863. The couple lived together until Louisa's death on November 1, 1868. Before her death, on March 5, 1868, Louisa and Asa executed a mortgage on the lands to secure a loan from Anna B. Cohrs. This mortgage included a clause that released all homestead rights. Following Louisa's death, the property was foreclosed upon, and a sale was executed under a decree in favor of the mortgagee. After several transactions, the property eventually came into the possession of William Largent, who became the defendant in this ejectment action brought forth by Louisa's heirs—James Bozarth, Mary L. Bozarth, and Ida B. Cook—seeking to recover the property.	The plaintiffs, as the heirs of Louisa Bozarth, argued that they held a rightful claim to the land, with a vested interest in the property as Louisa's heirs. They contended that the foreclosure sale was invalid and that any interests held by their father, Asa, should not affect their ownership rights derived from their mother, Louisa. Essentially, they sought recovery of the land based on the assertion of their legal rights as heirs.	The defendant, William Largent, contended that the foreclosure sale was valid and that he held rightful title to the property. He argued that Asa Bozarth had acquired an estate by the curtesy upon Louisa's death, entitling him to an interest in the land, which was subject to seizure and sale under execution for his debts. Largent asserted that the plaintiffs could not recover the property since their father's life estate allowed Largent continued possession until the life tenant's death.

Virginia B. Lochnitt initiated a replevin action against Charles Stockon and others in 1889 in Christian County, Illinois. The dispute arose over the rightful ownership of a set of fence rails. The case was initially heard by a justice of the peace, who ruled in favor of Lochnitt against Stockon and Newitt, but dismissed the case against Hill, who was a landlord claiming interest in the rails. Stockon and Newitt appealed the judgment, leading to a new trial in the Circuit Court, where the court considered the case de novo. During this trial, the issue of ownership was central, particularly since the rails were in temporary possession of Newitt, who did not claim ownership. The testimony of a witness, Bennett Lochnitt, regarding the ownership of the rails was also scrutinized, especially concerning statements about their return to Hill. Despite conflicts in evidence, the jury ultimately sided with the defendants, supporting the claim that the property belonged to Hill.	Virginia B. Lochnik's primary argument was that she had the rightful ownership of the fence rails and sought their return through the replevin process. She contended that the defendants, particularly Stockon and Newitt, were wrongfully retaining her property. Lochnitt requested the court to order the return of the rails and argued against the defendants' testimonies that contradicted her claims of ownership.	Charles Stockon and the other defendants argued that the ownership of the fence rails was not with Lochnitt but belonged to Hill, who had expressed his claims during the proceedings. They contended that Lochnitt failed to provide adequate evidence to support her ownership and emphasized the jury's finding that supported their defense. The defendants requested the court to uphold the jury's verdict, thereby maintaining possession of the property and denying any claims from Lochnitt.

The case "John B. Heustis et al. v. Daniel G. Johnson et al." arose in the year 1876 in Kendall County, Illinois. The plaintiff, John B. Heustis and others, initiated the suit against Daniel G. Johnson, who served as the executor of an estate. The central issue was that Johnson was accused of failing to fulfill his responsibilities as an executor by not properly accounting for the estate and not making a timely final settlement. The plaintiffs contended that Johnson had used various excuses to evade his obligations. A writ of error was filed, challenging a prior ruling from the circuit court, which had dismissed the case after sustaining a demurrer to the plaintiffs' bill in chancery. The plaintiffs sought intervention under the chancery jurisdiction, claiming that the situation warranted such action due to Johnson's inaction.	The plaintiffs argued that Daniel G. Johnson, as executor of the estate, was negligent in his duties by failing to promptly administer and settle the estate, thereby harming the beneficiaries. They alleged that he had used various excuses to avoid accountability. They sought relief from the court, contending that the matter warranted the chancery court's intervention due to the failure of the executor to act properly and timely.	The defendant, Daniel G. Johnson, contended that the circuit court did not err in sustaining the demurrer. He argued that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate adequate grounds for the chancery court’s jurisdiction over the estate administration, as such matters should typically be handled by the probate court. The defendant asserted that the county court had the jurisdiction and necessary powers to address the relief sought by the plaintiffs, and thus the chancery bill was inappropriate.

In 1868, in Sangamon County, Illinois, George B. Richardson brought a legal action against Uriah Mann and Daniel Bailey, who were acting as commissioners of highways. The case arose from a public road project in which the commissioners sought to lay out a roadway across Richardson's land. When the commissioners and Richardson could not agree on the compensation due to Richardson for the land taken, they submitted the matter to arbitration as per an agreement dated September 3, 1868. This agreement outlined that the arbitrators would determine the damages and make an award by a specified deadline. Subsequently, an award was made on September 5, 1868, directing Mann and Bailey to pay Richardson $650, but it was not sealed as required by the conditions of their bond. The legal action followed when Richardson sought to enforce this award. The case ultimately questioned whether the commissioners could be held personally liable for the award, as they acted in an official capacity without clear authority to arbitrate such public concerns.	The plaintiff, George B. Richardson, claimed that the defendants, Mann and Bailey, were personally liable for the arbitration award of $650 made in his favor. He argued that their actions, as commissioners of highways, constituted a contract, and hence they should abide by the award or be held accountable for failing to do so.	The defendants contended that they had no authority to submit the matter of damages to arbitration, as their role was a personal duty imposed by law, which could not be delegated. They argued that since the award was not made in accordance with the bonding conditions, and crucially, it was not executed under the seals of the arbitrators, they could not be held personally liable.

In 1831, Lewis Bailey, the administrator of the estate of Stephen Benedict (deceased), brought a case against James B. Campbell in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over a farm which was originally public land where improvements had been made by Bailey. The improvements included cultivation and the erection of a dwelling house, which Bailey sold to his intestate (Stephen Benedict). Benedict then leased the property to Bartholomew, who subsequently leased it to McKernan. McKernan ultimately sold the improvements to Campbell, who occupied the farm from 1829 to 1831. The case was tried in the La Salle Circuit Court, where the jury ruled in favor of Campbell. The central legal question revolved around whether Bailey, or his intestate, could claim for use and occupation without being recognized as the owner or having a contractual agreement for rent payment with Campbell.	The plaintiff, Bailey, contended that he was entitled to recover rent for the use and occupation of the farm based on the improvements made upon it, arguing that either he or his intestate owned the property or that there was an implied contract requiring Campbell to pay rent for his occupancy. He sought to reverse the judgment against him for costs, arguing that the court had misapplied the law concerning the relationship of landlord and tenant.	Campbell, the defendant, argued that there was no legal basis for the claim regarding rent since he had acquired improvements with the expectation of ownership, and not as a tenant. He maintained that the plaintiff failed to establish ownership of the land or an express contract for rent. Therefore, he requested that the judgment in favor of the defendant be upheld and costs be awarded to him.

In 1853, in Kane County, Illinois, a slander case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court by Henry Petrie against William Sloan. The incident involved Sloan allegedly making slanderous remarks that accused Petrie of perjury. Sloan pleaded not guilty and additionally submitted a special plea of justification. During the trial, Petrie provided evidence to support his claim that Sloan did, in fact, speak the slanderous words. Sloan attempted to justify his statements with evidence, claiming his remarks were warranted. However, the trial court instructed the jury that if they believed Sloan's justification failed, they should consider the plea as an aggravation of damages. This instruction was based on differing legal precedents regarding whether unsuccessful justifications can exacerbate damages. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of Petrie, resulting in a judgment against Sloan.	Henry Petrie, the plaintiff, argued that William Sloan made defamatory statements accusing him of perjury, which constituted slander. Petrie sought damages for the harm caused by these allegations, asserting that the remarks were false and damaging to his reputation. The crux of his claim was substantiating that the words Sloan spoke were slanderous, requiring the jury to consider the impact of the statements in assessing damages.	William Sloan, the defendant, contended that his remarks were justified and that he acted in good faith when making them. He pleaded not guilty and claimed a special justification for his statements. Sloan's defense relied on evidence purportedly supporting his belief that the accusations were true. He argued that the trial court erred in instructing the jury to treat his failed justification as an aggravation of damages, asserting that the motivation behind his plea should be considered, and maintained that the attempt to justify was made sincerely.

In April 1860, the case "Samuel P. Baily, Appellant, v. Martha and Mary Doolittle, and Isabella Sampson, Appellees" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered on the partition of a piece of land, where the appellees (Martha and Mary Doolittle, and Isabella Sampson) claimed ownership of two-thirds of the property, based on a previous agreement and title confirmations. Samuel P. Baily, the appellant, claimed his ownership through a tax deed received from a sheriff's sale for unpaid taxes on the land, dated May 7, 1847. He presented evidence of tax payments made from 1847 to 1856 and his possession of the land during that time. However, the court required a valid foundation for the tax deed, including an accurate judgment and precept, which was claimed to be defective as no dollar amounts were specified. The court also noted that Baily had entered into a purchase agreement with R. S. Doolittle, wherein he was responsible for paying future taxes, effectively undermining his claim to the land through the tax title alone.	The plaintiffs, Martha and Mary Doolittle, and Isabella Sampson, claimed ownership of two-thirds of the land, substantiating their title with evidence and a legal petition for partition. They presented a compelling case in the Tazewell Circuit Court that affirmed their rights to the property, which Baily contested on the grounds of his tax deed.	Samuel P. Baily argued that his tax deed provided him with a legitimate claim to the land despite the title challenges. He presented evidence of taxes paid over several years and argued that he had possessed the premises. Baily contended that the deed operated as a color of title, which under the limitation act, could bar the plaintiffs from recovering the property. However, the court highlighted the inadequacies in Baily's evidence regarding the judgment and precept related to the tax sale.

The case of *Phoenix Insurance Company of Brooklyn v. Chester B. Lebcher* took place in 1886, following a fire incident that occurred on February 11, 1884, in Miles City, Montana. The plaintiff, Chester B. Lebcher, held an insurance policy from the Phoenix Insurance Company, which stipulated that any claims must be made within twelve months of the fire incident. After the fire, Lebcher attempted to negotiate a settlement with the insurance company's adjuster, W. L. Wilder. Discussions ensued regarding the compensation for the loss, with conflicting amounts mentioned—Lebcher claiming he was entitled to more than Wilder's offer of $600 or $750. After several correspondences, Lebcher ultimately decided to pursue legal action, but he did not file the suit until August 25, 1885, well past the one-year limit established by the policy. The insurance company defended against his claim, citing the expiration of the limitation period as a valid defense.	Lebcher claimed that he was entitled to recover the losses incurred from the fire under the insurance policy. He argued that negotiations with the insurance company's agent had been ongoing, which should have prevented the limitation period from expiring. Lebcher sought compensation for his claim despite filing suit after the twelve-month deadline set forth in the insurance policy.	The defendant, Phoenix Insurance Company, argued that the limitation clause in the policy was valid and enforceable, barring Lebcher’s claim as he filed the lawsuit after the stipulated twelve-month period. They contended that the negotiations conducted by their agent did not constitute a waiver of the limitation clause since no credible promise or indication was given to delay the filing of the claim indefinitely. Thus, they requested the case be dismissed.

The case of Andrew Huls v. James Buntin was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1868, regarding a land dispute in Crawford County, Illinois. The case arose from an action of ejectment filed by Andrew Huls (the plaintiff) against James Buntin (the defendant) over the northeast quarter of Section 29, Township 6 North, Range 10 West. The trial took place in April 1867 and involved competing claims to the same parcel of land, with both parties asserting that their ownership derived from the same original title holder, Samuel Shaw. Huls tried to introduce evidence to support his claim that Shaw had purchased the land, but the court excluded that evidence on procedural grounds. Huls introduced deeds from Shaw’s heirs to back his claim, while Buntin relied on a deed from Shaw's administratrix that was contested due to questions regarding its validity. The administratrix's marital status at the time of the deed's execution and the jurisdiction of the court that authorized the sale were central issues during the trial. The case turned on whether proper legal procedures were followed and whether the defenses raised by Buntin were sufficient to bar Huls's claim.	Andrew Huls argued that he was the rightful owner of the land based on valid conveyances from the heirs of Samuel Shaw. He contended that the deed from Shaw's administratrix to Buntin was invalid due to lack of jurisdiction and failure to comply with statutory requirements, particularly regarding her marital status at the time of execution. Huls sought to demonstrate that both parties claimed title from the same source, which absolved him from having to trace title further back.	James Buntin maintained that he had valid title to the property through a lawful deed from Shaw's administratrix, despite her change in marital status. He argued that the administratrix possessed the legal authority to convey the land in her fiduciary role and claimed a statutory bar through more than twenty years of possession and payment of taxes. Buntin contended that Huls could not assert a claim against him due to the statute of limitations and that the evidence Huls attempted to introduce regarding the minority of Shaw’s heirs was improperly rejected by the court.

The case, "The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy R. R. Co. v. The People of the State of Illinois," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875. The action was initiated in McDonough County, Illinois, on May 21, 1874, where the plaintiff, representing the People of Illinois, brought forth an action of debt to recover penalties under a law aimed at preventing extortion and unjust discrimination in transportation rates. The plaintiff alleged that the railroad company charged extortionate rates and engaged in unjust discrimination against freight charges. The declaration included twenty counts, primarily focused on extortion; the last count was for unjust discrimination. The defendant railroad company submitted special pleas, which were ultimately rejected by the court, leading to a trial without a jury where the evidence was presented. The court imposed a $1,000 penalty for violations of the statute and the defendant appealed, claiming the declaration was defective as it did not account for a specific established schedule of reasonable rates, which was a requisite under the statute.	The plaintiff's main argument centered on the assertion that the railroad company committed extortion by charging rates that exceeded reasonable standards, as defined by the act established for regulating transportation costs. The plaintiff requested penalties for this extortion, claiming that there had been both unreasonable rates charged and unjust discrimination in freight charges. The charges were outlined in detail in the declaration, specifying the excessive rates in contrast to what was deemed fair and proper.	The defendant contended that the declaration was fundamentally flawed due to the lack of averments regarding the existence of a schedule of reasonable maximum rates established by the Board of Railroad and Warehouse Commissioners. According to the defendant, without this essential element, the charges of extortion were not valid, as penalties could only apply once such a schedule was provided and exceeded by the company’s rates. Hence, the defendant requested the court to overrule the judgment based on these procedural and substantive inadequacies.

In 1841, in Kane County, Illinois, Stephen Archer appealed against Daniel Bogue after a judgment was rendered against him in a trial stemming from a dispute concerning a financial agreement. Bogue brought the initial action against Archer before a justice of the peace, which was subsequently escalated to the Circuit Court. Bogue aimed to recover a total of $60, based on a $30 promissory note allegedly assigned to him and the damages arising from Archer’s failure to fulfill a contract to break 60 acres of prairie land for Bogue and a third party, Peck. Bogue successfully produced the note and additional testimony, despite Archer’s objections regarding the assignment's validity. It was found that Archer had broken only a part of the prairie land as agreed upon and had not received the remaining sum. The court initially ruled in favor of Bogue, awarding him the total claim amount. Archer contested this decision on the grounds that the assignment of the note should have been proven and that Bogue alone could not claim damages for breach of the joint contract since both Bogue and Peck were involved.	Bogue's main claims were rooted in a $30 promissory note that he argued was assigned to him from Archer, and damages due to Archer's failure to perform work as per a joint agreement with Peck. Bogue maintained that he was entitled to recover the total amount of $60, which included the note amount and damages for the incomplete prairie breaking.	Archer contended that the court erred on two grounds: first, by admitting evidence related to the assignment of the note when he believed this was not in issue since he had not formally denied it by affidavit. Secondly, he argued that Bogue had improperly sought damages alone for a breach of a joint contract, asserting that any claim should involve both parties to the contract, Bogue and Peck.

The case "Mary L. M. Ditch et al. v. John S. Sennott et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 12, 1886. It involved a dispute over land in Monroe County, Illinois, originally owned by Stephen W. Miles, Sr. The land in question was divided into two tracts: one of 114 acres and another of 80 acres. Miles' daughter, Amanda C. Sennott, married James Sennott, and in 1851, a deed was executed to transfer the land to her, which was later contested based on whether it was delivered. Amanda died intestate in 1854, leaving her husband James and her two brothers, Stephen W. Miles, Jr. and Alonzo N. Miles, as heirs. James Sennott later died in 1862, having occupied the land since at least 1851, and his heirs continued to claim ownership posthumously. Stephen W. and Alonzo N. Miles eventually claimed the land as heirs of their father, but they faced opposition from Sennott's heirs, who argued that the will of Stephen W. Miles, Sr., which bequeathed the land to James Sennott, was valid and accepted by Stephen and Alonzo when they accepted provisions in their father's will.	The plaintiffs, Mary L. M. Ditch and others, claimed they were entitled to the two tracts of land based on the deed from Stephen W. Miles, Sr. to Amanda C. Sennott. They argued that upon Amanda's death, her shares of the land should have descended to her brothers, Stephen W. and Alonzo N. Miles. The plaintiffs sought partition of the land based on their inherited rights.	The defendants, John S. Sennott and others, contended that the title to the land did not pass to Amanda C. Sennott due to lack of proper delivery of the deed. They argued that the land remained the property of Stephen W. Miles, Sr. and, upon his death, was properly bequeathed to James Sennott under the will. The defendants asserted that the long-time possession of the land by Sennott and his heirs, coupled with the acceptance of the will's terms by the Miles brothers, effectively forfeited any claims the plaintiffs had to the land.

On June 19, 1870, in Chicago, Robert Moir, part of the firm Robert Moir & Co., sold 200 barrels of high wines to Wilson Ames, who had the right to demand delivery within a specific timeframe. Due to a fire that destroyed their supply, Moir instructed commission merchants Phillips & Carmichael to procure wines in the market if necessary. When Ames demanded delivery on July 18, Phillips & Carmichael purchased 100 barrels from other suppliers, delivering them to Ames' store. However, upon returning the following morning to collect payment, they discovered the wines had been stolen. Following attempts to recover the stolen wines through legal measures, the funds received from a subsequent sale of the wines to Shufeldt were paid to the National Bank of Commerce, which had asserted a superior claim to the wines. This case arose as Phillips & Carmichael sought compensation from Moir & Co. for the money resulting from that sale.	Phillips & Carmichael argued that they were entitled to the funds resulting from the sale of the high wines, as they were acting within the customary practices of their trade and followed the directives provided by Moir. They claimed they had exercised due diligence as agents and therefore should be compensated for their actions that resulted in the transaction with Shufeldt.	The defense, led by Moir & Co., maintained that Phillips & Carmichael failed to uphold their duty as agents by allowing the wines to be delivered without proper security for payment. They argued that the loss was a result of Phillips & Carmichael’s negligence in following appropriate instructions and the customs of the industry, which mandated a more cautious approach to handling the sale and delivery of high wines.

John McAllister filed a legal case against Gilman W. Avery, arising from a financial dispute in Peoria, Illinois, concluding on December 4, 1885. This case revolves around a promissory note for $500 that was executed by a third party, Lenhart, and assigned to McAllister after its maturity. McAllister contended that Avery was a guarantor for this note. The core issue was whether the alterations made to the note—specifically, the removal of the bank's name as the payee and the insertion of Perry Frazer—occurred before or after Avery endorsed the note. During the proceedings, both Avery and Lenhart provided testimony. Avery asserted that the bank's name was the original payee when the note was signed. The jury ultimately sided with Avery, leading to a verdict and judgment in his favor, with the court affirming the decision based on the evidence presented.	McAllister argued that the note, with Avery's endorsement, was genuine and that the alterations made to the payee must have taken place after the endorsement by Avery. He claimed that this alteration, which favored the defendant, should not invalidate Avery's obligation as guarantor and sought enforcement of the payment under the terms of the note.	Avery's primary defense was that the alterations to the note were made after he had endorsed it, which placed the burden of proof on McAllister to demonstrate that the changes had been made prior to that endorsement. He maintained that there was no credible evidence to support McAllister's claims regarding the timing of the alterations and asserted that the presumption under law favored his position regarding any material changes to the document.

In the case of George W. Spahr v. John Tartt, the events unfolded in Madison County, Illinois, culminating in a court decision on June 7, 1887. The dispute arose from a replevin action, where George W. Spahr sought the return of animals he claimed were wrongfully detained by John Tartt. Tartt, as the defendant, asserted that he had taken the animals because they were causing damage on his property, thus invoking a legal right to detain them under Illinois law (Section 21, Chapter 54, Starr & C. Ill. Stat). However, Tartt's legal arguments, presented via pleas in response to Spahr's declaration, were contested in court for being improperly structured and lacking foundational facts. The court, presided over by Judge William H. Snyder, ultimately ruled on the validity of these defenses as Spahr pursued his claim for the return of his animals.	The plaintiff, George W. Spahr, claimed that John Tartt wrongfully detained his animals on Tartt's premises. Spahr sought the return of the animals through the legal action of replevin, arguing that Tartt's defense was insufficient and failed to meet legal pleading standards.	John Tartt, the defendant, attempted to justify the detention of the animals by asserting they were taken damage feasant, relying on statutory provisions that allow property owners to detain animals causing damage. However, his pleas were deemed defective as they merely stated conclusions of law without supporting factual details, which led to a general demurrer being upheld by the court.

At the Illinois Supreme Court, in January 1869, the case of John S. Williams v. Robert H. Ives emerged following a mortgage foreclosure proceeding initiated by Ives against Williams. This case traces its origins back to March 8, 1862, when the first writ of scire facias was issued in Piatt County, intended for the sheriff, but was returned marked “not found.” A subsequent alias writ was issued on August 4, 1862, which also met the same fate. In the absence of the defendant's appearance in court after the writs were returned, the circuit court entered a default judgment against Williams, assessing damages and awarding a special execution for the sale of the mortgaged premises. The case reached the Supreme Court on a writ of error, argued on two grounds: the sheriff's early return of the writs and the claim that the judgment was improperly in personam rather than in rem.	The plaintiff, Robert H. Ives, contended that the foreclosures were justified given the returns of the writs provided by the sheriff, which indicated that Williams could not be found. Ives maintained that two “nihil” returns allowed for the entry of a default judgment under the law governing such cases. Consequently, Ives sought a monetary recovery of $35,875.60 along with costs, and an execution order for the sale of the mortgaged property.	John S. Williams, the defendant, argued that the judgement entered against him was invalid because the writs were returned prematurely, prior to the scheduled return dates. Additionally, Williams contended that the judgment constituted an in personam ruling, which he believed was inappropriate for a case of mortgage foreclosure that should have been treated as in rem.

In February 1886, Douglass S. Low initiated a legal action against Susan H. Greenwood in Cook County, Illinois, which centered around false imprisonment and malicious prosecution. The events leading to this case began in February 1885 when Greenwood executed a chattel mortgage to Low and another party to secure a debt totaling $161.18. Later, in March 1885, Greenwood provided a second chattel mortgage on the same property for a different amount, due in July 1885. By late August 1885, Low claimed to have taken possession of Greenwood's furniture, alleging that she had directed him to do so. Low subsequently instructed his attorney to consider arresting Greenwood if the furniture was not returned. Following this instruction, Greenwood was arrested on charges of obtaining money under false pretenses, but those charges were dismissed by the court in September 1885. During the trial, evidence was presented regarding the existence of probable cause for Greenwood's arrest, as well as indications that Low may have opposed the arrest despite what had transpired.	Greenwood, the plaintiff, argued that she was wrongfully arrested, constituting malicious prosecution. Her main claims rested on the assertion that the arrest was made without probable cause, motivated by reasons other than bringing her to justice, and that the charges against her were unjustified. She sought damages for false imprisonment and malicious prosecution, contending that the real motive for her arrest was related to a dispute over the return of furniture, which she claimed was wrongly taken from her.	Low, the defendant, contended that there was probable cause for Greenwood's arrest based on the circumstances surrounding the mortgage agreements and the alleged theft of property. He argued that the claims against him failed to demonstrate a lack of probable cause or malice and that his actions were legally justified in attempting to retrieve his property. Additionally, Low maintained that the deposition used in court was improperly admitted and prejudicial, asserting that it influenced the jury against him.

On August 8, 1887, in East St. Louis, Illinois, George H. Recker, the owner of a grocery stock, sold the goods to Wendelin Huschle, his father-in-law. Shortly after the sale, the stock was levied by writs of attachment due to Recker's creditors, with Harry Morris serving as the constable. Huschle replevied the goods from Morris, initiating legal proceedings. The City Court ruled in favor of Morris, leading Huschle to appeal the decision. The case revolved around whether there was a legitimate transfer of possession from Recker to Huschle that was valid against Recker's creditors. The court determined that the chattel mortgage created as part of this transaction did not protect Huschle against claims from Recker’s creditors, as the possession of the stock remained with Recker. The judge directed a verdict for the defendant, stating that the evidence was insufficient to warrant a finding for the plaintiff.	Wendelin Huschle claimed that he had purchased the stock of groceries from George H. Recker, asserting that the sale was legitimate and entitles him to possess the goods against the attachment initiated by Recker’s creditors. He requested the court to reverse the City Court's judgment and affirm his ownership of the stock.	Harry Morris, the defendant in this case, argued that Huschle's claim of ownership was fraudulent in law as the possession of the goods had not been transferred accordingly. Morris contended that the chattel mortgage did not secure Huschle's interest as long as Recker retained possession and continued to sell the goods, thus invalidating Huschle's claims against the creditors.

In September 1873, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed the case of "The Anchor Line et al. v. Philip W. Dater et al." based in Cook County, Illinois. The case arose when Philip W. Dater, Edward P. Whaling, and William J. Whaling, partners representing The Union National Bank of Chicago, filed an action against the Anchor Line and several associated transportation companies as common carriers. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants failed to deliver 200 barrels of flour, which were destroyed in a fire at the defendants’ warehouse during the Great Chicago Fire. The flour was delivered to the defendants’ agent late on the evening of October 7, too late to load onto the propeller that day, and it was stored in a supposedly safe warehouse. The plaintiffs asserted that the defendants’ bill of lading, which contained clauses limiting the carrier's liability, was not sufficient to absolve them of responsibility since the shippers had not given their informed consent to those terms, which they were unaware of. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding damages of $1,400, prompting the defendants to appeal on grounds that the liability limitations were valid and enforceable.	The plaintiffs contended that the defendants, as common carriers, were liable for the loss of their goods, arguing that the bill of lading’s terms limiting the carrier’s liability were not fairly presented or accepted. They maintained that the lack of clear understanding and assent to those limitations did not constitute a binding contract, and thus they sought compensation for the destroyed flour, leading to the court's original decision in their favor.	The defendants claimed that the bill of lading was a valid contract that clearly limited their liability for loss due to fire while the goods were in transit or at depots. They argued that the plaintiffs, by accepting the receipt for the goods, should be assumed to understand and consent to its terms. The defendants also contended that the judgment against multiple companies was erroneous, asserting that the action should have only been brought against The Erie and Western Transportation Company, the primary operator.

In 1885, in Henderson, Illinois, A. D. Briggs, the appellee, held an insurance policy from The Security Live Stock Insurance Association (the appellant) which covered certain livestock, including a mare that died. Briggs submitted a claim to the insurance company for the mare's value. The appellant's agent, Thomas Junk, communicated with Briggs, conveying that they were willing to settle the claim through arbitration. As a result, an agreement for arbitration was established, involving four arbitrators who were to determine the value of the mare. This agreement was signed by both Briggs and Junk. However, two of the original arbitrators could not come to a consensus, prompting the inclusion of a fifth arbitrator, which was mutually consented to by both parties to resolve the impasse.
