Mason argued that these points were vital for assessing the validity of the claim and that they warranted a reversal of the judgment according to the established legal standards regarding writings and promissory notes.

The case "The Citizens' National Bank of Indianapolis v. Mary E. Dayton, Admx." took place in Illinois and concluded on January 22, 1886. The key individuals involved were Mary E. Dayton, serving as administratrix of the estate of the deceased mortgagee Mary D. Dayton, and the Citizens' National Bank of Indianapolis, a foreign corporation. The case revolves around a mortgage made by Joseph Dayton to Mary D. Dayton, which was initially intended to secure a debt. Following Mary D. Dayton’s death, Oliver E. Dayton, as the administrator of the mortgage, initiated a foreclosure case, which eventually transferred to Mary E. Dayton after his passing. The main legal issue emerged from the bank's assertion of a prior lien on the mortgaged property due to a judgment against Joseph Dayton that predated the mortgage. The court also considered the reformation of the mortgage due to an erroneous description of the property it covered. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Mary E. Dayton, affirming the right to correct the mortgage and granting a decree of foreclosure.	The plaintiff, Mary E. Dayton as administratrix, claimed the right to foreclose on the mortgage initially executed by Joseph Dayton. She sought to reform the mortgage to correct an error in the description of the mortgaged property, asserting that the correction was necessary and legally justified as incidental to the foreclosure process. The administratrix argued that the heirs of the deceased mortgagee had no claim to the property involved in the foreclosure and that the bank had notice of the mortgage due to existing record information.	The Citizens' National Bank defended its position by stating that they held a prior lien on the property by virtue of a judgment entered against Joseph Dayton. They argued that the administratrix was not entitled to reform the mortgage, claiming that any mistake in the documentation could not be corrected at this stage and contending that the heirs of Mary D. Dayton should have been included in the proceedings. Additionally, they maintained that their interest in the property should supersede that of the administratrix.

In 1871, the case of Joel G. Morgan et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois, for the use of Thomas Lewis was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Alexander County, Illinois, where the plaintiff, Morgan, alleged breach of duty by a sheriff in executing a sale of property. The sheriff had a bond, and it was claimed he failed to obey an order from the plaintiff to suspend the sale of shares worth $5,000, despite being notified of this intent through a telegram. The plaintiff had previously satisfied the execution associated with the sale, apart from costs. The case examined whether a sheriff could ignore the plaintiff's instructions and the validity of defenses raised by the sheriff, such as actions taken under attorney direction and the sheriff's legal obligations during an execution. The heart of the matter focused on whether the sheriff was liable for selling the property after being instructed to suspend the sale.	The plaintiffs, led by Joel G. Morgan, claimed that the sheriff acted unlawfully by selling shares of stock after being ordered to suspend the sale. They argued that the sheriff had received clear instructions to halt the sale, and his failure to follow these orders resulted in damages. They sought to hold the sheriff liable for breaching his duty as outlined in the sheriff's bond, asserting that the delay caused financial harm due to the improper sale.	The defendant, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, asserted several defenses. They contended that the sheriff acted under proper procedures and claimed that no official order to suspend the sale was in place at the time of the execution. Additionally, they argued that the execution was lawfully executed based on the attorney's directions, which should absolve the sheriff from liability. The defense highlighted that the telegram instructing the suspension should not bind the sheriff unless he had explicit evidence of such orders.

In September 1875, a legal dispute arose in Illinois involving William B. Fowler as the appellant and John L. Donovan and others as appellees. The case centered around a contract that stipulated the parties would cover the costs associated with hiring substitutes for individuals drafted for military service during a call for three hundred thousand men. The evidence presented demonstrated that one of the parties, Carey, was indeed drafted. He reported as required and paid $750 for a substitute, which was accepted. This situation prompted Fowler to seek recompense from the other parties for their share of the costs incurred. The case was initially heard in the Circuit Court of Iroquois County, presided over by Honorable N. J. Pillsbuby.	William B. Fowler claimed that under the terms of the contract, he was entitled to reimbursement for the costs of the substitute he had hired when drafted. He argued that the contract was valid and enforceable, supported by the precedent set in Wilson v. McClure, which allowed for proof of the contract's execution through parol evidence. Fowler contended that the agreement did not breach public policy, thereby warranting payment from the other parties.	The defendants, represented by Egbert Doyle, contended that the contract was not enforceable or valid under public policy. They argued against the interpretation of the contract stipulated by Fowler, suggesting that the situation might differ based on prior legal determinations, particularly citing Michigan case law. The essence of their defense was possibly rooted in the contention that no obligation arose apart from the contract's terms.

In 1872, in Illinois, Phoebe Thomas rented land to Morgan S. Thomas, who cultivated corn that was to be partially sold to Rufus Calef. A contract was made for the sale of two-thirds of the crop, but delays resulted in the transaction not concluding until March 1873. Following this, Phoebe Thomas rented the land to John Thomas starting March 1, 1873. Calef failed to remove the corn in a timely manner, leading to conflicts over the use of the land. In May 1873, he finally began removing the corn, but only using ox teams, which Phoebe opposed due to potential damage to her land. Tensions escalated when she burned approximately sixty shocks of corn stored on her property. Calef sought legal action against Phoebe, claiming malicious mischief. The grand jury ignored the charges against her, leading Phoebe to file a lawsuit claiming damages for malicious prosecution initiated by Calef. The jury awarded her $1,055.55, which Calef appealed.	Phoebe Thomas argued that Rufus Calef acted maliciously by prosecuting her for burning his corn, which she claimed was necessary to allow her new tenant to cultivate the land. She sought damages for the emotional and financial distress caused by the wrongful prosecution.	Rufus Calef countered by asserting that he had probable cause to believe Phoebe maliciously destroyed his property. He claimed that his actions were justified as he had acted upon the advice of legal counsel. He sought to prove that he did not act with malice and that the prosecution was warranted given the circumstances.

In September 1870, the legal case "Jacob Esty et al. v. James C. Grant" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a trial in the Superior Court of Chicago, presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gary. The plaintiff, James C. Grant, brought an action of assumpsit against defendants Jacob Esty, S. M. Waite, Joel Bullard, and Beilly Burdett. Grant claimed compensation for labor and services he performed, as well as materials he provided, all requested by the defendants. Instead of a jury trial, the defendants waived their right to one, leading to a court trial which resulted in a judgment favoring Grant. The defendants subsequently appealed the verdict, arguing that it was not supported by the evidence presented during the trial.	The plaintiff, James C. Grant, asserted that he was owed payment for labor and services he had rendered to the defendants, along with materials he had supplied at their request. He sought a judgment in his favor based on the common counts for work done and materials furnished.	In response, the defendants contended that the verdict was not backed by sufficient evidence. They argued for the reversal of the judgment issued by the lower court, claiming that the evidence presented did not validate the verdict in favor of Grant. Their appeal hinged on the assertion that the bill of exceptions did not encompass all the evidence required to support their claim.

The case "John G. F. Powell v. John Hyndman" occurred in 1888 in Greene County, Illinois. It was an action of replevin, where the plaintiff, John Hyndman, sought to recover possession of goods allegedly worth $615, based on an affidavit he filed to obtain a writ of replevin. However, during the trial, evidence was presented indicating that the actual value of the goods exceeded $1,000, specifically valued at $2,900. This discrepancy raised concerns regarding the jurisdiction of the County Court, as it could not handle cases involving amounts greater than $1,000. The defense objected to the court's jurisdiction on these grounds, but the court overruled the objection. After a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, the defense motioned for a new trial highlighting the jurisdiction issue, which subsequently prompted an appellate review. The appellate court found that the County Court had exceeded its jurisdiction by ignoring the evidence of the goods' value.	The plaintiff, John Hyndman, claimed that he was entitled to the return of his goods that he valued at $615, as per his affidavit for the writ of replevin. He sought a judgment in favor of his ownership, asserting that the defendant was wrongfully in possession of his property.	The defendant, John G. F. Powell, argued that the County Court lacked jurisdiction to hear the case since the actual value of the goods in question exceeded $1,000. He maintained that the court should have dismissed the case due to this jurisdictional issue, as evidenced by testimonies indicating the goods' worth was $2,900.

The legal case "Harry E. Holmes v. Ariel Nooe" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on July 3, 1884. The case arose in Coles County, Illinois, and involved the plaintiff, Harry E. Holmes, who brought a suit against the defendant, Ariel Nooe, under the Dram Shop Act. Holmes claimed that his wife suffered injuries to her property and her means of support due to the habitual intoxication of her husband, which was allegedly caused by Nooe's sale of intoxicating liquors to him. The key individuals involved included Holmes, his wife, and Nooe. While the evidence presented during the trial suggested that there was habitual intoxication by the husband, it was inconclusive regarding its direct cause being the liquor sold by Nooe. The jury found in favor of Holmes, awarding him $754, but the court later determined that this amount improperly included exemplary damages, as there were no aggravating circumstances proven to justify such damages.	The plaintiff, Harry E. Holmes, argued that due to Ariel Nooe's sale of intoxicating liquors to his husband, his wife experienced harm to her property and stability. Holmes sought compensation for actual damages incurred as a result of this intoxicating behavior, requesting both actual and exemplary damages based on their claims of habitual intoxication that resulted in financial damages.	The defendant, Ariel Nooe, contended that the jury erred in awarding exemplary damages since they were not warranted by the facts of the case. Nooe argued that there were no aggravating circumstances that would justify such a penalty. He maintained that if the jury determined damages were owed to the plaintiff, the findings should have been limited strictly to actual damages without any additional exemplary compensation. Nooe's defense included the contention that his actions did not meet the threshold for willful or wanton behavior necessary for awarding exemplary damages.

In De Soto, Illinois, on December 27, 1877, Andrew Friedline executed a promissory note for $100, promising to pay the Board of Trustees of Carthage College with an interest rate of 10% per annum. The note was intended to secure funds for the college's endowment. After Friedline's death, his estate was notified of the outstanding debt, leading the Board of Trustees to present a claim against the estate in the County Court of Jackson County. The court ordered the allowance of $152.58 as a seventh-class claim against the estate. The administrator, Frank Friedline, appealed this decision to the Circuit Court, which resulted in a jury verdict favoring the college for $100 in damages and court costs. The case revolved around the legal obligation of Friedline's estate to honor the promissory note, with discussions regarding the note's terms, the endowment fund conditions, and the claims regarding the validity of the evidence presented during trial.	The Board of Trustees of Carthage College (the plaintiff) argues that the promissory note executed by Andrew Friedline obligates his estate to pay the specified amount, despite Friedline's death. They assert that the right of action resides with the Board as the named payee and that the conditions related to the endowment fund do not absolve the estate of its liability. The plaintiff seeks the court to affirm the lower court's decision in allowing the claim against Friedline's estate and to award the amount stated in the promissory note as enforceable.	Frank Friedline, Administrator of the estate (the defendant), contends that the note's validity is compromised due to several factors, including the assertion that the right of action was not properly vested in the plaintiff as the payee was termed generically ("Treasurer of the Board of Trustees"). The defendant also argues that the death of the note's maker should revoke the obligation, claiming that the note was contingent upon raising a total endowment of $50,000, which had not occurred. Additionally, the defendant emphasizes that no evidence was presented showing advancements or liabilities incurred after Friedline's death based on the note.

In December 1851, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, John G. Metzger filed a lawsuit against John J. Miller. Metzger obtained an attachment against Miller's assets, prompting Miller to respond with a plea in abatement at the March 1852 court term. This plea resulted in a verdict in favor of Metzger. Miller challenged the verdict, and the case continued through several court terms, with multiple motions filed by both parties, including motions to dismiss, change of venue, and suppress evidence. During the trial, Metzger sought to prove the loss of a writing obligatory by allowing secondary evidence, which Miller objected to but the court permitted the amendment to the declaration on condition that Metzger pay costs. Additionally, Miller filed an affidavit alleging prejudice by the court against him but was denied a change of venue. Eventually, a jury trial resulted in a verdict for Metzger, and Miller's motions for a new trial and arrest of judgment were overruled. The case was heavily disputed over procedural motions and evidentiary issues before progressing to appeal.	John J. Miller, the plaintiff in error, claimed that the circuit court made several erroneous rulings, including: overruling his motion to dismiss the suit, allowing Metzger to amend his declaration during the trial, denying his motion for a change of venue, allowing certain depositions to be read as evidence, and denying his motions for a new trial and in arrest of judgment. He sought to reverse the judgment on these grounds.	John G. Metzger, the defendant in error, argued that the circuit court did not err in its procedural decisions. He contended that Miller's delay in raising objections (such as the authority of his predecessor to file the suit) was unacceptable and that the court rightfully allowed Metzger to amend his declaration during the trial. Metzger maintained that the evidentiary decisions made by the court were appropriate and that sufficient evidence supported the jury's verdict.

In June 1865, in Cairo, Illinois, the firm Gaff, Cochran & Co., represented by Thomas Gaff, James W. Gaff, and George W. Cochran, sold a steamboat named "Ella" to the firm of Musson & Culley. Joel S. Byington guaranteed the payment for this sale through a promissory note amounting to $2,500. Following the sale, the boat was delivered to Culley alone, prompting Byington to assert that this action constituted a breach of the sale agreement. Byington claimed that the original contract required the boat to be conveyed to both Musson and Culley as a partnership rather than to one individual. The legal dispute centered on whether Gaff, Cochran & Co. had abandoned the contract by transferring the boat solely to Culley, thus releasing Byington from his guarantee. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court after an earlier judgment was made at the Court of Common Pleas of Cairo.	The plaintiffs, Gaff, Cochran & Co., argued that the sale of the "Ella" was valid and the transfer to Culley was pursuant to the original agreement made with Musson & Culley, despite the bill of sale being directed solely to Culley. They contended that there was no abandonment of the contract for the sale of the boat and therefore sought to recover the amount specified in the note, asserting that Byington remained liable as the guarantor.	Byington, the defendant, claimed that the original agreement was breached when the plaintiffs sold the boat exclusively to Culley without his knowledge or consent, thereby releasing him from his guarantee obligations. He argued that the contract was for a sale to the firm as a partnership, and that any transfer to an individual without notifying him invalidated the guarantee. Byington insisted that the plaintiffs had abandoned the contract, and therefore he should not be held liable for the payment.

In September 1872, the case "School Directors et al. v. Trustees of Schools et al." was heard at the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Livingston Circuit Court. The plaintiffs, a group of school directors, sought to restrain the township treasurer from allocating funds collected from certain lands to newly formed school districts, an action taken by the trustees in 1870. In 1869, the school trustees had created nine school districts in township 28 north, range 8 east, but during their 1870 annual meeting, they restructured the districts to seven, effectively abolishing two districts. The plaintiffs claimed this reorganization did not reflect the will of the majority of the township's inhabitants and that it was not done with their convenience in mind. The case revolved around the discretion granted to the trustees under Illinois school law to create districts suitable for the community's needs. The plaintiffs alleged that the actions of the trustees were marked by fraud and injustice.	The plaintiffs argued that the trustees had improperly re-districted the township, causing inconvenience to a majority of the township's inhabitants. They claimed that the creation of the seven new districts violated the community's needs and wishes. The plaintiffs sought to prevent the distribution of funds to the newly formed districts and to have the court declare the trustees' re-districting invalid, asserting that it was not executed legally or fairly.	The defendants, the township trustees, contended that they acted within their legal authority to district the township under the school law, emphasizing their discretion in this matter. They denied the allegations of fraud or corruption, asserting that the process followed was consistent with legal procedures. The trustees claimed that the plaintiffs had not provided sufficient evidence of wrongdoing and argued that the court should not interfere with their administrative discretion unless clear violations of law were demonstrated.

In 1870, the legal dispute "Anna Burton v. Martin Gleason" was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a property title claim in La Salle County, Illinois. The case stemmed from events dating back to 1835 when one McQuon purchased a quarter section of land from the United States. In November 1850, McQuon conveyed a twenty-acre portion of this land to Charles Hallam, with the deed properly recorded. Following a series of property transfers, including a deed from Hallam to Samuel Burton in 1855, the property eventually came into the possession of Martin Gleason through multiple conveyances. The crux of the conflict arose when, after Samuel Burton's death in 1863, his widow, Anna Burton, claimed she had lost the unrecorded deed. She obtained a new deed from Hallam conveying the land to her, ostensibly to replace the lost document, which Gleason alleged was fraudulent. Gleason filed a suit in chancery seeking to restore his title and requested an injunction against Anna from further dealing with the property. Initially, the court granted the injunction and did not dismiss the case, leading to an appeal by Anna Burton.	Martin Gleason, the plaintiff, argued that he held the full title in fee simple for the twenty acres of land in question. He claimed that Anna Burton's deed was fraudulent because it was executed in the absence of a recorded deed, which created uncertainty regarding the ownership. Gleason sought a court order requiring Anna to convey the title back to him and requested an injunction to prevent her from conveying or incumbering the land while the case was pending.	Anna Burton's defense revolved around the legitimacy of her deed, which she claimed was a corrective measure for the loss of the original unrecorded deed belonging to her late husband, Samuel Burton. Her argument centered on the assertion that the deed was intended to ensure rightful ownership despite it not being recorded. Additionally, she highlighted that Gleason was out of possession and contended that he had a legal remedy available through an action of ejectment, thus questioning the equity of Glyson's claims in chancery.

The case of James T. Cooper et al. v. The People, for the use of Madison County took place in 1877 in Illinois, USA, specifically in the Circuit Court of Macoupin County. The suit was initiated regarding the surety bond executed by the county sheriff. The plaintiffs argued that the sheriff failed to properly pay into the county treasury the commissions he retained from collecting revenue, which exceeded the allowable amount set by the county board. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the obligations tied to the sheriff's bond and addressed whether the sureties on that bond could be held accountable for the sheriff's failure to pay over certain funds. The Chief Justice noted the importance of strictly interpreting the obligations of the surety, emphasizing that the specific bond in question covered general duties of the sheriff, while the responsibilities related to collecting and remitting taxes necessitated a separate bond. This distinction was critical to the court's analysis.	The plaintiffs claimed that the sheriff, acting in his capacity as an ex officio tax collector, did not remit all collected revenue to the county treasury but instead retained excess commissions. They argued for recovery of these improperly held funds, asserting that the bond executed by the sheriff covered these financial responsibilities.	The defendant contended that the bond in question only covered the sheriff's general duties and did not extend to the specific obligations of collecting and remitting taxes. The defense argued that separate bonds were required for different duties, and thus the plaintiffs were pursuing the wrong bond for their claims related to tax collection.

In January 1871, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case between the St. Louis, Vandalia & Terre Haute Railroad Company (appellant) and James H. Brown (appellee). This legal matter arose in Bond County, Illinois, where the railroad company sought to condemn a right-of-way over a 90-acre tract of land owned by Brown. Within this tract, Brown had previously released the rights to a portion of the land (the east 40 acres) to the railroad without seeking damages. The core issue emerged during the trial in the circuit court, where the railroad company attempted to present evidence regarding both the advantages and disadvantages that the entire 90 acres would experience due to the construction of the railroad. However, the circuit court restricted this evidence, permitting only an assessment of the benefits and damages related to the specific lands over which the railroad would run. The trial returned a judgment in favor of Brown, granting him $360, prompting the railroad company to appeal the decision.	The St. Louis, Vandalia & Terre Haute Railroad Company, as the plaintiff, claimed that during the condemnation proceedings, the trial court erroneously limited the consideration of the benefits to only the specified lands affected by the railroad. They argued that both the advantages and disadvantages should be evaluated comprehensively, including how the construction of the road might benefit other nearby lands owned by Brown, seeking a reassessment of damages that would account for these factors.	James H. Brown, the defendant, contended that the court's limitation was justified and consistent with the provisions of the railroad's charter. He argued that benefits to the land from which he had released the rights, as well as benefits to other tracts not directly affected by the railroad, should not be considered in assessing damages. Brown maintained that the damages should only reflect the specific 40-acre tract over which the railroad was constructed, thereby opposing any amendments to the ruling of the lower court.

The case "Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company v. Susan A. Asbury, Admx." took place in January 1877, involving the fatal injury of Joseph T. Asbury, a brakeman employed by the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company. The incident occurred while he was attempting to couple railroad cars on a special train transporting a circus company. The unsafe condition of the draw bars and couplings used for the cars was highlighted during the proceedings, as the coupling mechanism was deemed unsuitable for the task, leading to Asbury being caught between the cars and fatally injured. The jury found evidence of negligence on part of the railroad company for utilizing dangerous equipment. However, Asbury had extensive experience as a brakeman, and it came into question whether he exhibited negligence himself by putting himself in a perilous position. Ultimately, the case examined the responsibilities and duties of both the railroad company and Asbury concerning workplace safety and negligence.	The plaintiff, represented by Susan A. Asbury, claimed wrongful death and sought damages for the death of her husband, asserting that the railroad company was negligent in providing unsafe equipment for coupling the cars. She argued that the draw bars were defective and insufficiently designed, creating a risk of injury and leading to her husband's tragic accident. The plaintiff requested compensation for the damages caused by this negligence.	The defendant, Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company, contended that the equipment in question was in common use and not unusually hazardous. They argued that even if there was slight negligence on their part, the deceased's own negligence contributed significantly to the accident. The company insisted that Asbury was experienced and should have been aware of the risks involved in coupling the cars and thus should be held responsible for his actions that led to his death.

Horace Billings and Charles Sprague were involved in a legal dispute originating from an injunction case filed on February 27, 1866, in Cass County, Illinois. Frederick Potter, initially part of the case, conveyed certain real estate to Parker in trust to secure a $510 note owed to Sprague. The bond involved in this transaction required both Potter and Billings, the surety, to pay Sprague any due amounts and associated costs. After the injunction was dissolved, a suit was filed against Billings on this bond. The circuit court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding the amount of the note and attorney fees. The court justified the inclusion of attorney fees based on the provisions of the bond and the nature of the injunction. The case was eventually appealed, focusing on whether the amount awarded by the jury was appropriate given the nature of the bond and the dissolution of the injunction.	The plaintiffs, Charles E. Parker and Charles Sprague, argued that Horace Billings, as the surety on the injunction bond, was liable for the payment of the $510 note plus attorney fees due to the dissolution of the injunction. They maintained that it was within the court's discretion to include these fees within the judgment as part of the bond's conditions, reinforcing that the surety must respond to the bond’s obligations.	Horace Billings contended that the circuit court erred in including the amount of the note in the judgment, arguing that the fees awarded were recoverable but the note amount should not have been included. He also claimed that the jury should not have been directed on the specific amount to find, suggesting this instruction was erroneous and could serve as grounds for reversing the judgment.

This legal case revolves around an accident that occurred on May 1, 1882, in Buffalo, a small village in Sangamon County, Illinois, which had a population of around 400-500 residents. The plaintiff, Lafayette Hicks, as the administrator for the estate of John T. Lanliam, claimed that Lanliam was killed due to the negligence of the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company. At approximately 6:20 AM, Lanliam was driving his team and wagon across the railway tracks near the depot when he was struck by a fast-moving freight train, known as the "cannon ball," traveling approximately 35 miles per hour. The plaintiff alleged that the company was negligent in several ways: by running the train at an improper speed, failing to provide the required auditory signals (whistling/bell ringing), and allowing freight cars to obstruct visibility of the approaching train. Given that the village had no speed regulations for trains, and considering local knowledge of the train’s schedule, questions arose concerning whether the plaintiff’s allegations of negligence were valid. Ultimately, the case came to the Illinois Appellate Court for appeal after a trial judge ruled in favor of the plaintiff.	The plaintiff argued that the railway company was negligent for causing the death of John T. Lanliam through various points of negligence. These included operating the train at a dangerous speed and failing to give proper signals before approaching the crossing. The plaintiff also contended that the presence of freight cars on the side track obstructed the view of the oncoming train, compromising Lanliam's ability to assess the safety of crossing. The plaintiff sought damages for wrongful death resulting from these alleged negligent actions.	The railway company defended itself by arguing that the speed of the train, while fast, was not negligent given it was below the speed of many other trains and was within an acceptable speed range for traversing sparsely populated areas. The defense further contended that Lanliam himself acted negligently by disregarding safety measures, as he failed to look or listen for the train before crossing the tracks, despite being an experienced teamster familiar with the area. They claimed that any negligence on their part was not a proximate cause of the accident, emphasizing that Lanliam's own lack of care led to the incident.

In 1836, in Madison, Illinois, the case of Eli Foster v. Harvey Filley arose when Filley filed an action of assumpsit based on a promissory note in the Madison Circuit Court. The key individuals involved included Eli Foster as the plaintiff and Harvey Filley as the defendant. During the proceedings, the defendant (Filley) entered a plea of non assumpsit, which means he denied the obligation to pay the note. Subsequently, Filley agreed that a judgment by default could be entered against him if he failed to file a specific paper by a designated day. When Filley did not file the required document, the court entered judgment by default the following day. This led to an appeal, where Foster argued that there was an active plea that had not been resolved when the judgment was rendered. The case was ultimately reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court in the February term of 1836, presided over by Judge Sidney Breese.	The plaintiff, Eli Foster, claimed that the judgment entered against Filley was erroneous because he believed that his opponent's plea of non assumpsit should have been considered before the judgment was given. Foster argued that there were procedural issues that required the court to address the plea before entering judgment by default.	The defendant, Harvey Filley, contended that he had waived his plea of non assumpsit by agreeing to the terms that allowed for judgment by default if he failed to submit the required paper. Filley maintained that since he did not fulfill this obligation, the court's entry of judgment by default was justified and correct.

Jonathan J. Lyman filed a legal case against Lucy Russell and her family (Frank and Lora Russell) in 1867, seeking to contest a mortgage on a piece of land located in Iroquois County, Illinois. The mortgage in question was executed by William Bandy and his wife to O. L. Davis on January 20, 1858. Prior to this mortgage, Bandy had sold the same land to Samuel Lyman on July 27, 1855, who, along with his successors, had been in actual and visible possession of the land continuously since that time. This possession included agricultural activities observable from a public road. Lyman contended that the defendant should have been aware of this possession and should have questioned the legal authority under which the mortgage was granted. The Circuit Court previously dismissed Lyman's complaint, leading to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, which ultimately found merit in Lyman's claims regarding notice and possession of the land.	Jonathan J. Lyman claimed that the mortgage executed by William Bandy on the property was invalid because he had previously sold the land to Samuel Lyman. He argued that Samuel Lyman's continuous and open possession of the land constituted sufficient notice regarding the true ownership of the property, which should have been recognized by O. L. Davis when the mortgage was taken. Lyman sought to have the mortgage and all proceedings related to its foreclosure set aside.	The defendants, Lucy Russell et al., denied any knowledge of the prior deed from Bandy to Samuel Lyman until after the mortgage foreclosure had occurred. They asserted that they were unaware of any rights or claims that Lyman or his predecessors had in the property at the time of the mortgage's execution. The defendants, therefore, argued that the mortgage and its foreclosure should remain in effect.

The case, "The County of Vermilion v. William Knight," took place in the year 1833 in Vermilion County, Illinois. William Knight, a physician, entered into a contract with the County Commissioners to provide medical services to a pauper named Ludington. The agreement stipulated that Knight would only be compensated if his medical services benefitted Ludington; otherwise, he would receive no payment. Knight treated Ludington, claiming to have provided significant relief and thus sought $300 as reasonable compensation for his services, outlined in three counts in his declaration: the first for breach of contract, indicating the services were rendered and benefitted the pauper; the second for the county's promise to pay $180 for the same services; and the third as a quantum meruit claim for the services rendered. The county’s defense included a general issue plea and a special plea arguing that the County Commissioners’ Court held exclusive jurisdiction over establishing compensation due for services rendered. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Knight, allowing parol evidence when a formal record of the contract was lacking, and sustained the demurrer against the county’s argument.	William Knight contended that he had entered into a contract with the County Commissioners to provide medical assistance to a pauper, which he fulfilled, thus entitling him to compensation. He effectively claimed under three counts: first, for breach of contract due to the county's failure to pay for services that benefitted Ludington; second, for a promised payment of $180; and third, for a quantum meruit claim for the medical services rendered, asserting that the county owed him for the relief provided to Ludington.	The County of Vermilion argued primarily that the Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction, as only the County Commissioners’ Court could determine compensation for the services Knight rendered. The county also raised several errors including a misjoinder of parties and claims, along with arguments against the admissibility of parol evidence in the absence of a written contract. They maintained that the Circuit Court had erred in its instructions, contending that the evidence presented did not meet the legal requirements necessary to bind the county contractually.

The case "The Allerton Packing Company v. John Egan" took place in Illinois, with incidents occurring around November 1, 1874. John Egan, the employee, was injured due to an explosion of a steam tank operated by The Allerton Packing Company. The plaintiff argued that the explosion resulted from the unsafe construction and inherent defects of the tank and associated machinery. However, evidence presented by the defense included testimonies from the tank's manufacturer, indicating that the tank was well-constructed with quality materials. Additionally, the engineer on duty prior to the explosion noted that the safety-valve was functioning correctly. Despite these claims, Egan contended that the safety-valve’s adjustment could potentially have led to the explosion, but he denied any interference on his part. Throughout the trial, no evidence was found linking negligence or improper construction to the explosion, leading to the assessment of whether Egan's actions contributed to his own injuries.	The plaintiff, John Egan, claimed that the explosion of the steam tank was the result of its unsafe and defective construction, arguing that this constituted negligence on the part of his employer, The Allerton Packing Company. Egan sought damages for his injuries, asserting that the employer had a duty to provide safe machinery for his use and had failed to fulfill this obligation.	The defendant, The Allerton Packing Company, rebutted the claims by providing evidence that the steam tank was constructed using high-quality materials and was maintained properly. They argued that the explosion could not be attributed to any lack of care regarding the tank's construction or its operation. Furthermore, they contended that Egan may have caused the accident himself by altering the safety-valve, which, if proven, would absolve the company of liability.

In April 1859, in Joliet, Illinois, J. H. Brown appealed a judgment rendered by the County Court regarding a special assessment of taxes on his real estate for street improvements along Jefferson Street. The city collector, Philip Filer, had filed a list of properties with unpaid special taxes and sought a judgment to collect these taxes due. The County Court ruled in favor of the City of Joliet, leading to Brown’s appeal to the Circuit Court of Will County. During the proceedings, Brown argued that the evidence for the tax assessments was insufficient and that there were procedural errors concerning the jurisdiction of the County Court. The Circuit Court initially ruled against Brown, issuing a judgment for $172.89 and costs, without specifying judgments against the individual lots or blocks. Brown then appealed this decision, contesting various aspects of the legal proceedings and the specifics of the tax assessments.	Brown, the appellant, alleged that the County Court lacked jurisdiction to enter the judgment against his properties. He contended that improper evidence was accepted during the trial, challenging the adequacy of the evidence presented regarding the assessment. Brown argued that no clear assessment in dollars and cents had been made against his property, and thus the court's judgment was not legally valid. He requested the judgment be reversed and asserted that the case should have been dismissed with costs awarded in his favor.	The City of Joliet, represented by the city collector, maintained that the assessment and subsequent legal proceedings adhered to the statutory requirements. They argued that the court had the jurisdiction to render judgments concerning property taxes and that the procedures followed were appropriate. They contended that the judgment should be upheld as it was done in accordance with the statutory criteria.

Tarleton W. Chiles was employed as a bookkeeper by The Belleville Nail Mill Company in Illinois. The employment was initially on a monthly basis, but Chiles sought a long-term contract and submitted a written proposition to work for one year on January 20, 1870. The board of directors accepted this offer, agreeing to pay him $150 per month until the mill was operational and $200 per month thereafter. However, before the one-year term concluded, Chiles was discharged without reasonable cause. He claimed that the dismissal stemmed from a personal disagreement with the company's president, unrelated to his work performance. After being paid for the duration he worked up to his dismissal, Chiles filed a lawsuit to recover wages for the remaining unexpired portion of the contract, asserting that he was entitled to his wages for the entire year since he was wrongfully terminated. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court for resolution.	The plaintiff, Tarleton W. Chiles, argued that he was wrongfully discharged from his position as bookkeeper before the expiration of his one-year employment contract. He claimed that there was no reasonable cause for his dismissal, and sought to recover wages for the remaining months of his contract following his termination. Chiles maintained that the board's acceptance of his proposal constituted a valid contract for the entirety of the year.	The defendant, The Belleville Nail Mill Company, contended that the plaintiff was not entitled to any additional wages since he had only been paid for the time he actually worked. They argued that the dismissal was justified due to personal conflicts between Chiles and the company's president. Furthermore, the defendant maintained that the contract could not be interpreted as guaranteeing employment for the entire year, thus contesting the basis of Chiles' claims for unearned wages.

Jacob Greenhood brought a suit against Jerman S. Keator regarding the sale and delivery of a safe, which was part of a transaction initiated by an agent named Barclay. The events took place in the jurisdiction of Illinois, and the case reached the Illinois Appellate Court on February 5, 1885. Greenhood claimed that Keator had not paid for the safe, as the payment was made to Barclay rather than to himself. The defense, presented by Keator, argued that he had indeed paid Barclay the agreed-upon price of sixty dollars. The case had previously been appealed, and the court found that Barclay did not have the authority to collect payments on behalf of Greenhood. During the trial, it was revealed that Barclay had misappropriated the funds, which he had collected from Keator for his own benefit. The court noted that Barclay's original contract with Greenhood did not grant him such authority and that there was a lack of evidence supporting Keator's claim that the payment was valid.	The plaintiff, Jacob Greenhood, argued that he was entitled to the payment for the safe sold to Jerman S. Keator, asserting that Keator had improperly made the payment to an unauthorized agent, Barclay. Greenhood claimed that despite providing written directions for how the payment should be made, Keator failed to follow those instructions and did not remit the payment to him directly.	The defendant, Jerman S. Keator, maintained that he had paid the full purchase price of the safe to Barclay, who presented himself as an agent with authority to collect the payment. Keator argued that the previous court ruling in his favor supported his position and asserted that the evidence presented did not substantiate Greenhood's claims.

On January 14, 1888, John Ensch, a miner at the Starnes coal shaft, was a passenger on the lightning express train operated by the Wabash Railway. The train was traveling from Springfield to Starnes, a small settlement with minimal infrastructure, primarily consisting of miners’ homes. Ensch was returning from receiving his pay and positioned himself on the rear platform of the car to exit the train at the platform, which was the usual stop despite the train not being scheduled to halt there. As the train approached the platform, he placed a jug he was carrying on the platform and was in the process of disembarking when the train suddenly jerked forward, causing him to be thrown between the train and the platform, resulting in severe injuries. The case arose from Ensch’s claim of negligence against the railroad for not stopping long enough for passengers to disembark safely. The jury found in favor of Ensch, awarding him $82,500 in damages.	The plaintiff, John Ensch, contended that the Wabash railway was negligent by failing to stop the train long enough for him and other passengers to safely get off at Starnes station. He argued that the sudden start of the train without adequate time for disembarking caused his injuries, asserting that the train had indeed stopped at the platform before the incident occurred. He sought damages for the injuries sustained as a result of this alleged negligence.	The defendant, John McNulta, Receiver of the railway, claimed that the train did not come to a full stop at the station where Ensch attempted to exit, arguing that it only slowed down. He contended that the injury resulted from Ensch's own recklessness in attempting to disembark while the train was still moving. The defense emphasized that the train subsequently stopped at a different location where all other passengers were discharged safely, suggesting that any negligence claimed was unfounded.

The case of Henry L. Daggett v. David A. Gage arose in April 1866 in Chicago, Illinois. The dispute began when Daggett filed a suit against Gage concerning a promissory note that Gage had executed. The note was originally made payable to Henry T. Helm and later assigned to Daggett. The court proceedings were presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gary in the Superior Court of Chicago. During the trial, it was established that Gage had given the promissory note as security for the temporary release of a man named Reese, who was under arrest. The note stipulated that Reese would surrender to the sheriff by a specific date, which was later extended by agreement between the involved parties. On the final agreed surrender date, Reese attempted to present himself to several sheriff deputies, but they refused to take him into custody. Daggett claimed that Gage should still be responsible for the note despite the circumstances surrounding Reese's surrender.	Daggett argued that Gage was liable for the amount stated in the promissory note despite the conditions surrounding its execution. He maintained that Gage's note was a binding contract and sought the court's judgment to affirm the debt owed to him.	Gage contended that his obligation under the promissory note was contingent upon Reese's surrender to the sheriff, which he did in accordance with their agreement. Gage asserted that since Reese's surrender was made pursuant to the conditions agreed upon and was communicated to Daggett's attorneys, he should not be held liable for the promissory note due to the circumstances of the sheriff's refusal to accept Reese.

In 1866, Paul Beuninger issued a promissory note to Peter Wilding for $645.65, due in one year with a 10% interest rate. After Beuninger's death in 1869, the note became part of his estate, and Peter Wilding initiated a lawsuit in 1875 against Beuninger's heirs. By 1878, Frederick Rhein, acting as the administrator of Beuninger's estate, was named as the defendant. Rhein contended that he settled the estate in 1872 without any outstanding claims and had paid the heirs. Wilding's claims, however, included that Rhein failed to properly inventory estate properties, particularly a piece of land worth $1,000, which was discovered later. Following several court proceedings, including demurrers and replications, the case was brought to the Illinois Appellate Court after the plaintiff's death, where Maria Wilding, as executrix, continued the lawsuit. The focus centered around the interpretation of statutory limitations regarding claims against an estate, specifically whether the plaintiff's claim could still be pursued given when it was presented relative to the estate's settlement.	Maria Wilding, as the plaintiff, argued that the promissory note was never presented for payment to the probate court during Rhein's administration and highlighted that the administrator had failed to inventory all estate properties, specifically the land worth $1,000. Furthermore, Wilding claimed that a presentation of the note to the administrator occurred within the statute's timeframe, asserting that Rhein's failure to acknowledge this claim created grounds for the lawsuit.	Frederick Rhein contended that he was properly discharged from liability after making a full settlement of the estate in 1872. He argued that the suit was filed beyond the one-year statutory limit set by Illinois law, claiming that no claims were made against him after the estate was settled. Rhein maintained that the legal timeframe for any claims had expired, thus barring the current lawsuit.

The case revolves around a fire insurance policy issued by The Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company to James C. Whitehill. The policy was entered on March 29, 1859, providing coverage for a two-month period. The incident in question occurred on April 3, 1859, when Whitehill's property was allegedly damaged by fire. The lawsuit was initiated on July 27, 1860, after a claim was filed. The defendant, The Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company, argued against the validity of the claim, contending that the suit was initiated after the expiration of the twelve-month limit set in the policy conditions, which prescribed that any legal action must be commenced within twelve months of any loss or damage. Additionally, the defendant claimed negligence on the part of Whitehill, asserting that he failed to act diligently to save the property, did not properly notify the company about the loss, and did not provide adequate proof of loss as required by the policy. Despite these defenses, the trial court ruled in favor of Whitehill, leading to an appeal from the insurance company.",	Whitehill, the plaintiff, claimed that he sustained a loss due to the fire and sought recovery under the insurance policy. He contended that he had complied with the policy conditions regarding the notification of loss and the submission of proof of loss. He argued that the insurance company was liable to pay the claimed amount of $1,056 for damages caused by the fire, asserting that the company had no valid defenses against his claim.",	The defendant claimed that Whitehill's lawsuit was barred by the policy's stipulation requiring that claims be filed within twelve months after a loss. They contended that the fire occurred more than twelve months before the suit was filed. Additionally, the company asserted that the fire resulted from Whitehill's own negligence and wrongful actions, and that he did not fulfill the policy terms regarding notification and proof of loss. The company maintained that it should not be compelled to pay the claim based on these defenses.",

The case of Riley Ross et al. v. Alexander Demoss took place in 1867 in Illinois. The dispute arose from a mortgage agreement executed by Alexander Demoss in April 1858, which was to secure a debt of $68. Subsequently, a second mortgage for $300 was executed by Demoss in September 1858 on a different tract of land. In October 1859, the land was advertised for sale by William Ross, who sold it to his son, Riley Ross, and shortly thereafter, Riley reconveyed the land to his father for a small sum. Following the death of William Ross in September 1860, claims regarding the status of the mortgage arose. The plaintiff, Alexander Demoss, claimed that he had satisfied the debts related to the mortgages and sought to have the mortgage satisfied and the lands reconveyed to him. The evidence presented in court was conflicting, but witnesses testified that it was understood that Demoss had more time to redeem the land, and that significantly less was owed than the amount secured by the mortgages. After careful examination of the facts and testimonies, the court was faced with the question of whether the original mortgage obligation was still valid and whether Demoss had the right to redeem the land.	Alexander Demoss, the plaintiff, argued that he had fully satisfied the debts secured by the mortgages, which were originally agreed upon. He asserted that the sale conducted by William Ross was not intended as a foreclosure and that he was granted additional time to redeem the property. Demoss requested the court to declare the mortgages satisfied and to have the land reconveyed to him based on the understanding of the original mortgage terms and subsequent payments he had made.	The defendants, consisting of Riley Ross and others, contended that the mortgages were still valid and had not been satisfied. They argued that the sale was properly executed and that there was an outstanding debt remaining on the mortgages. Their claim was based on the assertion that the properties were sold under the legal power of sale granted in the mortgage agreements and that Demoss had failed to resolve the debts associated with those mortgages.

George E. Ayers filed a trespass on the case against the City of Chicago, stemming from an incident that occurred on December 11, 1881. The incident took place on the north-west corner of Washington and Clark streets in Chicago, Illinois. Ayers alleged that while he was walking along the sidewalk, he fell into a dangerous and uncovered light shaft adjacent to the sidewalk, resulting in severe injuries, including a broken leg that required amputation. He claimed the city failed to adequately guard or cover this dangerous opening, thus neglecting their duty to protect pedestrians from harm. The case progressed through the judicial system, initially resulting in a ruling by the Superior Court of Cook County, which sided with the defendant. The ruling was appealed to the Appellate Court for the First District, maintaining the judgment of the lower court. Ultimately, the case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for review, focusing on the adequacy of the plaintiff’s claims and the evidence presented.	Ayers claimed that the City of Chicago was negligent in its duty to cover or protect the light shaft located adjacent to the sidewalk. He asserted that the city, as occupier of the premises where the dangerous pit was situated, had a responsibility to safeguard the public from potential injuries. He sought damages totaling $20,000 for his injuries, medical expenses, and loss of business due to the incident.	The City of Chicago contended that there was no evidence to support Ayers' claims that they owned or were in control of the premises surrounding the light shaft. They argued that Ayers' injury resulted from his negligence in venturing away from the designated sidewalk into an area not owned or managed by the city. The defense maintained that the city could not be held liable as the evidence failed to demonstrate their possession or occupancy of the site where the injury occurred.

In 1870, Hiram Jones was involved in a legal dispute with The Chicago and Iowa Railroad Company concerning the condemnation of a right-of-way over certain lands he owned. The case unfolded in Ogle County, Illinois, but it did not reach trial in the circuit court until April 1873. The railroad sought to acquire a specific strip of land from an eighty-acre tract owned by Jones. While the evidence indicated that Jones owned additional adjacent lands, the court clarified that damages could only be assessed for the specific land described in the initial petition. This ruling was based on prior case law, which mandated that to seek damages for contiguous lands, Jones should have filed a cross-petition. The court reinforced that the railroad was required to maintain sufficient fencing to prevent livestock from accessing the track, but it ruled that this did not constitute a valid basis for damages in this case. Rulings regarding the treatment of farm crossings and the assessment of damages for potential fire hazards were also addressed. Ultimately, Hiram Jones's claims for a broader scope of damages and considerations related to fence maintenance were limited by the precedents established in earlier cases.	Hiram Jones, as the plaintiff, argued that the railroad's construction of the right-of-way caused damage not only to the specific strip of land outlined in the petition but also to his adjacent properties. He sought compensation for this damage, emphasizing the impact of the railroad's operations.	The Chicago and Iowa Railroad Company contended that they had adhered to legal requirements concerning fencing and maintenance along their track. They argued that the damages should only pertain to the land specifically identified in the condemnation petition and not encompass adjacent properties. The company maintained that there was no evidence presented that might substantiate additional claims for damages.

The case "George Sparling v. E. N. Marks" took place in September 1877 in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute centers around the ownership of a finger-ring that George Sparling sought to reclaim through a replevin action, originally initiated before a justice of the peace. Sparling argued that he was misled into believing that he purchased a diamond pin from E. N. Marks' associate, Eager, when in fact, the pin was merely a crystal of negligible value. Sparling asserted that the ring was provided as security for the $100 he intended to pay for the pin. Following an initial judgment in Sparling's favor, Marks appealed to the circuit court, which upheld the judgment for $150 in damages and costs against Marks for refusing to return the ring. Throughout the proceedings, the credibility of evidence concerning representations made about the pin was tested, leading to the court’s ruling based on a perceived breach of warranty regarding the nature of the pin sold.	George Sparling, the plaintiff, claimed that he was induced to believe he was purchasing a diamond pin due to positive assertions made by Eager. He argued that the assertion constituted a warranty, which was false, as the pin turned out to be worthless. His legal requests included the return of the finger-ring, which he had placed as security while negotiating the purchase of the pin, as well as damages for failing to return it upon request.	E. N. Marks, the defendant, contended that there was no evidence to support the judgment in favor of Sparling and argued that Eager had warned Sparling to inspect the pin before agreeing to the purchase, which implied no fraud was committed. Marks sought to have the court reverse the judgment by asserting that the legal action taken by Sparling was not appropriate, particularly argued on the grounds that the question of ownership should have been resolved with Eager before bringing the action against Marks.

In the case of James M. Petty v. The People, the proceedings took place in 1886, involving the appeal of a judgment issued by the Adams County Circuit Court. The case revolved around a forfeited recognizance entered into on October 18, 1881, which required the principal, Thomas J. Petty, to appear at the January term of court in 1885. This was deemed valid despite the intervening civil term, as ordered by the court. The surety, represented by J. N. Sprigg and the firm of Carter & Covert, argued multiple points of objection regarding the service of the writ and the legitimacy of the recognizance. The court ruled on various pleas submitted by the defendants—most of which were found to be inadequate. Ultimately, procedural aspects regarding the recognizance's returnability and the authority of the clerk to correct erroneous file marks were addressed. The case hinged on whether the recognizance sufficiently indicated the court's jurisdiction, which the appellate court upheld.	The plaintiff, represented by the People, argued that the forfeited recognizance was valid and enforceable, asserting that procedural flaws raised by the defendants did not invalidate the obligations stipulated in the recognizance. They contended that despite minor discrepancies in documentation, such as the name used and the misinterpretation of court jurisdiction, the recognizance met legal requirements.	The defendants' primary defenses included claims that the sheriff's return was insufficient, challenges to the approval and certification of the recognizance, and the assertion that the recognizance did not mandate an appearance in the correct jurisdiction. They argued for the dismissal of the forfeiture judgment, citing defects in the recognizance’s filing and discrepancies in its terms, asserting that these points merited a resolution in favor of the defendants.

Vaughn Williams filed an appeal against Daniel Corbet concerning an action in assumpsit that originated in Peoria County, Illinois. The case traces back to a dispute over the sale of cattle, where Williams was alleged to be the guarantor for a payment to Corbet made by another party, Caldwell. Although Caldwell received the cattle from Corbet, Williams contended that his agreement was an original undertaking to pay for the cattle directly. A justice of the peace initially ruled in favor of Corbet, leading Williams to appeal the decision to the County Court of Peoria County, where he was awarded $50 and costs. Corbet then appealed this decision to the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1862. The Supreme Court had to examine whether Williams’s promise constituted an original promise outside the statute of frauds.	The plaintiff, Vaughn Williams, claimed that he had an original undertaking to pay for the cattle he received from Daniel Corbet, not merely acting as a surety for Caldwell. He argued that the agreement was not subject to the statute of frauds and requested an affirmatory judgment regarding his obligation to pay for the cattle directly owed to Corbet.	Daniel Corbet contended that Williams’s promise was a collateral undertaking, which would fall within the scope of the statute of frauds, thus making it unenforceable without a written agreement. He believed that the proceedings leading to the judgment were flawed, particularly regarding the treatment of written pleas and the presumption of the statute of frauds being referenced in the lower court.

The case of Marcus Walker v. Oramel S. Hough, decided in September 1871 by the Illinois Supreme Court, involves a dispute over a land sale in Chicago. The key individuals are the plaintiff, Marcus Walker, and the defendant, Oramel S. Hough. The background of the case centers on a transaction in which Hough sold certain lots in Chicago to Walker in exchange for stock in the Chicago Patent Wood Hangings Company. Walker alleged that he was induced to make this exchange based on false and fraudulent representations made by Hough regarding the value of the company’s stock. Walker claimed that Hough misrepresented critical financial details, including the company's profitability and the status of stock sales. In court, it was found that Walker's claims of fraud rely heavily on his assertion of Hough's deceit, while Hough contested these allegations by insisting that Walker had personally investigated the company. The case was brought to the Supreme Court after a lower court decreed Walker's favor, ordering the return of the lots to him upon the return of the stock certificates.	Marcus Walker, the plaintiff, claims that Oramel S. Hough made false and fraudulent statements regarding the financial status and future prospects of the Chicago Patent Wood Hangings Company, which led him to convey his lots in exchange for worthless stock. He requests the court to cancel the sale and reconvey the lots back to him contingent upon the surrender of the stock certificates, arguing that the representations made were essential for his decision and that he relied on them completely.	Oramel S. Hough, the defendant, denies all allegations of fraudulent representation, contending that Walker thoroughly investigated the patent and the business of the company before proceeding with the trade. Hough asserts that any claims made regarding stock value or company success were either substantially true or irrelevant. He argues that Walker executed the trade in good faith and expresses that the transaction occurred after Walker was satisfied with his inquiries about the company's business. Hough seeks a dismissal of the case based on the lack of proof supporting Walker's fraud claims.

In 1889, the case of The Continental Insurance Company v. Stephen Ruckman arose in St. Charles County, Missouri. The plaintiff, Stephen Ruckman, sought a legal remedy against the Continental Insurance Company, based in New York. Ruckman had taken out an insurance policy on March 24, 1884, which insured his one-story frame dwelling and a log barn against fire damage. The policy was obtained through Harry Milne, a representative of the local agents Whipple & Smiley. During the policy negotiation, Ruckman, who was illiterate, discussed the terms of rent and vacancy with Milne, who assured him that the buildings could remain vacant for up to thirty days without affecting the insurance. However, this provision was not included in the final policy. When the insured buildings were destroyed by fire on November 1, 1886, while unoccupied, the insurance company refused to pay Ruckman’s claim, citing a breach of the occupancy condition. Ruckman subsequently filed a bill in chancery for the reformation of the policy and for damages incurred due to the loss.	Ruckman argued that the insurance policy should be reformed to reflect the terms verbally agreed upon with Milne, allowing for a thirty-day vacancy without jeopardizing coverage. He claimed that Milne’s assurances constituted a binding contract and requested that the court order the Continental Insurance Company to pay him the claimed damages of $1,049.50 plus interest, asserting that he had complied with the necessary proofs of loss.	The Continental Insurance Company contended that Milne was not authorized to create a clause allowing for vacancy without notice and claimed that the lack of occupancy invalidated the insurance coverage. They argued that Ruckman failed to fulfill the policy's condition regarding preliminary proofs of loss, alleging that any defects in the proofs excused their non-payment. Furthermore, they insisted that Milne was merely an employee of the local agency and lacked the authority to stipulate any terms on behalf of the company.

In the case of *William Cline et al. v. Matilda A. Jones et al.*, which took place in Illinois, the dispute arose following the death of John Cline, the common ancestor of the parties involved. John Cline passed away intestate on February 7, 1882. Prior to his death, on February 19, 1879, he executed a deed of a three-acre tract of land in favor of his daughter, Matilda Jones, citing "filial love and affection" and indicating that it was meant to equalize the property he had given to his other children, whom he had previously bestowed with financial gifts and land. After his death, the other heirs contested the validity of this deed, arguing that the land should be part of the estate to be divided among all heirs. Matilda Jones maintained that she was the rightful owner of the land conveyed to her through the deed, although it had never been formally delivered to her. The case highlights the legal complexities surrounding the delivery of deeds and the intentions of the grantor.	The plaintiffs, William Cline and others, contend that the deed executed by John Cline to Matilda Jones was ineffective due to a lack of delivery. They argue that since John Cline retained possession of the deed until his death and made statements indicating the land would be Matilda's upon his death (conditional upon her living on the land), the deed must be considered void. They seek partition of the land as part of the estates' assets to be distributed among all heirs.	Matilda A. Jones argues that the deed executed by her father was valid, asserting that it was intended as a voluntary settlement to equalize the distribution of property among all his children. She claims that the deed, even if retained by her father, should still be considered effective due to his intentions to convey the land immediately. Jones posits that the retention of the deed does not invalidate it, particularly in cases of voluntary settlements, and requests the court to affirm her ownership of the land.

In December 1845, in Menard County, Illinois, John K. Kincaid was involved in a legal case against Starling Turner in the Illinois Supreme Court. Turner had sued Kincaid for trespass, claiming that Kincaid negligently set fire to the prairie, leading to damage on Turner's property. Kincaid pleaded not guilty and asserted that prior to the lawsuit, both parties agreed to settle their dispute through arbitration involving three arbitrators. During the arbitration, the issue arose regarding whether the parties had consented to allow a majority of the arbitrators to make a decision. Evidence was presented that the arbitrators, after deliberation, indicated they could either withdraw their bond, select new arbitrators, or allow a majority to decide. Two of the arbitrators ultimately issued an award, which Kincaid later contested in court, contending that the jury's verdict was not supported by the evidence. The case underwent a trial by jury which found in favor of Turner, resulting in a monetary award of $150. Kincaid's request for a new trial was denied, leading to his appeal.	Turner, the plaintiff, argued that Kincaid's negligent actions in setting fire to the prairie led to the destruction of his property. He sought damages for the losses incurred as a result of Kincaid’s alleged negligence. Turner maintained that the arbitration award made by the majority of arbitrators was valid and should be recognized, despite Kincaid's silence during the arbitration process which Turner interpreted as consent to the awarded decision.	Kincaid, the defendant, contended that the case should be dismissed due to the prior arbitration agreement, asserting that the parties had mutually agreed that a majority of the arbitrators could render a decision. He argued that the jury’s verdict was not supported by the evidence, positing that the arbitrators’ award was binding. Kincaid claimed that without any objection from Turner during the arbitration process, his silence indicated acceptance of the majority's decision.

In 1861, the case of Henry Myers et al. v. Joseph Ladd took place in Peoria County, Illinois. The dispute arose from an act of trover, initiated by the plaintiffs, Henry Myers and others, against the defendants, Joseph Ladd and others, for the alleged conversion of goods and chattels, specifically machinery located in a mill owned by Randolph Ross, Jr. The plaintiffs claimed that they had a mortgage on the equipment, which included a twelve-inch by-engine, a thirty-four-foot boiler, and a double Child sawmill, valued at two thousand dollars. During the trial, the plaintiffs introduced the mortgage as evidence, but the defendants objected, citing that the mortgage stated Randolph Ross lived in Tazewell County, which they argued made the evidence inadmissible for identifying the property mortgaged. The court faced challenges in determining the validity of the claims based on the mortgage descriptions and location of the property.	The plaintiffs asserted that the machinery mentioned in the mortgage was located in a mill they had a rightful claim to. They contended that the description provided in the mortgage was sufficient for identification purposes and sought to introduce parol evidence to clarify any potential misinterpretations regarding the geographical location of the property. They argued that the intention of the parties involved, as expressed in the mortgage documents, should prevail to prove ownership and entitlement to the machinery.	The defendants primarily argued the inadmissibility of the mortgage due to inaccuracies in the geographical description. They contended that the indication of Randolph Ross's residence in Tazewell County was incompatible with the plaintiffs' claims about the property being situated in Peoria County. The defendants requested the exclusion of parol evidence, claiming it lacked relevance to the mortgage and did not establish identification of the property in question.

Anton Neustadt v. Cyrus Hall is a legal case that took place in January 1871 in Alton, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Anton Neustadt, the plaintiff and a captain in the 144th regiment Illinois infantry, and Cyrus Hall, the defendant and a colonel commanding the same regiment. Neustadt claimed that he had entrusted Hall with $1,000 in United States treasury notes for safekeeping until another individual, Col. Kuhn, returned. After a portion of the money was returned to Neustadt, he alleged that Hall kept the remaining $800 without justification. Hall contended that the money was meant as a payment for allowing recruits to be added to the regiment, asserting that this arrangement was legitimate since it was discussed with Mr. Ferguson from Monticello, who initiated the request for adding recruits. The testimonies of both parties were conflicting, with Neustadt insisting that the money was merely for safekeeping, while Hall argued it was part of a recruitment deal. The court was faced with evaluating the credibility of their accounts to determine any rightful claim to the funds.	The plaintiff, Anton Neustadt, argued that the $800 was his money entrusted to Cyrus Hall for safekeeping, asserting that Hall had no legal claim to retain the funds. Neustadt requested to recover the amount, emphasizing that it was provided for services related to military recruitment, which had already been performed, and claimed that Hall’s retention of the money was unjust and lacked legal standing.	The defendant, Cyrus Hall, contended that the agreement involving the payment of $1,000 was for recruiting services as arranged with Mr. Ferguson. Hall maintained that since the arrangement had been established for the benefit of the regiment, he was justified in handling the money as he did. He requested that the court dismiss Neustadt's claims based on the assertion that the agreement itself was invalid and therefore unenforceable as it violated public policy.

In the spring of 1879, George M. Warring owned 160 acres of land in White County, Illinois, which he had under a mortgage. After the mortgage was foreclosed, the land was sold in August 1878 to Parker, who obtained a certificate of purchase. Warring had a statutory right of redemption that expired on August 10, 1879. Subsequently, Warring rented out the land for the crop year of 1879, agreeing with tenants John Moore and William Coker to pay rent in corn per acre harvested. On November 14, 1879, Parker served notice to Moore and Coker demanding payment for rent directly to him instead of Warring. Parker conveyed the land to John Epley on December 11, 1879, after which Epley demanded the rent corn from Moore and Coker. The case centers on the dispute regarding the ownership of the 2,200 bushels of rent corn, primarily between Epley and Warring, as the corn was harvested after the foreclosure but before Epley acquired the title.	The plaintiffs, represented by John Epley, asserted that they were entitled to the 2,200 bushels of corn harvested by Moore and Coker, based on the argument that the rent accrued due to the lands being sold and that the rights of redemption had already passed. They contended that the rent was part of the reversion of the land and automatically passed to Epley when he acquired the land from Parker.	The defendant, George M. Warring, claimed that he was the rightful owner of the rent corn, asserting that the rent had not yet matured at the time of the foreclosure sale, and therefore should not have transferred to Epley. Warring also argued that the agreement for the rent payment had been made prior to the sale and that he retained rights to the crops due to the timing of their harvest and the status of redemption.

The case involves a legal dispute between the County Court of Madison County and The Toledo, Wabash & Western Railway Company in Illinois, dated January 1871. The conflict began when an act was passed by the General Assembly in 1867 that allowed the Decatur & East St. Louis Railroad Company to be incorporated. This company proceeded to build a railroad, which was completed before the current proceedings started. In 1869, the company's charter was amended to permit Madison County and others to subscribe to its capital stock, up to $100,000, and issue bonds for it. The Madison County Court proposed a subscription of $50,000 to the railroad’s capital stock, which was approved by a later election. However, when the Toledo, Wabash & Western Railway Company (which was formed from a consolidation of the Decatur & East St. Louis Railroad Company) requested the county to issue bonds and provide the subscribed stock, the county court refused. The county contended that a subsequent election indicated voters were against the subscription, effectively challenging the legal validity of the prior actions. The case revolved around the issues of statutory compliance, election validity, and constitutional adherence regarding the county's ability to incur this debt.	The Toledo, Wabash & Western Railway Company, as relator, argued that Madison County was legally obligated to issue $50,000 in bonds and transfer stock due to a favorable electoral vote and subsequent compliance with all requirements stipulated in the relevant acts.
