They contended that all prerequisites for the subscription to the railroad's capital stock had been met and sought a writ of mandamus to compel the county to fulfill this obligation based on the earlier electoral approval.	Madison County's defense hinged on the claim that the legislative act allowing them to subscribe to the railroad’s capital stock violated the Illinois Constitution. They argued that the election purportedly approving the subscription was invalid, asserting that the territory designated lacked corporate status and that the subscription process was unconstitutional. The county also claimed that the contractual terms imposed an unfair burden on the citizens, especially regarding the inadequate consideration involved in transferring stock for a nominal fee of one dollar.

Daniel P. Elston et al. v. Robert Dewes was a legal case that took place in 1862, specifically in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois. The case stemmed from an action of assumpsit initiated by the defendant in error, Robert Dewes, against the copartners Daniel T. Elston, Orin J. Rose, William H. Davis, and Otho Klemrn, doing business as "D. Elston & Co." The legal proceedings started with the filing of the precipe and declaration on June 16, 1858. Dewes sought judgment on a promissory note dated May 14, 1857, amounting to $10,000, which was due thirteen months later and accruing interest of ten percent per annum from July 14, 1857. A judgment by default was entered against Elston and Rose on June 30, 1858, as they failed to appear in court, resulting in damages assessed at $10,975. This judgment was contested nearly four years later, with the plaintiffs in error arguing it was excessive by $13.87.	The plaintiffs in error argued that the final judgment amount exceeded the damages stipulated in the promissory note, asserting a discrepancy of $13.87. They claimed that the judgment was wrongly computed and sought its correction. They relied on precedents indicating miscalculations in judgments that could be addressed through motions in the original court rather than appeals.	The defendant's position emphasized that the judgment was appropriate and within the context of the law. They argued that since the damages were assessed within the bounds of the original claim and that any potential error was due to the clerk's miscalculation, not the court's decision. The defendant maintained that the plaintiffs should petition the original court for redress regarding the amount rather than relying on the Supreme Court for an appeal.

The case "James E. Tyler et al. v. Ozias Bailey" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873. The context involves Ozias Bailey, the plaintiff, who alleged that he purchased seven land warrants (or Agricultural College scrip) from James E. Tyler and John H. Wren, operating as surviving partners of James J. Ullman. Bailey contended that these warrants were counterfeit. The dispute centered around whether the evidence sufficiently proved that Bailey acquired these specific warrants and whether he was entitled to recover the money paid. Bailey notified the defendants when he learned the warrants were counterfeit and promptly offered to return them. The defendants argued that the government had treated the warrants as genuine for years, and thus the obligation to replace them with genuine ones shifted. However, the law implied that the sale included a warranty of genuineness. Therefore, the trial involved the validity of Bailey's claim for a refund based on the non-genuine nature of the land warrants.	The plaintiff, Ozias Bailey, claimed he suffered a total failure of consideration due to purchasing counterfeit land warrants from the defendants. He sought to recover the money paid for these warrants, plus interest, on the basis that they were not genuine, thereby nullifying the contract. Bailey asserted that he timely notified the defendants upon discovering the warrants were counterfeit and offered to return them, demanding a refund.	The defendants, James E. Tyler and John H. Wren, contended that the plaintiff did not sufficiently prove that the specific warrants purchased were the same as those he later claimed were counterfeit. They argued that having previously used the warrants, the government recognized them as genuine, thus the obligation to return counterfeit warrants should not have fallen on them. Additionally, they maintained that Bailey's subsequent purchase of other scrip did not impose liability on them for the counterfeit warrants.

The case "Frank W. Palmer v. The Nassau Bank" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. The dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, and involved Frank W. Palmer, the appellant, and The Nassau Bank, the appellee. The lawsuit was based on a promissory note that Palmer was alleged to have executed. The Superior Court of Cook County had initially struck Palmer's plea from the files due to the lack of an affidavit of merits, subsequently rendering a judgment against him by default. Palmer contested this decision, raising three primary objections regarding the sufficiency of the affidavit submitted by the bank and the issues surrounding the title of the note. His claims hinged on procedural concerns regarding the affidavit's completeness and the legal standing of the bank’s indorsement of the note. Mr. Justice Sheldon delivered the court's opinion, examining the objections raised by Palmer and finding that the affidavit was sufficient and that possession of the note, indorsed in blank, implied legal title.	The plaintiff, The Nassau Bank, claimed that Frank W. Palmer owed payment on a promissory note. They argued that Palmer's objections to the validity of the affidavit were unfounded, asserting that the affidavit was sufficient to establish their claim. Additionally, the bank contended that possession of an indorsed note in blank is adequate evidence of title, and they claimed to have appropriately received and endorsed the note in question.	Frank W. Palmer, the defendant, argued against the judgment granted in favor of The Nassau Bank. His key defenses included the assertion that the affidavit filed by the bank was insufficient, lacking critical details that would validate its claims. Furthermore, he contended that the title to the note was not properly demonstrated because the bank’s indorsement appeared to be incomplete. Palmer also raised concerns over the legality of the bank’s president, B. F. Allen, acting as both buyer and seller in the transaction, which he argued compromised the legitimacy of the indorsement.

David T. Bonnell filed a case against Charles H. Bowman in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1870. The case arose in Jersey County, where Bowman served as the sheriff. Bonnell had obtained an execution against one Barber and others, which Bowman was responsible for collecting. However, Bowman returned the execution stating "no property found," despite claims that Barber had sufficient property to satisfy the debt. During the trial, evidence confirmed that Barber possessed personal property, but the defense argued it was exempt from execution. A deputy sheriff had previously levied on this property, but Bowman, as sheriff, ordered its release. When the jury ruled in favor of Bowman, Bonnell appealed, contending that the sheriff failed to levy on Barber's property without adequately proving its exemption from execution.	Bonnell argued that Bowman, as the sheriff, was liable for failing to seize Barber's property to satisfy the execution. He claimed that Barber owned property sufficient to cover the debt and contended that the jury's verdict was against the weight of the evidence. He requested the court to reverse the lower court's ruling and to hold Bowman accountable for his failure to act on the execution.	Bowman maintained that he was justified in not levying on Barber's property, arguing it was exempt. He claimed that Barber had returned the property under an exemption claim and contended that the evidence presented did not demonstrate that the property was subject to execution. Bowman requested the court to uphold the jury's verdict in his favor and to dismiss Bonnell's claims.

Talmon F. Hanford filed an action of replevin against Jacob Obrecht, the sheriff of Kankakee County, Illinois, in September 1868. The case stemmed from a levy executed by Obrecht on property belonging to Hanford, following an execution in favor of Otto Immelt. The dispute centered around household furniture that had previously been mortgaged by their father, Talmon Hanford Sr., to his son Stephen F. Hanford in April 1862. The mortgage specified that if Stephen paid $550 with interest by April 1864, it would be voided, allowing him the right to seize the property upon default. After Stephen took possession due to non-payment, he sold the furniture to Talmon F. Hanford in April 1864, following proper advertising of the sale. The defendant moved to exclude the mortgage and bill of sale due to alleged procedural irregularities, but the court denied this motion. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of the defendant.	The plaintiff, Talmon F. Hanford, argued that he rightfully purchased the property from his brother, Stephen F. Hanford, after the proper sale processes were followed for the foreclosed mortgage. He contended that the sheriff's actions in levying on the disputed property were unjustified, as he claimed he had legitimate ownership through the bill of sale.	Jacob Obrecht, the sheriff, defended against Talmon F. Hanford's claims by asserting that he acted within his duties under the execution and argued that the bill of sale was inadmissible due to its lack of a revenue stamp and procedural inconsistencies in the preceding sale under the mortgage. He claimed no personal interest in the dispute and emphasized that his actions were justified under the law.

The case "Potter et al. v. Board of Trustees" was filed in 1882 and took place in Madison County, Illinois. The plaintiffs were the Trustees of Schools, who initiated a lawsuit against the appellants, including Potter, who served as the township treasurer. The bond in question was executed by Potter as principal with Gerke and Volk as sureties when Potter was reappointed to his position on October 9, 1876. The core of the case revolved around allegations that Potter had unlawfully converted over $10,000 in school funds to his personal use during his tenure as treasurer. This misappropriation reportedly occurred over a twelve-year period before the execution of the bond. The plaintiffs claimed damages amounting to $4,068.32. The case highlighted the complexity of financial accountability and liability for public officers and their sureties, particularly regarding misappropriations that occurred during previous terms of office. Ultimately, the court had to consider whether the sureties were liable for Potter’s actions that were alleged to have occurred prior to the bond's execution.	The plaintiffs argued that Potter, as the township treasurer, had a duty to demand, receive, and properly manage funds that belonged to the township and its school districts. They sought damages against the sureties for Potter's failure to replace the misappropriated funds that he unlawfully converted to his own use during his previous terms as treasurer. Their claims centered on the belief that the sureties were liable for deficiencies arising from Potter's actions while in office.	The defendants, Potter's sureties Gerke and Volk, contended that they were not liable for the misappropriated funds because the alleged defalcations occurred during previous terms of office, prior to the issuance of the bond in question. They argued that the responsibility for such misappropriations rested with the sureties who were bonded during those earlier terms. The defendants maintained that no legal obligation was imposed upon them to cover defaults that took place outside of their contractual obligations, and the evidence presented primarily related to actions beyond their liability.

In 1885, Hezekiah McLaughlin was involved in a legal dispute concerning a charge of bastardy, which led to his arrest and subsequent appearance before a justice of the peace. During the proceedings, McLaughlin entered into a recognizance agreement with an appellant to ensure his appearance on a later date. However, he failed to appear as required, prompting the justice to note this default on the docket. Subsequently, a civil action for debt was initiated against both cognizors in the county court of Jefferson County, Illinois. The case was presided over by Judge William B. Anderson. Although the proceedings included various legal arguments regarding the process and the admissibility of the justice's transcript, the county court ultimately ruled in favor of the plaintiffs. An appeal was filed challenging the county court's decision, focusing on procedural technicalities and the admissibility of evidence.	The plaintiff, represented by Hr. William II. Green, claimed that McLaughlin's failure to appear constituted a breach of the recognizance agreement. They sought judgment for the amount due under the recognizance, asserting that legal processes were properly followed, and that the justice's records substantiated their claims for damages.	The defendant, represented by Hr. George B. Leonard, argued that the county court erred by allowing the justice’s transcript to be admitted as evidence without it being a full and formal document. They contended that the records lacked a seal and did not adequately demonstrate forfeiture of the recognizance, and raised additional technical objections regarding the form of the judgment as one for damages rather than for debt and damages.

In 1874 in Illinois, the case of John Mohler et al. v. Joseph Wiltberger was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court concerning the procedural rights of a complainant in a chancery case. The crux of the dispute revolved around whether John Mohler (the complainant) could dismiss his bill before a hearing. Background information included that a final decree had been rendered in the case in 1866, but it was reversed by the court in 1870, leaving the cause pending as if no decree had been made. The key individuals involved were John Mohler, the complainants represented by attorneys Harding, McCoy & Pratt, and Joseph Wiltberger, the defendant represented by Ayer & Kales. The Supreme Court dealt with the question of the complainant's right to dismiss the case after a decree had been reversed, ultimately affirming the decision of the Superior Court, which allowed the dismissal.	The plaintiff, John Mohler and others, argued that they had the right to dismiss their bill without prejudice at any time before a final decree was rendered. They asserted that since the previous decree had been reversed, the case should be treated as if it had never been decreed, thus reinstating their ability to dismiss the case freely.	The defendant, Joseph Wiltberger, contended that the complainant's motion to dismiss was untimely, as the decree had already been rendered before the reversal. Wiltberger argued that the case should continue forward unless the dismissal was agreed upon by all parties involved.

In 1870, Walker Evans, living in Franklin County, Missouri, authorized Richard J. Hughey, an agent from Mattoon, Illinois, to sell his farm of 343.5 acres. They agreed on a sale price of $30 per acre, with Evans to pay Hughey $500 for his services. If Hughey sold the land for more than $30 per acre, he would keep the excess commission. Hughey successfully sold the farm to John B. Rigney and Hugh J. Rigney for $35 per acre, totaling $12,015.75, with payments structured over several years. However, Hughey neglected to record the mortgage securing the first payment of $3,000. Due to this oversight, prior judgment liens were placed on the property, which began to affect Evans after he foreclosed the mortgage. Evans subsequently had to pay these liens to clear the title, believing that he had suffered damages due to Hughey's negligence. The suit commenced in September 1873 when Evans sought compensation for the excess commission Hughey believed was owed. The lower court found in favor of Hughey, awarding him $2,216.25, which Evans appealed.	The plaintiff, Richard J. Hughey, claimed that Walker Evans owed him the agreed commission under their contract for selling the farm, specifically seeking the excess amount earned from the sale above the stipulated price of $30 per acre. Hughey's position centered on the legitimacy of the commission agreement and his contention that he performed his responsibilities per the contract's terms.	The defendant, Walker Evans, argued that the lawsuit was premature as he had not yet received the full amount due under the contract, specifically the $30 per acre and denied liability for the excess amount claimed as commission. He contended that Hughey had mingled the excess $5 per acre into notes made payable to him rather than retaining it as commission, and thus, he should not owe anything until the notes were paid in full. Additionally, Evans raised the point that any losses from the recording neglect were not applicable in this case as they arose from a separate transaction not covered in the original contract.

The case titled "The Board of Supervisors of LaSalle County v. Cornelius W. Reynolds" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. It originated in the Circuit Court of La Salle County where Cornelius W. Reynolds filed an action of assumpsit for $125 against the board of supervisors of La Salle County. Reynolds provided medical services to William and Orin Woodbury, who were suffering from small pox and could not afford care. The overseer of the poor of South Ottawa, upon receiving complaints, employed Reynolds to assist the sick individuals. Although Reynolds' charges were initially approved in part by the township's authorities, the board of supervisors subsequently reduced the compensation to $50, which Reynolds rejected. The argument centered on whether the county was obligated to pay for the medical services provided under the provisions of the pauper act, which stipulates that counties have a duty to assist individuals who are sick and without means. The case was appealed after a jury ruled in favor of Reynolds, determining that the necessity of care for the Woodburys established the county's liability for medical expenses despite their not being classified as "paupers" under the law.	Reynolds asserted that the board of supervisors was legally obligated to compensate him for the medical services rendered to the Woodbury brothers under Section 4 of the pauper act. He argued that, regardless of their classification as paupers, since the individuals were residents without means and capable of falling ill, the county was liable for the medical aid provided. His primary legal request was for the court to affirm the jury’s verdict and award him the full amount claimed for his services.	The Board of Supervisors contested their liability, arguing that the overseer’s contract for medical assistance was not binding as they reduced the payment, asserting that they could determine what constitutes a reasonable allowance. They claimed that if the county established a "poor house," this absolved them of providing support for non-paupers. The defense maintained that a contract's enforceability depended on adherence to statutory provisions regarding pauper assistance.

Preston Wing v. Elton C. Cropper and wife is a legal case that originated in the Circuit Court of Rock Island County, Illinois, in the late 1850s. On July 29, 1856, Elton C. Cropper executed a promissory note for $575 to Preston Wing and secured it with a mortgage on a portion of land that was his family's homestead, meaning it was exempt from forced sale under Illinois law. After the note was not paid, Wing filed a foreclosure suit in August 1859, which the defendants did not answer, resulting in a decree of foreclosure taken as confessed. The property was then sold at auction on November 21, 1859, with Wing as the purchaser. In January 1861, Cropper and his wife moved to set aside the sale, arguing that the property was exempt from the judicial process under the homestead law. The court found merit in their motion, as the sale had overlooked the homestead status. The court ruled in their favor, leading to an appeal by Wing, claiming the trial court erred in setting aside the sale.	Preston Wing, the plaintiff, argued that the homestead act did not restrict him from foreclosing on the mortgage, which was valid. He contended that the sale was conducted under a court decree and, therefore, constituted a legal forced sale. Wing insisted that the homestead status had been legally waived by the defendants through the execution of the mortgage and that any exemption claims made after the fact could not apply. He sought to reverse the decision that set aside the sale.	The defendants, Elton C. Cropper and his wife, asserted that the property was their homestead, protected from forced sale under the homestead exemption law. They claimed that the mortgage did not waive their rights and that they had timely moved to contest the sale, highlighting that the presiding court had previously erred by not recognizing their homestead claim when awarding the foreclosure. They sought to maintain their homestead exemption and set aside the sale of the property.

Jacob Darst filed a case against the State of Illinois regarding damages to his property due to the construction of a lock and dam on the Illinois River near Copperas Creek, which was completed on October 21, 1877. Darst claimed ownership of approximately 850.58 acres of land in Peoria County, most of which had been cultivated prior to the dam's construction. He alleged that the dam raised the water level in the river, causing extensive flooding on his land, rendering it almost worthless for cultivation. By his estimation, 797.71 acres were adversely affected, and he sought $10,343.60 in damages. However, the state’s Attorney General contended that Darst's claim was invalid due to the statute of limitations, which required claims against the state to be filed within two years of their occurrence. Darst filed his petition on April 28, 1880, well after the two-year period had elapsed since the dam's completion.	Jacob Darst claimed that the State of Illinois caused significant damage to his property by erecting a dam that raised the water level of the Illinois River, resulting in his land becoming largely submerged and worthless for agricultural use. He argued that he was entitled to compensation for the damage, amounting to $10,343.60, for 797.71 acres of his land that had suffered severe flooding.	The State of Illinois, represented by the Attorney General, defended against Darst's claims by invoking the statute of limitations. It was argued that Darst’s claim was filed more than two years after the cause of action arose, specifically after the dam was completed in 1877, thus barring his claim from any consideration or compensation.

The case "Samuel Marshall v. John C. Ender" was decided on November 8, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute revolves around the ownership of a bond valued at $4,000, initially executed by Carl H. Carlson in favor of Francis Bradley and secured by a deed of trust on certain lands in Chicago. After Carlson's death, the bond was transferred through a series of agreements, and eventually came into the possession of John C. Ender, who purchased it from Charles A. Schmidt for $2,000. Samuel Marshall claims to have invested the same amount through Schmidt to secure the bond, but due to various extensions and dealings, he could not prove his claim convincingly. Marshall alleged that he had arranged for the purchase of the securities through Schmidt, however, he lost track of them after Schmidt took possession on his behalf. The court found that the ownership of the securities had shifted legally to Ender, who acted as an innocent purchaser, leading to the core of the legal dispute: whether Marshall had any rightful claim to the bond in the face of Ender's possession.	Samuel Marshall, the plaintiff, argued that he had a rightful ownership interest in the bond and the attached deed of trust, having entrusted the purchase to his brother-in-law, Charles A. Schmidt. He claimed that he had invested $2,000 in the securities and presented a narrative where Schmidt misled him regarding the transactions and the ownership of the securities. Marshall sought a decree from the court affirming his ownership of the bond and deed of trust, challenging Ender's claim over the same securities.	John C. Ender, the defendant, contended that he had purchased the bond and securities from Schmidt as the legal owner and holder, having no knowledge of any competing claim from Marshall at the time of purchase. Ender argued that he was an innocent purchaser and that any uncertainty in Marshall's claims should not undermine his ownership rights. He requested the court to uphold the validity of his purchase and dismiss Marshall's claims.

In 1855, the case of Henry McClure v. Jacob Engelhardt was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a dispute over property in St. Clair County, Illinois. The case centered on the northwest quarter of the southwest quarter and the southeast quarter of the northeast quarter of Section 5 in Township 2 North, Range 7 West. The factual background involved a series of transactions concerning the land beginning in January 1839, when William Cobb acquired it. In January 1840, Cobb transferred the property to Jefferson Shores. Subsequently, in October 1841, Shores lost the property following a court judgment against him, which led to a series of executions that were improperly processed. There was a failure to file necessary certificates for the levy on the property. Engelhardt later acquired the land in 1843 through a transaction with Shores, unaware of the issues surrounding the earlier execution process. The initial trial in 1849 resulted in a judgment against McClure's claim to the property, which was a crucial point of contention in this appellate case.	McClure, the plaintiff, argued that he had rightful ownership of the disputed land based on the chain of title originating from Cobb through Shores. He contended that the execution levied against Shores was valid and believed that the subsequent sale to Engelhardt should not affect his claim if proper legal procedures had not been followed. McClure pleaded for the court to reverse the trial court's decision, which ruled in favor of Engelhardt, and sought recovery of the property.	Engelhardt defended against McClure's claims by asserting that he held a valid title to the property through his purchase from Shores, compliant with legal formalities. He indicated that McClure's claim failed because the required certificate for the levy on the property was never filed, rendering the earlier execution ineffective as a lien against the property. Engelhardt aimed to uphold the lower court's judgment, arguing that he was a bona fide purchaser without notice of any claim by McClure.

In December 1844, the case "Thomas Morgan v. Young Griffin" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a judgment that Griffin had recovered against individuals named Gunn and Fox. An execution on this judgment was levied on property claimed by Morgan. When the right of property was tried before the sheriff in Scott County, the sheriff found against Morgan's claim. Subsequently, Morgan appealed to the Circuit Court, where a motion to dismiss the appeal was presented. The sheriff provided an uncontradicted affidavit indicating that the property had been sold with Morgan’s assent and that the proceeds were held by the sheriff for Morgan’s benefit. The Circuit Court dismissed the appeal and ordered Morgan to pay the costs. This decision prompted Morgan to appeal to the Supreme Court.	Morgan's primary argument was that the Circuit Court erred in dismissing his appeal and rendering a judgment against him for costs. He contended that the matter in dispute had been resolved after the initial trial before the sheriff and argued that the appeal should not involve costs against him.	Griffin's defense hinged on the sheriff's affidavit, which indicated that the property had been sold with Morgan's agreement after the sheriff's trial. Griffin asserted that, due to this settlement, there was no further subject matter to be litigated, and therefore the Circuit Court correctly dismissed the appeal. Furthermore, Griffin contended that the costs should not be automatically assigned to either party due to the compromise.

In the case of Abraham H. Graff v. David M. Simmons, the legal proceedings originated in January 1871 in Illinois. The appellant, Abraham H. Graff, had initiated the lawsuit against the appellee, David M. Simmons, for the enforcement of a promissory note that Simmons had executed in favor of the Winnesheik Insurance Company. This note was intended to cover the cash premium for an insurance policy issued to Simmons on his property. The insurance policy was issued in February 1866, and Graff, acting as the agent for the insurance company, allowed Simmons to execute a note for the premium, due on July 1 of the same year. When Simmons failed to pay the note at maturity, Graff advanced the funds to the company and subsequently took an assignment of the note for himself. During the trial, the defense for Simmons claimed that the consideration for the note had failed since the insurance company was allegedly insolvent at the time the note was executed, thus rendering the policy worthless. However, Graff argued that at the time of the policy's issuance, the company was solvent and had honored all claims made against it. There were further disputes over the evidence regarding the company's financial status, leading to an appeal after the circuit court ruled in favor of Simmons.	Graff's primary argument rested on the assertion that the promissory note was valid and enforceable. He contended that he fulfilled his obligations by paying the premium to the insurance company on behalf of Simmons when the latter failed to do so. Graff requested the court to reverse the lower court's judgment that ruled in favor of Simmons, claiming the jury's verdict was contrary to the weight of the evidence, and also contested the validity of jury instructions provided during the trial.	Simmons maintained that the promissory note was invalid due to a failure of consideration, asserting that the insurance company was insolvent at the time the note was executed, which made the insurance policy worthless. He also relied on testimonies indicating that the company was viewed unfavorably and that Graff himself had expressed doubts about the company's legitimacy. Simmons appealed for the court's ruling to uphold the previous verdict favoring him, arguing that there was insufficient evidence proving the company's solvency at the time the note was issued.

The case involves the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company (Appellant) and Elias Minard et al. (Appellees) and dates back to April 1858, in La Salle County, Illinois. The dispute arose when Minard initiated a claim against the railroad company for damages related to the loss of corn that he had delivered to the company for transport to Chicago. The initial claim was presented to a justice of the peace, which ultimately led to an appeal to the La Salle County Circuit Court after the justice ruled in favor of the plaintiff. During the trial in the Circuit Court, a jury awarded damages amounting to $60, though the plaintiff later remitted $5, resulting in a judgment of $55 plus costs awarded to Minard. The railroad company contested this decision, prompting an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Elias Minard, claimed damages from the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company for their failure to transport corn, which he had entrusted to them. His legal request sought compensation for the loss, ultimately leading to a jury ruling in his favor for $60, reduced to $55 after a remit.	The defendant, the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company, argued that the judgment awarded by the Circuit Court exceeded the amount specified on the summons. They claimed an error occurred because the judgment was for an amount greater than what was indicated. The defense's request was for a reversal of the judgment or, at the very least, for a new trial on the grounds of this alleged error.

The case "James Welsh et al. v. The People" took place in June 1856 in Chicago, Illinois. The defendants, James Welsh and others, were indicted for larceny after they were accused of participating in a fraudulent betting scheme known as the "ball and safe game." The primary victim, Hall, loaned money to the defendants, thinking it would be used for placing bets. At the time of the trial, the defendants had already been convicted and sentenced to three years in the penitentiary by the Recorder's Court in Chicago during the September term of 1855. The legal questions discussed centered on whether the defendants had retained possession and title of the money after it was loaned, and if larceny was truly committed, given that the owner willingly parted with the possession of the funds. The court examined various legal instructions provided regarding larceny and the intentions surrounding the loan.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants engaged in a fraudulent scheme to obtain money under false pretenses, which amounted to larceny as they did not intend to return the money loaned to them by Hall. The plaintiffs sought to affirm the conviction of the defendants, asserting that Hall had not legally transferred ownership of the money and that the defendants acted with felonious intent to permanently deprive Hall of his property.	The defendants contended that the money lent by Hall was part of a legitimate gamble and that they believed he intended for them to keep it, effectively arguing that no larceny had taken place since the money had been loaned and they had assumed legal ownership. They requested that the court acquit them, highlighting that Hall had willingly given up possession of his money without the expectation of its return.

In September 1867, the case of John Yocum et al. v. Fanny Benson was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following an action of assumpsit against John Yocum and several partners related to a note issued by the American Protective Union. The plaintiffs accused the defendants of being liable as partners for a debt, despite the fact that sixteen other defendants were defaulted in the case. The core issue revolved around whether the appellants (Yocum and three others) were indeed partners in the venture as claimed by the plaintiff. During trial, the court allowed the introduction of a list of stockholders, purportedly evidencing the appellants' involvement, but this list had been created without their knowledge by a former clerk of the association, raising questions about its validity. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff, leading the four defendants to appeal the decision based on the contention that the evidence was inadmissible and that the plaintiffs failed to prove the existence of the partnership necessary for liability.	The plaintiffs asserted that the defendants were liable as partners in trade under the American Protective Union. They sought to recover debts incurred by the association, arguing that the appellants' names were included in a stockholder list, indicating their status as partners. They requested a judgment against the defendants for the amount stated in the promissory note in question.	The defendants, particularly the appellants, denied any partnership with the other defendants and contended that a paper listing them as stockholders was inadmissible evidence since they had no knowledge of it and did not authorize their names to be included. They maintained that without proving the existence of the alleged partnership among all defendants, the plaintiffs could not succeed in their claim.

In 1828, Guyard & Morehouse made improvements on two lots in Galena, Illinois, which entitled them to a preemption claim under the relevant congressional acts. In November 1829, Guyard transferred his interest in the property to William A. Phelps via quitclaim deed. Subsequently, Guyard disappeared, leading Morehouse to administer Guyard's estate. Morehouse later claimed a preemption for half of the lots on behalf of Guyard's legal representatives, as well as for himself. The claim was decided in favor of representing entities, and a preemption certificate was granted. Ultimately, Phelps sought to claim the undivided half of the lots as Guyard's legal representative, while Morehouse insisted that he had acted as the true representative when he pursued the claim before the commissioners. The crux of the legal dispute was whether Morehouse was indeed the legal representative entitled to the land, as the jury instructions implied, resulting in an important question regarding the true legal representative's identity.	Phelps contended that he holds the undivided half of the lots as Guyard's legal representative, claiming rights under the patent issued that recognized the legal representatives of Guyard. He argued that the proceedings before the commissioners did not consider his claims and that he was the rightful heir to the rights transferred by Guyard. He requested the court to recognize his status as Guyard's legal representative and to grant him ownership of the property.	Morehouse argued that he rightfully pursued the claim as Guyard’s administrator and was designated by the commissioners as the legal representative of Guyard in their decision. He contended that the judgment should remain with him because of this designation and the instructions given to the jury, which suggested that Phelps could not recover ownership since the commissioners intended to grant the preemption to Morehouse, the administrator.

In 1869, a written contract was established between D. W. Tamblyn & Co., Henry Cease, and Washington Cockle in Mason City, Illinois, for the sale of 20,000 bushels of shelled corn at a price of $13,000. The contract specified the corn was to be of good quality and needed to be delivered on board of cars at Mason City by July 1, 1870. The agreement required partial payments, with $9,300 already advanced, but only 8,209 bushels were delivered by May 1873. Following this breach, Washington Cockle initiated legal action against Henry Cease, seeking damages for the deficit in the corn delivery. The case highlighted the death of D. W. Tamblyn before the delivery deadline and disputes over the terms of delivery. The defendant, Cease, contested the verdict, leading to an appeal after Cockle was awarded damages.	Washington Cockle argued that Henry Cease breached the contract by failing to deliver the full amount of corn, despite substantial payments made. He sought damages for the difference between the amount contracted and the amount delivered, totaling a judgment of $1,347.75. Cockle maintained that the original agreement stipulated specific performance of the delivery, and Cease's failure constituted a violation of that obligation.	Henry Cease contended that he was merely a surety for part of the delivery and that a subsequent agreement indicated that 10,000 bushels were to be delivered in Chicago instead of Mason City. He argued that due to this agreement, he was justified in not delivering the corn at Mason City, suggesting that the trial court should exclude certain evidence relating to suretyship and the delivery terms. He maintained that because Cockle did not pay for the corn that was ready for delivery, he was not liable for the non-delivery of the full contracted amount.

In the case of Marion County v. Isaiah D. Lear, which took place in Illinois and culminated on January 22, 1884, the dispute arose after Lear, the sheriff of Marion County, submitted a claim to the county board of supervisors for fees owed to him for services in criminal cases where defendants were acquitted or discharged without costs. The board denied his claim, prompting Lear to appeal to the Circuit Court of Marion County, which ruled in his favor. The case was then escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court primarily on grounds concerning the constitutionality of a statute governing sheriff compensation from county funds. The statute in question stipulated that sheriffs should be compensated from the county treasury under specific conditions, including cases where defendants were found not guilty. The court's central issue was to determine if the statute conflicted with the Illinois Constitution, which stipulated that county officers’ compensation should only be paid from fees actually collected. The ruling assessed the potential conflict between this statute and constitutional provisions regarding public officer compensation.	The plaintiff, Isaiah D. Lear, argued that he was entitled to compensation for his services as sheriff from the county treasury based on the statute that required counties to pay fees to sheriffs in criminal cases where the defendants were acquitted. He applied for these fees after having received a fixed salary and additional allowances for deputy hire and expenses. Lear claimed that despite the salary being ample, the additional fees were necessary to fully compensate him for the work performed under the stipulated conditions, thus rendering the statutory provision valid and enforceable against the county.	Marion County, the defendant, contended that Lear’s claim for fees was unwarranted as he had already received his full salary and allowances, totaling amounts that exceeded necessary compensation for his services as sheriff. The county argued that the statute was inconsistent with the Illinois Constitution by allowing compensation for fees that had not been actually collected. Consequently, they asserted that since the sheriff’s total earnings had surpassed his established salary, he was not entitled to claim additional fees from the county treasury as per legislative provisions and constitutional limits.

In the case of D. W. C. Gooding v. Anna King, Administratrix, filed on June 16, 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, appellant D. W. C. Gooding sought to enforce a judgment he had obtained against Claude B. King for $1,076 and costs from the Superior Court of Cook County. At the time of the filing, some of King's interests were tied to the Montello Granite Company, a copartnership with James H. Anderson, where assets were managed by a court-appointed receiver, H. H. Hibbard. Due to King's judgment being returned unsatisfied, Gooding's creditor's bill aimed to reach King's equitable interest in the firm assets. Claude B. King passed away on November 11, 1884, after which his wife, Anna King, became administratrix of his estate and asserted that the estate was largely insolvent. Despite a widow's award fixed at $1,975 for Anna, it was claimed that the estate's debts would preclude any payments to Gooding. The lower court initially dismissed Gooding's creditor's bill, ruling that his claims did not carry sufficient equity.	D. W. C. Gooding argued that he had a right to the equitable assets of Claude B. King through a creditor's bill due to a judgment that was unsatisfied. He contended that his lien on King’s equitable interests in the Montello Granite Company should survive King's death and asserted that Anna King's widow's claim should not negate his superior lien on the estate’s assets.	Anna King, as administratrix, defended against Gooding's claims by asserting that her husband's estate was insolvent and that any assets in the receiver's hands would be insufficient to cover both her widow's award and Gooding's claim. She argued that the creditor's bill was improperly filed and contested the existence of Gooding's lien on her late husband's assets, indicating that no justifiable claim against the estate remained.

In December 1858, a legal case was initiated in the Lake County Circuit Court, Illinois, involving key individuals including Daniel Billings, Ann Billings, William J. Robinson, Sarah Robinson, Thomas Attridge, Mary Attridge, James Swanton, John Swanton, and Martha Swanton. The dispute centered on a trust claim concerning 124.64 acres of land in Lake County. The conflict arose after Robert Swanton, who had originally settled on the land, passed away in June 1839. His family continued to occupy the land until Mary, the widow, remarried Thomas Attridge in 1841. The land had been purchased by James and Thomas Cole, who claimed that their pre-emption rights were valid and independent of Swanton's interest in the property. The plaintiffs argued that Robert Swanton's estate had an equal share in the land, while the defendants contended that the Cole brothers had a clear title to the land, having been conveyed directly from the government. The legislation and circumstances surrounding land ownership and familial relations complicated the case further, eventually leading to litigation on the matter of rightful ownership and trust.	The plaintiffs, Ann and Sarah, alleged that their late father Robert Swanton had an agreement with the Cole brothers, granting them an equal undivided interest in the land. They claimed that any payments for the land should have been attributed to Swanton's estate, arguing that the Coles took advantage of their father's death to acquire the rightful property without compensating his heirs.	The defendants, led by Thomas Attridge and the Cole brothers, argued that the plaintiffs had no legal basis for their claims. They maintained that the land had been purchased legitimately by the Coles from the government, and that Swanton had no pre-emption rights. The defense emphasized that there was no binding agreement regarding the land's interest, and that any funds used for the purchase were from Mary Attridge, not the estate of Swanton. The Coles contended that their purchase of the land was valid and free of any encumbrance from Swanton’s heirs.

Charles MacRitchie and Michol entered into a contract with the City of Lake View in 1889 to furnish and lay an inlet-pipe for the municipal waterworks on the bottom of Lake Michigan. The contract required the contractors to follow detailed plans and specifications created by the town’s engineer, with work subject to the engineer’s supervision. The conditions stipulated that the contractors would ensure the pipe remained in good condition for one year after acceptance. After the completion of the project, a break was discovered in the pipe, resulting in significant repair costs for the city. The city filed an action against the contractors based on a bond binding them to the contract. The key contention for the contractors was that the break in the pipe was not due to their workmanship but rather due to flaws in the plans provided by the engineer, namely the insufficient number of flexible joints required to accommodate the shifting lakebed.	The City of Lake View claimed that MacRitchie and Michol breached their contractual obligations by failing to ensure the inlet-pipe remained in good condition as guaranteed for one year. The city argued that this warranty made the contractors liable for repairs regardless of whether the break was due to defective workmanship or poor material, emphasizing their responsibility to indemnify the city for any costs incurred.	MacRitchie and Michol contended that the break was not a result of faulty workmanship or materials but rather due to the engineer's inadequate planning and instructions. They argued that since the engineer directed how to lay the pipe and its joints, they should not be held liable for defects stemming from the design. They sought the court's recognition that the warranty only covered defects in workmanship and materials actually provided, not liabilities arising from the plans created by the city’s engineer.

The case "Commissioners of Highways of Town of Dayton v. Commissioners of Highways of Town of Rutland" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1876. The dispute arose when the commissioners of highways for Dayton sought to recover half the costs of repairing a bridge over the Fox River, which served as the boundary between the towns of Dayton and Rutland. The bridge was built in 1853 through private donations and had been used by the public until it was carried away by ice in 1857. Following its destruction, a new bridge was constructed with funding from both towns and private sources. Over the years, actions taken by the commissioners, such as opening roads and managing the bridge's upkeep, indicated that they recognized and accepted the bridge as a public structure. However, when the bridge fell into disrepair in 1868, the commissioners of Rutland attempted to prevent travel over it. After Rutland failed to assist in repairing the bridge despite a notice from Dayton's commissioners, Dayton undertook the repairs and sought reimbursement for half the expenses in court. The trial initially resulted in a judgment favoring Rutland, leading to the appeal.	The commissioners of highways of the Town of Dayton claimed that they were entitled to reimbursement for half the costs of repairing the public bridge after the commissioners of Rutland failed to respond to their request for assistance. They argued that the actions of both towns' commissioners demonstrated an acceptance of the bridge's dedication to public use and that, legally, both towns were responsible for sharing the repair costs.	The commissioners of highways of the Town of Rutland contended that they did not accept the legal responsibilities associated with the bridge and disputed the suggestion that their actions constituted an acceptance of its dedication. They claimed that any legal intent related to their actions should not bind the town without clear evidence of acceptance. The Rutland commissioners argued that the evidence presented by Dayton did not satisfy the legal standards necessary to establish their liability for the repair costs.

In February 1868, in Sangamon County, Illinois, Samuel Haines sold a tract of land to Shadrack Wilburn for $2,400. Wilburn paid $500 upfront and executed two promissory notes for $950 each, due in one and two years, with a 10% interest rate payable annually. As part of the agreement, Haines provided a bond that stipulated if Wilburn paid the notes on time, Haines would transfer the deed for the property. After one year, when Wilburn failed to pay the first note and interest, Haines requested possession of the land, which Wilburn refused. Consequently, Haines filed an action of forcible entry and detainer against Wilburn to gain possession of the property. The case raised the question of whether Haines could maintain such an action under the law concerning vendor-vendee relationships.	Haines argued that Wilburn's failure to pay the first note constituted a breach of their contract, justifying his demand for possession of the property. He cited a 1861 amendment allowing a vendor to take action against a vendee who refuses to comply with contractual obligations after taking possession. Haines asserted he was entitled to regain possession without needing to return any payments, as the law permitted such actions under these circumstances.	Wilburn contended that Haines had no right to reclaim the property without first putting him in statu quo, asserting that Haines needed to rescind the contract officially. He argued that there was no evidence that Haines had intended to rescind the agreement or had provided notice of such an intention. Wilburn maintained that the bond was a simple contract without a clause of forfeiture and that time was not made the essence of the contract, thus requiring compensation rather than rescission.

In March 1883, Jacob Johnson, the payee of a promissory note for $1,500, endorsed the note and provided a guaranty for its payment. Joseph O. Glover, the defendant, was taken to court for failing to fulfill this guaranty. The case was tried at the Superior Court of Cook County in Illinois, with a jury verdict ultimately favoring the plaintiff, Glover. The court ruled in favor of Glover for $1,710 after a reduction of the total from $1,784.93. During the trial, the defendant requested a continuance due to the absence of a key witness, W.H. Bullen, which was denied by the court based on a lack of demonstrated diligence in securing the witness’s presence. The defendant's other motions for continuance and objections to amendments made to the declaration were also denied. Ultimately, the court found no material errors in the record, leading to the affirmation of the judgment.	Glover, the plaintiff, argued that as the guarantor of the promissory note, the defendant was obligated to pay the amount due upon its maturity. He claimed that Glover's failure to make the payment constituted a breach of contract. The plaintiff sought a judgment for the amount owed under the guaranty, successfully demonstrating that the defendant had not fulfilled his payment obligations.	Joseph O. Glover, the defendant, contended that he was unjustly denied a continuance that would have allowed him to present crucial witness testimony to support his case. He argued that he was not adequately prepared for trial and sought to introduce pleas regarding a failure of consideration related to the promissory note, claiming that the plaintiff was not entitled to recover because the note was purchased after maturity. However, the court noted that the defendant had failed to establish sufficient diligence or justification for his requests, leading to the denial of his defenses.

In 1876, a legal case titled "Thomas W. Williams et al. v. Bayard Chalfant" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Marion County, presided over by Judge Amos Watts. The plaintiffs, led by Thomas W. Williams, formed a suit in assumpsit against five defendants. The court initially found that service of process had been completed for all defendants and rendered a judgment against them. However, it was later revealed that one defendant, James W. Bobb, had not been served, leading to the conclusion that the judgment rendered was erroneous. The court emphasized that a judgment against all defendants is invalid if there is no service on even one defendant, citing precedents from earlier rulings. Additionally, an issue arose concerning a special deputy sheriff's service of process relating to another defendant, Tucker. The court ruled that the return on the summons, which included both the sheriff's and the deputy's names and was sworn to by the deputy, complied with statutory requirements. Due to these errors and clarifications, the judgment against the defendants was reversed and remanded for further proceedings.	The plaintiffs, Thomas W. Williams and others, contended that a valid judgment should be rendered against all named defendants. They claimed that service of process had been correctly executed and sought to hold all defendants accountable for the obligations in the suit.	The defendants argued that the judgment was erroneous because one of their number, James W. Bobb, had not received service of process, which invalidated the entire judgment against all defendants. They maintained that due process had not been observed, and thus, the judgment should be set aside.

In June 1853, the Illinois Supreme Court examined the case of William Dixon v. John H. Dunham concerning a dispute over the delivery of goods. The case took place between Buffalo, New York, and Chicago, Illinois. Dixon, the plaintiff, was a merchant and the consignee of certain goods shipped on the propeller "Illinois," which was captained by Dunham, the defendant. These goods were transported from Buffalo to Chicago, with a delivery obligation outlined in a bill of lading. Upon arrival in Chicago, Dunham delivered the goods to the wharf of Dole, Rumsey & Co., as was customary in the port. However, Dixon refused to accept the goods at that location, insisting they be delivered directly to his own wharf. Unable to reach an agreement, Dunham tendered freight payment and retained the goods, prompting Dixon to file a replevin action to reclaim them. The case revolved around the customary trade practice at the port regarding delivery obligations and the implications of the bill of lading.	Dixon argued that according to the explicit terms of the bill of lading, the goods were to be delivered to him at his wharf in Chicago. He contended that since he was doing business at this location, it was the defendant's obligation to fulfill the delivery there. Dixon demanded the court recognize his claim to the goods based on the assumption that the terms of the contract were clear and unambiguous, requiring delivery at his designated location.	Dunham countered Dixon’s claims by highlighting an established custom and usage of trade in Chicago. He asserted that it was customary for goods to be delivered at the dock selected by the vessel's master, rather than directly to the consignee’s designated wharf. Dunham maintained that Dixon was aware of this custom when he shipped the goods and that he had a legal obligation to accept the delivery at the customary location where Dunham had placed the goods. Dunham sought to have the court uphold the established usage, which he argued would govern the terms of the delivery.

In 1875, in Mason County, Illinois, Caleb W. Slade, Stephen Sexton, and George W. Henninger, operating under the partnership name Henninger, Slade & Sexton, were involved in a legal dispute with Robert D. McClure, Thomas Culter, Jared B. Wing, and Charles P. Culter of the firm McClure, Culter & Co. The case originated from a promissory note, for which the plaintiffs sought payment from Slade after he was the only partner served with process, as the others could not be found. Slade requested a continuance of the trial due to the absence of his partners, who had absconded, taking critical partnership documents with them. This request was initially granted, but a subsequent request for a continuance based on the same reason was denied by the court. The trial proceeded, resulting in a judgment favoring the plaintiffs, which led Slade to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, McClure, Culter, Wing, and Culter, contended that Slade was liable for the debt outlined in the promissory note. They argued that Slade's continued requests for a trial delay due to his partners' absence were unreasonable, especially since he had already received a prior continuance. Their claim aimed to uphold the initial judgment rendered in their favor.	Slade, as the appellant, argued that the circuit court committed errors by denying his request for a second continuance and refusing to grant a new trial based on the surprise caused by a witness's testimony. He maintained that the absence of his partners and their potential testimony was crucial for his defense. Slade claimed that the judgment against him should be reconsidered due to these procedural issues.

In the case of George Babel et al. v. Adam Babel et al., which took place in Illinois, the legal proceedings began on December 8, 1886. The case involved a dispute over an indebtedness of $475.95, initiated by Lord, Stoutenburg & Co. through an attachment against George Babel and Catherine Beauchamp. Adam Babel and Freeman E. Pettit were summoned as garnishees. Following the initial judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, a trial without a jury led to a further examination of the answers provided by the garnishees. The central issue revolved around the ownership of warehouse receipts tied to forty barrels of whisky, which had been placed in Pettit’s custody by Adam Babel for sale. The plaintiffs asserted that the receipts were under Adam Babel's agency because they were originally entrusted by them to him, while Adam Babel countered that he had purchased the receipts in good faith. The evidence presented was conflicting, leading the court to uphold the initial ruling based on standard judicial principles regarding conflicting evidence.	The plaintiffs, Lord, Stoutenburg & Co., claimed they were entitled to the $687.93 held by Freeman E. Pettit, alleging that the warehouse receipts for the whisky were merely held by Adam Babel as their agent. They asserted that the true ownership of the receipts and the proceeds from their sale remained with George Babel and Catherine Beauchamp.	Adam Babel argued that he had legitimately purchased the warehouse receipts from George Babel and Catherine Beauchamp for value and in good faith. He maintained that the receipts and the money derived from their sale rightfully belonged to him, thus contesting the plaintiffs' claims.

In April 1859, in Cook County, Illinois, an action of assumpsit was initiated by Joel Seymour and others (the appellees) against William T. Shufeldt and William S. Littell (the appellants). The legal action involved a promissory note made in the name of “W. T. Shufeldt & Co.” The plaintiffs asserted that the defendants were co-partners and, therefore, collectively liable for the note, which promised payment to Seymour & Woodruff. William T. Shufeldt responded by filing a plea of non-assumpsit, which included an affidavit denying the execution of the note and the existence of a partnership. The case proceeded without a jury, with the plaintiffs presenting witness testimony confirming Shufeldt's signature on the note. Despite efforts from Shufeldt to prove that William S. Littell was not part of the partnership, the court sustained objections and ruled that the partnership issue was not adequately raised. Shufeldt's subsequent motion for a new trial was denied, leading to an appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants, under the partnership name “W. T. Shufeldt & Co.,” executed a promissory note promising payment to them. They argued that the defendants were liable due to their partnership and provided evidence, including a witness who testified to Shufeldt's signature on the note. They sought a judgment against Shufeldt for the amount specified in the note, which totaled $102.28.	The defendants contended that the execution of the promissory note was denied and claimed that the existence of a partnership was not established. Shufeldt argued that the trial court erred by not recognizing the necessity to prove the partnership in order to establish liability. He objected to the court's refusal to allow him to present evidence about the firm's composition and asserted that the judgment entered against him was erroneous.

The case "Isaac Howland v. The City of Chicago" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 23, 1884. It arose from a situation where Isaac Howland was a livery stable keeper in Chicago, managing a business that involved hiring out six carriages. The city of Chicago accused him of operating without the necessary licenses for his carriages, violating section 1146 of the city’s revised ordinances, which explicitly required a license for anyone hiring out vehicles. After Howland was found guilty by a police justice and fined $50, he appealed the decision, which was subsequently upheld by the Criminal Court of Cook County and later by the Appellate Court for the First District. The case was escalated to the Supreme Court of Illinois due to the significance of the legal questions raised regarding the authority of the city to impose such licensing fees.	The plaintiff, the City of Chicago, argued that Howland was in violation of city ordinances that mandated a license for keeping and hiring out carriages. The city maintained that these ordinances were authorized by state law, which allowed for the taxation and regulation of livery stables. The plaintiff sought to affirm the fines imposed on Howland for his non-compliance and to uphold the legitimacy of the licensing requirements instituted by the city.	Isaac Howland contended that the ordinances under which he was convicted were not properly authorized by the state and that, if they were, they violated the constitutional provisions concerning taxation. He argued that the licensing requirement was not uniformly applied to all livery stables and thus was unconstitutional. Howland sought to have the judgment against him overturned and the fines dismissed, asserting that the city lacked the legal authority to impose such mandates on his business.

Charles Fabri brought a legal case against Thomas B. Bryan and others in September 1875, in Illinois. The dispute arose from Fabri's occupation of premises leased from Bryan. Fabri allegedly did not surrender possession after the lease expired and failed to pay rent for a significant period. Despite being notified to vacate the premises, he refused. Consequently, Bryan and his associates entered the premises and removed Fabri's belongings. Fabri then launched an action for trespass, alleging wrongful entry and removal of his goods. The case was tried before a jury, which found in favor of Bryan and the other defendants. Following this verdict, Fabri appealed the decision, questioning the legality of the defendants' actions under the lease agreement.	Fabri contended that the defendants committed trespass by unlawfully entering his premises and removing his property. He argued that their actions were unauthorized and not justified under the terms of the lease. Fabri sought legal remedy for the alleged trespass and requested a new trial on the grounds that the jury's verdict was improper.	The defendants, led by Bryan, claimed that their actions were justified under a provision in the lease that allowed them to enter the premises and remove any occupant, using force if necessary, if the tenant held over after the lease expired. They argued that Fabri's failure to pay rent and refusal to vacate the property legally warranted their actions. The defendants maintained that they had a right to regain possession of the premises under the lease terms and that no excessive force was used.

The case of Clarence Pomeroy v. Paul Villavossa took place in 1889 in Cook County, Illinois. The events began during an auction where Clarence Pomeroy, the plaintiff and auctioneer, conducted the sale of furniture at a private residence. The defendant, Paul Villavossa's wife, bid on several items, but after disputing her bill, she attempted to take a pile of silver coins that she had not paid for. Pomeroy, unfamiliar with the Villavossas, intervened to retrieve the coins. This action led Villavossa to come to his wife's defense, resulting in both of them leaving the premises without surrendering the money. Subsequently, Pomeroy accused Villavossa of larceny and obtained a warrant against him. However, during the judicial hearing, Villavossa was discharged as there was no evidence proving guilt. The case revolves around whether Pomeroy had probable cause for his actions against Villavossa.	Pomeroy claims he was a victim of malicious prosecution due to Villavossa's actions which led to an unwarranted arrest. He argues that he had reasonable grounds and probable cause to suspect theft based on the circumstances surrounding the auction and the conduct of Villavossa and his wife. Pomeroy seeks damages for the malicious prosecution he endured as a result of Villavossa's alleged wrongdoings.	Villavossa argues that Pomeroy acted without probable cause in initiating criminal proceedings. He contends that the prosecution was baseless and that the circumstances did not warrant the belief that he or his wife were committing theft. Villavossa asserts that Pomeroy's lack of familiarity with them should not have led to his actions and requests that the court dismiss the plaintiff's claims based on the lack of probable cause for prosecution.

In November 1853, in La Salle County, Illinois, Alexander M. Bruen and Louisa J. Bruen initiated a chancery suit against Herman Bruen, a non-resident, and Philo Lindley. The plaintiffs sought to cancel a deed for lands that Herman Bruen had recorded through Lindley. A decree was rendered by default against Herman Bruen due to his absence at the hearing, with the only notice being a publication. In November 1855, Herman Bruen filed a petition to have the decree set aside, claiming he had no knowledge of the proceedings. The petition was eventually accepted, and the case was transferred to Grundy County. Multiple notices of the proceedings were served, and Herman Bruen was allowed to file a cross-bill, in which the default against Alexander M. Bruen and Louisa J. Bruen was eventually taken. The court later ruled in favor of Herman Bruen, which led to a reevaluation of the original decree.	The plaintiffs, Alexander M. Bruen and Louisa J. Bruen, argued that the decree issued against Herman Bruen should be upheld since it was properly rendered in accordance with the applicable Chancery Code. They contended that the original decree was correct as they believed Herman Bruen had been appropriately notified of the proceedings through publication practices.	Herman Bruen, the defendant, claimed that the original decree was unjust due to his lack of knowledge and absence during the proceedings, as he had not been served with process or informed of the lawsuit appropriately. He requested the court to set aside the decree and allow him to answer the original complaint, arguing for his rights based on the Chancery Code provisions regarding notice and jurisdictional issues.

The legal case, "Eldridge S. Janney v. Johnson J. C. Birch, Administrator, etc.," took place in January 1871 in Illinois. The key individuals involved are Eldridge S. Janney, the plaintiff, and Johnson J. C. Birch, the defendant, who served as the administrator of the estate of Sarah E. Peake. The case centers on Janney's alleged indebtedness for two promissory notes, dated April 24, 1855, and April 24, 1856, for amounts of $525 and $1002.50 respectively. These notes were purportedly given to Mrs. Peake, who died in 1858. After her death, Janney's wife, the only child and heir of Mrs. Peake, also passed away, leading Janney to seek letters of administration on Mrs. Peake’s estate in February 1859. Janney claimed that he had previously settled with the defendant in 1861, during which the defendant allegedly denied owing the notes and became angry. The defendant contended that, during another settlement, he paid off a different note due to the estate and maintained that he was not informed of any other outstanding debts. The court ruled in favor of Birch initially, leading to Janney’s appeal.	Eldridge S. Janney argues that he does not owe the money represented by the notes as they were settled prior and never presented as claims against Sarah E. Peake’s estate. He claims that any potential debts were settled with the defendant in 1861, during which the defendant denied liability for the notes. Janney further asserts that he refrained from pursuing legal action due to his late wife's wishes and later filed suit only after being provoked by anonymous letters.	Johnson J. C. Birch contends that the notes in question were never executed by him and submitted a special plea denying their execution. Birch argued that the notes were settled previously and that if they existed, they were paid off during the 1861 settlement. He provided witness testimony that contradicts Janney's assertions and pointed out that Janney failed to account for the notes as administrator of Mrs. Peake’s estate. Birch requests that the judgment of the lower court be upheld based on the preponderance of evidence in his favor.

In 1872, in Illinois, a legal action was commenced by a married couple, Michael Vogel and his wife Mary Vogel, against William Hennies and his spouse, pertaining to allegations of assault and battery against Mary Vogel. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Livingston County, where the Vogels claimed that they suffered from personal injuries inflicted by the defendants. The court initially ruled in favor of the Vogels, awarding them damages of $1,112.50. This case also highlighted the legal principle concerning married women’s rights to sue for personal injuries as a separate property. The prior ruling in the case of C. B. and Q. R. R. Co. v. Dunn established that a married woman must sue alone for personal injuries, given that any right of action due to injuries sustained is her individual property. Furthermore, it noted that while the husband may experience losses due to his wife's injuries, he holds a separate remedy for such losses. The case was appealed, leading to a reassessment of the court's previous judgment.	The plaintiffs, Michael and Mary Vogel, claimed that Mary was subjected to assault and battery by the defendants, resulting in personal injuries. They sought damages for these injuries incurred, asserting that Mary possessed the right to sue on her own behalf as the injuries were her separate property under Illinois law.	The defendants contended that the husband, Michael Vogel, lacked a cause of action for the injuries sustained by his wife. They argued that any recovery for damages should not include the husband since the right of action belonged solely to the wife, and thus, her husband had no independent claim regarding the injuries.

In 1885, a legal case was brought in the Circuit Court of St. Clair County, Illinois, involving Margaret Spies and her children against The Covenant Mutual Benefit Association of Illinois. The case centered around a membership certificate that promised to pay $5,000 upon the death of Charles Spies, the deceased husband and father. The association had claimed that the certificate was cancelled in December 1882 due to Charles Spies' violation of terms that prohibited the use of alcoholic stimulants to the extent of impairing health. The circuit court trial found in favor of the plaintiff, leading to damages being assessed as specified in the certificate. This decision was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court for the Fourth District, which underscored that the primary issues revolved around factual determinations regarding the contract's terms and conditions.	The plaintiffs, Margaret Spies and her children, argued that the membership certificate, which assured them $5,000 upon Charles Spies’ death, remained in effect despite the defendant's claims of cancellation. They contended that proper notice of nonpayment of fees was not given, thus asserting their entitlement to the benefits outlined in the certificate. Their legal requests included the fulfillment of the payment due based on the terms stipulated in the membership agreement.	The defendant, The Covenant Mutual Benefit Association of Illinois, argued that the membership certificate was cancelled due to Charles Spies' failure to comply with the requirement of annual dues and the alleged use of alcoholic stimulants that led to a breach of contract. They requested the court to affirm the cancellation of the membership, thus denying liability to pay the benefits claimed by the plaintiffs.

The case "First National Bank of Centralia, for use, etc. v. Henry W. Strang et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1874. It originated when the payors of a promissory note delivered it to an agent named Ervy, intending for it to be discounted at the First National Bank of Centralia. However, the bank refused to accept the note for discounting, which meant that it never acquired any interest in it. Ervy then sold the note to Smith, who subsequently sold it to Gillespie, initiating the suit on behalf of the bank against Strang and others. The key question was whether the note had ever become a valid instrument binding the defendants. The court found that without delivery to the payee, the note was incomplete and therefore void. The defendants, having received a non-negotiable instrument, could not be held liable.	The First National Bank, through Gillespie, argued that it was entitled to recover the amount on the promissory note based on its supposed transfer from the payors via the agent, Ervy. The bank claimed that despite not having formally accepted the note, it had a right to be compensated for the amount due under it.	The defendants contended that the note was never valid because it was not accepted by the bank and therefore was not binding upon them. Specifically, they argued that the lack of indorsement and proper delivery rendered the note void. They asserted that since the bank had no legal title to the note, it could not maintain a suit to collect the amount.

The legal case "The Mobile and Ohio Railroad Company v. The People of the State of Illinois" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on April 22, 1890. It arose from a conflict regarding the operational and locational obligations of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad Company (the defendant), which took over the management of a railroad line originally created by the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company. The case was initiated due to the removal of a station at Hodges Park, a small village in Alexander County, Illinois, which had relied on the station for its economic activity and connectivity. Residents argued that the relocation of the station to a site north of Hodges Park increased travel distance for the local community, thus reducing their access to the railroad services that were critical to their livelihoods. The legal dispute centered around whether the railroad company had a responsibility to maintain the Hodges Park station, and whether the public's demand and the needs of the community mandated this service.	The plaintiff, represented by the Attorney General, sought a writ of mandamus against the Mobile and Ohio Railroad Company, claiming that the company was legally obligated to maintain the depot and stop its trains at Hodges Park. The plaintiff argued that the station had been established based on prior agreements and public necessity, emphasizing that the citizens of Hodges Park and surrounding areas had made considerable investments in real estate and business with the expectation that the railroad would remain a vital transportation link.	The defendant, the Mobile and Ohio Railroad Company, contended that there was no binding agreement mandating the maintenance of the Hodges Park station. It argued that the decision to relocate the station was made based on operational efficiency and to better serve the wider public needs, demonstrating that the new location was more central and advantageous for the majority of users, rather than just the residents of Hodges Park. Moreover, the defendant stated that maintaining two stations in close proximity was not justified by the low volume of business at Hodges Park.

In 1883, the case "The City of East St. Louis v. Elizabeth H. Underwood, Ex’x" arose in St. Clair County, Illinois. The proceedings were initiated by Elizabeth H. Underwood, acting as the executrix for William H. Underwood, to enforce the payment of a judgment obtained from the city regarding bonds and interest owed. The city failed to levy taxes for the fiscal year commencing March 15, 1879, and only initiated a tax levy just before the court hearing, which was not sufficient to cover the owed amount. Underwood's petition, filed on November 29, 1879, sought a peremptory writ of mandamus to compel the city to pay her judgment from the city treasury and to levy additional taxes if necessary.
