The court found that the city had not levied tax in accordance with its charter requirements and had wrongfully allocated funds that should have been used to pay the judgment. The trial court ruled that a portion of the subsequently levied tax should be applied to Underwood's judgment.	The plaintiff, Elizabeth H. Underwood, claimed that the City of East St. Louis had sufficient funds to pay her judgment for the bonds and coupons owed to her deceased husband. She sought a writ of mandamus demanding that the city council pay the judgment from these funds. Additionally, the plaintiff requested that if the current treasury funds were insufficient, the city be compelled to levy a tax in accordance with its charter to ensure full payment of the judgment, interest, and costs.	The City of East St. Louis defended itself by arguing that its powers to levy taxes were limited by its charter, which restricted general tax levies to one percent of property value for all municipal purposes. The city claimed that the judgment payment obligations were merged into the judgment itself, thereby disputing the classification of the original debt. It also emphasized that there were insufficient funds in the city's treasury to satisfy the judgment based on the current tax levy, suggesting that mandates for payment should not strain municipal finances.

In 1876, in McLean County, Illinois, Philip Crose filed a lawsuit against Andrew S. Rutledge for the seduction of his wife. The case was presided over by Judge Thomas F. Tipton in the Circuit Court of McLean County. The plaintiff, Crose, argued that Rutledge had engaged in an unlawful relationship with his wife, which led to significant emotional and reputational harm. During the trial, evidence was presented about Rutledge's character, but the court later ruled that such evidence regarding the defendant’s general character for chastity was inadmissible in this particular context. The jury found in favor of Crose, awarding him damages of $1,500. Following the verdict, Rutledge sought to overturn the decision through a writ of error, claiming various legal errors in the trial court's handling of evidence and jury instructions.	The plaintiff, Philip Crose, claimed that Andrew S. Rutledge seduced his wife, causing him emotional distress and harm to his reputation. He sought damages of $1,500, arguing that Rutledge's actions had culpably undermined the sanctity of his marriage and led to his public humiliation.	The defendant, Andrew S. Rutledge, contested the claims made by Crose, asserting that the trial allowed prejudicial evidence regarding his character that was not relevant to the charges of seduction. He argued that the evidence of his past conduct was too remote and inadmissible. The defendant also sought to reference the divorce record between Crose and his wife as part of his defense, although the court ruled it could be considered only for mitigating damages.

Joseph E. Otis et al. v. Thomas S. Beckwith et al. is a legal case originating from the city of Chicago, Illinois, and it revolves around a life insurance policy assigned by Edward Sacket to Thomas L. Beckwith as trustee for Sacket's three sons on February 18, 1862. Sacket had a policy worth $3,000 from the New York Life Insurance Company, which he intended to assign for the benefit of his sons, Hobart S., George B., and Frederick A. Sacket, while his youngest son, Walter D. Sacket, was to inherit from their mother. Following Sacket's death on January 17, 1866, the family administrator, Joseph E. Otis, refused to surrender the policy, arguing that it was part of Sacket's estate. The case went to the Superior Court of Chicago, where it was established that Sacket's intention was to provide for his sons, and the assignment was valid even if the policy was not physically delivered to the trustee. The case highlights the complexities of trust laws and the obligations of administrators of estates.	The plaintiffs, represented by Thomas L. Beckwith, argue that Sacket legally and equitably transferred ownership of the life insurance policy to him as a trustee for the benefit of his three sons. They claim that Edward Sacket intended for the policy to be assigned to Beckwith, who accepted the trusteeship. Beckwith demands the surrender of the policy from the administrator, Otis, as he believes he has rightful ownership as the trustee for the children, and seeks general relief in court.	The defendants, including the administrator Joseph E. Otis and Sacket's widow, assert that there was never a valid assignment of the policy to Beckwith. They argue that the assignments were not delivered, being merely voluntary acts without consideration, and hence did not create any legally enforceable trust. The defendants contend that the policy remained under Sacket's control until his death and should be considered part of his estate rather than a separate trust for the children.

In late 1868, in Cook County, Illinois, Charles Thompson and his partner sought legal advice from Joseph S. Reynolds and his partner regarding a release of property outlined in a deed. Reynolds' partner initially suggested they had no interest in the property and could execute a release without harm. Later, they consulted Reynolds and another attorney, James Dunne, who determined that Thompson and his partner did have an interest in the property. Subsequently, the parties entered into an agreement whereby Reynolds would initiate necessary legal proceedings to assert Thompson's claims, with the understanding that he would cover all expenses in exchange for half of any recovery. During the legal proceedings, Thompson and his partner compromised and received approximately $10,000 from various defendants. However, in May 1871, they terminated these proceedings without Reynolds' consent, conveying the properties in question in exchange for $7,500. Reynolds then sought to recover half of this amount, leading to legal action. A jury initially found in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $1,500, but the case was appealed on the grounds of the legality of the initial agreement.	The plaintiffs, Charles Thompson and his partner, claimed that they had entered a legal agreement with Reynolds to pursue their claims regarding property rights, and that Reynolds was entitled to half of any recovery based on this agreement. They argued that the termination of the legal proceedings and subsequent property conveyance they undertook was illegal as it was done without the agreement or knowledge of Reynolds.	Joseph S. Reynolds contended that the original agreement with Thompson was champertous and, therefore, illegal under common law, making the contract void. He argued that the arrangement breached public policy by allowing an attorney to share in the profits from a legal claim without bearing any of the risk or expense. This, he claimed, undermined the integrity of legal advice and practice.

In the case of Charles W. Moore v. Wiley House, which took place in June 1872 in Illinois, the dispute revolves around a labor compensation issue in the construction of a railroad. Selah Chamberlain had contracted with the Belleville and Southern Illinois Railroad Company to build forty miles of track. He subcontracted to Wiley House and his partner, who further subcontracted four miles of work to Daily & Tufts. Charles W. Moore was hired by Daily & Tufts to perform labor on this project. Despite completing the work, Moore sought payment from Wiley House after failing to collect from Daily & Tufts. Initially, Moore sued both Wiley House and his partner before a justice of the peace but lost the case. He appealed to the circuit court, where he successfully obtained a judgment in his favor against Wiley House, leading to this appeal. The core of the case centers on whether Moore could sue Wiley House for unpaid wages, given that his agreement was primarily with Daily & Tufts. The court must determine the implications of the contractual agreements involved and whether Moore had the right to pursue payment under the circumstances.	The plaintiff, Charles W. Moore, argues that he is entitled to recover wages for the work he performed while employed by Daily & Tufts, claiming that he has the legal standing to sue Wiley House as the prior contractor for the payment owed. Moore contends that the contractual provisions between Chamberlain and Wiley House create an obligation that allows him to claim wages directly from them, despite his contract being with Daily & Tufts. His main request is for payment of the outstanding balance owed for his labor, which totals $139.80.	The defendant, Wiley House, asserts that Moore's contract was with Daily & Tufts and that he looked solely to them for payment. They argue that the contractual relationship did not extend to Moore as he was not a party to the original contract and therefore lacks the legal ground to sue them directly. Wiley House also contends that the nature of their agreement with Chamberlain was meant to protect Chamberlain's interests, not to create a liability to Moore. They request that the circuit court's judgment in favor of Moore be overturned.

In 1888, a legal case arose in Chicago, Illinois, involving Portia Gage and others (plaintiffs) against Patrick Caraher (defendant). The case was a petition filed under the Burnt Records Act by Caraher, seeking to confirm his title to certain lots after the destruction of vital land records in a fire in 1871. Caraher asserted that he was the rightful owner, having lost essential deeds that established his chain of title. In their responses, Portia Gage and others claimed ownership of the same lots based on tax deeds recorded after the fire. They alleged that prior tax sales had taken place, which were conducted legally. The court needed to establish the validity of the competing claims in light of the destroyed records.	Caraher, the plaintiff, argued that the destruction of land records prevented him from proving his title directly, but he maintained ownership through established chains of title prior to the fire. He petitioned for confirmation of his title to the disputed properties, asserting that the tax deeds held by Gage and others were invalid due to the lack of an existing legal basis given the destroyed records. His primary legal request was to have the tax claims against his properties removed.	The defendants, led by Portia Gage, contended that the tax deeds recorded after the fire were valid and that they had legitimate ownership claims to the lots. They argued that Caraher should not be granted relief without compensating for taxes and other payments they had made upon acquiring the properties through tax sales. Their main position was that the plaintiff's petition was insufficient to void their tax deeds without demonstrating their invalidity clearly.

In 1834, in Jackson, Illinois, Phineas C. Hall and Samuel B. Hall initiated a legal action against Augustine Byrne & Co. for the foreclosure of a mortgage on land. The mortgage involved was secured by a nominal payment of one dollar, with a larger debt of $997.74 owed by James Hall, Jr., due to the mortgagee. In response to the foreclosure action, Byrne & Co. submitted three defenses: a lack of consideration for the mortgage, a complete failure of consideration, and a partial failure of consideration. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after the Circuit Court sustained the Halls' demurrer to these defenses and ruled in their favor for the amount due, allowing the sale of the mortgaged land.	The plaintiffs argued that the defenses presented by the defendants concerning the mortgage were unfounded. They maintained that a mortgage, when executed and recorded per statutory requirements, should not permit defenses related to consideration, as these do not apply to a mortgage in foreclosure actions. They sought to have the judgment from the lower court affirmed, which ruled that the mortgage was valid and enforceable regardless of the claims made by the defendants.	The defendants contended that there was no valid consideration for the mortgage, alleging either a complete failure or a partial failure of consideration. They argued that these points should be sufficient to defeat the foreclosure action initiated by the plaintiffs. Their primary request was for the court to reverse the decision made by the Circuit Court that denied these defenses.

Thomas Snell v. James De Land et al. is a legal dispute that took place in January 1867 in De Witt County, Illinois. The parties involved were Thomas Snell, the defendant, and James De Land, Edward De Land, Jonathan Hall, and the Magill brothers (Henry, Robert, Samuel, and William), who acted as the plaintiffs. The case originated from a contract made on July 1, 1864, where the plaintiffs sold Snell thirteen thousand pounds of wool at eighty cents per pound, to be delivered within a reasonable timeframe. The plaintiffs claimed to have delivered a total of thirteen thousand nine hundred and forty-nine and a half pounds of wool by August 1, 1864. Snell contested this through a plea of non-assumpsit, alongside invoking a possible set-off against the claims. The court found that at the time of delivery, wool prices ranged from one dollar to one dollar and five cents per pound, and that Snell was financially harmed by the failure to fully execute the contract. The matter was initially decided in favor of the plaintiffs in the De Witt Circuit Court, where the damages assessed amounted to $729.60. Snell appealed this judgment, arguing procedural inaccuracies regarding the joint contract and the sufficiency of proof presented by the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs asserted that they entered into a legitimate contract with Snell for the sale of wool, which they claimed had been fulfilled with the delivery of the wool as stipulated in their agreement. They sought damages based on the differential in price caused by Snell's non-compliance with the delivery terms, arguing their entitlement to the assessed damages of $729.60 due to the failure of Snell to adhere fully to the contractual obligations.	Snell contended that the plaintiffs were improperly joined in the lawsuit, arguing that they failed to demonstrate a joint interest in the contract as required by law. He maintained that the plaintiffs consisted of separate partnerships that were not unified in their contractual obligations toward him. Additionally, he challenged the sufficiency of the evidence supporting the plaintiffs' claims, particularly questioning whether all plaintiffs had rightful claims related to the wool contract. Snell sought to have the judgment reversed based on these arguments and procedural issues regarding the trial court's findings.

The case "Jevne & Almini v. Uri Osgood et al." took place in September 1870 in Joliet, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Jevne and Almini, entered into a contract with the defendant, Uri Osgood, for the purchase of a lot for $1,000. The payment structure included $400 for painting and fresco work on a church, followed by cash payments of $200 each in September of 1859, 1860, and 1861, with interest. They completed the painting to Osgood’s satisfaction and received a receipt. However, they were unable to make the initial cash payment, leading to a mutual agreement to end the contract, which was not formally canceled. Osgood later initiated a lawsuit for the amount owed and after negotiations, a new agreement was allegedly made involving partial payments and work to be done by the plaintiffs. Osgood, however, did not dismiss the original suit, and the plaintiffs did not fulfill all settlement conditions. Eventually, a judgment for over $800 was entered against them without their knowledge, which they claimed was fraudulently obtained. They filed a bill for an injunction to prevent enforced payment. The defendant countersued with a cross-bill for damages and the owed amounts.	Jevne and Almini claim that the contract was effectively rescinded due to mutual agreement and that the judgment against them was fraudulently obtained. They seek an injunction to prevent the collection of the judgment, arguing that they fulfilled their responsibilities under the contract and asserting that they were not notified about the judgment until it was too late.	Osgood defends himself by acknowledging the original sale and work completed but argues that the plaintiffs did not fulfill the contract's conditions or formally rescind the agreement. He claims that the plaintiffs failed to return the contract as agreed, continued to hold him liable, and did not pay the costs associated with the suit or surrender the contract. He seeks to enforce the judgment against them.

Isaac Shackeltow brought a legal case against William M. Sebree and others concerning a dispute over an eighty-acre parcel of land in Illinois. Several years before his father-in-law, John S. Sebree, passed away in April 1873, Shackeltow entered into possession of the land with Sebree’s consent, making significant improvements valued between $600 and $700. After the death of Shackeltow's wife, he surrendered possession back to Sebree without removing the improvements. Once Sebree died intestate, his estate passed to his widow, children, and grandchild. Subsequently, Shackeltow recorded a deed from Sebree to himself, dated September 21, 1870, indicating the deed wouldn’t take effect until after Sebree’s death. The defendants argued that this deed was a forgery, void as an attempt to convey a future interest, or constituted a testamentary paper not properly executed. The court examined various testimonies regarding the deed’s validity and the circumstances of its execution before coming to a decision.	Shackeltow's main claim was that the deed he recorded from John S. Sebree was valid and should convey ownership of the eighty-acre land upon Sebree's death. Shackeltow argued against the defendants' assertions that the deed was forged or legally invalid, asserting that it was executed properly and expressed the intention of both parties.	The defendants contended that the deed was a forgery, as it lacked proper execution requirements and was intended to take effect in the future, which they argued would make it void. They also challenged the evidence surrounding Shackeltow's claims, suggesting that the testimony supporting the deed's execution was unreliable and that Sebree was inebriated at the time of the deed's execution, thus rendering it invalid.

John H. Harris owned an eighty-acre tract of land in Tazewell County, Illinois, as of December 1, 1835. On that date, he and his wife conveyed twenty acres of this land to the county commissioners of Tazewell County, under a deed that included covenants of warranty. This conveyance was made in consideration of the location of the county seat on the property. The Illinois legislature had authorized the location of the county seat on privately owned land, provided that the proprietor donated a sufficient amount of land to the county. Harris accepted the terms, believing the location would increase the value of the remainder of his property. For 15 years, the county used the property for its courthouse and public functions. However, in February 1849, the legislature passed a law allowing the county seat to be moved, resulting in its relocation to Pekin in July 1850. As a result, Harris sued to recover the land he had conveyed, claiming the change in use removed his original agreement's purpose.	John H. Harris, as the plaintiff, argued that the county seat's relocation to Pekin meant that the land he donated could be returned to him. He contended that the original agreement implicitly presumed the county seat would remain indefinitely at Tremont. He requested that the court recognize his entitlement to the twenty acres based on the changed circumstances.	The defendants, Joseph L. Shaw and others, contended that the deed Harris executed was absolute and irrevocable, conveying the land in perpetuity for the public good. They argued that the delegation of authority to change the county seat was within legislative rights and that no condition existed that would cause the land to revert to Harris. The defendants maintained that since the property was still being used for public purposes (exclusively for education), they had not violated any agreement, and thus they sought a judgment in their favor.

Wesley Best brought a legal action against James A. Beal and two others, J. M. Buck and C. P. Buck, in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1877. The case originated in the Macoupin County Circuit Court. The plaintiff alleged that the defendants had jointly made a promissory note, which Best subsequently endorsed and delivered to Holden, who then assigned it to the plaintiff. As the case progressed, the court noted that initially, judgments were rendered by default against Buck and C. P. Buck due to their lack of appearance. Best was then made a party to that judgment through a scire facias procedure. The court reviewed the contents of the declaration, which included special counts indicating that the defendants along with Best were liable to the plaintiff for sums specified in the endorsed note. The record does not detail the exact evidence presented but indicated that the suit was based on an instrument in writing for the payment of money. The court, noting that Best’s status as a party to the default did not violate any procedural rules, ultimately upheld the presumption of joint liability among the defendants.	The plaintiff, Wesley Best, claimed that he should be paid for a promissory note endorsed and transferred through legal procedures from the defendants. He asserted that the defendants had jointly created the note for payment, and due to their default and failure to appear, they were liable for the amount specified in the writing. Best requested the court to recognize the validity of this claim and to enforce payment based on the note in question.	The defendants, while not appearing in the proceedings, implied by their default that they did not contest the claims made by the plaintiff. The primary defense was predicated on the notion that the evidence required to refute the plaintiff's claims was not recorded, and thus, the court must presume that the defendants shared equal liability based on the facts well pleaded in the declaration.

In 1885, George Panton was involved in a legal case against The People of the State of Illinois, which was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from Boone County, where Panton faced charges of murder. The trial included discussions on the principles of self-defense and the standards of insanity as a legal defense. The court examined various jury instructions given during the trial, particularly focusing on the accuracy and legality of the self-defense justification. One significant aspect was whether the danger faced by Panton was immediate and pressing, essential for claiming self-defense. Additionally, the court evaluated whether the jury had been instructed correctly regarding the defendant’s state of mind and the consequences of their findings. The judgment revealed that misleading jury instructions were given, leading to confusion regarding self-defense and the potential verdicts of murder or manslaughter. Ultimately, these erroneous instructions prompted the court to reverse the initial judgment.	The plaintiff, George Panton, claimed that he acted in self-defense when he fatally injured another individual. He argued that the trial court provided misleading jury instructions that improperly restricted the jury's ability to consider self-defense. Panton contended that the instructions failed to align with the legal standards regarding imminent danger and allowed bias against his defense. He sought a reversal of the judgment based on these procedural errors, advocating for a fair assessment of self-defense rights under the law.	The defendant, representing The People of the State of Illinois, argued that Panton's actions constituted murder, as he did not adequately demonstrate that he acted in self-defense. The defense maintained that the trial's jury instructions were appropriately aligned with legal standards regarding insanity and self-defense. They insisted that any claims related to jury confusion were unfounded and that the evidence supported a verdict of murder rather than manslaughter. The defense requested the court to uphold the original judgment due to the sufficiency of the evidence against Panton.

In February 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of David Dows et al. v. Byron J. McCleary et al. involves a dispute where plaintiffs David Dows & Co. seek to recover the value of eight carloads of corn they alleged was converted by the defendants, McCleary, Smith & Co. The central issue concerns a contract made on December 17, 1879, between Dows & Co. and Morse & Lilley, wherein the latter were to procure corn on behalf of the former. Evidence was presented at trial showing that Morse & Lilley acted as agents, storing the corn in cribs marked with Dows & Co.'s name, while Dows provided funds for purchasing the corn. However, the plaintiffs failed to conclusively prove that the contract was formally executed. Instead, it was established that Morse & Lilley, operating in the corn business, shipped five carloads of corn to the defendants, who sold it and returned the proceeds without knowledge of any ownership dispute. The court originally sided with the defendants in this conversion action, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiffs, David Dows & Co., claim that the corn stored in the cribs marked with their name was their property. They argue that the defendants, McCleary, Smith & Co., converted this property by selling it without consent. They seek compensation for the value of the corn, asserting that a valid contract existed between them and Morse & Lilley granting them ownership of the corn stored and sold by the defendants.	The defendants, McCleary, Smith & Co., argue that they were not liable for conversion as they transacted in good faith without knowledge of the plaintiffs' claims to the corn. They contend that Morse & Lilley acted within their authority as custodian to sell the corn and that no binding contractual obligations existed between Dows & Co. and Morse & Lilley that would prevent the sale. Therefore, since the transaction was in the normal course of business, they request that the plaintiffs' claims be dismissed.

In September 1868, the case of *August Wallbaum v. Edwin Haskin et al.* was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from actions taken in the Superior Court of Chicago. The plaintiff, August Wallbaum, brought the suit under the guise of "assumpsit" (a legal term for a type of contract dispute) against Edwin Haskin and others. The case arose from an earlier trial set for December 27, 1867, which the defendant had prepared for but subsequently challenged. On December 9, the plaintiffs filed an affidavit stating their belief that Haskin's defense was merely for the purpose of delaying the case. They notified the defendant that they intended to move the trial date up to December 16. When the case was called on the new date, the defendant objected to this expedited trial, claiming it contradicted established legal practices. However, the court overruled Haskin's objections and permitted the trial to proceed, ultimately resulting in a judgment against him. Following the trial's conclusion, the defendant appealed the ruling, contesting the legality of the court's procedures allowing for an earlier trial date.	The plaintiff asserted that the defendant's actions were primarily aimed at delaying the proceedings. They utilized a court rule that allows for a trial to be expedited if a belief is presented that the defense is merely a tactic for delay. Wallbaum contended that this rule was valid within the Superior Court's jurisdiction and sought immediate resolution of the dispute.	The defendant, Haskin, contended that the court's rule permitting an expedited trial was unlawful and not in accordance with established legal procedures. He argued that the trial should not have been altered from its original scheduling and that his defense was made in good faith, contrary to the plaintiff's claims. Haskin objected to the expedited process, asserting that it undermined the judicial practices that govern such cases.

Jacob Mussulman and others entered into a joint and several recognizance in 1853, in the Massac Circuit Court, Illinois, promising to ensure the appearance of a person named Lane to answer a criminal charge. Following a forfeiture of this recognizance, a scire facias was issued against the individuals who acknowledged the recognizance. Mussulman and another individual, Jack, responded to the process. Mussulman attempted to plead that Jack, being an attorney and counselor at law at the time the recognizance was executed, was not liable. However, the court demurred this plea, indicating that even if it were valid, Mussulman remained bound by the recognizance. The court's previous rulings in related cases, such as Passfield v. The People and Sans v. The People, further supported that a joint obligor cannot shield themselves by claiming another is not liable. Subsequently, Mussulman sought a writ of error after judgment was rendered against him for the amount of the recognizance.	The plaintiffs, led by Jacob Mussulman, argued that the court erred in not recognizing Jack's status as an attorney when the recognizance was executed, implying that this should absolve both from liability. They sought to overturn the judgment made against Mussulman, contending that the obligations of the joint recognizance should not apply due to Jack’s attorney status.	The People, serving as the defendants, maintained that Mussulman remained liable regardless of Jack's legal profession. They argued that the law stipulates that the defense pertaining to Jack's status as an attorney was personal to him and could not be used by Mussulman. The defendants also claimed that there was no error in the court not addressing Jack's liability since the matter directly pertained to Mussulman's obligations as a co-signatory.

In December 1852, the case of Stephen Abrams v. John Lee was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in Scott County, Illinois, and involved two copartners, Abrams and Lee, who entered into an action of account under the statute. Following a previous judgment, where the court had ruled in favor of Lee after reviewing errors assigned by both parties, Abrams appealed to have the case returned to auditors for an accounting between the partners. The circuit court, presided over by Judge Woodson, denied Abrams' motion to recommit the case for further proceedings. Subsequently, the matter was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for review and judgment.	Abrams, the appellant, argued that the circuit court erred by not allowing the case to be recommitted to auditors for an account statement. He sought a reversal of the previous judgment and requested that the court order an accounting of the partnership's financial matters to determine the appropriate resolution.	Lee, the appellee, contended that the circuit court's judgment was correct and supported the earlier ruling that the case had been fully decided, rendering further proceedings unnecessary. He maintained that there was no basis for the appeal, as the prior decision should stand, maintaining that the case was res judicata.

In September 1871, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed a legal dispute in Cambridge, Illinois, between Elizabeth Palmer (the plaintiff) and James A. Converse (the defendant). The case arose from a deed executed by Converse that conveyed a lot to Palmer, described as having a depth of eighty feet. Palmer contested this deed, asserting that she intended to purchase a lot that extended to a fence approximately one hundred and ten feet from the front. The case involved testimony from several key individuals, including an agent for Palmer, Samuel Horn, who claimed Converse had indicated the fence as the rear boundary of the lot during negotiations. However, Converse denied discussing the size of the lot. The court delved into the conflicting testimony regarding the property line and the execution of the deed. It became apparent that there were discrepancies between what Palmer believed she was purchasing and what was documented in the deed. The evidence ultimately led the court to question whether there was sufficient basis to reform the deed based on Palmer's claims.	Elizabeth Palmer argued that the deed she received from James A. Converse should be reformed to extend the property line to the fence, which was about one hundred ten feet from the front, rather than the eighty feet stated in the deed. She contended that the agreement made through her agent was based on the understanding that the lot would include the area up to the fence, which she believed constituted the true boundary intended in the purchase. Palmer sought a court decree to enforce this boundary as reflective of the actual contract she had agreed upon.	James A. Converse contended that no specific discussions were had regarding the lot's size during the negotiations. He maintained that the deed accurately reflected the agreed terms, stating the property to be eighty feet deep. Converse highlighted that Palmer had acknowledged and accepted the terms of the deed without objection. He argued that the court should not reform the deed to reflect something entirely different from what was written, emphasizing the need for clear and satisfactory evidence to support any reformation.

In 1867, a legal dispute arose in Morrison, Whiteside County, Illinois, between Edward McFadden and Edward L. Worthington. The case centered on a title claim by McFadden, who sought to quiet his title to certain real estate lots. The conflict originated from a cloud on his title, which was caused by a prior deed executed to Worthington. After a judgment for costs was entered against a mutual party, Caswell, the lots were sold, leading to McFadden's claim. The Circuit Court of Whiteside County, presided over by Judge W. W. Heaton, ultimately dismissed McFadden's bill. Following this, McFadden brought his case to the Illinois Supreme Court, alleging the dismissal constituted an error regarding the nature of judgment liens on real property.	McFadden argued that the judgment for costs against Caswell should not affect his title to the lots since the deed from Caswell to him was executed before the judgment. He contended that the plaintiffs in the cost judgment were not creditors as defined under the applicable Illinois statutes, and therefore, their claims did not create a valid lien upon the property in question.	Worthington maintained that the judgment for costs constituted a valid lien on the property since it was entered before McFadden's deed was recorded. He argued that McFadden's claim was flawed because the plaintiffs in the original judgment were indeed creditors. Thus, they had prior legal rights to the property despite McFadden's unrecorded deed and should be protected under the conveyance act.

John C. Mehlman filed a lawsuit against The Commercial Insurance Company in September 1868, stemming from a previous judgment made by the Superior Court of Chicago during the April term of 1866. The case involved two insurance policies: one dated September 11, 1865, for $600 insuring a one-story frame building, and another dated October 9, 1865, for a total of $1,400 covering groceries, provisions, and meat stock. Key to this case was a clause in the policies that voided them if the insured kept prohibited items, such as gunpowder or saltpetre, in quantities exceeding specified limits without written consent. The defendants sought to change the venue on claims of local prejudice, but this request was denied. A jury ultimately ruled in favor of the plaintiff. When the defendants appealed, they raised several points including the denial of their motion for a change of venue and the validity of their policy due to alleged violations by the plaintiff.	Mehlman argued that the Commercial Insurance Company breached their insurance contract by refusing to pay for his losses following a fire, despite his compliance with the clauses of the policies. He asserted that the presence of saltpetre was customary in his business and did not pose a risk that would void the insurance policy. The plaintiff's request was for judgment in his favor, reflecting the jury's verdict that confirmed the validity of his policies.	The Commercial Insurance Company contended that the insurance policies were voided due to Mehlman's improper storage of saltpetre, which was expressly forbidden in the policies. They argued that keeping saltpetre for sale constituted a significant breach of the agreement, and that a change of venue was necessary to ensure a fair trial, as prejudice against them existed due to their corporate status versus Mehlman's individual status.

In the legal case of William A. Golder et al. v. Peter Bressler, which was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 31, 1883, the dispute arose from the ownership of a property in Sterling, Whiteside County, Illinois. Peter Bressler claimed ownership of an undivided third part of Block 43 in that area and initiated a bill for partition against William A. Golder and Moses Dillon. Mary Wallace also claimed ownership and filed a cross-petition asserting title to the entire property. The defendants, Golder and Dillon, denied the allegations, and Bressler denied Wallace's claims. The court, after considering the testimony and evidence, determined that Bressler indeed owned an undivided third part of a specified segment of the property while affirming he had no claim to the remaining portion. This case reached the Supreme Court as the plaintiffs contested the lower court's decree based on the sufficiency of evidence regarding the title transfer from the State Bank of Illinois to Bressler.	The plaintiff argued that Bressler's claim to ownership was improperly supported and challenged the legitimacy of evidence presented regarding the transfer of the property title from the State Bank of Illinois to him. They maintained that the evidence was insufficient to establish Bressler’s title and sought a reversal of the lower court's decree that favored Bressler.	Bressler defended his title by asserting the legal sufficiency of the evidence he provided, which included legislative acts and board meeting minutes demonstrating compliance with statutory requirements for property assignment. His defense relied on arguing that the appointment of trustees and the subsequent actions were valid under the law, and any objections raised by the plaintiffs lacked substantive merit, thus supporting his claim of ownership.

In the case of Henry Knoll v. Suffrien Mayer, decided on July 27, 1883, the conflict arose in La Salle County, Illinois, between two neighboring landowners: Henry Knoll, the plaintiff, and Suffrien Mayer, the defendant. The dispute centered around an eighty-acre tract of land owned by each party, where Knoll claimed that Mayer constructed a large embankment along the boundary of their lands. This embankment allegedly obstructed and diverted the natural flow of water from Knoll's property onto Mayer's, thus rendering a portion of Knoll's land unfit for cultivation and harming his crops. During the trial, the jury found in favor of Mayer, resulting in a judgment against Knoll for costs. The case explored crucial issues related to water flow and land use, particularly how agricultural practices may affect natural drainage patterns.	Henry Knoll alleged that Suffrien Mayer's embankment obstructed the natural flow of water from his land, resulting in damage to his crops and making a part of his land unsuitable for farming. He sought compensation for these damages, arguing that Mayer was responsible for interfering with the water drainage that had historically flowed on Knoll's property.	Suffrien Mayer denied the allegations, asserting that he did not create an embankment that would redirect the water flow from Knoll's land. Mayer contended that any embankment, if it existed, was minor and a natural result of his farming activities rather than a deliberate obstruction of water. Additionally, he argued that Knoll had altered the natural drainage patterns by digging ditches and plowing his land in a way that increased the flow of water onto Mayer's property, justifying his actions in creating the embankment.

In the 1867 case of Hiram Pitts et al. v. Philander L. Cable et al., the dispute arose from a transaction involving a mortgage on real estate located in Rock Island County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were plaintiffs Hiram Pitts, Elias S. Gilbert, and Daniel Phelps, and defendants Philander L. Cable, Ransom R. Cable, and Stillman W. Wheelock. The plaintiffs had incurred substantial debt to Mitchell and Cable and sought to resolve this by selling portions of their property. To cover an outstanding amount of $3,556, it was agreed that they would execute a mortgage on a specific property. They also provided Philander L. Cable with a warranty deed and a bond for a reconveyance of the property upon payment, set for September 1, 1860. The core of the plaintiffs' argument was that the transaction was intended as a mortgage, while the defendants contended it was a sale with a right to repurchase. The complexity arose when the plaintiffs failed to make the repayments by the due date, prompting further legal disputes regarding the nature of the original agreement and subsequent ownership transfers involving the property.	The plaintiffs argued that the transaction was a mortgage arrangement intended as security for their debt of $3,556. They sought to redeem the property, claiming that the defendants exercised improper control over the property after the repayment deadline. The plaintiffs asserted that the nature of the deed and bond indicated a mortgage agreement, which entitled them to reclaim ownership upon payment.	The defendants countered that the transaction was meant to be a valid sale rather than a mortgage. Philander L. Cable acknowledged the existence of usury in the original debt but maintained that the true nature of the arrangement was a purchase agreement, with the right to reclaim ownership under certain conditions. They argued that the plaintiffs failed to fulfill the agreed-upon terms and timelines, and thus should not be entitled to any relief.

In August 1830, in Morgan County, Illinois, Ignatius R. Simms, the appellant, was summoned by the sheriff in a case brought against him by Joseph Klein, the appellee. Klein filed an action of assumpsit based on a promissory note and successfully secured a judgment by default after Simms failed to respond. The court proceedings included the assessment of damages by the clerk following the default judgment. The sheriff's return indicated that Simms had been adequately summoned; however, there were discrepancies in how his name was recorded, which later became points of contention in the appeal. Multiple errors were cited by Simms challenging the validity of the judgment against him, leading to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Klein, the plaintiff, claimed that Simms had defaulted on a promissory note, thus arguing for enforcement of the note through a judgment. He sought to uphold the judgment that had already been rendered in his favor due to Simms’ failure to respond adequately after being summoned.	Simms, the defendant, contended that the sheriff's return of service was insufficient and incorrectly referred to him in a truncated manner. He also argued that the declaration claiming the unpaid sum was insufficient, that no evidence supported the damages assessed by the clerk, and that the judgment lacked a detailed enumeration of costs. All these points were deemed frivolous and unsubstantiated by the court.

The case "Arthur Keithley v. William Stafford" revolves around a will contest following the death of Edmond Heaton, who passed away on February 20, 1887, while seriously ill. The events unfolded in Peoria County, Illinois, at the trial in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the final judgment occurring on November 15, 1888. The plaintiff, Elizabeth James, the daughter of Edmond Heaton, through her conservator William Stafford, initiated a bill in chancery to challenge the validity of her father's will. She argued that the will, which primarily bequeathed all property to Arthur Keithley, the deceased's attorney and legal adviser, was not valid since Edmond was supposedly lacking testamentary capacity due to his debilitated mental state caused by illness. During his last days, he was reported to have high fever and delirium. The will was executed in the presence of witnesses just days before his death, and it contained provisions that favored Keithley, leading to allegations of fraud and undue influence. The core of the dispute lay in whether Edmond Heaton was mentally competent to execute the will at that time and whether proper procedures were followed during its drafting.	Elizabeth James, as the plaintiff, contended that the will executed by her father was invalid on three main grounds: first, that he lacked the mental capacity to understand what he was doing at the time of the execution due to illness; second, that Keithley exerted undue influence and employed false representations to benefit himself through the will; and third, that Keithley failed to read the will to Edmond before it was signed, so he did not know its contents. She requested the court to declare the will invalid.	Arthur Keithley, the defendant and proponent of the will, refuted the plaintiff's claims, asserting that the will was valid and that Edmond Heaton was of sound mind when he executed it. Keithley argued that the plaintiff had failed to provide substantial evidence proving that Heaton was incompetent at the time of signing the will. He sought to uphold the will as legally binding and disputed the allegations of fraud and undue influence.

Elliott A. Tarbell, the plaintiff, brought a legal action against Amos Page and other members of the Crystal Lake Ice Company in Illinois in April 1860, seeking unpaid salary. Tarbell had worked for the company as a superintendent, earning an annual salary of $1,200, but after a few months, the company ceased to provide him with employment. The lawsuit was grounded in claims of individual liability under the Illinois General Manufacturing Law of 1849, which stipulated certain conditions for holding stockholders accountable for a corporation's debts. The court presiding over the case was the Illinois Supreme Court, with Judge Manniere in charge. The lower court ruled in favor of the defendants after a demurrer was sustained against the counts in Tarbell’s declaration. As per statutory requirements, it was determined that for a plaintiff to recover against stockholders, a suit against the corporation had to be initiated within one year of the debt’s due date, which had not occurred in this case.	Tarbell argued that he was entitled to receive the balance of his salary from the stockholders of the Crystal Lake Ice Company, relying on the individual liability provisions of the Illinois General Manufacturing Law of 1849. He contended that the company’s insolvency or failure to comply with certain legal formalities regarding its incorporation left the individual stockholders liable for the unpaid salary he earned while employed by the company. Tarbell sought a legal remedy to recover the owed amount.	The defendants, led by Amos Page, countered that Tarbell's claims were invalid as he had failed to file a suit against the company within the required one-year period following the debt’s due date. They maintained that the statutory provisions clearly mandated such compliance for any recovery action against individual stockholders. The defendants also argued that the dissolution of the corporation did not automatically render them liable for its debts beyond the statutory limits and that the company's insolvency did not waive the requirement for a timely suit against the corporation.

In March 1879, John Rung, the plaintiff, was employed as a yard switchman by the Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company, located in Chicago, Illinois. While he was coupling coal cars in the company’s yard, an unexpected movement of a locomotive engine, caused by a malfunctioning throttle valve, resulted in Rung's right hand being caught between the cars. This tragic incident led to the crushing of three fingers on his hand and the amputation of one of them. Following the injury, Rung filed a lawsuit against the railroad company in the Superior Court of Cook County, claiming damages for the negligence that led to his injury. After a trial, a jury ruled in favor of Rung, awarding him $2,000 in damages. The railroad company appealed the decision to the Appellate Court for the First District, which affirmed the judgment, prompting the railroad to take the case to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, John Rung, asserted that the Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company was negligent in failing to maintain the locomotive engine in good and safe condition. He claimed that the company knew, or ought to have known, about the defective throttle valve that caused the unexpected movement of the locomotive while he was performing his duties. Rung sought compensation for the injuries sustained due to this negligence, specifically demanding damages for the loss of one of his fingers and the related suffering.	The Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company contended that the evidence did not support the claims of negligence as alleged by Rung. They argued that the issues involved were factual determinations that should not result in a judgment against them. In their defense, they filed a general issue plea and challenged the admissibility of certain testimony, suggesting that the jury instructions and the trial process were flawed. Ultimately, they requested the court to reverse the lower courts' judgments.

The case, "American Merchants' Union Express Co. v. Isaac M. Wolf et al," took place in September 1875 in Illinois, with a focus on a transaction involving a shipment of goods. On October 8, 1872, goods valued at $65.70, intended for the Greeley club, were delivered to the American Merchants' Union Express Company in Chicago, consigned to W. A. Seib in Atchison, Kansas, under C.O.D. terms (collect on delivery). After the express company received the goods, the consignee, Seib, initially refused delivery due to lack of funds, promising to accept them later. Despite this, the agent failed to notify the Chicago office or the consignor of the consignee’s refusal until November 4, 1872, which left the goods in limbo. The plaintiffs, Wolf and Perlinsky, eventually sought to recover the value of these goods after discovering the delivery failure. A Cook County jury ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $48.68, prompting the express company to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, Isaac M. Wolf and Perlinsky, claimed that the American Merchants' Union Express Company failed in its duty as a common carrier by not properly delivering the goods or notifying them about the refusal by W. A. Seib. They argued that the express company had a responsibility to deliver the goods to the consignee and to inform the consignor if the consignee did not accept them. The plaintiffs sought compensation for the value of the goods, which was established at $65.70.	The defendant, American Merchants' Union Express Company, contended that they had fulfilled their responsibility as a common carrier by attempting to deliver the goods to the consignee. They argued that once the consignee refused acceptance, their obligation to store the goods safely relieved them of further responsibility, thus seeking a reversal of the judgment based on assumed compliance with carrier duties. The company also maintained that the evidence did not support the plaintiffs’ claims that they were required to collect the payment for the goods.

The case "Albert B. Voorheis et al. v. Hugh L. Bovell, Adm’r, etc." was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court on November 24, 1886. The dispute centers around the management of a clothing store known as the Robinson Clothing House. The background dates back to the spring of 1879, when Lutes and his brother, who previously operated a clothing business, failed and assigned their assets for the benefit of creditors, leaving the appellants, Albert B. Voorheis and others, as major creditors. The appellants purchased the assets of Lutes Bros. and opened the Robinson Clothing House, appointing Lutes as the general manager. Lutes maintained the business and managed the accounts until December 1, 1884, and after his death in March 1885, his estate sought compensation for Lutes' services in managing the store. The appellants argued that Lutes was entitled to compensation based on an agreement for half of the net profits, which was part of a conversation with a witness, Gr. W. Harper, about his role in the business. The court's examination focused on the existence of any express contracts regarding Lutes' compensation, the admissibility of evidence regarding the store's profits and losses, and how the absence of a specific agreed amount affected the interpretation of the contract.	The plaintiff, represented by Lutes' administrator, claimed that Lutes was owed compensation for his services as the general manager of the Robinson Clothing House. The basis for this claim was that Lutes' compensation should be measured by an agreement wherein he would receive half of the net profits from the store's operations. The plaintiff contended that this understanding was reached through conversations that indicated a clear expectation of profit-sharing despite the lack of a formally signed contract.	The defendants contended that Lutes' involvement was under an agreed arrangement where he would manage the store and receive half of the profits in exchange for paying off the creditors’ claims. They argued that there wasn't a clear, express contract regarding a fixed compensation amount and that Lutes' compensation should be interpreted in light of the business's performance. Additionally, the defendants sought to limit the evidence presented regarding the business's profits, suggesting that the court should not admit certain financial records that could indicate higher profits.

In December 1840, the legal case "Aaron Tyler v. Richard M. Young et al." was decided in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a promissory note originally made payable by the defendants to Charles C. Perry on January 26, 1837. This note was endorsed to Aaron Tyler, the plaintiff in error. The action was initially brought in the Morgan Circuit Court and then transferred by consent to Sangamon County. The defendants contested the plaintiff's claims and put forth several defenses, including the argument that the consideration for the note was invalid due to various failures related to a bond that was meant to convey certain land as part of the agreement. The Circuit Court ruled partially in favor of the defendants, leading Tyler to seek a reassessment of the judgment in the Illinois Supreme Court.	Aaron Tyler, as the plaintiff, argued that the promissory note he was assigned was valid and enforceable, despite the defendants’ contentions. He maintained that the assignment of the note should be upheld, and he sought a judgment declaring the defendants liable to pay the amount specified in the note.	The defendants countered with several defenses, asserting failure of consideration for the promissory note. They argued that the note was assigned after it had become due, and that there were outstanding judgments against Perry, which impeded his ability to convey the promised land. They contended that these factors negated the possibility of fulfilling the obligations of the promissory note, thus relieving them of liability.

The case involves the City of Chicago as the plaintiff and Benjamin B. Adams as the defendant, arising during April 1860 in Chicago, Illinois. The legal matter centered on an assessment that was levied by the City for the purpose of macadamizing West Randolph Street from Halsted Street to Union Park. The City of Chicago sought to collect this assessment through legal proceedings. During the initial trial held in the Superior Court of Chicago, a default judgment was taken against Adams. However, Adams subsequently filed a motion, supported by an affidavit, requesting the court to set aside this default judgment. The Superior Court granted his motion, allowing him to present a defense against the assessment, paralleling arguments from a related case (The City of Chicago v. Burtice).	The City of Chicago claimed that it was entitled to collect an assessment for the improvement of West Randolph Street. The City sought to uphold the default judgment taken against Adams, asserting that it had followed proper legal procedures for levying the assessment.	Benjamin B. Adams contended that the default judgment should be set aside, challenging the validity of the notice he received regarding the proceedings, which was only by constructive notice through newspaper advertisement. He argued that such notice was inadequate for his defense, and therefore, the court's discretion in setting aside the default was warranted.

In 1857, in Chicago, Illinois, an action of assumpsit was initiated by Nathaniel L. Williams against George C. Smith, who was impleaded with Frank Swick and Richard N. Cowan. The lawsuit arose from three promissory notes executed by the firm Frank Swick & Co., which was comprised of Smith, Swick, and Cowan. Smith was the only one served with process for this action. The case revolved around whether Smith was a member of the firm when the notes were issued. Testimonies were conflicting, with some witnesses asserting that Smith was part of the firm while others disagreed. The trial took place on June 30, 1858, and the jury was directed by the court to assess damages, which initially they did not fully execute. Eventually, the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff, assessing damages at $334.22 based on the notes and the interest calculated at six percent. Smith contested the court’s instructions, but the court found no fault in its actions.	The plaintiff, Nathaniel L. Williams, sought recovery based on three promissory notes issued by the firm Frank Swick & Co. He argued that Smith was liable for the amounts specified in the notes, totaling $334.22, including interest. Williams maintained that the evidence presented supported his claims and sought a judgment in his favor for the full amount due.	George C. Smith, the appellant, pleaded non-assumpsit, asserting that he was not a member of the firm Frank Swick & Co. at the time the notes were executed. He claimed that the evidence was insufficient to establish his involvement, and he challenged the court's instructions regarding the assessment of damages, requesting a new trial and a reconsideration of the judgment.

In 1879, Henry Memory, a merchant based in Chicago, engaged in a contract with the Bremen-based company Schmidt & Fuhrken, represented by Hermann Niepert, to deliver 250 boxes of American bacon. The contract, facilitated through Memory’s broker, Fred. Eggena, stipulated a price of 25 marks for 110 English pounds, with shipment intended for December 1879 or January 1880. However, the defendant failed to deliver the bacon, leading Memory to file a lawsuit for damages. The court trial occurred without a jury, and evidence favored Memory, who was awarded $4,919.96 in damages. Key aspects of the case involved the interpretation of the written contract, the application of the statute of limitations, and the appropriateness of damage calculations based on Bremen market values instead of Chicago's.	Henry Memory claimed damages for the failure of Hermann Niepert to fulfill the contract for the delivery of 250 boxes of bacon. He argued that the contract constituted enforceable terms and that the action was brought within the appropriate time frame despite the defense's claims related to the statute of limitations. He sought to recover the financial losses incurred due to the non-delivery of the goods.	Hermann Niepert contested the lawsuit on grounds including the assertion that the statute of limitations had expired, as more than five years had passed since the expected delivery date. He argued that the written agreement lacked an explicit acceptance or consideration from the plaintiff, rendering it unenforceable. Additionally, Niepert claimed that any implied agreement for adjustments amounted to a new contract, which superseded the original.

In May 1881, the West Chicago Park Commissioners initiated a petition in Cook County to condemn land owned by the McCormicks and others for the establishment of a 250-foot-wide boulevard from Douglas Park to the Illinois and Michigan Canal. A jury awarded $6,657.60 as compensation for the McCormicks' property on November 29, 1882. However, in March 1886, Patrick Flaherty and Lorin C. Collins Jr. claimed they owned part of the condemned premises and were not included in the original proceedings. They filed a petition asserting that they were entitled to a portion of the compensation due, $2,221.29. The Park Commissioners acknowledged Flaherty's claims but asked the court to hold the money until it determined the rightful parties. The McCormicks sought dismissal of the petition, contending that the court lacked jurisdiction. Hearing both parties on May 15, 1886, the county court ordered the Park Commissioners to pay the compensation into the court for distribution, a decision subsequently appealed by the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs, primarily represented by Leander J. McCormick and others, argued that the county court lacked jurisdiction over the case and dismissed the petitions filed by Flaherty and Collins. They contended that the original judgment highlighted their right to the compensation awarded and sought to have the payment made directly to them or to the county treasurer as stipulated by the Eminent Domain Act.	The defendants, represented by the West Chicago Park Commissioners, requested the court to allow them to pay the awarded compensation into court rather than directly to any party. They acknowledged Flaherty's claim and sought a resolution without engaging in disputes between the McCormicks and Flaherty, emphasizing their compliance with legal obligations to settle the money due.

The case "The City of Chicago et al. v. Timothy Wright" took place in September 1873 and was filed in the Cook Circuit Court, Illinois. The key individuals involved included Timothy Wright, the plaintiff, and the City of Chicago along with Mancel Talcott, the police chief, as defendants. Wright claimed ownership of a strip of land (Elizabeth Street) that he alleged had never been dedicated to public use, while the city maintained that this land had been used as a public street for over twenty years. The dispute arose when Wright attempted to take possession of the land and fence it, which he was prevented from doing by city authorities. The case was centered on a bill in equity, filed on June 24, 1872, seeking an injunction to stop the city and its police from interfering with his attempts to reclaim the land. The lower court granted a temporary injunction, which was later made perpetual, leading to the appeal by the defendants to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Timothy Wright, the plaintiff, argued that the strip of land known as Elizabeth Street had never been dedicated to the public and that he held rightful ownership. He claimed that attempts to take possession of the land were thwarted by city officials, and he sought a court injunction to prevent the city from interfering with his rights, asserting exclusive control over the property.	The defendants, consisting of the City of Chicago and its police chief, contended that the land in question had been publicly used as a street for over twenty years and was legally in their possession. They argued that Wright was attempting an illegal forcible entry onto public property and that an injunction preventing the city from exercising its police powers and maintaining public use was unwarranted and detrimental to public order.

In the case of John C. Yates et al. v. Alice M. Dodge, Executrix, the legal proceedings originated from an appeal filed in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the final decision delivered on June 29, 1887. The case arose in Peoria County, Illinois, where John C. Yates presented fraudulent claims against the estate of William M. Dodge, who was deceased. The dispute involved a debt that Yates had allegedly contracted through deceitful means by falsely claiming to be the guardian of two minors, Jennie and Ida Watrous. This representation led to Dodge disbursing a substantial amount of money to Yates, believing the claim to be legitimate. A previous ruling had reversed an earlier judgment, leading to a new trial during which it was determined that Yates' fraudulent statements were sufficient to maintain a legal attachment on the debt claimed. Additionally, there was a complication involving an interpleader claim made by Freeman, who asserted ownership of property levied under an assignment from Yates, which had not been recorded prior to the attachment. The court ultimately reinforced earlier findings regarding both the attachment and the fraudulent acquisition of the debt.	The plaintiff, Alice M. Dodge as the executrix of William M. Dodge’s estate, claimed that John C. Yates incurred a debt through fraudulent misrepresentation. The plaintiff argued that Yates falsely claimed to be the guardian of the minors, which induced Dodge to provide significant financial resources. The plaintiff sought to uphold the attachment against the debt, asserting that the fraudulent nature of the debt permitted the attachment under the Illinois Attachment Act.	The defendant, John C. Yates, contended that the writing associated with the transaction did not sufficiently support the attachment. Yates claimed that the statements made were not fraudulent or actionable under the terms of the Attachment Act. Furthermore, in response to the interpleader claim by Freeman, Yates argued that the prior assignment was valid despite not being recorded before the attachment was levied, and that the previous ruling should be honored without regard to the attachment.

In the case of Gregory Vigeant v. D. B. Scully, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, in 1889, the conflict arose from Vigeant's role as an architect responsible for supervising the construction of buildings overseen by Scully. The key individuals involved were Gregory Vigeant, the architect, and D. B. Scully, the owner of the buildings. Problems arose shortly after the completion of the masonry work executed by a contractor named Kaiser, wherein the dwarf walls began to show signs of sinking and structural failure. Scully claimed that these issues were due to Vigeant’s negligence in properly supervising the construction. The case previously came to court, resulting in a verdict in favor of Kaiser against Scully, which established the contractor had fulfilled his contractual obligations. This prior judgment became critical in assessing the current claims as it suggested Scully could not seek damages from Vigeant for the same alleged issues with Kaiser’s work, as the case documented prior had already settled those matters of liability.	Gregory Vigeant claimed that he should not be held liable for damages related to alleged negligence in supervising the construction of the buildings. He argued that the previous judgment in the case between Scully and Kaiser precluded Scully from pursuing further claims against him, as it established a resolution regarding the same facts and damages at play.	D. B. Scully contended that Vigeant's failure to adequately supervise the construction resulted in defects for which he was liable. Scully maintained that the issues with the dwarf walls were directly linked to Vigeant’s negligence and that as the owner, he was entitled to seek damages from Vigeant due to the losses sustained from the construction failure.

The case "The Schooner Constitution v. Nelson Woodworth" dates back to December 1838 and took place in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved are Nelson Woodworth, the plaintiff who provided services aboard the schooner Constitution, and Gurdon S. Hubbard and Henry G. Hubbard, who represented the schooner as appellants. Initially, a justice of the peace issued an attachment in favor of Woodworth against the schooner for $49.50 related to the services he provided. Following this judgment, the Hubbards filed an appeal to the Municipal Court of Chicago. However, during the hearing, the Municipal Court dismissed the appeal on Woodworth's motion and ruled that the Hubbards were liable for costs. The case subsequently moved to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the main issue revolved around the legality and process of the appeal from the justice's decision.	The plaintiff, Nelson Woodworth, claimed the outstanding payment for the services rendered on the schooner Constitution. After the judgment in his favor was dismissed in the Municipal Court, he argued that the judgment should stand, and he should not bear any costs due to the appeal.	The defendants, represented by Gurdon S. Hubbard and Henry G. Hubbard, contended that the appeal they filed was improperly dismissed. They argued that an appeal was permissible under the relevant statutes and that they should have the opportunity to contest the judgment issued against the schooner Constitution. However, they were unable to comply with the statutory requirements, as the act concerning the attachment mandated they should be parties to the original suit to properly appeal.

John K. Pollard initiated a legal suit against David Rutter in the Cook County Circuit Court, Illinois, which commenced prior to an appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court. The initial judgment favored Pollard, prompting Rutter to appeal. However, on February 1, 1889, the Circuit Court dismissed the appeal due to "want of prosecution," a decision supported by a court rule that had been made accessible to all attorneys. This rule, similar to one previously upheld in Hinckley v. Dean, stipulated that matters must progress timely unless there was a valid reason for delay. The court noted that Rutter's various objections concerning the dismissal and the amendments made to the bill of exceptions were unfounded; thus the court maintained that the dismissal followed established judicial protocols. The case ultimately hinged on whether the Circuit Court had adhered to its rules and whether the amendments regarding the dismissal were appropriate.	The plaintiff, John K. Pollard, argued that he had been wrongfully denied a continued hearing due to Rutter's failure to prosecute the appeal. He maintained that the dismissal met the procedural rules established within the Circuit Court, as these rules had been documented and accessible to all parties involved. Pollard therefore sought affirmation of the lower court's judgment, asserting the validity of the dismissal.	David Rutter contended that the dismissal of his appeal was improper and suggested that the Circuit Court had overstepped its authority in allowing amendments after the time for filing had lapsed. He argued that these amendments introduced uncertainty into the proceedings. Rutter requested reversal of the Circuit Court's judgment and reinstatement of the appeal process.

In 1889, in Chicago, Illinois, a legal case arose involving taxpayer William McCoy and the City of Chicago, alongside the German-American Publishing Company. McCoy filed a bill to prevent the City from entering into any contract with the Publishing Company for publishing city legal notices in the German language. The primary legal question was whether the City had the right to use taxpayer funds for such publications. The case referenced various pieces of legislation, including provisions from the City’s charter and prior acts enacted in 1867 and 1869, which aimed to ensure that municipal publications were in the German language. However, subsequent legislation implied a requirement for English-language publications based on the Illinois Constitution, which strictly mandated that all official documents and legislative proceedings be conducted, preserved, and published only in English. McCoy asserted that the City was not permitted to expend funds for publications in any language other than English, effectively challenging the legality of any contracts for such purposes.	McCoy contended that it was unconstitutional for the City of Chicago to use taxpayer money to publish legal notices in the German language, arguing that such publications must strictly adhere to the Illinois Constitution, which states that all official writings and proceedings should be in English. He sought an injunction to stop the City from entering any contract concerning publications in German.	The City of Chicago, defending against McCoy's claims, contended that there was a historical precedent and legislative support for publishing in German, given the large German-speaking population in the city. They argued that the City had the discretion to publish in a language beneficial to its residents based on general powers granted to the City Council. Their defense aimed to show that the constitutional prohibition did not apply to municipal publications and that the long-standing practice should be respected.

In September 1875, a legal dispute arose in Peoria, Illinois, involving a mechanic's lien case between Alexander F. Miller and Moses Dusenbery (the appellants) and Joseph Botto, John Waugh, and Thomas S. Dobbins (the appellees). Joseph Botto owned a property for which he contracted John Waugh to build a brick store. Waugh hired Miller and Dusenbery to perform the masonry work. The main issue in the case was the interpretation of the contract between Miller, Dusenbery, and Waugh concerning payment for the masonry work. The appellants claimed they should be paid $10 per thousand bricks laid, with deductions for the brick supply, while the court determined that they were entitled to $3 per thousand based on the contract's language. The case was heard without a jury, and the circuit court ruled in favor of the appellants for a total of $216.44, leading to the appeal for a re-evaluation of the decree.	The plaintiffs, Miller and Dusenbery, argued that the circuit court misinterpreted their contract with John's Waugh. They contended that they were entitled to $10 per thousand bricks for their labor, minus the $7 per thousand for the bricks provided by Waugh. They sought a reevaluation of the payment due to them based on their interpretation of the contract.	The defendants, led by Joseph Botto and represented by John Waugh, maintained that the contract explicitly stated that Miller and Dusenbery should be compensated at the rate of $3 per thousand bricks laid, after accounting for the cost of the bricks. They argued that the construction of the contract as claimed by the plaintiffs was mistaken and contrary to its evident intent.

The case of Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company v. George W. Neikirk occurred in Mason County, Illinois, and was decided on September 21, 1883. The plaintiff, George W. Neikirk, owned a farm that included a right-of-way operated by the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company. In 1881 and 1882, Neikirk's cattle and hogs were allegedly killed and injured by the company’s trains. Additionally, in 1882, three of Neikirk's horses were struck and killed while attempting to cross the railroad track on his property, resulting in damage to their harness. Neikirk filed suit seeking damages for these losses and attorney's fees, claiming that the railway failed to properly fence its tracks and operated its train carelessly and without proper warning. The initial judgment in favor of Neikirk awarded him $750, leading the railway company to appeal the decision.	Neikirk argued that the railway company failed to erect and maintain adequate fencing along its right-of-way, allowing his livestock to stray onto the track, which is a violation of Illinois law. He also asserted that the railroad's train struck his horses at a reckless speed without issuing any warning signals, constituting negligence. His legal request included compensation for the value of the livestock killed and injured, the destroyed harness, and attorney's fees for bringing the suit.	The railway company contended that it had complied with all fencing requirements and had erected proper gates at the crossing on Neikirk's property. They argued that there was no statutory obligation to provide warning signals at private crossings and that the train's speed was within legal limits. The railway also claimed that Neikirk had not provided sufficient evidence to support his claims regarding the alleged negligence and failure to maintain adequate fencing.

In June 1874, the case of J. W. Peers v. The Board of Education of School District No. 3 was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a written order dated January 18, 1873, where the Board of School Directors was supposed to pay J. W. Peers $267.88 for materials supplied for the construction of a school house in Collinsville, Illinois. This construction was part of a larger contract between the Board and Wm. H. Phillips & Brother, involving a total payment of $23,512, with specific timelines and conditions for payment. Peers contested that the school board had accepted the order he presented, thereby creating a liability. The trial court, however, ruled in favor of the Board, prompting Peers to appeal. The legal questions raised involved whether the school directors had the authority to bind the district by such orders and whether there was an actual acceptance of the order.	J. W. Peers argued that the Board of Education had accepted his order, thus creating a right of action against them for the payment. He claimed that the Board's retention of the order implied acceptance, and he sought payment for materials supplied for the construction of the school house, contending that the school district had benefited from the materials even though they were procured through a separate contract with Wm. H. Phillips & Brother.	The Board of Education, represented by their attorney, contended that they had no legal authority to accept the order or issue payment for it, as their powers were strictly defined by statute. They asserted that orders must be issued by the township treasurer and that previous arrangements for payments had followed the legal procedures set forth. The Board's position was that any order acceptance could potentially conflict with the school funds and exposed them to unnecessary liabilities. They argued that Peers had no standing to demand payment since they had not contracted directly with him.

In the case of Charles F. S. G. Hazeltine v. Jeremiah J. Fourney, heard before the Illinois Supreme Court on May 12, 1887, Jeremiah J. Fourney initiated a legal action in Cook County Circuit Court against Charles F. S. G. Hazeltine. The case revolved around a trust deed executed by Sarah Fourney, the wife of the plaintiff, on May 9, 1881.
