The plaintiff sought to vacate this trust deed and enforce a previous trust agreement made between him and Sarah on October 19, 1876, concerning the disputed property. Evidence showed that the plaintiff originally purchased the property and conveyed it to his wife under a trust agreement stating that if Sarah died before him, the property would revert to him, and vice versa. However, shortly before her death, Sarah executed a deed transferring the property to a third party in trust for her infant son from a previous marriage. This deed violated the existing trust agreement with her husband. The court had to determine the validity of the trust agreement and whether the deed made by Sarah should be set aside.	The plaintiff, Jeremiah J. Fourney, argued that the trust deed executed by his late wife Sarah shortly before her death was invalid as it violated their prior trust agreement. He requested the court to vacate the deed and enforce the trust arrangement that stipulated the property should revert to him if Sarah predeceased him, asserting that she had no right to transfer the property to another party.	The defendant, Charles F. S. G. Hazeltine, contended that the evidence did not sufficiently support a decree in favor of the plaintiff and highlighted that he was a minor at the time the decree was rendered. He questioned the validity of the trust agreement based on the absence of the original document, arguing that the claims should be dismissed due to insufficient evidence of the contract's existence and terms.

In 1888, the City of East St. Louis was involved in a legal case titled "The City of East St. Louis v. The People ex rel. Phillip M. Gundlach." This case originated when Gundlach sought a mandamus to compel the city to levy a special tax on its real and personal property. The purpose of this tax was to pay a judgment of $1,074.94 that Gundlach had previously won against the city in September 1886. The judgment stemmed from a bond issued by the city on July 26, 1873, along with eight annual interest coupons, as part of an ordinance to fund the city's floating debt. The city was required to provide a tax to fulfill its obligation to pay the aforementioned judgment due to a conflict between its charter limitations and the constitutional requirements following the 1870 Illinois Constitution. The city council's concerns were whether the constitutional provisions altered the city's bonding and tax-related responsibilities established previously.	Phillip M. Gundlach, as relator, claimed that the City of East St. Louis failed to levy an adequate tax to meet its debt obligations, which conflicted with the provisions of the Illinois Constitution. He sought a writ of mandamus requiring the city to impose a tax sufficient to cover the judgment against it and ensure the collected tax was used exclusively for this purpose.	The City of East St. Louis contended that its charter imposed certain limitations on taxation, asserting that the Constitution's provisions did not abrogate its existing charter powers regarding the extent of municipal indebtedness. They argued that the city had not exceeded its charter limitations and that the constitutional requirements should not compel them to act beyond what their charter allowed.

The case of John C. Cochrane v. Jane L. Tuttle took place in September 1874 and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose when Tuttle, who claimed she had a verbal agreement to rent Cochrane's house for one year and board his family, found herself unceremoniously evicted. Under differing interpretations of their agreement, Tuttle believed she had exclusive rights for one year, while Cochrane claimed the arrangement could be terminated at any time by either party. After Tuttle began to board her own guests, she left for a business trip to New York, leaving a housekeeper in charge. Upon her return, Cochrane informed her that he would no longer rent the house and had taken possession. He offered to pay her hotel bill but she refused, instead attempting to retrieve her possessions. A dispute ensued, including allegations that Tuttle had left behind a pocketbook containing a significant amount of money, which she claimed was stolen. Eventually, the jury awarded Tuttle $1,250 for damages, which Cochrane contested.	Tuttle claimed that she had a verbal contract with Cochrane that allowed her to occupy the house for one year and that he wrongfully evicted her. She argued that her eviction caused her emotional distress and additional losses, seeking substantial damages as compensation for what she asserted was unjust treatment and infringement upon her rights.	Cochrane's primary defense was that the arrangement with Tuttle did not create a landlord-tenant relationship and could be terminated by either party at any time, as per their understanding. He argued that the damages awarded by the jury were excessive, noting that Tuttle had not demonstrated any actual damages, as she left the house willingly and reclaimed all her personal belongings. Cochrane sought a reversal of the jury's decision, asserting there was insufficient evidence to validate Tuttle's claims.

The case "Thomas Cowen and Patrick Cowen v. The People" originated in July 1852 at the Recorder’s Court in Chicago, Illinois. Thomas and Patrick Cowen were indicted and tried for deceitful actions against Ransom Wilkinson. The Cowens were accused of selling a watch to Wilkinson, falsely claiming it was a gold watch worth $125, while in reality, it was a galvanized watch with minimal value, approximately $5. The prosecution argued that the Cowens engaged in fraudulent representations to cheat and defraud Wilkinson out of his money. The case was presided over by Judge R. S. Wilson, and the plaintiffs argued against the admissibility of certain evidence and the conduct of the jury instructions during their trial.	The plaintiffs asserted that the Cowens intentionally deceived Ransom Wilkinson by misrepresenting the quality and value of the watch they sold. Their primary claim was centered on the notion that the Cowens’ false pretenses directly led to Wilkinson parting with his money. They sought the court's judgment to uphold his conviction, supporting the findings of the Recorder’s Court regarding the fraudulent nature of the transaction.	The Cowens, through their counsel, argued against the jury instructions that they claimed were improperly modified by the court. They contended that the jury should have been instructed that if Wilkinson could have avoided being deceived through ordinary caution and prudence, then they should be acquitted. They also highlighted that not all false pretenses needed to be charged for a conviction, and they questioned the legitimacy of the evidence used against them regarding their intent and the clarity of the indictment against them.

The case "City of Chicago v. Andrew Garrison" took place in September 1869, with the location centered in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Andrew Garrison, the plaintiff, and the city of Chicago, represented by their attorney Mr. S. A. Irvin. The case arose from an incident in which Garrison sustained injuries after falling from steps that were part of the sidewalk. He filed a lawsuit against the city to recover damages. The trial resulted in a verdict and judgment favoring Garrison, prompting the city to seek a reversal through a writ of error, claiming that the evidence established the sidewalk was safe and the city had no notice of any issues. Garrison represented himself in the case, while the city contended that the preponderance of evidence did not support the jury's decision. The court found that the evidence was conflicting, and it refused to overturn the jury's verdict based on the established judicial respect for jury determinations.	Andrew Garrison claimed that the city of Chicago was liable for his injuries due to the unsafe condition of the sidewalk steps from which he fell. He sought financial compensation for the damages incurred because of the city's negligence in maintaining safe public walkways. Garrison argued that the city had either actual or constructive notice of the unsafe conditions and failed to take appropriate actions to rectify them.	The city of Chicago, represented by Mr. S. A. Irvin, argued that evidence showed the sidewalk was not unsafe and that the city had no notice of any potential danger related to the steps. They contended that Garrison himself was negligent, contributing to the incident. The city's legal team sought a reversal of the initial verdict on the grounds that the jury's decision was not supported by the weight of evidence.

In 1882, a legal case titled "Nathan Robbins et al. v. George J. Arnold" arose in Schuyler County, Illinois. The dispute centered around a trust deed connected to properties in West Virginia and Illinois. In 1851, land was devised to Samuel Clothier and his wife, Bachel. After Bachel’s death in 1864, Samuel sold the lands to Nathan Robbins (the appellee) in 1865 while also agreeing to obtain conveyances from their children once they reached adulthood. Samuel later executed a trust deed in 1865 to George J. Arnold, contingent upon repayment conditions related to interests in the West Virginia lands held by his children. By 1874, Arnold paid Eliza Clothier, the youngest heir, $1,030 for her release of interest in these lands, as Samuel Clothier was unable to do so. Robbins sought to contest the foreclosure of the trust deed, claiming he had rights over the land due to his purchase and that Arnold wrongfully forestalled this right by dealing directly with Eliza. The case ultimately made its way to the Illinois Appellate Court after Robbins appealed a lower court ruling favoring Arnold.	Nathan Robbins, as the plaintiff, argued that he had the right to acquire Eliza Clothier’s interest in the lands pursuant to the original agreement made by Samuel Clothier. Robbins alleged that Arnold's actions—purchasing Eliza’s interest—prevented him from exercising his rights and discharging the lien on the land. He sought to have the court reverse the foreclosure and recognize his claim over the property, essentially arguing that Arnold acted without his consent and disrupted his legal rights.	George J. Arnold, the defendant, countered Robbins' claims by insisting that he was justified in purchasing Eliza Clothier's interest when notified she had reached the age of majority. Arnold maintained that he acted solely to protect his own interests and that Robbins had no entitlement to notice or opportunity to purchase the interest before Arnold took action. He requested reimbursement for the sum paid to Eliza, asserting that he had properly followed the obligations outlined in the trust deed.

In 1867, in Putnam County, Illinois, a legal proceeding was initiated against Andrew C. Nixon for bastardy, which is a legal term pertaining to the recognition of a child born out of wedlock and the responsibility of the putative father. The case was brought forth in the name of the People of the State of Illinois. During the course of the lawsuit, the mother of the child passed away. The Circuit Court ruled that the death of the mother automatically abated the bastardy proceeding, leading to the dismissal of the case. This decision prompted an appeal by the People, questioning whether the death of the mother should extinguish the proceeding that had been initiated while she was still alive.	The plaintiff, representing the People of the State of Illinois, argued that the death of the mother should not abate the bastardy proceeding. They contended that the primary objective of the statute was to protect both the public interest and the mother by holding the putative father accountable for the support of the child. The proceedings were deemed necessary to secure public liability for the child's welfare, even in the absence of the mother.	Andrew C. Nixon's defense maintained that the Circuit Court's initial ruling was correct and that the death of the mother understandably abated the suit. They posited that she had been a necessary party to the proceedings, and her passing altered the legal dynamics of the case, warranting its dismissal.

In January 1869, in Madison County, Illinois, Daniel Gillham brought a legal case against The Madison County Railroad Company. The conflict arose after the railroad company constructed a large embankment across Gillham's land, which obstructed the natural flow of surface water that originally drained from higher lands onto his property and into a natural lake. Gillham claimed that this action created a rainwater blockage, causing water to back up on his land rather than flow away as it would naturally. He argued that the railroad company acted negligently by failing to provide an opening in the embankment for the water to escape. The case raised significant questions about property rights regarding surface water and the responsibilities of landowners in managing water flow.	Gillham claimed that the railroad company's embankment violated his rights by preventing the natural flow of surface water from his land. He sought legal recognition that the railroad's actions were negligent and damaging to his property rights and requested that the court reverse the lower court's demurrer, which had dismissed his case.	The railroad company's defense centered around the argument that they had the right to modify their land and that such modifications did not constitute negligence. They maintained that the law in certain jurisdictions allowed for the blocking of surface water flow under these circumstances and denied liability for the flooding issues that affected Gillham's property as a result of their embankment.

The case of Richard Seaton v. Henry Ruff took place in Quincy, Illinois, with a decision issued on November 23, 1888. The dispute centered around a chattel mortgage executed on June 30, 1884, by James T. Balthorpe and one Bushnell for a loan of $2,600. The mortgage secured various vehicles and equipment located in a livery stable. Following proper acknowledgment and recording, L. and C. H. Bull transferred the mortgage to John H. Duker in September 1884. Duker took possession and subsequently sold the property to Henry Ruff. Over time, the property was managed by Balthorpe, who was employed by Ruff, although he did not claim ownership. In October 1885, Ruff sold the property on credit to Hatcher, who later surrendered it to Ruff. The contested ownership led to a replevin action initiated by Seaton to reclaim the property after it was levied under an execution against Balthorpe. The plaintiff challenged the legality of the transfers and the claim of ownership by Ruff, asserting fraud and disputing the nature of the transfers.	The plaintiff, Richard Seaton, argued that the transfers of the mortgaged property were fraudulent and merely colorable. Seaton claimed that Balthorpe remained the true owner of the property throughout the transactions and that Ruff's claim of ownership was invalid. He sought to reclaim the chattels through the replevin action, arguing that the legal rights and the nature of the transfers should not have permitted Ruff to retain possession after the levy.	The defendant, Henry Ruff, contended that the transactions involving the mortgage and subsequent sale were valid and conducted in good faith. Ruff argued that he acquired legal title to the property both through the mortgage provisions and by the acquiescence of the original mortgagor, Balthorpe. He maintained that there was no evidence of fraud in the transfers and that the actions taken were permissible under the law related to chattel mortgages.

James A. Chadsey and Benjamin Harrison, along with Jonathan D. Manlove, formed a partnership in 1848 to construct and sell a raft of saw logs, which they intended to send down the Illinois and Mississippi rivers to St. Louis, Missouri. Chadsey agreed to oversee the construction and transportation of the raft but later incurred expenses exceeding the sales proceeds, leading to a net loss of $231.98. Chadsey claimed that, as a partner, Harrison was liable to pay his share of the loss. After a trial in the Schuyler Circuit Court, the jury ruled in favor of Harrison, leading Chadsey to appeal, claiming that the court erred in sustaining Harrison's demurrer to the special claim regarding the partnership’s financial obligations.	Chadsey argued that Harrison, as a co-partner, was obligated to pay his share of the losses incurred from the partnership venture. The plaintiff contended that there had been an agreement by Harrison to reimburse Chadsey for the expenses related to the raft after the partnership's completion. Chadsey's claims were founded on the premise that he had paid out more than his share without proper adjustment of partnership accounts.	Harrison contended that partners cannot sue each other for matters related to partnership concerns unless there has been a complete and final settlement of all partnership transactions. He argued that the claim failed to show such a settlement, and thus, no payment was owed to Chadsey. Harrison maintained that the partnership's financial affairs had not been fully reconciled, and therefore, Chadsey's demand lacked a legal basis.

In the early months of 1870, the case of Ivory H. Pike v. Elizabeth Baker was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from a dispute over the ownership of a horse. The case originated in McLean County, Illinois, where Elizabeth Baker filed an action of replevin against Ivory H. Pike, a constable who had seized the horse under an execution against her husband, William Baker. Elizabeth Baker claimed that the horse was her separate property, acquired through her own funds after her husband traded their property for it. The evidence presented included testimony from both Elizabeth and William Baker, supporting her claim of ownership. The horse had been recognized as belonging to Elizabeth, and prior to the seizure, William Baker had departed, taking the horse with him but later sending it back to Elizabeth. The court was to determine the rightful ownership of the horse, particularly in light of the execution and the timing of its delivery.	Elizabeth Baker claimed that she had purchased the horse using her own money and that it belonged to her as separate property, despite her husband's involvement in the transaction. She argued that the execution issued against her husband did not attach to the property as the horse was already out of the county when the levy was made. Elizabeth sought the court's recognition of her ownership and the return of the horse, asserting that the sale had been finalized and completed legally.	Ivory H. Pike's defense contended that the horse had belonged to William Baker and that the execution was valid and constituted a legal claim to the horse. His defense included a plea of justification for seizing the horse under the execution, arguing that the property had been traded without acknowledgment of the wife’s ownership. The defense ultimately requested the court to uphold the execution and find in favor of the seizure.

Edward Seckel et al. v. Emerson W. Scott et al. is a legal case that took place in September 1871 in Chicago, Illinois. The case arose after the plaintiffs, Edward Seckel and others, entered into a contract to buy 250 firkins of butter from the defendants, Emerson W. Scott and others, for fourteen cents per pound. Upon finalizing the sale, the parties agreed that the buyers would take 100 firkins immediately and pay earnest money of $2 for each of the remaining firkins, with the obligation to pay the remainder of the price within thirty days. However, after taking possession of 141 firkins, a devastating fire occurred on October 8-9, 1871, destroying the remaining butter still in the sellers' possession. The plaintiffs subsequently demanded the remaining firkins but were refused delivery on the basis of the destruction of the goods. The plaintiffs then filed a lawsuit claiming non-delivery of the goods they had purchased. The case focused on whether the sale was sufficiently completed at the time of the agreement to transfer the title—and thus the risk of loss—to the buyers before the fire occurred.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had completed a sale for the butter and asserted that the defendants failed to deliver the remaining firkins as previously agreed. They argued that despite the fire's destruction of the goods, they were entitled to recover damages for non-delivery due to the claim that the contract had vested them with ownership before the goods were lost.	The defendants contended that the title and risk of the butter had passed to the plaintiffs upon the completion of the sale, meaning they were not liable for the goods’ destruction in the fire. They requested the court to instruct the jury that the title to the goods passed to the plaintiffs as soon as the sale was completed, regardless of whether the goods had been physically delivered or weighed.

Virgil H. Eachus, the plaintiff, filed a case against The Trustees of the Illinois and Michigan Canal in 1856, concerning the flooding of his lands located in Lake County, Indiana. The flooding was reportedly caused by a dam constructed on the Calumet River to supply water to the Illinois and Michigan Canal. Eachus claimed damages amounting to $2,500, arguing that since the incident occurred during his mother's lifetime and persisted after her death, he was entitled to compensation as her heir at law. The action was initiated in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas, though objections were raised regarding the court's jurisdiction, as the cause of action was deemed local to Indiana. A general and special demurrer was filed against the claims, which was upheld by the court below, prompting Eachus to bring a writ of error, challenging the decision.	The plaintiff asserted that the defendants were liable for damages resulting from the flooding of his lands in Indiana due to the erection of the dam. He argued that the court had jurisdiction to hear his case and sought the stipulated damages of $2,500 for the nuisance affecting his inherited property.	The defendants contended that the action should not be maintained in Cook County nor under Illinois law as the injury occurred to real estate situated in Indiana. They argued that, according to established legal principles, claims arising from local injuries must be adjudicated in the jurisdiction where the injury occurred. Therefore, the defendants requested the dismissal of the case based on these jurisdictional grounds.

In September 1876, Madison Y. Johnson sued John H. Von Kettler over a case of false imprisonment that stemmed from actions taken during the administration of estates. The initial incidents occurred in Stephenson County and were later moved to Winnebago County for trial. The plaintiff, Johnson, claimed that his imprisonment was executed under an order from the county court that he argued was void. The case had previously been brought to the Illinois Supreme Court on multiple occasions, highlighting issues about the jurisdictional powers of the county court and the legality of the imprisonment. The core of the dispute centered around whether the county court had the authority to imprison individuals for failure to comply with its orders, with the court affirming that such powers were limited and specified by statute. Ultimately, the court ruled that Johnson’s imprisonment was unlawful based on previous rulings and that Von Kettler had acted without proper authority.	Madison Y. Johnson claimed that John H. Von Kettler unlawfully imprisoned him without cause, arguing that the order under which he was detained was void and beyond the powers granted to the county court. He sought damages for the false imprisonment, asserting that he suffered harm as a result of the unlawful actions of Von Kettler.	John H. Von Kettler contended that the county court had the appropriate jurisdiction and authority to imprison Johnson in relation to estate settlement matters. He argued that the imprisonment was justified under the statutory provisions relating to court orders and that the evidence presented did not support Johnson's claims of unlawful imprisonment. Von Kettler maintained that the jury should have been instructed on the necessity of proving lack of reasonable cause.

The case of B. Oswald v. John Mollet took place in Madison County, Illinois, with the appeals court's final decision rendered on October 19, 1888. The legal dispute originated from a lease agreement made on June 1, 1886, between Fridolin Oswald and John Mollet for agricultural land. The lease stipulated a rent payment of $300 for a term running from March 1, 1887, to March 1, 1888, with different terms for land sown with small grains. To secure the rent, Mollet executed three promissory notes assigned to Oswald. Following a series of financial complications, including the foreclosure of the property due to outstanding mortgages, Fridolin Oswald assigned his interest in the lease and related rent notes to B. Oswald. However, confusion arose as John Mollet expressed a desire to pay rent in the form of a share of the crop rather than cash. The primary legal question revolved around whether this arrangement constituted a valid landlord-tenant relationship post-assignment. The court's task was to determine if the actions of the parties amounted to an attornment, which recognizes the new party to whom rent is owed.	B. Oswald, the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to the rent derived from the lease after he received an assignment of both the lease and the promissory notes from Fridolin Oswald. He argued that Mollet, by acknowledging the assignment, was obligated to pay the agreed-upon rent and should not alter the payment method to a crop share. The plaintiff sought to enforce the payment of rent according to the original terms set forth in the lease.	John Mollet, the defendant, contended that he did not consent to the assignment of the lease and thus did not recognize B. Oswald as the rightful creditor. He emphasized his preference to settle his rent dues with a portion of the crops rather than cash, which indicated his lack of agreement to the terms imposed by the plaintiff. Mollet sought dismissal of the claims against him based on this assertion of non-recognition following the assignment.

In the case of Martin v. Beatty et al., decided in January 1870 by the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute arose from a mortgage foreclosure situation. The case took place in McLean County, Illinois, and involved key individuals including the appellant, Martin (the mortgagee), and the appellees, Beatty and Cox (the mortgagor and subsequent grantee). The central issue was whether a mortgagor or their grantee, who made improvements to mortgaged property after the mortgage was established, could claim priority for those improvement expenses over the mortgagee's claim. The lower court ruled that Cox, the grantee, was entitled to reimbursement for these improvements from the proceeds of the sale of the mortgaged property, effectively placing him in a better position than the mortgagee. This decision prompted Martin to appeal the ruling.	The plaintiff, Martin, claimed that as the mortgagee, his rights should take precedence over any claims by Cox regarding improvements made to the mortgaged property after the mortgage was executed. Martin argued that he should be fully reimbursed from the sale proceeds before any payments were made to Cox, asserting that no legal principle allows a mortgagor or his grantee to gain an advantage over the mortgagee by expending money on improvements.	The defendants, specifically Beatty and Cox, did not present an extensive defense in the appeal process, having failed to provide a brief or substantial argument regarding their claims to the improvements. They maintained, however, that the improvements should warrant some level of reimbursement from the sale proceeds, which led to their preferred position over the mortgagee in the lower court's ruling.

In the case of William Ogle v. Ananias Coffey, who is suing on behalf of John Beck, a legal dispute arose regarding a judgment rendered in the Madison Circuit Court in the state of Kentucky. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision dated December 1835. The primary issue at hand was whether there was a proper service of summons to the defendant, Ananias Coffey. The actions leading to the case occurred on October 18, 1832, when the return from the sheriff was submitted, indicating that the summons was executed as commanded. However, the dispatch did not clarify whether the date referred to was for the day of service or the return of the summons. Additionally, the specifics of how the summons was delivered were ambiguous, making it unclear if it was read to the defendant or a copy was provided. Due to these uncertainties, the case references prior rulings that highlight the need for demonstrable compliance with service of process regulations in similar cases.	The plaintiff, William Ogle, contended that the judgment against him was invalid due to improper service of the summons. The main argument focused on the ambiguity of the sheriff’s return, which did not adequately detail how the service was executed, nor did it comply with the legal requirements for effective summons delivery. Thus, Ogle sought to have the judgment reversed on the grounds that due process was not properly followed.	The defendant, Ananias Coffey, claimed that the service of summons was valid as per the return provided by the sheriff. The argument was largely centered on the sufficiency of the sheriff's statement of execution, holding that it could be interpreted as having met the necessary legal standards for service at that time. Coffey's request was for the court to uphold the previous judgment in his favor against Ogle.

Miles Hewett filed a legal action against John T. Johnson in the Circuit Court of Jefferson County, Illinois, in June 1874. The case revolved around a promissory note dated February 5, 1870, in the amount of $250, which was due eight months later and granted an interest rate of ten percent. The note was originally given by Johnson to Jas. B. Drake and was transferred to Hewett without recourse before it was due. Johnson contested the claim on the basis of fraud, asserting that he was misled into signing the note. The case went to trial, where a jury ruled in favor of Johnson, leading to a judgment against Hewett. Subsequently, Hewett appealed the jury's decision, claiming the trial court had improperly refused certain jury instructions and had incorrectly allowed some of Johnson’s instructions.	Hewett's principal argument was that he purchased the promissory note for a valuable consideration before it was due and without any notice of defenses against it. He contended that there had been error in the trial court's refusal to give specific jury instructions that would have instructed jurors regarding the circumstances of his purchase and the nature of Johnson's previous engagements, as well as the admission of evidence regarding Johnson's acknowledgment of the debt.	Johnson's defense centered on the assertion that the note was obtained through fraudulent means. He denied knowingly agreeing to or executing the note, claiming the circumstances surrounding his signature were deceptive. Johnson maintained that the trial court rightly accepted the plea of fraud, asserting that when fraud is proven to have occurred in the execution of a note, it serves as a valid defense regardless of the holder's innocence.

In September 1874, the case "William W. Kimball et al. v. George G. Custer" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in Cook County, Illinois, where George G. Custer, the plaintiff, accused William W. Kimball and two others (Woodruff and Chadwick) of trespassing. Custer claimed that the defendants unlawfully entered his home and took possession of a piano valued at $650. The events leading to the case began when Custer purchased the piano from Kimball in 1867, paying a total of $596 before the defendants attempted to reclaim it. After efforts to collect further payments had failed, the defendants devised a plan involving a fraudulently induced entry into Custer's home. An individual posing as an insurance agent tricked his way into the house and subsequently allowed the defendants to enter and remove the piano. Custer had consistently locked his house against the defendants’ access and maintained that their entry constituted trespass. The court had to determine the legitimacy of the defendants' entry and their claim to possession based on a prior rental agreement, which was disputed due to a lack of clarity following a fire that destroyed the original contract.	George G. Custer, the plaintiff, claimed that the defendants committed trespass by unlawfully entering his home and taking the piano without his consent. Custer argued that the defendants’ entry was obtained through fraud and deceit, and sought damages for the wrongful taking of his property. He maintained that despite the existence of a rental agreement, it did not grant the defendants the right to remove the piano without his explicit authorization, asserting that he retained ownership of the instrument despite outstanding payments.	The defendants, William W. Kimball, Woodruff, and Chadwick, contended that Custer had granted them permission to retrieve the piano, relying on the terms of the rental agreement. They argued that their actions did not constitute a trespass because they believed their entry was authorized, and emphasized that the person who initially entered the home did so peaceably, claiming they were acting as agents of Kimball. They asserted that since the piano was initially rented, they had a right to take it back upon alleged defaults in payments.

Royal E. Barber v. W. B. Hawley is a legal case decided on January 25, 1886, in Ontario, Illinois. The case involves an appeal from a judgment made by the Appellate Court for the Second District, which had previously upheld a decision from the circuit court. The circuit court had ruled on a claim for board and services originating from a probate court regarding the estate of a decedent. The trial was held before the circuit court without a jury, and no specific legal questions were presented for consideration. Instead, the case hinged on disputed facts regarding the amount of the claim, particularly in relation to the Statute of Limitations, which was applied to portions of the claim prior to five years before it was filed. The Appellate Court affirmed the lower judgment, leading to this appeal. The court's ruling clarified that since no legal questions were raised concerning the statute, it could only review factual sufficiency regarding the claim.	The plaintiff, Royal E. Barber, claimed compensation for board and services rendered, which he believed were owed from the decedent's estate. His arguments were primarily focused on presenting evidence that his claim was valid and should not be barred by the Statute of Limitations, particularly for the portion of the claim that was made within five years of filing.	The defendant, W. B. Hawley, contended that the portion of the claim prior to five years before it was filed was barred under the Statute of Limitations. Hawley's defense did not raise any legal questions but focused on disputing the sufficiency of the proof provided to bypass the statute's limitations, arguing that the claim was not actionable for part of its duration.

In 1887, the case took place in Jersey County, Illinois, involving the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company and a plaintiff named John H. Stamps. Stamps was injured while attempting to cross the railroad track in an open spring wagon drawn by a horse. As he approached the crossing, the horse became frightened by a fire along the highway, causing it to jump and ultimately leading to Stamps being thrown from the wagon. Witnesses indicated that Stamps became unconscious after the fall and was later found lying in the highway, away from the railroad track. Evidence presented included the condition of the wagon seat and its potential role in Stamps' injuries, with some suggesting that the seat was defective and contributed to the accident.	Stamps claimed damages for the injuries he sustained due to the incident at the railroad crossing. He argued that the railroad company was responsible for maintaining safe conditions at the crossing and that their negligence contributed to the accident. His main legal request was for compensation for his injuries, citing the dangers presented by the conditions at the crossing and claiming that the railroad company failed to ensure safety.	The railroad company contended that the evidence did not support Stamps' claims and argued that the accident was more reasonably attributed to the defective condition of Stamps' wagon seat rather than any shortcomings on their part. The defense pointed to the nature of the wagon's seat as a contributing factor to the injuries sustained by Stamps and requested that the court dismiss the claims against them based on insufficient evidence.

Warner L. Clark, the owner of the steamboat Uncle Toby, initiated legal action against Nathaniel Smith in June 1853 in Illinois. The case arose after Smith sued Clark through an attachment for $387.30 owed on a promissory note issued by the steamboat. Smith claimed damages for supplies such as coal, firewood, and other materials furnished to the boar. The lawsuit took place at the Jo Daviess Circuit Court during the August term of 1852, where a jury returned a verdict in favor of Smith. Clark's legal representatives, Higgins and Strother, argued for a new trial, asserting that the supplies provided were not meant for the boat's operation but rather as merchandise to be resold. The court's opinion underscored that the validity of the attachment depended on whether the supplies were genuinely used for the boat's navigation and operation, challenging the legitimacy of the claims made by the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, Nathaniel Smith, claimed that he supplied materials and coal necessary for the operation of the steamboat Uncle Toby. He argued that the supplies were essential for navigation and sought recovery of the amount owed under the promissory note executed on behalf of the boat. Smith maintained that the debt incurred was valid and justly owed by the boat, thereby supporting his claim for damages through the attachment.	The defendant, Warner L. Clark, contended that the supplies, particularly coal, were purchased with the intent to resell rather than for the boat's consumption. Clark's attorneys argued that the evidence demonstrated that the primary use of the supplies was speculative commerce rather than operational necessity. They asserted that since the supplies were not used or consumed on the boat, the claim for damages could not be sustained under the relevant legal provisions, which dictate that only supplies actually used in the vessel's operation could be recoverable.

In June 1872, in Randolph County, Illinois, the case of George Harmon v. Penina Harmon arose following the death of Absalom Harmon. Penina Harmon, as the administratrix of her deceased husband’s estate, initiated the action for trover against George Harmon, claiming that certain personal property belonged to Absalom Harmon and had been wrongfully converted by the defendant. The plaintiff established that the property in question was originally owned by her husband before their separation. During the trial, the plaintiff demonstrated the property’s value and detailed her demand for its return, which George Harmon refused. The defendant countered by presenting a bill of sale allegedly executed to him by Absalom Harmon after Penina had left, but he failed to provide proof of payment or consideration for the property. Additionally, testimonies revealed that Absalom exercised ownership over the property while living with the defendant. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Penina, awarding her $500, leading to George’s appeal against the judgment.	Penina Harmon, the plaintiff, argued that the disputed personal property belonged to her deceased husband and was wrongfully retained by George Harmon. She asserted her legal right to reclaim the property as the administratrix of Absalom's estate, claiming that the bill of sale presented by George was invalid due to the lack of consideration and intention to defraud creditors.	George Harmon contended that he possessed a valid bill of sale from Absalom Harmon, which he claimed transferred ownership of the disputed property to him after Penina's departure. He argued that this transaction was binding and that the plaintiff lacked grounds to question its validity as there were no existing creditors at the time of the sale. He sought to have the jury's verdict overturned and the case dismissed.

The case "The President and Trustees of the Town of Tamaroa v. The Trustees of the Southern Illinois Normal University" took place in June 1870, in Perry County, Illinois. The key individuals involved in this case were the President and Trustees of the Town of Tamaroa, who served as appellants, and the Trustees of the Southern Illinois Normal University, who served as appellees. The dispute arose when the trustees of the university decided to locate the university at or near Carbondale, Jackson County. The Town of Tamaroa sought to prevent this decision by filing a bill in chancery, requesting an injunction to restrain the trustees from commencing operations at the proposed site and compelling them to select Tamaroa instead. A temporary injunction was granted initially, but the university trustees moved to dissolve it. The lower court ultimately dismissed the bill due to a lack of equity, leading the trustees to claim damages related to their attendance and legal expenses incurred in the case. They sought a decree for a total amount of $1,220, which included attorneys' fees and other related costs. The court ruled on various aspects of damage claims, scrutinizing the legitimacy of the expenses and the necessity of attendance by the university trustees.	The plaintiff, the President and Trustees of the Town of Tamaroa, claimed that the Southern Illinois Normal University trustees had improperly chosen to locate the university at Carbondale instead of their town. They sought an injunction to restrain this action and requested that the court compel the trustees to locate the university near Tamaroa. Following the dissolution of the injunction, they appealed, arguing that the damages awarded to the defendants were excessive and not properly supported by the evidence.	The defendants, the Trustees of the Southern Illinois Normal University, defended against the claims by emphasizing the lack of necessity for the plaintiff's requested injunction. They contended that their attendance and expenses related to the case were legitimate claims for damages under the relevant statute. They argued that the assessments, including $720 for attending court and other expenses, were justified despite the plaintiff's objections and sought recovery based on these costs and damages incurred due to the delay caused by the injunction.

The case "Julius K. Rose et al. v. Elnathan L. Sanderson" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1865. The plaintiffs, Julius K. Rose and his wife Ellen A. Rose, were involved in a legal dispute concerning the attachment of Julius's life estate in lands that belonged to Ellen. The events leading to the case unfolded after a legislative act aimed to protect married women’s separate property came into effect on April 24, 1861. Specifically, Julius's life estate was under a levy due to a judgment against him, and the Roes contended that under the new law, Ellen's property should be exempt from any claims against her husband. The claim involved interpretations of the act regarding the rights of married women and the implications for property held by their husbands prior to the law's passage. The Circuit Court of Iroquois County initially dismissed the Roes' case, leading to their appeal to the Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Julius and Ellen Rose, argued that the land in question, which constituted Julius's life estate, was exempt from execution or attachment due to the law protecting married women’s property rights. They claimed that Ellen's property was her sole and separate property and should not be subject to her husband’s debts. The primary legal request was for the court to set aside the levy against Julius's life estate.	The defendant, Elnathan L. Sanderson, contended that the life estate held by Julius was subject to execution since it had vested before the protective law was enacted. Sanderson argued that the law could not retroactively apply to property rights already vested in Julius, maintaining that legislative authority does not extend to nullifying existing property rights through broad interpretations. He sought to affirm the dismissal of the case by the lower court.

Louise Stuber initiated a legal case against Franz Schack in September 1876 in Cook County, Illinois. The case arose from an action of assumpsit based on a promissory note. Stuber claimed that Schack failed to fulfill his obligations under this note. The case was presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gary in the Superior Court of Cook County. The defendant Schack provided a plea, but the court struck this plea from the files due to the lack of a sufficient affidavit of merits, which is a legal declaration that a party has a valid claim or defense. The court indicated that when Schack filed a second affidavit, he effectively abandoned the first, which prevented any assessment of its sufficiency from being considered. This led the court to find that Schack did not have a substantive defense regarding the matter at hand.	Louise Stuber, the plaintiff, argued that Franz Schack had breached the terms of a promissory note. She asserted that as a creditor, she was entitled to the enforcement of the note and any associated payments. Stuber effectively requested that the court hold Schack accountable for his obligations and enforce the terms laid out in the promissory note.	Franz Schack, the defendant, claimed that there was a lack of sufficient consideration for the promise to forbear debt collection, asserting his argument through a plea that was later struck down by the court. Schack attempted to provide facts in his defense, which he believed justified his position; however, the court found that these facts did not constitute a valid defense and concluded that Schack had no legitimate grounds to contest the enforcement of the note.

In 1876, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal case was initiated involving Thomas H. Halsey and others as plaintiffs against The People, represented by Julian S. Rumsey. The case arose from a request by the county collector of Cook County for judgment allowing the sale of certain lands and lots due to delinquent taxes and special assessments from the year 1872. The plaintiffs objected to this judgment on various grounds, primarily contesting the adequacy of the delinquent list and the proper processing of the tax equalization by the county board. Specifically, they argued that the list did not properly state the names of the property owners and questioned whether the equalization was performed in accordance with statutory requirements. The lower court evaluated these objections and delivered a judgment favoring the collector's application to sell the properties for tax arrears.	The plaintiffs claimed that the delinquent tax list was deficient as it did not adequately list the names of the property owners as required by law. They also argued that the county board did not equalize the taxes correctly and raised concerns that the park taxes being collected were unlawful, as they were extended to properties benefiting from services not shared with the town of West Chicago.	The defendant contended that the delinquent tax list was sufficient as it included a column indicating the names of the owners, even if not all names were fully known. The defense argued that the equalization of taxes occurred as legally required, asserting that the meeting of the county board was continuous and that actions taken by the committee of the board were valid and constituted the board’s resolution. Furthermore, they maintained that the park taxes were lawful and could be allocated appropriately within the town.

In January 1869, the case of City of Springfield v. Henry Le Claire arose in Springfield, Illinois. The plaintiff, Henry Le Claire, initiated a lawsuit seeking damages after falling into a sewer that was under construction in one of the city's streets. The City of Springfield was responsible for maintaining safe public streets as mandated by its charter, which granted the city control over streets, alleys, and highways. The core issue was whether the city had fulfilled its legal duty to ensure the safety of the public during the sewer construction. The circuit court ruled in favor of the plaintiff by sustaining a general demurrer against the defendant's special pleas, suggesting that the city bore primary responsibility for any damages resulting from negligence.	The plaintiff, Henry Le Claire, argued that the City of Springfield failed to keep its streets safe for the public by allowing a hazardous condition to exist during the sewer construction. He contended that this negligence directly caused his injuries when he fell into the inadequately safeguarded excavation. Le Claire sought damages amounting to $2,000, asserting that the city was liable under the legal duty imposed upon it to maintain safe public walkways.	The City of Springfield, represented by the defendant, sought to absolve itself from liability through two special pleas. The first plea attempted to shift responsibility to the contractor responsible for constructing the sewer, arguing that the city should not be held liable for the contractor's actions. The second plea referenced a clause in the city's charter, which stated the city could not be liable for injuries related to street conditions unless the supervising officer had been notified and failed to act. However, the court deemed both pleas insufficient defenses against the plaintiff's claim.

In 1889, the case of Nellie Lynn et al. v. Ellen Lynn, Adm’x et al. took place in Cook County, Illinois. The case revolved around the estate of George Lynn, who passed away leaving behind real estate that was at the center of a dispute. George Lynn was the beneficiary of a will from his ancestor, William Lynn Sr., who died in 1874. Following William's death, a will that designated George as the beneficiary was established in a prior court decree after the original will was wrongfully destroyed. Meanwhile, a deed was executed on June 5, 1873, inadvertently misdescribing the property to be conveyed in trust for the support of William’s deceased daughter and then for the benefit of her children. The deed had originally indicated a section number incorrectly, leading to questions of its validity. The core issue before the court was whether this deed could be reformed to correctly convey the intended properties, despite a lack of valuable consideration behind the deed.	The plaintiffs, represented by Nellie Lynn and others, contended that the deed should be reformed to correctly describe the premises intended to pass to George Lynn. They sought to assert that the equity of the situation warranted a reformation of the deed despite its non-valuable consideration since it was intended to benefit family descendants.	The defendant, Ellen Lynn, as administratrix of George Lynn’s estate, argued that the deed could not be reformed due to its lack of valuable consideration, adhering to established legal principles that a deed without a valuable consideration cannot be reformed, regardless of the circumstances. She asserted that the original will gave George Lynn a good title to the property, and the Probate Court’s decree for the sale of the real estate to pay off debts was thus proper.

In September 1872, the case "Tyler McWhorter et al. v. The People ex rel. The Chicago and Rock River Railroad Company" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a dispute over a municipal subscription to a railroad company's capital stock. The events originated in Whiteside County, Illinois, when the Chicago and Rock River Railroad Company, incorporated in May 1869, sought to compel the town of Montmorency to subscribe $50,000 to its capital stock following a vote by the town's legal voters. During an election on August 28, 1869, a majority voted in favor of the subscription. Subsequently, on February 12, 1872, the railroad company demanded the town issue bonds for this subscription, but the town officials refused, citing various pretexts. This case arose after the circuit court of Whiteside County was petitioned, and venue was changed to Rock Island County to determine the town's obligations concerning the subscription and bond issuance.	The plaintiffs, representing the Chicago and Rock River Railroad Company, argued that the town of Montmorency was legally required to subscribe $50,000 to the company's capital stock following a favorable vote from the town's legal voters. They highlighted that the railroad charter provided the necessary authority for such a subscription and sought a writ of mandamus to compel the town's officers to fulfill this obligation.	The defendants, representing the town of Montmorency, contended that the subscription authorization was misapplied, as the vote was related to a specific division of the railroad rather than the company as a whole. They argued that the election results were improperly influenced and that the conditions for the bond issue outlined in the election notice were not met, rendering the election null and void. They claimed there was no legal obligation for the town to issue the bonds.

The legal case "Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Joseph Brelsford" dates back to early October 1880, when Joseph Brelsford shipped a mare and colt from Racine, Wisconsin, to Onarga, Illinois, via the Illinois Central Railroad. He properly loaded and secured the animals, ensuring they would be well cared for during transit. They reached Chicago before dawn the next day, and he provided them with food and water before departing back home. However, later that evening, the same car transporting the mare and colt was observed at Kankakee, Illinois, with the mare in distress, struggling to stand. Despite the conductor's efforts to assist her, the mare grew worse and ultimately died before noon the following day. Brelsford subsequently sued the railroad for $115, claiming they failed to ensure the safety and care of the mare during transit. Expert testimonies in court differed over the cause of the mare's death, with the plaintiff’s witnesses suggesting an injury due to violence, while the defendant's witnesses attributed it to flatulent colic. Consequently, the jury was instructed on the liability of the carrier in cases of live freight, which became a focal point in the appeal.	Brelsford argued that the Illinois Central Railroad was liable for the mare's death due to negligence in caring for and safely transporting the animals. He asserted that the mare was in good condition before being shipped and that the defendant had an implied responsibility to deliver the animals without injury. He sought monetary compensation for the loss of the mare, believing that the railroad failed in its duty of care during the transportation.	The Illinois Central Railroad countered that there was no negligence on their part regarding the mare's transportation. They contended that any injury sustained by the mare was not due to their carelessness but rather attributable to the mare's own nature or improper loading by Brelsford. The defense maintained that the transportation was conducted smoothly, with minimal stops and careful handling, thus arguing against any liability for the purported loss.

Jonathan Browder, the appellant, brought a legal action against Jeremiah Johnson, the appellee, in the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1825. The dispute arose in Washington, Illinois, relating to a covenant for rent. Browder was dissatisfied with the verdict rendered against him in the lower court, which he argued was not in accordance with the law and the evidence presented. He cited that the damages awarded were excessive and claimed that the jury may have been misled regarding the rights of the parties involved. Following the verdict, Browder applied for a new trial. However, the court refused this request due to inconsistencies and irregularities in the record, including issues with the pleadings that complicated the matters at hand. The court highlighted that the details surrounding the trial were difficult to review properly because the essential evidence was not part of a formal bill of exceptions. Additionally, an affidavit presented by a juror was deemed improperly included in the record, which the court stated it could not consider. Ultimately, the court affirmed the judgment without delving into the procedural errors, concluding that the materials necessary for a comprehensive review were not appropriately presented.	The main arguments from Jonathan Browder, the plaintiff, centered around his dissatisfaction with the initial trial's verdict. He contended that the verdict was contrary to the law and the evidence, alleging that the awarded damages were excessive. Browder claimed the jury had acted under misconceptions about the rights of the involved parties, which he believed affected the outcome. His legal request was for the court to grant a new trial based on these assertions of error and injustice.	In response, Jeremiah Johnson, the defendant, argued against Browder's claims by emphasizing the validity of the trial court's verdict. The defense maintained that Browder's appeal lacked a sufficient basis for claiming errors, particularly due to the procedural deficiencies in how his arguments were presented. Johnson requested that the court uphold the lower court's ruling, asserting that the record did not properly substantiate Browder's claims of error or excessive damages, and thus the refusal of the new trial application was justified.

In 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, Maud and Edward Lyons were indicted on charges of felony for allegedly obtaining money through a confidence game. They were arraigned and pleaded not guilty, leading to a trial that was agreed to be conducted without a jury, contrary to legal requirements. The presiding judge found them guilty and sentenced Maud to three years and Ed to five years in the penitentiary. Following their imprisonment, the Lyons filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, asserting they were unlawfully imprisoned. The sheriff returned with the judgment copies, stating it was the cause of their detention. The key legal issue revolved around whether the court had the authority to try the case without a jury when the law explicitly required a jury of twelve men to determine guilt in felony cases. This raised questions about the constitutional guarantees of due process and the proper legal proceedings in criminal trials.	The plaintiffs, Maud and Edward Lyons, argued that their trial was invalid because it was conducted without a jury, which was a constitutional requirement for felony trials. They requested that the court review the legality of their imprisonment and ultimately sought their release based on the argument that the judgment against them was void due to lack of jurisdiction and due process.	The defendant, Sheriff Seth F. Hanchett, referred to the judgment rendered by the criminal court, asserting that the prisoners were lawfully detained based on a valid court process. The defense maintained that the judge’s actions were proper and that the agreement to waive a jury was acceptable, although he did not contest the statutory requirement for a jury trial in felony cases.

In the case of Charlotte A. Whitford v. Johanna Drexel et al., which was filed in the Circuit Court of Rock Island County, Illinois, the legal proceedings began with Charlotte A. Whitford, the plaintiff, seeking possession of two specific lots (lots 3 and 8) in the town of Cordova. This case was decided on November 13, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court. Whitford based her claim on a deed she obtained on December 2, 1860, which she believed granted her ownership of the lots. However, at the time of the trial, it was revealed that she only possessed all of the lots except for a narrow strip on their eastern side, which was occupied by defendants Johanna and Frank Drexel, who owned adjacent lots 4 and 7. Evidence showed that the Drexels had fenced in and possessed the strip since at least 1856. Whitford’s claims hinged on her color of title, possession, and payment of taxes for seven years, which she argued entitled her to the strip. However, the court found that she had never established actual possession of the disputed strip and that it remained under the adverse possession of the defendants. Ultimately, the trial court directed the jury to find for the defendants, leading to a judgment against Whitford.	Charlotte A. Whitford argued that she was entitled to recover possession of lots 3 and 8 based on her claim of title through a deed, her payment of taxes for seven consecutive years, and her color of title. She contended that the possession of part of the lots should extend to the whole under the law, despite the defendants holding the disputed strip. Whitford sought to overturn the jury's verdict that favored the Drexels, asserting that she should be granted possession of the property as per her claims.	Johanna and Frank Drexel, the defendants, contended that Whitford had failed to establish her legal possession of the disputed strip of land. They argued that their continuous and adverse possession of the area, which had been fenced since at least 1856, negated Whitford's claims. The Drexels maintained that even though she had paid taxes and had a deed, these factors alone did not qualify her for recovery as she had never claimed possession of the strip in question.

The case of Samuel Cable v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in January 1868 in Illinois. The appeal was made from the Morgan Circuit Court concerning a default judgment rendered on a scire facias—a legal writ requiring a person to show cause why a judgment should not be enforced—related to a recognizance, which is a legal agreement where a party promises to pay a penalty for failure to comply with the terms, often associated with bail. Samuel Cable was the appellant challenging the judgment, and Chief Justice Breese delivered the court's opinion. The main contention involved whether a judgment of forfeiture had to be established before issuing the scire facias against the cognizors associated with the recognizance, highlighting previous cases for reference. The court confirmed that the required judgment of forfeiture was indeed pronounced properly and that the writ of scire facias was a logical and legal follow-up to the proceedings.	The plaintiff, Samuel Cable, argued that a judgment of forfeiture was required before a scire facias could be issued against the cognizors. He referenced prior cases to support his claim that the court had erred in not adhering to this requirement, suggesting that the judgment rendered was improper due to the absence of such a prior forfeiture.	The defendant, represented by the Attorney General, contended that the necessary conditions for issuing a scire facias were met. They argued that since the cognizors were duly called and failed to appear, a judgment of forfeiture was rightfully entered. The court’s findings were in alignment with established legal precedents demonstrating that the issuing of the scire facias followed valid legal procedures.

The case, "The Richards Iron Works v. Thomas Glennon et al.," arose in September 1873, in Cook County, Illinois, and was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff, The Richards Iron Works, sold three steam boilers to the defendants, Thomas Glennon and others, and initiated a legal action to claim payment for these boilers, as well as for associated work and materials. The trial was conducted without a jury, and during the proceedings, the defendants raised issues of non-assumpsit (a denial of undertaking) and set-off (a claim to reduce or cancel a debt). The core of the defendants' complaint focused on their inability to secure the presence of a critical witness, prompting a request for a continuance of the trial. The court ruled that the defendants failed to demonstrate reasonable diligence in securing the witness's attendance, which is outlined in the relevant statutes. Additionally, the court admitted certain letter-press copies of contract proposals as evidence despite a request for the originals, establishing that the plaintiff's claims regarding indebtedness were sufficiently substantiated.	The Richards Iron Works argued that they were owed money for the sale of three steam boilers and for additional work and materials provided to the defendants. They contended that the defendants failed to fulfill their payment obligations and sought a judgment to recover the outstanding amounts owed.	The defendants, led by their attorney, challenged the trial proceedings by requesting a continuance based on the absence of a material witness. They argued that this absence adversely affected their ability to present a valid defense. Furthermore, they contested the admissibility of secondary evidence consisting of letter-press copies of contract proposals, positioning that these should not have been considered without the original documents being presented.

In the case of John Fay et al. v. Charles Richards, Administrator, the legal dispute arose in Peoria, Illinois, centering around the estate of Henry W. Burk after his death. The case was filed on December 8, 1888. Burk, prior to his passing, had entered into a series of financial transactions involving John Fay and his wife, Juliana Fay. In particular, Burk had purchased an undivided half interest in a malt-house property from John Fay for $12,000, initially paying $1,200 in cash and financing the remaining balance through three promissory notes, each for $3,600 and secured by a mortgage on the property. In October 1884, Burk sold his interest back to Fay, with the same notes being a point of contention. The estate of Burk, represented by Charles Richards, sought to enforce the payment of a recently created note dated April 28, 1885, amounting to $700, which was signed by John and Juliana Fay. The defendants contested the claim by asserting lack of consideration for the note, that it was merely accommodation paper, and included several claims for offsets based on prior transactions and obligations. A jury trial determined a judgment in favor of the plaintiff, leading to the appeal from the defendants.	The plaintiff, represented by Charles Richards, the administrator of Henry W. Burk's estate, claimed that the defendants owed a sum of $700 based on a promissory note dated April 28, 1885. The plaintiff argued that the note had valid consideration and was not merely accommodation paper. The plaintiff requested enforcement of the payment for the full amount of the note through the court, rejecting the defendants' claims for set-offs based on previous transactions.	The defendants, John and Juliana Fay, contended that the promissory note in question lacked consideration and characterized it as an accommodation note, which would not warrant enforcement. They claimed several set-offs related to notes and accounts that, according to them, amounted to more than the amount owed on the note. They sought to have the judgment overturned, arguing that the evidence presented did not support the plaintiff's claims and that the set-offs were valid.

This case, Phebe A. Woodburn v. James H. Woodburn et al., was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court and decided on November 11, 1887. The case originated following the death of George W. Woodburn on June 19, 1872, who left behind a will instructing his executor, Peter Ege, to sell his real estate to create a fund that would provide Phebe A. Woodburn, his widow, with an annuity of $1,000 annually. However, disagreements arose over an agreement made on March 13, 1873, in which Phebe relinquished her claim to this annuity in exchange for the interest on a reduced sum of $8,000, believing that there was a cloud on the title to the real estate. James H. Woodburn, her son, was the purchaser of the property in question and had certain rights to the estate as well. After various legal actions, including a bill for partition and claims from both Phebe and James H., the courts were tasked with determining the validity of the agreement, issues surrounding the notes secured by her mortgage, and the rightful financial entitlements as per the will.	Phebe A. Woodburn claimed that the agreement made with James H. Woodburn was fraudulent and sought to have it set aside, asserting that she had been misled into relinquishing her rights to the rightful annuity outlined in her husband's will. She also contested the handling of notes and mortgage payments related to the estate, seeking a greater claim against the estate for her financial support.	James H. Woodburn contended that the agreement was valid and should be upheld, asserting that there was sufficient consideration for the relinquishment made by Phebe. He argued that the Appellate Court erred by interpreting the agreement in a way that benefitted her beyond what was originally intended, specifically regarding the payments due for her annuity and the handling of the notes she secured through a mortgage.

In April 1865, the case of Charles M. Chase v. The Sycamore and Courtland Railroad Company was addressed by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in DeKalb County, Illinois, where Chase, who had subscribed to stock in the railroad company, claimed that the company owed him. The central issue arose from a subscription agreement that Chase signed, committing to purchase one-half share of stock valued at fifty dollars. However, the subscription was made contingent upon the company raising a total of five thousand dollars for the specific purpose of purchasing a locomotive engine. No evidence was presented during the trial to show that any funds had been raised by the company to fulfill this condition, leading to uncertainties regarding the execution of the contract. The court was tasked with unearthing the implications of this conditional subscription, whether Chase was a legitimate member of the corporation, and if necessary demands were made prior to initiating the legal action.	Charles M. Chase contended that he had a valid subscription to the stock of The Sycamore and Courtland Railroad Company. He argued that he was entitled to enforce the agreement against the company, claiming it was responsible for fulfilling the conditions laid out in their subscription terms, specifically the need to raise five thousand dollars for a locomotive before he had to pay his share. Chase requested that the court confirm his obligation and upholding of the stock subscription.	The Sycamore and Courtland Railroad Company argued that Chase's subscription was conditional and, as such, did not constitute a binding commitment until the specific condition—raising five thousand dollars—was met. They contended that no effective fundraising had occurred, and thus Chase was not legally obligated to pay any amount related to the stock. The company also claimed that Chase had not obtained membership status in the corporation, which relied on actual payment or receipt of a stock certificate.

In 1887, a legal case titled Frank W. Harvey v. Carlos A. Cook was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court, following a trial in the Superior Court of Cook County. The case involved Frank W. Harvey and his brother, who ran a clothing business under the name Harvey Brothers, and Carlos A. Cook, who served as an agent tasked with procuring advertising contracts. Cook claimed that he had successfully obtained 362 advertising contracts for the Harvey Brothers from various newspaper publishers in accordance with a contract dated October 6, 1882. He sought a commission of $5 for each contract secured. During the trial, it was revealed that although Cook provided acknowledgment receipts from Harvey Brothers for some batches of contracts, there was no evidence verifying the authenticity of the signatures of the publishers on the contracts. A key point of contention was whether Cook had fulfilled his obligations as an agent. The jury initially ruled in favor of Cook, awarding him $1,810 in damages, though this was later reduced to $810 after a remittance order. The case ultimately required an appeal due to questions about the validity of the jury instructions regarding the burden of proof and the genuineness of the signatures.	Carlos A. Cook, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to commissions for the procurement of 362 advertising contracts, as specifically authorized by the Harvey Brothers' contract. He contended he had delivered contracts that met the requirements set forth in the original agreement, and therefore, he claimed $5 for each contract secured. Cook relied on two receipts to establish that he had indeed delivered batches of contracts to Harvey Brothers.	The defendants, represented by the surviving partner of Harvey Brothers, disputed Cook's claims by asserting that he failed to provide evidence of the authenticity of the signatures on the advertising contracts. They contended that Cook's performance was lacking, alleging misconduct and fraud, and claimed that the contracts received were materially altered without their consent. The defendants argued that these defects exempted them from paying commissions owed to Cook.

In 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal case was initiated titled "Louis Jaeger v. Jacob Dieden." The case stemmed from a trespass incident wherein Louis Jaeger, the plaintiff, accused Jacob Dieden, the defendant, of unlawful actions against him. The proceedings were held in the Superior Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Thomas F. Tiptoe. During the trial, a jury was tasked with evaluating the evidence presented. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of Jaeger, awarding him $800 in damages. However, the court expressed dissatisfaction with the awarded damages. As a result, Jaeger agreed to remit $500 of the damages, leading to a new judgment reflecting the reduced amount. Dieden subsequently appealed the verdict, contesting whether the jury's decision was supported by adequate evidence.	Louis Jaeger claimed that Jacob Dieden committed trespass against him, leading to damages amounting to $800. He sought a verdict in his favor from the jury, which ultimately occurred when the court sided with him, leading to the initial damages award. Following the court’s suggestion of a remittitur, Jaeger complied, adjusting the damages claim while still pursuing the overall judgment for the balance.	Jacob Dieden, through his counsel, William T. Butler, filed a general issue and the plea of "molliter manus imposuit," indicating a denial of wrongful action. Dieden contested the jury's verdict, arguing that the evidence presented was conflicting and did not support the damages awarded. He sought a reversal of the judgment on appeal, claiming that the conclusions drawn by the jury were not substantiated by the evidence presented during the trial.

William Bradish v. George R. Grant is a legal case decided on November 13, 1886, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a dispute in Cook County, Chicago, over the possession of the west forty feet of lots 7 and 8 in block 60 of Bussell, Mather & Boberts' addition to the city. George R. Grant, the plaintiff, initiated an action of ejectment against William Bradish, the defendant, to recover these lots. The plaintiff demonstrated his title through a decree from a previous chancery suit under the "Burnt Records" act, indicating that the title to the property was held by Fernando Jones at the time of the decree in 1875. The plaintiff also provided evidence of a subsequent deed from Jones to himself. Meanwhile, the defendant attempted to challenge the evidence presented by the plaintiff, claiming he had not been properly served in the original chancery suit and questioning the jurisdiction of the court. Ultimately, the court had to determine whether the plaintiff's legal title was valid against the defendant's claims.	The plaintiff, George R. Grant, argued that he had a proper title to the disputed property, established through a decree from a previous chancery suit, which confirmed Fernando Jones as the owner at the time. He requested the court to affirm his title and grant possession of the lots. He presented evidence of the previous court's findings and the deed transferring the property from Jones to himself, asserting that these legally binding documents established his right to eject the defendant.	William Bradish, the defendant, contended that the court had no jurisdiction over him in the prior suit and argued that the decree determining the title was invalid since he allegedly did not receive proper service. He sought to introduce evidence suggesting that the plaintiff's title was flawed but was unable to present this effectively in court. His key argument was rooted in claims of fraudulent entry and service, which he asserted should invalidate the plaintiff's claims to property ownership.

In January 1869, Sarah J. Preston and others brought a lawsuit against Samuel P. Hodgen in the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a dispute over mortgage and promissory notes linked to several tracts of land in Logan County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Enoch Preston and James Maltby, initially purchased these tracts from James Primm for $6,000 and executed three promissory notes and a mortgage to secure the purchase. However, a mistake occurred when the mortgage mis-described one tract. The case arose after Primm assigned one of the notes to John F. Smith, who attempted to foreclose the mortgage and sold the property to Ousley. The remaining notes were later transferred to Hodgen, who redeemed the property before the expiration of the redemption period, leading to the current suit. The plaintiffs alleged various claims, including mistakes in the mortgage documentation and failure to pay taxes. The case involved multiple parties, including heirs and other creditors claiming interests in the property.	The plaintiffs claimed that due to a mistake in describing the notes and a failure by the defendants to pay taxes and the principal amount owed, they were entitled to amounts due under the mortgage. They requested an accounting of the total amount owed, including taxes paid by Primm and Hodgen, and sought the sale of the property to satisfy the debt if payment was not made.	The defendant, Hodgen, argued that he had a legal right to redeem the property to protect his interest as the assignee of the notes. He contended that the previous foreclosure by Ousley did not bar his right to foreclose again, as he became vested with all rights through his redemption.
