He also claimed that the facts alleged in the bill were not sufficiently proven, particularly regarding the mistakes and payments referenced, especially in the case of the minor defendants, and he sought the reversal of the decree due to these errors.

The case, "The People of the State of Illinois, for the use of Nancy J. Ingram’s Administrators v. Aaron G. Cloud et al.," was heard in June 1869 by the Illinois Supreme Court. This legal action originated in the Hamilton Circuit Court, where the plaintiffs, representing the estate of Nancy J. Ingram, pursued a debt claim against the sureties of a defaulting administrator on his bond. The case had its roots during the October term of 1866, when the defendants initially filed a general demurrer to the declaration, which was sustained by the court, granting the plaintiffs the opportunity to amend their claim. The proceedings were continued multiple times over the following terms until April 1868, when the defendants attempted to dismiss the case due to alleged lack of a bond for costs. This motion was granted by the court, resulting in a judgment against the plaintiffs for costs. The plaintiffs contested this decision, asserting that the motion to dismiss came too late and was improper given that they had already responded to the merits of the case. Upon review, the Supreme Court focused on procedural matters and past precedents regarding motions and costs, ultimately finding the previous court's judgment erroneous.	The plaintiffs contended that the dismissal of their suit for failing to provide a bond for costs was inappropriate, claiming that the motion was filed too late after they had already responded to the merits. They argued that established case law indicates such motions should be made promptly and that any delay would waive the right to dismiss on that basis. Furthermore, they asserted that the judgment for costs against them was improper, as it should not fall on the State when acting in the plaintiffs' capacity.	The defendants argued that the dismissal of the case was justified due to the plaintiffs' failure to provide a bond for costs, claiming that the plaintiffs had missed the proper timing to object to this requirement. They maintained that their original demurrer remained valid and that the court had the authority to dismiss the case based on procedural grounds. Additionally, they sought to confirm the judgment for costs against the plaintiffs as appropriate.

In the case of Levi A. Richardson et al. v. Ambrose S. Hadsall, which was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 10, 1883, a dispute arose from a mortgage executed by Levi A. Richardson to William Hadsall on December 1, 1865, in Will County, Illinois. The mortgage was meant to secure the payment of two promissory notes totaling $2360.29. The defendants, Hadsall and others, admitted to the execution of the notes and mortgage but claimed that certain payments had been made that extinguished the notes, leaving a balance owed to them of $1362. They also filed a cross-bill requesting the cancellation of the mortgage and a decree for any amount they believed was due to them. The court appointed a master to assess the accounts between the parties, who ultimately reported that Levi A. Richardson owed $2656.29 after accounting for all credits. The defendants contested this report, asserting that they were not duly credited for certain payments. However, their objection was ultimately overruled, and the court ordered a sale due to the sum owed by the complainant. The findings of the master's report were affirmed upon appeal to the Appellate Court.	The plaintiff, Levi A. Richardson, claimed that the defendant Hadsall was owed a sum secured by the mortgage due to the non-fulfillment of the mortgage agreement by the defendants. He contended that despite the payments asserted by the defendants, the total outstanding amount owed after accounting for credits was $2656.29. The plaintiff sought foreclosure on the mortgage and an order of sale based on this owed amount.	The defendants argued that they had made payments that should extinguish the obligations under the mortgage. They contended that the payments, if properly accounted for, would leave a balance in their favor rather than against them. Their key requests included the cancellation of the mortgage and a decree against the plaintiff for the amount they claimed was owed to them, which they argued should reflect the payments made.

The case "The State Savings Institution v. John A. Nelson" involves a dispute that traces back to October 3, 1865, in Chicago, Illinois. The State Savings Institution filed a lawsuit against John A. Nelson, who was the sheriff of Cook County at the time. The lawsuit claimed that Nelson failed to pay over $1,500 collected on execution, resulting in a judgment in favor of the State Savings Institution. Over two years later, on February 10, 1868, Nelson motioned to have this judgment set aside, which the court accepted. This action prompted the State Savings Institution to seek a review of the lower court's decision, ultimately contesting the validity of the order that nullified the original judgment. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, which examined the lower court’s authority after the expiration of its term during which the judgment was issued.	The State Savings Institution, as the plaintiff, argued that the lower court improperly set aside the original judgment rendered against John A. Nelson for $1,500. The plaintiff contended that the court lacked the authority to reverse the judgment more than two years after its issuance, except for clerical corrections or formal amendments. Therefore, the plaintiff requested the higher court to reverse the decision made by the lower court and reinstate the original judgment against Nelson.	John A. Nelson, as the defendant, sought to have the judgment against him set aside on the grounds that he believed there were valid reasons for contesting the original ruling. While specific arguments are not detailed in the case description, it can be inferred that he relied on the motion that led to the judgment nullification. Nelson's legal representatives argued for his right to relief from the judgment and urged the court to maintain the lower court's decision to revoke the ruling.

In September 1875, the case of Artemus Carter v. Lewis D. Webster was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in Cook County, where Artemus Carter, a real estate agent, claimed he was employed by Lewis D. Webster to sell a specific tract of land. Carter argued that he successfully procured an offer for the land through his efforts with other real estate agents, which Webster accepted. However, Webster maintained that their agreement required Carter to sell a larger portion of land at a specified price, asserting that no sale was completed at that rate. The case was characterized by conflicting testimonies regarding the extent of Carter's involvement in the sale and whether the local custom among real estate agents—which allowed for cooperation and commission sharing—was applicable. The jury ultimately found in favor of Carter, suggesting that he played a critical role in facilitating the sale through his network of agents.	Carter's main arguments centered on the assertion that he was employed by Webster to sell or procure offers for the land. He claimed his efforts directly led to the eventual sale by introducing interested parties. Carter sought the commissions due to him for the sale of the property, relying on the local custom among real estate agents that allows for shared commissions when multiple agents contribute to a sale.	Webster's defense rested on his claim that Carter did not fulfill the original agreement, which involved selling an entire quarter-section of land at a specific price of $350 per acre. He argued that Carter failed to effect a sale or find a willing buyer at the agreed price, contending that no commission should be awarded since the sale was not conducted under the terms initially established.

The case "Trustees of the Independent Presbyterian Church and Society of Buffalo Grove and Polo v. Robert Proctor" originated in 1872 in Winnebago County, Illinois. The involved parties were the trustees of an independent church organization and their pastor, Robert Proctor. The church operated autonomously, without affiliation to any larger religious denomination. The custom of this church allowed for the annual election of a pastor, a practice that resulted in Proctor being elected in November of 1868, 1869, 1870, and re-elected in 1871. Despite being re-elected, the church session and trustees later determined that Proctor should not continue in his role. Proctor, however, chose to remain in his position, which prompted the trustees to file a bill in chancery seeking an injunction to prevent him from officiating. The trustees claimed that the church session had the exclusive power to employ a pastor, a point that they were ultimately unable to substantiate through constitutional or written evidence, relying instead on the particular customs of their society. The court's role was to assess whether it should intervene to remove Proctor, whose presence was based on a majority vote of the church members.	The plaintiffs, the trustees of the Independent Presbyterian Church, argued that they had the right to terminate Robert Proctor's role as pastor, asserting that the church session alone possessed the authority to employ a pastor. They sought an injunction to restrain Proctor from continuing his duties in the church, contending that his refusal to step down was detrimental to the church's governance according to their established rules and customs.	Robert Proctor, the defendant, contended that his election as pastor was valid and based on the majority vote of the church society, supported by the customs of the church which allowed for such democratic processes. He argued that the trustees’ claim of exclusive authority was unfounded, as it was not backed by any formal written rules or constitutional provisions. Proctor maintained that any decision to remove him must align with the majority's wishes, which he believed currently supported his position.

On December 10, 1855, Chancellor Martin executed a promissory note for $2,000, payable one year later to Richard H. McGoon, alongside a deed of trust on real estate to secure the payment. By March 1, 1863, after failing to pay the principal and remaining interest, Martin offered McGoon $2,040 in legal tender and gold, which McGoon refused. Following Martin's death in 1864, J. Addison Crain was appointed as his administrator. In 1866, McGoon, having assigned the note to his son Henry, requested the sale of the property to satisfy the debt. Crain and other plaintiffs filed to prevent the sale and seek an account of the payment. After examining the evidence, a jury found that the amount due was $2,040 and confirmed that a tender had been made but not kept good. Subsequently, McGoon sought a foreclosure decree on the property through a cross-bill. The Circuit Court ultimately dissolved the injunction and ruled in favor of McGoon.	The plaintiffs argued that the tender made by Chancellor Martin on March 1, 1863, discharged the mortgage, despite it not being kept good after the refusal of acceptance by McGoon. They claimed that since the tender was made in a timely manner and the subsequent actions were rooted in equity, the court should prevent the foreclosure of the property.	The defendants, led by Henry S. McGoon, contended that the tender was invalid as it was not kept good after the refusal of acceptance. They maintained that the plaintiffs had not fulfilled their obligation to ensure that the funds remained available for the payment, thus justifying the enforcement of the foreclosure.

In September 1874, the case of Joseph Busch v. George W. Huston was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from a dispute in Mercer County, Illinois. The case centers around the deceased John Dewitt, Sr., who died intestate on April 6, 1846, leaving his assets, including certain lands, to his four heirs: Benjamin Dewitt, John Dewitt, Jr., and Betsey Shoemaker (married to John Shoemaker), along with Joseph Busch, the grandson of John Dewitt, Sr., through his daughter Jane. Joseph Busch claimed a one-fourth share of these lands as an heir, positioning himself as the only surviving child of Jane. The appellant, George W. Huston, argued that he acquired the land through a chain of title from the heirs of John and Betsey Shoemaker. The court deliberated on whether Limitation Laws barred Busch's claims, particularly relating to possession and ownership interests in the land, which Huston contended were handed down via various deeds and transactions initiated over the years. Ultimately, the court evaluated the legitimacy of the claims and the manner in which the possession of land passed through the generations, leading to this significant legal decision concerning property rights.	Joseph Busch, the appellee, alleged that he was entitled to a one-fourth share of the lands that he claimed as an heir of John Dewitt, Sr. He argued that he had not been effectively barred from his rights due to the passage of time, as he maintained a vested interest in the estate and its properties. Busch sought a partition of the property to ensure his rightful claim was recognized and to reclaim his share of the lands in question.	George W. Huston, the appellant, contended that Busch's claim should be barred by the statute of limitations due to his long inaction concerning the property rights. He asserted that the deed he possessed from John Dewitt, Jr. was a valid color and claim of title to the property, maintaining that he acquired and maintained possession of the land in good faith, and had fulfilled his obligations such as paying taxes on the property. Huston argued that because he held the property under lien and payment of dues, Busch's claim lacked the necessary evidence to overcome the defenses based on adverse possession.

The case of Charles W. Cilley et al. v. Nancy J. Hawkins took place in the state of Illinois, with a decision delivered by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. The dispute arose from a breach of contract regarding a lease for a farmland between the plaintiffs, Charles W. Cilley and others, and the defendant, Nancy J. Hawkins. The lease, intended for three years, outlined that both parties would contribute teams, grain, and implements necessary for farming. In March 1866, the plaintiffs entered the farm and began breaking ground but were subsequently denied permission by the defendant to proceed with their farming operations. This led the plaintiffs to bring an action to recover damages for the breach of contract. During the proceedings, issues arose regarding a tender of damages made by the defendant and the assessment of speculative damages sought by the plaintiffs. Ultimately, the jury found a tender had been made for fifty dollars but also assessed the plaintiffs' damages at thirty dollars.	The plaintiffs' primary claim was for damages resulting from the defendant's breach of the farming lease contract. They argued that they incurred losses after being denied possession of the farm to cultivate it, despite having begun preparations. They sought compensation beyond the amount of the initial tender, arguing that their damages reflected not only the value of the labor already performed but also the potential earnings lost from not having access to the farm.	The defendant contended that the plaintiffs had abandoned the contract due to their declaration regarding sub-letting the farm. She maintained that a valid tender of fifty dollars was made to the plaintiffs for the work done, thus mitigating her liability. The defendant argued against the admissibility of the plaintiffs' claims regarding speculative future damages, asserting that they were not provable under the existing terms of the contract.

The case "I. C. Persels v. James McConnell et al." was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on August 7, 1885. The legal dispute arose in Grundy County, Illinois, where the appellant, I. C. Persels, a constable, was involved in a replevin action against the appellees. The case originated when Persels received an execution to collect a judgment of $58.67, rendered by Justice of the Peace I. B. McGinnis in favor of George W. Brown & Co. against Bichólas Henson. On May 10, 1884, Persels went to Henson's residence to collect the amount owed or levy the execution. While there, he noted the property at issue: eighteen acres of growing oats and an old bay mare. He indorsed a levy on the oats but left the mare with Henson. The court addressed whether Persels had a valid claim to pursue replevin based on not having made a sufficient levy on the property as required by law. The court ultimately assessed the appropriateness of excluding evidence introduced by Persels regarding the property and his actions during the execution process.	Persels argued that he had a valid claim for replevin against the appellees based on his position as a constable with an execution in hand. He sought to replevy the eighteen acres of oats and the mare, claiming he was entitled to the property as a result of the execution. He contended that the evidence he sought to admit was relevant to establishing his right to maintain the action, despite not having formally taken possession of the property.	The appellees defended against Persels' claims by arguing that he did not have the legal right to maintain an action of replevin because he failed to make a valid levy on the property in question. They asserted that merely noting a levy without taking possession did not confer any rights to Persels. The defendants maintained that there was no sufficient evidence to prove Persels' ownership or rights to the property, as he did not fulfill the necessary legal requirements of a levy.

William H. Mason brought a legal action against Frances H. Jones (formerly Mrs. Boach) in the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1864, following a dispute regarding a debt. Mason claimed Jones owed him approximately $106 for goods that he had sold and delivered. Concurrently, Jones held a $300 mortgage note against Mason, which she had sold to a third party, Drake, in 1861. It was understood at the time that Mason's account with Jones would cover the interest on the mortgage note. In August 1861, Drake secured a decree against Mason for $402.50, which included the total amount of the note plus accrued interest, and then sold the certificate of purchase to another individual, Hults. Mason's suit aimed to recover the unpaid account from Jones, but the defense argued there was a fraudulent collusion between Mason and Hults. A verdict was initially reached in favor of Jones, leading Mason to appeal the decision based largely on a legal question regarding the admissibility of Drake's deposition as evidence.	Mason's primary claims were based on the assertion that Jones was indebted to him for $106 for goods sold and delivered. He sought recovery of this amount through the court, arguing against the defenses presented by Jones. Mason contended that Drake, who claimed not to have interest in the case, improperly served as a witness against him and that the overall judgment in favor of Jones was flawed.	The defense by Jones included claims that Mason had engaged in fraudulent collusion with Hults, which invalidated Mason's claim. They cited the fact that Drake, who was deemed to have financial interest in the case, provided a deposition that they argued supported their position. The defense maintained that the evidence presented by Mason was insufficient to change the outcome of the previous court’s ruling, thus justifying the prior judgment in favor of Jones.

About noon on August 8, 1884, West, Andress & Co. sold 5,000 bushels of corn to George B. Dickinson & Co. on the Chicago Board of Trade, with payment to be made via two checks totaling $2,332.34 drawn on the Hide and Leather National Bank. Instead of presenting the checks that day, West, Andress & Co. deposited them in their own bank for processing the next day. Later that day, Dickinson & Co. transferred the same warehouse receipts for the corn to the Hide and Leather National Bank to obtain credit, having previously overdrawn their account. However, by the next morning, Dickinson & Co. had failed and the checks were not honored. West, Andress & Co. demanded their property back from the bank, but the request was denied, prompting them to file an action of trover against the bank for the wrongful conversion of the warehouse receipts. The court found in favor of the plaintiffs initially, but the case was appealed.	West, Andress & Co. alleged wrongful conversion of their warehouse receipts for corn by the Hide and Leather National Bank. They asserted that when they sold the corn for cash, the delivery of the receipts was contingent on the payment being secured by the checks, which subsequently bounced when Dickinson & Co. failed.	The Hide and Leather National Bank claimed that they were a bona fide purchaser of the warehouse receipts for a valuable consideration and without any prior notice of the transaction details between West, Andress & Co. and Dickinson & Co. The bank argued that they acted in good faith and should not be held liable for the alleged wrongful conversion.

The case of Mary McClurkin v. Samuel Ewing took place in November 1866 within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff, Mary McClurkin, alleged that the defendant, Samuel Ewing, slandered her by accusing her of being the mother of a child found in a basket at a neighbor's door. The suit was filed in the Circuit Court of Washington County, wherejury trial resulted in a verdict favoring the defendant. After the verdict, McClurkin's legal team motioned for a new trial, but this motion was denied without stated reasons. The case was then brought to the Supreme Court on the basis of the instructions given to the jury, as documented in the bill of exceptions. Throughout the proceedings, issues arose regarding the adequacy of evidence and the instructions influencing the jury's perception of slander suits.	Mary McClurkin claimed that Samuel Ewing falsely accused her of being the mother of an abandoned child, which constituted slander. She contended that Ewing's statements harmed her reputation and sought legal redress through a slander action. The plaintiff argued that the jury should have favored her based on the evidence presented, particularly concerning her character and the implications of Ewing's statements.	Samuel Ewing's key defense was that the statements he made did not constitute slander, as they did not directly accuse McClurkin of fornication nor meet the legal threshold for such a claim. The defense pointed out that the jury should find in favor of Ewing unless it was proven that he explicitly charged McClurkin with the alleged conduct. The defendant emphasized the absence of sufficient evidence from the plaintiff's side, suggesting that the jury had valid reasons to doubt the testimony that purportedly supported the slander claim.

On December 1, 1867, an incident occurred involving the St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad in Tazewell County, Illinois. Warren Kilpatrick, the plaintiff, owned a horse that was killed by a train of the defendant, St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad Co. At the time of the incident, the railroad was under the control of the defendant, which had a responsibility to operate its trains with due care. The plaintiff alleged that employees of the railroad had carelessly left a fence down and opened the enclosure where the horse was confined, allowing the horse to escape onto the train tracks. The railroad's train subsequently struck the horse, leading to its death. The case was brought to court, where the plaintiff claimed damages for the loss of his horse.	The plaintiff, Warren Kilpatrick, claimed that the defendant was negligent in operating the railroad, specifically by failing to secure the enclosure of his horse and allowing it to escape onto the tracks. He requested compensation for the value of the horse that had been killed due to this negligence.	The defendant, St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad Co., contended that the declaration made by the plaintiff was insufficient due to a lack of specific allegations regarding the time and place of the incident. They asserted that the plaintiff’s claims did not adequately establish a basis for liability, indicating that they believed the court should dismiss the case based on these technicalities.

Martha Smith filed a case against William Curry and another defendant in December 1854. The events leading to the legal action took place on September 8, 1852, in Brown County, Illinois. Smith possessed a teaching qualification certificate from the school commissioner, which entitled her to payment from the local school fund. She taught at a common school from September 9 to September 27, 1852, and maintained a schedule of her students. On September 28, 1852, she submitted the schedule to the school directors, including the defendants, requesting them to examine it and issue a certificate for payment from the township’s school fund. However, the directors refused to examine her schedule or provide the necessary certification. The case was tried before a jury, which ruled in favor of Smith. Nonetheless, the court later arrested the judgment and ruled in favor of the defendants, resulting in dismissal and imposition of costs on Smith.	Martha Smith claimed that she was entitled to receive $5 from the township school fund as her distributive share, alleging that she met all legal qualifications and that the defendants failed to perform their duty by not examining her schedule and certifying it to the treasurer. She argued that her qualifications and the actions taken fell within the statutory requirements necessary to receive payment.	The defendants contended that Smith did not satisfy the statutory requirement of presenting her teaching qualification certificate before the school commenced. They argued that previous court rulings stated that school directors are not obligated to examine and certify schedules if the requisite certificate was not presented prior. Thus, they claimed they had not breached any duties concerning Smith's request.

The case of The City of Springfield v. Mahlon H. Mathus et al. was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 28, 1888. It arose in Springfield, Illinois, where the city sought to implement a special assessment for the construction of a sewer on College Street. The city council passed an ordinance directing the installation of a two-foot inside diameter sewer with necessary manholes and inlets for surface drainage. However, certain lot owners objected to this special assessment, leading to the case being brought before the county court of Sangamon County. The primary contention was whether the ordinance adequately described the proposed improvement, particularly regarding the location of the manholes, which some objectors claimed was insufficiently detailed for legal compliance. The court had to determine whether the ordinance met statutory requirements that mandated specifying the nature, character, locality, and description of improvements.	The City of Springfield claimed that the ordinance sufficiently described the sewer improvement, including necessary specifications about the materials and construction. They argued that, despite objections regarding the description of manhole locations, the term "necessary man-holes" was a definitive description that allowed a civil engineer to determine their placement. The city requested that the court overturn the county court's dismissal of the special assessment and allow the construction to proceed.	The defendants, represented by the objecting lot owners, contended that the ordinance failed to provide a clear description of the sewer improvement, specifically regarding the location of the manholes. They cited previous cases to support their argument that without specific designations for manhole placements, the ordinance did not fulfill statutory requirements. The defendants sought to uphold the county court's order dismissing the special assessment proceeding based on these insufficiencies.

The case, *School Directors v. Charles R. Miller*, took place in January 1869 in Sparta, Randolph County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Charles R. Miller, was involved in a legal dispute with the School Directors of District No. 2. The case arose after the school district was divided in April 1863, leading to the establishment of a new district, District No. 6. In October 1864, Districts No. 2 and No. 6 were consolidated back into one, known again as District No. 2. Miller, who served as a director in District No. 6, claimed that the school directors owed him money based on a promissory note for funds borrowed to construct a school building in District No. 6. The funds borrowed were exclusively utilized for the benefit of District No. 6, with no financial benefit to District No. 2. The case gained traction as it progressed through various courts, with both the recorder’s court and the circuit court ruling in favor of the plaintiff before the defendants appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court. The Supreme Court ultimately questioned the legal obligation of District No. 2 to repay debts incurred exclusively by District No. 6, considering both districts had distinct identities and liabilities.	The plaintiff, Charles R. Miller, claimed that the School Directors of District No. 2 were liable to repay a promissory note for money borrowed to build a schoolhouse in District No. 6. He argued that since the debt was executed for school purposes and that he was a director during that time, the school district should fulfill its financial obligations to him.	The defendants, the School Directors of District No. 2, contended that they were not liable for the debts incurred by District No. 6 because District No. 2 had not benefited from the borrowed funds. They argued that the debt belonged solely to District No. 6, and unless a clear legal obligation had been established, District No. 2 should not be held accountable for those debts. They also pointed out that the existing statute required a proper division of liabilities when districts are restructured, which had not occurred in this case.

In December 1857, John Hamilton purchased a tract of land comprising three lots of eighty acres and a two-acre lot from a man named Bubach. In 1860, Hamilton reconveyed two of the eighty-acre lots back to Bubach but denied that the two-acre lot was included in that conveyance. Several years later, in 1866, a man named Britt approached Hamilton to buy the two-acre lot for $40, which was to be paid in rails. Hamilton verbally agreed, allowing Britt to build a house on the lot. However, when Britt sought a deed after constructing the house, Hamilton informed him that the title to the property remained with Bubach. Britt subsequently pursued a deed from Bubach, who provided a bond for a deed in exchange for $45. Britt later sold his interest to Garver, who then transferred it to Thomas Rook, the appellee in this case. In 1870, Hamilton filed a lawsuit against Rook, seeking an injunction to prevent Rook from removing the house from the lot. In defense, Rook cited his bond from Bubach and argued a mistake in the original deed reconveyance. The Circuit Court initially denied Hamilton's claims but later granted Rook relief based on the verbal contract with Britt.	The plaintiff, John Hamilton, claimed that he maintained ownership of the two-acre lot despite his previous reconveyance to Bubach. He sought an injunction to prevent defendant Thomas Rook from removing the house built by Britt and requested the court to recognize his rights to the property.	The defendant, Thomas Rook, countered that he had a valid claim to the two-acre lot through the bond for a deed he received from Bubach. Rook argued that the verbal contract between Hamilton and Britt granted Britt an equitable interest in the property, which he inherited through Britt’s subsequent sale to Garver. Rook sought the court's recognition of this agreement and contended that he had acted in good faith.

In January 1871, in the town of Havana, Illinois, Lewis W. Ross initiated an action of ejectment against Levi Coat concerning a disputed lot in block ten. The suit was brought in the Mason Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Charles Turner. The issue at hand revolved around the title ownership of the lot. Ross claimed to have established title through mesne conveyances from the original patentee, but Coat, defending as a terre-tenant, asserted a bar to Ross's title based on the statute of limitations. The conflict centered on questions of possession, tax payments, and the relevant sections of the Conveyance Act that dictate property rights when taxes are involved. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendant, Levi Coat. The case was subsequently appealed, raising legal questions about the validity of tax payments over several years and whether the conditions for a title bar were met.	Lewis W. Ross claimed to have established a legal title to the lot through a series of conveyances from the original patentee. He argued that despite the defendant's possession, he had paid taxes on the property, contending that this constituted a legal claim to the title under the relevant provisions of the Illinois Conveyance Act.	Levi Coat claimed that he had satisfied the conditions under the statute of limitations, asserting that there had not been continuous payment of taxes by the plaintiff for the requisite seven years. He argued that the actions of the guardian of the heirs, who also paid taxes during the time, disrupted any claim Ross had to the title. Coat insisted that without the legal criteria met for continuous possession and tax payment, Ross's title claim was barred.

On May 23, 1863, William Lewis, a resident of Knox County, Illinois, executed four promissory notes totalling $874.08 to a firm named C.S. Colton & Sons, securing the notes with a trust deed on two forty-acre tracts of land. The deed authorized the trustee, Milo D. Cooke, to sell the property in case of default on the payments. After Lewis paid the first three notes and interest, he confronted C.S. Colton about the last note due in May 1867. By agreement, the principal amount remained unpaid for an additional year. However, when Lewis attempted to settle the remaining balance, C.S. Colton and his son were unavailable, leading to a situation where the trustee sold Lewis's land to Stoddard for a fraction of its value without Lewis's knowledge. Lewis filed suit in the Knox County Circuit Court, claiming fraud and collusion between Stoddard and Colton, seeking to set aside the sale and reclaim his property. The court found in favor of Lewis, setting aside the sale. The defendants then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court.	William Lewis argued that the sale of his property was fraudulent, asserting that there was collusion between Stoddard and C.S. Colton to deprive him of his equity in the land. He maintained that he made diligent efforts to pay off the debt but was thwarted by the Coltons' evasive actions and a lack of proper notice. Lewis requested that the court set aside the sale and deeds associated with the trust deed, allowing him to redeem his property.	The defendants, including Solomon F. Flint who acquired the property from Stoddard, contended that they were bona fide purchasers without notice of any fraud or prior interest Lewis held in the land. Flint argued that he believed the transaction to be legitimate and asserted that Lewis’s failure to pay on time justified the sale under the trust deed’s provisions. They also challenged the claim of inadequate notice, claiming that procedural requirements were met in executing the sale.

The case "Johnston & Deverill v. David Salisbury" was decided in September 1871 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from a contractual dispute involving the plaintiffs, Johnston & Deverill, and the defendant, David Salisbury, concerning a contract under seal. The plaintiffs delivered a horse, buggy, and harness to Salisbury as part of the agreement, in exchange for the promise of a lot of land in Chicago. However, the plaintiffs contended that Salisbury had failed to fulfill his obligations under the contract, leading them to file an action of assumpsit to recover the value of the delivered items. The case was presided over by Judge John G. Rogers in the Circuit Court of Cook County.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant had refused to perform their contractual obligations regarding the conveyance of the lot in Chicago. They sought recovery for the value of the horse, buggy, and harness, which had been delivered under the terms of the sealed contract. The legal basis for their claim was an action of assumpsit, asserting that the defendant’s failure to perform constituted a breach of contract.	The defendant's primary argument was that the action of assumpsit was not appropriate in this case, as the plaintiffs failed to provide evidence of a sale or conversion of the delivered items into money or money's worth. The defendant contended that without such proof, the proper legal recourse for the plaintiffs would be to pursue a different legal action—either a covenant on the sealed instrument or treating the contract as rescinded and seeking recovery of the property via trover or replevin.

On October 6, 1868, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, Orlin H. Gillett, serving as the administrator of the estate of Benoni R. Gillett, deceased, filed a claim against the estate for $1,900.86, asserting it as an outstanding balance owed to him. Madison Y. Johnson, an appointed administrator pro tem, represented one of the heirs and contested the claim's validity. The county court of Jo Daviess rejected Gillett's claim. Subsequently, Gillett sought to challenge this decision by bringing the matter to the circuit court through a certiorari, as the window for appeal had closed. The circuit court allowed Gillett’s claim, prompting Johnson to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, which scrutinized the administration of the estate and the procedures followed by the county court. The Court evaluated whether Gillett had sufficiently proven his claim and detailed the previous settlements and claims against the estate during the administrator's lengthy management.	The plaintiff, Orlin H. Gillett, argued that he has a rightful claim against the estate as the administrator. He asserted that after exhausting the personal assets available, he was entitled to seek payment for the amount owed to him in light of prior settled claims against the estate. He contended that his claim was valid and should be honored in accordance with the statutory provisions for estate administration.	Madison Y. Johnson, representing the heir’s interests, argued that the claim should not be allowed because Gillett had failed to show that the estate had been fully settled before filing his claim. Johnson sought to contest Gillett’s allegations and emphasized that the administrator had not presented sufficient formal judgments or processes to justify the legitimacy of the claim, asserting that the county court's rejection of the claim should stand.

The case "Asa D. Wright, Probate Justice of Menard County, for the Use, &c., Plaintiff in Error, v. John Bennett et al., Defendants in Error" took place in Illinois in December 1845. It stemmed from a previous ruling where Richard E. Bennett was convicted of being the father of an illegitimate child with Jane Davidson. He was ordered to pay $40 annually for seven years for the child's support, maintenance, and education, and had entered into a bond with his security, John Bennett. On June 8, 1844, Richard demanded custody of the child from the mother, who refused to surrender it. The defendants later claimed they offered Wright $3.55, the amount due under the bond, before the lawsuit was initiated. The case involved the interpretation of the relevant statute governing the maintenance of illegitimate children. The court had to decide if Richard was required to execute another bond to obtain custody and whether he would be discharged from his financial obligations if the mother refused to relinquish the child.	The plaintiff, Asa D. Wright, argued that Richard E. Bennett was in breach of the bond conditions by not making the required payments for the child's support. Wright maintained that a further bond with security was necessary before custody could be transferred from the mother to the father. The plaintiff requested that the court enforce the bond's terms and compel the defendants to fulfill their financial obligations toward the child.	The defendants, Richard E. Bennett and his security, John Bennett, contended that upon Richard's demand for custody of the child, and the mother's refusal to comply, he was released from any further obligations of payment under the bond. They argued that the statute only required one bond, which they had already provided, and that the law favored the father's right to custody once he demanded it.

In the case of **William M. Dorman et ux. v. L. C. Tost**, which was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1851, the origins trace back to the early 1800s. Christopher Robinson died intestate in 1819, leaving behind substantial real and personal estate. After a settlement with the Probate Court in 1826, it was revealed that the estate had a balance of $1,008.87 owed primarily to the Bank of Illinois. In January 1827, John Lane, who had connections to Robinson's estate through marriage to his widow, was authorized by the legislature to sell land to cover this debt. Lane sold parcels of land for $1,057; however, subsequent legal actions allowed Robinson's heir to reclaim this land through ejectment. After many years, in 1841, Lane was appointed administrator of the remaining estate and sought court permission to sell more land to settle old debts. The case was complicated by the absence of any current debts against the estate at the time of Lane's petition. Ultimately, legal proceedings determined that there was no justification for the land sale, as the previously owed debt had been paid and no other claims were made against the estate.	The plaintiffs, William M. Dorman and his wife, contended that the attempt by John Lane (and later L. C. Tost as administrator) to sell real estate was unjustified. They asserted that the original debts of the estate had been satisfied with the proceeds from past land sales. They argued that since there were no existing debts against the estate to necessitate the sale, the court should reject the administrator's petition and uphold their rights to the property in question.	The defendant, represented by L. C. Tost as administrator, argued that the sale of the real estate was necessary to settle the outstanding balance owed to John Lane personally, and that previous sales and settlements did not resolve the estate's obligations. The administrator sought approval for the sale of real property to ensure that any remaining debts could be paid, relying on previous endorsements to justify his actions.

In the case of Joseph Mills v. Charles C. Buffin, filed on February 9, 1883, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the dispute arose in Putnam County, Illinois, involving two key individuals: the plaintiff Joseph Mills and the defendant Charles C. Buffin. Mills initiated the lawsuit based on a quantum meruit claim, demanding compensation for work and labor he had performed. The defendant, Buffin, countered by asserting that Mills had breached an express contract to work for a specified term, quitting prematurely without just cause. Buffin presented evidence indicating that Mills’ departure was unjustified, citing the plaintiff’s slight illness as insufficient grounds for leaving. Mills defended his decision by explaining he had been unwell but anticipated returning to work immediately thereafter. Nevertheless, Buffin disputed the validity of Mills' stated reasons and attempted to present testimony to challenge Mills' reputation for truthfulness, which the court ultimately rejected as untimely. The court's admission of Mills’ medical excuse and refusal of Buffin's impeachment evidence were pivotal points of contention, leading to an examination of whether the initial judgment was appropriate.	Joseph Mills claimed compensation for labor performed based on a quantum meruit theory, arguing that he was entitled to payment for his work. He contended that his resignation was justifiable due to sickness. Mills sought a ruling that acknowledged his right to recover the value of his services rendered during his employment with Buffin.	Charles C. Buffin defended against Mills' claims by asserting that there was an express contract for a defined work term, which Mills breached by quitting without valid cause. Buffin argued that Mills' sickness was not continuously affecting him when he left and that any claims made regarding his illness did not justify abandoning the contract. Furthermore, Buffin sought to introduce evidence to diminish Mills' credibility, although this attempt was ultimately barred by the court.

In November 1866, the case of "James Sullivan v. Johanna Sullivan" was deliberated by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a legal dispute over the partition of property located in Cairo, Illinois. The action was initiated by Johanna Sullivan, the mother of Jeremiah Sullivan, who had passed away in May 1861. Jeremiah left behind no immediate family—no wife, child, or father—but did leave Johanna and several siblings as his only heirs. Johanna filed a petition for partition or, if necessary, for the sale of the property, asserting that her late son’s estate should be divided among his heirs. At the time of the filing, James Sullivan, one of the defendants, had not been served a summons, and a public notice was made only 59 days prior to the court term. A guardian ad litem was appointed for minor defendants whose names were not specifically mentioned. The case saw motions from both sides regarding the validity of the summons and the appointment of guardians. Chief Justice Walker presided over the matter and ultimately addressed procedural issues related to the adequacy of service, appointment of commissioners for partition, and the handling of the report regarding property division.	Johanna Sullivan contended that she and her siblings were entitled to specific shares of the deceased Jeremiah's estate, as they were his heirs. Her legal requests included the partition of the property or, alternatively, its sale under the statute should a partition not be feasible without causing harm to the parties involved.	James Sullivan argued that the court erred in rendering a decree before all defendants were properly before the court, emphasizing that he was not adequately served and that the publication notice was insufficient. He challenged the validity of the guardian ad litem appointment, citing a lack of proper identification of the minor defendants. Additionally, he contended that the commissioners appointed to oversee the partition acted without the required authority, as their actions preceded their formal appointment.

James M. Gooch filed a trespass action against John M. Tobias, claiming that Tobias destroyed certain goods belonging to him. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, and the events leading to the lawsuit took place in Clark County. The court proceedings concluded with a verdict favoring the defendant, John M. Tobias, after a motion for a new trial was overruled. The judge, Wall, P. J., noted that while circumstantial evidence is competent, the plaintiff was required to prove their case sufficiently for the jury to convict the defendant. The instructions given to the jury were deemed problematic, as they set a standard of proof higher than the law requires in civil cases, thereby potentially prejudicing the plaintiff’s position.	The plaintiff, James M. Gooch, argued that John M. Tobias unlawfully destroyed his goods and sought to hold him accountable for this alleged trespass. Gooch contended that the evidence presented should sufficiently satisfy the jury of Tobias's wrongdoing and requested that the jury find in his favor based on the circumstantial evidence available.	The defendant, John M. Tobias, maintained that there was insufficient evidence to prove his involvement in the destruction of Gooch’s goods. Tobias's defense hinged on jury instructions that emphasized the need for the plaintiff to meet a higher standard of proof to establish guilt, arguing that unless the jury was convinced by a preponderance of evidence, they should return a verdict of not guilty.

This case, "George Virgin v. William Gaither, Administrator," took place in Tazewell County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1866. William Gaither, as the administrator of the estate of the deceased Worthington Enslow, filed a trover action against George Virgin to recover certain horses, mares, and colts that were allegedly the property of Enslow prior to his death. The context of the situation involved Enslow enlisting in the army during the Civil War, at which time he instructed an acquaintance, Hynes, to deliver his horses to Virgin. Enslow wanted Virgin to care for the animals, promising compensation, and if Enslow did not return from the war, Virgin was to keep the horses as his own. After Enslow's death in the army, and with outstanding debts against his estate amounting to approximately $406, issues arose regarding the actual ownership of the horses. The Tazewell Circuit Court instructed that the administrator had the right to claim all personal property of the deceased unless there was evidence of a valid gift to Virgin. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Gaither, the plaintiff, awarding him $500 for the animals in question, despite Virgin claiming ownership through the gift.	The plaintiff, William Gaither, asserted that the horses belonged to Worthington Enslow at the time of his death, and as the administrator of the estate, he had the legal right to reclaim them. He argued that the horses were essential assets of the estate that should be returned to satisfy creditor claims. Gaither maintained that any alleged gift from Enslow to Virgin was invalid under the circumstances, particularly given the existence of creditors and the estate's debts.	George Virgin contended that the horses were gifted to him by Worthington Enslow, which he believed was a valid transfer of property made in anticipation of possible death during the war. Virgin claimed that there was no intention for the gift to be contingent upon Enslow's return, and he argued that Gaither's claim disregarded the validity of the gift considering Enslow’s intentions. Virgin emphasized that the horses should remain with him as part of the inheritance from Enslow.

This case, Addie Rothschild v. Charles J. Bruscke et al., was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 21, 1890. It originated from an action of assumpsit filed on May 14, 1887, in the Superior Court of Cook County. The plaintiffs, initially S. Kuhn & Sons, were bankers who had discounted a note for $1000 signed by the defendants under the firm name of Bruscke & Bicke on December 23, 1886. After discounting the note in February 1887, S. Kuhn & Sons demanded payment from the endorser, Addie Rothschild, in March 1888, and received $1066.81 from her. Subsequently, the plaintiffs transferred the note to Rothschild and sought to continue the suit in her name. The case proceeded with Rothschild as the plaintiff after the defendants filed several pleas. The trial was heard without a jury, resulting in a judgment favoring the defendants. This judgment was later affirmed by the Appellate Court.	Addie Rothschild's main argument was that she owned the note and was entitled to collect the $1000 from the defendants. She claimed that the defendants could not assert any defenses related to Rothschild & Sons and sought the court to exclude the defendants' testimony attempting to demonstrate their defenses, particularly their assertion that Rothschild & Sons owned the note in question.	The defendants argued that Addie Rothschild was merely a nominal plaintiff and that the actual ownership of the note was with R. Rothschild & Sons. They filed a plea of set-off claiming that Rothschild & Sons owed them substantial sums on several promissory notes, and thus, they were entitled to offset this debt against the claim brought by Rothschild regarding the $1000 note.

In the case of Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Ry. Co. v. Pauly, the events unfolded in 1886 in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, Pauly, brought an action against the defendant, Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company, following an incident where Pauly’s horses and harness were injured while crossing the railway tracks at a public street intersection on 55th Street. The plaintiff alleged that the injury resulted from the negligence of the railway company, specifically its agents and servants. During the trial, evidence was presented aiming to establish negligence on the part of the defendant; however, this was contested by the defendant, who argued that the driver of Pauly's team was not exercising ordinary care at the time of the accident. The jury was instructed to consider if the railway company’s flagman, who was supposed to give warnings of oncoming trains, was absent or negligent in their duties during the incident. The court eventually found issue with the jury instruction provided, stating it did not adequately consider the driver's conduct regarding care. The case concluded when the appellate court reversed the judgment and remanded the case for further consideration.	The plaintiff, Pauly, claimed damages amounting to one hundred and eighty dollars for the injury to his horses and harness, which he attributed to the negligent actions of the railway company. He argued that the company failed to provide a flagman at a crucial intersection to warn of approaching trains, which was necessary for the safe operation of the railway. The plaintiff sought a jury instruction that would hold the railway company accountable for this negligence if it was determined that their failure to provide adequate warning directly caused his damages.	The defendant, Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company, countered the claims by contesting the evidence of negligence and claiming that the driver of Pauly's team may not have been exercising ordinary care. They argued that the driver’s conduct should be scrutinized, suggesting that the plaintiff bore some responsibility for the accident. Additionally, the defendant claimed that the jury instruction given by the trial court was flawed and did not properly address the critical issue of the driver's care during the incident.

Dick H. Phelps filed a lawsuit against Joseph McGee concerning a contract for the sale of corn. The contract, dated June 23, 1854, stipulated that Phelps would sell five thousand bushels of corn to McGee, to be delivered at Point Isabel, Illinois, on or before August 15, 1854. The contract specified that McGee would pay thirty-four cents per bushel and would incur storage fees if the corn was not taken on time. The case took place in Cass County, Illinois, where Phelps resided. McGee, while residing in Fulton County, contended that the lawsuit should not proceed in Cass County. The legal dispute revolved around whether the contract was executed and the cause of action accrued in Cass County, allowing Phelps to sue there. Ultimately, after a trial where evidence was presented regarding the execution of the contract, the jury found in favor of Phelps for damages, determining he was owed $1,131. The defendant appealed this judgment.	Phelps argued that he had fulfilled the contractual obligations to sell corn to McGee. He claimed damages resulting from McGee's refusal to accept delivery of the remaining corn, which was in breach of their contract. Phelps contended that the action was properly brought in Cass County because the contract was made there and the cause of action arose from that contract. Moreover, he asserted that he had made a demand for delivery of the remaining corn and was willing to pay the agreed storage fees.	McGee’s defense hinged on the argument that the lawsuit should not have proceeded in Cass County, as he resided in Fulton County, and therefore claimed that he could not be sued there. He pointed out that the contract did not explicitly obligate him to accept delivery in Cass County. Additionally, McGee contended that Phelps did not suffer damages as claimed, asserting that he had delivered much of the ordered corn prior to the lawsuit and argued that any demand made after the contract's delivery date did not constitute a breach.

In 1843, Thomas Culbertson sold a barrel of whiskey on the wharf in Galena, Illinois, without possessing the necessary license to vend or retail merchandise. Subsequently, the City of Galena pursued legal action against him, claiming he had violated a city ordinance prohibiting unlicensed sales. Initially, the case was brought before R. F. Barry, a justice of the peace for Jo Daviess County. However, Culbertson appealed the case to the Circuit Court, arguing that Barry had not properly filed the required bond to legally act in his capacity as a justice of the peace. The court denied this motion. During the trial, the jury found Culbertson guilty and awarded a judgment against him amounting to twenty dollars. Culbertson subsequently sought a new trial and raised legal objections, which were also dismissed by the court. The case was marked by debates over the authority of the justice and the sufficiency of the evidence presented.	The City of Galena, as the plaintiff, claimed that Thomas Culbertson had violated a city ordinance by selling whiskey without a license. The city sought to recover a penalty for this purported violation, arguing that the ordinance prohibited unlicensed sales within its jurisdiction. The evidence presented at trial included testimony about Culbertson's sale and the assertion that he was subject to the penalties outlined in the ordinance.	Thomas Culbertson, the defendant, contended that the judgment against him was unfounded because the justice of the peace, R. F. Barry, was not legally authorized to preside over the case due to the absence of a filed bond. He argued that the trial was flawed as there was no clear evidence proving that he had violated the city ordinance, and hence the verdict was unsupported. Culbertson requested the court to dismiss the ruling and reverse the judgment, asserting that the legal foundations of the trial were invalid.

In 1884, the case of The People, for use of Christian County, v. Henry Davis took place in Christian County, Illinois, presided over by Judge Jesse J. Phillips. The action was initiated to recover delinquent taxes from Henry Davis, who, on May 1, 1875, was alleged to be the owner of substantial personal property, including moneys and credits, controlled by his agent, Henry D. Davis, in Taylorville. The county assessor requested Henry D. Davis to provide a statement of this property for taxation, but he refused. Consequently, the assessor estimated the property's value at $142,707, leading to a total personal property tax of $2,554.67 for the year 1875. The town collector attempted to collect this amount but reported it as delinquent due to the absence of Davis's personal property. Over the years, the tax continued to accrue, and the county collector made efforts to attach the tax debts to real property owned by Davis in Mosquito Township. Despite multiple court judgments against Davis's land for unpaid taxes, he never paid the amounts assessed or any part thereof, prompting the People to seek legal action to recover the owed taxes.	The plaintiff, representing Christian County, contended that Henry Davis failed to pay delinquent taxes totaling $3,804.50, which had been lawfully assessed against his personal property and subsequently attached to his real estate. They argued that the defendant was liable for these taxes due to his ownership of the property and that his refusal to settle the debt justified the action taken.	The defendant, Henry Davis, contended that the plaintiff's claims were invalid due to a lack of proper legal foundation in the complaint. He argued that the plaintiff failed to adequately demonstrate his residence at the location where the property was assessed and that the taxation was improper as it did not sufficiently prove that he had actual control of the property at that location, thus invalidating the tax claims made against him.

On January 8, 1876, bonds amounting to $15,000 were issued by the town of Honey Creek in Crawford County, Illinois, to the Paris and Danville Railroad Company. These bonds were set to pay interest at a rate of ten percent per annum, with annual payments beginning on January 1 of the following year. On March 14, 1881, a decree was entered in the circuit court of Crawford County, declaring the bonds void in a case brought by tax-payers led by George H. Maxwell against the county collector. The court issued a perpetual injunction prohibiting the collection of taxes from these tax-payers to pay the bond interest. Notably, the bondholders were not made parties to this case. Subsequently, on March 4, 1882, a bondholder named Preston obtained a judgment in a Federal court against the town of Honey Creek regarding certain bond coupons. He petitioned for a mandamus against the county collector to collect taxes necessary for bond interest. The county court denied the collector's request for judgment on these taxes due to the previous injunction. The collector appealed, claiming the court erred.	The plaintiffs, led by George H. Maxwell, claimed that the bonds were void and that taxes levied for their interest payment should not be collected. They argued that the county court's injunction against tax collection was valid and binding on the county collector.	The county collector, Isaac D. Mail, contended that the county court erred in refusing to grant a judgment for the collection of taxes, asserting that the Federal court's mandamus should take precedence. He argued that the bondholders were not parties to the prior injunction and should not be protected by it.

In 1869, a group of grain dealers in Rochelle, Illinois, entered into a written agreement for a partnership to control the grain trade, named Richard C. Craft, E. P. Sexton, Dr. John McConoughy, C. B. Boyce, and William Wiswell. The contract outlined arrangements for each firm to conduct business independently while sharing profits according to their respective shares. Following the death of one of the partners, John McConoughy, his son, James O. McConoughy, took his place under the agreement by mutual consent. However, the nature of the contract soon became questionable, as it facilitated a secret collaboration among the parties, effectively eliminating competition in the market. The firms controlled all warehouses and coordinated prices and operations in clandestine meetings. This arrangement, while appearing as separate businesses to the public, was deemed a conspiracy to monopolize the grain trade, raising concerns over its legality under public policy. The case ultimately raised two legal questions regarding the contract's validity due to potential restraint of trade and whether a court of equity could enforce any accounting of profits from an illegal contract.	The plaintiff, James O. McConoughy, argued for accounting and distribution of the profits derived from the partnership. His claims were based on the assertion that the contract, despite its alleged illegality, should be honored, as he believed the partnership operated on mutual consent and expectation of profit-sharing, especially after his father's passing.	The defendants, including Richard C. Craft and others, countered the claims by asserting that the contract was fundamentally unlawful and in restraint of trade, which rendered it void under public policy. They contended that the formation of the partnership had effectively suppressed competition, contravening legal principles. Furthermore, they argued that a court of equity should not assist in distributing profits from an illegal agreement since all parties were equally complicit in the unlawful combination.

John Nelson v. Ole M. Oren is a legal case that took place in April 1866 in Chicago, Illinois. The case originated from an action of covenant initiated by Ole M. Oren, the assignee of a lease, against John Nelson, the assignor of that lease. Oren had entered into a lease agreement with the original lessor, Gillmore, starting on April 1, 1861, and extending for five years. On March 24, 1864, Nelson assigned this lease to Oren for a payment of fifty dollars, with a written agreement that he would deliver possession of the premises by May 1, 1864. However, when Oren demanded possession on the due date, Nelson informed him that a barber was still occupying the premises and could not vacate until several days later. Oren, unable to take possession as agreed, sought an alternative arrangement with Gillmore, who then allowed Oren to lease directly from him. After some delay, Oren moved into the premises under this new lease. The case culminated in a judgment against Nelson for fifty dollars, which he appealed, arguing that he should not be held liable for damages since he offered to deliver the premises shortly after the assigned date.	Ole M. Oren claimed that John Nelson failed to deliver possession of the leased premises on the agreed date of May 1, 1864. He argued that Nelson’s breach of the contract caused him trouble and financial inconvenience, specifically related to his shoe-making business that he intended to operate from those premises. Oren requested damages for the delay in possession.	John Nelson contended that he should not be liable for the full amount paid by Oren because the delivery of possession was a separate part of the covenant. He argued that once the lease was assigned, Oren had already received part of the consideration (the right to occupy the premises), and thus the obligation to deliver possession by May 1 was not a condition precedent for Oren to recover the money. Nelson also offered a pro-rated compensation for the delay and argued against the interpretation of the covenant as one entire agreement dependent on possession delivery.

William Maxwell filed a legal case against William D. Vansant in September 1867 in Illinois, specifically in the Circuit Court of Marshall County. The case emerged from a dispute involving promissory notes that were assigned to Maxwell, who resided in Marshall County. Vansant, the original signer of the notes, lived in La Salle County, which becomes significant in terms of jurisdiction. The legal action was initiated with a process sent from Marshall County to La Salle County for service on Vansant. The defendant challenged the court's jurisdiction, resulting in a trial where the court ruled in favor of Vansant. This ruling was based on the court’s opinion that the Circuit Court of Marshall County did not have the jurisdiction to send the summons into La Salle County where the defendant lived, based on past precedents concerning similar cases involving jurisdiction and the assignment of notes.	The plaintiff, William Maxwell, claimed that as the assignee of certain promissory notes, he was entitled to enforce the notes against the defendant, William D. Vansant. Maxwell argued that the process was properly initiated by sending the summons to the appropriate county. He sought to overturn the judgment made in the lower court that favored the defendant, asserting that the defendant's plea in abatement regarding jurisdiction was not valid.	William D. Vansant contended that the Circuit Court of Marshall County lacked the jurisdiction to serve process in La Salle County where he resided. He argued that the notes in question were executed and endorsed in La Salle County, and therefore, the Marshall County court could not lawfully send its summons outside its jurisdiction. The defendant requested that the court uphold the judgment of the lower court, which found in his favor based on these jurisdictional grounds.

In December 1872, attorney John S. Davis entrusted Isaac N. Bassett and James H. Connell with four promissory notes for collection against Allen W. Bratton and William H. Loman. On February 24, 1873, the attorneys filed a lawsuit in the Mercer Circuit Court to collect on the notes, simultaneously seeking a writ of attachment against Bratton's property. While Bassett was in California, Connell filed a petition for a writ of ne exeat against Bratton, which was later approved by the master in chancery. A bond was posted, leading to Bratton’s arrest on March 7, 1873. He was held in jail until he could secure a bond. Ultimately, on April 15, 1873, judgment was entered against Bratton, leading to a series of appeals and further legal proceedings. On August 1874, Bratton initiated a malicious prosecution suit against Bassett and Connell, which resulted in a verdict favoring him on one count, although he was unsuccessful on others.	The plaintiffs, Bassett and Connell, faced claims of malicious prosecution, alleging their wrongful role in Bratton's arrest and imprisonment under the writ of ne exeat. They contended that the arrest was made without sufficient grounds, and thus sought damages for the unlawful conduct.	The defendants argued that they were not liable for trespass because the writ of ne exeat was issued under the authority of a master in chancery, who had jurisdiction over the issuance of such a writ. They maintained that the legal process had been correctly followed, and any errors made had to do with the merits of the allegations presented, not jurisdiction.

In June 1870, the case of Charles Freeman et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Monroe Circuit Court. The case involved a debt action initiated by Cordelia A. Merriman against Charles Freeman and others, where the claimed amount was $500, stemming from a bastardy bond with the same penalty. The defendants were served with legal process but failed to respond appropriately, resulting in a default judgment against them. The trial court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding her $500 for the debt and an additional $17.50 for damages. However, this judgment was challenged by the defendants upon appeal, arguing that the judgment was erroneous due to its failure to conform to established legal practices regarding penal bonds.	The plaintiff, Cordelia A. Merriman, claimed that the defendants owed her a total of $517.50, which consisted of a $500 debt from the bastardy bond and $17.50 in damages. She sought the court's enforcement of this judgment, arguing that the amount awarded was correct based on the bond's penalty and the defendants' default in responding to the claims.	The defendants contended that the judgment was erroneous for allowing recovery of both the debt and damages, which violated established practices regarding penal bonds. They argued that the plaintiffs should only receive the penalty amount as the debt, and any damages should not exceed that sum. The defendants appealed the judgment, seeking a reversal based on this legal principle.

John C. Schnebly and other heirs of Henry Schnebly initiated a legal case against Elizabeth M. Schnebly, the widow of Henry Schnebly, after his death on August 4, 1858. The case was brought before the Peoria Circuit Court in Illinois, where the plaintiffs sought a legal assignment of the widow’s dower in the deceased’s estate. Henry, prior to his death, held certain lands in fee simple, and Elizabeth renounced her claims under his will to claim dower instead. After the court appointed commissioners to assign her dower, a report was generated. This report allotted her a fractional interest in specific tracts of land, including their homestead. The plaintiffs contested this report, leading to further judicial proceedings regarding the legality of the dower assignment based on statutory provisions regarding unimproved and improved lands.	The plaintiffs claimed that the assignment of dower to Elizabeth M. Schnebly was improper because it included unimproved and wild lands, which they argued were not subject to dower under Illinois law. They further contended that the commission's report failed to equitably assign the widow's dower across all applicable properties, arguing that the division should reflect one-third of the total property value rather than only the tracts they designated.	The defendant, Elizabeth M. Schnebly, defended the assignment of dower by asserting that she was entitled to her dower rights in both improved and unimproved lands as stipulated by the relevant statutes. She acknowledged the commissioners' report and sought to uphold their assessment of dower, emphasizing the statutory framework which supports the provision of dower regardless of the property's condition at the time of the husband's death.

In September 1871, the case of The People of the State of Illinois v. Ezekiel H. Palmer was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The proceedings took place against the backdrop of allegations concerning the conduct of Ezekiel H. Palmer, a practicing attorney. The allegations included gross mismanagement of funds belonging to clients, primarily involving three individuals: McAboy, Forhner, and Richards. Palmer had been entrusted with significant sums of money and notes for collection, which he failed to return or account for appropriately. Over a span of five years, he collected money on behalf of McAboy but delayed payment, ultimately forcing McAboy to litigate to recover the owed amount. Similarly, Palmer retained funds collected for Forhner and Richards for extended periods without settling their accounts, making it necessary for them to pursue legal action. The court examined the evidence showcasing Palmer’s refusal to return collected funds and documents, revealing patterns of evasion and deceit. Palmer's claim of doubt regarding clients’ requests was perceived as a tactic to avoid fulfilling his professional obligations.	The People of the State of Illinois claimed that Ezekiel H. Palmer exhibited misconduct in his capacity as an attorney by failing to pay over collected funds to his clients, thus breaching the trust inherent in the attorney-client relationship. They argued that his actions were not just unethical but violated statutory duties that warranted disciplinary measures. The state's attorney sought to have Palmer's name stricken from the roll of attorneys due to his clear malfeasance and neglect of professional responsibilities.	Ezekiel H. Palmer's defense rested on questioning the legitimacy of the claims made against him. He argued that he did not recognize the signature on the demand letters from Forhner's legal representatives, which he proposed as a reasonable doubt. Palmer also presented a narrative involving the misplacing of a draft belonging to Richards as an excuse for his failure to return the funds. He contended that any disagreements regarding the amounts owed were honest differences in interpretation of his obligations.

In 1856, in Stephenson County, Illinois, Thomas F. Goodhue, the appellant, was involved in a legal dispute with Frederic Baker, the appellee, concerning the ownership of Lot 5, Block 14, in Freeport. The action of ejectment commenced on September 12, 1856, after Goodhue had reportedly built a house on the property in 1848 and lived there since around 1849 or 1850. The lawsuit moved to Jo Daviess County due to a change of venue and was tried on March 11, 1858. The jury ultimately returned a verdict favoring Baker, indicating that Goodhue was unlawfully withholding the property. Goodhue sought a new trial, claiming that the evidence was insufficient to establish that he was in possession of the property when the suit began. He also challenged the jury's verdict as insufficient to warrant a judgment, but both of his motions were overruled by the court.	Frederic Baker, the appellee, claimed that Thomas F. Goodhue was unlawfully withholding the property from him. His key argument centered on establishing the legitimacy of his ownership and possession rights over Lot 5 in Block 14, Freeport. Baker sought to have the court confirm his estate in fee over the disputed lot through the action of ejectment.	Thomas F. Goodhue, the appellant, contended that the evidence presented did not prove he was out of possession at the time the lawsuit commenced. He argued that the jury's verdict was insufficient to support a judgment against him and motioned for a new trial on both common law grounds and statutory provisions, claiming errors in the trial process and in the verdict delivered by the jury.

The case, "Leah Martin et al. v. William Hargardine," took place in January 1868, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal dispute arose following the execution of a mortgage by Christopher Orenduff, who, during his lifetime, mistakenly described the north-east quarter of a certain section in the mortgage instead of the intended south-east quarter. After Orenduff's death, Hargardine, the purchaser of the property, filed a bill in chancery against Orenduff's widow and minor heirs to correct the alleged mistake and demanded the sale of the land. The court took the case pro confesso against the widow, leading to the appointment of a guardian ad litem for the heirs, ultimately resulting in a decree to correct the mortgage and order the sale of the property, while also attempting to cut off the widow's dower rights. The widow and heirs later contested this ruling, leading them to pursue a writ of error, claiming deficiencies in the service of summons and the absence of proof of release of dower.	The plaintiffs, Leah Martin et al., argued primarily that the sheriff’s service of summons was inadequate, as it indicated only one copy was served upon all defendants. They contended that the record did not contain sufficient evidence regarding the proceedings and that the lands had been sold as a lump sum without following appropriate procedures. They maintained there was no valid relinquishment of dower by Leah Orenduff, which was essential for the legitimacy of the decree concerning her rights.	The defendant, William Hargardine, defended against the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that the sheriff's return indicated adequate service to all defendants, since he documented serving a true copy to each individual named. Hargardine argued that the court had sufficient evidence and that the land was appropriately sold as a whole after a failed offer of separate parcels. He insisted that the legal requirements for correcting the mortgage had been satisfied and that any errors regarding acknowledgment of dower were non-fatal to the overall ruling regarding the heirs.

The case of Mary Ann Sisk v. John H. Smith revolved around the application filed in December 1844 by John H. Smith, the administrator of the estate of Absalom H. Sisk, who had passed away.
