The court proceedings took place in Pope County, Illinois, where Smith sought judicial approval for the sale of Mary Ann Sisk's dower interest in her deceased husband’s lands to satisfy his debts. Mary Ann, as the widow and relict, contested the legal right of the administrator to obtain such an order, arguing that her claim to dower should not be subordinated to the payment of her husband's debts. Initially, her challenge to the petition was overruled, leading her to seek a writ of error in the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal inquiry involved understanding the nature of dower rights under common law and whether the widow’s claim could be legally defeated by her husband's debts, against the backdrop of statutory provisions that aim to protect her entitlement.	Mary Ann Sisk, the plaintiff, asserted that her legal entitlement to dower in her deceased husband's lands should not be challenged or sold off for the payment of his debts. She claimed that her right to a third of the estate, established under common law, was sacrosanct and should be preserved, irrespective of her husband's financial obligations. She requested that the court reverse the order permitting the sale of her dower and recognize her legal rights as a widow.	John H. Smith, representing the estate, contended that the court had the authority to order the sale of Mary Ann's dower interest to satisfy her husband’s debts. He argued that the statutory provisions allowed for the sale of a deceased's property under certain conditions, which included settling outstanding debts. Thus, he sought to affirm the lower court's decision allowing the sale of the dower.

In 1873, the case of The Town of Lake View v. The Rose Hill Cemetery Company took place in Lake View, Illinois, located near the lake shore and approximately seven miles north of Chicago. The Rose Hill Cemetery Company was established in 1859, authorized to acquire land for cemetery purposes up to 500 acres. The town's authorities had previously enacted an ordinance and subsequent legislation that prohibited the cemetery company from using certain lands for burial, claiming these lands fell outside the defined cemetery boundaries. The dispute arose over whether the state could restrict the cemetery company's use of its chartered lands. The town maintained that the legislation was a necessary exercise of the police power to protect public health and welfare, while the cemetery company argued that the law constituted an unconstitutional impairment of their rights under the charter.	The plaintiff, Town of Lake View, claimed that the Rose Hill Cemetery Company's use of lands for burial purposes was in violation of state law and public health regulations. They argued that the compliance with the 1869 legislation, which restricted the cemetery's boundaries, was essential for the comfort and welfare of the community and maintained that the state had the authority to impose such restrictions under its police power.	The defendant, Rose Hill Cemetery Company, contended that the legislation prohibiting the use of their lands for burial constituted an arbitrary infringement of their charter rights, which had been granted by the state. They argued that there was no evidence that their operations constituted a nuisance or affected the health of the community and asserted that the state lacked the authority to revoke or impair their contractual rights without due compensation.

The case "Prentiss D. Cheney et al. v. Frederick H. Teese et al." was filed on January 19, 1884, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The matter revolves around the will of Edward A. D'Arcy, who died on April 25, 1863, leaving two daughters, Ann Caroline D. Teese and Catherine M. Cheney, and a provision in his will that grants a fee simple of his lands in Christian County, Illinois, to his grandchildren, born of these daughters. Each daughter was given a life estate with the understanding that they would enjoy the land until their death, after which the grandchildren would take possession. The dispute arose when Mrs. Cheney passed away on April 23, 1877. Following her death, her husband, Prentiss D. Cheney, and son, Alexander M. Cheney, sought to establish their right to the land, which they claimed should pass to them for five years after Mrs. Cheney's death and then would go to Mrs. Teese for her remaining lifetime. Mrs. Teese, however, claimed the right to use all the lands. This disagreement over the rights to the land led to an appeal from the circuit court's decree, which initially ruled in favor of Mrs. Teese.	The plaintiffs, Prentiss D. Cheney and Alexander M. Cheney, assert their right to the enjoyment of half of the lands allocated to Mrs. Cheney after her passing. They argue that the will's provisions regarding the use and possession of the land should allow them access to their deceased mother’s share for five years following her death. They aim for a court interpretation that would affirm their claims as heirs to Mrs. Cheney's estate.	The defendants, Frederick H. Teese and Ann Caroline Teese, contend that the will established a right of survivorship between the two daughters, meaning that upon the death of Mrs. Cheney, her rights to the property automatically transferred to Mrs. Teese. They argue that the grandchildren have only a contingent remainder and counter the claim that the plaintiffs have any rights to the property during the asserted five-year period after Mrs. Cheney's death.

In the case of Oscar N. Case v. A. B. Lyman, the legal proceedings took place in September 1872 in Kankakee County, Illinois. Oscar N. Case, the plaintiff, issued a promissory note dated April 24, 1868, promising to pay $75 to C.D. Roberts, who was the agent of the Clough Refining Company, and this note was subsequently endorsed to A. B. Lyman. The case revolved around the validity of the note and whether Lyman had the right to collect the payment. Evidence presented indicated that the patent associated with the note for refining sugar was considered worthless, raising questions about the legitimacy of the claims made by Lyman. The matter of who Lyman truly represented—whether he was an agent for the company or had a separate claim—was central to the case. The court faced disputes over the admissibility of correspondence related to the case and the status of Lyman’s authority in dealing with the note. Ultimately, the decision hinged on whether evidence affirming Lyman's agency could be admitted, which the court controversially denied.	The plaintiff, A. B. Lyman, contended that he was entitled to enforce the promissory note originally drawn by Oscar N. Case. He argued that the note was valid and should be paid despite the claim that the underlying patent was worthless. Lyman requested that the court uphold the validity of the note and grant judgment in his favor against the defendant for the amount specified in the note.	The defendant, Oscar N. Case, presented several defenses asserting that the note was invalid due to factors such as its endorsement after maturity and that it was executed under the condition that the Clough Refining Company successfully delivered on the promised patent right, which they failed to do. Case argued that Lyman was merely acting as an agent for the company and that the real party in interest was the company itself, thus claiming that Lyman had no rights to the note’s enforcement given the failure of consideration.

In December 1832, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Peter Menard, Jr. against Joseph Marks, who was the administrator of George Love, deceased. The legal dispute originated from a scire facias issued by Menard to foreclose a mortgage held against the property of Love, who had passed away. The proceedings took place in the Peoria Circuit Court, where Menard sought to enforce his mortgage rights under the statute established on January 17, 1825, which allowed for such actions. After Love's death, Marks pleaded in abatement, arguing that the scire facias was issued within one year of Love's demise, which he claimed was in violation of the legal framework governing the administration of estates. The Circuit Court agreed with Marks, leading to a judgment that quashed the scire facias. Menard then sought to reverse this decision in the Illinois Supreme Court, bringing the case to this higher court for review.	Peter Menard Jr., the plaintiff, argued that the issuance of the scire facias to foreclose on the mortgage was a valid proceeding that should not be delayed until after the one-year period following Love's death. He contended that the law allowed him to pursue foreclosure since a mortgage provides a specific lien on the property, which should not be affected by the insolvency status of the decedent's estate. Menard sought a reversal of the Circuit Court's judgment to allow the foreclosure proceedings to continue.	Joseph Marks, as the administrator of George Love's estate, defended by asserting that the scire facias was improperly issued within one year of Love's death, referencing the statute that aims to protect administrational proceedings during this timeframe. He maintained that the foreclosure must be delayed until the one-year period had lapsed, thereby preventing Menard from pursuing his claim against Love's estate until that time had passed.

In January 1871, the case of Lewis Riggs v. Richard Henneberry took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered around a quarter section of land that was owned by Richard Henneberry, who held the paramount title granted by the government and was in actual possession of the land. Subsequently, Richard Henneberry’s co-defendant, John Paine, and others with only color of title unlawfully entered upon the land, claiming rights as trespassers. Riggs, the rightful owner, initiated actions of ejectment against the trespassers, contending that their entry was unlawful despite their claims of having paid taxes on the land for seven years while it was unoccupied. The circuit court ruled in favor of Riggs, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiff, Lewis Riggs, argued that he was the rightful owner of the land based on his actual possession and legal title. He maintained that the defendants, having only color of title and having trespassed on his property, could not use the statute of limitations as a defense. Riggs sought the court’s protection against the unlawful entry and requested a judgment for ejectment to restore his rightful possession of the land.	The defendants, Richard Henneberry and John Paine, claimed that their payment of taxes on the land for seven years constituted a colorable title and argued that this gave them a legal basis to defend their possession. They contended that the plaintiff's appropriate remedy should be an action for forcible entry and detainer rather than ejectment. Their defense rested on the assertion that their entry, though considered unlawful, should be protected under the statute of limitations by virtue of their payment of taxes.

The case "Indiana, Bloomington & Western Railway Company v. Henry Craig" occurred in McLean County, Illinois, following an incident on March 17, 1883. The plaintiff, Henry Craig, alleged that a stack of hay owned by him was burned by sparks from a locomotive associated with the Indiana, Bloomington & Western Railway Company, which was drawing a passenger train at the time. The fire originated in a field belonging to Mr. Long before spreading to Craig's property where the haystack was located. Although no witnesses saw the fire start, the evidence suggested it began outside the railway's right of way.  The circuit court initially ruled in favor of Craig, accepting that the sparks from the locomotive had caused the fire. However, the railway company contended that it had taken necessary precautions to prevent such incidents, as demonstrated by the maintenance and functioning of their smoke stack and spark arrester. Their engineer was described as experienced and capable of managing the locomotive safely.  Case proceedings ultimately led to an appeal hearing on February 5, 1884, with the appellate court ultimately considering whether the initial verdict against the railway company should stand or whether it should be overturned based on the evidence presented.	Henry Craig claimed that the railway company was liable for the destruction of his haystack due to negligence, asserting that the sparks emitted from their locomotive directly caused the fire. He sought compensation for the value of the burned hay, relying on a statutory presumption of negligence due to the fire being started by the locomotive’s sparks.	The Indiana, Bloomington & Western Railway Company argued that they had implemented all necessary safety measures to prevent such an incident, including equipping their locomotive with established spark arresting appliances. They provided evidence demonstrating that the smoke stack was in good condition, having undergone inspections immediately before and after the incident. Additionally, they emphasized that their engineer was competent and fulfilled his duties properly, seeking a reversal of the trial court's judgment favoring the plaintiff based on a lack of evidence supporting negligence.

The case of "The Ottawa, Oswego and Fox River Valley Railroad Company v. Jacob P. Black et al." was decided in September 1875 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case revolves around a contract dated October 3, 1867, in which Jacob P. Black and F. A. Black promised to pay the Ottawa, Oswego and Fox River Valley Railroad Company $3,000 upon the completion of rail construction from Wenona to Yorkville, Illinois. The payments were to be made in installments with accrued interest, and upon full payment, the railroad was to issue stock certificates corresponding to the amount paid. The plaintiffs claimed that the Blacks failed to pay the pledged sum. The defense presented by the Blacks hinged on allegations that the railroad company failed to fulfill its obligations stipulated in the contract, especially indicating that the construction of the railroad was not completed as required. An important aspect of the defense was the claim that the company had transferred part of its railroad ownership to another entity, thus nullifying the agreed conditions for payment.	The plaintiff, Ottawa, Oswego and Fox River Valley Railroad Company, argued that the Blacks were obligated to pay the $3,000 promissory note based on the construction agreement. They asserted that the consideration for the note was valid and that the obligations outlined in the contract were not fulfilled by the defendants, and thus they sought recovery of the owed amount along with interest.	The defendants, Jacob P. Black et al., countered by claiming that the consideration for the note had failed. They asserted that the railroad never completed the project from Wenona to Yorkville as required and that the company's actions—including the sale of part of the railroad to another company—had significantly devalued their stock and rendered it worthless, thus constituting a failure of consideration. They argued that this meant their obligation to pay the noted sum was void.

Moses Deere v. Isaac Cole et al. is a legal case from the Illinois Supreme Court decided on October 6, 1886. The case arose in Sidney, Champaign County, Illinois, where Moses Deere owned the southwest quarter and the west half of the southeast quarter of section 4. Deere filed a bill in equity against the commissioners of highways of the town of Sidney, seeking to prevent them from opening a highway that they had laid out, arguing that the proposed road deviated from the authorized section line. The highway in question was supposed to run from the northeast corner of the west half of the northwest quarter of section 10 and intersect another road located between sections 4 and 5, and sections 8 and 9. Deere claimed that the highway was incorrectly surveyed and was being opened on his neighboring land rather than on the designated section line. The dispute focused on the exact location of the western terminus of the road, which involved conflicting evidence regarding a lost corner landmark crucial for proper land demarcation. After a hearing in the circuit court, the court found in favor of the defendants (the commissioners) and dismissed Deere's case. This decision was later upheld by the Appellate Court.	Moses Deere's main argument was that the highway being opened by the commissioners was not on the properly designated section line, as mandated by the petition and survey documents. He sought an injunction to stop the commissioners from proceeding with the opening of the highway, claiming they were encroaching on his land by surveying north of the established section line. Deere contended that the petition and ensuing survey specified the road should only be opened along the section line and that any deviation constituted an illegal taking of property.	The defendants, represented by the commissioners of highways, argued that the road was indeed located on the section line as per the survey and that the lands they entered were correctly identified as within that line. They maintained that they acted within their authority as outlined in the original petition and survey. The commissioners contended that recognizing Deere's claims would disrupt the valid establishment of the highway, and they requested the court to affirm the validity of their actions and dismiss Deere's bill.

In 1856, an action of ejectment was initiated in the Circuit Court of Marshall County, Illinois, between James A. Smith (the defendant) and William Rankin (the plaintiff). The dispute centered around the N.E. quarter of section No. 19, township 13 N., range 9 E. of the 4th Principal Meridian. The case arose from conflicting claims to the land, with Rankin claiming possession through a series of ancient deeds dated 1819 and 1825, while Smith had taken possession and erected a house after throwing Rankin's lumber off the property. The court faced issues about the admissibility of the ancient deeds without sufficient evidence of their execution and possession. The court ultimately ruled on the merits of the evidence presented regarding these deeds and their validity.	William Rankin, the plaintiff, argued that he had a legitimate claim to the land based on two ancient deeds. He sought to prove ownership by introducing the deeds without sufficient proof of their execution, arguing they were ancient documents over thirty years old and therefore presumed genuine. He further claimed that he had taken initial possession of the land and intended to build a house thereon.	James A. Smith, the defendant, contested the admissibility of the deeds cited by Rankin. He argued that the deeds failed to meet legal standards for ancient deeds, lacking proper acknowledgment and recording, especially the 1825 deed, which had no subscribing witness and was recorded after a significant delay. Smith maintained that he recognized Rankin's claim and had taken possession of the land based on a different deed obtained from Lombard. Therefore, he sought dismissal of Rankin's claims based on the flaws in the evidence presented.

In 1868, in Scotland Township, McDonough County, Illinois, Andrew Allison and John Allison petitioned for the establishment of a public highway. The petition was posted on May 8, 1868, and officially filed with the town clerk on August 22, 1868, the same day that the commissioners of highways filed their order to establish the road. After the order's filing, a writ of certiorari was granted by the circuit court in response to the Allisons' petition, aimed at reviewing the commissioners' actions. However, the defendants, the commissioners, filed a motion to quash the writ, which the circuit court denied. Following a hearing on the merits, the circuit court dismissed the petition at the petitioners' expense, prompting the Allisons to appeal, arguing that the proceedings to establish the highway were flawed due to improper timing and jurisdiction issues.	The plaintiffs contended that the commissioners failed to establish the highway in a timely manner, as the order was not filed with the town clerk within thirty days of posting the petition. They claimed that the commissioners lost jurisdiction by not adjourning their proceedings and that the established highway's route differed from what was petitioned without allowing for public objections.	The defendants argued that the timeline for filing the order was within a reasonable time frame, citing that no specific statutory timeline exists for such procedures. They maintained that the appeal process to supervisors granted jurisdiction and that procedural irregularities were not jurisdictional and thus could be waived. Additionally, they asserted that the established road line correlated with the proposed route, only varying slightly to accommodate obstacles.

In January 1871, the case "Christian Herkelrath et al. v. James M. Stookey" was filed in the Illinois Supreme Court following an action of replevin. The plaintiffs, Christian Herkelrath and others, sought the return of personal property seized by the defendant, James M. Stookey, who served as the sheriff of St. Clair County, Illinois. The property in question had been seized under the authority of an execution order issued by the St. Clair Circuit Court in December 1869, based on a judgment involving Lewis Geisler and the Klug family (John, Charles, and A. L. Klug). The plaintiffs claimed ownership through a chattel mortgage executed in September 1869, which was intended to secure the payment of several promissory notes. However, the sheriff contested this by pleading non detinet, claiming that he acted legally under the execution order. During the trial, the plaintiffs attempted to introduce evidence related to the mortgage and the promissory notes; however, their submissions were met with legal objections and were ultimately rejected by the court, which concluded that the acknowledgment of the mortgage was not valid according to statutory requirements.	The plaintiffs argued that they were the rightful owners of the disputed property based on a chattel mortgage executed by John Klug. They contended that the mortgage was valid and should have been acknowledged by the police magistrate. They sought the return of their property that the defendant improperly seized without acknowledging their ownership rights through the mortgage.	The defendant, Stookey, claimed that he acted under proper authority as the sheriff when he seized the property based on a court-ordered execution. He argued that the acknowledgment of the chattel mortgage was invalid because it did not comply with statutory requirements. As a result, he contended there was no legal basis for the plaintiffs’ claim to the property.

In 1859, Joseph Stout and others filed a bill in chancery against Isaac Cook to set aside a sheriff's deed concerning a property in Chicago, Illinois. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1870. The issues arose from the plaintiff's contention that the sheriff's deed was invalid, leading to a final hearing where the relief they sought was initially granted. However, the case was subsequently appealed, leading to a review by the Supreme Court, where various points of contention, including evidence on the value of coal and the accounts of rents and profits, were examined. The court found that the evidence regarding coal values supported the lower court's rulings, and the claims concerning interest on payments were also upheld. Furthermore, the court ruled against the defendant's claims for allowances regarding improvements made to the land, establishing that the defendant was not entitled to compensation for improvements made by a tenant for which he had not paid. The Supreme Court ultimately affirmed the previous ruling of the lower court, asserting that no errors had been presented in the case.	The plaintiffs argued that the sheriff's deed was invalid and sought to have it set aside. They requested an accounting of rents and profits derived from the property in question and applied for the court to affirm their right to relief concerning these financial matters.	The defendant, Isaac Cook, contended that he should be compensated for improvements made on the property. He argued that the court erred in not allowing for these enhancements in the accounting process. Additionally, he maintained that the evidence presented at trial was mishandled and questioned the legitimacy of certain accountings and actions related to the evaluation of profits and rents.

In January 1873, the case of William H. Richardson et al. v. Lucius Mills et al. was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in the Circuit Court of McLean County, where a foreclosure of a mortgage was being contested. Both the mortgage and the corresponding note were executed on June 20, 1867. However, a clerical error in the court record inaccurately recorded the note's date as June 20, 1868. On September 30, 1870, the circuit court issued a decree that acknowledged the date of the note and mortgage, but the appellants claimed the decree incorrectly calculated interest based on the erroneous date. The court reviewed the records, found the claim of the appellant to be based on this error, and concluded that the actual date of the note and mortgage was indeed June 20, 1867. The court noted that correcting the clerical error would not harm the appellant's case. The ruling highlighted that reversing the decree would impose undue hardship on the appellee, who had already taken measures to satisfy a prior mortgage to secure recovery.	The plaintiffs (appellants) argued that the initial decree of foreclosure was flawed because it incorrectly stated the date of the note as June 20, 1868, rather than June 20, 1867. They contended that this clerical error inflated the decree amount as they calculated interest based on the erroneous date. They sought to have the decree reversed due to this alleged miscalculation, arguing that it constituted a significant error that warranted a reconsideration of the judgment.	The defendants (appellees) maintained that the date in question was clearly a clerical error that did not affect the overall rights of the parties involved. They argued that the proper date was well-documented in existing records, and as such, the actual decree amount was justified. The appellees further asserted that reversing the decree would result in significant hardship for them, as they had incurred additional costs to protect their interests in light of the foreclosure.

In the case of **John T. Major et al. v. John Collins et al.**, the events unfold in Illinois, with the decision rendered on December 4, 1885, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The case involves a mechanic’s lien petition initiated by John Collins against John T. Major, related to five buildings erected on separate lots owned by Major. Collins claimed lien rights for materials and labor provided under a contract, and the case was later complicated by the involvement of Edward A. Hartwell, who asserted his own claim against the proceeds of the lien as an assignee of Collins. The court initially granted Collins a lien of $3,085, but this was later reversed due to errors related to the sale of all properties as one unit rather than separately, as initially intended. After some time, the properties were sold to Hartwell for $4,283.36, but subsequent petitions led to further hearings regarding lien distribution and ordering a new sale.	The plaintiffs, Collins and Hartwell, initially sought to enforce a mechanic's lien for the payment of $3,085 for materials and labor. Following the reversal of the initial decree, they filed a supplemental petition requesting that Hartwell be allowed to cancel his certificate of purchase, recover surplus funds totaling $329.54 from the master, and that a new lien be established. Their primary argument centered on the validity and equitable distribution of the lien proceeds from the property sale, as well as Hartwell's rights as the purchaser from the previous decree.	The defendants argued that the previous sale and the decree confirming it should be upheld and that Hartwell’s challenge to its validity was improper. They contended that the reversed decree did not invalidate the sale to Hartwell and that any action to set aside or dispute the sale needed to be initiated by the defendants themselves. The defendants also sought to establish that they were entitled to a proper allocation of any resulting surplus funds from the sale.

In 1879, William Wittenmyre, a resident of Cook County, Illinois, died intestate, leaving behind his widow, Susan C. Wittenmyre, and two children from a previous marriage, Sallie A. Young and Charles A. Wittenmyre. Following his death, Susan was appointed administratrix of his estate in Cook County, and later in Iowa, where William had substantial personal property associated with his business. As administrator, Susan collected enough assets in Iowa to cover all estate debts, including an allowance from the estate. However, instead of using these funds to pay off debts in Illinois, she distributed a significant amount to herself and the heirs. Subsequently, she sought permission from the Cook County court to sell real estate to cover the widow’s allowance due to alleged insufficiency of assets. The court found that personal assets in Iowa were sufficient, and ruled that Susan could not sell estate property in Illinois when sufficient personal property in Iowa remained.	The plaintiffs, Sallie A. Young and Charles A. Wittenmyre, argued that Susan C. Wittenmyre, as administratrix, wrongfully distributed assets from the estate in Iowa without settling debts in Illinois. They contended that there were sufficient personal assets to cover all debts, particularly the widow’s allowance, and sought the court to reverse the order for selling real estate.	Susan C. Wittenmyre defended her actions by asserting that the sale of real estate was necessary due to insufficient personal assets within Illinois. She argued that she had properly fulfilled her administrative duties and that the distribution made to heirs was justified under the circumstances.

The case of Hankerson Watkins v. Jonas R. Gale took place in December 1851 in Illinois, during a trial conducted in the Circuit Court of Mason. The main individuals involved were the appellant, Hankerson Watkins, and the appellee, Jonas R. Gale. The dispute arose from Gale cutting trees on land owned by Watkins. The evidence presented indicated that the defendant, Gale, was aware that the land he cut the trees from was not his own, as the land was entered by Watkins after he had claimed the property. Gale had a license to operate on a neighboring property owned by Henry R. Green but still proceeded to cut timber that was on Watkins's land, even after Watkins's agent notified him of the trespass. The case hinged on whether Gale's actions could be considered willful and if he was liable for the penalties prescribed by law for cutting timber without the owner's permission.	Hankerson Watkins, the plaintiff, argued that Jonas R. Gale knowingly cut trees from his land without permission, thereby committing an act of trespass. Watkins sought penalties as provided by statute for this wrongdoing, asserting that the law presumes willfulness when the defendant cuts timber knowing full well it is not his own. He sought the court's instruction that could lead to a favorable judgment in favor of his claims if the jury found that Gale acted with knowledge of the trespass.	Jonas R. Gale, the defendant, contended that he believed he was cutting trees from land that was either his or legitimately licensed to him by Green. He argued that the jury should find in his favor if they believed he was acting under a mistaken belief regarding his property boundaries. Gale maintained that he did not willfully cut the trees on Watkins's land, and that any conduct he exhibited could not be deemed willful trespass since it was based on a reasonable belief that he was not infringing upon Watkins's rights.

Patrick L. Garrity and Edward S. Dreyer initiated legal proceedings against the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company et al. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, where an injunction had been granted in favor of the appellants (Garrity and Dreyer). This injunction was subsequently made perpetual. However, the defendants sought a writ of error from the Supreme Court, which resulted in the reversal of the Circuit Court's judgment. Following this, the Circuit Court permitted the defendants to present suggestions for damages, ultimately assessing the plaintiffs for reasonable attorney's fees amounting to $500. The decision of the Circuit Court was appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court, which had to determine whether the Circuit Court had jurisdiction to assess damages post-dissolution of the injunction, following the Supreme Court's directive.	The plaintiffs, Garrity and Dreyer, contended that the Circuit Court exceeded its jurisdiction when it assessed damages upon the dissolution of the injunction, arguing that the writ of error constituted a new suit rather than a continuation of the original case. They asserted that the court should not have granted damages to the defendants after the Supreme Court's intervention.	The defendants argued that the Circuit Court was within its jurisdiction to assess damages due to the dissolution of the injunction as directed by the Supreme Court. They maintained that the plaintiffs' claims regarding jurisdiction were unfounded and that the damages assessed were fully supported by evidence. The defendants sought to uphold the assessment of damages set at $500 for the reasonable value of their attorney's services.

The case "St. Louis, Jacksonville and Chicago R. R. Company v. John C. Hamilton" took place in January 1868 and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved included the plaintiff, John C. Hamilton, who was seeking to recover damages, and the defendant, the St. Louis, Jacksonville and Chicago Railroad Company. The background of the case revolves around an incident where a cow owned by Hamilton was killed by a train operated by the railroad company. The crux of the matter is a legal dispute concerning allegations made in Hamilton's declaration against the railway. The case was appealed from the Circuit Court of Morgan County, where the Honorable D. M. Woodson presided. The railroad company challenged the declaration through a demurrer, arguing that it lacked certain essential allegations. However, the Circuit Court found that the declaration was, in fact, adequate in substance, resulting in the demurrer being overruled.	Hamilton's primary claim was for damages resulting from the death of his cow caused by the railroad company's train. He contended that the declaration filed contained all necessary allegations even in the face of the railroad's demurrer, which claimed otherwise. Hamilton sought monetary compensation for the loss of his property, asserting that the railroad company was liable for the incident.	The St. Louis, Jacksonville and Chicago Railroad Company defended itself by filing a demurrer to Hamilton's declaration, arguing that it did not include certain necessary allegations to substantiate the claim. The railroad company challenged the adequacy of the facts presented by Hamilton, which they claimed were essential to establish liability. They requested that the court dismiss Hamilton's claims based on this alleged insufficiency.

The case "John Connolly v. Almond Cottle" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1830. The action originated in the Jo Daviess circuit court in October 1828, where Almond Cottle sued John Connolly on a written obligation dated April 27, 1821. This document required the signers to pay certain debts to the creditors of Samuel B. Smith, including a sum due to Cottle of approximately $350. The plaintiff, Cottle, claimed that Connolly was liable for this amount. During the trial, the defendant Connolly pleaded non assumpsit and challenged the admissibility of the written instrument on the grounds of variance and the lack of a stated consideration for the promise. The jury found in favor of Cottle, awarding him $350 plus costs. Connolly appealed the decision, arguing for a reversal based on the alleged defects in the declaration and instrument.	Almond Cottle, the plaintiff, asserted that he was entitled to payment under a written instrument obligating Connolly and others to pay the debts owed to the creditors of Samuel B. Smith, specifically including a sum of $350. Cottle argued that the writing constituted a valid debt obligation despite Connolly's defenses and maintained that the verdict in his favor should be upheld.	John Connolly, the defendant, contended that the judgment should be reversed due to two primary reasons: the absence of an averment of consideration for the promise in the declaration, which he argued was fatal to Cottle's claim, and a crucial variance between the written note declared upon and the one produced at trial, which he claimed invalidated the judgment. Connolly claimed that the note produced was a joint promise to multiple creditors, rather than a separate promise to pay Cottle individually.

In 1867, Franklin McVeagh initiated a legal case against the City of Chicago in the Cook Circuit Court, Illinois, to challenge the collection of taxes imposed on his shares of stock in the Commercial National Bank of Chicago. The basis of his complaint was that the act passed by the General Assembly on June 13, 1867, was unconstitutional and invalid. He argued that the assessment of his bank shares for taxation was unlawful because it was not included in the valuation of his personal property and that such shares were assessed at a higher rate than other monetary capital without allowing deductions for any debts owed by shareholders. The Circuit Court sustained a demurrer to his bill, ruling against him and affirming his responsibility for the costs, prompting McVeagh to appeal the decision on the grounds that the court erred in sustaining the demurrer. The Illinois Supreme Court considered various arguments raised by both sides regarding the constitutional validity of the tax assessment, the timing of assessments, and whether any discrimination occurred in taxation practices.	Franklin McVeagh claimed that the act allowing the taxation of bank shares for the year 1867 was unconstitutional, asserting that the assessment violated principles of equality and uniformity outlined in the constitution since it did not account for the personal property value at the correct valuation date. He argued that the law was defective and that the assessments were void because they imposed a greater tax burden than imposed on other moneyed capital, lacking proper deductions for debts owed by shareholders.	The City of Chicago argued that the law was constitutional, stating that McVeagh did not demonstrate any injury resulting from the timing of the assessments. Defendants maintained that the legislature had the power to enact a special law to address any discrepancies in tax assessments for the year 1867. They contended that the system established by the 1867 act for assessing bank shares was independent of the general revenue system and allowed for assessments without needing to provide deductions for debts owed by the shareholders.

In the case of Edward Handy v. The People of The State of Illinois, decided on May 29, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the controversy arose from the actions of Edward Handy, who was accused of unlawfully keeping a dram-shop within the incorporated limits of the village of Bluffs, Illinois. Prior to the issuance of his license on June 20, 1887, Handy executed a bond of $3,000, which was approved by the village. The village board had passed an ordinance allowing dram-shops, and Handy applied for and received a license to operate his establishment. The license was valid for ten months and required advance payments, which Handy complied with for the first two quarters. However, shortly after the second payment, the village board attempted to revoke the license, which Handy refused to accept as valid due to the absence of official revocation. The central legal issue revolved around whether the license issued to Handy was valid under the laws relevant to dram-shop licenses, specifically the requirement of advance payment for the entire license period, as established by state law.	The plaintiff, represented by The People of The State of Illinois, asserted that Edward Handy was unlawfully exercising the franchise to operate a dram-shop without a valid license. The claims were focused on the accuracy of the licensing procedure and alleged that the advance payment requirement had not been met fully according to state law, which stipulates that the entire fee for the license must be paid upfront. The plaintiff sought a judgment of ouster against Handy, resulting in the prohibition of his operations and a financial penalty.	Edward Handy contested the claims stating that he had complied with the licensing requirements by paying the fees as stipulated at the time of application. He argued that the actions of the village board in tendering back the second payment did not equate to a formal revocation of his license, and hence he retained the legal right to operate the dram-shop under the license issued to him. Handy also raised procedural objections regarding the appropriateness of using quo warranto proceedings against him in this context, asserting that the legal remedy pursued by the plaintiff was inappropriate.

Anson Blake and James F. Fash were involved in a legal dispute that reached the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. The case originated in the Peoria Circuit Court and was later transferred to Marshall County. The conflict arose over a parcel of land that had previously belonged to Ann Davis, who conveyed it to Henry W. Sargent in 1840. Sargent later attempted to transfer the title to Fash based on the assertion that he had bought the land from Davis. However, this deed was never recorded, and Sargent eventually destroyed it before issuing a new deed directly to Fash in 1847. The crux of the case revolves around the legitimacy of this later deed, with both parties claiming title through Sargent. At issue was not only the contents of the lost document but also whether secondary evidence could be used to establish the title after its destruction. The case included discussions about equitable estoppel and the nature of real estate deeds, particularly focusing on the timing of their effective delivery.	The plaintiff, Anson Blake, claimed that he had obtained a valid title to the land through Ann Davis's transfer of ownership. He argued that the destruction of the original deed did not invalidate the legitimate transfer of title and asserted that secondary evidence could confirm the validity of his claim to the property. Blake's legal request was for the court to affirm his ownership of the land based on this evidence.	The defendant, James F. Fash, disputed Blake's claims by arguing that Blake was estopped from asserting his title due to having recorded a deed that misrepresented the date of its delivery. Fash contended that this public record created an inequitable situation for purchasers who relied on it. Additionally, he challenged the admissibility of secondary evidence to prove the contents of the lost deed and claimed that the tax receipts and other evidence presented did not support Blake's ownership claim.

In September 1867, in Chicago, Illinois, an action of ejectment was initiated by Frank Porter against William Hague regarding the possession of lot 73 in the canal trustees' subdivision of section 7, township 39 north, range 14 east. The case was tried in the Superior Court of Chicago without a jury, with Judge Joseph E. Gary presiding. The court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, Frank Porter, who presented evidence of a clear title linked from the State through a series of conveyances concluding with a deed to himself. The defendant, Hague, appealed the decision, arguing that the plaintiff had not established a proper chain of title, particularly questioning the validity of a certificate of magistracy related to a deed. The court reviewed various legal arguments regarding certificates and the powers of clerks, ultimately affirming the legitimacy of the plaintiff's title.	Frank Porter, the plaintiff, claimed ownership of lot 73 based on a clear chain of title derived from the State and through subsequent conveyances. He argued that the only viable objection regarding the validity of a deed's certificate was unfounded, as clerks have the authority to certify deeds properly. The plaintiff sought to establish his rightful possession of the property.	William Hague, the defendant, contended that the plaintiff had failed to demonstrate a valid title to the property. He raised concerns about the certificate of magistracy included in the chain of title, asserting it was invalid due to being executed by an inappropriate official. Hague requested that the court reverse the lower court's judgment on the grounds that the plaintiff did not adequately prove his legal claim to the property.

In September 1868, the case of David R. Breese v. George L. Schuler took place in Illinois, presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court. The core of the dispute arose from a judgment against E. C. Anderson, in which Breese and Hiram Baker were sureties. Schuler, who had initially obtained a judgment against Anderson, desired a larger recovery but was impacted by Anderson's testimony. Soon after, Schuler had Anderson indicted for perjury, leading Anderson to evade the legal process. In this context, Schuler received a note from Mills, valued at five hundred dollars, which was the entirety of Anderson's property, in exchange for not pursuing the indictment. Breese sought relief, arguing that the transaction between Schuler and Anderson was illegal, as it involved compounding a felony, and he requested that the note's proceeds be applied to settle the judgment against him as a surety.	Breese claimed that the illegal transaction between Schuler and Anderson should not harm him as an innocent surety. He argued that since Schuler obtained the entire estate of Anderson through this illegal deal, equity required that Schuler apply the proceeds from the Mills note toward the payment of the judgment against him. Breese requested the court to reverse the lower court's decision, asserting his right to relief from the obligation as a surety due to Schuler's unjust actions.	Schuler’s defense centered on the legality of the transaction and argued that Breese, as a surety, was liable for the obligations incurred. Schuler contended that Breese had no standing to claim relief based on the illegal dealings between Schuler and Anderson, emphasizing that the surety's responsibilities remained intact, irrespective of the transaction's nature.

Excy D. Shufeldt v. John Gillilan is a legal case that took place in Kane County, Illinois, with the decision rendered on May 9, 1888, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case revolves around a promissory note dated December 13, 1877, wherein John Gillilan promised to pay Dolly Clauson $1,885 with interest. This note was subsequently indorsed to Excy D. Shufeldt by Dolly Clauson but did not contain words of negotiability. After Dolly Clauson's husband, Henry Clauson, passed away, Dolly was given the use and control of his estate, with the remainder directed to be divided amongst their children upon her death. An arrangement was made whereby Dolly Clauson would receive interest payments from Gillilan for his children’s share, with the principal to be destroyed upon her death. When Dolly Clauson died, she transferred the note to Shufeldt without Gillilan’s consent. Gillilan, having already settled the estate debts and arrangements, argued the note was never properly delivered. The circuit court ruled in favor of Gillilan, and this decision was upheld by the Appellate Court.	The plaintiff, Excy D. Shufeldt, claims that she is entitled to collect the debt from John Gillilan based on the promissory note indorsed to her by her mother, Dolly Clauson. Shufeldt argues that despite the lack of formal delivery of the note, the indorsement makes her the rightful holder, and she requests enforcement of the debt against Gillilan.	The defendant, John Gillilan, contends that the note was never delivered and that it was part of an arrangement wherein he was to pay interest only during Dolly Clauson’s lifetime, and the note was to be destroyed upon her death. He asserts that Shufeldt received the note without consideration and was aware of the stipulations attached, making it invalid as a collectible debt. Gillilan seeks dismissal of the claim based on these defenses.

Newton P. Holden v. Edgar Terhune et al. is a legal case that was adjudicated on June 14, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arises from a mortgage agreement initiated by Edgar Terhune, who borrowed $500 from Newton P. Holden on April 17, 1882, secured by a mortgage for a three-year term. The context includes the fact that Terhune was a partner with Holden’s son, both of whom were practicing lawyers. The primary issue at hand is whether a payment of $300 made by Terhune on April 3, 1884, was valid, as it was allegedly paid to Holden’s son, not directly to Holden. The trial court determined that, despite Holden’s son passing away on December 1, 1884, sufficient evidence supported that he had the authority to receive the payment on behalf of Holden. During a June 1885 interview, Holden acknowledged that if the payment was made, it was acceptable, although he expressed doubt about its occurrence and requested a receipt. The court focused on witness credibility and preponderance of evidence, ultimately affirming the trial court's finding.	The plaintiff, Newton P. Holden, claims that he is entitled to the balance remaining on the mortgage after a partial payment of $300 made by Edgar Terhune. Holden asserts that the payment was not authorized since it was received by his son, and therefore, he contends that Terhune still owes the remaining unpaid residue of the debt secured by the mortgage.	The defendant, Edgar Terhune, argues that he made a legitimate payment towards the mortgage through Holden's son. Terhune claims that the acknowledgment from Holden during the June 1885 conversation indicates acceptance of the payment. He contends that because Holden’s son was a partner and acted on Holden's behalf, the payment should be considered valid, thus reducing or eliminating the balance claimed by Holden.

The case involves The Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad Company and John Collins and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1870. The events transpired around July 16-17, 1867, in Chicago and Walcott, Iowa. John Collins, a Chicago grocer, claimed that he had checked his trunk as luggage for transport from Chicago to Walcott. Upon arriving at Walcott, he alleged that he could not locate his trunk. The railroad's agent indicated that the trunk had been left on the platform after his absence and was subsequently stolen. Testimonies were presented by various individuals, including Collins himself, who provided details about the trunk's contents, which included two revolvers valued at $25 each. The case turned on the credibility of Collins's claims, with evidence suggesting he may not have been the actual owner of the trunk, but rather an accomplice of Thomas Duggan, who was believed to have taken the trunk without authorization. The court considered a letter from Duggan to a relative, detailing their intentions to deceive the railroad, which was significant in determining the real ownership of the trunk and its contents. Ultimately, evidence from the case showed substantial coordination between Collins and Duggan, suggesting a conspiracy to defraud the railroad.	John Collins claimed that the railroad company was liable for the value of his lost trunk and its contents, which he alleged had been checked as his baggage and that he had attempted to recover it at both Walcott and Chicago, but had never been successful. He sought monetary compensation for the trunk and contents, including two revolvers.	The defendant, the railroad company, argued that Collins was not the true owner of the trunk, positing that it actually belonged to Thomas Duggan, who had taken the trunk without the knowledge of the railroad agent. They presented evidence indicating that Collins had provided false testimony regarding his whereabouts and actions related to the trunk. The defense urged that Collins’s claims were part of a conspiracy to defraud the railroad company, thus challenging the legitimacy of Collins's request for damages.

In the case of Lemuel J. Anderson v. Walker Donaldson, which took place in Menard County, Illinois, the dispute arose in 1890 regarding the sale of hogs. The plaintiff, Lemuel J. Anderson, accused the defendant, Walker Donaldson, of breaching a warranty related to the sale of these hogs. Anderson claimed that the hogs were sold while harboring a disease that he was unaware of at the time of purchase. The issue escalated as Anderson alleged that this concealed condition led to an infection in his other hogs. The case featured a voluminous amount of evidence and testimony, including unclear statements regarding warranties made by the defendant during the sale. The jury was tasked with determining whether a warranty existed and if it had been breached as well as evaluating the resulting damages. Ultimately, they sided with Anderson, resulting in a judgment against Donaldson for $247.80.	Anderson's main argument revolved around the claim that Donaldson had breached an express warranty regarding the health of the hogs sold to him. He contended that Donaldson fraudulently concealed the diseased conditions of the hogs, causing significant damages to his own herd when the infection spread. Anderson sought compensation for these damages, asserting that he relied on the defendant's assurances that the hogs were sound at the time of sale.	Donaldson defended against the claims by disputing the presence of an express warranty in the sale agreement. He argued that the evidence did not substantiate Anderson's claims of deceit regarding the hogs' conditions. Donaldson maintained that there was no clear indication of a warranty and that any implied expressions made during the sale did not meet the legal standards for establishing one. He requested the court to dismiss the case based on these grounds, insisting that the jury's interpretation of the evidence was flawed.

William Thomas v. Delia Sayles et al. is a legal dispute that took place in Illinois and concluded in January 1872. The conflict revolved around a small parcel of land that Thomas claimed based on a deed from Thomas Church, the original patentee. This deed, dated September 15, 1832, described a six-acre tract, establishing boundaries that Thomas argued included the land in controversy. The central issue was the accurate determination of the south line of the property, which was long lost, complicating the surveying process. The land in question measured 43 feet wide at one end and 41 feet at the other, making it crucial to ascertain if it fell within the described boundaries. The defendants, descended from Church’s successors, asserted that Thomas's land claim did not include the disputed area. They attempted to determine the boundary by referencing a subsequent deed between Joseph Duncan and Forsythe & Buckner from 1836, claiming it created a necessary starting point for the survey. The case centered on historical surveying practices, territorial rights, and the implications of long-term property occupancy.	William Thomas contended that he was rightful in claiming the land based on his interpretation of the 1832 deed from Church to Filson, asserting his "paper title" allowed recovery of the land. He argued against the defendants' claims by stating that surveys indicated the parcel fell within his lines, thus entitling him to ownership according to the deed's description and his long-standing possession.	The defendants, represented by Henry E. Hummer, countered Thomas’s claims by arguing that to determine the boundaries accurately, the deed from Duncan to Forsythe & Buckner had to be examined. They maintained that any claim to the land would need to originate from the conditions established in that deed, implying that Thomas had no valid claim to the property as per their readings of historical deeds and surv ey results.

The case "The Village of Melrose v. Daniel E. Bernard" took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the final judgment being filed on November 15, 1888. The case arose when the Cook County treasurer, acting as the ex officio collector of taxes, sought judgment for a special tax that had been levied by an ordinance of the Village of Melrose. The tax in question was claimed to be delinquent against a specific lot owned by Daniel E. Bernard. In response to the treasurer's application, Bernard and other lot owners filed numerous objections to the proposed judgment. After a hearing, the county court ruled in favor of the treasurer, granting judgment for half of the delinquent tax, amounting to $19.30, while denying judgment for the other half. The Village of Melrose appealed this decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, challenging the division of the tax and the county court's ruling that permitted only partial judgment.	The Village of Melrose argued that the county court incorrectly sustained objections to one-half of the special tax deemed delinquent against Bernard’s lot. They contended that the court erred in dividing the tax obligations and requested that the entire amount of the special tax be upheld.	Daniel E. Bernard contended that the county court did not have the authority to reduce the amount of the special tax and that the absence of a complete record or a bill of exceptions meant that the judgment rendered by the court should be affirmed. He maintained that the current records did not demonstrate any error that would warrant a change in the court's decision.

In 1858, Edward L. Gilson filed a trespass action against William Wood in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from an incident where, shortly after the death of George W. Gilson, his personal property was taken from a farm that was occupied by Edward Gilson as a tenant. About a month before the trespass, Ransom claimed to be the agent of Mrs. Gilson (the deceased's widow) and sold the property to Edward. On the day of the trespass, Wood and others took the plow, wagon, and harness from the farm. The dispute primarily centered around ownership and possession of the property, with complex relationships among the parties, including agreements on crop sharing for the farm's usage. The trial occurred in a County Court after an initial judgment in a justice's court ruled against the defendant for costs. The County Court jury awarded the plaintiff $68 in damages.	Edward L. Gilson argued that he had possession of the personal property at the time it was taken by the defendant, which provided prima facie evidence of ownership. He maintained that the property belonged to him and that the defendant, along with others, unlawfully took it. The plaintiff sought damages reflecting the worth of the property at the time it was unlawfully taken.	William Wood contended that Edward Gilson's possession of the property did not imply ownership since the plaintiff was merely a tenant under an arrangement with George W. Gilson, who had passed away. The defense asserted that the plaintiff had no rightful claim to the property, asserting that the sale conducted by Ransom, as agent for Mrs. Gilson, was invalid unless she had proper authority to sell the estate's property.

In 1841, in Rock Island, Illinois, John H. Sullivan sold two tracts of land to Lemuel Andrews and the other defendants for $990, receiving an initial payment of $400 and a promissory note for $590, due on June 8, 1842. Sullivan was unable to convey the property by the due date due to unexpected delays in business travel. After missing the deadline, the defendants had money ready to pay but did not tender payment or pick up the title. Sullivan later returned, prepared the deed, and requested payment, which was refused. Sullivan then filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The case was initially heard in the Rock Island Circuit Court before being moved to the Warren County Circuit Court, which found in favor of Sullivan but the case had several procedural issues that were highlighted by the defendants.	The plaintiff, John H. Sullivan, claimed that the defendants failed to tender payment for the tracts of land as per their agreement, despite having the money available. He sought specific performance of the contract, requesting that the court enforce the original terms and order the defendants to pay the owed amount of $749.88 alongside costs.	The defendants argued that the court lacked jurisdiction as Sullivan had a complete remedy at law. They contended that time was of the essence of the contract and Sullivan's failure to perform on time constituted a default, justifying their refusal to complete the transaction. They asserted that they had abandoned the premises without notifying Sullivan and challenged the validity of the specific performance claim.

John Welborn et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois is a legal case that occurred in 1875 and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case traces its roots back to February 1869, when William Spicer was indicted for larceny in Shelby County. The court set his bail at $300. Following his arrest on August 19, 1869, Spicer was committed to jail due to his inability to post bail. On October 19, after his arrest, he entered into a recognizance agreement before the sheriff, with John Welborn acting as his surety. This agreement allowed Spicer to be released from jail, and it was filed with the clerk of the circuit court. However, during the subsequent court term, Spicer failed to appear, leading to a forfeiture of the recognizance. The legal proceedings involved an appeal concerning various arguments about the variance between the scire facias (a legal order) and the recognizance, as well as claims regarding the sheriff's authority and the validity of the record.	The plaintiffs, represented by John Welborn, claimed that there was a variance between the scire facias and the recognizance, arguing that the document indicated a joint and several liability that did not exist in the original recognizance. They also contended that the court improperly sustained a demurrer against their third and fourth pleas, which sought to challenge the validity of the record related to the recognizance.	The defendant, The People of the State of Illinois, argued that the claims regarding variance were raised too late, as the recognizance had been accepted without objection in the circuit court. The People contended that the sheriff had the authority to accept the recognizance even after Spicer's arrest and that the approval of the recognizance was evident in the court records. They asserted that the pleas questioning the validity of the record were legally inadequate and that the record itself should be upheld as it stood.

In December 1828, the legal case "Greenup and Conway v. Philander Woodworth" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose in Randolph County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs, Greenup and Conway, acting in error, disputed a judgment against them. The key individuals involved were Justice Smith, delivering the opinion of the court, and representatives for both the plaintiffs and the defendant. The controversy stemmed from a legal action where a judgment was secured against the plaintiffs in their representative capacity by confession, while in their personal capacity, the judgment resulted from a default due to lack of a plea. The plaintiffs sought relief in equity, arguing that due process had not been followed in their case. The court examined the grounds for relief, concluding that the plaintiffs had not provided valid reasons for their request and that any defenses should have been raised during the original proceedings.	The plaintiffs, Greenup and Conway, contended that they were entitled to relief from the judgment obtained against them, as they alleged that the process had not been just. They argued that there were grounds for a legal defense that were not adequately explored during the initial proceedings. Their legal request sought redress from the judgment, claiming that the situation warranted the equitable powers of the court to intervene.	Philander Woodworth, the defendant, maintained that the plaintiffs' request for equity was unjustified, reaffirming that a proper legal defense could have been made earlier in the process. The defendant asserted that the plaintiffs had effectively admitted their liability through prior confessions, thus undermining their current claims for relief. The defendant argued that the court should not entertain relief requests when the plaintiffs had previously defaulted on their legal obligations.

In May 1858, in Clinton, Illinois, Justin H. Hill began purchasing lumber, lath, doors, and shingles from John Bishop and others, with no specific payment timeline agreed upon at the time of sale. The agreement allowed for a six-month deferment of payment starting from August 20, 1858. Hill utilized the materials to construct a house on a lot owned by him. Eventually, Hill owed $197.47 for the materials but failed to make timely payments. Elisha Stephens later claimed some interest in the property involved. The plaintiffs filed a bill requesting an accounting of the amount due, asserting that it should be established as a lien on the property with a prayer for foreclosure if payment was not made. The case proceeded against Hill and Stephens, with the Circuit Court initially finding Hill in default and ordering payment, raising errors submitted by Stephens regarding the validity of the mechanics' lien and Joint liability for the payments.	The plaintiffs claimed that Hill owed them for the materials used in constructing a house, asserting a total due of $197.47 with interest. They sought to establish a mechanics' lien on the property and requested a decree to allow for the sale of the house and lot should the payment not be made, along with general relief.	The defendants argued that the petition was insufficient to support a mechanics' lien, claiming that the purchase was made on an open account without specific reference to its use in building, thus invalidating any lien on the property. They contended that there was no clear showing of indebtedness from Stephens, suggesting the Circuit Court should have dismissed the case and awarded costs to the defendants.

The case "Erastus L. Clark et al. v. Henry Whitbeck" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1853. The dispute began when Henry Whitbeck sued Erastus L. Clark and Edwards before a justice of the peace in Cook County. Whitbeck claimed a total amount of $100, which comprised a promissory note for $36 and an account for $66. The justice issued a judgment against the defendants for $80. Clark and Edwards appealed this decision, arguing that the justice lacked jurisdiction. In the subsequent trial in the circuit court, they filed a motion to dismiss the suit based on the same jurisdiction argument, which was overruled. The case was then tried on its merits, resulting in a judgment against the defendants for $25. The defendants maintained their argument regarding the jurisdiction of the justice throughout the proceedings.	The plaintiff, Henry Whitbeck, claimed that he was owed $100 from the defendants based on a promissory note and an account. He argued that the justice of the peace had the authority to adjudicate the case based on the actual amount owed, which was less than the claimed amount. Whitbeck sought the court to recognize the legitimacy of the justice's jurisdiction in assessing his claim, ultimately requesting that the judgment against the defendants be affirmed.	The defendants, Erastus L. Clark and Edwards, contended that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction to hear the case because the claim exceeded the maximum amount allowable for such a court. They requested the circuit court to dismiss the suit on this basis, asserting that the jurisdictional question hinged on the claim amount stated in the initial filings rather than the actual debt evidenced during the trial.

In September 1873, Nicholas Troesch, a switch conductor for the Columbus, Chicago and Indiana Central Railway Company, suffered severe personal injuries while performing his duties in Chicago, Illinois. Troesch was directing the movement of a train loaded with railroad iron and was standing at the front of the forward car when he signaled the engine-driver to slow down. The driver’s response resulted in a sudden jerk that threw Troesch onto the tracks, leading to the loss of one leg and one arm. The case had been brought to trial twice, with the jury's previous verdict in favor of Troesch being overturned on appeal for lacking evidence of negligence on the part of the railway company. In this appeal, further examination revealed that the evidence presented did not sufficiently establish the claims of negligence against the company regarding the engine's condition or the driver's competency.	The plaintiff, Nicholas Troesch, claimed that the railway company was negligent in two primary ways: first, by providing a poorly constructed engine that was unfit for business, and second, by employing an unskillful engine-driver. Troesch argued that the company either knew or should have known about these issues, which contributed to his injuries while he was exercising due care at the time of the incident. He sought damages for the personal injuries sustained due to this alleged negligence.	The Columbus, Chicago and Indiana Central Railway Company defended itself by arguing that Troesch's injuries were not a result of its negligence. The company maintained that it had exercised ordinary care in selecting its employees and providing equipment. Additionally, they claimed that Troesch was injured due to the negligence of a fellow servant, which, under established legal principles, did not warrant liability for the employer. The company also pointed out that Troesch had not sufficiently proven that the machinery was defective or that it had failed to meet its duty of care regarding his safety.

The case "Ezra W. Bancroft v. Harry E. Eastman" was decided in December 1845, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated in Jo Daviess Circuit Court, where the plaintiff, Eastman, initiated a suit against the defendant, Bancroft, using a capias—a type of writ. The capias was supported by an affidavit from Ben. C. Eastman but lacked specific details, such as the exact amount due and whether the plaintiff was a non-resident. Bancroft's attorney motioned to discharge the bail and convert the capias into a summons, which the court denied, prompting an exception to be taken. Following this, Bancroft filed a plea in abatement claiming another suit between the same parties was pending. This plea, however, was struck from the record due to improper verification—specifically, it was not sworn by the defendant himself. The court subsequently entered a default judgment against Bancroft for damages amounting to $114-16. Bancroft then appealed the decisions made in his favor, focusing particularly on the claims regarding the capias and the striking of his plea.	The plaintiff, Eastman, argued that the capias was properly issued and contested Bancroft’s motion to discharge the bail. He maintained that the procedures adhered to by the court were correct and stated that Bancroft's plea in abatement was invalid due to improper verification.	Bancroft’s defense centered around multiple points: he contended that the court erred by not discharging the bail bond and allowing the capias to be treated as a summons. He argued that the affidavit was insufficient and did not legally establish the grounds for holding him to bail. Moreover, he claimed that the sua sponte dismissal of his plea in abatement was unjust, asserting that it was filed in a timely manner and sufficiently verified by the affidavit of his attorney, arguing that the law did not mandate personal verification by the defendant.

In December 1866, Abram Lumbard purchased land from Matthew Abbey in Whiteside County, Illinois, including specific defined plots. After executing a deed for these parcels, an error occurred in the description; the deed mistakenly referenced land in the southwest quarter instead of the southeast quarter. By 1870, Mitchell obtained a judgment against Abbey, subsequently leading to a sheriff's levy on the 20 acres Lumbard had purchased. To prevent the sale and rectify the deed's error, Lumbard filed a bill in chancery. The circuit court dismissed his claim, prompting Lumbard to appeal. The key issue debated was whether Mitchell’s judgment created a lien against Lumbard's land, given the circumstances of its recording and Lumbard's long-term possession and use of the property, including paying taxes and utilizing it as a wood lot.	Lumbard, through his executrix, claimed that the deed's description error caused an unjust lien against his property. He sought to correct the deed description and prevent the sale of the land by demonstrating clear evidence of his ownership through possession, use, and tax payments. Lumbard argued that Mitchell should have been aware of his interest in the land due to the longstanding occupation and use of the property.	Abbey contended that the judgment lien against him attached to all lands recorded in his name. He argued that Lumbard's possession did not provide sufficient notice to Mitchell regarding Lumbard's rights in the disputed property. Abbey maintained that the deed mistake was irrelevant once the judgment was recorded, asserting the primacy of the recorded claim over Lumbard's possessory rights.

David Nichols, the appellant, brought a case against A. Guibor, the appellee, in 1857, in Bureau Circuit Court, Illinois. The dispute arose from the sale of a plow that Nichols claimed he sold to Guibor. Nichols alleged that Guibor did not pay for the plow and sought recovery of the payment through an action initiated before a justice of the peace. Initially, the judgment was in favor of Nichols, so Guibor appealed to the Bureau Circuit Court. During the proceedings, Guibor raised several points of alleged error, specifically contesting the admissibility of the testimony of Linton, Nichols' agent, and the denial of a motion for a new trial. The case was tried with a jury and presided over by Judge Ballou. Ultimately, the court affirmed the previous judgment, ruling against the appellant, Nichols, throughout all raised points.	David Nichols, the plaintiff, claimed that he sold a plow to A. Guibor and sought recovery of the payment for this sale. He argued that he was entitled to the payment as the transaction should not have been based on any implied warranty of quality, and reiterated that Guibor was responsible for returning the plow if it did not meet his expectations.	A. Guibor, the defendant, argued that the testimony of Linton, who was Nichols' agent, should have been inadmissible since any potential damage to the plow while in Linton's possession could not impose liability on Guibor. Guibor also contended that the court erred in denying a motion for a new trial.

In 1882, in DeKalb County, Illinois, the case Appollos C. Edgerton v. Cornelia R. Weaver et al. arose. Appollos C. Edgerton, acting as the surviving executor of the estate of Gurdon H. Edgerton, filed a claim against the estate of Norman Weaver, who was deceased. The claim was based on a promissory note signed by Norman Weaver in 1860, promising to pay $1,240 with ten percent annual interest by June 1, 1866. Edgerton sought to recover the due amount, including interest on the interest claimed to be owed. A series of payments on the note were documented, but the county court found that nothing was due to Edgerton. This decision was appealed to the Circuit Court, which ruled similarly against the claimant. Edgerton then took the case to the Appellate Court, where he assigned errors such as the refusal of proper evidence and the judgment being against the weight of evidence. The Appellate Court upheld the Circuit Court's judgment, prompting Edgerton to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Appollos C. Edgerton, argued that he was entitled to recover interest on the interest owed based on an alleged contract. He claimed that forbearance constituted a valid consideration for this agreement and that proper evidence supporting his claim was wrongfully denied by the lower courts. His legal requests included a reversal of the lower court rulings and a judgment confirming his entitlement to the claimed amounts.	The defendants, represented by Cornelia R. Weaver and others, contended that the plaintiff failed to prove the existence of a binding contract to pay interest on the interest. They argued that forbearance, which was claimed as a consideration, did not meet the legal thresholds needed to support the alleged promise. They maintained that the evidence presented did not substantiate Edgerton's claims and that the lower courts rightfully found in their favor.

In the early 1860s, a legal dispute arose in Hancock County, Illinois, involving Ebenezer Rand and Bryant T. Scofield. The case was an action of ejectment, where Scofield sought recovery of seven-ninths of a tract of land. Scofield proved ownership via a title derived from the original patentee, while Rand defended his claim by asserting that he had color of title and had paid taxes on the property for seven consecutive years. The trial occurred without a jury, and later evaluations revealed confrontational evidence regarding tax payments. Key testimonies were provided by Henry Merrill, who claimed to have paid taxes on behalf of his brother, Alonzo Merrill, the previous owner of the land. Discrepancies in tax receipts were addressed through testimonies and explanations, yet the core question boiled down to whether the taxes had been paid on behalf of Rand, or for the benefit of Alonzo Merrill and his heirs.	Scofield, the plaintiff, asserted ownership of seven-ninths of the land based on a valid title from the original patentee. He argued that the defendant could not sufficiently prove the claim of a rightful title stemming from his tax payments. The plaintiff contended that the evidence presented by Rand did not convincingly demonstrate that the tax payments were for his benefit.	Rand defended his claim by presenting evidence of tax payments made for seven consecutive years. His key argument was that he had color of title to the property and had been paying taxes through an agent, which he contended should uphold his claim. Rand also pointed out that the irregularities in the tax receipts did not definitively disprove his assertions regarding the payments being made on his behalf, thus supporting his ownership rights.
