She argued that the city failed to provide adequate evidence of the ordinance's passage, specifically challenging the admissibility of the certified copy of the ordinance presented by the city in the lower court. Lindsay sought to prove that the city council proceedings were not properly recorded, which invalidated the special assessment confirmation.	The City of Chicago defended the confirmation of the special assessment by presenting a certified copy of the ordinance that purportedly authorized the paving of Canalport Avenue. The city argued that such a certified copy served as adequate proof of the ordinance's passage, as allowed by statute. They contended that the appellant had the burden to present the city council's journal if she disputed the ordinance's validity. The city maintained that the evidence it offered met the legal requirements necessary to confirm the special assessment.

In August 1859, Clancey J. Dempster purchased land from John H. Kedzie for $34,095, partially paid with properties and notes secured by a mortgage. Due to financial difficulties, Dempster negotiated with Kedzie to reduce the outstanding amount owed, resulting in restructuring of the payment plan. Following failed attempts to secure necessary funds, Kedzie had to retain the mortgage, while Dempster accrued debt primarily through unpaid interest. In January 1862, Dempster communicated his need to sell the land, which he believed would prevent further financial loss. Despite this, Dempster failed to make payments or upkeep the property for nearly seven years. In October 1869, after two installments of interest were due, Dempster elected to sell the property, whereby Kedzie facilitated the sale to Dempster for $1,500, with the intention of managing the mortgage obligations. Dempster later sought to set aside the sale, claiming it was invalid due to the circumstances under which the sale was executed, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiff, Charles West, argued that the sale of the property was voidable since Dempster held the debt while facilitating the sale. He claimed that the mechanism of removing the assignment allowed Dempster to purchase the property inappropriately, expressing the need for a legal redemption of the land as he asserted the sale was inequitable and against established legal principles.	The defendants, Clancey J. Dempster and John H. Kedzie, maintained that the sale was legally conducted as Kedzie had the rightful authority to manage the sale under the mortgage agreement. They argued that no fraud or undue influence had taken place, asserting that Dempster's purchase was valid, and there was no justification for West’s delay in seeking redemption or contesting the sale, as such delays amounted to laches in equitable terms.

The case "The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company v. The Wiggins Ferry Company" took place in 1876 in East St. Louis, Illinois. The Wiggins Ferry Company filed an action for forcible detainer against the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company, seeking possession of premises that had been leased on May 10, 1873, for a term of eight months. The lease was set to expire on January 10, 1874. Following the expiration of the lease, the Wiggins Ferry Company alleged that the railroad company remained in possession of the premises without consent. On October 4, 1875, the Wiggins Ferry Company formally demanded possession in writing. The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company responded by filing a general demurrer, arguing issues with the complaint's sufficiency regarding possession and the nature of the tenancy established post-lease. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after being heard in lower courts.	The Wiggins Ferry Company claimed that the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company unlawfully held over the premises after the lease expiration. They argued that once the lease term expired, the railroad company was obliged to vacate the premises, and their refusal to do so constituted unlawful detainer. The plaintiff requested that the court affirm their right to regain possession.	The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company contended that the complaint was defective because it failed to demonstrate that the Wiggins Ferry Company was ever in possession of the premises. They argued that the tenancy had implicitly transitioned to a month-to-month arrangement, which required prior notice to terminate. Additionally, they claimed that the premises were not adequately described in the complaint, raising issues about the complaint's overall sufficiency.

In the case of "The Trustees of Schools in Township No. 23 v. Richard H. Snell et al.," the events unfolded in Pekin, Illinois around the year 1857. The Trustees of Schools, acting as plaintiffs, sought to foreclose a mortgage on several lots owned by Richard H. Snell and others due to an outstanding debt of $405. A court decree was issued to facilitate the sale of these lands. The mortgage-related property included lots in both school section No. 16 and block 73. The procedure required the appointed commissioner to advertise the sale in a public newspaper for four consecutive weeks. The advertisement, published on December 4, 1856, stipulated that the sale would occur on January 2, 1857. However, the sale resulted in what was described as an "enormous sacrifice," with lots sold at nominal amounts, raising concerns regarding the effectiveness of the notice provided. One of the defendants, John Wightman, motioned to set aside the sale at the April 1857 term of the Tazewell Circuit Court, arguing that the advertisement's provisions were insufficient and that the lands were worth significantly more than the amounts bid.	The plaintiffs argued that the sale of the mortgaged properties should be validated as per the court’s decree, which mandated proper notification for the auction. They maintained that the process followed by the commissioner, who advertised and conducted the sale, complied with legal standards. Therefore, they sought to uphold the results of the foreclosure sale, which they believed was executed correctly according to the guidelines laid out by the court.	The defendants contested the validity of the property sale, arguing that the lands were undervalued and sold for a mere fraction of their worth, which was as high as $600. They highlighted several procedural inadequacies: (1) the advertisement did not correctly specify that the sale occurred four weeks after it was published; (2) the notice failed to set a definitive time for the sale, which could have permitted bids at unreasonable hours, potentially infringing on bidding fairness. They requested that the court set aside the sale and order a re-sale of the property under appropriate conditions.

In the legal case of James N. Longan v. George W. Taylor et al., decided on October 31, 1889, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the liability of sureties on an official bond associated with a township treasurer of schools. The case arose in Logan County, Illinois, and involved key individuals including James N. Longan, the township school treasurer, and his sureties, William Atteberry and Joseph F. Fisher. The bond in question, dated June 2, 1886, stipulated that Longan was responsible for accounting for all funds that came into his hands after the bond's date. The central issue at trial was whether Longan had fully accounted for the funds in his possession on the last day of his service and whether the sureties could be held liable for any shortages. The circuit court had previously refused to accept the plaintiffs' claims regarding entries in Longan's books and reports made at the end of his term. This ruling was contested, leading to appeals regarding the estoppel effect of Longan’s accounting records and the liability of the sureties based on the terms of the bond.	The plaintiff, James N. Longan, claimed that the defendants (the sureties) were liable for any funds that he failed to account for as stipulated in the bond. He argued that the entries in his official records should be considered conclusive evidence of the amounts in his possession at the time, effectively preventing the defendants from contesting these records. He sought to hold the sureties accountable based on these claims in court.	The defendants, George W. Taylor and others as sureties, contended that Longan had already accounted for all funds when the bond was executed and any shortages were the responsibility of prior sureties in place at the time of the discrepancy. They argued that the bond's terms limited their liability to only the actual funds that came into Longan’s hands after the bond's date. Therefore, they sought to be absolved from liability for any claimed shortages by asserting they could challenge the accuracy of Longan's reports and accounting entries.

The case "The People, &c., ex relatione George Dixon, v. Bela Shaw et al." was decided in June 1853 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from an information filed in the Stephenson Circuit Court on March 30, 1850, due to a venue change from Winnebago County. The case involved the Rockford Bridge Act, established on February 25, 1847, which required the election of four bridge commissioners at the annual general elections. The defendants, Bela Shaw and others, were elected as commissioners on August 6, 1849, but the relator, George Dixon, argued that the election was invalid because the election day had been changed by the new constitution to November. Dixon claimed that the defendants usurped their positions by holding office without a legitimate election and intended to levy an illegal tax on local taxpayers. The court examined the legality of the election dates and the interpretation of the statute, as well as the validity of the defendants’ claims to their positions.	George Dixon, representing the people, argued that the defendants unlawfully held the position of bridge commissioners without being elected at the designated general elections, as required by the Rockford Bridge Act. Dixon contended that their election on August 6, 1849, was not valid due to changes in the voting date and that they intended to levy an unlawful tax. The claims aimed to oust the defendants from their positions and prevent the tax levy based on alleged illegitimacy.	The defendants contended that they were duly elected at the election held on the first Monday of August, 1849, under the provisions of the Rockford Bridge Act. They argued that their election was legitimate and that they had held the office lawfully since their election and taken the required oath. The defendants sought to dismiss the information brought against them, claiming compliance with the statute.

In 1852, the legal case of Ebenezer Marsh v. John A. Chesnut took place in Macoupin County, Illinois, concerning a dispute over land ownership. The case arose when Chesnut initiated an action of ejectment against Marsh to reclaim the east half of the southwest quarter of section twenty-one in township ten north, range seven west, comprising eighty acres of land. During the trial, Chesnut presented evidence, including a judgment from the Macoupin circuit court from May 1840, documenting a tax judgment that led to the sale of the property due to unpaid taxes from 1839. This sale was formalized by a sheriff's deed issued to Chesnut in July 1842. It was acknowledged that the land had initially been acquired by the defendant from the patentee, without any outstanding taxes at the trial's outset. However, the defendant contended that the 1839 assessment was invalid since it was not reported until June, violating the statutory deadline of May 1 established by Illinois law. The jury ultimately sided with the plaintiff. Marsh later sought a writ of error to contest the judgment.	The plaintiff, John A. Chesnut, argued that he legally acquired the title to the disputed land through a valid tax sale due to unpaid taxes. He maintained that the court should uphold this transaction based on the tax judgment and sheriff's deed from 1842. Chesnut's primary request was to affirm his ownership and regain possession of the property.	The defendant, Ebenezer Marsh, contended that the assessment of the property for taxation in 1839 was invalid due to the failure of the assessor to return the assessment by the legal deadline, which was mandatory under state law. He argued that this defect rendered the tax sale and subsequent sheriff's deed invalid, thereby protecting his claim to the land. Marsh sought the court's acknowledgment of the invalidity of the tax title that Chesnut relied upon.

On October 13, 1884, The First National Bank of Michigan City filed a suit in attachment in the Superior Court of Cook County against William Mellors & Son, who were residents of Indiana. The lawsuit sought to recover an indebtedness of $2,074.02 for goods sold and delivered. The attachment writ was served on the defendant as garnishees; the First National Bank was served on October 18, 1884, and another garnishee, Einstein & Rosenthal, was served on October 13, 1884. Interrogatories were filed by the plaintiffs to be answered by the garnishees, and after the garnishees answered, the plaintiffs traversed those answers. Mellors & Son failed to defend against the claim, resulting in a judgment by default against them for the full amount owed. The issues regarding the garnishees were submitted for trial without a jury, which ruled in favor of the plaintiffs after rejecting requests for a new trial. The bank was ordered to pay $1,683.68, while Einstein & Rosenthal was ordered to pay $1,540.08. An appeal was made to the Appellate Court of the First District, which affirmed the judgment of the Superior Court. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court based on the appeal by the garnishees.	The plaintiffs, The First National Bank of Michigan City, claimed ownership of the money and effects in the hands of the bailees, Einstein & Rosenthal. They asserted that the transfer assignment or bill of sale executed by Mellors & Son to the bank was valid and entitled them to subject the funds to satisfy their debt. They sought to enforce the attachment suit against the funds in question and demanded judgment for the amounts owed.	The defendants, represented by Einstein & Rosenthal, contended that the money and goods held were rightfully the property of Mellors & Son and not subject to the claims of the First National Bank. They challenged the validity of the transfer to the bank and the chattel mortgage, asserting that the assignment made for the benefit of creditors was legitimate and effectively separated the disputed assets from the bank’s claims.

The case "Wallace R. Condict v. James M. Flower et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 20, 1882. It centered around a dispute involving Charles G. E. Prussing, a debtor, and several creditors including Wallace R. Condict. The case arose from the failure of Prussing, who proposed an agreement on April 4, 1874, to convey real estate properties on State Street in Chicago, subject to certain existing liens, to be managed by a trustee selected by the creditors. Key individuals included Prussing, Henry Greenebaum (the appointed trustee), and the Wartman Brothers, who sought a mechanic's lien for unpaid debts for services rendered. After a fire destroyed the buildings on the property, the trust property was sold under a prior mortgage, leading to multiple claims and defenses relating to the personal liability of the creditors under the agreement and the alleged mechanic's lien held by the Wartmans. The legal complexities questioned whether the creditors bore personal liability for the debts incurred by Prussing, the validity of the lien, and the trustee's accuracy in managing the trust.	The plaintiff, represented by the Wartman Brothers, claimed a mechanic's lien against the property and argued that under the agreement made on April 4, 1874, the other creditors should be held financially responsible for payments owed to them. They contended that the understanding among the creditors was that they would assume liability for all outstanding debts, including those to the Wartmans if they maintained their lien status.	The defendants argued that they were not personally liable for the Wartmans' claim, as the agreement clearly stated that they would not assume a personal liability for such debts. They contended that the Wartmans' lien was defeated by the prior mortgage on the property, and that the agreement did not contain provisions that bound them to pay off the Wartmans' claim. The defense emphasized that any advance for clearing liens was only among themselves and not intended as an overarching obligation toward third-party claims.

The case "Donald McKinnon v. The People ex rel. Henry Malzacher" was filed on June 13, 1884, and took place in Du Page County, Illinois. The controversy arose from the election for the office of town clerk in South Chicago, held on April 3, 1883. Donald McKinnon, representing the Republican Party, contested the election results after it was declared that Henry Malzacher of the Democratic Party won the election. The critical issue was that ballots were mistakenly printed with the name "Joseph Malzacher" instead of the correct name "Henry Malzacher." This confusion arose because there was no candidate named Joseph Malzacher, and the votes for this name were allegedly cast in error, intending to support the legitimate candidate. The County Court of Du Page County initially ruled in favor of Henry Malzacher, stating that the votes for Joseph should be counted as votes for Henry. McKinnon appealed the decision in hopes of overturning the ruling.	Donald McKinnon, the plaintiff, argued that the election results were incorrectly recorded due to the mistaken appearance of "Joseph Malzacher" on the ballots. He maintained that the ballots should not have been considered valid and that he was the rightful winner of the election. McKinnon sought legal recognition as the legitimately elected town clerk, challenging the validity of the votes cast for the incorrectly printed name.	Henry Malzacher, representing the defendants, contended that the votes cast in the name "Joseph Malzacher" were intended for him, the legitimate Democratic nominee. The defense relied on evidence demonstrating that no individual named Joseph Malzacher existed in the relevant area, asserting that the intention of the voters should dictate how the ballots were counted. Malzacher argued that the inclusion of the erroneous name did not undermine the election's legitimacy, and the ballots should be counted as votes for him.

The case "The City of Dixon v. Eli B. Baker" occurred in September 1872 before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from the City of Dixon's decision to raise the grade of a street and sidewalk, which caused surface water to flow into the basement of Baker's property, resulting in damage to the building and cracks in the walls. Prior to the elevation, Baker's building was two feet above the street grade, and it had adequate drainage. However, post-alteration, the surface water was not properly managed, leading to water entering Baker's property. This raise affected Baker's property significantly, raising concerns that municipalities could alter street grades without considering their impact on adjacent property owners. Baker claimed that the city did not provide adequate drainage, which could have prevented the damage he incurred. The case draws upon past rulings which established that municipalities are liable for injuries to private property caused by their actions regarding public streets, especially when negligence in infrastructure leads to harm.	Eli B. Baker, the plaintiff, claimed that the City of Dixon was responsible for damages resulting from the flow of surface water into his property due to the city's decision to raise the street grade. He argued that the city failed to provide sufficient sewerage to manage surface water, thus affirming their liability for the damages inflicted on his property. His legal request was for compensation for the injuries sustained to his building as a direct consequence of the city’s actions.	The City of Dixon, as the defendant, argued that municipal corporations should not be held liable for incidental damages caused by the natural flow of surface water when altering street grades. They contended that any damages incurred by Baker were incidental and did not arise from negligence on the part of the city. The city sought to establish that they exercised discretion regarding street grade adjustments, and thus could not be held responsible for the subsequent effects that these alterations had on Baker’s property.

In September 1874, the case of Elizabeth Nispel et al. v. William B. Laparle et al. took place in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose over three promissory notes executed by Elizabeth Nispel, a married woman who ran a saloon using her own separate funds. The defendants challenged her liability based on the plea of coverture—arguing that as a married woman, she could not enter into contracts. They claimed that there was an agreement to extend the payment time for the notes that involved giving new notes secured by a mortgage on real estate. The plaintiffs contended that Elizabeth purchased goods for her business with her own means and without her husband's interference. Following a trial, the court entered a judgment in favor of the plaintiffs for $299.80, dismissing the defendants' claims and defenses based on the legal standing of married women in business at that time.	The plaintiffs, represented by Elizabeth Nispel, claimed that the promissory notes in question were valid contracts. They argued that Elizabeth purchased goods with her own money for her own business and, therefore, had the capacity to bind herself contractually despite being married. They sought payment on the notes totaling $299.80.	The defendants presented multiple defenses, including the argument that coverture protected Elizabeth Nispel from liability on the notes. They also asserted that there was an agreement to extend the payment of the notes contingent on providing new notes and a mortgage on property, which they claimed was not properly fulfilled. However, they did not provide adequate proof that the mortgage secured valid property or addressed the objections raised by the plaintiffs regarding the value and title of the real estate.

James M. Lowman v. George A. Lowman et al. is a legal dispute that dates back to the late 19th century, specifically starting from 1884 when James M. Lowman sought to foreclose a mortgage originally assigned to him by Branson Lowman. The case stems from a series of financial transactions involving promissory notes and mortgages between members of the Lowman family and Samuel Burge & Co., starting with a $5,000 note secured by a mortgage dated July 26, 1872, executed by William Lowman and George A. Lowman. This was followed by a mortgage of $400 by George A. Lowman in favor of Branson Lowman. The transactions led to conflicts over the satisfaction of the debts and the enforcement of the mortgage rights. Key individuals involved include James M. Lowman as the plaintiff, who claims the right to enforce the mortgage; George A. Lowman, a defendant and former partner; and Samuel Burge, who holds the conflicting mortgage interests. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court on June 8, 1886, after being originally filed in the Circuit Court of Stark County.	James M. Lowman claims that he is entitled to foreclose on the $400 mortgage originally held by Branson Lowman. He argues that the mortgage was legally assigned to him and that he has the right to collect the debt purportedly owed, despite the assertion made by George A. Lowman regarding the satisfaction of the notes and mortgages. Lowman seeks a judgment of foreclosure to enforce his lien on the property secured by the mortgage.	The primary defense presented by George A. Lowman is that the notes and mortgages had been settled, with claims that the $400 mortgage was satisfied before it was assigned to James M. Lowman. Additionally, the defendant argues that any arrangement involving partnership assets should not serve private debts, particularly given the financial insolvency of the firm. George A. Lowman further asserts that previous legal decisions support his position concerning the satisfaction and merger of the mortgage.

In 1852, Peter Cruce passed away intestate in Union County, Illinois. At the time of his death, he was the guardian of minor children, Lucinda and Philip Cruce, and held funds totaling $346.83 belonging to them. His widow, Sophia Cruce, received a separate property allowance of $675.25, which exceeded the total of the personal estate valued at $247.60, leading to a deficit. The administrator of Peter Cruce's estate sold the deceased's real estate in 1853 for $388 to pay outstanding claims. The administrator initially paid debts classified as first and second class and allocated the remaining funds to Sophia rather than to the wards, whose claims remained unpaid. The case examined the legality of prioritizing the widow's claims over those of the wards, given that the wards were entitled to the funds held by their deceased guardian.	The plaintiffs, represented by the guardians of Lucinda and Philip Cruce, claimed that they were entitled to the proceeds from the sale of Peter Cruce's real estate. They argued that their claims, which were of the third class, should take precedence over the widow's claims due to the specific nature of the funds being held as guardian trust money.	The defendant, Adam Cruce, as the administrator, contended that the widow's claims should be prioritized over those of the wards. He argued that the widow's statutory allowances were due despite the funds belonging to the wards categorizing their claims as third class, seeking to uphold the initial decision that favored satisfying the widow's claims first.

In April 1866, the case of John Wallwork v. William M. Derby et al. arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving two tracts of land previously owned by Charles Boadnight and transferred to Henry S. Monroe, a trustee. Monroe was given the authority to sell the property to cover Boadnight's unpaid notes to Derby. Wallwork later purchased the land from Boadnight, but the sale conducted by Monroe at public auction resulted in Derby winning the bid for one of the tracts. However, the trustee mistakenly conveyed both tracts to Derby, which Wallwork contested, claiming that he owned the remaining tract. Wallwork sought to set aside the sale, arguing that the conveyance exceeded the authority granted to the trustee. The case revolved around the interpretation of the deed and whether Derby had a rightful claim to both pieces of land.	Wallwork, as the plaintiff, contended that the sale and conveyance made by Monroe to Derby should be invalidated due to the trustee's improper conveyance of more property than was purchased. Wallwork argued that he was misled about the land's ownership and sought a decree that would set aside the sale, asserting that he had a legal right to the remaining tract of land based on his purchase from Boadnight.	The defendants, Derby and Monroe, argued that the sale should not be invalidated as the deed of trust authorized the trustee to sell the entire property and Derby was entitled to both tracts since they were advertised as a single offering. They claimed that the correct interpretation of the deed indicated that both parcels were sold together and that any alleged misconduct by the trustee should not affect Derby's title as he paid for the entire property as listed.

The case "Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company v. Annie Ward" arose from an incident that occurred on April 29, 1886, at a railway crossing on Root Street in Cook County, Illinois. Annie Ward, the plaintiff, was waiting to board a Rock Island suburban passenger train when she moved south of Root Street to secure a seat on the approaching train. In doing so, she stood between the new-main and in-main tracks while another train was backing slowly on the new-main track. As she attempted to avoid the draft from the train, she was struck and injured by the train's tank. The location of the crossing had multiple tracks, and while the trains had historically stopped at Root Street to accommodate passengers, the defendant, Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company, denied that Root Street was an official station, claiming that the plaintiff was trespassing when she was struck, since there was no designated platform or ticket sales at that location. Courts considered the long-standing practice of stopping at that location and the obligations of rail companies regarding passenger safety, setting the stage for Ward's claims of negligence against the railroad.	Annie Ward claimed that her injuries were the result of negligence on the part of the Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company. She argued that the company had established a practice of receiving passengers at Root Street, creating a reasonable expectation of safety for those waiting for trains. Ward sought damages for the personal injuries she sustained due to what she deemed the railway's failure to provide a safe waiting environment and sufficient warnings regarding the potential dangers present at the crossing.	The defendant, Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company, asserted that Ward was a trespasser since there was no official station at Root Street, which was not advertised as a stopping point for passengers. They contended that Ward had moved into a dangerous area between the tracks and that the company had no liability for her injuries. The railway argued that it was not legally bound to ensure safety where it had not designated a formal station and that any stopping of trains at Root Street was solely for convenience related to nearby stockyards, not for passenger accommodation.

In 1866, William Mooney brought a legal action against Dennis McCarthey in the Recorder’s Court of Chicago, Illinois. The case arose from Mooney's claims regarding unpaid labor and services he provided to McCarthey, which included loading and unloading vessels with grain. The declaration included various counts for work and labor, goods delivered, and a stated account. Following a trial by jury, a verdict favored Mooney with an award of $230. However, McCarthey appealed the decision, asserting several grounds for reversal, including a motion for a continuance due to supposed inadequacies in the bill of particulars. The court heard the case and ultimately ruled on the merits of the appeal, focusing specifically on whether the evidence presented supported the verdict.	The plaintiff, William Mooney, claimed that he was owed $230 for labor and services rendered to the defendant, Dennis McCarthey. He argued that the evidence demonstrated he performed work for McCarthey, despite McCarthey disputing the specifics of the transactions and the validity of the claim. Mooney's main legal requests included enforcing the judgment in his favor based on the jury's verdict.	The defendant, Dennis McCarthey, contended that the evidence presented by Mooney was insufficient to support the verdict. He moved for a continuance, stating that he had not received a sufficient bill of particulars outlining the claims against him and argued that the trial court erred in not granting this motion. Furthermore, McCarthey asserted that the evidence did not prove he owed Mooney the amount claimed, emphasizing the need for more definitive proof of the labor performed and its value.

In the case of John Telford et al. Administrators v. Susannah Boggs, which was decided in June 1872, the events took place in Marion County, Illinois. The matter arose following the death of Spruce A. Boggs, who died intestate, leaving behind both real and personal estate. Susannah Boggs, the widow of the deceased, and the appellants, who are the administrators of the estate, were the key individuals involved. The probate court appointed appraisers to assess the value of the estate’s personal property, where a total valuation of $388.75 was assigned to specific articles for Susannah's use. However, Susannah executed a document relinquishing her claims to the initially specified items and chose to retain different items of equal value as per the appraiser's estimates. Later, after the administrators sold the other personal property, she sought a larger allowance from the administrators, which resulted in a jury verdict in favor of Susannah for $350 in the circuit court. The case was subsequently appealed by the administrators to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Susannah Boggs, the plaintiff, argued that the initial appraisal and the selection of property allowed to her as a widow were insufficient and did not meet her needs. She requested a larger allowance after relinquishing her initial claim, claiming the right to choose other property of greater value than what had been appraised.	The defendants, John Telford et al. as administrators, argued that the proceedings and evaluations carried out regarding the personal property were regular and lawful. They contended that Susannah had legally exercised her option to select the property she wished to retain at the appraised value, and thus there was no legal basis for her claim for a larger allowance, especially in the absence of any evidence of fraud or misconduct on their part.

On September 27, 1832, in Morgan County, Illinois, plaintiffs William Reihle and Joseph Bains initiated a writ of attachment against the estate of Samuel P. Judson, which was executed upon certain personal property claimed by David Sheldon. Following the sheriff's levy, a jury was convened to determine the rightful ownership of the property, which resulted in a verdict favoring Sheldon, the claimant. Reihle and Bains subsequently appealed this decision to the Circuit Court of Morgan County, filing an appeal bond through their attorney, Stephen B. Sexton. A change of venue was later made to the Madison Circuit Court, where Sheldon sought to dismiss the appeal on various grounds, including the alleged improper execution of the bond. However, the circuit court denied his motion, allowing the case to proceed. During the trial, the defendants presented the writ of attachment, which Sheldon contested but was admitted as evidence. The jury ultimately ruled that the title of the property belonged to Judson, leading to a judgment in favor of Reihle and Bains.	David Sheldon, the plaintiff in error, argued that the appeal bond was improperly executed and claimed that the bond did not meet legal requirements for an appeal, as it lacked proper authorization from the appellants. He requested the court to dismiss the defendants' appeal on these grounds, asserting that the evidence presented did not substantiate the defendants' claim to the property.	William Reihle and Joseph Bains, the defendants in error, contended that the appeal bond was valid and executed by a duly authorized attorney. They argued that the writ of attachment and accompanying documents were admissible evidence, supporting their claim that the property in question rightfully belonged to Samuel P. Judson. The defendants maintained that the jury's finding effectively negated Sheldon’s title to the property based on the attachment.

In 1876, the case of Augustina Hahn v. Joseph Huber and others was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The matter originated from a lawsuit filed by Joseph Huber seeking to foreclose on two trust deeds executed by Philip Hahn and his wife, Augustina Hahn, in Peoria County, Illinois. The first trust deed was executed on September 13, 1868, and the second on December 16, 1870, with the first securing the purchase money for the property involved. An intermediate mortgage had also been given to Joseph Miller on June 26, 1869. After the execution of the mortgages, Philip Hahn was declared insane, and a conservator was appointed for him on October 2, 1871. Both Hahn and Miller were made defendants in the case. Following Philip Hahn’s death on December 1, 1874, a supplemental bill was filed to include Augustina as the administratrix. She claimed her husband was insane during the execution of the trust deeds and stated that she had never released her dower rights in the property. The case continued through various hearings and motions concerning evidence, the role of a jury, and the management of the hearing process until reaching judgment.	Joseph Huber, as the plaintiff, sought the foreclosure of the trust deeds executed by Philip and Augustina Hahn. He argued that the necessary deed and notes were valid and that foreclosure was necessary to recover the debts owed to him secured by these mortgages. Despite challenges raised by Augustina regarding her husband’s mental state at the time of the deeds' execution, Huber contended that the documentation supported his claims.	Augustina Hahn, as the defendant, primarily claimed that her late husband was insane at the time the trust deeds were executed and argued that she retained her dower rights in the property. She contended that the court erred on several procedural grounds and sought a reversal of the decree based on alleged technical mistakes. This included her arguments against the court's handling of evidentiary references and the denial of requests to have questions of fact, such as Philip’s mental state, submitted to a jury.

In 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, John McBean filed a legal action (assumpsit) against Thomas McLean related to services performed for the grading and paving of Washington Street in Chicago during 1858 or 1859. The work was reportedly done at the request of property owners, including McLean's father, Thomas McLean, Sr. The evidence indicated that despite the project being valued at $1,600, no payment had been made by the elder McLean before his death in 1865. After the death of McLean Sr., the property was inherited by Thomas McLean, Jr. and his sister. In the early 1870s, McLean, Jr. allegedly agreed to pay $400 to McBean, reflecting the terms of a settlement made by another property owner, Mr. Peck. However, McLean, Jr. later denied making any such promise. The case led to a trial without a jury, resulting in a judgment favoring McBean for $400.	John McBean claimed he was entitled to payment for the work he performed on Washington Street, asserting that Thomas McLean, Jr. had both acknowledged a debt and promised to pay it. His legal requests were based on what he believed to be verbal agreements made by McLean, Jr. in which he agreed to settle the outstanding amount.	Thomas McLean, Jr. contested the claims by denying he had ever promised to pay McBean for the work done. His defense included arguments citing the absence of enforceable liability under Illinois law, as McLean, Jr. argued he was not legally responsible for his father's debts without evidence that the father's estate was unable to pay such debts. Furthermore, he contended that any claims based on verbal promises were unsupported by consideration.

In 1871 in Livingston County, Illinois, Mason B. Loomis filed a legal action against Joseph Gerson regarding a property dispute. The case arose from a mortgage secured by Peter I. Neilson to Nelson Anderson for a debt of $350, which led to Neilson's conviction for selling liquor without a license in 1869. Following this conviction, the sheriff levied on Neilson's property, which included a homestead he occupied with his family. The property was sold at a sheriff's sale to Loomis, who subsequently became involved in a legal dispute over the legitimacy of that sale. Gerson, who claimed to have acquired the property from Neilson prior to the sale, contended that the sale violated homestead protections under Illinois law, arguing that Neilson was the head of a household and that the property was improperly seized. The Circuit Court initially set aside the sheriff's sale, leading Loomis to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, Joseph Gerson, claimed that the sheriff’s sale of the property was invalid due to the homestead protections afforded to Neilson as a head of family. Gerson argued that Neilson’s residence on the property constituted a homestead, which should not have been subject to sale under a judgment for criminal penalties. He requested that the court declare the sale invalid and remove the cloud on his title from the sheriff's sale.	The defendant, Mason B. Loomis, contended that the sale was conducted legally and claimed ownership of the property acquired through the sheriff’s execution sale. Loomis argued that the sale should not be set aside entirely, suggesting that the court permit him to retain the title if he compensated Gerson with $1,000, countering Gerson’s assertions regarding the illegitimacy of the sale.

In January 1862, in Hancock County, Illinois, Reuben and Susan Weider (plaintiffs in error) were involved in a legal dispute with Benjamin Clark (defendant in error). The case originated as a mortgage foreclosure. Clark had previously held a mortgage on a tract of land owned by Samuel Moore, which he valued at $1,400. Weider entered into discussions to purchase Moore's land, along with another tract owned by Clark, for $4,600, intending to pay $1,000 upfront and the remainder through notes and a mortgage. The plaintiffs argued that the mortgage was executed to secure this purchase money, while Clark contended that the plaintiffs could not claim a homestead exemption to prevent the property's sale. The dispute intensified, leading to a cross-bill where the defendants claimed a homestead exemption. After changing the venue to McDonough County, both parties engaged in legal proceedings regarding the legitimacy of the claims and defenses surrounding the mortgage and the homestead exemption.	The plaintiffs contended that the notes and mortgage given to Clark were solely for the purchase price of the lands involved in the transaction. They argued that since the mortgage covered the purchase, they should not be subject to a foreclosure due to the homestead exemption law. They maintained that they did not owe any mortgage debt to Moore, as payment for the purchase was directed to Clark, making their obligation a direct one to him.	Clark, the defendant, claimed that the entire transaction constituted a straightforward sale of land, asserting that the plaintiffs indeed owed him the debt secured by the mortgage. He argued that the purchase money was legally given to Moore, and as such, the homestead exemption could not be invoked to challenge the foreclosure. Clark maintained that as the head of a family living on the premises, any claims made under the homestead exemption were invalid because the mortgage was for the purchase price of the properties.

Peter Hoener filed a lawsuit against John W. Koch and Gaylord D. Beebe in the Circuit Court of Adams County, Illinois, in January 1877, alleging malpractice as surgeons. The case stemmed from a surgical operation for a strangulated hernia that Hoener underwent, which he claimed was performed unskillfully and unnecessarily, leading to serious injury. Koch entered a plea of not guilty, while Beebe did not respond, resulting in a default judgment against him. During the trial, the jury returned a verdict of not guilty in favor of Koch. Following the trial, the jury was presented with testimony from witnesses, but the plaintiff raised concerns about the admissibility of evidence, particularly regarding the expert testimony that seemed to guide the jury’s decision. The court ultimately ruled against Hoener, demanding costs from him, but he appealed the decision, arguing that there were significant errors in the trial proceedings.	Hoener's main arguments revolved around the alleged malpractice of the defendants, claiming that the surgical treatment he received for his hernia was unnecessary and conducted without proper skill or scientific basis. He sought to establish that Koch and Beebe, as surgeons, were liable for his serious injuries resulting from their actions. Hoener's legal request centered on reversing the trial court's decision and holding the defendants accountable for their alleged malpractice.	The defendants, particularly Koch, contended that they were not guilty of malpractice. Koch maintained a not guilty plea, and the testimony presented during the trial suggested that the medical actions taken were appropriate based on the circumstances. Furthermore, they argued that the plaintiff had not met the burden of proof necessary to demonstrate malpractice, and they requested that the court affirm the trial’s verdict and dismiss the plaintiff’s claims.

The case "George R. Archer et al. v. William Claflin et al." took place in April 1863 in Illinois, presided over by Judge John S. Thompson. The dispute arose from a promissory note, with William Claflin and others (who were the defendants in error) initiating an action of assumpsit against George R. Archer and others (the plaintiffs in error). The case presented questions regarding a potential variance between the note described in the declaration and the one used for assessing damages. The declaration specified a note dated November 3, 1856, but a copy submitted with the declaration bore the year 1860. However, the original note used in court corresponded to the date stated in the declaration. The initial judgment was in favor of the defendants, prompting the plaintiffs to seek a writ of error to contest this ruling.	The plaintiffs argued against the earlier judgment and contended that there was no significant variance between the note detailed in the declaration and the original note presented for damages. They sought to affirm that the assessment of damages was correctly based on a valid note matching the description in their declaration.	The defendants maintained that the discrepancy between the dates of the copy of the note and the original note created a substantive variance that could invalidate the plaintiffs' claims. They argued that this variance should lead to the dismissal of the case, as the original note did not match the filed copy appropriately.

In 1876, Woodford G. McDowell and multiple plaintiffs filed a legal case against Samuel Stewart in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over a chattel mortgage linked to a bond executed during a replevin action concerning property claimed by the sheriff due to three writs against Robert J. Johnson, the original debtor. The issue centered around whether the chattel mortgage from Johnson to McDowell was valid, specifically regarding its acknowledgment according to the legal requirements. The case unfolded in Livingston County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs contended that the mortgage, despite being executed, lacked the necessary acknowledgment as Johnson was not present when it was certified by a justice of the peace. This misrepresentation called into question the mortgage's validity against third parties who were creditors acting in good faith. The case presented by McDowell's party challenged the legal standing of the mortgage and sought to reclaim their rights over the supposedly mortgaged property.	The plaintiffs claimed that the chattel mortgage executed by Robert J. Johnson was valid and that they were entitled to possession of the property specified in the mortgage. They argued that the sheriff's claim to the property was invalid because the mortgage had not been acknowledged in accordance with statutory requirements, asserting their rights over the property as rightful holders of the mortgage.	The defendant, Samuel Stewart, maintained that the mortgage lacked proper acknowledgment and, thus, had no binding effect against third parties, including the sheriff. Stewart contended that since the acknowledgment was falsely certified without Johnson's presence, the plaintiffs could not assert rights over the property against creditors, particularly given the legal precedent that a false acknowledgment renders a mortgage void against third parties acting in good faith.

The case "Eleanor Stribling et al. v. Benjamin S. Prettyman" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1870. The case stemmed from an ejectment action initiated by Prettyman against Casey to recover possession of a property in Tazewell County, Illinois. The heirs of Jacob Haas were permitted to defend the action as parties to the lawsuit. The initial trial took place in February 1865, where the court found in favor of the defendant (Casey). In February 1866, the plaintiffs sought to join the defense based on an affidavit stating a connection of the title of their ancestor to the land in question. Throughout the proceedings, there were arguments regarding the sufficiency of the initial affidavit and the ownership of the property derived from previous transactions. The court ultimately focused on aspects of title, the role of the sheriff’s deeds, and statutory limitations affecting the validity of the judgments and executions associated with the land.	The plaintiffs contended that their ancestor, David C. Alexander, had a valid title to the land through a series of deed transfers. They argued that a prior court judgment against their ancestor was improperly considered a nullity due to the lapse of time before execution. The plaintiffs requested that the judgment be reversed and that they be granted the right to defend their claim to the property.	The defendant, Prettyman, maintained that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a rightful interest in the property and challenged the validity of their title based on the execution process and the timeline of judgments. The defendant argued that the sheriff’s deed was properly admitted as evidence of ownership, as the execution had been appropriately issued. They requested that the court uphold the existing judgment in their favor.

Archibald P. Willis was indicted for larceny during the July term of 1837 in the Gallatin Circuit Court, Illinois. The indictment alleged he stole a pair of shoes valued at $1.75, with the trial occurring in September of the same year. The owners of the stolen shoes were identified only by their initials, "T. D. Hawke and E. Dobbins," a designation deemed insufficient by subsequent court review. Willis was convicted and sentenced to pay a $10 fine and serve one month in county jail. Willis contended that the court should have arrested the judgment due to the vague identification of the owners and that the jury was misdirected regarding an affidavit he had submitted, which was accepted as evidence. The case was appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court to review these issues and the legality surrounding the initial judgment.	Willis's primary arguments included that the Circuit Court erred by not arresting the judgment based on the inadequately described owners of the goods, violating the requirement for precise identification in indictments. Additionally, he claimed that the trial court misdirected the jury concerning the affidavit he provided, which should have been acknowledged as conclusive evidence rather than subject to contradiction.	The defense, represented by the state's attorney, maintained that the affidavit submitted by Willis should not have been treated as definitive evidence. They argued that the jury was correctly instructed to weigh the affidavit among other evidence and could consider it as they deemed appropriate, supporting the position that the indictment was valid, despite the complaints about identification.

On July 4, 1883, Michael Cleary, a single man and the brother-in-law of the appellant Michael Geelan, was brought to the boarding house of Isabell Reid after suffering a severe leg injury due to a train accident. Following the accident, two physicians were called to amputate Cleary's leg. The next morning, Geelan arrived at Reid's boarding house to see Cleary and allegedly promised Reid that he would ensure she was paid for the care she provided. Reid cared for Cleary until August 28, 1883, when Geelan took him away. The core of the dispute revolved around whether Geelan indeed made this promise. Reid claimed he did, while Geelan denied it. The case involved jury deliberation to assess the credibility of witness testimony regarding the promise. The court had to evaluate whether the promise, if made, was valid under the Statute of Frauds.	Isabell Reid, as the appellee, claimed that Michael Geelan promised to pay for the board and care provided to his brother-in-law, Michael Cleary, while he was under her care. Reid requested the court to hold Geelan accountable for the costs incurred during Cleary's stay at her boarding house, arguing the promise was valid and enforceable despite being verbal.	Michael Geelan, the appellant, argued against the existence of the promise, asserting he did not make any commitment to pay for Reid's services. Additionally, Geelan contended that even if he did make such a promise, it was merely collateral and thus void under the Statute of Frauds due to the lack of a written agreement. He maintained that the law did not bind him to Reid's claim.

In the case of Peter Howe v. W. J. Clark, decided on May 27, 1887, the dispute arose in Illinois over a landlord-tenant relationship. Peter Howe was the landlord who leased premises to tenant George Hutson for the period commencing March 1, 1885, to March 1, 1886. During the lease, Hutson removed crops from the leased premises and sold these crops to the defendant, W. J. Clark. Subsequently, Howe sought to recover $117.50, the unpaid rent owed by Hutson, from Clark, arguing that a statutory lien existed on the crops for the unpaid rent. However, the trial court ruled in favor of Clark, leading to Howe's appeal. The central legal issue was whether Howe could enforce the landlord's lien against Clark, who had purchased the crops without actual notice of the lien.	Peter Howe claimed that he was entitled to recover the $117.50 owed in rent for the premises leased to Hutson. He argued that the crops harvested by Hutson were subject to his statutory lien as a landlord. Howe contended that this lien should apply even after the crops were sold to Clark, regardless of whether Clark had knowledge of the lien at the time of purchase.	W. J. Clark defended himself by arguing that he was a bona fide purchaser of the crops without any notice of the landlord's lien held by Howe. Clark maintained that since he had no knowledge of the lien at the time of purchase, Howe could not impose the lien against him. The court's decision suggested that a bona fide purchaser is not liable for liens they are unaware of when acquiring property unless they had some constructive notice or inquiry.

In August 1842, in Scott County, Illinois, Murray McConnel and his wife, along with Holloway W. Vansyckle and his wife, executed a deed to Stark Fielder, which included a legal covenant. The covenant stated that their heirs, executors, and administrators would warrant and defend the title to the property against lawful claims. On October 9, 1845, Stark Fielder conveyed the same property to Lewis Rufner, who recorded the deed. However, on July 10, 1847, a court case was initiated by William Richardson and others against McConnel and other grantors asserting a paramount title. This resulted in a decree in September 1850 confirming that McConnel and others did not defend the title, and as a consequence, Rufner was evicted from the property. Rufner subsequently filed a lawsuit for broken covenants against McConnel and others in the Scott Circuit Court, which ruled in favor of the defendants by sustaining their demurrer, leading Rufner to seek a writ of error. This case, styled 'Lewis Rufner, Plaintiff in Error, v. Murray McConnel et al., Defendants in Error', was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1852.	Lewis Rufner argued that the covenant made by McConnel and the other grantors assured the defense of the title and claimed that they had breached that covenant, resulting in his eviction. He sought a remedy for this breach and contended that the grantors should be held liable for not honoring their obligation to defend the title.	The defendants contended that the covenant did not impose personal liability on the grantors to defend the title but rather required their heirs, executors, and administrators to do so. They argued that Rufner, therefore, did not have a legal right of action against the grantors. The defense maintained that the appropriate remedy would be against the grantors' legal representatives and that any alleged mistake in the deed should be addressed in equity.

The case of Fanny, a woman of color, against Montgomery and others took place in December 1828 within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. Fanny was subjected to acts of trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment, as she sought to assert her right to freedom. The defendants claimed that Fanny and others were captured and brought before a justice of the peace in Bond County, Illinois, because they allegedly owed labor to John Housten in Kentucky. The justice, therefore, issued a certificate allowing Housten to reclaim Fanny on the basis of this alleged debt of service. The defendants maintained that they only assisted Housten under this legal certificate. Fanny's legal team questioned whether the justice had the appropriate jurisdiction to issue such a certificate and whether the defendants acted within legal bounds. Errors were identified in the defendants' plea, particularly regarding the insufficient proof of jurisdiction, and the failure to specify to whom the certificate was granted. This led to a legal dispute wherein Fanny appealed the circuit court's judgment in favor of the defendants.	Fanny's primary arguments revolved around contesting the legality of her capture and the jurisdiction of the justice of the peace who issued the certificate allowing her to be taken back to Kentucky. She asserted that the defendants lacked the necessary legal authority to detain her, claiming that they failed to demonstrate that the justice had jurisdiction or that she owed service at the time the certificate was issued. The plaintiff requested the court to reverse the judgment made in the lower court which had favored the defendants.	The defendants asserted that they acted in accordance with a valid certificate issued by a justice of the peace, claiming that they were justified in assisting Housten in reclaiming Fanny. They contended that as long as their actions were limited to what was necessary under the certificate, they bore no liability for the charges of trespass and false imprisonment. The defendants requested the court to uphold the circuit court's judgment, maintaining that they were within their rights based on the certificate granted to Housten.

In 1873 in Scott County, Illinois, Thomas C. Coffey initiated a legal suit against Joseph B. Fosselman. The case originated as a small claims matter before a justice of the peace and was scheduled for trial on July 31, 1873. Coffey requested a continuance to August 21, 1873, which was granted. After the trial in August, judgment was ruled in favor of Fosselman. Subsequently, Coffey appealed this decision, filing a bond with the justice of the peace on September 6, 1873. The case was then heard in the county court, where Coffey again sought a continuance, citing the absence of key witnesses who resided in an adjoining county. However, this request was denied. The court ruled in favor of Fosselman again, with a judgment amounting to $40.20 entered against Coffey. The appeals process continued, leading to this case reaching the Illinois Supreme Court.	Coffey contended that the county court wrongly denied his motion for a continuance, which he believed was necessary due to the absence of witnesses who could support his case. He argued that the court’s decision to grant judgment without allowing him the chance to present these testimonies was unjust and called for a reversal of the lower court's judgment as a legal remedy.	Fosselman, on the other hand, asserted that Coffey's failure to diligently secure the presence of his witnesses was inadequate grounds for a continuance. The defense maintained that there was no evidence showing efforts were made by Coffey to obtain witness depositions or subpoenas. Fosselman argued that the county court acted within its jurisdiction to deny the continuance and affirmed the validity of the judgment rendered against Coffey.

John W. Marsh, acting as the administrator of the estate of Caroline A. Sturges, brought this case to the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The case originated in Cook County, where Sturges filed a bill in equity against Charles H. Morton, Henry C. Clement, and George R. Clarke. Sturges sought to prevent the sale of certain properties in Chicago based on nine trust deeds securing promissory notes totaling $50,000. The trust deeds allowed the holders to declare debts due if interest payments were not made. The lower court dissolved an injunction initially placed to halt the sale, which led to the assessment of $865 in damages against Sturges, comprising trustee fees, attorney fees, and printing costs for the sale notices.	The plaintiff, John W. Marsh, argued that the principal debt secured by the trust deeds was not due and sought to maintain the injunction against the sale of the properties. However, this argument was ultimately abandoned, conceding the defendants' right to declare the debt due upon failure to pay interest. The appellant contested the assessment of damages awarded to the defendants upon the dissolution of the injunction.	The defendants, represented by Morton, Clement, and Clarke, contended that they had the correct legal right to declare the debt due due to the failure to pay interest, justifying the decision to proceed with the sale. They claimed the assessed damages were appropriate, including the costs for printing nine notices of sale and trustee fees, asserting that no irregularities occurred in their process.

In the case of William Borden v. Catharine M. Croak, Administratrix, the events unfolded in Chicago, Illinois, where William Borden leased a store located in Borden Block to Thomas P. Croak, a merchant tailor. The lease stipulated that Borden would have a first lien for unpaid rent on the property associated with Croak. Croak passed away on June 3, 1886, with two months' rent owed at that time. Following his death, Borden communicated with Croak's estate and entered into a lease agreement with another tenant, explicitly stating that he waived none of his rights under the original lease. In November 1886, Borden sought to claim the rent due for June and July through the Probate Court, requesting that this amount be declared a first lien on the estate's assets, which were ultimately inadequate to satisfy the widow's award. The court addressed whether the lien was valid based on the terms of the lease and pointed out ambiguities regarding the definition of “property” for the lien's applicability.	Borden claimed that he was entitled to a first lien on the assets of Croak's estate for the rent due for June and July 1886, as established in the lease agreement. He argued that the lease contract clearly granted him this right, asserting that the lien was valid against Croak’s estate and specifically against the administratrix, Catharine M. Croak.	The defendant, Catharine M. Croak, through her role as administratrix, challenged the validity of Borden's claimed lien, stating that the lease's language was too broad and ambiguous to establish a clear lien on after-acquired property. The defense argued that without proper identification of the property, any lien Borden claimed was uncertain and thus invalid. They contended that the lien was merely equitable and could not be sustained without clearly specified property.

In the case of Oliver W. McKenzie v. Joseph M. Remington, which took place in September 1875 in Bureau County, Illinois, the plaintiff, Oliver W. McKenzie, brought an action of trespass against the defendant, Joseph M. Remington. The dispute arose over damage caused by Remington's cattle to McKenzie's crops, which included 20 acres of corn, 16 acres of oats, and 3 acres of Hungarian grass. Evidence indicated that between July 3 and August 21, Remington’s cattle and horses were found feeding on McKenzie’s crops on several occasions, resulting in significant damage. The trial resulted in a jury verdict in favor of McKenzie, awarding him $116 in damages. The case hinged on conflicting evidence regarding whether there was a valid arbitration concerning earlier damages and whether all instances of trespass were adequately covered by it. While Remington claimed a settlement through arbitration for an earlier trespass incident, McKenzie and his son asserted that the authority of the arbitrators to assess earlier damages had been revoked. The issue also involved procedural disputes about jury instructions and the timing of the arbitration.	McKenzie primarily argued that Remington’s cattle trespassed multiple times into his crops, causing extensive damage. He sought damages totaling $116 based on the estimated loss to his agriculture. McKenzie contended that there was no valid arbitration agreement for damages prior to August 18, as he had revoked any previous authorization for arbitrators to assess those damages.	Remington's defense rested on the assertion that the damages had been settled through arbitration for an earlier incident, where an arbitrator assessed the damages at $23.40. He also disputed the evidence presented regarding the number and timing of the trespasses, arguing that a prior agreement should negate further claims for damages. Additionally, he contested various procedural aspects of the trial, including the integrity of jury instructions and the refusal of a new trial based on newly discovered evidence regarding the arbitration timing.

Charles S. Morton, the appellant, and John Gateley, the appellee, were involved in a legal dispute stemming from a case initially presented before a justice of the peace. The case was then appealed to the Circuit Court of Coles County, Illinois, during the April term of 1835. The conflict arose from financial transactions related to labor performed jointly by Morton, Gateley, and a third individual in constructing a building. Gateley claimed that Morton received compensation for work that was supposed to be shared among the three but obtained the full payment without Gateley’s knowledge or consent. Morton’s appeal followed a judgment against him in the Circuit Court, where he was ordered to pay $47.50 along with court costs. The key individuals involved were Morton, Gateley, and the presiding judge Justin Harlan, alongside their respective attorneys.	The plaintiff, Charles S. Morton, argued against the Circuit Court’s refusal to instruct the jury that there was insufficient evidence supporting Gateley's claim of money received for work. Morton requested that the jury be directed to disregard the allegations concerning the financial arrangement and the existence of partnership between him, Gateley, and the third party.	John Gateley, the defendant, contended that compensation for the labor performed was rightfully shared according to their agreement. He asserted that Morton had received funds that were due to Gateley's share without authorization, thus justifying his claims for money had and received. Gateley sought affirmation of the Circuit Court’s decisions regarding jury instructions on the grounds that sufficient evidence existed for the jury to consider.

In April 1865, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the case of Abraham L. Winne v. David S. Hammond et al., originating from Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Abraham L. Winne, had been employed by Lewis Lillie to manage the sale of fireproof safes in Chicago under an agreement stipulating his compensation and responsibilities. Winne was to receive an annual salary of $1,200 and a percentage of the sales as commissions, along with additional sums under certain conditions. He was responsible for leasing a store, hiring clerks, and conducting the business while covering expenses with business proceeds. A dispute arose when the defendant, Sheriff David S. Hammond, and his deputy, John A. Kelson, levied an attachment on the safes, claiming them to be Lillie's property, which Winne argued violated his rights as a factor holding a lien on the goods for the debts owed to him for services rendered and advances made. Winne filed a trespass action against Hammond due to this alleged wrongful seizure.	Winne contended that he was acting as a factor under the contract with Lillie, asserting that he held a lien on the safes in his possession due to unpaid commissions and other advances related to the sale of the safes. He sought damages for the trespass, claiming that the court erred in instructing the jury that he was not a factor and therefore did not hold any lien on the property in question.	The defendants argued that Winne was an employee of Lillie, not a factor, and claimed that he had no legal lien over the property in question. They contended that the court's instruction to the jury was correct, leading to the jury's verdict in favor of the defendants, concluding that Winne was not entitled to any claims regarding the safes.

Samuel J. Hayes filed a legal case against The Ottawa, Oswego & Fox River Valley Railroad Company regarding the condemnation of his land for railroad use. This case took place in LaSalle County, Illinois, and the proceedings were conducted in September 1870. Hayes's land was situated within the town of Farm Bidge, where the railroad company planned to construct a line from Streator to Ottawa. During the trial, an agreement signed by representatives of the railroad company was presented, stating that several infrastructure improvements, including depots and farm crossings, would be established as part of the railroad's construction. Disputes arose regarding the admissibility of evidence pertaining to the potential benefits of the railroad to Hayes's property and the location of the depot, which were deemed pertinent for assessing compensation for the condemned land. The jury was instructed to consider both the value of the land taken and the potential damages, which led to a conflicting opinion about the treatment of benefits in relation to compensation. Consequently, the case hinged on the interpretation of state law regarding land condemnation and the assessment of damages and benefits.	The plaintiff, Samuel J. Hayes, argued that the compensation offered for his condemned land did not adequately reflect its full value. He contended that the jury should only consider the value of the land at the time of condemnation, rather than potential future benefits from the railroad’s construction. Furthermore, Hayes claimed that erroneous jury instructions allowed benefits derived from the railroad to offset the damages owed to him, which he believed contradicted state law regarding compensation for condemned land.	The defendant, represented by The Ottawa, Oswego & Fox River Valley Railroad Company, asserted that the potential benefits of the railroad to Hayes's remaining land should be considered when determining compensation. They argued that evidence about the anticipated location of a depot, which could favorably impact property values, was relevant for assessing the overall impact on Hayes's land. The railroad company contended that the jury's consideration of these benefits was appropriate under the circumstances, and they sought to uphold the validity of the jury's decision based on this framework.

In June 1868, the case of Christopher H. Preisker v. The People of the State of Illinois was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from an indictment with two counts against Christopher H. Preisker. The first count charged him with rape, while the second count accused him of assault with intent to commit rape. During the trial, it became evident that there was insufficient proof supporting the first count. The evidence regarding the second count was also deemed unsatisfactory. A significant point of contention arose from a jury instruction given by the court, which stated that if the jury believed the defendant not guilty of the first count but guilty of an attempt on the second, they should convict him under that count. The defense argued that this wording was misleading as the second count did not accuse Preisker of an attempt, but rather an actual assault with a specific intent. The jury found Preisker guilty, leading to the appeal on the basis of the erroneous jury instruction. The court ultimately ruled on this appeal.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Preisker was guilty of the charges as outlined in the indictment. They maintained that despite the lack of evidence for the first count, the evidence surrounding the second count warranted a conviction for assault with the intent to commit rape, as the intent behind the assault was clear, despite the vague jury instructions. The plaintiff sought a conviction based on the jury’s findings.	The defendant, Christopher H. Preisker, contended that the jury instruction concerning the second count was misleading and improperly stated. The defense argued that the instruction suggested a different charge than that which was brought against him, specifically by implying that an attempt was involved when the charge was solely for an assault with intent. They asserted that the jury's verdict was flawed due to this erroneous instruction and sought to have the judgment reversed.

The case "Clark Roberts et al., Adm'rs, etc., v. Daniel K. Draper" occurred in January 1886 in Wheeling, Cook County, Illinois. The case was initiated by the administrators of the estate of Timothy Hubbard, who had passed away without a will. They issued a citation against Daniel K. Draper, who was Hubbard's step-son, demanding that Draper pay over $650 that Hubbard had entrusted to him before a trip to his hometown in Amherst, Massachusetts. Hubbard had instructed Draper to ensure that $600 of this money was donated to the Foundlings’ Home and $50 allocated for a depot construction project if he did not return. After a court hearing in the probate court, Draper was ordered to pay $600 to the administrators. Upon appealing this decision to the circuit court, Draper testified that the money was meant to be held in trust until Hubbard’s death, which he anticipated could happen during his journey. Following a trial and a jury verdict in favor of Draper, the administrators appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court, seeking a new trial based on claims regarding the nature of the moneys given to Draper.	The plaintiffs, as administrators of Timothy Hubbard's estate, argued that Draper was obliged to hand over $650 from the estate because it was intended for charitable donations. They contended that the money was not a gift but rather a conditional payment contingent upon Hubbard's death during his journey. Their request was to overturn the lower court's judgment favoring Draper and to have the funds returned to the estate.	Draper argued that the funds in question were not a gift but a conditional deposit, with possession held with the intent to fulfill Hubbard's request only in the event of his death during the trip. He maintained that since Hubbard returned safely and made no formal gift transfer or will specifying otherwise, the funds remained his to hold. Draper sought to have the circuit court's verdict upheld, thereby allowing him to retain the funds.

In January 1868, in Hancock County, Illinois, Noah Cook and Martha Reason filed a case against Robert Sinnamon in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case was brought before the court following a judgment from the lower circuit court that ruled in favor of Sinnamon. The legal action was an ejectment case, which is typically used to regain possession of property. The plaintiffs’ declaration included three counts: the first alleging title in Noah Cook, the second joint title in Noah Cook and Martha Reason, and the third solely in Martha Reason. The key issue revolved around a patent granted to Martha Reason and the other heirs at law of James Reason, deceased. The court needed to determine whether this patent was adequate evidence to support Martha Reason's claim to title, and crucially, whether she could be considered the sole heir at law of James Reason without further proof of other heirs.	The plaintiffs, Noah Cook and Martha Reason, claimed that the patent issued to Martha Reason and the other heirs of James Reason established their title to the property in question. They argued that the circuit court erred in its judgment by failing to recognize Martha Reason's rights derived from the patent, which they believed should have been sufficient evidence for their claim.	Robert Sinnamon, the defendant, contended that the evidence presented by the plaintiffs was insufficient to support their claim. He argued that the patent, which named Martha Reason and the other heirs, did not conclusively establish Martha as the sole heir of James Reason. The defendant maintained that without proof that Martha was the only heir, the court could not determine the extent of her legal title to the property.

In April 1866, the case of James H. Reese v. John G. Mitchell was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from events that took place earlier in 1860 in Chicago, Illinois. James H. Reese (the plaintiff) filed a replevin action against John G. Mitchell (the defendant), seeking the recovery of personal property that had been seized. Reese's claim was based on a chattel mortgage executed by Thomas Sim, which was designed to secure a promissory note of $680.50 due on November 14, 1859. According to the mortgage, Sim was allowed to retain possession of the property until he defaulted on the payment. However, on November 16, 1860, Mitchell seized the property under two executions issued against Sim, just two days after the note's maturity. The case was presented to the court without a jury. The key issue was whether Reese was guilty of laches, or delay, in taking possession of the property before Mitchell's levy. The court ultimately found for the defendant, asserting that Reese's inaction did not protect his property from the executions.	James H. Reese argued that he held a valid chattel mortgage that entitled him to the possession of the property, asserting that the note was not yet due since it was customary among bankers and business people to allow days of grace after the maturity date. He contended that Mitchell's levy was improper as he (Reese) had not defaulted on enforcing the mortgage before the seizure occurred.	John G. Mitchell contended that he legally seized the property under execution warranted by valid judgments against Sim. He argued that Reese failed to act promptly to reclaim his property after the note's maturity, rendering the possessions subject to the levy. The court upheld this argument, stating that allowing the mortgaged property to remain with the mortgagor after the default was fraudulent toward creditors.

Stephen R. Moore filed a legal action against The Illinois Central Railroad Company in September 1873, concerning an alleged overcharge in passenger fare.
