The incident occurred on July 2, 1871, when Moore, after boarding a passenger car in Chicago, intended to travel to Kankakee, a distance of fifty-six miles. He offered the conductor a fare of three cents per mile, which was consistent with a proposed statute. However, the conductor refused to accept this amount and demanded the established fare of two dollars and forty cents for the entire trip. To avoid being removed from the train, Moore paid the higher fare under protest. The case began before a justice of the peace and later went to the circuit court, where it was determined that the railroad commissioners had not yet classified the railroad under the relevant legislative act (April 13, 1871) that would establish maximum fares. The circuit court ruled in favor of the railroad company, and the case was subsequently appealed.	Stephen R. Moore claimed that he was wrongfully charged a fare exceeding the allowable rate of three cents per mile as stipulated by the legislation enacted in April 1871. He sought to recover the amount he paid over the legally established fare, arguing that the railroad company’s demand for the higher fare was unlawful due to the lack of assignment for their road under the said act at the time of travel.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company defended against Moore's claims by arguing that at the time of the incident, its road had not been assigned to any specific fare class by the railroad commissioners, which meant that there was no violation of any fare regulations. They asserted that the charges imposed were reasonable and consistent with the company's pre-established rates, and therefore, the conductor had the right to demand the usual fare as a condition for carrying Moore as a passenger.

Frances W. Hervey filed a bill against Asahel Gage in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, in 1884. Hervey claimed ownership of specific parcels of land and sought to invalidate two tax deeds that purportedly transferred property to Gage. She argued that the deeds clouded her title. The court found that Hervey was in possession of the property at the time of the suit and had sufficient interest to maintain her claims. The first tax deed was deemed void due to constitutional provisions, and while the second deed was initially contended as valid by Gage, the court noted flaws in the affidavits supporting its legitimacy. Specifically, the notice of purchase was improperly served, as it did not fulfill statutory requirements for both parties involved in the taxation. This led to the conclusion that the second deed, too, could be set aside as a cloud on Hervey's title, provided she reimbursed Gage for the amounts he paid at the tax sales and related taxes, along with interest.	Frances W. Hervey asserted that she was the rightful owner of the property and sought to cancel the tax deeds held by Asahel Gage, as they were a cloud on her title. She claimed that the deeds were invalid due to improper notice and failure to comply with statutory requirements, which did not allow Gage to claim legal title. Her legal request aimed for a decree that would establish her ownership unequivocally by nullifying Gage's tax deeds.	Asahel Gage contended that the second tax deed was a valid transfer of property and argued that he had followed legal procedures to acquire it. He maintained that the affidavits he filed demonstrated compliance with statute requirements and asserted that the court should sustain the validity of his tax title. Gage's key requests included dismissal of Hervey's claims and reaffirmation of his ownership based on the tax deeds.

Alonzo A. Hill filed a case against Jaba Bell et al. in the Illinois Appellate Court regarding a judgment he sought for services rendered in threshing or hulling clover. The case was heard on September 21, 1888, at the County Court of Brown County, presided over by Judge J. J. McBohxold. The key issue at hand was related to the operation of a threshing machine powered by a horse, which utilized tumbling rods. Hill provided this service using a machine that did not comply with the state statute requiring that all sections of the tumbling rod, except the section nearest the horse power, be safely boxed or secured while in operation. The statute aimed to prevent accidents during the use of such machines. During the trial, it was determined that while some protection was offered at the joints of the rods, there was no substantial compliance with the statute's requirement to secure the entirety of the tumbling rods, leading to an evaluation of whether Hill was entitled to any recovery for his services. The court found no evidence demonstrating that the device used sufficiently mitigated dangers associated with the unprotected sections.	The plaintiff, Alonzo A. Hill, claimed compensation for services rendered in threshing clover. He argued that the work was performed using a threshing machine fit for service and thus sought legal remedy for the payment owed to him as per the work done. Hill maintained that the defendant's failure to secure the tumbling rods as required by statutory law should not limit his right to recovery for the performed services.	The defendants contended that the plaintiff's claim for compensation should be barred due to non-compliance with the statutory requirements regarding the safety of tumbling rods linked to horse-powered machinery. They argued that the failure to properly secure the rods would void any claims for damages or services rendered. Given that there was no pretense of compliance with the statute, the defense maintained that Hill could not seek legal remedy for the services he rendered due to his negligence in following safety protocols.

The case "George Stinson et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. The key individuals involved included George Stinson, Thomas Perkins, W. H. Farmer as defendants, and the People of the State of Illinois as the plaintiff. The events in question took place on a railroad train traveling from Detroit to Chicago, notably during a portion of the journey in the State of Indiana. The defendants orchestrated a scheme involving a wager where Stinson (A) wagered money against an express package containing supposed funds, which was later revealed to be filled with waste paper. Perkins (B) acted as a stakeholder for the wager. Following the transaction, Perkins refused to return the wagered money to Stinson upon discovering the fraud. The parties were subsequently arrested in Chicago, where the money was found in the possession of Perkins. The case hinges on the alleged larceny and the legal interpretation of whether possession and title to the money had been fraudulently obtained.	The plaintiff, representing the State of Illinois, argued that Stinson, Perkins, and Farmer participated in a fraudulent scheme that constituted larceny. The prosecution claimed that Perkins conspired with Stinson and Farmer to deprive the prosecutor (the original owner of the wagered money) of his property through deceitful means. They maintained that Perkins did not act as a mere stakeholder, but rather as a participant in the felonious design to misappropriate the money by claiming it was staked against something of value, which turned out to be fraudulent.	The defendants contended that there was no felonious intent behind their actions. They argued that Perkins, as a stakeholder, was merely acting as an intermediary in a wager, and that the original transaction was a voluntary act consenting to the wager made by Stinson. They claimed the lack of prior acquaintance or conspiracy among themselves nullified any implications of wrongdoing, and therefore, there was no larceny as Perkins had no intention to deprive Stinson of his money.

In 1819, a legal case arose in Madison County, Illinois, involving appellants François Coleen and Abraham Claypole against appellee Daniel Figgins. The case stemmed from a writ issued by the Madison circuit court on March 31, 1819, which was intended to be returnable to the May term of the court. However, this writ was deemed void because the act establishing the circuit courts had not taken effect until April 1, 1819. Consequently, the writ was invalid as it was returnable to a court that did not yet exist at the time of its issuance. The court ruled that no appearance by the parties could rectify this issue, determining that the writ constituted a fundamentally flawed process. Therefore, the lower court was required to quash the writ due to its significant deviation from legitimate legal process. Ultimately, the court refrained from addressing any other errors noted in the appeal, as the resolution of this primary issue determined the case's outcome.	The plaintiffs, François Coleen and Abraham Claypole, contended that the writ issued by the Madison circuit court was null and void as it was based on an act that was not yet in effect. They argued that the court was obligated to quash the void writ, which was improperly issued, and that the irregularity in the process could not be cured by any appearance made by the defendant. They sought a legal clarification affirming that improper process cannot be validated through appearance and pleading.	The defendant, Daniel Figgins, argued that any irregularity in the process was irrelevant due to his appearance in court. He maintained that an appearance would typically cure minor defects in process, even if the process was void. Figgins' defense hinged on the assertion that the presence of the defendant in court, regardless of the preceding irregularities, was sufficient to allow for the case to proceed and that the error involving the writ did not invalidate the process overall.

In the case of *George F. Sturtevant et al. v. Church Sturtevant*, decided on March 27, 1886, the dispute arose in Stark County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, George F. Sturtevant and others, sought to set aside two deeds executed by Church Sturtevant, the defendant. Church, who was nearly 80 years old and in failing health, had conveyed significant property to his nephew George, under the agreement that George would care for and support him. The conveyance occurred on May 13, 1881, after George persuaded Church to allow his family to move to the farm, assuring Church he would provide for him in his declining years. Church's condition at the time was a concern, as he was described as having both physical and mental frailties, exacerbated by isolation and family neglect. The plaintiffs alleged that the deeds were executed under undue influence, failing to meet legal standards of mental competency and consideration due to deceitful practices by George. Following the transaction, the plaintiffs claimed George did not fulfill his obligations to care for Church, consequently leading to the legal challenge against the deeds they believed were fraudulently obtained.	The plaintiffs claimed that the deeds should be annulled for several reasons: they alleged undue influence by George over Church at the time of the transaction; Church lacked the mental competency to engage in such legal agreements due to his age and condition; the deeds were made without valid consideration, as Church was deceived; the deeds weren't properly delivered; and lastly, George had failed in his contractual duties to care for Church. They sought the court to declare the deeds void and restore Church's ownership of the property.	In defense, George Sturtevant asserted that the deeds were executed voluntarily and that Church was of sound mind and understanding. George denied any wrongdoing, stating that he had a genuine intent to care for Church and that any supposed influence was not undue; rather, it was based on their familial relationship. He refuted claims of deception, claiming that all conditions were met, including care and support following the move onto the property. Furthermore, he contended that the deeds were delivered appropriately in line with legal requirements.

In 1856, in Pike County, Illinois, Benjamin Sigsworth (the appellant) was involved in a legal dispute with John Coulter (the appellee) concerning a promissory note. The underlying matter revolved around a lawsuit Coulter had initiated against Sigsworth's brother, John Sigsworth, for the loss of a cow. In a prior justice court proceeding, Coulter sought to recover damages for the cow which he claimed was lost due to John's fault. To settle this dispute, Benjamin Sigsworth provided a note to Coulter for $45, dated May 1, 1854, which was due in fifteen days. After an adverse ruling in the justice court, Benjamin appealed to the Pike Circuit Court. During the appeal, the plaintiff, John Coulter, submitted the promissory note as evidence. In response, Benjamin attempted to challenge the validity of the note by introducing testimonies that questioned Coulter's original claim regarding the cow's loss, arguing that Coulter had no legitimate basis for suing his brother. However, the court found that the note was given as part of a valid compromise to settle a suit initiated in good faith, rendering Benjamin's arguments insufficient.	The plaintiff, John Coulter, maintained that the promissory note given by Benjamin Sigsworth was valid and supported by a lawful consideration—the resolution of the attachment suit regarding the loss of his cow. He argued that the note represented a settlement of a genuine contractual dispute and sought to enforce its payment in court.	Benjamin Sigsworth contended that the note should be void as there was no actual cause of action against his brother, claiming that he should not be compelled to fulfill an obligation arising from a settlement that lacked a legitimate basis. He introduced evidence trying to show that Coulter had no rightful claim, arguing that the note was given without valid consideration.

Thomas Morgan, the appellant, filed an appeal against William D. Smithson and the County Commissioners of Scott County in 1847 following a decision made by the County Commissioners’ Court regarding the assessment of his property for taxes for the year 1845. Morgan sought a reduction of his property assessment, but his application was denied. He subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court, where he requested to dismiss the appeal. However, the court refused his request and dismissed the appeal instead. The case revolves around the interpretation of the 26th section of the 89th chapter of the Revised Statutes, which allows individuals aggrieved by property assessments to seek reductions through the County Commissioners’ Court within a limited timeframe. The decision emphasizes that the discretion exercised by the County Court in such matters cannot be reviewed by other courts, confirming that the Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction over the case. The case was presided over by the Hon. Samuel D. Lockwood during its dismissal at the November special term in 1846.	Thomas Morgan claimed that the assessment of his property was too high and requested a reduction from the County Commissioners’ Court. Following the court's denial, he appealed to the Circuit Court, asserting that he was aggrieved by the decision, and sought the court's intervention to lower the tax assessment. Morgan argued for the right to dismiss his appeal in the Circuit Court.	The defendants, led by William D. Smithson and the County Commissioners of Scott County, contended that the Circuit Court did not have jurisdiction to review the County Court's discretionary decision regarding property assessments. They argued that the assessment process was solely within the County Court's jurisdiction and that Morgan had no right to dismiss his case in the Circuit Court because the appeal was unauthorized. The defense requested the court to affirm the dismissal of Morgan's appeal.

In June 1851, the case of Reuben Vose et al. v. James Hart was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The action originated from a replevin case that took place in the Lake Circuit Court, where the plaintiffs, Reuben Vose and others, sought the recovery of goods allegedly taken by the defendant, James Hart. The trial, overseen by Judge Dickey, concluded with a verdict favoring Hart, awarding him damages of $15.85 plus costs, and a return of the property in question. The plaintiffs then filed a motion for a new trial, which was overruled, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant illegally took their goods and requested a return of these goods along with damages. They contended that the taking of the goods was unauthorized and sought legal redress through the replevin action.	The defendant, James Hart, argued against the plaintiffs' claims by filing a plea of "non cepit," which denied the allegations of taking the goods as stated by the plaintiffs. In essence, Hart contended that, regardless of the ownership claims, the question at hand was whether he had taken the goods, which he denied.

John Chilton v. The People, etc., for use of Anna E. Jones is a legal case that took place in January 1873 in Madison County, Illinois. The case originated from a bastardy prosecution against John N. Chilton, which was brought before a justice of the peace. Following the hearing, the justice required Chilton to enter into a bond of $700 to ensure his appearance at the next term of the circuit court. During that term, it was determined through a trial that Chilton was indeed the father of the child in question. As a result, he was ordered to enter another bond for payments of $100 to the child's mother in the first year and $50 for each subsequent year over the next nine years, as well as cover the costs of the case. However, after this ruling, Chilton failed to enter into the required bond and left the court without permission. The appellant sought to contest the terms of the bond, leading to a demurrer based on alleged deficiencies, including the lack of a seal which is mandated by statute for such bonds. The circuit court initially ruled against Chilton, leading to an appeal.	The plaintiff argued that John N. Chilton was liable for breaching the conditions of the bond he executed, which required him to remain at the court without departing. The plaintiff contended that his failure to remain constituted a breach of the bond's terms, thus entitling the plaintiff to the penalty stipulated in the bond. The claims included seeking payment based on the bond and enforcing the conditions set forth during the original trial regarding child support payments.	John Chilton's defense centered on the argument that the document he signed should not be construed as a valid bond since it lacked a seal, which is a statutory requirement. The defense maintained that without a seal, the instrument was not binding as a bond and, therefore, should be declared void. Chilton's legal team also contended that the matter was mischaracterized in the proceedings, suggesting that it was not treated properly as a formal bond issue.

In this legal case, "David Hutchinson v. Louis Oswald," the events unfolded in White Hall, Illinois, culminating in a judgment rendered by the Illinois Appellate Court on August 20, 1885. The dispute centers around the ownership of two spring wagons that were the subject of an action of replevin brought by the plaintiff, David Hutchinson, against the defendant, Louis Oswald. Prior to the legal action, Hutchinson had ordered the wagons from the Studebaker Wagon Company, and although he was initially involved in the sale of farm machinery, his business had ceased by June 1882. Hutchinson maintained possession of some articles, including the wagons, in the warehouse of Absalom Mitchell, from whom he had ordered the wagons. In January 1883, Mitchell sold the contents of the warehouse, including the two spring wagons in question, to Oswald. Hutchinson claimed he had not sold the wagons and sought to reclaim them, leading to the trial where conflicting claims regarding ownership arose.	David Hutchinson, the plaintiff, argued that he had rightful ownership of the two spring wagons and did not consent to their sale to Louis Oswald by Absalom Mitchell. He claimed that the wagons were wrongfully taken from him, asserting that he had not transferred ownership to Mitchell nor permitted him to sell them. Hutchinson sought the return of the wagons and damages for their detention.	Louis Oswald, the defendant, contended that he purchased the wagons in good faith from Absalom Mitchell, who appeared to be the owner due to his possession. Oswald argued that, under the circumstances, he was not legally obliged to inquire further about the true ownership of the wagons and maintained that he acquired a good title to the property. He requested the court to uphold the judgment in his favor, underscoring the principle that one who lacks title cannot transfer ownership.

In September 1871, in Cook County, Illinois, Edwin L. Gowen engaged in a business transaction involving the sale of a three-story brick building situated on a leased lot. At the time of the transaction, Gowen was in the process of relocating the building when Edward Kehoe allegedly purchased it. Following the sale, Kehoe took control of the building and the workers tasked with its movement. However, a dispute arose regarding the nature of the sale. Gowen argued it was an absolute sale, while Kehoe maintained it was conditional, contingent upon Gowen proving ownership and the absence of any liens. Just after the sale, on October 9, 1871, the building was destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire, complicating matters further. The court was tasked with determining whether the sale was indeed absolute or conditional, based on the conflicting evidence presented.	The plaintiff, Edwin L. Gowen, claimed that he sold the brick building to Edward Kehoe outright. He sought a judgment affirming the sale was absolute, contending that any condition related to ownership verification or lien status had been waived. Gowen argued that the nature of the sale should be recognized as final and that the control transferred to Kehoe was definitive and legitimate at the time of the alleged sale.	The defendant, Edward Kehoe, argued that the sale was conditional, hinging upon Gowen's proof of ownership and the absence of liens on the building. Kehoe contended that because the sale was made under these conditions, and since the building was destroyed shortly after the transaction, he believed he was not liable under a sale he deemed imperfect. He requested the court to overturn the judgment in favor of Gowen based on his interpretation of the sale's terms.

The case "Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company v. S. S. Peterson" took place in McDonough County, Illinois, and was decided on November 23, 1889. The key individuals involved were S. S. Peterson, the plaintiff, who was employed as a section hand by the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, the defendant. On the day of the incident, which was between five and six o’clock in the afternoon, Peterson and his fellow workers were using a handcar on the railroad while returning home. An extra freight train, operated by the defendant, was moving in the opposite direction on the track. Neither the crew of the train nor the men on the handcar were aware of each other’s presence until shortly before the collision occurred. The engineer of the train took all reasonable actions to prevent the collision by signaling and braking, but ultimately, the handcar was struck. Peterson sustained injuries as he attempted to evade the train but inadvertently moved in a dangerous direction. The case revolved around allegations of negligence on the part of the train crew versus contributory negligence by Peterson.	The plaintiff, S. S. Peterson, claimed that he was injured due to the negligent management of a locomotive engine by the employees of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company. He alleged that while executing his duties and exercising due care with the handcar, the train struck him due to the train crew's failure to recognize and prevent the impending collision. Peterson sought compensation for his injuries, arguing that the railroad company’s negligence was the direct cause of the accident.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, argued that their train crew acted within the bounds of standard operating procedures and took all reasonable measures to prevent the collision once they became aware of the handcar's proximity. They contended that there was no negligence on their part, as they had no reason to expect the handcar on the track and were not notified of its presence. The defendant also hinted at possible contributory negligence on Peterson's part, suggesting that his actions in the moment of danger contributed to the injuries he sustained.

In January 1870, the case "John Fetrow v. Reuben H. Merriwether" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered around an eighty-acre tract of land in Macon County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Reuben H. Merriwether, claimed ownership of the land based on a title he originally deduced from the general government, presenting a chain of title during the trial. The defendant, John Fetrow, challenged this claim by attempting to assert a paramount outstanding title. He introduced a mortgage from E. M. Thorpe, through whom Merriwether derived his title, to J. Park, citing a breach of condition in the mortgage that allowed him to retain possession of the land. The defense hinged on the assertion that the mortgage should be deemed valid if certain promissory notes associated with it proved to be worthless; however, Fetrow did not provide evidence confirming the insolvency of the note makers. The trial was overseen by Judge Arthur J. Gallagher, without a jury, resulting in a judgment for the plaintiff, Merriwether.	The plaintiff, Reuben H. Merriwether, aimed to recover ownership of the eighty acres based on his title derived from the general government. He argued that the defendant failed to prove any breach of condition related to the mortgage Fetrow attempted to rely on to assert his claim. Merriwether maintained that he was a bona fide purchaser and did not need to prove the value of the consideration for his property acquisition.	The defendant, John Fetrow, contended that he was entitled to retain possession of the land due to an alleged breach of condition in the mortgage associated with the land. He argued that various promissory notes secured by the mortgage had become worthless, which would validate his claim under the terms of the mortgage. Additionally, Fetrow claimed that the deeds transferring the property from Thorpe to Merriwether were in fraud of the creditors, asserting that Merriwether was not a good faith purchaser.

The case "St. Louis & Terre Haute R. R. Co. v. Rose" was decided on November 24, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court, under docket number No. 51. The key individuals involved are the St. Louis & Terre Haute Railroad Company (the defendant) and Rose (the plaintiff). The dispute arose when a carload of hoops, intended for a specific consignee, was wrongfully delivered by the railroad company to another individual. This situation raised questions about the responsibilities of common carriers regarding the delivery of freight and their liability for incorrect deliveries. The original court, presided over by Judge David J. Baker, ruled in favor of the consignee, which led to the appeal by the railroad company.	The plaintiff, Rose, claimed that the St. Louis & Terre Haute Railroad Company had negligently delivered a shipment of hoops to the wrong individual rather than to the designated consignee as stated in the bill of lading. Rose sought compensation for the value of the hoops, arguing that the company’s wrongful delivery constituted a violation of their duty as a common carrier.	The defendant, St. Louis & Terre Haute Railroad Company, argued against the claim, likely contending that they had followed proper procedures in their delivery process or that there were extenuating circumstances influencing the situation. They requested the court to overturn the decision of the lower court, which had ruled in favor of the plaintiff.

Ralph Plumb v. Abner Taylor et al. is a legal case that arose from a contractual dispute between the parties, with the incident tracing back to an agreement dated October 10, 1878, concerning shares of stock in the Decatur & State Line Railway Company. The plaintiffs, comprised of partners under the firm name Snell, Taylor & Co. (including Abner Taylor, Thomas Snell, James T. Snell, and Henry H. Porter), were to assign $700,000 in shares of this stock to Plumb in exchange for a payment of $42,600, due on or before July 1, 1879. The agreement stipulated that certain stock certificates would be held in trust by Solon Humphreys until Plumb made the payment. However, Plumb failed to make this payment by the May 1, 1879 deadline, and the plaintiffs contended that they had fulfilled their obligations by delivering the stock to the trustee. Subsequently, the plaintiffs filed a suit when Plumb refused to pay, with the court finding in favor of the plaintiffs. The trial was conducted without a jury, and the court determined damages based on the failure of the defendant to perform their contractual obligation.	The plaintiffs argued that they had executed the terms of the contract by assigning the stock certificate to a trustee and were therefore entitled to the $42,600 payment from Plumb. They maintained that delivery of the stock to Humphreys was sufficient to constitute performance of their contract, and they sought the recovery of the amount owed plus interest, ultimately claiming $88,040.73 in damages.	The defendant, Plumb, contended that the plaintiffs failed to perform their part of the contract by not tendering the stock certificates to him directly. Plumb asserted that he was not obligated to fulfill his payment due to the plaintiffs' lack of a valid tender, and he claimed that he had renounced the contract well before the payment was due. The defendant argued that the plaintiffs had not established a right to collect the payment due to these failures.

In the case of John M. Williams v. Margaret Crean, which occurred in Chicago around 1860, the central issue revolved around a dispute over a canal lot. John M. Williams had acquired a certificate of purchase for the entirety of the lot under a pre-emption claim based on improvements made to the land prior to a set regulatory date. Margaret Crean, the complainant, claimed an equitable right to half of the lot, arguing she had previously owned the east half, and tendered one-half of the purchase price. Her claim was based on her possession and improvements made while living there. The case escalated after Williams initiated an ejectment suit, seeking to remove the occupants from the lot. Testimonies indicated a lack of a clearly asserted pre-emption right by Crean, and specific details about prior transactions affecting the property came to light during proceedings. The Illinois Supreme Court was called to review the matter for a resolution.	Margaret Crean argued that she was entitled to the east half of the lot in question, having previously made improvements and occupied it. She tendered one-half of the purchase price to Williams and sought relief from his ongoing ejectment suit. Crean's legal request included a restraining order against Williams to prevent him from further prosecuting the ejectment suit and for the court to compel Williams to execute a deed for her share.	John M. Williams contended that Crean did not have a legitimate right to claim any part of the lot under pre-emption statutes. He emphasized that her inactivity in asserting a claim for over two years after the ejectment notice weakened her position. Williams maintained that she had only purchased the house and did not intend to acquire any pre-emption rights. He argued that since she did not actually possess any such rights, the court should dismiss her equity claims.

William Jones filed a legal action against Barney Nellis in April 1866, in the Illinois Supreme Court, after a seven-thirty government bond worth $500 was stolen from him. The bond had been stolen from Jones' safe by a third party named Joslyn, who was later convicted for the theft. Joslyn sold the stolen bond to the defendant, Nellis, who bought it in good faith, believing it to be legitimate and without any knowledge of its stolen status. The case centered around whether Nellis, as an innocent purchaser, could retain ownership of the bond despite it being stolen. The court examined the common law principles regarding title to stolen property and the implications of Illinois’ Criminal Code sections that define larceny and the rights of owners to recover stolen property.	Jones claimed he was the rightful owner of the stolen bond and sought recovery of its value from Nellis, arguing that ownership rights to property stolen and sold, regardless of the good faith of the purchaser, should allow him to reclaim his property.	Nellis defended against the claims by citing common law principles that allow a bona fide purchaser of a stolen item to gain title if they bought it in good faith and without knowledge of its stolen status. He also referenced the Illinois Criminal Code, asserting that it did not alter the established law that recognizes the rights of innocent purchasers of negotiable instruments.

In January 1867, the case "The People of the State of Illinois v. James N. McCall et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Fulton County, where the auditor of public accounts appealed the decision of the board of supervisors of Fulton County, which had released shares of stock in the First National Bank of Canton from taxation for the years 1865 and 1866. The shares were assessed for taxation at half their nominal value by the town assessor in 1865. However, after an appeal by shareholders, the board abated the assessment. The auditor, unaware of this abatement, listed the shares on the assessment list for 1866 at their full value, leading to further disputes about the tax liability of these shares. The issue revolved around whether the shares should be considered taxable property under state law, particularly in the context of national banking regulations. The Supreme Court had previously held in related cases that shares in national banks could be assessed for taxation, leading to the conflict in this case about the legitimacy of the board's decision to release the shares from taxation.	The plaintiff, represented by the auditor of public accounts, claimed that the shares of stock from the First National Bank of Canton should be assessed and taxed according to Illinois law. They argued that prior cases established the principle that such shares constituted personal property liable to taxation, and therefore, the board's decision to release these shares from taxation was inappropriate and should be overturned.	The defendants, represented by Mr. G. Barrere, contended that the abatement of the tax assessment by the board of supervisors was justified and in accordance with prior judicial decisions. They asserted that the shares in question were exempt from taxation as established by the ruling in the case of Bradley v. The People, which upheld the idea that shares of bank stock are effectively protected from taxation as part of a contract between the banks and the state, a principle supported by federal law.

Charles Waterman and William E. Dundee were indicted for forgery in Cook County, Illinois, in 1872. The charges stemmed from an attempt by Waterman, under the alias T.H. Wiley, to use a forged letter purportedly written by H.A. Ponda, the superintendent of a railroad, to obtain a free pass on the Chicago, Rock Island, and Pacific Railroad. The letter was intended to solicit "courtesies" from railroad officials, suggesting a promise to reciprocate kindnesses. However, the case hinged on whether this letter could legally fall under the definition of forgery. During the trial, evidence indicated that Waterman presented the letter in Chicago, aiming to exploit it for personal gain. The indictment contended that the letter was false and intended to deceive. Waterman contested the validity of the indictment, arguing that the letter’s contents did not establish any legal obligation or liability, and thus could not constitute forgery.	The plaintiff (the state) charged Charles Waterman with attempting to commit forgery by presenting a false letter that was meant to defraud the Chicago, Rock Island, and Pacific Railroad Company. The plaintiff asserted that Waterman knowingly tried to pass a counterfeit document to secure a free railroad pass, thereby committing a criminal offense under the laws of Illinois.	The defendant, Charles Waterman, argued that the document in question was not subject to forgery charges because it lacked any legal validity or consequence. His defense maintained that the letter was merely a letter of introduction seeking courtesies and that it did not impose any legal rights or obligations. Therefore, the defendant contended that since the letter could not subject anyone to legal liability, no indictment for forgery could be sustained.

In September 1857, in Tazewell County, Illinois, William and Joseph Lincoln were indicted for the theft of a large iron gray horse. The crime reportedly occurred on the night of September 29. Various witnesses testified that they had seen the defendants in Groveland around the time of the theft, although many claimed they had only a slight acquaintance with the Lincolns and could not confidently identify them. Testimonies included those of John Smith, A.J. Davis, and others, who described seeing similar-looking individuals in the area. Despite these claims, witnesses for the defense, including Moses Dooley and Jacob S. Brown, provided alibi evidence asserting that Joseph Lincoln was engaged in work during the time the horse was stolen. A jury ultimately found the defendants guilty, leading them to move for a new trial on the basis of the questionable identification by the prosecution witnesses and the definitive alibi provided by their witnesses.	The plaintiffs, representing the People of Illinois, argued that William and Joseph Lincoln were guilty of larceny, as identified by various witnesses who had seen them near Groveland on the night the horse was stolen. The state's evidence aimed to establish the Lincolns' presence at the scene during the crime.	The defendants contended that they were not guilty, emphasizing that many eyewitness accounts were unreliable due to the witnesses' lack of familiarity with them. They presented significant alibi witnesses who testified to Joseph Lincoln's presence elsewhere during the crime. Their primary request was for a new trial based on the insufficiency and uncertainty of the prosecution’s identification evidence.

The case of Sanders v. Robinson took place in Illinois, with the final judgment issued on September 2, 1886. The key individuals involved include Henry A. Sanders (deceased), Charles Haward (administrator of Sanders’ estate), and the defendant, Robinson, who was appointed as the new administrator after Haward's death. The legal proceedings began when the plaintiffs sought to compel Haward to inventory property belonging to Sanders' estate. After Haward's death, Robinson became the defendant and filed a motion to dismiss the case on the grounds that it abated due to Haward's passing. The case was heard without a jury on November 18, 1885, but the specific evidence presented was not recorded in detail. The lower court heard the case based on the evidence before it but did not resolve Robinson's motion to dismiss, which led to questions regarding the propriety of the original judgment.	The plaintiff's main arguments revolved around the need to inventory certain property alleged to belong to the estate of Henry A. Sanders, which they contended should be accounted for by the administrators of the estate. They insisted that the proceedings should continue despite the death of the original administrator, Haward, and challenged the legitimacy of dismissing the case based solely on the administrator's death.	The defendant, Robinson, argued that the case should be dismissed because it had abated upon the death of the original administrator, Haward. Robinson maintained that the lower court's failure to dispose of his motion to dismiss indicated that the claim against him should not continue, and he insisted on an affirmation of this position throughout the proceedings.

On January 26, 1881, Philip Snell owned land in the La Salle County, Illinois, which served as his homestead where he lived with his wife Ellen J. Snell and their two minor children. On this date, Philip mortgaged the property to his mother, Jane Snell for $1839.87, with Ellen joining in the deed. Due to an error, the property was described as being located in section 20 instead of section 27. Following the mortgage, on February 9, 1884, Philip and Ellen executed another mortgage on the same property to the Northwestern Mutual Life Insurance Company for $3000. On August 16, 1884, Philip passed away, leaving Ellen and their children as his only heirs. Jane Snell subsequently filed a bill in the La Salle circuit court in October 1885 to correct the mortgage description and foreclose on the property, with the widow and children as parties. The court granted Jane's request. In December 1886, the property was sold to Byron D. Snell via a master’s deed. On February 9, 1887, Ellen J. Snell and her children filed a new bill seeking to establish their homestead rights in the land. The court ruled in their favor, prompting the defendants to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, Ellen J. Snell and her children, argued that they were entitled to a homestead interest in the property following Philip Snell's death. They claimed that despite the prior mortgages, they had a legal right to have the estate of the homestead set off and assigned to them according to existing laws, as their claims were based on their status as heirs.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs' claim to a homestead was invalidated by the mortgages already placed on the property. They argued that the previously executed mortgages should remain effective and that the plaintiffs are bound by the court's earlier decree that reformed the property description, therefore denying them any rights to a homestead.

Vinton G. Harbaugh v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in April 1866 in Warren County, Illinois. The case involved Vinton G. Harbaugh, who was indicted for keeping a "common gaming house" by permitting individuals to use his billiard tables for profit. The indictment argued that Harbaugh unlawfully allowed people to gather and play billiards for money, in violation of a statute meant to suppress gambling. During the trial, evidence presented showed that players often paid a small fee for using the tables but that there was no manipulated gambling scheme as per the law's strict definition. Despite this, the jury found Harbaugh guilty, and he was fined $25. Harbaugh's defense contended that his establishment was merely for amusement, not illicit gambling, leading to an appeal and further examination of the case.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, claimed that Harbaugh was operating a common gaming house by allowing people to play billiards for money on his premises. They argued that he was facilitating gambling and profiting from it, which violated the Illinois Criminal Code's prohibition against maintaining a gaming establishment.	Harbaugh’s defense contended that he was merely providing a space for individuals to enjoy billiards for entertainment. They argued that the bettors were only determining who would pay a nominal fee for table use and that there was no substantial gambling taking place according to the law's definition of a common gaming house. Thus, they sought to demonstrate that the allegations did not warrant a conviction.

On October 20, 1882, Leander J. McCormick filed a partition bill against Cyrus H. McCormick and Patrick Flaherty in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, seeking to partition lands he claimed to have co-owned with Cyrus McCormick. The filing alleged that Flaherty was a squatter on the property without any legal title. The defendants, including Cyrus McCormick, acknowledged the claims in the bill and filed a cross-bill, seeking the same relief. Flaherty contested their claims, asserting that he had adverse possession of the property for over twenty years. The lower court ruled in favor of the McCormicks, ordering partition. Upon appeal, the Illinois Supreme Court reversed the lower court's decree, upholding Flaherty's claim to the land. Subsequently, after Cyrus H. McCormick's death, his heirs attempted to reassert their claims but were met with legal challenges from Flaherty. A series of motions and contentious filings occurred, culminating in disputes over the rights and validity of various bills and cross-bills, which were further complicated by procedural issues surrounding their dismissal.	Flaherty's primary argument was based on his assertion of adverse possession of the land for over twenty years, denying the McCormicks' equities in the case. He sought to have the court recognize his legitimate claim to the property and maintain his ownership despite the prior partition attempts by the McCormicks.	The McCormicks' defense relied on the assertion that Flaherty was a squatter without legal title to the property, emphasizing that their interests stemmed from a legitimate purchase from Samuel J. Walker. They claimed they were entitled to a partition of the land and requested the court to declare Flaherty's claims invalid.

In 1876, the case "Newton Smith v. Sylvester S. Newton et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in Bureau County, Illinois, when appellant Newton Smith filed a bill in chancery to foreclose a mortgage on an eighty-acre tract of land. The mortgage, executed by Charles W. Shinkle, secured a note for $520 originally payable to John W. Dickinson. Subsequently, Dickinson sold and assigned the mortgage and note to Smith. At the time of negotiation, Newton (the defendant), who owned the land under the mortgage, allegedly informed Smith that the mortgage was valid and binding and expressed willingness to pay it off, which Smith relied on to purchase the note and mortgage. However, Newton later denied making such representations. The case hinged on conflicting testimonies regarding whether Newton assured Smith of the mortgage's validity. A jury trial determined that Newton had not made those representations, leading to a decree dismissing Smith's bill, which Smith subsequently appealed.	The plaintiff, Newton Smith, claimed that he was misled by the defendant, Sylvester S. Newton, regarding the validity of the mortgage and note for the land in question. Smith argued that he relied on Newton's representations when purchasing the mortgage, believing it to be secure, and sought a foreclosure on the property to recover the unpaid money.	Sylvester S. Newton contended that he did not assure Smith of the mortgage's validity and that Smith never inquired about the mortgage's legitimacy prior to purchase. Newton asserted that the underlying consideration for the note failed, as it was based on a sale of land he had no title to. He claimed that since the mortgage was purchased after maturity, it was subject to all defenses.

Elijah Booth made a proposition to the Moline Plow Company on July 12, 1882, to take charge of its foundry at a salary of $1,000 per year. This proposition was accepted, leading to a binding contract for one year's services. Booth fulfilled his duties under the contract and continued working beyond the initial year. He was discharged on January 31, 1884, without cause. Following his termination, Booth claimed he was wrongfully discharged and asserted that he was entitled to damages based on a supposed contract for a second year of service from July 1883 to July 1884. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, with a jury verdict in favor of Booth, awarding him $416.65 in damages for the breach of contract. The court noted that employees who continue working after the expiration of their contracts could be considered under the original terms unless there is proof of a new agreement.	Elijah Booth claimed that he was wrongfully discharged from his position as foreman of the foundry, arguing that since he had an implicit contract to continue for a second year of service, he was entitled to damages for its breach. Booth sought compensation for the salary he would have earned during the second year of his supposed employment.	The Moline Plow Company defended against Booth's claims by asserting that there was no explicit agreement for continued employment beyond the first year. The company contended that the original contract ended after the first year and claimed that Booth's continued employment did not constitute a renewal or creation of a new contract. They denied liability for any alleged breach of a non-existent contract.

John A. Roebling's Sons' Company filed a legal action against The Lock Stitch Fence Company in the Illinois Supreme Court on October 31, 1889. The case arose from a breach of contract dispute regarding the sale of 500 tons of galvanized fence wire. The contract was established through a series of letters exchanged between the two companies, with shipping to commence after prior orders were fulfilled. The parties operated as follows: Roebling's Sons, based in Trenton, New Jersey, was engaged in the manufacture of the wire, while Lock Stitch, based in Joliet, Illinois, was in the business of selling barbed wire. After shipping 120 tons of wire, the Lock Stitch Fence Company instructed Roebling's Sons via telegram on April 27, 1885, to halt shipments and cancel the remaining order due to dissatisfaction with the wire's quality. Subsequently, Roebling's Sons refused to cease shipments and continued to send additional wire, which Lock Stitch refused to accept. Roebling's Sons later sold the unsold wire at public auction and sought damages for the difference between the contract price and the sale price.	The plaintiff, John A. Roebling’s Sons’ Company, claimed that The Lock Stitch Fence Company breached the contract by refusing to accept further shipments of wire after April 27, 1885. Roebling's Sons argued that despite the defendant's refusal, they were prepared to fulfill the contract and continued to ship the remaining wire. They sought damages for unaccepted shipments and the resulting financial loss incurred from selling the wire at public auction.	The defendant, The Lock Stitch Fence Company, contended that their refusal to accept additional shipments was justified based on the quality of the wire, which they claimed was subpar. Lock Stitch argued that the plaintiff failed to prove readiness to perform contractual obligations as they halted shipments after April 21, 1885. They maintained that their notice to revoke the order constituted a legitimate breach of contract by Roebling's Sons, thus releasing them from liability for further performance.

In June 1851, the case "Lester H. Magher, survivor, &c. v. Calvin W. Howe et al." came before the Illinois Supreme Court. The origins of the case trace back to a promissory note signed by Lester H. Magher and Noah W. Birge, which included a warrant of attorney permitting a confession of judgment. A judgment was sought against Magher as the surviving debtor after Birge's death. The judgment had been entered by the McHenry Circuit Court, where plaintiffs presented the note and the warrant demanding acknowledgment of judgment. The court allowed the confession despite Birge’s posthumous involvement, leading Magher to appeal, arguing that it was erroneous to admit a confession given a warrant signed after Birge's decease. The proceedings focused on the validity of the warrant and whether the execution by both parties was necessary and properly documented.	The plaintiffs argued that the promissory note, which included provisions for a judgment by confession, was valid and enforceable. They contended that according to the statutes and legal precedents, the warrant of attorney allowed for judgment against a surviving debtor, regardless of the joint nature of the original agreement. They requested the court to uphold the judgment entered by the Circuit Court, asserting that the procedural matters regarding the death of Birge were irrelevant as proper authority was established.	Magher, the defendant, claimed that the judgment entered against him was irregular, specifically because the warrant of attorney that authorized the confession was executed prior to Birge’s death. He maintained that the warrant must be strictly adhered to under law and insisted that the lack of proper documentation in the record undermined the legitimacy of the court’s action. He requested that the court reverse the judgment on the grounds of procedural error related to the execution of the warrant.

In December 1836, the case of John Jones, Thomas Jones, and William Jones, appellants, against John Doe ex dem. Betsey Bramblet and Nancy Bramblet, appellees, was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict arose from a claim to the Southeast quarter of Section 14 in Township 8, South of Range 6 East, located in Gallatin County, Illinois, following the death of John Brown, who passed away in March 1830. Brown's will stated that the land would be equally bequeathed to his two infant granddaughters, Betsey and Nancy Bramblet, on the condition that they continue to live with his wife, Sarah Brown, until they were married. Sarah Brown died in 1832, and the appellants, related to Sarah, claimed ownership of the land after taking possession as her heirs. The appellants argued that the will's conditions were not met and sought to establish their title to the land. The jury at the Circuit Court found in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to the appeal by the defendants.	The plaintiffs claimed that the condition in John Brown's will, requiring Betsey and Nancy Bramblet to live with Sarah Brown to inherit the property, was no longer valid after her death. They argued that, as stipulated in the will, the bequest to the Bramblet sisters should take effect since the condition of living with Sarah had become impossible due to her passing. The plaintiffs requested a ruling affirming their right to possession of the specified land.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs were bound to the conditions set forth in the will and argued that the Circuit Court erroneously admitted improper parol testimony while rejecting their valid evidence. They asserted that the jury's verdict was inconsistent with the law and the evidence presented during the trial. Additionally, they claimed that the will's language was insufficient to support the plaintiffs' assertion of a fee simple ownership, as it only created a life estate.

The case of Adrian W. Paul et al. v. The People ex rel. John Gillen was adjudicated in June 1876 in Illinois. Key individuals involved include plaintiff Adrian W. Paul and defendant John Gillen, representing the People. The case arose when an affidavit was filed to initiate a quo warranto proceeding against the plaintiffs, accusing them of illegally occupying the position of trustees in the town of Coulterville without legal authority. The plaintiffs argued that the town had never been incorporated according to Illinois law, and thus their claims to the office of trustees were invalid. The court proceedings included the submission of multiple pleas by the defendants, claiming that they had been duly elected to their positions as trustees. However, the court ruled against the defendants, finding them guilty of unlawfully holding office, which led to their ouster and an order for them to pay court costs. Notably, there were issues concerning the lack of a proper trial or agreement on facts, as records indicated the defendants and their attorneys were not present during the judgment.	The plaintiffs contended that they were illegally removed from their positions as trustees of the town of Coulterville. They argued that the town was never legally incorporated, making any claim to the trusteeship invalid. Their legal request was to contest the court's judgment that ousted them from office without a proper trial or legal proceedings.	The defendants asserted that they had been elected as trustees through a lawful election process, supported by the proper notice and voting procedures conducted by their clerk. They raised pleas arguing the legitimacy of the election and claimed that the court acted improperly by ruling against them without a trial, the presence of counsel, or a valid issue of fact.

The case "The Village of Carterville v. Samuel Cook" took place in 1889, in the village of Carterville, Illinois. The incident involved a fifteen-year-old boy, Samuel Cook, who, while walking along a public sidewalk, was jostled by another boy and pushed off the sidewalk, which was elevated six feet above the ground without any railings or safeguards. As a result, Samuel sustained serious injuries to his limb due to the fall. The case centers around the village's duty of care regarding the safety of the sidewalk and whether they were liable for the injuries sustained by Samuel as a result of the fall caused by a third party's actions.	Samuel Cook, represented by his attorneys, claimed that the Village of Carterville was negligent for failing to provide proper safety measures, such as railings, for the elevated sidewalk. He argued that, despite the involvement of another boy's negligent actions that pushed him, the village still bore responsibility for creating an unsafe condition that led to his injuries. Samuel sought damages for the injuries he sustained as a direct result of this negligence.	The Village of Carterville, represented by its attorneys, contended that they were not liable for Samuel's injuries because the primary cause of the accident was the unforeseen and careless act of the other boy who shoved him. They argued that the city had acted within its rights in not providing railings since the risk of such an incident was not predictable and that accidents caused by third parties should relieve them of liability. The village requested that the court dismiss the claim against them.

The case of George F. Dart and A. J. Lothery v. Christopher Hercules took place in 1864, in Livingston County, Illinois. The legal dispute originated from an action of ejectment initiated by Christopher Hercules against the defendants, George F. Dart and A. J. Lothery, concerning a specific tract of swamp land (the N.W. N.E. 18, T. 27 N. R. 8 E., 3rd principal meridian). The action commenced with service of the declaration and notice to the defendants on May 21, 1863. Throughout the subsequent court proceedings, the defendants contested jurisdiction due to claimed deficiencies in service and attempted to have the case dismissed. After a series of pleas and motions, the case went to trial in March 1864, during which evidence regarding the plaintiff’s ownership and the validity of the land transfer was presented. Key evidence included a certified copy of the swamp lands list and a deed executed by a county-appointed commissioner. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of the plaintiff, affirming his ownership of the land in question, prompting the defendants to appeal the decision based on various alleged legal errors.	Christopher Hercules, the plaintiff, argued that he was the rightful owner of the swamp land in question based on evidence including a certified copy of the state auditor's list of swamp lands, which he asserted served as valid title documentation. He maintained that the county had legally appointed a commissioner to convey the lands and that all procedural requirements had been met, allowing him to recover possession of the property.	The defendants, Dart and Lothery, contended that the court lacked jurisdiction due to insufficient service of process and that Hercules could not pursue the claim without presenting a patent from the U.S. government for the swamp land. They also argued that the conveyance should have been executed by the county clerk rather than a special commissioner and raised objections regarding the qualifications of jurors selected for the trial.

The case of *The Chicago City Railway Company v. The People ex rel. Allan C. Story* was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The legal dispute originated when the Chicago City Railway Company, incorporated in 1859, was charged with usurping its franchises to operate a railway on Indiana Avenue without the necessary authorization. The City of Chicago had initially granted the company permission to lay down tracks along this avenue, contingent on obtaining consent from the owners of two-thirds of the property fronting on the street and requiring completion within fifteen months. The company completed a track from Twenty-second Street to Thirty-first Street but failed to extend the railway to the city limits within the stipulated time. Following a series of legal proceedings, the matter escalated to the state supreme court, where it was examined whether the consent from property owners had been appropriately obtained and whether the timeline for construction could be extended by a subsequent ordinance passed by the city council.	The plaintiff, representing the people of Illinois, claimed that the Chicago City Railway Company did not obtain the required consent from two-thirds of the property owners along Indiana Avenue. They argued that the company had also neglected its obligation to complete the railway to the city limits within the stipulated timeframe. As a result, the plaintiff sought a judgment declaring the forfeiture of the company's franchises on Indiana Avenue.	The Chicago City Railway Company contended that they had obtained the necessary consent from the property owners and maintained compliance with city ordinances. The company argued that an amended ordinance passed in 1871 extended the time for completing the railway and confirmed their rights on Indiana Avenue. They claimed that any alleged failure to meet the original timeline should not result in forfeiture, highlighting that the city had the authority to waive strict adherence to the conditions imposed.

In 1872, in Union County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving William R. Patton, who served as the jailer for Union County. The legal matter originated from a proceeding initiated by Patton to retrieve fees he claimed for his services in maintaining the county jail. After Patton's claims were initially adjudicated in the county court, the case was appealed to the circuit court, where a jury ruled in Patton's favor, awarding him $811.60 in fees. The county, dissatisfied with this judgment, further appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, leading to the examination of the legal statutes governing sheriff fees and the implications of the newly adopted constitution of 1870 on such fees.	William R. Patton contended that he was entitled to recover specific fees for services rendered as the keeper of the jail. He argued that, despite the changes in law due to the constitution adopted in 1870, he was entitled to these payments as previously established under special laws regulating sheriff fees.	The county, represented in court, argued that the fees claimed by Patton were no longer applicable due to the explicit repeal of special compensation laws by the constitution of 1870. They contended that since the constitution abolished fees established by special laws, Patton, as a mere jailer, could not claim any sheriff's fees for his services in housing and managing prisoners.

In 1887, in Alton, Illinois, William H. Hayden filed a lawsuit against Alton National Bank to recover $504.04. The plaintiff claimed he deposited this amount into the bank, opening an account in the name "William H. Hayden, agent" while acting on behalf of his brother, George D. Hayden, who had disappeared and left his business in disarray. The bank asserted that the funds were, in fact, George D. Hayden's, thus giving them the right to set off his debts against the deposited amount, which included three notes owed by George D. Hayden, totaling $3,300. The trial court, hearing the case without a jury, found in favor of the defendant, concluding that the amounts deposited were indeed considered property of George D. Hayden, and that since he was indebted to the bank, they had the right to apply the balance of the deposit toward his debt. William H. Hayden’s appeal followed, claiming the deposits were his.	William H. Hayden argued that the deposit he made with the bank was his personal property and that the bank had no legal right to set it off against the debts of George D. Hayden, as he deposited the money intending it to be kept separate for specific purposes. He maintained that the bank accepted his deposit in his name and should not apply it toward George D. Hayden's outstanding obligations.	Alton National Bank contended that the money deposited was actually George D. Hayden's and that they were informed of this when the account was opened. They claimed the plaintiff was merely acting as an agent, and thus, the funds were subject to set-off against George D. Hayden's debts. The bank argued that they were legally entitled to offset the amount owed by George against the plaintiff's claim since the debts arose from the same transactions.

In December of 1839, the case of Joseph Emerson v. George W. Clark took place in Illinois. This legal dispute arose from a motion to dismiss Emerson's appeal regarding a judgment that was believed to be final and exceeded twenty dollars, exclusive of costs. Key individuals involved included Joseph Emerson, the appellant, and George W. Clark, the appellee. The Circuit Court's requirement was that the defendant must verify specific trial papers via his own affidavit within twenty days to have them included in the bill of exceptions. This case was being heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, which was examining the procedural aspects of the appeal to determine if the conditions set by the Circuit Court were appropriate.	Joseph Emerson, the appellant, contended that his right to appeal should be upheld without the additional conditions imposed by the Circuit Court. He argued that the statute grants the right to appeal in cases where the judgment is final and meets the monetary threshold. Emerson sought to maintain his appeal on the basis that the Circuit Court's requirements for verifying the papers were unnecessary.	George W. Clark, the appellee, defended against the appeal by highlighting the conditions set by the Circuit Court, arguing that the verification of the trial papers was a lawful requirement for the appeal to proceed. He requested that the court uphold the Circuit Court's decision to dismiss the appeal until the specified verification was completed.

On March 16, 1838, Arraham Brookbank initiated a lawsuit against Joseph Smith in Bureau County, Illinois, before a justice of the peace. The justice ruled against Brookbank, ordering him to pay $7.50 plus court costs. Brookbank then appealed to the Circuit Court, filing a new bill of particulars that included additional claims totaling $21.45 beyond what was presented in the initial trial. However, the Circuit Court, at the defendant's request, rejected the inclusion of these additional items. During a trial presided over by Hon. Dan Stone in June 1838, the court ruled in Brookbank’s favor and granted a new trial. At the subsequent March term in 1839, presided over by Hon. Thomas Ford, further evidence from Brookbank was presented but was rejected by the court. The judgment favored Smith, and Brookbank was ordered to pay six cents. Brookbank then appealed the Circuit Court's decisions to the Illinois Supreme Court, alleging that the Circuit Court's rulings constituted errors.	The primary argument from Arraham Brookbank is that the Circuit Court erred in rejecting the evidence related to the additional items presented in his bill of particulars. He contended that he should be allowed to amend his claims and present all relevant evidence that could substantiate his case. Brookbank sought to overturn the judgment favoring the defendant and to be compensated for the full amount originally claimed, including the additional items.	Joseph Smith's defense primarily focused on the procedural aspects of the case, arguing that the additional claims presented by Brookbank in the Circuit Court were not permissible based on the statutes. Smith maintained that the Circuit Court correctly rejected the new items since they differed from the claims presented at the initial trial before the justice of the peace. His argument also asserted that exceptions could not be made for the Circuit Court's decision to grant a new trial.

In the case of Sarah Pinneo v. Francis Goodspeed et al., the legal dispute arises from the estate of Horace Haff, who died intestate in 1866, leaving behind his widow Sarah Ann Haff and children Sarah Fargo and Edwin G. Haff. Following his death, a partition of Haff's estate was executed, wherein Sarah Fargo received a parcel of 300 acres of land. In a related divorce decree, Orange T. Fargo, Sarah Fargo's husband, was ordered to pay her alimony. After Orange T. Fargo's death in 1874, his estate was administered by executors Goodspeed and Elizabeth M. Fargo, who mismanaged the estate by paying unjust claims from the estate's funds. A series of legal actions ensued regarding possession of the land and the proper accounting of rents collected from it. A supplemental cross-bill was filed by Sarah Pinneo (formerly Sarah Fargo), claiming her rights to rental income and challenging the management of the estate by the executors. The case escalated through various rulings and appeals until it reached the Illinois Supreme Court, which faced complexities over rent evaluations and payments made under a mistaken belief about property ownership.	Sarah Pinneo claims entitlement to the 300 acres of land belonging to the estate of Orange T. Fargo and seeks an accounting of the rents collected from that land by the executors, alleging improper payments to others while neglecting to satisfy her claims and alimony decree. She argues that the executors should not profit from purchasing a mortgage secured on the land and that previous payments made to her under a mistaken belief should be accounted for against the estate's income, which properly belongs to her.	The defendants, including Francis Goodspeed and Elizabeth M. Fargo, argue that the payments and management of the estate were conducted in good faith based on misinterpretations of property ownership. They assert that the payments made to Pinneo constituted alimony, which ceased upon her ex-husband's death, and therefore she should not claim further from the estate. They maintain that all accounting was appropriately handled according to the law and equity standards, and they seek to justify deducting costs incurred in managing the estate and rents collected from the land.

The case titled "The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. Andrew Redman v. Nicholas Wren, Clerk of the County Commissioners’ Court of Adams County," was adjudicated in December 1843 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The specific issue arose in the context of a newly formed county, Marquette, created from the territory of Adams County by a legislative act. Andrew Redman claimed to have been elected as the justice of the peace for the Columbus precinct, which was situated within the newly delineated area of Marquette, on August 7, 1843. However, the precinct of Columbus was located in the still-unorganized county of Marquette. Nicholas Wren, as clerk of Adams County, did not acknowledge the election, prompting Redman's application for a writ of mandamus to compel Wren to issue a certificate of his election. The central legal question was whether the jurisdiction of Adams County extended over Marquette for county government purposes at the time of the election, given that Marquette had not yet organized. The Illinois Supreme Court needed to assess the legislative intent regarding the new county's formation and its implications for elections and governance.	Andrew Redman, the relator, argued that the legislative act creating Marquette County explicitly formed a new county, bestowing certain rights and capacities, including his election to a judicial office. He claimed he had been legally elected and sought a mandate to compel Wren to issue his election certificate, asserting that the legislature's intent was clear in establishing the new county and that he should be recognized in his official capacity.	Nicholas Wren, in defense, contended that the creation of Marquette County did not confer jurisdiction over it until the county was formally organized through the election of officers. He argued that, without organization, Marquette was still under the jurisdiction of Adams County. Wren maintained that Redman’s election was invalid as no county government was established to support it, and thus he had no obligation to issue the election certificate.

On March 6, 1878, in Whiteside County, Illinois, the plaintiff, represented by the firm of Charles E. Langford, filed a petition against Duncan Mackay and others to enforce a lien for materials (sawed and dressed lumber and shingles) provided to a man named Wilson for the construction of a house. Wilson had borrowed $11,000 from Mackay and had executed a deed of mortgage on his farm as security. The agreement with Langford’s firm for the lumber involved delivery over a series of days in February and May 1877, with a total cost of $141.87. The central dispute revolved around the payment terms: whether payment was due six months after the full delivery of materials or from the date of the contract. The circuit court found that the claim was barred by the statute of limitations since the petition was filed beyond the allowed time frame if calculated from the contract date. Nonetheless, it recognized the lien on Wilson's interest, ordering a sale of the premises if payment was defaulted, while dismissing the claim against Mackay.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were owed $141.87 for materials delivered to Wilson for building a house. They argued that payment was due six months after the complete delivery of the materials. They sought to establish a lien on Wilson’s property based on the delivery and sought to claim precedence over Mackay’s mortgage regarding the building, aiming for the material costs to be covered first before any mortgage claims were satisfied.	The defendants, particularly Mackay, contended that the plaintiffs' claim was barred by the statute of limitations since the legal action was taken too late if calculated from the date payment was due per the contract. They asserted that the plaintiffs did not establish their claim within the required time frame and that the lien should not take precedence over their existing mortgage on the property, maintaining that the court’s decision to dismiss the claim against Mackay was justified.

In 1886, Edward E. Blagden, employed by the Chicago & Eastern Illinois Railroad Company, became the subject of a garnishment proceeding initiated due to a judgment against him. The garnishment writ was served on the railroad company on June 18, 1886. Blagden’s employer reported that they owed him only $6 in wages at the time of the writ’s service. Over the years, the case saw various continuations and interrogatories to gather further details about Blagden’s wages, which were allegedly $60 per month, though he had received advances totaling $84. In September 1888, the justice court ruled against the railroad company (garnishee), ordering them to pay $103 to the plaintiff, based on the judgment against Blagden and other claims. The garnishee appealed the ruling to the Superior Court of Cook County, where further interrogatories were submitted' showing that no further wages were due to Blagden from June 1886 onwards, except the reported $6. The case took complex turns regarding the nature of advance payments to Blagden in a potential attempt to circumvent the garnishment.	The plaintiff maintained that the garnishee owed Blagden money at the time of the writ's service and sought to recover a total judgment amount of $103. The plaintiff argued that the garnishee’s advance payments to Blagden were an effort to avoid fulfilling the garnishment and intended to prove that more than just $6 should be recoverable from the garnishee.	The defendant, Chicago & Eastern Illinois Railroad Company, argued that at no point, including the service of the garnishment writ, were they indebted to Blagden for more than $6. They contended that the advance payments made to Blagden were legitimate and lawful, aimed at regularizing his salary without any intent to defraud the plaintiff. They requested the court to overturn the judgment against them, emphasizing that no evidence contradicted their claim that the garnishment was improperly applied.

In September 1872, a legal case arose in Whiteside County, Illinois, involving plaintiff Adaline Dallum and defendants Charles Birdsall and others. The case centered around a transaction where a stove was purchased for Dallum by her sister-in-law, who specifically paid for it as a gift. At the time of the purchase, Dallum was present, assisting her sister-in-law in selecting the stove. The plaintiff asserted that the vendor had made a verbal warranty regarding the quality of the stove, promising to take it back and refund the payment if the stove failed to meet the quality claims. After experiencing issues with the stove, Dallum sought to return it and recover the money paid. The case was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court, which evaluated the legal standing of the claim regarding the warranty and the payment arrangement.	Adaline Dallum, the plaintiff, claimed that the defendants provided a verbal warranty regarding the quality of the stove and agreed to refund the purchase price if the warranty proved untrue. She argued that, despite the stove being purchased by her sister-in-law, she had been involved in the decision-making process and had the right to enforce the warranty, as the promise was made for her benefit.	The defendants contended that the action could not be maintained as it was improperly initiated before a justice, asserting that there was no jurisdiction. They also argued that the warranty was given to Dallum's sister-in-law and therefore did not extend to Dallum herself. The defendants maintained that since the payment was made by another person, Dallum did not have a legal claim to recover the funds.

In November 1860, the case of Henry R. Dickinson v. James W. Breeden was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in Hancock County, Illinois, where James W. Breeden, the plaintiff, initiated an action of ejectment against Henry R. Dickinson, the appellant. The crux of the case revolved around the validity of a deed from James J. Dozier to Elisha L. Conant, dated October 8, 1835, which Breeden claimed as part of his title to certain premises. During the trial, Breeden offered a copy of this deed into evidence.
