However, the original deed was not available, prompting concerns about the adequacy of proof regarding its existence and subsequent unavailability. Breeden’s affidavit stated that he had never possessed the original deed and had made diligent efforts to retrieve it from Conant, who resided in Indiana. The court's acceptance of the copy of the deed was challenged by Dickinson, indicating the high stakes involved in proving authentic land titles and the risks of forgery without the original documents.	The plaintiff, James W. Breeden, claimed ownership of the disputed land based on his purchase from Elisha L. Conant, who had received the property title through a deed from James J. Dozier. Breeden argued that the absence of the original deed should not impede his ability to prove ownership and sought to have the deed's copy admitted as evidence, relying on his affidavit about efforts to obtain the original deed, which he alleged was lost.	The defendant, Henry R. Dickinson, contended that the court should not have accepted the copy of the deed without sufficient evidence establishing the existence of the original deed and its loss after diligent search. Dickinson's defense relied on the argument that allowing copies of deeds without rigorous proof creates risks for land ownership validity and opens potential avenues for fraud. He pointed to Breeden's failure to secure the original deed and demanded a review of the court's decision allowing the copy as valid proof.

In 1867, in Chicago, Illinois, Isaac Cook brought an ejectment action against Jehiel E. Norton, his wife Emily M. Norton, Grace J. Clarke, and Julia Wilkie to recover a portion of two lots within the city. Isaac Cook had originally purchased one-third of the premises from James Byan in May 1845. Subsequently, Byan lost two-thirds of the property to a judgment lien in favor of one Ballingall, who later acquired Byan's interest in the lot through an execution sale. In July 1860, Cook sought a sheriff's deed to the lot from Ballingall, which was granted, giving him a basis for his claim. The property had since passed through various owners, with Emily M. Norton and her daughter Grace J. Clarke eventually participating in the suit, as they had a vested interest through prior ownership. The action was consolidated due to the related interests of the defendants. The court assessed whether the defendants had established their claim to possess the land by demonstrating continuous payment of taxes for seven years and proved possession under a claimed title.	Isaac Cook claimed ownership of a two-thirds interest in a Chicago lot by virtue of a sheriff's deed obtained after an execution sale of Byan's interest. He argued that he had valid title based on the prior ownership and conveyances leading back to the original purchase from Byan. Cook also contended that the defendants had failed to maintain valid claims to the lot, particularly due to issues concerning the timely payment of taxes and proper possession requirements.	The defendants claimed they had valid ownership through subsequent conveyances and tax payments. They argued that the prior owner, Clark, had taken possession and paid the necessary taxes for seven successive years, thus establishing a claim under the law. They contended that they met the statutory requirements for property ownership and asserted that Cook’s claims were weak due to the alleged failure to complete the necessary elements for title through continuous tax payment and physical occupation of the premises.

The legal case of L. Knowles v. Village of Wayne City took place in 1889 in Wayne County, Illinois. The central issue arose when L. Knowles was charged with violating a village ordinance prohibiting the use of profane and obscene language. Knowles was tried in a justice court and was acquitted of these charges by a jury. Following the acquittal, the Village of Wayne City appealed the decision in the Circuit Court, claiming they had the right to do so despite the acquittal. The appeal was based on the argument of the village having jurisdiction to enforce the ordinance, and thus being entitled to challenge a lower court's ruling. The Circuit Court, presided over by Judge C. C. Boggs, examined whether it had jurisdiction to consider the appeal after Knowles had been acquitted. The court determined that the initial action was a civil matter regarding the village ordinance and that Knowles's acquittal concluded the case, preventing the village's appeal from moving forward.	The plaintiff, the Village of Wayne City, contended that Knowles had violated a specific ordinance against profanity and sought to recover penalties through the legal appeal process. They argued that the appeal was valid and within the rights afforded to municipalities under Illinois law, despite Knowles's prior acquittal in the lower court. The Village sought to overturn the acquittal and enforce its ordinance.	The defendant, L. Knowles, maintained that he had been acquitted of the charges in the justice court, which should prevent the village from appealing. Knowles argued that the nature of the case was clearly civil rather than criminal, and since no penalties had been adjudicated against him, the village had no grounds for appeal. He emphasized that the appeal was not permissible under the law, as no adverse judgment had been rendered against him in the initial proceedings.

William H. Grubey filed a lawsuit against The National Bank of Illinois in the Illinois Appellate Court concerning a promissory note for $1,000. The case was heard on February 12, 1890, in Cook County, Chicago. Grubey claimed that the note was tied to transactions that he asserted were gambling-related losses incurred at the Board of Trade, where he engaged in trading commodities such as stocks, grains, and pork through his broker, Charles Henrotin. The court found that Grubey had not provided sufficient evidence to support his claims, particularly regarding the legality of the transactions underlying the promissory note. The court's examination centered on the admissibility of evidence about conversations and transactions between Grubey and Henrotin, ultimately determining that the rulings made during the trial were appropriate, and Grubey had failed to demonstrate that the note’s consideration was based on illegal gambling activities.	Grubey argued that the promissory note was invalid because its consideration was derived from gambling losses related to transactions on the Board of Trade, asserting that these types of transactions violated Illinois law. He requested the court to dismiss the action for collection of the note based on this claim of illegality.	The National Bank contended that it had no involvement with or knowledge of any alleged gambling or illegal transactions linked to Grubey and maintained that the promissory note was valid. The defense argued that even if part of Grubey's debt to Henrotin arose from gambling activities, it did not affect the bank's right to enforce the collection of the note, as the bank was a legitimate creditor unaware of the nature of the underlying transactions.

The case "Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Co. v. Melson J. Davis et al." took place in Illinois, culminating in a court decision on May 29, 1885. The plaintiffs, Melson J. Davis and his partners, were engaged in business under the name Davis Brothers & Porter. They sought to recover damages for the loss of certain barrels of refined oil that leaked during transportation from Buffalo, New York, to Chicago via the defendant's railroad. The oil was delivered to the defendant on April 28, 1881, in good condition, but by the time it arrived in Milwaukee on May 21, 1881, one barrel was entirely empty, and the others were leaking. The defendant, Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company, attributed the delays and leakage to a strike by switchmen, which hampered their operations during that period. The plaintiffs contended that the loss was due to negligence in handling the oil, while the defendant maintained that they took all necessary precautions but were hindered by the unavoidable circumstances of the strike.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendant was liable for the loss of their oil due to leakage during transit, claiming that the delay caused by the defendant's operations led to shrinkage and ultimately the damage they incurred, assessed at $141.20. They sought full recovery of these damages, asserting that the conditions limiting the defendant's liability outlined in the bill of lading were not properly communicated or agreed upon by the plaintiffs, thus making them irrelevant in this case.	The defendant contended that they were not liable for the oil's leakage and loss because the delays were a direct result of a general strike by switchmen, an uncontrollable circumstance. They argued that the terms of the bill of lading permitted them to limit their liability for certain losses or damages, which were agreed upon by the plaintiffs at the onset of the shipment. The defendant sought a dismissal of the case, arguing the plaintiffs' claims were unfounded due to the provisions of the bill of lading and the unavoidable delays during the strike.

In the case of Garrett P. Atchison v. William Dullam, the events occurred in Boone County, Illinois, during September 1881. Plaintiff Garrett P. Atchison and the defendant William Dullam, along with an acquaintance named George A. Stanley, went hunting together. On the day of the incident, Dullam took possession of Stanley's double-barreled shotgun, which he cocked as they proceeded on their hunt. After Dullam shot a bird, he attempted to break down the gun to reload it. However, while fumbling with the weapon and turning towards Atchison, the gun accidentally discharged, striking Atchison in the leg below the knee. The injury was severe enough to necessitate amputation. Following this, Atchison initiated legal action against Dullam, claiming negligence in handling the gun that led to the injury. The initial trial resulted in a verdict favoring Dullam, prompting Atchison to file for a writ of error.	Atchison's claims against Dullam included allegations of negligence in the handling of the firearm. He argued that Dullam had carelessly pointed the gun at him while it was cocked, leading to its negligent discharge and Atchison's subsequent injury. The plaintiff sought damages for the injuries sustained due to this negligence.	Dullam's defense relied on the assertion that the gun's discharge was accidental and constituted a misadventure. He claimed that he had not pointed the gun at Atchison intentionally and that he was not at fault for the incident. The fundamental argument was that the circumstances surrounding the gun's discharge were unavoidable and did not result from any negligence on Dullam's part.

In September 1873, in Livingston County, Illinois, William Hennies and Annie Hennies were prosecuted for assault and battery. The case began in a justice of the peace court, where both defendants were found guilty. Following the conviction, both defendants appealed the ruling to the circuit court, which upheld the decision and imposed fines on each of them. The critical point of the case was whether formal pleadings were necessary for the appeal. The court determined that no formal pleadings were required either before the justice or in the circuit court, allowing the case to proceed. Additionally, the legality of a judgment against the surety on the appeal bond was debated, with the court ultimately affirming the judgment against both the defendants and their surety based on existing statutory provisions.	The plaintiff, representing the State of Illinois, argued that the trial's procedures were correct and that the defendants were properly found guilty. They maintained that no formal plea was required before either the justice of the peace or the circuit court. Furthermore, they contended that the appeal bond complied with statutory requirements and called for enforcement of the judgment against the surety alongside the defendants.	The defendants contended that the court erred in rendering judgment against the surety on the appeal bond, citing the bond's potential non-compliance with statutory form requirements. They argued that the bond did not meet the exact conditions stipulated by the 1845 act and that the judgment against the surety was unconstitutional. They sought to overturn the judgment based on these statutory interpretations.

The case, Churchill Edwards et al. v. John H. Vandemack, was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1852. The dispute originated from a legal action initiated before a justice of the peace and subsequently appealed to the Lake Circuit Court. The appeal was dismissed by the Circuit Court due to a claimed lack of jurisdiction over the case, which revolved around the plaintiffs’ demand for payment not exceeding one hundred dollars. The record indicates that while there was a summons issued by the justice, it did not adequately clarify the nature of the action taken against the defendant. A critical issue raised was whether the Circuit Court had the authority to hear the appeal, particularly since there are specific cases, as specified in the statute, where such appeal is not permitted. The court noted that the dismissal was based on procedural grounds concerning the jurisdiction of the lower court and that the absence of a bill of exceptions in the case further complicated any review of the Circuit Court's decision.	The plaintiffs, Churchill Edwards and others, claimed that there was a wrongful failure to pay a demand not exceeding one hundred dollars. They sought to appeal the decision made by the justice of the peace to the Circuit Court, arguing that their case should be heard in that higher court.	The defendant, John H. Vandemack, argued that the Circuit Court lacked the jurisdiction to hear the appeal from the justice of the peace's decision. He contended that the appeal was improper, supporting the dismissal of the case on jurisdictional grounds as dictated by state law regarding appeals from judgments made by justices of the peace.

In the legal case "Bloom v. The People," decided on December 8, 1886, the proceedings took place in the Criminal Court of Cook County, Illinois. The case was highlighted as a bastardy proceeding, with the key individuals involved being the relator, Josie Hovak, and the appellant, Jacob Bloom. During the trial, which was conducted without a jury, a direct conflict arose between Hovak's and Bloom's testimonies regarding the facts in question. Despite the presence of additional witnesses for Bloom, their testimonies were deemed irrelevant to the issue at hand. The trial judge's findings were based primarily on the conflict of the testimonies between Hovak and Bloom, emphasizing that no facts were presented that would impact the credibility of Hovak's claims. The resolution of the pivotal issues in the case was determined through this evidentiary conflict.	Josie Hovak, the plaintiff, claimed that Jacob Bloom was the father of her child, asserting a bastardy claim against him. Her main argument centered on establishing Bloom's paternity and holding him responsible for the child's support, requesting appropriate legal remedies under Illinois law for bastardy proceedings.	Jacob Bloom, the defendant, argued against the claims made by Hovak, contesting the assertion that he was the father of her child. He presented witnesses to support his defense; however, their testimonies did not effectively challenge Hovak's credibility nor provide substantial evidence to counter her claims. Bloom's request was to dismiss the claims made against him due to lack of supportive evidence.

Thomas Kergin, the appellant, was involved in a legal case in Illinois during December 1844 against Robert Dawson, the appellee. The case originated when Robert Dawson, who had secured a judgment against William Buchanan in a suit by attachment for $207.67, summoned Kergin as a garnishee. Kergin was questioned on whether he possessed specific property belonging to Buchanan—namely the woodwork of two wagons, a set of blacksmith’s tools, and a stand. Kergin confirmed having possession of the items, stating they were entrusted to him as security for an appeal bond for Buchanan's prior case. A jury was tasked with adjudicating the validity of Kergin's answer, which led to a finding against him, ultimately establishing that he improperly received at least some of Buchanan's tools. Kergin's motion for a new trial was denied by the Circuit Court, resulting in his appeal.	The plaintiff, Robert Dawson, argued that Kergin's answer to the interrogatories was evasive and insufficient to protect him against the judgment, alleging that the tools were valued higher than Kergin stated. Dawson requested the court to reject Kergin's claims and allow him to execute the judgment against the property Kergin was thought to possess.	Kergin contended that the property in his possession was pledged to him by Buchanan as security for an appeal bond, giving him a right to retain the property until his obligations were fulfilled. Kergin maintained his answer was truthful and complete, asserting that the tools’ value did not exceed the amount he had already paid on behalf of Buchanan. He requested that the court respect this legal right and reverse the previous judgment against him.

The case "Milton Dickie et al. v. James H. Carter" took place in November 1866 in Illinois, originating from the probate court of Alexander County. The key individuals involved were James H. Carter, the defendant, and the plaintiffs, who were the nearest blood relatives of Elizabeth Burnett, the deceased. Carter presented a document to the court, claiming it to be Burnett's last will and testament, and requested its recording. The probate court, however, found that the document was not sufficiently attested and that Burnett lacked the mental capacity to create a valid will. Consequently, Carter appealed this decision to the Circuit Court, where a jury ultimately ruled in favor of establishing the document as Burnett's will. The plaintiffs argued against this verdict, leading to further appeals and legal discussions concerning the will's validity, including claims of improper influence and lack of sound mind by Burnett at the time of signing.	The plaintiffs contended that the document presented by Carter was not a valid will, arguing that the statutory requirements for a will's execution had not been met. They questioned the soundness of Burnett's mind at the time she allegedly signed the will and raised the issue that the will was drafted under the undue influence of Carter, who stood to benefit from its provisions. The plaintiffs requested that the court reverse the Circuit Court's decision and declare the disputed document invalid.	The defendant, James H. Carter, argued that the will was validly executed and that the requirements for probate were satisfied according to the law. He maintained that the subscribing witnesses had established the sanity of Burnett during the execution of the will. Carter contended that there was no evidence of fraud or undue influence in the process and requested the court to uphold the ruling from the Circuit Court, affirming the will's validity.

On July 19, 1881, the case of Pennsylvania Company v. Patrick H. Boylan was initiated in the circuit court of Cook County, Illinois. The incident in question occurred on July 20, 1879, at the Forty-seventh Street crossing in Chicago, where the plaintiff, Patrick Boylan, was injured by a piece of plank that was struck by a passing locomotive of the Pennsylvania Company. The plaintiff claimed that the railway company's negligence led to the planks being left unfastened and lying crosswise on the railroad track, which culminated in his injury. Testimonies were presented from Boylan's mother and a neighbor, Dennis Larkin, who suggested that the railway workers were actively repairing the culvert just before the accident. In contrast, witnesses for the defendant asserted that no work had been done on that day and that the culvert had been properly maintained the previous September. This conflicting evidence centered on whether the railroad company had shown negligence in maintaining the culvert or whether proper protocols were observed, leading to the initial ruling that favored the plaintiff before being appealed by the defendant.	The plaintiff, Patrick H. Boylan, argued that the Pennsylvania Company failed to properly secure the planks over the culvert at the railroad crossing, which resulted in the dangerous condition that led to his injury. He claimed that the defendant's negligence in allowing the planks to remain unfastened constituted a breach of duty that directly caused his damages. The plaintiff sought compensation for his injuries stemming from this alleged negligence.	The Pennsylvania Company contended that they were not negligent as they had performed thorough repairs on the culvert nine months before the incident. The railroad company argued that their workers were not present at the Forty-seventh Street culvert on the day before the accident and that the planks were in good condition. They also emphasized that the circuit court erroneously excluded critical testimony that could counter the plaintiff's claims and that the evidence presented by the defense demonstrated they acted responsibly in maintaining the railroad crossing.

In 1877, the case of James Condon v. Joseph N. Besse arose in La Salle County, Illinois. The conflict began when Joseph N. Besse filed a note along with a power of attorney that led to a judgment by confession being entered against James Condon. This judgment was filed in the circuit court on January 7, 1876. Condon, illiterate and unable to read or write, claimed that Besse misrepresented the nature of the note to him, stating it was for $100, but in reality, it was for $185. He also asserted that he was not made aware of the power of attorney that would allow the judgment to be entered without proper evidence. Furthermore, Condon contended that Besse claimed the note would not be payable for two years while it was actually due within one year. Following the judgment, Condon motioned to set it aside during the court's January term, supported by affidavits from himself and other witnesses outlining the alleged fraud and misrepresentation. However, Besse and a witness testified that the documents had been read to Condon prior to their execution, resulting in conflicting evidence that necessitated a more thorough trial. The case highlights the issues surrounding the administration of justice when judgments are obtained through potentially fraudulent means.	James Condon, the plaintiff, argues that the judgment against him should be set aside due to fraudulent misrepresentation regarding the terms of the promissory note. He claims that Besse misled him about the amount owed and the repayment terms. Condon requests the court to allow him to challenge the judgment, positing that the circumstances under which the note and power of attorney were executed were deceptive, warranting a full trial to examine the validity of his defense.	Joseph N. Besse, the defendant, maintains that the judgment was valid and asserts that the documents were properly explained to Condon before he signed them. Besse argues that the affidavits supporting Condon's motion create irreconcilable conflicts that do not constitute sufficient grounds to set aside the judgment. He requests the court to uphold the judgment by confession, asserting that the claim of fraud lacks credible evidence.

In the case of Henry S. Carpenter et al. v. The First National Bank of Joliet, the dispute arose in Joliet, Illinois, with significant events occurring around June 19 and June 20, 1884. The case involved the sale of corn, where Henry S. Carpenter and partners purchased corn from Woodruff & Jones, with conditions pertaining to the quality of the corn upon inspection in Chicago. Upon supplying a promissory note as part of this transaction, Carpenter and partners later faced issues when they realized the corn shipped did not meet the expected quality. This led to a judgment by confession being entered against them, which they contested. The judgment was subsequently opened, allowing the defendants (Carpenter et al.) to plead their case in front of a jury, where they argued that the corn was conditionally sold. The jury trial highlighted procedural matters, such as the amendment of the declaration and the control the court had over the proceedings after the defendants were allowed to plead.	The plaintiffs, represented by the First National Bank of Joliet, asserted that Carpenter and his partners owed money as secured by the promissory note related to the corn purchased. The plaintiffs maintained that the note provided prima facie evidence of the amount due and contended that the defendants had an opportunity to understand their obligation under the note.	The defendants argued that the sale of corn was conditional upon an inspection of the grain and claimed that they had been misled regarding the quality of the corn through false statements made by the sellers, Woodruff & Jones. They contended that the court erred in procedural aspects concerning who had the opening and closing arguments in court and challenged the validity of the instructions given to the jury which they claimed did not adequately consider their defense.

In the case of George Railton v. John Lauder, the events took place in Chicago, Illinois, culminating on November 15, 1888. The plaintiff, George Railton, initiated a legal suit against John Lauder through the process of attachment, claiming that Lauder was a non-resident of Illinois. Railton's action involved publishing a notice of the legal proceedings in a newspaper, the “Chicago Daily Law Bulletin.” A default judgment was entered against Lauder, who later sought to have this judgment overturned. Lauder’s argument centered on the publication of the notice, claiming that it was not printed in a "secular newspaper of general circulation" as required by state statute. The case moved through circuit court proceedings and was affirmed by the Appellate Court for the First District, which also allowed for an important certificate that led to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, George Railton, claimed that the notice regarding the legal proceedings was properly published in the “Chicago Daily Law Bulletin” in accordance with statutory requirements. Railton sought to uphold the default judgment entered against Lauder, arguing that the newspaper fulfilled the legal criteria of being a secular newspaper of general circulation in Chicago, thus ensuring proper notice was given to the defendant.	John Lauder, the defendant, contended that the notice was not published in a recognized secular newspaper of general circulation as mandated by law. Lauder's legal team attempted to present evidence challenging the classification of the “Chicago Daily Law Bulletin,” asserting that the newspaper did not meet the necessary statutory qualifications. Their objective was to set aside the default judgment based on this alleged procedural error.

In 1858, Alexander N. Fullerton brought an action of ejectment against John Stoetzell and others in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas, seeking possession of a parcel of land located within Wolcott’s addition to Chicago, Illinois. The dispute centered around a lot originally owned by Charles Butler, who sold it to Fullerton on June 26, 1837, establishing a clear title for Fullerton. During the trial, the defendants presented evidence from a previous Circuit Court case where Fullerton had been found liable to Charles B. Beed and Nathaniel Church, resulting in a judgment that allowed Beed and Church to acquire the property through execution. The defendants argued that a quitclaim deed from 1857 further supported their claim to the property. Central to the case was the fact that Nathaniel Church had died before judgment was rendered in the earlier case, leading to the argument that this rendered the judgment void and without effect. The trial court ultimately found for Fullerton, affirming his ownership of the property.	The plaintiff, Alexander N. Fullerton, claimed ownership of the property based on the conveyance from Charles Butler in 1837. He sought to recover possession of the property from the defendants, asserting that the earlier judgment against him was invalid due to the death of one of the plaintiffs, Nathaniel Church, before the judgment was entered. Fullerton argued that the absence of a suggestion of death on the record meant the earlier proceedings were void, thereby affirming his rightful claim to the property.	The defendants contended that the earlier judgment against Fullerton was valid despite Church's death, as it had not been challenged in a manner that abated the suit. They argued that the death of Church should have been pleaded in abatement during the original action. The defendants maintained that Fullerton's claims were undermined by this failure and that they had legitimate title to the property based on the sheriff’s deed resulting from the previous judgment.

The case, 'The People of the State of Illinois, ex relatione Charles R. Matheny appellants v. Mordecai Mobley, appellee', took place in Illinois during the year 1835, particularly around the month of May. The key individuals involved in this case were Charles R. Matheny, who served as the clerk of the Circuit Court of Sangamon County, and Mordecai Mobley, who claimed the same position under an appointment made by Judge Stephen T. Logan. On May 4, 1835, Matheny was allegedly unlawfully displaced when Mobley, having been appointed by Judge Logan under a new legislative act passed on January 7, 1835, assumed the role of clerk. The dispute centered around the validity of Mobley’s appointment compared to Matheny's prior appointment, which Matheny argued was still in effect as the court had not been abolished or his position legally vacated. This case raised significant questions about the powers of appointment granted to judges under the Constitution of Illinois and the legitimacy of a clerk's tenure once appointed. The actions leading to this legal challenge stemmed from the definitions of appointments and removals as established by law and constitutional provisions at the time.",	Charles R. Matheny, the plaintiff, argued that he was the legally appointed clerk of the Circuit Court of Sangamon and had held that position since February 14, 1827. He claimed that his appointment had not been revoked and that he had not been removed from office by any court judgment. Matheny asserted that Mordecai Mobley was unlawfully holding the office without authorization, constituting a usurpation of his legally established role. He requested the court to restore him to his position and address the validity of Mobley's appointment.",	Mordecai Mobley, the defendant, contended that his appointment as clerk was valid under the provisions of the legislative act passed in January 1835, which allowed Judge Stephen T. Logan to appoint clerks for Circuit Courts. Mobley argued that his appointment was lawful and had been established properly according to the laws of Illinois. He maintained that he was exercising his office under legitimate authority, having taken the required oaths and executed the necessary bond.",

In December 1847, the case John Bean et al. v. John Doe, ex dem. James McNutt was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered around an action of ejectment for the recovery of a specific piece of land located in Adams County, Illinois, specifically the southwest quarter of section eleven in township thirteen south, range eight west of the fourth principal meridian. The plaintiff, John Doe, and the other parties involved were appealing a decision from the Adams Circuit Court, where they had previously claimed ownership of the land based on an Auditor’s deed. During the trial in April 1846, the defendants (the appellants) sought to introduce evidence of the Auditor’s deed, which had been executed on December 19, 1845. The deed acknowledged a tax sale from January 4, 1832, but the plaintiffs objected, asserting that the Auditor lacked the authority to issue deeds following the enactment of the Revenue Act of 1833. The court sustained this objection, leading to a verdict in favor of the plaintiffs and a judgment that the defendants were not entitled to the property.	The plaintiffs, led by John Doe, claimed rightful ownership of the land based on the court’s prior ruling. They argued against the validity of the Auditor’s deed presented by the defendants, contesting the Auditor's capacity to execute such deeds after the 1833 Revenue Act. Their legal requests were focused on maintaining their claim to the property and ensuring that the deed offered by the defendants was excluded from evidence.	The defendants, represented by John Bean and others, contended that the Auditor's deed was valid and should be admissible as evidence. They argued that the deed was consistent with legal precedents established in previous cases, specifically referencing the case of Bruce v. Schuyler, where a similar deed was upheld. They requested that the court reverse the lower court’s ruling that excluded the deed and allow for a re-hearing of the case based on this evidence.

Nathaniel K. Beasley and his brother filed a legal case against William H. Webster in September 1872 in the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from a contract dated March 14, 1867, regarding the construction of a house in Monmouth, Illinois. Under this contract, Webster was to build the house for Charles Wilcox, who was responsible for certain payments. As the construction completed by May 1, 1867, Wilcox still owed $450 by June 4, 1868. Prior to this, Wilcox, indebted to the Beasley brothers for $700, attempted to secure this debt through a mortgage on the property. However, they declined a mortgage, leading to Wilcox assigning his title bond to the Beasleys instead, under the condition that they would cover his debt to Webster. The Beasleys eventually secured a deed for the property but did not pay Webster’s claim nor recognized his lien. A lawsuit ensued when Webster sought an injunction to prevent the Beasleys from selling the property until they paid what they owed him. Subsequent hearings led to an injunction against the Beasleys from selling the lot until they satisfied Webster’s claim.	Webster claimed that the Beasley brothers failed to acknowledge and pay his mechanic’s lien for the $450 owed to him for constructing the house. He requested an injunction to prevent the Beasleys from selling the property and demanded that they pay the owed amount along with interest and legal costs. He based his claims on the contract made with Wilcox and the subsequent agreement with the Beasleys regarding payment for the debt.	The Beasleys argued they were not notified of Webster's lien and denied any agreement to pay his claim. They contended that the contractual payment timeline extended beyond one year from the completion of the work, thereby nullifying Webster's lien. They asserted that they had no contractual obligation to Webster and maintained that they did not agree to take on Wilcox's debts.

In 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, James W. Brockway served as the duly elected recorder of deeds. Under his role, Brockway was supposed to receive a salary of $3,000 per year, with the requirement to pay all additional fees and emoluments into the county treasury. However, Brockway received $500 more than authorized, which he refused to remit to the county. Subsequently, Cook County filed a suit against him to recover this sum. The case was tried without a jury, relying on Brockway's written reports to the county board and his oral testimony. Evidence revealed that, while Brockway was engaged in his official duties, he also operated a business making and selling property abstracts. This activity drew substantial profits, but the county argued that his extra earnings should rightfully belong to the county treasury. The court heard no defense evidence as Brockway pleaded "nil debet," stipulating the plaintiff could introduce any evidence in defense admissible under special pleas. The trial concluded with a judgment favoring Cook County for the amount sought.	Cook County argued that under Illinois law, Brockway was only to receive his fixed salary as compensation for performing his duties as recorder and that any excess earnings derived from fees and profits, including those from his abstract-making business, were meant to be paid into the county treasury. The county contended that it had no legal authority to grant Brockway additional compensation outside of his official salary, making his retention of the $500 both legally and contractually impermissible.	Brockway claimed that the earnings from the abstract-making business did not fall under his statutory duties as recorder. He contended that since the business of creating and certifying abstracts was not part of his official responsibilities, he was entitled to keep those earnings as they were derived from services rendered outside of his role as recorder. Furthermore, he asserted that the county had no legal authority to engage in the abstract business, which meant it could not claim any share in the profits made from those transactions.

On April 29, 1884, in Jackson County, Illinois, J. M. Scurlock (the defendant) placed a written order with the Havana Press Drill Company (the plaintiff) to manufacture and ship two grain drills, priced at $850 each, by July 1, 1884. Although the drills were delivered on July 17, they were never used or sold by Scurlock, who claimed they were defective and not what he ordered. A warranty in the contract stipulated the drills had to be well made and of good material, with provisions for defects to be reported within two days. Scurlock notified the company about issues with the drills immediately upon receipt and again on September 11, highlighting the unfit condition of the drills and requesting a remedy. However, the plaintiff failed to send anyone to address these concerns. Scurlock formally refused to pay in December and attempted to return the drills, but an agent from the plaintiff refused to accept them. The case went to a Justice of the Peace and was later appealed to the Circuit Court of Jackson County, where Scurlock was awarded judgments for the costs of the suit in both trials.	The plaintiff, Havana Press Drill Company, argued that Scurlock was liable for payment despite not returning the drills, stating that the contract required Scurlock to give the drills a two-day trial. They maintained that the drills had been supplied as per the agreement and emphasized that Scurlock's failure to return them invalidated his refusal to pay.	Scurlock's defense was based on asserting that the drills were defective and did not meet the warranty terms outlined in the contract. He argued that the plaintiff failed to comply with their obligations by not sending someone to remedy the defects once notified. Scurlock asserted that he was not required to return the drills because the warranty had been breached, rendering them worthless, and he was justified in refusing to pay due to the plaintiff’s failure to fulfill their contract.

In 1882, in Mercer County, Illinois, a legal action was initiated involving B. F. Brock, the supervisor of the town, as the plaintiff against H. R. Morrison and others, who were sureties on the official bond of Thomas F. McClintock. McClintock served as the treasurer for the town, initially appointed in the spring of 1876, and continued to serve in this role until his death in 1881. The case arose from claims that McClintock, who had failed to account for certain funds, was a defaulter for the year 1878. The defendants contended that the alleged defalcation occurred in 1877, a time before they had agreed to serve as sureties. The matter was brought to trial in the Circuit Court of Mercer County, where this factual issue was contested. After the court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, the case was appealed to the Appellate Court, which also upheld the decision, thus affirming the finding that the defalcation indeed occurred in 1878, making the sureties liable under the bond for that year.	The plaintiff, B. F. Brock, claimed that Thomas F. McClintock was a defaulter regarding his duties as treasurer for the year 1878. Brock sought to enforce the surety bond against the defendants, asserting that they were liable for the default because it occurred during the period covered by their bond.	The defendants argued that the alleged defalcation took place in 1877, prior to their assumption of liability as sureties for the bond in 1878. They contended this temporal distinction exempted them from responsibility for McClintock's failure to account for the funds in question.

The case "William Barks et al. v. Delilah Woodruff" took place in Bureau County, Illinois, with the judgment rendered on December 28, 1882. The key individuals involved include Delilah Woodruff, the plaintiff, and her husband, Nathan S. Woodruff, along with the defendants, who were Barks, Kies, and Banschbank, who sold intoxicating liquor to Woodruff. On February 26 and 27, 1881, Nathan Woodruff became intoxicated after consuming various alcoholic beverages. On his return home from Princeton, he fell out of a sled while intoxicated, which led to his team of horses straying away. Due to the severe weather conditions, which included a snowstorm, one of the horses owned by Delilah perished after becoming entangled in a snowbank. Delilah claimed that the defendants’ actions (the sale of alcohol to her husband) resulted in the loss of her horse and jeopardized her means of support for her family, including her minor daughters.	Delilah Woodruff's primary argument was that the defendants contributed to her husband Nathan's intoxication by selling him alcoholic beverages, which led to his negligence in controlling their team of horses. This negligence resulted in the death of one horse, which belonged to Delilah, significantly affecting her means of support as the horse was essential for farm work. She sought damages for the loss of her horse and the negative impact on her ability to support her family.	The defendants argued that the intoxication of Nathan Woodruff was a separate issue and that they could not be held liable for the subsequent injuries and damages he caused due to his actions after consuming the alcohol. They contended that because Nathan was sober the following day and displayed the ability to recover the team, his later intoxication was not relevant to their liability for the initial sale of alcohol. Additionally, they asserted that one of the defendants, Banschbank, did not contribute to the intoxication that led to the subsequent events.

The case of J. H. Tedens et al. v. J. B. Schumers took place in Lemont, Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a court decision on April 15, 1883. The principal individuals involved were the plaintiff, J. B. Schumers, and the defendants, J. H. Tedens and Thormahlen, who operated a store. The dispute arose over a due-bill for $2,100 given to Schumers by the defendants on June 1, 1879, reflecting his accumulated salary during his employment as a clerk. The defendants later accused Schumers of stealing goods from the store, claiming he admitted to these thefts when confronted. In an alleged settlement, Schumers agreed to surrender the due-bill in exchange for the defendants' silence concerning the alleged theft, although he contested the existence of such an agreement. The defendants testified that Schumers's thefts amounted to more than the amount of the due-bill, while Schumers denied the allegations, arguing he had taken goods under an arrangement to purchase them at cost. The case was brought to a jury, which found in favor of Schumers, awarding him $2,758, though he subsequently remitted half of this amount.	The plaintiff, J. B. Schumers, argued that he had not committed any theft and that the goods taken from the defendants' store were acquired under a prior arrangement to buy them at cost. He contended that he surrendered the due-bill to avoid false accusations of larceny and that the defendants had agreed to his conditions regarding the investigation of the goods taken. Schumers sought to recover the amount stated in the due-bill along with interest.	The defendants, J. H. Tedens and Thormahlen, claimed that they discovered Schumers had been stealing goods from their store over a period of nearly four years and argued that Schumers admitted to his wrongdoing. They presented evidence that indicated these thefts exceeded the amount of the due-bill. The defendants contended that the surrender of the due-bill constituted an accord and satisfaction for the stolen goods, thus negating any claim for the due-bill's payment.

In December 1819, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed a criminal prosecution for a riot involving James A. Whitesides and others as plaintiffs in error against the People of the State of Illinois, defendants in error. The case arose out of an incident in Pope County, Illinois. The plaintiffs were accused of creating a significant disturbance that allegedly constituted a riot. The court examined three points of error raised by the plaintiffs regarding the indictment: 1) the indictment failed to specify the year of the offense, 2) it did not adhere to the constitutional form required for such prosecutions, and 3) the charges described were too vague and did not adequately demonstrate that a riot, as legally defined, had occurred.	The plaintiffs contended that the indictment was defective on multiple grounds. They argued that the indictment did not state the year in a legally accepted manner and did not include the necessary phrasing that identifies the prosecution in the name and authority of the State of Illinois. Furthermore, they claimed that the allegations concerning the noise and disturbance were too vague and did not meet the legal standards for defining a riot.	The defendants maintained that the indictment was valid, asserting that the allegations presented were sufficient to demonstrate the occurrence of a riot. They argued that the prosecution had followed the necessary legal procedures and that any technical deficiencies in the indictment did not significantly impact the assessment of the plaintiffs' guilt.

The case "Elias R. Bowen v. Florence McCarthy et al." took place in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 15, 1888. Elias R. Bowen had been in possession of a specific lot in Chicago for many years, initially as a tenant under a lease with Sidney P. Walker, who owned the property. Bowen paid rent directly to Walker, and after their written lease expired, he continued to occupy the land while making improvements. In April 1866, Walker and Bowen entered into a settlement where Walker purportedly agreed to lease a portion of the lot to Bowen for five years, though no formal lease was signed. In 1874, Walker owed Bowen $4,600, leading to the execution of a chattel mortgage by Walker to secure the debt. This mortgage included a clause about applying rent from the property to the loan repayment. Walker passed away in January 1884, and in the following August, Florence McCarthy initiated foreclosure proceedings against Bowen and other mortgage holders. The circuit court ruled that while Bowen could remove his improvements, his claim for a lien on the lot was denied. This decree was affirmed by the Appellate Court. Bowen argued that the language in the chattel mortgage constituted an equitable mortgage, seeking rights over the property based on the rent payments.	Bowen claimed he had a lien on the north thirty feet of the lot based on the chattel mortgage's provisions that allowed him to apply rent payments toward the debt owed by Walker. He argued that this created an equitable mortgage on the property, thereby entitling him to rights as a mortgagee over the real estate.	McCarthy's defense revolved around the argument that the clause in the chattel mortgage did not create any lien on the property. The court found that Bowen’s security was limited to the chattels mortgaged and that there was no legal foundation for Bowen's claim to extend the mortgage to the real property based on the provided language in the chattel mortgage.

In September 1871, a legal dispute arose in DeKalb County, Illinois, involving Cornelia Misner as the plaintiff and David Huftalin as the defendant. The case was brought forth due to a forcible entry and detainer action, with Misner seeking to regain possession of approximately one hundred acres of land. Misner had previously rented the premises to a tenant named Wyatt for a year, after which she moved some of her belongings onto the property, indicating her intentions to occupy it. Upon her return to the premises, Misner discovered that Huftalin had taken possession and her belongings were left outside. The case progressed through the justice of the peace and the Court of Common Pleas of Aurora, where Huftalin was found guilty. Huftalin subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, contesting issues regarding the proof of demand for possession and the extent of Misner's previous possession.	Misner's main arguments centered around her rightful possession of the land and the legality of Huftalin's entry. She asserted that she had made a written demand for possession before the lawsuit started, which adequately supported her claim. Additionally, she presented evidence indicating that she had returned to occupy the premises after the lease expired and had performed actions suggesting she had control over the property. Misner sought to affirm her ownership rights and reclaim possession of her land.	Huftalin's defense focused on contesting the validity of Misner's claims, arguing that there was insufficient proof of her demand for possession prior to initiating the lawsuit. He claimed that Misner only occupied a portion of the premises and challenged the claim that she had actual possession of the whole property. Furthermore, Huftalin attempted to introduce evidence of a mortgage to assert his entry under that agreement, which was denied by the court. He sought a dismissal of the suit based on these points and requested that the jury consider certain facts around tenancy and possession.

William N. Wickliff initiated a legal case against Jamison Robinson and others in St. Clair County, Illinois, around December 1856. The case arose after Wickliff had obtained a judgment against Robinson and another party, Pelham. While this judgment was paid in full except for approximately thirteen dollars in costs, a clerk from the circuit court issued an execution for these costs without the authority of Wickliff or his attorney. This execution led to the sale of land, belonging to Robinson, valued at over one thousand dollars, to the clerk. The sale was facilitated through an arrangement between the sheriff and the clerk, wherein they would share the benefits of the purchased property. Under Illinois law at the time, public officers, such as sheriffs and clerks, were prohibited from purchasing property at sales they conducted, rendering the sale void. The legal framework aimed to ensure fairness in judicial sales and prevent any conflicts of interest or corruption among public officers.	Wickliff's primary argument centered on the illegality of the execution and subsequent sale of the land conducted by the clerk without his authorization. He asserted that the sale was void due to the clear statutory prohibition preventing officials from purchasing property in such contexts. Wickliff sought to have the execution and the sale set aside, thereby reclaiming the rightful ownership of the land or its value.	The defendants, including Robinson, contended that the execution and sale were valid undertakings conducted under the necessary legal protocols. They may have sought to frame the sheriff's and clerk's arrangement as permissible or to argue for the legitimacy of the costs due as a reason for the sale. However, specifics of their legal arguments weren't extensively documented in the description.

On December 23, 1852, in Bureau County, Illinois, Edward D. Kemp filed a bill against John G. Reed for specific performance of a contract. The contract, dated July 12, 1851, involved Reed binding himself to deliver a deed for land in exchange for $65 paid by Kemp. The bond was recorded, but alterations were made to the document while in Kemp's possession; it was also noted that there were issues regarding the acknowledgment of the contract. After the suit started, Reed had conveyed the property to another individual, Atkinson, which complicated the case. Atkinson claimed he purchased the land without notice of Kemp's contract and later sold it to the Duffield Mining Company. As the case progressed, both Reed and Atkinson filed cross claims but failed to effectively follow through, leading to legal disputes over the validity of the contract and the alterations made to it.	The plaintiff, Edward D. Kemp, argued for the specific performance of the contract with Reed, emphasizing that Reed had a legal obligation to deliver the deed for the land as per their agreement. Kemp pointed out the alterations made to the bond and asserted that these changes should not invalidate the contract. He maintained that his recording of the agreement served as constructive notice to any subsequent purchasers, including Atkinson and the Duffield Mining Company.	The defendants, John G. Reed and Atkinson, contended that the original contract was intended as security for a debt rather than a sale. They argued that the alterations made to the contract were immaterial and that Atkinson had purchased the land without any actual notice of Kemp's claims, which should therefore protect their interests. Atkinson claimed that he conducted due diligence by checking the records before purchasing and was unaware of Kemp's contract until after the purchase was concluded.

The case "Mary S. Mitchell v. The City of Chicago" took place in April 1866 in Chicago, Illinois. The primary individuals involved were Mary S. Mitchell, the plaintiff, and The City of Chicago, the defendant. The case originated from a proceeding to condemn land due to the non-payment of an assessment, which was purportedly for the improvement of a street in the city. A default judgment was rendered against Mitchell for failing to respond appropriately to the assessment proceedings. Subsequently, she filed a motion to set aside the default judgment based on an affidavit claiming irregularities. The only matter for consideration was whether the court had erred in refusing to vacate the default judgment.	Mary S. Mitchell argued that the default judgment against her should be set aside due to alleged defects in the assessment proceedings that were revealed only through her affidavit. She contended that the court had not addressed these irregularities and requested the court to reconsider its decision regarding the default judgment.	The City of Chicago maintained that the court below acted correctly in refusing to set aside the default judgment. They asserted that no exceptions were taken to the report or notice that led to the judgment, and prior court decisions established that such decisions by the lower court could not be contested as errors.

The case of Joseph Honnard v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in 1873 in Jackson County, Illinois. Joseph Honnard, a practicing physician, was indicted for manslaughter in relation to the death of Jane Stevenson, a pregnant woman suffering from bilious fever. Honnard was attending to Jane while her husband was incapacitated and under the care of another physician. On September 7, 1873, Jane experienced a miscarriage, and Honnard was called to assist in the procedure. He attempted to remove the fetus using improvised tools but ultimately left the case to another physician, Dr. Mahoney. After the miscarriage, Jane received no professional medical care for several days. Complications led to her developing puerperal fever, and she died on September 16, 1873. While the court heard evidence regarding Honnard's care, it became apparent that the physician did not contribute to the initial miscarriage and acted with care during the procedure. The deliberation centered around whether Honnard's actions were sufficient grounds for a manslaughter conviction.	The plaintiffs contended that Joseph Honnard was responsible for Jane Stevenson's death due to his alleged negligence during her miscarriage. They argued that his methods in attempting to aid the delivery were insufficient and that his failure to ensure proper care ultimately contributed to Jane's demise from puerperal fever.	Joseph Honnard's defense rested on the argument that he did not instigate the miscarriage and acted responsibly while providing care under difficult circumstances. Evidence demonstrated that he did not administer strong medications or take any actions that would have directly caused the complications leading to Jane's death. Honnard maintained that even if he had not exercised the utmost skill, there was no evidence that his actions led to the adverse health outcomes.

Murray McConnel initiated a legal action against Jarius Kibbe in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1864. The case arose in Jacksonville, Illinois, concerning a brick tenement divided between McConnel, who owned the upper stories, and Kibbe, who owned the ground-floor rooms. McConnel had previously leased his part of the property to a tenant named Fox for ten years. The dispute began when Kibbe allegedly removed a partition wall that supported McConnel's premises, leading to damage in the form of cracks and structural instability. The trial revealed that the removal of the wall occurred before McConnel's lease to Fox, which became a pivotal point in the court's judgment. The jury ultimately found in favor of the defendant, Kibbe.	McConnel claimed that the removal of the partition wall by Kibbe constituted an infringement on his property rights, damaging his reversionary interest in the tenement. He sought to recover damages for both the nominal harm inferred by law due to the wrongful act and any actual damages subsequently incurred as a result of the injury caused by Kibbe's actions.	Kibbe defended himself by asserting that the removal of the wall occurred before McConnel leased the upper floors to Fox, arguing that McConnel was not entitled to damages since the act leading to the alleged harm did not occur while Fox was in possession. His counsel maintained that the legal prerequisites for a successful claim were not satisfied, particularly regarding the timing of the actions in relation to the lease.

The case "The Chicago and Wilmington Coal Company v. Andrew R. Liddell" was decided in September 1873 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It arose in Will County, Illinois, where Andrew B. Liddell brought a lawsuit against the Chicago and Wilmington Coal Company. The dispute centered around a verbal contract in which Liddell was to supply boarding services for the coal company’s miners. The plaintiff claimed that the company failed to pay for these services after initially agreeing to do so at the rate of five dollars per week. The case was tried before a jury, which found in favor of Liddell, prompting the defendant to appeal. The primary contention of the defendant was that the contract, being verbal and not written, was void under the Statute of Frauds. However, the court noted that this statute was not explicitly claimed by the defendant and ruled that the undertaking was primary, not collateral. Additionally, the court established that the lack of a specified duration for the contract allowed either party to terminate it with notice, which was not provided by the defendant. The court upheld the jury's verdict and affirmed the judgment in favor of Liddell.	Andrew B. Liddell, the plaintiff, claimed that the Chicago and Wilmington Coal Company breached their verbal contract to pay for boarding services he provided to the miners employed by the company. Liddell sought compensation for the unpaid boarding fees, asserting that the company had a primary obligation to pay for these services, according to their agreement. He contended that the contract was valid despite being verbal and argued that the absence of written documentation did not negate the company’s responsibility to fulfill their financial commitment.	The Chicago and Wilmington Coal Company, the defendant, argued primarily that the verbal contract was void under the Statute of Frauds, claiming it should not be enforceable because it was not in writing. They also contended that the contract did not specify a duration, therefore allowing them to terminate it without notice. Additionally, the defendant maintained that a refusal to pay at a specific time invalidated the contract, implying that they should not be held liable for the boarding costs incurred by the plaintiff.

In 1883, Selina Gilmore and David Gilmore executed a mortgage in Will County, Illinois, to secure a promissory note for the sum of $2,969.15 to Wm. Findley. This note was due on October 24, 1884, and carried an interest rate of eight percent per annum. After Findley assigned the note and mortgage to Martin C. Bissell, Bissell filed a bill against the Gilmores seeking foreclosure due to the non-payment. The Gilmores acknowledged the execution of the note and mortgage but raised issues of usury, claiming deductions based on previous transactions with Findley that involved charging interest on previously due interest. They contended that the interest charged was excessive, referencing prior notes from 1875 and 1878, which included adjustments that resulted in a higher interest rate than initially agreed. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court in December 1887.	The plaintiff, Martin C. Bissell, claimed that the Gilmores owed the full amount of the promissory note and asserted that the entire sum was due following the assignment of the mortgage from Findley. Bissell sought to foreclose on the mortgage based on the non-payment of the debt, arguing that the transactions were legal and compliant with interest laws.	The defendants, Selina and David Gilmore, argued that the mortgage agreement was usurious due to the excessive interest charged and the practice of charging interest on previously accrued interest. They claimed these practices rendered the contract void and sought deductions related to the usury, questioning the validity of the foreclosure proceedings based on these allegations.

John M. Clark v. Charlotte F. Clark is a legal case that took place in 1888 in Vermillion County, Illinois. The case involves a bill for divorce filed by Charlotte F. Clark against her husband, John M. Clark, who was charged with incest with their daughter, India Clark, and desertion. Following previous attempts at divorce by Charlotte, which she dismissed after receiving $2,000 from John for attorney's fees and alimony, she revived the charges, claiming that the prior dismissal did not condone John's actions. The trial revealed conflicting evidence regarding the incest allegations, particularly concerning statements made by their daughter India, which raised questions about her credibility. The Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of Charlotte, and John Clark brought the case to the Illinois Appellate Court, contesting various aspects of the evidence and procedural decisions made during the trial.	Charlotte F. Clark's primary claims in her divorce petition included allegations of incest against her husband, John M. Clark, specifically regarding their daughter India. She argued that the nature of John's conduct warranted a divorce and that previous attempts to resolve the matter did not absolve him of his actions. Charlotte sought legal remedy from the court in the form of a decree for divorce based on these allegations.	John M. Clark defended against the allegations by challenging the admissibility and relevance of certain evidence, including witness statements and claims of bias regarding prior jury appearances. He argued that the court erred in excluding specific evidence and that there was a lack of sufficient proof to support Charlotte's claims. John contended that the dismissal of the previous divorce petition amounted to condonation of any alleged offenses and sought to have the case dismissed based on these defenses.

Clarissa Wren filed a legal case against William S. Moss and others in December 1844, after her husband Aquilla Wren's death. The case originates from a divorce decree obtained by Aquilla against Clarissa during proceedings in the Peoria Circuit Court in May 1844, where the issue of alimony was postponed for a later term. Shortly after the divorce was decreed, Aquilla Wren passed away, resulting in the abatement of the alimony suit. Before his death, Aquilla executed a will profiting his daughters with Sarah Bobo and assigning his remaining estate to Thomas Wren, with William S. Moss as the named executor. The case involved a motion by Clarissa’s counsel to issue a writ of scire facias to Aquilla's executor, challenging the prior divorce ruling and to ensure that her claims for alimony would not be forfeited. Other parties, including heirs and devisees, were also made defendants in this matter. The core issue revolved around whether Clarissa could still claim her rights to alimony and dower despite the abatement of her case due to her husband's death.	Clarissa Wren argued that the divorce decree and her husband’s death should not bar her from receiving alimony or her dower in his estate. She requested the court to issue a writ of scire facias against Aquilla's executor and to review the divorce decree, contending that the abatement of the suit concerning alimony denied her financial support from Aquilla's estate.	The defendants, led by William S. Moss, contended that the divorce decree effectively terminated Clarissa's rights to dower and alimony. They argued that the personal nature of the divorce suit means that it cannot survive against executors, heirs, or devisees, thereby suggesting that her claims to alimony are invalid due to the previous court ruling and her husband's death.

The case "Stephen P. Lunt v. John M. Stephens" originated in Cook County, Illinois, around September 1874, involving multiple parties, including the Balback Smelting and Refining Company and its officers, as well as the plaintiff Stephen P. Lunt and defendant John M. Stephens. The dispute arose from a claim by Lunt for unpaid labor and materials he provided for construction work on the company's facilities. He alleged that he was contracted to perform all masonry, stone, and brick work and to furnish materials, which he completed by July 10, 1872. Lunt claimed that after accounting for all payments, he was owed $2,768.25 with interest that was still unpaid. The property in question was originally owned by Lawson S. Warner and others but was sold to the company under a verbal contract. The case became complicated as several intervening creditors claimed prior liens, including mortgages established prior to the work done by Lunt. A legal battle ensued over the validity of these liens and the mechanics’ lien that Lunt sought to enforce.	Stephen P. Lunt claimed that he was entitled to a mechanic’s lien for the work and materials provided to the Balback Company, which amounted to $2,768.25, alleging these were due after his work was completed. He argued that the work performed in 1871 and 1872 constituted a single contract, which should not be barred by timelines related to the fire that disrupted the company’s operations. Lunt’s legal request involved enforcing this lien against the property, allowing him to recover the unpaid amount.	The defendants, including John M. Stephens, argued that Lunt's mechanic’s lien could not be enforced because the petition for the lien was not filed within six months post the alleged completion of work. They contended that the work completed by Lunt before the fire in October 1871 was distinct and therefore not applicable to the claims made afterwards. Additionally, they insisted that prior mortgages held by creditors took precedence over Lunt's lien, denying the continuity of Lunt's claims in light of intervening creditor rights.

Charles B. Phillips was involved in a legal case against Joseph L. Wilson, the administrator of the estate of Erastus B. Williams, and E. W. Blatchford. The case originated in Cook County, Illinois, and stemmed from an action of assumpsit initiated on behalf of Blatchford against Phillips. The original lawsuit was filed on January 23, 1884, but Phillips was defaulted, leading to a judgment against him. Subsequently, on January 26, 1884, he was allowed to plead with the judgment standing as security. Following the death of Erastus B. Williams on January 3, 1885, the court allowed the action to continue in the name of Wilson, as the administrator. Phillips's motions to vacate the order that allowed this substitution and to alter the plaintiff were denied by the court. The trial resulted in a verdict against Phillips, but he did not file a bill of exceptions, and his appeal included errors related to the substitution order and the proceeding in Wilson’s name.	The plaintiff, represented by Joseph L. Wilson, argued that the lawsuit could be continued in the name of the administrator following the death of the assignor, as permitted by Illinois law. The plaintiff maintained that the court's actions—allowing the case to proceed in the administrator’s name and denying Phillips's motions—were appropriate and did not prejudice Phillips’s ability to defend against the claims made.	Charles B. Phillips contended that the suit should not have continued in the name of Wilson, following the death of Williams, arguing that he was deprived of certain rights by the court's decisions. He sought to vacate the order that substituted the administrator for the deceased plaintiff and wished to have a different party recognized as the sole plaintiff, claiming that the court's decisions improperly affected his defense.

The case "Illinois Starch Company v. Ottawa Hydraulic Company" took place in Ottawa, Illinois, with the final judgment issued on June 13, 1887. The Illinois Starch Company, originally named the Ottawa Starch Company, had entered into a lease agreement with the Ottawa Hydraulic Company on March 1, 1856, for a water power source and a tract of land. This lease stipulated a rent of $2,500 per year for a term of 999 years but allowed for specific conditions where the Hydraulic Company could declare the lease void if the Starch Company failed to pay the rent or adhere to lease conditions. The dispute arose when the Ottawa Hydraulic Company sought to foreclose for unpaid rents. The Hydraulic Company identified that over $88,000 was owed; however, the Starch Company was found to be insolvent, with properties insufficient to cover the debt. After a court hearing established the overdue rents and the debtor's insolvency, foreclosure was ordered. The court found that the properties owned by the Starch Company would not yield enough to satisfy the debt, leading to a strict foreclosure ruling.	The Ottawa Hydraulic Company claimed that the Illinois Starch Company failed to pay rent due under their lease agreement. They sought foreclosure for unpaid rents combined with interest, citing a total outstanding amount of $88,964.11. The Hydraulic Company argued that they had a first lien against the property and the machinery, and appealed for a decree that would allow them to take possession of the property if the debt was not settled within 100 days.	The Illinois Starch Company contested the foreclosure, asserting that the lease granted them a secure and long-term leasehold which they had relied upon for significant investments in improvements on the property. They argued that the evidence did not justify a strict foreclosure due to the presence of other creditors and that the property was worth more than the debt. Furthermore, they maintained that the calculation of the property's value did not adequately reflect its previous worth or the significant investment made in it.

The case of H. B. Wickersham, Assignee, etc., v. Charles H. Beers took place in 1886 in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, H. B. Wickersham, acted as an assignee for Mark D. Shay, who had become insolvent, having substantial debts around $80,000. Shay had a judgment entered against him by the National Bank of Illinois for $5,457.76. On June 21, 1884, a sheriff's sale of Shay's stock was arranged due to the creditors' concerns over asset value, with Beers and his associate Coney purchasing the goods under a trust agreement. They received $2,148.93 from Shay, which they claimed to use for the bank judgment, further complicating the matter of whether this transaction constituted a loan. Wickersham's suit, asserting claims against Beers for repayment of that amount, was based on two counts: one regarding a promissory note that Beers and Coney allegedly issued, which had since been destroyed, and another related to an instrument promising repayment. The trial ended with a jury verdict favoring Beers, leading to the present appeal on various instructional errors and misapplications of law by the trial court.	The plaintiff, Wickersham, claimed that Beers and Coney borrowed $2,148.93 from Shay, promising to repay this amount via a promissory note dated June 19, 1884. He argued that Beers was liable for the repayment despite the absence of the original note and asserted that evidence supporting the claim of an acknowledgment of liability had been overlooked. Wickersham sought a judgment for the amount owed on the promissory note along with interest.	The defendant, Beers, contended that any transactions with Shay were made as trustees representing their interests in a legal arrangement, not personal borrowing. Beers argued that the instructions given to the jury appropriately communicated the burden of proof resting with Wickersham to establish the legitimacy of his claims. He maintained that since the plaintiffs could not prove the note's validity or provide solid evidence of a loan, Wickersham's claims were unfounded.

The case Union Drainage District Number One v. Francis J. O’Reilly took place in 1889 in Iroquois County, Illinois. The Union Drainage District was authorized to manage drainage for agricultural and sanitary purposes. After completing their system, the drainage commissioners discovered that the outlet was inadequate to handle the accumulated water. They sought permission to extend the outlet through O'Reilly's farmland but could not reach an agreement on compensation. Consequently, a petition was filed for the court to assess damages, resulting in a verdict of $223.97 for O'Reilly. After this compensation was paid, the commissioners constructed a deepened channel across his land, complicating his farming operations. O'Reilly repeatedly requested the commissioners to construct a bridge over the newly deepened ditch, but they refused to do so or enter into a contract with him for its construction. The legal dispute focused on whether the drainage district was obligated to build this bridge according to the applicable drainage statutes.	O'Reilly asserted that the drainage district had a statutory obligation to construct a bridge over the drainage channel that now crossed his land. He argued that without the bridge, he could not effectively farm his property. He maintained that the failure of the drainage commissioners to build the bridge hindered his access across the ditch, causing undue hardship. He sought a writ of mandamus to compel the drainage district to fulfill its duty to construct the necessary bridge as mandated by law.	The drainage district contended that the court should not compel them to build the bridge as they had not initially included the cost of the bridge in the damage compensation during the condemnation proceedings. They argued that a statutory requirement (Section 74) did not impose a bridge-building obligation for ditches outside the district. The district claimed that O'Reilly's farming access could be addressed without constructing a bridge, thus seeking to dismiss the complaint for the mandamus.

In 1875, the case of Leonard Morris v. The Indianapolis, Bloomington and Western Railway Company took place in Illinois. Leonard Morris was the original owner of a tract of land through which the defendant's railway was constructed. Prior to the railway's construction, Morris entered into a contract with the Danville, Urbana, Bloomington and Pekin Railroad Company (which later consolidated with the defendant) that granted the railroad the right to enter, build, and maintain its railroad on Morris's land, provided that the company would build and maintain fences and provide a crossing. The railroad began operations in 1870 based on this agreement. The dispute arose when Morris sought to eject the railway company from the right of way, alleging a breach of contract by the railroad due to non-compliance with certain conditions (such as fencing). However, the court determined that the conditions in the agreement were all subsequent and that failure to comply did not justify revocation of the railroad's right to occupy the land.	Leonard Morris claimed that the Indianapolis, Bloomington and Western Railway Company breached the written contract by failing to meet its obligations, such as maintaining fencing and providing a crossing. He sought to recover possession of the strip of land occupied by the company, arguing that the failure to fulfill the contractual obligations entitled him to revoke the railroad's license to use his property.	The defendant, represented by the Indianapolis, Bloomington and Western Railway Company, argued that the agreement provided an irrevocable license to occupy the right of way and that any alleged breaches of the conditions of the contract did not invalidate that license. They asserted that the conditions were subsequent, meaning that the plaintiff could claim damages but could not revoke the license or recover the property. The company maintained that because they were entitled to the right of way based on the contract, Morris's action for ejectment should be dismissed.

On July 21, 1854, William B. Doolittle died, leaving a will that divided his estate among several beneficiaries, including the children of his deceased brother Irwin, Mary Marie Doolittle and Irwin B. Doolittle, and his brothers Amaziah and George W. Doolittle. The will stipulated that if either child of Irwin died before reaching adulthood, their share would go to the survivor. It also stated specific provisions for the children of Hawley S. Doolittle. In September 1855, a partition suit was filed, and a decree was issued that divided the estate among the living beneficiaries. After the death of Hawley S. Doolittle in May 1864, Samuel G. Doolittle, who was born after the original partition, sought to claim his share of the estate. The court had to determine whether the phrase “the children” of Hawley included Samuel, who was born after William’s death. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for resolution.
