The plaintiffs, Mary Handberry and Martha Conklin, argued that the will did not entitle Samuel G. Doolittle to any portion of the estate since he was not born at the time of their father’s death, and that the previous partition decree should stand as it limited their rights as tenants in common to the land appointed to them.	The defendant, Samuel G. Doolittle, contended that the will’s provisions should include him as a child of Hawley S. Doolittle. He argued that the language of the will allowed for after-born children to inherit since it created an estate that did not vest immediately to the living children but was held until the youngest child reached adulthood, thus entitling him to a share as a member of the class referred to in the will.

In 1868, in Tazewell County, Illinois, George S. Smith and others (the plaintiffs) filed an action of assumpsit against Perry Frazer and his associates (the defendants) for damages resulting from the defendants' failure to fulfill a contract to repair and ensure the good working order of a still apparatus used for alcohol manufacturing. The plaintiffs alleged that the contract, made on February 20, 1868, stipulated that the repairs would be completed within six weeks. However, during the trial, it was revealed that the contract was, in fact, made on March 1, 1868, with a promised completion time of thirty days. This led to a dispute regarding a variance between the alleged terms of the contract and what was presented as evidence. The plaintiffs claimed damages due to loss of use of the machinery during the period it remained unrepaired. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, leading the defendants to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants had breached their contract by failing to repair the machinery within the agreed timeframe. They asserted that they suffered damages from the loss of use of the still, claiming prospective lost profits from potential alcohol production during the downtime. The plaintiffs sought compensation for these damages.	The defendants argued that there was a substantial variance between the contract alleged in the declaration and the contract proved at trial, claiming that the differences were significant enough to impact their liability. They also contended that the measure of damages claimed by the plaintiffs was not valid, as it was based on prospective gains that had not been substantiated by any existing contracts for the alcohol to be produced. Consequently, they requested a reversal of the judgment against them.

The case "Archibald D. Moore et ux. v. Charles W. Hunter et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal from a decree rendered by the Madison Circuit Court in November 1843. The appellants, Archibald Moore and his wife Betsy, filed their initial complaint in November 1841, amended in May 1842, requesting a court mandate for defendants Charles W. Hunter and William Russell to relinquish their claims to a specific tract of land, the North West fractional quarter of Section 13, Township 5 North, Range 10 West. This tract, which is approximately 532.51 acres, had a complex ownership history dating back to its original entry in 1814 by Andry Dunnegan. Over the years, the land was sold multiple times, eventually leading to claims by both the complainants and defendants. The appellants assert ownership through a chain of conveyances originating from the deed of Dunnegan to John Bates, the decedent of Betsy Moore. The defendants, on the other hand, claim title through a patent issued to Rufus Easton, who had purchased the land under circumstances that the appellants contest. The Circuit Court ruled against the Moore's claims, leading to the present appeal.	The plaintiffs, Archibald and Betsy Moore, argue that they hold superior title to the disputed land based on a legitimate chain of conveyance culminating from the original entry by Dunnegan. They contend that the land was bought with Bates' funds and they seek a court order compelling the defendants to concede their rights to the property and account for any profits derived from its use.	The defendants, Charles W. Hunter and William Russell, maintain that their claim to the land is valid under the patent issued to Rufus Easton, which they argue was acquired legally. They assert that the plaintiffs' claims are based on unsubstantiated equity and that they, as bona fide purchasers, were unaware of any competing equity. They request the court to affirm their legal title and provide them compensation for their costs.

In September 1874, the case of Michael J. Eich et al. v. August Sievers was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from two promissory notes with a warrant of attorney attached, on which judgment was initially confessed but later set aside to allow the defendants to present their defense. After the death of Peter Eich, the principal maker of the notes, Michael J. Eich was substituted as the administrator of Peter's estate. As the proceedings continued, the defendants asserted that the notes were obtained through willful misrepresentation and that a significant portion of the consideration for the notes related to illegal sales of intoxicating liquors. However, the court found a lack of evidence supporting the defendants' claims about misrepresentations. The burden of proving that parts of the consideration were illegal rested on the defendants, who failed to provide concrete evidence regarding the exact amount that was allegedly for illegal liquor sales.	The plaintiff, represented by Michael J. Eich, claimed that the promissory notes were valid and enforceable despite the defenses presented by the defendants. They requested that the court affirm the validity of the notes and sought judgment for the principal amount without the deductions being sought by the defendants, maintaining that any potential illegal consideration did not bar recovery.	The defendants, including the surviving maker of the notes and Peter Eich's administrator, argued that the notes were obtained through false representations. They claimed that a substantial portion of the notes' consideration was illegal, specifically for intoxicating liquors sold contrary to Illinois statutes. They requested the court to recognize the alleged illegality as a valid defense to reduce or negate the enforceability of the notes due to the lack of lawful consideration.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois, for use, etc., v. Oliver Smith et al." took place in Richland County, Illinois, with the final judgment issued on January 10, 1889. The key individuals involved were William Bhode, who recovered a judgment against Gottlieb Schmoker in 1881, and John Wolf, an administrator for William Stuckey, who had also obtained a judgment against Schmoker in 1887. Several executions were issued following these judgments, with Smith being a constable who carried out one of the judgments. The dispute arose when Smith levied on a horse belonging to Schmoker under an execution from Wolf, realizing $35 from its sale. Bhode contended that, since his execution was senior to Wolf's, Smith should have applied the sale proceeds to his judgment instead. Evidence was presented regarding the arrangements and agreements made between constables Miller (who handled Bhode's execution) and Smith, including alleged verbal agreements about which execution they would levy first. However, the case highlighted the implications of execution priority and the responsibilities of the officers involved.	The plaintiff, represented as William Bhode, claimed that the $35 from the sale of the horse should have been applied to his senior execution against Schmoker. He argued that Smith, as the constable handling the junior execution in favor of Wolf, acted improperly by keeping the proceeds instead of forwarding them to fulfill the senior judgment.	Oliver Smith, the defendant, contended that he acted within his rights as the constable with a valid execution. He argued that the agreement to levy the executions together was not binding and that he had followed the legal procedures applicable for his junior execution. Smith maintained that Miller, holding the senior execution, failed to take appropriate action despite being present when the horse was sold.

The case of V. W. Panton v. Hannah S. Collar was adjudicated on February 9, 1883, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose in Kane County, Illinois, where appellee Hannah S. Collar sought to recover a judgment of $757.65 against Knox and Ann Mitchell, after execution attempts revealed no recoverable property. The litigation involved several individuals, including Wm. Panton, the father of the appellant, V. W. Panton, who owned a mill property. A complex series of debts and foreclosures ensued, with Thomas Mitchell initially securing a mortgage on Panton’s mill for $7,000 and subsequently having a mortgage on his own farm foreclosed due to insolvency. Appellant Panton entered into contracts with Ann Mitchell, agreeing to hold her harmless from the judgment owed to Collar, which he later contested. After hearing the conflicting evidence, the court had to decide whether Panton's actions constituted a breach of contract that would necessitate payment of Collar's judgment.	The plaintiff, Hannah S. Collar, claimed that the appellant, V. W. Panton, should be compelled to satisfy her judgment against Ann Mitchell. She argued that Panton had assets and a contractual obligation to protect Ann Mitchell from the judgment's impact. Collar requested that Panton pay the judgment amount from any funds belonging to Ann Mitchell or have her interests sold to satisfy the debt.	The defendant, V. W. Panton, asserted that he had not agreed to pay Collar's judgment against Ann Mitchell in his transactions. He described his agreement as one of indemnity solely benefitting Ann Mitchell, asserting that he had full rights over the properties purchased while denying any obligation to satisfy Collar's claim. He contended that the judgment should not be satisfied through his actions as he was not directly responsible.

In 1880, Octavius Pierce acted as an agent for the Firemen’s Insurance Company of New Orleans to procure a fire insurance policy for Stina Wiggins in Cook County, Illinois. This policy insured Wiggins's property against fire for one year from June 1, 1881, for the sum of $1000. At the time of this transaction, the Firemen's Insurance Company was a foreign company that had not complied with Illinois insurance regulations, which required foreign insurance companies to appoint a local attorney and obtain a certificate of authority to conduct business in the state. Following a trial in the Superior Court of Cook County, the court found Pierce liable under the Illinois Insurance Act of 1869, which imposes penalties for parties aiding foreign insurance companies in transacting business without proper authorization. Octavius Pierce appealed this judgment, resulting in a case brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, where the core issue was whether Pierce acted as an agent for the insurance company or the insured.	The plaintiff, representing the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that Octavius Pierce violated the Illinois Insurance Act by acting as an agent for the Firemen’s Insurance Company without the necessary authority. The plaintiff sought penalties as outlined in the legislation, asserting that Pierce's actions were illegal and contrary to public policy because the insurance policy was issued by a company not authorized to do business in Illinois.	Octavius Pierce defended himself by arguing that he was acting solely as the agent for Stina Wiggins, the insured, and not as an agent of the Firemen's Insurance Company. He contended that the contract he facilitated should be considered valid and enforceable since it was made in Louisiana where the company was based and that the Illinois statute prohibiting such transactions was unconstitutional as it infringed upon citizens’ rights to contract with foreign entities.

Ann Fitzpatrick and others brought a case against The Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company, arising from an incident that occurred in 1888 in Chicago, specifically at the Dearborn station managed by the railroad company. John Fitzpatrick, employed by the Pullman Palace Car Company, was killed when a tool fell from a roof under construction at the station, possibly due to negligence by workers employed by subcontractors. The plaintiffs, as executors of Fitzpatrick's estate, sought damages related to the financial loss suffered by his next of kin due to his death. The case examines whether the railroad company could be held liable for the alleged negligence of the subcontractors, given that Fitzpatrick was lawfully present on the property.	The plaintiffs contended that the railroad company should be held responsible for the wrongful death of John Fitzpatrick, arguing that the company had a duty to ensure safety precautions on the construction site. They claimed that the negligence of subcontractor employees, which resulted in Fitzpatrick's death, ultimately reflected a failure on the part of the railroad company to oversee the work effectively, as it was their responsibility to prevent such hazards.	The defendant, The Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company, argued that it could not be held liable for the negligence of the subcontractor’s employees. They maintained that the workers were not their employees and that the railroad company had merely reserved the right to inspect the work, which did not equate to them being responsible for the subcontractor’s actions. They asserted that the plaintiffs' claims were unsupported by the existing legal precedents established by prior judicial rulings in Illinois.

Joanna E. Wallace, as executrix of the estate of Joel Eiee, was appointed by the Adams County Court in Illinois on September 21, 1878. Shortly thereafter, she scheduled a court term to present and adjust claims against the estate, notifying relevant parties as required by law. However, Alfred Gatchell filed a claim for $1,416.10 on September 14, 1880, which was not presented during the court term Wallace had established. The claim was filed within two years of the letters testamentary but went without proper notice until June 1, 1881, which was beyond the two-year limit set for claims against the estate. The county court allowed Gatchell’s claim as a seventh class claim, to be paid from non-inventoried estate assets. Wallace appealed the decision to the circuit court, which affirmed the claim, leading to further appeal by Wallace to the Appellate Court, which also upheld the prior rulings. The core legal issue revolved around whether Gatchell's claim was properly exhibited to the court within the statute's two-year limit.	Joanna E. Wallace, the appellant, claimed that Alfred Gatchell's filing of the claim was not valid because it did not strictly adhere to the statutory requirements for presenting claims against an estate within the required two-year limit. She argued that without timely notice and a summons being issued within that timeframe, the claim should be barred from allowance.	Alfred Gatchell, the appellee, contended that his claim, although filed late in terms of subsequent notice, was valid under the law, having been properly exhibited by being filed with the clerk of the county court within the two-year period following the issuance of letters testamentary. Gatchell argued that the statute allowed for the claim to be considered as properly presented and maintained that the challenge to the claim's allowance did not have merit based on procedural grounds relating to notice.

In 1855, the Illinois Central Railroad Company laid out the town of Wenona in Marshall County, Illinois, filing a plat that was recorded. However, the acknowledgment of this plat was improperly executed, only being authenticated by a notary public. In 1863, the railroad sold a section of this land to Thomas A. Hill, explicitly reserving the streets and alleys as per the recorded plat. In March 1885, the Wenona city council vacated one such alley, which was acknowledged to have been part of the plat. In July 1887, the railroad company issued a quitclaim deed of its interest in this vacated alley to Edward L. Gould. Gould then initiated an ejectment action against Charles Howe, who derived title through Hill. The trial proceeded without a jury, and a ruling was issued in favor of the defendant.	The plaintiff, Edward L. Gould, argued that the deed from the Illinois Central Railroad Company to Hill should be considered as if it involved a statutory dedication. He claimed that the streets and alleys should have vested in the municipality due to the plat, asserting that the vacation of the alley by the city meant that Gould retained rights to the property, as he had acquired the title through the quitclaim deed.	The defendant, Charles Howe, contended that the acknowledgment of the plat was invalid, preventing the streets and alleys from passing to the municipality, and thereby negating Gould's claims. Howe asserted that the railroad company had no interest in the alleys to convey to Gould since the streets and alleys were dedicated under common law and their vacation did not reinstate any title to the railroad for further transfer.

In 1843, in St. Clair County, Illinois, Jacob Swiggart and others initiated an ejectment action against Henry Harber and additional defendants to recover possession of multiple tracts of land. The case revolved around the land originally owned by Joseph Cornelius, whose heirs conveyed the title to the plaintiffs through deeds after his death. The defendants, on the other hand, claimed their title through a mortgage Cornelius had executed in 1822, which was foreclosed through legal proceedings against his administrator, William A. Beaird, after Cornelius's death. The court allowed various evidence into the trial, including a judgment against Beaird, a special writ of fieri facias, and a deed indicating the sale of the property. A jury ruled in favor of the defendants. The plaintiffs appealed, arguing that the court erred by admitting the evidence related to the mortgage and its foreclosure proceedings.	The plaintiffs contended that the judgment against administrator William A. Beaird was invalid as it did not pertain directly to the mortgaged premises. They argued that the proceedings which led to the defendants' claims did not comply with the relevant statutory requirements, making the judgments and decrees used by the defendants inadmissible. The plaintiffs sought the reversal of the lower court's ruling and the recovery of the land in question.	The defendants maintained that they legally acquired the title to the land through the mortgage executed by Cornelius. They argued that the judgments and execution documents were valid evidence of their right to the property, contesting the plaintiffs' objections as unfounded since the mortgage foreclosure process and related sales complied with the law. They requested the court to uphold the jury's verdict and affirm the judgment for the costs incurred during the trial.

On July 9, 1866, in Illinois, William Clawson owed Merritt Munson $3,000, evidenced by three promissory notes. To secure the payment of these notes, Clawson and his wife, Jane, mortgaged certain real estate to Munson. In January 1870, Munson, acting for the benefit of Andrew Crawford, initiated a writ of scire facias to foreclose the mortgage due to non-payment. The jury's verdict favored Munson, and the court subsequently entered judgment, allowing for the sale of the mortgaged property. The appeal was undertaken by Clawson, who contested the court's acceptance of evidence regarding reasonable attorney’s fees linked to the collection of the debt, arguing that such fees should not be recoverable in this case.	The plaintiff, Merritt Munson, claimed that he was entitled to foreclose on the mortgage due to the non-payment of the loans and that he should recover attorney’s fees based on the mortgage agreement, which stipulated that the mortgagor would cover all costs associated with the collection of the secured sum. Munson sought to establish that the addition of attorney’s fees was justified under the terms of the mortgage.	The defendants, William Clawson and his wife, countered that attorney’s fees could not be recovered in a scire facias proceeding, as they were not due at the lawsuit's commencement and had to be determined outside of simple computation. They argued that the recovery of attorney’s fees was inappropriate given the nature of the claim, suggesting that the court erred in admitting evidence for such fees during the foreclosure process.

Victor Larson brought a legal action against Samuel A. Murphy for malicious prosecution in 1875. The case stemmed from a dispute over lumber that Larson and his brother, Olin, claimed they had the right to remove from a farm they were renting. Murphy contended that he had purchased the lumber along with the farm. On March 14, 1874, an altercation occurred when Murphy caught Larson dismantling a shed to remove lumber. Convinced he needed legal counsel, Murphy sought advice from local attorneys, including a man named Payne, who was not a licensed attorney. Relying on Payne's advice, Murphy obtained a warrant for Larson's arrest, charging him with larceny. The justice of the peace dismissed the charges against Larson prior to trial. As a result, Larson filed suit against Murphy. During the trial, Olin was dismissed from the case, leaving Larson as the sole plaintiff. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Larson, leading to an appeal from Murphy.	Larson's claims centered around malicious prosecution, arguing that Murphy had acted without probable cause when he instigated the criminal charge of larceny against him. He sought damages for the wrongful prosecution, highlighting that he had been wrongfully accused and had suffered reputational harm and legal expenses as a result of Murphy's actions.	Murphy's primary defense was that he had acted in good faith based on the advice of counsel, believing that he had consulted a competent attorney. He argued that his reliance on the legal advice he received should absolve him from liability for malicious prosecution. Murphy contended that, while he may have acted mistakenly, he did so with the intention of following proper legal procedures to defend his property rights.

John Whiteside and his wife (plaintiffs) filed a legal action against John Divers (defendant) in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1843, following an incident that occurred in November 1838. The case revolved around allegations that Divers unlawfully cut and felled trees on land owned by the Whitesides. The plaintiffs provided evidence that Sarah Whiteside had purchased the land at the Kaskaskia land office, including a patent dated November 10, 1840. However, the defendant challenged the admissibility of an official certificate of purchase issued by the land office, which the circuit court excluded. Ultimately, despite evidence showing the trees were cut without permission, the jury ruled in favor of the defendant, leading the plaintiffs to seek a new trial, which was denied by the circuit court.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were the rightful owners of the land where the timber was cut, as evidenced by the patent and their purchase records. They argued that the exclusion of the land office certificate as evidence was erroneous, impacting their ability to prove title ownership essential to their case. They sought a new trial due to the circuit court's decision to exclude important evidence that would support their ownership claim.	The defendant contended that the plaintiffs failed to establish their legal title to the land from which the trees were cut. He argued that the exclusion of the certificate was appropriate and maintained that the plaintiffs could not rely on evidence of possession to satisfy the burden of proving title ownership as required under the statute for the action of debt for cutting timber. The defense's key request was to uphold the initial verdict of the jury in favor of the defendant.

Julius A. Willard v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in 1843 in Illinois. The case arose after Willard was indicted for secreting Julia, a mulatto girl and slave belonging to Sarah W. Liles from Louisiana, during a journey from Kentucky to Louisiana. Liles was traveling with Julia when the latter allegedly escaped without her knowledge or consent while in Illinois. Willard demurred to the indictment, which was overruled by the court, leading to a fine being imposed on him. The case raised significant legal discussions surrounding the laws of slavery, human rights, the constitutionality of certain statutes, and the implications of harboring a slave in a free state. The court had to consider the role of state legislation in relation to fugitive slaves, the constitution of the United States, and the interpretations of the Illinois constitution and the ordinance of 1787.	The plaintiff, Julius A. Willard, claimed that the indictment against him for harboring Julia was unconstitutional. He argued that the Illinois criminal code, which penalized the harboring of slaves, violated federal law and the Constitution. He asserted that by the laws of the state, all persons should be presumed free. Furthermore, he contended that having Julia in Illinois for the purposes of transit should not constitute her as a slave under state laws, thus he should not be penalized.	The defendant, the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Willard knowingly harboring a slave, Julia, was in violation of state law as outlined in the criminal code. The prosecution contended that the law recognized the existence of slavery in other states and mandated the penalties for harboring a slave owing labor to someone else. Furthermore, they claimed that the legislation was a necessary police regulation to maintain order and that it did not contravene federal laws regarding fugitive slaves or the Illinois Constitution.

The case of James Tisdale v. The President and Trustees of the Town of Minonk took place in September 1867 in Minonk, Illinois. The dispute originated from a proceeding initiated before a Justice of the Peace in Woodford County regarding the violation of a town ordinance. In the original proceedings, Tisdale was found guilty and fined for making loud and unusual noises deemed disturbing to the peace of the town. The case was subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court, where the lower court's decision was upheld. Throughout the appeal, Tisdale questioned the legal organization of the town of Minonk and the jurisdiction of the Justice of the Peace, arguing that there were procedural deficiencies in the complaint process. However, the court maintained that the town's ordinances were validly enacted and within the authority of municipal corporations. The Illinois Supreme Court, overseen by Chief Justice Breese, affirmed the lower court's judgment, firmly rejecting the arguments raised by Tisdale regarding jurisdiction and the ordinance's publication. The decision highlighted the established doctrines surrounding the authority of municipal corporations and the necessity of raising jurisdictional challenges at the earliest opportunity in legal proceedings.	James Tisdale, as the appellant, claimed that his conviction and fines were unwarranted based on questions regarding the legal organization of the Town of Minonk and alleged jurisdictional issues within the original case. He sought to overturn the ruling of the lower courts, arguing that the ordinance under which he was prosecuted was invalid due to procedural deficiencies, including the lack of a written, signed, and sworn complaint as well as a proper warrant.	The President and Trustees of Minonk countered Tisdale’s claims by asserting that the legal organization of the town could not be challenged collaterally. They argued that the Circuit Court had jurisdiction and that Tisdale's jurisdictional objections were raised too late. Furthermore, they defended the validity of the ordinance, explaining that it fell within the powers granted to the municipal corporate authorities and was properly published in a newspaper of general circulation despite being printed in another town.

In 1883, Alonzo L. Baker (the appellant) and Louis Rockabrand (the appellee) negotiated an exchange of properties; Baker owned a tract of land near Aurora, Illinois, while Rockabrand owned an eighty-acre tract in Macon County, Missouri. Baker's land was under a mortgage of $700, while Rockabrand's land had a $600 mortgage. Baker was in possession of his land, while Rockabrand's Missouri land was occupied by a tenant named Carr. Baker was assured that he could take possession of the Missouri land by March 1, 1884, after Carr's lease ended, which Rockabrand confirmed. The exchange occurred on September 14, 1883, with both parties assuming the respective mortgages. However, upon visiting the Missouri property, Baker discovered that Carr's lease actually extended until March 1, 1886, and Carr demanded compensation for early surrender. After Baker learned this, he sought to rescind the contract shortly after the exchange but was met with Rockabrand's refusal to reconvey the land. Baker then filed a bill in chancery in the city court of Aurora to compel Rockabrand to reconvey the Missouri land and enjoin the ongoing forcible entry and detainer suits initiated by Rockabrand in Kane County.	Baker argued that he was misled by Rockabrand's false representation regarding the lease status of the Missouri land. He claimed he relied on these statements to finalize the exchange and requested the court to rescind the contract, restore him to his original property rights, and compel Rockabrand to reconvey the land.	Rockabrand contended that he did not misrepresent the lease status of the Missouri land and insisted that the relevant lease had, in fact, expired as stated. He argued that Baker should have been aware of the true status of the lease and thus sought dismissal of Baker's claims.

The case "John H. Markillie v. George W. Ragland" arose in January 1875 in Scott County, Illinois, concerning the estate of Benjamin Ragland, Sr., who had recently passed away. The key individuals involved were his widow, Susan Ragland, and John H. Markillie, a purchaser of real estate sold by her. Benjamin's will indicated that Susan was entitled to the entirety of his estate during her lifetime, allowing her to manage and sell the property at her discretion. However, upon her death, the remaining estate was to be inherited by his heirs, unless Susan remarried, in which case her share would diminish to a dower interest. After Benjamin's debts were settled, Susan sold various parcels of the estate. John H. Markillie acquired part of the property in 1861, confirmed by some heirs, but George W. Ragland, one of the heirs and son of Benjamin, contested this sale, claiming a share in the property. He filed a petition for partition of the land following his mother’s death, leading to a court finding that Ragland was entitled to a portion of the land, resulting in an order for its sale and partition among the heirs.	George W. Ragland, the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to ownership of an undivided share of the property sold to John H. Markillie. He argued that the sales of the estate by his mother, Susan Ragland, were made without proper authority from all heirs and sought partition of the land to secure his rightful inheritance.	John H. Markillie, the defendant, contended that he obtained a valid title to the property based on the terms of Benjamin Ragland, Sr.'s will. He argued that Susan Ragland had the authority to manage and sell the property without needing consent from all heirs, as she held a life estate with the power to sell the property outright during her lifetime. He requested the court to uphold the validity of his title against Ragland's claims.

In April 1859, the case of Miles W. Conway, Plaintiff in Error, v. Covell Case, Defendant in Error, was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a contract involving a promissory note for $1,680, dated March 5, 1856, which was to be paid on or before October 10, 1857, at the Rock Island Bank. Conway, the plaintiff, was obligated to convey a piece of land to Case, the defendant, free of any encumbrances, as part of the agreement associated with the note. When the payment day arrived, Case attempted to tender the money, along with a request for a warranty deed for the property. However, Conway's agent demanded a deed that was free of a mortgage, which had not been resolved and remained on the property. The entire transaction took place in the city of Rock Island, Illinois, and the disagreement hinged on whether Case had properly tendered the payment while being entitled to an unencumbered title.	The plaintiff, Conway, claimed that the defendant, Case, failed to fulfill the conditions of their contract because he could not provide an unencumbered title to the property as stipulated. Conway sought payment based on the promissory note and argued that the existence of the mortgage meant that Case was not entitled to accept a deed for the property.	The defendant, Case, argued that he was ready to pay the amount due and had tendered the payment in the necessary amount at the due date. He contended that the mortgage should have been considered in the transaction and that since the property was encumbered, he was not obliged to execute the payment. Case maintained that the contract allowed him to withhold payment until he received a warranty deed free from any encumbrances.

The case "Ernest Treishel v. David McGill" was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court on July 20, 1888. It originated in Iroquois County, presided over by Judge Alfred Sample. The plaintiff, Ernest Treishel, and the defendant, David McGill, were involved in a legal dispute in which specific details of the case are not fully enumerated in the provided documentation. However, the court proceedings reveal that there was a bill of exceptions—a legal document detailing points of law taken during the trial—requested by the appellant (the party appealing the case). The court found that the bill of exceptions was stricken from the record, thus eliminating the basis for evaluating the appellant’s claims. As a result, the Appellate Court could not assess the merits of the appeal based solely on the remaining procedural record.	Ernest Treishel, as the appellant, argued for a reversal of the judgment rendered against him, suggesting that errors occurred during the trial process. He contended that there were legal and procedural missteps that warranted a different verdict. His primary legal request was for the Appellate Court to review these supposed errors in order to possibly overturn the trial court's decision.	David McGill, represented by his attorneys, maintained that the issues raised by the plaintiff were not valid for appeal since the necessary bill of exceptions had been stricken from the record. The defendant argued that without this essential document, the court could not accurately evaluate the claims made by the plaintiff, thus supporting the validity of the original judgment. Essentially, the defense requested that the court affirm the previous ruling in his favor based on the evidential insufficiency presented by the appellant.

The case arose from an incident in which The Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company was sued by Daniel Parker and others after a train on their line killed a steer on or near the railway. The lawsuit began in 1868 when the plaintiffs sought compensation for the loss of their livestock. Initially, the case was heard by a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment against the railway company. This judgment was appealed to the circuit court of Iroquois County, where a similar outcome occurred. Following this, the railway company again appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court. The primary argument revolved around the instructions given to the jury, particularly regarding the locations where the incident occurred and whether the railway company had complied with the requirement to fence portions of their line. Evidence indicated that the steer was killed in a location where the company was legally bound to maintain a fence. The court examined witness testimonies and the circumstances surrounding the recovery of the animal after the incident.	The plaintiffs claimed that the railway company was negligent in failing to properly fence its railway line, resulting in the death of their steer. They argued that the company's actions directly led to their financial loss and asserted their right to compensation for the animal. The plaintiffs maintained that they had a reasonable period to take possession of the steer to mitigate damages, which the railway company violated by burying the animal before they could respond.	The railway company contended that the court erred in its jury instructions, which did not account for locations excluded from fencing requirements. They argued that the evidence allowed for speculation that the incident could have occurred in a village, thus invalidating the jury's verdict. Additionally, the company claimed that the plaintiffs should have acted swiftly to recover the animal and convert it into profit, implying that the plaintiffs bore some responsibility for their loss.

William H. Burt filed a lawsuit against C. J. Warrington on January 27, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose from transactions that occurred on the Board of Trade, a formal trading exchange primarily for commodities in Chicago, Illinois. Burt alleged that Warrington, acting as his agent, sold certain grain without providing notice, resulting in financial losses for Burt. The case went to a jury trial, where the jury ultimately found in favor of the defendant, Warrington. The plaintiff appealed the decision, arguing that the sale was improper without notification. The defendant contended that the trades were validly closed due to the plaintiff’s failure to provide necessary margins, and that Burt had effectively waived any right to claim damages by deciding to pay the alleged outstanding balance without protest while having full knowledge of the circumstances. The conflicting evidence presented led the jury to side with Warrington, and the appellate court concluded that the jury's decision was supported by the evidence.	The plaintiff, William H. Burt, claimed that the defendant, C. J. Warrington, violated his duty as an agent by selling grain without notifying Burt, which caused damage to him. Burt sought to recover damages for the alleged misconduct due to Warrington's actions regarding the transactions on the Board of Trade.	The defendant, C. J. Warrington, defended himself by arguing that the trades were properly closed because Burt had failed to submit required margins. Furthermore, he claimed that the plaintiff had waived any right to pursue the claim by paying the balance for margins without raising any objections while being aware of the full circumstances surrounding the situation.

In the case of Edward H. Turner et al. v. Lucius B. Mantonya, a legal dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment on December 7, 1888. The litigation stemmed from an agreement between the parties concerning a lease of premises. The appellee, Lucius B. Mantonya, had leased the property from Farwell & Company and sublet part of it to the appellants, Edward H. Turner and others. A fire occurred on November 5, 1885, which Mantonya claimed made the premises unfit for occupancy, prompting him to attempt to terminate his lease. However, the Farwells disagreed, leading to a compromise regarding the lease termination. The appellants contended they had reached an agreement to cancel their lease with Mantonya and paid all due rents following a supposed surrender of the property on November 6, 1885. They also argued that the fire's destruction warranted the lease’s termination. However, evidence suggested only water damage and no substantial destruction of the premises. The matter was brought before a jury to determine if the lease had indeed been canceled or if the appellants were liable for the rent that accrued following the fire.	The plaintiff, Lucius B. Mantonya, claimed that the fire rendered the leased premises unfit for occupancy, justifying the termination of the lease. He argued that prior to his lease termination with the Farwells, he had made all reasonable attempts to surrender the lease effectively, negotiating with the appellants to vacate their area. Mantonya sought to recover $179.89 for unpaid rent from the appellants following the claimed termination of their lease.	The defendants, Edward H. Turner et al., presented two main defenses: first, they asserted that an agreement had been reached with Mantonya for the cancellation and surrender of their lease, thus absolving them of rent obligations beyond November 6, 1885. Secondly, they contended that the fire on November 5, 1885, had destroyed the leased premises to such an extent that it legally terminated their lease. They argued that without a lease provision relieving them from paying rent due to the premises’ destruction, they should not be liable for rent after the fire.

In 1883, Marvin S. Robinson was arrested under a capias ad satisfaciendum in Cook County, Illinois, due to a judgment against him for $800 by a plaintiff named Blumenthal. Following his arrest, Robinson sought discharge through the county court under the Insolvent Debtor’s law. The court scheduled hearings but ultimately dismissed his petition for discharge at the September 17 hearing. Robinson then appealed but failed to prosecute the appeal in the circuit court, leading to further complications regarding his custody. Subsequent habeas corpus petitions filed by Robinson were dismissed by the circuit court and the Superior Court of Cook County. The legal proceedings revolved around whether Robinson had been legally imprisoned and the nature of his release under bond, given that the hearings had been delayed beyond statutory limits. Robinson argued that he was wrongfully imprisoned following his bond release, claiming it constituted a legal "escape." However, the court maintained that the sheriff’s authority to re-arrest Robinson was valid due to the continuance process not undermining the jurisdiction of the court.	The plaintiff, represented by the state through the relator Marvin S. Robinson, argued for his release from imprisonment. He claimed that his bond and subsequent appearances were valid, and that he should be discharged from custody based on the procedural inconsistencies and alleged violation of jurisdiction stemming from the longer than permitted adjournment of his hearing.	The defendant, in this case the sheriff, countered that Robinson was legally imprisoned under the rules of execution and custody, and that his bond did not represent a lawful escape from his obligations. The sheriff argued that the continued custody was permissible under the laws governing insolvent debtors, and that any procedural problems raised by Robinson were insufficient grounds for his release.

The case "The Culbertson & Blair Packing and Provision Company v. City of Chicago et al." was decided on November 17, 1884, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, surrounding the construction of a viaduct on Eighteenth Street over the tracks of the Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne and Chicago Railway Company. The plaintiff, Culbertson & Blair Packing and Provision Company, claimed damages to their property caused by the construction of this viaduct, asserting that the new structure had resulted in financial loss. The initial judgment in the trial court favored the plaintiff, awarding $5,000 in damages against the city. This judgment was affirmed by the Appellate Court, leading to the current appeal. Central to the case were debates over the admissibility of evidence regarding the value of property and the liability of the city in relation to an ordinance that allowed the railway company to contribute financially to the project.	The plaintiff argued that the construction of the viaduct had caused significant damage to their property, leading to a decrease in its market value. They contended that the city should be held liable for these damages based on evidence of harm caused by the viaduct's erection. The plaintiff claimed that the city improperly structured its ordinances, which allowed for the construction of the viaduct without adequate consideration of the damages inflicted on surrounding properties. They sought compensation for the financial losses incurred, requesting the court to affirm the judgment awarded by the trial court.	The defendants, the City of Chicago and the railway company, presented arguments asserting that the city bore no responsibility for the damages claimed by the plaintiff. They contended that the viaduct construction was a lawful public improvement and that any financial contributions made by the railway company did not impose liability on it for damages resulting from the project. The defendants argued that the city had complied with all legal requirements in the construction process and that any deficiencies in property value should not reflect liability for the public improvement, emphasizing the absence of contractual or tortious duties owed to the plaintiff.

In the case of Felix Johannes v. Elizabeth Kielgast, a legal dispute arises regarding a rental agreement for premises located at 59 Archer Avenue, Chicago. The lease term began on November 1, 1877, and was set to end on November 1, 1882. The defendant, Felix Johannes, agreed to pay $35 per month in rent. However, Johannes failed to pay the rent for August 1878, prompting the plaintiff, Elizabeth Kielgast (the landlord), to serve a notice of termination of the lease on September 15, 1878, allowing five days for payment. As the rent remained unpaid, Kielgast initiated a forcible detainer action in February 1879, successfully obtaining a judgment for possession of the premises. The current action, initiated on March 5, 1886, concerns the recovery of unpaid rent for the months after the lease was terminated. The crux of the legal debate revolves around whether a landlord can collect rent for months accruing after the termination of the lease due to non-payment. The judgment by the lower court awarded Kielgast damages for the unpaid rent from August 1878 through January 1879, which Johannes sought to reverse, arguing the covenant for rent ceased after lease termination.	Elizabeth Kielgast claims entitlement to recover unpaid rent for the months following the termination of the lease agreement, asserting that the lease provisions kept the rental covenants alive despite the tenant's unlawful retention of the property after the lease was terminated. She argues that even after the termination and related court proceedings, Johannes should be liable for the rent entitled under the lease.	Felix Johannes contends that the lease was effectively terminated when the landlord issued a notice to terminate due to missed payments. He argues that following the lease's termination, he cannot be held liable for rent accrued in subsequent months, stating that the landlord cannot maintain an action for rent that would have been due if the lease had continued. He asserts that any action for recovery should involve mesne profits or damages for wrongful retention, not rent as contracted.

In April 1860, the case of Samuel B. Bancroft v. Thomas Speer was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following an error from the Superior Court of Chicago. The issue at hand stemmed from an insufficient return of service by the sheriff regarding a summons against Samuel B. Bancroft. The summons was allegedly served by reading it in the hearing of Bancroft on June 21, 1858. However, the return did not clarify whether the date indicated the time of service or the return, and it failed to explicitly state that Samuel B. Bancroft was indeed the intended person named in the summons. This ambiguity raised concerns since the initials "S. B." could apply to others, creating doubt about whether proper service was executed. The Supreme Court reviewed the flaws in the service process and determined that the lack of clear identification and the insufficient information rendered the service invalid.	The plaintiff, Samuel B. Bancroft, argued that the sheriff’s return was insufficient due to its ambiguity, claiming it did not properly identify him or indicate if the service occurred correctly. Bancroft sought to have the decision from the lower court reversed based on these procedural deficiencies, asserting that valid service of the summons was essential for any judgment to be rendered.	The defendant, Thomas Speer, did not present substantive arguments against the claims but relied on the procedural ruling regarding the service of the summons. His defense was essentially dependent on the insufficiency of the summons return, challenging the validity of the proceedings that led to the judgment against him.

In April 1861, the case of Henderson v. Morgan was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a dispute over a chattel mortgage. The key individuals involved were Charles M. Henderson, the appellant (mortgagee), and Nathan Morgan, the appellee (creditor). Henderson had claimed ownership of certain property based on a chattel mortgage that was acknowledged by a justice of the peace in North Chicago. However, the mortgagor, the individual who took the mortgage, resided in a different town. Morgan, as a creditor of the mortgagor, seized the property using a landlord's warrant for unpaid rent while the property was still in the possession of the mortgagor. The Circuit Court ruled that the mortgage was invalid because it did not meet the specific statutory requirement regarding the acknowledgment of such mortgages. As a result, the court found in favor of Morgan, leading Henderson to appeal the decision.	Charles M. Henderson, as the appellant, claimed that the property in question was rightfully his by virtue of a valid chattel mortgage. He argued that the acknowledgment of the mortgage was sufficient and sought the court's intervention to replevin (recover) the property from Nathan Morgan, who had seized it for unpaid rent owed by the mortgagor.	Nathan Morgan, the appellee, contended that the chattel mortgage claimed by Henderson was invalid because it was not acknowledged according to statutory requirements. He asserted that the acknowledgment must occur before a justice of the peace in the election district where the mortgagor resided. Since the acknowledgment was in a different district, Morgan argued that he rightfully seized the property as a creditor.

In September 1874, in Chicago, Illinois, John Cunningham, a laborer employed by the Illinois Central Railroad Company, suffered a severe injury resulting in the loss of his hand. The incident occurred while Cunningham was attempting to make repairs under a railroad car on a side track. Before starting his work, he positioned a colleague nearby to alert him of any approaching vehicles. The defendants, John T. Noble and Francis B. Little, operated a lumber yard and sent employees to move railroad cars to load lumber. Their employees attempted to move the cars to facilitate the loading process but failed to control the car that was set in motion. This car collided with another car, crushing Cunningham's hand. The core issue revolved around whether the defendants’ employees acted negligently in moving the car without proper precautions, thereby leading to Cunningham's injury. The case was submitted to a jury in the Superior Court of Cook County, which ruled in favor of Cunningham and awarded him $3,000 for damages.	The plaintiff, John Cunningham, claimed that the defendants’ employees acted negligently in moving the railroad cars without proper care or safety measures. He argued that their failure to ensure the cars could be safely moved resulted in his injury, as they did not check if the brakes were functional or whether anyone was near the cars. Cunningham sought damages for the injury sustained, which he contended was the result of the defendants' negligence.	The defendants, Noble and Little, contended that the jury's verdict was not supported by sufficient evidence. They argued that their employees had not been negligent and claimed they should not be held liable for the actions of their employees during the incident. Furthermore, they maintained that they had made adequate preparations to avoid any potential accidents and that the injury was unforeseeable. They requested that the court overturn the jury's decision in favor of Cunningham.

In September 1874, the case of William H. Stuart v. The People of the State of Illinois was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Lee County, Illinois, where William H. Stuart was indicted and convicted for the larceny of a horse. During the trial, Stuart claimed he had traded for the horse with the owner's son, who had temporary possession of it. The crux of the case rested on whether Stuart's actions constituted larceny or merely aggravated trespass. The evidence presented was contradictory; while there was some indication of an attempted transaction involving the horse, the court found it difficult to ascertain if Stuart acted in good faith or if he was merely concealing his theft. The issue was further complicated by the public manner in which he obtained the horse, casting doubt on the nature of the offense. Ultimately, the question of whether Stuart was guilty of larceny "beyond a reasonable doubt" became central to the court's deliberation.	The plaintiff, representing the People of the State of Illinois, argued that William H. Stuart had committed the crime of larceny by illicitly taking possession of the horse. They contended that his actions were deceitful and violated the law. The plaintiff sought the upholding of Stuart's conviction, asserting that his conduct demonstrated a clear intent to commit theft, which warranted punishment under criminal law.	The defense, represented by Stuart's attorneys, argued that there was insufficient evidence to prove he committed larceny. They stressed that the taking of the horse was done openly and in the presence of others, which suggested that it may not have constituted theft. Instead, they proposed it could only be characterized as aggravated trespass. The defense asserted that Stuart believed he had traded for the horse in good faith, and urged the court to reverse the conviction due to the lack of clear evidence proving his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

In 1876, the case of Lizzie E. Ladew v. William L. Paine et al took place in Bloomington, Illinois. Lizzie E. Ladew, the plaintiff, was the wife of A. P. Ladew. The legal dispute arose over a mortgage executed on the St. Nicholas Hotel, which was part of Lizzie's separate estate, to secure a debt of $518.55 owed by her son, George H. Ladew. The mortgage was executed jointly by Lizzie and her husband, with Paine as the grantee. Lizzie filed a bill in chancery to set aside the mortgage, claiming she was influenced unduly by her husband, alleging that this influence amounted to coercion. Her contention was that she executed the mortgage against her will, with the knowledge of Paine, who she argued was complicit in the undue influence exerted by her husband. Despite the proper documentation, including notarized acknowledgments, Lizzie sought relief as she believed her consent was not freely given. The circuit court dismissed her claims after hearing the merits of the case.	Lizzie E. Ladew argued that her husband exercised undue influence that compelled her to execute a mortgage against her separate property without her genuine consent. She claimed that William L. Paine, the mortgagee, was aware of this undue influence, thereby making him complicit in the coercion. She requested that the court set aside the mortgage on the grounds that it was a product of coercion rather than her free will.	The defendants, represented by William L. Paine, contended that they were not involved in any wrongdoing. They argued that Mrs. Ladew had executed the mortgage willingly, as evidenced by her acknowledgments in the presence of both Paine and a notary public, who confirmed that she did so without any indications of distress or coercion at the time of signing. They maintained that since the mortgagee was unaware of any undue influence, the mortgage should remain valid.

In 1853, in the town of Aurora, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Thomas Newlan and the President and Trustees of Aurora. Newlan was accused of violating a municipal ordinance that prohibited the sale of liquor without prior compliance with specific publication requirements. The proceedings began with an action of debt initiated by the town against Newlan for this violation. The case was initially heard before a justice of the peace in Kane County and subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court of Kane County, where it was tried before a jury in May 1852. The clerk of the corporation testified that the relevant ordinance had been posted in three public places for over ten days prior to the lawsuit, and a witness confirmed that Newlan had sold liquor about a week before the suit was filed. However, the timeline raised questions about whether the ordinance was in effect at the time of Newlan's sale, leading to the trial and eventual appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, represented by the town of Aurora, claimed that Thomas Newlan violated the local ordinance by selling liquor without proper compliance with the ordinance’s publication requirements. They contended that the ordinance was effective at the time of the sale and sought to impose penalties for the violation.	Newlan's defense centered on the argument that the ordinance was not validly in effect when he sold the liquor. They contended that the evidence did not clearly demonstrate that the ordinance took effect prior to the sale, suggesting instead that the sale occurred before the ordinance was operational. As such, they argued that he should not be liable for any penalties associated with the alleged violation.

In 1886, in Madison County, Illinois, Katherine Kundert filed a claim against the estate of Balthasar Schneider for a legacy bequeathed to her in his will, along with a financial transaction involving a certificate of deposit. Rudolph V. Grafenreid, the executor of the estate, had assigned a certificate of deposit for $1,800 to Kundert, who paid him an additional $800 in cash. The intention was that this transaction would cover her legacy of $1,000, but the bank associated with the certificate failed before it matured. Kundert claimed she was misled by Grafenreid, who assured her he would honor the certificate, and that she was unaware of the legal implications due to her inability to read English. The trial court initially ruled in her favor, awarding her a total of $1,612.35 against the estate. Grafenreid appealed this decision.	Katherine Kundert argued that she was misled into accepting the certificate of deposit and paying $800 by Grafenreid's representations that he would ensure the certificate would be honored. She claimed this constituted her legacy payment and sought recovery based on these assurances, asserting her entitlement to the legacy payment despite the bank's failure.	Rudolph V. Grafenreid contended that the transaction was valid and legally binding. He claimed he had explained the terms of the certificate to Kundert, asserted that she willingly accepted the certificate, and stated that the estate was not liable for payments without necessary court procedures such as the requirement of bonds for legatees. Grafenreid maintained that Kundert's claim should not be honored since she accepted the certificate with full knowledge of its terms.

Andrew Schneider v. Henry Westerman is a legal case from April 1861, set in Illinois. The case revolves around a replevin suit where the plaintiff, Andrew Schneider, asserts ownership over sixteen beer tubs allegedly in the possession of the defendant, Henry Westerman, and claims they are being unlawfully detained. The suit was initiated following a recorded chattel mortgage executed by Auguste Winkle in favor of Schneider in December 1859. This mortgage was for ten large and six small beer barrels, valued at $350, meant to secure certain promissory notes. The case involved testimonies regarding the circumstances around the production of the beer tubs and the outstanding debts of the deceased owner, Henry Ewalt. Notably, Ewalt died in January 1859, and Winkle married Ewalt’s widow shortly after. Evidence was presented regarding Winkle's financial dealings associated with Ewalt’s debts, indicating he might have paid off significant amounts owed by Ewalt. The case was complicated by Westerman’s claims as the administrator of Ewalt’s estate, raising questions about whether Winkle had the authority to sell the beer tubs after Ewalt's death. Ultimately, a jury found in favor of the defendant, leading to the appeal by Schneider.	Schneider's main arguments consist of asserting his legal ownership of the beer tubs based on the chattel mortgage, claiming that the property was unlawfully detained by Westerman. He contended that the title to the personal property had not vested in Ewalt's estate at the time of his death, as the beer tubs remained uncompleted and not ready for delivery. He requested that the court grant him possession of the beer tubs that he believes rightfully belong to him.	Westerman's key arguments included denying the claims of taking and detention of the beer tubs. He argued that he had a legitimate claim to the property as the administrator of Ewalt’s estate. Additionally, he contended that the ownership of the beer tubs did not automatically pass to Schneider due to the incomplete nature of the sale and production at Ewalt’s death. He sought to maintain possession of the beer tubs and argued against plaintiff’s claims to recover them.

John Frasure v. Jas. A. Zimmerly is a case that dates back to November 1860, arising in Edgar County, Illinois. The action was initiated by the plaintiff, John Frasure, against the defendant, Jas. A. Zimmerly, concerning the deceitful sale of a horse. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant misrepresented the condition of the horse, specifically stating that its eyes were sound when, in fact, they were unsound. This deceit allegedly induced the plaintiff to purchase the horse under false pretenses. The trial was held at the Edgar County Circuit Court, overseen by Judge Harlan, where the jury was impaneled to hear the case. Prior to the trial's progression, the defendant requested the court require the plaintiff to post security for costs, citing concerns about the plaintiff's residence status after learning he had moved to Kentucky. The court denied this motion. Ultimately, evidence presented revealed contradictions, but the jury generally found that the defendant had indeed represented the horse as sound, despite knowing about its condition. The case hinged on whether the plaintiff could recover costs related to the horse's ineffectiveness for a trip to Kentucky, as the plaintiff claimed to have discovered the deception only post-purchase.	The plaintiff, John Frasure, claimed that the defendant, Jas. A. Zimmerly, falsely represented the condition of a horse, asserting that its eyes were healthy when they were, in fact, diseased. Frasure argued that he was deceived into purchasing the horse based on this misrepresentation and sought to rescind the contract after discovering the fraud. He requested the return of the purchase price and compensation for related expenses, including the costs incurred for transporting the horse to and from Kentucky and its upkeep.	The defendant, Jas. A. Zimmerly, argued against the claims made by Frasure by asserting the general issue in his plea. He contended that the court should not have required him to provide security for costs after the jury had already been empaneled. The defendant suggested that the circumstances and factual determination surrounding the sale, particularly the nature of the horse's disease before the trip to Kentucky, should have been left to the jury's discretion, thereby challenging the trial court's instructions on admissibility of evidence and claim recovery.

On December 27, 1872, around 6:00 PM, an accident occurred at Venice crossing, Illinois, involving William Hillmer and the Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Company. Hillmer was attempting to cross the railroad tracks with a pair of horses and a wagon when he was struck by a locomotive pulling passenger cars. The collision resulted in the death of his horses, destruction of his wagon and harness, and serious injuries to Hillmer. He claimed that he was exercising due care while crossing and that the railroad company was negligent for failing to signal the approaching train appropriately. The case was brought to trial, where a jury found in favor of Hillmer, awarding him $1,681 in damages. The defendant, the railroad company, appealed the decision, arguing that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence regarding their compliance with signaling laws.	William Hillmer contended that the railroad company was liable for the accident due to their negligence. He argued that the company failed to ring the bell or blow the whistle, as required by law, and that the train was traveling at an excessive speed over a known dangerous crossing. Hillmer maintained he took necessary precautions by listening and looking for oncoming trains before attempting to cross. He sought damages for the loss of his horses and compensation for his injuries.	The Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Company asserted that they had complied with signaling requirements by ringing the bell and blowing the whistle. They claimed the train was not speeding and argued that it was not their duty to reduce speed at the crossing given the circumstances. The defendant also suggested that the plaintiff's testimony lacked reliability compared to their own witnesses, establishing a defense against the negligence claims made by Hillmer.

In September 1870, the case "John Wilson et al. impleaded, etc. v. John Loomis et al." was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute began when the defendants purchased property from Mrs. Rosette Roe, while an execution on a valid judgment against her husband, Cornwell S. Roe, was in effect. The property was later seized by a deputy sheriff due to this execution, prompting the defendants to sue for its recovery. The central issue revolved around whether Mrs. Roe, under the Illinois act of 1861, could engage in trade with her husband as the managing agent without exposing the business's assets to her husband's creditors. The business had been profitable during its operation, but the court needed to determine if the separate estate of Mrs. Roe could be preserved from her husband's debts given that he had significantly contributed his labor and skills to the business. The court explored precedents and legislative intent behind the 1861 statute, ultimately examining the implications of allowing a married woman to conduct business while shielding her husband’s earnings from creditors.	The plaintiffs, represented by John Wilson, argued that the property in question should belong to them as they made a legitimate purchase from Mrs. Roe. They contended that the seizure of the property under the execution was improper and that the property should be returned to them as it was bought in good faith without knowledge of the underlying debts of Cornwell S. Roe.	The defendants asserted that the property was rightfully seized as it was part of the assets owned by Cornwell S. Roe, which were subject to his creditors' claims. They maintained that the profits generated from the lumber business were primarily due to the husband’s labor and expertise and that, regardless of Mrs. Roe's initial investment, the assets of the business should be vulnerable to Cornwell S. Roe's debts.

On April 4, 1885, M. C. Campbell and others took judgment against Leroy A. Goddard for $1,390.80 before the clerk of the Circuit Court of Williamson County, Illinois. This judgment was based on a promissory note that was dated December 13, 1884, which had a principal amount of $1,359.14, was due ninety days later, and carried an 8% interest from maturity. The note included a power of attorney that allowed for judgment to be confessed for the amount due along with a reasonable attorney's fee. In May 1885, the defendants filed a motion to modify the judgment, which was denied. The appeal followed, focusing on whether the judgment, particularly the inclusion of a $25 attorney's fee, was equitable and just given the circumstances.	The plaintiff, Leroy A. Goddard, contended that the judgment was properly entered according to the promissory note's terms, which clearly allowed for a reasonable attorney’s fee. They argued that the defendants had acknowledged the correctness of the amount due and that the primary concern was the legality of the attorney's fee included in the judgment.	The defendants argued that the attorney's fee was not explicitly detailed in the note and asserted that there were equitable grounds to invalidate or modify the judgment. They maintained that the judgment should not include this fee, and that since the case involved significant contention and contradictory evidence, the court should reconsider the judgment to determine the propriety of the attorney's fee.

In January 1863, the case of John Corgan and Jacob Readleman v. Cornelius Anderson was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court following a trial in the Union Circuit Court, which was moved to Pulaski. The plaintiffs, Corgan and Readleman, were partners involved in the sale of goods, including barrels of whisky, to the defendant, Cornelius Anderson. The plaintiffs sought payment for these goods through a legal action known as indebitatus assumpsit. The defendant responded with several defenses, including non-assumpsit, a counterclaim for goods sold to the plaintiffs, and a payment assertion. A jury trial resulted in a verdict favoring the defendant for five hundred dollars. The plaintiffs filed a motion for a new trial, which was denied, although the defendant later remitted a portion of the judgment. The case was appealed primarily on grounds related to the admissibility of a deposition and other procedural issues surrounding the evidence presented at trial.	The plaintiffs asserted that they were owed payment for goods sold and delivered to the defendant, including barrels of whisky, and sought judgment against Anderson for the outstanding amount. They challenged the verdict and sought a new trial based on several legal objections, including the alleged improper use of a deposition and other evidentiary issues during the trial.	The defendant claimed that he had provided goods to the plaintiffs amounting to a set-off against their claims, arguing non-assumpsit, which denied the allegations of the plaintiffs. He also contended that payment had already been made and sought to introduce a deposition as part of his defense, which the plaintiffs contested. His main requests included the preservation of the jury's verdict in his favor and the denial of the motion for a new trial.

Charles Leyenberger filed a lawsuit against James R. Paul for malicious prosecution in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois. The case was presided over by Judge Rollin S. Williamson, with a jury trial taking place. The events began when Leyenberger was arrested on a warrant issued based on a complaint by Paul, who accused him of embezzlement for failing to pay insurance premiums collected under the Mutual Benefit Life Insurance Company's policies. Leyenberger provided a bond for his appearance, but the case against him was ultimately dismissed without trial. Following this dismissal, Leyenberger initiated the malicious prosecution lawsuit against Paul, seeking damages resultant from the initial arrest. The jury found Paul guilty of malicious prosecution, and the verdict awarded Leyenberger $5,000 in damages. Paul appealed this decision, leading to the hearing in the Illinois Appellate Court.	Leyenberger's primary argument was that James R. Paul had acted maliciously in bringing the embezzlement charge against him, which resulted in his arrest. He claimed that the prosecution lacked probable cause and was subsequently dismissed, constituting malicious prosecution. He requested the court to hold Paul liable for damages inflicted by this allegedly wrongful prosecution.	In his defense, Paul asserted that there existed probable cause for the arrest of Leyenberger, and thus, any prosecution stemming from it could not be deemed malicious, regardless of his motives. He contended that even if he acted with malice—such as revenge or hatred—his liability was negated by the presence of probable cause. Paul argued that the jury was misled by improper instructions regarding the definition of malicious prosecution, which he maintained incorrectly emphasized the relevance of his motives over the necessity of probable cause.

Melinda Anderson filed a case against William E. Stone after entering into a limited partnership with G. W. H. Gilbert in Peoria, Illinois, on December 20, 1883. Anderson contributed $2,750 to the partnership, which was supposed to be treated as a cash payment, while Gilbert contributed goods valued at $10,450. The partnership aimed to continue the business in hats, caps, and furs. However, the partnership became financially troubled, leading to its assets being reassigned to an assignee in July 1885. Subsequently, Stone, a creditor to the partnership, filed suit based on two promissory notes totaling $1,500, of which $729.20 remained unpaid when the case was heard. The Circuit Court ruled against Anderson, finding her liable for the unpaid balance, despite her claims that she was a limited partner and therefore not generally liable for the firm’s debts.	The plaintiff, William E. Stone, argued that Melinda Anderson should be held liable for the unpaid balance on the promissory notes. He maintained that under the partnership arrangement, she could not avoid liability despite her designation as a limited partner, as the affidavit related to the partnership contained false representations regarding her cash contribution and its application.	Melinda Anderson contended that she was a limited partner and, as such, her liability should be confined to her initial cash contribution of $2,750. She argued that the money was used to pay off existing debts rather than being part of the capital of the new firm, thereby protecting her from general liability for the partnership’s debts. Anderson asserted that the court failed to recognize the legal implications of her limited partnership status.

The case "Thomas Worthington, Appellant, v. The County of Pike, Appellee" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1860. The primary issue revolved around an appeal taken by Thomas Worthington against a decision made by the board of supervisors of Pike County. Worthington had applied for an abatement of an assessment on his property, claiming it was exempt from taxation. However, the board of supervisors denied his request, determining that the property was indeed liable for taxes. Following this unfavorable decision, Worthington sought a remedy through a Circuit Court appeal, arguing that the board's ruling should be reversed. The case's legal arguments focused on whether such an appeal was permissible under the relevant revenue law, specifically the 33rd section, which outlines the parameters for tax exemptions and appeals.	Thomas Worthington, the plaintiff, argued that the board of supervisors' decision to hold his property subject to taxation was erroneous. He claimed that the property in question should be exempt, and therefore, he requested the Circuit Court to reverse the board’s determination and grant the abatement of the assessment.	The County of Pike, as the appellee, contended that no appeal could lie from the decision of the board of supervisors regarding property assessments. Their argument was based on the stipulations of the revenue law, which indicated that the board’s ruling on tax liability was conclusive once a decision was made to deny the abatement request. Thus, they requested the court to uphold the board’s decision and dismiss the appeal.

The case of Daniel Lawrence v. Preston Yeatman and Germanicus Kent was decided in December 1839 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from an action of debt initiated by Yeatman & Kent against Lawrence in St. Clair County, Illinois, to recover a debt of $339.75 plus damages. The plaintiffs sought to attach Lawrence’s estate through an attachment bond, which was executed by their agent, A. Cowles. Lawrence, however, was not served with this attachment; instead, notice was published, leading to a default judgment against him during the August term of the Circuit Court in 1838. The judgment awarded the plaintiffs $320 in debt and $253 in damages, based on an assignment made by Lawrence of a writing obligatory from Hardy Robinson, which had become the subject of prior litigation. Lawrence contested the proceedings, arguing multiple defects in the affidavit and bond that initiated the attachment, pointing out the lack of legal authority of the agent and the insufficient description of the court procedure involved.	The plaintiff, represented by Preston Yeatman and Germanicus Kent, argued that they were owed a debt of $573.35 for a writing obligatory assigned to them by Lawrence. They contended that Lawrence’s failure to appear led to a default judgment in their favor, which they sought to enforce through the attachment process.	Daniel Lawrence, the defendant, raised several objections to the plaintiff's claim, primarily emphasizing the insufficiency of the affidavit and attachment bond. He claimed that the affidavit did not identify the agent's authority, lacked proper details about the court processes, and was fundamentally defective. Furthermore, Lawrence argued that the form of action was misconceived and that the damages awarded were excessive, exceeding legal interest on the debt.

Washington Wear v. John Killeen is a legal case that took place in Peoria County, Illinois, with the original judgment rendered on September 22, 1864. The case began as an action brought by John Killeen against Washington Wear before a Police Magistrate in Peoria County, where Killeen was awarded a judgment of $82.25 against Wear. Following this judgment, Wear appealed to the Circuit Court. In December 1864, Killeen filed a motion to dismiss Wear's appeal, which was granted without any resistance. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, and a procedendo was issued to the Magistrate to act as though no appeal had occurred. On December 22, 1864, Wear requested for the dismissal order to be set aside and filed a cross-motion to submit a better appeal bond. However, on December 23, these motions were denied.
