Subsequently, Wear appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, which eventually reviewed the procedural aspects of the case concerning the adequacy of his appeal bond.	The plaintiff, John Killeen, claimed that the appeal made by Washington Wear should be dismissed based on the assertion that the appeal bond was informal and lacked the necessary seals. Killeen's request was to sustain the Circuit Court's earlier dismissal of the appeal, thereby enforcing the judgment originally made in his favor against Wear.	The defendant, Washington Wear, contended that the dismissal of his appeal was improper since the court failed to follow statutory procedures regarding the appeal bond. Wear argued that the Circuit Court did not adequately provide him with the opportunity to rectify the bond issue by not setting a specific deadline for filing a sufficient bond, as mandated by the law. He requested the court to reinstate his appeal and allow him to present a proper bond.

In the case of The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company v. Richard N. Wilcox, the events took place on September 19, 1878, in Illinois, specifically concerning the operation of a freight train that allegedly carried passengers. Richard N. Wilcox, a resident of Ottumwa, Iowa, was on the train traveling to Biggsville for a fair. He paid for his passage upon being approached by the conductor. While attempting to disembark at the Biggsville station, the train did not come to a complete stop, and Wilcox refused to jump off at the conductor's urging. The conductor subsequently physically forced him off the train, resulting in significant injuries. Wilcox later filed a lawsuit against the railroad company for negligence in operating the train during his dismount. The case went to trial without initial objection to procedural issues, and the trial court eventually ruled in favor of Wilcox, prompting the railroad company to appeal the decision.	Wilcox claims that the railroad company acted negligently by failing to safely stop the train at Biggsville. He alleges that this negligence was the direct cause of his injury when the conductor improperly forced him off the train while it was still moving, resulting in severe injuries and incurred medical expenses amounting to $300. He argues that the railroad had a duty to ensure the safe disembarkation of its passengers and failed to uphold that duty.	The railroad company contended that Wilcox's claims were barred by the Statute of Limitations, as the injury occurred on September 19, 1878, and the summons was not served until September 27, 1880, exceeding the two-year limit. Additionally, they argued that there was a fatal variance between Wilcox's allegations and the evidence presented, asserting that the claim of negligence in operating the train did not align with the actual proof, which indicated he jumped off at his own volition, not due to any fault of the conductor.

This case, "Western Union Telegraph Co. v. Thaddeus Fairbanks et al.," was decided on January 6, 1885, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated from a telegraphic message sent by Thaddeus Fairbanks, an agent of the firm Fairbanks, Morse & Co., from Sioux Falls, Dakota Territory, to the Michigan Pipe Company in Bay City, Michigan. The message, sent on April 21, 1882, was intended to order specific wooden pipes for the Dakota Territorial Penitentiary. However, due to an error in transmission, the message was altered and resulted in the shipment of incorrect materials. Fairbanks and his firm sought to recover damages associated with the erroneous order. It was established that no claim for damages was made within the contesting thirty-day period required by the telegraph company's policy, and the original message documentation had been destroyed before the claim was presented.	The plaintiffs contended that they were entitled to damages for the erroneous transmission of their message, which resulted in the shipment of the wrong pipes. They argued that the Western Union Telegraph Company was liable for the mistake, and they sought financial compensation for the costs incurred related to the incorrect order and shipping.	The Western Union Telegraph Company defended itself by asserting that the plaintiffs failed to present their claim within the stipulated thirty-day period outlined in their terms and conditions, which barred any claims for damages. The defense claimed that the plaintiffs were bound by these contractual terms, whether they had explicit knowledge of them or not. They urged the court to dismiss the case on the grounds that the plaintiffs did not follow the required procedure for claiming damages.

The case "The Village of Marseilles v. George Howland" arose from an incident that took place on September 10, 1883, when George Howland sustained an injury while crossing a bridge over the Illinois River in Marseilles, Illinois. The village of Marseilles, incorporated in 1861, was responsible for maintaining public safety on its roads and bridges, including the aforementioned bridge constructed by the Marseilles Bridge Company in 1865. In March 1878, the bridge company sold the bridge to the towns of Eutland and Fall River, converting it from a toll bridge to a public one. Following the sale, the local commissioners of highways managed the bridge's repairs. However, the village of Marseilles did not take any action regarding the bridge's maintenance, claiming it never officially accepted the bridge or assumed responsibility for its condition. The bridge was, at the time of the incident, deemed unsafe, and Howland's injury was reportedly not due to his negligence. The principal issue was determining whether the village had a legal obligation to maintain the bridge's safety, given the legislative powers it received through its charter.	George Howland, the plaintiff, claimed that the village of Marseilles was negligent in maintaining the bridge, which was unsafe at the time of his accident. He argued that the village was responsible for the repairs and upkeep of all public highways and bridges within its corporate limits, regardless of the prior management by highway commissioners. Howland sought damages for his injury, asserting that the village failed to fulfill its legal duties to ensure public safety.	The defendant, the Village of Marseilles, contended that it did not have an obligation to maintain the bridge because it was never formally accepted as part of the village's infrastructure. The village argued that the management and repairs were the responsibility of the commissioners of highways and that these officials acted without jurisdiction concerning the incorporated village's bridges. The village requested that the court dismiss the claims based on the assertion that it was not liable for the bridge's unsafe condition.

In 1874, Urial Mills and Adaline Mills executed a trust deed to secure a promissory note owed to Samuel W. Brown, giving him the power to sell the property in case of default. After Brown's death, David Brown, as the administrator of Samuel W. Brown's estate, sought to substitute a trustee and initiate a sale of the property, which occurred on April 13, 1874. The property was sold for $2,110 to David Brown in trust for the heirs of Samuel W. Brown. George Rice, the defendant, was in possession of the property under Urial Mills. The case began when David Brown, desirous of reclaiming possession, filed a forcible entry and detainer action against Rice, asserting that Rice refused to surrender possession after a written demand was made. The circuit court ruled in favor of Brown, leading Rice to appeal.	The plaintiff, David Brown, claimed that as administrator of Samuel W. Brown's estate, he was entitled to possession of the property based on the successful trustee sale executed under the trust deeds. He argued that Rice, as the occupant under Urial Mills, was bound by the trust deed and that the demand for possession was valid, asserting that Rice's continued possession constituted unlawful detainer.	The defendant, George Rice, contended that the action should not have been brought against him, arguing that he was not a party to the trust deed and that the demand for possession was incorrectly directed. He challenged the legitimacy of the sale, positing that it should be considered a foreclosure under a court decree, which would have granted him a right of redemption that was not expired at the time of the suit. Additionally, he asserted defects in the sale process, claiming that not all required parties were notified and that the notice of sale was improperly posted, which invalidated the demand for his removal.

The case "The Rockford, Rock Island & St. Louis R. R. Co. v. Edward Rogers" took place in January 1872 in Madison County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Edward Rogers, brought an action against the Rockford, Rock Island & St. Louis R. R. Co. for damages caused by a fire that burned his fences and grass. The incident occurred when the railroad company's locomotive, while ascending a heavy grade, threw sparks that ignited a significant growth of dry grass on the railroad's right of way. This fire then spread to Rogers' property, leading to substantial destruction. During the trial in the Madison Circuit Court, evidence suggested that the railroad company had failed to maintain its right of way by allowing dry grass to accumulate, which was a violation of the legal requirement for railroad companies to prevent such hazards. The jury ruled in favor of Rogers, determining that the company was negligent in their upkeep, resulting in a verdict of four hundred dollars in damages.	Edward Rogers, the plaintiff, claimed that the railroad company was negligent in failing to clear dry grass from its right of way. He argued that this negligence directly resulted in the fire that damaged his fences and grass. Rogers sought compensation for the damages incurred, amounting to four hundred dollars, as he contended that if the company had adhered to their duty of maintenance, the fire would not have occurred.	The Rockford, Rock Island & St. Louis R. R. Co. contended that they were not negligent and that the fire may not have originated from their locomotive. They introduced the general issue plea but primarily focused on disputing the evidence suggesting that the fire began on their right of way. The defendant argued that external factors may have contributed to the fire and thus requested the court to overturn the jury's verdict.

The case "The Hartford Fire Insurance Company v. John Walsh" took place in Alton, Illinois, in 1868-1869. John Walsh owned two houses, a two-story and a one-story frame dwelling, which he insured with The Hartford Fire Insurance Company for $1,200 and $500, respectively, on June 4, 1866. The policy was renewed twice over the following years. On December 23, 1868, both houses were destroyed by fire. Walsh notified the company of the loss in January 1869 and provided proof, but the company failed to pay the claimed insurance amount. The Hartford Fire Insurance Company contended that the insurance policy had become void due to conditions purportedly violated by Walsh, arguing that the two-story house had been unoccupied for over thirty days without notice to the company, and that the one-story house had been converted into a dry goods store, thus increasing the risk covered under the insurance. Walsh, however, maintained that adequate notice had been given to the agents prior to the loss and contended that the policy remained valid.	John Walsh, the plaintiff, claimed that The Hartford Fire Insurance Company had failed to pay the insurance amount due for the loss of his two houses after a fire. He argued that he complied with all policy requirements, including providing notice of the loss and proof thereof, and that the insurance policy was still in effect despite the defendant's assertion of violations regarding occupancy and use of the insured premises.	The Hartford Fire Insurance Company, the defendant, argued that the insurance policy was void. They contended that Walsh failed to notify them when the two-story house became vacant for over thirty days and that he changed the use of the one-story house, which increased the risk covered by the policy. They claimed these actions violated the contract's terms, which included conditions regarding occupancy and the necessity of obtaining consent for any changes in risk.

In 1872, in Chicago, Samuel J. Walker borrowed $7,000 from the International Bank, with a repayment due by April 15, 1873. As collateral, he endorsed a note from Bryan Philpot for $8,750, secured by a trust deed on certain real estate. The Bank sold Walker’s note and Philpot’s collateral to Levi Abt. A legal proceeding commenced in the Cook Circuit Court to foreclose the trust deed, which led to a decree in favor of Abt against Walker and Philpot. They were defaulted in their responses, and while the International Bank also had an interest due to its collateral agreement with Walker, it was involved in the case as a defendant and could claim the surplus from the sale after Abt's debt was settled. The court found substantial debts owed by Walker and Philpot and ruled on how to distribute any surplus from the property sale, which was confirmed without objections.	The plaintiffs (Levi Abt) sought to foreclose on the trust deed due to unpaid debts on the notes provided as collateral. They claimed a total amount owed of $9,158.32 on Walker's note and $12,301.10 for Philpot's note. They requested the court to decree the sale of the mortgaged property and distribute the proceeds as outlined in the findings.	The defendants, particularly Walker, argued that the bank should not have been allowed to claim surplus from the property sale without filing a cross-bill. They contended that the decree improperly granted relief to the bank by enabling it to appropriate the surplus towards Walker's debts, despite the bank not being a claimant in the same manner.

In December 1841, the case of Lee v. Hicks was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The proceedings took place in Illinois, where various legal arguments were presented by the parties involved. F. Forman represented the defendants, and a motion was filed to take a supersedeas bond from the court files. This bond was critical for initiating further legal action concerning alleged breaches of its conditions. The court approved the motion, allowing a copy of the bond to remain on file while granting the defense the opportunity to pursue their claims against the bond's terms. The background revolves around the legal disputes and proceedings that emerged from actions taken or conditions pertaining to the bond, setting the stage for the resolution of the case.	The plaintiff, Lee, asserts claims based on the alleged breach of the conditions surrounding the supersedeas bond. Lee's primary argument revolves around the legal enforceability of the bond and the actions taken by the defendants that allegedly violated these stipulated conditions. The plaintiff seeks restitution or damages as a result of these breaches, requesting that the court uphold the bond's conditions and enforce accountability from the defendants.	The defendants, represented by F. Forman, argue against the plaintiff's claims by seeking permission to take action against the supersedeas bond due to the plaintiff's alleged breaches, thereby turning the focus onto the obligations of the plaintiff. The primary defense seeks to establish that any claims made by the plaintiff are unfounded or improperly substantiated, as they request the court to allow them to pursue their case against the bond itself, suggesting the plaintiff's responsibilities in the circumstances.

In December 1842, the case of John Doe, ex dem. Murray McConnel v. Maro M. M. Reed was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a dispute over a lot of land located in Jacksonville, Illinois. Murray McConnel, the plaintiff, claimed ownership of the land based on a chain of titles stemming from a certificate of entry and various deeds from Thomas Arnett. On the other hand, the defendant, Maro M. M. Reed, presented evidence including a deed from Arnett to Rixford, which included the same lot of land and was executed prior to the relevant deeds held by McConnel. The defendant proved that he and his predecessors had exercised continuous adverse possession of the property since 1829, further bolstered by improvements made on the land. The case was tried without a jury, and after considering both parties' evidence, the court reviewed the validity of the claims and the consequences of the recording laws in Illinois concerning land ownership.	The plaintiff, McConnel, contended that he held clear title to the property via a quitclaim deed from Arnett, asserting that the earlier title held by Reed's predecessor was invalid due to the conditions of the recording statutes at the time. McConnel argued that the prior deeds were either not sufficiently executed or recorded, and thus he should prevail in reclaiming his title to the lot in question.	The defendant, Reed, challenged the validity of the plaintiff's claims by demonstrating that his title derived from a prior conveyance from Arnett, which was executed and recorded before McConnel's deed. Reed argued that by operation of the recording laws, his title should be superior due to prior execution and evidence of actual possession of the property, which McConnel was aware of, thus negating his status as a bona fide purchaser.

In March 1853, Jeptha Dunlap filed a lawsuit against James Buckingham, concerning a bill of exchange dated June 18, 1842, which had been drawn by Buckingham in favor of Dunlap and subsequently protested for nonpayment. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, specifically arising from the Morgan Circuit Court. The key individuals involved were Dunlap as the plaintiff and Buckingham as the defendant. The court addressed the issue of whether the statute of limitations applied to the case, as Buckingham claimed that Dunlap did not initiate the lawsuit within the required time frame after the enactment of an amendment to the laws concerning limitations of actions. The court's initial ruling favored the defendant, leading to serious consideration of the application and interpretation of the relevant limitation acts.	Dunlap argued that the defendant’s plea regarding the statute of limitations was invalid because the limitation act did not include provisions for bills of exchange, specifically asserting that the time limit for filing the action had not yet lapsed. Dunlap sought judgment against Buckingham for the amount owed as specified in the bill of exchange, contending that despite no explicit consideration being stated in the instrument, the law implied that a good consideration existed for the transaction.	Buckingham contended that Dunlap's claim was barred by the statute of limitations, which mandated that any action based on the bill of exchange must be filed within five years from when the cause of action accrued. He maintained that Dunlap did not commence the suit within the required two-year period following the amendments to the limitation act. The defense emphasized that the plaintiff could not maintain a valid action of debt based on the bill of exchange due to the absence of an expressed consideration.

In the late 19th century, specifically in 1886, a legal dispute arose between Charles E. Rose and John Day in Calhoun County, Illinois. The case originated in the Circuit Court and involved a small strip of land used by Rose, which lay between Day's store and the Mississippi River. For five years, Rose had reportedly utilized this land without any formal rental agreement, claiming it was a place from which to ship apples and where he had stored wood. John Day had possessed the land for sixteen years prior, during which he paid all taxes and asserted ownership based on a deed he believed conveyed the property to him. The issue was whether Rose could maintain an action for "use and occupation" of the land without a clear contract stipulating rent. The court considered the implications of implied agreements for payment when no explicit contract existed and examined the existing relationship between the parties regarding the land.	Charles E. Rose contended that he had a right to occupy the strip of land in question and claimed damages for its use. His argument centered on the assertion that he had utilized the land for years, and he argued for an implied agreement that he would pay rent for the occupation of the land, despite the absence of an express contract.	John Day defended against Rose's claims by asserting that he had lawful possession and ownership of the land for sixteen years, supported by evidence of tax payments. He argued that Rose was using the land without the consent of the true owner and claimed there was no existing landlord-tenant relationship. Day contended that the law would not support Rose's claims as he had no rights to the land nor was he an authorized occupant.

The case of "The Unknown Heirs of Asahel Langworthy, deceased v. Jonathan H. Baker, Administrator of Asahel Langworthy, deceased" was handled by the Illinois Supreme Court and reached a decision in January 1860. The case originated from the probate court of McDonough County, Illinois, where Jonathan H. Baker was appointed as the public administrator for Asahel Langworthy's estate after Langworthy's passing on September 24, 1834. Court records indicated that Langworthy died intestate and that his estate had significant debts. In 1855, notice was given to settle claims against the estate, during which David P. Wells filed a promissory note demanding $1,607.52 from the estate. The County Court allowed the claim and subsequently authorized the sale of Langworthy's real estate to pay this debt. However, significant procedural issues arose, lacking evidence that no relatives or creditors were present in Illinois, and insufficient notice was provided to interested parties, including the heirs. The plaintiffs, being the unknown heirs, argued that the proceedings were fraudulent and lacked jurisdiction.	The Unknown Heirs of Asahel Langworthy contended that the County Court did not have jurisdiction over the estate as it failed to establish that there were no relatives or known creditors in Illinois. Furthermore, they argued that the debt had become stale due to a delay of 27 years, effectively waiving any claim against the estate. They claimed that the probate proceedings were fundamentally flawed and constituted fraud, seeking to invalidate the sale of the real estate which resulted in the loss of their inheritance.	Jonathan H. Baker, as the administrator, maintained that his actions followed the legal procedures for estate administration and that the court had the authority to sell the real estate to satisfy debts of the decedent. The defense thus argued for the validation of the proceedings and the authority of the County Court to adjudicate claims against the estate, asserting that the sales and the resulting distribution were lawful under the applicable statutes.

The case "Aquila H. Pickering v. John A. Lomax et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 22, 1887, concerning land disputes in Cook County, Illinois. Aquila H. Pickering, the plaintiff, sought to recover two parcels of land that he claimed ownership of through a series of conveyances traceable to a treaty between the United States and certain Native American tribes, specifically regarding property granted to Alexander Bobinson and his children. The case arose when the plaintiff filed an action of ejectment against John A. Lomax and William Kolze, the defendants. The trial was held without a jury, with the plaintiff presenting evidence, including the 1829 treaty, various conveyances, and a patent from the United States that prohibited the alienation of the land without presidential permission. The trial court ultimately ruled in favor of the defendants, declaring that the evidence supported the conclusion that no valid title had passed from the original grantor due to noncompliance with the alienation condition.	The plaintiff, Aquila H. Pickering, claimed ownership of the disputed land based on a chain of title that included conveyances from the original grantee, Alexander Bobinson, whose land was granted under a treaty with specific restrictions. He argued that subsequent approvals by the President of the United States indirectly validated the transfer of title despite the lack of prior approval at the time of the initial deed. The plaintiff requested that the court recognize his legal right to the land and grant possession.	The defendants, John A. Lomax and William Kolze, contended that the deed from Joseph Bobinson (part of the plaintiff's chain of title) to John F. Horton was void because it violated the treaty condition requiring presidential permission for any transfer of the land. They argued that no valid title passed through the conveyances made without this approval, therefore asserting that the plaintiff's claims were baseless, and they requested the court to uphold the ruling in their favor.

The case of "The Erie Railway Company v. Adalbert J. Wilcox" took place in 1876 in Illinois. The facts involve the shipment of goods by the plaintiff, Adalbert J. Wilcox, through the Erie Railway Company to a destination marked as "Eckly, Iowa." The goods were received by the Erie Railway at Friendship station and were marked for transportation. However, there was a mistake in the direction, as there was no place known as "Eckly, Iowa," but rather a place called "Ackly, Iowa." The goods were safely delivered to the Illinois Central Railroad Company for further shipment to their intended destination but were not accepted because the station did not exist on the Shippers' Guide. During the time that the goods remained with the Illinois Central Railroad, a fire broke out and destroyed the goods while they were still in a safe location. The issue arose as to whether the delays and subsequent loss of Wilcox's goods were due to negligence by the Erie Railway and the connecting carrier companies.	The plaintiff, Adalbert J. Wilcox, argued that the Erie Railway Company was responsible for the loss of his goods due to negligence in handling the shipment. He claimed that the railway company should have ensured that the goods were shipped to a valid destination and that they failed in their duties as a common carrier. Wilcox sought compensation for the loss of the goods, as they were damaged in the fire while under the carrier's custody.	The Erie Railway Company contended that they were not liable for the loss of the goods due to the agreement signed by the plaintiff, which released them from liability for damages, delays, or losses under normal circumstances. The company maintained that they had fulfilled their obligation by delivering the goods to the connecting carrier and that the delay was caused by instructions given by Wilcox himself, which contained the erroneous destination. The defendant argued that there was no actual negligence on their part and that the loss occurred while the goods were held safe, thus absolving them of responsibility.

The case of Toledo, Wabash & Western Railway Company v. David Prince took place in January 1869, in Jacksonville, Morgan County, Illinois. David Prince, a surgeon, was called by the station agent of the Toledo, Wabash & Western Railway to attend to a railway employee who had been seriously injured, necessitating an amputation. After providing his professional services, Prince sent a bill to the general superintendent of the railway company, who denied payment. Prince subsequently filed a lawsuit against the railway company, claiming unpaid fees for his medical services. The key individuals involved included the plaintiff, Dr. David Prince, and representatives of the defendant, the Toledo, Wabash & Western Railway Company, with the case being presided over by Judge Charles D. Hodges.	The plaintiff, David Prince, argued that the station agent’s decision to engage his surgical services should be considered ratified by the railway company since they failed to object to the agent’s actions after being informed about them. He sought compensation for the medical services he provided to the injured employee, asserting that his services were necessary and that the railway company was liable for the costs associated with them.	The defendant, Toledo, Wabash & Western Railway Company, contended that they were not legally obligated to provide medical attendance for injured employees and that the engagement of the surgeon was unauthorized. They argued that since the general superintendent was not informed of the situation until later and did not formally reject the engagement, they should not be held responsible for the surgeon’s bill.

The legal case "William W. Pickering vs. Fletcher Misner and William L. F. Jones" took place in June 1850, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The origin of this case was an appeal from a judgment rendered by a justice of the peace in Kendall County. During the initial trial, one of the plaintiffs testified that he had no witnesses to substantiate his claim regarding a note made by the defendant. The defendant, when called as a witness, could not recall whether he was credited for the note in a previous settlement. Despite objections, the court allowed a plaintiff to testify regarding the note's credit status, which led to the challenge of this decision in the appellate court. The case raised questions about the application of statutes around witness testimony and the boundaries of common law.	The plaintiff, William W. Pickering, argued that he had a valid claim against the defendants regarding a note that should have been credited in a prior settlement. He asserted that the only witnesses available were either the plaintiff himself or the defendants, and sought to testify on his own behalf after the defendant's testimony was found to be inconclusive.	The defendants, Fletcher Misner and William L. F. Jones, contended that the court erred in allowing Pickering to testify as a witness because the statutory provisions governing such cases were not properly adhered to. They argued that since the defendant had testified without refusing to provide information, the plaintiff should not have been permitted to become a witness in this matter.

In January 1875, Mary J. Gobble filed a lawsuit against John M. Linder in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a contract for the exchange of farms. The agreement stipulated that if either party failed to execute the deed at the appointed time, they would forfeit and pay $1500 as damages. Gobble was prepared to fulfill her part of the contract but alleged that Linder did not provide the necessary deed. The case was brought forward to recover the stipulated damages. The court faced a critical question regarding the nature of the stipulated sum—whether it was liquidated damages or a penalty. The resolution involved interpreting the intent of the parties involved in the contract. After evaluating precedents and the circumstances surrounding the agreement, the court had to determine which classification the specified sum fell under.	Gobble argued that Linder's failure to deliver the deed constituted a breach of their contract, which entitled her to recover the agreed-upon sum of $1500 as damages. She asserted that the sum was intended as liquidated damages, considering the complexities and uncertainties involved in measuring actual damages from the breach of the agreement.	Linder contended that the $1500 provision should be classified as a penalty rather than liquidated damages, implying that the actual losses incurred by Gobble were significantly less than the stated amount. He argued that the court should limit any recovery to actual damages, which he claimed did not exceed $50, highlighting the distinction between a penalty and genuine liquidated damages in contractual agreements.

In June 1871, Charles W. Colehour and Grant & McLain jointly purchased sixty acres of land in Cook County, Illinois, for $50,000. They made an initial payment and financed the remaining amount through notes and mortgage. The land was conveyed to Wm. H. Colehour in trust for them. Later that year, they sold forty acres of the land to Guyton for $50,000, with cash and assumed obligations for the remaining balance. After dividing the proceeds from the sale and settling accounts, they found a remaining debt of $16,000 from loans taken to make the initial land payment. In April 1872, they sold the remaining twenty acres to Thomasson for $25,500, generating more discussions on the division of debts incurred. Disputes arose, particularly regarding the amounts owed to Henry Clews & Co. and whether Charles W. Colehour was liable for specific debts in connection to the settlement. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court upon appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County, focusing on the accounting and distribution of payments related to their partnership agreement.	The plaintiffs, Charles W. Colehour and Grant & McLain, claimed that their accounting set forth that they owed $16,000, of which $4,000 should be paid jointly, with Colehour responsible for $5,000 and Grant & McLain for $7,000. They sought clarification on the distribution of debt payments and the validity of their financial obligations concerning the debts acknowledged during their settlement.	The defendants contended that the actual debt owed to Henry Clews & Co. was only $5,000 instead of the claimed $12,000. They argued that Colehour should not be responsible for this larger amount. Additionally, they insisted that the error in the court's understanding of the liability divided among them supported their case, asserting that they did not agree to the debt obligations claimed by the plaintiffs during the accounting.

The case involves David S. Hammond, the Sheriff of Cook County, against The People, represented by Joseph Vacaro and Paul Cella. The events took place in Cook County, Illinois, in March 1863. The plaintiffs, Vacaro and Cella, alleged that they were wrongfully imprisoned by the sheriff. They claimed they were arrested under a writ issued by a justice of the peace, which they argued was not applicable to them as they had different surnames in the lawsuit. Specifically, Vacaro was arrested on a writ for a judgment against a “Joseph,” while he had always been known as “Joseph Vacaro.” Vacaro stated that he was misidentified and that the arrest did not have a proper legal basis. Both plaintiffs filed for habeas corpus relief to challenge their detention, which resulted in a hearing before the Circuit Court. The court discharged them from custody, asserting that they were arrested improperly. The sheriff’s position was that he acted under the authority of the existing writ.	The plaintiffs, Joseph Vacaro and Paul Cella, claimed that their imprisonment was illegal because the writ under which they were arrested did not apply to them. They argued that they were misidentified in the legal process, as the judgments were pronounced using names that did not accurately reflect their identities. They sought discharge from custody through a writ of habeas corpus, asserting improper legal grounds for their arrest and claiming they had always been known by their true names, which were not the ones used in the court proceedings.	The defense, represented by Sheriff David S. Hammond, maintained that the arrests were lawful because they were executed based on valid writs issued from the court, regardless of the naming discrepancy. The sheriff contended that he acted in accordance with the statutory authority provided to him and that the judgments from the lower court were valid since the plaintiffs were present and had received summons, thereby establishing jurisdiction.

Harriet Steele brought a petition for dower against Haines H. Magie in 1868, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over a property originally purchased by a man named Wright from the State in 1833. Wright sold the property to Coles before fully paying for it or obtaining the legal patent. Coles then conveyed the property to Harriet Steele’s husband, who in turn transferred it to another party. The legal complications stemmed from the fact that Wright had not completed the payment or obtained his patent before these transactions occurred. The court highlighted that Steele never had a legitimate legal or equitable title to the property, as he merely possessed an incomplete equity that did not qualify under the law for a right of dower. The court referenced previous rulings to substantiate that without the husband holding an executed equitable estate, the wife could not claim a right of dower.	Harriet Steele argued that she was entitled to a dower in the property based on her husband's ownership and prior conveyances. She contended that because the property had been conveyed to her husband, she should have the right to claim a share, regardless of the technicalities regarding the legal title.	Haines H. Magie's defense relied on the argument that Harriet Steele’s husband never held a legal or equitable title to the property that would grant her a right of dower. The defendant asserted that the earlier transactions and the incomplete status of the property’s legal title meant that no dower rights could accrue to Steele, as her husband had transferred what little interest he had before acquiring any substantial title.

In the case of August F. Albright v. Joseph Bruner, decided on February 29, 1884, the dispute arose from damage caused by Bruner's cattle to Albright's crops. The two parties owned adjacent lands divided by a fence that had been built about 17 years prior to the trial. A verbal agreement existed regarding the maintenance responsibilities for the fence, which was made known to Albright when he acquired the property. The key issue was whether the fence was maintained adequately to prevent Bruner’s cattle from getting through, which they allegedly did on several occasions. Albright claimed that the fence was not in sufficient repair, while Bruner contended that it was well-maintained on his side. The court examined the evidence, including the height and condition of the fence, which was found to be slightly under the legal height requirement. Ultimately, the court highlighted that the burden of proof was on Albright to demonstrate that the cattle damage was not due to his own failure to maintain the fence in good condition.	Albright claimed that Bruner's cattle had damaged his crops due to Bruner's failure to maintain the fence properly as per their agreement. He sought damages for the losses incurred and argued that the fence was inadequate, which led to the breach by the cattle.	Bruner's defense rested on the assertion that the cattle did not pass through his portion of the fence, which he maintained in good condition. He argued that any breaches occurred due to Albright's inadequate maintenance of his own part of the fence and insisted that the fence was sufficient to keep ordinary stock contained.

In January 1868, the case of William McMullen v. Mary Gable was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, following actions taken in the Circuit Court of Sangamon County. The conflict began when a judgment was awarded to Morse against Gable, leading to a sheriff's execution due to the absence of collectible property. The sheriff then levied a thirty-six and a half-acre tract of land owned by Gable. During a sale on June 11, 1863, the land was sold to Morse for $23.58, which covered the judgment debt and costs. Gable later contested the sale in December 1864, claiming the land was worth around $1,000, suggesting that it could have yielded a better price had it been sold in smaller parcels. Gable alleged fraud and argued improper handling by Morse and the sheriff. The defendants maintained the sale's legality and denied any misconduct, asserting the property was not valuable due to its poor condition and susceptibility to flooding. The court evaluated whether inadequate sale price or failure to divide the land warranted the sale's annulment.	The plaintiff, Mary Gable, claimed that the sheriff's sale of her land was fraudulent and should be annulled. She argued that the property, valued at $1,000 and capable of division, was sold improperly without being divided into smaller parcels, which could have fetched a higher price. Gable requested the court to set aside the sale, contending that fraud was involved, and thus the sale should be deemed invalid.	The defendants, William McMullen and Morse, countered Gable's claims by asserting that the sale was conducted legally and regularly. They argued no fraud occurred during the execution or sale of the property, asserting that the land's value was significantly less than Gable claimed, which was corroborated by multiple witnesses. The defendants contended that the sheriff acted appropriately in selling the land as a whole and that there was no evidence showing that a division would have resulted in a better sale price.

Nathan F. Gardner filed a lawsuit against the Town of Chambersburgh in Pike County, Illinois, stemming from a case that originated before a justice of the peace in September 1850. Gardner was previously sued by William Todd, the overseer of roads for Chambersburgh, for failing to perform road labor, resulting in a judgment against him for $4.13, which Gardner appealed. The Circuit Court dismissed his appeal, leading Gardner to seek further legal recourse. In subsequent proceedings, Gardner sought recovery of costs associated with this earlier lawsuit, which he argued the town was liable for. Initially, a judgment for $35.41 was rendered against the Town by the justice, which the town subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court, resulting in a lower judgment of $5.54 for Gardner, alongside a split in court costs. Gardner then challenged this finding, claiming the town was responsible for additional costs. His claims were presented before the Illinois Supreme Court.	Gardner argued that the Town of Chambersburgh was liable for the recovery of costs related to the prior suit initiated by Todd, the overseer, based on the notion that the town, as a corporate entity, should bear the expenses incurred from legal actions that involve its officers. He requested full payment for the total amount owed, which he claimed had been validated in prior legal proceedings.	The Town argued that the overseer of highways does not have the inherent authority to initiate lawsuits that bind the town financially without proper authorization. They asserted that the legal framework under which the overseer operates does not grant him such powers and that the suit should be conducted in the name of the town, rather than that of the overseer. They sought to limit the town's liability and argued that the costs claimed by Gardner were not the town's responsibility.

Caroline Werner v. Emil F. Werner is a legal case from the Illinois Appellate Court, decided on February 13, 1889. The case centers around a marital dispute between Caroline Werner and Emil F. Werner, who were married in 1868 and lived together in Philadelphia until October 1882, when Emil deserted Caroline. In March 1887, Caroline moved to Chicago and discovered that Emil was living with another woman and had obtained a divorce from her in Indiana in December 1881, a fact she was unaware of until Emil presented the divorce decree during a bigamy prosecution. Caroline filed a bill against Emil, seeking to have the divorce declared void, asking for maintenance and general relief. The court took note of Emil's alleged fraudulent acquisition of the divorce, highlighting that his residency in Indiana was questionable and that the divorce was obtained without proper notice, violating Indiana law, particularly concerning the requirement to provide notice by mail.	The plaintiff, Caroline Werner, claims that the divorce granted to her husband, Emil, is void due to lack of proper notice, as he did not comply with the statutory requirement to mail her a marked copy of the notice. She argues that the Indiana court lacked jurisdiction since Emil was not a bona fide resident there, asserting that the divorce was obtained fraudulently. Caroline requests that the divorce be set aside, seeks maintenance from Emil, and demands any other relief deemed appropriate by the court.	The defendant, Emil F. Werner, does not contest the evidence regarding the divorce process but attempts to validate his actions based on the divorce decree obtained in Indiana. His defense rests on the argument that he followed the necessary legal proceedings according to the Indiana law at the time. However, the court recognized the significant legal flaws in his claims, primarily focusing on the alleged fraud and jurisdiction issues that rendered the divorce invalid.

The case "Emerson, Talcott & Company v. Rozella Marks" took place in Champaign County, Illinois, with the decision filed on February 17, 1887. The key individuals involved are David Shirk, the testator who bequeathed land in his will, and his daughter, Bozella Marks, the devisee. Shirk's will granted Bozella an eighty-acre tract of land to hold for her lifetime, explicitly prohibiting her from selling it. The legal question arose regarding whether her interest in the land could be sold under a court execution due to debts. Bozella had maintained possession of the property since her father’s death, and the court had to determine if the will's stipulations preventing the sale of the land could be enforced against creditor claims. The court upheld the testator's intention to protect the property from execution sales.	Emerson, Talcott & Company, as the plaintiff, argued that Bozella Marks' interest in the land should be subject to sale in execution for debts owed to them. Their primary claim focused on the legal interpretation of the will's provisions regarding the inability to sell the property, contending that this limitation should not restrict creditors' rights to pursue debts owed.	Rozella Marks, the defendant, contended that the will clearly stated her interest in the property was not subject to sale or execution. Her defense was based on the legal enforceability of the will's terms, asserting that the limitations imposed by her father were valid and should preclude any sale under execution, thereby protecting her interests from creditors.

Ninian W. Edwards filed an action against Elijah Hill in 1848, claiming penalties for the unauthorized cutting of timber on land. The case was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court, with the initial trial occurring in St. Clair County. The plaintiff, Edwards, alleged he was the owner in fee of the property, while the evidence revealed that he only held title to six-sevenths of the land in question. The case raised significant legal questions regarding the ownership and rights associated with the recovery of statutory penalties for timber cutting. The court instructed the jury that because Edwards did not have full ownership, he could not recover damages or penalties. This decision ultimately set the stage for Edwards’ appeal to the higher court.	Edwards argued that he was entitled to penalties for the cutting of trees on his land without permission, as stipulated by applicable statutes. He maintained that his ownership of the property justified his claim for recovery against Hill.	Hill's defense was centered on the claim that Edwards did not hold the full title to the land, thereby invalidating his right to recover penalties. Additionally, Hill argued that all co-owners of the land must join the action in order to pursue recovery under the statute. He implied that the statute allows for no division of the penalty between multiple owners.

In the case titled "Samuel Stookey et al. v. John D. Hughes et al.", decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1856, the dispute arose over a promissory note for $925 related to a real estate transaction. The key individuals involved were Samuel Stookey, the appellant, and John D. Hughes, the appellee. The incident occurred in Belleville, Illinois, where Stookey purchased land from Hughes. Stookey asserted that Hughes, through an agent, falsely represented the title of the land as being clear of encumbrances and that boundaries were properly delineated. After Stookey discovered that the land had been platted into streets and alleys, which diminished the land's value by approximately $800, he claimed that the consideration for the note had failed. The case revolved around whether Stookey’s plea was sufficient to answer the allegations made against him regarding the promissory note.	The plaintiffs, Stookey et al., argued that they were misled by false representations from Hughes regarding the title of the property they purchased. They contended that the representations made influenced their decision to buy the land and to execute the promissory note. As such, they claimed that the true value of the property was significantly diminished due to the existing platting, which failed to fulfill the terms of their agreement. Therefore, the plaintiffs sought judgment enforcing the payment on the promissory note.	The defendants, Hughes et al., argued that the plea made by Stookey to defend against the promissory note was inadequate as it only partially addressed the plaintiff's claims. They asserted that Stookey had failed to allege any fraud or warranty regarding the title, and according to established legal principles, all parties assume the risk regarding property title unless fraud is demonstrated. They requested that the court dismiss the plaintiff's claims due to the insufficient grounds presented in the defense plea.

In December 1848, the case of William Reece v. William H. Allen was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The matter originated from a legal conflict regarding a deed that William Reece had executed, conveying property to John F. Darby as a trustee for Richard H. McGill. The case arose from an ejectment action initiated by Allen, the administrator of James Mason, deceased, against Reece and others, concerning the legality of the deed's proof and its classification as a mortgage or a trust deed. At the March term of the same year, Allen dismissed his suit against all except for Reece, leading to a jury trial that found in favor of Allen. Reece subsequently appealed the decision, claiming that the acknowledgment of the deed was insufficient and that the necessary legal title had not been established in order for Allen to prevail in the ejectment claim.	The plaintiff, William H. Allen, argued that the deed from Daniel Reece to John F. Darby lacked a proper acknowledgment and did not serve as a legal guarantee of title necessary for recovery in ejectment. Allen maintained that he had a valid claim as the administrator of Mason and sought to establish possession of the property.	William Reece, the appellant, contended that the proof of the deed was sufficient and that it conveyed an absolute legal title. He argued that the court could not inquire into the conditions of the trust deed compliance by the trustee in a simple ejectment proceeding. Reece asserted that the deed was not a mortgage but rather a trust deed, and thus, Allen's claims should be dismissed on those grounds.

The case "Laura D. Mott et al. v. The Danville Seminary et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 15, 1889. It involved multiple parties, primarily the plaintiffs, Laura D. Mott and others, who claimed ownership of a one-third undivided interest in a parcel of real estate. The case's background dates back to March 21, 1888, when the plaintiffs allege they received their interest through a conveyance from Melissa B. Lamon, the original owner of the property. The land in question was originally conveyed by Lamon and her husband to the Board of Trustees of the Danville Seminary in 1850 as a donation for educational purposes. The seminary operated as an institution until its dissolution in 1880 due to inactivity and a legal proceeding. The plaintiffs argued that upon the seminary's dissolution, the property reverted back to Lamon and subsequently to them because the seminary had no legal authority to convey the land afterward. The defendants, including the new Danville Seminary corporation, contested this claim by asserting their title through subsequent, albeit disputed, deeds. The case revolved around legal interpretations of property ownership and corporate rights after the dissolution of the original seminary.	The plaintiffs claimed they were the rightful owners of a one-third interest in the property originally conveyed to the Board of Trustees of the Danville Seminary. They argued that since the seminary was dissolved in 1880 and did not have the legal authority to convey the land afterward, the ownership rights reverted back to the original grantor, Melissa B. Lamon. The plaintiffs sought the removal of subsequent deeds as clouds on their title and requested partition of the property, asserting their rightful claim based on the dissolution of the seminary.	The defendants, representing the Danville Seminary, argued that the plaintiffs' claims were unfounded as the deed transfers made by the old Board of Trustees were valid and not mere acts to circumvent the reverter. They contended that the “possibility of reverter” to Lamon was extinguished through valid conveyance before the dissolution. The defendants sought to maintain their title against the plaintiffs' claims, asserting that the previous transfers had legally vested ownership in them.

In 1861, an ejectment action was initiated in the Lawrence Circuit Court of Illinois by Joseph P. Bowman and William Harrow against Geo. W. Wise, regarding the recovery of lot twenty-one in the town of Lawrenceville. William Thomas, claiming ownership of the property as trustee for the Bank of Illinois, was permitted to join the case as a defendant in place of Wise and pleaded 'not guilty.' The trial was held without a jury, resulting in a verdict in favor of Bowman and Harrow. Thomas claimed an equitable title to the lot and had previously engaged in a chancery suit against the heirs of Touissant Dubois and Wise for partitioning the property. Thomas's previous court ruling established his title to the lot. However, following a redemption by Bowman of the lot sold during a sheriff's sale (following a judgment against the heirs of Dubois), Bowman and Harrow were deemed to hold fee title over the property. This led Thomas to appeal the court's subsequent decision, which favored Bowman and Harrow, claiming trespass and ejectment against him.	The plaintiffs, Joseph P. Bowman and William Harrow, argued that they acquired a valid title to the lot after having redeemed it from a prior execution sale. They maintained that Thomas's acceptance of redemption money indicated his acknowledgment of their legal standing and that he lost any claim to the property by allowing the sale to occur.	William Thomas contended that he retained ownership of the lot as established by prior court rulings. He argued that Bowman's claims to redeem did not confer a title because the heirs of Dubois held no actual interest in the property. Thomas further asserted that the acceptance of the redemption funds should not affect his title, especially as he acted in a fiduciary capacity as trustee. He emphasized that his title was established prior to Bowman's transactions and that Bowman could not claim ownership without a valid title from Dubois's heirs.

In 1874, the case of Ira Heath v. Samuel F. Hurless was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict originated in Whiteside County, Illinois, where Samuel F. Hurless filed a bill against several parties, including Heath and Henry Deihl, concerning land ownership. Hurless had purchased certain lands from Walter Harmon in January 1865, for a substantial sum and later conveyed these lands to Deihl. Heath claimed a prior interest in the land through a deed received from Harmon, asserting that he owned part of it. Tensions arose when Heath threatened Deihl with an ejectment suit, asserting his ownership. Hurless, facing potential liability from Deihl due to the situation, sought a court declaration to clarify the title and prevent Heath from pursuing legal action against Deihl. The court examined the claims surrounding the alleged misrepresentation of the land’s boundaries and whether Heath had committed fraud regarding the sale.	Hurless's main arguments centered on his right to the land and the need to confirm whether Heath's claims were legitimate. He requested the court to determine the ownership of the land and prevent Heath from pursuing any ejectment action against Deihl. Furthermore, he sought the return of the purchase money if the court found Heath's claims valid against any portion of the property.	Heath's defense was that he had legitimately acquired a portion of the land in question prior to the transactions between Hurless and Deihl. He denied knowledge of the dealings between Hurless and Harmon, but acknowledged that he held a deed for part of the land from Harmon. Deihl, meanwhile, asserted that he relied on Heath’s representations regarding the boundaries of the land he purchased and claimed that he should be compensated for his reliance on what he believed to be true regarding his property rights.

The case "Mitchell & Parrish et al. v. James L. Byrns et al." was adjudicated in January 1873 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal proceedings originated in the circuit court of Edgar County, Illinois, where plaintiffs Mitchell & Parrish, identified as creditors, filed a complaint against the defendants, led by James L. Byrns. The plaintiffs had previously obtained judgments against Byrns and other connected parties. Following the issuance of execution against Byrns, no property could be found to satisfy these judgments, leading the plaintiffs to allege that Byrns was concealing property intentionally. A specific point made was that Byrns’ father had conveyed property to Byrns' wife for $10,000 in consideration, a considerable part of which was alleged to be paid by Byrns himself. Furthermore, Byrns allegedly improved this property using funds drawn from his firm, which was insolvent at the time of the judgment. The plaintiff claimed an equitable interest in the property to satisfy the outstanding judgments. Upon hearing, the circuit court sustained a demurrer to the plaintiffs’ bill and dismissed it for lack of equity, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal.	The plaintiffs asserted that they held valid judgments against the defendants and that the defendants possessed property they were concealing to evade paying their debts. They alleged that the transfer of land from Byrns' father to his wife was fraudulent, as Byrns had used funds from an insolvent firm to pay for and improve this property. The plaintiffs requested the court to compel the defendants to provide a discovery of the concealed property and to allow for the sale of this property to satisfy the judgments against them.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs' claims lacked sufficient equity to necessitate an answer, leading to their demurrer. They argued that the concealment of assets, as alleged, had not been sufficiently substantiated in the plaintiffs' bill. The defendants also maintained that legal proceedings should not be used to delve into past transactions that might lead to potential criminal charges, hinting at protections against self-incrimination.

On May 6, 1878, William F. McLaughlin initiated a lawsuit in assumpsit against William MacLachlan, David MacLachlan, and Matthew T. Campbell in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, for goods sold and delivered, amounting to $829.52. The defendants failed to appear in court following personal service on May 6 and 7, 1878, leading to a default judgment against them. An execution was issued on June 6, 1878, but went unsatisfied. Subsequently, on November 6, 1882, an alias execution was issued, prompting the defendants to appear in court, seeking to stay the execution and set aside the judgment. The defendants had filed for bankruptcy on May 7, 1878, and were discharged from their debts on October 6, 1879. The court had to consider whether the defendants' discharge from bankruptcy would invalidate the judgment rendered against them, especially as they had not sought to stay the proceedings during the bankruptcy process.	McLaughlin claimed that he was owed the amount from the sale due to the successful judgment against the defendants. He argued that, despite the bankruptcy proceedings, the judgment should remain in force as the defendants made no effort to seek a stay of proceedings during their bankruptcy, thus contending that their subsequent discharge did not negate the judgment.	The defendants contended that they had been discharged from their debts through bankruptcy, asserting that this discharge should invalidate the previous judgment that McLaughlin obtained while they were bankrupt. They argued that their failure to appear in initial proceedings was a consequence of their adjudication as bankrupts and that they could not be held accountable for a judgment rendered without their defense being heard.

In May 1882, H. G. C. Miller began working for William Beard, who was in charge of a coal mining operation that involved sinking a coal shaft. On December 15, 1882, while Miller was being hoisted to the top of the shaft, the machinery malfunctioned, causing a sudden stop. The operatives instructed Miller to grab hold of a partition, but as he did so, the machinery unexpectedly resumed, resulting in Miller falling approximately 250 feet to his death. R. C. Maxwell, acting as the administrator of Miller’s estate, filed a lawsuit against Beard. The case was heard in Logan County Circuit Court, where it was alleged that Beard was negligent in maintaining the machinery and providing safe working conditions. The court found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding $1500 in damages, a decision that was later upheld by the Appellate Court for the Third District.	The plaintiff, R. C. Maxwell, claimed that William Beard was negligent in providing safe machinery which ultimately led to the death of H. G. C. Miller. The declaration highlighted defective and unsafe equipment, particularly an old and worn-out engine, as critical factors in the incident. The plaintiff sought damages for Miller’s death, arguing that the conditions of the work environment contributed to the fatal accident.	William Beard, the defendant, pled not guilty to the charges of negligence. His key arguments included contesting the validity of the claims regarding the machinery’s condition and the safety measures in place at the operation. Beard maintained that the instructions given to the jury were flawed and that any errors made during the trial did not affect the outcome. He sought to have the judgment overturned and the case dismissed.

In 1886, the case of James A. Kirk et al. v. The L. Wolf Manufacturing Company took place in Illinois. The dispute arose from a contract for the manufacturing of copper tanks and their associated connections. The plaintiff, L. Wolf Manufacturing Company, sought to recover costs for producing these items, claiming that the agreed price was fifty cents per pound, resulting in a total of approximately $3124.25 when including additional charges for extra work. The defendants, James A. Kirk and others, contested this claim, asserting that their total expenditures for the project did not exceed $1250. The case centered around whether a special contract regarding the price existed, as both parties claimed different amounts owed. The trial initially resulted in a jury verdict favoring the plaintiff for $3177, which prompted appeals from the defendants, arguing that the evidence pertaining to reasonable value was inadmissible due to the alleged existence of a quoted price contract.	The plaintiff asserted that they manufactured and delivered copper tanks based on a verbal agreement for payment at a rate of fifty cents per pound, plus additional costs for extra services rendered. They sought to recover the full amount of $3177 as owed under the agreement, arguing that the defendants accepted and retained the tanks and were therefore liable for the payment irrespective of the contested price details.	The defendants contended that there was no agreement on a definite price, claiming that the estimated amount of $1250 was merely an estimation and not a binding contract. They maintained that there was a misunderstanding regarding the contract terms, which should lead to a dismissal of the plaintiff's claims. Additionally, they argued that the evidence concerning what constituted a reasonable price should be excluded, as they claimed an agreed-upon price must prevail.

In 1856, the Illinois Central Railroad Company had ownership of land in Coles County, Illinois (now Douglas County). The company made a contract with E. S. Terry, W. T. Mulhollen, and T. S. Cornelius to purchase 160 acres of the land for the town of Tuscola. The company reserved the right of way for railroad purposes in the sale. Over the years, the Indiana and Illinois Central Railway Company (the appellee) planned to build its road, which would cross the appellant's track. In 1872, the two railroads discussed constructing a crossing, which eventually occurred without issue. However, in 1875, the Illinois Central Railroad Company began constructing a switch to connect its tracks with an elevator near its right-of-way, which interfered with the appellee's plans. The appellee obtained an injunction to prevent the switch's construction, leading to this legal dispute.	The Indiana and Illinois Central Railway Company (appellee) argued that the Illinois Central Railroad Company (appellant) had no legal right to build a switch on the reserved land, as it had previously permitted the appellee to lay tracks across its right-of-way. The appellee sought a permanent injunction to stop the construction of the switch, claiming it had acquired rights to the land through implied permission from the appellant.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that it retained the title to the land indicated in the reservation, asserting that no agreement or conveyance had legally transferred any rights to the appellee. The appellant argued that the appellee had no claim to the land, as it was not included in any formal contract or agreement, and it emphasized that the crossing was permitted only as a courtesy and did not constitute a transfer of land rights.

In the case of Catharine Paris v. Thomas Lewis, dated September 1877, the dispute arose over an eighty-acre parcel of land located in Cook County, Illinois. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court after Catharine Paris (the appellee) petitioned to establish her title to the property. The petition referenced the act aimed at addressing the consequences of losing public records due to fires or other disasters. Thomas Lewis (the appellant) contested this claim, asserting his own title to the land. The court's inquiry focused primarily on whether Paris had presented sufficient evidence to prove that she had paid taxes on this land for seven consecutive years, which was a requirement for validating her title under the law. It was noted that Lewis held a superior paper title due to the inability of Paris to connect her title back to the original patent from the United States, but Paris had been in continuous actual possession of the property since 1863. The court ultimately examined a series of transactions and tax payments made by previous holders of the title to determine the legitimacy of Paris's claim.	Catharine Paris, as the plaintiff, argued that she had established her claim to the land by demonstrating continuous actual possession since 1863 and by providing evidence of tax payments over a period of seven consecutive years under the title she acquired in good faith. She contended that these actions complied with the legal requirements to substantiate her title even though her connection to the original patent was not established. Paris requested the court affirm her title to the property.	Thomas Lewis, as the defendant, maintained that he held the superior title to the property based on documented ownership and transactions that predated Paris's claim. He argued that the evidence presented by Paris regarding tax payments was insufficient to demonstrate the necessary continuity and authorization of those payments. Lewis contended that since he had not been in possession of the property, which remained vacant until Paris's acquisition, the legitimacy of her claims was undermined.

Fred Bennitt and others initiated a legal action against The Wilmington Star Mining Company and others, arising from a complex dispute related to a mechanic's lien. This case dates back to January 7, 1886, in Illinois, specifically in Grundy County. The legal contention began with a mechanic’s lien filed by the Coleman Gas Works Manufacturing Company on September 14, 1875, against the Coalfield Coal Company, which involved multiple parties. The Coalfield Coal Company conveyed its title to the hotel premises involved in the case after the lien petition was filed but before service of process for the lawsuit was completed. The plaintiffs asserted their legal claims based on this action amid competing interests in the property among different parties, including the mortgagee and the purchaser after the lien filing. The court also addressed issues of proper party representation, focusing on the requirement that trustees involved in trust deeds should be included in such liens and the application of the doctrine of res judicata, which asserts that earlier judgments related to the matter should be honored in subsequent suits.	The plaintiffs, Fred Bennitt et al., claimed ownership rights over the disputed property, alleging that the mechanics lien obtained by The Wilmington Star Mining Company is invalid. They requested an injunction to prevent the enforcement of the lien and aimed to clear the title of any clouds resulting from previous judgments. Essentially, they sought legal validation of their interests in the property based on assertions of fraudulent conduct regarding the lien and the judgment linked to it.	The defendants, including The Wilmington Star Mining Company, contended that the prior judgments and the mechanic’s lien were valid and should protect their property interests. They argued against the claims of the plaintiffs by insisting that the plaintiffs lacked standing as they had missed the opportunity to challenge the lien during the previous proceedings. They also asserted that the transactions involving the ownership and claims over the property were conducted appropriately, maintaining that the lien and accompanying judgments were binding.

In the case of Henry Siegel et al. v. Chicago Trust and Savings Bank, which was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on May 29, 1889, the dispute revolves around a financial instrument issued by Siegel, Cooper & Co. to D. Dalziel. The document, dated March 5, 1887, promised the payment of $300 for advertising services to be rendered over a three-month period starting May 15, 1887. The main question at hand was whether this document constituted a promissory note that could be enforced by an assignee even if the underlying consideration (the advertising services) had not yet commenced and was potentially at risk of failure. The court had to determine the validity and enforceability of commercial paper under these circumstances, balancing the interests of business practices against legal standards for enforceability. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving key parties including Henry Siegel and the Chicago Trust and Savings Bank.	The plaintiffs, Henry Siegel et al., argued that the instrument in question was indeed a promissory note. They maintained that as an assignee who took the note for value before the consideration began, and without any notice of potential failure of consideration, they should be able to recover the owed amount. Their legal request was to affirm the enforceability of the promissory note in the context of commercial transactions.	The defendant, Chicago Trust and Savings Bank, contended that the document could not be treated as a promissory note due to the lack of consideration at the time of the assignment and claimed that the payment was contingent upon the completion of advertising services that had not yet started. They argued for a ruling in their favor stating that the lack of consideration undermined the enforceability of the note.

In 1868, in Lee County, Illinois, John A. Peck, on behalf of George M. Deland, initiated a legal action against Leonard Brewer and his associates over a contract concerning the lease of six hundred and eighteen sheep. The agreement stipulated that Peck would provide Brewer with the sheep for three years, during which Brewer was required to deliver a specified amount of wool annually and return the same number of sheep in good condition at the end of the lease period. Disputes arose over the condition of the sheep upon their return, particularly regarding a contagious disease known as foot rot, which was alleged to have infected the flock upon delivery. The case saw considerable procedural complexity, with numerous pleas from the defendants and only a few key matters at issue being addressed regarding the sheep's health. The jury ultimately examined the evidence presented, leading to a significant verdict favoring the defendants.	The plaintiff, Peck, claimed that Brewer failed to return the sheep in good marketable condition as required by the contract. He argued that Brewer's refusal to accept the sheep upon their return indicated a breach of the contractual obligations. Peck sought damages resulting from this alleged breach, insisting that he was entitled to receive healthy sheep as part of the agreement.	The defendants, led by Brewer, contended that they had been misled by Peck regarding the health of the sheep, asserting that Peck had fraudulently represented the sheep as sound and free from disease at the time of delivery. They maintained that Brewer had exercised reasonable care and had made efforts to control the disease amongst the sheep, which impacted their condition by the end of the contract. Brewer argued that given these circumstances, he fulfilled his contractual obligations to the extent possible and was not liable for the deteriorated health of the sheep.

In December 1838, in Illinois, a legal case titled "Alfred Edwards and Benjamin F. Bosworth, appellants v. Augustus Todd, appellee" arose involving a dispute over the transportation of goods. The case stemmed from an action of assumpsit where the plaintiffs, Edwards and Bosworth, sought to recover the agreed freight payment for transporting merchandise from Buffalo, New York, to Chicago, Illinois. The Circuit Court of Cook County had initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $354.66 plus costs. The defendants, Todd, contested this judgment, claiming that due to the plaintiffs' negligence, a significant portion of the goods was lost during transport. During the trial, the defendants attempted to introduce evidence to demonstrate their losses as a set-off against the freight claimed by the plaintiffs. However, this evidence was rejected by the Circuit Court, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to recover the full amount of freight due for the portion of the merchandise that had been safely transported and delivered. They maintained that the loss of other goods, which the defendants cited as being due to the plaintiffs' negligence, should not affect the freight payment for the items that were delivered.	The defendants contended that a portion of the goods transported was lost through the negligence and improper conduct of the plaintiffs. They sought to introduce this evidence to either set-off the lost goods' value against the claimed freight or to reduce the amount owed by the plaintiffs. They argued that since the losses were a direct result of the plaintiffs' negligence, they should not be liable for the total freight amount claimed.

The case involves the will of Esther E. Tuller, who passed away on March 6, 1874. Esther had previously been married and had three children from that marriage. She executed her will on May 20, 1869, while she was a widow, and later married Marcus Hosmer on September 2, 1869. Esther divorced Hosmer on December 16, 1873, and after her death, her will was contested. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court after a lower court ruled against admitting the will to probate, stating that her marriage to Hosmer revoked the will. The central legal question revolved around whether marriage automatically revoked a woman's will, given the existing laws at the time regarding married women's property rights.	Lydia A. Cole, as the residuary devisee and legatee under Esther Tuller’s will, argued that Esther's will should be admitted to probate and that the marriage to Hosmer did not result in the revocation of the will. She cited the statutes allowing married women to devise their property and claimed that the previous legal rules regarding revocation by marriage were no longer applicable under the law.	The defendant contended that the marriage between Esther and Hosmer served as a revocation of her previously established will in accordance with common law. They argued that under the statutes in place at the time, marriage created a presumption that the testator's intentions had altered, thus revoking the will. They also highlighted that a subsequent statute from 1872 deemed marriages as automatic revocations of prior wills.

In the case of Christopher B. Bouton v. A. B. Dement et al., dated June 28, 1887, Bouton was involved in legal proceedings regarding an alleged breach of an undertaking connected to his shares in the Empire Fire Insurance Company of Wheaton. The events leading up to the case date back to January 25, 1875, when Bouton acquired shares amounting to $14,000 but had not paid for them. A crucial event occurred in January 1877, when the insurance company issued an insurance policy to Dement, Clark & Israel that subsequently led to a fire damaging their property in February 1877. Due to the insolvency of the insurance company, a general assignment was made for the benefit of creditors, leading the plaintiffs to seek recovery through a creditor's bill. This process began with judgment creditors who sought to enforce their claims after the company failed to pay the owed amounts. Amongst various parties involved, Cole represented the interests of the creditors as the assignee. The evidence highlighted Bouton’s fraudulent actions, including manipulation of promissory notes and stock that ultimately detrimentally affected the company's creditors.	The plaintiffs, represented by Dement, Clark & Israel, claimed that Bouton breached his financial obligations to the Empire Fire Insurance Company. They sought relief through a creditor's bill, arguing that Bouton's actions, including his improper acquisition and manipulation of shares, had directly caused financial harm to the creditors of the insolvent company.
