They requested the court to mandate Bouton to pay the sums owed, which amounted to $17,584.92, reflecting damages and related costs.	Bouton contested the claims by asserting that the assignee, Cole, was not a proper complainant in the cross-bill filed against him. His defense also suggested that the company and its assignee lacked the legal standing to pursue him for repayment of the shares, arguing that the transactions regarding the stock should not impose any liability upon him. He sought to challenge the evidence presented, maintaining that any claims made by the plaintiffs were unfounded.

The case "Robert Lawson et al. v. Adelaide M. Funk" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 23, 1884. The case arose in Ogle County, Illinois, involving Robert Lawson, who was a debtor, and Adelaide M. Funk, the plaintiff and a creditor. The issue at hand was a conveyance made by Lawson to his two sons, John and George, on May 6, 1879, just prior to a judgment obtained by Funk against Lawson for the amount of $1,166.26. Funk claimed that the conveyance of property to Lawson's sons was fraudulent and intended to hinder her ability to collect on the judgment, as the conveyance appeared colorable and without actual consideration. Evidence presented indicated that Lawson had transferred his only real estate, which was a homestead, and a significant amount of personal property without adequate compensation. Following a trial in the Ogle Circuit Court and an appeal, the courts examined both the intent behind the conveyance and whether it legally constituted a fraudulent act against creditors, especially considering that Lawson was insolvent at the time of the transfer. The case ultimately centered around whether the conveyance could be considered a legitimate transaction or merely a tactic to defraud creditors.	Adelaide M. Funk, the plaintiff, claimed that Robert Lawson's conveyance of property to his sons was fraudulent from its inception. She argued that the transaction was intended to hinder and delay collections from creditors, specifically her claim, given that Lawson had no equity left after this conveyance. Funk sought a court ruling to declare the conveyance null and void as it served as a means to prevent the collection of her judgment against Lawson.	The defendants, Robert Lawson and his sons, defended the conveyance by claiming it was made in good faith and for adequate consideration. They admitted Lawson's insolvency but maintained that the transactions were legitimate and intended to settle any debts that Lawson had accrued, including claims for wages owed to his sons for their work on the farm. They argued that the agreements made regarding services rendered constituted valid consideration for the conveyance.

Samuel Flower filed a case against Albert J. Brumbach in the Illinois Appellate Court, which was decided on March 13, 1889. The events leading to this case began prior to December 28, 1883, when Flower placed an order for goods worth $513.05 with Brumbach's agent. Brumbach, based in Reading, Pennsylvania, expressed caution in fulfilling the order, asking Flower for a statement regarding his ability to pay, as he had experienced financial losses from prior dealings. In response, Flower sent a letter detailing his business's financial standing, including assertions about his sales and assets. Relying on these claims, Brumbach sent the goods; however, Flower failed to pay for them subsequently. Evidence presented showed that Flower had substantial debts that he did not disclose in his letter. The case had previously been reviewed, and issues from that decision were not subject to review in this appeal. Overall, the court was tasked with determining whether Flower's letter had involved false representations and whether he intentionally misled Brumbach.	The plaintiff, Samuel Flower, argued that his response to Brumbach's inquiry about his financial condition was honest and did not mislead. He sought to maintain that he was entitled to receive the goods ordered and claimed that he had provided a satisfactory account of his business finances, believing he had a legitimate basis for doing so.	The defendant, Albert J. Brumbach, contended that Flower's letter contained false representations regarding his financial state, arguing that it was misleading and that he acted on Flower's assurances when sending the goods. Brumbach requested the court to uphold the position that Flower's misrepresentation nullified any obligation for the defendant to fulfill the sale and maintain any claim against him.

Edward S. Mulliner sued Charles M. Bronson in the Illinois Appellate Court on January 22, 1884, over a dispute regarding a contract for lumber. The case arose after Mulliner supplied Bronson with lumber from a sawmill established on Crank's land, beginning around October 1, 1881. Mulliner was contracted to saw approximately 220,000 feet of sycamore lumber, with specific dimensions and rates for various widths, to be completed by January 1, 1882. The contract's terms dictated that Mulliner had to deliver the lumber after a six-month seasoning period and that Bronson would measure and pay for the lumber under conditions set forth in the contract. Mulliner claimed delivery of 263,839 feet of lumber, while Bronson contended that only a certain quantity met the quality standards laid out in their agreement. The core issue centered on Bronson's belief that he had overpaid Mulliner and that a significant amount of the lumber was unacceptable according to the contract stipulations.	Mulliner claimed that he delivered more lumber than was acknowledged by Bronson, including approximately 260,000 feet of sycamore lumber. He sought the balance of $1,088.96, asserting that Bronson was responsible for paying for all acceptable lumber delivered. Mulliner argued that Bronson's rejection of some lumber did not negate his obligation to compensate for what was accepted under the terms of their contract.	Bronson countered that only the lumber meeting contractual specifications was acceptable, claiming he had paid $3,669.05 for the amount delivered, which led him to believe he had overpaid by $120.16. He argued that the lumber deemed unsuitable should not be compensated and that his contractual obligation was only to pay for lumber that met the specified quality, which he contended Mullen failed to deliver entirely. Bronson requested a judgment that reflected these claims.

The case involves an incident that occurred on January 21, 1883, when a locomotive engine belonging to the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company derailed at the Heeleyville switch in Illinois. Arnold Schevers, the administrator of a deceased fireman who worked on the engine, initiated the lawsuit following the fatal accident. The engine jumped the track and overturned, killing the fireman immediately. The plaintiff claimed that the cause of the accident was a defect in the switching apparatus, specifically a misplacement of the sliding rails due to a broken steel pin that was part of the switching mechanism; this defect was not visible to the naked eye. Evidence suggested that prior to the accident, the apparatus had failed multiple times, indicating that something was amiss. The jury returned a verdict in favor of the plaintiff for $5,000.	The plaintiff argued that the accident which resulted in the fireman's death was due to the negligence of the defendant in maintaining the switching apparatus. The claim centered on the assertion that the defendant failed to discover and rectify a defect in the switching mechanism, which ultimately caused the derailment. The plaintiff contended that the broken steel pin and misalignment of rails were defects that should have been detected with ordinary care, leading to the tragic outcome.	The defendant contended that there was no evidence of negligence in maintaining the switching apparatus and that the fireman's death might have resulted from the negligence of his fellow worker, the engineer, who allegedly operated at too high a speed without proper lookout. The defendant maintained that the switching apparatus was approved, well-made, and initially functioned correctly, claiming that any defect would not have been discoverable. They asked the court to direct a finding in their favor based on these arguments.

The case "John S. Miller et al. v. George G. McManis" took place in September 1870 in the Bureau Circuit Court of Illinois, presided over by Judge Edwin S. Leland. George G. McManis, the plaintiff, initiated two debt suits against defendants John S. Miller and Jacob Chritzman regarding the use of his patent for manufacturing and selling the "Luper Patent Corn Cultivator." The plaintiff claimed rights to the patent in the counties of Bureau, Knox, Henry, and Stark, backed by two contracts: a written agreement from 1864 and a subsequent verbal contract made in 1866. Under these contracts, McManis was entitled to payments ranging from $2.50 to $6.00 per machine sold. The suits were consolidated for trial, and a stipulation was made allowing either party to present evidence related to the state of the accounts without formal pleadings. A jury ultimately found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him $1,200, prompting the defendants to appeal the ruling, asserting that errors in the proceedings led to an excessive verdict.	The plaintiff, George G. McManis, argued that he was entitled to recover $2 for each corn cultivator manufactured and sold by the defendants in specified counties under a verbal contract. He based his claims on previous contracts that outlined his rights to the patent and established the amount owed for the machines sold during the designated timeframe. McManis sought payment for the use of his patent and contended that the defendants had failed to adhere to the agreed-upon terms.	The defendants, John S. Miller and Jacob Chritzman, contested the plaintiff's claims by arguing that no binding contract existed because the alleged verbal agreement was never formalized. They maintained that they manufactured the machines without intention to infringe upon McManis's patent. Additionally, they argued that the jury's verdict was excessive, as the amount awarded did not appropriately reflect the terms of the original contracts and included machines sold outside the designated territories.

The case of William B. Clarke v. The Board of Supervisors of Hancock County originated in the early 1860s in Hancock County, Illinois. The legal dispute arose from a series of actions taken by the county regarding its subscription to two railroad companies—the Mississippi and Wabash Railroad Company and the Warsaw and Rockford Railroad Company. In 1855, a significant election was held where county electors voted on whether the county should subscribe a total of $200,000 in stock for these railroad projects. The election resulted in a majority favoring the subscription. Consequently, the Board of Supervisors ordered the issuance of bonds to fund this subscription, which were signed by the county judge, J. M. Ferris. However, after the issuance of the bonds, Clarke, as the plaintiff, contended that the bonds were illegal as they were not issued by the proper authority—claiming that the Board of Supervisors alone had the power to issue these bonds. This led to a trial in the Circuit Court of Hancock County, where the court ruled in favor of the defendant (the Board of Supervisors), prompting Clarke to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	William B. Clarke argued that the bonds issued by Hancock County were invalid because the county's actions violated procedural rules governing such decisions. He claimed that the Board of Supervisors, although they ordered the election for railroad subscription, did not have the authority to delegate the signing and execution of the bonds to the county judge. Clarke sought legal enforcement to penalize the county for refusing to pay the interest coupons attached to the bonds, asserting that the bonds were void due to these procedural errors.	The Board of Supervisors contended that their actions were legally valid despite any procedural irregularities in how the election was conducted and how the question was presented to the voters. They argued that the issuance of the bonds should not be deemed void, particularly since they were legally issued in accordance with the majority’s vote, and the public had acquiesced in the bond's issuance and payment of interest. Their defense emphasized that while procedural correctness is essential, the existence of plausible authority and subsequent acceptance of the bonds by the community validate their existence.

In June 1876, the legal case of Eliza Klein v. M. D. Wells took place in Illinois, specifically in the Circuit Court of Clinton County. The presiding judge was Amos Watts. The action involved was a claim of assumpsit, which typically concerns the breach of a promise or contract. The central issue was a special count on a promissory note and the common counts. The defendant, M. D. Wells, faced a demurrer to the special count while also contesting the general issue pleaded to the common counts. The court initially overruled the demurrer, defaulted the defendant, assessed damages, and rendered judgment without fully determining the issue related to the common counts. This procedural misstep led to an assessment of damages despite pending factual issues in the case.	Eliza Klein, the plaintiff, primarily argued that the court incorrectly assessed damages without resolving the outstanding issues on the common counts. She sought a reversal of the judgment rendered against her, based on the claim that the proper judicial procedure was not followed, specifically regarding the treatment of the special count and the unresolved general issues.	The defendant, M. D. Wells, maintained that the court acted improperly by assessing damages while factual issues remained unresolved. His legal position hinged on the assertion that the demurrer to the special count should have been ruled on before any damage assessment occurred, and thus, he requested that the lower court's judgment be overturned.

Northwestern University, incorporated by special charter in 1851 and having its charter amended in 1855 to exempt its property from taxation, found itself in a legal battle concerning the taxation of several lots owned by the university. The case took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the appeal originating from a judgment of the County Court presided over by Judge Martin E. M. Wallace. The dispute revolved around the tax assessment for the year 1875, amounting to $6,644.15, levied against properties held by the university. Although some of these properties were utilized for educational purposes, others were rented out, contributing to the financing of teaching and related expenses. Central to the case was whether the property, not directly used for the university's educational mission but generating income, qualified for tax exemption under the Illinois Constitution of 1848.	The plaintiff, represented by Louis C. Huck, sought to uphold the tax assessment against Northwestern University's properties, asserting that the properties in question were not directly engaged in educational activities. The plaintiff argued that the state legislature's attempt to exempt the university's properties from taxation, especially those generating profit, was unconstitutional under the provisions of the 1848 Constitution, which did not allow such exemptions for properties held for profit that were not directly aiding the educational purpose of the institution.	Northwestern University, through their attorneys, maintained that their properties should be exempt from taxation based on their amended charter stipulating that all properties owned by the university were forever tax-exempt. The university contended that regardless of the income-generating nature of some properties, the ultimate use of profits for educational expenses aligned with the charitable objectives of the institution, thus warranting their exemption from taxation.

John Palmer initiated a legal case against David T. Douglas and James S. Pearson in the Illinois Supreme Court to redeem land following its execution sale and to remove a cloud on the title. This case originated in 1877, when Douglas lent Palmer $80 secured by a mortgage on ten acres of land. Subsequently, a third party, Steadman, secured a judgment against Palmer, leading to a sheriff’s sale where Douglas acquired the parcel for $76, later assigning the purchase to his father-in-law, Pearson. Palmer claimed that Douglas deceived him regarding the timeline for redemption and provided false assurances that he would have more time to reclaim the property. Palmer, who was illiterate and an aged blacksmith, relied on Douglas’s representations, believing he had until July 14, 1880, to redeem his land. However, by the time Palmer sought to redeem it, he learned that the period had already elapsed, which he attributed to Douglas's misrepresentation and manipulation. The McLean Circuit Court dismissed Palmer's complaint, prompting his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	John Palmer alleged that David T. Douglas and James S. Pearson conspired to defraud him, as Douglas misled him about the redemption timeline for the mortgaged land. Palmer argued that Douglas's false promises and reassurances caused him to delay redeeming the land, which led to an improper loss of his property. He sought equitable relief to redeem the property and to rescind the sheriff's deed, which he argued was obtained through fraud, claiming he was not informed adequately about his legal rights throughout the process.	David T. Douglas contended that he never agreed to extend the redemption period and denied any wrongdoing. He asserted that the sale was executed lawfully and that Palmer was aware of his obligations regarding the mortgage. Douglas claimed that Palmer's statements lacked validity and that he should have taken legal action sooner regarding his rights. Pearson, as the assignee of the purchase, maintained that he was a bona fide purchaser and thus had rights to the property acquired through the sheriff's sale.

Smith Frye v. Nathan Tucker et al. is a legal case that dates back to April 1860, originating in Peoria, Illinois. The key individuals involved are Smith Frye, the appellant, and Nathan Tucker along with Henry Mansfield, the appellees. The dispute arose from a promissory note for $225 dated March 11, 1858, which Smith Frye issued to the Peoria & Oquawka Railroad Company. The railroad company later assigned the note to Tucker and Mansfield. A default judgment was made against Frye when he failed to appear in front of a justice of the peace, resulting in an award of $226.40 in damages and costs to the plaintiffs. Frye appealed the case to the Peoria Circuit Court, where the jury found in favor of Tucker and Mansfield, awarding them $235.50. Frye's appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court was based on several alleged errors, including the claim that the plaintiffs did not establish a valid assignment of the note and that the note was executed without good consideration.	The plaintiffs, Nathan Tucker and Henry Mansfield, claimed that they were the rightful holders of the promissory note originally issued by Smith Frye to the Peoria & Oquawka Railroad Company. They argued that the note was validly assigned to them, and they sought recovery of the specified amount along with damages incurred from Frye's default. The plaintiffs maintained that all legal requirements concerning the negotiation and assignment of the promissory note had been fulfilled.	Smith Frye, the defendant, argued several key points in his defense, claiming that the promissory note presented in court was not the same as the one described in the justice's transcript and that there had been no valid assignment of the note from the railroad company to the plaintiffs. Additionally, he asserted that the note was executed without any good consideration, which the plaintiffs were aware of at the time they received it. Frye requested that the court grant a new trial based on these objections and errors he claimed were made during the earlier trial.

Bernard Donnelly filed a case against Robert Harris et al. in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from an incident that occurred during a dispute in Galena, Illinois, in August 1862. The altercation initiated over claims related to volunteer bounties and escalated when Harris physically assaulted Donnelly without provocation. Donnelly sustained significant injuries and was subsequently arrested without a warrant by John C. Hawkins, leading to his imprisonment in the county jail and later, in Camp Douglas for a few months. The case was brought before the Circuit Court of Jo Daviess County, where the jury found in favor of the plaintiff but awarded only $50 in damages. Donnelly contended that this sum was inadequate and sought a new trial based on perceived jury misdirection and the small verdict amount.	Donnelly claimed that he was wrongfully assaulted and falsely imprisoned by the defendants. He argued that the court erred in instructing the jury regarding the impact of words on determining damages and claimed the jury was misled about their authority to award exemplary damages. He requested a reversal of the judgment and a new trial due to the inadequate damages awarded.	The defendants maintained a plea of not guilty, arguing against Donnelly's claims of assault and false imprisonment. They contended that the circumstances surrounding the altercation should mitigate their liability and asserted that their actions were justified. The defense argued that the instructions given to the jury were appropriate and aligned with the standard legal interpretations of damages.

The case of John H. Morgan et al. v. Joshua J. Evans et al. was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1874. The dispute arose in Effingham County, Illinois, revolving around the possession of a parcel of land. The appellants (plaintiffs), led by John H. Morgan, sought to recover the land from the appellees (defendants), Joshua J. Evans, who were then in possession of it. The contested title originated from Joshua B. Whitney, who had conveyed the land to James H. Whitney via a warranty deed in September 1860. Following this, the appellants initiated an attachment suit against the non-resident James H. Whitney due to a judgment of $1,096.25 obtained against him in April 1862. An execution against the property was delayed and was not issued until July 3, 1863, over a year after the judgment. The attached land was sold by the sheriff in a sale that occurred in December 1864, and the appellants acquired the sheriff's deed. The core legal issue revolved around whether the delay in issuing the execution rendered it void or merely voidable, as the original judgment process was deemed regular up to that point.	The plaintiffs, John H. Morgan and others, claimed that they rightfully acquired the land through the execution of a sheriff's deed, which was issued following a valid judgment against James H. Whitney. They argued that the delay in issuing the execution beyond the year was not a matter that invalidated their claim, as the execution was voidable but not void. Therefore, they sought to recover possession of the land based on their purchased title, which should be recognized as valid under the circumstances.	The defendants, led by Joshua J. Evans, contended that the execution against the property was void due to the failure to issue it within one year after the judgment against James H. Whitney. They argued that this lapse rendered the execution invalid, and consequently, they should retain possession of the property. They requested the court to rule in their favor by dismissing the plaintiffs' claims based on the invalidity of the execution and the ensuing sheriff's deed.

On December 7, 1888, Sarah Rosenthal filed a case against M. C. Boas and other defendants in Cook County, Illinois. The case arose from an injunction that had been issued to prevent the defendants from proceeding with certain lawsuits in justice court against Rosenthal that aimed to collect alleged unpaid rent. The defendants demurred to Rosenthal's bill, leading to the dissolution of the injunction and the dismissal of Rosenthal's case. The court assessed damages against Rosenthal for the wrongful issuance of the injunction, despite little actual evidence of damages suffered by the defendants, aside from one defendant, Edmund O. Boas. The ruling criticized the damages calculated for the alleged rent loss and the lack of evidence supporting the assessment of attorney's fees. The court also highlighted that no loss by the other defendant, M. C. Boas, was shown during the proceedings.	Sarah Rosenthal claimed that the injunction was improperly issued, restricting the defendants from suing her for overdue rent. She sought to prevent the enforcement of those lawsuits, asserting that the injunction was necessary and justified. Her legal requests included the continuation of the injunction to halt further legal proceedings against her.	The defendants, including M. C. Boas, contended that the injunction was unwarranted and caused them unjust delays, thereby seeking damages for the wrongful issuance of the injunction. They maintained that they should be compensated for the troubles and costs incurred due to the injunction, particularly emphasizing the assessment for lost rent and attorney's fees.

Mary A. Ward filed a lawsuit against the City of Chicago in 1884, stemming from an incident that occurred on October 11, 1880, at the intersection of West Jackson Street and Throop Street in Chicago. At the time, West Jackson Street was undergoing macadamization and was left in an unfinished state, with small broken rocks covering the surface and a deep gutter next to the curb. There were no proper bridges or barricades to direct pedestrian traffic, and the area was poorly lit. On the evening of the incident, as it was getting dark, Ward attempted to navigate from the curb across the gutter to a plank lying nearby. Unfortunately, she fell and severely sprained her wrist. Ward asserted that she was exercising ordinary care at the time of the accident. After the plaintiff presented her evidence, the trial court directed the jury to find for the defendant, ruling that there was insufficient evidence to support her claims. Subsequently, Ward appealed the decision.	Mary A. Ward's primary claim against the City of Chicago was for damages resulting from personal injuries sustained due to the city's alleged negligence. Ward argued that the city's failure to properly maintain West Jackson Street, leaving it in an unfinished and hazardous state without adequate lighting or barriers, directly contributed to her injury. She sought compensation for the injuries she sustained from the fall, asserting that she was taking reasonable care in navigating the dangerous conditions at the intersection.	The City of Chicago, represented by its counsel, contended that there was insufficient evidence to support the claims of negligence made by Ward. The defendant argued that the trial court acted appropriately in instructing the jury to find a verdict for the city, as the evidence presented did not prove that the city was negligent or that such negligence caused the injury. The city's defense relied on the notion that there were no material allegations proven that warranted the jury's consideration.

In February 1856, in McHenry, Illinois, Franklin Safford and Norman J. Safford (the plaintiffs) were involved in a financial transaction with Micah Vail (the defendant) that led to a legal dispute over a promissory note. Vail had initially loaned $500 to Henry Stephens, who issued a note for $600 based upon a usurious agreement. Subsequently, Vail and the Saffords entered into a new contract where they executed a note for $720 to replace the original obligation. The plaintiffs argued that the terms of these transactions violated Illinois usury laws, which limit interest rates to 10% per annum. The plaintiffs claimed the agreement imposed interest rates well above the statutory limit. This case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following errors alleged in the lower courts regarding the judgment and proceedings on the case.	The plaintiffs contended that the note for $720 was given for $500 borrowed under a corrupt and usurious agreement. They argued that the original transaction between Vail and Stephens involved interest rates exceeding the legal limit of 10% per annum and sought to have the court recognize this usury as a valid defense against the enforcement of the note. They requested that Vail's claim for payment be dismissed and that they not be held liable for the excessive interest.	The defendant, Micah Vail, argued against the plaintiffs' usury claims by asserting that the plaintiffs were not entitled to raise a defense of usury because they were parties to the new note. Vail maintained that the transaction was valid and enforceable, emphasizing that the plaintiffs had benefitted from the refinancing agreement and therefore could not disavow their obligation. He requested the court to uphold the validity of the contract and allow him to collect the owed amount along with costs.

In January 1876, in Mason County, Illinois, William Brannon and his wife, along with other plaintiffs, brought a legal action against Caroline Silvernail. The core of this case centered around the claim that Silvernail sold intoxicating liquors to Brannon, which led to his habitual drunkenness and, consequently, caused serious injuries to his wife. The court case arose from issues surrounding the impact that the sale of liquor had on Brannon’s behavior and the subsequent effects on his wife, highlighting the significant social concerns related to alcoholism and its consequences on families during that era.	The plaintiffs, particularly Mrs. Brannon, claimed that the defendant's sale of liquor to her husband led to his intoxication, which resulted in her sustaining serious injuries. They argued that the defendant was responsible for causing Brannon's habitual drunkenness and resulting harm to their family life. The specific legal requests included compensation for damages experienced due to the defendant's actions, which the jury found to amount to $300.	The defendant, Caroline Silvernail, argued that there was a variance between the allegations made by the plaintiffs and the evidence presented in court. Specifically, the defense contended that the evidence showed the liquors sold only partially contributed to the husband’s condition, thus reducing liability. Furthermore, the defense argued that existing legal precedents did not allow for exemplary damages against saloon keepers when they face potential criminal charges for their actions.

In April 1859, in Peoria, Illinois, the case of Francis W. Smith, using Alexander Allison, as the plaintiff in error against Henry Pries and others as defendants in error, arose from an action on a replevin bond. The condition of this bond required that if the court ordered the plaintiff to return property that had been replevied, he must do so. However, during the trial, the plaintiff sought to prove that the property had not been returned as mandated by the bond. The presiding Judge Powell denied his attempt to introduce this evidence, claiming it was irrelevant because there was no formal writ of returno habendo issued and returned from the prior case involving Pries and Allison. This refusal became a crucial point of contention for the plaintiff, as it blocked his ability to substantiate his claims regarding the return of the property.	The plaintiff, Francis W. Smith, argued that Henry Pries breached the replevin bond by failing to return the property as the court required. Specifically, Smith contended that Pries did not return the goods and chattels to Allison or any other designated individual. His main legal request was to prove that the property had not been returned according to the conditions stipulated in the bond, seeking justice for this failure.	The defendant, Henry Pries, contended that the evidence about the non-return of property should not be admissible since there was no writ of returno habendo issued in the related case of Pries v. Allison. By emphasizing this procedural point, Pries sought to defend against the claims of breach associated with the replevin bond and requested that the court uphold the ruling preventing the introduction of evidence regarding the return of property.

In the case of William H. Todd v. Mary A. Todd, which was decided on May 14, 1886, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute centers around a quarter section of land located in Moultrie County, Illinois. The land was originally entered by John Todd in 1854, who died intestate later that year, leaving behind a widow, Mary A. Todd, and several heirs, including William H. Todd. Following John Todd's death, Mary A. Todd claimed to have taken possession of the land, made improvements, and paid taxes on it. William H. Todd alleged that as an heir, he was entitled to half of the property and sought to partition it. He argued that Mary A. Todd's possession of the land was not adverse and did not interrupt his ownership rights under the statute. The issue of Mary A. Todd claiming possessory rights for over 20 years, invoking the Statute of Limitations as a defense, emerged as a key point in the case, raising questions about adverse possession among co-tenants.	William H. Todd claimed that he was entitled to half of the land inherited from John Todd, and he sought its partition. He alleged that Mary A. Todd had collected rents from the property from 1869 to 1881 and should account for those rents with reasonable interest. He argued that her occupation of the land did not amount to adverse possession as required to bar his right to recovery, citing the lack of sufficient evidence showing exclusive and notorious possession.	Mary A. Todd defended her claim by asserting that she had positively held the land in question by making improvements and paying all taxes since John Todd’s death. She appealed to the Statute of Limitations, stating that her possession had been adverse for over 20 years. However, her defense relied on insufficient evidence, as it failed to establish the nature of her possession or demonstrate that it was adverse, which was necessary to support her claims of exclusive ownership.

In December 1854, the case of Oliver Oakes v. Ann Oakes, Administratrix of John Oakes, deceased, was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal matter arose from an action of assumpsit filed by Oliver Oakes against Ann Oakes. The case originated in the probate office of Scott County, where an account was filed on January 5, 1854, related to various items—including a horse, saddle, bridle, wagon, and rent for a farm occupied by the defendant's deceased father, John Oakes, from 1848 to 1853. The plaintiff claimed damages stemming from these items and the rent, set at $300 per year. The trial was conducted with a jury, leading to a verdict and judgment for the defendant. The plaintiff's claims were based on provisions for the usage of property and the expectation of rent, but the defense countered with the statute of limitations and other arguments questioning the existence of a formal agreement.	The plaintiff, Oliver Oakes, claimed compensation for a horse, saddle, bridle, wagon, and unpaid rent from his son, John Oakes, who occupied Oakes' farm for five years. Oakes argued that despite a lack of an express agreement for rent, there was an implied expectation of payment due to the nature of the occupancy. He contended that the occupier could not remain rent-free and sought a recovery reflecting the reasonable value of the rent.	The defendant, Ann Oakes, argued against the claims, raising a defense of non assumpsit, which suggests that the allegations were not valid or legally binding. She also cited the statute of limitations, asserting that the plaintiff could not recover compensation for the horse and other items due to the lapse of time since the transactions. The defendant claimed that there was no express contract for rent and that the circumstances did not warrant an implied agreement for payment.

In 1875, William Wray was indicted for burglary at the Criminal Court of Cook County, Illinois. During his initial trial on June 25, 1875, the jury was unable to reach a verdict, resulting in his remand to jail. The prosecution relied heavily on the discovery of a stolen coat and burglar's tools found in Wray's possession shortly after the burglary. On July 15, after weeks of incarceration, Wray was informed by the State's Attorney that his attorney had abandoned his case. The court then scheduled a new trial for the following day without allowing sufficient time for Wray to prepare a defense. Despite Wray’s attempts to secure new counsel and witnesses, they could not be found in time due to the short notice. Wray filed a motion for continuance supported by an affidavit detailing the circumstances of his attorney's abandonment and the materiality of his witnesses' testimonies, which was ultimately denied, and he was convicted and sentenced to five years in prison.	Wray argued that the denial of his motion for continuance was erroneous. He asserted that he was unaware of his counsel abandoning the case until the day before the trial and that he had made reasonable efforts to prepare for the trial by issuing subpoenas for his witnesses. He maintained that the witnesses’ testimonies were crucial to his defense, and that the rush to trial without adequate representation constituted a violation of his rights.	The State's Attorney contended that Wray was given adequate notice of his trial and had enough time to prepare his defense. They argued that the prosecution's evidence, particularly the stolen items found in Wray's possession, was sufficient for a conviction, and Wray's claims of surprise and inadequacy of counsel did not justify a continuance.

In 1883, the case of Adelaide M. Funk v. Robert Lawson et al. arose in the Illinois Appellate Court. The plaintiff, Adelaide M. Funk, was seeking to enforce a judgment against Robert Lawson and Samuel H. Shoop. The crux of her claim was that certain lands and properties had been fraudulently conveyed by Robert Lawson and his wife to their sons, John and George Lawson, in an attempt to hinder repayment to creditors, particularly to her. Prior to the conveyance, Robert Lawson and Shoop had defaulted on loans which led to Funk obtaining a judgment for the debts. After several transactions and associations proving insufficient to cover the debts, the conveyance was executed during a period of financial distress for Robert, who was also ill and died shortly afterward. The conveyance claimed to transfer significant tracts of land and various personal properties, with Funk asserting that such transfers were illegitimate as they served to deprive her of her rightful claim to collect her judgment against Robert.	Adelaide M. Funk claimed that the conveyance of property from Robert Lawson to his sons was fraudulent and intended to protect these assets from her creditor claims. She argued that the conveyance was executed while Robert was still indebted, thus making it a vehicle to hinder her from collecting the judgment awarded. Funk requested that the court declare the conveyance void, asserting that it was a clear attempt to defraud her as a creditor.	The defendants, John and George Lawson, contended that at the time of the property transfer, they had no knowledge of Robert Lawson's debts. They claimed that the conveyance was made in good faith for valuable consideration, which included the release of their claims against Robert and their agreement to provide him and their mother with support during their lives. They argued that since they were not aware of any existing creditor claims against their father, there was no intent to defraud Funk.

In May 1870, John Johnston leased three lots in Chicago to a tenant named Pyle for a term of five years at an annual rent of $1500. Pyle sublet a small portion of the property to a third party, Armstrong, and later assigned his lease to Worth, who collected rent from Armstrong and paid Johnston until Worth defaulted in February 1871. Following this, Johnston legally terminated the lease and obtained a judgment in a forcible detainer action that allowed him to reclaim possession, except for the portion held by Armstrong. The rights to Armstrong's sublease transferred to Patchell & Turner, who were then sued by Johnston to recover possession. The lower court ruled against Patchell & Turner, prompting them to appeal the decision.	Patchell & Turner contended that the forcible detainer action was inappropriate under the old act of 1845, which primarily addressed lease terminations due to expiration. They also argued that under the 1865 amendment, the law did not permit actions against sub-tenants like themselves. Patchell & Turner sought to challenge their eviction by asserting these legal points and requesting the court to overturn the lower court’s judgment.	Johnston maintained that the forcible detainer action was valid under the 1865 amendment which recognized the landlord's rights to evict tenants for non-payment of rent, thus extending legal actions to sub-tenants. He argued that the legal framework allowed him to reclaim possession from sub-tenants in cases where the original tenant’s lease had been forfeited. Johnston also contended that the consent he provided for sub-letting did not alter the legal relations or impact the present suit.

In 1873, in Wayne County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose in the case of John A. Campbell et al. v. James W. Whitson et al. The case involved John A. Campbell's widow and heirs seeking to set aside a deed as a cloud on their title to certain lands. The original deed was executed by James Dagg to Campbell in 1848 but was alleged to have been made fraudulently to evade judgments against Dagg. The Campbell family had acquired the lands from Dagg in 1852, believing their ownership was secure without knowledge of the earlier conveyance. The plaintiffs, claiming they had been unaware of the 1848 deed for over twenty years, argued that it was not valid because Dagg had misused it for the purpose of defrauding creditors. The Wayne Circuit Court ruled in favor of the Campbell family, declaring the deed to Campbell void; however, the defendants, represented by Whitson, sought to contest this decision by appealing the ruling.	The plaintiffs claimed that a deed executed by James Dagg to John A. Campbell was fraudulent, alleging it was intended to defraud Dagg’s creditors and that Campbell did not pay for the land. They argued that following the resolution of Dagg’s previous debts, the deed should not effectively impair their title to the property. They sought to have the deed set aside, claiming their position as rightful owners without any wrongdoing.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing to challenge the deed as they were merely volunteers and failed to demonstrate any bona fide interest in the property. They argued that the deed from Dagg to Campbell was valid between the parties unless rectified by a bona fide purchaser for value, which the plaintiffs did not represent. They also maintained that the plaintiffs had no legal basis to claim ownership or have the deed annulled after a significant period of ownership had passed.

John L. Beveridge filed a lawsuit against William Wagner, acting for the use of James Young, in September 1868 in Illinois. The case arose from Wagner's role as a sheriff who allegedly failed to execute a court judgment. It was claimed that he made a levy on personal property but failed to collect the money owed, instead returning the writ with a false claim that the case had been appealed. The case presented two key counts against Wagner: the first accused him of claiming that he could not collect due to an appeal, and the second asserted that he neglected to levy on other known personal property that belonged to the defendant in the writ. The case was prosecuted in the Superior Court of Chicago before being escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court where the legal arguments centered on the sheriff's alleged failure to meet his duties.	The plaintiff, John L. Beveridge, argued that Sheriff Wagner failed to carry out his official duty by neither executing the levy on personal property nor collecting the owed money following the execution. Beveridge claimed deceptive practices in Wagner's return of the writ, asserting that it was wrongfully and deceitfully returned as unsatisfied due to a non-existent appeal. He sought accountability for this negligence and demanded satisfaction for the damages incurred due to Wagner's inaction.	Sheriff Wagner contended that the return on the writ was accurate and argued that the plaintiff's declaration failed to establish a cause of action against him. His defense presented the assumption that the claims should be dismissed since the plaintiff did not allege the falsity of Wagner's return explicitly and directly. He sought the court's acknowledgment that the declaration lacked sufficient grounds for the action.

The case of The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway Company v. Arthur C. Harper was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the final decision rendered on May 16, 1889. The dispute arose from events that took place in Cook County, Illinois, where Arthur C. Harper, the plaintiff, brought a case against the railway company. The crux of the matter revolved around the jury selection and the conduct of one of the jurors during the trial. During the proceedings, a juror attempted to cross-examine witnesses, leading the defendant's counsel to claim that this indicated potential prejudicial bias. They moved to exclude the juror from the panel, arguing that his actions implied an inability to remain impartial. The trial judge denied this motion, stating that there was no evidence of bias. The case was appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court from the Appellate Court for the First District, which had upheld the trial court's ruling regarding the juror's conduct and the matter of the jury instructions that were not properly entered into the record.	Arthur C. Harper, the plaintiff, claimed that the defendant's juror conduct compromised the trial's fairness. He argued that the juror's attempt to engage in cross-examination demonstrated potential prejudice against the defendant, thus warranting the juror's removal from the panel. Harper sought to uphold the trial's integrity and maintain the verdict in his favor.	The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway Company, the defendant, contended that the court erred by denying their motion to exclude the juror who had acted improperly during the trial. They argued that the juror’s questions raised concerns about his impartiality and made him unfit to serve. Additionally, the defendant claimed that the jury instructions provided to the court were erroneous and should be regarded as part of the record, but the court determined that the instructions were not properly included in the bill of exceptions.

John F. Smith initiated a legal action against Charles A. Knight, William Baker, Walter F. Cobb, and James Hennersheets in 1873 in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois. The case emerged from a business transaction involving a partnership dispute. The background highlights that Hennersheets had a written agreement with Knight, Baker & Co. for advancing funds to aid his commission-based business. The crux of the case concerned whether Knight, Baker & Co. operated as partners with Hennersheets, which would make them liable for Smith's claims. A default judgment was entered against Cobb and Hennersheets due to their absence, while Knight and Baker contested the partnership claims. The court determined that the evidence presented by Smith failed to establish a partnership between Hennersheets and the defendants, as their agreement explicitly stated that Knight, Baker & Co. wouldn't be responsible for any losses, and the intention to form a partnership was absent.	John F. Smith contested that Knight, Baker & Co. were partners with Hennersheets and thus liable for debts incurred during business transactions. He argued that he conducted business with Hennersheets under the belief that he was dealing with a legitimate partnership, and sought to hold Knight and Baker accountable based on this alleged partnership. Smith contended that the trial court made errors by excluding vital evidence in support of his claims and admitting evidence that negatively affected his case.	The defendants, Knight and Baker, countered Smith's claims by asserting that no partnership existed between them and Hennersheets. They introduced a written agreement outlining that their relationship was one of loaning funds rather than forming a partnership, with clear stipulations that they would not be liable for any losses incurred by Hennersheets. They requested the court to affirm the lack of partnership and ruled in favor of their defense, emphasizing that Smith bore the burden of proof to establish the partnership.

In 1874, Elizabeth Nispel brought a legal suit against Isaac Wolff and John C. Hispel in Cook County, Illinois. The case was initially filed before a justice of the peace, where Nispel was awarded a judgment of $95.68 plus costs against Wolff. Subsequently, Nispel appealed this judgment to the Superior Court of Cook County. However, during the July term of the same year, her appeal was dismissed due to a lack of prosecution, leading to a procedendo issued to the justice of the peace. Nispel later attempted to vacate this dismissal and reinstate her appeal by filing a motion supported by affidavits; however, the court denied this motion. The court justified its decision based on Nispel's failure to demonstrate due diligence in prosecuting the appeal, noting that her counsel was absent when the case was called for trial, having chosen instead to attend another trial. The absence of an effective excuse and the failure to properly respond to the case's scheduled trial led to the court's dismissal of Nispel's appeal.	Elizabeth Nispel claimed that her appeal from the judgment of the justice of the peace should not have been dismissed for lack of prosecution. She argued that the Superior Court erred in denying her motion to vacate the dismissal and reinstate her appeal, contending that her attorney was engaged in another trial and unable to be present for her case. Nispel sought to have the Superior Court's dismissal reversed and the original appeal reinstated.	Isaac Wolff contended that the dismissal of Nispel's appeal was justified due to her counsel's negligence. The defendant argued that the decision to deny the motion to reinstate the case was within the court’s discretion and that there was no abuse of discretion since the affidavits presented by Nispel did not adequately show diligence in prosecuting the appeal. Wolff maintained that the procedural regularity was upheld and that Nispel had forfeited her right to pursue her claim based on her attorney's lack of preparedness.

The case involved an action of ejectment brought by Cook County against the Calumet and Chicago Canal and Dock Company regarding a disputed piece of land in Illinois, specifically the south-west quarter of section 7 in township 37 north, range 15 east of the third principal meridian. It began with a judgment rendered for the plaintiff on March 1, 1886, but was complicated by subsequent motions regarding costs. On September 16, 1886, the defendant paid what was believed to be all accrued costs to the plaintiff’s attorney, who then allowed the issuance of a satisfaction certificate for the payment. However, a new trial was granted on January 25, 1887, based on the assertion that all costs were paid. After a motion to vacate this new trial order was filed by the plaintiff, the court overruled the motion, which eventually led to a trial on the merits where judgment was entered in favor of the defendant. The plaintiff's motions and submissions were challenged, and the legitimacy of the payments and the trial process were central to the court's decisions throughout the proceedings, culminating in a ruling in 1890 by the Illinois Supreme Court.",	The plaintiff, Cook County, claimed title to the land based on swamp land legislation passed by Congress and state laws from the 1850s. They argued that the title was valid as the acts stipulated that such lands granted to the state were to be conveyed to the counties, affirming their ownership against the canal company. The plaintiff’s primary legal requests included upholding their claim to the land based on prior legal statutes and challenging the subsequent new trial granted to the defendant.",	The defendant, Calumet and Chicago Canal and Dock Company, countered that the land in question was originally granted for the construction of the Illinois Central Railroad, and thus their claim was legitimate. They provided evidence of continuous payment of taxes and argued that the plaintiff could not prove their claims to ownership as the land had been entered previously through a lawful process that preceded the swamp land acts. The defense requested to maintain their standing on the property based on their deemed title and previous ownership transfers.",

On the evening of January 10, 1885, a fire originated from an engine of the Indiana, Bloomington & Western Railway Company while passing through Champaign County, Illinois. The fire spread either from dry grass on the railway's right of way or from stubble in an adjacent field, ultimately consuming three stacks of hay owned by Daniel Nicewander and George H. Lutz, located approximately 40 rods north of the railway track. The plaintiffs argued that the railway company failed to maintain its right of way, in violation of certain statutes that require railroads to clear their paths of hazardous materials. The railway's defense pointed to their prior actions in cutting and burning grass on the right of way in the fall, claiming compliance with maintenance requirements. Evaluating the evidence, including testimonies about the fire's source, the court concluded it was up to the jury to determine whether negligence occurred. Significant to the case was the duty of the railway to maintain safety conditions year-round, as the court stated that summer maintenance alone did not suffice for winter safety.	The plaintiffs, Nicewander and Lutz, claimed that the Indiana, Bloomington & Western Railway Company was negligent for failing to keep its right of way free from dangerous combustibles, specifically dry grass, which directly caused the fire damaging their hay stacks. They relied on specific statutes that impose a duty on railroad corporations regarding the condition of their right of way, seeking damages for the losses incurred due to the fire.	The railway company contended that they had taken appropriate steps to manage the risks by cutting down and burning the grass on their right of way prior to the incident, demonstrating diligence and compliance with relevant safety regulations. They asserted that any negligence should not be presumed simply due to the occurrence of the fire, emphasizing that the engine operated properly under the supervision of a competent engineer and was equipped with effective spark-arresting technology.

Charles Shevalier executed a will on January 23, 1886, at his residence in McDonough County, Illinois, while suffering from severe cancer and experiencing significant pain. He died on February 12, 1886, shortly after his will was probated. Some of his heirs contested the will in the circuit court, claiming that the testator was of unsound mind and memory when he made the will and that undue influence was exerted on him by his brother John, who was a principal beneficiary. The circuit court allowed a jury to decide whether the document was indeed the decedent's will. The jury, after extensive testimony highlighting a conflict in witness accounts regarding Charles's mental capacity at the time of the will's execution, ultimately determined that he was not of sound mind. The circuit court upheld this verdict after denying a request for a new trial, leading the proponents of the will to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, dissatisfied heirs of Charles Shevalier, claimed that the deceased lacked the testamentary capacity to create a valid will at the time it was executed. They argued that he was suffering from severe illness, which impaired his ability to think clearly and make rational decisions. They alleged that the will's execution was the result of undue influence exerted by John Shevalier.	The defendants, including John Shevalier, contended that the will was valid and claimed that the jury's decision was not supported by the evidence presented. Their defense also emphasized that the evidence indicating Charles's mental competency was substantial and contradicted the claims of undue influence, asserting that the jury's findings were unfounded and should be overturned.

In January 1832, Amasa Barbour owned land in Marshall County, Illinois, and conveyed it to the complainants, Ambrose C. Hankinson and others, via warranty deed. Following Barbour's death in 1833, their deed was not recorded. Ambrose C. Hankinson later acquired conveyances for parts of the land from Barbour's heirs, allegedly knowing that the complainants already had a valid claim to the property. The plaintiffs argued that Hankinson's actions were deceitful and fraudulent, as he procured these conveyances without acknowledging the complainants' rights. They had been paying taxes on the land for over 25 years and contended that it was well-known in the community that they owned the property. They sought to have the later deeds set aside as fraudulent and void. In the court's examination, it was determined that Hankinson, through his agent Greenleaf, had sufficient notice of the prior unrecorded deed, which should have prompted inquiry about the complainants' ownership rights.	The plaintiffs, Hankinson et al., argued that they held a valid deed to the land, having received it from Amasa Barbour in 1832. They claimed that Hankinson, with full knowledge of their ownership, attempted to defraud them by acquiring subsequent conveyances from Barbour's heirs. They requested that the court declare these conveyances void and affirm their ownership of the land.	Hankinson denied any knowledge of the plaintiffs' deed and claimed to have purchased the land in good faith from the heirs, without knowledge of prior claims. He rejected the notion that the plaintiffs had openly acknowledged ownership or paid taxes on the land. Hankinson maintained that he believed the land's value was significantly less than what the plaintiffs claimed and upheld that his conveyances were legally valid and not fraudulent.

In 1877, the case of Chicago and Alton Railroad Company v. Richard W. Ragland unfolded in McLean County, Illinois. Richard W. Ragland was an employee of the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company. The legal dispute arose when Ragland's wages were garnisheed by a creditor while Ragland was the head of a family. Under Illinois law, specifically Section 14, Chapter 62 on garnishment, wages amounting to $25 or less were exempt from garnishment for individuals who were heads of families residing with them. The railroad company was subsequently judged in favor of Ragland, as it failed to claim the exemption on his behalf despite knowing about his family status. The corporation contended that they had no obligation to intervene, arguing their paymaster had no knowledge of Ragland’s domestic situation. However, it was noted that other employees were aware of it, and the court remarked on the railroad company's responsibility to protect their employees' rights and interests. This case highlights the obligations of employers in ensuring their employees can benefit from legal protections regarding wage garnishment.	Ragland claimed that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company should have declared his status as the head of a family to invoke the legal exemption from garnishment. He argued that the wages owed to him, being under the exempt amount of $25, were wrongfully garnished, as the company failed to advocate for his rights as an employee. Ragland sought the court's intervention to uphold the exemption afforded by law and recover his wages that were paid out despite being exempt.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company argued that it had no relation or responsibility to disclose Ragland’s family situation during the garnishment process. They maintained that their paymaster lacked the knowledge required to intervene on behalf of Ragland concerning the garnishment. Essentially, they contended that it was not their duty to assert the legal exemptions available to Ragland.

In 1887, in Chicago, Illinois, Herman Krueger filed a lawsuit against the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad Company after sustaining a personal injury while performing his job. At the time of the incident, Krueger was washing the exterior of passenger cars on the company's tracks. The accident occurred when he was walking between car-trucks and was struck by a moving car that had separated from an engine and was rolling by its own momentum. The defendant railroad had a practice of uncoupling cars and letting them roll down the tracks without personnel to manage them or warn of their approach. Although the plaintiff claimed to have looked for approaching cars and saw none, the defendant argued that he was negligent for taking a more dangerous path. The situation involved conflicting evidence regarding the practices of the railroad and the actions of the plaintiff, leading the jury to determine negligence based on the standards of ordinary care.	Krueger claimed that the railroad company was negligent for allowing a moving car to traverse the track without proper supervision or warning. He argued that it was the company's responsibility to ensure a safe working environment, especially by either stationing personnel to prevent accidents or by warning employees of approaching dangers. He sought damages for the injuries sustained, amounting to $3,000.	The railroad company contended that Krueger was at fault for not being sufficiently cautious and for choosing a more dangerous route while moving between cars. It argued that his negligence contributed to the incident, as he did not adequately watch for approaching cars. The defense also pointed out the lack of custom or obligation to provide a warning to Krueger, as he was not supposed to be in close proximity to the northern track where the accident occurred.

Frederick W. Burnham initiated a legal case against The City of Chicago in April 1860, concerning a special assessment levied for the graveling of South Street in Chicago. Burnham, as the appellant, contested the legality of the assessment imposed on his property and others, citing a range of procedural and substantive issues. The Superior Court of Chicago, where this case was heard, had undergone recent reorganization, which led to questions surrounding its authority to hold special terms. Multiple objections were raised against the assessment process, including claims of valuation discrepancies, lack of proper notice, and alleged excessive charges applied to the assessments. Despite Burnham's arguments that the assessments were unconstitutional and inflated by fraudulent intent, the lower court ruled in favor of the city, prompting his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Burnham's main arguments centered around the assertion that the special assessment was unconstitutional and void due to several factors. He claimed that the assessment was not based on the actual value of the properties but rather on the perceived benefit from the improvements. He argued that the properties were assessed at two to three times their true value, exceeding reasonable taxation limits. Additionally, he maintained that proper legal procedures were not followed, such as failing to publish an assessment roll and not having the requisite financial contributions before commencing the work.	The City of Chicago defended its position, asserting that the assessment was legal and valid under their charter, which grants the common council authority to levy such assessments for public improvements. They argued that the term "pavement" encompassed various forms besides rigid materials, justifying the graveling work done on South Street. The city maintained that their assessment process was fair and in good faith, dismissing claims of fraud and procedural missteps as unfounded, particularly since the lower court found the assessment reasonable.

The legal case "Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railroad Company v. Henry Lenz and Pauline Lenz" was decided on February 12, 1890, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs, Henry and Pauline Lenz, claimed that their property was adversely affected by the erection of a viaduct on 18th Street over the railroad tracks owned by the defendant, the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railroad Company, and other railroads. They alleged that this construction, along with the defendant's laying down railroad tracks across 18th Street and in Blackwell Street, diminished the market value of their lots. The jury initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $10,000 in damages, prompting the defendant to appeal. The main issue under consideration was the liability of the railroad company for damages resulting from the viaduct's construction, with discussions focusing on various ordinances and contracts governing the construction and maintenance of the viaduct, as well as the relationships between the involved parties.	The plaintiffs claimed that the construction of the viaduct on 18th Street and the laying of railroad tracks nearby caused a significant depreciation in the value of their property. They argued that the defendant should be held liable for these damages due to its financial contributions for the construction and its involvement in the relevant ordinances. Essentially, the plaintiffs sought compensation for the loss in market value of their lots, which they attributed directly to the construction activities of the defendant.	The defendant, Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railroad Company, contended that it was not liable for the damages claimed by the plaintiffs. They argued that they did not actually build the viaduct, although they contributed to the costs associated with its construction. The defense maintained that the damage to the plaintiffs’ property was not solely due to the viaduct's construction as it was also influenced by other factors, including the existence of railroad tracks on the property that the plaintiffs could not legally recover damages for. Additionally, they argued that the jury instructions were misleading and allowed for the inclusion of improper damage assessments.

In September 1868, in Kane County, Illinois, George Baker was indicted for assaulting William Warner with a gun, intending to inflict bodily injury. The indictment included two counts, both validated by a motion to quash. During the trial, the jury found Baker guilty based on the second count, which described Baker's actions with detailed language, asserting he committed an assault using a gun charged with gunpowder and loaded with shot. Following the verdict, a motion to arrest the judgment was denied, and Baker was sentenced to a fine of $25 plus costs. Baker subsequently appealed the decision, arguing the indictment was flawed.	The plaintiff, represented as the state through the prosecution, claimed that George Baker had committed an assault with a deadly weapon, specifically a gun, intending to cause bodily harm. They maintained that the circumstances of the assault justified the charges brought under the Criminal Code.	George Baker's defense primarily challenged the validity of the indictment, arguing that it failed to meet mandated legal criteria. Specifically, they contended that the indictment did not sufficiently demonstrate that there was no considerable provocation for the assault or that the circumstances indicated an "abandoned and malignant heart.

In the case of Samuel M. Rothschild v. Otto Meyer et al., filed on February 3, 1885, in Cook County, Illinois, the plaintiff, Samuel M. Rothschild, had purchased dry goods worth $8,324 from the defendant, Otto Meyer, without any false representations. However, Rothschild had not paid for these goods. On December 27, 1884, the defendants, knowing that Rothschild was not liable for the debt and that he could not be lawfully arrested for it, instigated a legal process intending to injure and oppress him. They filed an affidavit claiming Rothschild had obtained credit through false representations and caused a judge to issue a capias ad respondendum for his arrest. Consequently, Rothschild was arrested and imprisoned for 24 hours until he was forced to post bail. Rothschild argued that the affidavit was willfully false and the actions of the defendants were malicious and unlawful. The proceedings led to him suffering significant damages.	Rothschild’s primary arguments revolved around claims of malicious prosecution and abuse of process. He alleged that the defendants initiated a civil suit without probable cause, leading to his wrongful arrest and imprisonment. He asserted that the actions taken by the defendants were maliciously intended to oppress him, and he sought damages amounting to $30,000, citing significant injury to his liberty and reputation as a result of their wrongful actions.	The defendants argued that the plaintiff's declaration did not sufficiently allege that the original suit had been terminated. They contended that in cases of malicious prosecution, it is generally required to demonstrate that the previous suit had concluded, which Rothschild failed to do. The defendants maintained that the actions taken were legally valid under the use of a capias ad respondendum and thus did not constitute an abuse of process, contending that their affidavit was justified by the circumstances.

Gilman M. Sargent was indicted for forging a receipt, allegedly changing the amount from $20 to $200. The events transpired in a marketplace setting, specifically involving Sargent and the prosecuting witness, Dimmoek. On the day in question, Sargent visited Dimmoek's office to make a payment, which was allegedly only $20. However, a receipt reflecting a payment of $200 was claimed to have been issued, which led to the charge of forgery. The jury found Sargent guilty and sentenced him to one year in prison, despite concerns regarding the validity of the evidence presented. The case revealed conflicting testimonies, with Dimmoek and his son asserting the payment was only $20, while Sargent's witnesses indicated he had paid $200. The court noted that the jury's verdict seemed compromised, calling for a review of the trial's fairness. Ultimately, the court decided to reverse the original judgment and remanded the case for a new trial.	The plaintiff, represented by the State of Illinois, claimed that Gilman M. Sargent committed forgery by altering a receipt to inflate a payment amount from $20 to $200. The prosecution presented witnesses who testified that the actual amount paid was only $20, suggesting Sargent had malicious intent in modifying the receipt to indicate a larger sum. The legal request was for a guilty verdict based on the evidence presented.	The defendant, Gilman M. Sargent, argued that the evidence against him was insufficient to warrant a guilty verdict for forgery. His defense consisted of testimony from witnesses who confirmed that he had indeed paid $200, including both cash payments and receipts. Sargent contended that the prosecution's witnesses had personal motives to testify against him and that their accounts were not credible. He sought a reversal of the verdict and a new trial due to the inconsistencies and biases in the testimonies presented by the prosecution.

On January 19, 1864, in Clinton County, Illinois, Morgan was appointed conservator of an individual referred to as Watkins, who was legally declared an idiot. Morgan, along with George M. Richardson as surety, executed a conservator’s bond to the People of the State of Illinois. Morgan received $500 belonging to Watkins while serving as conservator but was later removed from this role. At the time of his removal, it was discovered that Morgan had $250.36 belonging to Watkins which he failed to pay to his successor, Kile, or to John W. Dugger, who was appointed later as the new conservator. Following Morgan's death, Dugger and the heirs of Richardson sued for the recovery of the funds. The defendants demurred, but the court overruled the demurrer. The central issue was whether Dugger, as the successor conservator, had the right to sue for the recovery of the funds that Morgan had not paid over, given the bond executed.	The plaintiffs, represented by John W. Dugger, argued that the conservator's bond executed by Morgan and Richardson should be valid despite claims of technical deficiencies in the approval and filing. They contended that Dugger, as the rightful successor, was entitled to recover the remaining funds from the bond because Morgan had failed in his duties as conservator. They sought a judgment against the defendants for the amount left unaccounted for from Watkins’ estate.	The defendants argued that the bond was void because it had not been properly approved by a circuit court and claimed that only Kile, the immediate successor to Morgan, had the right to sue on the bond upon Morgan’s removal. They contended that Dugger lacked standing to bring the action since his immediate predecessor was not provided the funds, and they questioned the legal effectiveness of the bond itself, asserting that it should have been made payable to the county treasurer instead of the State.

In December 1839, the case of Darius B. Holbrook v. The Peoria Bridge Company was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following a judgment by default rendered in the Peoria Circuit Court. The key individuals involved were Darius B. Holbrook, the plaintiff, and The Peoria Bridge Company, the defendants. The case arose from a legal dispute over the issuance of process in a suit commenced in Fayette County. The plaintiff argued that the process to the foreign county was executed improperly, as the declaration did not contain necessary averments to authorize such action. This procedural issue became central to the dispute, leading to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, which aimed to clarify the rules governing suits involving corporations and the issuance of process.	The plaintiff, Darius B. Holbrook, claimed that the judgment by default rendered against the Peoria Bridge Company in the Peoria Circuit Court was erroneous. He argued that the process served in this case was improper as it lacked the necessary legal grounds to enable the issuance of process to a foreign county where the defendant was based, thus violating established legal procedures.	The Peoria Bridge Company, represented by attorneys W. Frisby and G. T. Metcalf, contended that the judgment by default was justified under the existing legal framework. They argued that the rules governing the issuance of process in favor of corporations should align with those applicable to natural persons. They maintained that the procedure followed in the Peoria Circuit Court adhered to these standards, defending the validity of the judgment against Holbrook's claims of error.

Gustave Manowsky initiated a legal case against James Conroy in the Illinois Appellate Court in Cook County. The background of the case involves a construction contract where Manowsky was supposed to build a house for Conroy valued at $1,300, with an agreement for payment in installments. By the time of the garnishment action, $900 had already been paid, leaving a remaining balance of $400. However, Manowsky had not completed the work, and Conroy claimed that various subcontractor liens, amounting to approximately $350, had been placed on the property, which had not yet expired. Conroy indicated in his response to the garnishment summons that he intended to retain the remaining funds until the liens were resolved. The court proceedings included evidence of an unpaid judgment against Manowsky. The trial ended with the court instructing the jury to find in favor of Conroy, leading to an appeal from Manowsky.	The plaintiff, Gustave Manowsky, claimed that he was entitled to the remaining $400 owed for the construction project. He argued that Conroy's assertion regarding the liens was unjustified and that the funds should not be withheld based on purported claims against the property.	The defendant, James Conroy, contended that he had a valid reason to withhold the remaining $400 based on the contractor's failure to complete the work and the existence of liens filed by subcontractors against the property. Conroy maintained that, under state lien law, he was entitled to protect himself from these claims by retaining the funds owed to Manowsky.

In Pleasant Valley, Illinois, on October 25, 1875, Delilah Deeds executed a written promissory note acknowledging a debt of $2,000 to her niece Mary J. Williams. The note stated that it was for a loan of $50 and for "sundry services and acts of kindness" performed by Mary. Delilah, then 63 years old, lived on a sizable stock farm and was cared for by her niece during times of illness. The note was drawn up by a neighbor named Reuben Mickel, who brought the $50 to Delilah from Mary. Witnesses testified regarding the nature of Mary’s assistance to Delilah, particularly during her illnesses. After Delilah’s death, a legal dispute arose over the validity of the promissory note which led to an appeal against a judgment rendered in favor of Mary for $2,800 by the county court, arguing that the services were rendered without compensation expectations.	Mary J. Williams claimed that the promissory note constituted a valid acknowledgment of debt owed to her by Delilah Deeds for both the loaned amount of $50 and the services provided over time. She requested the court uphold the judgment from the county court in her favor, asserting that the note was legally binding and reflective of a mutual understanding regarding compensation for her care and assistance.	The defendant contended that the services provided by Mary were acts of kindness rather than work expecting payment, suggesting that no valid contract existed. The argument was made that upon the execution of the note, there had been no express or implied obligation on Delilah's part to pay Mary. Additionally, the defense presented testimonies that suggested Mary was not present or did not provide care as claimed, thus challenging the basis of the promissory note's validity.

Jacob Fitzsimmons v. Benjamin Allen’s Administrator and Heirs is a legal case that took place in 1866 in Illinois. The case arose when Fitzsimmons, who had purchased 180 acres of land, sought a conveyance of 80 acres from Benjamin Allen.
