Fitzsimmons applied for a loan from Johnson to cover the outstanding balance on his land, leading to an agreement where Johnson would hold the title pending Fitzsimmons' debt payment. In 1855, Fitzsimmons and Allen agreed to exchange land; Allen would receive the controversial 80 acres in exchange for the 180 acres, with Allen taking over Fitzsimmons' debt to Johnson. After this exchange, Fitzsimmons occupied the 80 acres for nearly 18 months. However, he left the area for four to five years, during which Allen took possession of both the land and Fitzsimmons' property. A critical document in the case was a receipt signed by Fitzsimmons' attorney acknowledging payment from Allen, which the defendants claimed was a release of Fitzsimmons’ claim to the land. The Circuit Court dismissed Fitzsimmons' complaint, leading him to bring the case to a higher court.	Fitzsimmons claims he is entitled to the 80 acres of land based on his earlier agreement with Allen. He argues that he has paid his debts and fulfilled the conditions of their arrangement, and therefore seeks a court order to compel the conveyance of the land from Allen's estate. Additionally, he requests an accounting of the rents and profits from the land since the initiation of the suit.	The defendants, representing Allen's estate, argue that a receipt signed in 1857 by Fitzsimmons' attorney, which indicates the receipt of $240, releases Allen from any claims regarding the land. They contend that this document extinguishes Fitzsimmons' claim and assert that the case falls under the statute of frauds, implying there is insufficient evidence of a completed sale or agreement for the land.

In September 1869, the case "The City of Chicago v. Charles Johnson" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from an incident that occurred in August 1867 on Milwaukee Avenue in Chicago. Charles Johnson, the plaintiff, was driving his wagon along the street when his horse fell into a deep ditch that had been excavated for the purposes of street repair and paving. This ditch was left unmarked and unguarded, leading to Johnson being thrown from his wagon and sustaining serious injuries. He subsequently sued the City of Chicago for negligence, alleging that the city failed to provide proper warnings, guards, or barricades around the excavation. Johnson was awarded $1,000 in damages by the lower court, prompting the city’s appeal on several grounds regarding the sufficiency of the evidence and the legal responsibilities of the city.	The plaintiff, Charles Johnson, claimed that the City of Chicago was negligent for failing to secure a ditch that was dug during street repair activities, resulting in his injury. He argued that proper maintenance and safety measures, such as barricades or lighting, were not in place, which was a violation of the city's duty to keep public streets safe. Johnson sought damages for his injuries, ultimately obtaining a verdict of $1,000 in his favor.	The defendant, the City of Chicago, contended that there was insufficient evidence to prove that the city or its authorities had specifically instructed the excavation, and they argued that the plaintiff bore some responsibility for his injuries due to his knowledge of the ongoing street repairs. The city also challenged the jury instructions regarding the ownership and duties associated with the streets. Further, the city asserted that it was not liable for injuries if it could not be conclusively shown that it had notice of the existing conditions leading to the accident.

In 1877, John Lemley entered into an agreement to sell his newspaper, "The Golden Censer," to Charles E. Mandeville and Olin R. Brouse in Rockford, Illinois. This agreement included a covenant that Lemley would not establish or interfere with any similar newspaper for one year after the sale. However, in April 1878, Lemley moved to Albany, New York, and began publishing a new paper, "Zion’s Watchman," while illegally taking a copy of the subscription list of "The Golden Censer." He solicited some of the former subscribers, leading to a significant loss in subscriptions. The situation escalated as Mandeville and Brouse accused Lemley of misconduct, resulting in a trial that initially acquitted him. Despite this, disputes continued, and by May 1879, Mandeville and Brouse sought legal recourse, filing a bill against Lemley for damages, alleging breach of covenant and requesting the cancellation of a promissory note related to the sale. The case underwent multiple hearings in the equity court.	The Golden Censer Co. claimed that John Lemley breached the covenant by taking the subscription list and soliciting former subscribers for his new publication, resulting in significant financial damage. They requested that the court declare the promissory note given by the company as paid due to this breach and sought an injunction against the assignment of the note, along with ancillary relief pertaining to damages suffered from lost subscriptions.	John Lemley defended himself by asserting that the court had no jurisdiction over the matter and that there was no substantial evidence of damages caused by his actions. He argued that even if there were breaches, they did not amount to a failure of consideration for the promissory note, claiming that he had met his contractual obligations with the sale of the newspaper and its associated assets. Additionally, he maintained that the losses incurred by "The Golden Censer" could not be attributed solely to his actions.

On March 31, 1890, the case of Richard Lancaster et al. v. The Waukegan and Southwestern Railway Company was filed at the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Cook County, Illinois, presided over by Judge Francis E. Clarke. The plaintiffs, Richard Lancaster and others, took legal action against the Waukegan and Southwestern Railway Company. As the case reached the court, it was noted that no abstracts or briefs had been filed by the appellants by the required deadlines, which risked a dismissal of their case. After a motion for an extension was granted, the appellants still failed to submit the necessary documents and did not assign any errors upon the record for consideration. This led to the enforcement of the court's rules, resulting in the affirmation of the prior judgment from the lower court.	The plaintiffs, represented by Messrs. Ennis & Mason and Mr. C. L. Heydecker, claimed that the defendant (the railway company) acted improperly, seeking remedies through legal proceedings. Specifically, their arguments rested on procedural aspects of presenting their case, including the need for an extension on filing necessary documentation to support their claims.	The defendant, represented by Messrs. Williams, Holt & Wheeler, argued that the plaintiffs had failed to comply with procedural requirements set by the Illinois Supreme Court, specifically the rule mandating the timely filing of abstracts and briefs. They maintained that the failure to submit these documents justified the affirmation of the lower court's judgment without consideration of the merits of the plaintiff's case.

Amos H. Cox filed a lawsuit against J. W. Straisser in January 1872 in the McLean circuit court, Illinois, concerning a promissory note for the purchase of a horse. The central issue involved a conversation where Cox, wishing to sell a gray mare, engaged with J. W. Straisser and his associate Samuel Johnson. During this discussion, Johnson asked if Straisser would sign a note to secure the transaction. Straisser allegedly agreed to consider signing the note but ultimately testified that he never executed it. The plaintiff claimed that he had a verbal agreement for the note based on those discussions. The jury heard conflicting testimony, notably that while Straisser agreed in principle, he did not ultimately sign the note. Cox's claim relied on proving that the note was validly executed by Straisser. The trial concluded with a jury verdict in favor of Straisser. Cox then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the issues were not adequately addressed by the trial court during the proceedings.	The plaintiff, Amos H. Cox, asserted that J. W. Straisser agreed to sign a promissory note to secure the purchase of a horse he sold to Johnson and claimed that he delivered the horse based on this agreement. Cox requested compensation for the sale price of the horse, asserting that the defendant's endorsement on the promissory note was an integral component of the sale agreement.	J. W. Straisser's defense was based on two major points: he contended that he never executed the promissory note in question and provided sworn testimony to that effect. Additionally, the defense maintained that even if there was an agreement to sign the note, it required a written document to be binding, which was not present in this case. Therefore, Straisser argued that the plaintiff failed to prove his claims and requested the court to rule in his favor.

The case, titled "The People ex rel. Michael Evans v. Bernard Callaghan," took place in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision rendered in September 1876. Michael Evans was the relator who alleged that he was duly elected as the town collector of South Chicago during the annual election on April 4, 1876. Following this election, he received a plurality of votes, was certified as the winner, and swore an oath to assume the duties of the office. Subsequently, a board of appointment comprising town justices, the supervisor, and the town clerk questioned the legality of the election, suggesting possible fraud and determining that there had been a failure to elect town officers. Thus, they appointed Bernard Callaghan as the town collector. Evans contended that Callaghan's appointment was illegal and that he was unlawfully usurping the office. The relator sought permission from the court to file a legal action (in the nature of quo warranto) against Callaghan to challenge his claim to the office. The court initially denied this request, leading to the appeal.	Michael Evans, the plaintiff, claimed that he rightfully won the election for the town collector and was credentially certified for the position. He argued that despite assertions of election irregularities and fraud, there hasn't been an official contest of his election by any competent authority. Evans sought legal recourse to challenge Bernard Callaghan's appointment to the collector's position as unlawfully usurped and requested the court to allow him to file an information in the nature of quo warranto against Callaghan.	Bernard Callaghan, the defendant, maintained that he was legally appointed by the town board of appointment after they declared there was a failure to elect due to alleged election fraud. He argued that the board had the authority to fill the position based on their findings, and consequently, his appointment was valid. Callaghan resisted the motion to allow Evans to file the information, asserting that the petition did not adequately prove the essential facts of his possession of the office he was accused of usurping.

Charles H. Sutphen filed a lawsuit against William H. W. Cushman in April 1864, seeking to redeem property from an alleged mortgage executed between them on February 19, 1856. The transaction at issue involves a deed for several tracts of land in La Salle County, Illinois, which Sutphen contended was intended as security for his debts rather than a complete sale. At the time of the deed, Sutphen owed Cushman significant money based on a bond and promissory note with interest due. The court proceedings examined the nature of this transaction, with Sutphen asserting it was a mortgage and Cushman claiming it was a conditional sale. Historical debts, payments made, and collateral that changed hands were scrutinized during the case. Sutphen alleged substantial erroneous charges during the account settlement between them, which led to the legal dispute.	Sutphen’s primary claim was that the deed he executed to Cushman was not an outright sale but should be recognized as a mortgage, allowing him to redeem the property by paying a lesser sum than what was demanded. He argued the amount claimed by Cushman was inaccurate and sought a court determination facilitating his redemption of the property.	Cushman contended that the transaction was a valid conditional sale, not a mortgage, and insisted that Sutphen should adhere to the terms stated in the deed. He argued that the deed provided for an absolute estate recognizing dealings and statements made post-deed prohibited Sutphen from contesting its characterization or claiming redemption based on his alleged understanding.

In the fall of 1884, David H. Harts and Stephen A. Foley (the plaintiffs) contracted with Jacob Mangas to create 100 corn plows for the price of $15.50 each. Payments totaling $9 were to be paid in cash, with an additional $6.50 credited against an account Mangas owed Harts and Foley. The contract stipulated that payment would be made as the plows were completed. By spring of 1885, Mangas indicated that the plows were completed, and the plaintiffs visited to assess the work. They found 70 plows in a rented building known as the Primm Building and 30 additional plows on Mangas' lot, where they were noted to be unfinished. After settling accounts in February 1885, the plaintiffs believed the plows were their property. During this period, Mangas sold 18 plows with the plaintiffs' authority. When the defendant creditors levied executions on the property, the plaintiffs sought recovery through a writ of replevin. The Circuit Court found that there had not been a sufficient delivery to substantiate the plaintiffs' claim against Mangas' creditors, as the property remained under Mangas' control.	Harts and Foley claimed ownership of the corn plows, asserting that a contract of sale had been completed, entitling them to the property. They argued that the sequential payments and the subsequent settlement demonstrated their entitlement to the plows. The plaintiffs sought return of their property through a writ of replevin, insisting that sufficient delivery had been executed, which should ideally shield them from Mangas' creditors.	The defendants, James S. Jones and James A. Emmons, contended that Mangas retained control of the plows and had not effectively transferred possession. They argued that any sales by Mangas were valid as he was still in control of the property, negating the plaintiffs' claims. The defense maintained that without a clear transfer of possession, the plows remained liable for Mangas’ debts, which gave them the right to execute claims against the property.

In March 1885, Michael Keating entered into an agreement with William P. Nelson to undertake the painting and glazing of two buildings being constructed on Vernon Avenue in Chicago. The contract price for the work was set at $823. By April 23, 1886, approximately two-thirds of the work was completed, at which point Keating's brother sought a payment from the project's architect. The architect insisted on a formal written contract stipulating that future payments would be made in two installments, with the architect's certificates required for payment. Although Keating's brother signed this contract, it was acknowledged that Keating himself was neither aware of nor had consented to the terms before the dispute arose. The architect held the written agreement but lacked the authority to make binding decisions for Keating. Once the work was finished, the architect refused to provide a certificate for the remaining balance due, citing poor work quality as the reason. The case hinged on whether the terms of the written contract could be enforced against Keating, who had not explicitly agreed to them.	Michael Keating (the plaintiff) argued that the written agreement, signed by his brother with the architect, did not represent a valid contract between him and William P. Nelson (the defendant). He claimed he was entitled to payment for the services rendered despite the architect's refusal to issue a payment certificate, as he had not consented to the final decision dictated by the architect, nor had he agreed to the specific terms laid out in the written agreement.	William P. Nelson (the defendant) contended that the written contract, which made the architect's decision final regarding any disagreements, was binding. He argued that since the architect did not issue a certificate for payment due to alleged poor workmanship, Keating could not recover any payment. The defendant maintained that the requirements of the written agreement must be fulfilled before payment was warranted, and that Keating was bound by its terms.

John Warnock, the appellant, brought a legal action against William Russell, the appellee, in the Municipal Court of the City of Alton, Illinois, in October 1837. The case arose after Russell filed a precipe in a lawsuit against Warnock on the same day. Warnock's attorneys subsequently filed a bond for costs, stating, "The Same v. The Same," which was vague and did not adequately identify the parties involved. A motion to dismiss the case was filed by Warnock, asserting that the bond did not meet the required legal standards as he was a non-resident. Judge William Martin presided over the case and initially denied the motion to dismiss. The legal issue centered on the sufficiency of the bond filed as security for costs, which ultimately lacked clarity about the parties and case details.	The plaintiff, William Russell, contended that the bond for costs filed by John Warnock was valid and sufficient for the proceedings to continue. Russell argued that the Municipal Court should allow the case to proceed based on the bond that was submitted by Warnock's attorneys, despite any perceived deficiencies in the bond documentation.	John Warnock's defense was predicated on the argument that he was a non-resident and that the bond for costs was insufficient due to its vague title and failure to clearly indicate the parties involved in the legal action. He maintained that because of this deficiency, the Municipal Court should have dismissed the case when it was brought to their attention.

The case "Oramel S. Hough v. Cook County Land Company" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving the plaintiff, Oramel S. Hough, and the defendant, the Cook County Land Company. Hough conveyed certain lands to the Cook County Land Company in exchange for 365 shares of its stock and a loan equivalent to 80% of the stock's value, with the stock pledged as collateral. Following the transaction, Hough learned through legal counsel that the Cook County Land Company may have exceeded its corporate powers as defined by its charter, particularly concerning its ability to acquire real estate. Hough argued that the company's primary purpose, as stipulated in its charter, was limited to purchasing land for irrigation and improvements, and thus it lacked the authority to engage in the transaction that occurred. Hough filed a bill in equity seeking to set aside the conveyance and cancel the stock issued to him, claiming the underlying contract was void due to the company's overreach of its chartered powers.	Hough claimed that the Cook County Land Company illegally acquired the land and issued stock beyond its permitted corporate powers, which violated pertinent statutes. He sought to rescind the contract and reclaim the property he conveyed, arguing that the company's actions were unlawful because its charter only allowed for specific types of land transactions focused on irrigation and improvement.	The Cook County Land Company defended against Hough’s claims by asserting that the conveyance was valid and that it had adhered to its corporate charter concerning real estate transactions. The company argued that Hough, as the grantor, could not unilaterally rescind the contract merely based on allegations of misapplication of its charter powers. It suggested that any disputes regarding the nature of its corporate powers should be resolved by the state or in different legal proceedings, not by allowing a grantor to negate a valid conveyance.

John D. Wilson and his wife were involved in a legal dispute with William C. Kinney regarding the title to a tract of land. The case unfolded in November 1852, specifically revolving around a will left by the deceased William Kinney. The plaintiffs claimed that they were the rightful heirs to the land because they were named as legatees in Kinney's will. However, William Kinney's heir did not fully admit to this claim, stating that the complainants may or may not be the devisees. The case was submitted to the Illinois Supreme Court after being decided at May term of 1846 in the St. Clair Circuit Court. The Supreme Court found that the plaintiffs failed to provide sufficient proof supporting their claims regarding the will, which was critical for their request to obtain the land title. The court noted that since the will was not properly filed as evidence, the decree originally granted to the plaintiffs was unauthorized and required reversal.	The plaintiffs contended that they were the sole devisees of William Kinney and therefore entitled to the legal title of the land in question. They submitted a bill that included a reference to Kinney's will, asserting their right to the property based on this document. They sought legal recognition of their claim to the tract of land as outlined by the deceased's wishes in the will.	The defendant, William C. Kinney's heir, did not outright deny the plaintiffs' assertion but instead stated that their claim to be the devisees was uncertain. The defense highlighted the lack of proper evidence supporting the legitimacy of the will, arguing that the plaintiffs failed to provide a certified copy of the will at the hearing, which was essential to substantiate their claims. Consequently, they contended that the plaintiffs had not adequately proven their entitlement to the land.

Rebecca McGarvey v. Harvey Darnall et al. took place in Sangamon County, Illinois, with a legal decision filed on November 23, 1889. The case began with a petition on August 21, 1883, submitted by Harvey Darnall and Agnes Darnall against McGarvey and other heirs of Amelia Darnall, who died intestate on February 18, 1883, in Henry County, Iowa. The petition sought the partition of certain lands located in Sangamon County, which Amelia owned at her death. McGarvey responded with a cross-bill, asserting that letters of administration were granted for Amelia's estate in Iowa. McGarvey claimed a judgment against the estate for a sum of $82,545, which had been affirmed by the Iowa Supreme Court and remained unpaid. Evidence showed that Amelia Darnall had minimal personal property in both states, leading McGarvey to argue that if partitioning was not possible, proceeds from a potential sale of the land should first cover this judgment. However, the court ruled that evidence submitted by McGarvey regarding the judgment was incompetent. The court ultimately had to decide if jurisdiction was appropriate given the cross-bill's claims and the nature of submitting claims not presented within two years after administration was granted.	McGarvey claimed that she was a creditor of Amelia Darnall's estate, seeking to be paid from the proceeds of the land partitioned in Sangamon County. She maintained that a judgment against Amelia’s estate had been properly obtained in Iowa and should be honored in Illinois. McGarvey asserted that since the estate had no other significant personal property, the land's sale proceeds must be directed towards satisfying her judgment.	The Darnalls contended that McGarvey's evidence regarding the claim was inadmissible, as jurisdictional and procedural issues surrounding the claim's validity were significant. They argued that a judgment against the administrator in Iowa held no weight against the administrator of the same estate in Illinois. The Darnalls sought to have the court dismiss McGarvey's claims and proceed with the partition of the land as originally petitioned.

In the case of Amos Castner et al. v. James Walrod, the events stem from a land purchase made on October 27, 1849, when Amos Haskins (the father of the plaintiffs) bought a tract of land from Owen Hall for $140. Haskins provided promissory notes for the purchase, receiving a bond that promised conveyance upon payment. Haskins occupied the land and made some improvements. Tragically, Haskins lost the bond but it was later found by his son, Asa Haskins. On October 16, 1850, Asa assigned the bond to Walrod in exchange for a loan, an arrangement he testified enabled him to pay the first note. Following Haskins' death on November 4, 1850, Walrod acquired the deed from Hall on November 19, 1850, and took possession of the land, making extensive improvements and paying taxes. The plaintiffs, aware of Walrod's acquisition of the title, did not take any legal action to assert their claim until January 20, 1869, almost nineteen years later.	The plaintiffs claimed that the equitable title of the land belonged to them and sought a court order to compel the conveyance of the property from the defendant, alleging that Walrod acquired the title through improper means. They argued their lengthy delay in filing was justified given their circumstances and the complexities of the case.	The defendant, James Walrod, contended that the plaintiffs’ claim was barred due to laches because they waited nineteen years to assert their rights despite having full knowledge of the facts. Walrod also highlighted that he had obtained the deed legally and made substantial improvements to the property. He argued that the statutes of limitations should apply, and that the plaintiffs did not prove any fraud that would excuse such extensive delay.

James A. Collins, as the administrator of the estate of William H. Witham, deceased, filed a case against Greenleaf C. Robinson. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court following a November term in 1839 at the Morgan County Circuit Court. The dispute arose from a written promise made by Robinson on April 20, 1835, in Morgan County, where he agreed to deliver due bills on responsible endorsers amounting to $568.74 to Witham on January 1, 1836. This promise was made in exchange for certain goods sold to Robinson by Witham. However, the declaration did not indicate that Morgan County was the plaintiff's residence, leading to jurisdictional issues. A plea in abatement was filed by the defendant, which the court below overruled, resulting in the dismissal of the suit. The case ultimately hinged on whether jurisdiction was properly established given the provisions of the applicable state statute regarding suing defendants outside their county of residence.	The plaintiff, Collins, argued that the defendant, Robinson, failed to fulfill his written promise regarding the delivery of due bills as agreed in their contract. The plaintiff sought to enforce this contract, claiming that the necessary legal processes were initiated within the appropriate jurisdiction, despite the court's ruling to the contrary.	The defendant, Robinson, contended that the jurisdictional requirements were not met, as the declaration did not demonstrate that the Circuit Court of Morgan County had authority over him. He maintained that a subsequent agreement to make the contract payable at a specific location did not confer jurisdiction to initiate the lawsuit outside of the county where he resided. Hence, he filed a plea in abatement, asserting that the case should be dismissed due to these jurisdictional deficiencies.

Joseph Snell brought a case against The People of the State of Illinois in 1888, following an indictment related to disturbances of peace laws. The events occurred in Wayne County, Illinois, where Snell was accused of creating a nuisance that affected Lucy Mix's family and the neighborhood. The indictment contained two counts that broadly charged Snell with disturbing the peace through loud and boisterous language, threats to fight, active fighting, and other disorderly conduct. Snell’s legal team argued that some claims were too vague and that key elements lacked specificity, prompting a motion to quash the indictment. The primary legal focus was whether the language used in the indictment sufficiently charged Snell with offenses under the Criminal Code. The presiding judge, E. C. Kramer, overseen the initial proceedings in the County Court, which ultimately led to the appeal before the Illinois Appellate Court.	The plaintiff, Joseph Snell, argued that the indictment was improperly filed, particularly contending that the phrase “and by other disorderly conduct” was too vague and did not adequately specify charges against him. Snell's defense sought to have the indictment quashed, asserting that the legal language used failed to conform to the standards of clarity required for a criminal allegation.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by State's Attorney J. R. Creighton, maintained that the indictment effectively charged Snell with disturbances of peace by using statutory language. They contended that even if the phrase in question could be considered surplusage, the core charges of threatening and fighting were sufficiently clear to uphold the indictment. The defendant argued that challenging the indictment on these grounds was invalid since the essential components of the alleged crime were present.

In 1882, a deed for a piece of real estate was granted to Jane Kelly in Cook County, Illinois. In 1885, a two-story house was purchased and moved onto the lot, which was subsequently improved. In 1886, the property, including the building, was sold to the Chicago and Great Western Railway Company for $7000, with both Jane and her husband, Patrick Kelly, signing the conveyance. Following this, Patrick Kelly filed a suit in the Superior Court of Cook County against his wife and the attorney managing the sale, Ruel W. Bridge. He alleged that the property was bought with joint funds and asserted that he was entitled to at least half of the proceeds from the sale, arguing that the title should have been in both their names, with Jane acting merely as a trustee. A jury initially found in his favor, attributing $1500 of the total sale proceeds to him. However, this verdict was later vacated by the court, which settled instead on the claim that all but $35 of the purchase money for the land was paid by their adult daughter, Mary Kelly, with the minor daughter, Jennie, contributing the $35.	Patrick Kelly contended that he had equitably contributed to the purchase of the real estate, believing that he deserved a greater share of the proceeds from the sale. He sought to have the funds held in trust with the implication that he was entitled to a 50% stake, arguing for recognition of his equitable interest based on his contribution to the purchase money.	Jane Kelly and her attorneys maintained that the real estate was solely acquired by the financial contributions of their daughters, negating Patrick's claims. They argued that as the property title was in Jane's name, any claims to equity from Patrick were unfounded and that the original sale proceeds should not be subject to Patrick’s claims.

The case "The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company v. Wilson S. Watson et al." was decided in June 1877 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It involved the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company, located in Illinois, and several parties who had provided labor and materials to subcontractors working on the railroad construction. These parties sought to establish a lien on the railroad property under a statute designed to protect contractors, subcontractors, and laborers from non-payment. However, the central issue in the case was whether the statute allowed for liens in favor of those who had supplied materials to subcontractors, as opposed to directly contracting with the railroad company or its primary contractors. The court addressed the legislative intent of the lien statute and cited prior cases that clarified that the right to a lien did not extend beyond first-level subcontractors. Consequently, the court determined that the plaintiffs in this case were not entitled to claim a lien against the railroad property based on the statute in question.	The plaintiffs, comprising parties who provided labor and materials to subcontractors on the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad project, claimed that they were entitled to a lien on the railroad property under an Illinois statute protecting contractors and laborers. They argued that their contributions warranted a legal claim to the property to secure payment for their services and materials provided.	The defendant, the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company, contended that the plaintiffs had no valid claim to a lien against the railroad property because the statute did not extend to parties who supplied materials to subcontractors. The railroad argued that the law only recognized liens for direct contractors, which did not include the plaintiffs, as they had neither contracted with the railroad nor with the primary contractors directly.

The case "The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company v. The People ex rel. R. P. Hanna" took place in Illinois and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 18, 1888. The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company, a corporation chartered under Illinois law, operated a railroad from East St. Louis to the Wabash River, crossing into Indiana. The People, represented by R. P. Hanna as relator, filed an information in the nature of a quo warranto against the company, asserting that the majority of its directors were not residents of Illinois, contrary to state law. The relator argued that this situation caused the company to forfeit its franchise and privileges. The railway company admitted it was incorporated under Illinois law but contended that its majority non-resident directors were permissible due to provisions in earlier laws allowing such a structure after its consolidation with other companies in Indiana and Ohio. The circuit court initially sustained a demurrer regarding the first count of the information but overruled it for the second and third counts. The company was ultimately found guilty and fined $1,000, leading to an appeal.	The plaintiff, represented by R. P. Hanna, claimed that the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company had forfeited its rights to operate in Illinois because it violated the state law requiring a majority of its directors to be residents of Illinois. The plaintiff argued that the company, by having a majority of non-resident directors, was operating contrary to the laws of Illinois, thus justifying the quo warranto action.	The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company defended itself by asserting that it was properly incorporated under Illinois law and that the majority of its directors being non-residents was permissible under the laws that governed its formation and subsequent consolidation with rail companies from Indiana and Ohio. The company contended that the relevant constitutional provision did not apply to it, as it operated under the acts that allowed corporations formed in different states to consolidate, thereby possessing rights to elect directors from outside Illinois.

On May 13, 1869, James G. Blunt executed a trust deed on a property in Chicago to secure a loan of $5,500 from Mrs. Gurley, facilitated by agents Wright & Tyrrell. The loan required semi-annual interest payments of 10%. Following the initial interest payment in November, the second installment due in May 1870 was not paid. Consequently, the property was sold by the trustee, George Scoville, on June 29, 1870, to the Princeton Loan and Trust Company, which had purchased the underlying debt from Mrs. Gurley. Meanwhile, Blunt had sold the property to Parnell Munson, who assumed the mortgage with exceptions regarding the interest installment. Munson filed a lawsuit to nullify the sale, claiming there was an agreement to extend the interest payment deadline which was not proven in court. He alleged trustee misconduct and fraud associated with the sale. The case ultimately reached the Illinois Supreme Court.	Munson, the plaintiff, claims that the sale of the property should be set aside because there was an alleged prior agreement for an extension of the interest payment due on May 13, 1870, which was not honored. He argued that the trustee did not provide proper notice of sale and claimed misconduct and fraud in how the sale was conducted.	The defendant, Princeton Loan and Trust Company, contended that the trustee acted within the provisions of the trust deed that governed the sale and that no personal notice to the debtor was required beyond the public notice stipulated in the deed. They argued that there was no evidence of an actual agreement for an extension of the payment and that the trustee did not violate any duties regarding the sale proceedings. The company also maintained that the allegations of fraud were unfounded.

On February 19, 1879, John Hamlon and Fanny Sullivant entered into a lease agreement concerning the north half of section nineteen in township twenty-four, range nine, east of P. M. for agricultural use. The lease stipulated a rental of $400 per year, with $200 due on August 1st and another $200 due on December 15th. In addition, Hamlon was responsible for paying all taxes on the land during the lease term, running from March 1, 1879, to January 1, 1881. However, when Sullivant sought payment for the year 1880, Hamlon refused, leading Sullivant to file a complaint to reform the lease. She claimed there was a mutual mistake in writing the lease, as the $400 rental amount for 1880 was accidentally omitted. This entire matter unfolded in Illinois, and the case was ultimately heard by the Illinois Appellate Court.	Fanny Sullivant, the plaintiff, argued that the lease executed between her and John Hamlon omitted the agreed rental payment of $400 for the year 1880 due to a clerical error. She sought a court order to correct the lease to reflect the mutual understanding of the rental terms, asserting that the rental for the third year was mistakenly left out and that both parties initially intended for it to be included.	John Hamlon, the defendant, denied that he was obligated to pay any additional rents beyond what was stipulated in the existing lease. He contended that no mistake was made in the lease terms, arguing that the agreement clearly reflected their understanding, and there were no additional stipulations that would require modification. Hamlon maintained that the lease accurately represented their contractual agreement.

In 1871, in Kane County, Illinois, the case of Charles H. Force & Co. v. The Town of Batavia arose regarding bonds that were supposedly voted by the Town of Batavia to support the construction of the Ottawa, Oswego & Fox River Valley Railroad. The plaintiffs, Charles H. Force & Co., claimed that they were entitled to the bonds as they had earned them through the construction of the railroad. They sought an injunction to prevent the delivery of these bonds, alleging that the election for issuing the bonds was improperly called. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, issuing a perpetual injunction against the delivery of the bonds. The Town of Batavia appealed, asserting that the evidence was improperly admitted and that the court had erred in its findings, particularly in relation to the authority that called the election.	The plaintiff, Charles H. Force & Co., argued that the bonds in question were improperly voted on due to the election being called by an unauthorized person, contrary to the requirements set out in the Illinois statute regulating such elections. They claimed that the town clerk, and not the town supervisor, had the legal authority to call the election for the bond issuance. Consequently, the plaintiffs requested the court to uphold the circuit court's decision and maintain the injunction against the bonds.	The Town of Batavia contended that the election was valid and claimed that the actions taken were within their rights as local authorities, despite the manner of calling the election. They argued that the bonds were necessary for supporting the construction of the railroad, asserting that the plaintiffs’ claims overlooked the legitimacy of the voting process even though it was called by the supervisor. They requested the appellate court to overturn the circuit court's decree and allow for the bonds to be issued.

On February 14, 1870, a legal dispute arose in Knox County, Illinois, involving James Thompson and Briggs W. Sornberger. Sornberger filed a complaint for forcible entry and detainer, asserting that Thompson unlawfully entered and dispossessed him of a strip of land he had occupied for over twenty-five years. The legal proceedings initially took place before a justice of the peace but later transferred to multiple courts due to venue changes. Eventually, the case was heard by a jury in Warren County, which ruled in favor of the plaintiff, Sornberger. The defendant, Thompson, subsequently appealed the decision, aiming to overturn the jury's verdict and the judgment issued by the circuit court.	Sornberger claimed that Thompson forcibly entered the land, which Sornberger had peacefully possessed and had an estate of freehold in. He sought restitution of the premises and costs associated with the complaint, arguing that Thompson's entry was unlawful and against the statute governing forcible entry and detainer in Illinois.	Thompson's main defense was that he did not unlawfully enter any land that Sornberger was actually possessing at the time of the alleged entry. He contended that while Sornberger might claim title to the strip of land, he was not in actual possession of it, which is required to sustain a claim for forcible entry and detainer. Thompson also argued that the complaint was improperly framed, as Sornberger sought to claim more land than he could prove he possessed.

In the case of Alfred Dormueil et al. v. Henrietta Ward et al., the events transpired in Chicago, Illinois, with the business operations of Charles and Henrietta Ward under the firm name of Ward & Co. commencing on May 15, 1881, and concluding by November 22, 1882. The business was primarily conducted by Frederick Ward, who was the husband of Henrietta Ward. The plaintiffs, who are creditors of the Ward firm, claim they are owed $2,481.02 for goods sold to the firm, of which $617.26 was due at the time of the judgment, and the remainder would become due in 1883. Charles Ward's departure to Dakota left him considered irresponsible, with no property available for execution, except the partnership assets. The plaintiffs allege Charles sold his interest in the firm to Henrietta in January 1882 for $8,500, which was allegedly a fraudulent act designed to evade creditors. Ultimately, a judgment in favor of Charles was confessed by Henrietta, allowing for the execution against her business's stock, which the plaintiffs argue was made without consideration and therefore void. The plaintiffs contend that various fraudulent activities were conducted to prevent proper debt recovery.	The plaintiffs claim that Charles and Henrietta Ward engaged in fraudulent practices to hinder and delay their ability to collect just debts owed to them. They argue that a significant portion of the sold goods were purchased from them, and they insist that the funds obtained from the sale of goods should be directed to satisfy their claims. They request the court to recognize that these transactions were fraudulent and that they have a rightful claim to the proceeds.	The defense argues that the plaintiffs lack the legal basis to pursue a creditor's bill without first obtaining a judgment at law. They contend that the plaintiffs have not shown any equitable element in their claim, and as such, cannot invoke the jurisdiction of a court of equity. The defense emphasizes that past transactions were not fraudulent, asserting that legal remedies must be pursued before equity can be claimed.

The case of Lavinia Creel v. Nancy E. Kirkham involves a legal dispute concerning a crop of wheat that was growing on a tract of land devised by Benjamin Creel through his last will in April 1866. The case took place in Clinton County, Illinois, and reached the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1868. Following Benjamin Creel's death, the land was devised to Haney E. Kirkham, who became embroiled in a conflict with Lavinia Creel, Benjamin's widow. The crux of the matter centers around a contractual agreement Benjamin had with another individual named Hahn, which permitted Hahn to cultivate the wheat crop in exchange for sharing the produce. Benjamin’s executor appraised the harvested wheat and delivered it to Lavinia as part of Benjamin’s estate. The trial, which was conducted without a jury, ruled in favor of Haney E. Kirkham, leading Lavinia to appeal the decision. The plaintiff’s claim revolves around ownership of the wheat crop, arguing it should pass with the land. The key issue presented to the court was whether the wheat became an asset of the estate or transferred alongside the devised land.	The plaintiff, Haney E. Kirkham, argues that under the terms of Benjamin Creel's will, the portion of the wheat crop that belonged to Benjamin should pass to him as the land's devisee. He contends that despite an agreement with Hahn, the growing crop is tied to the land, and thus its ownership should accompany the transfer of land upon Benjamin's death. He seeks the value of the wheat that was delivered to Lavinia, claiming it rightfully belongs to him as part of the estate.	The defendant, Lavinia Creel, asserts that the wheat should be considered personal property belonging to the estate, and not part of the inheritance that passed to the plaintiff. She argues that since the wheat was appraised and delivered to her as the executor's decision, it should remain with her. Lavinia contends that the legal principles of tenancy and property rights applied in this case dictate that the crop does not automatically transfer with the land if there is no specific provision in the will for its transfer.

In April 1865, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Jacob Saylor et al. v. Seth F. Daniels, originating from an action of assumpsit brought at the January term of 1864 in the Superior Court of Chicago. The case revolved around a promissory note that Daniels sued Saylor on. Saylor defended against the claim by invoking usury, which he argued had tainted the underlying financial transaction. The events of the case involved a loan of $400 at an interest rate of 15 percent, with various payments made over time and new notes issued as part of a continuous transaction. Saylor contended that payments made should have been applied to counteract the usurious interest instead of solely reducing the principal. The court faced the question of whether these prior payments could offset the amount Daniels claimed was owed on the disputed note, leading to a deeper examination of usury law as it pertains to ongoing transactions and the treatment of assignments of such notes.	The plaintiff, Seth F. Daniels, argued that he was entitled to recover the amount of $277.32 on the promissory note executed by the defendant, Jacob Saylor. He contended that the payments made had been correctly applied and that the defendant was indebted to him. Daniels maintained that he acquired the note as collateral for a pre-existing debt owed to him by Barber, thereby asserting his rights as a holder for valuable consideration.	The defendant, Jacob Saylor, claimed that the note was tainted with usury due to excessive interest charges and sought to have the payments he made earlier account for the usurious interest. Saylor argued that the law allowed him to defend against the note by offsetting the usurious payments made during the same transaction. He contended that the fact that new notes had been issued did not alter the ongoing nature of the original transaction and sought dismissal of the plaintiff's claim based on these assertions.

In the case of Wesley Best v. Permelia Farris, et al., decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on May 21, 1886, the legal issue revolved around the interpretation of a will left by George W. Farris, who passed away in 1865. The will bequeathed all lands to his wife, Haney, for her natural life with a provision for the lands to be sold and the proceeds equally divided among his heirs upon her death. After Haney's death in 1882, a dispute arose over whether the heirs would inherit the estate per stirpes (by branch) or per capita (equally among all). Wesley Best, representing the interests of the grandchildren of a deceased daughter, appealed the lower court's decision, which ruled in favor of per stirpes distribution. The appellate court had to determine the proper method of estate distribution under the intent expressed by the words used in the will.	Wesley Best, as the appellant, contended that the phrase "equally divided among my heirs" in the will should be interpreted to mean that the estate must be divided per capita. Best argued that the intent of the testator was clear, and because the will did not specify proportions or limitations, it should follow the standard legal interpretation that uses “equal” to imply equal shares among all heirs.	The appellees, represented by Farris and Wall, argued that the distribution should be made per stirpes, referencing precedents where devises to a class of heirs typically result in per stirpes division. They asserted that the language in the will did not unequivocally indicate a per capita distribution and that the context as a whole could lead to supporting a per stirpes outcome, thus justifying the trial court's ruling.

The case "The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. v. Orson Morgan" took place in January 1874 and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The key parties involved were the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company (appellant) and Orson Morgan (appellee). The case arose from allegations made by Morgan against the railway company, claiming damages due to fires allegedly caused by sparks from the company’s locomotives. Specifically, the plaintiff asserted that sparks from the railway's coal-burning engine resulted in the destruction of wheat stacks situated approximately 40 to 50 rods away and damaged fences on his farm. Additionally, Morgan claimed that the construction of the railroad obstructed natural drainage on his land, causing it to flood. Throughout the proceedings, the validity of the claims became disputed—particularly concerning the distances involved and the feasibility of the engines igniting fires at such distances.	Orson Morgan, the plaintiff, claimed that the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company was responsible for three types of damages: the destruction of wheat stacks due to fire allegedly caused by sparks from the company’s locomotive, the destruction of a fence on his property, and damages caused by the obstruction of drainage due to the railroad's construction. Morgan requested compensation for these damages, arguing that the railway company’s actions were negligent.	The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company defended against Morgan’s claims by arguing that the evidence presented did not support any of the plaintiff's allegations. They contended that the distances involved made it impossible for sparks to ignite anything as far away as the stacks and the fences. Furthermore, the railway company maintained that Morgan did not own the land when the railroad was constructed and thus could not claim damages incurred by his predecessor's property ownership. They highlighted the lack of satisfactory evidence supporting Morgan's claims and requested the court to deny the plaintiff’s requests for damages.

The case "James H. Bowen et al. v. Mary Bond et al." was adjudicated in September 1875 by the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a land dispute in Cook County, Illinois. The principal parties involved were James H. Bowen and others (the appellants) and Mary Bond and others (the appellees). The controversy centered on the east half of the northeast quarter of Section 31 in Township 37, Range 15 East. Bowen and his co-plaintiffs sought to enjoin a suit in ejectment filed against them and to quiet title to the disputed land. The plaintiffs claimed they acquired the land through an administrator’s sale conducted in 1852 under an order of the circuit court of Ogle County, following the death of Ezra Bond, whose heirs were the defendants in this case. The appellants contended that the order for sale was valid despite missing files and papers, arguing that the recitals in the order were sufficient to establish jurisdiction. The defendants, heirs of Ezra Bond, challenged the validity of the original sale order and raised objections regarding jurisdiction and compliance with statutory requirements.	The plaintiffs, Bowen et al., asserted that they rightfully owned the property through valid mesne conveyances stemming from an administrator’s sale ordered by the circuit court of Ogle County. They claimed this sale, executed on July 20, 1852, was valid and sought to quiet title against claims made by Ezra Bond's heirs. The plaintiffs argued that the court had sufficient jurisdiction and that all legal requirements were met during the sale process, asserting that the objections raised by the defendants did not negate their title.	The defendants, Mary Bond et al., contended that the sale conducted by the administrators was void due to a lack of jurisdiction over the heirs and the subject matter. They argued that the records necessary to establish jurisdiction had been lost, and hence the recitals in the order of sale could not provide sufficient proof. Additionally, they claimed that the authority to sell the property had lapsed as all debts had been paid before the sale took place, thus extinguishing the need for the sale.

Mary Finch appealed a decision made by William T. Brown, the Clerk of the County Commissioners’ Court of Madison County, in a case involving property redemption. The events of the case trace back to June 1844, when two tracts of land were sold due to unpaid taxes from the year 1842. At the time of the sale, these lands were owned by Joel Finch. He passed away on February 19, 1846, without redeeming the lands. Following his death, on October 26, 1846, Mary Finch, as his widow, sought to redeem the lands by submitting an application to the clerk along with the necessary payment. However, her application was denied. Consequently, she petitioned the Circuit Court for a mandamus to compel the clerk to accept her redemption. The Circuit Court sustained a demurrer against her petition, leading to her appeal. The legal context involves the provisions of the "Act concerning the Public Revenue," which specifies the rights of property owners or their representatives to redeem their properties post-sale under certain circumstances. The case raises important legal questions about redemption rights for widows and the definition of "femes covert" under Illinois law.	Mary Finch's main argument is that as the widow of Joel Finch, she should have the right to redeem the property despite the expiration of the two-year period typically allowed for tax sale redemption. She contends that the applicable law allows redemption for women who held title as “femes covert” at the time of sale, asserting her right to reclaim the land as Joel Finch's widow.	The defendant, William T. Brown, maintains that Mary Finch is not entitled to redeem the lands because the statutory period for redemption under the 38th section of the "Act concerning the Public Revenue" has already expired. He argues that the 39th section, which addresses redemption rights for "femes covert," only applies to married women who owned the land in their own right at the time of sale, and Mary Finch does not meet this criteria since her interest was merely contingent upon her husband’s ownership and her not actively holding the title at that time.

In March 1865 in Mason County, Illinois, John B. Wright obtained a judgment against O. G. Millison for the sum of $152.50. Wright attempted to collect this debt via garnishee summons against Eli O. Fisk, the township treasurer, and the school directors of District No. 4, where Millison was employed as a teacher. When the garnishee process was served, Fisk reported that he held funds amounting to $104.59 that were to be used for scheduled payments to Millison for his teaching duties. During the proceedings, it was established that the funds were not yet appropriated for Millison’s payment, as they remained under the treasurer's control until the school trustees made their apportionment. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendants, discharging them from liability under the garnishee process due to the nature of the funds being in the custody of the law.	The plaintiff, John B. Wright, contended that Eli O. Fisk, as township treasurer, should be subject to garnishee process for the money owed to Millison for his teaching services. Wright argued that since there were funds available, Fisk should fulfill the debt obligation to Millison, asserting that the garnishee process could effectively seize these funds to satisfy the judgment against Millison.	Eli O. Fisk and the other defendants argued that the funds in question were in the hands of a public officer and thus in the custody of the law, making them exempt from garnishee process. They asserted that without a prior appropriation of the funds for Millison’s payments, there was no debt owed to him at the time the garnishee process was served. Fisk emphasized that the funds were held in a common pool for distribution according to the school trustees' direction, affirming that neither he nor the school directors had any personal liability regarding Millison’s wages until such an order was made.

The case "Mary L. Burt et al. v. The Batavia Paper Manufacturing Company" took place in September 1877 in Illinois. The case arose after the Chicago Fiber and Paper Company, organized in Kane County, went bankrupt in January 1870 after issuing bonds totaling $75,000. The bonds were secured by a deed of trust executed to George B. Moss, the company's president. The plaintiffs, Mary L. Burt and others, purchased three of these bonds. They sold two but retained one to enforce payment through this legal action. The original trust deed was canceled, and a new trust deed was executed, but the promised exchange for the bond held by the plaintiffs was never made. In July 1870, an assignee sold the company's assets to the defendant for $90,000, who claimed to be a bona fide purchaser without notice of the existing bond. The plaintiffs' attempts to collect on the bond were complicated by actions of their agent, who failed to present their claim during the bankruptcy proceedings. The lower court dismissed the case for lack of equity, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant should be held liable for the payment of the bond they held since it was secured against the property sold during the bankruptcy. They argued that the defendant had constructive knowledge of the bond's existence because some of its incorporators were previously involved with the Chicago Fiber and Paper Company. They sought to reverse the lower court's dismissal of their claim and enforce payment for the bond based on its legal standing.	The defendant maintained that they were a bona fide purchaser of the property and that the sale was conducted free from any encumbrances, including the plaintiffs' bond. They contended that the plaintiffs had failed to prove the existence of the bond's liability at the time of their purchase and argued that they had no actual or constructive notice of any incumbrance due to the trust deed release. The defendant requested that the court affirm the dismissal of the plaintiffs’ claims based on the absence of notice and the validity of their purchase.

In June 1874, the case of Grand Tower Manufacturing and Transportation Company v. John S. Hawkins took place in Illinois, focusing on an incident that occurred at a wharf boat owned by the appellant company. The incident took place on the night of July 17, 1870, when John S. Hawkins (the appellee) arrived at Grand Tower aboard the steamer "Rubicon." Due to coal barges blocking the wharf, he could not retrieve his carpet-sack, which he had previously entrusted to a porter. He employed a clerk from the wharf boat to assist him. Later that evening, as Hawkins sought his property, he attempted to access the wharf boat, which was closed for the night as per usual practice. The wharf boat only opened for business when the steamboat arrived. In the dark, Hawkins fell into a circular hole on the after-guard of the wharf boat, measuring approximately two feet in diameter, resulting in a serious back injury. The wharf boat had no obligation to maintain an open access path after hours nor to keep all areas safe. Hawkins failed to notify anyone about his intentions before approaching the boat and chose a route not designated for passenger use.	The plaintiff, John S. Hawkins, claimed damages for the injuries sustained from falling into the hole on the wharf boat, arguing that the Grand Tower Manufacturing and Transportation Company was negligent in maintaining safety and providing a safe passageway for the public. He sought legal recourse for his injuries, asserting that the company should be held liable for the unsafe conditions that led to his fall.	The defendant, Grand Tower Manufacturing and Transportation Company, contended that there was no negligence on their part, as they were not a common carrier of passengers and had no obligation to keep the wharf boat accessible at all times. They argued that Hawkins was himself guilty of a high degree of negligence, as he chose to navigate an unsafe route in the dark and did not attempt to communicate his intentions to the company's staff. The defendant requested the court to reverse the judgment in favor of Hawkins, asserting that the injuries were a result of Hawkins's own imprudence rather than any fault of the company.

John C. Brockenbrough filed a legal case against Parker Dresser and additional defendants in 1873, in Champaign County, Illinois. The case was presided over by Judge A. J. Gallagher in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute revolved around the title to a piece of land, with Brockenbrough seeking to assert his claim against the defendants. The central issue in the case was the admissibility of certain documentary evidence, specifically copies of judgments and executions related to the land in question. The court noted that the evidence necessary to support Brockenbrough's claims was not properly included in the record, as it lacked necessary certification and did not meet evidentiary requirements.	Brockenbrough argued that the documentary evidence, including copies of judgments and executions related to the land, was critical to his case and should be considered by the court. He sought to prove his claim to the land and to take action against the defendants who allegedly held conflicting claims to the title.	The defendants, represented by attorneys Jokes & Gardher, contended that the evidence presented by the plaintiff was improperly included in the record and could not be considered by the court. They argued that the absence of required certification and factual statements from the decree rendered the plaintiff's case invalid.

William Winkelman, an attorney, faced suspension from practice by the St. Clair Circuit Court during its March 1868 term. The presiding judge ruled against him based on allegations that after a bill in chancery was filed for an injunction, Winkelman had unlawfully interlined and altered the injunction to extend its reach to additional parties without authorization. In his response to the court's rule, Winkelman did not deny making the changes but asserted that he had no fraudulent intent or aim to harm anyone. Following the hearing, the court made the suspension ruling absolute, extending it across the judicial circuit that included St. Clair and two other counties. Winkelman appealed this order, raising questions about the legitimacy of the appeal itself and the circuit court's authority to suspend an attorney.	Winkelman contended that the circuit court exceeded its authority by suspending him from practice across multiple courts. He argued that only the Supreme Court holds the power to strike an attorney from the roll or impose a permanent suspension. Winkelman claimed the circuit court's actions were inappropriate and not warranted by law, asserting that any disciplinary action should rightfully originate in the Supreme Court.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by the Attorney General, maintained that the circuit court acted within its authority due to Winkelman's alleged grave misconduct, which included altering legal documents without permission, constituting contempt. They argued for upholding the suspension based on these serious allegations and that disciplinary measures were necessary to maintain the integrity of the legal profession.

Willard Graves filed a legal case against Herman Bruen and others in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1849. The case originated from an action of ejectment brought before the Adams Circuit Court, concerning the northeast quarter of section number thirteen in township one south of the base line, in range seven west of the fourth principal meridian. Graves (acting on behalf of the plaintiffs) sought to reclaim possession of the land, asserting rights derived from a deed issued by the Auditor of State, which reflected a sale for unpaid taxes dated January 10, 1833. The plaintiffs argued that the Auditor’s deed was prima facie evidence of their title. The defendants, in response, admitted possession but contested the validity of the plaintiffs' title by pointing out procedural deficiencies in the tax sale process, primarily that the necessary listing of the land for taxation was not properly established. This led to a trial without a jury presided over by Judge Minshall, who initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs. Following a denied motion for a new trial by the defendant, the case advanced to the Illinois Supreme Court on appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed to have legal title to the property based on an Auditor's deed, which they claimed demonstrated the regularity and legality of the tax sale. They requested the court to recognize their claim and award them possession of the land in question.	The defendant contended that the Auditor’s deed was invalid because it was not supported by a legal listing of the land for taxation, a requirement under Illinois law. They argued that without evidence of such listing, the tax sale was unauthorized and void, thereby challenging the legitimacy of the plaintiffs' claim to title.

In November 1853, the case of Thomas P. Ayers v. William M. Grider took place in Marion, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Thomas P. Ayers, the plaintiff, and William M. Grider, the defendant, who served as the town constable. The conflict arose when Grider arrested Ayers for allegedly breaching municipal ordinances, during which he confiscated Ayers' knife. Shortly after, Ayers accused Grider of stealing his knife, money, and purse, framing these accusations in a slanderous context. Grider defended himself by stating that he returned the knife to a third party, Pulley, and that the accusation of theft was understood by witnesses to refer to the context of the arrest, not as a criminal act. The trial featured a dispute over a jury instruction that would clarify the legal ramifications of the words spoken by Grider about the alleged theft. The refusal of this instruction became a focal point for the court’s eventual decision.	Ayers claimed that Grider had stolen his knife, money, and purse, articulating that the words used by Grider in response to his accusations implied criminal conduct. He argued that this constituted slander, leading to reputational damage, and requested the court to find Grider guilty of such defamation. Ayers sought remedy for the alleged wrongful accusation as well as an instruction for the jury that would support his claims of malice and actionable words.	Grider's defense centered on the assertion that the words he used were not actionable since they referred to a known act (the arrest) that did not constitute a felony in the eyes of the law. His main argument was that the accusations made by Ayers were understood by all witnesses as pertaining to a lawful arrest rather than any criminal theft on his part. Grider requested the court to dismiss Ayers’ claims on the grounds that the comments made were not slanderous, as they were rooted in the lawful actions taken during the arrest.

In January 1859, the case of "James Thompson and John L. Thompson, Appellants, v. Thomas Lee, Appellee" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from an action of assumpsit initiated by Thomas Lee against James Thompson and John L. Thompson in the Cass Circuit Court. The legal dispute revolved around a promissory note dated December 15, 1856, in which the defendants promised to pay Lee the sum of $2,025, with interest, on April 1, 1858. The note was signed by both appellants, but the signature of James Thompson included a character resembling a letter "B" or "R" between his first and last names. This signing raised questions during the trial regarding the authenticity and admissibility of the note. The court allowed the note to be admitted into evidence, resulting in a judgment for the plaintiff, Thomas Lee. The defendants sought a new trial, which was denied, leading to their appeal based on alleged errors in trial procedures related to evidence presentation and the handling of the note.	The plaintiff, Thomas Lee, contended that the defendants were liable for the amount stated in the promissory note they jointly signed. He argued that despite the middle character in the signature of James Thompson potentially causing confusion, it should not impede the recognition of the note's validity. Lee sought to enforce the payment of the $2,025 as agreed upon within the stipulated timeframe, asserting the legitimacy of the note and the defendants' obligations under it.	The defendants, James Thompson and John L. Thompson, defended against the claim by arguing that the note's presentation did not meet the necessary legal standards for admissibility. They claimed there was a variance between the note and the declaration filed, specifically regarding the representation of their names and signatures. They contended that the court erred in allowing the note into evidence and subsequently failed to grant their motion for a new trial. The defendants requested that the judgment be reversed in their favor, asserting that the inconsistencies invalidated the plaintiff's claims.

In 1876, W. F. Coolbaugh, J. W. Odell, and C. T. Wheeler filed a legal complaint in Cook County, Illinois, against Louis C. Huck and others regarding a tax assessment on shares of stock in the Union National Bank, located in South Chicago. The town assessor had initially valued the bank's shares at $34 each. At the county board's meeting in July 1876, without lawful authority, the board increased this valuation to $40.80 per share, a change that was deemed illegal by the plaintiffs. They argued that the assessment process was improperly executed since the county board had no jurisdiction to alter valuations established before the fourth Monday of June when the assessment review process was completed. The plaintiffs sought to enjoin the collection of taxes based on the increased valuation. The ongoing legal process included appeals to the Illinois Supreme Court, which was asked to determine the validity of the increased assessment and the county board's authority.	The plaintiffs claimed that the county board unlawfully raised the already assessed valuation of their bank shares after the established review period, violating the relevant statutory procedures. They argued for the injunction on the collection of taxes based on the unjust increased valuation. They contended that the increase of $6.80 per share was not supported by a valid complaint, notice, or lawful authority, rendering the tax assessment excessive and illegal.	The defendants asserted that the county board had the authority to raise the valuation based on complaints made regarding the assessments. They presented evidence claiming proper notifications were given prior to the meeting that resulted in the valuation increase, contending that the board acted within its lawful jurisdiction to protect the interests of taxpayers who deemed the original assessment too low.

The case "The Chicago West Division Railway Company v. Sereno W. Ingraham" occurred in Chicago in 1890. The dispute arose from an incident where Sereno W. Ingraham was riding in a buggy drawn by a single horse along west Twelfth Street. During the ride, the buggy was struck by a railway car operated by the Chicago West Division Railway Company. Ingraham claimed to have been exercising due care when the accident occurred, as the railway company's employees negligently operated the train, leading to the collision. As a result of the accident, Ingraham sustained severe personal injuries, and his horse and buggy were damaged. He filed a lawsuit seeking damages for these injuries and property losses. The trial resulted in a jury verdict of $1,000 in favor of Ingraham, which was later affirmed by the Appellate Court, prompting the railway company to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Sereno W. Ingraham, the plaintiff, claimed damages due to injuries sustained from a collision caused by the negligence of the railway company's employees. He argued that the accident occurred while he was acting with due care and that the company was liable for both personal injuries and property damage to his buggy and horse. Ingraham sought compensation for his medical expenses, lost wages, and the damages sustained to his property.	The Chicago West Division Railway Company, as the defendant, contended that the trial court erred in its instructions to the jury and the admission of certain evidence. They argued that the damages for personal injury and property damage should not be recovered under a single count as they were separate injuries. The defendant claimed that Ingraham was partially negligent, which contributed to the accident. They requested that the jury be instructed accordingly, emphasizing their rights to use the track and suggesting that Ingraham had failed to yield appropriately.

The case "Andrew M. Wiley et ux. v. Clementius Ewalt et al." was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. It arose from a deed of trust executed by John Ewalt in January 1861, shortly before his second marriage. This deed established a trust for his four daughters — Mary, Susan, Lucy, and Harriet — and outlined their inheritance of his property, along with provisions for his widow and a payment to his daughter Martha. The deed was contested by the heirs on the grounds that Ewalt lacked the mental capacity to execute it due to his advanced age and susceptibility to influence. The plaintiffs claimed that Wiley and others took advantage of Ewalt’s condition to benefit themselves at the expense of other heirs and the widow. Angered by the perceived injustice, they sought to annul the deed and partition the land among all heirs. The court's proceedings included extensive testimonies reflecting on Ewalt's character, mental faculties, and intentions, concluding that while his memory had diminished, his overall judgment remained intact.	The plaintiffs, led by Andrew M. Wiley, claimed that John Ewalt was mentally incompetent when he executed the deed due to age-related decline and undue influence from his sons-in-law. They argued that the deed unfairly favored his daughters while depriving the other heirs, particularly Ewalt's widow, of their rightful inheritance. The plaintiffs sought to set aside the deed and partition the estate equitably among all heirs.	The defendants contended that John Ewalt executed the deed voluntarily and with full understanding of its implications. They argued that he was mentally competent at the time, possessing sound practical judgment despite minor memory lapses. They pointed out that no undue influence was exerted, emphasizing that Ewalt independently decided the trust's beneficiaries based on long-held intentions. Consequently, they requested dismissal of the plaintiffs' claims and affirmation of the deed's legality.

In 1883, Wilson Morrow relocated to Mt. Carmel, Illinois, and established a partnership with Geo. W. Hicks. Morrow transferred the ownership of his business, which saw its inventory increase drastically, yet he had incurred debts amounting to $5,700. After a disagreement, Morrow dissolved the partnership and made a purported sale of his inventory to his kinsman, Francis M. Cowling, on January 2, 1884. This sale occurred when Morrow's creditors were pressing for payment. The goods were sold without cash payment and under suspicious circumstances, raising concerns of fraudulent intent towards Morrow's creditors. Subsequently, Cowling was accused of participating in this fraudulent scheme to hinder and delay Morrow's creditors. The Circuit Court of Wabash County found in favor of Cowling initially, but the case was appealed based on claims of fraudulent conveyance and the implications of Cowling's role in the sale. The court ultimately focused on whether the transaction was executed with fraudulent intent, leading to a detailed examination of the circumstances surrounding the sale.",	The plaintiff, Benjamin F. Estes, contended that the sale of goods to Cowling was fraudulent and intended to defraud Morrow's creditors. Estes argued that Cowling had participated in this fraud, knowing that Morrow was heavily indebted and seeking to evade his obligations. Estes's legal request centered around setting aside the sale transaction, asserting that Cowling's actions contributed to hindering his ability to collect debts owed by Morrow.",	Cowling, the defendant, responded with several defenses, including claims of having a license to acquire the goods, and that he was unaware of any fraudulent purpose behind Morrow's sale. Cowling argued that he acted in good faith and as an innocent purchaser, claiming that no particular reason indicated that Morrow sought to defraud his creditors at the time of the sale. Additionally, the defense emphasized the legitimacy of the transaction under the circumstances of Morrow's financial status and his right to sell the goods.",

William Long passed away intestate on July 4, 1877, in Illinois, leaving behind several heirs, including his children and grandchildren. His grandson William P. Long, one of the heirs, claimed that he had not received any advancements from his grandfather. William R. Long, the appointed administrator of the estate, filed reports in the county court stating that certain heirs had received advancements during the deceased’s lifetime.
