Johnson, the defendant, contended that her husband, William, could not maintain a lawsuit against her for the recovery of personal property due to the legal principle that a husband and wife are considered one person in law. She argued that the evidence provided by William was insufficient to prove that the horse was her separate property under the Married Woman’s Act of 1861.

In April 1866, the case titled "Anonymous" was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The court proceedings focused on the procedural aspects of rehearing motions. The specifics of the dispute are not outlined in the provided information, but it indicates a legal issue relevant to the process of appealing court decisions. The case emphasizes that an oral motion for a rehearing is not necessary, as the mere filing of a petition and proper docketing after due notice are adequate to bring a matter to the court's attention. These procedural clarifications aimed to streamline legal processes and assure parties involved that their cases could be heard without requiring unnecessary additional motions, reflecting an evolving understanding of judicial processes during that era.	The plaintiff's specific claims are not detailed in the case description. However, it can be inferred that the plaintiff sought a rehearing of a previous decision or ruling and presented a petition to the court in accordance with procedural guidelines. The aim was likely to challenge a prior ruling or order and seek a reconsideration by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The defendant's defenses are not explicitly stated in the case documentation. Nevertheless, it seems that the defendant's position could revolve around contesting the need for an oral motion for rehearing or arguing the sufficiency of the procedural steps taken by the plaintiff. Any specifics regarding the defendant's arguments or requests are not available in the provided summary.

In 1876, in White County, Illinois, the case of Louis Kahn et al. v. Emma B. Wood arose when Emma B. Wood sued for damages after her personal property was seized and sold under a writ of attachment issued by a justice of the peace. The attachment was part of a legal proceeding where Kahn and others were plaintiffs and Emma's husband, Marcus B. Wood, was the defendant. Emma claimed that the property was her sole and separate property, protected from seizure for her husband’s debts. In the jury's verdict, Emma was awarded $198.40, of which she remitted $27, leading to a final judgment of $171.40 in her favor. However, the court scrutinized the evidence Emma provided to prove that the property was indeed hers, emphasizing that the plaintiff needed to satisfactorily demonstrate the ownership of the property as required by law, particularly regarding the separate property rights of married women.	Emma B. Wood's main argument was that the personal property seized and sold was her separate property, thus exempt from her husband's creditors under Illinois law. She contended that the items had been given to her by her father upon her marriage and were also purchased with funds from her father's estate. Her legal request was for compensation for the wrongful seizure and sale of her property, which she argued was unlawfully taken due to her husband's debts.	The defendants, led by Louis Kahn, argued that the burden of proof lay with Emma to clearly establish that the seized property was her separate property, as stipulated by the law concerning married women. They contended that Emma failed to provide sufficient evidence regarding her ownership, particularly the timeline of her marriage and when she received the money from her father. They further asserted that since Emma had consented to her husband controlling the money from her father's estate, it became his property, thus negating her claim to the seized items.

The case 'Benjamin T. O. Hubbard v. Thomas Rankin, Sr.' took place in September 1873 in Illinois. It was an appeal from the Circuit Court of Warren County, presided over by Judge Arthur A. Smith. The key individuals involved were Benjamin T. O. Hubbard, the plaintiff, and Thomas Rankin, Sr., the defendant. Hubbard was suing Rankin based on a promissory note that had been assigned to him. Rankin claimed that the execution of the note was obtained through fraud and circumvention; he believed he was simply appointing an agent to sell a patented grain separator rather than signing a promissory note. The jury found in favor of Rankin, and the judgment for costs was determined against Hubbard, leading him to appeal the decision.	Hubbard's main argument was that the promissory note he received from Rankin was valid and enforceable, regardless of the circumstances surrounding its execution. He sought to have the court overturn the Circuit Court's judgment in favor of Rankin and to enforce the note, which he contended was properly assigned to him.	Rankin's defense rested on the claim that the note was void due to its execution being procured through fraudulent means. He asserted that he had no intention of signing a note when he allegedly appointed an agent for the sale of the patent. Furthermore, he argued that it did not matter whether Hubbard, as a bona fide holder, had notice of the alleged fraud or offered to restore any consideration received under their supposed agreement.

The case titled "The People ex relatione Joseph A. Philmot v. Anthony C. Hessing" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1862. The case originated in Cook County, Illinois, where Joseph A. Philmot (the relator) petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that he was unlawfully detained by Anthony C. Hessing, the sheriff of Cook County, under accusations of burglary. Philmot argued that although he was committed on a burglary charge, a grand jury had been convened and, after examining evidence, decided not to indict him. He asserted that since the grand jury did not find any evidence against him, he was entitled to be released from custody. Hessing, acting on a mittimus issued by a justice of the peace, returned the writ indicating Philmot's detention was lawful. The Circuit Court upheld the detention, prompting Philmot to appeal the decision.	Joseph A. Philmot, as the plaintiff, contended that his continued confinement was illegal due to the lack of an indictment from the grand jury. He argued that all evidence had been presented, and the grand jury had opted not to charge him. Therefore, he requested the court to issue a writ of habeas corpus to secure his release from the unlawful detention.	Anthony C. Hessing, the defendant, maintained that Philmot's detention was legitimate based on the existing mittimus issued by a justice of the peace. Hessing argued that the law does not automatically require a discharge simply because a grand jury did not return an indictment unless it is proven that they had considered evidence against Philmot. He contended that the presumption should favor the Circuit Court's ruling, which upheld the validity of the mittimus.

Thomas Newlan brought a legal action against Lombard University in September 1871 after the university was created from the Illinois Liberal Institute, the original entity that had a promissory note executed by Newlan for a scholarship. The transition of names was sanctioned by an act of the Illinois legislature, which enabled Lombard University to assume all rights and obligations of the Illinois Liberal Institute, including the ability to sue for outstanding debts. The appeal arose from a dispute over the notes associated with this scholarship and the claim that the matter had been submitted to arbitration, thus allegedly merging the promissory note into the award given by arbitrators. The case involved testimony from both Newlan and O. P. West, the financial agent of the university. Ultimately, the jury sided with West's account over Newlan's, leading to a decision reflecting their finding. The court determined that there were no grounds to question this jury decision or the record, leading to an affirmation of the judgment without error.	The plaintiff, Thomas Newlan, claimed that the promissory note was merged into an award from arbitrators, which should nullify the obligation to pay. He argued that any claims against him should be dismissed due to the arbitration process and requested a reversal of the judgment against him due to this alleged waiver of rights.	Lombard University's defense centered on the validity of the promissory note despite Newlan's claims regarding the arbitration. They emphasized the importance of the new arrangement testified by West, asserting that any purported arbitration was either nonexistent or waived through subsequent agreements. The university maintained its right to collect the debt, arguing that it had the legal standing to pursue the claim after the name change.

In the case of Thomas Althrop v. Charles H. Beckwith, which took place in 1884 in Illinois, the plaintiff, Beckwith, sought damages of $2,000 from the defendant, Althrop, based on an alleged verbal contract concerning the sale of business assets. The background involves a partnership that Beckwith was a part of, which was dissolving. An arbitrator awarded Beckwith the right to pay off the company's debts and take the assets. Subsequently, Beckwith and Althrop entered into a verbal agreement on November 1, 1881, where Althrop would purchase Beckwith's interest in the business for $2,500. Beckwith claimed Althrop failed to pay $2,000 owed as part of this agreement. During the trial, Beckwith provided evidence from a previous litigation, where a verdict had favored him for non-payment related to a separate claim against Althrop. Althrop contested the existence of the contract, and the court had to examine whether the earlier judgment could serve as an estoppel regarding the current case.	Beckwith claimed that there was a verbal contract in which Althrop agreed to purchase his business assets for $2,500, with an upfront payment and subsequent installments. He argued that Althrop's failure to pay the agreed amount constituted a breach of contract. To support his claims, Beckwith introduced evidence from a previous lawsuit where he had won a verdict against Althrop, alleging that the earlier court ruling established the existence and nature of their contract.	Althrop disputed the existence of any such verbal contract, arguing that no binding agreement had been made. He maintained that his discussions with Beckwith had not resulted in a contract but were merely proposals. Althrop also contended that the prior judgment and verdict could not be used to estop him from contesting the current claims, as it did not conclusively determine the validity of the alleged contract in this case.

In 1865, in Chicago, Illinois, Joseph McPherson entered into a contract with Rufus C. Hall to sell 5,000 bushels of oats at a price of 614 cents per bushel. The agreement stipulated that the oats were to be delivered during March 1865. However, Hall failed to demand the delivery of the oats within that timeframe. On March 31, McPherson attempted to tender warehouse receipts for the oats at Hall's office but found that Hall's agent, Stiles, was absent. McPherson's lawsuit sought damages due to this failure to take delivery of the purchased oats. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case, particularly focusing on the definition of a sufficient legal tender in this context, as the lower court's instruction did not comply with established legal precedents regarding tendering and the legitimacy of warehouse receipts.	McPherson claimed that Hall's failure to take delivery of the oats as per their agreement constituted a breach of contract. He argued that he had made a legal tender by being present with the warehouse receipts for the oats and was therefore entitled to damages due to Hall's inaction.	Hall contended that McPherson’s tender was insufficient because it lacked proof that the warehouse receipts were genuine and that the oats were free from any charges. He argued that without the defendant being present to accept the tender, no legal tender had effectively occurred. Moreover, Hall maintained that no actual harm was proven to have resulted from the alleged deficiency of the tender instructions.

The case, "The Board of Trustees of the Illinois and Michigan Canal v. Daniel Lynch," was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1849. The central figures were Daniel Lynch, a contractor who had performed work on the Illinois and Michigan Canal, and the Board of Trustees overseeing the canal's construction. Lynch entered into a contract with the Board that stipulated the chief engineer would evaluate the work and determine payments. After some time, the contracts were mutually abandoned, and Lynch was paid based on the chief engineer's estimates, which included a retained percentage. Lynch, however, claimed that there were errors in the estimates and that there was an understanding that the work would be re-measured to account for any discrepancies before final payment. The court proceedings revealed conflicting testimonies regarding the absence of any agreement to revisit the estimates after the contract was relinquished, which led to Lynch's lawsuit for the additional compensation he believed he was owed.	Lynch claimed that he was owed additional payment for work done on the canal, arguing there were mistakes in the chief engineer’s estimates. He asserted that there was a mutual understanding that, upon the contracts' abandonment, the work would be re-measured and payment would be made for any excess work that was identified. Lynch sought recovery based on these claims.	The Board of Trustees contended that Lynch had already been paid in full based on the estimates provided by the chief engineer and that there was no agreement to re-measure the work. They argued that both Lynch and the chief engineer confirmed that the payments made were final. The Board's position was that Lynch had not demonstrated any agreement for re-measurement at the time of settlement, thereby invalidating his claims for additional payment.

Isaac Gilham and others filed an appeal against Caldwell Cairns in June 1826. The case originated from the Monroe circuit court, which acted as a chancery court. The issue at hand involved a bill against the heirs of Gilham concerning a specific performance of a contract made by their ancestor with Jacob A. Boyce for the conveyance of land in Monroe County, Illinois. The plaintiffs contended that the court had not included Boyce, whose interests were directly impacted by the contract, as a party in the suit. The court's decision to dispense with Boyce was contested, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court to review whether the proper parties had been accounted for in the decree.	The plaintiffs argued that the circuit court had erred in not including Jacob A. Boyce as a party to the suit. They contended that Boyce's interests were significantly affected by the case's outcome and stressed that the absence of all materially interested parties rendered the decree problematic. They sought a reversal of the circuit court's decision and an amendment to the bill to include Boyce as a proper party.	The defendant, Caldwell Cairns, maintained that the circuit court had the discretion to decide which parties should be involved in the case. Cairns argued that as the appellants had not sufficiently demonstrated why Boyce's absence impacted the proceedings or the decree itself, the circuit court's actions were justified. Cairns also contended that it was inappropriate for costs to be assigned to the defendants, as they had not refused to fulfill any obligations regarding the land transaction.

The case of William H. Rhawn et al. v. Thomas A. Pearce et al. was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 19, 1884. It involved an action of assumpsit, where the plaintiffs, who were residents of Pennsylvania, brought a suit against John Landenberger, another Pennsylvania resident, by attaching his debts owed by John V. Farwell & Company, a Chicago-based firm. The plaintiffs initially secured a judgment on February 13, 1883, against Landenberger and in favor of the plaintiffs against the garnishees for an outstanding amount of $4,259.91. However, this judgment was vacated following an interpleader filed by the garnishees, asserting the involvement of trustees appointed under Pennsylvania's insolvency laws. These trustees claimed to be vested with the debtor’s estate, including all debts due at the time, per Pennsylvania law. The matter posed significant legal questions regarding the applicability of Pennsylvania's insolvency laws and how they interact with Illinois law, particularly involving non-resident creditors seeking to claim debts within Illinois.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to the garnished funds based on their status as attaching creditors under Illinois law. They contended that the Pennsylvania statute appointing the trustees and vesting them with the debtor's estate could not operate extraterritorially to affect the rights of creditors who were pursuing legal claims in Illinois courts.	The defendant’s primary argument, represented by the interpleader filed by the garnishees, was based on the Pennsylvania statute's authority, which they claimed granted the trustees rights over the funds since the statutes were designed to protect the creditor's interests in insolvency cases. They contended that the plaintiffs, being non-residents of Illinois and also creditors in the Pennsylvania insolvency proceedings, could not hold a superior claim against the funds.

In May 1884, M. C. Tingley, a school teacher, engaged in discussions with the directors of a school district in Franklin County, Illinois, about teaching their school for five months beginning October 1, 1884, at a rate of $50 per month. After reaching this agreement, he was informed by a director that he had been employed as the teacher. However, a resolution adopted by the board on September 2, 1884, declared the agreement void due to dissatisfaction in the district. The board expressed concerns following Tingley's arrest on July 8, 1884, for allegedly assaulting a woman, Lizzie Murray, with intent to commit rape, a charge that became known within the district and instigated public dissatisfaction regarding his teaching. Tingley attempted to clarify the accusations and presented evidence to the board; however, when the school was to commence, the directors refused to accept him as the teacher, claiming they had hired another individual. Tingley subsequently sued the directors for the contractual amount he believed he was owed.	The plaintiff, M. C. Tingley, argued that he had been unlawfully terminated from his teaching position based on a binding contract reached with the school directors. He sought to recover damages amounting to the full five-month salary he would have earned, totaling $250, asserting that the directors' cancellation of the contract was unjustified and based on his prior arrest rather than any actual findings of immorality.	The defendants, represented by the school board directors, contended that they had sufficient reason to annul Tingley's contract due to his arrest on serious charges, which had prompted public concern about his character. They presented two main arguments: firstly, that the contract was void as Tingley’s conduct raised questions of morality that disqualified him from teaching, and secondly, that the public notoriety surrounding the assault charge warranted their decision to revoke the contract before he commenced teaching.

On August 7, 1885, in Warren County, Illinois, the Illinois Appellate Court heard the case of Stein, Block & Co. v. Penrose D. Good. The dispute originated from a judgment by confession entered in favor of Stein, Block & Co. on December 26, 1884. This judgment amounted to $4,093.69, based on four promissory notes that included a warrant of attorney allowing for confession of judgment without process. On December 30, 1884, Good sought to quash this execution and vacate the judgment, claiming various procedural issues, including the absence of proof regarding the execution of the warrant of attorney at the time of the judgment's entry. Judge John J. Glenn granted a stay of proceedings until January 1, 1885, whereupon Good’s motion was heard and allowed, resulting in the execution being quashed and the judgment vacated. Stein, Block & Co. subsequently appealed this decision.	Stein, Block & Co. argued that the judgment by confession was valid and should be upheld. They contested Good's claims, insisting that the proper legal procedures were followed when the judgment was entered. They sought to have the lower court's ruling overturned, restoring the original judgment in their favor.	Good maintained that the judgment was void due to a lack of proof regarding the execution of the warrant of attorney, which was essential for jurisdiction. He requested that the court uphold the lower court’s decision to quash the execution and vacate the judgment, alleging that procedural deficiencies invalidated the confession of judgment and that no jurisdiction was obtained without the required proof.

William L. McCann filed a lawsuit against Prudence Atherton and others regarding a property dispute in Illinois, with the case originally initiated in 1882. McCann's claim stemmed from a life estate held by Atherton, whom he accused of preventing waste on the premises. Following her death, McCann filed a supplemental bill seeking a partition of the property and aimed to invalidate a previous deed made by Amos Rutledge to R. F. Dickerson. McCann contended that the deed had not been delivered under terms that had been fulfilled. During the hearing, McCann’s appeal was to disqualify the deed and assert his rights to the land after demonstrating Rutledge's testimony was necessary to support his claim. However, the court found that Rutledge was an incompetent witness due to his direct interest in the outcome. The decree for partition favored the initial parties identified in the first supplemental bill and dismissed McCann's broader claims.	McCann claimed that the deed from Amos Rutledge to R.F. Dickerson was not valid as it had not been delivered under the conditions agreed upon, contending that the absence of Rutledge's wife's signature invalidated the transfer. McCann requested the court to set aside the previous deed and demanded a partition of the property, arguing that he had a rightful claim once the deed was annulled.	The defendants, including Prudence Atherton's heirs, asserted the validity of the deed to Dickerson based on its proper execution and recording. They highlighted that McCann's claims lacked substantial evidence—particularly as the supposed agreements regarding the delivery were not recorded and depended on uncorroborated statements. The defendants sought to dismiss McCann’s claims, maintaining that the deed was acknowledged, recorded, and therefore legally established.

In September 1873, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Leonard W. Volk et al. v. James A. Roche was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a promissory note for $1,250, which was issued by the defendants—Leonard W. Volk, John Feeny, and Edward Burkhardt—to James A. Roche, the plaintiff. The note had a specific condition that any amounts received by Roche as a co-partner of the defendants, not recorded in the partnership's books, should be deducted from the amount owed with 10% interest. Roche filed a suit for the repayment on the note. In defense, the defendants asserted that Roche had received significant sums as a partner that had not been charged, and they also presented a plea of set-off for payments made on Roche's behalf. Following a trial, the jury found in favor of Roche. The defendants appealed the decision, arguing that the jury instructions were misleading and that the court had erred by not adequately considering their defenses and evidence related to the set-off.	James A. Roche's primary claim centered on the enforcement of the promissory note for $1,250 plus 10% interest. Roche argued that the amount owed was valid and that the defenses presented by the defendants regarding payments not charged to the partnership books were insufficient to negate the payment due on the note.	The defendants, Leonard W. Volk, John Feeny, and Edward Burkhardt, contended that Roche had received large sums of money as a co-partner that were not accounted for in the firm's books and therefore should be deducted from the amount owed on the note. They also raised a plea of set-off, asserting they had made payments on behalf of Roche, which entitled them to recover those amounts against the claim made by Roche.

In the case of Drainage Commissioners v. John Hudson et al., which took place in 1881 in Champaign County, Illinois, a significant legal proceeding was initiated regarding a special assessment for drainage works. The Drainage Commissioners made an initial assessment for the construction, maintenance, and repair of drainage systems on June 18, 1881. However, this assessment proved to be inadequate for completing the necessary work. Consequently, on December 18, 1882, the commissioners issued an additional assessment for the same lands under the authority provided by Section 32 of the Drainage Act. The defendants, John Hudson, John H. Hudson, and Frank M. Koch, contested the new assessment and appealed to supervisors, who ruled against the initial assessment for the Hudsons and reduced Koch's assessment. The commissioners subsequently appealed this decision to the county court, where a jury trial ensued. The jury ultimately reduced the assessments substantially. Additionally, the commissioners challenged the procedural validity of the appeals, asserting that Koch did not properly object to the assessment prior to his appeal. This series of events ultimately led to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The Drainage Commissioners, as plaintiffs, argued that the additional assessments levied on the defendants’ lands were justified and necessary for the completion of the drainage works under the statutory framework. They contended that the assessments had been determined equitably and aligned with the benefits that the properties would receive from the drainage improvements. They sought to overturn the decisions made by the supervisors and county court that had scaled back the assessments.	The defendants, John Hudson, John H. Hudson, and Frank M. Koch, argued that the assessments imposed by the commissioners were unjust and exceeded the actual benefits their lands would receive from the drainage improvements. They maintained that the supervisors acted correctly in reducing the assessments and that the commissioners failed to adequately substantiate their claims regarding the benefit-to-cost ratios of the assessments. They requested that the court uphold the supervisors' and county court's decisions while affirming the reduced assessment amounts.

On February 11, 1853, the Illinois General Assembly enacted a law holding dog owners liable for damages caused by their dogs. This case, "Kinower Wormley v. John Gregg," emerges from an incident that occurred on March 14, 1869, in the village of Mendota, Illinois. The plaintiff, Kinower Wormley, claimed that John Gregg, the defendant, owned a dog known to be fierce and dangerous. Wormley alleged that the dog ran out of Gregg's property and attacked his team of horses on a public street, causing the team to panic and run away, resulting in the death of one horse and damage to his wagon and harness. The case was initially brought in the LaSalle circuit court in November 1869, where a jury ruled in favor of the defendant. Wormley subsequently moved for a new trial, asserting the discovery of new evidence regarding Gregg's knowledge of the dog's dangerous nature. However, this motion was denied, which led to Wormley appealing the decision.	The plaintiff, Kinower Wormley, argued that he suffered damages due to John Gregg's negligence in allowing his known fierce dog to roam freely. Wormley contended that Gregg was aware of the dog's vicious nature and that his failure to secure the dog led to the attack on his team of horses. He sought damages for the death of his horse and the injury to his wagon, insisting that the jury should have found Gregg liable.	The defendant, John Gregg, argued that the evidence presented did not sufficiently prove that the dog's actions directly caused the plaintiff's damages. Gregg maintained that the plaintiff had not established the necessary legal requirement of proving his knowledge of the dog's dangerous propensity, as the action was based on common law rather than the veterinary act. He also contended that the newly discovered evidence presented by Wormley was merely cumulative and did not warrant a new trial.

In 1876, in Warren County, Illinois, the case of J. Frank Caldwell et al. v. Adolph E. Lawrence was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The lawsuit centered around a promissory note originally payable to D. K. Kness, which was indorsed and delivered to the plaintiffs, J. Frank Caldwell and others. The defendants contested the lawsuit by arguing that the plaintiffs had returned the note to the payee for a valuable consideration and thus relinquished their rights to it. The plaintiffs endured the claim that they still possessed the legal title to the note, despite its equitable ownership potentially lying with Kness. The court primarily reviewed technical objections to the judgment, ruling that those did not influence the merits of the case. The final decision focused on whether the defendants presented a valid defense to the promissory note.	The plaintiffs asserted that they were the legal owners of the promissory note, and thus had the right to sue for repayment. They contended that the defendants' special plea—that the note had been returned to the payee—failed to establish a valid defense against the note, as the title remained with the plaintiffs. Their request was for the court to affirm their right to recover the amount owed under the note.	The defendants claimed that the plaintiffs lost their right to enforce the note by returning it to the payee, arguing that this action transferred all rights associated with it back to D. K. Kness. They contended that since the plaintiffs no longer held an interest in the note, they should not have been able to sue for repayment.

In the case of Timothy Moshier v. David Norton et al., decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on February 29, 1884, the central issue revolved around the foreclosure of a mortgage held by Timothy Moshier on land belonging to David Norton. The backdrop of the conflict includes multiple appeals to the Supreme Court concerning the legitimacy of a mortgage agreement that had been contested by Norton based on claims of usury. Initially, the circuit court found the contract usurious, ruling that Moshier had already collected sufficient rents and profits from the property to satisfy the debt owed, except for a small remaining sum. However, upon appeal, the Supreme Court reversed the ruling, declaring that no usury existed and established guidelines for calculating the rents and profits due. Upon subsequent trials, further evidence was presented regarding the rental values and income from the property over several years (1862-1879), but the courts struggled with determining the actual value and profits received by Moshier. The court ultimately found inconsistencies in the methods used to calculate the rental income, leading to credit applied in favor of Norton.	The plaintiff, Timothy Moshier, claimed that he was entitled to foreclosure rights over the property based on the mortgage agreement. He argued that the circuit court erred on various counts relating to the assessment of rents and profits and that insufficient weight was given to evidence of actual receipts from the property. Moshier sought the court to recognize his rights under the mortgage and to deny the claims of usury raised by the defendant.	David Norton, the defendant, countered with claims that the mortgage agreement was usurious from the outset, hence voiding Moshier’s entitlement to the foreclosure. He asserted that Moshier had profited significantly from the rents received over the years, which exceeded the debt amount owed. Norton argued that due consideration must be given to the actual income generated by the property, as opposed to speculative rental values, laying a foundation for his claim for a rebate of interest due.

Louisa S. Glade v. Kasper G. Schmidt is a legal case that took place in Chicago, Illinois, with the judgment rendered on June 25, 1884. The case involves Louisa S. Glade, who was the executrix of her deceased husband Herman O. Glade's estate, and Kasper G. Schmidt, her husband’s former business partner in a lager beer manufacturing company. At the time of Herman's death on February 12, 1882, the partnership owed $1,881.93 to Herman. After his death, Louisa filed a complaint in chancery to wind up the partnership's affairs, which led to an agreement between her and Schmidt regarding the sale of the brewery and payment of liabilities. This agreement was documented and included provisions that Schmidt would pay the debts of the firm. However, Schmidt did not formally sign the deed and bill of sale. Louisa later brought a lawsuit against Schmidt to recover the debt owed, arguing that Schmidt had assumed responsibility for it. The case went to trial without a jury, where the court had to decide if the liability was enforceable and if the earlier equity decree barred Louisa from claiming the amount due to her husband.	Louisa S. Glade claimed that Kasper G. Schmidt was legally obligated to pay the $1,881.93 owed to her husband at the time of his death, due to an agreement they made after Herman's death during a chancery suit. She argued that Schmidt had assumed this obligation and that she was entitled to recover the debt through this lawsuit. Louisa asserted that the earlier court decree did not bar her claim since the duty to pay was created after the decree and was a legal obligation enforceable in a legal action.	Kasper G. Schmidt contended that he cannot be held liable for the debt since he did not formally sign or seal the deed and bill of sale that contained the payment obligations. He also argued that the previous chancery decree effectively barred Louisa from pursuing her claim in this case because any claims should have been raised in that proceeding. Schmidt maintained that the legal duty, which Louisa claimed he was responsible for, arose solely from the context of the decree, suggesting it could not be litigated separately.

In September 1874, the case of John P. Weber v. Andrew Anderson was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a property dispute over a land lot in Cook County, Illinois. The case began when Andrew Anderson, the plaintiff, filed an action of covenant against John P. Weber, the defendant, for breaching a covenant of seizin which involved a tract of land. The origins of the case date back to 1846 when a 40-acre tract of land was conveyed to Daniel Elston, who later subdivided the land into blocks and lots. One of these lots became known as the “Tollgate lot.” In 1849, Daniel Elston sold part of this lot to the Plank Road Company while inadvertently not conveying a 10-foot strip on the north side of the lot. The Plank Road Company took possession of the entire lot and claimed ownership until they sold it to Weber in 1863. Weber held possession until he sold the entire lot to Anderson in 1870. In 1873, Anderson acquired a quitclaim deed for the disputed 10-foot strip from Elston's heirs and subsequently sued Weber claiming breach of covenant. The case revolved around the legal question of whether the possession of the land by the Plank Road Company could adversely affect the original owner's title and whether Weber’s possession could be linked to the earlier possessors to establish a continuous adverse possession.	Andrew Anderson claimed that John P. Weber breached the covenant of seizin regarding the Tollgate lot, as the title failed to include a 10-foot strip of land. He requested damages amounting to $731, reflecting what he believed was the value of the title needed to protect himself from eviction and any expenses incurred in asserting his rights over the property.	John P. Weber’s defense centered on challenging the jury instructions given during the trial, arguing they were erroneous regarding the nature of continuous possession and the transfer of possession rights without a deed. Weber contended that the court's instructions misled the jury about the requirements for establishing adverse possession and the measure of damages in the absence of eviction.

In 1875, Thomas J. Cox entered into a loan agreement with the Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company in Bloomington, Illinois, borrowing $3,000 at a ten percent interest rate, which was then the maximum legal rate. Cox paid a commission of $150 to Tillotson, the agent who facilitated the loan. Five years later, in 1880, Cox approached Tillotson for a loan renewal. This time, Cox took another loan for $3,000 at an eight percent interest rate, with no cash disbursed, and paid Tillotson a commission of $75. The mortgage securing this second loan was the subject of a foreclosure proceeding. It was established that Tillotson was an independent agent who acted without the company’s consent, and the commissions paid by Cox were solely between him and Tillotson. The case revolved around whether this arrangement constituted usury.	Thomas J. Cox claimed that the loan agreement should be deemed usurious because he had paid commissions to Tillotson, implying that he was charged more than the maximum legal interest permitted. He sought to contest the foreclosure of his property based on this assertion, contending that the loan agreement was invalid due to the alleged usury.	The Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company defended itself by arguing that the commissions paid to Tillotson by Cox were without their knowledge or consent, and thus did not constitute usury. The company maintained that the transactions were legitimate and that Tillotson acted as an independent agent in facilitating the loan without any wrongdoing on the part of the company itself.

In August 1873, Thomas Higgins was involved in an accident while using a ferry boat operated by Wiggins Ferry Company in East St. Louis, Illinois. Higgins drove a two-horse team and a wagon loaded with approximately 6,000 pounds of iron onto the ferry. The captain instructed him to make a short turn to drive onto the other end of the boat. During the maneuver, Higgins fell, and the fore wheel of his wagon rolled over his foot, injuring him. As a result of this injury, Higgins was confined to bed for several weeks and was unable to work for about two and a half months, during which he lost wages of $40 per month. He also incurred medical expenses amounting to $25 for treatment and additional costs for medicine and board. The jury ruled in favor of Higgins, awarding him $140 in damages. Despite a motion for a new trial by the defendant, the judgment was upheld, leading to the appeal by Wiggins Ferry Company.	Thomas Higgins argued that the accident was caused by the unsafe conditions on the ferry when making the turn, including a narrow space and a depression on the ferry's floor. He claimed that he had warned the captain about the dangers involved. Furthermore, Higgins sought compensation for lost wages due to his inability to work, medical expenses from the injury, and other related costs.	Wiggins Ferry Company contended that the location was safe and that similar turns had been made without incident in the past. They suggested that the accident was primarily due to the unsafe nature of the wagon's seat that Higgins was using, rather than the conditions of the ferry. The company argued that the jury instruction regarding punitive damages was incorrect and claimed that the lower court failed to appropriately assess the evidence presented.

Henry Root v. Thomas Sinnock is a legal case decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on August 26, 1886. The case revolves around the Union Bank of Quincy, which was incorporated under a public law in Illinois on March 26, 1869. The bank operated from June 1, 1883, until May 15, 1884, engaging in banking activities, including accepting deposits in a savings department. During this period, the bank accrued debts amounting to $7,200 to the plaintiff, Henry Root, who had made several deposits and was also owed $500 in interest. When the bank closed its doors on May 15, 1884, it assigned its assets for the benefit of creditors, including Root. Root held 100 shares of the bank's capital stock, valued at $100 each, and sought to recover the amount owed to him, citing the liability of stockholders as stipulated in the bank’s charter. The court was tasked with determining the individual liability of stockholders under this charter, particularly whether the liability extended beyond the capital stock they subscribed for.	The plaintiff, Henry Root, argued that as a stockholder in the Union Bank of Quincy, he was liable to repay the debts of the bank due to the provisions of the bank's charter. He claimed that he was owed $7,200 for his deposits and an additional $500 in interest, and that this obligation persisted following the bank's closure. Root requested that the court recognize his claim and enforce the liability provisions of the bank's charter, requiring Thomas Sinnock, as a stockholder, to cover the bank’s debts.	The defendant, Thomas Sinnock, contended that the charter provisions regarding liability did not impose an additional financial obligation on stockholders beyond their subscribed shares. He argued that since he had paid for his stock at its par value, he should not be held personally liable for any debts of the bank. Sinnock sought to have the case dismissed by claiming that there was no legal basis for Root's allegations of unpaid debts, as he believed the liability provisions were misconstrued.

Harvey D. Ashley initiated a legal action against Horace I. Johnson and O. C. Kilbury regarding alleged false arrest. The case took place in Livingston County, Illinois, with the significant event occurring on October 27, 1871, when Ashley was driving a herd of cattle near Fairbury. During this time, six cattle belonging to Johnson inadvertently mixed with Ashley's herd. Upon realizing his cattle were missing, Johnson pursued Ashley to Fairbury, attempting to recover his cattle but without success initially. Later, Johnson, accompanied by a constable, caught up with Ashley two miles outside Fairbury, resulting in Ashley's arrest. He was taken to a justice of the peace and briefly detained before being released. The following day, Kilbury arrested Ashley again, but after a trial before the same justice, Ashley was discharged. The case progressed through the circuit court and led to a jury trial where Johnson was found not guilty, while damages of $25 were assessed against Kilbury. The plaintiff's requests for a new trial were based on improper evidence and the verdict being against the weight of the evidence.	Ashley claimed that he was falsely arrested first by a constable at Johnson's behest and later by Kilbury. He argued that the evidence admitted during the trial was improper and that the jury's verdict of not guilty for Johnson was contrary to the evidence presented. Ashley sought to reverse the judgment against him based on these claims and requested a new trial.	The defendants, specifically Johnson, argued that the legal proceedings for Ashley's arrest were justified and adhered to proper legal protocols. They contended that the evidence supporting Ashley's claims of false arrest was insufficient, and the jury's verdict was a reasonable outcome based on the presented evidence. They maintained that the findings should not be disturbed as the evidence was conflicting and the jury had fulfilled its duty in reconciling the evidence.

In June 1826, the case of Alsworth Baker v. Samuel Whiteside arose in Madison, Illinois, involving a dispute over a covenant for a deed of property. The key individuals in this case were Alsworth Baker, the appellant, who claimed to have fulfilled his part of the agreement by paying $125 to Samuel Whiteside, the appellee, as stipulated in a written contract. The contract required Whiteside to provide a deed for a lot in Edwardsville upon receipt of the payment by a specified date, October 1. Baker alleged that despite his payment and repeated requests, Whiteside failed to execute and deliver the deed. In response to Baker’s claim, Whiteside put forth two defenses in his pleadings. He argued that Baker did not formally demand the deed and mentioned that he was always prepared to complete the deed. Additionally, he claimed that he did offer to create the deed, but Baker indicated that he would request it only when needed. The court's role was to assess these defenses against Baker's claims.	Alsworth Baker's principal argument centered around his assertion that he had complied with the terms of their written agreement by paying the agreed amount of $125 to Samuel Whiteside. Baker contended that Whiteside neglected to fulfill his obligation to execute and deliver the deed for the property, which he had paid for as per their covenant. Baker's legal request was aimed at compelling Whiteside to perform his contractual duty by delivering the deed.	Samuel Whiteside's primary defenses highlighted the alleged lack of a formal demand for the deed from Baker. He maintained that he was always willing and prepared to execute the deed, which he claimed Baker did not request timely. Furthermore, Whiteside suggested that he made an offer to complete the deed, but Baker dismissed it by stating that he would apply for the deed when he chose, which constituted a waiver of the terms.

Coleman Olmstead, the plaintiff, and Jacob Burke, the defendant, were involved in a legal dispute following a lease agreement for a twenty-acre piece of land with a house on it, located in Illinois. In the spring of 1860, Olmstead had agreed to lease this land to Burke, who was supposed to cultivate it with the assistance of a team of horses and equipment provided by Olmstead. However, Burke used the team for hauling trees instead of preparing the land for crops, which led to a breach of their agreement. On May 2, after Burke failed to plough the land as required, Olmstead evicted him but allowed him to continue living in the house located on the property. The case went to court, where Burke contended that he deserved damages for his eviction despite not having planted any crops or completed necessary preparations for them. The trial resulted in a jury verdict in favor of Burke for $100, which he later remitted to $80. Olmstead challenged this decision by appealing to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Jacob Burke, claimed that he was wrongfully evicted from the leased land by Coleman Olmstead. He sought damages for this eviction, alleging that his expected value from the crop he could have potentially harvested constituted a loss due to the premature termination of the lease agreement. Burke did not specify any special damages in his declaration but argued for general damages as compensation for the eviction.	Coleman Olmstead, the defendant, argued that Burke had failed to fulfill the lease agreement by not using the team as intended for agricultural purposes, instead engaging in unrelated work that earned him $3 per day. Olmstead contended that since Burke had not cultivated the land or planted any crops, he could not claim damages for lost profits or speculative future gains. He aimed to overturn the trial court's decision by asserting that improper testimony regarding potential crop value was admitted without basis and that the original claim for damages was unfounded.

The legal case of La Salle National Bank of La Salle v. Tolu Rock and Rye Company took place in La Salle, Illinois, with the final judgment rendered on February 12, 1884. The dispute arose from an assumpsit action initiated by La Salle National Bank, which was the indorsee and holder of a bill of exchange. This bill was alleged to have been drawn by the De Steiger Glass Company and accepted by the Tolu Rock and Rye Company. The draft, valued at $825, was dated December 13, 1882, and was signed by Phil. R. De Steiger, who identified himself as the president of the De Steiger Glass Company. The Tolu Rock and Rye Company accepted this draft, and its treasurer, F. E. Davis, also endorsed it. The conflict arose when the bank sought to introduce the draft as evidence; the Tolu Rock and Rye Company contended that it was not liable due to the alleged personal nature of the draft and lack of proper endorsement from De Steiger. The trial court ruled against the bank's attempts to admit the draft into evidence, leading to a verdict and judgment for the Tolu Rock and Rye Company.	La Salle National Bank argued that the draft was indeed intended to represent the De Steiger Glass Company and should be viewed in this capacity. The bank contended that parol evidence should be admissible to demonstrate that De Steiger, as the president of the company, had the authority to bind the company through the draft. The bank sought recovery based on this drafted obligation, asserting that it was justified in its belief that it held a valid claim against the Tolu Rock and Rye Company for payment.	The Tolu Rock and Rye Company claimed that the draft did not constitute the company's obligation as it was executed by Phil. R. De Steiger without proper endorsement and should be viewed as his personal draft. They objected to the admissibility of parol evidence, asserting that it could not be used to interpret an instrument that was clear on its face. The defendant maintained that there was a variance between the instrument declared upon and the draft offered into evidence, leading to the assertion that they were not liable under the draft.

On July 18, 1888, in Chicago, Illinois, Edward T. Singer, the appellee and manager of a theatrical company, entered into a contract with Baker, the owner of a theatre being built on Wabash Avenue, to perform for one week starting December 10, 1888. Under this agreement, Singer was to receive 70% of the gross receipts, with a guarantee that his earnings would be at least $2,500. Before the engagement began, Baker made a voluntary assignment of the theatre for the benefit of his creditors. The assignee sought permission from the court to continue operating the theatre and fulfilling the contract with Singer, which the court granted. After completing the performance week, Singer filed a petition claiming $1,019.80 was due to him. The court ordered the assignee to pay this amount from available funds after covering administrative expenses, but reserved the question of whether this claim should be paid from property sales. An appeal was filed concerning this order.	The plaintiff, Edward T. Singer, argued that he was entitled to payment for his performance at the theatre based on the contract approved by the court. He contended that since he provided services to preserve the theatre's value during its management under the assignee, his claim should be prioritized over ordinary creditors.	The defendant, represented by the assignee, argued that while the court allowed expenses incurred in the operation of the theatre to be paid, it reserved the right to determine the source of payment from the property's assets. They emphasized that the court had the discretion to manage claims and debts associated with the property and had not abused that power in its ruling.

The case "The Chicago West Division Railway Company v. Mary L. Lambert" occurred in Chicago, Illinois, with the decision rendered on January 25, 1887, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff, Mary L. Lambert, a midwife and operator of a private lying-in hospital, and the defendant, The Chicago West Division Railway Company, which operated a street railroad in the city. The incident that sparked the legal claims took place while Lambert was attempting to alight from one of the railway company's cars, which was negligently started suddenly, causing her to fall and sustain injuries. The case progressed through the Cook County Circuit Court and was later appealed to the Appellate Court for the First District, which upheld the lower court’s judgment in favor of Lambert.	Mary L. Lambert claimed that the railway company acted negligently by suddenly moving the car while she was in the process of getting off, which resulted in her being thrown to the ground and sustaining injuries. She sought damages to compensate for her injuries and concluded that the railway company's actions directly contributed to her inability to work, thereby affecting her income as a midwife.	The Chicago West Division Railway Company defended against Lambert's claims by arguing that her testimony regarding her earnings was improper since she was not a licensed midwife, and thus sought to exclude evidence of her income from midwifery services. The defendant contended that any uncertainty regarding her potential earnings should be considered against her claim and tried to invoke a jury instruction that would lead to a verdict in favor of the defendant if the evidence was equally balanced.

John Tanton and John E. Van Alstine were involved in a landlord-tenant dispute concerning a forty-acre tract of land in Woodford County, Illinois. The case arose from an oral agreement made in 1878 or 1879, where Tanton rented the land to Van Alstine for $50 per year. The exact length of the lease was not specified, but it was agreed that either party could terminate the lease with notice. Van Alstine occupied the land and paid the annual rent consistently until March 1, 1884. Tanton filed a lawsuit to recover $50 for rent due for the year ending March 1, 1885, after a Justice of the Peace ruling against him. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Van Alstine, leading to this appeal by Tanton. Evidence was presented regarding whether Van Alstine used the land in 1884; he claimed he did not, but testimony indicated he had pastured cattle on it. The court analyzed the implications of the previous tenancy and whether proper notice to terminate had been given by either party.	Tanton argued that he was entitled to recover $50 for rent due under the express terms of their verbal agreement, asserting that Van Alstine's failure to pay for the year 1884 was unjustified because he was certified to give statutory notice if he intended to terminate the tenancy.	Van Alstine contended that since the contract was verbal and made in the late 1870s, he was not responsible for the 1884 rent unless he had occupied the land that year. He denied using the land in 1884 and claimed that the jury was misinformed regarding his rental obligations, specifically that he was not liable unless he actually occupied the premises.

In March 1867, Nicholas Schaeffer, a soap and candle manufacturer based in St. Louis, consigned 200 boxes of star candles to James L. Kirk and others, who were manufacturers and dealers in the same products located in Chicago. The defendants were appointed to sell these candles on behalf of the plaintiff. Prior to receiving the candles, the defendants had insured their own goods but did not obtain insurance for the candles after they were received. By May 17, 1867, the defendants had sold about 40 boxes from the shipment. However, on that day, a fire occurred which destroyed the remaining candles along with the defendants’ goods. Schaeffer subsequently filed a lawsuit seeking compensation for the loss of his candles, asserting that it was customary for commission merchants in Chicago to insure consigned goods, and thus the defendants should have insured the candles. The defendants countered that they were not commission merchants and therefore had no obligation to insure the goods, as established by precedent in bailment law.	The plaintiff, Nicholas Schaeffer, claimed that the defendants had a duty to insure the 200 boxes of star candles that he consigned to them for sale. He argued that this duty arose from customary practices involving commission merchants in Chicago. Schaeffer sought to recover the value of the candles destroyed in the fire, insisting the defendants should have acted to insure his property during the consignment period.	The defendants, represented by James L. Kirk, contended that they were not commission merchants and thus were not bound by the customs regarding insurance for consigned goods. They argued that they had no express or implied authority from Schaeffer to procure insurance for the candles. The defendants maintained that they merely acted as factors or agents for hire and were not liable for failing to insure the goods. As there was no contractual obligation to insure, they requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

In January 1874, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of George C. Stoolfire vs. Hiram A. Royse. The dispute centered around a covenant agreement where Stoolfire was to purchase 160 steers from Royse, selected from a herd of 190, to be delivered by November 1, 1866. The purchase price was set at 4½ cents per pound, to be paid with a mortgage and notes totaling $9,180, along with Royse agreeing to pay an additional $1,000 on demand. However, the cattle were neither delivered nor tendered on the agreed date. The contract was signed by an agent of Stoolfire but was deemed void unless Stoolfire notified Royse of his approval. Discrepancies arose as Stoolfire's son attempted to claim the cattle on the delivery date without finding Royse. A series of communications about the contract's ratification were made, but Royse denied receiving notice. Additionally, Royse contended he was released from the contract obligations because the mortgagor had sold a portion of the associated land before the mortgage was recorded. The jury ultimately found in favor of Royse, leading to an examination of whether Stoolfire had fulfilled his legal obligations under the contract.	George C. Stoolfire claimed that Hiram A. Royse had breached the covenant by failing to deliver the cattle as stipulated in their agreement. Stoolfire argued that he had complied with his obligations, including leaving the necessary paperwork for ratification with a bank and attempting to demand the cattle on the agreed date. He sought damages resulting from this breach.	Hiram A. Royse defended that he was not obligated to fulfill the agreement because Stoolfire had not complied with his part of the contract by not tendering the mortgage and notes in order to secure the cattle. Royse asserted that the sale of the mortgaged property prior to the mortgage recording invalidated the arrangement, exonerating him from delivering the cattle. He emphasized that mutual and dependent covenants required compliance from both parties, which had not occurred.

On November 23, 1882, Theodore Gardner, a 19-year-old German immigrant living with the family of John B. Welter in Mason County, Illinois, was indicted for the murder of Mary Welter, which occurred on November 14. Gardner, who did not understand English, was arraigned and pleaded guilty without counsel present. His plea was facilitated through an interpreter, H.B. Nortrup, who expressed doubts about Gardner's comprehension of the legal proceedings and his situation. The court sentenced Gardner to death on January 12, 1883. On December 14, 1882, after being appointed counsel, Gardner sought to withdraw his guilty plea, but the presiding judge denied the request, citing lack of jurisdiction since he did not try the case. The Illinois Supreme Court later reviewed the circumstances of the plea and noted multiple irregularities in the court's process, including the absence of proper legal advice for Gardner.	Gardner’s primary argument centered on the assertion that his plea of guilty was entered without adequate understanding of the nature of the charges against him, due to his language barrier and lack of counsel. He argued that the procedure violated his rights, as he was not of mature age and was not familiar with the legal system, thus demanding an opportunity to withdraw his guilty plea and enter a plea of not guilty.	The defense represented by the state maintained that Gardner had confessed to the killing, and the court's acceptance of his plea was justified based on this admission. They argued that effective communication had been established through the interpreter, and that Gardner had adequately indicated his understanding of the charges during the arraignment.

The case 'William Brownfield et al. v. Thomas Brownfield' was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1871. The case stemmed from an injunction bond dispute in Champaign County, Illinois, presided over by Judge A. J. Gallagher. The plaintiffs, William Brownfield and others, had sought an injunction against the defendant, Thomas Brownfield, to prevent him from claiming certain personal and real estate. The bond in question had a penalty of $1,000 and stipulated that if the injunction was dissolved, the obligors would pay any costs and damages awarded against them. Following the dissolution of the injunction, the court ordered costs against the complainants but no damages. While the defendant incurred $2,700 in attorney fees defending the injunction, the court ruled that the plaintiffs had not suggested damages at the time of dissolution, which meant there was no breach of the bond conditions. Consequently, the judgment of the lower court, which had awarded the penalty of the bond, was reversed, highlighting the necessity of an award for damages as a prerequisite for recovery on the bond.	The plaintiffs claimed the right to the injunction to protect their interest in certain personal and real estate from being claimed by the defendant. They argued that the bond provided them protection and that they were not liable for damages as none were awarded upon the dissolution of the injunction.	The defendant asserted that the plaintiffs were liable under the terms of the bond for all costs and damages incurred due to the injunction. He argued that since he had incurred significant attorney fees in defending against the injunction, the bond should be enforced to cover those expenses. However, he also contended that without an awarded damage, the bond condition was not breached, which should preclude liability.

In June 1870, the case of John L. Elder v. Felicia Cordray was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Jasper County, Illinois, involving key individuals: Felicia Cordray, the plaintiff, and John L. Elder, the defendant, who was acting as a sheriff. The case centered on the ownership of certain horses that had been levied upon by Elder under an execution for debts owed by Felicia's husband, Henry Cordray. Felicia contended that the horses belonged to her as separate property and were not subject to seizure for her husband's debts. The court examined the evidence, including testimony from the former owner of the horses, who indicated that they were exchanged for property owned by Felicia. She testified that she acquired the funds for the property and the construction of the house from her uncle’s estate, implicating that the horses were her lawful property. A jury was waived in the trial, and the lower court ruled in favor of Felicia, confirming her ownership of the horses.	Felicia Cordray claimed that the horses were her separate property, not subject to being seized for her husband's debts. She argued that the horses were obtained through her transactions and that the funds for these transactions originated from her own inheritance, thus establishing her independent ownership.	John L. Elder, as sheriff, argued that the horses were the property of Henry Cordray, Felicia's husband, and therefore subject to levy under the execution for Henry's debts. Elder sought to challenge the ruling of the lower court, claiming that the transaction regarding the horses should be deemed invalid regarding Felicia's separate ownership.

John L. Griswold appealed against The Board of Trustees of the Peoria University in April 1861, after a ruling obtained in the Circuit Court following a trial held in November 1860. The case originated in Peoria County, Illinois, where Griswold, a subscriber, had pledged $600 for the purpose of erecting buildings and supporting the operation of the Peoria College under the Synod of Illinois. Following a legal process that began before a justice of the peace, the case was elevated to the Circuit Court, which found in favor of the plaintiff Griswold for $300. The heart of the dispute concerned whether the subscription was binding and whether it constituted sufficient evidence for the court to uphold the claims. Griswold had contributed $300 of his total pledge and, after a building was destroyed, refused to pay the remaining $300. The court had to assess the validity of the subscription agreement in light of objections regarding the establishment of the corporation and the lack of formal assessment procedures for payment.	Griswold argued that the subscription document he signed constituted a valid and binding commitment, claiming that the board of trustees had incurred liabilities on the belief of his pledge. He sought to enforce his right to the remaining $300 based on the financial obligations incurred by the trustees of Peoria University and asserted that the university could be the rightful beneficiary of the subscription.	The Board of Trustees challenged the enforceability of the subscription based on several grounds: they asserted that there was no proper incorporation of the plaintiff (the university), that no formal assessments had been documented, that the subscription was not payable to them, and that the agreement lacked necessary consideration. The defendant also argued that there was insufficient evidence to prove the document's execution and that the subscription appeared altered. They requested the court to dismiss the claims based on these points of contention.

The case "The St. Louis Bridge and Tunnel Railroad Company v. The People ex rel. James D. Baker, Collector" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court on April 5, 1889, in Mt. Vernon, Illinois. The key individuals involved included James D. Baker, who served as the collector for the people, and the St. Louis Bridge and Tunnel Railroad Company, the appellant. The dispute arose from the application made by Baker at the May term of the county court of St. Clair County in 1888 for judgment on a delinquent tax list for the year 1887, which included property belonging to the railroad company deemed to be delinquent. The railroad company filed objections to this judgment, claiming that the property assessment was fraudulent, inconsistent with assessments of similar properties, and that a special road and bridge tax had been unlawfully levied. The court grappled with the validity of these objections, focusing particularly on the assessment process conducted by the State Board of Equalization and the legality of the tax levies made by local authorities.	The St. Louis Bridge and Tunnel Railroad Company, as the plaintiff, asserted that the valuation of its tracks and the tax assessments imposed were fraudulent and illegally conducted. Specifically, the plaintiff contended that the assessment was significantly higher than that of similar railroad properties in the area, indicating unfair treatment. The plaintiff sought to challenge the special road and bridge tax as having been unlawfully levied by the highway commissioners.	James D. Baker, representing the State's interests as the collector, argued against the claims made by the railroad company. The defense maintained that the assessment performed by the State Board of Equalization was quasi-judicial and could only be contested on grounds of fraud or lack of jurisdiction, neither of which were sufficiently proven in this case. Furthermore, the defense contended that the tax levies were valid and adhered to statutory requirements.

In this case, titled "Tom Pickard et al. v. H. C. Hopkins," the legal proceedings took place in 1885 in Woodford County, Illinois. The dispute arose over the ownership of a horse originally owned by a debtor named Taylor. On June 20, 1884, Hopkins, the appellee, purchased the horse from Taylor to settle an old debt. However, after leading the horse a short distance, it escaped and returned to a pasture owned by Strawhacker, the agister holding the horse. Hopkins decided to leave the horse in the pasture until further notice from Taylor. Crucially, neither party notified Strawhacker of the sale, which is a key point in the litigation. On July 19, a constable levied an execution on the horses due to a judgment favoring the appellants against Taylor. The case focuses on whether there was a valid transfer of possession necessary for the title to be obtained by the vendee against creditors and whether the delivery was adequately executed to establish ownership. The court ultimately found that the delivery was insufficient and defined the necessary conditions for transferring ownership and possession.	The plaintiffs, Tom Pickard and others, argued that the sale of the horse from Taylor to Hopkins was not valid against the creditors because there was no substantial change of possession. They claimed that the mere act of leading the horse for a short distance did not constitute adequate delivery of possession, thus allowing the execution against Taylor's property to stand.	The defendant, H. C. Hopkins, contended that he had legally purchased the horse in good faith and claimed that since he had taken the horse's mane to lead it, he had established possession. He requested that the court recognize the sale as valid, positing that he should maintain ownership of the horse despite the creditors' claim against Taylor.

The case "Myra A. Price et al. v. The Dime Savings Bank et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 26, 1888. The dispute arose from a series of financial transactions beginning in May 1872, when Henry C. Reed purchased stock from a group that included Levi Kelsey. To secure payment for the remaining debt owed to Kelsey, Reed provided various collateral, including a bank stock certificate. Over the years, Reed exchanged collaterals, including the original notes, which were also extended multiple times without the original owner's consent, William K. Beed. The core issue hinged around whether the bank stock, which Beed had pledged as collateral, was released due to the alterations in the financial agreements made without his knowledge. The parties involved included Myra A. Price and Lydia A. Cramb (the plaintiffs), and several defendants, including Henry C. Reed, the Dime Savings Bank, and William K. Beed. The Illinois Supreme Court was tasked with determining the validity of the claims against Beed's stock in the Dime Savings Bank.	The plaintiffs, Myra A. Price and Lydia A. Cramb, claimed that the fifty shares of stock in the Dime Savings Bank should be considered collateral for the payment of a promissory note made by Henry C. Reed. They sought a court order declaring the shares subject to a lien and requested their sale to satisfy the debt owed.	The defendants, particularly William K. Beed and the Dime Savings Bank, defended against the claims by asserting that the bank stock belonged to Beed and had been pledged as collateral for Reed's debt without Beed’s consent. They argued that the multiple extensions and renewals of the notes took place without their knowledge, thus invalidating the collateralization of Beed's stock, which was used in lieu of other debts.

In the case of *George S. Bowen, Admr. v. Anna Shay et al.*, the events unfolded in Cook County, Illinois, during the administration of the estate of Jefferson B. Shay, who had passed away. George S. Bowen, the administrator of the estate, sought to settle the estate's accounts in probate court. While most items in his account were approved, a claim for $7,019.58 was disallowed by the probate court. Bowen appealed this decision, first to the circuit court and then to the Appellate Court, but both affirmed the probate court's ruling. The dispute centered around a private sale of the estate's assets, which comprised a stock of goods and other personal property needed to pay the estate's debts. Bowen had been granted an order by the probate court to proceed with this private sale to W. A. Shay and F. F. French. Although Bowen took steps to sell the assets, the buyers became insolvent, leaving a portion of the sale price as uncollectible. The core question for the courts was whether Bowen, as administrator, was liable for this loss due to not taking security for the credit extended during the sale, despite being authorized for a private sale.	George S. Bowen, as the administrator of the estate, claimed that he should not bear the loss from the uncollectible amount from the sale to Shay and French. He argued that the probate court's order did not require him to take security for the credit sale. Therefore, he requested that the court recognize his position and allow the claim of $7,019.58 against the estate.	The defense, representing Anna Shay and other parties, contended that the administrator had a legal obligation to take security when selling estate assets on credit, whether at public or private sale. They maintained that since Bowen failed to secure this, he was liable for the loss incurred due to the insolvency of the purchasers. They requested that the court affirm the lower court's decision disallowing the claim.

In November 1858, a legal case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court involving William G. Bowman as the appellant and Milton Bartley as the appellee. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Gallatin County, Illinois, where Bartley initiated an action of debt against Bowman. The writ and declaration claimed a total of seventy-six dollars and twenty-five cents in debt and an additional fifty dollars in damages, amounting to a total request of one hundred and twenty-six dollars and twenty-five cents. In response, Bowman filed a general issue and two pleas of partial payment. After hearing evidence, the Circuit Court ruled in favor of Bartley, ordering Bowman to pay a judgment of seventy-nine dollars and ninety-four cents along with court costs. However, details of the judgment did not specify the division between the debt and damages, leading Bowman to appeal the decision citing this as a significant error.	Milton Bartley, the plaintiff, claimed a debt of seventy-six dollars and twenty-five cents along with damages amounting to fifty dollars. He sought a total judgment of one hundred and twenty-six dollars and twenty-five cents from William G. Bowman, questioning his obligation under the terms of the debt and damage claims presented in the original court declaration.	William G. Bowman, the defendant, argued that the Circuit Court erred by failing to distinctly separate the judgment into amounts for debt and damages. He asserted that the conflated judgment of seventy-nine dollars and ninety-four cents did not comply with legal precedents that require clarity in debt-related judgments. His appeal centered around this failure to specify, which he claimed rendered the judgment erroneous.

In January 1885, the legal dispute arose in Patoka, Illinois, involving Robert E. Allen as the plaintiff and George W. Bowen and Nancy Hall as the defendants. The case centered on an ejectment action filed by Allen to reclaim possession of the north two-thirds of lot 12 in block 10 of the railroad addition to the town. The foundation of Allen's claim rested on a will from 1870, which he argued bequeathed the property to him. After the death of the testatrix, Ann Quinn, in 1876, her heirs sold their interests in the property to Nancy Hall. The will was admitted to probate in 1881, leading to a series of legal evaluations addressing its validity and the property's rightful ownership. The relevant issues included the acceptance and implications of the will's provisions, particularly after changes and delays regarding its probate and whether the described property correctly identified the intended bequest.	The plaintiff, Robert E. Allen, argued that the will of Ann Quinn, which specified the north two-thirds of lot 12, solidified his ownership rights to the property. He contended that the probate of the will affirmed its legal standing and should thus be honored in court, regardless of subsequent transfers of interest by the other heirs. Allen sought a ruling that would grant him recovery of the disputed property based on his interpretation of the will's legitimate claims.	The defendants, George W. Bowen and Nancy Hall, contended that the will was not valid or enforceable due to delays in probate and the interference of subsequent marriages, which they argued could revoke the will’s claims. They also implied that relying on the will's current description created ambiguity, resulting in contradictory claims that might undermine Allen’s request. Bowen and Hall sought to have the court dismiss Allen's claims on the grounds that he had no rightful claim given these contentions over the will’s intent and validity.

The case of Ferdinand Darmstædter v. Philip D. Armour et al. was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 16, 1885. The background of the case centers around an appeal made by Ferdinand Darmstædter, who was seeking to quash a judgment rendered against him by a justice of the peace. The judgment amounted to $174.62 in favor of Armour and others, for goods that Darmstædter allegedly obtained fraudulently and wrongfully converted for his own use. Darmstædter did not appear or defend himself during the initial hearing, citing his own recent insolvency and an expectation that the appellees could only recover in an action in assumpsit, not trover. He claimed he had no knowledge of the judgment until after a subsequent arrest. The appellate court found that his petition for certiorari was insufficient as he did not show that the judgment was unjust or that he was incapable of making an ordinary appeal.	The plaintiffs, Philip D. Armour and others, argued that the judgment from the justice of the peace was valid and was based on rightful claims for goods sold and delivered to Darmstædter. They contended that the appellant's claims of fraud were unfounded and that he simply owed the amount rendered, which was less than what was due. The plaintiffs maintained that Darmstædter's petition showed no substantial injustice and that he had failed to engage in the legal process to appeal the judgment in a timely manner.	Ferdinand Darmstædter, as the appellant, claimed that he had not been guilty of fraud in obtaining goods from the plaintiffs. He argued that he had intended to contest the judgment but was misled by the failure of the summons to specify the claim type (assumpsit or trover). Additionally, he suggested that his insolvency should have allowed for a more lenient treatment in the legal proceedings, yet he did not demonstrate any actionable grounds for contesting the original judgment.
