Bennett maintained that the withdrawal of Delano’s attorney did not dismiss the case from the court’s agenda and insisted on the right to pursue the trial.

The case, "The New Home Life Association of Illinois v. Emma Hagler et al.," was decided on June 7, 1887, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose when Abram Hagler, a member of the New Home Life Association, died on January 19, 1885. In exchange for a membership fee of $12, Hagler was issued a certificate promising a death benefit of $4,000 to his wife and children, contingent upon satisfactory proof of his death. Following Hagler's death, his family filed a suit against the association to recover the claimed benefit. The association contended that Hagler's death resulted from suicide and that no satisfactory proof of death was provided within the stipulated timeframe. The case involved pivotal testimonies regarding the presentation of Hagler's death to the association and the nature of the death itself.	The plaintiffs, comprising Hagler's wife and children, asserted that the New Home Life Association had a legal obligation to pay the $4,000 death benefit as specified in the membership certificate. They claimed that satisfactory proof of Hagler's death was submitted within the required ninety days and that his death was due to congestion of the stomach, not suicide, thereby contradicting the defendant's rationale for refusal to pay.	The defendant, New Home Life Association, defended against the claims by arguing that they were only liable for the amount assessable from members after proof of death was provided. They asserted that Hagler’s death was self-inflicted, thus nullifying the insurance claim, and contended that the plaintiffs had not provided satisfactory proof of his death as outlined in their policy terms. Furthermore, the defendant claimed that the lawsuit was brought prematurely before the stipulated ninety-day period for claims submissions.

In January 1867, in Adams County, Illinois, Cornelia A. Streeter filed a lawsuit against her husband, Elijah S. Streeter, concerning two promissory notes valued at $50 and $100. The dispute arose from an agreement regarding the possession of certain properties, which included a house, a cistern, and fruit trees, claimed to be under lease to Cornelia. Cornelia alleged that the two notes were given as part of an agreement to surrender possession of the properties, which she claimed Elijah failed to do. The agreement stated that upon execution of the notes, Elijah was to deliver the properties back to her in their original condition. However, Elijah allegedly caused damage to the premises by allowing the house to burn, contaminating the cistern, and killing the fruit trees. This condition resulted in claims for damages against the notes. The case went to trial, leading to conflicts over the evidence and interpretations of the agreement.	Cornelia A. Streeter argued that the defendant, Elijah S. Streeter, breached the agreement to return possession of the property in good condition upon the execution of the notes. She claimed that due to his negligence, damages occurred, amounting to $500, which she requested as a set-off against the amounts owed on the promissory notes.	Elijah S. Streeter contended that Cornelia did not uphold her part of the agreement, allowing him to retain possession for a few days as needed and ultimately asserting that the damages caused were irrelevant to the agreements regarding the promissory notes. He maintained that the allegations of damages by Cornelia were immaterial and should not affect her ability to claim on the notes.

In the case of John Dawson v. Jane Dawson, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the legal proceedings stemmed from a divorce decree previously obtained by Jane Dawson against her husband, John Dawson. The decree mandated John to pay Jane $150 per month for alimony and child maintenance. In 1885, Jane filed a petition to increase her alimony from $150 to $175 per month, as well as requesting $200 for her solicitor's fees. The court granted these requests, prompting John to appeal the decision. Following the appeal, Jane submitted further requests for additional funds to cover the expenses related to the appeal process. The court again ruled in her favor, requiring John to pay her $80 for printing expenses and an additional $150 for her solicitor. This appeal was subsequently brought before the Illinois Appellate Court after John contested the payment order. The case eventually reached the Supreme Court, which ruled that there was insufficient justification for Jane's petitions and clarified that she should bear her own legal fees.	Jane Dawson claimed that due to increased financial needs, her alimony should be raised from $150 to $175 per month. She argued that John Dawson should also cover her solicitor’s fees and additional costs incurred while filing for these changes, thereby requesting financial support of $200 for her attorney, $80 for appeal-related costs, and subsequent fees.	John Dawson contended that the requests made by Jane Dawson for increased alimony and legal fees were unfounded. He argued against the necessity of her petitions, asserting that the substantial increase in alimony and payment for her solicitor's fees were unwarranted and sought to reverse the orders set by the court.

The case "P. C. Hanford Oil Company et al. v. First National Bank of Chicago" took place in 1887, following events that started in October 1884 in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiffs were the P. C. Hanford Oil Company and other creditors of Ferris & Avery, a firm that operated as dealers in oils and paints. Initially, Ferris & Avery were in good financial condition, having borrowed $1,500 from the First National Bank of Chicago, for which they provided a promissory note and a warrant of attorney as security. This agreement was intended to create a preference that would favor the bank over other creditors. However, by December 11, 1884, Ferris & Avery became aware of their insolvency and decided to make a general assignment of their property to benefit their creditors. Shortly thereafter, Mr. Ferris informed the bank of their financial troubles, leading to the bank entering judgment on the note before the assignment was completed. The bank's lien was contested by the assignee chosen to manage the assignment, leading to legal proceedings to determine the validity of the bank's claim against the goods of Ferris & Avery.	The plaintiffs claimed that the execution lien held by the First National Bank was invalid. They argued that the acts leading to the creation of the lien occurred after Ferris & Avery's decision to make a general assignment, which would constitute an unlawful preference under the Voluntary Assignment Act. They sought a declaration from the court that the bank's actions were improper because they allegedly colluded with Ferris & Avery to create a preference in violation of the law.	The defendant, First National Bank of Chicago, defended its position by asserting that the promissory note and warrant of attorney were created before Ferris & Avery decided to assign their property and were intended to secure a bona fide debt. The bank argued that there was a legitimate understanding with Ferris & Avery that would allow the bank to act on the note in case of financial trouble, and therefore, the lien was valid regardless of any subsequent actions taken by the debtors.

In the case of John J. Clause v. The Bullock Printing Press Company, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the legal proceedings began on July 2, 1884. The dispute originated from a contract dated May 19, 1882, in which the Bullock Printing Press Company was contracted to construct folding machines for John J. Clause. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant failed to properly construct the machines specified in the contract, particularly for clients like the “Boston Herald” and the “Philadelphia Press Company.” As the case progressed, Clause filed multiple suits against the defendant for damages associated with breach of contract and for two promissory notes owed to him. The cases were consolidated, and various motions were filed, including a plea for set-off by the defendant, which was ultimately denied by the court. The trial focused on establishing damages for the failure to perform under the contract, particularly regarding the folder for the “Boston Herald.” The matter drew attention to the legal requirements for a recovery on contracts and the general issue surrounding set-off in breach of contract cases.	The plaintiff, John J. Clause, argued that the defendant, Bullock Printing Press Company, breached their contract by failing to deliver properly constructed folding machines as agreed. He sought damages amounting to $1,935.48, which included the total due on two promissory notes. In support of his claims, Clause emphasized the importance of the timely fulfillment of his orders and the resultant financial impact due to the defendant's failure to deliver the contracted goods.	The defendant, Bullock Printing Press Company, contended that the plaintiff failed to take necessary delivery of the machinery, specifically the folder intended for the “Philadelphia Press.” They sought to introduce a plea of set-off to counter Clause's claims by referencing damages from the plaintiff’s breach of contract. However, their requests to file this plea and to admit evidence concerning unliquidated damages were denied by the court, as the defendant could only recover for specific damages related to the contract’s breach.

The case "Alois Podrasnik and Charles H. Ehlebracht v. R. T Martin Company" was decided on January 25, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The controversy centered around two promissory notes issued by the partnership of C. H. Ehlebracht & Company, which consisted of Charles H. Ehlebracht and Alois Podrasnik. The notes, totaling approximately $601.87, were dated March 1 and March 15, 1886, and were supposed to be paid four months thereafter. The issue arose when the plaintiff, R. T. Martin Company, sought to recover the amounts due on these notes after Ehlebracht became insolvent and assigned his assets to creditors. Podrasnik had previously been a partner in the business but ceased to be involved around February 1, 1886, right before the debts were incurred. The court examined whether Podrasnik, despite retiring from the partnership, could still be held liable for the debts resulting from transactions occurring while he was a partner. The court noted that Podrasnik did not provide proper notice of dissolution to the public, which played a crucial role in determining his liability.	The plaintiff, R. T. Martin Company, claimed that both partners of C. H. Ehlebracht & Company were jointly responsible for the promissory notes executed for goods ordered while Podrasnik was a partner. They argued that since the goods were ordered before the dissolution of the partnership, Podrasnik remained liable for the debts. The plaintiff requested recovery of the owed amount, contending that the notes were valid obligations of the partnership, despite Podrasnik's claims of retirement from the business.	The defendants, Alois Podrasnik and Charles H. Ehlebracht, asserted that Podrasnik should not be held liable for the debts incurred after the dissolution of the partnership and maintained the position that no public notice of the dissolution was required for Podrasnik as a dormant partner. They argued that because Podrasnik took no active role in the management and was not advertised as a member of the firm, he should not be held accountable for obligations arising from orders placed after he exited the partnership. Ultimately, they sought dismissal of the claims made against Podrasnik.

In the case of Elisha B. Steers v. William J. Brownell, dated January 18, 1888, the legal proceedings took place in Illinois. The dispute arose in the Circuit Court of McLean County and was subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case involved Elisha B. Steers as the plaintiff and William J. Brownell as the defendant. Steers filed claims against Brownell based on common counts in assumpsit, seeking to recover debts. Brownell responded with several defenses, including general issue, payment, the Statute of Limitations, and a plea of set-off, indicating he had debts owed to him that could counter Steers' claims. The legal interaction included multiple replications and rejoinders regarding the set-off claims connected to the statute of limitations. Ultimately, after trial, the court found in favor of Brownell, with a verdict favoring him on his set-off amounting to $342.65, against which Steers contested the ruling.	The plaintiff, Elisha B. Steers, contended that the claims presented in the defendant's plea of set-off should be excluded because they were barred by the Statute of Limitations. He argued that the various causes of action related to the set-off had not accrued within the five years preceding the initiation of the lawsuit. Steers sought a ruling that the defendant be entitled to a set-off only to the extent that any amount was found due on his own claim.	The defendant, William J. Brownell, countered that the claims in his set-off were held and owned at the time they became barred by the statute limitations. He emphasized that the plaintiff's claims were under his ownership prior to the barring of his own claims. Brownell sought to have his set-off plea accepted and argued for a judgment that included any excess amount beyond the plaintiff's claims, thereby allowing him to recover the total amount he was owed.

On September 1, 1869, William Ross, the owner of approximately 1,100 acres of land in Edgar County, Illinois, faced foreclosure on a mortgage which resulted in the sale of his land for $8,674.46 to William M. Coler, who subsequently assigned the purchase certificate to Richard B. Sutherland. After this transfer, Ross and Sutherland entered into three agreements regarding the redemption of the property. Initially, Ross was granted an extended redemption period until December 1, 1870. On November 20, 1870, this period was further extended to February 1, 1871, for a fee where Ross had to pay Sutherland the sale amount plus interest and an additional $200. Subsequently, on January 21, 1871, Ross conveyed 122 acres of his land to Sutherland, who agreed to convey 820 acres to Ross's sons under specific financial conditions. Eventually, on September 29, 1871, Ross arranged for O.W. Levings to pay Sutherland $13,538 to cover his debts, based on Sutherland's representation. However, on February 24, 1874, Ross filed a lawsuit alleging fraud and overpayment against Sutherland after Sutherland's refusal to proceed as promised, seeking equitable relief for the alleged injustices experienced. The lower court dismissed Ross's claims, prompting him to appeal the decision.	William Ross claimed that Richard B. Sutherland engaged in fraudulent and oppressive behavior regarding their contractual agreements. He asserted that he had overpaid Sutherland under the terms of their final contract and sought relief through the courts for the emotional and financial distress caused by Sutherland's actions, insisting that the contract was unfairly manipulated to his disadvantage.	Richard B. Sutherland defended himself by stating that the contracts were clear, voluntary, and legally binding. He argued that Ross had multiple opportunities to redeem the property and that he had fully complied with the terms agreed upon, including the proper disclosure of amounts due and that the payment made covered all obligations. Sutherland contended that there was no evidence of fraud or undue advantage that could invalidate their agreements or justify Ross’s claims of overpayment.

Bennett Jacobson filed a case against Samuel Gunzburg, which was presided over in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the judgment delivered on January 18, 1888. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, under the jurisdiction of Judge John P. Altgeld. The dispute between the two parties involved conflicting evidence concerning a specific event or series of events; however, the details of what transpired were not explicitly stated in the summary provided. The case's appeal centered around the validity of the jury's findings, which ultimately favored Gunzburg. The opposing legal teams included Messrs. Blum & Blum representing Jacobson and Mr. Robert H. McMurdy representing Gunzburg.	The plaintiff, Bennett Jacobson, argued against the verdict rendered by the jury and sought a new trial based on the introduction of what he considered newly discovered evidence. His claims hinged on the assertion that this evidence could potentially prove beneficial to his case, although it was argued to be merely cumulative and not conclusively decisive.	The defendant, Samuel Gunzburg, contended that the evidence presented by Jacobson was insufficient to merit a new trial. His defense pointed out that the jury's verdict was sound, given the conflicting nature of the evidence, and he argued that the introduction of additional testimony did not fundamentally alter the facts that had been settled.

George K. Shoenberger (plaintiff) filed a legal case against John McEwen (defendant) in 1884 in Cook County, Illinois. The case was based on a promissory note for $386.24 that McEwen issued to Shoenberger as part payment for two tubular boilers Shoenberger manufactured. Shoenberger's proposal for the boilers included specific details about the construction and the quality of materials to be used. The proposal was accepted by McEwen, and the boilers were built according to these specifications. However, one of the boilers failed due to a defect in the iron used to construct its shell, which was caused by improper rolling at the furnace. During the trial, McEwen claimed damages resulting from the defective boiler, while Shoenberger argued that he had used appropriate materials as specified in their agreement and did not know of the defect. The jury ultimately deducted $222 from McEwen's claimed amount and ruled in favor of Shoenberger for the remaining balance.	Shoenberger argued that he complied with the agreed-upon specifications for the boilers, having used the specified brand of iron and performing necessary tests before delivery. He contended that the failure of the boiler was due to an inherent defect in the material and not a result of any negligence or fraud on his part. He sought enforcement of the promissory note and payment of the remaining amount owed by McEwen.	McEwen argued that the boiler was defective due to the unsound quality of the iron, which he claimed impliedly warranted that Shoenberger should be responsible for the material used. McEwen's defense included evidence of damages incurred due to the boiler's defect and asserted that Shoenberger should be held liable for the substandard materials provided, regardless of whether he had prior knowledge of the defect.

On January 1, 1840, in Adams County, Illinois, Basil D. Stevenson (the appellant) executed a note for $800 in favor of his brother, Samuel Stevenson, promising to pay the amount in Baltimore bank notes with an interest rate of twelve and a half percent after three years. Additionally, he secured the note with a mortgage on specific land. After Samuel Stevenson passed away, Abdiel Unkefer (the appellee), serving as executor of Samuel's estate, initiated foreclosure proceedings on May 15, 1849, regarding the mortgage to recover the amount due on the note. The key legal issue arose around whether the interest rate was usurious according to the applicable statute. The circuit court rendered a judgment in favor of Unkefer, allowing recovery of $1,273.20 plus costs. Stevenson subsequently appealed this decision.	The plaintiff, Abdiel Unkefer, claimed that the loan executed by Basil Stevenson included a legal interest rate even though it was phrased as receiving twelve and a half percent interest in repayment. Unkefer sought to foreclose the mortgage to recover the total amount due as per the terms outlined in the note from the deceased brother Samuel Stevenson.	The defendant, Basil D. Stevenson, argued that the agreement carried an excessive interest rate that violated the anti-usury statute, asserting that the terms could classify the transaction as usurious. His defense was primarily focused on challenging the legality of the stipulated interest rate on the grounds of usury, claiming it rendered the contract invalid.

In September 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Mary E. Jones v. George V. Byrd was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. Mary E. Jones initiated a lawsuit against George V. Byrd through an attachment process, which required notifying the defendant by publication due to the lack of personal service. Byrd did not initially respond to the suit and was defaulted. However, he later appeared in court to contest the default judgment made against him, seeking to have it set aside. The judge presiding over the case was Hon. Josiah McBobebts. The lower court awarded Jones damages amounting to $463.65 plus costs. The case hinged on whether Byrd's appearance to challenge the default constituted a general appearance, which would allow for a personal judgment against him.	The plaintiff, Mary E. Jones, claimed that she was entitled to recover damages of $463.65 from George V. Byrd based on a default judgment that had been rendered in her favor. She argued that the process of attachment and notification by publication was sufficient to proceed with the judgment.	George V. Byrd contended that the appearance he made in court to challenge the default did not equate to a general appearance, which would allow the court to issue a personal judgment against him. Byrd maintained that without personal service, any judgment granted should be limited to in rem only and not include personal liabilities.

The case "The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Co. v. Joseph A. Clutter" took place in 1876 in Illinois. The plaintiff, Joseph A. Clutter, owned eight head of cattle that were either killed or injured due to an accident involving a train operated by the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company. Clutter accused the railway company of negligence for failing to maintain adequate fencing along its tracks, which is required by state law. It was established during the trial that the fence intended to keep livestock away from the railroad tracks was insufficient and had been in disrepair for a prolonged period, indicating that the company must have been aware of this issue. The negligence established that the plaintiff had not been at fault regarding the care of his cattle, leading to his claim for damages amounting to $200 for the loss of the livestock.	Joseph A. Clutter claimed that the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company was liable for the death and injury of his cattle due to their failure to maintain suitable fences along the railroad tracks as mandated by statute. Clutter argued that the negligence of the railway company in not properly safeguarding the tracks directly resulted in his cattle being killed or injured, leading to monetary damages that he sought to recover in the amount of $200.	The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company defended itself by contesting the sufficiency of the evidence regarding the value of the cattle killed. The company’s legal representatives pointed out that some elements of the plaintiff's declaration could be seen as surplusage. They may have also argued that the plaintiff's claims regarding the condition of the fencing did not directly establish their liability or warranted the amount of damages sought.

In July 1885, James O. McConaughy, a real estate broker located in Bochelle, Ogle County, Illinois, was engaged by Cordelia A. Mahannah, a local farm owner, to assist in selling her 241-acre farm. They agreed that McConaughy would advertise the property in two local newspapers, with Mahannah paying for the advertisement in one paper and McConaughy in the other. McConaughy was to receive a 2% commission on the sale price, which was initially set at $35 per acre. After advertising, Cary J. White made an offer of $30 per acre. Mahannah expressed interest in the offer but instructed McConaughy to negotiate better terms with a potential buyer, Peter Smith. However, after some time, White independently purchased the farm for $32 per acre. After Mahannah refused to pay McConaughy the agreed commission of $154.50, he sought to recover this amount through legal proceedings. He initially won the case in a lower court, but Mahannah appealed and the case eventually reached the Illinois Appellate Court.	McConaughy claimed he was entitled to the 2% commission for successfully finding a buyer for Mahannah's farm and argued that the commission was due upon the sale being completed, regardless of the changes in terms. He emphasized that his efforts resulted in the sale to White, and thus he should receive compensation as per their agreement.	Mahannah contended that McConaughy did not fulfill his contractual obligations because the farm was sold under new terms, and he had failed to sell it at the originally stipulated price. She argued that since the sale was not completed according to the agreement, McConaughy was not entitled to any commissions. Furthermore, she maintained that the broker could not demand a commission for a sale brought about through the efforts of another.

The case "Sisters of Loretto, of Chicago, v. The Catholic Bishop of Chicago" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1877. The dispute centers on a property in Chicago that was originally held by the Catholic bishop for parish use. Between 1863 and 1869, the Sisters of Loretto occupied this property for educational purposes. In 1869, the Sisters incorporated as "Sisters of Loretto, of Chicago." After the bishop became incapacitated, a temporary administrator attempted to reconvey the property to the bishop, which raised questions about the authority to do so. The Sisters invested in the property during their occupancy, making improvements and assuming debts. However, due to the illness of their leader, the organization was suggested to be abandoned by the bishop. A deed was executed in 1871 that transferred the property back to the bishop. Shortly after, most of the Sisters left the property, with only one, Mother Ferdinand, pursuing the matter later in court. Mother Ferdinand ultimately filed to cancel the deed, arguing that it was not a voluntary act and that her signature was forged. This led to a protracted legal battle until her death before the case was resolved.	The plaintiff, represented by Mother Ferdinand, contended that the deed reconveying the property to the bishop was invalid. She argued that it was not voluntarily signed by the grantors and claimed that her signature on the deed was forged. The plaintiff sought to have the deed canceled as a cloud on the property title, claiming undue influence was exerted by the bishop and that proper procedures were not followed in executing the deed.	The defendant, the Catholic Bishop of Chicago, maintained that the reconveyance was legitimate and properly executed. The bishop argued there was no evidence of undue influence or coercion during the signing of the deed. The defendant asserted that the president and secretary of the corporation had validly signed the deed, and that abandonment of the property by the other members signified acceptance of the transfer. The bishop denied any allegations of threats or misconduct and requested that the court dismiss the claims made by the plaintiff.

The case of "School Directors of District No. 5 v. School Directors of District No. 1" arose in Illinois, with the initial bill filed on September 6, 1880. The plaintiff, School Directors of District No. 5, alleged that between 1870 and 1873, their taxes meant for school purposes, totaling $1981.63, were mistakenly credited to School District No. 1 due to confusion between the two districts. Consequently, the treasurer of the township, misplacing funds, paid out the money to District No. 1 instead of its rightful owner, District No. 5. The plaintiff sought to recover these misappropriated funds after several years had elapsed, but their initial win in the circuit court was overturned by the Appellate Court. This case was then brought before the Illinois Supreme Court to determine whether the statute of limitations barred the recovery of those funds.	The plaintiff argued that the funds were misallocated school taxes belonging to their district, and they sought recovery of the sum of $1981.63, claiming it constituted public trust funds that should not fall under the statute of limitations. They contended that the township treasurer's mistake led to unjust enrichment on the part of District No. 1, which received and utilized these funds without levying any taxes during the relevant years.	The defendant, School Directors of District No. 1, claimed that the statute of limitations barred the recovery since more than five years had passed since the last payment. They argued there was no trust relationship established that would exempt them from this limitation since the funds were received without fraud or notice of their misallocation. The defendant maintained that the case should be dismissed based on these grounds as it amounted to a personal claim.

Charles W. Thomas et al. v. The People, for use of John Joiner is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 7, 1883. The case originated in St. Clair County, Illinois and involved Charles W. Thomas, who was the master in chancery for the county, and John Joiner, who had been presumed dead after disappearing for over seven years. During this time, Joiner’s brother applied for and obtained letters of administration on Joiner’s estate, believing him to be deceased. While acting as the administrator, Thomas paid Joiner’s share of proceeds from a partition sale to his brother, the administrator. When Joiner reappeared alive, he sought to reclaim the money from Thomas, resulting in a legal dispute over the validity of the actions taken under the administration granted based on the presumption of death. The case raised questions about the jurisdiction of the probate court and whether administration can be granted for a living person's estate.	The plaintiff, John Joiner, argued that the grant of administration on his estate was null and void since he was alive at the time it was issued. He claimed that Charles W. Thomas improperly paid his estate’s money to the administrator (his brother), based on a faulty grant of administration, and thus demanded the return of the $703.87 that Thomas had paid.	Charles W. Thomas, the defendant, contended that the probate court had acted within its authority upon the application for administration, and therefore its grant should be binding. He argued that the jurisdiction was not affected by Joiner's later reappearance and that actions taken under the administration were valid due to the court’s initial engagement with the case.

In 1883, Henry H. Swaim, a wholesale grocer in Bloomington, Illinois, sold a stock of groceries worth $540 on credit to Arnspiger & Lovell, retail grocers in the same city, who mortgaged their stock to secure the debt. Following the sale, the sheriff of McLean County seized the goods on December 20, 1883, under a judgment and execution favoring one of Arnspiger & Lovell's creditors, N. Winslow. Swaim sought the return of the goods, asserting they were fraudulently obtained by Arnspiger & Lovell. The core issue was whether Arnspiger & Lovell's representations during the sale were fraudulent. The jury ruled against the sheriff, leading to an appeal. The case was presided over by the Illinois Appellate Court, with the question of ownership of the goods central to the dispute.	Swaim claimed that the groceries were sold to Arnspiger & Lovell under false and fraudulent representations regarding their financial standing and ability to pay. He argued that these misrepresentations allowed the defendants to unlawfully retain possession of the goods after the execution and sought legal recovery of the groceries based on the fraudulent nature of the sale, asserting his ownership at the time of the suit.	The sheriff, represented by William E. Hughes, contended that Arnspiger & Lovell were the rightful owners of the goods purchased under a legitimate sale agreement. The defense argued that there was insufficient evidence to prove the fraudulent nature of the sale, asserting that the representations made by Arnspiger were not false, and thus the court should uphold the possession of the sheriff pursuant to the execution against Arnspiger & Lovell.

In early 1863, the case of Henry Carpen v. H. H. and R. Hall arose in Morgan County, Illinois. The central figures involved are Henry Carpen, the plaintiff in error, and H. H. and R. Hall, the defendants in error. The dispute emerged from a transaction in which both parties employed the same cattle broker, Florence, to sell their respective cattle. After the sale, the broker allegedly overpaid one party while underpaying the other; specifically, he paid too much to the Halls and too little to Carpen. Carpen then sought legal recourse against the Halls for what he considered money had and received. The core issue of the case was whether Carpen could recover the amount he believed was owed to him due to the broker's payment error.	Henry Carpen alleged that the Halls had received money from the cattle broker that rightfully belonged to him. He argued that the Halls were unjustly enriched by the broker's mistake and requested the court to order the return of the overpaid amount.	The Halls contended that Carpen did not have a legitimate claim to the money in question, as it was not specifically his but belonged to the broker. They argued that the nature of the transaction meant Carpen's claim should be against the broker and not them. They maintained that since the money was not commingled and did not rightfully belong to Carpen, he lacked grounds for his lawsuit seeking recovery from them.

In the case of Timothy Dunn v. Patrick Keegin, which took place in the St. Clair Circuit Court in Illinois, the legal proceedings began at the February term of 1840. Dunn, along with his co-defendants, was engaged in a lawsuit initially filed by Patrick Keegin, who sought a settlement of partnership accounts. On December 26, 1839, a subpoena was served to Dunn and his co-defendant William Doorley. In subsequent court sessions, Dunn filed various legal motions, including a demurrer and a plea in bar, claiming that a full and final settlement had been made with Keegin before the lawsuit was initiated. Throughout the case, Dunn sought to contest the claims against him and requested that the Court set aside defaults and allow him to file a complete answer. However, multiple attempts were made to strike his motions or declarations, with the court maintaining that proper procedure had not been followed, particularly regarding the need for affidavits to support motions. The case continued to evolve through several court terms, culminating in a final hearing in September 1841, where a decree was rendered against Dunn.	Patrick Keegin, the complainant, argued that Dunn and his co-defendants failed to adequately settle their partnership accounts as required. He claimed that proper legal procedures were not followed by Dunn in his responses to the lawsuit. Keegin sought relief by asking for the court to take the bill as confessed against Dunn due to his defaults and lack of sufficient response, thereby requesting a decree affirming his claims for settlement against Dunn and the other defendants.	Timothy Dunn contended that a complete and final settlement had already been achieved with Keegin prior to the initiation of the lawsuit. He filed a plea in bar to substantiate this claim but did not provide the required affidavit to verify his plea. Dunn also argued that his rights were violated when the court ordered the bill to be taken as confessed without due consideration of his plea. He requested that the court set aside the default judgment against him and allow him to file a more complete answer.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. Harless v. Ozias M. Hatch, Secretary of State; Same, ex rel. Keyes v. Jesse K. Dubois, Auditor of Public Accounts" arose in 1863 in Illinois. Key individuals involved included Thomas Harless and Charles A. Keyes as relators seeking writs of mandamus against state officials. The controversy revolved around whether a bill to incorporate the Wabash Railway Company had become law. The bill was presented to the governor on June 12, 1863, but was neither signed nor returned with objections within ten days. The relators argued that the general assembly was in session on the days in question, specifically June 23 and 24, despite the governor's adjournment proclamation on June 10. The court proceedings evaluated the existence of a legislative session and whether the timeline of the governor's actions complied with constitutional provisions.	The plaintiffs, Thomas Harless and Charles A. Keyes, claimed that their respective rights entailed valid compensation and official certification of the bill to incorporate the Wabash Railway Company. They argued that the bill had become law because the governor did not return it with objections within the stipulated time frame, and that the general assembly had not been properly adjourned, thus they were entitled to the legal recognition of the bill and compensation for their legislative service.	The defendants, Ozias M. Hatch (Secretary of State) and Jesse K. Dubois (Auditor), contended that the general assembly was legally adjourned on June 10, 1863, and thus the session concluded before the governor's ten days elapsed to act on the bill. They argued the evidence did not support the existence of a legislative session on June 23 and 24, and the governor's action was supported by the constitutional provision regarding adjournment in cases of disagreement. They maintained that the bill did not become law because it was not returned to the house where it originated.

The case of Isaac Graveson et al. v. Charles Tobey et al. took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the court's final judgment rendered in September 1874. The key individuals involved were Isaac Graveson and his partners (the plaintiffs) who contracted with Charles Tobey and others (the defendants) for stone cutting work on a five-story business building. The contract, made on April 22, 1872, required the plaintiffs to provide and install stone materials and complete their work by August 1 of the same year. However, due to delays caused by the defendants in their previous work, the plaintiffs could only begin their work around the contract's completion date, ultimately finishing on November 6, 1872, and contested by the defendants as completed only in December. The plaintiffs were paid $19,550 for their work, but claimed a remaining balance of $3,510.40 was owed. The defendants countered the claim, arguing that the plaintiffs' delays caused additional damages amounting to $1,570.40 due to the impact on subsequent construction schedules. A trial without a jury resulted in a court decree awarding the plaintiffs $2,000 after accounting for the defendants' claimed damages.	The plaintiffs, Isaac Graveson et al., asserted that although they faced delays due to the defendants' prior work, they completed the stone cutting as per the terms of their contract. They claimed that they were owed $3,510.40 after the $19,550 payment received and sought to enforce a mechanic’s lien against the building for the outstanding amount.	The defendants, Charles Tobey et al., contended that the plaintiffs acted in a dilatory manner, which caused significant delays in the project's completion, leading to greater damages. They argued that the plaintiffs were responsible for delays impacting the entire construction timeline and sought to deduct their assessed damages of $1,570.40 from the plaintiffs' claim.

M. M. Thompson and David Lipe initiated a legal case against J. F. Duff in 1887 in Jackson County, Illinois. The suit was filed in the circuit court as an action in replevin, seeking to recover possession of a portable saw-mill and its accompanying fixtures. During the trial, the jury found in favor of the defendant, J. F. Duff, resulting in a judgment against the plaintiffs. This verdict was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court for the Fourth District. The primary issue at the trial revolved around the question of ownership of the saw-mill, which the court deemed a factual matter. The evidence presented was conflicting regarding ownership. After reviewing the trial and Appellate Court records, the Illinois Supreme Court found no serious errors related to evidence admission, evidence rejection, or jury instructions. The assertion that sufficient grounds did not exist for one of the defendant's instructions was addressed, determining that the judge's prior instructions to the plaintiffs were adequate. Thus, the court did not consider it necessary to repeat content from other instructions.	The plaintiffs, M. M. Thompson and David Lipe, claimed ownership of a portable saw-mill and filed a replevin action to reclaim possession of the property. They argued that the evidence supported their ownership rights and sought to overturn the trial and Appellate Court judgments in favor of the defendant, aiming for a ruling that would return the saw-mill and its fixtures to their possession.	The defendant, J. F. Duff, contended that the plaintiffs did not have valid ownership rights over the portable saw-mill. He argued that the evidence presented during the trial supported his claim and the jury's verdict in his favor. Duff's defense highlighted that the Appellate Court's findings were conclusive, and he maintained that the initial verdict should stand, asserting that there were no significant legal errors in the trial court's handling of evidence and jury instructions.

The case "Abraham Irvin and Elizabeth Irvin, his wife, plaintiffs in error v. George Wright, defendant in error," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1834. The dispute originated in the Gallatin Circuit Court, where an action of assumpsit was brought by George Wright against the Irvins, specifically for compensation related to work performed for Mrs. Irvin while she was still single. The court proceedings were overseen by Judge Thomas C. Browne. The jury ruled in favor of Wright, awarding him $55.25. The Irvins attempted to set off a judgment they had recently recovered against Wright against the damages in this case, but this was met with a demurrer from Wright, which the Circuit Court sustained.	The plaintiffs, Abraham and Elizabeth Irvin, contended that they should be able to set off a judgment they had obtained against George Wright against the damages he claimed from them in his suit. They argued that their statutory provisions allowed for this kind of set-off to include claims or demands that arose after the initiation of the suit, suggesting that the statute's language was broader than comparable English laws.	George Wright, the defendant, maintained that the judgment he had received after the suit had started could not be used as a set-off against the claims made by the plaintiffs. He argued that the relevant statutes regarding set-offs were constructed similarly under Illinois law and English law, and thus, only debts or demands that existed prior to the action could qualify for such treatment. The Circuit Court agreed with Wright and sustained the demurrer to the Irvins’ claim.

The legal case "Canute R. Matson, use, etc., v. John L. Swanson et al." took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the judgment delivered on January 21, 1890. The case originated from an action of debt initiated by Canute R. Matson, the sheriff of Cook County, against John L. Swanson and others. The dispute arose following a writ of capias ad satisfaciendum issued in favor of John Carlson against Henry Bodelsen, who was held in custody by Matson. On January 7, 1887, Bodelsen petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and was subsequently released from custody after entering a recognizance bond, with Swanson and Charles A. Florence as sureties. However, Bodelsen failed to appear in court as required, leading to the forfeiture of the bond. Matson sought to recover the forfeited amount, claiming the defendants had breached their obligation. The Appellate Court initially reversed the circuit court's judgment citing issues with the declaration and the validity of the bond.	Canute R. Matson claimed the defendants, John L. Swanson and Charles A. Florence, failed to fulfill their obligations under a recognizance bond. Matson argued that the bond, which was forfeited due to Bodelsen's failure to appear in court, was valid despite the defendants' assertions to the contrary. He sought recovery of the $4,000 specified in the bond, asserting that their refusal to pay totaled to damages that warranted a debt action.	The defendants, Swanson and Florence, denied owing the amount claimed by Matson, asserting multiple defenses. They argued that the bond was not valid as it was not their deed and contended that the underlying writ was based on an improper or illegal custody arrangement. Additionally, they claimed that the bond was executed under a void consideration, as it was allegedly for the wrongful release of Bodelsen, who was unlawfully let go by Matson. They contended that the conditions of the bond were not legal and therefore, Matson should not be entitled to the amount demanded.

In September 1867, in Chicago, Illinois, Charles Gretzner filed a lawsuit against the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company following a collision between the railroad's train and Gretzner's wagon. As a result of this incident, Gretzner sustained serious injuries. The case was initiated in the Superior Court of Chicago, where the plaintiff claimed that the collision was due to the negligence of the railroad company. Specifically, he contended that the train was operated at an excessive speed, that a flagman was not present at the street crossing, and that the train did not ring its bell as required. The jury initially ruled in favor of Gretzner, awarding him $7,500. However, upon appeal, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the evidence, which indicated that the railroad company did ring its bell continuously and that the train was moving at a reduced speed. Witness testimonies from both sides were heavily scrutinized, revealing significant deficiencies in the evidence supporting the plaintiff's claims.	Charles Gretzner alleged that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was negligent for several reasons. He claimed that the train was traveling at an unsafe speed and that there was no flagman present at the crossing to warn him of the oncoming train. Additionally, he asserted that the train did not ring its bell, which further constituted negligence. Gretzner sought damages for the injuries he sustained due to this alleged negligence.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company defended itself by arguing that it had adhered to all safety protocols, including ringing the bell before the collision and operating the train at a safe speed. They provided testimonies from various crew members and bystanders confirming that a flagman was present and signaling appropriately at the time of the incident. The railroad contended that the evidence overwhelmingly favored their position and claimed that any negligence was attributable to Gretzner's actions, as he failed to observe proper caution while approaching the crossing.

In January 1863, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case originating from Morgan County, Illinois, involving parties Isaac Scarritt and Samuel Carruthers. The case arose from an action in assumpsit over a promissory note made by the defendants, Carruthers, which the plaintiffs, Scarritt and others, claimed had been executed by them. At trial, the defendants pleaded non-assumpsit, disputing the validity of their signatures on the note. Witnesses testified for both sides regarding the authenticity of the signatures, with some supporting the plaintiffs' claim and others denying it. The jury ultimately found in favor of the defendants, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal the verdict to the Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs argued that the signatures on the promissory note in question were genuine and that they were therefore entitled to the money indicated in the note. They contended that evidence presented in the trial supported their position, and they requested that the jury's verdict be overturned in their favor.	The defendants maintained that the signatures on the promissory note were not their own, presenting witness testimony to support their claims. They argued that the evidence did not sufficiently prove the authenticity of the signatures and requested that the jury's verdict in their favor be upheld.

In the case of Harman Brown v. The People of the State of Illinois, which took place in January 1866 in Madison County, Illinois, the defendant, Harman Brown, faced an indictment for manslaughter. This incident occurred when Brown was at his home during the night. He was alerted that his brother and another individual, Burnet, were coming to confront him. When they arrived, they forcibly broke into his home through the door and window. In response to this violent intrusion, Brown struck the deceased with a poker, leading to the latter's death the following day. Brown was initially found guilty and sentenced to one year in prison, but he appealed the decision, arguing that he acted in self-defense to protect his home during a riotous and violent attack.	The plaintiff, representing the State of Illinois, maintained that Brown's actions constituted unlawful manslaughter, asserting that he should be held accountable for the death resulting from the altercation. The claims revolved around the notion that Brown lacked justification for his use of deadly force against the deceased.	Brown's defense centered on the argument of justifiable homicide, emphasizing that he was acting in defense of his habitation. He contended that he had been warned of the imminent violent entry by the deceased and others, which rightfully justified his defensive action. Brown maintained that his response was necessary to protect himself and his home from an aggressive attack, which satisfied the conditions of self-defense outlined in the Criminal Code.

The case of J. Young Scammon v. The City of Chicago took place in April 1866, in Chicago, Illinois. The legal matter centered on a proceeding to condemn certain lots in the city for unpaid special assessments levied to fund the paving of a section of Wabash Avenue. The plaintiff, J. Young Scammon, appealed a judgment against the lots, contending that the legal requirements for notice regarding the assessment were not properly followed. Specifically, the law mandated six days of publication of the notice in the city's corporation newspaper after filing the assessment roll. A key issue arose regarding a publication made on Sunday, which was one of the days counted toward the required notice. The court had to address if such a publication could be valid since the common law viewed Sunday as an inappropriate day for legal proceedings and notifications. The Supreme Court of Illinois ultimately focused on the strict adherence to legal notice requirements, asserting that the law concerning the publication and timing was not followed properly.	The plaintiff, J. Young Scammon, argued that the notice requirements for the publication of the assessment roll were not satisfied, as one of the days counted was a Sunday. He claimed that according to the charter of Chicago, the publication had to occur on six different days, and counting a Sunday publication violated the strict legal standards required for such proceedings.	The City of Chicago, represented by the defendant, contended that the publication on Sunday should be considered valid. They might have argued that the notice was sufficient under the circumstances and that following through on the assessment was important for municipal operations and funding.

The case "Charles J. Johnson et al. v. Whiteside County" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 19, 1884. It originated in August 1882 during a term in the Whiteside Circuit Court, where four individuals were indicted for forgery. Unable to afford legal counsel, the court appointed Charles J. Johnson and others as attorneys to represent the defendants. After representing two of the accused, who were subsequently convicted, Johnson and his co-plaintiffs sought compensation from the Whiteside County's board of supervisors for their legal services, amounting to $100. The board denied this request, leading Johnson and his colleagues to file a lawsuit against the county. The circuit court ruled in favor of the county, prompting an appeal to the Appellate Court, which upheld the circuit court's decision. The case thus reached the Illinois Supreme Court, where the central question was whether the county had a legal obligation to pay for the services of court-appointed counsel defending indigent defendants in criminal trials.	The plaintiffs argued that as court-appointed attorneys, they were entitled to compensation for their legal services rendered in defense of individuals who could not afford counsel. They claimed that the county had an obligation to pay for services provided in accordance with the court's assignment, as this duty stemmed from the legal framework governing criminal defense.	The county contended that it was not liable for compensation to attorneys assigned by the court. The defense maintained that the prosecution was conducted on behalf of the state, not the county, and that the attorneys were fulfilling a duty without formal employment by the county. The county asserted that there was no statutory or common law obligation requiring it to compensate for legal defense of indigent defendants.

On April 29, 1885, the Englewood Connecting Railway Company filed a petition in the Cook County court, seeking to construct a railroad crossing over the tracks of the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company in the town of Lake, Illinois. This crossing was deemed essential for the Englewood Railway's operations, allowing a connection from the Chicago, St. Louis and Pittsburgh railroad to another rail line. The Englewood Railway Company offered to fund the construction and maintenance of the necessary crossing at its own expense. However, the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company opposed this, citing the proposed crossing as harmful to its operations, arguing that it would diminish the value and capacity of its railroad and cause financial losses. The case went to trial before a jury, resulting in a judgment favoring the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company.	The Englewood Connecting Railway Company's main argument was that the crossing was required for its railroad operations and that they were willing to bear all costs associated with its construction and maintenance. The plaintiff sought just compensation to be assessed by a jury for the right to cross over the existing railroad tracks.	The Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company's defenses included asserting that the proposed crossing would greatly hinder its operations and diminish the value of its railroad. The defendant argued that any damages resulting from the crossing should not be limited to just physical injury, and they sought the right to demonstrate how their capacity to conduct business would be impaired as a result of the new crossing.

Abraham Bernstein initiated a legal case against William Patterson in 1889 in Cook County, Illinois. The case arose from Bernstein's claim that he had overpaid for goods purchased from Patterson, totaling $70, for which he had given notes secured by a chattel mortgage. Bernstein, who was unable to read or write, stated that he had relied on a third party to assist him in accounting for his payments. He claimed to have paid the first two notes shortly after they were issued and continued making payments over the next sixteen months, allegedly totaling over $8120. However, he was only able to provide receipts amounting to $860.20, which he argued entitled him to a refund of $860, assuming he had overpaid after deducting the value of goods taken back under the mortgage. Bernstein was the only witness for his side, and his credibility was challenged, particularly since the constable who assisted him was not presented in court. The defendant's representatives disputed Bernstein's claims and provided contradictory testimony regarding the transaction.	Bernstein claimed that he had overpaid for the goods purchased from Patterson, seeking recovery of the alleged surplus amount he had paid. He argued that due to his inability to read or write, he trusted a third party to handle the calculations related to his payments and claimed that he had actually paid more than what was owed, thus justifying his request for a refund.	Patterson did not appear in court to defend himself, which limited the representation of his side of the case. However, the appellant's attorney disputed Bernstein's claims, arguing that the testimony provided by Bernstein was not credible and that the evidence did not warrant a recovery in his favor. The defense essentially challenged the validity of Bernstein's assertions regarding overpayment.

In December 1835, a legal dispute arose in Gallatin County, Illinois, between Oliver C. Vanlandingham (the appellant) and Thomas Lowery (the appellee). The case stemmed from two actions instituted in the Circuit Court of Gallatin, where both parties agreed to refer their cases to a jury of twelve disinterested individuals. The jurors were to be summoned by the sheriff or constable, with a meeting scheduled in Shawneetown after the regular Circuit Court proceedings. Both parties were required to give a week's notice before this jury convened. The proceedings were conducted under a specific agreement, which was affirmed in subsequent court terms after being unaddressed. The jury rendered verdicts for both cases, which were then presented to the Circuit Court. Despite some objections raised regarding the judgments on these verdicts, the court found no evidence of any irregularities in the process or deviations from the agreed procedures. Consequently, the Circuit Court presumed the proceedings were properly conducted and regular.	The plaintiff, Oliver C. Vanlandingham, contended that there were errors in the judgment rendered by the Circuit Court in favor of the defendant, Thomas Lowery. Vanlandingham appealed the decisions from the Gallatin Circuit Court, asserting that the judgments against him were erroneous and required reconsideration.	The defendant, Thomas Lowery, maintained that the proceedings were conducted in accordance with the mutual agreement between the parties and defended the regularity of the jury's selections and the judgments rendered. Lowery's position rested on the lack of evidence from Vanlandingham to substantiate any claims of irregularity in the process used, arguing that the onus was on the plaintiff to provide proof of any alleged misconduct before seeking to set aside the proceedings.

George S. Poppers sued Mary J. Meager after a distress warrant was filed against him on April 6, 1887, in Cook County, Illinois. The distress warrant was executed by agents Baird & Bradley, resulting in the levying of Poppers' goods on May 3, 1887. Poppers contested this action, arguing that the rent for which the warrant was issued had already been paid pursuant to a previous Circuit Court decree enforcing a lease renewal. The key issue at trial was Poppers' alleged indebtedness. The jury trial allowed a witness to testify about Baird & Bradley's agency status on behalf of Meager, despite Poppers' objections. Subsequently, a verdict was rendered in favor of Meager for the costs associated with the custody of the seized goods, which Poppers appealed. The case hinged on interpretations of the landlord-tenant laws regarding costs and agency.	Poppers contended that he owed no debt, as the rent for which the distress warrant had been issued was paid in compliance with a previous court order. He argued the jury was improperly allowed to determine costs related to the custody of the levied goods and asserted that the expenses should have been assessed by the court rather than the jury.	Meager argued that the agency of Baird & Bradley was established by their actions under the distress warrant, thus making the costs associated with the custody of the levied goods recoverable. She maintained that the jury's decision to grant her these costs was appropriate and aligned with statutory guidelines concerning landlord-tenant law.

In the case of Prussing Vinegar Company v. John S. Meyer, the events took place in Cook County, Illinois, surrounding an employment and promissory note dispute. John W. Prussing was employed as a traveling salesman for the Prussing Vinegar Company, starting on August 1, 1884, with an agreement to be paid $3,000 yearly plus expenses. After a few months, Prussing fell ill and was unable to perform his duties from December 12, 1884, for about five months. During this period, the company continued to credit him his full salary, which led to a buildup of a debt amounting to $328.01 during his illness. Prussing subsequently received a promissory note from the company on December 29, 1884, for the aforementioned debt, which was due four months later. However, after Prussing's illness, the company later contested this debt, arguing he should not have been credited for his wages during that period. Following a series of assignments of the note and a waiver of jury trial, the case was tried, and the plaintiff was awarded damages based on their claims related to the promissory note.	John S. Meyer, as the plaintiff, claimed that the Prussing Vinegar Company owed him the amount of the promissory note ($578.01) for salary and expenses that were due. He argued that the company had previously acknowledged the debt and settled it by crediting him the full wage despite his illness. Meyer sought recovery of the amount stipulated in the note along with necessary costs incurred.	The defendant, Prussing Vinegar Company, defended against the plaintiff’s claims by asserting non-assumpsit, a failure of consideration, and a set-off. They argued that Prussing’s salary payments should not have been made during his illness, and hence sought to contest the validity of the promissory note based on those grounds. They claimed the understanding of the employment agreement had changed due to Prussing’s alleged lack of service during his sickness.

The case "The Germania Fire Insurance Company v. Emil Klewer" took place in Illinois, with the court proceedings occurring in the late 1880s, particularly culminating on October 31, 1889. The dispute arose after a fire destroyed a house owned by Emil Klewer in Norwood Park, Illinois, on November 15, 1885. Klewer had taken out multiple insurance policies for the house and its contents, including a policy from the Germania Fire Insurance Company dated October 16, 1885. The key individuals involved were Emil Klewer (the plaintiff) and the Germania Fire Insurance Company (the defendant).	The plaintiff, Emil Klewer, argued that the Germania Fire Insurance Company's policy was valid and should cover the damages from the fire that took place after the previous policy expired. He contended that at the time of issuing the Germania policy, the earlier Hartford policy was void due to the house being vacant without consent, and thus it should not affect his right to collect under the Germania policy. Additionally, he claimed the defendant's other defenses regarding other insurance and vacancy were unfounded, asserting that the insurance company had waived those conditions through its agent's actions.	The Germania Fire Insurance Company defended itself by asserting that Klewer's claim was invalid due to several reasons: (1) the existence of another insurance policy (the one from Hartford) at the time the Germania policy was issued, which breached the contract terms; (2) that the house laid vacant for over ten days prior to the issuance of their policy, a condition that voided their coverage; and (3) the allegation that Klewer himself set the fire, which they maintained needed to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt due to its criminal nature.

Franklin Sawyer v. Susanna Martins is a legal case that took place in Chicago, Illinois, with the final decision rendered on March 28, 1888, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose from an incident on May 11, 1885, when Thomas B. Martins, the plaintiff's minor son, was injured due to the negligence associated with the removal of a sign-board from a building owned by the defendant, Franklin Sawyer. The removal of the sign was initiated by Charles D. Bockwood, a person who had a conversation with Sawyer about the signs left by a previous tenant. Sawyer claimed that the signs did not belong to him and had been abandoned, suggesting that anyone could take them down. On the day of the incident, employees of Bockwood, assisted by Sawyer's 15-year-old son, attempted to remove the signs when one of the sign-boards fell and struck Thomas, resulting in severe injury, including a broken leg. The jury found both Sawyer and Bockwood liable for the injuries but assessed different damages against them. The case presented complex issues around negligence and liability given Sawyer's claims of non-involvement in the removal of the signs.	Susanna Martins, the plaintiff, claimed that her son was injured due to the negligence of the defendants while they were removing the sign-boards from Sawyer's building. She sought damages for the loss of services and expenses incurred as a result of her son's injuries, which directly resulted from the actions of the defendants and their servants during the sign's removal.	Franklin Sawyer's defense centered around the assertion that he was not liable for the injury sustained by the plaintiff's son, as the removal of the signs was not conducted under his authority or instruction. Sawyer maintained that he had given no directions for the signs to be taken down and argued that any actions taken by his son or other persons during the incident were outside the scope of his employment and responsibility, thus negating the applicability of the legal doctrine "respondeat superior.

John M. Easton filed a legal case against G. M. Mitchell, which took place in Charleston, Illinois. The case revolved around a lease agreement executed on March 11, 1879, allowing Mitchell, who had been appointed postmaster of Charleston, to rent a room from Easton for use as a post office. The initial lease was for the duration of Mitchell's term as postmaster, which lasted four years, until April 1881. Before the lease expired, Easton informed Mitchell that after the term ended, he would need to vacate the premises or pay increased rent. However, Mitchell continued to occupy the building for an additional fifteen months after his initial term expired. The case arose when Easton claimed that the lease ended in April 1881, and he sought a recovery based on quantum meruit for the time Mitchell occupied the premises after the lease expired. The lower court excluded relevant evidence and instructed the jury to favor Mitchell, leading to Easton's appeal.	The plaintiff, John M. Easton, argued that the lease agreement with G. M. Mitchell had expired with the conclusion of Mitchell's first term as postmaster in April 1881. Easton contended that, after this expiration, he was entitled to compensation for Mitchell's continued occupancy of the property based on a claim of quantum meruit. He sought to have the court determine a reasonable amount due from Mitchell for the time he unlawfully occupied the premises.	G. M. Mitchell, the defendant, contended that the lease should be interpreted to extend beyond the initial term set in April 1881 because he was reappointed postmaster and continued to occupy the space under that assumption. He argued against the plaintiff's claim for additional rent or compensation and claimed that the lease was valid for the duration of his service as postmaster, implying that no additional rent was owed after the expiration of the first commission.

In June 1857, in Sycamore, De Kalb County, Illinois, Charles O. Boynton and George Walrodt, along with Hiram E. Whitney, faced litigation involving an injunction bond. The case arose when a court-ordered injunction was dissolved, resulting in claims that the associated judgment had not been paid. Boynton and Walrodt, as sureties for the bond, argued they were misled by Whitney. They asserted that Whitney, perceived as financially irresponsible, was induced by the plaintiffs to dismiss his bill in chancery, thereby forcing the sureties to become liable on the bond. The plaintiffs were said to have conspired with Whitney, corruptly agreeing to dismiss the injunction in exchange for delaying payment on an old debt owed by Whitney’s father. This supposed collusion aimed to unjustly shift financial responsibility to the sureties, violating ethical legal principles. The case ultimately reached the Illinois Supreme Court, where the complexities of fraudulent inducement and liability would be thoroughly examined.	The plaintiffs, Boynton and Walrodt, claimed that their obligation as sureties arose from the purportedly valid execution of the bond. They requested enforcement of the bond, asserting that the dissolution of the injunction was legitimate and that the dismissal of the bill was done without unlawful inducement from them.	The defendants countered with multiple pleas, arguing that the dissolution of the injunction was fraudulent, having been obtained through collusion between the plaintiffs and Whitney to harm the defendants. They claimed that the plaintiffs’ corrupt agreement to dismiss the bill was executed without their knowledge, making any resulting liability on the bond void. They sought judgment to dismiss the action against them based on this fraudulent conduct.

John Powers initiated this legal action against Thomas Cavenaugh in 1885, seeking to recover a judgment for rent and associated matters. The case began in a lower justice court where Powers initially won a judgment of $97 against Cavenaugh. However, Cavenaugh sought to appeal this decision, resulting in a trial at the circuit court level. During this trial, the jury found in favor of Cavenaugh, awarding him a verdict of $77, which was later reduced by remittitur to $68, leading to a judgment entered against Powers. The plaintiff, John Powers, subsequently appealed the circuit court's decision, arguing that the jury's verdict was significantly contrary to the evidence presented. The case was presided over by Judge Lyman Lacey in Mason County, Illinois, during a time when legal procedures and jury trials were evolving.	John Powers argued that the jury's verdict was against the weight of the evidence, claiming that there was enough credible evidence in his favor warranting the original judgment. He requested that the appellate court set aside the jury’s verdict and grant a new trial, asserting that the trial court failed to adequately correct the incorrect verdict.	Thomas Cavenaugh maintained that the jury's verdict was appropriate and just, given the conflicting evidence. He argued that the jury was properly instructed on the law during the trial and therefore their conclusions should not be disturbed. Cavenaugh sought to affirm the judgment of the circuit court, dismissing Powers' claims as unfounded.

The case of The Pennsylvania Railroad Company v. William J. Connell arose in 1884, stemming from an incident that took place on December 16, 1880, at Tacona, a station near West Philadelphia. The plaintiff, William J. Connell, had purchased a coupon ticket from the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company for travel from Omaha to New York, which was to include passage on the Pennsylvania Railroad. Later, upon boarding the Pennsylvania Railroad train, the conductor refused to accept Connell's ticket, demanding fare instead. When Connell did not comply and refused to leave the train, the conductor forcibly expelled him. Connell subsequently filed a lawsuit against the Pennsylvania Railroad Company in the Cook County Superior Court, seeking damages for the forcible removal. The jury ruled in favor of Connell, awarding him $15,000, a decision that was upheld by the Appellate Court. The case ultimately reached the Illinois Supreme Court for appeal.	Connell claimed that he had a valid ticket for his journey and sought damages for being forcibly removed from the train. He argued that by selling him the ticket, the Wabash company acted as an agent of the Pennsylvania Railroad, which was obligated to honor the ticket. Connell contended that he was entitled to compensation for the wrongful expulsion, loss of time, and any injuries incurred as a result.	The Pennsylvania Railroad Company contended that the Wabash company acted as an agent when selling the ticket and was not liable for Connell's transportation beyond its own road. The defendant argued that the conductor's refusal to accept the ticket was justified due to instructions received from superiors, and that Connell should have either paid the fare or exited the train. They maintained that the force used to remove Connell from the train was appropriate given his non-compliance.

In 1872, the case of Jefferson A. Davis et al. v. John H. Wilson arose in the town of Olio, Illinois, during an election. The plaintiffs, led by Jefferson A. Davis, were involved in what they claimed was false imprisonment during the election proceedings. The defendants, John H. Wilson and others, acted as judges of the election and alleged that the plaintiffs behaved disorderly at the polls. After fining Davis $20 for his conduct, the judges ordered that he be taken to jail when he refused to pay the fine. Constables called for assistance from the defendants to enforce this order. Davis resisted, leading to his alleged wrongful confinement. The case proceeded through the Woodford circuit court, where the jury found in favor of the plaintiffs and awarded $5,000 in damages. The defendants appealed the decision, arguing that the lower court erred in adjudicating the validity of their actions under the election laws.	The plaintiffs claimed that their wrongful imprisonment was unjust. They argued that the actions of the defendants, in fining Davis without proper written orders and detaining him, constituted false imprisonment. They contended that the judges of the election failed to follow the necessary legal procedures, such as issuing a written mittimus, which led to a violation of their rights. The plaintiffs sought compensation for the damages incurred due to this wrongful act.	The defendants defended their actions by asserting that as judges of the election, they were legally obligated to maintain order and ensure the proper conduct of the election. They claimed that Davis's disorderly conduct justified their actions in issuing a fine and facilitating his detention when he refused to comply. They argued that their pleas were valid, despite the lower court's ruling on various procedural discrepancies, asserting that they acted within their authority and followed the necessary procedures under election law.

The case "Caleb H. Booth v. Josephine C. Smith" originated in Cook County, Illinois, with proceedings taking place in the Superior Court. The dispute arose from a series of representations made by Oliver H. Parsons, the president of the Western Indiana Coal Company, to Josephine C. Smith's husband, leading to Smith's purchase of 392 shares of the company’s stock for $4,000. Parsons had falsely claimed that the company was successfully operating a coal mine, making it attractive for investment, asserting the stockholders had invested more than they actually had, and stating that the mine was profitable. Smith alleged that these representations led her to be deceived into paying for stock that was essentially worthless. Further complications arose when Booth, a shareholder, made a claim against the company for $2,000, which Smith asserted was without merit and part of a larger pattern of collusion among the company's directors. The case highlights issues of misrepresentation and fraudulent inducement concerning corporate investments.	Josephine C. Smith claimed that she was defrauded by Parsons' false representations concerning the profitability and value of the coal mine owned by the Western Indiana Coal Company. She sought restitution for the $4,000 she paid for the shares, accounting from the company, and requested the court to enjoin Booth from pursuing his claims against the company. Additionally, she wanted a receiver appointed to manage the company’s assets and argued for further action against Parsons and Booth for their respective roles in the deception.	Caleb H. Booth’s defense contested the allegations made by Smith, arguing that she did not rely on Parsons' representations when purchasing the stock, as her agent had conducted independent investigations. Booth maintained that he was a rightful shareholder and that the stock sale was conducted with the understanding that part of the payment was to be treated as a loan to the company. He denied any fraud or misrepresentation and sought to have the court dismiss Smith's claims against him due to a lack of evidence tying him to the alleged fraudulent actions.

In 1886, in McLean County, Illinois, the legal dispute arose in the case of Margaret A. Haldeman v. Perry F. Sennett. The case was initiated by Margaret A. Haldeman, who brought an action of assumpsit against Perry F. Sennett, seeking to recover an outstanding balance of $40.39 that she claimed was owed to her. The fundamental issue revolved around this alleged debt, with the defendant countering the claim. The jury ultimately rendered a verdict for the defendant, deciding in his favor on the plea of set-off, which indicated that Sennett had a valid reason or claim that reduced or negated Haldeman's claim. A motion for a new trial filed by Haldeman was denied, and the court upheld the jury's findings, indicating that while evidence was conflicted, there was sufficient basis for the verdict. The legal proceedings highlighted the importance of evidence and jury instructions, as the court found no grounds to overturn the judgment based on the objections raised by Haldeman's side.	The plaintiff, Margaret A. Haldeman, claimed that she was owed a balance of $40.39 from Perry F. Sennett. She sought recovery of this amount through legal action, asserting that the defendant had defaulted on the payment. Haldeman's main argument centered on the validity of her claim and the assertion that the evidence presented warranted the jury's verdict in her favor.	Perry F. Sennett, the defendant, responded with pleas of non-assumpsit and set-off. His defenses included contesting the debt claimed by Haldeman and arguing that there were offsets due to obligations or claims against her.
