The jury found in favor of Sennett, suggesting that he had a legitimate defense that justified the reduction of the amount claimed by Haldeman.

In the case of Benjamin F. Fridley v. Edwin A. Bowen, which took place in September 1877 before the Illinois Supreme Court, the plaintiff Benjamin F. Fridley was involved in a legal dispute regarding a foreclosure. The case originated from a mortgage taken by Edmund D. Taylor, which was intended to secure a promissory note of $10,000 payable to Edwin A. Bowen at the National Bank of Mendota, with interest of ten percent per annum. Fridley was made a defendant in this foreclosure action, and when he failed to appear in court, a default judgment was entered against him along with other defendants as per the court's rules. Fridley subsequently filed a motion to set aside this default, asserting that he had acted in good faith and believed, based on prior communications, that no steps would be taken in the case until after January 15, 1877. Despite his motion being supported by affidavits, the court found that while Fridley had made a sufficient cause for setting aside the default, his answers did not provide a valid defense against the underlying bill.	The plaintiff, Benjamin F. Fridley, claimed that he was wrongly defaulted in the foreclosure proceedings initiated by Edwin A. Bowen due to a misunderstanding regarding the timeline for taking legal steps. He requested the court to set aside the default judgment against him, asserting that he acted in good faith and believed there was an agreement with Bowen's counsel regarding a delay in proceedings. He filed an answer to the merits of the bill, seeking to be allowed to contest the foreclosure.	The defendant, Edwin A. Bowen, contended that the default judgment entered against Fridley was justified. In addition, Bowen argued that the mortgage in question was void due to violations of banking laws, claiming that the national bank could not legally accept real estate as collateral for loans. Bowen asserted that the mortgage to one of the bank's officers was effectively a loan made to the bank itself, which contravened the provisions of the national banking laws.

The case "Andrew Wheeler v. Stephen P. Mather" took place in September 1870 in Will County, Illinois, and was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a contractual agreement made on April 1, 1861, where Stephen P. Mather (the defendant) agreed to sell real estate to Andrew Wheeler (the plaintiff) in exchange for a total payment of $1,892. This payment was to be made in installments, with particular amounts due by specified dates, and the agreement stipulated that timely payment was essential. The contract also granted Mather the right to declare it void if Wheeler failed to meet his payment obligations. Wheeler made an initial payment but subsequently defaulted on further payments. In August 1862, Mather issued a notice declaring the contract void due to Wheeler's defaults. Wheeler sought to recover the money he had already paid, claiming entitlement despite his payment failures. The trial revealed that Wheeler lacked any defense against his defaults and did not allege any wrongdoings by Mather.	Andrew Wheeler claimed that he was entitled to recover the money he had already paid under the contract because he believed that Mather's declaration of the contract's termination was unfounded. He argued that, since Mather had terminated the contract, he should return the payments made by Wheeler. Wheeler contended that the contract did not specify a forfeiture of the amounts paid upon termination and that the jury should consider his claims irrespective of his prior defaults.	Stephen P. Mather contended that Wheeler's failure to make timely payments constituted a breach of the contractual terms, allowing him to rightfully terminate the agreement. Mather argued that since Wheeler was at fault and failed to fulfill his payment obligations, he was not entitled to recover any funds. Mather asserted that the contract explicitly granted him the right to declare it void due to Wheeler's non-compliance, reinforcing that he had acted within his legal rights as stipulated in the agreement.

The case, titled "The Teutonia Life Insurance Company v. Mary Mueller et al.", was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875. The action originated in Tazewell County and involved a life insurance policy held by Charles Mueller, who had passed away. Initially initiated by Aloes Maier, the administrator of Mueller’s estate, the case saw a change in plaintiffs as the court permitted Mary Mueller and the heirs of the deceased—Mary Maier, Kate Mueller, Millie Mueller, Carrie Mueller, and Henry Mueller—to be substituted as the legal representatives of the claim. The legal proceedings centered around a life insurance policy issued on August 12, 1873, through the "Bismark Bund" association, which provided life insurance to its members in exchange for weekly dues, later to be paid in quarterly premiums. After Mueller's death, the insurance company refused payment, citing that he was in arrears with his dues to the organization and claiming that no premiums had been paid. This refusal was contested in court.	The plaintiffs argued that the life insurance policy was valid and enforceable despite any dues owed to the Bismark Bund, asserting that the insurance company could not contest the policy's validity due to their obligation to pay for the premiums on behalf of the members of the association. They contended that all necessary premiums for the insurance coverage had been paid by the Bismark Bund and that the company’s refusal to honor the policy following Mueller's death was unjustified.	The defendant, the Teutonia Life Insurance Company, claimed that the policy should not be enforced because Charles Mueller was in arrears regarding his dues to the Bismark Bund at the time of his death. They argued that this failure constituted a valid ground to refuse payment on the insurance policy, suggesting that the contract could be rescinded due to the non-payment of dues to the association which established the insurance coverage.

In the case of Warren R. Buckley et al. v. Thomas B. Holmes, decided on June 9, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the dispute arose from a breach of contract involving the sale of corn. The plaintiffs, Warren R. Buckley and others, had directed the defendant, Thomas B. Holmes, to purchase 40,000 bushels of corn for future delivery. The transaction was supposed to take place on September 20, 1885. However, on that date, Holmes failed to make the purchase as agreed. Buckley had prior sold 20,000 bushels of corn at a price of fifty-five cents per bushel, anticipating the execution of the contract with Holmes. When Holmes later notified Buckley that he had not fulfilled the purchase, Buckley proceeded to buy corn at a higher price of fifty-seven and one-quarter cents per bushel to cover his previous sale. The trial court initially awarded Buckley damages, but the case hinged on the appropriate measure of damages for the breach of contract and the scope of what could be claimed under that breach.	The plaintiffs contended that they suffered significant financial losses due to the defendant's failure to execute the purchase of corn as agreed. They asserted that the price increase in corn from the contract date to the date they had to buy in order to fulfill their sale caused them to incur substantial damages, which should be compensated. They argued for a measure of damages that included not only the difference between the contract price and the market price at the time of delivery but also for special damages related to the direct consequences of the breach.	The defendant argued that the plaintiffs' claims for significant damages were unfounded. He maintained that the proper measure of damages should be limited to the difference between the contract price and the market price at the time of delivery, which did not amount to a loss since the market price fell. Holmes contended that the plaintiffs were responsible for their own losses due to their prior sale of corn and that no legitimate special damages were adequately claimed or proven in the pleadings.

Reuben Putnam filed a legal action against Case Wadley in Kankakee County, Illinois, in 1866, seeking to recover on a lost promissory note dated September 17 or 18, involving an amount of fifty-eight dollars and fifty cents plus interest. The case began before a justice of the peace and was subsequently moved to the Circuit Court due to an appeal. Putnam presented an affidavit claiming to have held the note, which he alleged was lost. In response, Wadley denied having executed the note through his own affidavit. The trial revealed conflicting testimonies surrounding the execution of the note. The jury ultimately found in favor of the defendant, Wadley, after reviewing the evidence that suggested doubts about the note's validity.	Putnam's primary claims included that he had possession of a valid promissory note from Wadley, which he summarized in his affidavit. He sought to recover the lost note's amount, asserting its legitimacy and requesting a ruling in his favor to enforce the note and secure judgment for the sum owed.	Wadley's defense centered around denying the execution of the note. He provided evidence that supported his claim, indicating that during a conversation about an old store account, Putnam never mentioned any note, implying that the claim was unfounded. Furthermore, Wadley challenged the adequacy of the proof presented by Putnam in establishing the note’s authenticity, emphasizing that familiarity with his handwriting was necessary for valid testimony.

Sarah M. Palmer v. Thomas Snell is a legal case that originated in the Circuit Court of DeWitt County, Illinois. The dispute centers around a mortgage foreclosure involving three small tracts of land. The mortgage, initially executed by Smith Taylor and his wife, was intended to secure a debt of $4,500 and later transferred to multiple parties, ultimately ending with Thomas Snell. While all defendants were served and agreed to the claims except for Sarah M. Palmer, who appeared, answered, and filed a cross-bill. Palmer acknowledged the mortgage's existence but contended that her late husband, Ezekiel H. Palmer, had purchased a ten-acre tract after the mortgage was executed, relying on an alleged verbal agreement for its release upon payment of a portion of the debt—an agreement she claimed was honored by her husband, with payment having been made. The case progressed through various court levels, including an initial favorable ruling for Palmer that was subsequently overturned by the Appellate Court, which led to the case being remanded back for re-evaluation. Ultimately, the Circuit Court ordered a foreclosure on all mortgaged premises, but allowed the ten-acre tract to remain free of the mortgage. This decision was affirmed on appeal, prompting Sarah M. Palmer to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court for a final judgment on the matter.	Sarah M. Palmer's main arguments were based on the assertion that a verbal agreement existed for the release of the ten-acre tract from the mortgage upon payment, which she argued was fulfilled by her late husband. She claimed that the mortgagee's failure to provide the release despite the payment constituted inequitable treatment. Palmer sought to cancel the mortgage with respect to the ten acres, insisting that the legal agreement and the circumstances surrounding the transaction warranted such cancellation. Furthermore, she asserted her status as the executrix and sole devisee of her husband's estate, thus reinforcing her standing in the case.	Thomas Snell, the defendant, contended that the alleged agreement for the release of the ten acres was too vague and indefinite to be enforceable in court. He argued that the testimony supporting Palmer's claims relied primarily on the mortgagor's statements, which failed to establish a clear and binding agreement. Snell also stated that any transaction involving the ten acres after the mortgage was executed did not rely on the supposed agreement, as the property was acquired through a sheriff's sale, not a direct purchase contingent upon a release. Furthermore, he maintained that the foreclosure process should be executed without delay and that Palmer had no legal grounds for her claims according to the Rules of Equity that govern mortgage foreclosures.

In 1888, in Adams County, Illinois, Jerry Shea, a physician, brought a lawsuit against Jacob A. Wagner to recover payment for medical services rendered. Shea initially received a judgment for $30 from a justice of the peace. However, Wagner appealed the decision, contesting the judgment on the grounds that there was an express contract stipulating a perfect cure for his catarrh, which was claimed to be defective. The key individuals involved were Jerry Shea, the plaintiff, who acted as the physician, and Jacob A. Wagner, the defendant, who was the patient disputing the effectiveness of the treatment. The case primarily revolved around the conflicting testimonies of the two parties regarding the existence and terms of the alleged contract for medical services.	Jerry Shea claimed that he provided medical services to Jacob A. Wagner and was entitled to payment for those services amounting to $30. He argued that the contract for his services did not stipulate a guarantee of a perfect cure, and sought to affirm the initial judgment rendered in his favor by the lower court.	Jacob A. Wagner maintained that there was a special contract whereby Shea was to provide a perfect cure for his catarrh for a fee of $25. He contended that since the promised outcome was not achieved, he was not liable for the full payment claimed by Shea. Wagner’s defense was based on the assertion that the services were rendered under the terms of this defective contract.

Isaac Wilson v. James McDowell took place in 1869 in Livingston County, Illinois. The case was tried without a jury and presided over by Judge Charles H. Wood. The legal proceedings arose from a dispute between the two parties; however, the specifics of the incident leading to the case are not detailed in the court documentation. The case was brought to the circuit court, where the appellant (Isaac Wilson) was represented by the law firm of Payson & Perry, and the appellee (James McDowell) was defended by Fleming, Pillsbury & Plumb. Due to the incomplete bill of exceptions, which did not include all the evidence presented, the appellate court found itself unable to review the factual findings made in the lower court.	The plaintiff, Isaac Wilson, sought to challenge the judgment made by the lower circuit court, arguing against the findings that were detrimental to his case. His main legal request was to have the appellate court review the case's evidence and findings, which he claimed were not accurately represented in the bill of exceptions presented.	The defendant, James McDowell, maintained that the appellate court should not review the findings because the bill of exceptions did not contain all evidence necessary for such a review. McDowell's argument centered around the procedural aspect, claiming that without a complete record of the proceedings, the court could not assess or overturn the lower court's judgment.

The case of Mary Bainter v. George Lawson took place in Hancock County, Illinois, and was presided over by Judge William Marsh. The dispute arose in 1887, stemming from an action of distress for rent filed by the plaintiff, Mary Bainter, against the defendant, George Lawson. The conflict centered around the payment of rent under the terms of a lease, specifically whether the rent, paid in the form of corn, was to be delivered on the farm or transported to La Harpe. During the trial, the defendant denied owing rent to the plaintiff, leading to a jury verdict in favor of the defendant. The plaintiff subsequently appealed, raising various points of contention regarding evidence and jury instructions, particularly focusing on the nature of the rent payment and the validity of the defendant's actions regarding a conversation about the sale of corn.	The plaintiff, Mary Bainter, argued that the defendant, George Lawson, had failed to fulfill his obligations under the lease agreement by not properly paying rent. She claimed that relevant evidence was improperly excluded during the trial, specifically regarding the defendant's potential to maximize his crop yield through good husbandry. Bainter sought a judicial review to overturn the jury's verdict and establish her right to the owed rent.	The defendant, George Lawson, maintained that he did not owe any rent to the plaintiff, supporting his position with evidence that indicated a dispute over the actual terms of the lease regarding rent payment delivery. Lawson argued that the trial court's decisions concerning the admissibility of evidence and jury instructions were correct. He contended that the underlying facts did not warrant intervention from the appellate court, as the jury's conclusion was not significantly undermined by any alleged evidentiary errors.

On March 14, 1885, in De Witt County, Illinois, Julia A. Parker conveyed her life estate in certain lands to her son, Matthew Parker, through a quit claim deed. The arrangement stipulated that Matthew would pay Julia $150 annually for her lifetime, along with specific future obligations based on her survival. Subsequently, on March 20, 1885, creditor John W. Cain obtained a judgment against Julia for unpaid groceries and supplies from prior years. Unable to collect his debt through execution on Julia's property, Cain filed a creditor's bill to challenge the validity of the conveyance, arguing it was fraudulent. The case raised questions about whether the conveyance was a legitimate sale or merely a means to escape creditor obligations, given the structured payments depended on Julia's survival.	The plaintiff, John W. Cain, contended that Julia A. Parker's conveyance of her life estate to Matthew Parker was fraudulent and amounted to an improper transfer designed to protect her assets from creditors. He sought to have the conveyance set aside, asserting that it was made solely to secure future support for Julia and therefore should be deemed invalid against the interests of her creditors.	Matthew Parker defended the transaction by claiming it was a legitimate conveyance in exchange for future support obligations. He argued that the payments were sufficient consideration for the life estate and maintained that the conveyance should be sustained as it did not violate any creditor rights, since Julia was free to manage her estate as she saw fit.

In 1873, in McLean County, Illinois, Franklin Kimler obtained a judgment against Walter Vanscoyoc and O. H. P. Vanscoyoc. Following this, a sheriff’s sale of a tract of land owned by Vanscoyoc was conducted to satisfy the judgment. The land, which was encumbered by previous mortgages exceeding its value, was sold on March 17, 1873, to the plaintiff’s attorneys, K.E. Williams and H. Burr, for $484.28. In September 1874, the attorneys moved to vacate the sale, claiming they had been misled regarding the land's encumbrance status. The court initially agreed with them, setting aside the sale and restoring all rights to Kimler while issuing an alias execution. However, the case was appealed on the grounds that there were no misrepresentations made by the debtors at the time of the sale.	The plaintiff's primary argument was that the attorneys believed the land was free from encumbrances when they purchased it at the sheriff's sale. They presented affidavits to support their assertion that the land had significant mortgages that exceeded its value. They sought to have the court vacate the sale due to these conditions and restore their rights as if the sale had never occurred.	The defendants contended that there were no misrepresentations about the condition of the land at the time of the sale. They argued that the principle of "caveat emptor" should apply, meaning that the buyers must take responsibility for the purchase. They asserted that they made no guarantees regarding the title and that the purchasers, being the plaintiff's attorneys, had the opportunity to investigate the title but chose not to. Therefore, the sale should remain valid.

The case of Altja R. Heeren v. William Kitson et al. took place in Illinois, culminating in a judgment delivered on December 8, 1888. The central figures involved were Altja R. Heeren, the plaintiff, and defendants William Kitson and his son John F. Kitson. The dispute arose after Heeren obtained a judgment for $8,980 against William Kitson and another party, C. M. Moody, in the Rock Island County Circuit Court. However, Kitson had made a deed to his son, John, for certain real estate, allegedly to defraud Heeren from collecting on her judgment. Heeren claimed that this deed was fraudulent and aimed at preventing her from satisfying the judgment owed to her. William Kitson was said to have been the legal owner of specific property before this transfer, and the deed was made shortly after Heeren’s claim had been established. Heeren further alleged that there was no true consideration for the deed and that John, the recipient, was not financially stable enough to warrant such a transfer. The mortgage agreement between the Kitsons and a third party, Simeon B. Stoddard, was also brought into question, although Heeren later dropped claims regarding its fraudulence. The Circuit Court heard testimonies, examined evidence, and ultimately upheld the deed transaction's validity, finding no evidence of fraudulent intent.	Altja R. Heeren's primary claims centered around the assertion that the deed executed by William Kitson to his son John F. Kitson was fraudulent. Heeren sought to have this deed annulled in order to recover her judgment against Kitson. She argued that the transfer was made without actual consideration and specifically to hinder her ability to collect on her legitimate claim. Heeren's complaint included demands that the court declare the deed and accompanying mortgage void due to their fraudulent nature, asserting that they were executed with the intent of defrauding her as a creditor.	The defendants, William and John F. Kitson, denied any wrongdoing, asserting that the deed was a genuine transaction made in consideration of an outstanding debt for services rendered by John to William. They claimed that the deed was not intended to defraud anyone, stating that William owed John approximately $2,190 for years of unpaid labor. The Kitsons argued that the evidence provided by Heeren did not meet the burden of proof necessary to establish fraud and contended that they were entitled to have their deed upheld as valid. They requested that the court dismiss Heeren's complaint entirely and sought to recover their reasonable legal costs.

John Fryrear, the appellant, faced off against Garrett L. Lawrence and others, the appellees, in a legal dispute regarding the estate of the deceased James Lawrence, who died intestate in Missouri. The case was initiated on February 19, 1846, in the Scott Circuit Court, Illinois. The appellees, claiming to be the only heirs at law—brother and sister of James Lawrence—sought to lay claim to his estate, which included both land and personal property. They alleged that Fryrear, the administrator of the estate, along with his wife Betsey, fraudulently appropriated funds and property belonging to the estate, knowing they were not entitled to it. Fryrear denied the plaintiffs' claims of heirship, asserting that he and his wife were the true heirs due to a supposed lawful marriage and by claiming a substantial amount was owed to him from the estate for his administration services. The conflict escalated as evidence and testimony were presented, leading to a decree in favor of the appellees for $159 at the October term of 1847.	The plaintiffs (appellees) asserted in their bill that they were the only legal heirs of James Lawrence and therefore entitled to his entire estate. They accused Fryrear and his wife of fraudulently acquiring significant sums from the estate while claiming a lawful relationship with Lawrence that would entitle them to the estate. They sought a decree confirming their heirship and demanded the recovery of financial assets that they argued rightfully belonged to them.	The defendant, Fryrear, contended that he and his wife were legally married and thus entitled to the estate. He claimed that due to an official settlement of the estate in Missouri, he was owed a balance as the administrator, which he believed took precedence over the claims made by the plaintiffs. Fryrear's defense included a demand for evidence to substantiate the plaintiffs' claims about their heirship, which he argued was based solely on the testimony of one witness, and an assertion that he had not benefitted from the estate as claimed.

The case "Peter R. Leonard, Plaintiff in Error, v. Administrator of John Villars, Defendant in Error" took place in January 1860 in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a circuit court ruling from Vermillion County. The plaintiff, Peter R. Leonard, borrowed money from John Villars, executing four promissory notes of $700 each due in one to four years, with a ten percent annual interest rate, and secured by a mortgage on real estate. Leonard's wife, Sarah R. Leonard, also executed the mortgage. Leonard defaulted on payments due by May 26, 1855, prompting Villars to file a foreclosure bill in court. The lower court ruled against Leonard due to his failure to answer the claims and ruled that Leonard owed $1,836.80, comprising principal and interest. Villars further sought to sell the mortgaged property if Leonard did not pay within twenty days. Subsequently, Leonard appealed the decision, asserting that his wife was a necessary party in the foreclosure case, among other claims about the court's computations and procedures.	The plaintiff, Peter R. Leonard, asserted several claims on appeal. Primarily, he argued that his wife, a party to the original mortgage, was a necessary party to the foreclosure proceedings, which the lower court erred in failing to include. Additionally, Leonard contested the court's decision to impose compound interest and interest on overdue amounts without explicit contractual provision for such actions. He also argued that the court should not have decreed foreclosure for an installment that was not due at the time the bill was filed and called for the possession of the land to be returned without any request for that relief in the original bill.	The defendant, through the administrator of John Villars, emphasized that the original ruling to foreclose the mortgage was justified based on Leonard’s failure to make payments as due. The defense asserted that it was appropriate for the court to order the sale of the mortgaged property to satisfy the debt, claiming that the other arguments raised by Leonard on appeal were without merit or irrelevant to the remanding of the foreclosure decree.

In September 1867, in Chicago, Illinois, Ralph Hanson and another individual (plaintiffs) entered into a transaction with Frederick Busse (defendant) to sell him 110 barrels of apples. The plaintiffs claimed the apples were good quality and similar to previously purchased fruit. Upon inspection, the defendant, who had limitations due to rheumatism, examined a few barrels with the help of a clerk. He was shown good-quality apples in the samples presented to him. However, upon receiving the full shipment, it was revealed that the apples were decayed and worthless. The defendant refused to pay for them, leading to the legal dispute. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court after a jury sided with the defendant during the initial trial.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant was liable for the price of the 110 barrels of apples sold, asserting that they had represented the apples to be good quality and were relying on those representations in making the sale. They argued that the defendant had an obligation to pay since the sale was completed based on their assertions.	The defendant contended that he should not be held responsible for the payment because the apples received were not as represented and were unmerchantable. He argued that he had relied on the samples shown to him before purchase, and since the apples were defective, he was entitled to return them and not be liable for the price paid.

William B. Keep et al. v. Andrew J. Griggs was a case filed in 1883 in Illinois, concerning a lawsuit for malicious prosecution. The plaintiff, Andrew J. Griggs, alleged that the defendants, William B. Keep and others, wrongfully caused a search warrant to be issued for his home in South Chicago. This search was conducted in the belief that goods belonging to the Chicago Match Company had been stolen or embezzled by Griggs. The case was tried in the Superior Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Elliott Anthony, where Griggs’ wife was allowed to testify in his favor despite objections based on her incompetency as a witness in a suit against her husband. The jury found the defendants guilty and awarded Griggs $1,000 in damages. The defendants appealed this decision.	The plaintiff, Andrew J. Griggs, claimed that the defendants acted with malice and without probable cause in causing him to be prosecuted, leading to the issuance of an improper search warrant for his home. He argued that the actions taken against him were unjustified and, as a result, sought damages for the allegations and the related repercussions of the malicious prosecution.	The defendants contended that they had reasonable grounds for their suspicions regarding Griggs' alleged theft of the property in question. They argued that, while they may have initiated the search warrant, it was based on honest convictions derived from the circumstances present at the time. Furthermore, they objected to the wife's testimony on the basis of legal incompetency, asserting that allowing her to testify violated the general legal rule concerning spousal testimony in such cases.

The case of Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company v. John Darst took place in 1869 in Woodford County, Illinois. The central figures involved were John Darst, the plaintiff, who owned livestock, and the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, the defendant responsible for operating the railway. The legal action arose when Darst sought compensation for damages after his cattle were allegedly killed by a train belonging to the railway company. The claim contended that the portion of the railway where the incident occurred was not adequately fenced, thus allowing the cattle to stray onto the tracks. The case progressed through the Circuit Court, which ruled in favor of Darst, leading to a judgment against the railway company for $90 in damages plus costs. Subsequently, the railway company appealed the decision, questioning the sufficiency of the plaintiff's declaration regarding liability and the conditions of the railway's fencing.	John Darst claimed that the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company was liable for killing his livestock because the railway was not fenced properly at the location of the incident. He argued that the lack of fencing constituted negligence, which directly resulted in the death of his cattle. Darst requested damages amounting to $90 along with the costs associated with the lawsuit.	The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company contended that the plaintiff's declaration was insufficient to establish liability. They maintained that the declaration failed to prove that the railway was unfenced where the cattle strayed onto the tracks. Furthermore, they argued that the declaration inadequately represented the circumstances surrounding the fencing of the railway and the timing of when it had been open. The railway company requested that the court reverse the lower court's judgment.

The case "Nelson Burnham v. John D. Roberts" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873. The dispute arose in Peoria County, Illinois, where John D. Roberts (the plaintiff) claimed that he sold certain claims against the estate of John W. Proctor to Nelson Burnham (the defendant) for $825. Roberts asserted that there was an agreement for him to have these claims probated against the estate, after which Burnham would pay him. However, Burnham disputed the existence of such a contract, stating that he had purchased a piece of land at an administrator's sale that he had previously sold to Proctor, intending for the money for the claims to be paid to Roberts by the administrator. The court examined testimonies from both parties and the estate's administrator, highlighting discrepancies in their accounts regarding the payment and agreement terms. The evidence suggested a lack of clarity over whether the claims had indeed been sold or transferred, as Roberts had not executed a formal assignment allowing Burnham to pursue the claims.	John D. Roberts claimed that Nelson Burnham owed him $825 for claims that were allegedly sold as part of an agreement for Burnham to pay him after the claims were probated against John W. Proctor's estate. Roberts maintained that the transaction was valid and that Burnham had a contractual obligation to pay for the claims, which he argued had been fulfilled by proving their existence.	Nelson Burnham countered that no sale or agreement ever took place regarding the claims. He argued that any discussions were about the purchase of land, for which he had paid $900 to the administrator rather than paying Roberts directly for the claims. Burnham asserted that the responsibilities surrounding the claims and their collection had not been formally transferred to him, making any claim for payment invalid.

The case titled "Biggs and others v. Postlewait and others" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1826. The action was initiated by Joseph Payne, one of the heirs of the deceased John Payne, against Postlewait, who was serving as the administrator of John Payne's estate, along with his sureties. The plaintiff alleged that the administrator failed to return an inventory or sale bill, and instead wasted the estate's assets. The case revolves around the obligations and liabilities associated with an administration bond, which is designed to secure the interests of the deceased’s estate and its heirs. The plaintiff claims that a significant amount of property passed into the administrator's hands; however, he did not present any prior judgment against the administrator establishing a breach of duty. The court had to determine if the administrator's sureties could be held liable without a demonstrated failure (devastavit) established through a previous suit against the administrator. Ultimately, the court affirmed the lower court's decision regarding the administration bond.	The plaintiff, Joseph Payne, claims that the administrator of the estate of John Payne did not uphold his duties under the administration bond by failing to return necessary documentation and mismanaging the estate's assets. However, the plaintiff has not established a judgment against the administrator or a prior finding of waste (devastavit), which he argues should allow him to recover losses from the administrator’s sureties.	The defendants, represented by Postlewait and his sureties, contend that the plaintiff has failed to meet the necessary legal requirements to pursue a claim against the sureties. They argue that the plaintiff must first obtain a judgment against the administrator to demonstrate that he has indeed failed in his duties towards the estate, and that without such a judgment, the sureties cannot be held liable for the administrator’s actions. They maintain that no action can be taken against them until the prerequisite devastavit has been established through a separate legal proceeding.

In 1875, in Morgan County, Illinois, Louis Reinback filed a legal action against John C. Crabtree and Abram C. Woods regarding a promissory note. Reinback sought to recover the amount he claimed was due on the note. The central issue arose from Crabtree's defense, which was that he had paid usurious interest on the amount due, exceeding the allowable legal limit. Crabtree maintained that this higher interest effectively satisfied the debt, rendering Reinback's claim moot. The jury found in favor of the defendants after examining the circumstances, including the nature of the interest payments made. The trial court, under Judge Cyrus Epler, presided over the proceedings, which led to further examination of the alleged usurious agreement and the instructions provided to the jury.	Louis Reinback argued that he was entitled to receive payment under the promissory note despite the assertions of the defendants. He contended that the interest claimed was legally justified and did not constitute usury as defined under the law. Reinback sought the court's affirmation of the validity of the promissory note and demanded recovery of the amount due.	John C. Crabtree and Abram C. Woods contended that the payments made exceeded the legal interest rate of ten percent, claiming they had already satisfied the debt through the payment of usurious interest. The defendants requested that the court acknowledge this excess as a credit towards the principal of the promissory note, asserting that this constituted a complete defense against Reinback's claim.

The case "The Village of Princeville v. Peter Auten et al." dates back to January 1875 and was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The village of Princeville, originally laid out in 1837, included a central block designated as a public square which remained blank and undivided, indicating no lots were allocated for development. The village board intended to move the town hall to this public square, but this action was challenged. The public square had been recognized as public grounds, with lots adjacent to it sold at enhanced prices, implying its intended use as a communal area. After years of remaining unoccupied for community use, the plaintiff sought to prevent the village trustees from appropriating the square for corporate buildings contrary to the wishes of local citizens. The legal question that arose was whether the village trustees had the authority to convert the square into a site for municipal buildings.	The plaintiff, representing the community, argued that the public square was originally intended to remain a communal space for the residents of the village. They claimed that the village trustees lacked the authority to repurpose it for a town hall without explicit permission or evidence demonstrating a change in its intended use. The plaintiff sought the court's intervention to prevent the trustees from moving forward with their plans and to uphold the original purpose of the square as a public area for the benefit of all villagers.	The defendant, represented by the village trustees, contended that they had the right to utilize public lands for municipal purposes. They argued that the absence of specific restrictions in the original layout allowed them to make decisions regarding the square's use as they saw fit, including the establishment of a town hall. The defendant also pointed to customary practices in similar cases to justify their proposed actions, claiming that such use was consistent with the development of public facilities.

The case of City of Beardstown v. Charles D. Moody arises from an ordinance enacted by the City of Beardstown on April 14, 1864, which imposed a wharfage fee of one dollar on the owner or master of any steamboat landing at its wharf. Additionally, Section 14 of this ordinance mandated that if a steamboat departed the city wharf without paying the fee, the owner or master would forfeit a penalty of fifty dollars. The case was tried during the September term of the Circuit Court in 1864 in Cass County, Illinois, presided over by Judge James Harriott. The city sued Moody to recover the penalty after he allegedly left without making the required payment. During the trial, the city attempted to present the wharf-master as a witness; however, the court deemed him incompetent due to a potential conflict of interest, as he was entitled to a percentage of wharfage fees collected. The court’s ruling on the wharf-master’s competency was challenged on the grounds that the penalty being pursued was distinct from wharfage fees.	The City of Beardstown claimed that Charles D. Moody had violated the city ordinance by permitting his steamboat to leave the wharf without paying the required one dollar wharfage fee. As a result of this violation, the city sought to collect a penalty of fifty dollars as stipulated by the ordinance. The city argued that the wharf-master's testimony was relevant and that he should have been allowed to testify about the collection of fees.	Charles D. Moody contended that the wharf-master was an incompetent witness due to his financial interest associated with the case, as the ordinance entitled him to a commission on collected wharfage fees. Moody argued that the attempted recovery of the penalty should not be processed if the main witness could not provide valid testimony, thus challenging the city's ability to prove its case and transfer liability for the penalty.

The case titled "The Mobile & Ohio Railroad Company v. The People of the State of Illinois" originated in September 1887 in Jackson County, Illinois. It involved a legal action where the People of the State of Illinois, represented by the State's Attorney, accused the Mobile & Ohio Railroad Company of violating specific statutory requirements regarding train stoppage at crossings. The pertinent law, as outlined in Sections 75 and 76 of Chapter 114 of the Illinois Statutes, mandated trains to come to a full stop a certain distance from railway crossings. The legislation had been amended on June 19, 1885, which changed the requirements of stopping distance for trains. The original statute required a stop at least 200 feet away from the crossing, while the amendment allowed stopping within 800 feet. The court examined the declarations made against the railroad and concluded that they were based on the outdated version of the statute that no longer applied, leading to the reversal of the original judgment.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that the Mobile & Ohio Railroad Company failed to abide by the train stoppage regulations as mandated by the statute prior to its amendment. They argued that the railroad's failure to stop its trains at the required distance constituted a violation of the law, which they believed justified legal action under the original statutory provisions.	The defendant, the Mobile & Ohio Railroad Company, contended that the claims against them were based on an outdated version of the law. They argued that the legal requirements concerning the stopping distance for trains had changed with the amendment in June 1885, making the basis of the plaintiff's claims invalid. They requested the court to reverse the judgment due to the misapplication of the law.

In 1871, in the city of Beardstown, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between John Baugan (the appellee) and John Mann (the appellant). The case involved an injunction filed by Baugan to prevent Mann from constructing a building on a portion of block 10, which Baugan claimed was an alley associated with a sub-lot he owned. The origin of the alley dates back to around 1848 when Charles Sprague, the then-owner of lots 9 and 10 in block 10, divided them into sub-lots and supposedly dedicated the alley for use by the sub-lot owners and the public. For many years, this area had been utilized as an alley until Mann began excavating it in May 1868 for a new building. Baugan asserted he derived his ownership title from Sprague. Mann, in response, argued that a prior judgment from the Cass Circuit Court regarding the legal existence of the alley was conclusive against Baugan’s claims and also contended that he held title to the land in question. The case was heard based on pleadings and available evidence, ultimately leading to a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, John Baugan, argued that the portion of land Mann was attempting to build on constituted an alley that had been dedicated to public use and usage by sub-lot owners following a subdivision made by Charles Sprague in 1848. Baugan sought a perpetual injunction to restrain Mann’s construction activities, asserting entitlement to use of the alley based on a historical claim of dedication and possession.	The defendant, John Mann, contended that the prior judgment from the Cass Circuit Court regarding the existence of the alley barred Baugan from asserting his claims. Mann also challenged Baugan’s evidence regarding the alleged dedication to public use, asserting that no proof existed that the alley was validly dedicated or that Baugan had any legitimate claim to it, contending he owned the title to the property in question.

The case "The City of Aurora v. Jackson Reed et al." took place in Aurora, Illinois, and reached the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision rendered in September 1870. The plaintiffs, Jackson Reed and others, owned a building on River Street, which had been affected by surface water runoff due to changes made by the city. Prior to the construction of their building, water from the west side of the street naturally flowed toward the river, but the erection of adjacent buildings obstructed this flow, resulting in an increased volume of water draining into the plaintiffs' premises. On multiple occasions of heavy rainfall, water flooded the basement of their building, causing damages and disruption to their grocery and dining operation. In 1862, a prior property owner had an agreement with the city to install a gutter, but this was not fully executed, leading to further accumulation of water. The issues brought forward by the plaintiffs included the city’s negligent street grading practices that diverted water into their property.	The plaintiffs argued that the City of Aurora was responsible for the damages to their property caused by surface water due to its negligent grading of the adjacent street. They claimed that the city’s actions had directly caused water to flow into their building, resulting in financial losses. Their legal request was for the city to compensate them for the damages incurred due to the flooding.	The City of Aurora defended itself by asserting that it had the authority to control street grading and did so according to proper procedures. The city argued that the plaintiffs had not adequately proven a direct causal link between its actions and the flooding damage. Additionally, the city claimed that the plaintiffs had a responsibility to protect their property and could have taken measures to prevent the water damage themselves.

In May 1861, Catharine Tannear purchased a quarter section of land in Marion County, Illinois, executing promissory notes and a deed of trust to secure the purchase money. Shortly after, she sold the land to Loyd, subject to the existing deed of trust. Loyd then conveyed the east half of the tract to Johnson A. Power (the appellant) and the other half to George Briscoe (the appellee), with both sales explicitly subject to the deed of trust. Loyd arranged for a potential release from the deed of trust upon paying half of the overall purchase price. When Briscoe was about to sell his land to cover the owed debt, he offered to pay his pro rata share, but Edgar L. Briscoe (the note holder) declined the payment and proceeded with the sale of Briscoe's land, purchasing it himself. Subsequently, Briscoe filed a suit to set aside that sale, arguing the property owned by Power was also liable for the debt. The circuit court agreed to set aside the sale, a decision that was affirmed by the Illinois Supreme Court. Eventually, after paying off the last promissory note in full, Briscoe sued Power to recover his pro rata share, claiming that Power should be liable for the debt.	George Briscoe argued that Johnson A. Power was personally liable to pay his pro rata share of the promissory notes, as the land owned by Power was subject to the same financial obligations. Briscoe contended that he should be reimbursed for covering the entire debt owed when Power did not contribute his share. He described the circumstances wherein he had consistently paid his dues in good faith and asserted that Power was obliged to repay the proportionate amount.	Johnson A. Power contended that there was no personal liability or express promise on his part to repay Briscoe for any money paid regarding the promissory notes. Power argued that the relationship did not establish a debtor-creditor arrangement, emphasizing that Briscoe could not impose a debt merely by paying on behalf of someone else without a request. He maintained that he only had a liability concerning the land itself, not to Briscoe personally.

In 1873, in Danville, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving a promissory note for $150 written by F. M. Welsh and endorsed by John C. Short & Co. The note stipulated that it was to be repaid ten months after its execution, along with 10% interest and an attorney's fee of 10% in case of collection efforts. John C. Short endorsed the note to Michael D. Coffeen, who subsequently endorsed it to John C. Short & Co., the appellee in this case. After the jury was waived, the trial was held before the court, leading to a judgment in favor of John C. Short & Co. for $186.89, which exceeded the amount of the original note, including the interest. The court found sufficient evidence to hold the endorsers liable but recognized that the awarded judgment was too high based on the established legal framework for recovery in cases involving promissory notes. The legal ceiling for recovery is the amount of the note plus interest, making the court conclude that the judgment should be reversed due to the error in the judgment amount.	John C. Short & Co. claimed that Michael D. Coffeen, as an endorser of the promissory note, was liable for payment. They argued that the note entitled them to collect the principal amount plus interest and an attorney’s fee in the event of a default, setting a precedent for recovery against endorsers.	Michael D. Coffeen contended that the judgment rendered by the lower court was excessive and not in accordance with the legal limits regarding the recovery amount allowed for endorsements of promissory notes. He argued that the recovery should not exceed the total of the original note and interest, and raised objections regarding the inclusion of the attorney's fees previously outlined in the note.

In April 1856, William W. Low, the plaintiff, initiated a legal case against William J. Getty, the defendant, in the Marshall Circuit Court of Illinois. The dispute revolved around a contractual agreement concerning the delivery of corn. Low alleged that Getty was obligated to deliver this corn at specific locations if Low could not procure a boat for transportation. A subsequent agreement was made, where Getty would not shell or thrash the corn until Low provided sacks for its packaging. Low claimed that he would furnish the sacks and direct Getty on the delivery schedule by August 1, 1849. After a trial, the jury found in favor of Getty, leading Low to appeal the verdict to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the defenses put forth by Getty were insufficient to support the ruling.	The plaintiff, William W. Low, contended that the pleas submitted by Getty lacked a sufficient consideration to validate the contract for corn delivery. Low asserted that there was an existing agreement detailing Getty's obligations to deliver corn, contingent upon Low supplying the necessary materials for the transaction. The main argument was centered around the assertion that the defendant's pleas were inadequate and did not support a legitimate legal basis for denying delivery.	William J. Getty, the defendant, maintained that the pleas he presented were sufficient and that the jury's verdict in his favor reflected a correct interpretation of the contractual obligations. Getty contended that despite the appellant's arguments, the evidence corroborated his position, and the instructions given to the jury regarding the pleas were appropriate. Getty sought to uphold the jury's decision and affirm the judgment rendered by the lower court.

The case "George T. Lovejoy, Impl'd, etc. v. Edward T. Steele, Assignee, etc." took place on February 3, 1886, in Illinois, specifically within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose from a legal action concerning an appeal bond related to a judgment against Hebron Clafiin, which was secured by Klink, an assignee in bankruptcy of the estate of W.A. & W.H. Butters. After Klink’s death in 1877, Edward T. Stelle was appointed as the new assignee in bankruptcy and attempted to bring forth a legal claim using the bond that had been executed with George T. Lovejoy as a surety. However, the defendants contested the legitimacy of the action, arguing that it was not brought in the name of the proper party since Klink was the original obligee and had died. The evidence presented led the court to determine that the lawsuit was improperly initiated by Stelle, who was not the legal representative of Klink’s estate that would have been required to maintain the action.	Edward T. Stelle, as the new assignee in bankruptcy of the estate of Butters, asserted that he could file a lawsuit using the appeal bond established when Klink was alive, and that he had the right to seek payment for damages owed under that bond for the use of Wesley H. Sisson. Stelle's core argument was based on his appointment as Klink's successor and his assertion that the bond constituted a legal right to recover the amounts due under the preceding judgment.	The defendant, Lovejoy, maintained that the lawsuit was improperly initiated because it was brought in the name of Stelle instead of Klink’s estate administrator. Lovejoy argued that Klink was the sole obligee of the bond, and upon his death, Stelle did not have the legal authority to enforce the bond or to claim the penalties associated with it as the assignee. The defense emphasized that neither the judgment nor the related amounts qualified as assets of the bankrupt estate, thereby nullifying Stelle's claim.

The case involves Andrew Johnson as the plaintiff and John Weedman as the defendant, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1843. The conflict arose when Johnson bailed a horse to Weedman for the specific purpose of agistment and feeding. Weedman, without obtaining permission from Johnson, rode the horse for fifteen miles. Shortly after this ride, the horse died, but the court noted that this demise was not a result of Weedman’s actions while riding it. Johnson claimed that Weedman’s actions constituted a conversion of the horse, while Weedman defended himself by arguing that since there was no actual damage incurred due to the ride, Johnson was not entitled to compensation. The jury initially found Weedman not guilty, and Johnson’s motion for a new trial was denied, leading to a judgment for the defendant.	Andrew Johnson's main arguments revolved around the assertion that John Weedman's unauthorized riding of the horse amounted to conversion, making him liable for damages. He claimed that regardless of the outcome regarding the horse's health, the unlawful use of his property warranted compensation for the non-permission of use. Johnson sought a new trial after the jury’s verdict of not guilty, which he argued was incorrect on the basis that Weedman had exercised ownership over the horse without permission.	John Weedman contended that his actions did not amount to conversion as defined by law, particularly since his riding of the horse did not result in any injury or damage to it. He argued that, under legal principles, without any measurable damage, Johnson could only recover nominal damages at best. Therefore, the jury's finding of not guilty was justified, and Weedman maintained that a new trial was unnecessary as there were no grounds for asserting a conversion.

In 1883, within Champaign County, Illinois, the case "Adeline C. Moore, Ex’x. v. The People ex rel. Thomas A. Lewis" arose concerning a legal application from the county collector for a judgment due to non-payment of two special assessments against a 420-acre tract of land owned by Adeline C. Moore. The assessments stemmed from the Union Drainage District No. 2. Through the assessments, the district levied a gross sum of $600 against Moore's entire property, which she contested as unauthorized, contending the law necessitated separate assessments for distinct tracts of land. The drainage commissioners were also accused of levying a second assessment of $1,812 without proper justification, as the original assessment was alleged to be adequate. Moore further claimed that certain properties, notably a railway and public highways benefiting from the assessment, were not included. Ultimately, the case involved complex interpretations of the Drainage Act and the proper procedures for levying assessments.	The plaintiff, Adeline C. Moore, argued that the special assessments against her land were void as they violated the legal requirements of separate assessments for different tracts of land. She maintained that the first assessment of $600 was unauthorized and that the second assessment lacked necessary justification and rationale documented by the drainage commissioners. Moore contended that this lack made the second assessment unlawful. Additionally, she claimed that the assessment unfairly excluded the right-of-way of the railroad and public roads that were also benefitted by the drainage work.	The defendant, representing the drainage district, maintained that the assessment was valid as per the provisions of the Drainage Act. They argued that the assessment method used was consistent with legal standards, as all of Moore's land was located in the same section and could be fairly assessed as a single entity. The defense contended that the procedural objections raised by Moore were not timely made before the drainage commissioners at the required meetings, asserting that the commissioners acted within their authority and discretion. Furthermore, they asserted that no fraud was determined in how the assessments had been levied.

Harmon Phenix v. Phebe Castner is a legal case that took place in Stark County, Illinois, during the March term of court in 1883. The plaintiff, Phebe Castner, brought an action against the defendant, Harmon Phenix, for verbal slander, claiming that Phenix made several derogatory remarks about her. Specifically, on June 27, 1882, Phenix allegedly used phrases that labeled Castner as a "dirty bitch" and a "dirty whore," implying that she had been guilty of adultery. Furthermore, during the funeral of Castner's child, Phenix made slanderous comments describing the deceased child as a "bastard" and making derogatory remarks about Castner's character. The trial concluded with a jury verdict awarding Castner $1,500 in damages. Phenix's subsequent motion for a new trial was denied, leading him to appeal to the Appellate Court for the Second District, which affirmed the earlier judgment. The case moved to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the judges evaluated the trial's proceedings and the validity of jury instructions.	Phebe Castner claimed that Harmon Phenix's statements constituted verbal slander, damaging her reputation and causing emotional distress. She pointed to specific instances of Phenix’s remarks, which not only insulted her character directly but also defamed her deceased child. Castner sought damages for the slanderous statements made in public, asserting that these allegations impacted her social standing and moral reputation.	Harmon Phenix, through his counsel, responded with a plea of not guilty and attempted to justify his statements by claiming that Castner was, indeed, a "whore" who had committed adultery. Phenix also contested the credibility of the witnesses against him and objected to jury instructions that he claimed would mislead the panel regarding the evaluation of witness testimony and the acceptance of evidence.

In 1888, Edward Welch, the appellee, sued Jacob K. Zerger, the appellant, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The lawsuit originated from a partnership dealing in livestock between the two parties. The key issue at hand was whether Welch had made a payment on a promissory note on behalf of Zerger, which should be considered a partnership liability. The note, payable to one Bennett, was related to a property purchase made by Zerger. Although Zerger had also signed a separate note for joint purchases, he contested the nature of the liability, arguing that Welch had partnership funds under his control. The court proceedings involved examination of various checks and claims relating to their business dealings, culminating in a jury determining that the payment Welch made was indeed for Zerger’s benefit. The case was presided over by Judge Lyman Lacey in the Circuit Court of De Witt County before being appealed.	Welch claimed that he was owed $706.14 from Zerger, which comprised a payment he made as surety on a promissory note and the value of livestock he had sold to Zerger. He argued that these payments were legitimately incurred obligations and sought to recover those amounts, asserting that the funds used were a mix of personal and partnership money.	Zerger contended that the payments were mischaracterized by Welch as he believed they were partnership debts. He raised objections against the admissibility of various evidence types Welch presented, particularly relating to their business partnership and financial contributions. Zerger sought to dismiss the claims based on the premise that they were improperly categorized as personal liability instead of partnership liability.

On August 2, 1872, Almon G. Sanford executed a bond in favor of the United States Mortgage Company for $10,000, secured by a mortgage on real estate in Cook County, Illinois. The bond stipulated payments of interest at a rate of nine percent, with provisions for the mortgage company to sell the property upon default. On December 4, 1874, Henry J. Hubbard purchased two interest coupons from this mortgage, believing them to be secured by the mortgage. However, the mortgage company later claimed a default had occurred and elected to foreclose, selling the property on December 28, 1876, to its president, Samuel D. Babcock. Hubbard, who still held the coupons, was refused payment by the mortgage company, which argued he was merely an agent of Sanford in the transaction. Hubbard filed a bill seeking to establish a lien on the property, demand payment for the coupons, or have the property sold to satisfy the debt owed to him, alleging a fraudulent conspiracy between the mortgage company and Babcock.	Hubbard contended that he rightfully owned the interest coupons and was entitled to recovery from the mortgage company's proceeds from the foreclosure sale. He sought a decree to establish a lien on the mortgaged premises, payment of the amounts due from the mortgagee, or, alternatively, an accounting for the unpaid amounts, arguing that the sale to Babcock was invalid due to a lack of authorization in the mortgage for the mortgagee to purchase the property.	The mortgage company argued that Hubbard had an adequate remedy at law, rendering the equity court without jurisdiction, and claimed his suit was barred by both the Statute of Limitations and laches. They maintained that Hubbard acted as an agent for Sanford in his purchase of the coupons and thus had no standing to collect directly from them.

Alexander L. Thorne et al. v. L. M. Prentiss is a legal case that took place in Chicago during June 1873. The key individuals involved are Alexander L. Thorne, the plaintiff and a large dealer in provisions, and L. M. Prentiss, a defendant who, along with his partner, engaged in the curing of hams. The dispute arose from the sale of 3,000 smoked hams, where the plaintiff claimed that the defendants misrepresented the quality and condition of the hams. The plaintiff alleged that the defendants assured him that the hams were “strictly first class” and suitable for sale. However, after the purchase, the hams were found to be of inferior quality and damaged, leading the plaintiff to sue for deceit. The case was heard at the Illinois Supreme Court after an appeal was filed by the defendants following a judgment in favor of the plaintiff for $2,000.	The plaintiff, Thorne, argued that the defendants engaged in deceit by falsely stating the quality of the hams during the sale. Thorne claimed that he was led to believe that the hams were exceptional when in fact they were inferior. He sought damages amounting to $2,000, contending that the defendants’ false representations induced him to make the purchase, which resulted in financial loss.	In defense, the defendants, Prentiss and his partner, denied making any false representations regarding the hams’ quality. They claimed that they had informed the plaintiff that the hams were second class and did not guarantee their quality. They also stated that the sale was conducted under the rules of the board of trade, which included provisions for inspection, and argued that the plaintiff could not claim deceit since he had the opportunity to inspect the goods.

James S. Beaumont, the appellant, was involved in a legal dispute against Yantz, the appellee, in July 1820, in Illinois. The case arose when Yantz filed an action of trespass de bonis asportatis against Beaumont, alleging that Beaumont unlawfully took and conveyed away four horses belonging to Yantz, valued at three hundred dollars. Beaumont responded to the action by demurring to the declaration on two grounds: first, that the horses were not described with sufficient particularity, and second, that the value of each horse should have been explicitly stated. The lower court overruled Beaumont's demurrer, leading him to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Yantz, claimed that Beaumont had unlawfully taken four horses, which were his property. Yantz argued that the collective valuation of the horses, as stated in the declaration, was sufficient for the legal claim. He contended that there was no requirement for individual descriptions of the horses used in the trespass action.	The defendant, Beaumont, contended that the declaration did not meet legal standards because the horses were not described sufficiently. He argued that the value of each horse should have been clearly stated rather than just the total value of the horses combined. Beaumont's defenses centered on these points in his appeal.

John Jones v. Sarah Jones took place in January 1874 in DeWitt County, Illinois. The case centers around a domestic dispute where John Jones, the defendant, confronted Sarah Jones, the plaintiff, in his home. After asking her to leave, she refused, which led to John employing physical force to remove her. The incident escalated as he allegedly struck her and physically forced her out of his property, utilizing excessive and brutal means. The court had to determine if John’s actions were justified or if he exceeded the necessary force required to remove Sarah, thereby committing an assault and battery. Evidence was presented in favor of Sarah, corroborating her account of the events, while John denied the severity of his actions. The case was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court, and the issues revolved around instructions given to the jury, the assessment of damages, and the costs incurred during the trial.	Sarah Jones claimed that John Jones assaulted her while forcibly trying to remove her from his premises. She argues that his use of physical violence was excessive and unjustified, constituting a battery. Sarah sought compensatory damages for injuries sustained and punitive damages due to the willful nature of John's actions. She maintained that her testimony and corroborating evidence should see her compensated adequately for the assault.	John Jones contended that he had the legal right to use reasonable force to remove Sarah from his property after she refused to leave when requested. He argued that he did not exceed what would be considered necessary force and denied the severity of the actions alleged against him. John sought to have the jury instructed that the force he used was justified and contested the method of assessing damages, claiming they were excessive and unwarranted.

The case "Danforth S. Clark et al. v. Osman J. Wilson et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1889. The dispute arose in La Salle County, Illinois, involving key individuals including Danforth S. Clark and Osman J. Wilson. The plaintiffs, who were judgment creditors of Osman J. Wilson, brought a bill in aid of the assignee for the benefit of Wilson's creditors. They sought to set aside various transactions—including deeds, mortgages, and notes made by Wilson shortly before he executed a deed of assignment—claiming these were fraudulent and aimed at defrauding creditors. During the trial, it was revealed that Wilson had transferred property to his son, Abram Wilson, and subsequently, Abram transferred it to Henry Boozel. The plaintiffs argued that these transfers were made in fraud of their rights, as they believed Wilson had no ownership interest in the property he transferred. However, the circuit court ruled that the plaintiffs failed to prove that Wilson owned the Lot at the time of the transfer. The subsequent appeal questioned the validity of several transactions executed just before Wilson's assignment.	The plaintiffs claimed that key transactions made by Osman J. Wilson, specifically a deed to Abram Wilson and a $1000 promissory note to his son John T. Wilson, were fraudulent and aimed at evading creditors. They sought to have these transactions set aside, arguing that they were made in contemplation of insolvency and were thus void under fraudulent conveyance laws. The plaintiffs requested the court to reverse the lower court's decisions that supported these potentially fraudulent transactions.	The defendants, including Boozel and John T. Wilson, contended that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated that Osman J. Wilson held any legitimate ownership interest in the property in question at the time of the purported fraudulent conveyance. They argued that the evidence presented was insufficient to prove the existence of a valid claim against the property, emphasizing that they had complete title to the lot, which had always been held by Abram Wilson and not Osman. The defendants requested the court to affirm the lower court's ruling in their favor, reinforcing their legitimacy in possessing the property.

The case "Manufacturers and Merchants Mutual Insurance Company v. William Gent" was decided on July 27, 1883, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in Winnebago County, Illinois, where William Gent applied for fire insurance from the Manufacturers and Merchants Mutual Insurance Company, a mutual insurance company that was in the process of being organized. In June 1880, a group of individuals in Rockford, Illinois, signed a statement expressing their intention to form this insurance company in compliance with the mutual insurance laws of Illinois. Gent's application for insurance was submitted after the company had solicited enough applicants to meet the initial capital requirement. However, the insurance company had not received the final certification from the Auditor of Public Accounts that would allow them to legally commence business and issue policies. Gent's property was destroyed by fire on February 5, 1881, shortly before the company was certified to do business. The issue at hand was whether the company held any liability for Gent's loss before their official licensing.	William Gent claimed that he was entitled to recover $1,000 from the Manufacturers and Merchants Mutual Insurance Company for the loss of his property due to fire. He argued that he had completed an insurance application and had been assured by the company's soliciting agent that he was insured from the date of the application. Gent contended that the company should be held liable for his loss as he understood that he was already covered under their insurance arrangement.	The Manufacturers and Merchants Mutual Insurance Company defended against Gent's claims by asserting that they were not liable for his loss because the company had not yet completed the organization process required by the statute at the time of the fire. They argued that any contract of insurance was not binding since they had not yet received the final certification to commence operations. The company maintained that Gent was aware of the lack of authority to issue a policy and contended that the application and premium note submitted by Gent did not constitute an enforceable agreement for immediate coverage.

The case "Martin S. Robison and J. H. Robison v. Alexander Hardy and W. H. Metzger" was initiated on May 16, 1884, in Cook County, Illinois. Plaintiffs Martin S. Robison and J. H. Robison, brokers and seed merchants based in Logansport, Indiana, employed several brokers to purchase a total of 40,000 bushels of flaxseed during 1883. These purchases resulted in warehouse receipts. The defendants, Hardy & Metzger, were also involved in seed merchant operations in Chicago and had entered into a written contract with the plaintiffs on November 30, 1883, to store the flaxseed and deliver it upon navigation opening. However, a dispute arose when the plaintiffs demanded the delivery of the flaxseed on April 22, 1884, claiming the defendants wrongfully converted the seed for their own use. This led to the plaintiffs filing a trover action seeking damages for the alleged conversion. The case was tried before a jury, resulting in a verdict against the defendants for $6,121.05, prompting their appeal on various grounds regarding the jury instructions and the exclusion of evidence regarding an alleged oral agreement.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants wrongfully converted 40,000 bushels of flaxseed that was stored under a contract. They argued that they had a right to immediate possession of the flaxseed and asserted that the defendants failed to deliver it upon demand once navigation opened. The plaintiffs requested compensation for damages caused by the defendants' alleged wrongful acts, establishing that the defendants sold or disposed of the seed without their consent.	The defendants contended that they had an oral agreement allowing them to use the flaxseed for their dealings and that the plaintiffs had waived their right to immediate possession. They argued that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated the ability or readiness to pay for the flaxseed when it was demanded. The defendants requested the court to admit evidence regarding this oral agreement and to reverse the decision based on the claim that the jury instructions were flawed and did not consider essential elements necessary for recovery in trover.

The case "Granderson R. Phares v. Norris S. Barber" took place in Peoria County, Illinois, with the decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871. The dispute arose from a promissory note issued on January 30, 1857, by Granderson R. Phares, Thomas J. Huffman, and William Croka, promising to pay Norris S. Barber $314, due for value received. The key individuals involved included the appellant Phares and the appellee Barber, with Huffman and Croka also being parties to the matter. The appellant and Croka acted as sureties for Huffman in securing the debt. Phares claimed that they were released from their obligations due to an agreement with Barber, which Barber denied. Following the trial, a jury ruled in favor of Barber, leading to Phares's appeal, indicating errors in the lower court regarding the admissibility of evidence related to their release from obligation. The appeals court identified shortcomings in the handling of critical cross-examination questions that could have influenced the jury's understanding of the case.	The plaintiff, Norris S. Barber, argued that the defendants Phares and Croka were liable for the payment of the promissory note despite their claims of having been released. Barber contended that he did not agree to release the sureties and argued that the note was valid and enforceable. He sought to uphold the prior judgment that required Phares and Croka to pay the amount due.	The defendants, notably Granderson R. Phares, presented several defenses, asserting that they were merely sureties and had been released from their obligations by Barber. They claimed that Barber extended the payment timeline without their consent and accepted alternative security (a chattel mortgage) that should discharge them from the note. Phares sought to reverse the trial court's decision and legally affirm their release from the note.

In 1863, in Clay County, Illinois, James C. Gill was indicted for assaulting Sullivan Hubble with the intent to kill. The trial took place at the October Term of 1864, during which the jury found Gill guilty of assault with a deadly weapon, specifically with the intent to inflict a bodily injury. Following the verdict, the court imposed a fine of twenty-five dollars and costs. Gill’s counsel moved for a new trial and to arrest judgment, claiming that the jury's verdict failed to provide necessary specifics about the assault that would classify it under the lesser offense for which he was found guilty. However, the court overruled both motions, and no bill of exceptions was preserved, which hindered Gill’s ability to appeal effectively.	The plaintiff, represented by the State of Illinois, contended that the jury's verdict against Gill correctly found him guilty of a lesser offense based on the indictment for assault with intent to kill. They supported the original verdict and the resulting judgment, arguing that the court's ruling and fine were justified given the circumstances of the trial.	Gill’s defense centered around the argument that the jury's verdict amounted to an acquittal of the original charge as it did not specify the circumstances necessary to differentiate between the greater offense of attempted murder and the lesser assault charge. Gill's attorneys claimed the verdict failed to clarify key elements such as substantial provocation or malicious intent. They maintained that the motion for a new trial was improperly dismissed without necessary documentation.

In 1884, the case "The Commissioners of Highways v. Thomas Harrison" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a dispute over the width of a highway in Clay County, Illinois. The controversy arose when the plaintiff, Thomas Harrison, contended that the highway's effective width should be limited to forty feet. He sought an injunction against the commissioners of highways, who were threatening to remove obstructions beyond this width.
