Mortimer contended that he had already sufficiently paid off the debt through both direct payments to Wells and payment for the lumber used in improvement of the property. He argued that the payment for lumber should count as a credit against his financial obligation, asserting that it was essentially a valid payment made at Wells's direction for the benefit of the wards.

The case of Eugenie De R. Rice v. The Illinois Central Railroad Company took place in 1887, stemming from an incident on the defendant's railroad while Rice was traveling from Chicago to New Orleans. During the trip, an accident occurred when a bridge over a creek at Duck Hill, Mississippi, collapsed, causing a baggage car and two additional cars to fall into the creek, injuring Rice and damaging her baggage. At the time of the accident, Rice had paid for a sleeping berth on the train, although her ticket was under the name "Mrs. E. Price," which was registered due to a mistake. Despite this, she maintained that she was traveling legitimately and that the company accepted her baggage without fraud. Following the incident, the defendant moved to exclude Rice's evidence, which led to the case being decided in their favor by the lower court, prompting her to appeal.	Rice claimed compensation for personal injuries and damage to her baggage resulting from the accident on the railroad. She argued that there was a presumption of negligence on the part of the Illinois Central Railroad Company due to the nature of the accident. She contended that her status as a passenger, despite the name error on the pass, did not negate the company's responsibility for her safety and the care of her baggage.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company asserted that Rice was a trespasser on the train, as she was traveling under a pass not issued in her name, which they contended exempted them from liability. They argued that the evidence showed she engaged in fraudulent behavior by using a pass intended for another person. Additionally, they maintained that there was no proof of negligence on their part, claiming that they were not liable for the damages to her baggage as she traveled without a contract of hire.

On May 16, 1874, in Chicago, William Dewar received his share of his father's estate, totaling $7,721.80. He loaned $1,500 to James Warrack, the British vice-consul at the time and an employee of Dewar. Warrack was a client of the Bank of Montreal, of which Dewar was aware. Dewar then sought to deposit his remaining funds at the bank and was offered 4% interest, but Warrack claimed he could secure a better rate. After negotiations, they agreed that the Bank of Montreal would pay 5% interest on the deposit under Warrack's name. Dewar questioned the reasoning behind the deposit being in Warrack's name, to which Warrack assured him it was not an issue as he would endorse it over to Dewar. Dewar, trusting Warrack, placed the endorsed certificate of deposit in a safe. However, on August 4, Warrack took the certificate without Dewar’s consent and withdrew the funds for his own account. Upon discovering this, Dewar protested but continued to treat the situation as a loan to Warrack over the next three years. In 1878, Dewar sued the Bank of Montreal, claiming the bank wrongfully converted the deposit certificate. The case eventually reached the Illinois Supreme Court after several trials and appeals.	Dewar claimed that the Bank of Montreal wrongfully converted his certificate of deposit when it paid Warrack, who had no authority to withdraw the funds. He argued that the bank acted negligently by allowing this payment to happen without ensuring proper authorization, and sought recovery of the amount due under the converted deposit certificate.	The Bank of Montreal contended that Dewar had effectively given Warrack apparent authority to access the deposit through his actions and had acquiesced to Warrack's control over the funds for over three years. They argued that Dewar treated the transaction as a loan to Warrack during that time and therefore had no right to recover the funds. The bank maintained that their actions were justified under the circumstances.

In the case of John E. Weiner v. Nicholas Heintz and Valentine Miller, dated December 1855, the legal dispute arose in Madison County, Illinois. John E. Weiner executed a mortgage in 1840 for certain lands to Nicholas Miller, to secure payment on two promissory notes of $920 each. After Miller transferred his interest to Nicholas Heintz, Heintz initiated foreclosure proceedings in 1843 for the note that was due. A court decree allowed Heintz to sell the mortgaged lands but ruled that the sale was subject to the remaining mortgage for the other note not yet due. Heintz purchased the land at a sale for $1,043 and subsequently conveyed it to Valentine Miller, who inherited the land after Nicholas Miller's death in 1852. Weiner later attempted to redeem the property by offering to pay the full debt but was denied by Miller and Heintz. Weiner filed an equitable suit seeking to redeem the mortgaged lands and prevent Heintz from enforcing the note that was not yet due while claiming that the decree of sale was void, alleging various rights held in equity.	Weiner claimed he had the right to redeem the lands as the previous decree of sale was void. He alleged that he had tendered full payment of the mortgage debt but was refused by the defendants. Weiner sought to be allowed to redeem the property and requested an injunction against Heintz from further collection of the note associated with the mortgage.	Heintz and Miller defended against Weiner’s claims by arguing that the decree of sale was valid and that Weiner no longer held the right to redeem the lands following the sale. They maintained that the land had been sold to satisfy the debt and, instead of being entitled to reclaim the property, Weiner should be held liable for any amounts due following the sale. They essentially asserted that the legal debt had merged with the property after Heintz took ownership.

In April 1866, Charlotte A. Dickey filed a lawsuit against John McDonnell in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from an alleged incident that occurred in Cook County, Illinois. The nature of the case was an action for assault and battery, during which Dickey also claimed that McDonnell attempted to commit rape against her. The case was characterized by contradictory testimonies. Dickey asserted that McDonnell physically attacked her, choked her, and threatened her life, leading to visible bruises on her body. During the trial, a key issue arose regarding jury instructions provided by the court at McDonnell's request. The jury was instructed to consider whether Dickey's actions indicated consent, in the context of whether her eventual compliance came after coercive violence. This instruction suggested that if Dickey had delayed consent due to fear or violence but ultimately assented, it could absolve McDonnell of responsibility for his earlier actions. The court ultimately deemed the jury's consideration of such factors improper, raising significant legal questions about consent and the nature of violence against women.	Charlotte A. Dickey claimed that she was subjected to an assault and battery by John McDonnell, which also involved an attempt to commit rape. She sought justice for the physical harm inflicted upon her, asserting that the application of force and threats was illegal and unjustifiable regardless of any consent given after such violence. Dickey's arguments emphasized that previous violent actions could not legally excuse any eventual compliance or consent to sexual advances, highlighting the need for legal protection against coercive behavior.	John McDonnell contended that the incidents described by Dickey did not constitute a valid claim for assault and battery. He argued primarily that Dickey had willingly accompanied him in his carriage despite allegedly knowing his intentions. McDonnell requested that the court instruct the jury to find for him if they believed Dickey's resistance was feigned or motivated by a desire to extort money. His defense hinged on the assertion that Dickey's actions indicated consent, which would absolve him of liability for any subsequent actions.

Benito Tojo filed a trespass lawsuit against the Illinois and St. Louis Bridge Company in the St. Clair County Circuit Court in February 1882. The events that led to this case occurred on July 1, 1881, at the Illinois and St. Louis Bridge, which spans the Mississippi River. The plaintiff, Tojo, claimed that while driving his wagon over the bridge, he was violently pulled from his wagon by an employee of the defendant and unlawfully taken into Missouri, where he was imprisoned. Additionally, Tojo alleged that the defendant unlawfully seized his wagon and two horses. The case involved legal questions about the justification for Tojo’s arrest and whether the policemen exercised their authority within the bounds of the law and local ordinances. The defendant contended that Tojo had violated an ordinance prohibiting the speed limit on the bridge and that the arrest was lawful under that context.	Tojo's primary claims centered on allegations of assault and unlawful imprisonment against the defendant. He maintained that he was wrongfully seized and carried into Missouri without just cause, constituting a kidnapping. In his second claim, Tojo demanded the return of his wagon and horses, claiming that the defendant had unlawfully taken and converted his property for their own use. He sought legal remedies for these trespasses.	The defendant argued that Tojo had been driving dangerously over the bridge, which was in violation of a city ordinance restricting the speed limit. They maintained that the arrest was lawful, conducted by a watchman appointed by the city, and was justified due to Tojo’s misdemeanor. The defendant asserted that the actions taken were necessary and appropriate within the bounds of the law, as Tojo had been found guilty of violating the ordinance and was subsequently fined by a magistrate.

David L. Hough filed an appeal against Harvey Leonard following a judgment rendered by a justice of the peace in La Salle County, Illinois, in 1850. Leonard had initiated the action against Hough, with a demand for fifty dollars marked on the summons, alongside additional fees for the justice and constable. After a trial, the justice ruled in favor of Leonard, awarding him a total of fifty dollars plus costs. Hough appealed to the La Salle Circuit Court, seeking to dismiss the suit due to lack of jurisdiction by the justice of the peace. The motion was denied, and during the Circuit trial, evidence showed Leonard's bill of particulars exceeded fifty dollars. However, Leonard proposed allowing credits to reduce the amount claimed, which was accepted by the court. The jury ultimately found in favor of Leonard, awarding him $48.55. Hough's subsequent motion for a new trial was also denied, prompting him to bring the case before the Illinois Supreme Court, questioning the Circuit Court's authority regarding jurisdiction in initial proceedings.	Hough's primary argument was that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction in the case due to deficiencies in the summons and initial proceedings. He contended that the Circuit Court erred in denying his motion to dismiss the case based on the supposed lack of jurisdiction appearing on the face of the papers. Hough sought to have the judgment against him overturned due to these claims.	Leonard argued against Hough's claims by demonstrating that, during the trial, he amended his bill of particulars to comply with jurisdictional requirements, thus maintaining that the justice of the peace had jurisdiction over the matter. He contended that the Circuit Court correctly handled the case by allowing for amendments to reduce the claimed amount to fit within the justice's jurisdiction limits. Leonard sought to uphold the Circuit Court's judgment in his favor.

In 1834, in Madison County, Illinois, William P. Bryan and Timothy M. Bryan filed a lawsuit against George Smith and David Smith to account for the rents and profits of a mill and tract of land, which the plaintiffs claimed they co-owned as tenants in common with the defendants. The plaintiffs argued that the defendants admitted to their co-tenancy prior to the lawsuit. However, the defendants denied this claim, asserting that they were not bailiffs of the plaintiffs and contending they did not hold the land in common. The case was heard before Judge Theophilus W. Smith, who ruled in favor of the defendants. The plaintiffs subsequently appealed the judgment to the Illinois Supreme Court, leading to a further examination of evidence regarding the affinity of their co-tenancy claim and the validity of the executions related to their ownership rights.	The plaintiffs asserted that they had legitimate claims to the land as tenants in common with the defendants and sought accountability for the rents and profits from the property. They attempted to provide verbal evidence of the defendants' prior admissions regarding their shared ownership and introduced past legal judgments and execution writs to substantiate their case.	The defendants countered that the plaintiffs could not prove their claim to the land through parol evidence while paper title existed, as official documentation was necessary to establish ownership. They maintained that the executions presented by the plaintiffs were inadmissible because they did not correspond to legal precedents fitting the requirements for establishing property title and argued against the validity of the plaintiffs’ claims based on the lack of proper legal issuance of the writs.

Robert S. Ingalls brought a case against Joseph C. Allen, which was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 29, 1890. The dispute arose from Ingalls’s employment as a ranch manager for Allen in Kansas from January 1, 1885, to November 1, 1887. Ingalls claimed he was to receive a wage of $40 per month, alongside board and travel expenses, under an agreement with Allen. After returning from Kansas in the spring of 1886, Ingalls asserted he worked at Allen's hotel and livery stable in Oak Park at the same wage but without a new contract. Allen contested this assertion, denying any agreement regarding Ingalls's wages during the Oak Park employment and arguing that Ingalls was not competent to manage the ranch. The case hinged on whether Ingalls's continued work at Oak Park could be regarded as an extension of the original employment agreement and whether the wage rate from that initial contract should apply.	Ingalls claimed he was entitled to recover unpaid wages for his services at both the Kansas ranch and the Oak Park hotel, totaling $150 for a promised amount on a farm sale. He argued there was an implied agreement for the same wage as established previously despite the change in location and nature of work.	Allen's defense relied on the assertion that there was no valid contract regarding wages once Ingalls returned from Kansas. He contended that Ingalls was merely using the livery stable and had no formal employment at Oak Park, denying the existence of any compensation agreement for the services provided subsequently.

The case, "The People ex rel. The Springfield and Illinois Southeastern Railway Co. v. The County Board of Cass County," dates back to January 1875 and took place in Illinois. The key individuals involved included the Springfield and Illinois Southeastern Railway Company as the plaintiff, and the County Board of Cass County as the defendant. The case originated when the railway company sought to enforce a subscription for $50,000 in county bonds that had been voted upon favorably on February 15, 1870. The company argued that it relied upon this vote to borrow money and begin construction, believing the county had a legal obligation to fulfill the subscription. The circuit court of Sangamon County presided over the case after a change of venue from Cass County. The case revolved around whether the county board had the legal authority to issue bonds based on the prior vote when conditions had not yet been met, as the board argued they had discretion not to subscribe despite the favorable vote.	The plaintiff, Springfield and Illinois Southeastern Railway Company, claimed that the County Board had a legal obligation to issue the $50,000 in bonds as per the positive vote taken on February 15, 1870. They argued that their reliance on this vote constituted a basis for a contractual obligation, as they had begun construction on the railway using funds borrowed based on this anticipated support from the county.	The defendant, County Board of Cass County, contended that it had the discretion to withhold the subscription to the bonds despite the favorable vote. They argued that the original vote did not constitute a binding contract because the subscription was conditional upon specific requirements being met, which they claimed had not occurred. Therefore, they maintained that no legal obligation to issue bonds existed, allowing them to refuse the request without being compelled by mandamus.

In 1889, in St. Clair County, Illinois, George Wombacher, a former farmer with limited experience in mining, worked for The Consolidated Coal Company in a machine-operated coal mine. The work environment was divided among various roles, and on the night of his injury, Wombacher was waiting for a coal-cutting machine in the entries where he had been loading coal. With no work available, the night foreman directed him to a different area with coal to load. After working for three hours there, the mine roof collapsed, seriously injuring him and resulting in paralysis of his lower body. Following his injury, Wombacher was awarded $2,500 by a lower court, prompting an appeal from the coal company.	Wombacher claimed that his severe injury was due to the negligence of his employer, The Consolidated Coal Company. He argued that the night foreman, who directed him into a dangerous work area without warning him about potential hazards, acted in a supervisory capacity, making the company liable for the incident. Wombacher sought compensation for his injuries, asserting that he was placed in a situation beyond the normal risks of his employment without adequate information or warnings.	The Consolidated Coal Company contended that Wombacher was injured due to the negligence of the night foreman, who was not acting in the capacity of a supervisor but rather as a fellow employee. They argued that Wombacher had assumed the risks of his employment, and the foreman's direction did not equate to a legal responsibility for the company. The company requested the reversal of the judgment awarded to Wombacher, maintaining that there was a failure to show negligence on the company's part, particularly regarding the night foreman's knowledge of the work area’s safety.

In 1889, in Upper Alton, Illinois, Martha L. Wyman and Edward Wyman were the owners of an educational institution called “Wyman Institute.” They filed a bill of complaint seeking an injunction to prevent the collection of taxes levied for the year 1887 on the real estate and personal property associated with the institution. After Edward Wyman's death, his administrator was substituted as a party complainant. The case was heard under an agreed state of facts, with Mrs. Wyman's deposition considered in the proceedings. The major issue was whether the property was exempt from taxation under Illinois law, which can exempt property used for educational purposes. However, it was established that the property was owned personally by Mrs. Wyman and jointly by her deceased husband, and profits were being generated from the operation of the institute, which ultimately supported their livelihood. The court scrutinized the legal ownership and use of the property, concluding that it did not qualify for tax exemption, illustrating that the designation of an “institution of learning” alone does not shield property from taxation if it is not owned by a recognized institution and is used with a profit motive.	The plaintiffs claimed that the real estate and personal property of the Wyman Institute were exempt from taxation under Illinois law. They argued that their property was used exclusively for educational purposes, which should qualify for an exemption. They sought a perpetual injunction against the tax collector from collecting the taxes owed.	The defendant, P.H. Montgomery and other tax collectors, contended that the Wyman Institute was a private school operated for profit and therefore not eligible for tax exemption. They argued that the property was owned by individuals (the Wymans) rather than a recognized educational institution, and the operations generated profits that benefitted the Wymans personally. They requested the court to dismiss the plaintiffs' complaint and allow the collection of taxes.

In the case of Jerry M. Cox v. Allen M. Pierce, which took place in Illinois and culminated in a decision on May 12, 1887, the legal dispute involved a partnership disagreement between the two parties. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court following prior proceedings in the Appellate Court and Circuit Court of Stark County. The plaintiff, Jerry M. Cox, alleged issues regarding the accounting of partnership dealings. Initial proceedings involved a master in chancery being appointed to take evidence and state the accounts between the parties. Following this, multiple reports were submitted, and exceptions to these reports were filed by the appellant (Cox). The master disallowed these exceptions, leading to further courtroom proceedings where the court sustained the exceptions initially and referred the matter back to the master for re-statement of accounts. When the final report was submitted, further exceptions by the appellant were denied by the court. Throughout the proceedings, the appellant sought to introduce additional oral evidence to contest the master’s accounting, but the court repeatedly denied this request, leading to a legal interpretation of the rights to introduce evidence in actions before a master in chancery.	Jerry M. Cox, the plaintiff, argued that the partnership accounting prepared by the master in chancery was incorrect. He filed exceptions to the master’s reports claiming inaccuracies in the accounts and sought the right to introduce oral evidence to challenge the findings of the accounting presented by the master. The plaintiff’s primary request was for a correct restatement of the partnership accounts.	Allen M. Pierce, the defendant, contended that the master’s accounting was accurate and had already been properly reported to the court. He argued that the court did not err in denying the plaintiff's attempts to introduce additional oral evidence after the master had concluded his report, maintaining that the statutes governing chancery proceedings were appropriately applied.

William Phelps v. John G. Conover is a legal case adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision rendered in January 1861. The case stems from an execution sale of real estate that took place on July 23, 1859, by Sheriff John H. Havinghost. Phelps had obtained a judgment against Conover in 1858 for $1,621.61, which led to the sale of Conover's land to satisfy the debt. Conover's land consisted of several tracts scattered across different locations, most notably a section cultivated as his homestead. Despite the land being offered for sale in smaller parcels of 40 acres, it received no bids. Eventually, the sheriff sold the entire property en masse to the plaintiff for $1,726.48, a price considered to exceed one-third of its real value. Conover filed a motion in the Mason Circuit Court to set aside this sale, arguing it was irregular as the land should have been sold in parcels. The case involves intricate issues surrounding property execution, obligations under the Homestead Exemption Act, and the rights of creditors and debtors in such sales.	The plaintiff, William Phelps, claims that the sale conducted by the sheriff was valid and should not be set aside. Phelps argues that the sheriff acted within his authority when he offered the properties for sale, first in smaller parcels and subsequently as a whole due to lack of bidders. The plaintiff insists that the sale’s price should reflect the market value and that the court does not have grounds to invalidate the sale based on procedural objections presented by the defendant.	John G. Conover, the defendant, contends that the sheriff's sale was improperly conducted, arguing three main points: (1) the land was sold as a single entity rather than in divided parcels, which violated statutory requirements; (2) the property sold included his homestead, thus subject to protections under the Homestead Exemption Act; and (3) the notice and procedural aspects of the sale were not handled correctly. He requests the court to set aside the sale and remedy the resulting costs incurred from the plaintiff's actions.

The case "The Peoria & Rock Island Railway Company v. James M. Rice, Admr." involves proceedings that began after the Peoria & Rock Island Railway Company sought to condemn certain lands owned by Thomas Bryant for its right of way. The case took place in Peoria County, Illinois, with the initial actions occurring around 1869. Once the damages were assessed by appointed commissioners, both the railway company and Bryant appealed the decision to the Circuit Court. After several legal maneuvers and the death of Bryant in May 1872, the case was continued, and transferred to his administrator, James M. Rice. The appeal from the railway company was dismissed due to their counsel’s absence at a January 1874 court session. The court initially ordered that the $5,000 deposited by the railway company be paid to the administrator, but later rescinded this order. In March 1874, the railway company attempted to vacate the dismissal but the court denied this motion. The legal arguments revolved around whether the administrator had the right to prosecute the case against the railway company post-Bryant's death, given that the heirs would inherit the land.	The plaintiff, James M. Rice, as administrator of Thomas Bryant, argued that he had the right to pursue compensation for the land condemned by the railway company. He contended that the damages assessed by the commissioners entitled him to the funds previously deposited by the railway company, following the procedural rules of the condemnation statute.	The defendant, Peoria & Rock Island Railway Company, contended that the suit should not proceed in the name of Bryant's administrator since the land title had descended to Bryant's heirs upon his death. They argued that the administrator was not a proper party to the lawsuit, as no vested right to recover for the land existed at the time of Bryant's death, and that any actions regarding the property should involve the heirs.

The case titled "The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Co. v. Antoinette T. Curtenius" was adjudicated in September 1872 in Illinois. The central individuals involved were Antoinette T. Curtenius, the widow of a deceased husband whose estate is in question, and The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, which purchased the estate of her minor children at a guardian's sale. The transaction occurred under a court order, where the railway company believed they were acquiring a perfect title to the estate, based on their assumption that Curtenius had consented to the sale, despite her entitlement to dower rights. A critical aspect of the dispute revolved around whether her advisory role in the sale estopped her from claiming her dower rights in the property. The case examined the validity of the sale process as it related to her interests and the responsibilities of the buyers concerning her claim to dower.	Antoinette T. Curtenius, as the plaintiff, argued that she was entitled to dower rights in the estate inherited by her children, which the railway company purchased. She claimed that her advisory role in the sale did not constitute a waiver of these rights, asserting that there was no legal relinquishment of her dower. She maintained that the purchasers were aware of her dower interest and emphasized that they should have inquired about her rights before proceeding with the purchase. Curtenius requested the court to affirm her entitlement to dower and to prevent the defendants from denying her claim due to their misconceptions about the ownership transfer.	The defendant, The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Co., contended that Curtenius was estopped from asserting her dower claim based on her advice and consent to the sale, arguing that she should have asserted her rights if they were indeed valid. They also claimed that she should be required to seek her dower rights against the funds obtained from the sale. Their key argument revolved around the notion that she had played a part in the transaction, which led the company to believe that they had adequately handled the title rights, while asserting that they were unaware of her dower interest at the time of purchase.

The case "William Ennor, Impleaded with John W. Luke et al. v. Henry Welch" took place in September 1868 in Illinois. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff Henry Welch and defendants William Ennor, John W. Luke, and others. The case stemmed from a dispute over a note for $150, which Welch alleged was given merely for usurious interest related to two other notes. Welch sought to compel Ennor to cancel certain securities he held against Welch and a deed of trust involving a note for $400. The defendants, Ennor and Trevarthan, demurred to the bill, asserting misjoinder of parties and a lack of equity. However, the demurrer was overruled, and when the case was heard, it was determined that the main issue was whether there was sufficient evidence to support the finding that the note was given for usurious interest, as claimed by Welch. The circuit court found that the evidence favored Welch's position, leading to the appeal from Ennor.	Henry Welch claimed that the $150 note was unauthorized because it was for usurious interest related to previous loans. He requested the court compel Ennor to cancel and surrender certain securities and a deed of trust securing a separate note. Welch argued that the circumstances surrounding the transactions indicated that the note lacked validity due to its usurious nature.	William Ennor and his co-defendants primarily contended that the note in question was valid, asserting that it was given for an additional loan rather than solely for usurious interest. They argued that the evidence presented by Welch did not successfully impeach the validity of the note and requested the court to dismiss the claims against them.

In 1869, in Jersey County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between James J. Haycraft and Benjamin F. Davis regarding a promissory note made by James Brown. Davis, the payee of the note, initiated an action of detinue against Haycraft to recover the value of the note after he claimed it had been pledged as security for debts owed to him. The case was brought to the Jersey Circuit Court, where a jury trial was held. The jury found in favor of Davis, leading to a judgment that required Haycraft to either deliver the note or pay Davis its value, which was determined to be $1,112.07. Haycraft appealed, contending that the verdict was contrary to the law and evidence. Central to the dispute was whether the note had been pledged solely for Davis’s endorsement of a $300 note to a third party or if it also secured Haycraft’s additional debt of $93 for whiskey received. The jury's decision was challenged due to the significant discrepancy between Haycraft's testimony and that of three other witnesses, including two disinterested parties.	Davis argued that the promissory note was pledged not only for the $300 debt to Yaughan but also as security for an additional $93 debt owed by Haycraft for whiskey. His claim was supported by testimonies from three witnesses, including two who were disinterested, thereby asserting that he had a rightful claim to the note's value.	Haycraft asserted that the note was pledged solely to secure Davis’s endorsement for the Yaughan note, dismissing any claim for the additional whiskey-related debt. He appealed the ruling based on the argument that the evidence overwhelmingly supported his position, and that the jury’s verdict was against the preponderance of evidence presented.

Lewis W. Pitcher filed a case against The Board of Trade of the City of Chicago, which is a corporate entity established by an act of the Illinois legislature on February 18, 1859. Pitcher became a member of the Board eight years prior to the expulsion incident. On March 16, 1886, a complaint was filed against Pitcher by another member, alleging fraudulent behavior in business dealings. Following the complaint, the Board of Directors appointed a committee to investigate the claims. The committee reported specific allegations of dishonorable conduct by Pitcher. During a trial conducted by the Board, Pitcher appeared and pleaded not guilty. However, on May 11, 1886, the Board voted to expel him, which deprived him of membership rights and access to the Board's facilities, valued at $10,000. Pitcher subsequently sought a mandamus order from the circuit court to restore his membership, arguing that the expulsion was unauthorized and illegal on several grounds, including improper delegation of power and procedural violations.	Pitcher claims that his expulsion from the Board was illegal. He asserts that the Board of Trade's charter vested the power of expulsion in the entire membership rather than the Board of Directors, making their action a violation of trust. Additionally, he argues that the required quorum for expulsion was not met and cites procedural unfairness during the trial as grounds for his appeal. Pitcher requested the court to restore his membership and prevent any further exclusion until a proper hearing could occur.	The Board of Trade's defense highlighted that the expulsion process was conducted according to the rules and by-laws established under the corporate charter. They maintained that the Board of Directors was authorized to expel members when necessary, and that the required procedures were duly followed during Pitcher's trial. They argued that the issues of equitable relief sought by Pitcher were not appropriate for consideration by the chancellor, referencing prior cases that placed jurisdiction elsewhere.

Charles A. Walker filed a case against Julius Schum in January 1867, concerning the property located in Miller’s addition to Carlinville, Illinois. The case originated in the Macoupin Circuit Court as an action of ejectment, where Walker sought to reclaim lot No. 8. The plaintiff relied on a master’s deed associated with a previously foreclosed mortgage. During the trial, he presented evidence including the foreclosure decree and the sale of the premises. However, he refrained from offering proof of court approval for the master’s sale. The court, disputing the admissibility of the master’s deed, excluded it from the evidence. Subsequently, the jury favored the defendant, leading to the plaintiff's motion for a new trial being denied. Walker then appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, challenging the trial court’s ruling on the exclusion of his evidence and arguing that the legal requirements for the master’s deed were met.	Charles A. Walker argued that the master’s deed, executed under the foreclosure decree, should have been admitted as evidence in the ejectment case. He claimed that excluding the deed hindered his legal right to establish ownership and possession of the property. Walker sought to have the appellate court reverse the previous judgment and allow the entry of the master’s deed to prove his rightful claim to the property.	Julius Schum contended that the validity of the master’s deed was contingent upon prior court approval, which Walker did not provide. Schum argued that the decree only allowed for the sale of the mortgagor's interest, not the land itself if it deviated from the terms outlined. His defense emphasized that Walker's failure to contest the sale until after the redemption period had expired waived any minor objections, maintaining that all proper procedures were followed in the sale.

The case "The Racine & Mississippi Railroad Company v. The Farmers’ Loan and Trust Company et al." was brought to trial in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1877. The dispute originated from the Farmers’ Loan and Trust Company filing a bill in equity on December 31, 1864, seeking to foreclose a mortgage to recover payment for 680 bonds valued at $1,000 each, issued by the Racine and Mississippi Railroad Company. An initial decree allowed for the sale of the railroad property to satisfy the mortgage, with subsequent appeals leading to modifications in the original ruling. After significant legal back-and-forth, including objections and procedural issues related to a sale that occurred in 1867, the court reconvened to address claims regarding whether the foreclosure sale should be set aside and the proper accounting for profits generated during the relevant period. Key parties included the Farmers’ Loan and Trust Company, the Racine & Mississippi Railroad Company, and the Western Union Railroad Company, which acquired the property during the proceedings. After delays and motions filed over the years, the court ultimately addressed the waiver of rights regarding contesting the sale and issues of laches due to the extensive delay in contesting the sale.	The plaintiff, the Farmers’ Loan and Trust Company, claimed that the Racine and Mississippi Railroad Company was entitled to an accounting for profits earned from the railway during the period it was owned by the bondholders, which was relevant to the redemption from the mortgage sale executed under the circuit court decree. The plaintiff argued that the court should modify prior decrees to allow for proper accounting regarding the profits earned and sought to confirm the legality of the sale that took place.	The defendants contended that the court erred in refusing to set aside the sale of the railroad property. They argued that the significant delay in filing their motion to vacate the sale constituted a waiver of their right to contest it. They pointed out that this inaction allowed the sale to stand, and the request to have an accounting done should rightfully not exceed the date of the master’s deed, further emphasizing that the sale had occurred under clear and legal conditions, entailing full possession by the Western Union Railroad Company.

In 1886, Samuel E. Holtzman filed a lawsuit against Joseph Hoy, a physician and surgeon, in Illinois alleging malpractice regarding the treatment of a serious leg fracture. The case originated in the circuit court of Livingston County and was subsequently reviewed by the Appellate Court for the Second District. Holtzman claimed that Hoy's negligence and lack of skill in treating his leg resulted in injury, seeking damages of $2,500. During trial, a key issue arose when the court excluded testimony from one of Hoy's witnesses regarding Hoy's reputation as a physician. The central question of law was whether a physician's professional skill could be established through evidence of reputation rather than specific conduct in the case at hand. The Illinois Supreme Court was asked to review the lower court's decision, particularly the legal standard regarding the burden of proof related to the physician’s skill in a malpractice claim, focusing on the proper evidence required to establish claims of negligence.	Holtzman claimed that Hoy acted negligently and unskillfully in treating his leg fracture. He argued for damages of $2,500, asserting that the standard of care expected from a physician was not met, thus leading to injury. The plaintiff contended that he should be able to present evidence regarding Hoy's general reputation in the medical community to support his claims of inadequate skill.	Hoy defended himself by arguing that the plaintiff failed to establish the necessary proof of negligence in treatment. He maintained that general reputation evidence was inadmissible and that the burden of proof lay with Holtzman to demonstrate Hoy's lack of skill specifically in the treatment provided. Hoy's legal team asserted that the court correctly excluded evidence regarding his reputation as a skillful physician since it did not directly correlate to the actions taken in the case under consideration.

In 1861, the case of W. W. Willard v. James Bassett was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The appellant, W. W. Willard, an attorney, alongside Minerva Merrill, the widow of the deceased N. C. Merrill, originally took out letters of administration on the estate of N. C. Merrill after his death. However, they both resigned their positions, leading to James Bassett being appointed as administrator de bonis non. Willard later submitted a claim for $218 against the estate, primarily for legal services he had provided as the administrator in legal matters involving the estate. The County Court denied this claim but allowed a total of $150 for both Willard and Minerva Merrill for their administrative services, which was above the standard fee. Following this, Willard appealed to the Circuit Court of Marion County, which upheld the County Court's ruling and ordered that the allowed amount be divided between Willard and the administratrix. Willard then escalated the case to the Illinois Supreme Court, disputing the Circuit Court's affirmation of the County Court's decision and seeking compensation for his legal services to the estate.	W. W. Willard argues that as an attorney and former administrator of the estate, he is entitled to remuneration for the professional legal services he provided in handling the estate's legal matters. He claims that the lower courts erred in not allowing his fees and seeks to overturn the decision that denied him compensation for his services rendered during his administration.	James Bassett contends that an attorney serving as an administrator cannot claim fees against the estate for legal services rendered in that capacity. He asserts that any services performed must be considered a gratuity, as allowing attorneys to charge for such services could lead to unethical practices and undermined the beneficent nature of fiduciary roles. The court decisions are defended on the grounds of maintaining professional integrity and preventing conflict of interest.

In 1875, in the city of Chicago, a legal case arose involving Zebina Eastman and other plaintiffs against The City of Chicago. The case was initiated after an ordinance was enforced requiring dealers of second-hand goods to obtain a license. The plaintiffs, operating as booksellers, contended that their business predominantly focused on new books, with the trade of second-hand books being an incidental part of their operations. They argued that the definition of a "dealer in second-hand goods" as laid out in the city ordinance was incorrectly applied to their retail book shop. The ordinance sought to regulate businesses engaged in the sale of second-hand clothing and junk. The defendants maintained that their trade in second-hand books should not fall under the purview of this ordinance. A stipulation indicated that their purchases of old books were minimal compared to their total stock, which largely consisted of new goods. The case raised the question of whether a bookseller, whose primary business is new books, could be considered a dealer in second-hand goods due to their incidental transactions involving old books.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were not "dealers in second-hand goods" as defined by the city ordinance. They argued that the majority of their business involved new books, and only a small portion corresponded to second-hand books. They requested the court to reverse the conviction that imposed penalties under the ordinance for failing to obtain a license for selling second-hand goods.	The defense argued that the application of the ordinance to the plaintiffs was unjust. They contended that the ordinance was intended to regulate junk dealers and those primarily engaged in trading second-hand clothing, not booksellers whose primary business involved new and rare books. The defendant requested that the court dismiss the case against them, asserting their activities in second-hand book trading were incidental and did not warrant the penalties outlined in the ordinance.

The case "The Michigan Life Ins. Co. v. Wm. H. Beaver" took place in 1887 in Bloomington, Illinois. The dispute arose from a promissory note dated February 8, 1886, whereby Wm. H. Beaver issued a note for $116.81 to the Michigan Life Insurance Company, payable nine months later. Beaver claimed that the note was intended for an endowment policy on his life worth $3,000. However, support for Beaver's position rested on his assertion that he did not deliver the note to the company due to an arrangement with F. A. Niles, the plaintiff's agent, who was to hold the note pending payment from commissions Beaver expected to earn. Beaver testified that the agreement included provisions for Niles to make him a member of the local board of control, which did not materialize, and that he requested the return of the note when he learned of Niles' relocation. The defendant, represented by Niles, denied the agreement and characterized the transaction as valid. The jury ultimately found in favor of the defendant based on the conflicting testimonies regarding the note's delivery.	The Michigan Life Insurance Company, as the plaintiff, claimed that Wm. H. Beaver had issued a promissory note that he was obligated to pay. The company argued that the note was validly delivered, and thus Beaver owed the amount as stipulated in the note. They sought to enforce the payment and recover the $116.81 mentioned in the promissory note through legal action.	Wm. H. Beaver's defense rested on the argument that the promissory note was never delivered to the Michigan Life Insurance Company due to an agreement with the plaintiff’s agent, F. A. Niles. Beaver contended that the note was to be held by Niles until certain conditions were met regarding commission payments from policies written. He argued that without proper delivery of the note, no binding contract existed, making any claim by the plaintiff unenforceable.

Charles A. Williams brought a case against the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company concerning an incident that occurred when he was plowing in a field adjacent to the defendant’s railroad track, nearby a public highway crossing. The event took place in McLean County, Illinois. Williams alleged that a train approached suddenly from the northeast without giving the required statutory signals—meaning they failed to whistle or ring the bell at least eighty rods before reaching the crossing. Due to a curve in the track and the presence of trees and vegetation, Williams could not see the train until it was alarmingly close. His horses became frightened by the sudden appearance of the train, which led to Williams sustaining serious bodily injuries. The crux of the allegation was that the railroad company had a duty to warn individuals in proximity, specifically by sounding the whistle and ringing the bell. Williams contended that the railroad was negligent for not fulfilling this duty as prescribed by statute, thereby causing his injuries.	The plaintiff, Charles A. Williams, argued that the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company was negligent for failing to give the statutory signals when approaching the railroad crossing. He claimed that this negligence directly caused his injuries when the horses he was using became frightened as the train approached unexpectedly. Williams sought compensation for his bodily injuries, asserting that the railroad's failure to follow safety regulations constituted grounds for liability.	The defendant, Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, contended that the statute requiring signals was intended to protect individuals who are crossing the railroad tracks at highway intersections, not those working nearby. They argued that Williams was not in imminent danger of crossing the tracks and that the statutory duty to provide warnings did not extend to individuals in adjacent fields. Thus, they requested dismissal of the case, asserting that the claim did not meet the legal requirements for negligence as outlined by the relevant statutes.

Hannah Ashbaugh filed for divorce in 1855 against her husband, Oliver T. Ashbaugh, after a period of married life that began in Canada in 1849. The couple lived together as husband and wife until 1852, when Oliver deserted Hannah willfully and without cause. Following the desertion, he moved to Illinois and resided there for three years before the divorce filing. Throughout this time, he refused to support Hannah and denied her attempts to re-establish their relationship. Hannah claimed that Oliver's desertion lasted for more than two years, continuing up to the time of her filing for divorce. However, the Circuit Court dismissed her case on the grounds that she had not resided in Illinois for a full year prior to filing, which was a requirement under Illinois law for divorce cases.	Hannah Ashbaugh claimed that her husband, Oliver, deserted her for over two years and refused to live with or support her. She sought a divorce on the basis that this desertion constituted a legal ground for divorce within the State of Illinois because it completed while Oliver was residing in the state, despite the initial act occurring in Canada.	Oliver Ashbaugh did not directly contest the desertion claim but relied on the technicality of residency laws. He argued that Hannah’s filing for divorce should be dismissed because she had not lived in Illinois for one whole year before submitting her bill for divorce, which is a prerequisite under Illinois law.

The case "Marenus P. Stull et al. v. Charles H. Hance" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871. The dispute originated from a lawsuit filed by Charles H. Hance against Marenus P. Stull and others, concerning payment for services rendered and money loaned related to the construction of a schoolhouse in McHenry County, Illinois. Hance, a carpenter, was employed by Stull from August 1868 until July 1869. During his employment, he became concerned about receiving payment for his work, which led him to quit temporarily in April 1869. Upon returning, he continued working under Stull, who supervised the construction. After the project was completed, Hance claimed he was owed $59.50 for his work and $25 for money he lent to Stull to pay other workers. Hance sought payment from Stull, who he believed was his employer, and did not initially recognize the other appellants as liable. The appellants, designated as sureties in an agreement with Stull regarding the schoolhouse's construction, contended that their responsibility was limited strictly to their surety status rather than being joint contractors.	The plaintiff, Charles H. Hance, claimed he was owed a total of $84.50, which included $59.50 for labor performed and $25 loaned to Stull. Hance sought to recover these amounts from Marenus P. Stull and the other appellants, arguing that they were jointly responsible for his payment due to their contractual agreement to build the schoolhouse.	The defendants, Marenus P. Stull et al., asserted that they were not liable for Hance's claims as they were merely sureties in the agreement with Stull, who was identified as the principal contractor. They argued that the contract clearly designated Stull as the contractor, and their role was strictly collateral, guaranteeing Stull's performance of the contract rather than performing construction themselves. The defendants emphasized that they had no involvement in hiring Hance or managing the work on the schoolhouse, and they contended that the legal instruction given to the jury incorrectly classified them as joint contractors.

The case "The People ex rel. Louis C. Huck v. The Graceland Cemetery Company" took place in 1877 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved include Louis C. Huck, representing the People, and the Graceland Cemetery Company as the defendant. The dispute arose when the company contested taxation on two large tracts of land it owned, which it claimed were exempt due to their charter provisions for cemetery grounds. The properties in question included a 46.67-acre tract and a 107-acre tract, which had been platted and recorded as cemetery grounds but were not used for burial purposes. The county court initially supported the cemetery company’s claim of exemption from taxes for these lands. However, the lands were used for non-burial purposes, such as housing for employees and pasturing horses, and there had been no intention to utilize them for burials in the immediate future. The Illinois Supreme Court had to determine whether the lands could be considered "subservient to burial purposes" as per the exemption criteria in the company's charter.	The plaintiff, Louis C. Huck, argued that the Graceland Cemetery Company was inappropriately claiming tax exemption for lands that were neither in actual use for burial purposes nor were they held for the general use of lot holders. Huck maintained that the company had not demonstrated a legitimate need for the two tracts of land to be exempt from taxation, as they had not been utilized for any burial activities or related cemetery functions.	The Graceland Cemetery Company contended that the two tracts of land were indeed exempt from taxation under the terms of its charter, which allowed for properties held for burial purposes, or subservient to such purposes, to be tax-free. The company asserted that since the land was platted and recorded as cemetery grounds, it qualified for this exemption, regardless of current usage. They argued that the lands could be used for cemetery expansion in the future.

Olof Johnson and Samuel Remington brought a forcible detainer action against Jonathan H. Baker in April 1865 in Henry County, Illinois. The case initially commenced before a justice of the peace but was later appealed to the Circuit Court. Johnson and Remington had obtained a judgment against Baker for $214.45. An execution was issued and levied on the disputed property, which they redeemed from a sheriff's sale linked to a judgment favoring Ezekiel Husted. However, the redemption process faced complications when the sheriff's sale resulted in no bids exceeding the redemption amount, prompting the sheriff to convey the property to the plaintiffs. During the proceedings, the plaintiffs sought to introduce a transcript from the justice of the peace judgment, but this was rejected by the court. The plaintiffs noted that Baker had only been served with the summons two days before the judgment was rendered, thus questioning the validity of the judgment and subsequent sale. The court ruled that the insufficient service meant the justice lacked jurisdiction over Baker, rendering the initial judgment void and making all subsequent steps based on it equally invalid.	The plaintiffs claimed the right to recover possession of the property under the 1861 amendatory act of the forcible entry and detainer law. They argued that they had lawfully redeemed the property and contended that the sheriff's sale was valid, seeking to uphold their claim as junior judgment creditors. They argued that their purchase, following the redemption, should allow them to recover possession, despite the defendant’s objections.	The defendant, Jonathan H. Baker, contended that the initial judgment rendered by the justice of the peace was void due to improper service of the summons. Baker noted that the plaintiffs should have been aware of the jurisdictional issues and that the invalid judgment could not form a legal basis for the plaintiffs’ claim regarding the property. He argued that since the original judgment was invalid, all subsequent actions, including the sale and the plaintiffs' claims, were consequently void.

The case "Hector J. Humphrey et al. v. Henry C. Newhall" took place in September 1868 in Illinois. It was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after proceedings in the Circuit Court of Henry County, presided over by Judge Ira O. Wilkinson. The case revolved around a mortgage foreclosure initiated by Newhall against Humphrey and several other defendants—Turner, Flanain, Allen, and Peterson—due to a note executed for $1,750. Humphrey, a non-resident, was served by publication while the other defendants were served personally. The case escalated in the lower court when a rule was established requiring the defendants to respond to Newhall's complaint, which they failed to do, leading to a pro confesso decree entered against them. Humphrey appealed, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction over him due to the alleged insufficiency of the affidavit supporting the publication service.	The plaintiff, Henry C. Newhall, claimed foreclosure of a mortgage secured by a note executed by Humphrey and Turner. Newhall contended that all defendants were properly served and failed to respond to the court proceedings, warranting a decree in his favor.	The defendant, Hector J. Humphrey, asserted that the court did not have jurisdiction over him, as the affidavit of non-residence, which was the basis for the publication service, was insufficient. He argued that this lack of proper jurisdiction should lead to the reversal of the decree against him.

The case "The Elgin, Joliet and Eastern Railroad Company v. James M. Fletcher et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 16, 1889. The dispute arose from a condemnation proceeding under the Eminent Domain Act, initiated by the railroad company to acquire about 9 1/2 acres of land from the appellees' 314-acre farm for the construction of a railway line. The land taken split the farm into two parcels: 184 acres on the east side and 120 acres on the west side. During the trial, there were significant disputes regarding the damages incurred on the remaining land. A jury assessed the value of the land taken and the damages at a total of $3,700. Testimony was presented regarding the land's value, and the railroad company made a stipulation in open court to fence the right of way and maintain an underground crossing on or before May 1, 1888. The trial court provided specific jury instructions concerning the stipulation and damages, leading to contention over whether statutory duties regarding fencing applied in this case.	The plaintiff, the Elgin, Joliet and Eastern Railroad Company, sought to condemn the land necessary for its right of way and requested damages pursuant to the Eminent Domain Act. The plaintiff argued that the jury should assess damages based solely on the land taken and the additional damages to the remaining land, exempt from considering future failures in maintaining fences or crossings as expressed in the stipulation. They contended that the damages should reflect any stipulations made in open court regarding the timely enclosure of the right of way.	The defendants, James M. Fletcher and Mark W. Fletcher, contended that the railroad company was obligated to maintain fencing for the right of way within six months of the railway's opening. They argued that the railroad's stipulation did not negate the statutory requirements, asserting that any potential damage claims should include consideration for the delays and lack of proper fencing until such obligations were fulfilled. They insisted that the jury's instructions should allow for damages arising subsequent to the stipulated deadline for fencing.

In January 1860, Joseph E. Norwood took out a $10,000 life insurance policy with the Manhattan Life Insurance Company, payable to George W. Pulsifer. In August 1865, Pulsifer assigned this policy to Elizabeth Norwood, Joseph's wife. Due to financial difficulties, Elizabeth endorsed the policy in blank, allowing Joseph to use it as collateral for a loan of $1,200. In June 1867, a mutual arrangement was made between Joseph, Guerdon, and Kimball, where Joseph would pay his debts, including a $5,000 note to Guerdon. Guerdon paid off the loan to Sturges and received the policy as security. When the annual premium of $524.90 became due in January 1868, Guerdon was misinformed that Joseph had partially paid it. Consequently, a new policy was issued to Elizabeth, and Joseph later paid the remainder of the premium. After Joseph’s death in April 1868, Guerdon sought to claim payments from the insurance proceeds to satisfy his debt, leading to a legal battle with Elizabeth and the insurance company regarding the validity of his claim on the new policy.	Guerdon claimed entitlement to the insurance proceeds under the newly issued policy, arguing that the policy had effectively renewed the original assignment and that he should retain his interest as a creditor. He contended that Joseph’s financial arrangements had been made in good faith, asserting that he had relied on representations from Norwood and the insurance agent regarding the payment of the premium.	Elizabeth Norwood contended that she did not consent to assign the policy to Guerdon and was misled by her husband's actions. She argued that her endorsement of the policy was not a formal assignment, emphasizing that she did not understand the implications of her signature and that Guerdon should not benefit at her expense. The defense claimed that the insurance policy's assignment was invalid as it was done without her informed consent.

The case "City of Chicago v. James Glanville" took place in Chicago, Illinois, with the final judgment issued on January 27, 1886. The plaintiff, James Glanville, brought a lawsuit against the City of Chicago, claiming that he sustained personal injuries due to the city's negligence in maintaining its sidewalks. The incident occurred on West Indiana Street, where Glanville alleged that the sidewalk was in disrepair, specifically pointing to broken and unfastened planks. During his transit, he tripped and fell as a result of the defective sidewalk. The evidence presented during the trial revealed that the plaintiff was familiar with the sidewalk's condition but contended that the city failed to properly maintain it, which ultimately led to his injury. The lower court ruled in favor of Glanville, ordering the city to pay $1,500 in damages, prompting the city's appeal on the grounds of improper jury instructions regarding its liability.	The plaintiff, James Glanville, claimed that the City of Chicago was negligent in failing to keep the sidewalks in a safe condition. He asserted that the city allowed a portion of the sidewalk on West Indiana Street to remain unsafe, which directly caused his injuries when he tripped on the defective walk. Glanville's legal request included seeking damages for his injuries incurred due to the alleged negligence of the city in maintaining the sidewalk.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant, contended that it was not liable for the injuries sustained by Glanville. The city argued that municipal corporations are not insurers against accidents occurring on their streets and sidewalks. The defense emphasized that the key issue was whether the city had exercised reasonable and ordinary care to keep the sidewalk in safe repair, and not merely the existence of a defective sidewalk. The city maintained that the jury instructions mistakenly implied absolute liability based on the mere existence of a defect without considering the city's due diligence.

In the case of Marshall Field et al. v. Nicholas H. Ridgely et al., which was decided on March 27, 1886, in Springfield, Illinois, the litigants were involved in a dispute concerning the creditors of Ember, Ragsdale & Co., who had been operating a substantial business in Springfield prior to their suspension on January 12, 1883. Prior to their suspension, Ember and Ragsdale executed judgment notes totaling $28,500 to the appellees, who were seeking to secure their debts through mortgages on the firm's real estate—mortgages that went unrecorded. On the morning of the firm's suspension, the appellees took a judgment by confession on their notes, securing an execution that was levied on a valuable stock of goods owned by Ember, Ragsdale & Co. After a general assignment was made for the benefit of creditors, the assignee sold the levied goods for $39,295.08. The appellants, who were also creditors, contested this sale, claiming that the execution lien of the appellees was invalid and sought recovery of the proceeds distributed under the county court's order, arguing that they should be applied to satisfy their own claims.	The plaintiffs, Marshall Field et al., argued that the judgment against Ember, Ragsdale & Co. was entered without legal authority, rendering it invalid. They contended that because the judgment and subsequent execution were improper, the funds paid to the appellees from the sale of goods should be returned and distributed among all creditors equitably, including themselves.	The defendants, Ridgely et al., maintained that their judgment and execution against Ember, Ragsdale & Co. were valid and superior to the claims of the other creditors due to a proper lien established before the general assignment. They argued that the plaintiffs were bound by the county court's distribution orders and had not presented sufficient evidence of fraud to warrant a different distribution of the proceeds from the sale of goods.

In 1871, in Jefferson County, Illinois, William Carpenter leased land from Samuel Carpenter, his father, to grow a crop of wheat. Following the planting, William, along with Jonathan C. Jones and others, purchased the entire tract of land from Samuel, which was conveyed to them in a deed without mention of the wheat crop. William then sold his undivided fifth interest in the property to D.T. Phillips. When the wheat was ready for harvest, Jonathan, Phillips, and others cut and harvested it. A legal dispute arose when William claimed wrongful taking of the wheat, arguing he still owned it despite having sold his interest. The case was tried in the Jefferson Circuit Court, where a jury returned a verdict for the defendants, leading William to appeal on the grounds that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence.	William Carpenter claimed that he was wrongfully deprived of his wheat crop by the defendants, who harvested it after he had previously rented the land. He argued that he retained rights to the crop even after selling his interest in the land and sought to have the jury's verdict set aside, requesting a new trial on the basis that the verdict was inconsistent with the evidence presented.	The defendants, including Jonathan C. Jones, contended that William Carpenter had no rights to the wheat after selling his undivided interest in the land without reserving the crop in the deed. They argued that the absence of mention of the wheat in any of the conveyances indicated that William abandoned his claim to it. The defendants maintained that the jury's verdict was justified based on the evidence and the circumstances surrounding the property transactions.

Edward Houts and Susan Houts were married on January 18, 1883, and had one child during their marriage. The case arose from an incident on March 1, 1885, when Edward left their home, which led Susan to file for separate maintenance in the Circuit Court of Wabash County, Illinois on April 8, 1885. She alleged that Edward deserted her and their child without any fault on her part, leaving them without support. Edward countered that Susan had refused to live with him and had actually abandoned him. The case was primarily concerned with determining whether Edward's departure constituted desertion or if Susan's refusal to accompany him to a different residence was the cause of their separation. The court evaluated testimonies from both parties, noting that Edward claimed to have provided a suitable place for them to live and that Susan's refusal was not justified. The trial court initially ruled in favor of Susan, leading to Edward's appeal.	Susan Houts claimed that Edward Houts willfully deserted her and their child without any valid reason, resulting in their abandonment and lack of support. She sought separate maintenance, arguing that his actions constituted wrongful desertion, as she had not faulted him in their separation.	Edward Houts denied the allegations of desertion, asserting that it was Susan who had willfully abandoned him. He testified that he only left their home because he was required to move by the landlord and that he had asked Susan to accompany him, which she refused, citing the ill will of a third party as the reason.

In 1817, in St. Clair County, Illinois, David Everett became the security for Isaac J. Bailey, who sought to purchase goods on credit from William Morrison through Morrison's agent, William Padfield. Morrison refused to extend credit to Bailey directly but was willing to sell goods, valuing at $46.50, on the condition that Everett acted as surety. After goods were sold, Bailey failed to make payment. Subsequently, in 1819, Everett informed Padfield that Bailey had property and requested that he seek payment, yet Morrison failed to collect from Bailey. Everett later received a receipt for a separate account, which added complexity to his liability. The case transitioned from a judgment in favor of Everett by a justice of the peace to a reversal by the circuit court in favor of Morrison, prompting Everett to appeal this decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	David Everett claimed that as a surety based on a verbal agreement, his liability was not binding due to the statute of frauds and perjuries, which requires certain contracts to be in writing. He contended that no written agreement existed to enforce the promise of payment, thus asserting that he was not liable for Bailey’s debt to Morrison.	William Morrison defended against Everett’s claims by asserting that the undertaking was valid and binding under the circumstances. Morrison argued that the credit was primarily given to Everett, not merely as a security for Bailey’s debt, thereby making his promise enforceable. The testimony indicated that Morrison wouldn’t have sold the goods without Everett’s assurance, challenging the claim that the agreement fell under the statute of frauds.

In the fall of 1838, a minor, the son of John Thompson (the defendant), traveled to Jacksonville, Illinois, to visit friends with his father's approval. Initially, he was well-provided with clothing; however, by the spring of 1839, his apparel had become worn out and inadequate due to the prolonged visit. Samuel Hunt (the plaintiff) provided the minor with a new suit of clothes and sought payment from the father. The son was boarding at a tavern and had accumulated debts deemed excessive by his friends, who informed the father, John Thompson, that he would not be responsible for these debts, although Hunt was unaware of this notification. The case was heard without jury intervention, and a judgment was rendered against the plaintiff, leading to this appeal.	Samuel Hunt argued that John Thompson, as a father, had an obligation to provide for his son, which included paying for necessary clothing. Hunt contended that although there was no express authority to contract from the father, the circumstances suggested an implied promise, as John had previously supported his son.	John Thompson defended against the claims by asserting that he had not given express authority for his son to make the purchase, and there were no circumstances indicating he impliedly agreed to cover such expenses. He argued that since the son was living apart from him and had not informed his father of any need for clothes, Thompson was under no obligation to pay for Hunt's services. The son voluntarily abandoned his home, which affected his right to support.

In the case of Anne Montague v. Theodore Selb et al., the legal dispute arose in Illinois, with the final decision issued on March 30, 1883. Anne Montague, the plaintiff, was the widow of Daniel Montague, who had died intestate while occupying a homestead property. After his death, the property was sold to the defendants, Theodore Selb and others, by the estate's administrators to pay debts. Montague claimed her rights to dower and homestead in the property. The significance of the case revolves around complex issues of property rights, mortgages, and the equitable principles regarding claims against co-tenants. The defendants argued that Montague's claims to homestead and dower should be subject to prior mortgages on the property, which included a release of her rights to dower and homestead. Initially, the trial court sided with Montague, granting her claims, but that decision was reversed upon appeal, leading to further legal proceedings.	Anne Montague argued that as the widow of Daniel Montague, she was entitled to homestead and dower rights in the property that had been sold by the estate administrators. She maintained that her deceased husband's prior debts should not impair her rights and that she had continued to occupy the property as a homestead. Her legal requests included a decree to have her homestead and dower rights assigned to her, along with general relief concerning her claims.	The defendants, Theodore Selb and others, contended that Montague's claims were invalid as the property was subject to prior mortgages, which had released her dower and homestead rights. They asserted that they acquired a legitimate interest in the property through the administrator's sale and were entitled to deductions for the amounts owed under those mortgages before any assignment of benefits to Montague could occur. They requested the court to enforce their position regarding Montague's obligation to contribute toward these debts associated with the property.

Nelson Braxon and others held land adjoining the north bank of the Bock River in Illinois, where a dispute arose regarding the stones quarried from the riverbed. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. The plaintiffs, landowners, claimed that the defendant, Isaac N. Bressler, had unlawfully taken rock from their property in the river. The river, measuring about 1300-1400 feet wide at the point of contention, is classified as navigable but above the tidal influence. The court needed to determine the extent of the plaintiffs' property rights to the riverbed and whether they had the authority to protect their land from trespassers. The major legal principle in question was whether riparian owners had ownership of the riverbed up to its center when the river is navigable above tide water.	The plaintiffs argued that they had ownership rights over the land up to the centerline of the Bock River due to the common law principle establishing riparian ownership. They contended that as the river was navigable in fact, yet above the tidal flow, their rights were not affected and granted them authority to protect the riverbed from unauthorized removal of materials, such as rock or gravel.	The defendant maintained that the public has an easement over navigable streams for passage and that this should restrict the rights of the plaintiffs concerning the riverbed. Bressler argued that the ownership of land adjacent to the river did not grant exclusive rights to the material of the riverbed, as public navigation should take precedence over individual property rights in this context.

In January 1873, a legal case emerged in McLean County, Illinois, involving Ebenezer D. Churchill and The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company. Churchill had purchased a ticket to travel from Chenoa to Chicago. After traveling to Joliet, he procured a lay-over ticket for a 30-day period. When he sought to continue his journey after the lay-over period, he was denied passage by the conductor, who refused to accept his expired lay-over ticket. As a result, Churchill was forcibly ejected from the train despite his attempts to present his ticket. This case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after a lower court judgment ruling in favor of the railroad’s demurrer to Churchill's claims regarding the second count of his declaration.	Churchill argued that the lay-over ticket he received authorized him to travel at any time on the railroad's cars. He claimed the railroad company had no authority to impose limitations after the purchase of the ticket. Additionally, he contended that the manner in which he was ejected from the train was excessive and violent, and he sought damages for this wrongful ejection.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company defended its actions by asserting that it had the right to establish terms for lay-over tickets, which did not legally bind them to honor the expired ticket. The railroad argued that the conditions of the lay-over ticket were agreed upon by both parties, and since Churchill did not use the ticket within the specified time, he had no grounds for recovery. They maintained that the ejection was justified and responded appropriately to Churchill's failure to pay his fare.

Jonathan Sharp was involved in a legal case regarding an assault charge against Thomas J. Locey, which took place in the Clinton Circuit Court, Illinois. The incident occurred prior to November 1862, during which Sharp was accused of stabbing Locey multiple times with a knife, allegedly intending to inflict serious bodily harm. Testimony during the trial revealed that shortly before the assault, Sharp had made threats indicating his intention to hurt the Locey family if he got into any difficulties with them. The introduction of this testimony was contested but ultimately allowed in court. The jury had to consider whether Sharp acted in self-defense, as he claimed he had retreated and warned Locey to desist before the confrontation escalated. The case was brought forth after he was found guilty of the assault. The court deliberated on the evidence presented, including Sharp's behavior during the confrontation, and ultimately affirmed the jury's verdict.	The plaintiff, or in this case, the state (People), claimed that Jonathan Sharp was guilty of assaulting Thomas J. Locey with the intent to cause serious bodily injury. They presented evidence of Sharp's prior threats towards the Loceys to establish intent and context for the assault. The prosecution argued that Sharp's actions were not justifiable as self-defense, highlighting the severity of the injuries inflicted.	Jonathan Sharp defended himself by claiming he acted in self-defense during the confrontation with Locey. He argued that he had retreated from the fight and issued warnings to Locey to back off before the stabbing occurred. Sharp contended that the evidence could support an acquittal based on his claim of self-defense, seeking a new trial on these grounds.

The case "Thomas Watt et al. v. William McGalliard et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1873. The case centers around a dispute involving a fractional half-quarter section of land, totaling 141 acres, located in Logan County, Illinois.
