The court initially struck down the defendant's pleas due to an insufficient affidavit.	Samuel S. Hays argued that the affidavits filed by Edgar Loomis were inadequate and that his claims should be upheld. He sought to have the court deny Loomis’s defenses, stating there was a lack of sufficient grounds for the latter's claims. As part of his legal requests, Hays aimed for a judgment that would affirm his original claims and secure a remedy against the defendants for breaching their alleged obligations.	Edgar Loomis contended that his affidavit of merits, despite lacking a formal caption, met the legal requirements outlined in Illinois statutes. He argued that the contents of the affidavit sufficiently identified his case and provided a solid basis for a defense against Hays's claims. Loomis maintained that the evidence he presented backed his assertion of a meritorious defense, thus seeking to have Hays's claims dismissed and have the court recognize the validity of his defense.

Edgar Loomis v. William Cowen is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 16, 1883. The case involves a dispute over the ownership of a tract of land, specifically lot 17, originally owned by Winchester Hall. Hall had a mortgage for approximately $20,000 with Ayers and Hamilton and entered into a contract with Joseph Smith to sell the west half of the tract for about $18,000. After Smith failed to pay, he reconveyed the property back to Hall, who subsequently conveyed the entire tract to Louis Bush. William Cowen, having entered into a contract with Smith, had taken possession of the lot in the spring of 1857 and made partial payments under that agreement. In 1871, Cowen paid Bush to obtain a deed for the lot. Meanwhile, the mortgage debt had been partially paid by Hall and was subject to a sale prompted by non-payment. The ownership of the lot was further complicated by a series of sales under the mortgage, which ultimately led to Edgar Loomis acquiring the title through mesne conveyances. The crux of the case revolved around whether Loomis could claim the title against Cowen, who had an earlier claim stemming from his contract with Smith.	Edgar Loomis, the plaintiff, contended that he held the legal title to lot 17, having acquired it through the legitimate chain of ownership and valid mesne conveyances from previous owners, including the original mortgagor. Loomis asserted that all sales under the mortgage had been completed, and therefore, Cowen's claim to the lot was invalid since the mortgage sale did not pass any title to him. He sought a judgment of ejection against Cowen to reclaim legal possession of the property.	William Cowen, the defendant, argued that he had a valid claim to the property based on his earlier contract with Smith and subsequent payments made for the lot. He maintained that his possession was rightful and established through agreement and payment. Cowen pointed out that Loomis could not recover simply based on the previous decisions concerning the mortgage since those decisions were now res judicata (a matter already judged). He asserted that Loomis had failed to present a title that could overcome his prior claims.

In November 1852, in Menard County, Illinois, Thomas Reed filed a lawsuit against Archibald Johnson claiming trespass due to Johnson's cattle damaging his growing corn. Reed pursued the case before a justice of the peace, arguing that the injury to his crops warranted compensation. The circuit court, however, dismissed the suit, asserting that it did not have jurisdiction over such a matter because growing corn was considered real estate, thus not within the purview of a justice's jurisdiction, which was limited to cases involving personal property under the law. This case raised the critical legal question of whether growing corn should be classified as personal property, and thus actionable before a justice of the peace. The court noted the historically evolving definitions of personal property and acknowledged the practical implications of allowing justices to handle such cases for efficiency and fairness.	The plaintiff, Thomas Reed, contended that his growing corn should be recognized as personal property for the purpose of filing a trespass lawsuit against Archibald Johnson after his cattle damaged it. He sought to have the case reinstated, arguing that allowing justices of the peace to exercise jurisdiction over such disputes would provide easier access to justice for those with minor claims while maintaining the ability to assert his rights against the defendant.	Archibald Johnson defended against Reed's claims by arguing that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction because the injury was to an item classified as real estate. Johnson's position was based on a strict interpretation of the law that limited justices' jurisdiction to actions involving personal property and not on growing crops, which were deemed part of real estate due to their immobility and perishable nature.

The case of Jonathan H. Baker et al. v. The Bishop Hill Colony took place in the state of Illinois, heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1867. The dispute arose over a mortgage executed by John I. Hall to the Bishop Hill Colony. In the mid-1850s, Hall gained possession of land and later purchased a tax title for it. On March 20, 1858, he executed a mortgage in favor of the Colony, securing two promissory notes. Following complications over payments and titles, an agreement was struck in June 1860 between Hall and the firm of J.H. Baker & Co. (composed of Jonathan H. Baker, David Lawson, and David P. Wells), which reportedly included a quitclaim to the land and other financial adjustments. However, this arrangement occurred without the knowledge or consent of the Colony, which led to a foreclosure against Hall by the Colony due to non-payment. The case revolves around the rights of ownership, the validity of the mortgage, and the arrangements made by the parties involved, with significant emphasis on the transactions and legal standing related to the property.	The plaintiff, the Bishop Hill Colony, primarily argued that they held a legitimate mortgage on the property executed by John I. Hall, and thus had the right to foreclose on the mortgage due to Hall's failure to pay. They sought a decree of foreclosure to sell the mortgaged premises and recover the owed amounts. The plaintiff asserted that their rights were superior to those of J.H. Baker & Co. regarding the property based on the equitable interests at stake.	The defendants, J.H. Baker & Co., contended that their agreements and transactions with Hall established claims to the property that predated the Colony's mortgage. They argued that Hall's default was mitigated by their arrangement, which transferred control back to them. The defense claimed that the Colony had no standing to enforce the mortgage without addressing their competing equities, suggesting that the rights established by Baker & Co. took precedence over the Colony's claims.

On April 18, 1885, a financial transaction took place involving Ira Holmes, who had his promissory note for $5,000 discounted by Avery, Hillabrant & Co., guaranteed by Henry V. Bemis. Holmes received a portion of the proceeds, while the rest was used to set off an existing debt. As collateral, Holmes assigned a $10,000 promissory note from his wife, Virginia B. Holmes, to this company. After Holmes defaulted on the $5,000 note, Bemis paid it and subsequently took a judgment by confession against Virginia for $12,312.48 on February 24, 1887. Virginia sought to vacate this judgment, which was partly successful—resulting in a reduction of the amount to $3,807.50—before the case was taken to the Illinois Supreme Court for further review on appeal from the Appellate Court for the First District.	Virginia B. Holmes, the plaintiff, argued that the confession of judgment should be vacated because it was not authorized by the power of attorney included in the promissory note. She contended that the judgment was improperly taken in the name of Bemis, claiming it fell outside the intent and scope of the originally granted power of attorney.	Henry V. Bemis, the defendant, maintained that the power of attorney explicitly allowed for any attorney of any court to confess judgment in favor of the assigned holder of the note. He argued that the inclusion of "& Bro." did not negate the validity of the power, as the intent of the power was to benefit both the payee and the assignee. Bemis contended that the judgment made in his name as assignee was justified and should not be invalidated.

In the case of Crane Brothers’ Manufacturing Company v. Kraft, Gross & Company, taking place in Illinois, the legal dispute arose regarding a contract for the sale of goods, which was entered into between the parties. The case was initiated by the Crane Brothers’ Manufacturing Company, who claimed that Kraft, Gross & Company failed to uphold their contractual obligations. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, and the proceedings were conducted without a jury. Over the course of the trial, three primary issues of fact were identified: whether the appellant, Crane Brothers, actually made the contract, whether there was a breach of said contract, and what the resulting damages were. The trial court's findings were contested, primarily due to conflicting evidence presented from both sides. However, the appellate court ultimately conducted a thorough examination of the record and concluded that the trial court's findings were correct.	The plaintiff, Crane Brothers’ Manufacturing Company, asserted that Kraft, Gross & Company had breached a contract concerning the sale of goods. They claimed that the defendant had not fulfilled their obligations as specified in the contract, leading to financial damages. As a result, the plaintiff requested compensation for these damages and sought to establish the legality of their claims regarding the contract's existence and terms.	The defendant, Kraft, Gross & Company, contended that they had not breached the contract and questioned the validity of the contract itself. They asserted that the evidence presented by the plaintiff was insufficient to prove the existence of a binding agreement. The defendant's primary request was for the court to dismiss the claims brought against them due to lack of evidence substantiating the plaintiff's allegations.

The case involves two brothers, Charles Johnston (originally Abijah Edmonds) and Charles Edmonds, hailing from Massachusetts. The elder brother, Charles Johnston, changed his name and moved to Illinois, leaving the responsibility of caring for their aging parents to the younger brother, Charles Edmonds. For nearly thirty years, Charles Edmonds supported their parents with minimal financial help from Johnston. At one point, Johnston expressed a desire to reimburse Edmonds for half of the expenses incurred in this support, which led to a note of $3,129.59 being executed in favor of Edmonds in 1850. Over the years, the brothers maintained a trusting relationship, with Johnston allowing Edmonds to manage his affairs and property freely. In 1852, Johnston confessed judgment for the note amount to Edmonds, but both parties intended for it not to be enforced during Johnston's lifetime. After Johnston’s death, Edmonds presented the judgment against his estate, which was allowed as a valid claim by the County Court of Clark County. The executors of Johnston's estate appealed to the circuit court, leading to the present case.	Charles Edmonds, as the plaintiff, claims reimbursement from the estate of his deceased brother, Charles Johnston, for care he provided to their parents over several decades, supported by a judgment created via a confession of judgment. He argues that this judgment is valid and should be honored, thus seeking a payment of $7,105.88, which includes interest on the original judgment amount.	The executors of Johnston's estate argue that the original judgment is void and has been fully paid. They contend that the judgment was intended to defraud other creditors and that it was improperly recorded without relevant documents being presented at trial. They also insist that the significant lapse of time suggests the judgment was satisfied, and thus they should not be liable for the payment.

In April 1857, the case of William W. Low et al. v. William Martin was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from a dispute over a quantity of corn. The plaintiffs, William W. Low and others, claimed that the corn in question was their property, which had been stored with the defendant, William Martin, who operated as a common warehouseman. Martin countered by asserting ownership of the corn, claiming his lien for storage fees. The plaintiffs contended that the defendant had fraudulently issued receipts for grain that he did not have in store for them, which led them to believe that their grain was securely held in storage. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of the defendant, rejecting the plaintiffs’ claims.	The plaintiffs argued that the corn stored with the defendant was their property and that they had been misled by the defendant's fraudulent issuance of warehouse receipts for grain they did not own. They sought recovery of their corn through a replevin action, asserting that they had a rightful claim to the specific property stored with Martin.	The defendant contended that he was a common warehouseman and had a lien on the corn for storage fees, which justified his retention of possession. Martin argued that the intermingling of the corn with other grain occurred with the consent of the plaintiffs, thereby preventing them from making a claim to specific corn. He further maintained that the issuance of false receipts did not negate his right to retain the stored property for unpaid charges.

In April 1863, the case of George O. Banks v. Louisa L. Banks was deliberated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The background of the case dates back to May 9, 1861, when a summons was served to George O. Banks. The document indicated that he acknowledged receiving a copy of the summons. The summons, dated May 8, 1861, was part of a chancery bill filed by Louisa L. Banks against George O. Banks in the Recorder's Court of Peru, Illinois, presided over by Judge William Chumasero. The primary legal question in the case was whether the court had jurisdiction over George O. Banks, given the debated sufficiency of the service of process. The court found that the defendant was served properly, emphasizing the need for written acknowledgment of service. However, George O. Banks contended that no valid service occurred, arguing that the acknowledgment was not proven to be his signature. The court ultimately had to affirm or dismiss the decree based on the legitimacy of the summons service.	Louisa L. Banks, the plaintiff, argued that the court had properly obtained jurisdiction over George O. Banks through the acknowledged service of the summons. She contended that the acknowledgment was formal and legally sufficient as evidence that George O. Banks received notice of the proceedings, allowing for the bill to be taken as confessed when no answer was filed.	George O. Banks, the defendant, contended that the court lacked jurisdiction due to insufficient service of the summons. He argued that the acknowledgment of service was not adequately proven to be his signature, and therefore the court could not take jurisdiction over his person. The defendant maintained that jurisdiction must be displayed affirmatively in the court record, and since it wasn't, the decree should be reversed.

In 1887, the legal case of "The Town of Aurora et al. v. The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company" was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose when the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company sought to prevent the Supervisor of the Town of Aurora from reallocating funds collected through a special tax, known as the “registered bond tax.” This tax was levied in 1872 specifically to pay off bonds issued by the town to aid in constructing a local railroad. The tax had generated a surplus in funds that the Town's voters, during an annual town meeting in April 1883, directed the Supervisor to allocate to the highway commissioners for bridge repairs. The Railroad Company contested this decision, asserting that the funds were intended solely for the purpose of repaying the bonds, and thus should not be used for any other purposes. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the Railroad Company by issuing a decree that prohibited the town from diverting the funds, affirming that the tax constituted a trust fund meant for a specific purpose. This ruling was upheld by the Appellate Court, leading to further appeal.	The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company argued that the funds raised by the “registered bond tax” needed to be preserved exclusively to pay the bonds specifically tied to the railroad's construction. The plaintiff claimed that the town's attempt to redirect the tax funds to a bridge fund violated the original purpose of the tax and amounted to an unlawful diversion of a designated trust fund.	The defendants, representing the Town of Aurora and its supervisor, contended that since the bonds were declared void by both state and federal courts, they possessed the authority to allocate the collected tax funds for local improvements, like bridge maintenance. They argued that the town meeting's resolution to repurpose the funds for the bridge fund was lawful and appropriate under the circumstances.

On March 5, 1874, Benjamin R. Frohock leased a farm to Frederick Taylor, Alexander G. Howe, and Joseph B. Taylor for a term of five years, contingent upon the property not being sold. The agreement stipulated an annual rent of $960, payable in two equal installments. If the farm was sold to a third party, Frohock was to compensate the tenants with "reasonable damages," while they were required to vacate the property after harvesting their crops. The tenants occupied the farm without issues until March 1875 when Frohock demanded possession due to a sale of the premises to another party. The tenants complied and surrendered the farm. Subsequently, Taylor and the others initiated a legal action against Frohock to recover the last rental installment for their time on the farm. The defendant argued that they suffered damages as a result of the early termination of the lease, including increased costs associated with relocating and leasing a new property.	The plaintiff, Frederick Taylor et al., claimed that they were entitled to recover the unpaid last installment of the rent for the farm they occupied. They asserted that the lease agreement was clear and required the defendants to pay the owed rent despite the early termination of the tenancy due to the sale of the property.	The defendants contended that the sale of the farm before the end of the lease term caused them financial damage, including difficulties and expenses incurred in finding and renting a new farm. They sought to prove that the market value of the property had increased and that they were entitled to damages for being forced to vacate prematurely.

In March 1869, in Ogle County, Illinois, George Baugh sold a half section of timbered land to his son, Athe B. Curtis, for $11,840. Athe paid $3,000 upfront and agreed to pay the remaining $8,840 using notes secured by a trust deed on the property. After Athe quit-claimed his interest in the land back to his father, George, the latter attempted to sell the timber separately to raise funds for his son's obligations. Despite objections, George provided a trust deed to indemnify the vendor against losses due to timber removal, allowing the sale to proceed. Approximately 83 acres of timber were sold, generating $2,201.16. However, George subsequently enjoined any further sales and when Athe’s debts were unpaid, he sold the land for $6,278, but still owed George approximately $4,936. George filed a bill in court to determine damages and compel the sale of Athe's land to satisfy the debt. The court concluded that George suffered damages amounting to $3,500 due to the timber sale.	George Baugh (the plaintiff) argued that he sustained damages due to the removal of timber from the land without proper compensation. He sought to quantify the damages caused by the timber's sale and requested that Athe's land be sold to recover the amount owed, claiming that the measure of damages should reflect the actual loss incurred from the timber's removal rather than the unpaid notes.	Athe B. Curtis (the defendant) contended that the notes provided as collateral security were not valid claims since he had no existing debt to George at the time of the trust deed. He argued that the measure of damages should not exceed the actual value of the timber sold. Athe maintained that George's claim for damages was excessive and not aligned with the actual financial loss incurred from the timber removal.

Cornelia P. Richey, as the administratrix of B. W. Bichey’s estate, filed a claim against J. Marion Fort, the administrator of Thomas G. Bichey's estate. This case dates back to January 7, 1888, and took place in Henderson County, Illinois. The issue at hand revolves around a financial agreement made on August 5, 1881, when B. W. Bichey transferred a quarter section of land to his son, Thomas G. Bichey, for $5,000. Thomas paid $2,500 upfront and agreed to make annual payments of $175 for his father's support for the remainder of B. W. Bichey’s life, along with a provision that additional funds could be provided if needed, without exceeding the principal sum. Following the death of both B. W. Bichey in 1885 and Thomas G. Bichey in 1886, Cornelia claimed the remaining balance owed from Thomas's estate. The County Court initially ruled in her favor, but the Circuit Court dismissed the claim, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiff, Cornelia P. Richey, contended that the agreement constituted a valid promissory note for $2,500, which became due upon the death of her father and demanded payment of the remaining balance owed by Thomas G. Bichey’s estate. She argued that the payments made during Thomas's lifetime were insufficient to settle the full amount owed, and thus, the estate had an obligation to honor the remaining payment.	The defendant, J. Marion Fort, argued that the agreement functioned as a composition agreement and that all payments were intended to cease upon the death of B. W. Bichey. He contended that any remaining balance at the time of R. W. Richey's death would not be owed to his estate, thus absolving Thomas's estate of responsibilities for any unpaid sums. The Circuit Court upheld this interpretation, leading to the dismissal of the claim.

The case "The People, &c., ex relatione Theron D. Brewster and Henry Jones v. Patrick M. Kilduff" took place in Peru, Illinois, in June 1854, following a mayoral election held on April 1, 1854. The key individuals involved were Theron D. Brewster, the plaintiff and candidate for mayor, and Patrick M. Kilduff, the defendant and acting mayor. Brewster won the election, receiving 162 votes to Kilduff’s 116, which constituted a clear majority. However, the election results were contested due to the manner in which the ballots were presented; Brewster's supporters used white paper while Kilduff's used a slightly tinted paper, leading Kilduff and some lawmakers to unlawfully invalidate Brewster's votes on the grounds of ballot legality. After the election, Kilduff acted as if he were still mayor and refused to recognize Brewster's election, resulting in Brewster and colleagues attempting to resume city council functions. The conflict over the control of the city seal and formal authorizations became central, as Brewster sought a writ of mandamus to regain possession of the seal.	The plaintiffs, Brewster and Jones, argued that the election laws were violated when Kilduff discarded valid ballots based on spurious claims of their illegality. They contended that the ballots were compliant with the election statute, as they were indeed white paper, and that the rejection of ballots constituted a fraud against the voters. As a remedy, they sought a writ of mandamus compelling Kilduff to deliver the city seal to Jones, the elected city clerk, ensuring Brewster could officially assume his duties as mayor.	Kilduff defended himself by asserting that Brewster was never legitimately elected and thus lacked the right to the mayor's office. He argued that the assembly led by Brewster was not a functioning city council because it included members who were not duly recognized. Kilduff claimed that the election returns and ballots were properly handled according to regulations, insisting on his right to control the city seal and denying the legitimacy of the plaintiffs' claim to it. He also suggested that any legal challenge to his conduct should be pursued via a quo warranto proceeding rather than mandamus.

George W. Miller filed an action of ejectment against Abram M. Pence and others in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois. The case revolves around a dispute over certain lands that Miller claims to own in fee. Initially, the trial resulted in a judgment favoring the defendants, which was upheld by the Illinois Supreme Court. After this affirmation, Miller paid the costs and sought to have the judgment vacated and a new trial granted. This new trial featured the same evidence as the first trial, but the court directed the jury to find a verdict for the defendants based on the validity of the title held under the Aughinbaugh judgment, which was not disputed. While the plaintiff attempted to introduce evidence to challenge the defendants' title based on the Brahmstadt and Miller judgment, the court found it immaterial, as the title under the Aughinbaugh judgment was sufficient to defeat Miller's claim. The proceedings highlight key issues in property law, such as the effects of judicial sales and validity of titles arising from them.	Miller's main argument was that he owned the land in question and sought to recover possession through the ejectment action. He attempted to challenge the validity of the defendants' title, claiming possible errors in the previous judgments that had led to the sale of the property.	The defendants argued that their title to the property was valid and uncontested, based on the Aughinbaugh judgment. They asserted that the plaintiff's claims of error regarding the Brahmstadt and Miller judgment did not affect the validity of the title derived from the Aughinbaugh judgment, thus justifying the court's instruction for the jury to find for the defendants.

In September 1870, the case of The Commercial Insurance Company v. Henry Ives et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from an insurance policy issued to Henry Ives and his associates regarding their frame steam flour mill located in El Paso, Woodford County, Illinois. The Ives had an existing insurance policy with additional coverage amounting to $8,000 from other companies. They applied for a new policy with the Commercial Insurance Company through an agent named J. P. Holmes. Holmes filled out the application and signed it on behalf of the Ives without their direct communication, making specific assertions about the property's status. After a fire destroyed the insured property, the Commercial Insurance Company denied the claim, arguing that the policy was void due to several stipulations. These included a requirement for written consent regarding other insurance and accurate disclosure of the insured's interest in the property, which was falsely represented in the application. The company contended it relied entirely on its own knowledge of the facts and the conduct of its agents.	The plaintiff, the Commercial Insurance Company, argued that the insurance policy was void due to several breaches of the policy's conditions. They claimed that the prior insurance coverage was not disclosed in writing and that the application contained false statements regarding the ownership and interest in the property at the time the policy was issued. The company sought to have the court declare the policy invalid, thereby denying the claim made by the defendants for coverage.	The defendants, Henry Ives and his associates, maintained that the policy was valid and should be honored by the insurance company. They argued that the application was filled out by the company’s agent, Holmes, without proper behavior that would implicate them in the inaccuracies. They contended that the company cannot deny coverage based on faults in the application initiated by its agent and claimed that they acted in good faith without knowledge of the alleged misstatements in the application process.

The case "Merchants National Bank v. Augustus W. Ritzinger et al." was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on June 16, 1886. The plaintiffs, Augustus W. and Frank L. Ritzinger, operated as a partnership under the name Bitzinger & Co. They initiated an assumpsit action against Merchants National Bank of Chicago concerning a bill of exchange or check for $2,000 that was originally drawn by A. & J. C. S. Harrison, a banking firm from Indianapolis, Indiana, and made payable to William Haerle, who then indorsed it to the Ritzingers. The check was dated July 19, 1884, and was presented to the bank on July 28 and again on August 1, 1884, but payment was refused both times. At the time of the check's presentation, A. & J. C. S. Harrison's account with the bank showed a balance that would have covered the check; however, the account was subsequently charged to settle an unrelated note due from another party. The case revolved around whether the bank had the right to apply the depositor’s funds to an other obligation that was not yet due, and the nature of the check concerning the funds' availability.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to recover the amount of the check for $2,000 plus interest due to the refusal of the Merchants National Bank to honor the check. They argued that at the time of presentation, there were sufficient funds in the account of A. & J. C. S. Harrison to cover the check. The plaintiffs contended that the bank acted improperly in applying the funds toward a different obligation rather than paying out the check.	The defendant, Merchants National Bank, contended that they had a right to apply the funds in A. & J. C. S. Harrison's account to an outstanding note that was not yet due, arguing that their action was legally justified. They also pointed to the nature of the check as a foreign bill of exchange, suggesting that the plaintiff could not maintain a suit without an acceptance of the check by the bank.

In 1890, in Cook County, Illinois, T. B. Baker and Sophronia Baker faced insolvency issues, leading to a voluntary assignment of their estate. The legal matter involved a dispute concerning orders made by E. H. Gary, the judge of Du Page County, regarding the management of Baker's Theater, which was part of the assigned estate. The appellants, Baker and his wife, contended that the orders were improperly issued without the proper authority, as they claimed Judge Gary was not requested to oversee matters. Furthermore, they argued that one of the orders was made at his private office and not in a legitimate court setting. Despite these claims, the court record affirmed that Gary was indeed presiding appropriately at the request of the Cook County judge. The court's orders allowed the assignee to complete the theater, issue necessary financial instruments, and lease the property, all aimed at maintaining and optimizing the estate's value for creditors. The court ultimately believed that all procedures followed were valid and in line with its discretion to support the creditors' best interests.	The plaintiffs, T. B. Baker and Sophronia Baker, argued that the orders issued by the assignee concerning the management and leasing of Baker's Theater were improper. They claimed that Judge Gary lacked proper jurisdiction to make those orders since he was not requested by the Cook County judge to preside over the case. They attempted to introduce parol evidence to invalidate the orders, asserting that they were made outside the bounds of appropriate judicial oversight.	The defendant, represented by Edward T. Singer, the assignee, maintained that the orders made by Judge Gary were valid. They argued that, according to the court record, Gary rightfully presided over the assignment case and that the decisions supported the optimal management of the insolvent estate to benefit the creditors. The defendant emphasized that no evidence demonstrated a manifest abuse of discretion by the court, reinforcing the legitimacy of the orders in question.

William F. Mahon and Joseph J. Mahon were partners in the wholesale millinery business alongside James H. B. Daly. On August 27, 1872, they executed an agreement to dissolve their partnership. This agreement stipulated that Daly would transfer his interest in the business to the Mahons in exchange for indemnification against the firm's liabilities and guaranteed employment until January 1, 1873, at a specified salary of $1,250 per month, payable semi-monthly. Daly began his role as a salesman and clerk following the dissolution. However, on October 1, 1872, the Mahons discharged him from his position. In response to his termination, Daly initiated a lawsuit seeking compensation for the wages owed for the period he had served. The case was tried without a jury, and the court had to evaluate conflicting testimonies regarding Daly's conduct at work, including allegations of inattentiveness and intoxication. Ultimately, the court found in favor of Daly, assessing damages at $573.90, leading the Mahons to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, James H. B. Daly, claimed that he was wrongfully discharged by the Mahons before the agreed employment period ended. He argued that according to the contract, he was entitled to pay for the time he actually served, which was supported by the agreement made when the partnership was dissolved. Daly sought to recover the wages owed to him based on the contract terms.	The Mahons contended that they had justifiable reasons to terminate Daly, asserting that he committed breaches of his implied obligations by being inattentive and appearing under the influence of intoxicants during work. They aimed to justify their decision to discharge him and disputed the rightful payment for the period Daly claimed he was owed wages.

In April 1867, in Stephenson County, Illinois, Augusta Young, an unmarried woman, initiated a slander lawsuit against Ludwig Baker and Caroline Baker, his wife. The plaintiff alleged that Caroline Baker had maliciously accused her of being "in the family way" and stated that she had been taken to a Chicago doctor to have a child “worked off.” These statements were considered damaging to Young’s reputation. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after the jury found the Bakers guilty in a prior trial and awarded Young $800 in damages. The trial involved witness testimonies that corroborated Young's claims about Caroline Baker's statements. The defense argued various points related to the words spoken and the validity of evidence.	Augusta Young claimed that Caroline Baker made false and slanderous statements about her being pregnant and implied fornication. She requested damages for the emotional and reputational harm caused by these statements. The plaintiff presented evidence from witnesses who had heard Caroline Baker's remarks, arguing that the words spoken met the legal criteria for slander and justified a verdict in her favor.	Ludwig and Caroline Baker contended that the plaintiff had not proven the specific words laid out in the declaration and argued that additional words mentioned by witnesses did not constitute a valid variance. They also challenged the instructions given to the jury during the trial, asserting that they misled the jury regarding the implications of the statements and the qualifications for assessing damages. The defendants requested that the court overturn the jury’s verdict and either grant a new trial or dismiss the case based on these arguments.

The case of Edward M. West et al. v. The Madison County Agricultural Board took place in June 1876 in Illinois. The Madison County Agricultural Board, a corporation, owned fairgrounds where it held annual exhibitions. In a meeting, the board unanimously resolved that its treasurer could borrow up to $2,000 to finance the construction of a new exhibition hall and the reconstruction of an amphitheater. The treasurer, alongside the president, borrowed the funds from Edward M. West and attempted to execute a trust deed on the fairgrounds to secure the loan. However, the trust deed was executed in the names of the president and treasurer, not explicitly in the corporation's name, leading to a dispute. West filed a bill seeking to correct this execution error, foreclose on the deed of trust, and obtain a sale of the property if payments were not made. The court had to consider whether the agricultural board had the authority to execute the trust deed and whether the execution error could be remedied through equitable relief.	The plaintiffs, led by Edward M. West, argued that the trust deed executed by the agricultural board was improperly formalized as it did not correctly represent the corporation. They sought to correct this informality through a court order to reform the deed of trust, initiate foreclosure, and allow for a sale of the property if the agricultural board failed to repay the loan.	The Madison County Agricultural Board contended that they were not authorized to execute the trust deed as it was not reflected in the corporation's name. They argued that the execution error meant the obligation for the loan could not stand, as the deed was not validly created. The board's defense was based on the claim of lack of authority to secure the loan in the manner performed by their officers.

In 1870, John C. Smith borrowed $2,500 from James W. Osborne and secured the loan with a mortgage on his property in Kane County, Illinois. After his death in 1872, John’s estate passed down to his widow, Clarinda Smith, and five children from two marriages. The mortgage remained unpaid, and in 1873, Osborne initiated foreclosure proceedings. By December of that year, he purchased the property for $3,021.12 after a court-ordered sale. Christopher C. Smith, the eldest son, managed the family property interests and contacted Samuel McNair, Osborne's agent, to negotiate the purchase of the certificate of purchase. In November 1874, a deal was struck where Smith would pay a $100 premium to McNair and later redeem the property by paying an additional $3,400. However, Smith failed to secure the funds in time and ultimately tendered the amount in March 1874, but McNair refused to accept the payment, claiming it was too late. The case revolved around the terms of their agreement and whether Smith could enforce his rights to the property.	The plaintiffs, Christopher C. Smith and others, claimed that they were entitled to redeem the property based on the agreement made with McNair, asserting that they complied with the terms by tendering the necessary amount before the legal redemption period expired. They sought to compel Osborne to accept the payment of $3,400 and transfer the property title to them.	The defendants, including Osborne and McNair, contended that the plaintiffs missed the deadline to redeem the property according to their agreement. They argued that the $100 premium paid by Smith was forfeited due to his failure to pay the required redemption money in a timely manner, asserting that Smith's claims were not valid as per the terms of the agreement.

The case titled "Louis Brizzolara et al. v. William H. Mosher et al." took place in Chicago, Illinois, with proceedings commencing in July 1872. Key individuals involved included plaintiffs Louis Brizzolara and Guiseppe Botto, along with defendants William H. Mosher, David Cole, and Charles D. Cole. The dispute arose from a contractual agreement regarding the sale of real estate located at 535, 537, and 539 West Madison Street. On July 8, 1872, Brizzolara and Botto authorized D. Cole & Son as their agents to sell the property for $18,000, which included a substantial down payment. After adjusting the terms on September 26, 1872, Mosher made an earnest money payment of $200, with expectations of a warranty deed upon settlement. However, disputes arose regarding the title to the property, as the sellers were unable to provide a perfect title, leading Mosher to refuse further payments. In response, Brizzolara and Botto sought legal action through the Superior Court of Cook County to clear the title and enforce their contract. The case eventually reached the Illinois Supreme Court for resolution.	The plaintiffs, Brizzolara and Botto, argued that the contract executed through their agents constituted a valid agreement for the sale of the property. They claimed that they had tendered a general warranty deed to Mosher and demanded payment, which Mosher refused, leading to their assertion that he was obligated to proceed with the purchase. The plaintiffs requested the court to affirm the decree to remove the cloud on their title resulting from Mosher's refusal to fulfill his contractual obligations.	The defendant, William H. Mosher, contended that the plaintiffs were unable to provide a good title as stipulated in the sales agreement, which included a clause allowing for the refund of money if the title proved unsatisfactory. Mosher argued that due to these contractual terms, he had the right to refuse payment, believing the title issued was not in compliance with the agreement. Moreover, Mosher's defense emphasized the claim that there had been significant adjustments to the terms of the sale that could potentially invalidate the contract.

In September 1875, the case of The Knickerbocker Insurance Company v. Samuel A. Tolman et al. was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving a fire insurance policy for $25,000 obtained by the appellees (Tolman et al.) from the appellant (Knickerbocker Insurance Company). The policy covered a stock of drugs and related articles housed in a brick building located at 35 South Water Street, Chicago. Following a fire that destroyed the property insured under the policy, the Knickerbocker Insurance Company refused to compensate the appellees for their loss. Subsequently, the appellees initiated legal proceedings against the appellant to recover the amount due under the policy. The appellant contended that the trial court erred by not granting a change of venue due to alleged prejudice in Cook County and raised additional objections regarding the sufficiency of the plaintiff's claims regarding the valuation of the property and conditions of the policy. The trial held in the Circuit Court concluded with a judgment against the insurance company, prompting them to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, Samuel A. Tolman and others, claimed that the Knickerbocker Insurance Company failed to fulfill its contractual obligation under the fire insurance policy after a fire destroyed their insured property. They argued that the insurance policy explicitly covered their loss and sought a legal remedy in the form of monetary compensation for the amount insured as specified in the policy.	The defendant, Knickerbocker Insurance Company, presented several defenses, including the assertion that the plaintiffs did not adequately specify the value of the destroyed property in their complaint. They claimed that the declaration lacked necessary details regarding other insurance policies covering the same property and argued for a change of venue, claiming that the local jurors were prejudiced against them. They contended that the refusal of this motion by the court was an error and insisted that such a change was a statutory right that should not have been denied.

In September 1867, Lewis Russell filed a lawsuit against David W. Paine in the Whitesides Circuit Court, located in Illinois. The case originated from a dispute over a mortgage on specific lands. Russell sought to foreclose the mortgage, but Paine responded by denying the execution of the note associated with the mortgage and claimed that Russell had no grounds for a decree in his favor. After a hearing, the court dismissed Russell's bill at his costs, prompting him to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court. The court noted that the evidence presented was contradictory and inconclusive, making it challenging to arrive at a definitive conclusion regarding the merits of the case. The court suggested that due to the conflicting evidence and the nature of the claims, it would be prudent to form an issue of fact and submit the matter to a jury for determination.	Lewis Russell, the plaintiff, argued that he had rightful grounds to foreclose a mortgage on certain lands due to a note that he believed Paine had executed. Russell requested the court to reverse the lower court's dismissal of his case, thereby allowing him to proceed with the foreclosure of the mortgage.	David W. Paine, the defendant, countered Russell's claims by asserting that he had never executed the note referenced in the lawsuit. He maintained that Russell did not have the legal standing to seek a foreclosure decree and requested that the court uphold the dismissal of the case.

In the case of Chicago and Alton Railway Company v. Abraham Buck, which took place in Logan County, Illinois, on the night of October 21, 1882, Abraham Buck owned a farm adjacent to the railway's tracks. Buck had twenty-two horses in a pasture on his property. By the next morning, four of these horses were found badly injured after they escaped through a gate onto the railroad tracks, resulting in their subsequent death. Buck brought a lawsuit against the Chicago and Alton Railway Company, alleging that the negligence of the railroad's employees in handling the trains led to the deaths of his horses. The key individuals in the case included Abraham Buck, the plaintiff, and representatives from the railway company as defendants. The lawsuit was initially tried in the Logan Circuit Court, where a jury found in favor of Buck, prompting the railway company to appeal the decision, claiming the verdict contradicted the evidence presented.	Abraham Buck claimed that the railway company was negligent in its duty to safely operate its trains and maintain its property. He argued that the fastenings on the gate to his pasture were insufficient, allowing his horses to escape onto the tracks, ultimately leading to their death. Buck sought damages for the value of the horses lost due to the alleged negligence of the railroad’s employees in managing the train operations.	The Chicago and Alton Railway Company contended that they could not be held liable for the incident as they had employed commonly accepted fastenings for the gate that were deemed sufficient for preventing livestock from escaping. They argued that any negligence should be attributed to Buck, who failed to secure the gate adequately or to prevent his horses from straying onto the tracks. The railway asserted that the burden of proof for negligence lay with Buck, and the evidence did not support his claims, especially since the company maintained a proper lookout and management of their trains.

In 1882, the case of David Preston et al. v. Jesse Spaulding et al. arose from a financial dispute in Chicago, Illinois. The complainant, Jesse Spaulding, engaged in the lumber trade and sold significant amounts of lumber to the firm of Hair & Odiorne, comprised of James A. Hair, Samuel G. Hair, and William H. Odiorne. As of October 31, 1882, Hair & Odiorne had accrued a substantial debt of $247,322.89 to Spaulding. This debt stemmed from various fraudulent financial statements the firm provided, which misrepresented their financial condition and omitted significant liabilities. On October 31, under impending insolvency, Hair & Odiorne executed judgments in favor of select creditors to preferentially pay them before filing a general assignment for the benefit of all creditors. This legal maneuver occurred just hours before their insolvency declaration, leading Spaulding to file a bill in court seeking to rescind the lumber sales and prevent creditors from executing their judgments, citing fraud and inadequate disclosures from Hair & Odiorne regarding their financial status.	Jesse Spaulding claimed that Hair & Odiorne provided fraudulent financial statements that misrepresented their true indebtedness, thereby inducing him to extend credit and continue selling lumber to them. He requested the court to rescind the sales of lumber made after September 30, 1882, and to recover the value of that lumber as well as declare the judgments against Hair & Odiorne fraudulent and void since they were executed without proper notification and were part of a scheme to defraud creditors.	The defendants, Hair & Odiorne and their preferred creditors, argued that the judgments were valid and that Spaulding had notice of the financial issues, which negated his claims of fraud. They stated that the execution of judgment notes was a legitimate effort to resolve their debts. Furthermore, the defense contended that Spaulding had not exhausted all legal remedies before resorting to equity and that his claims to rescind the contracts should be barred due to his negligence in investigating Hair & Odiorne’s financial condition before extending credit.

The case revolves around Benjamin R. McCleary, who is the administrator of the estate of Jennie and Effie Hicks, and Henry Menke, who was a surety on the guardian’s bond for Edwin Howe. The events date back to April 14, 1865, when William M. Hicks passed away intestate in Cass County, leaving behind a widow and three minor children. Edwin Howe was appointed as the administrator of the estate and later became the guardian for the minors. On August 12, 1867, Howe reported receiving $3731.52 from settling the estate, which included a distribution intended for the minors. However, Howe failed to account for the funds as required and improperly used the money. The two minors, Jennie and Effie, died in 1869, and after a series of legal developments, including a citation for Howe to account for the funds in court, it was determined that he only properly managed a fraction of the money that was reported. The Illinois Supreme Court had to decide whether the prior court's findings were binding regarding Howe's obligations to the Hicks' estate.	McCleary, representing the interests of Jenny and Effie Hicks, claimed that Edwin Howe had breached his fiduciary duties as a guardian by failing to properly account for and distribute the funds allocated to the minors. He sought to hold Henry Menke, the surety, liable under the guardian's bond for the sums reportedly misappropriated.	Menke's defense, articulated through the plea of "nil debet," contested the claims by arguing that the previous court had already found Howe’s accounting adequate and that the plaintiffs' claims were irrelevant since the legal proceedings had not involved those representing Jennie and Effie directly. Menke asserted that the judgment from earlier hearings should be considered final and conclusive regarding Howe’s obligations.

In December 1844, the case of William F. Bradshaw v. Gurdon S. Hubbard et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The original trial occurred at the Lee Circuit Court during the September term of 1842, overseen by Judge Thomas O. Browne. The case involved an assumpsit action regarding a bill of exchange initially drawn by Bruner in favor of Bradshaw for $500, payable ten days after sight. Bradshaw claimed that he had indorsed and delivered the bill to the defendants and that after presenting it for payment, the amount was refused by Bruner. The jury initially found in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $593.94. Subsequent legal maneuvers included a motion for a new trial and an arrest of judgment, both of which were denied. Testimonies raised issues regarding the admissibility of certain evidence, including the protest by a Notary Public and the status of witness Alexander Charters, who had also been an indorser. The case centered on procedural matters and the admissibility of claims regarding the non-payment of the bill.	The plaintiff, William F. Bradshaw, argued that he was entitled to payment under the terms of the bill of exchange after presenting it for payment and receiving notice of non-payment. He claimed that proper procedures were followed, as the bill was presented for acceptance, and he provided testimony supporting this. Bradshaw sought judgment against the defendants for the amount due under the bill of exchange and additional costs associated with the trial.	The defendants contended that the plaintiff's claims were invalid due to procedural errors, including the lack of sufficient averment of the bill's presentment and acceptance. They argued that the Court allowed inadmissible evidence and that a juror, Gilbraith, was improperly seated due to being an indorser and a security for costs. Thus, they sought a new trial and the arrest of the judgment based on these contentions.

In the case of Samantha Gardner v. Peter A. Ladue, which took place in January 1868, the action originated in the Hancock Circuit Court, Illinois. The dispute involved a parcel of land in Hancock County, described as the southeast quarter of section 35, town 7, north range J, west of the fourth principal meridian. The plaintiff, Peter A. Ladue, sought to eject Samantha Gardner from the property, claiming ownership based on a will from Isaac J. Blauvelt, which he produced as evidence. The will, dated September 16, 1825, bequeathed all of Blauvelt's estate to his wife, Sarah, and had been duly admitted to probate in New York. The court was tasked with determining the validity of this will amidst objections raised by the defendant, Gardner, regarding its introduction and the manner of its proof. It was established that a certified copy of the will was admissible under Illinois law, and the case bore some intrigue as both the plaintiff and defendant were connected to different individuals named Isaac Blauvelt, who had claims to military bounty land. Ultimately, the court concluded that the plaintiff's title claim was valid and that the objections raised by the defendant did not hold sufficient merit.	The plaintiff, Peter A. Ladue, claimed ownership of the disputed property based on a will from Isaac J. Blauvelt, asserting that he had established a legitimate legal title through his documentation, including a certified copy of the will which was duly probated. Ladue argued that the land was rightfully his, as supported by historical evidence linking him to the estate in question, and that the court should rule in his favor in ejectment proceedings against Gardner.	The defendant, Samantha Gardner, objected to the introduction of the will, questioning its validity on procedural grounds and arguing that it was only proved by one of the subscribing witnesses, which she contended was not sufficient under the circumstances. Gardner maintained that the will should not serve as a reliable basis for Ladue's claim, thus requesting that the court dismiss his arguments in support of his ownership.

In 1889, the case Allemania Fire Insurance Company v. Willys G. Peck et al. was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated from a fire that resulted in a loss covered by an insurance policy held by Willys G. Peck. Following the incident, negotiations between Peck and the general agent of Allemania Fire Insurance Company took place, where the company expressed doubts about liability but offered a partial settlement of $500. The plaintiff contended that the defendant's ongoing negotiations created a reasonable expectation for an adjustment, which delayed his decision to file a lawsuit within the six-month period stipulated by the insurance policy. The court reviewed evidence indicating that the insurer's actions had indeed deterred Peck from commencing legal proceedings. The Judge, Gary, P.J., determined that if time was consumed in negotiations, it should extend the period allowed to file a claim. The matter had previously been addressed in a prior appeal, which the court indicated could not be reconsidered.	The plaintiff, Allemania Fire Insurance Company, argued that they had a valid liability under the insurance policy, despite the defendant's claims that certain conditions were violated. They contended that the negotiations held by the defendant created a situation where Willys G. Peck was discouraged from filing a lawsuit within the required timeframe. The plaintiff sought a declaration of their right to recover based on the policy terms and showed that the negotiations effectively extended the time permitted due to the reasonable belief that a settlement was imminent.	The defendant, Willys G. Peck, maintained that the insurance company had disclaimed liability under the policy due to alleged violations. They argued that the offered settlement of $500 did not represent acknowledgment of full responsibility for the loss. The defense asserted that the plaintiff was not justified in delaying the suit, arguing that they had enough time to file after receiving the company's last correspondence. They requested the court to dismiss the claim based on the alleged failure to comply with the lawsuit timeframe outlined in the policy.

In January 1860, the legal case of Jesse T. Newman and Simon P. Newman against James Bennett took place in Illinois. The central issue involved a dispute over the ownership of cattle, specifically two cows, two calves, and two steers. Bennett, the defendant, was alleged to be wrongfully holding the property that rightfully belonged to him as a minor, living under the care of H. R. Gillespie, who was acting in loco parentis. Gillespie had made a formal demand for the cattle before the lawsuit commenced, asserting that the demand sufficed for the plaintiffs' claim. The defendants contested the legitimacy of this demand and the overall claims made against them. After presenting their arguments, the jury found in favor of Bennett, determining that the property belonged to him.	The plaintiffs claimed ownership of the cattle and argued that H. R. Gillespie’s demand for the cattle was legitimate, as he acted as a parent figure for minor Bennett. They insisted that a general demand for "Bennett's stock" was sufficient under the circumstances, and the lack of specificity should not invalidate their claim.	The defendant, James Bennett, contended that the demand made by Gillespie lacked legal authority since he was not the legally appointed guardian of the plaintiff, Bennett. The defendant's key argument was that for the demand to hold weight, it must be made by a legally recognized guardian, and that the circumstances did not support the validity of the claim.

The case "City of Nashville v. Henry Weiser et al." took place in June 1870 in Nashville, Illinois. The city of Nashville sought a judgment from the county court of Washington County to sell lands and town lots for unpaid taxes that had been levied for school and other municipal purposes. The county court granted the judgment authorizing the sale of these properties. However, the defendants, represented by Henry Weiser and others, appealed to the circuit court, which reversed the county court's judgment and ruled in favor of the defendants. This appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court was concerned with whether the city had the authority to appeal and whether the proper procedures were followed in the assessment process, including the notification of affected taxpayers and their opportunity to object to the tax assessment.	The city of Nashville contended that the county court's judgment should be sustained, asserting that their charter provided the necessary authority to both levy taxes and appeal judgments related to these taxes. They argued that the appeal bond was valid as it was made payable to the city, which would benefit from the collection of the tax proceeds.	Henry Weiser and the other defendants argued that the city had failed to comply with legal requirements, such as providing taxpayers the opportunity to contest their assessments adequately. They contended that crucial procedures were overlooked by the city council, including notifying taxpayers and holding hearings, thereby rendering the tax judgments invalid. The defense also claimed that their appearance in the county court to contest the judgment did not waive their right to argue these procedural violations.

In June 1870, Walter Williams filed a case against John H. Schmidt in the St. Clair Circuit Court. The dispute arose after Williams leased a coal mine from Schmidt in 1868 for a ten-year term. Williams operated the mine for approximately four months but failed to pay rent and did not manage the mine to Schmidt’s satisfaction. Consequently, Schmidt terminated the lease and reclaimed possession of the mine. Following this, both parties engaged in disputes over claims related to rent, tools, damages caused by poor mining practices, and other costs. The parties initially agreed to arbitrate their differences, with each selecting two arbitrators. However, only two individuals were selected by Williams, and Schmidt disputed the validity of this arbitration process, arguing it lacked the required formal structure and that he was not appropriately notified about the proceedings. Ultimately, a jury trial led to a verdict favoring Williams, awarding him $700, which Schmidt contested.	Walter Williams (plaintiff) claimed compensation for the mining tools and equipment that Schmidt took when he reclaimed the mine. He also sought payment for horses and mules used in the mine operations, as well as the costs incurred for constructing a blacksmith shop and other buildings. Williams argued that he was entitled to these amounts based on the initial lease agreement and the circumstances surrounding the mine's operation.	John H. Schmidt (defendant) countered by asserting that Williams should owe him money for unpaid rent, freights associated with coal shipments, tools, and for damage inflicted on the mine due to unskillful work by Williams. Schmidt maintained that the arbitration process initiated by Williams was invalid since it was not constituted as agreed, lacked proper notice to him, and unfairly barred him from presenting his side. He insisted he should be able to recoup losses stemming from Williams' breach of the lease terms.

On February 14, 1868, in Kane County, Illinois, James T. Hards, along with Smith and Wright, executed multiple mortgages on parcels of property to secure debts totaling over $20,000. The financial arrangements became complicated as mortgages were assigned to different parties, including Tuthill and Wells, and later, John Burton, who sought to foreclose on the properties due to unpaid debts. Hards filed a cross-bill, claiming an agreement with Smith and Wright allowed them to divide the mortgaged property, which included a custom mill. They had assumed responsibility for the debts on the property while conveying the custom mill to Hards. Hards sought to prevent the sale of the custom mill, a move he argued was unjust considering the agreement. The lower court ruled in favor of the defendant, initiating a sale of the property without adequately considering Hards's claims or conducting an accounting of the debts owed. Hards, along with his wife, pursued a writ of error to have the decision overturned.	The plaintiffs, Hards and his wife, contended that an agreement among the mortgagors had been made to divide the property, wherein Smith and Wright would pay the encumbrances on the custom mill. They argued that the court should restrain the sale of the mill as it was not justly assessed in terms of incumbrances and sought an accounting for profits related to the property from the mortgagee to be deducted from the debt before any decree was made.	John Burton, the defendant, argued that the existing agreements between Hards, Smith, and Wright regarding property division and payment of debts did not concern him as the mortgagee. He maintained that the court was correct in permitting foreclosure as he was entitled to ensure the debts were paid through the sale of the mortgaged properties. Burton contended that the plaintiffs had failed to adequately request an accounting and could not complain about the court's actions in the absence of such requests.

In the case of **Sjoerd Tunesma v. Peter Schuttler**, filed on May 15, 1885, in Ottawa, Illinois, the litigation arose from a dispute over the liabilities of stockholders in the insolvent German Savings Bank of Chicago. The appellant, Sjoerd Tunesma, claimed that he was owed $2,624.88 as a depositor in the bank, invoking the 9th section of the bank’s charter which held stockholders individually responsible when defaults occurred. The case unfolded in Cook County Circuit Court and the appellate proceedings clarified the context of the bank's insolvency stemming from events beginning on December 7, 1877, when the bank ceased operations. A receiver was appointed, and various creditors, including the plaintiff, pursued their claims against the bank and its stockholders to recover their funds. A series of legal maneuvers were made through the courts concerning the assets and the liabilities of the stockholders until a decree was established regarding the obligations of the stockholders.	Sjoerd Tunesma, as the plaintiff, argued for the recovery of the amount due to him from Peter Schuttler, the defendant and stockholder of the insolvent German Savings Bank. He claimed that the bank's charter imposed liability on stockholders for any debts incurred by the institution. Tunesma contended that the previous judicial proceedings confirmed the bank’s insolvency and established the stockholders' obligations to satisfy claims from the depositors, including his. He insisted that he should be entitled to recover the outstanding balance owed to him pursuant to these established liabilities.	Peter Schuttler, the defendant, countered the plaintiff's claims by asserting that the plaintiff should not proceed with his lawsuit because he was not part of the earlier proceedings regarding the bank's insolvency and the distribution of its assets. Schuttler argued that a previous court ruling had already adjudicated the liability of stockholders under the amended supplemental bill, thus shielding him from further lawsuits. He contended that any claims against him are barred due to the comprehensive final decrees previously issued, which settled the liability and the distribution of funds among the stockholders.

The case of The Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company v. Allen N. Merrill took place in September 1868 in Illinois. The legal dispute arose when Allen N. Merrill, the consignor, shipped goods marked for John L. Page, care of the American Express Company, and specified as "C. O. D." (Cash on Delivery). The goods were transported by the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company from Geneva to Winnebago and were successfully delivered to Page, who subsequently became insolvent. Unable to recover the price of the goods from Page, Merrill initiated a legal action against the railway company, asserting that they were liable for the value of the goods under the terms of transportation. A circuit court verdict favored Merrill, prompting the railway company to appeal the judgment.	Merrill, the plaintiff, argued that the railway company had an obligation to collect the price of the C. O. D. goods upon delivery to the consignee, Page. He sought damages for the value of the castings, claiming that the railway company had failed to fulfill this duty after delivering the goods to an insolvent recipient. Merrill contended that the company was responsible for collecting payment because the goods were marked for C. O. D., which implied an arrangement for collection.	The Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company contended that their liability only extended to the safe transportation and delivery of the goods to Page, the named consignee. They argued that their receipt did not indicate any obligation to collect payment and that they had not undertaken the role of a collecting agent. Furthermore, they pointed out that no bill for the price of the goods had been provided to them by the consignor, making it impossible for them to collect any dues from Page. The company requested the court to reverse the lower court's judgment.

Thomas H. Wheeler filed a case against Eleanor Wheeler, the administratrix of the estate of O. B. Wheeler, in December 1888. O. B. Wheeler, who passed away on March 15, 1886, had issued a promissory note for $2,000 to his son, Thomas, dated April 1, 1878. After O. B. Wheeler died, Thomas filed a claim against the estate based on this note. Initially, the County Court disallowed the claim, leading to an appeal in the Circuit Court, where the same outcome was reached. The defendant's main argument revolved around the assertion that the note was issued without consideration, as it was given in the context of impending bankruptcy, and that O. B. Wheeler had received a discharge in bankruptcy. However, Thomas countered this by claiming a subsequent promise made by his father to pay the note after the bankruptcy proceedings had begun, as well as asserting that he had provided valuable labor for his father, which constituted consideration for the note. The case presented complex legal issues involving bankruptcy discharge and valid consideration for debts.	The plaintiff, Thomas H. Wheeler, argued that the note was valid and claimed a subsequent promise from his father to pay the debt despite O. B. Wheeler’s bankruptcy. He contended that this promise, made after filing for bankruptcy but before being discharged, revived the original note. Additionally, Thomas asserted that his work and labor for his father provided sufficient consideration for the note, challenging the defendant's claims of lack of consideration and the implications of the bankruptcy discharge.	Eleanor Wheeler, as the defendant, presented two primary defenses against the claim. Firstly, she argued that the note was issued without proper consideration, asserting it was meant to preserve the estate amid O. B. Wheeler's anticipated bankruptcy. Secondly, she claimed that the discharge obtained during the bankruptcy proceedings released O. B. Wheeler from any debts incurred prior, thereby nullifying the enforceability of the note.

Franklin D. Sweetser was engaged in the agricultural implements business in Ottawa, Illinois, prior to January 8, 1886. During this time, his half-brother, J. Howard Sweetser, was involved in a similar business in Streator, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Benjamin H. Warder et al., were manufacturers and sellers of agricultural implements in Chicago, having business dealings with both Franklin D. and J. Howard Sweetser. J. Howard Sweetser had an outstanding debt of approximately $1,200 to the plaintiffs, of which Franklin D. was unaware. To address his health issues, Franklin D. signed a contract with J. Howard on January 8, 1886, outlining the transfer of business duties. J. Howard took charge of the business, which operated under the name of F. D. Sweetser & Co., until the partnership dissolved in August 1886. Franklin D. returned to find that J. Howard had mismanaged the firm's funds, leaving Franklin D. with debts exceeding $5,000. The plaintiffs had also received funds and notes from J. Howard Sweetser without Franklin D.'s knowledge. Franklin D. sought relief through the courts, arguing for an accounting of the funds and claims made against the business.	The plaintiffs claimed that J. Howard Sweetser had wrongfully used partnership funds to satisfy his personal debts, thus requesting an equitable accounting of all moneys received and applied against their claims. They aimed to have the funds collected by J. Howard Sweetser, taken from the partnership assets without consent, be credited towards any debts owed by the partnership to them. Their petition sought discovery of all financial dealings and the application of those funds against the debts due from the firm F. D. Sweetser & Co.	Franklin D. Sweetser contended that he was unaware of J. Howard's misappropriation of funds and that any agreements or representations made by J. Howard regarding the use of partnership funds to pay his personal debts were conditional, not absolute. He disputed the claims of ratification of J. Howard's actions and further argued that he was not legally obligated to cover J. Howard's individual debts with partnership assets since he had no knowledge of those transactions.

On May 15, 1879, John Hoover obtained a legal judgment against John and Benjamin Redmond, which established a lien on their lands for seven years. Approximately a month prior to this judgment, John Redmond conveyed land to his mother, Rachel Redmond (appellee), for $2,400; however, the deed incorrectly described the property due to a clerical error, stating the east half instead of the west half. In August 1881, the cleric attempted to amend this mistake, but a year later, on December 14, 1883, the land in question was sold under execution due to Hoover’s judgment against John Redmond. Rachel Redmond claimed she took possession of the land shortly after purchasing it. However, she did not reside there until months after Hoover's judgment had become a lien. The case escalated to the Illinois Appellate Court, where Rachel sought to invalidate the sale and clear the title, arguing the land was rightfully hers despite the lien. The key issue revolved around whether Rachel’s possession of the property was sufficient to alert Hoover to her claim of ownership.	Rachel Redmond (appellee) contended that the sale of the contested land to John Hoover (appellant) was invalid due to the previous erroneous deed and that she should be recognized as the rightful owner. She asserted that she had taken possession and made improvements to the property, thereby warranting relief from the judgment against her sons. Rachel requested the court to set aside the sale and clear the title, claiming her rights were not properly acknowledged during the execution process.	John Hoover (appellant) argued that the lien from his judgment was valid and should stand as legal notice against the property. He maintained that Rachel’s possession of the land was neither open nor exclusive at the time the lien was established, indicating he was an innocent purchaser unaware of any claims to the property. Hoover contended that the evidence of possession presented by Rachel was insufficient to alert him to her interest in the land, thus defending the legitimacy of his purchase and seeking to uphold the original court's ruling.

The case of James H. Carr v. Anson Rising et ux. arose in September 1871 in Illinois, involving a dispute over property transactions between James H. Carr (plaintiff) and Anson Rising and his wife (defendants). The case began when Mrs. Rising executed a trust deed to secure a loan for her husband in December 1857, amounting to $2,057.23. After the loan became due in December 1858, the defendants transferred the property to a middleman, Myers, who then sold it to Carr in March 1859 for $2,395. Subsequent to this transaction, Carr provided a bond for reconveyance of the property to the Risings, contingent upon payment. The Risings occupied the property until August 1860, when Carr successfully removed them through forcible detainer. In December 1862, the Risings filed a bill in chancery, asserting a homestead right and claiming that the deed to Carr was merely a mortgage; they sought to redeem the property. Carr denied any obligation to reconvey, arguing he had purchased the property outright. The first court ruling rejected the Risings' homestead claim but found the deed to be a mortgage, leading to further litigation. In 1867, the Risings filed another bill, again requesting redemption and an account of rents, resulting in a decree requiring Carr to reconvey the property upon payment. This case emerged from complex ownership claims and the parties' diverging perspectives on the nature of their transactions.	James H. Carr contended that he had purchased the property outright and denied the Risings' claims of a mortgaged obligation. He argued that they had abandoned any homestead rights by relocating to Nebraska, and sought to cancel their previous claims by confirming his title as an absolute fee simple. Carr maintained that their inability to prove the transaction was intended as a mortgage justified his ownership of the property.	Anson Rising and his wife claimed that the conveyance of the property to Carr was a mortgage rather than an outright sale. They argued for their right to redeem the property and requested an account of the profits and rents derived during their occupancy. The Risings asserted that Carr had not actually lent them money but instead was holding the property only as security for their debt, thus requiring him to reconvey it upon repayment.

In the case of Samuel L. Fox v. John Virgin et al. and Samuel L. Fox v. Christopher Hodgson, which was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on October 24, 1882, Samuel L. Fox was involved in disputes over land use and public access. The events leading to this case centered on a tract of timber land that was vacant and uninclosed up to the year 1874, when Fox first fenced the property. The central issue was whether the public could establish a right to a road over this land based solely on usage over a period of twenty years. Fox had fenced his land and informed public authorities of his intended use for the property, maintaining a clear and hostile position toward the establishment of any roadway. The court noted that the prior judgment related to this issue had already addressed similar claims, indicating a longstanding legal contention over the public's right to access and use the property.	Samuel L. Fox, the plaintiff, claimed that his property was being unjustly claimed for public use, arguing that the public could not acquire road rights over his land without clear proof of intention to dedicate the area for such purposes. He sought a reversal of previous judgments that might have unintentionally recognized a public road on his property without sufficient evidence or legal grounds.	The defendants, John Virgin and Christopher Hodgson, presumably contended that a public road had been established through long-term use and had sufficient implied dedication by the previous owner. They likely argued that the public had acquired a right to the road despite Fox’s fencing and stated intentions, disputing the claim that no right had been established.

In the case of Samuel Best et al. v. Lorenzo Y. Jenks et al., filed at Mt. Vernon, Illinois, on January 20, 1888, the crux of the dispute revolves around the ownership of a fifty-five-acre tract of land after the death of Susan Best (formerly Jenks) in March 1880. The case involves multiple parties, including the plaintiff Lorenzo Y. Jenks, who was married to Susan, and various heirs related to Susan's family.
