Susan died intestate, and her heirs included her half-sister, Caroline Lemen, and several nieces and nephews from her deceased brothers. The plaintiff claimed that Susan was the rightful owner of the land at her death due to her prior ownership and residence there. The appellants (defendants) argued that her mother, Ann Hogan, owned the land at her time of death, thereby disputing Susan's ownership. Throughout the proceedings, it was established that the land had a history of inherited claims, partitions, and claims to dowers and homesteads. The original court ruling favored the plaintiff's position regarding dower and homestead rights resulting from Susan’s marital relationship and her familial connections, leading to an appeal from the defendants.	The plaintiff, Lorenzo Y. Jenks, argued that he was entitled to one-half of the fifty-five acres as an heir of his wife Susan, who died intestate and without issue. He contended that Susan had a valid claim to the land before their marriage and that he was entitled to dower and homestead rights in the other half of the land as her surviving spouse. Additionally, he sought a partition of the property according to the respective interests of all involved parties.	The defendants, including Caroline Lemen and others, contested the plaintiff's claims by asserting that Susan Best did not own the fifty-five acres at her death. They argued that the land rightfully belonged to Ann Hogan based on her ownership at the time of death, and consequently, the inheritance should not favor Jenks. They requested the court to dismiss Jenks’ claim of ownership and partition based on their assertion of intestate inheritance laws and the history of the property.

In September 1871, the case "George C. Bestor v. William Moss et al." was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Peoria County, presided over by Judge S. D. Puterbaugh. The legal dispute arose from a financial matter where the plaintiff, George C. Bestor, claimed that the defendants, William Moss and others, owed him a debt. The central issue was whether the defendants had sufficiently demonstrated that they had paid the debt in question, or at least the portion for which they were liable. The trial involved conflicting evidence presented by both parties, all of whom were sworn. The jury ultimately found in favor of the defendants, affirming that they had indeed paid the debt. The evidence presented, some of which was objected to by the plaintiff, was deemed admissible, and the court concluded that even if it might have been considered irrelevant, it did not impact the jury's verdict.	The plaintiff, George C. Bestor, claimed that the defendants had not fulfilled their obligation to pay a debt owed to him. He sought a judicial ruling to enforce payment, arguing that the evidence clearly indicated the defendants were still liable for the owed amount. Bestor contested the findings of the jury and sought a new trial based on claims of improper evidentiary rulings and the jury's alleged misinterpretations of liability.	The defendants, represented by Messrs. Johnson & McCoy, argued that they had indeed paid the debt in question, and the jury's verdict should stand. They contended that the evidence provided, although conflicting, supported their case of having fulfilled their financial obligation. The defense maintained that any evidentiary issues raised by the plaintiff were irrelevant to the jury's findings and requested that the court uphold the jury's decision and deny the plaintiff's motion for a new trial.

In January 1875, an incident occurred in Atlanta, Illinois, involving a train operated by the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company, which resulted in the tragic death of a young boy named Frederick Becker, aged between six and seven. On the day of the accident, Frederick was sent to Sunday school with his older brother. The boys had to cross the railroad track, but visibility was obstructed, making it difficult to see an oncoming train. The train was confirmed to be exceeding the legal speed limit of four miles per hour, with witnesses estimating its speed between twelve to eighteen miles per hour. During the attempt to cross, Frederick stumbled and fell onto the tracks, leading to him being struck and killed by the train. The case raised significant issues surrounding negligence and the appropriate standard of care expected from both the railroad company and the parents of the deceased.	The plaintiff, representing Frederick Becker's estate, argued that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was grossly negligent for operating the train at a speed exceeding legal limits in the town, therefore contributing to the accident. The plaintiff contended that Frederick was exercising due care and that he, being a child, could not be held to the same standard of caution expected of an adult. The legal claim sought damages for the death of the boy, highlighting the loss suffered by the family.	The defendant, Chicago and Alton Railroad Company, countered the claims by arguing that the evidence presented was insufficient to support a finding of negligence that would warrant recovery. They claimed the damages awarded were excessive, suggesting that the jury's decision might have been influenced by bias or emotions rather than legal standards. The railroad maintained that the accident did not occur due to any wrongdoing on their part, ultimately requesting the court to overturn the judgment made in favor of the plaintiff.

In December 1853, a legal dispute arose in Fulton County, Illinois, involving Richard Motsinger, acting as the guardian of Paschal Taylor and other minors, against William D. Coleman in a case that proceeded through various courts. The matter stemmed from three promissory notes signed by Paschal Taylor, Eli Taylor, and John Taylor, which were payable to the deceased John Coleman. Initially, these notes were presented in the county court where the administrator, Thomas F. Wolf, was present and did not object to their allowance. Subsequently, Motsinger, representing the minor heirs, successfully moved to contest this allowance. The county judge ruled against the claimant, leading to an appeal in the circuit court. However, significant procedural errors occurred, including a lack of notification to Motsinger about the appeal, which ultimately resulted in a default judgment against Wolf in the circuit court, where the jury assessed damages and rendered judgment without the guardian's presence.	The plaintiff, Motsinger, argued that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction to proceed with the appeal because there was no service of process against him or the minor heirs. He claimed that the clerk of the circuit court failed to issue a summons for the minor heirs, thus invalidating the proceedings. Motsinger maintained that the administrator’s default and the subsequent judgment were erroneous, as they deprived the minor heirs of their right to contest the claims appropriately.	The defendant, Coleman, contended that the circuit court's actions were justified, arguing that the process followed was standard. He asserted that the administrator's failure to appear warranted a default judgment, claiming that the circuit court properly assessed damages based on the evidence at hand. The defense emphasized that the judgment was valid and should be upheld despite the procedural challenges raised by Motsinger.

In June 1825, the case of Richard W. Chandler v. John H. Gay came before the Illinois Supreme Court. The proceedings originated from an arbitration under a statute enacted on February 25, 1819, which regulated arbitration processes. The plaintiff, Chandler, sought to overturn an arbitration award that had previously ruled in favor of the defendant, Gay, awarding him $38.75. Chandler argued that the award was uncertain, lacked mutuality, and did not address all submitted matters. The circuit court initially considered Chandler’s motion to set aside the award but ultimately ruled against him, confirming the award to Gay and directing that the bond and award be filed. The controversy centered around whether the circuit court correctly followed statutory procedures and whether it erred in confirming the award before resolving Chandler's motion.	The primary argument made by Chandler, the plaintiff in error, was that the circuit court had erred by not setting aside the arbitration award based on grounds of uncertainty and lack of evidence regarding mutual compliance. Chandler contended that the award did not encompass the whole matter submitted and was therefore invalid. He requested that the court reverse the lower court's decision and declare the award null due to these claimed defects.	The defendant, Gay, maintained that the proceedings followed the proper statutory protocol, asserting that the circuit court acted within its authority by confirming the award and that there were no valid grounds for Chandler's motion to set it aside. Gay argued that the statute specifically required compliance with the award and that the lower court’s actions were justified, as Chandler had not provided sufficient evidence for his claims of uncertainty or misconduct concerning the arbitration.

In April 1862, Cyrus H. McCormick initiated a legal case against Edward J. Moss, Gilbert Hathaway, and John Moss in Peoria County, Illinois. The case emerged from an execution delivered to Moss, who served as a constable but had his term expire before he could begin the collection process. Following his re-election, Moss was required to give a different set of securities for his new bond. During his second term, he did manage to levy the execution and collect the money; however, he failed to account for or pay it over. The suit revolved around the legal question of which set of securities was liable—the first set tied to Moss's initial bond or the second, which was mandated for his re-election term. The lower court found in favor of the defendants, leading McCormick to pursue the case further.	Cyrus H. McCormick, the plaintiff, argued that the securities of E.J. Moss's first bond should be held liable for the funds collected on the execution. He contended that the execution was initiated during Moss's first term and asserted that the law indicated the bond from that term remained applicable until the execution was completely addressed.	The defendants, led by Hathaway and John Moss, countered that the liability should fall on the second bond's securities. They argued that since the levy and collection occurred during Moss's second term, the securities associated with that term were accountable, dismissing any claims against the first bond's securities.

In June 1877, in Union County, Illinois, Stephen Modglin was involved in a legal case against the Illinois Central Railroad Company. The plaintiff claimed that while he was operating a handcar on the railroad, the railroad's construction train, negligently and carelessly run by its agents, collided with him, resulting in injuries. Modglin sought damages amounting to five thousand dollars for the incident. A jury trial led to a verdict against the railroad company, awarding Modglin two thousand and five hundred dollars. The defendants' legal team filed a motion for a new trial, arguing that the verdict was inconsistent with the evidence and that the jury had been misdirected. The appeal made by the defendants brought the case before the Illinois Supreme Court, where the central issue of negligence was scrutinized, as well as the appropriateness of the court's instructions to the jury.	Modglin argued that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent in the operation of their construction train, which ultimately led to his injuries while he was performing his job duties safely. He maintained that he deserved compensation for the damages he incurred due to their failure to exercise proper care.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that Modglin had prior knowledge of the train's movement and, thus, was negligent for not clearing the track in a timely manner. They argued that their actions did not constitute negligence as Modglin had a responsibility to ensure the track was clear for passage and that he failed to do so.

On April 9, 1867, an election was held in Cass County, Illinois, to determine whether the county seat should be removed from Beardstown to Virginia. The election, authorized by a state legislative act, permitted any legally eligible voter to contest its legality. H. H. Littlefield, as the contestant, claimed that the election process was flawed. Specifically, he argued that a total of 2,820 votes were cast in Virginia, well above the population of the precinct, which was only about 1,700, with only approximately 450 legal voters. The poll books showed dubious voting patterns, suggesting possible fraud, including evidence that fraudulent or fictitious names were registered without a legitimate voting process. Littlefield's contest emphasized that the irregularities were severe enough that the legitimacy of the vote could not be established. William Green, as the contestee, appealed the decision made by local justices of the peace who initially favored Littlefield. The primary contention revolved around the validity of votes from the Virginia precinct amidst claims of widespread electoral fraud, affecting the final decision on the removal of the county seat.	H. H. Littlefield contended that the election results from the Virginia precinct were fraudulent and invalid due to the casting of illegal votes. He argued that the overwhelming total of 2,820 votes reported could not be legitimate given the precinct's legal voter count of only 453. Littlefield sought to have the entirety of the Virginia precinct vote disregarded, asserting that the irregularities presented, such as the suspicious ordering of the vote tally and the admission of fictitious names, rendered the election results unreliable.	William Green, the contestee, argued that there were enough legal votes to support the removal of the county seat, despite the irregularities. He maintained that as many as 400 legal voters had cast their ballots in favor of the move, asserting that these votes should be counted irrespective of the alleged misconduct by election officials. Green contended that the misconduct should not disenfranchise legitimate voters and insisted that the process in Virginia should not be entirely disqualified.

In 1887, in Cook County, Illinois, Will H. Lyford filed a legal action against the Hutchinson Furnace and Smoke Consuming Company. The case revolved around allegations of fraud in the sale of certain shares of capital stock that Lyford had purchased from the company. The trial was overseen by Judge Eollin S. Williamson, and it culminated with a jury verdict in favor of Lyford, who claimed to have been misled by the defendant in the stock transaction. Upon review of the evidence and legal arguments during the appeal process, it was determined that the trial's proceedings contained no legal errors, and the evidence supported the jury's finding.	Will H. Lyford, the plaintiff, asserted that the Hutchinson Furnace and Smoke Consuming Company engaged in fraudulent practices during the sale of capital stock. He sought damages corresponding to the amount he paid for the shares along with interest, arguing that the misrepresentation or deceit had caused him financial harm.	The Hutchinson Furnace and Smoke Consuming Company, the defendant, contended against the claims made by Lyford. While the details of their arguments were not fully outlined in the case summary, the defendant likely sought to challenge the allegations of fraud and attempted to demonstrate that the sale was conducted adequately and without intention to deceive.

The case, titled "The City of Peoria v. John H. Calhoun," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1862. The dispute arose in the city of Peoria, where John H. Calhoun was charged with violating local ordinances that restricted the sale of fresh meats outside of designated market areas. Calhoun had been found guilty by a lower court and fined five dollars. He subsequently appealed the decision to the Circuit Court, which resulted in a verdict and judgment favorable to him. The case then reached the Illinois Supreme Court, where the city presented its charter and the relevant ordinance as evidence. The defendant admitted to selling fresh meats outside of the Central Market, explicitly stating he was doing so in violation of the ordinance. The case centered on the legal authority of the city to issue such ordinances and whether these ordinances constituted a restraint of lawful trade.	The City of Peoria argued that it had the authority, under its charter, to regulate the sale of fresh meats and that the ordinance prohibiting sales outside the Central Market was valid. The city maintained that because Calhoun admitted to violating this ordinance by selling fresh meats outside the designated area, he should be found guilty and fined accordingly.	Calhoun’s defense contended that even if the city had the authority to establish such ordinances, the specific ordinance in question restrained lawful trade, which meant it should not be enforced. The defense argued that the jury should find for Calhoun unless they deemed the ordinance to be a legal and valid regulation. Additionally, they asserted that the city council had no right to create such restrictions or fix market stall rents at exorbitant rates.

Thomas Cox, the appellant, was involved in a legal case against John McFerron, the appellee, in July 1820 in the Randolph circuit court, Illinois. The action was initiated by McFerron through a writ of scire facias to foreclose a mortgage that Cox had executed in favor of McFerron. During the proceedings, the court received two nihils—returns indicating that the process could not be served on the defendant, Cox. The central issue was whether these two returned nihils should be considered equivalent to actual service of process, which would allow the court to assert jurisdiction over Cox and proceed with the mortgage foreclosure. The court ultimately ruled that the return of two nihils sufficed as service and thus authorized the judgment in favor of McFerron.	McFerron, as the plaintiff, claimed that the mortgage executed by Cox should be foreclosed. He sought to proceed with the foreclosure despite the lack of personal service on Cox, arguing that the returns of two nihils constituted sufficient legal basis for the court's jurisdiction.	Cox's defense was based on the assertion that proper personal service had not been executed, thus contesting the jurisdiction of the court to proceed with the foreclosure. He focused on the necessity for personal service in such cases and challenged the legitimacy of the court's actions based on the returned nihils.

Josiah T. Betts, the appellant, and Pierre Menard, the appellee, were involved in a legal dispute in Illinois that culminated in a Supreme Court decision in December 1831. The case originated from Betts operating a ferry near Menard's established ferry on the Kaskaskia River. Menard, the owner of the existing ferry, sought penalties against Betts for running his ferry without proper authorization, arguing that the county commissioners’ court of Randolph County invalidly granted a ferry license to the trustees of Kaskaskia, where Betts operated. Initially, the justice of the peace ruled in favor of Betts, but this decision was reversed in the circuit court, which found that Betts had not obtained a legitimate license and ordered him to pay penalties amounting to ninety dollars. Betts appealed this ruling to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the license granted to the trustees was valid and that the circuit court's decision was incorrect.	The plaintiff, Pierre Menard, claimed that Josiah T. Betts operated his ferry without a valid license, which constituted an infringement on Menard's established ferry business. Menard sought recovery of penalties through legal action, asserting that Betts' operation violated the regulations set forth for maintaining ferry services in the area. Menard contended that the license granted by the county commissioners to Betts was void and therefore, Betts had no lawful right to operate his ferry.	In response, Josiah T. Betts argued that the license granted to the trustees of Kaskaskia by the county commissioners’ court was valid and provided him the right to operate the ferry. Betts contended that the county commissioners had jurisdiction to issue such licenses and that the decision made by this court should not be reversed on appeal. He maintained that despite any errors in judgment, the license was lawful, and thus he should not be subjected to the penalties sought by Menard.

In July 1865, John N. Shuler, a commission merchant based in Chicago, Illinois, was solicited by Edward F. Pulsifer in Ottawa, La Salle County, to consign grain on his behalf. Pulsifer indicated that if Shuler changed commission houses, he would consider shipping grain to Pulsifer's firm. Subsequently, in October 1865, Shuler shipped approximately 5,800 bushels of corn to Pulsifer for sale. Along with the shipment, he instructed Pulsifer to deposit $2,500 into a bank in Chicago. When the corn was sold in New York, after paying all expenses, there was a shortfall of $433.82 that Shuler claimed was owed to him. Shuler filed a lawsuit in Cook County to recover this amount, leading to a legal dispute over jurisdiction since the contract was claimed to have been made in La Salle, not Cook County.	The plaintiff, John N. Shuler, argued that he was entitled to recover the $433.82 deficit resulting from the sale of the corn. He claimed that the contract for the shipment was valid and that the jurisdiction of the Cook County court was appropriate despite the defendant residing in La Salle County. Shuler requested that the court affirm his right to the amount owed.	The defendant, Edward F. Pulsifer, contended that the court lacked jurisdiction as the contract was made in La Salle County, where all related actions occurred. He argued that since the contract was not made in Cook County, the lawsuit should not have been filed there. Pulsifer’s defense included a plea to the jurisdiction, asserting that the agreement was not enforceable in the jurisdiction claimed by the plaintiff.

Cornelia Martin v. Wilson H. Stubbings is a case decided on December 8, 1886, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The case revolved around a judgment by confession for $3,630.83 obtained by plaintiff Wilson H. Stubbings against Cornelia Martin, who was appearing on behalf of her deceased husband, Neal K. Martin. Stubbings claimed this amount based on a promissory note executed by Neal and Cornelia Martin, dated January 1, 1886, but signed on April 16, 1886. The note was connected to a partnership between Stubbings and Neal K. Martin, which was ongoing at the time of the note's execution. Cornelia claimed she had no interest in the business and only signed the note at her husband's request, without knowing the content, believing it was conditional pending a partnership accounting. She noted that no accounting had been conducted to ascertain the true balance owed. After Stubbings obtained judgment by confession against her, Cornelia filed a motion to vacate the judgment, asserting she possessed a valid defense, which was initially denied by the court.	The plaintiff, Wilson H. Stubbings, claimed that the promissory note executed by Neal K. Martin and Cornelia Martin had a legal basis for the judgment. He argued that the note was due under their partnership agreement and represented the balance owed by Neal at the time of his death. Stubbings asserted that the note was a valid instrument, supported by the partnership's financial dealings, and he sought to uphold the judgment for the amount outlined in the promissory note.	Cornelia Martin, the defendant, contended that she had not received any consideration for her signature on the promissory note and claimed she was merely acting at her deceased husband's request. She argued that no accounting had occurred to define the actual balance owed and that any contractual obligations related to the partnership were not enforceable until such an accounting was completed. Furthermore, she stated the note was effectively a conditional promise, subject to future evaluation of the partnership's financial status. Consequently, she requested the court to vacate the judgment and allow her to present her defense.

In February 1869, in Illinois, Perry Powell authorized Asahel Pierce and others as real estate agents to sell 21 acres of land for $1,500 per acre, with a payment plan that required one-third in cash and the remainder spread over one, two, and three years, with interest applied to the unpaid balance. The agents were to receive a 2.5% commission on the sale. On March 1, 1869, the agents received a $1,000 deposit from James B. Rathburn, which was to apply toward the purchase price if he finalized the purchase; otherwise, the amount would be forfeited. Rathburn, however, had no obligation to proceed with the purchase and eventually decided not to buy the land, leading to the forfeiture of the deposit. As Powell attempted to reclaim the deposit, he also requested that the receipt which clouded his title be removed. The agents claimed ownership of the deposit, arguing it served as a commission for the sale or because they helped procure the related quit claim deeds. The core issue revolved around the absence of a completed sale since Rathburn held no binding agreement to purchase the land.	The plaintiff, Perry Powell, argued that he was entitled to recover the $1,000 deposit forfeited by Rathburn, as no sale was completed per the agreement with the agents. He claimed that the actions of the agents did not entitle them to retain the deposit either as a commission or for procuring the quit claim deeds since a sale had not been finalized, thus he sought a judgment in his favor to reclaim the deposited amount.	The defendants, Asahel Pierce and the other agents, contended that they were entitled to keep the $1,000 as they were owed a commission on the intended sale that was valued at $31,500. They also argued that they had, in fact, facilitated the quit claim deeds for Powell. Their defense hinged on the position that since Rathburn had made a deposit related to the property transaction, it was rightfully theirs as compensation for the services they purportedly provided.

Elizabeth M. Gleason filed a legal case against the Village of Jefferson and its street commissioner in September 1875. The events took place in Jefferson, Illinois. Gleason sought to enjoin the village from grading and improving specific strips of land designated as streets. She claimed ownership of the disputed premises in fee simple. However, during the hearing, she failed to provide evidence of her title to the land, such as deeds or any documents proving ownership or possession. The court at the initial hearing dissolved the temporary injunction against the street improvements and dismissed her case. Gleason appealed the decision, arguing that the village had admitted her possession of the land, which she believed should suffice for her request for an injunction. However, the court highlighted that mere possession does not prove ownership and a party must establish a clear right to relief before the court can intervene.	Gleason's main argument was that she was the rightful owner of the land in question and therefore entitled to a perpetual injunction against the village's street improvements. She contended that possession, as asserted by the defendants' response, indicated her claim to the property. Gleason sought to reverse the lower court's dismissal of her case, asserting that her legal rights should protect her from the village's actions concerning the land.	The Village of Jefferson argued that Gleason did not conclusively prove her ownership or even possession of the land in dispute. They maintained that she had not submitted any legal documentation or evidence to substantiate her claims. Moreover, they contended that merely showing possession was insufficient to warrant an injunction that would prevent public improvements, which could benefit the community at large.

In September 1875, the case of Emil Horner v. Jesse B. Spelman et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after being decided in the Superior Court of Cook County. The case originated from a prior judgment rendered by the Superior Court of Hartford County, Connecticut, regarding damages sustained by the plaintiff, Emil Horner, due to frauds and wrongs committed by the defendant, Jesse B. Spelman. The legal proceedings involved Horner seeking to recover a debt from the defendant based on this previous judgment. The defendant raised several defenses including a claim that there was no valid court record (nul tiel record), allegations of payment, and claims of accord and satisfaction concerning the original judgment. The trial was conducted without a jury, resulting in the court finding in favor of Horner for the amount of the previous judgment, leading Spelman to appeal the decision.	Emil Horner's main argument was based on a judgment previously obtained in Connecticut for damages due to fraudulent actions by Jesse B. Spelman. Horner claimed that despite the defendant's assertions, there was no legitimate basis for the defenses raised, and that the court should upholding the previous judgment and award the claimed damages, including accrued interest.	Jesse B. Spelman contended in defense that the record of the Connecticut judgment was not properly authenticated, argued that the debt had been paid through an arrangement involving a third party, Tobias Kohn, and claimed that his bankruptcy discharge should absolve him of this judgment. However, the court found that these defenses were not substantiated, noting that evidence did not support the payment claim, and the bankruptcy discharge was not pleaded.

In 1868, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Imozens Moser et al. v. David Kreigh et al. took place. The dispute arose when David Kreigh and Company filed an action of replevin against Moser and Wild for a quantity of soap, lard, oils, and candles. The key individuals involved were the plaintiffs, David Kreigh and Company, and the defendants, Imozens Moser and Wild. The case centered around the ownership and possession of the specified goods, which Moser had pointed out to Kreigh, indicating their separation from a common stock. The court proceedings began in the Circuit Court, where the plaintiffs asserted their right to the goods and were awarded damages of one cent after a judgment was rendered in their favor. The defendants sought to overturn this judgment by appealing on several grounds, primarily questioning the admissibility of evidence concerning a receipt they had provided.	The plaintiffs claimed their rightful ownership and lawful entitlement to possess the goods in question. They argued that the defendants, Moser and Wild, had previously acknowledged Kreigh's ownership of the property by pointing it out and separating it from the general stock. They requested the court to affirm their right to recover the property through replevin.	The defendants contended that the receipt they issued should not have been accepted as evidence in the trial. They argued that there were specific objections to the relevance of the document that should have been raised. They sought to establish that the transaction could not confer ownership to Kreigh and Company and attempted to dispute the evidence supporting the claim.

The case "The Town of Oran, etc., v. The People ex rel. etc." took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered on January 6, 1886, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose after the town of Atlanta incurred a debt of fifty thousand dollars related to a railroad subscription and subsequently issued bonds to cover this debt. After this liability was established, a portion of Atlanta's territory was transferred to the town of Oran under a statutory procedure. Following the transfer, it became the responsibility of the supervisors and assessors of both towns to meet, adjust their affairs, divide the assets, and apportion the debts based on taxable property assessments. However, a decade passed without the required meeting taking place. Consequently, the supervisor of Atlanta served notice to his counterparts in Oran to convene, but the Oran officials disregarded this request. Atlanta then initiated a mandamus action to compel the meeting for apportionment of the debt, which led to a ruling in their favor in the lower court. The case was appealed, and the central issue raised by Oran was the Statute of Limitations, which claims that the right to take action had expired.	The Town of Atlanta, as the plaintiff, claimed that the town of Oran had a legal obligation to meet and discuss the apportionment of the indebtedness resulting from the territory transfer. Atlanta sought a mandamus order to compel Oran to follow statutory procedures and resolve the debt apportionment, arguing that the obligation was not only necessary but also a mandated duty under the law.	The Town of Oran presented a defense primarily based on the Statute of Limitations, asserting that more than five years had elapsed since the cause of action arose before Atlanta filed their petition. They contended that the matter at hand was a private right rather than a public right or trust, which should allow them to invoke the statute as a defense to the claims made by Atlanta.

The case of "The People ex rel. John C. Richberg v. The Trustees of Schools T. 39 N., R. 13 E." took place in 1877 in Cook County, Illinois. It involved John C. Richberg, a resident, legal voter, and tax payer in Chicago, who also served as the president of the Board of Education. The case arose when Richberg filed a petition in the Superior Court, seeking a writ of mandamus to compel the trustees of schools in township 39 north, range 13 east, to allocate a portion of the school fund derived from a specific section of land (16th section) to the city of Chicago for school use. This demand stemmed from an 1869 legislative act that incorporated sections of territory from the adjacent township into the city. Richberg alleged that, since the incorporation, the school trustees had managed the funds without considering the rights of the new residents in the area taken into the city. The court subsequently examined the validity of his petition and the authority of the trustees over the school fund after the township division.	The plaintiff, represented by John C. Richberg, claimed that the school trustees were obligated to equitably apportion and distribute the school funds resulting from section 16 for the benefit of the residents of Chicago. He argued that the 1869 act changed the township boundaries and that the residents of the newly incorporated area had vested rights in the school fund. Richberg sought a court order (writ of mandamus) compelling the trustees to allocate the rents, profits, and interests from the school fund to the educational use of the city's inhabitants.	The defendants, the Trustees of Schools, contended that the petition lacked merit. They argued that Richberg had no vested right to the school fund as a resident of the newly incorporated area. The trustees maintained that the division of the township effectively meant that the remaining part retained all rights to the school fund. They asserted that legislative authority permitted changes to school fund administration based on township boundaries, ultimately claiming that the merged municipal area had its own educational resources that far surpassed those available in the rural township.

In 1882, in Sullivan, Illinois, a lawsuit arose when Robert M. Miller, the plaintiff, sought damages from the Peoria, Decatur & Evansville Railway Company after his cow was killed by a locomotive at a train crossing. Miller had previously tied the cow's head to one of her hind feet because it was "breachy" (escaping from enclosures) and let her roam, violating a town ordinance. The accident occurred at a crossing equipped with a planked surface, where one plank had become loosened, exposing a spike. When a train approached, the engineer spotted the cow near the tracks and sounded the alarm whistle. However, the cow was later found entangled by the rope on the spike, making it impossible for the train to stop in time despite emergency measures taken by the engineer. The plaintiff contended that the engineer’s speed was grossly negligent, while the defendant argued that the crossing was appropriately maintained, and the plaintiff’s actions were in violation of local laws regarding livestock control.	Miller claimed that the engineer was grossly negligent for operating the train at a speed that did not allow for a safe stopping distance when the cow was sighted. He also alleged that the railway company failed to maintain the crossing safely, resulting in conditions that caused the accident. He sought compensation for the value of the cow, arguing that negligence on the part of the railway resulted in his loss.	The railway company contended that it operated the train at a normal speed appropriate for the area, which was sparsely populated, and that the engineer acted reasonably under the circumstances. They argued that the situation was exacerbated by Miller's actions of turning the cow loose while it was hobbled, violating local ordinances, and that any negligence on the railway's part was minimal compared to Miller's own negligence.

In September 1872, a legal case titled "The Board of Trustees, etc. v. Electa S. Davison et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following a bill in chancery filed in the Woodford Circuit Court. The plaintiffs, The Board of Trustees, sought to foreclose two mortgages on real estate owned by the defendants, husband and wife, Ezra D. Davison and Electa S. Davison. The first mortgage, executed on December 16, 1867, secured a loan of $400 but was found to be void concerning the wife due to defects in acknowledgment. The second mortgage, executed on July 22, 1868, secured a loan of $800 and was properly acknowledged. The case centered around the plaintiffs’ attempt to collect debts secured by these mortgages, despite the defendants’ claims that the mortgages were void or defective. The court had to determine if they could proceed with foreclosure before the debts were officially due, focusing on statutory regulations regarding such loans and mortgages.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to foreclose on both mortgages due to a breach of conditions when additional security was requested by the Board of Trustees and not provided. They contended that the statutes governing public loans required the mortgages to comply with specific acknowledgment requirements and asserted that the original debt should be considered due since the defendants failed to meet those security requirements. The plaintiffs sought a judgment allowing them to foreclose the mortgages to recover the outstanding debts.	The defendants claimed that the first mortgage was void regarding the wife due to improper acknowledgment and that the second mortgage needed reforming to be enforceable. They maintained that while an action at law could be pursued on the covenants, a bill for foreclosure could not be filed until the debt was due. The defendants also argued that the husband had no substantial interest in the property beyond what he had as the husband of a wife holding a separate estate, thus contesting the legitimacy of the mortgages.

Matthias Hosher filed a petition against the State of Illinois in the Illinois Court of Claims on October 20, 1879. The case arose from Hosher's ownership of an eighty-acre tract of land located in Woodford County, Illinois, specifically the southeast quarter of the northeast quarter of section twenty-one in township twenty-eight, north of range three west of the 3d P. M. This land, situated in the flood plains of the Illinois River, was typically dry enough from May to October to support profitable grain cultivation. However, after October 1877, a dam constructed by the State of Illinois raised the water level in the river by approximately three feet, subsequently flooding Hosher's lands and preventing proper drainage, thus diminishing their agricultural value. Evidence was presented showing Hosher sustained some damages due to the dam construction, although there was also evidence suggesting minimal damage.	Hosher claimed that the construction of the state dam led to flooding of his land, rendering it less viable for farming and reducing its overall value. He sought compensation for the damages incurred, arguing that the state was responsible for altering the natural flow of the Illinois River and negatively impacting his property.	The State of Illinois contended that while a dam was constructed, there was insufficient evidence to prove that Hosher suffered significant damages as a result of the water level increase. They argued that Hosher might not have experienced any substantial loss in value or use of his land due to the dam's construction.

Frederick W. Hunerberg filed a case against the Village of Hyde Park regarding an ordinance passed on September 4, 1888, that involved the grading and paving of Champlain Avenue. This municipal improvement was set to cost $14,446, funded by special assessments. Hunerberg owned a portion of the property where the proposed improvement was to be located and objected to the assessment, claiming the ordinance intended to use part of his land for public use without proper compensation. The case was tried in the Cook County court, where Hunerberg argued he possessed ownership of the east thirty-three feet of his property. In contrast, the Village claimed that street had long been established through common law dedication and was already public land. The county court overruled Hunerberg's objections and confirmed the assessment, leading Hunerberg to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court seeking to reverse the lower court's judgment.	Hunerberg argued that the assessment placed on his property was invalid due to part of the contemplated roadway encroaching upon his private land. He claimed he had not been compensated for the use of his property and asserted that the Village did not acquire the necessary title to the land designated for public use before imposing the assessment. Furthermore, he contended that he should not be assessed for improvements that would occur on property that rightfully belonged to him.	The Village of Hyde Park defended its actions by asserting that the street in question had been utilized by the public for many years and was maintained by the village, constituting a common law dedication. They maintained that since the necessary assessments were made according to statutory provisions, the objections raised by Hunerberg were unfounded. The Village argued that the lack of evidence proving Hunerberg's ownership or a claim that the assessment exceeded the benefits conferred onto his property justified the confirmation of the assessment by the court.

George Long passed away on September 4, 1876, in Jacksonville, Morgan County, Illinois. At the time of his death, he was survived by a widow but no children or descendants. Just a few months prior, on July 3, 1876, he executed a will that primarily bequeathed his estate to Caroline Smith, his niece, and Carroll C. Mayhew, a close friend, both of whom witnessed the will. Additional minor bequests were made to other parties. The will was admitted to probate on September 11, 1876. However, on November 2, 1876, Elias Long and others contested the will's validity, claiming that George Long lacked the mental capacity to create a will at that time and that undue influence was exerted by Mayhew and Smith during its execution. The case was heard in the Morgan Circuit Court, which ultimately found in favor of the will's validity based on a jury's verdict. This decision was later upheld by the Appellate Court for the Third District, prompting the plaintiffs to seek further review from the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Elias Long and others, contested the validity of George Long's will, arguing that he was not of sound mind when he executed it and that undue influence had been exerted by the principal beneficiaries, Caroline Smith and Carroll C. Mayhew. They sought to have the will declared invalid, claiming that it was improperly executed due to these factors.	The defendants, Caroline Smith and Carroll C. Mayhew, defended the will's validity by asserting that George Long was of sound mind when he executed the will and that there was no undue influence involved in its creation. They argued that the jury's finding in favor of the will was correct and sought affirmation of the circuit court's ruling to uphold the will's validity.

M. M. Blake v. The People, for use of A. Caldwell took place in Illinois in the late 19th century, with the final judgment delivered on March 26, 1884. The case stemmed from a special assessment imposed on a tract of land owned by Blake, which was part of the "Sny Island Levee Drainage District." This district was established under a law enacted on May 29, 1879, allowing the construction and maintenance of drainage systems for agricultural, sanitary, and mining purposes. Blake contended that the act enabling this drainage district was unconstitutional and therefore invalid, arguing that it violated various provisions of the Illinois Constitution, such as having multiple subjects and improperly allowing the county court to form the corporation without landowners' consent. His objections required a thorough review of the legislative framework and procedural compliance related to the establishment of the drainage district.	The plaintiff, M. M. Blake, argued that the Drainage Act of May 29, 1879, was unconstitutional on two grounds: firstly, that it embraced multiple subjects, contrary to section 13 of article 4 of the Illinois Constitution, and secondly, that the county court was improperly empowered to create the drainage district instead of the landowners. He sought to declare the special assessment invalid due to these alleged constitutional violations.	The People, represented by A. Caldwell, contended that the Drainage Act was constitutional and valid. They maintained that the act's purpose was singular— to protect lands from surplus water, thereby justifying various methods employed. The defense also asserted that procedural requirements for forming the drainage district were followed, including the requisite court findings, and that the existence of an acting de facto corporation negated Blake's claims against the assessment.

On August 30, 1861, in Pulaski County, Illinois, Morgan Trahern obtained a judgment of $911.85 against William A. Hughes, the surviving partner of Hughes & Bro. This judgment was assigned to Trahern's attorney, John Dougherty, on December 9 of the same year. After Trahern's death, his widow, Sarah B. Trahern, was appointed administratrix of his estate and sought to enforce the judgment against Hughes. At the same time, Hughes had a claim against Trahern's estate for $438.78, which was recognized in a subsequent judgment against the estate. Hughes filed a bill in chancery, seeking an injunction to set off his judgment against the estate against Trahern's judgment against him. The estate was found to be insolvent. Hughes argued that the assignment of Trahern's judgment to Dougherty was fraudulent since Dougherty was aware of Trahern's debt to Hughes and thus sought equitable relief to address the debts directly tied to the parties involved.	The plaintiff, William A. Hughes, contended that due to the insolvency of Morgan Trahern's estate, he should be allowed to set off his judgment against the estate (for $438.78) against the judgment obtained by Trahern during his lifetime (for $911.85). Hughes claimed that Dougherty, the assignee of Trahern's judgment, had notice of Hughes’ claim and that allowing the estate to collect the judgment against him while indebted to Hughes constituted inequitable treatment.	The defendant, Sarah B. Trahern, administratrix of the estate, defended the claim on the basis that the debts were not mutually settable, as they arose from different legal positions. Dougherty argued that the assignment of the judgment was valid, asserting that Hughes was attempting to leverage the insolvency of the estate to evade his obligations under the earlier judgment.

In 1873, the case of William F. Durant v. Henry J. Rogers took place in Cook County, Illinois. The suit was brought by Henry J. Rogers against William F. Durant in the Illinois Supreme Court. The essence of the case revolves around whether Rogers could recover money that he had paid on behalf of Durant without any formal obligation or request. Rogers claimed that he paid the amount at Durant’s request while acting as a surety for a firm that included Durant. The dispute arose after a previous lawsuit in which partners of the firm were held liable for trespass. Rogers, having paid a judgment stemming from that suit, sought to reclaim that money from Durant. However, Durant contended that he never requested Rogers to make those payments, causing a direct conflict in testimonies. The court had to determine the validity of Rogers' claims based on their discussions, obligations under the law, and the requisite evidence of a contract or promise to pay.	Henry J. Rogers, the plaintiff, argued that he should be entitled to recover money he paid at the request of William F. Durant for benefits that Durant received. He asserted that his payment was made under the impression that Durant would refund him, relying on the assertion that a request for payment had occurred. Rogers maintained that since he was compelled to cover a judgment related to the firm that included Durant, he had a right to seek reimbursement for that amount.	William F. Durant's defense was centered around the argument that he never requested Rogers to make any payments on his behalf, denying any liability for the money paid. He contended that since there was no formal obligation or evidence that he agreed to cover the debts arising from the prior laws, Rogers could not claim reimbursement. Additionally, Durant highlighted that the payment was made as a surety for a debt of another (the firm) and argued that he could not be held responsible for obligations that were not expressly requested or agreed upon, especially those involving wrongful actsone partner committed against another.

The case "Robert Black v. The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision rendered on September 27, 1884. The dispute originated in DeWitt County, Illinois, during the summer of 1881 when the plaintiff, Robert Black, a farmer and stock shipper, arranged for the transportation of his cattle and hogs from Midland City, Illinois, to Chicago. Black contacted Cicero Lane, the station agent of the railway company, to negotiate shipping rates. Initially quoted a higher rate, Black was later informed that a lower rate of $25 per car was available. Black loaded 94 head of cattle and 55 hogs onto the railway cars and signed a contract, which he claims he did without a full understanding of its terms, believing it was merely a pass. Upon arrival in Chicago, several cattle were reported lost or harmed, prompting Black to seek damages from the railway company. However, the railway company relied on a clause in the contract which required claims to be made in writing within five days. Black failed to comply with this provision. The circuit court ruled in favor of the railway company, stating that Black's claims were invalid due to the contract stipulations, a decision that was affirmed by the Appellate Court. Black appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, challenging the trial court’s rulings regarding evidence and the binding nature of the contract.	Robert Black contended that the railway company was negligent in transporting his livestock, leading to injuries and losses. He argued that the stipulation within the shipping contract, which required him to submit claims in writing within five days, was unreasonable and conflicting with public policy, thus invalid. Black claimed he was misled into signing the contract under the pretense it was simply a pass for the transportation, not a binding agreement with restrictive conditions. He sought damages for the loss and injury to his cattle, asserting that the company’s negligence warranted compensation.	The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company defended against Black's claims by pointing to the contract he had signed, which included a stipulation that prohibited any claims unless made in writing and verified within five days of loss. The defendant argued that Black's ignorance of the contract terms was not a valid excuse, as he signed it as an adult of sound mind and should have understood the contents. The railway company insisted that the contract was binding and that Black did not comply with the stipulated procedures for filing claims. Furthermore, they provided evidence to refute Negligence in the transportation process.

In September 1868, the case of *Dennis Beach et al. v. George C. Bestor et al.* was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated after George C. Bestor filed a bill in chancery seeking to access a fund held by a receiver to satisfy a $50,000 judgment he had won against Richard B. Morgan in 1858. After Morgan's judgment was assigned to Dennis Beach and another party, creditors of Morgan—King, Sharps, Allen, and Berkins—contested the assignment, arguing it was fraudulent and sought to participate in the fund. The case stems from complex transactions surrounding the assignment of Morgan's judgment, which were intended to distribute the funds among specified creditors while allowing Beach and Beckham to retain a portion as part of their repayment for the notes given to Morgan. The matter became complicated with claims that the assignment should be set aside, leading to multiple hearings and ultimately a decree dismissing the creditors' petitions.	The plaintiffs, represented by Dennis Beach and others, contended that the assignment of Morgan's judgment was legitimate, aimed at ensuring a fair distribution of the collected amounts. They argued that the arrangement did not constitute a general assignment that would be fraudulent to other creditors, and insisted that the terms of the assignment, including reservations for creditors, were lawful under the rules governing sales of choses in action, not general assignments.	The defendants, primarily the intervening creditors of Morgan, argued that the assignment of the judgment was fraudulent as it reserved a portion of the proceeds for the assignor (Morgan), which excluded them. They maintained that this exclusivity violated the principles governing general assignments for the benefit of creditors. Therefore, they requested the court to declare the assignment void, allowing them to participate in the fund created by the judgment.

The case "The Firemen’s Insurance Company v. Charles E. Peck" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision rendered on November 15, 1888. The dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, where Charles E. Peck, the plaintiff, initiated legal action against The Firemen's Insurance Company, the defendant. Peck sought to compel the company to transfer thirty shares of its capital stock to him and claimed damages amounting to $5,100 for the company's refusal to fulfill this request. The case was first tried in the Circuit Court of Cook County without a jury, where Peck secured a favorable judgment. The defendant's subsequent motion for a new trial was denied, leading to an appeal to the Appellate Court, which affirmed the judgment. The Supreme Court, upon reviewing the case, upheld the decisions of both the Circuit and Appellate Courts, emphasizing the procedural requirements for appeals and the competency of Peck as a witness despite the death of prior stockholders involved in the transaction.	Charles E. Peck claimed that The Firemen's Insurance Company wrongfully refused to transfer thirty shares of its stock to him, despite being the holder of the stock. He argued that this refusal caused him significant financial damages, totaling $5,100. Peck sought a court order to compel the transfer of the stock and requested monetary compensation for the damages incurred due to the company's actions.	The Firemen's Insurance Company contended that the trial court erred in denying its motion for a new trial and sought to challenge the sufficiency of the evidence supporting Peck's claims. The company argued that the procedural requirements for appealing the trial's findings were not properly executed, as it did not appear that a proper bill of exceptions was filed. Additionally, the insurer asserted that Peck's testimony was inadmissible due to possible conflicts of interest, which the court addressed by ruling him competent as a witness.

In 1867, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Edward Bulger et al. v. Theodore Hoffman emerged as a legal dispute over an issue of forcible detainer initiated by Hoffman against Bulger and Walsh. The matter began at the local level before a justice of the peace and subsequently progressed to the Circuit Court of Cook County. During the proceedings, the Circuit Court dismissed the case, prompting an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The appeal was scrutinized for procedural compliance, particularly regarding the necessity of a bill of exceptions, which was not present in the record, leading to the presumption that the dismissal was made due to compliance failures with the court's orders.	The plaintiffs, Edward Bulger and Walsh, sought to overturn the dismissal made by the Circuit Court ruling against them in the forcible detainer action initiated by Theodore Hoffman. They argued for the appeal's reconsideration, challenging the court’s decision based on the assertion that the grounds for dismissal were improperly established as there was no bill of exceptions retained to indicate the reasons for the dismissal.	Theodore Hoffman, the defendant, contended that the appeal was rightfully dismissed due to the plaintiffs' failure to meet procedural requirements, particularly the absence of an affidavit of merits within the stipulated timeframe. He argued that the rules of the court were justly applied and that the plaintiffs had not preserved the necessary points for their appeal.

In October 1865, the canal boat Gibraltar was transporting cargo when it collided with Crotty, another canal boat that had sunk in the Illinois and Michigan Canal near Lockport, Illinois. The incident occurred around eleven o'clock at night in darkness, without any warning signals from the sunken vessel, which was associated with its owners who were in the process of raising it. The collision led to the Gibraltar sinking. George W. Adler, the owner of the Gibraltar, subsequently sued The Board of Trustees of the Illinois and Michigan Canal for damages resulting from the collision. Following a trial, a judgment was initially rendered in favor of Adler, prompting the defendants to appeal. The primary legal question revolved around whether the Board of Trustees could be held liable for not maintaining the canal and consequently causing injury to fisherman.	George W. Adler claimed that The Board of Trustees of the Illinois and Michigan Canal was negligent for failing to maintain the canal and allowing a sunken boat to create a hazard, leading to the collision and damages to his canal boat. He sought monetary compensation for the repairs and losses incurred as a result of this negligence.	The Board of Trustees contended that they could not be sued for the incident based on previous case law indicating that liability for negligence in maintaining the canal rests solely with the State Canal Trustee, not the Board of Trustees. They argued that since the law established them as a body corporate without the capacity to be sued for the claims brought by Adler, the court should not hold them accountable for the incident.

In June 1871, the First Rational Bank of Knoxville held a past due note for $1,000 against L. P. Robinson and Daniel Robertson. The bank agreed to extend the payment deadline if satisfactory additional security was provided. L. P. Robinson was the principal borrower, and Daniel Robertson acted as a surety. A new note was created, which Daniel presented, and it was signed by himself, L. P. Robinson, and Elsia Robertson. However, the bank's president, Mr. Runkle, required assurance about Elsia's financial responsibility before accepting the note. Daniel approached Deatherage, who stated that Elsia was as financially reliable as anyone in the county. Believing he was only guaranteeing Elsia, Deatherage signed the note. When the note defaulted, Elsia and Daniel paid the debt, and Elsia then sued Deatherage for contribution. After a trial, a jury ruled in favor of Deatherage, leading Elsia to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, Elsia Robertson, claimed that Deatherage was liable for contribution as he had co-signed the note. Elsia contended that Deatherage's agreement to sign the note implied acceptance of being a co-surety alongside Daniel Robertson, hence making him liable for sharing the payment of the debt when it became due.	The defendant, Deatherage, argued that he only intended to be a surety for Elsia and did not agree to be a co-surety for the entire debt. He maintained that he was misled about the nature of the agreement, asserting no prior agreement existed that would make him liable to contribute to payments for a note he believed was solely between Elsia and the principal borrower, L. P. Robinson.

In the case of Alexander T. Miller et al. v. Sarah A. Kingsbury, which was decided on April 5, 1889, the events unfolded in Adams County, Illinois. The legal conflict arose after the death of Albert B. Kingsbury, who died intestate on May 16, 1886. Following his death, Sarah A. Kingsbury was appointed as the administratrix of his estate on May 25, 1886. Subsequently, she filed a bill in chancery on June 11, 1886, against Alexander T. Miller—the surviving partner in the firm Miller & Kingsbury—requesting a settlement of the partnership's affairs and the appointment of a receiver. To support this action, a bond was executed by Miller and his sureties, promising to fulfill his duties as the surviving partner and to account to Sarah for any funds due to the estate after paying off partnership debts. The bond stipulated that the payments would be made at the direction of the circuit court. However, Miller failed to comply with a court order regarding the payment of $3,772.59 to the firm's creditors, prompting Sarah to pursue legal action for damages related to Miller's breach of contract.	Sarah A. Kingsbury claimed that Alexander T. Miller did not faithfully fulfill his obligations as the surviving partner of Miller & Kingsbury. She argued that Miller had a responsibility to promptly pay the partnership debts and that his failure to pay the identified creditors, as mandated by a court order, constituted a breach of the bond. She sought compensation of $1,818.47 as damages resulting from Miller's failure to comply with the court's directive.	Alexander T. Miller contended that the bond's main provisions were conditional upon an order from the circuit court, asserting that he should not be held liable until such an order was issued directing payment. He argued that the plaintiff could only sue in her capacity as administratrix of the estate, challenging the legitimacy of the action filed under her individual name. Additionally, Miller questioned the sufficiency of evidence supporting the damages awarded to the plaintiff.

In the case of Roxana Shelton v. Daniel Blake, the events leading to the legal dispute occurred around the execution of property deeds in the 1870s and 1880s. Roxana Shelton and her husband, Charles E. Shelton, owned property in Livingston County, Illinois. A significant incident happened when Charles Shelton allegedly executed deeds to Richard D. Parkin, conveying this property in 1876. However, evidence presented in court suggested that these deeds were actually executed in January or February of 1881 and backdated to defraud creditors. By that time, Charles Shelton had already declared bankruptcy and failed to list this property among his assets. When Daniel Blake, claiming rights to the property through a sheriff’s deed obtained from a sale related to a judgment against Charles, sought to establish his title, it raised questions regarding the validity of the earlier property conveyances. The judges deliberated on the authenticity of the deeds and the nature of their execution to ascertain whether they were legitimate or part of a scheme to hide assets from creditors. Ultimately, the court found evidence of bad faith in Charles Shelton's actions, particularly focusing on the lack of transparency surrounding the conveyance of the property.	Roxana Shelton, as the plaintiff, argued that the deeds executed by her husband to Richard D. Parkin were fraudulent, backdated, and aimed at evading creditors. She sought to have the court recognize her title to the property and set aside the sheriff's deed held by Daniel Blake, asserting that her deeds were valid and superior to Blake’s claim.	Daniel Blake, the defendant, contended that his sheriff's deed was valid and that he had obtained the certificate of purchase rightfully, claiming no need to prove he paid for it since the sale supported by a proper judgment was adequate. He argued that Roxana Shelton had not established her rights to the property, alleging that the conveyances to her were not executed as claimed and were predicated on fraudulent intent to mislead creditors.

In June 1875, a loan application was received by lawyer Edward Sanford from a man claiming to be William Robins, who was temporarily residing in Chebanse, Illinois. The application was submitted along with an abstract of title, purportedly demonstrating Robins' ownership of 80 acres of land in Will County. The correspondence was conducted entirely through letters and involved a loan of $1,500, which was agreed upon by Sanford and another party, Hoge. After verifying the details with a local surveyor, a draft was issued by the Grundy County National Bank to the order of William Robins and sent to him. The draft was cashed on the indorsement of a man who falsely represented himself as William Robins, who subsequently defaulted on the loan. The real William Robins from Lockport, Illinois, later discovered the fraud and had his property freed from the mortgage. In March 1879, after realizing they had been defrauded, Hoge and Sanford demanded reimbursement from the First National Bank, arguing that the draft had been paid based on a forged endorsement. The Superior Court of Cook County ruled in favor of the bank, prompting the appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court.	The plaintiffs, Hoge and Sanford, contended that they had been defrauded because the indorsement of the draft they issued was not made by the genuine William Robins but by someone who had falsely used his name. They sought to recover the amount of the draft from the First National Bank on the grounds that it had been paid on a forged indorsement and claimed that they had acted reasonably in their negotiations.	The First National Bank defended itself by arguing that the draft was paid to the exact individual who had executed the note and mortgage, whom they believed to be William Robins. They maintained that the endorsement was valid since it was made by the person present in the minds of the parties involved. The bank asserted that there was no evidence of negligence on their part, as they acted in good faith by paying the draft as authorized.

Laban G. Russell filed an appeal against Edward Pickering following a judgment rendered on July 28, 1851, by a justice of the peace in Edwards County, which ordered Russell to pay Pickering sixteen dollars. After twenty days, Russell sought to appeal the judgment by removing the case to the Circuit Court through a certiorari. However, the Circuit Court dismissed his appeal due to an insufficient petition. Russell's petition did not adequately demonstrate the required legal elements: showing that the prior judgment was unjust or erroneous, not resulting from the applicant's negligence, and that an ordinary appeal wasn’t possible. Russell claimed that he sought an appeal through the justice but was denied due to insufficient security. He subsequently attempted to appeal to the Circuit Court but was turned away because it was a Sunday. The court determined the petition lacked necessary details to validate the appeal, including proof of the security's worth and that the clerks were not obligated to process appeals on Sundays.	Russell argued that the judgment against him was unjust and that he had attempted to appeal both through the justice of the peace and the Circuit Court, but was hindered by the refusal of his offered security. He sought to challenge the judgment on the grounds that he did not have a viable alternative to appeal in the regular manner and that procedural issues denied him the opportunity to defend himself properly.	Pickering contended that Russell's petition for appeal did not fulfill the statutory requirements as it failed to convincingly show that the judgment was erroneous and not due to Russell's negligence. The defendant highlighted that the security Russell offered might not have been adequate and emphasized the proper conduct expected from the justice of the peace regarding appealing judgments. Moreover, Pickering pointed out the procedural nature of the issue, including the refusal of the clerk to process the appeal on a Sunday.

The case involves Benj. J. Prettyman as the Plaintiff in Error against the Supervisors of Tazewell County and associated defendants in Error. The case originated in Tazewell County, Illinois, but was moved to McLean County. The events began when, on an unspecified date in 1853, a majority of legal voters in Tazewell County voted for subscriptions to the stocks of two railroad companies: $75,000 to the Mississippi and Wabash Railroad and $25,000 to the Peoria and Oquawka Railroad. Following this, on July 1, 1857, the board of supervisors scheduled another election for August 22, 1857, to decide on an additional subscription of $100,000 to the Tónica and Petersburg Railroad Company. Prettyman, a taxpayer and resident of Tazewell County, claimed that the county's subsequent actions lacked authority due to previous subscriptions and raised concerns about the legality and fairness of the election process, alleging that illegal votes were cast and legal voters were intimidated. He contended that this violated constitutional prohibitions against aiding corporations through the state’s credit.	Prettyman's primary arguments focused on his assertions that the Tazewell County board exceeded its authority both by attempting to subscribe to additional railroad stock and by holding a flawed election. He argued that the court must prevent the issued bonds from being utilized to support the Tónica and Petersburg Railroad Company, claiming that the legislative act permitting such expenditures contravened the Illinois Constitution. Prettyman sought a permanent injunction against the county supervisors, aiming to stop them from issuing bonds or making subscriptions related to the railroad company.	The defendants, including the Tónica and Petersburg Railroad Company and the board of supervisors, contended that they acted within their legal authority and properly followed legislative procedures. They maintained that Tazewell County was legally permitted to subscribe to the capital stock of the railroad company, having met the necessary threshold of a majority vote from the legal electorate. Additionally, they asserted that any allegations of election fraud were not substantiated and that such claims, if valid, should have been raised promptly, which had not occurred.

In the case of Gordon M. Richardson v. Adolph Ascher et al., the events took place on April 10, 1889, in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved are Gordon M. Richardson, the appellant and attachment creditor, and Adolph Ascher, among others, as the assignees of the voluntary assignment made by Simon Richter. On the same day that Richter executed a voluntary assignment of his assets for the benefit of creditors, Richardson sought to enforce a writ of attachment before the stock of goods owned by Richter could be levied by the sheriff under an existing attachment from the Superior Court in favor of Moore Brothers. Although Richardson claimed his attachment had priority based on a notation made by a constable, evidence presented indicated that the sheriff was not notified of the attachment until after the assignment was recorded, leading to ambiguity regarding the exact timing of the levies. The County Court ultimately dismissed Richardson’s petition for priority after evaluating the evidence.	The plaintiff, Gordon M. Richardson, argued that he held precedence over the assets of Simon Richter due to an attachment he placed before the recording of the assignment to Ascher and other assignors. He sought a judicial declaration that his attachment lien took priority over the assignment made for the benefit of Richter's creditors.	The defendants, Adolph Ascher et al., contended that the recorded assignment of Richter’s assets was valid and took precedence over Richardson's attachment. They argued that the sheriff was not notified of Richardson's attachment until after the assignment was executed and filed, thus rendering any claims to priority by Richardson moot. They requested the court to uphold the dismissal of Richardson’s petition.

On August 27, 1885, in Cook County, Illinois, Andrew Lehn conveyed real estate to Helmont Kasch and Arie Van Deursen through an absolute warranty deed for $5,000. This transaction occurred amid Lehn’s substantial debts to multiple creditors, totaling approximately $658.29, which included unpaid loans and taxes. The deed was allegedly executed with the intent to defraud these creditors, with rumors that a secret agreement existed that would label the conveyance a mere mortgage rather than a legitimate sale. Following failed attempts by John G. Lobstein, a creditor who had previously obtained a judgment against Lehn, to collect the debt, he filed a complaint in September 1886. Lobstein claimed that the deed facilitated Lehn’s efforts to hide assets from creditors and requested the court to void the deed and sell the property to cover his judgment. The courts had to examine both the intention behind the conveyance and the actions of Kasch and Van Deursen, determining whether they acted in good faith or were complicit in Lehn's fraudulent scheme.	John G. Lobstein claimed that Andrew Lehn executed the deed to Kasch and Van Deursen to defraud his creditors, including himself. Lobstein sought to have the deed declared null and void, asserting that it was executed without legitimate consideration and with the intent of hindering the collection of debts. He requested that the property be sold and that the proceeds be used to satisfy his judgment against Lehn.	Kasch and Van Deursen contended that they acted in good faith when acquiring the property from Lehn. They asserted that the deed was executed based on a written agreement whereby they took the property subject to existing liens, intending only to secure their claim while allowing Lehn to benefit from the property. They denied having any fraudulent intent and sought to have their claim honored based on the terms of their agreement.

Cortez B. O’Hair and William H. Wilson were opposing candidates for the position of town clerk in Seven Hickory, Illinois, during the election held on April 5, 1887. The canvassing board awarded the election certificate to O’Hair, prompting Wilson to contest the election’s results. The county court in Coles County determined that both candidates received an equal number of legal votes, leading the court to order them to draw lots to resolve the tie. Wilson won through the drawing, which established his right to the office. O'Hair filed an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing against certain findings regarding the legality of votes cast for both candidates. The appeal centered on conflicting evidence concerning the legality of specific voters, particularly James McCoy and others who voted for O’Hair, as well as Ed Sharp, who voted for Wilson. Ultimately, the Illinois Supreme Court examined the trial court’s decisions regarding voter qualifications and the counting of ballots, affirming the lower court's ruling.	Cortez B. O’Hair claimed that several votes counted against him were cast by individuals who were not legal voters. He argued that the county court's finding that these individuals were not eligible was incorrect, and he sought to challenge the legitimacy of the votes that favored Wilson. O'Hair contended that, given the proper consideration of these votes, he should have been awarded the office of town clerk.	William H. Wilson’s defense rested on the assertion that he was declared the rightful candidate after the lots were drawn, following a tie in the number of votes counted. He countered O’Hair's claims by defending the legality of Ed Sharp's vote and argued that the irregularities raised by O’Hair concerning voter eligibility were unfounded. Wilson contended that the method of resolving the tie by drawing lots was in accordance with the law and maintained that the county court's decisions on the matter were correct.

The case "William C. Goudy et al. v. John Hall" originated in 1861 in Fulton County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs, William C. Goudy, S.C. Judd, and T.A. Boyd, initiated an action of ejectment for the recovery of specific land parcels in Township 6 North, Range 2 East. The claimed properties were originally owned by John Fridley, who died intestate in the 1840s, leaving several heirs. Following Fridley's death, the land was sold by an administrator in a court-administered process, which the plaintiffs contested. During the trial, the plaintiffs presented historical patents and quitclaim deeds to assert their title, while the defendant, John Hall, defended his ownership by referencing decrees and the established chain of title from prior sales. The initial trial culminated in a ruling favoring the defendant, which prompted the plaintiffs to seek a new trial, alleging improper evidence and a verdict contrary to the law.	The plaintiffs claimed title to the disputed land by presenting patents and evidentiary deeds showing their ownership stemming from the heirs of John Fridley. They argued that the court below made erroneous findings regarding jurisdiction and improperly admitted evidence that supported the defendant. They requested a new trial on these grounds, asserting that the initial verdict should be reversed due to these alleged errors.
