The defendant contended that the court possessed jurisdiction to authorize the sale of the disputed properties, supported by valid decrees asserting that notice was given prior to the land sale. He argued that even if errors were made in admitting evidence against the plaintiffs' claims, the findings were still binding, as jurisdiction was established. He requested the court to affirm the lower court's ruling in his favor, asserting that the plaintiffs had failed to demonstrate contrary evidence.

The case "The City of Galena v. Henry Corwith" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. The dispute arose in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, where Henry Corwith, the defendant in error, initiated an action against the City of Galena, the plaintiff in error. The action was based on two bonds issued by the city, each amounting to $500. Corwith argued that the city was obligated to honor these bonds. The city, on the other hand, contended that it lacked the authority to issue the bonds and raised defenses including want of consideration. A jury trial resulted in a verdict for Corwith amounting to $1,182.50, which led the city to file a motion for a new trial, claiming error in the trial court's decisions. The case addressed the broader issue of whether municipal corporations have the inherent power to fund their debts, even if their charters impose specific conditions on borrowing money.	The City of Galena claimed that its charter limited the power to borrow money specifically for improvements and did not allow for the funding of existing debts. The city argued that it could not validate the bonds issued in this context and sought to overturn the jury's verdict which ordered payment to Corwith.	Henry Corwith contended that the city was legally obligated to honor the bonds it had issued, regardless of its charter limitations. He argued that municipal corporations inherently possess the power to pay their debts, including the authority to convert existing debts into bonds that bear interest. Corwith sought to uphold the jury's verdict and the court's judgment in his favor.

In the case of John H. Conlon v. Eliphalet W. Blatchford et al., decided on December 4, 1885, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the dispute arose from a promissory note for flax seed. The key individuals involved included John H. Conlon, the appellant (defendant), and Eliphalet W. Blatchford and others, acting as the appellees (plaintiff). The events leading to the case began in the spring when a party named Dement sold flax seed to the appellants, taking a promissory note payable to the appellees. The note outlined an agreement that the appellants would sow the flax seed, harvest it, and sell the yield to the appellees at a price lower than the market rate. Concurrently, Dement was to provide a threshing machine and manage the straw involved in the process. However, Dement failed to deliver the thresher, which resulted in poor-quality flax and significant waste since the crop was not threshed timely. The straw was also considered a total loss. Conlon defended against the note by arguing that the appellees should be held liable under Dement's contract and claimed damages due to his failure to fulfill the threshing obligations. The lower court ruled that the contracts were separate and not binding on the appellees, leading to the current legal dispute.	The plaintiffs, represented by Eliphalet W. Blatchford and others, claimed that they were entitled to recover the amount due on the promissory note taken for the flax seed. They argued that the obligations outlined in the note were independent of any agreements made between the appellants and Dement regarding threshing, indicating that the defendants were responsible for the payment regardless of any failures on Dement’s part.	The defendant, John H. Conlon, contended that the obligations were interconnected and that the plaintiffs should bear responsibility for Dement's failure to supply the threshing machine, which directly affected the quality of the crop and resulted in damages. Conlon sought to offset the damages incurred against the amount owed on the promissory note.

In September 1872, the case of Patrick Ahern et al. v. Thomas S. Evans was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County, overseen by Judge Lambert Tree. The dispute arose when Thomas S. Evans, a contractor, sought to establish a mechanic’s lien against the properties owned by Patrick Ahern and Daniel A. Walsh for labor and materials provided by Evans. The initial ruling granted Evans the relief he sought, leading Ahern and Walsh to file an appeal. The key issue revolved around the interpretation of the mechanics' lien law enacted in 1869, which was being contested regarding its applicability to subcontractors and whether Evans, as a sub-contractor, could claim a lien.	Thomas S. Evans argued that he had a right to establish a mechanic’s lien on the defendants' property for the work he had performed. His primary legal request was for the court to uphold the initial decree that granted him the mechanic’s lien, asserting that the labor and materials he provided warranted a claim under the relevant laws.	Patrick Ahern and Daniel A. Walsh contended that the mechanics' lien law of 1869 did not extend the rights of lien holders beyond the first sub-contractor. They argued that since Evans was a subordinate contractor, he was not entitled to maintain a lien against their property. They challenged the validity of the initial ruling that favored Evans, seeking to have it reversed.

The case "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Wilson Allen" took place in Illinois, with the suit being initiated on August 19, 1859, in the Circuit Court of De Witt County. The primary parties involved were Wilson Allen, the plaintiff, and the Illinois Central Railroad Company, the defendant. The core issue began when Allen alleged that the railroad company caused significant harm by obstructing an ancient drainage system, resulting in the creation of a stagnant pond that affected his family's health and enjoyment of his property. Additionally, he claimed that a different tract of land was harmed due to mud and sediment washing onto it, linked to the railroad's construction practices. The defendant countered with a defense of "not guilty," asserting prior recovery and satisfaction from a similar issue claimed by Allen in a previous case. The court proceedings led to a jury verdict in favor of Allen for $25, which prompted the railroad to appeal, arguing that the earlier settlement barred his current claims, and that his own requests contributed to the alleged drainage issues.	Wilson Allen, as the plaintiff, asserted that the Illinois Central Railroad Company's obstruction of a drainage system caused a pond that negatively impacted his family's health and deprived him of the enjoyment of his land. He sought damages for these grievances, arguing that the railroad's actions also led to damage from mud and sediment affecting another tract of land he owned.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company defended against Allen's claims by stating that a previous agreement and settlement from a related lawsuit precluded any further action regarding the drainage issues. They asserted that the original injuries claimed existed prior to Allen's ownership of the affected land, thus his claims lacked merit. Furthermore, the defendant contended that any injuries were a natural result of their lawful construction and that Allen had requested a change to the drainage that exacerbated the situation.

The case "John Fahey v. President and Trustees of the Town of Harvard" was decided in September 1871 in Illinois, involving a legal dispute stemming from an incident on September 1, 1869. The key individuals in this case were John Fahey (the plaintiff) and the President and Trustees of the Town of Harvard (the defendants). The case arose when Louis Lackner fell into an unmarked pit that had been dug on the street by Fahey, without the town's consent. This pit remained open without warning for both day and night, leading to Lackner's injuries. Lackner later settled with the town for $300 and associated costs before any trial took place against Fahey. The primary issue in the court was the legal liability of the town towards Lackner, as Fahey contended that the town should be held liable only if it had actual or implied notice of the nuisance created by his excavation. The court ultimately had to decide whether the town could recover the amount paid to Lackner from Fahey, given the lack of evidence that the town was informed of the pit before the settlement.	The plaintiff, President and Trustees of the Town of Harvard, claimed that Fahey was liable for damages resulting from his negligence in creating a hazardous situation by leaving an excavation open without warnings. They sought to recover the $300 paid to Lackner as damages for his injuries, arguing that the town had to be compensated for the liability encountered due to Fahey's actions.	Fahey's defense was primarily that the town should not have settled with Lackner without informing him, and therefore, the town could not claim damages from him. He argued that the town was not liable unless it had actual notice of the pit or if it had lingered long enough for such notice to be implied. Fahey asserted that the declaration against him lacked sufficient allegations to prove that the town had any prior knowledge of the nuisance, rendering the town's claim void.

John C. Grier v. Jacob Gibson is a legal case that originated in Peoria County, Illinois, with a declaration filed on January 21, 1864. The case revolved around an action of assumpsit initiated by Jacob Gibson, the indorsee of four promissory notes, against John C. Grier, the maker of those notes. Following the filing on January 21, Grier filed a plea on February 4, challenging the first special count and common counts while demurring to the subsequent counts. A series of pleas and motions for continuance ensued, with Grier's plea of the general issue upheld against the complaint until the trial commenced on March 2, 1864. Gibson presented the promissory notes during the trial, but Grier objected to their admissibility, which the court overruled. The court ultimately ruled in Gibson's favor, holding Grier liable for an amount of $587.88, leading Grier to appeal the decision on several grounds including the refusal of his motion for continuance and the evidentiary challenges presented.	The plaintiff, Jacob Gibson, asserted that he was the indorsee of four promissory notes issued by the defendant, John C. Grier. He claimed the total sum of $587.88 owed to him based on these notes. Gibson's legal request included upholding the admission of the promissory notes into evidence and arguing against Grier's motion for continuance based on allegedly not having copies of the notes filed.	The defendant, John C. Grier, contended that the court erred by not granting his motion for continuance due to the absence of copies of the promissory notes in the filed declaration. Grier also argued that the assignment of the notes should have been proven, as he had not received any affidavit denying it, and he objected to the notes being considered as evidence without such proof. Furthermore, he claimed the court did not properly address his demurrer to the declaration before proceeding.

The case of County of Christian v. Charles V. Rockwell took place in 1887 in Christian County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Charles V. Rockwell, was a surgeon who provided emergency medical services to an eleven-year-old boy named Eobert Watts, who had suffered a serious gun injury. Watts was described as a pauper; his mother was deceased, and his father was deemed an idle and worthless individual who neglected to care for him. At the time of the incident, Watts was staying with a farmer named Wright, who arranged for Rockwell to treat the boy. Due to the severity of the injury, an amputation was required immediately, and Rockwell performed the operation promptly, enabling a quick recovery. The surgical services were valued at $125, but the plaintiff sought to recover a judgment of $50 from the County of Christian instead. The county objected, citing that Watts had an undivided interest in land valued at $75, arguing he was not a proper subject for county support. The court trial was conducted without a jury, and judgment was rendered in favor of the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, Charles V. Rockwell, claimed he was entitled to compensation for his emergency medical services provided to Eobert Watts, arguing that the services rendered were necessary and urgent due to the boy's pauper status. Rockwell contended that the health crisis justified immediate action without prior consultation with county officials, and he sought to recover at least a portion of his fee from the county, asserting that the boy's limited property was insufficient to cover the medical expenses.	The defendant, the County of Christian, asserted that since Eobert Watts had a property interest valued at $75, he was not eligible for support under the applicable statute governing county assistance. They argued that the existence of any property disqualified the boy from being considered a pauper under the law, and therefore, the county should not be liable for the payment of Rockwell's charges. They also contested the judgment against the county for the costs incurred during the suit.

In 1869, Annie Harris, a widow with two children, and her brother Neil McIntyre jointly purchased a 152T8^- acre farm (known as the Bellows farm) for $2,100 in Carroll County, Illinois. Annie contributed $1,600, while Neil provided $500. They agreed to hold the land as tenants in common. However, Neil took the title solely in his name without Annie's knowledge, and they subsequently lived on the farm as one family. Although Annie was the housekeeper, Neil managed the premises. Over time, Neil borrowed against the farm without Annie's consent. In 1879, Neil conveyed the land to another brother, Daniel McIntyre, to settle debts, with additional financial transactions involving a trust deed secured to Henry Ashway. Annie, who occupied the land until 1881, filed a complaint in 1881, asserting her equitable interest and seeking partition of the property, claiming that her rights were ignored through Neil's actions.	Annie Harris claimed that she and her brother intended to hold the farm as tenants in common and that she had contributed significantly to its purchase. She argued that Neil's sole possession and title taking were fraudulent, maintaining that he held the land in trust for her. She sought legal recognition of her equitable interest in the farm, partition of the land, and the removal of the liens placed by Daniel and Ashway against her claim.	The defendants, including Daniel McIntyre and Ashway, contended they had no knowledge of Annie's claim to the farm and asserted their reliance on the recorded title which showed Neil as the sole owner. They claimed that Annie's long-term presence on the property did not establish her equitable rights because she had not acted to assert them even when aware of the title. Daniel specifically denied that Annie had ever had an equitable interest in the land.

In January 1864, Thomas W. Berry was indicted in St. Clair County, Illinois, for gaming, specifically for playing cards for money. The case originated during the March term of the St. Clair Circuit Court but was tried later at the October term of the same year. The trial revealed that Berry was found guilty of violating a local ordinance against gaming set by the city of Belleville. During the trial, the defendant introduced evidence concerning the city’s charters, claiming that the city had exclusive control over gaming laws. Berry's defense argued that he could not be convicted under state law when the city charter allowed for the licensing and regulation of billiard tables and gaming houses. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court through a writ of error on the ground that the local ordinance should take precedence.	The plaintiff, represented by the State's Attorney, argued that Berry was guilty of the offenses charged under state law prohibiting gaming activities. They maintained that his actions violated the Illinois Criminal Code and that the local ordinance did not exempt him from state prosecution.	Berry's defense contended that the city of Belleville’s charters provided exclusive authority to regulate and punish gaming activities. They argued that since the city council had enacted ordinances governing these activities, the state could not impose penalties for the same actions. They asserted that the conviction was improper as the city had the jurisdiction to handle such matters first, and hence the state should not prosecute for the same offense.

The case "The First National Bank of Quincy, Illinois, v. Henry F. J. Ricker" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1874. The case arose after a series of transactions involving checks that turned out to be forgeries. On June 24, 1873, Hundrack & Co. deposited three checks at the First National Bank, including one allegedly from Manning Bros. The tellers were not familiar with the signature, yet the check was indorsed by an employee of the bank after assurances of payment were given. Later that same day, it was discovered that the checks were forgeries, prompting the First National Bank to seek the return of the funds paid. The court examined the actions and knowledge of the individuals involved, including the teller who noted doubts about the signature and the context under which the check was presented for payment. The case factored in principles from previous rulings concerning the presumption of knowing a correspondent's signature and the obligation of the parties involved in the transaction.	The First National Bank claimed that it should be entitled to recover the money paid for the forged check presented by Hundrack & Co. They argued that the drawee (the bank) is presumed to know the signature of their correspondent (in this case, Manning Bros.), and as such, they should not be held liable for losses due to the forgery when there is no demonstrated fraud by the bank itself.	Henry F. J. Ricker, the defendant, contended that the bank had received the check in good faith and without suspicion of it being forged. Ricker argued that the bank's teller noted uncertainty about the signature and only paid the amount after the check was indorsed by an employee from the First National Bank. He emphasized that the bank should have exercised due diligence in verifying the authenticity of the checks they presented for payment, and since they failed to disclose their doubts about the check’s validity, they could not claim the right to recover the funds after paying it.

On May 1, 1878, a lease was executed between Magie & Tree and Lawrence & Martin for a ten-year term for a tract of land in Cook County, which allowed lessees to use the property only for a trotting park or race course. Lawrence & Martin subsequently entered a contract with Willoughby, Hill & Co., granting them advertising rights for the fences and buildings on the property for five years, extendable to a total of ten years if the lessors continued to occupy the land. Willoughby, Hill & Co. constructed a fence at a cost of $2,700, of which only $400 was paid by Lawrence & Martin. Following the completion of the fence, a corporation named the "Chicago Jockey and Trotting Club" was formed, to whom Lawrence & Martin assigned their lease rights. The Jockey Club refused to allow Willoughby & Hill to exercise their advertising rights as stipulated in their agreement, prompting Willoughby & Hill to file a lawsuit seeking injunctive relief against Lawrence & Martin and the Jockey Club for obstruction of their contractual rights. The case included various appeals, complexities related to corporate structure and insolvency, and rights relating to real estate contracts that were recorded.	The plaintiffs, Willoughby, Hill & Co., claimed they were barred from using the fences and buildings for advertising purposes as per their contract with Lawrence & Martin due to the actions of the Chicago Jockey and Trotting Club. They sought an injunction to prevent interference with their rights under said contract and demanded compensation for damages incurred from being denied these rights.	The defendants, including Lawrence & Martin and the Chicago Jockey and Trotting Club, argued that the agreement with Willoughby & Hill did not confer an enforceable right to use the premises due to a clause that prohibited sub-leasing or assignment of the lease. They contended that the rights should not be enforcible against the subsequent assignees who had not received proper notice of the appellants' claimed rights.

In 1875, in Morgan County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Alfred Andreas and others (the appellants) and Isaac J. Ketcham (the appellee). The case initially began before a justice of the peace, where the appellants sought to recover $89 for a map of Morgan County, which included a view of Ketcham's residence and additional views as per their agreement. The appellants had succeeded in obtaining a judgment, but Ketcham appealed the decision to the circuit court of Morgan County. During the trial, evidence was presented including subscription contracts that Ketcham signed, detailing the payments and additional views promised. However, during the proceedings, it became evident that Ketcham claimed the rendering of his residence was incorrect, presenting a conflict over the accuracy of the map and the description of his business location. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Ketcham, leading to the appellants' motion for a new trial being overruled. The case was defined by factual determinations of the correctness of the depiction of Ketcham's residence and the validity of the subscription agreement.	The appellants, Alfred Andreas et al., claimed that Ketcham owed them $89 for the subscription to a county map, which included a view of his residence as well as additional views. They argued that Ketcham had entered into a binding contract to pay for the services rendered and provided tangible evidence of the agreement and the services they delivered.	Ketcham, acting in his own defense, contended that the views presented in the map were incorrect, which he argued invalidated the basis of the contract. He maintained that inaccuracies in the map and the business card's description harmed the validity of their agreement. Ketcham asserted that because the plaintiffs failed to honor the contract terms regarding accurate representation, he was not liable for payment.

In May 1871, the Union Mutual Life Insurance Company loaned $60,000 to Elizabeth Kirchoff, her husband Julius Kirchoff, and her mother, Angela Diversy, secured by a trust deed on several parcels of land, including specific lots within the Canal Trustees’ subdivision. By 1878, defaults occurred, leading to negotiations where Angela conveyed most of her land to the company, while Elizabeth and Julius transferred all of theirs, with an agreement that Elizabeth could buy back two specific lots for $10,000 over an uncertain nine-year period at 6% interest. Elizabeth later filed a bill to enforce this agreement, which was dismissed in the Circuit Court. The case hinged on whether the company’s actions could be interpreted within the constructs of mortgage law and equity, especially regarding the right to redeem property.	Elizabeth Kirchoff claimed that the Union Mutual Life Insurance Company had agreed to allow her to redeem the two lots for $10,000 and sought to enforce this agreement through the court. She asserted that the agreement was valid and aimed to reclaim her property by fulfilling the payment terms as stipulated in their negotiations.	The Union Mutual Life Insurance Company argued that the agreement was not enforceable because of uncertainties in the terms regarding payment timelines and interest rates. They contended that the legal title was passed to them via the trust deed, which included the right of redemption for the entirety of the mortgage rather than a part of it, claiming that the law does not allow for partial redemption based on a verbal contract.

In January 1885, a legal dispute arose in Cass County, Illinois, involving John C. Lamb and William Campbell et al. The case centered on the Virginia Coal and Water Company, which was facing foreclosure on certain bonds secured by a trust deed that covered its lands and machinery. The defendants, holders of the bonds, initiated the foreclosure proceedings. Lamb, as a defendant in the case, claimed that under a contract dated October 1883, he had provided the company with machinery, thereby acquiring a prior lien on the property. This claim was backed by a decree from the Cass County Circuit Court, which recognized his lien before the trust deed. However, during the subsequent legal proceedings, it was revealed that the lien Lamb sought to enforce was filed after the trust deed was recorded, and the beneficial owners of the trust deed were not made parties to Lamb’s lien enforcement petition. Consequently, the court had to determine the validity and precedence of the competing liens.	The plaintiff, John C. Lamb, argued that he had a prior lien on the Virginia Coal and Water Company's properties due to machinery he supplied under a contract from October 1883. He contended that his lien should take precedence over the bondholders' claims secured by the trust deed since he had obtained a court decree affirming his lien prior to the bondholders' foreclosure action. Lamb sought to have the court recognize his lien as superior.	The defendants, holders of the trust deed bonds, contended that their lien was superior to Lamb's mechanics lien. They maintained that Lamb's lien was invalid because he failed to include the beneficial owners of the trust deed in his enforcement proceeding, as required by Section 28 of the Lien Law. They argued that since the proper parties were not joined in the action, Lamb's claim could not affect or prejudice their right to foreclose on their lien.

The legal case known as "The Bishop Hill Colony, Appellant, v. Lycurgus L. Edgerton et al., Appellees" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1861. The participants in this case involved the Bishop Hill Colony, the appellant, and Lycurgus L. Edgerton, along with additional appellees, who were associated with a financial transaction involving a promissory note and the sale of broom corn. The dispute arose when the Bishop Hill Colony failed to pay a debt of $550 on a promissory note made to Solomon Shoup, dated April 1, 1858, which became due after six months. The appellees included Shoup’s creditors, who sought compensation for the debt owed to them. After an agreement to resolve an additional sum of $885.95 for the sale of broom corn, Shoup released the Colony from further payments to him. This transaction and subsequent calculations of interest at ten percent and six percent respectively led to a verdict in favor of the appellees in the lower court, prompting the Colony to appeal multiple claims of judicial error.	The appellees, led by Edgerton, asserted that the Bishop Hill Colony owed them a total of $1,435.95, encompassing both the amount from the promissory note and the proceeds from the broom corn sale, along with interest after the maturity of payments. They argued that the agreement concerning the broom corn was clear and effective, and that the debts needed to be settled as per the contractual terms they had established.	The Bishop Hill Colony contested the lower court's decisions, claiming that several judicial errors had occurred, including the overruling of motions to quash the summons, for continuance, and for a new trial. They argued that the clerk’s signing of the summons was insufficient as it only contained initials, and they maintained that improper evidence was presented during the trial. The Colony sought the reversal of the lower court's judgment on these bases, contending a fundamental misunderstanding of the contractual obligations and interest calculations.

In March 1871, John Adkisson passed away intestate, leaving behind 234 acres of land in DeWitt County, Illinois, to his widow, Gorilla, and three sons: Thomas B., Horace, and Frank, the latter being a minor. To prevent a forced sale of this land to settle estate debts, in 1874, the family borrowed $2,000 from Albigence H. Brown, facilitated by Charles F. Emery, securing the loan with a trust deed on their interest in 139 acres of land. In 1875, they initiated Circuit Court proceedings for dower and partition, proposing the sale of a ten-acre lot to cover the debt. The court divided the land into five parcels, and the ten-acre lot was later sold, generating proceeds that did not fully satisfy the debt. In 1876, multiple transactions occurred concerning the conveyance of various lots, culminating in the widow’s payment of $450 toward her debt share, while the remaining debt led to further actions against various defendants. Brown and Emery were later included in a bill seeking contributions from the other landowners for the debt. The court found against the defendants, examining the intricate transactions and the implications of a prior partition decree, leading to complexities regarding liability and contributions among co-tenants.	Albigence H. Brown and Charles F. Emery, as plaintiffs, sought a contribution from the other landowners for their financial responsibilities regarding a loan secured by a trust deed on the land. They claimed that the sale executed by the trustee and the receipt of proceeds did not extinguish their entitlement to the debt's remaining balance. Additionally, they requested the court to set aside the sale deed to John Warner and demanded repayments of certain payments made under the trust deed, asserting that equity and fairness justified their claims for contribution from the other defendants.	The defendants included various parties who contested the plaintiffs' claims, arguing that the partition decree had extinguished the obligation associated with the trust deed. They maintained that the plaintiffs, Brown and Emery, had ratified the actions taken under the partition proceedings, thereby relinquishing their rights to claim further contributions from them. The defense also contended that the sale undertaken by the trustee was unauthorized and illegal, asserting that the plaintiffs had no valid basis to demand further compensation from the remaining landowners due to prior agreements.

In the case of John Evans v. Horace Landon, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1839, the legal dispute arose from a promissory note dated January 29, 1838. John Evans, the appellant, promised to pay Horace Landon the sum of six hundred and fifty dollars, which could be paid in good bank paper. The case was initially heard in the Circuit Court of Greene County, where Evans filed a petition under a newly established state statute designed to simplify debt collection proceedings. The defendant, Landon, responded with a general demurrer to dismiss the petition, arguing that the legal remedy sought was inappropriate. The Circuit Court, however, overruled Landon’s demurrer and ruled in favor of Evans, granting him the judgment for the debt amount along with damages and costs. This prompted Landon to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, challenging the appropriateness of using the petition process for collection under the statute.	The plaintiff, John Evans, claimed that he was entitled to payment as per the terms of the promissory note he issued to Horace Landon. He argued that the petition filed followed the statutory procedures designed for debt collection, contending that his allegation of the unpaid debt was sufficient to warrant court action without further averments regarding the payment method. Evans sought the court to uphold the Circuit Court's ruling to enforce his claim and recover the owed amount plus damages and legal costs.	The defendant, Horace Landon, contended that the petition process was not applicable to the case because the promissory note did not straightforwardly mandate payment. He argued that according to a related Kentucky statute, additional averments of non-payment were necessary when the note involved specific conditions (like payment in good bank paper), and thus the remedy sought by Evans was inappropriate. Landon sought to have the Circuit Court's judgment overturned, claiming that the statute should be strictly construed.

The case of Jacob Zimmerman v. Peter Zimmerman was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1853. The origins of the dispute date back to an action brought before a justice of the peace in Jackson County, where Jacob Zimmerman sought recovery on a promissory note for $20.39, which was initially judged in his favor. Following this judgment, Jacob appealed to the circuit court, where, after a trial without a jury led by Circuit Judge W. A. Denning, he was awarded $40.90 and costs. However, the defendant, Peter Zimmerman, contested this decision, presenting evidence of a prior judgment against Jacob, which was recorded in the docket of Justice Napoleon Collins. This prior judgment stated that after hearing both parties, Jacob was ordered to pay the costs, which the defendant claimed constituted a valid bar against Jacob’s current action. The case then focused on whether parol evidence could be used to change or reinterpret the recorded judgment.	Jacob Zimmerman argued that the prior judgment in his case merely mandated the payment of costs and should not hinder his action to recover the amount owed on the promissory note. He presented evidence of the note and included the testimony of the justice who had originally ruled in the matter, trying to clarify the intent behind the judgment.	Peter Zimmerman contended that the earlier judgment was definitive and constituted a complete bar to Jacob's current claim, asserting that it had been ruled against him in the past. He argued that parol evidence should not be allowed to alter the formal record of the justice's judgment, emphasizing the importance of having immutable records in legal proceedings.

In December 1850, the legal case "Nicholas A. Garland v. Isaac S. Britton" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case stemmed from a chancery suit initiated by Garland seeking to foreclose a mortgage against Britton. The issue arose when the summons issued against the defendant, Britton, was not under the seal of the court. As a result, during the November term of 1847, the bill was taken as confessed, and a decree of foreclosure was entered without the proper judicial procedures being followed. The absence of the required seal led to the court's inability to enforce the decree, prompting Britton to challenge this ruling by filing a writ of error.	The plaintiff, Nicholas A. Garland, contended that the proper judicial procedures were upheld as he successfully had the decree of foreclosure established in the lower court. Garland argued that the absence of the seal, which is mandatory for all court processes, did not invalidate the process he initiated. He sought to uphold the foreclosure that had been previously established against Britton.	The defendant, Isaac S. Britton, argued that the summons served to him was invalid due to the lack of the required judicial seal, rendering the service ineffective and the resulting decree unauthorized. Britton maintained that all court processes must adhere to the statutory requirements and therefore sought to have the earlier decree reversed based on procedural deficiencies.

In December 1837, the case of Matthew Stacy, administrator of Samuel Hitt, deceased, v. Robert E. Baker was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Morgan Circuit Court, where Baker filed a suit against Stacy related to promissory notes. These notes, executed in Kentucky in 1826, promised payment of $300 each to William Miller, Jr. The notes were later assigned to Baker in 1828. The defendant, Baker, argued several defenses in response to the claims brought by Stacy, who was representing Hitt's estate after Hitt's death. During the legal proceedings, the court considered various pleas presented by Baker, particularly focusing on the laws governing contracts in Kentucky, where the notes were executed. This case highlights the complexities of cross-state contract law and the implications of shifting jurisdictions on legal obligations.	The plaintiff, Matthew Stacy, claimed that Baker was liable for the amounts specified in the assigned promissory notes. He argued that the notes were valid contracts that should be enforced despite the defendant’s claims regarding the lack of consideration. Stacy sought to obtain the amounts due under the promissory notes, along with damages and court costs.	The defendant, Robert E. Baker, raised several defenses, including the argument that the consideration for the notes was invalid due to a lien held by William Miller, Sr. at the time of the sale of property in Kentucky. Furthermore, he contended that the laws of Kentucky allowed him to argue the notes were executed without consideration, thus defending against the enforcement of the contract. Baker requested that the court overturn the prior judgment that favored Stacy based on these pleas.

John Stone filed a lawsuit against The Fairbury, Pontiac and Northwestern Railroad Company in the circuit court of Livingston County, Illinois, around September 1873. The case arose due to the construction and operation of the railroad along Walnut Street, directly in front of Stone's residence. Stone claimed that the railroad's daily operations, particularly the smoke and cinders emitted by its locomotives, caused significant damage to his property. The court initially sustained a demurrer (a dismissal based on a lack of legal basis) against Stone's declaration, leading to a judgment requiring him to pay costs. Stone then appealed the decision, questioning whether his declaration was sufficient to establish a cause of action for damages. Ultimately, the court examined the allegations, referencing the Illinois Bill of Rights, which protects property owners from damage caused by public use without compensation, concluding that Stone had a valid claim of direct physical injury due to the railroad's operations.	John Stone argued that the Fairbury, Pontiac and Northwestern Railroad Company caused significant damage to his property through the emission of smoke and cinders from its locomotives, impacting his quality of life. He asserted that the railroad's construction and operation on the public street directly violated his rights as a property owner under the Illinois Bill of Rights, which ensures compensation for damages incurred due to public use.	The railroad company contended that the damage claimed by Stone was not sufficient for a legal remedy since property owners must accept certain inconveniences when a railroad is established near their properties, as these are considered incidental to the public interest served by railroads. The defendant argued that the court should dismiss the case based on these grounds, maintaining that the declaration did not demonstrate a direct cause for damages that warranted recovery.

On December 10, 1861, in Cook County, Illinois, Benjamin F. Brookfield and several co-plaintiffs filed a bill in chancery against Grant Goodrich and others concerning a series of financial transactions dating back to March 1, 1856. The defendant John McCaffery borrowed $14,000, secured by twenty-one bonds with varying values, and executed two deeds of trust on the same property to protect these bonds. The first deed secured seven bonds of $1,000 each, while the second secured fourteen bonds of $500 each. The plaintiffs held some of the $500 bonds and alleged that the trustee (Goodrich) inaccurately claimed priority of the first deed over their interests. The plaintiffs feared that a sale of the property would occur, disadvantaging their claims, as McCaffery was insolvent. They asserted that both deeds were part of a single transaction and sought an injunction to prevent the trustee from selling the property, claiming equal lien status under the secured deeds. The case revolved around determining which deed held priority based on the record-keeping practices of the recorder’s office.	The plaintiffs argued that both deeds of trust constituted a single transaction, claiming that there was no priority between them. They sought to prevent the trustee, Goodrich, from selling the property in a manner that would favor the holders of the $1,000 bonds over their own claims on the $500 bonds. The plaintiffs prayed for an injunction to restrain the trustee from proceeding with the intended sale and insisted on having equal lien rights against the property.	The defendants contended that the recording law favored the deed first filed and recorded, which was the one securing the $1,000 bonds. They argued that the trustee acted correctly as per the law, believing the first recorded deed had priority over the second. The defendants maintained that the plaintiffs' failure to confirm the recording order before investing in the $500 bonds reflected their negligence. They requested the dismissal of the plaintiffs' claims and the affirmation of the priority of the first deed.

Justin Butterfield filed an appeal against James Kinzie following a decision made in March 1838 by the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, presided over by Judge John Pearson. The case was brought to the Supreme Court of Illinois. The dispute arose from an action concerning a promissory note or bill of exchange, which required interpretation of legal principles regarding the necessity of proving a demand for payment at the specified location. The Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of Kinzie, meaning they accepted the requirement that the plaintiff needed to prove a demand for payment. Butterfield contested this ruling, arguing that such proof was not necessary to maintain his case.	Butterfield's primary argument was that, in actions against the maker of a promissory note or the acceptor of a bill of exchange, it is not mandatory for the plaintiff to allege or prove that a demand for payment was made at the specified location. He sought to have the Supreme Court reverse the lower court's decision, contending that established legal precedent supported his position on this issue, and requested a trial on the merits of the case.	Kinzie’s defense rested on the argument that the Circuit Court's ruling was correct, asserting the necessity for the plaintiff to prove a demand for payment at the specified time and place. The defendant relied on the affirmative of the legal proposition, suggesting that without such evidence, the plaintiff’s claim could not proceed under the law governing promissory notes and bills of exchange.

Nathan Cromwell and Enoch C. March were involved in a legal dispute that led them to agree on arbitration to resolve their differences. This agreement, made prior to the court's involvement, stated that the arbitration award should be entered as a rule of court in the Morgan County Circuit Court. The agreement also asserted that this award would have the same force and effect as a judgment. Following the arbitration process, March filed a notice to apply for judgment based on the award, which resulted in the Circuit Court entering a default judgment in favor of March during its April term in 1829. Cromwell challenged this decision by filing a writ of error to reverse the judgment, questioning whether the Circuit Court had the jurisdiction to award a judgment on the arbitration. The Illinois Supreme Court assessed the validity of the Circuit Court's jurisdiction within the context of the state's regulations on arbitrations and awards, notably a law from January 6, 1827, aimed at ensuring proper protocol for arbitrations.	Cromwell argued that the Morgan County Circuit Court lacked the jurisdiction to issue a judgment based on the arbitration award. He relied on the stipulations of the 1827 legislative act regarding arbitration, asserting that the agreement made by both parties did not properly establish jurisdiction for the court to act on the award, thereby rendering the judgment invalid.	March contended that the arbitration agreement allowed for the award to be entered as a rule of court, claiming it fell within the provisions of the statute. He sought to maintain the validity of the judgment issued by the Circuit Court, asserting that proper procedures were followed and that the court acted within its authority in rendering judgment based on the arbitration award.

In the case of Joseph Kelley v. John Inman, the dispute arises from an ejectment action filed by Inman on April 20, 1840, in the Adams Circuit Court, Illinois. Kelley was notified prior to the filing that the declaration would be presented on the second day of the April term. Following the notification, a rule was established requiring Kelley to respond within twenty days, but he neglected to file a plea within this timeframe. When Kelley attempted to enter his plea at the July term, the court dismissed his motion citing his previous noncompliance with the rule. Kelley contended that he was not adequately notified as he believed no further actions had occurred at the term's start. He later submitted an affidavit claiming he had hired counsel who attended the initial court session, yet no declaration was filed on that day; hence he argued he was surprised by the rule that followed. The Circuit Court ultimately ruled in favor of Inman, leading Kelley to appeal the decision. The Illinois Supreme Court examined the statutory requirements relating to pleadings and defaults in ejectment cases to resolve whether Kelley had a right to plead after the expiration of the rule.	The plaintiff, John Inman, claimed that Joseph Kelley failed to comply with the court’s rules regarding pleading deadlines. He argued that Kelley was duly notified of the need to appear and plead but neglected to do so within the stipulated twenty-day period following the declaration's filing. Consequently, Inman sought a judgment by default to recover possession of the premises.	The defendant, Joseph Kelley, maintained that he had a valid defense and was improperly denied the opportunity to plead after failing to comply with the original deadline. He claimed surprise and lack of proper notice regarding the filing of Inman’s declaration, supported by an affidavit stating he attended court as required but received no proper communication of any subsequent action. Kelley sought to have his late plea accepted and the previous default judgment overturned.

The legal case "The Pennsylvania Co. v. Henry Marshall" took place in Chicago, Illinois, and was decided on January 6, 1886. The key individuals involved were Henry Marshall, the plaintiff, and The Pennsylvania Company, the defendant. The case arose after Marshall's son was fatally injured by a train operated by the defendant's railroad. The incident occurred as the train—consisting of over twenty freight cars and an engine—was being moved in reverse through a busy area near Grove and 18th streets without any warning signals or precautions to alert pedestrians. The plaintiff alleged that the carelessness and negligence of the defendant's employees were the primary causes of the accident, as there was no one stationed to account for the safety of passers-by. A jury trial was held, which resulted in a verdict for the plaintiff, awarding him $2,999 in damages.	The plaintiff, Henry Marshall, claimed that the Pennsylvania Company was responsible for the death of his son due to the negligent operation of its train. He argued that the defendant failed to take necessary safety precautions, such as using warning signals or having personnel to alert pedestrians in the busy area where the accident occurred. Marshall sought damages for the wrongful death of his son as a result of this negligence.	The defendant, The Pennsylvania Company, contended that it was not liable for the accident and that the actions taken by its employees did not constitute negligence. The defense likely argued that the operation of the train was within standard practices and that the absence of a flag or signal did not necessarily equate to negligent behavior. The specific details of their defense strategy were not extensively detailed in the summary.

John Fagan v. Theodore Schultz et al. is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The case arose in Jefferson, Cook County, Illinois, involving key individuals including John Fagan, his guardian Frank Wulf, and the purchaser Theodore Schultz. The dispute centered around a contract and a deed of conveyance concerning a tract of land that was Fagan's homestead, which he inherited from his father, James Fagan, through a will that left the property for his benefit until he turned 21. After reaching adulthood, Fagan sold the property to Schultz for $1,000, which was significantly less than its market value of $2,800 to $3,000. Fagan claimed he was misled about his rights by his guardian, Wulf, who allegedly made him believe he only owned one-eighth of the land and influenced him into making the sale under false pretenses. Fagan argued that this arrangement was fraudulent and aimed to defraud him of his rightful inheritance.	The plaintiff, John Fagan, argued that he was misled regarding his ownership rights by his guardian, Frank Wulf, who led him to believe he owned only a small portion of the property. Fagan claimed that this deception, combined with the influence of Wulf and Schultz—who were involved in a partnership—meant that the sale was fraudulent. Fagan requested the court to rescind the sale and cancel the deed, asserting that the transaction did not reflect a fair market value and was marred by Wulf's undue influence.	The defendants, including Theodore Schultz and Frank Wulf, contended that the sale was legitimate and that there was no fraud involved. They argued that Fagan was of sound mind when he made the sale, having consulted a lawyer who advised him regarding the title. The defendants emphasized that there was no conspiracy or intention to defraud Fagan, and they maintained that the purchase was made at a price that, while low, was not so unfair as to warrant rescission. They asserted that Wulf was honest in his dealings and had not influenced Fagan’s decision inappropriately.

The case of James C. Gault et al. v. Julien S. Hoagland et al. was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1861. The plaintiffs, Gault and Smeetzer, originally executed a mortgage for $2,400 to the defendants, Hoagland and Ricketts, to secure a debt. The mortgage arrangement involved the delivery of 300,000 bricks, which were to be valued at market price upon delivery, to partially pay off the debt. The plaintiffs admitted to delivering the bricks but contended that a note for $601 remained unpaid. However, key documentation, including the obligations related to the bricks and the promissory note, was not submitted for evidence. Following the default of the defendants to respond to the complaint, a decree pro confesso was entered against them in July 1858 for $622. The plaintiffs argued on appeal that the court's decree was issued without sufficient evidence about the value of the bricks and their obligations, ultimately leading to an error in the judgment.	The plaintiffs claimed that the court erred in granting a decree pro confesso without sufficient evidence. They argued that the bill filed lacked essential averments, including the market value of the bricks delivered and the exact amount owed after accounting for this value. The plaintiffs contended that since no obligations or notes substantiating the claims were filed, the decree should not stand and requested that the case be remanded for further proceedings to allow for amendments.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs' bill was fundamentally flawed due to its failure to establish a definite and certain amount owed. They highlighted that the mortgage and related documents did not properly exhibit the obligations relating to the bricks or the promissory note. The defendants argued that the ruling by the court to impose liability was unwarranted as there was no solid evidence presented regarding the value of the bricks or any substantial claims that warranted the amounts demanded by the plaintiffs.

In February 1861, Samuel Ogden became involved in a legal dispute in Peoria, Illinois. The case arose when Harrison & Bennet purchased liquors from Henry Amsler, who owned a hotel and was selling the liquors at his bar. They executed notes totaling $793.25 and secured the payment with a chattel mortgage on the goods purchased. Amsler remained with them for about ten days and witnessed them selling the liquors without objection. By the end of July 1861, following a fire that destroyed their tavern, Harrison & Bennet sold the remaining liquors to Ogden. Shortly after this sale, the defendants—James Stewart and John A. J. Murray, representing Amsler in a writ of replevin—seized the liquors from Ogden. Ogden then brought a replevin action against the defendants, asserting his legal right to the goods. The case details showcase arguments surrounding property rights, mortgages, and the implications of Amsler's consent and knowledge regarding the sales that Harrison & Bennet conducted.	Samuel Ogden's main argument was that he lawfully acquired the remaining liquors from Harrison & Bennet, who had the authority to sell them, despite the mortgage agreement with Amsler. He contended that Amsler's ongoing acquiescence to these sales indicated a waiver of his rights to reclaim the goods after they were sold. Ogden sought the return of the liquors that were unlawfully seized by the sheriff under the writ of replevin.	The defendants, Stewart and Murray, contended that the liquors were still the property of Amsler and that they had the right to seize them based on the existing chattel mortgage. They argued that the sheriff acted within the law under the writ of replevin issued in favor of Amsler, negating Ogden's claim to ownership of the liquors.

In 1839, Elisha Davis was appointed as the collector of Brown County, Illinois. As required by law, he entered into a bond with sureties, including S. W. Miller. The Illinois legislature passed an act on January 7, 1841, which extended the deadline for Davis to settle the revenue owed for 1839 until September 1, 1841. In March 1842, the State of Illinois filed a lawsuit against Davis and his sureties for the non-payment of county revenue for 1839. The sureties claimed that the need for payment arose after the extension provided by the legislature, and asserted that this extension discharged them from liability. The Circuit Court dismissed this defense, leading to a judgment against Davis and the sureties for the bond amount and damages totaling $6,305.15. The sureties then sought to reverse this judgment, arguing that the extension without their consent invalidated their obligations.	The plaintiffs, representing the State of Illinois, claimed that Elisha Davis failed to pay the county the owed revenue for 1839 as stipulated in his bond. They argued that Davis and his sureties breached their contractual obligations and sought the payment of the penalty of the bond along with damages for the breach.	The defendants, Davis and his sureties, contended that the legislative act extending the payment deadline effectively discharged them from further liability. They argued that the act, passed without their consent, materially altered the original terms of their bond, thereby absolving them of responsibility for payment until the new deadline set by the legislature.

In the legal case of P. Q. Harrison v. Ann Hart and Francis Hart, Executors, the events unfolded in Morgan County, Illinois, with the judgment being rendered on December 1, 1886. The case arose from a scire facias action, which sought to make P. Q. Harrison a party to a previous judgment issued in May 1881 against Benjamin Berry and him. The plaintiff, Ann Hart, argued that a former judgment made against them was valid. Harrison, the defendant, disputed the validity of the original judgment, claiming that he was never properly served process and that the court lacked jurisdiction over him at the time of the judgment. He presented two pleas: the first asserting the court’s lack of jurisdiction and the second asserting that he neither executed nor owed any obligation related to the promissory note at the center of the case. The Circuit Court of Morgan County rendered judgments based on the original action against Berry alone, and when the demurrers were sustained against Harrison's defenses, judgment was entered against him, leading to an appeal.	The plaintiffs, represented by Ann Hart and Francis Hart, contended that the previous judgment issued in May 1881 was valid and that P. Q. Harrison should be held accountable as a party to this judgment. They asserted that Harrison had been properly served with process, and thus the court had jurisdiction over him when the original judgment was rendered. The plaintiffs moved to have Harrison made a party to the earlier judgment.	The defendant, P. Q. Harrison, countered the claims by asserting that he had not been properly served with process, leading to the conclusion that the court lacked jurisdiction over him. He argued that the judgment rendered in the original case was void due to lack of jurisdiction. Additionally, he challenged the validity of the promissory note, stating he neither executed it nor owed any debt to Matthew Hart as alleged. Harrison claimed that the return of service was false and maintained that the judgment could not be enforced against him.

Luke Nevin took legal action against the Pullman Palace Car Company in a dispute concerning their refusal to allow him and his wife to occupy assigned sleeping berths on a train. This incident occurred on August 5, 1881, in Dubuque, Iowa, where Nevin had purchased three first-class tickets from the Illinois Central Railroad for himself, his wife, and his niece. Upon boarding the train, he engaged two lower berths for himself and his wife through the conductor. After waiting for the berths to be prepared, Nevin temporarily stepped out onto the platform. Upon his return, he discovered the conductor had locked the doors and prevented him from re-entering, subsequently ejecting his belongings to another car. Nevin was forced to sit in a common passenger car for the journey, resulting in physical discomfort and humiliation. The circuit court of McLean County ruled against Nevin after sustaining a general demurrer to his case, and the Appellate Court upheld this decision. Nevin appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Nevin contended that his ejection from the sleeper berth constituted a wrongful act by the Pullman Palace Car Company and was a breach of their contractual obligation to provide him with the promised accommodations, based on the payment he had tendered. He argued that even if a special contract existed, it did not negate the possibility of pursuing an action on the case because the company's actions represented tortious conduct that caused him harm.	The Pullman Palace Car Company maintained that their conduct amounted to a mere breach of contract rather than a tort, arguing that the plaintiff misconceived the nature of his action. They contended that since the refusal to let Nevin occupy the berth was based on the condition that it had not yet been prepared, their actions fell within the scope of the contractual arrangement rather than constituting a tortious wrong against Nevin.

In the case of John P. Harris et al. v. Paul Cornell et al., the plaintiffs, John P. Harris and three others, claimed to be heirs of Benjamin Harris, who had passed away in 1863. The dispute centers around land that Benjamin Harris acquired from Mark Noble, Jr., in 1836 through misconstrued deeds. The legal conflict originates from these transactions and subsequent events, including a judgment against Noble that led to a sale of the land to Jefferson Gardner in 1840. The plaintiffs argue that the land's transfer was illegitimate, asserting that Gardner knew he lacked lawful title and that his subsequent grantees (Cornell and Fellows) were aware of the situation. The case highlights issues of fraud, witness perjury, and jurisdictional questions relating to prior court proceedings. This intricate history involves the plaintiffs’ claim of a recorded deed from Noble to Harris, against which the defendants argue their title rights derived from previous judgments and sheriff sales. The intricate web of property transfers, bankruptcies, and legal filings shaped the dispute, leading to a resolution process in the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs argue that they have rightful ownership of the land due to a previously recorded deed which proves their ancestor, Benjamin Harris, owned the land prior to it being wrongfully sold due to fraudulent practices. They seek to have the court set aside the previous decree that denied their title, declare the sheriff's deed void, and assert that the land should be returned to them, maintaining the rightful heirship and property claims.	The defendants, Paul Cornell and Elisha C. Fellows, contend that they obtained title to the land through lawful judicial proceedings and assert that the plaintiffs’ claims are baseless since they are trying to overturn a decree obtained years prior. They argue that the plaintiffs' ancestor had no legal standing in the original case due to bankruptcy and lack of valid title at that time, thus rendering any claim by the plaintiffs invalid.

In 1881, Candace Sands, a 73-year-old woman living on a 126-acre farm in Whiteside County, Illinois, executed a deed transferring a 40-acre portion of the property to her son, Marcus Sands. Candace had been ill during this period, and evidence suggests her mental faculties were impaired due to her sickness. After executing the deed, which she believed would not take effect until recorded, she destroyed it later in the summer of the same year. The farm had been improved through joint labor with her husband, John P. Sands, and their eight children, and Marcus resumed working on it after returning home. Upon the death of John P. Sands in 1883, Marcus did not account for or pay rent to Candace. The deed's execution and subsequent destruction became the source of conflict between mother and son. Candace contended she had been unduly influenced by Marcus, who allegedly misled her regarding the deed's validity while taking advantage of her illness. This situation led to legal proceedings initiated by Marcus, who sought to compel Candace to reexecute the deed.	Marcus Sands claimed that his mother, Candace, executed a valid deed transferring a 40-acre tract of land to him on June 3, 1881, for valuable consideration. He alleged that he took possession of the land, made substantial improvements, and that Candace wrongfully destroyed the deed without his knowledge. He sought a court order compelling Candace to reexecute the deed and for general relief.	Candace Sands admitted executing the deed but asserted she did so while mentally impaired and under the undue influence of her son. She claimed that she believed the deed would not be valid unless recorded and that she had only handed it to Marcus for safekeeping. She also asserted a homestead claim on the property, sought to invalidate the deed, and requested an accounting of rents and profits from Marcus.

Robert Dawson, as the plaintiff in error, was involved in a legal dispute with Abel Harrington, the defendant in error, regarding a mechanic's lien. The case emerged from a series of events that began in September 1847 when Harrington was allegedly employed by G. W. Robbins, who was purportedly acting as an agent for Dawson, to work on a mill that Dawson was constructing. Harrington claimed he worked for 100 days at a wage of $1.83 per day, which amounted to a total of $143 owed to him after receiving $30. In response, Dawson argued that Robbins had constructed the mill under a direct contract with him, denying Robbins had any authority to hire Harrington on his behalf. The jury trial presented conflicting testimonies, including Harrington's assertion that his work was worth $90, but there was no concrete evidence regarding the timeline of services rendered. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of Harrington, awarding him $106, leading Dawson to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, Harrington, claimed he was entitled to payment for labor performed on a mill constructed by Dawson. He argued that he was hired by Robbins, who he believed was acting as Dawson's agent, and that as a result, he did work worth $143. Harrington sought enforcement of a mechanic's lien based on his claim for unpaid wages for the 100 days of labor he provided.	The defendant, Dawson, countered that Robbins was not his agent and had no authority to hire Harrington. He maintained that Robbins had a direct contract with him to construct the mill and had been fully paid for the work, which included Harrington's labor. Dawson's defense rested on the assertion that Harrington could not make a claim against him for wages since he was employed by Robbins, thereby denying Harrington's allegations of entitlement to payment.

The case, "The Anchor Line v. John C. Knowles," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. The central issue arose when John C. Knowles filed a claim against The Anchor Line after a shipment of goods was destroyed by fire. The goods had been transported via water and land as per a bill of lading issued by The Anchor Line. The shipment was successfully delivered and stored in a warehouse; however, a significant fire occurred the following day, leading to the destruction of the goods. The court considered stipulations about the carrier's liability as outlined in the bill of lading, which exempted The Anchor Line from liability for loss or damage occurring after delivery. The case was examined without a jury, and the decision was influenced by prior cases and legal standards regarding a carrier's responsibilities.	The plaintiff, John C. Knowles, argued that The Anchor Line was liable for the loss of his goods based on the stipulation that they typically provided notice of arrival. He claimed that the failure to notify him when the goods arrived contributed to his losses and that the circumstances warranted compensation for the damages incurred.	The Anchor Line contended that the terms of the bill of lading specifically exempted them from liability for loss or damage due to fire after the goods were safely stored at the warehouse. They asserted that since the goods had been properly delivered and stored, and the destruction by fire occurred outside their control, they were not liable for the loss. Even if there was a duty to provide notice, the fire occurred before such notice could be reasonably given.

The case, titled "Wm. K. Reed and The Dime Savings Bank v. Lydia A. Cramb and Myra A. Price," was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 11, 1886. It arose in Bureau County, Illinois. William K. Reed, the appellant, had pledged fifty shares of stock from the Dime Savings Bank as collateral for loans made to H. C. Reed. The shares were pledged to Levi Kelsey, the father of appellees Lydia A. Cramb and Myra A. Price, as security for the debt totaling around $3,300. The stock had initially replaced a $1,000 note and mortgage held by Kelsey, which had been placed without Kelsey knowing H. C. Reed was not the true owner of the mortgage. Disputes arose when Kelsey renewed the debts without the knowledge or consent of William K. Reed. The court had to determine if the collateral was adequately protected under the law of sureties. The case presented arguments concerning the treatment of collateral and whether the renewal of notes without consent released the lien on the stock.	The plaintiffs, Lydia A. Cramb and Myra A. Price, argued that the fifty shares of Dime Savings Bank stock were never owned by H. C. Reed but were instead the property of William K. Reed, meant to secure his own mortgage. They contended that the original agreements were violated when Levi Kelsey made changes to the terms of the note without the consent of William K. Reed. They sought to foreclose the lien against the stock to recover the amounts due from H. C. Reed.	The defendants, William K. Reed and the Dime Savings Bank, claimed that the lien on the stock was released due to the unauthorized renewals of the notes and that the stock functioned as collateral only when the original agreements were intact. They argued that since Kelsey had prior knowledge of the ownership of the stock and the collateral's intended purpose, any changes made in the contractual obligations without Reed's consent invalidated the lien.

The case of Henry J. Chase v. Moses Gray Palmer was tried in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision made in April 1862. The events stem from a legal dispute regarding the validity of a deed related to a parcel of land located in Peoria, Illinois. The action of ejectment commenced in the Peoria Circuit Court following a jury trial that occurred in November 1861. The jury rendered a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, Henry J. Chase, awarding him an undivided fourth of the south-east quarter of Section thirty-three, Town ten north, Range seven east. The defendant, Moses Gray Palmer, sought to appeal this decision. A critical issue in the appeal was the validity of the deed, which lacked the name of a grantee at the time of execution, a fundamental requirement for a valid deed under Illinois law. The ruling focused on the deed's preparation, which was deemed improperly executed since no grantee was named when it was acknowledged, leading to further scrutiny of its acceptance in the initial trial.",	The plaintiff, Henry J. Chase, claimed ownership of an undivided fourth interest in a specific tract of land and sought to enforce his rights through the action of ejectment. His main argument rested on the validity of the deed presented as evidence, asserting that it legally transferred the property interest to him. Chase contended that any deficiencies or procedural errors regarding the deed should be rectified through proper evidence, maintaining that he had a legitimate claim to the land.",	Defendant Moses Gray Palmer contended that the deed presented by the plaintiff was invalid due to the absence of a grantee's name at the time of its execution. Palmer argued that since the deed was prepared with blank spaces intended to be filled later, it did not satisfy legal requirements for a valid property transfer. He requested that the court recognize the deed's invalidity, asserting that it should have been excluded from evidence, thereby questioning the legitimacy of the plaintiff’s claim to the property.",

John J. Fentz v. Mary C. Meadows was a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1874. The case originated in the Richland Circuit Court and involved a lawsuit initiated by Mary C. Meadows against John J. Fentz, relating to the provisions of a statute enacted on July 1, 1872, that aimed to address issues stemming from the sale of intoxicating liquors in Illinois. Mary C. Meadows alleged that John J. Fentz, through his establishment, unlawfully sold intoxicating liquors to her husband, who was a chronic drunkard. Meadows sought damages for the supposed harm caused to her as a result of this sale. The jury ruled in favor of Meadows, awarding her $500 in damages. Fentz appealed the judgment, arguing that the trial court had erred in its instructions and the interpretation of the statute. The case underscored the strict interpretation required for claims made under the penal statute regarding sales of intoxicating liquors, which led to complexities in establishing actual damages as a basis for exemplary damages.	Mary C. Meadows claimed that John J. Fentz, through his establishment, sold intoxicating liquor to her husband, who was known to be a chronic drunkard, thereby causing her harm. She sought $500 in damages under the Illinois statute designed to protect wives from the negative consequences of their husbands' alcoholism, asserting that the sale of alcohol directly impacted her well-being and support.	John J. Fentz defended himself by arguing that Meadows failed to prove any actual damages resulting from the sale of alcohol to her husband. He contended that he had, in good faith, instructed his employees not to serve intoxicating liquors to chronic drunkards, and that the server's disobedience should mitigate any exemplary damages. Fentz also highlighted that the statute provided grounds for action only if actual harm to the plaintiff could be established, which he claimed was not demonstrated in this case.

In the case of Caroline Eimer v. George J. Eimer et al., which took place in June 1868 in St. Clair County, Illinois, the dispute centered around the real estate inheritance of the deceased Simon Eimer. Caroline Eimer, the widow of Simon Eimer, sought a legal remedy concerning the partition of the property inherited by the heirs and the assignment of her dower rights. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, which appointed commissioners to assess the parties' rights regarding the real estate. However, it was determined that neither a partition could be made nor a dower assigned. Consequently, the court ordered the sale of the property and empaneled a jury to ascertain the yearly value of Caroline Eimer's dower, which was then decreed as a lien on the property until payment was made. Following the property sale, the solicitors for Caroline Eimer moved for the payment of their professional fees from the sale proceeds. The associated amount of $500 was ordered, but the legality of this payment was contested, leading to an appeal.	Caroline Eimer, the plaintiff, claimed the right to a fair partition of the inherited real estate and proper assignment of her dower from the estate of her deceased husband. She sought the court's intervention to ensure her claims were recognized and fulfilled, ultimately resulting in the sale of the property to uphold her financial rights.	The defendants contended that the court erred in allowing attorney's fees out of the proceeds of the sale, arguing that under statutory guidelines, only costs that are specifically taxable should be allowed, and that the payment of solicitor's fees was not authorized. They requested the reversal of the decree that ordered the payment of these fees.

The case "Daniel T. Foster and John Eddy v. Richard W. Hart" was decided on November 23, 1888, by the Illinois Appellate Court. It involved a replevin suit concerning a wagon valued at approximately $200. The wagon was originally owned by McBean & Foster, a partnership engaged in a bus line and transportation business in Bloomington, Illinois. After the death of partner Isaac McBean on March 30, 1887, Daniel T. Foster, the surviving partner, and Mary J. McBean, Isaac's executrix, sold the partnership's undivided interest in the business and the wagon to John Eddy on June 1, 1887. However, Richard W. Hart claimed he had purchased the wagon two weeks before McBean’s death. On June 11, 1887, Hart replevied the wagon from Foster and Eddy. The critical issue in the case was whether Hart's testimony regarding his purchase from the deceased Isaac McBean was permissible since it involved statements made in the absence of the surviving partner, Foster.	The plaintiffs, Foster and Eddy, argued that Hart did not have a legitimate claim to the wagon since, as an adverse party, he should not be allowed to testify about conversations with the deceased McBean without Foster being present. They contended that Hart's testimony was not competent under Illinois law and emphasized that the sale of the wagon by the executrix was void since the surviving partner had sole authority over the partnership’s assets after McBean's death.	The defendant, Hart, maintained that he had indeed purchased the wagon from McBean before his death and sought to validate his claim through testimony regarding that transaction. He argued that he should be permitted to testify regarding the circumstances of the purchase, suggesting that such matters should not be restricted by the absence of the surviving partner during past conversations.

On June 3, 1859, Joshua C. and Wilson M. Jenkins obtained a judgment against Henry and Martin L. Bush for $299.40 plus costs. Subsequently, Henry Bush sold real estate to Lucy H. Doolittle for $1,000, intending to settle certain debts, including the Jenkins judgment. A third party, Allen, was given $1,500 by Doolittle to compromise these debts but only managed to pay about $700, failing to settle the Jenkins judgment. On February 5, 1866, Henry Bush, assuming the debts had been settled, conveyed the property to Doolittle. The Jenkins plaintiffs, misled by Allen's assurances of payment, delayed enforcing their judgment until the lien duration expired. In a prior court ruling, a vendor's lien was incorrectly decreed for Bush, which was later reversed by the Illinois Supreme Court, asserting that Allen held Doolittle’s funds in trust for creditors. The matter returned to the lower court for further proceedings and the bill was amended to include Allen as a party. Following additional evidence, the bill was dismissed, leading to the plaintiffs’ appeal.	The plaintiffs, Joshua C. and Wilson M. Jenkins, argued that they were entitled to enforce their judgment against the property sold to Doolittle, asserting that Allen, who received funds to pay off their judgment, failed to do so, thereby preventing them from collecting the amount owed. They requested the court to decree that Allen should pay the remaining amount of the judgment, arguing he held the money in a trust for their benefit as creditors.	The defendant, Lucy H. Doolittle, contended that she paid Allen to settle the debts of Bush and was misled by Allen regarding the satisfaction of the Jenkins judgment. She maintained that she fulfilled her obligation under the purchase agreement, and any issues regarding the payment of the Jenkins judgment were Allen's responsibility, asserting that the plaintiffs had no claim against her for the unpaid judgment.

Thomas Eagan v. Susan Connelly is a legal case from 1883 adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning an ejectment action in Ford County, Illinois. The case revolves around a dispute over land ownership for the west half of the southeast quarter of section 25 in township 28 north, range 9 east. The plaintiff, Susan Connelly, produced several pieces of evidence to support her claim of rightful ownership, including a patent from the United States and subsequent deeds transferring title from previous owners. The defendant, Thomas Eagan, challenged the admissibility of these deeds, arguing that the acknowledgments did not confirm the personal identification of the grantors by the officer who took the acknowledgment. Upon objection from Eagan, Connelly introduced an Ohio statute to validate the deeds, which the court accepted despite Eagan's opposition.
