Eagan's defense also included the claim of title based on a tax deed resulting from a tax judgment, which Eagan argued was valid. However, Connelly contended the tax judgment lacked proper certification and therefore did not confer a valid title. The trial court ruled in favor of Connelly, affirming her ownership claim and excluding Eagan's tax deed from evidence as inadequate.	Susan Connelly's main arguments included the legality of her title based on a chain of deeds, acknowledged as valid according to both the U.S. patent and Ohio’s statutory requirements, which she demonstrated in court. She maintained that the tax deed alleged by Eagan was not supported by a valid judgment and precept, as it lacked proper certification by the county clerk, rendering it void. Her legal request was to affirm her right to the land and seek possession against Eagan.	Thomas Eagan primarily contended that the deeds relied upon by Connelly were invalid due to inadequate acknowledgments. He argued that the acknowledgment certificates did not prove that the grantors were personally known to the officer, thus challenging their status as legitimate legal documents. Eagan also asserted that the tax deed he held should confer legal title, claiming compliance with tax sale procedures. He requested that the court recognize the tax deed as valid against Connelly's claim.

In the case of Frederick Baker et al. v. Mary S. Scott, the legal dispute arose from a will left by Orestes H. Wright, which specified the distribution of his estate among his wife, Mary M. Wright, and their two children. Upon the death of Orestes, his daughter, Mary Sophia, married John Scott and executed a deed to Frederick Baker for a tract of land that her father had bequeathed to her. The transaction involved a sum of $875, with Baker executing two notes and a mortgage on the land to secure part of the purchase price. When Baker failed to make payments, Mary S. Scott initiated a foreclosure suit to sell the land and barred Baker's wife from asserting any dower rights. Baker acknowledged the mortgage notes but contended that Mary only had a life estate in the land, based on her father's will, which he argued should impact the amount owed under the notes. The case was decided in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871, with the central legal question revolving around whether Mary Sophia had received a fee simple or merely a life estate through the will.	Mary S. Scott, as the plaintiff, claimed that the terms of her father's will granted her a fee simple estate in the land. She requested foreclosure on the mortgage for failure of payment and sought a decree to sell the property, subsequently barring the defendant's wife from entering any claim against the estate.	Frederick Baker, the defendant, contended that Mary Sophia only inherited a life estate from her father's will, citing that her conveyance to him transferred only that limited interest. He requested that the court compel Mary to account for the present value of the estate he purchased, which he argued resulted in no outstanding balance on his notes or mortgage. Baker also filed a cross-bill seeking cancellation of the notes and discharge of the mortgage.

In the case of Lester P. Wood v. John Clark et al., the events took place in Somonauk, De Kalb County, Illinois. P. H. Evans, who was engaged in selling agricultural equipment and other goods, left town on January 29, 1885, leaving his brother, John F. Evans, in charge of his business. P. H. Evans was financially distressed and had secured sureties, John Clark and Stephen D. Wright, for several notes. After leaving, P. H. Evans authorized John F. Evans to handle his affairs in a letter dated January 26, 1885. Shortly thereafter, John F. Evans, in an effort to secure debts owed, arranged a meeting with Clark, Wright, and a representative of the Somonauk Bank to secure them for P. H. Evans' debts, which amounted to $4,197. On February 5, 1885, John F. Evans transferred about $4,696.86 worth of property to these creditors in exchange for their loans, under the authority granted to him. The property was under their possession when it was seized by other creditors on February 7, 1885, under writs of attachment. This led to the replevin action to settle the ownership of the property in question.	The plaintiff, Lester P. Wood, contended that the transfer of property by John F. Evans was fraudulent and intended to hinder and delay creditors of P. H. Evans. They argued that John F. Evans did not have legitimate authority to dispose of the property as he did and sought to reclaim the property based on these assertions, highlighting the involvement of other creditors in the analyses of the legitimacy of the transaction.	The defendants, John Clark et al., argued that John F. Evans was fully authorized to act on behalf of P. H. Evans, which included securing debts with the property in question. They maintained that the claims against them were unfounded and that the transaction was proper and conducted in good faith to settle debts owed. The defendants requested that the court uphold the validity of their claim to the property transferred, emphasizing that the sale was not fraudulent as alleged.

The case "Frederick C. Porter et al. v. Charles Triola" took place in September 1876 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Frederick C. Porter, the plaintiff, and Charles Triola, the defendant. The background of the case reveals that Porter initiated an action of trespass against Triola, claiming that Triola unlawfully took certain goods that Porter purchased from Triola's debtors. The primary legal contention revolved around whether Porter’s purchase was valid against the creditors of his vendors.  During the trial, the defendants raised an objection to the verdict, asserting that the court erred in their handling of certain procedural matters, particularly regarding a motion for a continuance caused by the sudden illness of the appellants' attorney. They argued that this illness hindered their preparation for trial and the presentation of crucial evidence.  The Illinois Supreme Court, led by Justice Dickey, examined the evidence and procedural issues, expressing doubts about the merits of the defendants' arguments but ultimately confirming that the lower court's actions did not warrant a reversal of the judgment.	The plaintiff, Frederick C. Porter, claimed that he was the rightful owner of certain goods taken by the defendant, Charles Triola, arguing that he had lawfully purchased these goods from Triola's debtors. Porter maintained that his purchase was valid and sought compensation for the unlawful taking of the goods, contending that the defendants questioned the validity of his purchase unfairly.	The defendant, Charles Triola, provided several key defenses, including challenging the validity of the plaintiff's purchase against the creditors of his vendors. Triola argued that the plaintiff's claims were unfounded and insisted that the court erred by not granting a continuance due to the sudden illness of their attorney. This illness, they claimed, impeded their ability to present adequate evidence, leading to a denial of a fair trial. They requested a new trial based on these asserted procedural errors.

Obadiah Arnold v. A. J. Ludlam is a legal case that took place in April 1865 in McLean County, Illinois. The case began when Obadiah Arnold (the plaintiff) sought to recover penalties after A. J. Ludlam (the defendant) allegedly drove Arnold's cattle from their usual range. The situation arose when Ludlam was driving his herd of cattle, and Arnold's cattle mixed with the drove. There was clear evidence that Ludlam knowingly included Arnold's cattle, as he branded them and castrated a bull belonging to Arnold. He then moved the cattle twenty-five miles away through densely populated areas, where multiple habitations existed. Arnold first won a judgment in the local justice court, but the defendant appealed to the Circuit Court, which ruled in Ludlam's favor. Arnold then appealed this ruling, claiming that the Circuit Court erred in its instructions to the jury regarding the definition of a drover and the application of the relevant statute.	The plaintiff argues that Ludlam violated a statute aimed at protecting cattle owners by knowingly driving Arnold's cattle off their premises and past a significant distance, which entitled Arnold to recover damages. He claims that Ludlam's actions constituted a clear case of cattle driving under the statute, justifying the penalties Arnold initially sought in the justice court.	The defendant contends that he was merely moving his cattle within the same neighborhood and therefore should not be classified as a drover under the statute, which would exempt him from the penalties. Ludlam claims that the jury was misled by incorrect legal instructions regarding these definitions, and his arguments rely on the assertion that Arnold's claims do not satisfy the legal thresholds necessary for penalties.

The case "The Board of Supervisors of Cumberland County v. Andrew J. Edwards" was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875. The legal dispute arose from an action of assumpsit filed by the Board of Supervisors of Cumberland County against Andrew J. Edwards, who served as the county treasurer and collector. The main issue involved the collection of taxes for the years 1871 and 1872, where the board sought to recover funds that Edwards allegedly retained beyond what was legally allowed. The case examined whether the charges Edwards made for his services were consistent with the statutory provisions governing county treasurers and collectors. The evidence indicated that Edwards had collected significant amounts of money but retained a greater commission than permitted by law, leading to questions regarding the accuracy and legality of his financial reports to the board. The court scrutinized the applicable laws regarding commissions for tax collection, which specified different percentages for various amounts collected and stipulations for paying over funds to successors.	The plaintiff, the Board of Supervisors of Cumberland County, claimed that Andrew J. Edwards retained commissions that exceeded the legal limits based on state law. They provided evidence indicating that Edwards collected a total of $15,843.62 and improperly charged more than the allowed commissions for his services as county treasurer for the years 1871 and 1872. The board sought to recover the overcharged amounts, highlighting that the amounts reported by Edwards included fees not sanctioned by law, thus violating their legal entitlements.	Andrew J. Edwards, the defendant, asserted that the charges made to the board were justified based on his interpretation of the applicable laws regarding commissions. He argued that the board, by approving his financial reports, had estopped themselves from later claiming that the fees were illegal. Edwards maintained that his compensation was in line with the complexity of his duties and the relevant statutes in effect during his tenure as county treasurer and collector. He requested that the court uphold the validity of his commission claims.

Isaac H. Gray brought an action against the Fuller Electrical Company in 1886, seeking to recover commissions from the sale of electrical apparatus. The case was tried in the Illinois Appellate Court without a jury, presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gary. The transactions in question involved Gray acting as an agent for the Fuller Electrical Company. The trial concluded with a judgment favoring the defendant, Fuller Electrical Company. Notably, the trial proceedings did not include any exceptions to the court's findings or judgments, which are critical for any appeal. This lack of exceptions ultimately limited the appeal process and the court's ability to review the evidentiary basis for the ruling. The case reflects typical proceedings of the era in commercial disputes, emphasizing the roles of agents and commission in sales of electrical equipment during the late 19th century.	The plaintiff, Isaac H. Gray, claimed that he was entitled to certain commissions for sales of electrical apparatus, asserting that he acted as the agent of the Fuller Electrical Company. He sought to recover these commissions through an action of assumpsit, asserting that the defendant had an obligation to pay him for the sales he facilitated.	The Fuller Electrical Company, as the defendant, claimed that there were no grounds to award commissions to Gray. They successfully defended against the claims, leading to a court ruling in their favor. The judgment stated that the findings made by the trial court were not subject to challenge due to the absence of recorded exceptions to those findings, which aligned with established legal principles.

In April 1866, Charlotte A. Dickey filed a lawsuit against John McDonnell in the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from an alleged assault and battery incident that occurred in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff accused the defendant of attempting to commit rape against her. The trial featured conflicting testimonies from both parties. Dickey claimed that McDonnell physically assaulted her by throwing her to the ground, choking her, and threatening her, leading to visible bruises on her body, corroborated by her sister's testimony. McDonnell’s defense included an instruction that, if the jury found that Dickey consented to ride with him despite suspecting his motives were sexual, and if her resistance was feigned to extract money, the verdict should favor him. The court assessed these instructions and the context of violence used during the encounter in their deliberations.	Charlotte A. Dickey argued that John McDonnell committed assault and battery against her, especially by using physical force and threats in an attempt to coerce her into submitting to sexual advances. She sought damages for the violence she experienced and contended that consent obtained through such means should not absolve McDonnell of liability for his actions.	John McDonnell's defense centered on the argument that Dickey voluntarily accompanied him, suggesting that any later resistance was feigned to extract money from him. He contended that if the jury believed that her ultimate consent followed acts of violence, the law required a verdict in his favor. McDonnell requested that the court instruct the jury that consent, even if coerced by prior violence, did not negate his defense against the claims of assault.

William Thompson v. Luther Dearborn et al. is a legal case filed in Illinois, with its decision rendered on March 29, 1883. The case stemmed from a dispute concerning a transaction dating back to February 20, 1877, involving a mortgage on a property located in Mason County, Illinois. William Thompson was the grantee in a deed of trust executed by Absalom C. Funk and Chloe E. Funk, which conveyed 560 acres of land to him. In the deed, Thompson reportedly assumed responsibility for a mortgage of $3,500, which was part of the consideration for the property. The plaintiffs sought a money decree against Thompson for the mortgage debt based on the assumption clause within the deed. The central issue was whether the deed's language sufficiently established Thompson's personal liability to pay the mortgage. The court examined whether Thompson had assented to the mortgage assumption clause and whether his default in the case admitted the necessary facts to support such liability.	The plaintiffs contended that the deed executed by Funk and his wife clearly established that Thompson had assumed the mortgage debt as part of the property transaction. They argued that the deed’s language constituted a binding contract that created personal liability on Thompson for the payment of the mortgage debt. As such, they sought a monetary judgment against him for the amount owed, which was alleged to be $3,168.67.	Thompson's defense rested on the argument that the plaintiffs failed to establish that he had accepted or assented to the terms of the deed, specifically the clause requiring him to pay the mortgage. They maintained that merely stating that the land was sold and conveyed did not suffice to create a personal obligation for him to pay the mortgage debt. The defendant contended that, without evidence showing his assent—such as his signature on the deed or proof of acceptance—he should not be held liable for the mortgage indebtedness.

In 1854, Horace Smith, for the use of George C. Lamb, initiated a legal action against Abraham H. Smith and John W. Hull in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas. This case stemmed from a judgment rendered on January 14, 1842, in the Superior Court of New York, where a debt of $6,087.34 was owed by the defendants under the New York “Joint Debtor Act” of 1830. The process of a capias (a court order to seize a person) was served on Abraham H. Smith successfully; however, the capias concerning John W. Hull was returned as “not found.” During the court proceedings, Abraham H. Smith filed two pleas against the plaintiff's declaration: "nul tiel record" (no such record) and "nil debet" (none of the debt). The plea of nil debet was later withdrawn, and the case was presented solely on the plea of nul tiel record, questioning the validity of the joint judgment alleged by the plaintiff against both defendants. The case was overseen by Judge J. M. Wilson at the October term in 1855, focusing on the acceptable presentation of the New York judgment in relation to the defendants' liability.	The plaintiff's main argument was that the judgment rendered against both defendants in New York was valid and should bind them in the current action. They sought to enforce this judgment in Illinois against Smith and Hull, asserting that the judgment was properly adjudicated under the jurisdiction of New York, despite Hull not being served with process. The plaintiff contended that the other party (Smith) had an obligation to recognize the joint judgment and was estopped from disputing its legal effect as it pertained to him.	The defendant, Abraham H. Smith, argued primarily through the plea of nul tiel record, asserting that there was no valid joint judgment against him and Hull, as the record of the New York judgment did not demonstrate that Hull had been served process or appeared in the action. Smith contended that the lack of proper service on Hull made the purported judgment against both invalid, effectively null, and that he should not be bound by an unenforceable judgment. His position was that the record exhibited a variance that should prevent the admission of the judgment as proof of joint liability.

In the case of Frona Ann Ransom v. Samuel E. Henderson et al., the proceedings took place in 1885 in Brown County, Illinois. The case originated as a partition action brought forth by Samuel E. Henderson, Owen P. Thompson, and William H. Barnes against Hiram E. Henry, Robert Ransom, Frona Ann Ransom, and others. The land in question originally belonged to Jesse Orr, who died intestate on January 1, 1876, leaving a widow and seven children. Following the death, some heirs conveyed their interests in the property to Hiram E. Henry, Robert Ransom, and Frona Ann Ransom, which turned them into tenants in common. The plaintiff parties claimed to have purchased and acquired additional interests from other heirs, leaving only one-seventh interest owned by Lorano Caroline Orr. The defendants, including Frona Ann Ransom, denied the plaintiffs' claims, asserting that Frona Ann Ransom owned six-sevenths of the property and contested any right of the complainants. Ultimately, the court found that the plaintiffs held one-seventh interest, while Frona Ann Ransom was awarded four-sevenths of the property. Due to the inability to partition the land physically, the court ordered it to be sold, with proceeds distributed according to the established interests.	The plaintiffs claimed that they owned specific interests in the property previously held by Jesse Orr's heirs. They argued that titles and ownership were established through various conveyances, including tax sales. Their legal request was for partition of the property among the rightful owners, contesting Frona Ann Ransom's claims to a greater share than what was established by law.	Frona Ann Ransom and her co-defendants contested the plaintiffs’ claims, asserting that they were the rightful owners of larger portions of the property than claimed. Frona Ann Ransom's defense stated that she owned six-sevenths of the land and challenged the validity of the plaintiffs' titles derived from the other heirs, with the argument that the necessary precept for tax sales was not presented as evidence, thus questioning the legitimacy of the plaintiffs' claims.

In February 1889, in Gallatin County, Illinois, John Price was indicted for murder after a violent incident in Shawneetown. He became concerned about his ability to receive a fair trial due to widespread prejudice against him in the local community, which had been exacerbated by media coverage portraying him negatively. On February 8, 1889, his counsel filed a petition requesting a change of venue, citing fears of bias among the county's residents, supported by several affidavits from local citizens. The prosecutor opposed this request with counter-affidavits denying the existence of prejudice. However, on February 12, the circuit court denied Price’s petition for a change of venue. Following various procedural activities related to continuances and trial preparation, Price was ultimately convicted and sentenced to be executed, leading him to appeal the decision based on multiple assigned errors.	John Price's primary claims in the appeal included the assertion that the circuit court erred in denying his request for a change of venue, thereby compromising his right to a fair trial. He argued that he had provided sufficient evidence of local prejudice that warranted a change of venue as a matter of right, according to Illinois statutes. Price also contended that the court improperly denied his motions for a continuance and incorrectly modified jury instructions related to self-defense.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by the prosecution, defended against Price's claims by arguing that the judge acted within his discretion in denying the change of venue request based on the evidence presented. They asserted that the affidavits provided by the defense did not adequately demonstrate a reasonable apprehension of bias. The prosecution contended that the court's determinations regarding motions for continuance and jury instructions were appropriately handled, and thus the trial had been fair despite any purported local prejudice.

In 1858, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between John H. Dart and several defendants, including John Horn. The case revolved around a writ of replevin for five stacks of hay, of which the sheriff was able to recover only two and one-eighth stacks. The plaintiff, Dart, originally filed two counts: one for the two and one-eighth stacks that were taken, and another for the remaining two and seven-eighths stacks that were not found. The defendants, including Dart, Sutherland & Gould, claimed ownership of the hay through various pleadings asserting property rights in the names of Charles and Martin Horn. The issue was joined on these pleas, and the plaintiff was granted permission to add a count in trover to include the missing stacks. The trial, overseen by Judge J. M. Wilson and conducted by a jury, resulted in a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, finding that Dart was the owner of the hay and awarding damages of two hundred and eighty dollars. The defendants then filed a motion for a new trial, which was denied, prompting their appeal.	The plaintiff, John H. Dart, argued that he was the rightful owner of the five stacks of hay and sought damages through replevin for the loss of the hay. In court, Dart successfully demonstrated ownership of the two and one-eighth stacks that were recovered and sought compensation for the remaining two and seven-eighths stacks that were unaccounted for. He requested the jury to assess damages based on his ownership claims.	The defendants contended that they were rightful owners of the hay, raising several defenses based on property ownership attributed to Charles and Martin Horn. They argued against the assumption that all defendants were liable for the claimed property, asserting that it should be clarified whether all parties were involved in the removal of the hay. Their defense included a plea of “not guilty” to the charges in the added count in trover.

John S. Wheeler v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in Madison County, Illinois, with key events occurring around March to May 1864. The case arose when two individuals, James Finley and Edward Kelten, were indicted for larceny. Wheeler acted as Finley's surety, entering into a recognizance for $500 to ensure Finley's appearance in court. On May 2, 1864, after Finley's failure to appear, the court declared the recognizance forfeited, prompting a scire facias to be issued against both Finley and Wheeler. A general demurrer was filed by Wheeler against this scire facias, which led to a judgment ordering Wheeler to pay the forfeited amount due to Finley’s default. The matter was subsequently appealed, with Wheeler contesting the legality of the forfeiture on the grounds of service and indictment procedures.	The People of the State of Illinois claimed that Wheeler, as the surety for Finley’s recognizance, was liable for the forfeited amount due to Finley's failure to appear in court. They asserted that the recognizance was enforceable despite Wheeler’s argument that no indictment was offered at Finley's scheduled appearance, contending that the recognizance did not require such an indictment to establish liability.	John S. Wheeler contended that he could not be held liable for the forfeiture because no indictment had been presented against Finley at the relevant court term. He argued that since the recognizance was conditioned upon Finley appearing to answer an indictment that was not actually preferred, there was no breach of the undertaking. Wheeler's defense included references to prior case law, asserting that execution against him could not proceed unless all defendants were duly served.

The case "City of Centralia v. Joseph Krouse" occurred around June 1872 in Centralia, Illinois. The incident arose following a disastrous fire on December 14 or 15, 1870, which destroyed eleven buildings in the city, including one owned by the plaintiff, Joseph Krouse. The sidewalk in front of the damaged structures was made of plank, rendering it almost impassable due to fire damage. Approximately eight to ten days after the fire, Krouse attempted to navigate the damaged sidewalk to retrieve fuel from his premises and fell, sustaining serious injuries. The central issues were whether the city was negligent for failing to repair the sidewalk promptly after the fire and whether Krouse himself exhibited contributory negligence by attempting to use the dangerous walk. The court found that the city had acted reasonably under the circumstances, having erected temporary guards and that Krouse was fully aware of the risks yet chose to proceed over the hazardous sidewalk.	Joseph Krouse, the plaintiff, claimed that the City of Centralia was negligent in failing to repair the damaged sidewalk in a timely manner, which he argued led to his personal injuries. He contended that the city had a duty to ensure public safety by making necessary repairs to the sidewalk within a reasonable time after the fire.	The City of Centralia defended itself against the claims by asserting that it had exercised reasonable diligence in addressing the sidewalk's condition. They argued that the officials had erected a temporary fence for public safety and that adverse weather conditions made it impractical to conduct repairs. Additionally, they maintained that Krouse exhibited contributory negligence by choosing to walk on the damaged sidewalk despite the apparent dangers and the availability of safer alternatives.

In January 1886, Edward Bates, a merchant facing financial difficulties in Mansfield, Piatt County, Illinois, had already paid one creditor approximately $1,600 from his stock. On January 30, 1886, D. P. Erwin & Company, another creditor of Bates, began attempts to attach his remaining goods. On that same day, Doggett, Bassett & Hills Company, through their attorney, T. J. Smith, executed a contract to purchase Bates' entire stock of goods worth $1,288.03. The agreement specified that after deducting the expenses related to the sale, any surplus should be returned to Bates. Following the sale, the appellants were served as garnishees in the Erwin attachment suits and maintained that they had taken possession of and sold the stock. However, a trial led to a judgment against them for $2,500, as they were not allowed to deduct their debt from the sale proceeds, due to the contract being mischaracterized by the court. The court allowed the testimony of some incompetent witnesses regarding the value of the goods sold.	The plaintiffs, represented by D. P. Erwin & Company, claimed that Doggett, Bassett & Hills Company wrongfully retained funds from the sale of Edward Bates' stock and failed to properly account for the proceeds, which should have included covering their own debt and returning any surplus to Bates. They sought a judgment for the claimed amount resulting from these actions.	Doggett, Bassett & Hills Company argued that their contract with Bates was valid as a chattel mortgage, thus allowing them to sell his stock to secure their debt. They contended that the lower court erred by not recognizing their right to deduct their owed amount from the sale's proceeds and improperly allowed incompetent witnesses to testify about the value of the goods. They requested a reversal of the judgment against them and a proper accounting of the surplus after the sale.

In January 1867, a legal case titled "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Abram Middlesworth" was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court following an incident in Shelby County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Abram Middlesworth, a local resident, had been keeping a large herd of mules in a pen adjacent to the railroad owned by the Illinois Central Railroad Company. On occasion, the mules broke loose and strayed onto the railway track, leading to a collision with a passing train that resulted in the death of twenty-two mules, valued at $2,840. Middlesworth brought an action of trespass against the railroad company, alleging negligence for failing to properly fence the track and for the negligent operation of the train and its cars. The defendant, the Illinois Central Railroad Company, contended that the plaintiff's negligence—specifically, his failure to properly contain the mules—was a contributing factor to the incident. The case went to trial where the jury favored the plaintiff, leading to a verdict against the railroad company for damages.	Abram Middlesworth claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent for not fencing their track, which led to the death of his mules. He presented three counts in his declaration—one for the failure to fence the track and two related to the negligent management of the train and cars that resulted in killing his livestock. He sought damages amounting to $2,810 based on the loss of his mules.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company argued that even if they were negligent in operating the train, the burden of the accident also fell on Middlesworth due to his lack of reasonable care in managing the mules. They emphasized that he should have taken more precautions, knowing the mules' behavior when frightened. The railroad contended that without clear evidence of gross negligence on their part, Middlesworth could not recover for the damages claimed. The company requested the court to provide specific jury instructions reflecting this comparative negligence principle.

In January 1869, in McLean County, Illinois, George W. Knotts and Matthew A. Steers, former business partners, filed a lawsuit against Charles H. Preble in the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiffs claimed that Preble owed them money due to losses incurred from a fire that destroyed their store, which they asserted began because of a defective flue in Preble's building. Knotts persuaded Preble that he had a valid claim against him, arguing that he could prove Preble's negligence contributed to the fire. Under this impression, Preble issued a promissory note to Knotts. However, during the trial, it was revealed that Knotts provided false representations regarding the fire's origins and failed to substantiate his claims. The jury ultimately found no evidence linking Preble to the cause of the fire, leading to a verdict in favor of Preble.	The plaintiffs claimed that Preble was liable for their financial losses due to the fire, which they contended was caused by a defective flue in his building. They argued that Preble had an obligation to contribute to their losses and requested enforcement of the promissory note he had issued.	Preble's defense centered on the lack of consideration for the note, asserting that he was misled by Knotts' false claims about his liability for the fire. He maintained that there was no moral or legal obligation for him to pay the plaintiffs, as they failed to prove any connection between his property and the cause of the fire.

The legal case "The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company v. Albert Adler, Admr." took place in 1889, in Joliet, Illinois. The case involved Albert Adler, the administrator of the estate of William Beuck, who died as a result of a collision with a train at a public railroad crossing. Beuck was riding in a top buggy along Fourth Avenue when he approached the crossing at Eastern Avenue and was struck by a southbound train. The crossing was obstructed by various buildings and railroad cars, which limited visibility of the approaching train. Witnesses gave conflicting accounts regarding the presence of a flagman who was supposed to warn travelers of oncoming trains. The trial court found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding $2,400 in damages, leading to an appeal by the railroad company, which claimed negligence on the part of Beuck in failing to exercise ordinary care.	The plaintiff claimed that the railroad company was negligent, asserting that their failure to provide sufficient warning or a flagman at the crossing contributed to the accident. The plaintiff's argument focused on the allegation that the train did not sound its horn or ring its bell as it approached the crossing, and that the lack of visibility at the crossing due to obstructions increased the risk of the accident.	The defendant, the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company, contended that the deceased was grossly negligent while attempting to cross the tracks, claiming he failed to properly look for an approaching train despite the expectation of doing so. The railroad argued that the burden of proof was on the plaintiff to show that Beuck was exercising ordinary care for his personal safety when he approached the crossing.

In 1857, a bond was executed in Carlinville, Macoupin County, Illinois, involving key individuals John Hall, Nicholas Boice, and George W. Hamilton as the signers, with Samuel S. Gilbert, the County Judge, and two justices, George A. W. Cloud and George Judd, as the obligees. The bond was for $1,000, contingent upon Hall, having been elected as a constable, fully discharging his duties and accounting for all funds received in that capacity. A dispute arose when it was discovered that Hall failed to return executions associated with judgments he was responsible for. The case began before a justice of the peace and was subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court, where the plaintiffs sought to use the bond as evidence against Hall for failing to perform his official responsibilities. The Circuit Court admitted the bond in evidence and ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, prompting the defendants to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court regarding the legality and admissibility of the bond as a statutory obligation.	The plaintiffs, Nicholas Boice and George W. Hamilton, argued that the bond executed by John Hall was a valid legal instrument binding him to perform his duties as constable, and they sought to enforce it for damages resulting from Hall's failure to return executions. They claimed that Hall's negligence in accounting for the funds constituted a breach, making the defendants liable for the full penalty as outlined in the bond.	The defendants, including Samuel S. Gilbert and others, contended that the bond was not properly executed as a statutory bond because it was payable to individuals rather than the County Court, thus lacking validity. They argued that the justice court did not have jurisdiction over such a bond as it exceeded the penalty limitations stipulated for justices, and raised multiple objections regarding the admission of evidence and the legality of the judgments rendered.

In September 1877, the case of A. B. Smith et al. v. The People ex rel. Louis C. Huck arose in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute involved a special assessment for the South Park, which was determined to be necessary by law. The lands in question were reported as delinquent by the South Park Commissioners, leading to further action by the county collector. The plaintiffs, A. B. Smith and others, contended that the return to the county collector regarding the delinquent status of the lands should legally have been made by a designated collector appointed by the South Park Commissioners, rather than the commissioners themselves. This case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court after an appeal from the county court's judgment against Smith and his associates regarding their lands.	The plaintiffs argued that the return of the delinquent lands must be made by a collector appointed by the South Park Commissioners as per the law. They maintained that the return made by the commissioners themselves was not valid and that this invalidity should affect the judgment issued by the county court against their lands.	The defendant, represented by the People ex rel. Louis C. Huck, countered that the South Park Commissioners are authorized by the Park act to make the delinquent returns themselves. They argued that the statutes clearly state that the corporate authorities are responsible for returning the list of delinquent properties to the county treasurer, thus affirming the actions taken by the commissioners were legally sound.

On June 20, 1884, James A. Hearn was walking on a sidewalk in South Canal Street, Chicago, when the cover of a coal-hole gave way, causing him to fall into the cellar below and resulting in personal injuries. The defective cover, measuring approximately two and a half feet by four feet, was only loosely resting on the curb wall and a supporting joist, lacking secure fastenings to prevent it from moving. Evidence suggested that this condition may have persisted for several months prior to the incident. Hearn filed a lawsuit against the City of Chicago, claiming the city's negligence was due to the unsafe sidewalk, which violated local ordinances regarding the proper construction and maintenance of coal-hole covers. The case was tried in the Superior Court of Cook County, where the city was represented by attorneys H. Washburn and Clarence A. Knight. The court excluded certain ordinances from evidence that may have been pertinent to demonstrating the city's responsibility for the sidewalk's safety. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of the defendant (City of Chicago) during the trial.	James A. Hearn claimed damages for personal injuries sustained from the alleged negligence of the City of Chicago related to a defective sidewalk cover. He argued that the city violated its own ordinances requiring all coal-hole covers to be safely constructed and maintained, which contributed to the unsafe conditions of the sidewalk. Hearn sought to include these ordinances as evidence to highlight the city's responsibility for the safety of its sidewalks and to demonstrate negligence in their enforcement.	The City of Chicago defended itself by asserting that it could not be held liable for latent or unseen defects in the sidewalk that were not preventable through reasonable care. The city claimed that the cover was in a reasonably safe condition at the time of Hearn's injury, based on the standards of diligence expected from city officers responsible for such maintenance. Additionally, the defendant questioned the admissibility of the ordinances as evidence, arguing that the plaintiff did not provide sufficient proof regarding their relevance or current status.

In the case of Samuel Isaacs v. Luke Lee Steel, originating in Illinois, the litigation commenced in September 1836 in the Montgomery Circuit Court. The plaintiff, Samuel Isaacs, filed an action of ejectment against the defendant, Luke Lee Steel, seeking possession of a specific parcel of land described as the east half of the northwest quarter of section twenty-three in township eight north, range four west of the third principal meridian. Steel, having settled on the land in 1824, argued that he made substantial improvements to it over the years, thereby qualifying for preemption rights under U.S. law. Isaacs, aware of Steel's claim, fraudulently induced land office officers to allow him to enter the land, claiming no one resided there. Following the filing of Steel's injunction, the courts granted him relief and initially ruled against Isaacs. Ultimately, the case involved intricate interpretations of rights to preemption and possession under applicable acts of Congress, leading to multiple judicial considerations over time.	Samuel Isaacs contended that he had a right to eject Steel from the property based on an entry he made at the land office after claiming he was unaware of Steel’s occupancy and cultivation of the land. Isaacs argued that he had validly obtained the duplicate receipt for the land, which he considered a lawful claim of ownership and requested the court to affirm his rights and trespass against Steel’s existing claim.	Luke Lee Steel asserted that his longstanding occupation and continuous cultivation of the land entitled him to preemption rights, per the preemption acts of 1830 and 1834. He maintained that Isaacs had acted fraudulently by misrepresenting the occupancy status of the land to the land office. Steel sought an injunction to prevent Isaacs from proceeding with the ejectment action and expressed that the prior rights should prevail based on lawful occupancy and improvements made to the property.

John Brennan was jointly indicted and tried alongside two others in the Christian County Circuit Court, Illinois, for burglary on September 9, 1881. The indictment included two counts, and the defendants were convicted based on the second count, which accused them of willfully entering an open freight railroad car with intent to commit larceny. The case was appealed on the grounds that the second count of the indictment was insufficient because it failed to explicitly state that the doors and windows of the car were open. Brennan's legal team asserted this objection after the trial, but the court presumed the evidence during the trial showed that the doors and windows were indeed open, as a conviction would not have been possible otherwise. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the procedural aspects of the indictment and ultimately found that the indictment was sufficient for the charge of burglary.	John Brennan, as the plaintiff in error, argued that the second count of the indictment was flawed due to its failure to specify that the doors and windows of the freight car were open at the time of the unlawful entry. He requested the court to reverse the conviction based on this technicality, arguing that the count was fundamentally inadequate and that he could not be properly tried for the alleged offense.	The defense, representing the People of the State of Illinois, contended that the objection regarding the indictment's wording should have been raised before the trial or through a motion after the conviction. They argued that since there was no such objection during those stages, it could not be valid now on appeal. Furthermore, they maintained that the evidence presented at trial must have supported the conclusion that the car's doors and windows were open at the time of entry, thus validating the conviction.

John Davis filed a lawsuit against The Michigan Southern and Northern Indiana Railroad Company in 1859, claiming the loss of his luggage during travel. The incident occurred after Davis checked two bags, a trunk and a carpet bag, which he asserted were lost while in transit to Chicago. Upon reaching Toledo, checks were exchanged, but Davis later discovered that his baggage was missing upon arrival at his destination. He testified in court about the contents of the lost items, claiming their total value to be $915.25. The defendant, the railroad company, contested his claims, with evidence presented by their general passenger agent, George M. Gray, indicating that Davis initially reported only diplomas and family relics in the trunk, later adding claims of gold and other valuables. The trial was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court after an unfavorable ruling in a lower court, which had initially granted Davis a $100 judgment.	Davis claimed that the railroad was liable for the loss of his baggage, presenting checks as evidence of the responsible custody during transport. He sought damages to cover the value of lost items, including diplomas and personal belongings amounting to $915.25, asserting that the delivery of the baggage check indicated that the company should have assumed care for his luggage.	The railroad company argued that Davis failed to provide accurate information regarding the contents of his luggage. They indicated that he initially mentioned only diplomas and family relics during conversations about the lost baggage and later exaggerated the value by claiming it contained significant amounts of cash and valuables. The defendant also pointed out that company policy limited liability for baggage over a certain value unless disclosed, and contended that the money was not appropriate baggage content. They sought to have the claims dismissed on these grounds.

The case of *Nicholas Hunsaker, Sheriff of Alexander County, and the County Court of Alexander County v. John H. Wright and Charles Davis, Trustees* took place in January 1863 in the city of Cairo, Illinois. In 1860, the defendants filed a bill in the Alexander Circuit Court seeking an injunction to prevent the plaintiffs from collecting county taxes on property located within Cairo's corporate limits. The bill claimed that the city of Cairo, as per its charter established in 1857 and amended in 1859, is exempt from county taxes on property, provided that the city supports its paupers and pays expenses related to its Circuit Court criminal cases. The county had imposed taxes at the same rate on Cairo properties as those outside the city, despite this exemption clause. The initial court ruling was in favor of the defendants, leading to a legal challenge from the plaintiffs who argued that the exemptions violated the state constitution regarding uniform taxation.	The plaintiffs contended that the provisions of the charter exempting Cairo properties from county taxes were unconstitutional, asserting that the General Assembly lacks the power to create such tax exemptions. They maintained that taxes must be levied uniformly and argued that the previous court's ruling that granted a perpetual injunction against tax collection was erroneous.	The defendants claimed their right to the tax exemption based on the language of the city charter passed by the legislature in 1859. They argued that the county's imposition of taxes on city properties contravened the charter provisions and that compliance with obligations to support local paupers and criminal court expenses justified their exemption from county tax responsibilities. They asserted that the initial court’s ruling was correct and that the law of the land supported their position.

In 1887, in Vandalia, Illinois, John S. Barton was involved in a legal dispute against The Farmers and Merchants' National Bank concerning a promissory note for $300, which was due six months after its issuance on December 10, 1886. Barton and co-makers promised to pay the bank with interest at eight percent after maturity. The note included a provision that required payment of a $30 attorney's fee if the note was placed in the hands of an attorney for collection due to non-payment. When the note was not paid at maturity, the bank sought to collect the amount and included the attorney's fee in their claim. Initially, the trial court ruled in favor of the bank for the principal and interest but excluded the attorney's fee. The case then progressed to the Appellate Court, which reversed the trial court's decision, leading to an appeal by the bank to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, John S. Barton, argued that the $30 attorney's fee stipulated in the promissory note was usurious and therefore unenforceable. He contended that the fee was without consideration, contrary to public policy, and in violation of the relevant Illinois statutes regarding interest on loans. Barton asserted that since the fee would effectively increase the cost of borrowing beyond the legal limit on interest, its enforcement should be barred.	The defendant, The Farmers and Merchants' National Bank, maintained that the attorney's fee was a legitimate provision intended as indemnification for the actual loss incurred due to Barton’s default. They argued that the fee did not constitute additional interest but was intended to cover reasonable expenses arising from the collection process. The bank contended that the inclusion of the attorney's fee within the note was valid and should be enforced, as it did not violate usury laws under the given circumstances.

In September 1866, the Board of Supervisors of Kankakee County, Illinois, appropriated $500 from the county treasury to the Circuit Court judge for official services. Felix Beauchamp, a taxpayer, filed a bill in the Circuit Court to obtain an injunction to prevent payment of this appropriation and the associated tax collection. An initial injunction was granted. However, the defendants moved to dissolve it, raising objections about the form of the order and the bond's sufficiency. The court agreed to dissolve the injunction but allowed Beauchamp to motion for a new one, which he did immediately. Despite this, the court denied the request after the defendants provided evidence that the clerk's order had been returned. The court ultimately dismissed Beauchamp's bill and awarded the defendants $150 in damages for attorney's fees.	Felix Beauchamp claimed that the appropriation made by the Board of Supervisors was illegal and sought an injunction to prevent both the payment of the clerk's order and the collection of taxes for that purpose. He argued that the facts presented in his bill warranted the issuance of an injunction.	The defendants argued that the injunction should be dissolved due to technical inaccuracies in the form of the order and the insufficiency of the injunction bond. They contended that the board of supervisors had acted within its authority and that Judge Starr's actions concerning the returned clerk's order negated the need for a new injunction.

In 1843, John C. Stickney and associates brought a legal action against Jacob Cassell in Gallatin, Illinois, regarding a written contract related to carpentry work on a building. The contract specified that Cassell's workers would be employed at a daily rate to perform all necessary carpentry tasks, with specific prices outlined for various jobs, including the creation of window and door panels. Stickney claimed that he sustained damages because Cassell did not allow him to complete additional work needed on the building beyond what was specified in their agreement. Despite the plaintiff's claims, the record indicated irregularities in the proceedings, complicating the determination of the issues addressed. A jury originally ruled in favor of Stickney, awarding him $600 in damages. However, the defense brought forth several pleas, including non assumpsit and special defenses, leading to confusion over the legal standing of the case and the contract's interpretation.	The plaintiff, Stickney, asserted that he was entitled to complete the building's carpentry work as per the contract, which he believed included provisions for additional work beyond the agreed specifications. He claimed that the defendants' refusal to allow him to complete this work resulted in lost profits and damages amounting to an unspecified sum.	The defendant, Cassell, argued that the contract did not explicitly obligate him to let Stickney finish the building, nor was there any evidence that he prevented Stickney from completing the work. Cassell contended that the nature of the contract gave him discretion regarding the scope of work and was not a binding agreement to allow Stickney additional tasks beyond what was specified. The defendant also challenged the sufficiency of the evidence presented in court to support the plaintiff's claims.

John S. Rand v. Charles D. Wilber et al. is a case that originated in 1886 in Aurora, Illinois. The key individuals involved are the plaintiff, Nancy Wilber, and the defendant, John S. Rand. Wilber owned a lot with a dwelling house that had been their home for several years. Rand owned the adjacent lot, and conflicts arose when he began constructing a vault for a privy within proximity to Wilber's property. The privy was planned to be located within five feet of Wilber's lot line, posing a potential nuisance to her family and compromising their health due to the close proximity to their well, which supplied water for domestic use. Wilber filed a bill in equity to enjoin Rand from continuing the construction, arguing that it would cause irreparable harm, diminish the value of her property, and constitute a nuisance. A temporary injunction was granted while the case proceeded. Despite Rand’s claims that he was not constructing a privy, it was revealed that he had completed the vault intended for that use. The case ultimately focused on whether a court of equity had jurisdiction in such matters and whether the allegations of nuisance were substantiated.	The plaintiff, Nancy Wilber, asserted that John S. Rand was building a privy too close to her property line, which would violate city ordinances and create a nuisance. She argued that the construction would endanger her family’s health, interfere with their enjoyment of property, and potentially cause irreparable damage, particularly affecting their well, which was located nearby. The complaint sought an injunction to prevent Rand from using or constructing the privy as planned.	John S. Rand, the defendant, denied building a new privy and argued that any structures on his property had been converted into part of his dwelling and would actually serve as an ash pit. He contended that he had the right to build on his lot as he saw fit and claimed that the plaintiffs had a sufficient legal remedy and that equity should not intervene without a prior legal determination of nuisance.

The case of George F. White et al. v. John E. Liston was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on April 28, 1886. The relevant events unfolded in Illinois, involving the appellants, George F. White and others, and the appellee, John E. Liston. The case was brought forth as a legal dispute, the details of which are not entirely specified in the provided description. However, the evidence presented in the court appeared to support the jury's verdict, indicating that a legal question was not evidently raised in the record, which was significant to the court's ruling. The case was overseen by Judge Joseph E. Gary, and the attorneys representing the appellants were Messrs. Munn & Wheeler, while the appellee was represented by Mr. Wm. J. Manning and Mr. Percy Y. Castle.	The plaintiffs, George F. White and others, likely claimed that they had suffered damages or injuries due to the actions of John E. Liston. They requested that the court affirm the jury's verdict, which presumably favored their position and sought redress for any grievances they had endured.	The defendant, John E. Liston, likely contended that the evidence did not establish liability on his part and maintained that the verdict was not justified. He may have requested that the court dismiss the claims brought by the plaintiffs, upholding his position against any allegations presented.

William Green petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Deputy Sheriff Bradley in the Illinois Circuit Court in 1870. The case arose after Gustav Fischer, the sheriff, absconded from the state without intent to return, which left the office vacant and created uncertainties about the authority of those acting under him, including Deputy Sheriff Bradley. Green claimed that Bradley was not empowered to detain him because the sheriff’s office was effectively vacant due to Fischer's absence. The court needed to determine whether the deputy was acting lawfully or if the coroner should assume the responsibilities of the sheriff during this vacancy, as defined by the statutes. The case highlighted significant legal principles concerning de facto officers, the authority of deputies, and the conditions that constitute a vacancy in public office.	Green argued that since Sheriff Fischer had absconded, his office should be deemed vacant, which meant Bradley, as deputy, no longer had the legal right to detain him. He maintained that the coroner should be the one authorized to detain prisoners under these circumstances and requested his immediate release from custody.	In response, Deputy Sheriff Bradley contended that he acted as a de facto officer and thus his authority should remain valid despite Fischer’s absence. He argued that the legal framework surrounding de facto officers protects their actions unless a court formally declares their authority invalid. Furthermore, Bradley insisted that he could fulfill the duties of sheriff due to the lack of an official replacement.

In September 1872, Leonard Rothgerber brought a legal action against Aaron N. Dupuy in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a construction project in Chicago. The dispute began when Dupuy was contracted by Ann Hyman to build a house on her property. Dupuy employed John Milne as a sub-contractor, who in turn hired Rothgerber to perform the necessary labor for the project. Rothgerber sought recovery for unpaid wages amounting to $67.35 through the Mechanic's Lien Law, which allows those who perform labor in construction to claim a lien for unpaid labor. Initially, Rothgerber won a small judgment in the justice's court, but Dupuy appealed the decision. In the circuit court, the jury upheld the original judgment, and Dupuy continued to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Rothgerber, the plaintiff, claimed the right to recover unpaid wages based on the Mechanic’s Lien Law of 1869, asserting that he was entitled to payment since he performed labor on the construction of the house. Rothgerber contended that even though he was a sub-contractor of Milne, the statute should allow him to claim payment from Dupuy, whom he believed should be held partly responsible.	Dupuy, the defendant, argued that he could not be held liable as a subcontractor of a subcontractor was not explicitly included in the Mechanic’s Lien Law provisions. He maintained that the law only extends protection to direct subcontractors and did not cover further extensions of subcontracting. In addition, Dupuy contended that any representations regarding ownership made after Rothgerber's engagement with Milne could not be used to impose liability on him.

In the case of Genafeva Mueller v. Emma Newell, the events transpired in 1888 in Cass County, Illinois. The legal matter involved a forcible detainer action initiated by Genafeva Mueller, who was represented by her husband. The dispute centered on the right to possession of certain premises, which were claimed to be leased to an individual named Thompson at the time the lawsuit was filed. The plaintiff's husband, acting as her agent, testified regarding the existence of a lease, although the defending party contended that this documentation only constituted an agreement to lease, not a formal lease. Notably, the court observed that the evidence presented did not substantiate the plaintiff's claim to maintain possession against her husband, as her entitlement to the premises was questioned based on the lease status. During the proceedings, important details regarding jury instructions were omitted, leading the court to disregard any arguments related to those instructions.	Genafeva Mueller, the plaintiff, argued that she was entitled to the possession of the leased premises against Emma Newell. She asserted that the evidence, particularly the lease documentation, supported her claim to reclaim possession. Mueller's legal team aimed to demonstrate that the lease with Thompson was valid and enforceable, entitling her to seek the forcible detainer action.	Emma Newell, the defendant, argued that the plaintiff could not maintain the action for forcible detainer as she was not entitled to possession. The primary contention was that the lease presented by the plaintiff's husband was merely an agreement and lacked the formal status of a lease, undermining the plaintiff’s claim. The defendant's legal team sought to affirm the judgment in their favor, emphasizing the shortcomings in the plaintiff's argument and the absence of sufficient evidence to support her claims.

The case "William H. Broadwell et al. v. The People for the use of Morgan County" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875. At the heart of the matter was William H. Broadwell, the sheriff of Morgan County, who had been elected in November 1872. He executed a bond as the county collector for the year 1872. Morgan County was not organized under a township structure at that time. The county court had set Broadwell's compensation at $2000 annually, prompting a dispute over whether he was entitled to retain commissions as collector beyond this fixed salary or if he was obligated to remit such excess to the county treasury. The legal interpretation focused on the phrase "county board," and the authority granted to the county court in determining officer compensation under the state's constitution. The implications of this case hinged on the correct identification of the "county board" as defined by the constitution, particularly how such definitions applied to counties not under township organization.	The plaintiffs, representing Morgan County, claimed that Broadwell was bound by the constitutional requirement to pay all commissions from his role as collector into the county treasury if such amounts exceeded his fixed compensation of $2000 per year as sheriff. They argued that the county court had the authority to determine officer compensation and that Broadwell's dual roles did not create a jurisdiction where he could collect additional compensation without remitting the excess.	Broadwell, through his attorneys, contended that he was entitled to keep the commissions accrued as a collector, arguing that his roles as sheriff and collector were functionally distinct and that he should not be penalized by the fixed compensation as sheriff restricting his collector's earnings. He claimed the compensation scheme established by the county court was improperly applied and sought to maintain his right to the commissions.

In June 1868, in Crawford County, Illinois, William Adams was indicted for the murder of Thomas Bostic. During the trial, the jury convicted Adams of manslaughter, sentencing him to ten years in the penitentiary. Adams filed a motion for a new trial, supported by his own affidavit and those of two witnesses, claiming jury misconduct and newly discovered evidence. The court denied this motion, leading Adams to appeal the verdict. Key individuals involved included Chief Justice Breese, who delivered the court's opinion, and attorneys J.C. Allen and E. Callahan representing Adams, while Robert G. Ingersoll served as the Attorney General for the People. The court remained focused on whether the original trial appropriately handled evidence and jury instructions concerning self-defense and the nature of Adams' actions leading to Bostic’s death.	The plaintiff, representing the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Adams attacked Bostic with malicious intent, highlighting the fact that he could not claim self-defense if he provoked the altercation. They contended that the jury was justified in finding Adams guilty of manslaughter based on evidence suggesting he sought out the conflict, and therefore he should be held accountable for his actions.	Adams' defense claimed that he acted in self-defense, asserting that the court erred in modifying jury instructions regarding self-defense and introducing certain qualifications. They argued that the newly discovered evidence could potentially alter the outcome of the trial and called for a new trial on those grounds. The defense maintained that the jury was influenced by misconduct, which prejudiced Adams’ right to a fair trial.

In 1882, in Galesburg, Illinois, Henry A. Biederman and Michael O'Conner entered into a contractual agreement in which O'Conner promised to deliver 10,000 bushels of corn to Biederman for twenty cents per bushel. The terms stipulated that Biederman was to pay $1,000 in cash upon the signing of the contract for the agreement to take effect. However, Biederman could not produce the cash and instead offered a check, which O'Conner rejected. The parties eventually agreed that the contract would only be binding if Biederman paid the $1,000 by eight o'clock the following morning. When Biederman returned without the cash, claiming to have an amount in gold but failing to complete the payment, O'Conner refused to honor the contract. The Knox circuit court ruled in favor of O'Conner, leading Biederman to appeal to the Appellate Court, where the judgment was upheld, resulting in further appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Biederman contended that O'Conner failed to deliver the corn as per the contractual agreement and sought damages for this failure. He claimed that the special pleas filed by the defendant were immaterial and contended that he was entitled to enforce the contract despite O'Conner’s objections.	O'Conner argued that no binding contract was formed due to the lack of payment from Biederman, asserting that the agreement was contingent upon the upfront cash payment. He maintained that the contract was never delivered because Biederman took possession of the contract without fulfilling the payment conditions, and thus could not legally enforce it. He further contended that the conversation preceding the contract signing indicated no intent to create a binding agreement without immediate payment.

Nelson Maloney v. The People of the State of Illinois is a legal case that took place in April 1865 in Illinois. The case arose from a prosecution against Nelson Maloney for bastardy, which is a legal proceeding to compel him to provide support for an illegitimate child allegedly fathered by him with Maria Owen. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court following a trial in the Circuit Court of Woodford County, where the presiding judge was Hon. S. L. Richmond. Following the trial, Maloney was found guilty of the charges against him and subsequently appealed the decision. His core argument on appeal was centered on the claim that the court erred in not instructing the jury that a finding of guilt required a standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt, which he argued was necessary in any criminal proceeding.	The plaintiff, representing the State of Illinois, argued that Nelson Maloney should be held accountable for the support of his illegitimate child, stating that the burden of proof required to establish guilt in a bastardy case should be a preponderance of evidence rather than the higher standard of beyond a reasonable doubt typically required in criminal cases. The plaintiff's main legal request was to maintain the conviction and ensure Maloney's obligation to support the child.	Nelson Maloney, the defendant, argued that the prosecution for bastardy constituted a criminal proceeding that required a conviction based on proof beyond a reasonable doubt. He claimed that the refusal of the Circuit Court to provide the jury with this instruction constituted a significant error that warranted a reversal of his conviction. His request was for the court to overturn the lower court's decision based on this alleged error.

The case "The Chicago Dredging and Dock Company v. John McCarty" arose in Cook County, Illinois, with the initial judgment delivered by a justice of the peace prior to an appeal. The plaintiff, The Chicago Dredging and Dock Company, filed a lawsuit against the defendant, John McCarty, resulting in a judgment in favor of the plaintiff. Following this, McCarty appealed to the Circuit Court of Cook County by filing an appeal bond on August 9, 1878. However, on May 19, 1882, the circuit court dismissed the case for lack of prosecution at the request of McCarty, which resulted in an order for costs against the Dredging Company. The dismissal occurred despite the non-appearance of the plaintiff or any representative in court. Notably, the appellate court found that the court action was improper due to a lack of jurisdiction, as no service of summons was completed to McCarty nor had he made an appearance in writing.	The Chicago Dredging and Dock Company contended that the dismissal of their case in the circuit court was erroneous due to a lack of jurisdiction over them since there had been no service of process. They argued that the circuit court had no authority to dismiss the case or award costs against the plaintiff, citing relevant legal precedents that supported their position.	John McCarty's defense was predicated on the appeal for dismissal due to the plaintiff's lack of action. He sought to have the case dismissed on the grounds that the plaintiff had not appeared in court nor prosecuted the appeal, even after filing the appeal bond.

In the case of Samuel Johnson v. Robert A. Donnell, which took place in December 1853, the Illinois Supreme Court was asked to examine a bill for the foreclosure of a mortgage. The plaintiff, Samuel Johnson, sought foreclosure based on non-payment of a mortgage, alongside claims that the mortgaged premises lacked sufficient value to cover the outstanding debt and associated costs. This situation arose amid a period when Johnson, as the mortgagor, was insolvent, and the property in question would not yield enough to repay the mortgage amount upon sale. The court had to consider whether it had the right to decree a strict foreclosure under Illinois law, especially since a new statute had attempted to standardize foreclosure processes but did not explicitly eliminate the power for courts to grant strict foreclosures. After a thorough consideration of the facts and legal precedents, the court concluded that granting a strict foreclosure aligned with the interests of both the mortgagor and the mortgagee. The decision followed a hearing where the bill was allowed to be taken as confessed due to the defendant's non-appearance.	The main argument advanced by Samuel Johnson centered on the execution of a mortgage and the subsequent non-payment of the debt owed. Johnson claimed that a strict foreclosure was necessary, emphasizing that the mortgaged property would not sell for enough to cover the mortgage amount and costs. Consequently, he argued that since he had no means to pay any remaining balance post-sale, a strict foreclosure would relieve both parties of unnecessary further financial burdens.	The defendants, led by Robert A. Donnell, contended primarily that the court lacked jurisdiction to decree a strict foreclosure due to regulatory changes. They argued under the Illinois statute that required properties to be sold in foreclosure cases, claiming that this legislative change implied the removal of the court’s power to grant strict foreclosures. Thus, they sought the court to overturn the decree for strict foreclosure, insisting that a sale was mandated given current legal standards.

The case "George D. Williamson v. John Hogan" originated in January 1868 in the city of Cairo, Illinois. George D. Williamson filed a replevin action against John Hogan, who was the city marshal at the time. The dispute involved the steamboat Cumberland. On September 20, 1866, an attachment warrant was issued in a separate case by the Clerk of the Court of Common Pleas in Cairo, directed towards the Cumberland for a debt owed by the River Transportation Company to Samuel Wilson for supplies. Hogan, acting under this warrant, seized the Cumberland while it was docked in Cairo. After seizing the boat, Hogan released it back to its owners upon the execution of a bond. Later, a judgment was obtained against the Cumberland for a different debt, and subsequent execution processes led to the boat being sold at public auction. Williamson purchased the Cumberland at this auction and claimed peaceful possession until Hogan's later seizure. This case examined legal questions regarding the applicability of jurisdiction and the validity of claims under the attachment law and maritime statutes.	George D. Williamson argued that he legally acquired ownership of the steamboat Cumberland through a public auction conducted by the sheriff based on valid executions against the boat. He asserted that he maintained peaceable possession of the boat, and Hogan's seizure constituted unlawful interference. Williamson sought a judgment to reclaim the Cumberland, challenging the validity of the attachment and Hogan's actions as the city marshal.	John Hogan, as the defendant, contended that his seizure of the Cumberland was lawful as it stemmed from a valid attachment warrant for a debt owed by the River Transportation Company. He argued that he acted in accordance with the law and that any claims Williamson had were ineffective due to the prior lien resulting from the attachment process. Moreover, Hogan requested that the court dismiss Williamson's claims on the grounds of this alleged prior claim to the vessel and the propriety of his actions as city marshal.

Jeriel Wilday filed a case against George M. McConnel, executor of the estate of Murray McConnel, following a series of judgments by default entered against him in the Illinois Circuit Court in April 1869. Wilday claimed he had not been properly served with the court process concerning several notes owed to the deceased, for which he had already made substantial payments. At that time, the court ruled against him, prompting an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered around whether Wilday had sufficient notice of the judgment and whether he had indeed made payments that were not credited, totaling at least $1400. The court noted that there was conflicting evidence regarding the service of process, and crucially, Wilday argued he discovered receipts for some payments only after the judgment was entered. The Illinois Supreme Court, recognizing potential errors and the possibility of an unjust judgment, ultimately decided to reverse the lower court's decision and remand the case for a new trial, stating that it would be inequitable for Wilday to face double payment without having had a chance to present his defense.	Jeriel Wilday contended that he was not properly served with the legal process regarding the notes due to the late Murray McConnel, and as such, never had a fair opportunity to defend against the judgment. He asserted that he had made payments on the notes amounting to at least $1400, yet these were uncredited due to the mislaid receipts. Wilday sought a perpetual injunction to prevent the collection of the judgment until a fair hearing could be held, arguing that failure to address these funds may lead to him being compelled to pay the same debt twice, contrary to principles of equity.	George M. McConnel, as executor, defended against the claims by maintaining that the judgment was valid and was predicated on the fact that Wilday had accepted service of the summons. The defendant’s position was that, despite Wilday's claims of not being served properly, the evidence indicated that proper legal procedures were followed. Furthermore, McConnel did not have awareness of any payments made by Wilday, which were supposedly discovered only after the judgment was rendered. The defense contested the validity of Wilday's arguments concerning missing receipts and maintained that the judgments sought were justly obtained.

Hiram Gould et al. v. Mary E. Steinburg, decided in September 1876, involves a series of events that began in Will County, Illinois, before 1859. Hiram Gould executed seven notes with a partner, Bicherson, for liabilities associated with Bicherson. In November 1859, Gould conveyed two separate parcels of land to his brother-in-law, Jackson, which were recorded on December 1, 1859. Later, judgments were entered against both Bicherson and Gould for those notes, leading to the levying and sale of parts of Gould's property under execution. In May 1870, a bill was filed, asserting the conveyances to Jackson were fraudulent, aimed at hindering creditors. An amendment to the bill claimed that a subsequent deed from Jackson and his wife back to Gould was fraudulently altered to change the grantee's name from "Hiram" to "James" and not recorded until after the bill was filed. The plaintiffs sought to set aside these conveyances and remove the cloud on their title. The circuit court found the deeds fraudulent and declared the title belonged to Steinburg, leading to the appeal by Hiram and James Gould. The evidence was contradictory, but the circuit court’s reliance on witness testimony supported the finding of fraud in the conveyances, established to delay creditors’ claims.	The plaintiffs, Hiram Gould and James Gould, claimed that the conveyances made to Jackson in 1859 were fraudulent, intended to delay and hinder creditors. They argued that the deed from Jackson back to Hiram Gould was altered fraudulently, changing the grantee's name from "Hiram" to "James." They sought to have these fraudulent transactions set aside to clear the title of the property, as the deeds created a cloud on their ownership.	The defendant, Mary E. Steinburg, denied all allegations of fraud regarding the conveyances. She contended that the deed from Jackson and his wife was originally made to "James Gould," and never included "Hiram Gould" as a grantee. Steinburg's defense focused on maintaining that these transactions were legitimate and any claims of fraud were baseless, thus requesting the court to uphold the validity of her ownership as established through the sheriff's deeds.
