The case, "Daniel Carr v. John Welch, Executor, etc.," took place in LaSalle County, Illinois, with the final judgment being rendered in September 1867 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The central issue revolved around a promissory note originally issued by Thomas Welch, now claimed by his executor, John Welch. It was alleged by John Welch that Daniel Carr had failed to repay the promissory note, which was written in black ink and due in six months without interest. The controversy arose due to the addition of the phrase "ten per cent, after due," written in red ink at the lower right corner of the note. The defendant, Daniel Carr, contended that this addition constituted a material alteration, making the note void. However, John Welch argued that the addition was merely a memorandum without any intent of fraudulent alteration. The court needed to assess whether this addition materially altered the obligations under the note.	The plaintiff, John Welch, as the executor of Thomas Welch's estate, claimed that Daniel Carr was liable for the debt represented by the promissory note. Welch contended that the note, despite the addition in red ink, was valid and should be enforced as it did not constitute a material alteration that would render the note void. He sought a judgment affirming the enforceability of the note and requiring Carr to fulfill his payment obligation.	Daniel Carr, the defendant, argued that the addition of "ten per cent, after due" in red ink constituted a material alteration of the promissory note, thereby nullifying its validity. He maintained that this change was significant enough to charge him with interest post-maturity, which was not originally stipulated in the note. Carr sought a dismissal of the claim, asserting that the altered note should not be enforced against him.

The case of Sophia A. Bostwick et al. v. Mark Skinner et al. took place in Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a court decision in September 1875. The plaintiffs, including Sophia A. Bostwick, were heirs and descendants of John Bostwick, who had executed a mortgage in 1855 to Mark Skinner for a significant sum of $19,000, securing a parcel of land near Chicago. Following Bostwick's death in September 1855, intestate, the plaintiffs contested the validity of a sale of the property by the county court which had been administered by Benjamin F. Downing. They argued that the county court lacked jurisdiction due to Bostwick's alleged residence in Madison County rather than Cook County, where the estate was being administered. The appellants sought to redeem the property from the mortgage held by Skinner and requested other equitable relief. However, the court ruled against the appellants, asserting that Bostwick's legal title to the property was held in trust for another party, John M. Krum, who financed the original purchase. The court's findings concluded with a decree favoring the defendants and denying the appellants' claims.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had the right to redeem the mortgaged property following John Bostwick's death and contested the legitimacy of the Cook county court's jurisdiction over Bostwick’s estate. They argued that since the administrator granted possession of the property was appointed incorrectly due to jurisdiction issues, the sale was void and sought other equitable relief related to the property.	The defendants, including Mark Skinner, maintained that John Bostwick was only a trustee and had no equitable interest in the property he mortgaged, as he acted under an agreement with John M. Krum, who financed the purchase. They argued the sale conducted by the county court was valid, and that jurisdiction had been properly exercised under the belief that Bostwick resided within Cook County at the time of his death. They requested that the plaintiffs' claims be dismissed and affirmed the legitimacy of their own title to the property.

In the case of "Henrietta Farnan v. William B. Borders," filed on January 25, 1887, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the background dates back to April 5, 1884, when Henrietta Farnan (the widow of Dr. James Farnan) filed a bill seeking partition of certain lots in Sparta, Illinois, and assignment of her dower rights. Dr. Farnan had passed away intestate in October 1877, leaving behind his widow and four step-children. After Dr. Farnan's death, Henrietta initially lived on the premises with her step-children but relocated to St. Louis in August 1878. They later rented out the homestead while Henrietta continued to live in St. Louis, Quincy, and Milwaukee. The case's crucial issue was whether the widow had effectively abandoned her homestead rights by moving away and without the intention to return. The court examined evidence from both parties regarding Henrietta's intentions about the homestead.	Henrietta Farnan (the appellant) claimed that she had not abandoned her homestead in Sparta and in fact intended to return at some point. She argued her relocation was necessary for the purposes of educating her step-children. Furthermore, she contended that she maintained some connection to the homestead by reserving a room and furniture there for a time.	William B. Borders (the appellee) asserted that Henrietta had indeed abandoned her homestead by moving to St. Louis and not returning, as evidenced by her actions and statements over the years. The appellee contended that the widow's change of residence and eventual sale of her furniture indicated a clear intent to remain away from Sparta permanently, thus forfeiting her homestead rights. He maintained that he owned a larger share of the property and sought the affirmation of this ownership.

This case involves Lucius T. Benham and other plaintiffs who brought a lawsuit against the Chicago & North Western Railway Company in January 1888, in Cook County, Illinois. The litigation arose from the defendant's failure to transport and deliver certain goods that they had received as a common carrier. The court trial was conducted without a jury, and after the proceedings, the court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them damages amounting to $400 along with court costs. The defendant subsequently sought to challenge this judgment by filing a writ of error, citing several alleged errors including the admission of improper evidence, the ruling in favor of the plaintiffs, and the denial of the defendant's motion for a new trial. However, the appeals court faced a significant procedural hurdle due to a lack of a properly signed bill of exceptions, which is necessary to review the purported errors.	The plaintiffs asserted that the Chicago & North Western Railway Company had failed to fulfill its obligations as a common carrier by not transporting and delivering their goods. They sought compensation for the damages incurred due to this failure, ultimately receiving a judgment of $400 in their favor.	The defense argued that there were errors in the trial process, specifically challenging the admission of certain evidence and the court's refusal to grant a new trial. They contended that the record did not contain a valid bill of exceptions as required to substantiate their claims of error. This procedural flaw meant that the appellate court could not consider the defense's arguments.

In 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, the case "Marie A. Youngs v. Phineas R. Youngs" arose where Marie Youngs sought a divorce from her husband, Phineas Youngs. The case was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court, presided over by Judge Lorin C. Collins. Marie alleged two statutory grounds for divorce: habitual drunkenness and extreme and repeated cruelty. Evidence was introduced claiming that Phineas had a morphine habit that made him behave drunkenly and helplessly. Although this behavior included acts of cruelty, it was argued that these behaviors occurred under the influence of morphine, rather than achieving the legal definition of habitual drunkenness that pertains to alcohol consumption. Additionally, claims of physical violence and excessive sexual demands were made, but the court found that these acts had been condoned by Marie since they occurred prior to her seeking divorce and there was a lack of ongoing abusive treatment after December 1886, when the last act of cruelty occurred.	Marie A. Youngs claimed that her husband, Phineas R. Youngs, exhibited habitual drunkenness due to his morphine addiction and exhibited extreme and repeated cruelty. She argued that Phineas’s behavior, including physical violence and coerced sexual relations, constituted grounds for a divorce. Marie sought a legal separation from Phineas based on these claims and requested the court to grant her the divorce as her marriage was intolerable due to such conduct.	Phineas R. Youngs defended against the claims by arguing that the alleged habitual drunkenness from morphine use did not meet the statutory definition of drunkenness as described in divorce law, which typically applies to alcohol. He contended that any actions interpreted as cruel occurred under compulsion from his morphine addiction. Furthermore, he supported the notion that any claims of violence or coercive sexual conduct had been condoned by Marie, as there was no evidence of persistent abuse leading to her decision to seek divorce.

In 1849, in La Salle County, Illinois, a legal proceeding commenced in the La Salle Circuit Court involving The Board of Trustees of the Illinois and Michigan Canal and John V. A. Hoes, among others. The case arose after the canal's construction obstructed established public highways that had been in use since as early as 1832-1835. Hoes and other local residents petitioned the court to compel the Canal Trustees to build a bridge over the canal to restore public access. The Circuit Court issued an alternative writ of mandamus, which commanded the trustees to construct the bridge or provide a valid reason for not doing so. However, the trustees did not respond, leading the court to award a peremptory writ of mandamus. The trustees challenged the decision, claiming that the original writ was improperly issued and lacked substantial legal basis to enforce the construction of the bridge.	The plaintiffs, represented by John V. A. Hoes and others, argued that the construction of the Illinois and Michigan Canal obstructed several established public roads, which had been laid out and used for years. They sought a court order compelling the trustees to construct a bridge over the canal to restore access to these public highways. They contended that it was the responsibility of the Canal Trustees to maintain the functionality of these highways, which they believed should be preserved even with the canal's construction.	The defendants, The Board of Trustees of the Illinois and Michigan Canal, argued that the alternative writ of mandamus was fundamentally defective and did not properly set forth facts supporting the plaintiffs' claims. They asserted that there was no legal obligation requiring them to construct the bridge, as the responsibility to maintain highways belonged to the counties, and that the writ unjustly demanded action without establishing a clear legal right or necessity for such action.

In 1873, Elbanis C. Myers and Abraham Fry, along with others, signed a note for $500, which was a debt owed by Olden Myers, who was believed to be financially stable at the time. However, Olden soon became financially troubled. In the following year, a renewal note was executed, which appellant Fry later paid in full, totaling $850.95 including interest and costs by July 22, 1880. Subsequently, Fry sought contribution from the other signatories, including Myers, but only Fry was served. During the trial, Fry testified that he initially refused to sign the last note due to Olden's insolvency but was persuaded to sign as a surety for Elhanis Myers, which he claimed was a limitation of his liability. The jury believed Fry's testimony, which led to a ruling in his favor as the court instructed that Fry's assertion could serve as a valid defense, resulting in a judgment for his costs.	Elbanis C. Myers, the appellant, contended that the renewal note signed was presumed to maintain the previous co-surety relationship, implying that Fry remained a co-surety for the renewed obligation alongside him. He argued that Fry's liability should not have changed without his consent, asserting that the law protects sureties from alterations in their obligations being imposed by a co-surety without their agreement.	Abraham Fry, the appellee, contended that he limited his liability to acting solely as a surety for Elhanis Myers and not for Olden Myers during the signing of the renewal note. He testified that his understanding and agreement were conditional upon the financial soundness of Elhanis and not Olden, thereby arguing that this limitation should prevent the maintenance of Myers's action for contribution against him.

In January 1873, the case of Matthew Patton v. Leander Gates was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Sangamon Circuit Court. The dispute arose from a previous judgment obtained by Matthew Patton against Walter Kirkpatrick and Robert N. Allen for $380.21 and costs. Patton sought to collect this debt through garnishment, arguing that Gates owed money to Kirkpatrick, which should be available to satisfy the judgment. During proceedings, Gates disclosed that he had purchased 80 acres of land from Kirkpatrick's wife, paying partly in cash and with a $300 note bearing interest. Patton countered that the financial arrangement was a ploy to protect Kirkpatrick's assets from creditors. Testimony revealed debates over the source of the funds Kirkpatrick used in his business, with claims that the money was originally contributed by his wife, a contention countered by Allen, who argued Kirkpatrick had operated as if the funds were his own. The court ultimately ruled on the legitimacy of the garnishment in the context of these conflicting accounts.	Matthew Patton, the plaintiff, argued that the funds owed from Leander Gates were rightfully garnishable to satisfy the outstanding judgment against Kirkpatrick and Allen. Patton contended that the financial arrangement between Kirkpatrick and Gates, involving transactions with Kirkpatrick's wife, was designed to evade creditor claims, asserting that these funds should be considered available for the repayment of debts incurred by Kirkpatrick and Allen's partnership.	Leander Gates, the defendant, argued that he owed no money to Kirkpatrick, pointing out that the property was rightfully transferred to Kirkpatrick's wife and that any debt should not attach to the note he issued. Gates maintained that the financial arrangements were legitimate, disputing the assertion that they were structured to defraud creditors. Consequently, he requested the dismissal of Patton's garnishment action based on his assertion of no liability.

The case "Alanson E. Davis et al. v. Samuel C. Kenaga" took place in Kankakee County, Illinois, with a decision rendered in September 1869 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a loan agreement where Alanson E. Davis and others (plaintiffs) loaned a quantity of corn to Samuel C. Kenaga (defendant). After a contention over the return of the corn, which was allegedly done in a lesser quality than agreed upon, the plaintiffs sought to recover damages claiming the value of the corn. Initially, the trial court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, resulting in a judgment that they claimed owed payments and interest; however, the defendants appealed the verdict, leading to this higher court case.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to the value of the corn loaned to the defendant, asserting that the defendant returned the corn but in an inferior quality. They claimed damages due to the breach of contract and sought interest on the amount due from the time they demanded the return of the corn.	The defendant contended against the award of interest, asserting that the court erred in allowing the jury to determine interest based solely on the return of inferior quality corn. The defendant argued that the matter of unreasonable and vexatious delay, which is a requirement for interest recovery under Illinois law, should have been submitted to the jury as a question of fact.

Charles Waterman and Reuben Barrett filed an appeal against Frederick T. Peet and Samuel H. Hitchcock concerning a legal matter arising in the Kane Circuit Court, Illinois, in December 1849. The case concerned a promissory note payable at the office of Ed. E. Harvey in Elgin, Kane County, Illinois. The plaintiffs sought to recover the amount of the promissory note, which was affirmed as payable in Kane County, thus establishing jurisdiction there. The defendants, Peet and Hitchcock, resided in the counties of Stephenson and Winnebago. They contested the validity of the promissory note, claiming it was fraudulently obtained for $100 more than owed, with the involvement of Harvey as an agent of the plaintiffs. The defendants attempted to introduce evidence from Harvey's statements made to a witness about the execution of the note, which was ultimately excluded by the court. The case was heard by Judge Theophilus L. Dickey, and a judgment for $357.50 was rendered against the defendants, prompting their appeal.	The plaintiffs, Waterman and Barrett, argued that the promissory note was valid and made specifically payable in Kane County, thus establishing sufficient grounds for the court’s jurisdiction. They contended that procedural objections raised by the defendants concerning the note’s validity and the admittance of certain evidence were without merit.	The defendants, Peet and Hitchcock, contended that the promissory note was fraudulently obtained owing to overstated amounts, aided by Harvey as the plaintiffs' agent. They sought to prove their claim by introducing Harvey's prior admissions regarding the acquisition of the note. However, their attempts to present this evidence were rejected by the court.

In September 1873, the case of August Wischover v. German Mutual Fire Insurance Company of North Chicago was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The proceedings took place in Cook County, Illinois, presided over by Judge William A. Portee. The legal conflict arose after a previous trial involving a similar case pertaining to a premium note issued by the insurance company. The focus of the current case included the qualifications of a juror who had served in the earlier trial and had reportedly formed an opinion concerning a written resolution of the company. This resolution was presented as evidence in both cases. The issue at hand was whether the juror's prior knowledge disqualified him from participating in the current trial. The court sustained the juror’s competence, concluding that the resolution's interpretation was a legal matter for the court, not a personal opinion that would disqualify the juror.	August Wischover, the plaintiff, contended that the juror's previous exposure to the case and the resolution constituted a disqualifying opinion that could bias the jury. This claim was built on the assertion that the juror had formed an opinion regarding the interpretation of the company's resolution during the prior trial.	The German Mutual Fire Insurance Company, as the defendant, argued against the challenge to the juror's competency. The defense maintained that the resolution's construction was a legal question for the court to decide and that the juror did not hold a personal opinion disqualifying him from serving on the jury. They urged the court to affirm the decision that upheld the juror's competence.

The case of *International Bank v. Joseph Jones et al.* took place in Cook County, Illinois, with its final judgment issued on January 6, 1885, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The parties involved included the plaintiff, Joseph Jones & Sons, and the defendant, International Bank. The plaintiffs sought to recover the amount of a check that had been drawn on the bank by John D. Oakford in their favor. The key legal question revolved around whether there were sufficient funds in Oakford's account at the time the check was presented for payment. The case was heavily influenced by a prior related case, *Richardson v. International Bank*, where it was established that the burden is on the plaintiffs to show the bank had enough funds to honor the check at the time of its presentment. Evidence indicated that deposits made by Oakford on the same day were not proven to have occurred before the check was presented, creating a legal complication concerning the validity of the payment.	The plaintiffs argued that there were sufficient funds available in Oakford's account at the time their check was presented for payment. They aimed to recover the amount of the check based on the assertion that the bank had improperly denied payment due to an overdraft situation, which they contended did not take into account relevant deposits made by Oakford.	The defendant, International Bank, contended that the plaintiffs failed to provide adequate evidence showing that there were sufficient funds in Oakford's account to cover the check at the time it was presented. The bank maintained that simply showing deposits made on the same day was insufficient as it did not prove the timing of those deposits relative to the presentment of the check, thereby justifying their refusal to honor it based on existing overdraft accounts.

In January 1876, a legal case arose involving the St. Louis, Vandalia and Terre Haute Railroad Company and a nine-year-old boy named Robert Bell in Highland, Illinois. On a pleasant Sunday, Bell and a group of other boys discovered a turn-table belonging to the railroad company. While playing on it, Bell was seriously injured. The turn-table was described as a skeleton structure without a covering and lacked adequate safety measures. It was not located near any public street or thoroughfare where people typically passed. Although the turn-table was latched to prevent accidental rotation, it was not locked, allowing the children to open it and engage in dangerous play. Following the incident, Bell's guardians brought an action against the railroad company, claiming negligence in constructing and maintaining the turn-table. A verdict initially favored Bell, but the case was appealed due to concerns over the railroad's duty of care.	The plaintiff, Robert Bell, argued that the St. Louis, Vandalia and Terre Haute Railroad Company acted negligently in its duty to ensure the safety of the turn-table, leading to Bell's serious injury. The claims were based on the assertion that the railroad failed to properly secure the dangerous structure and that the lack of adequate safety measures constituted a breach of care owed to the public, particularly regarding the safety of children playing in the surrounding area. Bell sought damages for his injuries resulting from the incident.	The defendant, St. Louis, Vandalia and Terre Haute Railroad Company, contended that the turn-table was situated in an isolated location, far from public access and habitual passage. The company argued that it took reasonable precautions by latching the turn-table, even though it was not locked. This defense emphasized the position of the turn-table and suggested that the company could not be held liable for Bell's injuries, as they had not acted with negligence due to the lack of proximity to populated areas and common foot traffic.

In the case of **David B. Haworth v. Abijah Taylor**, the legal proceedings took place in the **Illinois Supreme Court**. The case arose in **1883** concerning land ownership disputes involving **David B. Haworth** and **Abijah Taylor**. The conflict began after **Mary E. Taylor**, Abijah's former wife, conveyed property to Haworth on **December 26, 1866**, despite having previously granted title to Taylor. Taylor's previous deed was filed but not recorded in a timely manner, which led to questions regarding notifications and rights over the property. Ownership complications were further amplified by a sheriff's sale of land that included Taylor’s life interest, sold for an inexplicably low bid of just **five dollars**. Taylor, unaware of the sale due to misleading record entries, pursued legal action to reclaim the property. The case involved multiple court hearings, with Taylor initially challenging the validity of Haworth’s title in an ejectment suit beginning in **1872**, which was repeatedly favored for the defendant (Haworth) leading to the filing of this current bill by Taylor to adjudicate his rights. The circumstances surrounding the dealings and the evidence presented became central to the judicial decisions made.	The plaintiff, **Abijah Taylor**, claimed that the deed from Mary E. Taylor to Haworth was invalid due to prior unrecorded deeds of ownership and the misleading records regarding the sheriff's sale. He sought to have the deed set aside and to redeem his rights to the property, arguing that he was not afforded proper notice of the sale and that there were irregularities affecting his ownership claim. He contested that he should be allowed to reclaim the land due to the gross inadequacy of the sale price and the lack of timely recording of relevant deeds.	The defendant, **David B. Haworth**, defended against the claims by asserting that he had acquired ownership legally through the conveyance from Mary E. Taylor, arguing that he was an innocent purchaser. He pointed to the lack of timely recording and asserted that he was not on notice of Taylor's prior claims. Haworth sought to maintain his title to the property, reinforcing that he had proceeded under a sheriff’s sale and was entitled to the benefits associated with it despite Taylor's claims to redemption.

Margaret E. Hoodless borrowed $7,000 from Simon Reid, Thomas Murdoch, and Frederick Fischer on October 31, 1876, agreeing to pay 8% annual interest over five years. This arrangement was formalized through a promissory note and further secured by a mortgage deed executed in favor of L.C. Paine Freer as trustee. The repayment included ten semi-annual interest coupons. By defaulting on several interest payments in 1878 and 1879, Hoodless triggered a provision in the mortgage that allowed for immediate repayment of the full debt upon default in interest payments. Consequently, Freer sold the mortgaged property at a trustee's sale on July 1, 1879, to Reid, who was among the creditors. Hoodless challenged the validity of this sale, asserting several objections regarding the sale procedures, notice, and the adequacy of the sale price, claiming her right to redeem the property and the need for Reid to account for rents received.	Hoodless claimed that her right to redeem the mortgaged property was infringed upon when the property was sold at a trustee's sale after she defaulted on interest payments. She argued that the separation of interest notes and the manner in which they were treated constituted an improper acceleration of her debt. Furthermore, she requested that the court require Reid to account for any rents collected from the property and to return the property to her.	The defendants maintained that Hoodless was in default of her loan obligations, justifying the trustee's sale under the terms of the mortgage. They argued that the separate interest coupons did not represent a payment of interest for the entire term and that the sale was conducted in accordance with the law, with sufficient notice given. The defendants contended that the sale price, although lower than market value, was not so inadequate as to render the sale fraudulent or erroneous. They requested the court to uphold the validity of the trustee's sale and dismiss Hoodless's claim.

In February 1865, a contractual dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, involving John H. Gale (the plaintiff) and Joseph McPherson and Elias B. Stiles (the defendants). Gale claimed that he entered into an agreement with the defendants for the sale of 5,000 bushels of No. 1 oats, priced at 61.25 cents per bushel, to be delivered at the buyers' option during March 1865. Despite Gale's readiness to deliver the oats by presenting warehouse receipts on March 31, 1865, the defendants failed to accept the delivery and did not pay for the oats. Gale sought legal remedy, and the matter proceeded through the court system, culminating in a judgment by the Illinois Supreme Court. The court was tasked with determining whether Gale's actions constituted a sufficient legal tender under the terms of the contract made in the context of the grain market in Chicago.	The plaintiff, John H. Gale, asserted that he had a valid contract with the defendants to sell 5,000 bushels of oats and that he had fulfilled his obligations by being prepared to deliver the warehouse receipts for the oats on March 31, 1865. Gale claimed that the defendants' refusal to accept the receipt constituted a breach of contract. He argued that the legal acknowledgment of his readiness to tender the oats should entitle him to recover damages in the amount of $1,000.	The defendants, represented by McPherson and Stiles, contended that the plaintiff's method of tendering the oats was insufficient. They argued that mere readiness to deliver warehouse receipts, especially without proof that Gale had the oats in his possession and control at the time, did not constitute a legal tender of the contract. Thus, they sought to challenge the validity of the plaintiff's claim while denying responsibility for the alleged breach.

The case "School Directors v. John Parks" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1877. The lawsuit originated in Clinton County, Illinois, where W. H. Schnyder and Caspar Krone, school directors of District Number Four, filed a suit against John Parks. The dispute arose over two orders drawn by the other school directors in favor of Parks for services rendered—$12.50 for eight days of labor repairing the schoolhouse and $18 for six cords of wood provided to the school. Both payments were disbursed by the township treasurer from school funds on February 19, 1874. The plaintiffs sought to recover the funds disbursed to Parks, arguing that the orders violated school law, which prohibits school directors from being interested in any contract made by the board. The plaintiffs asserted that Parks was likely acting as a director at the time the labor was performed and the wood was provided, rendering the payments unlawful.	The plaintiffs, school directors Schnyder and Krone, claimed that the payments made to John Parks were improper under Illinois law. They contended that since Parks had drawn payment for services performed while he was a director, it constituted a violation of the prohibition against directors benefiting from transactions made while serving. Their main request was to recover the amounts improperly paid to Parks from the school fund.	John Parks contended that the evidence did not sufficiently prove that he was a director at the time the labor and wood were provided. He argued that the presumption of law favors the legality of actions, and thus any claims against him would need to be substantiated with clear evidence that the payments were for services rendered while he was in office. Parks pointed out that the burden of proof lies with the plaintiffs to demonstrate that he was indeed a director when the transactions occurred, or else the payments were lawful.

Timothy O’Brien and William Hanley entered into a partnership in Lockport, Will County, Illinois, focused on boat building, repairing, and running a dry-dock and saw-mill, which lasted from December 6, 1869, until January 1873. The partnership was dissolved when Hanley sold his interest in the business to another party. Following the dissolution, O’Brien filed a bill for an accounting, claiming funds due to him. Hanley countered with a cross-bill, asserting that he was owed money as well, leading to a dispute regarding the financial accounts of the partnership. The court referred the matter to a master in chancery to review the accounts. The master reported that there was a balance of $368.48 owed from O’Brien to Hanley, which led to exceptions being filed against this report. O’Brien argued that the court erred by not recognizing the validity of his time records for labor rendered and for not compensating him sufficiently for his individual contributions to the partnership. After thorough examination of the evidence, the circuit court upheld the master's report.	O’Brien contended that the master in chancery improperly accounted for the partnership's expenditures. He argued that the inclusion of payments for 320 days of labor that he claimed were unrendered was erroneous and contested the exclusion of payment for his own labor. O’Brien maintained that he should be compensated for his services rendered during the partnership, claiming his contribution entitled him to a just accounting of the partnership’s finances.	Hanley countered O’Brien’s claims by asserting that the books kept by Marcy, which documented employee labor, were authoritative and binding. He argued that O’Brien failed to successfully challenge the validity of these records and that he was equally responsible for the management and integrity of those accounts. Additionally, Hanley contended that there was no express agreement pertaining to payment for O’Brien's individual services, and that any claimed compensations were not supported by the partnership agreement.

In 1850, in La Salle, Illinois, Jeremiah Crotty (the appellant) and Edward Collins (the appellee) engaged in a verbal agreement regarding the lease of forty acres of land owned by Collins. They agreed that Collins would allow Crotty to occupy the land for one or two years at an annual rent of twenty dollars, with Collins responsible for repairs. However, before Crotty could take possession, Collins insisted on a written contract, which included Crotty’s mother as security. In April 1850, Crotty attempted to enter the field to plow, but Collins forbade him, saying he could not do so until the lease was finalized. Despite this, Crotty, along with his servant, began plowing the land. Collins intervened, and both parties proceeded to cultivate parts of the crop simultaneously. Eventually, Collins impounded Crotty's horses and took control of the entire corn crop, valued at approximately three hundred dollars. The case emerged from Crotty's subsequent claim against Collins for trespass relating to the contested use of the land.	Crotty claimed that he had a valid lease agreement and asserted he was entitled to recover damages for trespass after Collins forced him to abandon possession of the field. He contended that he was lawfully in possession of the premises at the time of the alleged trespass, asserting that Collins's actions to prevent him from entering were unwarranted.	Collins defended against Crotty's claims by arguing that he never allowed Crotty to take lawful possession of the land, emphasizing that he had notified Crotty that a written contract and security were prerequisites for any lease agreement. He maintained that Crotty's attempts to cultivate the field were unauthorized and constituted a trespass, as Collins had actively resisted Crotty's entry and maintained control over the land.

The case of Indiana, Bloomington & Western Railway Company v. Eno Hinshaw took place in 1886, specifically on November 20, in the jurisdiction of the Illinois Appellate Court. The key individuals involved in the case were Eno Hinshaw, the plaintiff, and the Indiana, Bloomington & Western Railway Company, the defendant. The case arose from an incident in which a cow owned by Hinshaw was killed on the railway company's road. This incident led Hinshaw to seek damages for the loss of his cow, which resulted in the legal proceedings against the railway company.	Eno Hinshaw, the plaintiff, claimed that the Indiana, Bloomington & Western Railway Company was liable for the loss of his cow, which had been killed while on the railway's property. He sought judgment for $10 in damages, arguing that the railway company had a responsibility to prevent such accidents and was negligent in its operations that led to the death of his cow.	The Indiana, Bloomington & Western Railway Company, as the appellant, contested the judgment awarded to Hinshaw. Their defense was primarily focused on challenging the evidence presented in the case, claiming that the issues at hand were fundamentally based on conflicting facts. The railway company's legal representation did not present a strong counter-argument regarding liability but aimed to highlight the discrepancies in the evidence rather than deny the incident itself.

In June 1872, the case of Silas M. Phelps v. Illinois Central Railroad Company was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict arose over a contractual agreement for the purchase of a tract of land by Silas M. Phelps from the Illinois Central Railroad Company. The key individuals involved were Silas M. Phelps, the appellant and purchaser, and the Illinois Central Railroad Company, the appellee and seller. The case centered around Phelps’ failure to make timely payments as required by the contract. Specifically, the contract stipulated that prompt payment was essential, and any failure to comply would result in the forfeiture of all rights associated with the contract. After repeated delays in payment, the railroad company declared the contract null and void, asserting that all rights pertaining to the transaction had ceased. Phelps subsequently invoked the court's power to compel specific performance of the contract.	Silas M. Phelps, the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to specific performance of the purchase contract for the land. He argued that the railroad company had not formally surrendered the notes owed nor declared proper forfeiture regarding the payments. Phelps asserted that he was prepared to fulfill his obligations under the contract and contested the railway's right to declare a forfeiture based on his failure to make payments on time.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that Phelps was indeed in default as the contract explicitly outlined that time was of the essence. The company maintained that the contract provided for automatic forfeiture in the event of non-compliance with payment deadlines, rendering all rights associated with the contract void without requiring formal surrender of notes. The railroad insisted that even prior acceptance of late payments did not absolve Phelps from meeting his financial obligations as required.

In 1866, the case "William Bailey v. William B. West" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a property dispute. The key individuals involved are William Bailey, Jr. (the deceased), his widow Lydia (who later married William Low), and William Bailey, Sr. (the father). The property in question was conveyed to William Bailey, Jr. by Thomas R. Green in February 1849 as security for a loan. After William Bailey, Jr. died, Lydia executed a deed conveying the property back to William Bailey, Sr. in 1854. Subsequently, William Bailey, Sr. conveyed the land to Frederick W. Bailey, who later sold it under a trust deed to Wm. J. Hunt, from whom West purchased the property. Lydia Low disputed the validity of the deed and her dower rights, particularly after remarrying. Given the complexities of trust law concerning dower rights and the necessary parties in the case, multiple parties were involved, and the court was called to address the proper distribution of the property ownership and enforceability of the deeds.	The plaintiffs, William B. West and Hira Barrett, claimed that they were entitled to the property based on the legal conveyances made after William Bailey, Jr.’s death. They sought a decree requiring the defendants to either pay them the amount they paid at the trust sale or have the land conveyed to them, asserting that the legal titles had been properly transferred in accordance with the law.	The defendants, including Lydia Low and others, contended that Lydia’s right to dower had not been properly addressed and that her separate conveyance of the property after her marriage with Low was invalid as it lacked his participation. They argued that the nature of the trust and the various deeds executed prior did not validly transfer ownership, maintaining that Lydia had a legitimate claim to the dower until the corresponding rights were established.

The case "Megill v. Megill" was decided on July 28, 1886, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff, Mrs. Megill, and the defendant, Mr. Megill, who were husband and wife. The case arose in response to a bill filed by Mrs. Megill against Mr. Megill seeking a divorce. The grounds for her request included accusations of extreme and repeated cruelty as well as adultery by Mr. Megill. A hearing was conducted where both parties presented their testimonies before the chancellor. However, the court found that the claims made by Mrs. Megill were not substantiated by a preponderance of the evidence, leading to a dismissal of her divorce petition.	Mrs. Megill, the plaintiff, claimed that her husband, Mr. Megill, had engaged in extreme and repeated cruelty towards her, alongside committing adultery. She sought a divorce based on these allegations, hoping to have the court validate her claims and dissolve her marriage.	Mr. Megill, the defendant, denied the allegations of cruelty and adultery made by Mrs. Megill. He argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiff did not sufficiently support her claims. Consequently, he requested the court to dismiss the divorce action based on the lack of credible proof to substantiate the accusations.

On July 9, 1844, Christopher Sammis and his business partners, merchants in New York City, sold a bill of goods to Ralph Clark, a merchant in Peoria, Illinois, for a total of $283.51. The order was initiated by Clark who had originally sent a request to another merchant in New York. By May 29, 1845, Clark made a partial payment of $160 towards the account. The plaintiffs shipped the goods as per the order, with the invoice indicating a six-month credit period for payment. The plaintiffs introduced evidence showing that it was common practice among New York merchants to charge interest on overdue accounts, and that Clark was aware of this customary practice. There were related dealings where Clark himself charged interest in an account with another merchant. The case was ultimately brought to the Illinois Supreme Court following Clark’s appeal after a jury found him liable for the debt including interest and awarded damages based on interest charges. The court had to determine whether the jury was justified in including interest in their verdict.	The plaintiffs claimed a total of $162.23 in debt for the goods sold, along with damages of $38.82, which represented interest on the account. They argued that under both customary practices among New York merchants and the specifics of the Illinois statute regarding the recovery of interest, they were entitled to receive interest on the outstanding amount after the due date.	The defendant contended that the plaintiffs were not entitled to recover interest based on the Illinois statutory rules governing interest recovery. He argued that there was no express agreement to pay interest and that no substantial evidence indicated that there was a vexatious delay in payment on his part. The underlying premise of the defense was that the mere passage of time did not constitute grounds for claiming interest without specific contractual or statutory basis.

The case "City of Havana v. Milroy Vanlaningham" was presented in the Illinois Appellate Court on October 5, 1885. It arose in Mason County, Illinois, where Milroy Vanlaningham operated a livery stable. The city of Havana enforced an ordinance requiring individuals to obtain a license to operate as common carriers for hire within city limits. The ordinance aimed to regulate carriers to prevent extortion and protect the interests of the public. The plaintiff, the City of Havana, claimed that Vanlaningham violated this ordinance by allowing his teams to be used for transporting goods for hire without the necessary license. However, Vanlaningham maintained that he was not functioning as a common carrier; rather, he had merely rented out his teams to another party for a short-term task involving ice. The court needed to determine whether Vanlaningham's actions fell under the purview of the ordinance.	The City of Havana contended that Milroy Vanlaningham violated the city ordinance concerning common carriers, which requires licensing for transporting goods for hire. They sought to impose penalties on Vanlaningham for operating without a license, as the ordinance aims to regulate carriers and protect the public from potential abuse.	Milroy Vanlaningham defended against the claims by arguing that he was not a common carrier under the ordinance's definition. As the owner of a livery stable, he claimed that he only rented out his teams temporarily for a specific task of hauling ice, which did not constitute operating as a common carrier. Consequently, he argued that he should not be subjected to the penalties outlined in the ordinance since he was within neither the terms nor the spirit of the law.

In November 1861, in Perry County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Harrison Rayburn and co-appellant Jesse Barbre (who was not served with process) against George W. Day and other appellees. The case centered on the enforcement of a promissory note and the associated mortgage on 240 acres of land, which was executed by Barbre after the dissolution of their partnership. This note was intended to secure payment for an outstanding account. However, during the trial, the note was deemed inadmissible as evidence, leading the appellees to attempt to prove that the account existed independently of the note and mortgage. Ultimately, the court ruled in favor of the appellees, awarding them $1,279.73 in damages plus costs. The appellants contested the decision, claiming that the mortgage and note constituted a settlement that absolved them of the debt; they argued that since these had been executed after the partnership had ended, they should not be held liable.	The plaintiffs, George W. Day et al., maintained that the promissory note and mortgage executed by Jesse Barbre did not extinguish the underlying account owed by the partnership. They argued that the note was not intended as a release from liability and contested the claim that it satisfied the partnership’s debt. They sought recovery of the amount due on the account, which they believed was valid and enforceable despite the execution of the note.	The defendants, Harrison Rayburn and Jesse Barbre, contended that the execution of the promissory note and mortgage, which secured the account, released them from further liability. They insisted that the note was intended as complete satisfaction of the account and should preclude any judgment against them. Additionally, they challenged the court's decision to allow the inclusion of interest on the account, arguing that there was no evidence that they had been informed of a custom charging interest after accounts became overdue.

Joseph W. Peck and John Ledwidge entered into a lease agreement for a steam mill in Illinois in 1859, with Ledwidge as the lessee for a term of twelve months. The lease stipulated a rental payment of $500 per annum to be paid quarterly and required the lessee to return the mill in good repair, excepting reasonable wear and unavoidable accidents. During the lease, Ledwidge incurred $160 in repair costs due to damage to the mill's boiler, which he attributed to unavoidable circumstances. He deducted $95 from the rent owed to Peck for these repairs and filed a claim for the remaining $65. Peck countered by seeking payment for unpaid rent amounting to $156.91. The case proceeded to trial where Judge Caton presided over the proceedings, considering the responsibilities outlined in the lease and whether a verbal or other agreement for repairing costs existed. Ledwidge testified about his repairs, while witnesses confirmed that the damage was not his fault. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of Ledwidge, awarding him $65 for repairs, leading to Peck filing an appeal due to disagreements over the jury instructions regarding liability for the repairs and rental obligations.	Ledwidge claimed that he was entitled to compensation for the repairs he made to the mill, which he argued were necessary due to damage caused by unavoidable circumstances, not negligence. He asserted that by undertaking these repairs, which he believed Peck or his agents had implicitly authorized, he should recover the costs from Peck. Ledwidge sought a judgment for the value of the repairs after crediting Peck with unpaid rent.	Peck contended that under the lease agreement, he was not responsible for repairs while the mill was rented. He argued that the rental payments should continue regardless of any repairs needed, as the lease did not stipulate such an obligation on his part. Furthermore, he claimed that since there was no explicit agreement for him to cover the repairs, he should not be liable for the amounts Ledwidge sought. Peck’s defense emphasized that any claims for repair costs were not contractually warranted.

Jane Holloway et al. filed a case against James Galloway et al. in 1869, in La Salle County, Illinois. The dispute arose after certain heirs of James Galloway sought to set aside the probate of his will, claiming that he was mentally incompetent at the time the will was created. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, where various arguments were presented regarding the admissibility of witness testimony and the burden of proof concerning the mental capacity of the testator. The court evaluated the legality of allowing James and Archibald Galloway, named defendants in the case and beneficiaries of the will, to testify. The complainants contended that the witnesses should not have been allowed to take the stand due to a statutory provision aimed at ensuring fair proceedings in cases involving parties with an interest in the outcome. After a thorough examination of the case, including evidence presented and instructions given to the jury, the court determined its findings based on precedents and relevant statutes.	The plaintiffs, heirs of James Galloway, claimed that their father lacked mental capacity when he made the will. They sought to have the will set aside on these grounds, arguing that the necessary legal standards concerning the testator’s competency had not been met during the probate proceedings. Their key points revolved around the admissibility of testimony from defendants who were also heirs.	The defendants, heirs and beneficiaries under the will, argued that the testimony of James and Archibald Galloway was admissible as it concerned facts that occurred after James Galloway’s death. They contended that the plaintiffs did not meet their burden of proof to establish mental incapacity, pointing to the presumption of competency established by the testimony of subscribing witnesses at the will’s probate. They requested that the case be dismissed based on the plaintiffs’ failure to demonstrate the testator's incompetence.

Thomas Sheeran filed a lawsuit against The Chicago and Milwaukee Railway Company in September 1868. The case originated in Lake County, Illinois, but was later moved to the Cook County circuit court, where it was presided over by Hon. Ebastus S. Williams. The suit was based on allegations of negligence on the part of the railway's servants, specifically concerning the operation of a train that resulted in damages to Sheeran. The case revolved around conflicting testimonies regarding the incident, necessitating legal examination by the courts. The trial court ruled in favor of the defendant, leading Sheeran to appeal the decision, claiming that the verdict contradicted the evidence presented.	Thomas Sheeran contended that the railway company acted negligently, resulting in damages that warranted compensation. He sought to reverse the trial court’s decision, arguing that the conflicting testimonies presented during the trial should have been viewed more favorably towards his claims of negligence.	The Chicago and Milwaukee Railway Company, represented by Mr. H. W. Blodgett, argued that the verdict rendered by the jury was justified, given the conflicting nature of the testimonies. They maintained that the jury, having observed the witnesses and the evidence presented, arrived at a reasonable conclusion, and thus, the verdict should not be disturbed under established court principles. They requested that the appellate court uphold the trial court's decision.

The case "Peter Jensen and Theodore Johnson v. William C. Fricke and Charles P. Dose" took place in Cook County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 2, 1889. The plaintiffs, Peter Jensen and Theodore Johnson, initiated legal action against the defendants, William C. Fricke and Charles P. Dose, in front of a justice of the peace, where they were awarded $8,114. The defendants subsequently appealed the judgment to the Superior Court. During the June term of that year, the court required the appellants (defendants) to file an affidavit of merits, but they failed to comply with this order. Consequently, the Superior Court dismissed their appeal for non-compliance. The court's action was viewed as inconsistent with a previous case ruling (Martin v. Hochstadter, 27 Ill. App. 166), prompting the appellate court to reverse the dismissal and remand the case for further proceedings.	The plaintiffs, Jensen and Johnson, claim that the initial judgment rendered in their favor by the justice of the peace should be upheld. They argue that the defendants' failure to file an affidavit of merits does not justify the dismissal of their appeal and that the original ruling awarding them $8,114 should stand.	The defendants, Fricke and Dose, maintain that the appeal from the justice court should be dismissed due to the plaintiffs' failure to adhere to procedural requirements, specifically the court's order to file an affidavit of merits. They argue that the dismissal aligns with the procedural guidelines for the appeals process.

T. Judson Hale filed a legal action of ejectment against Levi Gladfelder and others in September 1869 in Illinois. The dispute centered around the ownership of a specific parcel of land, described as the southeast quarter of section fourteen in township twelve north, of range four east. The case emerged from prior transactions where Hale had acquired a claim and color of title to the land from James Stewart, who paid taxes on it from 1838 to 1853. Following this, Hale sold the property to David Swickard, who took possession and made improvements but eventually abandoned the land in 1858 without Hale's consent. Afterward, the land remained vacant until Gladfelder took possession. Hale's lawsuit aimed to recover this land. During the trial, the jury ruled in favor of the defendants, leading Hale to appeal the decision based on his entitlement under the Illinois limitation act of 1839, which he argued established his right to recover the land due to previous possession and tax payments.	Hale argued that he had a valid claim to the property based on color of title, long-term payment of taxes, and rightful possession through Swickard. He asserted that his legal rights were established and that the court had erred in its instructions to the jury, which he claimed misled their judgment. Hale sought a reversal of the lower court's ruling, emphasizing that he met the criteria set forth in the limitation act to reclaim the land.	Gladfelder and the co-defendants contended that Hale's claims were invalid, arguing that Swickard's abandonment of the land eliminated any claim Hale had to possession. They argued that the statutory bar of the limitation act did not apply because Swickard had effectively forfeited any rights by leaving the property, which had since become vacant. The defense requested the court to uphold the initial ruling, asserting that due legal process had been followed in determining the rightful possession of the land.

In 1890, in Cook County, Illinois, George Sindelar, a partner in a dry goods business, found himself embroiled in a legal dispute with James H. Walker. Sindelar and his partner, Hubka, had incurred a debt of $2,000 to Walker, prompting them to execute a chattel mortgage on their business assets. This mortgage allowed the partners to retain possession of the property until default, but it also granted Walker the right to take immediate possession if he felt insecure about the collateral. Before the debt was due, Walker allegedly colluded with Hubka to falsely claim foreclosure on the chattel mortgage. As a result, Walker entered the premises, took possession of the goods, and ousted Sindelar, causing him to lose access to the property. Sindelar claimed that Walker had no reasonable cause to feel insecure and that the foreclosure was enacted without justification, representing a conspiracy to harm him. The court had to determine whether a single partner could sue a third party for actions that were consented to by the other partner without the partnership being dissolved or accounts settled.	George Sindelar argued that James H. Walker, in collusion with Hubka, wrongfully foreclosed on the chattel mortgage, thereby unlawfully taking possession of firm property and ousting him from the premises. Sindelar contended that Walker lacked sufficient reason to consider himself unsafe regarding the mortgage, and he sought legal remedy for the wrongful foreclosure, emphasizing that both he and Hubka were partners and that no settlement of partnership accounts had occurred.	James H. Walker countered that since both Sindelar and Hubka, as partners, were involved in the arrangement, Sindelar could not maintain an action against him for a trespass to firm property. Walker argued that one partner cannot recover damages for actions taken with the assent of the other partner. He emphasized that the partnership remained intact without the debts being settled, and thus Sindelar had no separate claim against him regarding the foreclosure.

The case of James Holliday v. Thomas Swailes took place in June 1837 in Morgan County, Illinois. The dispute revolved around the responsibility for maintaining a partition fence that divided the lands of Holliday and Swailes. On June 14, 1837, justices Samuel S. Brooks and Matthew Stacy ruled in favor of Swailes, ordering Holliday to pay $58.80, which was a portion of the estimated cost for the division fence. Holliday claimed he was not present before the justices during the proceeding and therefore did not have the chance to defend himself. Subsequently, Holliday appealed the decision to the Circuit Court, where he sought to reverse the judgment based on the lack of notification regarding the proceeding. However, the Circuit Court dismissed Holliday's appeal, stating that the statute under which the judgment was given did not require notification to the defendant or provide for an appeal. This led to Holliday escalating the case to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the validity of the initial proceedings was contested. The Supreme Court ultimately addressed the necessity of notification to the defendant in judicial processes and the right to appeal under the relevant statutes.	James Holliday, the appellant, claimed that he was denied due process because he was not notified of the proceedings against him regarding the partition fence. He argued that this lack of notification deprived him of the opportunity to defend himself adequately. He sought to have the judgment rendered by the justices reversed and contended that an appeal should be allowed based on existing statutes that require notification to defendants.	Thomas Swailes, the appellee, maintained that the law under which the justices rendered their judgment did not require any notification to the defendant regarding the proceedings. He argued that the judgment against Holliday was final and valid, emphasizing that the statutes governing the matter did not provide for an appeal in this type of case. Swailes sought to have Holliday's appeal dismissed, asserting that the justices acted within their jurisdiction.

James H. Taylor v. Samuel Beck took place in Illinois with the case commencing on August 3, 1850. The dispute arose from a written agreement where James Beck was to sell and deliver an entire lot of broom brush to Thomas Freeman, with Taylor acting as a surety. The terms specified that the broom brush was to be delivered by March 1, 1851, at Freeman's shop in Rushville, Illinois, with a payment of $350 to be made in installments. After the agreement was executed, Beck claimed to have delivered the material except for a minor quantity. However, Freeman failed to make multiple installment payments, leading Beck to file a legal action for debt against both Freeman and Taylor in the Schuyler Circuit Court. The defendants filed several pleas regarding non-performance due to various claims related to the delivery of the brush, including insufficient quality and quantity, as well as accusations of fraudulent representations regarding the amount of brush raised. The case ultimately went to trial after various legal maneuvers and was heard in September 1851.	The plaintiff, James Beck, argued that he had fulfilled his contractual obligation to deliver the broom brush and sought to recover the unpaid installments totaling $150. He claimed that Freeman had accepted the deliveries made, although he had not delivered a minor portion of the contract. Beck asserted that multiple counts of non-payment constituted breaches of the contract terms, further asserting that he was entitled to the judgment based on his complete contractual adherence.	The defendants, particularly Taylor and Freeman, contended several defenses, including claims of non-performance by Beck, arguing that not all of the brush was delivered in merchantable condition, and alleging that some of the brush was damaged. They also made claims of fraud, asserting that Beck misrepresented the amount of brush raised. Taylor specifically asserted that Beck failed to act with due diligence in pursuing the collection from Freeman after being notified of defaults, which they argued led to losses and should relieve them of liability under the contract.

James Holliday was indicted in the Perry Circuit Court in Illinois during September 1844 on five counts for administering poison to procure an abortion. After initially seeking to quash the indictment—succeeding only regarding the first count—Holliday pleaded not guilty and requested a venue change to St. Clair County. The trial convened at the May term of 1846, where Holliday was notably absent when the jury returned a verdict of guilty, sentencing him to one month of imprisonment in the penitentiary and a $100 fine. Holliday subsequently filed motions to set aside the verdict due to its inconsistency with the evidence and for being pronounced in his absence, both of which the court denied. After appealing this decision, the case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court.	Holliday contended that the indictment should have been quashed due to deficiencies in several counts. He argued the verdict was improperly received without his presence, violating common law principles, and claimed a new trial was warranted since the only witness contradicted the allegations. He also asserted that the judgment should be overturned, as it failed to meet procedural standards regarding the indictment's transmission.	The defense, representing the People of Illinois, maintained that the indictment contained at least one valid count, sufficient to sustain the verdict. They asserted that the verdict could indeed be received in the defendant's absence for a misdemeanor charge. Furthermore, they argued that the decision to deny the motions for a new trial and in arrest of judgment was within the discretion of the Circuit Court and thus not subject to Supreme Court review.

Prentice J. Douglass v. Alexander X. Parker and George M. Plumbe was a case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1867. The case originated in the Coles County Circuit Court, presided over by Judge James Steele. The dispute arose when non-resident plaintiffs, Parker and Plumbe, filed a lawsuit against Douglass in October 1866, initiating an action of assumpsit. On the same day, the plaintiffs' attorney filed a bond for costs, which was officially acknowledged by the court clerk. However, Douglass’s counsel contested the sufficiency of this bond, leading to a motion to dismiss the case for lack of a proper bond. The plaintiffs then sought permission to file a new bond, which the court granted, while it overruled the defendant's motion to dismiss. This led to the trial, where the issue was found in favor of Parker and Plumbe.	The plaintiffs, Parker and Plumbe, claimed that they had properly filed a bond for costs in accordance with legal requirements. They argued that although the initial bond was contested, the court allowed them to file a valid new bond, affirming their right to pursue the lawsuit. Their legal request included seeking the court's affirmation of the trial court's decision to let them amend the bond and to allow the case to continue to trial.	The defendant, Douglass, contended that the bond filed by the plaintiffs was inadequate and thus sought dismissal of the case on those grounds. Douglass's legal arguments challenged the court's decision to allow the plaintiffs to file a new bond and included claims that evidentiary questions raised during the trial were improperly handled. Douglass requested that the court review these alleged errors and dismiss the case due to the purported lack of a valid bond.

In the case of Henry Potwin v. William T. Johnson, Collector, the events unfolded in 1882 at Cook County, Illinois. The county court was involved in a legal proceeding regarding the sale of real estate to address certain delinquent special assessments. The court published a notice for the judgment's application at its July term, 1882. Property owners were given until the 12th of July to file objections. As no objections were filed, the court ruled in favor of the collector on the 19th of July, confirming the judgment against the real estate. On the 26th of July, Potwin, the plaintiff, sought to set aside this judgment, but the court denied his motion. The case revolves around the legal intricacies of the notices and demands purportedly related to the special assessments and whether the county collector had the appropriate authority to apply for the judgment before the required term.	Henry Potwin's primary argument centered around the jurisdiction of the county court to render the judgment for the collection of special assessments. He contended that the only demand for the assessments was communicated via a postal card, and the timing of the advertisements was improper, as they preceded the demand. Potwin further asserted that the inclusion of costs in the demand was invalid and that the collector lacked the power to apply for the judgment at the time.	William T. Johnson, the collector, defended the judgment by arguing that the court had jurisdiction to render the judgment, as the special assessments were correctly processed following the procedures mandated by the relevant laws. Johnson contended that the notices provided, albeit through a postal card, met the legal requirements for informing property owners about the assessments. He maintained that the legal framework allowed for such judgments to be applied for without the plaintiff's objections, and thus, the court’s ruling should be upheld.

The case, "The Highway Commissioners of the Town of Rutland v. The Highway Commissioners of the Town of Dayton," took place in LaSalle County, Illinois, and culminated in a judgment delivered on September 1, 1871, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The two towns involved, Rutland and Dayton, are adjacent and separated by the Fox River. A bridge was constructed over this river in 1853, forming part of a highway that became essential for public travel. The commissioners of highways from Rutland claimed that the bridge was a public structure requiring joint maintenance. When the bridge fell into disrepair, they notified the Dayton commissioners about its unsafe condition and requested their cooperation in repairs. They subsequently threatened to proceed with repairs themselves if Dayton did not contribute to the costs. The Dayton commissioners denied that the bridge was a public bridge and refrained from participating in the repairs. Following this dispute, the Dayton commissioners repaired the bridge and sued Rutland for reimbursement of half the expenses, resulting in a jury ruling in favor of Dayton for $1,317.36.	The plaintiffs, representing the Highway Commissioners of Dayton, argued that the bridge had become a public structure that required both towns to maintain it. They contended that after several notifications about its unsafe condition, Rutland failed to contribute to necessary repairs. Consequently, Dayton performed the repairs and sought reimbursement for half the costs incurred, asserting that Rutland was legally obligated to share the financial responsibility under the township organization laws.	The defendants, representing the Highway Commissioners of Rutland, contended that the bridge was never constructed as a public bridge but rather by private means. They argued that Rutland was not liable for the repairs, as they claimed the bridge was a private structure, and they had no legal obligation to contribute to its maintenance. The defendants challenged the manner by which the plaintiffs filed the suit and the admissibility of evidence during the trial, suggesting that procedural errors warranted a reversal of the judgment.

In 1869, in La Salle County, Illinois, Joseph Mosher brought a case against Asa Griffin and others for services rendered in training a horse for a race. The case arose when Mosher claimed he should be compensated for efforts related to the horse's preparation—specifically for training, shoeing, and feeding. The issue at hand was whether these services were legally recoverable, given the context that the race had money bet on it, which raised questions about legality under gambling statutes. The County Court ruled in favor of the defendants, leading Mosher to appeal the judgment. The Illinois Supreme Court considered the nature of the claims and the context in which the services were provided.	Joseph Mosher contended that he was entitled to compensation for services in training a horse for a race, alongside reimbursement for expenses incurred for shoeing and feeding the horse while it was under his care. He argued that even if the race did not occur, the services provided were necessary and should be paid for, thereby claiming recovery for both training and associated care costs.	Asa Griffin and the other defendants argued that the services provided by Mosher were part of a gambling transaction, which violated state law. They maintained that because the training was for a race with money bet on it, the claim was unenforceable. Thus, they requested that the court dismiss Mosher's claims on the grounds that any recovery associated with the race was prohibited by statute.

The case of Gardner S. Chapin et al. v. Moses W. Dake revolved around a legal dispute that occurred in September 1870 in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved included Moses W. Dake, the plaintiff, and Gardner S. Chapin along with J.J. Gore, who were the defendants operating as partners under the firm name Chapin & Gore. Dake had originally drawn two drafts for $1000 each from the Fifth National Bank of Chicago, which were payable to him and then indorsed to another party, John Donaldson. Dake lost both drafts while gambling, having staked them and receiving cash in exchange for his gambling losses. After attempting to claim the drafts back from Chapin & Gore, the situation escalated to a court case to determine the rightful owner of the drafts following Dake's assertion that the indorsements were void due to the gambling nature of their original transaction. The court ultimately had to determine whether the drafts, in the hands of Chapin & Gore, could legally be held due to the illegality attached to their endorsement resulting from gambling.	Moses W. Dake claimed that the two drafts he had initially drawn were lost through gambling and that the indorsements made to Chapin & Gore were void under Illinois gambling laws. He sought the return of the drafts and the cancellation of his indorsements, arguing that since the transfers were made in connection with a gambling transaction, they should provide him with legal grounds to reclaim ownership without any obligation to repay any amount received, such as the $500 he had received during the gambling transaction.	Chapin & Gore contended that they were bona fide holders of the drafts and should therefore be entitled to keep them, regardless of Dake’s claims regarding their endorsement being void. The defendants argued that as innocent parties who had received the drafts through legitimate trade, they should not be compelled to surrender them simply because of Dake’s prior gambling losses. They maintained that the law should protect them as rightful possessors.

In the case of William Jack et al. v. F. D. Weiennett, Collector, filed at Ottawa on November 14, 1885, the key individuals involved are William Jack and Leslie D. Putekbatjgh as the appellants representing creditors, and F. D. Weiennett, the county tax collector, as the appellee. The dispute arose in Peoria, Illinois, involving Day Bros. & Co., merchants who were assessed for taxes amounting to $1,827 for the year 1884. After selling their stock of goods in September 1884, they made a general assignment of the remaining assets, valued at approximately $25,000, to Jack and Putekbatjgh for the benefit of the creditors. The tax collector claimed that the taxes due on the property were a priority charge on the funds held by the assignees, prompting the collector to petition the county court to direct the assignees to pay the taxes before any distributions to creditors. The county court agreed to the petition, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiffs (appellants) argued that the tax collector’s claim for payment of the taxes should not take precedence over the rights of the creditors since the tax was not a lien at the time the assignment was made. They maintained that taxes should not be treated as an ordinary debt and that the rights of the creditors to the assigned assets should be protected.	The defendant (tax collector) contended that the tax claim had paramount priority over all other claims; thus, the assignees were obligated to pay the taxes due before any distributions to the creditors. The collector argued that as a governmental claim, taxes should always take precedence over ordinary debts, emphasizing the necessity of ensuring the state’s revenues for public needs.

Nehemiah Simons, the plaintiff, initiated a legal action in Kane County, Illinois, before a justice of the peace against John S. Waterman, the defendant. The case was originally heard in Kane County, where the court ruled in favor of the defendant, ordering Simons to pay $88.46. Simons appealed the decision, leading to a change of venue to DeKalb County. During the October term at the DeKalb Circuit Court, the case was decided by the court without a jury, resulting in a judgment for Waterman with damages assessed at $97.66. The trial centered on two promissory notes presented as evidence by Waterman, which were executed by Simons. The defendant attempted to introduce evidence indicating that the plaintiff was not the rightful holder of the legal interest in the notes, arguing that Simons was incorrectly named as "John C. Waterman," while the relevant party was "James S. Waterman." The court sustained an objection to this evidence, which became a critical point of contention in the appeal.	The plaintiff, Nehemiah Simons, argued that he had legal rights to the promissory notes in question. He contended that the evidence presented by Waterman should not be admissible because it questioned his legal standing by suggesting that he was not the real party in interest. Simons requested the court to uphold the initial ruling in his favor and allow the original judgment to stand.	John S. Waterman, the defendant, maintained that the plaintiff did not possess the proper legal standing to enforce the promissory notes. He argued that the plaintiff’s name was incorrectly stated and that the rightful holder of the notes was someone else, specifically James S. Waterman. Waterman sought to have the evidence regarding the true ownership of the notes admitted, which would invalidate Simons's claims.

In 1853, Daniel Pile initiated an action of ejectment against John and Hugh McBratney to regain possession of a parcel of land, specifically the southwest quarter of section 25 in Adams County, Illinois. The defendants were in possession of the property at the time the suit was filed. Pile presented evidence including a patent dated October 13, 1817, from the United States to a previous owner, Carr Mastín, and two subsequent deeds transferring ownership to him from John Sample (dated February 6, 1849, and October 29, 1850). The deeds were connected to a chancery suit where Pile was the complainant, and it aimed to resolve issues regarding Mastín’s heirs, who were claimed to be unknown. The chancery bill alleged that Mastín had sold the property to Sample in May 1818, and due to Mastín’s demise, Pile sought to compel the defendants to convey the property rights. The legal proceedings included affidavits and notices regarding the unknown defendants and culminated in a decree that appointed a commissioner to convey the property to Pile. However, the court ruled against Pile, leading him to appeal the decision. The primary legal issue examined involved the validity of the title transfer and jurisdiction over unknown heirs.	Daniel Pile's primary arguments rested on the assertion that he was the rightful owner of the property based on a chain of title leading back to Carr Mastín. He claimed that despite the defendants being in possession, he had legal grounds to reclaim the property through the deeds he possessed, which he argued were legitimate and valid. He sought to compel the defendants to convey the property and emphasized that proper notice was given to all interested parties, including the unknown heirs of Mastín.	The defendants, John and Hugh McBratney, contended that Pile's legal arguments were insufficient to establish his rightful ownership. They emphasized that the original conveyance from Mastín to Sample was ineffective due to lacking essential deed formalities, specifically that it was not under seal, resulting in Sample holding only an equitable title. Consequently, they argued that no legal interest passed to Pile, defeating his claims to possession.

The case "City of Dunleith v. Reynolds, Saulpaugh & Co." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1869.
