The dispute arose in Dunleith, Illinois, involving the firm Reynolds, Saulpaugh & Co., which consisted of Elisha P. Reynolds, Thomas Saulpaugh, and others. The plaintiffs were contractors engaged in the construction of railroad bridges, specifically a bridge spanning the Mississippi River. During the construction process in 1868, the plaintiffs had various construction materials and equipment within Dunleith, including rock, engines, flat boats, and derricks. The city of Dunleith claimed that the plaintiffs owed $186 in taxes on the personal property used for the bridge project, which the plaintiffs argued was illegal and paid under protest. The city’s collector demanded the tax payment and attempted to levy the plaintiffs' property when they refused, ultimately leading to a court case after the plaintiffs paid the tax under duress and sought to recover the amount in court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the tax assessed on their personal property by the city of Dunleith was illegal. They argued that since they were non-residents and the property was temporarily situated for use in a specific project, it should not have been subject to city taxation. The plaintiffs sought to recover the $186 they paid under protest to the city, asserting that the tax was improperly levied.	The city of Dunleith's defense centered on the assertion that the property was rightly taxed as it was located within the city's limits and was in active use in a project benefiting from municipal services. The defendant argued that their charter granted them the authority to impose taxes on all property, real and personal, regardless of the owner's residency, provided it had an established physical presence within the city for a sufficient duration. They contended that the plaintiffs' use of the property in the construction project qualified it for taxation.

In the case of Francis Longwith v. Milton W. Riggs et al., decided on November 8, 1887, by the Illinois Supreme Court, the matter originated from the estate of Thomas Longwith, who had passed away leaving a will that devised his estate to various beneficiaries, including his four children: Francis, Huida, Julia, and Lavina. Notably, Lavina was granted her share in trust, as she was recognized to be feeble-minded, only able to receive the income generated by her share during her lifetime. Following Thomas Longwith's death, his three other children filed a bill in the circuit court requesting the appointment of a trustee to manage Lavina’s share. A trustee, Milton W. Riggs, was duly appointed and was tasked with ensuring Lavina’s support using her trust fund. Over a span of nearly seven years, the trustee spent not just the income from the trust fund but also some of the principal to support Lavina. After her death, it was found that Lavina had accrued debts including medical expenses. Julia Longwith, another sibling, claimed compensation for the care provided to Lavina. The case involved examining the jurisdiction of the court regarding the trust fund and the extent to which the trust's principal could be used for Lavina’s maintenance.	Francis Longwith, one of the plaintiffs, contended that the court erred by allowing expenditures from the principal of Lavina's trust fund for her care and maintenance, thus questioning the distribution of the trust after Lavina's death. The plaintiffs sought clarification and adjustment of the expenses charged against the trust fund, arguing for the limitations specified in the will regarding how the trust was to be managed.	Milton W. Riggs, as the trustee, along with Julia Longwith, defended the position that the court holds the authority to use the principal of the trust fund if necessary for the maintenance of Lavina, especially given her feeble-minded condition. They argued that the intention of the testator was to ensure Lavina’s support, and that the court’s intervention was justified under those circumstances to prevent her from suffering due to insufficient funds. They requested that the court uphold the payments made for Lavina's necessary support and medical care from the trust.

The case of The Bank of Chicago v. Charles J. Hull took place in September 1874, in Cook County, Illinois. The Bank of Chicago (plaintiff) brought a lawsuit against Charles J. Hull (defendant) in the Circuit Court, with Judge Lambert Tree presiding. The dispute arose over an alleged balance due on a deposit account. The plaintiff submitted an affidavit and attached a bankbook, which included entries made by the defendant, clearly showing the amount owed. The plaintiff contended that the documentation fulfilled the necessary statutory requirements to support its claim for the owed balance, while the defendant failed to provide an affidavit of merits to support his plea.	The Bank of Chicago claimed that Charles J. Hull owed them money from a deposit account. They argued that their affidavit, evidencing the nature of their demand and the owed amount, combined with the attached bankbook reflecting the defendant's entries, constituted a sufficient "bill of particulars." They requested the court to affirm their judgment based on compliance with statutory requirements for filing the suit, which they believed the defendant failed to contest appropriately.	Charles J. Hull's defense centered around the argument that the plaintiff's affidavit did not meet the statutory conditions, suggesting that it should have been executed by the plaintiff themselves. Hull did not provide an affidavit of merits to support his defense against the claim made by the Bank of Chicago. As such, his plea was rendered ineffective, leading to his argument being struck from the records.

In September 1869, Orrin Forsyth, Willard Abbott, and Joseph F. Forsyth, partners operating as Forsyth & Co. in Rochester, New York, became defendants in an attachment suit initiated by William C. Warren in the Superior Court of Chicago, Illinois. Warren claimed that the defendants owed him $230.60 for services rendered and commissions. As they were not residents of Illinois, Warren filed an affidavit to establish jurisdiction and sought a writ of attachment against their estate. The notice of the attachment was published in the Chicago Republican for four consecutive weeks. Despite challenges, including the computation of the sixty days required between the publication and court term, the court subsequently entered a judgment against the defendants for $238.65, including costs, after the defendants failed to appear in court. The decision led the defendants to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	William C. Warren argued that he was entitled to judgment based on the defendants' failure to appear following the publication of the notice. He maintained that all procedural requirements for the attachment were met, including the proper notice, and emphasized that the only outstanding debt was the claimed amount stated in the affidavit. Warren sought enforcement of the judgment in his favor along with costs incurred.	The defendants contested the judgment on several grounds, arguing that the publication notice had a fatal defect due to an erroneous date and that the judgment exceeded the amount specified in the affidavit plus accruing interest, which they claimed was impermissible. They asserted that they had not waived their rights by appealing the judgment, emphasizing that their appeal was within the same term of court and should therefore be considered valid to challenge the errors.

George G. Shepardson initiated a legal case against Thomas Stevens in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1874, following a dispute concerning a trust deed on certain lands in Ford County, Illinois. Shepardson previously owned the land and sold it to John Conley on October 24, 1870, accepting two promissory notes as part of the payment. On February 9, 1871, Conley executed a trust deed to secure those notes, which was not recorded until February 17, 1871. Just days before the trust deed was recorded, on February 13, Conley conveyed the land to Stevens, whose deed was recorded on February 14. The core issue was whether Stevens had notice of the trust deed when he purchased the land from Conley, or if he was aware of facts indicating he should have inquired about any existing liens. The court examined the evidence that suggested Stevens was aware of Conley’s debts and the arrangement surrounding the sale, establishing that he failed to conduct the necessary due diligence before the purchase.	Shepardson's primary argument was based on his assertion that the trust deed executed by Conley was valid and should be upheld, thus allowing him to foreclose on the property due to non-payment. He alleged that Stevens, when purchasing from Conley, should have been aware of the existing lien from the trust deed and therefore could not justifiably claim ownership without acknowledging Shepardson's rights stemming from the original transaction.	Stevens contended that he was unaware of the trust deed's existence at the time of his purchase. He argued that he did not have any actual notice and that the circumstances did not provide him with sufficient reason to inquire about any potential liens on the property. Stevens maintained that the lack of recorded notice and his own ignorance of the sale terms between Shepardson and Conley should protect him from the claims made by Shepardson.

John B. Moffett filed a bill in chancery against John Clements in the Macon Circuit Court, seeking the specific performance of a written agreement from April 29, 1834, which stipulated that Clements would convey a tract of land upon Moffett's payment of a $100 promissory note. This note was dated April 9, 1834, and was due sixty days after its issuance. The case revolves around a prior arrangement from 1832 where Moffett leased a stock farm to Clements, with each party sharing in the sales of stock. The defendant provided an inventory of about $1200 in stock sales on March 29, 1836, and Moffett offered to credit Clements for the land note in exchange for the land's conveyance, which Clements refused. Clements eventually paid a sum to Moffett's attorney but declined to accept an offer to settle the note. The Circuit Court concluded that Moffett failed to pay the purchase money properly, leading to a dismissal of the bill. An appeal was made by Moffett, stating a general error, claiming that the decree should favor him instead of Clements.	Moffett's primary claim was that he had fulfilled his obligation by paying the $100 promissory note, warranting the specific performance of the land conveyance contract. He argued that scheduling was not essential to the contract since the payment was made on the due date and sought enforcement of the agreement.	Clements contended that Moffett had not made any payment towards the purchase price of the land. He maintained that the allegations made by Moffett were unsupported by the evidence, asserting that the offer to settle was made significantly after the note's due date, and thus Moffett had not complied with the agreement.

In September 1873, in the town of Leepertown, Illinois, the defendants, Samuel J. Russell and Miles Masters, serving as highway commissioners, advertised for bids to construct two bridges. The advertisement stipulated that the contract would be awarded to the lowest and most responsible bidder according to the specifications available at the town clerk's office. Samuel J. Russell, the plaintiff, submitted the lowest bid of $238 for each bridge, totaling $476, and his bid was accepted by the defendants. However, after Russell procured the necessary materials worth $300 in reliance on this acceptance, he was forbidden by the defendants from proceeding with the work. This led to Russell claiming damages for breach of contract. A trial resulted in a judgment against Masters and Bussell for $50, which they subsequently appealed. The court found errors in the trial’s jury instructions regarding the existence of a binding contract due to lack of proper evidence and authority among the commissioners.	The plaintiff claims that he submitted the lowest bid to construct two bridges after the defendant commissioners advertised for such bids. He argues that once his bid was accepted, he acted upon this acceptance by acquiring materials necessary for the contract's execution. Therefore, he seeks damages amounting to $300 for the defendants' alleged breach of contract when they forbade him from completing the work as agreed.	The defendants contend that there was no formal contract as the bid was never finalized since the plaintiff did not appear for an arranged meeting after his bid was accepted. They argue that there was insufficient proof that any advertisement or specifications were communicated to the plaintiff and that one commissioner could not bind the others without their authority. Consequently, they request a reversal of the lower court's decision.

In 1888, in Cook County, Illinois, James Irwin filed a lawsuit against Arthur Christian in the circuit court. The case arose from a personal injury incident in which Irwin, while riding in a buggy with another man on Des Plaines Street, was struck by a horse and wagon driven by Christian's servant. The collision occurred at the intersection with Van-Buren Street, resulting in severe injuries to Irwin. Following the incident, Irwin claimed that the injuries were due to the negligence of Christian's servant. During the trial, Irwin presented evidence that suggested he was exercising due care at the time of the accident. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Irwin, awarding him damages of $2,500. Christian's subsequent motions asking for a verdict to be set aside and for a new trial were denied, leading to an appeal to the Appellate Court, which upheld the trial verdict. Christian then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court for further review of the case.	James Irwin claimed that he sustained personal injuries due to the negligence of Arthur Christian’s servant, who was driving the horse and wagon that collided with the buggy in which Irwin was a passenger. Irwin asserted that he was exercising due care at the time of the accident and sought compensatory damages for his injuries, which were evaluated at $2,500 by the jury after concluding the defendant was liable.	Arthur Christian contended the jury's damage award was excessive and sought to challenge the jury’s assessment of the facts. He claimed that the trial court failed to adequately instruct the jury regarding the issue of whether Irwin and the driver of the buggy exercised ordinary care to avoid the accident. Christian argued that any negligence on the part of his servant should not fully impose liability if the plaintiff also failed to take proper precautions.

The case of D. P. Good v. Chas. A. Allen took place in Iroquois County, Illinois, with the decision rendered on January 16, 1885. The central issue involved a promissory note executed on July 5, 1877, by the defendant, Chas. A. Allen, and another individual named Irwin, which was due on October 1 of the same year. The note, amounting to $54.75, was allegedly made payable to D. P. Good, the plaintiff. The defendant testified that the note was given under duress, as it was tied to the release of his cousin, who had been fined $40 for selling liquor and imprisoned. Allen, claiming to be the city attorney, allegedly offered to release the cousin from confinement in exchange for the note. The underlying judgment against the cousin remained unsatisfied. The trial court found in favor of the plaintiff, leading to the defendant's appeal, thus contesting the validity of the note and the authority under which it was executed.	The plaintiff, D. P. Good, claimed that the defendant owed the amount specified in the promissory note, which was executed under the premise of releasing the defendant's cousin from imprisonment for a municipal offense. Good argued that the note constituted a valid agreement and demanded repayment of the $54.75.	The defendant, Chas. A. Allen, contended that there was no legal consideration for the note since the underlying circumstances involved an improper release from a legally imposed penalty. He argued that the village attorney had no authority to accept a note in place of the fine or compromise the judgment against his cousin, asserting that any such agreement was illegal and invalid.

On September 16, 1842, in Galena, Illinois, Hezekiah H. Gear executed a promissory note for $1,900 payable to Nathaniel J. Brown, maturing 18 months later. After its maturity, the note was indorsed to John Lowery, who filed a lawsuit against Gear on September 12, 1860, in the Circuit Court of Jo Daviess County. The defendant asserted two defenses in response: the statute of limitations and a failure of consideration. The plaintiff claimed that two payments were made on the note—one for $30 on June 1, 1844, and another for $15 on January 29, 1848—implying a new promise to pay that would extend the statute of limitations. The trial jury found in favor of the defendant, leading Lowery to appeal the decision.	John Lowery claimed that since he was the holder of the promissory note, Hezekiah H. Gear was obligated to pay. Lowery argued that the payments made on the note within the prior sixteen years constituted an implied new promise to pay, which should bar the statute of limitations defense raised by Gear. The plaintiff sought to recover the full amount due on the note.	Hezekiah H. Gear's primary defense was that the statute of limitations barred Lowery's claim, as more than sixteen years had passed since the note's maturity. Furthermore, Gear contended there was a failure of consideration, arguing that the payments made did not constitute an acknowledgment or new promise to pay the debt. He asserted that any acknowledgment of payments made was unauthorized and did not bind him.

Thompson Tomlin (the appellant) initiated a legal action against The Tonica and Petersburg Railroad Company (the appellee) in Illinois, centering on a subscription for stock in the railroad company. The dispute arose in Mason County Circuit Court during its October term in 1859, with the plaintiffs claiming damages amounting to $1,500. Tomlin allegedly contracted to subscribe ten shares of stock, valued at $1,000, on August 1, 1857. However, he contested the validity of the subscription based on claims of fraudulent representations made by the railroad's agents regarding the route of the railroad, asserting that the railroad would run through a farm which ultimately was not the case. The case involved multiple counts in the declaration, including special counts detailing the subscription and common counts asserting general obligations. During the trial, issues arose regarding the legitimacy of the calls for payment on the stock owed by Tomlin, with the defense arguing that these calls were invalid, resulting in a jury verdict against Tomlin for $990. Following this, Tomlin contested the verdict and subsequent judgments on several grounds, including the introduction of improper evidence and the mishandling of the jury instructions.	Tomlin's primary claims included that he had legally subscribed to the stock on the condition that the railroad would run through a certain farm, which was critical to his investment. He argued that the railroad did not fulfill this condition and that he was misled by agents of the railroad company regarding the construction of the line. The plaintiff requested damages for the failure of the defendant to comply with the contractual obligations concerning the stock subscription.	The defense, representing The Tonica and Petersburg Railroad Company, contended that the subscription was void due to fraud, asserting that Tomlin was induced to sign the subscription based on misleading statements about the railroad's route made by the plaintiffs' agents. The defense argued that the calls for payment were invalid and not legally sufficient as they lacked proper notice as required by the corporate charter. Additionally, they maintained that the court had improperly admitted evidence supporting the plaintiff's claims.

In 1886, a legal dispute arose in Cairo, Illinois, involving a real estate matter concerning lots 30 and 31 in block 53. The case was initiated by Eugene E. Ellis against Angus Leek as a suit in ejectment, with Ellis being the real party in interest. Both parties claimed title to the properties through Henry B. and Thomas B. Ellis; Ellis held the title through a mortgage resulting from a strict foreclosure, while Leek claimed it via a tax deed. A strict foreclosure decree was issued after Holmes B. Kelly, the complainant in the initial case, successfully prayed for the foreclosure against the Ellis defendants, who admitted the allegations and consented to the decree. The decree allowed the defendants 90 days to pay a sum owed, failing which they would lose all rights to the properties, which would then vest entirely in Kelly. The court found the properties were not worth the debt owed. After Kelly transferred his legal title to Ellis on January 18, 1887, Leek attempted to assert his claim through a tax deed, but the lower court excluded this evidence, ruling that Ellis maintained valid title through Kelly's ownership.	The plaintiff, Eugene E. Ellis, contended that he rightfully obtained ownership of the properties through the decree of strict foreclosure, which vested the title in Holmes B. Kelly, who subsequently conveyed it to him. Ellis argued that the procedures followed in the foreclosure were consistent with Illinois practice and that the previous foreclosure decree sufficed to establish his legal title to the properties.	Angus Leek, the defendant, argued primarily that the plaintiff's evidence failed to establish a legal title. He contested the lower court's exclusion of his affidavit and tax deed as valid evidence for his claim. His defense centered on the idea that the foreclosure decree did not sufficiently convey title since it lacked a final order searching for compliance with the payment terms.

John C. Jones v. John W. Neely is a legal case that commenced in chancery court on September 4, 1869, relating to a dispute over land conveyance. The events trace back to April 13, 1868, when John W. Neely sold 117.6 acres of land to Henry A. Ash for $2000, structured through four promissory notes and a commitment from Ash to support Neely until the debt was settled. Neely entrusted the notes and bond to Ash for safekeeping, under the condition that Ash would return them. However, Ash failed to meet these obligations, refusing to return the documents despite Neely's repeated requests, and subsequently neglected to support him as promised. Furthermore, Ash allegedly fraudulently obtained the property deed by deceiving Neely, as he was believed to be a minor at the time of the transaction. Ash later conveyed the land to Jones without any consideration. The matter escalated with Jones answering to the court after Ash failed to appear, and the court ultimately ordered the cancellation of both deeds. Jones appealed the decision, claiming the court overstepped its jurisdiction.	Neely, the plaintiff, asserts that Ash obtained the deed through fraud and deceit, failing to deliver the promised notes and bond while neglecting his duty to support Neely. Neely contends that the court has the authority to annul the deed due to this fraudulent conduct. He seeks the cancellation of the land conveyances as the fraudulent actions invalidated the transaction, a remedy which he believes is justifiable under equitable laws concerning fraud.	Jones, the defendant, argues that the court erred by granting equitable relief since Neely's claims against Ash, who defaulted, could have been adequately addressed in a legal context. He contends that the allegations do not warrant the court's assumption of jurisdiction as there exists a sufficient remedy at law. Additionally, Jones asserts that his answer to the bill should not constitute evidence, and notes the absence of a formal replication as a reason for the decree to be challenged.

The case, "The Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company v. Robert Johnston," takes place in Iroquois County, Illinois, in September 1874. Robert Johnston, the plaintiff, initiated legal action against the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company following an incident where the railway's negligence allegedly led to the death of his livestock. The main issue at hand was whether the railway company had failed to adequately fence its tracks, resulting in the animals being killed. The appellant railway company sought to argue that Johnston was guilty of contributory negligence, claiming that he allowed the animals to roam freely. However, the evidence presented indicated that the livestock escaped from their pasture without Johnston’s fault.	The plaintiff, Robert Johnston, claimed he suffered damages due to the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company's negligence in failing to maintain proper fencing along their tracks. He sought compensation for the value of the livestock that was killed, asserting that he should not be held accountable for any contributory negligence, as the animals escaped without his fault. Moreover, Johnston believed that interest should be awarded on the assessed damages from the date of the livestock's death.	The defendant, Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company, argued that Johnston was contributorily negligent because he let the livestock run at large. They contended that the damages awarded to Johnston were excessive, as they believed the assessed value was significantly lower than what the jury determined. Additionally, the railway company challenged the court's instruction allowing interest on the damages, stating that it was incorrect and not supported by precedent.

In June 1850, M. McConnell purchased the Morgan House (now known as the Mansion House) in Jacksonville, Illinois, from the heirs of the late Governor Duncan. The property included a description and reservation concerning mutual use of the partition wall shared with an adjacent one-story brick building. In 1858, P. B. Price acquired the land next to the Mansion House, where the old building stood, and replaced it with a new three-story structure. In constructing this new building, Price improperly utilized the Mansion House's west wall as part of his structure, making alterations that caused damage to McConnell's property, including structural injuries due to unauthorized joist insertion and modifications to the foundations. McConnell subsequently sued Price for the consequential damages incurred during the construction, leading to this legal dispute.	McConnell, the plaintiff, claimed that Price's construction efforts caused significant damage to the Mansion House, violating the reservation rights detailed in his property deed. He argued that Price had no legal right to use portions of the wall beyond what was previously designated as a partition wall and sought compensation for damages amounting to $500, asserting that Price's actions constituted an infringement on his property rights.	Price, the defendant, contended that he had acquired rights to use the entire west wall of the Mansion House as a partition wall through his deed of conveyance and argued that his construction was necessary and appropriate for the new building. He sought to reverse the judgment rendered against him in favor of McConnell, advocating for the legality of his use of the wall and asserting that no damages should be awarded.

The case, County of La Salle v. William R. Milligan, was decided on February 8, 1890, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The legal dispute arose in La Salle County, Illinois, involving the sheriff, William R. Milligan, and the county, represented by the County of La Salle. The sheriff sought recovery for fees and expenses he claimed were due as part of his office's operations. Concurrently, the county accused the sheriff of unlawfully receiving a substantial sum from the county treasury, which they asserted exceeded the legitimate fees due to him. The disputes were consolidated for trial without a jury, resulting in a verdict against the sheriff for $1,891.89. The trial considered multiple transactions and accounts over four years, indicating a total of over $90,000. Central to the case were claims regarding what constituted legitimate expenses of the sheriff’s office and the validity of previous financial settlements between the sheriff and the county.	The plaintiff, the County of La Salle, claimed that the sheriff, William R. Milligan, had received payments that were illegal and exceeded the actual fees due for his services. They argued that considerable sums had been paid out of the county treasury for expenses that were not legitimate costs of the sheriff's office. Therefore, the county sought to recover these alleged overpayments and emphasized that prior settlements should not prevent them from retrieving these funds.	The defendant, Sheriff William R. Milligan, contended that the county had indeed settled accounts with him, accepting his statements of fees and expenses paid over time. He argued that according to the principles of estoppel, the county was barred from seeking repayment of the amounts they had previously approved. Milligan maintained that the payments he received were legitimate expenses allowed under statutory provisions, and he challenged the county's claims regarding what constitutes allowable expenses for his office.

In 1871, a legal proceeding began in St. Clair County, Illinois, involving the estate of John Scheel, who had served as the guardian for minor heirs of Adam Eidman. The case was initiated by William, Margaret, Michael, and Louisa Eidman to determine the amount owed to them from Scheel’s estate concerning funds from the sale of a tract of land previously partitioned among them. The guardian Scheel was supposed to manage these funds but failed to separate or account for them individually. This legal action sought to recover a total of $1,444, which included money received by Scheel as guardian, specifically $624.86, plus interest calculations. The case evolved through multiple rulings, with the original judgment favoring the surviving heirs Michael, William, and Margaret Eidman. The executors of Scheel’s estate contested this ruling on technical grounds, questioning the legitimacy of a joint claim and the judgment's wording, which did not specify the executors. Over time, it became complicated due to the death of one supposed heir, Louise, and the court had to navigate the claims for her share, complicated by lack of sufficient evidence regarding her status as an heir.	The plaintiffs, the surviving heirs, argued that they were entitled to the full amount of funds that their guardian had failed to account for. They asserted that the claim was valid as it involved a joint amount due to all four wards, necessitating that they collectively pursue the claim against Scheel’s estate. They sought a judgment acknowledging their rights to the assets that came into Scheel's control during his guardianship tenure, claiming that the guardianship relationship entitled them to recover their shares along with accrued interest.	The defendants, representing the estate of John Scheel, contended that the claim brought jointly by the plaintiffs was improper, asserting that each heir should have pursued their claims separately as it was not a valid joint claim. They also raised procedural issues, arguing that the judgment was incorrectly directed against the estate rather than the executors. Additionally, they disputed the calculation of interests awarded by the court and sought to prevent the recovery of the deceased heir’s portion, claiming the plaintiffs did not adequately prove their entitlement to that share.

In the fall of 1863, in Fairview township, Fulton County, Illinois, James Headen sued Leonard H. Rust for trespass, claiming damages from Rust's hogs that had entered Headen's corn field. The incident occurred over several months when Rust's hogs, allowed to roam freely, destroyed $25 worth of corn in Headen's duly fenced field. During the initial trial before a justice of the peace, Headen was awarded $7.50 but appealed the decision to the Circuit Court. Evidence presented by Headen claimed that his fence was sufficient to keep out non-breachy hogs, while Rust’s defense countered this by asserting that the fence was inadequate, allowing hogs to enter freely. The jury ultimately sided with Rust after the court refused to accept certain jury instructions requested by Headen. This led Headen to motion for a new trial, which was denied. He subsequently brought the appeal before the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the lower court erred in its jury instructions regarding the responsibility of landowners to maintain sufficient fencing.	Headen's main argument centered around the assertion that his fence was adequate to keep Rust's hogs out, and thus he should be compensated for the damages to his corn crop. He contended that regardless of the fence's condition, he had a right to recover damages for the trespass caused by Rust's hogs. He requested the court to direct the jury to assess the damages incurred due to the hogs' destruction of his corn.	Rust argued that the law in Illinois does not require landowners to keep their livestock contained and asserted that Headen's fence was not sufficient to keep out the hogs. Rust's defense requested the court to instruct the jury that for Headen to recover damages, he needed to prove his field was sufficiently fenced. Therefore, if the jury found the fence inadequate, they should rule in favor of Rust.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois, for use, etc., v. James H. Leaton et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on September 27, 1887. The origin of the case lies in a debt action concerning an appeal bond related to a judgment from the Circuit Court of McLean County. This appeal was granted under the condition that the appellants, Leaton and others, file a bond in the sum of $2000 with sufficient security approved by the circuit clerk within thirty days after the judgment. However, the executed bond omitted the name of one of the appellees as a payee. The clerk, without approval of the bond from the circuit court, accepted and transmitted the bond to the Appellate Court for review. A demurrer raised against the declaration was sustained by the circuit court, and this judgment was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court. The Supreme Court then reviewed the case in light of statutory provisions related to appeals and the duties of clerks regarding bond approval.	The plaintiff claimed that the circuit clerk improperly approved the appeal bond, which lacked the necessary formalities, specifically the omission of an appellee's name. They argued that this lack of compliance should invalidate the bond and the appeal itself. The plaintiff requested the court to uphold the circuit court's decision to sustain the demurrer and affirm the inadequacy of the bond.	The defendants contended that the clerk's approval was limited strictly to the sufficiency of the security provided for the bond. They argued that the omission of the appellee's name did not impact the bond's validity in terms of securing the appeal. Furthermore, they asserted that approval of the security did not make the bond invalid, and any alleged errors did not arise to a level that would deny their right to appeal.

On January 18, 1840, the Illinois General Assembly authorized Hezekiah H. Gear to maintain a ferry across the Mississippi River, providing him the rights to operate at a designated point for ten years, later extended to thirty years in 1849. On August 10, 1862, John H. Bullerdick obtained a license from Jackson County, Iowa, allowing him to operate a ferry from Whiteside’s Landing in Iowa to Jo Daviess County, Illinois. Bullerdick ran his ferry and collected fares, occasionally from Illinois passengers. The Gears, claiming that they held an exclusive franchise for three miles up and down the river from their established ferry, contended that Bullerdick's operations infringed on their rights. Consequently, the Gears forcibly took Bullerdick's ferryboat and relocated it to Galena, leading Bullerdick to file an action of replevin for the return of his property in the Jo Daviess Circuit Court.	The primary argument of John H. Bullerdick is that he operated his ferry under a valid license granted by the proper authorities in Iowa, which entitled him to carry passengers and freight legally across the Mississippi River to Illinois. Bullerdick maintained that the Gears had no lawful grounds to seize his boat without a court's determination of any forfeiture for operating within their claimed territory.	The Gears claimed that they held an exclusive right to operate a ferry within a defined area along the Mississippi. They argued that Bullerdick was running his ferry without valid authority and infringing on their established franchise. Asserting that the boat had become forfeited due to Bullerdick's illegal operations, they sought a declaration of ownership and return of the seized ferryboat.

In 1876, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between William C. Poleman and Nels Johnson. The case centered around an alleged fraudulent transaction in which Poleman sold eighteen shares of stock in the Chicago Metallic Cement Manufacturing and Roofing Company to Johnson. Johnson claimed that Poleman deceitfully induced him to believe the stock was valuable, while in reality, it was worthless, and that Poleman was aware of this fact at the time of sale. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, with Mr. Justice Dickey delivering the opinion. After examining the evidence, the court found that there was no significant proof to support Johnson's allegations of fraud against Poleman. As a result, the court found that the evidence did not constitute a case against the defendant.	Nels Johnson, the plaintiff, argued that William C. Poleman engaged in deceit by selling him stock that was represented as valuable when it was, in fact, worthless. Johnson claimed that Poleman had purposely misled him about the stock's value, knowing it to be worthless at the time of sale. He sought damages for the alleged fraud.	William C. Poleman, the defendant, countered Johnson's claims by asserting that the evidence presented by the plaintiff did not substantiate the allegations of fraud. Poleman requested that the court exclude the plaintiff's evidence from jury consideration, arguing that there was a lack of proof to support any essential allegations made by Johnson. The defendant sought a verdict in his favor based on the absence of sufficient evidence.

In the year 1854, in Naperville, Illinois, Jesse B. Ketchum was involved in a legal dispute with his neighbor, James B. Stolp. The case arose from a dispute over the construction of a partition fence that Ketchum was legally obligated to build between his property and Stolp’s. After being notified, Ketchum failed to construct the fence within the required timeframe, prompting Stolp to take legal action. The initial proceedings occurred before justices of the peace, who ordered Stolp to build the fence and directed Ketchum to pay for it. Stolp constructed the fence using a combination of new materials and existing posts but did not meet a town resolution specifying that the fence must be four and a half feet high. Ketchum contested the payment, asserting that Stolp had not built the fence according to local standards, despite evidence that the fence was functional for its intended purpose. The case eventually escalated to the Circuit Court of Kane County after moving through the legal system.	Ketchum argued that Stolp was not entitled to payment because the fence he built did not conform to the town's specified height requirement of four and a half feet as established by local voters. Ketchum sought to argue that since the fence did not meet this resolution, it was not a lawful fence and, therefore, Stolp should not receive any compensation for its construction.	Stolp maintained that the fence he constructed was adequate for its purpose and met the legal standards outlined in the order of the justices, which did not specify the height of the fence. He argued that Ketchum was obligated to pay for the fence he had built, regardless of its height, as it was functional and served the intended purpose of fencing in cattle. Stolp contended that Ketchum's objections were overly technical and disregarded the practical nature of neighborhood laws designed to resolve such disputes equitably.

On September 30, 1852, in Marshall County, Illinois, Benjamin L. T. Bourland entered into a contract with William Sickles and others for the sale of land, specifically the northeast quarter of Section 29 in Township 12 north, Range 8 east. The agreement stipulated that Bourland would provide a quit-claim deed upon receipt of $200, payable in four installments of $50 each on January 1 of the years 1853, 1854, 1855, and 1856, with the addition of interest. On March 13, 1858, Bourland tendered a deed to Sickles and demanded the remaining purchase money and interest. Sickles, however, refused to accept the deed or make the payment. Bourland subsequently initiated a legal action of debt against the defendants for breach of contract. The court proceedings involved a demurrer filed by the defendants, which the court sustained, leading to a judgment against Bourland for costs. Bourland contested this judgment, which prompted the writ of error process leading to the appellate review by the Illinois Supreme Court.	Bourland's main argument revolved around the enforcement of the contract for the sale of land and the validity of his tender of a deed along with a demand for payment. He contended that the defendants' refusal to accept the deed constituted a breach of their contractual obligations. He sought to overturn the lower court's judgment that sustained the defendants' demurrer, thereby allowing him to pursue the original claim for the recovery of the unpaid purchase money.	The defendants' primary defense rested on the assertion that Bourland's declaration was fundamentally flawed due to the lack of a clear tender of the deed as required by the contract terms. They argued that without indicating where the purported amendment to the declaration should be inserted, the amendments were ineffective and led to obscurity in the plaintiff's claims. This confusion justified their demurrer, which the court upheld, leading to the conclusion that Bourland could not recover the unpaid amount since he did not aver an unequivocal offer to perform his part of the contract.

In May 1887, in Cook County, Illinois, William S. Lane and Maud B. Lane were involved in a divorce case. The appellee, Maud B. Lane, filed a bill for divorce against the appellant, William S. Lane, citing habitual drunkenness and extreme cruelty. She claimed that she was without means to support herself and their child and requested temporary alimony and legal fees. Evidence was presented from both sides regarding Lane’s ability to earn a living and support his family. The chancellor presiding over the case ordered Lane to pay Maud $50 for solicitor’s fees and $5 weekly in advance as temporary alimony. Upon appeal, Lane argued that the order was an abuse of judicial discretion, citing his lack of money and property. The case raised questions about the ability of a husband to provide support even when he appears destitute.	Maud B. Lane claimed that William S. Lane was habitually drunk and cruel, which justified her request for a divorce. She alleged that he had the capacity to earn a good living and support her and their child but chose not to do so. She applied for temporary alimony and solicitor's fees, emphasizing her lack of financial resources.	William S. Lane defended against the claims by asserting his lack of money and property, arguing that the chancellor’s order to pay temporary alimony was an abuse of discretion. He contended that the evidence from his affidavit clearly demonstrated his inability to support his wife and child financially, challenging the need for such an order.

In the case of Archibald Williams v. Richmond Merritt, the events date back to the early 19th century, with key transactions occurring around 1820. Williams, the plaintiff, claimed a title to a land parcel located in Hancock County, Illinois, which had been granted as a military bounty following the War of 1812. The dispute arose from a series of land transactions initiated by Nathaniel Abbott and other property owners, who engaged Abraham Beck as their land agent to facilitate the sale of their land. Although a power of attorney was issued to Beck, it was limited in scope, requiring him to secure a mortgage on the properties sold. However, Beck sold the land to William O’Harra without obtaining such collateral; he obtained only a personal covenant instead. After nearly four decades, in 1859, Archibald Williams sought recovery of the land, leading to a court trial where he faced a plea of not guilty from Merritt, who had acquired title through subsequent transactions involving O’Harra. The trial was conducted in the Hancock Circuit Court by Judge Sibley, and the court found in favor of Merritt.	Archibald Williams contended that the sale of the land to O’Harra by his agent, Abraham Beck, was invalid due to the breach of the conditions outlined in the power of attorney. He asserted that Beck’s sale exceeded the authority granted to him, making the transaction null and void. Williams aimed to recover the land based on the argument that the principal, Abbott, had not ratified Beck's unauthorized act, and thus he requested the court to declare the title in his favor.	Richmond Merritt’s defense relied on the argument that the original landowners, including Abbott, had effectively ratified Beck's sale through their long silence and inaction over the years. Merritt claimed that the power of attorney had been executed and utilized properly according to acknowledged practices in real estate transactions at the time. He contended that since sufficient time had passed without objection from Abbott, the transaction should be viewed as valid. Merritt requested the court to affirm his title to the land based on this acquiescence.

In April 1858, in Winnebago County, Illinois, Frederick Brown, an attorney, found himself imprisoned due to a contempt ruling made by Justice of the Peace John Garver. The incident occurred on January 23, 1858, during a court proceeding where Brown allegedly made a significant disturbance and refused to comply with orders to cease. As a consequence of his actions, Justice Garver fined Brown five dollars for contempt and ordered his imprisonment until the fine was paid or he was released by lawful means. Following his arrest on the morning he filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, Brown's case was presented to the Circuit Court, where Judge Sheldon denied his motion for discharge and upheld the fine and commitment order.	The central argument presented by Frederick Brown was that the imprisonment resulting from the contempt ruling was unjust. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, seeking to be released from imprisonment on the grounds that the justice of the peace lacked the authority to imprison him until he paid the fine. Brown's legal team maintained that the imprisonment for contempt was not a lawful exercise of power.	The defense, represented by State’s Attorney W. Bushnell, argued that the justice of the peace possessed the requisite authority to impose fines and enforce the payment through imprisonment. They contended that the ability to fine and imprison those found in contempt was essential for the proper administration of justice and that limiting this power would undermine the court's authority and effectiveness.

On October 18, 1884, Edward C. Huling entered into a partnership with Simeon Farwell and Stephen Lasky as merchants in Chicago, forming the firm Farwell, Huling & Go. By the summer of 1885, conflicts arose within the partnership, leading Huling to file a bill for an accounting. Following this, a master was appointed to assess the firm’s finances, presenting a report on October 28, 1888. The report indicated that the firm incurred a total loss of $8,234.79 and assigned a value of $5,000 to Huling's interest in the firm's goodwill. The master ultimately found that Farwell and Lasky owed Huling $1,596.70. Huling raised several objections to the master’s findings, contending that the goodwill’s value should have been set at $25,000, that the evidence considered was unreliable, and that the report contradicted the weight of the evidence. The appellees countered by asserting that the goodwill had no value at all. After reviewing the exceptions to the master’s report, the court ultimately ruled in favor of the appellees, resulting in a decree against Huling.	Edward C. Huling, the plaintiff, argued that the master undervalued his interest in the goodwill of the partnership, claiming it should be $25,000 instead of the reported $5,000. He contended that the master relied on incorrect evidence and made errors in assessing the losses, maintaining that the business, contrary to the master’s finding, was profitable at the relevant time. Huling sought a revised accounting and payment of the amount he claimed was owed to him.	The defendants, Simeon Farwell and Stephen Lasky, argued that the master’s evaluation of Huling’s goodwill was justified and properly calculated. They contested Huling's claims about the partnership's profitability, insisting instead that the partnership incurred a significant loss. The defendants sought to uphold the master’s report and maintain that Huling should not be credited with any value for goodwill, contesting his assertions about the erroneous evaluations.

In December 1854, the case of Cyrus H. McCormick v. Daniel Elston et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal dispute originated from a contract related to the sale and delivery of 100,000 bricks, which Elston, one of the plaintiffs, had entered into with McCormick. The bricks were to be delivered at McCormick's factory in Chicago, with an agreed price of four dollars and fifty cents per thousand bricks. The plaintiffs argued that the contract was for the delivery of quality bricks, but McCormick claimed that the quantity and quality stipulated were not delivered as promised. The defendants sought to establish a partnership in the brick business, raising the issue of whether they could pursue a joint action to enforce the contract with McCormick, who had only signed with Elston. The trial took place after the delivery of the bricks began in August and ended in October or November of 1851, with the suit filed in December of the same year. The proceedings included various evidence attempts regarding the partnership and proper documentation of the transactions.	The plaintiff, Cyrus H. McCormick, claimed that Daniel Elston, one of the appellees, breached the contract for the sale and delivery of 100,000 bricks by failing to provide the proper quantity and quality at the agreed times and locations. McCormick sought damages for the inadequate delivery of goods and compensation for work and labor incurred due to the breach. He requested that the court enforce his claims against Elston and Sleight, asserting that they could not join in the action since the contract was made solely with Elston.	The defendants, Daniel Elston and Sleight, contended that the contract was made with Elston alone, and they argued that they were entitled to a joint action based on their ownership interest in the bricks. They raised defenses concerning a set-off for damages resulting from the alleged breach of the contract, asserting that McCormick had not been delivered the agreed quantity or quality of bricks. They requested the court to consider their partnership and the established amounts due as a legitimate defense to McCormick's claims.

On January 20, 1882, in Cornell, Livingston County, Illinois, a constable (appellee) levied executions against an individual named Dodwell. The levy was placed on approximately five hundred bushels of corn and a buggy in a railway car belonging to the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company, which the constable claimed was the property of Dodwell. However, it was disputed whether the constable took actual possession of the goods or had control over them at the time of the levy. After the levy, the railway car containing the goods was shipped out the following day, allegedly under Dodwell's direction. The plaintiff initiated a trespass suit against Dodwell and another party, Benjamin Burt, resulting in a jury verdict against the defendants for $342. The trial court denied their motion for a new trial, and they subsequently appealed the ruling. It was later determined that the corn was never owned by Dodwell nor in his possession during the levy, as it belonged to a third party, Francis Carpenter, who had sent Dodwell money to purchase the corn on his behalf.	The plaintiff, a constable, claimed that he had a valid levy on the corn and buggy as the property of Dodwell and sought compensation for the trespass committed by Dodwell and Burt when they removed the goods from the railway car without permission. The argument hinged on the assertion that the plaintiff had rightful possession at the time of the alleged trespass and that the defendants had acted unlawfully in retaking the property.	The defendants argued that the goods taken by the plaintiff did not belong to Dodwell, as he did not possess them at the time of the alleged levy. They maintained that the corn was owned by Carpenter and that the plaintiff had no right to seize it since it was not the property of Dodwell. They also contended that the constable's actions amounted to a trespass since he attempted to levy against property that he had no right to.

The case "William M. Kilgour et al. v. John B. Crawford et ux." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1869. The case took place in Whiteside County and involved a dispute over a 40-acre parcel of land that descended from Ezekiel J. Kilgour. Key individuals include William M. Kilgour, Elizabeth G. Kilgour, Haney Crawford, and John B. Crawford. Haney Crawford and his wife initiated a partition proceeding against William M. Kilgour and Elizabeth G. Kilgour, claiming rights to the land's division. The court found that the land could not be physically divided based on its dimensions and configuration. Consequently, a sale of the property was decreed. William M. Kilgour appealed this decision. During the proceedings, various procedural issues arose regarding the filing of answers and objections to the court's actions, including a disputed mortgage against the property.	The plaintiffs claimed a right to partition the land based on their ownership interests. They argued that the court's determination should ensure that all parties' rights regarding the property, including any existing mortgages, were clearly defined and that the sale took place without ambiguity regarding liens against the property.	The defendants contended that the court made procedural errors in the required filings and in the handling of the mortgage associated with the land. They argued that the court failed to adequately address the mortgage during the proceedings and did not make sufficient findings regarding the financial interests tied to that mortgage. The defendants maintained that the sale should either clarify these liens or discharge the property from them.

The case of The Chicago Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company v. John Notzki took place in Peoria, Illinois, occurring on May 18, 1871. The plaintiff, John Notzki, was involved in an accident at a public street crossing where a train operated by the defendant, Chicago Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company, collided with his team as he attempted to cross the tracks. This collision resulted in severe injuries to Notzki, including a tragic amputation of his hand, the death of his horse, and significant damage to his wagon. The negligence attributed to the defendant included failing to ring a bell or sound a whistle at the time of the accident, operating the train at excessive speed in violation of city ordinances, and allowing trains and cars to obstruct the view of the approaching train. Notzki frequently crossed the tracks at this location, raising questions about his awareness of the potential dangers at the crossing. During the trial, the defendant attempted to introduce evidence regarding the customary practices of various railroad companies in the area, which was denied by the court, along with a defense instruction aimed at shifting some blame onto Notzki. The trial ruled in favor of Notzki with a verdict awarding him $5,500.	The plaintiff, John Notzki, claimed that he suffered severe injuries due to the negligence of the Chicago Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company. He argued that the defendant failed to ring a bell or sound a whistle when their train approached the street crossing, and that the train was operating above the permitted speed limit. Furthermore, he contended that by allowing trains to block the view of the tracks, the company created an unsafe situation that directly led to his accident and injuries, which included the amputation of his hand.	The defendant, Chicago Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company, defended against the claims by arguing that the jury was improperly instructed regarding the liability related to whistle and bell signals. They asserted that the instruction should have required proof that the negligence (failure to sound the signals) was directly related to the plaintiff’s injury. Additionally, the defendant contested that Notzki, being familiar with the crossing, was aware of the dangers presented by the presence of a switchman who signaled the train, suggesting that he also bore some responsibility for the accident.

Thomas E. Melvin et al. v. Charles D. Hodges is a case tried in January 1874 in Greene County, Illinois. The case arose when Charles D. Hodges filed a lawsuit against Thomas E. Melvin and Henry Rainey to recover $500 allegedly owed under a promissory note. Hodges claimed that Rainey approached him to borrow the money, offering Melvin as surety. Hodges prepared the note, which Rainey returned after having it signed by Melvin. During the trial, the jury found in favor of Hodges, deciding that Melvin was responsible for the amount due on the note. Melvin, who had exclusively been served with process, contested this decision by asserting defenses regarding the sufficiency of the evidence proving his execution of the note. After the trial court denied his motion for a new trial, Melvin appealed the ruling.	The plaintiff, Charles D. Hodges, argued that he had a valid promissory note signed by both defendants, Thomas E. Melvin and Henry Rainey. He claimed that the note was executed validly and that Melvin was liable as the surety for Rainey’s debt of $500. Hodges requested the court to enforce the payment of the amount due on the note, including any accruing interest.	Thomas E. Melvin’s main defense was grounded in the assertion that the execution of the promissory note was not sufficiently proven. He claimed procedural errors during the trial concerning the admissibility of the note into evidence and the basis for the identification of his signature. Melvin sought a new trial, arguing that the evidence presented did not support the jury's verdict and requested the court to overturn the prior ruling.

This case, titled *Henry F. McCloskey v. Cyrus H. McCormick et al.*, was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1865. The action originated from a sheriff's sale in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, where a warehouse and its contents were sold as part of an execution against the previous owner, John Bennett. The defendants, Henry McCloskey being the primary, reached an agreement with the plaintiffs, who were Cyrus H. McCormick and his associates, to purchase the warehouse and its contents for $1200. A written memorandum, acting as a bill of sale, listed various movable items, explicitly excluding “442 tierces and 100 barrels of salt.” However, it was claimed that fifty barrels of salt were mistakenly included in the bill of sale. The dispute arose when the plaintiffs alleged that McCloskey wrongfully retained the fifty barrels of salt, which they argued were never meant to be sold. A trial took place, during which oral testimonies were presented alongside the written bill of sale, leading to arguments about the legitimacy of the evidence and the interpretation of the contract. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of the plaintiffs for $142.50, leading to further legal proceedings concerning the evidence admitted during the trial.	The plaintiffs claimed ownership of the fifty barrels of salt that they argued were not meant to be included in the sale to McCloskey. They sought legal remedy for the wrongful retention of the salt, claiming that the written bill of sale had been executed in mistake and did not accurately reflect the agreement between the parties. The plaintiffs contended that the evidence presented by McCloskey was inadmissible as it contradicted the written agreement, which they believed was a clear agreement of sale that should not be modified by parol evidence.	The defendant, McCloskey, argued that the bill of sale had been executed due to a mistaken understanding and that the evidence provided in court should include oral testimony to clarify the actual intent regarding the sale of the salt. McCloskey's defense centered around the premise that the plaintiffs should not be permitted to exclude parol evidence that could showcase that the salt was not intended to be sold. He asserted that oral evidence was essential to explain the transaction's details, which he claimed could demonstrate that the bill inaccurately represented the items sold. McCloskey requested a new trial based on these assertions after the jury's initial verdict.

Alexander M. Jenkins, the appellant, brought a case against Daniel H. Brush, the appellee, in the Jackson Circuit Court in Illinois during the May term of 1844. The case revolved around an agreement made on May 3, 1839, where Brush was tasked to collect various notes, accounts, and judgments owed to Jenkins, retaining half of the collected amounts as compensation. Jenkins claimed that Brush failed to utilize due diligence, resulting in significant financial losses. Throughout the trial, evidence showed that while Brush had collected a portion of the debts, Jenkins had also controlled many claims, affecting the recoverable amount. The jury found in favor of Brush, awarding him $335.60, which Jenkins contested, seeking a new trial on the grounds that the jury's verdict contradicted the evidence presented. Ultimately, Brush agreed to a remittitur, further reducing the verdict amount to $79.25, and the court upheld the jury's original decision, citing sufficient evidence supporting the payment claims.	Jenkins claimed that Brush did not exercise proper diligence in collecting debts owed to him, leading to considerable financial loss. He argued that Brush had collected $2,000 but failed to pay him half of the sum due, seeking restitution for the amounts he believed were mismanaged or unreturned.	Brush countered Jenkins's claims by asserting that he had used due diligence in collecting the debts. He presented a defense grounded in mutual accountability, proving that Jenkins had received considerable payments and that many of the debts were either uncollectible or had already been settled. Brush sought to establish that he owed Jenkins an amount substantially lower than what Jenkins claimed.

In the case of **John Gilmore v. Ephraim Gilmore et al.**, the events took place in McLean County, Illinois, following the death of Nathaniel Gilmore on November 22, 1855. The deceased left behind his widow, Mary, and eight children: John, Craig, Eliza J., Albert, William, Ephraim, Mary Ann, and Johnson, who were his only heirs. After Nathaniel's death, the family continued to live together on their homestead, known as the "Empire farm," which consisted of 300 acres, while also owning another farm, the "Downs farm," under a purchase contract. The dispute arose as Ephraim Gilmore filed a bill for partition against his mother and siblings, seeking a division of the two farms and assignment of dower. John Gilmore, claiming to have a right to reimbursement for taxes and improvements paid for the properties, filed a cross-bill. The case was reviewed, revealing that extensive family labor and profits from the farms contributed to improvements and payments owed on the properties. The court had to determine the rightful distribution of assets among the heirs, the widow's dower, and the impact of past agreements made among the surviving family members.	Ephraim Gilmore, the plaintiff, sought the partition of the Empire and Downs farms and the assignment of dower from his deceased father's estate. He argued that the widow and other siblings had either agreed to or acquiesced in arrangements that undermined his rightful interest in the properties and rental profits generated from them. His claims were based on assertions of equitable treatment and fair distribution of the estate’s assets among all heirs, particularly in light of past settlements that he deemed unfair.	John Gilmore, the defendant and one of the heirs, contended that he had certain equities against Ephraim and Albert Shaver due to payments made for taxes and significant improvements on the farms. John asserted that the contributions made on the Downs farm should be reimbursed proportionately among the heirs. He emphasized that the arrangements made in 1870 established the framework for compensation and division of the estate, which he claimed should hold in the current proceedings. John's defense was based upon his interpretation of familial agreements and the joint nature of labor that benefited the entire family.

In April 1868, private bankers McCann & Smith in Nebraska ordered twelve pieces of "Agricultural College scrip" from plaintiffs Stephen P. Lunt et al., who were also private bankers in Illinois. The plaintiffs procured the scrip from defendants John H. Wrenn and another party, offering it for sale at $160 each. The plaintiffs complied with the order and paid a total of $1,920 for the scrip, which authorized holders to locate land in the United States. However, when the scrip was presented to the U.S. General Land Office for patents, six pieces were pronounced counterfeit and worthless in early 1872. Consequently, members of McCann & Smith assigned the scrip to a man named Walker, who later sued them for the money paid due to its counterfeiting. In May 1875, McCann won a judgment against plaintiffs Lunt et al. for $2,025.84 related to this incident, which they then paid. In 1878, Lunt et al. brought action against Wrenn to recover the amount they had paid; however, the Statute of Limitations became a focal point in the ensuing legal battle.	The plaintiffs contended that they were entitled to recover damages from the defendant Wrenn due to the sale of counterfeit scrip, alleging a breach of an implied warranty of genuineness. They sought recovery of $2,025.84, the amount they had to pay McCann as a result of the initial transaction involving the counterfeit scrip. The plaintiffs argued that their legal claim was not barred by the Statute of Limitations when they initiated the lawsuit.	The defendant, Wrenn, defended the case primarily by asserting the Statute of Limitations, arguing that the plaintiffs failed to bring their action within five years of discovering the counterfeit nature of the scrip, which they were aware of as early as January 8, 1872. Wrenn’s position was that the action was barred because the plaintiffs were notified about the worthless scrip prior to the commencement of their lawsuit.

The case "The People ex rel. Highway Commissioners v. The Board of Supervisors of McHenry County" was decided on May 19, 1884, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The controversy originated in McHenry County, Illinois, where the Highway Commissioners petitioned the county board to appropriate $4,100 as half the cost for constructing a bridge over the Fox River in McHenry. The commissioners argued that they acted under the provisions of the 110th section of the Road and Bridge law, which allows towns to seek county aid for bridge construction if the cost is too burdensome for the town to bear alone. However, during the hearings, the circuit court dismissed their petition, stating that the town had already completed the bridge using its own funds without applying for county assistance prior to construction. This ruling was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court of the Second District, leading to the appeal to the Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, represented by the Highway Commissioners, claimed that under the Road and Bridge law, they were entitled to request county aid for half the costs of the bridge due to the financial burden on the town. They maintained that their actions complied with the statutory requirements, thus establishing the county’s obligation to provide financial support for the bridge they constructed.	The defendants, represented by the Board of Supervisors, argued that the county had no legal obligation to pay for a bridge that had already been constructed without prior request for assistance. They contended that the plaintiffs acted under a different section of the statute that did not invoke the county's liability, as the necessary procedures for applying for county aid were not followed. The defendants asserted that the case should be dismissed since the plaintiffs failed to comply with the statute's requirements.

In 1845, an order for payment was drawn by the defendants, Samuel Robinson, on behalf of Strawbridge & Bower, in East Fork, Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The bill was to be paid to Robinson for the sum of $110 and was presented to Smith & Carter for payment. Although the parties involved were all residents of Illinois, it was established that the instrument was executed in Wisconsin. As a result, a legal dispute arose regarding whether the bill was an "inland bill" governed by Illinois law or a foreign bill subject to different rules. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1849. The court had to determine the implications of the bill's classification and whether reasonable notice of non-payment had been properly given.	The plaintiff, representing Robert C. Buzan, argued that the bill of exchange should be classified as an inland bill governed by Illinois law. They asserted that a reasonable notice of non-payment was provided, allowing them to recover the amount due. The plaintiff sought to uphold the jury's finding in their favor for $134.20, claiming that the defendants were liable for the payment under the agreed terms of the bill.	The defendants contested that the bill should be treated as a foreign bill due to its execution in Wisconsin, which would affect the determination of liability and damages. They argued for the necessity of formal protest for non-payment because of the bill's foreign nature. The defendant contended that any laches by the plaintiff failed to meet the conditions precedent for recovery on the contract, specifically pointing to the absence of a protest and the lack of timely presentment for payment.

On May 1, 1865, in Chicago, Illinois, a partnership was formed between William Evans, Ralph Hanson, and John M. Moore for a produce and commission business under the name Hanson, Evans, and Moore. The partnership agreement stipulated that the total capital investment would be $25,000, equally divided among the partners. Hanson and Moore contributed a portion of this capital, reportedly totaling $10,850.34, while Evans contributed $10,235.08. Each partner had limits on withdrawing funds from the partnership, with a provision for all partners to commit their time solely to the business. Discrepancies arose when Evans withdrew significant sums from the firm after expressing his intent to leave. Following the dissolution of the partnership, Hanson and Moore sought to settle the financial matters related to the firm, leading them to file a bill in chancery against Evans in the Superior Court of Chicago to take account of the partnership's finances. The lower court found that Evans had overdrawn his entitled distribution from the firm’s assets and was ordered to pay Hanson and Moore a specific sum in compensation.	The plaintiffs, Ralph Hanson and John M. Moore, claimed that William Evans had overdrawn his share from the partnership’s assets upon its dissolution. They demanded a thorough accounting of the partnership's finances and sought payment for expenses incurred during the winding up of the partnership, alleging that Evans owed them specific amounts based on the settlement of accounts.	William Evans contended that the trial court made errors in its accounting and distribution and argued that the $2,000 he paid to join the partnership should remain his property. He also claimed that any expectations of profits tied to the partnership should be considered in the final accounting. Ultimately, he requested the reversal of the lower court's decree regarding the accounting and the amounts he was ordered to pay.

About mid-September 1871, a contract was established between Stephen W. Rawson (the defendant) and Robert Clark et al. (the plaintiffs) for the manufacture and installation of iron work for a building located at the corner of Madison and Dearborn streets in Chicago, Illinois. The agreement stipulated that 85% of the payment would be made as the work progressed upon receiving a certificate from the architects, with the remaining 15% payable upon completion. Unfortunately, on October 8, 1871, before the installation of the iron work could commence, the building was entirely destroyed by fire. The plaintiffs, whose iron work was completed but not yet installed, sought to recover the costs associated with the iron work. Following a trial in the Circuit Court of Cook County, the plaintiffs achieved a favorable verdict and were awarded $206. The defendant appealed the decision, arguing against the plaintiffs' right to recover the costs based on the terms of the contract.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had fulfilled their contractual obligations by manufacturing the iron work and were ready to install it within the time specified in the contract. They argued that their inability to complete the installation was due to the defendant's default, as he failed to make the building available. They sought to recover $206, the agreed amount for the iron work, contending that they were entitled to this payment regardless of the building's destruction since their performance had already been completed.	The defendant argued that the contract required an architect’s certificate as a condition precedent for any payment, which could not be issued since no work was placed in the building due to the fire. He further contended that, based on the contract's terms, the plaintiffs had assumed the risk of the materials until the work was fully completed, which included the readiness of the building. Thus, he maintained that he was not liable for the payment of the iron work following the destruction of the building.

John Higgins v. Bridget Halligan is a legal case that took place in LaSalle County, Illinois in 1866. The case involves Bridget Halligan, acting as the executrix of her deceased husband Patrick Halligan, who filed a lawsuit against John Higgins, who had been a tenant of the Halligan property in LaSalle for three years, paying a yearly rent of $500. On July 11, 1866, Halligan provided Higgins with written notice that the tenancy would terminate on September 10, 1866. Subsequently, on July 17, 1866, Halligan offered to re-let the premises at a higher rate of $700 per annum, provided that Higgins signed a new lease within five days. However, Higgins failed to surrender the property by the deadline and continued to occupy the premises after the tenancy had legally ended. Halligan claimed that Higgins owed $1,000 per year for the time he held over the premises, demanding payment of $250, which was due. The plaintiff filed her suit in February 1867, leading to a trial in which the court ultimately found in favor of Halligan, awarding her damages for the unpaid rent.	The plaintiff, Bridget Halligan, claims that John Higgins failed to vacate the premises after receiving proper notice to terminate the tenancy. She argues that despite her offer to re-let the property at an increased rate, Higgins continued to occupy the premises without signing a new lease. Halligan seeks damages for the use and occupation of the premises at the rate of $1,000 annually, with $250 already due and unpaid.	John Higgins, the defendant, contends that the tenancy was not properly terminated and that the notices provided were insufficient to end his legal rights as a tenant. He states that he was only liable for the amount tendered, specifically $125, which he claimed was the full extent of what he owed. Furthermore, he argued that the acceptance of this tender should entitle him to a judgment for costs. Higgins also questioned the proper construction of the lease terms and the timing of the notice given by Halligan.

In June 1876, the case of Matthew E. Hamilton et al. v. Sylvanus Johnston was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated when Samuel Stookey, who held a promissory note secured by the Baumans, required a new note as he was unsatisfied with the original security. The new note was executed by the defendants (including Hamilton) and accepted by Stookey, but it only bore the signatures of the defendants, with the names of Hamilton and others written on its back. Separate judgments were obtained against the defendants as makers and against Hamilton and others as guarantors. Hamilton paid over $1,000 on this judgment and subsequently filed a lawsuit to recover the amount. The case revolved around whether Hamilton, by signing the back of the note, was a guarantor or a co-surety with the other defendants. Hamilton claimed he did not intend to be liable. The court analyzed the relationships and legal standings of the parties involved, particularly focusing on the perceptions of liability and intentions surrounding the signing of the promissory note.	The plaintiff, Matthew E. Hamilton, argued that he signed the back of the promissory note as a guarantor, not as a co-surety, asserting that he did not intend to assume any liability beyond what was agreed upon with the principal makers. He sought to recover the amount he paid on judgment against him and the other unnamed parties, contending that he was not liable for the debts of the other defendants in the way they claimed.	The defendants, including Sylvanus Johnston, contended that Hamilton's signature on the back of the note made him liable as a co-surety. They argued that he was aware of the relationship among the parties when he agreed to sign and therefore could not claim to be merely a guarantor. They asserted that Hamilton should not recover the amount he paid, as he willingly participated in the transaction under the belief of being a co-surety.
