In April 1858, the case of Thomas W. Baird et al. v. William Evans et al. was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court, following an action of assumpsit initiated in the La Salle County Court. The core of the case revolved around a contractual dispute over a lease agreement made on November 28, 1854, wherein William and James F. Evans (the plaintiffs) leased their farm to Thomas W. Baird and Benjamin M. Graham (the defendants) for one year, from March 1, 1855, to March 1, 1856, for the sum of $400 payable on October 1, 1855. According to the agreement, the plaintiffs were obligated to provide suitable stable room for three spans of horses, sufficient grain storage, break unplowed prairie sod, dig a stock well, and fence the property legally. The plaintiffs claimed that they fulfilled their contractual obligations but that the defendants failed to pay the agreed rent. The defendants contested this, leading to a trial by jury, which resulted in a verdict for the plaintiffs for $330. Following the verdict, the defendants motioned for a new trial, which was denied, prompting an appeal.	The plaintiffs, William and James F. Evans, argued that they had fulfilled their contractual obligations under the lease, including building adequate facilities, breaking prairie sod, and fencing the farm legally. Their primary claim was that the defendants failed to pay the agreed rent of $400 following the lease term. They sought recovery of the owed amount under both the special count concerning the written agreement and a common count for use and occupation.	The defendants, Thomas W. Baird and Benjamin M. Graham, contended that the plaintiffs did not fully comply with the lease conditions, specifically claiming that they failed to dig the required stock well and did not break all the necessary prairie sod. The defendants maintained that since these obligations were conditions precedent to their duty to pay rent, the plaintiffs could not recover the rent without having proven full performance of their contractual obligations. They requested a reversal of the judgment that awarded damages to the plaintiffs.

In the case of William T. Davis v. Stephen Gossnell et al., filed on January 22, 1885, in Mt. Vernon, Illinois, the dispute arose over land ownership following a tax sale. William T. Davis, the plaintiff, claimed title to a parcel of land through a tax deed. However, for such a deed to be valid under Illinois law, an affidavit must confirm the proper service of notice to the occupant regarding the tax sale and the redemption period. In this case, the affidavit stated that a notice was served on the occupant but lacked detail on the manner of service, failing to meet constitutional and statutory requirements. This procedural deficiency led to a challenge of the deed's validity, emphasizing the necessity for personal service and specific affidavit content as prerequisites for establishing a legitimate claim of title through a tax deed.	The plaintiff, William T. Davis, contended that he held title to the land based on a tax deed. He argued that the notice of the sale and the redemption expiration must have been properly served to the land occupant, as per statutory and constitutional requirements. Davis insisted that the affidavit associated with the deed was sufficient and that it established his rightful ownership of the property.	The defendants, represented by Stephen Gossnell and others, argued that the plaintiff's tax deed was invalid due to fatal defects in the associated affidavit. They maintained that the affidavit failed to specify how the notice was served, which is a requirement for establishing proper service under Illinois law. The defendants emphasized that the lack of detailed information on the service method rendered any claim to title through the deed unauthorized and that the constitutional requirement for personal service was not met.

The case of Thomas Davis v. Isaac Scarritt was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1855. The legal proceedings took place in Morgan County, Illinois, and stemmed from a breach of contract dispute involving a promissory note. The plaintiff, Isaac Scarritt, claimed that Davis and his partner, William Pankey, operating under the name "Pankey & Davis," issued two promissory notes in 1851—one for $340.41 and another for $622.04. Scarritt claimed that the defendants failed to fulfill their payment obligations under these notes. The case became complicated when Davis filed a non-assumpsit plea, asserting that he was not bound by the notes as he was not a partner with Pankey at the time the notes were executed. The circuit court initially ruled that Davis did not adequately challenge the existence of the partnership or the execution of the note, leading to an appeal by Davis.	Isaac Scarritt, the plaintiff, argued that he was owed payments from the promissory notes signed by Pankey & Davis, claiming that both defendants were jointly liable as partners. His legal request was for the court to enforce the payment stipulated in the notes, asserting that the signatures reflected a legitimate partnership between Pankey and Davis at the time of the notes' issuance.	Thomas Davis contended that he was not a partner with William Pankey at the time the promissory notes were created and therefore could not be held liable for the debts claimed by Scarritt. He supported his argument with a verified affidavit claiming non-assumpsit and asserted that the court should not presume the existence of the partnership or his liability without adequate proof.

The case "The Prairie Farmer Company v. Alva B. Taylor et al." was decided in September 1873 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a contract for the sale of a printing press. The Prairie Farmer Company, the plaintiff, engaged Alva B. Taylor and others to supply a four-roller, drum-cylinder printing press for $4,000, with stipulations for its installation in complete running order within seventy days. The contract specified that the company would have thirty days post-installation to decide whether to keep the press. The press was installed, and the Prairie Farmer Company continued to use it for nearly a year before it was destroyed in a fire. The company did not formally notify the defendant of its intention not to keep the press within the thirty-day period. Consequently, the case examines whether the payment for the press was conditioned on the performance of the additional obligations outlined in the contract.	The Prairie Farmer Company argued that Alva B. Taylor and his associates were obligated to deliver the printing press in complete running order and to keep it maintained as per the terms of the contract. The plaintiff maintained that it had the right to recover the total contract price, insisting that the performance of obligations by the defendant was independent, allowing for recovery without needing to demonstrate full performance of every condition from the defendant.	The defendants contended that the obligations outlined in the contract were interdependent. They argued that the plaintiff was required to prove full performance of all conditions before being entitled to recover any amount. They asserted that since the plaintiff had failed to provide notice indicating an intention not to keep the press, the contract's terms meant that the right to recover was conditional upon fulfilling all obligations, which the defendants claimed were not satisfied.

James Common v. The People of the State of Illinois is a legal case stemming from a bastardy proceeding that began in October 1886 when Carrie Winkle filed a complaint accusing James Common of being the father of her child. The case took place in Iroquois County, Illinois, with the initial trial occurring before a justice of the peace. After being bound over to the County Court, a judgment of guilt was rendered against Common, leading him to appeal this judgment to the Circuit Court. The main issue in the trial was the paternity of Carrie Winkle's child, born on February 26, 1887. Winkle provided testimony claiming that Common was the father, but there was a lack of corroborating evidence to support her claim. Instead, numerous testimonies indicated inconsistent statements from Winkle about the child's paternity. Common consistently denied having sexual relations with Winkle. Compounding the case was Common's motion for a continuance, supported by affidavits asserting that he could not procure the attendance of key witnesses who might testify that Winkle had claimed another man, Richard Heisler, was the actual father. The trial court denied this motion and subsequently also denied Common's motion for a new trial.	The plaintiff, represented by Carrie Winkle, accused James Common of bastardy, claiming that he was the father of her illegitimate child. Winkle's primary argument relied on her testimony asserting that Common was the father, despite the absence of corroborating evidence. She sought to have the court affirm the paternity accusation and enforce liability on Common for the financial support of the child.	James Common, the defendant, argued that the trial court improperly denied his motion for a continuance aimed at securing the testimony of crucial witnesses who could support his claim that he was not the father. Common maintained that these witnesses would testify that Carrie Winkle had previously confessed that another man, Richard Heisler, was responsible for her pregnancy. He requested that the court grant a new trial based on the perceived errors surrounding witness testimony and the denial of a fair trial.

In the case of Moline Paper Co. v. Union Printing Co., which was adjudicated in the Illinois Appellate Court, the dispute dates back to the years 1880 and 1881, with additional dealings occurring in the first half of 1882. The conflict arose in Illinois, where the Union Printing Co. purchased paper from Moline Paper Co. amounting to between $5,000 and $6,000. Throughout this period, various payments were made by the printing company; however, Moline Paper Co. claimed that a balance of $306.02 remained unpaid. The Union Printing Co. contended that their account was settled completely. The central issue stemmed from differing interpretations of payment records, particularly involving a shipment of paper and the associated invoices. Testimony was provided regarding inconsistent invoicing; deliveries made via street car sometimes lacked accompanying invoices. The matter was further complicated when a letter from the printing company stated that their account had been balanced, except for a portion bought on a ninety-day credit. The trial court ruled in favor of the Union Printing Co., leading to an appeal by the Moline Paper Co., claiming errors in the admission of evidence and the weight of the trial court's findings.	The Moline Paper Co., as the appellant, claimed that the Union Printing Co. owed them a balance of $306.02 for paper purchases that had not been fully paid. They argued that various items charged for paper had not been credited by the printing company. The plaintiff sought to overturn the trial court's ruling that found the account settled, citing improper testimony admitted during trial and contending that the trial court's findings were not supported by the evidence presented.	The Union Printing Co. argued that their account with the Moline Paper Co. had been paid in full, asserting that a letter sent on July 19, 1881, confirmed their payment that balanced the account inconsistently mentioned. They contended that the burden of proof was on the Moline Paper Co. to establish that any additional quantities of paper were delivered, and the evidence provided was insufficient. The defendant requested that the trial court's findings be upheld, asserting that the evidence was conflicting and did not warrant a reversal of the judgment.

The case "James M. Samuels et al. v. The Drainage Commissioners" was decided on June 14, 1888, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Mason County, Illinois, and involved James M. Samuels and Matilda Samuels, who were defendants in a foreclosure action initiated by the Commissioners of the Central Special Drainage District. The drainage commissioners sought to foreclose a lien for drainage assessments on lands owned by the defendants. This legal proceeding was initiated under a specific statute relating to drainage for agricultural and sanitary purposes, which allowed the commissioners to file a petition for a foreclosure if assessments were not paid by a certain date. The defendants did not respond to the complaint and defaulted, leading the court to consider the allegations as confessed, thus allowing the court to proceed with foreclosure. The case was referred to a master in chancery to report on proofs, and the court found that every material allegation of the complaint was true, thereby granting the foreclosure.	The plaintiffs, the drainage commissioners, asserted that all necessary steps for the creation of a lien against the defendants' property were fulfilled as per the drainage assessment statute. They argued that the lien for the assessment was valid and enforceable since the defendants had failed to respond to the complaint and had not paid the assessments. Their legal request was for the court to foreclose the lien on the property due to the non-payment of drainage assessments, thus allowing for the sale of the land to satisfy the debt.	The defendants claimed that the lien claimed was not foreclosed according to the requirements of the law and argued that the assessment was void because it was made by individuals without proper authority. They also contended that the proceeding should align with the law concerning tax lien foreclosures. The defendants did not file any answer to the complaint, and their arguments were essentially conceded due to their default.

In the case of Harry Byrne v. J. D. O’Neill, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the proceedings were held in February 1890 before the Illinois Appellate Court. The trial was initially entered upon by a judge without a jury, but was postponed by agreement of both parties to allow for further proceedings. When the trial was scheduled to resume on the agreed date, the plaintiff, Harry Byrne, was absent, although his counsel was present. This absence was due to a misunderstanding regarding whether he was to be notified of the trial's resumption, a miscommunication attributed to either Byrne or his attorney. As a result of his absence and the absence of any justification for it, the court proceeded with the trial in his absence and subsequently rendered a judgment against him. Following the judgment, Byrne filed a motion to set it aside and requested a new trial, but this motion was denied by the court. The court found that Byrne's lack of diligence and negligence led to his absence during the trial proceedings, which were not excused. The court ultimately concluded that there were no sufficient grounds to overturn the judgment rendered against Byrne.	The plaintiff, Harry Byrne, claimed that the judgment rendered against him in his absence should be set aside due to a misunderstanding with his counsel about notification to resume the trial. He argued that this miscommunication resulted in his failure to appear, thus justifying his request for the court to grant him a new trial. Byrne sought to demonstrate that he had a reasonable defense against the claims of the defendant, J. D. O’Neill, which warranted a reconsideration of the judgment.	The defendant, J. D. O’Neill, contended that the trial was properly conducted and that Byrne’s absence did not merit a delay in proceedings. O’Neill's counsel highlighted that his side was present and prepared for trial, and the plaintiff’s failure to attend was due to his own neglect and misunderstanding, not a fault of the defendant or his legal team. The defendant argued that there was no abuse of discretion by the court in denying the motion to set aside the judgment, asserting that the original decision should stand.

In December 1837, in Chicago, Illinois, William Bell was indicted and convicted of larceny by the Municipal Court of the City of Chicago. The indictment was signed by the City Attorney and indicated that the grand jury was composed of individuals chosen from both the City of Chicago and County of Cook. Upon arraignment, Bell's counsel moved to quash the indictment, arguing that the grand jurors were not solely selected from the municipal limits of Chicago, as required by law. The court overruled the motion and proceeded with the trial, resulting in Bell's conviction and sentencing to the penitentiary. Following the conviction, Bell appealed, asserting that the indictment was improperly constituted due to its mention of both the city and county in the selection of jurors, thus questioning the jurisdiction of the Municipal Court.	The plaintiff, William Bell, claimed that the indictment against him was invalid because it was based on a grand jury that included jurors from the County of Cook, rather than exclusively from the City of Chicago, as stipulated in the relevant legislation. He argued that this improper selection violated his legal rights and sought to have the indictment quashed.	The defendants, representing the People of the State of Illinois, contended that the Municipal Court had the jurisdiction to hear the case and that the indictment, while not signed by the appropriate State’s Attorney, was valid as it was signed by the City Attorney, who was authorized to prosecute in that court. They argued that the inclusion of jurors from the county was acceptable and did not invalidate the proceedings.

The case "Beadle County National Bank v. Sigmund Hyman et al." originated in Huron, Dakota Territory, where the Beadle County National Bank and S. Hyman & Co. were creditors of the insolvent firm L. Adler & Co. A letter dated November 20, 1884, indicated that Hyman & Co. authorized assistance for a Mr. M. F. Moss, allowing the bank to hold them responsible for any favors extended to him. The bank later sold its claim against L. Adler & Co. to Moss in exchange for a promissory note, which included an indorsement allowing for a 30-day extension for payment. The central issue of the case pertains to whether the letter constituted a guarantee by Hyman & Co. for the payment of Moss’s debts to the bank. While the plaintiff, Beadle County National Bank, asserted it held the letter during the execution of the note, the defendants disputed both its possession at the relevant time and its implied obligations.	The Beadle County National Bank contended that the letter signed by Hyman & Co. constituted a guaranty for the payment of Moss's promissory note. The bank argued that regardless of the timing of possession, it held the letter when the extension of the note was granted. They sought to hold Hyman & Co. liable based on this perceived guarantee.	The defendants, represented by Hyman & Co., maintained that the letter did not authorize the bank to sell a bad debt to Moss or act as a guarantor for him. They argued that the context of the letter was misinterpreted, and the facts did not support the bank's claim of liability. They requested that the court reject the bank's arguments based on the evidence presented.

In December 1831, the legal case of David G. Bates v. Thomas Jenkins took place in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The dispute stemmed from an attachment sued out by David G. Bates against Jenkins and his partners—Thomas McCraney and Charles Galloway—alleging they owed him $600 for goods sold and delivered. Bates claimed that the defendants had left the state with the intention to evade their debts. Jenkins, one of the partners, contested this by filing a plea in abatement, asserting that he had not departed from Illinois but was present in Galena at the time the attachment was issued. The case was complicated by procedural delays, as it was continued multiple terms before moving forward. Ultimately, after Jenkins was allowed to enter his appearance and file his plea, the court ruled in his favor, leading to a nonsuit against Bates. This judgment was then appealed by Bates.	Bates argued that Jenkins and his partners had left the state, attempting to avoid their debt to him. He sought to impose an attachment based on his assertion that the defendants owed him $600 for goods provided. Bates contended that the attachment was valid because it was claimed under the premise of the defendants' supposed departure from the state with the intent to evade debt.	Jenkins contended that he had not left the state at the time the attachment was issued and was not attempting to evade the debt. His defense included a plea in abatement, which argued against the validity of Bates's claims, asserting that the court should quash the attachment because Jenkins was physically present in Illinois. The court's acceptance of this plea was a critical aspect of Jenkins’s legal strategy, as it led to the dismissal of Bates's claims.

The case of Augustus O. Garrett v. Andrew Stevenson et al. originated in the Circuit Court of Peoria County, Illinois, in October 1841, when Stevenson & Wardwell filed a lawsuit against A. O. Garrett to enforce a mechanic’s lien related to construction work done on certain lots in Peoria. The venue was subsequently changed to Tazewell County, where the case continued to be heard. The dispute was based on a contract made on March 3, 1840, but the proceedings extended until a final decree was issued in April 1846. The key individuals involved were Augustus O. Garrett, the appellant, and Andrew Stevenson as the primary appellee, along with Mary G. Garrett. The disagreement centered around payments for materials supplied and work performed under the contract, with the plaintiff arguing that the defendant had refused to pay for services rendered, thus justifying the enforcement of the lien. During the course of the trial, a jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to an appeal by Garrett.	The plaintiffs, Stevenson & Wardwell, claimed the right to enforce a mechanic’s lien against Garrett for unpaid work and materials supplied under the contract. They argued that they had performed their part of the contract but were denied payment by Garrett, which constituted a breach. They requested the court to recognize their lien and award them the amount owed for labor and materials, totaling $2,595.20.	Garrett's defense was twofold. Firstly, he contended that the plaintiffs could not enforce the lien because the suit was not filed within three months of the payment being due, as required by previous law. Secondly, he claimed to have made significant payments to the plaintiffs and argued that they provided work that was unskilful and unworkmanlike, which justified a set-off against any amounts owed. He sought a dismissal of the claim and a reduction of any judgment against him.

The case revolves around Mary Kelly, a married woman, who filed a lawsuit against the City of Chicago in 1873. The incident occurred when Kelly was walking along a sidewalk in Chicago with her sister and stepped on a loose or defective plank, causing her to fall and sustain personal injuries. Initially, she felt the primary injury was in her foot and managed to walk to her sister's house nearby. However, a couple of days later, she experienced a dull, heavy feeling in her side, which lasted for three weeks, ultimately leading to a miscarriage. Prior to the incident, Kelly had eight children and had been in good health. Although she was able to give birth to a living child after the miscarriage, her health declined post-incident. The jury awarded her $4,050 in damages, which the court later found excessive, leading to an appeal by the city, which sought reversal of the verdict on the grounds that it was disproportionate to the injuries sustained.	Mary Kelly claimed personal injury due to a fall caused by a defective sidewalk. She argued that the accident resulted in significant physical pain, particularly from a miscarriage attributed to the injuries from her fall. She sought compensatory damages for the injuries she suffered, including the pain and suffering associated with her condition after the incident.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant, argued that the damages awarded to Kelly were excessive and disproportionate to the actual injuries sustained. They maintained that the incident could largely be attributed to an accident rather than wilful negligence on their part, asserting that municipal corporations are not liable for vindictive or exemplary damages unless gross negligence is proven, which was not established in this case. They sought to have the jury's verdict reversed due to the excessive amount awarded.

This case involves Francis Mattingly filing a replevin action against Cornelius Crowley in the Jasper Circuit Court in Illinois during November 1866. The dispute centers around the recovery of a cow, a calf, a yearling calf, and a steer. Mattingly claimed he purchased the animals from Joseph Sitzelman, who had originally owned them, and that Sitzelman saw the cow in Crowley’s possession. The case was tried without a jury, and the court ruled in favor of Crowley regarding the ownership of the property, with Mattingly successfully arguing other issues. Mattingly's motion for a new trial was denied, and the original court ordered him to return the property and pay the costs. Mattingly then appealed the judgment, seeking to overturn the decision.	Francis Mattingly's primary claims included a challenge to the ownership of the animals, asserting that he had purchased them from Joseph Sitzelman. Mattingly argued that he did not wrongfully possess the property and was seeking its return. He contended that the legal procedures concerning the property rights were not adhered to properly by the defendant, Crowley. Mattingly requested the court to reverse the original judgment and allow him to retain possession of the cows.	Cornelius Crowley defended by asserting property rights to the animals based on his possession and the lack of proper legal documentation regarding the posting of the cattle. He argued that Mattingly had no legal grounds to claim the animals since they were not properly replevied, particularly concerning the steer that was missing at the time of the replevin. Crowley requested that the court uphold the original ruling that favored him and validate his ownership of the livestock in question.

In 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Edward J. Hill et al. v. John D. Parsons et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiffs were surviving members of the firm Weed, Parsons & Co., who were suing defendants Edward J. Hill and Henry S. Austin over two promissory notes totaling $1,350, plus interest. These notes were issued as part of a settlement regarding debts owed by Hill to the firm for printing and binding four volumes of "Hill's Illinois Digest." The defendants countered the claims with various defenses, alleging issues such as delay in project completion, overcharges on certain volumes, and defective workmanship. The jury in the Superior Court found in favor of the plaintiffs, and this judgment was subsequently upheld by the Appellate Court. The case centered on whether the defendants could successfully assert set-off claims regarding the alleged delays and defects after having provided the notes in question.	The plaintiffs argued that the promissory notes represented a settlement of all amounts due after accounting for any alleged set-offs or claims. They maintained that the notes were valid contracts and that the defendants were precluded from contesting them because any claims related to delays or overcharges were known at the time the notes were signed. The plaintiffs requested the court to enforce payment based on the full amount of the promissory notes.	The defendants contended that they were entitled to set-offs due to delays in completing the books, which caused financial damages. They argued that the plaintiffs failed to meet their contractual obligations regarding the timeliness and quality of the work. Additionally, they claimed that overcharges beyond the agreed contract price occurred and sought to have these matters recognized as defenses against the plaintiffs' claims.

George S. Russell filed a case against Edward G. Harris in 1885 in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose over a sum of $420.69, which represented the balance of an account for lumber that Russell's firm had delivered to a contractor named Frank Stewart. Stewart was engaged in the construction of two houses for Harris. Russell claimed that Harris promised to pay for the lumber in proportion to what he paid to other suppliers before the delivery occurred; however, Harris denied making any such binding promise. The only witnesses in the case included Russell's clerk, who testified that he interpreted Harris's remarks as a promise to pay, while Harris indicated that he merely expressed a willingness to pay voluntarily but refused to make a formal promise. It was established that Harris had paid other suppliers based on orders from Stewart and that he paid over $400 to Russell's firm before he received notice of the remaining balance. The case was presented to a jury, who ultimately sided with Harris.	The plaintiff, George S. Russell, argued that Edward G. Harris had a contractual obligation to pay the balance of $420.69 for the lumber delivered. He claimed that Harris had made a promise to pay for the materials provided to the contractor, which formed the basis of his legal request. Russell sought a judgment against Harris to recover the owed amount, asserting that Harris’s denial undermined the contract formed by the agreement regarding the payment for materials.	Edward G. Harris maintained that he never made any legally binding promise to pay Russell's firm for the lumber. He contended that any statements he made were not intended as commitments and that he would fulfill obligations to suppliers only as directed by the contractor, Stewart. Harris provided evidence that he did not receive notice of any outstanding balance before he made payments to the lumber firm, which were based on existing orders rather than an agreement to pay for all expenses.

In January 1869, the case of Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company v. William Apperson was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident occurred while William Apperson was traveling on a train operated by the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company. During this journey, the train car Apperson was seated in derailed and overturned due to poor track conditions, resulting in serious injuries to him. Apperson subsequently filed a lawsuit against the railway company, claiming negligence. The case underscored the critical responsibilities of the railway company regarding the maintenance and safety of its tracks, with the court noting the extremely hazardous state of the railway track where the accident occurred. The rails were reported to be worn and inadequately secured, with significant gaps and broken ties, leading to a jury’s verdict of $1,000 in favor of Apperson.	William Apperson, the plaintiff, asserted that the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company was negligent in maintaining its railway tracks. His main argument was that the unsafe condition of the tracks directly caused the train accident, which resulted in his severe injuries. Apperson sought damages for his injuries, emphasizing that the company’s gross negligence in track maintenance warranted a significant compensation.	The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company, the defendant, contended that the plaintiff's claims regarding the condition of the railway tracks were not entirely accurate. The defense raised objections regarding the role of an employee known as the “section boss” in the situation and questioned whether he was informed about the track's condition prior to the accident. They argued that the responsibility for track maintenance should not be solely placed on the defendant without considering these factors.

In 1872, in Springfield, Illinois, Franklin C. Bushway entered into a contract with Lucy F. Wright, the widow of Erastus Wright, for a monument to be erected over his grave in Oak Ridge Cemetery. The contract specified the dimensions and materials for the monument, with a total cost of $1,200, to be paid from Erastus Wright's estate. Following the death of Erastus Wright, the county court of Sangamon ruled in favor of Bushway, ordering the estate’s administrator, Stephen A. Foley, to pay the amount after Bushway claimed the costs associated with the monument. Foley appealed the decision. He argued that the estate should not be liable for the monument's cost as he had not contracted for its erection nor had approved the arrangement made by the widow, pointing out that the contract binding the widow did not create any legal obligation on the estate. The court considered whether the administrator's prior knowledge of the contract imposed any limitation on his right to object later. Ultimately, it assessed that the widow's contract was individual and that the estate was not liable for it.	Franklin C. Bushway claims that he is owed $1,200 for the construction of a monument placed over the grave of Erastus Wright, which was agreed upon under contract terms with his widow, Lucy F. Wright. He contends that since the contract for the monument was validly made, the estate of Erastus Wright should fulfil the obligation to pay for the monument.	Stephen A. Foley, the administrator of Erastus Wright's estate, contends that the estate cannot be held liable for the contract made by the widow. Foley asserts that he did not authorize or approve the agreement for the monument and that Lucy F. Wright lacked the legal authority to bind the estate for expenses incurred under her personal contract. He argues that since the agreement is hers alone, any obligation to pay rests solely with her.

William H. Ralston, the plaintiff, brought a case against John Hughes in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1851. The case originated from a previous action of ejectment concerning a quarter section of land located in Adams County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a series of property transactions and a mortgage foreclosed by the Adams County Circuit Court in 1844, involving multiple parcels of land across various counties. Ralston claimed ownership through a master’s deed from the foreclosure case, while Hughes, who had been in possession of the property since 1841, contended that he had rights stemming from a tax deed he obtained. During the trial, Ralston provided historical deeds linking the land to the original mortgagor, while Hughes attempted to present evidence of his tax title to contest Ralston's claims. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Hughes, which prompted Ralston to appeal the decision.	Ralston's main argument centered around the validity of the foreclosure decree that he contended vested him with the rightful title to the property in question. He asserted that the Circuit Court of Adams County possessed jurisdiction to foreclose the mortgage, despite the involved lands being spread across multiple counties. Ralston sought to overturn the lower court's judgment, aiming to establish his ownership based on the master’s deed obtained through the court-approved sale following the foreclosure.	Hughes' defense was built around the claim that he held a legitimate tax title to the property derived from unpaid taxes during his possession. He argued that the tax deed was valid, and thus, he maintained rights to the land that superseded Ralston's claim through the foreclosure proceedings. Hughes contended that the court incorrectly admitted evidence related to the foreclosure suit and that the jurisdictional questions surrounding the foreclosure decree cast doubt on Ralston's title claims.

Christian Thomas sued Louisa Fischer in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1874, stemming from slanderous statements allegedly made by Fischer. The incident took place in Adams County, Illinois, where Fischer purportedly accused Thomas, a married woman, of being a whore, using slanderous words in German that translated into English conveyed an imputation of lewdness and adultery. The context for these statements arose from an altercation related to a life insurance policy concerning Thomas's husband, which had been canceled without notice. During the trial, conflicting evidence emerged as to whether the exact words were spoken as claimed. Ultimately, the jury found for Thomas, awarding her $1,600 in damages, which she subsequently reduced by half. Fischer appealed the decision, contesting the sufficiency of evidence and the jury’s handling of damages.	Thomas claimed that Fischer's statements were slanderous and damaging to her reputation. She argued that the words used imputing lewdness were not only false but also maliciously repeated by Fischer after the initial altercation, indicating a deliberate intent to harm. Thomas sought monetary compensation for the emotional distress caused by these accusations, with the jury initially awarding her $1,600, which she later reduced to $800.	Fischer denied the allegations of slander, asserting that the specific words charged by Thomas were not proven to have been spoken as claimed. Fischer argued that the remarks, made in a heated moment, should be viewed with leniency and contended that the plaintiff's decision to remit part of the damages signified an admission of excessive amounts awarded. Additionally, she believed the court erred in its jury instructions regarding the proof of slander.

The case "C., B. & Q. R. R. Co. v. Blake" took place in Illinois, with the incident occurring around the first of March in 1881. The key individuals involved were the C., B. & Q. R. R. Co. (the appellant) and Blake (the appellee). Blake, a farmer, claimed that three of his horses were killed and one was injured when they were struck by a locomotive belonging to the railroad company on his property. The basis for the lawsuit was the railroad company's alleged failure to maintain legally required fences on either side of its tracks, which was asserted to be the reason for the horses being on the tracks. After the case was brought to trial, the jury found in favor of Blake, leading to the railroad company appealing the decision.	Blake's main arguments centered on the negligence of the railroad company in maintaining the necessary fencing along its tracks. He contended that this failure directly resulted in the death and injury of his horses, thereby causing him significant financial loss. Blake sought to recover the value of the three horses that were killed and the damages associated with the injured horse.	The railroad company contested the claims by arguing that they had no liability for the incident, implying that Blake may have contributed to the circumstances leading to the horses being on the tracks. They likely asserted that they had adhered to all relevant laws and regulations concerning railroad operations and maintenance. The railroad requested the court to dismiss the claims and overturn the jury's verdict in Blake's favor.

Hiram Reed v. Salome C. West et al. took place in Kane County, Illinois, with the Illinois Supreme Court rendering its decision in September 1873. The case revisits a prior judgment involving a dispute between Reed, the appellant, and West, the appellee, regarding the relationship of mortgagor and mortgagee. The core issue revolved around the equity of redemption of the mortgagor, which the court found to have been extinguished for valuable consideration. The opinion by Mr. Justice Scott stated that there was no fraud or undue influence involved in the transaction, and the reasons provided for the rescission of the sale were inadequate. The current judgment affirms the earlier decision, retaking no new legal ground, confirming that the differences raised by the appellant were not substantial enough to warrant a different outcome.	Hiram Reed, the plaintiff, contended that there had been errors in the previous ruling and argued for a reconsideration of the facts related to his rights as a mortgagor. He sought equitable relief, claiming that the circumstances surrounding the transaction were unjust and that the sale should be rescinded due to alleged misunderstandings regarding the equity of redemption.	Salome C. West et al., the defendants, maintained that the court's prior judgment was conclusive and should be upheld. They argued that the equity of redemption had been satisfactorily and legitimately extinguished. The defendants emphasized that there was no evidence of fraud or undue influence in the mortgage transaction, and contended that the plaintiff was barred from challenging the previous court's findings, as insufficient grounds were presented for altering the judgment.

William J. Mettler filed a lawsuit against Jonathan T. Miller on November 4, 1885, in the Ogle Circuit Court, Illinois, as part of an ejectment action. Mettler sought to recover a one-fourth interest in two lots located in Palmer's addition to Bochelle, Illinois. The disputed land had a complex title history that began with Sheldon Bartholomew, who purchased a squatter's claim in the 1840s and obtained a patent for the land. Upon Bartholomew's death in 1846, his widow and daughter became key figures in the inheritance, with the daughter eventually marrying Isaac Boss. Mettler's claim was based on subsequent transfers of the land interests from the heirs of Bartholomew to himself. Conversely, Miller's defense was rooted in the chain of prior ownership, which he maintained through various conveyances and tax payments. The court considered the germane history of ownership, the widow’s dower rights, and the claims of the heirs before deciding on the legal rights of Mettler and Miller regarding the contested lots.	Mettler claimed that based on a series of conveyances, he held a valid title to an undivided one-fourth interest in the disputed lots. He argued that the estate by curtesy held by Isaac Boss, husband of the original heir, did not adversely affect his claims. Mettler sought a determination from the court affirming his ownership rights and requesting the court to grant him possession of the property in question.	Miller contended that he had superior ownership based on a long-standing possession under various prior legitimately executed deeds from the heirs of the land’s original owner. He claimed that his possession and payment of taxes for many years entitled him to the property under the applicable limitation laws. Miller argued that Mettler's claims were invalid because they were subordinate to the legitimate title held through the succession from the original parties.

The case of "The Supreme Lodge of the Ancient Order of United Workmen et al. v. Florentine Zuhlke" took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered on January 16, 1889. The key individuals involved included Florentine Zuhlke and representatives of the Supreme Lodge of the Ancient Order of United Workmen. The dispute stemmed from the expulsion of Edward Zuhlke, the husband of the plaintiff, from his lodge without prior notice. Following his death, the plaintiff sought to claim benefits under a beneficiary certificate that was to be paid to her. The defendant organizations argued that any liability lay solely with the Grand Lodge of the State, contending there was a misjoinder of defendants. The court had to consider the nature of the expulsion and whether proper procedures were followed, particularly regarding notification. Ultimately, the court ruled on aspects of contract law concerning the beneficiary certificate, examining the bylaws of the mutual benevolent society involved and the implications of expelling a member without notice.	The plaintiff, Florentine Zuhlke, argued that her husband's expulsion from the lodge was invalid due to a lack of notice, rendering it void. She maintained that this void expulsion should not preclude her from claiming the death benefits under the beneficiary certificate, which was meant to be payable to her upon her husband’s death. The plaintiff contended that the rules of justice required an opportunity for defense, and without notice of expulsion, she had continuing rights to the benefits assigned to her.	The defendants argued primarily that the beneficiary certificate did not create a joint liability between the lodges involved. They claimed that if there was any liability, it was only on the part of the Grand Lodge, not the subordinate lodges. They also pointed to the absence of a verified plea denying the execution of the certificate and asserted that the expulsion, while possibly procedural, had been acted upon in good faith. The defendants asserted that the plaintiff had not exhausted all available remedies within the organization before bringing her claims to court.

In the case of D. W. Norris v. Nelson Rogers, which took place in Illinois, a co-partnership was formed on October 13, 1877, between Nelson Rogers and D. W. Norris. The partnership was created for the purpose of manufacturing and selling "incased glass vessels" under letters patent owned by Norris. Rogers contributed $1,000 in capital, while Norris provided the patent's use. An initial partnership agreement was established in writing, followed by supplementary articles signed on June 6, 1879. Although some business was transacted, the precise extent remains undetermined. A key event leading to litigation occurred when Norris, having sold a one-fourth interest in the patent to Mr. Burgess, and later granting Riessner & Co. exclusivity to manufacture and sell wares under the patent, notified Rogers of the partnership’s dissolution effective September 11, 1879. Rogers then filed for an accounting of royalties received by Norris from Riessner & Co., asserting his entitlement to a portion of future royalties. The dispute primarily revolved around the interpretation of partnership agreements and the calculation of profit-sharing after Norris's declaration of dissolution.	Nelson Rogers argued that he was entitled to an accounting of the royalties paid to Norris by Riessner & Co. due to their partnership agreement. He sought to establish his share in the preceding and future royalties, claiming that under the original partnership terms, he was entitled to three-eighths of the total royalties resulting from sales made by Riessner & Co., following the dissolution of their partnership.	D. W. Norris contended that upon his declaration of dissolution, Rogers had no right to any further royalties as they originated from an exclusive contract with Riessner & Co. Norris maintained that the partnership agreement allowed either partner to terminate the partnership with notice, and therefore Rogers was not entitled to any profits stemming from the contract beyond the dissolution date. He challenged the interpretation of their agreement regarding the sharing of royalties and sought to dismiss Rogers's claims.

The case "J. Irving Pearce v. Ira Foote" was decided on February 7, 1885, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a dispute involving a promissory note worth $5,000 made by the trustees of the Couch estate, which had been assigned to S. G. Hooker & Co. by the payee, Ira Foote. Foote, who had engaged Hooker & Co. as brokers, had contracted with them to speculate on grain options without any intention of actual purchase or sale of the commodities. The agreement was characterized as a gambling contract, and losses were incurred, leading Foote to pay Hooker & Co. approximately $22,000 in settlement of such losses, including notes for future payment with a guaranty from Foote. Hooker & Co. later assigned one of these notes to Pearce, which prompted Foote to sue Pearce for recovery after he demanded the note back and was refused. The trial court found in favor of Foote, prompting Pearce's appeal.	The plaintiff, Ira Foote, argued that the contract with Hooker & Co. was a gambling contract, which was illegal and therefore void under Illinois law. He contended that the assignment of the promissory note to Hooker & Co. did not confer valid title due to the illegal nature of the consideration. Foote sought to recover the value of the note from Pearce, asserting that he was entitled to the property as it was originally lost in a gambling transaction.	The defendant, J. Irving Pearce, contended that the contract between Foote and Hooker & Co. was valid and that any implications of it being a gambling contract should not affect the ownership of the note now assigned to him. Pearce requested the court to dismiss Foote's claims, arguing that Foote could not recover the note based on an illegal contract, and maintained that his status as an assignee should have protected him from liability for prior dealings.

In December 1876, Alexis Rivard executed a trust deed in Kankakee County, Illinois, transferring a tract of land to Charles Blain to secure a promissory note held by Camille Blain. The deed included covenants for tax payments and specified that in the event of default, the grantee could take possession of the property and collect rents. By 1879, Rivard had defaulted on the note and taxes owed, prompting Blain to attempt a foreclosure sale. During this time, Rivard had leased the property to Xavier Fortier, who was paying rent in the form of a share of crops. After the attempted sale in July 1879, Rivard sued Blain for the value of the rent corn collected from Fortier, claiming entitlement to the payment. The case progressed through the circuit court, where Rivard successfully argued for a judgment of $195 against Blain, leading to this appeal. However, the court noted several inconsistencies, particularly regarding the validity of the acknowledgment of the deed and the rights transferred through the trust deed.	Rivard's main argument was that he was entitled to the value of the 1879 rent corn that Fortier delivered to Blain, asserting that the foreclosure was ineffective, and thus, he retained his rights as the mortgagor. He sought a monetary judgment for the amount of the rent corn collected by Blain, laying the basis for his claims on procedural deficiencies in the foreclosure process.	Blain contended that as the trustee under the trust deed, he had the right to collect the rents due from Fortier after the foreclosure attempt. He argued that Fortier's payment of rent to him was valid, as the tenant had effectively attorned to him given the circumstances. Blain claimed that Rivard had no cause of action, citing the ineffective nature of the foreclosure and the failure to prove any entitlement to the rent corn after the legal title transferred.

In December 1845, the case of Chester Hitchcock et al. v. Daniel S. Haight was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court after being initially filed in the Boone Circuit Court. The case revolved around a promissory note made by Daniel S. Haight to H. B. Potter, which was due in September 1841 and subsequently assigned to the plaintiffs in January 1842. The plaintiffs claimed that the note represented a valid debt, while the defendant raised various defenses. Haight argued that the note was contingent upon promises made by W. E. Dunbar, who acted as an agent for Potter, regarding the construction and fitting of a courthouse that had not been fulfilled. The case went through multiple trials and verdicts, with contentious legal maneuvers regarding the validity of the defenses and the basis of the plaintiffs' claims.	The plaintiffs contended that the promissory note issued by Haight was valid and due. They argued that the money was owed for the purchase of a courthouse as part of a subscription agreement, which Haight had pledged to support financially. The plaintiffs maintained the position that Dunbar was not authorized to make any detrimental representations regarding the terms of the note and that the note itself was a binding contract requiring payment.	The defendant, Daniel S. Haight, asserted that the consideration for the note had completely failed as the conditions laid out by Dunbar, regarding the construction and suitability of the courthouse, were not fulfilled. Haight contended that Dunbar had made representations that influenced his decision to subscribe, which were unfulfilled, rendering the promise invalid. Additionally, he claimed that the note was assigned after it became due, which further negated its enforceability.

In 1887, a legal case was initiated in Cook County, Illinois, between William Scharnweber (the plaintiff) and Benjamin F. Felix (the defendant). The dispute arose over a royalty agreement concerning a patent for an improved "rope reel," of which both parties were joint proprietors. According to their written agreement, Felix was granted the exclusive rights to manufacture and sell the rope reels, and was required to pay Scharnweber a specified royalty for each reel sold. The primary contention in court was whether the reels sold by Felix fell under the scope of their written contract. During the trial, a jury ruled in favor of Scharnweber, leading to a judgment that was subsequently upheld by the Appellate Court for the First District. Felix sought further appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, raising issues regarding the number of reels that were properly covered under the royalty agreement and the admissibility of certain evidence. The court noted that the factual determination of the number of reels sold was not within its purview for review, as that had been resolved by lower courts.	Scharnweber contended that Felix breached the agreement by failing to pay the required royalties on the rope reels manufactured and sold. He argued that the reels sold were indeed covered under their contract, and he sought damages corresponding to the unpaid royalties. The plaintiff also claimed that it was relevant to show improvements he suggested that were adopted in the production of the reels, bolstering his position regarding the contract.	Felix defended himself by asserting that the reels he sold were not the ones stipulated in the contract and argued that he was only responsible for royalties on the reels explicitly covered by the agreement. He sought to prove that the machines sold were new inventions and argued against the admissibility of certain testimonies regarding improvements suggested by Scharnweber. Felix also attempted to leverage claims of collateral issues surrounding the invention to diminish his liability.

Henry B. Truett filed a case against Charles B. Wainwright and others after a judgment in favor of Wainwright & Co. was made against him in Jo Daviess County Court during the July term of 1845. The conflict arose from a judgment that Truett claimed was obtained without his proper authorization, asserting that an attorney who was not authorized acted on his behalf. Following the initiation of this case in October 1845, Truett submitted a bill seeking to set aside the judgment and requesting discovery of certain facts relevant to the case. The defendants filed a demurrer, which was sustained by the County Court in July 1846, leading to the dismissal of Truett's bill and the dissolution of the injunction he sought. Truett contested the court's decision, arguing that the court had sufficient jurisdiction and that his claims warranted a response from the defendants instead of dismissal.	Truett argued that the judgment against him was fraudulent as it was procured by an unauthorized attorney representing him. He sought to set aside the preceding judgment, requesting the court to provide the discovery of certain facts and to prevent the enforcement of the judgment via an injunction. His claim was rooted in allegations of fraud and misrepresentation regarding the powers granted to the unauthorized attorney.	Wainwright and the co-defendants contended that the court of law had adequate jurisdiction to address the issues raised by Truett's claims, positing that a court of equity should not intervene unless a party cannot obtain sufficient relief in a legal court. They maintained that the proceedings followed were proper, and the demurrer was correctly sustained, which led to the dismissal of Truett's bill.

Jasper Weidekin and Copenbarger, the appellants, were involved in a legal dispute with James Snelson, the appellee, concerning alleged damages to Snelson's land caused by the obstruction of drainage. The case arose in Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 4, 1885. Snelson owned two forty-acre tracts of land, while Weidekin owned a forty-acre tract south of Snelson’s, and Copenbarger owned land east of Weidekin’s. Snelson's land naturally drained southward, funneling water into a pond on Weidekin’s property. When Weidekin and Copenbarger later installed a tile drainage system, Snelson argued it disrupted the natural flow of water, damaging his land's rental value and crop yield in 1881, the year the drainage was installed. The trial jury initially awarded Snelson $300, but the case was appealed by the defendants, who contended they had not obstructed any natural drainage. The court examined the history of the land’s drainage and determined that the irrigation practices did not legally bind Weidekin or infringe upon Snelson's rights.	Snelson's main arguments rested on the assertion that Weidekin and Copenbarger had unlawfully interfered with an artificial drainage system developed by Snelson and Copenbarger. He claimed their actions obstructed the proper flow of water, which had led to damages on his property, specifically a decrease in rental value and loss of corn crops. Snelson sought compensation for these damages, arguing he had a right to maintain the drainage and, based on the earlier established system, that his land should remain unaffected by Weidekin and Copenbarger's changes.	The defendants claimed that any obstruction caused by their actions was a natural right to manage water flow on their land, as Weidekin was not originally a landowner at the time the ditch was constructed. They contended that there had been no formal agreement to maintain the artificial drainage and that Snelson had no clear legal claim based on prescription or visible burdens on their property. The defendants argued that Snelson's losses were not due to their drainage modifications but to unrelated factors. Moreover, they maintained that Snelson's claims did not meet the legal standards necessary to impose liability, asserting that any harm suffered was "damnum absque injuria" (loss without injury).

Thomas Y. Bates filed a bill in equity against Erastus Wheeler in December 1832, seeking specific performance of a written contract for the conveyance of certain real estate located in Illinois, specifically within the military tract. Bates alleged that he had fully paid for the land as per the contract and had made frequent demands for the deed from Wheeler. The Circuit Court, however, ultimately dismissed Bates' bill, ruling that he failed to meet the necessary conditions to compel the specific performance he was seeking. Evidence presented during the trial indicated that while Bates had delivered a mare as part of the consideration, he had not sufficiently proven the delivery or payment of a five-dollar note, which was also a part of the agreement. The court indicated that compliance with all aspects of the agreement was essential for Bates to secure a decision in his favor.	The plaintiff, Thomas Y. Bates, claimed that he had fulfilled all obligations under the contract by paying the full consideration for the land, which included delivering a mare and a five-dollar note. Bates requested that the court compel Erastus Wheeler to perform the contract by conveying the land to him as promised.	The defendant, Erastus Wheeler, contended that the plaintiff had not complied with the contract fully, particularly failing to establish the payment or offer of the five-dollar note, which was crucial for a valid claim. Wheeler maintained that without proof of this payment, Bates had no right to demand the specific performance of the contract.

The case "The Chicago & Pacific Railroad Company v. Solomon Stein et al." took place in September 1874 in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Solomon Stein and Morris M. Hirsh, were partners who owned property adjacent to the north branch of the Chicago River. They brought action against the Chicago & Pacific Railroad Company, claiming damages suffered due to the construction and maintenance of a bridge across the river by the railroad. The plaintiffs argued that the bridge obstructed navigation and caused difficulties in accessing their property. A jury trial resulted in a verdict against the railroad company, awarding the plaintiffs $2,692.51 in damages. The case involved procedural questions related to the plaintiffs' amendment of their declaration to include a count in trespass and the defendant's motion for a continuance, which were both topics of debate throughout the proceedings. The court found that no sufficient basis existed for the damages claimed, leading to further examination of the nature of damages attributable to the bridge.	The plaintiffs claimed that the construction of the railroad bridge had caused damage to their property by obstructing navigation on the Chicago River, thereby preventing boats from easily landing at their dock. They sought compensation for loss incurred due to these impediments, specifically totaling $4,500, based on the costs of dredging and the potential rental income lost. They also contended that the bridge diminished the value of their property.	The defendant, Chicago & Pacific Railroad Company, argued that the river was a public navigable stream, and any consequent damage due to the bridge construction should be viewed as damnum absque injuria (damages without injury). They claimed that since the bridge was built with proper authority from the state and city, the plaintiffs could not claim damages. They also contended that the evidence provided by the plaintiffs was speculative and lacked substantial basis, ultimately questioning the validity of the damages awarded by the jury.

On November 1, 1881, Frederick A. Howe purchased several lots in Chicago from Matthew Laflin under a written contract. The agreement stipulated a purchase price of $400 per front foot, with an initial payment of $25,000 and the balance due in five months with interest. The contract included a provision that specified the sale was subject to existing leases on the property and did not convey any rights to buildings not owned by Laflin. After appraising the buildings, the total value was determined at $5400. Howe later made additional payments, ultimately paying a total of $60,000 for the lots. However, upon receiving the deed, Howe discovered that one of the buildings for which he had paid $1,000 did not belong to Laflin. When Howe demanded a refund for the misrepresented building, Laflin refused. Consequently, Howe initiated a legal action against Laflin for recovery of the money paid for the building.	Howe's main argument was that he was entitled to recover the $1,000 he paid for the Frazer building, as Laflin had no ownership of that building, and thus no title was transferred. He asserted that the transaction was premised on misrepresentation of ownership, and in equity and good conscience, Laflin should not retain the payment for a building he did not own.	Laflin contended that the contract had been executed in full through the delivery of the deed, and that any claims for money had and received were invalid because the contract merged into the deed. He argued that Howe had no basis for recovery since the deed encompassed all aspects of the contract regarding the lots and any claims related to the buildings were implicit in that conveyance, therefore denying Howe's claim for refund.

On April 5, 1872, in Cook County, Illinois, D. C. Campbell & Co., a banking firm, sent a telegram to L. T. Smith, S. Coffman, and N. B. Beam, seeking confirmation to honor a draft drawn by A. Harper for $2,300. The following day, they received a reply stating that they would pay the draft for stock. Harper subsequently drew the draft, which was presented to the defendants but was refused acceptance. The case was filed by D. C. Campbell & Co., alleging that the defendants were liable for the amount of the draft due to their telegram acceptance. The defendants contended that their acceptance was conditional upon the shipment of stock, which did not occur. The case went to trial, where a jury ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to an appeal by the defendants who argued that the acceptance of the draft was not clear and conditional. The court's consideration centered on whether the defendants’ acceptance was conditional on stock being shipped.	The plaintiffs, D. C. Campbell & Co., claimed that the defendants had provided an unconditional acceptance of the draft by affirmatively agreeing to pay the specified amount. They argued that the terms of the telegram did not convey any conditions related to the shipment of stock and as such, they were entitled to recover the amount of the draft from the defendants based on their reliance on the defendants' acceptance.	The defendants contended that their acceptance of the draft was conditional, asserting that the payment was contingent on the receipt of stock purchased by A. Harper. They claimed that since the stock was not shipped, they were not liable for the payment of the draft. Additionally, they argued that the language of their acceptance implied a requirement for stock to be involved, which was not met in this case.

George W. Mullinix was indicted in 1875 by the Moultrie Circuit Court for selling intoxicating liquor to a man named Harding, who was described as "a person in the habit of getting intoxicated." The indictment included several counts, and during the trial, the jury found Mullinix guilty on the first two counts. The court subsequently sentenced him to twenty days in the Shelby County jail and imposed a fine of $80 plus costs. Mullinix appealed the judgment through a writ of error, arguing that the trial court had erred in various instructions to the jury and in its handling of the charges. He claimed that the jury instruction regarding defining someone in the habit of drunkenness was misleading and not precise. Furthermore, he contended that the jury's conviction was based on improper instructions about the responsibility of a liquor seller for the actions of their employees. The court reviewed these arguments, scrutinizing the legal definitions involved and the implications of both the evidence and the jury instructions given during the trial.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, argued that Mullinix had violated liquor sale laws by selling to an individual (Harding) who was known to be in the habit of getting intoxicated. They maintained the legality of the indictment and insisted that proper jury instructions supported the conviction. Specifically, they contended that it was sufficient for the court to establish that Harding's behavior fell within the legal definitions of intemperance and that Mullinix, as an employer, was responsible for the actions of his clerks without needing to demonstrate direct knowledge of their illegal sales.	Mullinix contended that the jury was misled by the trial court's instructions, which conflated intemperance with habitual drunkenness. He argued that the trial court erred in its legal interpretations and instructions regarding the agent's actions, asserting that he should not be held liable for sales made by his employees unless he had prior knowledge of their unlawful actions. Additionally, he argued that the court's judgment was flawed in its handling of sentencing, citing that he deserved a separate sentence for each count of the indictment rather than a combined one.

On July 20, 1850, in Menard County, Illinois, the inhabitants of a school district voted to levy a tax of $500 for the construction of a schoolhouse. The election process and the tax were subsequently certified by the district clerk to the county clerk by October 15, 1850. However, William M. Cowgill and Frackelten were later charged $28.26 related to this tax, leading the collector to distrain their property for payment on May 14, 1851. The plaintiffs filed a chancery bill against the collector to prevent the sale of their property while their suit was pending. On January 21, 1853, an act was passed declaring that the tax voted by the school district in July 1850 was valid, despite the improper timeframe of the vote. The plaintiffs contested the legality of the tax based on the timing of the voting and certification. Ultimately, the case was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court for final resolution.	The plaintiffs claimed that the tax levied for the erection of the schoolhouse was invalid, as it was voted on after the legally designated date for tax certification, which was supposed to be prior to July 1. They argued that the collector's actions to distrain their property were therefore unlawful, seeking an injunction to prevent the sale of their property until the case was resolved.	The defendant contended that the legislative act passed on January 21, 1853, retrospectively validated the tax and corrected any prior defects in its voting and certification process. They argued that the legislature had the authority to rectify such issues while the tax remained uncollected, maintaining that the action to collect the tax was lawful and justified.

Alexander B. Moore v. Abram Bruner was a legal case decided on June 15, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in Massac County, where the key individuals involved were the plaintiff, Abram Bruner, and the defendant, Alexander B. Moore. The dispute arose from a guardianship bond in which both men, along with two others, acted as sureties. The guardian of a ward died leaving a debt of $500 to the ward, leading to a judgment against the guardian's estate. Due to insolvency, this amount could not be recovered, prompting a suit against Bruner and Moore, resulting in a $500 judgment against them. Bruner paid the full amount owed and sought contribution from Moore, claiming he was entitled to $269.45, as the remaining sureties were insolvent or deceased. The court initially ruled in favor of Bruner, awarding him $260, which Moore appealed on the grounds of a miscalculation regarding the proportionate liability among the sureties.	The plaintiff, Abram Bruner, argued that he was entitled to contribution from Alexander B. Moore, his co-surety, for the payment made to satisfy the judgment against them. Bruner contended that due to the insolvency of two other sureties, he should be able to recover a greater proportion than the one-fourth typically apportioned among the four sureties. His primary legal request was for Moore to pay him the amount of $269.45 as contribution.	Alexander B. Moore contended that he was only liable for one-fourth of the debt paid by Bruner, which equated to approximately $129.72, regardless of the insolvency of the other sureties. He argued that under the prevailing legal standards, the insolvency of co-sureties should not influence the calculation of contribution owed. Moore requested the court to overturn the previous judgment against him, asserting that he owed Bruner only a fraction of what had been awarded.

In April 1862, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Robert Pullian et al. vs. George W. Nelson, stemming from a conflict over an alleged debt. Robert Pullian and his business partners, operating under the name Pullian, Wills, Rankin & Co., filed an affidavit on December 24, 1859, stating that Nelson was indebted to them for goods worth $124.63, and claimed that he was a non-resident of Illinois. This affidavit led to a writ of attachment being issued. Nelson was accused of being non-residential at the time of the suit's commencement. Nelson disputed this claim, asserting that he was indeed a resident of Illinois, thereby prompting legal proceedings. A trial took place where the jury ultimately found in favor of the defendant, leading to a judgment on November 15, 1860, that required the plaintiffs to cover Nelson's court costs. The case hinged on the issues regarding Nelson's residency status as defined by legal standards and procedural correctness concerning witness testimonies during the trial.	The plaintiffs argued that George W. Nelson was indebted to them for $124.63 for goods sold and delivered. They contended that Nelson was a non-resident of Illinois, which justified the issuance of a writ of attachment against his property to secure the debt. They requested that the court confirm their claims and rule in favor of enforcing the attachment based on his alleged non-resident status.	Nelson's defense centered on his claim of residency in Illinois at the time the suit commenced, which the defense asserted negated the basis for the attachment. He challenged the validity of the plaintiffs' affidavit, arguing it was defective because it did not demonstrate that he was a non-resident when the suit was initiated. They sought to have the suit dismissed, asserting that the plaintiffs failed to prove their claims adequately.

In 1886, the case of George H. Fergus et al. v. Seth Wilmarth et al. was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case stemmed from a trust deed executed on June 26, 1871, by George H. Fergus and his wife, which was meant to secure a $12,000 loan made to Fergus by Alexander H. Rice, payable to the order of Seth Wilmarth. The trust deed required Fergus to insure the buildings on the mortgaged property in Chicago for $7,500, with the insurance proceeds payable to the trustee in the event of loss. A significant fire in October 1871 destroyed the buildings, and the trustee collected $7,500 from the insurance company. Fergus and his wife later contested that the full amount owed on the loan should be reduced by the insurance proceeds. Fergus argued that he was entitled to credit for the full insurance amount against the mortgage debt since it had been improperly retained by the trustee. The case initially went to the Cook County circuit court, which ruled in favor of Wilmarth. The matter was appealed, leading to further consideration by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, George H. Fergus and his wife, claimed that the trustee should have credited the $7,500 insurance proceeds against their mortgage debt. They argued that as the mortgagors, they had fulfilled their obligation by insuring the property, and that the proper application of the insurance funds would necessitate a reduction in the amount owed on the loan. Fergus maintained that the trustee had acted improperly by using the insurance funds for purposes he had not consented to.	The defendant, Seth Wilmarth, contended that the trustee acted correctly by not applying the insurance money towards the mortgage debt without Fergus's consent. Wilmarth argued that until there was default on the mortgage or the principal became due, the trustee had a duty to hold the funds for the security of the debt rather than disbursing them to the mortgagor. The trustee's actions were consistent with the trust deed's provisions, which did not allow for the funds to be used without consent from both the mortgagor and the mortgagee.

Jacob Williams entered into two premium notes with the German Mutual Fire Insurance Company of North Chicago, dated March 17, 1868, and June 21, 1870, promising to pay the company $125 and $62.30, respectively. The company brought an action of assumpsit against Williams to recover these amounts after an assessment was levied due to significant losses the company suffered during the Great Chicago Fire of October 9, 1871. The case escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court after the lower court ruled in favor of the insurance company. Key individuals involved included Jacob Williams, the plaintiff, and representatives from the German Mutual Fire Insurance Company. The case focused on the validity of the notes, the assessment process, and procedural nuances regarding the language in which the notes were written.	The German Mutual Fire Insurance Company claimed that Jacob Williams failed to pay the amounts due on the premium notes. They argued that the assessment applied to the notes was valid and necessary due to the company's substantial losses from the Chicago Fire. The plaintiff requested the court to uphold the validity of the assessment and enforce the payment of the amounts owed by Williams under the terms of the premium notes.	Jacob Williams contended that the admission of the premium notes in German constituted a variance since the court had not established that they were made in that language. He also challenged the validity of the assessment, arguing that not all directors were notified properly, and questioned whether the evidence presented adequately demonstrated the company's right to levy the assessment. He sought to reverse the lower court's decision and dismiss the claims against him.

Wilson P. Hall v. William C. Kimball is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1871. The case originated in the Morgan Circuit Court, where it was presided over by Judge Charles D. Hodges. The action was initiated by surviving partners William C. Kimball and Ezekiel Kimball against Wilson P. Hall and partner Elizabeth McHatton, based on a promissory note for $5,000 signed by Hall and his firm. The litigation centered around a plea in abatement concerning the non-joinder of a third party, William L. Nugent, who was claimed to be a dormant partner. There was a contention about his status, with the plaintiffs stating they were unaware of Nugent's partnership, while the defendants argued he was a known partner. After various procedural amendments, including Nugent being added as a defendant, the trial proceeded without a jury, resulting in a judgment favoring the plaintiffs. The case was then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Wilson P. Hall and Elizabeth McHatton, contended that the addition of William L. Nugent as a defendant was appropriate under the act of 1869, which allows for amending pleadings to include new defendants. They sought a judgment on the promissory note and goods sold, and claimed that they were entitled to interest on the amount owed.	The defendants, Hall and McHatton, presented several defenses, including a plea of non assumpsit (i.e., they did not assume or accept the obligation) and a plea of payment, asserting that the debt had been settled. Additionally, they argued that allowing an interest rate exceeding that permissible under Illinois law was an error given that there was no specific interest rate agreed upon in the note or supported by evidence of the rate applicable where the debt was incurred.

On January 1860, in Hancock County, Illinois, Harrison H. Barnes served as a constable who levied and sold property belonging to John Rogers under an execution. Rogers claimed the property, specifically sixty bushels of wheat, was exempt from such levies as he maintained he was the head of a family and resided with them at the time of the levy. Rogers filed a trespass action against Barnes, arguing that Barnes had wrongfully seized his property.
