On the following day, four defendants entered their appearance, and subsequently, a default judgment was entered against these defendants for not pleading. However, there was no judgment or order regarding the remaining two defendants who had been served but did not appear. The plaintiffs sought a writ of error to reverse their own judgment, arguing that it was erroneous to render judgment against part of the defendants while neglecting the others. The case was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court, which found that the initial judgment was flawed and that all defendants should be addressed together in line with common law principles.	The plaintiffs claimed that the judgment entered against only part of the defendants was erroneous and sought to have it reversed. They argued that rendering judgment against some defendants while leaving others unaddressed violated the legal requirement that all parties involved in joint obligations must be treated together. The plaintiffs requested that the judgment be overturned due to this procedural error.	The defendants had not entered an appearance or made any formal defenses since the judgment was entered against only those who appeared. They indicated that the judgment should not have been entered without addressing the remaining defendants. The defendants maintained that the court had erred by failing to serve all parties properly and by not allowing for a complete determination of the case before entering judgment.

In October 1804, Rachael, a free negro woman aged twenty-three, entered into an indenture with Joseph Cornelius, binding herself to serve him for fifteen years. This indenture stipulated that Cornelius would provide Rachael with necessities including food, lodging, and clothing, but it was only signed by Rachael. Betsy, a negro girl born to Rachael in fall 1805, became the subject of the legal dispute when Cornelius sought to reclaim her services. The defendant, Thomas Cohen, challenged the validity of the indenture, arguing that Cornelius had no legal claim to Betsy's services due to the indenture not being executed by him. The circuit court's jury was instructed to consider these points, but the court later decided they should have been directed to rule in favor of Cohen based on the indenture's invalidity. An appeal was made by Cornelius following a judgment of nonsuit by the circuit court.	Joseph Cornelius claims that the indenture entered into with Rachael grants him the legal right to the services of Betsy. He argues that under the laws governing slavery and indentures, he is entitled to enforce the agreement even though it was not signed by him, as Rachael’s entries were sufficient for the time period and context. Cornelius seeks the court’s decision to prevent Cohen from keeping Betsy and to affirm his right to her services.	Thomas Cohen argues that the indenture is entirely void since it was not executed by Cornelius, asserting that without his signature, there is no legal binding agreement. Cohen contends that the earlier laws resulted in the indenture being non-enforceable and that the claim to Betsy’s services under the thirteenth section of the 1807 Act is inadmissible because the proper legal process was not followed, as Rachael and Cornelius failed to formalize the agreement in accordance with the law. Cohen requests the court to rule in his favor, confirming that he rightfully retains Betsy.

On March 3, 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, Frank P. Reynolds filed a bill of complaint against William Gordon and his spouse, Mary Gordon, as well as Charles Gordon. Reynolds had previously secured a judgment of $2103 against Charles Gordon, which remained unsatisfied due to "no property found" upon execution. The core of the complaint centered around a 1876 transaction in which Charles Gordon purportedly transferred ownership of a valued property in Chicago to his son, William, for a nominal sum of $500. Reynolds alleged that this conveyance was fraudulent, intended to hinder and delay creditors, as it involved a secret trust that benefited Charles. The property was claimed to be held in trust for Charles, with an understanding that he would receive support from William. Despite William's claims of having paid for the property, Reynolds sought to have the conveyance nullified, asserting that it was structured to protect Charles’s assets from creditors. The case involved various legal processes including demurrers, answers to bills, and supplementary filings, which led to a hearing where the court ultimately found the transfer necessary to address Reynolds's claims of fraudulent conveyance.	Reynolds claimed that the alleged conveyance of property from Charles Gordon to William Gordon was fraudulent and intended to thwart creditors. He argued that the transfer was void due to lack of consideration and the existence of a secret trust arrangement. Reynolds sought the court to set aside this pretended conveyance and have the property subjected to the payment of his judgment, asserting that the true nature of the transaction was to protect Charles's assets from legitimate claims against him.	William and Mary Gordon argued that the property was legitimately sold to William for $997.67 and denied allegations of fraud. They contended that the payment was valid and asserted that Reynolds was merely a nominal complainant. They also claimed a conspiracy between Reynolds and Charles to deprive them of the property. The defendants sought to uphold the validity of the conveyance and asked for the dismissal of Reynolds’s claims against them.

In 1860, Elisha D. Carter, the plaintiff in error, engaged in a legal dispute with Adolphus Lewis and others in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a series of debts owed by Carter to multiple creditors, including Lewis & Rosenham and Samuel Hale. Before November 12, 1859, Carter was significantly indebted to these creditors, and despite judgments being entered against him in 1858, he failed to satisfy them. Instead, in an attempt to avoid paying his debts, Carter executed a fraudulent mortgage on his real estate valued at ten thousand dollars, claiming he owed David Schmick $8,000—this purported debt was fabricated to mislead his creditors. Creditors subsequently filed a bill alleging the mortgage was fraudulent, aimed at delaying the collection of their claims. After jurisdiction was changed to DeWitt County, Carter failed to respond adequately, resulting in the court taking the bill for confessed and issuing a decree demanding payment of specific amounts owed to the creditors.	The plaintiffs—creditors of Carter—claimed that he engaged in fraudulent actions by creating a mortgage without real consideration, intending to frustrate their efforts to collect on their debts. They requested that Carter and Schmick be compelled to answer to the allegations and that the mortgage be deemed void. Ultimately, they sought a decree that would allow for the sale of Carter's real estate to satisfy the debts owed to them.	Carter's defense revolved around the argument that the court's handling of the procedural aspects, such as striking their demurrer and rendering a decree by default, was erroneous. They contended that the decree against Carter imposed an indefinite amount due to the lack of claimed interest or costs. Carter also claimed that the decree for the $700 owed to Emerson and Cassell was vague, as it stated “and upwards.”

The case "Eugene Patneaud v. Hyppolite Claire" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on July 1, 1889. It involved two adjacent landowners: Eugene Patneaud, who owned the west half of the northeast quarter section 6 in Township 27, Range 13 W, and Hyppolite Claire, who owned the east half of the northwest quarter of the same section. In the 1860s, both owners, originally purchasing their lands from the Illinois Central Railroad, constructed a ditch to facilitate water drainage across their properties. Over the years, both parties maintained the ditch until Patneaud unilaterally filled it and constructed a dam, obstructing the natural flow of water from Claire’s land onto his. This action resulted in flooding 20 to 30 acres of Claire's land. The court addressed whether Patneaud had the legal right to alter or obstruct this drainage system given its historical significance and mutual agreement regarding its maintenance. Patneaud asserted ownership of the ditch while denying any easement rights of Claire, leading to the case being appealed after the Circuit Court ruled in favor of Claire, awarding him $18 in damages.	The plaintiff, Hyppolite Claire, claimed that Patneaud's actions in filling the ditch and erecting a dam violated his right to allow water from his land to flow naturally over Patneaud's property. Claire argued that the ditch was established with the understanding and agreement of both parties to facilitate drainage, constituting an implied easement that Patneaud could not legally obstruct. He sought damages for the flooding caused by Patneaud's actions.	Eugene Patneaud contended that he had the right to manage the drainage on his property as he deemed fit, asserting separate ownership over the ditch and the ability to fill it in without any obligation to maintain it for Claire's benefit. He challenged the existence of any legal easement that would afford Claire rights over his land, claiming that the historical arrangement did not grant Claire any legal claim to the continued use of the ditch after their respective ownerships shifted.

In December 1827, in Clinton County, Illinois, Henry Curtis was indicted on two counts: one for assault with a loaded gun intending to kill James Tilton, and the second for a physical assault against Tilton. The grand jury's indictment asserted that Curtis had discharged the gun at Tilton, causing a dangerous wound, contrary to Illinois statutes. At the September term of the Circuit Court, Curtis was tried and found guilty, leading to his sentencing to pay a $50 fine and serving 20 days in prison. Following the verdict, Curtis appealed the decision, arguing that the indictment had several formal defects, including the omission of the word “oaths,” the indictment's language differing from the statutory requirements, lack of a charge for "intent to commit murder," and that a general verdict of guilty could not stand due to the first count's alleged defects.	The plaintiff, referred to as "The People," argued that Curtis was guilty of the charges against him as laid out in the indictment. They asserted that the evidence presented during the trial sufficiently demonstrated Curtis's intent and actions were contrary to the laws of Illinois regarding assault and battery.	Curtis's defense focused on several points challenging the validity of the indictment. He claimed that it did not confirm that the indictment was presented upon the oaths of the grand jury, it varied from statutory language, and it failed to charge him appropriately with the intent to murder. His defense maintained that the two counts of the indictment were flawed, and since the first count was defective, a general guilty verdict could not be substantiated legally.

Ignatius R. Simms, the appellant, was involved in a legal dispute with Nelson H. Clark and Sarah W. Clark, the appellees, during the year 1849 in Morgan County, Illinois. The case arose from Simms's payment of a judgment amounting to $684.08 owed to the Clarks, during which he mistakenly paid a counterfeit $50 banknote. The Clarks lived in Mississippi but had an agent, Branson, who facilitated the transaction in Jacksonville, where Simms resided. After Simms paid the debt, the counterfeit note changed hands several times but was eventually identified as fake by the Auditor of Public Accounts in Springfield. The Clarks' claims hinged on the notion that they had notified Simms of the note's counterfeit status within a reasonable time frame, while Simms argued he should not be obligated to take back the note since it had not been returned to him in a timely manner after its counterfeiting was established. The jury found in favor of the Clarks, leading to Simms appealing the verdict.	The plaintiffs, the Clarks, claimed that Simms had made a payment using a counterfeit $50 banknote as part of his settlement for the outstanding debt. They asserted that the note was returned to Simms within a reasonable time after it was discovered to be counterfeit and requested that he fulfill his obligation to return the money paid.	Simms, the defendant, contended that he had fully satisfied the debt and argued that the Clarks had failed to notify him promptly about the note's counterfeit status. He insisted that due diligence was not exercised in confirming the note's legitimacy and maintained that the time taken to notify him of the counterfeit bill discharged him of any obligation to pay it back.

In 1865 in Peoria County, Illinois, Drury Dalton entered into a recognizance before two justices of the peace to answer an indictment for larceny. William W. O’Brien and others signed as sureties for Dalton. When Dalton failed to appear for his court date, the recognizance was forfeited, prompting a scire facias issued on April 20, 1865, to enforce the recognizance. This led to legal proceedings questioning the conditions of the recognizance and the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court, given that the term scheduled for Dalton's appearance was exclusively for civil business according to Illinois law. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court after an appeal challenging the lower court's judgment on the demurrer related to the scire facias.	The People of the State of Illinois argued that the scire facias did not need to allege an indictment by the grand jury at the term stated in the recognizance, citing prior case law to support their claim. They contended that the condition of the recognizance should be interpreted in light of the law governing court terms, insisting that Dalton was expected to appear at the next term that allowed criminal proceedings.	The defendants contended that the recognizance was contingent upon Dalton appearing at a term of the Circuit Court where it was impossible for him to do so, as it was a civil term. They argued that this made the recognizance void, and the indictment could not be criminally processed at the scheduled term, which did not allow for criminal cases, thus challenging the efficacy of the scire facias.

The case of Andrews v. Board of Trade of Chicago took place in 1886, within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Appellate Court. The appeal was led by the plaintiff, Andrews, against the Board of Trade of Chicago, following a jury verdict that ruled against him. The legal proceedings aimed to address the claims brought forth by Andrews, who was unhappy with the outcome in the lower court decided by Judge Rollin S. Williamson. During the trial, the plaintiff failed to establish a sufficient cause of action. As a result, the court was tasked with reviewing the jury's verdict and the circumstances surrounding the case to determine the validity of the claims made by Andrews.	The plaintiff, Andrews, claimed that he had valid grounds for his lawsuit against the Board of Trade of Chicago. He sought to overturn the jury's verdict from the lower court, asserting that the decision was incorrect and that he had sufficient evidence to prove his case. Andrews requested the appellate court to reverse the judgment, claiming failure on the part of the Board to respond adequately to his allegations.	The Board of Trade of Chicago, as the defendant, maintained that the plaintiff did not establish a cause of action that warranted a judgment in his favor. They argued that the jury's verdict was justifiable based on the evidence presented during the trial. The Board requested the appellate court to affirm the lower court's judgment, emphasizing that the plaintiff had failed in meeting the necessary legal standards to support his claims.

In December 1825, the case of Willis Hargrave v. The Bank of Illinois was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, located in Gallatin, Illinois. The key individuals involved were plaintiff Willis Hargrave and the Bank of Illinois as the defendant. The case revolved around Hargrave's challenge to the Bank's claim of legal existence as a corporation in a lawsuit related to the recovery of funds owed. The court was tasked with determining whether the Bank was required to provide evidence of its corporate status in order to pursue legal recourse for its claims. The case arose from previous rulings and discussions regarding the prerequisites for a corporation to engage in litigation, notably the necessity of proving incorporation at trial.	The plaintiff, Willis Hargrave, argued that the Bank of Illinois failed to provide adequate evidence of its incorporation during the trial. He contended that without proving its legal status as a corporation, the Bank was not entitled to pursue its claims in court. Hargrave sought to have the court reverse the previous judgment that permitted the Bank to proceed without such proof.	The Bank of Illinois, represented by its counsel, maintained that the act of indorsing a bill to the bank amounted to an admission of its corporate status, thereby alleviating the need for further evidence of incorporation. They argued that the court's instruction to require evidence of incorporation was unnecessary and incorrect, asserting that their actions sufficiently demonstrated the Bank's existence as a corporation.

The case "Parnell Munson v. Charles B. Farwell et al." took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the final judgment issued on April 8, 1885. The case involved Parnell Munson as the defendant and Charles B. Farwell along with others as plaintiffs. The plaintiffs brought a lawsuit under the action of assumpsit, claiming that Munson owed them $803.32 for goods, wares, and merchandise sold and delivered, as well as for money paid on Munson’s behalf at his request. The specifics of the claim centered around an agreement made in 1877, where the parties involved were creditors of Sibley and Chester, who had claims against various insurance companies following a fire. Farwell and others were appointed as trustees to prosecute claims against those companies. Munson, along with these other creditors, was to pay his share of the attorney fees and disbursements for the litigation. A trial was held in the absence of Munson, where a jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to a judgment against Munson for the claimed amount. Munson later sought to vacate this judgment, prompting this appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that they were owed $803.32 from the defendant for his pro rata share of attorneys’ fees and costs incurred in the prosecution of insurance claims assigned to them by Sibley and Chester, in which Munson was also a creditor. They contended that Munson had agreed to pay this amount for the joint benefit of all involved parties and that he had promised to pay multiple times but had failed to do so.	The defendant contended that the evidence presented by the plaintiffs did not sufficiently prove that any money was paid out by the plaintiffs on his behalf. He argued that the witness testimony did not establish that plaintiffs had incurred any actual expenses or liabilities that would warrant the claim. Munson maintained that since the plaintiffs did not demonstrate a valid claim for payment under the contract or any relevant law, the judgment rendered against him should be reversed.

In the case of Samuel T. Songer et al. v. James Partridge, the legal dispute took place in the Circuit Court of Wayne County, Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 7, 1883. The case revolved around a series of transactions involving Jasper Partridge, Isaac Fitzgerald, Titus Buffington, and Samuel T. Songer. In 1867, Fitzgerald, burdened by debts and facing potential bankruptcy, executed a deed transferring properties (lots 17 and 19 in Fairfield) to Buffington in what was intended to be a protective measure. However, the transaction was viewed as potentially fraudulent, prompting creditors to seek its cancellation. Following bankruptcy proceedings, the deed was vacated, and Fitzgerald settled with his creditors, receiving a full discharge. He then surrendered the notes for the property to Buffington in exchange for Buffington relinquishing all claims to the lots, leading to a subsequent claim by Songer for possession of these properties. The court had to determine the legitimacy of the agreements between Fitzgerald and Buffington and whether these could be enforced post-bankruptcy discharge.	The plaintiffs (Fitzgerald and Partridge) argued that the original deed from Fitzgerald to Buffington was fraudulent, and they sought to have it nullified to reclaim ownership of the lots. They claimed that after Fitzgerald settled his debts, Buffington agreed to return all rights he had in the properties, thus asserting their current rights over the lots due to this agreement.	The defendants (Songer and Buffington) contended that the original conveyance was legally binding despite its fraudulent appearance concerning Fitzgerald's creditors. They argued that since Fitzgerald settled his debts and canceled the initial agreement, the subsequent contract allowing Buffington to relinquish his claim was invalid. Additionally, they posited that the actions taken after the bankruptcy should not aid the plaintiffs in regaining the properties, emphasizing that allowing the plaintiffs to reclaim property after an agreement would undermine the principles of equity.

In 1875, in Lee County, Illinois, Levi Compton was indicted by a grand jury for selling liquor without a license. During the May term of court, it was ordered that Compton be held to bail in the amount of $500. Compton and his surety, Joel Compton, entered into a recognizance in open court, acknowledging their obligation to appear before the circuit court on October 26, 1875, to respond to the indictment. The matter became a part of the court's record. However, Levi and Joel Compton later contested the validity of this recognizance through a scire facias, an order issued to bring a party before the court. They raised defenses claiming that the recognizance was never formally recorded and that there was no such crime as listed in the indictment under Illinois law. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court after a series of motions and rulings in favor of the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs, Levi and Joel Compton, argued that the scire facias on which the recognizance was based was flawed because it did not show that the recognizance was entered into before an authorized officer or court and lacked proper description of the crime. They contended that these deficiencies invalidated the action against them, leading to a request for a dismissal or reversal of any judgment against them.	The defendants, representing the People of the State of Illinois, maintained that the plea of "nul tiel record" effectively challenged the record of the recognizance and argued that the interpretation of the scire facias was sufficient to confirm the existence of a valid recognizance. They claimed that past precedents supported the validity of the language used in the scire facias, contending that even if the indictment's language had deficiencies, the court should presume it pertained to the statutory offense.

Adam B. Robbins filed a lawsuit against Kate L. Crandall, stemming from a dispute about a bill for merchandise sold. The events took place in September 1873 in Grundy County, Illinois, involving two firms: one named Green & Co., which operated the “Mazon Store” across the river from Morris, and another firm in Morris called H. B. Green & Son. The case arose to determine which firm was liable for the payment, as the goods in question were delivered to the “Mazon Store” but were ultimately purchased by H. B. Green & Son. The evidence presented in court indicated that the goods were sold to H. B. Green & Son, as they were responsible for payment and had solicited the order. The testimony revealed that the order was fulfilled under the name of H. R. Green & Son, corroborating that the transaction was correctly attributed to them despite the goods being delivered to a different location. The background involved complex relationships between the firms and an apparent bankruptcy that led to the legal dispute.	Adam B. Robbins, as the appellant, claimed that he was owed payment for the merchandise sold and delivered. He argued that the sale was made to Green & Co. and sought to recover the owed amounts based on the delivery and solicitation of the goods that were sold to his firm, asserting that they were rightfully entitled to payment.	Kate L. Crandall, representing Green & Co., contended that the goods were not sold directly to their firm but were instead purchased by H. B. Green & Son, who were responsible for fulfilling the obligation. The defendant maintained that since the goods were for the other firm that had already paid, Green & Co. should not be liable for the sales price, emphasizing that no fraudulent activity occurred and that Robbins was aware of whom he was dealing with during the transaction.

In September 1841, James Gray successfully proved his entitlement to a preemption right for a tract of land in Quincy, Illinois, and made the corresponding purchase. However, in November 1841, S. S. White, acting as administrator for Edward White's heirs, applied for the same land, but his application was referred to the Commissioner of the General Land Office by the register and receiver. In December 1841, the Commissioner suspended Gray's entry pending investigation. In May 1842, both Gray's and White's claims were deemed invalid by the register and receiver, leading to the cancellation of Gray’s entry in June 1842. In March 1844, James A. McCance made a successful entry for the same land based on a new preemption claim. Gray contested McCance's claim, arguing it was invalid. Following further investigations, the Commissioner affirmed McCance's right to the land. In October 1848, Gray initiated a chancery suit against McCance to assert his claim, but his bill was dismissed. The case ultimately escalated when Gray sought a writ of error.	James Gray, the plaintiff, argued that his initial proof of preemption and payment secured his legal title to the land, and asserted that neither the land officers nor the Commissioner had the authority to invalidate his entry or sell the land to another party. He referenced various precedential cases to support the notion that once a valid right of preemption is established, it must stand unless conclusively invalidated according to legal protocols.	James A. McCance contended that the proceedings of the register and receiver were appropriate and ultimately validated his claim to the land. His defense leaned on the assertion that both Gray's and White's claims were rightfully investigated and subsequently dismissed based on a lack of merit. McCance maintained that the decisions made by the land officers were conclusive and final in determining preemption rights, which negated Gray's attempts to claim the land.

In November 1886, in Bureau County, Illinois, an accident occurred involving a railroad crew loading gravel onto trains operated by the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company. The deceased, Henry Blank, was part of a group of approximately twenty-seven men working under the conductor, William Henry. On the day of the accident, as the train, consisting of twenty-two flat cars and a caboose, backed towards the gravel pit, the conductor ordered the men to switch from the caboose to a flat car. Before all men had safely transitioned, the conductor instructed the brakeman to uncouple the caboose and signaled the engineer to set the air-brakes. This caused a sudden jerking motion, which resulted in Blank and another worker being thrown off the flat car. Blank was tragically struck and killed by the following cars. The suit was brought forth by his widow for damages, alleging the conductor's negligence in the timing of the order and lack of warning before the sudden movement of the train.	The plaintiff, Charlotte Blank, claimed that the conductor, acting on behalf of the railroad, was negligent in his orders that directly led to her husband’s death. She argued that he failed to provide adequate time and notice for all workers to safely transition cars before pulling the coupling pin. The suit sought damages amounting to $2,150 for the loss of support and the wrongful death of Henry Blank, asserting that his death was the result of gross negligence from the conductor.	The defendant, represented by the railroad company, contended that the conductor had followed proper procedure and that the deceased should have anticipated the typical jerking motion associated with slowing trains. They argued that Blank had sufficient time to move to safety and that the conductor's actions were standard for their customary practices. The defense also claimed that if any negligence occurred, it was on the part of the deceased rather than the conductor, seeking to absolve the railroad of liability.

Jonathan Taylor initiated a legal case against Michael Sprinkle in the Illinois Supreme Court, with proceedings dating back to December 1819. The case originated in Gallatin County. The crux of the dispute revolved around a covenant, where issues emerged regarding the validity of a plea asserting that the consideration for a note had failed. The plaintiff Taylor and the defendant Sprinkle were central figures in this legal dispute. Ultimately, the case focused on the technicalities of the plea and whether the defendant sufficiently demonstrated the failure of consideration.	The plaintiff, Jonathan Taylor, contended that the plea filed by Michael Sprinkle regarding the failure of consideration was insufficient. Taylor argued that under legal statutes, any special plea must clearly articulate the grounds for avoiding the obligation, which the defendant failed to do. Taylor requested the court to sustain the demurrer against the defendant’s plea and affirmed the obligation under the original covenant.	The defendant, Michael Sprinkle, based his defense on the assertion that the consideration for the covenant had indeed failed. He contended that his plea was valid under the statutes and sought to demonstrate that there were grounds that justified the plea. Sprinkle argued that the case deserved careful consideration of the new remedy introduced, which could potentially exempt him from the obligations of the covenant.

The case titled "Delavan Martin, Administrator of Albert Houston, deceased, Appellant, v. James Charter, Administrator of Jonathan Charter, deceased, Appellee" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1862, following an action of trespass initiated at the October term of the McDonough Circuit Court in 1856. The case revolves around the taking and subsequent sale of a horse that was originally the property of Albert Houston. During the proceedings, both parties involved passed away. The defendant, James Charter, who was acting as a constable, claimed that the horse was taken under an execution for a debt owed by Knowles and McGee, asserting that the horse was liable due to its ownership by Knowles at the time. The plaintiff contended that the constable had already levied other property, sufficient to satisfy the execution, and that the horse had been sold to Martin following the execution's initiation. This led to legal complexities regarding the sufficiency of the levy and the corssitutionality of the statutes in play.	The plaintiff, Delavan Martin, argued that the constable had levied an execution on two other horses and a threshing machine, which were sufficient to satisfy the execution debt owed by Knowles and McGee. Subsequently, the constable took a delivery bond from Knowles for those properties, thereby leaving them with Knowles and permitting him to sell the horse in question to Martin. The plaintiff's central claim was that the horse had been rightfully sold to him and sought to challenge the defendant's actions post-levy.	The defendant, James Charter, maintained that he acted as a constable under a valid execution for a debt. He claimed that at the time of the supposed trespass, the horse belonged to Knowles and was consequently liable to seizure for that debt. The defendant's primary defense rested on this assertion of authority under the execution, contesting the validity of the plaintiff's ownership claim and responding to the plaintiff's replication with a demurrer, which was ultimately sustained by the court.

In 1831, John Bustard and Charles Nooe obtained a judgment against John Edgar in the Randolph Circuit Court for $839. After two years, an execution was issued on this judgment, which was replevied with Robert Morrison acting as surety. Subsequent executions were returned unsatisfied. Edgar, who was found to be insolvent at the time of his death, owned lands in Randolph, Jackson, and Perry counties that were sold to various defendants, but these lands remained subject to Bustard and Nooe's judgment. The plaintiffs sought a perpetual lien on the properties and requested that the land be sold to satisfy their judgment. However, the defendants filed a demurrer, leading to the court's review of the applicability of their claims, particularly concerning the jurisdictional limits of the Circuit Court's judgment and the remedies available in equity.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to a perpetual lien on the lands owned by Edgar and sought the sale of these lands to satisfy their judgment arising from the unpaid execution. They contended that their judgment created an enforceable lien despite Edgar's insolvency and subsequent death, and they maintained that the court should allow them to pursue their claim through equity since their attempts in law had been thwarted by the insolvency of Edgar.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs were mistaken in seeking a remedy in equity, as a court of law should enforce its own judgments. They argued that judgments create liens only on the lands within the jurisdiction where the judgment was rendered. They further asserted that if the plaintiffs lost their lien due to time elapsed or negligence, they could not seek equity to extend it, and thus, the matters of judgment enforcement were purely legal, not appropriate for chancery consideration.

In 1836, in Warren County, Illinois, the legal case of Abraham Johnson v. Thomas Moulton originated before a justice of the peace and was subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court. The dispute centered on claims made by Moulton against Johnson regarding improvements made on public land. During the trial, a jury found in favor of Moulton, awarding him damages of $21.65. Johnson appealed this decision, arguing that the judgment was against the weight of the evidence presented, that improper evidence was admitted, and that the jury had been incorrectly instructed about the nature of the contract regarding the improvements. The Circuit Court Judge, Richard M. Young, presided over the case, which included discussions on whether there was an express or implied contract between the two parties concerning the land improvements.	The plaintiff, Thomas Moulton, claimed that he had a right to recover damages for the improvements he made on public land, arguing there was either an express promise or an implied agreement from Johnson to pay for these enhancements. Moulton sought a judgment affirming his claim and additional costs incurred during the trial, asserting that he had fulfilled the requirements of the law regarding contracts for public land improvements.	The defendant, Abraham Johnson, countered Moulton's claims by asserting multiple errors during the trial. He argued that the jury's verdict was against the weight of the evidence and that the trial court wrongfully allowed certain testimony to be admitted. Additionally, Johnson claimed that the jury instructions misrepresented the legal standards regarding contracts, particularly in regard to implied agreements, challenging the legality of the judgment in favor of Moulton.

In 1860, Abram Van Wormer, formerly a partner in a saw-mill with De Clausel, sold logs to the firm for which De Clausel and Francis Wittram were partners. The partnership of De Clausel and Wittram was formed after Van Wormer left, and they dissolved their partnership on January 1, 1861. On December 20, 1860, De Clausel issued a note for $979.86 as payment for the logs sold by Van Wormer, which he later indorsed. Van Wormer argued that the payment was due to him, while Wittram contended he was unaware of the note's existence, claiming that the logs were part of De Clausel's contribution to the capital of their partnership. The case raised the question of whether the logs were sold to De Clausel personally or to the firm, and whether the note constituted a valid obligation of the firm.	The plaintiff, Abram Van Wormer, claimed that De Clausel issued a promissory note to him for the balance owed for logs sold upon the dissolution of the old partnership. He argued that the note represented a valid debt owed to him by the partnership of De Clausel & Wittram, asserting his right to payment as a creditor of the firm.	The defendant, Francis Wittram, contended that he was never made aware of the note until the lawsuit began and maintained that the logs were contributed to the partnership as part of De Clausel's capital investment. Wittram argued that one partner cannot bind the firm to a debt incurred for a personal liability, and therefore claimed that the firm was not responsible for the note issued by De Clausel.

In 1866, in Monticello, Illinois, John W. White entered into a written agreement, promising to pay the Monticello Railroad Company $50, with payments to be made in installments assessed by the company's directors. Over the following years, White made multiple payments based on assessments but eventually refused to pay a later assessment. Charles W. Smith, the defendant, was involved as the party refusing to pay the final assessment made in January 1869. The legal case escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court after the initial court ruled in favor of the plaintiff. The primary legal question revolved around whether the instrument constituted a valid negotiable promissory note. The court examined the validity of White's instrument under the applicable legal definitions and case law precedents.	The plaintiff, John W. White, claimed that the written promise was a valid negotiable promissory note. He argued that he had fulfilled his obligations by paying earlier assessments, and the remaining amount due, as required by the assessments made by the directors of the Monticello Railroad Company, constituted a legitimate claim for payment.	The defendant, Charles W. Smith, contended that the instrument could not be considered a valid negotiable promissory note because its payments relied on future actions by the railroad's directors, rendering the payments subject to contingencies. He argued that this uncertainty meant the promise was not enforceable, as it could lead to situations where the payment might never become due.

The case "Off & Co. v. Givens" took place in Illinois, with the judgment rendered by the Illinois Appellate Court on June 8, 1886. The key individuals involved were Charles J. Off & Co., the plaintiff, and D. F. Givens, the defendant, along with W. D. Lomax, another party referenced in the original judgment. The case arose from a request made by Off & Co. in February 1885 during the Knox Circuit Court term to amend the record of a judgment issued in October 1883. Off & Co. sought to correct the record to reflect a judgment of $153.29 against D. F. Givens, instead of the judgment incorrectly noted against W. D. Lomax. The crux of the issue was whether Givens was rightfully included as a party in the trial and whether the original jury verdict applied to him. The court examined the records and found a lack of definitive evidence showing that Givens was indeed a party to the previous trial or that a judgment had been rightfully entered against him.	The plaintiff, Off & Co., argued that there was an error in the original judgment that mistakenly listed W. D. Lomax as the party liable instead of D. F. Givens. They sought to amend the court record to correctly reflect a judgment against Givens for the amount of $153.29, asserting that Givens should have been held accountable based on the jury's findings.	The defendant, D. F. Givens, contended that there was insufficient evidence to support the claim that he was a party to the original trial and that the jury had rendered a verdict against him. Givens argued against the amendment of the judgment, stating that the records did not clearly indicate his involvement or liability in the trial proceedings.

In December 1845, a case known as Lewis Hatch v. John S. Potter et ux. was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from the Circuit Court of McHenry County. The core issue involved slanderous statements made by Lewis Hatch (the appellant) against John S. Potter's wife. Specifically, Hatch was alleged to have stated that Mrs. Potter had slept with him before her marriage, implying she engaged in fornication. The statements were made on July 21 and on multiple occasions thereafter, prompting Potter and his wife (the appellees) to file suit. The trial included testimonies and objections regarding the admissibility of evidence, particularly concerning the intent behind Hatch's remarks and the circumstances of their publication. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of the appellees, awarding them $425 in damages, leading Hatch to appeal the decision to the higher court.	The plaintiffs, John S. Potter and his wife, contended that Lewis Hatch made defamatory statements that harmed their reputation. They argued that the published words amounted to slander, as they imputed a charge of fornication against Mrs. Potter. The plaintiffs sought damages for the emotional and reputational harm suffered due to Hatch’s allegations.	Lewis Hatch maintained a defense largely focused on the context and intent of his statements. He argued the words were spoken in jest and claimed that he did not intend to be taken seriously, thus denying liability for slander. Hatch also objected to the introduction of certain testimonies that he believed were prejudicial and irrelevant, particularly regarding witness interpretations of his intent when making the statements.

John Buckingham et al. v. August Fisher is a legal case decided in September 1873 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident occurred in the context of a warehouse operated by the appellants, Buckingham and his associates, who had leased it from the Illinois Central Railroad Company. The warehouse was situated on the bank of the Chicago River, with a dock for lake vessels receiving grain for shipment. In April or early May 1871, August Fisher, the appellee, sent his team to retrieve grain purchased from the warehouse. While waiting for a loading ticket in the office, the horses, hitched to a 22-pound clog, backed over the edge of the wharf and drowned in the river. The plaintiff claimed the defendants failed to provide necessary safety measures, such as guards or fenders on the wharf, and adequate facilities for hitching teams. The case highlighted a dispute over responsibility for the accident, particularly regarding the duty of care owed by the warehousemen.	The plaintiff, August Fisher, argued that the defendants were negligent for failing to place guards or fenders on the edge of the wharf to prevent teams from falling into the river. Fisher contended that the lack of protection constituted a breach of duty and sought damages for the loss of his horses, wagon, and harness.	The defendants, Buckingham and his associates, contended that they owed no legal duty to provide guards or hitching facilities at their private warehouse. They argued that the situation did not fall under the obligations of common carriers, who are held to a higher standard of care, and that the accident was a result of the negligence of the plaintiff's teamster, who failed to secure the horses properly. The defendants requested the court to dismiss the case based on these arguments.

In the case of C. O. Reynolds v. J. J. Phillips, which took place in 1883 in Clay County, Illinois, the dispute arose from a trespass action wherein the defendant, Reynolds, killed the plaintiff's dog. The incident occurred on a public street when the plaintiff's dog attacked the appellant, barking and snapping. Reynolds believed that the dog intended to bite him, prompting him to kill the dog in self-defense. However, the court noted conflicting testimony regarding the dog’s nature—whether it was truly dangerous or accustomed to attacking people was at the heart of the matter. The jury received instructions that a person may not kill a dog unless it presents a clear threat, which seemed to place an undue burden on the defendant to prove the dog was ferocious. The case revealed procedural errors when the jury was instructed, and evidence regarding the dog's prior bad habits was excluded from consideration. Ultimately, these factors led to the reversal of the judgment and a remand for further proceedings.	The plaintiff, J. J. Phillips, claimed that Reynolds unlawfully killed his dog without justification, thus constituting a trespass. He sought damages to compensate for the loss of his property (the dog) and incurred costs associated with the incident.	The defendant, C. O. Reynolds, argued that he acted in self-defense when he killed the dog, which he perceived as a threat. He maintained that he believed the dog intended to attack him, and thus his actions were justified. Additionally, Reynolds contended that evidence regarding the dog's bad habits should have been permitted to mitigate any damages awarded.

Asad Udell brought a legal action against Henry W. Howard, the sheriff of McHenry County, Illinois, in a case dated December 8, 1888. The case arose from a dispute over property that Howard purportedly sold in violation of the law. Udell claimed that certain personal property amounting to $1,300, which included oats, harness sets, a corn sheller, scales, and hay, was exempt from levy and sale due to its nature and his family circumstances. Howard was executing a court order in favor of Charles Herrington for a debt of $498 when he attempted to levy on Udell’s property. During the execution process, Udell asserted his exemptions, but the sheriff insisted on selling the property, leading to disagreements over which items were levied. The court found in its initial judgment that Udell was entitled to receive double damages for the unlawful sale of his property.	Udell asserted that the property sold by Howard was exempt from execution under the law, and he sought damages amounting to the value of the unlawfully sold property, which he claimed was over $1,300. His lawsuit was focused on recovering double the value of the property sold, as permitted by statute due to the sheriff's failure to honor his exemptions.	Howard contended that Udell did not properly assert his exemptions and failed to comply with the legal requirement to turn over the remainder of his property to satisfy the execution. He argued that Udell's claim for double damages should be dismissed because he could not show that he fulfilled the necessary conditions to invoke the statutory protections.

The case 'Archibald McAllister, Plaintiff in Error, v. Zebulon S. Ely, Defendant in Error' took place in Chicago, Illinois, around July 10, 1852, when a promissory note was executed by Jacob E. Depuy and Zebulon S. Ely, payable to Enoch Ely and Archibald McAllister, the plaintiff, which was due ninety days later. Following the maturity of the note, the case commenced on June 20, 1856, almost two years after a written notice was given to McAllister to put the note in suit due to concerns about Depuy's potential insolvency. The defendant's argument was based on the claim that he was a security for Depuy, the principal debtor, and that McAllister, the payee, failed to act within a reasonable time after being notified. This resulted in the defendant believing he was barred from recovering against him as the creditor did not take timely action to collect the debt. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court and stemmed from a previous ruling where the Common Pleas Court had sustained a demurrer against the defendant's plea.	Archibald McAllister's primary argument was that as a surviving payee of the promissory note, he had the right to recover the owed amount from Zebulon S. Ely as the surviving maker of the note. McAllister contended that the appropriate legal action was valid and enforceable, asserting that the failure to act promptly did not provide sufficient grounds for the defendant to evade responsibility.	Zebulon S. Ely's main defense was that he was merely a security for the principal debtor, Jacob E. Depuy, and claimed that McAllister had been duly notified to initiate legal proceedings once the note became due, which he failed to do within a reasonable timeframe. Ely asserted that this lack of action on McAllister’s part barred him from recovering the debt, in accordance with the relevant statutes regarding creditor-debtor relationships and securities.

Adam Seibert, appointed by Sheriff Hiram L. Pierce, served as the jailor for Logan County at a monthly wage of $40. Over nine months, he worked diligently in this role and submitted a total compensation claim of $360 to the Board of Supervisors of Logan County. However, the Board refused to pay this claim. Following this rejection, Seibert appealed to the circuit court, where the judge ruled against him, ordering Seibert to pay the costs of the court proceedings. Unsatisfied with this decision, Seibert proceeded to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking to reverse the judgment made by the circuit court.	Seibert contended that, as a jailor appointed by the sheriff, he was entitled to the wages promised to him by the sheriff and argued that the county should be financially responsible for his compensation. He sought a reversal of the circuit court's decision and the allowance of his claim for wages.	The Board of Supervisors and the sheriff's representatives argued that the county was not legally obligated to compensate Seibert, emphasizing that the jailor is considered a deputy of the sheriff. They maintained that Seibert should seek payment solely from the sheriff, who appointed him, thus refuting any claim against the county itself.

In January 1867, the case of St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago R. R. Co. v. Trustees of Illinois Institution for the Education of the Blind was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Jacksonville, Illinois, concerning a dispute over property belonging to the State, specifically grounds used for the Illinois Institution for the Education of the Blind. The St. Louis, Jacksonville and Chicago Railroad Company sought to condemn a portion of these grounds for depot purposes, claiming rights based on a law that allowed them to prioritize land for railroad construction. However, this property was permanently required for the educational institution, which had been supported by the State both financially and politically, indicating that the state had no intent to abandon it. The institution, pivotal for educating unprivileged individuals, had existed for years with state backing, and approbation for its operation. The Supreme Court evaluated the legislative intent behind the railroad's claim and the nature of the property as already occupied and dedicated by the State.	The Trustees of the Illinois Institution for the Education of the Blind claimed that the St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad's attempt to condemn state property was unauthorized and illegal. They argued that the property had been permanently allocated for the education of the blind, which the State had historically supported through appropriations. The Trustees asserted that any legislative grant intended to benefit the railroad should not infringe on property already dedicated to a state institution.	The St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad contended that they had the legal right to appropriate state property for their operational needs under an act of the general assembly. They argued that the law allowed the railroad company to take possession of any necessary land to construct and operate the railroad effectively, claiming that the property's use for the institution did not exclude this right. They sought to overturn the court's earlier ruling that denied their attempt to condemn the property for use as a depot.

The case, "The Board of Education of District No. 3, etc. v. Gotlieb Neidenberger et al.," took place in June 1875 in Illinois. It involved the plaintiff, The Board of Education of District No. 3, and the defendants, Gotlieb Neidenberger and J. George Gerding, who were partners in the firm Neidenberger & Co. The plaintiffs filed a petition against the Board of Education seeking enforcement of a mechanic’s lien for materials alleged to have been provided by the defendants as sub-contractors. The Circuit Court of Madison County ruled in favor of the defendants, determining there was a lien for $1,265 and ordering payment within thirty days, failing which the school property would be sold. However, the case raised significant legal questions regarding whether a mechanic’s lien could be attached to property used for public school purposes.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to a mechanic’s lien for materials they provided as sub-contractors for the construction or repair of school property. They argued that under the relevant Illinois statute, they should be compensated for the labor and materials supplied, and sought judicial enforcement of the lien against the school district to secure payment.	The defendants contended that the mechanic’s lien statute did not extend to property held for public school purposes. They argued that the law was designed to protect public schools from losing their property to lien claims, thereby preserving their resources for public education. They requested that the court reverse the previous ruling that granted the lien, emphasizing that such property should not be subject to mechanic’s liens based on the statutory provisions and public policy considerations.

The case "Blandford, Fowler & Company v. Wing Flour Mill Company" arose in 1887, involving commission merchants (Blandford, Fowler & Company) based in Baltimore, Maryland, and a flour manufacturer (Wing Flour Mill Company) from Charleston, Illinois. The plaintiffs received two consignments of flour from the defendant, which were intended to be sold on behalf of the defendant in the Baltimore market. The defendants drew two drafts totaling $1,100.75, which were paid by the plaintiffs. Upon arrival, a bonded inspector assessed the flour and determined it was unsound, preventing its sale at regular market prices. Consequently, the plaintiffs informed the defendant of the situation and attempted to negotiate but faced a lack of response. After three weeks, unable to execute a profitable sale, the plaintiffs sold the flour for less than the amounts advanced to the defendant. The plaintiffs initiated this lawsuit to recover the difference. The initial jury trial led to a verdict in favor of the defendant, prompting the plaintiffs to contend that the court had erred by not overturning the verdict, as the evidence substantiated their claims regarding the flour's unsound condition.	The plaintiffs assert that they were entitled to recover the difference between the amounts realized from the sale of the unsound flour and the advances made on the drafts issued by the defendant. They argue that the flour did not pass inspection and was marketed in line with local customs, which implied that they should be protected from losses incurred by receiving unsound goods. The plaintiffs seek compensation for the financial loss they experienced due to the inability to sell the product at market value.	The defendant contends that evidence presented indicated that at least one of the flour samples was not unsound at the time it was shipped. They argue that the plaintiffs did not exercise due diligence in their sales efforts and infer a lack of good faith. Moreover, the defendant requests the court to uphold the jury's verdict, maintaining that the plaintiffs were properly informed and that the sale efforts were inadequate.

The case of *The Carondelet Iron Works v. George S. Moore et al.* was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1875. It originated in St. Clair County, Illinois, involving George S. Moore and his partner George D. Morris, who operated as George S. Moore & Co., as the plaintiffs, and the Carondelet Iron Works as the defendant. The legal dispute arose from a contract between the two parties dated July 27, 1872, wherein the iron works agreed to sell the entire product of iron fabricated at their furnace from August 1, 1872, to December 31, 1872. The plaintiffs alleged they purchased 610 tons of iron, which they were led to believe was mill iron, but claimed it was actually inferior white-mottled iron. They asserted that they paid $27,450 based on this misrepresentation. Following a jury trial, the jury ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $14,228. The defendant subsequently appealed, seeking to overturn the judgment on the grounds that the plaintiffs failed to prove their claims regarding the classification and quality of the iron delivered under the contract.	The plaintiffs, George S. Moore & Co., claimed that they were misled regarding the quality of iron they purchased under the contract. They contended that the defendant knowingly represented 610 tons of delivered iron as mill iron while it was actually white-mottled iron, an inferior grade of iron. As a result, they demanded restitution of the overpaid amount based on this misrepresentation and failure to deliver the quality of product that was guaranteed in the contract.	The Carondelet Iron Works defended itself by arguing that the plaintiffs did not provide sufficient evidence to support their claims of misrepresentation and fraud. The defendant contended that the plaintiffs had opportunities to inspect the iron before payment was made and that the designation of the iron as mill iron on the bill was merely a statement of opinion, not a binding warranty. Additionally, the defendant argued that any right to reject the inferior iron was forfeited due to the plaintiffs' delay in asserting their claims.

On June 20, 1855, Walter S. Gurnee entered into a contract with Dexter Broad for the sale of ten acres of land under specific payment terms. The contract allowed Gurnee to declare a forfeiture if payments were not made. After Broad's untimely death in 1856, the estate was managed by administrators who continued to make partial payments on the contract, incurring further debts. The estate notably included two contracts: one with Gurnee and another known as the Springer contract. Upon the death of Broad, Sarah C. Broad, his widow, and their posthumous child, Sarah D. Broad, inherited the estate alongside Orville D. and Edward H. Smith, Sarah's half-brothers. Disputes arose over property rights and claims to the estate when Sarah D. Broad, as the heir at law, sought to assert her claim over the property. The Smith brothers, under the belief that valid forfeiture procedures were followed, contested this. The case ultimately brought before the Illinois Supreme Court revolved around the determination of heirs’ rights and the validity of the forfeiture declaration regarding the land.	Orville D. Smith, the plaintiff, argued for a partition of the ten-acre land, asserting that he, his brother Edward, and their sibling Sarah D. Broad each owned one-third of the property according to the deeds executed. The plaintiffs contended that the declaration of forfeiture was justified due to the failure to comply with payment terms stipulated in the contract, thereby establishing their claim to the land.	The defendants, primarily represented by Sarah D. Broad, claimed that the conveyance of the land was erroneous and should have been conveyed entirely in her favor as the sole heir to Dexter Broad. They argued that the prior deeds held no validity since they did not recognize her claim and that the forfeiture declaration was not properly grounded. Furthermore, they maintained that the existing agreements did not dissolve her rights to the property.

In 1875, in Mercer County, Illinois, the case of Sophia C. Newman v. Wells Willitts arose from a dispute over land ownership. The plaintiff, Wells Willitts, sought a forcible entry and detainer against the defendant, Sophia C. Newman, concerning a parcel of land that included a homestead worth over $1,000. The matter was first heard in front of a justice of the peace before being appealed to the Mercer circuit court. The circuit court determined that Mrs. Newman held a life estate in the land and decreed that she was entitled to retain a homestead portion, which comprised ten acres including her dwelling and farm buildings. The sheriff was ordered to sell the remainder of the property. After the land was sold, Willitts brought action for possession after Newman refused to vacate. The issue revolved around the legality of the homestead set-off under Illinois law, as the valuation of the land played a crucial role in determining Newman’s claims to the property.	Sophia C. Newman, the defendant, argued that she was entitled to the entire forty-acre tract of land claimed by the plaintiff, Wells Willitts. She sought to have the homestead established in her favor extended to cover the entire parcel rather than just the ten acres assigned to her. The plaintiff contended that the entirety of the land was worth more than $1,000, which, per the statute, entitled her to a larger claim than what was allocated.	Wells Willitts, the plaintiff, defended the circuit court's decision, asserting that the legal procedure had been followed correctly in setting off the homestead. He argued that the court had properly found that Mrs. Newman was only entitled to the homestead portion worth $1,000 and that the remaining land could be sold to satisfy the judgment against her. The defense relied on the statute that allows for the distribution of property in accordance with its valuation, affirming that the exemption applied to only part of the land.

The case of Christian Troutman et al. v. Lorentz Schæffer was decided in April 1863 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated in Tazewell County, where a chancery court had entered a decree to foreclose a mortgage. The mortgage was intended to cover a specific piece of real estate—the south half of the southwest quarter of Section 28, Township 26 north, Range 4 west of the third principal meridian. However, the decree mistakenly directed the sale of a different property, namely, the south half of the southeast quarter of the same section, which was not specified in the mortgage. The plaintiffs, represented by Mr. B. S. PeettymaN, contested this error, claiming that the foreclosure order was based on a clerical mistake that made the decree invalid under the law.	The plaintiffs, Christian Troutman and co-plaintiffs, claimed that the decree issued by the lower court was erroneous because it directed the sale of a property not included in the mortgage. They argued that this mistake, likely clerical in nature, invalidated the foreclosure process and sought to have the judgment reversed and remanded for further proceedings to accurately address properties under the mortgage agreement.	Lorentz Schæffer, the defendant, defended against the foreclosure decree by emphasizing that the court below had erred in its decision. The defense pointed out that there was neither allegation nor proof that the property decreed for sale—the south half of the southeast quarter—was intended to be included within the terms of the mortgage. They argued that any decree of foreclosure must be based on premises explicitly covered by the mortgage.

In the case of Dennis Ryan v. George W. Newcomb et al., which was decided on May 27, 1887, in the Illinois Appellate Court, Dennis Ryan (the appellant) entered into multiple loan agreements with George W. Newcomb (the appellee) as part of a money-lending arrangement. These transactions involved loans of $1,700, $1,200, and $600 secured through trust deeds, with claims of usurious terms impacting their validity. In the course of these dealings, Ryan failed to pay back the loans, leading to the sale of land tied to the loans under the power of a trustee. The situation escalated when Ryan executed a warranty deed transferring land to a third party, Kinsella, which was intended to be conveyed back to Newcomb as part of a settlement. During a court hearing, Ryan sought to overturn previous agreements and reclaim his land by disputing the validity of the deed he executed to Kinsella. The case revolves around issues of property settlement, estoppel, and the effect of usury on the transaction. Ultimately, the court examined whether Ryan had effectively waived claims of usury through prior agreements and transactions.	The plaintiff, Dennis Ryan, argued that the quit-claim deed to Kinsella was inoperative due to a lack of delivery and acceptance. He sought redemption of the land by paying off any outstanding amounts, excluding usurious penalties, claiming that the transactions were unfairly structured against him.	The defendant, George W. Newcomb, contended that Ryan’s execution of the warranty deed to Kinsella was valid and constituted a complete settlement of all prior claims. Newcomb maintained that after the execution of the quit-claim deed, Ryan was estopped from contesting the usurious nature of the original loans or seeking to invalidate the earlier arrangements, emphasizing that the transactions were ambiguous and that Ryan had accepted the conveyance.

The legal case titled "The People, etc., for use of John F. Schuchert et al. v. Catharine Phelps, Admx" took place in June 1875 in Illinois. The key individuals involved included Catharine Phelps, the administratrix of the estate of Benjamin F. Phelps, who had recently passed away. The case arose from a dispute over the management of Benjamin's estate, particularly regarding the handling of a life insurance policy. The plaintiff, represented by John F. Schuchert and others, contested the account rendered by Catharine Phelps, claiming that she failed to account for the life insurance proceeds, which she had previously collected. This omission was significant as the plaintiffs believed these funds should be treated as assets of the estate, subject to distribution among creditors. The circuit court had initially upheld the county court's order approving Catharine's account, which led to the appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that the life insurance proceeds collected by Catharine Phelps should have been included in the estate's assets for the benefit of creditors. They contended that her failure to account for this money altered the distribution scheme for paying claims against the estate, leading to an unfair advantage for certain creditors over others. The plaintiff's legal request sought to have the administratrix's account amended to reflect the inclusion of the insurance proceeds and to ensure that all claims were paid pro rata among creditors.	Catharine Phelps, as the defendant, defended her conduct by asserting that she had appropriately managed the estate's funds and fulfilled her obligations to creditors. She argued that the payment of certain claims in full was justified and within her authority as administratrix. Catharine maintained that the life policy's proceeds were intended for her as the legal representative of the deceased, and thus, the distribution to creditors was not prejudiced.

In November 1823, the case of William B. Whiteside v. John Bartleson took place in Madison County, Illinois, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved were William B. Whiteside, the plaintiff and a sheriff, and John Bartleson, the defendant. The action was based on a common count for money had and received. The lower court rendered a judgment against Whiteside, assessing damages in favor of Bartleson without involving a jury. This judgment arose after Whiteside returned an execution as sheriff, which was documented in writing and filed in the clerk's office. The core issue centered on whether liability could be determined solely by this written return, bypassing the jury's role in assessing damages.	William B. Whiteside contended that the lower court's judgment was erroneous for assessing damages without a jury. He argued that the right to a trial by jury should not be abridged, as the nature of the evidence, while potentially supporting his liability, should still be evaluated by a jury rather than the court alone.	John Bartleson maintained that the court's judgment was justified based on the written return of execution by Whiteside, interpreting it as sufficient evidence to support liability for the money had and received. He argued that the assessed damages were appropriate given Whiteside's failure to properly execute his duties as sheriff.

In June 1853, the case "Horatio Newhall v. Nancy J. Turney, Administratrix of John Turney, deceased" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, where Nancy J. Turney, representing the estate of her deceased husband John Turney, filed a debt action against Horatio Newhall. The dispute centered around a promissory note originally owed to John Turney, who had been the administrator of the estate of William Smith, also deceased. This action took place after John Turney’s passing, and before any formal settlement of his estate had occurred. Turney had accepted the note as part of a transaction for selling goods from Smith's estate, raising questions about the legal standing of the note after Turney's death and whether Turney's successor or the administratrix could claim it. Several legal arguments emerged over the rightful party to maintain the action, particularly concerning the authority of an administrator de bonis non (an administrator appointed to manage any unadministered assets).	Nancy J. Turney, as the administratrix of John Turney's estate, asserted that the legal title to the promissory note had transferred to her upon her husband's death. She claimed the right to sue for the amount due on the note, arguing that it was a legitimate asset that should be recoverable for the benefit of William Smith’s estate.	Horatio Newhall's defense challenged Turney's right to sue, arguing that the note should be asserted by the newly appointed administrator de bonis non of William Smith’s estate, not by Turney's widow. He also presented pleas seeking to set off a debt that Smith’s estate owed him, claiming that his financial claims should offset against what he owed on the note.

In December 1857, the Illinois Supreme Court handled a legal dispute involving Edward F. Adams as the plaintiff and Otho Bishop and others as defendants, concerning a land title in Adams County, Illinois. The case originated in the Adams Circuit Court during the March term of 1857, where Adams sought to reclaim ownership of a parcel of land identified as S.W. 32, Township 2 S., 8 W. The property had a complex history involving multiple transactions dating back to its initial patent from the United States to Adam Storm in 1818. Adams claimed a chain of title transfer through a series of deeds, including one executed by Levi James in 1827. The trial, overseen by Judge Sibley without a jury, evaluated the validity of these deeds and the proper acknowledgment procedures as dictated by Illinois law. A significant point of contention arose around the acknowledgment of the deed from James to Charles Whipple, which the plaintiff contended was valid based on Ohio law, where the acknowledgment had occurred. Ultimately, the Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendants, rejecting the deed's introduction into evidence and deciding the legal implications surrounding the acknowledgment process.	The plaintiff, Edward F. Adams, argued that he held valid title to the disputed land based on a series of deeds leading back to its original patent. He sought to introduce a deed from Levi James to Charles Whipple as evidence of his ownership. Adams maintained that this deed was properly executed in compliance with the laws of Ohio, thus entitling him to recover the property and requested a judgment declaring him the rightful owner.	The defendants contended that the deed from Levi James to Charles Whipple was improperly acknowledged, failing to meet the requirements outlined in Illinois law. They argued that the acknowledgment process must adhere strictly to the state’s recognized procedures and that any variance, particularly in the acknowledgment of identities and procedures, rendered the deed inadmissible. The defendants sought to have this deed excluded from the proceedings and requested a ruling in their favor.

Richard Rainforth was prosecuted in September 1870 in Cook County, Illinois, for obtaining money through false pretenses. The key individuals involved were Richard Rainforth, the plaintiff in error, and Alexander L. Smith, the prosecuting witness who claimed to have been defrauded. Rainforth allegedly convinced Smith that he possessed substantial inventory, including nine thousand feet of weather strips and two hundred fifty dozen nutmeg graters, leading Smith to invest $200 in the business. However, it was later established that Rainforth did not own the mentioned items or the claimed profitable business. During the trial, evidence was presented including advertisements and letters related to the business, but the court refused to permit certain cross-examination questions regarding the actual inventory received by Smith. The jury ultimately found Rainforth guilty, resulting in a four-month prison sentence. Rainforth appealed the judgment, highlighting issues regarding the admissibility of evidence and the jury's access to written materials.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, claimed that Rainforth obtained money through fraudulent representations. They argued that he falsely pretended to own a significant quantity of goods and misled Smith regarding the profitability of the business. The prosecution sought to prove that Rainforth knowingly defrauded Smith to illegally acquire funds.	Richard Rainforth's defense argued that critical evidence, which could substantiate his claims and demonstrate the truthfulness of his representations, was improperly excluded from consideration during the trial. They contended that the prosecution's case relied heavily on alleged false pretenses, asserting that all evidence relevant to directly challenge this narrative should have been made available to the jury.

In September 1877, the case of Isaac Evans v. Thompson P. Bouton was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court, emanating from a lower judgment in a replevin action concerning a black mare in Peoria County, Illinois. The case started when Evans sought to regain possession of the mare, which he claimed was wrongfully detained by Bouton. The initial hearing took place before a justice of the peace, where the defendant did not appear. Subsequently, the case was appealed to the circuit court, where proceedings were postponed multiple times until the defendant filed a motion to dismiss the case, citing the absence of a required affidavit from Evans proving ownership and entitlement to the property. The court analyzed whether the defendant's motion was timely, ultimately concluding that since the action was not called for trial prior to the defendant's motion, and considering he was not obligated to appear earlier, his motion was valid. The court upheld that the absence of the mandatory affidavit rendered the justice of the peace without jurisdiction to act on the case.	Isaac Evans, the plaintiff, argued that he was the rightful owner of the black mare and claimed that the mare was being wrongfully withheld by Thompson P. Bouton. Evans sought the court's intervention to replevy the mare, asserting his entitlement to its possession and arguing that the justice of the peace had jurisdiction over the matter based on his assertion of ownership and wrongful detention.	Thompson P. Bouton, the defendant, contended that the case should be dismissed due to the lack of an affidavit, which is mandated by statute before a justice of the peace can issue a writ of replevin. He asserted that since Evans did not submit the required affidavit demonstrating ownership and lawful possession, the justice lacked jurisdiction to make any ruling in the case. Bouton requested that the court recognize the absence of jurisdiction and dismiss the action.

The case, "James Dalton et al. v. Cyrus Bentley, Administrator," was decided in June 1854 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from a contractual dispute between the plaintiffs, James Dalton and others, and the defendant, Cyrus Bentley, who was acting as an administrator. The case arose from an agreement whereby the Daltons were to deliver lumber produced at their mill to Bentley & Orr at White Lake for a set price of $5.50 per thousand feet, with $100 paid upfront upon executing the contract. The Daltons subsequently failed to deliver the lumber as agreed, prompting Bentley & Orr to sue for breach of contract, which resulted in their favor with a judgment for damages. Following this, Bentley & Orr sought to recover the initial deposit of $100 from the Daltons in a new suit for money had and received. The main procedural issue was whether the previous judgment from the breach of contract case barred this new claim for the return of the advance payment.	The plaintiffs, Bentley & Orr, argued that they were entitled to recover the $100 paid as part of the original contract because the Daltons did not deliver the lumber as promised. They contended that after the breach of contract, they had the right to seek a return of the money paid under the presumption of an implied agreement that the payment should be refunded.	The Daltons claimed that the prior judgment in favor of Bentley & Orr constituted a complete bar to the current action for the return of the advance payment. They argued that since the breach of contract had been addressed in the earlier suit, Bentley & Orr could not pursue a different cause of action for the same payment, and should be estopped from denying the existence of the contract under which the money was paid.

The case "The People ex rel. Samuel T. Mayo v. Charles E. Lippincott" took place in Illinois in January 1876. It involved a petition for a writ of mandamus filed by Samuel T. Mayo, representing the People, against Charles E. Lippincott, the Auditor of Public Accounts. The core issue revolved around the Auditor's refusal to register a new bond issued by Macoupin County. This bond was meant to replace an old bond related to debts incurred before March 26, 1872, but after February 13, 1865.
