They cancelled $25,000 of this debt in exchange for an assignment of notes and accounts from Beak & Bucher, which were estimated to be worth approximately $25,000 but only about $19,000 had been collected by the time of the decree. On the same day, Michael Sampter and his associates, creditors of Beak & Bucher, were owed $7,716.40, which was later reduced to $4,773.00. The core issue arose from whether the Wight Brothers held the assigned notes and accounts in trust for Sampter and his associates. The parties involved included Wight Brothers, M. Sampter Sons & Co. (comprised of Michael, Otto, Arnold, Morris Sampter, and Sigmund Simon), and Beak & Bucher. The agreement established that both creditor groups would advance funds to Beak & Bucher in reliance on mutual interests while agreeing on the priority of claims. However, conflicts arose over the trust status of the assigned conditions and the collection efforts. The Wight Brothers contended they were entitled to the full benefit of the assigned notes and accounts, emphasizing that no formal agreement to prefer Sampter's claims was established in their negotiations leading up to the assignment.	The plaintiffs, M. Sampter Sons & Co., argued that they were entitled to prioritization in the repayment of their debt by Beak & Bucher. They claimed that the Wight Brothers were acting as trustees and, therefore, should apply the proceeds of the assigned notes and accounts toward their debts first, before addressing their own claims. They alleged that this fiduciary duty existed due to an agreement made on August 10, 1885, which guaranteed a portion of their debt and established a trust-like relationship, especially in respect of the accounts collected by Wight Brothers.	The defendants, Wight Brothers, denied that they held any obligation to prioritize the claims of M. Sampter Sons & Co. They contended that the agreement did not impose a trust relationship and that the assignment of accounts was legally valid and primarily for securing their own claims. They argued that there was no evidence of an agreement to prefer the claims of the Sampters, and thus their collection of debts from Beak & Bucher was lawful and binding.

On May 28, 1858, in Illinois, William P. C. Whiting and his co-defendants were sued by James E. Fuller and Myers. The lawsuit stemmed from two promissory notes: one for $461.20, due in sixty days, made by Whiting & Co., and another for $64.05, made by Whiting & Go., due upon presentation. The defendants filed a plea of general issue in response to the plaintiffs’ declaration on June 7, 1858. Accompanying this plea, Whiting provided an affidavit asserting a belief in a good defense to the lawsuit. However, on June 10, 1858, the court struck the defendants' plea from the record, citing an insufficient affidavit of merits, which led to a default judgment against the defendants for $516.87 in damages and costs. The judgment was entered by the Cook County Court of Common Pleas, prompting the defendants to appeal, arguing the court's action was erroneous.	The plaintiffs claimed they were owed payment under two notes, asserting that the defendants had breached their obligations. They requested that the court enforce the payment due from the notes and grant judgment in their favor for the stated amounts, along with incurred costs.	The defendants argued that the affidavit of merits provided was sufficient to support their plea of general issue and that it was inappropriate for the court to strike the plea from the file. They contended that only one defendant needed to file an affidavit for the plea and that the plea made a valid defense against the claims. Their main request was to have the court's decision reversed and to restore their plea.

On February 11, 1865, in Illinois, Mary E. Rixford married William H. Rixford, who had enlisted in the army days before and received a bounty of $400. Shortly after the marriage, on February 21, Mary loaned $365 of this bounty to William, executing a note for it. The dispute arose when William sought to enforce this note through legal means, claiming it was his property as the husband. The defendant, Rixford, demurred to the first count of the declaration, arguing he was not a party to the promise in the note. He subsequently presented special pleas claiming the note was Mary’s separate property due to living separately and that the funds were not Williams's. The court overruled the demurrer, leading to a trial by jury where the jury ultimately ruled in favor of Mary, awarding her $320 owed on the note. An appeal followed regarding various rulings of the trial court.	Mary Rixford argued that the note, executed for the money loaned to William, was her separate property. She contended that the funds were hers due to the marital property law that recognized a married woman’s right to hold and control property independently from her husband. Mary sought the law’s enforcement to recover the owed amount from her husband and requested the court to find the funds and note as her own, arguing it was not a gift from William.	William Rixford countered that the note was not enforceable by Mary, asserting that it was essentially his property. He maintained that any funds she claimed as her own were actually given to her by him, and he contested the court’s rulings regarding the special pleas concerning the nature of the note and the ownership of money. He argued that the note was a gift which, legally, was revocable and thus sought to reverse the judgment in favor of his wife.

John Clifford filed a lawsuit against John Waldrop on October 8, 1857, in Montgomery County, Illinois, for the recovery of a debt amounting to fifty dollars stemming from a promissory note. The note was related to an agreement in which Clifford promised to cure Waldrop's eyesight; if he failed, the note was to be void. After a judgment in favor of Clifford was issued by a justice of the peace, Waldrop later petitioned the master in chancery, claiming that the judgment resulted from his lack of awareness and not from negligence. He asserted that the justice misled him regarding being informed of the outcome of the case. Waldrop believed he would be notified if the judgment went against him, so he did not appeal in the defined timeframe. His petition was sworn and led to the issuance of a certiorari to review the prior judgment. The case went through various legal motions, with Waldrop's pleas ultimately being argued in the Circuit Court, where he sought to have the judgment overturned due to what he described as insufficient evidence against the claim of negligence on his part.	John Clifford argues that Waldrop's petition for a writ of certiorari is insufficient as it fails to demonstrate that the original judgment did not arise from Waldrop's negligence. Clifford asserts that Waldrop had a duty to attend the trial and defend against the claims. He claims the verdict should stand and moves for dismissal of Waldrop's appeal based on these insufficiencies.	John Waldrop counters that the judgment against him was erroneous and resulted from his misunderstanding of the proceedings, citing the justice's failure to inform him properly. He contends that he was led to believe that he would be notified only if the judgment was adverse to him, thus missing the opportunity to appeal within the designated time. Waldrop claims that the judgment was unjust because it was based on a promissory note tied to Clifford's failure to cure his eyesight.

The case "Benjamin L. Cleaves v. Phillipine Herbert" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871. It originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Benjamin L. Cleaves, was involved in a legal dispute concerning a chattel mortgage related to property that included various goods such as wines, liquors, and saloon fixtures. The mortgagor, Kutz, had defaulted on the payment of the mortgage note, prompting the plaintiff to take action to reclaim the property through a replevin suit. The case hinged on the admissibility of evidence concerning the nature of the mortgage and whether it established a sufficient property right for the plaintiff to claim possession of the disputed goods. The defendant contested aspects of the evidence presented against them, including the claim about the mortgagor's residence and the nature of the demand for the property. The court had to determine whether the mortgage terms allowed for repossession and whether the plaintiff's claims about property ownership were valid based on the chattel mortgage agreement.	The plaintiff, Benjamin L. Cleaves, claimed that he had a right to repossess the goods mortgaged under chattel mortgage law. He argued that the mortgage, despite being forfeited due to default on a note, demonstrated a special interest in the property necessary to support his action for replevin. The plaintiff maintained that his demand upon the sheriff for the property was adequate, regardless of the noted objections regarding his claims about the specific property identified in the demand.	The defendant, Phillipine Herbert, raised several defenses including the argument that the chattel mortgage evidence was inadmissible because it implied only a qualified right to the property, not an absolute right. The defense also contended that proper preliminary proof regarding the mortgagor's residence was lacking, and claimed that the demand made by the plaintiff was insufficient. Additionally, the defendant argued that the mortgage was fraudulent and void against creditors because it permitted the mortgagor to use the property for sale in the ordinary course of business.

In January 1875, in Macoupin County, Illinois, residents from townships 10 north and 9 north petitioned for the formation of a new school district. The petition, conforming to the state school law, was granted by the trustees of township 9 but denied by the trustees of township 10. In response, the petitioners filed for a mandamus to compel the trustees of township 10 to approve the formation of the new district. The trustees filed a demurrer, denying the petition's alignment with legal requirements and arguing that it would harm educational interests and increase costs. A trial followed with a waiver of jury consent, where the court found in favor of the petitioners. The case highlighted the conflict over the discretion of trustees in forming school districts against residents’ rights when filing a lawful petition.	The plaintiffs, represented by Abraham Travis, claimed that they had complied with the legal requirements for forming a new school district, which included having all necessary legal voters sign the petition. They sought a court order mandating the trustees of township 10 to grant their petition for the creation of the new district, asserting that such action was in line with the expressed will of the voters.	The Trustees of Schools in township 10 argued against the petition, asserting that it was not signed by all legal voters and that the formation of the new district would violate several provisions of the law. They contended that the proposed district would be too close to an existing schoolhouse, would not serve the educational interests of the community, and would unnecessarily raise the costs of education in the area.

On January 21, 1873, in Chicago, William Reed purchased a sleeping car ticket for berth No. 4 on the Pullman Palace Car Company's train from Chicago to Crestline. After boarding the train and exhibiting his ticket to the porter, Reed lost the ticket and informed the conductor about the situation, requesting to ride on his berth. The conductor insisted he must either show a ticket or pay the fare again. After that, Reed attempted to procure a duplicate ticket through the company's agent, who issued an order to the conductor. Nevertheless, the conductor refused the order, stating it was not a valid pass. Reed insisted he should be allowed to remain in his berth, but the conductor forcibly removed him, transferring his belongings to the adjacent passenger car. Ultimately, the conductor found Reed's original ticket the next morning and returned it to him. Reed claimed damages for this wrongful ejection.	William Reed argued that he was wrongfully ejected from the sleeping car despite having purchased a valid ticket. He claimed that the ejection was improper and sought damages amounting to $3,000 for the humiliation and inconvenience of being forced from his berth.	The Pullman Palace Car Company maintained that the conductor acted under a reasonable doubt concerning Reed's ticket ownership and sought to enforce company rules requiring either a ticket or payment. They argued that the conductor's actions, which involved no violence or abusive language, were simply an honest mistake. Additionally, they contended that the damages assessed were grossly excessive given the circumstances.

John W. Connett filed a lawsuit against The City of Chicago concerning an incident that occurred on September 6, 1869, when his wife suffered an accidental injury due to a defective sidewalk in Chicago. Connett initially pursued the case in 1874 through an action of assumpsit, seeking to recover expenses associated with her treatment after the injury. This action was later amended to a negligence claim in 1876, accusing the city of failing to maintain the sidewalk. The city responded with several defenses, including objections regarding the timing of the claims. A trial occurred on March 20, 1876, where Connett won a judgment of $1,500. Before the city could perfect its appeal, a settlement agreement was reached to submit specific legal questions to Judge W. K. McAllister. Ultimately, Judge McAllister ruled in favor of the city in June 1876 regarding the validity of the city’s defenses. In January 1878, the city sought to enjoin the collection of the original judgment, prompting further legal proceedings. The circuit court supported the city’s motion, which was later upheld by the Appellate Court. Connett appealed this decision, leading to the current case before the Illinois Supreme Court.	Connett alleged that the City of Chicago was negligent in maintaining the sidewalk where his wife was injured. He sought compensation for the medical expenses incurred while caring for her due to the injury. His main argument centered on the assertion that the city should be held liable for failing to repair the sidewalk, resulting in his wife's injury.	The City of Chicago's defenses included the general issue plea, arguing that the statute of limitations barred the claims based on the timing of the lawsuit as it did not accrue within the required five-year period prior to the change of action. The city contended that the original agreement submitted to arbitration by the city attorney was invalid and that the city was not bound by it, questioning the authority of the attorney to make such an agreement.

The case of William P. Grimsley and Laurison Levering v. Joseph Klein took place in the Sangamon Circuit Court during the October term of 1836. The primary legal question revolved around the right of property as it pertained to goods distrained by a landlord, Joseph Klein, for unpaid rent owed by his tenant, Bailey. After Klein seized Bailey's goods for rent dues, these same goods were later taken in execution by Grimsley and Levering, who were execution creditors. During the trial, the court allowed Klein to introduce a lease agreement with Bailey as evidence to establish his claim over the goods. Grimsley and Levering objected to the admissibility of this lease due to a lack of proof of its execution, as they were not parties to the lease and had not signed it. The trial judge overruled the objection and ultimately ruled in favor of Klein, affirming his right to the goods based on the lease. However, Grimsley and Levering appealed the decision, leading to the examination of the legal standards for evidence in property claims.	Grimsley and Levering, the appellants in the case, argued that Klein did not possess the legal standing to claim the distrained goods as he merely had an interest in them as a landlord. They objected to the admission of the lease as evidence, claiming it lacked proof of execution and therefore should not be considered. The plaintiffs requested that the court dismiss Klein's claims to the goods based on these grounds.	Klein, as the appellee, contended that he had the right to distrain the goods for unpaid rent and sufficiently established his interest in the goods through the lease agreement. He chose to present the lease to demonstrate Bailey's debt to him, which warranted his claim over the goods in question. Klein argued that the trial court correctly admitted the lease as evidence, contending that the provision of the lease was appropriate given the circumstances, despite the objections raised by the appellants.

The case of Samuel Davidson v. William Porter et al. took place in 1870 in Illinois. The dispute arose over ownership of a parcel of land claimed by both the plaintiff, Samuel Davidson, and the defendant, William Porter. Davidson alleged that he had purchased the land from Shellswick, an agent of the Illinois Central Railroad Company, and had taken possession of it, cultivating and fencing the land since the spring of 1867. He argued that he paid a total of $360 for the land in several installments and contended that Porter had either actual or constructive notice of his claim. In contrast, Porter claimed he purchased the land from another agent, Sill, having entered into a binding agreement with the railroad company prior to Davidson’s supposed purchase. Porter maintained that he had no knowledge of Davidson's claim until after his own purchase. The railroad company denied that Shellswick had the authority to sell the land and stated that Porter’s purchase was executed before Davidson’s application for the land was considered.	Samuel Davidson claimed that he had a legitimate purchase agreement for the land with Shellswick, having paid the required amount and taken possession. He requested the court to compel the railroad company to convey the title to him, arguing that he was the rightful owner based on his prior transactions, while asserting that Porter was aware of his claim.	William Porter argued that he purchased the land first and that Davidson had no official contract with the railroad company. Porter contended that he conducted due diligence before buying and had no notice of Davidson's claim. He sought to have the suit dismissed, asserting his legitimate ownership of the land based on his earlier transaction.

Michael Neubrecht v. Louisa Santmeyer et al. is a legal case that originated in 1869 in Hancock County, Illinois. The key individuals involved include Michael Neubrecht, the appellant (defendant), and Louisa Santmeyer, the widow of Henry Auer and administratrix of his estate, along with their children Caroline and Louisa Auer, the plaintiffs. The case arose when the heirs of Henry Auer sued Neubrecht to recover $200 that was loaned to him by Louisa in her capacity as the administratrix of Auer's estate. Neubrecht was alleged to have made a verbal promise to return the money to the Auer children when the youngest reached the age of 21. After Louisa and Neubrecht divorced before the youngest turned 21, the children initiated legal proceedings for recovery of the funds. The initial judgment was ruled in favor of the children for $80.66 and costs in the Circuit Court, prompting Neubrecht to appeal, raising several points of error concerning evidence and witness competency.	The plaintiffs, Caroline and Louisa Auer, claimed they were entitled to recover $200 loaned to Neubrecht, made by their mother while acting as the administratrix of their father’s estate. They argued that Neubrecht had verbally promised their mother to return the money to them upon the youngest reaching the age of 21. After this age was reached, they initiated legal proceedings against Neubrecht to reclaim their portion of the loaned amount, having won a judgment at the lower court that they sought to uphold.	Neubrecht, as the defendant, contended several defenses, including the argument that the testimony of his divorced wife regarding the debt was inadmissible, asserting that a spouse cannot testify against the other in a legal matter. He further claimed that the Auer children had no direct legal claim to the money as it was loaned to him in a transaction involving their mother, who, as administratrix, had not obtained a court order for distribution of the estate assets. Neubrecht sought to have the circuit court’s judgment reversed based on these grounds.

On June 9, 1845, Artois Hamilton initiated an action of assumpsit against Joshua J. Moore in Hancock Circuit Court, Illinois. A summons was issued to the sheriff of Peoria County but returned "non est inventus," indicating Moore could not be found. On June 17, Hamilton filed a bond and affidavit and obtained an attachment in aid of the original case, which was levied on Moore's real and personal property. Notice of the attachment was published, but no personal service was made on Moore, nor did he appear in court. At the October 1845 session, Moore was found to be in default, and damages were assessed at $145.74, leading to a judgment for Hamilton to be executed against the attached property. Moore subsequently filed a writ of error, seeking to overturn the judgment due to lack of personal service.	Hamilton, the plaintiff, argued that the attachment was a valid adjunct to his original action of assumpsit, allowing him to seek damages based on the original claims. He maintained that the absence of personal service was not critical and that proceedings could continue under the attachment.	Moore contended that the judgment against him was unwarranted because he was not personally served in either the original action or the attachment proceedings. He argued that the attachment action was inseparable from the initial suit, and without personal service, the court lacked jurisdiction to render judgment against him.

James D. Lehmer filed an appeal in September 1875 with the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a judgment from the Cook County Court related to a special assessment on certain real estate for improvements on Parker’s Avenue. The court ruling involved the collection for a delinquent special assessment, which was reported by H. B. Miller, the Collector. Judge Mártir E. M. Wallace presided over the initial county court proceedings. Lehmer's appeal contended that various objections to the application for judgment should have been considered, including potential errors relating to the nature of Parker’s Avenue, whether it was public or private. However, the court noted that previous objections related to the assessment process were res adjudicata, meaning they could not be reopened for investigation, and that judgment for taxes and special assessments conforms to statutory provisions under the General Revenue Law.	The plaintiff, James D. Lehmer, argued against the validity of the special assessment and contested the application for judgment, presenting several objections. He insisted that the nature of Parker’s Avenue should have been addressed before judgment, questioning whether it was classified as a public street. Lehmer sought to challenge various decisions made leading up to the confirmation of the assessment and aimed to have the original judgment invalidated.	The defendant, represented by H. B. Miller, the Collector, contended that all matters preceding the application for judgment were res adjudicata and should not be examined again. They argued that the objections raised by Lehmer were either invalid or too delayed to be considered, emphasizing that clerical errors in the assessment rolls did not affect the rights of Lehmer. The defense maintained that any disputes about the public or private status of Parker's Avenue should have been made prior to the confirmation of the assessment.

In 1877, John H. Altrogge was elected treasurer of Randolph County, Illinois, and was re-elected in 1879. His term was extended by legislation for another year, during which he executed an official bond in December 1881. Following his death on May 27, 1882, B. G. Detrich was appointed as his successor and tasked by the county board to examine Altrogge's accounts. Detrich's investigations revealed significant discrepancies: Altrogge received over $18,000 more than he disbursed in the first term, about $28,000 in the second term, and approximately $15,000 more than his receipts during his extended term. The county initiated lawsuits against the sureties of Altrogge’s bonds due to the identified defalcations. These cases were referred to R. H. Mann, Esq., as a referee, and, despite exceptions raised by the plaintiffs against the referee’s findings, the judge upheld Mann’s report which concluded that the plaintiffs were owed $1,718.12. The court determined that the plaintiffs did not sufficiently prove their case for further evidence or to dismiss the conclusions reached by the referee.	The plaintiffs, Gustavus Pape et al., argued that the referee's findings regarding the liability of the sureties on Altrogge's last bond were incorrect. They contended that the defalcation occurred in earlier terms and not during the last term for which the bond was executed. The plaintiffs sought to re-refer the case for additional evidence that they believed would demonstrate their claims.	The defendants, representing the sureties on Altrogge's bonds, asserted that the evidence presented was sufficiently comprehensive to justify the referee's conclusion. They argued that the law presumes defalcation occurs in the last term in the absence of evidence indicating otherwise. Additionally, they maintained that the plaintiffs did not meet the burden of proof needed to challenge the referee's report or to show that the trial court abused its discretion in denying further examination of evidence.

David D. Hull v. John Peer et al. is a legal case concerning a dispute over a parol agreement for the sale of land. In August 1855, Billingsby Bowen filed a bill in the Circuit Court of Pike County, Illinois, claiming that he and Hull entered into an agreement around 1850 for Hull to sell him the east half of a quarter section of land for $150. Bowen contended that he would assume Hull's debt of $100 to the township’s school fund, effectively reducing the sale price to $50, to be paid later. Bowen alleged he paid the debt and tendered the remaining balance, but Hull refused to convey the land. Hull denied the agreement altogether, although he acknowledged the payment of his note by Bowen. The court found Bowen had made improvements on the land and had been in continuous possession. The testimony from multiple witnesses supported Bowen's claims against Hull's denials. The case grappled with competing assertions regarding the existence and terms of the alleged contract for the land, leading to a significant judicial determination regarding equitable remedies.	The plaintiff, Billingsby Bowen, argued that there was a valid parol contract between him and Hull for the sale of land, which Hull refused to fulfill despite Bowen's performance by paying off Hull's debt and making improvements on the property. Bowen sought specific performance of the agreement, demanding that Hull convey the land to him based on their mutual understanding, which included the tender of the remaining balance owed for the land.	The defendant, Hull, denied any agreement to sell the land, referring to the arrangement as an informal proposal rather than a binding contract. He claimed Bowen's payment of the debt was unauthorized, asserting that Bowen had never fulfilled the conditions necessary for the sale of land and that he never recognized Bowen's claim of ownership or contract rights over the property in question. Hull maintained that any improvements made were not made under any sale agreement but were part of an alternate understanding regarding labor compensation.

William Gilbert v. Strew M. Emmons is a case that took place in April 1866, in Cook County, Illinois, and was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from an action for malicious prosecution brought by Strew M. Emmons against Gilbert and his partner Frank S. Palmer, who were accused of wrongfully instigating a larceny charge against Emmons. During the proceedings, it was established that the grand jury found no basis to indict Emmons, effectively declaring him not guilty of the alleged offense. The lower court had initially convicted Gilbert after a jury found in favor of Emmons, awarding him $5,000 in damages. However, Gilbert contested the decision, arguing that the legal basis for claiming malicious prosecution was flawed since there had been no jury trial or subsequent acquittal in the strict sense. The Supreme Court examined the plaintiff's claims and the precedent regarding malicious prosecution and jury requirements, particularly whether mere knowledge of an impending wrongful act could render Gilbert liable, especially as he might not have directly instigated the arrest but simply consented to his partner's actions.	The plaintiff, Strew M. Emmons, claimed that he was wrongfully prosecuted for larceny based on a warrant that was allegedly obtained maliciously and without probable cause by the defendants, Gilbert and Palmer. Emmons asserted that the grand jury's refusal to indict him affirmed his innocence and served as evidence of his wrongful prosecution. He sought damages for the harm caused by the false charges, citing emotional distress and reputational damage resulting from the defendants' actions.	The defendants, particularly Gilbert, argued that there was insufficient evidence to support Emmons' claims of malicious prosecution. They contended that the legal precedent required a jury trial and verdict of acquittal for such an action to be viable. Moreover, Gilbert claimed he had not directly participated in causing Emmons' arrest but rather had passive awareness of Palmer's decisions. According to the defense, mere knowledge and consent to an unlawful act were not enough to establish liability for malicious prosecution.

In September 1868, the case of Augustus T. Johnson et al. v. Anning O. Campbell et al. was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in the town of Byron, Illinois, where the town had levied a tax intended to pay off debts incurred from bounties given to volunteers, a necessity due to the Civil War draft. The plaintiffs, including Augustus T. Johnson and others, filed a bill in chancery to prevent the collection of this tax, arguing that it was invalid. The tax was authorized by a legislative act dated January 18, 1865, which allowed towns to raise revenue to reimburse individuals who had voluntarily contributed funds to support enlistment efforts for the war. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs by enjoining the tax collection, prompting the defendants to appeal the decision, thereby bringing the case to the Supreme Court for review.	The plaintiffs contended that the town's tax to pay for the bounties was unlawful. They argued that funds raised through taxation could not be utilized for purposes that were not deemed corporate, and they sought a judicial decree to stop the collection of the tax intended for reimbursing the contributions made for volunteer bounties.	The defendants, including Anning O. Campbell and others, argued that the legislature had the authority to permit the taxation for the purpose of refunding money advanced for public welfare in emergencies. They maintained that the bonds issued to volunteers and the funds raised by subscription were both binding debts that the town was obligated to repay, claiming that reimbursement through taxation was lawful and justified.

Frank Field sued The Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company in January 1874. The case was initially brought to the circuit court of Peoria County, Illinois, but was later moved to Tazewell County. Field, the plaintiff, had filed thirty-two counts related to different shipments of flour he sent to New York City via the defendant’s railroad. He claimed that due to the defendant's negligence, his flour was not transported safely and was delayed for four months, resulting in two thousand dollars in damages to the goods. The defendant contended that they fulfilled their responsibilities as a common carrier by delivering the flour to the Michigan Central Railroad at Joliet. The terms of the receipt or bill of lading, which Field's clerk completed, specified that the railroad's responsibility ended once the goods were delivered to another carrier. During the trial, it was argued whether Field had knowledge and consented to the terms outlined in the bills of lading, which limited the railroad's liability. The court ultimately found that Field had sufficient notice and understanding of these terms.	Frank Field claimed that The Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company failed to transport and deliver his flour in a reasonable timeframe as required by their agreement. He argued that the defendant's negligence resulted in significant delays that caused damage to his shipments amounting to two thousand dollars. Field requested compensation for the losses resulting from what he claimed was the railroad's failure to uphold their obligations as a common carrier.	The Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company argued that they had fulfilled their contractual obligations by delivering the flour to the Michigan Central Railroad company, and that their responsibility ceased at that point, as specified in the receipt that Field accepted. They maintained that the terms of the bill of lading were made clear, and that Field had knowledge of and consented to these terms. The defendant requested that the court uphold the limitations on their liability outlined in the shipping contract.

John Durham was indicted for forgery at the November term of the Sangamon Circuit Court in 1843, in Sangamon, Illinois. The forgery charge arose from Durham's alleged alteration of an order drawn by Grubb on the firm J. Irwin & Co., intending to defraud its members. He was initially arraigned, tried, and acquitted on the first indictment. Shortly after, another indictment closely mirrored the first but referred to the firm as “composing the firm of John Irwin & Co.” Durham pleaded autrefois acquit, asserting he should not be tried again for the same offense since he had already been acquitted. The court, however, sustained a demurrer to his plea and subsequently, Durham pleaded guilty to the second indictment. As a result, he was sentenced to one year in prison. Expressing disagreement with the circuit court's handling of the autrefois acquit plea, the case was appealed, leading to scrutiny over whether the two indictments charged the same offense.	John Durham, the plaintiff in error, argued that the circuit court erred by not sustaining his plea of autrefois acquit, claiming that he was being tried twice for the same offense, which violated his rights against double jeopardy. He contended that the two indictments, despite minor differences in description, referred to identical offenses, as the material facts necessary for conviction were the same, making the subsequent indictment invalid.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by Attorney General J. A. McDougall, defended the court's decision to sustain the demurrer to Durham's plea, arguing that the two indictments were not for the same offense and justifying the legal distinctions between them. The prosecution maintained that the description within the second indictment warranted legal scrutiny and that the plea of autrefois acquit was not appropriately pleaded.

Elkanah Brush, a minor, represented by his next friend D.H. Brush, brought a legal action against Israel Blanchard in November 1856, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Jackson Circuit Court during September 1854, where it was tried without a jury. The plaintiff's claims stemmed from services that Brush rendered, which he believed entitled him to compensation. The background of the case reveals that Blanchard had married Brush's mother, a widow, at the time of the marriage, and Brush lived with them as a member of their family. The pivotal issue in the case revolved around whether Blanchard, as a step-father, was obligated to pay for the services rendered by Brush while he was part of their household. The relationship dynamic was essential in determining the legal implications regarding obligations of the step-father towards his step-son.	The plaintiff, Elkanah Brush, argued that he was entitled to payment for the work and services he provided while living with his step-father, Israel Blanchard. He claimed that despite living in the same household as Blanchard, he had the right to compensation just like any other service rendered to a family member. Brush sought a court ruling to require Blanchard to pay for the labor he performed.	Israel Blanchard, the defendant, contended that as a step-father, he was not legally obligated to support Brush or pay for any services rendered, given that the relationship established through marriage did not imply a financial obligation to his step-children. He maintained that the presumption under the law recognizes that there is no implied contract for compensation for services between step-parent and step-child unless explicitly agreed upon. Blanchard argued that since no express contract existed, he should not be held liable for payment.

In 1867, in the City of Belleville, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving Russel Hinckley, a banker, and the city council regarding licensing requirements. The city had passed an ordinance mandating that bankers obtain a license, which involved a fee of $100. Hinckley was found guilty of not complying with this ordinance, resulting in a $50 fine imposed by a police magistrate. Following his conviction, he appealed to the Circuit Court of St. Clair County, where the case was tried based on an agreed statement of facts. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the city, imposing a fine of $100 plus costs on Hinckley. Hinckley subsequently sought further appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court to challenge the city council's authority to impose such licensing requirements.	Russel Hinckley, the plaintiff, argued that he was wrongly penalized under the city's ordinance requiring bankers to obtain a license. He maintained that the ordinance was not applicable to his business activities and thus contested the legitimacy of the fine imposed on him.	The City of Belleville, as the defendant, contended that the city council held the authority to regulate and license bankers under the powers granted by the state legislature. They argued that the term "banker" as used encompasses all related financial activities, including those of a money-changer, and thus Hinckley was indeed required to obtain a license as per the city ordinance.

On April 21, 1885, in Lincoln, Illinois, Charles F. Gerard and partner Isaac Wert operated a livery and stock business under the firm name of Wert & Company, with Gerard holding a three-fourths interest and Wert one-fourth. On that date, Gerard exchanged a half section of land in Nebraska, valued at $3,200, for two-thirds of his interest in the firm, transferring one-half of the total firm stock to Danley by bill of sale. Following this, Danley joined the firm. The partnership lasted until June 18, 1885, when Danley's interest was sold due to executions for debts. Subsequently, Erastus W. Bates, holding an unrecorded mortgage on Danley’s interest, sought advice from Gerard on purchasing Danley’s interest at the execution sale to protect his lien, which Gerard supported, estimating a potential value of $1,400. After purchasing at the execution sale, Bates claimed ownership of an undivided half interest in the firm stock, while Gerard contended the interest was conditional based on the land value. Bates filed a bill against Gerard and Wert for an accounting and other relief. The case proceeded with evidence and appointments of a receiver to oversee sales and payments, resulting in the court determining the shares owed to each party.	The plaintiff, Erastus W. Bates, claims absolute ownership of an undivided half interest in the firm stock, which he asserts should be shared according to their respective debts. He seeks an accounting of the firm’s assets and for the court to recognize his claims to these assets notwithstanding the executions and debts, which he argues should not exempt him from participation in the firm's total assets.	The defendant, Charles F. Gerard, contends that Bates's claim is unsubstantiated, asserting that Danley’s interest was contingent upon the land value and that Bates should not profit from sales of firm property not explicitly subject to execution levies. Gerard argues that the decree allowing Bates to receive a share of proceeds from the sale of assets violates his claim over the guarantee of Danley’s interest and that Bates was fully informed about the contingent nature of his claim.

In September 1867, in Livingston County, Illinois, The Stephenson Insurance Company faced a lawsuit brought by John Dunn concerning an insurance covenant. The case arose when Dunn sought to recover $180 for a loss he claimed was covered under his policy with the company. However, the significant legal issue revolved around whether the Circuit Court of Livingston County had jurisdiction over the defendant, Stephenson Insurance Company. The company’s principal office was located in Freeport, in Stephenson County, while the legal action occurred in Livingston County, where the contract was claimed to have been made. The court examined the validity of the service of process to the defendant, which had been directed to the president of the company in a different county, rather than serving local agents. Chief Justice Breese delivered the opinion, focusing on the jurisdiction implications tied to the improper process serving.	John Dunn, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to recover insurance payments for his loss as defined under the policy with The Stephenson Insurance Company. He maintained that the insurance policy was valid and enforceable, thereby asserting the jurisdiction of the Livingston County Circuit Court to address his claims based on where the contract had been executed.	The Stephenson Insurance Company countered by asserting that the Circuit Court did not possess jurisdiction over it due to improper service of process. The company contended that service directed at the president while he was in another county was invalid. They argued that proper procedure would require serving process in the county where the plaintiff resided or issuing it to an appropriate local agent, thereby contesting the court's authority to adjudicate the matter.

The case "Cyrus Aldrich et al. v. Stephen Aldrich et al." took place in La Salle County, Illinois, with the final judgment delivered by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1865. The dispute originated from a military bounty land warrant located by William S. Joscelyn in 1849. This warrant was initially canceled by the Commissioner of Pensions in May 1851 for suspected fraud. However, this cancellation was later rescinded in May 1853, restoring the warrant’s validity. Despite this, the cancellation of the land entry itself was not rescinded, leading to uncertainty regarding land ownership. Cyrus Aldrich, who was the Receiver of the Land Office at the time, entered the land and received a patent in 1856, subsequently selling it to Harvey Morgan. However, Stephen H. Aldrich and Irwin Palmer claimed rights to the land through Joscelyn’s heirs, as the land had been occupied since 1854 under the Joscelyn title. This led them to file a bill against Aldrich and Morgan to compel the conveyance of the legal title to them. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiffs, Stephen H. Aldrich and Irwin Palmer, claimed lawful rights to the land based on the original entitlement under Joscelyn’s military bounty land warrant. They argued that the earlier cancellation of the warrant was invalid when subsequently rescinded, thereby reinstating their claim to the land. They maintained that since the land was under the Joscelyn title and had been continuously occupied since 1854, they were rightful claimants and sought to compel Aldrich to convey the legal title to them.	Cyrus Aldrich and Harvey Morgan contended that the entries made under Joscelyn's name had been officially canceled, which they argued justified their subsequent patent and ownership of the land. They maintained that after the cancellation, Aldrich’s acquisition of the patent should stand valid as there were no rights to restore the entry posthumously. Their defense emphasized the legality of the transactions based on the government’s actions and the presumed validity of the patent they received.

The case, titled "Smith v. Race," was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1862. The key individuals involved were Benjamin F. Smith, Alexander Thompson, and William H. Cooper, who represented minors affected by the case, versus Job A. Race. The dispute centered around land ownership involving the south-west quarter of Section 35 in Macon County. Plaintiffs claimed rights to the land based on a guardian's sale to Alonzo Lapham, which subsequently passed to Race. The historical backdrop includes the death of John E. French in 1841, whose heirs became central to the case. In 1860, the heirs attempted a separate legal action for recovery, which was dismissed prior to this case. The court proceedings involved trials at multiple terms, including trials held in July and November of 1861, ultimately resulting in the judgment rendered by the court regarding the legitimacy of the guardian's sale and the claims of the current land possessors, Race being a critical player in the question of title.	The plaintiffs argued that the title to the land in question was improperly sold by the guardian of John E. French's heirs, alleging that the legal proceedings against the minors were invalid due to their not being made parties to the action. They sought the court to acknowledge their ownership and reinstate their claims to the land, emphasizing the need for proper legal recourse due to procedural errors in the previous filings concerning the guardianship and property sale.	The defendant, Job A. Race, contended that the guardian's actions and the subsequent sale of the land were legitimate and lawful, asserting that the court had acquired jurisdiction over the matter. Race's defense relied on evidence that the necessary legal requirements were met during the guardianship process and the sale was sanctioned through proper decrees. Race requested the court to affirm the validity of the title derived from the guardian's sale and to dismiss the plaintiffs' claims which were deemed baseless and unsubstantiated.

The case, titled "The Chicago West Division Railway Company v. Leo Patrick Ryan," took place in Chicago, Illinois, and was initiated on July 31, 1886, following an incident that occurred on October 1, 1885. The plaintiff, Leo Patrick Ryan, a minor aged just under seventeen months at the time of the incident, was struck by a horse-drawn streetcar operated by the defendant, Chicago West Division Railway Company, at a street crossing on Indiana Street. As a result of the accident, the child suffered a significant injury; one of his feet was crushed, necessitating amputation shortly after. The plaintiff's family, who operated a small grocery store nearby, had entrusted the child to his older brother for care. The plaintiff claimed that the driver of the streetcar failed to exercise ordinary care to avoid the accident once he became aware of the child in danger. The jury for the trial court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding damages of $1,750, which was subsequently upheld by the Appellate Court before reaching the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, through his legal representative, argued that the railway company was negligent in its operation of the streetcar, particularly because the driver failed to stop or slow down upon noticing the child in a dangerous position. They contended that even if the child’s older brother had exhibited negligence by allowing him to wander into the street, this did not absolve the railway company of its responsibility to exercise ordinary care to prevent the injury once it was aware of the child's peril.	The defendant, represented by its attorneys, countered the plaintiff's claims by asserting that the actions of the child's custodian (the older brother) contributed to the child's unsafe position. They argued that the plaintiff should not recover damages as the circumstances of the accident indicated that the child acted negligently by running into the path of the streetcar without giving the driver adequate notice to avoid the collision.

On August 4th, 1872, Christopher Rafferty was arrested in Chicago, Illinois, when he was approached by two policemen, Patrick O’Meara and Scanlan. The policemen, acting without lawful authority, attempted to seize Rafferty. O’Meara pointed Rafferty out to Scanlan, after which Scanlan informed Rafferty that he had a warrant for his arrest. Despite initially acquiescing, Rafferty threatened to shoot anyone who tried to touch him. The situation escalated, resulting in Rafferty shooting O’Meara, leading to O’Meara's death. During the trial that followed, it was revealed that the warrant was improperly issued. The magistrate had signed blank warrants that were filled in by police officers without proper authority. The legality of the arrest was central to the case, as it affected the nature of the homicide charge against Rafferty, who argued that he had acted in self-defense against an illegal arrest.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Rafferty's actions constituted murder, as he had killed a police officer engaged in the lawful execution of his duty. They maintained that the police were justified in attempting the arrest and that Rafferty's use of deadly force was unwarranted.	Rafferty, the defendant, claimed that the arrest was illegal and that the warrant used was a nullity, as it had not been duly authorized. He argued that he was justified in resisting the unlawful arrest and contended that his actions should be classified as manslaughter rather than murder. His defense emphasized the importance of the legality of the arrest and the validity of the warrant in determining culpability.

In 1872, in Cook County, Illinois, John Heaney purchased a portion of a lot in Chicago from James O. Humphrey. Subsequently, in 1867, the property was sold for unpaid taxes, and a deed for the land was issued to Asahel Gage in 1869. During the spring of 1869, Heaney hired Samuel B. Chase and his associates, who were engaged in generating title abstracts for real estate, to prepare an abstract of title for his property. Heaney paid $25 for this service. However, the defendants failed to include a critical judgment against the property for tax arrears in the abstract, which Heaney was unaware of at the time. Consequently, Heaney could not redeem the property before the deadline, ultimately leading him to pay $1,300 to clear the title's cloud created by the omitted judgment. Heaney subsequently filed a lawsuit for negligence against Chase and his co-defendants for failing to accurately perform their duty in preparing the abstract.	Heaney argued that the defendants, by neglecting to properly include the judgment against his property in the abstract, failed to meet the standard of skill and care required in their professional duties. Heaney claimed this negligence caused him financial harm, as he had to pay the judgment amount to resolve the issue and restore a clear title to his property. His legal request sought compensation for the damages incurred due to the defendants' failure to provide an accurate abstract of title.	The defendants contended that there was insufficient evidence proving that the judgment and sale were properly recorded at the time the abstract was prepared. They argued that they should not be held liable since there was no explicit contract for a complete abstract and claimed that the lack of a specific notice regarding possible limitations of liability absolved them of responsibility. Furthermore, they asserted that Heaney was guilty of contributory negligence for failing to verify the accuracy of the abstract.

Marcus C. Stearns v. Patrick Reidy is a case that took place in October 1881 in a quarry operated by Patrick Reidy in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Marcus C. Stearns, was injured while working under the foreman's orders at the quarry, specifically by an explosion stemming from a dynamite charge in what is known as a "missed hole," which refers to a charge that did not explode as intended. The primary factual dispute between the parties revolved around the orders given by the foreman regarding that "missed hole." The appellant (Reidy) argued that the order was to clean out a missed hole using a scraper, while the appellee (Stearns) contended that he was instructed to drill a hole in a rock. Throughout the litigation, there were multiple jury trials and conflicting evidence. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of Stearns, leading to discussions regarding the admissibility of evidence, legal instructions, and whether the foreman’s negligence in giving a dangerous order contributed to the plaintiff's injuries. Stearns sought damages for his injuries, which resulted in his blindness.	The plaintiff, Marcus C. Stearns, claimed that he suffered severe injuries, specifically total blindness, due to an explosion in a quarry when he followed the orders of his foreman, who was aware of the inherent dangers associated with the "missed hole." He argued that he had no knowledge of the potential risks involved in following the foreman’s directive to drill a hole and sought damages for the negligence displayed by the defendant, Patrick Reidy. The case hinged on the premise that Stearns should be compensated for the injuries sustained as a direct result of obeying an unjust and dangerous order given by a superior.	The defendant, Patrick Reidy, contended that there was a significant variance between the claims made in the initial pleadings and the evidence presented, specifically regarding the nature of the foreman's orders. Reidy maintained that the plaintiff was instructed to clean out a hole, rather than drill a new one, which created a discrepancy in the case's factual basis. Additionally, Reidy raised a plea of the statute of limitations against Stearns's amended claims, asserting that the new allegations regarding the nature of the order were barred due to the time elapsed since the incident. The defense focused on emphasizing these legal technicalities, arguing they should undermine the plaintiff's case.

Alvis Sharp and Spencer Smitherman were involved in a legal dispute in Illinois in December 1873 concerning mill property ownership. At that time, Sharp owned an undivided third of the mill, while Smitherman and Levi Berry co-owned the remaining two-thirds. Sharp and Berry operated the mill as partners. Due to Sharp's debts, which Smitherman secured as a guarantor, Sharp and his wife executed a warranty deed, transferring their interest in the property to Smitherman for $2,000. Sharp claimed that this deed was intended merely as a mortgage to secure additional funds for his debts, while Smitherman contended that it represented an absolute sale. The legal question centered around whether the deed should be considered a mortgage, despite its clear language of sale.	The plaintiff, Alvis Sharp, argued that the warranty deed he executed was intended as a mortgage, not a complete transfer of property rights. He contended that the deed should be considered a security for repayment of debts Smitherman would cover on his behalf. Sharp sought a decree to affirm his ownership claim over the undivided third of the mill property, challenging the characterization of the deed as an outright sale.	The defendant, Spencer Smitherman, argued that the warranty deed was an absolute conveyance of property rights and not merely security for a debt. Smitherman claimed that the clear and unconditional terms of the deed indicated an intent for a complete sale. He contended that the evidence provided by Sharp was insufficient to overturn the presumption of an absolute transfer contained within the deed and insisted that the initial court's ruling be upheld.

In 1871, James Steel, formerly the secretary of the Piute Mining Company of Chicago, obtained a judgment against the company in Cook County, Illinois. Following the failure to collect on this judgment, he initiated legal action against James Dunne, whom he alleged was a stockholder in the Piute Mining Company. The statute governing such companies stated that stockholders are personally liable for the financial obligations of the company up to the amount of their shares. The key issue in the case was whether Dunne was a stockholder at the time the debt was incurred. Evidence presented indicated that no stock certificates were ever issued to anyone, and Dunne had not subscribed to stock in the original company. The original company was short-lived, transitioning into the Piute Silver Mining Company with a new name and directors, in which Dunne was a stockholder. However, Steel had no judgment against the new entity, complicating his claims against Dunne.	James Steel claimed that as a stockholder of the Piute Mining Company, James Dunne was personally liable for the debts owed by the company. Steel argued that despite Dunne's position, he had an obligation to pay the outstanding judgment, as the liability should extend to all stockholders according to the relevant statutes of Illinois.	James Dunne contended that he was never a stockholder of the Piute Mining Company; instead, he was a stockholder only in the reorganized Piute Silver Mining Company. Dunne argued that the company had never issued stock certificates, nor had he subscribed to any stocks that would render him liable under the law. He maintained that without proof of stock ownership in the original company, there could be no basis for recovery against him.

In 1883, in McDonough County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Israel Jared and the partners Vanvleet & Johnson. Prior to this case, Jared had filed a lawsuit against Anthony Vanvleet in a justice of the peace court regarding an open account. During that trial, Vanvleet attempted to set off his counterclaim, but a significant portion of it was ruled inadmissible due to it being a partnership account belonging to Vanvleet & Johnson. Following this, Vanvleet & Johnson initiated a lawsuit against Jared to recover for the items previously disallowed. As a defense, Jared invoked the Statute of Limitations, arguing that his right to action regarding most of the claims had expired, as they accrued over five years before the commencement of this suit. There was a debate regarding an admission made by Jared during the first trial that allegedly could remove the statute's bar, but the court found that the admission was narrowly defined and did not revive the previously barred claims.	The plaintiff, Vanvleet & Johnson, claimed they were entitled to recover amounts owed by Israel Jared on the disallowed partnership accounts from the earlier trial. They argued that the admissions made by Jared during the first suit should negate the Statute of Limitations defense, asserting that he acknowledged the debts as existent and unpaid, thus entitling them to relief.	Israel Jared contended that the claims brought forth by Vanvleet & Johnson were barred by the Statute of Limitations, asserting that the debt collections for the items in question were initiated more than five years after they accrued. He maintained that his admissions during the previous trial did not sufficiently renew any expired claims and that the agreement made regarding the statute should not be interpreted to apply to this subsequent suit.

The case involves Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company and William Sierer. The incident took place on the night of October 24, 1883, approximately five miles east of Monmouth, Illinois. During this night, a train on the railroad killed five horses belonging to Sierer. The horses had entered the railroad's right of way through a sliding gate that was part of a farm crossing on adjacent property owned by Mrs. Eilenberger. The plaintiff asserted that the railroad company negligently failed to properly maintain the gate, which had been found open. The safety measures for the gate, including its regular inspection, were supposed to be the company’s responsibility, though it was not specifically proven that the company had left the gate open. Witness testimony indicated that the gate was seen open intermittently on the day of the incident, yet there was a lack of evidence that it had been left open for an extended period prior to the accident.	The plaintiff, William Sierer, claimed that the railroad company was negligent by knowingly allowing a farm crossing gate to remain open, leading to the death of his horses. He argued that the company had a legal duty to keep the gates closed and safe, and by failing to do so, it caused his financial loss. He sought damages amounting to $550 for the loss of the horses due to what he contended was clear negligence on the part of the railroad company.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, contended that they had fulfilled their obligations by ensuring that the gate was closed and in good repair earlier that day. They argued that there was no actual notice of the gate being open, and thus, they could not be held responsible for an event that occurred without their awareness. The defendant emphasized that maintaining the gate's condition was not solely their responsibility, but also a shared duty with landowners. They requested the court to dismiss the case, asserting that the evidence did not support the plaintiff’s claims of negligence.

In 1882, Frank Cihak, intending to purchase the east half of lot 19 in Chicago, engaged the services of John Gunzenhauser, who had been managing a series of lots for William Wilder. Gunzenhauser subdivided the lots and marked out an alley that was intended for access to these lots, particularly benefiting Cihak’s prospective property. After careful negotiations and assurances from Gunzenhauser regarding a plat he promised to record, Cihak finalized his purchase of the lot. Cihak subsequently built a structure on his property that relied on the alley for deliveries and access. However, following his purchase, several property owners (the defendants) attempted to close off the alley, leading Cihak to seek legal action. He filed a bill in June 1884 to prevent the obstruction of the alley, arguing that he had an easement entitling him to use this alley, which had been established as beneficial for both his lot and others.	Cihak claimed that he had an easement right to access and use the alley behind his property, which was established during the initial platting and subdivision of the lots. He argued that the alley was essential for the enjoyment of his property and that its closure without his consent violated his rights. Cihak sought a court order to prevent the defendants from obstructing the alley.	The defendants contended that the alley was intended only for the use of their lots and that Cihak could not claim any right to it. They argued that since the alley was designated as a "private alley" in the recorded plat, it implied that its use was restricted. They requested the court to uphold the closure of the alley and deny Cihak’s request for injunction.

The case "F. M. Chapman v. The Drainage Commissioners of District No. 3" took place in Iroquois County, Illinois, with the decision being rendered on May 28, 1888. The central figures involved were F. M. Chapman, the plaintiff, and the Drainage Commissioners of District No. 3, the defendants. Chapman was concerned about the classification and assessment of certain sections of land within the newly formed drainage district. He alleged that two sections of land had not been classified, and one was wrongly classified as lying within the district when it actually did not belong to it. Chapman sought legal recourse to compel the commissioners to provide accurate records of their classification and assessments, arguing that the failure to properly classify the lands resulted in significant damages to him. The drainage commissioners contended that due to a change in the drainage route, the two sections in question would not benefit from the drainage project and, therefore, would have been classified at zero. They believed there was no merit to Chapman's claims, citing a lack of injury resulting from their actions.	F. M. Chapman claimed that the drainage commissioners failed to properly classify two sections of land according to the drainage laws and included land that did not belong in the district while omitting land that did. He argued that this process was illegal and caused him significant damage. As part of his lawsuit, he requested a full transcript of the records related to the drainage district and sought for those proceedings to be quashed in court.	The Drainage Commissioners defended against Chapman's claims by stating that the two sections would not be benefited by the drainage project due to changes in the planned ditch route; thus, they would have been classified at zero with no tax assigned. They argued that Chapman's petition was based on an informal complaint that did not harm any substantial rights and indicated that the timing of his complaint was too late to be addressed effectively. They also noted that significant steps regarding the drainage project had already been taken, including assessments collected and contracts let for the work.

In 1886, in Cook County, Illinois, Samuel S. Chisholm entered into an agreement with the Circulating Boiler Company, represented by its president, Alexander J. McDonald, to advance funds for a boiler installation. The company lacked sufficient funds and Chisholm agreed to provide $1,200 as an advance, with the understanding that further business would be arranged if the boiler's installation proved successful. As collateral, they assigned patents to Melville E. Dayton. Chisholm was to receive a promissory note from both the company and McDonald, due ninety days after the date of the note. Despite disputes over the regularity of these notes and the timing of Chisholm's judgment entry, the court noted that the notes’ formalities, including the corporate seal, rendered them prima facie valid. By January 13, 1887, Chisholm entered judgment against the company and McDonald for the advances made. The case involves subsequent efforts by McDonald and the company to challenge this judgment, arguing for relief based on what they claimed was unjust enrichment and the wrongful enforcement of the judgment against them.	Chisholm argued that he had validly entered a judgment based on the promissory notes issued by McDonald and the Circulating Boiler Company, which he claimed were executed properly under Illinois law. He sought to maintain the enforcement of his judgment against the company and McDonald and contended that he should be prioritized for repayment from the funds obtained from property levied under execution. Chisholm asserted that the company and McDonald had no grounds to divert payments owed to him, and he requested that the court uphold his right to the proceeds derived from the property used to secure his advances.	McDonald, representing the Circulating Boiler Company, argued against the validity of the judgment entered by Chisholm, contending that the notes did not adhere to proper procedures and that the advancing of funds constituted an unjust enrichment to Chisholm. The defense claimed that there were irregularities in the execution of the notes and questioned the legality of the confession of judgment prior to the notes' maturity. They sought relief from the judgment, requesting that the court enforce a revision of its orders and prevent Chisholm from receiving the proceeds from the levied property until their claims were properly adjudicated.

The case of Rosa Lazovert v. Morris Lazovert took place in the year 1884 in Illinois. Rosa Lazovert and Morris Lazovert were married in New York City. While living there, Morris committed numerous acts of cruelty against Rosa, which led her to seek a divorce. After these acts of cruelty, he deserted Rosa and moved to Montreal, Canada. When Rosa and her father traced him there, he disappeared entirely and was never heard from again. More than a year before filing her divorce petition, Rosa moved to Chicago, Illinois, to live with her father and his family. Despite her residence in Chicago, the court ruled that Rosa's legal residence followed Morris's, meaning she had not established the legal residence necessary for the Illinois court to have jurisdiction over her divorce case. As a result, the lower court dismissed her divorce petition, leading Rosa to appeal this decision.	Rosa Lazovert, the plaintiff, argued that she was entitled to a divorce based on the grounds of extreme and repeated cruelty from her husband, Morris Lazovert. She sought legal relief and contested the dismissal of her divorce petition, insisting that she had established her residence in Illinois, which should grant the court jurisdiction to hear her case.	Morris Lazovert, although not actively involved in the legal proceedings due to his disappearance, had the implication of the defense that the court lacked jurisdiction to grant Rosa a divorce since he had never resided in Illinois, and therefore, her residence could not confer jurisdiction based on the existing legal principles.

In the case of David Jones v. The People of the State of Illinois, decided on September 27, 1884, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the background involves an indictment against David Jones, the operator of the White Oak coal mine in St. Clair County, Illinois. The indictment was based on Jones's failure to install track scales at the coal mine, as mandated by an 1883 statute titled "An act to provide for the weighing of coal at the mines." This statute required coal mine operators to install scales to weigh all coal before it was loaded onto transport vehicles, ensuring accuracy in calculating wages based on the coal mined. During the trial, Jones sought to present evidence showing that the miners at the coal mine had long been satisfied with a payment arrangement of forty cents per box of coal mined, and they did not desire weighing scales. However, this evidence was excluded by the court. Subsequently, Jones was found guilty and fined $40, prompting him to appeal the decision, arguing the constitutionality of the statutory requirements.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, claimed that David Jones, as the coal mine operator, violated the state law requiring track scales at coal mines to accurately weigh coal. The statute was intended to protect miners and ensure proper wage calculations based on coal weight, as stipulated in the law.	The defendant, David Jones, contended that the statute was unconstitutional as it interfered with his right to contract freely, asserting he had an agreement with the miners that did not necessitate the use of scales. He argued that the law deprived him of property rights by mandating conditions for wage determination that contradicted existing contracts. He sought to prove that the miners preferred their current payment method and had no interest in the scales, which were costly to install.

In 1859, Lester Underwood and George H. West entered into an agreement to exchange real estate in Ottawa, Illinois. Underwood believed he would receive an undivided half of the Fox River house property along with certain lots, while he would convey eighty acres of land and some cattle to West. After both parties executed their respective deeds and made a transfer through Arthur Lockwood, Underwood learned that two key lots, identified as lots six and ten, were not included in the deed he received. Convinced that he was entitled to these lots based on their discussions and the nature of the property shown to him, Underwood refused to accept the deed due to its incompleteness. West, on the other hand, argued that he had fulfilled his obligations under their agreement. The case was initially dismissed in the Circuit Court of La Salle County, prompting Underwood to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court to seek the rescission of the contract due to what he claimed amounted to fraudulent misrepresentation by West.	Underwood’s primary argument hinged on the assertion that West had misrepresented the properties included in the agreement. He contended that the terms of their contract implied the inclusion of lots six and ten in the conveyance of property. Underwood sought to rescind the agreement and set aside the conveyance of the property due to fraud, claiming that West's actions led him to believe he was acquiring all relevant lots, aside from one that was explicitly excluded.	West defended himself by asserting that he had duly executed the agreement and conveyed all the lots that were expressly included in the deal. He argued that Underwood did not have any right to contest the deed since he had received everything that had been agreed upon and insisted that he acted in good faith throughout their transaction. West contested Underwood's claims of fraud, maintaining that Underwood had misunderstood the agreement rather than being misled.

In 1885, in Cook County, Illinois, William E. Hinchliff initiated a legal battle against George W. Prins through a suit by attachment, seeking to recover an outstanding debt of $661.50 for goods sold and delivered. Hinchliff claimed that Prins had either left the state with the intention of removing his assets or had fraudulently conveyed or concealed his property in a manner that hindered his creditors. The sheriff's return noted that Prins could not be found in the county, prompting Hinchliff to publish a notice as per statutory requirements. With Prins failing to appear, the court rendered a default judgment against him for the claimed amount and costs. However, it was later determined that the affidavit supporting the attachment was faulty, failing to state the residency status of the defendant or to include proper allegations as prescribed by law.	The plaintiff, William E. Hinchliff, argued that he was owed $661.50 for goods sold to George W. Prins. He claimed that Prins had fled the state or concealed his assets to evade repayment, justifying the need for a writ of attachment to secure the judgment against him.	George W. Prins did not appear in court to defend against the claims, leading to default judgment against him. However, the defense could argue that the affidavit for the attachment was improperly formulated, as it did not meet legal requirements by failing to clearly state the grounds for the writ or his residency status. This lack of proper procedure was pivotal in challenging the legitimacy of the judgment.

In December 1854, in Madison County, Illinois, Stacy Taylor brought a lawsuit against Gilbert Cottrell and Madison Marcum. The case arose after Cottrell sold a wood boat called the Star Boat to A. Polly without disclosing the sale to Taylor, who later purchased the boat from Cottrell for $156.50. After Polly replevied the boat from Taylor, Taylor had Cottrell arrested in St. Louis for swindling him. While in custody, Cottrell and Marcum executed a promissory note for $176.50, which Taylor claimed was to satisfy the debt for the boat and related expenses. The defendants argued that the note was obtained under duress, as Cottrell was in a position of vulnerability while arrested. Initially, the Madison Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendants, but Taylor appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Taylor contended that the promissory note was valid and constituted a legitimate demand for payment owed to him by Cottrell relating to the sale of the boat. He argued that the defendants' claim of duress was unfounded, as he was merely pursuing legal remedies for the sale and ownership of the boat. Taylor sought to have the judgment of the lower court reversed and for the enforcement of the promissory note.	Cottrell and Marcum defended their position by claiming that the note was executed under duress, given that Cottrell was under arrest at the time and was pressured to sign the note for his release. They maintained that the circumstances surrounding the note’s execution were unjust, alleging that Taylor had improperly used the legal process to coerce Cottrell. The defendants requested that the court uphold the original ruling, thus dismissing Taylor’s claims.

The case "The Central Military Tract Railroad Company v. William Spurck et al." took place in April 1860 in Illinois. The dispute arose from an action of assumpsit brought by William Spurck and another individual against the Central Military Tract Railroad Company. The plaintiffs claimed they had performed labor under a contractual agreement for excavation work and were entitled to payment. They alleged that the railroad company failed to pay 80% of the contract price according to the monthly estimates and unlawfully hindered them from completing their work. The railroad company's defenses included a plea of payment and claims that the plaintiffs had not fulfilled their part of the contract and had abandoned the work before its completion. A trial was conducted, resulting in a jury verdict favoring the plaintiffs for $939.16, prompting the defendants to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to payment for work performed based on the contract, claiming they had completed a portion of the excavation required. They asserted that the railroad company refused to approve and estimate the work completed and wrongfully discharged them, thus denying them rightful payments. Their primary legal request was for recovery of the contract price for the labor performed, amounting to an unfulfilled payment.	The Central Military Tract Railroad Company contended that they had made payments according to contract stipulations, arguing that the plaintiffs abandoned their work prematurely and failed to complete the required excavation quantity. They claimed the plaintiffs were not justified in their abandonment of the contract and that any estimates from their engineers were accurate, affirming no dues were owed to the plaintiffs. Their request was for the court to reverse the lower court's judgment and deny the plaintiffs' claims.

The case of "The City of Ottawa v. The Trustees of the Free Church" took place in the city of Ottawa, Illinois, with the legal proceedings initiated in April 1858. The City of Ottawa was seeking to enforce a special assessment against various lots within the city that benefited from sewer improvements on Jefferson Street. Albert F. Dow, the city collector, reported that certain lots remained unpaid in terms of their assessments.
