His affidavit confirmed that no payments had been made on the delinquent list since its return on January 18, 1858, and he was unable to find goods belonging to the owners for levy. The city had published a notice detailing the improvements, the properties assessed, and the related valuations. The defendants, in turn, filed objections against the assessment, stating that some of the lots were church property, which they argued should be exempt from these kinds of assessments.	The plaintiff, The City of Ottawa, argued that the assessments were valid and necessary for the funding of public improvements, namely the sewer. They maintained that church properties could be assessed for special purposes even if they were exempt from ordinary taxes, based on past legal precedent. The city requested the enforcement of the assessment and a judgment to collect the due amounts from the property owners involved.	The defendants, The Trustees of the Free Church, contended that some of the lots in question were church properties that should not be subject to assessment. They argued that since church properties are exempt from ordinary tax liabilities, they should likewise be exempt from special assessments imposed for local improvements. They requested dismissal of the claims against those properties.

This case, "The Galena and Southern Wisconsin Railroad Company v. William Ennor," originated in January 1886 in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The legal issue stemmed from a prior judgment of $5,678 against William Ennor, adjudicated on June 30, 1879, for the subscription price of eight first mortgage bonds of the Galena and Southern Wisconsin Railroad Company. Ennor had signed a subscription agreement in February 1877, committing to purchase the bonds, contingent upon 100 bonds being subscribed for in total. However, Ennor later claimed that he had never received the bonds or shares subscribed for and alleged that the railroad company was insolvent and unable to provide them after a foreclosure sale of its assets. Ennor, imprisoned for a significant period due to the judgment against him, filed a bill in chancery seeking relief against the judgment. He accused the railroad company of fraud in their representations about the subscriptions. Initially dismissed by the circuit court, the appellate court later reversed this decision, granting Ennor a new trial. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case, focusing on the validity of the judgment based on the subscription agreement and the claims of fraud.	William Ennor claimed that the judgment obtained by the Galena and Southern Wisconsin Railroad Company was invalid because he was unaware that not enough bonds were subscribed to make his commitment binding. He argued that he had been misled by the company’s false representations regarding the number of bonds subscribed and that he had been unjustly imprisoned for over fourteen months due to the judgment. Ennor requested an injunction to prevent the company from collecting the judgment, a new trial to be granted, and a set-off against the judgment for a promissory note he held against the company.	The Galena and Southern Wisconsin Railroad Company contended that the judgment was valid and that Ennor had the opportunity to defend himself in the original trial. They argued that the claim of fraud was unsubstantiated, as the subscription issue was a matter that could have been addressed during the initial proceedings. The company posited that the subscription agreements were complex, and that the existence of secret agreements among other subscribers did not invalidate the overall subscription process. They requested the court to uphold the original judgment against Ennor.

The case of The Belleville Nail Mill Company v. Tarlton W. Chiles emerged from a disagreement concerning the employment of Chiles by the Belleville Nail Mill Company. The incident took place in St. Clair County, Illinois, and the legal proceedings began with a lawsuit filed by Chiles against the company on February 17, 1871. Following a series of trials, the case was initially tried with a verdict favoring the defendant. However, upon appeal, the Illinois Supreme Court reversed that decision, establishing that Chiles had indeed been employed as a bookkeeper for the company for a year. Upon retrial, the jury ruled in favor of Chiles, allotting him $1,775 as compensation for his services over the agreed period, based on the court's acknowledgment of the evidence presented regarding his employment. The proceedings noted that there were no significant discrepancies in the testimony regarding the employment relationship, and the court found the awarded amount to adequately reflect the value of services rendered.	Tarlton W. Chiles claimed that he was employed by the Belleville Nail Mill Company as a bookkeeper for one year and sought compensation for his services. He argued that the employment was established and that he was entitled to monetary damages amounting to $1,775, representing the fair value of his work during that year.	The Belleville Nail Mill Company, in defense, contended that the action was improperly initiated before the cause for the action arose and argued that a demurrer was pending when the trial commenced. They sought to challenge the validity of Chiles' claims and disputed the adequacy of damages assessed by the jury, although they faced difficulties in proving their case during the retrials.

In 1878, Frederick P. Burgett and two others filed a lawsuit against John S. Paxton, the sheriff of Mercer County, and Frank H. Bernard, the execution creditor. The plaintiffs sought to block the sale of land that had been levied against Wells Willets due to an execution against him. To initiate their case, the plaintiffs executed a bond with an additional appellant as surety, committing to pursue the injunction suit and cover all associated costs. A subsequent assignment of the judgment against Willets, referred to a Shadrach C. Burlingim, led to Burlingim being included as a co-defendant. After the court dismissed the injunction and the appellate courts upheld this decision, Bernard and Paxton sought damages by filing a suit against the obligors of the bond, claiming substantial costs incurred during the case. After waiving a jury trial, the court found in favor of the plaintiffs and ordered the appellants to pay $567 in assessed damages. The defendants appealed, questioning whether the bond's terms allowed for recovery of damages incurred solely by Burlingim and whether the plaintiffs had actually sustained any damages.	The plaintiffs, John S. Paxton and Frank H. Bernard, claimed damages due to an injunction that prevented a sale of land levied under an execution against Wells Willets. They sought recovery for costs incurred in solicitors’ fees and the expenses from the circuit, appellate, and supreme courts, totaling approximately $1,500. Their declaration focused on the financial hardships they faced due to the delay in executing the sale along with the loss of interest accrued during that period.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs had not incurred any damages because they had no standing or interest in the original judgment against Willets when the injunction was filed. They argued that Burlingim, not the plaintiffs, had assumed responsibility for legal costs and any damages associated with the injunction suit. Thus, the defendants asserted that they could not be held liable for damages claimed by someone who was not a party to the bond and that the bond did not cover Burlingim's incurred expenses.

In September 1875, the case of David Dreyer et al. v. Henry C. Durand et al. was filed in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a bill in equity where the complainants, Henry C. Durand and associates, sought to claim goods owned by David Dreyer to satisfy a previous judgment against him. Durand’s firm contended that Dreyer was fraudulently concealing his property by using Leo Lefman as a cover for the goods in question, which were stored at 219 Cottage Grove Avenue in Chicago. The complainants alleged that these goods belonged to Dreyer, despite being managed by Lefman, and requested the court to prevent any liens or assignments on the property and sought the appointment of a receiver. Dreyer and Lefman denied the allegations, claiming that the goods were actually Lefman’s property, and that Dreyer was merely acting as his agent following a financial disaster in 1871 that left him nearly destitute. The situation stemmed from a familial arrangement where Lefman provided support to his nephew Dreyer by purchasing the goods, which Dreyer sold to support himself and his family.	The plaintiffs claimed that David Dreyer was fraudulently concealing his assets to avoid settling debts owed to them. They asserted that the goods in the store were actually owned by Dreyer and requested the court to intervene by preventing anyone from creating a lien on the goods, barring any assignment of property by the defendants, and appointing a receiver to manage the situation.	The defendants, David Dreyer and Leo Lefman, countered the claims by asserting that the goods belonged to Lefman and not Dreyer. They maintained that Dreyer was simply acting as an agent to sell the goods on behalf of Lefman. They argued that the arrangement was legitimate and that the goods could not be claimed by the plaintiffs to satisfy Dreyer's debts, as the plaintiffs were aware of Dreyer's agency status. They provided evidence and testimony that corroborated their claims of ownership.

The case "The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company v. Mary E. Michie, Admx." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1876. The background involves Mary E. Michie, the administratrix of her deceased husband, Joseph B. Michie, bringing a lawsuit against the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company. The incident occurred when Joseph, a passenger on the railroad’s train traveling from Chicago to St. Louis, died due to what the plaintiff claimed was the negligence of the railroad company. The trial took place in the Superior Court of Cook County, where the jury awarded Mary E. Michie $5,000 in damages. However, the railroad company contested the decision, leading to an appeal. Throughout the proceedings, fundamental issues arose regarding the status of Joseph Michie as a passenger and whether he was riding in compliance with the rules of the railroad.	The plaintiff, Mary E. Michie, argued that her late husband was a passenger on the defendant's train and claimed that the railroad company had a duty to transport him safely. She presented several counts in her declaration, asserting that he had paid fare and that his death was a result of the company's negligence. She requested compensation for the damages incurred due to her husband’s untimely death.	The defendant, the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company, contended that Joseph Michie was not a legitimate passenger but was riding unlawfully on the engine in violation of company rules. They argued that there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the claims made by the plaintiff, emphasizing that the deceased was traveling without permission and therefore the company held no liability for his death. They maintained that any claimed relationship of carrier and passenger did not exist due to his unauthorized presence on the train.

In 1865, in Cairo, Illinois, Charles D. Arter, a merchant, sold a quantity of powder and shot which raised suspicion from Joel S. Byington, the defendant. Byington believed these items were intended for the use of the rebel States during the Civil War. He seized the goods while they were being loaded at night and attempted to arrest the individuals involved, but they managed to escape. Subsequently, Byington confronted Arter and threatened to shut down his store and report him to the United States marshal unless he paid a bribe of $1,000. Arter, seeking to avoid legal repercussions, paid the requested amount. Later, he initiated a lawsuit to recover the bribe he had paid, resulting in a trial where the jury ruled in his favor in the Circuit Court. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for appeal.	Arter claimed that he was entitled to recover the $1,000 he paid to Byington, arguing that the payment was made under duress and constituted a bribe to prevent exposure to authorities regarding his supposed illegal actions during the Civil War.	Byington contended that if Arter was engaged in unlawful commerce with the enemy and paid a bribe to avoid being reported, he could not subsequently claim to recover the money. The defendant argued that the law should not provide relief to parties involved in illegal activities, emphasizing the principle of "ex turpi causa, non oritur actio," which states that a party cannot seek legal remedy for a wrong that arises from their own illegal act.

The case "City of Rockford v. Margaret Hollenbeck" took place in Rockford, Illinois, with the injury incident occurring on November 12, 1886. The plaintiff, Margaret Hollenbeck, a 69-year-old woman, was walking along a defective sidewalk on Rockton Avenue after attending a funeral. The sidewalk, located in a sparsely populated area, had a significant structural issue where a 16-foot board was improperly laid along the sidewalk. As Hollenbeck was walking, another person accidentally stepped on one end of the board, causing it to tip and trip Hollenbeck, resulting in her falling forward onto the sidewalk. As a result of the fall, she sustained severe, long-lasting injuries, including paralysis in her left hand and persistent pain. Evidence indicated the city had neglected the sidewalk for years, allowing its dangerous condition to persist without proper repair.	Hollenbeck claimed that the City of Rockford was negligent in maintaining the sidewalk, which had been in disrepair for several years. She argued that the city failed to ensure the safety of pedestrians and allowed the sidewalk to become a trap for unsuspecting individuals. Hollenbeck sought damages for the injuries she sustained from her fall, asserting that such negligence directly led to her substantial injuries and suffering.	The City of Rockford denied negligence, contending that the sidewalk was situated in a remote area of the city, thus warranting less stringent maintenance standards. The defense argued that they could not be held liable for incidents occurring on less frequented paths. Additionally, the defendant claimed that the plaintiff may have demonstrated contributory negligence for not observing the condition of the sidewalk beforehand. They requested a reversal of the judgment in favor of the plaintiff based on these assertions.

In the case of Daniel B. Brant v. Benjamin E. Gallup et al., decided on May 15, 1886, the legal proceedings took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. Daniel B. Brant filed an appeal against defendants Benjamin E. Gallup and others regarding a prior decision made by the Appellate Court for the First District. The case began with a motion by Brant for a rehearing of the court's previous judgment, which he claimed was unfavorable. During the September term of 1884, a rehearing was initially granted, leading to an opinion filed on January 22, 1885, which affirmed the judgment of the Appellate Court. After several months and a March 1885 term where no further action occurred, Brant sought additional consideration for his case. However, he failed to comply with the court's required procedures for filing a rehearing petition within a specified time frame. Brant's affidavits indicated that he had sought advice from his attorney right after the last opinion was filed, but was incorrectly informed that no further actions could be taken, resulting in a missed deadline. The court noted that public policy necessitates finality in legal decisions and denied Brant's request for another rehearing.	The plaintiff, Daniel B. Brant, argued that he was entitled to file a petition for a rehearing of the case after a decision was rendered against him. He claimed that he misunderstood his rights based on the incorrect advice from his attorney regarding the possibility of seeking further review after the original decision. Brant requested the court to allow the filing of his petition for rehearing despite the missed timeframe, citing an alleged error in communication.	The defendants, represented by Messrs. Paddock & Alois, contended that Brant's failure to comply with the established rules regarding the timeline for filing a rehearing petition should preclude any further consideration of the case. They argued that Brant's situation did not merit an exception to the rules of court, as there were no new grounds or errors in the prior judgments. They requested the court to deny Brant’s motion for leave to file his petition for a rehearing, emphasizing the necessity of adhering to procedural rules to ensure public policy and judicial stability.

In the case of Moses S. Trader and Tegal Trader, appellants, against Moses McKee, appellee, the legal proceedings stem from actions that took place in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, in 1838. The plaintiff, Moses McKee, brought forward judgments that he had obtained from a justice of the peace in Indiana against the defendants, Moses S. and Tegal Trader. The defendants objected to the admission of the transcripts of these Indiana judgments into evidence, arguing that no concrete evidence demonstrated that the Indiana justice had jurisdiction over them or the subject matter involved. Despite their objections, the Circuit Court accepted the transcripts as evidence and ruled in favor of McKee. The case was subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, which examined whether the prior judgments could be legitimately introduced without proper demonstration of the Indiana court's jurisdiction, as established by Indiana law. Several procedural and jurisdictional concerns were raised by the appellants regarding the validity of the transcripts and the certification process, ultimately leading the Supreme Court to re-evaluate the case.	The plaintiff, Moses McKee, claimed that the transcripts of the judgments from the Indiana justice of the peace should be admissible as valid evidence in the Illinois court. He requested enforcement of these judgments, asserting that they were duly certified, although he did not produce sufficient legal grounding for the jurisdiction of the Indiana justice over the defendants or the subject matter of the original actions.	The defendants, Moses S. and Tegal Trader, contended that the admission of the Indiana judgments was improper. They argued that McKee failed to demonstrate that the Indiana justice had jurisdiction to make the rulings and that the processes followed to certify the judgments were flawed. They sought to have the prior ruling in favor of McKee reversed on the basis of these failings, particularly emphasizing the necessity of proving jurisdiction affirmatively in cases involving justices of the peace from another state.

On July 15, 1885, Adolphus Miller filed a legal action against C. D. Cook and another party in the Circuit Court of Jefferson County, Illinois. Miller claimed to hold a mortgage on a portion of a lot in Mt. Vernon, Illinois, securing a $3,000 loan to D. C. Warren. Though Warren paid the taxes for several years, the collector failed to discharge them, allowing a tax judgment that resulted in the sale of the lot to Cook for $228.56 on June 8, 1883. Miller alleged that he was not notified about these proceedings and that the sale would destroy his security interest in the property. He sought a perpetual injunction to prevent Cook from obtaining a tax deed and requested that the sale be declared void. The Circuit Court initially found in favor of Miller, but Cook appealed the decision, contending that the tax sale was legally valid and that the prior judgment from an earlier case should bar Miller's claims.	Adolphus Miller asserted that he possessed an interest in the property due to his mortgage with D. C. Warren. He claimed that the issuing of a tax deed to Cook would irreparably harm his rights and requested an injunction to prevent Cook from taking out the deed. Miller offered to pay all outstanding lawful taxes to protect his interest in the property and aimed to have the sale declared void.	C. D. Cook defended against Miller's claims by stating that the tax sale was legally executed after all relevant notifications were served. Cook claimed that Miller was barred from bringing forth his case due to a previous court decision where Warren, the original mortgagor, had already litigated regarding the same subject matter. Cook argued that Miller's allegations were unfounded as there were sufficient securities underlying the mortgage, and that no irreparable harm would occur.

In 1877, in Piatt County, Illinois, the case of Alvin Caldwell et al. v. Silas A. Evans et al. arose when the defendants, Evans and others, removed certain fences belonging to the plaintiffs, Caldwell and others. These fences were treated as a division fence between the two properties. The removal of the fences created gaps that allowed the plaintiffs’ cattle to escape into their corn, leading to actual damage. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants acted without the required statutory notice and justification, particularly since it was not demonstrated that a public road had been legally established in the area. Although one defendant owned adjacent land, their defense was based on acting under the order of the highway commissioners to open a public road. However, the court ruled the evidence supporting this establishment of a road was inadmissible, and no lawful right to remove the fences was demonstrated.	The plaintiffs, Alvin Caldwell et al., argued that the defendants unlawfully removed their fences without proper legal authority or notice, directly causing damage to their corn by allowing cattle access. They sought compensation for the actual damages incurred due to the actions of the defendants.	The defendants contended that they had a right to remove the fences based on an order from the highway commissioners to open a public road. They argued that their actions were justified under this claim, despite the lack of evidence for a legally established highway. Furthermore, they supported their case by stating that the removal aimed at fulfilling public interest.

On February 11, 1853, the Illinois General Assembly incorporated the Randolph County Plank Road Company, granting authority to use public highways for construction. The plank road connected Chester to Sparta, eventually becoming essential for local travel. By February 1854, the charter was amended, allowing the company to neglect the initial five-year completion requirement and to borrow against the road. The legislature further allowed the sale of the company's properties in 1859, while obligating the company to maintain the roadway. By January 3, 1868, the company announced intentions to cease road maintenance due to high costs and poor conditions, warning that access would be restricted if not purchased by the public by April 1, 1868. In response, the county's State Attorney filed a bill against the company to prevent obstruction of the road, as it was deemed a public nuisance for impeding public travel. The defendants admitted the existence of their charter but argued that the public highway had not been legally vacated and thus remained travelable. Ultimately, the court dealt with the question of the public's right to use the plank road and the responsibilities of the company to maintain it.	The plaintiff, on behalf of the public, claimed that the defendants intended to enclose a public roadway which would obstruct travel, constituting a public nuisance. The plaintiff sought an injunction to restrain the defendants from interfering with the road and its bridges, emphasizing that such actions would cause irreparable harm to the traveling public.	The defendants contended that not all parts of the plank road graced public highways; rather, most of it was constructed over private lands. They denied that the old public highway had been legally vacated and asserted that if any enclosures occurred, they were unauthorized actions by the public. They also argued that the public interest was not at risk since the old highway still had open sections for travel.

Benjamin Bates, the appellant, and Isaac West, the appellee, were involved in a legal dispute that took place in Griggsville, Illinois. The case stems from a transaction on March 24, 1838, in which Bates conveyed a property lot to West for $150. The deed included full covenants ensuring that Bates would warrant and defend West’s title to the property. However, on March 5, 1856, West was evicted from the premises based on a superior title claim. Following this eviction, West initiated a legal action against Bates on March 6, 1856, claiming breaches of covenant related to the warranty. Bates, as a defense, cited a prior discharge in bankruptcy granted to him on March 24, 1843, arguing that this discharge protected him from liability on the warranty that was not violated until after the bankruptcy.	West's primary claim was that Bates failed to uphold his covenants by not defending West's title to the property against the eviction. He sought damages for this breach, which were assessed by the lower court to be $323.80.	Bates countered West's claims by asserting that his discharge in bankruptcy effectively absolved him of the obligation to honor the warranty because the breach had not occurred until after his bankruptcy discharge. He contended that the covenant was a contingent and uncertain demand, which was covered under the bankruptcy protections.

The case of G. Bessey v. J. B. Ruhland, decided on April 17, 1889, involves a legal dispute that originated from an appeal taken from a justice of the peace in Cook County, Illinois. The defendant, Bessey, filed an appeal on December 1, 1882, challenging a judgment made against him. However, due to delays, the necessary paperwork was not entered into the Circuit Court until September 28, 1887. The court subsequently dismissed the appeal on May 7, 1888, during a preliminary call because Bessey failed to appear, resulting in an adjudication of costs and damages against him. Bessey then sought to reinstate the case but was denied in July 1888, prompting him to appeal this dismissal. The case revolved around procedural issues related to the timing and manner in which Bessey's appeal was filed, particularly focusing on whether the dismissal was appropriate given the lack of a formal appearance from the appellee, Ruhland.	The plaintiff, G. Bessey, asserted that the Circuit Court erred in dismissing his appeal without proper consideration of the legal requirements outlined in Section 68 of the act of 1872 regarding appeals. He contended that, since the appellee did not file a written appearance in a timely manner, the court should have allowed the appeal to proceed. Bessey sought reinstatement of his appeal and reversal of the Circuit Court's dismissal, arguing it was unjust and unsupported by established legal precedents.	The defendant, J. B. Ruhland, maintained that the dismissal of the appeal was justified based on procedural grounds. Ruhland's key argument centered on the absence of a written appearance filed before the term, which he claimed negated Bessey’s ability to prosecute his appeal. Consequently, he requested that the dismissal be upheld and argued for the enforcement of the costs and damages adjudged against Bessey as a result of the dismissal.

The case involves The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company and others as plaintiffs against Hindman, Michælis & Co., with the proceedings taking place in Jackson County, Illinois. The original action was a writ of error aimed at overturning a circuit court judgment. The plaintiffs sought to enforce an attachment against defendants Fleming & Lacy, with the railroad company and H. H. Payson & Co. named as garnishees. During the proceedings, it was determined that the errors cited did not exist upon reviewing a complete record. As a result, the writ of error was dismissed concerning the railroad company, thus distancing it from the claims made by Hindman, Michælis & Co. In contrast, the court considered the matter of the payments or debts owed by Payson & Co. However, the presence of prior suits complicated their ability to declare any debts clearly owed to Flemings & Lacy, leading to further deliberation.	The plaintiffs claimed that the garnishee process against the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company and H. H. Payson & Co. was valid. They argued that there was clear indebtedness from these companies to Fleming & Lacy that warranted the attachment. Specifically, they sought to hold the garnishees accountable for any amounts owed at the time the garnishee process was served.	The defendants, including the garnishee H. H. Payson & Co., contended that prior lawsuits existed which left the nature of any possible debts uncertain. They asserted that it was impossible to declare any specific amounts owed since the results of those prior litigations needed to be resolved first. They also argued that lacking a clear basis for their liability, they should not be held responsible under garnishment rules.

In September 1850, in Jefferson County, Illinois, Shadrick Alvis initiated a lawsuit against Jordan McKinney in a justice of the peace court over a claim related to a transaction involving eight hundred rails, originally owed by McKinney to a deceased individual named Piper. Alvis asserted that he had acquired Piper's claim to the rails and demanded that McKinney deliver them to him. Alvis obtained a judgment for $7 after McKinney failed to fulfill this contractual obligation. McKinney subsequently appealed to the Jefferson Circuit Court, which upheld the lower court's decision in December 1851 despite McKinney's motions for a new trial and to arrest judgment being denied. This brought the case to the Illinois Supreme Court for further review, where the central issue revolved around the legality of Alvis maintaining the action in his own name without proper assignment from Piper.	The plaintiff, Jordan McKinney, contended that Alvis could not sustain the lawsuit in his name because the debt was not properly assigned to him. McKinney cited the legal principle that "dioses in action," which are non-negotiable claims, are not assignable as a matter of law without a communication and agreement between all parties involved to extinguish the original debt. He argued there was no evidence of communication between Piper and himself and that Alvis did not legally assume responsibility for the claim against McKinney.	The defendant, Shadrick Alvis, maintained that he was entitled to enforce the claim for the rails based on an express verbal promise from McKinney. Alvis argued that this promise constituted an exception to the general rule regarding non-assignable debts. However, he faced challenges in demonstrating that the original obligation owed to Piper had been properly extinguished or assigned, and he acknowledged the absence of any solid evidence supporting his claim.

The case "Mullanphy Bank et al. v. Otto G. Schott et al." was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on February 4, 1890. The case originates from a chancery suit filed in the Madison Circuit Court involving the Brookside Coal & Coke Company, amidst claims of insolvency and fraudulent acts by its officers. Key individuals included Martin J. Schott, who was both a director and the treasurer of the company, and Louis Schlosstein, who intervened in the case claiming hold of certain promissory notes secured by a mortgage from the company to Schott. The case arose when various creditors sought a ruling on the order of payment for their claims, with the primary dispute focusing on the priority of Schott's mortgage over other liens derived from subsequent mortgages and judgments. The court assessed the credibility of the claims, including whether Schott, due to his dual role as an officer and creditor, was estopped from asserting his priority, and evaluated the admissibility of certain resolutions from the company records that purportedly indicated the intention to prioritize the second mortgage.	The plaintiffs, including Mullanphy Bank and others, claimed that Schott's mortgage was rendered subordinate due to certain resolutions indicating that all debt, including Schott’s, would be addressed through a subsequent deed of trust. They asserted that this effectively altered the priority of liens and implied that Schott should be estopped from claiming a first lien on the properties.	The defendant, represented by Schott, argued that his mortgage was a valid first lien on the properties in question, supported by proper documentation and recorded prior to opposing claims. He contended that the subsequent mortgages and the declarations made by the company's president did not legally impact his lien, as there was no evidence of fraud or misleading conduct. Schott maintained that the actions taken at the board meeting did not bind him or alter his rights as a secured creditor.

In the case of Edward G. Mason, Executor, etc. et al. v. Gustavus H. Bauman, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871, the key parties involved included Edward G. Mason, acting as executor for the estate of Charles R. Starkweather, and Gustavus H. Bauman, a former tenant of Starkweather. The background of this case stems from transactions made in 1858 when Bauman, who was heavily indebted, devised an arrangement with Starkweather aimed at alleviating his financial burdens. This included the transfer of various securities to Starkweather, including a deed of trust and an assignment of a mortgage, aimed at ensuring the payment of Bauman's debts. Over time, Starkweather sold parts of Bauman's property to settle some of his debts. However, disputes arose surrounding the validity of these transactions and whether Starkweather acted as an agent or a trustee. In particular, there were claims regarding the sale of a mortgage on a property that Bauman had assigned to Starkweather, which subsequently passed through several hands. Bauman contended that Starkweather’s actions were fraudulent and asserted the right to redeem the property after Starkweather’s eventual foreclosure of the mortgage. The case culminated in significant discussions regarding agency, trust, and the rights arising from these relationships.	The plaintiffs, led by Edward G. Mason as the executor of Starkweather's estate, claimed that Starkweather had been acting as a trustee rather than as an absolute owner of the mortgage in question. They argued that Starkweather's failure to disclose a better sales offer, which he concealed, constituted fraud. Consequently, they requested leave to redeem the property based on the idea that Starkweather did not obtain a full title due to his alleged fraudulent actions.	In defense, Gustavus H. Bauman and the subsequent purchasers argued that Starkweather acted within his authority and had no obligation to disclose the previous offer. They asserted that the sale of the note and mortgage was executed properly and that the purchasers acquired the title in good faith, free from any claim of fraud. They contended that Bauman had no right to redeem the property since Starkweather had executed his duties lawfully as Bauman's agent.

In the case of Harmon Myer et al. v. William McDougal, which took place in January 1868, the dispute emerged over the ownership of a piece of land located in Illinois. The property had originally belonged to Robert Hayden, who died in November 1856, leaving behind a will that devised the land to Elizabeth Hayden. Elizabeth later sold the land to Barney M. Hayden. At the time of his death, Robert was indebted to several creditors, and the land was sold under a court's execution due to these debts, with a redemption period still in effect. Barney M. Hayden, as the purchaser, sought to redeem the land by paying part of the debt and issuing promissory notes to the original creditor, William McDougal, who had taken a mortgage on the property. However, the mortgage executed by Barney did not specify the county or meridian details of the land. Following this, Barney obtained letters of administration on Robert's estate and filed a claim for the amounts he had paid. In 1862, the county court directed the sale of the land to settle the existing debts, with the property ultimately purchased by Myer and Bracken without any knowledge of McDougal's mortgage. The contention arose over who held the superior claim to the land, with McDougal asserting priority due to the mortgage, while Myer and Bracken claimed ownership via the administrator's sale.	The plaintiff, William McDougal, argued that he held a prior and superior lien on the property through the mortgage he recorded, which should be recognized despite the subsequent sale to Myer and Bracken. He contended that the land, even though sold to new buyers, remained subject to the debts of Robert Hayden, thereby asserting that his mortgage should take precedence over their claim.	Defendants Harmon Myer and Bracken contested McDougal's claims by asserting that they acquired paramount title to the property through the legal sale conducted by the administrator of Robert Hayden's estate. They maintained that the sale was legitimate and that they were unaware of any fraud or improper claims associated with the transactions regarding the estate. Furthermore, they argued that even if some claims were fraudulent, this should not affect their title as they had no direct involvement in the alleged wrongdoing.

In 1820, in White County, Illinois, George Naught initiated a slander lawsuit against Hezekiah Oneal. Naught claimed that Oneal had made defamatory statements that harmed his reputation. Oneal responded by asserting the defense of the statute of limitations, arguing that the alleged slanderous remarks did not occur within one year prior to the filing of the lawsuit. The central legal dispute revolved around whether the plaintiff's claims fell within the permissible time frame outlined by the statute of limitations. Naught countered that the lawsuit was filed within a year of the enactment of a new limitations statute, which he believed should apply to his case. The case was heard in the circuit court of White County, where the court decided in favor of Oneal by sustaining his demurrer to Naught’s claims. Naught subsequently appealed the decision, leading to a writ of error being filed.	George Naught argued that the statements made by Hezekiah Oneal were slanderous and detrimental to his reputation. Naught contended that the remarks were not made within one year before the lawsuit was filed, thus claiming that the statute of limitations should not bar his action. He maintained that he initiated legal proceedings within a year of the passage of the act of limitations, invoking the new statute in support of his case.	Hezekiah Oneal's primary defense was the invocation of the statute of limitations. He argued that the cause of action did not accrue within the one-year period prior to the commencement of the suit, which should preclude Naught's claim. Oneal demurred to Naught's assertion regarding the timing of the statements, asserting that the plaintiff's argument was insufficient under the law.

The case "Josephus Scott v. Job White" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1874. It originated in Edgar County, Illinois, where Josephus Scott, the plaintiff, worked for Job White, the defendant, on a corn crop that was cultivated on land rented by a third party named Clawson. Scott and Clawson formed a partnership for the crop, with Scott entitled to a quarter of it in exchange for his labor. However, Clawson had previously mortgaged the crop to White to secure rent owed, which complicated matters when the crop was harvested. After the mortgage was foreclosed, White took possession and sold the corn, promising Scott payment for his labor if Scott refrained from claiming a right to the crop. Scott's testimony supported that White promised to pay him for his labor, but White denied this, claiming there was no consideration for such a promise. Issues arose regarding whether Scott, being a minor at the time of labor, could recover payment without his father's claim. The court had to evaluate the evidence and the legal implications surrounding these claims, including the Statute of Frauds and the concept of emancipation.	Josephus Scott, the plaintiff, claimed that Job White, the defendant, promised to pay him for his labor in raising a corn crop. He argued that he had a right to one-fourth of the crop's proceeds and sought a judgment for $100, reflecting the value of his work. Scott contended that White's promise was valid consideration and that his rights were infringed when White took possession of the crop and sold it without fulfilling the promise to pay. Scott's case relied on testimonial evidence from several witnesses who supported his claims of the agreement.	Job White, the defendant, denied having made any promise to pay Scott for his labor. He argued that there was no contract or consideration for such a promise, asserting that Scott, being a minor, could not recover wages without his father's involvement. White also contended that the agreement was void under the Statute of Frauds due to lack of written documentation, asserting that the proper legal protocols had not been followed in their arrangement.

The case "The Town of Partridge v. John Snyder" took place in 1875 in Illinois. The action was initiated before a justice of the peace, following a complaint made by William Crank, a commissioner of highways for the Town of Partridge. The town sought to recover a penalty from John Snyder for allegedly obstructing a public highway, as defined under section 58 of the act concerning "Roads and Bridges" in the Revised Statutes of 1874. A trial was conducted, resulting in a verdict favoring the defendant, John Snyder. The town subsequently appealed this decision to the circuit court. However, the circuit court, upon a motion from Snyder, dismissed the appeal. The key issue for the Illinois Supreme Court was whether the town had the right to appeal the justice of the peace's judgment in this particular case.	The Town of Partridge argued that it was entitled to appeal the judgment issued by the justice of the peace because the action was a civil case about recovering a penalty for obstructing a highway. They contended that under existing statutes, appeals should be allowed in all cases where the action of debt or assumpsit can be pursued, and the penalty suit fell under that jurisdiction. The town requested the Illinois Supreme Court to reverse the dismissal of their appeal so they could have their case re-heard in a higher court.	John Snyder contended that the appeal should be dismissed as it had been improperly filed. He insisted that the appeal bond was executed by Crank, the commissioner of highways, rather than the supervisor of the Town of Partridge, which Snyder argued was required by law. He maintained that because the proper procedure was not followed, the town forfeited its right to appeal the judgment rendered by the justice of the peace regarding the penalty for obstructing the highway.

In 1874, in Illinois, James C. Morrison sued the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company after the railway's construction caused water to overflow onto his property. Prior to the railway's construction in 1869, surface water that typically accumulated near Morrison’s premises flowed naturally away from it. However, the railway's embankment and ditches obstructed this natural flow, directing surface water to run towards Morrison's land via a culvert, resulting in damage to his property. Morrison claimed damages for the overflow that occurred in 1870 and 1871. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Morrison, leading the railway company to appeal the decision, contending errors in jury instructions related to the case. The court had given all the plaintiff's requested instructions and refused those of the defendant concerning the standard for the railway’s construction practices.	Morrison argued that the railway company had wrongfully diverted surface water onto his property through its construction methods, violating his property rights. He requested damages for the harm caused by the flooding as a result of the railway’s embankments, emphasizing that the railway company had no right to obstruct the natural flow of surface water.	The railway company contended that it constructed the railway in a prudent and skillful manner and is not liable for damages as these arose from proper construction activities. They argued that damages could only be recovered if proven that the railway was built negligently or unskillfully, which Morrison failed to demonstrate. The company maintained that no law made them liable for any consequential damages resulting from the lawful construction of their railway.

John W. Israel initiated a legal case against James S. Brooks in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1860, following an incident involving malicious prosecution. The case arose after Israel accused Brooks of stealing approximately $200. He made a complaint to John Amos, a justice of the peace, who subsequently issued a warrant for Brooks’s arrest based on Israel's allegations. After some time, a justice examined the situation and discharged Brooks, which sparked Israel's lawsuit alleging he was wrongfully prosecuted. The action was viewed cautiously by the courts due to concerns about discouraging legitimate criminal prosecutions. During the trial, Israel sought to prove that Brooks had acted without malice or probable cause, claiming his good character as a defense against Brooks's accusation.	Israel claimed that Brooks initiated a malicious prosecution against him, arguing that Brooks had no probable cause for the accusations. He requested monetary damages amounting to $600, asserting that the prosecution's basis was fabricated and that Brooks's actions caused him undue harm and distress.	Brooks defended himself by arguing that there was sufficient cause for the prosecution, asserting that Israel had admitted he did not hold Brooks blameworthy for his actions. He contended that his own conduct was reasonable, given the circumstances, and requested the court to dismiss Israel's claims based on the assertion that probable cause for the prosecution was present.

The case "J. W. Dulin et al. v. Ezra M. Prince" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 28, 1888. It involved a legal dispute between J. W. Dulin and others who acted as plaintiffs and Ezra M. Prince as the defendant. The case originated from a contract whereby Prince agreed to procure a homestead right to a twenty-acre tract of land in Trego County, Kansas, for Dulin and his group. However, Dulin contended that Prince had never been capable of fulfilling this obligation as he lacked the title to the land and the right to a homestead. Evidence presented during the trial showed that both parties intended to secure government land under U.S. law for settlers. Dulin's abandonment of the contract occurred before Prince had the chance to secure the homestead right, leading to a situation where the right was rendered unavailable to Dulin. Although there was an objection raised by the plaintiffs regarding the non-compliance of Prince with the contract, the court found that the specific performance of the contract could not be granted since the plaintiffs had previously abandoned their obligations under it. The ruling finally affirmed the circuit court's decree, which directed that the contract be upheld despite the plaintiffs' claims of variance between the allegations and their proofs.	The plaintiffs, J. W. Dulin and others, claimed that they were entitled to specific performance of the contract for Prince to secure a homestead right in Kansas. They argued that Prince had failed to demonstrate his ability to procure the necessary rights and that their original agreement had not been fully honored. The plaintiffs sought judicial enforcement of the contract stipulating that Prince should procure title to the land.	Ezra M. Prince, representing himself, argued that the plaintiffs had abandoned the contract and that he had never been in a position to perform his obligations as he did not hold any title to the homestead. He contended that the failure of the Dulin party to comply with the contract terms prior to his performance made any claims for enforcement of the contract moot. Prince submitted that the plaintiffs' objections regarding variances between their claims and the evidence were too late and should have been made before the initial trial court, not at the appeal stage.

The legal case 'The American Fire Insurance Company v. Brighton Cotton Manufacturing Company' occurred in Brighton Park, Cook County, Illinois, and was decided on December 14, 1887. The plaintiff, Brighton Cotton Manufacturing Company, had an insurance policy with the defendant, American Fire Insurance Company, to cover their cotton mill, which included machinery and fixtures. The policy was issued on January 4, 1885, for a period of one year, protecting against damages or loss by fire, up to $3,000. A fire occurred on July 16, 1885, destroying the mill. Following the fire, the plaintiff sought compensation under the policy. During the trial, it was revealed that the mill was temporarily idled for repairs from July 8 to July 16 due to supply issues and repairs needed for the factory machinery. The defendant contested that this stoppage breached the policy conditions, rendering the insurance void. However, the court found that the temporary cessation was permissible under the policy's terms, and the leasing of the premises to Baker & Kelly was disclosed and approved by the insurance company.	The plaintiff's main arguments rested on the assertion that the insurance policy was valid at the time of the fire. They claimed that the temporary suspension of factory operations was necessary for repairs, which was permitted under the policy. The plaintiff sought damages for the loss incurred from the fire, amounting to $2,692.82, and maintained that there was no breach of the insurance contract.	The defendant contended that the policy became void due to violations of specific conditions, arguing the temporary factory shutdown increased the risk of insurance loss and constituted a breach of the agreement. They asserted that the factory was vacated, which contradicted the insurance terms, and that proper notification about stopping operations wasn’t provided. The defendant requested the trial judgment to be reversed based on these claims.

In April 1865, in Bloomington, Illinois, the case of **The American Express Company v. David D. Haggard** was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose when David D. Haggard, a hardware merchant, sought to recover $170.30 from the American Express Company after a package of money sent to him was not delivered. The package was sent by an agent from Clinton, DeWitt County, and was supposed to be delivered to Haggard at his store in Bloomington. The American Express Company was sued as a corporation. Upon service of the summons, their agent, Luther A. Fuller, denied knowledge of such a corporation, prompting a legal back-and-forth regarding the company's corporate status. The defense subsequently admitted to operating under the name of the American Express Company but denied corporate existence. The issue of whether the delivery occurred was central to the case; Haggard's clerk, a minor at the time, had unknowingly receipted for the package, thinking it was for castings. After the package's loss, Haggard’s father repaid the amount to him without being explicitly requested. The trial examined various procedural points, including the admissibility of witness testimony and the legal implications of receipt signing.	David D. Haggard, the plaintiff, asserted that the American Express Company failed to deliver a package containing $170.30, for which he expected compensation. He claimed to have proved to the court that the package was entrusted to the company and that the clerk had mistakenly received it under the assumption it was for a different delivery. Haggard sought to recover the lost amount while arguing that the payment made by his father to him did not extinguish his right to sue the express company.	The American Express Company, as the defendant, denied being a corporation and questioned the validity of the service of process. They filed a plea in abatement, arguing that they were merely a partnership doing business under that name. They contended that the delivery of the package was complete since a receipt was signed, thus discharging them from liability. The defense also claimed that any liability was extinguished by the payment made by Haggard's father.

The case of "John Fitzgibbon et al. v. David J. Lake et al." took place in April 1862 in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, John Fitzgibbon and his siblings, claimed the property known as lot 29 in block 4 of Fort Dearborn Addition to Chicago. They alleged that they were wrongfully ejected from their property by the defendants, David J. Lake and others, on August 1, 1860. The case was initiated as an action of ejectment and was tried without a jury in the Superior Court. The plaintiffs presented evidence, including their deceased father Patrick Fitzgibbon's will and a government patent for the property, to support their claim of ownership. The defendants, on the other hand, contested the plaintiffs' claims by presenting records of a guardian's sale executed by Edmond Fitzgibbon, the plaintiffs’ testamentary guardian. The trial court ruled in favor of the defendants, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal the decision. Their core arguments revolved around the validity of the guardian’s sale and whether proper legal procedures had been followed.	The plaintiffs argued that the guardian's sale of the property was invalid due to several alleged deficiencies: the minors (plaintiffs) were not parties in the proceedings; there were irregularities in the execution of the sale; and the application of funds from the sale was improper. They sought to have the sale declared void and to regain possession of the property that they claimed belonged to them.	The defendants contended that the guardian’s sale was valid, asserting that the court had jurisdiction over the matter and that the proper protocol was followed in the sale. They argued that the previous dismissal of the proceedings did not negate the legitimacy of the sale post-confirmation. Furthermore, they maintained that any shortcomings in the proceedings did not invalidate the transactions, and they sought to uphold the trial court’s ruling in favor of their ownership of the property.

Benjamin A. Mink filed a legal action of trover against Daniel F. Crilly and Charles H. Blair to recover the value of certain fixtures, furniture, and utensils located in a meat market previously occupied by William C. Ogden. The incident took place in 1884, when Ogden rented the meat market from the defendants. The property in question belonged to Mrs. Eliza Ogden, who purchased the fixtures with her own funds to assist her husband in his business. After Ogden's business failed in June 1885, the defendants seized the property under a distress warrant, which they later sold. Mink claimed to have bought the property from Mrs. Ogden after Ogden’s failure but was denied access to retrieve it due to the defendants locking the premises. The case revolved around the ownership of the fixtures and whether they could be subjected to Ogden's debts. The court explored the legal implications of the property being loaned to Ogden by his wife and examined the relevant statutes concerning a married woman’s property rights.	Mink argued that he had legitimately purchased the fixtures from Mrs. Ogden and that the defendants acted unlawfully by seizing the property under a distress warrant for Ogden's debts. He sought the value of the fixtures as compensation, asserting that ownership remained with Mrs. Ogden, and thus the property should not have been subject to the husband's obligations.	The defendants contended that the fixtures could be distrained for Ogden's debts, claiming that a marriage relationship alters property ownership rights such that property loaned by a wife to her husband for business purposes could be considered part of his assets. They argued that the property was rightfully seized under the distress warrant due to Ogden's failure to pay his debts.

John Corbett filed an action against Phineas L. Underwood in 1876, following a series of grain transactions in Chicago. Corbett, a resident of Jerseyville, deposited a total of $4,500 as margins with Underwood, a commission merchant operating under the firm name Underwood & Co. On May 15, 1873, Corbett authorized Underwood to purchase 50,000 bushels of corn, initially assigned to be delivered in August of that year. Subsequently, on September 1, an additional order for another 50,000 bushels for October delivery was placed. However, by mid-June and mid-September, due to a market decline and failure to maintain sufficient margin deposits, Underwood sold the corn at a loss without giving Corbett prior notice of the sale. Ultimately, Underwood provided Corbett with an account detailing a remaining balance of $157.42, which Corbett later withdrew. The case revolved around whether Underwood had a legal obligation to provide notice before selling the corn and the classification of their transactional relationship.	Corbett claimed that Underwood, as a commission merchant, failed to provide adequate notice before selling corn purchased on his behalf when the required margins were not maintained. He argued that a pledge relationship existed that necessitated a notice before any sale could occur. The plaintiff sought to recover his losses from the grain transaction and claimed that the sales were improperly executed without his knowledge.	Underwood contended that the sales were justified as the margins had fallen short, and he had adequately informed Corbett of the need for additional funds to protect the contracts. He argued that the nature of their agreement did not establish a pledge, as no corn was in his possession to secure the debt. Underwood maintained that as per the rules of the board of trade, it was permissible to sell the grain when margins were insufficient, and he requested that the court recognize his actions as lawful under their contractual obligations.

In January 1873, in Illinois, Robert C. Sallee served as the township treasurer and was succeeded by Warren M. Fales. Following the conclusion of Fales’s term, both he and Sallee met with the trustees to settle the accounts concerning funds held in the office. It was agreed upon that a specific amount was due to the trustees. In the settlement, Sallee assigned a promissory note from a third party, Carpenter, to Fales, indicating that Fales would be responsible for payment if Carpenter failed to pay the note within a specified time frame. When Carpenter did not pay the note, Fales initiated legal action against Sallee, leading to a recovery judgment in favor of Fales. However, during the judicial review, it was determined that the judgments made were flawed due to improper application of legal statutes regarding the roles and responsibilities of the parties involved. The court concluded that the debt was owed to the trustees and that any claims concerning the account should have been brought forth in their name. Therefore, the matter was reverted to the lower court.	The plaintiff, Warren M. Fales, argued that Sallee had a responsibility to pay the amount specified in the promissory note given the agreement established with the trustees. Fales contended that since Carpenter had not paid, Sallee should fulfill the obligation as per their agreement, reflecting a formal transaction regarding the financial responsibilities they shared post-tenure.	Robert C. Sallee asserted that the case against him should not stand because the evidence did not support the special claims outlined in the lawsuit. He maintained that the agreement regarding the promissory note was misrepresented and that the actual financial obligation lay with the trustees, who were not a party to the suit. Sallee argued that any potential recovery under the common counts was inappropriate since the trustees were the holders of the note due.

George A. Seaverns and others (the plaintiffs) filed a legal action against Joseph W. Tribby (the defendant) in September 1868. The case arose from a dispute regarding the sale of 77 tons and 542 pounds of broom corn, which the plaintiffs alleged was sold to the defendants at a price of $140 per ton. The transaction included a written contract, and the corn was reportedly delivered and accepted by the defendants. The plaintiffs claimed there was still a balance due after accounting for payments made to them, while the defendants contended that the full amount had been paid. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, which evaluated the instructions given to the jury during the trial. It was determined that the instructions were misleading as they assumed facts about the amount due and the price to be paid, which were in dispute. The court's evaluation also involved examining the admissibility of evidence related to weights of the delivered goods and noted issues regarding the documentation and testimony presented regarding these weights.	The plaintiffs argued that they were owed a balance for the broom corn sold under the contract despite payments already made. They sought a judgment that would confirm this amount after deducting any applicable credits for payments received, claiming to have delivered the corn per the contract's terms.	The defendants contended that they had fully paid the amount due for the broom corn. They challenged the jury instructions during the trial, arguing that they incorrectly assumed a balance was still owed and improperly directed the jury regarding evidentiary weight and the quantity of corn delivered.

The legal case "Charles L. Bonney v. Mary E. Stoughton et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 11, 1887. The case arose from a partnership between Charles H. Crowell and Edward G. Bowzer, which was dissolved on May 21, 1879, through mutual consent. After the dissolution, Bowzer believed there was a financial settlement where Crowell owed him $1,230.06. However, no formal settlement was finalized, and the partnership was deemed completely dissolved. Crowell passed away on December 18, 1881. Bowzer filed a claim against Crowell's estate in the probate court in August 1882, but this claim was rejected. After appealing to the circuit court, the ruling was upheld on November 2, 1884. On January 20, 1885, Bowzer's assignee, Charles L. Bonney, filed a bill seeking an accounting, but this was challenged by the defendants on the grounds that the statute of limitations had expired, as more than five years had passed since the cause of action accrued at the time of dissolution.	The plaintiff, Charles L. Bonney, contended that he was entitled to an accounting for partnership affairs and believed that the amount due from Crowell had been previously agreed upon. Bowzer's argument was that he acted under a legitimate belief that the partnership accounts had been settled. He sought to have the court intervene to settle the accounts and recover the money he believed was owed to him.	The defendants, represented by Mary E. Stoughton and others, argued that the plaintiff's claim should be barred by the statute of limitations, which was five years from the date the cause of action accrued upon dissolution of the partnership on May 21, 1879. They emphasized that there was no fraud or concealment preventing Bowzer from taking action sooner. The defendants asserted that the death of their debtor did not halt the statute's progression and that Bowzer's failure to act within the limitations period precluded any relief.

The case "Ely York’s Adm’rs v. Bashaby York’s Adm’r" arose in November 1865, in Hamilton County, Illinois, following the deaths of Ely York and his widow, Bashaby York, who died intestate. Ely died on June 23, 1863. Shortly thereafter, Bashaby, who was left without children or immediate family, passed away on July 3, 1863. Administrators for Ely’s estate were appointed on July 11, 1863, while Bashaby’s estate was administered by John Davis, who was appointed on July 11, 1864. Prior to her death, John Davis filed a claim for the value of specific property allowed to Bashaby under Illinois law, meant to provide for widows of intestates. The County Court initially disallowed this claim, which led to an appeal to the Circuit Court, where a verdict favored Davis, awarding him $246. The appellants contended that the estate was not liable, arguing procedural shortcomings regarding the appraisers and claiming the widow’s rights to specific property did not materialize because the estate was administered after her death without a proper allocation of property.	The plaintiff, John Davis, as administrator of Bashaby York's estate, claimed that his late wife was entitled to specific articles of property as allowed under Illinois law for widows of intestates. He argued that upon her husband's death, the lawful title to those articles passed to her, and thus, after her death, his claim to those articles or their value was legitimate. He sought a judgment affirming this value from Ely York's estate based on statutory entitlements.	The defendants, the administrators of Ely York's estate, disputed that they were liable for the claim made by Davis. They argued there had been no widow at the time administration of Ely's estate was granted, hence the appraisers had no authority to set aside specified property. They further asserted that the statutory rights of the widow did not vest until she actively claimed the property, which they believed did not occur in this case due to the widow's subsequent death and lack of proper administration prior.

The case "The Chicago & Western Indiana Railroad Company v. William J. Slee" originated in January 1881 in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, William J. Slee, owned two lots (eleven and twelve) in Wilder’s north addition. Slee purchased these lots in 1868 and later conveyed them through trust deed to secure a note for $4,500. Due to a default, the property was sold to the Union Mutual Life Insurance Company, which subsequently conveyed it to Albert J. Averill. The Chicago & Western Indiana Railroad Company entered the premises, accompanied by a deputy sheriff, and undertook actions that included tearing down fences, filling the lots with dirt, and laying railroad tracks, claiming to possess the land under Averill’s title. Slee contested the railroad's entry, asserting that they lacked authority, as a certain writ of possession did not include the described premises. The case revolved around whether the railroad had a legal right to possession and the validity of its claim against Slee's ownership rights, which had been supported by previous documentation involving the trustee and insurance company.	William J. Slee claimed that the Chicago & Western Indiana Railroad Company unlawfully trespassed on his property by entering without authorization and making significant alterations. He sought damages resulting from the rental value of the premises taken, maintaining that his legal ownership had not been lawfully transferred and that the defendant's entry and activities constituted a wrongful taking of property.	The Chicago & Western Indiana Railroad Company defended its actions under the legal doctrine of "liberum tenementum," asserting that its entry was justified based on the title held by Averill, whom they recognized as their agent. The defendant contended that legal documentation supported their right to possession, and thus the plaintiff's claims should be dismissed. They requested the jury to return a verdict in their favor, emphasizing that the plaintiff’s rights in equity did not affect the legal title in this case.

The case "Samuel Gerrish et al. v. Marshall Ayres et al." took place in the Brown Circuit Court, Illinois, and was decided in December 1841. The key individuals involved were Samuel Gerrish and others as plaintiffs, and Marshall Ayres and others as defendants. The dispute originated when the defendants erected a dam across McKie's Creek, negatively impacting the plaintiffs' mill situated upstream and destroying their ford across the creek. The plaintiffs claimed ownership of the mill and land as of May 1, 1837, while the defendants constructed the dam on June 1, 1837, and it has remained in place since July 17, 1839. The plaintiffs filed their claim during the April term of 1840 after issuing a writ on March 7, 1840. The defendants countered with a plea of not guilty and a special plea claiming that the matter had been submitted for arbitration the previous August, resulting in an award that addressed the issues between the parties.	The plaintiffs argued that their action was legitimate as it stemmed from damages sustained to their mill due to the defendants’ dam, constructed after their ownership of the mill. They contended that the arbitration agreement was only meant to cover past grievances and not future injuries arising from the continued presence of the dam. Therefore, they requested compensation for damages caused since the arbitration submission, claiming that the arbitration only resolved previous disputes and did not bar their current claims.	The defendants contended that the issues raised by the plaintiffs had already been resolved through arbitration, where an award was made directing them to lower the dam and pay the plaintiffs $10 as full satisfaction for all claims. They argued that the arbitration settled all potential disputes arising from the dam’s erection, effectively barring any subsequent lawsuits concerning the same matters, including the plaintiffs’ current claims for damages sustained after the award was rendered.

In June 1870, a legal dispute arose involving a chattel mortgage in Clinton County, Illinois. The case was initiated by Charles Feikert and Joseph Speckart as plaintiffs, with Paul Chipron acting as the defendant. The mortgage in question was executed by Theophile Detro, officially acknowledging a debt of $426 to the plaintiffs. The mortgage was acknowledged before Joseph Hanke, a police magistrate in Trenton, Clinton County. However, the defendant challenged the mortgage's validity based on the acknowledgment process, claiming it was improper since the mortgagor did not reside in Trenton at that time. The case proceeded through a justice of the peace and then appealed to the circuit court, where it was tried before a jury. The plaintiffs maintained possession of the property covered by the mortgage, which was critical to their claims. The case ultimately centered on the admissibility and validity of the chattel mortgage evidence against the defendant’s objections regarding the acknowledgment. The court upheld the circuit court's decision, which had validated the mortgage despite the challenges presented by the defendant.	The plaintiffs, Charles Feikert and Joseph Speckart, claimed a right to the property in question based on a chattel mortgage that was duly executed and acknowledged by Theophile Detro. They argued that their possession of the property should protect their interests from any claims made by the defendant, as they held the proper documentation even if there were defects in the mortgage acknowledgment process. Their legal request was for the court to affirm their right to the property based on their established claim under the mortgage.	Paul Chipron, the defendant, contended that the chattel mortgage was invalid due to an improper acknowledgment, as the mortgagor was not a resident of Trenton at the time of its acknowledgment. He argued that this defect undermined the plaintiffs’ claims, asserting that the evidence of the mortgage should not be admissible under these circumstances. The defendant sought to challenge the plaintiffs' right to hold the property and requested the court to reverse the circuit court's judgment and rule in his favor.

George T. Hopkins filed a legal action against Ethan Walter, junior, in 1850 in Illinois. The case originated when Hopkins sought to enforce a debt based on a judgment that Walter had previously confessed to before another justice of the peace. The situation escalated to a higher court after Walter appealed a ruling made at the justice level. The case was brought before the Kendall Circuit Court in November 1849, where it was heard without a jury, with Judge Spring presiding. The court was tasked with determining the validity of the earlier judgment, focusing on the authority of a justice of the peace to issue a judgment based on a party's confession of indebtedness.	Hopkins claimed that there was a valid judgment against Walter based on his confession of indebtedness, which was within the jurisdiction of the justice of the peace. He sought to affirm this judgment, arguing that a confession of debt serves as solid evidence of indebtedness and should thus be upheld.	Walter's defense revolved around challenging the validity of the judgment rendered against him. While specific arguments made by Walter are not detailed, he appealed the initial judgment, suggesting dissatisfaction with the ruling at the justice level. His request was for the court to reconsider the judgment, presumably seeking to have it overturned.

In January 1868, the case of Charles Peine v. Wendelin Weber was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a dispute over a lease agreement. Charles Peine, in partnership with August Scheineman, was engaged in a saloon business in Adams County, Illinois. The issue arose when Peine and Scheineman allegedly failed to deliver possession of a leased property to Weber, the lessor, on the agreed date of June 2, 1866. The lease allowed for liquidated damages of $500 if the premises were not vacated on time. While Peine did not personally sign the lease, it was established that he had authorized Scheineman to sign on their behalf with a full understanding of the lease's provisions. Following Scheineman's departure from the partnership, Peine continued to occupy the premises and pay rent but ultimately did not vacate as stipulated, leading Weber to sue for damages claimed under the lease. The case involved the interpretation of the lease’s terms and the legal standing of the lease in light of its execution.	Weber, the plaintiff, argued that Peine and Scheineman breached the lease by failing to deliver possession of the premises on the required date. Weber claimed that he was entitled to liquidated damages of $500 as stated in the lease, due to the non-performance of the tenant's obligations. The plaintiff emphasized that the lease was valid regardless of Peine's lack of personal signature, as it was executed for the benefit of the partnership.	Peine, the defendant, contended that the lease was not validly executed because he did not personally sign it and argued that any authority given to Scheineman was merely verbal and insufficient for a sealed instrument. He claimed that the stipulation for liquidated damages was excessive and should be viewed as a penalty rather than genuine liquidated damages. Peine sought dismissal of the claims against him based on these arguments.

In April 1867, the case of Frederick Beckman et al. v. John P. Kreamer et al. was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose on a tract of land near a small lake approximately seven miles from the Kankakee River. The plaintiffs, Frederick Beckman and others, claimed ownership of the land surrounding the lake, which was known to be rich in fish. The defendants, John P. Kreamer and others, entered the lake with boats and fishing equipment to fish, despite the plaintiffs’ objections. This unauthorized entry constituted a trespass, prompting the plaintiffs to seek legal recourse, initially winning a small award in a justice court, which was subsequently reduced to five dollars on appeal in the Circuit Court. The defendants contested the court's decision regarding the apportionment of costs incurred during the proceedings.	The plaintiffs contended that they held either a legal or equitable title to the land and the exclusive right to fish in the lake, which they claimed was on their property. They argued that the defendants’ entry onto their land to fish constituted a clear trespass. The plaintiffs sought to have the court recognize their rights and recover damages for the unauthorized actions of the defendants.	The defendants argued against the apportionment of costs ordered by the Circuit Court, claiming it was not in line with statutory requirements. They sought a revision of the cost allocation, asserting that the court's decision to impose a disproportionate burden on the defendants, given the circumstances of the case and the outcome, was erroneous.

Horace A. Hurlbut brought a case against Frederick M. Kantzler and others, including the Board of Education of the City of Chicago, seeking specific performance of a lease assignment. The case originated in Chicago, Illinois, stemming from a lease agreement dated May 12, 1876, in which the Board of Education leased property to Kantzler for nineteen years at an annual rent of $4,100. This lease included a covenant requiring consent from the board for any assignment, as well as a provision mandating Kantzler to erect a building worth at least $40,000 within a specified timeframe. Kantzler attempted to assign the lease to Crilly & Blair while also negotiating with Hurlbut for a separate assignment. Hurlbut believed he had a valid agreement with Kantzler; however, Kantzler ultimately chose to assign the lease to Crilly & Blair after refusing to proceed with Hurlbut. An injunction was sought by Hurlbut to stop this assignment, but it was eventually dismissed. Hurlbut contended that the Board accepted a surrender of the lease, allowing them to issue a new lease to Crilly & Blair, which effectively nullified his claims. The court ultimately considered several factors including legal rights, contracts, and the board’s authority before rendering a decision.	Hurlbut's main arguments were based on the premise that he had a valid contract with Kantzler for an assignment of the lease, which he believed should be enforceable, despite the requirement of the Board's consent. He sought a court order for specific performance to compel the assignment of the lease from Crilly & Blair, asserting that they were not bona fide lessees and that their actions constituted a breach of Kantzler's obligations to him. Hurlbut requested that Crilly & Blair be declared trustees for him with respect to the leasehold estate.	The defendants, including Kantzler and Crilly & Blair, contended that Hurlbut had no legal or equitable right to enforce an assignment of the lease due to the explicit requirement for the Board's consent, which had not been given.
