They argued that since the Board had awarded a new lease to Crilly & Blair after Kantzler surrendered his lease, it was impossible for the court to grant specific performance as requested. Additionally, they claimed that any rights Hurlbut might have possessed had been forfeited and that he could not compel the Board to approve the assignment.

In June 1876, the case of Emily Allmon et al. v. Thomas Pigg et al. was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Marion County, Illinois, where Emily Allmon and others challenged the will of Hiram Allmon after his death. The plaintiff argued that the will and specific conveyances made by Hiram's widow, the principal beneficiary of the will, were influenced by undue pressure and fraud. Central figures in the case included Hiram Allmon, his widow, and their son Thomas, who had a legal judgment against him. The plaintiffs contended that Thomas's influence over Hiram affected the creation of the will, which aimed to protect the estate from being used to satisfy the judgment against Thomas. The court was tasked with determining whether the will represented Hiram's true intentions, free from any coercive influence.	The plaintiffs argued that Hiram Allmon’s will was invalid due to undue influence exercised by his son Thomas, which coerced Hiram into making a will that favored his wife disproportionately. They requested the court to set aside the will and the related transactions, claiming they were products of fraud and manipulation that compromised Hiram’s free will.	The defendants contended that Hiram Allmon created the will of his own volition while in full possession of his faculties, demonstrating no signs of undue influence or coercion on the part of Thomas. They argued that the will was reasonable and reflected Hiram's genuine intentions regarding the distribution of his property, asserting that Thomas’s prior knowledge of a judgment did not compel him to alter his father’s decision.

John Baines v. Theresa Kelly is a legal case that took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the Illinois Supreme Court rendering its judgment in September 1874. The case originated from actions taken following an appeal from a justice of peace's ruling. Baines filed the appeal on May 19, 1874, the day after the May term of the circuit court began. During the appeal process, the circuit court, presided by Judge Lambert Tree, ordered an additional bond to be filed and subsequently dismissed the appeal for non-compliance with that order. The dismissal occurred before the beginning of the next court term set for June 15, 1874. Baines argued that the court had no authority to dismiss the appeal out of term and that any claims of perjury against the surety of the appeal bond should not confer jurisdiction to dismiss the appeal.	The plaintiff, John Baines, contended that the circuit court acted improperly by dismissing his appeal before the commencement of the term to which the appeal was taken. He argued that the court had no jurisdiction to require an additional bond or dismiss the case out of term, asserting that the existing legal provisions did not permit such actions. Baines sought a reversal of the dismissal of his appeal and the opportunity to have his case heard.	The defendant, Theresa Kelly, maintained that the appeal should be dismissed due to alleged perjury concerning the surety's affidavit of solvency related to the appeal bond. Kelly argued that such perjurious behavior justified a summary dismissal to protect her rights. However, the court held that the mere charge of perjury did not grant jurisdiction to dismiss the appeal if proper jurisdiction had not been established in the first place.

The case "George Harney et al. v. D. K. Laurie" took place in Franklin, Illinois, with a decision rendered on September 21, 1883. The plaintiffs, George Harney and his partners, were engaged in the corn trade and sought to have their corn shelled. They partnered with IT. S. Hannon, who owned an engine and aimed to shell corn using an old machine (corn sheller) that the appellants did not consider valuable. Hannon proposed to shell the corn for a fee of one cent per bushel and, after initial work, suggested that the plaintiffs back him financially for a new sheller, despite the plaintiffs advising him to purchase a better model. Ultimately, Hannon acquired a second-hand sheller through the defendant, D. K. Laurie, who warranted that the machine would perform satisfactorily. However, once the sheller was obtained, it failed to work properly, leading the plaintiffs to refuse payment for it. The defendant then sued for the payment, resulting in a judgment against the plaintiffs for $160, the agreed price of the defective sheller. The issue at hand was whether the plaintiffs were liable for payment given the breach of warranty and the circumstances surrounding the purchase.	The plaintiffs argued that they were not liable for the payment for the sheller because Hannon—who purchased it—was not acting as their agent but rather for his own benefit. They contended that their obligation only arose if the sheller worked satisfactorily, as outlined in the guarantee they provided to Hannon. Given the machine did not perform as warranted and was not returned, they claimed they should not be held liable for the purchase price.	The defendant, D. K. Laurie, maintained that the plaintiffs were liable for the payment because they had guaranteed the payment assuming the sheller worked satisfactorily. The defendant argued that the promise made by Hannon to return the defective machine if it failed was binding as it was a condition in their contract. Based on this, the defendant asserted that the plaintiffs had failed to fulfill their obligation by not ensuring the machine was returned, thus affirming their liability.

Joseph Evans brought a legal action against Milton Anderson in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Iroquois County, presided over by Hon. N. J. Pillsbury. The dispute revolved around a promissory note originally given by Anderson to John W. Jones, which had been assigned to Evans. The defendant, Anderson, raised a defense claiming a failure of consideration and asserted that the note was made in Indiana. He argued that according to the laws of Indiana at the time of the note's issuance, he was entitled to all defenses against the assignee that he could assert against the original payee. Evans countered this by stating that he received the note in Illinois for a valuable consideration before its maturity and pointed out that at the time of the assignment, Anderson was a resident of Illinois. The court found merit in Anderson's argument regarding the governing law of the contract being determined by Indiana law.	Evans argued that the promissory note was assigned to him in Illinois for a valuable consideration and prior to its maturity. He contended that because Anderson resided in Illinois at the time of the assignment, local laws applied and should favor his claim against the defendant.	Anderson's key defense was based on the assertion that the note was made in Indiana, and therefore, the defenses available under Indiana law should govern the case. He claimed that the law in Indiana provided him with certain defenses against the note, which he believed invalidated Evans' claim. The defendant's argument rested on the principle that the obligations of contracts are governed by the laws of the state where they are made.

In 1877, in Hyde Park, Illinois, a legal case arose involving Thomas H. Ricketts and the Village of Hyde Park regarding a special assessment for the construction of water supply pipes. The assessment was conducted under a local ordinance. Ricketts objected to several aspects of the ordinance and the assessment process. He claimed that the ordinance was void because it encompassed two distinct improvements, that it improperly mandated the assessment for work already completed, and that the hydrants used did not comply with the specified requirements. The publication of notice regarding the assessment was also contested, as it was published in a newspaper printed in Chicago rather than within the village. The court had to determine the validity of the special assessment imposed by the village based on the objections raised by Ricketts.	Ricketts asserted that the ordinance under which the special assessment was levied was void because it combined two distinct improvements for the water supply system. He argued that assessing property for work already completed exceeded the corporate authority's power and that the hydrants used were not the ones specified in the ordinance. Additionally, he contested the validity of the publication of notice for the assessment.	The Village of Hyde Park defended the ordinance by arguing that the improvements defined in the ordinance constituted a single and essential enhancement to the water supply system, necessary for maintaining water purity. The village contended that the ordinance allowing for special assessment for work already done was valid and supported by statutory provisions. Furthermore, they claimed that any discrepancies in the hydrants used were inconsequential since the alternative hydrants, while not named, were of superior quality. The defense also addressed the notice publication, insisting that it met the legal requirements.

The case "Smith v. Newland" took place during the April Term of 1865 in Illinois, specifically before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case centers around a writ of error intended to reverse a decree made in a chancery proceeding. The principal issue revolved around a deposition of a witness that had been suppressed during earlier hearings. This deposition had been included in the record but was challenged in this court as improperly entered. The discussion highlighted the complexity of chancery practice, where exceptions do not need to be formally taken as in common law. The court clarified that even when a deposition is suppressed, it remains part of the proceedings and can be reviewed by the Supreme Court to determine the propriety of the suppression order.	The plaintiff, Smith, argued that the suppression of the deposition was erroneous and sought to have the deposition included in the record to review its impact on the case. Smith contended that the deposition should be considered part of the proceedings as it stands, despite being suppressed, to allow the Supreme Court to assess the court's ruling.	The defendant, Newland, maintained that the deposition had been justly suppressed and argued that a motion to strike the deposition from the record was appropriate. Newland's stance was based on the rules of chancery practice, which do not require technical exceptions and argue that the inclusion of such evidence was erroneous in light of the suppression order.

In June 1872, the case of Elias Hibbard v. Henry Molloy was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal dispute originated from an appeal by Elias Hibbard, identified as the surviving partner of L. N. Nutz, who contested a judgment rendered in the Alton City Court. The plaintiff, Henry Molloy, sought to recover payment for a quantity of coal he claimed to have delivered to the partnership of Hibbard & Nutz during Nutz's lifetime. Following a trial, a verdict favored Molloy, resulting in a judgment against Hibbard. However, Hibbard argued that this verdict was clearly against the evidence presented at trial.	Henry Molloy's primary argument centered around the assertion that he was owed payment for coal deliveries made to the partnership of Hibbard & Nutz. He maintained that the partnership was legally recognized at the time of the transactions and sought monetary compensation for the goods provided during Nutz's lifetime, leading to the original judgment in his favor.	In response, Elias Hibbard contended that there was no valid partnership existing between himself and Nutz at the time the majority of the coal was delivered. Hibbard's defense was that the jury's verdict was unsupported by the evidence, suggesting that the claims made by Molloy lacked legitimacy. Therefore, Hibbard sought to overturn the lower court's judgment, arguing for a reversal and remand of the case.

The case titled "The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Co. v. James M. Hatch et al." took place in Chicago, Illinois, and was decided in September 1875. The incident involved a train belonging to the Chicago and Northwestern Railway that collided with a one-horse wagon containing stoves and cement, owned by the plaintiffs, James M. Hatch and others, as it crossed the railway's track. The events leading to the collision occurred at a location where the railway had established three tracks on a city street. The teamster driving the wagon, familiar with the dangerous crossing, failed to take proper precautions before attempting to cross. Although there was some evidence suggesting that the train was not running at an unsafe speed and one witness claimed to have alerted the driver to the approaching train, the driver denied receiving such a warning. The case raised issues of negligence on both sides and required the jury to determine the responsibilities and rights of the parties involved.	The plaintiffs claimed that the railway company was negligent in operating its train without adequate warnings and for running the train in a manner that led to the collision. They sought damages for the losses incurred from the accident, arguing that the railway company had an obligation to ensure safety at crossing points and that its failure to do so constituted negligence.	The defendant, Chicago and Northwestern Railway Co., argued that both the plaintiffs and the railway had equal rights to use the crossing and that the teamster was negligent for failing to exercise reasonable care before crossing the track. The railway contended that the teamster, aware of the crossing's danger, did not take necessary precautions. The defendant requested the jury to find in their favor based on the claim that the teamster's negligence was the primary cause of the accident, precluding recovery for the plaintiffs.

The case "The Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. Edward Hempstead et al." was adjudicated in September 1870 in Illinois. The central figures involved were the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company and the owners of the Illinois River elevator, specifically Edward Hempstead, among others. The dispute arose when the owners of the elevator sought a writ of mandamus to compel the railway company to deliver bulk grain consigned to their facility located in Chicago. The railway company had established a policy in 1866 that limited grain deliveries to several specific elevators, thus refusing deliveries to the Hempstead elevator despite its location on the line. The court examined the operations of various divisions of the railway and the legal obligations concerning freight delivery, particularly analyzing whether the elevator's connection to the railway constituted a duty for the company to make deliveries there.	The plaintiffs argued that the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company had a legal obligation to deliver bulk grain to their elevator, which was connected to the company's line via sidetracks. They claimed that the railway company's refusal to deliver grain constituted discriminatory practices against their facility, thereby undermining their rights as common carriers mandated by law.	The defendant contended that their policy of delivering grain exclusively to selected elevators was based on contracts established with those specific facilities, which they claimed justified their refusal to deliver to the Hempstead elevator. They also argued that delivering to the Hempstead elevator would cause substantial additional expenses and operational inefficiencies, thus claiming they were not obligated to alter their established delivery customs.

On March 31, 1861, Samuel Harper and his wife executed a warranty deed for a lot in Chicago to John L. Hancock, with a stated consideration of $600. However, on April 11, 1863, Hancock sold the lot to a third party, Able, for $2,000. Harper filed a complaint on October 24, 1874, claiming that the warranty deed was intended as a mortgage for a loan of $588.23 made by Hancock to Harper, which was supposed to be repaid within a year. Harper sought an accounting for the proceeds from the sale of the lot to Able, asserting he was entitled to the excess over the alleged mortgage debt. Throughout the proceedings, evidence was presented regarding Harper's intoxication during the signing, his inability to pay outstanding notes secured by a trust deed on the property, and his knowledge of the deed's nature over time. Harper contended that the deed was a mortgage, while the court noted that such claims must be backed by clear evidence, which was lacking. The case hinged on whether Harper's claims were timely, as too much time had passed since the sale and apparent knowledge of Hancock's actions.	Harper argued that the warranty deed executed to Hancock was not a true conveyance but a mortgage meant to secure a loan of $588.23. He requested an accounting for the sale of the lot, asserting he was entitled to the difference between the sale price of $2,000 and the loan amount. Harper emphasized that he was intoxicated during the transaction and believed he was granting a mortgage rather than selling the property.	Hancock's arguments focused on the nature of the transaction, claiming it was an absolute sale rather than a mortgage. He contended that Harper had not made any payments or expressed intentions to redeem the property for over a decade, indicating the absence of a mortgage agreement. Hancock also raised the defense of the statute of limitations, asserting that Harper's claim was barred by the five-year limit for actions concerning money recovery, which had long lapsed.

In the 1850s, in Chicago, Illinois, Betty M. Clark, the plaintiff, was engaged in a legal dispute with Buckner S. Morris and others over a property deed. The case arose from a trust deed executed by her brother, Lewis W. Clark, which transferred the property to a trustee, I. H. Burch, to settle debts owed to creditors. Betty claimed that she held an unrecorded deed for the property, which was purportedly given to her by her brother before he assigned his interests to the trustee. The family history revealed that Lewis supported their parents and Betty, and it was claimed that Betty had been in possession of the property between November 1845 and March 1850. However, upon a serious quarrel, she was required to leave, and her claim to the property surfaced only after her departure. The court found the record cumbersome with numerous testimonies, most of which were biased as they came from family members. Ultimately, Betty’s claim was challenged because of lack of sufficient evidence demonstrating her legal possession and ownership of the property, as well as the overwhelming debt and financial circumstances faced by Lewis at the time of the deed's execution.	Betty M. Clark argued that she was the rightful owner of the property based on an unrecorded deed from her brother, Lewis W. Clark. She contended that her possession of the property at the time the trust deed was executed should have given notice to the trustee and other parties of her claim. She asserted that her prior residence on the property and contributions to its upkeep constituted sufficient grounds for her claim against the defendants, who had benefitted from the property following Lewis's financial difficulties and subsequent death.	The defendants, led by Buckner S. Morris, argued that they were unaware of Betty's alleged ownership or possession of the property. They contended that the claim was based on an unrecorded deed, and relevant parties had no duty to inquire about her ownership interests. They maintained that possession presented by Betty was not adverse, exclusive, or sufficient to put anyone on notice regarding her claims. Morris emphasized that he purchased the property to protect his interests in debts owed by Lewis and claimed that Betty's failure to disclose her interest in the property was detrimental to her case.

Jeptha N. Jackson v. Mary A. Crenek took place in Whiteside County, Illinois, with the court's decision filed on July 1, 1889. The case involved the plaintiff, Mary A. Crenek, who was employed by the defendant, Jeptha N. Jackson, as a domestic worker, commonly referred to as a "hired girl." Crenek was hired for a term of eight months at a wage of $3 per week and worked from March 1 until early July. A dispute arose when Jackson requested that Crenek refrain from allowing her suitor to visit late at night, as it disturbed his sick wife. Following a heated argument on a Sunday morning, in which both parties exchanged sharp words, Crenek claimed that Jackson ordered her to leave. She subsequently quit her job and sought recovery of her wages, filing a lawsuit when Jackson refused to pay her for the four months she had worked. The case had previously undergone multiple trials with varying outcomes.	Mary A. Crenek claimed that she was entitled to wages for her work as a domestic servant for four months at the agreed rate of $3 per week. She argued that the termination of her employment was not voluntary, as she contended that she was effectively ordered to leave by Jeptha N. Jackson during their dispute. Crenek sought compensation for the services she had rendered and requested that the court uphold her claim for unpaid wages.	Jeptha N. Jackson contested Crenek's claims, maintaining that she willingly abandoned her employment due to personal disagreements rather than any actionable dismissal on his part. Jackson argued that Crenek had left her position on her own accord and that he was not liable to pay her for the remaining term of her contract. He requested that the court dismiss Crenek's claims for unpaid wages based on her voluntary departure from the job.

On September 1869, the case of Jesse C. Boyd v. George Merriell was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. It stemmed from an action of assumpsit, wherein the plaintiff, Jesse C. Boyd, sought to recover the value of services rendered while examining silver mines in the Colorado Territory. Boyd had been employed by a group that included George Merriell to perform these services, which included traveling to Colorado and incurring expenses. Merriell was the sole defendant present in the court as the other defendants failed to appear, resulting in a default judgment against them. Boyd's declaration included common counts for work and labor as well as money paid and expenses incurred. Merriell contested his liability, claiming he was not jointly liable with the other defendants. The trial took place without a jury, and after examining testimonies, including that of James Barman, who confirmed Boyd’s employment, the court found in favor of Boyd.	The plaintiff, Jesse C. Boyd, claimed that he provided valuable services related to the examination of silver mines in Colorado, which were requested by Merriell and the other members of the association. Boyd sought compensation for the work done, specifically the amount agreed upon at the association meeting—$50 per week plus expenses. He asserted that he met the burden of proof demonstrating his employment and the value of the services rendered.	George Merriell, the defendant, filed a general issue plea and claimed a lack of joint liability with the other defendants. He argued that his co-defendant, James Barman, was improperly included, asserting that Barman's wife should have also been a defendant and that he had signed her name without authority. Merriell contended that since Barman was not an official member of the association and thus could not bind him, he should not be held liable for Boyd's claims.

In 1851, a legal case known as "Valentine Owens et al. v. The People" unfolded in Illinois, specifically in the Massac Circuit Court, with proceedings later taken to the Marion Circuit Court. The plaintiffs, Valentine Owens and Thomas Hobbs (a man of color), were involved in a legal action concerning a bond executed to the State of Illinois. The bond was conditioned on Hobbs's behavior and stipulating that he would not become a charge on the county. There were claims that Hobbs was brought into the state as a slave without the necessary documentation of freedom. The defendants, led by the People and representing Massac County, contended that the bond was void because Hobbs failed to present a certificate of freedom as mandated by state law prior to signing the bond. The issue raised from the action began with Hobbs needing to prove his freedom and produce appropriate documentation before being allowed to reside in Illinois. The case focused on the legality of the bond considering the statutes governing the residence of black and mulatto individuals in Illinois during that period.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants failed to uphold the conditions of the bond, resulting in the county incurring expenses for Hobbs's maintenance. They emphasized that the bond, executed at the time of Hobbs's entry into the state, was valid and should be enforced, seeking reimbursement for the costs incurred by Massac County due to Hobbs's support needs after the bond's execution.	The defendants presented several key arguments, asserting that the bond was void since Hobbs had not provided the legally required certificate of freedom and that he was, in fact, a slave at the time the bond was executed. They claimed the bond did not meet the legal requirements set forth by the statute concerning the residence of negroes and mulattoes. Furthermore, one defense posited that the law under which the bond was taken was unconstitutional, rendering it invalid.

On November 27, 1885, the Illinois Appellate Court addressed the case of Truman S. Crissey v. John Alsop. The case arose in Illinois and involved legal disputes between the two parties. The case was brought forth in a time when courts were particularly hesitant to disturb the verdicts of juries, especially in cases with smaller amounts of money at stake. The trial's key individuals included the plaintiff Truman S. Crissey and the defendant John Alsop, along with their respective legal representatives, Mr. J. H. Gwin for the appellant (Crissey) and Messrs. Wood Bros. for the appellee (Alsop). The core issue in dispute hinged on the validity of the original judgment, specifically whether it contradicted the evidence presented during the trial. This reluctance to interfere with jury decisions highlighted the court's inclination to acknowledge the jury's role in the justice system, even when substantial interests were at stake.	Truman S. Crissey, the plaintiff, argued that the judgment made in his case was not supported by sufficient evidence, which justified an appeal. He sought to have the previous ruling overturned to rectify what he believed was an erroneous decision that failed to account adequately for the evidence presented during the trial. Crissey's legal appeal hinged on demonstrating the appropriateness of revisiting the jury's verdict in light of the evidence supplied.	John Alsop, the defendant, contended that the original jury's verdict should stand, arguing that it was consistent with the evidence presented during the trial. His legal team urged the appellate court to respect the jury's decision and uphold the judgment, emphasizing that the case's circumstances did not merit a reversal and uncovering the judicial reluctance to disturb established verdicts, particularly in cases where both parties faced potential loss.

Alfred Daniels initiated an action of ejectment against Peter Burso in the Kankakee Circuit Court, Illinois, around April 1866. The case revolved around the possession of lot eight in block nine of Kankakee city. Daniels claimed ownership based on a sheriff's deed acquired from a tax sale for unpaid taxes from 1858, with the deed recorded on October 30, 1861. In the trial, Burso provided a receipt from the tax collector indicating that taxes for the property had been paid before the sale, which Daniels contested. The jury found in favor of Burso on two occasions, leading to a judgment against Daniels for costs. Daniels subsequently appealed, marking a significant legal confrontation regarding property rights based on tax deeds and the validity of evidence presented in the case.	Alfred Daniels argued that his possession of the property was lawful based on the sheriff’s deed from the tax sale. He contended that this deed served as prima facie evidence of ownership, claiming no taxes had been paid before the sale. Daniels requested the court to recognize his ownership and overturn the verdict that ruled against him, citing various errors in admitting evidence and jury instructions that he believed misrepresented the law.	Peter Burso countered Daniels's claims by offering evidence that the taxes for the property had been paid prior to the sale, thus challenging the validity of the sheriff's deed. Burso argued that the receipt provided was sufficient evidence to imply that the property in question had been redeemed from tax obligations. He contested the admissibility of Daniels’s evidence and maintained that the burden of proof was on Daniels to establish ownership, requesting the court to affirm the jury's verdict in his favor.

The case of "Jacob Frye et al. v. Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Co." arose from events dated June 13, 1872, in Illinois, specifically at the Union Stock Yard of Chicago. The plaintiffs, Jacob Frye and others, alleged that the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company wrongfully brought eighty head of Texas cattle and sixty head of Cherokee cattle into Illinois. The plaintiffs purchased these cattle and later placed them on Frye's farm in Peoria. It was claimed that these cattle transferred a fatal disease to the plaintiffs’ native cattle, resulting in their deaths. The dispute revolved around a law enacted on April 16, 1869, which prohibited the importation of Texas and Cherokee cattle into Illinois outside specific dates and without proper acclimatization. The case included five counts against the defendants, asserting violations of this statute. The defendants responded to the claims by providing a demurrer, leading to a judgment in their favor in the Superior Court of Cook County, which prompted the plaintiffs to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs contended that they incurred damages due to the defendants' unlawful introduction of Texas and Cherokee cattle into Illinois. They argued that the cattle were brought into the state contrary to the specific operating regulations and that they were misled into believing these cattle were legally introduced. They sought damages for the loss of their native cattle caused by a disease contracted from the improperly imported cattle.	The defendants maintained that the plaintiffs had no grounds for their claims, asserting that the plaintiffs had violated the same law they were trying to invoke by purchasing and owning cattle that had not been brought into the state during the legal timeframe established. The defendants argued that the law did not support the plaintiffs’ cause of action since their possession of the cattle was unlawful, making them co-transgressors. They urged the court to affirm the lower court's demurrer ruling.

William Mehrle v. Patrick Dunne et al. is a legal case from September 1874, adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, where William Mehrle, the owner of a property, was involved in a construction project contracted to George L. Cross and William B. Champion. The original contractors were hired to perform all mason work and plastering on a brick building, as per their contract dated August 12, 1872. However, they failed to complete the work on time, leaving it unfinished by the deadline of November 1, 1872. In the interim, sub-contractors Patrick Dunne and John F. Scanlan filed a petition seeking to enforce a mechanic’s lien for $586.11, which represented the unpaid materials they supplied to the original contractors for use on Mehrle's property. Upon notification of the unpaid amount, Mehrle contested the lien due to unresolved payments and claims from other lien holders not included in the petition. The case hinged on whether Mehrle was liable for any amount under the contract and the requirement to name all entitled lien holders.	The plaintiffs, Patrick Dunne and John F. Scanlan, claimed a mechanic’s lien against Mehrle for $586.11, reflecting the cost of materials supplied for the construction project. They requested enforcement of their lien, arguing that they were entitled to payment for the materials provided, which were vital for the building's construction, as per the statute governing mechanic’s liens in Illinois. They contended that timely notice had been given regarding the unpaid materials even after the contractors defaulted on completing the work.	William Mehrle, the defendant, argued that the plaintiffs failed to frame their petition correctly under the relevant statute, particularly noting that the original contractors did not fulfill their obligations, which diminished his liability. He maintained that he should only be liable for the work and materials reasonably worth according to the original contract price after accounting for any payments already made and the damages incurred due to the contractors' failure to complete the project. Furthermore, he highlighted that other lien holders were not included in the proceedings, which was a procedural error that affected the case's viability.

The legal case 'Hinckley v. West' was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1847. The case originated from an action of debt filed in the St. Clair Circuit Court by Benjamin J. West (the appellee) against Timothy Hinckley and Sargent (the appellants). The debt stemmed from a writing obligatory executed on June 3, 1839, wherein the appellants and A. W. Snyder (now deceased) agreed to indemnify West against any liabilities related to the firm T. Hinckley & Co. The complaint alleged breaches of this agreement due to a prior judgment obtained by Henry West against Hinckley and another individual, which involved debts arising from the time the writing obligatory was made. Hinckley and Sargent contested the suit, claiming various defenses including non est factum (not my deed) and payment. The matter was brought to a jury, which assessed damages of $154 in favor of the plaintiff. The court ultimately ruled in favor of West, demanding that the appellants pay the stipulated penalty unless they cleared the jury's verdict. Subsequent motions for a new trial were denied, leading to an appeal by the appellants based on arguments about the validity of certain legal pleas.	The plaintiff, Benjamin J. West, claimed that the defendants had breached a contractual obligation to indemnify him for debts incurred by the partnership of T. Hinckley & Co. He asserted that he had paid a judgment concerning those debts, amounting to $154 in damages, and sought recovery of the total penalty of $6000 as stated in the writing obligatory.	The defendants, Hinckley and Sargent, argued that the court erred in accepting West's claims, contesting the validity of the declaration and the alleged breaches. They presented defenses including the non-existence of debts that would trigger the indemnity agreement and claimed that they were owed a set-off of $1000 based on amounts West had collected from the firm, which they argued should offset his claims. They maintained that the jury's verdict should have included a finding of the debt amount, asserting procedural errors in how the court handled their defenses.

In the case of Samuel McCarty v. The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Co., filed in 1889, the dispute arose in the City of Aurora, Illinois. The plaintiff, Samuel McCarty, owned a hotel known as the Tremont House, situated at the intersection of La Salle and Main streets. The railroad company extended its tracks and switches in front of McCarty's hotel between 1883 and 1889, which he claimed damaged his property. He alleged that the addition of the double track, moving of one of the tracks, and related installations had harmed his hotel's market and rental value, as well as impeded access to the property. The case involved various testimonies regarding the impact of these changes on the property value, with conflicting assessments from witnesses regarding the extent of damages. Ultimately, after deliberation, a jury found in favor of the defendant, stating that there was insufficient evidence to support McCarty's claim of damages.	McCarty's primary arguments centered around the assertion that the installation of the railroad's double track and associated structures caused significant damage to his hotel property. He claimed that the construction diminished the rental value of his hotel, disrupted access, and introduced unsightly features like a flag station. McCarty requested compensation for the damages he believed resulted from these changes, alleging that the railroad's actions affected the market value of his property.	The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad argued that McCarty did not present sufficient evidence to prove that he suffered damages due to their actions. They contended that the installation of the double track may have even benefited McCarty's property, as it resulted in increased rental income and overall property values in the area. The defense maintained that the jury was properly instructed on the damages and that the verdict of one cent was justified based on the evidence presented.

The case "Charles A. Helmle et al. v. Mary Queenan et al." was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 4, 1885. The litigation arose from the Springfield Savings Bank, which was incorporated in 1867 with a capital of $100,000. The bank operated successfully until it suspended payments on December 17, 1877, leading to its insolvency. By April 1879, the bank made a general assignment of its assets under the statute. Mary Queenan and Theodore Merger, both depositors, filed a suit against the bank’s stockholders in January 1880 to recover the amounts owed to them, as well as to ascertain the stock holdings of the defendants. They charged that the stockholders were liable for losses to depositors under a specific amendment to the bank’s charter. Several other depositors intervened, and the case was referred to a master to identify stockholders and claims. After extensive proceedings, the court found that there were significant losses and decreed that certain stockholders were liable for the debts incurred prior to the bank’s suspension.	The plaintiffs, Mary Queenan and Theodore Merger, contended that the stockholders of the Springfield Savings Bank were liable for the amounts they had deposited, totaling $5,000 (with Queenan losing $4,000 and Merger losing $1,000). They sought to determine the defendants' respective stockholdings and the amounts due to them and other creditors. The plaintiffs argued that since they were depositors, the stockholders’ liabilities were primary and absolute according to the bank’s charter, asserting that the stockholders should be held accountable for the full amount due at the time of the bank's suspension.	The defendants argued against the characterization of their liabilities as primary, contending that "loss" should be understood to involve the determination of what could still be recovered from the bank's remaining assets. They maintained that the stockholders’ liabilities were conditional upon the exhaustion of the bank's assets and alleged that the plaintiffs had not shown sufficient diligence in their attempts to recover debts owed from those assets.

The legal case "The People, on the relation of Henry Warren Loomis and Selden M. Bronson, v. Ira O. Wilkinson, Judge of the Sixth Circuit" took place in June 1852 in Illinois. It involved Henry Warren Loomis and Selden M. Bronson as the petitioners seeking a remedy against Judge Ira O. Wilkinson of the Sixth Circuit Court. The case arose when the petitioners had obtained a writ of capias ad respondendum against Henry W. Sims, leading to his arrest by the sheriff. At Sims' request, he was brought before the county judge, who held an ex parte hearing and discharged Sims without notifying the plaintiffs. This action was taken under the assumption of acting in compliance with the insolvent laws, which the judge had exceeded, as he could only proceed with such cases while sitting in an official court capacity. The petitioners later filed a motion requesting the issuance of a writ of certiorari to review the county judge's actions, but this was denied by Judge Wilkinson initially, citing a lack of jurisdiction for issuing such a writ. The matter was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for decision.	The plaintiffs, Loomis and Bronson, contended that the county judge exceeded his jurisdiction by discharging Sims without providing notice to them, thus violating their right to contest the insolvency claim. They argued that formal proceedings were necessary for the discharge, which were not adhered to in this case. The plaintiffs sought a peremptory writ of mandamus to compel the county court to properly adjudicate the discharge in accordance with jurisprudential requirements.	Judge Wilkinson, the defendant, argued that the circuit court did not have the jurisdiction to issue the writ of certiorari. He initially denied the motion for the writ, claiming that the petitioners had not followed the necessary legal protocols. Furthermore, Wilkinson acknowledged the submission of the case to the Supreme Court for advice, interpreting it as a potential consent for the issuance of the writ if the Supreme Court concluded that the circuit court held the authority to do so.

Lansing W. Wells (the plaintiff) and Patrick Hogan (the defendant) were involved in a legal dispute that took place in the town of Galena, Illinois, in December 1830. The case originated as an action for forcible detainer, initiated by Hogan, who claimed ownership of a house and lot occupied by Wells. Hogan alleged that Wells refused to vacate the premises despite receiving written notice to do so. The initial complaint was brought before two justices of the peace in Jo Daviess County, where Hogan's claim was affirmed. An appeal was made to the circuit court, where a verdict was again found against Wells for being "guilty of a forcible detainer." Following this decision, the circuit court granted Wells time to file a bill of exceptions and issued a ruling that Wells must post a bond of seven hundred dollars within fifteen days to avoid eviction from the property. Wells contested the legality of the original complaint, arguing that it failed to satisfy jurisdictional requirements as it did not adequately establish the landlord-tenant relationship or proper grounds for a forcible detainer action.	Wells argued that the complaint filed against him was insufficient to establish jurisdiction for the justices of the peace. He claimed that the necessary elements to prove a forcible detainer were absent in Hogan's complaint, specifically the requirement to show that Wells held over the premises after the expiration of a lease under a landlord-tenant relationship, which Hogan failed to demonstrate.	Hogan contended that the proceedings were valid and that there was no requirement for a specific form of judgment from the circuit court. He claimed that the order to issue a writ of restitution unless Wells paid the bond was sufficient grounds for the court's action. Hogan argued that the justices had the jurisdiction to hear the case based on his original complaint.

In the case of Henry W. Leman v. Edwin Sherman et al., decided on February 23, 1886, the dispute arose from the estate of Francis C. Sherman, who died in Chicago on November 7, 1870. He left behind a will that entrusted the management of his property, including the Sherman House, to a trustee, Joshua L. Marsh. The will specified that in case of the trustee's death or inability to act, a new trustee would be appointed by the Cook County Court. Following Marsh's resignation in 1875, George Taylor was appointed as trustee by the county court and continued until his death in 1881. After Taylor's death, Martha S. Marsh petitioned the county court to appoint Henry W. Leman as the new trustee, which was done without any conveyance from Marsh to Taylor. Edwin Sherman, one of the beneficiaries and an infant at the time of the proceedings, brought a suit in the Cook County Circuit Court challenging the validity of the county court's power to appoint a new trustee due to it lacking chancery jurisdiction.	The plaintiff, Edwin Sherman, asserted that the county court did not have the legal authority to appoint a new trustee as the will stipulated, which required the court to have jurisdiction over such matters. He sought a declaration from the court about the invalidity of the previous appointment, requested the removal of Leman as trustee, and requested the appointment of a new trustee who would act in accordance with the provisions outlined in Sherman’s will.	The defendant, Henry W. Leman, argued that he was validly appointed as trustee by the county court according to the provisions of the will. He contended that the appointment was carried out legally and that as trustee, he had been fulfilling his duties appropriately. Leman also requested the court to affirm his status and dismiss the challenges brought by Edwin Sherman.

In September 1873, in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Mary E. Rounds and Edward Kehoe et al. regarding a piano. The action in question was initiated by Rounds to recover possession of the piano through a replevin. Unfortunately, before the case could be tried, a fire in October 1871 destroyed the entire court record. On January 11, 1873, Rounds was granted permission to submit a copy of the original declaration, which included a count in trover for the piano's conversion. Rounds filed an affidavit alleging ownership and the requirements for replevin, but the affidavit appeared not to have been properly sworn before an official. A new writ of replevin was subsequently issued, which neither defendant contested, resulting in a default judgment that favored Rounds. The court later assessed damages as the property was reportedly not recovered by the officer. Discrepancies arose regarding the legitimacy of the affidavit in replevin and whether the property was retrievable, which played a crucial part in the court's considerations.	Mary E. Rounds, as the plaintiff, claimed ownership of the piano and sought its return through replevin. She argued that the original court records were destroyed, which justified her filing a substantial copy of the declaration and an affidavit to reinstate her claims. Rounds requested a judgment for the value of the piano under the count in trover due to the officer's inability to recover the property.	The defendants challenged the validity of the process because the affidavit in replevin was not properly sworn to, questioning the jurisdiction of the court to enter judgment. They argued that there was no sufficient basis to assess damages since the court did not have evidence of the officer's actual return regarding the retrieval of the piano. The defendants sought to have the default judgment reversed due to procedural errors, including inadequate restoration of the record following the fire.

The case of McCumber v. Gilman dates back to August 4, 1842, when Calvin McCumber purchased a lot in Belvidere, Illinois, with a bond for conveyance and subsequently secured a loan from William H. Gilman, involving a mortgage on the property. After McCumber's death in 1845, his heirs inherited the property, which was burdened with debts. Gilman pursued a foreclosure, obtaining a judgment in 1846, and subsequently purchased the property at a sheriff's sale following the redemption period. By 1849, Gilman made significant improvements to the property, replacing a wooden building with a new one and undertaking various repairs. The case arose from disputes regarding the appropriateness and reimbursement for these improvements, particularly considering the financial situation of McCumber’s heirs, who had limited means to redeem the estate. The Illinois Supreme Court ultimately had to decide on the legitimacy of Gilman's claims for reimbursement based on the improvements made while he was in possession of the estate.	The plaintiffs, heirs of Calvin McCumber, argued that any financial burden from improvements made by Gilman should not be imposed on them. They claimed that the expenses for enhancements like the new building were excessive and unjust, given their precarious financial condition after inheriting only a mortgaged property with outstanding debts. They sought relief from having to pay for these improvements when they were not involved in the decision-making process regarding the enhancements.	William H. Gilman maintained that he rightfully made improvements on the property while in possession, believing he had a valid title after acquiring it via foreclosure. He argued that the improvements were necessary to prevent the property from falling into disrepair and that he should be reimbursed for these enhancements upon allowing the heirs to redeem the property from the mortgage. Gilman contended that the enhancements should be seen as a way to increase the overall value of the estate, regardless of the heirs' ability to pay.

In 1872, in Chicago, Illinois, the case of F. Kranert v. Leopold Simon et al. arose from a dispute over goods purchased by Buttner from the plaintiffs, Kranert and another party. Buttner made fraudulent claims about his financial stability, misrepresenting his assets and liabilities, which led the plaintiffs to sell him goods trusting his statements. Kranert, who claimed to have taken a chattel mortgage on the goods to secure debts owed to him by Buttner, was subsequently implicated in the fraudulent transaction. The plaintiffs filed an action of replevin to reclaim the goods, arguing that no title had passed to Buttner due to his fraudulent representations and that Kranert had participated in the fraud. The case also involved discussions around the merchant practices in Chicago, particularly the risks involved in extending credit based on a buyer's self-reported financial status. Kranert's defense was based on his claim as a bona fide creditor unaware of the fraud at the time of taking the mortgage. The case was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs argued that Buttner purchased the goods based on fraudulent representations about his financial situation. They claimed that since Kranert participated in the fraud or had knowledge of it, he could not maintain his status as an innocent purchaser. They sought recovery of the goods and damages for their conversion based on the fraudulent actions.	Kranert contended that he acquired the chattel mortgage in good faith and without knowledge of any fraud committed by Buttner. He argued that as a bona fide creditor, he was entitled to the goods and that the plaintiffs could not recover them from him after he took the mortgage, as he was an innocent purchaser protected under the law.

In 1883, in Gibson County, Indiana, Hiram Knowles and Riley Knowles, brothers, became embroiled in a legal dispute following the death of their father, Marvel Knowles. Marvel had debts owed by Riley amounting to $2716, secured by promissory notes and a mortgage on Riley's land. In April 1883, Marvel surrendered these notes and executed a release of the mortgage after Riley relinquished his claim to his father's estate. Following Marvel's death and the probate of his will, which equally divided his estate among his three sons, Riley claimed part of the estate despite his earlier relinquishment. The dispute escalated when negotiation attempts to settle the estate's distribution led Riley to execute two promissory notes worth $300 each to Hiram. Hiram sued Riley to recover the amount of these notes, leading to this case being heard before the Illinois Supreme Court after a lower court judgment was appealed.	Hiram Knowles, the plaintiff, claims that he is owed the amount specified in two promissory notes executed by his brother Riley Knowles. Hiram argues that the notes were executed in a valid transaction and requests the court to enforce the payment, seeking to recover the total of $669.70 plus costs incurred due to the legal proceedings.	Riley Knowles, the defendant, contends that the promissory notes lack consideration and were executed based on fraudulent misrepresentation by Hiram's attorneys regarding his claimed obligations to the estate. Riley argues he was misled into believing he owed the estate money and requests the court to dismiss Hiram's claim, asserting that no valid debt exists.

The case of Smith S. Ventres et al. v. Junius B. Cobb et al. revolves around a dispute regarding the sale of two tracts of land located in Englewood, Illinois, stemming from an execution of a trust deed by D. H. Pike to secure a debt of $4,000 owed to creditor Wenham. The alleged events took place leading to the sale of the properties on February 25, 1879. Ventres and his co-plaintiff Haskell purchased the land from Pike and assumed responsibility for the remaining debt which was partially paid. On the eve of the scheduled sale, Ventres allegedly agreed with Wenham to buy one of the blocks to fully settle the lien, contingent upon receiving a certified check. However, upon Ventres' return with the check shortly thereafter, it was reported that both blocks had already been sold by Cobb, the trustee, under questionable circumstances. Ventres claimed that the sales occurred within an unreasonable timeframe and without due consideration of his prior agreement to keep the sale open. This led to accusations of misconduct and unfairness against Cobb, who was expected to act in the best interests of all parties involved. Following lower court proceedings, the bill brought by Ventres was dismissed, prompting them to appeal.	The plaintiffs, Ventres and Haskell, argued that the trustee, Cobb, acted unlawfully and did not honor the agreement to postpone the sale while Ventres secured financing. They claimed the sales were executed quickly and at unfair prices, oppressing their rights. They sought to nullify the sales, asserting that they had validly tendered payment sufficient to cover the debt and costs before the sales were finalized.	The defendants, led by Cobb, maintained that the sales were conducted according to established procedures and that Ventres did not fulfill his obligation to procure the certified check within an acceptable timeframe. They contended that the terms of the sale were legitimate and that Cobb, as trustee, followed the obligations required of him without malfeasance. They argued the sales should stand as they were conducted under the authority granted to Cobb.

In the case of **Reynolds v. Henderson**, which took place in Illinois during the 1840s, the conflict arose between Ivey Reynolds, serving as the administrator for William McFatridge, who had died insolvent, and John M. Henderson, the administrator of John Henderson, who had previously obtained a judgment against McFatridge. The underlying issue stems from a judgment that Henderson won against McFatridge in 1830 for $624.64, which was followed by several attempts to execute the judgment. However, this execution was blocked by an injunction filed by McFatridge in 1831, which lasted until 1840. John Henderson died in 1839, and after McFatridge also died in 1840 without settling the debt, a scire facias was filed by Henderson's administrator to enforce the judgment against McFatridge's heirs and estate. Legal proceedings were carried on, and a demurrer was filed by McFatridge's heirs but was eventually overruled by the court. The case examined the legitimacy and enforceability of the scire facias process in relation to an insolvent estate and the continuation of judgment liens after the debtor’s death.	The plaintiff, John M. Henderson (administrator for John Henderson), contended that he was entitled to enforce the previously obtained judgment against the lands owned by William McFatridge at the time of his death. He argued that the lien created by the judgment continued to exist after McFatridge's death. Henderson sought execution of the judgment against McFatridge's real property, claiming that the process was valid despite the estate being insolvent and that both the administrator and the heirs were appropriate defendants in the scire facias action.	The defendants, led by Ivey Reynolds, raised several defenses against Henderson's claim. They argued that a scire facias could not proceed against McFatridge's heirs until the administrator had been notified with a nihil return. They maintained that given McFatridge's insolvency, it was only the administrator who had the right to manage and sell the estate's assets for debt payment, and that execution against the heirs would improperly bypass the administrator's control. They also claimed that the lien of the judgment did not authorize the sale of McFatridge's land after his death, especially since an administrator existed to handle the estate.

On April 17, 1877, George Hamilton and James C. Hamilton entered into a contract with William Scully for the sale of 4141 acres of land in Sangamon County, Illinois, for a total price of $215,297.40. The payment was structured in multiple installments, with significant amounts due upon the execution of the contract and at the delivery of the warranty deed, while the remaining balance was to be secured by Scully's note and mortgage. The contract allowed either party the right to conduct a survey of the land to determine the exact acreage. If the survey showed more acres than initially stated, Scully would pay the difference; if it showed fewer acres, the amount would be deducted from the purchase money. Despite fulfilling his payment obligations by April 1, 1878, Scully did not conduct a survey until January 1884. The survey revealed an excess of approximately 68 acres, prompting Hamilton to file a lawsuit on February 16, 1885, to recover the value of these acres, claiming Scully owed him money for the excess land.	The plaintiff, George Hamilton, contended that Scully owed him for the excess acreage identified in a survey performed nearly seven years after the sale was completed. He requested payment for the value of the excess land discovered, arguing that the contract stipulated Scully was responsible for such costs if the survey revealed more acres than originally agreed.	William Scully, the defendant, argued that the survey conducted by Hamilton was invalid due to its late timing, occurring after he had already fulfilled all his payment obligations by March 1, 1878. Scully claimed that the contract included no specific timeframe for conducting the survey, but asserted that it should have been completed within a reasonable time, which Hamilton failed to do. Thus, he maintained he had no obligation to pay for any purported excess land.

On December 11, 1886, the Illinois Appellate Court presided over the case of William Dodge v. John C. Yates. The case took place in Peoria County, Illinois, involving William Dodge, who was the guardian of minor heirs Jennie and Ida Watrous. On July 22, 1885, Dodge reported having $1,941.41 belonging to his wards and tendered his resignation as their guardian, which was accepted by the court. Subsequently, John C. Yates was appointed as the new guardian. On August 7, 1885, Yates visited Dodge's office, claiming that he had filed the necessary bond and was officially qualified as guardian. He presented a receipt signed as “succeeding guardian” to Dodge, who then paid him the settlement based on the assumption that Yates was indeed the lawful guardian. However, Yates never filed a guardian’s bond nor qualified for the post actually and later absconded to Canada. Dodge later initiated a lawsuit in November 1885, asserting Yates had fraudulently induced him into paying over $1,923.84 under false pretenses about his status as guardian. The issue was whether Yates' representation was fraudulent and whether Dodge had grounds for an attachment under the relevant Attachment Act.	William Dodge, the plaintiff, contended that John C. Yates misrepresented himself as the duly appointed guardian of Jennie and Ida Watrous, which led him to wrongfully pay Yates the sum of $1,923.84. Dodge argued that if he had not relied on Yates’ fraudulent claims, he would not have made the payment. He sought recovery of the amount wrongly paid, asserting that the transaction was tainted by fraud and therefore should be rendered invalid under the law.	John C. Yates, the defendant, denied the accusations of fraud. He contended that he did follow the necessary procedures to become the guardian and claimed that Dodge should have verified Yates' claims independently before making the payment. Yates argued that there was no substantial basis for the claim of fraud since Dodge received documentation that should have assured him of Yates' status. Therefore, his request was to dismiss the case altogether on the grounds that the plaintiff lacked sufficient evidence of wrongful conduct on his part.

In November 1860, in Kane County, Illinois, Myron V. Hall and his brother executed a note for $2,000, with an interest rate of 10%, in favor of John Jones. Alongside the note, they signed a warrant of attorney, allowing Jones to confess judgment against them personally for the sum due under the note. The note and a cognovit, signed by an attorney named A.M. Harrington, accompanied the declaration filed on November 20, 1860. The Kane Circuit Court entered a judgment against Myron V. Hall for $2,020, which included attorney fees and costs. On February 10, 1863, Hall filed a motion to vacate this judgment, citing affidavits that questioned the validity of the warrant of attorney and its execution. The affidavits claimed that the cognovit had been signed without Harrington's authorization. The court, however, found the motion unmeritorious, ruling that sufficient evidence existed to support the original judgment and affirming it based on the judicial act of the court and the affidavits provided.	The plaintiff, John Jones, argued that the judgment against Myron V. Hall was valid based on the note and the warrant of attorney, which allowed for the confession of judgment. He asserted that the necessary legal procedures had been followed, and no legitimate defenses had been presented by Hall to warrant vacating the judgment.	Myron V. Hall contended that the judgment should be vacated due to issues regarding the execution of the warrant of attorney and the validity of the cognovit. He claimed that the cognovit was signed without proper authorization and that there was a procedural error in entering the judgment without an actual demand for payment. He sought to have the judgment set aside in order to present a defense.

Daniel Neal v. Israel Blanchard et ux. is a legal case that took place in Jackson County, Illinois, around November 1863. The primary individuals involved include Daniel Neal, the defendant, and Israel Blanchard, along with his wife, as the plaintiffs. The case arose when Blanchard and his wife filed an ejectment action against Neal to recover ownership of two lots in Murphysboro, claiming title derived from the United States through multiple predecessors, specifically as heirs of a deceased individual named John Logan. The conflict over the property stemmed from a previous suit involving Logan, wherein he had incurred costs and against which a fee bill (a legal document to collect costs) was issued by the court. This fee bill was used to sell the disputed lots after being improperly issued against Logan, leading to the sale of the property to Brush and Hanson. Neal attempted to assert a claim to part of the lots based on this sale but faced challenges in admitting evidence to support his claim. Eventually, the jury sided with Blanchard, leading to a denial of Neal's motion for a new trial and affirming the jury's verdict.	The plaintiffs, Israel Blanchard and his wife, argued that they had valid title to the property based on their claims as heirs of John Logan. They contended that the fee bill issued against Logan for costs was void and, therefore, any resulting sale from it was also void. They sought recovery of the lots and demonstrated the chain of title derived from the United States.	Daniel Neal, the defendant, claimed that he held title to one-half of the property in question through a deed from Brush and Hanson, who acquired it under the contested fee bill. He argued that the fee bill issued against Logan was a legitimate process for collecting owed costs, thus validating the transactions that followed. Neal sought to have the jury consider the validity of the fee bill and the subsequent sheriff's deed, which would substantiate his claim to the property.

In October 1882, William H. Maher owned a lot in Cossit’s addition to Chicago and owed $500 to Margaret Collins, the mother of Anna Maher (the appellee). After Maher arranged the release of a mortgage held by Collins, he agreed to use the money owed to create a home for Anna. In 1883, Maher purchased another lot on Macalester Place for $1,200, subsequently constructing a $5,000 building divided into flats. Anna and her family moved in and she managed the property's rental income while fulfilling financial responsibilities like tax payments. In December 1885, a judgment of $610.72 was entered against William Maher. In January 1886, a deed transferring the lot to Anna was recorded, although Anna was unaware of it until after William's death in December 1886. The Circuit Court had removed the judgment as a lien on Anna's title, prompting the appeal.	The plaintiffs, Michael Myers and Cornelius Griffin, argued that the judgment lien against William Maher impeded Anna Maher's title and sought the removal of this lien. They claimed that the deed transferring the property to Anna was valid, and they contended that she possessed the properties under an unrecorded deed, asserting an equitable interest that was not recognized by the judgment creditors.	Anna Maher, the appellee, defended against the judgment lien by claiming that she was in possession of the property under an unrecorded deed and raised the argument of a resulting trust, suggesting that as the funds to purchase the property were her mother’s, she was entitled to ownership. Additionally, she requested subrogation to the previous liens after paying off associated debts on the property.

The case "Ambrose P. Edwards et ux. v. William Patterson" took place in 1848 and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Mason County, where a legal dispute arose regarding an execution—an enforcement of a court judgment—issued against William Patterson. The plaintiffs, Ambrose P. Edwards and his wife, challenged this execution due to the absence of a seal on the document. During a hearing presided over by Judge Samuel D. Lockwood in the Mason Circuit Court, the plaintiffs filed a motion to amend the execution to correct this oversight. However, their motion was denied, while the defendant's motion to quash the execution and set aside the sale made under it was granted. This procedural decision led to the plaintiffs appealing the judgment to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the focus was on whether the execution was valid without the required seal and the implications of the lack of included evidence in the record.	The plaintiffs claimed that the execution against them was invalid because it lacked the required seal. They contended that this technicality rendered the execution legally inadequate and sought to amend the execution to rectify this issue. They challenged the Circuit Court's decision to quash the execution and set aside the sale made in reliance on it, asserting that their rights had been infringed upon.	The defendant, William Patterson, argued that the execution was indeed improper due to the absence of a seal, which is a necessary component for its validity. He requested the court to quash the execution and to set aside the sale resulting from it, effectively contending that the plaintiffs had no valid claim to enforce the execution as it stood.

In September 1864, the schooner T. Y. Avery, while carrying a load of lumber bound for Chicago, collided with a propeller in Lake Michigan, resulting in significant damage. The propeller towed the schooner to Mackinaw, the nearest port of refuge, where the crew made minor repairs and then towed the vessel first to Milwaukee for more extensive repairs and subsequently to Chicago. Upon arrival in Chicago, the lumber was delivered to David Goodwillie, the consignee, who signed a general average bond, thereby indicating that he understood there may be shared expenses due to the accident. The case arose when Goodwillie was sued to cover a portion of the heavy expenses incurred while bringing the vessel and cargo to Chicago, amounting to $1,666.17. Goodwillie contended that since the cargo could have been offloaded at Mackinaw, leading to lower expenses, he should not be required to contribute to costs deemed more beneficial for the vessel than for the cargo.	The plaintiff, David Goodwillie, argued that the expenses incurred in transporting the damaged cargo to Chicago were primarily for the benefit of the vessel, suggesting that unloading the cargo at the safe harbor of Mackinaw would have been a more prudent and less expensive course of action. He sought to be exempted from liability for the general average contribution associated with these high expenses, asserting that the master of the vessel was obligated to protect the cargo by adopting this alternate course.	The defendant, Dennis McCarthy, maintained that the master of the vessel acted as an agent for both the ship owner and the cargo owner, making decisions in good faith for the safety of both interests. He argued that the incurred expenses resulted in a joint benefit and common safety of both the ship and its cargo, and thus, the plaintiff was liable for his share of the general average costs. The defendant contended that the route taken was necessary and appropriate given the circumstances.

Jonathan Tullis appealed a decision from the Circuit Court of LaSalle County, Illinois, following a case involving the administrators of a deceased individual named Yoder, who was allegedly killed by the Rock Island Railroad Company. During an ongoing trial, the court permitted the jury to visit the site where Yoder's death occurred, with the agreement of both parties. While the jury was examining the scene, the court continued with other cases on the docket. Tullis's case was among those called, but his counsel was absent. Consequently, the court dismissed Tullis's case for lack of prosecution. Tullis subsequently filed an appeal, challenging the dismissal of his case and the court's of proceedings during the other trial.	Jonathan Tullis, the appellant, argued that the court improperly dismissed his case while it was in progress due to the absence of his counsel. He contended that the court should have suspended all proceedings and waited for the jury to return before proceeding with other cases. He sought to have the dismissal overturned and for his case to be reinstated.	Andrew W. Henderson, the appellee, asserted that the court acted appropriately by moving forward with the docket while the jury was absent. He contended that litigants bear the risk of absence and that the court has the discretion to manage its docket without requiring a pause for the pending trials. The defendant sought to uphold the lower court's dismissal of Tullis's case.

In the case of John Ley v. Lorenz Reitz, decided on January 7, 1888, at the Illinois Appellate Court, the conflict arose from a series of financial transactions involving a promissory note and a chattel mortgage executed by Lawrence P. Ley in favor of his father, John Ley. In February 1886, Lawrence Ley executed a $1,200 note to John, secured by a chattel mortgage on various livestock and farming equipment. This transaction occurred after William Deering had previously won a judgment against Lawrence Ley for $250 in an unrelated suit. In July 1886, Deering’s judgment led to a levy on the mortgaged property by Lorenz Reitz, the county sheriff. Subsequently, John Ley replevied the property and sought to regain possession through legal proceedings. The core issue became whether the chattel mortgage was fraudulent, aimed at impeding Deering’s ability to collect his debt. A jury found in favor of Lorenz Reitz in the replevin suit, establishing that the mortgage’s intent was to hinder Deering’s recovery.	John Ley, the appellant, contended that the chattel mortgage was legitimate and properly executed. He argued that the sheriff’s actions in levying the property were wrongful, seeking the return of the mortgaged assets based on the assertion that he had a secured interest, and requested reversal of the jury's finding in favor of the defendant.	Lorenz Reitz, as the appellee and sheriff, defended the position that the chattel mortgage was fraudulent and made with the intent to deprive Deering of his legal claim against Lawrence Ley. He argued that the mortgage did not serve legitimate interests but rather was designed to hinder the collection of Deering’s debt. Reitz requested that the court uphold the jury's verdict affirming his position regarding the legitimacy of the levy and the intent behind the mortgage.

The case of The Ridgely National Bank v. Patton & Hamilton occurred in Springfield, Illinois, culminating in a decision on March 26, 1884. The plaintiffs, Patton & Hamilton, were attorneys representing Lewis Coleman & Co., who were owed money by Kimber, Ragsdale & Co., a local merchant. On January 11, 1883, Kimber, Ragsdale & Co. deposited funds with the Ridgely National Bank and subsequently issued a check for $1018.23 to Patton & Hamilton to settle the claim. The following day, when Patton & Hamilton presented the check at the bank, payment was refused as the bank applied Kimber, Ragsdale & Co.'s entire deposit to settle a different debt owed to N. H. Ridgely & Co. The plaintiffs notified the drawer of the non-payment and initiated a suit against Kimber, Ragsdale & Co. for the original claim while the bank denied any liability regarding the check. The Appellate Court affirmed a lower court decision in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to the appeal by the bank to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Patton & Hamilton's main argument centered on the assertion that the check issued by Kimber, Ragsdale & Co. constituted a valid instrument for the payment of the debt owed to Lewis Coleman & Co. They claimed the check's refusal was improper since it was payable immediately on presentation and that as attorneys (with standing as trustees for their clients), they had the right to sue the bank for the full amount of the check.	The Ridgely National Bank countered that the check was not valid due to the wording “for account of Lewis Coleman & Co.,” which they argued diminished plaintiffs' interest, perceiving them as mere collecting agents with no legal standing to enforce the check. They maintained that the legal proceedings commenced by Lewis Coleman & Co. through an attachment against Kimber, Ragsdale & Co. precluded the plaintiffs from pursuing the check payment, claiming that procedural inconsistencies should bar the claim.

In Logan County, Illinois, a public highway ran between the towns of West Lincoln and Sheridan. Following the destruction of an old wooden bridge over Sugar Creek due to floods in February 1883, the highway commissioners decided to replace it. In the spring of 1883, they contracted a new wooden bridge, but when it was found that building it was impracticable, they opted to construct an iron bridge on stone abutments instead. The new bridge, which cost $4,360, was completed in December 1883. The commissioners petitioned the Logan County Board for financial assistance, seeking half of the costs; however, the Board only appropriated $1,000 initially, later refusing a request for an additional $1,180 after the bridge was completed. The highway commissioners filed for a mandamus in circuit court, claiming the county had a legal obligation to fund half the cost after an emergency had arisen for constructing the new bridge. The circuit court ruled in their favor, leading to an appeal to the Appellate Court, which upheld the lower court's decision.	The plaintiffs, the Commissioners of Highways of West Lincoln and Sheridan, argued that the Logan County Board had a legal duty to provide financial support for the bridge construction under the relevant Illinois statutes. They claimed there was an emergency justifying the request for county aid after the old bridge's destruction, and that the petition submitted met all legal requirements, warranting the full appropriated amount for the cost of the new bridge.	The Board of Supervisors of Logan County contended that the request for additional funds was untimely and did not meet the statutory requirements. They argued that the existence of a public road as defined in the relevant law had not been proven sufficiently and objected to the application being presented after the work was completed, challenging the legitimacy of the emergency claim and the means by which the commissioners sought funding.

The legal case "The Rosencranz & Weber Company et al. v. Seth F. Hanchett et al." took place in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision being rendered on January 16, 1889. The case involved the Rosencranz & Weber Company (the plaintiffs) and Seth F. Hanchett, who acted as a sheriff in executing a judgment against a jewelry store owner, Shute (the defendant). The plaintiffs claimed that the jewelry found in Shute’s possession rightfully belonged to them, arguing it had been delivered to Shute as an agent for sale on their behalf. According to their arrangement, Shute was to sell the jewelry at no less than the invoice price, retaining any excess as commission. The situation arose when Hanchett levied an execution on the jewelry based on a debt owed by Shute, prompting the plaintiffs to seek replevin of the goods. The trial was conducted without a jury, and the findings went against the plaintiffs' claims regarding the arrangement's legitimacy.	The plaintiffs argued that they were the rightful owners of the jewelry because it had been delivered to Shute solely as an agent for sale, not as a sale to Shute himself. They maintained that the jewelry remained their property and was to be sold for cash, with Shute required to return either the unsold goods or their sale proceeds. The plaintiffs sought to reclaim the jewelry that had been seized by the sheriff based on a debt of Shute, asserting that the arrangement was a legitimate bailment, not a sale.	The defendants contended that there was no evidence of actual fraud regarding the arrangement between the plaintiffs and Shute.
