They argued that the transaction was a bona fide consignment, where Shute was to sell the jewelry on the plaintiffs' behalf and return either the proceeds or the unsold goods. They emphasized that all terms were followed and the arrangement was not a cover for selling goods to Shute in order to benefit from a fraud in law. The defendants requested the court to uphold the levy as legitimate.

In 1890, the legal case of William F. Hair v. Nels Johnson took place concerning a contract for building a viaduct over Kinzie Street at Ashland Avenue in Chicago, Illinois. Hair had hired Johnson to supervise the masonry work, for which Johnson was to receive 40% of the net profits from the project. The contractual agreement stated that Johnson would manage various aspects of the masonry work while Hair would provide the necessary materials and ensure timely progress without delays. After completing his responsibilities, Johnson filed a bill seeking his share of the profits. Hair contested this by claiming there was a mistake in the contract, arguing that Johnson should only receive 40% of the profits from the portion of the work he specifically supervised, rather than the entire project. Hair submitted a cross-bill for reformation of the contract, claiming the same mistake, which was dismissed by the Superior Court. The court initially focused on the written terms of the agreement and the nature of evidence regarding the alleged misunderstanding between the parties.	The plaintiff, Nels Johnson, claimed that he was entitled to 40% of the net profits from the entire viaduct construction as per the contract. He argued that he had fulfilled his obligations by supervising the masonry work as outlined in their agreement, which justified his claim for payment. Johnson sought legal relief to enforce the terms of the contract and obtain the profits derived from the work completed.	The defendant, William F. Hair, contended that there was a mistake in the contract regarding the profit-sharing arrangement. He argued that Johnson was meant to receive 40% only from the portion of the work he directly supervised. Hair filed a cross-bill for reformation of the contract, seeking to amend the written terms to reflect this understanding. His position was that the contract, as written, did not accurately represent their agreement and that he should not be held responsible for the profits from work beyond Johnson's supervision.

In January 1863, a legal dispute arose involving Darius Runkle and William Pollock (the appellants) against Amos M. Johnson and others (the appellees) in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case stemmed from an agreement dated June 19, 1858, in which the appellees sold a parcel of land to the appellants for $1,500, payable in three installments. The payments were scheduled for December 1 of each year from 1858 to 1860, making the completion of payments essential to the contract. The appellees covenanted to convey the title to the land upon full payment. However, the appellants contended that the appellees were unable to convey a valid title to the land because they never owned the patent title necessary for the transaction. The matter escalated to the Fulton Circuit Court, where the appellees filed a lawsuit for the outstanding debt and damages. The court initially sustained a demurrer against the appellants' pleadings, which focused on the appellees' lack of title. This error was cited as the basis for appeal, ultimately leading the Illinois Supreme Court to evaluate the validity of the original agreement and the defenses presented by the appellants.	The plaintiffs, Amos M. Johnson et al., claimed that Darius Runkle and William Pollock owed them $1,500 for the purchase of land, which was to be paid in three installments. They asserted that following the completion of the payments, they made a tender of a deed to convey the title of the land to the appellants, as stipulated in their agreement. The plaintiffs sought recovery of the unpaid balance and damages for breach of contract.	The defendants, Runkle and Pollock, argued that the plaintiffs could not enforce the contract because they never held the patent title to the land being sold. They contended that the entire agreement hinged on the plaintiffs’ ability to convey a valid title, which constituted a failure of consideration. They maintained that because the plaintiffs admitted to not owning the necessary title at the time of the contract's execution, they were entitled to a judgment dismissing the plaintiffs' claims.

In the case of Morrison v. Smart, which was decided on April 15, 1886, the events took place in Greenfield, Ohio. The key individuals involved included the appellant, Morrison, who executed a promissory note for the sum of $286.36 to the appellee, Smart, on May 6, 1872. This note was due six months later. Years later, during the February term of the 1884 Circuit Court of Marion County, Smart initiated legal action to recover the amount due on the note. Morrison, in response, filed several defenses including a plea of set-off, which included claims of indebtedness against Smart. However, Smart countered this plea on the basis of the five-year Statute of Limitations, leading to a legal dispute regarding the applicability of the statute to the case at hand. The central issue revolved around whether Morrison's set-off claims were valid given that they were potentially barred by the statute of limitations at the time of the note's execution.	The plaintiff, Smart, claimed that Morrison owed him the amount due on the promissory note, which was executed in 1872. Smart's primary argument rested on asserting that Morrison’s claims of set-off were invalid due to the statute of limitations. He contended that any claims for set-off were already barred and, therefore, he sought the recovery of the outstanding amount on the note.	The defendant, Morrison, argued that he was entitled to a set-off against Smart’s claims, based on items of indebtedness that he believed should offset the amount due on the promissory note. Morrison referenced the statute of limitations, claiming that it should protect his rights to present set-off claims despite the passage of time. However, Smart argued that Morrison’s claims were barred by the statute due to the time elapsed, specifically pointing out that the original debts associated with his set-off were already extinguished by statutory limits.

The case "The People ex rel. John M. Sullivan v. Herman G. Weber" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1877. The case took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, involving John M. Sullivan, who claimed to be the city treasurer, and Herman G. Weber, the county collector of St. Clair County. Sullivan's petition sought a writ of mandamus to compel Weber to pay him $15,351.45, which represented city taxes collected by Weber under his role as county collector, purportedly belonging to the city tax levy of 1876. The situation arose after the city council had rejected Sullivan's appointment by the mayor due to the removal of the previous treasurer, Franz. The council's refusal to recognize Sullivan as the city treasurer and their failure to approve his bond rendered Sullivan's position legally doubtful. Furthermore, the city council issued a resolution instructing Weber not to disburse the collected taxes to anyone, including Sullivan, since they did not recognize him as the treasurer. The court had to determine whether Sullivan had the standing to compel Weber to pay the city taxes he claimed were owed to him.	John M. Sullivan, as the petitioner, argued that he was the rightful city treasurer entitled to collect the city taxes from Herman G. Weber. He requested the court to issue a writ of mandamus to compel Weber to pay him the sum of $15,351.45, which he claimed was collected in taxes on behalf of the city. Sullivan contended that as treasurer, he had a legal right to the funds, and the city council's refusal to recognize him was unwarranted, thus requiring judicial intervention.	Herman G. Weber, the defendant, contended that he was justified in retaining the funds collected since the city council had issued a directive not to pay them to Sullivan or anyone else. Weber argued that the council's resolution, passed by a two-thirds majority despite a mayoral veto, effectively nullified Sullivan's claim to the position of city treasurer. Additionally, Weber pointed out that Sullivan was not legally recognized as treasurer due to the rejection of his appointment by the city council, which invalidated any claims to the office and the funds associated with it.

In December 1853, the Illinois Supreme Court heard a case involving Charles L. Pate (Appellant) against the People of the State of Illinois (Appellees) in Vermilion County. The case arose from a recognizance signed on July 22, 1851, which entrusted Pate and Johnson W. Pate with a bond of $150. This bond was a requirement after Johnson faced charges for larceny involving a stolen steer from John Bailey. The recognizance mandated Johnson to appear in court on October 3, 1851, and comply with court orders regarding his charges. However, Johnson failed to appear, leading to a forfeiture that the court entered against Charles L. Pate as well. C. L. Pate then appealed, aiming to challenge whether an action of debt could be maintained against him regarding the recognizance and its forfeiture without further detailed allegations. The court considered if C. L. Pate could be liable under this bond and whether results from previous proceedings could influence the outcome.	The People claimed that the conditions of the recognizance were not met due to Johnson W. Pate's failure to appear in court, which constituted a default. They sought to hold Charles L. Pate responsible for the forfeiture stated in the recognizance, which was a straightforward obligation to pay a predetermined sum of money as stipulated in the bond.	Charles L. Pate's defense argued that the action of debt could not be sustained against him without additional specific averments that demonstrated the plaintiffs' claim was valid and legally actionable under the established recognizance. His position centered on the legal authority surrounding the bond and asserting that procedural inadequacies in addressing these matters should absolve him from liability.

The case "William Wilborn v. Timothy B. Blackstone et al." took place in Cook County, Illinois, and was initiated in April 1866. The action began as a forcible entry and detainer case, where William Wilborn was the defendant against Timothy B. Blackstone and others. Initially, a judgment by default was entered against Wilborn by a justice of the peace. Wilborn appealed this decision to the Circuit Court of Cook County. The plaintiffs subsequently moved to dismiss the appeal, arguing that Wilborn's affidavit of merits was insufficient, specifically citing that it did not explicitly state the title of the court or the term. However, the court maintained that despite this technicality, the affidavit was reasonably adequate and clearly linked to the relevant case. Chief Justice Walker presided over the case, emphasizing that strict technicalities should not hinder a party's right to present a meritorious defense. The case put significant focus on ensuring fairness in legal proceedings. Ultimately, the Circuit Court had dismissed the appeal, which Wilborn contested.	The plaintiffs, represented by Timothy B. Blackstone and several others, claimed that Wilborn's affidavit of merits was inadequate, leading to the dismissal of his appeal from the judgment entered by the justice of the peace. They argued that without a sufficient affidavit, Wilborn should not be allowed to pursue his appeal and sought to uphold the lower court's dismissal and the judgment against Wilborn.	Wilborn countered the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that he had a good defense to the merits of the suit. His primary argument hinged on the assertion that the technical deficiencies in his affidavit did not warrant the dismissal of his appeal, as the courts should allow parties with meritorious defenses a chance to contest judgments. He contended that the dismissal was unjust given that the underlying facts of the case and his necessary defenses were adequately presented, even if the affidavit lacked formal specifics.

Sanford Richards v. William C. Betzer was a legal dispute that originated during the November term of 1868 in the case court of Champaign County, Illinois. The case centered around two promissory notes, dated October 5, 1867, which were initially executed by William C. Betzer in favor of S. D. Mandeville. They were endorsed to Sanford Richards, who sought to enforce their payment. Both notes were due ten months after their issuance, with one valued at $1000 and the other at $584, accumulating 10% interest from the date of issuance. The defendant, Betzer, presented two special pleas arguing that the notes were void due to misrepresentations made by Mandeville regarding a flock of sheep sold to him. He claimed Mandeville had fraudulently stated that the ewes were not bred and were not with lamb when, in fact, they were, resulting in a significant loss for Betzer. The matter went to trial, concluding with the court's decision to rule in favor of Richards with a verdict amount of $1300. Betzer appealed against this judgment, prompting a review by the Illinois Supreme Court.	Sanford Richards argued that he rightfully held the promissory notes endorsed by S. D. Mandeville and was entitled to payment as the legal assignee. He contended that the defendant had failed to show that the notes were transferred after their maturity and emphasized the lack of evidence proving that any misrepresentations made by Mandeville were fraudulent. Richards sought to collect the total amount owed based on the notes, plus interest.	William C. Betzer's defense relied on the claim of a partial failure of consideration due to fraudulent misrepresentation by Mandeville regarding the condition of the sheep he purchased. He asserted that Mandeville had falsely claimed that the sheep were not bred, which led to a significant financial loss when many of them died. Betzer insisted that Richards had knowledge of these misrepresentations when he acquired the notes and therefore requested the court to invalidate the debt based on these grounds.

In late 1852, in Kane County, Illinois, Franklin C. Cook filed a lawsuit against William A. Lake seeking payment on a promissory note dated July 25, 1849, for $290, which was due one year later. The lawsuit included a warrant of attorney that Lake had signed, permitting Cook to confess judgment without further notice. The court initially ruled in favor of Cook, awarding him $370. However, in February 1853, Lake sought to overturn this judgment, claiming the note was obtained fraudulently and without consideration. Lake asserted he was unaware of the judgment until much later and wanted to defend against claims made by Cook. Witness testimonies from Lake and others supported his claims that the note was executed under duress and was not valid. However, Cook testified that the note was for valid consideration relating to rent and the sale of goods. The court denied Lake's motion to set aside the judgment initially, leading to the case being taken to a higher court where further examination of the merits was sought.	Lake claimed that the promissory note was fraudulent and that he had not received any consideration for it. He asserted that Cook had pressured him into signing the note and that significant facts surrounding its execution had been misrepresented. Lake requested the court to vacate the judgment in Cook's favor and allow him to present a full defense.	Cook contended that the promissory note was valid and legally executed in exchange for rent and goods provided to Lake. He argued that Lake's claims of fraud and coercion were unfounded and unsupported by credible evidence. Cook sought to maintain the judgment and execution against Lake, asserting that the terms of the warrant of attorney precluded any further contest.

Asa Tallmadge initiated a legal case in the Illinois Supreme Court during April 1858, seeking to reverse a portion of a prior decree concerning his disputes with Elisha A. Kirk and other defendants, originally connected to the case of Ferguson et al. v. Tallmadge, which was also decided at the same term. The matter took place in Winnebago County, Illinois, where Tallmadge alleged errors in the dismissal of his bill against Kirk and Smith, two of the original defendants. The case revolves around the actions and decisions of the lower court regarding these defendants.	Tallmadge's primary argument was that the dismissal of his bill against Kirk and Smith was erroneous and should be reversed. He sought to have the court reconsider the dismissal and to allow his claims against these defendants to proceed, as he believed the lower court had made a mistake in their judgment.	The defendants, Kirk and Smith, contended that the dismissal of the bill was appropriate and that the lower court's ruling should stand. They argued that the previous case's findings necessitated the dismissal of all claims against them, thereby maintaining that the court acted correctly in its original judgment.

The case "The East St. Louis Packing and Provision Co. v. Barney McElroy" took place in 1889 in East St. Louis, Illinois. Barney McElroy, who was employed as a laborer at the East St. Louis Packing and Provision Company, sustained personal injuries while working. The incident occurred when McElroy was positioned at the lower end of a conveyor slide, responsible for receiving and removing ice being delivered from an upper story to a cooler below. Due to alleged negligence, a large piece of ice, due to the unsafe conditions of the slide, fell and struck McElroy, causing injuries. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant failed to provide safe appliances, creating a hazardous work environment. The defendant, however, argued that McElroy was familiar with the setup and had assumed the risk of injury. The jury initially found in favor of McElroy, awarding him damages, but the case was appealed by the defendant.	The plaintiff, Barney McElroy, claimed that his injuries were due to the negligence of the East St. Louis Packing and Provision Company. He argued that the conveyor slide was improperly constructed and lacked sufficient safety features to prevent ice from falling off during operation. McElroy asserted that he was performing his job duties in the course of employment and that the defendant failed in their responsibility to provide safe working conditions and equipment, leading to his injuries. He sought damages for the injuries he suffered as a result.	The defendant, East St. Louis Packing and Provision Company, contended that McElroy was familiar with the machinery and conditions under which he was working and had voluntarily assumed the risks associated with his job. They argued that the slides had been in use for many years without incident, asserting that there was no negligence on their part. The defendant emphasized McElroy's contributory negligence, stating that he was aware of the dangers of the work environment and had chosen to assume that risk, thereby absolving the defendant of liability for his injuries.

In the case of Joshua C. Sanders v. Walter L. Peck et al., the legal proceedings began on October 9, 1874, in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute revolved around a bill filed by the appellees seeking to reform and foreclose a trust deed known as the Jewett trust deed, which secured bonds amounting to $1,000,000. The appellant, Joshua C. Sanders, was a defendant in the case and owned 301 lots of land in Riverside that were subject to the lien of the Jewett trust deed. He also held 195 bonds of the Great Western Railroad Company, which he believed he could use to redeem his lots from the trust deed. After various legal arguments, cross-bills were filed, and the case involved multiple defendants asserting different claims regarding their interests in the property. The litigation went through extensive court hearings, including decisions from the Supreme Court that reversed prior judgments and required further proceedings. After 14 years of litigation, Sanders claimed that significant changes affecting the parties and property occurred since the initial filing of the bill, impacting his position. The core issue was whether Sanders could redeem individual lots from the trust deed by surrendering the appropriate number of bonds, a claim initially rejected by the Circuit Court.	Sanders argued that, as the rightful owner of the lots and bonds, he was entitled to redeem his lots from the trust deed by surrendering the bonds corresponding to the schedule price of the lots he wished to redeem. He contended that the court had previously erred by requiring him to redeem all 301 lots at once in exchange for his 195 bonds. Sanders sought a decree to allow him to choose which lots to redeem individually based on the bonds he was willing to surrender.	The defendants, led by Jewett, argued that the terms of the trust deed required the redemption of all the lots if any were to be redeemed. They maintained that Sanders had previously tendered all his bonds for the release of all 301 lots, and thus was obligated to surrender all bonds for this purpose now. The defendants contended that allowing Sanders to choose fewer lots to redeem would contradict the terms of the agreement and the prior court rulings.

In the case of Joseph A. Brown et al. v. The City of Chicago et al., dated May 15, 1886, the plaintiff, Joseph A. Brown, alongside other property owners, filed a bill in chancery in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois. The case arose from the city’s intention to collect a special assessment for the improvement of Main Street in Chicago, which the plaintiffs sought to contest. The plaintiffs argued that the county court lacked jurisdiction to confirm the assessment because the required ten-day notice was not adequately provided as per the statutes governing city assessments. It was claimed that notices were posted and published in a daily newspaper starting on January 30, 1885, but that the first day of the next term of court was February 9, 1885, leading to their assertion of insufficient notice. Moreover, they maintained that the city council had previously agreed to defer action on the improvements for two years, and therefore, the confirmation was unauthorized. The case was ultimately dismissed in favor of the defendants after the court determined that the plaintiffs had failed to show lack of notice and did not file their objections in a timely manner.	The plaintiffs claimed that the county court did not have jurisdiction to confirm the assessment due to inadequate notice being given as required by law. They argued that sufficient time was not allowed before the confirmation hearing and that prior agreements made by the city council to postpone the proceedings for two years should have invalidated the assessment. The plaintiffs sought a judicial order to prevent the collector from selling their lots for non-payment of the assessment.	The defendants contended that the notice for the assessment was adequate under the required legal framework, as computed correctly, allowing sufficient time prior to the confirmation of the assessment. They argued that the plaintiffs failed to show that they did not receive proper notice or did not have the opportunity to object to the assessment. The defendants maintained that the plaintiffs had the opportunity to present their objections at the time of the confirmation but neglected to do so.

In the case of James F. Farmer v. Eliza J. Farmer, which was tried in January 1874 in Morgan County, Illinois, the dispute centers around the ownership of a horse. Eliza J. Farmer, the plaintiff, brought an action of replevin against her father, James F. Farmer, the defendant, to recover a horse she claimed belonged to her. The court trial was conducted without a jury, and the issue was decided in favor of Eliza. During the proceedings, it was revealed that in 1868, James promised Eliza a colt if she stayed home and cared for her ill mother. Over time, James traded the colt for a sorrel horse, and subsequently for a horse named "Wild Bill," which was later traded for the horse in question. Witnesses testified that James consistently stated that the horse belonged to Eliza. The defendant argued against the judgment, claiming it contradicted the evidence and challenged the court's refusal to postpone the proceedings until he could summon more witnesses.	Eliza J. Farmer claimed that her father, James, agreed to give her a sucking colt in exchange for caring for her mother. She presented evidence, including testimonies from multiple witnesses, stating that James acknowledged her ownership of the contested horse on various occasions. She requested the court to affirm her ownership and recover her horse.	James F. Farmer contested the judgment, arguing that the ruling was contrary to the weight of the evidence presented. He also sought to postpone the trial to procure a witness after the evidence had been heard, a request the court denied, claiming that it was a matter of discretion and that James had failed to subpoena the witness.

Citizens Gaslight and Heating Co. v. A. O. Granger is a legal case heard by the Illinois Appellate Court, with the final decision dated February 25, 1886. The case arose in McLean County, Illinois, involving the Citizens Gaslight and Heating Company, a corporation dedicated to gas manufacturing, and A. O. Granger, who represents the appellees in the case. The central issue pertains to the provision of certain machinery and apparatus necessary for gas production; specifically, the machinery was required to replace equipment lost in a fire. The appellees argue that they supplied the machinery under the representation that the fire was caused by the bursting of a pipe, as conveyed by the company's secretary, C. D. Hank. However, they later discovered that the pipe had not burst, which raised disputes over whether they were entitled to compensation for the replacement. The court trial concluded with a jury verdict favoring the plaintiffs by awarding them $1,215.18, despite the defendant's contentions regarding the evidence admissibility and the form of action.	The plaintiffs, represented by Granger, claim that they are entitled to compensation for the machinery and labor provided to replace equipment damaged in the fire. They assert that the replacement was agreed upon based on the defendant's representations regarding the fire's cause. The plaintiffs argue that they fulfilled their contractual obligations by supplying the replacement machinery and that the benefit of this machinery was received and utilized by the defendant.	The defendant, Citizens Gaslight and Heating Co., denies any obligation to compensate the plaintiffs, contending that the representations made about the cause of the fire were not accurate. They argued that no such admissions were made by their agent, and thus, the plaintiffs cannot claim compensation based on those statements. Furthermore, they challenged the admissibility of certain statements made by their superintendent as evidence. The defendant also contended that the action should not have proceeded as assumpsit, claiming that the form of action was misconceived.

The case Thompson Weir v. Andrew Leibert was decided in September 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originates from Jo Daviess County, where the contingent for volunteers in the Civil War was set at 556 men. In February 1865, the town of Woodbine, with Thompson Weir as supervisor, appointed a committee to recruit volunteers, offering a bounty of $600. Andrew Leibert enlisted under this offer. Later, in March 1865, the county's board of supervisors passed resolutions that included a plan to borrow $111,200 to pay a bounty of $200 to each volunteer fulfilling the county's quota. An amendment prohibited any township from paying a bounty exceeding $400. The board's intent was to prevent a draft by encouraging volunteer enlistment. Weir received funds from the county to distribute as bounties, but Leibert claimed he was entitled to an additional $200 as a bounty under the resolutions, arguing that it should have been paid directly. The case revolves around the interpretation of the resolutions and whether they were intended to apply to recruits like Leibert, who had already enlisted.	Andrew Leibert, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to a $200 bounty under the resolutions passed by the Jo Daviess County board of supervisors. He claimed that the funds should have been paid to him due to his enlistment under the earlier offer, asserting that the board's resolutions intended for all volunteers to receive an equal bounty, regardless of when they enlisted.	Thompson Weir, on behalf of the defendant, contended that the resolutions intended to provide additional funds strictly for volunteers who enlisted after their adoption. He argued that the money was meant for reimbursement to the townships and that paying Leibert an extra bounty would contradict the resolutions' aim to maintain equality and prevent inequity among volunteers who had already received varying amounts.

In the case of Parker v. Allen, dated June 8, 1886, the setting is Illinois where the dispute arose over two promissory notes amounting to $100 and $650. The appellee (plaintiff) brought a lawsuit against the appellant (defendant), Mrs. Parker, in the Illinois Appellate Court, alleging that she had executed the promissory notes in question. The defendant was a married woman at the time of execution, and her husband signed the notes on her behalf. The crux of the case revolved around the defendant's denial of her husband's authority to execute the notes, either express or implied. The case's evidence suggested that her husband operated the farm independently rather than in service of his wife's interests, leading to doubts about any implied authority. Ultimately, the court found errors in the way the case was submitted regarding implied authority and noted that despite the plaintiff’s claims, the evidence for the defendant's personal authorization for the notes was weak.	The plaintiff, Mr. Allen, claimed that the defendant owed him money based on two promissory notes signed by her husband. He sought recovery of the amounts due as outlined in those notes. The primary issue was the enforceability of the promissory notes, contingent upon whether Mrs. Parker had granted her husband the authority to sign them on her behalf.	The defendant, Mrs. Parker, argued that she never executed the promissory notes herself and that her husband did not have the authorization to sign them in her stead. She contended that there was no express or implied authority as her husband operated independently rather than on her behalf. Additionally, she expressed willingness to pay the $100 note, indicating acknowledgment of that specific debt but not the larger claim.

In the case of James H. Woodburn v. Phebe A. Woodburn et al., dated January 25, 1886, the situation revolves around financial transactions involving promissory notes. The key individuals involved are James H. Woodburn, the appellant, and Peter Ege, the executor of the estate of George W. Woodburn, deceased. The case takes place in Whiteside County, Illinois. Woodburn held four promissory notes, totaling $8000, all dated March 14, 1873, with varying terms of repayment. After making partial payments, Woodburn claims to have paid off the remaining balance on March 13, 1880, by providing Ege with a check for $8000 and simultaneously securing a new loan of $8000 at a lower interest rate of 8%. However, the arrangement was conducted in such a way that no actual money changed hands, as the check was essentially worthless due to Woodburn having no funds in the bank. The court focuses on whether the debts represented by the original notes were indeed paid. The lower court ruled that the original notes remained unpaid, thus resulting in the current appeal.	James H. Woodburn, the plaintiff, argues that he fulfilled his obligation by allegedly paying the $8000 owed on his four promissory notes on March 13, 1880. He claims that through a check agreement with the bank’s cashier, he effectively settled the debt while simultaneously obtaining a new loan. Woodburn requests the court to acknowledge this payment and discharge the original notes and mortgage associated with the notes, solidifying his new loan agreement.	The defendants, represented by Peter Ege, contend that the arrangement between Woodburn and the bank was merely a subterfuge designed to change the interest rate from 10% to 8% without any actual payment being made. Ege argues that since no money changed hands and the original notes were never surrendered or canceled, the original debt remains unpaid. Ege requests the court to affirm that the four notes are still valid, and Woodburn's claims of payment are invalid.

Harvey T. Pace, the plaintiff, owned a school-house built on his land in Mt. Vernon, Illinois, which was listed for taxation for the year 1856 by an assessor. The school-house was constructed with Pace's own funds for the specific purpose of a female school, and it operated as such for two years under the supervision of qualified school directors. The teacher received appropriate certifications and was compensated by Pace, who also provided her with board and lodging. However, the school had been unoccupied for four years following its last session, and Pace attempted to rent it for educational purposes, though school directors never expressed interest in doing so. The County Court determined that the property was subject to taxation, a decision upheld by the Circuit Court of Jefferson County. Pace then appealed, seeking a reversal of the judgment based on claims that the building should be exempt from taxation under the revenue laws in effect at that time.	The plaintiff, Harvey T. Pace, contended that the school-house should be exempt from taxation under the revenue law of 1853, which provides tax exemptions for properties designated for school purposes. He argued that the property was used as a public school-house and should not be subject to taxation since it had been employed for educational activities and was available for rental for such purposes.	The defendants, the County Commissioners of Jefferson County, argued that the property did not qualify for tax exemption under the revenue statutes. They maintained that Pace did not donate the property for school purposes, nor did he convey it to the school directors. The defendants asserted that, although the property was temporarily used for educational activities, ownership remained with Pace, who could utilize the property as he saw fit, which indicated an intention to derive income from it, thereby undermining his claim for tax exemption.

On September 3, 1878, in Adams County, Illinois, a written lease was executed between Elizabeth Hulse and the appellees, John P. Cadogan and Matilda Cadogan, granting Ernst Disselhorst the right to occupy 240 acres for a period of one year, starting from March 1, 1879, with a stipulated rental payment of $8,700—half payable on November 1, 1879, and the remainder by March 1, 1880. Disselhorst maintained his occupancy and continued making rental payments, even after the death of Hulse in March 1883, and under verbal agreements until March 1, 1884. However, during this period, the property underwent partition proceedings resulting in a sale to Henry Glaser on July 28, 1883, with the deed executed on October 22, 1883. Disselhorst paid Glaser the due installment despite being aware of Cadogan's claims to the rent. The case arose when Cadogan's heirs filed suit against Disselhorst for unpaid rent after he refused to acknowledge their claim. The legal arguments centered around the validity and implications of the partition sale and the relationship between the original lease and subsequent property sale.	The plaintiffs, John P. Cadogan and Matilda Cadogan, claim that they are entitled to the rent payment owed by Disselhorst based on their ownership rights following the partition sale. They argue that the sale did not diminish their entitlement to rent since it should have been reserved as an incident of the reversion rights they held as lessors. They contend that the sale to Glaser was conditional and did not fully convey the right to the rents accruing until the end of the lease.	The defendant, Ernst Disselhorst, defends by asserting that the property was sold unconditionally, with the right to receive rent passing to Glaser as the new owner. He argues that the partition sale and subsequent deed adequately conveyed all rights of the original lessors, and as such, he is not liable for any rent that the plaintiffs claim is due. Disselhorst emphasizes that his obligations were fulfilled by paying the purchaser after the sale and that he was not made a party to the partition proceedings.

In December 1853, a legal dispute arose in Illinois concerning land ownership between Alanson Noakes and Stephen W. Martin. Both parties claimed title under Philip W. Hackett, their common grantor. The appellant, Noakes, based his claim on an older deed dated December 15, 1818, which was recorded in Madison County. Conversely, the appellee, Martin, relied on a junior deed from Hackett to Romulus Riggs, dated April 22, 1818, recorded in Pike County on December 30, 1821. Both deeds, however, were improperly acknowledged per Illinois law at the time of recording, meaning their registration did not hold legal significance. Despite the defendant, Martin, having taken possession of the land in 1849 under a purchase contract from Riggs—while Noakes remained inactive—the trial court ruled in favor of Martin, awarding him a writ of possession. Noakes subsequently appealed this decision.	The plaintiff, Stephen W. Martin, argued that despite the deeds being unacknowledged, his claim to the property was valid due to being in possession of the land. He asserted that he had paid taxes on the land since its acquisition and had established his rights through continuous possession.	The defendant, Alanson Noakes, contended that his deed, being the oldest in date, conferred superior title over Martin’s claim. He argued that any legislative changes regarding the validity of the recording of deeds did not retroactively alter existing rights and that the lack of proper acknowledgment invalidated Martin's claim to priority in this case.

In January 1859, the case of William Essington v. Thomas M. Neill was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court following an action of trespass quare clausum fregit initiated in the Clinton Circuit Court. The plaintiff, William Essington, alleged that the defendant, Thomas M. Neill, unlawfully took seven pieces of lumber belonging to him from land he had built a frame house upon in February 1858. Essington claimed rightful ownership of the land through a connected chain of title from the U.S. government. The defendant, Neill, contended that he acted as an agent for James Russell, who had a color of title and claimed possession due to a tax deed from 1846. Additionally, Neill argued that Russell's wife had given him permission to take the lumber as she had put up a small building on the property shortly before Essington's house was constructed. The trial was conducted by the court without a jury, where both sides presented evidence and claims regarding ownership, possession, and the validity of the tax deed.	The plaintiff, William Essington, argued that Thomas M. Neill unlawfully trespassed on his property by taking his lumber without permission. Essington asserted that he had built a house on the land and provided evidence of his ownership through a legitimate connected title from the U.S. government. He sought redress for the removal of his property and contended that the defendant's claims of ownership through James Russell were unfounded and legally insufficient.	The defendant, Thomas M. Neill, claimed that he was justified in taking the lumber as he acted under the authority of James Russell, who had purportedly owned the land and had permission from his wife to occupy and act on it. Neill argued that Russell had established a claim to the property by paying taxes and having possession of it for seven consecutive years prior to the lawsuit. He provided evidence of tax receipts and a tax deed to support his defense, asserting that the trespass was lawful.

On January 1, 1871, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed the case of Elizabeth W. Mason v. William Ainsworth, originating from a dispute over land titles. In this case, both parties claimed ownership of the land in question, tracing their title back to Darius L. Ball. In August 1854, Ball and his wife sold the land to Reuben Hankinson via a warranty deed. Following this transfer, Hankinson and his wife sold the premises to the appellant, Mason, in November 1858. Conversely, the appellee, Ainsworth, based his claim on a mortgage from Ball to Alonson Reed, dated December 14, 1853, which aimed to secure an indebtedness of $110. Reed later assigned the mortgage and related rights through a series of transactions to various parties, ending with Jacob F. Coppel. In 1860, Coppel attempted to foreclose the mortgage, selling the property to Luther Dearborn, who then transferred it to Ainsworth. Central to the court's decision was whether Coppel, as an equitable assignee, could legally execute the power of sale contained in the mortgage without the original mortgagee's consent, as the secured debt had never actually been assigned in a legally recognized way.	Elizabeth W. Mason argued that she held rightful title to the property based on her chain of title from Darius L. Ball, asserting that the procedures followed by Jacob F. Coppel to execute the power of sale were improperly conducted as he lacked the legal authority to do so. Mason contended that the mortgage was never assigned in a manner that allowed Coppel to execute the sale, and thus, she sought a ruling that would affirm her ownership of the property.	William Ainsworth defended his claim to the land based on the mortgage signed by Darius L. Ball, asserting that the power of sale within the mortgage was executed legitimately by Coppel. Ainsworth argued that the chain of assignments from Reed to Coppel entitled him to enforce the sale, despite the lack of traditional legal assignments of the underlying debt.

The case "Henry Brand et al. v. William F. Henderson et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 14, 1883. The origins of the case trace back to late 1880, when W.F. Henderson & Co., grain factors based in Danville, Illinois, received orders from Henry Brand & Head to purchase 20,000 bushels of No. 2 red wheat for delivery at Toledo in January 1881. Evidence presented suggests that both parties understood the wheat was never to be physically delivered; rather, they intended to settle the price differences between the market rates at the time of the order and the scheduled delivery date. Subsequently, after the wheat's price declined, Brand & Head refused to settle the loss as agreed. Henderson & Co. tried to recover $21,000 through a financial arrangement that involved tendering warehouse receipts that supposedly represented the wheat. Brand & Head contested this offer, leading to the current legal dispute. The case became complicated by the nature of the agreement, as Henderson & Co. had not actually owned the wheat nor paid any amounts, raising questions about the legitimacy of their claims.	The plaintiff, W.F. Henderson & Co., argued that they had acted as agents for Brand & Head in purchasing the wheat and sought to recover the difference between the purchase price and market value under common counts. They asserted that Brand & Head unjustly refused to settle their losses as agreed upon in writing.	The defendants, Henry Brand & Head, contended that the agreement constituted a gambling contract with no intention of actual delivery of the wheat. They claimed the transactions were void under the statute due to their gambling nature and argued that Henderson & Co. failed to prove ownership or payment for the wheat, and thus could only claim commissions as agents, not the actual losses.

John W. Corgan v. Aaron A. Frew is a legal case stemming from a contract dispute that unfolded in Perry County, Illinois. The case was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court, with the judgment delivered in November 1865. The central figures in this dispute included John W. Corgan, the defendant, and Aaron A. Frew, the plaintiff. The conflict originated when Mason F. Woods executed a promissory note on December 6, 1861, for $500, payable to C. P. Christian, which was subsequently indorsed to Corgan and later to Frew. Frew contended that Woods was insolvent from the note's maturity on May 20, 1862, until the suit's initiation, making legal collection impossible. The plaintiff initiated the lawsuit against Corgan, challenging the non-payment of the note. During the trial, Corgan objected to the note's admission as evidence, leading to disputes over its validity and the insolvency claims regarding Woods. The court deliberated on various legal principles surrounding the assignment of notes, the competency of witnesses, and the requirements for proving an effective sale of property against creditors.	The plaintiff, Aaron A. Frew, argued that he was the rightful assignee of the promissory note originally made by Mason F. Woods. He claimed that Woods had been insolvent from the date the note became due until the initiation of his lawsuit, thus rendering any attempts to collect the debt ineffective. Frew requested that the court recognize the validity of the note and hold Corgan accountable for the amount outlined in the note, which was $500 plus interest.	The defendant, John W. Corgan, countered the plaintiff's claims by asserting that the instrument in question was not a valid promissory note, challenging its assignability. Corgan argued that the necessary elements for a legitimate sale of any property were not fulfilled given the alleged insolvency of Woods. He insisted that Woods had retained ownership of personal property sufficient to settle the debt and that Frew should have made efforts to levy on those assets before pursuing this legal action. Ultimately, he sought to have the case dismissed on these grounds.

The case "Dwelling House Insurance Company v. John A. Butterly, Jr." was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 2, 1889. It originated in Cook County, Illinois, where John A. Butterly, Jr. had obtained an insurance policy from the Dwelling House Insurance Company. The policy was issued based on an oral application and covered various types of property, including livestock and farming implements. A critical condition of the policy stipulated that if the insured property was mortgaged or if the assured's interest became less than perfect legal ownership, the policy would be void. Following the issuance of the policy, certain portions of the insured property were mortgaged. Unfortunately, a fire occurred, damaging both mortgaged and unencumbered property covered under the policy. The central issue in the case was whether the existing mortgages rendered the entire insurance policy void or only affected the property specifically incumbered. The court reviewed the valid legal interpretations of insurance policies concerning the sale and encumbrance of property and determined the nature of the coverage that existed between the insured and the insurance company.	The Dwelling House Insurance Company argued that the policy was void due to the breaches of its terms, specifically related to the title of the property that was covered. They contended that since portions of the insured property were mortgaged, the policy should not be considered enforceable for any property under such encumbrances. Their main legal request was to declare the insurance policy void based on these conditions, arguing that the presence of chattel mortgages on parts of the insured property voided the insurance coverage altogether.	John A. Butterly, Jr. maintained that the insurance policy remained valid despite the encumbrances on some assets. He argued that the provision in the policy should be interpreted to allow coverage for property that was not specifically encumbered by mortgages. Essentially, Butterly contended that the policy only became void concerning the properties that were directly mortgaged, not for the entirety of the covered insurance. He aimed to affirm the judgment that recognized this nuanced interpretation of the coverage and requested the court to uphold the validity of the insurance contract for the unencumbered property.

In September 1868, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Samuel McCarty et al. v. William H. Carter arose involving a dispute over a mechanic's lien. The key individuals involved were Samuel McCarty, his wife Emily A. McCarty, their daughter Lucy J. Davis, and the contractor William H. Carter. The issue centered on a contract made by McCarty for improvements to a property owned by Lucy, which was subject to Emily's right of dower. Carter, who executed a written contract with Samuel McCarty, sought to establish a mechanic’s lien against the property for his work. The court faced questions about the enforceability of the contract, given that Lucy was a minor at the time it was made, raising concerns over the legality of contracting on her behalf without her authority. Furthermore, the court examined the implications of Lucy's receipt of rents from the property once she gained majority, evaluating whether that could retroactively validate the contract or create a lien against her property. Ultimately, the court's analysis focused on the binding nature of contracts involving minors and the conditions under which a lien could be established.	The plaintiff, William H. Carter, claimed a right to a mechanic's lien on the property owned by Lucy J. Davis based on a contract he had entered into with Samuel McCarty for construction work. Carter argued that the contract was valid and binding, despite not having Lucy's name included or her explicit consent, and that her receipt of rents from the property after reaching the age of majority constituted a ratification of the contract. He sought to enforce the lien for any amount owed for the work performed under this agreement.	The defendants, including Samuel McCarty, Emily A. McCarty, and Lucy J. Davis, contended that the contract was invalid due to Lucy being a minor at the time it was made, asserting that minors cannot be bound by such contracts, especially those concerning property improvements. They argued that her subsequent actions, such as receiving rents after reaching adulthood, did not equate to ratifying the previous contract. Moreover, they emphasized that any lien claimed by Carter was unenforceable since he did not contract directly with the property owner or have the owners' consent.

The case of "Columbus C. Smith v. Sarah J. Brittenham" dates back to August 14, 1874, when Sarah Brittenham filed a lawsuit in DeWitt County, Illinois, against Columbus Smith. The central issue involved a conveyance of 237 acres of land that Brittenham had made to Smith in January 1869. Brittenham requested the court to set aside this conveyance, claiming it was obtained through fraud perpetrated by Smith and her husband, John A. Brittenham. Sarah alleged that Smith and her husband colluded to undervalue a stock of goods that was exchanged for the land. After several court proceedings over the years, with judgments and appeals, the circuit court initially ruled in favor of Brittenham. However, complications arose when Brittenham conveyed her interest in the property to Harvey E. Husten, who was also her attorney, before the legal proceedings could reach a conclusion. The Supreme Court of Illinois ultimately examined the history of the case and the issue of who held the legal rights to the land, highlighting the necessity of proper parties being involved in such a case. The complexity of actions, conveyances, and appeals ultimately led to further scrutiny of the case.	Sarah Brittenham, the plaintiff, contended that the conveyance of land to Smith was fraudulent. She accused Smith and her husband of misrepresentation regarding the value and quantity of the goods exchanged for the land. Sarah claimed she was led to believe the stock was worth $14,000 while it was actually worth much less, inducing her to sign over her land. She sought rescission of the conveyance and asserted that she was entitled to have the contract voided due to the alleged fraud.	Columbus Smith, the defendant, denied all allegations of wrongdoing and asserted that the transaction was valid. He argued that Sarah lacked the standing to sue since she had transferred her interest in the land to Husten prior to the proceedings. Furthermore, Smith maintained that the amended bill filed by Sarah did not present a solid basis for the claims, and even if there were issues regarding the valuation of the goods, the legal proceedings could not continue without properly establishing parties in interest.

Albert H. Guild and James T. Durant, the appellants, were involved in a legal case against Seth Johnson, the appellee, which took place in December 1837 in the Municipal Court of the City of Chicago, Illinois. The action was centered around a debt claim brought forth by Johnson against the appellants. The lower court had ruled in favor of Johnson, awarding him damages along with costs associated with the suit. The decision led the appellants to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing against the judgment rendered against them.	The plaintiff, Seth Johnson, claimed that he was owed a debt by the appellants, Guild and Durant. He sought compensation for damages incurred due to the non-payment of this debt, as well as the costs associated with bringing the action to court.	The defendants, Albert H. Guild and James T. Durant, challenged the judgment rendered by the Municipal Court. Their key argument was that the judgment for damages was incorrect and warranted a reversal. They requested that the Illinois Supreme Court correct the error made in the lower court's ruling and provide a proper judgment in their favor.

The case "George Karnes v. The People ex rel. J. S. Rumsey" arose from an application for the sale of delinquent lands in Cook County, Illinois, for unpaid taxes from the year 1871. The county treasurer and ex-officio collector, J. S. Rumsey, filed the petition at the county court's February term in 1873. The defendants opposed the sale, arguing that procedural errors occurred regarding the timing of the court sessions. Specifically, they contended that the Cook County Court was improperly convened on the first Monday instead of the mandated third Monday of the month. The notice of the pending sale was also said to have been issued too late. Despite these objections, the county court authorized the tax sale, prompting the appellants to appeal to the circuit court, which upheld the decision. This appeal was launched to the Illinois Supreme Court, focusing on procedural validity and interpretation of relevant laws governing court operations and tax collection procedures.	The plaintiff, represented by the county treasurer J. S. Rumsey, claimed that the procedures followed for the sale of delinquent lands were in accordance with the applicable laws and regulations. They argued that the Cook County Court was authorized to convene on the specified dates as per current legal provisions, and the notice of sale complied with the requirements set forth in the revenue law. The plaintiff sought affirmation of the county court's judgment to proceed with the sale of the delinquent properties.	The defendants maintained that the county court's actions were unlawful based on two main arguments: one, that the court had wrongly convened on the first Monday when it should have met on the third Monday; and two, that the notice of sale failed to comply with statutory requirements regarding the proper timing of notifications. They requested that the Illinois Supreme Court reverse the circuit court's judgment, asserting that the legal grounds for the tax sale were not properly established.

Peter L. Frame was appointed the administrator of the estate of William Frame, deceased, on September 23, 1835, in Morgan County, Illinois. Following his appointment, he conducted various estate proceedings, including appraisements and inventories, which were filed with the county court. However, despite conducting preliminary and final settlements on January 24 and May 30, 1837, the official records failed to capture these settlements. In late 1853, a citation was issued requiring Peter L. Frame to appear and make the estate settlement, prompting him to seek an amendment of the court records to include the previously unrecorded settlement documents. The county court permitted the amendment, but this decision was subsequently reversed by the circuit court of Morgan County upon appeal by Rebecca Frame and others, leading to Peter L. Frame's appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1854.	Peter L. Frame argued that the evidence presented was sufficient to warrant the inclusion of the settlements in the court records as they had been formally conducted and certified by the probate judge. He requested that the Illinois Supreme Court reverse the circuit court's decision, allowing the records to reflect the established settlements.	The appellees, represented by Rebecca Frame and others, contended that the circuit court correctly reversed the county court’s decision, arguing that the evidence and procedural grounds did not support the inclusion of the settlements in the record. They sought to uphold the circuit court's decision as valid.

In November 1824, a legal dispute arose in Madison, Illinois, involving plaintiffs James and Paris Mason and defendant Christian Eakle. The case centers around a contract where the plaintiffs were to pay a sum of money with an agreed interest rate of twenty percent. Following a judgment rendered in favor of Eakle, an execution was issued against the Masons for the amount owed, including the interest. The plaintiffs contended that the execution was improperly issued, given that after obtaining a judgment, the terms of the original contract are overridden by statutory regulations governing judgments.	The plaintiffs argued that the execution against them was erroneous because the statutory interest rate applicable to judgments is six percent, not the twenty percent stated in their original contract. They requested the court to set aside the execution, claiming it did not comply with statutory requirements concerning the interest rate applicable to judgments.	The defendant contended that the court's decision to enforce the original contract's interest terms was justified. They argued that the execution was valid based on the agreement between the parties, implying that the higher interest rate of twenty percent should be honored. The defendant sought to have the court uphold the execution as legally sound.

Joshua T. Cox v. The People of the State of Illinois is a legal case from 1884 where the court addressed a bastardy claim stemming from an incident on July 4, 1881. The plaintiff, Rhoda Hallock, accused Cox of being the father of her illegitimate child, born on March 9, 1882. Hallock claimed that she had sexual intercourse with Cox twice on the night in question, leading to her pregnancy. Cox denied these allegations, asserting that due to a physical malformation, it would have been impossible for him to have had sexual relations with Hallock. The case initially went to the circuit court of Livingston County, where a judgment mandated that Cox pay $550 for the child's education and support. This judgment was then appealed to the Appellate Court for the Second District. During the trial, the jury received an instruction indicating they did not need to find Cox guilty beyond a reasonable doubt, which the Supreme Court found to be erroneous.	The plaintiff, Rhoda Hallock, argued that Joshua T. Cox was the father of her illegitimate child, claiming that their interactions on July 4, 1881, resulted in her pregnancy. She sought financial support for the child’s education and upbringing, leading to a court order for Cox to pay a total of $550 over a span of ten years. Hallock's claims rested primarily on her testimony regarding the nature of their relationship.	The defendant, Joshua T. Cox, denied the allegations, contending that he did not engage in sexual intercourse with Hallock, citing a physical condition that rendered it impossible. Furthermore, Cox contended that the jury was misled by an erroneous instruction that diminished the required standard of proof, arguing that his rights were prejudiced as a result.

The case of John H. McMillan and Julius F. W. Thomsen v. Cyrus H. McCormick, Jr. was located in Chicago, Illinois and the proceedings were filed in the Superior Court of Cook County. The case originated from a bill in equity intended to enjoin the foreclosure of a trust deed related to two parcels of land in Chicago. John H. McMillan and Julius F. W. Thomsen claimed ownership of these parcels under Sheriff’s deeds resulting from judgments against Samuel J. Walker. Specifically, McMillan acquired his property from a judgment in July 1875, and Thomsen through a judgment in September 1874. The defendant, Cyrus H. McCormick, asserted a legal claim to the trust deed originally executed by Henry H. Walker in 1868 to secure a promissory note of $20,000. The bill contended that the foreclosure of the trust deed was barred by a statute (section 11 of chapter 83 of the Revised Statutes), and thus, the trust deed constituted a cloud on the titles of McMillan and Thomsen. After the bill was taken pro confesso against Foreman, who was involved as a trustee, McCormick demurred, arguing that the facts did not support a claim for foreclosure. The court ultimately dismissed the bill, leading the plaintiffs to appeal.	The plaintiffs, McMillan and Thomsen, asserted that the right to foreclose the trust deed had been lost and perpetually barred under section 11 of chapter 83 of the Revised Statutes. They claimed that the trust deed no longer constituted a valid lien on their properties and argued that it created an unjust cloud on their titles. They sought an injunction to prevent the foreclosure of the trust deed, claiming their ownership rights were being infringed upon.	Cyrus H. McCormick defended against the plaintiffs' claims by demurring, asserting that the facts presented in the plaintiffs' bill did not substantiate their right to prevent the exercise of power under the trust deed. He contended that the power of sale and liability of the land to foreclosure remained intact despite the plaintiffs' claims regarding the statute, arguing that the section relied upon was not applicable to the prior executed trust deed.

The case "George Purinton et al. v. The Northern Illinois Railroad Company" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1867. The dispute arose from an agreement on May 3, 1861, involving the construction of a railroad from Freeport to Savanna. The Northern Illinois Railroad Company sought to acquire a right-of-way over a specified tract of land owned by George Purinton and Abraham T. Green. In exchange for one dollar and the construction of a side track, the landowners consented to allow the railroad company to build over their land, with the condition that the company pay the agreed amount within a year. The railroad company built on the land and claimed it had tendered payment of the dollar. However, Purinton later initiated an action for ejectment to reclaim the land. The key legal question involved determining whether the railroad company could enforce its rights under the agreement, especially regarding the conditions of payment and construction obligations.	The plaintiffs, the Northern Illinois Railroad Company, argued that they had entered into a valid agreement with Purinton and Green for the right-of-way, fulfilling their obligations by beginning construction within the specified timeframe. They asserted they had tendered payment and sought specific performance of the contract, claiming the defendants had failed to execute a deed for the conveyance of the land as required.	The defendants contended that the true consideration of the agreement was not merely the one dollar, but also the obligation of the company to fill a sluice and build a side track, which they claimed was not completed. They argued that the company had not been put in possession of the land, asserting that the agreement should be forfeited due to non-compliance with these conditions. They also claimed the contract was too vague to be enforced.

In January 1883, John Morrison purchased about $2,500 worth of goods on credit from Seneca D. Kimbark, a wholesale dealer in iron, in Chicago, Illinois. Morrison represented his financial condition falsely, claiming he had minimal liabilities and significant assets. After confessing a judgment to his brother for $2,500, Morrison's financial status deteriorated, leading him to attempt to assign his property to Kelley, Maus & Co. The plaintiffs, in this case, were the sheriff of Cook County acting on behalf of Kelley, Maus & Co., who had acquired a replevin bond after Kimbark initiated an action to reclaim the goods. Kimbark argued that the sale to Kelley, Maus & Co. was fraudulent and intended to conceal assets. Initially, a jury ruled in favor of Kimbark, and the Appellate Court upheld this decision. After a successful appeal for a rehearing, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed evidence concerning Morrison's alleged fraud and the circumstances surrounding the sale. The key individuals involved included Kimbark as the seller, Morrison as the buyer, and Kelley and Maus as the purchasers of the goods from Morrison.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were owed the value of the goods based on the replevin bond executed by Kimbark. They argued that Kimbark's attempt to reclaim these goods was without merit because Kelley, Maus & Co. believed they had acquired valid title to the goods purchased from Morrison. They sought to recover the value of the goods from Kimbark on the basis that the sale was legitimate and that Kimbark had no rightful claim to the goods.	Kimbark contended that the initial purchase by Morrison was fraudulent, asserting that there was intent to defraud his creditors. He claimed that Kelley, Maus & Co. should have been aware of Morrison's financial deception at the time of their transaction, making them complicit in fraud. Kimbark sought a judgment confirming his right to rescind the sale due to these fraudulent circumstances, asserting that the goods should be returned to him.

In the case of Daniel F. Shirk v. The People of the State of Illinois, which took place in 1885 in Stephenson County, Illinois, Daniel F. Shirk was tried and convicted for the crime of uttering and publishing a fictitious instrument with the intention to defraud. The incident involved Shirk allegedly presenting a false document claiming to be a bill for the purchase of a marble gravestone from a non-existent individual, Morton Walldecker, to Harvey F. Perkins. The indictment was based on a section of the Criminal Code prohibiting the use of fictitious instruments for financial gain. Shirk was sentenced to two years in prison. He subsequently filed for a writ of error to review the conviction, arguing that the instrument presented did not align with the legal definition of a fictitious bill, note, or check as outlined in the statute. The core issue was whether the contract was a 'writing' constituting a form of a negotiable instrument. The Supreme Court of Illinois, while deliberating Shirk's appeal in May 1887, focused on the nature of the instrument involved.	The People of the State of Illinois claimed that Daniel F. Shirk had committed the crime of uttering and publishing a fictitious instrument intended to defraud Perkins. They maintained that the presented instrument fell within the statutes governing fraudulent instruments, despite acknowledging that it was not a bill, note, or check in the traditional sense. The prosecution sought to uphold Shirk's conviction and suggested that the terms of the statute should be construed to include various types of written contracts, thereby rendering the indictment valid.	Daniel F. Shirk contended that the instrument he allegedly published did not meet the specific definitions outlined in the criminal statute regarding fictitious bills, notes, or checks. He argued that the document was merely a contract for future delivery of a monument and did not constitute a promise to pay money unconditionally, as required by the law. Shirk's defense sought to have the indictment quashed, asserting that the prosecution's interpretation of the statute was overly broad and misapplied to an executory contract that included contingencies.

In 1885, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Arthur T. Howe et al. v. E. G. Frazer was initiated as an assumpsit action to recover a debt of $8,358.33 owed for a quantity of lime sold by the plaintiffs to the defendant. The defendant, E. G. Frazer, responded by presenting a plea of set-off, claiming a contractual agreement with the plaintiffs that entitled him to sell their Marble Head lime exclusively in a designated territory for five years. He contended that the plaintiffs had breached this contract, ceased to fulfill their obligations since December 1, 1880, and that he incurred expenses totaling $10,000 while creating a market for their product, from which the plaintiffs had benefitted, accruing profits of $12,000. The contract was also asserted to be in writing, although the plaintiffs denied this and challenged the validity of the defendant’s claims under the Statute of Frauds. The case had prior legal proceedings, leading to a jury trial in which the defendant was awarded $3,000, further complicating the trial dynamics and procedural motions related to filing requirements.	The plaintiffs, Arthur T. Howe et al., claimed that the defendant owed them for the sale of lime, asserting a general denial of the claims raised in the defendant’s plea of set-off. They contended that the alleged contract was not in writing, as required by the Statute of Frauds, and sought to have the defendant's plea struck from the record for failing to comply with statutory requirements regarding the filing of the contract and account, as well as opposing the validity of the jury's finding in favor of the defendant.	The defendant, E. G. Frazer, defended against the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that he had entered into a valid written contract allowing him exclusivity over the sale of the plaintiffs' lime. He argued that he had fulfilled his contractual obligations and that the plaintiffs had failed to honor the agreement since December 1, 1880, causing him financial loss. Furthermore, he claimed compensation for the value of the rights he lost due to the plaintiffs' breach of contract.

The case, titled "The Chicago Mutual Life Indemnity Association et al. v. George Hunt, Attorney General," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1889. The legal dispute arose in Chicago, where George Hunt, the Attorney General of Illinois, initiated proceedings against the Chicago Mutual Life Indemnity Association, a corporation established on January 13, 1885. The Attorney General claimed that the association had engaged in fraudulent practices and had failed to comply with statutory requirements governing mutual benefit societies under the Illinois Mutual Benefit Society Act of 1883. Specific allegations included the filing of a false financial report, mismanagement of the association's funds, and admitting minors to membership contrary to the association's bylaws. The proceedings were initiated after the Auditor of Public Accounts had conducted an examination and reported findings to the Attorney General. The case involved determining whether the various misconduct allegations warranted the removal of the association’s officers and potentially the dissolution of the corporation.	The Attorney General's main arguments included the assertion that the Chicago Mutual Life Indemnity Association had willfully submitted false financial statements, mismanaged funds intended for death benefits, and issued membership certificates to ineligible candidates, including minors. He claimed that these actions constituted fraud and violations of the law, which justified compelling the association's officers to show cause for their removal, or, alternatively, for the association to be dissolved and its assets distributed.	The defense argued that the Attorney General lacked the authority to bring forth proceedings without a sufficient initial report from the Auditor. They maintained that the Auditor’s report did not meet the statutory requirements, asserting that the communication to the Attorney General was merely a collection of conclusions without factual support. Furthermore, they contended that the membership of minors did not violate any existing statutes governing the organization.

In September 1874, the case of Charles B. Knox, Administrator versus The City of Sterling took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. The initial incident involved a man named Thomas who suffered personal injuries after falling into an excavation on a public street in Sterling. The excavation was made without permission by William Edwards, who was constructing stores on his property adjacent to the street. Edwards was notified of Thomas's lawsuit against the city prior to its trial. In May 1870, Thomas secured a judgment against the city amounting to $850, which was upheld by the Supreme Court following an appeal. Subsequently, after Edwards's death in December 1871, the city sought to recover the amount it paid to Thomas from Edwards's estate, claiming the sum as damages and costs. However, the county court disallowed this claim. The city then appealed to the circuit court of Rock Island County, where it was successful, obtaining a judgment of $1,174 against the estate. The administrator of Edwards's estate later appealed this judgment, and the central question was whether the cause of action persisted against the estate after Edwards's passing.	The plaintiff, Charles B. Knox, as the administrator of Edwards's estate, argued that the action initiated by the city was unfounded as it stemmed from tort law and therefore did not survive Edwards's death. He maintained that the judgment against the city relating to the public street incident should not impose liability on Edwards's estate.	The defendant, The City of Sterling, contended that they should be allowed to recover the damages paid out to Thomas because Edwards was responsible for creating the dangerous condition in the street. They asserted that because the city was not at fault, it had a right to seek reimbursement from Edwards's estate for the injury caused by his actions.

Charles K. Harland filed an ejectment lawsuit against Henry B. Eastman in Cook County, Illinois, seeking to recover property (lot 45, block 47, school section addition to Chicago) on January 3, 1882. Harland claimed title to the property through his possession and a line of conveyances from the heirs of Abraham B. Adams, who had been in possession since at least 1855 until his death in 1873. Following his death, ownership was claimed by his widow until her death in 1881. Eastman defended against the suit by alleging that a demand for possession had not been made prior to filing the suit and also put forth other defenses questioning Harland's ownership. The trial resulted in a judgment in favor of Harland, which Eastman appealed. The appellate court granted a rehearing and affirmed the prior ruling that the tax judgment on the property was invalid due to excessive amounts and an improper inclusion of costs.	Harland's principal argument was based on his proof of possession under a claim of ownership, supported by the historical possession of the property by Adams and his heirs. Harland contended that he had demonstrated sufficient title through the evidence provided and that since the parties were claiming independent hostile titles, no notice to quit or demand for possession was required before filing the suit.	Eastman's primary defense was the assertion that no demand for possession of the property was made before the lawsuit commenced. He also argued that Harland's evidence was insufficient to establish ownership. In addition, Eastman challenged the validity of the tax title that had been used against the property, claiming the tax judgment was for an amount exceeding what was legally permissible, rendering the tax deed void.

The case "Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company v. Enos Ayres" took place in Illinois and was decided on May 10, 1883. The central individuals were Enos Ayres, the plaintiff, and the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company, the defendant. The dispute arose after the railroad company constructed railway tracks in front of Ayres' property along Wallace Street, a public road. Ayres owned approximately seven and a half acres of land that had previously been ten acres, with limited access to the road due to the railroad's construction, which raised the ground significantly. The construction of the tracks cut off Ayres' access to Forty-ninth Street, shortly after he had sold a strip of his property to another railway company. Ayres claimed that the railroad's actions had unjustly restricted his access and damaged the usability of his property, resulting in financial harm. The case was tried without a jury, and after the court ruled in favor of Ayres, it was appealed to the Appellate Court, which upheld the judgment.	Enos Ayres, the plaintiff, argued that the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company wrongfully constructed railway tracks in front of his property, infringing on his access to the public road and causing significant damage. He claimed the construction led to various nuisances, including dust and smoke, and destroyed the street's usability as a public highway. Ayres sought compensatory damages to cover the financial loss incurred due to the railroad's actions, amounting to $3,000.	The Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company contended that their actions were lawful and carried out with the necessary permissions from local authorities. They argued that any damages experienced by Ayres were shared with the general public, and thus he could not recover for such general inconveniences. The defendant maintained that the tracks were essential for public use and that the damages claimed by Ayres did not warrant compensation under legal standards.

The case 'The Chicago Building Society et al. v. Elizabeth Haas et al.' originated on July 11, 1874, in Cook County, Illinois. Elizabeth Haas filed an original bill against the Chicago Building Society and Luther L. Greenleaf to prevent the sale of her two lots due to alleged fraud and usury related to loans. During the legal proceedings, it was revealed that her attorney, D. J.
