Leary, had acted without her consent by entering into a stipulation allowing the building society to obtain a decree for a sum much larger than what she owed. This stipulation, made in late 1874, was signed under the pretense that Leary had her authority, which he did not. As a result of this fraudulent action, the Chicago Building Society obtained a decree on December 14, 1874, against Haas for $24,785.56. Subsequently, Haas and her husband appealed, seeking to invalidate the decree based on the claim of fraud perpetrated by their solicitor and the society. They argued that their solicitor had no authority to compromise their interests, leading to a legally questionable decree that granted the society a larger claim than legitimately owed. The case progressed through the legal system, ultimately leading to a review by the Illinois Supreme Court, which had to assess the validity of the previous actions taken based on the compromised stipulation.",	The plaintiffs, Elizabeth and Valentine Haas, claimed that the original decree against them was obtained through fraud and collusion orchestrated by their attorney, D. J. Leary, who wrongfully acted without their knowledge or consent. They asserted that the money claimed by the Chicago Building Society was significantly overstated due to usurious interest rates, maintaining they only owed a fraction of the claimed amount. They requested that the court annul the prior decree, set aside the mortgage sale, and take a proper accounting of the actual sums due with lawful interest.",	The Chicago Building Society contended that the stipulation entered into by D. J. Leary was valid and had been made in good faith. They argued that the attorneys acting for the Haas couple had given consent through their actions and that the society had no reason to suspect any wrongdoing. Moreover, the society sought to uphold the original decree and the effects of the sale, asserting that the procedural steps taken were legally sound.",

Philip Fusselman appealed against Thomas Worthington in a case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1852. The case originated in Pike County, where William Fusselman was a tenant of Worthington from April 1849 until March 1852. During this period, Philip Fusselman lived on the premises with William's consent. Philip initially entered with the understanding that he was a tenant under Worthington. However, when the time came for William to vacate, Philip refused to surrender possession, claiming he had bought the land from a third party. The court examined whether Philip was right in his claim to possess the property despite disavowing Worthington's title. The court found that Philip's assumption of ownership and refusal to acknowledge Worthington’s title constituted a forfeiture of his tenancy rights.	Philip Fusselman (the plaintiff) argued that he rightfully possessed the property due to a purchase from a third party, which he claimed extinguished the existing lease tied to Worthington. He contended that this purchase warranted his continued possession of the premises contrary to the landlord's requests.	Thomas Worthington (the defendant) argued that as a landlord, he had the right to reclaim possession of the property since Philip had negated the original conditions of the lease. Worthington maintained that the tenancy was invalidated when Philip disavowed the lease and claimed ownership, thereby allowing him to pursue a summary proceeding for forcible detainer to regain possession.

In April 1859, the case regarding the settlement of the Estate of Seth S. Whitman was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court following the death of Seth S. Whitman, who left behind a significant real and personal estate. His widow, Matilda Whitman, along with two executors, Samuel Bennett and Hiram Whitman, were appointed to manage the estate. They sought authority from the Boone County Circuit Court to sell part of Whitman's real estate to pay debts and to support the family, as stipulated in his will. After selling property and accumulating funds for estate expenses, a conflict arose regarding Matilda Whitman's obligation to account for funds received. The Probate Court initially found a balance of $1,787.77 in her hands and ordered her accountable for this amount. Upon appeal, the Boone Circuit Court upheld the Probate Court's decision. Matilda and Bennett challenged this judgment, arguing that the will's provisions exempted her from accounting until their youngest child reached adulthood.	The plaintiffs, Matilda Whitman and Samuel Bennett, claim that the widow should not be held accountable for the estate's residue until the youngest child attains majority. They seek a reversal of the Boone Circuit Court's decision, asserting that according to the will’s clauses, the funds held by Matilda were not due for distribution until the specified time for the remaining estate distribution.	The defendants argue that Matilda Whitman is indeed accountable for the funds she holds from the estate. They contend that as executors, they have fulfilled their duties according to Whitman’s will and that the funds in question should be subject to court order for distribution. They maintain that the Probate Court correctly determined Matilda's liabilities and their finding should be upheld.

In September 1870, a legal case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court involving the Board of Supervisors of Stephenson County and Pells Manny, the owner of shares in the Second National Bank of Freeport. The case concerned the recovery of taxes assessed on Manny's stock for the years 1865 and 1866. The plaintiff, the Board of Supervisors, argued that Manny had an obligation to pay the taxes based on Illinois law, which mandated that every person or corporation must pay taxes in proportion to their property value. Although the assessment process was claimed to be informal and not strictly compliant with the statute, it was determined that Manny still had a legal responsibility to pay the taxes. The court was asked to review whether the payment of taxes could be recovered back, focusing on the legality of the assessment and the challenges to it.	The Board of Supervisors contended that Manny was obligated to pay the assessed taxes on his stock holdings. They argued that despite any irregularities in the assessment process, the taxes were lawfully assessed under the principles of equity, as Manny’s shares represented taxable property. The plaintiff sought to retain the tax payments made by Manny, asserting that they were justified based on the legal obligations set forth by the state’s constitution and revenue laws.	Manny's defense presented the arguments that the taxes were assessed improperly and that under the Illinois law and the act of Congress regarding national banks, the capital stock—not the shares—should have been subject to taxation. Manny claimed that taxing the shares resulted in double taxation and pointed out the alleged illegality of the tax assessment process. He requested that the court recognize the irregular nature of the tax assessment and allow for recovery of the taxes paid back to him.

The case of Lemuel Anderson v. Eliza Friend took place in January 1877 in Illinois. The dispute arose when Lemuel Anderson claimed that two of his large hogs were stolen, allegedly by Eliza Friend and her husband. Anderson reported his suspicions to the prosecuting attorney but was initially advised that the evidence was insufficient for a conviction. After receiving further corroborating information, he returned to the attorney, who then deemed the evidence adequate to initiate prosecution. Anderson subsequently procured a warrant for the arrest of Eliza Friend and her husband. They were arrested and taken before a justice of the peace, who discharged them after a hearing due to a lack of probable cause. Following this, Eliza Friend filed a lawsuit against Anderson for damages related to the arrest, alleging it was false and malicious. The defendant raised the general issue which led to a trial, resulting in a jury verdict in favor of Eliza Friend, prompting Anderson to appeal the decision after his motion for a new trial was denied. The overarching issue concerned whether Anderson had grounds for his claims and whether he acted in good faith based on the legal advice he had received.	Eliza Friend, the plaintiff, claimed damages against Lemuel Anderson, alleging that his actions in initiating the prosecution were false and malicious. She argued that Anderson did not have reasonable or probable grounds for believing that she and her husband were guilty of the theft of the hogs, which constituted malicious prosecution. She sought compensation for the wrongful arrest and its repercussions.	Lemuel Anderson, the defendant, argued that he acted in good faith and upon the advice of a reputable attorney after presenting all pertinent facts. He maintained that he had reasonable grounds to believe that his allegations were true at the time of filing the complaint. Anderson contended that the acquittal of Friend and her husband did not negate the probable cause for his prosecution, emphasizing that the advice from the attorney shielded him from claims of malicious prosecution.

The case of The Winnesheik Insurance Company v. George H. Holzgrafe took place in January 1868 in Mason County, Illinois. George H. Holzgrafe, the plaintiff, filed a bill in chancery against the Winnesheik Insurance Company, seeking compensation for a loss incurred due to a fire covered by his insurance policy. The summons for the case was issued from the Circuit Court of Mason County, but the service was carried out by the sheriff of Stephenson County, who served the summons to the President of the Insurance Company in his jurisdiction. During the hearing, the court ruled in favor of Holzgrafe, leading to a default judgment against the Insurance Company due to their failure to respond. The defendant then appealed, asserting that the Circuit Court of Mason County lacked jurisdiction over the case because the summons had been improperly served from a different county.	Holzgrafe claimed that he was entitled to recover damages for his fire loss under the insurance policy with the Winnesheik Insurance Company. He asserted that proper legal proceedings were initiated when the summons was served, and therefore the default judgment against the Insurance Company was valid, supporting his request for relief.	The Winnesheik Insurance Company, represented by their attorney, contended that the Circuit Court of Mason County did not possess jurisdiction in this matter. They argued that the service of the summons from one county to another was not legally valid, and therefore the default judgment issued against them should be reversed based on the lack of jurisdiction over the defendant.

John Farrell and Amelia Farrell were involved in a legal case concerning separate maintenance. The case was initiated in 1886 and came before the Illinois Appellate Court on May 28, 1888, following proceedings in the Circuit Court of Peoria County, presided over by Judge T. M. Shaw. The appellant, John Farrell, was accused of improper treatment towards his wife, Amelia Farrell, which included jealousy over compromising letters she received from other men. Despite his claims, the evidence suggested no proof of wrongdoing on Amelia's part, as she did not respond to the letters or engage in inappropriate behavior. The case was referred to a master to gather evidence, which concluded that Amelia was entitled to separate maintenance from John, who was found to possess significant assets valued between $15,000 and $20,000. John's cruelty was highlighted through threats and intimidation involving his gun, leading to Amelia fleeing in fear. The master's recommendation included a monthly payment of $20 for Amelia's support.	Amelia Farrell's primary claim was for separate maintenance from John Farrell, citing his cruel treatment and threats against her safety. She argued that the allowance of $20 per month was inadequate, given the evidence of her husband's financial capability and the distress his behavior caused her.	John Farrell defended against the claims by asserting that the accusations were unfounded and that the reported evidence was against the weight of the facts. He argued that his treatment of Amelia was justified and contended that the master's findings and the proposed financial support were excessive given the circumstances.

The case "The Gilman, Clinton and Springfield Railroad Company v. Jonathan Spencer" took place in January 1875 in DeWitt County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Jonathan Spencer, filed a lawsuit against The Gilman, Clinton and Springfield Railroad Company to claim damages for the killing of his hogs by the railroad's engines. The railroad was not subject to statutory liability for such incidents because its tracks had not been operational for six months. Initially, a judgment of $31.50 was awarded to Spencer by the Circuit Court, highlighting the railroad's potential negligence in managing its trains. This decree was contested by the railroad company, which initiated an appeal, claiming that the instructions given to the jury were flawed and led to an unfair finding against them. Specifically, the railroad argued that the court had excluded the necessity for the plaintiff to prove that the injuries could have been avoided through ordinary care, rendering the case particularly sensitive to erroneous judicial instruction.	The plaintiff, Jonathan Spencer, argued that the railroad company's engine was responsible for the deaths of his hogs. He sought damages, claiming that the company had failed to exercise ordinary care when operating its trains. He presented testimony from himself and another witness, noting the absence of warning bells during the incidents. Spencer requested compensation for the losses he sustained due to the railroad's alleged negligence.	The defendant, The Gilman, Clinton and Springfield Railroad Company, contended that they were not liable for the damages claimed by Spencer since their tracks had been used for less than six months, which exempted them from statutory liability. They argued that the plaintiff had not sufficiently proven negligence on their part and that the jury instructions were incorrect, as they did not require a demonstration that injuries could be prevented through the exercise of ordinary care. The railroad's defense requested that the judgment be reversed and the case remanded for a new trial.

David Hyman initiated a legal action against Sigmund Coen in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the case heard on June 28, 1887. The origins of the case traced back to transactions involving goods sold by A. Goldsmith to Coen, with the account assigned to Edward JST. Marks, who then transferred it to Hyman. The disputed items included diamond earrings and a gold watch, with Coen admitting to a debt of $455, but contesting the remaining amount. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Coen, resolving the conflict based on the evidence presented. It was determined that the jury was adequately instructed on the issues, and the court upheld the jury's verdict.	David Hyman, as the plaintiff, argued that he was owed a total debt for goods sold and delivered, including diamond earrings and a gold watch. He claimed that Sigmund Coen's admission of $455 indicated acknowledgment of a portion of the debt, and sought the full amount alleged in the account. Hyman requested that the court recognize his claim for the disputed sum.	Sigmund Coen, the defendant, acknowledged a debt of $455 but disputed the remaining balance claimed by Hyman. Coen's defense was centered on the notion that the amount of the bill was not correct and that mere silence when presented with a bill should not be interpreted as an acceptance of its accuracy. He argued that the burden of proof rested with the plaintiff to establish the correctness of the claimed amounts.

Upon the request of George Reddick, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case involving John Ross and Job Ross, the plaintiffs, in an action of trespass quare clausum fregit. The incident took place in Peoria County, Illinois, with the trial occurring during the September term of 1832. The plaintiffs were accused of trespassing on land described in the legal declaration by its section, township, and range. A significant point of contention arose during the trial as the plaintiffs proved that the trespass occurred but failed to demonstrate that the land lay within Peoria County. The county itself had been established by a legislative act passed in January 1825, which also defined its boundaries through public surveys. Given the legal framework, the Circuit Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $8 and costs. The case was characterized by the introduction of evidence from the Register of the Land Office, which substantiated the claim of pre-emption rights over the disputed land.	The plaintiffs, John Ross and Job Ross, contended that they had rightful ownership of the land in question and that the defendant, George Reddick, committed trespass. They introduced evidence from the Register of the Land Office proving their pre-emption rights to the property described in the legal declaration. The plaintiffs sought judgment for damages incurred due to the trespass, ultimately resulting in a court ruling in their favor.	The defendant, George Reddick, objected to the plaintiffs' introduction of the Register's certificate as evidence, arguing that it did not adequately demonstrate that the land was located within Peoria County, a crucial requirement for the trespass claim. Furthermore, it was asserted that one of the pleas raised by the defendant was left unanswered, which he argued should have a bearing on the case's outcome.

The case of The Pittsburgh, Cincinnati and St. Louis Railway Company v. James McGrath, Admr. was filed in the Illinois Supreme Court on November 14, 1885. It arose from an incident where the intestate of the plaintiff, Thomas Kelly, was killed when struck by a train operated by the defendant railway company. The case was based on claims of negligence against the railway company for the incident. The plaintiff, represented by attorney M. J. Dunne, sought damages for the alleged negligence leading to the death. The legal proceedings initially took place in the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Kirk Hawes, and were later appealed to the Appellate Court for the First District, which affirmed the judgment in favor of the plaintiff. A significant point of contention during the trial was the exclusion of a deposition from a deceased witness, deemed inadmissible due to the lack of opportunity for cross-examination. The court navigated various legal interpretations relating to negligence, particularly concerning the definitions of slight and gross negligence, along with instructions given to the jury regarding the care obligations of the deceased.	The plaintiff claimed that the railway company was negligent in their operations, leading to the death of Thomas Kelly. They contended that the company failed to ensure the safety of workers in the railway yard. The plaintiff sought compensatory damages for the wrongful death of the intestate as a result of the defendant's alleged negligence.	The defendant railway company argued that the plaintiff's claims were unfounded, asserting that the deceased had a duty to take reasonable care for his own safety. They contested the exclusion of a witness deposition taken before a coroner's inquest, arguing that it should have been admissible as evidence. The defendant also sought to establish definitions of negligence, asserting that the definitions of "slight negligence" and "gross negligence" previously given were incorrect and that the jury's instructions regarding the deceased's responsibility should not have been modified.

The case, "The Empire Car-Roofing Company v. Silas N. Macey," was filed in 1885 in Cook County, Illinois. The action began as an original attachment brought by Silas N. Macey, the surviving partner of Macey & Brown, against the St. Louis Galvanizing Company, a Missouri corporation. Macey sought this legal remedy for an outstanding debt claimed to be at least $2,500, based on a balance for goods sold. On October 2, 1884, a default judgment was entered against the St. Louis Galvanizing Company for $2,693.75, with interest accruing, though the company did not contest this judgment. The Empire Car-Roofing Company was summoned as a garnishee. After the initial proceedings, the garnishee answered a series of interrogatories regarding the company's assets but failed to provide sufficient evidence of a debt due to the Galvanizing Company. A trial ensued without a jury, culminating in a judgment against the garnishee for $1,499.50, which prompted the garnishee to appeal to the Appellate Court. The primary issues at hand involved whether the garnishee's defenses were valid and the extent to which it could contest the original judgment against the Galvanizing Company. The Appellate Court affirmed the lower court's judgment, leading to this appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Silas N. Macey, asserted that the Empire Car-Roofing Company had not accurately disclosed the assets of the St. Louis Galvanizing Company that were in its possession or owed to it at the time the writ was served. Macey's main argument revolved around the garnishee's failure to respond adequately to interrogatories regarding money and property that could satisfy the judgment against the Galvanizing Company. Macey aimed to establish that the garnishee was liable for the amounts owed and sought to recover the outstanding judgment.	The defendant, the Empire Car-Roofing Company, contended that the court lacked the authority to enter a judgment exceeding the amounts stated in the initial affidavit for the attachment. It argued that the original judgment against the St. Louis Galvanizing Company was unauthorized due to insufficient evidence of the debt. Additionally, the garnishee claimed it had a right to question the validity of the proceedings and sought to maintain that any evidence presented in its favor was not properly traversed by the plaintiff’s replications, thus establishing that its claims should be taken as true.

On September 1875, in Cook County, Illinois, John M. Adams initiated legal proceedings against Charles Gardner, claiming damages after Gardner collided with Adams' phaeton, causing extensive damage to the vehicle. The damage included broken shafts, a bent dashboard, and warped axles, leading Adams to file for damages amounting to $500 for necessary repairs. During the trial, Adams testified regarding the costs incurred for repairs, amounting to $17.50, and claimed the phaeton's value was diminished by at least $100 post-repair. The trial court ruled in favor of Adams, granting him the requested amount. However, Gardner appealed the decision, arguing that part of the evidence presented by Adams—specifically about diminished value and loss of use of the vehicle—was inadmissible based on the legal rules of pleading, which dictate that specific damages must be explicitly stated.	John M. Adams claimed that due to the collision with Charles Gardner, his phaeton sustained significant damage requiring repairs costing $17.50. He argued that the injury decreased the vehicle's overall value by at least $100 and emphasized that while his phaeton was being repaired, he incurred a loss due to its unavailability for use. Adams sought compensation for these damages in his claim.	Charles Gardner contested the judgment, asserting that evidence related to the loss of use and the phaeton's diminished value after repairs was inadmissible since Adams did not explicitly state these damages in his declaration. Gardner maintained that the only permissible claim was for the repair costs incurred, totaling $17.50, and not for any special damages not previously specified.

La Roy Griffin filed a lawsuit against Charles Larned in February 1883, in Cook County, Illinois. The case revolved around a promissory note, where Griffin claimed that Larned owed him money. During the trial, the jury delivered a verdict in Griffin's favor, assessing his damages at $1,467.88. However, a procedural issue arose as the jury's written verdict, which was sealed and delivered to the court clerk, omitted the word "dollars." The court later read the verdict aloud in court, including the amount, to which the jurors confirmed it as their verdict before being dismissed. This case was ultimately reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court, which evaluated whether the court erred in rendering judgment based on the jury's verdict. The key focus was on the validity of the verdict delivered orally and the implications of its written form. The Supreme Court affirmed the ruling of the Appellate Court, indicating the jury's oral confirmation in open court solidified the verdict's validity despite the earlier omission.	The plaintiff, La Roy Griffin, claimed that the jury had correctly assessed his damages at $1,467.88 in the case of the promissory note. He requested an affirmation of this judgment, asserting that the jury's verbal confirmation of the verdict in open court should be considered valid regardless of the discrepancies in the written verdict presented earlier.	The defendant, Charles Larned, argued that there were procedural errors regarding how the verdict was handled, particularly concerning the written form and its discrepancies. Larned requested that the court find an error in the judgment rendered based on an allegedly flawed verdict that lacked clarity due to the absence of the word "dollars" in the jury's written document.

The case "The Town of Pleasant v. Solomon Kost" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1863. It originated in Fulton County, where the Town of Pleasant brought an action against Solomon Kost for failing to fulfill a road labor tax requirement. Kost, a resident of the town and categorized under road district No. 2, was assessed for two days of road labor by the commissioners of highways for 1861. Despite proper notice for him to work, Kost refused to participate or pay the commutation fee. The plaintiff established its case by demonstrating that all legal requirements had been met prior to the assessment and that Kost had been duly notified. Kost defended himself by asserting that he lived in the town of Ipava, which was incorporated separately and claimed jurisdiction over its own road labor requirements. Both parties agreed to consider specific facts established during the trial, with the key legal question revolving around whether Kost was exempt from the road labor tax due to his residency in an incorporated town. The Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of Kost, leading to the Town of Pleasant appealing the decision.	The Town of Pleasant claimed that Solomon Kost was liable for failing to work or pay the assessed two days of road labor as required by the town's commissioners of highways. They argued that all legal procedures had been followed for the tax assessment, and Kost had been duly notified about his obligations under the law. The plaintiff sought to have the previous ruling overturned and for the court to enforce the labor requirement.	Solomon Kost contended that he was a resident of the incorporated town of Ipava, which had jurisdiction over roadwork within its boundaries. He argued that according to the relevant legal provisions, he was exempt from the road labor tax imposed by Pleasant for work outside the corporate limits of Ipava. The defense maintained that the law exempting incorporated town residents from such taxes was constitutional, and therefore, Kost should not be liable for the assessment made by the Town of Pleasant.

The case "Asa H. Danforth et al. v. Jacob Semple, et al." was heard in September 1874 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved included Asa H. Danforth and other plaintiffs who were the payees of a loan agreement, and Jacob Semple, the principal debtor, along with his sureties. The dispute arose from a loan of $1,500 made to Semple in September 1869. The sureties, Breese, Zeigler, and Fawcett, had no knowledge of an arrangement made by Semple to extend the loan's repayment period after the note's maturity. Semple, through the agent Merchant, made payments for six months' interest and an extension fee, which the payees accepted as part of a binding agreement. The sureties believed this extension should release them of further liability since they were not informed about it.	The plaintiffs argued that the arrangement for extending the time of payment of the loan was invalid since it was made without the consent of the sureties. They claimed that, according to established law, such an arrangement releases the sureties from liability. The plaintiffs requested that the court rule in their favor based on these legal principles.	The defendant, Jacob Semple, contended that the payments made for extending the time on the note constituted a valid and binding agreement. Semple argued that the sureties’ release was unfounded since the money (including the extension fee) was paid to obtain the extension, and the receipt provided a clear acknowledgment of this agreement. He maintained that this arrangement complied with legal standards and did not warrant the sureties’ release.

This case, titled "George E. Gifford v. Charles Wilkins, Administrator," was decided on December 9, 1887, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose from a 1881 promissory note for $600 dated January 28 and due two years later, made out by Charles Wilkins, the appellant, in favor of George E. Gifford's wife, Jane Spanswick, who is now deceased. Gifford, as the administrator of his wife's estate, initiated the suit to enforce the note. The appellant claimed a set-off of $800 for providing care to Gifford’s in-laws, Timothy and Priscilla Spanswick (his deceased wife's parents). Gifford contested this, citing the statute of limitations on the set-off claim and asserting the lack of consideration for the agreement to pay for boarding. The jury's verdict favored Gifford, awarding him $671.55. The appellant's motion for a new trial was denied, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiff, George E. Gifford, contended that the promissory note for $600 was valid and that he was entitled to recover this amount as the administrator of his deceased wife's estate. He argued that the appellant failed to substantiate his claim for a set-off related to board and lodging provided to Gifford's in-laws and that any such claims fell outside the statute of limitations.	The defendant, Charles Wilkins, argued his entitlement to a set-off of $800 for the care he provided to Gifford’s in-laws, claiming that this constituted a valid defense against the note. He sought to introduce testimony from his wife regarding the arrangement but faced limitations on her competency as a witness. Additionally, he argued that limitations should not apply due to the circumstances surrounding the debt.

In June 1874, a legal case titled "Jane McArthur v. Sarah E. Howett" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. This case originated in Illinois, where Jane McArthur filed a replevin suit—an action to recover personal property—against Sarah E. Howett for the possession of a sewing machine. The initial trial took place in a justice's court, where Howett was found guilty and thus lost the case, which prompted her to appeal the verdict to the county court. During the appeal, Howett claimed the suit should be dismissed due to the absence of a replevin bond in the documents filed. The county court dismissed McArthur's suit and awarded damages of $25.78 to Howett instead. This led to further litigation, including the assessment of damages, with both parties presenting evidence about the ownership and usage rights of the sewing machine. McArthur's legal team attempted to introduce evidence indicating that Howett had only acted as a pledgee of the machine. However, the court barred this testimony, resulting in McArthur appealing once again.	Jane McArthur, the plaintiff, claimed ownership of the sewing machine and requested its return through the replevin suit. She argued that the county court erred in dismissing her suit and in excluding critical evidence showing that Howett was merely a pledgee, not the rightful owner, which was pertinent to the question of damages for the use of the machine.	Sarah E. Howett, the defendant, argued that the suit should be dismissed due to the lack of a replevin bond in the relevant court documents. She contended that as the appellant in this case, McArthur had failed to provide the necessary paperwork to support her claim. Additionally, Howett maintained that her damages for the detention of the sewing machine should be assessed based solely on the value of its use, asserting ownership and opposing McArthur's claim.

Dee McReynolds et al. v. The Burlington and Ohio River Railway Company was a legal case filed in the county court of Macoupin County, Illinois, culminating on March 29, 1883. The case revolved around the Burlington and Ohio River Railway Company's petition for the condemnation of strips of land belonging to the plaintiffs, who were the owners of two farms measuring 256 acres and 420 acres. The railway sought to acquire a 90-foot wide strip from the smaller farm and a 66-foot wide strip from the larger one. In response, the defendants filed a cross-petition claiming damages to both parcels of land. The jury assessed damages of $404.20 to the smaller tract and $859.50 to the larger, totaling $1,263.07. The defendants subsequently appealed the assessment, arguing that the verdict did not align with the evidence presented, especially regarding the opinions of witnesses on damages.	The plaintiffs, McReynolds et al., contended that the railway's construction would cause significant damage to their farms, seeking compensation for the diminished value and operational challenges posed by the railway dividing their properties. They argued that the overall inconvenience and potential dangers from the railroad constituted legitimate claims for damages, which they believed were not adequately represented in the jury's assessment.	The defendants, represented by the railway company, maintained that the jury's assessment was excessively low and not reflective of the damages supported by substantial evidence. They argued that the opinions of witnesses regarding damages were variable and unreliable, claiming that the assessments should account for potential dangers and inconveniences brought by the railway's operation. The defendants sought a new trial based on these claims and contended the lower court's rulings regarding evidence and jury instructions were erroneous.

In September 1875, the case of John Warne et al. v. Byron Kendall was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, having originated in the Circuit Court of Kane County with Judge H. H. Cody presiding. The case involved a dispute over a writ of attachment that had been issued against a debtor, Kosina Brown. Byron Kendall, the plaintiff, claimed to have a judgment against Brown and sought to attach the property of garnishees (appellants), John Warne and others, who were alleged to owe money to Mrs. Brown. The core of the issue arose from the procedural irregularity wherein the issue was framed between the attaching creditor and the garnishees, rather than between the debtor (Mrs. Brown) and the garnishees. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff, but the appeal focused on whether this trial setup was appropriate and whether there was actual indebtedness owing from the garnishees to Mrs. Brown.	The plaintiff, Byron Kendall, contended that the garnishees were indebted to his debtor, Kosina Brown, and therefore requested that the court uphold the judgment in favor of his original claim. He argued that under the garnishment process, he should be able to hold the garnishees responsible for the debt they allegedly owed to Mrs. Brown.	The defendants (garnishees) argued that no judgment could be rendered against them, as they did not owe any money to Mrs. Brown at the time the garnishment process was served. They maintained that the issue should have been between them and Mrs. Brown, rather than the plaintiff, and emphasized that the transactions related to a negotiable note had been properly assigned to a bank prior to maturity, meaning they were not liable to Mrs. Brown.

Western Union Telegraph Co. v. Harris & Comstock is a legal dispute that arose in Peoria County, Illinois, involving a telegram mishap that occurred on August 10, 1882. The plaintiffs, who were grain and commission merchants, sent a telegram to the Paris Flouring Company in Portland, Maine, offering to sell ten cars of new oats at fifty-six and one-half cents per bushel. However, due to an error in transmission, the message delivered only stated a price of fifty and one-half cents per bushel. After the Paris Flouring Company accepted the message, the plaintiffs incurred financial damages when the price of the oats changed unfavorably. They later sought to recover damages from Western Union, claiming negligence in the transmission of their telegram based on the erroneous message delivered. This case was adjudicated in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision rendered on December 29, 1885.	The plaintiffs argued that Western Union was liable for damages due to its negligence in transmitting the telegram, which caused them to incur losses from the sale of the oats at a price lower than intended. They sought damages amounting to six cents per bushel for 9,187 and one-half bushels, totaling $551.25, which they needed to repay to the Paris Flouring Company. They maintained that the provisions limiting damages in the message blanks were unreasonable and against public policy, as they did not account for the negligence or misconduct of the telegraph company's employees.	Western Union contended that it should not be held liable for the damages claimed by the plaintiffs, arguing that the limitations set forth in their night message contract exempted them from liability for errors in transmitting messages, as these errors resulted from causes beyond their control. They claimed that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated that Western Union was aware of the critical nature of the message and thus, any damages claimed should be limited to the specified provisions in their contract concerning night messages.

On July 27, 1881, Archibald M. Rogers, in partnership with Dunn and Harvey, shipped five cars of cattle from Aledo to Chicago via the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company. Rogers received a permit to accompany the stock on the train along with his son. Upon reaching Leland, Illinois, around 1:00 AM, the train stopped with the locomotive positioned east of the depot, leaving the rear of the train several hundred feet away from the depot grounds. The conductor had gone to the depot, while a brakeman remained with Rogers and his son. After receiving information from the brakeman about the duration of the stop, Rogers decided to check on his cattle. While holding a lantern, he walked forward on the track, focusing the light on the cattle rather than the path ahead. Consequently, he fell into a culvert and was injured. Initially, a jury awarded him $1,000 in damages after remitting part of a larger judgment. The case proceeded to appeal, questioning the judgment based on alleged negligence.	Rogers claimed that the railroad was negligent, leading to his accident and subsequent injuries. He argued that there was a duty of care owed to him as a passenger and caretaker of the livestock. He sought compensation amounting to $1,000 after the remittitur, asserting that the injuries he sustained were due to the railroad's failure to maintain a safe environment for him to perform his duties effectively.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy R. R. Co., contended that there was no willful tort or gross negligence on their part. They argued that the plaintiff did not exercise ordinary care by failing to use his lantern to assess the conditions of the track while walking. The defense emphasized that since the plaintiff’s lack of ordinary care contributed significantly to the accident, it precluded any recovery for the plaintiff.

In September 1875, the case of Alphonso Yates et al. v. The Village of Batavia was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. This legal dispute arose in the Village of Batavia, Illinois, where several lawsuits had been initiated against the plaintiffs, Alphonso Yates and others, for allegedly violating an ordinance aimed at regulating the sale and distribution of intoxicating liquors. The plaintiffs sought to legally challenge these lawsuits by filing a bill in court to prevent the further prosecution of the suits and to question the validity of the village ordinance in question. The presiding judge at the Circuit Court of Kane County was Hon. Hikam H. Cody. The case raised significant questions about the jurisdiction of the court and the appropriateness of filing such claims in a court of chancery.	The plaintiffs argued that the provisions of the village ordinance that led to their lawsuits were unjust. They requested the court to enjoin the further prosecution of the actions against them, thereby seeking relief from what they perceived as illegitimate enforcement of the ordinance. They aimed to settle the legality of the ordinance and questioned whether a court of law or a court of chancery had jurisdiction over the matters pertaining to the ordinance's enforcement.	The Village of Batavia contended that the court of chancery lacked jurisdiction over the subject matter of the litigation. They argued that any defenses against the actions initiated by the plaintiffs could be effectively resolved in a court of law, where these cases were originally filed. The defense also maintained that the jurisdictional questions posed by the plaintiffs could not be waived by the parties involved, asserting that the court properly dismissed the case to allow it to be handled in a more appropriate legal forum.

In September 1885, in Clayton, Illinois, James F. Long entered a contract to sell a saw mill to Lothaire B. Cockern for $1,200. As security, Cockern provided a mortgage on a piece of land he claimed to own, although it actually belonged to his wife, Emily S. Cockern. The mortgage was to also include the sawmill. After some negotiations, Cockern added the saw mill and associated equipment to the mortgage in the absence of his wife. The saw mill was installed on the land, which was primarily valuable for its timber. The mortgage note matured in April 1886, but Cockern failed to make payment. Long sought to recover the mill through a replevin suit in June 1886, which initially granted him possession but was dismissed a year later when he could not settle satisfactorily with Cockern. Cockern was later found to have sold the mill to J.W. Metcalf, despite Long's claims of mortgage ownership. Long subsequently filed a suit for foreclosure against the property, seeking to prevent Cockern and Metcalf from removing the mill, asserting that it remained under the lien of his mortgage.	The plaintiff, James F. Long, argued that the saw mill should be included in the foreclosure because it was affixed to the mortgaged land and was part of the security agreement. He requested the court to restrain the defendants from removing the saw mill and other equipment from the property, for a receiver to be appointed for the mill, and for a foreclosure of the mortgage on the property, seeking any deficiency judgment against Lothaire B. Cockern.	The defendants, particularly Lothaire B. Cockern, claimed that the saw mill had been placed on the land under the agreement with his wife and did not constitute part of the mortgage since it was considered personal property. They contested the validity of Long’s mortgage concerning the saw mill, and J.W. Metcalf argued that he purchased the mill in good faith without knowledge of Long's claim, thus asserting his rights to the property.

On September 1869, in Cook County, Illinois, William Severin and his wife, Caroline Severin, initiated a legal action against William H. Eddy. Caroline sustained severe injuries after falling through a hatchway door on the sidewalk that was associated with Eddy's premises. The Severins claimed that the hatchway had been left in an unsafe condition due to Eddy's negligence, causing Caroline significant pain and ultimately crippling her for life. The case followed a prior lawsuit in 1866 where the Severins had sued the city of Chicago for the same injuries. The city won that case, leading to a judgment that the city should not be liable to the Severins anymore, and the city provided notice to Eddy as part of the defense. However, the court found that the prior judgment against the city did not preclude the Severins from pursuing a separate claim against Eddy for the same incident.	The Severins argued that William H. Eddy was negligent in maintaining the hatchway door, which led to Caroline's fall and injuries. They sought damages for the pain, suffering, and permanent injury Caroline sustained as a result of Eddy's failure to ensure the safety of the sidewalk's hatchway.	Eddy's defense relied on a plea that the prior judgment in favor of the city barred the Severins from pursuing a case against him for the same injuries. He contended that since he was not a party to the earlier suit, the judgment absolved him of liability. Eddy claimed that the Severins had already received a legal determination regarding the incident that should preclude them from making further claims against him.

The case of Seth F. Hanchett v. The First National Bank of Chicago took place in Chicago, Illinois, culminating in a court decision on January 25, 1888. The central individuals involved were Seth F. Hanchett, the Sheriff of Cook County, and the First National Bank of Chicago, which sought damages for alleged negligence. The background of the legal conflict stems from a writ of attachment issued by the bank against the Garden City Warehouse Company. The warehouse company was in possession of numerous goods, many of which belonged to third parties. The bank claimed that Hanchett, in his capacity as Sheriff, wrongly surrendered the attached goods to unknown parties, thereby failing to secure the bank's interests in accordance with the law. The allegations included that Hanchett did not adequately attach or keep the goods in a manner necessary for further legal proceedings. The case revolved around the interpretation and execution of the writ of attachment against a company that held property as a bailee.	The First National Bank of Chicago argued that Hanchett had a duty to secure the attached goods but failed to do so by surrendering them improperly. The bank claimed damages of $2,783.43, which it stated were lost due to the Sheriff's negligence in managing the attachment. They contended that the Sheriff was responsible for ensuring the property remained liable for attachment and that his actions denied them the opportunity to benefit from their legal right.	Hanchett defended himself by arguing that he acted under the guidance of the bank’s attorney and that his actions were consistent with these directions. The defense maintained that the goods in question were not subject to attachment due to the nature of the warehouseman's lien over the stored property. Furthermore, the defendant asserted that there was no negligence on his part as he followed the attorney's instructions, emphasizing that the money collected from the storage was not subject to attachment.

In 1869, in Illinois, Daniel T. Elston and others (plaintiffs) engaged in a legal dispute with Caroline Kennicott and others (defendants) regarding property ownership. The case involved claims pertaining to the payment of property taxes and title to a lot of land. The parties had previously faced the court, where a judgment was reversed and the case remanded for a new trial with additional evidence. The two parties agreed to submit their case without a jury, using evidence from both prior trials. A significant aspect of the case was whether the plaintiffs could prove they had paid the necessary taxes for a consecutive period of seven years to assert their claim under the statutory limitation law. During the trial, it was established that Hong, who had previously owned the property, testified to his continuous payment of taxes over more than seven years. However, the court had to evaluate the sufficiency of evidence surrounding these payments to rule on the claims. After reviewing testimonies and tax receipts, the court aimed to ascertain whether the conditions required by the statute were fulfilled, particularly focusing on whether payments during the owner’s tenure were documented adequately.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had the legal title to the property based on their continuous payment of property taxes for over seven years. They argued that this entitled them to the statutory benefits of adverse possession and requested the court to recognize their ownership of the specified lot due to their adherence to the conditions outlined in the relevant property laws.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs failed to provide sufficient evidence of uninterrupted tax payments for the required duration. They argued that the tax receipts presented were unreliable and did not adequately prove that all taxes had been paid as claimed. Consequently, the defendants requested the court to dismiss the plaintiffs’ claims on the grounds that the statutory requirements for adverse possession were not met.

The case "William Taussig et al. v. Simon Reid et al." was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on March 10, 1890. It stemmed from a contractual arrangement involving a guarantee made by William Taussig and others (the appellants) for debts incurred by Mrs. Mathilde Zuckerman, a retail grocery store owner in Chicago, who had signed a guarantee for goods purchased on credit worth up to $1,500 with interest. The appellants were involved because they had guaranteed payment for Zuckerman's debts resulting from these purchases. The relationship between the parties was established as follows: the wholesale grocery business (appellees) sold goods on credit to Zuckerman while relying on the guarantee from Taussig and the other appellants. Disputes arose when Zuckerman defaulted on her payments, leading to a series of uncollected debts totaling over $2,700, accumulated between the dates of January and November 1887. The appellants claimed they were unaware of Zuckerman's defaults due to a lack of notification from the creditor, which they argued deprived them of the chance to secure their interests. The case raised legal questions regarding the nature of continuing guarantees and the necessity of notifying guarantors regarding defaults.	The defendants, William Taussig and others, sought to challenge the judgment requiring them to pay $1,680.34, claiming they were entitled to notice of Mrs. Zuckerman’s defaults in payments before being held liable under the guarantee. They argued that the failure to provide such notice constituted a waiver of their obligation because it deprived them of the ability to mitigate any potential losses caused by Zuckerman’s insolvency.	The plaintiffs (appellees) maintained that under the law, no notification of default was necessary when it comes to a collateral continuing guaranty like the one in this case. They asserted that the appellants’ liability was fixed irrespective of whether notice was provided about Zuckerman's failure to pay. They contended that the terms of the guarantee were clear and did not require any additional verification or demand for payment to engage the appellants' liability for Zuckerman's debts.

In 1871, Albert B. Shannon and James B. Webb, executors of the will of Samuel L. Beady, filed a bill in equity in the Wabash Circuit Court to foreclose a mortgage on certain lots in Mt. Carmel, Illinois. The mortgage had been executed by William T. Page to Beady in his lifetime. During the proceedings, it was established that the principal and accrued interest on the note secured by the mortgage were unpaid since November 1, 1865, although Page had paid interest annually until that date. The mortgage documents were recorded, but they were later destroyed in a courthouse fire in 1857. James Hall, who purchased the premises, claimed no knowledge of the mortgage. The case involved multiple defendants who similarly purchased the lots without any notice of the mortgage, despite it being recorded earlier. The court, reviewing these facts, determined that the equities favored the defendants and dismissed the complaint.	The plaintiffs argued that the mortgage was duly recorded, which provided notice to all parties of its existence. They asserted that the destruction of the record by fire did not extinguish their rights or the notice encompassed by the recording. They contended that the original mortgage was sufficient to protect their interests and that the defendants' lack of knowledge regarding the mortgage should not negate the plaintiffs' claims.	The defendants countered by claiming they purchased the property in good faith without any notice of the mortgage and had paid a valuable consideration. They argued that the long lapse of time since the mortgage's execution and the destruction of the record should favor their position. Moreover, they pointed out that the previous owner, Beady, had notice of Hall’s occupation, which undermined the plaintiffs' assertion of entitlement based on the recorded mortgage.

Matthew Kingman filed a lawsuit against Patrick Harmon and others in the Illinois Supreme Court seeking to foreclose two mortgages executed by Harmon, acting as the guardian for William and Mary Boylan. The case originated in Peoria County, with actions occurring between 1880 and 1881. The mortgages were secured for loans made to the guardian, totaling $2,000 and $925 for two separate loans. William Boylan, the father of the children involved, died in December 1866, bequeathing his estate to his children contingent upon the youngest reaching the age of twenty-one. The youngest child, Mary, reached this age on June 30, 1888, long after the mortgages were executed. At the heart of the matter was whether the children were legally entitled to the property at the time the mortgages were made. The Appellate Court found the mortgages invalid due to the children's lack of title when they were executed.	Kingman, the plaintiff, contended that he was a creditor with valid security interests in the form of mortgages, executed by Harmon as the guardian for William and Mary Boylan. He argued that the guardian was authorized, under county court orders, to mortgage the lands for the benefit of the wards. Kingman sought foreclosure of the mortgages, asserting his right to recover the loaned amounts.	The defendants, including Harmon, contested the validity of the mortgages, arguing that the will of their deceased father established that the land could not be mortgaged until the youngest child turned twenty-one, which had not occurred at the time of execution. They claimed mismanagement of the child’s assets by Harmon as guardian and that the funds were not used for their intended purposes. Therefore, the mortgages lacked legal backing and should not be enforced.

In January 1868, in Macon County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Ira Stockton (the plaintiff) and Henry Churchman (the defendant), who served as a constable. The case was initiated by Stockton as an action of trespass, claiming that Churchman unlawfully seized property that Stockton asserted was exempt from execution. The property in question was taken during a levy executed against Stockton, purportedly under a valid execution captioned in favor of John H. Clark and others. Stockton claimed damages equivalent to three times the value of the seized property, invoking a statute meant to protect individuals from losing exempt properties. The case was eventually brought to the Illinois Supreme Court for review after a jury verdict in favor of Stockton was rendered by the Circuit Court, which also declined to grant a new trial. The central issue revolved around whether Stockton had consented to the seizure of the property without asserting his exemption rights at the time.	Ira Stockton claimed that Henry Churchman unlawfully seized property that was exempt from execution. He argued that the seizure was without legal justification and sought to recover three times the value of the property, as allowed under the applicable statute. Stockton maintained that he did not consent to the seizure and that his rights had been violated due to Churchman's actions as a constable.	Henry Churchman contended that he acted within the scope of his duties as a constable and that the property had been taken with Stockton's consent. He argued that Stockton had not claimed exemption at the time of the seizure, which negated any statutory penalty for the sale of the exempt property. Churchman requested the court to reverse the judgment against him, asserting that the jury's verdict was not supported by the evidence.

In December 1846, the case "Same v. Same" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after a judgment in the Circuit Court was rendered against a surety, Sans, based on a recognizance for one Jordan, who was to answer a criminal charge. The key individuals involved in this case were Sans, the plaintiff in error, and the People, represented by the Attorney General, D. B. Campbell. Following the Circuit Court's ruling, Sans sought a writ of error, contesting the judgment. The Illinois Supreme Court reversed the lower court's decision, allowing Sans to challenge the subsequent fee bill issued by the clerk for the costs associated with the appeal process. The fee bill included a variety of costs, and Sans moved to quash it, arguing that he was not liable for the fees charged.	Sans, as the plaintiff in error, contended that he should not be responsible for the fees included in the clerk's fee bill following the reversal of the Circuit Court's judgment. He argued that costs associated with certain services rendered on behalf of the People should not be taxed against him, asserting that he was only responsible for costs he incurred in the prosecution of his writ of error.	The People, through their attorney, contended that the fee bill was justified and that Sans should be liable for all reasonable costs associated with the prosecution of the writ of error. They referenced a previous decision (Carpenter v. The People) that presumably supported their position that Sans bore responsibility for the costs incurred during the appeal process.

David L. Hough initiated a legal case against Michael Coughlan and others in April 1866, which was originally filed as a bill in chancery in La Salle County, Illinois, and later moved to the Circuit Court of Lee County. The case concerned the specific performance of a contract for the conveyance of a tract of land. Hough claimed rights based on a bond executed on October 2, 1849, by Michael Goughian to Timothy Horgan, which Hough received on January 25, 1862, over twelve years later. Throughout the period leading up to the assignment, Horgan publicly disclaimed any interest in the land, while Coughlan's grantees occupied, cultivated, and improved the property. The Circuit Court ultimately dismissed Hough’s complaint, leading to Hough's appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, which reviewed key issues related to the long lapse of time and the established possession rights of the defendants.	Hough's primary argument was that he was entitled to specific performance of the contract to convey the land based on the bond assigned to him. He sought to enforce his rights under the contract despite the significant time lapse since its execution. His legal requests included the transfer of the land and an acknowledgment of his equity in the matter.	Coughlan and co-defendants contended that the bond was never delivered and that the assignment was taken with full awareness of their rights. They highlighted that significant time had passed without any action from Horgan or Hough to assert their claims, coupled with the ongoing occupations and improvements made by parties claiming title through a warranty deed from Goughian since 1851. They argued that Hough’s request for specific performance should be denied on the grounds of gross laches and adverse possession by Coughlan's grantees.

On January 14, 1878, in Cook County, Illinois, Sarah B. French filed a trespass lawsuit against Henry W. and Ella M. Savage, claiming that they forcibly broke into her home and unlawfully took her personal property. The plaintiff contended that this act constituted a trespass, which, under Illinois law, focuses on the breaking and entering aspect as the primary grievance, with the taking of goods only as ancillary aggravation. Following this incident, the plaintiff pursued a replevin action in a justice's court on January 15, 1878, to recover her property. This suit resulted in a judgment favorable to her, asserting ownership of the goods in question and awarding her nominal damages. The defendants responded to the trespass claim by asserting the replevin judgment as a defense against any further recovery relating to the same goods. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, where the legal interpretations of actions and judgments in replevin versus trespass were pivotal.	The plaintiff, Sarah B. French, claimed that the defendants trespassed by breaking into her home and taking her goods. She argued that the act of taking her property was directly related to the act of breaking and entering, thereby forming a single cause of action. French asserted that the defendants' previous replevin case judgment did not bar her claim for trespass, as the nature of damages recoverable in the two types of actions differed, specifically that replevin would not allow for vindictive damages.	The defendants, Henry W. and Ella M. Savage, defended against the trespass claim by arguing that the replevin judgment established a legal bar to any further recovery for the same cause of action, as the original cause was merged into that judgment. They maintained that the prior replevin suit, which focused on the recovery of the same goods, settled the matter, and additionally claimed justification for entry under a valid chattel mortgage held by them, which they argued allowed for the entry on the property.

John Yowell filed a trespass lawsuit against Jacob Braden and others, who were commissioners and overseers of highways, for entering his property and cutting down approximately eighty trees and saplings. This incident occurred in the fall of 1881. The case was tried four times, with the first three juries returning verdicts in favor of the defendants. However, two of these verdicts were set aside due to being against the law and the evidence. The final verdict was allowed to stand only because the court's ability to grant new trials on similar grounds had been exhausted. Yowell's witnesses confirmed the extensive tree cutting, which they estimated caused damages between $10 and $35, with an average of about $22. The defendants argued they acted in good faith under the assumption they were clearing a public highway, but no substantial evidence supported their claim of proper authorization.	The plaintiff, John Yowell, argued that the defendants unlawfully entered his land and caused significant damage by cutting down timber. He sought damages from the trespass, asserting that the cutting of the trees was uncontested and that the damages incurred were substantial. He maintained the defendants were aware of his objections prior to their actions, highlighting their disregard for his warning.	The defendants, represented by Jacob Braden and others, contended that they acted in good faith as highway officers, believing they were clearing what they thought to be an established public highway. They claimed the damage inflicted on Yowell's property was minimal, arguing that there was no malicious intent behind their actions and that they had assumed the legality of their actions based on their interpretation of the land's status.

In 1860, Daniel Ward filed a case against Joseph Stout and Samuel A. Summers in La Salle County, Illinois, over a dispute regarding a promissory note for $300 dated November 25, 1857. The note was for money loaned, and both Summers and Stout were makers of the note. Ward claimed that Stout was equally liable. However, Stout contended that he only signed the note as a surety for Summers, who was the principal debtor. Stout asserted that he had requested Ward to collect the debt from Summers rather than pursue him. The matter proceeded through various legal arguments regarding the sufficiency of the pleadings and the relationship between the parties to the note preceding the court's judgment.	Daniel Ward claimed that both Samuel A. Summers and Joseph Stout were liable for the debt outlined in the promissory note. He argued that Stout should be held equally responsible as a maker of the note and sought to recover the $300 owed plus any applicable interest.	Joseph Stout's defense was based on his assertion that he signed the promissory note solely as a surety for Samuel A. Summers, who was the main borrower and thus the principal debtor. He contended that Ward was aware of this relationship and failed to take reasonable steps to collect the debt from Summers, despite being notified to do so. Stout claimed that because Ward extended the payment term without his consent, he was discharged from liability.

The case "Christian Linck v. Walter Scheffel, by Next Friend, etc." took place in Montgomery County, Illinois, on November 28, 1887. The central event involves Christian Linck, a seven-year-old boy who was passing by the residence of Walter Scheffel while riding a hand-sled on a slightly inclined sidewalk. As Linck attempted to coast down the incline, Scheffel's dog attacked him, biting him in the hip. There was an attempt to argue that Linck had provoked the dog by either kicking it or attempting to do so just before the bite occurred; however, the jury found no evidence of this. They determined that the dog had a history of biting people, and Scheffel was aware of this behavior. After the jury ruled in favor of Linck, awarding him $75 in damages, the case was appealed by Scheffel, who claimed issues with the jury instructions, particularly regarding the measure of damages and the child's alleged provocation of the dog.	The plaintiff, Christian Linck, asserted that he was bitten by the defendant's dog and claimed damages for that injury. He argued that at the time of the incident, he was only seven years old, and thus should not be held to the same standards of care as an adult. Linck sought compensation for the injuries inflicted by the dog, asserting that the dog's biting behavior was dangerous and that the defendant was aware of the dog's prior aggressive incidents.	The defendant, Walter Scheffel, contended that the dog was provoked by Linck, who allegedly attempted to kick the dog. He requested that the jury find him not guilty of negligence on the grounds that the dog’s actions were a result of Linck's provocation. Scheffel also sought to introduce evidence showcasing the dog’s generally peaceful nature and argued that the jury should consider the behavior of the minor plaintiff when determining negligence.

In December 1842, in Illinois, the case of Zalmon Young v. James Bennett arose regarding slander. The plaintiff, Zalmon Young, claimed that the defendant, James Bennett, had made false statements accusing him of stealing wheat. Young alleged Bennett stated, "I know that Bennett stole [my wheat]," among other similar accusations. This case involved testimonies from multiple witnesses, including a key witness named Jacob Bruner, who testified about conversations with Bennett regarding the allegations. Bennett pleaded justification, asserting that Young had indeed stolen one bushel of wheat. The jury found in favor of Young, awarding him $250 in damages. Following the verdict, Bennett sought a new trial, citing improper testimony from Young's witnesses and excluding his own evidence. The court denied this motion, but Bennett appealed, seeking to overturn the verdict based on legal errors in the trial.	Zalmon Young, the plaintiff, claimed that James Bennett made false and slanderous statements against him, asserting he stole wheat. Young demanded compensation for damages caused by these defamatory statements, which he argued harmed his reputation. He presented witness testimony that supported his accusation of slander and objected to the exclusion of evidence that could bolster his case.	James Bennett, the defendant, contended that his statements about Young were justified, claiming Young had stolen wheat from him. He tried to introduce evidence to establish Young's bad character and a neighborhood rumor suggesting that Young was guilty of the allegations. Bennett sought a new trial, arguing that the court improperly admitted evidence for Young while excluding materials that supported his defense.

In 1877, O. S. Richardson and others (the plaintiffs) brought a legal action against E. K. Akin (the defendant) in the Illinois Supreme Court as stockholders of The Illinois Steam Forge Company, a corporation formed in 1857. Akin had subscribed to twenty-five shares of $100 each, fully paid in 1869. The claim arose from debts incurred by the company in late 1873. Akin moved to dismiss the suit on grounds of lack of jurisdiction, which the lower court upheld, citing changes in the law effective July 1, 1872, regarding creditor remedies against stockholders. The court had to determine whether a court of law had jurisdiction to hear the case when the indebtedness occurred after the enactment of new legislation limiting creditor remedies to courts of equity. The plaintiffs contended their rights were vested in the previous statute, while the defendant argued the 1872 act amended the legal environment that governed creditor claims against stockholders.	The plaintiffs argued that the prior legislation from 1857, which held stockholders individually liable for corporate debts, created vested rights that could not be altered without their consent. They maintained that the changes made by the 1872 act could not legally diminish their right to sue Akin for the debts accrued by the corporation.	The defendant contended that the court lacked jurisdiction since the debts in question were incurred after the effective date of the 1872 act, which limited creditor actions to equity courts. He argued that the plaintiffs were not creditors until the debts were created, hence their claims were not protected by the repealed rights from the earlier act. Akin asserted that legislative changes regarding remedies did not violate any vested rights, allowing the court's dismissal of the case.

James R. Long was involved in a legal case against The People, which took place in February 1890 in Jasper County, Illinois. The charge against Long was assault with a deadly weapon, specifically intended to cause bodily harm, under circumstances where no considerable provocation was evident. The case arose when Long sought a continuance in court, claiming that he needed additional time due to the absence of a crucial witness, Albert Hutson. Long asserted that Hutson could provide evidence that the complainant, Chezem, had previously threatened him. However, the court found the affidavit supporting the continuance insufficient as it did not establish that Hutson's testimony was necessary or credible. Moreover, Long's lawyer claimed that another attorney, James W. Gibson, was unavailable, which the court also dismissed. The original information against Long was lost, prompting the state's attorney to file a copy. Long moved to quash the substituted information, which the court rejected, affirming its jurisdiction despite the loss of the original document. After considering several assignments of errors related to the trial proceedings, the court ruled that no errors were found, and the charges against Long proceeded in the absence of the original information.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, focused on the allegation that Long committed an assault with a deadly weapon without provocation. The state asserted their right to proceed with the trial even after the original information was lost and replaced with a copy. They argued that the court had the authority to accept this substitute and that Long's motions to dismiss based on technicalities should be denied.	The defendant, Long, contended that the trial court erred in refusing his request for a continuance, arguing that the absence of a key witness, Hutson, compromised his defense. Long also challenged the validity of the substituted information filed by the state's attorney, asserting that there was no proper proof that the copy was a true and accurate representation of the lost original. His defense relied on the procedural mishaps he claimed deprived him of a fair trial.

In 1864, in Christian County, Illinois, Robert North filed a suit in chancery against Abial Pope and his wife, Catharine H. Pope, to foreclose a mortgage they executed. While both were named as defendants, only Abial Pope participated in the proceedings by confessing the bill's allegations. A decree was issued against Abial, directing him to pay the owed money, with the property to be sold if he failed to comply. Catharine was not served or notified during the proceedings, leaving her rights unaddressed and intact. The court had no means to effectuate any claims against her due to her absence from the litigation, leading to the decision that her rights remained unaffected by the foreclosure decree. Catharine retains the ability to reclaim her interest in the property through future legal actions.	Catharine H. Pope, the plaintiff in error, contended that the foreclosure proceedings were improperly executed without her presence or service, essentially arguing that the decree, which only addressed her husband, should not affect her rights. She sought to reverse the foreclosure decree on the basis that she was not properly a party in the case and that no default had been entered against her.	Robert North, the defendant in error, focused on the fact that Catharine was neither served nor involved in the court proceedings. He argued that since the decree did not overstep or encroach upon Catharine's rights, she had no valid basis to maintain a writ of error against the ruling on the foreclosure. Essentially, he maintained that the court's actions did not impact her legal standing regarding the mortgage.

In May 1872, in Chicago, Illinois, Cass F. Maurer leased the first story of a two-story frame building located at 113 West Washington Street from Samuel Glickauf and Joseph Lederer, who owned the property. Maurer operated a wholesale and retail cigar store on the premises. A short time before the incident, the defendants contracted a carpenter to install skylights on the roofs of the building and adjacent ones. The carpenter began the work on May 24 and completed the carpentry by noon on May 26. However, the roofers, who were supposed to cover the openings after the carpentry was done, failed to arrive, leaving the building exposed. That night, a severe rainstorm occurred, leading to significant flooding in Maurer's store and damaging his inventory. Maurer sued Glickauf and Lederer, ultimately winning a judgment that led to their appeal, arguing that they were not liable due to hiring an independent contractor.	The plaintiff, Cass F. Maurer, argued that the defendants were negligent in their duties as landlords. He claimed that they failed to adequately protect his goods from water damage after allowing work on the roof to leave the store exposed to rain. Maurer sought compensation for the damages incurred, which amounted to $1,133, claiming that the defendants should be held responsible for the negligence of the contractor they hired.	Glickauf and Lederer defended themselves by asserting that they were not legally responsible for the damages since they had hired an independent contractor to perform the work. They cited a legal precedent which held that an owner of property is not liable for incidents resulting from a contractor's negligence if the owner surrenders control of the work. They also claimed that the damages awarded to Maurer were excessive and questioned the trial court's refusal to permit testimony regarding the independent contractor's control over the work.

The case "Harvey Sandusky et al. v. Exchange Bank of John C. Short & Co." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1876. It arose from an action of debt initiated by Harvey Sandusky and co-plaintiffs against the Exchange Bank of John C. Short & Co. concerning an appeal bond associated with a prior judgment in the Circuit Court of Ford County. The appeal bond had been executed to secure an appeal taken by Sandusky following a judgment rendered against him. The crux of the case hinged on a plea made by both the principal (Sandusky), who had been declared bankrupt, and the surety on the bond. They contended that the judgment from the circuit court had already been affirmed and considered that bankruptcy proceedings absolved them of further liability. The court was tasked with deciding if the plea constituted a valid defense against the surety. The circumstances included the assertion that the plaintiffs had effectively collected the debt from Sandusky's estate through bankruptcy proceedings, thus releasing the surety from the bond. The court ultimately ruled on the validity of the plea and its implications for both defendants.	The plaintiffs claimed that the surety on the appeal bond remained liable for the debt, as the appeal had not been effectively prosecuted by Harvey Sandusky. They argued that the mere filing of the judgment in bankruptcy did not equate to payment of the judgment, as it was not an action that extinguished the obligation of the surety. The plaintiffs sought to enforce the appeal bond to collect the judgment amount.	The defendants (Sandusky and the surety) contended that the affirmation of judgment and subsequent bankruptcy proceedings were sufficient grounds to absolve them of further liability under the appeal bond. They claimed that, due to the bankruptcy, the plaintiffs were estopped from recovering any additional amounts against the surety. Their joint plea argued that since the principal's bankruptcy had been adjudicated, the surety's liability should be diminished or entirely negated.

In January 1866, Charles L. Hancock entered into a lease agreement with the Chicago Literary Association, a de facto corporation based in Chicago, Cook County, Illinois, for a term of five years. The lease included covenants for the Association to pay a yearly rent of $2,400 and maintain the premises in good condition. The agreement specified that the covenants were to be performed by the Association, which was represented by its trustees, including John Yunker, for the second party. By September 1876, Hancock claimed that the Association owed him rent and interest amounting to $3,212.33.
