At the heart of the conflict was whether the property measurements and conveyed titles were properly constructed, especially concerning the location of fences and the interpretation of the original deed. The case involved scrutiny over previous tax payments made by both parties and the concept of "color of title," which refers to documents that appear to confer a title but may not do so legally. The trial had elapsed since the original action was brought on October 26, 1880.	The plaintiff, James D. Sherman, asserted that he held rightful ownership of the six-foot strip of land, having acquired it through a valid conveyance from Augustus Garrett. He argued that despite never having actual possession of the land, his legal title was established through official documents. Sherman emphasized that the adjacent property owner placed a fence incorrectly and that his investment in tax payments substantiated his claim to ownership.	The defendant, represented by Bolden and Stevens, contended that they had made tax payments on the disputed land for several years, demonstrating possession and good faith in their claim to the property. They argued that the description in the deed they received, despite minor discrepancies in measurements, was sufficient to give them color of title. Furthermore, they challenged the credibility of Sherman's evidence regarding tax payments and the absence of supporting documentation to assert their ownership effectively.

F. M. Atkinson v. Frank Foster is a legal case presided over by the Illinois Appellate Court, decided on July 3, 1888. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, when Frank Foster, acting as a receiver, was appointed following a creditor's bill filed against F. M. Atkinson. Atkinson had a judgment against him, and after an execution failed to find property, the court appointed a receiver to manage Atkinson's assets. The receiver discovered that Atkinson owned 450 shares of stock in the Chicago Tyre and Spring Works, which he argued were crucial to the interests of the creditors and the value of the company. The receiver needed a proxy or written power of attorney from Atkinson to vote those shares at an upcoming stockholders’ meeting. Atkinson, however, filed a response claiming the debt underpinning the creditor's bill had already been paid. The case involved discussions of the court's authority to compel Atkinson to execute necessary documents to protect the stock's value amid internal corporate disputes and Atkinson's alleged indifference to the corporation's well-being.	The plaintiff, represented by Frank Foster (the receiver), claimed that without Atkinson's proxy to vote on the stock, the receiver could not adequately protect the interests of the stock or contribute positively to the company during a tumultuous period involving internal strife and rival boards of directors. The receiver requested that the court compel Atkinson to either provide a proxy to vote the stock or to directly issue new stock certificates in the receiver's name, emphasizing the urgency to ensure the stock did not become worthless.	Atkinson's defense was centered on his assertion that the judgment leading to the creditor's bill had been satisfied, and therefore, he did not owe any obligations related to the case. He also contested the need for issuing a proxy or transferring stock certificates, arguing that the claims made by the receiver were unfounded and insufficient justification for the court's intervention.

In February 1886, Elijah S. Alexander passed away intestate in Chicago, Illinois. His siblings, Josephine P. Waldron and Edwin Walker, were appointed as administrators of his estate by the Probate Court of Cook County. In April 1887, Serotia A. Alexander, the deceased's sister, filed a claim against the estate seeking compensation for 18 years of service caring for their elderly parents in Brattleboro, Vermont, a role she undertook under a verbal contract with her brother. The claim initially sought $18,000 for her services and an additional $12,299 in interest. After being partially granted $9,500 by the Probate Court, Serotia appealed to the Circuit Court, which ultimately resulted in a jury verdict of $41,800 after a remittitur of $14,953. The appellants contested this amount, arguing against the validity of the claim based on the statute of limitations and various evidentiary issues. The case focused on whether the deposit of her earnings with her brother constituted an ongoing obligation that exempted her claim from the limitations period.	Serotia A. Alexander claimed she provided substantial caregiving services to their parents under a contractual agreement with Elijah S. Alexander, who promised to compensate her. She argued that payments made over the years maintained the validity of the claim, making it exempt from the statute of limitations and that the payments he provided were acknowledgments of the debt owed to her for her services.	The administrators of Elijah S. Alexander's estate contended that many portions of Serotia's claim were barred by the statute of limitations, as they accrued more than five years prior to her filing. They argued that there was no written contract to support her claim and challenged the admissibility of evidence related to the value of her services. Moreover, they sought a reversal of the judgment in favor of Serotia, asserting that any payments made did not necessarily revive the specific debt she was claiming.

Philemon Cadwell v. Silas H. Sherman was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1867. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Lake County, where Silas H. Sherman, a minor represented by his next friend Joel S. Sherman, brought an action of trover against Cadwell for the recovery of two war fund bonds. Sherman claimed that these bonds, which he held as a minor, were unlawfully taken by Cadwell. The jury found Cadwell guilty and assessed damages at $226.12. Cadwell appealed this decision, resulting in a review of the evidence presented during the trial, including the question of whether the verdict was against the weight of that evidence. The court reaffirmed the jury's decision, determining that the evidence supported Sherman's ownership of the bonds.	The plaintiff, Silas H. Sherman, asserted that he rightfully owned two war fund bonds, which he claimed were taken unlawfully by the defendant, Philemon Cadwell. He requested the court to recognize his ownership of the bonds and sought to recover their value, which was determined to be $226.12 after a jury trial concluded in his favor.	The defendant, Philemon Cadwell, contended that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence presented. He appealed the decision, arguing that the case did not present any significant questions of law and sought a new trial on the grounds that the jury’s finding was unreasonable. However, he ultimately could not convince the court to overturn the jury's verdict.

The case "Nathaniel Smith v. Frederick Binder" arose in La Salle County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The dispute involved Frederick Binder, an agent for The Fireman’s Insurance Company, and Nathaniel Smith, who had engaged Binder to insure his property valued at $3,500. Smith paid a premium of $127 for this insurance. However, following the Chicago fire on October 9, 1871, both insurance companies Binder represented became insolvent. Shortly after the disaster, Binder informed Smith that he had not forwarded the premium to the companies and was holding it instead. Smith sought the return of his premium after learning the policies were no longer valid due to the insolvency. Binder initially refused to return the money, arguing his position as an agent protected him from liability. Subsequently, Smith filed a lawsuit to reclaim his premium, which was initially brought to a justice of the peace and later moved to the circuit court, where Smith won a favorable verdict. Binder appealed this decision, claiming the verdict contradicted the evidence and challenged the jury instructions given.	Nathaniel Smith claimed that he was entitled to recover the premium he paid to Frederick Binder since the insurance policies provided were rendered worthless due to the insolvency of the insurance companies. He argued that Binder, while acting as an agent, failed to forward the premium to the insurers and should be liable for returning the amount he had paid. Smith insisted that the circumstances surrounding the insolvency of the insurance companies released him from any obligation regarding the policies, and thus he should be entitled to a refund.	Frederick Binder defended himself by asserting that he was merely an agent of the insurance company and, as such, should not be personally liable for the premiums collected, especially after the failure of the insurance companies. He contended that the verdict was contrary to the evidence provided during the trial and criticized the court's jury instructions that favored Smith. Binder maintained he was justified in withholding the funds and argued that Smith's failure to surrender the insurance policies diminished his claims.

In 1843, Elisha Riggs initiated an action of ejectment against George Savage in the Warren Circuit Court, Illinois, seeking possession of a 160-acre parcel of land in Warren County. Riggs claimed ownership, but after a trial in June 1844, the jury found in favor of Savage, rendering a verdict of "not guilty" and awarding costs to Savage. Following this, at the November term of 1844, Riggs' attorney moved to reinstate the cause on the docket, which the court granted upon proof that the costs were paid. However, in November 1845, Savage's attorney moved to strike the cause from the docket, and Riggs' cross motion to amend the record was denied. The court subsequently struck the case from the docket, leading to Riggs' request to try the cause despite its dismissal. This motion was also overruled, resulting in a judgment against Riggs for costs. Riggs appealed, claiming multiple errors in the court's decisions regarding the reinstatement and subsequent proceedings.	Riggs contended that the circuit court made several errors, including improperly overruling his cross motion to amend the reinstatement order, wrongly sustaining Savage's motion to strike the cause from the docket, and denying his motion to try the cause after it had been struck. Riggs argued that the judgment should have been in his favor considering he had paid the costs and followed the necessary legal procedures as per the statute regulating ejectment actions.	Savage maintained that Riggs failed to make the proper motions within the required timeframe, asserting that the court acted correctly in striking the cause from the docket. Savage argued that since a year had passed without Riggs vacating the prior judgment, and no substantive action was taken to contest the ruling, the court's decisions were justified, and costs were rightly awarded against Riggs.

In the case of W. Scott Marshall v. Christian Yoos, taking place in Marion County, Illinois, in July 1886, the dispute centers around a cow owned by the plaintiff, W. Scott Marshall. The cow was in the care of Marshall's father-in-law when the defendant, Christian Yoos, acting as pound-master, impounded her. Marshall claimed ownership and sought the cow's return through a replevin action, asserting that Yoos had no right to possess the cow. The legal proceedings followed a complaint made to a justice of the peace after the cow's impoundment, leading to a trial in which the circuit court found Yoos not guilty, failing to address the return of the cow to Marshall. Marshall maintained that he had the rightful claim to his property, despite the defendant's attempts to justify the impoundment under local bylaws which, upon review, were not adequately followed by the pound-master.	The plaintiff, W. Scott Marshall, argued that he was the rightful owner of the cow and that the defendant, Christian Yoos, wrongfully impounded it without following the necessary legal procedures outlined in the local bylaws. He requested the court to restore possession of the cow to him, claiming that as the owner, he had the right to recover the animal on demand. Marshall asserted that Yoos, as pound-master, failed to adhere to the legal requirements for impounding property, which undermined his justification for retaining the cow.	The defendant, Christian Yoos, contended that he impounded the cow as part of his duties as the pound-master. He attempted to justify the impoundment by claiming compliance with the relevant bylaws. Yoos maintained that he had acted within his authority and that the cow was impounded legally, although he struggled to demonstrate full adherence to the procedural requirements mandated by law. Ultimately, he sought confirmation from the court that his actions were justified under the law.

In 1850, James B. Hoyne took possession of a tract of land under a tax-title and sold it to William K. Ware, who held the land thereafter through tenants. In 1857, Cratty acquired the patent title through a sale from the land’s original patent holder and simultaneously mortgaged the property to secure the purchase. By 1859, Cratty filed actions of ejectment against Ware's tenants, seeking recovery of possession, while Ware initiated foreclosure proceedings based on the mortgage held against Cratty for unpaid notes. A series of legal actions ensued, with Ware ultimately purchasing the property at a court-ordered sale in 1860. After a jury ruling against Cratty in 1861, he later filed a bill in equity to compel Ware to account for rents and profits, claiming the mortgage debt should be credited with those payments. Following Ware's death in 1870, Cratty sought to further amend his complaint. However, the circuit court ruled in Cratty's favor, prompting an appeal from Ware's heirs.	Cratty asserted that he had fully paid off the mortgage debt with the rents and profits collected by Ware during his possession of the property. He requested that Ware be required to account for those profits to apply against the mortgage debt and sought to have the foreclosure decree opened to allow for evidence regarding the rents. Cratty also aimed to secure legal title to the property through the court.	The heirs of Ware responded by contesting the legitimacy of Cratty's claims, arguing the mortgage was extinguished by a prior foreclosure sale and the resulting decree. They contended that Cratty's claims lacked merit since no fraud had been alleged, and previous opportunities to challenge the foreclosure had not been acted upon. The defendants sought dismissal of Cratty’s bill, asserting it lacked equity and grounds for relief.

In July 1881, Philetus Sawyer and George F. Harding filed a bill in the Cook County Circuit Court, claiming to quiet title and clear clouds from the title to lot 2, located in Cook County, Illinois. The defendants included Ambrose Campbell, who claimed ownership of the land through trust deeds dating back to 1868 and related sales. The case arose in part because land records were destroyed in a fire in 1871, complicating ownership claims. Sawyer and Harding contended their title derived from a quitclaim deed involving Alonzo J. Sawyer and others, but the court found their claims to be subordinate to the established titles held by Campbell resulting from valid sales under the trust deeds. The evidence demonstrated a clear lineage of title that traced back to Charles W. Clayton, and the court's consideration of past rulings and structures revealed a solid legal basis for Campbell’s ownership.	The plaintiffs, Sawyer and Harding, argued that they possessed lawful title and sought to remove any clouds from their claim to the property, contesting Campbell’s title based on alleged defects in his claims. They sought relief from the circuit court to affirm their ownership and question the validity of Campbell’s claims, which they believed were linked to prior trust deeds.	Ambrose Campbell, the defendant, argued that he held valid title through properly executed trust deeds and subsequent sales, asserting that Sawyer and Harding's claims were subordinate to these established titles. Campbell maintained that the plaintiffs had long been aware of their financial obligations regarding the trust deeds and had failed in their attempts to honor them, thus forfeiting any superior claim they might have had to the property.

On October 18, 1843, John Taylor filed a bill in Chancery against John Wright in the Circuit Court seeking to foreclose a mortgage executed by Wright on March 6, 1841. This mortgage was intended to secure three promissory notes totaling $672.08, due at one, two, and three years, respectively. While the first note had been paid, the second note was unpaid by the time of proceedings. Taylor claimed the right to collect the remaining amount, stating that he had made a payment to the State Bank of Illinois for the note after its assignment by Taylor to the Bank. Wright admitted the execution of the note and mortgage but contended that he retained the right to pay the debt using the depreciated paper of the Bank due to the assignment, which he claimed affected the value of the note due to its devaluation. The Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of Taylor, allowing him to foreclose the mortgage and recover the amount due. This triggered Wright's appeal based on the assertion that he should only be liable for the depreciated value of the note.	Wright argued that he should only be required to pay the specie value of the Bank's paper at the time it was advanced by Taylor, including interest from that date. He claimed that Taylor, having paid the Bank in depreciated currency for the note without his consent, had no right to collect more than the depreciated value.	Taylor maintained that he had the right to collect the full amount of the note and that his actions were legitimate under the circumstances. He argued that upon the assignment of the note to the State Bank of Illinois, he succeeded to the rights of the Bank and had the legal authority to enforce the debt. He sought to uphold the Circuit Court's decree that required Wright to pay the outstanding amount.

In the case of Seth F. Hanchett v. Charles Williams, the events unfolded in 1887, in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute involved Seth F. Hanchett (the plaintiff) and Charles Williams (the defendant), who served as a Sheriff. The conflict arose when Hanchett had four barrels of wine, approximately 220 gallons in total, stored in a liquor dealer's shop owned by Howe. Despite Howe's request for Hanchett to remove the wine, he failed to do so, and the barrels remained in the store. Subsequently, Williams, acting as the Sheriff, levied the goods in Howe's store under an execution against Howe and sold them. Hanchett sought legal recourse, initiating an action of replevin, which evolved into a summons in trover after the goods were not found. A judgment against Williams was rendered by a Justice of the Peace, prompting Williams to appeal to the Circuit Court, where the case went to trial without a jury. The Circuit Court found for Hanchett, affirming that Williams incorrectly levied Hanchett's property as part of Howe’s estate.	The plaintiff, Seth F. Hanchett, claimed that the Sheriff, Charles Williams, wrongfully took possession of his four barrels of wine while executing a judgment against Howe. Hanchett argued that the Sheriff’s actions constituted conversion, wherein his property was sold without proper legal basis. He sought a reversal of the initial judgment and reparation for his lost goods.	The defendant, Charles Williams, contended that there was no demand made for the return of the goods prior to initiating the action in trover, which he argued was a necessary component for a recovery claim. He also maintained that the details regarding the sufficiency of the transcript should preclude Hanchett's claims since both parties participated in the Circuit Court trial without raising disputes concerning the evidence presented.

The case of John D. McIntire v. John C. Yates et al. was adjudicated in 1882 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The central figures in the case were John D. McIntire, a creditor, and John C. Yates, who held a mortgage as a trustee for the Mechanics’ National Bank of Peoria and Kingman, Blossom & Co. The background involves a series of financial transactions and mortgages concerning T. J. McGrew, a partner in the firm Neill, McGrew & Co., which was indebted to the aforementioned banks. McGrew executed a mortgage to Yates for $75,000 to secure debts owed to the banks, while also arranging for notes with T. Neill, which were intended for investment in property that was never completed as planned. Subsequently, McGrew also executed a mortgage to McIntire to secure an individual debt after these transactions. The legal proceedings included attempts to foreclose various mortgages, with arguments revolving around the validity, consideration, and priority of these mortgages in relation to the debts owed by McGrew and the implications for the rights of his wife, Almira McGrew.	The plaintiff, John D. McIntire, filed a cross-bill seeking to foreclose the mortgage given to him by McGrew. He argued for a priority lien based on the grounds that his claim was for McGrew's individual debt, which should take precedence over partnership liabilities owed to other creditors. McIntire contended that the individual property of McGrew should be liable for his separate debts before any claims by partnership creditors.	John C. Yates, along with other defendants, contested McIntire's claims by asserting that the mortgage was valid and secure in accordance with the debts owed to the banks. They argued that McGrew could not question the validity of the notes due to his own actions, which presumably estopped him from raising certain defenses concerning lack of consideration or misuse of the proceeds from the mortgage transactions. They maintained that the mortgages were validly executed to secure essential partnership debts and that the decree should affirm these priorities.

The case of *The Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Co. v. Michael Conroy* arose in September 1873 and was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. Michael Conroy, the plaintiff and administrator of John Conroy's estate, brought the action against the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company, alleging that the death of John Conroy was due to a defective bridge managed by the railway company. During the trial in the Peoria circuit court, it was established through witness testimonies that the bridge, built approximately fifteen years prior, was in a deteriorated state. Despite prior knowledge of the bridge's unsafe condition, the railway company had performed only minimal repairs and failed to conduct a thorough inspection. The jury ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding damages of $1,500. The railway company subsequently appealed the decision, claiming errors in trial procedures and evidence presentation.	The plaintiff claimed that John Conroy died due to negligence on the part of the railway company, specifically citing the defective condition of the bridge. The plaintiff argued that the railway company failed to maintain the bridge properly, despite being aware of its deteriorating state. They requested damages for the wrongful death caused by this negligence.	The defendant, Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company, contended that the jury's finding of negligence wasn't supported by sufficient evidence. They argued that the condition of the bridge did not demonstrate that it was the direct cause of the accident, asserting that the train may have derailed before reaching the bridge rather than due to defects in the bridge itself. Additionally, the defendant claimed that any negligence could be attributed to a fellow employee, asserting that they should not be held liable for the actions of their employees in this context.

The case "Commercial Insurance Company v. Isaac S. Robinson" took place in Chicago, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. The dispute arose from a fire damage claim made by Isaac S. Robinson, the plaintiff, against the Commercial Insurance Company. Robinson held an insurance policy that included specific clauses about the company's liability concerning fire damage caused by explosions. After a fire damaged Robinson's property, he sought compensation from the insurance company. The case centered on the interpretation of the insurance policy language, particularly regarding whether the company could deny liability for fire damage that resulted from an explosion occurring elsewhere. The court reviewed the language of the policy and assessed previous case law, ultimately leading to a thorough analysis of the intentions behind the policy clauses.	Isaac S. Robinson, the plaintiff, argued that the Commercial Insurance Company should be liable for the fire damage to his property caused by an explosion, as outlined in his insurance policy. He claimed the policy did not exclude coverage for fire resulting from an explosion and stated that he had complied with the requirements set forth in the policy regarding the inventory of damaged goods.	The Commercial Insurance Company contended that the insurance policy explicitly protected them from liability for any fire damage caused by explosions. They argued that the interpretation of the policy should consider the specific language used, which distinguished between losses caused directly by explosions and those merely involving fire. The company also claimed that Robinson had not properly complied with the policy's requirements concerning the inventory of the damaged property.

On June 20, 1864, Robert W. Hyman, a real estate dealer in Chicago, and Edward Mott Robinson, from New York, entered into a contract to purchase land in Cook County, Illinois, for a joint account. Hyman took title but relied on Robinson for financial advances, including the initial cash payment and further costs like taxes. Following Robinson's death in 1865, he left the property to trustees under his will. Despite the original agreement, the dynamics changed after Hyman died intestate in May 1885, leaving unresolved obligations to various creditors, including a debt of approximately $100,000 to the Exchange National Bank of Norfolk, Virginia. The bank’s receiver subsequently filed a bill in the Circuit Court seeking a sale of the property, claiming Hyman's equitable interest and alleging that the executors refused to sell despite being tasked with this duty under the agreements. The court was compelled to consider Hyman's role, the terms of the contracts, and the fiduciary obligations of the surviving executors towards both Hyman's estate and the bank's receiver.	The plaintiffs, represented by the receiver of the Exchange National Bank, claimed that Hyman held an equitable interest in the land purchased under the agreements with Robinson. They argued that both Robinson and Hyman intended for their partnership to result in shared profits from the property, emphasizing that Hyman owed debts that could be satisfied by the property's sale. Therefore, they requested that the court compel the sale of the land and distribute the proceeds after reimbursing the executors for their advances.	The defendants, consisting of Robinson's executors, contended that Hyman had no legal interest in the land, asserting he acted solely as an agent for selling it on behalf of the partnership. They maintained that the contracts expressly limited Hyman's role to that of a service provider without ownership rights and thus opposed the sale, arguing for their discretion to retain the property until they deemed it appropriate to sell.

Ralph A. Gillett and Daniel J. Avery, for the use of Amos Smith, commenced this case against Peter Sweat in the Peoria Circuit Court in December 1844. The dispute arose concerning a promissory note dated November 14, 1838, where Sweat, along with Amos Smith, promised to pay Gillett & Avery $500. The plaintiffs alleged that they were entitled to payment based on this note. Sweat countered that he had already paid the note, and it had been improperly altered by removing Smith's name after its execution. Gillett and Avery, both parties in the case, testified about their lack of interest and their consents for Smith's involvement in the suit. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of the defendant, Peter Sweat, leading to further claims of judicial error regarding the admissibility of testimonies from Gillett and Avery.	The plaintiffs argued that they were owed the amount specified in the promissory note since it was signed by Sweat and Smith. They sought to prove that Smith's name remained relevant to the note's enforceability, contending that they followed proper legal procedures in bringing the suit and were entitled to recover the $500.	Peter Sweat's defense centered on the allegations that the note had been paid by Amos Smith, thereby discharging any liability. Sweat also argued that the removal of Smith's name constituted an alteration that invalidated the note's enforceability against him. Additionally, he highlighted that both Gillett and Avery had no legitimate standing to testify or pursue the claim as they were nominal plaintiffs with no stake in the outcome.

Charles Medler, a 69-year-old resident of Mount Carroll, Carroll County, Illinois, passed away shortly after publishing his last will and testament on December 31, 1882. His will included provisions for the distribution of his estate, chiefly to his friend Margareth Dunz, designating various properties including homestead, land parcels, a sum of $3,000, and all loose property in and around his homestead. After his death, an administrator was appointed, who managed the estate. Medler's sisters, who resided in Saxony, Germany, claimed they were the only heirs to his estate and petitioned the county court to distribute the remaining assets, aside from those specifically bequeathed to Dunz, alleging that Medler's gifts to Dunz were invalid. The case moved through the court system, being dismissed in the circuit court and later affirmed by the Appellate Court for the First District. The central legal question revolved around the interpretation of Medler's will and his intent regarding the distribution of his estate.	The plaintiffs, Medler's sisters, contended that the residuary estate, which included approximately $2,000 and uncollectible notes, should rightfully belong to them as the heirs-at-law. They argued that the gifts made to Dunz were limited to specific items and, therefore, did not extend to the entire estate, claiming disinheritance without an express devise. Their legal request sought to overturn the previous decisions and obtain a favorable distribution of the estate in their favor.	Margareth Dunz, the defendant, maintained that the will of Charles Medler clearly expressed his intent to bequeath all of his estate to her. Her defense relied on the presumption that a testator intends to dispose of their entire estate unless expressly stated otherwise. Dunz argued that the language of the will, particularly the clause stating “all other property of every kind,” indicated a comprehensive intention to include all remaining estate assets, thereby rejecting the plaintiffs' claims of inheritance.

In this legal case, Andrew Wettig appealed against a judgment made by the St. Clair Circuit Court, where John B. Bowman was the plaintiff in an action of ejectment. The case dates back to January 1868 and took place in Illinois. The dispute arose over land ownership, with Bowman holding the paramount title and Wettig claiming a tax title under the limitation act of 1839. The court had to consider whether the sheriff's deed introduced by Wettig constituted a valid color of title that could support his claim. The essential requirements under the act were that a claimant must show not only good faith color of title but also continuous possession of the land for seven years and payment of all legally assessed taxes during that time. Wettig was found to have not paid the taxes for the year 1858, which was critical, as the court determined that even if he had valid color of title and possession, the lack of tax payment meant he did not meet the statutory requirements to bar Bowman's recovery of the land.	The plaintiff, John B. Bowman, argued that he held the paramount title to the land and contested Wettig's claim based on the sheriff's tax title. He asserted that Wettig failed to meet the statutory requirement of continuous possession and the payment of taxes for seven consecutive years as mandated by the limitation act. Therefore, Bowman requested the court to uphold the judgment in his favor, affirming his legal ownership of the property.	Andrew Wettig contended that he had acquired color of title through a sheriff's deed and claimed to have been in continuous possession of the land for more than seven years. He argued that the act for the relief of certain persons in the American Bottom absolved him from the tax payment obligation for the year 1858 and that the assessment of the taxes for that year should be questioned. Wettig sought to overturn the judgment in favor of Bowman, asserting his legal claim to the property based on his possession and the validity of his color of title.

The case of William Welge et al. v. John D. Batty et al. took place in Waverly, Illinois, where the appellees, a milling firm, sold two carloads of corn to the appellants, a business firm in Hillsboro, on December 8, 1881. The transaction included the preparation of a sight draft for $600 drawn on the appellants by the appellees on December 16, shortly after the corn had been shipped. The draft was endorsed for collection by the appellees' bank, Waverly bank, to Haskell, Harris & Co., the bankers of the appellants at Hillsboro. After the corn arrived on December 24 and was weighed at $629.56, the bank presented the draft for payment. The appellants had enough funds in their account and directed the bank to pay, leading to $600 being charged against their account. Subsequently, they also sent an additional payment of $29.56 to the appellees, satisfying the total due for the corn. However, two days later, the bank failed, and the draft issued to the Waverly bank was dishonored. The case was brought to determine whether the appellants were still liable for the corn purchase despite the bank's failure.	The plaintiffs, Welge et al., claimed that the defendants, Batty et al., failed to pay for the corn sold and sought the $600 they asserted was due for the transaction. They contended that despite the failure of the bank, the defendants remained liable for the debt as the payment had not been validly completed.	The defendants, Batty et al., argued that they had made valid payment for the corn by directing their bank to charge the draft to their account, effectively discharging their liability at the time of the transaction. They asserted that since the bank held legal possession of the funds and was authorized to collect the draft, the risk of bank failure should not continue to place them liable for the debt to the plaintiffs.

In 1865, in Bloomington, Illinois, a division occurred within a Presbyterian church that had been established in 1833. The congregation initially attached to the "new school" denomination switched to the "old school" in 1848. However, in 1865, a significant majority of the church voted to return to the "new school." A dissenting minority that preferred the "old school" elected new trustees and filed a bill in chancery against the trustees elected by the majority, claiming that the church property rightfully belonged to them. The circuit court assessed the number of members and pew-holders, decreeing a sale of the property with provisions for purchase by either party, and determined the financial shares of both groups. Disputes arose over the legitimacy of votes and the voting rights of non-church members, leading to appeals and cross-errors from both parties regarding the court's decisions on property rights and voting rules.	The plaintiffs (the minority group) argue that their rights to the church property should be upheld, emphasizing that a majority cannot abandon their religious tenets and still control property dedicated to their faith. They assert their right as the original trustees to maintain control over the property they believe is rightfully theirs.	The defendants (the majority group) counter that the withdrawal from the old school denomination was a legitimate action that did not constitute an abandonment of the church's original beliefs. They argue that the property, which had been acquired under varying affiliations, should be divided equitably based on membership contributions, including pew-holders, irrespective of their formal church membership status.

In 1886, the case of Robert Stubblefield v. Pelig Soule took place in McLean County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a lease agreement between the plaintiff, Robert Stubblefield, and the defendant, Pelig Soule. The plaintiff claimed that the premises leased to the defendant were in good repair when the lease began. However, he asserted that the defendant failed to uphold their end of the agreement by damaging the property and neglecting to maintain certain aspects as stipulated in the lease, such as trimming hedges and removing manure. The defendant countered by claiming that prior to signing the lease, the plaintiff misrepresented the condition of the property's roof, stating it was in good condition when it was, in fact, leaky. The leak purportedly caused damage to the defendant's furniture and carpets, which led to the defendant vacating the premises before the lease term ended. The trial court excluded this evidence from consideration, leading the defendant to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, Robert Stubblefield, claimed that Pelig Soule failed to maintain the leased property as required by the lease agreement. He argued that the premises were left damaged during Soule's tenancy and requested damages for the breach of lease covenants.	The defendant, Pelig Soule, argued that prior to entering the lease, Stubblefield misrepresented the condition of the roof as being good, when it was not. Soule asserted that this misrepresentation resulted in damage to his belongings, and he should be allowed to present evidence of this fraud as a recoupment against Stubblefield's claims.

This case, "Horace Billings v. Kankakee Coal Company," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1873. The dispute concerns tracts of land located in Will County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Horace Billings, initiated an action of ejectment to regain possession of specific land parcels. He claimed ownership derived from the United States. The defendant, Kankakee Coal Company, countered with a tax deed they had received from the sheriff in 1848, which documented a tax sale from 1842. This sale had resulted from unpaid taxes on the land for 1841, and the defendant asserted that the deed provided a legitimate chain of title, asserting continuous tax payments from 1848 to 1854 by James Hervey, who had acquired the land through the sheriff's sale in 1848. The defendant's position included claims that the land description in the deed was sufficient and asserted that the conveyance was made in good faith, despite challenges concerning the deed's validity because it named a person who had passed away by the time of the deed's execution.	Horace Billings argued that he was the rightful owner of the tracts of land, having title traced back to the United States. He contended that the tax deed produced by the defendant was inadequate as a legitimate claim to the property, bringing into question issues of good faith and the sufficiency of the property description in the deed. Billings sought a court ruling to recognize his claim and restore his possession of the land.	The Kankakee Coal Company defended its claim by presenting a tax deed obtained from a sheriff's sale, contending that it constituted valid color of title. They asserted that any ambiguities in the description of the land could be clarified through evidence, connecting the land to Will County. The defendant argued that the tax payments made over several years were indicative of good faith and challenged the sufficiency of Billings's claims to ownership. They maintained that the deed was valid even though it named a deceased individual, as it was executed with the intent of transferring rights to James Hervey, who was connected to the property.

The case of Springfield Marine and Fire Insurance Company v. John L. Tincher and Joseph G. English took place in 1861 in Springfield, Illinois. It arose from a financial dispute between the insurance company, acting as the plaintiff in error, and the defendants, Tincher and English. The central issue was related to a draft or bill of exchange issued by the insurance company for the amount of $610.30, which was supposed to be paid in "currency." The plaintiffs presented evidence that this draft was not honored by the banking firm H. A. Tucker & Co. due to their refusal to pay in depreciated currency worth about sixty-five cents to the dollar at the time of presentation on June 5, 1861. The plaintiffs claimed that the refusal constituted a dishonor of the draft, leading to a legal action for the owed amount. The defendants argued that the draft's holder failed to present it within a reasonable time, specifically arguing that early June was too late and that the expected funds were available until May 18, 1861.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants dishonored a currency draft due to their refusal to pay it in appropriate funds and demanded the payment of $730.44. They asserted that they had adequately presented the draft for payment within a reasonable timeframe. The plaintiffs argued that the terms of the draft required payment in currency that passed at par as cash and that the defendants had failed to honor that obligation, leading to damages they seek through their legal claim.	The defendants contended that the plaintiff, as the holder of the draft, did not act with due diligence by presenting the draft too late, after a significant depreciation in the currency had occurred. They asserted that if the draft had been presented by the end of May, it could have been paid in full value. They sought to demonstrate that, due to this delay, the drawee sustained a loss that should negate the plaintiff's claim for damages.

John Frink and another individual filed a case against Jacob Darst concerning the possession of certain land in Peoria, Illinois. The matter was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, where the action of ejectment was initiated by Frink and Walker against Darst. The case was tried at the May term of 1852 in the Peoria Circuit Court, with Judge Kellogg presiding. The plaintiffs argued over the implications of a quitclaim deed made by John L. Bogardus to Isaac Underhill, which purported to convey all of Bogardus's rights and interests in a specified parcel of land, including a ferry. The core issue was whether the deed could transfer any title acquired by Bogardus after the deed was executed, given that Bogardus had no interest in the land at the time of the transaction. The circuit court ruled in favor of Darst, prompting Frink and Walker to seek a writ of error to the Illinois Supreme Court for further consideration on this legal point.	The plaintiffs, Frink and Walker, claimed that the quitclaim deed executed by John L. Bogardus should vest any subsequently acquired title to the land in Isaac Underhill, as they argued that the deed conveyed a full interest in the property. They requested that the court overturn the lower court's judgment and recognize their rightful claim to the land based on the implications of the prior deed.	Jacob Darst, the defendant, maintained that the quitclaim deed in question did not transfer any interest to Underhill because Bogardus had no title at the time of the execution. He argued that the deed merely conveyed whatever interest Bogardus had, which was none, thus any later-acquired title by Bogardus could not be claimed by Underhill. Darst requested that the court uphold the lower court ruling in his favor.

Frederick Koch, Sr. and Mary E. Quick were involved in a legal dispute that was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on March 1, 1889. The case originated from a contract between John Pruitt and the drainage commissioners of the Columbia Drainage and Levee District No. 3 in Monroe County, Illinois, for work that Pruitt had performed. Pruitt had instructed the commissioners to issue bonds worth $552 to Quick against the amount owed to him for his labor. After presenting this order, Quick was assured by the commissioners that she would receive the payment owed to Pruitt upon the determination of the final measurement of his work. However, Pruitt soon ceased work and left the state, leaving a balance of $316.80 due for his labor. Koch, a commissioner, claimed acknowledgment of the amount owed to him instead. The subsequent trial in the Circuit Court of Monroe County found in favor of Quick, leading Koch to appeal the decision.	Mary E. Quick claimed that she was entitled to the bonds and money owed from the work done by John Pruitt, as instructed by the drainage commissioners. She argued that the order given to commissioners represented an equitable assignment of funds in her favor and that she should receive the amount due to Pruitt without dispute. Quick requested the court to affirm her right to recover the payment for the labor performed and sought a judgment in her favor for the sum of $327, which included interest.	Frederick Koch contended that the action should be dismissed, arguing that Quick misconceived her cause of action and that only the legal title holder of the bonds, which he claimed were actually delivered to him, could sue. Koch asserted that the trial court erred in allowing Quick's claim and that the amount she sought was excessive and unsupported by evidence. He argued that since he did not receive any funds belonging to Quick directly but rather the bonds originally issued to Pruitt, Quick was not entitled to recover under the current form of action.

The case "Chicago and Alton Railroad Company v. Elsie Bragonier, Adm’x" took place before the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision filed on September 28, 1883. It arose from McLean County, Illinois, involving the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company and the administrator of the estate of a deceased employee, Elsie Bragonier. The plaintiff claimed damages due to the death of Bragonier's husband, who suffered fatal injuries while coupling railroad cars. The pivotal issue was determining whether the railroad company was liable for the injuries, focusing on the distinction between potential negligence on the company's part and actions attributable to fellow employees, which would exempt the company from liability. An earlier decision had been reversed by this court, which emphasized the need for clarity regarding the responsibilities of the railroad and the actions of its employees. A significant error in the most recent trial occurred when the plaintiff's counsel introduced an article disparaging railroad companies, leading to an argument about its prejudicial impact on the jury's impartiality.	The plaintiff, Elsie Bragonier, sought damages for the death of her husband, claiming that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was liable due to negligence. She argued that her husband's fatal injuries occurred while he was performing duties in the railroad's service, specifically relating to a defect in the equipment he was using at the time of the incident, namely, the brake rod. The plaintiff contended that the railroad company failed to ensure the safety of its employees and claimed the introduction of an irrelevant article during trial was improper.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company defended itself against the claims by arguing that the injuries were caused by the actions of a fellow employee, which would absolve the company of liability under the doctrine of fellow servant rule. They contended that the plaintiff's portrayal of the company’s negligence was unfounded and that the injury resulted from the deceased's own failure to check the brake equipment prior to use, thus mitigating any responsibility of the railroad company. They also objected to the introduction of prejudicial articles during the trial.

In September 1874, the case of Herman Heiman v. Theodore Schrœder was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a trial in the circuit court of Cook County. The central issue involved a suit to enforce a mechanic’s lien initiated by Herman Heiman against Theodore Schrœder. Heiman alleged that he had been hindered and prevented from completing contracted work on Schrœder's property, which he had commenced under a written agreement specifying payments for the work. A jury trial resulted in a verdict and judgment favoring Heiman, prompting Schrœder to appeal the decision. The appellant contended that the jury instructions were erroneous and questioned the sufficiency of the pleadings regarding the duration of the work and payment periods as mandated by statute. The court evaluated the instructions given to the jury and the details of the written agreement underpinning Heiman’s claims, assessing whether valid legal grounds existed for recovery under the mechanic's lien statute.	The plaintiff, Herman Heiman, claimed that he was entitled to recover for work done under a contract despite the work not being entirely completed due to interference from the defendant. He sought the full amount alleged to be owed for the work performed, along with interest as stipulated by the contract. He argued that his plea adequately encompassed the legal interest on funds due, even if not explicitly claimed in the petition.	The defendant, Theodore Schrœder, countered the claims by asserting that Heiman could not recover for work that was incomplete, arguing the jury instructions misled the jury regarding this point. Additionally, Schrœder contended that the plaintiff's petition lacked sufficient averments concerning the timing of the work completion and payment, which were required under statutory provisions.

The case "Jonathan L. Christie et al. v. Thomas Hale" was decided in September 1867 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated in the De Kalb Circuit Court, where Thomas Hale filed a bill in chancery against several defendants, including Jonathan L. Christie and Harman K. Wells, to prevent the sheriff from selling certain land under an execution. The background involves a series of transactions related to 160 acres of land in De Kalb County, which was initially conveyed by James L. Ball to Thomas Hale in January 1854 to secure debts owed by Ball and his brother. Although this deed appeared absolute, Hale had also provided a memorandum indicating its purpose as security for the debt. When debts remained unpaid, Hale sought to foreclose the mortgage in 1855. A subsequent judgment by Otis and Ogden against the Balls led to complex interactions involving new mortgages and foreclosures. Eventually, Hale obtained a sheriff’s deed following his judgment, while Christie and Wells sought to enforce their claims to the land under their judgment for the Balls. Hale disputed these claims, leading to the current injunction suit to clarify ownership and restrain the defendants from acting on their judgment execution.	Thomas Hale, the plaintiff, argued that he held a valid mortgage on the property that took priority over the claims of the defendants, Christie and Wells. He sought an injunction to prevent the defendants from selling the land under their execution, asserting that his rights to the property were superior due to prior transactions and that any attempt by the defendants would unjustly cloud his title.	The defendants, Christie and Wells, contended that they had acquired a valid judgment lien against the property through their actions following the judgment against the Balls. They argued that Hale's re-conveyance of the property and subsequent mortgage could not diminish their rights under their judgment, and therefore, they should be allowed to proceed with the sale of the land under execution as they had a legitimate claim to it.

The case "Frey Brothers v. Harrison & Atchison and J. H. Harrison" was decided on November 23, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. It arose in McLean County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs, Frey Brothers, initiated a replevin action to recover goods they claimed were obtained through fraudulent representations made by the defendants, Harrison & Atchison, along with J. H. Harrison. The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants sold the goods to J. H. Harrison to satisfy a debt, despite their claim that the sale was invalid due to the fraud. The court conducted a trial without a jury, where the plaintiffs argued that J. H. Harrison was aware of the fraudulent nature of the transaction, which should have nullified his title to the goods. However, the court found against the plaintiffs' claims, as it determined that the evidence did not support the allegation that J. H. Harrison had the requisite notice of the fraud that could undermine his ownership of the goods.	The plaintiffs asserted that they were entitled to recover the goods because those items were obtained fraudulently by the defendants. They contended that the subsequent sale of the goods to J. H. Harrison was void due to the fraudulent misrepresentations and that J. H. Harrison had notice of the fraud, which should have prevented him from obtaining valid title to the goods. The plaintiffs requested the court to disaffirm the sale made by the defendants to J. H. Harrison and to restore possession of the goods to them.	The defendants refuted the plaintiffs' claims by arguing that J. H. Harrison purchased the goods in good faith and without knowledge of any fraud. They contended that the evidence presented did not prove that J. H. Harrison had notice of the alleged misrepresentations at the time of purchase, thereby validating the transaction. The defendants requested the court to uphold the sale to J. H. Harrison and dismiss the plaintiffs' claims.

The case of The Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Co. v. Thomas Sweeney took place in April 1866 in Iroquois County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included Thomas Sweeney, the plaintiff, who had livestock that was killed, and the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company, the defendant, accused of negligence. The incident arose when Sweeney's cattle were killed after they wandered onto the railway tracks. The railway company had not fenced the railway, which led to the cattle accessing the tracks. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court following a verdict rendered in favor of the plaintiff in the lower court, challenging the necessity of fencing given the presence of an embankment along the railway.	The plaintiff, Thomas Sweeney, claimed damages for the loss of cattle killed by the railway. He argued that the railway company was negligent for not fencing the railway, as evidenced by the presence of the cattle on the tracks. Sweeney sought compensation for the full value of the cattle, highlighting that they were found in a state unfit for beef due to the warm weather, which contributed to their swollen condition when located.	The defendant, Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Co., contended that there was no need for fencing due to the 12 to 20-foot high embankment along the railway, suggesting this should have prevented cattle from accessing the tracks. They argued that the damages claimed were excessive and sought to have the judgment against them reversed, asserting that the fencing requirement was not justified in this context.

Absalom Nixon was indicted for assault with the intent to commit murder against Adam, a man of color, who was described as a deformed person unable to move or communicate effectively. The incident occurred on October 23, 1838, in Wayne County, Illinois. Nixon allegedly forced Adam out of a wagon onto the freezing ground and left him there, exhibiting malicious intent to kill. The case was tried at the April term of the White Circuit Court in 1839, where Nixon was convicted and sentenced to seven years in the penitentiary. Nixon subsequently sought to overturn his conviction through a writ of error, arguing that the indictment was flawed and that the court had erred in denying his motions for a new trial and in arresting judgment.	Nixon claimed several errors regarding the indictment, asserting that it did not adequately describe the offense he was charged with, failed to specify the location where Adam was abandoned, neglected to detail the means of the alleged assault, and argued that the court wrongfully denied his motion for a new trial. He maintained that these alleged deficiencies warranted a reversal of his conviction.	The defense, representing the People of the State of Illinois, maintained that the indictment was valid under the state's statutes and sufficiently detailed the criminal act committed by Nixon against Adam. They argued that the evidence presented at trial clearly established Nixon's guilt and that the court acted appropriately in affirming his conviction.

The case "The Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company v. Jeremiah O’Connor" took place on July 14, 1881, in Cook County, Illinois. The incident involved the plaintiff, Jeremiah O’Connor, who was severely injured while standing on a railroad track operated by the defendant, the Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company. During this time, the railroad's employees neglected to ring a bell or sound a whistle as required. Consequently, a train struck O’Connor, resulting in the loss of his leg and other serious injuries. O’Connor filed a lawsuit claiming damages for his injuries. The case began in the Superior Court, resulted in a $5,000 judgment for O’Connor, but was appealed by the defendant. O’Connor later died in 1883 from unrelated causes, after which his son was substituted as the plaintiff. The Appellate Court then reversed the Superior Court's decision and remanded the case for a new trial. The case included legal arguments regarding whether the action could continue posthumously and the admissibility of evidence from the initial trial.	The plaintiff, represented posthumously by his administrator, argued that the defendant was negligent in managing and operating its train, which led to O’Connor's injuries. The claims included the defendant’s failure to provide adequate warning of the train's approach, as required by law, and that O’Connor had acted with due care. The lawsuit sought damages for severe injuries, including the loss of a leg, pain and suffering, lost earnings, and medical expenses, amounting to $10,000.	The defendant’s primary defenses included the assertion that the plaintiff's injuries were a result of his own mistake regarding the train’s track, which they argued absolved them of liability. They also contended that the plaintiff was injured solely by the negligence of his foreman, a fellow employee from another railroad company, and sought instructions to the jury that would support these claims. Additionally, the defendant argued procedural issues regarding the continuance of the case after the plaintiff's death.

In 1882, Dennis Geary was employed as a night watcher for the Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company at their crossing on Thirty-five street in Chicago. His responsibilities included overseeing the tracks to ensure safety and reporting any obstructions. On the evening of March 6, while a freight train passed on track No. 2, Geary stepped out of his flag-house with a lantern to speak with a brakeman and was subsequently struck by a train of empty cars being backed up on track No. 1. The rear car of this train, which lacked a warning light or a crew member at the back, knocked him down and crushed his elbow. Geary filed a lawsuit against the railroad company, claiming negligence for the lack of proper safety measures that led to his injury. The circuit court ruled in favor of Geary, leading to an appeal by the railroad company, which argued that errors had occurred in the lower court’s rulings.	Dennis Geary claimed that the Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company was negligent in ensuring the safety of their operations, specifically by not providing adequate warnings or personnel to protect against the risks while trains were being operated. His lawsuit sought damages for the injuries sustained due to the negligence he attributed to the railroad’s operational practices, arguing that had sufficient safety measures been in place, his injury could have been prevented.	The Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company contended that Geary was injured as a result of the negligence of his fellow-servants within the crew responsible for operating the train. The railroad argued that it was not liable since the crew acting under their supervisor was not improperly staffed at the time of the incident, and Geary had voluntarily accepted the risks associated with his employment. They maintained that Geary, being aware of the working conditions and risks, could not hold the company responsible for the actions of fellow-servants.

In September 1843, in Grafton, Illinois, the case Paris Mason, for the use of Sarah Mason, Guardian, &c. v. John R. Caldwell arose from a real estate transaction involving the sale of two town lots. Paris Mason acted as the attorney for Sarah Mason, the guardian of Martha Maria Mason, who was a minor at the time of the sale. A bond was executed stipulating that Caldwell would pay a specified amount for the lots, and failure to do so within ten days would void the bond, preventing him from claiming the lots. Caldwell did not make the payments as agreed, arguing later that the transaction was void as the guardian lacked authority and the necessary legal processes were not followed. He claimed the consideration for his notes had failed and thus he was exonerated from his obligations. The case saw several pleas from Caldwell and subsequent responses from Mason. The trial initially sided with Caldwell, granting judgment in his favor, leading to the appeal.	Paris Mason, representing Sarah Mason, contended that despite the claims from Caldwell regarding the void nature of the sale, the issues pertaining to the validity of the contract were settled in their favor. They argued that after Martha Maria Mason reached adulthood, she married and adopted the previous sale, thereby making the contract valid. They sought to enforce the terms of the bond based on this adoption and the later tender of a deed which Caldwell refused, insisting Caldwell had been given a chance to redeem the contract by completing his payment.	John R. Caldwell raised multiple defenses asserting that the sale was invalid due to the lack of authority from Sarah Mason, as the necessary statutory provisions were not followed, and that the bond became void once he failed to make the required payments. Caldwell maintained that he was freed of any liability since the consideration for the contract had entirely failed, and he had no obligation to proceed with the purchase due to the circumstances surrounding the contract's validity.

On March 27, 1881, in Chicago, Illinois, Henry Marshall, acting as the administrator, brought a lawsuit against the Pennsylvania Company following the tragic death of his son, James Marshall. James was run over by a train operated by the Pennsylvania Company at the intersection of Grove and Eighteenth streets. The plaintiff argued that the defendant's train management was negligent and sought damages on behalf of the deceased. Initially, a jury awarded $2,000 to the plaintiff, a verdict that was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court. In the ensuing appeal, the primary legal issue centered on an instruction provided to the jury by the Superior Court, which the defendant claimed was erroneous. The plaintiff’s case hinged on the assertion that James was exercising due care at the time of the accident, and the jury was instructed to assess damages based solely on pecuniary loss without considering emotional grief. The court's ruling examined whether the jury instructions adequately addressed the issue of comparative negligence.	Henry Marshall contended that the Pennsylvania Company was responsible for the wrongful death of his son due to negligence in the operation of its train. He argued that the jury should hold the defendant liable since James was exercising due care when he was struck by the train. The plaintiff specifically contested the negligence of the train operators and sought compensatory damages strictly for the financial impact of the incident.	The Pennsylvania Company defended against the claims by asserting that the instructions given to the jury were erroneous as they failed to address comparative negligence adequately. They claimed that if it were proven that James did not take proper care, including not looking out for the train before crossing the tracks, he was at least partly responsible for the accident. The defendant requested that jury instructions reflect this potential negligence on the part of the deceased.

In December 1852, the case of Joseph Capps et al. for the use of Philemon B. Price against Josiah Gorham was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a note dated November 1, 1850, in which Gorham promised to pay $100 to Capps and others for the purpose of purchasing a lot and building a church for the Methodist Episcopal Church in West Jacksonville. The terms stipulated that payment could be made in lumber to be delivered at current cash prices. The plaintiffs claimed that $50 had been credited on the note by Bordwell, one of the original payees, to settle a debt owed to Gorham, which effectively reduced the amount owed on the note. Testimony indicated that there was an understanding between the parties regarding this credit, but there was contention regarding whether Price, who had acquired the note, had notice of this credit. The trial court ultimately ruled in favor of the plaintiffs for the remaining $50 due on the note, leading to an appeal by Price.	The plaintiffs' main argument was that despite the credit of $50 against the note, they were entitled to collect the remaining balance owed on the note from Gorham. They maintained that the assignment of the note to Price was subject to the previous credit that had been applied while the note remained in the possession of Bordwell and McCord, and contended that they had the right to collect the full $100 as the legal holders of the note.	The defendant, Gorham, contended that the previous credit of $50 should be honored, thereby reducing the total amount owed on the note to $50 at the time Price took possession. He argued that a payment made on a note is valid against any subsequent holder and that Bordwell’s endorsement of the credit on the note effectively discharged his liability for the amount. Gorham maintained that he fulfilled his obligations by recognizing this credit, and thus owed nothing more to Price.

On September 1, 1868, Alexander H. Hanley and his wife, Elizabeth K. Hanley, executed a mortgage deed to Selwin Easton and J. Lester Easton to secure an indebtedness. Some debt was paid, but the mortgage was not foreclosed, and payments of interest continued sporadically over several years. The debt was later assigned to Charles B. Hosmer, who subsequently sold the mortgaged property in October 1879 to Anson W. Jenks, who passed it on to defendant Charles Bogardus. David McConneaughey claimed ownership of the equity of redemption concerning the property and sought to contest the validity of the sale. He attempted to redeem the property by offering to pay the total outstanding debt but was denied this opportunity. The circuit court dismissed his claims, prompting McConneaughey to appeal, arguing the sale was invalid for several reasons, including improper sale location and the nature of the payment.	McConneaughey's primary argument was that the sale of the property under the mortgage was invalid. He contended that the sale violated legal statutes by being conducted in a county different from where the property was located. He also claimed that although he paid interest on the mortgage, an extension of payment terms had been agreed upon, thereby challenging the legitimacy of the sale and seeking to redeem the property by paying off the remaining debt.	Charles Bogardus and the other defendants argued that the sale was legally conducted under the conditions set forth in the original mortgage. They stated that the mortgage's power of sale was valid as it was executed before the relevant statute took effect and that the arrangements regarding payment extensions did not alter the validity of the mortgage. They further argued that the sale was conducted for cash, as the purchaser provided a valid check for the amount, thus satisfying the sale requirements.

In 1835, in Coles County, Illinois, a legal action was initiated by Gideon S. Bailey and his wife, Julia Bailey, acting as administratrix of the estate of James J. Jones, who had passed away. The plaintiffs filed a case against Charles S. Morton, seeking to recover amounts that they claimed were owed to Jones's estate. Bailey's argument revolved around the fact that after Julia Bailey was appointed administratrix, Morton submitted a claim to the Probate Judge for debts he claimed Jones owed him for various services, including work, goods sold, and loans. After a default judgment was awarded to the plaintiffs, Morton contested the legality of this judgment. The case was argued before the Illinois Supreme Court, which primarily addressed whether the administratrix was barred from pursuing the case due to Morton’s previous claim and whether Morton could object to evidence during the default judgment process.	The plaintiffs asserted that the administratrix had the right to recover debts owed to the estate by Morton, despite his earlier claim. They contested that Morton's claim in the probate court did not bar them from seeking payment, as there was no statutory requirement for the administratrix to set off any debt before pursuing their claims against Morton.	Morton argued that by submitting his claim before the probate judge, he effectively barred the administratrix from pursuing additional claims in court. He maintained that the plaintiffs should have set off their claims against him during the probate proceedings. Additionally, he contended that he should be allowed to raise objections to the evidence presented during the trial, despite having a default judgment against him.

In January 1869, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Christopher Shaffer v. Stephen Sutton. The case originated from the Morgan Circuit Court, where Stephen Sutton, as the administrator of Jacob Emerick's estate, secured a default judgment against Christopher Shaffer for $1,100. The default judgment was based on allegations that Shaffer had received money belonging to Emerick's estate. An execution was issued on this judgment and levied on Shaffer's property. In response, Shaffer filed a bill of complaint to enjoin the execution, claiming he had no notice of the suit and believed the process served was merely a subpoena for him to appear as a witness, which he could not do due to illness. The administrator, Sutton, countered that he had indeed served process and that Shaffer had received money from Henderson, a third party, shortly after Emerick's death. Evidence suggested that Shaffer had received the money and was responsible for distributing it among the heirs of Emerick, making his claims questionable. The court ultimately found the judgment against Shaffer just and equitable.	Christopher Shaffer argued that he had not received proper notice of the lawsuit and that the process served on him was misinterpreted as a harmless subpoena. He maintained his position that he owed nothing to Emerick's estate and sought to enjoin the execution and all proceedings related to the default judgment against him.	Stephen Sutton contended that he had duly served process on Shaffer and that Shaffer had received $1,025 from Henderson after Emerick's death. Sutton argued that Shaffer's claims of misunderstanding were unfounded, emphasizing that evidence presented demonstrated Shaffer’s acknowledgment of the debt and his responsibility for the money in question.

In 1857, James O'Donald owned several lots in Bloomington, Illinois. He entered into a bond for a deed to Martha Watson, the wife of Samuel Watson, for $2,550, partially payable through a secured note. After Martha's death in February 1859, she transferred this bond back to O'Donald in exchange for a different lot, which was conveyed to her daughter, Sarah Watson. Following Sarah's death in 1860, Samuel Watson was appointed as her estate's administrator. He sought to sell the property to pay debts owed by the estate. Concurrently, Asahel Gridley had obtained a judgment against Samuel Watson, leading to an execution and the sale of the same property under this judgment. The dispute arose when Watson filed a bill in chancery aimed at removing the cloud over the title caused by Gridley's claim. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case, which involved complex transactions around property ownership and the validity of the lien held by Gridley.	Samuel Watson, as the administrator of Sarah Watson's estate, claimed he needed to remove a cloud on the title of the property to ensure it could be sold to pay off debts. He argued that Gridley's prior claim on the property was invalid because Samuel Watson, at no time, held legal title to it. He sought the cancellation of the sheriff's certificate issued to Gridley.	Asahel Gridley contended that the property was purchased using funds belonging to Samuel Watson and that the transactions were aimed at defrauding creditors. He argued that his judgment against Samuel Watson created a legal lien on the property, which entitled him to pursue the claim despite any subsequent transactions involving Sarah Watson. Gridley sought a decree confirming his title to the property as valid.

In the case of Board of Supervisors of Peoria County v. Austin H. Gordon, which took place in Illinois, the origins of the conflict date back to an act passed by the General Assembly on February 13, 1853, to lay out a State road from Peoria to Rock Island. The commissioners appointed under this act assessed damages to Austin H. Gordon, whose land was affected, at $50. However, upon appealing this assessment in 1856, Gordon won a judgment against Peoria County for $548 and costs. This judgment was reaffirmed by the Illinois Supreme Court in 1857. Years later, on October 22, 1872, Gordon, although he no longer owned the land, filed a petition for a writ of mandamus to compel the Board of Supervisors of Peoria County to pay the judgment from 1856. At that time, the road had not been constructed on Gordon's property, which had since been fully fenced. The case later escalated to an evaluation of whether the Statute of Limitations barred Gordon's claim, based on the time lapse since the original judgment.	Austin H. Gordon, as the plaintiff, sought a writ of mandamus to compel the Board of Supervisors of Peoria County to pay the sum of $548 as per the judgment awarded in 1856. He argued that, despite the passage of time, the county still owed him this payment for the damages assessed against his land for the state road that had never been built.	The Board of Supervisors of Peoria County defended against Gordon's claim primarily on the grounds of the Statute of Limitations, which stipulates that actions based on judgments must commence within sixteen years. They contended that the original judgment was rendered over sixteen years prior to Gordon's petition in 1872, thus barring his claim. Additionally, they argued that simply filing an appeal did not suspend the timeline for the Statute of Limitations.

This case involved Thomas Payne (the defendant) and John K. Webster (the plaintiff) in an action of assumpsit regarding a promissory note executed on April 7, 1854. The note was made jointly by Payne and Calvin A. Warren, promising the sum of $1,000 to Frederic Woodward, with an obligation to pay after one year, plus 10% interest. The dispute arose after the note was assigned to Webster, who initiated legal proceedings against Payne when the amount was not paid. On June 8, 1857, the case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court. The crux of the issue lay in whether Payne, who claimed he signed the note as a security for Warren and not as a principal borrower, was liable for the amount due on the note. Payne argued that the plaintiff failed to take timely action to enforce the note per statutory requirements, thus forfeiting his right to collect from him, as per the law governing security agreements. The court's decision ultimately revolved around the interpretation of this statutory plea and the obligations of the parties involved in the promissory note.	John K. Webster, the plaintiff, contended that Thomas Payne was liable for the repayment of the promissory note, alleging that Payne had signed the note without any stipulation that he only acted as a security for Warren. Webster sought to collect the full amount due under the note, including accrued interest, thereby claiming Payne's liability under the assumption that he was a co-maker of the note.	Thomas Payne argued that he was only a security for the principal borrower, Calvin A. Warren, and not the main obligor on the note. He maintained that all consideration for the note was received by Warren and that he had notified Webster in writing to proceed with a suit against the principal before a reasonable time had lapsed, which Webster failed to do. As per the applicable statute, he claimed that this failure by the plaintiff forfeited any claim against him, as he was not liable unless the plaintiff acted expediently.

The case of David Atkins v. William A. Hinman took place in 1845 in Schuyler County, Illinois. This action of ejectment began when William A. Hinman filed a suit against David Atkins for the recovery of a tract of land defined as the south half of section five (5) in township three (3) north of range four (4) west. Hinman based his claim on a judgment that had been entered at the March term of 1840 regarding unpaid taxes on the property, following a series of legal proceedings aimed at recovering tax debts through the sale of the land. During the trial, Hinman presented various documents, including the original judgment for taxes and a sheriff's deed conveying the property to him. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Hinman, and the court awarded him a writ of possession. Atkins appealed the decision, challenging the admission of evidence and the validity of the judgment under which Hinman's title was based.	Hinman argued that he had legally acquired title to the property through a proper sheriff's sale conducted under Illinois tax law. He pointed to the judgment from 1840, claiming it supported his right to the land due to the previous owner's failure to pay taxes.
