Hinman's legal requests included recognition of his title and possession of the property based on the sheriff's deed obtained from the sale.	Atkins contended that the judgment under which Hinman's title was derived was void due to procedural deficiencies, including missing dates and descriptions necessary for jurisdiction. He argued that the original judgment did not follow statutory requirements and therefore failed to legally transfer the property to Hinman. Atkins sought to have the evidence supporting Hinman's claims excluded and ultimately aimed to overturn the judgment in favor of Hinman.

In 1873, the case of Daniel Knecht v. James Mitchell occurred in St. Clair County, Illinois. The dispute involved a forcible detainer action brought by Daniel Knecht, who claimed that James Mitchell had entered the premises as his tenant under a verbal lease for two years. Knecht contended that Mitchell had occupied the property and paid rent throughout the lease period, which expired on August 1, 1872. Following the expiration of the lease, Knecht made a written demand for possession of the premises on August 8, but Mitchell refused to vacate. During the trial, Knecht sought to present evidence of the verbal lease and the payment of rent; however, the court initially rejected this evidence, arguing that the lease was void under the statute of frauds and that the tenancy had reverted to a year-to-year basis, requiring a sixty-days' notice for termination.	Daniel Knecht argued that James Mitchell entered into a valid verbal lease for two years, during which Mitchell occupied the premises and paid rent. Knecht claimed that since the lease had been fully executed, no further notice was necessary to terminate the tenancy after the lease expired. He sought to regain possession of the property after Mitchell's refusal to vacate.	James Mitchell contended that the verbal lease was void due to the statute of frauds, resulting in a tenancy from year to year. He maintained that under such circumstances, Knecht was required to provide a sixty-days' notice to terminate the tenancy. Consequently, Mitchell argued that he was not obligated to leave the premises without proper notice.

In September 1874, the legal case "Truman W. Steele v. Levi D. Boone et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Superior Court of Cook County. Truman W. Steele, the appellant, sought to enjoin (prevent) the sale of certain real estate in Chicago, threatened by a deed of trust. Steele contended that no deed of trust had been executed by the parties he claimed to be the grantors. He argued he was a good-faith purchaser without knowledge of any prior deed. The defendants included Levi D. Boone among others, who opposed Steele’s claims through sworn answers and supporting affidavits. The court initially dissolved the injunction, leading Steele to dismiss his bill and subsequently appeal the decision. Evidence indicated that the original deed of trust had been executed, despite the prior owners' claims to the contrary. Due to a fire that destroyed county records, the absence of recorded notice of the deed raised complications in Steele's case. The factors examined played a key role in the court's deliberations regarding the legitimacy of Steele's claims and the enforceability of the deed.	Truman W. Steele, the plaintiff, claimed that a deed of trust under which a sale of property was threatened had not been executed. He asserted that he had purchased the property in good faith and without notice of the deed, and thus requested the court to enjoin the sale, arguing that he was entitled to equitable relief.	The defendants, including Levi D. Boone, countered Steele's claims by asserting the legitimacy of the deed of trust, emphasizing that it was duly executed and filed before Steele's purchase. They contended that Steele, despite the destruction of records, should have been aware of the deed's existence due to its execution and filed record. Furthermore, they filed affidavits supporting their defense and sought the dissolution of the injunction initially granted to Steele.

The case "Frank Sturges et al. v. Samuel L Keith" took place in Cook County, Illinois, and was decided in September 1870 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved included the plaintiffs, Frank Sturges and others (part of a banking firm), and the defendant, Samuel L. Keith. In May 1864, the plaintiffs were engaged in banking under the name Solomon Sturges' Sons. The defendant, a customer of the bank, deposited certificates for 250 shares of stock from the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company as alleged collateral for his debts amounting to approximately $13,000. The arrangement concerning the stock's deposit was disputed—while the plaintiffs claimed it was for safe keeping, the defendant believed it was merely collateral. A power of attorney was granted to William Sturges (not a partner but a managing agent) to sell and transfer the stock. The stock was subsequently sold in January 1865 without the defendant's consent. In March 1866, the defendant sought the return of the stock and later filed suit for wrongful conversion against all members of the Sturges firm. During the trial, various legal principles regarding the liability of partners, bailment, and the definition of conversion were debated.	The plaintiff claimed wrongful conversion of the 250 shares of stock, arguing that the defendants, as partners, had a duty to safely keep the stock following its deposit. They contended that the stock was wrongfully sold by William Sturges and that all partners were liable for this conversion, regardless of their withdrawal from the partnership or involvement in the sale.	The defendants argued that they were not liable because the stock was left with William Sturges who had the power of attorney to manage it. They claimed that the plaintiff did not prove that the stock was left as a special deposit for safekeeping, and thus, they had no duty under law to safeguard it. Additionally, the dissolved partnership negated any collective liability by the remaining partners after the withdrawal of some members.

In 1882, Charles S. Kilbourne, the owner of a cheese and butter factory in Barrington, Cook County, Illinois, entered into an agreement with Ludwig Werner and twenty-five other farmers and dairymen. The arrangement involved Kilbourne receiving milk from the complainants and converting it into butter and cheese, which would then be sold under a "dividend plan." This plan compensated the farmers based on the quantity of milk supplied, after deducting Kilbourne's costs. On April 4, 1882, Kilbourne executed a deed of trust to secure payments to the farmers for the milk and proceeds from the factory's products. However, between August and October 1883, Kilbourne failed to pay the complainants for the milk they provided. On October 14, 1883, while knowing he was insolvent, Kilbourne allegedly conspired with Alfred Bosworth to secretly remove the butter and cheese produced from their supplied milk. Some complainants managed to intervene and seize the products through legal means. The First National Bank of Elgin, claiming rights over the factory's premises and products due to an outstanding loan of $6,700 from Kilbourne, contested the validity of the deed of trust securing the complainants' interests and sought to have their claim prioritized.	The complainants argue that they did not sell their milk to Kilbourne but rather delivered it to him under an agreement to manufacture butter and cheese, retaining ownership of the products and the right to their proceeds after sales. They claim that Kilbourne's fraudulent actions denied them rightful payment for their contributions and seek an accounting for what is due to them, along with the foreclosure of the deed of trust on the factory's premises to recover their losses.	The First National Bank of Elgin maintains that the deed of trust is invalid, asserting that the complainants' dealings with Kilbourne constituted outright sales of milk. They argue that Kilbourne had legally mortgaged the factory and assigned his rights to the butter and cheese to the bank, making the bank the rightful claimant. The bank's cross-bill sought to have the complainants' seizure of the products declared unlawful and to establish the bank’s mortgage as the primary lien.

In April 1866, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case of Simeon B. Chittenden et al. v. Thomas S. Rogers et al., originating in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose from the execution of multiple judgments against Rogers and his associates, following a series of legal processes concerning property attachments. Chittenden and other plaintiffs sought to enforce judgments obtained in earlier cases against Rogers, asserting that the proceeds from property sales should be allocated to satisfy their claims. The plaintiffs moved the court to compel the local sheriff to use sale proceeds to cover their damages owing to prior judgments, arguing that the sheriff failed to properly levy debts against attached properties. The court previously dismissed their claim for lack of equity, prompting the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. A key legal focus was on whether the sheriff had conducted proper legal levies and whether the attachments had created valid liens on the property in question.	The plaintiffs, led by Simeon B. Chittenden, claimed that the sheriff failed to levy the necessary executions on property that was effectively in the custody of a designated custodian. They argued that the court should have ordered the sheriff to pay them from the sale proceeds of the attached property to cover the judgments awarded to them against the defendants.	The defendants, represented by Thomas S. Rogers, contended that no sufficient levy was made on the property during the relevant timeframe due to procedural errors and inconsistencies in how the sheriffs managed the attachments. They argued that the executions on subsequent judgments were not properly applied, resulting in the plaintiffs losing their priority claims to the property's proceeds.

In the case of Wesley Misner et al. v. J. Murray Bullard, filed in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867, several taxpayers from the town of Fox in Kendall County sought to challenge the collection of a special tax. This tax was levied to pay bounties for volunteers to the U.S. Army, aiming to meet a required quota and avoid a military draft. On January 23, 1865, the town clerk announced a special meeting for February 3, 1865, to vote on a loan to support these bounties. The election yielded 58 votes in favor and 4 against the tax. Subsequently, some citizens pledged amounts as loans to support the volunteer efforts, leading the town's board of auditors to certify the tax, which amounted to 3% on all taxable property in Fox for the year. The town collector, J. Murray Bullard, was preparing to collect these taxes when the lawsuit was initiated to prevent the collection. The plaintiffs argued that none of them were liable for the draft, as many were over 45 years old or had served in previous conflicts. The circuit court dissolved the initial injunction that restrained the tax collection, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed that the special tax for volunteer bounties was unconstitutional and a violation of their rights. They argued that the levied tax was not for a legitimate town purpose, as most complainants were not draft-eligible and had historical service records that distinguished them from being liable for the draft. Their legal request was to enjoin (prevent) the collection of the tax assessed by the town for the purported bounties.	The defendant, J. Murray Bullard, contended that the town had legally and appropriately levied the tax pursuant to existing statutory authority. He argued that the tax was necessary for a corporate purpose, specifically to raise funds for war volunteers as authorized by Illinois law. The defense also claimed that the town auditors properly audited and allowed claims for the money borrowed to pay bounties, and therefore, the tax procedures were valid. Furthermore, Bullard sought damages amounting to $100 for attorney fees incurred due to what he described as the wrongful issuance of the injunction.

In 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, Asahel Gage and others (the plaintiffs) discovered that their land had been improperly subdivided without their consent by John E. Gardner. This unlawful subdivision resulted in the plaintiffs' property being assessed for taxes under Gardner's unauthorized layout. The plaintiffs were unaware of this situation until they attempted to pay their taxes and found that their land did not appear on the assessment rolls. Following this revelation, the plaintiffs learned that a significant portion of their land had been sold for taxes due to the invalid assessment. They subsequently filed a bill in equity in the Superior Court, seeking to annul the tax sale and prevent the issuance of a deed for the sold property. The court had to determine whether the unauthorized subdivision and subsequent assessment were legally valid.	The plaintiffs argued that their land was wrongfully subdivided by Gardner, who had no ownership or authority to do so. They requested the court to annul the tax sale that resulted from the invalid assessment and to enjoin the issuance of any deeds related to that sale.	The defendant's primary argument revolved around the validity of the assessment based on Gardner’s subdivision. They contended that the assessment was correct despite the contention that the subdivision was unauthorized. The defendant moved to dismiss the plaintiffs’ claims regarding the annulment of the tax sale, asserting that the assessment should stand.

In 1877, in Randolph County, Illinois, the case of James M. Gregson v. Minor Allen et al. emerged from a dispute over the possession of two stacks of wheat. The plaintiffs, Minor Allen and Theodore Phillips, initiated the suit in replevin against the defendant, James M. Gregson, before a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment against him. Seeking to challenge this decision, Gregson filed an appeal, providing the required appeal bond. When the case was set for trial, the plaintiffs moved to dismiss the appeal, claiming that Gregson had not entered the name of an attorney on the court docket as required by a local court rule. However, Gregson was present in court, declared his readiness to proceed without counsel, and expressed his desire to try his own case. Despite his statements, the court denied him the opportunity and dismissed his appeal, prompting him to assign this as error in the circuit court.	The plaintiffs argued that the appeal should be dismissed because the defendant had failed to comply with a rule requiring the entry of an attorney's name on the judge's docket before the first Tuesday of the court term. They requested the dismissal of Gregson's appeal on these grounds, emphasizing adherence to established court rules.	Gregson contended that he had the legal right, under Illinois statutes, to represent himself and try his own case without being forced to have an attorney listed on the docket. He maintained that the dismissal of his appeal was erroneous and that the court's actions unjustly infringed upon his statutory rights as a party in the lawsuit. He sought the reversal of the dismissal and the opportunity to proceed with his appeal.

In the case of Charles Wicker et al. v. Benjamin F. Ray, the proceedings began in April 1886 in Cook County, Illinois. Benjamin F. Ray was in possession of land and claimed ownership, negotiating a sale with appellants Charles G. Wicker and Charles H. Smyth for $12,800, payable in installments. However, upon examining the title, the purchasers found it unsatisfactory and refused to proceed with the sale. In response, Ray filed a bill in the Superior Court of Cook County to compel specific performance of the contract, asserting that he had a valid agreement with Wicker and Smyth. The lower court decided in Ray's favor, leading to an appeal by the defendants which was heard by the Appellate Court for the First District. The ruling centered on the interpretation of a will left by Lewis Whiteman, from which Ray deduced his title to the land, specifically concerning whether the beneficiaries, Jenny and Eliza Carson, received a fee simple or a life estate as part of the inheritance. The court analyzed various clauses in the will to determine the nature of the estate transferred to the Carsons and ultimately concluded that they held a fee simple estate in the land.	The plaintiff, Benjamin F. Ray, argued that he had a valid contract with the defendants for the sale of land and sought specific performance of that contract. He contended that the issues regarding the title were irrelevant to the enforceability of the sale agreement. Ray claimed that the lower court's decree confirmed his rightful ownership based on the interpretation of the will that outlined the transfer of property rights to beneficiaries.	The defendants, Wicker and Smyth, contended that they were justified in refusing to complete the purchase due to unsatisfactory title examination. They argued that the court should not enforce the contract for specific performance, as the title did not meet the legal standards necessary for a transfer of ownership. They requested the court to reverse the lower court’s decision affirming Ray's claim and dismiss the complaint.

In December 1826, in St. Clair County, Illinois, Eli B. Clemson (the plaintiff in error) brought a legal action against Henry Kruper (the defendant in error) for a case of assumpsit, which typically concerns breach of a contract. The trial was presided over by the St. Clair circuit court, where the jury rendered a verdict in favor of Kruper. Following the verdict, Clemson requested a new trial, arguing that the damages awarded were excessive. However, the court dismissed this motion. As a result, Clemson filed a writ of error, seeking to reverse the court’s judgment based on the claim that the trial court had erred in denying his request for a new trial. The primary legal issue revolved around the validity of the bill of exceptions—essentially a formal objection to a court decision—which Clemson attempted to submit as part of his appeal.	The main argument presented by Eli B. Clemson was that the St. Clair circuit court erred in its decision to deny his motion for a new trial, asserting that the damages awarded to the plaintiff (Kruper) were excessive. He aimed to have the original judgment overturned and to secure a new trial.	Henry Kruper, as the defendant in this case, contended that the denial of a new trial cannot be properly assigned as an error for the appellate court's consideration. His defense was grounded on the legal principle that a bill of exceptions must be taken during the trial and that the exceptions made by Clemson were not properly presented. Consequently, he requested that the court affirm the lower court's ruling.

The case "William G. Kase, Admr. v. Sarah Painter" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1875. It arose in St. Clair County, Illinois, concerning a claim filed by Sarah Painter against the estate of Ruth McLaughlin, who had passed away. Sarah Painter, a married woman, sought compensation for services rendered to the deceased during 1868 and 1869, which included housekeeping, nursing, and providing food and board until the time of death. The initial claim, filed in the county court, detailed various expenses totaling $1,982, but following a trial, the jury awarded Sarah Painter $1,056 and court costs. The focus of the case was on the legal rights of married women to receive payment for their earnings, particularly before and after the enactment of a law in 1869 that allowed married women to recover their earnings independently.	Sarah Painter claimed compensation for her services to Ruth McLaughlin, amounting to $1,982. She argued that she provided substantial care, including housekeeping and nursing, and requested that she be compensated for these services rendered prior to and following the 1869 law that recognized married women's rights to their earnings. The plaintiff sought to uphold the jury’s verdict, which awarded her $1,056.	The defense, represented by the administrator of Ruth McLaughlin's estate, contested the claim based on the earnings prior to the 1869 law, asserting that a married woman could not recover for services rendered before that law was enacted. They argued that the evidence did not support the jury's verdict and that the claims should be dismissed for lack of legal standing based on the law at the time.

In 1889, the case of Merrimac Paper Company v. Illinois Trust and Savings Bank took place in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included representatives from the Merrimac Paper Company and a broker named Spaulding. The situation arose when the Merrimac Paper Company, based in Massachusetts, manufactured a lot of paper and shipped it to Chicago for delivery to customers who ultimately refused to accept it. Spaulding, the broker, stored the paper in a warehouse under his name. While in Boston, Spaulding received an offer from a potential buyer, Beers, to purchase the paper at a specific price, contingent on his creditworthiness. Spaulding communicated this offer to the Merrimac Paper Company, which approved the sale if Beers was financially sound. After Spaulding's clerk assessed Beers and deemed him responsible, the sale was executed, and Beers received the warehouse receipts in exchange for notes. However, after the sale, doubts arose regarding Beers' credit, leading the Merrimac Paper Company to pursue legal action to reclaim the paper stored in the warehouse. The court initially ruled in favor of the defendant, prompting the plaintiff to appeal the decision.	The Merrimac Paper Company claimed that the sale conducted by Spaulding and his clerk was invalid because Beers did not meet the stipulated condition of being a buyer of first-class credit. They argued that Spaulding lacked the authority to finalize the sale without adhering to the company's requirements, which specified that the sale was contingent on Beers’ financial credibility. The company sought to recover its paper from the defendant.	The defendant, Illinois Trust and Savings Bank, contended that the decision regarding Beers' creditworthiness was left to the judgment of Spaulding's clerk, who acted in good faith and without fraud. They argued that the authority to sell and deliver the goods was valid as long as Beers met condition of being of good credit, which was reasonably determined by the clerk. They asserted that the ownership of the paper passed to Beers because the sale complied with the agent's discretion, rendering the plaintiff's claims unfounded.

In January 1884, Jane Fallin sustained injuries from a fall caused by a defective sidewalk in Mattoon, Illinois. The incident occurred between Western Avenue and Prairie Avenue while she was en route to church, accompanied by a friend. The fall resulted from a loose plank on the sidewalk, which tilted and caused her to fall, leading to serious injuries, including a broken arm that, due to Fallin's advanced age (she was 75), would not heal properly and led to permanent suffering. She subsequently recovered a judgment of $1,000 in the Circuit Court of Coles County against the City of Mattoon for neglecting to maintain the sidewalk. The city appealed the decision, claiming a discrepancy in the location of the accident as stated in Fallin's declaration compared to where the evidence allegedly pointed to. Despite these claims, the court upheld the trial court's findings and emphasized that procedural objections to the evidence should have been raised earlier, which would have allowed for potential amendments to Fallin's declaration. The Supreme Court decision was made on March 30, 1885.	Jane Fallin claimed damages of $1,000 from the City of Mattoon due to injuries sustained from a fall caused by a negligently maintained sidewalk. She argued that the city was at fault for allowing the sidewalk to become defective, which directly resulted in her significant injuries. The permanent nature of her injuries and her advanced age further underscored her suffering and the need for compensation.	The City of Mattoon contended that the evidence presented did not adequately establish negligence on its part since the incident's declared location did not match where the accident occurred, suggesting a variance between the allegations and the proof. They claimed that if this discrepancy had been addressed during the trial, it could have influenced the jury's decision and requested the court to reverse the previous judgments based on these arguments.

In January 1876, a legal dispute arose in Illinois involving Joseph Drew and other parties (the plaintiffs) against John Mason and others (the defendants). The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court and stemmed from a petition by the plaintiffs to enforce a mechanic's lien related to a lightning rod that had been installed on a building. The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to compensation for the materials and labor they provided in the installation of this lightning rod. However, the case was originally decided in the Circuit Court of Mason County, where it was presided over by Judge Lyman Lacey. The lower court sustained a demurrer to the plaintiffs' petition and dismissed their bill, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Joseph Drew et al., claimed that they had the right to enforce a mechanic's lien for the labor and materials provided in the installation of a lightning rod on a building. They argued that this work should fall within the protections of the Mechanic’s Lien Law, which typically applies to parties involved in building, altering, repairing, or ornamenting a property.	The defendants, John Mason et al., contended that the work done by the plaintiffs did not meet the statutory definitions of construction work as outlined in the Mechanic’s Lien Law. They maintained that furnishing materials and labor for a lightning rod installation does not qualify as building, altering, repairing, or ornamenting a house, thus invalidating the plaintiffs' claim for a mechanic's lien.

In 1879, a contract was established between the Chicago & Alton Railway Company and William B. Suffern et al., allowing for the construction of a switch that enabled coal cars from their line to be transported to a coal mine owned by the appellees. This arrangement continued until 1887. That year, another company constructed an alternate rail line which provided the appellees access to their own coal mine via switches allowing cars from this new line to connect with the Chicago & Alton Railway's tracks. The Railway Company, citing safety concerns about potential accidents with the other company's cars on their tracks, discontinued the switch connection to the coal mine. In response, the appellees sought a writ of mandamus to compel the Railway to restore the switch connection and provide cars for transporting coal as previously done. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, which was tasked with determining whether the Railway had the legal duty to maintain the switch connection based on prior conduct and statutory stipulations.	The plaintiffs, Suffern and associates, argued that the Chicago & Alton Railway had an obligation to restore the switch connection based on their previous business practices and various legal statutes. They contended that the constitutional provision mandates railroad companies to permit connections to their tracks for the transportation of coal, and claimed that the Railway's discontinuation of the switch was unjust and unlawful, thereby seeking the court's intervention through mandamus to compel restoration of the switch and the provision of coal cars.	The Chicago & Alton Railway Company denied the plaintiffs' claims, asserting that the provision in question was not self-executing and that the manner of maintaining such connections is at their discretion. They argued that discontinuing the switch was necessary for the safety of their passengers and property due to potential trespassing risks presented by the other company’s access. Furthermore, they maintained that the plaintiffs did not have a clear legal right to the switch connection and that mandamus was not an appropriate remedy for the plaintiffs’ request.

In December 1832, a legal dispute arose in Jackson County, Illinois, involving John Bowers as the plaintiff in error and Clark Green as the defendant in error. The case originated when Green sued Bowers before a justice of the peace to recover a penalty of $5 for allegedly taking excessive tolls, contrary to the "Act regulating Mills and Millers," which was enacted on February 9, 1827. The justice ruled in favor of Green, resulting in a judgment that Bowers appealed to the Circuit Court of Jackson County. The Circuit Court upheld the justice's ruling for $5. Bowers then brought the case to the Illinois Supreme Court by writ of error, challenging both the judgment and the jurisdiction of the justice of the peace. The Supreme Court needed to address preliminary objections regarding jurisdiction concerning the amount in question and whether a writ of error was applicable given the judgment was under $20. After considering these points, the Court turned its attention to the substantive issue regarding the jurisdiction of justices in penal actions.	The plaintiff, John Bowers, argued that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction over penal actions, contending that the statute did not grant such authority to inferior courts. He sought to have the previous judgments overruled, claiming they were invalid due to this jurisdictional issue and emphasized the nature of statutory penalties as punishments rather than contractual obligations.	The defendant, Clark Green, maintained that the justice of the peace appropriately ruled on the matter and claimed entitlement to the penalty as per the statute. He argued against the plaintiff's assertion regarding jurisdiction and upheld the Circuit Court's affirmation of the justice's decision, consequently seeking to sustain the judgment awarded to him.

The case "Cornelius H. Tunnison et al. v. Franklin Field et al." was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1859, originating from the Madison Circuit Court. The dispute arose after Cornelius H. Tunnison and others (the plaintiffs) initiated an attachment procedure seeking to recover a debt of $8,358.76 from Franklin Field and Barton (the defendants). This debt was claimed to result from work and materials provided for the North Missouri Railroad under a contract dated June 25, 1856. The plaintiffs contended that they had fulfilled their contractual obligations, thus entitling them to payment. However, the defendants moved to dismiss the case, citing a purported failure to provide a sufficient declaration. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendants, dismissing the suit on the grounds of insufficient declaration, prompting the plaintiff to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs argued that they were owed a specific sum for work and materials they had provided under a valid written contract. They asserted that their declaration was adequate and that they had fully performed their contractual obligations. They requested the court to reverse the dismissal of their suit, contending that the Circuit Court erred in sustaining the defendants' motion to dismiss without adequate proof of their claims.	The defendants maintained that the plaintiffs had not filed a proper declaration that met the requirements necessary for the case to proceed. They argued that the dismissal was justified due to this alleged inadequacy in the declaration and requested the court to uphold the dismissive ruling made by the Circuit Court.

In 1882, in the state of Illinois, Henry F. Merrill, the appellant, filed a lawsuit against Henry Dibble, the appellee, claiming damages for alleged trespass on Merrill's property. Over the years, both parties occupied neighboring farms, with Dibble occupying land owned by his mother, while Merrill owned his farm. The dispute arose from a partition fence that had fallen into disrepair, allowing Dibble's cattle and horses to frequently enter Merrill's fields. Despite Merrill's notifications to Dibble regarding this issue, Dibble failed to address it. Additionally, Merrill claimed that Dibble and his servants used a private lane on Merrill's property without permission. The case revolved around whether Dibble had any legal justification for his actions, with the jury ultimately ruling in favor of Dibble, which led Merrill to appeal the decision.	Merrill claimed that Dibble's cattle damaged his property by trespassing due to the dilapidated state of the fence between their lands. He argued that Dibble neglected to maintain the fence despite being informed. Merrill sought to recover damages for the trespass and contended that Dibble's use of a private lane on his property was also unauthorized.	Dibble defended against the claims by asserting that he had a license or prescriptive right of way over Merrill's property, arguing that Merrill failed to prove actual damages beyond nominal amounts. His counsel maintained that the jury should consider the motive behind Merrill's lawsuit, suggesting that it was driven by a desire for revenge rather than actual harm.

In the case of "John N. Shuler v. Edward F. Pulsifer et al.," a legal dispute arose in September 1868, involving parties from La Salle and Cook counties in Illinois. The plaintiff, Edward F. Pulsifer, operated a grain commission business in Chicago, while the defendant, John N. Shuler, resided in La Salle County. The conflict began when Shuler was solicited by Pulsifer to consign grain. On October 24, 1865, Shuler shipped approximately 5,800 bushels of corn to Pulsifer's firm for sale. Shuler instructed Pulsifer to deposit $2,500 in a trust account, which was done. However, after selling the corn in New York, there remained a deficit of $433.82 from the transaction. Pulsifer filed a suit in Cook County to recover the shortfall. The defendant challenged the jurisdiction of the Cook County court, asserting that the contract was made in La Salle County where all relevant actions occurred, rather than in Cook County.	The plaintiff, Edward F. Pulsifer, claimed that he was entitled to recover $433.82 due to a deficit resulting from the sale of consignments. He argued that the contract was validly formed in Cook County since the granary’s proceeds were directed to a bank there, thus justifying the lawsuit being filed in Cook County.	The defendant, John N. Shuler, contended that the court in Cook County lacked jurisdiction, asserting that the contract was made in La Salle County where he resided and where all actions tied to the contract were conducted. He argued that the essential elements of the contract were executed in La Salle, thus invalidating any claim brought in Cook County.

The case of "William Kennedy, Administrator, et al. v. William Wikoff et al." arose in 1886, stemming from a legal dispute involving creditors of John R. Snyder, a banker located in Chenoa, McLean County, Illinois. Snyder had created a deed of trust for all his assets on September 30, 1883. Shortly thereafter, on October 4, 1883, several creditors, including William Wikoff and Alfred R. Kidwell, initiated attachment lawsuits against Snyder. Multiple judgments were obtained against Snyder at the same term of court. The attachment claims were subsequently denied as Snyder’s judgment was appealed, and during the proceedings, various garnishments were executed against Snyder's property, which had been consolidated into one case. By November 1884, the plaintiffs dismissed their attachment claims, and by September 1885, the attachments were fully dismissed. Despite garnishment proceedings retrieving some assets, it remained insufficient to satisfy all judgments owed to the creditors. The court was later asked to distribute the proceeds from the assets, leading to contention over whether the appellants (plaintiffs in this case) were entitled to participate in the distribution of property obtained through garnishment.	The plaintiffs, including William Kennedy as the administrator, argued that they were entitled to share in the proceeds from the garnished property based on the provisions of Section 37 of the Attachment Act. They contended that since they had obtained judgments against Snyder, they should have a right to participate in the distribution of proceeds from the garnished assets.	The defendants contended that Section 37 of the Attachment Act did not apply to the garnishment process initiated under Chapter 62, and therefore, the plaintiffs were not entitled to share the seized property. They argued that the garnishee proceedings should allow each creditor to claim their share of the recovered assets independently and that the plaintiffs’ claims lacked validity given the prior dismissal of the attachment.

In October 1885, the case of E. C. John Cleaver et al. v. Christian Burcky et al. was adjudicated in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case stemmed from a financial agreement involving a promissory note for $9,366.92 executed by Frederick Burcky to Christian Burcky in October 1877, secured by a deed of trust on lands in Cook County, Illinois. The arrangement allowed Christian Burcky to pay taxes on the property and have that amount added to the principal, if Frederick failed to pay the taxes. In August 1882, Frederick transferred these premises to E. C. John Cleaver, who explicitly assumed the debt from Christian Burcky. This deal was valued at $19,000, less any debts secured by the deed of trust. The plaintiffs, Cleaver and another party, alleged that the original promissory note contained usurious interest and sought to have that claim applied to reduce the debt secured by the deed of trust. The court found that the defenses based on usury could only be asserted by the original debtor, Frederick Burcky, and denied the plaintiffs’ claims, ultimately concluding that any oral agreement attempting to contradict the written deed was invalid.	The plaintiffs claimed that the promissory note executed by Frederick Burcky contained unlawful and usurious interest that should be applied to reduce the amount owed under the deed of trust. They argued that Cleaver, authorized by Burcky, had the right to raise this defense, and sought an injunction to stop the foreclosure proceedings until the alleged usurious interest could be resolved.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs, as grantees who had assumed the obligations of the deed of trust, could not assert the defense of usury. They argued that the written agreement explicitly obligated Cleaver to pay the indebtedness and that any verbal agreement attempting to assert the usury defense was invalid as it contradicted the terms of the deed. The defendants maintained that the plaintiffs had no standing to claim usury.

In 1853, in Macoupin County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between the County of Macoupin and Henry Edwards concerning a contract for the care of paupers. Henry Edwards had entered into an agreement with the county court to receive and support every pauper sent to him, specifically to properly feed and clothe them for a set fee of $1.37 per week for each individual. The controversy emerged when the county sent three insane individuals to Edwards, whom he claimed were more troublesome and required a higher fee due to their condition. The case was heard in the Macoupin Circuit Court, where it was established that the plaintiffs qualified under the broader legal definition of "pauper," which includes individuals unable to earn a living due to mental incapacitation. The circuit court ruled in favor of Edwards, leading to the appeal by the County of Macoupin.	Henry Edwards argued that the insane individuals sent to him were not within the terms of his contract as "paupers." He asserted that caring for these individuals warranted compensation beyond the agreed-upon fee because their additional care needs led to increased costs and burdens on him.	The County of Macoupin contended that the contract explicitly covered all paupers, including those with mental health issues. They maintained that since the individuals were sent under the definition of "paupers," Edwards was only entitled to the predetermined fee stated in their agreement, regardless of any additional challenges presented by their insanity.

Jonathan K. Greenough and others filed a case against Edmund D. Taylor and others in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision reached in June 1856. The case stems from a mortgage agreement established on June 12, 1838, where James Whitlock owed Taylor, Breese & Payne a sum of $3,537.65 for merchandise sold and secured it with notes and a mortgage on certain real estate. After Whitlock's death, his estate, including minor heirs, allegedly failed to pay any of the debt. The plaintiffs claimed that the full amount, along with interest, remained unpaid. Throughout the proceedings, a master in chancery was involved to calculate the exact amount due, leading to a report that indicated substantial payments made to certain creditors, purportedly on behalf of Whitlock. However, the court later scrutinized the sufficiency of evidence regarding these payments and the various endorsements on the involved documents.	The plaintiffs argued that the amount due under the mortgage agreement was unpaid, including interest since the mortgage's execution. They highlighted specific payments made to creditors, claiming they were authorized by the mortgage agreement. The plaintiffs sought the total amount owed, which included principal and accrued interest, contending that proper processes had not been followed by the defendants in addressing these debts.	The defendants contended that the evidence presented by the plaintiffs was insufficient to substantiate the claims, particularly regarding the endorsements indicating payments on the mortgage. They argued that the payments made did not have proper legal backing and that the plaintiff’s reliance on the notes and endorsements should not lead to an unfounded assumption of debt liability. The defense insisted that strict proof was necessary, especially since minors were involved as heirs to the deceased. They requested that the court find in favor of the defendants due to these inadequacies in proof.

On October 7, 1855, in LaSalle County, Illinois, Joshua Cushing executed a $1,600 promissory note to Orville N. Adams, secured by a deed of trust on certain real estate, with Adams as the trustee. In May 1856, Adams owed Young & Van Kleek an amount of $1,828 and transferred the note and the trust deed to their attorneys as security for this debt. By November 27, 1856, Cushing conveyed the property to Adams as it remained unpaid. Lycurgus Edgerton had previously obtained a judgment against Adams, leading to a sale of the property on August 25, 1857, which was conveyed to him. Young & Van Kleek later sought to foreclose the trust deed, arguing the lien was lost due to the sale. Edgerton, claiming a paramount title, contested the foreclosure, stating he had no knowledge of any assignment since the record only reflected a direct deed from Cushing to Adams, leading to this legal battle. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Young & Van Kleek, prompting Edgerton to appeal.	The plaintiffs, Young & Van Kleek, claimed that they were entitled to foreclose on the trust deed because the note had not been paid. They argued that Edgerton's acquisition of the property did not extinguish their lien and that despite the conveyance of the property from Cushing to Adams, the mortgage should remain valid. They requested that the premises be sold if Edgerton did not pay the owed amount on the note.	Edgerton and Adams contended that the judicial sale effectively created a paramount title over the property, thus nullifying the mortgage held by Young & Van Kleek. They argued that there was no recorded deed from Adams to Young & Van Kleek, and therefore the mortgage should not apply. Edgerton claimed that he purchased the property under the impression that the mortgage had been satisfied, seeking a reversal of the foreclosure decree.

In June 1867, in Bond County, Illinois, a legal case titled *James M. Miller v. John S. Jenkins* was initiated in the County Court and later moved to the Bond Circuit Court. The plaintiff, John S. Jenkins, brought an action of assumpsit against the defendant, James M. Miller, claiming for unpaid work and labor. The jury found in favor of Jenkins, awarding him $182.25. Following the verdict, Miller filed a motion for a new trial citing several grounds, including the rejection of proper defense instructions and alleged jury misconduct. However, Jenkins contended that the grounds for new trial were invalid as they were not supported by a properly sealed bill of exceptions. The court denied Miller's motion, leading him to appeal the ruling claiming errors in the trial process.	The plaintiff, John S. Jenkins, argued that he was owed compensation for work and labor performed, as noted in the common counts of his declaration. He asserted that the defendant’s appeal was based on insufficient grounds, particularly claiming that the bill of exceptions lacked a seal, rendering it invalid for consideration.	The defendant, James M. Miller, contended that the trial court erred by refusing proper jury instructions, which negatively affected the trial's outcome. He claimed that the jury disobeyed the court's instructions and alleged inappropriate communication between the jury and the officer in charge. In support of his request for a new trial, Miller filed affidavits addressing these issues.

In the case of James Funk v. Rosell M. Hough et al., the legal proceedings took place in McLean County, Illinois, with the final ruling issued in April 1862 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a special contract concerning the purchase and sale of cattle. The plaintiff, James Funk, was originally found in default for failing to deliver one hundred head of stall-fed beef cattle to the defendants, who had already advanced a significant payment of $1,705. The plaintiffs (Hough et al.) attempted to enforce the contract, claiming they were ready and willing to accept delivery and pay for the cattle as per their agreement. A summons was issued to Funk, which was executed by the sheriff, resulting in a default judgment against him for $2,192.50 in damages. Funk appealed the decision, contesting the sufficiency of the sheriff’s return to the summons and the validity of the special counts in the declaration. The court examined the details surrounding the return of the summons and the circumstances of the contract, ultimately affirming the lower court's judgment.	The plaintiffs argued that they had entered into a valid contract for the purchase of one hundred head of cattle, which were to be delivered between January and February of 1861. They claimed to have advanced a part of the purchase price and were fully prepared to pay the remainder upon delivery. The plaintiffs contended that the defendant had failed to deliver the cattle as agreed and sought recovery of the amount paid along with damages in accordance with the contract.	The defendant, James Funk, contended that the sheriff’s return on the summons was insufficient, which he argued undermined the court's jurisdiction over him. He challenged the validity of the special counts in the plaintiff's declaration, asserting that they were fundamentally defective as they did not demonstrate an offer or tender of payment for the cattle. Funk maintained that the plaintiffs' claims were without merit, arguing that the court's judgment was not supported by law.

In January 1859, in Morgan County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between William H. Smucker and Thomas J. Larimore. The conflict originated from a public auction where Larimore intended to sell personal property, including a mule, to satisfy a financial award he was owed by Smucker. Before the sale, Smucker and Lewis HatfieldRequested Larimore to allow Hatfield to purchase the goods using a note payable in sixty days instead of immediate cash. Larimore agreed to this new arrangement with the understanding that it would resolve any ongoing disputes between the parties. Hatfield successfully bid on the property, paid with his note, and thus entered into a contract to waive all errors related to the case. This agreement was intended to conclude all litigation concerning the matter. A legal challenge followed regarding the validity of this contract and the plea of release of errors presented by Larimore.	Smucker's key argument was that the contract and agreement made with Larimore and Hatfield were invalid, asserting that the release of errors was not supported by sufficient legal consideration. He aimed to challenge the enforcement of the plea that claimed all disputes were resolved by the arrangement made at the auction and sought to overturn the judgment rendered by the Morgan Circuit Court.	Larimore contended that the arrangement reached with Smucker and Hatfield constituted a valid and binding contract, supported by adequate consideration. He argued that the agreement to accept Hatfield's note instead of cash, which resulted in a disadvantage for him, served as sufficient justification to support the plea of release of errors. Larimore maintained that since the terms of the sale were altered at Smucker's request, the arrangement effectively resolved all litigation, and thus the court should uphold the judgment.

The case "Joseph E. Otis et al. v. Thomas S. Beckwith et al." was decided in September 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It arose from a dispute over a life insurance policy executed by Edward Sacket in favor of his children. Sacket, who was a resident of Chicago, obtained a policy from the New York Life Insurance Company valued at $3,000, and he later assigned this policy to Thomas S. Beckwith, naming him as trustee for his three sons from a previous marriage. Following Sacket's death on January 17, 1866, his administrator, Joseph E. Otis, alongside his widow, Hannah L. Sacket, and other heirs, refused to surrender the policy to Beckwith, claiming it as part of Sacket's estate. The case involved allegations that the assignment was never completed due to a lack of proper delivery and consideration, which prompted Beckwith to seek legal intervention, asserting his right to the insurance policy for the benefit of the children, especially as their father intended. The core of the dispute centered on the legal and equitable standing of the policy after Sacket's death.	The plaintiff, Thomas S. Beckwith, claimed that he was the rightful trustee of the life insurance policy assigned to him by Edward Sacket for the benefit of Sacket's three sons from a prior marriage. Beckwith argued that all actions required to effectuate the assignment were completed, including notifying the insurance company and providing his written acceptance of the trusteeship. He requested the court to compel the administrator, Joseph E. Otis, to surrender the policy to him and to declare him the legal and equitable owner of the policy as the designated trustee.	The defendants, led by Joseph E. Otis, contended that the assignment of the life insurance policy was invalid due to the lack of actual delivery and that the policy remained an asset of Edward Sacket's estate. They claimed that the supposed assignments were not executed properly, lacked consideration, and were not delivered to Beckwith. Furthermore, they asserted that Sacket retained control over the policy up until his death, making any claims by Beckwith without legal standing.

The case "Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Co. v. Amos L. Merriman" took place in September 1869 in Peoria, Illinois. The plaintiff, Amos L. Merriman, brought a legal action against the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company due to the company's failure to deliver a box of goods he had entrusted to them for transport to Washington, D.C. The goods were delivered to the railroad company's agent at Peoria with a bill of lading issued for their transportation, highlighting that it was a through freight contract. However, Merriman's goods did not reach their intended destination, prompting him to seek compensation for their value. The railway company's defense was based on their claim that they were not liable for deliveries beyond the terminus of their railroad, which ended at the state line between Illinois and Indiana. They argued that since it wasn't demonstrated that the loss of the goods occurred on their line, Merriman could not recover damages. The case was initially heard in the Peoria circuit court, where the jury found in favor of Merriman.	Merriman's main argument centered on the assertion that the railway company's failure to deliver his goods constituted a breach of the agreed terms of the through freight contract evidenced by the bill of lading. He sought recovery of the value of the goods, insisting that the railway company had a responsibility as a common carrier to ensure their delivery to Washington, D.C.	The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company's defense hinged on the argument that they limit their liability to deliveries made only within the confines of their railway line. They contended that, as goods were not proven to have been lost on their route, they could not be held accountable. The company maintained that their liability ended at the state line, and they had not undertaken to carry the goods beyond this point.

In 1830, in St. Clair County, Illinois, Adam W. Snyder entered into a transaction with Baptiste Laframboise and Louis Pingonneau for the purchase of a tract of land. Snyder claimed to have paid $150 and received a quitclaim deed from the defendants, which explicitly stated that the sellers did not warrant the land against claims from anyone but themselves. However, during the trial, it became evident that the defendants had no rightful title to the land, and Pingonneau made comments suggesting that he was aware Snyder was wary of dealing with him due to concerns about potential deception, asserting a preference for conducting business with Pingonneau instead. The case revolved around the validity of Snyder's assertions that he had been misled, specifically questioning whether there was fraud involved in the sale of the land. The jury found in favor of Snyder, leading to an appeal by Laframboise.	Snyder argued that he was entitled to recover his purchase money due to misrepresentation by the defendants regarding their title to the land. He contended that the defendants sold land without holding valid title and that their actions constituted fraud. Consequently, he sought a judgment for the return of his $150 investment, claiming that they did not disclose critical information about the title that would have influenced his decision to purchase the land.	The defense, represented by Laframboise, contended that there was no fraud or false statements made regarding the title of the land. They argued that the principles of caveat emptor (let the buyer beware) applied, implying that without any fraudulent actions or misrepresentations, Snyder had no grounds to recover the purchase money. The defense also insisted that any statements made by Pingonneau were inadmissible as evidence against Laframboise since he was not present during these statements.

David Siegwald passed away on October 13, 1862, in Chicago, Illinois, leaving behind a contested will. His will bequeathed all his real and personal estate to his wife, Antonia, in "fee simple absolute forever," but also specified that upon her death, their son, Anton, would inherit what remained. The will was admitted to probate, and letters testamentary were granted to Antonia. Shortly thereafter, Antonia sought to sell the real estate, valued at approximately $13,000, to address a $3,000 encumbrance placed on it during David's lifetime. Anton, then a minor, filed a bill in chancery claiming that his mother was only granted a life estate by the will and that the fee simple title belonged to him, subject to her life estate. The initial court upheld Anton's claim by denying Antonia's request to sell the property and issued an injunction against her. Antonia then filed a writ of error, contesting the ruling. The dispute centers on interpreting the will's language regarding the estate's vesting and the limitations imposed on it.	Anton Siegwald claimed that the will of David Siegwald only granted his mother, Antonia, a life estate in the real property with the remainder going to him after her death. He argued that the language in the will clearly indicated that, while Antonia could enjoy the estate during her lifetime, the fee simple estate was vested in him, and thus he requested the court to restrain Antonia from selling the property.	Antonia Siegwald contended that the will conferred upon her a fee simple absolute interest in the real estate, integrating the language that she could enjoy its benefits until her death. She argued that the limitations placed on her ownership were either repugnant or inoperative, thereby asserting her right to sell the property. Following the initial ruling against her, she sought to have that decision overturned through the writ of error.

The case "T. & H. Smith & Co. v. Charles Yargo" was decided on May 25, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute originated in the County Court of Cumberland County, Illinois, where T. & H. Smith & Co. (the plaintiffs) sought to enforce a promissory note against Charles Yargo (the defendant). The plaintiffs initiated an attachment suit, which involved levying real estate to satisfy the debt owed by the defendant. However, the County Court dismissed the case, asserting it lacked jurisdiction to hear attachment cases concerning real estate when there was no personal service of process on the defendant. The plaintiffs argued that the County Court had the same jurisdiction as Circuit Courts when it came to actions on promissory notes. They contended that the attachment statutes permitted such proceedings and that the County Court could enforce its judgments in all ways permitted by the attachment act.	The plaintiffs, T. & H. Smith & Co., claimed that the County Court had the jurisdiction to issue a judgment against the defendant's real estate in their attachment suit. They argued that the legislative statutes allowed for this procedure, despite the absence of personal service on the defendant, asserting that the court's jurisdiction should not be limited in this manner.	Charles Yargo, the defendant, maintained that the County Court did not have the authority to grant a judgment against his real estate without personal service. He contended that jurisdiction in attachment cases involving real property was limited, and thus the suit should be dismissed based on this lack of jurisdiction.

Robert O’Niel v. Christopher Orr et al. is a legal case from December 1842, held in Peoria, Illinois. The lawsuit involved Robert O’Niel and Andrew Gray, who initiated an action of replevin to recover a steamboat named The Tennessee from Christopher Orr and others. Initially, Gray objected to his participation in the suit, leading to his withdrawal and O’Niel proceeding as the sole plaintiff. The crux of the case lay in the legitimacy of O’Niel's purchase of the steamboat. O’Niel testified that the previous owner, Phillips, sold the boat for a total of $1,000, with $500 paid upfront and the remainder secured through a deed of trust for future payment. The defendants claimed rights to possess the steamboat because of a lien from an execution against Phillips, which was allegedly in the sheriff's hands at the time of O’Niel’s purchase. A significant point of contention was whether the steamboat was in Missouri when the sale occurred, impacting the execution of the lien. During the trial, the court instructed the jury that a bona fide purchaser must pay the consideration upfront, a point that was contested by O’Niel.	Robert O’Niel claimed that he was the bona fide purchaser of The Tennessee, arguing that he paid part of the total purchase price and that the transaction was legitimate since he was unaware of any existing execution lien against Phillips at the time of sale. He requested the court to instruct the jury that his purchase should be recognized as valid, irrespective of the fact that the outstanding balance was secured for future payment, which he believed would exempt the steamboat from being seized under the execution.	The defendants argued that they had rightful possession of The Tennessee due to a lien from an execution against Phillips. They contended that since the execution was in effect at the time of sale, the sale to O’Niel could not be deemed bona fide unless the full purchase price had been paid upfront. They highlighted that the court's instruction to the jury regarding the necessity of actual payment for a bona fide purchase was appropriate and valid.

The case "Marquis D. Lusk et al. v. Henry Harber" was initiated as an action of ejectment in the Madison Circuit Court in June 1844. The plaintiffs, Lusk and Meeker, sought to recover a tract of land encompassing 400 acres (claim 1833, survey 675) from defendant Henry Harber. To support their claim, the plaintiffs presented a judgment from the Madison Circuit Court favoring the State of Illinois, related to unpaid taxes on the property for the year 1840. They also produced a deed from the sheriff to the plaintiffs, confirming their ownership after the sale of the land due to tax delinquency in October 1841. During trial, the plaintiffs established that Harber was in possession of the disputed land at the time of the action. In defense, Harber presented a patent from the U.S. to Nicholas Jarrot, along with a series of deeds that traced ownership from Jarrot's heirs to Leopold Carrier. The defense also aimed to prove that the land was not properly assessed for taxes. The court trial concluded with the jury favoring Harber, leading the plaintiffs to seek a new trial on the grounds of perceived legal irregularities.	The plaintiffs argued that they had established a prima facie case by demonstrating ownership through a sheriff's deed derived from a valid judgment and precept. They maintained that Harber's possession of the property at the action's commencement did not legitimize his claim against their established title. The plaintiffs requested the court to instruct the jury that any irregularity in the assessor's reports did not invalidate the judgment or the sheriff's deed.	The defendant, Henry Harber, contended that the assessment of the land for taxes in 1840 was invalid due to irregularities in the assessment process. He argued that without a proper and legal assessment, the subsequent sale and the sheriff's deed should hold no weight in establishing title. Furthermore, Harber claimed to have possession of the land and suggested that because of the defective assessment, the jury should rule in his favor.

The case of *The Peoria and Pekin Union Railway Company v. John Clayberg, Admr.* took place in Peoria, Illinois, and culminated in a judgment delivered by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 20, 1883. The incident involved the death of Fred Clark, an errand boy, who was struck and killed by a moving train while crossing the defendant's railroad tracks at a street crossing just after dark. The location had notable traffic, as many pedestrians used the crossing during peak hours. The railway company was accused of negligence due to their failure to provide adequate warnings, such as sounding a whistle or ringing a bell before moving their cars across the street. The case underwent a series of legal proceedings, resulting in appeals that kept the central issues revolving around the alleged negligence of the railway company and the conduct of the deceased. The court had to address errors of law following a jury's verdict in favor of the plaintiff at the lower court.	The plaintiff, representing the estate of Fred Clark, argued that the railway company was liable for negligence leading to Clark's death. The plaintiff claimed the defendant failed to take necessary precautions, such as warning pedestrians at the crossing where the accident occurred. It was asserted that the defendant knew the crossing was frequently used, especially during specific hours, and yet did not implement measures to prevent accidents. The plaintiff’s stance also included that Clark was not guilty of contributing negligence which could absolve the defendant from liability.	The defendant, the Peoria and Pekin Union Railway Company, contended that the plaintiff's deceased was not exercising due care at the time of the incident. They wanted to introduce evidence suggesting that Clark had a habit of boarding trains unsafely, but the court ruled it inadmissible as irrelevant and harmful. The railway company also argued that the plaintiff's instructions to the jury exaggerated the defendant's responsibilities while neglecting to clarify the duties expected of the deceased. They asserted that the deceased may have been trespassing or acting recklessly, thus potentially relieving them of liability.

The case "Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Ry. Co. v. W. H. Purviance" was brought to the Illinois Appellate Court and was decided on May 22, 1884. The dispute arose in Logan County, Illinois, where W. H. Purviance, the plaintiff, claimed that eight hogs belonging to him were killed by a train operated by the Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railway Company, the appellant. Purviance sought compensation for the value of the hogs, as well as attorney's fees pursuant to statutory provisions. During the trial, a jury found in favor of Purviance, rendering a verdict of $78.50 against the railway company. The railway company subsequently appealed this judgment, asserting that the evidence presented did not demonstrate that the railroad had been open for use for six months prior to the incident involving the hogs, a requirement for recovery as established in prior cases. The appellate court found that there was no evidence to support that assertion, leading to a reversal of the lower court’s judgment.	The plaintiff, W. H. Purviance, claimed the railroad company was liable for the value of the eight hogs killed by its train. He argued that statutory provisions entitled him to recover both the value of the livestock and attorney's fees due to the negligence of the railroad. Purviance contended that the necessary legal requirements for his claim had been met despite the railroad company's defenses.	The defendant, Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Ry. Co., argued that the case should be dismissed because there was no evidence that their railroad had been operational for six months prior to the hogs' death. They claimed that without proof of this critical requirement, which was based on established legal precedents, Purviance was not entitled to any recovery. The defendant requested the court to reverse the judgment entered against them.

In 1860, in De Witt County, Illinois, Elijah W. Swearingen brought a lawsuit against the Illinois Central Railroad Company after three of his horses were killed on the railroad tracks. The plaintiff claimed that the deaths resulted from the railroad's failure to maintain the fence along its tracks, which allowed his horses to escape from his pasture onto the track. The plaintiff alleged that he had not erected or agreed to erect the required fence but was later found to have built it under a contract with the railroad company, which supplied the materials and paid for the construction. A series of events led to the damage claim as one horse was killed on a Saturday night and two others on the following Monday, after which the fence that had been in good repair was discovered broken. The defense was based on the assertion that the railroad company acted reasonably regarding fence repairs and that the legal obligations did not transfer to Swearingen merely by the nature of their agreement.	The plaintiff, Elijah W. Swearingen, claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company's negligence in maintaining the fence led to the deaths of his horses. He argued that the company owned the responsibility to keep the fence functional and that his employment to build it didn't transfer that duty to him. He sought damages in the amount of $287.50 for the loss of his horses.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company defended itself by asserting that the fence had been adequate at the time of the incidents and that any damages caused were due to factors outside its control, such as trespassing or an accident. They argued that Swearingen had built the fence under their contract and, therefore, should not hold the company liable. The defendant also requested certain instructions to the jury regarding their responsibility and the timing for repairs that were refused by the court.

In late 1840, the case of Wickliffe Kitchell et al. v. The County of Madison arose in Madison County, Illinois. Key individuals involved included Wickliffe Kitchell, who served as the attorney-general; Miller, the sheriff; and Brown, the clerk. They sought payment for their services related to the prosecution of John Smith and others indicted for larceny. The county commissioners court refused their fee bills, as the defendants were insolvent and unable to pay court costs. The case was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court to address whether there is a legal obligation for the county to pay these fees, given the defendants' inability to cover the costs of their prosecution. The Illinois statutes at the time, specifically a repealed act from 1821, previously allowed for payment of these fees in certain circumstances, but the current law indicated no such obligation remained.	The plaintiffs argued that the county had a legal obligation to pay the fees incurred by law enforcement officers during the prosecution, regardless of the defendants' insolvency. They claimed that previous statutes authorized such fees to be paid by the county when defendants were either acquitted or unable to pay costs, pressing for an allowance of their fees for services rendered in the aforementioned larceny case.	The defendant, the County of Madison, contended that there was no legal requirement to pay the claimed fees because statutory provisions allowing for such payments had been repealed. They maintained that the obligation to pay costs falls on the convicted individual, and since the defendants were insolvent, the county commissioners were correct in denying the allowance. The defense cited existing laws indicating the county is not bound to cover prosecution fees in cases of conviction and that any fees payable must be requested from the defendant's estate, risking non-recovery in cases of insolvency.

On August 18, 1886, in a railroad excursion incident near Petersburg, Illinois, Theodore Fisher became a passenger on a Chicago and Alton Railroad train that was running an excursion to Ashland. During the return journey, the plaintiff experienced overcrowding on the train, which led to dangerous conditions as many passengers crowded onto the platforms and aisles. The plaintiff tried to board one of the rear cars but ultimately ended up on the crowded front step of the smoker car. As the train approached Petersburg, a rush to exit caused him to be pressured off the train and he tragically fell onto a heavy truck positioned too close to the platform, which resulted in significant injuries, though no bones were broken. Fischer was unconscious for several days and required six weeks to recover, although his condition was not fully resolved by the time of the trial. Witness testimony varied, with some suggesting he voluntarily exited the train, while others indicated he was pushed off due to the crowding and pressure from other passengers. Evidence pointed to inadequate accommodations by the railroad company, which had failed to anticipate the high passenger numbers for the soldier reunion event.	The plaintiff, Theodore Fisher, claimed that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was negligent for allowing their train to become overcrowded, which created unsafe conditions that led to his injuries. He argued that the company had prior notice of the expected high passenger volume due to the soldiers' reunion and failed to provide adequate room and safety measures, including allowing a heavy truck to be placed dangerously close to the train platform. Fisher sought damages for the injuries he sustained during the incident.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company contended that there was no negligence on their part since the injuries were a result of Fisher's own actions. They argued that he voluntarily stepped off the train rather than being forced by the crowd. The defense also maintained that they were only required to exercise reasonable diligence to accommodate passengers during an extraordinary demand and questioned the admissibility of certain evidence regarding the anticipated crowd size, suggesting it did not constitute valid notice to necessitate additional accommodations.

On September 1875, in Chicago, Illinois, a legal case arose between Alfred Berrington and Michael F. Casey regarding a lease agreement for a house and lot. The written lease, dated December 7, 1871, specified that Casey was to rent a store for $100 per month until May 1873, having provided an advance payment of $10. However, following this agreement, Casey leased the same premises to another individual, McLaughlin, for $125 per month, thereby putting McLaughlin in possession. Upon returning from New York, Berrington sought to pay the remaining rent and reclaim possession, but Casey refused. Consequently, Berrington filed a lawsuit to recover damages for the breach of lease, leading to a trial in which a jury ruled in favor of Berrington for $450 in damages. Casey then sought a reversal of this judgment through a writ of error.	Berrington argued that Casey breached the lease agreement by subleasing the premises to McLaughlin, thereby preventing Berrington from occupying the property as contractually intended. Berrington claimed damages for this breach, asserting that he was entitled to monetary compensation without needing to formally tender the rent he owed, as Casey's refusal to accept payment constituted a waiver of the requirement to pay.	Casey contended that the lease agreement was not enforceable as it lacked certain covenants, particularly a provision for possession and quiet enjoyment by Berrington. He argued that the suit instituted by Berrington was improper, asserting that Berrington should have made a formal tender of the rent due to pursue his claims. Casey maintained that the jury's verdict and the award of damages were unjustified based on the claims presented.

In the year 1837, James Heaton entered into a contractual agreement with Joseph Kemper regarding the operation of a tanning business. The contract stipulated that Kemper would manage the tanning business for one year and was responsible for ensuring no hides spoiled or suffered damage during his tenure. In exchange, Heaton agreed to compensate Kemper with various provisions, including $200, a residence, firewood, flour, and essential tools necessary for the business. In June 1840, Heaton filed a lawsuit against Kemper in the Edgar Circuit Court, claiming that due to Kemper's negligence, a significant quantity of hides valued at $1,000 was ruined. The central issue was whether Kemper performed his covenants. Kemper contended that he adhered to the contract, while also arguing that Heaton had failed to provide certain necessary tools and materials, which impeded his performance. The case was presented to a jury, who ultimately found in favor of Kemper, leading to Heaton's request for a new trial, citing a refusal of the court to provide specific jury instructions related to the case.	James Heaton, the plaintiff, claimed that Joseph Kemper had neglected his responsibilities under their agreement, resulting in the spoilage of hides worth $1,000. He sought remedial action based on the assertion that he had upheld his part of the covenant, specifically by providing the necessary provisions and expecting Kemper to fulfill his obligations, including taking proper care of the hides.	Joseph Kemper, the defendant, argued that he fully complied with the covenant's terms and showcased that any failure of performance was attributable to Heaton's neglect to provide essential tools and materials that were necessary for the tanning process. Kemper's defense was twofold: first, he maintained that he performed his duties as stipulated in the contract, and second, he alleged that Heaton's failure to furnish requested tools hindered his ability to meet his contractual obligations.

In November 1860, the case of George P. Uhl v. Andrew J. Dighton was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Piatt Circuit Court. The dispute arose from Uhl's claim against Dighton for trespass de bonis asportatis, which pertains to the wrongful taking of personal property. The background of the case involved a lease between Dighton and a tenant named Smith for a farm, with an annual rent of $360 due. Uhl, claiming not to be Dighton's tenant but a sub-lessee under Smith, argued that the corn seized by Dighton and the sheriff was his property, asserting that under Smith's lease, the rent was not due until after a specific date in December 1859. Dighton contended that the corn belonged to Smith, and since Uhl was not the tenant, Dighton had the right to seize the corn for the unpaid rent. The court had to decide whether the landlord's right to distrain for unpaid rent could extend to the crops grown by a sub-tenant.	George P. Uhl argued that he was a sub-lessee of the farmland and not a direct tenant of Andrew J. Dighton. Uhl claimed that the corn seized was his property and was grown during the year 1859 under the terms of the lease from Smith, which stipulated that rent was not due until December 25, 1859. Therefore, Uhl requested that the court recognize his rights to the property and invalidate Dighton's seizure.	Andrew J. Dighton contended that as the landlord, he had the authority to seize any personal property within the demised premises to cover rent owed. Dighton argued that since the corn was considered part of the estate, he lawfully distrained it due to the unpaid rent by Smith, the original tenant. He requested that the court uphold his right to seize the crops, emphasizing that Uhl's claims as a sub-lessee were insufficient to protect his interests.

David F. Hamsher died on February 15, 1889, in Decatur, Illinois, leaving behind a will and no direct descendants. His estate included two town lots and 160 acres of land. His only heirs were his widow, Anna Hamsher, and his father, William Hamsher. Following the terms of the will, Anna was entitled to an annuity and a homestead lot, while William was allocated a lesser annuity.
