Anna filed a legal action on May 23, 1889, seeking the assignment of her homestead rights to one of the lots, the partition of the other town lot, and the partition of the 160 acres, claiming her interest as an heir and through her renunciation of the will's provisions. In response, William Hamsher filed a cross-bill alleging that a bequest to the Young Men’s Christian Association was void because it exceeded the legal limit for land ownership by a religious corporation. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Anna and dismissed William's cross-bill, leading to an appeal by William to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Anna Hamsher, as the plaintiff, argued that due to her renunciation of the will, she was entitled to half of the estate, including a right to partition the properties. She sought legal recognition of her claims to the homestead, along with a partition of the remaining estate, which she contended should be divided equally among the rightful heirs, including herself and the executors of the estate.	William Hamsher, the defendant, argued that the claim made by Anna was incorrect based on the position that the land bequeathed to the Young Men’s Christian Association was invalid due to the organization's status as a religious corporation, which under Illinois law was restricted from owning more than ten acres of land. He contended that this rendered additional land belonging to the estate intestate and therefore rightfully his as the sole heir.

Timothy Wright filed a legal case against The City of Chicago, which was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1870. The case originated from a lawsuit related to tax issues concerning Wright in the city of Chicago. During the proceedings, a judgment was rendered against Wright in the lower court, leading him to appeal the decision. The case involved several key individuals, including Mr. Daniel L. Shobey, who represented Wright as the appellant, and Mr. M. F. Tuley, who represented the City of Chicago as the appellee. The central issue at hand revolved around the tax obligations and whether the judgments of the lower court were just.	The plaintiff, Timothy Wright, argued against the judgment rendered against him in the lower court concerning tax liabilities. He sought to contest the decision and was looking for a reversal of the judgment, claiming that the taxes assessed were unjust or incorrectly handled.	The defendant, The City of Chicago, maintained that the lower court's judgment against Wright was sound and well-founded. Their primary argument was that the proceedings complied with established legal precedents in similar cases, specifically referencing prior rulings like Dunham v. The City of Chicago. They requested the court to affirm the judgment of the lower court.

In 1873, in Cook County, Illinois, Myron J. Amick initiated a replevin action against George H. Young and Timothy M. Bradley, the latter serving as the county sheriff. The case revolved around a framed building originally a barn that had been purchased from Finney and was converted to a dwelling. Amick claimed ownership or right to possess the building, which had been the subject of a judgment against Charles B. Foster in favor of Young. The case involved questions regarding the lease of land to Foster, the purchase and relocation of the barn, and who was responsible for its renovations. Two juries had previously found that Carpenter leased the lot to Foster, who had claimed the barn and paid for its movement and conversion into a dwelling. The court examined testimonial evidence regarding possession and actions indicating ownership, concluding that such evidence could affect the determination of rightful ownership. Multiple legal arguments regarding jury selection, evidence admission, and appeal bond requirements were also presented.	Myron J. Amick argued that he had rightful ownership or the right to immediate possession of the framed dwelling. He challenged the judgment made by the lower court favoring the defendants, claiming errors regarding the acceptance of evidence and jury instructions that potentially influenced the outcome against him.	The defendants, particularly Timothy M. Bradley as the sheriff, defended their actions by asserting the legitimacy of the property seizure under an execution issued for a debt owed by Foster to Young. They argued that the existence of Foster's claims and actions over the barn, including payment for its relocation and renovation, indicated that Foster had rightful possession. The defendants contended that the jury's findings were justifiable based on substantial evidence.

The case involves The Chicago, Milwaukee & Saint Paul Railway Company and The Chicago & North-Western Railway Company against Mary A. Snyder, Administratrix, and it took place in Illinois, culminating in a court decision on December 7, 1888. This incident traces back to a fatal accident that occurred in October 1882 on a foggy morning. At that time, the tracks of the North-Western Railway ran east and west, intersecting with the tracks of the St. Paul Railway at an acute angle. Both companies had trains waiting to cross the tracks when the conductor, Snyder, was involved in the accident. The safety of the crossing relied on signals shown at a semaphore near the location. Two juries had previously ruled on the case, suggesting the negligence could have originated from either company's crew or the semaphore operator. After examining various testimonies and instructions given to juries, it was established that the conductor’s death resulted from an accident that might have involved negligence on the part of both railway companies.	Mary A. Snyder, as the administratrix, claimed damages for the wrongful death of her husband, who was a conductor for one of the defendant railway companies. She argued that the negligence of the employees operating the semaphore signal contributed to the fatal accident, holding both railroad companies liable for this negligence and seeking compensation for the resulting damages.	The defendants, The Chicago, Milwaukee & Saint Paul Railway Company and The Chicago & North-Western Railway Company, contended that any negligence leading to the accident was solely the responsibility of the semaphore operator, who had been employed and discharged by the Chicago & North-Western Railway Company. They argued that since the operator's actions were isolated to one company's trains, they could not be held liable for the accident that involved the conductor employed by the other company.

In 1876, in Illinois, Elizabeth Yazel and her late husband John Yazel conveyed their homestead property to Ezekiel H. Palmer. As part of this transaction, Palmer executed a bond promising to pay Elizabeth $2,000 from the proceeds of the property's future sale. After selling the property for $1,700, Palmer made payments amounting to nearly $1,000 to John Yazel, who was then deceased, without explicit authority from Elizabeth. The case centers on Elizabeth's claim to the remaining funds and the rights governed by the Harried Woman’s Act of 1861, which protected her dower rights. The court considered her unwillingness to release her rights without securing funds for another homestead and examined whether Palmer had the authority to pay her deceased husband. As the contract was deemed valid as long as no creditors objected, the focus was on the obligations Palmer had towards Elizabeth following the property sale.	Elizabeth Yazel's primary argument was that Ezekiel Palmer wrongfully paid her deceased husband John Yazel without authorization, violating the terms of the bond, which was intended to secure her rights. She sought the remaining balance of the sale proceeds, asserting that the obligation explicitly required payment to her and that she had not consented to any payments made to her husband. Elizabeth maintained that the bond created a trust in her favor, and she was entitled to recover the funds as they constituted her separate property, protected under the law.	Ezekiel Palmer contended that he acted in good faith when he made payments to John Yazel, inferring that the obligation to pay the proceeds was effectively a responsibility of the husband, even though the bond was payable to Elizabeth. He argued that since Elizabeth's interest in the property was bound to her husband's estate, he had no obligation to pay her directly. Palmer claimed that any payments made to the husband were justified under the assumption that he had agency to act on behalf of his wife, and thus he sought to retain the funds until disputes regarding the property title were resolved.

Samuel S. Hake filed a case against Isaac J. Strubel, which culminated in a legal dispute over the proper handling of a bill of exceptions concerning a trial decision made in St. Clair County, Illinois. The case was considered by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 20, 1887, stemming from a judgment rendered in the St. Clair Circuit Court on April 21, 1886. Hake's counsel had requested an extension of time to file the bill of exceptions after the trial court's term had adjourned. The trial judge had initially granted a fourteen-day extension in writing, but the issue arose regarding whether the judge had the authority to make this extension after the court term had ended. The court needed to determine whether the judge's actions in extending the filing period and signing the bill of exceptions were valid under the law.	Hake argued that the trial judge’s extension of time to file the bill of exceptions was valid, claiming it allowed him to preserve the record of the trial's proceedings for appellate review. He contended that the necessary actions taken by the judge qualified the bill of exceptions to become a part of the official court record despite the expiration of the original filing period.	Strubel contended that the trial judge did not have the authority to extend the time for filing the bill of exceptions after the end of the court term. He argued that the bill of exceptions, having been filed beyond the allowed time after the court term had concluded, should not be admitted into the record of the case, rendering it a nullity.

In the case of Joshua C. Sanders v. Walter L. Peck et al., heard by the Illinois Supreme Court on October 31, 1889, the dispute originated from a complex series of legal actions involving land and bonds. Joshua C. Sanders had purchased 195 bonds from the Chicago and Great Western Railroad Company and acquired 301 lots at Riverside from the Chicago and Great Western Railroad Land Company. He made these purchases intending to secure the release of these lots from the lien of a trust deed held by trustee John N. Jewett, which had specific provisions for such a release upon the tender of certain bonds. However, when Sanders tendered his bonds to Jewett for the release, the trustee refused to accept them. This led to a series of legal filings, including Sanders' cross-bill against Walter L. Peck and others, who sought to foreclose on the trust deed. Initially, the circuit court found that Sanders' deeds were procured by fraud, which was later reversed by the appellate court, affirming Sanders' right to the release of the lots upon fulfilling certain conditions. The matter involved significant legal complexities and previous court decisions spanning nearly 14 years of litigation.	Sanders claimed that he was entitled to a release of his lots from the trust deed's lien upon surrendering his bonds to the trustee. He argued that he had made a valid tender of his bonds, which should enforce his right to redeem the lots. Sanders insisted that the foreclosure proceeding would cause him unjust harm and that he was entitled to relief per the express terms of the trust deed, specifically requesting that the court compel Jewett to execute the release of his lots upon his bond surrender.	The defendants, including Peck and his associates, argued against Sanders' claims by pointing out that the trust deed’s provisions required strict adherence to its terms, which included the surrender of bonds and the payment of taxes before any release could be granted. They contended that Sanders’ claims were based on the invalidity of the bonds and that the previous court decrees had already dismissed the possibility of such a release due to purported fraud in the acquisition of the lots. They maintained that his tender lacked legal standing, asserting that he had not complied with the decree’s requirements, which justified the dismissal of his claims.

In April 1851, Frederick Vogt and his wife Christiana filed a bill in equity against John V., John C., and Martha Hess, minors, over a shared property in Butterfield’s addition to Chicago. The petitioners claimed lawful ownership of an undivided fourth of the property, seeking a partition due to its indivisibility. The court appointed a guardian ad litem for the minors and, following a master’s report, decreed the property to be sold rather than divided. The sale took place for $185 to Arno Voss, who later occupied it. In a subsequent bill, the Hess family accused Christiana of fraudulent actions and claimed improper sale and valuation of the property, asserting it was worth $800 at the time of sale. They contended that Voss, as the attorney, manipulated the proceedings and that no just reason existed for the sale. They sought to reverse the prior decree, declare the sale void, and obtain an account of rents and profits.	The plaintiffs argued that the previous partition and sale of the property were fraudulently procured by Arno Voss. They maintained that the property was sold for far less than its true value and claimed that the sale was improperly conducted, lacking competitive bids due to fears of illegality. They requested the court to reverse the previous decree, declare void any deeds or mortgages tied to the property against them, and seek an accounting for any rents and profits accrued since the sale.	The defendant, Arno Voss, contended that the proceedings were lawful and the sale was executed correctly. He denied allegations of fraud, asserting that the property was sold at a reasonable price and that he acted in good faith during the sale. Voss claimed that the minors were appropriately represented at every step and that the allegations of impropriety were unfounded. He also argued that the court’s actions were supported by evidence and the procedures adhered to proper legal standards.

In September 1874, the case of Sanford B. Parkhurst v. Eliakim P. Vail, Admr., etc. was tried in the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Cook Circuit Court. The parties involved included Sanford B. Parkhurst, the defendant, and Eliakim P. Vail, the plaintiff, representing the estate of Micah Vail, who had passed away. The legal dispute centered around a promissory note dated July 18, 1857, for the sum of seven hundred dollars, which was executed by Henry A. Parkhurst and Robert L. Wilson. The note was guaranteed by Sanford B. Parkhurst, who indorsed it on the back. The core issue was whether Parkhurst’s signature was written before or after the note was delivered to the payee, Micah Vail. The trial revealed conflicting testimonies regarding the delivery and consideration for the note. The jury ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding the amount of the note plus interest, leading to Parkhurst's appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, represented by Eliakim P. Vail, claimed that Sanford B. Parkhurst had guaranteed the payment of a promissory note executed in 1857. Vail argued that Parkhurst, by signing the note, assumed liability to pay the sum if the original makers failed to do so. The case was based on the presumption that Parkhurst's guarantee was made with the same consideration as the note if his signature was placed on it before its delivery. Vail sought to enforce the payment against Parkhurst.	Sanford B. Parkhurst contended that his signature was placed on the back of the note after it had been delivered to the payee, Micah Vail, implying no legal consideration for the guarantee. He argued that because the note was not paid at maturity, no obligation existed for him unless a new consideration was proven. Parkhurst also raised objections regarding the jury instructions and claimed that Vail's delay in bringing suit invalidated the claim against him.

Joseph Liness sought the position of clerk of the police court in Chicago and sent a letter dated April 7, 1865, to Anthony C. Hesing. In his letter, Liness enclosed twenty dollars, requesting Hesing to use his influence to secure Liness's nomination for the position, with the promise of an additional twenty dollars if the nomination was successful. However, instead of using his influence in Liness's favor, Hesing acted against him, leading Liness to file a lawsuit to recover the twenty dollars. The case originated in the justice court of Cook County, then was appealed to the Circuit Court, which ruled in favor of Hesing. Following this, Liness filed a writ of error to challenge the decision. The key legal principle at stake was that courts will not recognize transactions aimed at influencing public office nominations through improper financial incentives, as exemplified by the maxim "ex turpi causa non oritur actio" (no action arises from a base cause).	Liness’s main argument revolved around the claim that he had sent twenty dollars to Hesing with the expectation that he would use his influence for Liness's nomination to a public office. Liness contended that, since he provided the money on the premise of securing the office, he was entitled to recover the amount when Hesing did not act in his favor but instead worked against his nomination.	Hesing’s defense focused on the improper nature of the transaction, asserting that he did not use his influence for Liness because the arrangement was unethical. He argued that the legal principle of "ex turpi causa non oritur actio" should apply, implying that the law does not provide remedy for claims deriving from immoral or illegal acts, and therefore, Liness should not recover the money since it involved an attempt to influence public office through financial inducement.

Jacob Johnson v. Joseph O. Glover is a legal case heard by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 17, 1887. The dispute arose in connection with a promissory note for $1500 executed by Nelson & Bullen, which was guaranteed by Joseph O. Glover (the defendant) upon its execution on March 6, 1883. After some time, Glover sold the note to Lawrence Carton at a discount and wrote his name across the back of the note twice. Carton then transferred the note to the First National Bank of Ottawa, which subsequently sent it to the Union National Bank of Chicago for collection. Johnson (the plaintiff) brought an action of assumpsit against Glover, arguing that he intended to guarantee the note. During the trial, evidence was presented that Glover had agreed to guarantee the note when he sold it to Carton, but Glover disputed this. The case hinged on whether the repeated signing indicated a different intent regarding his liability.	The plaintiff, Jacob Johnson, claimed that Joseph O. Glover acted as a guarantor for the promissory note when he sold it to Carton and, by signing his name twice on the back of the note, accepted liability for its repayment. Johnson contended that he had purchased the note in good faith and without notice of any issues regarding its enforceability, seeking recovery based on Glover's guarantee.	The defendant, Joseph O. Glover, argued that he was not liable under the note, asserting that the evidence of his intent to guarantee was improperly admitted in court. He maintained that the two signatures did not indicate an intention to assume different obligations and argued that parol evidence should not contradict the written contract. Additionally, Glover claimed that the note was paid after its maturity, which would extinguish his obligation as a guarantor.

In February 1874, Robert Greenhalgh from Galesburg, Illinois, was shipped a box of goods valued at $250, marked “C. O. D.” by the consignors, Grismer & Buxbaum, through the American Express Company. Upon arrival, the agent at Galesburg offered the goods to Greenhalgh, who refused to accept or pay for them, though he paid the express charges and requested the goods be returned to the consignors. Subsequently, the consignors filed a lawsuit against Greenhalgh in March 1874, and by August, the court ruled in their favor, granting them a judgment for the goods' value. On the following day, based on the consignors' attorney's instructions, the express company shipped the goods back to Grismer & Buxbaum, who received them. Around August 24, Greenhalgh demanded the goods from the express company without offering payment. The company refused to deliver them, leading Greenhalgh to file a trover action to recover the goods' value. During the trial, it was acknowledged that the judgment from the county court granted Greenhalgh absolute title to the goods. However, the court ruled against him, stating that the express company was justified in delivering the goods based on the circumstances around the return order.	Greenhalgh claimed that he was entitled to the value of the goods following the county court judgment, which should have vested him with absolute title to the goods. He argued that the express company failed in their duty by not delivering the goods after the judgment was rendered, despite his repeated demands for their return without an offer to pay the required charges.	The American Express Company contended that they acted correctly by returning the goods to the consignors as instructed and that they were not liable for damages to Greenhalgh. They maintained that the consignee (Greenhalgh) had previously directed the return of the goods and failed to notify the company of any changes to that order. The company asserted that liability for delivering the goods lay with the consignors, and they had delivered the goods to the true owners as per legal standards.

The case "Village of Hyde Park v. William J. Slee et al." took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the decision rendered on October 23, 1883. The key individuals involved included the Village of Hyde Park as the plaintiff and William J. Slee among the defendants. The dispute arose surrounding certain actions or decisions made by the defendants that were contested by the plaintiff. The case's significance lies in its connection to a similar case involving George L. Thatcher, which was decided at the same term, prompting the court to treat the legal questions similarly. The proceedings were presided over by Judge Sidney Smith in the Superior Court of Cook County.	The Village of Hyde Park claimed that the defendants, including William J. Slee, were responsible for actions or omissions that harmed the interests of the municipality. They sought legal remedy through the court, requesting reversal of prior judgments and a ruling in favor of the village based on the precedence set in similar cases, arguing that their rights and public interests were infringed upon.	The defendants, represented by attorney Consider H. Willett, contended that the plaintiffs' claims were unjustified and that the previous judgments should be upheld. They argued that the legal principles from prior case precedents did not apply to their situation. Their main request was for the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims and affirm the previous ruling in their favor.

In September 1870, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Peter Kern et al. v. August Zink et al., originating from a bill for partition filed by some of the children of Peter Kern, who was deceased. The case took place in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiffs, who are the co-heirs of Peter Kern, sought to partition the inherited land among themselves. The defendants included Peter and Emma Kern, who were also heirs, and Robert J. Allison, who was a lessee claiming rights to a part of the premises. A significant issue arose regarding a lease that Allison held; the plaintiffs argued it was a cloud on their title. The court had to examine the validity of the lease and the rights of the various heirs, while a writ of error was prosecuted by the defendants against the partition proceedings. The court ultimately found that the lease claimed by Allison was void, and that the other co-heirs had rightful claims to the partition of land, which they subsequently received.	The plaintiffs, consisting of some of Peter Kern's children, claimed that the lease held by Robert J. Allison was invalid and constituted a cloud on their collective title to the inherited property. They requested that the lease be set aside and that the court award them a writ of possession to the lands in question. They asserted their rights as co-heirs entitled to a fair partition of the property.	The defendants, particularly Robert J. Allison, argued against the validity of the court's decree awarding possession to Caroline Russer without a cross bill. They contended that the writ of possession granted in favor of Russer provided her with affirmative relief that was inappropriate under the circumstances. The defense claimed that the lease was valid and that it should not have been set aside.

In 1859, in Monroe County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose over a seventy-acre tract of land known as the “John M. Hull Tract.” The plaintiffs, Ellender C. Masterson et al., were the heirs of Benjamin F. Masterson, who had lived on the land for twenty years before his death in 1853. The defendants, Samanda E. Cheek et al., were connected to Silas T. Cheek, who had entered the property after Masterson’s death. The plaintiffs introduced a deed dated December 5, 1831, from John M. Hull to Benjamin Masterson, and contended they had rightful ownership of the land. The defendants, however, claimed that the title to the property had been granted to an illegitimate son of Benjamin Masterson, Andrew J. Masterson, and that this grant was valid despite the child’s death before reaching maturity. The court examined evidence surrounding the intentions of the grantor and the existence of an outstanding title in another party, which played a critical role in determining the outcome of the case.	The plaintiffs contended that they had a valid title to the land based on the deed executed by John M. Hull to Benjamin F. Masterson, and argued that they should be able to recover possession of the seventy acres. They sought a judgment confirming their ownership and requested to overturn the lower court's decision that favored the defendants, asserting that the existence of an alleged prior deed to an illegitimate son was not sufficient to void their claim.	The defendants maintained that a legal and subsisting title to the land existed in the form of a deed that granted the property to Andrew J. Masterson, the illegitimate son of Benjamin Masterson, whom they argued was a legitimate grantee despite being an infant when the deed was executed. They argued that the presumption of acceptance applies to infants, meaning that they believed this deed effectively conveyed ownership and thus defeated the plaintiffs' claim. Furthermore, they requested the court reaffirm the lower court's decision, ruling that the plaintiffs had no rightful claim to the land.

The case "Edmund S. Holbrook v. John Nichol, and Benjamin S. Prettyman" took place in the state of Illinois, with relevant events occurring during the years leading up to and including 1864. The plaintiff, Edmund S. Holbrook, sought to recover property located in Tazewell County, specifically the west half of the northeast quarter of Section 35 in Township 25 North, Range 5 West. Holbrook initiated an action of ejectment against John Nichol, who was represented by Benjamin S. Prettyman as his landlord. The action was moved to the Circuit Court of Woodford County for trial. Holbrook claimed ownership based on a title derived from James B. Campbell, who had allegedly conveyed the property to him after being declared bankrupt in 1842. However, the defendants contended that Campbell had previously transferred the property to another party, Lee, in 1836, which would undermine Holbrook's claims. The court addressed questions surrounding the validity of documents and the acknowledgment of deeds, including the legitimacy of a power of attorney associated with the case. The trial concluded with the defendants prevailing initially, prompting Holbrook to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff's primary argument was that he had established ownership of the property through sufficient evidence, claiming that James B. Campbell was the rightful owner when he acquired the property in 1850 via a sale conducted by Campbell's bankruptcy assignee. Holbrook argued that Campbell, despite declaring bankruptcy, had a legitimate title to the land that he could convey through the power of attorney. Holbrook sought a verdict that would confirm his ownership and evict the defendants from the property.	The defendants contended that Campbell had already transferred his interest in the property to Lee in 1836, prior to his bankruptcy, thus rendering any subsequent claim to the property invalid. They argued that Holbrook could not establish legal title to the premises, stating that the validity of the documents he produced was questionable. The defendants maintained that even if they were in possession of the property, the burden was on Holbrook to prove his title, which he failed to do, and thus requested a judgment in their favor.

Maurice Clifford filed a legal case against Christian Luhring and others in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, in September 1873. The dispute arose over payment for plastering services provided to Luhring on a building in Chicago. The work was initially contracted by Luhring to a primary contractor named Gruís, who subcontracted the plastering work to Clifford and his associates. When Gruís failed to fulfill his contractual obligations, Clifford informed Luhring of the situation and expressed his intention to stop working. Luhring, however, assured Clifford that he would pay for the work if they continued. The case involved conflicting testimonies regarding Luhring's promise to pay, which the jury resolved in favor of the plaintiff. The Illinois Supreme Court later upheld the jury's verdict, noting that discrepancies in testimony should not lead to overturning the jury's decision, especially regarding contract enforceability and the Statute of Frauds.	Maurice Clifford argued that Christian Luhring had made a direct promise to pay for the plastering services after the primary contractor's failure to perform. Clifford maintained that this promise constituted an enforceable original undertaking and should not be dismissed under the Statute of Frauds because it served Luhring's own interest in completing the building for rental purposes.	Christian Luhring contended that his alleged promise to pay was not enforceable under the Statute of Frauds, asserting that he was merely offering a collateral promise to cover Gruís's obligations rather than making an original commitment. Luhring argued that since the promise served the interests of the primary contractor, it should not be binding. He requested dismissal of the plaintiff's claims on these grounds.

In the spring of 1861, William H. W. Cushman, a banker based in Ottawa, engaged in banking transactions with B. F. Carver & Co., a banking firm located in Chicago. Prior to May 7, 1861, Cushman had a significant balance of approximately $7,500 held by Carver & Co. At this time, the currency of numerous Illinois banks was under scrutiny due to doubts about their solvency, leading to a depreciation of their banknotes. Aware of this issue, Cushman sent a letter on April 29, 1861, to Carver & Co., specifying the types of currency he would accept for remittances. On May 7, the bank sent Cushman a package containing the $7,500, which included depreciated currency not specified in Cushman's earlier communication. After receiving the package, which he initially stored unopened, Cushman later discovered that it contained lower-quality currency. He communicated his dissatisfaction to Carver, stating he would withdraw his funds and would not handle the inferior currency. However, Carver claimed that the deposits were returned in the currency previously agreed upon. This led to a legal confrontation over the treatment of the remitted funds.	Cushman argued that he should not be held liable for the full nominal value of the depreciated currency sent to him by Carver & Co. He contended that the funds were not represented in a form he had specifically requested, and thus he should only be accountable for their actual diminished value at the time of receipt. He sought to recover the difference between the nominal value of the currency and its actual worth due to depreciation.	Carver & Co. defended their actions by asserting that they acted according to the terms set by Cushman in his previous letter, as they sent back the balance in the forms of currency specified. They claimed that, since there was implicit agreement on the remittance conditions, Cushman had waived his right to dispute the nominal value by failing to act promptly upon receiving the funds. The bank argued that the delay in Cushman's response indicated acceptance of the currency sent.

On November 2, 1882, Taylor Boyce executed two chattel mortgages on a steam threshing engine to secure loans totaling $1,615. The first was to the J. I. Case Threshing Machine Company for $1,175, recorded on November 3, 1882, and the second to the Northwestern Manufacturing and Car Company for $440, recorded on September 15, 1882. The mortgages were acknowledged before David H. Sample, a police magistrate located in Harvel, Montgomery County, Illinois. The core issue of the case arose from the validity of these acknowledgments since Boyce resided in the township of Harvel but not within the village itself. After Boyce defaulted, the plaintiffs, R. S. Nelson and others, purchased the property under a constable's sale and brought an action of trover against the defendants, Thomas G. Kessinger and others, claiming ownership of the steam threshing engine. The case was brought to the Illinois Appellate Court due to the exclusion of the notes and mortgages from evidence in the lower court, which ruled against the defendants.	The plaintiffs contended that they had legal ownership of the steam threshing engine based on a constable’s sale and execution. They argued that the acknowledgments of the chattel mortgages were invalid, as the magistrate who acknowledged them did not reside in the same township. Consequently, they sought to affirm their ownership and recover the engine's value from the defendants.	The defendants argued that the acknowledgments of the chattel mortgages were valid and that the mortgages constituted prior liens on the property. They claimed that the magistrate, David H. Sample, was an officer de facto and had the authority to take the acknowledgments, making the mortgages effective. The defendants sought to have the evidence from the excluded notes and mortgages admitted to court, aiming to overturn the lower court’s judgment.

On March 19, 1863, Lewis Morrell was indicted for perjury in Marion County, Illinois, specifically for allegedly making false statements in an affidavit submitted in an effort to secure a continuance in a court case. The affidavit was supposed to be sworn before Jacob O. Chance, who identified himself as the clerk of the Marion Circuit Court. The charges claimed that Morrell falsely affirmed the truth of the statements in the affidavit, which were related to the application for a continuance of a case in which the state of Illinois was the plaintiff and Morrell was the defendant. Following the indictment, Morrell sought to quash the indictment, arguing that it was defective as it failed to adequately allege the materiality of the sworn facts. A trial ensued, resulting in a verdict of conviction against Morrell, and his subsequent request for a new trial was denied.	The plaintiff, represented by the state of Illinois, contended that Lewis Morrell committed perjury by making false statements in an affidavit in a judicial proceeding. The prosecution argued that the affidavit was significant as it was related to a motion seeking a continuance in a legal case, thus making Morrell's alleged falsehoods material to that process.	Lewis Morrell's defense asserted that the indictment was flawed because it did not demonstrate that the facts deposed in his affidavit were material to the case or that a motion for continuance had been properly filed based on that affidavit. Additionally, Morrell challenged the validity of the oath, stating there was no proof that Jacob O. Chance was legally authorized to administer the oath, as required by law.

On March 27, 1886, in Shelby County, Illinois, the case of Joseph Chesshire et al. v. The People ex rel. Robert Harper was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case stemmed from a legal proceeding initiated by State's Attorney William G. Kelley, suggesting that Chesshire, Barr, and Smith wrongfully claimed to hold the positions of school directors for a supposed School District No. 9. This claim was based on the assertion that proper legal protocols for forming such a district had not been followed, specifically that the district contained insufficient families as required by law. Robert Harper, the relator and individual bringing the complaint, was a taxpayer who contended that the formation of District No. 9 was unlawful. The case delved into the legitimacy of the school district's formation and whether the defendants had any lawful claim to their positions.	The plaintiff, representing the People of the State of Illinois through Robert Harper, argued that Joseph Chesshire, William Barr, and Isaac Smith had usurped their positions as school directors of a non-existent School District No. 9, following an unlawful division of School District No. 3. They claimed that the attempted formation did not meet legal requirements, specifically that District No. 9 lacked the necessary population threshold of families mandated by law. The plaintiff sought a judgment of ouster against the defendants based on this alleged usurpation of office.	The defendants contended that there were no faults in the way the information was presented and argued that the issues raised in the claim were not valid under the law. They maintained that the relator, Robert Harper, lacked standing because his interest in the district was not clearly demonstrated. The defendants filed a general demurrer and sought to have the claims dismissed, asserting that the proceedings against them were unfounded.

John Nichols filed a suit against Samuel Ruckells before a justice of the peace, seeking to recover an account amounting to $50.23. The trial jury found in favor of Ruckells, leading Nichols to appeal the decision to the Circuit Court. In the Circuit Court, Nichols proved his claim for the original amount, while Ruckells presented a larger counterclaim of $675, including an item for $150 related to damages from hired labor during a period of being unemployed due to a contractual obligation concerning rent of a mill between Nichols and Ruckells. Nichols objected to this counterclaim being admissible in the current action, specifically arguing about the nature of the setoff and the jurisdictional boundaries of the justice of the peace. The court allowed the evidence and ultimately ruled in favor of Ruckells, resulting in a judgment for $61.14 against Nichols. The dispute raised important questions regarding unliquidated damages and the jurisdiction of justices in contractual disputes.	John Nichols contended that the claim for damages presented by Ruckells amounted to unliquidated damages and was improperly included as a setoff in his action. He argued that these claims should be treated as separate legal matters outside the jurisdiction of the justice of the peace, and he sought to uphold his initial claim for the amount due.	Samuel Ruckells maintained that the setoff claim, though exceeding $100, was valid since the balance he was pursuing against Nichols did not surpass the jurisdictional limit. He argued that the unliquidated damages arose from a contractual agreement and therefore constituted a legitimate matter for setoff under the law.

In the case of "Jane A. Brooks v. The People, use, etc.", presided over by the Illinois Appellate Court, the plaintiff was Stanley B. Sexton, who was represented by the state against Jane A. Brooks, the widow and heir of Joseph P. Brooks, deceased. The legal dispute centered around a guardian's bond for Henry M. Curtis, who was appointed guardian of Sexton. The bond, executed on January 3, 1873, was for $120,000 and signed by Brooks, George E. Bissell, and Henry E. Seelye as sureties. The court examined whether Curtis, as guardian, had appropriated funds improperly, leading to a final judgment against him. After a court process, including a judgment by a county court confirming the amount due from Curtis to Sexton, Brooks contested the execution of the bond. The key question became whether the bond was properly delivered during Brooks's lifetime, as he died before the proceedings concluded. The court investigated the events surrounding the bond's presentation and whether its delivery to the judge constituted legality given that it was taken away by the sureties without completing the appointment process. Ultimately, the court ruled on the nature of obligations under the bond and the implications of its delivery.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, asserted that Brooks, as a surety on the guardian's bond, owed $120,000 due to the misconduct of the guardian, Henry M. Curtis. The plaintiff emphasized that a prior judgment from the county court confirmed the amount due from Curtis to Sexton, meaning Brooks and the other sureties should be held liable. They argued that the bond should be enforced as it was essential in providing the financial security for Curtis's responsibilities as guardian.	The defendant, Jane A. Brooks, contended that the bond had not been delivered legally and therefore should not be enforceable against her. Brooks’s defense focused on the timelines and circumstances around the bond's purported delivery, arguing that without valid delivery, the bond did not legally bind her or her husband at the time of his death. Furthermore, any claims against her were invalid as there had been no fraudulent or collusive actions from their side during the guardian's appointment process.

In June 1876, the case of Robert Gardner et al. v. Eugene Eberhart et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following a forcible detainer action originating in Jersey County. The case involved a dispute over the ownership of a parcel of land sold at a sheriff's sale, which the plaintiffs, Robert Gardner and others, claimed title to via a sheriff's deed resulting from an execution issued on October 21, 1869. The execution stemmed from a judgment in favor of White and Smith against Gardner. The land, part of a larger farm owned by Gardner, was sold to White and Smith who subsequently assigned the deed to Eberhart and Ruedin. The plaintiffs contended that proper demand requirements were met to assert their claim to the land. Their claim was supported by four written demands, with one being produced as evidence, which the defendants argued was merely a copy rather than an original. The court's trial did not include a jury and ultimately favored the plaintiffs based on the sufficiency of their demands and evidence, leading to the appeal by the defendants.	The plaintiffs claimed ownership of the land in question based on a sheriff’s deed derived from a legal sale following a judgment against Gardner. They argued that the demands for possession were properly issued and evidenced, insisting that the objections raised by the defendants regarding the nature of the demand documents and the procedure for the execution sale were unfounded. The plaintiffs sought affirmation of their title to the property and requested to uphold the sheriff’s sale as valid.	The defendants contended that the sheriff's sale was void due to a lack of proper notice and demand for payment before executing the levy, which they argued violated statutory provisions. They claimed that the land sold was part of Gardner's homestead, which was exempt under the law without appropriate procedures to set it off. Additionally, they objected to the admission of the demand evidence, asserting that the paper presented was merely a copy and not an original.

In December 1829, David Ingalls brought a case against George T. Allen in the Illinois Supreme Court, after having previously received a jury verdict in his favor for slander, resulting in a judgment of fifty dollars against Allen. The incident arose when Allen allegedly accused Ingalls of forging the indorsement on a promissory note, changing its amount dishonestly. The case was set in Morgan County, Illinois, where Ingalls claimed that Allen's statements had damaged his reputation. The trial included testimonies from several witnesses who claimed to have heard Allen make remarks about Ingalls altering the note’s indorsement or credit. The core of the argument was centered around whether Allen's words constituted actionable slander, given their ambiguous nature. Ultimately, the court decided that the statements made by Allen were not considered actionable slander, as they did not directly accuse Ingalls of illegal activity nor did they unambiguously accuse him of a crime.	David Ingalls claimed that George T. Allen slandered him by accusing him of forgery related to a promissory note. Ingalls argued that the statements made by Allen were damaging to his reputation and sought damages of fifty dollars in compensation for the harm caused by these alleged slanderous remarks.	George T. Allen defended against the slander claims by stating that his accusations were ambiguous and did not amount to a definitive charge of wrongdoing. He contended that the language used was not actionable, as it suggested no concrete evidence of forgery or criminal intent. Thus, Allen sought to have the jury's verdict overturned, arguing that the statements did not meet the legal threshold for slander.

Henry Blanck v. Edward Pausch is a legal case that took place in the town of Lebanon, St. Clair County, Illinois, arising from a contested election for the position of town clerk. The case was filed on January 22, 1885, and heard by the Illinois Supreme Court after an appeal from the County Court of St. Clair County, presided over by Judge William J. Underwood. The election in question occurred on April 1, 1884, following a previous vote to adopt township organization, where Pausch claimed to have been duly elected for the office. However, Blanck also asserted that he had won the election, alleging that valid votes were cast for him at a location in the city of Lebanon—a location that had not been authorized as a voting place. Pausch's petition argued that the votes cast for Blanck were illegal and requested that he be declared the legitimate town clerk, as he contended that he had received the majority of valid votes. The initial ruling from the county court favored Pausch, but Blanck's appeal sought to contest that decision.	Edward Pausch, the plaintiff, claimed to be a citizen and resident of Lebanon and stated that he received the majority of votes for town clerk in the April 1, 1884 election. He asserted that Blanck's election was invalid due to votes being cast at an unauthorized location, thus making them illegal. Pausch requested to be declared the lawful town clerk and sought to oust Blanck from office based on these claims.	Henry Blanck, the defendant, argued that the petition contesting his election was fatally defective because Pausch failed to aver that he was an "elector" of the town of Lebanon. Blanck maintained that while the petition described Pausch as a "citizen and resident," this did not fulfill the legal requirement to establish his standing to contest the election. Consequently, he contended that the court should uphold the outcome of the election and not recognize Pausch's claims.

The case of *Philip Campbell v. Sarah Harris* took place in Illinois, with the action commencing on February 22, 1861. The dispute revolved around a promissory note executed by Philip Campbell, which promised to pay Isaac Harris $75 by December 25, 1841. The central issue was whether the statute of limitations barred the collection of this debt. Campbell argued that the promissory note's cause of action accrued beyond the state's limits before applicable statute limitations enacted prior to April 13, 1849. This case involved a complex interplay of several statutes, including acts from 1845, 1849, and 1851, which were examined by the Illinois Supreme Court. The Circuit Court originally ruled in favor of Sarah Harris, sustaining her demurrer against Campbell's plea, leading to a judgment for the amount owed plus damages.	Sarah Harris, as the executrix of Isaac Harris's estate, asserted that Philip Campbell owed $75 based on a promissory note executed in 1840. Her claim was that despite the complexities of the statutes of limitations, the debt was valid and collectible under Illinois law. She filed a general demurrer against Campbell's plea, seeking to affirm the court's authority to enforce the note despite the defendant's arguments regarding the statute of limitations.	Philip Campbell contended that the cause of action was barred by various statutes of limitations that applied to promissory notes executed outside of Illinois. He argued that the note was executed and the cause of action accrued prior to significant legislative changes in 1849, which would have limited the time within which Harris could sue for the debt. Campbell maintained that no subsequent statutes applied to revive or affect the limitations concerning his case, making his plea valid.

On April 18, 1864, in Will County, Illinois, George Chase was involved in a deadly incident while incarcerated in the penitentiary. The victim, Joseph Clark, was a deputy warden responsible for prison discipline. During the events that unfolded, Clark attempted to discipline Chase, who was among four convicts temporarily taken out of their cells. Tension escalated when Clark called Chase out of his cell; instead of cooperating, Chase threw a stone that struck Clark's head, fracturing his skull. This was followed by a physical struggle where Chase obtained Clark's revolver and shot at him multiple times. Clark managed to shoot back at Chase before collapsing. He eventually died from his injuries on May 1, 1864. Chase's defense included an assertion of insanity, but this was deemed insufficient. He was found guilty of murder, leading to his appeal based on several alleged judicial errors, primarily concerning juror qualifications and the nature of evidence presented.	The prosecution's case focused on establishing that George Chase committed murder against Joseph Clark while both were in the penitentiary. The claim asserted that Chase acted willfully and with malice, and no legal justification existed for his actions. The prosecutor maintained that the evidence clearly indicated that the stone throwing and subsequent use of the revolver resulted in Clark's death, fulfilling the criteria for murder.	George Chase's defense argued primarily on two fronts: the alleged insanity at the time of the incident and the disqualification of a juror based on alienage. The defense claimed that Chase was not in a sound state of mind, which should negate the culpability for murder. Furthermore, they contended that one of the jurors, identified as Francis Nicholson, was not qualified due to being an alien, which rendered the jury's verdict invalid. Ultimately, their request was for a new trial based on these arguments.

In the legal case of David A. Barry et al. v. Alexander E. Guild, Jr., decided on November 15, 1888, at the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute arose over a mortgage foreclosure in DuPage County, Illinois. The parties involved included David A. Barry and Budolph Nunnemacher (appellants) against Alexander E. Guild, Jr. (appellee), who held the purchase-money mortgage. The case originated from a sequence of property transactions starting in 1868, involving multiple parties and complicated property descriptions. Martin Sauber and Charles Freihauf initially owned a 48-acre lot and conveyed a portion to Charles Fitzsimmons. Later, John Atkinson, holding a warranty deed for the entire tracts, conveyed half of these to Guild. Barry, later acquiring an interest through a special warranty deed from George E. Gindele, secured his transaction with promissory notes for $4,000. When Guild initiated foreclosure proceedings due to non-payment, Barry and Nunnemacher sought to defend against the foreclosure, alleging failure of title due to the complicated series of deeds and undisclosed interests. The trial court ruled in favor of Guild for the full unpaid amount and a solicitor's fee.	The plaintiff, Alexander E. Guild, contended that he was owed the full balance of the purchase money under the mortgage agreement, asserting that the defendants' claims of a failure of title were unfounded. Guild requested the court to uphold the foreclosure of the mortgage and grant the claimed solicitor's fee of $100, arguing that the defendants had not sustained valid defenses to counter the foreclosure based on the conditions of the original deeds.	The defendants, Barry and Nunnemacher, argued that they were entitled to a reduction in the purchase price due to failure of title concerning the property. They contended that Atkinson, the original seller, had conveyed the property with certain deficiencies that should relieve them of the obligation to pay the full purchase money. They claimed that Guild was not justified in collecting the unpaid amounts under the circumstances of the concealed title issues related to the deed's covenants.

This case, titled "Gideon H. Rupert et al. v. David Mark," was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision rendered in June 1854. The case originated when Rupert and Haines filed an ejectment action against Mark on April 7, 1851, seeking to recover possession of a lot located in Pekin, Illinois. The plaintiffs presented evidence showing that David Bailey was the owner of the lot as of July 15, 1831, and that the defendant, Mark, was in possession of the property at the time the lawsuit began. The plaintiffs provided a deed transferring the lot from David Bailey to Samuel G. Bailey, as well as proof of inheritance from Samuel G. Bailey’s heir, Emily B. Bailey. They also showed a power of attorney that allowed Emily to sell the lot, which she did on January 2, 1851. Conversely, Mark produced evidence of his possession of the lot for three or four years prior, alongside several deeds, including one granting him a quitclaim deed of the property. The trial court ultimately ruled in favor of the defendant, Mark.	The plaintiffs, Rupert and Haines, claimed title to the entire lot based on their purchase from Emily B. Bailey. They argued that their legal rights were established through the recorded deed and that as bona fide purchasers from an heir, they should prevail over any unrecorded competing claims. They contended that the evidence did not support the defendant's claim as he had no superior title to the property.	The defendant, David Mark, argued that he had been in actual possession of the lot for several years and presented multiple deeds supporting his claim, including a quitclaim deed from Daniel M. Bailey. He raised the issue of the plaintiffs possibly having notice of his prior unregistered interests in the property at the time of their purchase, suggesting that this knowledge negated their claim to the lot's title.

On February 12, 1890, the Illinois Appellate Court dealt with the case of Thomas Lord et al. v. Mary E. Owen, arising from a contractual agreement made on July 4, 1876, between the plaintiff, Mary E. Owen, and the defendants, wholesale druggists based in Chicago. Under this contract, Owen granted the defendants exclusive rights for ten years to manufacture and sell a patented medicine, "Owen’s Compound Fluid Extract of Buchu." The defendants were required to adhere to specific conditions, including the use of specified molds for bottling, effective advertising and promotion, and returning materials such as molds and receipts to Owen upon contract expiration. When the contract ended, Owen sued the defendants for failing to comply with the terms, alleging they did not adequately market the product and did not return the proprietary materials. During the trial, contentious evidence regarding the interpretation of the phrase "vigorously pushing" was allowed in, which led to a verdict of $6,000 in favor of Owen. The defendants appealed, arguing against the admittance of such evidence and the basis for calculating damages.	The plaintiff, Mary E. Owen, claimed that the defendants breached their contract by failing to use the specified molds for bottling the medicine and not promoting its sale as required. She sought damages for these breaches, asserting they undermined the sale and success of the product. Owen also claimed the defendants did not return important proprietary materials at the end of the contract, which contributed to her losses.	The defendants contended that the trial court improperly admitted evidence on the interpretation of "vigorously push," which influenced the jury's decision. They argued that there was no established business practice regarding this phrase, implying that the success of advertising in the manner suggested was not guaranteed. They challenged the basis of calculated damages as overly speculative and unsupported by solid evidence, claiming that the actual losses were minimal, primarily involving the failure to return the molds valued at only $34.

In 1868, the case "Moses Robison v. Josephus Hibbs" arose in Warren County, Illinois. The dispute originated from a suit initiated by Moses Robison, who sought to recover a small balance owed from an account in the local justice court. The trial concluded with a judgment favoring Josephus Hibbs, the defendant. Robison then appealed the decision to the circuit court, where a jury also ruled in favor of Hibbs, awarding him forty dollars. Following this, Robison attempted to overturn the verdict through a motion for a new trial, which was denied. The issue at hand was whether the circuit court erred in allowing Hibbs to present a counterclaim for damages resulting from Robison's hogs trespassing and damaging Hibbs's corn. The court allowed this claim despite Robison's objections, which centered on the assertion that the damages were unliquidated and not appropriately set off in the contract action.	Moses Robison, the plaintiff, contended that the circuit court erred in permitting Josephus Hibbs to introduce evidence regarding unliquidated damages related to the alleged trespass of Robison's hogs on Hibbs's property. Robison argued that since the exact amount of damage was not contractually agreed upon, these damages should not have been applicable as a counterclaim in the recovery of the account balance.	Josephus Hibbs maintained that the damages from the trespass were liquidated and that he was entitled to prove these damages as part of his defense against Robison’s claim. Hibbs argued that the evidence demonstrated a specific amount of damage due to the destruction of his corn, thus asserting that set-off was appropriate despite Robison's challenge to the court's admission of such evidence.

The case of Valentine H. Marshall et al. v. Elijah Barr took place in Warren County, Illinois, in 1864. The primary individuals involved were Elijah Barr (the plaintiff) and Valentine H. Marshall, along with James Dickson (the defendants). The dispute arose from an action of ejectment initiated by Barr against Marshall and Dickson, seeking recovery of land described as the northeast quarter of section twenty-one in township eight, north of range one west of the fourth principal meridian. Barr's claim was based on a deed from Marshall, executed on May 2, 1860. However, the defendants challenged the validity of this deed, arguing that it was inoperative as it had not been signed by Marshall's wife, which was required by the homestead law in effect at the time. In court, evidence was presented showing that the land in question was indeed the homestead residence of Marshall and his family, who had lived there continuously, and that the deed was essentially a mortgage intended for securing a debt rather than a legitimate transfer of ownership. The lower court found in favor of Barr, prompting the defendants to file an appeal, questioning whether Barr could recover based solely on the deed lacking the necessary spousal consent.	The plaintiff, Elijah Barr, claimed rightful ownership of the property based on a deed from Marshall, asserting that he was entitled to recover possession. He argued that the deed established a legitimate title to the land, despite the defendants’ objections regarding the lack of Marshall's wife's signature. Barr contended that his ownership was valid, relying solely on the deed for recovery.	The defendants, Marshall and Dickson, contended that the deed was invalid because it lacked the necessary signature of Marshall's wife, thereby violating the homestead law, which mandates that both spouses must consent to the transfer of homestead property. They sought to demonstrate that the land was a homestead and that the deed should be treated as a mortgage meant only for securing a debt, not a transfer of ownership. They argued that because the deed was inoperative, the plaintiff could not prevail in ejectment based solely on that document.

The case "William Ripley et al. v. The People’s Savings Bank et al." was adjudicated on January 25, 1887, in Illinois, specifically in the Superior Court of Cook County, followed by the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved included plaintiffs William Ripley and Bradford W. Bipley, who initiated a suit in attachment against John Monaghan. As part of the proceedings, certain parties were served as garnishees, admitting that they held money derived from the sale of railroad ties and cedar posts. The People’s Savings Bank of Michigan interpleaded, claiming ownership of these funds. Eventually, the lower courts found that the funds rightfully belonged to the bank based on contracts detailing the ownership and handling of the sales. The critical legal question in the appeal concerned the admissibility of certain evidence introduced by the interpleader, particularly contracts that defined the ownership of the funds in question.	The plaintiffs argued that the funds in the hands of the garnishees belonged to John Monaghan, the attachment debtor, and sought to have the court recognize their claim over these funds. They maintained that the bank lacked rightful ownership and contested the bank's claim, seeking a judgment in favor of their attachment suit.	The People’s Savings Bank contended that the funds were legitimately theirs based on written contracts with the defendant, which specified that the proceeds from the sale of the railroad ties and cedar posts would reimburse the bank for its financing. The bank sought to uphold the lower court's ruling that confirmed its claim over the funds, arguing that the evidence provided, including contractual agreements, supported its ownership rights.

Jonathan B. Salisbury was involved in a legal case concerning an application for a writ of habeas corpus. This case took place in June 1855 in Illinois, specifically under the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. Salisbury was held in custody due to three writs of capias ad satisfaciendum, which were issued against him related to a judgment from the Supreme Court of New York. The case alleged fraudulent activities where Salisbury was accused of transferring significant amounts of real and personal property to others to evade creditors. The affidavit outlined evidence suggesting that Salisbury had been involved in fraudulent transactions to put his assets out of reach from creditors, including selling property at prices significantly below their actual worth. The actions taken by Salisbury in December 1853, particularly with respect to various partnerships and property transactions, were said to be aimed at delaying and hindering his creditors’ claims.	The plaintiff’s main arguments were centered on asserting that Salisbury had engaged in fraudulent transfers of property intended to defraud his creditors. They sought the enforcement of the capias writs against him, highlighting the inadequacy of the sales he conducted and suggesting that he had concealed assets to avoid fulfilling his financial obligations stemming from a judgment against him.	Salisbury’s defense contended that he could not be discharged from custody under one of the writs since it was issued from a court with proper jurisdiction and the affidavit supporting the writ was legally sufficient. However, regarding the writ from the Cook County Common Pleas, Salisbury argued that the absence of a requisite affidavit rendered the issuance of that writ improper, thus seeking his discharge from that particular imprisonment.

In September 1868, in Chicago, Illinois, a legal dispute arose in the case of Charles H. Hapgood et al. v. Cornelius Cornwell et al. The key individuals involved were Charles H. Hapgood, acting as a trustee for Amory Bigelow's wife, and Amory Bigelow, who was a partner in a business alongside Gilbert F. Bigelow and David Burr. The conflict originated after Hapgood loaned a significant amount of money to Amory Bigelow, which had been inherited from his wife's grandfather. Concerned about the safety of these funds, Hapgood urged Bigelow to buy out his partners to secure the money. Bigelow proceeded with this suggestion. However, the partnership's creditors, having obtained a judgment, filed a bill in chancery against Hapgood and the partners, leading to a court decree ordering Hapgood to pay the creditors' judgment. Hapgood appealed this decision, questioning whether he had acted fraudulently by facilitating the purchase of partnership assets to secure an individual debt.	The plaintiffs, in this case, were the creditors of Bigelow's partnership who claimed that Hapgood had essentially conspired to defraud them by helping Bigelow secure the firm's assets. They argued that this transaction denied them their rightful claims to the partnership property and violated the principles of equitable lien that entitled them to repayment from the firm's assets before any personal creditor's claims were addressed.	Hapgood, the defendant, maintained that he acted legally and ethically by accepting the partnership assets in satisfaction of a legitimate debt owed to him, as he was a purchaser for valuable consideration without notice of any superior claims. He argued that the firm creditors did not have a direct lien on the partnership property since the partners could agree to a buyout and that any promises made by Bigelow to their creditors were personal obligations, not creating any lien or preventing Bigelow from using the goods to settle his personal debts.

The legal case "The City of Paris v. Daniel R. Cracraft" occurred in January 1877, in Illinois, involving a dispute between Daniel R. Cracraft and the city of Paris. Cracraft claimed that the city was negligent in its construction of a sewer system, which he alleged caused water to flow onto his premises, resulting in damages. The situation was exacerbated by the actions of a neighboring landowner, Mr. Jones, who filled his lot and obstructed a natural drainage path, leading to increased water flow that the city's sewer system could not handle during heavy rains. The Circuit Court of Edgar County ruled in favor of Cracraft, awarding him $50 in damages. The city of Paris sought to appeal the decision, arguing that the jury should have been instructed to consider the apportioning of fault due to Jones's actions.	The plaintiff, Daniel R. Cracraft, claimed that the city of Paris was responsible for flooding his property due to the construction of an inadequate sewer system. He sought damages for the injury caused to his premises, asserting that the city's negligence significantly contributed to the flooding that occurred during heavy rainfall.	The city of Paris, as the defendant, argued that the flooding of Cracraft’s property was not solely due to their negligence but was also caused by Mr. Jones filling in his lot, which blocked a natural drain. The city requested the court to instruct the jury that if they found Jones's actions contributed to the injury, the city should not be liable for the entire amount claimed by Cracraft.

On September 5, 1857, in Chicago, the appellants Ira Y. Munn and others, grain merchants, sold wheat to a buyer named Bissell, who arranged payment through C. Wright. Wright issued a check for $6,500 on Burch & Co., the bank where he held an account, as part payment to Munn. The same day, Munn deposited this check with George Smith & Co., his own bank. On the following Monday morning (September 7), Smith & Co. presented the check to Burch & Co. for payment. At that time, it was confirmed that Wright had sufficient funds in his account to cover the check. However, Wright had met with Burch & Co.'s clerks on that morning, discussing his accounts. Subsequently, due to a financial crisis involving Wright's principal, Holly, the bank decided to return the check unpaid. Munn, having repaid Smith & Co. for the dishonored check, brought legal action against Burch & Co. to compel payment. The lower court dismissed Munn's bill, prompting an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Ira Y. Munn et al., claimed that Burch & Co. wrongfully refused to honor the check drawn by C. Wright, despite the check being properly deposited and the funds being available. They argued that the customary practice among banks allowed them to expect payment on checks drawn by depositors with sufficient funds. The plaintiffs requested a decree for the amount of the check plus interest.	Burch & Co. defended their actions by asserting that the bookkeeper’s entry of the $6,500 check was unauthorized and did not obligate the bank to honor the check. They contended that the customary banking practices did not apply here due to the instructions given to their staff. Essentially, the bank argued they acted within their rights based on the timing and circumstances surrounding the presentation of the check.

Jacob Darst, the appellant, initiated the case against Israel M. Marshall, the appellee, in an ejectment action at the Knox Circuit Court during the September term of 1855. The dispute centers around the northwest quarter of section thirty-two, township ten north, range one east of the fourth principal meridian in Illinois. Darst claimed rightful ownership based on a chain of title originating from the United States. Marshall, the defendant, admitted possession of the land but presented a series of deeds and an agreement with the Illinois Land Company to establish his claim. The contested land had been improved by Marshall since he initially settled there in 1835, making various enhancements such as fencing and planting. The trial was conducted without a jury, wherein both parties presented evidence for their claims. The court found for the defendant Marshall at the trial conducted at the April term of 1857, leading Darst to appeal this decision.	Darst argued that he possessed a valid title to the land derived from a continuous chain of conveyances from the United States to himself. He contended that, despite the defendant's occupancy, his ownership was established and legally recognized. The plaintiff sought recovery of the property, claiming that the defendant's possession did not confer a valid title and that the deeds submitted by Marshall were insufficient to challenge his ownership claims.	Marshall's defense hinged on several deeds he presented, which documented his ownership rights to the land. He argued that he held the land under a contract with the Illinois Land Company, which entitled him to the property following the completion of certain payments. Additionally, he claimed to have continuously paid taxes on the land since 1841, asserting this demonstrated a colorable title under Illinois law. Marshall maintained that his legal rights precluded Darst's claims, and he requested the court to affirm his ownership of the property.

In the case of J. Irving Pearce v. The Bryant Coal Company, the events unfolded primarily in Illinois, culminating in a Supreme Court decision on September 27, 1887. The Forsythe Coal Mining Company had incurred a significant debt to the Haskell & Barker Car Company, executing thirty-five bonds for $24,000 plus interest. To secure these bonds, a deed of trust was executed in favor of J. Irving Pearce. However, the Forsythe Coal Mining Company defaulted on the payments, leading to further complex dealings regarding the debt. In 1877, a promissory note of $35,000 was made by Forsythe to Haskell & Barker, secured by a deed of trust over the same property. This led to additional complications when, following default on this note, the property was sold to Haskell & Barker. The Bryant Coal Company acquired the property and sought to have the original deed of trust released by Pearce. After multiple requests and failure to secure the release, the Bryant Coal Company filed a bill against Pearce in the circuit court in March 1883, seeking the release. Pearce countered with a cross-bill claiming unpaid coupons, seeking reimbursement and asserting that he was due payments. The case revolved around the obligations of the trustee and the rights of the parties involved, presented with repeated appeals that ultimately led to the Supreme Court's judgment affirming the lower court's decisions.	The Bryant Coal Company, as the plaintiff, claimed that Pearce, as the trustee, had a duty to release the deed of trust related to the property after they had satisfied the underlying bonds with an alternate form of indebtedness. They argued that Pearce was unjustly withholding the release despite multiple requests and an offer to cover his reasonable costs. Furthermore, they contended that Pearce had no valid claim to the coupons in question, as any moneys he informed he advanced were considered paid and should not place encumbrances on the property.	Pearce, acting as the defendant, argued that he held rights to the coupons, asserting they remained unpaid despite claims to the contrary. He maintained that he had a vested interest in the debt secured by the deed of trust. Pearce's defense revolved around his assertion of subrogation rights, stating that because he paid the coupons, he was entitled to reimbursement and that the obligations were not satisfied, demanding the release of the financial claims against the property under his control.

The case involves Sarah Ann Prieto et al. as Plaintiffs in Error against John Duncan as Defendant in Error, with the legal proceedings taking place in April 1859 in Illinois. The background centers around a mortgage foreclosure suit initiated by Duncan against William Whaley, who had executed a mortgage before his death. Sarah Ann Prieto, as the wife of Whaley, was made a party to the proceedings. Whaley's estate was involved, and a default was entered against Mrs. Prieto, leading to a decree against her. The legal challenge revolved around the sufficiency of the sheriff's return of service for Mrs. Prieto, and whether it was adequate under the law. The court examined whether the service fulfilled statutory requirements and determined whether the acknowledgment of the mortgage by Mrs. Prieto was sufficiently established. Additionally, there were concerns about ordering payments from the estate of Whaley without his representatives being included in the case.	The plaintiffs, represented in error as Sarah Ann Prieto and others, argued that the service of the summons upon Mrs. Prieto was improperly executed and insufficient. They contended that the complaint failed to adequately allege Mrs. Prieto's execution of the mortgage and questioned the court's jurisdiction to decree the payment of any debt from the estate of William Whaley without proper parties being involved in the case.	The defendant, John Duncan, maintained that the service was valid as it was delivered to Mr. Prieto at his wife’s residence and presumed they lived together. He asserted that the mortgage filed indicated Mrs. Prieto's acknowledgment and execution. Duncan argued against the claims that the court lacked jurisdiction or that the execution of the mortgage was in question, asserting that all legal requirements were met in the proceedings.

The case "The East St. Louis Board of Trade v. The People ex rel. Robert S. McCormick" originated in East St. Louis, St. Clair County, Illinois, during the September term of 1882. The proceedings were initiated by the state through Robert S. McCormick against the East St. Louis Board of Trade, a corporation established under Illinois law. The crux of the case involved allegations that the Board of Trade unlawfully usurped the authority to appoint inspectors for grain storage facilities (class "B" warehouses) and charged fees for inspections from owners not part of the organization. The Board asserted that it derived its powers from the same legislative framework that governed the Chicago Board of Trade, claiming it had the right to conduct inspections based on its charter. However, the opposing party argued that the charter’s provisions did not legally empower the Board of Trade to enforce the inspection powers claimed. The trial court sustained a demurrer against the Board’s defense, which resulted in a judgment of ouster being entered against the Board, prompting the Board to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, represented by the People ex rel. Robert S. McCormick, claimed that the East St. Louis Board of Trade had unlawfully exercised powers not granted by law. Specifically, the plaintiff alleged the Board usurped the authority to appoint inspectors for class "B" warehouses and levied fees for mandatory inspections from non-member grain owners. The lawsuit sought a judicial determination that the Board's actions were unauthorized and demanded the cessation of these unlawful practices.	The East St. Louis Board of Trade argued that it was a legal entity formed under an act of the General Assembly, which conferred upon it the same powers as those held by the Chicago Board of Trade. The Board maintained that its rights to appoint inspectors and charge fees were derived from the powers outlined in its charter. The defense contended that the state’s regulations regarding warehouse inspections did not negate its purported authority. The Board requested that the court overturn the judgment of ouster and allow its continued operations.

In 1882, in Woodford County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Margaret Dunn and Pickard Brothers regarding the purchase of a two-horse, double-seated buggy.
