Benjamin Poyer contended that the previous court judgment contained an error regarding the jurisdiction of the circuit court to assess damages. He argued that the absence of documented continuances after the injunction should not nullify the jurisdiction, insisting that by operation of law, cases are presumed to be continued. His legal request included a reversal of the previous judgment and remand of the cause, thereby seeking rectification of the alleged error.	The Village of Des Plaines, represented by their legal counsel, countered Poyer's claims by asserting that the objections raised were unfounded. They argued that the case had remained on the docket legitimately, and thus, it had been correctly continued from one term to another. They maintained that no special order for continuance was required and that the court had jurisdiction to assess damages based on the filed suggestions, despite the objections about the timing of the filings.

The case "Henry Shoup et al. v. Benjamin F. Shields et al." originated in Sangamon County, Illinois, in 1886. The dispute involved Henry Shoup and others (plaintiffs) who accused Benjamin F. Shields and others (defendants) of trespassing by unlawfully entering their property and cutting down a hedge. The plaintiffs claimed that the hedge was located on their land, supported by evidence of possession and payment of taxes following the acquisition of the land through a deed from Joseph B. Royal dated October 19, 1844. The case was tried in the Illinois Supreme Court after the plaintiffs initially obtained a verdict and a judgment for $204 in damages from a lower court. The key issue was whether the plaintiffs could show legal title to the land based on possession or a continuous chain of title from the government, which they successfully demonstrated. The defendants argued otherwise, maintaining the hedge was either on a disputed line or that they had acted lawfully as highway commissioners. The court had to determine the rightful ownership of the land where the hedge was situated and whether the defendants had justification for their actions.	The plaintiffs, Henry Shoup and others, claimed that the defendants entered their land and cut down a hedge without permission, constituting trespass. They argued that they held legitimate possessory rights to the land based on a deed and years of uninterrupted possession and tax payments. They requested damages amounting to $204, asserting that the destruction of the hedge caused financial harm.	The defendants argued that the evidence did not support the judgment because the plaintiffs had failed to prove a clear title stemming from the government. They contended that the hedge was not exclusively on the plaintiffs’ land but rather on a line between adjacent properties. Additionally, they attempted to justify their actions by claiming they were carrying out duties as highway commissioners, suggesting the hedge was part of a public road. However, they presented inadequate proof that the hedge fell within the boundaries of the claimed road.

William J. Stewart was elected and qualified as the city marshal of Braidwood, Illinois. On June 23, 1883, he was arrested on the complaint of Samuel Jacobs for allegedly committing assault and battery while attempting to execute civil process directed to him as marshal by a justice of the peace within the city limits. He was fined $40 by a justice of the peace, but upon appeal and a trial de novo in the circuit court, the fine was reduced to $20. Stewart then sought a review of this decision, raising the central legal question of whether a city marshal has the authority to execute civil process. The relevant provisions from the Revised Statutes indicated that the city marshal is endowed with the same powers as a constable under state law, and this authority pertains specifically to the execution of civil processes. The court noted that the clarification of these powers is crucial for determining the legitimacy of the marshal's actions during the incident.	The plaintiff, William J. Stewart, claimed that he was acting within his legal authority as a city marshal when he attempted to execute civil process directed to him. He argued that the laws of Illinois conferred upon him the same powers as a constable, thereby justifying his actions during the incident in question. Stewart sought to reverse the lower court's judgment, asserting that the fine imposed was unjust based on his legitimate use of his office's powers.	The defendant, The People, contended that the marshal overstepped his authority in attempting to execute the civil process. They argued that the laws governing municipal officers do not explicitly provide for a city marshal to execute such processes and that any actions taken by Stewart could be deemed as unlawful conduct under the circumstances defined by local ordinances. They sought to uphold the lower court's decision to impose a fine for the alleged assault.

Marston Hefner and David Vandolah were involved in a legal dispute that took place in McLean County, Illinois in 1872 regarding a promissory note. The note in question was allegedly signed by Hefner and another individual, Coman, for the amount of $700, with a stipulated interest rate of 12%. Vandolah sought repayment based on this note. However, Hefner denied having made the note and claimed that he was being wrongfully implicated. He contended that he was not the original signer, arguing that certain declarations made by him should not render him liable. The court trial was held without a jury, and the evidence presented suggested that Hefner ultimately adopted and ratified the use of his name on the note. Despite having initially expressed doubt over the signature's authenticity, Hefner admitted it was his after careful examination, leading to the court finding in favor of Vandolah. The judgment amounted to $790.73 for damages after a motion for a new trial was overruled.	Vandolah, the plaintiff, asserted that he had a valid claim against Hefner based on the promissory note that appeared to carry Hefner’s signature. He argued that Hefner's subsequent admissions and actions constituted ratification of the forged signature, rendering him liable for the debt. Vandolah requested the court to enforce the repayment of the principal plus interest on the note.	Hefner, the defendant, contended that he did not sign the note and sought to escape liability by asserting that he should not be bound by a forgery. His defense relied on the argument that any admission he made was not sufficient to constitute an estoppel, as there was no formal authorization for Coman to sign on his behalf. Hefner further claimed that the interest rate stipulated in the note was usurious and thus invalidated the entire claim.

The case "Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company v. Martin Arnold" took place in 1865 in Tazewell County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Martin Arnold, brought an action of trespass against the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, claiming damages for livestock (a heifer and a hog) allegedly killed by the defendant's railroad due to inadequate fencing. The lawsuit was initiated on August 16, 1865, and it was established that the heifer was killed in October 1865, while the hog was killed in September 1865, one month after the commencement of the suit. The trial in the circuit court resulted in a judgment for the plaintiff, awarding $440 in damages. However, the railroad company challenged this decision in the Illinois Supreme Court, leading to a review of the circumstances under which the animals were killed and the nature of proof regarding the railroad's operation.	Martin Arnold, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to compensation for the livestock killed by the defendant's railroad due to its failure to maintain proper fencing. His primary request was to recover damages amounting to $440 for the loss of his heifer and hog. Arnold contended that the injuries to his livestock were directly caused by the railroad's negligence.	The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, as the defendant, contested the claims by asserting that part of the injuries incurred happened after the suit was filed, rendering any recovery invalid for those instances. They maintained that there was insufficient evidence proving they operated the railroad that caused the injuries, arguing that the inferred connection was not a definitive proof of liability.

The case, "The Moline Water Power and Manufacturing Company v. Lorain L. Nichols," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1861. The dispute arose in Rock Island, Illinois, where Lorain L. Nichols provided engineering services to the Moline Water Power and Manufacturing Company. Nichols was employed to create plans and oversee the improvements of the company’s infrastructure, submitting various plans to its board of directors, who ultimately accepted one for execution. Testimonies were presented by the company's secretary and several board members, affirming Nichols' role as the company’s engineer and demonstrating that he was actively involved in the project, including making estimates and supervising work done under the company’s contract with contractors. Evidence indicated that Nichols was consistently consulted by the board throughout the project and was acknowledged as the engineer in charge. Despite some questioning of his competency and the necessity for a formal contract, the company had retained him and continued to seek his input, implying recognition of his expertise.	The plaintiff, Lorain L. Nichols, claimed compensation for his services as an engineer, including a year’s salary of $2,000, along with various reimbursements related to travel, supplies, and assistance. He argued that he had acted under the authority of the company and that the work performed was essential to the company’s operations. Nichols contended that the evidence supported his employment status and his right to recover the claimed amounts.	The defendant, the Moline Water Power and Manufacturing Company, contended that the evidence did not support Nichols' claim of employment or the validity of his salary request. They argued that Nichols' plans were inadequate for the work required and that he lacked a formal written contract establishing his compensation. Furthermore, they asserted that the testimonies from certain witnesses presented was biased due to their interest in the case's outcome and that such evidence should not have been considered by the jury.

The case "Town of Dorr v. Town of Seneca" was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The dispute arose in McHenry County, Illinois, when the Town of Dorr sought to recover expenses incurred for maintaining a pauper whom they claimed was chargeable to the Town of Seneca. The primary question centered on the residence of the pauper at the time she became a charge. Evidence was presented regarding her living arrangements, including statements from the pauper herself and testimonies from her brothers-in-law, depicting various aspects of her residency prior to being a town charge. The pauper had consistently referred to the home of a man named Albright as her residence; she had left a child there and paid for her board while employed elsewhere. Testimonies suggested her intention to return to Albright's when not employed, indicating her connection to the location as more than temporary. In contrast, evidence also showed a period of employment in the Town of Seneca, raising questions about her actual residence and whether it was sufficient to deem the Town of Dorr liable for her support.	The Town of Dorr argued that the pauper was a resident eligible for support under their jurisdiction, as she had no permanent home and was, in their view, a chargeable individual. They sought to demonstrate that her actual residence was in Dorr, thereby holding Seneca responsible for her support based on statutory definitions of residence for paupers.	The Town of Seneca contended that the evidence presented was insufficient to support the claim that the pauper was a resident of Dorr at the relevant time. They argued that the pauper's apparent residence, having been employed in Seneca for an extended period, should attribute liability for her support to Dorr, thus denying the claims made by the Town of Dorr.

Charles Stockon filed a case against Bennett Lochnitt in 1889, before the Illinois Appellate Court, concerning the ownership of 1,200 fence rails. The conflict centered around a prior arrangement in which Lochnitt, with Hill's consent, removed the rails from Hill's property to aid in cultivating a hedge. While Lochnitt was expected to return the rails after their use, he instead used them to build another fence on a different property. Stockon, asserting his claim, initially brought an action of replevin against Lochnitt in a justice court, which was appealed to the Circuit Court. After the presentation of evidence, Lochnitt's motion to instruct the jury to find for him was granted, leading to a verdict for the defendant. Stockon objected to this decision, leading to further motions and an appeal to the higher court. The core issue revolved around whether Stockon had the right to claim the rails given their ownership and previous arrangements.	Stockon argued that he had ownership and the right to possession of the fence rails, claiming that they were wrongfully retained by Lochnitt. He sought the return of the property through replevin and contended that the trial court erred in instructing the jury to favor the defendant. He urged the court to recognize his entitlement to the rails and correct the trial court's judgment regarding ownership.	Lochnitt asserted that he lawfully retained possession of the rails, as they had been removed with the consent of Hill, the actual owner. He argued that Stockon lacked the standing to pursue the replevin since the arrangement allowed for the temporary relocation of the property, and thus, any claim should be made by Hill, not Stockon. Lochnitt sought to maintain the verdict in his favor and countered Stockon’s claims by emphasizing the law regarding possession and ownership rights.

In January 1871, the case of James Somerville v. Anthony Marks took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff, James Somerville, accused the defendant, Anthony Marks, of violating the Texas cattle law established on February 27, 1867, which prohibited the importation of Texas and Cherokee cattle into Illinois. Somerville claimed that Marks unlawfully brought these cattle into the state and that as a result, his own cattle became infected with disease, ultimately leading to their deaths. The circuit court found in favor of Somerville, leading to an appeal from Marks. The court affirmed the validity of the Texas cattle law and ruled that Marks, as a violator, was liable for the harm caused. The case hinged on issues of negligence, specifically whether Somerville had acted without gross negligence in his handling of his cattle, thereby allowing him to make a recovery.	Somerville's main argument was that Marks violated the Texas cattle law by bringing prohibited cattle into Illinois, which directly caused the infection and death of his cattle. He sought damages for these losses, asserting that even if there were some negligence on his part, it should not bar his right to claim damages unless it was gross negligence.	Marks contended that the jury was improperly instructed regarding negligence and that ordinary negligence on Somerville's part should prevent him from recovering damages. He argued that the court's directions were misleading and that he was wrongfully held liable for the situation, despite his claims that Somerville had contributed to the injury through his own negligence.

In the case "The People ex rel. Peter Greenwood et al. v. The Board of Supervisors of Madison County," filed on June 16, 1888, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute arose in Madison County, Illinois, involving Peter Greenwood and other appellants against the Board of Supervisors. The appellants, serving as the commissioners of highways for Wood River Township, sought a mandamus to compel the county board to appropriate funds for constructing a bridge over Wood River. The core of the case revolved around whether the commissioners had met the statutory requirements to justify their petition for county aid. They claimed that the construction was necessary, that it would impose an unreasonable burden on the township, and that they had provided half the required funds. However, the offered evidence was largely rejected by the court because it was not recorded in the official meeting minutes of the highway commissioners, which the law required. The case discussed the procedural aspects of jury selection, objections to the array of jurors, and the sufficiency of evidence in the context of municipal corporations and quasi-corporations.	The plaintiffs claimed that it was necessary to construct a bridge over Wood River and that the bridge's construction would impose an unreasonable burden on the township. They sought to compel the county board to appropriate funds under the relevant statute related to highway construction and maintenance, arguing that they met the jurisdictional requirements for financial assistance from the county.	The defendants, represented by the Board of Supervisors, argued that the plaintiffs failed to provide adequate evidence to support their claims, particularly regarding the legal prerequisites necessary for the county to allocate funds. They maintained that the commissioners of highways did not adhere to statutory requirements in their record-keeping, and thus the county board was under no legal obligation to provide funding for the bridge construction.

The case "Guy Turner and Harry A. Turner, by their next friend, v. Arthur L. Turner and Benjamin F. Turner" was adjudicated on June 14, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. It involves a dispute over a monetary claim against the estate of William E. Turner, who died in December 1881, leaving behind two infant children (the plaintiffs) and a widow. The claim in question, amounting to $1,080, was filed by Benjamin F. Turner (the father of the deceased) against William's estate for a loan he purportedly made to his son. Arthur L. Turner, another son of Benjamin and brother to the deceased, acted as the estate's administrator. The plaintiffs allege that the claim was allowed and paid out through fraudulent actions and collusion between Benjamin and Arthur. The evidence suggests that the claim was originally a gift rather than a loan, as it was not established with any documentation or proof when it was presented. Instead, conversations between the administrator and the deceased's mother raised concerns about the legitimacy of the claim. In 1884, prior to the claim being allowed, the administrator asserted that there would be funds available to distribute after settling debts. Eventually, the court dismissed the plaintiffs' bill on the grounds of insufficient evidence of fraud and collusion, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiffs, Guy and Harry Turner, assert that the claim filed by their grandfather Benjamin against their deceased father's estate was fraudulent. They argue that there was no actual loan made, but rather a gift, and the claim was allowed through collusion between the administrator, Arthur L. Turner, and Benjamin F. Turner. They seek recovery of the funds they believe were unjustly taken from their inheritance.	The defendants, Arthur L. Turner and Benjamin F. Turner, contend that the claim was legitimate and duly allowed by the court. They argue that the administrator acted within his duties when presenting the claim and that there was no fraud or collusion involved in the process. They believe that the claim was valid and should remain allowed, thus opposing the charges brought by the plaintiffs.

Thomas Gill filed a slander lawsuit against James Caldwell in December 1822 in Illinois. The case originated from charges made by Caldwell against Gill, alleging that Gill had sworn false testimony in a previous judicial proceeding presided over by Justice Thomas Kennedy. During the trial, the issue arose regarding whether Gill's swearing by an uplifted hand constituted a legal oath under the law. The Justice of the Peace, Kennedy, testified that he administered the oath to Gill without using a Bible, leading the defense to challenge the validity of this testimony by arguing that it did not prove that a legal oath was administered. The court below upheld the exclusion of Kennedy’s testimony, prompting Gill to appeal for correction of this decision.	Gill argued that the way he was sworn in by the justice was valid and legally recognized as an oath, even though it did not follow the traditional format of swearing on a Bible. He contended that the common law allows for oaths to be administered in a manner that reflects a person's conscience and beliefs. He sought to have the judgment of the lower court reversed, allowing the inclusion of Kennedy's testimony and the opportunity for new proceedings.	Caldwell's defense centered on the assertion that the oath Gill purportedly took was not legally acceptable, as it lacked traditional elements such as the use of a Bible. They argued that because the oath was administered without a Bible and without proper questioning, it did not meet the standards required for legal oaths. The defense requested that the court sustain the exclusion of Kennedy's testimony from the trial.

The case, John Doe, ex dem. Moose v. Samuel Hill, was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1829. The dispute involves a tract of land located in Monroe County, Illinois. The plaintiff, represented by John Doe as the administrator of the estate of Moose, is claiming land based on a confirmation deed issued by Arthur St. Clair, the governor of the Northwest Territory, to Nicholas Jarrot in 1799. This deed confirmed Jarrot's ownership and the associated rights over approximately 778 acres of land. The plaintiffs assert that Jarrot transferred this land to George Lunceford, whose heirs are the current plaintiffs. The defense revolves around the fact that Samuel Hill purchased a portion of the land from the U.S. government, which had put the land up for public sale following the rejection of the prior claim by Montgomery's board of commissioners. The jury found that if the law favored the defendant, he was not guilty; however, if it favored the plaintiff, the defendant was guilty of trespass, with an assessment of damages at one cent.	The plaintiffs argue that the confirmation deed granted by Governor St. Clair vested a fee simple title in Nicholas Jarrot, which could not be nullified by later governmental actions or Congressional legislation. They contend that Congressional movements recognized and validated these confirmations, asserting that the governor had the authority to grant such confirmations and maintain that any defects in the process were subsequently ratified by Congress.	The defendant Samuel Hill argued that Governor St. Clair exceeded his authority when issuing the confirmation deed, claiming that the governor was not empowered to grant confirmation titles. Hill further asserted that Congress had the right to nullify such acts, implying that the plaintiff lacked a valid title to the property. Additionally, he contended that the jury's verdict was flawed as it didn't clarify that the premises lay within the limits set by congressional resolutions.

In April 1863 in the State of Illinois, a legal case arose involving Henry R. Chittenden, representing the People of Illinois, against Charles H. Mellen, the Treasurer of the City of Warsaw. The case centered around a writ of mandamus sought by Chittenden to compel Mellen to pay an order drawn by the city’s mayor. The issue at hand was the constitutionality of a specific act passed by the General Assembly, titled "An act to repeal certain acts therein named." This act aimed to repeal the acts that incorporated the city of Warsaw and to reorganize the territory into a town, stipulating new governing provisions and the transfer of property and pending suits to the newly defined town structure. The law was contested on the basis that it violated the Illinois Constitution, which stipulates that local laws must express a singular subject in their title. Following extensive legal arguments, including the assertion that the act contained provisions beyond its enacted title, the court was tasked with determining its validity.	The plaintiff, Henry R. Chittenden, claimed that the acts passed by the General Assembly, particularly one aimed at repealing the incorporation of the City of Warsaw, were unconstitutional. He argued that the constitution explicitly requires that local laws must only embrace one subject that is clearly stated in the title. He requested the court to declare the law void, which would compel the treasurer to fulfill the payment order issued by the city mayor.	The defendant, Charles H. Mellen, maintained that the law passed by the General Assembly was valid and constitutional. He argued that the title of the law sufficiently described its intent, and thus the law should not be deemed void. Mellen contended that the legislative processes adhered to the necessary requirements of the Illinois Constitution, challenging the interpretation that the act undertook issues beyond its titled subject.

The case "The United States Express Company v. Albert M. Meints" took place in June 1874 in St. Clair County, Illinois. The dispute arose when August Angour delivered a chest of carpenter tools as collateral for a $30 debt to the appellee, Albert M. Meints. The tools were stolen and subsequently found in the possession of the United States Express Company in St. Louis. Angour authorized Davis, his agent, to reclaim the chest. Davis approached the express company’s agent, McMasters, and initially requested the chest. However, the agent claimed that Davis did not provide a written demand nor show a power of attorney at that time. Following their discussion, and after returning with a constable, Davis found that the chest had already been shipped away by the express company. Meints initiated a legal suit against the express company, which culminated in a judgment in his favor for $70 in the county court. The express company appealed this judgment, leading to proceedings in the circuit court and subsequently to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Albert M. Meints asserted that he had a valid lien on the tools and rightfully possessed them until his debt was settled. He claimed that the express company improperly retained possession of the chest without legal justification, despite demands made by his authorized agent. Meints sought recovery of damages equating to the value of the tools, which were wrongfully kept by the express company.	The United States Express Company contended that they were under no obligation to surrender the chest since the initial demand for the property was not presented in writing, and Davis failed to adequately demonstrate his authority to reclaim the chest. They argued that they acted in accordance with the law and that any failure to recover the property was a result of a lack of proper legal proceedings by Davis.

In October 1888, the firm Sues & Uhlendorf owed a significant debt to Kaufman Bros. & Co., ranging from $12,000 to $15,000. Growing concerned about the debt, Kaufman Bros. & Co. sought better security, leading to the creation of promissory notes with warrants of attorney for confession of judgments, initially signed by Sues alone but with Uhlendorf's approval. These were held in escrow by attorney Edmund Furthmann. Dissatisfied with the existing arrangement, Kaufman Bros. & Co. received new notes from Sues on November 15, 1888, again with the intention to improve security. On November 27, 1888, a judgment by confession was entered in favor of Kaufman Bros. & Co. Following this, Sues & Uhlendorf made a voluntary assignment of their property for the benefit of creditors, which led to legal issues regarding the validity of the judgment. Uhlendorf contested the judgment on multiple grounds, arguing that it was unauthorized and lacked his consent. The County Court later deemed the judgment an unlawful preference and ordered that it be set aside. Kaufman Bros. & Co. then appealed this decision, asserting the validity of their claims.	Kaufman Bros. & Co. contended that they legally acquired valid judgment rights against Sues & Uhlendorf based on the promissory notes executed by Sues and approved by Uhlendorf. They argued that the judgment was valid and that they were entitled to enforce their lien on the goods seized, asserting that the prior ruling from the County Court setting aside their judgment constituted an unlawful preference to Uhlendorf and should not have stood.	Uhlendorf, as the defendant, claimed that he did not authorize Sues to execute the judgment notes and that the judgment was therefore invalid as it lacked his consent. They further argued that the judgment represented an unlawful preference, as it occurred just before their voluntary assignment of property for creditors, and that the court should treat the judgment as void.

In 1883, in East St. Louis, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between The Wiggins Ferry Company and The East St. Louis Union Railway Company regarding the construction of a railroad track on Front Street. The East St. Louis Union Railway Company, incorporated under the state's Railroad and Warehouse Act, had received permission from the East St. Louis city council to construct its railroad along Front Street. However, The Wiggins Ferry Company, owning more than three-fourths of the adjoining property, sought an injunction against the railway company, arguing that it had not given its consent for the construction, thus claiming the ordinance was invalid. The railway company, on the other hand, admitted the facts but insisted it was legally permitted to lay its tracks under the city council's grant without the need for further approval from abutting property owners. The case highlighted the legal complexities surrounding municipal authority and the rights of property owners in urban settings, particularly regarding the necessary permissions required for railroad construction.	The Wiggins Ferry Company claimed that the East St. Louis Union Railway Company could not lawfully lay tracks on Front Street without obtaining consent from a substantial majority of the property owners, as required by the city charter. It argued that the ordinance permitting the railway's construction was invalid, alleging improper authorization and seeking an injunction to stop the railway from proceeding with its plans.	The East St. Louis Union Railway Company contended that it was fully authorized to construct the railroad tracks based on the city council's grant and that it did not need to obtain consent from the adjoining property owners, as the relevant statutes did not mandate such approval. The company maintained that its operations complied with the local laws governing railroads and asserted the legitimacy of its incorporation and intended activities.

On June 14, 1882, George Taylor obtained a judgment against Samuel G. Weagley and others for $6,282.87 in the Morgan Circuit Court, Illinois. On the same day, the defendants requested an appeal, which was granted pending the filing of a bond in the amount of $7,000 within 30 days. However, the bond was not effectively filed until July 15, 1882, and the defendants failed to submit the record to the appellate court. Subsequently, Taylor filed a short record, and the appellate court dismissed the appeal in January 1883, ordering damages of $314.14 and costs of $19.17 against the defendants. The defendants paid the original judgment amount on March 4, 1883, but later sought to have the dismissal and assessment of damages set aside, resulting in an unsuccessful motion in the appellate court. On April 24, 1884, Weagley and Boyce filed for an injunction in the Morgan Circuit Court to prevent the collection of damages and costs ordered by the appellate court. The case was tried, resulting in a decree that enjoined collection of the judgment. Taylor then brought the case to the appellate court to reverse this decree.	George Taylor, the plaintiff, argued that the defendants did not file their appeal bond in a timely manner and failed to take necessary actions to properly pursue their appeal. He claimed that due to their negligence, the appellate court correctly dismissed the appeal and assessed damages against them. Taylor sought to reverse the circuit court's decree that allowed the defendants to avoid paying the damages and costs arising from the dismissal of their appeal.	Samuel G. Weagley and the other defendants contended that their appeal should not have been dismissed, and they filed a bill in the circuit court seeking injunction against the enforcement of the appellate court's judgment for damages and costs. They argued that the circuit court had the jurisdiction to provide relief from the consequences of the appellate court's actions and alleged that their situation was equitable enough to warrant such relief.

In 1876, the case of Catlin Preston v. Joseph M. Williams was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a legal action to correct a mistake in the description of land conveyed by Peter G. Cooper to his three minor children, Melissa, Elizabeth, and Charles W. Cooper, via a deed dated May 9, 1864. The context of the deed involved a prior marriage dissolution between Peter G. Cooper and his wife Martha Cooper, during which Martha was awarded alimony due to the custody of their children. In March 1863, the court ordered Peter to pay Martha $50 biannually as alimony, which became a lien on his real estate. By signing the deed in question, Peter received $900 in exchange, ostensibly discharging his alimony obligation. The core of the litigation was triggered when the appellant claimed that the deed was a voluntary and consideration-free conveyance, arguing that a court of equity should not rectify mistakes in such situations. The appellees, the Cooper children, sought to affirm the validity of the deed and rectify any errors in its description.	The plaintiff's main argument focused on the assertion that the deed was executed with proper consideration, specifically that it was made in satisfaction of an alimony decree. They contended that the children were not mere volunteers in this transaction since the payment was made not only for Martha's benefit but also to secure the children's support. Therefore, the plaintiffs sought the court's affirmation of the deed's validity and correction of any descriptive errors, arguing that the deed should be enforceable based on the consideration provided.	The defendant contended that the conveyance was voluntary and devoid of consideration, citing the general principle that a court of equity should not assist in rectifying mistakes in voluntary contracts. The argument suggested that because the initial payment was not directly from the grantees, the deed was not enforceable. Additionally, the defendant claimed they had a rightful interest in the property and that any errors in the deed's description should permit them to benefit from the unclear circumstances surrounding the conveyance.

The case titled "The President, Directors, and Company of the State Bank of Illinois v. Thomas Batty, Jr., for the use of David A. Smith" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1843. The plaintiff, represented by the President, Directors, and Company of the State Bank of Illinois, claims that Thomas Batty, Jr. failed to fulfill his obligation regarding deposits made at the Jacksonville branch of the bank. The primary event that triggered the legal action occurred on July 7, 1842, when David A. Smith, authorized by Batty, presented a check at the bank demanding the payment of funds totaling $970 from deposits made by Batty on several earlier dates. The bank refused to honor the check. Evidence presented included a power of attorney allowing Smith to act on Batty’s behalf and the check itself, which was inaccurately signed without the "Jr." suffix. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff, assessing damages due to the non-performance of Batty's promises at $991.08. The court was tasked with determining the validity of the claims based on the evidence presented.	The plaintiffs argued that Batty had deposited funds with the bank and had authorized David A. Smith to demand payment on his behalf. They contended that the refusal of the bank to honor the check on July 7, 1842, constituted a breach of contract. The plaintiffs sought recovery of the deposited amount along with damages for the failure to perform the agreed-upon financial obligations.	The defendants contended that the refusal to pay was justified due to issues regarding the check's validity, particularly the omission of "Jr." from Batty's name. They argued that this omission created uncertainty regarding Smith’s authority to demand payment. Additionally, they questioned the sufficiency and formality of the verdict and maintained that errors were made in admitting evidence related to the power of attorney and the check into the court records.

In January 1868, the legal case Pulaski Scovil v. James P. Kelsey arose in Mason County, Illinois, involving Pulaski Scovil as the plaintiff and James P. Kelsey as the defendant. Kelsey had purchased a piece of land at a tax sale and subsequently sold it to Mrs. Connell, a married woman. However, her deed did not have the necessary signature of her husband, which was required under Illinois law at that time. Mrs. Connell then transferred the property to her husband, Scovil. After the land was redeemed, Kelsey received the redemption money from the county clerk but refused to pay it to Scovil. Kelsey argued that the right to the redemption money was tied to the certificate of purchase and that his previous deed only conveyed a contingent interest in the land. The court had to consider whether the equitable interest conferred by Kelsey’s deed to Mrs. Connell could be passed on to Scovil and whether the deed’s validity was affected by the lack of the husband’s signature.	Scovil claimed that he was entitled to the redemption money since the land was conveyed to him through Mrs. Connell. He argued that the conveyance should pass the equitable interest of the property and the rights associated with it, including the right to the redemption payment. He requested the court to enforce the transfer of these rights despite the legal inadequacy of Mrs. Connell's deed due to the absence of her husband's signature.	Kelsey defended his position by asserting that the redemption money right was intrinsically linked to the certificate of purchase, which must be assigned to the grantee for the rights to the redemption payment to transfer. Kelsey contended that his original deed had only passed a contingent interest to Mrs. Connell, not the right to the redemption money itself. He argued that since Mrs. Connell did not properly convey her interest due to lacking her husband's signature, Scovil could not claim any rights to the redemption money.

In September 1869, the case of Eliza A. Quinn, Administratrix of Bernard Quinn, deceased, v. The Illinois Central Railroad Company was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident took place when Bernard Quinn, part of a large funeral entourage, boarded a train in Cairo, Illinois, for a short journey. During the trip, Quinn stood on the train's platform while waiting to pay his fare. As the conductor was making change, a gust of wind blew away the paper money, prompting Quinn to try to reclaim it. In doing so, he lost his balance and fell, resulting in fatal injuries after being thrown under the train cars. The case centered on whether the railroad company was liable for his death or if Quinn's actions were solely responsible for the incident.	The plaintiff, Eliza A. Quinn, claimed damages for the wrongful death of her husband, asserting that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent. She argued that the company's failure to provide adequate seating for the passengers in the crowded train contributed to the conditions that led to her husband's tragic fall. The implication was that the company should have foreseen the potential dangers posed to passengers standing on the platform.	The defendant, the Illinois Central Railroad Company, contended that Quinn's death was the result of his own negligence rather than any fault of the company. They argued that there was standing room available inside the train and that Quinn voluntarily placed himself in a dangerous position. The defense maintained that the conductor’s alleged oversight did not rise to the level of negligence necessary to hold the company liable, as Quinn's actions were recklessly negligent given the circumstances.

In the legal case of John D. Kedzie et al. v. The West Chicago Park Commissioners, which was filed in Ottawa, Illinois, on June 13, 1885, the parties involved were the plaintiffs, John D. Kedzie and others, against the quasi-municipal corporation known as the West Chicago Park Commissioners. The case arose from actions taken by the Park Commissioners regarding the special assessment of property benefits tied to the establishment of a boulevard. The plaintiffs contested the authority of the West Chicago Park Commissioners to levy such assessments, claiming that the procedures followed had legal deficiencies. The Illinois Supreme Court was brought into the matter after an appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County, where these issues had been previously addressed.	The plaintiffs claimed that the West Chicago Park Commissioners lacked the statutory authority to levy assessments on properties for the boulevard project. They argued that the assessments were not executed according to the established legal framework and violated constitutional rules requiring uniformity in benefit and burden. They sought to have the assessments declared void and requested the court to enjoin the collection of these assessments based on insufficient legal notice and the alleged lack of authority in conducting the assessments.	The defendant, West Chicago Park Commissioners, maintained that they were authorized under specific sections of the Illinois statute to levy special assessments for park purposes, including boulevard construction. They argued that the law provided them with the necessary powers to carry out these assessments appropriately and that all necessary procedures had been followed legally. They contended that the Circuit Court had proper jurisdiction during the confirmation of the assessment, and any objections raised previously should have been dealt with at that stage rather than through a bill in chancery.

Josiah H. Lombard v. Gwinthlean H. Kinzie is a legal case decided in September 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case revolves around a claim of dower made by Gwinthlean H. Kinzie in connection to accreted land that was once owned by her late husband, Robert Kinzie. The property in question is situated in Cook County, Illinois, and is associated with a previous case, Kinzie v. Winston. Robert Kinzie had an interest in a piece of land, identified as "Sand street," which remained his until it was sold by his assignee in bankruptcy. The Court's opinion clarifies that Kinzie held sufficient title to the land during his marriage, giving his wife the right to claim dower in both the land and its accretions. The legal argument focuses on whether the dower right extends to subsequent accretions formed after Kinzie's death and subsequent sale of the property. The Court examined the legal principles relating to dower rights, particularly in regards to property ownership and rights of surviving spouses.	Gwinthlean H. Kinzie, the plaintiff, asserted her right to dower in the accretions to “Sand street,” maintaining that as the widow of Robert Kinzie, she was entitled to inherit rights to the land and any subsequent land formed by natural processes. She argued that her dower rights remained valid despite the sale of the land by her husband's assignee, as her claim was based on the title held by Robert Kinzie during their marriage.	The defendant's position, represented by the assignee in bankruptcy, was that Kinzie's sale of the property limited Gwinthlean’s claim and that any rights to the accretion could not be conferred to her given the sales made on the street during Kinzie’s lifetime. They contended that she could not claim dower rights over property that was no longer in her husband's possession and highlighted the alleged rights of purchasers of the lots sold on “Sand street.”

In June 1876, the case of George W. Hall et al. v. Catharine Barnes took place in Illinois. The plaintiff, Catharine Barnes, brought an action against George W. Hall and others under the "Act to provide against the evils resulting from the sale of intoxicating liquors" that had been enacted on July 1, 1872. The lawsuit stemmed from the alleged intoxication of her husband, which she claimed was caused by the defendants' actions. The case was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, and the presiding judge was Amos Watts from the Circuit Court of Marion County. The dispute centered around the effects of her husband's drunkenness on her life and the family, leading to significant financial and emotional consequences. Barnes sought remedies for these damages, arguing that the defendants contributed to her husband’s condition through their selling of liquor.	Catharine Barnes argued that the defendants were responsible for her husband's repeated intoxications, which caused serious disruption to her family and loss of support. She requested the court to hold the defendants accountable under the relevant Illinois law, seeking damages of $300, which was awarded to her by the jury.	The defendants contended that the court made several errors during the proceedings, including the denial of their request for a change of venue and that the testimony presented by Barnes was irrelevant. They argued that her evidence should have been excluded and claimed that the evidence against them was not sufficient for the jury’s decision. They sought to reverse the judgment awarded to the plaintiff.

In 1865, in the Vermilion Circuit Court, Jane C. Crane filed a bill in chancery against her husband, William H. Crane, and the widow, heirs, and administrator of Oscar F. Harmon, deceased. Jane sought to set aside a deed executed in 1856, which transferred 16.5 acres of land from her to Harmon. She claimed that the deed was obtained under duress, threats, and coercion. The case arose after Jane alleged that the acknowledgment of the deed was invalid, asserting it was taken before the wrong officer, instead of the clerk of the Vermilion County Court. Key testimonies included those from Jane’s daughter and another witness, arguing that improper influence was used during the execution. However, testimony from the official who took the acknowledgment stated that Jane executed the deed voluntarily. Ultimately, the Circuit Court dismissed her bill, leading Jane to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Jane C. Crane contended that the deed transferring her property to Oscar F. Harmon was void due to being executed under duress, and that it was improperly acknowledged. She argued that the deed was extorted from her through threats and coercion, and requested that the court set aside the deed.	The defendants, led by William H. Crane and the heirs of Oscar F. Harmon, asserted that the deed was executed voluntarily and properly acknowledged. They argued that Jane's later actions—accepting property in exchange for the deed and receiving $700 for her interest—demonstrated her approval of the transaction and negated her claims of duress.

In 1860 in Chicago, Josephine Spear, who owned a lot (lot 13, Canal Trustees), married Sidney P. Walker. They had one child, Mary Louise Walker, born in 1863. Josephine died in 1864, leaving Mary Louise as the sole heir. Sidney Walker was appointed guardian of Mary Louise's estate in 1872. Elias R. Bowen began renting the lot in 1857 and continued to occupy it after the lease expired, paying rent to Sidney Walker. In 1874, Walker borrowed money from Bowen and used personal property as collateral via chattel mortgages, which referenced the lot's rent or mortgage payments. After Mary Louise turned eighteen, Sidney obtained a quitclaim deed from her for the lot, along with a promissory note to secure the transaction. However, Bowen claimed that these chattel mortgages constituted an equitable mortgage on the property to secure Walker's debt to him. Meanwhile, the estate experienced multiple transactions, including other loans secured by mortgages on the lot. The court was asked to foreclose a trust deed as a mortgage and to determine the equities between the various creditors.	Bowen argued that the chattel mortgages he executed with Sidney Walker created an equitable mortgage on lot 13, asserting that these mortgages secured Walker's previous debts to him. He contended that his claim of equitable mortgage should take precedence over the other encumbrances on the property, citing the nature of the agreements and the timeline of the transactions.	The defendants, including McCarthy and others, contended that Bowen's claims were invalid since Sidney Walker had no legal estate in the property when the mortgages were created. They argued that as guardian of Mary Louise's estate, Walker held no substantial interest to mortgage the property and that the later-acquired title after Mary Louise's majority did not benefit Bowen as he alleged. They emphasized that Bowen was aware of his subordinate position in the claims against the property.

In April 1862, the case "John S. Oxford v. David Peter" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Iroquois County. The conflict arose when John S. Oxford directed a young boy, living with him and approximately thirteen years old, to go into his field and drive out any cattle present. During this task, the boy successfully drove out a steer but then pursued other cattle that were nearby in a lane. This pursuit resulted in the death of one of the cattle. The plaintiff, David Peter, subsequently brought a legal action against Oxford to recover the monetary value of the animal that died, leading to a trial where a verdict was rendered in favor of Peter for twenty dollars. Oxford appealed the decision, arguing that the damage occurred when the boy exceeded his specific instructions.	The plaintiff, David Peter, claimed that John S. Oxford was responsible for the death of his cattle due to the actions of Oxford's servant. Peter's legal argument centered on the assertion that the servant acted within the scope of his employment by attempting to drive the cattle out of the field, which resulted in damages for which Oxford should be liable. Peter sought compensation for the loss of the animal, amounting to twenty dollars.	John S. Oxford, the appellant, contended that the servant had exceeded his authority by chasing the cattle beyond the boundaries of the field, and therefore, he was not liable for the damages that ensued. Oxford's defense relied on the principle that if a servant acts beyond specific directions provided by the master, the master is not responsible for those actions. He argued that his instructions were explicitly limited to driving cattle out of the field and did not include any pursuit of the cattle outside its confines.

In December 1847, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, the case of Johnson Ginn et al. v. Charles Rogers arose from a Forcible Entry and Detainer action initiated by Rogers against the appellants, Ginn and others, before a justice of the peace. The attempt to resolve this dispute involved a jury trial, but the jury could not reach a verdict, leading to their discharge. Subsequently, both parties' attorneys agreed to transfer the case to the Jo Daviess County Court, stipulating that they would not object to this transfer in any future proceedings. After the County Court's jury returned a verdict favoring Rogers, Ginn's team filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that the County Court lacked jurisdiction, as it can only gain jurisdiction through an appeal from a justice's judgment—something that did not occur in this case. The County Court’s jurisdiction was established by statute, and it was unclear if the attorneys’ agreement was sufficient to confer jurisdiction in this context. The primary legal question was whether the County Court had jurisdiction over the matter.	The plaintiff, Charles Rogers, asserted that he had the right to recover possession of the disputed property through the action of Forcible Entry and Detainer, which is generally initiated at the level of a justice of the peace. He maintained that the case was properly transferred to the County Court for trial after the initial jury could not reach a verdict.	The defendants, led by Johnson Ginn, contended that the Jo Daviess County Court did not have original jurisdiction over the Forcible Entry and Detainer case, as such jurisdiction lies exclusively with the justice of the peace. They claimed that the case had not been properly appealed, and thus the transfer to the County Court was invalid. Ginn also argued that he had not agreed to the transfer, and his attorney lacked the authority to bind him to such an agreement.

Jonathan Clark and Levi Roberts were involved in a legal dispute originating from an attachment lawsuit in Madison County, Illinois, in June 1826. Roberts claimed that Clark owed him $100 and was in the process of moving his property out of the county, which justified the issuance of an attachment. Initially, the case was decided in favor of Roberts by a justice of the peace. Clark appealed the judgment to the circuit court, where he attempted to quash the attachment while Roberts sought to amend his affidavit. The court allowed the amendment but later shifted the trial venue to Montgomery County due to an unclear jury verdict. Ultimately, a jury in Montgomery County ruled in favor of Roberts again, awarding him the original claim amount. Clark contested this outcome by alleging multiple errors regarding the attachment and the amended affidavit.	Clark maintained that the attachment against him was improperly issued and felt that the affidavit on which it was based did not meet statutory requirements. He sought to have the attachment quashed and argued that the amendments made to the affidavit did not cure its initial defects, thus invalidating the subsequent proceedings.	Roberts contended that the affidavit was sufficient to establish the court's jurisdiction and that the attachment was valid. He argued against Clark's motions to quash the attachment and emphasized that the amended affidavit complied with legal standards, which justified the court's decision to uphold the attachment.

Thomas B. Murphy filed an action of ejectment against Henry Riemenschneider and others on July 25, 1873, concerning the possession of lots 1 and 2 in block 1 of Honore’s re-subdivision in Chicago, Illinois. The focal point of the dispute is the boundary line between Murphy's lots and the defendants' lots (3 and 4). The block is triangular, with Ogden Avenue on one side. Historical subdivisions complicate the matter, as no measurements for the corner lots were marked on the initial plat. Both parties provided conflicting evidence regarding the actual dimensions of Murphy's lot 1—while Murphy claimed it had a frontage of 100 feet, the defendants argued it was only 55 feet. The original recorded plat of the subdivision was destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, further complicating the proofs. The stipulation in court acknowledged Murphy's ownership of lots 1 and 2 and the defendants' ownership of lots 3 and 4, but the trial focused on the boundary between these lots.	The plaintiff, Thomas B. Murphy, claims that he is entitled to possess lots 1 and 2, asserting that lot 1 has a frontage of 100 feet on Ogden Avenue and lot 2 has a frontage of 24 feet. He argues that since the boundaries were originally staked out, these dimensions should be upheld. Murphy maintains that the defendants' claim over the adjoining lot encroaches on his properties.	The defendants contest Murphy's claim by asserting that the actual frontage of lot 1 is only 55 feet. They argue that their possession, starting 79 feet from the corner, does not infringe upon Murphy's lots. The defendants provided evidence from surveys conducted to support their position, countering the original stakes mentioned by Murphy and suggesting that those stakes are inconsistent with established mapping.

The case, referred to simply as "Anonymous," took place during the April Term of 1865 in Illinois. The details surrounding the specific events leading to the case are not provided, but it involves a legal question regarding the procedure of filing an amended abstract. The key individual involved is Mr. B. C. Cook, who posed a question to the court about the necessity of obtaining permission to file such an amended document. The Illinois Supreme Court needed to clarify the rules regarding the right to file amended abstracts, which is an essential aspect of legal documentation and court processes. The case represents procedural legal considerations in the mid-19th century American judicial system.	The plaintiff's claims, though not explicitly detailed, center around the inquiry of whether it is mandatory to seek leave from the court in order to file an amended abstract. This reflects the plaintiff's concern regarding adherence to procedural rules and their rights correspondingly.	The defendant's defenses, while not explicitly stated, can be inferred from the court’s response that either party has the authority to proceed with the filing of an amended abstract without needing to obtain leave. This suggests that the defendant was possibly arguing against the necessity of such permission, asserting a lack of procedural barriers for filing.

In June 1867, in Livingston County, Illinois, the county court’s treasurer sought judgment against a list of delinquent lands for unpaid taxes from the previous year, which included properties owned by the appellants, John Stilwell and others. The appellants objected to this action on two grounds: first, that the treasurer's application for judgment was made during the June term instead of the earlier May term, and second, that the list of lands was not filed five days prior to the term's commencement. The court upheld the latter objection and denied the treasurer’s request for judgment. In August 1867, the treasurer made a second attempt to obtain a judgment for the same lands, which the appellants again resisted, asserting lack of jurisdiction and citing the previous refusal to render a judgment at the June term. Despite the appellants' objections, the court ruled in favor of the treasurer and approved the sale of the lands to satisfy the tax debts. Subsequently, the case was appealed to the Circuit Court, which affirmed the county court's judgment, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, which addressed jurisdiction under the relevant revenue laws.	The plaintiffs, represented by the county treasurer, argued that the delinquent lands were subject to tax judgments due to unpaid taxes from the previous year. They claimed that the county court had jurisdiction to render these judgments at any regular term following April, regardless of the specific term schedule mentioned in prior notices. This meant the application for judgment could be appropriately made during any term that followed the delinquency notice.	The defendants, John Stilwell and others, contended that the county court lacked jurisdiction since the treasurer's judgment application was improperly made during the June term instead of the May term. They also argued that the court's prior refusal to grant judgment at the June term barred any subsequent judgment application during the August term for the same properties.

In the case of William B. McCrosky v. Drury C. Leach et al., which took place in Jersey County, Illinois, a legal action known as "assumpsit" was initiated in January 1872. The plaintiff, William B. McCrosky, sought damages resulting from alleged fraudulent activities by the defendant, Drury C. Leach. The venue changed from the circuit court of Jersey County to the Alton city court by mutual consent. The core of the case centered around a deed executed by Leach and his wife on April 5, 1869, which conveyed real estate to Robert W. Leach, acting as a trustee for Mrs. Leach. McCrosky argued that this conveyance was aimed at hindering and delaying creditors, a claim supported by a statute from February 1865 that allowed for attachments in cases of such fraudulent conveyances. However, prior to the lawsuit and the issuance of an attachment, the deed in question was voluntarily withdrawn and destroyed, as all parties agreed it was done in good faith to provide for Mrs. Leach. During the trial, evidence indicated that the conveyance was never properly recorded and was retracted before legal action began. Consequently, the court needed to determine the validity of McCrosky's attachment based on these facts.	The plaintiff, William B. McCrosky, claimed that Drury C. Leach had fraudulently conveyed property to avoid paying his debts, thereby violating the Illinois statute that allows attachments in cases of such behavior. McCrosky contended that this conveyance hindered his ability to collect on a debt owed to him and sought the court's approval of the writ of attachment to secure the claimed assets before the court.	The defendant, Drury C. Leach, denied any fraudulent intentions behind the property's conveyance. He asserted that the deed to the trustee was executed in good faith to protect his wife's interests amid potential financial difficulties. Leach argued that since the deed was withdrawn and destroyed before any legal action was initiated, there was no existing legal title to hinder the collection of any debts. This premise supported his plea in abatement, which aimed to quash the writ of attachment filed by McCrosky.

In February 1884, in Kane County, Illinois, Lafayette Reed filed a motion appealing a decision regarding an execution issued against him and his co-defendant, J. Wesley Morris, who had passed away prior to the execution's issuance. At the time of judgment, J. W. Morris owned 280 acres of real estate, and the court had rendered a decree against both defendants. However, the execution and fee bill had not been revived against Morris's heirs or executors, as required by statute after his death. The case arose after the sheriff seized Reed's property, and it was sold, with a certificate of purchase issued to Reed. The motion was brought forth by F. G. Garfield (the appellee) who sought to quash the execution on the grounds that it was invalid against him due to the failure to properly revive the judgment against the deceased's estate. The court agreed and quashed the execution, asserting that fundamental legal procedures had not been followed.	The plaintiff, Lafayette Reed, argued that the execution against him was valid despite the fact that J. W. Morris was deceased. Reed asserted that the levy on his property and the resulting sale were legitimate actions based on the judgment rendered against both defendants. Reed claimed that the failure to issue a revival against Morris's estate did not negate the execution against the surviving defendant, particularly since his property was involved in the initial judgment.	The defendant, F. G. Garfield, contended that the execution against him was void because it had not been revived as required by law after the death of J. W. Morris. Garfield emphasized that notice had not been given to the executors of Morris's estate regarding the existing judgment, making any execution levied on his property invalid. He maintained that the legal foundation for the execution failed due to non-compliance with the statutory provisions.

Charles P. Swigert, Auditor, et al. filed a case against the County of Hamilton concerning the state's handling of funds related to municipal bonds. The case stemmed from events that began in October and November of 1871 when Hamilton County issued $200,000 in bonds to the St. Louis and Southeastern Railway Company, supposedly payable in twenty years with a 7% interest rate. These bonds were registered with the Illinois Auditor of Public Accounts. In June 1888, the Illinois Supreme Court declared these bonds void, a fact communicated to the relevant authorities. Following this, in June 1888, the Hamilton County Board passed a resolution requesting the Auditor to issue a warrant for approximately $17,500 collected from taxes intended for the interest payments on the now-invalidated bonds. However, the Auditor refused to comply, arguing that funds from taxes collected could only be applied to valid bonds still outstanding. The resolution was interpreted within the context of an act from June 10, 1885, which provided instructions for the handling of surplus funds related to municipal bonds. The legal proceeding initiated sought a mandamus order requiring the Auditor to draw his warrant and release the funds to the county.	The plaintiffs, represented by the Hamilton County Board, claimed that the Auditor unlawfully refused to issue a warrant for $17,500 collected from taxes intended for payments on the voided bonds. They argued that since the bonds had been declared void and there were no valid bonds to which the funds could be allocated, the funds should be refunded to the county. The plaintiffs sought a writ of mandamus to compel the Auditor to draw the warrant for this amount and release the funds.	The defendant, Charles P. Swigert, the Auditor of Public Accounts, contended that he was legally obligated to consider all registered bonds from Hamilton County, including separate valid bonds that had not been declared void. He argued that there existed no specific ascertainable amount regarding the surplus funds since some taxes had to be applied towards these valid bonds. Thus, he claimed it was not his duty to issue a warrant for unknown amounts and that mandamus could not be invoked in this situation.

In January 1868, the case "John Byler et al. v. John Asher" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from an election held on November 6, 1866, in Adams County. The plaintiff, John Asher, a white man residing in the precinct, sought to vote in that election but was denied by John Byler and Charles F. Talcott, the judges of the election. Asher’s name was not registered, which led to his denial. He alleged that his lack of registration was a misunderstanding as he was a longtime resident who had previously voted. Despite submitting an affidavit claiming his right to vote, the judges refused to accept it, arguing that he had left the state to evade a military draft. In the lower court, Asher was awarded $5 for damages; however, Byler and Talcott appealed, contesting the decision and presenting claims of legal errors regarding the denied evidence and instructions given to the jury.	Asher claimed his right to vote was infringed upon by the election judges' refusal to accept his ballot. He asserted that he had resided in the precinct for many years and was known to the judges. Asher sought legal redress arguing that their refusal violated his rights as a citizen eligible to vote, despite lacking formal registration at the time of the election. He presented his affidavit to support his claim and requested damages for this infringement.	The defendants, Byler and Talcott, argued that they were justified in refusing Asher’s vote due to his lack of registration. They contended that under the act of 1865, he was required to present proof, including an affidavit from a registered householder, which he failed to do. Moreover, they sought to introduce evidence about Asher’s military status and reasons for leaving the state, which the court excluded. They maintained that their actions were within their authority and that they were not liable for damages as their refusal was based on the legal requirements of the voting process.

In September 1847, Augustus H. Evans owned 220 acres of land and verbally agreed to sell it to James C. Clement through an intermediary, Smith. Evans intended to execute a quitclaim deed for the land, which was to be held in escrow by Smith until Clement provided a deed of trust to secure a $1,000 note payable to Evans. On October 22, 1847, Evans prepared the quitclaim deed and entrusted it to Smith alongside the deed of trust. Evans accepted a partial payment of $77.17 from Clement in November 1848. However, during the process, Smith and Clement conspired to defraud Evans by delivering the quitclaim deed to Clement without completing the required terms of the transaction. This led Evans to seek legal redress, claiming fraud, and requesting the return of the land, an accounting for rents earned by Clement, and a full execution of their original agreement. The case ultimately went to the Illinois Supreme Court after a ruling by the Scott Circuit Court found in favor of Evans but required Clement to perform actions that the higher court later deemed excessive.	Evans, the plaintiff, argued that Clement fraudulently obtained a quitclaim deed for his property by not fulfilling the agreed-upon conditions set forth in their transaction. He claimed that the deed should be declared null and void because it was delivered under false pretenses and without his authorization. Evans requested restoration of the property, an accounting for any rents and profits Clement earned from the land, and other equitable relief as deemed appropriate by the court.	Clement, the defendant, contended that he had rightful claims to the land and alleged that he should be compensated under the original contract of purchase made with Evans through Smith. He argued that even if the deed was fraudulently obtained, he still possessed rights to land he might have acquired otherwise. Therefore, he resisted the complete surrender of any property rights and sought the specific performance of the original contract, despite having previously repudiated it.

In September 1870, the case of Luther Stone v. James C. Fargo et al. was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court. The events leading to the lawsuit took place primarily in Chicago, involving key individuals: Luther Stone, the plaintiff; James C. Fargo and Edward A. Rucker, the defendants, among others. Stone had purchased property from Caroline Clarke through Rucker, giving notes for part of the payment and receiving an indemnity bond from Clarke to protect against claims on prior notes owed to another vendor, Charles G. E. Prussing. After Clarke's death, Rucker, who had become the trustee, sold the property to Fargo for a significantly lower price than its value, without notifying Stone, who was still involved in legal disputes regarding the notes. This sale, which occurred while a related lawsuit was pending, was conducted under questionable circumstances that led Stone to allege fraud. He sought both to set aside the sale and to offset his obligations on the notes against the losses he incurred from the indemnity bond.	Luther Stone claimed that the sale of the property held under the trust deed was wrongful and fraudulent due to bad faith and a lack of notice on the part of the trustee, Rucker. He argued that the price obtained was grossly inadequate compared to the property's value and that he should be allowed to set off his claim for damages arising from the bond against the notes he owed, as the estate of Clarke was not insolvent and allowing the set off would not harm other creditors.	The defendants, represented by Rucker and Fargo, asserted that the sale was legitimate, arguing that Stone had not raised his claims timely and contended that allowing a set-off would interfere with proper distribution among other creditors of Clarke’s estate. They emphasized the legality of the sale itself, despite the circumstances surrounding it.

The case "Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Daniel Fishell" took place in 1889 in the village of Ludlow, Illinois. The central individuals involved were Daniel Fishell, the plaintiff, and the Illinois Central Railroad Company as the defendant. The incident in question involved Fishell's wagon, which was loaded with corn, colliding with a train at a crossing. Fishell claimed that the train was traveling faster than the local ordinance allowed, which was set at ten miles per hour between cattle guards and fifteen miles per hour outside them. The collision resulted in damages to Fishell's wagon, load, and one of his horses. During the trial, evidence around the speed of the train was considered conflicting, yet there was sufficient support for the claim that the train exceeded the speed limit at that location. Furthermore, Fishell argued that he had exercised due care by looking and listening for trains before crossing, although some argued that he failed to stop due to the obstructed view caused by nearby parked cars.	Fishell claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent for violating the village's speed ordinance, which directly caused the damage to his property. He sought compensation for the damages amounting to $116. Fishell maintained that he had taken reasonable precautions while crossing the tracks, suggesting that the accident was not due to any negligence on his part.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company defended against the claims by arguing that the plaintiff's failure to stop and properly look and listen before crossing the tracks constituted contributory negligence, which should bar his recovery. They pointed out that his limited ability to hear and see the train due to environmental factors did not excuse his obligation to ensure safety. Additionally, they questioned the sufficiency of the evidence proving that the ordinance was in force at the time of the incident.

In the case of William C. Shirley v. Enoch Howard and Corydon Weed et al., the legal proceedings took place in January 1870 in Illinois. The case involved promissory notes where William C. Shirley, the plaintiff, acted as the endorsee or assignor of the notes in question, which were issued by the defendants Enoch Howard and Corydon Weed. The primary issue revolved around the legality of the promissory notes, specifically the argument made by the defendants that the consideration for these notes stemmed from a wager on the outcome of the last presidential election, suggesting that the notes were therefore not valid. The case was presided over by Judge Benjamin S. Edwards in the Circuit Court of Sangamon County before being appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, William C. Shirley, claimed that the promissory notes were valid and that he was entitled to enforce them as the endorsee. He argued that the notes were issued for valuable consideration and that the reasons for their issuance (involving a wager) should not be a valid defense when the notes were acquired in good faith and before maturity.	The defendants, Enoch Howard and Corydon Weed, contended that the promissory notes were invalid due to their underlying consideration, which involved a wager on the outcome of the presidential election. They maintained that this constituted a basis for disputing the enforceability of the notes, asserting that a wager should render the notes void against the claims of an assignee.

In June 1870, Charles C. Mœller, a resident of a railroad area approximately fifty-five miles from Chicago, engaged Alexander McLagan, a commission merchant in Chicago, to purchase 10,000 bushels of wheat for him. Mœller agreed to pay McLagan a commission of one-half cent per bushel, along with a margin of ten cents per bushel, to be held to secure his advances. The contract specified that McLagan would store the grain and charge Mœller for any storage fees and interest until the wheat was sold. Following the purchase, wheat prices began to decline, and McLagan notified Mœller of the situation, requesting instructions on whether to sell the wheat as the margin was being exhausted. Despite several correspondences and requests for additional margin, Mœller did not provide further funds, leading McLagan to sell the wheat at a loss. Disputes arose over whether McLagan had the right to sell without Mœller's consent due to the margin being depleted.	Mœller claimed that McLagan failed to fulfill his duties as a commission merchant by selling the wheat without proper instructions and before giving Mœller a fair opportunity to provide additional margin. He sought damages for the losses incurred from the sale made by McLagan.	McLagan argued that he was within his rights to sell the wheat after Mœller's margin was exhausted. He maintained that he had communicated adequately with Mœller regarding the market situation and requested further funds, which Mœller failed to provide. Thus, McLagan contended that his actions were justified as they followed standard practices for managing such agreements in the commission market.

The case of Elisha Buck v. The People ex rel. Charles P. Swigert took place in September 1875 in Kankakee County, Illinois. The proceedings involved the county treasurer seeking judgment against delinquent lands and town lots for unpaid taxes for the years 1873 and 1874. The county court previously ruled against Buck, who raised several objections regarding the validity of the tax sale. Buck argued that the notice for the tax sale was not sufficient to confer jurisdiction, that the taxes were not legally assessed, and that the descriptions of the lands were inadequate. However, the court found Buck's objections to be mere technicalities without merit. The court emphasized the importance of taxpayers fulfilling their obligations and deemed the objections raised by Buck as unjustified.	Elisha Buck, as the objector, claimed that the tax notice and application were insufficient for jurisdiction, that the taxes were improperly assessed and described, and that various statutory requirements were not met. Buck did not claim he was unfairly assessed but contended that the tax collection process was flawed. He sought the court to overturn the judgment that approved the sale of his lands due to these alleged irregularities.	The People, represented by the treasurer, countered Buck's claims by stating that the notice of the tax sale was valid and conformed to legal requirements. They asserted that the objections raised were merely technical and did not affect the substance of the tax itself. The defense argued that the essential procedures were followed, and the taxes were necessary for county functions and public services, emphasizing that the court should enforce the collection of taxes to maintain governmental operations.

George W. Campbell filed an appeal against Abel S. Conover in April 1861 before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from an action in which Conover sought to recover three times the value of property that Campbell, acting as a constable, had levied upon.
