The Snowells contested that they had not unequivocally promised to pay rent for the full year and asserted that the amendment to the complaint made by Moss should not have been permitted after the cause was submitted. They argued that this amendment could potentially mislead their defense against the claims made by Moss.

This case, George D. Williamson v. John Hogan, was an action of replevin concerning the steamboat Cumberland, initiated by George D. Williamson against John Hogan in January 1868 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated when Hogan, the city marshal of Cairo, executed an attachment warrant on September 20, 1866, issued in favor of Samuel Wilson for unpaid supplies to the boat, which was owned by the River Transportation Company. Hogan seized the Cumberland as part of this warrant, but purportedly released it to the owners upon the execution of a bond. Following a lawsuit initiated by Williamson, in which he secured judgments against the boat through two separate executions, the vessel was ultimately sold to him at public auction for $4,200. The case revolved around the legal interpretations of both the bond conditions and the rightful ownership of the boat following the seizures and sales. The lower court ruled in favor of the defendant at one point, which led to Williamson appealing the judgment.	The plaintiff, George D. Williamson, asserted that he had purchased the Cumberland through lawful means after it had been seized under separate legal processes which ultimately favored him. Williamson claimed he was in peaceful possession of the boat when Hogan took it unlawfully from him, and he contended that the bond executed by the River Transportation Company effectively discharged any liens against the vessel, thus validating his ownership.	John Hogan, the defendant, defended his actions by arguing that he acted within the scope of his authority as the city marshal executing a valid attachment. He contended that he was entitled to seize the boat for the debt owed to Wilson and that his actions were justified based on the legal framework under which he operated, including the validity of the initial attachment warrant.

The case of James Ingraham v. Henry Luther took place in Warren County, Illinois, with the decision rendered in September 1872 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a promissory note that was allegedly payable to "H. Luther." The plaintiff, James Ingraham, brought an action of assumpsit against the defendant, Henry Luther, seeking to recover the amount owed on the note. During the trial, the defendant offered evidence to prove that the note was actually executed and delivered to a different individual, Hulbert Luther, and not to the plaintiff. However, the trial court rejected this evidence, allowing the note into evidence after the defendant admitted he had signed it. The jury returned a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, leading the defendant to appeal the judgment, claiming that the plaintiff did not have the legal right to maintain the action.	James Ingraham claimed that he was entitled to enforce the promissory note, which he asserted was payable to him. He contended that the defendant's argument regarding the note being payable to another individual should have been addressed through a plea in abatement for misnomer rather than being a question of variance. Ingraham sought damages based on the note, affirming his position as the rightful party to sue.	Henry Luther, the defendant, argued that the plaintiff did not possess the legal ownership of the promissory note, as it was payable to Hulbert Luther, not to Ingraham. Luther maintained that under the general issue plea, he had the right to prove that the note was not in the plaintiff's name, which constituted a fatal variance to Ingraham's claims. The defendant's request was for the court to reverse the decision of the lower court based on this evidence.

In March 1851, an incident occurred at a ferry crossing on the Illinois River at Lacon, involving William Fisher and Levi F. Clisbee. Fisher's servant, Kuhn, was attempting to cross the river on Clisbee's ferry with a horse hitched to a buggy. During the crossing, the horse became restless and backed off the ferry into the river, resulting in the horse's drowning and damage to the buggy and harness. Fisher claimed damages from Clisbee, who was the owner of the ferry. The Circuit Court found in favor of Fisher, leading Clisbee to appeal the decision, arguing that Fisher's servant failed to properly manage the horse and thus contributed to the incident.	The plaintiff, William Fisher, argued that Levi F. Clisbee, as the ferryman, had a duty to ensure the safe transportation of passengers and their property. Fisher claimed that the horse, which was under Clisbee's responsibility during transit, was lost due to the negligent management of the ferry by its owner and operators, resulting in significant damages to both the horse and the buggy.	The defendant, Levi F. Clisbee, contended that his ferry was well constructed and that Fisher's servant, Kuhn, failed to heed instructions to unhitch the horse from the buggy. Clisbee argued that if Kuhn had followed the directions, the horse would not have backed off the ferry. The defendant claimed that the responsibility for the loss lay not with him but with Fisher's servant, who did not act appropriately to prevent the accident.

In 1867, in the State of Indiana, Mary Cox, a married woman, purchased a horse using her own funds. After she and her husband, Alfred Cox, moved to Illinois, her husband mortgaged the horse to John Tinkler, who had signed a note as security. Tinkler later claimed that he gained the absolute title to the horse after paying off the note and a separate debt to Cox. The subsequent dispute arose when Mary Cox initiated a replevin action against Tinkler for the horse, arguing that it was her separate property. The case was first heard before a justice of the peace in Marion County, then appealed to the Circuit Court, where she won. Tinkler then appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the horse's ownership was incorrectly attributed to her based on marital property laws at the time of purchase.	Mary Cox contended that the horse was her separate property, asserting that she purchased it with her own means and that her husband had no claim over it. She maintained that Tinkler had wrongfully taken possession of the horse, and she sought its return through legal action.	John Tinkler's defense was centered on the argument that the title to the horse was vested in Alfred Cox, as per the common law in effect at the time of the purchase. He claimed that the sale and subsequent delivery of the horse from Cox were valid, arguing that he obtained ownership rights because he had paid off the debt secured by the horse.

Lawrence Moore and others (the plaintiffs) filed a lawsuit against Helen R. Williams and others (the defendants) on April 22, 1890, in Mt. Vernon, Illinois. The case revolved around an ejectment action, which is a legal procedure used to regain possession of property. The Illinois Supreme Court was called to review a previous decision from the Circuit Court of Franklin County, presided by Judge George W. Young. The lower court had determined that the plaintiffs were barred from pursuing their current ejectment claim due to a prior equity decree involving the same parties and subject matter. This decree had established their title to the disputed land and placed them in possession, thus rendering the current suit moot in terms of the plaintiffs’ ability to recover any further judgment.	The plaintiffs argued that they should be entitled to a judgment in their favor regarding the property they were claiming, asserting that the prior decision through equity did not prevent them from winning the ejectment case. They contended that the pendency of their appeal did not erase their right to litigate the matter at law since they had already secured a writ of possession.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs were estopped from prosecuting the ejectment claim because of earlier judicial rulings that had settled the matter in equity. They maintained that the previous decree barred the present suit due to res judicata, stating that the plaintiffs had received the specific relief they sought in the earlier proceeding, including possession, and therefore were not entitled to any further claims.

In the case of George W. Hinckley v. Joseph Horazdovsky, a legal matter was brought forward in the year 1889 concerning a work-related injury. The incident took place in Cook County, Illinois, involving a twelve-year-old boy, George W. Hinckley, who was employed by Joseph Horazdovsky. While performing his work, Hinckley was directed by the foreman to oil a planing machine that was in motion. As he followed this instruction, he became caught in the machine and sustained severe injuries. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, where the details surrounding the circumstances leading to the injury were examined, including the relevant actions taken by both the foreman and the employer.	The plaintiff, George W. Hinckley, contended that he was injured due to the negligence of his employer, who instructed him to oil a moving machine. He sought compensation for the injuries sustained while he was fulfilling the orders given by a superior. Hinckley argued that the employer was liable for failing to ensure a safe work environment.	The defendant, Joseph Horazdovsky, argued that the court had erred in its handling of jury instructions and claimed that the jury's verdict was not supported by the evidence presented during the trial. He contended that the evidence was conflicting and that the court's general instruction to the jury did not accurately reflect the law. Ultimately, the defendant sought to have the verdict overturned.

In 1870, the legal case "Anthony S. Seely et al. v. Samuel Wells" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiffs, Anthony S. Seely and Hiram Parr, contested ownership of a tract of land in Greene County, Illinois, against the defendant, Samuel Wells. The case arose from a prior certificate of entry related to the land, recorded on March 6, 1867, by John W. Davis and signed by William F. Elkin, who was the Register of the Land Office in Springfield, Illinois. During the trial, the plaintiffs presented this certificate and a deed from Davis to support their claim to the land. However, the defendant countered this evidence with official certificates from the land office and the general land office in Washington, D.C., indicating that the land had previously been set aside for school purposes by Greene County authorities and that Davis's entry was canceled by federal order in May 1867 due to the land being designated for educational use. The circuit court ruled in favor of the defendant based on the evidence presented regarding the historical allocation of the land.	The plaintiffs argued that they held valid title to the land through a certificate of entry and a deed from John W. Davis, seeking possession of the disputed tract. They contended that their documented entry should be recognized by the court and requested the court to reverse the lower court's ruling that favored the defendant.	The defendant, Samuel Wells, countered the plaintiffs' claims by presenting certified evidence showing the land had been designated for school purposes before the plaintiffs’ entry. He asserted that the plaintiffs lacked any valid title due to this earlier designation and the subsequent cancellation of Davis’s entry. His request was to uphold the circuit court's judgment confirming his ownership.

In 1887, in Green County, Illinois, Sandwich Manufacturing Company (the appellant) brought a lawsuit against William C. Kelly (the appellee) regarding a promissory note for $105 related to the purchase of a reaper machine. Kelly had previously recovered a judgment for $114.46 against the company through a set-off claim. The reaper machine failed to perform as expected, leading Kelly to argue that he had tendered the machine back to the company after attempting to resolve issues over two seasons. The appellant countered that there was no warranty or contract that allowed for such a defense, and that Kelly should not be allowed to set off his claims since he had used the machine. The court examined the agreements made between the parties, concluding that they understood and bound by changes to the contract, thereby allowing Kelly to present his set-off. The court found that there was sufficient evidence for the jury to support his claims regarding the machine's performance and the resultant legal implications.	The Sandwich Manufacturing Company claimed that there was no warranty applicable to the reaper machine purchased by Kelly. They argued against Kelly's right to set off the amount he paid on another note assigned to Mosher, asserting that he had no legal grounds to return the machine after having benefited from its use for two seasons.	William C. Kelly contended that the reaper was defective and did not work properly despite multiple attempts to fix it. He asserted that he had acted in good faith while attempting to resolve the performance issues and that the contract’s warranty should apply to the machine he received. Kelly sought a set-off for the amount he was obligated to pay on the assigned note, arguing that his offer to return the defective machine constituted a rescission of the contract.

In September 1867, the case of Alice B. Smith v. Bartholomew Brown was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from an action filed by Bartholomew Brown against Alice B. Smith regarding goods sold and delivered. Brown claimed that he had presented the account to Smith multiple times and left it for her to review, during which she made no objections and repeatedly promised to make the payment. Smith, however, testified that she had not received all the goods listed on the account and contended that she owed significantly less ($585.65) than the claimed amount ($862.60). The conflict in testimonies between Brown and Smith represented the crux of the matter, with Brown supported by a disinterested witness.	The plaintiff, Bartholomew Brown, argued that Alice B. Smith failed to object to the account for the goods sold and had made promises to pay the full amount stated. Brown sought a judgment for the total amount claimed, which was $862.60, asserting that Smith's lack of objections and promises indicated her acknowledgment of the debt.	Alice B. Smith contested the claim by asserting that not all goods listed in the account were delivered to her. She argued that the correct amount owed was far less than what Brown claimed, specifically stating she owed only $585.65. Smith appealed for the court to reconsider the judgment, asserting that the evidence presented did not support Brown's claims in full.

In the case of Clifton H. Moore v. Sylvanus Shurtleff et al., heard by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 14, 1889, the dispute arises from a real estate transaction in DeWitt County, Illinois, involving lots 4 and 5 owned by Thomas B. Adkisson. The lots were encumbered by a trust deed of $458.27. Adkisson sold lot 5 to Andrew Hutchin on January 6, 1876, and subsequently, lot 4 to Clifton H. Moore on February 10, 1876. Hutchin then subdivided lot 5, selling parts to Sylvanus Shurtleff, P. H. Mills, and Jacob Yogel. In order to fulfill obligations under the trust deed, the part of lot 5 owned by Shurtleff was sold to satisfy debts amounting to $685.66, which Shurtleff later redeemed. He filed a bill for contribution, seeking to recoup costs associated with settling the trust deed. The circuit court ruled in favor of Shurtleff, ordering contributions from both Moore and Yogel. The case was appealed, focusing on how obligations were to be split between the parties involved in light of the trust deed encumbrance.	The plaintiff, Sylvanus Shurtleff, claimed entitlement to contribution for the costs incurred in settling the trust deed associated with the real estate. He argued that the circuit court was correct in ordering that both lots (4 and 5) contribute to the payment of the outstanding amount owed on the trust deed, and he sought to enforce this decree.	The defendant, Clifton H. Moore, contended that he should not be held liable for any portion of the debt until lot 4 had been found insufficient to cover the obligations. He argued that under the general rule of inverse order of alienation, his property should not be charged until the prior transfers of lot 5 had been exhausted, and he sought to avoid additional liabilities based on the existing agreements affecting the properties involved.

George T. Brown filed a legal case against John Malledy in December 1857 in Madison, Illinois. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court under the citation 19 Ill. 290. The core of the case arose from a situation where Brown took a voluntary non-suit in the lower court, which refers to a plaintiff's decision to withdraw their case, leaving the matter unresolved. The legal implications of this decision had significant bearings on the proceedings, as it meant that there was no longer an active controversy for the court to review or adjudicate.	George T. Brown's main argument revolved around the circumstances leading to his non-suit in lower court. He presumably believed that he had grounds for his case against John Malledy and sought to appeal the decision. However, upon taking a voluntary non-suit, he could not assert errors in the previous record.	John Malledy did not present specific counterarguments in the court's recorded opinion, as the focus of the judgment was primarily on the plaintiff's action to withdraw from the case. Consequently, Malledy's defense was implicit in the recognition that no appeal could be made following Brown's non-suit.

Eva Lawrence, acting as guardian, filed a case against the City of Chicago in September 1868. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court and stems from a prior case, "Wright v. The City of Chicago," suggesting a similar legal foundation. The judgement was presided over by Chief Justice Joseph E. Gaby of the Superior Court of Chicago. The specific details leading to the legal action by Lawrence are not provided, but they involve issues presumed to be related to the actions or policies of the City of Chicago that warranted legal scrutiny.	The plaintiff, Eva Lawrence, argued against the City of Chicago, seeking legal remedy under claims that mirror those in the prior case of Wright v. The City of Chicago. The precise details of Lawrence's legal requests or claims are not specified in the summary.	The City of Chicago, represented by attorney S. A. Irvin, likely raised defenses similar to those in the previous case of Wright v. The City of Chicago, challenging the claims made by Lawrence. However, specific arguments or requests from the defendant are not detailed in the provided information.

In the case of James K. Fisher v. Lillie G. Cook, which took place in 1887, the plaintiff, Lillie Gillette Cook, suffered personal injuries after falling into an elevator shaft of a building located on Michigan Avenue, Chicago, known as the Beaurivage. The incident occurred when Cook, alongside her family, was attempting to use the building's elevator. The elevator door was opened by an employee of the defendant, James K. Fisher, who was managing the elevator. Unbeknownst to Cook, the elevator was not at the ground floor, leading her to step through the opened door and fall into the shaft. The case commenced with Cook filing a declaration in 1879, explaining that Fisher, as the occupant of the building, had a duty to ensure the elevator door was safely managed. The matter went through various amendments and pleadings, particularly around the assertion that Fisher was not solely liable due to co-ownership with Archibald Fisher. Ultimately, a jury trial found in favor of Cook, awarding her damages of $3,000.	Lillie G. Cook claimed that James K. Fisher, the building's manager, was negligent in allowing the elevator doors to be inadequately guarded. She argued that the employee's action of opening the elevator door without the cab being present directly led to her accidental fall and injury. Cook sought damages for her injuries resulting from this negligence, asserting a legal duty on the part of the defendant to ensure the elevator's safe operation for the building's occupants.	James K. Fisher contended that he should not be held liable because the building's management was a shared responsibility with another co-owner, Archibald Fisher. He filed a plea in abatement claiming the non-joinder of the other owner, suggesting that both should be included in the lawsuit. However, this plea was not found to be a valid defense, and the court ultimately ruled against it, maintaining that Cook's claims were properly directed at Fisher alone.

In the case of Sarah Sevier v. Samuel L. Magguire et ux., which took place in September 1868, the legal dispute arose out of the Circuit Court of Woodford County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Sarah Sevier, the plaintiff, and Samuel L. Magguire along with his wife Harriet Gr. Magguire, the defendants. The background of the case involves a prior decree that subjected a tract of land, held in the name of Harriet Gr. Magguire, to the payment of a judgment owed to Sarah Sevier from Samuel L. Magguire. This prior decree was rendered by default and did not account for the homestead rights of Harriet Gr. Magguire. Consequently, both Samuel and Harriet filed a bill seeking to vacate the earlier decree citing obvious errors, such as the inappropriate inclusion of an unrelated judgment against Samuel favored by Edgerly, who was not a party to the initial suit. The original decree was fundamentally flawed because it failed to respect Harriet's homestead rights, and thus, they sought to enjoin the sale of the land.	Sarah Sevier claimed a right to enforce a judgment against Samuel L. Magguire, which resulted in a decree that her judgment would be satisfied through the sale of a property titled under Harriet Gr. Magguire. Sevier argued that the previous decree improperly included a judgment owed to Edgerly, who was not involved in the original proceedings, and contended that the decree ignored the homestead rights of Harriet and her children, which should exempt the land from sale.	Samuel L. Magguire and Harriet Gr. Magguire contested the original decree by arguing that it was flawed due to obvious errors, notably the inclusion of Edgerly’s judgment without his presence in the case. They maintained that the land in question was their homestead, which should not be sold to satisfy Sevier's judgment, contending that both the decree and the sale were invalid due to this lack of consideration for homestead rights.

In early 1882, located in Adams County, Illinois, Carl Prante, a carpenter, was employed to repair an ice house and brewery belonging to Frederick Schutte after they were partially destroyed by a fire on January 30, 1882. Following the repairs, there was a verbal agreement between Prante and Schutte regarding the rebuilding of the brewery, which was to be done at their joint expense. Schutte was to pay Prante $3,300 by June 1 and was to receive a deed entitling him to half of the property after the payment. However, the details of this agreement were not documented, leading to disagreements over the conditions. Prante performed work and provided materials based on this unformalized agreement, but when the time for payment arrived, Schutte did not fulfill his end. Consequently, Prante decided to sue Schutte for the labor and materials provided, leading to a trial that examined whether a valid contract existed and the specific terms agreed upon.	Carl Prante claimed that he completed work and provided materials for the repairs of the ice house and brewery, amounting to at least $1,086.50. He sought payment for these services, arguing that he had fulfilled his obligations as per their agreement. He maintained that the verbal agreement was valid and that he was entitled to compensation for the work done.	Frederick Schutte contended that the work performed by Prante was based on a special contract, which he argued had not been fully executed. Schutte claimed that the parties’ discussions about the terms were incomplete and unclear. He raised the issue of whether there had been mutual consent on the price to be paid and suggested that Prante had acquiesced to abandoning the agreement when he delayed action for nearly two years before filing the lawsuit.

Charles Carpenter v. Edward Burkhardt was a legal action that took place in 1885 in Cook County, Illinois. The case revolved around a contractual dispute regarding the construction of a stone-front building. The plaintiff, Edward Burkhardt, had performed work and supplied materials for the construction under a written contract, which specified that Carpenter was to pay Burkhardt following the approval of an architect's certificate. Burkhardt claimed to have completed the work according to the contract and was seeking payment. The defendant, Carpenter, argued that there were defects in the workmanship and colors of the stone, and he contested the necessity of the architect’s certificate, alleging issues related to the architect's dismissal before the project was completed. The case was presided over by Judge Sidney Smith, and after a trial, a jury found in favor of Burkhardt, awarding him $135.75. Carpenter appealed the decision.	The plaintiff, Edward Burkhardt, claimed he had fulfilled his contractual obligations by providing work and materials for the construction of a building. He argued that any failure to secure the architect's certificate was justified because the defendant had dismissed the architect during construction. Burkhardt requested the court to award him payment for the services and materials provided, totaling $135.75.	The defendant, Charles Carpenter, countered Burkhardt's claims by asserting that there were defects in the materials supplied and in the workmanship performed. He contended that Burkhardt was obligated to procure the architect's certificate before seeking payment and argued that since he did not secure this certificate, he was not liable for the payment. Carpenter requested the court to find in his favor, potentially allowing for a recoupment of damages due to alleged deficiencies.

John C. Birket filed a trespass lawsuit against Henry W. Williams in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision rendered on December 8, 1888. The case originated in Peoria County, Illinois, following an incident where Williams’ cattle trespassed onto Birket’s leased property, which he had been cultivating for nursery stock since March 1886. Birket claimed that Williams’ uncontained cattle damaged his nursery trees by eating them. The dispute centered around the adequacy of the fence separating their properties. Williams argued that the fence was not sufficient, thus absolving him of liability for the cattle’s actions. However, the court determined that under Illinois law, landowners must keep their cattle fenced in and be liable for any trespasses that occur, regardless of how the cattle escaped. The issue of damages was also contested, with Birket ultimately awarded $100 in compensation. The legal context included precedents establishing the responsibility of animal owners for their trespassing animals, drawing from both statutory and common law.	Birket's main argument was that Williams was liable for the damages his cattle caused to Birket's nursery trees. He claimed that since he had occupied the land and cultivated it for several years, he had the right to protect his investment. Birket sought financial compensation for the damage inflicted by Williams' cattle, which he quantified to be $100.	Williams contended that he should not be held liable for the damages because the fence separating their properties was not maintained to a sufficient standard. He argued that if the cattle escaped through a defective fence without any negligence on his part, he should be exempt from liability. Williams maintained that the law should allow for such defenses, challenging both the legal interpretations of liability and the sufficiency of the evidence provided by Birket.

In 1855, the General Assembly of Illinois incorporated The Joliet and Chicago Railroad Company, granting it the power to construct a railroad from Joliet to Chicago. This law allowed the company to enter and use private land for the railroad, provided they compensated landowners for damages. James A. Johnson, a non-resident landowner, had 60 feet of his property condemned for the railroad's use. In June 1858, he filed a trespass action against the railroad company, claiming that the company's entry onto his land was unlawful. The railroad defended itself by citing the special act under which it operated, which allowed for property condemnation without notice to absent landowners. The General Assembly had appointed commissioners to determine compensation, which was set at one dollar, a sum the railroad was ready to pay. The trial court overruled Johnson’s objections and held that the condemnation procedure followed by the railroad did not require notice to Johnson, leading to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Johnson argued that the condemnation of his land was invalid because the railroad did not provide him notice of the proceedings. He contended that the special act under which the railroad operated contradicted the Illinois Constitution, particularly regarding due process and the right to compensation for property taken. Johnson claimed that the lack of notice and the minimal compensation offered failed to meet the constitutional standards for taking private property for public use.	The Joliet and Chicago Railroad Company countered that the General Assembly's act granting them the power to condemn land was lawful and did not violate the Illinois Constitution. They argued that the law did not require notification for non-resident landowners like Johnson, and that the condemnation process was executed correctly, including the appointment of commissioners who assessed the damages. The company maintained that since they were willing to pay the assessed amount, they were not trespassers on Johnson's property.

In 1889, James W. Sykes was indicted in Cook County, Illinois, under the Warehouse Act for allegedly issuing fraudulent warehouse receipts without having the specified goods stored in his public warehouse. Sykes operated a warehouse in Chicago and was engaged in business as a warehouseman of class “C.” From February 1885 onward, he procured loans from Merchants’ Loan and Trust Company by providing them with warehouse receipts as collateral, which falsely represented that he was storing bags of timothy seed. However, at no point did he have these bags in his custody. The transactions involved issuance of receipts to the bank for goods he did not possess, and he may have intended these receipts to function as a mere formality for loans rather than legitimate warehouse documentation. The trial focused on whether Sykes issued these receipts with fraudulent intent. The jury found him guilty, but he contended that his intent and surrounding circumstances were improperly excluded from consideration during the trial.	The prosecution argued that Sykes illegally issued warehouse receipts under counts of the indictment that were specific to the Warehouse Act. They maintained that these receipts were false and fraudulent because no timothy seed was stored in his warehouse at any time. The state contended that the act of issuing false receipts represented a clear violation of the law and sought punishment under the statutory penalties established for such offenses.	Sykes's defense revolved around the argument that the issuance of these receipts was a misunderstood agreement with the bank; he claimed that they were intended as nominal security for loans rather than legitimate warehouse transactions. He asserted that the bank's officers were aware that no actual deposit was made and contended that evidence demonstrating his lack of fraudulent intent was improperly excluded from the trial. Sykes argued that the law was misapplied, asserting that his actions did not fulfill the criteria for criminal culpability under the Warehouse Act.

In 1873, David Coey entered into a written contract with Lavina A. Herrick, who was the guardian of certain minors, to construct a block of buildings in Chicago, with the contract requiring completion by December 15 of that year for a total of $50,750. Coey then contracted with George Lehman for mason work and plastering for the same buildings, agreeing to a payment of $13,750. Under this contract, payments were to be made based on certificates issued by L.B. Dixon, the architect supervising the project. Despite the work being partially completed, Lehman had received certificates for 85% of the payment but no certificate for the final 15% was obtained because the architect did not consider the work satisfactory. Consequently, Coey initiated legal action seeking payment for the extra work and materials provided. The case was tried without a jury, and the court initially ruled in favor of Coey for $1,132.22.	The plaintiff, David Coey, claimed that he was entitled to payment for the extra work and materials supplied for the masonry and plastering on the buildings. He argued that even if the architect had not formally accepted the work, payments should be made for the work performed and the materials furnished. He requested the court enforce the payment stipulated in the contract, asserting a balance due under the agreement.	The defendant, George Lehman, contended that the judgment should not stand because Coey had failed to comply with the contract's requirement of obtaining the architect's acceptance and necessary certification before pursuing a claim for payment. He argued that the contract expressly mandated that no payments were due until the architect had certified the completion and acceptability of the work, a condition that was not met. Lehman maintained that the terms of the contract must be enforced strictly according to their language.

On September 25, 1857, James Boggs, George Boggs, and Bedmond Cotter executed a mortgage on property in Chicago, Cook County, Illinois to secure four promissory notes, each for $1,400, with maturities ranging from one to four years. George and James Boggs later became the sole owners of the equity of redemption after Cotter transferred his interest. By September 25, 1861, the last note was due, but it remained unpaid along with part of the third note. Consequently, Elisha W. Willard, the assignee of the notes and mortgage, sold the property to George Smith on November 5, 1861, for $300 through a power of sale stipulated in the mortgage. Willard assumed possession and paid taxes on the property after the sale. George Boggs, who had left for New Orleans in May 1860, contested the sale in a chancery suit on October 26, 1868, claiming the sale was invalid due to his absence during the Civil War, arguing that his inability to pay due to the war suspended the contract. Lower court proceedings led to a pro forma decree in favor of Boggs, prompting the defendants to appeal.	George Boggs, the plaintiff, claimed that the sale of the property was void due to his absence in a territory occupied by Confederate forces during the Civil War. He argued that this situation suspended the contract of indebtedness, as well as the power of sale, making the recorded sale unauthorized. His main legal request was to redeem his half of the property, asserting that the sale was invalid because he was cut off from communication with Willard and unable to pay the debt.	The defendants, represented by Willard, argued that the sale and conveyance were conducted in strict accordance with the mortgage's power of sale and were valid despite George Boggs' absence. They contended that the claims made by Boggs had no legal standing as the laws of war did not suspend the collection of debts or the right to enforce contracts in this situation. They asserted that the sale was bona fide, conducted with the required notice, and that the lack of knowledge about Boggs’s whereabouts did not impose any obligation on them to delay the sale.

The case "Alfred A. Wright v. Gabriel K. Wright et al." took place in Illinois and was decided on March 13, 1889. The key individuals involved included Alfred A. Wright, the plaintiff, and Gabriel K. Wright along with others as defendants. The legal issue arose from allegations of libel made by Alfred A. Wright against the defendants. The plaintiff contended that the defendants had made defamatory statements, but the defendants claimed that their communication was privileged. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court after an initial ruling in the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Egbert Jamieson.	Alfred A. Wright claimed that the defendants committed libel against him through their statements. He argued that the defendants had misused the privilege of communication to express malice and that such use of privilege justified the need for the jury to consider his case. He sought a judgment that would recognize the wrongful nature of the defendants' actions and appropriate remedies for the harm done.	The defendants, represented by M. L. Rastree, argued that their statements were protected by the defense of privilege. They contended that the communication in question was made in a context that warranted such protection and denied the claim of malice, which, in their view, would negate liability for any alleged defamatory remarks.

In 1886, Bela M. Stoddard and David Filgur were involved in a legal dispute in Woodford County, Illinois, regarding water drainage rights on their adjoining properties. Stoddard owned the southeast quarter of Section Two in Minonk Township, while Filgur owned the southwest quarter. The conflict arose when a significant amount of surface water from Stoddard’s land flowed over Filgur’s land. In 1875, Filgur dug an open ditch on his land to accommodate this water. Stoddard later constructed a series of tile drains that directed water into this ditch. In 1885, Filgur initiated efforts to fill in the open ditch to the level of his property, prompting Stoddard to file a bill in court seeking an injunction to prevent this action. The underlying legal questions centered on the rights of the dominant (Stoddard) and servient (Filgur) estate owners, specifically regarding any license to drain water and the ability to stop Filgur from filling the ditch.	Stoddard, the plaintiff, argued that he held a right to drain surface water from his property into the ditch on Filgur’s land and claimed he had obtained a parol license to do so. He sought a legal injunction to prevent Filgur from filling up the ditch, asserting that the filling of the ditch would harm his property by altering the natural flow of water.	Filgur, the defendant, contended that Stoddard had no legal right to drain water into the ditch without express permission, as such acts could unjustly burden his property. He argued that even if there was an implied or verbal license, it was revocable, and he was entitled to fill the ditch at his discretion. Filgur maintained that the law supports his right to close the ditch since it was built for his benefit and could be changed without the consent of the adjoining landowner.

Pulaski Scovil v. Mary A. Connell was a legal case decided in January 1868 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from Mason County, where Pulaski Scovil filed an action of covenant against Mary A. Connell. The action sought to challenge a judgment rendered in favor of Connell by the Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Charles Turner. The central issue of the case revolved around the interpretation of the 1861 act aimed at protecting married women's separate property rights, specifically whether a married woman could convey real estate solely in her name, without her husband's involvement. The court's inquiry hinged on precedents regarding the requirements for a married woman to effectuate real estate transactions and the laws surrounding those transactions at the time.	Pulaski Scovil, the plaintiff, argued that under the 1861 act intended to protect married women in managing their separate property, Mary A. Connell should have been able to convey her real estate without needing her husband's consent or joinder. Scovil sought to reverse the previous judgment in favor of Connell, asserting that the language of the act granted women the rights necessary to conduct real estate transactions independently.	Mary A. Connell, the defendant, contended that the 1861 act did not permit a married woman to convey her real estate without her husband's participation. Connell's defense rested on the precedent established in the case of Cole v. Van Riper, which asserted that the husband must join in the conveyance for the deed to be valid. As such, the defendant requested the court to affirm the lower court’s judgment in her favor.

In 1870, an accident occurred in Chicago involving Edward C. Murray and Mason, large tobacco manufacturers occupying the buildings at 174 and 176 North Water Street. The two structures were connected via archways, creating a unified workspace. On April 15, 1869, the elevator was in use, transporting hogsheads of tobacco from the first to the fourth floor. During this time, a cooper named McLean, who often supplied kegs to the defendants, was found injured in the cellar beneath the elevator hatchway. Witnesses indicated he fell through the hatchway while the elevator was operational. After being discovered, he claimed not to know how he ended up there and received medical attention but died weeks later. His widow filed a lawsuit against Murray and Mason for damages, alleging negligence leading to her husband's death. The trial jury awarded her $5,000, which prompted the defendants to seek a new trial, arguing that the verdict was unsupported by the evidence.	The plaintiff, Jane McLean, as administratrix of her late husband's estate, claimed that the defendants were negligent in maintaining safety standards around the elevator hatchway, which led to her husband's fatal injury. She argued that the defendants failed to ensure the safety of individuals on their premises, particularly given the elevator's operation while the hatchway was unguarded. She sought damages for the wrongful death of her husband, asserting that the conditions contributed directly to the accident.	The defendants, Murray and Mason, contended that there was no culpable neglect on their part. They pointed out that the hatchway was located away from where non-employees would typically be found and was surrounded by safety rails when the elevator was not in use. They argued that the deceased had no legitimate business near the hatchway and that he had entered the area without a cause. The defendants requested the verdict to be overturned, stating that the evidence did not demonstrate their negligence and that they had taken reasonable safety precautions.

Phillip Byrne (the appellant) filed a legal case against Dickinson B. Morehouse and others (the appellees) concerning a dispute over property rights in Galena, Illinois. The core of the case revolves around a deed of partition executed on May 29, 1838, by McNulty, Smith, and Nagle, which addressed ownership rights to two lots previously certified for pre-emption by a government commission. The lots were entered by McNulty and Smith on July 26, 1837. Following a series of legal judgments, Byrne obtained rights to the property after redeeming Nagle's interest from a judgment filed by Wm. Navin. The main legal question was whether Nagle acquired a one-half or one-fourth interest in the property according to the terms of the partition deed. The trial primarily examined the legal implications of the deed and the rights of the involved parties, with conclusions showing that McNulty and Smith had retained the legal title, thus affecting Nagle's equitable rights.	The plaintiff, Phillip Byrne, claimed that he was entitled to an undivided half of lot No. 8 based on prior legal judgments and his right to redeem Nagle's interest in the property. He argued that the court erred in determining his interest as only one-fourth, rather than one-half of the property. Byrne sought a new trial and requested that the court address the misinterpretation of the partition deed's implications regarding property ownership.	The defendants contended that the partition deed and the legal title had established the ownership rights between the parties involved. They argued that the findings of the lower court were correct in determining that Nagle's interest was only one-fourth of the property, and they supported their claims based on the recitals within the deed, which they maintained were binding and conclusive. They effectively requested the court to uphold the original ruling regarding property interests as stated in the deed of partition.

The case "The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company v. The People ex rel. The City of Bloomington" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1874. It stems from proceedings in the Circuit Court of McLean County, presided over by Judge Thomas P. Tipton. The case involves a dispute between the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company (the appellant) and the City of Bloomington, represented by the People ex rel. The City. The critical issue was the issuance of a peremptory writ of mandamus that the lower court had awarded after the Illinois Supreme Court directed it to do so during a prior session in January 1873. The court determined that the circuit court correctly followed its prior ruling without the introduction of new evidence, leading to the current appeal regarding the enforcement of that writ.	The City of Bloomington, as the plaintiff, claims that the Railroad Company is obligated to comply with the issuance of a peremptory writ of mandamus as determined by the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff argues that the previous ruling of the court necessitates that the Railroad Company fulfill its legal obligations as outlined in that decision, thereby seeking enforcement of the writ.	The defendant, Chicago and Alton Railroad Company, contends that the judgment awarding the writ of mandamus by the circuit court should not be reviewed or overturned, as it merely followed the Illinois Supreme Court’s earlier directive. The appellant does not claim that any new evidence was introduced after the remand; rather, their position is that the court acted correctly in affirming the previous opinion.

On May 21, 1886, in Warren County, Illinois, George W. Brent (the appellee) obtained a judgment against Kenner Brent (the appellant) for the sum of $125 and associated costs, totaling $205.90. At the time of this judgment, Kenner Brent was indebted to his attorneys, Davidson and Norcross, who were owed legal fees surpassing the judgment amount. On July 24, 1886, Davidson and Norcross assigned the judgment to themselves and initiated collection actions through the Warren County Sheriff. Following this, Kenner Brent accused the Sheriff of misapplying the funds by not allowing him to set off multiple outstanding judgments he had against Kenner Brent against the single judgment owed to Davidson and Norcross. The appellant sought an order allowing the set-off during the September 1886 court term. On March 5, 1887, the court ruled in favor of Davidson and Norcross, which led Kenner Brent to appeal the decision, arguing that he should be allowed to offset his debts before the plaintiff's attorneys received payment.	The plaintiff, Davidson and Norcross, argued that they had a rightful claim to the proceeds from the judgment awarded to Brent as it was assigned to them before Kenner's request to set-off his judgments. They maintained that the set-off should not apply due to specific statutory exceptions that prioritized attorneys' claims for fees over the debtor's judgments against the creditor.	The defendant, Kenner Brent, contended that he had the right to offset his judgments against the amount owed to Davidson and Norcross. He claimed that the statutes allowed for such a set-off between the parties and sought to have the court recognize his independent judgments as valid against the attorneys' claim.

In the case of The Board of Supervisors of Livingston County v. William Henneberry, which took place in 1866 in Livingston County, Illinois, William Henneberry sought specific performance of a contract regarding the purchase of swamp land. Henneberry had paid $520 for the land and received a certificate of purchase, contingent upon fulfilling certain conditions. He alleged that he had met all obligations but had not received the deed to the property, as the county refused to issue it. The county's defense admitted the purchase but contested Henneberry's compliance with the contract's stipulations, including payment, necessary drainage, and improvements to the land. The swamp land commissioner testified that Henneberry had offered the purchase money and demanded a deed but declined to issue one due to uncertainty over competing claims to the property. The case was subsequently heard in the Livingston Circuit Court, where the court ruled in favor of Henneberry.	Henneberry's primary argument was that he had fulfilled all conditions as outlined in the contract for the purchase of swamp land from the county. He sought a court order for specific performance demanding the county to deliver the deed to the land for which he had already paid.	The Board of Supervisors contended that Henneberry had not paid the full purchase price or met other contractual conditions, such as performing necessary drainage and improvements on the land. They argued that these conditions were prerequisites for Henneberry to receive the deed and insisted that he had failed to comply with them.

The case "James S. Ward et al. v. Soloman Ware et al.; The Same v. William Sherrick" was tried in the Illinois Appellate Court and pertains to a legal dispute that occurred in Cumberland County, Illinois, with the final judgment rendered on May 25, 1888. Key individuals involved in the case include the plaintiffs James S. Ward along with unknown co-plaintiffs, and the defendants Soloman Ware and William Sherrick. The case proceeded without a jury, as both parties waived their right to one. The court considered the matter based on appeals from judgments rendered earlier. There were no objections raised concerning the judgments, and the record indicated that motions for a new trial were made and subsequently overruled. However, the details of these motions and any exceptions taken by the parties were not duly preserved in the bill of exceptions presented to the court. This lack of preserved exceptions meant that the court could not consider the errors claimed by the appellants.	The plaintiffs, represented by attorneys George W. Fithiak and W. S. Everhart, pressed their case without providing explicit details in the summary provided. Their main argument appears to have revolved around the trial court's denial of their motions for a new trial, contending that the procedural issues hinged upon how these motions were documented in the bill of exceptions. They likely sought a reversal of the trial court's judgments or a new trial based on the errors alleged.	The defendants, Soloman Ware and William Sherrick, were represented by attorneys P. A. Brady and L. M. Brewer. Their defense did not specifically counter the plaintiffs' claims in detail as noted in the summary. Instead, they maintained that the trial court's process and judgments were appropriate as the plaintiffs failed to preserve necessary exceptions in the bill of exceptions. The defense focused on the procedural validity of the trial court's rulings and argued that the plaintiffs could not assign error due to their failure to record any exceptions at the time of the trial.

The case "The City of Chicago v. Margaret Murphy" was adjudicated in September 1876 in Illinois, specifically within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. The case stems from an incident where the plaintiff, Margaret Murphy, sustained injuries due to a defect in a sidewalk. While walking along a sidewalk made of wooden planks, a man in front of her stepped on a loose plank, causing it to flip and strike her leg below the knee. This incident resulted in a painful injury, for which Murphy sought damages. The jury determined that the City of Chicago was liable, awarding her $750 in damages. However, the critical question in the case was whether the city was aware or should have been aware of the loose plank, as this would affect their liability for the injuries sustained by the plaintiff.	Margaret Murphy claimed that the City of Chicago was negligent by failing to maintain the sidewalk in a safe condition, which directly led to her injury. She argued that the city should have known about the loose plank due to previous incidents or complaints. Her legal request was for compensation for the injury caused by the defect in the sidewalk, which she felt was the city’s responsibility to repair and monitor.	The City of Chicago, represented by Mr. Egbert Jamieson, contended that it had no prior notice of the loose plank and therefore could not be held liable for the injuries suffered by Murphy. The defense asserted that reasonable diligence did not require the city to anticipate the defect, as there were no records or complaints indicating that the plank was loose before the incident. They maintained that since the city authorities were unaware of the condition that caused the injury, they should not be held responsible.

John C. Cover filed a legal action against William Armstrong in 1872 in the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a suit in attachment. The case arose from the allegation that Armstrong had departed from Illinois with the intention of removing his assets and causing harm to Cover. Cover, as plaintiff, contended that Armstrong was a non-resident, which justified the issuance of an attachment writ against him. In response, Armstrong filed a plea in abatement, asserting that he had not left the state with the intent to remove his property nor was he a non-resident. He argued that he was temporarily out of state for business and had sufficient assets within Knox County to cover his debts. The presiding judge at the Circuit Court in Knox County, Hon. Arthur A. Smith, handled the proceedings. The case turned on whether Armstrong’s plea sufficiently rebutted the allegations made by Cover regarding his residency and intentions at the time the writ of attachment was filed.	The plaintiff, John C. Cover, claimed that William Armstrong had left Illinois to evade his creditors and remove his property out of state. Cover sought the attachment of Armstrong's assets to protect his financial interests, asserting that Armstrong was a non-resident when the writ was issued. Cover filed a special demurrer against Armstrong’s plea, arguing that it failed to adequately address all allegations in his affidavit and was insufficient in form.	The defendant, William Armstrong, defended himself by asserting that he was not a non-resident and had not the intention of permanently leaving Illinois. He argued that he was only temporarily away for business purposes and that he maintained sufficient real and personal property in Knox County, which could cover any debts owed. Armstrong contended that Cover's claims were unfounded and requested that the court dismiss the attachment writ against him.

The case "Chicago, Milwaukee & St Paul Railway Company v. Sophia Wilson" originated from a tragic accident that occurred on August 4, 1887, in Chicago, Illinois. The incident involved Sophia Wilson, a married woman carrying her one-year-old baby and leading her three-year-old son, who attempted to cross Wood Street, which intersects with eleven railway tracks at a level grade. As Sophia waited for a passenger train on the north main track to pass, she stepped onto the south main track, unbeknownst that a locomotive was backing towards her at a speed of approximately six miles per hour. The train struck her and her children, resulting in severe injuries to Sophia and the death of both children. A flagman present was obscured from view, providing no warning of the impending danger. The railway company was not the owner of these tracks, but operated on the south main tracks where the accident occurred. The case is composed of multiple claims: one from Sophia for her injuries and separate claims from the administrator of her deceased children for damages. The jury ruled against the railway company, awarding damages of $5,000 to Sophia, $2,000 for the younger child, and $1,941.66 for the elder child.	Sophia Wilson claimed damages for her personal injuries sustained in the accident, asserting that the railway company was negligent in failing to provide adequate warning of the approaching locomotive. Additionally, the administrator of her children's estate sought compensation for the wrongful death of both children, arguing that the railway's negligence directly led to their deaths.	The Chicago, Milwaukee & St Paul Railway Company contended that there was no negligence on their part and argued that the verdicts for damages were excessive. They maintained that the presence of the tracks should have served as sufficient warning for Sophia Wilson and that the jury misjudged both the issues of negligence and due care.

Robert Scott v. The Town of New Boston pertains to a legal dispute that occurred in New Boston, Illinois, with the case judgment issued on February 29, 1888. The case arose when the Town of New Boston took legal action against Robert Scott for allegedly obstructing a public road known as the Hew Boston and Millersburg road, particularly at the Winters Creek crossing on Scott's property. The dispute began when the Highway Commissioners ordered Scott to remove various obstructions he had placed, including fences along the roadway and stakes in the creek, which allegedly undermined the bridge and damaged the surrounding road. The case passed through the Justice's court, where Scott was found liable for $100 and costs. Upon appealing, the verdict against him was reduced to $50 and costs in the Mercer Circuit Court. The core issue was whether Scott’s modifications to the land constituted a legal obstruction to the public highway, leading to the legal interpretation of rights concerning landowners adjoining public roads.	The Town of New Boston claimed that Robert Scott obstructed a public highway by building fences and placing structures that blocked the road and drained water in a manner that damaged the road and bridge. They argued that these actions violated Section 71 of the road law, which prohibits harming or obstructing public roads. The Town sought damages and penalties claimed under this section, which could amount to a fine for each day that the obstruction remained after being ordered to be removed.	Robert Scott defended against the accusations by arguing that he had the right to modify his property and that his fence and structures did not actually obstruct the road. He claimed that the section of the road in question was not actively used, and therefore, he was not responsible for an obstruction as defined by the law. Scott contended that if the road was established solely by user or prescription, the layout and modifications did not violate legal statutes, nor did it impact public travel in a meaningful way.

In December 1832, in Peoria, Illinois, the case of Mary Clifton v. John L. Bogardus unfolded in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated after a judgment in favor of Bogardus against Moses Clifton resulted in an execution being levied on property that Mary Clifton claimed belonged to her. During the trial concerning the rightful ownership of the property, Moses Clifton was called as a witness to help support Mary Clifton's claim. However, the Circuit Court rejected his testimony on the grounds that he was the debtor involved in the execution, which Mary Clifton argued was an error. The plaintiff maintained that there were no applicable disqualifications for Moses Clifton's testimony since the interest that could disqualify a witness must favor the party calling them, which was not the case here. The core issue revolved around whether the court was incorrect in disallowing his testimony, which was crucial for Mary Clifton's claim to the property.	Mary Clifton, the plaintiff, argued that the Circuit Court erred by rejecting Moses Clifton's testimony in the trial regarding the rightful ownership of the property. She contended that the witness's status as a debtor did not inherently disqualify him from testifying, as his interest did not favor the party producing him. Consequently, she sought the reversal of the prior judgment made against her.	John L. Bogardus, the defendant, defended the court's decision to disallow the testimony of Moses Clifton, asserting that as the debtor, he was disqualified from providing evidence that might undermine the basis of the execution. The defendant sought to uphold the judgment of the Circuit Court that ruled in his favor, maintaining that the trial adhered to legal principles concerning witness qualifications.

On January 21, 1890, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with a legal dispute involving Alexander J. McDonald, president of the Circulating Boiler Company, and Samuel S. Chisholm. The case arose from a contract signed on December 16, 1886, wherein Chisholm agreed to lend the Circulating Boiler Company a sum of $1,200 to construct a water tube boiler. The contract stipulated that McDonald and the company would secure the loan with a promissory note and a warrant for judgment. Chisholm advanced funds, but as he continued to do so, it was recognized that an additional $600 was required to finish the project. On January 11, 1887, while McDonald was bedridden, he allegedly authorized Chisholm to sign a $600 note on his behalf. Subsequently, judgment by confession was entered on both the $600 and the original $1,200 notes for the amounts owed. However, after the judgment was rendered, the boiler turned out to be defective. The plaintiffs sought to vacate the judgments against them and prevent the sale of certain patents related to the boiler design. The case was initially vacated in the Superior Court but was later reversed at the Appellate Court.	The plaintiffs, McDonald and the Circulating Boiler Company, argued that the confessions of judgment should be set aside. They contended that the notes were not properly executed since the corporate name was missing on the $1,200 note at the time of its original issuance, and McDonald claimed he did not authorize the signature used on the $600 note. They sought to have the judgments against them vacated and prevent the sale of patents associated with their invention.	The defendant, Chisholm, maintained that the notes were valid and binding, asserting that McDonald had the authority to execute them on behalf of the Circulating Boiler Company. Chisholm argued that the issuance of the judgments was justified as he had incurred expenses exceeding the judgments in furtherance of completing the boiler. He contended that the execution of the notes, including the power of attorney, was lawful and established a binding obligation on the corporation.

The case of Lawrence Looby et al. v. William D. Austin et al. took place in Menard County, Illinois, with a final decision rendered on February 25, 1886. The suit was initiated by Lawrence Looby and others against William D. Austin, the supervisor of roads, and the county commissioners of Menard County. The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants unlawfully destroyed their property by tearing down a fence, which subsequently caused destruction to their crops. The defendants contended that the fence was removed to establish a public and private road as authorized by the county commissioners. The plaintiffs argued that the necessary legal procedures were not properly followed and contested the validity of the defendants' claims concerning the establishment of the road and the authority claimed by the county commissioners.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants, by unlawfully removing their fence, committed trespass that resulted in the destruction of their crops. They asserted that the defendants failed to establish the proper jurisdiction for the road and questioned the legality of the action taken by the county commissioners.	The defendants maintained that the removal of the fence was justified because it was part of the establishment of a public and private road, authorized by the county commissioners. They argued that the original petition for the road gave them the necessary jurisdiction, and the record confirming the road's establishment should stand as sufficient evidence of their authority to act.

In this case, "Chicago & Alton R. R. Co. v. Benjamin C. Few," the incident occurred on February 1, 1883, at the railroad company's yard in Boadhouse, Illinois. The key individual involved was Benjamin C. Few, an employee of the railroad, who was working as a switchman when he sustained a serious injury. Few alleged that the railroad company failed to fulfill its duty to ensure safe working conditions, specifically by not blocking or wedging the frogs in the tracks. As a result, Few caught his foot in one of the frogs and was thrown onto the track, where a flat car wheel crushed his left arm, necessitating amputation. In response to Few’s lawsuit for damages due to negligence, the trial court ruled in favor of Few. The railroad company appealed the decision, raising objections regarding the admission of certain evidence and the overall fairness of the trial.	The plaintiff, Benjamin C. Few, claimed that the railroad company was negligent in its duty to provide a safe working environment. He argued that the company failed to block the frogs in the yard's tracks properly, which caused his injury when he caught his foot in one. He also cited negligence in the use of a defective automatic brake as a contributing factor to his injury. Few sought damages for the injuries he sustained due to the company’s negligence.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company contended that it was not negligent in its duties. They argued that the absence of wooden blocks was not a failure of duty, as the plaintiff had not proven that blocking the frogs would have been safe or necessary, nor that such practices were required by state law. The company also claimed that the evidence presented did not sufficiently establish that Few's injury was directly caused by the alleged negligence concerning the automatic brake or the frogs. Furthermore, they challenged the trial court's admission of evidence regarding Few's dependents, arguing it unfairly influenced the jury and led to an unjust verdict.

The case "Burton M. Ford, impleaded, etc., v. Charles H. Beckwith" was heard in September 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Erastus S. Williams. The primary individuals involved were Burton M. Ford and Charles H. Beckwith. The case arose from a scire facias proceeding meant to revive a judgment that had been rendered against Beckwith, which was categorized as nil dicit (meaning he did not contest the declaration). Beckwith contended that he had filed a plea against the declaration, which an attorney later withdrew without proper authority. As a result, judgment was entered against him. Ford pursued the revival of this judgment, leading Beckwith to challenge the propriety of the actions taken by the attorney, asserting that he was not properly notified of the judgment withdrawn.	Ford's main argument was that the judgment against Beckwith should be revived, as Beckwith had previously entered an unchallenged plea. Ford argued that Beckwith's actions, including his failure to challenge the attorney's withdrawal of the plea or to seek the judgment's dismissal in a timely manner, demonstrated his acquiescence to the judgment rendered against him.	Beckwith's defense rested on the assertion that his plea was improperly withdrawn by an attorney who lacked the authority to do so, which led to an unjust judgment entered against him. He claimed that his original plea should have been properly considered and that the judgment he faced was not valid due to procedural misconduct. Beckwith sought to have the court set aside the judgment against him based on these grounds.

Sarah Wolf filed a case against F.W. Michaelis in 1888, pertaining to a mechanic's lien in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a construction contract, which stipulated that Michaelis was to pay Wolf $5,450 for work and materials, to be paid in six installments, contingent on receiving certificates from the architect, Edward G. Elleock, confirming that the work met the agreed standards. Wolf claimed that work was completed and sought payment, but Michaelis contended that Wolf failed to secure the necessary certificates for the installments due. The lack of these certificates led to the legal contest over the validity of the mechanic's lien Wolf placed on the property. The central issue in the case was whether Wolf could maintain the lien without the required evidence from the architect regarding the work's compliance with the contract specifications.	Sarah Wolf argued that she was entitled to payment for work completed under the contract and sought a mechanic's lien for $1,450. She asserted that the work had been performed satisfactorily, despite the failure to obtain the architect's certificates, and consequently that Michaelis owed the payments as specified in their agreement.	F.W. Michaelis defended against the lien by asserting that Wolf did not obtain the architect's certificates required by the contract for the payment installments. He contended that without such certificates, the claim for payment was not valid, arguing that the stipulation in the contract about certification was non-negotiable and essential for any recovery.

In January 1873, the case of Andrew B. McConnell v. William T. Scott was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a dispute over a chattel mortgage. The events took place in Sangamon County, Illinois. The defendant in error, William T. Scott, had allowed N. J. Shropshire to occupy his farm, with Shropshire becoming indebted to Scott for unpaid rent. On January 5, 1871, Shropshire executed a chattel mortgage to secure the payment of his debts, including both past and future rent, although specific amounts were not designated. When Shropshire failed to pay the rent by the agreed date, Scott took possession of the property and sold it, having properly executed the mortgage transaction. However, Andrew B. McConnell subsequently levied an execution against Shropshire's goods, claiming a right to the mortgaged property. This legal action led to the dispute over the validity and execution of the chattel mortgage and the rights of the parties involved.	McConnell, the plaintiff in error, argued that the chattel mortgage was void because it did not specify the amount owed. Furthermore, he contended that Scott did not have the right to take possession of the mortgaged property until the rent for the year 1871 became due. He claimed that the notice of the sale was insufficient and requested that the court reverse the previous judgment against him.	Scott, the defendant in error, contended that the mortgage was valid, as it was given to secure bona fide debts for rent, even though the amounts were unadjusted. He argued that once the mortgagor failed to pay on the due date, he had the right to take possession of the property and sell it to satisfy the debt. Scott maintained that any procedural issues, such as insufficient notice, did not invalidate the sale and that McConnell had no standing to complain as the debts had not been paid.

In September 1874, a legal dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, between Daniel D. Schrœder and Joel D. Harvey, the assignee for Franklin Bank. This case stemmed from a claim for money had and received concerning twelve dividend warrants that were drawn by Thomas Buckley, the assignee in bankruptcy of the Home Fire Insurance Company. The warrants were treated like bank checks and were made out to various creditors of the bankrupt company. Schrœder cashed these warrants, which were drawn on the Mechanics’ Bank and subsequently deposited them with Franklin Bank. However, the named payees on the warrants were discovered to have forged signatures. When the forgeries were identified, the Mechanics’ Bank credited Buckley, returned the warrants to Franklin Bank, which then sued Schrœder for the amount paid on the warrants. The suit resulted in a judgment in favor of the Franklin Bank. Schrœder appealed the judgment claiming insufficient proof of forgery and alleging negligence on the part of the bank for failing to notify him promptly regarding the forgeries.	The plaintiff, represented by the Franklin Bank, contended that the payees' names on the dividend warrants were forged. They sought to recover the funds that had been paid to Schrœder upon the presentation of these forged warrants, totaling $721.05, insisting that Schrœder should be liable for the amount received as the transactions were based on fraudulent conduct.	Schrœder defended against the claims by arguing that there was inadequate evidence to prove that the payees' names were actually forgeries, except for three warrants. He also asserted that the Franklin Bank had been negligent in failing to notify him of the forgeries almost immediately after their discovery, suggesting that this negligence absolved him of liability for the funds he had received.

The case, Asa Knoles et al., Plaintiffs in Error, v. Parthena W. Hill, Administratrix, etc., Defendant in Error, was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1861. It originated in the probate court of Menard County, Illinois, and was subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court. The dispute centered around a promissory note for twelve hundred dollars, which was signed by the plaintiffs and stipulated an interest rate of ten percent. However, there was an additional memorandum on the same document stating “when due to draw fifteen per cent,” but this was placed below the signatures and not formally part of the note itself. The case questioned the validity of this memorandum and its impact on the enforcement of the note. The lower court had ruled in favor of the plaintiff, and the matter was brought to the higher court for reassessment.	The plaintiffs contended that the promissory note was valid and enforceable at the specified interest rate of ten percent. They argued that the additional memorandum regarding a fifteen percent rate was irrelevant and did not form part of the contractual agreement. Their primary request was for the court to uphold the judgment in their favor regarding the collection of interest at the established rate.	The defendant, represented by Parthena W. Hill as administratrix, maintained that the presence of the memorandum suggested an intention to charge a higher interest rate. The defense argued that this notation should be considered part of the contractual obligation, potentially raising the permissible interest above the ten percent stated in the note. They disputed the lower court's decision and sought to dismiss the claim or adjust the interest rate based on the memorandum.

In September 1871, the legal case of Asa White v. Moses Robinson was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over an arbitration award concerning matters submitted to three arbitrators, with the award signed by two arbitrators and a third umpire. The key issue in the case was the testimony of an absent witness who was sick; this witness's statement was recorded in writing by two arbitrators and presented for consideration. The opposing counsel did not object to this procedure during the arbitration process, and the court later ruled that the recording and presentation of the sick witness's statement did not invalidate the award. The absence of objection or evidence of fraud or misconduct led to the conclusion that the procedural irregularity was permissible, underscoring an evolved understanding of arbitration and its requirements.	The plaintiff, Asa White, argued that the arbitration award was valid and binding despite the absence of one arbitrator during the witness examination. White claimed that all parties involved, including their counsel, consented to the process by which the absent witness's testimony was handled. Thus, he requested that the court uphold the award as legitimate and enforceable, asserting that there was no harm or prejudice inflicted by the procedure followed.	The defendant, Moses Robinson, contended that the arbitration award should be set aside due to the procedural irregularity, specifically the absence of one arbitrator during the witness's testimony. Robinson's defense emphasized that this violation of protocol undermined the integrity of the arbitration process. However, the defendant ultimately argued based on a technicality, asserting that strict adherence to arbitration rules was necessary to protect the rights of all parties involved.

In 1865, in McDonough County, Illinois, Mary White was embroiled in a legal dispute over property ownership with Michael B. Clark and Martin I. Clark. The case arose from an action of ejectment brought against Mary White for possession of a three-acre homestead that had been owned by her husband, Thomas White, since 1855. Thomas conveyed the property to Stephen A. White in 1857 without Mary’s consent, as she did not join in the deed and thus retained her homestead rights. Following Thomas's abandonment of Mary in August 1860, she remained in occupation of the homestead. The plaintiffs presented evidence of a judgment against Thomas White and others, claiming to have purchased the property after a sale under execution. Mary maintained her claim over the property due to her continuous occupancy and assertion of homestead rights, supported by prior judicial decisions that protected such occupancy against the husband's unilateral actions.	The plaintiffs, Michael B. Clark and Martin I. Clark, argued that they were lawful purchasers of the property following a court judgment delivered against Thomas White and others, which justified their claim to ownership. They contended that the sale of the homestead was valid despite Mary's claims of occupancy and homestead rights since they had obtained possession through the execution of a judgment.	Mary White, the defendant, asserted her right to the homestead, arguing that her husband failed to legally transfer his ownership rights since she did not consent to the conveyance. She emphasized her continuous occupancy of the property as a family homestead, coupled with legal precedents indicating that a wife retains her homestead rights even if her husband abandons her.
