Mary argued that the plaintiffs did not provide sufficient evidence that their debt, which led to the property sale, fell within exceptions to the protections offered by the homestead law.

Peleg Matteson and W. W. Porter, acting as plaintiffs in error, were involved in a legal dispute with Aaron Kellogg and Hubbard Kellogg, the defendants in error, regarding a fiduciary debt and the proceeds from a financial transaction that occurred on May 19, 1836. On that date, George H. Wright, of Warren County, Illinois, received $400 from Sylvester Blish on behalf of Kellogg and his associates for the purpose of acquiring a quarter section of timber land in Vernon, Connecticut. However, Wright filed for bankruptcy on March 22, 1842, and was discharged from his debts later that year. Following his intestate death, Matteson and Porter filed a claim against Wright's estate for the funds, which had not been earmarked for any liability under the bankruptcy discharge. The county court allowed their claim, which subsequently led to an appeal by the administrators of Wright’s estate to the circuit court of Warren County, resulting in a judgment against the plaintiffs in error for approximately $828. This prompted Matteson and Porter to seek a reversal of the judgment, culminating in this case reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs argued that the $400 received by Wright constituted a fiduciary debt, as it was entrusted to him for a specific purpose—acquiring land on behalf of Kellogg and his associates. They asserted that Wright's misapplication of the funds constituted a breach of trust, thus rendering the debt unaffected by the bankruptcy discharge he received. They sought to have their claim recognized as valid and enforceable against Wright's estate.	The defendants contended that Wright's bankruptcy discharge relieved him of his debts, including the one claimed by the plaintiffs. They argued that since Wright had been officially discharged, the plaintiffs' claim against the estate was not valid, claiming it should not be considered a fiduciary debt under the general bankrupt law. Additionally, they maintained that the plaintiffs had not participated in the bankruptcy proceedings, which would have waived their right to assert such claims.

In the case of The Equitable Trust Company et al. v. Septimus Fisher, the events took place in Champaign County, Illinois, centered around a real estate transaction that began when Fisher borrowed $3,000 from the Equitable Trust Company in February 1877. To secure the loan, Fisher executed a trust deed on 246 acres of land, designating Jonathan Edwards as the trustee. Subsequently, in case of Edwards’ incapacity, other successors were appointed, including Harmon. Following a claimed default on the loan, Harmon advertised the property for sale and conducted the sale on August 26, 1880, which went to a bid of $1,200. Fisher later petitioned the court to vacate and set aside the sale, claiming Harmon acted without authority, as proper procedures outlined in the trust deed were not followed, including a thirty-day notice requirement. The Champaign Circuit Court ruled in favor of Fisher, setting aside the sale and allowing him to redeem the property. The case was then appealed by the defendants.	The plaintiff, Septimus Fisher, argued that the sale of the property was void due to unauthorized actions by Harmon, who acted as a trustee without the legally required notice or formal declination of Edwards and Bond. Fisher claimed that the sale was fraudulent and that he was entitled to redeem his property by settling the debts incurred under the trust deed. He sought an accounting of rents and profits generated from the property.	The defendants, represented by the Equitable Trust Company and Harmon, contended that Harmon was a legitimate successor trustee and that the sale was valid despite the issues raised. They argued that even if there were some failures in procedure, there was no fraud, and they requested upholding the sale and denying Fisher’s claims for redemption and accounting of profits.

In January 1873, in Illinois, William G. Sappington, the plaintiff, brought a lawsuit against Cyrus C. Carter, the defendant, in the Scott County Circuit Court. The case centered around Sappington's claims for unpaid debts regarding spirituous liquors sold to Carter. Sappington claimed an outstanding amount of $284.05 for goods sold and presented a due bill from Carter for $108.13. During the trial, it was established that the majority of the account, excluding approximately $50 for other grocery items, consisted of liquor sold in quantities less than one quart. Conversely, Carter, a wagon-maker, countered with a set-off for $306, asserting he had provided services and goods to Sappington. The case hinged on the legality of Sappington's claims under Illinois law, specifically a statute that voided accounts for retail liquor sales exceeding fifty cents if sold in quantities less than one quart.	Sappington asserted that Carter owed him $284.05 for goods sold, primarily spirituous liquors, and presented a due bill for $108.13. He claimed that the defendant's failure to pay constituted a breach of contract. Sappington appealed after a jury verdict favored Carter, arguing that the verdict was against the evidence and that improper instructions had been given during the trial.	Carter contended that Sappington's claim was invalid due to the Illinois statute that rendered any account for spirituous liquors sold in quantities less than one quart void if the total amount exceeded fifty cents. Carter also claimed a set-off of $306 for a new buggy and repair work done for Sappington. This defense asserted that the entire claim from Sappington for liquor was legally unenforceable, leading to the jury's verdict in his favor.

Edward Boynton filed a lawsuit against William Renwick in the Illinois Supreme Court due to a promissory note for $225.63 including attorney’s fees, which had been secured in favor of Boynton. The initial judgment was entered against Renwick at the April term of the Dellalb Circuit Court in 1866. After the court's executions were levied, an order was issued to stay execution based on Renwick's application to open the judgment and present a defense, which the court granted. Renwick subsequently filed four pleas, primarily arguing usury and claiming the note was assigned to Boynton after it became due. The jury trial found in favor of Boynton but only awarded him $43, which was the amount originally loaned. Boynton motioned for a judgment for the full note amount, which was denied, leading him to appeal the decision.	Boynton argued that the court erred by allowing Renwick to open the original judgment and plead his case. He contended that the reassessment of the judgment two terms after its entry lacked substantial grounds, as the original judgment was valid. Boynton sought to have the original judgment reinstated for the full amount of the note and interest, rather than the jury's reduced award.	Renwick contended that the judgment should be opened due to the usurious nature of the note and asserted that the assignment of the note was invalid since it occurred after its due date. He claimed that Boynton's special pleas did not sufficiently negate his arguments regarding the assignment, thus justifying the jury’s limited award of $43.

William Ennor entered an agreement in February 1877 to purchase eight bonds and forty shares of stock from the Galena & Southern Wisconsin Railroad Company. This agreement required at least one hundred bonds to be subscribed for before it became binding. Ennor subsequently refused to pay after the railroad company claimed that one hundred bonds were subscribed. The railroad sued Ennor and won a judgment of $6,568 in June 1879. Following this, Ennor was imprisoned for about fifteen months due to the judgment debt, eventually released on bail. After his release, he filed a new complaint challenging the judgment, arguing that the railroad had become unable to deliver the subscribed stock due to their own actions prior to the judgment. The case centered on the contention that the railroad's bankruptcy meant they could not meet their obligations, and Ennor claimed that the judgment was obtained through fraud or mistake. The court ultimately found the railroad unable to deliver since it had hypothecated the bonds and was effectively bankrupt, having no property to deliver to Ennor.	William Ennor claimed that the railroad company's actions made it impossible for them to deliver the subscribed bonds and stock, thus invalidating the judgment against him. He sought an injunction to prevent the collection of the judgment until the bonds and stock were available for delivery, asserting that the judgment was obtained through the company's fraudulent conduct.	The Galena & Southern Wisconsin Railroad Company contended that Ennor had not made a proper demand for the bonds and stock before filing his bill. They argued that any inability to deliver the bonds should have been raised during the trial of the original lawsuit. They maintained that if Ennor had demanded the stock before a certain date, he would have received it, and thus his claims were without merit.

In the case of William T. H. Brooks et al. v. Warrick Martin et al., which took place in September 1872, the central figures included William T. H. Brooks, the plaintiff, and Warrick Martin, the defendant. The legal proceedings occurred in the Winnebago Circuit Court in Illinois. The case revolved around a bill in chancery filed by Brooks to foreclose two mortgages that had been executed by DeLorma Brooks, a key party not directly involved in the lawsuit. These mortgages were initially given to Isaac N. Phelps and John A. Blanchard and later assigned to William T. H. Brooks. Warrick Martin contested this foreclosure in a cross-bill, claiming that the mortgages were fully paid and alleging that the assignment to Brooks was fraudulent. He argued this was a scheme to defraud him, as he had acquired ownership of the premises through a United States Marshal sale related to his judgment against DeLorma Brooks. The case was then brought to the Illinois Supreme Court by Brooks, seeking to reverse the circuit court's decree that favored Martin's cross-bill.	William T. H. Brooks contended that he was the rightful owner of the mortgages due to valid assignments from Phelps and Blanchard. He argued that the mortgages had not been fully paid and sought to foreclose on them. Brooks asserted that the evidence provided supported his claims of ownership and that the cross-claim of the defendant, which alleged fraud in the assignment, lacked solid proof and was based largely on hearsay.	Warrick Martin defended against Brooks' claims by asserting that the mortgages were fully paid by DeLorma Brooks, the original maker. Martin argued that the assignment of the mortgages to Brooks was fraudulent, intended to conceal assets from DeLorma Brooks’ creditors, of whom Martin was the principal. He maintained that the court had sufficient evidence to support his defense and that Brooks had not paid any consideration for the assignment, claiming it was a contrived operation to defraud his interests.

The case "Harrietta V. Helm v. John K. Webster" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1877, concerning property rights in Quincy, Illinois. The central issue involved a street, specifically the south half of Jersey Street, and who held the title to this land after it had been vacated by the city. The dispute began with Samuel Holmes, who, in 1855, conveyed land to the city for public street use, including a reversion clause stating that if the street was abandoned, the property would revert to the original owner or their heirs. After Holmes's interests were transferred to John K. Webster in 1865, Webster subdivided the land and it became part of the official city plat. In 1876, the city vacated Jersey Street, triggering the reversion clause. Harrietta Helm, who acquired her property through subsequent conveyances from Webster, claimed ownership of the land based on the city's actions and state statute. The critical legal question was whether the vacation of the street allowed Helm to claim ownership of the south half of Jersey Street.	John K. Webster, the plaintiff, argued that he retained ownership of the land based on the reversion provision in the deed from Holmes, which stipulated that the property would revert to its owner if the street was vacated. He maintained that the legal actions taken by the city did not divest him of his rights to the property. Webster sought a judgment confirming his ownership of the south half of Jersey Street following its abandonment by the city.	Harrietta Helm, the defendant, claimed that her ownership rights extended to the south half of Jersey Street due to the statutory provisions that stated adjoining lots would automatically extend to the centerline of vacated streets. She argued that her claims were valid because the city officially vacated the street, meaning the property should transfer to her under the law. Helm contested the interpretation of the original deed and the implications of the vacation.

In the case of Nathaniel McLain et al. v. Mary Isabel Van Winkle et al., filed in 1864 in St. Clair County, Illinois, Nathaniel McLain, acting as next friend for his children, initiated a legal action against Mary Isabel Van Winkle and other heirs of Miles Van Winkle, who was deceased. The legal proceedings stemmed from an earlier petition in 1860 related to the dower rights of Rebecca Clark, the widow of Miles Van Winkle. The court ruled in 1860 that while Mrs. Clark had dower rights, the property could not be divided or sold without harming the interests of the owners. Following procedural complexities, including the death of the originally appointed commissioner for the property sale and irregularities in the filings, a supplemental bill was filed to reapportion the land. Over the ensuing years, various orders and reports were presented, but crucial elements, such as the appointment of commissioners to partition the land and due resort to the essential statutory processes, were lacking. Instead, the property was sold without proper authorization, leading to exceptions being raised by the minor defendants. This culminated in the appeal of a lower court's decree approving the master's sale of the property.	The plaintiffs, represented by Nathaniel McLain, argued for the reinstatement of the original partition action, asserting that the land should be partitioned according to the rights of the parties involved. They requested that the dower of Rebecca Clark be acknowledged and that the property be sold to ensure fair distribution among the heirs, provided it could not be divided without prejudice.	The defendants contended that the procedures followed in the original sale were irregular and did not adhere to the statutory requirements for a proper partition process. They asserted that no formal order or decree for sale had been properly entered prior to the sale, and claimed that the master's report lacked the necessary evidential foundation to authorize any sale of the property, thereby rendering the sale invalid.

John Bauerschmitz filed an action of forcible entry and detainer against Patrick Bailey in 1888, specifically on November 30th, in Sangamon County, Illinois. The case arose from an incident where Bailey's wife unlawfully entered and occupied property belonging to Bauerschmitz. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant was complicit in the unlawful act, either through direct involvement or by acquiescing to his wife's actions. The dispute centered around the responsibilities of a husband for the actions of his wife, especially in cases where the wife is seen as an agent acting on behalf of her husband. The legal proceedings considered the nature of the defendant’s involvement and the legitimacy of the plaintiff's claims regarding the wrongful entry.	The plaintiff, John Bauerschmitz, contended that Patrick Bailey was responsible for the wrongful entry by his wife into Bauerschmitz's property. Bauerschmitz maintained that the defendant either directed or consented to the act of unlawful possession. He sought a legal remedy to regain possession of his property and claimed damages resulting from the forcible entry by the defendant's wife.	The defendant, Patrick Bailey, argued that he was not involved in the wrongful entry into Bauerschmitz's property, asserting that he simply acquiesced to his wife's actions. Bailey maintained that his wife acted independently and that he was not responsible for her unlawful occupation of the property. He requested that the court reverse the plaintiff's claim, emphasizing that the evidence did not sufficiently show his direct involvement in the entry.

In January 1889, in Chicago, Illinois, James K. Fisher and A. J. Fisher, the appellants, were involved in a legal case against Egbert L. Jansen, the appellee. The incident occurred at the Beaurivage flats, an apartment building owned by the appellants. The appellee was injured when he walked through an open door of the elevator shaft while the elevator cab was above, causing him to fall into the pit below. As a result of this accident, the appellee suffered significant bodily injury, leading to a degree of disability. The appellants were responsible for the elevator operation and employed the staff at the time of the accident. During the trial, the jury heard testimonies related to the safety measures, negligence, and the nature of the appellee's injuries. The trial court instructed the jury to consider whether the appellee had exercised reasonable care for his safety and if the defendants were negligent. The instructions given were challenged by the appellants, who claimed they assumed certain factual relationships and responsibilities that were not adequately supported by evidence.	The plaintiff, Egbert L. Jansen, argued that he was exercising reasonable care at the time of the accident, and the defendants were negligent in their duty of care regarding the elevator's safety. Jansen requested compensation for the injuries sustained during the fall, emphasizing the pain and suffering and the disability he would endure, alongside the financial expenses incurred for medical treatment as a result of the accident.	The defendants (James K. Fisher and A. J. Fisher) contested the claims on the grounds that the instructions provided to the jury improperly assumed a negligent duty owed to the plaintiff without established cause. They argued that there was insufficient evidence to demonstrate that their actions were negligent or that they had a duty of care towards the appellee at the time of the incident. The defendants sought to have the jury's instructions modified and ultimately disputed the findings on negligence and damages claimed by the plaintiff.

The case of A. Fred. Grassly et al. v. Lyman L. Adams took place in January 1874 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from an alleged defective service on the defendant, Lyman L. Adams, and the appropriateness of a note assignment in a legal declaration. A. Fred. Grassly and others (the plaintiffs) argued that the service of summons was not correctly executed against Adams. The case's backdrop involved the interpretation of legal documents, particularly focusing on the assignment of a note, which was claimed to be insufficiently stated in the declaration. During the appellate process, a request was made to amend the service record to correct these issues, which was allowed by the court. The court examined whether the amended return resolved the initial difficulties and whether the assessment of damages by a clerk constituted proper procedure under the law.	The plaintiffs claimed that the service of summons on Lyman L. Adams was defective and argued that the assignment of the note in question was inadequately documented. They contended that these defects should invalidate the case against them, requesting that the court overturn the lower court's judgment based on these errors.	The defendant, Lyman L. Adams, maintained that the service of summons was indeed defective, but the remedial actions taken by the circuit court to amend the return resolved this issue. He contended that the declaration was sufficient as it contained common counts that could support the assigned note, and argued that the clerk's assessment of damages did not follow proper court procedure but was nonetheless inapplicable as the judgment effectively stated that the court assessed the damages based on the evidence presented.

In March 1876, Truman W. Montague became security for defendants Arthur Hutton and Winston Hutton by signing a note for $2,000 to the Second National Bank of Charleston. When the Huttons failed to repay the loan, Montague arranged to provide them with a bond for a deed to 80 acres of land, which would be turned into the bank to secure the debt. Eventually, a plan was made wherein the Huttons would grow broomcorn on Montague's land, estimated at 120 acres, with agreements on the crop's proceeds to pay off their debt. The Huttons were responsible for labor and cultivation, while Montague supplied the seed and expenses. By spring 1882, the Huttons grew a crop amounting to sixty bales of broomcorn. However, in December of that year, Montague claimed that he had no knowledge when he learned the Huttons sold the crop to O.B. Ficklin. Montague argued that the legal title to the crop remained his, although he had authorized the Huttons' labor. The case focused on whether Ficklin had obtained a valid title through the Huttons despite Montague's claims, leading to a jury trial that found in favor of Montague.	Montague's main arguments centered around the assertion that he was the true owner of the broomcorn crop raised by the Huttons on his land. He argued that the arrangement made with the Huttons outlined that the proceeds from the sale of the crop should apply towards their debt to the bank, firmly establishing his claim to the crop. Montague sought damages for the unauthorized sale of his property by the Huttons to Ficklin.	Ficklin contended that he purchased the broomcorn in good faith, believing the Huttons had the right to sell the crop. He argued that the Huttons were either tenants or joint owners of the crop and claimed that he, as a buyer, was unaware of Montague's interest. Ficklin requested the court's instruction that he had acquired a good title through his purchase, reasoning that he acted without notice of Montague's rights.

Patrick H. Stack filed a legal action against the City of East St. Louis regarding an incident that occurred on or before February 26, 1873, in East St. Louis, Illinois. Stack owned a property located on Crook Street that became inaccessible due to an ordinance that allowed the Illinois and St. Louis Bridge Company to construct an approach to its bridge over Crook and other streets. This construction obtruded the street in front of Stack's property, making it permanently impassable and obstructing his ability to access his land. The obstructions also caused water to drain onto Stack's property, which filled the cellars and increasingly affected the living conditions for his tenants, ultimately leading to their departure. As a result of these actions, Stack's property became unproductive and sustained significant damage. Stack claimed that the city, holding a trust for the public use of the streets, had failed in its duty to maintain the street and protect property owners from harm caused by its decisions. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court after the circuit court sustained a demurrer from the city, leading to a judgment against Stack.	Stack's main legal argument centers around the claim that the City of East St. Louis, by authorizing the construction of the bridge approach, has obstructed public use of Crook Street and denied him access to his property. He contended that the city's actions led to the flooding of his land, the displacement of his tenants, and significant damage to his property, effectively rendering it unproductive. Stack sought a reversal of the lower court's judgment, arguing that the city should be liable for the damages caused.	The City of East St. Louis defended itself by stating that it held the fee to the street in trust for public use, allowing it to permit the construction of the bridge without liability. They argued that the construction did not constitute an infringement of Stack's rights, maintaining that the street remained available for public use, and thus, the city should not be held responsible for any negative impacts on Stack's property.

The case of The Pennsylvania Company v. Albert Frana took place in Chicago, Illinois, culminating in a judgment delivered by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 17, 1884. The plaintiff, Albert Frana, brought a lawsuit against the Pennsylvania Company after sustaining personal injuries while attempting to cross the company's railroad tracks with a wagon and team. Frana attributed his injuries to the negligence of the railroad's servants, specifically arguing that they failed to operate the train with the necessary care and did not provide a flagman at the crossing, as mandated by a city ordinance. The trial court initially ruled in Frana's favor, a decision that was upheld by the Appellate Court, prompting the defendant to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case primarily revolved around allegations of negligence, the responsibilities of individuals crossing railway tracks, and applicable local ordinances regarding rail safety.	The plaintiff, Albert Frana, argued that the Pennsylvania Company was negligent for failing to have a flagman present at the crossing, which he claimed was a violation of the city's ordinance. He maintained that he was exercising ordinary care when crossing and that the negligence of the railroad's employees directly led to his injuries. Frana sought compensatory damages for the injuries he sustained due to the alleged negligence of the defendant's train management and operations.	The Pennsylvania Company claimed that Frana himself was negligent by not exercising appropriate caution while approaching the railroad tracks. They contended he could have avoided injury by properly looking and listening for oncoming trains before crossing. The defense further asserted that even if the railroad's flagman had been absent, this failure should not absolve Frana of his responsibility for his own safety. They argued that the ordinance concerning the lumber yard where Frana worked had no bearing on the case and should not affect the determination of negligence regarding the crossing incident.

In 1867, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving Lewis H. Baldenwick and The Union National Bank of Chicago concerning a counterfeit $100 bank bill. Baldenwick, the plaintiff, initially filed his claim before a justice of the peace, asserting that he had been paid with a counterfeit bill by the bank. After a trial that favored Baldenwick, the bank appealed to the Superior Court, which upheld the initial judgment. The case was then brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, which examined whether the presented evidence could support Baldenwick's claim. The bank argued that it never received the bill, and admissible evidence concerning this assertion was not allowed in the lower courts. The court explored the implications of this exclusion and the reasonable time required to return the counterfeit bill after its discovery, ultimately leading to a reassessment of the evidence and its relevance in proving the case.	Lewis H. Baldenwick claimed that he received a counterfeit bill from The Union National Bank of Chicago and sought to recover its value. He asserted that the bank failed to provide sufficient evidence to counter his assertion that the bill was spurious.	The Union National Bank of Chicago contended that Baldenwick could not prove that the bank had paid him the counterfeit bill. They requested the court to consider additional evidence that the bank never received the bill, which was initially excluded by the lower courts. The bank also argued that Baldenwick failed to return the bill within a reasonable timeframe after identifying it as counterfeit.

The case "Alfred B. Safford v. Robert Miller et al." was heard in June 1871 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The roots of the case trace back to a legal action involving a debt obligation stemming from an injunction bond dated May 20, 1864, linked to William Barker, Robert W. Miller, and W. P. Halliday. This bond was executed to protect Barker from lawsuits filed by Miller and John Cheek, pending a court decision regarding the injunction. After prolonged legal proceedings, including those in the Alexander County Circuit Court and an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, which upheld the dismissal of Barker's complaint, the plaintiffs sought damages for the troubles and expenses incurred during the legal battles. Specifically, Miller claimed to have lost possession of his property and the associated rental income due to the injunction, amounting to significant damages. The plaintiffs presented multiple breaches of the bond, citing extensive legal fees and lost profits, totaling $4,600. The legal proceedings involved numerous amendments to pleas and demurrers, ultimately leading to a complex assessment of damages based on misjoinder of counts and the nature of the covenants involved.	The plaintiffs contended that due to the issuance of the injunction against them, they faced considerable financial strains, successfully incurring legal expenses amounting to $500 each and being deprived of $3,000 in rental income over 30 months. Their claims emphasized the breach of the bond's condition whereby Barker was required to compensate them for damages caused by the injunction. They argued that the court should hold Barker liable for these amounts, including interest, as outlined in the bond's terms.	The defendant, Alfred B. Safford, argued against the plaintiffs' claims by presenting multiple pleas. He contended that the plaintiffs were not legally entitled to the damages they sought, particularly asserting that the claims were improperly joined since some damages alleged resulted solely to one plaintiff (Miller). Safford highlighted that the assignments for damages needed to be separate rather than combined, as the legal interest of the plaintiffs was joint, creating a misjoinder of counts. Accordingly, he requested the court to dismiss the claims related to damages that he claimed were not applicable to the joint bond agreement.

In 1882, Peter P. Ayer, the plaintiff, entered into a business arrangement with Sidney B. Mead, the defendant, concerning the purchase of 5,000 bushels of wheat. The transaction was intended to take place on the Chicago Board of Trade, where Ayer and his associates would act as commission merchants. On August 24, 1882, Ayer received a written order from Mead to buy the wheat at the market price, with an agreement that Mead would provide a margin deposit of $250 as security against potential market losses. However, when the price of wheat declined, Mead failed to furnish the requested margins, prompting Ayer to sell the wheat on September 12, 1882, which resulted in a loss of $268.75. Ayer subsequently sued Mead to recover the loss and the commissions owed for the transaction. The case was tried in the Circuit Court of Cook County, where a jury ruled in favor of Ayer, leading to a verdict for $268.75.	Ayer claimed that he and his associates were authorized to buy wheat on behalf of Mead, who agreed to pay $12.50 in commissions and to provide a margin for protection against losses. Ayer sought to recover the amount lost due to Mead's failure to provide the required margins when the wheat prices declined, thus leading to a need for Ayer to sell the wheat to minimize losses.	Mead contended that there was insufficient evidence to support Ayer's claims, arguing that the written order did not establish authorization for Ayer to sell the wheat or a requirement for margins. He maintained that the terms of the order were unclear and were not consistent with the customs of the board of trade. Mead requested that the court dismiss Ayer's claims due to lack of evidence for the alleged agreement and the circumstances of the sale.

In the case of *James W. Martin v. Henry H. Gilmore et al.*, which took place in January 1874 in Fulton County, Illinois, James W. Martin initiated an action of ejectment against Henry H. Gilmore and S. Corning Judd to recover a quarter section of land. The conflict arose from competing claims to the land, with both parties asserting titles derived from a common previous owner, Joshua J. Moore. The case involved a series of judicial and transactional actions including a judgment against Moore in favor of Joseph C. Hoagland in 1854, followed by an execution sale of the land to Hoagland in 1856. In 1858, after the original marshal's term expired, another deed was executed by a new marshal, James W. Davidson, to Andrew Hoagland, which the defendants claimed was void under an earlier congressional act. The complexity of the case was amplified by subsequent dealings and legal decisions surrounding perceived defects in title, including challenges to the validity of prior court decrees affecting ownership rights and the absence or presence of notice to various parties involved in the chain of title.	James W. Martin claimed that he was the rightful owner of the land based on a deed he obtained from Andrew Hoagland in 1870, which he contended was valid despite the challengers’ claims. He argued that the judgment of the lower court was contrary to both evidence and law, primarily focusing on the validity of the United States Marshal's deed made to Andrew Hoagland and asserting that it did not undermine his ownership.	The defendants, Henry H. Gilmore and S. Corning Judd, contended that the deed from the marshal to Andrew Hoagland was void due to the expiration of the marshal’s term before the deed was executed. They argued that this voided the title Martin was claiming, asserting that their own title, based on a preceding foreclosure judgment against Moore, was paramount. They maintained that they were innocent purchasers without notice of any defects in prior transactions involving the land.

The case of *Thomas Young et al. v. Sarah A. M. Young et al.* took place before the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision rendered on March 30, 1885. The litigation arose from a deed executed on December 30, 1878, wherein John Young conveyed 130 acres of land in Shelby County, Illinois, to his son, Samuel Young. Disputes began in 1873 when John and his wife, Gilla Young, faced marital difficulties, eventually leading to Gilla filing for divorce. During negotiations for settlement, the couple transferred 200 acres of land to Joseph Prickett, who subsequently transferred 70 acres to Gilla and 130 acres to Samuel at John Young's request. After Samuel's death in 1881, his heirs became defendants when John Young sought to reclaim the land, arguing that the deed was invalid due to inadequate consideration, false representations, and undue influence by Samuel. The case revolved around the legitimacy of the transactions between John and Samuel, focusing on John’s intentions and mental competency at the time of the conveyance.	The plaintiffs, heirs of John Young, contended that the deed to Samuel Young should be vacated on several grounds: the consideration was inadequate, the transaction involved false representations, and undue influence exerted by Samuel over John. They argued that since Samuel did not provide proper compensation for the land, the deed lacked legal validity and that he misled his father regarding potential claims against him, coercing the deed under false pretenses. The plaintiffs sought to have the court declare the deed void and compel Samuel's heirs to convey ownership back to them.	The defendants, heirs of Samuel Young, argued that John Young had the legal right to gift the land to his son without requiring monetary compensation, based on natural love and affection. They maintained that the agreements and transactions were voluntary, and there was no evidence that any misrepresentations significantly influenced John’s decision to convey the land. The defendants contended that the claims of undue influence and false representations were unfounded, as John had repeatedly expressed his intent for Samuel to inherit the property, demonstrating his clear mental capacity and volition.

Isaac Cook and Elias Shipman were involved in a legal action of debt regarding a bond located in Chicago, Illinois in the 1860s. The bond in question was in the amount of two thousand dollars and was conditioned on the payment of one thousand dollars to the obligee, Shipman, once the Chicago common council passed an ordinance that would change the dock line in front of Cook's property. The intent of the bond was to secure a favorable alteration that would give Cook's lot a water front. During the proceedings, the defendant, Cook, argued through a plea of non est factum, claiming that the bond was illegal. He alleged that the bond was part of a corrupt agreement designed to influence a member of the council, Elihu Granger, who was also engaged as a city employee. Granger's role as an alderman, according to Cook, violated his duty, as both he and Shipman were involved in a scheme to coordinate efforts to impact the committee's decision for Cook's benefit. After a trial, a verdict was reached in favor of Shipman for one thousand dollars in debt and an additional amount for damages, prompting Cook to appeal the judgment.	The plaintiff, Elias Shipman, argued that the bond was valid and that he was entitled to recover the amount specified, claiming he suffered damages as a result of Cook's failure to fulfill the payment under the bond agreement. Shipman maintained that the bond represented a legitimate contract, which he was legally entitled to enforce despite the defendant's assertions regarding the alleged corrupt nature of the agreement.	The defendant, Isaac Cook, countered Shipman's claims by asserting that the bond was illegal and void due to its corrupt nature. Cook claimed that the bond was created as a means to bribe an official (Granger) within the common council to influence decisions favorably for Cook. He argued that this represented an unlawful inducement that undermined the integrity of public office, disqualifying the bond from being enforceable in a court of law. Cook requested the reversal of the judgment in favor of Shipman based on the pleas that established the bond's illegality.

On September 27, 1887, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Thomas H. Bush et al. v. James R. Stanley et al. in Springfield, Illinois. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County and involved a dispute over the legal title of a piece of land bought by John L. Wilson, who funded Isaac K. Palmer to purchase it from the U.S. government in 1836. Wilson alleged that the patent for the land was mistakenly issued to Palmer due to the loss of the original certificate. The legal entanglement involved various parties, including the city of Chicago and claims of a prior bankrupt status of Wilson, which affected his rights to the property. A series of amendments and cross-bills complicated the proceedings, with Bush and the Palmers defending their interests against Wilson's claims. The case revolved around whether Wilson could establish a resulting trust to reclaim his interest in the land after significant time and transactions had taken place, culminating in the long-standing dispute over ownership.	The plaintiffs, led by John L. Wilson, claimed that he had funded the purchase of land by Palmer on his behalf and sought to assert a resulting trust over the property. They requested that the court declare that Wilson had the equitable interest in the property, direct the legal title to be conveyed to him, and enjoin the ongoing ejectment action against him by Bush and others. They argued that the land was rightfully Wilson's, as he had financially supported the acquisition despite a lapse in clear documentation.	The defendants, including Thomas H. Bush and the city of Chicago, countered that Wilson's claims were barred by his earlier discharge in bankruptcy, contending he had no present interest in the property. They argued that the evidence supporting Wilson's claims was insufficient and that any agreements or transactions were invalid due to the bankruptcy discharge. Moreover, they invoked legal principles regarding laches and prior titles, asserting that there was no need for equitable intervention as Wilson had not exercised his interest in the property.

In 1883, William C. Wright, a cattle dealer from Colorado, sought to know the selling price of a lot of cattle shipped by Peacock to the Union Stock Yards in Chicago, Illinois. On May 31, 1883, he arranged for a telegram to be sent by Bensley, Wagner & Bensley, a commission firm, to inquire about the sale price of the cattle. The telegram was altered by Western Union Telegraph Co., which caused the sale price to be inaccurately reported as five-eighty rather than the correct four-eighty. After receiving the telegram, Wright purchased 140 head of cattle based on the incorrect information and incurred a loss upon sale due to the miscommunication. He initially claimed damages for negligence against Western Union, which denied responsibility. The case eventually reached the Illinois Appellate Court for appeal after Wright was awarded $666 in damages in the Circuit Court of Cook County.	Wright argued that he suffered financial damages due to the negligence of Western Union in transmitting an altered telegram. He claimed that he relied on the telegram's contents when making his purchase of cattle. Wright requested compensation for the losses he incurred as a direct result of the erroneous information provided in the telegram.	Western Union contended that Wright was guilty of contributory negligence. They argued that he received information from an independent source indicating the actual selling price of the cattle before making his purchase, which should have prompted him to verify the correctness of the telegram. Instead, they asserted that he acted on the presumption that Western Union guaranteed the message's accuracy, which was not the case.

The legal case "Lake Erie & Western Railroad Company v. Phillip H. Faught" took place in McLean County, Illinois, with the final judgment issued on January 21, 1889. Phillip H. Faught, the plaintiff, was contracted to perform grading work on the railroad company's road-bed under an agreement with the original contractors, J. M. Wright & Co., and sub-contractors. After a period of work, Faught became dissatisfied with the likelihood of receiving payment and refused to continue under the original contracts. He claimed that Mr. Perry, the chief engineer for the railroad company, had authorized him to proceed with the work, constituting a new independent contract. Conversely, the railroad company contended that Perry had no authority to bind the company and that his assurances were meant solely to guarantee payment from the contractors. The jury found in favor of Faught, leading to the appeal by the Lake Erie & Western Railroad Company.	Phillip H. Faught's primary argument revolved around the assertion that his work on the railroad's roadbed was authorized by Perry, who acted with the company's authority. Faught contended that his terms constituted a new contract with the railroad, thus entitling him to compensation for the work performed after his refusal to continue under the original contract.	The Lake Erie & Western Railroad Company argued that Perry, as the chief engineer, lacked both express and implied authority to bind the company to a new contract. They insisted that his communications were only assurances that payment would be made by the original contractors and did not represent an agreement between Faught and the company.

In the spring of 1871, the board of directors of the L. B. & M. R. R. Co., including William H. Pells, contracted with the firm Snell, Taylor & Co. for constructing a railway extending from Bloomington, Illinois, to the state line. The contract allowed Snell, Taylor & Co. to locate stations east of McLean County with approval from the chief engineer. Pells, who owned land near Sugar Creek in Vermillion County, sought to locate a station there with alleged agreement from Taylor. In October 1871, local residents, looking to secure a station at Sugar Creek, initiated a subscription for Pells, totaling $3,400, promising payment if a station was established. Snell and his firm were unaware of this arrangement until mid-1872. Controversy arose when Snell informed Pells that establishing a station at Pellsville would require payment, which Pells claimed he would raise. In June 1872, Snell sent a representative to secure a promissory note in lieu of the subscription, but the note was made payable to Pells, who later claimed the funds after selling it. After the case progressed through various legal stages, including a judgment favoring the defendant that was reversed by the Supreme Court, a new trial found Pells liable for the amount owed from the note based on his agency status in its collection.	The plaintiffs, Edgar Z. Pells and Charles Bogardus, administrators, claimed that Pells had a contract with Snell, Taylor & Co. to establish a station and collect funds from local residents for that purpose. They asserted Pells acted as their agent in receiving the subscription money and that Snell’s firm was entitled to payment for their services in constructing the station. The plaintiffs sought recovery of the funds represented in the promissory note as they argued Pells improperly appropriated the money.	The defendant, Thomas Snell, contended that there was no binding contract regarding the location of the station, claiming that any such agreements were void as against public policy, and that Pells was not acting as their agent when he collected the subscription funds. Snell also argued the limitations statute applied to bar the claims against him, asserting that the plaintiffs had no standing in their pursuit of the funds, as they lacked a legal basis for their claims.

In November 1852, in Illinois, William H. Walter sued William Kirk and others regarding a promissory note. The case stemmed from a note of $22.25, created on August 11, 1844, as a debt settlement between Walter's wife, who was the widow of Levi Bennett, and Reason Bennett, the administrator of Levi's estate. Walter's wife owed the estate this amount, and the note indicated that it would be paid for goods obtained from the estate. It was understood that if any funds were available due to the widow when the estate was settled, they would be credited against the note. The plaintiff proved to the probate court that the note had been reassigned to him in November 1844 for value received. The defendant attempted to introduce evidence suggesting that the plaintiff had previously recovered a judgment on the note and subsequently sold it as a bad debt, but this evidence was excluded during the trial. The trial court ruled in favor of Walter, awarding him the amount of the note plus interest.	The plaintiff, William H. Walter, argued that he had a valid claim to the amount stated in the promissory note, which had been assigned to him by Reason Bennett, the administrator of the estate. Walter sought to recover the full amount of $22.25, asserting that he was entitled to the sum as the note was duly executed and transferred to him before it became due. He claimed that the defenses raised by the defendant regarding the note’s validity were without merit, especially since the evidence presented by the defendant was ruled inadmissible.	The defendant, William Kirk, contended that the plaintiff had previously obtained a judgment on the note and sold it at a discount, implying that it was a doubtful debt without recourse. He sought to introduce this evidence to challenge the validity of the plaintiff's claim on the basis that the assignment was made with knowledge of defenses against the original note. Additionally, he argued that any claims about the settlement between his wife and the estate administrator should bolster his case against the assignment of the note to Walter.

The case "The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company v. Jonathan Peacock" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. It involved an incident on the trains of the Chicago and Northwestern Railway, where Jonathan Peacock, a passenger, was forcibly ejected from the train by the conductor after he refused to pay his fare. This incident occurred between stations on the railway line in Illinois. The key individuals involved were Jonathan Peacock, the plaintiff, and employees of the Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company, the defendants. Peacock's ejection from the train was deemed unlawful, as the law only permitted the conductor to remove a passenger at a usual stopping place. This led to claims of trespass against the railway company, as the conductor acted with excessive force outside the legal parameters established for such situations.	Jonathan Peacock, the plaintiff, argued that the conductor’s actions in forcibly ejecting him from the train constituted trespass. He claimed that the ejection was unlawful since the conductor was prohibited from removing him at a place that was not a designated stopping point. Peacock sought damages for the injuries he sustained during the ejection, alleging that the conductor’s use of force was unwarranted and violated his rights as a passenger.	The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company contended that the conductor was justified in his actions because Peacock had initially refused to pay his fare. They argued that since Peacock had acknowledged he would get off if the conductor stopped the train, his subsequent refusal to leave did not excuse the conductor from taking action. The defendant claimed that the law permitted them to eject passengers who refuse to pay their fares, although they faced legal challenges in justifying the method and location of the ejection.

John Lilly filed a legal action against Ormus Palmer regarding a promissory note for $280, dated November 18, 1865, and due on January 1, 1867. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1869, following a judgment from the Court of Common Pleas of the City of Aurora. The note in question was secured by a mortgage on certain lands in De Kalb County. Palmer had sold this land to Lydia A. Backer in January 1866 while it was still encumbered by the mortgage. This transaction was properly recorded. Backer later sold the land to Mary Puller, taking a mortgage from her that was eventually bought by Lilly. Following a series of transactions, Lilly effectively held both the mortgage and the land, implying an ownership that positioned him similarly to a mortgagee who had completed a strict foreclosure. The jury found for the defendant, ruling that the note had been paid. Lilly's efforts to overturn this judgment led to his appeal to the higher court.	John Lilly's primary claims included an assertion that the promissory note was still valid and owed. He argued that the conveyance of the land from Backer and Hall's assigned mortgage demonstrated his entitlement to recover the amount due under the note. Lilly contested the previous ruling, seeking a new trial on the grounds that the jury had erred in its decision.	Ormus Palmer's defenses were based on the argument that the promissory note had been effectively satisfied through the transactions involving the mortgages and land ownership changes. Palmer maintained that the jury correctly concluded that Lilly, by acquiring the mortgage and holding the appropriate deeds, had positioned himself as having paid off the mortgage debt. He requested that the court affirm the original judgment against Lilly, asserting that all actions regarding the mortgage and property transfers had been conducted properly.

On September 18, 1883, Augustus Lamb filed an action of ejectment against Nicholas Heinsen in Cook County, Illinois, seeking to recover a specific lot in South Chicago. The lot was part of a larger subdivision by the Calumet and Chicago Canal and Dock Company. The case went through various proceedings, and the suit was dismissed concerning most of the premises, retaining only a small portion actually possessed by the defendant. The case was heard before a jury in January 1886, ending in a verdict and judgment in favor of the plaintiff. The defendant then appealed this judgment to the Illinois Supreme Court. Throughout the proceedings, significant issues arose, including the admissibility of evidence concerning the plaintiff's title, especially an abstract of title that was introduced in lieu of missing original deeds due to a fire. The court ultimately had to consider the soundness of the procedures followed and the facts surrounding the evidence presented.	The plaintiff, Augustus Lamb, contended that he had title to the disputed property, relying on an abstract of title prepared by a recognized abstract company prior to the loss of original records. He maintained that this abstract sufficiently established his claim despite the destruction of the original deeds. Lamb requested the court to affirm the verdict and judgment in his favor, asserting that he had demonstrated rightful ownership backed by credible evidence.	Nicholas Heinsen, the defendant, challenged the admissibility of the abstract of title, arguing that it was not prepared in the ordinary course of business and thus should not be accepted as evidence. Heinsens' key arguments hinged on the stipulations regarding the necessity of the complete abstract being produced in court and the implications of missing acknowledgments of certain deeds. He sought to have the court strike the amended bill of exceptions and alleged that the trial court improperly directed the jury's verdict in favor of the plaintiff without allowing a fair consideration of evidence.

In December 1856, the case of Charles Chandler v. The Northern Cross Railroad Company was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a subscription made by Charles Chandler to purchase shares in the Northern Cross Railroad Company, amounting to $2,000 for twenty shares. The case originated in the McDonough Circuit Court, where Chandler claimed that the railroad company breached their agreement by not allowing him to vote and receive benefits associated with being a stockholder due to alleged non-payment of his subscription. The subscription was made under a charter of incorporation that did not require immediate payment of an initial installment. The court scrutinized numerous defenses raised by the railroad company, including several special pleas and general defenses asserting that Chandler had not satisfied the subscription agreement. Ultimately, the court found that Chandler's subscription was valid despite the absence of a certificate of stock, allowing the company to recover the funds he owed.	The plaintiff, Charles Chandler, argued that he had validly subscribed to shares in the Northern Cross Railroad Company and was entitled to vote and other stockholder rights. He claimed that the company had breached the subscription agreement by not recognizing him as a bona fide stockholder due to the implementation of a by-law that required upfront payment of an installment for voting rights, which was not stipulated in the company charter at the time of his subscription. Chandler sought to recover the amount due for his subscription based on the original agreement.	The Northern Cross Railroad Company countered Chandler's claims with multiple defenses, including a general assertion that he had not paid the required five percent installment on the stock subscription, thereby disqualifying him as a stockholder. They contended that their by-laws prohibited him from voting or recognizing him as a stockholder due to his non-payment. Additionally, they claimed that Chandler could not become a stockholder or receive a stock certificate under the charter and by-laws unless he had paid the stipulated installment.

In September 1873, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of John L. Cusick v. James Campbell, stemming from a labor dispute in Livingston County. The case revolved around a contract for labor performed by Cusick's son for Campbell. The plaintiff, John L. Cusick, claimed that his son worked for Campbell for eight months and five days, while Campbell argued that the son quit before completing the work they had agreed upon, specifically before finishing husking corn in November. This discrepancy regarding the timeframe of employment became the crux of the dispute. A jury initially rendered a verdict in favor of Cusick, awarding him $55, prompting Campbell to appeal the decision. The appeal focused on two main arguments: that the verdict was contrary to the evidence and the claim that the court had improperly refused to give a specific instruction that Campbell requested for the jury's consideration.	The plaintiff, John L. Cusick, claimed that his son had a valid contract to work for Campbell for a duration of seven to eight months and had fulfilled that contract for a total of eight months and five days. He sought compensation for the labor provided, arguing that the amount awarded by the jury was justified based on the evidence presented.	The defendant, James Campbell, contended that the jury's verdict was not supported by the evidence, asserting that Cusick's son did not fulfill the terms of their agreement as he quit work prematurely before finishing the corn husking project. Campbell also argued that the trial court erred by refusing his request for a specific jury instruction, claiming it would provide clarification on critical facts relevant to the case.

In December 1860, Ephraim Potter executed a will that divided his real estate and bequeathed his personal property to his wife and certain heirs. He died in January 1861, leaving behind both plaintiffs (James M. Potter and others) and defendants (John Potter and others) as heirs. The plaintiffs filed a suit in chancery in the Woodford Circuit Court to contest the will, claiming it was not written or dictated by Ephraim and that it was the result of a conspiracy by some of the defendants, specifically naming Abram, Elizabeth, and Marian Potter. They alleged undue influence exerted on Ephraim, indicating he had neither signed nor acknowledged the will. The defendants countered that the will was validly executed, maintained it was drafted at Ephraim's request, and was witnessed by two individuals. After a jury trial where evidence was presented, the jury found the will to be valid, and the circuit court dismissed the complaint.	The plaintiffs claimed that the will of Ephraim Potter was invalid due to a lack of proper execution and execution under undue influence from designated defendants. They argued that the will was not dictated or signed by Ephraim and stressed conspiracy among the defendants to appropriate his property unlawfully, seeking to have the will set aside and canceled.	The defendants argued that the will was executed in compliance with legal requirements, asserting that Ephraim requested it to be drafted, confirmed it through his mark, and had it witnessed as mandated by law. They denied all allegations of conspiracy, undue influence, or fraud, maintaining that the will accurately reflected Ephraim's wishes at the time of its creation.

In December 1828, the case of Joseph Duncan, Appellant, v. Ingles and Burr, Appellees, was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from the Jackson circuit court, where the defendants, Ingles and Burr, had obtained a judgment against the plaintiff, Joseph Duncan. The basis of this earlier judgment was a prior ruling from the state of Kentucky. Duncan filed a bill in chancery seeking to prevent the enforcement of this judgment. He argued that he had a valid defense against the Kentucky judgment but had not been able to present it effectively in that court. The case revolves around the procedural issues regarding whether Duncan could seek relief in equity after failing to assert his legal defenses at the proper time in the Kentucky suit.	Joseph Duncan asserted that he had grounds for a legal defense to the prior judgment made against him in Kentucky, which he believed warranted the intervention of the court of equity. He filed the bill to seek an injunction to prevent the enforcement of the judgment obtained by Ingles and Burr in the Jackson circuit court, questioning the fairness of the original judgment and seeking relief based on his claimed but unproven defenses.	Ingles and Burr argued that Duncan's appeal lacked merit and that he should have filed a bill for discovery during the initial proceedings in Kentucky if he had a legal defense. They maintained that since Duncan failed to act appropriately at the right time, he was ineligible to seek equitable relief now. The defendants contended that the law established that a party could not claim relief in equity if they neglected to assert their legal defenses earlier in the legal process.

The case "Abbott L. Adams et al. v. The Cross Wood Printing Company et al." was decided on September 19, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The plaintiffs were three separate firms challenging the Cross Wood Printing Company, which had conducted business in Chicago since at least December 17, 1883. The plaintiffs asserted that the printing company had become insolvent before this date and had engaged in actions intended to hinder the collection of debts owed to them. They claimed that on December 10, 1883, the company was aware of its insolvency but still allowed certain officers to execute judgment notes, which were later leveraged to falsely secure payments against the company's property. Notably, John E. Cross (pretending to be the company president) and Edward Richards (the treasurer) executed these judgment notes without proper authorization from the board of directors. The plaintiffs contended that the denial of their claims violated creditor rights and sought restitution for the value of seized assets, stating that the officers knowingly assumed positions of conflict and misused corporate assets.	The plaintiffs argued that the entries of judgment against the Cross Wood Printing Company were invalid due to the lack of proper authorization from the board of directors. They claimed that both John E. Cross and Edward Richards were aware of the company's insolvency and acted inappropriately by enforcing personal claims at the expense of other creditors. Their legal request was for accountability and restitution for the value of the property wrongfully taken under void executions.	In their defense, John E. Cross and Edward Richards denied knowledge of the company's insolvency and asserted that they executed the judgment notes with proper authority and for valuable consideration related to actual debts owed by the company. They argued that the judgments were valid, denying any misconduct or fraudulent intent in their actions concerning the company’s assets.

In December 1853, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of William Weer, Junior (Appellant) vs. Mary Hahn (Appellee) concerning a tract of land in Macoupin County, Illinois. The dispute began when Hahn, the plaintiff, brought an action of ejectment to recover possession of the land after Weer, the defendant, claimed ownership through a tax sale. Weer purchased the property following a judgment in June 1850 for unpaid taxes from 1849. The court trial examined the legitimacy of Hahn's ownership, evidenced by a chain of title starting from a U.S. government patent to Carson, which was then conveyed to Schaffer, and finally to Hahn. While Weer successfully introduced the sheriff's deed validating his tax sale purchase, Hahn contested it based on the legality of the notice requirement for such sales, arguing that the notice should have been published in the nearest newspaper, which in this case was not adhered to as the notice appeared in a paper further away. The court weighed the evidence, particularly the sufficiency of the notifications concerning the tax sale, leading to an in-depth analysis of legal requirements surrounding property tax sales.	The plaintiff, Mary Hahn, contended that she legally owned the property based on her chain of title starting from the U.S. patent through various deeds. She maintained that the defendant's claim to the land was invalid due to procedural errors in the notice requirements during the tax sale, specifically arguing the notice was not published in the nearest newspaper as mandated by the constitutional provisions.	William Weer, the defendant, argued that he lawfully obtained the title to the land via a sheriff’s deed after purchasing the property at a tax sale, complying with all necessary legal procedures. He asserted that he published notice about the tax sale in accordance with the law since no newspaper was published in Macoupin County, and claimed that he followed the statutory requirements in obtaining the deed, presenting an affidavit to support this claim.

In the case of Charles L. Ingersoll v. Daniel P. Banister, the events unfolded in De Kalb County, Illinois, with legal proceedings commencing in June 1865. Charles L. Ingersoll, the plaintiff, claimed that Daniel P. Banister, the defendant, owed him for a sale of grain consisting of wheat, oats, and corn, sold through Ingersoll’s agent, Norman Weaver. The total debt was roughly $437.04. Banister had acknowledged receipt of some of this grain but had not paid for it. In July 1863, Weaver and Banister formed a partnership that lasted until December 1864, during which the grain debt was recorded in their firm books. However, this arrangement was disputed; Weaver denied ever assuming the debt in favor of Ingersoll, asserting that the entries were incorrect. After a trial, the jury ruled in favor of Banister, prompting Ingersoll to seek a new trial, which the court denied. The case was then taken to the Illinois Supreme Court for review.	The plaintiff, Charles L. Ingersoll, argued that Daniel P. Banister was liable for the purchase of grain and sought compensation for the amount owed. Ingersoll maintained that the business arrangements between Weaver and Banister did not absolve Banister of his debt. He contended that even if there was an agreement regarding the partnership, it could not eliminate his right to recover the owed amount, as he was not a party to any such agreement.	The defendant, Daniel P. Banister, claimed that he entered an arrangement with Weaver which, he argued, effectively made Weaver liable for the debt to Ingersoll. Banister attempted to support his position by introducing evidence from the partnership's accounts, asserting that the debt had been transferred to Weaver’s account. He argued that since the debt was recorded in the firm books, Ingersoll should pursue Weaver for the payment, stating that he had been discharged from liability.

In September 1869, the case of John Forsythe v. John L. Beveridge took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. The central issue arose from a judgment obtained by attorneys Hurd, Booth, and Kreamer in the superior court of Chicago against defendants Turner and Nichols. This judgment was subsequently assigned to John Forsythe, who sought payment from John L. Beveridge, the sheriff who collected the funds. However, Hurd, Booth, and Kreamer claimed an attorney’s lien on that judgment, alleging they were entitled to payment for their fees before Forsythe could receive any money. The superior court upheld this claim, directing that the collected funds be kept in court until a jury determined the amount owed to the attorneys. The case focused on whether such a lien existed under Illinois law.	John Forsythe argued that he was entitled to the funds collected by the sheriff as the rightful assignee of the judgment against Turner and Nichols. He contended that the attorneys’ claim to a lien on the judgment for their fees was not valid under Illinois law, as the fees were neither taxed nor part of the judgment. Forsythe sought a court order compelling the sheriff to pay him the collected amount.	Hurd, Booth, and Kreamer defended their claim by asserting that they held a legitimate attorney’s lien for fees incurred in obtaining the judgment. They argued that irrespective of the classification of fees as taxable costs, their work entitled them to a claim on the judgment itself. They maintained that the liens existed based on various precedents from other jurisdictions that recognized such rights.

Anton Zarresseller was indicted on April 4, 1855, in the Marion Circuit Court for selling spirituous liquor without a license in Marion County, Illinois. The indictment accused him of selling one gill of liquor to a person named Tracy, which was less than one quart. Zarresseller moved to quash the indictment, arguing that the "act for the suppression of intemperance," approved on February 12, 1855, had repealed any laws requiring a license for such sales, along with the associated penalties for selling without a license. He contended that the indictment was also deficient as it failed to specify the type of liquor sold and that it did not conform to the constitutional language required for such indictments. The court examined the intent and provisions of the new act, noting that it would not take effect until the people voted on it later that year, and concluded that the laws regulating liquor sales remained in effect until such a vote occurred.	The plaintiff, Anton Zarresseller, claimed that the recently enacted act to suppress intemperance repealed the existing laws that required a license for selling spirituous liquor. He argued that since he sold less than a quart of liquor, and given the act’s conditions, he should not be prosecuted under the previous licensing laws. Additionally, he maintained that the indictment was insufficient because it did not specify the type of liquor sold and lacked the proper wording required by the constitution.	The defendant, represented by the state's attorney, contended that the act of February 12, 1855, did not repeal the requirement for a license to sell spirituous liquors. The defendant argued that the statute should be interpreted in a manner that preserved the existing licensing laws and penalties for violations. Furthermore, the prosecution insisted that the indictment was sufficiently detailed according to state law and that the way it was concluded was still within constitutional guidelines.

In September 1871, the case of Arthur Dyer v. Ezra Day et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following a dispute over a parcel of land located in Illinois. The case originated from an ejectment action where plaintiff Arthur Dyer claimed ownership of the land under two deeds: one executed by defendant Ezra Day and his wife to a third party, Bradley, and another deed from Bradley to Dyer. The core issue arose from Day's assertion that the deed to Bradley was fraudulent; he claimed it was made in exchange for a property in Missouri, which Bradley had misrepresented in terms of its value and character. Dyer maintained his legal claim to the property based on the deeds presented. The court had to consider the validity of Day's defenses, particularly his claims of fraud associated with the previous transactions. The case was heard in the Court of Common Pleas in Aurora, Illinois, with Judge Richard G. Montony presiding.	Arthur Dyer, the plaintiff, argued that he held a legal title to the property based on the deeds executed by Ezra Day and Bradley. He contended that the two deeds clearly established his ownership rights, and therefore, he sought possession of the land through the ejectment action. Dyer's main legal request was the affirmation of his title against any claims made by Day, irrespective of allegations regarding fraudulent representations made by Bradley regarding the Missouri property, as these were not pertinent to the legal title.	Ezra Day, the defendant, claimed that the deed he executed was made under fraudulent pretenses, asserting that Bradley had misrepresented the property in Missouri as a basis for the exchange. Day contended that Dyer had knowledge of the fraudulent representations. He sought to use this claim of fraud as a defense in the ejectment action. Furthermore, Day argued against whether his wife's relinquishment of her homestead rights to the property was valid, claiming she was misled into believing the deed was a mortgage.

In April 1867, in Kankakee County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Asahel H. Warner and Samuel H. Ostrander. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff, Samuel Ostrander, initiated an action of trespass against Asahel Warner for unlawfully levying and selling a quantity of personal property that belonged to him. This personal property consisted of grain and other farm produce, which was claimed to have been raised by Peter Ostrander, possibly for the benefit of the plaintiff. Warner, as the defendant, contended that the ownership claimed by Ostrander was merely a façade to avoid the property being sold to satisfy the debts of Peter Ostrander. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him damages of $500, but this decision was contested by Warner, leading to an appeal to the Supreme Court on various grounds, including a challenge to the instructions given to the jury during the trial.	The plaintiff, Samuel Ostrander, argued that the personal property in question was rightfully his and that the defendant, Asahel Warner, committed a trespass by unlawfully levying and selling that property under an execution order against Peter Ostrander. He sought damages for the wrongful sale, asserting that the property had greater value than the amount for which it was sold.	Asahel Warner's primary defense was that the ownership claimed by Samuel Ostrander was not genuine and was presented for the purpose of shielding the property from being sold to pay off debts owed by Peter Ostrander. Warner contended that since the property actually remained with the Ostranders and was disposed of by them, there was no legitimate claim for damages beyond the amount for which the property was sold under execution.

In September 1876, the case of Robert W. Hyman v. William Bayne was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following an action of assumpsit initiated by Hyman against Bayne in the Superior Court of Cook County. Hyman claimed that he had paid money for Bayne's use, alleging that Bayne owed him for these expenditures. Over the course of the proceedings, the defendant, Bayne, filed several special pleas, including one that invoked the Statute of Limitations, asserting that more than sixteen years had passed since the causes of action had accrued. Hyman countered by stating that he had not been within Illinois during that time. The court's discussion revolved around the application of the Statute of Limitations, particularly with respect to non-residents and actions arising in other states, notably Maryland and New York. The issues explored in the case included whether the claims were barred by the respective limitations laws of Maryland and New York, and the implications of the Illinois limitation statutes as they applied to non-residents. Multiple pleas and demurrers were raised, ultimately leading to a complex interaction between state laws and the rights allowed in litigation.	Hyman's primary arguments rested on his assertion that the Statute of Limitations should not apply since he had not been within Illinois during the entirety of the limitation period. He maintained that the claims arose during a time when both he and Bayne were non-residents, and thus, according to Illinois law, he should be allowed to pursue the action despite the passage of time under the statutes of other states. Hyman sought a judgment for the recovery of the money he claimed was owed to him.	Bayne's defenses were primarily grounded in the invocation of the Statute of Limitations, arguing that since the causes of action accrued in Maryland, and given the laws of that state, Hyman's claim had been barred for over three years prior to the initiation of the lawsuit. He contended that because both parties had continuously resided outside of Illinois, the legal framework mandated the barring of Hyman's claims. He requested the court uphold his defenses and dismiss the action based on these limitations.

In July 1865, in Lawrence County, Illinois, George W. Whitaker, then the sheriff, executed a levy under an attachment for Mark Sunthimer against Charles Wheeler and Robert Potter. The levy included 116 head of cattle and other personal property. Daniel Wheeler, claiming ownership of the property, was in possession and herding the cattle at the time of the levy. On July 21, 1865, Daniel Wheeler filed a notice requesting a trial of the right to the property, which resulted in a jury verdict affirming his ownership. Despite this, Whitaker sold the cattle as if they were perishable goods, stating he acted under section 23 of the attachment law. Daniel Wheeler subsequently initiated an action of trover against Whitaker for the unlawful taking and conversion of his property, leading to a trial that was moved to Marion County. The trial allowed the introduction of certain evidence objected to by the defendant, which became a central issue in the appeal.	Daniel Wheeler, the plaintiff, argued that Whitaker unlawfully took possession of his cattle and other personal property, converting it for his own use under a wrongful attachment. He sought damages for the unlawful levy and claimed ownership through the prior jury verdict in the right to property case, demanding $3,000.	George W. Whitaker, the defendant, contended that the introduction of the prior judgment as evidence was erroneous since he was not a party to that trial. He argued that certain depositions were improperly accepted and that the damages awarded were excessive. Whitaker claimed that based on the attachment law, the measure of recovery should only reflect the proceeds from the sale of the property.

In the case of George M. De Land v. The Dixon National Bank, the events transpired between 1873 and 1879 in Illinois. George M. De Land was a depositor at the Dixon National Bank for approximately four years. In April 1877, the bank provided De Land with a passbook and 42 vouchers detailing his transactions, indicating that his account was balanced with no outstanding dues. However, De Land did not contest this statement until he filed the lawsuit on October 17, 1879, claiming that there was a balance owed to him. The bank responded to his claim with a non-assumpsit plea, asserting that De Land owed them money due to two promissory notes he executed, totaling over $800. During the trial, the legitimacy of certain checks charged against De Land's account was disputed, with claims that he had not authorized them. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of the bank, leading to an appeal by De Land regarding the trial process, particularly concerning the instructions given to the jury.	George M.
