James M. Shackleford filed an action of ejectment against Samuel P. Bailey in Tazewell County, Illinois, for the recovery of a specific tract of land, the southeast quarter of the southeast quarter of section two, township four north of range five west, on April 13, 1858. During the trial, Shackleford presented a patent from the United States dated November 1, 1839, granting him the disputed land. The defendant, Bailey, acknowledged being in possession of the land at the lawsuit's commencement and introduced multiple deeds as evidence, including a tax deed from the sheriff of Tazewell County and related tax receipts. Shackleford objected to the admission of these deeds, citing insufficiencies in land descriptions. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of Bailey. Following the trial, Shackleford sought a new trial, arguing that the jury's verdict was improperly guided by the court’s instructions and the descriptions in the admitted deeds were void for uncertainty, as they did not accurately represent the land in dispute. The case marked a significant interaction between property rights and challenges regarding evidence admissibility in an ejectment action.	Shackleford argued that the deeds presented by Bailey were void due to ambiguous and conflicting descriptions of the land. He claimed that Bailey had no legal title or color of title to the disputed land, emphasizing that the actions of the trial court, particularly in allowing those deeds to be admitted as evidence, were erroneous. He sought a new trial, contending that the verdict returned by the jury should be set aside for these reasons and that a proper judgment be entered in his favor.	Bailey contended that he had color of title and had paid taxes related to the property according to the deeds presented. He maintained that he was a legal owner of the land due to the purported transactions, arguing that the plaintiff's objections were insufficient in light of the evidence submitted. He requested the court to uphold the jury's verdict in his favor, asserting that all procedural and evidentiary requirements had been satisfied.

In January 1865, Mary A. Stone owned a farm in Cook County, Illinois, which she conveyed to Beverly, who then transferred it to her husband Richard Stone on the same day. Mary A. Stone died intestate in April 1865. In 1871, Richard conveyed the property to his son Robert B. Stone and son-in-law Amos Wilbern, following tensions with his wife's children from a previous marriage. Afterward, Isabella Wilbern and her husband Amos filed a lawsuit to cancel the earlier deeds, claiming they were fraudulent. Richard countered with a cross-bill asserting he was subjected to fraud and undue influence by Robert and Amos. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court after a lower court dismissed both the original bill and the cross-bill.	Jane Stone, the wife of Richard Stone and sole devisee of his estate, sought to invalidate the deeds executed in January 1865 and to partition the contested property, arguing that the transfers were executed under fraud and undue influence affecting her husband, Richard, at the time of the transfer.	The defendants, Robert Stone and Amos Wilbern, contended that Richard Stone was mentally competent to execute the deed in question and that no undue influence or fraud was involved. They maintained that Richard willingly transferred the property to ensure its preservation for his children and that all parties acted in accordance with his wishes.

Sievert T. Gunderson and co-plaintiffs brought an action of assumpsit against Charles A. Sirborn in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois. The trial concluded on June 16, 1888, with a jury ruling in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding $419.75. The case was appealed, with the defendants (appellants) claiming that it was tried out of its order, violating procedural statutes. They attempted to raise objections to this effect but were unsuccessful as the trial court overruled their requests to address these objections before proceeding with the trial. The defendants did not clearly articulate what their objections were, attempting instead to bolster their case through an affidavit, which was deemed insufficient as it was not certified by the trial judge. The presiding judge did not validate the affidavit’s claims, and it was ultimately determined that there was sufficient evidence for the jury's verdict.	The plaintiffs argued that the trial was conducted appropriately, adhering to the procedural requirements. They sought to have the judgment in their favor affirmed, asserting that their case had sufficient legal grounding supported by evidence presented during the trial.	The defendants contended that the trial court erred by trying the case out of order, claiming this was a violation of legal statutes. They objected to the trial's progression and attempted to introduce an affidavit to support these objections; however, they did not have the affidavit's claims certified by the trial judge, which weakened their argument. Their main request was to have the verdict overturned due to these alleged procedural errors.

In the case of David Puterbaugh v. Charles Hammond, the legal dispute originated from an action of assumpsit filed by Charles Hammond against David Puterbaugh in the Circuit Court of Carroll County, Illinois, during the January term of 1881. The crux of the case involved a note for $2000 given by Puterbaugh to Hammond as indemnity against losses Hammond incurred as surety for Puterbaugh. The case began when Hammond sought to recoup various amounts he paid on behalf of Puterbaugh, including payments for legal costs and judgments. During the trial, it was revealed that in December 1878, Hammond had made an arrangement in which he paid $1600 to satisfy a judgment owed by Puterbaugh and subsequently assigned Puterbaugh's note to Samuel W. Treat. Puterbaugh argued that Hammond had sacrificed the note by selling it for less than its face value without his consent. The trial jury found in favor of Hammond, awarding him damages of $1177.85, which led to subsequent appeals and legal motions. In the appellate court, the judgment against Puterbaugh was upheld, leading to this case being brought before the Illinois Supreme Court.	Charles Hammond, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to recover payments made on behalf of Puterbaugh, including legal fees incurred in prior judgments against them. He contended that the note provided to him by Puterbaugh was meant as security for any losses he might endure due to his role as surety. Hammond sought to recoup amounts he had paid, including the sums used to satisfy a judgment and additional costs related to their legal proceedings, thereby emphasizing that he had acted within his rights under the indemnifying note.	David Puterbaugh, the defendant, claimed that Hammond had improperly assigned the note to Treat for a lesser amount without his consent, effectively forfeiting his rights to recoup the full amount owed on the note. He argued that the assignment constituted a detriment to him as the maker of the note and asserted that he was entitled to a credit for the difference between the amount paid by Hammond and the note’s face value. Puterbaugh's defenses revolved around the premise that Hammond acted without proper authority in sacrificing the note's value through the sale.

In September 1869, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the case of Lewis Kenton v. Philip Shreck et al. The dispute originated from a series of judgments against Smiley S. Keiser in Mercer County, which led to the sale of several parcels of land, including one that was of focus in this case. The sale occurred on November 5, 1859, with Elias Willits, an attorney for Samuel O. Donaldson, purchasing the contested land, allegedly for Donaldson despite the absence of formal payment. The land was encumbered by a mortgage in favor of William McCartney. In 1861, McCartney filed for foreclosure, and despite Donaldson not being formally served, his attorneys entered a general appearance for him. A decree of foreclosure was made that same year, which led to the sale of the land to McCartney. Lewis Kenton later acquired an interest in Donaldson's claims, filing a bill to redeem the property in 1867, six years post-foreclosure. Kenton's claim hinged on the argument that Donaldson’s initial appearance in the foreclosure case was without authority.	Lewis Kenton asserted that he was entitled to redeem the land despite having acquired it through Donaldson's interests. He argued that Donaldson’s appearance in the foreclosure proceedings was invalid as it lacked proper authority. Kenton sought the court's help to set aside the foreclosure and secure his right to redeem the property.	The defendants, represented by McCartney and their attorneys, contended that the foreclosure decree was valid due to the general appearance made by Donaldson’s attorneys. They maintained that sufficient time had passed since the foreclosure, during which the land had changed hands and had been improved upon, thus entitling them to the benefit of the judicial decree. Their main argument was that allowing Kenton to challenge the authority of Donaldson’s attorneys would undermine the title acquired by innocent parties.

Henry B. Drake and Thomas B. Perry were involved in a legal dispute concerning a promissory note. The case originated in Logan County, Illinois, in the early months of 1871. Drake originally gave a $50 promissory note to Kellogg and Squares, which was assigned to Perry prior to its maturity by someone impersonating their agent. When the note matured, Perry attempted to collect the debt through Justice Alsop. In this trial, Drake contested the collection by arguing fraud, circumvention, and lack of consideration, resulting in a judgment in favor of Drake. Following this, Perry attempted a second collection action by writing an assignment over the note and submitting it to Justice Benner, leading to a judgment against Drake. Drake appealed this second judgment, arguing that the previous judgment should bar the new suit. The central issue was whether the first judgment could be pleaded as a bar to the second suit, given that it remained in full force and was unreversed.	The plaintiff, Henry B. Drake, claimed that the promissory note had been obtained through fraud and lacked consideration. He argued that the initial judgment in favor of Drake from the first trial should serve as a defense against the second suit initiated by Perry, asserting it constituted res judicata.	The defendant, Thomas B. Perry, contended that the initial suit brought against Drake was improperly processed, as it was in the name of the payee rather than the proper holder, Perry. However, Perry did not challenge this procedural defect in the first trial and subsequently sought to collect the note in his name after withdrawing it from Justice Alsop.

In June 1826, in St. Clair County, Illinois, Nicholas Beaugenon filed an appeal against François Turcotte and François X. Valois regarding a financial obligation. The case arose when Beaugenon executed a note that he believed was payable in state paper, but he later argued that he was deceived about the currency indicated in the note and the language used. He alleged that both Turcotte and his agent were not present during the signing and thus could not be responsible for any fraud or misrepresentation. The lower court reduced the judgment to the value of state paper at the time the note was due, indicating some acknowledgment of his position without confirming any deception. The court emphasized the principle that a party seeking relief in equity must first do equity, and since Beaugenon admitted he was willing to execute the note, the court declined to disturb the lower court's decree, affirming the judgment reached there.	Beaugenon claimed that he was misled regarding the type of money the note was payable in, believing it to be state paper rather than specie. He sought relief from the judgment imposed on him, claiming that if he was deceived into signing the note under false pretenses, he should not be held liable for its full value in specie.	Turcotte and Valois defended themselves by stating that they had no knowledge of any fraudulent actions in obtaining Beaugenon's signature on the note. They contended that Beaugenon had willingly signed the note, assuming it to be for state paper, and therefore, it was equitable for him to pay the amount in accordance with how he understood the obligation at the time of execution.

The case "Pauline Friedman v. Rebecca Steiner et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 10, 1883. It arose from a dispute over the will of Henry Steiner, who died on December 22, 1879, owning real estate in Cook County, Illinois, as a tenant in common with Leopold Mayer. Henry's will included a provision that bequeathed his estate to his wife, Rebecca Steiner, with specific conditions regarding the distribution of the estate should she die intestate and without lawful heirs. The controversy centered on whether Rebecca was granted a fee simple estate in the property or a life estate with conditions attached. The Circuit Court had initially ruled that Rebecca held a fee simple estate and had total authority to convey it without limitation. Pauline Friedman, a beneficiary named in the will, appealed this decision, asserting that the will intended to limit Rebecca’s estate to a life estate, with a remainder to specified beneficiaries upon her death if she died without lawful issue.	Pauline Friedman claimed that the terms of Henry Steiner's will constituted an executory devise intended to limit Rebecca Steiner's interest in the property to a life estate. She argued that this limitation would prevent Rebecca from transferring the full ownership of the estate without adhering to the terms set forth in the will. The key requests from the plaintiff included a reversal of the lower court's decision and a correction to reflect that Rebecca's estate should not be considered a fee simple, but rather a life estate.	Rebecca Steiner and her co-defendants contended that the language used in the will conferred upon her a fee simple title without conditions prohibiting alienation. They argued that the proviso regarding her intestate death and lack of heirs was void as it contradicted the estate’s nature conveyed to her, thus allowing Rebecca full power to sell or will the property as she saw fit. They insisted that no limitations imposed by the will restricted her ownership rights.

The case of Benjamin L. Hunt et al. v. John K. Rowley et al. took place in September 1877, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over two entries made on a fractional section of land in township 37 north, range 14 east of the third principal meridian. John Holbrook applied for and received a certificate of entry for a parcel containing 109.33 acres on December 24, 1838, which he later conveyed to Joseph Hunt. This land remained vacant but had taxes paid by Hunt and his heirs. Willis M. Hitt subsequently made two applications between 1870 and 1871 for pieces of land he claimed were separate from Holbrook's entry. The main contention hinged on whether Hitt's claims overlapped with the land already entered by Holbrook. The question before the court was whether Holbrook's entry encompassed all the land between the navigable lake and the river or was restricted to that on one side of the outlet connecting both bodies of water.	The plaintiffs, representing the interests of Joseph Hunt and his heirs, argued that Holbrook rightfully entered and obtained title to the land as described in his application. They maintained that Hitt's entry conflicted with Holbrook's original entry and contended that the entire tracts were included in Holbrook’s application based on the proper survey and field notes. They sought a judgment affirming their ownership of the land in question based on these claims.	The defendant, Hitt, argued that his own application for land was valid and separate from Holbrook's entry. He contended that the tract he entered should not be considered part of the land Holbrook had purchased, thus asserting that he held a valid claim to the acreage he applied for. Hitt's defense hinged on interpreting the land descriptions and the boundaries delineated between the outlet and the river.

The case, "St. Louis, Alton and Rock Island R. R. Co. et al. v. John Coultas; Same v. Alexander J. Hawk’s Admr’s," was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1864. At the heart of the dispute was an obligation involving the St. Louis, Alton and Rock Island Railroad Company, which had undergone a name change from the Rock Island and Alton Railroad Company. The case arose from actions of debt initiated by several plaintiffs—landowners who were owed compensation for the condemnation of their land to secure a right of way for the railroad. The disputed instrument stated that the railroad company was bound to pay the landowners damages, amounting to a total of $3,000, according to their individual interests as assessed during the condemnation process. However, the plaintiffs did not note whether the damages for the other obligees had been assessed, nor did they specify the extent of their respective interests in the declarations. This omission sparked the legal debate regarding the sufficiency of the declarations and the nature of the obligations assumed by the railroad company.	The plaintiffs contended that they were entitled to recover damages as specified in the bond, which stipulated that the railroad company, upon assessment of damages related to the right of way, would compensate them according to their respective interests. They argued that the railroad failed to honor this obligation by not paying the assessed damages, thus seeking a legal judgment to enforce the payment stipulated in the bond.	The railroad company argued that the legal instrument in question was structured in a manner that required all obligees to join in the lawsuit, as the obligation was a joint one, rather than several. The company emphasized that without the necessary assertions regarding the interests of the other obligees included in the declarations, the claims were insufficient for recovery. Essentially, they maintained that each plaintiff could not individually recover without showing the total damages assessed for all obligees, which were necessary for a proportionate distribution of the $3,000 penalty.

John J. Manion was involved in a legal case against The People of the State of Illinois concerning an indictment for violating the dram-shop act. The relevant events occurred in Jefferson County, Illinois, during the May term of 1887, when a grand jury returned an indictment against Manion, stating it was a "true bill." Following this, Manion filed motions to quash the indictment, arguing that the grand jury was improperly selected and that the requisite number of grand jurors did not vote in favor of the indictment. His motions were contested in the Circuit Court, presided over by Judge C. C. Boggs. The court overruled Manion's motions at various stages, eventually leading to a trial, where he was found guilty and fined. This led to an appeal questioning the legality of the grand jury's actions and the proceedings.	Manion's principal claims rested on two arguments: first, that the grand jury that indictments were returned by was not chosen in accordance with statutory requirements, as he contended the records failed to demonstrate they were selected by the proper authority. Second, he argued that insufficient jurors voted to support the indictment since at least twelve members did not concur with the finding. He sought to quash the indictment based on these grounds.	The People of the State of Illinois defended against Manion's claims by asserting that the grand jury selection, as certified by the county clerk, complied with statutory requirements, despite any record discrepancies. They contended that the grand jurors had not violated legal protocols since the selection's certification served as competent evidence. Additionally, they argued that the affidavits submitted by Manion did not substantiate his claim that the required number of jurors had not concurred in the indictment's finding.

In December 1827, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case arising from the Clark circuit court involving Richardson and Haggatt, the executors of the estate of R. Crow, who had passed away, acting as appellants against Samuel Prevo, the appellee. The case stemmed from a request to restrain the collection of a legal judgment through an injunction. The circuit court dismissed the request for injunction before the defense was presented and subsequently issued a judgment against the appellants and their securities, requiring them to pay the original judgment amount along with interest and damages. The appellants appealed this decision, claiming errors in the court's handling of the injunction and the judgment against them.	The plaintiffs (Richardson and Haggatt) argued that the injunction should not have been dissolved prior to a full answer being heard because their bill presented sufficient equity. They contended that the circuit court erred in rendering a judgment against both the principals and the securities for the total amount originally enjoined, including damages and costs.	The defendant (Samuel Prevo) maintained that the dissolution of the injunction was appropriate, as the bill lacked sufficient equity to warrant relief. He argued that any legal defense should have been raised prior to the judgment, and highlighted that the judgment against both the principals and securities for the full amount was a justified ruling.

The case "Wiley S. Scribner et al. v. Samuel B. Chase et al." was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court and decided on June 13, 1888. The events leading to this case took place in Cook County, Illinois, beginning with a bill in chancery filed on February 25, 1886. The plaintiffs, comprising the firm of Handy & Company, were engaged in providing abstracts of title to real estate. The key issue arose when Wiley S. Scribner, the Cook County Recorder of Deeds, issued a notice on February 17, 1886, in compliance with a resolution adopted by the Cook County Board of Commissioners. This resolution directed the recorder to deny access to all abstract firms seeking to use the office for their private business, particularly in making copies or abstracts of original records. The plaintiffs claimed that this action would obstruct their work and cause them irreparable harm. They sought an injunction against the defendants, including Scribner, to guarantee their legal right to access these records without obstruction.	The plaintiffs argued that they had an absolute legal right to access original instruments and records within the Cook County Recorder's office for the purpose of conducting their business. They contended that the resolution from the board of commissioners, which barred them from using the recorder's facilities, was unauthorized and would lead to significant damages. Thus, they requested the court to issue an injunction to prevent the defendants from interfering with their access and to allow their clerks to make abstracts in the same manner as before.	The defendants, including Scribner and the county commissioners, contended that under existing law prior to the new statutes in 1887, abstract firms did not have a right to access the original instruments for private gain. They argued that maintaining control over the records was necessary for the effective operation of the recorder's office and to uphold public interests. They sought to have the court affirm the validity of the resolution and maintained that their actions were lawful and justified.

In 1869, the case of Dudley R. Roundtree, Administrator, v. Marvin Baker, Administrator was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a debt action related to a contract executed on October 10, 1833, in Kentucky, concerning the sale of a slave named Eliza. Dudley Roundtree sold Eliza to Turner Roundtree for the price of $400, payable in installments. Following Dudley Roundtree's death, the plaintiff, as his administrator, attempted to collect the debt owed for the sale of the slave. The defendant, Marvin Baker, contested the claim by citing several defenses, including the statute of limitations and the argument that the contract was void due to the consideration failing as it involved a slave, which was illegal in Illinois. The case was tried in the Knox Circuit Court without a jury, and the court ruled in favor of the defendant, prompting the plaintiff to file for a reversal of the decision.	The plaintiff claimed that the contract entered into in Kentucky was valid and enforceable under Kentucky law at the time of its execution. The plaintiff argued that the sale of the slave, Eliza, was legal in Kentucky, and thus the debt incurred by the sale should be collectible in Illinois based on the principle of comity. The plaintiff also contended that the statute of limitations had not expired, as the action was brought within sixteen years of the cause of action accruing.	The defendant’s key arguments included the assertion that the statute of limitations barred the claim, and that the consideration for the contract had failed since it was based on the sale of a slave, which was contrary to Illinois law and public policy. The defendant also argued that since slavery was no longer legal in Kentucky, the obligation of the contract should be considered void.

In the year 1840, in Illinois, John Yarwood and his partners were involved in a contract for work on the Illinois and Michigan Canal. They wished to purchase a twenty-horsepower engine owned by Allen but in the possession of William H. Stow. Before purchasing, they asked Stow if he had any claims against the engine, and he claimed he had none. After this, they purchased the engine and contracted Stow to repair it. Although repairs valued at approximately $500 were made, Stow failed to complete the contract, retaining parts of the engine and converting them for his own use. Yarwood and his partners sought legal recourse, resulting in a replevin action that recovered other parts of the engine. During the court proceedings, Stow argued that he had expended money repairing the engine. However, the trial judge refused to allow the jury to consider whether the defendants were owed for these repairs as a set-off against damages claimed by Stow for the conversion of property. The jury ultimately awarded Stow $725.	The plaintiff, William H. Stow, claimed that the defendants, John Yarwood and his partners, wrongfully converted his property (the engine and its parts) for their own use. Stow argued that he had a right to possession of the property at the time the suit was brought, and sought damages for the conversion. He asserted that the defendants should not have been allowed to use their repair claims as a defense in the ruling against him.	The defendants contended that they were entitled to recoup the costs associated with the repairs they performed on the engine against any damages Stow claimed for the conversion of the engine. They argued that the judge erred by not allowing the jury to consider their claims of indebtedness based on the work done and that these should offset Stow’s claimed damages. The central argument was that mutual demands arose out of the same subject matter and could be adjusted within one action.

In the case of Thomas M. Campbell v. The People of the State of Illinois, the events took place in Jackson County, Illinois, with legal proceedings beginning in December 1882. The indictment against Thomas Campbell was based on two counts: receiving stolen goods knowing they were stolen, and unlawfully concealing stolen property with knowledge of its stolen nature. After a hung jury in a trial at the March term of 1883, Campbell was retried at the August term 1883. He asserted a special plea of autre fois acquit, referencing a previous acquittal in Perry County for the same charges; however, the court overruled this plea. Campbell was ultimately found guilty and sentenced to three years in penitentiary. His case raised significant legal issues regarding jurisdiction, specifically the local jurisdiction for trials concerning criminal offenses, and whether a prior acquittal could be used as a defense in a different county.	The plaintiff argued that Campbell had knowingly received and concealed stolen goods, thereby violating the relevant statutes. They contended that the separate counts in the indictment were valid under the law and sought a guilty verdict that would lead to a conviction for both charges of receiving and concealing stolen property.	Campbell's defense centered on the assertion that he had been previously acquitted of the same offenses in Perry County, thereby filing a plea of autre fois acquit. He contended that the court had erred in not allowing this plea and claimed that the evidence presented against him was insufficient for a conviction. Additionally, he requested that certain jury instructions when denied by the court should have been given which would have favored his defense.

In September 1872, the case of Thomas Mowbry et al. v. Mary Ann Mowbry et al. was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in LaSalle County, Illinois, following the death of the complainants' father, who had made provisions for his family in his will. The father bequeathed his daughter Caroline a cow and devised the remainder of his estate to his son Thomas, with a stipulation regarding the support of his widow and minor daughters, Mary Ann and Elizabeth Jane. After the father's death, the widow, now married to George Hartman, was appointed as guardian of the minor children but reportedly did not receive any assets from the estate for their support. The family lived on a quarter section of land owned by the father, and after two years, the widow’s dower was determined and divided, creating issues regarding the support of the minor children during that time. The guardian sought to recover costs incurred for the support of the children from the estate, prompting questions about the legal obligations of the mother, step-father, and Thomas regarding their maintenance.	The plaintiffs, represented by their guardian, claimed that Thomas Mowbry should be held responsible for the support of Mary Ann and Elizabeth Jane. They argued that the will implied a charge for the children's support on the estate and sought a decree to secure funds for their upbringing and education based on the reasonable costs incurred during this period.	Thomas Mowbry contended that the existing legal obligations did not require him to provide for the minors since the children were living with their step-father, George Hartman, who had not formally adopted them. He argued that the support of the minor children could not legally be charged against his share of the estate, as their mother had a duty to support them and that there was no sufficient evidence to classify Hartman as being in loco parentis to the children.

In September 1868, in Chicago, Illinois, the case of James Keating v. Bridget Keating unfolded in the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff, Bridget Keating, initiated legal proceedings against her husband, James Keating, seeking a divorce. The trial court granted Bridget a divorce decree and awarded her alimony, which included full ownership (fee) of 205 Third Avenue, a property belonging to James, as well as a monetary sum. James Keating appealed this decision, contesting the nature and extent of the alimony awarded, particularly the granting of the property fee, which he argued was erroneous based on claims that the property was acquired with Bridget’s money—a assertion that he contended was unfounded. Throughout the appellate process, the court examined the validity of the lower court's decision and the implications of alimony allocation in divorce cases.	Bridget Keating's primary claim was that the decree should grant her a substantial form of alimony, which she argued included the ownership of the property as she believed it was purchased with her funds. She sought to uphold the lower court’s decision that awarded her the fee of the property along with a monetary sum.	James Keating's defense centered on arguing that the alimony decree was improper, particularly the awarding of the fee to Bridget. He contended that the property was not bought with her money and thus there was no legal basis to divest him of his ownership. James requested that the appellate court reverse the lower court's decree, modifying the alimony to either provide Bridget with a life estate or an annuity rather than ownership stake.

In 1875, in Montgomery County, Illinois, the case of Anthony Almond et al. v. David T. Bonnell arose involving a dispute over land ownership. The plaintiff, David T. Bonnell, filed an ejectment action against defendants Anthony Almond and Alice C. Almond, claiming he was the rightful owner of the property in question based on a sheriff’s deed obtained through a prior judgment against Anthony Almond. The disputed land was previously patented by the United States to Robert Stanley in 1851, who died without heirs, leaving his land to his surviving family members. Title to the property eventually passed through quitclaim deeds to Anthony Almond and his wife, Alice. The case was heard without a jury, and the court rendered a judgment favoring Bonnell for ownership of the land, awarding him an undivided half in fee simple and the other half for life to Anthony Almond.	The plaintiff, David T. Bonnell, claimed that he held the rightful title to the land in question based on a sheriff’s deed that followed a court judgment against Anthony Almond. He asserted his full ownership rights and sought recovery of the property through the ejectment action, arguing that he was seized in fee simple of the entire land, despite the involved complexities regarding the chain of title and how the property was conveyed to the Almonds.	The defendants, Anthony and Alice C. Almond, contended that the lower court erred by granting Bonnell ownership of only half the property and the other half for the life of Anthony Almond. They argued that since Bonnell's declaration claimed the entire fee, it was inappropriate to render a judgment for a fractional interest. Additionally, they asserted that the title was vested in them as tenants by the entirety, preventing any sale without the assent of both spouses, thereby disputing the legitimacy of Bonnell's ownership claim.

In February 1880, John Beaird and Charles Schroeder, partners of Beaird & Company, filed a lawsuit against the Illinois & St. Louis Railroad & Coal Company in the Circuit Court of St. Clair County, Illinois. At that time, the railroad operated a line from Belleville, Illinois, to the Mississippi River bank across from St. Louis, Missouri, with a branch extending to the land of Becherer. The railroad had connections with twenty coal mines and transported coal daily from these mines. Beaird & Company operated two coal mines along the railroad's line and claimed that from February 1880 until the commencement of the lawsuit, the railroad transported 5,000,000 bushels of coal for them, charging two and a half cents per bushel. Beaird & Company argued that the railroad charged them the same rate for coal transported a shorter distance (eight miles) as for coal from the Becherer mines transported a longer distance (sixteen miles). They contended this constituted unfair discrimination, seeking damages of $5,000 for what they described as unjust treatment under common law. The initial ruling by the Circuit Court favored the plaintiffs, awarding them $1,550, prompting the defendant to appeal.	The plaintiffs asserted that the Illinois & St. Louis Railroad & Coal Company engaged in unjust discrimination by charging them the same transportation fee for a shorter distance as it charged other coal operators for a longer distance. They claimed that this practice resulted in significant financial harm, amounting to a total alleged damages of $5,000.	The defendant, Illinois & St. Louis Railroad & Coal Company, argued that under common law, carriers are not obligated to charge higher rates for longer distances as long as the rates are not extortionate. They claimed that distance alone should not dictate charges and contended that the absence of proof that the rates were unjust or extortionate negated the plaintiffs' claims. Thus, they sought to have the judgment of the lower court reversed.

In September 1867, Walter N. Woodruff and Jackson E. Woodruff purchased a lumber yard along the south branch of the Chicago River from John R. Thorne and Alexander L. Thorne. The sale included a side railroad track extending several hundred feet along the yard, for which the Woodruffs paid $525. However, they later discovered that the railroad track actually belonged to the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company. As a result, the Woodruffs were forced to return the property to the railroad company, leading to their loss. They initiated legal proceedings seeking to recover the money paid for the track, arguing that an implied warranty of title had been breached when the Thorne defendants sold them the property without rightful ownership. The case focuses on whether the defendants sold the track and whether they had the legal right to do so.	The plaintiffs, Walter N. Woodruff and Jackson E. Woodruff, claimed that they purchased a railroad track along with the lumber yard from the defendants, John R. Thorne and Alexander L. Thorne, under the assumption that the sellers owned the track. They alleged a breach of the implied warranty of title, seeking to recover the $525 they paid for the track after discovering that it belonged to the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company.	The defendants argued that they had owned the side railroad track and provided evidence, including testimony from a railroad representative, supporting their claim of ownership. They contended that any lack of clarity regarding ownership was not due to a breach of warranty but rather related to unsettled accounts with the railroad company. Thus, they requested that the case be dismissed, asserting that the sale did not constitute a breach.

The case of The Hartford Fire Insurance Company v. Nancy Wilcox took place in September 1870 in Lacón, Marshall County, Illinois. The case arose from an action of assumpsit based on a verbal contract to insure a building owned by the plaintiff, Nancy Wilcox. The plaintiff’s son, Levi Wilcox, acted on her behalf during discussions with Howard, who was a clerk in the insurance office where the purported contract was negotiated. The plaintiff argued that Howard had the authority to bind the defendant to the insurance contract. However, it was revealed during the trial that Howard was merely a clerk under the authority of a commission held by Green and Black, with Black having died prior to this event. The court excluded important evidence regarding the written authority of the agents involved, which ultimately became a significant point of contention in the appeal process.	The plaintiff, Nancy Wilcox, claimed that a valid verbal insurance contract existed between her and The Hartford Fire Insurance Company, based on her discussions with Howard, whom she believed to be authorized to act on behalf of the insurer. She sought to recover damages for the alleged breach of this insurance contract.	The defendant, The Hartford Fire Insurance Company, contended that no valid contract was established due to the lack of authority on Howard's part, claiming he was merely a clerk without binding powers. They argued that the court erred in excluding evidence that could demonstrate the limitations of Howard’s authority and supported their motion for a new trial based on these exclusions and proper authority documentation.

In the case of Joseph J. Hunter v. James Mathewson et al., the legal proceedings took place in 1888 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Joseph J. Hunter, a live stock commission merchant based in Chicago, and James Mathewson and his business partner Haidle, who were engaged in farming and stock trading in Stanton, Nebraska. The dispute arose from the shipment of cattle on May 2, 1885, by a third party, C. Abrams, who purchased the cattle from the plaintiffs. Abrams shipped the cattle to Hunter for sale, while he owed the plaintiffs a portion of the purchase price, covered by a draft drawn on Hunter. The plaintiffs alleged that Hunter withheld proceeds from the sale, claiming a lien for his advances to Abrams without recognizing the plaintiffs' claim on the proceeds from the livestock sale. The case revolved around the nature of the transaction between the plaintiffs and Abrams and whether Hunter had notice of the plaintiffs' rights before selling the cattle.	The plaintiffs, Mathewson and Haidle, claimed that they sold cattle to Abrams and provided him with a draft on Hunter for the remaining balance. They sought to recover $1,311.69, asserting that they retained a right to the proceeds of the cattle sale since Hunter had no prior notice of any claims against the cattle before they were sold. The plaintiffs argued that the agreement constituted a valid sale, which entitled them to the funds from Hunter.	Hunter's defense rested on his assertion of a lien for advances he had made to Abrams, stating he was unaware of the plaintiffs' claims until after the sale. He contended that the factual arrangements between himself and Abrams justified the withholding of the proceeds to cover the debt owed to him by Abrams. Additionally, he argued that the court erred in excluding evidence that could demonstrate an agreement with Abrams regarding the payment from proceeds, thereby necessitating the jury's examination of whether he was a bona fide purchaser of the cattle.

Nathan P. Sanford filed a slander lawsuit against John V. Gaddis in December 1851 in Illinois. The case originated from a trial held on February 10, 1850, at the office of a justice of the peace in Fairview, Fulton County, where Sanford was the defendant and Gaddis was the plaintiff. During that trial, Sanford was sworn as a witness, with Gaddis consenting to his testimony without a preliminary oath. Gaddis allegedly made slanderous statements about Sanford in conversations concerning his testimony, claiming that Sanford had "perjured himself" and "swore false" in connection to the judicial proceedings. The Circuit Court dismissed several counts of Sanford's declaration due to an insufficient legal basis, leading to an appeal from Sanford regarding the court's ruling on selected counts, specifically the first, fifth, and seventh counts.	Sanford's primary argument was that Gaddis's statements constituted slander, specifically charges of false swearing during his testimony as a witness in the previous judicial proceedings. His legal request included the reversal of the lower court's decision that dismissed several counts of his declaration. Sanford contended that the comments made by Gaddis were actionable per se and did not require further elaboration regarding the context of their utterance or the jurisdiction of the justice involved in the original trial.	Gaddis's defense centered around the claim that the counts in Sanford's declaration were insufficient in law, arguing that the jurisdiction of the justice and the validity of the testifying process had not been properly established in Sanford's allegations. Gaddis maintained that the language used in his statements did not clearly impute perjury to Sanford, and therefore, he should not be held liable for slander as described in Sanford's complaint.

In the case of Emeline C. Ferry et al. v. Richard B. Moore, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, in 1882, Richard B. Moore entered into a written contract with Aaron D. Ferry to supply materials and labor to erect a building on a lot owned by Emeline C. Ferry, Aaron's wife. The contract specified a total payment of $3,123.30 for the completed building, with portions due during construction. Throughout the project, Emeline was actively involved, prepared the plans, and was present during construction, despite the title being in her name. The building was completed around December 25, 1882, after some changes requested by Aaron, leading to additional costs. However, Aaron Ferry, having claimed ownership, turned out to be insolvent without the means to pay Moore's claim. After Aaron’s death, Moore petitioned for a mechanic's lien against Emeline and others, asserting that Emeline should be estopped from denying liability as her husband acted as her agent under which the contract was made. Emeline and others contested this, leading to a legal proceeding.	Richard B. Moore claimed that the contract for the construction was effectively his and Emeline’s, as Aaron acted as her agent. He alleged that Emeline should be responsible for the outstanding balance of $560.19 owed to him as he had relied on representations that Aaron was the owner of the property. Moore requested that a mechanic's lien be established on the property to secure his claim, ultimately asserting that Emeline’s conduct amounted to an acknowledgment of Aaron acting on her behalf.	Emeline C. Ferry and the other defendants contended that the contract was solely between Moore and Aaron D. Ferry. They argued that Moore gave exclusive credit to Aaron and that Emeline was not liable for any payments because she had no transaction with Moore. They also claimed that after realizing Emeline's role as the true owner, Moore chose to pursue Aaron only, thus, they should be estopped from seeking relief against Emeline. The defendants requested the dismissal of Moore's petition.

William Barnes was convicted of horse theft in June 1855 at the Massac Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Parish. The case arises from the allegation that Barnes stole a horse owned by Dougal McGinnis, although McGinnis was also referred to as Dugald McInnis. The conflicting names led to questions about the adequacy of the indictment, but the court determined that the names were similar enough that jurors would likely not distinguish between them due to the principle of idem sonans. The court noted that sufficient evidence was present to prove McGinnis's ownership of the horse, especially since he had general ownership rights illustrated by actions like riding the horse and keeping it at an inn. The special property rights of the innkeeper, William Shuts, were also acknowledged but were not deemed sufficient to disprove McGinnis's ownership.	The plaintiff, William Barnes, argued that the indictment for horse theft was invalid due to the variance in names—claiming that the prosecution needed to prove that the horse belonged to the specific name stated in the indictment. He sought a judgment in his favor by challenging the adequacy of the evidence presented to support the ownership claim.	The People asserted that the names Dougal McGinnis and Dugald McInnis were sufficiently similar under the idem sonans rule, which means that the slight variance in names does not undermine the prosecution's case. They argued that there was adequate evidence of McGinnis's ownership based on his general possession and actions, and they contended that the court had properly rejected Barnes’s proposed jury instruction.

In November 1850, Christian Keaggy (the appellant) was involved in a legal case against Andrew Hite (the appellee) in the Marion Circuit Court, Illinois. The dispute arose over a promissory note and mortgage executed by Keaggy in favor of Marshal Wautland, which was subsequently assigned to Hite. The key issue at trial was whether the note and mortgage were delivered to Keaggy as a pledge for a debt or were intended to be canceled upon a future settlement. The evidence presented included testimony from a single witness who suggested that the note and mortgage were given as security. However, this evidence was contradicted by two other witnesses who confirmed that Hite had been asked by Keaggy to return the documents and had refused, indicating that the documents were received as part of a financial obligation. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of Hite, awarding him $200, which led Keaggy to appeal the decision.	Keaggy contended that the promissory note and mortgage were delivered to him as a pledge to secure a debt owed to Hite. He argued that the actions of the defendant indicated an acknowledgment that the documents should be returned. Keaggy sought to overturn the jury's verdict based on insufficient evidence supporting Hite's claim to retain the documents, positing that he was entitled to the full value of the note and mortgage due to their conversion.	Hite's defense rested on the assertion that the note and mortgage were delivered to him as part of a settlement for money owed by Keaggy. He presented witness testimony indicating that Hite believed he needed to account for the documents as they were related to a financial obligation owed to him by Keaggy. Hite contended that the jury's original verdict was justified based on the evidence, and he sought to uphold the decision of the lower court.

In the case of Richard L. Boggs v. Adolph Bindskoff et al., which took place in November 1859 in Illinois, the appellant, Richard L. Boggs, faced a legal action initiated by the appellees. The case stemmed from an attachment that was filed against Boggs by Bindskoff and others. The appellees claimed in their affidavit that Boggs was concealing himself and evading legal officers, making it impossible to serve him with regular process. The attachment was filed on April 22, 1858, and was enforced against Boggs’s property shortly thereafter. During the trial at the May term in 1859, a jury found in favor of the plaintiff after hearing evidence, but Boggs did not appear when damages were assessed. An amount of $2,120.93 was awarded to the appellees. The case revolved around the legality of the attachment and whether Boggs had indeed been avoiding service or if he had legitimate business outside of his county.	The plaintiff claimed that Richard L. Boggs was deliberately evading legal process by concealing himself, which justified the issuance of an attachment to secure payment of the debt owed. The primary legal request was to have the attachment upheld and to recover damages amounting to $2,120.93, as determined by the jury’s verdict.	The defendant, Richard L. Boggs, argued through a plea in abatement that he had not concealed himself or evaded service of process, asserting that he had been conducting legitimate business and was not obligated to remain in Clay County to facilitate legal actions against him. Boggs contended that the evidence did not support the plaintiffs' claims of absconding, emphasizing that there was no intention to evade creditors or legal obligations.

In January 1877, the case of Thomas Snell et al. v. Almond B. Ives took place in Illinois, specifically in McLean County, with the Illinois Supreme Court presiding over the matter. The dispute arose from an action of assumpsit initiated by Almond B. Ives, acting on behalf of Samuel T. Young and Abner S. Bacus, against the partners of Snell, Taylor & Co. The case centered around the financial dealings of the Lafayette, Bloomington and Mississippi Railroad Company, which had incurred debts including a $100,000 subscription issued by the township of Bloomington. In November 1870, Ives, who was both the supervisor of Bloomington and a director of the railroad company, delivered bonds related to this subscription. Despite a resolution passed in January 1870 to address the payment of interest coupons on these bonds, the railroad company lacked the necessary funds to fulfill these obligations, leading to Ives loaning money to the company. Subsequently, Snell, Taylor & Co. acquired all the assets and assumed the debts of the railroad company for $1,300,000. Ives sued Snell, Taylor & Co. for the owed amount, but the defendants alleged fraud on Ives' part. The initial judgment favored the plaintiff, prompting an appeal from the railroad company.	The plaintiff, Almond B. Ives, claimed that he was owed payment by the Lafayette, Bloomington and Mississippi Railroad Company for a loan he provided to cover unpaid interest coupons on bonds originally issued for the company’s subscription. He argued that Snell, Taylor & Co., having purchased the company's assets and assumed its debts, was liable for this payment. Ives sought to recover the amount due to him based on the agreement that transferred all debt obligations to Snell, Taylor & Co.	The defendants, particularly Thomas Snell and his partners, contended that Ives had committed fraud in the transaction. They argued that Ives had misled them regarding the financial status of the railroad company and the legitimacy of the claims he was making. They sought to overturn the initial judgment by discrediting Ives' claims and the validity of his loan to the company.

Michael Cunningham filed a case against Thomas W. Ferry and others in September 1874 in Cook County, Illinois. The case centered around a mechanics' lien for lumber that Cunningham had provided to Ferry for the construction of a house on Ferry's property. Cunningham alleged that the lumber, delivered within a specified timeframe, was used in the building of the house. The primary legal issue concerned whether Cunningham had properly filed the lien and whether there were any substantial variances between the allegations made and the evidence presented. The court examined the evidence and determined that there was no significant variance that would merit a reversal of the decision, asserting that an implied contract existed due to the circumstances surrounding the lumber's delivery and use.	Cunningham's main arguments were based on the enforcement of a mechanics' lien for the lumber he supplied for the construction of a house. He claimed that the lumber was provided at the owner's request, was used for the house, and that the lien was filed within the legally stipulated timeframe after the last payment was due. Cunningham sought to affirm the lien and secure payment for the lumber based on the implied contract.	The defendants, led by Thomas W. Ferry, argued that there were discrepancies between the allegations and the evidence presented. They contended that Cunningham failed to institute the lien within the required six-month period after the last payment was due for the lumber and that his claims were not supported by adequate evidence. They also challenged the validity of Cunningham's petition regarding the timeline of the payments and the filing of the lien.

In 1872, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Frank Wolf et al. and Catherina Boettcher regarding a seizure of goods. The town of Jefferson, alongside Frank Wolf, who served as the town’s constable, executed a judgment against Frederick Boettcher (the husband of Catherina Boettcher) to satisfy a debt owed to the town. The town claimed that the goods seized were the property of Frederick, allowing them to be taken under the execution. Catherina Boettcher argued that the goods were actually hers, leading to a trial where the plaintiff asserted their rightful claim. The defendants did not offer a plea in abatement but claimed justification based on the execution against Frederick. The trial resulted in a verdict against Frank Wolf and the town of Jefferson, leading to the appeal due to the belief that the town should not be held jointly liable for the actions of the constable regarding the seizure of the appellant's goods.	Catherina Boettcher, the plaintiff, claimed that her goods were wrongfully seized by the constable under the town’s direction during the execution of a judgment against her husband. She argued that the seizure constituted a trespass (de bonis asportatis) and sought damages for the unlawful action taken against her property.	The defendants, represented by Frank Wolf and the town of Jefferson, contended that the execution was properly executed based on the judgment against Frederick Boettcher, which deemed the goods subject to seizure. They argued that the town should not be held jointly liable in trespass with the constable under these circumstances, asserting that there was no evidence of the town's interference or assent to the officer's actions.

In 1884, in Lexington, Illinois, David H. Vandolah, a banker, was involved in a legal dispute with Addison Kanouse concerning a deposit made by Uzziel Kanouse, Addison's father, with Vandolah's banking firm, Vandolah & Harness. Uzziel had previously been found liable for violating a municipal ordinance, resulting in a judgment against him which was returned unsatisfied. Subsequently, the town of Lexington issued a writ of garnishment against Vandolah and his partner to recover the amount owed. Addison contested the garnishment, claiming ownership of the $400 deposit, which was credited to him. A trial was held resulting in a judgment against Vandolah and Harness for $194.60 in favor of Uzziel, which Addison appealed. The appellate court confirmed the judgment. The core of the case hinged on whether the earlier garnishment proceedings barred Addison’s subsequent claim to recover the full amount of the deposit.	Addison Kanouse, the plaintiff, claims ownership of the $400 deposit held by Vandolah’s bank, arguing that he is entitled to the full amount. He contends that the previous garnishment ruling does not preclude his claim since he was not the subject of that order. He seeks to recover the full amount of his deposit plus interest from Vandolah.	David H. Vandolah, the defendant, asserts that the prior garnishment and subsequent judgment against him establish a res judicata, barring Addison's current claim. He maintains that the earlier adjudication determined the rights concerning the deposit, and therefore, Addison cannot successfully litigate his claim. The defense emphasizes that they only owe the amount equivalent to the prior judgment and not the full deposit.

In the case of Albert W. Jansen v. Cornelia B. Grimshaw, which took place in Quincy, Illinois, the dispute arose from a promissory note executed on February 1, 1881, by three brothers—Albert W. Jansen, Frederick G. Jansen, and Charles C. Jansen—under the firm name F. W. Jansen & Son. The plaintiff, Cornelia B. Grimshaw, lent the brothers $2000. Albert withdrew from the firm in November 1881, but Grimshaw was allegedly unaware of this change. The note was renewed in February 1883, but payments ceased when the firm made an assignment in February 1886. Grimshaw filed an action against Jansen and his brothers to recover the full debt, leading to multiple legal maneuvers, including a request for the case to be moved to a Federal court. A judgment by default was entered against Frederick and Charles Jansen after they withdrew their pleas. Subsequently, the case was remanded back to state court, where Grimshaw successfully petitioned to vacate the judgment against the other two defendants. Several legal nuances were explored concerning the validity of the judgments and the continuation of partnership obligations after Albert's withdrawal.	The plaintiff, Cornelia B. Grimshaw, claimed that Albert W. Jansen was liable for the amount on the promissory note, asserting that she had given credit to the firm while Albert was a partner, and she had no notice of his withdrawal. Grimshaw requested the court to affirm the judgment against Jansen and recover the amount owed, which she believed was not discharged by the renewal note she had accepted.	Albert W. Jansen contested the plaintiff's claims by arguing that he was no longer a partner when the new note was executed and that he should not be held liable for debts incurred after his withdrawal. He also argued that the judgment against the other two Jansen brothers should bar recovery against him, as it constituted a joint obligation. Jansen requested the court to dismiss the claims against him based on these defenses.

In the case of L. S. Holderman et al. v. Edward C. Gray, decided on October 31, 1889, the events took place in Paxton, Illinois. The case centered around a dispute regarding ownership of four lots originally owned by James Mix. The lots were sold through a contract to J. R. Francis, who later transferred this contract to Shepardson. In 1867, Edward C. Gray acquired the contract and subsequently took possession of the lots, paying off the purchase price. In 1871, James Mix conveyed the property to Gray's wife, Frankie Y. Gray. On December 10, 1875, the Grays conveyed the lots to Charles H. Wyman. The Grays contended that the conveyance was part of an agreement wherein Wyman would hold the title for the benefit of the Grays depending on Frankie’s health; if she recovered, the deed would revert to her, and if she died, it would go to Edward. However, the defendants, who were Wyman's heirs, denied the existence of such an agreement, claiming the conveyance was straightforward and without trust. The court considered the evidence around these claims and the validity of the deed, particularly focusing on whether consideration was transferred.	The plaintiff, Edward C. Gray, argued that Wyman held the title to the lots in trust for himself and his wife Frankie, based on an agreement that if Frankie recovered from her poor health, the property would be returned to her. If she died, it would go back to Edward or anyone he directed. Gray contended that since Wyman failed to make any payment for the lots and did not possess or pay taxes on them afterward, the conveyance was effectively a trust without a lawful basis to stand as a sale.	The defendants, the heirs of Charles H. Wyman, asserted that no trust existed because they believed there was no valid agreement between Wyman and the Grays, and thus the conveyance was valid without any preceding trust. They argued that since any purported agreement to hold the property in trust would not meet the Statute of Frauds requirements without being in writing, the case lacked the necessary legal foundation to support Gray's claims.

The case of "The People, ex rel. the Warsaw and Rockford Railroad Company, v. R. W. Rickey" was addressed in April 1858 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It took place in Illinois, involving a legal dispute between the Warsaw and Rockford Railroad Company and R. W. Rickey. The nature of the case revolved around the railroad company's application for an alternative writ of mandamus, which is a court order compelling a party to execute a certain action, typically one that that party is legally obligated to perform. This case illustrates the legal mechanisms used by a corporation to enforce compliance with its rights or obligations in a matter deemed important for its operations.	The Warsaw and Rockford Railroad Company, as the plaintiff, sought an alternative writ of mandamus to compel R. W. Rickey to perform a duty or act as prescribed by law. The plaintiff likely argued that it had given the required notice of intent to apply for the writ, and thus was entitled to the court's intervention to ensure compliance from the defendant.	R. W. Rickey, as the defendant, may have raised arguments challenging the provision of the duty or obligation being enforced, possibly questioning the legitimacy of the mandamus application or the necessity of complying with the plaintiff's request. However, specific details on the defenses presented are not provided in the description.

In January 1874, the case of James H. Lewis v. John D’Arcy was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over a chattel mortgage involving property previously owned by Owen Sullivan. Lewis, the mortgagee, sought to reclaim possession of the property after it was levied upon by D’Arcy, acting as a constable, under two writs of attachment against the mortgagor. According to the terms of the mortgage, the mortgagor was to retain possession until the debt matured, unless the mortgagee felt "unsafe or insecure," at which point he could take immediate possession. The court examined whether Lewis had the right to reclaim the property in light of the levy and determined that the mortgage provisions allowed him to do so, as the conditions of the mortgage were deemed breached. Ultimately, the court recognized the validity of the mortgage contract and concluded that the mortgagee's right to reclaim the property superseded the constable's claim against it.	The plaintiff, James H. Lewis, claimed that he had the right to reclaim possession of the mortgaged property after it was wrongfully levied upon by John D’Arcy. Lewis argued that the mortgage contained a clause allowing him to take immediate possession if he felt unsafe regarding the debt, which was justified in this case due to the impending sale of the property resulting from the levy. He requested the court to affirm his right to reclaim the property in replevin.	John D’Arcy, the defendant, contended that he had a lawful claim to the property through the execution of the writs against the mortgagor. His argument centered on the idea that the mortgagor's possession granted them an interest subject to levy, which he believed should prevail over the mortgagee's rights. D’Arcy sought to uphold the legitimacy of the levy as valid and prevent Lewis from reclaiming the property.

In June 1853, in Illinois, the case "The People, &c., on the Exchange Bank, v. Thomas H. Campbell, Auditor, &c." arose when the Exchange Bank attempted to comply with the state’s banking regulations. The plaintiff, represented by T. S. Hayes, contended that on the first Monday in July 1853, they prepared a full statement of the bank's affairs as mandated by law. The statement was verified and published in a Chicago newspaper as required. However, due to an unfortunate delay, the statement was not deposited in the post office until July 19, 1853, and was received by the state auditor, Thomas H. Campbell, on July 21, 1853. The auditor refused to accept and file the statement since it was not received by the legally mandated deadline of July 20, insisting that this refusal led to the forfeiture of the bank's franchise. The court was asked to issue a mandamus to compel the auditor to file the report.	The plaintiff claimed that the Exchange Bank had complied with all necessary legal requirements except for the delivery timeline, which was affected by circumstances beyond their control. They requested that the court commands the auditor to accept and file their quarterly report, asserting that the forfeiture of the bank's franchise should not be enforced due to the delayed receipt.	The defendant, Thomas H. Campbell, acknowledged the facts presented by the plaintiff. He admitted that if the statement had reached him by the 20th, despite delays in mail service, he would have accepted it. His defense rested on the notion that the law mandates strict compliance with the reporting timeline, and since the auditor did not receive the statement on or before the specified date, he had no discretion to accept it post-deadline. He argued that the forfeiture of the bank's franchise was warranted due to this failure.

In September 1867, the case "Henry A. Mix v. Melville Beach et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Lee County, Illinois, stemming from a series of land transactions beginning in 1848. Josiah B. Williams sold property to Henry A. Mix, who then entered into agreements to sell the land to Jacob W. Thayer and subsequently transferred it to John E. Pearl. Pearl eventually assigned his interest to James W. Johnston, who sold the property to Melville Beach. Beach entered possession of the land and made improvements but did not receive the deed as the final payment was never made. Mix claimed a forfeiture of the contract due to the outstanding payment. The case was initiated when Beach sought enforcement of the contract against Mix, who had failed to procure the necessary legal title to the land from Williams at the time of the contract. Throughout the proceedings, questions of contract performance, proper parties, and compliance with legal obligations arose.	The plaintiffs, comprising Melville Beach and others, argued that they were entitled to specific performance of the contract with Henry A. Mix. They claimed that they had made payments towards the purchase price and sought a decree to compel Mix to convey the property to them, as Mix had failed to fulfill his part of the agreement by providing the deed. The plaintiffs contended that they were ready to pay the remaining balance in accordance with the contract terms and requested the court enforce the agreement.	The defendant, Henry A. Mix, contended that there had been a forfeiture of the contract because his co-defendant had not made the final payment on time. Mix argued he was unable to convey the property to Beach because he lacked legal title to it, as he had not secured a deed from Williams. Additionally, he contested the inclusion of Johnston's heirs as co-plaintiffs, arguing they had no vested interest in the case. Mix sought a reversal of the lower court’s decree that favored the plaintiffs.

William Dickhut filed a case against Thomas Durrell in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1849. The dispute arose from a contract where Durrell agreed to raft 110,000 feet of lumber, owned by Dickhut and Robert Bennison, from Hill’s mill on the Wisconsin River to the city of Quincy, for a payment of $370 by Dickhut upon delivery. The case reached trial after Dickhut claimed that Durrell failed to perform his obligations under the contract. Durrell contended that he was ready to deliver the lumber but Dickhut did not provide it as agreed. The initial trial took place in March 1842, where the jury ruled in favor of Dickhut, awarding him $284.25 in damages. Throughout the case, Durrell attempted to advance multiple defenses, but the court ultimately upheld the previous judgments without addressing the merits of several of the issues raised due to procedural errors in the bill of exceptions filed by Durrell.	Dickhut's claims centered around Durrell's failure to raft and deliver the contracted lumber as stipulated in their agreement. He argued that Durrell had not fulfilled his contractual obligations and thus sought damages for the breach of contract. The claims contended that Durrell failed to execute his end of the arrangement, resulting in the plaintiff's financial loss.	Durrell's primary defense argued that he was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract but that Dickhut failed to provide the lumber at the appropriate time. Additionally, he posited several procedural objections and claimed that previous rulings, including the jury instructions and demurrers, were improperly handled by the court. Durrell contended that the errors in these rulings should lead to a re-evaluation of the judgment against him.

The case "William L. Hambleton v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. Levi Young" was decided in June 1867 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The action arose in the Circuit Court of Pulaski County under Judge John Olney. William L. Hambleton, the appellant, was subject to an information in the nature of a quo warranto, which is a legal procedure used to challenge an individual's right to hold a public office. The process commenced when the court granted leave for a party to file this information, and a notice was sent to Hambleton, but he did not appear in court. A rule was entered requiring him to respond, but it was not served properly. Following the affidavit alleging that the rule was served, judgment of ouster was rendered against Hambleton for failing to comply. The case raised questions about the court's jurisdiction, specifically whether the proper legal processes were followed to bring Hambleton into the court system.	The plaintiff, represented by Levi Young, argued that the court had sufficiently notified William L. Hambleton of the actions being taken against him and had the legal authority to require a plea from him. They sought to have Hambleton ousted from his position based on the failure to respond to the court's rule.	William L. Hambleton, through his legal team, contended that the court lacked jurisdiction to enter the rule to plead since he had not been formally brought into the court. They argued that the notice he received did not constitute proper service of process and that without this, the court could not render a judgment against him.

In the case of Chicago, Burlington & Quincy R. R. Co. v. John Stafford, the incident occurred on June 11, 1883, in Peoria, Illinois. John Stafford was employed as a switch-man at the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad, working alongside engineer Robert Mack. They were engaged in switching operations when an accident transpired. Mack failed to stop the engine in time while coupling a passenger car, leading to an impact that caused Stafford to be caught between the locomotive and the car, resulting in severe injuries, including fractures to both femurs and other bodily harm. The case revolved around the allegations that Mack was negligent and incompetent as an engineer, with the plaintiff asserting that the railroad company was aware of Mack’s deficiencies but retained him in service, thus making the company liable for Stafford's injuries.	The plaintiff, John Stafford, argued that Robert Mack, the engineer, was habitually careless and unskilled in operating the engine, which ultimately led to the accident that caused his significant injuries. Stafford claimed that the railroad company had prior knowledge of Mack’s incompetence and negligence and that he, Stafford, was unaware of these issues. He sought damages for the injuries sustained, arguing that the company’s negligence in retaining an unfit employee resulted in his suffering.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy R. R. Co., contended that both Stafford and Mack were fellow servants under the same employer and thus argued that Stafford could not recover damages for injuries caused by the negligence of another servant unless the company itself had been negligent. They asserted that Stafford had knowledge of Mack's operating practices, implying he accepted the associated risks. The defendant maintained that there was insufficient evidence to hold the company responsible for the accident.

In the case of I. R. Snow v. A. J. Wiggin, which was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court on June 14, 1886, the lawsuit centers around a promissory note executed on March 27, 1883, by John Iglehardt for the sum of twenty dollars. The agreement stipulated repayment six months after the date without interest if paid timely, and an eight percent interest charge thereafter. The suit was initiated by I. R. Snow against A. J. Wiggin, who acted as the indorser of the note. Initially, a Justice of the Peace trial favored Wiggin after he denied endorsing the note under oath. Snow appealed the decision to the Circuit Court, which also ruled in favor of Wiggin, prompting this appeal. Key individuals involved include I. R. Snow (the appellant), A. J. Wiggin (the appellee), John Iglehardt (the maker of the note), and several bank officers who testified about the handwriting. The case resulted in multiple claims of error, particularly focusing on the exclusion of evidence, jury instructions, and the validation of the endorsement.	The plaintiff, I. R. Snow, argued that the court erred in denying admission of crucial evidence, which he believed was necessary to prove that A. J. Wiggin had endorsed the note. Snow sought a new trial on the grounds that the jury had not been correctly instructed regarding the legal implications of Wiggin's potential indorsement, arguing that the jury should find Wiggin liable regardless of his claims regarding knowledge of the endorsement.	The defendant, A. J. Wiggin, maintained that he did not endorse the note and argued that the trial court's decisions regarding evidence and jury instructions were appropriate. He contended that there was no evidence supporting a request for the jury to consider Wiggin's liability, as he explicitly denied signing the note. Wiggin emphasized the absence of conflicting evidence regarding his endorsement.

In the case of Joseph Gartside v. The City of East St. Louis, filed in January 1867, a legal dispute arose surrounding an ordinance enacted by the city of East St. Louis that mandated individuals hauling stone coal through the city to first obtain a license. Joseph Gartside, the plaintiff, was heavily involved in the coal industry, employing approximately sixteen four-horse teams for transporting coal from a depot in the city to a boat on the Mississippi River, which then shipped it to St. Louis. Gartside contended that the ordinance was unreasonable and infringed on his ability to conduct business. The case was brought in St. Clair Circuit Court, where Gartside sought an injunction to prevent the enforcement of the ordinance and alleged that it imposed an undue burden on his coal transportation activities. The city's charter allowed it to regulate the vehicles used for transportation within the city, leading to the ordinance in question. After the circuit court dismissed his bill, Gartside appealed the decision.	Joseph Gartside claimed that the ordinance requiring a license to haul coal was unreasonable and an infringement upon his trade rights. He argued that the ordinance was not authorized under the city's charter and sought an injunction to prevent the city from penalizing him for failing to comply with the licensing requirement. Gartside sought relief in the form of a ruling that the city could not enforce this license requirement, which he viewed as a restriction on his ability to conduct his business of transporting coal.	The City of East St. Louis, through its legal representatives, defended the ordinance by asserting that it was authorized under the city's charter, which grants the common council the power to control vehicles conveying loads within the city. The city contended that the ordinance was reasonable and necessary to maintain the streets in good condition due to the wear caused by heavy coal wagons. They argued that the licensing requirement was akin to similar regulatory practices in other areas, insisting that such a requirement was necessary for public welfare and the upkeep of city infrastructure and that it did not constitute an unlawful restraint on trade.

In 1877, in Randolph County, Illinois, Abijah Leavitte was involved in a legal dispute against Randolph County regarding the obstruction of a public highway. The case originated when the prosecution commenced before a justice of the peace and subsequently escalated to the circuit court, where a jury trial was conducted. The jury found against Leavitte, leading to a judgment rendered by the circuit court. Leavitte's counsel appealed this judgment, asserting that errors were made by the court in its instructions to the jury. However, the appeal did not include any evidence from the trial itself, which hampered the ability of the Illinois Supreme Court to assess the validity of the instructions given. The court pointed out the importance of presenting sufficient facts when appealing on instructional issues and concluded that without this evidence, it could not reasonably determine whether any legal errors had occurred.
