The plaintiff, Abijah Leavitte, claimed that the jury verdict against him was reached in error due to faulty jury instructions provided by the circuit court. Leavitte's legal team requested that the Supreme Court review the trial court's decisions regarding which jury instructions were given and which were refused, arguing that these instructions were improperly handled and ultimately impacted the jury's verdict against him.	The defendant, Randolph County, maintained that the circuit court correctly instructed the jury and that no errors occurred regarding the admission or rejection of testimony. They argued that the absence of evidence in the records regarding the facts presented during the trial made it impossible to assess or contest the appropriateness of the instructions given to the jury or those refused.

In the case of James G. Gill v. William Hopkins, decided on June 12, 1886, the events took place in Clay County, Illinois. The controversy arose from two promissory notes related to a loan. James G. Gill (the appellant) was allegedly a guarantor on a note for $50 that was presented to William Hopkins (the appellee) for a loan. The situation began when Sackrider, who was involved in the loan transaction, approached Hopkins with a note signed only by himself, asking to borrow money against it. This note was unsigned by Gill at the time but was later dated by Hopkins before the money was loaned. The absence of Gill’s signature led to a legal dispute when Sackrider vanished, presumably having drowned, leaving Gill to challenge the validity of the note he claimed he did not execute. The case reached the Illinois Appellate Court following a ruling from the Circuit Court of Clay County, where Judge C. C. Boggs presided.	The plaintiff, William Hopkins, claimed that Gill was liable for the $50 promissory note on which his name appeared. Hopkins argued that the addition of the date to the note upon its acceptance was not a significant alteration of the document's original terms. He maintained that Gill's involvement as a guarantor for Sackrider's loan was valid and that Gill should bear responsibility for the debt outlined in the note.	The defendant, James G. Gill, contended that he did not sign the note and had not authorized anyone to sign on his behalf. He claimed that the addition of the date by Hopkins constituted a material alteration that invalidated the note, thus he should not be held liable for its enforcement. Gill provided sworn statements denying the execution of the note and contested the legitimacy of any claims against him.

In the case of Daniel Paullin v. T. Judson Hale, which occurred in Knox County, Illinois, the action began in February 1866 when T. Judson Hale filed an ejectment suit against Daniel Paullin. The dispute centered around the ownership of a particular tract of land that Hale claimed. The trial found that Hale was in possession of the land, and a verdict was issued in his favor, affirming his fee title to the premises. Paullin subsequently appealed the judgment, arguing that the court had erred in its refusal to provide specific jury instructions he had requested and by not granting his motion for a new trial on the basis that the evidence did not support Hale's claim. During the trial, Hale substantiated his claim with a series of deeds leading back to the original patent, alongside proof of property tax payments over several years, while Paullin attempted to prove his own claim to the land with documentation of his title. The judge presiding over the original case dismissed Paullin's arguments challenging Hale's ownership.	Hale's claims centered on his ownership of the disputed land, supported by a historical chain of title stemming from a deed dated back to 1830 and further transfers culminating in his ownership. He presented evidence of maintaining taxes and utilizing the land, asserting a rightful claim based on both possession and adherence to the legal requirements for property ownership.	Paullin contended that Hale's claim to the land was not valid due to deficiencies in proof of ownership and occupancy. He appealed on the grounds that he should have been entitled to jury instructions pertaining to the validity of Hale’s title and standing. He argued that if Hale had never established legal possession and that Paullin's recognized rights were overlooked, the judgment must be reconsidered to reflect this argument.

In 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, George P. Barton brought a legal action against William Treutler to recover a balance allegedly owed on a contract for carpenter work, including claims for additional charges classified as "extras." The case involved numerous contested points between the two parties, leading to a complex and voluminous record presented in court. The trial was overseen by Judge Rollin S. Williamson, during which the jury ultimately provided a verdict favoring Barton. The court found that the jury's responses to special interrogatories supported their decision, indicating that they considered the facts presented thoroughly. A significant part of the defendant's argument was based on a prerequisite for a certificate from the architects, which the jury found was waived by the defendant, undermining Treutler's main contention.	George P. Barton claimed that there was a balance due under a contract for carpenter work performed by him, in addition to requesting compensation for various extras not included in the original agreement. Barton sought a ruling from the court affirming his right to recover the owed amount.	William Treutler argued that Barton could not maintain his action without producing an architect's certificate, which he claimed was a condition precedent to enforcing the contract. Treutler contended that this requirement must be met before any claims for payment could be validly considered by the court.

In April 1867, in La Salle County, Illinois, a legal case was initiated known as "Henry Mills et al. v. James McCabe". The plaintiff, James McCabe, brought the action against Henry Mills, Thomas Phillson, and Darius Fyffe, who were the judges at a general election. The case arose when McCabe's vote was refused, leading him to seek damages for this rejection. McCabe, an immigrant from Ireland, claimed to have been naturalized according to US laws prior to offering his vote. However, the defendants contested his claims, arguing that the court that naturalized him, known as the Marine Court of the City of New York, lacked the jurisdiction to do so. The central issue for the court was to determine whether the Marine Court fell under the authorized courts able to grant citizenship under federal law, as defined by the Naturalization Act of 1802. The Illinois Supreme Court was tasked with examining the legitimacy of the Marine Court's authority in naturalizing individuals and whether McCabe was a qualified elector entitled to vote.	McCabe claimed that he was a naturalized citizen and, therefore, a qualified elector who had the right to vote. He argued that his vote was wrongfully rejected by the judges, leading him to seek damages as permitted under the Illinois election laws. His primary legal request was for compensation due to the refusal of his vote.	The defendants, Mills, Phillson, and Fyffe, contended that McCabe was not a legally naturalized citizen because the Marine Court lacked jurisdiction to grant his citizenship. They asserted that McCabe did not meet the qualifications of an elector under the law, thereby justifying their refusal to accept his vote. Their main argument was that the plaintiff did not have a legal basis to sue because he was not a qualified elector.

John P. Fyffe v. Mary Fyffe is a legal case heard by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 16, 1883, concerning a dispute over the title to eighty acres of land in Lawrence County, Illinois. The primary individuals involved are John P. Fyffe, the plaintiff, and Mary Fyffe, the defendant, who is the widow of John P. Fyffe, the plaintiff's father. The case revolves around a deed executed on October 8, 1870, by William J. Mayo and his wife, which is claimed by both the plaintiff and defendant to convey property to John P. Fyffe. The plaintiff asserts that he is the grantee named in the deed, while the defendant contends that the deed was intended for her late husband, also named John P. Fyffe. During the trial, evidence was presented that supported both claims, leading to complications regarding the deed's intention. The plaintiff, then a minor at the time of the deed's execution, had no involvement in its procurement. The trial jury ultimately ruled in favor of the defendant, prompting the plaintiff to appeal the verdict.	The plaintiff, John P. Fyffe, argues that he is the legal owner of the eighty acres of land based on the deed executed in 1870, asserting that he is the named grantee in that document. He claims that the evidence supports his position as the rightful owner, having been designated as such in the deed despite his minor status at the time of execution. He requests the court to recognize his ownership rights and reverse the trial court's judgment favoring the defendant.	Mary Fyffe, the defendant, contends that the land was purchased and conveyed to her late husband, John P. Fyffe, rather than the plaintiff. She argues that the evidence demonstrates that the deceased husband treated the land as his own, occupying and managing it throughout his life. The defendant requests the court to uphold the jury's verdict, affirming that she is the rightful owner of the property based on her husband's ownership claim.

In 1852, in Kane County, Illinois, an action for trespass due to false imprisonment was initiated by Frederick Ashbaugh against Erastus Tefft, along with other defendants, Heath and Vining. Heath, a constable at the time, arrested Ashbaugh under a writ of capias ad satisfaciendum and held him for six to eight days until he was released via a habeas corpus proceeding. Evidence presented showed that Ashbaugh was received by the county jailer from Heath and that Heath's actions were conducted in his official capacity. Tefft, who was in New York during the arrest, claimed no involvement, stating that Baird, a clerk in his store, instigated the arrest. Ashbaugh's case included testimony regarding the value of legal services for his release, culminating in a jury verdict against Tefft for $73.75.	The plaintiff, Frederick Ashbaugh, claimed false imprisonment against Erastus Tefft and asserted that his arrest was unlawful. He sought damages for the wrongful imprisonment and the legal expenses incurred for his release. Ashbaugh presented evidence indicating that the arrest was initiated without proper legal grounds and sought to demonstrate Tefft's responsibility in the matter.	The defendant, Erastus Tefft, contended that the evidence presented by Ashbaugh was insufficient to warrant a verdict against him. Tefft argued that Heath was acting within his official duties as a constable and that there was no evidence linking Tefft to the wrongful arrest. He maintained that Ashbaugh failed to prove the unlawfulness of the arrest or establish Tefft's direct involvement, requesting the jury to find him not guilty based on the lack of evidence.

The case "Hubert Reynolds et al. v. The Milks Grove Special Drainage District et al." was filed in 1889 in Iroquois County, Illinois. The appellants, including Hubert Reynolds, filed a bill in chancery against the Milks Grove Drainage District and the holders of its bonds, claiming mismanagement and improper assessment related to the district's drainage project. The drainage district was organized to manage drainage through the construction of a singular main ditch; however, after its commencement, the commissioners decided to create additional lateral ditches, resulting in an increased cost of $20,000. The appellants argued that the tax assessment for these improvements was unjust, excessive, and uninformed, claiming they received no notice of the second levy for taxes. They sought an injunction to prevent the collection of said taxes. In response, the district's commissioners admitted to the need for these ditches and denied all claims of fraud or excessive taxation. The case ultimately hinged on whether the circuit court had jurisdiction over the enforcement of these assessments.	The plaintiffs contended that the second tax levy for the construction of additional lateral drains was unjust and disproportionate to the benefits received, violating both equity and constitutional limits on taxation. They claimed they were not given notice of the second levy and sought an injunction to halt the collection of the associated bonds until their grievances could be addressed.	The defendants, represented by the commissioners of the drainage district, asserted that they had followed proper legal processes and acted within their jurisdiction. They argued that the plaintiffs were aware of the additional drainage works and that the tax assessments were not excessive nor unjust. The defendants further maintained that even if there were irregularities, the circuit court lacked jurisdiction to intervene in the matter.

In the case of Fairbank Canning Company v. Maurice Weill and David Blum, the events took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the decision rendered on February 12, 1890. The Fairbank Canning Company operated a factory located at the Union Stock Yards in Cook County. The dispute arose from an alleged oral contract made around September 1, 1887, where a company vice-president, through an individual named Vogel, sold solder to David Blum. The amount of solder in question became a contentious issue, with the Fairbank Canning Company asserting that they sold 10,000 pounds, which they had delivered in four different loads. Conversely, Blum and his associates claimed that they had purchased all the solder available, estimating the total to be between 14,000 to 20,000 pounds. The plaintiffs were seeking damages for the failure to deliver more solder than what was claimed to have been sold. During the trial, controversy arose over the admissibility of testimony relating to a conversation Blum had with an unidentified man (referred to as "the hunchback") concerning the transaction, which the appellant contended was inadmissible and prejudicial.	The plaintiffs, Maurice Weill and David Blum, claimed that they entered into an oral contract to purchase all available solder from the Fairbank Canning Company, asserting that they were entitled to approximately 20,000 pounds. They argued that the defendant failed to deliver the full quantity agreed upon, which led them to seek damages for the shortfall in delivery. The key points of their claim revolved around the assertion that the sale was for the entire stock of solder and the impact of the defendant's failure to deliver as promised.	The defendant, Fairbank Canning Company, contended that the actual agreement only involved the sale of 10,000 pounds of solder, which they claimed had been duly delivered in multiple loads. They argued that any additional claims by the plaintiffs were unfounded and that the court had erred in admitting testimony that was not directly relevant to the contract or the parties involved. The defendant sought to have the verdict in favor of the plaintiffs overturned, contending that improper evidence influenced the jury's decision.

On September 20, 1880, Jacob Weidel borrowed $2,600 from the Bohemian American Building, Loan and Homestead Association in Cook County, Illinois, agreeing to pay $6.50 weekly until the principal amount and 8% annual interest were settled. To secure this loan, Weidel executed a trust deed on a property located in Cook County. Despite making regular payments, he later sought an additional $2,000 loan from the association, which led to complications involving a judgment note and a lack of payment to the association. In February 1884, after accruing debts, Weidel made an agreement with John Stelzich to pay the remaining balance owed to the association. Stelzich paid $400 and later settled the debt, after which the association transferred the mortgage to him at Weidel's request. However, after Weidel sold the property to Frank J. Mueller, the payment requested by Stelzich went unpaid. This prompted Stelzich to file a bill in the Superior Court seeking to foreclose the trust deed. The case involved several parties, including Weidel, his wife, and others, culminating in a ruling from the Superior Court, which dismissed Stelzich’s bill for lack of equity.	John Stelzich claimed that as the equitable assignee of the agreement following his payment to the association, he should have the right to foreclose the trust deed on the property. He contended that the Superior Court erroneously dismissed his bill, arguing that procedural defects regarding party inclusion did not justify dismissal for lack of equity.	The defendants, led by Frank J. Mueller, argued that Stelzich failed to prove his ownership rights to the agreement and trust deed because there was no formal written assignment. They maintained that the Superior Court's dismissal was proper, citing the absence of necessary parties and the claim that not all debts had been declared due per the original agreement terms.

Francis Hogg was involved in a legal case tried in the July term of 1884 in the County Court of Pope County, Illinois. He was indicted for selling intoxicating liquor in quantities less than one gallon without a legal license under the Dram Shop Act. The incident occurred on December 25, 1882, when Hogg was persuaded by a group of individuals to travel to Shetlerville and acquire a jug of whisky for a gathering at Jonathan Wallace's house, where people were assembled for dancing. The arrangement was such that Hogg would contribute thirty cents toward the whisky’s purchase, while others would cover the remaining cost. After collecting the funds, they shared the whisky among themselves in a barn. The court found Hogg guilty, resulting in a judgment that imposed a fine of $60 plus costs. However, the core of the case revolved around whether Hogg acted as a vendor or merely as an agent for the contributors in the procurement of the liquor.	The plaintiff (the People) argued that Hogg violated the Dram Shop Act by selling intoxicating liquor without a proper license. They contended that he participated in the distribution of alcohol to individuals at a social gathering, constituting illegal selling under the statute.	Hogg's defense posited that he was not a vendor of the liquor but rather acted as an agent on behalf of himself and others who contributed to the purchase. He argued that there was no intention to evade the law and that he had not acted in bad faith. Importantly, they maintained the legal relationship was one of principal-agent, not vendor-vendee, which should exempt him from liability under the indictment.

On June 15, 1872, David L. Crist executed a bond for a tract of land to James Worden, agreeing that Worden would pay $502.80 by May 20, 1873. This bond specified that if the payment was made on time, the conveyance would be by general warranty; otherwise, it would be by quitclaim deed. The land was sold to Alexander Campbell, Jr. due to a foreclosure, and the agreement was meant to facilitate the redemption of the property. On May 16, 1872, four days before the payment was due, Worden paid $500 towards the bond, but Crist was unaware of this when he subsequently paid the bond amount of $502.80. Howard C. Crist, son of David, received a master’s deed from the property, but when Worden later paid Crist for the land, Crist only provided a quitclaim deed, which Worden rejected. Worden then sold his bond for a conveyance to another party and claimed possession of the land. Crist's defense relied on an alleged agreement that the title would remain with him to indemnify against a loan he secured for which Worden was a surety. This case unfolded in the Illinois Supreme Court following disputes over the title and the validity of the claims surrounding the bond and agreement.	Charles Worden contended that he was entitled to a specific performance of the bond for the conveyance of the property after having paid the necessary sum. He argued that his assignation of the bond was valid and that he had no notice of any existing defense that Crist might assert regarding the title of the property. Worden requested the court to enforce the obligation of the bond such that he could obtain the legal title to the land as originally agreed upon.	Howard C. Crist argued that there was a pre-existing verbal arrangement in which Crist would hold the title to the property as indemnity for a loan taken out by James Worden, thus preventing Worden’s claim for specific performance. Crist claimed that this arrangement was intended to protect the estate of David L. Crist against loss until the debt was paid. Additionally, Crist contended that Worden, as an assignee of the bond, should have been aware of the actual condition of the title and was therefore bound by it.

In January 1870, the legal case "James Millikin v. Robert Taylor" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from Macon County, Illinois. The dispute involved two parties: Robert Taylor, the plaintiff, and James Millikin, the defendant. Taylor had obtained an assignment of a promissory note for $4,410, which was secured by a mortgage on a herd of cattle. The defendant, Millikin, held a secondary mortgage of $1,200 on the same cattle. Eventually, Millikin took possession of the cattle, sold them, and paid Taylor $1,000. Taylor subsequently filed a lawsuit to recover the remaining balance owed on the promissory note, which led to Millikin appealing the judgment after being ordered to pay. The case focused on determining whether Millikin had received sufficient funds from the sale to cover the amount owed to Taylor, with conflicting testimonies presented regarding the actual amount received by Millikin.	Robert Taylor claimed that James Millikin owed him money from the sale of cattle that Millikin had disposed of. Taylor contended that Millikin had received more than just the $1,000 already paid and sought recovery of the remaining balance on the promissory note, arguing that Millikin had received money linked to the cattle on which Taylor had a lien.	James Millikin contested the claims against him by asserting that he only received $2,500 from the sale of the cattle and had accounted for it. He maintained that he did not owe any additional money to Taylor beyond what was already paid and challenged the sufficiency of the evidence regarding the amounts claimed by Taylor.

Victoria Stewart filed a lawsuit against the School Directors after being terminated from her teaching position. The case took place in Jasper County, Illinois, with the initial suit brought before a Justice of the Peace. Stewart had been employed to teach for a term of four months starting in October 1885 at a rate of $25 per month. While she was fully compensated for the agreed four-month term, Stewart claimed that she was entitled to an additional month’s salary based on a purported special contract which she claimed provided for a five-month teaching term. The Board of Directors refuted this claim, stating the employment was only for four months. The case went through the Circuit Court where a verdict was returned in favor of the defendants, leading to Stewart appealing the decision. Key individuals included Victoria Stewart, members of the Board of Directors (including Towland and Clark), and a clerk named I.N.S. Clark who documented the meeting where Stewart was hired.	Victoria Stewart claimed she was wrongfully discharged after four months of teaching and sought recovery of salary for a fifth month based on her assertion that there was a special contract for employment for five months. She presented testimony from herself and two witnesses that supported her claim, implying the Board had agreed to grant her a fifth month if she provided satisfactory services.	The School Directors asserted that the only contract agreed upon was for a term of four months, with no binding agreement for a fifth month in place. They stated that any informal discussions regarding a fifth month did not alter the written contract. Additionally, one director informed Stewart that other board members were opposed to her continuing, indicating no wrongful dismissal had occurred since her term had officially ended.

The legal case "The Ottawa Gas-light and Coke Company v. Darlin Thompson" was heard in April 1864 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated on December 26, 1860, when plaintiff Darlin Thompson filed an action against the Ottawa Gas-light and Coke Company. The main issue revolved around alleged damages to Thompson's well water caused by noxious substances emanating from the company's gas manufacturing processes. Thompson claimed that these deleterious materials had polluted his well and created unpleasant odors and smokes, rendering his residence uncomfortable for habitation. The jury initially ruled in favor of Thompson, awarding damages of $414. However, the case was appealed, prompting the court to reassess whether Thompson had legitimate grounds to seek damages for the well, which was owned by another individual, James Graham. The court expressed confusion over whether the jury's verdict pertained to the well's injury or the nuisance violations. Ultimately, the court noted conflicting authorities on whether the nuisance constituted a private or public nuisance and aimed to determine the plaintiff's right to recover damages for an injury to property that he did not own.	Darlin Thompson, the plaintiff, argued that the Ottawa Gas-light and Coke Company was responsible for contaminating the water in his well with harmful substances resulting from the company's gas manufacturing processes. He claimed these actions not only spoiled the well water but also created a significant nuisance due to unpleasant smells and fumes, making his premises uninhabitable. Thompson sought legal remedies for both the injury to his well's water and the resulting discomfort and nuisance caused by the company's activities.	The defendant, Ottawa Gas-light and Coke Company, contended primarily that Thompson had no standing to recover damages for injuries to the well since it belonged to James Graham, not Thompson. They argued that Thompson's claim was invalid as he had only a verbal license to use the well, which did not confer any ownership or legal interest in the property. Furthermore, the company claimed that the alleged nuisance was a public nuisance, which could only be addressed through criminal indictment, not civil action initiated by an individual.

Samuel Hanna was indicted along with other individuals for an assault with intent to kill and murder John H. Arnold, taking place in Will County, Illinois. Following a trial, Hanna was convicted and sentenced to seven years in the penitentiary. During the trial, the regular jury panel became exhausted, prompting the court to summon additional jurors. However, Hanna objected to having the county sheriff, who was related to the prosecuting witness, serve this special venire. He requested that either the coroner or a special bailiff be appointed instead. The court denied this motion, leading Hanna to preserve an exception to the ruling. Additionally, Hanna sought a change of venue, claiming prejudice from the presiding judge towards him. His petition was verified by affidavits from two individuals declaring they believed the judge could not be impartial. The circuit court, however, found deficiencies in the petition, including its failure to list the affiants' names and affirm their qualifications. Despite these challenges, the petition's requirements were deemed satisfied as per legal standards.	The plaintiff's main claims centered around the wrongful conviction of Samuel Hanna due to procedural errors during the trial. Hanna argued that he was entitled to a fair trial and that his rights were violated when the court refused to appoint a special bailiff to summon additional jurors, given the sheriff's relation to the prosecuting witness. He also maintained that the change of venue should have been granted due to the presiding judge’s prejudice against him as affirmed by the affidavits he provided.	The defendant, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Hanna's petition for a change of venue was insufficient because it lacked necessary details, such as the names of the affiants who supported his claim of prejudice. They contended that the court acted within its rights by not appointing a special bailiff since the objections raised by Hanna were viewed as not substantial. Furthermore, they asserted that the jury instructions regarding common design were accurate as consistent with legal precedents.

The case of Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Cobb, Christy & Co. took place during the winter of 1864-1865 in Cairo, Illinois. The central individuals involved were the plaintiff company, Cobb, Christy & Co., which was contracted by the government to supply corn and oats to the army, and the defendant, Illinois Central Railroad Company, which was responsible for transporting these supplies. Cobb, Christy & Co. made significant purchases of grain through an intermediary named Fallis, who purchased the grain along the railroad’s route for delivery to Cairo. They had a contract with the government, effective January 10, 1865, to deliver large quantities of corn and oats. However, the Railroad Company failed to deliver the grain in a reasonable time, resulting in Cobb, Christy & Co. allegedly losing the opportunity to fulfill their contract with the government. Consequently, they sought damages from the Railroad Company for this breach of duty. Cobb, Christy & Co. won in the circuit court, prompting the Railroad Company to appeal.	The plaintiffs, Cobb, Christy & Co., argued that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was a common carrier that failed to deliver a significant portion of the corn in a reasonable timeframe, causing them to miss their contractual obligations with the government. They claimed damages based on the contract price for the corn, asserting that they had invested in the grain and had incurred losses due to the delivery failures.	The defendant, Illinois Central Railroad Company, contended that the plaintiffs did not own the corn being shipped until it passed inspection at Cairo, and thus lacked standing to sue. They also argued that military control during the war impacted their operations, suggesting that government orders contributed to delays that absolved them of liability for the late delivery. Additionally, the Railroad claimed that any delay in transportation was attributed to logistical challenges on their tracks, rather than their negligence.

In 1855, a group of property owners, including Frederick A. Bryan, Charles V. Dyer, John Sollitt, and Jacob Harris, signed an agreement regarding the potential construction of government buildings at the corner of Monroe and Dearborn streets in Chicago. This agreement promised payment to Dyer for his assistance if the government decided to erect the buildings there. Over time, the U.S. government indeed located these buildings by May 1860, preceding the actual suit's commencement and known to the signatories. Dyer initiated legal action against Bryan in the Superior Court of Chicago to collect the pledged amount of $500, which Bryan had officially subscribed to in the agreement. Bryan's defense focused on claiming that the agreement lacked consideration, was illegal, and was not binding since Dyer's influence was not needed for an already made governmental decision. The jury found in favor of Dyer, and Bryan was required to pay $234.68 in damages.	Bryan's claims against Dyer asserted that he had a valid contract wherein Dyer would pay him $500 if the wrongful erection of the government buildings occurred at the designated location. He contended that the government had duly located and built these structures by May 1860. Thus, he requested compensation per the contract.	Bryan's defenses revolved around the claims that the contract was void due to the purported lack of consideration since the decision to build was finalized before the signing. He argued that the contract was illegal as it sought to use personal influence over public decisions, which contradicted public policy. He also claimed he had an outstanding debt to Dyer, which should offset any payment obligation.

In May 1880, Daniel C. Lynn acquired land from his father-in-law, Caleb M. Lyerle, for $1,200. Instead of paying cash, Lynn gave five promissory notes, each for $200, to Lyerle’s daughters, and $200 was designated for Lynn's wife, who was also Lyerle's daughter. This transaction raised suspicions; it was alleged that it was aimed at defrauding creditors since Lyerle was a surety for debts incurred by an individual named Morgan, who later became insolvent. Creditors challenged the land's conveyance in court, and it was set aside, requiring the land to be sold to satisfy debts. Subsequently, an arrangement was made wherein Lyerle would pay off the creditors, and Lynn would later purchase the land. However, Lynn ultimately refused to fulfill this agreement after Lyerle settled the debts. The case then escalated to the circuit court, which ruled in favor of Lyerle, ordering Lynn to pay $1,003 or lose the land. Lynn appealed this decision.	Caleb M. Lyerle, the plaintiff, argued that the original conveyance of land was intended to defraud his creditors and, therefore, was void. He claimed that after paying off the judgments against the property, he had an understanding with Lynn that Lynn would compensate him for the land. Lyerle requested that Lynn pay the total owed or the property be sold to satisfy the debt.	Daniel C. Lynn, the defendant, contended that the initial transaction was binding between the parties, albeit void for creditors. He argued that Lyerle's payment to settle the judgments did not necessitate Lynn's obligation to pay him, claiming no agreement existed for Lynn to return the favor financially. Lynn sought to diminish his liability based on his payments to Lyerle’s daughters and requested a credit for a payment made to one of them toward his debt.

In September 1873, a legal case took place involving A. Green Coursen as the plaintiff and George Browning et al. as the defendants in Cook County, Illinois. The case arose from an appeal bond executed on July 23, 1873, which was filed in the Superior Court of Cook County. The bond was related to a previous judgment from that court. The action was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the validity of the appeal bond and the process pertaining to it became points of contention. The court proceedings included claims that the court had erred in handling the defendant's pleas and in determining the proper parties subject to judgment under the bond's terms. The judgment concerning the appeal was submitted for decision during the September term of 1873 and was affirmed on January 30, 1874, without conflict with any statutes or constitutional provisions, as indicated in the court's opinion.	The plaintiff, A. Green Coursen, argued that the appeal bond constituted a binding contract for payment and asserted his right to collect on this bond. Coursen filed an affidavit of claim supporting his declaration, contending that the defendant had failed to adequately respond by submitting an affidavit of merits with their pleas. Consequently, he requested that the court uphold the validity of his claims against the defendants based on the filed appeal bond.	The defendant, George Browning, contended that the declaration brought forth by Coursen was insufficient to support the judgment against him. The defense argued that one of the defendants had not been properly served and that the court's proceedings should have accounted for this. Additionally, they asserted that the court erred in striking their pleas from the files due to the lack of an accompanying affidavit of merits.

On December 2, 1889, a legal case known as "Canute R. Matson and J. M. Kelsey v. Robert K. Davies and J. M. Davies" was adjudicated in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated from the County Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Richard Prendergast. The dispute arose from a replevin suit, which is a legal procedure to recover personal property wrongfully taken or detained. The plaintiffs (Canute R. Matson and J. M. Kelsey) filed an appeal regarding the dismissal of their replevin suit, claiming that the dismissal occurred without notice to them. This lack of notice prevented their opportunity to respond or address the court adequately. The plaintiffs contended that they were entitled to the return of the property upon the dismissal of the suit, a principle they argued was supported by established law in Illinois. However, the court had made its decision without awarding a return of the property or providing evidence to the contrary regarding the plaintiffs' entitlement to it, which raised concerns about the fairness of the proceedings.	The plaintiffs asserted that the dismissal of their replevin suit by the County Court was erroneous, primarily because it occurred without their notification or opportunity for input. They claimed that upon dismissal, they were entitled to the return of the property, and the failure of the court to grant this return constituted a legal error. They sought a remedy for the wrongful dismissal and the lack of return of their property, advocating for their right as established by Illinois law.	The defendants argued that the presumption of correctness applies to the decisions made by the lower court, which was the County Court in this case. They contended that in the absence of a formal bill of exceptions demonstrating otherwise, the court's actions should be upheld. The defendants asserted that without evidence showing that the plaintiffs had a valid entitlement to the property, the dismissal and the accompanying judgment should be considered appropriate and not subject to challenge.

The case of George M. Fadner et al. v. E. B. Hibler took place in Cook County, Illinois, and was decided on May 31, 1888. The case revolved around a dispute over a contract for commissions related to orders for nursery stock. George M. Fadner and others were the appellants (plaintiffs) suing E. B. Hibler (the appellee) for an alleged balance due for commissions. The core of the dispute involved the terms of the employment contract between Fadner and Hibler, particularly concerning the commission structure and liability for order losses. Fadner’s witness testified that he had negotiated the terms with Hibler, stipulating that Hibler would receive thirty percent of the orders he sent in as long as losses did not exceed ten percent. A significant contention arose over a written contract presented in court, which Hibler claimed was signed by Fadner's agent, Meyers. Fadner disputed this, arguing that Meyers lacked the authority to bind the company in this instance. The court admitted the contract into evidence, which ultimately contributed to the case's controversy.	The plaintiffs, George M. Fadner and others, claimed that Hibler was owed a balance for commissions based on the terms of their employment agreement. They argued that according to the verbal agreement, Hibler was entitled to thirty percent of the orders he processed, contingent on order losses not exceeding ten percent. They sought to recover this amount based on the written contract they believed was validly executed.	The defendant, E. B. Hibler, contended that the contract proposed by the plaintiffs was inadmissible because it was signed by Meyers, who he claimed did not have the express authority from Fadner to sign such a contract on behalf of Fadner Brothers & Company. Hibler requested the court to disregard the written contract as evidence due to the lack of proof of Meyers' authority to bind the company, arguing that the admission of the contract was erroneous.

Frederick A. Bragg brought a legal action against Henry C. Walker regarding a claim for commissions linked to the sale of real estate. The events at the heart of the case took place in Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Appellate Court on July 27, 1887. The controversy arose when Walker purportedly told Bragg that he would pay him a commission of $5,000 if Bragg found a buyer willing to purchase his property for $100,000. Bragg successfully found such a buyer, but Walker subsequently refused to sell the property, leading to Bragg's claim for the promised commission. The case went to trial in the Superior Court, where a jury rendered a verdict in favor of Walker, prompting Bragg to appeal. The appellate court reviewed the evidence and noted a conflict in testimonies, particularly concerning whether Walker had previously withdrawn the authority for Bragg to sell the property.	The plaintiff, Frederick A. Bragg, claimed that he was entitled to a $5,000 commission for successfully finding a buyer for Walker's property at the agreed price of $100,000. He argued that Walker's refusal to sell the property after the buyer was secured constituted a breach of their agreement and that the jury’s verdict was against the weight of the evidence.	The defendant, Henry C. Walker, contended that he had communicated to Bragg the withdrawal of his authority to sell the property before Bragg found a buyer. Walker maintained that during a conversation prior to the sale, he explained changes regarding his property that prevented the transaction. He argued that the jury’s verdict in his favor was supported by the evidence, and thus, the court should not reverse the verdict.

Leander Douglas et al. brought a legal action against Samuel P. Whiting in April 1861 in the Knox Circuit Court in Illinois, seeking to recover their share of a tract of land. The case stemmed from a previous judgment entered in favor of Isaac Armstrong against Whiting for a debt of $324.50, which resulted in a sheriff's sale of the land following an execution on the judgment. The plaintiffs provided the court with evidence including the judgment record, an execution, and a sheriff’s deed. The defendant claimed that the service of the summons in the previous case was improper, asserting that the default service method used (reading the summons) did not comply with statutory requirements and rendered the judgment void. The trial progressed with the introduction of various legal documents and arguments from both parties.	The plaintiffs argued that they had a valid claim to the land based on the judgment against Whiting, which had been executed correctly according to the law. They presented evidence including the court judgment and the sheriff’s deed as proof of their ownership rights and entitlement to recover their share of the property.	The defendant contended that the service of summons in the original debt action was defective and did not meet statutory requirements. He argued that the judgment against him should be considered void due to this improper service. Additionally, he pointed out irregularities in the execution process that validated his claim to maintain possession of the land in question.

In the case of Jackson Long v. Samuel R. Barker et al., the events took place in Jasper County, Illinois, around April 1, 1875. Samuel B. Barker purchased a portable steam saw-mill from John T. Coville for $1,500, paying $600 upfront and issuing three promissory notes for the remaining balance. Barker asserted that Coville claimed ownership of the saw-mill, which had been irregularly acquired by Coville through a tax sale. Jackson Long contested this claim, asserting his ownership of the property and subsequently filed a replevin action. Barker sought an injunction to prevent Long from reclaiming the mill, arguing he would incur great and irreparable loss if Long removed it. The case escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court after Barker's bill was decreed in his favor, leading Long to appeal the decision, claiming that an adequate legal remedy existed for settling the property dispute.	Samuel B. Barker claimed that he rightfully owned the steam saw-mill purchased from John T. Coville and sought to prevent Jackson Long from interfering with his possession. He contended that the tax sale under which Coville obtained the mill was invalid and that Long's actions would cause him considerable harm. Barker requested the court to determine the ownership of the mill and to enjoin Long from removing or dealing with the property.	Jackson Long contended that he was the rightful owner of the saw-mill and that the irregular tax sale claimed by Barker did not transfer proper title. He argued that the matters related to ownership could adequately be settled through the existing replevin suit, asserting that there was no necessity for equity involvement. Long requested the court to reverse the lower court's injunction against him, defending his legal standing to reclaim the mill.

DeWitt C. Barber v. James Bell is a legal case that took place in the Circuit Court of Perry County, Illinois, with the decision rendered in June 1875. The case revolves around a promissory note given by E. C. Dawes & Co., originally made payable to DeWitt G. Barber, who endorsed it to James Bell prior to its maturity. The note was executed on September 2, 1872, and an initial six-month due date was extended several times, ultimately due in December 1874. The makers of the note, Dawes & Co., were residents of Ohio and not subject to jurisdiction in Illinois at the time the note was due. Bell filed the lawsuit against Barber as the indorser of the note after the makers had failed to pay. The plaintiff's claims included arguments about the insolvency of the makers and the fact that they were outside the jurisdiction of Illinois. The defendant argued that no recovery could be obtained without showing the note had been presented for payment where it was payable and claimed that Bell had failed to exercise due diligence to collect the debt. The case was tried without a jury, and Barber appealed the judgment after a ruling favored Bell.	James Bell, the plaintiff, asserted that as the indorsee of the promissory note, he was entitled to recover from DeWitt C. Barber as the indorser. Bell argued that since the makers of the note resided out of state when it matured, and had been deemed insolvent, he was justified in not pursuing collection efforts against the makers. He emphasized that the law allowed him to hold Barber liable without requiring proof that the note was presented for payment at the designated location, given the circumstances surrounding the maker's residency and insolvency.	DeWitt C. Barber, the defendant, contended that James Bell could not recover without providing evidence that the note was presented for payment at the specified location. Barber also argued that Bell failed to exhibit due diligence in attempting to collect the debt from the makers. He claimed that the presence of property belonging to the makers within Illinois required Bell to attach the property prior to holding him liable as an indorser. However, Barber ultimately recognized that maintaining such procedures was unnecessary due to the circumstances of the makers' residency and debt status.

The case "City of Bloomington v. Laura Annett" was decided on January 16, 1885, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The incident occurred in Bloomington, Illinois, where Laura Annett sustained injuries after falling through a defective covering over a cellar way on Madison Street during a visit to a store. The sidewalk measured twelve feet wide, and the cellar way created a dangerous opening that Annett and her companions encountered while admiring a display in the store's window. The platform covering the cellar had been constructed two weeks prior and was inadequately supported, leading to Annett's fall where she suffered significant injuries that required medical attention and confined her to her home for several months. The case was brought against the city, claiming negligence regarding the maintenance of the sidewalk.	Laura Annett, the plaintiff, claimed damages for her injuries caused by the fall on the defective sidewalk. She argued that the city was negligent for failing to repair the known unsafe condition of the sidewalk, leading to her injuries. Annett sought compensation for medical expenses, the cost of nursing services, and damages for pain and suffering. The jury awarded her $1,800 in damages based on her claims and the evidence presented.	The City of Bloomington, the defendant, contended that it had no prior notice of the allegedly dangerous condition of the sidewalk, thus unable to remedy it before the accident. They also contested the admissibility of certain testimony and instructions given to the jury that favored the plaintiff, suggesting that damages claimed by Annett were improper as they should solely belong to her husband, as he had incurred costs related to her medical care and household duties during her recovery.

In the case of "Susan R. Willdey et al. v. Angeline Webster et al.", the dispute originated from a contract signed on September 22, 1855, between Jonathan B. Willdey, the deceased husband of Susan R. Willdey, and Angeline Webster for the sale of a tract of land located in Tazewell County, Illinois. The agreement stipulated that Webster would pay $200 for the land, and in return, Willdey would convey the title through a deed with general warranty covenants. Following Willdey’s death, Susan and his heirs sought the enforcement of this agreement, claiming payment had been made but the land had not been conveyed before his passing. The case was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1866 after the lower court had ordered a conveyance of the land. The widow, Mrs. Willdey, denied the execution of the contract, raising doubts about its legitimacy. Key individuals in the case included the plaintiffs (Susan R. Willdey and others), the defendant (Angeline Webster), and witnesses who provided testimony regarding the agreement and execution of the bond.	The plaintiffs, led by Susan R. Willdey, argued that there was a valid contract for the sale of land and requested specific performance of the contract. They maintained that Jonathan B. Willdey had agreed to sell the land, that payment had been made, and the non-conveyance before his death was a failure to fulfill the contractual obligation.	The defendant, Angeline Webster, contested the validity of the alleged contract by asserting that it was not executed by her deceased husband and pointed out that he had died prior to the acknowledgment of the bond. Webster also claimed that the deed was effectively a forgery or obtained through fraud and that any informal communications regarding the land were insufficient to validate the claim against the estate, particularly concerning the rights of the minor heirs.

In the case of The Town of Old Town v. William H. Dooley, which was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1876, the dispute revolves around a public highway in McLean County, Illinois, where Dooley owned land on both sides of the road where it crosses the Kickapoo stream. Approximately three years prior to the lawsuit, the Town erected a bridge for public use. Subsequently, the highway commissioners allowed Dooley to connect his fence to the bridge approaches, which he proceeded to do. The case emerged when the Town claimed that Dooley's fences obstructed the highway. The Court, after a trial without a jury, ruled in favor of Dooley, concluding that no obstruction occurred because the public's right of way over the land retained the interests of the landowner, who still could use his property in ways consistent with that right, so long as it did not interfere with the highway.	The Town of Old Town alleged that Dooley had unlawfully obstructed the highway by failing to remove his fences connected to the bridge. They claimed that the consent given by the highway commissioners was insufficient, as it was only verbal and not officially recorded, arguing that this constituted a violation of the statutory requirement regarding highway management.	William H. Dooley contended that the highway commissioners had indeed granted informal consent to attach his fences to the bridge, which was permissible under the law. He argued that the consent did not need to be in writing, and the fences, examined and deemed satisfactory by the commissioners, did not obstruct the public's use of the highway. Dooley maintained that the right of passage did not entitle the public to access water sources on his land, and therefore, his actions did not violate any statutes.

George Watson brought a case against the City of Chicago regarding a special assessment levied on his property to fund the construction of a sidewalk along Bryson Street from Leavitt Street to Western Avenue. This legal conflict arose in Cook County, Illinois, with the court's opinion delivered on November 14, 1885. The total cost of the sidewalk improvement was approximately $639.54, with $589.05 being assessed on the property owned by Watson and others, while the city was responsible for the remaining $50.49. Watson objected to the assessment, claiming that his property would not benefit from the sidewalk's construction. A jury found that the assessment was appropriate, and Watson's motion for a new trial was denied. The case hinged on whether the property’s assessed contribution exceeded its benefit and addressed the legal authority of city officials in determining assessment amounts.	The plaintiff, George Watson, claimed that the special assessment placed on his property was excessive and did not reflect the benefits he would receive from the sidewalk improvement. He filed objections to the assessment, seeking a new trial based on the argument that the assessment was unfair and that the sidewalk would not enhance the value of his property. Watson sought to have the assessment overturned and to avoid the responsibility of paying the assessed amount.	The City of Chicago defended the special assessment by arguing that it was valid and in accordance with local ordinances governing such improvements. The city argued that the assessment was properly calculated and reflected the proportional benefits conferred upon the properties by the sidewalk construction. They maintained that the city council had the authority to determine the distribution of costs between private property owners and the public, thus upholding the integrity of the assessment process.

On May 8, 1857, James Berney sold a block of land in Chicago to William C. Yeaton and others, with a total consideration of $33,040 to be paid in five installments through joint promissory notes. These notes were payable to Berney at the office of S. H. Kerfoot & Co. in Chicago. At the time, Berney was a resident of Alabama, where he remained throughout the Civil War, holding onto the unpaid notes. The makers of the notes were divided: some were within Confederate lines and others remained in Union territory. While Yeaton and Duval were able to operate without breach of duty to the Union, Beverly and Skinner were not. The appellants had settled most of the debts but disputed $2,655.58 in interest that accrued due to unpaid funds during the war. They filed a bill seeking to have the mortgage declared satisfied, while Berney filed a cross bill for foreclosure over the unpaid interest. The original case was dismissed, leading the complainants to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs (Yeaton and partners) contended that the unpaid portion of the debt should not incur interest during the Civil War period. They argued that since some of the makers were ready to pay at the specified location, they should be relieved of any further interest obligations. They sought the discharge of the mortgage associated with these claims.	The defendant (Berney) maintained that the mechanics of the promissory notes did not require a formal demand for payment to sustain a foreclosure action. He argued that the creators of the notes residing within the Confederate territories had no legal barriers to making payments. Hence, he contended that the plaintiffs retained their obligations to pay the accrued interest, as circumstances did not preclude their legal responsibility.

Charles B. Farwell filed a suit in equity against Max A. Meyer and other parties in April 1864. The dispute arose from a promissory note for $750, guaranteed by Farwell as surety for Henry W. Zimmerman, who was the principal. The note was originally due on October 16, 1857, and was associated with a series of extensions granted to Zimmerman without Farwell's knowledge. The plaintiff claimed that the holders of the note, Rosenfeld & Rosenberg, unlawfully extended the payment terms multiple times, charging usurious interest rates, while Farwell was unaware of these arrangements. A judgment by confession had been entered in favor of Max A. Meyer without notice to Farwell, prompting him to seek an injunction to restrain the collection of the judgment and declare it void based on claims that he had been released from liability due to the unauthorized extensions. This led to hearings, witness testimonies, and legal arguments regarding ownership, authority of agents, and the nature of usurious agreements.	Farwell contended that he was unfairly bound by the judgment because Rosenfeld & Rosenberg had extended the due date of the note multiple times without his consent, which he argued discharged him from his liability as a surety. He sought an injunction against the collection of the judgment entered by Max A. Meyer and requested that satisfaction be recorded with respect to his obligations under the note.	The defendants, including Meyer and Rosenfeld, disputed Farwell's claims, asserting that he had given consent to the extensions and that Rosenfeld & Rosenberg had not misrepresented their authority over the note. They argued that Farwell was aware of the negotiations and supported the extensions. They denied any wrongdoing related to usurious practices and maintained that Farwell had been adequately informed about the status of the note, thereby indicating that he remained liable.

Edward F. Dutcher initiated a legal action against Moses T. Crowell in the Circuit Court during the May term of 1849, presided over by Hon. Hugh Henderson in the Ogle Circuit Court, Illinois. Dutcher sought an attachment to aid his suit, which was subsequently dismissed by the court because it was issued during vacation. The primary question for the Supreme Court was whether the Circuit Court erred in quashing this writ of attachment. The attachment was applied for under the provisions of the 30th section of the ninth chapter of the Revised Statutes, which had a historical context stemming from a misprint in the original Attachment Act of 1833 that changed the term "time" to "term." The Supreme Court examined the legislative intent behind this statute and concluded that it was reasonable to allow for the issuance of attachments any time, including during vacation periods, as there was no legislative intent to restrict the remedy to specific court sessions.	The plaintiff, Edward F. Dutcher, argued that the Circuit Court wrongly quashed the writ of attachment that he had applied for. He contended that the legislative intent behind the relevant statute permitted the issuance of such attachments during vacation periods, not just during court sessions. He sought to have the Supreme Court reverse the Circuit Court's decision and allow for the issuance of the attachment.	The defendant, Moses T. Crowell, contended that the lower court's dismissal of the attachment was proper due to the wording of the statute, which he argued explicitly limited attachments to "term" times. He maintained that the legal interpretation should reflect the term "term" as written in the Revised Statutes, thereby not allowing for attachments during vacation periods. He requested that the Supreme Court uphold the Circuit Court's decision to quash the attachment.

In the late 19th century, specifically during the years 1884 and 1885, the case arises from Chicago, Illinois, involving Frank P. Hawkins as the appellee and Commercial National Bank as the appellant. The Commercial Club and the Citizens Association, two patriotic citizen groups, engaged in discussions about acquiring land near Chicago for the State Militia. Hawkins was retained by these organizations to act as an agent to negotiate the sale of approximately 200 acres of land owned by the appellant, Commercial National Bank. Despite Hawkins' diligent efforts, including organizing an excursion for State Militia officers, he was unable to secure a sale. Ultimately, the land was purchased by the Commercial Club in October 1887 through a different series of negotiations completely separate from Hawkins' interactions. Hawkins later claimed that he earned commissions based on his supposed role in facilitating the sale, even though no evidence linked his actions to the eventual land transaction.	Hawkins claimed he was entitled to commissions for facilitating the sale of land on behalf of the Commercial National Bank, arguing that his efforts contributed to the eventual public sentiment favoring military presence in Chicago. He sought payment for these commissions based on the agency relationship he believed existed between himself and the bank regarding the sale of the property.	The Commercial National Bank contended that Hawkins did not have any connection to the eventual sale of the land and that his efforts did not influence the transaction. They argued that no evidence supported Hawkins' claims for commissions since the sale proceeded independently of his involvement and without any demonstrated benefit from his actions.

On February 1, 1865, in Kankakee City, Illinois, George W. Byrns and several other relators presented a bill for an injunction to the Judge of the 20th Judicial Circuit, C. K. Starr, to restrain certain parties from specific actions. Judge Starr refused to grant the injunction, endorsing the bill accordingly. A week later, on February 8, 1865, Judge B. R. Sheldon of the 14th Judicial Circuit allowed the injunction despite being aware of the refusal from Judge Starr. The necessary bond was executed, and the order was filed in the Kankakee Circuit Court. However, the next day, without the parties' knowledge, Judge Starr vacated Judge Sheldon’s order, claiming the authority to do so. When the relators sought the issuance of the injunction from the clerk of the Kankakee Circuit Court, John B. Welch, he refused, insisting on the prior ruling by Judge Starr. Following this refusal, the relators filed for a writ of mandamus with the Winnebago Circuit Court, which was granted, leading to this appeal.	The relators, led by George W. Byrns, contended that the clerk of the Kankakee Circuit Court unlawfully refused to issue the writ of injunction mandated by Judge Sheldon’s order. They claimed that the clerk was obligated to comply with the directive since it was a valid order that should not have been vacated by Judge Starr without legal basis. The plaintiffs sought a peremptory writ of mandamus to compel the clerk to issue the injunction.	John B. Welch, the clerk of the Kankakee Circuit Court, argued that he was justified in refusing the issuance of the injunction based on Judge Starr's earlier refusal and his endorsement on the bill. Additionally, he asserted the authority given to Judge Starr's rules that prohibited the issuance of injunctions under such circumstances, claiming that the order from Judge Sheldon was invalid.

In September 1875, in Cook County, Illinois, Barnum Blake and Christine Blake were involved in a divorce case. The court had previously issued a decree requiring Barnum to pay alimony and attorney’s fees to Christine. Barnum’s failure to comply with this order led to his imprisonment for contempt of court. This situation prompted Barnum to appeal the ruling, arguing that the decree was interlocutory and not final. The case raised important legal questions about the nature of the decree concerning the award for attorney’s fees and whether an appeal could be filed against it. The Illinois Supreme Court had not previously ruled on whether such a money decree could be appealed, but they examined the circumstances, the nature of the payments, and the potential implications for Barnum's liberty and property. Ultimately, the court found that the decree was more akin to a final ruling, justifying the appeal. The court then reviewed the allowance for attorney’s fees and described it as unreasonable based on the provided evidence, which influenced their decision to reverse the lower court's decree.	Christine Blake claimed that she was entitled to a specific amount for attorney's fees and other expenses related to her divorce proceedings. She argued that these fees were necessary for her to adequately defend her interests in the divorce case against her husband. The plaintiff sought enforcement of the original decree requiring Barnum to make these payments, insisting on the necessity of the funds for her continued legal representation and well-being.	Barnum Blake contended that the decree for attorney's fees was excessive and unreasonable. He argued that the court's order that led to his imprisonment for non-compliance was based on a final decree, which he challenged. Barnum's defense was built upon the assertion that the fees demanded by Christine were not justified by the services rendered and that the ruling should be reconsidered due to the undue burden it placed on him.

In September 1870, a legal case was filed in the Illinois Supreme Court involving the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company and Michael Adler. The case was a result of a breach of railroad laws, specifically concerning the failure of the railroad company to ring a bell or sound a whistle at a highway crossing with their engine and trains. The suit referenced the railroad law enacted on November 5, 1849, enabling citizens to claim penalties for such violations. During the trial, the jury rendered a verdict favoring Adler, awarding him $1,150 for several breaches of the statute. Key issues arose during the trial regarding juror competency and instruction, with the defense questioning the impartiality of several jurors who expressed bias towards the plaintiff. The case focused on whether the railroad company had indeed failed to provide the required signals at the crossing and involved examining various procedural and evidential matters, including the admissibility of witness testimony based on memoranda. Ultimately, the Illinois Supreme Court found significant errors in the proceedings below, particularly around jury instructions and the rights of jurors.	The plaintiff, Michael Adler, claimed that the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company failed to comply with statutory requirements by not ringing a bell or sounding a whistle when their engine crossed a public highway. This negligence resulted in several breaches deserving a penalty, and Adler sought penalties amounting to $1,150. Adler argued that the jury should find in his favor based on the evidence presented, maintaining that the railroad company’s negligence was clear and deserving of the statutory penalties established under the railroad law.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company's defenses included several arguments, primarily contesting the competency of jurors who exhibited bias against the defendant. The defendants also claimed procedural errors at trial, arguing that the court improperly instructed the jury, particularly regarding the requirement for the plaintiff to prove the existence of a public highway where the incident occurred. They requested that the court rectify these issues and sought a reversal of the trial court's judgment based on these alleged errors.

The case of Charles Drohn v. William Brewer took place in Macon County, Illinois, culminating in a ruling by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875. The events leading to the case began on March 29, 1873, when William Brewer, the plaintiff, was assaulted by defendant Charles Drohn. Drohn allegedly attacked Brewer without provocation, using a padlock chained to a heavy chain to strike Brewer multiple times on the head. The assault caused Brewer severe head injuries, which resulted in a dangerous illness, specifically erysipelas, and led to significant medical expenses. Brewer filed the action of trespass to seek damages for the physical harm he suffered. A jury awarded Brewer $2,750 in damages. The trial court upheld the jury's verdict and denied Drohn's motion for a new trial.	The plaintiff, William Brewer, claimed that he suffered severe physical injuries as a result of an unprovoked assault by Charles Drohn. Brewer argued that the assault caused him long-term damage and incurred significant medical expenses. He sought compensatory damages for his injuries, as well as for the pain and suffering endured due to the assault.	The defendant, Charles Drohn, raised several defenses in an attempt to reverse the judgment. He argued that the court erred in excluding certain testimony related to Brewer's habits of sobriety, which he claimed could be relevant to the case. Drohn also contended that the court improperly refused his proposed jury instructions regarding exemplary damages, claiming that the assault was provoked and lacked malice. Additionally, he asserted that the damages awarded by the jury were excessive and not justified by the evidence presented at trial.

The case of City of Danville v. Harry Vangundy took place in 1888 in Vermillion County, Illinois. The incident involved Harry Vangundy's horse stepping on a defective plank culvert that spanned a city street, causing the horse to break through the culvert and throw Vangundy, resulting in permanent injuries. Vangundy subsequently filed a lawsuit against the City of Danville, and at trial, he was awarded $200 in damages based on the jury's verdict. The court noted that the culvert's defect was not immediately apparent, but the city had recently made repairs to that area and may have been negligent for not conducting a thorough inspection to identify potential hazards.	The plaintiff, Harry Vangundy, argued that the City of Danville was negligent in allowing a defective culvert to exist unfixed, which led to his injuries when he was thrown from his horse. He asserted that the city had a duty to ensure the street and its infrastructure were safe and that the injury was a direct result of the city's failure to properly maintain the culvert.	The City of Danville contended that they had no prior notice of the defect in the culvert and classified it as a latent defect rather than a patent one. They argued that it would be unreasonable to hold the city liable for not knowing about a defect that was not obvious. The city further claimed their responsibility was to keep the streets reasonably safe under the law, which did not equate to ensuring complete immunity from accidents.

The case "The City of Ottawa v. George B. Macy et al." arose in April 1858 in Ottawa, Illinois, concerning an application by the city collector to the County Court of La Salle County for judgments against several lots for assessable improvements made to La Salle Street. The city assessed certain lots that were identified as benefiting from this street improvement, setting forth the valuation and unpaid sums due. The application followed a procedure where the collector certified the assessment list’s accuracy, claiming an inability to find goods belonging to the property owners. The city clerk verified that no payments had been made on the assessed lots from the time of return until the application for judgment. The case included various objections presented by the defendants regarding the assessment procedures and legality.	The City of Ottawa argued that the assessment levied on the properties was valid and justified under the charter provisions that allowed for assessing costs of public improvements on properties benefitting from such improvements. The city sought judgment against the specified lots for the unpaid assessments and contended that proper notice was given regarding the proceedings, in line with statutory requirements.	The defendants, including George B. Macy, raised several objections, asserting that the assessment lacked uniformity among the properties, the notice provided was inadequate, and the assessment process did not follow legal requirements. They questioned the constitutionality of the city's charter provisions utilized for the assessment and highlighted issues such as properties owned by minors and church properties not subject to assessment.

In the case of John T. Cool et al. v. Nathaniel Jackman et al., the events unfolded primarily between 1859 and 1883 in Madison County, Illinois. William and Deborah Cool were married on July 10, 1859, and lived together on a 600-acre tract of land owned by William. In November 1874, they mortgaged the land for $50,000, with Deborah releasing her homestead and dower rights. After William's death on July 17, 1877, the mortgage was foreclosed, leading to the appointment of Nathaniel Jackman as a receiver to collect rents from the property and manage the sale of the land. The land was sold, and the generated funds along with collected rents exceeded the amount needed to satisfy the mortgage decree. During the time prior to the land's redemption expiration, Deborah occupied the dwelling rent-free. A surplus of $1,659 in collected rents remained, prompting a legal dispute regarding the rightful recipient of these funds. A circuit court action led to a decree favoring Deborah Cool over the appellants, claiming she had the right to the surplus rents based on her vested dower interest rights under the law at the time of her marriage.	The plaintiffs, John T. Cool and others (William's heirs), argued that the entire surplus of rents collected should revert to them, as Deborah Cool had not made a formal demand for the assignment of her dower rights. They contended that a legislative repeal of the Dower Act's provisions altered her rights and that her claims were meritless unless she had sought legal recognition of her dower entitlement.	The defendant, Nathaniel Jackman as receiver, maintained that Deborah Cool had a vested right to the surplus rents as she had legally occupied the property without rent post-William's death. Deborah's counsel argued that her retention of the home and the derived rents were justified by her vested interests, which should be recognized despite the legislative repeal of the Dower Act.

In the case of Samuel G. Telford v. Julia E. Telford, which took place in Marion County, Illinois, the dispute arose from a promissory note made by W. H. Telford and others for which Samuel G. Telford was a surety. The case was brought to court to recover the amount due on that note, with Julia E. Telford as the plaintiff. While initially filed against multiple defendants, only W. H. Telford and Samuel G. Telford were served and remained involved in the proceedings. Samuel G. Telford appealed the decision after the jury found in favor of Julia E. Telford. The jury's verdict came after conflicting testimonies regarding the terms and conditions of the promissory note and the actions taken by both parties following its maturity. The trial emphasized that the jury's role was vital in evaluating credibility amidst contradictory accounts. Judge Reeves presided over the appeal, which was filed on June 15, 1889.	Julia E. Telford claimed that she was owed money on the promissory note and alleged that the defendants, including Samuel G. Telford, signed it as security. She maintained that, following the maturity of the note, there was no consent or knowledge from Samuel G. Telford when she extended the time of payment to W. H. Telford, which solidified her position to recover the amount due.	Samuel G. Telford's defense consisted of two main arguments. The first claimed that he and the other defendants were only acting as sureties for W. H. Telford and that he had not agreed to any extension of payment terms. His second defense argued that he had informed Julia E. Telford in writing after the note matured to initiate legal proceedings and that her delay in doing so relieved him of any liability.

Thomas H. O’Neal filed a legal action against The Wabash Avenue Baptist Church et al. in September 1868, regarding a dispute over a property in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved in this case included Thomas H. O'Neal, Stephen Bronson, Jr., and Sherman P. Tracy. In June 1852, Bronson executed a contract to sell a lot to O'Neal for $722.37, with the condition that O'Neal would pay taxes and assessments on the property and make the final payment by June 1855. However, O'Neal failed to make the final payment and did not pay the property taxes. On August 29, 1855, Bronson sold the property to Tracy and informed O'Neal of the conveyance. O'Neal later claimed that Bronson extended the payment deadline when they spoke in September 1855. Subsequently, in February 1865, Bronson executed a deed for the same premises to O'Neal. The crux of the dispute revolved around whether O'Neal had any legal claim to the property after Bronson had already sold it to Tracy before O'Neal's final payment was made.	O'Neal contended that he was entitled to the property based on the deed executed by Bronson in February 1865, which he argued should relate back to the original contract made in June 1852. He alleged that the contract was forfeited unfairly since he had been led to believe that the payment terms had been extended, and he maintained that Bronson's earlier conveyance to Tracy did not invalidate his claim. O'Neal sought to reverse the judgment that had favored the defendants and to reclaim the title to the property.	The defendants, represented by Tracy's legal team, argued that O'Neal's claim to the property was invalid because Bronson had legally conveyed the title to Tracy in August 1855, prior to O'Neal’s payment due date. They maintained that the contract between O'Neal and Bronson had been forfeited due to O'Neal's failure to fulfill the payment obligations. The defendants contended that once Bronson conveyed the property, he no longer had the authority to extend the payment deadline or to convey title to O'Neal in 1865. Therefore, they requested the court to uphold the validity of their title to the property.

Alexander B. Miller filed a case against Ross Houcke, Jacob C. Gauterman, and Jefferson Weatherford in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1838. The case originated from a trial that took place during the April term of 1838 in the Macoupin Circuit Court presided over by Judge Jesse B. Thomas. Miller had been ruled against in the Circuit Court, where the court awarded the defendants a judgment of $71 plus costs. The legal dispute appears to center on the admissibility of witness testimony where Miller challenged the court's decision to allow a certain question to be asked of a witness during trial. The record does not specify whether the witness answered the question or if the answer provided presented improper testimony.
