She argued that her previous statement of age in the deed did not legally bind her due to her minority status, and she sought recovery of the property based on these grounds.	The defendants contended that the evidence was insufficient to justify recovery against all of them, as there was no proof linking the other defendants to Anna C. Haas, who was directly involved in the property transaction. They asserted that the plaintiff was estopped from disaffirming the deed since it contained a statement that she was of age, thus claiming that she should be held accountable for her representations made at the time of the contract.

The case "The Western Union Telegraph Company v. Mary E. Satterfield" occurred in Jefferson County, Illinois, with a decision filed on March 1, 1889. The plaintiff, Mary E. Satterfield, brought an action of trespass against the Western Union Telegraph Company for cutting down trees on her property. The incident involved a line repairer employed by the telegraph company, Mr. Karberry, who, under his authority, directed that certain trees be removed as he judged they posed a danger to the company’s telegraph lines. Witnesses affirmed that Karberry was present during the cutting and that he specifically pointed out the trees to be cut. The court found no controversy regarding the fact of the injury or the damages resulting from the cutting, which amounted to $100. The central issue deliberated was whether Karberry was acting within the scope of his employment when he made the decision to cut the trees, essentially determining if the company could be held liable for his actions.	Mary E. Satterfield claimed that the Western Union Telegraph Company committed trespass by unlawfully cutting down trees on her property without permission. She argued that the company's actions resulted in damages, which she quantified at $100. The plaintiff sought compensation for the loss sustained due to the unauthorized removal of her trees.	The Western Union Telegraph Company contended that Mr. Karberry, as their line repairer, had the authority to remove trees that he deemed dangerous to the telegraph lines. They argued that any damage incurred was incidental to his duties and that he was acting within the scope of his employment when the alleged trespass took place. The company asserted that it could not be held liable for the actions of its agent if those actions were taken under the belief that they were necessary for the safety of the company's operations.

Sarah M. Parker, the widow and executrix of John C. Parker, initiated a legal case against the Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company following the death of her husband, which she attributed to the railroad's negligence. The case took place in Cook County, Illinois, and proceedings began with a trial under the plea of general issue. During the trial, after the plaintiff presented her evidence, the defendant's counsel requested a written instruction for the jury to find in favor of the defendant. The court complied, leading to a judgment against Parker. Unhappy with this outcome, Parker brought the case before the Illinois Appellate Court, seeking a review of the trial court's decision, particularly focusing on the propriety of instructing the jury to favor the defendant. Key issues in the trial included questions of negligence on part of the defendant and whether there was a lack of ordinary care exhibited by the deceased at the time of the accident. The appellate court noted that while evidence showed negligence by the defendant, it wasn't strong enough to absolve the plaintiff's deceased husband of ordinary care.	The plaintiff, Sarah M. Parker, sought damages for the death of her husband caused by the alleged negligence of the Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company. She argued that the railroad's failure to exercise ordinary care led to the tragic incident. Parker asserted that the court made an error in instructing the jury to decide in favor of the defendant without allowing a complete consideration of the evidence on negligence and ordinary care.	The defendant, Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company, contended that the evidence presented by the plaintiff did not sufficiently demonstrate negligence on their part or a lack of ordinary care by the deceased. The defense maintained that the trial court was correct to direct a verdict in their favor based on the evidence and the established legal standard requiring clear proof of culpable negligence to take the case from the jury. They argued that the plaintiff’s case needed strengthening and noted the impropriety of the supplemental bill of exceptions presented post-trial.

The case "Chicago & Western Indiana Railroad Company v. Barclay Roath" was decided on February 12, 1890, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The incident occurred at a railroad crossing on 68th Street in a thickly settled neighborhood near a school and depot. The plaintiff, a six-year-old boy named Barclay Roath, was injured when he attempted to cross the tracks and was run over by a freight train's cars. The case revolved around whether the railroad company had a duty to ensure safety at the crossing, particularly for children who might not appreciate the dangers of the train's approach. The jury found that while Roath had crossed in front of the train, he had not been struck by the engine itself but rather by one of the cars behind it. The case presented complex issues regarding negligence, particularly whether the boy's actions of attempting to climb onto the moving train constituted negligence and whether the railroad company could be held liable for failing to provide a flagman at the crossing.	The plaintiff, representing young Barclay Roath, claimed damages for the loss of his leg, which was crushed by moving freight cars at the 68th Street crossing. The plaintiff argued that the railroad company failed to take necessary safety measures, such as providing gates and a flagman at the crossing, despite the area being heavily trafficked and near a school. The claim emphasized Roath's age, suggesting he acted with the care expected of a child his age and lacked an understanding of the dangers posed by the train.	The railroad company contended that it owed no duty to protect individuals attempting to climb aboard a moving train and that the plaintiff's actions constituted negligence. The defense highlighted that the plaintiff was found attempting to climb onto the train at the time of the incident. Thus, they argued that the circumstances of the accident were due to the plaintiff's own actions rather than any negligence on the part of the railroad company, and requested the court to dismiss the claim based on this rationale.

John K. Stevens v. Christopher C. Brown et al., Ex’rs. is a legal case decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on February 12, 1884. The case arises from a lease agreement where John K. Stevens leased a property in Chicago for use as a photography gallery from John E. Owsley. The lease commenced on April 29, 1881, for one year. While Stevens occupied the property, Owsley began constructing a large brick building next door. To facilitate this construction, Owsley dug deep trenches next to Stevens's premises, which led to foundational issues with Stevens's building, causing damage to his property and photographic materials. Additionally, Owsley erected a one-story frame building to the south of Stevens's gallery, which obstructed light access necessary for Stevens’s photography work. Stevens filed a lawsuit alleging injuries due to Owsley's actions, originally against Owsley, but after Owsley's death, the suit continued against his executors. The case included multiple counts related to damages from both the excavation and the obstruction from the new building.	Stevens claimed that the actions of Owsley, particularly the excavation and construction next to his gallery, interfered with his use and enjoyment of the leased premises. He asserted that these actions resulted in significant damage, including structural issues with his building and damage to his photographic materials. Stevens requested damages for the losses incurred due to these alleged wrongful acts.	The defendants, representing Owsley's estate, contended that Stevens did not adequately prove his claims regarding the extent of the damages. They argued that the trial court's modifications to jury instructions were appropriate, placing the burden on Stevens to demonstrate unlawful possession interference, which they claimed he failed to do. Consequently, they sought to uphold the lower court's ruling in favor of the defendants.

The case "Jeffrey Robinson v. James D. Harlan" was decided in December 1835 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose in Wayne, Illinois, where Jeffrey Robinson, the plaintiff, pursued action against James D. Harlan, a constable, for failing to execute a legal process. Harlan had been entrusted with an execution order based on a judgment from a justice of the peace in favor of Robinson against John B. Gash. Despite this, Harlan returned with a report of “no property found” when attempting to retrieve funds and later returned a capias indicating Gash was “not found.” Robinson accused Harlan of willful neglect and sought damages amounting to $200. However, the court found that Robinson's case was improperly presented; it did not sufficiently establish the jurisdiction of the justice presiding over the original judgment, which is critical in justifying the constable's obligations. This led to a legal discussion about the limitations of a justice's jurisdiction and the responsibilities of a constable in executing lawful processes.	Jeffrey Robinson claimed that constable James D. Harlan failed to execute the legal processes properly concerning a judgment against John B. Gash, causing him financial harm. He argued that Harlan’s negligence resulted in a loss of $200 and sought damages as the plaintiff in the case, asserting that Harlan had an obligation to act on the lawful process issued by the justice of the peace.	James D. Harlan, the defendant, contended that he was not liable for failure to execute the processes due to deficiencies in Robinson's legal declaration. Harlan argued that the plaintiff did not adequately demonstrate that the justice of the peace had the rightful jurisdiction in the original matter, which is pivotal for holding the constable accountable. His defense included a demurrer to Robinson's declaration, which asserted that the lower court correctly sustained this demurrer, as the required legal foundation for such a claim was lacking.

The case of George S. Pidgeon et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in Pulaski County, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1864. The situation arose from an application by the county tax collector for a judgment against specific lands for delinquent taxes. The lands had been returned as delinquent, and a judgment was sought to sell these properties to collect unpaid taxes. Initially, the County Court had disallowed the defendants' defenses and ordered the sale of the lands to cover the taxes, interest, and costs. Following this, the case was appealed to the Circuit Court, where a trial was conducted that led to a judgment against the defendants for $149.37 plus additional costs and an awarded execution for collection. The primary legal question revolved around whether the Circuit Court erred by rendering a personal judgment against the defendants rather than following the specific statutory requirements that mandated judgments against the lands themselves.	The plaintiffs, represented by the county collector, argued that the court should enforce the collection of delinquent property taxes through the sale of the lands involved. They contended that the process followed was inline with the revenue law which stipulates that judgments for unpaid taxes should be against the property in question and that appropriate procedures had been followed in notifying the defendants about the delinquency.	The defendants contended that the judgment rendered by the Circuit Court was improper as it awarded a personal judgment and execution against them rather than sticking to the statutory requirement for judgments to be made specifically against the lands for tax collection. They claimed that the court overstepped its jurisdictional authority by deviating from the mandated process outlined in the revenue act, which only allowed for in rem judgments against the properties with unpaid taxes.

E. P. Saunders initiated legal proceedings against Thomas Bernard in a garnishee case, which was held in Clinton County, Illinois. The proceedings began when Lippincott and Cox, who were judgment creditors of Saunders, sought to claim debts owed to them by Bernard. The initial ruling by a justice of the peace favored Lippincott and Cox, resulting in a judgment against Bernard. Following this, E. P. Saunders appealed the decision to the Circuit Court of Clinton County. However, Lippincott and Cox filed a motion to dismiss Saunders's appeal, which was granted, leading to the appeal being dismissed. Saunders then brought the case to the Illinois Appellate Court, arguing that the dismissal of his appeal was erroneous. The court noted that no bill of exceptions was filed, meaning that the issues raised could not be considered due to procedural requirements.	E. P. Saunders claimed that the Circuit Court's decision to dismiss his appeal was in error. He sought to overturn the dismissal and continue with his appeal against the judgment rendered in favor of Lippincott and Cox. The essence of his argument rested on the assertion that due process was not fully afforded concerning his appeal rights.	The defendants, Lippincott and Cox, argued that the appeal should be dismissed as the necessary procedural steps had not been followed by Saunders. They maintained that without a bill of exceptions, the appellate court could not consider the claims and legal questions raised by Saunders, thus upholding the dismissal of the appeal.

In March 1859, David L. Hough filed a lawsuit in La Salle County, Illinois, for the foreclosure of a mortgage on property originally executed by Thaddeus H. Coburn on November 29, 1854. The mortgage secured a promissory note for $350 due to William E. Kent. Coburn, who had purchased the land for $850, claimed he had paid the balance secured by the note into the Bank of Ottawa before it became due. He alleged that this payment was wrongfully delivered back to Kent. Coburn deposited $371 at the Bank of Ottawa in November 1855 and requested that it be retained until the title to the property was perfect, against the backdrop of a defective title discovery. The bank collected the note but never applied Coburn’s deposit to it because the title was not cleared. The case hinged on whether Coburn's payment constituted a valid satisfaction of the promissory note or if it remained conditional based on title perfection.	The plaintiff, David L. Hough, argued that the promissory note was valid and had not been satisfied, despite Coburn's claims to have paid the amount into the Bank of Ottawa. Hough sought foreclosure of the mortgage, asserting that Coburn's conditional payment did not fulfill the terms of the note, thus allowing Hough to pursue the property as collateral for the debt owed.	Thaddeus H. Coburn contended that he had indeed paid the amount due on the promissory note into the Bank of Ottawa before the due date. He maintained that the bank was instructed to hold the payment until the title issue was resolved, and because the title remained defective, the bank was never authorized to apply the funds to settle the note. He requested that the court acknowledge his payment and dismiss Hough's foreclosure action.

The case "The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company v. Otway Watson et al." was decided on February 7, 1885, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It involved the Commercial National Bank and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company as key participants, who were seeking a resolution concerning ownership claims related to two tracts of land. The overarching issue stemmed from Samuel J. Walker, who had been a prominent real estate operator in Chicago and had become insolvent. Various creditors, including Watson and others, had obtained judgments against Walker, leading to the original bill filed in Cook County. The complainants sought to set aside a series of transactions involving Walker's interests in properties, including a private railroad street and land in Lake County, asserting these constituted fraudulent transfers designed to evade creditors. The assigned bankruptcy trustee, Jenkins, also pursued claims to retrieve assets for Walker's creditors. The proceedings included multiple judgments and executions, with Walker's interests being subject to various liens and sales that complicated the recovery by his creditors.	The plaintiffs, comprised of Walker’s judgment creditors, claimed that several transactions involving Walker's properties were fraudulent. They argued that ownership of the private railroad street should be adjudged as part of Walker's estate, unencumbered by the interests of the bank and its affiliates. They sought a legal declaration to set aside previous sales and judgments, asserting that these property claims were made to hinder and defraud them as legitimate creditors.	The defendants, including the bank and the railroad company, contended that their acquisitions of Walker's properties were legitimate and conducted under valid transactions. They argued that the sales and other legal proceedings followed due process and did not constitute fraudulent behavior aimed at evading creditor claims. They maintained that the prior liens and judgments had been correctly followed and executed, rendering the plaintiffs' claims baseless.

In April 1858, in Tazewell County, Illinois, a trial was held regarding the divorce case of John Turbitt and Margaret Turbitt. The couple married in 1855, and Margaret filed a bill alleging that John had committed extreme and repeated cruelty towards her. She claimed that he failed to provide adequate maintenance despite having significant financial means and that he left her without food and medical help during her pregnancy. Specifically, she noted that he abandoned her just days before she gave birth and did not return for ten days, during which time she relied on the charity of her neighbors. John Turbitt responded to these allegations by denying them and asserting that Margaret had exhibited problematic behavior as well. The case was significant enough to warrant a writ of error to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Margaret Turbitt claimed that her husband, John Turbitt, exhibited extreme and repeated cruelty by neglecting to provide sufficient maintenance and abandoning her during critical times, including her confinement. She highlighted his lack of support in essential needs and the impact this had on her well-being. Margaret requested a divorce based on these claims, arguing that his behavior constituted sufficient grounds under the law.	John Turbitt denied Margaret's allegations of cruelty and neglect. He argued against the claims of insufficient support and stated that the circumstances leading to any threats he made were not adequately presented. Additionally, he highlighted grievances against Margaret’s behavior, indicating that the issues were not solely one-sided. John requested that the court reverse the lower court's decision to grant the divorce.

In 1854, a legal dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, concerning the rightful occupation of the office of judge of the recorder's court of the city. The parties involved were W. T. Burgess, acting on behalf of The People as the plaintiff, and Robert S. Wilson, who was the defendant in error. The crux of the case revolved around whether Wilson was eligible to hold the office he was elected to during an election that took place on March 1, 1853. It was established that Wilson had been elected to this office under an act passed in February 1853 but had not resided in Illinois for the requisite five years prior to his election, as stipulated by the state constitution. The case was heard in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas, where Judge J. M. Wilson denied a motion for leave to file an information in the nature of a quo warranto, which led Burgess to seek a writ of error to challenge that decision.	The plaintiff, W. T. Burgess, contended that Wilson was unlawfully holding the office of judge of the recorder’s court. Burgess argued that Wilson did not meet the constitutional requirements for eligibility, specifically the stipulation of having resided in Illinois for five years prior to his election. The legal request was for the court to grant leave to file an information to determine Wilson's right to hold the office.	The defendant, Robert S. Wilson, maintained that he was duly elected to the recorder's court following a legal election process. He argued that the constitutional residency requirements applied solely to judges of courts established or recognized by the constitution, which did not include the recorder's court. Wilson asserted that the qualifications presented against him were misapplied and that he was entitled to hold the office given the context of the law under which he was elected.

On April 5, 1886, Denison F. Holmes filed a claim against the estate of Adam Burwell in the County Court of Carroll County, Illinois, seeking $470 for his share of expenses incurred during bankruptcy proceedings involving John W. Asay. Holmes had entered an agreement with other creditors to bear a proportionate share of these expenses. An objection was raised against the allowance of his claim, leading to a hearing where the court ruled in favor of the defendant estate. The plaintiff subsequently appealed the judgment to the Circuit Court of Carroll County. A jury trial resulted in a verdict for the defendant, prompting Holmes to appeal again, claiming errors in the trial court's jury instructions regarding the statute of limitations and the exclusion of certain evidence. The court reviewed the case, considering the implications of the statute of limitations and the specifics of the contract that Holmes had with the other creditors.	The plaintiff, Denison F. Holmes, argued that he was entitled to recover $470 as his share of costs associated with the bankruptcy proceedings involving John W. Asay, based on an agreement he entered with other creditors in 1874. He contended that the expenses were just and overdue despite objections regarding the statute of limitations, which he claimed should not apply due to the agreement being a continuing one.	The defendant, represented by Mary E. Burwell as the executrix of the estate, contended that Holmes' claim was barred by the statute of limitations. They argued that there was insufficient evidence to prove that the bankruptcy proceedings had not concluded more than ten years prior to Holmes filing his claim. The defense maintained that the payments Holmes sought were not related directly to the expenses of the bankruptcy proceedings and that the estate had already fulfilled its obligations through previous payments made to Holmes.

In December 1830, the case of Joseph Johnson, Plaintiff in Error, v. The People, Defendant in Error, was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The events leading to this case occurred in Madison County, Illinois, where Johnson faced an indictment during the October term of 1829 for violating a specific statute regarding the sale of spirits. The statute in question prohibited individuals without a legal tavern license from selling any alcoholic beverages in quantities less than one quart. Johnson was tried and found guilty, resulting in a court-imposed fine of twelve dollars. His legal team subsequently attempted to have the judgment arrested, but the circuit court denied their motion. The law at the time stipulated a maximum fine of ten dollars for such an offense, thus leading to Johnson's appeal against the imposed penalty and the judgment rendered against him.	Joseph Johnson argued that the fine imposed on him for retailing spirits without a license was excessive and violated the applicable statute, which capped the penalty for such an offense at ten dollars. He sought to reverse the circuit court's judgment and ultimately requested that the court either nullify the sentence or reduce the fine to comply with the statutory limit.	The People, represented by the state’s attorney, maintained the validity of the circuit court's judgment against Johnson. Their primary argument revolved around adherence to the legal statutes regarding unlicensed sale of spirits, asserting that the court acted within its jurisdiction and authority in imposing the fine for the alleged offense.

The case "William Bihler v. Amos Gockley" took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the decision being rendered by the Illinois Appellate Court on April 28, 1886. William Bihler, the plaintiff, was engaged to Fredricka Lieb, who, trusting Bihler's honesty, entrusted him with $43 for safekeeping before she was adjudged insane and committed to the Cook County Insane Asylum. During her treatment, Bihler paid for her care, which altogether exceeded the amount she had entrusted to him. After Fredricka was discharged from the asylum, Bihler provided her with a transparent account of his expenditures, and she expressed satisfaction without demanding any money back. However, after some time, Amos Gockley, the defendant and pastor of Bihler’s church, publicly accused Bihler of cheating Fredricka out of her money, suggesting he had mismanaged her funds and been dishonest in his accounting. Gockley made these derogatory statements in the presence of other congregation members, which led to a formal investigation by the church that ultimately ruled in Bihler's favor, declaring the allegations unfounded.	Bihler accused Gockley of slander, claiming that the defendant's statements were false, malicious, and damaging to his reputation. He argued that Gockley's public accusations implied he had committed larceny regarding Fredricka's funds, and he sought vindication through the court, requesting the judgment to dismiss the demurrer to the slander counts against Gockley.	Gockley's primary defense was that his statements were not defamatory nor sufficient to substantiate a claim of slander. He contended that the language used was not prima facie defamatory and that it should not be construed as implying criminal behavior. Gockley may have sought to dismiss the counts against him by arguing that the words could not be reasonably interpreted in the manner alleged by the plaintiff.

In 1874, Theodore Meeker and Elizabeth Bond, the appellants, contested the validity of the will and codicil of Joseph Meeker, who had passed away in January 1872. The trial took place in Cook County, Illinois, where it was revealed that Joseph Meeker, at the time of his death, was about 65 years old and had suffered multiple strokes, impacting his health and mental capacity. Elizabeth Meeker, the appellee, was his third wife, while the appellants were his children from a previous marriage. The will was executed on May 13, 1871, followed by a codicil on November 27, 1871. The appellants claimed that Joseph lacked the capacity to make the will and that undue influence from Elizabeth led him to make these instruments contrary to his true desires. After hearing testimonies from around forty to fifty witnesses, a jury determined that while Joseph had the capacity to execute the will, he lacked the capacity for the codicil. The trial court ultimately upheld the will and annulled the codicil, prompting the appellants to appeal this decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Theodore Meeker and Elizabeth Bond, claimed that Joseph Meeker was not of sound mind when he executed his will and codicil due to his medical condition. They argued he lacked the necessary mental capacity to make valid decisions regarding his estate and contended that Elizabeth Meeker exercised undue influence over him in the creation of these documents. They sought to have the will set aside and the codicil recognized as invalid.	Elizabeth Meeker, the defendant, contended that her husband was of sound mind when the will was executed, capable of transacting his affairs as evidenced by his business activities following the strokes. She argued that the claims of undue influence were unfounded and that the distribution of the estate reflected his independent decisions rather than manipulation. Elizabeth requested that the court affirm the validity of the will while setting aside the findings regarding the codicil.

The case "Capital City Mutual Fire Insurance Company v. George E. Detwiler" was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court, with a decision rendered on November 9, 1887. The dispute originated when George E. Detwiler, the plaintiff, alleged that he had been wrongfully discharged as the general agent of Capital City Mutual Fire Insurance Company, the defendant, on February 11, 1884. Detwiler claimed that he had been under a contract with the insurance company, which was established on September 29, 1882, and was to last for five years. He asserted that he fulfilled his part of the contract and sought compensation for services rendered, along with damages for the alleged wrongful termination of his employment. The defendant countered with a plea of accord and satisfaction, claiming an agreement was reached on April 21, 1884, that purportedly resolved all disputes regarding compensation. The case progressed without a jury to the trial court, where evidence was presented by both parties regarding the agreements and the plaintiff's claims for damages.	The plaintiff, George E. Detwiler, contended that he had offered services as an agent for the Capital City Mutual Fire Insurance Company based on a contract which entitled him to compensation. He claimed that he was wrongfully discharged during the term of the contract. In his lawsuit, he sought damages for unpaid wages and the wrongful nature of his termination, alleging that the contract had been breached by the defendant.	The defendant, Capital City Mutual Fire Insurance Company, asserted that there had been an accord and satisfaction following Detwiler's alleged wrongful discharge. They claimed that a new agreement was established on April 21, 1884, in which Detwiler accepted a settlement in lieu of further claims against the company. The defendant argued that this new agreement effectively resolved any issues concerning the prior claimed debt, dismissing Detwiler's allegations of wrongful termination, and insisted that the plaintiff's claims were thereby settled.

In September 1867, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Jacob Bunn et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. Matthew Laflin. The case arose from a legislative act that aimed to establish a new State house, appointing certain individuals as commissioners to oversee its construction. The plaintiffs in error, which included Jacob Bunn and several others, challenged the legitimacy of their appointment, arguing that these commissioners were, by definition, officers under the Illinois Constitution. The central question was whether the commissioners constituted "officers" as described in sections of the Constitution that restrict legislative appointments to such positions. The court considered various statutory and constitutional definitions, along with historical context, surrounding the nature of public office and the intentions behind the restrictions on legislative appointments.	The plaintiffs contended that the commissioners appointed to oversee the construction of the new State house were "officers" under the Illinois Constitution. They argued that their appointment violated constitutional provisions which prohibit the legislature from appointing officers, asserting that their roles involved continuous duties and responsibilities that warranted their classification as officers. The plaintiffs requested a judicial ruling to oust the commissioners on the grounds of this constitutional violation.	The defendants, comprising the commissioners, argued that they were not officers under the Constitution but rather employees tasked with a specific, single purpose—the completion of the new State house. They asserted that their duties did not exhibit the continuity or enduring nature characteristic of public office, as their authority would cease upon the completion of their designated duties. They requested that the court dismiss the action against them, affirming their appointments under the act.

In the case of Charles Aulger v. Asa S. Smith, which took place in Peoria County, Illinois, around April 1864, the legal conflict arose from an incident in which the plaintiff, Charles Aulger, accused the defendant, Asa S. Smith, of assault and battery, specifically alleging that Smith stabbed him with a knife. The legal proceedings began with a declaration charging Smith with the assault and seeking special damages. Smith entered a plea of the general issue and son assault demesne. During the trial, several pieces of evidence were pivotal, particularly the deposition of a deceased witness, Cicero S. Burns, which had been lost but previously read at an earlier trial concerning the same incident. The court allowed limited testimony regarding Aulger's previous statements in a related criminal trial but did not allow the entirety of his prior testimony to be presented, leading to an objection from Aulger's legal team. The jury ultimately found in favor of Smith, prompting Aulger to seek a reversal of this decision through a writ of error.	Charles Aulger's key arguments included a claim for damages resulting from the assault, specifically emphasizing the unfair exclusion of vital evidence, such as the content of the lost deposition given by the deceased witness Burns, which could have supported his claims. Aulger argued that the trial court's limitation on the testimony allowed from past proceedings unnecessarily prejudiced his case and that the overall process was unjust due to these evidentiary restrictions.	Asa S. Smith's primary defense rested on the general issue of the case, asserting that the claims of assault and battery were unfounded. He challenged the admissibility of certain evidence, including the exclusion of the complete testimony of Aulger from the prior criminal trial, and argued that limiting evidence did not undermine his defense. Smith maintained that the case was appropriately tried without the contested evidence and that the jury’s verdict in his favor was justified.

In 1868, in Winnebago County, Illinois, Israel B. Holmes and his wife (the plaintiffs) pursued legal action against John H. Holmes (the defendant). The case had previously been brought before the Illinois Supreme Court and was reported in 44 Ill. 169. At the crux of the case was a dispute over leasing land. The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to a lease for life on the east half of a quarter section of land owned by the defendant. The court had ruled in favor of the plaintiffs previously, granting them the lease. However, the defendant appealed this decision, arguing that there was no legal basis for the claimed lease as the land entirely belonged to him. The defendant contended that his promise to lease the land, which was not backed by consideration, was not legally enforceable under the statute of frauds. The case brought into question the existence of equitable grounds for the plaintiffs' claim to the land.	The plaintiffs, Israel B. Holmes and his wife, claimed an entitlement to a lease for life on the east half of the quarter section of land owned by John H. Holmes. They asserted that they had a legitimate interest in the property, as previously recognized by the court, which warranted the granting of a lease. The plaintiffs sought to compel the defendant to provide them with this lease based on their understanding of past agreements and interactions regarding the land.	John H. Holmes, the defendant, refuted the plaintiffs' claims by maintaining that the land in question was solely his property, and any verbal promise to lease it for life, made out of familial goodwill, held no legal force as it lacked consideration. He emphasized that the plaintiffs had previously rejected an offer for a lease, and thus he was under no obligation to provide the lease. The defendant argued that the plaintiffs were already compensated through the use of the land for many years and that their claim for a lease lacked legal and equitable foundation.

In the case of John H. Evans v. The People, the events unfolded in Warren County, Illinois, during the October term of the County Court in 1886. John H. Evans was initially tried before a jury, which rendered a verdict against him, resulting in a judgment on November 9, 1886. Evans sought to appeal this judgment and was granted leave to do so, provided he filed a bond of $800 within twenty days. The bond was filed on November 18 and subsequently approved by the county judge on November 19. However, on January 3, 1887, the Circuit Court dismissed Evans's appeal, which allowed him to withdraw his appeal bond. Subsequently, he re-filed the case in the County Court and the approval of the bond was made. The appeal was again dismissed in May 1887, leading to uncertainty over the validity of the appeals due to prior dismissals and whether the appeal process had been correctly followed according to procedural rules.	The plaintiff, The People, argued that the second appeal filed by John H. Evans was barred due to the first dismissal of the appeal, suggesting that the dismissal was a final disposition. They maintained that the procedural requirements for perfecting an appeal had not been met, notably concerning the approval of the appeal bond and the necessary documentation of prior proceedings.	John H. Evans contended that the first dismissal of his appeal was not a bar to his second appeal, asserting that it had been improperly dismissed without proper grounds documented in a bill of exceptions. He argued that the cases presented in the Circuit Court during the appeals were not sufficiently transparent to prevent his right to appeal. Evans claimed that the procedural rules regarding the appeal process were not properly applied and requested that the court reinstate his appeal and address the merits of his case.

In September 1872, a legal dispute arose in the Superior Court of Chicago, Illinois, involving August Bauer (plaintiff) and Gustav Gottmanhausen (defendant). The case centered on the boundary line of their properties in Lot 22 of Bronson's Addition to Chicago. Both parties claimed ownership of a strip of land, with Bauer owning the north half of the lot and Gottmanhausen claiming it belonged to the south half. The background revealed that a surveyor, Bradley, had made an error in placing the boundary stakes for the lots around 1845, which inadvertently designated the north lines incorrectly. This error was recognized over a period during which fences were established according to the mistakenly placed stakes. Despite a continuous boundary acknowledgment by both parties for 20 years, tensions escalated when, in a bid to claim the land, Gottmanhausen unlawfully removed a fence and trespassed on the disputed strip. Bauer sued for damages based on this invasion of his possession, leading to a trial that resulted in a jury's verdict favoring Bauer.	August Bauer's primary argument was that he had rightful possession of the disputed strip of land, as established by 20 years of continuous and open possession. He claimed damages for trespass under the action of quare clausum fregit, asserting that Gottmanhausen's actions unlawfully deprived him of his rightful property and caused damage to his business. Bauer sought not only the restoration of his property rights but also compensatory damages for his losses.	Gustav Gottmanhausen contended that the boundary line was positioned at the north side of the disputed strip and that his ownership claim to the north half included the area in question. He argued liberum tenementum (freehold), positing that he had a legitimate legal claim to the land based on the original survey despite the long-standing possession claimed by Bauer. He requested a dismissal of Bauer's claims on the grounds of his interpreted ownership rights.

Octavius Lumaghi v. Sebastian Neuber is a legal case that took place in Madison County, Illinois, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1873. The case revolves around a dispute regarding unpaid wages for services rendered. The plaintiff, Sebastian Neuber, was employed by Henry James to assist in sinking a shaft for the defendant, Octavius Lumaghi. Neuber was owed $69.50 for his work. Prior to quitting, he received a partial payment of $35 from Lumaghi, who also drafted an order for James to sign, which would authorize the payment of the remaining balance. However, the order was not signed until approximately six weeks later, and at that point, Lumaghi refused to pay the remaining amount. Following a trial, the jury ruled in favor of Neuber, awarding him $34.50. Lumaghi appealed the decision.	The plaintiff, Sebastian Neuber, argued that Lumaghi had promised to pay him for his services and had partially fulfilled this promise by paying $35. He claimed that Lumaghi was obligated to pay the remaining balance of $34.50 as per their agreement, regardless of whether Henry James had signed the order, since Lumaghi had the responsibility to withhold the payment from James for Neuber's wages.	The defendant, Octavius Lumaghi, contended that he should not be held liable for the entire payment due to the outstanding signature from James on the order. He argued that the delay in obtaining that signature impacted his obligation to make the remaining payment. Additionally, Lumaghi disputed the extent of Neuber's claims and sought to overturn the trial jury's verdict.

The case of William T. Robinson v. C. F. McNeill took place in September 1869, in Iroquois County, Illinois. The central issue revolved around a promissory note that McNeill had issued to Robinson, which was connected to the assignment of certain open book accounts. Robinson claimed that the accounts were unpaid and collectible, which McNeill later contested. The trial held in the Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Charles R. Starr, led to a verdict favoring McNeill. The court examined the nature of the assignment and found that while the transfer of accounts implied they were unpaid, it did not guarantee that they were collectible. The specifics of the contract made at the time of the assignment did not include any warranty regarding the collectibility of the accounts, highlighting a crucial element of the case.	The plaintiff, William T. Robinson, argued that C. F. McNeill owed him payment based on a promissory note linked to assigned book accounts, which he asserted to be unpaid and collectible. Robinson’s claims were rooted in the belief that the assignment of these accounts came with an implied warranty of their collectibility, which he sought to enforce through the legal action.	C. F. McNeill countered Robinson's claims by asserting that the accounts assigned were not collectible, which negated any obligations under the promissory note. McNeill argued that the only evidence of a warranty came from oral statements made at the time of the sale, which should not have been considered since a written contract outlining the terms of the assignment had been established, containing no warranty that the accounts were collectible.

In 1869, the case of Rosanna Heward v. Henry Slagle took place in Tazewell County, Illinois, over the estate of Nathan Dillon, who died on January 28, 1863. Rosanna Heward, a daughter and heir of Dillon, was dissatisfied with the final settlement of the estate conducted by his administrators, Mary Dillon (his widow) and Henry Slagle (her brother). Heward appealed the county court’s approval of the settlement, which included the discharge of the administrators and a distribution of a minimal amount remaining of a much larger estate. The case became complicated due to a lease agreement made between Dillon and Slagle that lasted until Dillon's death and a deed executed by the heirs to their mother that transferred property rights for her lifetime. The administrators claimed they acted based on the deed and that the estate had been settled accordingly. However, the appeal raised questions about whether the proper procedures were followed in administering the estate and if all assets had been fully accounted for, including a substantial amount of gold that was allegedly unaccounted for.	Rosanna Heward argued that the administrators had not properly settled the estate of her father, especially since a large part of the estate was missing or unaccounted for. She claimed that there was no necessity for administration due to the absence of debts, and she insisted that the settlement executed by the administrators was unfair and not in the best interest of the heirs. To resolve her grievance, she sought to reverse the lower court's approval of the settlement and gain a full and transparent accounting of the estate.	Henry Slagle and Mary Dillon contended that they had adequately administered the estate and claimed that the settlement done was in accordance with the deed executed by the heirs. They argued that the estate was settled based on the understanding of how the property would be managed and distributed, specifically under the terms of the deed that they believed granted full rights to the widow, thereby justifying their decisions as administrators. They asserted that any claims concerning undisclosed assets were unfounded and that they had complied with their duties in managing the estate.

The case "The City of Chicago v. Charles M. Edwards" took place in January 1871, within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. Charles M. Edwards was appointed as a police patrolman by the City of Chicago's board of police at the request of the board of health, starting from April 12, 1867, for a term of one year, with specific duties on the sanitary squad. Edwards served for approximately six months before his discharge was requested by the board of health, with no cause assigned for this removal. Following his discharge, Edwards sought to recover the salary for the remainder of his appointment, arguing that this termination breached the terms of the appointment, which he claimed constituted a contract that could not be legally rescinded without mutual consent.	Edwards, as the plaintiff, claimed that his appointment as a police patrolman created a binding contract with the City of Chicago for the duration of one year. He argued that his discharge without cause constituted a wrongful termination and sought to recover the salary for the remaining portion of his term that he had not been paid.	The City of Chicago, represented by the board of police, contended that under the city charter, specifically section 10 of chapter 10, the board had the right to remove Edwards at any time without assigning a reason. The defense maintained that the appointment did not constitute an irrevocable contract, and they argued that the law provided them with the authority to terminate the appointment in order to determine the necessity for police patrol services.

The case "John Knight et al. v. Bradley B. Begole" was handled in the Illinois Supreme Court and decided in September 1870. The dispute arose over a mechanic’s lien concerning property in Chicago, Illinois. In May 1869, a decree was made to sell premises due to an outstanding lien. The court ordered that unless the amount owed, including costs, was paid within ninety days, the property would be sold at public auction with prior notice. Subsequent to this, legislation was passed on March 30, 1869, allowing for a right to redeem real estate following such sales. However, this new law did not take effect until sixty days post-session, which meant it was not yet applicable at the time of the decree. The defendants challenged the decree on the basis that it precluded their right to redemption, which emerged after the passage of the new statute, but this statute was determined by the court not to have retrospective effect.	The plaintiffs, John Knight et al., claimed that they were entitled to enforce the mechanic's lien against the defendant, Bradley B. Begole, which included requesting a sale of the premises to satisfy the owed amount. They argued that the decree issued was valid and request the court affirm this decision in light of the circumstances regarding the lien and the subsequent failure of the defendant to redeem the property.	The defendant, Bradley B. Begole, contended that the decree was erroneous as it effectively revoked his right to redeem the property following the passage of the new statute allowing for such a right. He argued that even though the decree was proper at the time of issue, it became flawed with the introduction of the statute, which should grant redemption opportunities for interests acquired post-1865.

In January 1873, a legal dispute arose in Mason County, Illinois, involving James R. Walker and Adolph Krebaum. The case initially began before a justice of the peace and later progressed to the Circuit Court. The central issue centered on a promissory note that the defendant, Walker, had issued to the Kalamazoo Manufacturing Corporation. The note was subsequently endorsed by the corporation to Krebaum. During the trial, the defendant objected to the introduction of this note and its indorsement as evidence, arguing about the authority behind the endorsement. The court, however, permitted the presentation of the note and ruled in favor of Krebaum, leading to a judgment against Walker for the amount due on the note. Walker subsequently appealed the decision.	Adolph Krebaum, the plaintiff, argued that he was the lawful assignee of a promissory note originally made payable to the Kalamazoo Manufacturing Corporation. He maintained that the endorsement allowing him to collect on the note was valid, despite the defendant's objections regarding the authority of the person who reportedly endorsed it. Krebaum sought the payment owed on the note as his legal right as the assignee.	James R. Walker, the defendant, contended that the endorsement of the promissory note was insufficient because it did not clearly demonstrate that the person who signed it had the necessary authority to act on behalf of the Kalamazoo Manufacturing Corporation. He argued that it was the plaintiff's responsibility to prove the authority behind the endorsement, which he claimed was not sufficiently established in court. Consequently, Walker requested that the court dismiss the plaintiff’s claims.

Thomas Milnor filed a lawsuit against E. W. Willard and others in April 1864, seeking to enforce a contract for the purchase of a specific lot in Duncan's Addition to Chicago. The contract was originally made on June 15, 1854, between the defendants and the trustees of the South Chicago German Church, involving a sale price of $4,000 with payment terms that included a down payment of $400 and annual installments. Milnor acquired the contract from the original purchasers on June 12, 1855, and made payments totaling $2,673.96, leaving the final payment due on June 19, 1859. However, Willard declared the contract forfeited on October 6, 1861, due to non-payment. Milnor attempted to make a payment in April 1863 and subsequently filed his complaint on May 2, 1863. He claimed that his inability to meet the payment deadline was due to financial hardship but sought relief from the disappointment of the contract's terms. The court needed to assess whether this reason was valid enough to warrant specific performance of the contract.	The plaintiff, Thomas Milnor, argued that he should be granted specific performance of the contract despite a delay in payment, citing his financial struggles as the reason for his inability to comply with the payment terms. He sought to prevent the forfeiture of the contract and demanded enforcement of the agreement after offering to pay the outstanding amount, including interest.	The defendants, led by E. W. Willard, contended that the contract clearly stipulated that time was of the essence and that the failure to make timely payments constituted a breach of contract. They argued that Milnor's financial situation did not excuse his noncompliance and that enforcing the contract without due consideration of the payment timetable would undermine the obligations of purchasers in land contracts. They sought the affirmation of the contract's forfeiture, emphasizing that the late payments invalidated any claims for specific performance.

On January 15, 1886, the Charles Whittaker Manufacturing Company was established in Illinois with a capital stock of $100,000 for manufacturing goods. By November 3, 1887, the company became insolvent, a fact known to its board of directors: William L. Roseboom, Albert D. Ferry, Frank Scales, and Charles Whittaker. Roseboom, Ferry, and Scales, who were liable on promissory notes amounting to $23,591.57, sought to secure their interests by replacing these notes with a judgment note approved in a board meeting, even as they were aware of the corporation's insolvency. Subsequently, they caused a judgment by confession to be entered in their favor, allowing them to execute the judgment against the company’s assets. Following this, other creditors, including Childs & Co. and Everett & Post, initiated attachment suits against the corporation’s assets, which led to competing claims over the company's property. Whittaker and others filed a bill to set aside the judgment favoring Roseboom and his associates. The legal proceedings culminated in a decree that found the actions of Roseboom, Ferry, and Scales to be fraudulent, resulting in their judgment being vacated.	The plaintiffs, including Charles Whittaker and others, claimed the judgment obtained by Roseboom, Ferry, and Scales was fraudulent and sought for it to be vacated. They requested an injunction to prevent further proceedings on the judgment and the appointment of a receiver for the corporation's assets to ensure fair distribution among creditors. The plaintiffs argued that the actions taken by the directors to secure their own interests improperly prioritized them over other creditors.	The defendants, Roseboom, Ferry, and Scales, argued that their actions were valid, asserting that as creditors, they had the right to secure their debts against the corporation. They contended that the decree was erroneous in prioritizing the other creditors’ attachments over their claims. They also claimed procedural errors regarding the failure to include all creditors in the case, arguing that this invalidated the decree concerning the distribution of the corporate assets.

On April 19, 1866, Pitts and Wilson obtained a judgment against James W. Haworth in the circuit court of Macon County, Illinois. At that time, Haworth owned two lots in Decatur, Illinois, which he occupied as a homestead while being the head of a family. Subsequently, he executed two mortgages on these properties for $1,000. In December 1868, he filed for bankruptcy and, in August 1869, the court granted his discharge from debts, with the lots being set apart to him as exempt from debts under the bankruptcy act. Later, both mortgages were foreclosed, and the lots were sold. Haworth redeemed the property after his discharge and later mortgaged the lots again for $500. On August 10, 1870, under an alias execution sought by Pitts and Wilson, the sheriff appraised the lots at $2,000, exempting a portion worth $1,000 as his homestead and targeting the remaining value for sale. Haworth filed for an injunction to prevent the sale, claiming the property was homestead-exempt. The court granted a temporary injunction but eventually dismissed Haworth's bill after a hearing, which he subsequently appealed.	Haworth argued that his property was exempt from sale under judgment due to homestead protections, as it did not exceed a value of $1,000. He claimed that the lien from the judgment did not attach to the homestead property and sought to enjoin the sale under the execution by Pitts and Wilson.	Pitts and Wilson contended that the judgment lien remained effective regardless of Haworth's bankruptcy discharge and that the lien could extend to property valued over $1,000. They argued that the law allowed the lien to attach to any remaining value beyond the homestead exemption and that the sale under the execution should proceed as planned.

In 1883, the legal case of Patrick Kane et al. v. The People took place in Illinois. The plaintiffs, Patrick Kane and others, were involved in a dispute against the State (referred to as "The People"). The case arose when the plaintiffs filed an appeal against a decision in a previous legal matter, prompting challenges from the appellees regarding the procedures followed. Specifically, the appellees sought to have the court strike the bill of exceptions and dismiss the appeal, arguing that the motion was filed too late after the joinder in error had occurred. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court, which addressed these procedural issues in its ruling.	The plaintiffs contended that their bill of exceptions was valid and should remain part of the court's consideration. They were seeking to continue their appeal and assert their claims against the state regarding the outcome of a prior judgment that affected them.	The defendant, representing the interests of the state, argued that the motion to strike the bill of exceptions was filed too late, referencing legal precedents that supported their position. The defense requested that the court dismiss the appeal on these procedural grounds, stating that it did not comply with the required timing for such motions.

In 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, Henry Kuecken and Bertha Reinke filed a bill in equity against John Voltz, concerning a dispute over an alley that extended from two lots owned by the plaintiffs across two lots owned by the defendant, leading to Chicago Avenue. The origins of the alley's designation trace back to 1856, when George B. Chandler sold portions of his property, which included an exception reserving ten feet for an alley from the sold lands. Chandler's property underwent several transactions, with Kuecken and Reinke acquiring adjacent lots that contained similar exceptions. The plaintiffs argued that the exception was intended to benefit the owners of the adjoining properties, while the defendant contended that the reservation was personal to Chandler and not for the benefit of future property owners, leading to the dismissal of the plaintiffs' claims by the circuit court.	The plaintiffs, Kuecken and Reinke, argued that the reservation of the alley in the earlier deeds constituted an easement appurtenant that should benefit all subsequent owners of the adjoining lots. They sought to compel the opening of the alley, asserting that the intent behind the original reservation was to establish a right of way for all future landholders, which would enhance the property's usability.	The defendant, Voltz, through his counsel, argued that the reserved alley was a personal right granted only to Chandler, thus not transferable to future property owners. He maintained that the language of the deeds indicated no intention of creating an easement for the benefit of others. Additionally, he claimed the plaintiffs had lost their rights due to non-use and that he had established adverse possession over the alley for over twenty years.

The case takes place in Illinois and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1824. The key individuals involved are the administrators, widow, and heirs of T. Ernst, who are the plaintiffs in error, and the President and Directors of the State Bank of Illinois, the defendants in error. The background involves a mortgage loan of eight hundred dollars made by T. Ernst to the State Bank of Illinois on August 31, 1821. To secure the payment of this loan, Ernst executed a mortgage deed. When the debt remained unpaid, the bank sought a court order to sell the mortgaged premises via a writ of scire facias in the Fayette County circuit court. The plaintiffs, heirs of T. Ernst, claimed that the mortgage debt was released by a legislative act passed on February 18, 1823, stating that Ernst's estate was exempt from debts owed to the state, thus contesting the bank's claim to recover the debt.	The plaintiffs argued that a statute passed by the Illinois General Assembly released T. Ernst’s estate from all debts owed to the state, including the mortgage debt to the State Bank of Illinois. They contended that this statute, which aimed to protect estates from state debts, should apply to their case. They sought to reverse the lower court's judgment that upheld the bank's claim against Ernst's estate.	The defendants maintained that they were entitled to collect the mortgage debt as secured by the deed. They argued that the bank was merely acting as a trustee for the people of Illinois and thus should be able to collect debts owed to it. The bank contested the plaintiffs' claim of legislative release, claiming that the act was not applicable to their mortgage debt.

The case of Edwin S. Fowler v. Edward R. Pirkins was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875. The background of the case involves Edwin S. Fowler, who owned certain lands in Sangamon County, Illinois. The county collector of taxes, Edward R. Pirkins, initiated proceedings against Fowler's lands due to unpaid taxes as part of an application to the county court. Despite Fowler's objections to the imposition of a judgment against his lands, the county court ruled against him, leading him to appeal the decision to the circuit court. However, the circuit court dismissed Fowler's appeal, ruling that it lacked jurisdiction based on changes in the relevant laws after the appeal was filed. This dismissal was contested by Fowler, citing that the dismissal was erroneous and arguing about the correct interpretation of the statute concerning appeals in tax-related cases.	Edwin S. Fowler, as the appellant, argued that his objections to the judgment against his lands were valid and that the circuit court had jurisdiction to hear his appeal. He contended that the appeal was properly filed under the previous Revenue law, which allowed such appeals to the circuit court. Fowler sought to have the dismissal of his appeal overturned and to continue his challenge against the tax judgment imposed on his property.	Edward R. Pirkins, the appellee, maintained that the appeal filed by Fowler was invalid under the new law enacted July 1, 1874, which changed the jurisdiction for these cases, providing that appeals from the county court be made directly to the Supreme Court for certain matters, including tax judgments. Pirkins argued that the law had effectively repealed the previous provisions that allowed appeals to the circuit court, and therefore the circuit court had no jurisdiction to continue with Fowler's appeal.

In September 1871, the case of Chicago & Northwestern Railroad Co. v. Dennis Ward was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident occurred at the South Branch station where James Ward, an employee of the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad Company working as an ear-coupler and switchman, suffered fatal injuries while coupling freight cars. The accident was caused when a brake that was too low caught his foot, resulting in him falling onto the tracks and being run over by a train. The company regularly transported damaged cars for repairs and Ward was responsible for managing such cars, which meant he understood the risks involved in his job. The defense argued that the railway had taken all reasonable precautions, and that Ward accepted the inherent dangers of his employment.	The plaintiff, representing James Ward's estate, claimed that the railroad company was negligent in providing a safe work environment, particularly regarding the condition of the freight car involved in the accident. It was argued that the car was not marked for repairs, potentially misleading Ward and contributing to the incident. The plaintiff's main legal request was for compensation due to the alleged negligence of the company, suggesting that the railway did not fulfill their duty of care towards their employee.	The defendant, Chicago & Northwestern Railroad Co., contended that the employee had voluntarily accepted the risks associated with his job, which included working with potentially defective cars. The defense maintained that the injury occurred amidst normal operations for repair and was not due to any negligence on their part, arguing that the absence of a repair mark did not equate to liability. Furthermore, they emphasized that the employee was aware of the risks and had a duty to act cautiously given the nature of his work.

The case "The Riverside Company v. Augusta M. Townshend et al." involves a legal dispute regarding property rights and the validity of a tax deed. The case took place in Gallatin County, Illinois, and reached the Illinois Supreme Court on November 10, 1886. This was not the first time the case had been heard; it came forward for consideration after prior proceedings set a precedent for the issues at hand. The Riverside Company (plaintiff) sought to recover possession of real estate, claiming that the tax deed held by the defendants (Townshend et al.) was invalid. During previous proceedings, the court ruled that the tax deed was void, leading to a re-trial concerning the legal ownership of the property. The court found in favor of the Riverside Company, stating it possessed rightful ownership of part of the premises, invalidating the tax deed. However, the circuit court's judgment required the Riverside Company to pay the defendants a sum of money before regaining possession, which became a contentious point of legal interpretation in the appeal.	The Riverside Company claimed ownership of the property based on previous rulings that deemed the defendants' tax deed invalid. The company argued that the judgment requiring them to cover the amount paid for the tax deed as a precondition to recovering possession was improper and unconstitutional. They sought to overturn this judgment to facilitate their right to regain possession without the financial condition imposed by the lower court.	The defendants, represented by Townshend et al., contended that the tax deed was valid and that they were entitled to compensation for taxes and legal costs paid in relation to the deed, as stipulated under the Revenue act of 1885. They argued that the Riverside Company's claim was barred by previous judgments in related cases, such as forcible entry and detainer suits, which ruled in favor of the defendants.

In the case of B. S. Prettyman et al. v. L. H. Wilkey et al., originating in Pekin, Illinois, the legal dispute arose around two lots owned by Samuel P. Baily and James Baily in 1831. They deeded these lots to Daniel M. Baily in trust for their creditors. Shortly after, Daniel executed a power of attorney to Joshua R. Stanford, who sold these lots to Menard & Doolittle for $400, with their possession since the sale in 1831 indicating they claimed ownership. Over the years, ownership had changed hands multiple times, culminating in Prettyman acquiring the lots through Reeves after several transactions, despite acknowledgment of claims by Menard & Doolittle and their heirs to the original ownership. The case revolved around whether the legal title held by Prettyman could override the established equities stemming from the prior possession and claims of Menard & Doolittle. The court examined whether the conveyances made were valid or constituted a fraud upon the equities of the complainants, and the case was heard in 1857 by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the conveyance of lots from D. M. Baily to Reeves, and subsequently to Prettyman, was fraudulent and did not honor the prior equitable rights of Menard & Doolittle. They asserted they had rightful possessory title due to their long-term and continuous possession, which included important legal principles of adverse possession. They sought an injunction to enjoin the recovery of the lots by Prettyman and requested a court order to compel the defendants to convey the legal title to the lots to them.	The defendants acknowledged the original conveyance to D. M. Baily and admitted the subsequent transactions but denied any wrongdoing or fraudulent intent in the sale to Reeves and then to Prettyman. They argued that Menard & Doolittle held possession as tenants under the Baily brothers and had not claimed rightful ownership against the transactions leading to Prettyman’s acquisition. The defenses maintained that the conveyances were made in good faith and that the necessary legal titles had been properly established.

In 1886, Josiah Deyo filed a lawsuit against Edwin Ferris in Stark County, Illinois, concerning a verbal contract that involved the drainage of water across their adjacent lands. The plaintiff, Deyo, owned land that was primarily wet and contended that the defendant, Ferris, had agreed for a sum of $75 to dig and extend a ditch that would allow the water from Deyo's land to flow into a creek via Ferris's property. Deyo argued that he should not have to pay the $75 until he utilized the ditch by installing a drainage tile on his land. The trial initially took place in the Circuit Court after an appeal from a Justice of the Peace. The lower court ruled in favor of Ferris, asserting the validity of the contract and the right to pursue the financial claim for the work. However, Deyo contested that the findings were contrary to the evidence presented, leading to an appeal.	Deyo claimed that the contract for the drainage work was contingent upon the installation of a drainage tile on his property and therefore asserted that payment should not be owed until that work was completed. Deyo further argued that the contract was void under the Statute of Frauds since it implied a perpetual right to drain water across Ferris's property, which should have been documented in writing.	Ferris contended that the verbal agreement for a payment of $75 was valid and that he had fulfilled his obligations by digging the ditch as per their agreement. Ferris maintained that the contract was enforceable and that he was entitled to recover the agreed sum since he had performed the work.

The case of Thomas Moulding et al. v. George C. Prussing et al. took place in September 1873, in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved included Thomas Moulding, Edward Harland (the appellants), and George C. Prussing and Charles G. Mueller (the appellees). The dispute arose from a contract in which Moulding and Harland were to deliver 500,000 merchantable bricks at a price of $6.37 per thousand, to be delivered on Wabash Avenue south of Van Buren Street. However, only 35,000 bricks were delivered, leading to claims of breach of contract from the plaintiffs. The written agreements exchanged were found to be inconsistent and uncertain, contributing to the complexities surrounding the enforcement of the contract. The Superior Court of Cook County ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, resulting in an appeal by the defendants.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants breached their contract to deliver 500,000 bricks, having failed to deliver the remaining 465,000 after delivering only 35,000. They sought damages amounting to $2392.50, asserting that the defendants' failure to perform the contract entitled them to compensation.	The defendants contended that the written memoranda of the contract were void due to inconsistency and uncertainty regarding terms such as the quantity and delivery schedule. They argued that verbal evidence should not alter the written terms, and they claimed they were not obliged to deliver further bricks due to the plaintiffs' actions that allegedly halted the delivery.

In July 1820, the legal case of "James Mason, Plaintiff in Error, v. N. Buckmaster, Assignee of P. Mason, Defendant in Error" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Madison County, Illinois, where James Mason was the maker of a promissory note that was executed in favor of Paris Mason. This note was subsequently assigned to N. Buckmaster, who sought to enforce it through legal action. The trial court faced objections from the defendant, Buckmaster, regarding the plaintiff's declaration. Specifically, Buckmaster argued that there was no profert (production) of the note that was the subject of the lawsuit and claimed that the plaintiff had not stated a consideration for the note. The trial court rejected these objections and ruled in favor of the plaintiff, leading to Buckmaster's appeal to disturb the judgment based on the same concerns.	The plaintiff, Buckmaster, claimed that he was entitled to payment based on the promissory note assigned to him. He asserted that the trial court correctly dismissed the defendant’s objections regarding the need for profert of the written note and the requirement of stating a consideration, arguing that these were not necessary in actions involving assigned notes.	The defendant, James Mason, countered Buckmaster's claims by asserting that the trial court erred in its rulings concerning the objections raised. He argued that without profert of the note and without a stated consideration, the action to enforce the note should not proceed. Thus, he requested that the appellate court reverse the trial court’s judgment.

In September 1870, Joseph Knox and several co-defendants were involved in a legal case against The Winsted Savings Bank in Illinois. The case arose from a judgment rendered by confession against Knox and others based on a promissory note that they executed. The note was made payable to "Tucker & Ritchie" and was signed by a total of seven individuals, establishing joint and several liability. In July 1870, Knox and other appellants filed motions to vacate the judgment, claiming issues of usury and procedural errors, including that the judgment was improperly entered against them without including Tucker & Ritchie. The court held hearings on these motions, where both sides presented affidavits regarding the assignment of the note and the legitimacy of the judgment. Ultimately, the appeals highlighted whether the Superior Court should vacate the prior judgment based on technical errors or equitable grounds.	The plaintiffs, The Winsted Savings Bank, asserted that they were the bona fide assignee of the promissory note in question and that there was no valid defense against the enforceability of the judgment. The bank maintained that the motions to vacate the judgment were unfounded and that the appellants failed to provide compelling evidence to challenge the validity of the confession of judgment.	The defendants, Joseph Knox and his co-appellants, contended that the judgment should be vacated due to alleged usury and procedural errors, including that the judgment was improperly rendered since it did not include all parties to the note. They argued that the authority to confess judgment was not applied correctly, suggesting that the joint and several nature of the note required all makers to be treated equally under the law. They sought to have the judgment set aside based on these claims.

The case "The Pennsylvania Company v. George M. Sloan" began when George M. Sloan filed a lawsuit against The Pennsylvania Company in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, on July 3, 1874, seeking damages for personal injuries sustained on July 5, 1872. The incident occurred in Chicago, specifically on Eighteenth Street, where Sloan was riding in a buggy and was stopped by a train that obstructed his view of other tracks. After waiting for the train to pass, a flagman signaled Sloan to cross the tracks, not knowing that another train was backing up and hidden from view. This caused panic in Sloan's horse, leading to the buggy being jolted and, ultimately, Sloan jumping out to avoid further danger, resulting in his injuries. Sloan claimed negligence on the part of the railroad servants for signaling him to cross when it was unsafe. The case saw multiple trials and appeals after initial judgments, with the defendant's identity debated in terms of the Pennsylvania Company's prior corporate name and claims of statute of limitations being raised. After various legal maneuvers including amendments to the declaration and more trials, the courts deliberated on the actual party responsible and negligence by the railroad's employees.	George M. Sloan claimed that The Pennsylvania Company's employees were negligent in signaling him to cross the railroad tracks when it was unsafe to do so, given the presence of an unseen backing train. Sloan requested compensation for his injuries caused by this negligence, which he argued was directly linked to the railroad employees' actions and failure to ensure a safe crossing.	The Pennsylvania Company contended that the lawsuit was improperly initiated against the wrong corporate name (the Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne and Chicago Railroad Company) and that the statute of limitations had expired for the claims. They asserted that the action did not accrue within two years before the suit was brought and that any statute of limitations defense should apply since they were not properly impleaded as the defendant until 1877.

The case of Hector J. Humphrey et al. v. Orville H. Browning et al. took place in January 1868, in Illinois, where the plaintiffs, Hector J. Humphrey and others, filed a bill in chancery against the defendants, Orville H. Browning and others. The plaintiffs sought to establish a lien on certain real estate that had been recovered through an action of ejectment, claiming they were entitled to compensation for their legal services rendered in that action. This matter was originally heard by the Circuit Court of Hancock County, presided over by Judge Joseph Sibley. The case raised significant legal questions regarding whether an attorney has a lien on real estate recovered in an ejectment action.	The plaintiffs argued that as attorneys who successfully prosecuted the ejectment action on behalf of the clients, they were entitled to a lien on the real estate recovered for their legal fees. They contended that their contributions in securing the property warranted a claim to compensation, which should be secured against the real estate itself.	The defendants challenged the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that attorneys do not possess a lien on real estate recovered through legal action. They argued that the compensation for legal services is not secured by a lien on the property, focusing on legal principles and precedents that supported their position that liens only exist for taxable costs, not for general compensation.

In August 1871, Christian Brownfield executed a will that included two distinct clauses regarding the distribution of his estate following his death. The first clause bequeathed a 40-acre tract of land, which housed the family home and orchard, to his wife, Mary Brownfield.
