The second clause allocated the remainder of his real and personal property to his heirs, allowing them to share equally after the death of his wife. After the will was drafted, Christian's heirs, dissatisfied with the provisions, initiated legal action against his widow, alleging undue influence and questioning his mental competency at the time of the will’s signing. Later, they amended their complaint to request a construction of the will, arguing that Mary Brownfield only received a life estate from the estate. However, the original trial court concluded that the widow was entitled to only a life estate based on the interpretation of the will's clauses. She subsequently appealed this decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that she should have received full ownership based on the clarity of the first clause.	The plaintiff, Mary Brownfield, claimed that the language in the first clause of the will clearly bequeathed her a fee simple ownership of the 40-acre land. She contended that the second clause did not alter or limit the first clause and that the intent of the testator was to bestow upon her full ownership. Therefore, she requested the court to reverse the lower court's decision and establish that she held the land outright, not limited to a life estate.	The defendants, Mary Ann Wilson and the other heirs, argued that the second clause of the will had implications that limited the first clause. They maintained that the will taken as a whole indicated the testator’s intent to only grant Mary Brownfield a life estate, with the property to ultimately revert to the heirs upon her death. Thus, they requested the court to uphold the lower court's interpretation, which limited her rights to the estate.

The case "Joseph Silvey v. George Dowell et al." took place in January 1870 in the Mason Circuit Court of Illinois. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff, Joseph Silvey, and the defendants, George Dowell, John Welch, J.W. Stevenson, and Sheriff David B. Phelps. The case arose from a financial arrangement involving a promissory note for $250 executed by John Welch to William Claypool for the purchase of personal property. Silvey and Dowell were co-sureties on this note, which was to be secured by a chattel mortgage executed by Welch to them. Dowell assumed responsibility for the loan and paid half of it before arranging for Stevenson to purchase the note, which then led to Stevenson successfully suing both Dowell and Silvey for a claim of $147.19. Silvey sought to enjoin the execution process against him based on the assertion that Dowell, who had received substantial benefits and the funds to cover the obligation, should be liable for the debt instead. The court needed to resolve the equity of forcing Silvey to pay the debt while Dowell had assumed responsibility for it.	Joseph Silvey argued that he should not be held responsible for the debt associated with the promissory note, as his co-surety Dowell had received funds intended for the payment of the note and assumed the obligation himself. Silvey asserted that it would be inequitable to compel him to pay for a debt that his co-surety voluntarily undertook to cover, especially when it appears that all inequities favored Dowell.	The defendants, George Dowell and Stevenson, contended that Silvey was liable for the debt pursuant to the terms of the note. They disputed the facts alleging that Dowell had assumed responsibility, thereby leading to Silvey’s obligation remaining unchanged. They requested that the court affirm the judgment against Silvey and allow the execution on the property to proceed.

In December 1842, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case from Madison County involving William Russell and the Administrators of Wm. B. Whiteside. At the heart of the dispute was a tract of land originally entered under the name Samuel Jackeway, comprised of approximately 487 acres. In March 1829, Russell owned 146.4 acres of the land, while Whiteside owned 359.29 acres. Both properties were advertised for sale due to overdue payments, which, under land office regulations, necessitated redemption of the entire tract together. To save his own land from being sold, Russell paid the total amount of $108.16 in arrears, which was owed solely on Whiteside's portion. Despite being informed and requested to participate in this payment, Whiteside refused. Russell then initiated an action of assumpsit in the circuit court to recover the amount he paid on behalf of Whiteside. The trial culminated in a jury verdict favoring Russell, resulting in a judgment for $130.67. The underlying legal principles revolved around issues of land ownership, payment obligations, and rights in property redemption.	The plaintiff, William Russell, contended that he was compelled to pay $108.16, which was due solely on the portion of the land owned by Whiteside, to redeem the entire tract from foreclosure. He argued that since the payment was necessary to protect his own property, he was entitled to recover the costs from Whiteside. Russell's legal request centered on obtaining restitution for the amount he expended on the defendant's behalf, asserting that he had a rightful claim as a co-owner unable to separate the portions due to land office regulations.	The defendant, represented by the Administrators of Wm. B. Whiteside, argued primarily through the plea of non assumpsit, maintaining that he was not liable for the repayment. The defense claimed that any payment made by Russell was voluntary and could not be considered as a debt owed to Russell since there was no express consent or request from Whiteside for Russell to make the payment on his behalf. Furthermore, the defendant requested jury instructions emphasizing that a person cannot create a debt for another without their knowledge or consent.

The case "George W. Guild et al. v. Thomas M. Hull, Conservator, et al." was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision handed down on April 3, 1889. The legal dispute originated from a transaction involving John Warne, who transferred a significant portion of his property to his grandson, John W. Guild, in 1882, citing "natural love and affection" as well as consideration for services rendered. The transactions included a deed for 108 acres of land, a lease for his home farm, and a bill of sale for personal property, conditional upon Guild caring for Warne and his wife. Following Guild's demise in 1886, and with Warne dying in 1888, Warne's heirs initiated a legal challenge in 1887 against Guild’s estate, alleging that Warne was mentally incapacitated and that the property transfers had been procured through undue influence exerted by Guild. The circuit court's jury ultimately ruled that Warne was not of sound mind during the transactions and that undue influence had occurred, leading to an initial ruling to set aside the deeds in question.	The plaintiffs, John Warne's heirs, claimed that the deed, lease, and bill of sale executed by Warne to Guild should be invalidated due to Warne's alleged mental incapacity at the time of execution. They argued that Warne lacked the legal capacity to make such transactions and contended that Guild exerted undue influence over him, thereby misleading him into transferring his property.	The defendants, comprising Guild's estate's representatives, contended that Warne was mentally competent at the time of the transfers and that there was no undue influence exerted by Guild. They highlighted that Warne had sought legal advice and showed awareness of his property dealings. They also argued that the court improperly handled testimony and jury instructions regarding the presumption of sanity and the admissibility of certain evidence.

Uzziel Kanouse initiated legal action against Jacob A. Kanouse and Jacob C. Mahan in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1865, regarding a dispute over property ownership. The case arose from an arbitration arrangement between the parties, which involved a bond dated December 10, 1857, in the sum of $4,000, concerning property listed in a schedule "A." The arbitration was necessary due to ongoing disagreements about various properties and business relations. Uzziel claimed that J.A. Kanouse had failed to uphold the terms of the bond by not keeping the property secure and not paying him $720 awarded as part of the arbitration. The case was originally filed in Livingston Circuit Court but was later moved to Ford County. The bond provided conditions under which the property was to be safeguarded until the dispute was resolved, with the requirement that payment be made if property was sold before the award. The arbitrators eventually concluded that Uzziel was entitled to $720 and that J.A. Kanouse could retain the property only after making such payment. However, the trial court found in favor of the defendants, prompting Uzziel to appeal the decision.	Uzziel Kanouse argued that Jacob A. Kanouse failed to comply with the requirements of the arbitration award, specifically by not paying the determined amount of $720 and failing to preserve the property as per the bond's terms. He sought recovery of the awarded amount and claimed that J.A. Kanouse's failure to protect the property and subsequent sale of parts of it led to his entitlement to damages. Uzziel requested the court to overturn the previous judgment that dismissed his claims.	Jacob A. Kanouse and Jacob C. Mahan contended that they complied with the arbitration award and maintained the property appropriately. They denied any breaches of the bond's conditions and asserted that the arbitrators did not obligate Kanouse to pay Uzziel the $720. They also argued against the trial court's findings, maintaining that they had fulfilled their obligations and, therefore, should not owe the plaintiff any further compensation.

In 1886, Preston, a farmer in La Salle County, Illinois, hired Zimmerman to manage the rental of his farm in Rock Island County. Zimmerman rented the farm to Enright for one year beginning on March 1, 1886. Lacking housing for the tenant, Preston and Zimmerman arranged for the rental of a house from Harmon Marshall for $48 a year, with payment deferred until after the harvest of the first crop. Enright occupied the house as well as the farm. After the original rental was completed, Enright continued leasing the farm and house under the same terms but without a formal agreement. In June 1887, Preston assigned his property to Morey for the benefit of creditors, and in October of that same year, Morey sold the farm to Edward Wilson, the appellant. In April 1888, Wilson executed a new lease with Enright for the farm, which excluded Marshall from the agreement regarding house rent. Marshall, having received payment for 1887, filed suit against Wilson to recover rent for 1888. The case raised issues regarding Wilson's liability for rent owed to Marshall since Preston, the original landlord, had assigned his rights to Wilson while having a pre-existing obligation to Marshall.	Harmon Marshall claimed that Edward Wilson, as the new owner of the farm and the party benefiting from Enright's continued occupancy, was liable for the house rent owed for 1888. Marshall argued that because Enright remained in occupation of the house, Wilson implicitly assumed the rental agreement established by Preston for the house. He sought to recover the sum of $18 owed for the year 1888.	Edward Wilson contended that he had no legal obligation to pay Marshall for the house rent, as there was no express agreement between them, and the original lease had expired. Wilson argued that after he acquired the property, any prior agreements involving Preston and Marshall concerning the house rent were no longer enforceable against him. He maintained that Marshall was not a party to the new lease with Enright and thus had no claim against him for the rent.

The case "The St. Louis Bridge Company v. Sarah E. Fellows, Administratrix" took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, with the final decision rendered on November 1, 1889. The plaintiff, Sarah E. Fellows, brought the suit following the death of her son, who was employed as a switchman by the defendant, The St. Louis Bridge Company. The accident occurred when her son was operating a switch engine, and it derailed while moving from one track to another, resulting in him either jumping or falling off and subsequently being struck by the derailed engine. The plaintiff alleged that the death resulted from the company's negligence, specifically citing the dangerous and defective condition of the track, which was claimed to have been improperly constructed and maintained. Despite these allegations, testimonies presented during the trial suggested that the track was in good repair at the time of the accident, with experts supporting that it was constructed properly using the best materials available.	Sarah E. Fellows claimed that her son's death resulted from The St. Louis Bridge Company's negligence, specifically due to their failure to maintain and repair the roadbed and track adequately. She requested damages amounting to $5,000, arguing that the company's negligence directly caused the accident without any fault on her son's part.	The St. Louis Bridge Company contended that they were not liable for the accident, asserting that the track and engine were properly constructed and maintained. They emphasized that there was a lack of evidence to support the plaintiff's claim about the track being dangerously defective at the time of the incident. The defendant also sought a reversal of the lower court's judgment, arguing that the jury's findings were not substantiated by the evidence presented.

The case "C. M. Capen et al. v. The De Steiger Glass Company" was decided on September 28, 1882, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff, De Steiger Glass Company, engaged in a contract with the defendants, C. M. and J. S. Capen, to sell and deliver five hundred gross of Mason patent fruit jars at a price of $16 per gross. The defendants only received one hundred and forty-seven gross but failed to pay for fifty-four gross that had been delivered. Subsequently, the defendants asserted that the plaintiff did not fulfill their contractual obligations regarding the undelivered jars, resulting in damages. Initially, the jury in the circuit court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, assessing damages at $500. The defendants' motions for a new trial were rejected, and after a remittitur, the judgment in favor of the plaintiff was finalized at $450. The defendants appealed this ruling to the Appellate Court, which affirmed the trial court's decision.	The plaintiff claimed that they were owed payment for fifty-four gross of fruit jars delivered to the defendants, amounting to $864. They argued that the defendants had failed to fulfill their obligations, specifically the contractual agreement to purchase a total of five hundred gross jars. The plaintiff sought recovery of the unpaid amount and eventually received a judgment for $450 after overcoming the defendants' appeals and set-off pleas.	The defendants contended that the plaintiff had failed to deliver two hundred and ninety-nine gross of jars as stipulated in their contract. They claimed that this breach caused them damages, which they attempted to set off against the plaintiff’s claim. They asserted that they incurred additional costs by purchasing some jars at a higher price and calculated their total damages to exceed $1,000, which they attempted to claim in their defense.

In March 1868, in Sangamon County, Illinois, Sexton E. Smith initiated a legal action against Elizabeth Archer, the administratrix of William Archer's estate, due to damages caused by Archer's animals. Smith owned a cornfield adjacent to Archer's farm, where Archer's cattle, known to be unruly and "breachy," broke into Smith's cornfield and consumed a substantial amount of corn. Smith had repeatedly notified Archer about his cattle’s behavior, yet Archer failed to take measures to contain them. Following an appeal to the Circuit Court, the case continued under the same circumstances, leading to a jury verdict favoring the defendant. This prompted Smith to file for a writ of error, challenging the judgment that found no cause for action based on the nature of the claims.	Smith argued that Archer's cattle trespassed onto his property and caused significant destruction to his growing corn. He claimed that the act should qualify for damages under the law and sought to recover the value of the destroyed corn, asserting that Archer had a duty to maintain his cattle and prevent them from infringing upon Smith's property.	Archer's defense contended that a claim of trover (conversion of property) was inappropriate for Smith's allegations, as the destruction was caused by animals, rather than a direct act of conversion by Archer himself. The defense argued that if Smith had pursued the correct legal remedy, it should have been a trespass action, not trover, and thus requested dismissal of Smith's claims.

In 1857, James C. Stewart was appointed as the guardian of Thomas M. Shields by the County Court of Richland County, Illinois, with a bond executed by William Stewart, the appellee, as surety. In May 1866, following a final accounting, the County Court ordered that James C. Stewart pay Thomas M. Shields the sum of $324.97. However, Shields did not immediately file a suit against his guardian to recover the amount due. James C. Stewart passed away in 1875, and the estate was settled in 1878. In 1887, William Stewart was summoned to account for the guardianship, during which it was revealed that part of the amount owed from the guardian to Shields had not been paid. The case hinged on whether the statute of limitations barred Shields' claim against William Stewart, the surety, more than twenty-one years after he attained legal age. The court ultimately addressed whether the citation to account could revive the cause of action against the surety.	The plaintiff, Thomas M. Shields, claimed that after the County Court's order regarding the unpaid sum, he had the right to file a suit against his guardian for the money owed. He argued that the surety, William Stewart, should be held liable because, notwithstanding the statutory limitations period, the citation requiring the surety to account for the guardian's estate effectively revived his claim.	The defendant, William Stewart, contended that the statute of limitations barred any claims against him as the surety since more than twenty-one years had elapsed since Shields came of age. He argued that a mere citation to appear and state the account was not a legal action that could revive the claim that was already time-barred. Stewart maintained that his obligation as a surety could not be invoked after the expiration of the statute of limitations and that the court's order did not change this situation.

The case "The Mount Carbon Coal & Railroad Co. et al. v. I. Blanchard et al." took place in Jackson County, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1870. The Mount Carbon Coal & Railroad Company and Andrew C. Bryden filed a bill in chancery seeking an injunction against the school directors of School District No. 2 in the township. They aimed to prevent the collection of a tax they claimed was assessed illegally. On September 2, 1867, the school directors certified a tax rate of 3.5% on the district's taxable property for school purposes and a new schoolhouse's construction, which included an unauthorized rate of 2.5% following no election on the tax levy. The plaintiffs argued that only a 1% tax was legally permissible for school purposes and that the higher amounts were unwarranted. After their tax payment was refused by the collector, they sought the court's intervention. The directors demurred, claiming issues with party structure and the sufficiency of the claims. The circuit court dismissed the bill, leading the plaintiffs to appeal.	The plaintiffs contended that the tax levied against them was illegal and unsupported by law due to the absence of an electoral process for the higher rates. They argued that only a 1% tax was valid for school purposes, while the additional taxes aimed at constructing a schoolhouse were unauthorized without an election. They sought a court injunction to stop the tax collection, asserting they had attempted to pay the rightful amount, which was ignored by the tax collector.	The defendants, comprising the school district's directors, demurred to the plaintiffs' bill, arguing that the suit involved improper parties and was multifarious, suggesting that the claims did not contain sufficient matter for legal relief. They contested the joining of Bryden with other plaintiffs based on conflicting interests and questioned the validity of the bill due to its complexity and alleged lack of distinct matters.

The case of John S. Williams v. Robert H. Ives occurred in January 1869 in Illinois, specifically in Piatt County. The dispute arose from a proceeding by scire facias intended to foreclose a mortgage. The initial writ was issued on March 8, 1862, but the sheriff reported that the defendant (Williams) was not found. A second writ was issued on August 4, 1862, which was again returned with the same indication. Due to Williams's absence and lack of appearance in court, the circuit court entered a default judgment against him, assessing the damages and granting judgment for the amount due on the mortgage. Williams appealed the judgment, challenging the timeliness of the sheriff's return of the writs and the classification of the judgment as personal rather than against the property (in rem).	The plaintiff, Robert H. Ives, argued that the foreclosure proceedings were valid due to the failure of the sheriff to locate the defendant after multiple attempts, thus justifying the default judgment. He maintained that the statute allowed a judgment to be entered based on the returns of the writs, regardless of whether they were returned on the same day as the issuance. Ives sought the enforcement of the mortgage against the properties secured therein, asserting that the judgment should allow for the recovery of the amount due and facilitate a sale of the mortgaged premises.	The defendant, John S. Williams, contended that the writs were returned prematurely by the sheriff and argued that the judgment rendered was in personam (against him personally) rather than in rem (against the property). Williams requested a reversal of the judgment, asserting that proper procedures were not followed and that the court lacked jurisdiction due to the alleged improper execution and return of the writs.

Thomas Williamson v. The County of Cass took place in Cass County, Illinois, during the early 1870s, specifically beginning in March 1874 when a petition was filed to open a public road. The county commissioners appointed viewers to assess the proposed route, which they ultimately recommended for establishment. However, Williamson and other landowners whose properties were affected filed claims for damages. The county board then appointed a jury of six freeholders to assess these damages. Williamson requested a jury of twelve, but his motion was overruled. The jury of six assessed his damages at $235, which was subsequently approved by the board. Unsatisfied, Williamson appealed to the circuit court, where a jury awarded him $475. He then moved for a new trial, which was denied, leading to his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Thomas Williamson, argued that his constitutional right to a jury of twelve men was violated when the county board appointed only six freeholders to assess damages for the public road's establishment. He contended that the trial court's ruling on damages was also erroneous, asserting the jury's verdict was against the evidence.	The County of Cass defended itself by asserting that the county board had jurisdiction over the matter, and any procedural irregularities in appointing the jury were waived by Williamson when he chose to appeal to the circuit court. The defendant maintained that the circuit court conducted a fair trial where a jury of twelve did evaluate Williamson's claims regarding damages, and highlighted that jury assessments are primarily a matter of discretion for the jury based on the evidence submitted.

In the case of Frederick R. Wilson v. Thomas Raybould, which took place in Chicago, Illinois, the dispute arose from a lease agreement initiated on May 1, 1867. The plaintiff, Thomas Raybould, claimed that he was induced to accept this lease based on fraudulent representations made by the defendant, Frederick R. Wilson, who alleged that he owned water lot 45 in Kinzie’s Addition. Relying on these claims, Raybould erected a shop and installed machinery on the property. However, in November 1868, he was ejected from the premises due to a legal judgment favoring the actual titleholder of the land. Raybould then pursued legal action to recover damages, asserting that Wilson's misrepresentation had caused him significant financial harm. The case was brought before the Circuit Court of Cook County, where a jury initially awarded Raybould $2,500 in damages. The case ultimately reached the Illinois Supreme Court on appeal, focusing on the appropriateness of the measures of damages awarded.	The plaintiff, Thomas Raybould, argued that he suffered financial damages due to the defendant's fraudulent misrepresentation regarding property ownership, which led him to lease and improve the land. He requested compensation for expenses incurred while relocating his shop and machinery, the difference in costs for the new location, and interest on the invested capital during the business suspension caused by the eviction.	The defendant, Frederick R. Wilson, contended that the damages awarded to Raybould were improperly calculated. He challenged the jury's instruction on how to assess damages, arguing that it allowed for excessively broad recovery for moving expenses and rent, which should have been limited to necessary expenses and a reasonable rental value for a comparable property.

Abigail McGaha, the plaintiff, was driving a horse and buggy along a highway near a railroad crossing in Knox County, Illinois, when the incident occurred. On December 4, 1885, McGaha stopped to look and listen for an approaching train, as required by ordinary care. However, the view of the tracks was obstructed by weeds and brush on the defendant's right of way, and no warning signals were given by the train, such as a bell or whistle. Despite her precautions, a locomotive suddenly approached, frightening her horse and causing McGaha to be thrown from her carriage, resulting in serious injuries. She subsequently filed a lawsuit against the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, claiming negligence for failing to provide adequate warning and for allowing vegetation to obstruct the view of oncoming trains.	McGaha alleged that the railroad company was grossly negligent for not ringing a bell or blowing a whistle as their train approached the crossing. She also claimed that the defendant failed to maintain their right of way, allowing trees, brush, and weeds to grow, which prevented her from safely discerning the approach of the train. McGaha sought damages for the injuries sustained as a result of this negligence, ultimately winning a jury verdict for $750.	The defense argued that McGaha herself lacked ordinary care while approaching the crossing, suggesting that she should have taken further precautions to ensure it was safe to cross. They maintained that any injuries she sustained were due to her negligence and not the railroad's actions. The defendants requested that the jury rule in their favor, asserting that the evidence showed no gross negligence on their part.

In 1873, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of William A. Muller v. Mathias Benner, Guardian, arose when Mathias Benner, acting as the guardian for wards Matthew and Nicholas Schent, initiated an ejectment action against William A. Muller. The case focused on whether Benner, as guardian, had the legal authority to sue for the possession of real estate belonging to his wards. The trial court found in favor of Benner, establishing that the fee of the lands was indeed in the wards, which entitled the guardian to possession. However, Muller's appeal challenged the legitimacy of the guardian's right to bring the suit in his own name. The court evaluated Illinois statutory laws regarding guardianship and the specific powers granted to a guardian in relation to their wards’ real estate. The legal precedent in question hinged on whether a guardian could maintain ejectment actions independently or if they were required to do so in the name of their wards.	The plaintiff, Mathias Benner, claimed he was entitled to recover possession of the lands belonging to his wards under his guardianship. He argued that as the legal guardian, he had the right to bring an action of ejectment in his own name to reclaim the property for the wards.	The defendant, William A. Muller, contended that Benner, as the guardian, did not have the authority to maintain ejectment proceedings in his own name for the lands of the wards. Muller argued that Illinois law required such actions to be brought in the name of the guardians for the wards, stressing that guardianship did not bestow rights over real estate that would allow a guardian to bring lawsuits in their own name.

In 1877, in the state of Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Edward Spring and Edmund O. Kane concerning the title to a piece of property originally owned by Giles Spring, Edward's father. It was established that Edward Spring was the only surviving heir of Giles Spring. The contested title dated back to a sale conducted by Edward's guardian in 1853, which was authorized by a circuit court decree for the purpose of maintaining Edward and other minor heirs. Various technical objections were raised regarding the validity of the sale, primarily about supposed irregularities that emerged during the sale process. However, the court found that these objections did not affect the core merits of the case. Instead, it was determined that the guardian had appropriately obtained jurisdiction for the sale, as outlined by law, which involved the necessary publication of notice and the presentation of a written petition to the court, despite difficulties in proving the details due to records being destroyed by fire. Ultimately, the court ruled that the sale divested Edward of his title, regardless of who currently held it.	Edward Spring claimed that he was the rightful owner of the property in dispute due to his status as the sole heir of Giles Spring. He contended that the sale conducted by his guardian was invalid, asserting that procedural defects in the guardian's actions should nullify the decree that authorized the sale. Edward sought recovery of the property, arguing that the sale was not executed according to the legal requirements necessary to divest him of his inherited title.	Edmund O. Kane, the defendant, argued that the sale of the property, authorized by a court having proper jurisdiction, was valid and binding, despite the plaintiff's claims of procedural irregularities. Kane contended that any technical objections raised by Edward Spring did not undermine the legality of the original sale proceedings, as the court had jurisdiction of the subject matter and the parties involved. Kane asserted that a purchaser in good faith should not be affected by any alleged errors in the judicial proceedings, especially given the destruction of records and the long time elapsed since the original sale.

James Berry, the appellant, and William Hamby, the appellee, were involved in a legal dispute originating from a promissory note dated June 24th, 1837. The note was for $100 and was made payable to the Treasurer of Alexander County. Berry, the maker of the note, assigned it to Hamby on January 26th, 1838. The case was initiated in the Alexander Circuit Court, where the court found in favor of Hamby, ruling that the assignment was valid. Berry appealed the decision, claiming that the promissory note was void because the Treasurer of Alexander County did not have the legal authority to accept the note made payable to himself nor to assign it. The case ultimately brought into question whether a lawsuit could be maintained in the name of a County Treasurer.	The plaintiff, William Hamby, argued that he had a valid claim to the note based on the assignment made by the Treasurer of Alexander County. He asserted that the assignment entitled him to collect the amount due under the note, which was properly executed and in accordance with his rights.	James Berry, the defendant, contended that the promissory note was void and inoperative because the Treasurer of Alexander County had no authority to create or assign such a note. He claimed that, since the Treasurer could not legally hold or assign the note, the plaintiff had no legitimate claim to it, and therefore the action taken in the Circuit Court was erroneous.

In the case of John Kennedy et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois, which took place in Lee County, Illinois, the plaintiffs, John Kennedy and Daniel Kennedy, were jointly indicted in October 1884 for an assault with a deadly weapon on James Minnihan. The case was retried in September 1886 after a new trial was granted, resulting in the plaintiffs being found guilty of assault, while their brother James Kennedy was found not guilty. The court imposed a fine of $40 on John Kennedy and $25 on Daniel Kennedy, along with costs for the proceedings. The statute under which the judgment was rendered allowed for imprisonment until the fines and costs were paid. The plaintiffs contested this ruling, citing a constitutional provision that prohibits imprisonment for debt, hence arguing that costs in a criminal case should not constitute a debt that could lead to imprisonment.	The plaintiffs argued that the provision allowing jail time for non-payment of costs is in violation of their constitutional rights, particularly the clause prohibiting imprisonment for debt. They contended that the costs associated with their prosecution represented a debt, and therefore they should not be imprisoned until such debts were settled. They sought a reversal of the judgment that mandated their commitment for non-payment of fines and costs.	The defendants, representing the People of the State of Illinois, maintained that the statute allowing imprisonment for non-payment of fines and costs is constitutional. They argued that costs in criminal cases are not considered debts in the same manner as contract debts and that such provisions are necessary to uphold the law. They insisted that the plaintiffs were correctly convicted and liable for their prosecution costs, which arose from their criminal conduct.

In December 1826, in Illinois, John Flack, a justice of the peace, was involved in a legal case against Wiley O. Harrington. The case arose when Flack issued a warrant for the arrest of Harrington without proper legal grounds, such as a sworn complaint or personal knowledge of the events leading to the issuance of the warrant. Flack claimed that Harrington had committed a breach of the peace concerning an individual named Edward Valentine. Harrington filed a lawsuit against Flack for trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment, asserting that Flack had no legitimate reason to suspect him of wrongdoing when he issued the warrant. The trial revealed that the warrant had been served by Johnson, who was deputized by Flack, and the court ultimately ruled against Flack, finding him liable for the wrongful issuance of the warrant without due process.	Harrington, the plaintiff, argued that Flack acted unlawfully by issuing a warrant for his arrest without a proper affidavit or any personal knowledge of the alleged breach of the peace. He contended that Flack had no reasonable cause to suspect him of any wrongdoing and requested damages for trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment due to the irregular actions taken against him.	Flack and Johnson, the defendants, contended that they did not act unlawfully since Johnson had a special plea of justification supporting their actions. Initially, they demurred against Harrington's complaint, asserting that the legal standards for issuing a warrant had been misapplied and that any errors were technical in nature rather than substantive. However, the jury ultimately sided with Harrington.

The case titled "The City of Chicago v. Mary Ann Gallagher, Administratrix, etc." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. It involved the city of Chicago and Mary Ann Gallagher, acting as the administratrix of her deceased husband, Michael Gallagher. The incident that triggered the legal action was the drowning of Michael Gallagher, which occurred at a slip crossing in the city, specifically at Ogden’s slip. Gallagher fell into the unprotected and poorly lit area while navigating the bridge that spanned the slip. This area lacked safety measures such as railings or barriers, posing a significant risk to pedestrians, especially at night. After being tried twice in lower courts, both juries found in favor of Gallagher, initially awarding $1,000 in damages, which was later increased to $2,000. The city contested this decision, arguing that it was not negligent in this case.	The plaintiff, Mary Ann Gallagher, claims that the city of Chicago was negligent in failing to secure the street crossing, leading to her husband's death. She contended that the absence of proper lighting and protective barriers at the bridge over Ogden’s slip created a dangerous environment for pedestrians, particularly at night. Gallagher requested damages for the loss of her husband’s life due to this negligence.	The city of Chicago's main defense was that the evidence did not sufficiently prove that it was negligent. The city maintained that it fulfilled its obligations and argued against the claims of gross negligence related to the slip's unsafe condition. Furthermore, the city requested the court to reverse the lower court's rulings and the jury's verdicts that favored Gallagher.

The case of Mary New v. Jesse E. Oldfield took place in Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 19, 1884. The key individuals involved include Jesse E. Oldfield, the plaintiff and creditor, and Mary New, Nicholas New, and Michael New, the defendants. The case centers on a creditor's bill filed by Oldfield to enforce a judgment against Nicholas New related to a debt incurred in 1881. In a series of transactions beginning in November 1874, Nicholas New conveyed a property to his brother Michael New, who later transferred it to Nicholas's wife, Mary New, under suspicious circumstances. It was argued that these transfers were fraudulent, intended to protect Nicholas's property from creditors. The court examined whether the sale to Mary was genuine and whether it was a legitimate attempt to divest Nicholas of liability. The court found that the transactions did not follow the necessary ethical and legal standards to protect against creditor claims.	Jesse E. Oldfield claimed that the conveyance of property from Nicholas New to his brother Michael and subsequently to Mary New was fraudulent. He argued that the transactions were manipulative devices designed to shield the property from creditors and that they should be set aside to satisfy his judgment against Nicholas New. He requested that the court affirm the prior rulings allowing for the property to be subjected to the debt owed.	Mary New, representing her interests, contended that the transfers were legitimate and intended as bona fide purchases. She asserted that she obtained the property through lawful means and that it was not subject to the debts of her husband. The defense challenged the notion of the transfers being fraudulent, emphasizing that they followed lawful property transactions. They requested the court to reverse the lower courts' decisions and uphold the legitimacy of the property ownership.

William Dundy filed a case against Ezekiel Chambers and others in January 1860, which was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered around the transfer of a ferry franchise in Hancock, Illinois. The court was tasked with determining whether the ferry franchise should be treated as real estate, governed by the Illinois conveyance act, which required certain formalities for the transfer of property, or as a personal chattel, which could potentially have different transfer rules. Dundy sought to use a power of attorney as evidence for the franchise's transfer, which had purportedly been acknowledged but was done before the mayor of a town, a setting which the court later deemed insufficient according to the statutory requirements. The case involved complex legal arguments about the nature of ferry franchises and the proper execution procedures for legal documents related to property conveyances.	The plaintiff, Dundy, claimed that the ferry franchise was a form of real estate and argued that its transfer must adhere to the standards set forth in the Illinois conveyance act. Dundy sought to introduce a power of attorney as evidence to establish the legitimacy of the transfer, which he believed had been properly executed. He contended that the acknowledgment before a town's mayor should be considered valid for the purposes of his claim.	The defendants, represented by A. Wheat, argued that the power of attorney provided by Dundy was not acknowledged in accordance with the statutory requirements, as acknowledgments needed to be made before specific officers as prescribed by law. They contended that evidence of execution required either attestation by witnesses or acknowledgment in compliance with the statute, which was lacking in this case. The defense maintained that the court should reject Dundy's claims based on the procedural deficiencies in the evidence presented.

In the case of Esther E. Taylor v. Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company, the events unfolded in the late 19th century, specifically around May 8, 1889, in Cook County, Illinois. Esther E. Taylor claimed ownership of a twenty-five-foot wide strip of land adjacent to the right of way owned by the Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company. The railway had begun fencing this strip as part of its operations. Upon observing this activity, Taylor's husband initiated legal action by preparing a complaint and obtaining an injunction to prevent the railway from interfering with their perceived right to the land. However, before the legal process was finalized, the husband left for the premises, and the attorneys for Taylor proceeded to secure the injunction. The court later found that Taylor had effectively lost her claim to the land and dismissed her case, stating that the defenses raised were meritorious. The court's decision addressed procedural issues and the proper conduct regarding the rights of both parties.	Esther E. Taylor's primary argument was that she had a rightful claim to the strip of land being fenced by Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Company. She requested the court to issue an injunction to prevent the railway from disturbing her purported ownership and sought to maintain her possession of the land until the case was resolved.	The railway company, represented in court, contended that Taylor did not own the land in question and had not been in possession of it prior to obtaining the injunction. They argued that the injunction had been obtained through misleading claims and that the court should dismiss Taylor's bill as a result. The railway sought to recover its legal costs and maintain its right to the land without interference.

John B. Hoag filed a suit against James C. Starr and James H. Connell in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from an agreement made on March 4, 1871, regarding a mortgage that Hoag executed as security for a loan of $1,200 taken by his brother-in-law, Spencer Tompkins, from Starr. After Tompkins defaulted on the loan, Starr initiated foreclosure proceedings against Hoag's property, ultimately leading to a decree that Hoag owed Starr $1,538. As part of a settlement, Hoag agreed to pay Starr $1,903.33, offering a deed of trust on his 240-acre farm as security. However, after Hoag’s lands were sold at a foreclosure sale for $1,565, the case escalated due to disputes over the agreement's intent and Hoag's liability. Hoag contended that Starr's enforcement of the decree was unjust and sought to have the sale set aside, leading to court proceedings to clarify the parties' obligations and the validity of the earlier agreements.	Hoag claimed that the agreement made on March 4, 1871, was meant to settle all matters in controversy between himself and Starr, including disputes over the debt owed following the foreclosure. He sought to have the decree of foreclosure annulled, contending that the subsequent execution and sale were invalid and demanded that Starr fulfill his obligations as outlined in their agreement, including returning certain notes and contracts.	Starr’s defense rested primarily on the assertion that the agreement made on March 4, 1871, did not absolve Hoag of his obligations under the prior foreclosure decree. Starr argued that the agreement was valid and that Hoag remained liable for the debt as set forth in the new arrangement, which involved a deed of trust and new notes. Starr emphasized that Hoag had responsibilities to pay for expenses incurred to preserve the title to the mortgaged lands.

Jonathan Chestnutwood, Edmond Menard, and 190 other citizens and taxpayers from Randolph County filed a suit in the Circuit Court against Alexander Hood and others, seeking to restrain the county from delivering bonds to the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company. This legal action took place in November 1869 during the regular election for county officers, where the citizens voted on a proposition concerning the county's financial support to the railroad project. The county court had ordered this election to determine whether the county should subscribe to the railroad's capital stock and issue bonds for this purpose. A total of 3,210 votes were cast, with 1,278 votes in favor and 1,275 votes against the subscription. It was alleged that the railroad company misrepresented its authority and that the election conduct was flawed, as it was combined with regular county elections. The plaintiffs contended that a lawful majority was not achieved for the issuance of the bonds, which could negatively impact the county's financial health and taxpayers.	The plaintiffs argued that the county court lacked the authority to issue bonds to the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company due to insufficient legal voter approval. They claimed that the legislative provisions required a majority of all legal voters at the election, not just a majority of those who voted on the specific question. They requested an injunction against the delivery of the bonds and asserted that the proceeding of the county court, influenced by fraudulent representations, was unlawful and threatened the taxpayers' financial interests.	The defendants contended that the majority of votes cast on the particular subscription question should be sufficient to authorize the bond issuance. They argued that the election process followed statutory requirements and that their subscription to the railroad was valid based on the votes received. The defendants maintained that there was no need for a separate ballot for the bond issue as it was part of the duly called election and claimed that the court should uphold the action taken by the county court.

In 1868, the case of Margaret Fitzgerald v. John Forristal et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from Bureau County, Illinois. Margaret Fitzgerald filed a bill to prevent the foreclosure of a mortgage executed by her to Matthew O'Farrell, who had since passed away, with John Forristal acting as one of the executors of O'Farrell's estate. Fitzgerald claimed that the money used to finance the land purchase was provided by her mother when she was an infant, intending the land for Fitzgerald’s benefit. Following her mother’s marriage and later divorce, Fitzgerald maintained possession of the property, living there continuously with her children. Fitzgerald’s step-father, Jeremiah Hartney, also claimed rights to the land, leading her to execute a mortgage to protect her interests. The defendants sought to foreclose on the mortgage, asserting its validity despite Fitzgerald’s claims of it being executed without consideration and specifically to thwart Hartney’s claims. The court proceedings in the Circuit Court denied Fitzgerald's relief, leading to her appeal.	Margaret Fitzgerald claimed that the mortgage to O'Farrell was invalid as it was executed without consideration and was intended to defraud her step-father, Hartney, from claiming rights to the land. Fitzgerald sought an injunction to prevent the foreclosure proceedings on the mortgage, arguing that the defense could not be adequately addressed in a legal court and should be heard in equity.	The defendants, executors of O'Farrell's estate, countered that the mortgage was valid and rightfully due, asserting that Fitzgerald had no legal defense against it. They argued that she executed the mortgage voluntarily to defraud Hartney, and, as such, the mortgage was binding despite any alleged lack of consideration. They insisted that the mortgage was part of a legitimate transaction and that the allegations made by Fitzgerald were insufficient to warrant an injunction against the foreclosure.

In June 1854, the case "Morris Hadden v. David H. Shoutz" was decided in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over six acres of land in Kane County, Illinois, which included a dam and mill located on Big Rock Creek. Morris Hadden, the appellant, owned the land and sought to prevent Shoutz, the appellee, from constructing a new dam that would cause water to flow onto his land. The mill and dam were significant improvements on the land, and Hadden's claim was based on the contention that when Shoutz purchased the land, he should have been aware of the existing conditions, including the prior rights related to the use of the mill and the dam. The core legal issue concerned the interpretation of the deed from 1845, which conveyed the land with its "hereditaments and appurtenances." Ultimately, the court examined the intentions of both parties at the time of the conveyance and the practical implications of the dam’s presence.	Hadden claimed that the construction of a new dam by Shoutz would unlawfully direct water onto his land, infringing upon his rights to the land and its use. He argued that the deed under which Shoutz acquired the property included the right to the flow of water that the dam provided, asserting that this easement was implied and integral to the property conveyed.	Shoutz countered that the deed explicitly conveyed only the specified land without mention of the mill or the right to flood neighboring property. He argued that the absence of the mill in the deed indicated that it was not intended to be included in the sale. Shoutz maintained that he had the right to construct the dam, and hence, the water flow issue did not relate to the property that he owned.

In the case of Stephen Van Dusen v. The People of the State of Illinois, the events unfolded in Carroll County, Illinois in 1873, when an indictment for perjury was brought against Stephen Van Dusen by the grand jury. The charges stemmed from an affidavit he allegedly falsified before Samuel Lichty, the assessor of Wysox Township. The indictment included two counts: the first claimed that Van Dusen was owed $10,811 for money loaned on May 1, 1873, while the second stated he claimed only $1,000 was owed to him. After a change of venue to Whiteside County, Van Dusen was tried in August 1874, found guilty, and sentenced to three years in prison. Subsequently, he filed a writ of error seeking to reverse the judgment on the grounds that there was insufficient evidence supporting the charge of perjury, particularly contesting the validity of the oath taken outside the assessor’s jurisdiction and the lack of evidence regarding the details of the alleged loan.	The plaintiff, Stephen Van Dusen, argued that the oath administered by the assessor was invalid because it took place beyond the legal territorial limits of his authority. He claimed that there was no evidence proving that the oath had been administered in Carroll County and that the official acts taken by the assessor outside his township were illegal. Van Dusen sought a reversal of the judgment against him on the basis that the evidence presented was insufficient to establish a conviction for perjury.	The defense, representing the People of the State of Illinois, contended that the venue specified in the affidavit provided adequate proof that the oath was administered in Carroll County. They argued that the assessor had the authority to administer oaths related to property assessments in his township. The defense maintained that the evidence of perjury was corroborated by the claims made in Van Dusen's affidavit, and thus sought to uphold the jury's conviction and the sentencing imposed by the lower court.

In the case of Henry W. Merriwether and Robert L. Hill, impleaded with Richard B. Hill v. Samuel Smith, who sues for the use of Charles Gregory, the events took place in Greene County, Illinois during the August term of 1839. The lawsuit was initiated by Samuel Smith against the defendants on a promissory note. The defendants, Merriwether and Robert L. Hill, claimed that they executed the note based on Smith's representation that he was the owner in fee simple of a specific lot of land and that he would provide a good and perfect title to this land once the note was executed. However, they asserted that Smith never delivered a sufficient deed and, in fact, had no title to the lot at all, thus claiming that the note failed due to lack of consideration. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court after the lower court sustained a demurrer against the defendants’ special plea. The case involved the examination of the legal implications of the promissory note and the validity of the plea regarding the promised deed's execution and title ownership.	The plaintiff, Samuel Smith, claims that the defendants owe the amount stated in the promissory note. He argues that the defendants executed this note in consideration of his promise to convey a good title to the lot of land mentioned, which is central to the case. Smith contends that their assertion that he had no title is baseless and that the promissory note remains valid.	The defendants, Merriwether and Robert L. Hill, argue that their execution of the promissory note was contingent upon Smith's promise to provide a good title to the lot of land. They claim that Smith misrepresented his ownership of the property, as he never had a valid title to convey. Their defense highlights the failure of consideration due to Smith’s inability to deliver the promised deed and challenges the legal sufficiency of the plaintiff's claims based on these grounds.

The case centers around a dispute between The Springfield Engine and Threshing Company, located in Springfield, Ohio, and Edward W. Green, the appellee, who was involved in agricultural implements sales in Cerro Gordo, Illinois. The events began in January 1881 when Green entered into a contract to sell the company's threshing machines. In June 1881, he sold one machine to the appellee for $550 but didn't collect payment at the time. Later, in October, the company’s director, Yan II. Cartmell, visited Green to collect payment, resulting in two notes for $332.72 and $221.58. After complications arose regarding a supposed rebate agreement and the loss of one of the notes, Green faced allegations of forgery, leading to his arrest. The charges were ultimately dismissed after the prosecution could not sustain its claims. The appellate court examined the actions of the company's agents and questioned the authority under which they acted, ultimately finding that there was no basis for the claims against the company.	The plaintiff, Edward W. Green, claimed malicious prosecution against The Springfield Engine and Threshing Company. He argued that the company's agents wrongfully charged him with forgery, leading to his arrest and humiliation without just cause. He sought damages for the consequences of this malicious prosecution, totaling $5,000.	The Springfield Engine and Threshing Company contended that their agents acted without express or implied authority to prosecute Green for forgery. They argued that there was probable cause for the prosecution, thus negating the claims of malice. The defense highlighted that the agents' actions were personal and did not implicate the company, maintaining that the prosecution was unjustified in the context of its business interests.

In March 1839, James M. Archer was involved in a legal dispute with James H. Spillman and Edmund D. F. Reed in Edgar County, Illinois. The case was heard in the Edgar Circuit Court, presided over by Hon. Justin Harlan. The plaintiffs, Spillman and Reed, initiated an action of debt based on a sealed note against Archer. During the court proceedings, both parties made appearances through their attorneys; E. B. Webb represented Archer, while O. B. Ficklin represented Spillman and Reed. The court noted that although Archer filed a plea and the plaintiffs joined it, the actual plea and the joining had not been properly documented in the clerk’s office. As a result, the court was unable to establish how the issue was resolved since no jury was called to try the case, nor was there a record of any agreement to have the court conduct the trial. Consequently, the plaintiffs were awarded their debt and damages, but the court was later challenged for not allowing a jury trial, which was considered a significant error.	The plaintiffs, Spillman and Reed, claimed that Archer owed them a debt as per a sealed note and sought to recover this amount along with damages. They argued that the trial proceedings should uphold their claim, despite the lack of documented pleas, which they believed did not invalidate the original agreement.	Archer's defense centered on the procedural error of not having a jury trial to adjudicate the issues of fact, as required under the law. He contended that without the jury's examination of facts, the judgment was improper. Additionally, he requested the opportunity to file a new plea to address the lack of documentation and ensure a fair trial on the merits of the case.

In 1877, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Samuel Bailey, Jr. v. John R. Bensley et al., which involved a dispute over grain consignments between the appellant, Samuel Bailey, Jr., a grain buyer from Baileyville, Illinois, and the appellees, Bensley & Wagner, commission merchants based in Chicago. The case arose after Bailey began consigning grain to the appellees in 1868 and continued this practice until 1873. The controversy centered on the ownership and handling of warehouse receipts issued for the grain stored in public warehouses upon its arrival in Chicago. Bailey claimed that the warehouse receipts were his property and that Bensley & Wagner had a duty to retain these specific receipts even when instructed to hold the grain. Conversely, the appellees argued that, under the customary practices of the trade, they were not obligated to keep or maintain the original receipts, as grain was mixed and its identity lost once stored. The case’s origins date to disputes over monthly account statements and unpaid balances owed by Bailey to the commission mercantile firm, leading to Bailey's suit on April 6, 1874, against the appellees for $1,119.68.	Samuel Bailey, Jr. contended that the warehouse receipts representing his grain were his property, and he accused Bensley & Wagner of failing to retain the specific receipts for the grain they were instructed to hold. His main argument was that he should be entitled to the price achieved from the sale of his grain, calculated based on the original warehouse receipts, and sought to limit his liability for storage costs to a minimal amount accrued prior to the grain's sale.	Bensley & Wagner defended their actions by asserting that under the established customs of the Chicago grain trade, commission merchants were allowed to use warehouse receipts interchangeably without obligation to hold on to the exact receipts for each shipment. They maintained that their transactions were in line with industry standards and that Bailey was only liable for storage costs incurred up until the sale order was given, asserting that the receipts did not represent Bailey's ownership but were merely evidence of a debt owed to them.

In December 1857, the case of Eliab B. Kirby v. David B. Watt took place in Illinois, involving the parties in a dispute over the delivery of 205 bushels of wheat. The appellant, Eliab B. Kirby, initiated an action of debt against David B. Watt, the surviving partner of D. Watt & Son, regarding to whom the wheat was delivered—either to Watt as a joint benefit or his father individually. The crux of the dispute pertained to whether the wheat had been accounted for in a prior settlement between Kirby and Watt's father. The case was heard before Judge Wood-son with a jury, which ultimately ruled in favor of the defendant, David B. Watt. The jury had to determine the facts surrounding the delivery of the wheat and whether it had been included in past financial settlements.	Kirby claimed that he delivered 205 bushels of wheat intended for settlement with David B. Watt or his father. He argued that the wheat had not been properly accounted for in prior financial dealings and sought recovery based on this assertion. He maintained that the evidence presented, including his books, proved that the wheat delivery had not been settled correctly.	David B. Watt contended that the wheat was delivered to his father and denied any obligation for the amount claimed by Kirby. Watt argued that Kirby's books of account were not admissible as evidence since they lacked the necessary foundation to establish their correctness. Furthermore, Watt asserted that Kirby failed to present any legitimate evidence that would overrule the established account between the parties.

In January 1877, Henry Cobb brought a legal action against The People, stemming from a bond executed under the Dram Shop Act in Pike County, Illinois. The case revolved around claims related to the operation of a dram shop and the responsibilities it entailed. Cobb alleged that he suffered damages as a result of violations of this act. Notably, the case was tried not by a judge but by a member of the bar, which became a pivotal point in the subsequent court decision. The initial proceedings led to a judgment that raised questions about the allowed types of damages, as Cobb was seeking exemplary damages contrary to the provisions of the applicable section of the Dram Shop Act.	Henry Cobb's claims centered on seeking compensation for damages he believed were sustained due to the defendant's violations of the Dram Shop Act. He asserted that he was entitled to exemplary damages, reflecting the severe nature of the infringements. Cobb's main legal requests included a judgment awarding him these damages, arguing that the violations warranted a penalty beyond mere compensation.	The People, as defendants, contended that under the Dram Shop Act, only actual damages could be recovered, and exemplary or punitive damages were not permissible. They also raised procedural objections, specifically challenging the legitimacy of the proceedings on the grounds that the trial was conducted by a member of the bar rather than an appointed judge, which they argued violated judicial standards.

The case, "The Northern Illinois Railroad Company et al. v. The Racine and Mississippi Railroad Company," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. It stemmed from a legal dispute involving the Northern Illinois Railroad Company and the Racine and Mississippi Railroad Company over costs related to a prior decree in a mortgage foreclosure case. The key individuals involved were the representatives of both railroad companies, with Mr. Thomas J. Turner representing the appellants (Northern Illinois Railroad) and Messrs. Knowlton & Jamieson representing the appellees (Racine and Mississippi Railroad). The controversy centers on whether costs could be properly taxed against the Northern Illinois Railroad Company despite their claim that they were out of court due to the prior decree's sale order. The court found that the Northern Illinois Railroad Company remained in court and could still be assessed for costs as further actions might be required, thus allowing the case to progress to the next term for resolution.	The Northern Illinois Railroad Company, as the plaintiff, claimed that the court had wrongfully taxed them with costs associated with the previous mortgage foreclosure decree. They argued that due to the decree of sale, they were effectively out of court, and therefore, could not be subjected to costs at a subsequent trial term. They sought to reverse the part of the decree concerning the costs awarded against them.	The Racine and Mississippi Railroad Company defended against the claims of the Northern Illinois Railroad Company by stating that the decree had appropriately retained the company in court for the possibility of further actions. They argued that the court had the discretion to award costs in such matters and that the difficulties in assessing those costs did not warrant changes to the previous order. They requested that the original order regarding the taxation of costs be upheld.

The case, "The Merchants’ Savings, Loan & Trust Company v. Grant Goodrich, for use, etc.", was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. It arose in Cook County, Illinois, amid a public voting event related to the West Side Park Bill. The central figures in the dispute were The Merchants’ Savings, Loan & Trust Company, which served as a stakeholder, Grant Goodrich, acting on behalf of the vendors, and H. M. Shepard and F. L. Welles. The issue involved two certified checks, each valued at $2,500, totaling $5,000, deposited with the bank under a condition tied to the outcome of an election. Goodrich sought possession of the checks after a vote in favor of the West Side Park Bill, but the bank refused to release them based on instructions from Shepard and Welles. Goodrich filed a replevin action against the bank, resulting in a jury verdict that awarded him damages of $6,275 for the wrongful detention of the checks. The trial court upheld this verdict, prompting the bank’s appeal.	The plaintiff, Grant Goodrich, argued that he had a rightful claim to the two certified checks due to the favorable election outcome for the West Side Park Bill. He maintained that the checks were to be delivered to him as per the deposited agreement contingent upon the election result. Goodrich sought to replevy the checks from the bank, which he claimed wrongfully detained the property, and he requested damages for the loss incurred during the period of detention.	The defendant, The Merchants’ Savings, Loan & Trust Company, contended that the transaction was void as it was contrary to public policy, characterizing it as a wager dependent on the uncertain outcome of a public election. They maintained that as a mere stakeholder, they were following the instructions of the true owners of the checks (Shepard and Welles) to retain the checks until the rightful conditions were satisfied. The bank argued that because the underlying contract was void, Goodrich had no legal basis for recovering the checks or the damages awarded by the lower court.

The case, "William F. Johnson, Plaintiff in Error, v. John C. Dodge, Defendant in Error," was decided in June 1856 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It revolves around a dispute regarding the specific performance of a contract for the sale of land. On September 4, 1852, John C. Dodge, the landowner, purportedly entered into an agreement through his agent, N. P. Iglehart, to sell forty acres of land to Thomas C. Walters. Walters paid $50 as part of the down payment and agreed to pay the remaining balance in installments. After Walters assigned this contract to William F. Johnson, Johnson attempted to exercise his rights under the agreement by offering to pay the remaining amount and requesting a deed from Dodge. However, Dodge refused to comply, claiming the land's value exceeded the contracted price and asserting he had never authorized Iglehart to negotiate the sale. Despite evidence from Iglehart indicating he had the authority to sell the land, Dodge denied this and challenged the validity of the contract under the statute of frauds, leading to the lawsuit.	William F. Johnson, as the plaintiff, sought specific performance of the land sale contract he obtained from Walters. He asserted that both Walters and he had complied with the obligations stipulated in the agreement and formally tendered the remaining payment before demanding a deed from Dodge. Johnson argued that the refusal by Dodge to finalize the sale constituted a breach of contract, warranting judicial intervention to compel the performance of the agreement.	John C. Dodge, the defendant, rejected Johnson's claims by denying the existence of a binding contract. He asserted that he had not authorized Iglehart to sell the land, and thus, no valid agreement had been formed. Dodge further contended that the contract was void under the statute of frauds, emphasizing the lack of a written agreement binding him to the sale or signed by Walters. He claimed that Johnson's attempts to tender payment and demand a deed were insufficient and that he had been unaware that the land was being sold while he was actively managing other property transactions.

The case of John H. Crawford et al. v. Lantrom J. Clark et al. was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1854. The dispute originated from the delivery of a shipment consisting of iron and steel, which was transported from Cleveland to Chicago by a common carrier, the propeller "Granite State." On September 4, 1852, the plaintiffs delivered 12,048 pounds of iron and steel to the defendants, who accepted them for transportation with an expectation of delivery to the consignees, Dole, Rumsey & Co. However, upon arrival in Chicago, the defendants claimed the iron was delivered at their dock, in accordance with customary practice, but the plaintiffs alleged that the goods were lost because they were not delivered to the actual consignees, leading to the legal action. The issue raised was whether the customary delivery at the dock constituted sufficient delivery to release the carrier from liability.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants, as common carriers, failed to deliver their goods in accordance with the terms of the contract. They asserted that even though the shipment was received in Chicago, it was not delivered to Dole, Rumsey & Co., the designated consignees, resulting in a total loss of the iron and steel valued at $500. The plaintiffs maintained that the defendants were liable for the loss due to inadequate notice and failure to secure the goods.	The defendants contended that they followed established practices in the delivery of goods, claiming that the custom at the time mandated that deliveries be made at their authorized dock and that proper notice of delivery had been given to the consignees. They argued that this constituted a valid delivery that discharged their responsibilities as carriers. The defendants sought to demonstrate that the loss was not due to their negligence and that the delivery complied with customary practices in the shipping industry.

The case of Henry W. Billings v. John Detten took place in December 1853 in Madison County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Henry W. Billings, initiated an action of ejectment against the defendant, John Detten, seeking to recover possession of a specific parcel of land—specifically, the west half of the southeast quarter of section thirteen, township six north, range ten west. During the trial, it was established that Billings held a regular title to the property through a chain of conveyances originating from the patentee, with no outstanding taxes on the property. However, Detten was in possession of the land when the lawsuit commenced. The defendant presented evidence of a prior judgment from the Madison Circuit Court regarding taxes assessed on the property for the year 1845, which had resulted in a sheriff's deed transferring the property to him. Billings countered this by providing evidence from the assessor's books showing that the tax assessments were improperly filed, which hindered his ability to contest the assessment in court. The trial court ultimately found in favor of Detten, leading to a judgment against Billings.	Billings asserted that he was the rightful owner of the property due to a valid chain of title and argued that the tax assessment leading to Detten's possession was invalid, as the assessor failed to return the assessments within the legally mandated timeframe. He requested the court to recognize his ownership and eject Detten from the property based on this claim of invalid assessment.	Detten contended that the prior judgment and subsequent deed transferring the property to him were valid, citing the sheriff's deed awarded after the tax assessment was ruled upon. He maintained that the assessment, despite the alleged flaws in the timing and filing, had been properly executed and that subsequent legislation could not nullify the tax that had already been collected. Detten sought to uphold the lower court's ruling that permitted him to retain possession of the property.

The case "Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. v. Julia A. Brooks" took place in January 1876 in Illinois. Julia A. Brooks and a man she claimed was her husband boarded a train in Decatur, intending to travel to Danville. They did not purchase tickets or pay the required fare, with the husband asserting they had no money, despite evidence suggesting they had ample funds to cover the fare. It was brought to their attention that traveling without a fare was against the train company's regulations. The case had previously been discussed in this court term involving the same parties, leading to considerations about the fraudulent nature of their actions. During the trial, the court erroneously instructed the jury on the importance of fare payment, focusing on whether or not Brooks was aware of the regulations. However, the court concluded that her husband, as her agent, had knowledge of the rules, thus implicating her in his fraudulent actions.	The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. argued that Julia A. Brooks, along with her husband, engaged in fraudulent behavior by traveling on their train without paying the fare. Their claims emphasized that the railway company is not liable to individuals who knowingly induce conductors to carry them in violation of company regulations. They requested that any recovery for injuries sustained by the plaintiff should be barred due to this fraud.	Julia A. Brooks defended herself by asserting that she was not aware of the regulations prohibiting travel without payment. She sought to establish that her lack of knowledge should absolve her from the implications of her husband's actions. However, the court refuted this argument, citing that her husband's knowledge was pertinent due to his role as her agent during the transaction.

Hugh S. Martin was indicted in Fulton County, Illinois, for obstructing a road claimed as a public highway. The key individuals involved included Martin as the plaintiff in error, and the People of the State of Illinois as defendants in error. During the trial, questions were raised about whether the road had ever been worked or recognized as a public highway by local authorities, and if it had been used by the public as such. The defense argued that the prosecution needed to demonstrate adverse and uninterrupted use of the road for the appropriate duration to validate claims of public use. The opposition maintained that the public’s use must have been established as against the owner's use, and any failure by town or county authorities to maintain the road undermined the claim to public status. The case hinged on the nature of the road's use over time and whether it was merely a private right or a public highway.	The plaintiff, Hugh S. Martin, argued for the admissibility of evidence concerning the road's public status and whether it had been regularly maintained by local authorities. His main legal request was to challenge the indictment based on procedural grounds, asserting that the evidence was crucial to establishing the claims against him.	The defendants contended that their claims of public highway status could be justified through proof of longstanding adverse use. They maintained that should the road not have been used by the public uninterruptedly, it could not be classified as a public highway. Additionally, the defendants argued for the rejection of certain evidence and instructions provided to the jury which they believed misrepresented the situation regarding public versus private road usage.

In the case of Joseph McPherson v. Murray Nelson et al., which took place in April 1867 in Chicago, Illinois, the dispute arose from a contract entered into on February 25, 1865, between plaintiffs Murray Nelson and Enoch Stevens, doing business as Murray Kelson & Co., and defendants Joseph McPherson and Elias Stiles. The contract involved the sale of 5,000 bushels of oats to be delivered by the plaintiffs during March 1865 at a price of 61.5 cents per bushel. The plaintiffs claimed they were always ready and willing to deliver the oats but that the defendants refused to accept them. After the completion of the trial, the jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, leading the defendants to appeal the verdict, claiming that they had not been afforded proper instructions from the court and asserting that the plaintiffs were required to prove a tender of the oats in order to recover. The case ultimately revolved around nuances within contractual obligations, the requirement of tender, and the sufficiency of evidence presented during the trial.	The plaintiffs argued that they had fulfilled their contractual obligations by being ready and willing to deliver the oats. They asserted that an actual tender of oats was not necessary to maintain an action against the defendants for damages due to non-acceptance. The plaintiffs sought to recover damages amounting to $1,075 for the defendants' refusal to accept the delivery of the oats as per the contract.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs were required to prove an actual tender of the oats to recover. They argued that the plaintiffs' evidence did not suffice to demonstrate that they were ready and willing to deliver the contractual quantity of oats.
