The defendants sought to have the jury instructed that without proof of tender, the plaintiffs had no right to recover damages under the terms of the contract.

Edward Stevens v. The City of Chicago took place in September 1868 in Chicago, Illinois. The case arose from an action of debt for a penalty initiated by the City of Chicago against Edward Stevens, who was accused of operating a disorderly house. The police court issued a judgment against Stevens, imposing a fine of fifty dollars. Stevens appealed this judgment to the superior court. During the trial in the superior court, a jury found against Stevens, upholding the fifty-dollar penalty. Following this, Stevens filed a motion for a new trial, which was denied, leading him to further appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The central issue in this case hinged on the legal basis for the penalty—specifically, the absence of an ordinance establishing such a penalty for keeping a disorderly house in the city.	The City of Chicago, as the plaintiff, argued that Edward Stevens had violated city ordinances by keeping a disorderly house, which warranted a financial penalty. They sought to uphold the judgment from the superior court that imposed a fifty-dollar fine on Stevens for this violation.	Edward Stevens, as the defendant, contended that the judgment against him should be reversed because there was no evidence presented that a relevant city ordinance existed to enforce a penalty for keeping a disorderly house. His defense argued that without evidence of such an ordinance, the claims against him could not hold legal ground.

Josephine Lowery filed a lawsuit against Robert Niccolls in the Illinois Appellate Court on October 24, 1882. The case stems from a contract between the parties regarding the sale of a half section of land in Butler County, Kansas, executed on January 3, 1879. Niccolls received $1,000 from Lowery and agreed to perfect the title of the land within nine months. However, his attempts to secure a title were unsuccessful, ultimately leading to the foreclosure of the property due to mortgage issues. Lowery, after giving Niccolls sufficient time to perfect the title and after receiving no satisfaction, opted to elect a provision in their contract that allowed her to instead recover the purchase money from the collateral held by a third party. Lowery communicated her decision not to take the land and tendered a quitclaim deed back to Niccolls, which he refused. In March 1881, Lowery initiated a lawsuit to enforce her rights as outlined in the original agreement.	Lowery's primary argument was that Niccolls failed to meet his contractual obligation to perfect the title of the land within the specified nine-month timeframe. She sought a legal declaration enforcing her right to either recover the purchase money plus interest or to reconvey the property back to Niccolls. Lowery insisted that her election not to keep the land was timely and within the terms of their contract, and that she was entitled to the collateral funds held by Swan & Ellis.	Niccolls contended that he had made efforts to perfect the title and that Lowery was not entitled to rescission of the contract based on his actions. He argued that any delay in perfecting the title was justifiable and that Lowery's claims to rescind the contract were unwarranted since he was working within legal frameworks to secure the title. He requested the court to uphold the contract as binding and maintain that Lowery should proceed with taking the land.

In 1865, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Henry L. Swartwout v. Joseph Evans arose. The dispute centered around a reaping machine that Joseph Evans claimed belonged solely to him. The plaintiff, Joseph Evans, initially purchased the machine in 1839 for $75. In 1850, his son Richard sold an undivided half of the machine to the defendant, Henry L. Swartwout, for $25. Richard did not consider himself an agent of his father in this transaction, and upon informing Joseph of the sale, Joseph expressed dissatisfaction. However, for the subsequent two years, both parties used the machine as joint owners, with Swartwout paying half the repair costs. The conflict escalated to legal proceedings when Joseph demanded the return of the machine from Swartwout, which led Joseph to file an action for trover to recover damages for the alleged conversion of the machine. The case moved from a justice of the peace to the Superior Court of Chicago.	The plaintiff, Joseph Evans, claimed that he was the sole owner of the reaping machine and argued that Swartwout had wrongfully converted it. He sought damages for the conversion, exemplified by a demand for the machine that was subsequently refused by Swartwout. Evans presented testimony indicating that he considered himself the sole owner and that his son's sale of the machine was unauthorized.	The defendant, Henry L. Swartwout, contended that he was a joint owner of the reaping machine, having purchased half of it from Richard Evans. He argued that for two years, both parties acted as co-owners and that his claim to ownership had never been effectively disputed until the legal action commenced. Swartwout claimed that there was no valid demand made by the plaintiff before the lawsuit, asserting that Joseph's demand was more of a claim to sole ownership rather than joint possession.

James Sanders was indicted for perjury related to an affidavit he made during his trial for burglary and larceny in St. Clair County, Illinois. Sanders was accused of breaking into a home near East St. Louis on the night of October 22, 1886, along with two others, Schmidt and Tourville. During his trial on March 29, 1887, Sanders filed an affidavit for a continuance, claiming he could not proceed without a crucial alibi witness, H. T. Winchester. He stated that Winchester was the only person who could confirm his alibi for the night in question. However, this affidavit was later deemed false as the prosecution argued that Sanders knew of other witnesses who could corroborate his claim. The jury found Sanders guilty of perjury based on this false statement, leading to his sentencing to the penitentiary. Sanders appealed the conviction, citing errors like the refusal to quash the indictment and the improper handling of jury procedures.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Sanders committed perjury by making a false affidavit asserting that Winchester was the sole witness to prove his alibi. They maintained that this statement was material to the motion for a continuance and therefore substantiated the charge of perjury. The prosecution contended that Sanders had not exercised due diligence to secure Winchester's presence and highlighted that other witnesses were available to testify, undermining Sanders' claim.	Sanders' defense hinged on contesting the validity of the perjury charge, arguing that the statement made in the affidavit was not material to the case's outcome since he was acquitted of the burglary charges. They claimed that the indictment was insufficient and alleged that the court had improperly handled the trial, including the supervision of the jury. The defense also challenged the prosecution's remarks during the trial and the trial court's refusal to allow certain jury instructions.

The case of Andrew G. Lundberg v. William Boldenweck took place in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 2, 1889. Andrew G. Lundberg served as the town supervisor of Lake View from April 1888 to March 3, 1889. A taxpayer from the town filed a bill to prevent the town clerk from issuing a warrant for Lundberg's compensation, alleging that Lundberg had only attended to business for seven days during the entire period but had claimed compensation for 318 days of service inside the town and 42 days outside at inflated rates. The taxpayer contended that the claims were fraudulent and sought an injunction to stop payment. The town clerk recognized the discrepancies and confessed to the allegations, while Lundberg, the defendant, demurred, asserting his right to the claimed amount. However, upon examination, the court concluded that the case provided prima facie indications of fraud, ruling against Lundberg and affirming the decree to restrain the warrant's issuance.	The plaintiff, acting as a taxpayer, claimed that Lundberg had not legitimately performed the services for which he sought payment. They pointed out that Lundberg only engaged in town business for seven days, yet he sought compensation for an exaggerated total of 318 days in town and 42 days outside, which constituted a clear overstatement and implied fraud. The plaintiff requested the court to issue an injunction to prevent the delivery of the town warrant to Lundberg.	Lundberg, the defendant, contended that he was entitled to the compensation claimed for his service, arguing against the allegations of fraud presented by the plaintiff. Lundberg demurred, seeking to have the case dismissed based on his assertion of legitimate services rendered during his term as town supervisor, thereby claiming the right to the town warrant.

In 1868, Martin Keating brought an action for debt against The Albany City Fire Insurance Company before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Cairo, Illinois, where Keating sought compensation for a fire loss under an insurance policy he had purchased. Central to the case were allegations made by the insurance company that the risk had increased due to changes in the conditions surrounding the insured property. The insurance policy included a provision that allowed the company to cancel the coverage if the risk was deemed to have increased, provided they gave notice and refunded a part of the premium. The insurance company argued that on May 15, 1866, they notified Keating of their intention to cancel the policy and refunded a portion of the premium. They claimed that the construction of a city pump and works nearby increased the hazard of the insured building, as it changed its risk profile. They also argued that Keating had misrepresented the nature of the property when applying for the insurance, claiming it was occupied as more than just a dwelling and saloon, thus further increasing the risk. The trial court ruled in favor of Keating, leading to the appeal by the insurance company.	Martin Keating, the plaintiff, contended that The Albany City Fire Insurance Company was liable under the terms of the insurance policy for the fire loss he incurred. He argued that he had complied with all obligations under the policy and denied that any change in circumstances had occurred that would warrant cancellation of the insurance. Keating sought payment for his loss and disputed the insurer's claims regarding an increase in risk, asserting that the company had not properly exercised its right to cancel the policy.	The Albany City Fire Insurance Company, as the defendant, contended that they had a valid reason to cancel the insurance policy under the provision allowing for cancellation if the risk increased. The company argued that the erection of a city pump in close proximity to the insured building constituted an increased risk. They also claimed that Keating had misrepresented the occupancy of the property, which included using it as a boarding house, thus justifying their decision to terminate the policy. The company maintained that they had given the required notice and proper refund of the premium.

The case of *The Pittsburgh, Cincinnati and St. Louis Railway Company v. Isabella Knutson, Admx* centers around an incident that occurred on November 17, 1871, at the intersection of Kinzie and Desplaines streets in Chicago, Illinois. Severt Knutson was struck and fatally injured by a passing train while attempting to cross the tracks. The plaintiff, Isabella Knutson, serving as the administratrix of Severt's estate, filed a lawsuit claiming that the injuries and subsequent death resulted from the negligence of the railroad company's employees. The case was tried by jury, which awarded a verdict of $1,700 against the railway company. They subsequently appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing issues regarding ownership of the train involved and the degree of negligence attributed to both parties.	The plaintiff argued that Severt Knutson's injuries were due to the negligence of the railway company's employees. She claimed that the train was operated at a reckless speed of ten miles per hour in a busy area, violating city ordinances that permitted a maximum speed of six miles per hour. The plaintiff sought damages for the wrongful death of Severt Knutson, asserting that any negligence on his part was negligible compared to the company's gross negligence in operating the train at the prohibited speed.	The defendant, the Pittsburgh, Cincinnati and St. Louis Railway Company, contended that the evidence did not definitively prove that the train involved belonged to them. They argued that the deceased was complicit in the accident, suggesting that he was guilty of negligence for standing on the tracks and failing to observe the approaching train, which he could have seen from a distance. The railway company requested that the verdict be overturned based on these claims of insufficient evidence and alleged contributory negligence from the deceased.

In September 1870, in Henry County, Illinois, a legal action was initiated by Samuel W. Harlan for the use of Martin B. Harlan against John S. Buckles concerning a promissory note. The plaintiff contested that Buckles owed a certain amount based on this note. In response, Buckles entered a plea in abatement, claiming that there was another ongoing action with the same cause currently pending in the same court. This plea stated a request for the court to quash the writ and declaration associated with the current suit. However, the circuit court rejected this plea, deeming it ineffective due to a lack of correspondence between its initial and concluding requests. The court subsequently ruled in favor of Harlan, leading to a judgment against Buckles for the amount owed on the promissory note, with interest included. Buckles, seeking reversal of this judgment, filed an appeal.	The plaintiff, Samuel W. Harlan, argued that John S. Buckles owed money based on a promissory note. Harlan requested that the court enforce the terms of the promissory note and ultimately ruled in his favor for the payment of the owed amount, including interest.	The defendant, John S. Buckles, contended that there was another legal action pending for the same cause in Henry County, which justified his plea in abatement. He argued that the presence of two simultaneous lawsuits for the same issue was unjust and requested that the court quash the writ and declaration of the current case based on this argument.

In the case of William Duchardt v. The People ex rel., etc., decided on February 7, 1883, the incident took place in Cass County, Illinois. William Duchardt was the plaintiff who brought forth the case against The People, represented by the state. The dispute centered on the trial court's rulings during the proceedings led by Judge C. Epleb. Duchardt challenged various rulings made by the trial court, but the specifics of what those challenges were is not detailed in the case description. The legal arguments presented by Duchardt were encapsulated in his brief but faced an insurmountable procedural obstacle concerning the preservation of exceptions to the rulings made during the trial.	William Duchardt, the plaintiff, claimed that certain rulings of the trial court were erroneous and sought to have these judgments overturned. He argued that exceptions to these rulings had been taken, although the case notes did not properly document this according to the required legal procedure.	The defense, representing The People, countered that there were no valid exceptions preserved for the appellate court's review. They pointed out that the bill of exceptions signed by the trial judge did not show that any exceptions were taken to the trial court's rulings. Therefore, they argued that the appellate court should dismiss the plaintiff's claims due to a lack of proper procedural records.

Richard Clark and Frederick Miller were involved in a legal case against Samuel Marfield in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision rendered in January 1875. The case originated in Champaign County, Illinois, where Samuel Marfield filed a bill in chancery aimed at resolving a dispute over land ownership. The crux of the dispute centered on a forged deed that allegedly transferred the title of Clark's land to a third party, Reuben H. Simpson. The defendants, Marfield and his co-defendants, denied all material allegations. During the hearing, evidence was presented confirming that the deed was indeed a forgery and that Clark had never relinquished title to the land. Additional points of contention noted in the case were procedural issues related to the timing of the trial and the notification of the defendants regarding the change in the hearing date, which the court addressed in its ruling.	The plaintiffs, Richard Clark and Frederick Miller, claimed that the defendant, Samuel Marfield, along with others, had attempted to uphold a forged deed that falsely conveyed Clark's land title to Reuben H. Simpson. The plaintiffs sought the court's intervention to nullify the forged deeds and effectively reestablish their rightful ownership of the property in question. They asserted that the evidence conclusively demonstrated the deed was forged and hence invalid.	The defendant, Samuel Marfield, countered the plaintiffs’ claims by denying all material allegations in the complaint. He contested the trial's timing, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction to hear the case ahead of the date set by the clerk. Marfield's legal representation claimed that this procedural error compromised the defense and that there were failures in properly notifying all parties involved. They also argued regarding the sufficiency of notice served on Simpson, suggesting the publication notice was insufficient to confer jurisdiction.

In 1884, in Quincy, Illinois, Willis J. Montgomery, an experienced railroad switchman, sustained injuries while working in the yards of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company (appellant). At the time of the incident, a damaged freight car had been in the yard for several days and was being loaded for a long trip. Montgomery was uncoupling the cars when his hand and arm became caught, resulting in injury. The case hinges on whether the railroad company was negligent in ensuring the cars were safe for handling. The court noted that mere accidents do not presume negligence, and the injured party must prove the car was defective, that the injury resulted from this defect, and that the company had notice of such defect.	Montgomery claimed that the railroad company had a duty to maintain the cars in safe condition and failed to do so, which directly led to his injury. He argued that the circumstances of the accident suggested that the car was defective and that this defect could have been discovered by the company's employees. Montgomery requested compensation for the injuries sustained due to this alleged negligence.	The railroad company argued that Montgomery failed to prove any defect in the car or that any such defect was known to them or could have been discovered through ordinary diligence. They maintained that the burden of proof lay with Montgomery to demonstrate negligence on their part. Furthermore, they contended that since Montgomery was aware of the risks associated with the cars in the yard, he assumed responsibility for his own safety during the performance of his duties.

The legal case "The Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Co. v. Allen M. Eastburn" took place in Iroquois County, Illinois, beginning with a trial in January 1873. The plaintiff, Allen M. Eastburn, brought an action against the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company for the death of certain animals that were allegedly killed by the railway on its tracks. The county court found in favor of Eastburn, resulting in a monetary judgment of $371.12. The railway company appealed this verdict to the circuit court, which led to several proceedings. During the August special term of 1873, the case was submitted for hearing but held under advisement until January 9, 1874, when the circuit judge reversed the county court's judgment and ordered a new trial. However, at the November term of 1874, a different judgment was entered by the circuit court, leading to confusion with two judgments existing simultaneously, one for the plaintiff and one for the defendant. This situation raised questions about the validity of the judgments and the jurisdiction of the circuit court regarding the rendered decisions.	The plaintiff, Allen M. Eastburn, argued that the judgment of January 9, 1874, which reversed the county court's initial verdict against the railroad, was void. He maintained that the most recent judgment entered in November 1874 was without jurisdiction and requested that the Supreme Court validate the original verdict and monetary compensation for the deceased animals.	The defendant, Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company, contended that the judgment from January 9, 1874, was valid and should be considered final since no action was taken to set it aside at the subsequent court terms. They asserted that the November 1874 judgment, which was in their favor, was appropriate and should stand as lawful. The railway company challenged the jurisdiction of the circuit court in entering the later judgment, claiming it contradicted the procedural statutes governing judgment finality.

In 1879, William T. Johnson, the tax collector, assessed a quantity of lumber owned by Thomas R. Lyon, an agent and resident of Michigan. The lumber was shipped to a lumber yard in Cook County, Illinois, on May 1, 1879, and received on May 10, 1879. The case questioned whether this lumber was subject to taxation in Cook County for the year 1879, considering the assessment was made before July of that year. According to Illinois revenue laws, personal property is subject to taxation on May 1, based on the owner's residence or place of business. However, a specific statute provides that personal property moving into Illinois between May 1 and July 1 should be listed in the town where the owner resides unless previously assessed in another state. The court found that the lumber did not fall under these general tax rules since the owner resided in Michigan and thus was not subject to the tax effective for that year.	The plaintiff, William T. Johnson, contended that the lumber should be assessed for taxation in Cook County as it was received at the lumber yard after May 1, 1879. He argued that the tax was legitimate under the state's revenue laws, which allow for the taxation of personal property within the jurisdiction of the assessor.	The defendant, Thomas R. Lyon, argued that the lumber was not subject to taxation because it was owned by a non-resident who was not assessed for that year in Michigan. Lyon maintained that the assessment of the lumber was unlawful as it did not meet the conditions outlined in the state's revenue laws, specifically those concerning the taxation of personal property moving into the state.

In April 1866, the case of James M. Wiley et al. v. James A. Southerland was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Peoria County, where Southerland sought to enjoin the collection of a judgment rendered against him on garnishee process at the behest of Wiley. Southerland claimed that although the judgment indicated it was rendered on the same day he provided an answer to the garnishee process, it was actually entered much later, thereby denying him the right to appeal. Furthermore, Southerland argued that due to the delayed entry, the magistrate had lost jurisdiction over the case. The court ultimately considered the weight of the official magistrate's records and the principle that a judgment's date should be treated as absolute truth, making it ineligible for challenge through parol evidence. The legal arguments centered around the integrity of judicial records and their implications for the rights of the parties involved.	The plaintiffs, James M. Wiley and others, claimed that the judgment awarded against Southerland was valid and should be enforceable. They argued that Southerland's allegations regarding the timing of the judgment’s entry were unfounded and attempted to dismiss the judgment improperly.	The defendant, James A. Southerland, argued that the date on which the judgment was purportedly rendered was incorrect and that the official record did not reflect the true date, preventing him from exercising his right to appeal. He contended that because of the delay in entering the judgment, the magistrate lost jurisdiction, and therefore, the judgment should not be enforceable.

In December 1842, Charles Ballance filed a legal action in the Peoria Circuit Court against Jamison Samuel and Churchill Samuel, both non-residents of Illinois. The case concerned a bill of exchange drawn and accepted by the Samuels as partners. An attachment was placed on certain real estate. During the proceedings, it was revealed that Churchill Samuel had died after the lawsuit commenced, prompting the court to allow the continuation of the case against Jamison Samuel as the surviving partner. The defendants' counsel then moved to dismiss the suit for lack of jurisdiction, arguing that the property levied was solely owned by the deceased partner. A continuance was granted without a decision. Ballance later filed an affidavit regarding the non-residence of Churchill Samuel's heirs, leading to a scire facias issued against them, which the court quashed. The motion to dismiss was then granted because no jurisdiction existed over the property owned by the deceased. The court ruled in favor of the defendants, imposing costs on the plaintiff, who appealed.	Charles Ballance claimed that the partnership's obligations under the bill of exchange should allow him to secure a judgment against Jamison Samuel as the surviving partner. He contested the court's dismissal of the suit, arguing that appropriate procedures were followed and that the attachment could be pursued despite the death of Churchill Samuel. He sought the reversal of the judgment which ruled against him.	Jamison Samuel's defense centered on the argument that the court lacked jurisdiction since the attached real estate was solely owned by the deceased Churchill Samuel. The defense maintained that the case could not proceed against Jamison Samuel without proper service of the writ of attachment concerning his individual property. They also argued that the issuance of the scire facias against Churchill Samuel's heirs was improper, resulting in the dismissal being justified.

In July 1853, Claborn Ham faced an assault and battery charge, for which a justice of the peace imposed a fine. Within five days of the judgment, Ham and a surety executed an appeal bond that the justice approved. This bond was conditioned for the payment of any judgment that could arise from the appeal or its dismissal. However, in the circuit court, the State's attorney filed a motion to dismiss the appeal, to which Ham responded with a cross motion to amend the bond. The court dismissed Ham's motion to amend and upheld the State's motion to dismiss the appeal altogether, leading to the subsequent appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The court examined the relevant statutes regarding appeals from justices and determined that an appeal process had not been correctly initiated by Ham.	Ham, as the appellant, argued that the appeal bond was valid and that he should be granted the opportunity to amend it if necessary. He sought to overturn the earlier ruling that dismissed his appeal on technical grounds, allowing him to have his case heard in the circuit court on its merits.	The People's defense, represented by State’s Attorney J. S. Bailey, contended that Ham's appeal was defective due to improper execution of the appeal process regarding the bond. They argued that existing laws did not allow for the appeal to be amended after the initial five-day window had passed, asserting that there was no proper jurisdiction for the appeal and that it should be dismissed as a result.

The case "Cothran v. Ellis" was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court and culminated in a judgment filed on December 8, 1886. The primary parties involved in the case were the plaintiff, Cothran, and the defendants, Ellis and others as indicated by the initialism "Messrs. Trumbull, Washbuene & Robbins." The legal action revolved around a promissory note valued at $10,000, which Cothran had originally made payable to Smith, McCormick & Co. The note was subsequently indorsed to the defendant parties. The case was presented after several special pleas by the plaintiff were put forth, arguing that the only valid ground for the promissory note was its consideration; specifically, that the note stemmed from a gaming transaction and losses incurred through trading differences at the Board of Trade in Chicago. This pivotal argument gave rise to a conflict of evidence during the trial. The jury ultimately found in favor of the defendants, leading to an appeal by Cothran, which asserted issues around the validity of consideration in the promissory note given the circumstances of its origin.	The plaintiff, Cothran, claimed that the $10,000 promissory note was invalid on the basis that it represented a debt related to gaming losses and trades settled on differences, which he argued are unenforceable under the law. Cothran sought to establish that the only cause of action regarding the note was its questionable consideration, thus necessitating its dismissal or a ruling in his favor that protected him from liability.	The defendants contended that the promissory note was valid and enforceable. They argued against the plaintiff's claim regarding its gaming-related origins, insisting that the note was legitimate and that the consideration was sufficiently backed by evidence. Their defense relied on the argument that the jury's verdict, which favored the defendants, was well-supported by the evidence presented during the trial. They sought affirmation of the lower court's ruling.

In the case of Franklin D. Cummings et al. v. Michael J. Davis, decided on December 4, 1885, in Illinois, a dispute arose regarding the ownership of a Landau carriage. The key individuals involved included the plaintiff, Michael J. Davis, who claimed that he maintained ownership of the carriage based on a conditional sale, and the defendants, Franklin D. Cummings and another party, who asserted that they had purchased the carriage outright from Beale & Dwelle for $1,350. The plaintiff, Davis, argued that the sale was conditional; he retained possession and control of the carriage until full payment was made. The case went to trial where conflicting testimonies were presented, with Davis claiming continued ownership despite the actions of Cummings and Marsh after a chattel mortgage was executed without his consent. Ultimately, the jury sided with Davis, upholding the argument that the sale was indeed conditional and not final.	The plaintiff, Michael J. Davis, contended that the sale of the carriage to Beale & Dwelle was conditional, meaning that he retained ownership and control until the full purchase price was paid. He argued that the carriage was still his property and that the subsequent actions of the defendants, Cummings and Marsh, who acquired a mortgage on the carriage, were invalid given they had prior notice of his claim. He sought the return of the carriage and damages for its detention, which were assessed at $425.	The defendants, Franklin D. Cummings and Marsh, argued that they had acquired ownership of the carriage via an outright purchase from Beale & Dwelle, claiming that they had paid part cash and provided a note for the remaining balance. They contended that the plaintiff's claim of a conditional sale was unfounded, and that any actions taken by Davis to regain possession were inappropriate. Their requests included a reversal of the jury's decision and a new trial, asserting various legal errors had affected the outcome.

James M. Nixon v. George W. Noble took place in June 1872 in Chicago, Illinois. The case arose when George W. Noble, the landlord, sought to regain possession of a property leased to James M. Nixon. Nixon had been granted possession of the property under a written lease that expired on June 6, 1872. On June 7, 1872, Noble issued a written demand for possession through his agent, Joel Lull, which was served to Nixon on June 12, 1872. Nixon, however, refused to surrender possession of the property. The case was initially brought before a justice of the peace and subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge John G. Rogers. The main issue in the trial revolved around the validity of the written demand and whether the agency of Lull was adequately communicated to Nixon.	The plaintiff, George W. Noble, claimed that he properly served a written demand for possession through his agent, Joel Lull, as per the terms of their lease agreement. Noble argued that the demand was valid and that Nixon, having been informed of Lull's agency and the expiration of the lease, was legally obligated to return possession of the property. Noble sought an affirmation from the court that the demand for possession was sufficient and that he was entitled to regain possession of the property.	The defendant, James M. Nixon, argued that the demand for possession was flawed because it did not include a written notice regarding Lull's agency in the proper format. Nixon contended that he had no prior knowledge of Lull acting as an agent and claimed that there was a verbal agreement for a one-year lease extension, contradicting Noble's assertion. He sought to have the complaint dismissed on the grounds that the demand was insufficient and that he had rightful possession based on the alleged verbal agreement.

In March 1872, John Baldwin, Jr. filed a bill seeking to establish a mortgage executed by A. G. Morey and wife to Daniel Sager on real estate owned by the Chicago City Railway Company. The case's origins trace back to August 1867, when George A. S. Crooker executed a trust deed to secure notes payable to T. S. Dobbins. Over time, the properties changed hands, passing through various conveyances, ultimately to Baldwin. In February 1869, Morey secured a second mortgage for $4,000 to Sager, which was assigned to Baldwin later. The legal dispute arose when the lower court concluded that the assignment was a mere pledge to secure a debt Baldwin owed Sager, rather than an absolute transfer. The court held that the Morey mortgage remained a valid lien on the premises, thus ordering Baldwin to pay Sager to satisfy this lien or face the sale of the property. Key individuals involved included John Baldwin, Jr., Winnie J. Sager, A. G. Morey, and the Chicago City Railway Company.	John Baldwin, Jr.'s primary claim was to enforce his rights to the property and contest the validity of Sager's claims over the mortgage. Baldwin argued that the assignment of the mortgage was absolute and thus should satisfy the mortgage lien. He sought an order to establish that he held an equitable title free of any encumbrances and requested the court to uphold his ownership against Sager's claims.	Winnie J. Sager's defense centered on the argument that the assignment of the mortgage to Baldwin was merely a security pledge for a debt Baldwin owed him. Sager claimed that the assignment, although formal, did not signify an absolute transfer of rights and maintained that he had a valid lien over the property, which should not be extinguished despite Baldwin's assertions to the contrary.

John C. Holliday and Hiram Reed filed a replevin action against Henrietta Burgess, the executrix of James Burgess, in Kankakee County, Illinois, in April 1864. The dispute centered around the ownership of 1,200 bushels of corn kept in a crib. Holliday and Reed claimed they purchased the corn from Augustus T. Ingham, asserting him to be the rightful owner. In contrast, the defendant, as the sheriff, contended that the corn belonged to George H. Ingham. The corn was seized under an execution against George H. Ingham, thus complicating the ownership claims. During the trial, evidence was presented regarding the origins of the corn and the alleged purchase agreement between Holliday, Reed, and Augustus T. Ingham. However, the defense argued that a mere agreement to sell the corn, without further actions, did not constitute a completed sale. The court grappled with whether the evidence sufficed to demonstrate that the ownership was effectively transferred to Holliday and Reed through the sale agreement.	The plaintiffs, Holliday and Reed, argued that they had a valid claim to the corn based on their purchase from Augustus T. Ingham, who was allegedly the owner. They contended that the title to the corn was transferred to them at the time of purchase, and therefore they were entitled to recover the property in question.	The defendant, Henrietta Burgess, claimed that the corn belonged to George H. Ingham, and any execution against him allowed for the corn's seizure. The defense maintained that the agreement between Augustus T. Ingham and the plaintiffs did not constitute a completed sale, asserting that they failed to demonstrate sufficient evidence of ownership transfer, thus requesting a verdict in their favor.

In January 1872, the case of Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Co. v. James Holloway was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident occurred in Edgar County, Illinois, when James Holloway filed a lawsuit against the Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Co. He claimed that their train, operated by the defendant’s employees, had killed his cow while it was on the railroad track. Initially, the case was tried before a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment that awarded Holloway $50 and costs. The railroad company then appealed this decision to the Circuit Court of Edgar County, where a jury once again ruled in favor of Holloway, affirming the earlier award. The railroad company sought to reverse this decision, leading to the appeal to the state’s supreme court, which would ultimately evaluate the evidence of negligence by the train's operators.	James Holloway argued that the Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Co. was negligent in operating its train, leading to the death of his cow on the tracks. He maintained that the company’s employees failed to ring the bell or sound the whistle as required, which contributed to the incident. Holloway sought damages for the loss of his cow, successfully winning the previously awarded $50 during initial trials.	The Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Co. contended that the evidence was insufficient to establish that the injuries to Holloway's cow resulted from their negligence. They appealed the jury’s findings in the lower courts, arguing against the sufficiency of the evidence presented, and requested the Illinois Supreme Court to overturn the judgments favoring Holloway.

Frank Grundies filed a case against Simon Reid and others in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a dispute over ownership of a property in Chicago involving lots 19 and 20. The conflict stemmed from a loan transaction that occurred on December 2, 1875, when the defendants, Reid, Murdock & Fischer, provided a $4,500 loan to Conrad Eickenberg, secured by a trust deed on the disputed lots. The records indicated that the title of the property was held by Conrad Eickenberg, but Grundies claimed a superior title derived from a judgment rendered against Charles Eickenberg, a name sometimes used by Conrad Eickenberg. The case hinged on whether the defendants had notice of the judgment against Charles Eickenberg, as they relied on the record which showed a clear title under Conrad. The trial revealed that the defendants had no actual knowledge of any judgments against Eickenberg and that mere suspicion or constructive notice was insufficient to affect their title. Consequently, the court evaluated whether the defendants had been negligent in not investigating potential liens on the property before approving the loan.	Frank Grundies argued that he was the rightful owner of lot 19 and sought to have the claim of title held by Reid, Murdock & Fischer declared invalid as it constituted a cloud on his title. He based his claim on a judgment against Charles Eickenberg, asserting that the defendants should have been aware of this judgment since Conrad Eickenberg was known by both names. Grundies sought to assert his ownership and invalidate the defendants’ claim to the property based on this prior judgment.	The defendants (Reid, Murdock & Fischer) contended that they were bona fide purchasers who acted in good faith. They asserted they had no knowledge or reason to suspect that Conrad Eickenberg was also known as Charles Eickenberg. The defendants argued that their attorney had thoroughly examined the property records, which did not indicate any liens or judgments against Conrad Eickenberg, and that they should not be charged with constructive notice based on mere suspicion. They maintained their ownership interests in the property were valid.

William W. Low filed a legal action against Samuel Freeman and Elijah Freeman in Marshall County, Illinois, after they failed to deliver eight hundred bushels of corn as per a contract dated June 2, 1849, which required delivery by August 1. The contract stipulated a price of twenty cents per bushel and indicated that the corn could be delivered at specified locations. When the Freemans did not fulfill the contract, Low pursued a writ of replevin on August 9, 1849, leading to the sheriff seizing two hundred and eighty-three bushels of corn—fifty from the defendants' wagons and the remainder from Elijah Freeman's farm. The case was moved to Stark County for trial, where the jury found in favor of the defendants. The court ruled that the contract did not confer ownership of the corn to Low, as it merely obligated the defendants to deliver a specific quantity within a particular timeframe without conveying title to any specific lot of corn.	Low argued that he was entitled to the corn under the terms of the contract, which he interpreted as a sale of a defined quantity of corn. He claimed that since the defendants did not deliver the corn by the agreed-upon date, he was entitled to recover the seized property through replevin.	The defendants contended that the contract did not transfer ownership of the corn to Low at the time of the agreement. They asserted that until the corn was measured and properly prepared for delivery, the title remained with them. Additionally, they filed pleas arguing that they did not wrongfully detain the corn and maintained the property rights over it.

In 1889, in Clayton County, Illinois, the case of Voorheis & Miller v. Hugh L. Bovell, Administrator, arose after a judgment of $2,000 was awarded to Hugh L. Bovell, as the administrator of the estate of Howard B. Lutes, who had managed a store owned by Voorheis & Miller for nearly six years prior to his death in March 1885. The management arrangement followed the failure of Lutes Bros., whose assets were sold to Voorheis & Miller for $1,600, including both merchandise and cash. Various testimonies emerged about the terms of Lutes's compensation which included potential profit sharing and a fixed annual salary of $450. These conflicting accounts led to disputes regarding whether Lutes was entitled to a share of the profits or just his salary. The case escalated to appeal after the defendants contested the jury's finding, arguing that the evidence only supported their claim that Lutes's compensation was tied to profit-sharing with deductions for outstanding debts.	The plaintiff, Bovell, argued that Lutes was entitled to recover compensation for his management services based on a quantum meruit claim. The plaintiff contended that Lutes’s contributions to the store deserved recognition regardless of the specific terms of their agreement, thereby justifying the judgment for the services rendered over the statutory period. The plaintiff requested that the jury's finding affirming this compensation for Lutes’s management role be upheld.	The defendants, Voorheis & Miller, contended that the evidence did not support a fee recovery under quantum meruit, asserting that Lutes was supposed to receive no more than half of the net profits and that various deductions would render any claim for excess payments unfounded. They emphasized that the jury's decision was based on unreliable testimonies regarding the arrangement and that Lutes's estate was actually indebted to them. Their defense sought to overturn the judgment in favor of the plaintiff.

The case "Chicago, Burlington & Quincy R. R. Co. v. Charles S. Bartlett et al." took place in Chicago, Illinois, with a decision rendered on July 21, 1886. The case involved Charles S. Bartlett, who was paymaster for the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company. In March 1884, a sum of $26,850 belonging to the company was stolen from a safe that Bartlett was responsible for securing. Prior to the bond in question, Bartlett had worked without a bond for about ten years, handling significant amounts of money for the company. The bond required him to faithfully perform his duties and account for all funds received. Evidence presented in court included testimonies regarding whether Bartlett had locked the safe before leaving for lunch and the standard operating procedure regarding safe access. The safe was accessible from a room that had been temporarily left unsecured. The case ultimately hinged on whether Bartlett was negligent in securing the funds and if the defendants, who were sureties on the bond, were liable.	The plaintiff, the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, claimed that Bartlett had failed to secure the company's funds and that he was liable for the stolen amount. They argued that the bond required Bartlett to ensure the safety of the funds irrespective of the circumstances and that he should be held accountable for the loss caused by theft.	The defense, representing Bartlett and his sureties, contended that the bond did not make Bartlett an insurer of the funds against theft or accidental loss. They argued that if he exercised ordinary care and was not negligent, he should not be held liable for the theft. They also maintained that customary practice allowed safes to be left with the combination set to the last number, and thus, he should not be accountable for a crime that occurred without his negligence.

On August 13, 1855, David Gibson, representing himself and other creditors of Henry King, filed a suit in Cook County Court against the heirs of Edward Eldridge and Henry King in Chicago, Illinois. The purpose was to enforce payment of claims asserted as a lien against certain lots in Chicago arising from an assignment of property by King to Edward Eldridge for the benefit of King's creditors. Over the years, various legal proceedings occurred, including dismissals of claims, extensions for proving claims, and appointments of trustees to manage property. In 1856, the case was dismissed as to several defendants, and a decree was made, allowing claims against Henry King to be proved. As the case progressed, creditors of King, including claims assigned to James H. Rees, sought to attach liens on properties in dispute. Disputes ensued over the ownership of the lots and the validity of claims, which were further complicated by bankruptcy actions. By January 13, 1868, Gibson chose not to pursue the case, transferring responsibility for prosecution to Rees and others representing claims against King. This complex legal entanglement revolved largely around the properties initially assigned by King and who had rightful claims to them.	The plaintiff, David Gibson, claimed that certain properties in Chicago were subject to liens resulting from debts owed by Henry King. Gibson sought to enforce these claims and argued that the trust established with Eldridge intended to benefit all creditors, including those making claims against King. He also sought accountability for rents and profits accrued from the property and requested the appointment of a receiver to manage the property during litigation.	The defendant, James H. Rees, contended that any claims against the real estate could not be enforced because the trust had been revoked. Rees argued that the creditors had been inactive for an extended period, which led to a presumption that they had assented to the revocation. Thus, he maintained that Gibson's claims and the claims of other creditors had become stale and unenforceable, as they did not demonstrate timely action to establish their rights over the property.

In the case of John Feister v. The People of the State of Illinois, which was decided on June 16, 1888, in Watseka, Illinois, the defendant, John Feister, was charged with the attempted burglary of a storehouse owned by George Laub, who ran a saloon. The alleged incident occurred on a Sunday morning in May, around eleven o'clock. Feister had previously visited the saloon that morning and had consumed alcohol. Witnesses testified that they saw him trying to enter through a rear window, which had been left slightly open. When confronted, Feister claimed he sought merely to obtain more whisky. During the trial at the circuit court of Iroquois County, he was found guilty and sentenced to one year in the penitentiary. He later appealed the judge's ruling, stating that the jury's verdict was unsupported by the evidence. The prosecution's case hinged on the assumption of intent to commit theft versus Feister's explanation of seeking access to liquor due to his prior visit.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that John Feister acted with intent to commit burglary by attempting to illegally enter Laub’s saloon. The prosecution argued that Feister's actions constituted an attempt to break in and steal alcohol, which warranted his conviction and subsequent penalty.	John Feister's defense centered around the argument that his actions did not constitute an attempt to commit burglary. He claimed that his reason for attempting to access the saloon was solely to obtain more whisky, as he believed there were individuals inside who had previously refused him entry. The defense emphasized that the evidence did not support the assertion of criminal intent necessary for a burglary charge.

In April 1851, Edward D. Kemp and Hiram Humphreys entered into a written agreement in Illinois regarding the sale of a parcel of land, specifically the west half of the south-west quarter of section twenty-four. The agreement stipulated that Kemp would convey the land to Humphreys within three months for the sum of $110 plus interest at a rate of 10%, with the provision that failure to comply would nullify the agreement. Before the deadline, Humphreys sought to extend the payment deadline, which Kemp verbally agreed to, but the lack of written documentation made this extension questionable under the statute of frauds. On August 6, 1851, before the expiration of the extended deadline, Humphreys attempted to pay Kemp but was refused. Despite this refusal, Humphreys took possession of the land and made improvements, leading him to file a legal bill seeking specific performance of the contract. The case was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court in 1852.	Hiram Humphreys claimed that he had a valid agreement with Kemp to purchase the land and that they had mutually agreed to extend the payment deadline. He asserted that he had attempted to fulfill the terms of the contract by offering payment within the extended time frame and requested that the court compel Kemp to execute the deed for the property in question, invoking the principle of specific performance.	Edward D. Kemp admitted to the existence of the written agreement but denied that any valid extension of time for payment had been made, arguing that such an extension would be unenforceable under the statute of frauds. Kemp contended that Humphreys' failure to pay by the original deadline voided the agreement. He maintained that the written contract clearly made time of the essence and requested the court dismiss Humphreys' claims for specific performance, emphasizing that the contract's terms excluded such a remedy.

On May 27, 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, an injunction bond dated for $500 was executed between Morgan Burns and John P. Taylor (the obligors) and George A. Follansbee along with ten other parties (the obligees). The bond's condition required the obligors to pay for damages incurred due to the wrongful issuance of an injunction. Following the dissolution of the injunction, Follansbee and the other obligees claimed they incurred legal expenses totaling $500 for counsel in defending against the injunction, which they asserted the obligors had not compensated. However, at trial, the plaintiffs represented no evidence of payments made by all obligees, despite four of them contributing a total of $73.32. The court incorrectly instructed the jury that a partial payment from the plaintiffs was sufficient for recovery, leading to a favorable jury verdict for the plaintiffs. The ruling prompted an appeal by the defendants.	The plaintiffs claimed they were entitled to damages for legal expenses incurred while defending against a wrongful injunction issued against them. They argued that they had collectively incurred costs associated with retaining counsel to achieve the dissolution of the injunction, for which they sought recovery from the obligors under the penal bond agreement.	The defendants asserted several defenses, including "non est factum" and "nil clébet," contending that the plaintiffs lacked standing as all obligees did not join the action. They argued the plaintiffs failed to show that the damages claimed were jointly suffered, since only a portion of the obligees had incurred actual legal costs. The defendants contested the instruction given to the jury which allowed recovery based on contributions from just a subset of plaintiffs.

The case "P. E. Lewis et al. v. Nancy R Flowree, Administratrix, etc." originated in the County Court of Mason County, Illinois. The proceedings began with a petition from the administratrix, Nancy R Flowree, seeking leave to sell real estate to settle the estate's debts. An order was issued for the sale on October 8, 1888. The plaintiffs, represented by attorneys I. R. Brown and B. S. Prettyman, filed an appeal against this order following the approval of an appeal bond. On October 30, 1888, the defendants, including Eliza Lewis and Samuel Flowree, among others, also filed an appeal bond, which the Circuit Court deemed sufficient. However, the administratrix subsequently moved to dismiss the plaintiffs' appeal, arguing that the bond had not been filed within the required twenty days after the decree of sale. The Circuit Court agreed, dismissing the appeal, leading the plaintiffs to assign error to this ruling.	The plaintiffs claimed that the appeal they filed was valid and should not have been dismissed. They argued that the appeal process is governed by Sec. 122, Chap. 37 of the Illinois Revised Statutes, which allows appeals to be taken from final orders of the County Courts under conditions stipulated by the court. They contended that the timing of the bond filing should not preclude their right to appeal, as the order did not specify a time limit for filing.	The defendant, Nancy R Flowree, maintained that the plaintiffs' appeal was flawed due to the late filing of the appeal bond, which did not comply with the statutory requirement of being submitted within twenty days of the decree of sale. The defendant's key argument leaned on the precedent set in Darwin v. Jones, emphasizing that the appeal was not perfected in accordance with the law and thus should be dismissed.

The case titled "St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad Company v. James Thomas et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1868. The dispute originates from an incident on May 19, 1866, in Morgan County, Illinois, where the St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad Company, a corporation operating under Illinois state law, was accused of running locomotives and railroad cars that killed livestock owned by the plaintiffs, James Thomas and others. The plaintiffs claimed that the railroad company failed to maintain adequate fencing along its tracks to prevent animals from straying onto the railway, which contributed to the incident. Following another incident when seven hogs were killed on July 17, 1866, and a subsequent event resulting in the death of additional livestock on August 20, 1866, the plaintiffs filed a lawsuit seeking damages from the railroad company. The court proceedings began after the railroad company filed a demurrer against the plaintiff's claims, which was ultimately overruled.	The plaintiffs, represented by attorneys Morrison & Epler, asserted that the railroad company was negligent in failing to build and maintain proper fencing along its railway to protect livestock. They emphasized that the incidents were not in areas that were fenced or that had agreements for fencing, implying a clear liability on the part of the railroad. They sought to recover damages for the value of the livestock killed, arguing that the railroad's negligence directly led to their financial loss.	The St. Louis, Jacksonville & Chicago Railroad Company, represented by attorneys Ketcham & Atkins, defended against the claims primarily through a demurrer. They argued that the venue for the claim was improperly laid out in the declaration and challenged the assertion that the company was responsible for fencing. They contended that the declaration failed to meet formal legal standards and sought to have the court dismiss the claims based on these procedural arguments, insisting that the plaintiffs did not appropriately prove damages or value for the livestock in question.

William J. Fagan v. Valentine Fries is a legal case that took place in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, with a judgment issued on February 13, 1889. The case centers around a slander action brought by the plaintiff, William J. Fagan, against the defendant, Valentine Fries. The dispute arose during a previous lawsuit where Fries, as a witness, made statements that Fagan argued were slanderous and damaging to his reputation. The court, however, ruled that the words spoken by Fries were made in the context of his privileged role as a witness in a legal proceeding. When Fagan presented evidence in his favor, the court excluded it upon a motion from Fries. Ultimately, the jury returned a verdict in favor of Fries, leading Fagan to appeal the ruling concerning the exclusion of his evidence.	The plaintiff, William J. Fagan, claimed that Valentine Fries made slanderous statements against him while acting as a witness in a related lawsuit. Fagan argued that these statements caused him reputational harm and sought damages for slander. He contended that the words spoken by Fries were not protected under the privilege extended to witnesses, implying that they either were irrelevant or maliciously intended.	The defendant, Valentine Fries, argued that the statements he made while testifying were protected by witness privilege, as they were relevant to the case at hand. He maintained that the remarks were necessary to explain his actions regarding the discharge of Fagan from employment. Fries contended that since the statements were made in a legal context, they could not serve as the basis for Fagan’s slander claim and requested the court to uphold the exclusion of Fagan's evidence and affirm the jury's verdict in his favor.

In 1863, Delia Hartwell entered into a verbal agreement with Jacob P. Black to purchase a house and lot in Yorkville, Kendall County, Illinois, for $3,310 with a payment plan that included quarterly interest and taxes. Hartwell took possession of the property and claimed to have made improvements worth $50. However, when she attempted to advance a payment of $230 towards the principal in 1861, Black refused. On April 20, 1868, Black sold the property to Thomas, leading Hartwell to file a suit for specific performance against Black and Thomas. The case was initially heard in Kendall Circuit Court but was moved to DuPage Circuit Court, where the trial commenced and ultimately resulted in a decree favoring Black and Thomas, dismissing Hartwell's claims.	The plaintiffs, Delia Hartwell and others, asserted that they had a valid verbal contract with Jacob P. Black for the purchase of the property, claiming they had been paying rent and had made improvements. They sought the court's intervention for specific performance of the agreement, asking for a deed to the property after substantial payments had been made.	Jacob P. Black denied the existence of a valid purchase contract, asserting that the arrangement was instead a rental agreement. He claimed that Hartwell had paid rent, not the principal or any interest, and relied on the statute of frauds to argue that the verbal agreement was unenforceable. Thomas, the subsequent property buyer, also denied any fraud in his acquisition and claimed he provided adequate consideration for the property.

This case, John Jackson, ex dem. Murray McConnell v. De La Fayette Wilcox, was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1837, originating from the Circuit Court of Cook County. The dispute arose over a claim to a part of the South-West fractional quarter of Section 10, Township 39 N., Range 14 E., on which Fort Dearborn is located. The plaintiff, Murray McConnell, claimed possession of the land through pre-emption rights purchased from Beaubien, who had occupied and improved the land since 1817. The defendant, De La Fayette Wilcox, as a military officer, was in possession of the land at the time of the suit. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Wilcox, stating that Beaubien could not assert a right against the United States in this manner. McConnell appealed this decision, seeking to demonstrate the validity of his claim.	The plaintiff argued that he had a legal title to the land based on Beaubien's pre-emption rights, which he had legally acquired through proper procedures outlined by acts of Congress. The plaintiff sought to recover possession of the premises, asserting that the prior decision by the Circuit Court was incorrect and that his claim was legitimate due to Beaubien’s documented occupation and the applicable pre-emption laws.	The defendant contended that the land was reserved for military purposes and thus was not subject to pre-emption. Wilcox argued that the acts of the Land Office granting pre-emption rights to Beaubien were void since he had no jurisdiction over land reserved for military use. Additionally, the defendant asserted that the legal title to the land remained with the United States, and consequently, an action of ejectment could not be maintained against military occupancy.

The case revolves around an incident in 1852 involving Roswell E. Goodell and Charles D. Townsend. Goodell, the plaintiff, initiated a legal action against Townsend, the sheriff of La Salle County, following a situation where a convict named Cummings was sentenced to the penitentiary after being convicted of larceny in La Salle County. The venue for the trial was changed to Kendall County, where Cummings was ultimately convicted. After sentencing, the sheriff of Kendall County transported Cummings to the penitentiary and received payment from the State amounting to $78.46 for this service. Goodell, acting as the sheriff of La Salle County, sought to recover this amount from Townsend through an action of assumpsit, arguing that the payment was owed to him. The case was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court after the Circuit Court had ruled in favor of Townsend.	Goodell's primary argument was that he, as the sheriff of La Salle County, should receive the compensation of $78.46 for the transportation of the convict to the penitentiary. He claimed that under Illinois statutes, it was his duty to ensure the safe delivery of convicts sentenced from his county and, therefore, was entitled to the payment.	Townsend’s defense rested on the assertion that the responsibility and corresponding compensation for conveying convicts to the penitentiary lay with the sheriff from the county where the conviction occurred—Kendall County, in this case. He argued that the laws cited by Goodell did not apply to his situation and that the Circuit Court correctly ruled in his favor.

Ole H. Aarvig, representing Nels Olson, brought a case against N. H. Kellogg and others, following a judgment rendered by a Justice of the Peace in favor of Olson for $75.75 on January 24, 1879. After the execution of the judgment was returned with "no property found," Olson sought to recover the amount through garnishee proceedings initiated on May 7, 1885. The case was escalated to the Circuit Court by appealing the Justice's judgment. However, the Circuit Court ruled to quash the writ and dismiss the suit, citing that the judgment was barred by Section 15 of the Statute of Limitations due to the elapsed time since the original judgment. This case proceeded against the backdrop of a legal principle set forth in the Supreme Court case of Bemis v. Stanley, which established that certain foreign judgments were barred after five years. The key legal question centered on whether the judgment held by the Justice should be classified under the five-year limit or the ten-year limit outlined in Section 16 of the Statute of Limitations.	The plaintiff claimed that the judgment originally obtained from the Justice of the Peace was valid and should not be barred under the statute of limitations, arguing that it fell under the category of "other evidences of indebtedness in writing," which carry a ten-year limitation according to Section 16. The plaintiff sought to overturn the Circuit Court's dismissal and to recover the amount owed.	The defendant asserted that the action was barred by Section 15 of the Statute of Limitations, which limits actions on judgments to five years. They moved to dismiss the case based on the ruling in Bemis v. Stanley, contending that the original judgment was too old to enforce. The defendant argued for the application of the shorter limitation period to the judgment made by the Justice of the Peace.

In 1873, in Cook County, Illinois, an action of assumpsit was brought by lumber dealers Van DeMark and Chandler against Turlington W. Harvey. The plaintiffs had purchased a cargo of lumber shipped by a vessel named "Holmes" from the defendant. They claimed that the lumber was warranted to be of quality equal to or superior to that of the "Holmes." Upon inspection, Van DeMark found the lumber unsatisfactory and requested the defendant's agent to take it back. The agent suggested that they continue unloading and sorting the lumber, assuring them that he would cover any excess charges for unsatisfactory materials. The plaintiffs sorted approximately 120,000 feet of lumber while expressing ongoing dissatisfaction. Eventually, negotiations broke down over the price per thousand feet, leading the plaintiffs to present a bill for their labor, sorting, and dockage associated with the lumber, claiming the total for damages and expenses amounted to over $2,000. The jury initially awarded them $628 in damages, prompting the defendant to appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendant breached the warranty of the lumber's quality, claiming damages for work and labor associated with sorting the lumber, dockage fees, and the loss incurred from not receiving the expected quality of lumber. Their total demand included $148.20 for labor, $690.00 for dockage, and $2,000 for damages due to the unsatisfactory lumber.	The defendant argued that the contract had been mutually rescinded and claimed they had not been required to pay for dockage, which should have been explicitly outlined in a separate count. They pointed out that the jury's awarded damages were excessive given the conditions and circumstances of the contract's rescission. The defense asserted that the plaintiffs were only entitled to compensation for the actual work performed in sorting the lumber, which was limited to a substantially lower amount than what the jury awarded.

In 1839, in Greene County, Illinois, a legal case was initiated involving Henry Merriweather as the appellant and Charles Gregory as the appellee. This case arose from an action of debt regarding a promissory note that had been assigned to Gregory before it matured. Merriweather was accused of defaulting on this debt, prompting Gregory to file suit against him. The case was heard at the August term of the Greene Circuit Court, presided over by Judge William Thomas. The trial court ruled in favor of Gregory, awarding him $466.62 and costs. Merriweather appealed the judgment, claiming procedural errors during the earlier court proceedings related to the handling of his defense against Gregory’s claims.	Gregory, the plaintiff, argued that he was legally entitled to payment on the promissory note originally issued to him by Edward D. Baker. He maintained that the assignment of the note was valid, and Merriweather was liable for the debt due to the failure to repay the assigned amount as stipulated in the promissory note.	Merriweather's defense was centered around two special pleas. He contended that the note was given in consideration of a fraudulent sale of land by Baker, who misrepresented his ownership and the title to the property. Merriweather argued that since Baker had no legal title to the land at the time of the transaction, the consideration for the note had failed, making the note unenforceable. Furthermore, he claimed that Gregory had prior knowledge of these facts when he accepted the assignment.

William Hudson (Appellant) filed a case against Charles M. Dickinson (Appellee) in Illinois, which escalated from an initial trial before a justice of the peace to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the fall of 1850 when a promissory note was assigned to Hudson, but Dickinson objected to its validity, arguing that the assignment took place after the note had matured and involved a partnership transaction. Hudson’s claim revolved around the enforcement of this assigned note, while Dickinson sought to dispute the assignment's legitimacy. The trial took place in the Circuit Court without a jury, where the judge ruled on the admissibility of the evidence regarding the assigned note, ultimately leading to an appeal by Hudson to the higher court.	The plaintiff, William Hudson, claimed that he was entitled to enforce the promissory note assigned to him by demonstrating its validity in court. He argued that the assignment was lawful and sought a ruling that would allow him to collect on the note without the complications raised by the defendant regarding its due status and the nature of the assignment.	Charles M. Dickinson, the defendant, contended that the assignment of the promissory note was invalid as it occurred after the note had matured. He argued that the partnership context surrounding the transaction and a receipt given by one of the partners undermined the assignment’s enforceability. Dickinson asserted that a proper challenge to the assignment had not been made due to the lack of the required affidavit to form an issue on this matter, thereby requesting the court to dismiss Hudson's claims.

On April 23, 1856, in Chicago, Illinois, one Trussing sold a lot of land to Luther Stone for $4,620. Stone made an initial payment of $1,200 and provided three promissory notes for the remaining balance, due in 1857, 1858, and 1859. Concurrently, Trussing had a previous agreement with Mrs. Clark for the same property, for which he had not completed the payments. In December 1857, Mrs. Clark declared a forfeiture of her contract with Trussing due to his default. After the forfeiture, with Trussing's title lost, Stone was notified that the property was back on the market, leading him to buy it directly from Mrs. Clark while settling the owed amount to her. Trussing assigned the unpaid notes from Stone to plaintiffs Lull and Mayer as collateral; however, upon their maturity, Stone refused to pay. As a result, Lull and Mayer sued for the full amount of the notes, while Stone argued that Trussing's loss of title negated his obligation to pay. The case revolved around whether the failure of consideration justified Stone's non-payment.	The plaintiffs, Lull and Mayer, argued that they were entitled to recover the full amount of the promissory notes discounted due to the assignment from Trussing and contended that their position as innocent indorsees justified their claim, irrespective of the circumstances surrounding Trussing's forfeiture of the property.	The defendant, Luther Stone, contended that he was not liable to pay the notes because Trussing had lost his title to the land, which negated any obligation due to the failure of consideration. Stone asserted that he had fulfilled his obligations under the contract with Trussing until the latter's default and that he should not be compelled to pay for a property he never received due to Trussing's negligence.

Moses Garrett was involved in a legal case against John Doe, acting on behalf of Samuel Wiggins, regarding the ownership of a tract of land in Illinois. The case stemmed from a tax sale that took place on January 17, 1829, when the Auditor of Public Accounts sold Garrett's land due to unpaid taxes. Following the tax sale, Wiggins received a deed from the Auditor, which he presented as evidence of his title during the trial. The trial took place in the Circuit Court of Franklin County in April 1834, presided over by Judge Thomas C. Browne. During the trial, Wiggins' attorney requested jury instructions asserting that the Auditor's deed was sufficient evidence of title, while Garrett's counsel challenged the legality of the sale, arguing that proper legal procedures had not been followed for notifying Garrett of the tax sale. The jury ultimately ruled against Garrett, prompting him to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Samuel Wiggins, argued that the deed he received from the Auditor was valid and demonstrated the legality and regularity of the tax sale. He contended that under the relevant law, the deed served as adequate proof of title, and therefore the jury should find in his favor. Wiggins sought to maintain ownership of the land through the confirmation of his title in court.	The defendant, Moses Garrett, contended that the tax sale and resulting deed were invalid due to a failure to comply with statutory requirements, particularly regarding proper notice of the sale. He argued that the Auditor had not followed the necessary legal procedures to administer the sale, which, according to Garrett, invalidated Wiggins' title. Therefore, Garrett requested that the court recognize his rightful ownership of the land rather than sanction the sale to Wiggins.

On April 16, 1872, in Cook County, Illinois, Charles E. Brown obtained a divorce from his wife, Mrs. Brown, who continued to occupy a portion of their shared home after the divorce. Mrs. Brown invited her sister, Helena Smith, to stay with her in the house, which Brown found bothersome. Following his unsuccessful attempt to evict them, Brown consulted with his lawyer, John Mason, and was advised to lock them out of the house. On June 1, 1872, after Brown locked the doors and boarded up the windows to prevent their entrance, Mrs. Brown and her sisters forcibly re-entered the house. This led to Brown filing a complaint against them for malicious mischief with the police, resulting in their arrest. Smith subsequently filed a lawsuit against Brown for malicious prosecution.	Helena Smith claimed that Brown wrongfully prosecuted her for malicious mischief, arguing that his actions lacked legal basis and were motivated by malice. She sought damages for the alleged harm caused by the prosecution.	Brown contended that he acted on the advice of his attorney, asserting that there was probable cause for the prosecution based on the sisters’ unlawful entry. He argued that both Mrs. Brown and Smith were intruding upon his property rights, and hence, his actions were justified. He requested the court to dismiss the claim made by Smith.

The case "The Albany City Fire Insurance Company v. Martin Keating" took place in January 1868 and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a fire insurance policy that the Albany City Fire Insurance Company had issued to Martin Keating. The company claimed that Keating had increased the risk of loss by not disclosing changes around the insured property, specifically the erection of a city pump that heightened the fire hazard. They decided to cancel the insurance policy on May 15, 1866, citing provisions in the policy that allowed them to do so if the risk was increased. Despite the company’s claims, the court had to assess whether Keating had adhered to the policy conditions and if the company's cancellation was justified. The case showcases the legal complexities surrounding insurance agreements and the obligations of both parties regarding risk disclosures.	Martin Keating, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to payment for the fire loss covered by the insurance policy. He contended that the defendant's cancellation of the policy was invalid, as it did not follow the policy's terms correctly. Keating asserted that he had not concealed any information about the property that would have increased the risk, and that the company’s attempt to terminate the policy was unfounded.	The Albany City Fire Insurance Company, the defendant, claimed that they had the right to cancel the insurance policy due to increased risk from changes near the insured property, including the addition of a city pump. They provided evidence of notifying Keating of their decision to cancel on May 15, 1866, and offered to refund a portion of the premium. They argued that Keating's failure to disclose the fact that the property was being used as a boarding house also contributed to the increased risk.

Henry C. Strong brought an action of ejectment against Abner C. Harding in the Warren Circuit Court, seeking recovery of a property described as lot five in block one of Haley’s addition to the city of Monmouth, Illinois. The case was decided in April 1866, with both parties waiving their right to a jury trial, leading to a decision by the court. Harding pleaded not guilty, but Strong presented a deed as evidence asserting his claim to the property. Harding's objections to the validity of the deed were overruled by the court, which found in favor of Strong, stating that the acknowledgment of Monmouth's location in Warren County was adequate for the deed's validity.
