The court ruled that Harding was unlawfully withholding possession from Strong and awarded a writ of possession to the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, Henry C. Strong, argued that he held title to lot five in block one of Haley’s addition in Monmouth, Illinois, claiming he was the rightful owner of the property. He presented a deed as evidence of his claim and requested the court to affirm his title and grant him possession of the property, alleging that the defendant was wrongfully withholding it.	The defendant, Abner C. Harding, contended that the deed presented by the plaintiff was inadequate because it failed to specify the state and county where the property was located. He also argued that there was no proof of his possession of the premises at the start of the lawsuit. Harding requested that the court dismiss the action due to these alleged deficiencies in the plaintiff's case.

The case "The Chicago and Iowa Railroad Company v. William Baker" took place in DeKalb County, Illinois, and was decided in September 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose when the Chicago and Iowa Railroad Company unlawfully entered Baker's land to construct a railroad without his consent. As a result, Baker filed an action of trespass against the railroad company. The initial judgment from the DeKalb circuit court was in Baker's favor, but the railroad company appealed. The legal proceedings revolved around the implications of a default judgment, which admitted the occurrence of a trespass but did not automatically grant Baker more than nominal damages. The court's focus was on the circumstances of the trespass, specifically whether the railroad Company's actions were malicious or oppressive, as the law allows for exemplary damages only if such conditions were evidenced.	William Baker, the plaintiff, argued that the Chicago and Iowa Railroad unlawfully trespassed on his property and constructed a railroad without consent, claiming actual damages for the injury to his land. Baker sought not only compensation for the damage but also requested exemplary damages, believing that the railroad's actions were willful and malicious, warranting additional penalties.	The Chicago and Iowa Railroad Company, as the defendant, contended that the default judgment only admitted the factual occurrence of trespass without acknowledging any aggravating circumstances or entitlement to exemplary damages. The company asserted that Baker failed to present evidence demonstrating that the trespass was committed with malice or oppression, thereby limiting the damages to nominal compensation only.

In 1887, in Cook County, Illinois, the Circuit Court was tasked with admitting the will of John Noble, who was deceased. The case involved an appeal concerning the validity of depositions taken from the will's subscribing witnesses. The appellant, represented by H. O. McDaid and W. S. Cox, challenged the admission of these depositions, arguing that they did not comply with the legal requirements for being properly enclosed when submitted to the court. It was noted that after the appellant's motion to suppress the depositions, they were opened in the court's presence, indicating possible procedural missteps on the appellant's part. The court noted discrepancies in evidence concerning the wrapping of the depositions and held that the appellant should have raised concerns about their enclosure prior to having them opened. The trial court’s decision was further scrutinized regarding the instructions given to the jury regarding the credibility of a witness who had previously pleaded guilty to forgery, with the court asserting that the instructions were adequately clear. Ultimately, after evaluating the entire record, the reviewing court found no errors justifying a reversal of the trial court’s decision.	The appellant (claiming to represent the interests opposing the admission of the will) argued for the suppression of depositions on grounds of improper enclosure. They contended that this alleged procedural error invalidated the depositions' admission as evidence before the court and requested that the will not be probated on this basis.	The proponents of the will countered that the envelope containing the depositions, although challenged, did not show any signs of tampering or altering and that the appellant's late motion to suppress essentially waived their right to contest the enclosure issue. Additionally, they argued that the jury was properly instructed regarding the credibility of witnesses, including one with a criminal background, emphasizing that the definitions of incompetence and credibility were appropriately clarified in court.

Ichabod Mitchell and George Mayberry, the appellants, were involved in a legal dispute with The President and Directors of the State Bank of Illinois, the appellees, which culminated in a case heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1838. The conflict originated in Hamilton County, Illinois, where the State Bank initially sued the appellants on a promissory note amounting to $86.10. This note was given in exchange for two judgments in favor of the Bank against N. Janny and one judgment against Ichabod Mitchell in the Circuit Court. Mitchell and Mayberry claimed that their liabilities stemmed from judgments based on notes linked to bills of credit issued by the State Bank, which they argued were unconstitutional under the U.S. Constitution. They attempted to present evidence in the Circuit Court to prove that these judgments were void due to the considerations that violated federal law. However, the Court rejected the admissibility of their testimony regarding the judgments, maintaining that the original judgments were valid until reversed. The case subsequently moved to the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal from the Circuit Court's decision.	The plaintiffs, The President and Directors of the State Bank of Illinois, argued that the appellants were liable for the payment of the promissory note they signed. They asserted that the judgments obtained against N. Janny and Ichabod Mitchell were valid and binding. The plaintiffs sought to enforce the payment of the amount due, emphasizing that the original considerations for the judgments could not be disputed in this action.	The defendants, Ichabod Mitchell and George Mayberry, contended that the notes leading to the judgments were void as they were based on bills of credit issued by the State Bank, which they claimed violated the Constitution of the United States. They sought to introduce evidence to challenge the validity of the judgments that fueled their financial obligations, arguing that this evidence should invalidate their liability on the promissory note.

The case "The Chicago Planing Mill Company v. The Merchants’ National Bank" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1877. The background involves a legal obligation of the Chicago Planing Mill Company to respond to a financial claim by the Merchants’ National Bank. The Superior Court of Cook County had previously ruled in favor of the bank on July 6, 1876, awarding them $4,052.66. The original service of process was an issue, with the sheriff claiming to have served the company’s secretary, William H. Jenkins, instead of its president, who was not found at that time. Later, an amendment to the return of service was made to clarify this point. The main legal question arose regarding the adequacy of the service, specifically whether the president's absence needed to be expressly stated to validate the service on another officer. Various legal precedents concerning service of summons on corporations were explored, including the requirements for service and amendments to those returns.	The plaintiff, the Chicago Planing Mill Company, argued that the service of process was insufficient because the sheriff did not expressly indicate that the company’s president was not found in the county. Thus, according to the relevant laws, service on the secretary should not be considered valid. The plaintiff sought to reverse the judgment made against them by demonstrating that proper legal procedures were not followed in serving the summons.	The defendant, the Merchants’ National Bank, contended that the amendment to the sheriff's return was appropriate and should be upheld. They maintained that the court had the authority to allow the amendment even after the judgment was rendered. The bank's counsel argued that the service of process, as amended, met the legal requirements for serving a corporation and opposed the plaintiff's claims that the service was inadequate.

In January 1873, the case of Easton Whitton v. John H. Barringer took place in Illinois before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a financial dispute involving a promissory note executed by a principal named Brown and a surety, Cundiff. Brown paid a sum of $185 to Easton Whitton, who administered Cundiff's estate, to satisfy a debt that was allowed against the estate. Whitton, however, refused to pay the amount received from Brown to the plaintiff, John H. Barringer, arguing that the money belonged to the estate and asserting that Barringer should receive only a pro-rata share due to the insolvency of the estate. Barringer subsequently pursued legal action claiming the money had been received for his use, leading to a trial where he was awarded judgment for $190.43, prompting Whitton to appeal the decision.	John H. Barringer, the plaintiff, argued that the money received from Brown rightfully belonged to him. He contended that Whitton had no lawful justification for withholding the funds after Brown paid the debt, and he sought a judgment entitling him to the full amount paid by Brown. Barringer maintained that, regardless of Whitton's claims regarding the estate's liability, the money was due to him, as the holder of the promissory note.	Easton Whitton, the defendant, asserted that he was entitled to keep the funds received from Brown, claiming that the estate was liable for the debt. He contended that since the estate had been declared insolvent, Barringer should only receive a pro-rata share of his debt rather than the full amount. Whitton's defense relied on the argument that the money was estate funds, as the amount paid by Brown was conditioned by the estate's existing obligations.

The case of Holly R. Webb v. Absolum P. Lasater was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1843. The trial began in Hamilton County, where Webb initially sued Lasater before a justice of the peace and won a judgment for $11.21 and costs. Lasater appealed the decision, leading to a retrial in the circuit court, where the jury found for Lasater and rendered a verdict in his favor for $3.12. Key individuals involved were Holly R. Webb, the plaintiff in error, and Absolum P. Lasater, the defendant in error. Webb’s surprise and dissatisfaction primarily stemmed from the defense presenting an account that Lasater failed to disclose during the first trial. Webb's objection to the court's rulings on evidence and Lasater's eligibility to provide testimony regarding his own account became central to the proceedings. The plaintiff's attempts to argue against the use of Lasater's account and the way the trial was conducted ultimately led to the appeal to the higher court.	Holly R. Webb argued that the verdict in favor of Lasater was contrary to law and evidence. He claimed surprise due to the introduction of Lasater’s account, which he had not seen before the circuit court trial. Webb believed he could prove that Lasater owed him $7.50, as admitted by the justice of the peace after the initial ruling. His legal requests included a motion for a new trial based on these objections, specifically on grounds of surprise and newly discovered evidence.	Absolum P. Lasater’s defense revolved around the legality of the evidence presented against him and the right to file a new account during the second trial. Lasater argued that he possessed the right to introduce his account despite previously not filing it in front of the justice of the peace. He contended that the trial court conducted proper procedure in allowing him to testify and provide evidence regarding his own account.

In the year 1847, the case of Michael Carroll et al. against William Craine arose in Alton, Illinois. The dispute centers on a mechanics' lien petition filed by William Craine against Michael Carroll and others for unpaid work performed on a Catholic church. Craine alleged that several contracts existed for work on the church, including carpenter work, the installation of pews, and various extra tasks totaling $2,221.26. The contracts specified payments to be made within a year of completion. Craine claimed that he had not received any payments despite finishing the work on July 14, 1845. Carroll acknowledged the first contract but disputed the existence of the second contract and claimed that all payments owed added up to $1,500, of which he had partially paid $1,055.96. Carroll argued that there had been a final accounting and settlement made between him and Craine post-completion of the work, to which Craine had agreed upon the payment of $1,500 for all work done. The case was eventually heard at the Illinois Supreme Court after a decree had previously favored Craine in a lower court.	The plaintiffs, led by Craine, claimed that under the various contracts established, he completed work for which he had not been compensated. Craine sought to enforce a mechanics' lien to recover the payment for the work totaling $2,221.26 and argued that significant additional work was done that warranted further payment beyond the amounts originally agreed. He requested the court to affirm his lien against the church to recover the outstanding sums due.	Carroll, representing the defendants, admitted the contract terms but argued that Craine had been fully compensated for the work performed as per the agreed contracts. Carroll disputed the claims regarding the additional amounts Craine sought and contended that all work was already covered under the existing payment framework, emphasizing a prior settlement that concluded the financial obligations at $1,500. He maintained that the contracts did not support Craine's claims for additional compensation, thus limiting recovery to the amounts already paid.

In June 1877, the case titled "The City of East St. Louis v. Bridget Hackett" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a legal dispute involving an action of ejectment initiated by Bridget Hackett against the city of East St. Louis. The trial took place in the Circuit Court of St. Clair County, presided over by Judge William H. Skyder. The conflict centered around a claim made by Hackett regarding land described as a strip taken from the southeasterly end of two lots within H. Valle's subdivision. During the trial, a jury found the defendant, East St. Louis, guilty of unlawfully withholding possession of the land, leading to a judgment in favor of the plaintiff. However, the evidence presented indicated that the land actually claimed by Hackett was a narrower strip than what was described in her declaration, which raised issues pertaining to the validity of the verdict.	Bridget Hackett claimed that she was the rightful owner of a strip of land that the city of East St. Louis was unlawfully withholding from her. She sought to recover possession of the premises described in her declaration, asserting her rights to the property.	The city of East St. Louis argued against the claims made by Hackett, contending that the jury's verdict could not be sustained due to the lack of evidence supporting that Hackett owned all the land described in her declaration. They pointed out that Hackett’s actual claim involved a smaller strip of land than what was presented, implying that a proper judgment should reflect the true extent of her entitlement.

Sophronia M. Daugherty filed a case against Alexander L. Monroe that was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875, concerning a dispute over financial obligations stemming from the sale of the "Rockford Register" newspaper. On September 4, 1871, Daugherty won a substantial judgment against the Rockford Register Company and subsequently entered into a contract to purchase the printing establishment for $9,000. As part of this transaction, her existing judgment was to be deducted from the purchase price, and the remaining balance was to be paid over time with interest. This contract required that payments made by Daugherty be used to settle the company's debts proportionally among creditors. Daugherty later purchased debts owed to the company and was subsequently sued by the company for a $900 note related to these debts. The court case revolves around whether Daugherty's newly purchased note could be used as a set-off against the company's claim. Monroe, holding a $1,000 note from the company, argued that Daugherty's $900 note constituted a trust fund that should benefit all creditors, leading to the lawsuit to enjoin her from using this defense in her case.	Monroe claims that the $900 note Daugherty holds should be treated as a trust fund to which all creditors are entitled. He argues that there was an equitable lien created by the agreements made which entitled him to a proportional share of any funds derived from the note. Monroe insists that Daugherty should not be allowed to set off her obligations to the company by using the notes she acquired, as they are subject to the interests of all creditors.	Daugherty contends that the $900 note cannot be classified as a trust fund and that her purchase of the outstanding notes from the company was valid. She argues that the earlier agreements did not encompass the $900 note, which was explicitly created in a subsequent contract. Daugherty maintains she acted within her rights to set off the purchased notes against her debt to the company and that Monroe and the other creditors neglected to protect their interests in not notifying the trustee of their claims.

John G. Feldes v. James P. Duncan is a legal case that took place in La Salle County, Illinois. The action of trespass was initiated by the appellee, John G. Feldes, against the appellant, James P. Duncan, concerning the tearing down and conversion of a dwelling-house that Feldes claimed as his homestead. The house was built by Feldes on land owned by the priests of the congregation of the mission and located near a coal mine. Feldes was a coal miner, and in December 1884, following the death of his wife, he temporarily moved with his children to live with his married daughter in La Salle, leaving some belongings in the house. The house was subsequently levied and sold due to a judgment against him, after which Duncan purchased it and removed a significant portion of it for his own use in late 1885. The jury ultimately concluded that Feldes had not abandoned his homestead rights, and the case revolved around whether Feldes's homestead claim was valid and if he had indeed abandoned it.	Feldes argued that he had a valid right to the property as it was his legally recognized homestead under Illinois law. He contended that he did not abandon the homestead even after temporarily moving, as he left his belongings there and intended to return. His legal request sought damages for the unlawful conversion of his property, and he was awarded $250 by the jury for the trespass committed by Duncan.	Duncan defended himself by arguing that Feldes had abandoned his homestead rights before the levy and sale occurred. He maintained that Feldes's temporary absence from the property was indicative of relinquishing his interest and that the property was no longer his homestead. Duncan requested the court to affirm the validity of his actions, arguing that any claim Feldes had to the homestead had been extinguished due to abandonment.

In 1866, in Jersey County, Illinois, David T. Bonnell (the appellant) and Joshua Neely (the appellee) were involved in a legal dispute over real estate. Neely purchased property that was subject to a mortgage executed by Philip English. Bonnell had secured a judgment against English after the mortgage was placed. Following Bonnell's judgment, an execution levied on the mortgaged premises occurred on March 4, 1864, culminating in a sale to Bonnell on May 14, 1864. However, this sale was deemed irregular and was set aside in April 1866. Subsequently, a venditioni (a type of execution) was issued, which permitted the sheriff to conduct a new sale. On June 2, 1866, Bonnell bought the property again, and the sheriff treated this bid as a redemption of his earlier purchasing rights. Nonetheless, Bonnell declined to accept the deed, instructing the sheriff to resell the property instead. In response, Neely sought a court order to stay the sheriff's proceedings, initiating the dispute surrounding the rights tied to the property and the legitimacy of Neely’s intervention in the process.	Bonnell argued that Neely, not being a party to the execution proceedings, had no standing to file for a stay of execution under the 1845 Practice Act. He maintained that the law was intended solely for parties involved in the case and should not include third parties like Neely, who sought to assert rights through summary proceedings rather than the established legal processes.	Neely's defense relied on the assertion that his right to seek a stay of proceedings was valid under the statute. His argument centered on claiming adverse rights in the property at stake, despite not being directly involved in the original execution. He contended that the irregularities in the prior proceedings justified his intervention and his motion to quash the execution.

The case of Jesse S. Hildrup et al. v. Lorenzo Brentano et al. was decided on May 29, 1885, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose in Cook County, where Lorenzo Brentano, Adolph Loeb, and Theodore C. Brentano (the plaintiffs) sued Jesse S. Hildrup and Robert A. Childs (the defendants) over an injunction bond linked to a prior equity suit. The original injunction had been issued against the plaintiffs, and the bond required the defendants to pay costs and damages if the injunction was dissolved. During the trial, the plaintiffs claimed they incurred $500 in necessary fees and expenses to secure the dissolution of the injunction, which included solicitor fees and other legal costs. The evidence indicated that fees were specifically incurred by Lorenzo Brentano for services from his law firm in this process. The jury ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $150 as damages based on the bond. However, the case highlighted issues related to the bond’s conditions and whether individual expenses could be claimed by one plaintiff against a joint bond.	The plaintiffs contended that they suffered damages amounting to $500 due to necessary legal expenses incurred while defending against the injunction. They argued that the bond conditioned the defendants to be liable for all costs incurred by the plaintiffs, including attorney fees required to dissolve the injunction. The plaintiffs sought damages for the reasonable costs they believed they were entitled to under the terms of the bond.	The defendants challenged the claims by asserting that the evidence did not support the allegations of a joint expenditure on behalf of all plaintiffs. They argued that the damages claimed were incurred solely by one plaintiff, Lorenzo Brentano, and therefore did not qualify for compensation under the bond. Furthermore, they contended that individual expenditures were not covered by the bond’s conditions, which did not extend liability to damages sustained individually by one obligee.

In November 1861, Charles Henckler appealed a case that originated from the Monroe County Court regarding a constable’s bond. The case was brought before a justice of the peace and subsequently appealed to the Monroe Circuit Court. The action centered around George Scheuermann, a constable who was responsible for collecting a claim owed to John E. Schuetze and Charles F. Eggers against Dr. Hoffman. It was alleged that Scheuermann collected the owed amount without legal process, leading to the plaintiffs suing for the amount owed, which totaled one thousand dollars plus damages. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them the amount they claimed. The defendant, Henckler, who was one of Scheuermann's sureties, contended that the court erred on multiple grounds, particularly regarding the change of plaintiffs' names and the legal obligation of a constable to collect funds without court process.	The plaintiffs, represented by the County Court of Monroe County, asserted that Scheuermann, as a constable, was liable for the amount he collected on their behalf. They argued that, despite the lack of a lawsuit initiated for collection, the constable's bond should cover the funds collected. They sought to hold Henckler, as a surety on the bond, accountable for the debt incurred due to Scheuermann's actions.	Henckler, the appellant, contended that the Circuit Court made significant errors, including permitting a change in the plaintiff's name during the trial and ruling in favor of the plaintiffs without sufficient evidence that the constable was legally obligated to collect money without a process. He argued that the statute did not require a constable to collect funds except through formal legal proceedings and that any collection outside that framework did not implicate the sureties on the bond.

In 1865, I. Marshall Freese entered into a financial agreement with John B. Ideson, the owner of a saw mill in Wisconsin. Freese provided Ideson with $10,000 to be used for manufacturing lumber, and in exchange, Ideson agreed to deliver lumber to Freese for sale in Chicago for a specified period. The contract stipulated various terms, including Freese retaining his advances from the proceeds of lumber sales and specified commissions based on the mode of sale. A second agreement in April 1866 amended the first, establishing a partnership named "Ideson & Freese" for the sale and general trade of lumber. Freese was given the option to elect between two pricing methods for the lumber, which he did, thus solidifying his role as a purchaser rather than a partner in the venture. Through this election, Freese opted for more stability by agreeing to purchase the lumber at a dollar less than market rates, thereby avoiding involvement in the associated risks of manufacturing. After Ideson's death, disputes arose regarding the agreements and the nature of their partnership, leading to Freese's claims of having a greater stake than what was documented in the contracts.	Freese argued that the contracts established a partnership including the manufacturing of lumber at Ideson's mill, which would entitle him to a share of the profits. He contended that subsequent actions and communications between the parties implied a partnership that extended to the mill operations. Freese sought a court decision recognizing this partnership and demanded a fair distribution of profits according to his interpretation of the agreements.	Ideson's estate, represented by Margaret L. Ideson, maintained that the written agreements clearly outlined the transaction terms. They argued that Freese had willingly opted to receive lumber at fixed prices, which excluded him from participating in profits or losses associated with the mill's operations. The defense requested that the court uphold the contracts as written, arguing that Freese's claims were inconsistent with the agreements' explicit terms.

Grant Newell, as the administrator of the estate of Patrick Terry, deceased, brought this case against Catherine Montgomery and others in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated from the Probate Court of Cook County, Illinois, and was heard on January 16, 1889. The dispute arose over a lot in the city of Ottawa, which was originally owned by Robert Montgomery. After his death, the lot was sold under a Circuit Court decree, with ownership eventually conveyed to Patrick Terry. Terry had paid for the lot based on a friendly agreement with Montgomery’s widow, who was never formally conveyed the title. The main issue revolved around whether Terry held the lot in trust for Montgomery's heirs, a claim that was asserted by the defendants but lacked evidential support. The Probate Court's dismissal of Newell's petition to sell the lot due to the lack of personal estate in Terry's estate prompted this appeal.	The plaintiff, Grant Newell, claimed that there was a lack of personal estate to settle the debts of the deceased Patrick Terry, and thus requested leave from the court to sell the lot to cover these debts. Newell argued that the ownership of the lot was in Terry's name and that the defendants' assertion of a trust was unfounded due to the absence of any written evidence or prior arrangements indicating such a trust.	The defendants, led by Catherine Montgomery, argued that a trust existed in their favor concerning the property, asserting that the lot was purchased under an agreement involving Terry and Montgomery. They contended that Terry was meant to hold the property for the benefit of Montgomery and her children, and thus the sale of the lot should not occur without acknowledging this trust.

The case "The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway Company v. Benjamin Melville" took place in Lake County, Illinois, and was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. It revolved around a proceeding under the eminent domain act, where the railway company sought to condemn Melville’s land for the construction of a railroad right-of-way. A jury trial concluded with the jury determining Melville’s damages to be $1,450. Additionally, the jury imposed specific obligations on the railway company to provide and maintain crossings and fencing on Melville’s property. However, the court later found that the jury had exceeded their authority by requiring the performance of these additional actions, as compensation for land takeovers must be calculated solely in monetary terms. The case was subsequently brought to the Supreme Court on appeal, seeking review of the county court's judgment.	The plaintiff, Benjamin Melville, claimed that the railroad company’s actions in condemning his land required appropriate compensation for damages. He argued that the jury's ruling, which assessed his damages at $1,450 and mandated additional constructions like crossings and fencing on his property, should be upheld as a fair resolution for the taking of his land.	The defendant, The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway Company, contended that the jury overstepped their authority by including non-monetary obligations, like maintaining crossings and cattle-guards, in addition to the financial compensation for damages. They argued that compensation in eminent domain cases must only be determined in terms of money, thus challenging the supplementary provisions included in the jury's report and seeking a reversal of the county court's judgment.

The case "James C. Cloyd v. William Trotter" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 10, 1886. The lawsuit was initiated in the circuit court of Wayne County by William Trotter against James C. Cloyd, seeking to remove a cloud from the title to a property Trotter claimed to own. The defendant, Cloyd, was a non-resident of Illinois, living in New York. Service of the legal documents was executed by delivering a copy of the bill and notice of the suit to Cloyd at his residence. The circuit court found that the service met statutory requirements and rendered a decree accordingly. The defendant contested the validity of this service, arguing it was insufficient due to the lack of a signed notice and a summons. The court's jurisdiction over Cloyd's person was also challenged, as he lived outside Illinois. The case eventually progressed to the Supreme Court after Cloyd appealed the decree, primarily regarding jurisdictional issues and the court's authority to impose costs.	The plaintiff, William Trotter, claimed ownership of a property and filed a bill in chancery to eliminate any legal ambiguity affecting his title. He requested the court to decree the removal of the cloud on his title and establish his clear ownership, contending that the service of the bill was appropriately conducted according to statutory guidelines.	The defendant, James C. Cloyd, argued that the service of process was invalid because the notice was not signed and that no summons was properly issued. Cloyd contended that the Illinois courts lacked personal jurisdiction over him as he resided outside the state and had not appeared in court or made any legal representation. He sought to have the court's decree overturned, particularly the judgment concerning costs.

In 1849, Samuel Hanna loaned Jonathan Ratekin $200 to secure a pre-emption right to a parcel of land, which was registered in Hanna's name due to Ratekin's inability to enter the land himself. The loan agreement included a 15% annual interest rate. There were various settlements made between the parties regarding the accrued interest over the years. Notably, in March 1862, Ratekin conveyed 24 acres of land to Hanna for $240, after which Hanna lent him an additional $260. Eventually, the total amount owed, including interest, was calculated to be $1,732.77. A bond was executed, requiring the repayment of $2,232.77 within a year for the reconveyance of the land. When the note matured, Ratekin, who was in Oregon at the time, had his family attempt to pay Hanna with legal tender notes. Hanna refused this payment, insisting it had to be made in gold or silver. Consequently, Hanna's agents removed Ratekin's family from the land in spring 1863. In July 1864, Ratekin filed a bill in court seeking specific performance of the contract, reaffirming his desire to pay the debt.	Ratekin argued that he was ready and willing to fulfill his obligations under the contract by paying the outstanding amount. He claimed that Hanna's refusal to accept legal tender constituted a waiver of strict performance and that he should not be charged with laches as he made an offer to pay shortly after the note's maturity. He requested the court to enforce the specific performance of the contract.	Hanna contended that due to the refusal of payment in gold or silver, he was justified in not accepting the offered legal tender. He claimed that the circumstances led to an improper tender and that the plaintiff had insufficient grounds to seek specific performance, asserting that the original contract terms had not been adequately met.

In the case of Trustees of Schools v. John Stoltz et al., which took place in Tazewell County, Illinois, the legal proceedings were initiated on November 18, 1887. The case revolves around a dispute concerning a bill of exceptions that was filed with the Illinois Appellate Court, which reviewed the earlier ruling made by the Circuit Court presided over by Judge N. M. Laws. The central issue involved the omission of evidence from the trial record, specifically a missing entry in a book of accounts maintained by the defendant, John Stoltz. This missing entry was crucial as it potentially referred to a payment of interest made in April 1866, which the plaintiffs claimed was relevant to adjudicating their case, especially concerning the Statute of Limitations. The absence of this evidence led to speculation about its content and implications for the court's judgment. Ultimately, the court acknowledged the incomplete nature of the bill of exceptions but decided against speculating on the evidence's relevance in their ruling.	The plaintiffs, Trustees of Schools, argued that the missing entry in Stoltz's book of accounts was vital for their case, as it might demonstrate a timely interest payment that would exempt their claim from being barred by the Statute of Limitations. They contended that the inclusion of this evidence was essential for supporting their claims, and without it, they could not effectively argue that their case held merit under the law.	The defendants, led by John Stoltz, countered the plaintiff's assertions by arguing that the bill of exceptions, as it stood, did not require the missing entry to substantiate their defense. They maintained that sufficient oral evidence was presented to support the court's ruling and contested the plaintiffs' claim that the omitted evidence was determinative. The defense assumed that the incomplete record presumed in favor of the prevailing court judgment.

After the death of Richard Graham, his heirs, John R. Graham and James W. Graham, contested an administrator's sale of real estate, which occurred on February 26, 1853. George Sloan, the administrator and son of John Sloan, was responsible for the sale in Clark County, Illinois. The heirs claimed that the court's decree for the sale was invalid due to improper notice, which was supposed to be published for six weeks before the sale. Although the court's decree indicated that proper notice had been published, the heirs presented evidence that the notice was defective. The case centered on whether the findings of the court could be overruled by collateral evidence regarding the notice. The court also examined the implications of the administrator purchasing the property himself and the heirs' delay in contesting the sale, particularly focusing on the rules of equity and laches. Ultimately, while some aspects of the sale were found to potentially be voidable, the legal nuances regarding notice and timing led to a complex resolution.	The plaintiffs contended that the administrator's sale was void due to insufficient notice of the sale being published, which did not comply with statutory requirements. They argued this defect invalidated the court's decree and sought to set aside the administrator’s sale of the real estate to reclaim their inheritance.	The defendant, George Sloan, contended that the administrator's sale was valid as the court had recited in its decree that due notice had been given. He argued that even if the sale was voidable, the heirs had not acted in a timely manner to contest it, thus presuming their ratification of the sale due to their delay. Sloan maintained that he held color of title through his possession of the property and payment of taxes since the sale.

On February 4, 1864, Win. F. Spellmeyer and his wife, Sarah, executed a mortgage on 120 acres of land in Livingston County, Illinois, to secure a $100 note due in two years. After Spellmeyer's death, Sarah married James Warner, who lived with her and their three minor children—John, Laura, and Caroline—on the mortgaged premises. In December 1866, Van Sant filed a foreclosure action against them. The sheriff executed the summons but failed to specify the identity of the white person, James Warner, who received copies for the infant defendants, thus creating a jurisdictional defect. Despite the defects, a guardian ad litem was appointed, and a foreclosure decree was issued on January 30, 1867. The property was sold, leading to a series of deed transfers until the case resurfaced when the sheriff sought to amend his return in August 1882, after being alerted to the service deficiencies. The circuit court denied this motion, leading James H. Gaff (the appellant) to appeal, arguing the court had the power to allow the amendment needed to affirm prior actions.	The plaintiff contended that the foreclosure proceedings were improperly executed due to the sheriff's defective service of summons concerning the infant defendants. Gaff claimed that the lack of proper identification of the person who received the summons on behalf of the minors deprived the court of personal jurisdiction. Gaff sought leave from the court to amend the sheriff’s return to include accurate information regarding the service, asserting that allowing this amendment would correct a significant error that could rectify potential injustice.	The defendants, namely the appellees, argued that the sheriff's return was not merely an irregularity but a substantive defect depriving the court of jurisdiction over the infant defendants. They contended that the delay of sixteen years to request an amendment was excessive and questioned Gaff's interest in seeking such an amendment, suggesting he was neither a party nor in privity with the foreclosure suit. The motion to dismiss the appeal was also based on procedural grounds, asserting that the sheriff lacked the standing to appeal as he was not a party directly involved in the foreclosure proceedings.

Henry Mills filed a lawsuit against William Parlin, William J. Orendorff, another William Parlin, and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company in 1883, concerning a railroad switch track constructed in the street in Canton, Illinois. Mills alleged that steam engines running over this track, which connected to the main railroad, would cause substantial damage to his property located in close proximity. The circuit court initially granted Mills' request to prevent the operation of steam engines over the track. However, after the defendants appealed, the Appellate Court reversed the decision, directing the circuit court to dismiss Mills' bill. Mills subsequently brought the case to the Illinois Supreme Court. The pivotal issue was the city of Canton’s jurisdiction over the street and the legitimacy of the defendants' permit to operate the track.	Mills argued that the operation of steam engines over the track directly adjacent to his home would render his property essentially uninhabitable and cause irreparable damage. He sought an injunction to prevent the defendants from using steam engines on the track, claiming that the injuries he suffered were a private matter deserving of intervention by the court.	The defendants contended that the city of Canton had the authority to permit the railroad track's use in the street, as it owned the street's fee. They argued that any remedy for Mills' concerns would not lie in chancery but rather in a court of law. They also claimed that since the injury he alleged was common to all property owners on the street, Mills could not individually enjoin the use of steam engines.

The case "Charles W. Rigdon v. Elbert W. Shirk" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1889. The dispute arises from an agreement made on January 21, 1886, concerning ownership of a tract of land in Illinois, for which both parties sought to clarify their rights. Charles W. Rigdon, the plaintiff, had acquired options to purchase land, which he later assigned to Elbert W. Shirk, the defendant. Shirk was to hold these options for the joint benefit of both parties and promised Rigdon a share of the profits upon the sale of the property after certain conditions. The core of the case hinges on allegations that Shirk failed to uphold his obligations as outlined in their agreements, leading to Rigdon claiming that Shirk's actions created a "cloud" on his legal title to the land. The trial court's judgment was contested, leading Shirk to seek dismissal of Rigdon’s claims based on his assertions regarding the validity of their agreements and the nature of Rigdon's interest in the property.	Rigdon's primary argument was that Shirk had created an illegitimate "cloud" on his title to the land by not adhering to the agreements they made. Rigdon claimed a rightful share of the profits derived from the property transaction and requested the court to enforce the agreements between the parties, asserting that Shirk was to hold the property in trust for both parties, thus ensuring Rigdon’s entitlement to half of any profits after Shirk recouped his initial investment plus interest.	Shirk contended that the subsequent tripartite agreement entered into with a third party, Malcolm McNeill, effectively superseded any previous agreements with Rigdon, thus negating Rigdon's claims to any interest in the property or profits. He argued that since the venture intended to establish the hotel company failed, Rigdon lost his claims and Shirk was entitled to operate independently of any such obligations toward Rigdon set forth in earlier contracts.

The case 'John P. Pynchon, use, etc. v. Albert M. Day et al.' was decided on May 15, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Superior Court of Cook County. The plaintiff, John P. Pynchon, claimed that the defendants, Albert M. Day and another, failed to return money entrusted to them as margins for the purchase and sale of stocks and bonds. Pynchon alleged that he had paid the defendants a total of approximately $19,166.99 for investing in securities, but they had only returned approximately $9,011.01, leaving a claimed balance of around $10,390.98 owed to him. Throughout the dealings, Pynchon received monthly statements from the defendants, which he did not dispute at the time. When he finally sought a settlement, he accepted a check for $2,511.01 from the defendants, which he said constituted the remaining balance owed to him, yet he still pursued legal action claiming he was owed more. Notably, the legal dispute revolved around the defendants' refusal to provide full access to books that would show their entire account of transactions during their dealings with the plaintiff, particularly regarding stocks bought and sold not only for Pynchon but also for other clients.",	Pynchon argued that the defendants mismanaged his investments and failed to return the total owed after the stock transactions. He contended that his total payments to the defendants amounted to $19,166.99 while only $9,011.01 had been returned to him, thus asserting he was owed $10,390.98. He sought the production of the defendants' financial records to substantiate his claims and alleged that these records would prove that he was due more money based on the transactions where he was not adequately compensated.",	The defendants, Day and another, contended they had fulfilled their obligations and provided the plaintiff with accurate monthly statements for all transactions. They pointed out that Pynchon accepted the check for $2,511.01 as the final settlement of his account, which indicated his satisfaction with the transactions and amounts due. They argued that the court should not compel them to produce books that included transactions with other customers which were irrelevant to Pynchon's claims, and emphasized that the records pertaining to Pynchon's dealings had already been provided appropriately.",

On April 28, 1871, in Iroquois County, Illinois, a legal proceeding began when Charles W. Smith and others (appellees) initiated a suit by attachment against John Beaumont, leading to garnishment proceedings involving Peter Dieter (appellant). Dieter had secured a chattel mortgage on Beaumont's property, claiming it was worth more than Beaumont's debt to him. An initial judgment was rendered against Dieter in a lower court, prompting his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. During the trial, a jury found in favor of Dieter, determining that Beaumont owed him $65.56 and that the value of the mortgaged property was $130. However, the lower court later overturned this verdict and ruled against Dieter, which he contested as erroneous, arguing that the court lacked the authority to contradict the jury's findings.	The appellees claimed that Dieter was liable concerning the garnishee process, asserting the validity of their attachment of Beaumont's debts to Dieter. They contended that Dieter's possession of the mortgaged property, which exceeded the debt amount, established grounds for the garnishment. Their main request was for the court to uphold the judgment originally rendered against Dieter.	Dieter contended that he was not indebted to Beaumont at the time the garnishee process was served, as he held a valid chattel mortgage on the property in question, which was valued greater than the debt. He argued that the lower court acted improperly by setting aside the jury's contrary verdict. Dieter's request was for the Illinois Supreme Court to reverse the lower court's decision and reinstate the jury's verdict in his favor.

Benjamin Poyer v. Village of Desplaines is a legal case that took place in 1886 in Desplaines, Illinois. The case originated from a prosecution by the Village of Desplaines against Benjamin Poyer for allegedly violating a village ordinance that required a license for using real estate for picnic purposes if any compensation was received by the owner or manager. Poyer owned a grove used for picnics, which he permitted various organizations, such as churches and temperance groups, to utilize without charging a direct fee. Instead, he reserved the right to sell refreshments to the parties attending the picnics as a means of compensation. The ordinance in question was passed on June 7, 1886, and after a conviction and fine imposed on Poyer, he appealed the decision. During the appeal, the court examined whether Poyer had actually received any compensation for using the grounds since the ordinance's enactment, ultimately determining that the evidence did not support a violation.	The Village of Desplaines claimed that Poyer violated the ordinance by allowing his grove to be used for picnics without obtaining the necessary license, which was required when any form of compensation was involved. They argued that Poyer's actions of reserving the right to sell refreshments constituted obtaining compensation under the ordinance, thereby necessitating a license he failed to acquire.	Poyer contended that he did not actually receive any compensation for the use of his grove after the ordinance came into effect. He maintained that while he had the right to sell refreshments, it was not proven that he had done so nor that he had charged any fees for the use of the grounds. Therefore, he argued that there was no breach of the ordinance and that the judgment against him should be overturned.

John W. Laimbeer v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. William Swineburn is a legal case that took place in 1866 during a town election in Cicero, Cook County, Illinois. John W. Laimbeer was elected as a constable for the town during the November election of that year. His opponent, William Swineburn, who had lost the election, filed a lawsuit challenging Laimbeer's eligibility for office. The lawsuit was based on the assertion that Laimbeer had not been a resident of Cicero for the required one year prior to the election, as stipulated by the first section of Article 6 of the township organization law of 1861. The case was taken to court, where a jury was convened to determine Laimbeer’s residency status. After reviewing evidence and hearing testimonies, the jury found that Laimbeer had indeed not met the residency requirement, as his actual residence in Cicero only started in March 1866, well after the threshold period required for the election.	William Swineburn argued that John W. Laimbeer was ineligible for the office of constable because he did not meet the one-year residency requirement mandated by the relevant township organization law. Swineburn sought to oust Laimbeer from office by claiming that the election was invalid due to Laimbeer’s ineligibility based on his residency status.	John W. Laimbeer, represented by Messrs. Hurd, Booth & Kreamer, contended against the claims made by Swineburn, but was unable to provide sufficient evidence to support his claim of residency for the required year prior to the election. The defense aimed to maintain Laimbeer’s position as a constable, disputing the nature and implications of the residency requirement but ultimately failing to substantiate their claims.

On February 28, 1847, the Illinois legislature passed an act to fund interest on certain State indebtedness, allowing for the issuance of certificates for the interest. This led to a legal question regarding whether bonds or certificates issued under this act would qualify for a share in the two mill tax fund established by the Illinois Constitution in 1848. The case involves The People, on the relation of the Bank of Bloomington, and Jesse K. Dubois, the Auditor of Public Accounts. After the law began allowing these bonds to draw interest starting January 1, 1857, the Bank of Bloomington presented a bond to the auditor in January 1858 and demanded payment from the treasury funds collected under the two mill tax. Dubois refused to issue the warrant for payment, claiming he lacked the authority. As a result, the matter was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court to decide whether the bonds were considered "State indebtedness" eligible for the tax fund distribution.	The Bank of Bloomington, acting on behalf of the People, argued that the bond issued under the 1847 act should entitle them to a share of the funds raised under the two mill tax for State indebtedness. They contended that since the bond began drawing interest on January 1, 1857, it should be treated as principal indebtedness and thus qualify for payment from the tax fund.	Jesse K. Dubois, the Auditor, contended that the bonds, which only recently began to draw interest, should not qualify as “State indebtedness” under the terms of the constitution. He refused to issue the warrant for payment, asserting that he did not have the authority to do so given the status of the bonds at the time they were presented.

John A. Larimer brought a case against the Board of Supervisors of McLean County in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1868. The core of the case revolves around a bounty resolution adopted by the Board on December 23, 1863, promising a payment of $150 to each volunteer from McLean County who enlisted in the U.S. Army for a duration of three years or until the war ended, specifically before January 5, 1864. Larimer, a resident of McLean County, had previously served and been honorably discharged on December 31, 1863. The day after, he re-enlisted in the same regiment, a move for which McLean County received credit towards its quota of volunteers. Larimer claimed that he was entitled to the promised bounty of $150 upon his re-enlistment. The county's agents denied his claims, offering him only $50, which he accepted under the understanding that it did not waive his claims for the additional bounty. The case highlights disputes over the terms of volunteer enlistment and the county's obligations to fulfill their bounty promises, whether or not Larimer's re-enlistment met the established criteria.	John A. Larimer argued that he was entitled to the full bounty of $150 after re-enlisting in the U.S. Army, as he had met the conditions set forth in the resolutions enacted by the McLean County Board of Supervisors. He maintained that he had not received a prior bounty from the county and that his re-enlistment was legitimate under the terms of the resolution. Furthermore, Larimer claimed an additional bounty of $50, as per another resolution, which provided payments to volunteers who had not received any bounties.	The Board of Supervisors denied Larimer's claims by arguing that his re-enlistment was not regular because he was already in service at the time of enlistment. They contended that he should have provided notice of his enlistment prior to January 5, 1864, to be qualified for the bounty. Additionally, they disputed the legitimacy of his claim to the additional $50 bounty, asserting that he had not satisfied the conditions stipulated in their resolutions regarding eligibility for prior soldiers.

The case "Henry H. Shufeldt et al. v. Charles M. Henderson" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on May 31, 1888. It originated from a lease agreement made on December 20, 1878, between The Chicago Gas Light & Coke Company (the lessor) and the appellants, Shufeldt & Company (the lessees). The lease stipulated that the premises would be rented from January 1, 1879, to April 30, 1884, for an annual rent of $2,000, payable quarterly. On January 8, 1881, the lessor assigned the lease to the plaintiff, Charles M. Henderson, who was subsequently attorned to by the lessees, Shufeldt & Company. The lawsuit arose when the plaintiff sought to recover rent for one quarter under the lease, along with interest. The defendants appealed after the plaintiff secured a judgment in their favor in the lower court. The central issue in the appeal was related to the admissibility of the lease and assignment documents, as no copies were filed with the declaration and there was a challenge regarding their execution.	The plaintiff, Charles M. Henderson, argued that he was entitled to recover rent due from Shufeldt & Company based on the lease agreement and its subsequent assignment to him. He maintained that he had provided sufficient grounds for his claim, as the lessees had attorned to him following the assignment. The plaintiff's legal request was for the court to affirm the judgment for the owed rent and interest, as the defendants did not properly challenge the execution of the lease and assignment documents.	The defendants, Shufeldt & Company, contended that there were no copies of the lease or assignment filed with the declaration, and thus, these documents should not have been admitted into evidence without proof of their execution. They argued that their appeal was valid based on this procedural issue, claiming that they were not adequately given an opportunity to contest the execution of the documents since they had not filed an affidavit denying their authenticity.

On November 25, 1881, in Marion County, Illinois, Fales’ Sons & Co. obtained a judgment against William Lee & Sons for $177.85. Subsequently, on December 14, 1881, William Lee & Sons, facing financial difficulties, voluntarily assigned their stock in trade to Meigs R. Myer, the appellant. This assignment was properly signed, acknowledged, and delivered to Myer, who filed it for record in the county clerk's office on December 16, 1881. On the same day, before the assignment was recorded, Fales’ Sons & Co. obtained an execution against William Lee & Sons and ordered a constable to seize their property. The constable discovered the business was locked and learned about the assignment. The following day, the constable demanded enough goods from Myer to satisfy the execution, but he refused, claiming the goods belonged to him as the assignee. Subsequently, Fales’ Sons & Co. filed a petition in the county court, seeking to establish their claim as a prior lien and to have Myer pay the amount due from the sale of the assigned stock. The circuit court ruled in favor of Fales’ Sons & Co., prompting Myer to appeal the decision.	Fales’ Sons & Co. claimed that the assignment made by William Lee & Sons did not take effect until it was recorded. They asserted that since their execution was obtained after the assignment but before it was filed for record, they held a prior lien on the goods, which entitled them to payment from the proceeds of the assigned property.	Myer argued that the assignment took effect immediately upon its delivery, which occurred prior to the execution being issued. He claimed that the law did not require the assignment to be recorded before its effect, and therefore, no lien attached against the property due to the execution issued after the assignment was executed. Myer contended that the recording of the assignment was the responsibility of the assignee and did not affect the validity of his claim to the property.

In 1885, the legal case "City of Elgin v. Melissa Welch" was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court concerning the flooding of Welch's property, located at the intersection of Gifford Street and Division Street in Elgin, Illinois. The plaintiff, Melissa Welch, claimed her property was damaged due to improper grading of Gifford Street and the construction of sewers, sidewalks, and ditches by the city. Welch's premises were positioned lower than the surrounding land, making them a natural basin for drainage from adjacent properties. After extensive development of the streets and nearby lots, significant flooding occurred, particularly after a series of heavy rains in 1882. Welch inherited the property from her husband, E. H. Welch, who had previously notified the city's street commissioner about the poor drainage and its impact on their property. The case focused on whether the city was liable for damages caused by the flooding, stemming from both the street work completed prior to Welch's ownership and actions taken after she purchased the property. The lower court initially awarded Welch $250, reducing from an original $400 after remittance.	Melissa Welch argued that the city's actions—specifically the improper grading and construction of sidewalks—caused substantial flooding on her property. She claimed the city was liable for these damages because the flooding was exacerbated by the changes made to the street and adjacent properties. Welch sought compensation for the damages inflicted upon her premises and maintained that the flooding was a direct result of municipal negligence regarding drainage.	The City of Elgin contended that they were not liable for the damages as the issues arose from natural drainage conditions, which predated Welch's ownership of the property. They asserted that any damage from natural water accumulation was the responsibility of the previous property owner. The city argued that because the work leading to water accumulation was completed before Welch purchased the lot, she could not seek damages for that flooding. Furthermore, they claimed that the increases in flooding were primarily due to surface water that naturally flowed to her property, independent of their actions.

Mary A. Herdman filed a case against Charles T. Pace in June 1877 in Mt. Vernon, Illinois, concerning a mortgage she executed on January 2, 1871. The mortgage was taken out to secure four promissory notes totaling $2,910, made solely by Herdman without her husband William H. Herdman's involvement or acknowledgment. At the time of the mortgage's execution, state law required that her husband join in the mortgage for it to be valid. The Illinois Supreme Court noted that the acknowledgment of the mortgage was not in the required form and thus declared it void, referencing previous court decisions. The lower court had ordered the sale of part of the property to satisfy claims for purchase money, but it was determined that the decree was not supported by the allegations in the bill, which only sought to foreclose the void mortgage.	The plaintiff, Mary A. Herdman, claimed that the mortgage she executed was valid and sought a decree for foreclosure of the mortgage to recover amounts due on the promissory notes. She argued that part of the property should be sold to satisfy her claims, despite her mortgage being executed without her husband's involvement as required by law.	The defendant, Charles T. Pace, contended that the mortgage was void due to the absence of necessary endorsements and acknowledgments from the plaintiff's husband, William H. Herdman. He argued that there was no legal basis for the court to grant the plaintiff relief for the purchase money because the bill was only framed to foreclose a mortgage, which was itself invalid.

Peter Weist was involved in a legal case against The People of the State of Illinois, with the proceedings taking place in Madison County, Illinois, around January 1866. The prosecution was initiated before a justice of the peace in response to Weist allegedly selling spirituous or malt liquors within one mile of Shurtliff College in Upper Alton, a violation of Illinois law. The complaint was made by three members of the college's board of trustees, who believed that Weist had engaged in this illegal activity on or around July 2, 1865. Initially found guilty, Weist was fined $25 in one charge and $75 in another. He appealed to the Circuit Court, where he sought to amend his appeal bond. However, the court dismissed his appeal and did not allow the amendment. This decision led Weist to seek a reversal from the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that his right to amend his bond was unlawfully denied.	Peter Weist contended that the Circuit Court erred by dismissing his appeal and refusing to allow an amendment to his appeal bond. He argued that under the statute enacted on February 9, 1853, he had the right to amend any informality in the bond and that his appeal should have been heard on the merits of the case. He sought a reversal of the dismissal and a new trial.	The defense, represented by the State’s Attorney, emphasized the procedural correctness of the court’s decision to dismiss the appeal due to the alleged insufficiency of the appeal bond. The state maintained that the dismissal adhered to legal protocol and that the amendment of the bond was not warranted under the circumstances.

In 1887, a legal dispute arose in Rock Island County, Illinois, involving the city of Moline and the assessment of a toll bridge for taxation. The bridge, located a mile and a half south of Moline, categorized as owned by the city, facilitated transport across the Rock River, connecting the township of South Moline with the city. Moline collected tolls for its use, and after the local assessor included the bridge in the township's tax rolls for the year, the city sought to have this assessment abated, arguing that the bridge was not subject to taxation due to its ownership. The county board rejected the city's petition, prompting the city's appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The core legal question centered on whether property owned by municipal corporations, specifically a toll bridge situated outside city limits, was eligible for tax exemption under Illinois law and the constitutional provisions in place at that time.	The plaintiff, represented by the Auditor of Public Accounts, argued for the confirmation of the county board's decision that assessed the bridge for taxation. The plaintiff maintained that there was no law exempting the toll bridge from taxation and asserted that municipal property typically requires clear legislative exemption to be free from such obligations. The claim emphasized that property owned by a municipality is generally subject to taxation in the absence of explicit exemptions stipulated by law.	The defendant, the city of Moline, argued against the assessment of the bridge for tax purposes, claiming that municipal property should not be taxed unless a clear legal framework exists to justify such taxation. The city maintained that the toll bridge, as property utilized for municipal purposes, was exempt under existing laws. They sought the abatement of the tax assessment, contending that the property’s use and ownership fell under the categories which should be exempt from taxation.

The case, "Johnson v. Johnson," was heard in 1863 by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a legal proceeding in the Circuit Court of Shelby County, Illinois. The complainants, Melinda Johnson and others, were the children and sole heirs of Francis Johnson, who died intestate, owning certain real estate. Following his death, letters of administration were taken out, and after the administrator's death, John Middlesworth was appointed as administrator de bonis non. In January 1847, Middlesworth filed a bill seeking the sale of the real estate to pay the debts of the estate, naming the complainants as defendants along with other deceased parties. The summons for this case was executed, but the plaintiffs were minors with no proper representation initially. The court ordered the sale of the property without sufficient evidence or proper jurisdictional compliance, leading to the property being sold for a minimal sum and subsequently confirmed by the court in October. The plaintiffs claimed the court lacked jurisdiction because proper notice was not served as required by law; thus, they sought to impeach the previous decree.	The plaintiffs argued that the original decree ordering the sale of their deceased father's property was void because the court lacked jurisdiction over them and the subject matter. They asserted that no proper notice was provided as mandated by law, and the decree was obtained without supporting evidence. The plaintiffs sought to reverse the prior decree, remove the cloud on their title, and contest the legitimacy of the administrator's actions.	The defendants, while admitting that Francis Johnson died intestate and that John Middlesworth filed a bill for the sale of the property, contended that the plaintiffs were properly brought into court via the summons. They argued that although there were procedural failings, the court had jurisdiction because the plaintiffs received notice through summons. They denied any irregularities in the proceedings and claimed that Middlesworth's predecessor had followed statutory requirements, advocating for the dismissal of the plaintiffs' bill.

The case "The Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Company v. Cyrus W. Steele" took place in 1873 in the circuit court of Henderson County, Illinois. The involvement of key individuals includes Cyrus W. Steele, the plaintiff who brought the action of debt against the Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Company, the defendant. The central issue arose from a special contract alleged to be under seal between the two parties, along with the common counts added. The trial included a jury verdict, which ultimately favored Steele, resulting in a judgment for damages amounting to four hundred dollars. During the trial, the plaintiff focused on the common counts rather than the sealed contract, while the defense presented arguments regarding the validity of the contract and the performance by the plaintiff. The courtroom proceedings and subsequent judgment raised questions about the appropriate legal categorization of the outcome, particularly regarding the terminology used for the judgment of damages in an action traditionally characterized as one of debt.	Cyrus W. Steele, the plaintiff, claimed damages under the common counts in reference to a breach of contract involving the railroad company. He sought to recover financial compensation amounting to four hundred dollars, demonstrating that the company was liable for the contract and performance of duties relating to their agreement. The plaintiff did not pursue the claim based solely on the sealed contract but rather on the common counts, asserting that he was deserving of the damages due to the supposed failures on part of the railroad company.	The Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Company, the defendant, argued primarily on the grounds of "non est factum," which questions the validity of the alleged contract, and asserted that there was a failure of performance by Steele. The defense contended that there wasn't sufficient proof to hold the railroad accountable under the contract or for the cross-ties in question. Additionally, they highlighted an error concerning the judgment's phrasing in the context of debt, asserting it was inappropriate to render a judgment for damages in what should be classified as an action of debt, although they acknowledged this irregularity did not merit reversal.

In 1868, in Cook County, Illinois, Dennis McCarthy and William Mooney were involved in a legal case concerning a dispute over work and labor. Mooney, the plaintiff, filed suit against McCarthy, claiming he was owed payment for services rendered. The case had previously been tried in the Illinois Supreme Court, where the court had found the evidence insufficient and remanded it for a second trial. The retrial saw both parties testify under the new statutory requirements, and the jury ultimately found in favor of Mooney, awarding him $210. Following this verdict, McCarthy, the defendant, appealed the decision, disputing the validity of the jury's finding by arguing that the verdict was not supported by the evidence.	The plaintiff, William Mooney, asserted that he had completed work for Dennis McCarthy and was entitled to payment for his labor. He sought a judgment reflecting the compensation owed to him, which a jury initially affirmed by awarding him $210 after reviewing the evidence presented during the trial.	Dennis McCarthy, the defendant, contested the jury's award, claiming that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence. He argued that the evidence did not sufficiently support the jury's finding in favor of the plaintiff and requested the court to reverse the judgment, contending that the verdict was unjust.

The case titled "The Lafayette, Bloomington & Mississippi Railroad Company v. Charles M. Winslow et al." arose in September 1872, involving the condemnation of land in Bloomington, Illinois, for use by a railroad company. The city was a critical location, with the land situated near Main Street, which was the main thoroughfare of the city, connecting to various business establishments. The railroad company, chartered in 1867, sought to claim this land under the legislation from 1852 to establish their roadway. The proceedings led to the destruction of several buildings on the property owned by Winslow and others, who contended that the compensation offered was insufficient. After lengthy deliberations and testimony regarding the valuation of the property, a jury awarded the plaintiffs $12,000. The railroad company appealed, claiming that the damages awarded were excessive and arguing that they had only acquired an easement in the land, thus the valuation should reflect that.	The plaintiffs, Charles M. Winslow et al., argued that the Lafayette, Bloomington & Mississippi Railroad Company improperly acquired their property without just compensation, as mandated by the state constitution. They contended that the destruction of their buildings for the railroad’s use warranted a fair assessment of damages based on the actual value of the property lost. They requested the jury's assessment to consider the complete destruction of the buildings and the consequent loss suffered.	The defendants, the railroad company, argued that the jury had assessed excessively high damages for the property taken. Their key argument was that the law allowed them to take only an easement in the condemned land, and therefore, its valuation should only reflect that. They also raised concerns that improper evidence, detailing their violent entry into the property, had influenced the jury’s decision, potentially leading to unjust compensation in the form of vindictive damages rather than just compensation for property taken.

The case, "James Brown and Margaret Brown v. Miner, Frost & Hubbard," was decided on May 21, 1886, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute originated from a foreclosure bill filed by Miner, Frost & Hubbard, a banking firm, against James Brown and others, concerning a mortgage taken out on April 6, 1883, for $13,500, due in five years with an annual interest of seven percent. The plaintiffs alleged that the Browns had defaulted on the interest payment due on April 6, 1884, and had also failed to pay taxes on the mortgaged property for the year 1883. Margaret Brown claimed that her husband, James, was non compos mentis at the time of the mortgage execution and sought the appointment of a guardian ad litem for him. The court appointed a guardian, and during the proceedings, it was revealed that there were disagreements regarding the funds owed and the legitimacy of the mortgage due to James' mental state. The court eventually found that the taxes and amounts owed were valid claims, leading to a decree for foreclosure if payments were not made.	The plaintiffs, Miner, Frost & Hubbard, claimed that the Browns defaulted on the mortgage agreement by failing to pay interest and property taxes. They requested a decree for foreclosure on the mortgaged property unless the Browns paid the total amount due, which included the unpaid principal, interest, and any additional expenses incurred for tax payments and legal fees.	The defendants, primarily James and Margaret Brown, contended that James was mentally incapacitated at the time of executing the mortgage, and they argued that the consideration for the mortgage largely stemmed from debts owed by a partnership that included James. Margaret Brown also alleged that an agreement existed where funds for settling the debt were misappropriated without their knowledge. They sought dismissal based on the argument that the mortgage should not be enforceable due to James's alleged mental incompetence.

John B. Bowman et al. v. Louisiana St. John is a legal case that took place in January 1867, in St. Clair County, Illinois. The case arose from an action of trespass, assault, and battery brought by Louisiana St. John against John B. Bowman and Timothy Canty. The conflict revolved around Canty, as the city marshal, arresting St. John for allegedly obstructing a street in violation of a city ordinance. The ordinance defined the obstruction of streets as a misdemeanor but did not specify any penalties or grant jurisdiction to the city judge for imposing fines or issuing processes. The key individuals involved were Louisiana St. John, the plaintiff; John B. Bowman and Timothy Canty, the defendants; and the city judge who authorized the warrant for St. John's arrest. The case was presented at the St. Clair Circuit Court during the October Term of 1866, where the defendants’ justification plea was challenged.	The plaintiff, Louisiana St. John, argued that the defendants engaged in unlawful actions by arresting her based on a city ordinance that did not provide clear jurisdiction or penalties for obstructing the streets. St. John claimed damages for trespass, assault, and battery resulting from the arrest, asserting that the defendants had no legal grounds to justify their actions.	The defendants, represented by Bowman and Canty, contended that they acted under the authority of a city ordinance when arresting St. John for obstructing a street. They maintained that Canty, as city marshal, had the right to detain the plaintiff in accordance with the municipal regulation. However, their legal plea was challenged, as it lacked the necessary elements to establish a legal basis for the arrest due to the ordinance's vague nature.

In the legal case of Weir & Creig v. William M. Dustin, which took place in 1886 in Lincoln, Illinois, William M. Dustin formed a partnership with Charles A. Nicholson and his son, William L. Dustin, to operate a banking business under the name William M. Dustin & Company. After the banking firm failed in October 1886, Dustin assigned assets to Aaron B. Nicholson for the benefit of the bank's depositors. The plaintiffs, Weir & Creig, filed a suit in attachment, claiming that Dustin's transfer of property to Nicholson violated attachment laws due to its fraudulent nature. The case addressed the legality of this transfer and whether it constituted fraud against creditors. The plaintiffs maintained that the transfer intentionally preferred certain creditors, while the defendant argued that the conveyance was legitimate and executed in good faith to secure specific creditors, namely the bank depositors. The court assessed whether there was evidence of fraudulent intent in the deed's execution and ruled in favor of the defendant.	The plaintiffs' main argument centered around the allegation that the conveyance of real estate by William M. Dustin to Aaron B. Nicholson was fraudulent.
