Tuterwiler's main argument hinged on the assertion that the railroad's negligence resulted in the loss of his cattle, thereby warranting compensation for damages resulting from their death.	The Terre Haute & Indianapolis Railroad Company, as the defendant, contended that they were not negligent in the incident that led to the death of the steers. They argued that the cattle were running out on public commons and that the presence of the cattle on the track was an unavoidable circumstance. Further, the defendant highlighted evidence suggesting that their train engine rang the bell and sounded the whistle well in advance of the crossing and that the accident could not have been prevented even with this protocol. They requested the court to reverse the judgment against them based on a lack of evidence proving their negligence.

In the case of **James H. Woodburn et al. v. Thomas A. Gifford**, which was decided in September 1872, the dispute arose in Whiteside County, Illinois. The key individuals involved include James H. Woodburn, Susan Woodburn (his wife), and George W. Woodburn. The situation began when James H. Woodburn entered into a contract with Thomas A. Gifford for the construction of a building on a tract of land jointly owned by the Woodburns. The land in question comprised several tracts: the west half of the southeast quarter of section 20 and the west half of the northeast fractional quarter of section 29. It was alleged that these tracts were fenced together and used jointly, and thus, a mechanic’s lien should be placed on the entire area due to the construction. The defendants, however, argued that the tracts were practically divided and that the building was only on a portion of the land exclusively possessed by them. The court previously ruled, finding in favor of the plaintiff, and ordering that the properties be sold to satisfy the debt owed for the construction, despite the plaintiff's failure to connect George W. Woodburn to the contract, raising issues for the validity of the lien on the entire property.	The plaintiff, Thomas A. Gifford, argued that he was entitled to a mechanic’s lien on the entire tract of land, as the contract for the building was made with James H. Woodburn and Susan Woodburn. His claims suggested that separation of the land would result in detriment and requested that the court enforce the lien on the undivided half of the joint property to secure repayment of $666.84 owed for the work done.	The defendants (James H. and Susan Woodburn) contended that the tracts of land were used separately and that James H. Woodburn was the sole person contracted for the construction, denying any connection to George W. Woodburn regarding the contract. They argued that the court should limit the mechanic’s lien specifically to the land where the building was erected, which was 22.5 acres, and objected to the sale of the entire properties.

The case "Roseville Union Bank v. Frank P. Gilbert and John A. Gordon" took place in Roseville, Illinois, with the final judgment rendered on May 27, 1887. The dispute arose from a promissory note for $250, primarily made by Frank P. Gilbert, with John A. Gordon serving as surety. Gilbert sought an extension of the note, which had become due on May 15, 1876. He approached the bank's cashier, Seth F. Pratt, requesting an additional thirty days to pay the note in exchange for upfront interest. Gilbert did not inform Gordon about this extension, asserting he wanted to avoid troubling him. Gordon later contended he was unaware of any such extension and claimed he would not be held liable. The case hinged on whether Gilbert’s extension constituted an agreement that would legally discharge Gordon from his obligations. The jury found in favor of Gordon, citing discrepancies in the testimony regarding whether the cashier agreed to extend the note and whether the interest payment was valid. A significant point of contention involved the erasure of an indorsement related to the interest payment and the failure of the bank to produce relevant financial records.	The Roseville Union Bank (plaintiff) asserted that Gilbert had validly extended the payment due date of the promissory note and that Gordon, as surety, remained liable for the debt despite the bank's cashier’s actions. The bank contended that Gilbert's request and the associated interest payment constituted a binding agreement without needing Gordon's consent.	Gordon (defendant) defended against the claims by arguing that no valid extension agreement existed between Gilbert and the bank's cashier without his knowledge. He claimed the extension and the payment of interest were unenforceable, thereby releasing him from any liability on the note. The defendant highlighted discrepancies in the bank's evidence and the cashier's inability to produce essential financial records that could validate the claims.

In 1880, in Coles County, Illinois, several mortgagees, all residing in Ohio, engaged John Reese to oversee the foreclosure of mortgages on certain lands. The mortgages were executed by Perley K. Scott and not paid, leading to Reese working with attorney John Favorite to foreclose on them. After Reese bid on the property during a foreclosure sale, he had a verbal agreement with Favorite to find a purchaser for the property. However, Wallace later purchased one claimant's interest and completed several payments to redeem the property from the sale, assuming they were fulfilling an agreement with Favorite. Reese, who had accepted a fee for acting as the agent, later acquired the certificate of purchase but failed to transfer it to Wallace, compelling Wallace to seek an injunction against Reese's attempts to force the master in chancery to issue a deed to him instead. The case arose from Reese's dual role as an agent for the mortgagees and a personal claimant to the property.	Wallace, the plaintiff, argued that he rightfully purchased the claim against the property and that Reese, despite being paid to act as an agent for the mortgagees, was wrongfully attempting to retain the property for personal gain. Wallace requested the court enforce the transfer of the certificate of purchase to him, asserting that Reese held it in a trust capacity on behalf of all mortgagees.	Reese contended that he acted within his rights as he raised objections to the court's jurisdiction and cited the Statute of Frauds as a defense, claiming that the trust arrangement had not been formally executed. He maintained that he should not be mandated to transfer the certificate of purchase based on communications with Favorite and the failure of Wallace to secure his interest promptly.

In April 1867, in Stephenson County, Illinois, a legal case arose involving Alfred Poppen and Israel B. Holmes. Poppen was the defendant in an action of replevin brought by Holmes to recover a horse that Holmes claimed to be his property. The horse had been impounded by the pound-master of Bidott, a town with regulations prohibiting animals from running at large. The pound-master sold the horse without any prior judicial proceedings to determine whether any laws had been violated. The town's by-laws allowed for the impounding and eventual sale of such animals but mandated that a judicial inquiry must occur to establish if any penalties were indeed incurred. The case was appealed following a trial without a jury that ruled in favor of Holmes.	Holmes claimed rightful ownership of the horse and sought its return through the legal action of replevin. He argued that the sale conducted by the pound-master was invalid since it lacked a necessary judicial determination that a law had been violated, undermining the claim of title that was conditional upon a lawful process.	Alfred Poppen contended that the pound-master was authorized to sell the horse according to the town's by-laws, arguing that the sale was conducted following the rules set out for impounding animals. He maintained that the sale was justified to recover fines and associated costs due to the horse having been running at large, despite the lack of judicial oversight to affirm that a penalty had been incurred.

The legal case of William Harris v. William F. Whitmore occurred in LaSalle County, Illinois, and concluded in September 1872. The case arose from a dispute involving a financial agreement between the plaintiff, William Harris, and the defendant, William F. Whitmore. Harris sought to enforce a promissory note and an award made by arbitrators for payment related to that note. During the trial, which was conducted without a jury, Harris presented evidence of both the award and the promissory note. However, the court, presided over by Judge Charles H. Gilman, ultimately ruled in favor of the defendant, leading to an appeal based on the admissibility of the promissory note as evidence, given the claims regarding the uncertainty of the award.	The plaintiff, William Harris, argued that the court should recognize both the promissory note and the associated award made by arbitrators as valid claims for payment. He contended that even if the award was deemed void for uncertainty, the promissory note itself was still admissible as evidence and should be considered separately in the court’s judgment.	The defendant, William F. Whitmore, contended that the award was unacceptable due to its lack of clarity and therefore should not support Harris's claims. Whitmore’s legal counsel argued that since the award was void, it undermined Harris's case, suggesting that there was no sufficient reason for the court to accept the promissory note as evidence.

The case "George Metz et al. v. Jacob Albrecht" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1869. The legal action took place in Cook County, Illinois, involving plaintiffs George Metz and Edward Stege, who brought a suit against Jacob Albrecht. The core issue stemmed from an alleged breach of contract regarding the delivery of barley. Metz and Stege claimed that Albrecht failed to deliver 10,000 bushels of barley as agreed in their contract dated August 25, 1867, where Albrecht promised to deliver the barley at a rate of 1,000 bushels per week for ten weeks at the price of one dollar per bushel. Albrecht's defense hinged on the claim that the plaintiffs were to pay for the barley upon delivery. The dispute arose over the terms of the contract, primarily whether it required payment before or after each installment was delivered. The defendant had previously delivered barley to the plaintiffs but claimed that they were owed $871.90 for the barley delivered under the contract, which the plaintiffs allegedly refused to pay. The court focused on the interpretation of the contract regarding payment terms and the readiness of the plaintiffs to pay for the goods.	The plaintiffs, Metz and Stege, argued that Albrecht breached their contract by failing to deliver the agreed-upon barley. They contended that they had always been ready and willing to accept the barley and pay for it at the agreed price. The primary legal request from the plaintiffs was for damages totaling $4,000 due to the loss of potential profits from the non-delivery of the barley.	The defendant, Jacob Albrecht, contended that the contract indicated a cash-on-delivery arrangement and argued that the plaintiffs were in arrears regarding previous barley deliveries. Albrecht asserted that he was prepared to deliver additional barley at the time the suit was filed, but the plaintiffs refused to pay. He maintained that the plaintiffs had not fulfilled their obligations under the contract, which led to his non-delivery.

In December 1867, in Chicago, Honora Sweeney filed a lawsuit against the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company after the death of her husband, Michael Sweeney, a track repairer employed by another railroad company. The accident occurred at a highly trafficked location known as the "Galena Y," where multiple railroad tracks converged and trains frequently moved. Sweeney was familiar with the dangers of the area, having worked near it for years. On the day of the incident, he stepped onto the railroad track without looking and was struck by a train while it was backing onto the Fort Wayne railroad track. Witnesses indicated that Sweeney displayed reckless behavior, notably failing to use caution and not heeding an approaching train or a warning shout from the switchman, resulting in his death.	The plaintiff, Honora Sweeney, claimed that the railway company was negligent in ensuring safety at the railroad intersection, which led to her husband's death. She argued that the railway failed to take necessary precautions to avert such accidents, requesting damages for the loss of her husband due to the alleged negligence of the railway.	The defendant, Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company, argued that the deceased had acted negligently by failing to look for oncoming trains, despite his familiarity with the area. They contended that the train was moving slowly and that the usual signals and safety measures were in place, including a switchman monitoring the tracks. The company maintained that any negligence on their part was minimal compared to the gross negligence exhibited by Sweeney.

In the case of Elizabeth Campbell v. Amy Harmon et al., which took place in January 1867 before the Illinois Supreme Court, the central issue originated from a decree issued by the Circuit Court of Adams County in 1851. Elizabeth Campbell, a minor, was represented by her guardian who sought permission to sell certain real estate for her support and education. The guardian was Amy Harmon, who had been appointed by the probate court. The court had documented that Harmon had filed the necessary bond. The legal proceedings brought forth several questions, including whether Harmon had properly qualified as a guardian, if sufficient notice for the sale was provided, and if the court's decree was based on adequate evidence. A master reported that key facts substantiating the sale need were proven, such as Campbell not possessing personal property or a significant income. The case also addressed whether or not the guardian's actions needed to specifically report evidence and if all parties, including minors, needed to be included in the proceedings. The court aimed for a resolution that protected the established titles acquired through judicial sales, especially given the rapid increase in real estate value at that time.	Elizabeth Campbell, through her guardian, claimed that the decree allowing the sale of her real estate was improper due to various alleged errors, including the lack of proper qualification of the guardian, insufficient notice of the sale, and potential inadequacies in the evidence supporting the sale's necessity. The plaintiff requested that the court reverse the previous decree to protect her rights as a minor and ensure that her interests were adequately represented.	The defendants, led by Amy Harmon, contended that the legal requirements for a guardian's qualifications were met, as documented by the probate court's order and the filing of the bond. They argued that proper notice was provided legally and that challenges to the sufficiency of evidence were unwarranted, as the master had confirmed that the necessary facts for the sale had been proven. The defendants maintained that the guardian had discretion in managing the sale process, which aligned with legal standards, and urged the court to uphold the sale to safeguard the child’s welfare.

The case "Harvey Otter v. John S. Williams" took place in January 1859 in Illinois. Harvey Otter, the appellant, had entered into an agreement with John S. Williams, the appellee, on November 11, 1857. Under this agreement, Williams delivered fifty head of work oxen to Otter, who was to feed them until a specified date in April 1858, in exchange for a fee based on the increased weight of the cattle. In early January 1858, Otter paid Williams $100 as part of the agreement. However, in February, when Williams sought the cattle, Otter informed him that he had sold twenty of the oxen in Chicago for his own benefit, without Williams's consent, claiming he needed the payment for feeding them. Williams contended that Otter’s actions constituted an unlawful conversion of his property. The case was tried in the Coles Circuit Court, where Williams was awarded $1,050 in damages for the loss of his cattle, leading to Otter's appeal against this verdict.	The plaintiff, John S. Williams, argued that Harvey Otter wrongfully converted his cattle by selling twenty head without authorization and compensation. He claimed there was no evidence of any delinquent payment from his side regarding the feeding of the cattle, and asserted that Otter's actions constituted a significant breach of trust. As a remedy, Williams sought full damages for the value of the sold oxen at the time of their conversion.	The defendant, Harvey Otter, contended that he had the right to sell the oxen due to what he claimed were financial requirements stemming from the feeding costs. He alleged that the valuation used to determine damages was incorrect, as it did not adequately account for the feeding value added to the cattle during their care. Otter sought to prove that his actions were justified by the circumstances under which the agreement was made.

The case "William H. Shinn et al. v. Horace B. Shinn et al." originated in Illinois and was presided over by the Illinois Appellate Court, with an opinion filed on May 22, 1884. The dispute centers around a mortgage executed on January 6, 1865, by Clement L. Shinn to Horace B. Shinn for $5,000, collateralized by certain real estate. Prior to this, both Horace and Clement had co-owned the property, purchasing it from Ebenezer Hoyes in September 1864, and incurring a $3,000 mortgage. After a foreclosure decree on Hoyes's mortgage in 1869, Thomas B. Trower acquired the property and subsequently sold the certificate of purchase to William H. Shinn and Mary A. Kenney, who later received the property deed in March 1871. Horace B. Shinn filed a bill seeking to foreclose the mortgage claiming the deed was obtained with knowledge of his rights and financed by Clement's money. In contrast, defendants, including William H. and Kenney, counterclaimed the conveyance was legitimate. Further complexities arose when a cross-bill filed by Clement demanded accounting for an alleged partnership, and additional legal inquiries pertained to parties' rights concerning the property, particularly involving Austin M. Ward, a necessary party left out of earlier legal proceedings.	Horace B. Shinn claimed that the property purchased by William H. Shinn and Mary A. Kenney was acquired fraudulently, alleging it was financed with Clement L. Shinn's funds with full knowledge of Horace's mortgage rights. Horace sought to subject the title obtained by William H. and Kenney to the mortgage debt owed to him by Clement. He also argued that the new title held by the defendants should be invalidated to protect his interests as a creditor.	The defendants, including William H. Shinn and Mary A. Kenney, contended that they purchased the property legitimately and maintained that the mortgage from Clement to Horace lacked merit. They claimed that any implications of fraud or illegitimacy surrounding the property's acquisition were unfounded and that Mary A. Kenney was an innocent purchaser without prior notice of Horace's claims. Additionally, they pointed out procedural flaws, including the absence of necessary parties in the foreclosure suit.

On February 10, 1853, in Beardstown, Illinois, Benjamin E. Roney, a store owner, experienced a devastating fire that destroyed goods in his store. Roney was insured through the Delaware Mutual Safety Insurance Company, which had a policy covering some of his merchandise. Roney claimed a loss amounting to $6,805.50 and received a payout of $4,400.43 from the insurance company. However, it was soon discovered that Roney might have been involved in causing the fire to fraudulently claim insurance money. Under pressure from Sweat, an alleged agent of the insurance company, Roney was accused of arson and was forced to assign value of his goods back to the company as collateral for the disputed insurance claim. Following legal proceedings initiated by Roney in the Cass Circuit Court, the court focused on the legitimacy of Roney's claims and the role of the insurance company's actions in asserting fraud against him. The case turned on evidence suggesting that Roney had prepared for the fire, exaggerated his loss, and had a motive for committing fraud.	The plaintiff, Roney, claimed that he had suffered significant loss due to the fire and asserted that the Delaware Mutual Safety Insurance Company was responsible for the insured amount. He contended that the accusations of arson and fraud against him by the insurance company were baseless and coerced, arguing that the evidence did not support their claims. Roney sought relief from the court to declare the assignment of goods void, the appointment of a receiver for his remaining assets, and a resolution that would allow him to recover the full amount of his insurance claim.	The defendant, Delaware Mutual Safety Insurance Company, argued that Roney had intentionally caused the fire to inflate his claims for insurance payouts. The company provided evidence suggesting that Roney had committed fraud by exaggerating his losses and hiding some of his merchandise. They maintained that the assignment of goods, obtained under the pressure of threats from their agent, was valid and that they had acted within their rights as Roney’s fraud was proven beyond a reasonable doubt. They sought to uphold the legitimacy of their actions and the terms of the original insurance policy.

In 1886, in Union County, Illinois, a legal case arose between William C. Rich and David Gow concerning the re-location of a public highway over Rich's farmland. Rich owned a valuable farm that had been cultivated with the existing public highway running through it, which was re-located by county commissioners in 1878. In December 1884, the county board considered a petition presented by Gow to again relocate the highway. The board appointed viewers, two of whom supported the re-location while one opposed it. The majority's recommendation was adopted, and the board ordered the road to be opened, placing the burden of costs and damages on the petitioners. Rich argued that this condition effectively transferred control of the proceedings from the county board to the individual petitioners, leading to a potential for irreparable damage to his property. Following the board's order, Gow, as supervisor of roads, initiated legal actions for assessing damages against Rich. Rich sought an injunction to stop these proceedings, asserting the new road was unnecessary and posed a threat to his property. Initially, a temporary injunction was granted, but the circuit court later made it perpetual, prompting Gow to appeal.	Rich claimed that the re-location of the highway was unnecessary and would cause irreparable damage to his farm. He argued that the previous road was sufficient and could be maintained easily. Rich contended that the county board improperly delegated its statutory powers to the petitioners. He sought an injunction to prevent Gow and others from proceeding with the re-opening and assessment of damages associated with the new road.	Gow argued that the county board acted within its jurisdiction when ordering the re-location of the highway, and the procedures followed were in accordance with statutory requirements. He maintained that the public necessities warranted the new road and that the conditions imposed by the board did not invalidate its order. Gow's defense focused on the argument that Rich's claims were without merit and that the court had no grounds to interfere with the county board's decision.

On April 6, 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, Sheriff Seth F. Hanchett levied executions against Charles S. Munson's property, specifically the furniture and fixtures of the Massasoit House in Chicago, based on two outstanding judgments. The following day, Eliphalet W. Blatchford and Caleb F. Gates filed a replevin suit to reclaim the seized property from the sheriff. They claimed the property as secured by a chattel mortgage executed by Munson in 1881, which was set to expire soon. However, the mortgage was organized in such a way that they planned to sell the property back to Munson after taking possession. These actions led to a convoluted legal dispute, as their title to the property was contested, and the sheriff also had two executions against Munson. The court noted a procedural misdescription of a party in the bond but ultimately addressed that the defendants in the original replevin suit were not liable for the goods attached. The plaintiffs then brought a suit for damages, claiming the original replevin was insufficient on procedural grounds.	The plaintiffs, Blatchford and Gates, claimed that they had valid ownership rights to the property due to a chattel mortgage taken on it. They argued that subsequent to the sheriff's execution, their possession of the property was legitimate and that the replevin bond should be honored. They sought damages due to the sheriff's wrongful levying on the goods that they claimed were rightfully theirs based on their security interests.	The defendants contended that Blatchford and Gates were attempting to impose a liability on them that was not recognized under the bond's condition since they were attached as parties inappropriately. Additionally, they argued that the plaintiffs' claims to the property were fraudulent and designed to keep it in Munson's possession, thereby avoiding punishment from other creditors. The defendants sought dismissal of the claims based on these arguments and pointed out that the lawsuit had not proved the legitimacy of the plaintiffs' title to the property.

In the case of Dustin & Musick v. Samuel P. Hodgen, the dispute arose in Lincoln, Illinois, in the spring of 1861 between plaintiff Samuel P. Hodgen, a merchant, and defendants William M. Dustin and George Musick, who were bankers. The controversy centered around an agreement that allowed Hodgen to deposit proceeds from corn sales—termed "corn money"—with Hoffman & Gelpcke, a banking house in Chicago, to the defendants' credit. The defendants initially agreed to a deposit of $1,000; however, the plaintiff failed to make this deposit in a timely manner, doing so seven days later and subsequently depositing a total of $3,500 without the consent of the defendants. When the bank failed shortly thereafter, Hodgen sought to hold Dustin & Musick liable for the amounts deposited, claiming they acted as guarantors for the funds. The case was initially heard at the Logan Circuit Court and moved to the McLean Circuit Court, where the court ruled in favor of Hodgen, prompting the defendants to appeal.	The plaintiff, Hodgen, argued that the defendants had agreed to allow him to deposit "corn money" to their credit at Hoffman & Gelpcke. He contended that he followed through with the deposit as a means of settling debts owed to creditors, and he sought to hold the defendants liable for the total amount he deposited, alleging they acted as guarantors for those funds.	The defendants, Dustin and Musick, contended that they did not authorize the deposits beyond the initial $1,000 and argued that the plaintiff acted without their consent in making the additional deposits. They maintained that the delays in deposit placed the funds in a depreciated currency situation and that their agreement to allow a deposit was contingent upon it happening in a reasonable time frame. The defendants claimed no responsibility for any amounts deposited after the initial agreement due to the delays and the lack of consent.

In September 1872, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of William J. Ralph v. James Baxter arose concerning a judgment entered against Baxter. The judgment was based on a warrant of attorney, a legal document allowing a lender (Ralph) to confess judgment against a borrower (Baxter) without prior notice in case of default. Ralph initiated the legal action after Baxter reportedly failed to meet payment obligations. The Superior Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gary, was tasked with evaluating an appeal by Baxter, who sought to set aside the judgment on grounds of alleged irregularities and the inclusion of usurious interest in the debt amount. The court's decision focused on the validity of the warrant of attorney and whether Baxter demonstrated the necessary grounds to overturn the judgment.	Ralph contended that the judgment entered against Baxter was proper and based on a valid warrant of attorney, which was executed voluntarily and for good consideration. Ralph argued that while the judgment included some usurious amounts, he had voluntarily remitted the excess to remedy the situation. His request was for the court to uphold the original judgment and dismiss any efforts to set it aside.	Baxter's defense primarily claimed that the judgment should be set aside due to the inclusion of usury in the total amount. He argued that the warrant of attorney was not valid, suggesting it had either been obtained through fraud or was not given voluntarily. Additionally, Baxter noted that an agreement to extend the payment time existed, implying that the action could not be brought before this extension expired. He requested that the court formally annul the judgment.

In August 1886, in Benton, Illinois, Elias J. Brown obtained an insurance policy from The Niagara Fire Insurance Company, covering his stock of goods for $1,450 and his store fixtures for $50. On November 8, 1886, his store was destroyed by a fire, along with its contents. Following the fire, the insurance company refused to pay for the loss, leading Brown to file a lawsuit to recover the insured amount. The insurance policy contained a stipulation that required Brown to keep detailed records of his business in a fireproof safe; however, these records were lost in the fire. Brown's defense against the claim of non-compliance with this stipulation was that it was ultimately waived by the insurance company’s agent, J.F. Mason, who solicited Brown to renew the insurance and assured him that the safety requirement was not necessary for country stores. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court, where the determination of the policy's validity hinged on whether the stipulation had been waived.	The plaintiff, Elias J. Brown, asserted that the insurance policy was valid and that the stipulation regarding the safe keeping of his business records had been waived by the insurance company’s agent. He contended that he had informed the agent about his inability to comply with the requirement and that the agent assured him it was not enforced for country stores. Brown sought to recover the insured amount to cover his losses from the fire, arguing that the loss was genuine and that the company should be held liable.	The defendant, The Niagara Fire Insurance Company, argued that Brown did not comply with the stipulation of keeping his business records in a fireproof safe, which they claimed should void the insurance policy. They contended that this condition was material to the risk, and because Brown's records were destroyed in the fire, they refused to payout on the insurance policy. They maintained that the agent's actions did not constitute a waiver, and thus they were justified in denying the claim.

The case "Robert D. Noleman v. Jacob P. Weil" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1874. The legal action originated from the Marion Circuit Court, where Robert D. Noleman, the plaintiff, initiated an assumpsit action against Jacob P. Weil, the defendant. The dispute arose from a summons that was to be served to Weil. The sheriff indicated that the summons was served by the special deputy Thomas E. Ord, who stated he read the summons to Weil on August 1, 1873. At the return term of the court, the defendant's attorney filed a motion to quash the return of service, which the court granted, resulting in the dismissal of the suit. Noleman then appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, which was tasked with determining the correctness of the lower court's ruling regarding the return of service.	The plaintiff, Robert D. Noleman, argued that the dismissal of his suit due to the quashing of the return of service was incorrect. He contended that the service, as performed by the special deputy, was substantial despite its technical deficiencies. He sought the court's intervention to reinstate his case and allow it to proceed to trial.	The defendant, Jacob P. Weil, maintained that the service of the summons was inadequate, as the return did not indicate that a copy was delivered to him, which is a requirement per the statute. He argued that the special deputy's return was fundamentally flawed, justifying the dismissal of the suit, and sought to uphold the lower court’s decision.

In 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Ellis Kaufman v. Edgar Loomis centers around a promissory note for $3,000 executed by John R. Babcock and C. Q. Ten Broecke, which Loomis guaranteed. The note was held by the International Bank and endorsed to Kaufman for collection. Kaufman, representing the bank, filed the action after a verdict favored Loomis. The situation was complicated by Loomis’ liability on other notes, as well as collateral claims against two railroad companies for an alleged patent infringement, related to a patent that was later deemed invalid. A trustee, L. H. Bisbee, was involved in negotiations with the railroads to settle these claims but was hindered by the bank's president, Lowenthal, who refused to allow a sale of the claims despite significant offers from the railroad companies. This refusal ultimately rendered the collateral worthless when the patent was declared invalid.	The plaintiff, Kaufman, argued that Loomis was liable for the debt based on his guarantee of the promissory note. Kaufman contended that the bank's president's refusal to allow the sale of claims, which could have settled the debt, did not absolve Loomis of his guarantee responsibilities. They sought to hold Loomis accountable for repayment of the sum on the note.	The defendant, Loomis, claimed that he should not be held liable for the notes due to the interference of Lowenthal, who prevented the sale of valuable securities that could have settled the debt. Loomis argued that since the collateral became worthless due to the bank's actions, he was effectively released as a guarantor.

Edgar A. Hall initiated a legal action against John Kilderhouse in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, concerning the earned moneys from the schooner T. B. Pomeroy while operating between Chicago and Buffalo. At the time the earnings were generated, the schooner was owned by Hall & McGrew. A dispute arose regarding the rightful owner of the funds, leading to Hall filing a lawsuit while a separate case was ongoing in Erie County, New York, where Kilderhouse was appointed as the receiver. Despite an arbitrators’ decision awarding the funds to Hall, Kilderhouse failed to comply, paying the money to McGrew instead. Following a trial where a jury was waived and the case was heard by a judge, the Superior Court ruled in favor of Hall. Kilderhouse appealed this decision, only to find the judgment upheld by the Appellate Court, prompting him to bring the case before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case primarily revolved around the legality of the arbitrators' award and whether Hall was entitled to the funds held by Kilderhouse.	Hall asserted that the funds in Kilderhouse's possession rightfully belonged to him as determined by the arbitrators’ award. He requested that the court order Kilderhouse to pay the money to him, emphasizing that the arbitrators' decision was valid and binding, and that the ongoing partnership dispute with McGrew should not preclude his claim at law.	Kilderhouse contended that the award from the arbitrators was not binding due to a prior revocation of the submission agreement by McGrew, and he argued the issues surrounding the funds should be settled in the ongoing equity suit for partnership accounting between Hall and McGrew, rather than in this legal action. Kilderhouse sought to challenge the validity of the arbitrators’ award and maintain that a court of law should not resolve a matter pending in equity.

In 1848, in Hardin County, Illinois, Leonard White and his partner Sloo were involved in a commercial dispute with By Wilson. The case arose when Wilson initiated an action of assumpsit by attachment against White & Sloo due to an alleged debt. He claimed that the partners were about to remove their property—a quantity of pig iron—from Illinois, which would injure him financially. A writ of attachment was issued based on this allegation. In response, White & Sloo filed a plea in abatement, contesting the claim that property removal would be detrimental to Wilson. The court found against this plea, leading to a judgment that required the plaintiffs to respond with a plea of non assumpsit, which was also ruled against them. Critical evidence was excluded during the trial, specifically testimony indicating that one partner had sufficient unencumbered property within the state to satisfy Wilson's claim. The plaintiffs maintained that this evidence was essential to show that the removal of the iron would not cause any financial harm to Wilson.	The plaintiffs, White and Sloo, argued that the attachment against their property was unjustified, as the claims made by Wilson regarding their impending removal of property and subsequent injury were flawed. They sought to present evidence showing that one partner possessed other unencumbered personal property within Illinois that was more than sufficient to cover Wilson's debt. They contended that the removal of the pig iron in the course of normal trade would not negatively affect Wilson's ability to collect the debt.	Wilson's defense centered on his assertion that the plaintiffs were about to remove property from the state, which constituted a risk of injury to him financially. He argued that such actions warranted the issuance of an attachment under Illinois law, which allows creditors to secure debts by seizing property they believe may be removed to their detriment. The exclusion of evidence by the court that could counter Wilson's claims was seen as a critical aspect of his defense.

Nathan H. Farnsworth filed a legal action of ejectment against Milton M. Agnew in the Monroe Circuit Court, Illinois, on April 12, 1858. The case revolved around a dispute regarding a parcel of land located in Monroe County. Farnsworth, who was allegedly a non-resident of Illinois, submitted his declaration and a bond for costs on the same day. Shortly thereafter, he moved to compel Agnew to respond to his claim within twenty days. However, Agnew countered with a motion to dismiss the suit, arguing that Farnsworth failed to file the required bond for costs prior to initiating the suit, which was a necessity according to the pertinent statutory requirements for non-residents. The court considered affidavits from both parties regarding the timing and filing of the bond, which ultimately led to a ruling based on the interpretation of the law pertaining to non-resident plaintiffs and the timing of filing the necessary bond for costs.	Farnsworth's primary argument was that he had filed the required bond for costs in conjunction with his original declaration. He contended that the bond was either indorsed on the declaration or filed at the earliest point possible upon realizing he was classified as a non-resident, which should have satisfied the statutory requirement and allowed the suit to proceed.	Agnew's defense emphasized that Farnsworth's bond for costs was not filed before the suit commenced, which violated the statute requiring such security for non-resident plaintiffs. He pointed to the timeline of events and affidavits presented, arguing that since the bond was filed only after the declaration was served, the court did not have the jurisdiction to proceed with the suit, warranting dismissal.

On April 3, 1837, John C. Hugunin and Alexander Logan purchased an undivided half of a lot in School Section addition to Chicago from Leonard C. Hugunin for $2,000, giving promissory notes as payment. On May 20, 1837, the property was re-conveyed back to Leonard C. Hugunin, who returned the notes to the purchasers. Mary A. Hugunin, who was married to John C. Hugunin at that time, did not join in the re-conveyance. John C. Hugunin passed away on July 4, 1866, after which Mary A. sought the assignment of dower in the property on June 3, 1867. The court dismissed her petition, leading her to appeal the decision, questioning the legal rights concerning the property and the assignment of dower since the property had been re-conveyed to the original vendor.	Mary A. Hugunin claimed her right to dower in the lot after her husband's death, asserting that the property should be subject to her claim as she was the widow of John C. Hugunin. She argued that her husband's actions did not negate her right to dower and requested the court to assign her dower rights in the property.	Leonard C. Hugunin, the original vendor and defendant, contended that the lien he held as a vendor on the property was superior to any dower rights claimed by Mary A. Hugunin. He argued that since the land was re-conveyed to extinguish the promissory notes, it passed free from her dower claim, which the court maintained should take precedence over her rights.

The case "John R. Schnebly and Charles E. Rowcliffe v. Richard A. Culter" was ruled upon by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 11, 1886. The dispute stems from two partnerships involving Richard A. Culter and Cary E. Robinson. On January 1, 1883, Culter and Robinson formed a partnership named R. A. Culter & Company in Peoria, Illinois, focusing on the general hardware and tin business. Later, on September 23, 1884, Robinson entered into another partnership with Schnebly and Rowcliffe, which did not involve Culter. Under this new partnership agreement, Robinson was to provide a credit of $3,000 to his new partners through the original partnership. However, Culter claimed he was not informed that this credit was to be sustained for five years and contended that the full amount owed, $4,079.12, including the disputed $3,000, was not due until later. After the original partnership dissolved in July 1885, Culter sought to collect the debt from Schnebly and Rowcliffe through a bill in equity, asserting his right as a creditor following the dissolution of the partnership. The circuit court had to determine whether the appellants were liable for the entire debt and the conditions of the credit agreement.	The plaintiffs, John R. Schnebly and Charles E. Rowcliffe, argue that they are entitled to collect the debt of $4,079.12 from Richard A. Culter, which arose from transactions between their partnership and Culter's partnership with Robinson. They assert that the debt is presently due and that the partnership agreement Robinson had entered into concerning the credit did not exempt them from obligations to Culter. They request the court to recognize their right to recover the full amount owed plus interest, emphasizing that no proper credit agreement or extension was communicated regarding the timing of the debt's payment.	Richard A. Culter contends that he should not be liable for the amount claimed by Schnebly and Rowcliffe. He argues that the $3,000 component of their claim is not due until five years post-partnership initiation with Robinson, based on their partnership agreement, which he believes Schnebly and Rowcliffe should have been aware of. Culter asserts that equitable principles should preclude his obligation until the financial matters between the partnerships are fully resolved. He admits to a smaller liability of $1,079.12 but denies responsibility for the full amount claimed, arguing that he should not be held accountable for the miscommunication regarding the partnership's credit arrangement.

The case titled "The People ex rel. the Pekin, Lincoln and Decatur Railroad Company v. The Board of Supervisors of Logan County" centers around an election held on April 27, 1869, in Logan County, Illinois. The Pekin, Lincoln and Decatur Railroad Company sought to compel the Board of Supervisors to subscribe $300,000 to its capital stock following the election, which resulted in a claim of a majority in favor of the subscription. However, the Board of Supervisors refused to issue the bonds needed for this subscription, citing that the majority of votes were fraudulent and that the election's conduct was improper, as no judges of election were present in two townships. The Board argued that illegal votes significantly outnumbered the legitimate votes supporting the subscription, thereby invalidating the electoral process. The case was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court, which focused on the legality of the election and whether the Board of Supervisors had the authority to act under the alleged circumstances surrounding the voting.	The plaintiff, the Pekin, Lincoln and Decatur Railroad Company, claimed that the election held to determine the subscription was valid and that the Board of Supervisors had a legal duty to subscribe to the capital stock as stipulated in the amended charter. They requested a writ of mandamus to compel the Board to issue the bonds for the first installment of $100,000 based on the outcome of the election, despite the Board's refusal based on claims of fraud.	The Board of Supervisors of Logan County contended that the election was conducted illegally, with a significant number of fraudulent votes. They maintained that the majority in favor of the subscription was composed of illegal votes and that a majority of the lawful votes had actually opposed the subscription. Additionally, they asserted that the railroad company had prior knowledge of these irregularities, which should invalidate the claim for subscription and issuance of bonds.

On January 28, 1865, in Clark County, Illinois, the county board passed resolutions offering bounties to incentivize enlistment into the military during the Civil War, as a response to the impending draft. This bounty offered $100 to individuals who volunteered or who were drafted and provided a substitute. On February 7, 1865, the Illinois General Assembly enacted a law allowing counties to levy taxes for bounty payments up to $100,000 to support enlistments. Subsequently, on March 15, 1865, the county board confirmed prior resolutions to distribute these bounties and authorized the issuing of county orders for payment. However, some orders were issued invalidly due to the lack of statutory authority in prior resolutions. The county collected taxes to fund these payments, leading to a legal challenge by several individuals who sought to restrain the collection of this tax, claiming it was illegitimate due to the unauthorized issuance of certain orders before the law's passage.	The plaintiffs, consisting of Joseph S. Allison and others, argued that the tax levied for bounty payments was unauthorized, claiming that some orders issued for enlistments prior to the February law lacked legal grounds. They requested the court to restrain tax collection as it was being conducted to pay for these unauthorized bounties.	The defendants contended that the resolutions and subsequent legislative act provided the necessary legal authority to levy the tax and issue the county orders for bounties. They maintained that the bounties were valid and necessary to fill the county's military quota, arguing that the board acted within its rights based on legislative permission.

In 1857, the case of Julius A. Penn and his wife against David W. Heisey unfolded in the town of Paris, Edgar County, Illinois. The underlying issue involved a disputed lot sold by Gideon Minor, the guardian of Oliver Minor's minor children, including Eliza Penn, one of the plaintiffs. Although the sale occurred under state authority, it was not reported or confirmed by the court, rendering it void. Over time, the lot changed hands multiple times, ultimately coming into the possession of Heisey, who purchased it in good faith without knowledge of the title issues. The Penns sought to reclaim the lot based on their legal title, claiming rightful ownership. Heisey, however, filed for an injunction against their ejectment suit, asserting that he had acquired the lot legitimately and had utilized sale proceeds to benefit the Minor children, including purchases of additional lands. The Penns contested the legitimacy of this claim, denying the evidence presented by Heisey and questioning the origins of those land purchases.	The plaintiffs, Julius A. Penn and his wife, argued that they hold the valid legal title to the lot sold by Gideon Minor, their guardian. They claimed that the sale lacked proper court confirmation and that, as heirs of Oliver Minor, they were entitled to reclaim their rightful property. Their legal request included an order to oust Heisey from the lot and to establish ownership based on their claimed title.	David W. Heisey contended that he was a bona fide purchaser of the lot without notice of any title defects. He argued that the sale was conducted by the guardian, despite its failure to be reported or confirmed by the court, and that the Penns had benefitted from the proceeds of the sale through other land purchases. He sought an injunction to prevent the Penns from proceeding with their ejectment suit and requested a decree to quiet the title in his favor, citing equitable estoppel due to the Penns’ acceptance of benefits from the proceeds of the contested sale.

In September 1875, the case of Marcus Belden et al. v. John W. Woodmansee was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court following events in Knox County, Illinois. The case arose from a parol contract concerning the shelling of corn, primarily in Iowa. The plaintiff, Marcus Belden, claimed that he was contracted to shell 150,000 bushels of corn and as much more as possible before the onset of cold weather. However, due to delays caused by the defendant, Woodmansee, who allegedly ordered Belden to stop shelling the corn, only 81,602 bushels were shelled by November 6th. Belden argued that the defendants prevented him from completing the contract on time and subsequently promised to pay him for the lost time. After a trial, the jury ruled in favor of Belden, awarding him $1,000. The defendants contended that the court erred in various jury instructions and motions regarding the contract terms and the interpretation of the evidence presented.	The plaintiff, Marcus Belden, argued that he had a valid contract to shell 150,000 bushels of corn and that the defendants' actions prevented him from fulfilling this agreement within the stipulated time. Belden contended that despite the delays caused by the defendants requiring him to halt work, he was entitled to compensation for the time lost during these interruptions. He sought an affirmation of the jury's verdict for $1,000 against Woodmansee.	The defendant, John W. Woodmansee, maintained that the court made several errors regarding the jury's instructions and the interpretation of contractual obligations. The defendant argued that the plaintiff could not recover for lost time when he was ordered to stop shelling due to the corn not being ready. Woodmansee claimed that any promises made to pay Belden lacked consideration since the contract did not allow continued work regardless of the corn's condition.

Alexander K. Owen initiated a legal case against James McKean in the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a slander claim. The events took place in Morris, Grundy County, Illinois, around June 1853. The case stemmed from allegations made by Owen that McKean had “sworn falsely” in connection with a bill in chancery involving county commissioners. Owen claimed to have referred to McKean during discussions about the bill, asserting that he could substantiate his claims against McKean through court documents. However, McKean's defense presented witnesses who clarified that the words attributed to Owen were spoken in the context of a different location, and those words misidentified McKean as the person who had sworn to the bill, when it was actually McGrath, another commissioner, who had done so. During the trial, the court rejected several pieces of evidence Owen sought to introduce as a defense, focusing on the necessity of malice in the claim of slander. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of McKean, resulting in Owen's appeal of the verdict.	Owen claimed that McKean slandered him by asserting false statements regarding his actions connected to a legal bill. Owen sought to demonstrate that he believed these statements to be true at the time of speaking, indicating he had supporting documents to back his claims. He contended that he was wrongfully accused and express that the statements he made were made under a reasonable belief that they were accurate, which he wanted to utilize as a defense against the slander allegations.	McKean defended himself by arguing that the location and context of Owen's statements were misrepresented, as they were made in reference to a suit not connected to him but rather to another individual, McGrath. He contended that Owen’s testimony did not prove the statements were made maliciously, which is a crucial element in slander cases. Moreover, he sought to exclude Owen's attempts to introduce evidence aimed at proving the truth of his accusations in mitigation of damages.

The case of The Rockford Insurance Company v. Sarah Nelson took place in September 1872 in Illinois, specifically referred to by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from an insurance policy that covered a dwelling and boarding house owned by Sarah Nelson. Nelson's property, including household furniture and other belongings, was destroyed by a fire, leading her to claim compensation from the Rockford Insurance Company under the policy. The insurance company contested the claim, asserting a variety of defenses, including an alleged variance in the declaration regarding the ownership of the property, which they argued should have included a detailed account of the conditions within the insurance agreement. The case involved multiple legal intricacies, including interpretations of the insurance policy, the sufficiency of the pleadings, and the insurable interest that Nelson held in the property. Ultimately, the crux of the legal battle rested on whether Nelson had properly demonstrated her insurable interest and whether the company was liable for the destruction of her property under the insurance policy's terms.",	Sarah Nelson, the plaintiff, argued that she was entitled to recover damages for her losses due to the fire that destroyed her property, which was insured under a policy issued by the Rockford Insurance Company. She claimed to have an insurable interest in the property, meeting the requirements set forth in the insurance contract. Nelson contested the insurance company's objections regarding her ownership claim and asserted that the policy remained valid and enforceable, entitling her to compensation for the loss sustained.",	The Rockford Insurance Company, as the defendant, presented several defenses. They contended that there was a variance between the declaration and the actual insurance policy, claiming that the conditions necessary for recovery were not adequately set out in Nelson's case. Moreover, they argued that Nelson had not proven she held a fee simple title to the property but merely claimed an insurable interest—less than ownership. The company also raised issues related to questions of fraud and collusion between its agent and Nelson regarding the nature and use of the property by suggesting that the house was misrepresented as a dwelling rather than a public hotel.",

The case of *The City of Galesburg v. Erastus D. Higley* occurred in September 1871 in Galesburg, Illinois. The plaintiff, Erastus D. Higley, sustained injuries after falling into an unguarded opening on a city sidewalk. The incident happened in the evening between 8 and 9 PM when Higley was returning from the railroad depot. It was dark and raining, and he was running to avoid getting wet. While trying to navigate around large boxes on the sidewalk, he fell into an opening that was approximately three feet long, twenty inches wide, and eighteen inches deep, which had previously been covered by an iron grating that had been removed. The city's failure to secure or close this dangerous opening was central to Higley's claim that the city was grossly negligent. This dangerous condition had reportedly been known to city officials as multiple individuals had previously experienced similar falls into the openings. Higley suffered serious injuries, including a sprained wrist, and he claimed that the city officials were aware of the hazardous conditions without taking action to rectify them.	The plaintiff, Erastus D. Higley, claimed that the City of Galesburg was negligent in failing to secure the sidewalk opening and remove the large boxes that obstructed the path. He argued that the city officials had prior knowledge of the dangerous condition but took no steps to safeguard pedestrians. Higley sought damages for the injuries he incurred as a result of this negligence, asserting that his injury was serious and likely to require long-term medical treatment.	The City of Galesburg, as the defendant, contended that it had no prior notice of the boxes on the sidewalk and argued that they may have been moved there shortly before the incident. The city pointed to evidence that might suggest the boxes were not a permanent obstruction. Furthermore, the city argued that the injuries claimed by Higley might have resulted from improper medical treatment rather than the fall itself. The defendant contested the extent of Higley's claimed injuries and the amount of damages awarded, claiming they were excessive.

Lovell Kimball and others, plaintiffs, filed a case against Amasa G. Cook, the defendant, in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1844. The origin of the case stems from a mechanic's lien Cook sought to enforce regarding a contract dated June 3, 1838, in which he was to perform millwright work for Kimball on a flouring mill located in Marseilles, Illinois. Cook claimed he completed most of the work as per the contract but had not installed a corn cracker due to Kimball’s failure to provide it. Cook stated he had already received $2,400 in payments, with the same amount remaining due. Kimball, in response, contested that Cook had not fulfilled the contract, specifying various deficiencies. After a jury trial, the jury ruled in favor of Cook, awarding him the full amount he claimed, which was $2,400. The case was marked by complexities regarding the admissibility of evidence and the interpretation of proceedings related to mechanic's liens, which were primarily viewed through the lens of Chancery court rules.	The plaintiff, Amasa G. Cook, asserted that he completed the work outlined in the contract except for the installation of the corn cracker, which was contingent upon receiving the necessary materials from Kimball. He sought to recover the unpaid amount of $2,400, which he argued was due under the contract for the services rendered.	The defendant, Lovell Kimball, denied that the work was completed according to the contractual terms and asserted that no payment was owed to Cook. Kimball contested the admissibility of certain evidence presented by Cook during the trial, arguing that the work was not finished as agreed and highlighting several issues with the quality of the performed work.

In July 1820, in Madison, Illinois, a legal case unfolded between John Y. Sawyer and Benjamin Stephenson. The issue arose after the trial court granted a new trial to the defendant, Stephenson. During the original trial, a juror had provided additional testimony in the jury room that influenced the verdict in favor of the plaintiff, Sawyer. This juror's affidavit revealed that had this additional testimony not been presented, he would have returned a verdict for the defendant. Consequently, the trial court's decision to grant a new trial was challenged by Sawyer through a writ of error, seeking to overturn the previous ruling. The case was significant as it addressed the principles surrounding the awarding of new trials and the admissibility of juror affidavits regarding improper conduct.	John Y. Sawyer, the plaintiff, argued against the trial court's decision to grant a new trial. He contended that the new testimony introduced by a juror during deliberations was improperly admitted and that the original verdict should stand. Sawyer sought to reverse the ruling that favored granting a new trial and restore the initial decision that was in his favor.	Benjamin Stephenson, the defendant, maintained that the affidavit of the juror was valid and demonstrated that improper conduct during jury deliberation influenced the final verdict. Stephenson's legal argument revolved around the notion that a new trial was justified due to the juror's admission of receiving additional testimony that affected the deliberation process. He requested the court to uphold the decision to grant a new trial.

Alice B. Hendershott filed a suit against William S. Calhoun, resulting from a landlord-tenant dispute in Cook County, Illinois. The case traces back to February 7, 1882, when Hendershott executed a lease to Calhoun for a term of one year at a rental rate of $300, payable in monthly installments of $25. Due to an existing debt of $300 to James E. DeWolf, Hendershott instructed Calhoun to pay the monthly rent directly to DeWolf. Calhoun complied with these payments until he vacated the premises, having made all payments through November 1882 and half of December's installment. After paying off the debt to DeWolf, Hendershott received the original order. The case progressed through an appeal after the initial verdict favoring Calhoun at the circuit court. The jury was instructed that the payments to DeWolf barred Hendershott from recovering additional rent. The evidence presented included the claim that the premises were in disrepair when Calhoun vacated, although this issue was not directly addressed in the jury instructions.	Hendershott argued that the rental payments due under the lease had not been assigned to DeWolf in a way that prohibited her from recovering unpaid rent from Calhoun. She asserted that upon paying the debt, the assignment of rent was effectively extinguished, and therefore, Calhoun was still liable for the remaining rent payments.	Calhoun contended that the instruction given to the jury—claiming that the assignment of the rental payments to DeWolf barred Hendershott from recouping unpaid rent—was valid. He argued that as he had paid the rent to DeWolf as per the agreement, he was no longer liable for additional rental payments to Hendershott after vacating the premises.

The case "The Chicago and North Western R R. Company v. Charles L. Williams" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. The dispute arose in Winnebago County, Illinois, where plaintiff Charles L. Williams filed an action against the defendant, The Chicago and North Western Railroad Company. The plaintiff claimed that 2,269 pounds of iron, which he had entrusted to the railroad company for transportation from Chicago to Harvard, Illinois, was lost while in their custody. Key individuals involved included Mr. James M. Wight, representing the appellant (the railroad company), and Messrs. Lathrop & Bailey, representing the appellee (Williams). The central question was whether the evidence presented supported the jury's verdict regarding the liability of the railroad company for the lost iron. Witnesses testified that the iron was indeed placed in the company’s car, but it was later found to be missing, which led to the lawsuit.	The plaintiff, Charles L. Williams, claimed that the Chicago and North Western Railroad Company was liable for the loss of the iron that he had delivered to them as a common carrier for transportation. He argued that the evidence showed the iron had been loaded onto the railroad’s car and was, therefore, their responsibility. Williams sought compensation for the value of the lost iron, holding the defendant accountable for failing to safeguard the property entrusted to them.	The defendant, The Chicago and North Western Railroad Company, contended that the iron was never properly loaded into their car, disputing the plaintiff’s claim of possession at the time of the loss. They argued that the lack of evidence showing the iron’s presence in their facilities at the time of checking out meant they could not be held liable for the loss. The company maintained that they did not receive the iron legally transferred to their car, and thus requested the court to dismiss the claims against them based on insufficient evidence.

In April 1860, in Peoria, Illinois, Merritt D. Wood and another individual (the plaintiffs) initiated a lawsuit against George Goss and another party (the defendants). One of the plaintiffs was a non-resident of Illinois, which prompted the defendants to file a motion to dismiss the case due to the failure to provide a bond for costs as required by the Illinois Cost Act. The defendants argued that the presence of a non-resident plaintiff warranted the dismissal because the act stipulates that a bond must be filed if an action is instigated by a non-resident. The lower court initially sustained the defendants' motion, leading to the plaintiffs appealing the decision on the grounds that the dismissal was unauthorized. The controversy centered around the interpretation of the statute regarding solvency and residency of plaintiffs, and whether all plaintiffs needed to be residents or if one solvent resident plaintiff sufficed to prevent dismissal.	The plaintiffs' main argument was that the court should not dismiss their suit solely based on the presence of a non-resident plaintiff. They contended that the Cost Act allows for a lawsuit with one resident plaintiff who is solvent and capable of bearing the costs. They argued that since one of the plaintiffs was a resident, the statutory purpose of securing the defendant's costs was satisfied. Therefore, they sought to have the dismissal reversed.	The defendants maintained that the suit should be dismissed because one of the plaintiffs was a non-resident and did not file the necessary bond for costs as mandated by the Illinois Cost Act. They argued that the intention of the statute is to secure a defendant against potential costs resulting from the lawsuit. The defendants' position was that without a bond, the court had no choice but to dismiss the suit to uphold the legislative intent.

In the case of Ann Stillman v. Raymond Palis, which was filed in the Illinois Appellate Court, the events took place in St. Clair County, Illinois, culminating in a decision on February 4, 1890. The key individuals involved were Ann Stillman, the plaintiff, and Raymond Palis, the defendant. The dispute arose over a piece of land that both parties owned, which was adjacent to one another. The plaintiff, Ann Stillman, was in possession of the property in question when the defendant, Raymond Palis, forcibly entered her possession, claiming title to the land. Palis erected a wire fence on the property, leading Stillman to file a suit for forcible entry and detainer, asserting her right to the property she possessed.	Ann Stillman claimed that she was in rightful possession of the land in question. She argued that Raymond Palis's actions of forcibly entering the premises and constructing a fence were unlawful and amounted to a violation of her possessory rights. Stillman sought legal redress through the court to affirm her possession and to remove Palis's encroachment on her property.	Raymond Palis contended that he had a valid title to the land, which justified his forcible entry. He maintained that the description of the land in the complaint was insufficient and claimed that his actions were warranted due to his belief in ownership. His defense included a challenge to the plaintiff's right to file the suit without a prior demand for possession, arguing procedural shortcomings in Stillman's approach.

In 1865, the Illinois Supreme Court adjudicated the case of James L. Adams et al. v. James M. Robertson et al., which arose in the context of a legal dispute regarding a mortgage. The events date back to 1856 when James M. Robertson, then residing in Indiana, incurred debts totaling approximately $11,650 to the Prairie City Bank, secured by several bills of exchange connected to business transactions involving the shipment of livestock. Alongside this debt to the bank, Robertson also owed about $2,000 to the complainants, who operated under the name Graham & Buckingham. On March 20, 1856, Robertson executed a deed conveying several tracts of land to C. W. Barbour, president of the bank, with a concurrent defeasance that promised the reconveyance of the lands upon payment of both the bank's debts and any dues to Graham & Buckingham. The central issue in the dispute was whether the bank or Graham & Buckingham had priority over the proceeds from the sale of the mortgaged land, especially given conflicting interpretations of interest rates relevant to the debts, which invoked laws from Indiana and New York.	The plaintiffs, Graham & Buckingham, asserted that the Prairie City Bank had violated usury laws by reserving an interest rate exceeding the legal limits—specifically arguing that because the bank charged 7.5% interest on the bills of exchange, they were essentially void. They claimed a right to share equally in the mortgage security, which was intended to cover both the bank's and their debts, insisting that they should not be penalized for the bank's alleged illegalities. Their primary legal request was for the court to recognize their equal claim to the security and to ensure their interests were protected during the proceeds' distribution.	The bank contended that it held a priority claim over the mortgage security. It argued that the contract with Robertson was valid under the laws of Indiana, which permitted a 6% interest rate, and asserted that Graham & Buckingham were aware of the nature of the agreement. The bank claimed that no usury was present in the transactions and that its actions were lawful, emphasizing that they should not be penalized for the charged interest rates. Additionally, the bank sought to prove that the defeasance did not reflect any fraud, asserting its position based on the perceived agreement at the time of the contract.

In the case of St. Patrick’s Roman Catholic Church of East St. Louis v. Stephen Abst, which was decided in January 1875, the legal matter took place in St. Clair County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the St. Patrick’s Roman Catholic Church, represented by its trustees, and Stephen Abst, who was employed as the church's sexton. Abst had been hired by a majority of the church trustees to perform various duties over the course of nearly one year. These responsibilities included cleaning the church, maintaining its order, and assisting the priest with church-related errands. After the church received these services, a dispute arose regarding the payment owed to Abst, particularly disputes surrounding the adherence to the church’s by-laws, specifically whether the employment followed these rules correctly. The church had not objected to the services provided, but raised questions about the hiring process.	The plaintiff, Stephen Abst, claimed that he was entitled to payment for his services rendered as the sexton of St. Patrick’s Roman Catholic Church. His principal argument rested on the fact that he was employed by a majority of the church’s trustees and that the church had benefited from his services without objection for almost a year. He maintained that the financial arrangements, including contributions from the ladies of the Altar Society, did not affect his right to be compensated by the church itself for his undertaking.	The defendant, St. Patrick’s Roman Catholic Church, contended that it could not be held liable for Abst's wages based on sections 14 and 15 of the church’s organizing act from 1869 and the ninth section of its by-laws. The church argued that hiring a sexton was unrelated to its "temporalities" and management of assets, suggesting that the employment was not valid due to procedural issues. They posited that because the necessary by-law procedures were not followed, they should not be responsible for the payment owed to Abst.

Albion Wheeler executed a contract on December 22, 1883, to sell a patent for a new invention, a Loose Draft Equalizer, to Albert Fishell and others. The agreement specified that Wheeler, a resident of Iowa, would grant rights within certain U.S. territories, excluding several states and territories. In exchange for one dollar and a future payment of $1,000 upon delivering a deed, Wheeler transferred the rights to the invention. However, he did not apply for the patent until May 26, 1885, and the patent was not issued until January 5, 1886. On February 24, 1886, Wheeler executed a deed to the defendants, asking for the payment. The defendants contested that the deed had not been tendered and the patent was not secured within a reasonable time, leading to the initiation of litigation. The case was tried in Illinois, where a jury was waived, resulting in a judgment favorable to the defendants.	Wheeler argued that the contract served as an absolute assignment of the patent rights and contended that the defendants were bound to pay the $1,000 upon the tender of the deed. He asserted that since the defendants accepted the contract, although they did not sign it, they were obligated to fulfill its terms, including making payment once the deed was delivered.	The defendants claimed that the contract merely provided an option to purchase rather than a definitive sale. They contested that Wheeler did not properly execute the contract and argued that he failed to secure the patent and tender the deed within a reasonable timeframe. They maintained that this delay rendered the contract unenforceable and justified their refusal to pay.

Joseph O. Glover et al. v. Clara Benjamin is a legal case that took place in September 1874 in Illinois. The key individuals involved included Joseph O. Glover, Clara Benjamin, and George C. Campbell, among others. The case arose from a bill in chancery filed by Clara Benjamin and S. G. W. Benjamin against Glover and Campbell to foreclose a mortgage held by Benjamin on city lots that secured a promissory note. The note was originally given by Charles H. Scriven, who had sold the property to Campbell, leaving him with an equity of redemption. Glover was assigned an undivided half interest in the promissory note but did not wish to join the foreclosure as a complainant. The Superior Court initially ruled in favor of Benjamin and Glover but was later reversed when Glover contested that he did not consent to the decree. Upon remand, a new decree was issued requiring Campbell to pay the amount due or face the sale of the mortgaged property.	Clara Benjamin, the plaintiff, argued that Glover should be compelled to join the foreclosure proceedings since he had received an assignment of part of the mortgage. The claims centered around the enforcement of the mortgage due to the non-payment of the promissory note by Scriven. Benjamin sought a decree for the sale of the property to satisfy the unpaid debt, bringing forth her rights as a note holder in the foreclosure process.	The defendants, Glover and Campbell, contended that the initial decree favoring Glover was made without his consent and thus, he should not be held to any obligations under it. Glover specifically argued that he did not seek a foreclosure and should not be compelled to pay without his express consent. Campbell also felt that the decree represented a personal liability against him, which he contested.

The case "The First National Bank of Centralia et al. v. Edward B. Marshall" was decided on May 5, 1888, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The First National Bank of Centralia was established on March 23, 1865, with a capital stock of $80,000. By 1885, the bank was facing an impending expiration of its charter, prompting stockholders to vote on whether to liquidate the bank. At a meeting on January 30, 1885, all shareholders, including Edward B. Marshall, voted for voluntary liquidation, which took effect on February 25, 1885. Following this, the Old National Bank was chartered, with the same officers as the First National Bank, though Marshall did not become a stockholder in the new organization. Tension existed between Marshall and other shareholders, stemming from his previous attempts to establish a competing bank. After liquidation, Marshall received several dividends totaling sizable amounts from the disposed assets but later contested the actions as fraudulent and sought a share of the earnings from the newly chartered bank.	Edward B. Marshall, the plaintiff, claimed that the restructuring and liquidation actions taken by the First National Bank and its officers were intended to effectively "freeze him out" from his interest as a stockholder. He alleged that these actions were conducted without his consent and that the new bank had unlawfully benefited from the assets of the First National Bank. Marshall sought an accounting of the earnings of the Old National Bank, requesting a decree for payment corresponding to a proportionate share of its profits based on his initial shares in the First National Bank.	The defendants, comprising the First National Bank and the Old National Bank, argued that the voluntary liquidation and establishment of the new bank were legally executed with the agreement of the majority of stockholders, including Marshall, who had participated in the voting process. They contended that Marshall had received dividends and benefits from the liquidation process, thus estopping him from claiming any further rights or interests in the newly formed bank. The defendants maintained that the actions taken were in accordance with the National Bank Act and that no fraudulent conduct had occurred in the disposition of the bank's assets.

The case of Abraham Frank et al. v. Dora J. King et al. took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered on June 20, 1887, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiffs, a firm under the name A. Frank & Sons, initiated action by attachment against T. N. Humphrey and L. B. King, partners in T. N. Humphrey & Co., due to a debt. The plaintiffs claimed that L. B. King owned a piece of land that they sought to attach to satisfy the debt. The writ of attachment was issued on November 20, 1885, and the sheriff levied on the land believed to belong to L. B. King. On the defense side, L. B. King challenged the attachment's validity, and Dora J. King filed a plea of interpleader, claiming ownership of the land in question.
