The court allowed for a trial without a jury to determine ownership. Evidence presented indicated that L. B. King had conveyed the land to Dora J. King shortly before the liens were established, raising questions regarding the validity of the transfer as potential fraudulent conveyances intended to defraud creditors. The court ultimately ruled in favor of Dora J. King, establishing her title to the land and quashing the attachment.	The plaintiffs claimed ownership of the property attached, believing it to be the asset of L. B. King due to outstanding debts owed by him. They sought to have their claim recognized and the attachment maintained, arguing that the transfer of the property to Dora J. King was fraudulent and intended to place the property beyond the reach of creditors.	The defendant, Dora J. King, contested the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that she was the rightful owner of the property in fee simple. She contended that the transfer of the land to her was valid and that L. B. King intended to prefer her as a creditor. Furthermore, she sought to have the attachment quashed based on her rightful ownership of the property.

The case, titled "The Laflin & Rand Powder Company v. Mary Tearney," was decided on January 21, 1890, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident occurred in the town of Lake, on Archer Avenue, near the outskirts of Chicago, Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Mary Tearney, owned a dwelling, barn, and other outbuildings that were damaged due to an explosion caused by a powder magazine operated by the defendant, Laflin & Rand Powder Company. The explosion was significant enough to destroy Tearney's property. The Superior Court of Cook County initially ruled in favor of Tearney, and this judgment was upheld by the Appellate Court, which prompted the defendant to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case centered around claims of negligence related to the storage of explosives in close proximity to residential properties, affecting the safety and well-being of neighboring residents.	Mary Tearney claimed that the defendant's operation of the powder magazine constituted a private nuisance. She argued that the magazine was in a location that posed a substantial risk of harm to her property. Tearney sought damages for the destruction of her buildings due to the explosion, asserting that the defendant's actions were illegal under local ordinances governing the storage of explosives.	The Laflin & Rand Powder Company contended that the plaintiff did not sufficiently prove a cause of action and claimed that the explosion was not a result of any negligent acts on their part. They argued that the plaintiff assumed the risk of living near potential hazards, as other powder magazines existed in the area prior to her property acquisition. Furthermore, they maintained that the explosion might have been caused by an act of nature, such as lightning, and claimed that the plaintiff's complaint did not establish negligence or actionable harm.

The case "American Merchants’ Union Express Co. v. Horace H. Willsie" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. It originated in the Knox Circuit Court and involved a dispute over goods taken by Horace H. Willsie, acting as a constable on behalf of John B. Ellison & Sons, who had a legal claim against John A. Marshall. The goods in question, valued at $696.46, had been sent from a New York mercantile firm to Marshall and were marked C.O.D. (Collect on Delivery). The express company, represented by the American Merchants’ Union Express Co., withheld delivery until payment was made. Marshall falsely assured the express agent that his check would clear and induced him to release the goods without payment by presenting a check dated for future collection. However, at the time, Marshall was bankrupt, owing over $20,000 and had no funds. The express company claimed the goods were fraudulently obtained and sought their return. The jury initially ruled in favor of Willsie, leading to this appeal by the express company, which argued that the jury was misled regarding the fraudulent nature of the transaction.	The American Merchants’ Union Express Co. argued that the merchandise had been obtained by fraud as Marshall had no legitimate means to pay for the goods at the time. They contended that since Marshall's actions constituted fraud, he had no valid title to the goods, which meant that no lien could be created in favor of his creditors. The express company sought to recover the goods based on the fraudulent acquisition.	Horace H. Willsie, acting on behalf of his creditors, contended that the jury should not have focused solely on the fraudulent act but rather on prior transactions where goods were released without immediate payment. Willsie maintained that the express company’s agent had acted beyond his authority and that they failed to adequately prove fraud during the trial.

John H. Herrick filed a legal case against Jude P. Gary in the Illinois Supreme Court following issues that arose in the 1860s. The dispute was centered in De Kalb County, Illinois, where both parties owned adjacent farms. Herrick raised five hundred sheep that bordered Gary's property. The core of the conflict involved Gary's responsibility to maintain a division fence between their properties, which he neglected, allowing Herrick’s sheep access to his own diseased flock. Gary's sheep were afflicted with "scab" and "foot-rot," both contagious diseases, and despite being aware of their condition, he did not repair the fence after Herrick’s requests. As a result, Herrick's flock became infected, leading to sickness and death among his sheep, which incurred him considerable expenses. Herrick ultimately brought various claims against Gary based on a statute aimed at punishing the owner of diseased sheep if they let their livestock run at large. After a trial and appeal against a verdict favoring Gary, the case was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court due to procedural issues concerning jury instructions and the interpretation of liability under the law.	The plaintiff, John H. Herrick, asserted that Jude P. Gary was liable for damages caused by allowing his diseased sheep access to Herrick's flock due to Gary's failure to maintain the division fence. Herrick contended that Gary acted with negligence, as he knew his sheep were sick, yet continued to keep them contained in an area where they could infect the neighboring flock. Herrick sought damages resulting from his sheep becoming sick and dying, as well as coverage for additional expenses incurred while caring for his infected sheep, citing the statutory framework governing liability for diseased livestock.	Jude P. Gary, the defendant, claimed that he should not be held responsible as there was insufficient evidence to establish that his sheep directly communicated the disease to Herrick's flock. He argued that the jury's instruction regarding the burden of proof was too high and misled the jury into requiring an unreasonable standard. Furthermore, Gary suggested that Herrick's sheep might have contracted the disease from other sources and asserted that if Herrick's own sheep carried the illness into his flock, it diminished or eliminated his liability. He requested the court to uphold the verdict favoring him based on these principles.

In September 1871, John Wilson, the appellant, owned a tract of land in Warren County, Illinois, which The Rockford, Rock Island & St. Louis R. R. Co. (the appellee) sought to use for its railway. The company required a portion of Wilson's land for its right-of-way. In accordance with the statute, commissioners assessed the damages to Wilson at $350 and filed their report with the circuit court. Both parties appealed to the circuit court, which then moved the case to Knox County. There, a jury upheld the commissioners' valuation, awarding Wilson the same amount of $350 specifically for the right-of-way while denying any additional damages. Wilson contested the jury's verdict and sought an appeal, claiming that the jury's decision was against the weight of evidence, that improper evidence had influenced the jury, that erroneous instructions were given, and that the judgment did not comply with statutory requirements. The railroad company was incorporated under an act in 1865, and the petition for the right-of-way was presented in Warren County in September 1870, following the procedures outlined in the act of 1852.	John Wilson argued that the jury's verdict was against the evidence, asserting that his land's market value was significantly higher than the assessed $350. He contended that the compensation should reflect the true value of the land taken for the railroad and should not disregard the benefits accruing from its construction. Wilson sought to prove that the evaluation did not account for the true market price and raised issues with the evidence and jury instructions provided during the trial.	The Rockford, Rock Island & St. Louis R. R. Co. defended the jury's verdict, arguing that the assessment made by the commissioners was correct and properly reflected the value of the land taken. They contended that the trial followed the statutory requirements and that Wilson's argument regarding the jury's instructions and the evidence presented was unfounded. The defendant requested that the court uphold the jury’s decision and maintain the judgment in their favor.

In the case of The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company v. James C. Lackey, which was adjudicated in June 1875 by the Illinois Supreme Court, the background involved several incidents in Marion County, Illinois, during the year 1869, where three individuals were fatally struck by trains operated by the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company. James C. Lackey, serving as the coroner of Marion County at the time, conducted inquests for each fatality. The case arose when Lackey sought reimbursement for the total costs incurred from these inquests and subsequent burial expenses, amounting to $91.15, from the railway company. The legal issue centered around the interpretation of a law enacted by the Illinois General Assembly in 1855, which stipulated that railroad companies were liable for such expenses. The railway company contested this liability, claiming the statute was unconstitutional, as it imposed costs on them without requiring the establishment of negligence or fault on their part, which contradicted standard legal principles.	James C. Lackey, the coroner, claimed that as per the 1855 statute, the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company was liable for the expenses related to the inquest and burial of individuals who died due to incidents involving the railway. He sought a judgment entitling him to recover the total amount of $91.15 from the railway company, arguing that the statute granted him the right to sue for such costs regardless of any negligence or fault.	The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company argued that the 1855 statute was unconstitutional because it unjustly imposed liability on railroad companies for expenses arising from incidents where they had committed no violation of the law or exhibited negligence. The company contended that the costs associated with fatal accidents should typically fall to the deceased's estate or, in the absence of funds, to the county, and that it was unreasonable to place such burden solely on the railway companies without evidence of wrongdoing.

John Dunstedter v. Jacob Dunstedter is a legal case from 1875 that took place in Madison County, Illinois. The case involved a dispute between John Dunstedter (the plaintiff) and his son Jacob Dunstedter (the defendant) over the possession of a barn located on a town lot. Both parties claimed ownership of the barn, which had been built after the father sold an undivided interest in the property to his son in 1860. The father claimed he had permitted his son to build the stable, while the son contended that he built and paid for it himself. They both used the barn for a significant period, raising questions about the terms and understanding under which it was occupied. The case escalated to an appeal after the initial ruling favored Jacob Dunstedter. The Illinois Supreme Court ultimately examined the nature of their occupancy and agreements, or lack thereof, regarding the barn and property.	John Dunstedter claimed that he was the rightful owner of the barn and sought to regain possession from Jacob Dunstedter. He asserted that, despite having authorized his son to build the barn, an agreement regarding possession and occupancy had never been finalized, thus giving him the legal right to reclaim the property.	Jacob Dunstedter defended his possession of the barn by arguing that he either had permission from his father to build the barn or that he acted as his father’s agent. He maintained that their long-term shared occupancy implied a mutual agreement, although he failed to provide clear evidence of such an understanding. Jacob asserted that he had been given the resources by his father to erect the barn, which supported his claim to keep exclusive possession.

A. B. Stickney and James J. Hill, on behalf of Stickney & Co., brought a legal action against William C. Goudy in the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking damages for an alleged breach of contract. This case originated from contracts executed on May 28, 1880, which involved Goudy’s agreement to procure the right of way for a railway project and the associated financial arrangements with Stickney & Co. The dispute arose when Goudy failed to perform his obligations under these contracts. Stickney & Co. paid an initial amount of $20,000, but disputes over the performance led to multiple extensions and ultimately Goudy’s refusal to fulfill his obligations. The situation was complicated by allegations that Goudy sold trust-held shares and a promissory note without permission, effectively defrauding Stickney & Co. The case previously went to equity court, where it was argued that the issues of contract performance and the payment of damages had been previously determined. The Illinois Supreme Court had to evaluate whether the previous equity ruling barred the current action based on principles of res judicata.	The plaintiffs, A. B. Stickney and James J. Hill, claimed that William C. Goudy breached their contract by failing to perform his obligations regarding the railway project, leading to financial damages. They requested compensation for the sums previously paid and asserted that Goudy’s actions constituted fraud, as he disposed of trust property in violation of the agreements. The plaintiffs sought a legal determination to assess damages suffered due to Goudy’s alleged breaches.	William C. Goudy defended himself by arguing that the claims were barred due to a prior judgment in an equity case concerning the same contracts, which involved issues of performance and damages that had already been resolved in his favor. He contended that the equity court had found that the plaintiffs had no equitable claim, thus should not be permitted to relitigate the same matters in this case. Goudy asserted that all contractual obligations had been fulfilled per the terms of their agreements, and that any delays or failures were attributable to the plaintiffs.

In 1886, in Chicago, Illinois, Leopold Schlesinger and David Mayer filed a lawsuit against James B. Keifer and Nora B. Keifer for goods sold and delivered. The plaintiffs claimed that during September, October, and November of that year, they sold merchandise totaling $348.95 to Nora B. Keifer at her request, meant for the family’s expenses, which they argued made both defendants liable for payment. Only James B. Keifer was served with the summons, as Nora B. Keifer could not be found. The case was tried without a jury, and the trial court ruled in favor of the defendants, denying the plaintiffs’ request for a new trial and entering judgment for costs in favor of the defendants. Despite the Appellate Court affirming the ruling, they certified that the case involved significant legal questions warranting consideration by the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiffs presented evidence of the marriage status of the defendants and the nature of the goods purchased, while the defendants contended they were living separately during the purchase of the items, therefore not constituting a family needing supplies, and later divorced.	The plaintiffs sought recovery for the amount of $348.95 for goods sold to Nora B. Keifer, claiming that these purchases were necessary family expenses made at her request during the time when she and James B. Keifer were married and living together. They argued that both defendants should be jointly liable for the payment.	The defendant James B. Keifer contested the claims by pleading non assumpsit, asserting he was not jointly liable with Nora B. Keifer as they were living separately at the time the goods were purchased. He also highlighted that the trial court's decision regarding evidence and the legal interpretation of their marriage status was correct, reducing any liability in this case.

The case of "Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railroad Company v. The City of Chicago" was decided in September 1870 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The background of the case involves a special assessment levied for the improvement of Clark Street in Chicago, specifically for curbing and filling activities spanning from the south line of Twelfth Street to the north line of Eighteenth Street and from the south line of Eighteenth Street to the north line of Twenty-Second Street. Prior to the passage of the ordinance for this assessment, significant portions of the work had already been completed by private individuals and a railroad company. The ordinance included language that excluded portions of work deemed to have been done “in a suitable manner.” However, there was no formal determination by the city council regarding what constituted suitable work or what had been completed. The court found that responsibility for such determinations rests with the common council, asserting that the ordinance unintentionally conferred excessive discretionary power to the Board of Public Works, which could lead to potential fraud and favoritism. The court ultimately determined that the ordinance was void, leading to further legal challenges based on the assessment process and arrangements made by the Board of Public Works.	The Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railroad Company claimed that the special assessment imposed by the City of Chicago was not legitimate due to the absence of clarity regarding which portions of the work had been previously completed. They argued that the ordinance directing the assessment was void, as it improperly delegated authority from the common council to the Board of Public Works, which could result in unfair or fraudulent assessments. The plaintiffs requested the court to reverse the judgment stemming from the lower court's decision on the assessment.	The City of Chicago defended itself by asserting that the ordinance was valid and legally sound, adequately describing the intended improvements and exceptions for previously completed work. The defense contended that the assessment was made according to the established processes, and that evidence of prior work should not impact the legitimacy of the assessment. They sought to maintain the assessment and uphold the council's authority in this matter.

The case "The Trustees of Schools v. David Schroll et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 12, 1887. It originates from Morgan County, Illinois, revolving around Fractional Section 16, designated for school use. The Trustees of Schools claimed they owned a portion of this land, which had been platted and intended for sale since the mid-1800s, but no bids were received initially. They later sold specific lots to individuals, Edward Watson and Edward Lusk, who received patents for lots within the fractional section. The defendants, represented by David Schroll and his partners, argued that they possessed the property due to these sales and a claim of adverse possession for the past twenty years. The case hinged on the interpretation of land ownership rights concerning a body of water referred to as Meredosia Lake, determining whether the defendants had legal claim to it as riparian owners or based on other legal principles. The trial concluded with the defendants prevailing in the lower court, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiffs (Trustees of Schools) contended that they held legal rights to land in Fractional Section 16, which included areas adjacent to Meredosia Lake. They referenced an enabling act from Congress and an ordinance from the Illinois Constitutional Convention that enabled them to sell or lease school lands. They argued that the defendants lacked legal basis for their claims and contended that any such claims over the water body were unjust because the original land grants to the school trustees were clear and legitimate.	The defendants (Schroll, Boles & Co.) claimed ownership based on their long-held possession of the land and water claimed in the suit. They argued that historical sales of land adjacent to the lake carried with them rights to the water, as the grants were presumed to extend to the center of the lake. They also invoked the principle of adverse possession, asserting that their consistent possession over the contested area for over twenty years had established their legal claim. The defendants maintained that the plaintiffs had effectively sold the water rights when they sold the adjoining land.

In 1874, Roland Whitney filed a lawsuit against U. G. Stevens in the Circuit Court of Jasper County, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute over a tax title that Stevens had acquired for a quarter section of land in Jasper County. The land had been sold for non-payment of taxes in 1860, and Stevens subsequently obtained a deed from the sheriff in 1864. Despite the land being vacant until 1872-1873, Stevens consistently paid taxes for seven years before taking possession. Whitney's claim sought to set aside this tax title, arguing that irregularities in the sale process invalidated Stevens's title. The case was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court following the dismissal of Whitney's complaint by the circuit court, which found no grounds for Whitney to claim relief.	Whitney argued that the proceedings that led to the tax sale were flawed, which entitled him to challenge Stevens's title to the land. He maintained that the tax deed should be set aside as it constituted a cloud on his title. Whitney's legal request was to invalidate Stevens's ownership based on the alleged errors surrounding the tax sale procedure.	Stevens contended that he acquired the land through a valid tax deed obtained in good faith, having paid taxes consistently for seven years on the vacant property before taking possession. He asserted that even if the tax sale were technically flawed, the legitimate stream of tax payments and his sworn possession of the land established a clear title. Stevens argued that Whitney should seek resolution through an action of ejectment in a court of law, rather than through equity.

The case "Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Elizabeth Hutchinson, Adm’x, etc." took place in June 1868 in Cairo, Illinois. Elizabeth Hutchinson, acting as the administratrix for her deceased husband, Alexander Hutchinson, initiated a lawsuit against the Illinois Central Railroad Company in the Alexander Circuit Court. The claim stemmed from an incident where Alexander Hutchinson was killed by a train operated by the railroad while crossing the track. The accident occurred during the evening when it was dark. Hutchinson was reported to have been drinking, and his location at the time of the accident was disputed among witnesses. Testimony varied regarding whether the train’s bell was ringing or if a headlight was present on the locomotive, but consensus held that there was no headlight. The railroad company was accused of negligence for failing to take adequate safety precautions despite the public nature of the street along which their tracks ran.	Elizabeth Hutchinson argued that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent in its operation of the train, specifically for failing to utilize a headlight, ring a bell, or sound a whistle while the train was traveling along a public street. She contended that these failures contributed directly to her husband's death, and she sought compensation under the act of February 12th, 1853, which allows for recovery in cases involving wrongful death due to the neglect or wrongful acts of a company.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company maintained that Hutchinson was grossly negligent for placing himself on the tracks while intoxicated, especially in the dark. They asserted that if the jury believed he was drunk and failed to exercise care, he should be deemed responsible for his own death. The defense argued that unless it could be proven that company agents acted willfully or with gross neglect contributing to the accident, they should not be held liable.

In April 1866, the case of Walter E. Lewis v. The Galena and Chicago Union Railroad Company was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a shipment of grain, specifically barley, oats, and wheat, which were shipped from Lane Station on the Galena and Chicago Union Railroad. The key individuals involved in the case were Walter E. Lewis, a banker who had advanced money on behalf of the grain buyer R. P. Burlingame, and the commission merchants Campbell & Woodruff in Chicago. The grain was initially consigned to Campbell & Woodruff, but Burlingame intended for the proceeds to pay off drafts he had drawn that had been endorsed by Lewis. He attempted to change the destination of the shipment to Lewis to ensure payment of the drafts, following conversations implying such consent. However, the railroad company refused to alter the shipment direction, asserting they were obliged to deliver the grain to Campbell & Woodruff, resulting in Lewis not receiving the proceeds of the sale of the grain. The case focused on whether Lewis had the right to redirect the shipment to himself, considering the arrangements made with the involved parties.	Walter E. Lewis claimed that he was the rightful owner of the grain shipment and sought a replevin for its delivery. He argued that there had been an understanding that the proceeds from the grain would be used to satisfy his drafts that Burlingame had endorsed. Lewis maintained that the railroad company wrongfully refused to honor the change of shipment, leading to his financial loss as the grain was subsequently delivered to Campbell & Woodruff.	The Galena and Chicago Union Railroad Company defended its actions by asserting that it had fulfilled its obligations by delivering the grain to the original consignees, Campbell & Woodruff. The railroad company claimed that it had not been informed properly about the change in destination before the grain's delivery, stating that they were not authorized to redirect the grain without proper documentation or consent from the original consignees.

The case "The Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Co. v. Lorenzo D. Morris" took place in January 1873, in Illinois. Key individuals involved included Lorenzo D. Morris, the plaintiff, who provided care services, and The Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Co., the defendant, whose brakeman, O’Conner, was severely injured while on duty at the Paris station. Following his injury, the conductor of the train directed O’Conner to Morris's house for care and immediately communicated the situation to the company's officers. The subsequent legal action arose over whether the railroad company was liable for the expenses incurred by Morris for taking care of O’Conner, given their failure to notify Morris about their intention not to cover the cost of services rendered. The nature of the injury was severe, necessitating five weeks of care, which included an amputation of O'Conner's arm. The primary question was the company's liability for the medical services provided.	The plaintiff, Lorenzo D. Morris, claimed that he was entitled to compensation for the reasonable value of care services he provided to O’Conner at the request of the railroad company's conductor. He argued that since the company was informed about the situation and failed to communicate any intention not to pay for the services, it should be held liable. Morris initially sought $90, which was increased to $100 during the trial based on the extensive care required.	The defendant, The Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Co., contended that the damages awarded to Morris were excessively high and not adequately supported by evidence. They suggested that the company should not be held liable since they claimed no responsibility for the expenses incurred if they had not been formally notified about the care arrangements. However, they did not dispute the fact that Morris rendered the care required by O’Conner after the conductor's request.

Oliver C. Vanlandingham was the plaintiff in error in a legal case against Evan Huston, the defendant in error. The case began in June 1846 at the Gallatin Circuit Court, Illinois, before being transferred to the White County Circuit Court, where it was tried in April 1847. The key issue was a claim for compensation for work and labor performed by Huston. Vanlandingham entered a plea of the general issue, claiming that payment had been made and that he had not undertaken any obligations within the five years preceding the suit. Huston countered that Vanlandingham had indeed made an undertaking within that timeframe and also that he had been outside the jurisdiction of the court for much of that period. Following a trial, the jury found in favor of Huston, awarding him $1270. Vanlandingham subsequently filed a motion for a new trial, asserting that the court had given improper instructions, but the motion was denied. The focus of the legal proceedings primarily revolved around the interpretation of the Statute of Limitations and the correctness of the jury instructions provided by the court.	Evan Huston's main arguments revolved around his claim for compensation, asserting that he had performed services for which he was entitled to payment. He maintained that despite Vanlandingham’s claims about the Statute of Limitations, exceptions applied due to previous promises and his intermittent absence from the jurisdiction, which prevented the Statute from barring his claims.	Oliver C. Vanlandingham’s defense included a plea of the Statute of Limitations, arguing that the claims made by Huston were invalid as they had occurred more than five years prior to the lawsuit. He contended that his brief absences from Illinois for business did not affect the residence status necessary to invoke the Statute, which he argued should dismiss Huston's claims.

The case of John Titley et al. v. The Enterprise Stone Company was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1889. The dispute originated from a contract made on March 20, 1885, between the Enterprise Stone Company and J. & J. Titley for the delivery of rubble stone from the Company's quarry in Chicago. Under the agreement, the Titleys were to receive a specified quantity of stone at a rate of seven dollars per cord, with stipulations on delivery timing and payment. As the case progressed in the Superior Court of Cook County, the plaintiff (Enterprise Stone Company) claimed that the Titleys had failed to pay for the stone delivered as per their agreement. Conversely, the Titleys alleged that the quantity and quality of the stone delivered were inadequate and that the delivery delays had caused them damage due to a fall in market prices. The trial involved intricate factual disputes about the quantity, quality, and timing of the stone deliveries, with evidence presented regarding the Titleys' acceptance of the stone and their subsequent sales of it, as well as their payment behavior after deliveries were made.	The plaintiff, Enterprise Stone Company, claimed that it had delivered stone as per the contract and sought payment for the balance owed, amounting to $5,000. They argued that the Titleys had accepted the stone deliveries, did not raise any quality objections at the time of acceptance, and continued to sell portions of the stone, implying satisfaction with the quality provided.	The defendants, Titley et al., contended that the Enterprise Stone Company failed to deliver the quantity of stone specified within the agreed time, resulting in financial losses due to a declining market price for stone. They sought to recoup damages based on these alleged failures, arguing that the quality of the stone delivered was not what was agreed upon and that they were hampered in their operations due to these shortcomings.

In January 1876, the case of Theodore M. Walker v. Mary Jane Coleman was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in McLean County, Illinois, involving the plaintiff, Mary Jane Coleman, a married woman living separately from her husband. At the time of the events, she was residing with her husband and sought to purchase a farm. The defendant, Theodore M. Walker, was a real estate agent in Bloomington who facilitated the sale of the "Wilcox farm" and certain lands in Kansas. Coleman's husband acted as her agent in negotiating for the purchase, but misrepresented the price of the Kansas lands during the transaction. Coleman paid Walker $350 and signed a promissory note for $450, believing the lands were priced at $5 per acre, when in fact, they were only $2.50 per acre. When Coleman discovered the true price, she realized her husband had misappropriated the funds and the note without her consent. This led her to file a lawsuit against Walker for the money he received, claiming he acted in collusion with her husband, impacting her rights.	Mary Jane Coleman claimed that Theodore M. Walker had wrongfully received $350 from her and a promissory note for $450, which she never intended for her husband to obtain. She argued that Walker, as the seller's agent, should have known that her husband did not have authority to appropriate those funds for himself, thereby committing fraud upon her. Coleman sought to recover the money, asserting that Walker's actions constituted unjust enrichment.	Theodore M. Walker argued that he was not directly responsible for the misrepresentations made by Coleman's husband and denied any agency relationship with her. He maintained that he had acted in good faith based on the information provided by her husband, who claimed to have discussed the deal with Coleman. Walker contended that there was a legitimate transaction, as the husband had indicated Coleman was aware of the pricing and had consented to the arrangement.

In 1874, a property exchange took place between Simeon S. Burke and Betsey P. Grant in Cook County, Illinois. Simeon owned a Chicago lot mortgaged for $1,000 and acquired Grant's farm, which was under a $3,000 mortgage. As part of this transaction, both parties assumed each other's mortgages. After the exchange, Samuel W. Burke, Simeon's brother, visited the Grant farm and agreed to help Simeon with the mortgage on the Chicago lot. During this visit, it was claimed that he told Mrs. Grant that their personal property, which included livestock and farming equipment, would be compensated for by discharging the $1,000 mortgage on her property. The personal property was eventually sold to Simeon under the assumption that it would satisfy the mortgage debt. When the time came for payment, Mrs. Grant was not informed of any outstanding debts until several years later. The case arose when Betsey P. Grant sought a court declaration that the $1,000 mortgage was satisfied, arguing that Samuel Burke's actions and assurances constituted an agreement to release the mortgage.	The plaintiff, Betsey P. Grant, claimed that she had been led to believe by Samuel W. Burke that the mortgage on her property would be discharged in exchange for the transfer of her personal property to Simeon Burke. She argued that, based on Samuel's representations, it was inequitable for him to enforce the mortgage, which she believed had been satisfied through the transactions. Grant sought an injunction against the sale of her property and an official declaration that the mortgage was paid off.	The defendants, represented by Huldah E. Burke as administratrix of Samuel W. Burke's estate, argued that no formal agreement was made to release the mortgage. They contended that the transaction lacked the necessary legal documentation to invalidate the existing mortgage and asserted that the plaintiffs could not rely on verbal assurances to alter the legally binding mortgage agreement. Furthermore, they suggested that the evidence presented supported the notion that the mortgage remained in effect despite the discussions of release.

Sarah L. Savage v. Joseph Eakins, decided on January 21, 1889, involves a legal dispute concerning the sale of a stallion named Black Diamond. The case takes place in Le Roy, Illinois. John B. Savage sold the horse to Joseph Eakins for $1,200, which included $500 cash, a note for $500 secured by collateral, and another horse valued at $200. The plaintiff, Joseph Eakins, claimed that Savage provided a verbal warranty regarding the horse's quality at the time of sale, a warranty that was later documented in writing. The written warranty, executed on January 7, 1886, stated that Black Diamond was sound, a good covering horse, and capable of producing quality offspring. The transaction was complicated by the relationship between John B. Savage and his wife, Sarah L. Savage, who was identified as the horse's owner. The court had to determine whether John B. Savage acted as Sarah's agent with the authority to sell and warrant the horse. The jury concluded that he did, and ultimately, the court affirmed the jury's decision.	The plaintiff, Joseph Eakins, claimed that John B. Savage breached a warranty made for the stallion Black Diamond at the time of sale. Eakins asserted that the horse was not as represented and demanded compensation for the breach of warranty.	The defendant, Sarah L. Savage, argued that her husband did not have the authority to warrant the horse for sale, claiming that if he could sell, he had no authority to make claims regarding the horse's quality. Additionally, she contended that Eakins had given his husband exclusive credit, which should have absolved her of responsibility.

The case, "The People, for use of Logan County, v. William Toomey et al.", was filed on September 27, 1887, in the Illinois Supreme Court. It centers around William Toomey, who served as the county clerk of Logan County from December 1881 to December 1882. Following Toomey's term, C. M. Knapp was elected as his successor and took office on December 4, 1882. The legal dispute arose concerning Toomey's official bond obligations, specifically his actions regarding fees earned during his term. Toomey submitted a bill amounting to $2,133.18 for services rendered, which was presented to the Board of Supervisors by his successor, Knapp. Although Toomey made a report showing a surplus of $414.23 in fees, he received the full amount without repaying the excess into the county treasury. The board subsequently directed Knapp to draw an order for the full claim to Toomey. The plaintiffs aimed to hold Toomey's sureties liable for the unreturned funds after the end of his term.	The People, representing Logan County, claimed that the sureties on Toomey’s official bond should be liable for the payment of $2,133.78, which Toomey received after his term had ended. They argued that Toomey, having failed to remit fees back to the county treasury, left his sureties responsible under the terms of his bond, which required him to perform his duties faithfully throughout his term.	The defendants, Toomey's sureties, contended that they could not be held liable for payments made after Toomey's term of office had expired. They argued that the bond explicitly covered Toomey's performance during his term, and any obligations arising thereafter were beyond the bond's scope. In essence, they maintained that the county had improperly authorized the payment to Toomey, who was no longer in office, relieving the sureties of any responsibility for the unreturned funds.

Virgninus A. Turpin, as Receiver for the Fidelity Savings Bank, initiated an ejectment action against the Baltimore, Ohio and Chicago Railroad Company in 1882 in Cook County, Illinois. The case revolved around a strip of land located within lots 11 and 13 of Seip’s subdivision, which the railroad company occupied as a right of way since its construction in 1874. The key individuals involved included Virginius A. Turpin, Chauncey T. Bowen (the previous landowner), and various parties including the Fidelity Savings Bank, Honoré, and Abell, who were involved in property transactions related to the land. The dispute stemmed from Bowen's claim that he had verbally agreed to provide the railroad with the right of way, despite having a written contract for such an agreement dating back to May 13, 1874. The railroad utilized this access in operations, and the plaintiff contended that the land rights had not been legally transferred to the railroad.	The plaintiff, Turpin, argued that the railroad company's claim to the right of way was not valid as it relied upon a verbal promise made by Bowen, which he contended was revocable and lacked consideration. He asserted that the company should not have possession of the land since there was no formal grant or conveyance of the right of way, thus requesting the court to eject the railroad from the property occupying lots 11 and 13. The plaintiff's primary legal request was to regain possession of the land they claimed rights over.	The defendant, the Baltimore, Ohio and Chicago Railroad Company, countered that their possession of the land was based on a valid written contract with Bowen, which included provisions for the right of way. They maintained that Bowen had indeed agreed to provide the railroad access in the formal contract, and thus, their occupancy was legal. The railroad requested the court to affirm their right to remain on the land and dismiss the plaintiff's claims of ejectment on the basis that the plaintiff was not wrongfully kept out of possession.

The case, "The City of Chicago v. James Stinson," originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, on March 11, 1886, involving a dispute over a parcel of land in a subdivision in Chicago. The plaintiff, James Stinson, sought to recover a strip of land that was a part of lot 31 in his subdivision. The trial conducted without a jury concluded on October 22, 1887, with the court ruling in favor of Stinson. The core of the city's defense was based on the claim that the disputed land had been dedicated as part of a street (Jones or Paulina Street) due to its use over time, arguing for a common law dedication. The city contended that they had the right to the property because it had been utilized for public purposes and had a public road planned to connect with Archer Avenue, thereby impeding Stinson's ownership. The defense was weakened by evidence that Stinson had never granted permission for any street usage and that he paid taxes on the land in question for over twenty years.	Stinson claimed rightful ownership of the land, arguing that there was no clear evidence of his intention to dedicate the land to public use. He maintained that the city had no legal claim to his property, as he was unaware of any street existing on his lot. Stinson asserted the validity of his title and requested the court affirm his ownership over the disputed strip.	The City of Chicago contended that the strip of land in question had been dedicated as a public street through its long-term use by the public, asserting that the owner’s silence and inaction over the years indicated an intention to dedicate the land. The city argued that through historical usage and partial improvements of the lot, a common law dedication should be recognized, and thereby sought to prevent Stinson from claiming exclusive ownership.

The case of Village of Momence v. Charles B. Kendall took place in Kankakee County, Illinois, and was decided on February 29, 1884. The central issue arose from an excavation for a cellar at a property owned by Knightheart, which was located along Front Street. The village had permitted this excavation, and as a result, large rocks were placed in the sidewalk to deter pedestrians. On the night of March 13, 1882, the plaintiff, Kendall, who was well-acquainted with the site, attempted to cross a plank that had been laid across the cellar corner. The night was dark, and Kendall fell into the cellar, sustaining injuries. He claimed that the Village failed to properly secure the site, thus endangering pedestrians. The construction site posed an obvious hazard, yet Kendall chose to navigate it rather than use alternative routes.	The plaintiff, Charles B. Kendall, argued that the Village of Momence was negligent in not appropriately guarding the excavation site, which led to his fall and subsequent injuries. He claimed that the Village failed to place adequate barriers or warnings to protect pedestrians and sought compensation for damages amounting to $375.	The Village of Momence contended that Kendall was grossly negligent. They argued that he was fully aware of the excavation and its hazards, having helped to dig it and passed by it frequently. The defendant maintained that Kendall had options to avoid the danger and chose to cross the planks carelessly, thus rendering himself responsible for his own injuries.

In December 1851, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case of William Davis against Charles and Thomas Easley concerning an action of replevin for a quantity of boards. The events arose in Schuyler County, Illinois, beginning in February 1849, when two cherry trees were unlawfully felled from a tract of land owned by Davis. The defendants transported the cut trees to a sawmill and converted them into boards before they were recovered by a sheriff. Davis produced evidence including a deed dated April 19, 1836, confirming his ownership of the land, and receipts showing he had paid taxes on it from 1840 to 1848. Historically, Davis had been in possession of the land since 1837 and had made various improvements, including a cabin and orchard, asserting continuous ownership and dominion over the property. Despite this, the trial court excluded his deed and tax receipts from the jury's deliberation. The jury ultimately returned a verdict in favor of the defendants, leading to a judgment against Davis.	Davis argued that he was the rightful owner of the trees and, consequently, the boards made from them. He contended that the act of manufacturing the wood into boards did not change the ownership and claimed his right to recover property wrongfully taken from him. Additionally, he asserted that his evidence and long-term possession of the land under a valid title supported his claims, yet the trial court's exclusion of this evidence severely undermined his case.

The case "Robert McCornack et al. v. Horace L. Sage" was heard in September 1877 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from Knox County, Illinois, involving Robert McCornack as the defendant and Horace L. Sage as the plaintiff. The dispute centered around a written contract dated December 1, 1855, in which McCornack allegedly agreed to sell 20 acres of land to David McConkie. However, it was claimed that there was a misdescription of the property in the contract. Sage, as the assignee of McConkie, sought specific performance of the contract for the correct parcel of land. The defendant, McCornack, denied the execution of the contract and contended that he had not sold the land but had permitted the McConkie family to live on it due to familial obligations. The case was complex, involving issues of property rights, contract execution, and the mental health of Elizabeth McConkie, David's wife, who had been declared insane. The case revolved around whether the defendant had indeed entered into the contract and the validity of the alleged misdescriptions.	Sage argued that a written contract existed for the sale of the land, which mistakenly described the property. He requested the court to decree that McCornack convey the correct land as originally intended in the contract. Sage asserted that McConkie was in possession of the land under that contract, and he sought specific performance to fulfill the agreement.	McCornack denied that he ever executed the contract in question and claimed that he allowed the McConkie family to occupy the land without any intention to sell it. He further argued that the alleged contract was fabricated and that Sage had no legitimate interest in the land or the contract itself. Additionally, he highlighted the long delay in pursuing the claims and the lack of clear evidence supporting Sage's assertions.

The case "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Commissioners of East Lake Fork Special Drainage District" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 15, 1889. It involves the Illinois Central Railroad Company (the defendant) and the Commissioners of the East Lake Fork Special Drainage District (the plaintiff). The controversy arose over special assessments made against the railroad for drainage improvements that the commissioners claimed would benefit the railroad. According to the provisions of the Drainage Act of 1885, the commissioners assessed the railroad a sum in proportion to the benefits received from the drainage work—$200 for the main ditch work and $33.78 for work in a designated sub-district. The railroad company objected to these assessments, arguing that its tracks and property would not receive any benefit from the drainage improvements. The commissioners maintained that the assessments were just and equitable, and the railroad's failure to appeal their classification led to the confirmation of the assessments. The case centers on the legal framework of the assessments, the nature of benefits conferred, and the constitutionality of the statutes involved.	The Commissioners of East Lake Fork Special Drainage District claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company benefited from the drainage improvements made in the district. They argued that the railroad was subject to special assessments based on the benefits it received according to the Drainage Act of 1885, specifically asserting that the railroad should pay an assessment proportional to the benefits from the improvements.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that the assessments were invalid as the nature of its property (the tracks and right of way) could not be benefited for agricultural and sanitary purposes as intended by the Drainage Act. They raised constitutional objections, claiming that the statute under which the assessments were levied was void and that the assessments exceeded the actual benefits received. Additionally, they argued that the assessment process violated the principles of fairness under the law.

In December 1849, the case of Lucien B. Adams et al. vs. The County of Logan reached the Illinois Supreme Court following events in Logan County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, including Adams, had previously donated property and funds to establish the county seat in Postville, with the understanding that the county seat would permanently remain there. They had erected a courthouse and conveyed various lots as part of this arrangement. However, after the Illinois General Assembly authorized the permanent relocation of the county seat to Mount Pulaski, the plaintiffs contended that the previous donations should entitle them to recover damages or reimbursement for their contributions. They argued that the unconditional nature of their donations did not preclude them from claiming compensation upon the relocation. The county, meanwhile, maintained that the legislature had the authority to change the location of the county seat and that the plaintiffs had no legal claim to damages for the removal, as they had donated the property with an understanding of the potential for change.	The plaintiffs claimed they were entitled to compensation due to the relocation of the county seat from Postville to Mount Pulaski, arguing that their donations of property and funds were made with the expectation that Postville would remain as the county seat indefinitely. They sought a judgment for money lent, advanced, and received by the county to cover their losses incurred as a result of this relocation.	The defendant, The County of Logan, argued that the donations made by the plaintiffs were unconditional and did not guarantee the permanence of the county seat at Postville. They asserted that the legislature had the right to change the county seat based on the public good, which negated any claims the plaintiffs might have for damages. Additionally, the defendant contended that any supposed agreements regarding the return of property or funds would need to be explicitly stated in writing, which was not the case here.

William P. Henry brought an action of ejectment against Charles Halloway in September 1875, in La Salle County, Illinois. The case involved a dispute over the possession of lots 8 and 9 in block 49 of the State’s addition to Ottawa. The circuit court heard the case without a jury, resulting in a judgment that awarded Henry possession of lot 9 but ruled in favor of Halloway regarding lot 8. To establish his title, Henry introduced a deed from the trustees of the Illinois and Michigan canal to Andrew J. Galloway, followed by a deed from Galloway to himself. Halloway countered with a tax deed from the city of Ottawa, evidencing a property sale due to non-payment of taxes, which he argued established his rightful ownership of lot 8.	Henry claimed that he was the rightful owner of the disputed properties based on the deeds he presented. He contended that the tax deed introduced by Halloway was improper and that it violated constitutional provisions regarding notification and deed entitlement after a tax sale.	Halloway's defense relied on the validity of the tax deed he possessed, asserting it granted him rightful ownership of lot 8. He argued that the deed served as prima facie evidence of regular compliance with the law governing tax sales, which negated Henry's claim of ownership.

Samuel Holmes and William Stummel were involved in a legal dispute stemming from a contract regarding land clearing work in Illinois in the early spring of 1852. Stummel was hired by Holmes to "clear, grub, and pile the brush" on a specified plot of land south of a road, with the work expected to be completed by April 1, 1853. The agreed payment for Stummel's services was $278, to be distributed in two installments. However, Stummel neglected to grub an entire ravine on the property, which Holmes argued was a breach of their contract. The case was tried in the Marshall Circuit Court, where Stummel initially prevailed, obtaining a verdict for $193.19. The case was then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the contract's terms, the implications of the word "clear," and the necessity of grubbing the ravine were analyzed.	Samuel Holmes asserted that Stummel failed to comply with the contract by not grubbing the ravine, despite being contractually obligated to do so. Holmes argued that the contract explicitly required all areas to be cleared, including the ravine, and that Stummel's neglect constituted a breach. Holmes requested a reversal of the lower court's judgment and insisted on the proper performance of the contract terms without allowing for community customs to excuse Stummel’s failure.	William Stummel contended that he fulfilled his duties according to the contract and implied that Holmes had waived his right to insist on work in the ravine by not directly overseeing Stummel's work. Stummel's defense included evidence suggesting that it was not customary in the area to grub such ravines, asserting that leaving the ravine untouched was a common practice that added utility to the land. Thus, he argued that he should not be held liable for the work not performed in the ravine.

In November 1853, the case of Mary A. Casey v. John P. Baldridge et al. was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a contract that Mary A. Casey entered into with the inhabitants of a school district to teach a common school for one quarter. Casey claimed she was legally qualified to teach, as no objections were raised against her qualifications by the school directors, of which the defendants were members. After teaching according to the contract, she prepared a schedule to claim the school funds for her services but faced a refusal from the defendants to examine and certify the schedule, claiming it was due to a lack of proper certification of her qualifications. The case was heard at the May term of the Jefferson Circuit Court, where a demurrer to Casey’s declaration was sustained, leading to her appeal to the Supreme Court.	Mary A. Casey argued that she had fulfilled her contract to teach a common school and was entitled to the school funds belonging to the district. She claimed she was legally qualified to be a teacher, and there were no formal objections from the school directors concerning her qualifications. She requested the court to compel the defendants to examine and certify her schedule to receive the owed payment for her teaching services.	The defendants, led by John P. Baldridge, contended that Casey did not meet the statutory requirements necessary to receive payment from the school funds. They argued that the law mandated teachers to present a certificate of qualification to the school directors before starting their teaching, which Casey failed to do. Consequently, they maintained that they were not obligated to certify her schedule and denied any breach of duty.

George Hankins was convicted for keeping a gaming house in Cook County, Illinois, in violation of the state's Criminal Code. The conviction occurred at the Criminal Court, where Hankins was fined $250 for the first offense under Section 127 of the Criminal Code. This section outlines penalties for operating a gaming house, where a first offense incurs a fine of not less than $100, while a second offense incurs a significantly larger fine and potential jail time. The case was then appealed to the Appellate Court for the First District, which affirmed the conviction and fine, leading to further appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The defense raised several arguments, including challenges to the jurisdiction of the court, the validity of the imposed fine, and the nature of statutory interpretation regarding penalties. The court examined the legislative intent and the statutory language, concluding that while a minimum fine was set, this did not preclude the imposition of a higher fine under certain circumstances, particularly if necessary to reflect the gravity of the offense.	The primary argument from the plaintiff, represented by George Hankins, was that the Criminal Court exceeded its jurisdiction by imposing a fine greater than the $100 minimum stipulated in the statute for the first offense of keeping a gaming house. Hankins contended that the statute mandated a strict interpretation limiting fines to the minimum defined. Additionally, the plaintiff argued that previous cases established a precedent for interpreting penal statutes restrictively.	The defendant, representing the People of Illinois, contended that the imposed fine was valid and within the court's authority to determine penalties for offenses. They pointed out that the legislature intentionally set no maximum limit for fines for the first offense under the relevant statute, suggesting a broader interpretation of allowed penalties. The defense also emphasized that the discretion given to the courts regarding penalties reflects a legislative intent to allow for varying degrees of punishment based on the specifics of the case.

In the case of Amos J. Snell v. Emanuel J. Buresh et al., filed on November 11, 1887, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the conflict arose in Cook County, specifically in the village of Jefferson. The main parties involved are the plaintiff, Emanuel J. Buresh, and the defendant, Amos J. Snell. Buresh, along with other local property owners, initiated a bill in equity against Snell, who threatened to obstruct the intersection of Milwaukee Avenue and California Avenue by erecting a toll-gate. This action was considered a significant infringement on the rights of the public and property owners, as it interfered with the long-standing use of the avenues as public highways that had been frequented for over twenty years without obstruction. The plaintiffs claimed that Snell's proposed toll-gate would not only obstruct access but would also devalue their properties and disrupt their businesses. Snell maintained that he had the authority to establish a toll-gate as part of his rights acquired from the Northwestern Plank Road Company, which had operated the road for many years. The court had to evaluate whether Snell’s claim of authority to erect the toll-gate could be upheld in light of the potential harm to the local community and property owners.	The plaintiffs, led by Buresh, argued that Snell's erection of a toll-gate at the intersection would create a significant nuisance, obstruct public highways, and cause irreparable harm to their properties and businesses. They requested the court to issue an injunction preventing Snell from continuing with the construction of the toll-gate, asserting that it would adversely affect their access and diminish the value of their properties located near the toll-gate.	The defendant, Snell, contended that he had legal rights to construct the toll-gate based on a charter granted to the Northwestern Plank Road Company, which permitted the establishment of toll-gates along the road since it had been utilized as a toll-road for decades. Snell argued that his actions were in compliance with the law and requested that the court recognize his right to use and operate the toll-road as authorized by statute.

The case involves The Callender Insulating & Waterproofing Company as the appellant and Alpheus C. Badger as the appellee. The legal proceedings took place in April 1889 in Cook County, Illinois. The appellant filed a suit against the appellee, who acted as a guarantor of a promissory note made by Sheridan S. Badger. The promissory note was linked to the consideration of wire, which was central to another recent litigation involving the appellant against Sheridan S. Badger. The case under review had been delayed to give the appellant a chance to seek a review from the Supreme Court. However, the appellant chose not to pursue this option, leading the court to affirm the previous judgment.	The Callender Insulating & Waterproofing Company contended that as the appellant, they were entitled to enforcement of the promissory note against Alpheus C. Badger. They claimed that Badger, as the guarantor, should be held responsible for the debt arising from the promissory note related to the wire product, which had been the subject of previous legal action.	Alpheus C. Badger argued against the enforcement of the promissory note, likely highlighting that the claims made by the appellant were baseless or unjustified. He relied on the prior court decision regarding the litigation involving Sheridan S. Badger, suggesting that the ruling in that case affected the obligations under the guaranty.

In June 1861, in Cumberland County, Illinois, a transaction occurred between James Ewart and Uriah G. Walling. Ewart was indebted to Walling for approximately $700. To secure this debt, Ewart and his wife executed a deed of conveyance for certain town lots, which appeared to be an absolute transfer of ownership. Simultaneously, Walling executed a bond for reconveyance, stipulating that if Ewart paid back the debt with interest within three years, the lots would be returned to him. Ewart expressed concerns about potential legal actions that might lead to losing the property and wanted to secure Walling's interest while retaining the option to redeem the property. Despite the deed's apparent finality, evidence suggested both parties intended the transaction to serve as a mortgage rather than an outright sale. This belief was reinforced by the agreement that Ewart could occupy the property rent-free for three years, the considerable value of the property compared to the debt, and Ewart's ongoing possession of the property.	Walling claimed that Ewart executed the deed to secure the repayment of the debt. He sought a court order for an accounting of the amount owed to him and demanded that Ewart pay the balance. If Ewart failed to pay, Walling requested that the property be sold to satisfy the debt. Walling framed the transaction as a mortgage disguised as a conveyance.	Ewart admitted to the debt and the execution of the deed and bond but argued that the deed was not meant to be a mortgage. He claimed it was an absolute transfer of ownership in full satisfaction of the debt, asserting that he had the right to repurchase the property by paying back the original amount, which he believed mitigated the need for Walling to classify the transaction as a mortgage.

Jacob Ferkel, a town marshal or police officer for the town of Columbia, was indicted by the Grand Jury of Monroe County for extortion under the Criminal Code. The indictment stemmed from an incident on August 3, 1884, where Ferkel allegedly misrepresented having a justice of the peace summons against Frederick Take and extorted him of $12.15 by claiming this fee was due for serving said summons. The county court convicted Ferkel, fining him $25 and the costs of the proceedings after a trial where his motions to quash the indictment and for a new trial were denied. Ferkel appealed the decision, arguing that the indictment was faulty since it did not assert that he was authorized to charge fees for his services, a key requirement under the law. He maintained that the payment received was a result of deceit, not a legal fee for any service rendered. The case raised significant issues regarding the sufficiency of the indictment and the evidence pertaining to the alleged offense.	The plaintiff, in this case, represented the state, claiming that Jacob Ferkel engaged in extortion by fraudulently asserting the existence of a summons and collecting $12.15 from Frederick Take under the pretense of a legal fee. The indictment was based on Ferkel's actions that allegedly violated the Criminal Code by unlawfully demanding money without proper legal authority. The prosecution sought to uphold the conviction based on these claims.	Jacob Ferkel's defense centered around the argument that the indictment was fundamentally flawed because it failed to establish that he was legally authorized to charge fees as an officer. He contended that the actions described in the indictment did not constitute extortion under the law, as he had no summons to serve, and the payment was made under false representations about an alleged pending suit. Additionally, Ferkel's defense asserted that the jury’s verdict was against the weight of the evidence presented at trial.

The case titled "The St. Louis Bridge Company v. The City of East St. Louis et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 20, 1887. It originated when the St. Louis Bridge Company, a Missouri corporation that acquired ownership of the Mississippi River bridge connecting East St. Louis and St. Louis in 1879, filed an injunction to prevent the collection of city taxes levied by East St. Louis for the year 1885. The company contended that a significant part of the bridge was situated over the Mississippi River, which is not subject to municipal taxation as it lies over territory that cannot be improved by the city. The assessed value of the bridge and its approaches was $946,000, with city taxes totaling $15,136. The plaintiff argued incessantly that they had not received any municipal protection or services for the heavy taxes paid over the years, totaling $125,000, which they alleged were illegal for portions of the bridge over the river. The case examined the limits of municipal authority regarding taxation and the constitutional implications of taxing properties that are partially submerged under navigable waters.	The St. Louis Bridge Company argued that a large portion of their bridge was located over the Mississippi River and, as such, that this area should not be subject to city taxes because it could not benefit from municipal improvements. They claimed that they had paid substantial taxes to East St. Louis without receiving any protection or services from the city and sought an injunction against the tax collection, asserting that the taxes were levied illegally and unconstitutionally on the part of the bridge situated over the river.	The City of East St. Louis maintained that the taxes levied were valid and subject to constitutional provisions allowing municipal taxation within corporate limits, even over submerged property. The defendant argued that the bridge, though extending over the river, was still within the corporate boundaries of East St. Louis and was thus liable for taxation. They emphasized that the city had jurisdiction over the territory and that the ability to tax does not correlate to direct benefits received by the property owner.

The case "Edward C. Kehr v. William H. Snyder" took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, and was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 13, 1885. At the heart of the dispute was a triangular piece of land on the eastern bank of the Mississippi River, specifically part of lot 233 in the third subdivision of Cahokia commons, with the older boundaries dictated from a survey conducted in 1860. Over time, accretions had formed along the river, altering the original bank line. The plaintiff, William H. Snyder, owned lot 233, positioned north of lot 232, owned by the defendant, Edward C. Kehr. The central issue was the division of these accreted lands; if the original division line was extended to the river’s center without change, the land in dispute would belong to Snyder, whereas a deviation would favor Kehr. The conflicting interpretations of ownership rights concerning the accreted land led to legal arguments surrounding established property laws regarding land adjacent to rivers.	William H. Snyder, the plaintiff, claimed ownership of the disputed land based on the extension of the original boundary lines of his lot, allowing him to assert that under legal precedents, the accretions belonged to him. He argued that a line should be drawn at right angles to the middle thread of the river from the dividing point of lots 233 and 232, indicating that the land in controversy was indeed part of his property. Snyder sought a judgment to confirm his ownership of the land and to have Kehr's claim dismissed.	Edward C. Kehr, the defendant, contended that the accretions should be divided based on a different interpretation that favored his claim to the land. He argued for the adoption of a legal rule that was not only advantageous to him but also, according to his interpretation, was the correct application of the law governing riparian property rights. Kehr asserted that Snyder’s claims lacked substantial legal support and sought for the court to affirm his rights over the disputed land based on his legal arguments.

In the case of City of Bushnell v. Melville F. Metz, the incident occurred on the evening of December 20, 1881, in Bushnell, Illinois. The plaintiff, Melville F. Metz, was a commercial traveler visiting the city. The accident took place at the northeast corner of Main and Hurst streets, where there was an unguarded opening leading to a basement stairway. This opening measured approximately four by eight feet and had a stone coping around it. The railing around the stairway consisted of upright iron rods, which were sharpened at the top. At around 7 PM, during poor visibility due to mist and fog, Metz stumbled upon the coping and fell three or four steps, injuring his hand on the sharp railing. He was unfamiliar with the area and had not noticed the hazardous condition. Metz brought a lawsuit against the city of Bushnell and received a judgment in his favor of $800 for damages related to his injuries. The judgment faced an appeal, but the trial court's decision regarding the plaintiff’s claim and the amount awarded was largely upheld.	The plaintiff, Melville F. Metz, argued that the City of Bushnell was negligent in failing to adequately warn pedestrians about the hazardous and unguarded stairway opening on the sidewalk. He contended that the city was responsible for the lack of safety measures, such as proper lighting and a secure railing, which led to his fall and subsequent injury. Metz sought compensatory damages for the injuries suffered as a result of this negligence, ultimately claiming $800 in damages.	The City of Bushnell, the defendant, contended that the amount of damages awarded to the plaintiff was excessive. They argued that the case should be dismissed or that a lesser amount should have been awarded based on the evidence presented. The defense ultimately focused on questioning the plaintiff's evidence and the trial court's rulings regarding jury instructions and the admissibility of certain testimonies, asserting that the jury had potentially miscalculated the damages.

In 1862, Abner G. Murphy and others initiated a legal action against Hugh Orr in Lawrence County, Illinois, to reclaim a tract of land described as the northeast quarter of the southeast quarter of section nineteen of township three north of range twelve west. The plaintiffs, children of William Y. Murphy and Elizabeth Murphy, aimed to recover the entire premises in fee simple. They provided evidence of a prior transaction involving a judgment against their father that led to the land's sale to George Buchanan, who then conveyed it to the plaintiffs. However, key to the case was a prior decree in chancery that declared their title void due to fraudulent intent to evade creditors. The court of chancery had found that the deed from Buchanan to the children was made in fraud of creditors' rights, thus affecting Abner G. Murphy's claim to the land. Despite objections regarding the legitimacy of the prior decree's effect on Abner due to service issues pertaining to other children's titles, the court ultimately ruled on the basis of existing decrees and misjoinder of parties.	The plaintiffs argued that they held valid title to the land based on the deed from Buchanan. They contested the effectiveness of the prior chancery decree that declared their title void by claiming that procedural errors had occurred in bringing the other defendants to court. They sought legal recognition of their title to recover the land situated in Lawrence County.	The defendant, Hugh Orr, asserted that he held a superior title derived from the same source (William Y. Murphy) and argued that the prior decree in chancery, which voided the plaintiffs' title, was binding on Abner G. Murphy since he was a named party. Orr claimed that the plaintiffs were improperly joined in the action, and thus the case should not proceed as a recovery on their claims.

In the case of Henry H. Hall v. David M. Irwin, the legal proceedings took place in Illinois during December 1845, following a trial that occurred in July 1844. The case originated as an action of ejectment in the Circuit Court of Cass County before being transferred to Sangamon County. The dispute arose over a quarter section of land in Cass County following the death of Thomas Payne, who had made a will directing that his land should be sold for the benefit of his children but did not name an executor. After Payne's death, Benjamin H. Gatton was appointed as the administrator of the estate with the will annexed. Gatton believed he had the authority to sell the land and executed a deed in favor of Hall. However, the heirs of Thomas Payne challenged the validity of the deed, asserting that Gatton, as the administrator, lacked the power to sell the property under the terms of the will. The case hinged on whether an administrator without an appointed executor had the authority to convey the land.	The plaintiff, Henry H. Hall, contended that he had a valid title to the land based on the deed executed by Benjamin H. Gatton, the administrator of the estate. Hall argued that Gatton had the necessary authority to sell the land as the will directed the land to be sold for the welfare of the testator's children. Hall sought legal recognition of his ownership of the property.	The defendants, who were the heirs of Thomas Payne, countered Hall's claims by asserting that Gatton had no legal authority to sell the land since the will did not name an executor and did not explicitly provide such power to an administrator. They maintained that the deed executed by Gatton should be excluded as evidence, as it sought to convey land rights that Gatton lacked the power to convey.

The case of The Kaskaskia Bridge Company v. Joseph P. Shannon et al., decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1844, arose from actions relating to a bridge constructed across the Kaskaskia River. The plaintiffs, the Kaskaskia Bridge Company, were accused of insufficiently constructing the bridge, which had been designated for the defendants, Joseph P. Shannon and others. Legal actions ensued when the defendants filed an assumpsit against the plaintiffs, claiming that four drafts issued by the Kaskaskia Bridge Company for payments associated with the construction work were invalid. These drafts were for various amounts between $150 and $908.49, with claims that they lacked good and valuable consideration, that the bridge was defective, and that the drafts were obtained through fraudulent representations. The controversy unfolded in the Randolph Circuit Court, where evidence of the drafts, bills of exchange, and testimonies were presented, including claims of inadequate oversight and construction management by the plaintiffs. Ultimately, a jury ruled in favor of the plaintiffs for $1,540.11. Consequently, the defendants sought to reverse this decision through a writ of error.	The plaintiffs argued that they rightfully issued drafts based on authorized work completed, as represented by their agents, which entitled them to payment. They contended that the defendants had not validly proved their defenses concerning the drafting's legality and the quality of work done. Their legal request was for enforcement of payment as indicated by the executed drafts.	The defendants countered the plaintiffs' claims with multiple defenses: they asserted non-assumpsit, claimed the drafts were issued without valuable consideration, and provided evidence that the work performed on the bridge was negligently executed, rendering it entirely useless. They sought to establish a set-off for damages amounting to $10,000, arguing that the poor work quality sustained by the plaintiffs justified their refusal to honor the drafts.
