In 1851, Peter Gutzweller was residing in the city of Alton, Madison County, Illinois. He was indicted for unlawfully selling spirituous liquor in quantities less than one quart, violating Illinois state law. In March 1852, Gutzweller was found guilty at the Madison Circuit Court. The controversy revolved around a law enacted in 1851 that prohibited such sales and withdrew the city of Alton's authority to grant licenses for the sale of liquors. Prior to this law, Gutzweller claimed to have had a valid license from the city. However, the state argued that this license was invalid because it was issued after the new prohibitive law came into effect. Gutzweller’s conviction led to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court to determine whether the city retained the power to issue licenses despite the new statute.	Gutzweller's main argument was that he had a valid license issued by the city of Alton, which he believed granted him the authority to sell spirituous liquors. He contended that the law of 1851 did not revoke the city’s power to issue such licenses to its residents. Gutzweller sought a reversal of his conviction based on the legitimacy of his license.	The state, represented by "The People," argued that the 1851 law explicitly repealed the authority of any city, including Alton, to grant licenses for selling spirituous liquors. They contended that this legislation was clear in its intent to revoke any prior licensing authority and that Gutzweller's license was issued without legal authority. Therefore, they requested that the conviction be upheld.

Isaac W. Garvin filed a legal action against Willard Wiswell in September 1876 in DeKalb County, Illinois. The case revolved around a county bond originally payable to John Murphy, which Garvin claimed to own. Garvin testified that he had purchased the bond from Morris Holcomb in 1870, but he lost it in the same year. Wiswell, on the other hand, claimed he bought the bond from E. F. Dutton in July 1870, through his bankers Pierce & Dean, without any knowledge that the bond had been lost or that Garvin had a claim to it. The case turned on whether the legal title to the bond transferred to Wiswell by virtue of his purchase, as the bond was payable to Murphy or bearer, raising issues under Illinois' negotiable instruments statute. The court had to determine if Garvin’s failure to properly indorse the bond meant he retained legal title, despite his claim as the equitable owner.	Garvin's main argument was that he had the rightful ownership of the bond since he purchased it from Holcomb. He asserted that because the bond was payable to Murphy or bearer and had never been indorsed, the legal title had not passed to Wiswell. Therefore, he sought to recover the money Wiswell received from the county treasurer upon its redemption.	Wiswell maintained that he was an innocent purchaser of the bond, having acquired it in good faith from Dutton for full value without knowledge of any issues surrounding its title. He argued that under Illinois law, the legal title to a negotiable instrument could pass by delivery, and since he purchased it without notice of Garvin's claims, he should be protected from Garvin's assertion of ownership.

In September 1871, a legal case arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving Amanda F. Armstrong, the administrator of an estate, against the City of Chicago. The case centered on a special assessment warrant for opening a new street named Campbell Avenue. The plaintiff, Armstrong, appealed from a judgment of the Superior Court that arose from a collector's report. This report included a certificate of publication from the "Chicago Republican" newspaper, purportedly indicating that a notice for judgment had been published ten times between late September and early October 1870. However, evidence was presented that the signer of the certificate, Henry C. Cook, was not the publisher of the newspaper at the time of publication, but rather became the publisher only two months later. This discrepancy raised questions about the validity of the required notice and, consequently, the court's jurisdiction over the case.	The plaintiff, Amanda F. Armstrong, argued that the judgment based on the collector’s report was invalid because the necessary certificate of publication was not properly issued. Armstrong maintained that since the certificate was signed by someone who was not the publisher at the time of the notice's publication, the court lacked the jurisdiction to issue a judgment based on that report. She requested that the case be reconsidered due to this procedural error.	The City of Chicago, represented by Corporation Counsel Mr. M. F. Tuley, defended against the claims by asserting the validity of the notice and the legitimacy of the collector's application for judgment. The defense argued that all procedures had been followed correctly and requested that the court uphold the judgment rendered by the Superior Court, despite the contentions raised by the plaintiff.

Richard Dunnigan filed a case against Eli F. Stevens, administrator of the estate of the deceased O. R. Stevens, in 1886. The case originated from a series of promissory notes made by a man named Kisner to O. R. Stevens, amounting to a total of $7,500, secured by a mortgage on certain lands in Sullivan County, Indiana. These notes were dated January 1, 1881, and had varying maturity dates, the last set to mature on January 1, 1891. After Stevens's death, Dunnigan claimed the amounts due on the notes that had been indorsed to him. His claim was initially disallowed by the county court, leading to an appeal. The circuit court later acknowledged a claimed interest of $560 but denied the claim for the principal amount on the grounds that the notes were not yet due. A suit was also filed by John J. Brake, to enforce his rights on the notes held by him against Kisner and Dunnigan, resulting in a personal judgment for Dunnigan before the maturity of his notes. Dunnigan's claim in the circuit court hinged on whether he was entitled to the principal amount despite the notes not having matured.	Dunnigan's primary argument was that he was entitled to the principal amount of the promissory notes that had been indorsed to him by Stevens’s estate. He argued that the notes technically were negotiable instruments, and despite the fact that they were not yet due, the law in Indiana allowed for claims to be presented in such a manner. Dunnigan contended that even if the notes had not matured, the statutory provision in Indiana allowing creditors to present claims not due for allowance should apply to him.	The defendant's key argument was that the promissory notes were still contingent liabilities, not absolute claims, and thus could not be considered for allowance until due. The defendant pointed out that according to Indiana law, the indorser could not be held liable until the notes matured. Since the relevant legal proceedings and judgments did not modify Dunnigan's liability, the defendant maintained that there was no basis to grant the plaintiff’s claim for the principal amount prior to maturity.

The legal case "Joseph Griffin v. The City of Belleville" originated in June 1869 in Belleville, Illinois. The case arose when the City of Belleville sought judgment against certain town lots owned by Joseph Griffin due to a non-payment of a special assessment related to a sewer. This action was initially filed in the County Court of St. Clair County. Griffin appealed the judgment rendered against him, which subsequently led to a challenge in the circuit court. The City moved to dismiss the appeal, arguing that the appeal was improperly filed under the city charter and that the appeal bond submitted by Griffin was insufficient. The circuit court agreed with the City’s arguments and determined that the bond was not in the correct form and could not be amended as the discretion to allow amendments in such cases does not guarantee success. The appeal was dismissed based on these grounds.	Joseph Griffin, the plaintiff, argued that the city’s requirement for payment of the special assessment was unjust and contested the dismissal of his appeal against the judgment. His main legal request was to have the circuit court's decision reviewed and the appeal reinstated, which he believed was improperly dismissed due to a technicality regarding the sufficiency of the bond filed.	The City of Belleville, as the defendant, contended that the appeal filed by Griffin should be dismissed because the bond was insufficient as it was incorrectly executed. They maintained that the bond was not directed to the proper parties involved in the matter, such as the City or the state representatives. Additionally, they argued that the circuit court acted within its discretion when it refused Griffin's motion to amend the bond, as no statutory provision allowed for such an amendment in this context.

In 1869, in Chicago, Illinois, the case of *Samuel Chase et al. v. Charles E. Cheney* arose from allegations against Rev. Charles E. Cheney, the rector of Christ Church, for failing to comply with the Book of Common Prayer during infant baptisms. Cheney was accused of intentionally omitting the words “regenerate” and “regeneration” from the baptism service, based on his conscientious objections. The Bishop of Illinois issued a commission to investigate these claims, appointing three presbyters to present the charges against Cheney. The charges included violations of church law and his ordination vows. Cheney challenged the jurisdiction of the ecclesiastical court, arguing that the commission was improperly constituted and that he had not committed any offenses justifying a trial. The Superior Court of Chicago awarded an injunction to stop the ecclesiastical trial, leading to an appeal by the defendants seeking to dissolve the injunction and allow the church trial to proceed.	The plaintiff, Charles E. Cheney, contended that the ecclesiastical court lacked the authority to try him due to various procedural violations and questioned the legitimacy of the charges against him. He argued that the commission appointed by the Bishop of Illinois was invalid and that he had not received proper notice for the accusations. Cheney sought to enjoin the trial process initiated by the ecclesiastical court, asserting his right to challenge the accusations against him in a civil court.	The defendants, represented by the ecclesiastical court, maintained that the court legitimately had the authority to proceed with the trial based on the presentment made against Cheney. They argued that even if the Bishop could have disregarded the canons in appointing the commission, the ecclesiastical court still had jurisdiction over the matter. They emphasized that the technicalities raised by Cheney did not invalidate the church's authority to discipline its ministers and that the civil court should not interfere with ecclesiastical matters.

The case of Daniel Welker v. John O. Butler took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, with the judgment filed on October 10, 1884. Daniel Welker, the plaintiff, accused John O. Butler, the defendant, of slander, asserting that Butler had made false statements implying that Welker committed larceny. The case reached a jury trial, during which the court allowed details about Welker's general reputation to be introduced as evidence against him. After the jury's verdict favored the defendant, the court upheld the decision, rejecting a motion for a new trial. The court noted that while malice could be implied from the use of slanderous words, this could be countered by context. The instructions provided to the jury were a point of contention, especially regarding the implications of the statements made by Butler and whether they related to a known act that did not constitute felony theft.	The plaintiff, Daniel Welker, claimed that John O. Butler slandered him by accusing him of larceny, seeking damages for the harm done to his reputation. Welker argued that the words used by Butler were not only false but damaging to his character and standing in the community. Furthermore, Welker requested that the court consider the mental suffering he experienced as a result of Butler's statements in determining damages.	John O. Butler, the defendant, countered Welker's claims by arguing that the statements he made were justified and relevant to Welker's actions at the time, specifically that Welker was taking Butler's property with intent to convert it. Butler contended that the words used were not malicious and that the context of the statements mitigated their slanderous nature. He requested the jury find in his favor, asserting that sufficient evidence linked Welker's actions to the meaning of his words.

In September 1870, the case of William McLaughlin v. Lewis W. Thompson was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a legal dispute over property in Aledo, Mercer County. McLaughlin initiated an action of ejectment against Thompson, seeking to recover several lots. The case first went to the Mercer circuit court, where a plea of not guilty was filed by Thompson. The jury ultimately rendered a verdict in favor of McLaughlin, prompting Thompson to appeal the decision to the Supreme Court. The central issues revolved around the legitimacy of the tax title held by McLaughlin compared to Thompson's patent title. The court specifically examined the validity of a tax deed related to the property, questioning whether the tax had been correctly levied according to applicable laws. The court found that the county commissioners had improperly levied taxes at an unauthorized time, rendering the tax deed legally void.	McLaughlin claimed that he had established a valid tax title to the property in question. He argued that the tax deed was legitimate and that the jury should recognize his title, which entitled him to recover the lots from Thompson. McLaughlin requested the court affirm the previous ruling in his favor, contesting Thompson’s claims and underlying title.	Thompson's primary defense focused on the assertion that McLaughlin's tax title was not valid. He contended that the title was based on an illegally levied tax, which should negate any claim by McLaughlin. Thompson argued that he had an actual patent title and that he and those claiming through him had resided on the property for seven years, suggesting that this occupancy should protect his rights to the land regardless of McLaughlin’s claims. He sought to have the court reverse the lower court’s judgment due to these legal errors.

In 1855, the case of William H. Woodward v. William S. Blanchard was held in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a dispute over a piece of land located in Henry, Marshall County, Illinois. The legal proceedings began after Blanchard filed an action of ejectment against Woodward, claiming he was the rightful owner of lot number 280, as indicated in the town plat. The trial took place after Blanchard's claims were submitted for trial without a jury, resulting in the lower court ruling in favor of Blanchard, stating that he was seized of the property in fee simple. The plaintiff presented evidence of a patent for the land from the State of Illinois, obtained through a sale made for school purposes. The defendant, Woodward, also presented a deed from the Auditor of Public Accounts, claiming he acquired the property after the lot was stricken from tax rolls for non-payment and had held the property through his grantor, Chester S. Woodward. This case centered around the legal validity of the transfer of title under the state's laws regarding property and tax forfeiture.	Blanchard's primary claim was based on his ownership of the land through a patent granted by the State of Illinois and subsequent deed from Albert Reeves. He contended that he rightfully possessed the title and sought restoration of the property as he had been deprived of it. Blanchard asserted that his ownership and the evidence provided constituted lawful and sufficient proof of title under state law.	Woodward's defense rested on the assertion that he held a valid title acquired through a deed from the Auditor of Public Accounts, highlighting that he had possession of the lot for several years, paid taxes, and made improvements on the property. He argued that the statute of limitations protecting claims of title due to tax sales applied, and contended that the evidence presented by Blanchard was inadequate to prove a superior claim of ownership.

The case of Edwards County v. White County was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1877. The dispute arose over the boundary line between Edwards County and White County, located in Illinois. Edwards County claimed that its southern boundary should extend unbroken towards Bon Pas Creek or the Wabash River, in alignment with previous township boundaries. White County, however, argued that the boundary line followed the middle of township layers, resulting in what was known as a “jog.” This dispute was rooted in an act from January 22, 1829, which described the boundary but lacked clear designation for the terminus of the line. Chief Justice Scholfield delivered the opinion, noting that the boundary line's actual location was uncertain due to historical survey errors. In effect, the court examined the original legislative language and considered long-term recognition of the established line by public authorities. The situation was exacerbated by a lack of fixed monuments in the act, leading to ambiguity in the boundary's construction.	Edwards County contended that the disputed boundary line should be a straight extension from the established limits, ignoring the intervening jog where township lines did not align perfectly. They argued for a clear, continuous southwestern extension of their boundary line as originally intended by the legislative act.	White County maintained that the official boundary was the middle of the township tiers, resulting in a broken line or jog at specific ranges. They argued that they had exercised possession over the disputed territory for nearly fifty years, and therefore, they should not be challenged in their boundaries based on historical assumptions about the legislative intent.

The case "Deidrich Ehrich v. Warren White" took place in September 1874 in Kankakee County, Illinois. The key individuals involved include the plaintiff, Warren White, who is seeking damages for an injury sustained by his minor son, H. W. White, and the defendant, Deidrich Ehrich, owner of a saloon where the incident allegedly occurred. The case arose after H. W. White was reported to have become intoxicated after consuming alcoholic beverages, which he claimed he obtained from the defendant's saloon. In the initial trial, the jury ruled in favor of Warren White, awarding him damages of $25. However, during the appeal, the defendant argued that there was insufficient evidence to prove that he provided the liquor to the minor, supported by testimonies from his sons and other witnesses indicating that H. W. White had acquired alcohol from another location.	The plaintiff, Warren White, contended that the defendant unlawfully sold intoxicating liquor to his minor son, resulting in injury to the child. He sought damages for the alleged wrongdoing, asserting that the defendant's actions were negligent and directly caused H. W. White's intoxication.	The defendant, Deidrich Ehrich, argued that the evidence presented was inadequate to establish that he supplied alcohol to H. W. White. His defense was supported by testimonies from his sons, who denied any involvement in providing liquor to the minor, and Ehrich himself claimed he was absent from the saloon during the alleged incident, as he was working on his farm. The defendant sought to overturn the trial court's decision, asserting that the verdict was contrary to the evidence.

John H. B. Willoughby, acting in the interest of Morris M. Armstrong and others, filed a legal case against John S. Dewey in 1870 in Madison County, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute involving the sale of a field of growing wheat, which Willoughby, as a constable, sold under an execution that he had in his possession. Willoughby sought to recover payment for this sale from Dewey. The initial trial resulted in a verdict favoring Dewey, prompting Willoughby to appeal, claiming that the court had erred in rejecting essential evidence regarding the transaction. Specifically, Willoughby argued that the police magistrate's docket indicating the judgment and execution should have been admitted as evidence, contrary to the court's decision. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for review.	The plaintiff, Willoughby, contended that the police magistrate's docket was a necessary piece of evidence to demonstrate the validity of the judgment against Dewey, urging that the original docket, proven to be authentic, should be permissible in court. He requested the Supreme Court to reverse the trial court's judgment and allow the docket as competent evidence to support his claim for the recovery of the price of the wheat sold under execution.	The defendant, Dewey, maintained that the evidence presented by Willoughby, particularly the rejection of the police magistrate's docket, was sound and that the trial court acted appropriately. Dewey's defense focused on the assertion that even if the docket were admitted, it would not sufficiently establish the court's jurisdiction over the subject matter or the person involved. Dewey sought to uphold the verdict of the jury that ruled in his favor and requested that the court affirm the trial court's judgment.

The case of Elisha Freeman et al. v. Gustavus W. Morse was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1858. The dispute centers around a financial transaction involving a note made by G. W. P. and A. B. Bowman to Harris Hoyt, which Hoyt assigned to Morse. The appellants, Freeman and others, held a judgment against Hoyt and received the Bowman note from Morse with the understanding that any collected amount would be applied to their judgment. After collecting about $300 from the note, the appellants executed a judgment against Hoyt’s real and personal property. However, they claimed they could not collect all of Hoyt's property, specifically a melodeon and a carpet, which he refused to relinquish, claiming potential double payment concerning the note. Initially, the Kane Circuit Court ruled in favor of Morse, confirming the appellants' responsibility to remit the collected amount from the note, leading to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the central issue revolved around ownership and rightful collection of the funds from Hoyt's debts.	The plaintiffs, Elisha Freeman et al., asserted that they had a right to the proceeds from the Bowman note for which they provided services. They argued that Morse, who assigned the note to them, owed them the remaining funds collected from it after their judgment against Hoyt had been satisfied. The plaintiffs sought to justify their retention of some proceeds by claiming they had not received all the property from Hoyt during the execution of the sale, and therefore were entitled to compensate for these missing assets.	The defendant, Gustavus W. Morse, contended that the plaintiffs had received funds from the Bowman note but failed to apply it to the existing judgment against Hoyt as agreed. Morse claimed that the plaintiffs were attempting to avoid accountability for the portion of the funds they collected, arguing that the transaction involved was binding and that the plaintiffs had no grounds to retain the proceeds due to the execution sale method they employed.

In March 1870, Hugh Maher executed a note for $10,000 to Leopold Silverman for money loaned. To secure a later note of $15,000, Maher conveyed his property in Bridgeport to Silverman. Subsequent transactions led to the several renewals and extensions of these loans, with various deeds and conveyances involving the property. In June 1872, Maher conveyed the premises for the benefit of his wife, Mrs. Maher, indicating a loan of $25,000 from her, though valuing it higher during the deed transfer. Legal complexities arose over claims of usury, especially as Hugh Maher alleged he had paid interest rates of 1.5% per month, contrasted with Silverman’s claim of 10%. Simplifying matters, Mrs. Maher asserted that the transactions were usurious, while the mortgage and its lien were central factors in the court's deliberations. The Illinois Supreme Court had to determine the validity of the claims related to usury, the role of Mrs. Maher as a purchaser, and the implications of the mortgage extensions.	The plaintiffs, led by Mrs. Maher, claimed that the property should be free of liens due to usury in the original agreement between Hugh Maher and Silverman. They argued that since Mrs. Maher had taken ownership without knowledge of the encumbrance, any agreements made by Silverman with her husband should not hinder her rights to the property. They sought to reduce the amount due based on allegations of usurious practices, insisting they were not liable for payments that included unlawful interest rates.	The defendants, including Martin Lanfrom, contended that the original agreements and subsequent extensions were valid and should enforce the lien against the property. They argued that the extension of time for payment did not discharge the mortgage and that Mrs. Maher, having taken the property with legal notice of the mortgage, was subject to its encumbrances. They disputed the usury claims, asserting that the transactions did not meet legal standards for usury and that they were entitled to collect based on the terms of the original contract.

In January 1869, in Morgan County, Illinois, a legal case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court involving John C. Crabtree (the plaintiff) and James N. Reed (the defendant). The case arose from an incident where Reed acknowledged striking Crabtree's mule with a heavy stick, which resulted in the mule's death. The plaintiff, Crabtree, pursued legal action against Reed, claiming damages for the killing of the mule. The core dispute centered on the value of the mule and whether Reed's actions constituted liability for the death of Crabtree's property. The Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Charles D. Hodges, instructed the jury that the plaintiff bore the burden of proof to establish a clear preponderance of evidence in his favor to succeed in his claims. The jury found in favor of the defendant, Reed.	Crabtree's main arguments focused on seeking damages for the wrongful killing of his mule by Reed. He contended that Reed's actions were negligent and wrongful and requested the court to hold Reed liable for the loss of his property, emphasizing that evidence should support a probability of liability rather than requiring a clear preponderance to succeed.	Reed's defense hinged on the acknowledgment that he did strike the mule as a form of discipline, claiming justification for his actions on the grounds of the mule being unbroken to work. Reed contended that the evidence did not establish sufficient grounds for liability, arguing that the burden of proof was improperly placed upon the plaintiff. His key request was to have the jury find in his favor based on the evidence presented.

Robert Smith was involved in a legal case against John Irwin in Madison County, Illinois, which commenced with a suit by Irwin against Smith. Initially, a judgment was rendered in favor of Smith by a justice of the peace. Following this, Irwin appealed to the Circuit Court, which led to a summons being issued for Smith's appearance. However, attempts to serve Smith were unsuccessful, as the summons was returned “not found.” An alias summons was subsequently issued, but returned similarly. At the Circuit Court's March 1847 term, despite the lack of service, the appeal was tried, resulting in a judgment in favor of Irwin for $79.75. Smith contested this judgment through a writ of error, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction due to the failure to serve process upon him as required under the Revised Statutes. The case hinged on whether a valid trial could occur without the appellee present before the court.	Smith, as the plaintiff in error, claimed that the Circuit Court improperly proceeded with the appeal trial without proper service of process, thus lacking jurisdiction. He argued that according to the Revised Statutes, an appellee must be summoned or appear in court for a judgment to be valid. He requested the reversal of the Circuit Court's judgment rendered in favor of Irwin due to these procedural irregularities.	John Irwin, the defendant, maintained that the trial should proceed as the Circuit Court had conducted the appeal based on its interpretation of statutory provisions. Irwin contended that the court's actions were valid, and any errors claimed by Smith were unfounded, asserting that the case could be heard in absence of a formal summons. Irwin sought affirmation of the Circuit Court's judgment in his favor.

The case "Xavier L. Otis, Admr. v. Jefferson Gardner et al." took place in Illinois and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 31, 1883. The dispute arose over the ownership of one hundred shares of stock in the Calumet and Chicago Canal and Dock Company, originally owned by Sheridan Wait, who had passed away. In March 1875, Wait endorsed the stock certificates and delivered them to Chauncey T. Bowen while receiving a receipt stipulating that he had borrowed the shares and agreed to return them on demand. In November 1875, Bowen pledged these certificates as collateral for loans from Jefferson Gardner. The stock certificates, while possessing a blank assignment and power of attorney allowing transfer on the company's books, were never formally transferred. After Wait's death, Xavier L. Otis, as administrator of Wait's estate, sought formal transfer of the stock. He filed a suit against Chauncey T. Bowen, the Calumet and Chicago Canal and Dock Company, Jefferson Gardner, and George Van Zant, asserting that the stock rightfully belonged to Wait's estate. The circuit court dismissed Otis's claims, which led to an appeal that also affirmed the dismissal.	Xavier L. Otis argued that the stock certificates in question belonged to Sheridan Wait at the time of his death and should therefore be considered part of Wait's estate. He requested a declaration from the court that the stock belonged to Wait, that the old certificates be canceled, and new ones issued under his name, as well as an injunction against Gardner, Van Zant, and Bowen from interfering with the stock.	Jefferson Gardner contended that he acquired the stock certificates as collateral for money borrowed by James H. Bowen and did so in good faith, without knowledge of any prior claims related to the shares. Gardner maintained he did not have notice of any prior rights to the stock and insisted that the collateral agreement was valid as Bowen had the authority to pledge the stock, despite the formalities of transfer not being completed.

James R. Paul filed a lawsuit against Charles Leyenberger in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the case being decided on October 22, 1885. The legal dispute centered on a claim for malicious prosecution. Paul asserted that he had been wrongfully arrested and imprisoned by Leyenberger, resulting in actual damages of thirty-five dollars, which he presented as evidence during the trial. Despite the jury finding Leyenberger guilty, they awarded Paul only nominal damages of one dollar. Following the verdict, Paul sought a new trial, arguing that the jury had failed to consider the actual damages he incurred. The presiding judge, Hollín S. Williamson, denied the motion for a new trial, leading to an appeal from Paul on the grounds that the damages awarded were insufficient given the evidence of substantial harm he had suffered.	Paul claimed that Leyenberger's actions constituted malicious prosecution, and he provided evidence of actual damages amounting to thirty-five dollars. He contended that the jury's award of just one dollar in damages was inadequate, failing to account for the severity of his injuries from the false arrest. Paul requested a new trial, arguing that the jury erred in their judgement by not fully considering his evidence of damages.	Leyenberger defended against the claims by highlighting the jury's verdict of guilty and the nominal damages awarded. He maintained that the award, although minimal, indicated the jury did not find the circumstances of Paul's arrest to be as severe as asserted. The defense requested the court to uphold the jury's decision and deny any motions for a new trial, arguing that there was no basis for altering the jury's verdict.

Nannie E. Bedford, the plaintiff, was married to Benjamin F. Bedford and was also the sister-in-law of Stephen G. Bedford, who was the defendant in this case, represented by Lettie L. Bedford, the administratrix of Stephen's estate. The case revolves around the death of Amanda Bedford, Stephen's wife and Nannie’s sister, who passed away on June 5, 1883. Knowing she was dying, Amanda requested Nannie to care for her infant child, Walter, as she desired no one else to raise him. Stephen, present during this request, did not object and subsequently consented to Nannie raising Walter. For about 91 weeks, Nannie raised the child without any formal agreement for compensation from Stephen. During a period when Stephen lived with his brother Benjamin, he agreed to share living expenses but made it clear that these did not cover Nannie’s expenses for caring for Walter. Nannie’s claim against Stephen’s estate was initially ruled in her favor in County Court, followed by an appeal where the Circuit Court favored the estate, leading to this appeal in the Illinois Appellate Court.	Nannie E. Bedford claimed compensation for the care of Walter, who she raised for 91 weeks after Amanda Bedford's death. She argued that there was an implied promise from Stephen to pay for her services, as he had previously acknowledged the trouble and expense associated with raising Walter. The amount claimed was $6 per week, totaling $546. Nannie asserted that despite her familial relationship with Walter, she was entitled to compensation for the services provided.	The defense argued that an action against a parent for necessities provided for their infant child cannot be maintained without an express promise. They claimed that there was no enforceable contract regarding compensation, asserting that any supposed promises were insufficient given the familial ties and the nature of services provided voluntarily. Additionally, it was contended that since Nannie was married, she was incapable of entering into a legal contract without her husband's consent, an argument deemed legally irrelevant by the court for purposes of pursuing compensation from the estate.

William Hollingsworth initiated a legal case against O. W. Koon and others on March 27, 1885. The proceedings took place in the Illinois Supreme Court, and the case was filed in Iroquois County, Illinois. The conflict arose from a bill brought by Hollingsworth to redeem property from certain mortgages. After a hearing in the circuit court, a decree was issued fixing the amount due on the mortgages and allowing Hollingsworth to redeem the property upon payment of that amount. Dissatisfied with this outcome, Hollingsworth sought to reverse the decree by filing a writ of error to the Appellate Court for the Second District. However, the Appellate Court dismissed the writ, concluding that a freehold was involved in the case, which Hollingsworth contested. The Illinois Supreme Court was then petitioned to review the Appellate Court's decision, arguing that under precedents, no freehold was implicated in this situation.	The plaintiff, William Hollingsworth, claimed that the Appellate Court improperly dismissed his writ of error by incorrectly identifying the issue as involving a freehold. He sought to reverse the Appellate Court's decision and was requesting that the case be heard on its merits. Hollingsworth argued that the circuit court's decree regarding the redemption of the property from the mortgages was valid and should be reconsidered.	The defendants, represented by C. H. Wood, likely contended that the Appellate Court's dismissal was justified because a freehold was indeed involved. They would have argued that the legal process followed was appropriate and articulated reasons for maintaining the Appellate Court's decision.

Jeremiah O’Connor initiated a personal injury lawsuit against the Chicago & Eastern Illinois Railroad Company following an incident in which he sustained injuries. The case was originally heard in a lower court where the plaintiff secured a verdict in his favor; however, after the defendant appealed, the appellate court reversed this judgment, leading to a remand for a new trial. Tragically, Jeremiah O’Connor passed away shortly after the appeal. His son, Jeremiah O’Connor, Jr., was then substituted as the administrator of his father’s estate and continued the lawsuit. The defendant argued that the death of the original plaintiff extinguished the cause of action, claiming that O’Connor's death was not connected to the injuries alleged in the original complaint. The court struck down these claims, ruling that the action could survive even after the plaintiff's death and that the administrator was properly substituted. Following procedural disputes over the plaintiff's declaration regarding the permanence of the injury, the case moved to trial. A jury found the railroad company negligent and awarded the plaintiff damages of $2,250. The court upheld this verdict despite the defendant citing contradictions in the evidence.	The plaintiff, represented by Jeremiah O’Connor, Jr., argued that the injuries sustained by his father due to the defendant’s negligence resulted in significant damages that warranted compensation. He requested the court to hold the defendant accountable for the injuries suffered by his father, emphasizing that the death of the original plaintiff did not diminish the validity of the claims since it was unrelated to the alleged injuries.	The Chicago & Eastern Illinois Railroad Company contended that the death of the original plaintiff extinguished the cause of action, arguing that the injuries were not the cause of Jeremiah O’Connor's death. The defendant also sought to introduce a plea of not guilty and raise the Statute of Limitations as a defense, claiming that the lawsuit should have been barred due to a procedural change in the plaintiff's declaration.

In September 1869, a legal case took place in Illinois involving John D. Gardner and The Northwestern Manufacturing Company. Gardner, along with his alleged partner William D. Nichols, was sued to recover the value of goods sold and delivered on Nichols' order. Nichols defaulted, and Gardner defended himself by denying the existence of a partnership. The case involved testimony from Nichols and Crane, vice-president of the manufacturing company, to establish Gardner's joint liability. Nichols had claimed that Gardner was a "silent partner" when making the purchase, which the plaintiff used as evidence. However, Gardner's counsel objected to the admissibility of these statements, arguing that they should not bind Gardner as he did not authorize Nichols to make them. The court's treatment of this evidence, particularly concerning the definition and acknowledgment of partnership, became crucial in the trial. The judgment ultimately hinged on whether there was sufficient proof of a partnership between Gardner and Nichols.	The plaintiff, The Northwestern Manufacturing Company, argued that John D. Gardner was liable for the goods purchased by his partner, William D. Nichols, based on Nichols' representations that Gardner was a silent partner in the business. The plaintiff sought to recover the value of the goods sold and delivered, contending that the partnership formed the basis of Gardner's liability.	John D. Gardner contended that there was no partnership between him and Nichols and argued that Nichols' statements about his status as a silent partner were inadmissible. Gardner asserted that the court should not consider Nichols' declarations as evidence against him and insisted that the existence of a partnership had not been proven. His defense included a request for the rejection of the plaintiff’s evidence regarding the alleged partnership.

In 1889, in Henderson County, Illinois, a legal case titled "William Ross v. The People" arose when Florence Marshall accused William Ross of fathering her child. The case began in the County Court, where a jury found Ross guilty, confirming he was the father of Marshall's child. Ross appealed the decision, arguing that the evidence did not support the verdict. Florence Marshall claimed that the intimate encounter occurred on the evening of November 20, after a prayer meeting, leading to her pregnancy and the birth of the child on August 15, 1888. Ross tried to prove his innocence by presenting witnesses, mostly family members, asserting that he was at another location during the alleged incident and was physically incapacitated, as he had been walking on crutches following a horse accident. Despite his counsel's attempts to challenge the evidence, the prosecution's assertions remained largely uncontradicted as Ross did not testify. The jury ultimately affirmed the jury's belief in Marshall's testimony over Ross's alibi.	Florence Marshall claimed that William Ross was the father of her child, asserting that they engaged in sexual intercourse only once on November 20, 1888, which resulted in her pregnancy. She contended that her testimony was definitive and that Ross was the only man she had been intimate with, thereby holding him responsible for the child's paternity. Marshall sought restitution from Ross for his alleged role in the bastardy claim.	William Ross argued that the jury's verdict was unsupported by evidence, primarily by presenting alibi witnesses who claimed he could not have fathered the child due to being elsewhere on the night in question. Ross did not testify in his defense, which his counsel suggested weakened their case. They also maintained that the specific date of the encounter was material to his defense, insisting that Marshall's assertion as to the date negated his involvement. However, they acknowledged the failure of the evidence to conclusively absolve him.

The case of The Insurance Company of North America v. Thomas M. Hope was a legal dispute that took place in January 1871 in Alton, Illinois. Thomas M. Hope, the plaintiff, initiated the action against the Insurance Company of North America following a fire that destroyed his property. Hope sought damages under his insurance policy after the company denied payment for his loss. The insurance policy allowed the company to repair or replace the property damaged by fire, provided they notified the insured within thirty days of the proof of loss being submitted. The company claimed to have made this election within the specified time frame and conducted repairs to the property, which included hiring a carpenter and paying him $150 for the work done. However, the plaintiff contended that the repairs were unnecessary and conducted without his consent. He argued that the company did not give timely notice of their intent to repair. The trial led to conflicting evidence regarding the condition of the property post-repair and whether sufficient notice was given to Hope. The case ultimately went to the Illinois Supreme Court after an appeal from the company.	Thomas M. Hope claimed that the Insurance Company of North America failed to adhere to the terms of the insurance policy by not providing timely notice of its election to repair the damaged property. He argued that the repairs were unauthorized and not consented to, rendering the company's actions invalid. Hope sought recovery for the full amount of his loss, which he believed was justified under the policy, as the company did not fulfill its obligations according to the agreed terms.	The Insurance Company of North America contended that it had exercised its right under the insurance policy to repair the damaged property and claimed to have notified Hope within the required timeframe. The company argued that the repairs were appropriate and necessary to restore the property; hence, they should not be liable for the full amount of the loss claimed by Hope. They maintained that the objections raised by Hope regarding the repair process and the condition of the property were unfounded.

The case of Truman E. Andrews et al. v. Content F. Andrews et al. was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 13, 1884. The dispute arose concerning the will of Amzie Andrews, who passed away in 1876. The will included a specific clause concerning a block of land in Chester, Illinois, which he bequeathed to the First Presbyterian Church of Chester. The clause placed conditions on the land, including a prohibition on its sale for twenty-five years after the death of the last life tenant and specified that the income generated from the land was to be used to support the church and advance educational interests. The heirs of the testator challenged this clause, arguing that it created a perpetuity contrary to public policy and legal statutes. The circuit court dismissed their claims, leading to an appeal on the grounds that the will's provisions contravened legal regulations concerning property and charitable uses.	The plaintiffs claimed that the sixth clause of Amzie Andrews' will was void as it allegedly created an illegal perpetuity contrary to Illinois law, which restricts the duration of property interests. They argued that the provision against selling the land for twenty-five years exceeded the permissible limits and contravened public policy. The plaintiffs sought to have the clause of the will declared invalid, thereby allowing for the unrestricted sale and use of the land.	The defendants, representing the interests of the church, contended that the clause was valid because it fell within the exceptions of charitable uses as outlined in the statute of 43d Elizabeth, which permits conveyances for charitable purposes, circumventing traditional rules against perpetuities. They maintained that the clause aimed to promote religious activities and educational purposes, which are recognized as legitimate charitable uses. The defense requested that the court uphold the validity of the will's provisions.

In 1886 in Ludlow, Champaign County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between James C. Ware (plaintiff) and Lazarus Hirsch (defendant). The case originated when J. W. Jefferson, a debtor residing in Indiana, sold his general merchandise stock to a group of eight creditors, including Ware. Jefferson provided a bill of sale and authorized Ware to manage the business, allowing him to take possession, employ clerks, and conduct operations. Following this arrangement, a firm of creditors, which did not partake in the sale, filed a writ of replevin against Jefferson to reclaim goods that had been sold to him but were included in the stock sold to the other creditors. The sheriff, acting on the writ, seized these goods from Ware, leading him to sue for damages. The central issue was whether Jefferson's sale and the transfer of possession were sufficient to vest ownership in Ware.	The plaintiff, James C. Ware, argued that he had been given legitimate possession of the goods following a bona fide sale from Jefferson and that the seizure of these goods by the sheriff was unlawful. Ware claimed damages for the wrongful taking of the goods and asserted that the sale was made in good faith, thus supporting his entitlement to full damages for the items seized.	The defendant, Lazarus Hirsch, primarily contended that the transfer of possession following the sale was insufficient to establish Ware's title to the property. Hirsch argued there was no substantive change in possession that would legally support Ware's claim. He also claimed that Ware was not entitled to recover full damages, asserting that he could only recover based on his interest in the goods.

The case, "The People on the relation of Thomas R. Courtney v. Jesse K. Dubois," was decided in April 1857 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It arose in Ottawa, Illinois, where Thomas R. Courtney presented two five-dollar bills issued by the Bank of Ottawa for redemption. The bank, organized under the general banking law of 1851, refused to redeem the bills in gold coin, which Courtney requested. Instead, the cashier offered to pay in quarter dollars, a form of legal tender for more than five dollars under specific conditions. Frustrated with this refusal, Courtney had a notary public make a formal demand for payment in gold, which was likewise declined. This led to a protest from the notary, after which Courtney petitioned the auditor, Jesse K. Dubois, seeking a formal notice to the bank to comply with the redemption request as per the legal acts in effect. The auditor, however, justified his refusal to intervene by asserting that the bank's tender was indeed legal under existing laws.	Thomas R. Courtney, representing the plaintiff, contended that the Bank of Ottawa was obliged to redeem the bills in gold coin as it was a legal requirement. He claimed that the bank's tender of payment in quarter dollars was illegal, and he requested a peremptory writ of mandamus against the auditor to compel compliance with the law and ensure that the bank met its obligations to redeem the bills in the specified form.	Jesse K. Dubois, the auditor and defendant, maintained that the bank's offer of payment in quarter dollars constituted a legal tender according to the laws of the United States. He argued that there was no lack of compliance on the bank’s part, and that the protest did not establish that the bank was in default for not redeeming in gold. Consequently, he opposed Courtney’s request for the mandamus, asserting that the bank had met its obligations under the law.

Nathan A. King v. Thorett C. Bushnell et al. was a case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on September 27, 1887. The case stems from the death of Curtis Bushnell, who passed away intestate on April 24, 1859, leaving behind his widow Zerilda J. Bushnell and four minor children. At the time of his death, he owned 416 acres of land. Zerilda was appointed guardian of their children shortly after Curtis's death and held this position until Nathan A. King married her in February 1863. Following their separation in August 1865, Zerilda was reappointed as guardian. Curtis's estate sold the land through court decrees to pay debts. Zerilda purchased a portion of this land, allegedly with the intent to hold it in trust for her children. The evidence suggested that she had an agreement to convey the land to the children upon their reaching adulthood, which they did. The land's sale price was notably low, raising claims of it being held in trust for the children. Nathan A. King claimed a right to dower in the property after Zerilda's death, which was contested by the defendants, who argued that Zerilda held the property in trust for the children, and thus Nathan had no claim.	Nathan A. King, the plaintiff, contended that he was entitled to dower rights in the lands purchased by Zerilda Bushnell, asserting that he had a claim to these properties as her husband. He argued against the notion that the lands were held in trust for the children. He sought to recover a portion of the estate he believed was rightfully his.	The defendants, representing the interests of the minor children, argued that Zerilda had purchased the land in trust for her children and that the concept of dower did not apply since a trustee's spouse has no right to claim dower in trust property. They asserted that Nathan could not claim an interest in the land based on the principles of equitable trust and relied on the Statute of Frauds as a personal defense against claims of the verbal promise regarding land conveyance. They sought a dismissal of King's claims.

On December 13, 1859, Robert Fergus, along with his wife Margaret Fergus, executed a mortgage on their property located in Chicago. This property included several buildings and was mortgaged to secure a loan of $13,000 to David Sears, Jr. After the couple defaulted on the mortgage, the property was foreclosed and sold by a master in chancery to James H. Woodworth. Following the sale, Woodworth attempted to take possession of the property, claiming he had rightfully purchased it. The Fergus couple contested this, asserting that the property should be considered their homestead and thus exempt from foreclosure. A legal battle ensued, which included a reversal of a previous decree in their favor by the Illinois Supreme Court due to an erroneous amount stated in the foreclosure decree. This led to the Fergus filing a supplemental bill against Woodworth, alleging that his purchase was not bona fide and challenging the manner in which the property was sold (as an entire unit instead of in separate parcels).	The plaintiffs, Robert and Margaret Fergus, argued that the property in question was their homestead and should be protected from foreclosure under homestead rights. They claimed that they had not abandoned the property as their residence but were temporarily living elsewhere. The Fergus also contended that Woodworth's purchase was not bona fide and that the sale of the property en masse was improper, warranting the court to set aside the transaction.	James H. Woodworth, the defendant, denied the Fergus' claims of homestead rights, arguing that they had abandoned the property and had not lived there for several years prior to the foreclosure. He asserted that the foreclosure sale was conducted properly and disputed the plaintiffs' allegations regarding the nature of his purchase, maintaining that it was legitimate and in accordance with the law. Woodworth requested the court to affirm the sale and grant him possession of the property.

John A. Brown and Fred H. Luehrs were involved in a legal dispute originating in Cook County, Illinois, which culminated in a court case in September 1875. The background involves two promissory notes issued by Luehrs to Brown in 1868, with interest and various payments made over the years. However, Luehrs, claiming to have overpaid Brown, initiated a lawsuit in 1874 seeking $557.15 due to what he asserted was an erroneous payment. The controversy arose from a claimed payment of $1000 made by Luehrs on November 24, 1870. Luehrs left the payment with a commission merchant firm, Moeller & Busch, to be delivered to Brown, but there was uncertainty whether the money reached Brown. During the trial, both Luehrs and Brown denied the payment took place. After the defense won a judgment in favor of Brown, who received $793.44, Luehrs sought to vacate this judgment based on newly discovered evidence, which eventually led to an appeal and subsequent hearings concerning the matter.	Plaintiff John A. Brown sought to vacate and enjoin the collection of a judgment favoring him based on newly discovered evidence relating to a disputed $1000 payment claimed to have been made by Luehrs. Brown contended that this evidence, which included testimony indicating that the payment was made but not duly recorded, warranted a new trial. He requested relief from the judgment rendered in his favor due to the lack of clarity surrounding the circumstances of the payment.	Defendant Fred H. Luehrs presented the argument that the judgment in favor of Brown was based on a misunderstanding regarding whether the $1000 payment had been fulfilled. Luehrs asserted that newly discovered evidence demonstrated that the payment was indeed made, based on corroborated accounts from the commission merchants involved. He indicated that he had acted with due diligence regarding the evidence and maintained that the evidence presented could likely change the outcome of the original trial.

In April 1866, the case of Thomas Brennan v. Patrick Timmoney arose in the Superior Court of Chicago, Illinois. The action was initiated by Patrick Timmoney against Thomas Brennan and John O’Neill, who were alleged to be joint makers of a promissory note for $1,000, due twelve months after its execution, with interest at a rate of 10% per annum. The note was dated August 12, 1857, and although O’Neill was defaulted, Brennan contested the claims against him. During the trial, Brennan filed three pleas: first, a denial of the claims made in the declaration; second, an assertion that he only signed as the bookkeeper for O’Neill and had not made a joint promise; and third, a claim that the statute of limitations had expired, as the promise had not been made within five years of the suit. The court initially ruled in favor of Timmoney, interpreting the note as a joint obligation. However, evidence suggested that the connection between the names in the document was actually "pr." (per) instead of "&", indicating that Brennan was not jointly liable.	Patrick Timmoney argued that both Thomas Brennan and John O’Neill were jointly liable for a promissory note they allegedly signed together. He sought to recover the $1,000 stipulated in the note along with the accrued interest, asserting that the defendants had committed to the payment terms outlined in the document.	Thomas Brennan contended that he was not a joint maker of the note and claimed that the note indicated he signed as "pr." (per) for O’Neill, thereby asserting that he bore no financial responsibility. He also argued against the claims on the basis of the statute of limitations, stating that the promises outlined had not been undertaken within the time frame specified by law.

On August 1, 1872, the Illinois Masons Benevolent Society issued a life insurance certificate to Havilah B. Johnson, stating that upon his death, a specified sum would be paid to his wife, Judith Johnson, or his legal representatives. Judith Johnson passed away in 1877, which led to Mr. Johnson losing his home, as they had no children. Facing health issues and financial hardship, Mr. Johnson attempted to transfer the insurance benefits for support but was unsuccessful. On January 17, 1880, he surrendered the original certificate and obtained a new one naming Elizabeth L. Van Epps as the beneficiary with the insurer's consent. By then, Mr. Johnson was in a relationship with Van Epps, and they intended to marry after his divorce from his wife. He signed the new contract with the understanding that Van Epps would care for him and maintain the policy. Mr. Johnson died on October 25, 1881, and after his death, Van Epps claimed the insurance proceeds, leading to a legal dispute with Mr. Johnson's relatives, who asserted their rights to the funds.	The plaintiff, Elizabeth L. Van Epps, argued that she was the rightful beneficiary of the life insurance proceeds due to a legitimate change in beneficiary made with the insurer's consent. She maintained that Mr. Johnson had the right to designate her as the beneficiary after his wife’s death, as he had fulfilled his obligations under the contract through life insurance premiums. Van Epps claimed she provided care and support to Mr. Johnson before his death, justifying her claim to the insurance funds.	The defendants, John T. Johnson and other relatives of the deceased, contended that the original insurance contract could not be voided without their consent and that Mr. Johnson lacked the legal right to change the beneficiary to Van Epps. They argued that the transfer was invalid due to a lack of insurable interest, asserting that the policy's benefits should rightfully go to the deceased's estate, specifically to his heirs.

In 1864, Samuel Todd filed an action of trespass against The St. Louis, Alton and Terre Haute Railroad Company in the Circuit Court of Coles County, Illinois. The case was heard during the September Term, resulting in a judgment favoring Todd for $250 in damages, along with costs. Following the judgment, an execution was issued on October 25, 1864, which the sheriff levied on the company’s personal property. Prior to the sale of the seized property, the Railroad Company contended that the proceedings in the suit were erroneous and sought an injunction in Circuit Court to prevent the sale. They claimed that levies on real estate should precede those on personal property. The Circuit Court issued an injunction halting further actions related to the execution until the issue could be resolved. This decision led to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the central inquiry was whether the injunction effectively released any errors from the initial legal proceedings.	Todd's primary argument centered on the assertion that the issuance of the injunction effectively acted as a stay of the judgment at law and released any errors that occurred prior to it. He contended that the injunction could restrict the Railroad Company from executing further collection actions against him following the judgment.	The Railroad Company's defense hinged on the claim that the judgment proceedings leading to Todd's damages were erroneous. They argued that the granting of the injunction did not release any errors regarding the prior legal proceedings, as it only sought to stay subsequent actions without affecting the judgment itself.

In 1874, the case "John Fitch v. Elisha W. Willard" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following events beginning on December 14, 1867, regarding a contract for the sale of land located in Cook County, Illinois. John Fitch, the plaintiff, entered into a contract with Elisha Willard, the defendant, to purchase approximately 83 acres of land. The agreement stipulated that Willard would provide a quit-claim or special warranty deed and a satisfactory abstract of title. However, complications arose regarding the title, particularly concerning claims from George Boggs, who sought to reclaim ownership of the land. As the case progressed, it was discovered that Fitch had not acted on the contract or made efforts to comply with its terms for over five years, leading to a claim of laches against him. Willard contended he had fulfilled his obligations and sought to regain possession of the property after declaring the contract void due to Fitch's inaction.	John Fitch argued that he had entered into a valid contract to purchase the land, asserting that the title conveyed by Willard was deficient. He sought specific performance of the contract, requesting the court to compel Willard to convey the property to him as initially agreed.	Elisha W. Willard defended against Fitch's claims by arguing that the contract’s language indicated he bore no obligation regarding the title's quality, emphasizing that he only needed to convey the title he had and provide a satisfactory abstract. Willard also cited Fitch's inaction over five years as laches, arguing that this delay precluded any legitimate claim for specific performance.

In 1854, the Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company constructed an embankment and stone culvert over a small stream in St. Clair County, Illinois. Around June 1885, following heavy rainfall, the culvert became insufficient, causing backwater to flood Michael Wachter's brick-yard and damage property. The resulting damage was substantial, with Wachter claiming $600 in losses. The case was brought to court after Wachter sought compensation for the damages. The jury found against the railway company, stating that they were liable due to the inadequacy of the culvert to manage the water flow. Evidence from witnesses, including engineers from the railway company, supported the jury's conclusion that the culvert was not constructed or maintained adequately to prevent flooding. The court had to assess whether the railway company acted with due care, given their duty to ensure no harm came to adjacent property owners due to their infrastructure.	Michael Wachter, the plaintiff, claimed that the Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company's insufficient culvert caused flooding on his property, resulting in substantial damage to his brick-yard and other belongings. He argued that the company failed to maintain a proper outlet for the water flow, leading directly to his losses. Wachter sought compensation of $600 for the damages incurred.	The Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company contended that the culvert was adequately constructed for normal conditions and should not be held liable for extraordinary flooding. They argued that the plaintiff could not maintain the lawsuit since he was aware of the existing conditions when he placed his property there. Additionally, they claimed that a prescriptive right might exist due to previous instances of overflow without complaint, which would nullify Wachter's claims.

In the case of Perry McLaughlin v. Lorimer Johnson, which took place in Mercer County, Illinois, during the 1860s, the dispute revolved around the ownership and return of a set of fence rails. The original owner, Arnold, sold a 40-acre tract of land to Perry McLaughlin in 1861, and later, in January 1864, he sold the remaining portion of the quarter section to Lorimer Johnson. Prior to Johnson's purchase, McLaughlin was deployed in the military, and during his absence, Johnson, with the consent of McLaughlin's wife, removed fence rails from the property, intending to utilize them for his own land. Upon returning home, McLaughlin demanded the return of the rails, but Johnson claimed he had bought them with the land. The case escalated through the justice system, culminating in an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court following an unfavorable verdict in the Circuit Court. The central legal question was whether the rails, once temporarily removed, remained the property of McLaughlin or passed to Johnson with the sale of the land.	McLaughlin argued that the fence rails were his property and that they were only temporarily removed from the land. He claimed that since the rails were part of the property he purchased, Johnson was obligated to return them. His main legal request was to reverse the judgment of the Circuit Court, which ruled in favor of Johnson, and to reclaim ownership of the fence rails based on the premise that they remained part of the realty.	Johnson contended that he legally acquired the fence rails when he purchased the land from Arnold. He asserted that the rails had been temporarily borrowed with permission and that, upon the completion of the sale, they passed to him as part of the property. Johnson's defense rested on interpretation of property law regarding the ownership of fixtures and appurtenances, arguing that the removal of the rails did not constitute a permanent severance from the land and that they were inherently included in the sale of the property.

The case "The Board of Supervisors of Kendall County v. The People ex rel. Commissioners of Highways of Bristol" revolves around a dispute that occurred during the 1881-1882 period in Kendall County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the Board of Supervisors of Kendall County (the defendant) and the Commissioners of Highways of Bristol (the plaintiff). The controversy arose when the Commissioners sought financial assistance from the Board to construct a bridge across Fox River, which they claimed was necessary for local transportation. Initially, they requested $6,000, arguing that the total cost of $12,000 would be an unreasonable burden on the town. Following a rejection of their petition, they presented a second request, now estimating the bridge's cost at $20,000 and stating that they had secured half the funds required. The Board, however, denied their claim again, leading the Commissioners to file for a writ of mandamus to compel the Board to provide the requested financial aid.	The plaintiff argued that they had complied with all statutory requirements for receiving county aid for the bridge construction. They claimed that a valid election had been held to raise funds and that they indeed possessed sufficient funds to cover half of the construction costs. Their petition for mandamus requested the court to compel the Board of Supervisors to allocate the necessary financial support for the bridge, as stipulated under Illinois law.	The defendant contended that the plaintiff's assertions regarding the validity of the election and the claimed funds were untrue. They denied that the town had raised one half of the required finances legally and argued that the plaintiff had conducted the construction of the bridge improperly, without full compliance with the necessary procedures. The Board sought to have the mandamus request dismissed based on these denials.

In December 1847, the case of Henry B. Truett, the appellant, against Charles B. Wainwright and others, the appellees, was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated at the Jo Daviess County Court during the July term of 1845 when E. B. Washburne, an attorney, filed a warranty of attorney supposedly signed by Truett. This document authorized an attorney to confess judgment for Wainwright & Co. regarding a bill of exchange amounting to $640.195, leading to a judgment against Truett for $503.25. Truett later claimed that he had not authorized the confession of judgment and that the debt had already been paid from merchandise left with the plaintiffs. In April 1847, Truett sought to stay the execution and set aside the judgment, claiming he had not consented to the legal proceedings. A series of affidavits presented conflicting accounts related to the authority of Miers F. Truett, Henry's brother, who was said to have acted as his agent. The court ultimately ordered the suspension of the judgment, and a trial ensued in September 1847, leading to a ruling affirming the original judgment in favor of the appellees.	The plaintiffs, represented by Wainwright & Co., argued that they were entitled to the judgment based on the warranty of attorney executed by Miers F. Truett, which bore Henry Truett's signature. They maintained that they acted in good faith, relied on the authority given, and that the conditions under which the bond was drafted were sufficient under the law. The plaintiffs sought to affirm the judgment that had previously been made in their favor and argued against the claims made by Truett regarding lack of authority.	Truett contended that the judgment was improperly obtained as he had not granted the authority to confess judgment through the proper channels, believing the actions taken by Miers F. Truett were unauthorized and without his consent. He claimed that he had made efforts to settle the debt before his departure but was misrepresented by his brother. Truett requested that the court set aside the original judgment entirely, stating that the document's execution was flawed and that he had not been sufficiently notified of the actions against him at the time.

The case "Gaty, Cune and Glasby v. Charles Pittman" took place in Illinois, with proceedings dating back to May 1845. The action of ejectment was initiated by the plaintiffs Gaty, Cune, and Glasby to assert their claim to certain premises that were originally owned by John Berry Meacham. After several trials, the final trial in September 1849 resulted in a jury verdict in favor of the defendant, Charles Pittman, who claimed title through a deed acknowledged and recorded following an attachment levied by the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs presented evidence of attachments and a sheriff's deed, while the defendant provided a deed that was dated before the attachment but recorded afterward. The key issue revolved around the priority of the attached title versus the recorded deed. Ultimately, the plaintiffs' case rested on whether the sheriff had filed the required notice of the attachment, while the defendant sought to prove that his conveyance was bona fide and took precedence over the attachment.	The plaintiffs argued that their claim to the premises arose from two attachments levied against the property and subsequent judicial actions including judgments and a sheriff's deed. They contended that the deed from Meacham to Pittman was fraudulent, thus invalidating Pittman's title. They requested the court to set aside the jury's verdict in favor of the defendant due to alleged misinstructions by the court and to affirm their ownership through the recordings they produced.	The defendant, Charles Pittman, maintained that his recorded deed, which predated the plaintiffs' attachments, took priority over their claim. He argued that there was no evidence that the sheriff had complied with the requirement of filing a notice of the attachment with the recorder, which would have affected the enforceability of the attachment against his title. Pittman asserted that his conveyance from Meacham was valid and bona fide, and therefore sought to have the verdict upheld, affirming his rightful claim to the property.

On July 5, 1881, the Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railway Company received a mare and colt from Neely, the agent of Lawrence Harmon, for transportation from Ottawa, Illinois to Peoria, approximately seventy-five miles away. The animals were shipped in a box car under the supervision of Neely and the railway company's agent. Upon arrival in Peoria the following morning, the mare was reportedly overheated due to insufficient ventilation in the car and died the next day. The plaintiff claimed that the injuries resulted from the railway company's negligence in failing to maintain proper ventilation during transport. In contrast, the defendant argued that the overheating was due to external weather conditions and the inherent condition of the mare, rather than any negligence on their part. The case ultimately went to trial, where the jury was instructed on the responsibilities of a common carrier in such situations.	The plaintiff, Lawrence Harmon, contended that the railway company failed to provide a properly ventilated transport environment, resulting in the overheating and subsequent death of his mare. He asserted that the company neglected its duty to ensure the animals were delivered in good condition and sought damages totaling $433 for the loss of the mare and for the resulting harm to the colt.	The defendant, Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railway Company, argued that they had maintained appropriate care and provided a suitable car for transportation. They claimed that the overheating was due to the horse's inherent ailments and external weather conditions unrelated to any lack of care on their part. Furthermore, they maintained that they were not liable for damages resulting from conditions that were beyond their control, such as the mare's health decline after delivery.

In the case of Emanuel Kramer et al. v. George J. Ferry et al., which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the events leading up to the legal dispute began when the plaintiffs initiated a suit involving a promissory note. The suit was commenced with the service of a summons and continued with a declaration on the note. On February 3, 1885, the plaintiffs submitted a petition for the removal of the case to the United States Circuit Court for the Northern District of Illinois, which was approved by the Superior Court, allowing the transfer of jurisdiction. A bond was filed as required, and the order for removal was entered on February 4, 1885. However, the case experienced complications when, on December 10, 1885, the clerk of the United States Circuit Court certified that no transcript of the record was filed since February 1, 1885. Subsequently, the Superior Court, after the defendants failed to plead, reinstated the case and entered a default judgment against them for $2,673 on December 12, 1885. This series of events led to the appeal, questioning the jurisdiction of the state court after the removal order.	The plaintiffs argued that the Superior Court lost all jurisdiction over the case following the successful and proper removal of the cause to the United States Circuit Court. They contended that any further actions by the state court without being remanded by the federal court were void. Hence, they sought to have the judgment against them reversed, asserting that the matter belonged solely within the jurisdiction of the federal court due to the removal order.	The defendants, who did not appear in court, were represented by their attorney who maintained that procedural issues regarding the filing of the record in federal court were significant. They aimed to reinstate the case in the Superior Court, arguing that the initial jurisdiction could be re-established and that the judgment against them should not stand due to the lack of a filed transcript in the Circuit Court.

In January 1868, in Edgar County, Illinois, Nathaniel G. Chilcote filed a case against William Kile and others. The dispute centered around a debt of $200 owed by a third party, Lowry, to Chilcote. The defendants (Kile et al.) had received and sold Lowry's wool and were supposed to handle the proceeds. Chilcote attempted to collect the debt using an order drawn on Lowry, directing the defendants to save any funds for him. Additionally, Kile had loaned Chilcote $100, which he claimed was to be offset against the order drawn on Lowry. However, Kile denied this arrangement, leading to Chilcote's claims against them. It was argued that the defendants failed to present the order to Lowry and were negligent in their handling of the wool sale, resulting in a loss for Chilcote. The court, however, found that the defendants had not entered into a binding obligation to Chilcote, as they acted merely as agents without a formal agreement.	Chilcote alleged that Kile and the other defendants neglected their duties related to the sale of Lowry's wool, resulting in a lower sale price than expected. He claimed that they were responsible for the $200 debt owed to him by Lowry due to their actions. Chilcote sought compensation for his losses, arguing that he had a valid claim to the proceeds from the sale of the wool based on the agreement he believed was established.	Kile and the defendants countered that they were not liable for the debt owed by Lowry to Chilcote, as they acted as agents without any contractual obligation. They maintained that they had never accepted the order drawn upon Lowry unconditionally. They argued that since they were merely assisting Chilcote as a favor, they held no responsibility for any alleged negligence in handling the wool sale or for the associated debts.

Israel Underwood filed a replevin action against Miles White in the Circuit Court of Stephenson County, Illinois, during April Term 1867. Underwood sought to reclaim possession of cattle, hogs, and other property that he alleged were rightfully his. The case involved significant parties, including the plaintiff (Underwood) and the defendant (White), and included the involvement of attorneys Thomas J. Turner, James J. Neff for the appellant, and H. C. Hyde, Burchard & Barton for the appellee. The defendant responded with five pleas: non cepit, non detinet, that the property was not owned by the plaintiff, that the property belonged to the defendant, and that it belonged to third parties.
