A jury eventually found the issues for the defendant, leading to a judgment against Underwood.	Underwood claimed ownership of the cattle, hogs, and other property involved in the replevin action. He argued that he was entitled to exclusive possession of his property and requested that the court return the property to him, asserting his right against White's possession.	White's key defenses included asserting that the property was not in Underwood's ownership and that he (White) had a legitimate claim to the property in question. The jury's verdict favored the defendant, leading to an affirmation of White's right to the property, based on the multiple pleas filed against Underwood.

Samuel Gotts v. Barrett B. Clark is a legal case from September 1875, heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case involves Samuel Gotts (the plaintiff) seeking to recover the value of goods that were sold and delivered to the defendant's wife and minor daughter. The key individuals involved include Samuel Gotts, Barrett B. Clark (the defendant), and the defendant's wife and minor daughter, though their names are not explicitly mentioned in the case description. The goods in question were deemed necessary for the wife and daughter’s social status and comfort, thus raising the issue of the defendant’s liability for these purchases, particularly as they were charged to him. The case revolves around whether Barrett B. Clark should be held accountable for the goods purchased by his wife and minor daughter, highlighting both the legal standards regarding agency and the responsibility of a father for his minor child's purchases.	The plaintiff, Samuel Gotts, argues that he is entitled to recover the cost of goods sold to Barrett B. Clark’s wife under the premise that she had acted as her husband's agent in that purchase. He requests payment based on the necessity and appropriateness of the goods for his wife’s position in life. He also attempts to claim for the goods sold to the minor daughter, positing that they were required for her comfort.	Barrett B. Clark, the defendant, contends that he should only be liable for the goods purchased by his wife, as they were necessary and appropriate. However, he asserts a technical defense regarding the goods purchased by his minor daughter, arguing that there is no express promise or evidence indicating that she had the authority to make purchases on credit. Furthermore, he highlights that she was living independently, earning her own wages, and did not reside at home where he would have presumably provided for her needs.

William Tarble was tried in February 1882 at the Circuit Court of Kane County, Illinois, for robbery. The key individuals involved in the case were Tarble, Dr. Alfred Blood (the victim), and James Cook (a witness). The incident occurred on the evening of February 4, 1882, in the St. Cloud saloon in Aurora, Illinois. Blood consumed a drink that rendered him unconscious, and his belongings, including a diamond pin and a watch, were reported missing after he regained consciousness. Witness Cook testified that he saw Tarble taking Blood's pin. On the other hand, Tarble claimed he was at the saloon during the timeframe in question and had an alibi supported by three witnesses. During the trial, character witnesses for the prosecution indicated that Tarble had a poor reputation for honesty. Ultimately, Tarble was convicted and sentenced to six years in prison.	The plaintiff, William Tarble, argued that the evidence presented at trial was insufficient to justify his conviction for robbery. He contended that there were errors in the court's handling of evidence and testimony, including the admission of prejudicial character evidence against him. Tarble sought to reverse the conviction based on these claims and requested a new trial.	The defendant, representing the People of the State of Illinois, maintained that the evidence overwhelmingly supported the conviction. The prosecution pointed to witness testimonies that established Tarble's presence at the crime scene and his actions during the incident. Additionally, the prosecution countered Tarble's claims of insufficient evidence by presenting the testimony of multiple character witnesses who attested to Tarble's bad reputation for truthfulness in the community.

Matthias B. Denman filed a case against James Bloomer in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1849, arising from a transaction involving a raft of lumber. In July 1848, a man named Johnson claimed to represent Bloomer, who was purportedly the owner of the raft that had been taken from another man, Clinton, as payment for debts. Denman agreed to buy the raft from Johnson for $300, with the remainder to be paid upon measurement after removal. The raft was landed but eventually went missing, prompting Denman's agents to search for it. The raft was located at Hannibal, and Johnson returned to make arrangements regarding repayment. However, Johnson failed to honor a draft he issued payable to Denman, which led to Denman's claim against Bloomer, asserting he was responsible for Johnson's actions.	Denman claimed that Bloomer was liable for the money paid to Johnson since Johnson represented himself as Bloomer's agent in the sale of the raft. Denman argued that Bloomer should be bound by Johnson’s representations and sought to recover the amounts paid related to the raft, including the draft that was due from Bloomer.	Bloomer contended that he was not responsible for Johnson’s actions or any funds received by him. He argued that Johnson was acting as the agent of Clinton, the actual owner of the raft, and that as such, Denman had no privity of contract with him. Bloomer further maintained that Johnson lacked the authority to rescind the sale according to the agency rules, thus absolving Bloomer from any liability for the funds paid by Denman.

C. A. Lake filed a legal case against James Lower and others in the Kankakee Circuit Court. The appeal was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court on January 10, 1889. The key individuals involved included C. A. Lake, the plaintiff representing himself, and Mr. W. H. Richardson, representing the defendant, James Lower. The case revolved around the insufficiency of the abstract provided by the plaintiff, which failed to comply with the court's rules. The court emphasized the requirement for a complete abstract that would allow them to comprehend the entire case without needing to reference the original records. The abstract submitted was described as brief and imperfect, lacking critical details about the trial and the testimonies of witnesses. As a result, the court found itself unable to assess the merits of the case.	C. A. Lake, as the plaintiff, aimed to appeal a judgment from the Kankakee Circuit Court. His main argument rested on the validity of the trial process and the outcomes that stemmed from it. However, his claims were hindered by the inadequacy of the abstract presented to the court, which did not effectively summarize the evidence or the details of the case, limiting his legal requests and the court's ability to evaluate the appeal.	The defendant, James Lower, maintained that the case should not proceed due to the lack of a sufficient abstract from the plaintiff, which is a requirement under court rules for appeals. The defense argued that without a complete record, the court should affirm the judgment of the lower court, as the abstract was unable to provide a coherent understanding of the case and did not meet the standards set by rules regarding the submission of legal documents.

The case of Murray McConnel et al. v. David B. Ayres takes place in Illinois in the early 1840s, following a judgment that had previously been rendered against McConnel and Collins in the Morgan Circuit Court in July 1838. The judgment was issued in favor of John Kerr for a debt of $600 and $65 in damages. After Kerr's death, David B. Ayres was appointed as the administrator of Kerr's estate. Subsequently, McConnel and Collins appealed the judgment, claiming several errors. The case was then moved to the Sangamon Circuit Court via a change of venue. During this process, McConnel and Collins sought an injunction to halt Ayres from further proceedings under the judgment. The court granted the injunction, but it was later dissolved. The principal issue addressed by the Illinois Supreme Court revolved around whether the injunction acted as a bar against errors occurring in the original proceedings.	The plaintiffs, McConnel and Collins, argued that there were significant errors in the judgment rendered by the Morgan Circuit Court, which they wished to amend. They asserted that the previous judgment had been entered without due process, compounded by an erroneous appearance filed on their behalf. They sought an injunction to prevent the enforcement of the judgment against them while they pursued legal remedies to amend the mistake and reassess the merits of their case.	Ayres, the defendant and administrator of Kerr's estate, countered the plaintiffs' arguments by claiming that once the injunction was granted, it operated as a release of all errors in the proceedings. The defendant maintained that the plaintiffs had essentially chosen equity over law through their actions, and thus should be bound to the outcomes dictated by the equitable context. He asserted that the plaintiffs should not be allowed to pursue multiple remedies concurrently and that their appeal should be dismissed.

In 1865, William Messmore entered into a land purchase agreement with Samuel Kail, paying $600 in cash and providing four promissory notes of $300 each for the remaining balance. Disputes regarding the land title arose, prompting Messmore to withhold further payments until the title was secured. Subsequently, Kail borrowed $300 from Messmore, issuing a due-bill with Messmore as security. Kail later transferred two of Messmore's promissory notes to Severt Larson, the defendant, as security related to the due-bill, without Messmore's consent. The case went to trial, where the jury ruled in favor of Messmore after finding that Larson had not successfully proven his defenses of set-off and release. The trial revealed that the considerations for the notes Larson held had failed, which he was aware of at the time of receiving them. The trial took place in Knox County under Judge Arthur A. Smith and concluded with a judgment in Messmore's favor for $461.50.	William Messmore, the plaintiff, argued that the defendant, Severt Larson, had no valid claim on the due-bill as the consideration for his claimed set-off (the notes held against him) had failed. He contended that Larson failed to prove his defenses and sought judgment to recover the amount defined in the due-bill.	Severt Larson, the defendant, claimed a set-off based on the two promissory notes issued by Messmore to Kail for the land purchase, asserting his right to redeem the amounts due. He also claimed that he was released from his obligation on the due-bill due to arrangements made regarding the notes. Larson, however, bore the burden of proof, which he did not satisfy during the trial.

The case "Rosalia E. Kreitz v. Elisa B. Hamilton, Assignee, et al." was decided on May 25, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court concerning a property in Quincy, Adams County, Illinois. The central individuals involved were Rosalia E. Kreitz, the plaintiff, and Elisa B. Hamilton, serving as the assignee of the Union Bank of Quincy, among others. The dispute arose over the foreclosure of two trust deeds and associated promissory notes tied to a parcel of real estate owned by John M. and Mary P. Kreitz. The bank, through Hamilton, sought to foreclose on its mortgage, asserting that Kreitz's 1872 deed was fraudulent and that the associated debt had been paid in full. In response, Kreitz filed a cross-bill seeking to enforce her trust deed to recover a long-standing debt. Hamilton and other defendants demurred, claiming the cross-bill was barred by the statute of limitations. The Illinois Appellate Court's decision hinged on whether the statute of limitations had indeed expired and the effect this had on Kreitz's ability to foreclose on the property.	Rosalia E. Kreitz claimed that the trust deed executed in 1872 was valid, that the debt it secured was unpaid despite interest payments made until 1883, and that the defendants had no legitimate claim over the property. She contended that her trust deed should take priority over the Union Bank's mortgage and sought foreclosure on her interest in the property.	The defendants, led by Elisa B. Hamilton, contended that Kreitz's cross-bill was barred by the statute of limitations since more than ten years had passed since the cause of action accrued with the maturity of the promissory note in 1874. They argued that Kreitz's claims had become stale and were consequently unenforceable, calling for the dismissal of her amended cross-bill.

The case, "The Beaucoup Coal Company v. America J. Cooper," was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on April 13, 1883, following events that occurred on May 22, 1881, in a coal mine operated by the Beaucoup Coal Company in Perry County, Illinois. The key individuals involved include James M. Cooper, the deceased, who was the pit boss and also an agent for the company, and the Banyak Coal Company, the defendant. James M. Cooper was employed in operations at the mine, which utilized a shaft for hoisting and lowering a cage. On the day of the incident, while descending in the cage, the cable broke, leading to a fatal fall attributed to the company's failure to provide adequate safety measures, specifically a sufficient brake and spring catches. The plaintiffs, who were Cooper’s widow and heirs, initiated the action against the company, claiming damages due to the negligence of the defendant in adhering to safety regulations outlined by a mining safety act passed in 1879.	The plaintiffs contended that the Beaucoup Coal Company had a statutory duty to ensure the safety of operations by providing adequate safety mechanisms on the cage, specifically claiming that the company failed to install a proper brake and spring catches as mandated by law. They argued that this negligence was willful and led to Cooper's death, who was their sole provider. As a result, the plaintiffs sought $10,000 in damages for their loss, alleging that the defendant's failure to comply with the safety provisions directly contributed to Cooper's fatal accident.	The defendant, the Beaucoup Coal Company, provided two key defenses. Firstly, they argued that James M. Cooper, at the time of his death, was the company's agent responsible for the very duties he allegedly neglected, thereby claiming he was culpable for his own death due to his failure to enforce safety protocols such as installing the required safety catches. Secondly, they maintained that because Cooper had sufficient capacity and opportunity to manage these safety requirements, the company should not be held liable for his death, and thus, the plaintiffs should not recover any damages.

Michael McMahon was indicted for larceny in Cook County, Illinois, arising from an incident that took place in August 1886. At that time, McMahon was employed as a foreman for a roofing company called Wheeler & Thomas. He and his crew were working on the house of Adam Jaeger, located at 701 South Halsted Street in Chicago. After completing their work, it was alleged that McMahon stole a suit of clothes belonging to Jaeger. The accusation relied primarily on the testimony of John Hartig, a carpenter who claimed to have seen McMahon leave the premises with a large bundle wrapped in an old coat. This was corroborated by the discovery of the bundle on the wagon they used to leave. In his defense, McMahon argued that he did not take any clothes and presented witnesses, including Judson Jones, who testified that he was with McMahon during the entire episode and that McMahon had only his coat and vest. Additionally, several character witnesses spoke to McMahon’s reputation for honesty.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, claimed that McMahon committed larceny by unlawfully taking Jaeger’s suit of clothes. They argued that there was sufficient evidence, particularly Hartig's testimony, to support McMahon's conviction and requested that the court uphold the jury's decision.	McMahon asserted that he did not commit the crime, emphasizing that he was seen by a reliable witness, Judson Jones, who affirmed he did not take any items from Jaeger’s house. McMahon's defense included evidence of his good character and a challenge to the credibility of Hartig's testimony. He requested the court to overturn the conviction based on insufficient evidence to justify the guilty verdict.

In December 1857, the case of James M. Robertson v. James R. Hamet was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff, James M. Robertson, had taken legal action against the defendant, James R. Hamet, concerning a promissory note originally executed by Hamet to a third party, Murdock. The legal proceedings revolved around the transfer of the note through endorsements: it was endorsed by Murdock to Bragg, and then by Bragg to Robertson. After admitting certain payments that had been made against the note, Robertson claimed that the remaining balance was owed by Hamet. The court assessed damages, and following the defendant's general demurrer, which was overruled, the clerk of the court undertaken the assessment of damages based on the established claim of non-payment. The court ruled that it was not necessary for the plaintiff to specifically allege consideration for the various endorsements nor to indicate non-payment to prior holders of the note, as the legal framework governing negotiable instruments provided an adequate basis for the claim.	The plaintiff, James M. Robertson, contended that he was the rightful holder of the promissory note following its endorsements from Murdock and Bragg. He alleged that a balance remained unpaid on the note due to the defendant’s failure to settle it, thereby seeking damages based on the outstanding amount owed. The plaintiff asserted that the allegations of note execution, endorsements, and non-payment were sufficient to uphold his claim under the principles governing negotiable instruments.	The defendant, James R. Hamet, raised a general demurrer against the claims made by the plaintiff, arguing that the plaintiff had not adequately substantiated his claim regarding the necessary considerations for the endorsements and non-payment to prior holders of the note. By choosing to abide by his demurrer, Hamet essentially maintained his position that the claims were insufficient to warrant a judgment against him, seeking dismissal of the case based on these procedural grounds.

Abram L. Small v. Cyrus Brainard is a legal case that took place in 1867 in Kankakee County, Illinois. The case originated from an action of trespass filed by Cyrus Brainard against Abram L. Small. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant illegally dug a ditch, which caused water to flood his land. During the trial, Brainard presented his case, and a jury found in his favor, awarding him damages for the alleged trespass. Small, the defendant, subsequently appealed the verdict to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the jury instructions were flawed, particularly that they assumed the defendant had committed the trespass rather than leaving that determination to the jury. The Supreme Court reviewed the trial court’s decision, focusing on the adequacy of evidence regarding the damages awarded and the jury instructions given by the trial judge.	The plaintiff, Cyrus Brainard, claimed that Abram L. Small committed trespass by digging a ditch that caused water to overflow onto his property. He sought damages for the harm caused to his land due to these alleged trespass acts. Brainard argued that the jury should be instructed to award him all damages proven to have been sustained as a result of the trespass.	The defendant, Abram L. Small, pleaded not guilty to the claims of trespass and raised several special defenses during the trial. Upon appeal, Small contended that the jury instructions given were prejudiced, as they assumed the factual basis of the trespass without allowing the jury to determine whether the trespass had indeed occurred. He argued that this instruction led to misleading the jury regarding the basis for awarding damages.

John S. Cook v. Isadore F. W. Gillmore et al. is a legal case that was decided on October 23, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved include John S. Cook, the appellant and former trustee, and Isadore F. W. Gillmore along with other appellees. The dispute arose after Cook was appointed trustee for certain funds amounting to approximately $31,000, which were created from the sale of real estate and constituted trust funds for the appellees. The original trustee, Robert D. Wilson, had died, and Cook was appointed at the request of all the appellees. However, there was no provision made in the court order or trustee agreement for Cook's compensation for performing his duties as a trustee. After executing the responsibilities of the trust, Cook sought to be recompensed for his time and services. The case revolved around whether a trustee who accepts a trust without prior compensation agreement can claim remuneration for their efforts.	The plaintiff, John S. Cook, argues that as the appointed trustee, he is entitled to compensation for the time and services he dedicated to managing the trust following the death of the previous trustee. He claims that despite fulfilling the responsibilities associated with the trust, the absence of a prior compensation agreement should not preclude him from being reimbursed for his services rendered while executing the trust duties.	The defendants, represented by Isadore F. W. Gillmore and others, assert that under established legal precedents, a trustee is not entitled to compensation for their services unless explicitly stated in the agreement or court order. They argue that Cook accepted the role of trustee without any contract for payment and, therefore, cannot claim compensation for management of the trust funds. The defendants emphasize the strict legal rule that prohibits remuneration for a trustee without an agreed compensation scheme.

The case of John M. Wilson v. The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company took place in Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. The legal action arose from a complaint filed by John M. Wilson in June 1868, in the circuit court of Richland County, seeking to recover penalties under Section 38 of the 1849 railroad law, which mandated that locomotives use a bell or whistle while crossing roads to ensure safety. The statute specified a penalty of $50 for non-compliance, and Wilson's complaint included 1,115 counts, each claiming this penalty. However, while the case was pending, a new law was enacted in February 1869, which amended the penalty provisions and allowed a maximum penalty of $100 but included a clause that exempts ongoing lawsuits from its application. The pivotal legal questions revolved around whether the earlier statute was implicitly repealed by the new law and the implications of such a repeal on the pending case.	Wilson argued that the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company had incurred penalties for failing to adhere to the safety requirements set forth in the 1849 law. He contended that each instance of non-compliance warranted a penalty of $50 per the statutory requirement. Wilson sought to recover these penalties in full, totaling over $55,000 based on the multitude of counts in his complaint. He contested the application of the 1869 statute during the ongoing litigation, which he believed should not affect the penalties accrued under the earlier law.	The defendant, Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company, responded by invoking the 1869 amendment, which effectively altered the penalties for non-compliance. They contended that the new law repealed the 1849 statute regarding penalties and therefore sought the court to dismiss Wilson's claims based on the new legal framework, which provided a higher maximum penalty but did not apply to pending cases in the same manner. They argued that the saving clause in the 1869 law was intended to limit ongoing litigation actions, and hence, the penalties pursued by Wilson should be dismissed.

In January 1877, the case of Daniel L. Wells et al. v. Hiram Sandford et al. took place in the Edgar Circuit Court, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Daniel L. Wells and others, were partners under the firm name Wells, French & Co., and they pursued legal action against Hiram Sandford and others, who operated as the partnership H. Sandford & Co. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants owed them an alleged indebtedness of $18,000. They filed for a writ of attachment, asserting that within six months before the suit began, the defendants had fraudulently disposed of their property to hinder their creditors. In response, Sandford filed a plea in abatement to counter this claim. The central question arose over a previous court decree that appointed a receiver for Sandford’s assets, which the plaintiffs argued was a fraudulent transfer intended to obstruct creditors. The case revolved around whether the transfer of assets handled by a court-appointed receiver could be considered fraudulent under the law.	The plaintiffs contended that the defendants engaged in fraudulent activities by disposing of their property to evade creditors ahead of their suit. They sought a legal judgment confirming their right to collect the alleged debt and asserted that the property assigned to the receiver was subject to attachment due to this fraudulent conveyance.	The defendants argued that the transfer of their property to a receiver was executed under a valid court decree from a court that had full jurisdiction over the subject and parties involved. They contended that since the decree had not been appealed and was lawful, the transfer should not be deemed fraudulent or subject to attachment. Thus, they maintained that the plaintiffs had no grounds to attach the property in question.

The case "Estate of Michael Rapp v. The Phœnix Insurance Company" took place in Jacksonville, Illinois, culminating in a decision filed on March 30, 1885, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved were the estate of Michael Rapp, who was a surety in a bond, and the Phœnix Insurance Company. Rapp had signed a bond that obligated him, along with two agents, to financially guarantee the proper conduct of the agents in their dealings with the insurance company. Rapp passed away in March 1882, and after his death, the agents failed to settle accounts with the insurance company for the January and February of 1883. The court had to determine whether Rapp’s estate was liable for the defaults occurring after his death, given the nature of the bond and its binding effect after Rapp’s demise. The lower courts had allowed a claim of $188.90 against Rapp's estate but not for the February default.	The Phœnix Insurance Company, as the plaintiff, claimed that the estate of Michael Rapp was liable for the amounts due from the agents due to their failure to remit payments for January and February 1883. The company asserted that the bond executed by Rapp indicated a binding obligation despite his death, emphasizing that Rapp's estate should be accountable for obligations arising during the term of the bond.	The estate of Michael Rapp contended that the bond inherently ceased to be operational upon Rapp's death, arguing that liabilities could not extend beyond his life. They pointed to the nature of the bond being akin to a continuing guaranty, which they claimed invalidated further obligations after Rapp’s demise. The defense mentioned previous cases to support the assertion that a surety’s death nullifies their obligations regarding any subsequent transactions.

The case of Canton Masonic Mutual Benevolent Society v. Charles W. Rockhold originated in Peoria County, Illinois and was decided on March 20, 1888. The plaintiff, Charles W. Rockhold, was a member of the Canton Masonic Mutual Benevolent Society, a corporation established for the purpose of providing financial aid to the widows, orphans, and heirs of deceased members. The society, organized under Illinois law, was not classified as a life insurance company. Rockhold had joined the society in 1875, paying a total of $165.60 in assessments, and was entitled to receive $1,836 upon reaching the age of seventy, as stipulated in the society's constitution. However, the society's board of directors had subsequently altered its constitution to prohibit such payments to living members. After reaching the age of seventy, Rockhold demanded payment, but the society claimed it could no longer fulfill that obligation. The case was brought before the Circuit Court, which ruled in Rockhold's favor, leading to the appeal by the society.	Rockhold argued that the constitution of the Canton Masonic Mutual Benevolent Society constituted a binding contract which entitled him to receive $1,836 upon turning seventy years old. He claimed his consistent payment of assessments satisfied his obligations as a member, therefore making the society liable for the promised benefit. Rockhold maintained that subsequent amendments to the society's constitution, which prohibited payments to living members, were invalid and did not affect his entitlement under the original terms.	The Canton Masonic Mutual Benevolent Society contended that it lawfully ceased to have the power to make payments to living members under amendments to its constitution, which restricted benefits to the heirs of deceased members only. The society argued that any contract promising a benefit to a living member exceeded its authority and was void. Furthermore, it claimed that the amended constitution was known to Rockhold, and thus he could not claim benefits that the society was prohibited from providing without risking penalties against its officers.

John A. J. Kendig, Horatio Stone Jr., and Elizabeth A. Stone, as trustees, filed a lawsuit on March 3, 1883, in the Cook County Circuit Court against Emily H. Pratt, her husband James Pratt, and E.K. Smith. The case revolves around a dispute over property originally owned by Horatio O. Stone, who passed away in 1877, with titles affected by multiple prior litigations. The complainants sought a court order to quiet their possession of certain lots in Stone's subdivision, aiming to eliminate any claims or "clouds" on the title to the properties involved, and to issue a permanent injunction against further litigation related to these properties. Emily H. Pratt countered with a cross-bill asserting her ownership and requesting possession of the lots in question, as well as an accounting for any proceeds from previous sales. The Circuit Court ultimately decreed that the trustees held valid title to the lots and issued a permanent injunction against the Pratts' interference, declaring the deed from Emily H. Pratt to E.K. Smith as null and void.	The plaintiffs, the trustees for the estate of Horatio O. Stone, claimed rightful ownership of the disputed properties based on established legal titles from previous litigation. They sought to permanently enjoin the defendants from making any claims to the property or pursuing further legal actions that would interfere with their possession. They requested the court to recognize their title to the lots and to remove any legal impediments pertaining to their ownership.	The defendants, led by Emily H. Pratt, countered with arguments asserting their claimed ownership of the lots, presenting a cross-bill that contested the trustees' claims and sought possession. Their defense included appealing for the court to account for proceeds from property sales and rents collected by the trustees, as well as questioning the legality of the title transfers to the trustees.

In 1874, in Kankakee County, Illinois, George Laidlou and his business partner Humphrey Barber entered into a dispute regarding a contract with Frank Hatch and others, relating to work for the Kankakee and Indiana Railroad Company. M. C. Ott, a contractor with the railroad, subcontracted work to Laidlou and Barber for a fixed price. Following their agreement, Ott began work while Laidlou and Barber also commenced their tasks as per their agreement. Subsequently, Hatch and his associates obtained a judgment against Ott for $377.62, which Ott was unable to pay, leading them to issue a garnishee summons against the railroad company, seeking the money owed to Ott. Laidlou and Barber intervened, claiming that the railroad company owed them for the work performed. A verbal agreement was asserted wherein the railroad’s treasurer would pay Laidlou and Barber directly for their work upon completion. However, the railroad company contested this claim, stating that the conversation lacked the elements of a binding contract, particularly since it was not in writing, lacked consideration, and did not release Ott from his original contract with the company.	Laidlou and Barber, as the plaintiffs, claimed that a verbal agreement existed wherein the railroad company was to pay them directly for their work instead of paying Ott. They argued this arrangement was valid and sought the money owed to Ott as rightfully belonging to them, based on the presumed agreement that amended their original contract with Ott.	The railroad company, as the defendant, contended that there was no enforceable contract with Laidlou and Barber, citing the absence of a written agreement, lack of consideration, and the lack of any release or assumption of liability towards them. They maintained that the conversation held with the treasurer did not constitute a legal contract, merely serving as a request for payment directed to them at Ott's behest, which was insufficient to create a binding obligation.

In 1881, in Chicago, Illinois, Kittielia Howard filed a slander suit against Simon Heller, a local dry goods store owner, after a conversation that allegedly occurred in his store. Howard claimed that during this conversation, Heller implied that she was guilty of theft regarding a parasol in her possession. Heller had accused her of having the parasol that had been stolen from his store two weeks prior. The conversation was reportedly witnessed by several individuals, and it involved Heller stating that the parasol did not belong to Howard and that he would send it to the rightful owner for identification. Howard countered his claims by stating she had purchased the parasol for $1.75 from another store, offering evidence through a receipted bill. After a trial where the jury found Heller guilty of slandering Howard and awarded her $700 in damages, Heller appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court, challenging the trial court's rulings on jury instructions and the admissibility of evidence.	Kittielia Howard claimed that Simon Heller falsely accused her of stealing a parasol during a public conversation. She argued that these accusations were slanderous and damaging to her reputation. Howard sought damages for the emotional and reputational harm caused by Heller's statements, specifically claiming that such remarks implied she had committed larceny.	Simon Heller defended himself against Howard's claims by asserting that his comments did not amount to slander and contended that there was insufficient proof that the words allegedly spoken could be construed as a formal accusation of theft. Heller argued that the necessary extrinsic facts to support Howard's claims were not adequately established and that the instructions provided to the jury were erroneous. He requested that the case be dismissed or that a new trial be granted.

In September 1874, a legal contest unfolded regarding the election for the office of alderman in Joliet, Illinois. The case involved Henry Young, the appellant, and William Adam, the appellee. The core issue was whether the county court of Will County had the jurisdiction to review the election contest. Historical precedents in Illinois law indicated that for a county court to preside over an election contest for a city office, the city must be incorporated under the general law governing city incorporation. Significantly, Joliet was incorporated under a special charter, which ultimately influenced the court's jurisdiction. The case drew comparisons to a prior case, Brush v. Lemma, which established similar jurisdictional issues in the context of a mayoral election. As a result of these legal findings, the court had to determine the validity of the county court's involvement in the election dispute.	Henry Young, the plaintiff, argued that the county court should have jurisdiction to hear the contest for the alderman position. Young's primary claim hinged on the interpretation of laws concerning contested elections and the authority of the county court in such matters.	William Adam, the defendant, maintained that the county court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the election contest because Joliet was not incorporated under the general law of the State of Illinois. Instead, Adam argued that the city's incorporation under a special charter precluded the county court from making a legitimate ruling on the case, citing the precedent set in Brush v. Lemma.

On February 13, 1843, at a public land sale in Chicago, Wm. N. Davis purchased two tracts of land in Kendall County, initially under the name of Geo. A. O. Beaumont. On November 20, 1843, Beaumont conveyed these lands to Davis, but the deed was not recorded. In May 1848, Davis transferred the lands to Francis Howe. The dispute arose when S. B. Hopkins filed a bill in March 1849 against Davis, Howe, and Israel P. Vancleve, seeking a conveyance for these lands, claiming a prior agreement with Davis to purchase them. Vancleve had initially attempted to secure the lands through a loan agreement with Davis, where he proposed that Davis bid for the land on his behalf. The arrangement included terms of interest, and although Vancleve claimed to have paid Davis through work and cash, Davis refused to finalize the deed. Hopkins filed the bill after Vancleve conveyed part of his interest to him in 1848. Throughout the case, multiple testimonies and claims regarding the nature of the agreement, conveyance, and payments were presented, with the court tasked with determining the validity of Hopkins's claim over the lands.	The plaintiff, S. B. Hopkins, argued that he was entitled to a conveyance of the disputed lands based on a previous agreement with Wm. N. Davis that included a loan for the purchase of the land, with terms specifying a 20% interest rate. Hopkins alleged that Vancleve, who had an equitable interest in the land, and Davis entered into an arrangement regarding the bidding and payment for the lands, which Davis later misrepresented by taking the title in Beaumont's name. Hopkins sought a court order compelling Davis and Howe to convey the land to him as he had performed under the contract.	The defendants, Wm. N. Davis and Francis Howe, denied the material allegations in Hopkins's bill. Davis claimed that the contract implied by Vancleve and himself was unenforceable under the statute of frauds and that any agreement regarding the land was usurious. Davis maintained that the discovery of prior possession and the supposed loan arrangement lacked equity and that Vancleve's conveyance to Hopkins did not solidify any legitimate claim to the land. They further argued that any legal obligations had been extinguished by the passage of time and the failings of the previous claims.

The case titled "Green L. J. Haralson and Wife v. David Bridges" took place in November 1852 in Johnson County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Green L. J. Haralson and his wife, filed a suit against David Bridges for the recovery of rent that was due for a property leased from Mrs. Haralson prior to their marriage. The crux of the dispute centered around a payment made to Smith, who was Mrs. Haralson's husband before their divorce, for the rental fees. The plaintiffs contended that this payment was made collusively, aiming to prevent them from claiming their legal right to the rent due. They argued that Smith had abandoned Mrs. Haralson and was living separately from her, thereby invalidating his authority to receive the rent on her behalf. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendant by sustaining a demurrer against the plaintiffs' claims regarding the collusion of payment to Smith.	The plaintiffs argued that a payment made to Mrs. Haralson's former husband, Smith, should not discharge the defendant from his obligation to pay rent to Mrs. Haralson. They claimed the payment was fraudulent and collusive, facilitated to deny them their legal right to receive the rent. The plaintiffs sought a court ruling to hold Bridges accountable for the outstanding rent, asserting that Smith's abandonment of Mrs. Haralson during their separation invalidated his claim to receive the rent payments.	The defendant, David Bridges, maintained that the payment made to Smith was a legal discharge of his obligation to pay rent for the property, regardless of Smith's living arrangement with Mrs. Haralson. He argued that the legal rights remained intact, despite the couple living apart. Thus, Bridges contended that the payment to Smith upheld his liability and should protect him from any further claims for the rent by the Haralsons.

Benjamin L. Dorsey v. The St. Louis, Alton & Terre Haute R. R. Co. occurred in 1871 in Illinois. The case centers around a dispute over a covenant related to a land conveyance. On April 25, 1854, Dorsey sold a strip of land to the Terre Haute & Alton Railroad Company, including stipulations for the construction and maintenance of fences and a depot on the property. After the original company failed to uphold these terms, it sold its interests to the St. Louis, Alton & Terre Haute Railroad Company. Dorsey claimed that the new owner was liable for the covenant obligations despite the changes in ownership. The core legal question was whether the original covenant concerning the land "ran with the land," thus binding subsequent owners. The lower court dismissed Dorsey's claims, determining that the covenant was personal rather than real and did not extend to the new owner. Dorsey appealed, arguing that the covenant was perpetual and should apply to the purchaser.	Dorsey's main arguments were that the original covenant stipulating the maintenance of the fences and the depot was a real covenant that ran with the land, thus binding the new owner, St. Louis, Alton & Terre Haute Railroad Company. He asserted that the new company had received notice of the covenant when they acquired the land and therefore should uphold the obligations stated in the original agreement.	The defendant contended that the covenant was personal and did not run with the land, hence making them not liable for the obligations outlined in the original covenant as they were not signatories to that agreement. They argued that since the Terre Haute & Alton Railroad Company was not authorized to convey certain rights as a corporation, the covenant should not bind the new entity.

John B. Frink v. Pratt & Company took place in Macon County, Illinois, with the final judgment rendered on November 18, 1887. The case involved John B. Frink (the appellant), who brought an action of trover against Pratt & Company (the appellee) to recover the value of corn grown on land leased to a tenant. The tenant had sold the corn to the defendant. Frink claimed that he was entitled to one-third of the crop as rent for the land, supported by a statutory lien which he believed allowed him to pursue any party acquiring the crop from his tenant. The circuit court trial was conducted without a jury, and the judge ultimately ruled in favor of the defendant. The court found that while a landlord holds a lien on the crop, this does not confer the necessary right of possession to maintain a trover action against a third party purchaser.	The plaintiff, John B. Frink, contended that as the landlord, he had a statutory lien on the crop produced by his tenant, which entitled him to pursue recovery of the corn's value following its sale to Pratt & Company. Frink argued that he had an equitable interest in the crop and sought legal remedy to reclaim what he believed was rightly his due to his claim on the crop as rent.	Pratt & Company, the defendant, argued that they purchased the corn in good faith from the tenant and claimed that the landlord, by having only a statutory lien, did not possess the right of immediate possession required to maintain an action of trover. They contended that the tenant was regarded as the legal owner of the entire crop until the rent was deducted, thereby negating the landlord's claim to pursue the matter against an innocent purchaser.

In September 1872, the case "Reese P. Stitt v. Christian Brendel, Jr." was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from an action of replevin that originated before a justice of the peace. The dispute arose in JoDaviess County, Illinois, where Reese P. Stitt sought the recovery of property that he claimed belonged to him. At trial in the circuit court, a jury found in favor of Stitt, establishing the property as his and assessing damages at one cent for the use of the replevied property. Following the jury's decision, Brendel, the defendant, moved for a new trial and in arrest of judgment, both of which were overruled by the court. The presiding judge, Hon. William Brown, upheld the jury's verdict, stating that since no written pleadings or bill of exceptions were provided to contest the trial’s findings, the court could only review the verdict and ensure that the judgment aligned. Consequently, the court affirmed the judgment based on the jury's verdict.	Reese P. Stitt's primary argument was that he was the rightful owner of the property in question and sought its return through a replevin action. He argued for the acknowledgment of his ownership and the damages assessed by the jury, amounting to one cent for the use of the property. Additionally, he requested recovery for costs incurred in the litigation.	Christian Brendel, Jr., the defendant, contested the court's judgment by filing motions for a new trial and in arrest of judgment, arguing against the jury's verdict. However, in the absence of written pleadings and a bill of exceptions, the specifics of his defenses were not elaborated in the record. Compared to Stitt's claims, Brendel did not present a substantive defense that established his ownership or rights to the property.

The case "Hiram F. Bush v. Joseph H. Hanson" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873, concerning a judgment by confession against the plaintiff, Hiram F. Bush. The events leading to this case began when Bush executed a promissory note on September 8, 1871, which was payable six months later. Accompanying the note was a warrant of attorney that authorized an attorney to confess judgment on behalf of Bush. This judgment was confessed in court on September 30, 1871. The plaintiff later filed a motion on June 4, 1873, seeking to set aside the earlier judgment, asserting that the necessary testimony required by statute to justify such a judgment was not produced during the initial proceedings. The court ultimately addressed the issues surrounding the statutory requirements for confession of judgment and the jurisdiction of the court in handling the case.	The plaintiff, Hiram F. Bush, argues that the confession of judgment should be set aside on the grounds that the record does not offer evidence of compliance with the statutory requirements. Specifically, he contends that the plaintiff must provide testimony to prove that he was informed of the nature of the power of attorney, which allowed for the rendition of judgment before the note was due. He claims the circuit court erred by not acknowledging this lack of evidence.	The defendant, Joseph H. Hanson, contends that the necessary documents, including the warrant of attorney and affidavit, were properly filed before the court. The defendant argues that the court had jurisdiction to render the judgment and that the absence of the specific oral testimony required at the time of confession does not negate the court's authority to proceed with the judgment. The defendant asserts that the judgment should stand as there was sufficient proof provided to the court that warranted the judgment's confession.

In June 1860, a legal dispute arose in the Alexander Circuit Court, located in Cairo, Illinois. The case involved plaintiffs Nicholas Hunsaker and others (referred to as Plaintiffs in Error) and defendants B. S. Harrell and others (Defendants in Error). The background centers around a 1859 legislative act that stipulated that real and personal property in Cairo would be exempt from taxation for county purposes. However, at the March term of the Alexander County Court, a subsequent order was passed assessing taxes on all property, including that in Cairo. Hunsaker was set to collect these taxes, prompting the defendants, who were property owners in Cairo, to seek an injunction to prevent this collection, arguing that the tax assessment was in violation of the exemption provided by the earlier legislative act. The court granted the injunction and ruled against the plaintiffs' claims, leading to an appeal by Hunsaker to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs contended that the defendants' claims for an injunction were invalid, asserting that the tax was legally imposed despite the previous exemption legislation. They claimed the circuit court erred in granting the injunction and sought to overturn this decision through a writ of error, arguing that the bill of complaint against them lacked sufficient legal basis and that the decree should legally favor them rather than the defendants.	The defendants argued that as property holders in Cairo, their assets were exempt from tax under the 1859 legislative act. They maintained that the tax assessment imposed by the county court was unlawful and that Hunsaker's attempts to collect the taxes were unjustified. They sought a perpetual injunction to prevent the collection of these taxes, asserting that the court's previous ruling supported their legal arguments and right to exemption.

On February 28, 1863, in Springfield, Illinois, Richard H. Ridgway initiated a legal action against Alexander J. Hawk and John Gannon, claiming trespass vi et armis, which included allegations of assault and unlawful imprisonment. Ridgway sought $2,000 in damages. The case was presided over by Judge David M. Woodson in the Circuit Court of Morgan County. During the trial, the jury received instructions from the court regarding how to assess the defendants' actions. The defendants denied the claims and pleaded the general issue, and the jury subsequently found them guilty, awarding Ridgway $450 in damages. The defendants then appealed the decision, arguing that the court's instructions were erroneous, particularly those that influenced the jury's assessment of damages by considering the defendants' financial circumstances.	Ridgway asserted that Hawk and Gannon unlawfully restrained him, constituting false imprisonment. He maintained that the defendants' actions, regardless of whether they involved physical violence, amounted to deprivation of his liberty. Ridgway requested a monetary verdict reflecting the emotional and psychological distress suffered, seeking no more than $2,000.	The defendants contended that the jury instructions provided during the trial were flawed, particularly the instruction that suggested the jury consider their financial capacity in determining potential damages. They argued this assumption unduly influenced the jury's judgment regarding their guilt and the nature of the damages. The defendants sought to have the judgment overturned, asserting that the jury should have determined the guilt based solely on the evidence presented.

The case "Pittsburg, Fort Wayne and Chicago Railway Company v. Thomas Bumstead" took place in September 1868 in Cook County, Illinois. The incident involved a four-year-old boy, son of Thomas Bumstead, who was injured near a railway track owned by the Pittsburg, Fort Wayne and Chicago Railway Company in Gastello, Indiana. On the day of the accident, the boy's mother temporarily left him with his fourteen-year-old sister while she visited a neighbor. During her absence, the child wandered away and was struck by debris from a collision between an express train and a push car that had been improperly left on the track. The child sustained significant injuries, leading to a lawsuit by his father against the railway company for damages due to negligence. The jury awarded Bumstead $4,500, but after he remitted $3,000, a judgment was entered for $1,500 against the railway company. The railway company appealed the decision, contending negligence on the part of the parents and the child’s status as a trespasser.	Thomas Bumstead, the plaintiff, argued that his son was not a trespasser on the railway right of way and that the railway company was negligent in the management of their train, which resulted in the child's injuries. Bumstead claimed that the child's mother acted reasonably by leaving him in the care of his older sister. He contended that the railway company's negligence, particularly in loaning the push car to untrained individuals and failing to halt the train despite warning signals, was the direct cause of the accident. Bumstead sought damages to compensate for his son's injuries.	The Pittsburg, Fort Wayne and Chicago Railway Company argued that the child was a trespasser on their property and that his parents were grossly negligent for allowing him to wander unsupervised. They contended that the child’s wandering onto the railway right of way was an action that contributed to the accident, and that the parents should bear some responsibility for this negligence. Furthermore, they asserted that the employees operating the train did not act negligently, emphasizing that the child was in a position he shouldn't have been, and thus, liability should not fall on the railway.

In 1844, a legal dispute arose in Jersey County, Illinois, involving Elizabeth Hart as the plaintiff and Cyrus Tolman, the administrator of the estate of Urial Downey (deceased), as the defendant. The case centered around a bond related to a previous obligation concerning alimony payments. The bond stipulated that if Urial Downey was released from another penal bond related to an alimony obligation to Elizabeth Hart, he would pay her a specified amount of $200. Hart's claim was based on this bond, but the court found significant deficiencies in the declaration regarding the bond's conditions. Specifically, Hart did not include an averment that Downey had indeed been released from the original penal bond, rendering her claim invalid. The case was initially brought to the Jersey Circuit Court in September 1843, presided over by Judge Samuel D. Lockwood, who handled the initial demurrer to Hart's declaration.	Elizabeth Hart argued that she was entitled to $200 from Urial Downey based on a bond stipulation that required Downey to pay her upon being released from a previous penal bond concerning alimony. Her claims relied on the terms of the bond but were ultimately deemed insufficient due to missing allegations about Downey's release from the prior bond.	Cyrus Tolman, representing the estate of Urial Downey, contended that Hart's declaration was deficient as it failed to assert that Downey was released from the previous penal bond. The defense highlighted the lack of proper legal grounding in Hart's claims, suggesting that both counts in her declaration were inaccurate and loose, warranting the demurrer and subsequent dismissal of her claims.

The case "Orson W. Goit et al. v. Patrick Joyce et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871. It originated from the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Johst G. Bogers. The case involves a legal dispute regarding liability for certain goods that were purportedly purchased. The plaintiff, Orson W. Goit and others, claimed that the defendants, including Patrick Joyce, were liable for the costs associated with those goods. The court's review indicated that there was insufficient evidence demonstrating that one of the defendants, Curtis, had any obligation to pay for the goods or any knowledge of their purchase. As a result, the court determined that the evidence produced in the case at hand only indicated liability on the part of Goit, leading to complications regarding the judgment rendered against both defendants.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants were liable for the purchase of certain goods. They contended that there was an implied or express obligation for the defendants to pay for the items in question. They sought a judgment confirming this liability and requiring the defendants to compensate them for the goods.	The defendants, particularly Curtis, maintained that there was no evidence showing any liability for the goods. They argued that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate Curtis's involvement or any promise on his part to pay for the goods. They requested the court to reverse the judgment against both defendants, citing the lack of supporting evidence for liability.

In the case of H. C. Agnew et al. v. A. J. Brall, the dispute arose in McDonough County, Illinois, with the first court's ruling occurring prior to July 14, 1887. The case initially involved a municipal corporation's judgment that was being challenged by the appellants, H. C. Agnew and others. The plaintiffs argued that the settlement reached between the municipal corporation and the defendant, A. J. Brall, was improper and not aimed at resolving the underlying issues of the case, which focused on the collection of a judgment. The plaintiffs sought to clarify the motivations behind the Council's order that released the appellee (Brall) from the judgment, emphasizing that it was not a settlement but rather an act of clemency. The case had previously been reversed and remanded to the Circuit Court, which reaffirmed its decision in accordance with the appellate court's findings. The case was once again brought for review, focusing on whether the previous decision should be reconsidered.	The plaintiffs, H. C. Agnew et al., contended that the Council's order releasing A. J. Brall from the municipal judgment was not intended to settle the matter regarding the lawsuit. They emphasized that the Council's actions lacked the necessary intent to conclude the issues at hand or prevent an appeal. The plaintiffs sought clarity and legal relief from what they perceived as an inappropriate settlement arrangement that undermined their position.	A. J. Brall, the defendant, maintained that the actions of the Council were legitimate and that the order was meant as a gesture of goodwill towards the plaintiff. Brall contended that the plaintiffs' arguments regarding res judicata—previous judgments that bar further litigation—applied to their claims, asserting that the issues were already conclusively ruled upon in earlier proceedings.

In September 1873, in DeKalb County, Illinois, the legal case "Sarah Wade v. Reuben M. Pritchard" arose when Reuben M. Pritchard, interested in the estate of the deceased Elotia Pritchard, filed an affidavit in the county court requesting a citation to compel Sarah Wade to disclose any effects she possessed belonging to the estate. Wade and another individual, who was also cited, appeared before the court, waived the process, and underwent examination. While the other party was discharged, the court found that Wade possessed two notes belonging to the estate, leading to orders for their surrender to the estate's administrator. Wade subsequently appealed the decision to the circuit court, which upheld the original ruling. Wade appealed again to the Illinois Supreme Court, raising objections regarding jurisdiction and the rejection of her evidence regarding the title to the notes.	Sarah Wade claimed that the county court erred by not dismissing the proceedings for lack of jurisdiction, arguing that the affidavit did not adequately state Pritchard's interest in the estate. Furthermore, she contended that the court wrongfully rejected her evidence supporting her title to the notes, which she argued was pertinent to her defense.	Reuben M. Pritchard contended that the waiver of process by the parties led to the assumption of jurisdiction, effectively waiving any objections regarding the affidavit's sufficiency. He argued that the proceedings were valid under the Statute of Wills, which authorized the court to compel discovery of estate property, and asserted that both parties had the right to present relevant evidence during the inquiries.

In the case of Louisiana St. John v. William Quitzow, the dispute originated in the town of St. Clair, Illinois. The events leading to the legal action took place around 1874. The property in question was part of an old street that had been vacated. In 1859, Louisiana St. John, the appellant, leased a portion of her property to August Myer, which included the disputed area. William Quitzow, the appellee, later acquired the rights to this lease. The case involved complex issues of property ownership, particularly concerning an assignment of the lease and the transactions surrounding the vacated street. In 1863, St. John had sold lots including lot 63, which intersected with the disputed property, potentially affecting ownership claims. St. John vacated some streets legally in 1867, but there was contention around whether Quitzow, due to his possession as a tenant, could challenge St. John's title after purchasing the property from other parties. The primary legal questions revolved around the rights related to vacated streets and the limits of the tenant's ability to dispute the landlord's title.	Louisiana St. John claimed that she maintained ownership of the property, including the center of the vacated street, and sought to recover possession from William Quitzow under the assertion that he could not dispute her title as her tenant. She argued that any rights he may claim were invalid because she had not relinquished her interest and retained rights reserved in the transaction that allowed for the street's vacation.	William Quitzow contended that he could assert rights to a portion of the land based on his purchase of property from Rantenberg and Orbike, claiming it included rights to the center of the vacated street. He argued that St. John's actions in selling and vacating the property terminated her title, thus enforcing his claim to the disputed land. Quitzow maintained that, as the current owner, he had the right to challenge St. John's claim despite initially being her tenant.

In the case of H. G. Rouse v. Peter Mohr and Fred Glissman, the events unfolded in Peoria, Illinois, during the late 19th century, specifically on February 20, 1881, when a promissory note was issued. The plaintiff, H. G. Rouse, and his business partner George W. Bouse & Son accused Fred Glissman of embezzlement, leading to Glissman's arrest under a warrant. Subsequently, to secure Glissman’s release, Peter Mohr, Glissman's half-brother, was coerced into signing as surety on a promissory note. The police officer, Fahey, threatened Glissman with imprisonment if Mohr did not agree to sign the note. During the proceedings, allegations arose regarding the appropriateness of the officer's actions and the legitimacy of the note, which led to the legal dispute.	H. G. Rouse claimed that Mohr’s signature on the promissory note held legal validity and sought enforcement of the note, emphasizing that Glissman owed a debt due to embezzlement. The plaintiff argued that the note should be honored, and they sought compensation for the amount stated in the note plus interest and legal costs.	The defendant, Peter Mohr, contended that the note was void due to its illegal consideration. Mohr asserted that his signature was obtained under duress since the officer had no authority to take Glissman out of custody for the purpose of coercing Mohr to sign the note. He emphasized that the threat of prosecution against Glissman was unlawful and constituted an abuse of legal process, effectively rendering the contract void.

In 1868, a legal dispute arose in Morgan County, Illinois, involving the heirs of Jacob Strawn, a deceased landowner. The case, titled "Phebe G. Strawn et al. v. William Strawn et al.," was filed as a petition for partition and assignment of dower among the heirs and Jacob's widow, who served as the estate's administratrix. The contention centered around lands purchased by Jacob Strawn before his death. A deed for these lands arrived during his final illness but was not delivered prior to his passing. After his death, the widow, using estate funds, paid the vendor the purchase price and received the deed. The widowed plaintiff sought her dower rights in these lands while also claiming she was entitled to receive one-third of the paid purchase money as part of the estate's personal assets. The case was marked by significant disagreement over the proper division of the estate and the widow's claim.	The plaintiff, represented by Phebe G. Strawn, argued that as Jacob Strawn’s widow and administratrix, she was entitled to claim one-third of the purchase money paid for the lands purchased posthumously as part of her share of the estate’s personal property. Additionally, she sought the assignment of her dower rights in the properties purchased by her late husband.	The defendant, represented by William Strawn and co-heirs, contended that the widow was not entitled to the claimed sum of money as she had already recognized the validity of the estate's debts by paying them. They argued that the money disbursed for the land was a valid estate expense and that the widow should not be allowed to charge this payment against the heirs’ interests. Instead, they maintained that she should accept her dower rights from the acquired properties.

In 1889, in a bustling area of Chicago, an incident occurred involving the Chicago Hansom Cab Company and a man named John McCarthy. The case arose from an alleged act of negligence by the cab company's driver, who, while trying to maneuver into position in a line of cabs waiting for a bridge to close, accidentally struck McCarthy in the back with one of the cab's shafts. This incident led to McCarthy sustaining personal injuries, prompting him to file a lawsuit against the cab company. The case was reviewed by the Illinois Appellate Court after an initial ruling was made in the Cook County Circuit Court, with the Honorable Julius S. Grinnell presiding.	McCarthy, as the plaintiff, claimed that the cab driver acted negligently, resulting in his injuries. He argued that the driver’s reckless actions, amid a crowded street, directly caused the accident and his subsequent suffering. McCarthy's legal request was for compensation for the personal injuries sustained due to the cab driver's negligence.	The Chicago Hansom Cab Company, represented by attorneys Monroe & McShane, contended that the jury's verdict in favor of McCarthy should not be disturbed. They argued that there was conflicting evidence presented during the trial but maintained that there was no error in law that justified overturning the decision. The Cab Company sought to affirm the verdict, contesting the notion of negligence on part of its driver.

In December 1839, a legal dispute arose in Schuyler County, Illinois between William B. Warren, the plaintiff in error, and Samuel McHatton, the defendant in error. The case was heard before Justice Peter Lott during a special term of the Circuit Court. The action stemmed from a promissory note, and Warren sought to amend his petition and summons regarding the figures detailing the amount owed in the note. He requested to replace the figures "19" with "17," but the Court denied this request. Given the circumstances, the appeal focused solely on this refusal. The majority opinion acknowledged the discretionary power of the Court to grant or deny such motions and held that the refusal to amend the petition did not constitute a valid ground for error. Consequently, the Circuit Court's decision stood.	The plaintiff, William B. Warren, primarily argued that he should be allowed to amend his petition and summons pertaining to a promissory note to correct a numerical error in its description. Specifically, he wanted to replace the figure "19" with "17". His legal request was to challenge the Court's refusal to allow this simple amendment, contending that it was a matter of legal correctness.	The defendant, Samuel McHatton, maintained that the Circuit Court's refusal to grant the requested amendment was within its discretionary powers and did not amount to a reversible error. His defense focused on the procedural aspect of the case, asserting that the decision made by the lower court should be upheld since it properly exercised its discretion in denying the amendment.

In 1857, in the Randolph Circuit Court of Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Joseph B. Holmes (the appellant) and Joseph Sinclair (the appellee), who was suing on behalf of James Close. The case centered around the enforcement of two promissory notes. The first note involved both Holmes and Joseph Sinclair & Co. as joint makers, while the second note was exclusively issued by Holmes. During the trial, the plaintiff, Sinclair, presented the joint note as evidence against Holmes. Holmes objected to its admission, arguing that the note should not be valid without additional proof of its nature. However, the court overruled the objection, allowing the note into evidence. The trial concluded in favor of Sinclair, with a judgment of $185.64 against Holmes. Following the judgment, Holmes sought a new trial, claiming that the admission of the note was erroneous, but the court denied this request, forming the basis for his appeal.	The plaintiff, Joseph Sinclair, claimed that Holmes was liable for the amount stated in two promissory notes. He argued that the first note, executed jointly by Holmes and Joseph Sinclair & Co., and the second note executed solely by Holmes, clearly established Holmes's obligation to pay the debts specified. Sinclair sought a judgment in the amount due under these notes, which amounted to $185.64.	The defendant, Joseph B. Holmes, contended that the admission of the joint promissory note into evidence was improper without supporting proof of its nature as a series note solely belonging to him. Holmes asserted that if the name of the joint maker was fraudulent or unauthorized, his liability was limited, and he could not be held accountable under a joint action. He requested that the court grant a new trial based on the alleged error regarding the joint note.

The case of Arthur C. Ducat v. The City of Chicago emerged in September 1868 in Chicago, Illinois. The City of Chicago brought an action of debt against Arthur C. Ducat, acting as an agent for four insurance companies incorporated in New York. The city sought to recover taxes on insurance premiums collected by Ducat from those companies while they operated in Chicago. The city based its claim on the fifth section of the Revised Charter of the City of Chicago, which allowed for taxation on foreign insurance companies. The case initially faced a special plea from Ducat, which was demurred, leading to a trial on the general issue wherein the court ultimately decided in favor of the city, awarding $3,756.39 plus costs. Ducat appealed the ruling, focusing on the constitutionality of taxing foreign insurance companies versus domestic ones.	The City of Chicago's main argument was that it had the authority under its charter to tax premiums received by foreign insurance companies like those represented by Ducat. The city contended that such taxation was lawful and did not violate constitutional provisions regarding the treatment of corporations as citizens. The city sought to uphold the trial court's judgment and collect the owed tax amount.	Duane, as the representative of the insurance companies, argued that the taxation imposed by the City of Chicago was unconstitutional, claiming that it discriminated against foreign corporations while benefiting domestic corporations. He maintained that corporations should be treated as citizens and, thus, should not be taxed disproportionately compared to state-born entities. He requested the reversal of the trial court's ruling, emphasizing the inequity of the tax.

On November 19, 1884, in Muskegon, Michigan, the tugboat Alice E. Getty was preparing for a towing voyage to Pentwater, approximately 40 miles away. The tug's owner, Cullen C. Allen, contacted Lewis, an agent who had previously conducted fire insurance business with him, to procure marine insurance for the vessel. Allen paid Lewis a premium of $52 for this insurance, intended to cover the period from November 19 to November 30, 1884. However, the actual insurance contract was not concluded until November 20, after further communications through an insurance broker in Chicago, during which the premium increased to $60. Before the insurance certificate was delivered, the tug met with disaster during a storm on the morning of November 20 and was stranded. The court found that Lewis acted as an agent of the plaintiffs and lacked authority to bind the defendant, Continental Insurance Company, to an insurance contract. This lack of proper agency led to the question of whether the insurance was valid given the timing of the loss undisclosed to the insurer.	The plaintiffs argued that they had secured a valid marine insurance contract through Lewis on November 19, 1884, since they had paid the premium before the loss occurred. They sought to recover damages amounting to $5,348.47 based on the assertion that the insurance should be applicable retroactively to the date of the premium payment, despite the fact that the certificate was issued after the wreck.	The defendant contended that no valid insurance contract was made as Lewis was not authorized to act on behalf of the defendant. They also argued that the plaintiffs had knowledge of the tug's disaster before the insurance certificate was delivered and that the concealment of this information should void any liability. The defendant sought to have the court dismiss the claims based on these defenses.

In 1868, the case of Israel B. Holmes et ux. v. John H. Holmes took place in Illinois, representing a dispute regarding real property. The appellant, John H. Holmes, had ownership of a parcel of land and originally made a verbal promise to his father, Israel B. Holmes, to lease him the east half of this land for life. However, after refusing to formalize a lease agreement, the dispute escalated into legal action when Israel initiated a lawsuit to enforce this verbal promise. The case had previously been heard in April 1867, where the facts were thoroughly detailed. This led to an appeal after the initial court decree granted Israel a lease for life on the property. The defendant argued that the promise was not binding under the statute of frauds, stating that it lacked the necessary legal foundation, as there was no consideration provided for such a promise.	The plaintiff, Israel B. Holmes, claimed a right to a lease for life on the east half of the property owned by his son, John H. Holmes. He argued that the property should have been conveyed to him based on John's verbal promise, and sought legal enforcement to secure his title to the lease.	The defendant, John H. Holmes, contended that the verbal promise to lease the property was not legally binding under the statute of frauds, as it was made without consideration. He asserted that, as the sole owner of the property, he was under no obligation to honor his father's request for a lease, especially since the initial offer was declined and there were no equitable grounds to compel compliance.

John Boyd and Jacob Lammert are adjoining landowners in Illinois, involved in a legal dispute regarding a partition fence separating their properties. On September 5, 1885, Lammert served Boyd with a written notice indicating his intention to remove his portion of the fence after a year. Following this notice, Boyd filed a legal complaint on September 17, 1885, aiming to stop Lammert from removing the fence. The legal bill filed by Boyd was lengthy and included many irrelevant details. However, it effectively sought an injunction against Lammert's removal of the fence. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court after a demurrer was sustained against Boyd's complaint during the November term of 1885. The court examined the relevant state statutes governing partition fences, which stipulate that adjoining landowners must contribute to the maintenance of such fences unless one party decides to leave their land open.	Boyd's main argument centered on his assertion that Lammert should not be permitted to remove his share of the partition fence without mutual agreement or proper compensation for its value. He sought a legal injunction to prevent Lammert from carrying out his plan to remove the fence, emphasizing his right as a landowner to maintain the fence as part of their joint responsibility for property demarcation.	Lammert's defense rested on the legal provision allowing an adjoining landowner to remove their portion of a partition fence after providing one year's written notice. He argued that since Boyd had not ensured the appointment of fence viewers to assess the fence's value, there was no legal basis for Boyd's claims. Lammert maintained that he had the right to keep his land open without being compelled to contribute to the cost of maintaining the fence.

This legal case, "Henry B. Childs v. Frederick J. Fischer," took place in September 1869 before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case stemmed from a contract involving United States bonds worth $2,400, issued by the partners Henry C. Childs, J. C. Wheaton, and Erastus Gary. In the contract, the parties promised to repay Fischer either in United States bonds or in cash, with the stipulation of accruing interest at a rate of 10% per annum. The legal dispute arose when Fischer claimed that Childs had failed to meet the terms of their agreement by not disbursing the funds in the specified form at the appropriate time. During the trial, the court initially rejected the special counts under which Childs sought to recover the amount. However, it allowed evidence under common counts, ultimately determining the value of the bonds based on market prices as of August 15, 1867. The case focuses heavily on the interpretation of the debt agreement and the obligations set forth therein.	Henry B. Childs, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to receive the value of the bonds with interest accrued up to the date of the agreement, accusing the defendant, Frederick J. Fischer, of failing to execute the debt repayment specified in their contractual agreement.
