Childs contended that he should be compensated with the appropriate currency or equivalent value of the bonds as stipulated in the agreement, specifically asserting that he was wronged by not receiving the payment as outlined in the note.	Frederick J. Fischer, the defendant, asserted that Childs had failed to elect the form of bonds he wished to receive within the specified time frame. Fischer claimed that according to the contract terms, Childs was obliged to communicate his election to receive either five-twenty or ten-forty bonds, and since he did not do so before the note matured, Fischer was not required to fulfill Childs' later requests. Fischer argued that Childs's failure to make this election exonerated him from complying with Childs' claims.

In the case of William Fielding v. Ellen Fitzgerald et al., which was decided on October 31, 1889, the parties involved included William Fielding, the executor of Maurice Fitzgerald's will, and Ellen Fitzgerald, the widow of the deceased. The case arose in Sangamon County, Illinois, where Ellen Fitzgerald, along with other heirs, contested the validity of an instrument claimed to be the last will and testament of Maurice Fitzgerald, who had died at the time stated. On September 14, 1888, Fielding had probated the will in the county court. Fitzgerald's heirs, displeased with this development, initiated a bill to contest the will under the statutes concerning wills. Fielding admitted the probate of the will and his role as executor. However, part of the proceedings involved a jury trial that resulted in a verdict against the validity of the will, determining it was not the last testament of Maurice Fitzgerald. Following this trial and the subsequent motion for a new trial by the proponents of the will, further complications arose, including a contention over jurisdiction due to an appeal by Ellen Fitzgerald to the circuit court regarding the probate ruling. The court found no error in the initial ruling, particularly concerning the motion to amend the answer by adding that the appeal was pending, as the court deemed no evidence was provided to support this amendment.	The plaintiffs, led by Ellen Fitzgerald, claimed that the instrument presented by Fielding was not the valid last will of Maurice Fitzgerald. They requested the court to contest the will and declare it invalid, which would entail dismissing the prior probate ruling made by the county court. Their position was largely supported by the jury's verdict which found that the document in question did not represent the true last wishes of the deceased.	The defendant, William Fielding, maintained the legitimacy of the will and asserted that it had been duly probated. Fielding's main defense included an argument that there was a pending appeal regarding the will's probation, which should grant the circuit court no jurisdiction over the matter at hand. He sought to have the court dismiss the contesting bill, asserting that all challenges to the will should be resolved in the ongoing appeal process.

On August 21, 1872, in Le Boy, Illinois, William Murray and associated parties (appellees) delivered a lot of hogs to the Indianapolis, Bloomington and Western Railway Company (appellant) for transportation to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The hogs were placed in a double-deck car and were consigned to Sadler, Haven & Co. Upon reaching Indianapolis, the hogs were transferred to the Cleveland, Columbus, Cincinnati, and Indianapolis Railroad Company (the connecting line). According to established custom, the appellant's liability as a common carrier ceased once the hogs reached Indianapolis, ready for delivery to the consignee. The dispute arose when the consignee mistakenly paid proceeds from the sale of the hogs to another party, Chapman, who had shipped his hogs on the same train and had not accounted for the payment to the appellees. The appellees alleged that negligence on the part of the appellant led to their financial losses.	The plaintiffs, William Murray et al., claimed that the Indianapolis, Bloomington and Western Railway Company was negligent in failing to properly indicate or mark the way-bill to show that the hogs were consigned to them. They argued that this negligence resulted in the consignees incorrectly paying Chapman for the proceeds from the sale of their hogs, causing them financial loss. The plaintiffs requested compensation for damages incurred due to this miscommunication.	The defendant, Indianapolis, Bloomington and Western Railway Company, contended that they fulfilled their obligation as common carriers by delivering the hogs according to the directions given by the shipper. They argued that there was no contractual requirement for them to identify the consignors on the way-bill. Furthermore, they asserted that any negligence alleged by the plaintiffs was due to their own failure to safeguard their interests, and that the ultimate loss should not be attributed to the railway company but rather to the actions of the consignees and Chapman.

The case of *The Tug Montauk v. William H. Walker & Co.* took place in June 1868 and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a legal action initiated by William H. Walker & Co. against the steam tug Montauk in the Court of Common Pleas of Cairo, Illinois, during the October term of 1866. The plaintiffs claimed damages amounting to one hundred and nine dollars for supplies reportedly provided to the tug. The defendant argued that the court did not have jurisdiction to hear the case since it involved a maritime contract, which they contended fell exclusively under admiralty jurisdiction. The defendant's motion to dismiss the case based on this argument was initially overruled. Consequently, a judgment was rendered against the tug by default due to the defendant's lack of further defense in the matter. The appeal then progressed to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the jurisdiction of the court was scrutinized extensively.	The plaintiff, William H. Walker & Co., claimed that they were entitled to damages for supplies provided to the tug Montauk. They asserted that the Court of Common Pleas had the authority to hear the case under state law, specifically referencing the act of the Illinois legislature from 1857 related to proceedings against boats and vessels in rem, which provided them with a legal basis for their claims.	The defendant, the steam tug Montauk, contended that the contract in question was a maritime contract, thus falling under the exclusive jurisdiction of the admiralty courts. They argued that the supplies were related to maritime services and therefore should have been adjudicated in federal admiralty jurisdiction rather than in the state court. The defendant sought to have the judgment against them reversed on these grounds, asserting that the state court lacked jurisdiction over this maritime matter.

The case "The Board of Supervisors of DuPage County et al. v. The People, etc. ex rel. Willard Scott et al." was a legal dispute concerning the results of an election held in DuPage County, Illinois, in 1872, regarding a proposition for the removal of the county seat. Following the elections, a controversy arose, leading the parties involved to seek resolution through the circuit court in DuPage County. The case was subsequently transferred to the circuit court of Cook County, where it was presided over by Judge E. S. Williams. In the election, the judges of election had taken a one-hour recess for lunch, during which it was claimed that this action should not disqualify all the votes cast in the township since there was no evidence of impropriety, tampering, or any voter being deprived of their ability to vote. The key issues revolved around irregularities in the election process, particularly regarding the improper handling of votes from non-registered voters and the compliance with statutory requirements. The appellants appealed the decision of the circuit court, arguing that the rejection of the entire vote of the Winfield precinct was an error, while the appellees contested the validity of votes from the Milton township based on the statutes governing voting eligibility.	The plaintiffs, represented by Willard Scott and others, primarily claimed that the election results were valid and should not be set aside based on the judges' recess, arguing that no fraud or harm had occurred during the polling process. They contended that the rights of voters who acted in good faith should be preserved and that the entire poll should not be suppressed because of a minor procedural irregularity. They requested that all valid votes be counted and that the election result should reflect the true will of the constituents.	The defendants, including the Board of Supervisors of DuPage County, argued against the inclusion of votes from the Milton township due to a lack of proper proof of residency by non-registered voters who did not submit the required affidavits. They claimed that the statute explicitly stated that no ballot should be accepted without proper documentation from both the voter and a registered householder. Therefore, they requested the court to uphold the circuit court's initial decision that excluded these votes based on statutory non-compliance, asserting that this exclusion was necessary to maintain the integrity of the electoral process.

In the case of *Charles W. Thomas et al. v. Martha J. Burnett*, decided on April 5, 1889, the dispute arose in Randolph County, Illinois. Martha J. Burnett filed a bill against Charles W. Thomas, who was acting as an attorney for a creditor seeking to enforce a judgment against Burnett's son, James Burnett. The case centered on a forty-acre tract of land initially owned by James Burnett. On March 29, 1882, Martha purchased the land from her son for $1,600, but the deed was not recorded until October 22, 1884. In the interim, on October 10, 1883, an attachment was placed on the land due to a court judgment against James Burnett, leading to the property being sold to Thomas for $1,900. Martha sought to set aside the sale, claiming her ownership was valid despite the lack of recording since she had maintained possession through tenants who were aware of her ownership. The legal issue hinged on whether the attaching creditor (Thomas) had notice of the unrecorded deed at the time of the attachment.	Martha J. Burnett argued that she had rightful ownership of the land through a valid but unrecorded deed from her son, James Burnett. She claimed that Thomas, as the attaching creditor, should have been aware of her rights due to her continuous possession of the property before and after the sale to Thomas. She sought to have the court set aside the certificate of purchase held by Thomas, asserting that it constituted a cloud on her title and requested an injunction to prevent the sheriff from conveying the deed based on the sale.	Charles W. Thomas contended that he was an innocent purchaser without notice of Martha's unrecorded deed. He argued that he acquired a valid lien on the property when the attachment was levied since there was no actual notice of her claim. Thomas maintained that the unrecorded deed did not establish any rights against him and that the law protects creditors who act without notice of prior unrecorded conveyances.

In the case of **George Schneider et al. v. Voluntine C. Turner**, the legal proceedings unfold from events that took place in Cook County, Illinois, leading up to a decision on October 31, 1889. The principal parties involved are the plaintiffs, George Schneider, Walter L. Peek, and Ferdinand W. Peek, and the defendant, Voluntine C. Turner. The matter arose from an alleged contract for the sale of 1,786 shares of stock in the North Chicago City Railway. Turner, on November 11, 1885, issued a written agreement to sell the shares at $600 each, contingent on the plaintiffs taking possession by December 15, 1885. Schneider and his associates claimed to have tendered the total payment due for the shares before the deadline, but Turner reportedly refused to complete the transaction. The plaintiffs initiated legal action in the Superior Court of Cook County, seeking enforcement of the contract, but the case was met with several legal complexities concerning the nature of the agreement, leading eventually to appeals that addressed the contract's validity under state law regarding option contracts.	The plaintiffs' main arguments centered on asserting the existence of a valid and enforceable contract for the purchase and sale of the stock. They contended that Turner breached the contract by refusing to deliver the shares despite the payment being made. The legal requests included a claim for damages stemming from this breach and attempts to establish that the terms of the instrument constituted a binding contract rather than a mere option or offer for future sale.	The defendant, Turner, responded by arguing that the written agreement constituted an unenforceable option contract, thereby violating section 130 of the Illinois Criminal Code, which deems such contracts as void. He asserted that there was a lack of consideration for the agreement, and thus, no valid contract arose. Turner maintained that the plaintiffs could not present evidence contrary to the provisions of the written instrument, which he claimed did not establish a binding obligation for the sale of the stock.

In 1857, Jacob Whisler filed a replevin action against William Roberts in the Fulton Circuit Court of Illinois. The dispute revolved around a span of mares and a wagon that Whisler was alleged to have taken wrongfully. Roberts claimed ownership of the property based on a mortgage executed by John Strickland in February 1857. The situation became contentious when Strickland, facing multiple executions against him, was said to have transferred the property to Roberts prior to these executions being placed in the hands of the constable. The property was initially taken into custody based on the claim of rightful ownership, which led to various legal arguments about the sufficiency of the affidavit for the replevin and the rightful ownership of the property amid conflicting testimonies regarding the timeline of its possession. The case involved multiple testimonies, with the jury charged to assess the evidence and determine the rightful possessor of the property as the court weighed whether proper legal procedures were followed.	Whisler, as plaintiff, claimed that he had rightful ownership and was entitled to immediate possession of the mares and wagon. He argued that the property was wrongfully taken by Roberts, who was acting under an execution based on Strickland's debts. Whisler contended that the affidavit for replevin was valid and did not require an allegation of unlawful taking or detention per statutory requirements, thus requesting the court to affirm his ownership and order the return of the property.	Roberts, the defendant, argued primarily that the property belonged to Strickland, not Whisler. He claimed that he acquired the property through an execution initiated due to Strickland's debts, which gave him lawful possession. Roberts contended that Whisler's actions were unfounded as the property was not rightfully his after it was voluntarily returned to Strickland. He raised objections regarding the sufficiency of the affidavit and requested both dismissals of the suit and a new trial, claiming errors in the Circuit Court’s judgment and instructions provided to the jury.

The case "The President and Trustees of the Town of Jacksonville v. John Holland and Jonathan Neely" took place in December 1857 in Jacksonville, Illinois. The plaintiffs, represented by D.A. Smith, were the President and Trustees of the Town of Jacksonville, who took legal action against defendants John Holland and Jonathan Neely for selling liquor in violation of a local ordinance that deemed such sales a nuisance. The plaintiffs initially obtained a judgment for $40 from a justice of the peace; however, upon appeal to the Circuit Court, the verdict favored the defendants. The key issue in the case revolved around the partnership between the defendants and a third party, Eitzsimmons, which complicated the plaintiffs' claim since they needed to prove both defendants were jointly involved in the sale of the liquor. The Circuit Court instructed the jury accordingly, leading to a not guilty verdict for the defendants. The case was subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs argued that both defendants were liable for selling intoxicating liquor, which violated the town ordinance declaring such sales a nuisance. They contended that the ownership of the liquor by three individuals did not preclude them from holding the two defendants accountable. Additionally, they focused on the importance of properly publishing and adopting the ordinance in question.	The defendants contended that they could not be held liable unless it was proven that both were jointly interested in the illegal sale of liquor. They argued that there was a lack of evidence demonstrating their joint involvement. Furthermore, they claimed that the plaintiffs failed to adequately prove the publication and adoption of the ordinance in compliance with the town’s charter, which was essential for the plaintiffs' case to stand.

The case "Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company v. Herman Flint" takes place on March 18, 1885, in the western part of Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, Herman Flint, was a frequent commuter using the railroad to travel to work. On the day of the incident, he was hurrying to the train station after he realized the train he intended to catch had already departed. Instead of using safe pathways located on either side of the tracks, Flint walked through a narrow space between the two main tracks of the railroad. While navigating this space, he was struck by a freight train that was reportedly running at a speed faster than allowed by city ordinance. This led to serious injury, resulting in the loss of Flint's arm. The case arose from Flint's claim that the railroad company was negligent in their operations, primarily for running the train at excessive speeds and failing to ensure safety for individuals walking near the tracks. The accident sparked a significant dispute regarding the responsibilities of the railroad for passenger safety and the degree of care expected from Flint as a user of the tracks.	The plaintiff, Herman Flint, claimed that he suffered serious injuries due to the negligence of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company. He argued that the railroad was liable for running the train at a prohibited speed within city limits, which contributed to the accident and his subsequent injuries. Flint requested damages amounting to $10,000, asserting that the railroad failed to provide a safe environment for passengers and careless operational practices led to his injuries.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, contended that Flint was familiar with the area and failed to exercise ordinary care for his safety. They argued that Flint's decision to walk between the tracks, rather than using the designated pathways, constituted contributory negligence. Additionally, the railroad company requested that the court instruct the jury that Flint had assumed the risk of injury by being on the tracks and that they should not be held liable if Flint's own negligence was the primary cause of the accident.

In 1872, in Warren County, Illinois, The First National Bank of Monmouth initiated a legal action against James M. Whitman and Alexander G. Kirkpatrick concerning a promissory note for $1,000 dated June 8, 1867. The note was originally executed as a renewal of a previously extended debt. At the time the note was created, some collateral notes and a bond were left with the bank for security. Kirkpatrick, about to leave for Europe, appointed his brother as his attorney to handle his affairs. The dispute arose after the bank discounted a collateral note, resulting in several transactions involving funds related to the original note. The bank used part of the discounted sum to settle other debts of Whitman. The defense claimed these actions were unauthorized and constituted fraud, while the bank asserted that the collateral and subsequent dealings were done with the consent of Kirkpatrick's agent. After a trial where the jury sided with the defendants, the bank appealed, arguing that the jury was misdirected on key issues in the case.	The First National Bank claimed that the discounted collateral transaction was legitimate and done with valid consent from Kirkpatrick's attorney. The bank argued that Kirkpatrick remained liable for the note, as he had recognized his debt after returning from Europe and had not objected to the actions taken in his absence.	Whitman and Kirkpatrick contended that the bank acted fraudulently when it discounted the collateral note and misrepresented the security arrangements made for their debts. They asserted that Kirkpatrick, as surety, was released from liability due to the unauthorized actions taken by the bank without his personal consent during his absence, which released him from the obligation to pay.

In 1885, Martha J. Griffin was the owner of certain lots in Olney, Illinois. On October 17, 1885, she conveyed these lots to her son, Lemuel Griffin, for $8,550. Following this transaction, John Wolf, who had previously obtained a judgment against Martha J. Griffin for $8,376.46, sought to enforce his judgment through a fieri facias, claiming that the conveyance to Lemuel was made with the intent to hinder and delay him in collecting the judgment. The case escalated when Lemuel Griffin subsequently transferred the lots to his siblings. Wolf contended that these transactions were fraudulent and sought to subject the lots to a sale to satisfy his judgment. Martha and her family members denied any fraudulent purpose behind the transactions. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Wolf, leading to an appeal.	John Wolf, the plaintiff, claimed that the conveyance of the lots from Martha J. Griffin to her son was fraudulent, intended to delay him from collecting his judgment. He alleged that both the original transaction and its subsequent transfers to Lemuel’s siblings were done with a fraudulent purpose, thus seeking a court order to subject the properties to sale for satisfying his debt.	Martha J. Griffin and her son, as defendants, denied the allegations of fraud. They argued that the property transactions were legitimate and above board, with Lemuel acting in good faith to complete family property exchanges without knowledge of any indebtedness. They maintained that there was no evidence of fraudulent intent and that the separate transactions were conducted lawfully and correctly.

In September 1873, a legal case titled "Philip Larmon v. Philo Carpenter" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Cook County Circuit Court and concerned a chattel mortgage. The plaintiff, Philo Carpenter, filed an action of debt against the defendant, Philip Larmon, based on the terms of a chattel mortgage that was fully detailed in the declaration. Larmon demurred to the declaration, arguing that debt could not be pursued on a chattel mortgage because the instrument did not include an acknowledgment of indebtedness or a promise to pay. The circuit court overruled this demurrer and ordered judgment against Larmon for the debt claimed by Carpenter, who opted to abide by his demurrer instead of seeking further remedies. The case was subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, which addressed the nature and requirements of an action of debt concerning chattel mortgages.	Philo Carpenter claimed that he was entitled to recover a debt through an action based on a chattel mortgage. He argued that such an action is permissible, referencing legal texts suggesting that debt applies to various financial instruments, including mortgage deeds. Carpenter asserted that the mortgage should be viewed as a valid legal document supporting his claim to receive the owed amount.	Philip Larmon contended that the circuit court erred in permitting the action of debt to proceed based on the chattel mortgage, as he claimed it contained no promise or covenant to pay money. Larmon emphasized that the mortgage did not demonstrate any indication of indebtedness on his part. He maintained that the chattel mortgage, as described, operated more as a conditional sale and did not satisfy the criteria necessary for an action of debt.

The case revolves around Nancy E. Kirkham and her husband, John Kirkham, as defendants, and Jacob E. Boston as the complainant. It was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal from a decree made by the circuit court of Marion County in June 1873. The central issue involves property transactions and debts related to lands in Clinton County, Illinois. Haney E. Kirkham, a defendant, originally owned certain land and granted a deed of trust on a portion of it to secure a loan. She sold the land to Henry Albers, receiving promissory notes in return. Later, she purchased a farm from Jacob E. Boston, using those notes (which were lost but known to Boston) as partial payment, in addition to another note and collateral. The core dispute arises from Boston's claim for unpaid debts and the validity of the vendor's lien. The circuit court had ordered the defendants to pay Boston $1452, which led to the appeal contesting the claims regarding the lien and the responsibilities of the parties involved.	Jacob E. Boston, the complainant, argued that he was entitled to a vendor’s lien for the balance of the purchase money concerning the land transactions. He claimed that the defendants had an obligation to pay him the stated amount due to the unpaid notes secured by mortgage, which were transferred to him as part of the sale arrangement.	The defendants contended that the complainant was not entitled to enforce a vendor's lien, as it was not recognized by statute. They argued that by accepting the notes and mortgage, Boston had waived any lien for the unpaid purchase money. They also asserted that he had taken the notes at his own risk and that the contract terms did not obligate them to cover Boston's losses related to the notes.

In the case Lydia A. McKean et al. v. S. S. Vick, filed at Mt. Vernon on January 22, 1884, the central issue arises from a petition by the administrator of the estate of Evan T. Wiley, who had passed away. The petitioner sought permission to sell real estate to settle the debts owed by the estate. The widow and heirs contested the petition, arguing that the administrator had delayed the filing for nearly thirteen years after receiving letters of administration on May 16, 1870. This substantial delay was a focal point for the defense, who asserted that it constituted laches, which is an unreasonable delay in pursuing a right or claim. Despite the defense's arguments regarding the delay, the county court decreed the sale of the real estate. The court determined that the interests of the heirs had been damaged by the prolonged inaction, as accumulated debt had increased due to interest. Additionally, several attempts to sell the property had failed due to the widow's dower rights and the involvement of the partnership between the decedent and others, which had not yet been resolved.	The plaintiffs, represented by the estate's administrator, claimed that the sale of real estate was necessary to pay the debts of the deceased. They asserted that the substantial delay was justified by the complexities surrounding the estate's assets, including a town lot occupied by the widow under a dower claim. The administrator sought the court's approval to proceed with the sale despite the defense of laches posed by the widow and heirs of the estate.	The defendants, consisting of the widow and heirs of Evan T. Wiley, presented several defenses against the administrator's petition. They contended that the claim was barred by laches due to the seventeen-year delay in filing for the sale of real estate, which they argued had not been adequately explained. The heirs emphasized that the status of the property remained unchanged and questioned the necessity of selling under a new decree when existing debts had not been sufficiently proven to warrant such action.

The case "Benjamin Bernstein v. Moses Bernstein, for use, etc." was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the final opinion filed on December 7, 1887. The issue arose from a legal action against Moses Bernstein, who was the appellant and acted as the surety on an appeal bond. The case took place in Cook County, Illinois, and involved a dispute over the authenticity of a signature made by mark, with the appellant contesting the genuineness. The case featured conflicting evidence regarding this signature, which led to significant debate in court about its legitimacy. Mr. H. B. Stevens represented the appellant, while Mr. B. M. Shaffner acted for the appellee. The Honorable Richard Prendergast presided over the County Court where the action originated. The core of the case surrounded the interpretation of whether the signature was valid, raising questions about legal verification and evidence credibility.	The plaintiff, represented by Moses Bernstein, contended that the signature made by mark on the appeal bond was genuine. They sought to affirm the validity of the bond which had been challenged by the appellant. The plaintiff's primary argument emphasized the authenticity of the signature despite the denial of its genuineness by the defendant.	The defendant, Benjamin Bernstein, challenged the case by denying the authenticity of the signature used on the appeal bond. He argued that there was a clear conflict of evidence regarding the validity of the signature, suggesting that it should not be accepted as legitimate. The defendant sought to have the appeal bond invalidated based on this claim of non-genuineness.

In 1860, William H. Brooks, Jr. married Catharine Ewing Kearns. Prior to their marriage, property was conveyed to a trustee for Brooks' benefit, with Kearns consenting to its provisions. In 1861, the trustee released the property back to Brooks. In 1866, Kearns conveyed several Chicago lots to Brooks, claiming he paid her $3,500 as consideration for the property, which she denies. The couple divorced in Indiana shortly after, with Kearns filing a new bill charging Brooks with desertion. Following the divorce, Kearns filed a bill to set aside the deed from 1866, asserting that it was void under the law because a married woman could not convey property directly to her husband without her husband's joint consent. The court analyzed the jurisdiction to hear the case, the validity of the deed, and the nature of a contract made by Kearns' attorney during the divorce proceedings, concluding that the deed in question was indeed void.	Kearns argued that the deed conveying property to Brooks was void as it violated marital property laws that required joint consent to validly convey property. She sought to set aside the deed on the grounds that it created a cloud on her property title, asserting that no valid transaction occurred and that the deed should be canceled.	Brooks contended that he had validly purchased the property for $3,500 and insisted that he had paid Kearns in cash for the property. He argued that Kearns’ claims were unfounded and sought to maintain ownership of the land based on the transaction he believed to have occurred during their marriage.

In the case of Solomon Cole v. Henry Van Riper, decided in April 1867 by the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute arose in La Salle County, Illinois. The case was an action of ejectment brought by Henry Van Riper to recover possession of a tract of land in the town of Whitfield. The plaintiff, Van Riper, demonstrated title through a series of deeds, specifically one from John R. Snyder and his wife, Elizabeth H. Snyder, to James Van Riper, dated July 22, 1862. Solomon Cole, the defendant, occupied part of this land as a tenant of John R. Snyder. Van Riper's case relied on the validity of a deed from Ellen Cole (the defendant's wife) to himself. The defendant objected to the deed's admission into evidence, arguing that as a married woman, Ellen Cole could not convey real estate without her husband's consent. The court allowed the deed, and the jury found in favor of Van Riper. Cole thereafter moved for a new trial, citing the court's error in admitting the deed and contending that the law of Illinois did not permit a married woman to convey property without her husband's joinder.	Henry Van Riper, the plaintiff, claimed that he had obtained lawful title to the property in question through a series of recorded deeds, including one from Ellen Cole, the wife of the defendant. He argued that the court should allow the deed to be entered into evidence, which would validate his claim to the property and facilitate his recovery of possession, despite the defendant's objections regarding the legality of Ellen Cole's conveyance as a married woman.	Solomon Cole, the defendant, contended that Helen Cole, his wife, could not legally convey the property without his involvement, as mandated by Illinois law. He argued that the state statute protecting married women’s separate property did not extend to allow a married woman to convey real estate independently of her husband. Cole maintained that the deed was invalid because it failed to have his consent, thus challenging the court's admission of the deed into evidence and the resulting judgment.

In February 1889, the legal case of Ernest F. Smith et al. v. George R. Grant was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated from a transaction involving a sum of $375 that was paid by Hunter, acting as an agent for George R. Grant, to the defendants, Ernest F. Smith and others, in connection with a claim arising from a deal on the board of trade. While Grant was in Europe, he instructed Hunter to settle the claim but also sought a way to reclaim the payment upon his return, should it be determined he was not indebted to the defendants. Hunter testified that he communicated to the defendants that the payment was contingent on whether the defendants owed money to Grant, implying that if it turned out they didn’t owe him, the payment could be returned. The defendants disagreed with this characterization of the arrangement. The jury was given instructions regarding the burden of proof, which became a central issue, as the court later deemed that the plaintiff (Grant) had to provide evidence of his claims rather than rely on denying the defendants’ assertions.	The plaintiffs contended that they were entitled to recover the $375 paid to the defendants by Hunter, asserting that the payment was made based on an understanding that it would be returned if it was found that the plaintiffs owed nothing to the defendants. They argued that the defendants had a legal obligation to repay the amount once sufficient accounting substantiated the lack of indebtedness.	The defendants maintained that they were not liable to return the $375, arguing that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated that they were not indebted to them at the time the payment was made. They claimed the payment had been properly received under the circumstances, thereby disputing any obligation to refund the amount. They asserted that the burden of proof lay with the plaintiffs to establish their right to recover the funds.

In the case titled "Cyrus S. Kellogg v. Laura P. Hale et al.", filed on November 20, 1883, in Carroll County, Illinois, Cyrus S. Kellogg sought to regain ownership of 250 acres of land that he had conveyed to Philetus Peck in 1853 before moving to California. This conveyance, while absolute in wording, was intended to function as a trust, allowing Peck to manage the property for Kellogg's benefit. In 1857, Kellogg's wife, Laura P. Hale, presented a letter from Kellogg to Peck requesting the land be conveyed to her. This action was based on Kellogg's intent to provide for his wife, as he wished to ensure her financial security should he encounter difficulties. Over the years, Laura actively managed the property, paid taxes, and received rents until their separation in 1865 and her subsequent divorce from Kellogg in 1871. Kellogg's claim revolved around the argument that the original deed to Peck created a trust that should legally revert the title back to him under the Statute of Uses. The court assessed the nature of the trust and the lawful intent behind the conveyance amidst Kellogg's claims of eventual reinvestment of the title.	Cyrus S. Kellogg, the plaintiff, asserted that the original deed transferring the land to Philetus Peck was actually a conveyance in trust for his own use. He argued that his intent at the time was to maintain control of the property without relinquishing ownership. He requested the court to compel a conveyance of the 250 acres back to him.	Laura P. Hale, the defendant, contended that the property was rightfully conveyed to her based on her husband’s intentions to secure her future by transferring the title to her, free of debts and creditor claims. Additionally, she argued that the deed from Peck to her was valid and that Kellogg could not reclaim the property as it was a voluntary act intended as a provision for her.

In January 1890, a legal case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court involving Josiah M. Pearson (the plaintiff in error) and Ella Pearson (the defendant in error). The case arises from a series of real estate transactions concerning lands that Ella Pearson owned in La Salle County. After certain lands were sold at a sheriff's sale due to a lien against Ella, a judgment creditor named Starr redeemed the property, leading to a subsequent sale to Samuel Dunavan. An agreement was later formed where Josiah M. Pearson would receive a promissory note from Ella for $3,800, provide funds to redeem the property from Dunavan's sale, reclaim the lands, and later convey them back to Ella once her debts were settled. Although there was conflicting evidence, the court found that Ella had repaid Josiah all amounts owed. Consequently, Josiah was deemed unjustified in refusing to transfer the lands back to Ella, prompting her to seek judicial enforcement of the agreement.	Ella Pearson claimed that Josiah M. Pearson had wrongfully refused to convey the title of the lands and assign the promissory note back to her, despite having received full payment for her debt. She sought specific performance of the agreement made between them, asserting that the nature of their transaction was akin to a mortgage, where Josiah as the creditor should return the title to her upon repayment.	Josiah M. Pearson contended that he had valid reasons to hold onto the title and promissory note, arguing about the nature of the redemption and legal rights. He suggested that the agreement was designed to secure his interests and alleged potential fraud among the parties involved. Josiah sought the circuit court’s judgment in favor of retaining the property and denying Ella's claims.

In January 1860, the case "Daniel Rhinehart et ux. v. William J. Stevenson" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a legal action filed in the Circuit Court of Effingham County regarding the foreclosure of a mortgage on specific tracts of land. The plaintiffs, Daniel Rhinehart and his wife, initiated the case against the defendants, William J. Stevenson and others, seeking to foreclose on the mortgage. The Circuit Court issued a decree that allowed a redemption period of only twelve months after the sale of the property, which the plaintiffs argued was insufficient according to the law that provided for a fifteen-month redemption period. The decree mandated that if the property was not redeemed within the twelve months, the master in chancery would deliver an absolute deed to the purchaser. The plaintiffs contended that this decree contained errors detrimental to their rights as the law entitled them to a longer redemption period.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Circuit Court’s decree was erroneous because it set a redemption period of only twelve months instead of the legally mandated fifteen months. They argued that this error negatively impacted their rights regarding the mortgage, and they sought a reversal of the decree to ensure compliance with the legal parameters governing mortgage redemption periods.	The defendants did not present specific defenses in the provided extract, but it is implied that they relied on the validity of the decree as issued by the Circuit Court. Their main argument would likely have revolved around upholding the court's decision, asserting that the stipulated redemption period was adequate for the circumstances of the case.

In March 1884, in Madison County, Illinois, Christopher Faitz's son, aged twenty-one, was tragically killed when the wagon he was driving, pulled by two horses, was struck by a locomotive of the St. Louis, Vandalia & Terre Haute Railroad Company while attempting to cross the railroad tracks at a public crossing. The collision resulted in the death of Faitz's son as well as the destruction of the wagon and harness. The case had been tried twice in the Circuit Court of Madison County, with consistent verdicts. The key issue was about the negligence of the railroad's employees; specifically, they were accused of failing to ring a bell or sound a whistle as they approached the crossing, which was considered unusually dangerous due to obstructions like willow trees that impaired visibility from the public road. Despite some conflicting evidence regarding the actions of Faitz's son at the crossing, it was established that the railroad failed to provide adequate warning signals as it approached a known perilous crossing.	The plaintiff, Christopher Faitz, claimed damages for the loss of his son, the horses, and the wagon. He argued that the employees of the railroad acted negligently by not giving appropriate warnings (ringing a bell or sounding a whistle) before approaching the crossing, which directly contributed to the fatal accident. The plaintiff maintained that the crossing was particularly dangerous and that the railroad company's failure to provide signals constituted gross negligence.	The defendant, St. Louis, Vandalia & Terre Haute Railroad Company, argued that its employees were not negligent because they believed the crossing was approached with reasonable caution. They contended that the driver (Faitz's son) had a duty to exercise due care before crossing the tracks, as railroad crossings are recognized as dangerous. The defendant asserted that the son did not look or listen for an approaching train and thus exhibited negligence on his part, which should mitigate or eliminate the responsibility of the railroad.

The case "William Church v. George W. Noble" took place in April 1860 in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved were William Church, the plaintiff, and George W. Noble, the defendant. The dispute arose from a lease agreement dated March 22, 1858, concerning premises known as the "American House." The plaintiff claimed that after taking possession of the premises, the defendant exercised his rights under the lease to take down the west wall for rebuilding without appropriately compensating Church as stipulated in the covenant. Church argued that due to the construction, he was deprived of the use of several rooms for six months and sought damages amounting to $1,500 for this loss, as the defendant supposedly failed to pay this sum as per their agreement.	The plaintiff, William Church, claimed that George W. Noble breached the covenant in their lease by taking down the west wall of the premises without compensating him for the loss of use. Church argued that the actions of the defendant deprived him of several rooms for six months, which he valued at $1,500. He requested damages for this loss based on the covenant made in the lease, alleging that Noble had notice of the impact of his actions.	George W. Noble, the defendant, defended against the claims by contending that the covenant was too uncertain and, therefore, void. Noble argued that the contract's phrase regarding the payment included a blank for the amount, which meant that nothing was agreed upon for payment. He contended that due to this uncertainty, Church had no valid claim for damages, leading to his demurrer that was sustained by the lower court.

Joseph P. Griffin, as Executor of the estate of Ira Manville, filed a legal claim against John L. Kehrer. The case took place in October 1887 in St. Clair County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a claim made by Kehrer for work and labor he performed for the deceased, Ira Manville, during his lifetime, for which he had not received payment. Initially, Kehrer's claim was contested in the County Court where a jury ruled in his favor. Following this, Griffin appealed the decision to the Circuit Court of St. Clair County, where the jury again sided with Kehrer. The core of the dispute hinged on whether Kehrer's services were offered as a neighborly gesture without expectation of payment or as a legitimate claim for reimbursement for services rendered. Griffin's appeal questioned the jury's verdict, stating that it was against the weight of the evidence presented.	Griffin, representing the estate, claimed that the services rendered by Kehrer were gratuitous acts of kindness, not meant to be compensated. He argued that the jury's conclusion was not supported by substantial evidence and therefore sought to have the judgment against the estate reversed.	Kehrer maintained that his work was performed at the request of Manville, with an implied understanding of compensation. He contended that the jury had already ruled in his favor, affirming the service's legitimacy and the rationale for payment. Kehrer requested that the court uphold the previous jury's decisions and continue to affirm the validity of his claim against the estate.

In 1874, in Sterling, Illinois, a significant incident involving Frederick Mitchell, husband of the plaintiff Mary Mitchell, occurred. Frederick became intoxicated after purchasing liquor from the defendants, Matthias Schmidt and others. Later that night, while intoxicated and attempting to break into the property of Henry Friedenbach, he was shot in the thigh by Friedenbach, who was defending his home. Mitchell initially appeared to recover from the injury, but after several days, his condition worsened, leading to an amputation of his leg and ultimately his death a few days later. The case arose from Mary Mitchell's legal action against the defendants, claiming that their sale of intoxicating liquors to her husband led to his intoxication and the subsequent series of events that caused his fatal wound.	Mary Mitchell claimed that the intoxication caused by the defendants’ sale of liquors was the direct cause of her husband’s injuries and death. She argued that if he had not been intoxicated, he would not have attacked Friedenbach's house and consequently would not have been shot. Mary sought damages for the loss of her husband, emphasizing that his death was a direct consequence of the defendants’ actions in providing him alcohol.	The defendants contended that any injuries Frederick Mitchell sustained, and ultimately his death, were not a direct result of their actions but rather of his own misconduct after becoming intoxicated. They argued that Mitchell’s failure to follow the medical advice provided after his injury, particularly regarding the care of the wounded leg, led to the complications that resulted in his death. The defendants insisted that the death was caused by an intervening factor rather than the intoxication itself.

The case "The Union National Bank et al. v. The International Bank et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 19, 1888. It arose from a dispute involving two banks—The Union National Bank (the plaintiffs) and The International Bank (the defendants)—regarding the validity of mortgage agreements and issues of usury. The relevant events took place in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, as second mortgagees, claimed that the first mortgage held by the defendants contained usurious interest, which should affect the enforceability of the prior mortgage in a foreclosure proceeding. The case evaluated whether a subsequent mortgagee, who had not foreclosed their mortgage or gained possession, had the right to assert a defense of usury against the first mortgage secured by the International Bank.	The Union National Bank contended that the mortgage executed by the International Bank was usurious, arguing that this usury should prevent the enforcement of the first mortgage. They sought to introduce evidence of the usurious nature of the mortgage to nullify the claim for foreclosure made by the International Bank.	The International Bank argued that the plaintiffs, as second mortgagees, had no right to plead usury as a defense in the case of the first mortgage. They maintained that only the original borrower, and those in privity with the borrower, could interpose the defense of usury, which did not include the second mortgagee in this instance.

In September 1876, E. Follett Bull, a citizen, legal voter, property holder, and taxpayer of LaSalle County, petitioned the Illinois Supreme Court to compel the county's board of supervisors to construct a suitable jail. The current facility, situated in the basement of the county courthouse in Ottawa, was deemed grossly inadequate and unhealthy for the confinement of prisoners. Bull described the jail as a cramped hall with insufficient sunlight and ventilation, where conditions could become so foul that individuals became ill due to the atmosphere. Reports from grand juries over the past decade consistently condemned the jail's state, noting overcrowding and the mingling of various classes of offenders, contrary to legal mandates. LaSalle County was affluent, with financial resources sufficient for a new jail. However, despite these circumstances, the county board had failed to act upon numerous calls for improvements. The circuit court dismissed Bull's petition after the board filed a general demurrer, leading to an appeal for a writ of error.	Bull contended that the county's failure to provide a suitable jail violated the health and safety rights of those confined. He argued that the jail's conditions were hazardous, as evidenced by numerous grand jury reports condemning the facility. Bull requested the court to issue a mandamus order requiring the board to construct a new, suitable jail building, reflecting the financial capability of LaSalle County to afford such an improvement.	The board of supervisors asserted that while they had provided a jail, the suitability and conditions were matters within their discretion. They argued that the court had no authority to interfere with their judgment regarding the jail's structure and conditions. The board maintained that they were fulfilling their statutory duties and that mandamus could not be used to compel them to act according to someone else's standards of what constituted a 'suitable' jail.

The case "Great Western Railroad Company v. Samuel Morthland" revolves around an incident that occurred on October 16, 1860, near Decatur, Illinois. Samuel Morthland's horse was struck and killed by a train operated by the Great Western Railroad Company. The incident took place close to the city limits, specifically at a cattle-guard on the railroad track. Morthland claimed that the railroad company had failed to maintain necessary fences and cattle-guards to prevent animals from straying onto the tracks. He brought the case against the railroad in the Macon Circuit Court in November 1861. The plaintiff argued that due to the company's negligence in maintaining these safety features, his horse had wandered onto the track and met its fatal end. The evidence indicated that the horse was indeed on the track just outside the city limits, where the railroad company claimed no obligation existed to maintain fences since it was not required by law in that specific area. This legal principle regarding the fencing and cattle-guard responsibilities became central to the trial proceedings.	Morthland, the plaintiff, argued that the Great Western Railroad Company was negligent in failing to erect and maintain sufficient fences and cattle-guards along their railroad, which allowed his horse to wander onto the tracks. He claimed the company had a legal responsibility to protect against such incidents, particularly since the horse was valued at $150. Morthland contended that the company's failure directly led to the death of his horse, and thus he sought damages for negligence, citing both a lack of fencing in appropriate areas and the careless conduct of the train operators.	The defendant, Great Western Railroad Company, asserted that there was no negligence on their part and that their legal obligation to maintain fences did not extend to the area where the incident occurred—specifically, just outside the city limits of Decatur. The company's defense highlighted that the horse had strayed onto the tracks in a location where they were not bound to maintain fencing. They argued that any damage to the horse was not a result of careless operation of the train, emphasizing the lack of evidence proving negligence. Therefore, they requested the court to dismiss the case based on these points.

In December 1844, the case of Beeman Crandall v. Alexander Dawson took place in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a slander action initiated by Dawson against Crandall. The case originated in the McHenry Circuit Court, where it was tried by Judge Richard M. Young. Dawson’s claims stemmed from Crandall accusing him of perjury during a trial, which allegedly harmed Dawson's reputation. The jury found in favor of Dawson, awarding him fifty dollars. Crandall appealed the verdict, specifically contesting the trial court's refusal to instruct the jury that one witness, supported by corroborating testimony, could suffice for a justification of the slander charge.	The plaintiff, Alexander Dawson, claimed that Beeman Crandall slandered him by falsely accusing him of having perjured himself as a witness during a trial. Dawson's lawsuit sought damages for the injury to his reputation caused by these allegations. He presented evidence through witnesses corroborating the slander, asserting that Crandall's statements were untrue and harmful.	Beeman Crandall, the defendant, pleaded the general issue and claimed that he would prove the truth of his statements regarding Dawson. He argued that the trial court should have instructed the jury that the testimony of one witness, coupled with corroborating circumstances, was enough for a justification of the slander charge. Crandall contended that the jury's decision was flawed since they were misinformed about the evidentiary requirements needed to prove the charge of perjury.

In September 1868, John Fahs and his wife filed a lawsuit against the Ohio & Mississippi Railroad Company in Edwards County, Illinois, after Mrs. Fahs sustained injuries while a passenger on the railroad. They obtained a judgment against the railroad and later had an execution issued to Richland County, which was levied by the local sheriff on various railroad materials, including cord wood and bridge timber. This led the plaintiffs to file for an injunction to prevent the sale of these items, arguing that they were not subject to levy. Over the following years, the case underwent multiple hearings and decisions regarding the validity of the levies on the property and the original judgment. Eventually, the court dissolved the injunction for the cord wood while still under consideration for the bridge materials. The matter was further complicated by a supplemental bill claiming that the original judgment had been reversed in a higher court, challenging what property could be sold. The ultimate ruling centered around the appropriateness of the injunction and the legitimacy of the supplemental claims introduced after the original case proceedings.	The plaintiffs, John Fahs and his wife, argued that the cord wood, iron rails, and bridge timber on which the sheriff had levied were not subject to execution and, therefore, should not be sold. They sought an injunction to prevent the sale of these items, maintaining their position through the various procedural developments, including the claim that the original judgment against the railroad had been reversed.	The defendants, represented by the railroad company's legal team, contended that the injunction was improperly issued as the original bill did not provide a sufficient basis for an injunction. They argued that the subsequent reversal of the judgment did not affect the case's core issue regarding the property available for levy. Their request focused on the dissolution of the original injunction and the dismissal of the plaintiffs' case, while asserting that maintaining the injunction was inequitable to them given the purported baselessness of the plaintiffs' claims.

In December 1840, the case of George W. Little v. George Carlisle and William E. White was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. George Carlisle and William E. White, non-residents of Illinois, initiated the lawsuit against George W. Little based on a promissory note. Upon filing the lawsuit, they initially provided security for costs but later submitted a new instrument for cost security that lacked Little's name, rendering it ineffective. The court issued a summons to Little, which was never returned; subsequently, an alias summons was issued without any endorsement of service. On the fifth day of the November term, both parties appeared in court, where Little motioned to dismiss the suit due to insufficient security for costs, a motion that was denied. He was also not allowed to plead a defense related to the merits of the case. The court entered a judgment for the plaintiffs by nil dicit due to Little's alleged failure to file pleas on time, following a general procedural rule established at the commencement of the term.	The plaintiffs, Carlisle and White, claimed that the defendant Little owed them money based on a promissory note. They argued that they had complied with all court requirements regarding the security for costs necessary for non-resident plaintiffs. They sought a judgment for the amount due under the promissory note, as well as the associated legal costs.	Little contended that the plaintiffs did not meet the legal requirements for securing costs because their subsequent instrument for cost security was invalid. He argued that he was not bound to appear in court until correctly served and asserted that the court's refusal to allow him to file his pleas was unjust. He requested the dismissal of the suit on the grounds of lack of proper service and the plaintiff's inadequate security for costs.

In the case of Michael Butz et al. v. Thomas Kerr, decided on January 19, 1888, the location was Kankakee County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included the defendant Thomas Kerr, who filed the bill on behalf of himself and other taxpayers against the plaintiffs Michael Butz and August D. Ehrich, both commissioners of highways in Kankakee, alongside William F. Kenaga, the county clerk. The case revolved around a tax of sixty cents on each hundred dollars, which was levied by town authorities for road maintenance purposes. Kerr sought to restrain the collection of this tax, arguing that the city of Kankakee, established by a special charter in 1865, prohibited the town from levying such a tax within the city's corporate limits. The circuit court determined that if the city charter was in effect, the town had no authority to levy the tax, leading to a decree that prohibited its collection.	The plaintiff, Thomas Kerr, claimed that the city of Kankakee, governed by a special charter, had exclusive control over the roads and was empowered to levy taxes for maintenance within city limits. Kerr contended that the town authorities were expressly prohibited from levying any road tax within the city according to the provisions of the charter. He requested the court to enjoin the collection of the road tax imposed by the town, asserting that the tax was unauthorized and contrary to the existing municipal law.	The defendants, Michael Butz and the other town officials, argued that the law governing taxation should extend uniformly across the jurisdiction of the town. They contended that the provisions of the city charter conflicted with the constitutional requirement of uniformity in taxation for corporate purposes. They suggested that recent legislative changes might modify their authority to levy the road tax and that such changes should be reflected in the court’s interpretation of existing laws. They requested the court to overturn the previous ruling that prohibited the tax collection.

In January 1876, the legal dispute known as Hiram Baker v. The Town of Normal took place in Normal, Illinois. The case arose when Hiram Baker, the plaintiff, sought to impose a penalty on the appellant (defendant) for hitching his horse to a shade tree located in a public street, which violated a local ordinance. The trees in question had originally been planted by the prior owner of Baker's lot, intended to create a row between the sidewalk and carriageway. After the trees matured, the lot’s fence was moved back, allowing the trees to stand in public space. The defendant, who lived next to Baker, had been maintaining these trees. The circuit court found the defendant liable under the ordinance which broadly prohibited hitching horses to any shade trees in public streets and on private property. The legal interpretation of the ordinance was put to task, particularly regarding its reasonableness and applicability, culminating in a judgment for the penalty against the defendant.	Hiram Baker claimed that the town's ordinance prohibiting the hitching of horses to shade trees in public streets was within the town's rights to enforce and sought a penalty against the defendant for violating this local law. Baker argued that the defendant's actions not only infringed upon the ordinance but undermined the community's interest in protecting the public streets and decorations.	The Town of Normal contended that the ordinance was unreasonable, suggesting it unduly restricted property owners from using their own fences and trees. They claimed the ordinance's language could lead to interpretations that made sections of it void, arguing that such broad prohibitions lacked the necessary authority. Nonetheless, the town maintained that the control of the streets and the trees therein remained under its jurisdiction, which was not relinquished through individual property concessions.

In June 1874, in Chicago, Illinois, Minnie Herz was involved in an accident while walking on a dilapidated wooden sidewalk on Wabash Avenue. The sidewalk, built several feet above the street, was in poor condition, with reports of rotten stringers and loose boards. On the evening of June 16th, as Minnesota Herz crossed the sidewalk while carrying her child, she stepped on a rotting plank that gave way. The fall resulted in severe injuries, including a spinal fracture that left her paralyzed from the waist down. Despite her healthy condition before the injury, she suffered immense pain and was unable to stand or walk afterwards. The condition of the sidewalk had been known to city officials, with a policeman reporting its dangerous state shortly before the accident. The city's negligence in maintaining the sidewalk was a key issue in the case.	Minnie Herz, the plaintiff, claimed that the City of Chicago was negligent in maintaining the sidewalk, leading to her severe injury. She argued that the city failed to repair the sidewalk despite being aware of its dilapidated state, thereby creating a significant risk for pedestrians. Herz sought damages for her injuries, pain, and suffering, contending that the city's gross carelessness directly resulted in her irreparable harm.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant, argued that the verdict against them was not supported by the weight of the evidence. They did not raise any legal exceptions to the court's rulings regarding the handling of evidence or jury instructions. The defense suggested that the city had made a reasonable attempt to repair the sidewalk and questioned whether the level of negligence attributed to them warranted the damages awarded to the plaintiff.

Stephen W. Miles initiated the case against Thomas James and others, stemming from a lease agreement involving certain premises leased by Peter Warren for the years 1862 and 1863. The lease obligated Warren to pay an annual rent equivalent to one-third of the crop harvested. Warren sowed twenty-five acres of wheat in the autumn of 1862, which was growing on the leased land during both years of the lease. In March 1863, Lewis James obtained a judgment against Warren from a justice of the peace and subsequently levied an execution against the wheat in April 1863. This wheat was sold on July 25, 1863, to Lewis James, who later sold it to other parties. Meanwhile, Warren failed to pay Miles the rent due for 1862, leading Miles to distress the wheat to recover the rent owed for both years. The value of the wheat resulted in a surplus over the rent for 1863, but Miles argued he had a right to distress the wheat for the unpaid rent of 1862. The case was submitted to the Illinois Supreme Court to resolve whether the wheat could be distrained for the rent attributable to both years or just for the latter year.	Miles asserted that he was entitled to a lien on the wheat for the rent owed for 1862, as the crops were growing during both years of the lease. He argued that according to the applicable statute regarding landlord and tenant, he had a rightful claim to recover rent from the wheat that matured in 1863, as it was essential for the growth and maturation of the crop. Therefore, he sought judgment to enforce his lien for the unpaid rent.	The defendants contended that the wheat was not subject to distress for the unpaid rent of 1862, arguing that since the execution sale had occurred, it nullified Miles's right to claim the wheat for that year's rent. They maintained that the judgment rendered previously favored their position and requested the court affirm that judgment.

This legal case, titled "John H. Creager et al. v. William Blank," was adjudicated by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 16, 1889. The dispute took place in Du Page County, Illinois, primarily involving John H. Creager and associates as plaintiffs (appellants) and William Blank as the defendant (appellee). The conflict arose over a transaction concerning a "Gray tread power" stave cutter machine, which the plaintiffs claimed to have sold to the defendant for $222. The plaintiffs contended that the sale was final if the machine operated satisfactorily, akin to another machine sold to a third party, Barber. Conversely, the defendant alleged that he had only taken the machine on a trial basis with the option to return it if dissatisfied. This contention led to a contested factual dispute, presented before a jury, with testimonies from both sides. Ultimately, the jury ruled in favor of the defendant, affirming his claim of an implied trial agreement for the machine. The plaintiffs then appealed, challenging certain aspects of the trial proceedings, including procedural decisions made by the court.	The plaintiffs, led by Creager, argued that the machine's sale was absolute, contingent solely on its satisfactory performance compared to another similar machine. They sought to recover the payment of $222 based on their assertion that the defendant did not possess the contractual right to return the machine after trial. They maintained that the transaction terms were clear, and the defendant's claims of dissatisfaction were unfounded.	The defendant, William Blank, countered that he only agreed to take the machine on a trial basis, with an explicit option to return it if unsatisfactory. He argued that after testing the machine, it did not meet his expectations, and he made an offer to return it, which the plaintiffs refused. His defense was supported by witness testimonies asserting the trial arrangement, contradicting the plaintiffs’ version of the sale.

The case of John Faulds v. William Yates et al. took place in September 1870, in Illinois. The parties involved included John Faulds and two other partners, William Yates and Bunn, who were stakeholders in the Chicago Carbon and Coal Company, a corporation involved in mining operations. The corporation had leased valuable coal-bearing lands to a third party named Kirkland, who subsequently assigned the lease to Faulds, Yates, and Bunn. The partnership was formalized in February 1866, with each partner investing and managing the business with the expectation of sharing profits and losses equally. However, Faulds failed to meet his financial obligations and misrepresented the purchase price of additional land that was intended as partnership property. The situation led to a breakdown in their working relationship, prompting Yates and Bunn to sue for dissolution of the partnership, requesting an accounting of profits and the return of their shares in the partnership property, particularly concerning the “Sanger tract.”	The plaintiffs, Yates and Bunn, argued that Faulds had committed fraud and misrepresentation regarding the partnership agreements and the costs associated with acquiring the Sanger tract. They contended that Faulds failed to contribute his fair share to the mining operations, leading to financial losses for the partnership. They sought a court order for a dissolution of the partnership, an accounting of the partnership affairs, and a conveyance of their respective shares in the Sanger land.	Faulds defended against the claims by asserting that the partnership agreement was void for being against public policy and claimed that the alleged fraud did not support the plaintiffs’ arguments. He contended that there was adequate legal remedy available and that fraudulent intent was not proven. Furthermore, Faulds sought to have the court dismiss the plaintiffs' demands and argued that the management arrangement was lawful and in the interest of all shareholders.

In 1855, a legal battle arose in the Gallatin Circuit Court of Illinois involving Oliver C. Vanlandingham as the plaintiff and Ebenezer Z. Ryan, the surviving assignee of the Bank of Illinois, as the defendant. The case stemmed from a foreign attachment action initiated by Ryan to collect debts represented by two promissory notes, each worth $2,000, allegedly owed by Vanlandingham. The defendant, Vanlandingham, filed a multitude of twelve pleas in his defense, arguing points including a lack of consideration for the notes, prior recoveries in other jurisdictions, and non-viability of debt claims against the assignees. The court was tasked with determining the validity of these defenses and the enforceability of the promissory notes in question, examining multiple related legal principles. Throughout the proceedings, issues surrounding procedural elements and the sufficiency of pleadings emerged, particularly concerning earlier judgments that might bar further claims regarding the same debt.	The plaintiff, Oliver C. Vanlandingham, contended that the promissory notes for which he was being sued lacked consideration and that valid defenses existed based on previous rulings in separate lawsuits. He asserted that there were no debts owed at the commencement of the action, thus claiming that the action taken against him was not legally sound.	The defendant, Ebenezer Z. Ryan, maintained that the prior judgments in different jurisdictions had resolved the matter in Vanlandingham's favor, effectively barring any further claims on the same notes. Ryan's defense included arguments asserting that the underlying notes were void due to a failure of consideration and that there were no existing debts against the Bank or its assignees, which would validate the collection efforts.

In 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, Joseph B. Ditto and Caroline C. Hitchcock (the plaintiffs) were involved in a legal dispute with Louis L. Sharpe (the defendant) regarding the possession of certain goods. Ditto and Hitchcock appealed a decision from the Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Julius S. Grinnell, which revolved around a bill of sale and a writ of attachment concerning these goods. The plaintiffs had claimed that Sharpe had wrongfully taken possession of items from a man named Hall, who had left the city. The court found that Sharpe had indeed taken possession of these goods before the writ of attachment was levied, suggesting that he acted within his rights under the bill of sale. The appellate court was tasked with reviewing whether the lower court's finding of fact regarding possession and ownership was valid and supported by the evidence presented.	The plaintiffs, Ditto and Hitchcock, contended that Sharpe had wrongfully taken possession of goods that were rightfully theirs. They argued that the bill of sale from Hall to Sharpe was fraudulent and should be void as to creditors and purchasers, asserting that a vendor retaining possession after sale constitutes fraud. They requested that the court overturn the lower court's ruling, deeming Sharpe's possession of the goods unlawful and upholding their claim to ownership.	Sharpe, the defendant, contended that his possession was legitimate and that he had taken control of the goods under a valid bill of sale before the attachment was filed. His defense highlighted that there was no fraud imputed to him and that the lower court had correctly determined his rightful possession under established legal principles. He requested that the appellate court affirm the trial court's judgment in his favor.

The case "Andrew Frazier v. Seth Gates" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871. The dispute arose over a lot of land in Keithsburg, Illinois, following a series of financial transactions and legal actions concerning a mortgage. Seth Gates purchased the property on March 13, 1869, for $3,294, under a foreclosure decree against Andrew Frazier, who had executed the mortgage on May 26, 1866, to secure a loan of $2,500. Frazier continued to live on the premises despite the mortgage and received a written demand from Gates to vacate after the expiration of the redemption period. Frazier claimed to possess the lot through a tax deed obtained by Isaac N. Bassett in 1869, alleging that this gave him the right to occupy the property. However, Frazier failed to notify Gates about an ejectment suit arising from this tax deed, which resulted in a judgment against him. The case involved issues of possessor rights, notification responsibilities, and alleged collusion in the transfer of possession.	Seth Gates, the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to reclaim possession of the property since he had legally purchased it through the foreclosure process and had issued a written demand for Frazier to vacate. Gates argued that Frazier's failure to inform him about the previous ejectment suit and his subsequent agreement with Bassett to lease the property indicated bad faith and collusion, undermining Frazier's defense. Gates requested the court enforce his right to possession based on his ownership under the mortgage and the foreclosure decree.	Andrew Frazier contended that he had a legitimate claim to the lot due to the tax deed obtained from Isaac N. Bassett, which he used to justify his continued possession. He posited that the foreclosure and sale did not negate his rights derived from the tax deed and the ejectment judgment in his favor. Additionally, Frazier argued that Gates should have been aware of the ejectment proceedings and thus could not properly claim a right to possession after the court ruled against Frazier in that case.

The case "William M. Kilgour v. Levi Gockley" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1876. The dispute arose over property owned by Samuel Gockley, who passed away intestate in 1857, leaving behind his son Levi Gockley (the defendant) and three daughters (the plaintiff). The plaintiff claimed title to the disputed land, having received interests from the deceased's daughters. The defendant, however, produced evidence of a mortgage from Samuel Gockley to Galt in 1855, securing two notes for $200, with one note reportedly unpaid. The defendant asserted that he had acquired the mortgage and subsequently took possession of the land in 1860, which he maintained ever since. In the trial court, the jury was directed by the judge to ignore the mortgage as a defense, leading to an appeal on the grounds that the assignee of a mortgage has the right to defend possession under certain conditions. The case questioned whether the defendant, as the mortgage assignee, could legally defend his possession against the plaintiff.	The plaintiff argued that he derived valid title to the property from the intestate father's estate, as he inherited it along with his sisters. He brought the ejectment action to regain possession of the land, challenging the defendant's claim based on an outdated mortgage that he contended should be disregarded.	The defendant contended that he held a legal defense against the ejectment action due to his possession of the land secured by the mortgage, asserting that the mortgage and the note granted him rights to the property. He argued that the earlier court's instruction to ignore the mortgage while allowing the plaintiff’s claims was erroneous, and he claimed to have acquired title through a circuit court decree favoring him as the purchaser of the property.

On April 4, 1863, in Illinois, Robert Bellew executed a promissory note for $850, with a deed of trust on certain real estate to secure its payment, granting Matthew Henderson rights to the property. Patrick Bellew later purchased this land but knew it was subject to the deed of trust. After the note became overdue, the trustee planned to sell the property to pay off the debt. Patrick Bellew filed a bill to enjoin this sale, arguing that there was an agreement between Henderson and Robert Bellew establishing the interest rate at thirteen percent instead of the ten percent stated in the note, claiming a forfeiture due to usury. The case involved the examination of equity principles relating to usury and the obligations arising from the hypothetically hidden agreement regarding interest rates.	Patrick Bellew, the plaintiff, argued that the deed of trust was subject to a forfeiture due to usury, based on a purported agreement between Henderson and Robert Bellew that set an interest rate of thirteen percent, rather than the ten percent noted. He claimed that due to this usury, he should be allowed to pay only the principal amount, excluding the usurious interest, in order to halt the sale of the property.	Matthew Henderson argued that regardless of the private agreement on the interest rate, he was only entitled to enforce the original terms stated in the deed of trust, which allowed him to claim ten percent interest.
