Kratz had previously obtained a judgment against Patrick Bates, and later he redeemed a piece of property that was originally sold under a different judgment favoring Busey Bros. The land was sold after a failure to redeem under this prior judgment, and Kratz claimed that his redemption was lawful and gave him the right to retake possession of the land. However, the defendant, Eli Buck, contended that he had rights to the property as he was a tenant of Edward H. Bates, who acquired the property after the original sale. The case bounced between courts, and the county court ultimately ruled against Kratz, leading him to seek a writ of error to the Illinois Supreme Court to challenge the decision.	W. H. Kratz argued that he had legally redeemed the land from a prior sale conducted under a judgment against Bridget and Patrick Bates, which entailed a failure to redeem on their part. Kratz claimed that because he redeemed the property as a judgment creditor of Patrick Bates and was awarded a sheriff’s deed, he was entitled to recover possession of the land based on the statute concerning forcibly detaining individuals from property after a judicial sale.	Eli Buck contended that he was not a party to the original judgment under which the land was sold, and therefore, Kratz's action could not be maintained against him. Buck asserted that he was occupying the land legally as a tenant of his mother, Bridget Bates—who had been the original owner and possessed the property at the time of the judgment against her. Buck's defense rested on the notion that since he was not directly involved in the judgment against Patrick Bates, he couldn't be held liable for possession in this forcible entry and detainer action.

On October 3, 1868, Helson Hooker filed for divorce against Melissa Rooker in the Woodford Circuit Court, Illinois. Rooker responded with a cross bill seeking a divorce and alimony, making John T. Harper and others defendants. Following the hearing, the court granted Rooker a divorce and awarded her $12,000 in alimony. Additionally, Rooker initiated a separate suit for maintenance against Hooker, causing his arrest, with Harper serving as his surety on a ne exeat bond of $5,000. In connection with this, Emmet Hiekox provided Harper with $5,000 in U.S. bonds as indemnification for his surety and to cover attorney's fees for the ongoing legal matters. This case arose due to an appeal regarding an order for Harper and others to pay Rooker $4,578, which constituted a part of the alimony from the bonds after attorney's fees were deducted. The main contention was whether the ongoing separate maintenance suit could proceed after the court's decree in the divorce case had already addressed the relevant financial claims.	Rooker claimed she was entitled to alimony due to her divorce from Hooker and pointed out that the financial claims relating to her separate maintenance suit had been fully addressed in the divorce proceedings. She sought the approved amounts stipulated by the court to ensure her financial security.	Harper and the other defendants argued that the decree demanding they pay Rooker was erroneous since the separate maintenance suit was still pending without a formal disposition. They contended that the issuance of the alimony decree essentially barred any further claims in the maintenance suit, undermining their legal position and obligations.

In 1874, the legal case Peoria and Rock Island Railway Company v. Robert Mitchell arose in Stark County, Illinois. The Peoria and Rock Island Railway Company (the appellant) sought to assess damages for the appropriation of a portion of Robert Mitchell’s (the appellee) land intended for railroad purposes. Commissioners were appointed to evaluate the damages and submitted their findings to the circuit court. Following a subsequent appeal by Mitchell due to the findings, a default judgment was entered against the railway company as no representation appeared on their behalf during the trial. The railway company then filed a motion to set aside this default, claiming various procedural errors had occurred. The court reviewed the requests but determined the railway company’s application for a venue change was tardy and the default should not be overturned, culminating in the appellate process that brought the case before the Illinois Supreme Court.	Robert Mitchell argued that the railway company had taken a portion of his land without proper compensation and sought damages assessed by a jury. He contended that the company’s request for a change of venue and the motion to set aside the default were untimely and improper, hence, the court should affirm the damages awarded to him.	The Peoria and Rock Island Railway Company contended that the court erred in refusing to change the venue and set aside the default judgment. They claimed that their counsel was engaged in negotiations for a compromise which caused the delay in their appearance at trial. Additionally, they argued that the damages assessed were excessive and that the execution awarded was improper according to the charter provisions.

George J. Williams was indicted and convicted in 1887 by the Criminal Court of Cook County, Illinois, for practicing medicine without the required qualifications under an act that was in force on July 1, 1877. The act aimed to regulate the practice of medicine in Illinois, mandating that individuals practicing medicine must possess specified qualifications. Williams was assessed a fine of $200. The case focused on whether the provisions of this act were constitutional, particularly a clause exempting individuals who had practiced medicine for ten years prior to the act's enactment from its regulations. Williams contended that the law was unconstitutional special legislation as it allegedly granted exclusive privileges to a certain class of practitioners. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case, emphasizing the State's police power to regulate the medical profession for public health and safety.	George J. Williams argued that the act under which he was convicted was unconstitutional. He claimed it was special legislation that unfairly exempted practitioners with ten years of experience from being regulated, thereby granting them privileged status over other practitioners who had been examined or graduated. Williams sought to have his conviction overturned based on these constitutional claims.	The People of the State of Illinois contended that the law was a valid exercise of the police power of the State, designed to ensure that only qualified individuals can practice medicine, which is crucial for protecting public health. They argued that the exemption for ten-year practitioners did not confer any special privilege but merely recognized previous experience as a qualification. The defense maintained that Williams had the burden of proof to show compliance with the law.

John H. Boltz et al. v. A. C. Huston is a legal case from 1887 that originated in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose when A. C. Huston placed an order for 5,000 cigars through an agent, C. J. Miller, who mismanaged the order and had Huston receive a total of 10,000 cigars. Boltz, Clymer & Co., the appellants, shipped these cigars based on Miller’s order. After receiving the shipment, Huston, who was not home at the time of delivery, later found that Miller had not taken the remaining cigars in a timely manner. When Boltz, Clymer & Co. presented their bills for payment, Huston refused to pay for the excess cigars, claiming he only ordered 5,000. The case highlighted issues of agency, authority, and the responsibilities involved in conducting business transactions. Huston eventually paid for the first set of cigars but not for the additional 5,000. Consequently, Boltz, Clymer & Co. pursued legal action following Huston's refusal to pay.	The plaintiffs, Boltz, Clymer & Co., argued that Huston was contractually obligated to pay for all 10,000 cigars because they were shipped according to an order made by Miller, their agent. They maintained that Huston should have been aware of the authority of the agent and that he was estopped from denying acceptance since part of the goods had been used. They requested payment for the full amount owed for the cigars shipped.	The defendant, A. C. Huston, contended that he had only ordered 5,000 cigars and was misled by the agent regarding the order. He argued that Miller did not have the authority to accept additional goods on his behalf and therefore he should not be liable for the payment of the surplus cigars sent without proper authorization. Huston requested that the court uphold his refusal to pay for the excess cigars.

In a legal dispute titled "Frederick B. Suppiger et al. v. Gerhard W. Garrels et al.", dated January 8, 1887, the case arose in Jefferson County, Illinois. The central parties involved were Frederick B. Suppiger and others (appellants) as plaintiffs, and Gerhard W. Garrels and others as defendants. Prior to September 25, 1870, a relationship was established between F. Ryhiner & Co. located in Highland, Illinois, and Gruner, Haller & Co. in Berne, Switzerland, concerning loan agreements. On January 17, 1880, Ryhiner & Co. loaned $700 to Hardin, Barker, and his wife, securing it with three promissory notes. These were subsequently assigned to different parties. Disputes arose regarding the payments and rights associated with the notes, particularly concerning two notes held by Garrels. The appellants claimed to hold a superior interest due to the payment of a related note. Garrels filed for a foreclosure to reclaim the loan amount, leading to cross-claims regarding the rights to share in the proceeds from the sale of the mortgaged property.	The plaintiffs (appellants) contended that they were entitled to equal sharing with Garrels based on the subrogation doctrine, asserting that they were owed rights due to their financial contributions, particularly their payments on the note held by Mrs. Imer. They argued that these payments positioned them to claim part of the payments owed from the mortgage secured by the notes they were involved with, even if they asserted that their claimant status arose from an obligation related to their agency role.	The defendants (appellees) contested the appellants' claims, primarily arguing that Ryhiner & Co. were mere volunteers in making the payments, which disqualified them from claiming subrogation rights. They stated that the appellants had neither the legal obligation nor the standing to demand a shared distribution of the proceeds from the foreclosure, as their involvement did not establish them as legitimate holders of the notes with any enforceable claims against the security.

In 1873, in Will County, Illinois, Seth W. Hardin filed an ejectment action against Peter Rickey to recover a parcel of land in township 33 north, range 10 east of the third principal meridian. Hardin claimed ownership of the land. However, during the trial, the name of the defendant was changed to Samuel M. W. Gouveneur. The trial was conducted without a jury, and the court found the defendant not guilty, resulting in a judgment in favor of Gouveneur. Hardin appealed the decision. The key issue in the case revolved around the proof of ownership and the payment of taxes on the property. The defendant presented a deed as color of title and claimed to have paid taxes over several years, which were challenged regarding the validity of the payments made and the applicability of the color of title. Evidence was introduced during the trial, including a letter and tax receipts, which were scrutinized regarding their sufficiency to establish a defense against Hardin's claim.	Seth W. Hardin, the plaintiff, contended that he had rightful ownership of the disputed land and sought recovery through the ejectment action. He argued that the defendant, Gouveneur, failed to establish a valid defense through the introduction of the deed and tax payment evidence. Hardin aimed to demonstrate that the payments made were not under a lawful claim of title, therefore invalidating Gouveneur's claim to the property.	Samuel M. W. Gouveneur, the defendant, claimed ownership through a deed executed by John and Walter Lockwood, arguing that this constituted color of title. He presented tax receipts purporting to show that he had paid the taxes on the land for several years, which he asserted strengthened his defense against Hardin's ejectment claim. Gouveneur argued that the evidence, including a letter from a tax payer, should be sufficient to establish his claim to the property, despite Hardin's challenge regarding the legitimacy of the payments.

In 1876, the Chicago and North Western Railroad Company was engaged in a case against Bradford C. Church and others concerning the loss of goods during transportation. The plaintiff, Church, had shipped sixty-five barrels of flour and eighty-one bags of bran from Sterling, Illinois, to North Anson, Maine. The agreement was that the railroad would transport the goods and deliver them to the National Dispatch Freight Line in Chicago, who would then forward them to their final destination. However, the goods were improperly delivered to a person without proper authorization, leading to their loss. The case was tried in the Illinois Appellate Court without a jury, focusing on the nature of the contract between the railroad and the shipper, particularly regarding the extent of the railroad's liability given the bill of lading's stipulations.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Chicago and North Western Railroad Company was negligent in handling their goods, resulting in the loss of the shipment. They argued that the company was contractually obligated to ensure safe delivery to North Anson, Maine. The plaintiffs contended that the railroad failed in their duties as common carriers, invoking state statutes restricting a carrier's ability to limit liability through contractual clauses that would deny common law duties.	The railroad company contended that the terms in the bill of lading limited their liability to only the transportation of goods over their line to Chicago. They asserted that once the goods were delivered to the National Dispatch Line in Chicago, their responsibility ceased, and thus they were not liable for the loss of goods incurred beyond that point. The company argued that the plaintiffs accepted these terms knowingly, which should absolve them from further obligations.

John Johnson (Appellant) and Richard Ackless (Appellee) were involved in a legal dispute originating in St. Clair County, Illinois, in 1824 and culminating in an appeal in 1825. The case began when Ackless brought a suit against Johnson before a justice of the peace to recover a sum related to a property transaction involving land. Ackless had initially owed Johnson $800 for a tract of land, having already paid $400, but could not pay the remaining amount. During a prior trial, Ackless expressed his inability to pay and proposed that if Johnson would release him from the remaining debt, he would forfeit the payments made and return the land. Following this discussion, Johnson accepted, and the contract was rescinded. Johnson later sold the land to a third party, Divers, for $453, resulting in the current dispute over the sum he received above the $400 owed to Ackless. The circuit court of St. Clair County upheld Ackless's claim, leading Johnson to appeal the decision, arguing that there was no consideration supporting the contract as it constituted a mere promise without enforceable terms.	Johnson, the appellant, contested the circuit court's ruling in favor of Ackless, arguing that the contract lacked consideration and thus was invalid. He claimed that the promise made by Ackless was gratuitous and that the evidence demonstrated no binding obligation existed between the parties. He sought to have the circuit court judgment reversed, emphasizing that the petition represented a naked agreement lacking legal enforceability.	Ackless, the appellee, defended against Johnson's claims by asserting that there was indeed a lawful agreement between himself and Johnson. Ackless contended that although he could not pay the remaining balance, a valid negotiation had taken place wherein he relinquished his claim to the land in exchange for Johnson's forgiveness of the debt and the return of the payments made. He maintained that the circuit court's judgment was correct and should be upheld as it aligned with the established legal principles regarding contracts.

W. W. Crawford et al. filed a case against The People ex rel. Julian S. Rumsey in September 1876 in Cicero, Cook County, Illinois. The case stemmed from an ordinance adopted by the town's board of trustees to gravel a portion of Madison Street, which stipulated that $400 of the cost would be covered by the town, while $39,600 would be assessed on the properties deemed benefited by this improvement. The board of trustees determined that such real estate was beneficial, appointing commissioners to allocate the assessment proportional to the perceived benefits. However, there were concerns raised about the legal sufficiency of this assessment process, particularly regarding whether it violated the principle that property assessments should not exceed the benefits that accrue to that property from the improvement. The appellants argued that the process neglected to ascertain the actual benefits each parcel received and instead imposed a general assessment based solely on arbitrary determinations.	The plaintiffs claimed that the assessment process conducted by the town's trustees was flawed and legally insufficient. They argued that the commissioners were instructed to levy a specific amount of money without a proper evaluation of the actual benefits bestowed on each piece of property. Essentially, they asserted that the assessment violated established legal principles stipulating that property assessments for improvements should not exceed the actual benefits conferred upon the property.	The defendants maintained that the ordinance and the assessment procedure conformed to the legal requirements set forth by the town's charter. They argued that the board of trustees had the authority to determine the total special benefits and appropriately allocate the assessment among property owners. The defense contended that there was a proper examination of the benefits by trustees, which sufficed under legal standards, and that the commissioner’s actions were within the scope of their authority.

Michael O’Connor brought a legal case against Peter Leddy, which was heard in September 1872 in Illinois. The context involved a dispute regarding legal procedure in the superior court of Cook County. The court had previously struck down the defendant's plea of general issue due to the absence of an affidavit of merits, as mandated by a now-abrogated law specific to Cook County. This led to a default judgment against Leddy. The case raised important questions regarding the application of a new state constitution adopted in 1870, which required uniformity in legal practices across all courts of the same class. The constitution's provisions aimed to eliminate inconsistencies that previously existed, fostering a uniform legal environment. The Illinois Supreme Court ultimately had to consider whether the laws in question continued to hold after the constitutional changes.	O’Connor argued that the default judgment against Leddy was justified due to procedural noncompliance. His central claim was that Leddy failed to meet the requirements set forth under the now-abrogated Cook County act, leading to a rightful judgment in his favor. O’Connor's legal request centered on the enforcement of this judgment, asserting that Leddy's defenses were invalid under the new constitutional standards.	Leddy contended that the act requiring an affidavit of merits was inconsistent with the new state constitution, which mandated uniform operation of laws relating to courts. He argued that the plaintiff's claims should be dismissed on these constitutional grounds, asserting that this local law did not apply following the abrogation by the 1870 constitution. Leddy sought a reversal of the default judgment against him based on these legal interpretations.

In September 1875, the case of John C. Stewart et al. v. Cincinnatus C. Mumford arose in Knox County, Illinois. John C. Stewart had obtained a lease for certain lands for the mining of coal, where he invested significant resources to develop the site, including sinking a shaft and constructing machinery. The lease required him to pay royalty fees and employ twenty-five men. Stewart negotiated a sale of his interests to the Lathop Coal and Mining Company, but the company refused to honor the agreement due to disputes over lease terms. In anticipation of the pending litigation against the company, Stewart surrendered the possession of the mines back to his lessor, Dean. However, before the trial, Dean leased the mines to defendants Stewart and McFarland, who promptly took possession. In the interim, a fire destroyed much of Stewart's equipment, leaving the mines filled with water and largely worthless. Stewart claimed compensation for his investments and sought the court's help to execute an agreement with Stewart and McFarland regarding his interests in the mines, while the defendants argued that Stewart had abandoned his claim.	The plaintiff, John C. Stewart, claimed that he was entitled to compensation for the investments he made in the coal mines under his initial lease and subsequent negotiations. He argued that even though the lease with Dean was surrendered, he had an agreement with Stewart and McFarland for them to compensate him for his interests in the mines should he fail in his litigation against the Lathop Coal and Mining Company. He sought judicial intervention to have his contractual rights acknowledged and enforced.	The defendants, Stewart and McFarland, contended that the plaintiff had effectively abandoned his initial lease and the associated rights when he surrendered possession of the mines to Dean. They argued that the agreement for compensation expressed by Stewart was not valid and maintained that the lease with Dean was made with his consent. Furthermore, the defendants claimed the plaintiff should not pursue this matter in equity, as his claims arose from a contract and should be addressed in common law.

The case of *The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company v. Andrew J. Miller* took place in January 1875 in Illinois. The incident involved the tragic death of James D. Miller, a nine-year-old boy, who was riding in a wagon when it collided with a passenger train operated by the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company. The accident occurred at a railroad crossing that approached from the east and west. Andrew J. Miller, as the administrator of the deceased's estate, brought the lawsuit against the railway company, seeking damages for negligence. The plaintiff argued that the railway company was responsible for the accident due to improper conduct. During the trial, the jury sided with the plaintiff, awarding them $3,500 in damages. However, the railway company disputed the verdict and appealed the decision, leading to the case being scrutinized by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Andrew J. Miller, alleged negligence on the part of the railway company, asserting that their actions led to the fatal accident that caused the death of his son. He requested damages for the wrongful death of James D. Miller, maintaining that the railway company failed to exercise appropriate care in operating the train near the crossing.	The defendant, the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company, contended that the accident was primarily due to the negligence of the wagon driver, Jones, who did not exercise due caution while crossing the tracks. The defendant argued that the train was running at a normal speed and that the statutory requirements, such as ringing the bell, were adhered to. They maintained that the circumstances of the crossing in an open area did not necessitate the train's speed to be reduced, and thus requested the court to overturn the jury's verdict.

In the case of *Oliver Decker v. Homer Decker et al.*, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 20, 1887, the central issue revolved around the interpretation of the last will and testament of John Decker, who passed away leaving behind an estate comprising several tracts of land and over $8,000 in personal property. The key individuals involved included Oliver Decker, the deceased’s son and executor of the will, as well as his minor grandchildren, Bosina and Homer Decker, who were named as devisees. The will designated specific real estate to Oliver and his granddaughter, and set forth conditions for the distribution of any remaining money after debts and funeral expenses were paid. Disputes arose concerning the meaning of the phrase “any money remaining after my death,” particularly whether it referred solely to cash on hand or to the residue of the entire personal estate. Additionally, concerns were raised about the correct description of certain parcels of land mentioned in the will, leading to a detailed examination of the testator's intent regarding the estate's distribution.	The plaintiff, Oliver Decker, argued that the term “money remaining” should be interpreted to include all personal property available after settling debts and funeral expenses, rather than being limited to cash on hand at the time of the testator’s death. He asserted that the ambiguity in the will’s language justified his interpretation, claiming entitlement to the full residue of personal property in addition to the specific bequests of land.	The defendants, represented by Homer Decker and Bosina Decker, contended that the term “money remaining” strictly referred to the actual cash available at the time of John Decker’s death and did not encompass other forms of personal property. They argued that the interpretation sought by Oliver Decker would leave portions of the estate undisposed of, contrary to the presumed intentions of the testator, and that the ambiguities in the will were inherent and not subject to revision through the introduction of extrinsic evidence.

In September 1875, in Bureau County, Illinois, Robert M. Miller was involved in a legal case against Amanda Balthasser. The case stemmed from an allegation of trespass and assault made by Balthasser against Miller. The plaintiff, Amanda Balthasser, claimed that Miller unlawfully assaulted her while she was a maid in his household, using threats and personal violence to compel her to submit to sexual intercourse. The trial was conducted before a jury, which found in favor of Balthasser, awarding her $1,000 in damages. Following the verdict, Miller appealed the decision, contesting the jury instructions given during the trial and asserting that the evidence did not support the verdict. The case was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court, which examined the details surrounding the jury instructions and the credibility of the witnesses.	Amanda Balthasser alleged that Robert M. Miller assaulted her by threatening her and using personal violence to force her into sexual intercourse. She argued that the assault not only constituted a trespass but warranted compensation for the personal injuries she sustained. Balthasser maintained that if the jury believed her testimony, they should rule in her favor and assess damages up to $5,000, reflecting both her suffering and the need for punitive measures against Miller's actions.	Robert M. Miller denied the allegations of assault and claimed that the jury instructions created an unfair bias against him. He argued that the court erred by giving certain instructions to the jury and maintained that the decision was contrary to the evidence presented. Miller asserted that there was no wrongdoing on his part, and the jury should have found in his favor based on his testimony. He sought a reversal of the judgment and a new trial on the grounds that the original trial was flawed.

In the case of David K. Turley v. The People ex rel. Mayfield, Collector, dated March 27, 1886, the legal dispute arose in Logan County, Illinois, where David K. Turley challenged the assessment of his lands by the drainage commissioners under the provisions of the "Drainage Act" of 1879. The commissioners assessed benefits against several tracts of land owned by Turley, totaling $420, but when Turley appealed the assessment, it was affirmed without any changes by the county supervisors. Subsequently, a certified copy of the assessment roll was delivered to the treasurer of the drainage district, who returned Turley's lands as delinquent to the county collector. In a subsequent meeting, the commissioners altered the assessment's description in the absence of Turley, dividing the benefits among separate tracts without notifying him. Turley objected, claiming the amended assessment was void due to the lack of authority and proper procedure followed by the commissioners. The case thus revolved around the question of whether the commissioners had the power to change the assessment after Turley had already appealed and expressed objections.	Turley claimed that the drainage commissioners had acted outside their legal authority when they changed the description of the assessed lands post-appeal and that this change constituted a substantial amendment, thus voiding the new assessment. He argued that he had the right to contest the assessment of benefits assigned to each of his tracts of land, and he challenged the validity of the process followed in making the amendments, seeking a reversal of the judgment against his lands.	The defense, represented by the drainage commissioners and the county collector, asserted that the changes made to the assessment after Turley’s appeal did not exceed their powers despite the objections raised by Turley. They maintained that the amended assessment was valid and that the assessment process was conducted in accordance with the drainage law. The defense likely argued for the court to uphold the judgment against Turley’s lands.

The legal case "The Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company v. Allen N. Merrill" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. The dispute arose from a transaction involving a shipment of goods—specifically castings—sent via railway from Geneva to Winnebago, Illinois. The goods were consigned to John L. Page, with delivery instructions specifying American Express Co. as a point of care and indicated as C.O.D (Collect on Delivery). The railway transported the goods and successfully delivered them to Page upon receipt of freight payment. However, Page proved to be insolvent, and as a result, Allen N. Merrill, the consignor, sought to recover the value of the castings from the railway company, arguing that they had a responsibility to collect the payment at the time of delivery. Merrill had previously obtained a favorable judgment from the circuit court; however, the railway company appealed the judgment.	The plaintiff, Allen N. Merrill, claimed that the railway company was liable for the value of the goods as they were marked C.O.D. Merrill argued that the railway had an obligation to collect the payment from the consignee (Page) upon delivery and that their failure to do so rendered them liable for the loss incurred due to Page's insolvency. He sought financial compensation equal to the value of the castings shipped.	The defendant, the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company, contended that their responsibility ended upon the successful delivery of the goods to the consignee, Page. The railway argued that there was no evidence of them undertaking the role of a collecting agent and that the receipt given did not indicate any obligation to collect the price of the goods. Moreover, the company maintained that without being provided with a billing statement for the goods, they were unable to pursue collection if they had even desired to do so.

James D. Kilgore brought a legal action against H. B. Ferguson and other members of the board of supervisors of Ford County in Illinois in January 1875. The case originated after Kilgore was elected as the county treasurer and executed a bond, which was required for his position. Allegedly, the defendants conspired to injure Kilgore by urging his sureties to withdraw their support, which led to them notifying Kilgore of their desire to be released from the bond on July 25, 1874. As a result, Kilgore was required to file a new bond within a statutory timeframe. He presented what he believed to be a sufficient bond to the board on August 11, 1874. However, the defendants, knowing the bond was valid, falsely claimed it was insufficient, leading to a vacancy in Kilgore's office. Kilgore accused the officials of maliciously refusing to approve his bond, intending to harm him financially and reputationally. The case was appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court after a lower court ruled in favor of the defendants, who had filed a general demurrer against Kilgore's declaration.	Kilgore's main argument was that the defendants, as members of the board of supervisors, wrongfully and maliciously refused to approve his official bond, which he maintained was valid and sufficient according to legal requirements. He claimed this refusal resulted in his unlawful removal from office and sought damages for the harm caused by the defendants' actions.	The defendants contended that the declaration made by Kilgore was fundamentally flawed as it did not sufficiently allege facts that demonstrated the bond complied with statutory requirements. They argued that without a clear indication that the bond met the legal standards, they could not be held responsible for refusing to approve it. As a result, they requested the court to uphold the lower court's ruling in their favor, effectively dismissing Kilgore’s claims.

The case "Paul Nenninger et al. v. Sebastian Fietsam, Adm’r" took place in 1889 in St. Clair County, Illinois. The main individuals involved include Paul Nenninger (deceased) and Sebastian Fietsam, who served as the administrator de bonis non of Nenninger's estate. The dispute arose when Fietsam filed a petition in the Circuit Court seeking authorization to sell land belonging to Nenninger's estate to pay debts, primarily related to a judgment against the previous administrator, Frederick Rhein. The judgment, approved in 1881, demanded payment from any subsequently discovered assets of the estate. The defendants challenged the petition, arguing that it was deficient in facts and failed to establish the necessary jurisdictional conditions for the sale of real estate. The court initially sustained Fietsam’s petition, but the defendants filed for a writ of error, leading to further legal proceedings.	The plaintiff, represented by Fietsam, claimed that the estate had fully administered personal assets, leaving only land to satisfy the outstanding debt. The petition contended that the judgment against the estate allowed for the sale of any discovered assets to pay the debt. Fietsam sought a court decree authorizing the sale of the identified real estate, stating it was necessary to meet the obligations arising from the judgment approved in 1881.	The defendants contended that the petition was legally insufficient because it did not specify the dates of death, administration letters, or whether the claims were allowed within the required two-year period. They argued that real estate could not be sold to satisfy debts if personal assets were sufficient and emphasized that the necessary facts to support the sale were not adequately presented in the petition, thus contesting the court's jurisdiction to grant the sale.

Bridget Dougherty, as the administratrix of the estate of her deceased husband Bernard Dougherty, initiated a legal action against the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company. The incident that led to this case occurred on September 7, 1881, when Bernard Dougherty was killed at a railroad crossing on Columbus Street in the north part of Ottawa, Illinois, while attempting to cross with a team and wagon. The plaintiff's complaint alleged that the railroad company exhibited a lack of ordinary care, specifically by failing to ring a bell or sound a whistle, running the train at an excessive speed, and not providing a flagman at the crossing. A jury trial concluded with a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, awarding $5000 in damages. The case was subsequently upheld by the Appellate Court, prompting the railroad company to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, Bridget Dougherty, asserted that her husband’s death was caused by the railroad company’s negligence. She claimed the defendants failed to fulfill their duty of giving proper signals (bell or whistle) prior to reaching the crossing and ran the train at a dangerous speed without providing a crossing flagman. Bridget sought damages for the wrongful death of her husband.	The railroad company contended that it had complied with the statutory requirements regarding signaling at crossings by ringing a bell and sounding a whistle as mandated. They argued that any failure to avoid the accident was due to the deceased's own negligence. Furthermore, the defendant highlighted that the jury was misinstructed regarding their responsibility for giving warnings, which exceeded what the statute required, thereby seeking a reversal of the verdict based on this legal misstep.

On October 17, 1865, Maria Anapow acquired a $3,000 insurance policy from the Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company for her stock of tobacco and cigars stored in Albert Michelson's tobacco shop in Chicago. Michelson subsequently purchased an insurance policy for $4,000 for his own tobacco stock located in the same room as Anapow's. On January 4, 1866, Michelson bought Anapow's stock and received an assignment of her policy with the company's consent. However, on January 9, 1866, a fire destroyed all the tobacco, leading to Michelson receiving compensation from the Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company for his insured stock. The Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company refused to compensate for Anapow's policy, prompting Michelson to file a lawsuit on her behalf. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff for $3,090. The case was appealed, with the court examining the policy's terms, the concept of double insurance, and whether Anapow's stock became part of Michelson's insured stock after the purchase.	The plaintiff, Maria Anapow through Michelson, argued that the Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company was obligated to pay the $3,000 under the insurance policy for the stock destroyed by fire. The plaintiff contended that the terms of the policy had been met and that there had been no valid basis for the company’s refusal to pay.	The defendant, Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company, maintained that the policy included a clause stating that if other insurance existed on the same property without being noted on the policy, the policy would become void. They argued that after Michelson’s purchase of Anapow’s tobacco stock, it effectively became part of his insured inventory under another policy, which negated their liability for the loss claimed under Anapow's policy. They requested a review of the jury's instructions regarding the requirements for proving double insurance.

In January 1888, in Knox County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Robert L. Nelson and the plaintiffs, Charles S. Smith and Erastus Smith, over eleven hogs that the plaintiffs alleged were unlawfully detained by the defendant, Nelson. The Smiths discovered their hogs were missing and were informed by a neighbor that Nelson had them confined in his cornfield. When the Smiths approached Nelson regarding the hogs, he claimed to have taken them up due to damages caused by the hogs in his field. The Smiths offered to pay for damages amounting to $12.25, which Nelson refused, stating they had to reclaim the hogs legally. A Justice of the Peace was involved, and when the Smiths attempted to settle, they ended up suing Nelson for replevin after making a formal tender of the damage amount and costs. This matter was tried first in front of a Justice of the Peace and later in the Circuit Court, which ruled in favor of the Smiths. Nelson appealed the decision, bringing the case before the Illinois Appellate Court, which ultimately affirmed the previous judgment.	The plaintiffs, Charles S. Smith and Erastus Smith, claimed that they were entitled to the return of their eleven hogs, which Nelson had unlawfully detained. They argued that they made a proper tender of $12.25 to cover the damages he alleged, and therefore, upon demand for their hogs, they were entitled to regain possession of the property. Their legal request included the recovery of their hogs through an action of replevin.	The defendant, Robert L. Nelson, contended that the tender made by the Smiths was not kept good and asserted that they had not properly complied with the legal requirements for reclaiming the hogs. Nelson argued that he had a right to retain the hogs until he was settled for the alleged damages. Additionally, he raised objections regarding jury instructions related to the sufficiency of the tender and the burden of proof, suggesting that there were errors in how the case was tried.

In September 1871, the case of Peter Bressler et al. v. Frederick H. Kent was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a matter in Whiteside County, Illinois. The case involved Sabrina Bressler, a married woman, who executed a deed of trust on certain real estate owned solely by her to secure a promissory note. The note was for a debt incurred by both her and her husband. The legal question centered on whether Sabrina's deed could properly encumber the property she owned independently, without her husband's consent. Historically, married women had limited rights to convey property, requiring their husbands to join them in such actions. Although an act passed in 1861 allowed for married women to control their separate property, this privilege was confined to personal rights and profits, not extending to real estate without specific provisions allowing such powers. The court examined whether the property could be deemed a separate estate, capable of being compromised for debts, and noted principles from equity law which indicate that a married woman could not dispose of real estate without her husband's involvement.	The plaintiffs, Peter Bressler et al., argued that Sabrina Bressler validly charged her separate real estate to secure a debt, and thus sought to compel the sale of the property to satisfy the obligation. They contended that under the legislation enacted to protect married women’s properties, Sabrina should have the right to manage her own estate without the interference or consent of her husband.	Frederick H. Kent, the defendant, contended that the deed of trust executed by Sabrina was invalid because her husband did not join in the execution as required by law. He argued that without the husband's concurrence, the conveyance was void, and thus there was no valid lien created against the property. The defense emphasized that the statute governing the conveyance of a married woman’s property must be adhered to strictly, asserting that any implied powers for disposal of the property cannot be inferred and must be explicitly stated.

In December 1846, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed the case of E. B. Washburne, the Prosecuting Attorney for Jo Daviess County, against Thomas H. Campbell, the Auditor of Illinois. The background of the case stems from legislation passed on March 1, 1845, which established the Jo Daviess County Court and called for the election of a Prosecuting Attorney with a fixed annual salary of one hundred dollars. However, the Legislature failed to appoint anyone to this position. Subsequently, a joint resolution was passed on March 3, 1845, allowing the Governor to appoint a Prosecuting Attorney without any compensation from the state. Washburne was appointed the Prosecuting Attorney on the same day as the resolution's passage. The central issue was whether Washburne was entitled to the salary designated by the earlier law or if he held his position under the joint resolution without compensation. Key individuals involved included E. B. Washburne, Thomas H. Campbell, and the Illinois Legislature.	The plaintiff, E. B. Washburne, claimed that he was entitled to the annual salary of one hundred dollars for his services as the Prosecuting Attorney for Jo Daviess County, asserting that his appointment was valid under the Act passed on March 1, 1845. Washburne sought a mandamus against Campbell to compel the issuance of the salary payment from the state treasury, arguing that despite the later joint resolution, the intention of the legislature was to create a valid, compensated position.	The defendant, Thomas H. Campbell, argued that the resolution allowing the Governor to appoint a Prosecuting Attorney, which stipulated no compensation from the state, invalidated Washburne's claim to the salary. Campbell contended that the appointment could not legally fall under the earlier law since there was no vacancy created by the legislature's failure to elect an attorney, making the later joint resolution the basis for Washburne's position without financial entitlement.

Charles W. Boynton and Plowden H. Ball were involved in a legal dispute that reached the Illinois Supreme Court on March 28, 1883. The case originated when Ball filed an action of debt against Boynton in the Circuit Court of Stephenson County during the September term of 1877, seeking to recover a judgment from several years prior. In April 1878, Boynton was adjudged bankrupt by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. The trial commenced in December 1879, where Boynton did not contest the judgment against him and was ordered to pay the debt along with accrued interest. Following the judgment, Boynton received a discharge in bankruptcy but subsequently filed a motion in the Circuit Court to stay the proceedings based on his bankruptcy discharge. The court denied his motion, which he subsequently appealed. This led to further examination of the applicable bankruptcy laws and the validity of the judgment rendered against Boynton after his bankruptcy adjudication.	The plaintiff, Plowden H. Ball, argued that Boynton's bankruptcy discharge did not invalidate the judgment rendered against him because Boynton had failed to seek a stay of proceedings while the bankruptcy issues were determined. Ball maintained that the judgment was valid and enforceable, asserting that Boynton's own negligence and failure to act during his bankruptcy proceedings barred him from disputing the judgment after receiving his discharge.	Charles W. Boynton contended that he should be granted a perpetual stay of the judgment enforcement against him due to his bankruptcy discharge. He argued that according to the provisions of the Bankrupt Act of 1867, the debt underlying the judgment was extinguished upon his discharge, and that any actions seeking to enforce the judgment were improper because he had not been given a fair opportunity to defend against it due to the ongoing bankruptcy procedures.

In 1841, in Beardstown, Illinois, a man named Lindsay owned a lot of land. Lindsay's property was subsequently sold at a sheriff's sale in 1841 to a group named Ormsby, Hite, & Co. due to a default judgment against him, although no deed was made to them, only a certificate of purchase. In 1846, while still in possession of the lot, Lindsay arranged for the defendant, James Thompson, to buy the property on his behalf, resulting in Thompson receiving an assignment of the certificate of purchase from Ormsby, Hite, & Co. without any immediate payment. An agreement was made between Lindsay and Thompson that Thompson would hold the lot and its rents as security for a loan to Lindsay, which was not formally documented due to Lindsay's unexpected death. After Lindsay’s death, James Stephenson, who had a prior judgment against Lindsay and acquired the property through a sheriff's sale in 1848, filed a suit against Thompson seeking an accounting of rents and the title to the property. Stephenson alleged that Thompson was holding the property in trust for Lindsay, essentially asserting that Thompson's claim to the property was fraudulent and that his title was void.	James Stephenson, the plaintiff, argued that James Thompson's possession and title of the property were fraudulent and claimed that he was entitled to an accounting for rents collected by Thompson. He contended that, although his judgment allowed him to buy the property at sheriff's sale, Thompson should be compelled to return the property or account for any rents received, as Thompson had no legitimate claim upon the property based on an alleged secret trust arrangement with Lindsay.	James Thompson denied that any agreement or trust existed between him and Lindsay regarding the property. He claimed that he had purchased the property legitimately, using his own money, and disputed any assertion of fraud. Thompson argued that any claims of a verbal contract were invalid under the Statute of Frauds, which requires written contracts for the sale of real estate. He maintained that there was sufficient evidence to support his rightful ownership of the property, and he sought to dismiss the claims made by Stephenson.

In January 1864, the legal dispute arose in St. Clair County, Illinois, involving John Stewart and others as plaintiffs against George Peters. The case originated from a note allegedly executed by George C. Stout & Co. The summons for the trial included Stout, Stewart, and Shortridge, but only the latter two were judged. They contended that they had not signed the note. Stout did not contest the case, yet no judgment was sought against him. Stewart then appealed the decision to the Circuit Court, which upheld the judgment from the justice of the peace. However, the issue arose regarding the failure to ensure Stout and Shortridge were made parties to the appeal. According to the relevant provision, an appeal requires that all parties involved in the original judgment must be present in court either through service or appearance. The court highlighted the necessity of summoning all parties, indicating that judgment should be rendered against all or none in cases of joint liability.	The plaintiffs, led by John Stewart, argued that the two defendants, Stewart and Shortridge, had not executed the note, and thus, they should not be held liable. They contended that the Circuit Court's decision was erroneous due to not including Stout in the appeal. Stewart sought to reverse the lower court’s judgment, claiming that the process of the trial was not conducted according to legal requirements and that without all parties present, the judgment could not stand.	The defendants argued that they had not executed the note and thus claimed they were not liable under its terms. They emphasized that they were not properly summoned in the appeal process, which was a procedural requirement under relevant law. The defense maintained that a judgment should not have been issued without all parties having been brought before the court by proper notice or representation.

Gerhard Kuhnen v. William Blitz is a legal case that took place in September 1870 in Cook County, Illinois. The case originated from a lawsuit filed by plaintiff William Blitz against defendant Gerhard Kuhnen, alleging that Kuhnen committed a wrongful and willful act resulting in personal injuries to Blitz. The case was escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court following a jury trial at which the jury found in favor of Blitz, leading to the defendant's appeal. Kuhnen contested the jury's verdict, raising concerns about the trial court's instructions and the weight of the evidence presented.	The plaintiff, William Blitz, argued that he suffered injuries due to the wrongful actions of Gerhard Kuhnen. He sought compensation for these injuries, asserting that the defendant's actions were willful and resulted in harm. Blitz maintained that the jury’s verdict was justified and requested that the judgment in his favor be upheld.	Gerhard Kuhnen, the defendant, contended that the trial court erred in its instructions to the jury and argued that the evidence did not support the verdict reached by the jury. Kuhnen sought reversal of the judgment and argued for a new trial on the grounds of improper guidance provided to the jury and the overall lack of substantial evidence supporting the plaintiff's claims.

The case, Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company v. The President and Trustees of the Town of Chenoa, took place in January 1867 in Chenoa, Illinois. The town's president and trustees filed an action against the railway company for violating a local ordinance aimed at preventing obstruction of public streets. The ordinance, purportedly passed on October 20, 1865, prohibited allowing railway cars to remain on public streets for more than fifteen minutes. The plaintiffs claimed that the railway company had obstructed a public street by leaving its cars on the crossing from January 25 to January 26, 1866. Initially, the case was heard by a justice of the peace, who ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $98 for the obstruction. The defendant appealed to the Circuit Court of McLean County, where the court examined the validity of the ordinance and the town's authority to impose penalties.	The plaintiff, the town of Chenoa, claimed that the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company violated the local ordinance by allowing their trains to block public streets beyond the prescribed time. They introduced evidence that the ordinance set a penalty of $5 per hour for such obstructions, asserting that their actions warranted monetary compensation for the obstruction caused.	The defendant contended that the town lacked proper incorporation and authority to impose penalties under the ordinance. They argued that there was no evidence of a legally enforceable ordinance in effect at the time of the alleged violation, pointing to discrepancies in the documentation and the timing of the ordinances referenced in the case.

The case "The Town of Canoe Creek v. John McEniry et al." was decided on December 11, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute centers on alleged injuries to a public highway resulting from actions by the appellees, John McEniry and others, who excavated a ditch on their property that allegedly caused water to flow onto the road and cause damage. The appellant, the Town of Canoe Creek, claims that the appellees' actions violated Section 58 of a law concerning roads and bridges, which prohibits damage to public roads. This case began in 1881 when the Town issued a summons for payment related to the damages caused by washing and saturating the road. Following a judgment against them in an initial hearing before a Justice of the Peace, the appellees appealed to the Circuit Court, where a trial took place and resulted in a verdict favoring them. The lawsuit involved complex legal arguments regarding the existence and maintenance of the highway, the lawful digging of ditches by landowners, and proper notice requirements. The central issue revolved around whether the ditch excavation constituted an injury to the highway as defined by state law.	The Town of Canoe Creek, as the plaintiff, argued that the appellees caused damage to the public highway by digging a ditch and redirecting water flow, leading to the washing and saturation of the road. They contended that such actions violated Section 58 of the road law, which penalizes individuals for obstructing or injuring public roads. The Town sought a penalty for the damages incurred, amounting to an unspecified sum not exceeding $200.	The defendants, represented by McEniry, defended themselves by arguing that their land was not naturally subject to the water flow, thus allowing them to construct the ditch without legal repercussions. They claimed that the ditch did not cause the road to overflow except during extraordinary floods. Furthermore, they maintained that the Town could not seek recovery for the penalty mentioned in its filings since it was not explicitly included in the original writ, contravening due process requirements.

In the years 1862, 1863, and 1864, a special war fund tax was assessed by the county of McLean, Illinois, under legislation aimed at encouraging the formation of volunteer companies during the Civil War. The Board of Supervisors of McLean County appointed a disbursing agent and authorized township collectors to pay the collected war tax directly to this agent, bypassing the county treasurer. Thomas Fell was the county treasurer during this period and retained a two percent commission on the war fund tax after settling with the Board of Supervisors upon his retirement from office. However, the Board had directed the payments to the disbursing agent instead of the county treasurer, which led to a lawsuit against Fell on his bond, as the Board contested his commission claims. The Circuit Court allowed Fell to keep one percent of the commission, leading him to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, represented by the Board of Supervisors of McLean County, claimed that Thomas Fell was not entitled to the full two percent commission he retained from the war fund tax. They argued that according to the law, the war tax was a county tax that should have been deposited with the county treasurer, and as such, Fell should not have collected full commissions due to improper handling of the tax.	Thomas Fell contended that he was legally entitled to retain the two percent commission based on the existing law governing his role as the county treasurer. He argued that although the Board of Supervisors had given improper direction regarding the payment of the war tax, it was reasonable to assume he would have received and disbursed the funds if permitted, thus justifying his claim for the full commission.

The legal case "Herman G. Webber, U. S. Marshal, for use, etc. v. Mackey, Nisbet & Co. et al." took place in 1889 in the Circuit Court of Saline County, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute over property that had been levied upon by Jones, a sheriff, due to nine attachment writs filed against Thomas J. Crawford by his creditors. The plaintiff, Herman G. Webber, a U.S. Marshal, was seeking to enforce a replevin bond involving goods originally contested in the attachment suits. The plaintiff argued that the conveyances in question—specifically chattel mortgages made by Crawford to the defendants Mackey, Nisbet & Co. and Hinkle, Nisbet & Co.—were fraudulent, intended to hinder or delay other creditors. The case escalated through various courts, with the defendants claiming the mortgages were valid and had been upheld in prior rulings. Ultimately, the Circuit Court ruled against the mortgagees, declaring their title void in the eyes of the attaching creditors, leading to ongoing litigation over the ownership of the replevied property.	The plaintiff contended that the property in question had been fraudulently conveyed by Crawford to the defendants to hinder his creditors. He asserted that previous court decisions had rendered the defendants' claims to the property invalid, and sought recovery based on these claims. Specifically, the plaintiff maintained that the mortgages to Mackey, Nisbet & Co. and Hinkle, Nisbet & Co. were designed to obstruct creditor rights, and requested compensation for damages incurred due to the defendants' actions.	The defendants argued that they had acted in good faith when accepting the chattel mortgages and contested the allegations of fraud. They maintained that the mortgages were valid and that they took immediate possession of the mortgaged property as per the agreement, which should protect their interests. They requested that the court uphold their rights to the property based on the previous adjudication that had recognized their claims in earlier court rulings, opposing the plaintiff's assertion of fraud.

The case of Katharine Schneider et al. v. Conrad Seibert et al. arose in January 1869 in St. Clair County, Illinois. The legal dispute centered around the estate of Jacob Braun, who passed away in 1856 without a will, leaving a widow, Katharina, and several children, including Frederick Braun and Henrietta. The plaintiffs, Conrad and Henrietta Seibert, filed a bill in the St. Clair Circuit Court for partition and assignment of dower, claiming that Katharina was entitled to dower and the children each to an undivided sixth of the property. The court appointed a guardian ad litem for the minors and established rules for the defendants to answer. In a parallel filing, Jacob Weyhopt filed a bill of interpleader against Frederick Braun and Conrad Schneider, alleging fraudulent conveyance of Frederick's interest in the property to Schneider to evade debts. The court heard the case, and findings indicated the property could not be partitioned without injury to the owners. The master reported the yearly value of the widow's dower and ordered a sale of the property, with proceeds to be used as directed.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to a partition of the real estate and sought the assignment of dower for the widow, Katharina. They asserted that the estate had been rightfully inherited, with allegations that the legal interests of all heirs were being undermined by fraudulent actions related to conveyances made by Frederick Braun. Thus, they sought a court decree for the partition of the property according to each heir's share and resolution of the dower rights.	The defendant, Conrad Schneider, argued against the court's decree for partition, claiming procedural errors regarding the title and the filing of the bill of interpleader. Schneider contended that he should have been allowed to answer the original bill, and he objected to the appointment of commissioners, alleging that the necessary formalities were not adhered to. He sought to have the court's decree opened for him to answer these claims, arguing that he had insufficient notice of the interpleader's filing.

On November 18, 1869, Peter Hale and Jacob Burhyte, the owners of a lot in Dunleith, Illinois, conveyed the lot in trust to John Ollinger to secure five promissory notes, each for $500, payable to Nelson M. Brett. On December 19, 1877, Grover & Baker obtained a judgment against Hale and Burhyte, leading to the property being sold under execution to Grover, who received the sheriff’s deed on June 14, 1880. Subsequently, on August 16, 1880, the lot was sold under the trust deed by John M. Miller to pay an unpaid note balance of $356, and the property was deeded to Miller. Miller later sold the property to Margaret J. Hale on June 1, 1881, for $224, with no payments made on the purchase. The case arose when Grover filed a bill seeking to correct errors in the sheriff’s deed, set aside the trustee's sale, declare Ollinger’s deed to Miller void, and redeem the property. The circuit court's decree only partially granted Grover's relief regarding the sheriff’s deed and denied the remaining requests, leading Grover to appeal.	William O. Grover claimed that the sale of the property under the trust deed was invalid, as it was executed by an agent of the trustee instead of the trustee himself. Grover sought correction of the sheriff's deed, requested the trust deed sale to be set aside, asserted that Ollinger's deed to Miller was void, called for an account of amounts due under the trust deed, and aimed to redeem the property based on his equity of redemption.	The defendants, including Peter L. Hale and Margaret J. Hale, contended that Grover was not an immediate party to the sale thus could not challenge its validity. They argued that Margaret J. Hale was an innocent purchaser entitled to protection, having purchased the property in good faith without knowledge of any sale irregularities. Furthermore, they claimed that Grover's standing to contest the sale was undermined as he had not made a claim against them under these circumstances.

Glens Falls Insurance Co. v. R. S. Hopkins et al. is a legal case from the Illinois Appellate Court decided on January 16, 1885. The case centers on R. S. Hopkins and H. S. Nichols, who were partners operating a store in Ogden, Illinois. They held an insurance policy through Glens Falls Insurance Co. The key individuals involved were the general manager of the insurance company, Whitelock, and the partners, Hopkins and Nichols. On August 27, 1883, a fire devastated their store. However, the relevant insurance policy had expired just three days earlier, and there were disputes regarding whether there was a verbal agreement to renew it. Although Hopkins was authorized to countersign policies, a renewal was not performed before the fire, and the company refused to acknowledge the loss under the expired policy. The court examined the validity of the alleged verbal renewal agreement and the circumstances surrounding the issuance of a second policy, which was dated before the fire but executed afterward. The case was tried without a jury, leading to further scrutiny of agency authority within partnership contexts.	The plaintiffs, R. S. Hopkins and H. S. Nichols, claimed that a verbal agreement existed to renew their insurance policy prior to the fire, against which they sought recovery of insurance money. They argued that despite the original policy's expiration, a valid renewal had been agreed upon, and they requested the court recognize this contract for the purpose of recovering their loss from the fire.	The defendant, Glens Falls Insurance Co., contended that there was no valid renewal of the insurance policy since it had expired before the fire, and the second policy was invalid because it was issued after the property was destroyed. They argued that the authority given to Hopkins to bind his firm to contracts with himself could not apply in this case, and thus they requested the court dismiss the plaintiffs' claim for recovery based on these defenses.

Richard Webster filed a lawsuit against Philip Conley in September 1867 in Chicago, Illinois. The dispute arose from a lease agreement concerning property owned by Alice Radin, an infant, for which Conley served as guardian. The lease, executed for a five-year term, was not approved by the County Court, as required by law. After two years of Webster occupying the premises and making improvements, Conley's guardianship was revoked, and a new guardian, Sherlock, was appointed. Sherlock subsequently evicted Webster and offered him a new lease with significantly increased rent. As a result, Webster sought damages for breach of covenant, claiming losses equivalent to the difference between the original rent and the premises' current value at the time of eviction. Conley filed several defenses, which included the assertion that he acted solely in his capacity as a guardian and that the lease had no legal standing due to its lack of court approval.	Richard Webster claimed that the eviction was wrongful and sought damages due to Conley’s breach of covenant from the initial lease agreement. He argued that as a lessee who occupied the premises and made improvements, the financial loss incurred due to the eviction warranted compensation, specifically the difference between the original rent and the current market value of the property.	Philip Conley defended himself by stating that the lease was void because it lacked judicial approval, which is a requirement for guardians when leasing their ward’s property. He contended that he acted purely in his role as guardian and therefore was not liable for damages since the lease did not create any legal obligations or covenants due to its invalidity under the law.

The case "Andrew J. Cox v. John Montgomery" took place in Iroquois County, Illinois, and was addressed by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1867. The dispute arose from a contract involving an exchange of lands made in January 1862. The plaintiff, Andrew J. Cox, was accused of committing fraud against the defendant, John Montgomery, who discovered the alleged fraud around July 10, 1862. Following the discovery, Montgomery sought legal advice, which led to a delay in filing a lawsuit. Although he filed his first complaint on May 2, 1863, it was dismissed on November 27, 1863, prompting the filing of a new bill on the same day. The court had previously remanded the case to allow Montgomery to explain the delay in his lawsuit. Upon reviewing the explanations regarding the delay, including the advice of counsel and Montgomery's illness during 1862, the Circuit Court found that the delay was justified and that the contract should be rescinded.	Montgomery’s primary argument was centered on the fraud committed by Cox during the land exchange, which he claimed entitled him to rescind the contract. He filed a bill in equity seeking to set aside the conveyance of land, asserting that the fraud adversely affected his rights. His requests included the annulment of the original land exchange due to the fraudulent actions of Cox.	In response, Cox argued that he was entitled to compensation for improvements made on the property, estimated at $125, as well as interest on $300 and reimbursement for taxes. His defense was based on the claim that the time taken by Montgomery to initiate the lawsuit constituted a form of laches, which he believed should disallow Montgomery’s request for rescission of the contract.

The case of "Maria L. Kinney et al. v. Jacob Knoebel et al." emerged in June 1868 and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in St. Clair County, Illinois, following the death of William C. Kinney on October 24, 1858. Kinney had a farm located in St. Clair County, and upon his death, Jacob Knoebel was appointed executor of Kinney’s estate. The will authorized Knoebel to sell any lands outside St. Clair County to pay debts, but did not grant him authority over lands within the county. Following Kinney’s death, two judgments had been levied against him amounting to significant sums, which led to a sheriff's sale of the Kinney property, specifically section 12. The plaintiffs claimed the sale was invalid since it disregarded legal requirements, including the possibility of dividing the land into smaller parcels for sale, and argued that the property was sold under duress and misinformation. The key individuals involved were Maria L. Kinney and other heirs of William C. Kinney as plaintiffs, and Jacob Knoebel, the executor, along with Morrison, who purchased the property at the sheriff’s sale, as defendants.	The plaintiffs, Maria L. Kinney and others, argued that the sale of the land was conducted unlawfully by the executor, Jacob Knoebel, and the sheriff. They contended that the property was worth substantially more than the amount for which it was sold and claimed that Knoebel failed to sell the property in accordance with the will's provisions. The plaintiffs asserted that the sale was invalid due to the executor's lack of authority to sell the land within St. Clair County and alleged collusion among the defendant parties to prevent competitive bidding, which ultimately led to their loss of rightful ownership.	The defendants, Jacob Knoebel and Morrison, contended that the sale was legal and necessary to pay debts owed by the estate of William C. Kinney. They argued that Knoebel acted within the framework of the law and with the creditors' consent to sell the property to satisfy the estate's debts. Morrison claimed he was an innocent purchaser without knowledge of any wrongdoing and insisted that the sale price reflected the fair market value of the property, dismissing allegations of conspiracy and suppression of competition as baseless.

Edward S. McDonald was involved in a legal case against the People of the State of Illinois in 1888, arising from an indictment for conspiracy to defraud Cook County using false pretenses. The events took place in Cook County, Illinois, where McDonald, alongside co-defendants McGarigle, Schneider, and Faber, were accused of conspiring to obtain money from the county through deceptive methods regarding work and materials purportedly supplied for a normal school building. The indictment consisted of multiple counts, each detailing various fraudulent schemes. During the trial, evidence introduced by the prosecution involved not only the normal school bills but also relevant actions and conversations linked to other county institutions which were purportedly part of the same conspiracy. McDonald and his co-defendant were found guilty by a jury, resulting in a three-year prison sentence. After their conviction, motions for a new trial and to arrest judgment were rejected, prompting McDonald to file a writ of error that brought the case to the Illinois Appellate Court for review.	The plaintiff, represented by the State of Illinois, argued that McDonald and his co-defendants conspired to defraud Cook County through false pretenses related to billing for services not provided or overcharging for materials. The prosecution claimed that substantial evidence showed a coordinated effort to mislead county officials to obtain unauthorized funds. They emphasized that the scope of the conspiracy was expansive, involving numerous fraudulent activities and other conspirators, and asked for the conviction to be upheld based on the sufficiency of the evidence presented at trial.	McDonald and his defense team contended that the evidence presented was insufficient to prove his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. They asserted that many errors occurred during the trial, including the admission of irrelevant evidence and improper jury instructions. They claimed that the prosecution's attempt to introduce evidence not confined to the particulars of the indictment misled the jury and impeded a fair trial. McDonald denied involvement in the conspiratorial activities and argued that he had no knowledge of the fraudulent bills or actions attributed to Schneider, which they claimed were based solely on Schneider's uncorroborated testimony.

In April 1869, in Chicago, Illinois, a seven-year-old boy named Ferdinand Stumps was severely injured while attempting to climb onto a freight train operated by the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company. On April 17, while he and two companions were on their way to a planing mill to collect shavings, the incident occurred near the intersection of Brown and Walsh Streets. Witnesses to the event provided conflicting testimony about whether Stumps was climbing onto a detached car or one of the moving train's cars when he fell beneath the train and had both legs crushed below the knee. Plaintiff witnesses claimed negligence on the part of the train's crew for not seeing a stationary car ahead, whereas the train's crew testified there was no car on the track, and that the train was moving slowly, making every effort to ensure the safety of any nearby individuals.	The plaintiff, Ferdinand Stumps, claimed that the railroad company was grossly negligent for failing to see a car that was allegedly standing on the track ahead of the moving train. He argued that this negligence led to the accident and resulting severe personal injuries. The plaintiff sought damages for the injuries sustained, emphasizing the responsibility of the railroad to ensure safety in its operations.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, contended that there was no stationary car on the track at the time of the accident, and thus, they were not negligent. They argued that the train was under proper management with personnel assigned to monitor the situation. They asserted that Stumps was attempting to climb onto the moving train rather than a detached car, which was a violation of safety. The defendant's request was for the dismissal of the case based on the evidence of their adherence to safety protocols and the absence of negligence.

In 1881, in Lebanon, Illinois, James D. Baker served as the Township Treasurer overseeing school district funds. Baker faced a lawsuit from the Board of Trustees to recover mismanaged funds amounting to $3,500 that he loaned to Silas Smith without adequate security. The loan was made based on a request from the Board of Education of School District No. 3, which stated that the land used as security was "ample." However, the real estate offered as security did not meet the legal requirement of being valued at least double the loan amount, as mandated by Illinois law. The mortgage taken was later foreclosed, resulting in a loss for the school district, as the proceeds from the sale only covered part of the loan, leaving a significant amount unpaid. The plaintiff alleged Baker neglected his duty as treasurer to secure proper collateral, which led to the financial loss for the school district.	The Board of Trustees claimed that James D. Baker failed to adhere to his statutory duty as Township Treasurer by not securing the loan with adequate real estate collateral, which should have been valued at double the amount loaned. They argued that his actions amounted to a breach of his official bond, justifying the recovery of the financial losses incurred due to this breach and requested the court to hold Baker accountable for the deficiency in loan security.	Baker defended himself by asserting that he acted on the written request of the Board of Education to make the loan to Smith, believing their assessment of the security was warranted. He argued that since the request came from authorized school officials, he should not be held liable for the loss resulting from following their directions, which he deemed sufficient. He contended that the statute allowed loans to be made upon the Directors' written request and claimed he had acted in good faith.

The case "Lake Erie & Western Railroad Company v. John S. Scott" took place in 1889 in McLean County, Illinois. The case involved a farmer, John S. Scott, who owned a 216-acre farm adjacent to a public highway known as White Oak Grove Road. The railroad company's tracks were constructed in close proximity to the highway, which also bordered Scott's property. During the railroad's construction, a subcontractor removed soil from a small triangular area of Scott’s land without obtaining permission or condemnation, despite being warned by Scott not to trespass. The railroad argued the land was too small to warrant concern and promised to settle, but no agreement was reached. Consequently, Scott filed a lawsuit alleging damages due to reduced safety, unsightliness, and decreased value of his property because of the railroad’s construction and operations. A jury awarded Scott $500 in damages after a trial.	The plaintiff, John S. Scott, claimed that the railroad's construction and operation caused significant harm to his property. He argued that the excavation and subsequent proximity of the railroad made access to his land dangerous, diminished the aesthetic appeal of his farm, and reduced its overall value, which was approximately $6 to $10 per acre. Scott sought compensatory damages for both the direct physical injury to his land and for the broader reduction in value due to the ongoing operation of the railroad.
