The defendant, Lake Erie & Western Railroad Company, claimed that Scott had not demonstrated any unique damages, arguing that any harm he experienced was suffered in common with the general public. They contended that the injury did not arise from a physical invasion of his property but rather from the lawful operations of the railroad's right-of-way. The railroad maintained that it should not be liable, as the damages claimed were speculative and did not exceed the common injuries to public amenities.

The case of *Cleveland Co-operative Stove Company v. Canute R. Matson et al.* dates back to January 22, 1887, in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved include the Cleveland Co-operative Stove Company (the plaintiff) and W. L. Eisengart (the defendant), who was a retail hardware merchant. The dispute arose when the sheriff of Cook County levied an attachment on certain stoves in Eisengart's possession due to a debt owed to the appellants, which occurred after Eisengart absconded prior to the attachment. The plaintiff claimed ownership of the stoves, asserting they had been delivered to Eisengart under a sales agreement stipulating that the stoves were to remain the property of the plaintiff until sold to a bona fide purchaser. The agreement further dictated that the proceeds would belong to the plaintiff until certain conditions were met. The case questioned whether the delivery constituted a consignment for sale or a sale on credit, which would determine if the plaintiff had rightful ownership against Eisengart's creditors.	The Cleveland Co-operative Stove Company claimed ownership of the stoves taken by the sheriff, asserting that the stoves were delivered to Eisengart under a specific agreement that did not allow for the transfer of ownership until the stoves were sold to a bona fide buyer. They argued that the stoves remained their property and that Eisengart's absconding should not affect their rights to reclaim the goods.	The defendant, W. L. Eisengart, contended that the arrangement constituted a sale on credit rather than a consignment. He argued that the delivery of goods under the specified terms was meant to cover a sale and preserve a lien for the price, thus claiming that the plaintiff's ownership could not be established against his creditors.

In April 1862, Frederick Shafer initiated a legal action against Thomas Newlan in Aurora, Illinois. The dispute arose from an order given by Newlan to H. Buchanan, requesting the delivery of liquors to Shafer as part of a horse trade. Shafer subsequently presented this order to Buchanan but claimed that the liquors he received were adulterated and thus valueless. Despite his dissatisfaction, Shafer returned the liquors and later managed to retrieve the order from Buchanan. Following this, he filed a lawsuit against Newlan based on the order and additional common counts, alleging goods sold, money lent, and other expenses. The lower court ruled in favor of Shafer, granting him eighty dollars, which prompted Newlan to appeal the decision.	Shafer's principal argument centered on the order provided by Newlan to Buchanan for the payment of liquors. He claimed that Newlan had facilitated the transaction and owed him for the unsatisfactory liquors he received, which he argued were worthless due to adulteration. He sought a remedy through the courts, including recovery of the sum stated in the order and any ancillary relief allowed under the circumstances.	Newlan contended that the allegations laid out by Shafer in his declaration did not align with the evidence presented. He argued that when Shafer presented the order to Buchanan, it was fulfilled in full with liquors that Shafer himself selected and accepted, thereby nullifying Shafer's claims. Newlan requested the court to refute Shafer's claims and suggested that the evidence constituted a different case altogether, warranting dismissal of the action as presented.

Emanuel B. Deardorff, a nineteen-year-old brakeman employed by the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company, sustained a personal injury while coupling freight cars on January 16, 1880. The incident occurred at a sidetrack near Decatur, Illinois, on a foggy night. Deardorff was assigned to replace a sick brakeman and was tasked with making couplings for a train carrying coal cars loaded with extended iron rails. While attempting to make the coupling, Deardorff failed to notice the projecting iron rails, which hit him in the head. The lawsuit was initiated by Deardorff, through a next friend, and also included a claim from his father. The plaintiff alleged negligence on the part of the railway company for improperly loading the cars.	The plaintiffs claimed that the railway company was negligent in allowing the iron rails to project over the ends of the freight cars, which created a hazardous condition for the brakemen. They argued that this negligence led to Emanuel Deardorff's injury when he attempted to couple the cars. They sought compensation for the injuries sustained due to this alleged negligence.	The railway company contended that Deardorff's injury resulted from his own negligence and that he was a fellow servant of those who loaded the cars, absolving the company of liability. They asserted that the loading practice was standard and that Deardorff, being an experienced brakeman, was aware of the risks involved in making couplings under such conditions. The defendant requested a dismissal of the case based on these arguments, including their claim that no negligence existed.

In April 1864, the case of Holbrook v. Nichol is addressed in the Illinois Supreme Court arising from an ejectment action filed by Holbrook against defendants Nichol and Prettyman in the Circuit Court of Woodford County. During the trial, the defendants attempted to present a certified copy of a power of attorney as evidence. The plaintiff, Holbrook, contended that the submitted copy contained erasures, interlineations, and interpolations that were not present in the original document. He objected to the admission of this copy, but the lower court overruled his objection, leading to a judgment that was unfavorable to Holbrook. Subsequently, Holbrook appealed this decision, asserting that the Circuit Court erred in ignoring his objections and filed a motion with the Illinois Supreme Court for a ruling requiring the defendant Prettyman to produce the original power of attorney for the court’s inspection, citing its importance for the appeal process. Holbrook filed an affidavit explaining that the original document held significant evidence that was not reflected in the copy presented at trial, such as differences in handwriting, ink color, and other details.	The plaintiff, Holbrook, claims that the Circuit Court made a significant error by allowing the admission of a certified copy of the power of attorney which had erasures and interpolations not present in the original. He argues that these differences are crucial to the case and insists on having the original document examined by the court. Holbrook seeks a rule to compel defendant Prettyman to produce the original paper used during the trial for the Supreme Court to scrutinize, believing it essential to ensure a fair assessment of his claims.	The defendants, Nichol and Prettyman, maintain that the certified copy of the power of attorney presented during the trial was an acceptable form of evidence. They assert that Holbrook's objections are unfounded, as the copy is accurate despite claimed discrepancies. Prettyman's retention of the original document complicates the situation but does not diminish the validity of the copy used. The defendants oppose Holbrook’s motion to compel the production of the original, relying on the lower court's decision that previously admitted the evidence.

Hiram B. Scutt and Daniel Robertson were involved in a legal dispute relating to a license allowing the manufacture and sale of barbed fence wire. The case dates back to the time of the license agreement, which was initiated on December 18, 1878, when Scutt, after obtaining patents for barbed wire, entered a partnership with Robertson and another individual under the firm name H. B. Scutt & Co. They manufactured and sold barbed wire, generating royalties for their licensors, the Washburn & Moen Manufacturing Company. This partnership operated under various amendments to the agreement, including extensions of licensing terms, until its dissolution in 1882. Following the dissolution, disputes arose over the ownership and value of the license rights, particularly regarding an unutilized portion of the license for 1,000 tons per annum that Scutt allegedly applied to his own use. The case eventually reached the Illinois Supreme Court on appeal from an earlier decision rendered by the Appellate Court, which upheld certain conclusions about the nature of the license as a partnership asset.	The plaintiff, Daniel Robertson, argued that the license for manufacturing and selling barbed fence wire, although issued to Scutt, was essentially a partnership asset belonging to H. B. Scutt & Co. He claimed that any proceeds from the sale of the license or the products manufactured under it should be treated as partnership assets, and demanded Scutt account for the 1,000 tons of wire that he had retained for personal use, treating it as a valuable property right of the firm.	Hiram B. Scutt contended that the license was strictly a personal privilege granted to him and his associates, emphasizing that it was non-transferable and intended solely for their personal use. He argued that the refusal of his former partners to execute required agreements barred them from claiming any interest in the license or its proceeds after the dissolution of the partnership. Therefore, he requested the court to reject the claims made by Robertson.

In June 1876, the case of Robert T. Brock et al. Admrs. v. Allen M. Slaten was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court, regarding a claim against the estate of Isaac M. Piggott, who had passed away on February 11, 1874, at the age of 81. The claim was initiated by Allen M. Slaten, represented by administrators Robert T. and Mary Jane Brock. Slaten alleged that Piggott owed him $1,200 as part of a contract dated back to 1873, which stated that in return for moving his family to East St. Louis, he would be compensated. The claim was contested by the administrators during probate court proceedings. Initially, a judgment favored Slaten for $1,125, which included a later request for interest that brought the total to $1,320. The case moved to a jury trial, leading to a verdict for the plaintiff (Slaten), but the administrators sought to appeal the decision, arguing inconsistencies in the evidence regarding the alleged contract.	Allen M. Slaten claimed that he was owed $1,200 by the estate of his grandfather, Isaac M. Piggott, based on a contract that required him to move his family to East St. Louis. He argued that inducements were offered to facilitate this move, including a promise of monthly payments and land for a soap factory. Slaten sought to recover this amount, along with interest, from Piggott's estate.	The administrators of Isaac Piggott’s estate contended that the plaintiff had failed to substantiate his claims and that the testimonies of witnesses did not align with Slaten’s allegations. They argued that the alleged contract lacked clarity and specificity, with no witnesses corroborating the exact terms Slaten claimed. Furthermore, they highlighted the need for careful scrutiny of claims made against deceased individuals, especially those involving significant sums.

Patrick J. Sexton filed a legal action against the City of Chicago in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, regarding a dispute that arose in 1878 during the construction of a new city hall. Sexton, a contractor, was contracted to perform iron work for the city and based his bid on a set of plans provided by the city. He was awarded the contract, but issues arose when the city later declared the contract forfeited, claiming that Sexton failed to comply with requirements regarding specific materials and construction details, especially concerning the roof and sky-lights. Sexton contended that the city was responsible for discrepancies in the plans and that the contract should be construed according to the plans he used to bid. Disagreements ensued over the nature and specifications of the work, leading to subsequent appeals after the initial judgment favored the city.	Sexton's main arguments were centered on the assertion that the discrepancies in the construction plans provided by the city were due to the city's negligence. He claimed that he should not be penalized for refusing to construct elements, such as sky-lights, that were not adequately detailed in the plans he had bid upon. His legal requests included recovering the value of the work and materials he provided under the principles of quantum meruit, arguing that he fulfilled his contractual obligations based on the plans he had relied on when submitting his bid.	The City of Chicago defended its position by arguing that Sexton's refusal to construct the specified "T" iron rafters and sky-lights constituted a breach of contract, justifying the forfeiture of the agreement. The city maintained that the original plans should hold precedence over any copies given to Sexton and asserted that discrepancies, if any, were Sexton's responsibility to verify, as he had the opportunity to consult the original documents.

In August 1874, a young lieutenant in the United States Navy, Edwin S. Houston, arrived in Chicago en route to New York. He possessed a diamond ring of approximately three and a half carats. While in the Bryan Block, he encountered William B. Hayes, who expressed interest in Houston's ring. After negotiations, Houston agreed to sell the ring to Hayes for $250 and a city lot he claimed was worth $1,000. However, the lot, located fourteen miles from the courthouse and measuring only five by ten feet, was of no substantial value. After discovering this, Houston attempted to confront Hayes in December 1874 about returning the diamond and found his efforts fruitless. Consequently, Houston filed a lawsuit for the return of his ring, claiming fraud against Hayes. The case was heard in the Cook circuit court and later appealed by Hayes, who contended the verdict was against the evidence presented.	Edwin S. Houston's claims centered on the assertion that he was a victim of fraud perpetrated by William B. Hayes. Houston argued that Hayes misrepresented the value of the city lot and did not disclose its actual worthless nature. He sought a legal judgment to recover his diamond ring, emphasizing that he had made his purchase under false pretenses and had relied on Hayes's misrepresentations.	William B. Hayes defended himself by claiming that the jury's verdict was against the weight of the evidence, suggesting that the conflict in testimonies warranted a different outcome. He argued that there was insufficient basis for the jury's findings, particularly concerning Houston's attempt to negotiate a return of the ring. Hayes maintained that the evidence presented did not support a claim of fraud or misrepresentation and requested a new trial based on these grounds.

Charles Freeman v. The People of the State of Illinois is a legal case from June 1870, adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Monroe County, where it was presided over by Judge Silas L. Bryan. The prosecution involved a charge of bastardy against Charles Freeman, who was alleged to be the father of an illegitimate child. The trial included a jury verdict of guilty against Freeman. Subsequently, Freeman's legal counsel brought the case to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking to reverse the Circuit Court's judgment. The central issue in dispute was the competency of Freeman, as the putative father, to testify in his defense. During the trial, the lower court had denied his request to testify about his paternity and to deny having sexual relations with the child's mother, which Freeman contended was a critical error that warranted an appeal.	In this case, the plaintiff, representing the state, successfully secured a guilty verdict against Charles Freeman for bastardy. The primary argument made by the plaintiff was that Freeman's refusal to accept responsibility as the father of the illegitimate child warranted criminal prosecution under the law.	Charles Freeman's defense revolved around his assertion that he should have been permitted to testify in his own defense. He argued that the trial court erred in disallowing his testimony, which included claims that he was not the father of the child and that he had never engaged in sexual intercourse with the child's mother. Freeman sought to challenge the guilty verdict based on the court's decision to reject his testimony.

In September 1873, in Aurora, Kane County, Illinois, Mary Ann Tripp initiated a legal action against Daniel Freese, claiming damages for the sale of intoxicating liquor to her habitual drunkard husband, William Tripp. This case was brought forth under an Illinois statute enacted on January 13, 1872, which prohibited the sale of intoxicating liquors to minors and intoxicated persons. The statute allowed individuals harmed by the intoxication of another to file suit. Mary Ann sought $100 in damages, asserting that Freese’s sales contributed to her husband’s condition, which impacted her financial support and personal well-being. Initially, a justice of the peace ruled in her favor, granting her $100, prompting Freese to appeal to the Court of Common Pleas. The jury found Freese guilty, again assessing damages at $100. However, the trial judge refused an original verdict emphasizing exemplary damages and instructed the jury to reframe their verdict without specification. After re-evaluation, the jury returned a similar amount for the plaintiff. Freese contested the trial proceedings, arguing that the jury had been misled regarding the definitions of actual and exemplary damages, thereby prompting the appeal that resulted in the cancellation of the initial judgment.	Mary Ann Tripp claimed that her husband, William Tripp, suffered from habitual intoxication, which was exacerbated by Daniel Freese selling him alcohol. She argued that this resulted in injury to herself in terms of loss of support and personal distress, asserting rights under the Illinois statute that allowed individuals harmed by another's intoxication to sue for damages. She sought $100 in damages for this injury.	Daniel Freese defended against the claims by arguing that the jury instructions were erroneous and misleading, particularly regarding the assessment of damages. He contended that Mary Ann herself had a poor reputation and that the case may have been part of a plan to entrap him. Freese asserted that he should not be liable for exemplary damages without demonstrable actual damages sustained by Mary Ann, claiming that the statute requires proof of actual harm for any award of damages and argued that matters mitigating his responsibility, such as his alleged prohibition against selling liquor to William, were not sufficiently considered.

In the case of George W. Powell v. Joseph T. McCord, which took place in Chicago, Illinois, a legal dispute arose regarding four promissory notes totaling $3,500 executed by Powell in favor of McCord. The events were rooted in 1881 when McCord, operating as McCord & Co., was engaged in grain trading on the Chicago Board of Trade. Fred Gould, a middleman, received orders from Powell to buy and sell grain and transmitted these orders to McCord. There was a contentious relationship regarding whether McCord was acting as the principal or agent in these transactions. Powell alleged that their agreement was for trading without actual delivery of goods, focusing solely on the profits or losses on paper, which he claimed rendered the consideration for the notes illegal. Conversely, McCord contended that he had indeed purchased grain on Powell's behalf and was entitled to payment for incurred liabilities. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court after a jury sided with McCord in the Circuit Court. The jury found in favor of McCord, leading to Powell's appeal to the Appellate Court and further to the Illinois Supreme Court for review.	Joseph T. McCord claimed that the promissory notes executed by George W. Powell were valid and sought recovery of the amounts due on those notes. McCord argued that he had acted in good faith as a commission merchant, making actual purchases of grain on behalf of Powell, thus entitling him to reimbursement for the expenses incurred during the transactions. He maintained that the business dealings were legitimate and not gambling contracts, asserting that the notes represented a lawful obligation for his actions.	George W. Powell defended against McCord's claims by asserting that the consideration for the notes was entirely illegal. He argued that the transactions were merely speculative and amounted to gambling, as they did not involve actual delivery of grain. Powell contended that McCord had not provided evidence of cash expenditures related to the transactions and that any obligations were invalid due to the nature of the dealings. He also challenged the admission of certain evidence regarding his employment of convict labor, arguing that it was irrelevant and prejudicial.

Jeremiah Honnihan, the appellant, initiated this legal action against John Friedman, the appellee, in the Circuit Court of Peoria County, Illinois. The case stemmed from a sheriff's sale of Honnihan's farmland that occurred on March 18, 1881, following a foreclosure judgment entered on December 24, 1880, for the amount of $2,793.30. The land was sold for $2,937.15. Honnihan filed an equity bill on June 24, 1882, seeking to redeem the land. However, he did so after the statutory period of fifteen months for redemption had expired. Honnihan claimed that Friedman had made fraudulent misrepresentations regarding an extension of the redemption period, convincing him to allow the time to expire. Specifically, Friedman allegedly promised that Honnihan could redeem the property for an extended period beyond the statutory limit and would not take advantage of him regarding the expiration. Honnihan stated that he had relied on these representations, which ultimately led him to miss the opportunity to redeem the property. The lower court dismissed Honnihan's bill, prompting him to appeal the decision.	Honnihan argued that he was misled by Friedman’s fraudulent representations that he would have additional time to redeem after the legal deadline. He claimed that these misleading promises were made intentionally to deprive him of his property for an inadequate price. He requested the court to allow him to redeem the property despite missing the statutory deadline due to reliance on Friedman's promises.	Friedman contended that there was no enforceable agreement to extend the redemption period and claimed that Honnihan failed to allege a mutual agreement or consideration which would validate the supposed extension. He argued that Honnihan did not have a specific obligation to redeem the property within any defined timeframe and sought to uphold the lower court's dismissal of Honnihan's claims.

Gena Lancaster v. Ida M. Lancaster is a legal case that took place in 1888 in Illinois. The dispute arose from a divorce decree that ordered Ida M. Lancaster (the defendant) to pay Gena Lancaster (the plaintiff) monthly installments for the support of their infant child. The court involved was the Illinois Appellate Court. The defendant failed to pay the agreed monthly amount of $30, accumulating a total of $990 over a period of thirty-three months. Ida contended that Gena refused him access to their child, violating the terms of the divorce decree, which he claimed entitled him to withhold the support payments. The court determined that non-assumpsit was not a valid plea in the action of debt, and the conditions of the decree did not allow for the defendant to refuse payments based on his visitation rights. The court emphasized the legality of the plaintiff's right to recover the owed amounts for the child’s benefit.	Gena Lancaster claimed that she was entitled to recover $990 in unpaid child support installments as ordered by the divorce decree. She argued that the defendant's refusal to pay was unfounded since the decree did not permit him to withhold payment over visitation disputes. Her legal request was for the court to enforce the payment obligations set forth in the divorce decree.	Ida M. Lancaster's defense rested on the argument that Gena's refusal to allow him to see their child violated the terms of the divorce decree, thus surrendering his obligation to make support payments. He contended that due to this refusal, he should not be required to fulfill the financial decree. Additionally, he used the plea of non-assumpsit, which the court found inappropriate in this context.

In 1856, John M. Waugh owned around 480 acres at Richland Grove, Mercer County, Illinois, and was looking to build a steam flouring mill. He partnered with Benjamin T. Sisson, who was to have a half interest in the mill. In February 1858, Waugh sold half of the land to his brother-in-law, Henry B. Ellis, and together they mortgaged the mill to Sisson for $9,280. Waugh and Sisson acquired machinery from T.B. Ellis & Bros., creating debts that complicated the situation. In May 1858, T.B. Ellis purchased Waugh's concern, taking on debts including the Sisson mortgage. On September 30, 1858, T.B. Ellis made a contract to sell all the property to Waugh, Sisson, and John B. Rathbun, which was not fully consummated due to disagreements. In March 1861, T.B. Ellis filed a bill in chancery against Waugh, Sisson, and Rathbun, seeking to set aside existing mortgages and enforce the sale contract. In 1862, Sisson assigned his mortgage to Sumner & Co., leading to further litigation until several cases were consolidated in Peoria County. Ultimately, the complexities of debts and contracts resulted in a protracted legal dispute involving multiple parties.	T.B. Ellis claimed he was entitled to set aside the mortgages imposed on the property and sought the assurance of security for his paid-in interest from the property sale to Sisson and Rathbun. He argued that he had fulfilled his obligations under the agreement and had not rescinded the contract through his earlier suit, thereby necessitating the enforcement of his rights concerning the equity in the properties involved.	The defendants, particularly Sisson and Sumner & Co., argued that T.B. Ellis had failed to comply with the terms of the contract regarding the settlement of debts and the provision of authenticated invoices. They claimed that Ellis's previous suit functioned as a rescission of the contract, and they were entitled to the rights established by the mortgage held against Ellis.

The case titled "The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Julius J. Elmore" took place in Morgan County, Illinois, with the final judgment delivered on February 14, 1890. Julius J. Elmore, a local farmer, claimed damages against the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company after two of his horses were killed by a train on the night of August 1, 1888. The horses strayed onto the railroad tracks through a gate that the railroad allegedly failed to properly maintain. Elmore asserted that the company neglected to construct sufficient barriers at farm crossings to prevent animals from accessing the track. Additionally, on February 7, 1889, a fire originating from the railroad right-of-way spread to Elmore’s pasture, causing further damage. The suit, filed during the May term of 1889, consisted of two counts: one for the loss of the horses and another for the destruction of the grass due to the fire. A jury found in favor of Elmore, awarding him $396 in damages. The appeal arose after the railroad company contested the jury's verdict and various aspects of the trial, including the admissibility of testimony and jury instructions regarding the gate's condition.	Julius J. Elmore claimed that the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company failed to fulfill its duty to construct and maintain gates or barriers at farm crossings, which allowed his horses to access the tracks and be killed by a train. He argued that the railroad was liable for the deaths due to negligence regarding the gate's maintenance. Furthermore, he asserted that the company neglected to keep its right-of-way free from dead grass, which resulted in a fire that caused damage to his pasture. Elmore sought damages for both incidents in his legal claims.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company contended that the evidence did not support the claim of a defective gate and argued that any issues with the gate’s fastening did not exist long enough to establish their liability. They claimed that the conditions of the gate at the time of the incident were not as Elmore described. Additionally, the railroad argued that certain objections raised during the trial regarding testimonies and jury instructions were not valid as they had not been properly highlighted in a motion for a new trial. The railroad's main request was to reverse the judgment rendered against them.

Nathaniel Buckmaster initiated a legal action in the Circuit Court of Illinois on behalf of George W. Denham against Manning Beames and others, who are the defendants in this case. The events leading to the lawsuit transpired in 1845, with the key parties being Buckmaster as the nominal plaintiff and Denham as the plaintiff in interest. After the Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendant, Buckmaster appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court. In the course of the appeal, the defendants submitted an affidavit claiming that Denham was insolvent. They requested that Denham be required to provide security for costs, arguing that his financial situation could potentially affect the ability to recover costs in the case. The court's deliberation centered around whether further security was necessary given that Buckmaster was a resident of the state and thus liable for any costs associated with the case.	The plaintiff, Nathaniel Buckmaster, argued against the Circuit Court's ruling that favored the defendants. He sought to reverse the judgment and maintain the right to pursue the case on behalf of Denham, asserting that Denham’s insolvency should not undermine Buckmaster's ability to proceed as a legitimate claimant in the appeal.	The defendants, led by Manning Beames, contended that Denham's insolvency warranted a requirement for additional security for costs associated with the litigation. They highlighted the risk that Denham's financial situation posed to their ability to recover costs if they prevailed in the case, thereby justifying their request for protection against potential non-payment.

The case "John S. Medley et al. v. William Elliott et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1872. It originated from Fulton County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs, John S. Medley and others, were involved in a legal dispute with the defendants, William Elliott and others, concerning a mortgage. The principal issue was whether the grantees of a mortgagor could protect their title against the foreclosure of a mortgage by claiming possession and paying taxes for a certain period. The court needed to determine the nature of the relationship between mortgagors, mortgagees, and grantees, and how that relationship affected rights to the property and the applicability of the statute of limitations to foreclosures.	The plaintiffs argued that their possession of the mortgaged property, along with their payment of taxes, should protect their title against foreclosure. They claimed that such possession constituted an independent right, and that the limitations law of 1839 should prevent the defendants (the mortgagees) from foreclosing the mortgage due to the passage of time and their actions.	The defendants contended that the grantees (plaintiffs) of the mortgagor only inherited the rights of the mortgagor, which remained subject to the existing mortgage. They asserted that possession could not be deemed adverse or hostile because it was subordinate to the mortgagee's rights, and that the statute of limitations could not bar a foreclosure as long as the debt remained enforceable. The defendants requested that the court confirm their rights to foreclose on the mortgage.

On February 11, 1865, Mary E. Rixford married William H. Rixford, who had enlisted in the United States Army shortly before their marriage, receiving a bounty of $400. Shortly thereafter, on February 21, Mary loaned $365 of this money to William, formalizing the transaction through a promissory note. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court after William contested ownership of the note, arguing that it was his separate property. The plaintiff, Mary, had declared the note in an assumpsit action, claiming the balance due on the note. Key issues arose around whether Mary Rixford, as a married woman, could independently control the note and claim the funds. The court subsequently tried the case before a jury, which ruled in favor of Mary, awarding her $320.	The plaintiff, Mary E. Rixford, contended that the note was a valid obligation and that the money loaned to William was her separate property, derived from her husband’s gift. She sought a legal judgment for the remaining balance of the note, claiming an entitlement to recover funds due based on the agreement formalized in the promissory note.	The defendant, William H. Rixford, argued that the note was not valid as a legal obligation that he was responsible for, claiming it was Mary’s separate property. He presented multiple special pleas asserting that the loan was not made from joint funds and that Mary was conducting her own business separately, thus maintaining the claim that the note represented her exclusive ownership and not a joint obligation.

John H. Dunn filed a lawsuit against John D. Moore, William M. Kemp, and James W. Bunch in December 1854 after a disagreement regarding a promissory note dated July 21, 1852, which promised to pay Dunn $60 for teaching a school for three months starting July 26, 1852. Dunn claimed he commenced teaching the school as agreed; however, the defense provided evidence that the school only operated for one month. This case was initially heard in the justice court before being appealed to the Scott Circuit Court. Throughout the trial, both parties presented their understanding of the contract's terms, specifically regarding Dunn's entitlement to payment based on the duration he taught the school.	Dunn contended that he had fulfilled his obligation to teach for the full three months as outlined in the contract. He sought the remaining payment of $40 based on the original $60 agreement. Dunn's argument rested on the premise that the defendants owed him this sum upon the completion of the teaching term.	The defendants argued that Dunn had only taught for one month of the promised three-month period. Consequently, they maintained that Dunn was entitled to only a third of the total amount, equating to $20. They highlighted that since Dunn had already received $20, he had no valid claim for further payment, asserting that the obligation to pay was contingent upon completing the agreed teaching term.

In 1860, William Wheeler and Rosalie A. Bonner brought a case against the City of Chicago in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from an action of assumpsit in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas. The case arose after the city appropriated land for the extension of South LaSalle Street from Madison Street to Jackson Street. Wheeler was the owner of specific sub-lots in the area, and he argued that the city owed him $15,545 in damages, as assessed by commissioners appointed to determine benefits and damages caused by the street opening. The process began with the city council ordering a survey on October 15, 1855, followed by a notice given ten days later about the intention to take the land. The commissioners, after being appointed and sworn, assessed the property and returned their assessment to the council, which was confirmed on June 10, 1856. However, Wheeler claimed the city failed to pay him the awarded amount in a timely manner, leading to the case being brought to court after the city's demurrer was sustained regarding the plaintiff’s initial claims.	The plaintiffs argue that the City of Chicago, after following all legal protocols for the street opening and subsequent assessment, has failed to pay the awarded damages of $15,545. They assert that the city had a duty to promptly pay this amount after the assessment was confirmed but neglected to do so for an unreasonable period, lasting two years and eight months. This failure constitutes a breach of the city's obligation to the property owner, warranting the action of assumpsit based on the implied promise to pay the assessed damages.	The City of Chicago defended itself by filing a general demurrer against the plaintiff's claims, which was sustained by the lower court. The city argued that the assessment and the subsequent actions did not comply with the necessary legal framework and that the procedural timelines established were not adhered to, leading to potential voiding of the assessment. Thus, they contended that the plaintiffs did not establish a valid claim for the damages awarded, which affected their obligations regarding payment.

The case of *The City of Chicago v. Louisa Schmidt, Admx.* took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 16, 1883. The plaintiff, Louisa Schmidt, was the administratrix of her late husband, Frederick Schmidt, who died due to an incident involving a defective sidewalk. The accident occurred on May 5, 1873, when Frederick Schmidt was walking near the track of the Northwestern Railroad. After stepping into a hole in the sidewalk, he was thrown onto the railway track and fatally struck by a train. Following the initial trial in March 1875, which resulted in a verdict for the defendants (the City and the railroad), the plaintiff appealed and the case was subsequently retried multiple times. Over the years, various verdicts were reached, including one for $5000 against the city which was later set aside, and a mistrial. Eventually, by January 1882, after a total of five trials with differing outcomes, a jury found in favor of Louisa Schmidt, awarding her $3500 for damages. The city appealed the decision, prompting this case's review.	Louisa Schmidt, as the plaintiff, argued that the city was negligent for failing to repair a known defect in the sidewalk, leading to her husband's death. She claimed that he exercised due care while walking on the sidewalk when he fell into a hole, resulting in his being struck by the train. As a legal request, she sought damages for wrongful death, asserting the city's liability under the relevant statutes for causing his death due to negligence.	The City of Chicago contended that the plaintiff's claims were unfounded and that Frederick Schmidt's own actions contributed to the accident. The defense proposed that he may have stepped into the pathway of the train due to his hurried manner or failure to exercise sufficient caution near the railroad crossing, thereby arguing comparative negligence. They sought to have the judgment against them reversed and argued that the evidence supported the theory that Schmidt had assumed the risk of injury.

The case "Leander Choate v. Emily Blackford et al." took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the final judgment rendered on June 13, 1888. The suit was initiated through an attachment proceeding by Emily Blackford, who sought to recover rent owed by Charles H. Choate. The defendant, Leander Choate, along with others, was summoned as garnishees. The plaintiff's primary allegation was that the garnishee, Leander, had received property and financial advantages from Charles H. Choate that were not disclosed in response to the interrogatories presented. During the legal process, Leander contested these claims by asserting the legitimacy of transactions involving chattel mortgages and notes that he had received from Charles. The court's evaluation of the evidence revealed gaps in the plaintiff's claims about the garnishee's supposed indebtedness to the defendant.	Emily Blackford, representing the plaintiff, claimed that Charles H. Choate owed rent, and she sought to attach Leander Choate's assets as a means of recovering that debt. The plaintiff contended that Leander had not fully disclosed relevant property and financial transactions in his response to the interrogatories, which were crucial to establish any indebtedness owed to the defendant.	Leander Choate, as the garnishee, defended himself by asserting that he was not indebted to Charles H. Choate. He detailed transactions involving substantial loans and property transfers which he had engaged in with Charles. Leander argued that the plaintiff bore the burden of disproving his sworn statements regarding these transactions, and he certified that his answers to the interrogatories were accurate and complete.

The case "The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company v. Henry Lammert" took place in Illinois and culminated on April 13, 1883. The case involved a child, Henry Lammert, who was injured while attempting to board a moving train operated by the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company. The injury occurred when the train started moving as he was attempting to step onto it. Allegedly, Lammert was allowed to board the train by the railroad workers, which the railroad company denied. At the time of the incident, the child was only ten years old and deaf and dumb, raising questions about his ability to exercise due care. The court had to consider whether the railroad company was negligent and if the child had acted reasonably given his circumstances. Testimony was presented by several witnesses, including the child's mother, who aimed to establish the circumstances surrounding the injury and the conduct of the train's crew.	The plaintiff, Henry Lammert, through his next friend (likely a guardian or advocate), claimed that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was negligent in allowing the train to start moving while the child was attempting to board. He sought damages for personal injuries caused by the negligence of the railroad employees and argued that his status as a minor and his circumstances as a deaf and dumb child should be taken into account when assessing his ability to exercise care.	The defendant, Chicago and Alton Railroad Company, contended that there was no negligence on their part since the child was not allowed to board the train and that he acted on his own accord. They argued that the child assumed the risk by trying to board a moving train and that the engineers operating the train had no knowledge of his presence. Therefore, the railroad company claimed they should not be held liable for the child's injuries.

The case of "The Board of Supervisors of Jackson County v. Samuel T. Brush et al." took place in January 1875 in Jackson County, Illinois. The main individuals involved included the Board of Supervisors of Jackson County, plaintiffs seeking an injunction, and Samuel T. Brush, administrator of John M. Hanson's estate, along with other defendants including Hugh Crawford, John Ford, and the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company. The dispute arose over two series of undated bonds, each valued at $1,000, which were to be delivered to the railroad company under conditions set by elections held in June 1868 and July 1869. The plaintiffs argued that the bonds were improperly in the hands of trustees and demanded their return to county authorities, asserting that the bonds should not be issued until specific conditions had been satisfied. The circuit court initially issued a temporary injunction but later dismissed the case regarding the first series of bonds while granting a perpetual injunction for the second series. Both parties appealed, leading to this review by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The Board of Supervisors claimed that the two series of bonds for the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company were issued under conditions that had not been met. They sought to have the bonds returned to the county's corporate authorities and requested that the underlying orders authorizing the subscriptions be declared null and void. The plaintiffs argued that the authority to determine when these bonds could be issued rested solely with the county's official officers and could not be delegated to individual trustees.	The defendants contended that the necessary conditions for the issuance of the bonds had indeed been fulfilled and that the subscriptions had been legally authorized by prior votes. They maintained that the bonds were properly in the possession of the trustees and argued for the validity of the bond subscriptions, stating that the required procedures had been followed during the elections. The defendants sought to have the court uphold those subscriptions and allow the bonds to be delivered to the railroad company.

The case of James A. Cunningham v. John Stein was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 26, 1884, concerning a dispute in Danville, Illinois. James A. Cunningham, the plaintiff, owned a brewery, while John Stein, the defendant, owned a nearby starch factory. The conflict arose when the starch factory discharged slops into a stream that flowed past both businesses, which Cunningham claimed polluted the water and emitted unhealthy odors affecting his brewery. The plaintiff alleged that this pollution rendered the water unsuitable for making ice and contaminated the air, thereby adversely impacting the sale of his beer and causing discomfort. The case was initially ruled in favor of Cunningham by the Vermilion County Circuit Court, prompting Stein to appeal. The Appellate Court upheld the original decision, which further escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court. The main legal questions revolved around evidentiary rulings pertaining to the impact of odors on beer sales and whether the jury received appropriate instructions regarding burdens of proof and damage assessment.	Cunningham's claims focused on the damages incurred from the pollution caused by Stein's starch factory. He argued that the discharged slops polluted the nearby stream, negatively affecting the water quality required for making ice and contaminating the air with unpleasant odors. These factors, he contended, diminished the quality and sales of the beer produced in his brewery, leading to economic losses and rendering his living conditions uncomfortable.	Stein's key arguments revolved around challenging the assertions made by Cunningham regarding the causation between the factory's discharge and the alleged damages. Stein contended that the evidence presented was not conclusive enough to show that the pollution directly impacted Cunningham's beer sales and living conditions. He also raised objections about the jury's instructions related to the standard of proof required for Cunningham to establish his claims and questioned the fairness of the damages assessed.

In December 1852, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with a case involving the trustees of the State Bank of Illinois, plaintiffs in error, against Benjamin N. Gibson, defendant in error, regarding two lots located in Petersburg, Illinois. The case arose from an action of ejectment to recover possession of the lots. The plaintiffs had acquired the legal title to the lots on February 20, 1843. However, at the time the suit commenced, Gibson was in possession of the properties. During the trial, the plaintiffs objected to the defendant's presentation of evidence regarding a previous judgment dating back to June 1843, which involved taxes due for the year 1842 that led to the sale of the lots. The jury ultimately returned a verdict in favor of the defendant, leading to a judgment in his favor from the court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the lots were exempt from taxation as per their charter, arguing that since the State Bank of Illinois acquired the properties after the tax was levied, they should not be liable. They contended that the tax lien was not valid against their title and that the tax sale process was flawed, thus challenging the legality of the evidence presented by the defendant.	The defendant argued that he had valid title to the lots based on a sheriff's deed obtained from a tax sale, asserting that the plaintiffs were responsible for discharging the tax lien on the properties inherited from the previous owner. He maintained that any shortcomings in the tax collection process were not sufficient to invalidate the sale, and he claimed that the plaintiffs bore the burden to prove the invalidity of the tax title, rather than himself needing to validate it.

On April 9, 1855, Royal A. B. Mills initiated a legal action against Henry Graves in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, aiming to reclaim ownership of a piece of land located in Chicago. The case was heard without a jury before Judge E. S. Williams. During the trial, the defendant, Graves, sought to present evidence that Mills had transferred his interest in the property to a third party, Henry L. Rucker, on April 2, 1861—after the lawsuit had commenced. Mills' legal team objected to this evidence, but the court allowed its admission and subsequently ruled in favor of Graves, leading Mills to appeal the decision.	Mills contended that the conveyance of his title to Rucker while the lawsuit was pending should not undermine his claim to the property. He argued that under Illinois law, a plaintiff's right to recover in an ejectment action is determined by their title at the beginning of the lawsuit, regardless of any subsequent conveyance. Mills sought to overturn the lower court's judgment and restore his right to recover the land.	Graves argued that the transfer of the property title from Mills to Rucker invalidated Mills' claim to recover possession of the land in question. He maintained that the court should admit the evidence of the conveyance and that Mills' action for ejectment should fail based on the statutory provisions that govern such titles.

In the case of Charles Kennedy et al. v. Peter S. Stout, which was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court on March 20, 1888, the plaintiff, Peter S. Stout, accused Charles Kennedy and other defendants of engaging in unlawful gambling contracts. The events transpired at the Chicago Board of Trade, where the parties were involved in dealings regarding options on grain. Stout claimed he paid $914 as margins on these options, which he argued were effectively gambling contracts. The defendants, who were commission merchants operating on the Board of Trade, contended that the transactions were legitimate contracts for actual delivery of commodities. The case was tried without a jury, and the judge had to assess conflicting testimonies regarding the nature of the contracts and whether they were, in fact, gambling contracts as claimed by Stout. Ultimately, the evidence showed a pattern in the communications between the parties that suggested a mutual understanding to treat these contracts without intent for actual delivery, aligning with Stout's assertions. The court evaluated the situation and decided based on the evidence presented.	Peter S. Stout, the plaintiff, claimed that the money he paid to the defendants was for margins on illegal gambling contracts, which he sought to recover under Section 132 of the Criminal Code. His main arguments included the assertion that there was an express agreement to only deal in options and that the transactions were never intended for actual delivery, thus qualifying as gambling contracts. Stout requested the court to grant him recovery of the $914 he had paid.	The defendants, led by Charles Kennedy, argued that the transactions were valid contracts for actual delivery of commodities, not gambling contracts as claimed by Stout. They contended that Stout was well aware he was engaging in lawful contracts and that the money claimed arose from legitimate trading activities. The defendants raised a statute of limitations defense, claiming the action was filed too late, although they did not successfully assert this during the trial.

In 1867, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, an action of replevin was initiated by Samuel Dietrich against George Rumsey, seeking the recovery of two hogs. The case progressed through the legal system, starting at a justice of the peace and moving to the Circuit Court of Stephenson County. During the trials, both parties presented an equal number of witnesses to assert ownership of the hogs. Dietrich claimed that the hogs belonged to him, while Rumsey contended that they were his or belonged to a third party named Hunter. Witnesses on both sides confidently identified the hogs as belonging to their respective parties, leading to a significant conflict in evidence, which necessitated a jury's decision. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Rumsey, prompting Dietrich to appeal the decision based on the assertion that the verdict had no backing from the evidence presented.	Samuel Dietrich claimed ownership of the two hogs involved in the dispute. He argued that the evidence favoring his ownership was credible and requested a new trial on the grounds that the jury's verdict in favor of George Rumsey was contrary to the evidence provided.	George Rumsey defended his claim by asserting that the hogs belonged to him or to a third party, Hunter. Rumsey argued that the jury had the opportunity to assess the credibility of the witnesses and concluded correctly in favor of his claims. He requested that the court uphold the jury's verdict and affirm the judgment of the lower court.

In 1843, an action of replevin was initiated by John Frink in the Peoria Circuit Court, Illinois, concerning the ownership and possession of certain oak timber and logs, valued at approximately seventy-five dollars. The case was subsequently transferred to Stark County. Frink's agent, Curran Walker, filed an affidavit asserting Frink's rightful ownership of the property, which was allegedly unlawfully detained by John C. Flanagan. After multiple proceedings, Flanagan filed a motion to dismiss the case based on the inadequacy of Walker's affidavit. Frink sought permission to amend the affidavit but was denied by the court. The Stark Circuit Court, presided over by Hon. John D. Catón, ultimately ruled in favor of Flanagan, dismissing Frink's replevin action and ordering the return of the property, leading to Frink's appeal against this decision.	John Frink, through his agent, claimed that he was the legal owner of the disputed property and sought replevin to recover possession from John C. Flanagan, who was unlawfully detaining it. Frink argued that the affidavit submitted was sufficient and requested the court allow him to amend it to continue the proceedings.	John C. Flanagan contended that the affidavit provided by Frink's agent was insufficient to establish ownership, as required by the Replevin Act of 1839. He argued for the dismissal of the case, asserting that there was a lack of a proper basis for jurisdiction due to the deficient affidavit, and opposed Frink's request to amend the document.

On August 7, 1872, a legal dispute originated in the Cook County Criminal Court, Illinois, during a divorce proceeding titled Elizabeth Dinet v. Joseph Dinet. The court issued a consent order requiring Joseph Dinet, the defendant, to pay his wife’s solicitors, Joseph Pfirshing and Francis Adams, a total of $2,845 in attorney fees. This included immediate payments of $825 and $285, followed by a payment of $1,520 to Joseph Pfirshing as the surviving partner of Daniel Driscoll for services rendered from the suit's inception until a jury verdict. Joseph Dinet made a partial payment of $720 towards the $1,520 fee. Joseph Pfirshing then initiated an action against Dinet for the remaining balance of $800. Dinet's defense centered on his claim of full payment, leading to a demurrer to his plea being sustained. The case presented a crucial question of whether the $1,520 represented the total amount due for all services or was in addition to the previously ordered payments. After appeal, the court had to interpret the decree regarding the payment obligations.	The plaintiff, Joseph Pfirshing, claimed that Joseph Dinet owed an additional $800 based on the decree that required Dinet to pay $1,520 for legal services rendered by Pfirshing & Driscoll in the divorce proceedings. Pfirshing argued that the $1,520 should be interpreted as the total fee for all services, which included the $800 previously paid, and sought the court's enforcement of the payment.	The defendant, Joseph Dinet, contended that he had fulfilled his payment obligations by paying a total of $720 against the stipulated $1,520 and argued that the previous payments rendered the total amount due to be lower than claimed. Dinet maintained that the construction of the court's decree should account for prior payments, asserting that the language of the decree should reflect that the $1,520 was not an additional fee but inclusive of payments already made.

In January 1864, the case of Charles O. Nickerson et al. v. Amos C. Babcock was decided in the Illinois Supreme Court. The specifics of the time and location are detailed in the court records, which were part of the Illinois judicial system. Key individuals involved include Charles O. Nickerson and Amos C. Babcock, with Nickerson representing the plaintiffs. The case involves a dispute between the parties; however, the exact nature of the conflict and the events leading to the legal action were not detailed in the information provided. The court ultimately reviewed the case and referenced similar previous decisions in its judgment.	The plaintiffs, Charles O. Nickerson et al., presented arguments establishing their entitlement to a legal remedy against the defendant, Amos C. Babcock. Their claims likely involved grievances stemming from actions taken by Babcock that they argue violated their rights or obligations according to law. The specifics of their legal requests are not detailed, but they sought favorable judgment to resolve the issues raised in the case.	The defendant, Amos C. Babcock, raised defenses challenging the validity of the plaintiffs' claims. His arguments would typically center on disputing the assertions made by Nickerson and potentially highlighting legal principles or precedents that support his position. The detailed content of his defenses is not provided; however, it can be inferred that he sought to dismiss the claims or refute the plaintiffs' allegations.

In February 1858, in the La Salle Circuit Court, Illinois, a legal dispute unfolded between Roswell E. Goodell and Norman W. Woodruff concerning the sale of lumber. Woodruff, the appellee, claimed that Goodell owed him for lumber allegedly purchased for Goodell's farm. Before the sale, Goodell had contracted with Lighthall, the owner of a lumber yard, for lumber delivery. Upon selling the yard to Woodruff, it was agreed that Woodruff would fulfill these contracts with the understanding that Lighthall would benefit financially. Goodell's brother-in-law, Irvin, obtained about twenty thousand feet of fencing lumber from Woodruff's yard without Goodell having paid anything on his prior contract with Lighthall. Goodell denied responsibility for payment to Woodruff, asserting that his contract was exclusively with Lighthall. The jury ultimately ruled that the purchase was indeed made from Woodruff, despite Goodell’s contention. Following a jury trial where a verdict favored Woodruff, Goodell's motions for a new trial were overruled, leading him to appeal the decision.	Norman W. Woodruff claimed that Roswell E. Goodell owed him for lumber sold and delivered, which was utilized on Goodell's farm. Woodruff argued that the sale and contract for lumber were valid and that Irvin had acted as Goodell’s agent in procuring the lumber. Therefore, he requested the court to uphold the jury’s verdict in favor of his claims for the owed amount.	Roswell E. Goodell defended against the claim by asserting that his original contract was with Lighthall, not Woodruff, suggesting that he bore no responsibility to pay Woodruff for the lumber. He contended that he did not authorize Irvin to purchase lumber from Woodruff and maintained that any obligations should fall to Lighthall. Goodell sought to have the jury's findings overturned, claiming they were not supported by the evidence.

On January 17, 1882, in Chicago, Henry B. Lockwood, a merchant, declared bankruptcy and executed two judgment notes—one for $54,579.90 and another for $36,569.76—payable to members of Carter, Hawley & Co. He also assigned all sums due from his book accounts to Carter, Hawley, and Macy. Judgments were quickly entered on the notes, and Lockwood's goods were attached, resulting in a collection of $37,607.91. Later, on January 25, 1882, John W. Doane & Co. initiated an attachment against Lockwood's property over a debt of $1,101.42, naming Carter, Hawley, and Macy as garnishees. In the following month, Lockwood made a general assignment for the benefit of his creditors, appointing William L. Glass as the assignee. On January 13, 1883, during the attachment suit, Glass filed an interpleader to claim the property attached in the hands of the garnishees. The court proceedings revolved around whether the assigned book accounts could be garnished and the priority of claims among the parties involved.	The plaintiff, William L. Glass, claimed the property, credits, and effects seized from Henry B. Lockwood, arguing that the assignments to the garnishees were invalid and that the attached assets rightfully belonged to him as the assignee. He sought a judgment to reclaim these assets from the garnishees, asserting that the garnishees had no legal claim to the funds collected or the accounts assigned to them.	The defendants, John W. Doane & Co. and the garnishees, contended that their attachment had priority over the claims of the assignee. They argued that the transfers made by Lockwood were valid and that they had properly garnished the assets in accordance with the law. They maintained that the assignment of the accounts to them was intended as security for Lockwood's debt, hence giving them superior rights to the funds collected compared to the claims made by the assignee.

Julius Frank and others filed a lawsuit against Elizabeth Taubman in 1889 in Cook County, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute regarding a forcible detainer action, where the plaintiffs claimed an unlawful holding of property by the defendant. The plaintiffs contended that a new lease had not been executed, which the defendant argued was the basis of her possession of the property. To support their claim, the defendants sought to introduce evidence including an appeal bond and various receipts signed by Taubman, aiming to establish the legitimacy of Taubman's signature on the disputed lease. The court examined these pieces of evidence, determining their relevance and admissibility based on previous case law. Ultimately, it focused on whether Taubman’s signature was genuine and the legal implications surrounding tenancy agreements without a notice to quit for tenants holding over.	The plaintiffs, Julius Frank et al., claimed that the defendant, Elizabeth Taubman, wrongfully detained the property in question due to a lack of a new lease agreement. They argued that the defendant was not entitled to possession and sought a judgment to evict her from the property, insisting that the evidence presented by the defendant regarding a new lease and signature was irrelevant.	Elizabeth Taubman, the defendant, contended that she was in legal possession of the property due to having executed a new lease. She sought to validate her claim by presenting an appeal bond and receipts as evidence that would support the authenticity of her signature on the lease. Her main argument was that these documents could demonstrate her rightful tenancy despite the plaintiffs' claims.

In 1865, in Chicago, Illinois, John Mitchell (the plaintiff) sold 5,000 bushels of barley to William Saladin (the defendant) through broker Theodore D. Hall. The sale price was set at $1.33 per bushel, with an additional storage charge of two cents per bushel. Although Saladin took some barley, he did not pay for the total expected amount after the initial exchanges. By March 1866, Mitchell filed a lawsuit against Saladin to recover damages for the barley that was never taken or paid for. During the trial, the court ruled that the sale was valid, and Mitchell, as the owner, had the right to sue for the breach of contract through his broker. Saladin contended that there was ambiguity in the sale terms, and any contract was rescinded without consent from the plaintiff. The court examined the nature of the broker's authority and concluded that the contract for sale remained in effect despite the broker's actions.	The plaintiff, John Mitchell, argued that a valid contract existed for the sale of 5,000 bushels of barley, which Saladin had purchased. Mitchell claimed damages for the barley that Saladin did not accept or pay for, emphasizing that he had the right to sell the barley through his broker, Hall, and asserting that Saladin's failure to fulfill the contract constituted a breach.	William Saladin contended that his agreement was solely with the broker Hall and that he was not bound to the claims of the plaintiff. He argued that any contract was a mere proposal that had not been executed, suggesting that the terms included a promise that was not honored. Additionally, Saladin asserted that the contract could have been rescinded without Mitchell’s consent, claiming that there was no legal obligation to fulfill the payment as he had not taken ownership of the total barley.

The case of Francis Hopkinson v. The People took place in April 1857 in Bureau County, Illinois. The incident leading to the trial occurred in October 1855, involving Francis Hopkinson and John Cummings. On the night before the alleged assault, the two had a confrontation where Cummings physically restrained Hopkinson by choking him. The following day, they met again, and Cummings confronted Hopkinson about the previous altercation, urging him to "stand off." In response, Hopkinson drew a pistol and, after a brief exchange, fired at Cummings but missed. Cummings then chased him. Hopkinson was subsequently indicted for assault with intent to murder. The jury found him guilty, and the trial court denied a motion for a new trial. The case then progressed to the Illinois Supreme Court on appeal, where legal arguments revolved around the justifications for Hopkinson's actions and the adequacy of legal instructions given to the jury.	The plaintiff, Francis Hopkinson, argued that he acted in self-defense during the incident with Cummings. His main claims were centered on the premise that his use of the pistol was a necessary response to an impending threat posed by Cummings, who had previously assaulted him. Hopkinson requested that the jury consider the circumstances leading to the shooting, suggesting that a reasonable belief of danger justified his actions.	The defense, representing The People, maintained that Hopkinson's actions constituted an unlawful assault with intent to murder. They argued that Cummings was not a threat without having made any violent moves, and the use of a deadly weapon in this context was unjustifiable. The defense emphasized that even if Cummings had acted provocatively, it did not warrant Hopkinson discharging his firearm, and thus he should be found guilty of assault.

The case titled "George Bowen et al. v. Robert Prout" was decided in September 1869 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated in Bureau County, Illinois, and involved a legal action of ejectment brought by Robert Prout against George Bowen and another party to recover an undivided three-fifths interest in a specific piece of land—a quarter section described as the northeast quarter of a section in township number fifteen north, of range six east. The litigation arose over conflicting claims to the property, particularly regarding a complex chain of title and the legitimacy of various conveyances. The initial trial concluded with a judgment favoring Prout, who provided evidence of a connected chain of title. Following a writ of error filed by Bowen, arguments were made pertaining to the adequacy of the land description in the deed and an unrecorded prior deed that Bowen claimed constituted a paramount title.	Prout's main argument was based on his legitimate claim to the three-fifths interest in the property through a series of valid conveyances in the chain of title. He sought to establish his ownership and recover the specified portion of land, asserting that the legal description used in prior deeds was sufficient to support his claim. Additionally, Prout argued that he was a bona fide purchaser for value and had not received notice of any prior unrecorded deeds that could impair his title.	Bowen contended that an outstanding paramount title in the property existed due to a prior unrecorded deed from Prout's ancestor to a third party, James Warren. Bowen argued that this previous deed affected Prout's claim and sought reversal of the lower court's judgment on grounds of inadequate land description and the existence of this earlier title that superiorly claimed the same property interest.

In 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, Jacob Sankey and other plaintiffs filed a legal case against William C. Seipp and others regarding the cancellation of tax sale certificates. The plaintiffs asserted that they were the rightful owners of several unimproved and unoccupied lots, except for two properties that were being rented. They claimed these lots were wrongfully sold for taxes at an alleged tax sale conducted by the county collector, which was attended by the county clerk. They argued that the sale was illegal due to the clerk's failure to certify the sale as required by law, thus creating a cloud on their title. The plaintiffs sought to annul the tax sales and cancel the associated certificates. The case was initially dismissed by the Superior Court for lack of equity, a decision that the plaintiffs challenged, resulting in an appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed ownership of certain lots and argued that the tax sale conducted in 1884 was invalid because the county clerk failed to issue necessary certifications as mandated by statute. This failure rendered the tax sale illegal, creating a cloud on the plaintiffs' title. They sought the annulment of the tax sales and requested that the court declare the tax certificates void and prevent further actions based on those certificates. The plaintiffs also offered to pay any taxes or interest as required, suggesting their willingness to act in good faith.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs' bill was without equity and maintained that the certificates of sale were valid, having been issued following the tax sale. They argued the procedural correctness of the sale process and countered the assertion that the lack of certification invalidated the transaction. The defendants filed a plea claiming that deeds had been issued to them in connection with the certificates after the initial dismissal of the case, thereby asserting the legitimacy of their ownership.

In the case of Joseph T. Anthony et al. v. John C. Wheeler, the legal dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, culminating in a decision dated October 31, 1889. The appellants, who were in possession of a city lot, claimed their title through tax deeds and a quitclaim deed from Carrie Walker and her husband, Samuel O. Walker. The appellee, John C. Wheeler, asserted that he held the paramount title and initiated the action of ejectment in June 1886 in the Superior Court of Cook County. During the trial, both parties presented conflicting evidence regarding the ownership of the property. However, the judge directed the jury to return a verdict for the plaintiff, leading to a judgment in favor of Wheeler for the premises claimed. The defendants subsequently appealed, citing multiple errors in the trial court's proceedings, with the primary contention being that the court improperly instructed the jury to find for the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, John C. Wheeler, argued that he held a fee simple title to the property in question based on undisputed evidence from a common source. He contended that the defendants had constructive notice of his unrecorded deeds due to the legal requirements for recording deeds. By asserting his ownership and the validity of his title, Wheeler sought to recover possession of the city lot from the appellants.	The defendants contended that the trial court erred in instructing the jury to find in favor of the plaintiff. They claimed that their title was valid and, crucially, that Wheeler's deeds were not recorded until after their own quitclaim deed. They argued that an unrecorded administrator's deed would not serve as constructive notice to subsequent purchasers, including themselves, and that properly recorded documents should prevail in establishing rightful ownership.

On March 29, 1880, Thomas J. Sutherland entered into a lease agreement with Granville S. Ingraham for a property in Chicago. The lease was set for one year, starting on May 1, 1880, and included an option for Sutherland to renew for another year if Ingraham did not sell the property before the lease ended on April 30, 1881. Later, Sutherland either assigned the lease or sub-leased the property to the defendants, William D. Goodnow and others. In March or April of 1881, Ingraham entered into a written agreement to sell the property to Hiram Sibley, and possession was transferred to Sibley in May 1881. After Sibley took possession, Goodnow and the others continued to occupy the premises under Sibley without Sutherland’s involvement. Subsequently, Sutherland sent a notice demanding $3,600 for rent if the defendants held over into the next year. Sutherland later sued Goodnow and the others for rent for the second year, leading to a dispute over the interpretation of the lease agreement and the implications of the property sale.	Sutherland claimed that under the terms of the original lease, since Ingraham did not sell the premises before the expiration of the first year, he had the right to renew the lease for a second year. He sought damages for unpaid rent amounting to $3,600 from the defendants for holding over after the lease term.	The defendants argued that the lease stipulations were void due to the sale of the property before April 30, 1881. They asserted that Sutherland could not charge them for rent for a second year because they were no longer his tenants following the sale to Sibley and their subsequent agreement with him. They maintained that any right Sutherland claimed through the lease was transferred and no longer enforceable.

In the case of Henry Myers et al. v. Charles Walker, which took place in 1863 in Peoria County, Illinois, the parties involved were Henry Myers and Stanley J. Dawson, partners operating as H. Myers & Co., and Charles Walker, the surviving partner of Walker & Kellogg. The case originated in 1858 when Walker initiated an action of assumpsit against Myers and Dawson. The plaintiff alleged that Myers & Co. had breached multiple contracts regarding the purchase and delivery of corn and sought to recover a balance of $6,685.87 after accounting for various transactions. The defendants countered with their own set-off claims, asserting over $12,822.87 owed to them for various expenses related to corn. The trial took place initially in 1859 but led to a rerun that resulted in a reversed judgment in 1860, prompting further legal proceedings. Throughout the trial, issues arose including the competence of a witness related to the deceased partner and disputes over jury instructions and the admissibility of certain evidence. The case revolved around alleged contract breaches, financial claims, and whether proper legal procedures were followed in handling the evidence and witness testimonies.	The plaintiff, Charles Walker, claimed that Myers & Co. had failed to deliver the contracted amount of corn, as agreed upon in their contracts. Walker's primary argument revolved around damages tied to the alleged breaches of contract, claiming a balance due of $6,685.87. The claim included several counts for goods sold, money advanced for corn purchases, and other related financial matters, indicating Walker sought compensation for his losses resulting from the defendants' actions.	The defendants, Myers and Dawson, contended that they had fulfilled their contract obligations. Their defense included a counterclaim for $12,822.87 due to expenses incurred through storage, sacking, hauling, and commissions linked to the corn. They argued that Walker failed to collect the corn within a reasonable time frame, thereby causing additional costs and loss, which they claimed should not be assigned to them. They also raised objections regarding the qualifications of certain witness testimonies and argued about the adequacy of jury instructions provided during the trial proceedings.

Samuel A. Buckmaster v. James Gowen is a legal case that dates back to January 1876. It was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, where Buckmaster claimed against his former partner, Gowen, regarding a failed partnership agreement for constructing a railroad. On August 17, 1871, Buckmaster, Gowen, and another individual, Patterson, verbally agreed to form a partnership called Patterson, Gowen & Co. They planned to procure a contract with a railroad company for construction work, with Gowen responsible for providing necessary funds and profits divided equally among the partners. Buckmaster successfully secured a contract with the railroad company, but later alleged that Gowen failed to supply the required capital for the work. Additionally, Gowen reportedly canceled the contract with the railroad company, resulting in significant financial losses for Buckmaster, who detailed his contributions, including $1,000 of his own money and seven months of labor worth $10,000. Buckmaster claimed damages amounting to $50,000 due to Gowen's actions.	Buckmaster argued that Gowen's failure to provide financial support as agreed led to significant lost profits from the railroad contract. He stated that the firm could have generated substantial gains had Gowen fulfilled his funding obligations. He requested damages of $50,000 for the losses incurred due to Gowen's misconduct, which included canceling the contract with the railroad company.	Gowen's defense relied on a demurrer, claiming that the case should not proceed as a legal action between partners for internal misconduct. He maintained that the issues raised by Buckmaster could only be resolved through equity after a final settlement of their partnership affairs, rather than as a lawsuit. This argument aimed to assert that Buckmaster's claims were premature given the nature of their partnership.
