Neff, accused of threatening him. During the trial before a justice of the peace, Marlatt testified that Neff threatened to shoot him. However, it was alleged that Marlatt knowingly lied, as Neff did not make such threats. Upon indictment, Marlatt pleaded not guilty but was found guilty by the jury and sentenced to three years in the penitentiary. Marlatt’s counsel filed motions for a new trial and to arrest judgment, both of which were denied. The court subsequently examined the evidence and found insufficient grounds to uphold the conviction, determining that the jury ignored the legal standard requiring guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.	The plaintiff, represented by the State of Illinois, claimed that Willis Marlatt committed perjury by falsely testifying against Fletcher T. Neff, which resulted in a conviction. The state sought to uphold Marlatt's conviction and sentence him to the prescribed penalty for the crime.	Willis Marlatt, through his attorney, contested the verdict by arguing that the evidence presented was inadequate to warrant a conviction. He maintained his innocence, asserting that the jury's decision contradicted the legal requirement that guilt must be established beyond a reasonable doubt. His legal team requested a new trial based on the alleged errors in the trial proceedings.

The case of Robert M. Tarlton v. George Miller took place in November 1823 in Gallatin County, Illinois. It involves a legal dispute regarding a promissory note executed by a man named Squire Brown, who made the obligation to Robert M. Tarlton and subsequently assigned to George Miller. The issue arose when Miller sued Tarlton, claiming that despite a diligent search for Brown in Gallatin County at the time the note became due, Brown could not be found, and the note remained unpaid. Tarlton, as the assignor of the note, was argued to be liable under these circumstances. During the trial, Tarlton's defense sought to instruct the jury to dismiss the first count of Miller's declaration, arguing that it was defective because it failed to adequately demonstrate due diligence in locating the maker of the note. The trial court rejected this motion, leading to Tarlton's appeal of the judgment in favor of Miller.	George Miller's primary argument was that he had made diligent efforts to locate Squire Brown within Gallatin County at the time the promissory note was due but was unsuccessful. Miller contended that this constituted grounds for holding Robert M. Tarlton, as the assignor of the note, liable for the unpaid amount. He also included a count for money had and received against Tarlton.	Robert M. Tarlton's defense centered on challenging the sufficiency of the claims made by Miller. Tarlton argued that the declaration was insufficient in alleging due diligence since it did not explicitly state efforts were made to find Brown outside of Gallatin County. His defense emphasized that without clear evidence of due diligence or the absence of the maker of the note, he should not be held liable as the assignor.

The case of Micajah Chauncey v. John Jackson occurred in December 1847 in Illinois. Micajah Chauncey was the owner of the schooner General Thornton, while John Jackson served as its master for two months in 1838. The legal proceedings began when Jackson initiated an attachment against Chauncey, claiming unpaid wages for his services as master of the vessel. During the trial, evidence was presented showing that Jackson's services were valued at $50 per month, and that he had received $189 for freight earned by the schooner while he was in charge. The Circuit Court found in favor of Jackson, awarding him $100 and granting a special execution against the schooner, prompting Chauncey to appeal the judgment. The case addressed maritime law principles and the application of Illinois statutes regarding wage claims related to vessel services.	The plaintiff, John Jackson, claimed that as the master of the schooner General Thornton, he was entitled to wages for his services rendered during 1838. He alleged that he had provided labor and incurred expenses for the vessel, which entitled him to a total of $100. Jackson sought the court's judgment to affirm his right to payment for the wages claimed, along with the execution against the vessel for recovery.	The defendant, Micajah Chauncey, argued that Jackson, as the master of the vessel, was not entitled to proceed under the Illinois Attachment Act for recovery of wages. Chauncey contended that the Act did not authorize claims from masters and highlighted that maritime law does not grant a master a lien over the ship for wages. He also asserted that Jackson's claim was excessive and that the judgment rendered by the lower court was contrary to law and evidence.

The case "The People ex rel. Eli Frank v. Richard Prendergast, County Judge" took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the court's decision rendered on May 15, 1886. The primary individuals involved were Eli Frank, the relator and assignee of an insolvent estate, and Richard Prendergast, the County Judge. The dispute arose from orders issued by the county court on December 5 and 6, 1884, which mandated Frank to pay a sum of $2,387.95 to creditors and threatened him with imprisonment for non-compliance. This situation occurred following a composition agreement made between the insolvent estate's debtors and their creditors. After delivering what he believed constituted full payment, a contention arose regarding a promissory note that Frank had given to the creditors. When the county court found in favor of the creditors, Frank petitioned the Illinois Supreme Court seeking a writ of mandamus to enforce his right to appeal the county court's orders.	Eli Frank, as the relator, claimed that he was entitled to appeal the county court's final order requiring him to pay a specific sum to the creditors, arguing that the court's refusals to allow such an appeal were unjust. He contended that the order rendered by the county court was final and thus subject to appeal, as stated in state statutes regarding appeals from county court judgments. Additionally, he sought the court's intervention to mandate the exercise of his right to appeal.	Richard Prendergast, as the County Judge, defended against the writ of mandamus by asserting that the orders issued were not final judgments and therefore did not warrant an appeal. The defense implied that the requirements set forth by the statute for an appeal had not been met and raised questions regarding the nature of the orders and whether they indeed constituted an appealable decision. The judge maintained that the orders were valid and should remain enforceable without the need for appeal.

William Maxwell filed a case against William D. Vansant in September 1867, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from an action of assumpsit related to certain promissory notes that Maxwell, as the assignee, claimed from Vansant, the assignor. The notes in question were executed in La Salle County, Illinois, and at the time of the assignment, Maxwell lived in Marshall County while Vansant resided in La Salle County. The legal issue arose when the process was sent from Marshall County to La Salle County for service. Vansant contested the jurisdiction of the Marshall Circuit Court by filing a plea in abatement. After a trial, the Circuit Court sided with Vansant, ruling that it did not have jurisdiction to send a summons to La Salle County for service on him. Consequently, Maxwell appealed the judgment to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Maxwell's primary argument centered around the assertion that the Circuit Court of Marshall County had jurisdiction to bring the case against Vansant, as the assignee of the promissory notes. He contended that the transfer of the notes and their subsequent endorsement in blank justified the legal proceedings initiated in Marshall County. Maxwell sought to overturn the lower court's judgment in favor of Vansant.	Vansant's defense rested on the argument that the Marshall Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction. He maintained that the summons could not be executed in La Salle County, where he resided. He cited precedent that established jurisdictional protocols, emphasizing that the court could not transfer its summons outside its county boundaries when neither party resided there.

The case of The Sterling Bridge Company v. George Baker was initiated in September 1874 in Whiteside County, Illinois. The dispute arose when George Baker, the plaintiff, sought compensation from The Sterling Bridge Company, the defendant, for the use of eight jack-screws that were loaned to George Baker's agents for a period of thirty-three days. A representative of the defendant, Spencer, had sent Blair to obtain the jack-screws from the plaintiff for repairs on a bridge. Although the plaintiff's customary charge for the use of the jack-screws was twenty-five cents a day, Baker did not return one of the jack-screws, leading to claims for compensation. The case was initially heard before a justice of the peace and was later appealed to the circuit court, where the court ruled in favor of the plaintiff for $66. Baker subsequently remitted $7.50 of this verdict, resulting in a final judgment against the defendant. The case involved conflicting evidence and legal interpretations regarding the agent's authority and the appropriate charges for the use of borrowed equipment.	The plaintiff, George Baker, claimed that he was entitled to payment for the use of the eight jack-screws, as well as the value of one jack-screw that was not returned. He argued that the defendant, The Sterling Bridge Company, was bound by the terms communicated to their agent, Blair, regarding the daily rental fee for the jack-screws. Baker sought to affirm the judgment delivered by the circuit court, which awarded him compensation for the use of the equipment.	The defendant, The Sterling Bridge Company, contended that the charges for the jack-screws were not adequately communicated to them, as their agent, Blair, failed to inform Spencer about the rental fee. They argued against the applicability of the rental terms given to their agent, claiming that the instructions refused by the court were misaligned with their understanding of the situation. The defendant sought to overturn the circuit court's ruling, asserting that the judgment should not stand.

In September 1871, the case "Lucius B. Otis v. The City of Chicago" was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from events that occurred in Cook County, Illinois. This legal proceeding was initiated as an application by the city collector of Chicago for judgment on a special assessment warrant aimed at facilitating the widening of an alley from Clark Street to La Salle Street, traversing block 117 of the school section addition in Chicago. The case drew attention due to the collector's authority to seek a court order for the sale of real estate to recover delinquent taxes and special assessments. The Illinois Supreme Court examined several points of contention but fundamentally focused on the collector's lack of authority to apply for judgment, which had been nullified by a provision in the new state constitution. This decision aligned with the precedent from the case "Hills v. Chicago," confirming the necessity for a general officer of the county to undertake such actions post-constitutional changes.	The plaintiffs, Lucius B. Otis and Laban S. Major, contended that the city collector did not possess the legal authority to apply for judgment regarding delinquent taxes and special assessments related to the property sale. They argued that the actions taken were invalid due to constitutional provisions enacted in 1870 that mandated oversight by a general officer empowered to manage such financial recoveries.	The City of Chicago, represented by the city collector, argued that the application for judgment was in line with the existing city charter at the time of the request. They contended that the procedures followed adhered to the requirements for managing delinquent taxes and special assessments. The defense sought to uphold the judgment made by the lower court, asserting there was no basis for the reversal sought by the plaintiffs.

In January 1869, the case of Matthew McMillan v. John Andrew was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated over the ownership of a mare that McMillan claimed as his estray. John Andrew had taken possession of the mare and sought to establish his title under the state’s estray statute, which requires specific advertising and notification procedures to inform the rightful owner. In presenting his case, Andrew provided a notice where the mare was described as taken up by “John Anderson," instead of the correct name, “John Andrew.” This mistake was crucial, as it did not adequately inform McMillan about who had taken possession of his property or how to reclaim it. The locality description in the advertisement was vague, stating the taker's location as “about 3-½ miles from Coulter’s Mill," which further complicated McMillan’s ability to recover his mare. The court addressed the issue of compliance with the statutory requirements necessary for the owner to lose their title and highlighted that errors in the advertisement could lead to significant repercussions for both parties involved.	Matthew McMillan, as the plaintiff, argued that the advertisement John Andrew filed was fundamentally flawed due to the incorrect name and vague locality description. McMillan contended that these flaws violated the requirements of the estray statute, preventing Andrew from acquiring legal title to the mare. He asserted that because the advertisement did not meet the statutory standards, he retained ownership of the mare and sought a judgment in his favor.	John Andrew, as the defendant, claimed that he should not suffer from the error in the advertisement, which he argued was made by a clerk or justice. He contended that despite the mistakes, the law should allow him to claim ownership of the estray, asserting that the intention of the statute was served. Andrew sought to maintain his title to the mare and requested the court to uphold the validity of his claim despite the procedural errors.

In the case of Henry Walters v. Katie Walters et al., a legal dispute arose regarding a verbal contract between Henry Walters and his son, Charles Walters, regarding the management and eventual transfer of a farm in Tazewell County, Illinois. In 1877, Henry, with his wife’s agreement, offered Charles the opportunity to manage the farm for his lifetime in exchange for support and a promise of ownership after Henry’s death, provided that Charles would stay on the farm and surrender the proceeds of his labor to Henry. Charles diligently worked the farm for about ten years before passing away in April 1887, leaving behind a widow, Katie Walters, and two minor children. Following Charles' death, Katie and the children filed a bill in August 1888 against Henry, seeking to enforce the verbal agreement made by Henry with Charles. The court proceedings began swiftly and led to a default judgment against Henry, who was described as elderly and influenced by his family. The legal arguments centered on the enforceability of the verbal contract and whether the complainants had met their obligations under it.	The plaintiffs, Katie Walters and her children, claimed that they had a right to the farm based on the verbal contract between Henry and Charles. They argued that Charles had fulfilled his obligations by working the farm for many years and that Henry had acknowledged his indebtedness to them through a posthumous agreement to pay them $2000. They sought a legal decree to compel Henry to convey the property to a trustee for their benefit, raise the outstanding payment owed, and ensure that upon Henry's death, the property would vest in their favor, as stipulated in the original agreement.	Henry Walters, the defendant, did not formally answer the complaint, resulting in a default ruling against him. However, the defenses presented in the court outlined that the plaintiffs had not performed their part of the contractual obligations. Henry maintained that the verbal contract was not enforceable and that the plaintiffs had not offered to perform any unfulfilled obligations of Charles, especially as they had failed to manage the farm or prove they could continue with the terms of the contract after Charles' death. Henry also expressed concerns about the potential influence of his wife and sons on the property, suggesting that an injunction would suffice without placing the property under a trustee's control.

In January 1875, the case of Paulsen B. Bush v. William Scott et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, involving individuals from Edgar County, Illinois. Paulsen B. Bush, the plaintiff, had purchased multiple parcels of land from Samuel Scott for $1,300, paying an initial $500 and securing the remainder with notes backed by a mortgage on one of the tracts. Following Scott's death, his executors secured a foreclosure decree on the mortgaged property. The sale of the property did not fully satisfy the debt, leading the executors to obtain a judgment against Bush for $631.52, the remaining balance. Subsequently, the executors sold another of Bush’s properties under execution. In response, Bush filed a bill to have the latter sale annulled, claiming the land was his homestead. However, the court below sustained a demurrer and dismissed Bush's bill, prompting Bush to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, Paulsen B. Bush, contended that the land sold under execution was his homestead and thus should be exempt from the sale to satisfy the debt owed on the property. He sought to set aside the sheriff's sale of his land, arguing that the homestead protections should apply to his situation due to the misleading interpretation of his property rights.	The defendants, the executors of Samuel Scott, argued that the claim of homestead rights did not hold against the debt owed for the purchase of the land. They emphasized that the law clearly states that no homestead exemption exists for debts related to property purchase or improvement. They contended that the foreclosure proceedings were legitimate and should not be challenged, as they were acting within statuary bounds to recover the debt from Bush.

In the summer of 1865, Robert Stuart and Solomon McKichan entered into a partnership to pave streets in Chicago, initially including Andrew Gray. By 1869, disputes arose between the partners, particularly regarding financial dealings and the appropriated funds for their work. McKichan accused Stuart of misappropriating an estimate for the work done, leading McKichan to file a suit to prevent Stuart from negotiating this estimate. In response, Stuart filed a counter-suit seeking to investigate their partnership transactions and dissolve the partnership. The two suits were consolidated, and after extensive testimony, the case was referred to a master for accounting. However, much documentation was lost in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, necessitating the retaking of testimony and reconstruction of the account. The master submitted a report, to which Stuart filed multiple exceptions, all but one of which were disallowed by the court. The accounting relied heavily on partnership books, which were presumed to reflect accurate transactions unless disproven.	McKichan claimed that Stuart misappropriated funds related to the partnership's projects and sought an injunction to stop Stuart from negotiating the disputed voucher. He requested a fair accounting of the partnership transactions from 1865 to 1869 and confirmed that the expenses related to money raised for their business operations were validly charged against the firm’s account.	Stuart argued against the master's report, claiming that multiple exceptions he raised regarding the accounting were valid. He contended that McKichan improperly charged interest and expenses to the partnership that he had not objected to when the changes were made. Stuart's main defense emphasized that the firm's financial records contained inaccuracies and misrepresentations that were detrimental to his case, insisting that the court's ruling on the exceptions should be reversed.

In the case of William E. Hughes v. William Stubblefield and Joseph Ator, which took place in McLean County, Illinois, in the year 1886, the central issue revolved around a chattel mortgage. The dispute began when Joseph Ator, acting as the bailiff for landlord William Stubblefield, took possession of personal property belonging to John and William Bix based on a distress warrant for unpaid rent. While Ator held the property, Eix executed a chattel mortgage in favor of Hughes, which was duly acknowledged and recorded. Upon maturity of the mortgage, Hughes demanded the return of the property, but Ator refused, prompting Hughes to file a replevin action, seeking immediate possession of the property. The case was heard without a jury, and the trial court ruled in favor of the defendant, citing that no title had passed to Hughes as the mortgage was executed while the property was held by Ator under adverse possession.	The plaintiff, William E. Hughes, argued that the chattel mortgage he had received was valid despite the adverse possession of the property by Ator. He claimed that, as the rightful owner, he had the legal right to possess the property after the mortgage's maturity. Hughes sought a ruling that would enable him to reclaim the property taken by Ator under the distress warrant.	William Stubblefield and Joseph Ator defended against Hughes's claims by asserting that the chattel mortgage was executed while the property was in the hands of Ator, who held it under a distress warrant for rent. They argued that this situation created an adverse possession, invalidating any transfer of title through the mortgage to Hughes. The defendants contended that the landlord's lien needed to be perfected, and since it was not, the ownership claims by Hughes were legally inadequate.

The case "William F. Petillon v. Henry M. Wilmarth et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1877. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, where the plaintiff, William F. Petillon, brought an action of assumpsit against Henry M. Wilmarth and others to recover a balance for gas fixtures provided in the Pacific Hotel building. The testimony revealed that Petillon had a written contract with the hotel company to install specific gas fixtures in the building's basement. The defendants, who had leased the barber shop and bath rooms, were dissatisfied with the quality of the fixtures and entered into a separate agreement with Petillon to select better quality fixtures, agreeing to pay the difference in value between the chosen fixtures and those originally specified in the contract with the hotel company. During the trial, the defendants attempted to introduce the original contract as evidence, claiming it was relevant to the case. However, the court only allowed that evidence to counter a specific testimony given by Petillon. The court's refusal to admit the full contract and specifications as evidence was later seen as erroneous, forming the basis for the appeal.	The plaintiff, William F. Petillon, argued that he was entitled to recover payment for the gas fixtures provided upon the defendants’ request. He claimed that the defendants had agreed to pay him for the difference in value between the fixtures installed and those specified in the initial contract with the hotel company. His key legal request was for the court to uphold his claim for the unpaid balance owed for the fixtures.	The defendants contended that the gas fixtures provided by Petillon did not meet their expectations as they were of inferior quality compared to what had been agreed upon. They sought to admit evidence of the written contract with the hotel company to demonstrate the quality and specifications of the gas fixtures that Petillon had originally contracted to supply. The defense claimed that this evidence was critical for establishing the difference in value for which they were obligated to pay.

In the year 1838, in Will County, Illinois, an action of assumpsit was initiated by Rufus Colton against Ripley E. W. Adams. During the April term of court in 1838, Adams sought a continuance for the trial, asserting that he required the testimony of a witness, Joel Jenks, who had become unavailable after relocating without the defendant's knowledge. Adams believed Jenks could substantiate a claim of $150 related to an item in his account of set-off. Despite providing an affidavit detailing his attempts to locate Jenks and his expectation of obtaining his presence by the next court term, the court denied the motion for continuance. The case continued to trial, resulting in a jury verdict favoring Colton with an award of $422.70. Following the verdict, Adams filed a motion for a new trial based on the discovery of new evidence from another witness, Josiah Beaumont. The court also denied this motion. The case was subsequently escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court based on assigned errors concerning the motion for continuance and new trial.	Rufus Colton, the plaintiff, asserted that he was owed $422.70, representing the amount due from Adams in an action of assumpsit. Colton sought to establish his claim through the results of the trial, which concluded with a jury verdict in his favor, despite Adams’ claims of missing evidence that could influence the case.	Ripley E. W. Adams, the defendant, presented his key arguments by highlighting his inability to secure the testimony of a crucial witness, Joel Jenks, during the trial, which he claimed was essential to adequately defend against Colton's actions. Adams contended that the court's refusal to grant a continuance, despite his diligent efforts to secure Jenks' attendance, was unjust. He also sought a new trial after discovering new material evidence through Josiah Beaumont, which he argued could potentially overturn the verdict.

In the case of Henry Tetzner et al. v. Sarah Naughton, the action took place in Elgin, Illinois, on February 9, 1883. The case revolved around Sarah Naughton, who brought a lawsuit against several individuals, mainly saloon keepers, claiming damages for the loss of her means of support due to her husband, Thomas Haughton’s, demoralization and subsequent death. Naughton asserted that the defendants had sold intoxicating liquors to her husband, which led to his habitual intoxication, wasting his earnings and reducing him to a state of poverty before his death on September 23, 1881. The lawsuit was based on the state’s Dram Shop Act. During the trial, it was revealed that the jury found in favor of Sarah Naughton, awarding her $2,804, which included actual and exemplary damages. The suit was dismissed against some defendants due to a lack of evidence of sales made to Haughton, and the focus narrowed to the actions of certain saloon owners on the day of his death.	Sarah Naughton claimed that the defendants' sale of intoxicating liquors to her husband caused him to become an alcoholic, ultimately leading to his financial ruin and death. She sought compensation for the loss of support for herself and their six children, claiming that her husband’s addictions led him to neglect his responsibilities as a provider. The damages sought included both actual damages for loss of income and exemplary damages for the suffering caused by her husband's downfall.	The defendants argued that they were not responsible for the habitual intoxication of Haughton, asserting that his death was the direct result of his actions on the day in question, where he consumed liquor at various establishments. They contended that their involvement was limited to the sale of a small number of drinks over a long period, insufficient to establish liability for his habitual drunkenness or to link their actions directly to his demise. The key point of contention was whether the defendants could be held liable for an 'intervening act' leading to Haughton's death, mainly that his intoxication on the day of the incident was attributable to sales made by them that day, not his prior history of drinking.

Daniel H. Brush filed a lawsuit against The City of Carbondale in 1875 in Jackson County, Illinois. The case arose when the city officials ordered the removal of an existing sidewalk in front of Brush's property to replace it with a new sidewalk of different width. Brush claimed that he had contributed to the cost of the original sidewalk and that the existing one, with minor repairs, could serve its purpose for several more years. He argued that the new sidewalk would impose unnecessary financial burdens on residents through increased taxes and assessments. Brush's complaint was that the city's actions were illegal and without proper authority. The city’s officials, in response, filed a demurrer, which was sustained by the court, leading to the dismissal of Brush’s bill. Brush then appealed, seeking a reversal of this dismissal.	The plaintiff, Daniel H. Brush, claimed that the City of Carbondale lacked the legal authority to tear up the existing sidewalk and replace it, as it would impose unnecessary financial burdens through taxes on property owners. He asserted that the old sidewalk could remain with minimal repairs, making its removal unnecessary. Brush requested that the court issue an injunction to prevent the city from proceeding with plans to construct the new sidewalk, alleging that such actions would be illegal and unwarranted.	The City of Carbondale, represented by its legal team, contended that Brush's complaint was defective as it failed to demonstrate whether the city was incorporated or to refer to its charter. They argued that the city held proper authority to manage sidewalks and streets under its powers, and that Brush had an adequate legal remedy to contest any illegal taxes or assessments in law rather than through equity. The defense emphasized that the city’s actions were within the bounds of its discretionary powers and not subject to judicial interference unless there was a clear abuse of power detrimental to the citizens.

On April 1858, in La Salle County, Illinois, the case of Edward Neary v. James Cahill, Guardian, was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute revolved around the ownership of a certain mare that had been levied upon by a constable due to an execution issued from a justice of the peace. Edward Neary, the appellant, contended that he had a rightful claim to the mare, which was held as personal property among several owners. The property in question had been attempted to be seized based on an execution against one of the joint owners, without consideration for the shared ownership among multiple tenants in common.	The plaintiff, Edward Neary, argued that the mare could not be legally levied upon in its entirety due to the nature of joint ownership among the tenants in common. He maintained that the execution should have been limited to the interest of the judgment debtor only, as the law does not permit a complete seizure of jointly-owned property. Neary sought to recover the mare based on this assertion.	The defendant, represented by James Cahill, contended that the execution against one individual in a common ownership arrangement was valid. Their argument rested on the assertion that the constable's actions were standard procedure in such circumstances. However, they failed to demonstrate a legal basis for levying the entire property rather than just the debtor's share.

The case "Benjamin Kindig, et al., Executors, etc., of Benjamin Kindig, deceased. v. Anthony C. Deardorff, Administrator, etc., of William Henry Smith, deceased" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1866. The primary individuals involved include Benjamin Kindig's executors and Anthony C. Deardorff, the administrator of William Henry Smith's estate. William Henry Smith, one of Kindig’s grandchildren, died without issue at the age of twenty-one. The dispute arose after Deardorff petitioned the County Court to compel the executors of Benjamin Kindig to pay a legacy to Smith, as stipulated in Kindig's will. The County Court ruled in Deardorff's favor, and this decision was upheld by the Circuit Court. The core issue was the interpretation of the will, particularly regarding the conditions under which Smith’s legacy would be distributed in light of his death and the intended beneficiaries described by the testator.	The plaintiff, Anthony C. Deardorff, argued that as the administrator of William Henry Smith's estate, he was entitled to the legacy specified in Kindig's will. He contended that since Smith died without issue, the estate should pass to his personal representatives, despite the will's provision for the share to go to Kindig's children and surviving grandchildren in certain conditions.	The defendants, the executors of Benjamin Kindig, argued that under the terms of the will, the phraseology dictated that the legacy to William Henry Smith should not pass to his administrator because the conditions of dying without issue must be interpreted as requiring both specified events—dying under twenty-one and without issue. They maintained that Smith retained the legacy upon reaching the age of majority, aligning with the intended purpose of the will.

In 1873, the case of William C. Dawson v. Peter Hayden et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, focusing on an action of ejectment for certain lots in Peters-burg, Menard County. The appellant, William C. Dawson, executed a deed of trust on July 21, 1853, to secure debts owed to the appellees, Peter Hayden et al. Subsequently, the trustee sold the property to the appellees on December 15, 1859. Dawson claimed a homestead exemption regarding the property since his wife did not sign the deed of trust, and there was no provision releasing the homestead right. The case revolved around the interpretation of the homestead act of 1851 and the legalities surrounding the sale executed by the trustee. Key issues included the validity of the acknowledgment of the trustee's deed and whether the required notice prior to sale met legal standards. The court examined these circumstances, citing previous cases to support its rulings.	The plaintiff, William C. Dawson, argued that the homestead exemption protected him from losing the property since his wife did not join in the deed of trust. He contended that the trust deed and subsequent sale violated the protections established by the homestead act of 1851, which he believed prevented such a sale without a court order. He also raised objections regarding the validity of the trustee's deed due to alleged defects in acknowledgment and the notice period preceding the sale.	The defendants, Peter Hayden et al., countered that the homestead act did not apply to sales conducted under a trust deed, as this was not a sale enforced by a court order. They maintained that the sale executed by the trustee was valid, notwithstanding the acknowledgment issues raised by Dawson. They argued that the legal estate was held by the trustee and conveyed to them properly, asserting that any challenges regarding the specifics of the trustee's sale were irrelevant in an ejectment action.

The case of "The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. v. Edward H. Williams" took place in January 1875 at a union depot in Quincy, Illinois. Edward H. Williams, the plaintiff, purchased a ticket for travel from Quincy to Jacksonville. While waiting for the train in a room designated for passengers, he encountered E. E. Goodrich, a servant of the defendant railway company, who forcibly ejected him from the area. Williams claimed that he was insulted and beaten during this encounter. The court proceedings began after Williams filed a lawsuit against the railway company, alleging wrongful assault. The trial resulted in a judgment in favor of Williams, awarding him $50 in damages. However, the case hinged on whether Williams had a legitimate claim, given the context of his entry into a space reserved specifically for women, which was the "ladies' private room," where he was not permitted to be.	Edward H. Williams claimed that the defendant's servant, E. E. Goodrich, assaulted him while he was waiting in the ladies' private room at the train depot. Williams argued that the defendant was liable for the actions of its servant during his attempt to evict him. He sought damages, asserting that the treatment he received constituted wrongful conduct leading to emotional and reputational harm.	The defendant, The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co., contended that Williams had no valid cause of action. They argued he was inappropriately situated in the ladies' private room, which was clearly designated for women. Furthermore, the defendant asserted that their servant acted within reasonable bounds to maintain safety and order in the depot. They claimed that no actual physical injuries were inflicted on Williams, and thus, they should not be held liable for his removal from the premises.

In 1890, in Cook County, Illinois, Canute R. Matson, in his capacity as sheriff, seized and sold two carloads of paper that had been ordered from the firm of A. T. & F. W. Denison of Detroit, Michigan. The plaintiffs, George H. Taylor and Joseph T. Mix, claimed ownership of the paper, asserting that it had been consigned to them and that they were in the process of examining it to ensure it met the required quality before paying the freight and taking possession. However, just as they were about to finalize the transaction, the paper was levied upon under a writ of attachment at the request of a creditor of the Denisons. During the trial, the plaintiffs presented evidence of their order and inspection of the goods, but the court later instructed the jury to award a verdict in favor of the plaintiffs, resulting in an initial judgment for them. The appellate court, however, found issues with the evidence of ownership presented by the plaintiffs, noting inconsistencies regarding whether payment had been made for the goods and whether they were acting merely as agents for the Denisons. Consequently, the court determined it was inappropriate to take the matter away from the jury and ruled to remand the case for further proceedings.	The plaintiffs, George H. Taylor and Joseph T. Mix, claimed the right to the two carloads of paper, asserting that it had been ordered and consigned to them. They argued that they were about to complete the transaction by paying the freight when the sheriff seized the goods under a writ of attachment. Their main contentions revolved around the alleged ownership and the evidence indicating their entitlement to the goods at the time of the seizure.	The defendants, represented by Canute R. Matson (the sheriff), argued that the seizure was justified under the attachment writ. They contended that the presence of the writ should suffice, and claimed that the plaintiffs failed to prove their ownership or that they were entitled to recover the goods. The defense pointed out the lack of evidence regarding the plaintiffs' payment or any agreement to pay for the paper, thereby questioning the legitimacy of the transaction and the plaintiffs' claim.

On October 21, 1884, Thomas Turner died at the residence of Henry Booth in De Kalb County, Illinois. Prior to his death, Turner had made a will in May 1884, designating Booth and his brother, James Tabbernor, as residuary legatees following specific legacies. Turner's estate consisted of real estate valued at $1,000 and personal property, primarily promissory notes worth about $2,500. After the will was probated, in March 1885, Tabbernor filed a complaint in the De Kalb County Court, alleging that Booth, who was also an executor of the estate, possessed undisclosed goods including $250 in cash and various personal items that were not included in the inventory. Booth denied having possession of the money and claimed the items were given to him by Turner. The County Court ordered Booth to inventory the $250, leading to an appeal after a circuit court jury found in favor of the claim against Booth.	The plaintiff, Thomas Tabbernor, argued that Henry Booth failed to include certain assets belonging to the estate of Thomas Turner in his inventory. Specifically, he claimed that Booth possessed $250 in cash and several personal items that had belonged to Turner. Tabbernor sought a court order compelling Booth to account for these assets and formally inventory them as part of the estate.	Henry Booth contended that he was not a competent witness regarding facts occurring before Turner's death, arguing that he could not testify about the personal property allegedly given to his wife or son by Turner. He also maintained that there was no specific issue presented regarding those items in the trial. Booth contended that the plaintiff did not need to prove the existence of the exact money claimed and protested the denial of his request for a new trial based on claims of newly discovered evidence.

The case "A. F. Smart v. N. B. Morrison" took place in 1884 in Illinois, specifically in Marion County. The central figure in the dispute was A. F. Smart, the plaintiff, who entered a legal action against N. B. Morrison, the defendant, regarding a promissory note. The promissory note, valued at $286.36, was dated May 6, 1872, and signed by Morrison, promising payment to Smart six months after that date. The case was filed as an action in assumpsit, which is a legal term signifying a type of action for breach of contract. Morrison filed two pleas: the first was non-assumpsit (meaning he denied the obligation to pay), and the second asserted that the cause of action had not accrued within ten years prior to the initiation of the suit. The court ruled against the plaintiff by overruling the demurrer, which essentially upheld the defendant’s second plea. This led to a judgment against Smart, requiring him to pay the costs of the action. Smart subsequently appealed, and the appeal questioned the sufficiency of Morrison's second plea in light of applicable statutes concerning the statute of limitations.	A. F. Smart, the plaintiff, argued that N. B. Morrison was legally bound to fulfill the terms of the promissory note for $286.36. He contended that the statute of limitations permitting claims based on the note was not applicable as the cause of action had accrued prior to the enactment of the new limitation period. Smart was seeking to enforce the payment of the promissory note, believing that the previous sixteen-year statute of limitations should apply rather than the newly enacted ten-year limit that Morrison’s defense cited.	N. B. Morrison, the defendant, presented two main defenses against Smart's claims. First, he filed a non-assumpsit plea, effectively denying any obligation to pay the promissory note. Secondly, he emphasized that the cause of action on the note did not accrue within the ten years before the lawsuit was filed, given that the applicable statute of limitations had changed to a ten-year limit. Morrison requested that the court dismiss Smart’s claims based on this defense, asserting that Smart's suit was not timely under the new law.

In the autumn of 1873, Henry Harding, a 14-year-old boy from England, moved to St. Clair County, Illinois, after the death of his parents. He began working in the coal mines with his brother until his brother was killed in 1879. Due to his epilepsy, Henry struggled to find work and eventually became wholly incompetent to work alone. After living with his brother's widow, who was financially impoverished, Henry's condition worsened. In the early 1880s, Henry's family moved to Dakota, and he remained there for several years. In 1887, he returned to St. Clair County where he became a county charge. This lawsuit was initiated to recover a statutory penalty from William Harding for bringing Henry, as a pauper, back into St. Clair County. The case was argued in the Illinois Appellate Court, with testimonies regarding Henry's return and who was responsible for bringing him back being contested.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that William Harding should be held liable under Section 13, Chapter 107 of the Revised Statutes for bringing a pauper, Henry Harding, into St. Clair County. The plaintiff sought the statutory penalty for this act, contending that there was clear evidence of William Harding's involvement in Henry's return to the county.	William Harding, the defendant, argued that he had no responsibility for bringing Henry Harding into St. Clair County. His defense included testimonies asserting that he did not admit to having any role in Henry’s return, and there was insufficient evidence to support the claim that he brought Henry back into the county. The defendant contended that the evidence presented did not legally establish his liability for the statutory penalty sought by the plaintiff.

Thomas A. McLaurie and Jaques purchased lots 13 and 14 in the Illinois Central railroad addition to Urbana in 1855 for $500, which was financed partly by money from McLaurie’s wife and son, received from her father. McLaurie executed an unrecorded deed to his wife for half the property, but they later conveyed it to Robert McMurray to hold in trust for the wife and son after learning the deed was ineffective. Renovations to a brick building on the lots were funded by the wife and son’s money. Samuel Partlow, the defendant, obtained a judgment against McLaurie in November 1858, while McLaurie had conveyed the property to McMurray in April 1858. Partlow attempted to assert his judgment against the properties in Champaign County, but the deed to McMurray was recorded before Partlow's judgment, suggesting it was known to Partlow when the property was levied upon. The plaintiffs argue the conveyance to McMurray was a trust and was legitimate under the circumstances, asserting it was made without intent to defraud.	The plaintiffs, Thomas A. McLaurie and others, claim that the deed conveying the property to Robert McMurray was valid and served as a trust for the benefit of McLaurie's wife and son. They argue that the property was purchased and improved using the wife's and child's money, and therefore it should not be subject to the claims of Partlow, who had knowledge of the trust before levying his execution. They request the court to set aside Partlow's claim on the property, asserting their rights over it.	Samuel Partlow contends that McLaurie's conveyance to McMurray was a voluntary act meant to evade creditors, claiming that McLaurie, despite still holding title, should not have made an arrangement that shields the property from legitimate debts. He argues that since McLaurie incurred the debt before the deed to McMurray was made, the property should be available to satisfy the judgment. Partlow requests the court to uphold his claim on the property despite the trust situation presented by the plaintiffs.

On April 3, 1872, a legal action was initiated by Joseph J. Ironmonger against Henry B. Funk in the circuit court of Morgan County, Illinois. The case stemmed from a contract dispute, and the summons was initially issued but returned as not found. Subsequently, an alias summons was issued on August 31, 1872, which also went unserved. During the December 1872 term, the court decided to continue the case with another alias summons directed to Macon County, where it was eventually served on April 30, 1873. Funk, the defendant, responded by filing a plea in abatement, arguing that the suit should not have been brought in Morgan County. However, the court found the plea lacking because it did not state that Funk was not a resident of Morgan County nor that the contract had not been executed there. The court sustained a demurrer against Funk's plea, interpreting the statutes in force at the time to uphold that the service of summons was valid despite the defendant being served in a different county.	The plaintiff, Joseph J. Ironmonger, argued for the enforcement of a contractual agreement with Henry B. Funk. He maintained that the proper legal procedures were followed in initiating the lawsuit, despite the challenges in serving the defendant initially. The plaintiff sought damages based on the alleged breach of contract and requested that the court affirm the validity of the summons.	The defendant, Henry B. Funk, contended that the case was improperly filed in Morgan County since he was served in Macon County. His plea in abatement argued that the court lacked jurisdiction over the case due to the alleged improper service of summons. Funk sought to dismiss the case based on these procedural claims, asserting that the necessary legal grounds to bring the case forward were not met.

Jacob White initiated a lawsuit against George W. Hight in the Adams Circuit Court, Illinois, around November 1835. The case revolved around two counts: the first count concerned a promissory note for $403 dated January 26, 1819, and the second count was based on a written agreement from October 1, 1824, where Hight was to pay White $486.92, representing a balance on a previously held note that had been lost. Hight defended himself by filing three pleas, asserting that the statute of limitations barred White's claims. Specifically, he claimed non assumpsit (denying liability) and indicated the actions were barred after five years and sixteen years, respectively. White countered, stating he was a non-resident living in Ohio when the cause of action accrued, thus claiming exemption from the statute of limitations under Illinois law for non-residents. The Circuit Court upheld Hight's demurrer to White’s claims, ruling in favor of Hight, prompting White to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court. The primary legal question was whether the statute of limitations applied to non-resident plaintiffs.	Jacob White claimed that George W. Hight owed him money based on a promissory note and a written agreement. He argued that the statute of limitations should not apply to him as a non-resident living in Ohio when the cause of action arose. He sought judgment for the amounts specified in both counts of his declaration, asserting that he had a valid claim despite the time elapsed.	George W. Hight contended that White's claims were barred by the statute of limitations, arguing that the actions were not brought within the five or sixteen-year periods prescribed by law. He maintained that the earlier claims were invalid due to the expiration of the statute and hencely requested the court to sustain the demurrer to White’s claims, ultimately seeking a judgment in his favor.

On March 6, 1885, the appellees, Seth T. Sawyer and Robinson S. Sawyer, filed a bill in chancery in the Illinois Appellate Court, alleging a series of fraudulent transactions involving Geo. T. Brown, William P. Bradshaw, and Andrew W. Metcalfe. The background dates back to February 1879, when the Sawyers obtained a judgment against Brown for $8,160, establishing a lien on Brown's property, specifically lot 39 in the Penitentiary Plat Addition to Alton. Following an execution of the judgment, the Sawyers acquired the lot through a sheriff’s sale on November 29, 1879. However, prior to this, Brown had executed a deed of trust on the lot to secure a $3,000 note to Metcalfe & Bradshaw, which was claimed to be done with the intent to defraud the Sawyers, who were creditors of Brown. The Sawyers argued that the trust deed and subsequent sale to Bradshaw were fraudulent, requesting that these transactions be declared null and void, and sought to have the title of the lot vested in them. The case involved allegations of misrepresentation and illicit activities surrounding property transactions intended to hinder the Sawyers from collecting on their judgment against Brown.	The plaintiffs, Seth T. Sawyer and Robinson S. Sawyer, claimed that Bradshaw and Metcalfe engaged in fraudulent transactions by executing and maintaining a deed of trust on a property owned by Brown, which was intended to prevent them from collecting their legal judgment. They requested that the trust deed and all subsequent sales, including those to Bradshaw and Anna S. Clark, be declared null and void. They sought the vesting of the property title to themselves and requested an accounting of rents and profits from the date of the sheriff’s deed.	The defendants, Bradshaw and Metcalfe, contested the claims, arguing that the trust deed was executed in good faith for valuable consideration, and therefore was not fraudulent. They asserted that the Sawyers had accepted redemption money, thus affirming the validity of the trust deed and their right to the property. Bradshaw and Metcalfe maintained that the sale of the property was legitimate and that Clark, the subsequent purchaser, was an innocent buyer for value, denying any intent to defraud the Sawyers.

On June 16, 1880, in Custer County, Colorado, Walter H. Putnam and Ira F. Benson entered into a written agreement regarding the 'Milk Maid' mining claim. Putnam owned the claim and sought capital for its development, while Benson agreed to invest in exchange for a half interest in the mine. Following this agreement, Putnam conveyed the half interest to Benson for $2,500, with the stipulation that a good title would be provided. Tragically, Benson passed away shortly after, on July 5, 1880, leaving one child, Fannie M. Snyder, as his sole heir. Isabel Kelsey, claiming to have lent Benson significant sums of money over the years, filed a claim against his estate in the Grundy County court on September 3, 1880, which evolved over time to exceed $18,000. A critical point was Kelsey’s assertion that she used her funds to purchase the mining interest but the deed was executed in Benson's name. She later recouped a portion of her claim by assigning a part to Snyder for $2,000, purportedly as payment for the mine interest. Kelsey contested Snyder's deed, claiming deception in part of the transfer process. The judicial proceedings revolved around allegations of trust and improper conveyance following Benson's death.	Isabel Kelsey argued that she financed the purchase of the mining interest through Benson, asserting a resulting trust in her favor despite the deed being in Benson's name. She claimed that Benson fraudulently induced her into accepting a conveyance from Snyder instead of receiving ownership directly. Kelsey requested the court to enforce this alleged trust and validate her claim against the estate.	Fannie M. Snyder, as the heir and administrator, contended that Kelsey's claims were not substantiated by evidence. Snyder highlighted procedural defects regarding the admissibility of Kelsey’s deposition as witness testimony, asserting that Kelsey’s prior acceptance of notes as repayment negated any claim of a resulting trust. Snyder sought the dismissal of Kelsey’s claims, arguing she failed to prove the alleged fraud and could not reclaim her interest without returning the consideration from the deed.

Albert M. Pool filed a legal suit against John Roberts in the Illinois Appellate Court concerning a promissory note valued at $500, originally issued by J. L. Jones and guaranteed by Roberts. The note was dated February 13, 1882, and was scheduled to mature one year later. Pool, as the indorsee of the note, claimed that Roberts had guaranteed its payment, but when the note became due, the payment was not made. Roberts raised several defenses. The trial was conducted without a jury, and the court found against Roberts, ultimately holding him liable for the amount due on the note plus interest, totaling $592.22. The court’s decision to sustain Pool's demurrer to Roberts' various defenses was questioned by Roberts' claim of error, but the appellate court upheld the lower court's judgment.	Pool's main argument was that Roberts, as the guarantor, had an unconditional obligation to pay the amount due on the promissory note at maturity. Pool claimed that he was entitled to payment without being required to notify Roberts of any non-payment or to use diligence in collecting from the maker of the note, Jones.	Roberts presented several defenses, arguing that Pool had extended the payment schedule of the note without his consent and had failed to notify him of Jones' default. He contended that had he been notified about the non-payment, he could have taken steps to secure his position, as Jones was solvent at the note's maturity. However, Roberts’ pleas were deemed insufficient as they failed to demonstrate valid defenses against the unconditional guaranty.

In January 1868, the Illinois Central Railroad Company was involved in a legal case against Abram Middlesworth in the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident occurred in Shelby County, where a railroad train operated by the Illinois Central Railroad killed twenty-one mules owned by Middlesworth. The plaintiff alleged that the train's engineer was negligent in operating the train and failed to take adequate measures to stop it before colliding with the mules. The engineer, having seen the mules on the track near a culvert, attempted to scare them away by sounding the whistle; however, the mules ran along the track and were killed as the train continued forward instead of stopping. Middlesworth claimed that the negligence of the railroad employees led to the loss of his property. The court examined the evidence and found that the train driver exhibited gross negligence, asserting that he could have prevented the deaths of the mules with ordinary care. Additionally, while Middlesworth was acknowledged to have some responsibility for penning the mules in a location where they could escape, the court determined that this did not absolve the railroad of its responsibility to operate the train safely.	Abram Middlesworth contended that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was liable for the deaths of his mules due to gross negligence on the part of its train crew. He argued that the engineer could have prevented the accident by using ordinary care and proper attention while operating the train. Middlesworth claimed damages equivalent to the value of the mules killed and sought a verdict in his favor as he believed the railroad company's negligence directly caused the loss of his property.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company, represented by Mr. Charles Emerson, put forth arguments stating that the engineer was not negligent as per the legal precedents cited, asserting that railroad companies are not liable for stock killed on the tracks unless there is gross negligence. The defense claimed that Middlesworth's actions in penning his mules inappropriately contributed to the incident, suggesting that his negligence should diminish potential liability. They requested that the court dismiss the claims against them based on this assertion of comparative fault.

In April 1862, the case of Louis Steiner v. Benjamin Priddy was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after being appealed from the Circuit Court of Tazewell County. The legal dispute originated from a forcible detainer complaint filed by Louis Steiner against Benjamin Priddy over the ownership of two lots—five and six—pertaining to the estate of Isaac Perkins, located in Tazewell County, Illinois. The background of the case includes a series of judgments against Priddy. Initially, Jesse Fisher won a judgment against Priddy and David Shay for $1,201, leading to Fisher buying the lots at a sheriff's sale in July 1860. Subsequently, the Steiners secured a judgment against Priddy for a larger amount of $3,519.02 in February 1861. As Priddy failed to redeem the lots from Fisher's purchase within the statutory period, the Steiners redeemed the lots themselves, ultimately selling the property to Louis Steiner later that month. The core issue at the heart of the case was whether there was a legal justification for Priddy’s eviction, as it required either a forcible entry or a landlord-tenant relationship, neither of which were established in this case.	Louis Steiner, the appellant, claimed that he had acquired rightful ownership of the contested lots through a valid deed obtained after redeeming them from the sheriff's sale, following the failure of Benjamin Priddy to redeem them himself. Steiner argued that Priddy was unlawfully occupying the property and sought a legal resolution to evict him from the lots in question.	Benjamin Priddy, the appellee, contended that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction to order his eviction in this case since neither a forcible entry nor a landlord-tenant relationship was presented. Priddy maintained that the legal process invoked by Steiner was inappropriate and requested the court to affirm the previous judgment made in his favor.

Nora Wheeler filed a chancery bill against William Mortland regarding a life insurance policy. The case took place in Calhoun County, Illinois, and the judgment was delivered on August 26, 1886. The background of the case centers on a policy originally issued to Wheeler's husband, Arthur W. Argust, in June 1878, which was valued at $5,000 and intended for Wheeler's benefit. However, on May 25, 1884, Argust surrendered this policy without Wheeler's knowledge or consent and obtained a new policy in favor of their two children. After Argust's death, the proceeds from the new policy were paid to Mortland, who acted as the guardian of the children. Wheeler claimed that since she was the initial beneficiary of the original policy, she should receive the funds. The court ultimately deemed that there were no grounds to establish equity jurisdiction in this case, leading to a dismissal.	The plaintiff, Nora Wheeler, argued that she was entitled to the proceeds from the life insurance policy that her husband, Arthur W. Argust, had originally taken out in her name. She claimed that the subsequent surrender of that policy by Argust, which resulted in a new policy benefiting their children, was done without her consent. Wheeler sought an accounting of the insurance proceeds and requested that the guardian, Mortland, pay her the funds from the new policy.	The defendant, William Mortland, contended that the contract of insurance was solely between the insurance company and Arthur W. Argust, meaning he had the legal right to surrender the initial policy and obtain a new one for the children's benefit. Mortland argued that there was no legal relationship (privity) between Wheeler and him that would allow her to maintain a lawsuit against him for the policy amount. He asserted that the widow had no right to the proceeds given the circumstances of the policy's surrender and subsequent designation.

The case of Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Ezekiel Phillips took place in September 1868 at the Union Depot in Chicago, Illinois. The incident involved an explosion of the boiler from a railroad engine operated by the Illinois Central Railroad Company. Ezekiel Phillips, a bystander, was injured during the explosion, suffering a bruise on his head and confusion from the blast. Prior to the explosion, the engine had been withdrawn from service due to machinery injury, repaired, and tested under pressure without any defects being found. On the day of the explosion, the engine was used for freight service before it exploded without warning while Phillips was nearby. The explosion caused pieces of the boiler to be thrown considerable distances, leading to Phillips's injuries. He subsequently brought a suit against the railroad company, seeking damages. A jury found in favor of Phillips, awarding him $7,000 in damages, which prompted the railroad company to appeal the decision.	Ezekiel Phillips argued that the explosion was due to the railroad company's negligence in maintaining their engine and boiler, which he claimed were old, worn out, and unfit for use. He asserted that proper care was not exercised by the company's servants in managing the engine, leading to the explosion that caused his injuries. Phillips sought damages for the physical injuries he sustained, which he claimed resulted from the explosion as well as lasting effects like paralysis.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that they had exercised due diligence in the maintenance and operation of the engine and boiler, asserting that it had been examined thoroughly by qualified mechanics and was in good condition prior to the accident. They argued that the explosion was not due to any negligence on their part and that there were no evident defects that could have been discovered through reasonable inspection. The railway sought to have the trial court's judgment reversed, claiming that the evidence did not support Phillips's allegations.

In 1886, in Illinois, the case "Forsythe v. Merrick" was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case was overseen by Judge Thomas A. Moran, with attorneys James E. Munroe representing the plaintiffs and Edward Roby along with Boutell & Waterman defending the defendants. The specifics of the incident that initiated the legal dispute were not detailed in the court opinion, but it was noted that there were complexities that warranted the case's review by the Supreme Court. The court decided to focus on the jurisdictional restrictions and procedural matters, determining that analyzing the case's details was unnecessary due to these factors.	The plaintiffs contended that the defendants' plea in abatement was insufficient. They sought a legal remedy from the court, arguing for the sustenance of their demurrer against the defendants' claims, thus intending to have the lower court's decision overturned.	The defendants maintained that their plea in abatement was valid and should be upheld. They argued against the plaintiff's claims, supported by precedents and legal principles outlined in their counsel's brief, asserting that the conditions of the case warranted the judgment as per their defenses.

Sjur Ammondson v. Adelia Ryan is a legal case that took place in Chicago, Illinois, originating in the year 1874. Adelia Ryan loaned Sjur Ammondson $2000, secured by a trust deed on property. Ammondson failed to make interest payments, and in 1876, the accumulated interest was added to the principal, resulting in a total debt of $3000. This new amount was secured by a second trust deed. In October 1880, the property was sold for $2500 after the trust deed was foreclosed. In 1881, a deficiency judgment of $2597.50 was entered against Ammondson. In 1882, Ryan filed a creditor’s bill to set aside a fraudulent property conveyance made by Ammondson to his wife and sought to subject the property to satisfy her judgment. Ammondson responded with claims of usury and alleged that he was misled regarding the sale of the property. The lower court and appellate court dismissed his claims, culminating in an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Adelia Ryan, the plaintiff, argued that the conveyance of property from Ammondson to his wife was fraudulent and without consideration, thereby seeking its annulment to enable her creditor's claim to be enforced against the property. Ryan requested that the court uphold the foreclosure sale and the deficiency judgment against Ammondson, asserting her entitlement to collect her owed debt through the proceedings initiated by her creditor's bill.	Sjur Ammondson, the defendant, filed a cross-bill claiming the loan agreement was tainted by usury because he was charged commissions and fees on the loan. He contended that he was misled and secured by Ryan, and therefore, he had not been properly notified of the foreclosure sale. Ammondson sought to redeem the property from foreclosure, have the judgment set aside, and request an accounting for the alleged excessive interest charged.

Margaret A. McMahill and William McMahill were married on October 7, 1879, in Warren County, Illinois. Prior to their marriage, they entered into an ante-nuptial agreement stating that neither party would have a claim to the other's property during their lifetime, except for specified provisions. Margaret, a widow with two minor children from a previous marriage, was to be supported by William, and the agreement stipulated that if she outlived him, she would receive $1,000 from his estate in lieu of dower, homestead rights, and a widow's award. William died in June 1881, leaving Margaret and his children from a previous marriage. Following his death, the county court disallowed Margaret's claim for a widow's award based on this agreement, a decision affirmed by the circuit and Appellate courts. The case centers on whether Margaret’s ante-nuptial agreement barred her from receiving a widow's award from William's estate.	Margaret A. McMahill claims that the ante-nuptial agreement should not bar her entitlement to a widow’s award, arguing that such an award is a legal right provided for her benefit and that the circumstances of the agreement do not exempt her from receiving it. She seeks to have the previous rulings overturned, claiming that the court's decision disregards established precedents protecting a widow's statutory rights.	The Estate of William McMahill contends that the ante-nuptial agreement explicitly outlined the terms of property claims post-marriage, wherein Margaret agreed to forgo a widow's award in exchange for $1,000. They argue that since there were no children of the marriage between Margaret and William, his estate had no legal obligation to provide a widow’s award. The estate requests that the court uphold the previous rulings that disallowed Margaret's claims to the widow's award.

In September 1868, the case "Hiram A. Pool, for the use of Cyrus Niles, v. Elijah Marshall" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from an action of assumpsit initiated by Hiram A. Pool, representing Cyrus Niles, against Elijah Marshall. The dispute involved a shared land purchase that both Pool and Marshall had made from a common grantor, Baker. This purchase had a mortgage attached to it. At the time of the transaction, Pool retained a portion of the purchase money with the intention of paying off the mortgage. However, the mortgage was paid using funds that were not Pool's but rather belonged to Baker, the grantor. Pool argued that he was entitled to recover the amount that was equitably due from Marshall for the share of the mortgage associated with Marshall's ownership of the land. The case was presided over by Judge S. L. Richmond in the Circuit Court of Woodford County prior to reaching the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Hiram A. Pool, claimed that he and the defendant had purchased land that was encumbered by the same mortgage. Pool argued that he had to pay the entire mortgage debt and sought to recover from Marshall the equitable share that corresponded to Marshall’s interest in the land. Pool contended that he should be reimbursed for the amount related to Marshall's share of the mortgage obligation.	The defendant, Elijah Marshall, contended that the plaintiff, Pool, did not pay the mortgage debt from his own funds but used money retained from the purchase price that belonged to Baker, their common grantor. The defense argued that since the funds used to pay the mortgage were not Pool's own but rather Baker’s, Pool could not claim reimbursement from Marshall as there was no legal basis for the recovery of the payment made.

The legal case of The Omaha National Bank v. The First National Bank of St. Paul took place in 1871 before the Illinois Supreme Court. The events leading to the case began on September 14, 1868, when the First National Bank of St. Paul issued a letter of guaranty to C. W. Nash, allowing him to draw drafts up to $14,000 against a firm called Merriam & Wilder. Nash drew several drafts on this guaranty, including $6,000, $2,000, and $4,000 drafts, some of which were forwarded to the defendant bank for collection. The case was brought to court when a $6,000 draft was protested by the defendant after it had collected previous drafts totaling $12,000. The plaintiff, Omaha National Bank, argued that the defendant was still liable for the entire $6,000 draft based on the letter of guaranty. However, the case hinged on whether the defendant was released from liability due to the previous payments made on behalf of Nash.	The Omaha National Bank contended that the First National Bank of St. Paul was liable to pay the $6,000 draft under the letter of guaranty. The plaintiff argued that regardless of the previous drafts and their payments, the letter of guaranty remained valid and that the defendant's liability had not been completely discharged, allowing them to recover the full amount from the defendant.	The First National Bank of St. Paul claimed that its liability under the letter of guaranty had been discharged once Nash had drawn drafts totaling $12,000, which were paid. They argued that since the $6,000 draft was drawn without endorsement on the letter of credit, they could not be held liable for its payment. The defendant emphasized that the plaintiff was aware of the prior payments and therefore could not claim any additional amounts beyond the limit set in the guaranty.

George W. Yocum v. John T. Smith took place in early 1872 in Sangamon County, Illinois. The case arose from a promissory note originally made by Yocum to T. W. Barbour for $320, dated March 5, 1868. The note was indorsed to M. Matteson shortly after its execution, who subsequently sold it to John T. Smith. Smith informed Yocum of the purchase by mail and subsequently demanded payment by the due date, demanding payment again eleven days after it was due. Yocum contested the validity of the note, claiming that it had been altered from an original amount of $300 to $320 without his consent. Smith, however, maintained that he purchased the note in good faith, and the note showed no evidence of alteration at the time of purchase. The case was tried in the Circuit Court, where the lower court ruled in favor of Smith.	Smith, as the plaintiff, argued that he was a bona fide holder of the promissory note, having purchased it in good faith and for value in the usual course of business. He contended that he had notified Yocum of the acquisition and that there was no indication of an alteration in the note when he bought it. Smith requested the court to enforce the terms of the note and hold Yocum liable for the full amount due, plus interest.	Yocum, the defendant, claimed that the note had been altered to increase its value, asserting that he had never authorized such a change. He introduced evidence that the note's original amount was $300, based on the deed to a patent right that constituted the consideration for the note. By asserting the defenses of non est factum, Yocum requested the court to dismiss Smith's claims due to the alleged unauthorized alteration of the note.

In September 1869, in Cook County, Illinois, the case "The Commercial Insurance Company of Chicago v. Lehman Huckberger et al." arose when Huckberger and others filed a lawsuit against the Commercial Insurance Company to recover damages based on an insurance policy covering their stock of goods. The trial was presided over by Judge Erastus S. Williams, resulting in a jury's favorable verdict for the plaintiffs after extensive testimonies and evidence presentation. The defense revolved around allegations of fraudulent conduct and misrepresentation by the plaintiffs regarding their losses, which the insurance company claimed were untrue or exaggerated. However, the jury found the plaintiffs' witnesses credible, ultimately leading to an appeal from the insurance company following the judgment in favor of the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs, Huckberger and others, claimed that the Commercial Insurance Company failed to honor their policy following a loss they incurred, seeking recovery for the damages based on the submitted insurance policy. They argued that their testimonies and evidence sufficiently validated their claims and were credible. Their legal request was for the court to uphold the jury's verdict affirming their entitlement to damages.	The defendant, the Commercial Insurance Company, contended that the plaintiffs had misrepresented their losses, asserting that their statements during the claims process were not accurate or truthful. They challenged the jury's findings, arguing that the plaintiffs should be bound by their original account of the loss submitted and that any errors made during the examination under oath were inadmissible. They requested that the appellate court reverse the lower court's judgment and rule in their favor.

In September 1874, the legal case of Daniel W. Gammon v. Leonard Hodges et al. was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Cook County, Illinois, where Daniel W. Gammon filed a bill in chancery against Leonard Hodges and others, seeking to enjoin the sale of certain lots in the city of Chicago. The dispute arose over a trust deed related to the property in question. On November 22, 1870, Leonard Hodges had sold the property to Felix B. Higgins, who paid a portion upfront and executed promissory notes for the remaining balance secured by a trust deed naming Hodges as the trustee. The trust deed was recorded, but the records were destroyed in a fire on October 9, 1871. Gammon purchased the property from a subsequent owner, Francis Crocker, believing there were no encumbrances due to the destroyed records. The court was tasked with determining whether the original owner was required to re-record the trust deed after its destruction to protect his rights from subsequent purchasers.	Daniel W. Gammon argued that he should be protected as a subsequent purchaser of the property due to the destruction of the trust deed record. He sought to maintain the injunction against any sale of the lots, claiming that the original recording of the trust deed should not bind him as it was no longer recorded following the fire. His claim hinged on the premise that the destruction of the record adversely affected his ownership rights.	The defendants, represented primarily by Leonard Hodges, contended that the original recording of the trust deed fulfilled the legal requirements for notice. They argued that once the trust deed was recorded, it provided public notice of the title no matter the subsequent destruction of the records. The defendants maintained that Gammon purchased the property at his own risk and had no rightful claim to challenge the trust deed's validity based on the destroyed records.

Matilda Phillips filed a lawsuit against Henry C. Dickerson in January 1877, following an incident that occurred on June 30, 1875, at their residences in Illinois. Phillips was seven to eight months pregnant when Dickerson entered her home without permission and engaged in a violent confrontation with her husband, who was on the porch with a boy named Alladice. During this confrontation, Dickerson verbally abused both the boy and her husband, threatening violence and drawing a knife. While Phillips remained in bed inside the house, she ultimately suffered from great fear and pain, which led to her giving birth to a stillborn child a few days later.
