The key issue revolved around whether Dickerson’s actions were the proximate cause of Phillips's premature labor and its consequences, with arguments surrounding the foreseeability of such a severe outcome from his behavior.	The plaintiff, Matilda Phillips, claimed that Henry C. Dickerson's unlawful entry and abusive behavior directly caused her emotional distress, resulting in premature labor and the loss of her child. She sought damages for the suffering and loss she endured due to the defendant’s violent conduct, arguing that his actions were entirely responsible for her resulting medical and emotional trauma.	Henry C. Dickerson defended against the claims by asserting that he could not reasonably have foreseen that his confrontation with Phillips's husband would result in harm to Phillips, who was not present during the altercation. He argued that the damages claimed were too remote and did not directly stem from his conduct, as he had no knowledge of Phillips's condition or proximity to the incident.

The case, "The People of the State of Illinois v. The Utica Cement Company," was decided on December 11, 1886, in La Salle County, Illinois. The litigation arose after the Utica Cement Company was accused of causing damage to the Illinois and Michigan Canal due to the improper disposal of waste materials from their factory. The plaintiffs, represented by the State of Illinois, claimed that the company's actions led to the contamination of the canal's waters. The court examined the circumstances surrounding the damage, particularly focusing on whether the flooding that caused the pollutants' movement into the canal could be attributed to the company's negligence or was simply an act of Providence due to extraordinary weather events that could not have been reasonably foreseen. Key individuals involved included the plaintiffs representing the State of Illinois and the defendants from the Utica Cement Company.	The plaintiff argued that the Utica Cement Company was liable for damages caused to the Illinois and Michigan Canal due to waste material it deposited on its premises. The plaintiffs contended that this waste contributed to pollution of the canal, especially during ordinary floods. They sought legal compensation for the damages and argued that the defendants failed to take necessary precautions regarding their waste disposal, which would have prevented harm to the canal during typical flooding events.	The defendant, Utica Cement Company, claimed that any damage to the canal was caused by natural and extraordinary floods, which they argued were not foreseeable. They contended that they had the right to use their property for lawful purposes and not liable for any consequences stemming from acts of Providence beyond their control. They argued that the plaintiffs’ claim should not prevail unless there was clear evidence of negligence on their part and that their actions were reasonable under the circumstances.

In 1870, in Illinois, a dispute arose between Luke Flanigan (the appellee) and Jefferson Crull (the appellant) regarding a sewing machine that had been won in a New York lottery scheme in which both belonged to a group of twenty-three ticket holders. The arrangement involved sharing the prize among members of the association. Flanigan received notification that a sewing machine was drawn and he instructed its delivery after paying freight charges. Subsequently, the majority of ticket holders agreed to sell the machine at an auction held during a picnic. Flanigan sold the machine to Crull’s wife, who was also a ticket holder, for $51 and delivered it to her. Flanigan claimed that Crull promised to pay him the auction price, leading to the lawsuit. In court, it was argued whether the suit should have been filed in the name of all ticket holders. The jury found in favor of Flanigan, concluding that he had the authority to sell the machine on behalf of the group and could sue for the sale proceeds.	Flanigan's main arguments were predicated on the assertion that he was authorized by the other ticket holders to sell the sewing machine and, as such, he had the legitimate right to claim the auction proceeds. He claimed that Crull's wife purchased the machine with Crull's consent and that the sale was executed according to the majority's agreement, thus allowing him to seek payment directly from Crull.	Crull contended that the lawsuit should have been filed jointly by all ticket holders, claiming it was inappropriate for Flanigan alone to seek the auction proceeds. Additionally, he argued that since his wife was a participant in the lottery and a buyer of the machine, there was a conflict that invalidated Flanigan’s claim to the proceeds in a personal capacity without involving all members.

The case "The Tug Montauk v. William H. Walker & Co." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1868, stemming from an action initiated in the Court of Common Pleas of Cairo in October 1866. The plaintiff, William H. Walker & Co., sought to recover damages against the steam tug Montauk under the Steamboat Warrant Act of 1857, which allowed for proceeding in rem against boats and vessels. The defendant contested the trial court's jurisdiction, arguing that the matter involved a maritime contract that should be adjudicated in an admiralty court, thus moving to dismiss the case. However, the court overruled the motion and subsequently issued a default judgment against the Tug Montauk for $109, the sum claimed by Walker & Co. The defendant appealed, challenging the jurisdiction of the state court over what they claimed was a maritime contract.	The plaintiff, William H. Walker & Co., contended that they were entitled to recover payment for supplies furnished to the Tug Montauk. They argued that the state courts had jurisdiction based on the provisions of the Steamboat Warrant Act, which was designed to provide a remedy for such claims related to domestic vessels operating within the state. Their legal request was for the enforcement of the judgment awarded by the Court of Common Pleas.	The defendant, Tug Montauk, argued that the alleged contract was a maritime contract, which under the Constitution should be adjudicated solely in federal admiralty courts. They claimed the case lacked proper jurisdiction in the state court and asserted that the supplies were provided to a domestic vessel at her home port, and thus, the matter should be analyzed under maritime law. They requested the court to dismiss the case due to the lack of jurisdiction by the state court.

In March 1844, in La Salle County, Illinois, Edward D. Taylor, a property owner in Adams' addition to the town of La Salle, faced a legal challenge regarding unpaid taxes for the year 1843. The local tax collector reported a list of properties with taxes due and sought to sell these properties to recover the owed taxes. Taylor objected to the sale, arguing that the tax collector's report did not indicate whether the owner had no personal property in the county that could be levied to satisfy the tax debt. The Circuit Court ruled against Taylor's objections, affirming the collector's report and allowing the judgment against the properties to stand. Taylor then appealed the decision, claiming various errors related to the court's jurisdiction, the sufficiency of the tax collector's report, and the need for proper notice regarding the judgment against his properties.	Edward D. Taylor contended that the Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction because the tax collector's report was insufficient. He argued that the report failed to state whether the owners had no personal property available for levying taxes, did not provide adequate notice of the judgment application against his properties, and violated specific statutory requirements laid out in the Revenue Law of 1838-1839. Taylor requested that the court reverse the judgment.	The State of Illinois, represented by the Attorney General, defended the tax collector's report by asserting that it substantially complied with the necessary statutory requirements. They emphasized that the law did not require the collector to state the inability to levy personal property explicitly; instead, such a presumption was made if the report followed the proper format. The defense argued that the court had jurisdiction and that due notice had effectively been provided.

In the case of Lida K. Stelle et al. v. George T. Lovejoy, the events transpired in Illinois, culminating in a ruling by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 16, 1888. The case involved Lida K. Stelle and Edward T. Stelle, administrators of the estate of Leonard G. Klinck, who acted on behalf of William H. Sisson. The defendants, Hebern Claflin and George T. Lovejoy, were implicated in a debt case stemming from an appeal bond associated with a prior judgment against Claflin for a debt amounting to $174 and costs. The appeal had been dismissed on November 21, 1876, and Sisson had subsequently recovered costs in the circuit court from Claflin. The plaintiffs accused Claflin and Lovejoy (the surety) of failing to pay the judgment and associated costs stated in the bond. The central matter revolved around whether the statute of limitations barred the action upon the bond, as the plaintiffs sought to recover the judgment amount, interest, and costs following the dismissal of the appeal.	The plaintiffs contended that the defendants (Claflin and Lovejoy) failed to comply with the obligations set forth in the appeal bond after the dismissal of the appeal. They claimed the right to recover the amount of the original judgment (plus interest and costs) against Lovejoy as the surety. They argued that the defense's assertions relating to the statute of limitations were misplaced and indicated the action on the bond was valid, not subject to the shorter five-year limitation applicable to judgments before justices of the peace.	The defense, represented by Lovejoy, argued that the cause of action was barred by the five-year statute of limitations. They contended that because the action to recover on the original judgment against Claflin was time-barred, the same should apply to the action on the bond, claiming that any potential obligation under the bond should be similarly extinguished due to the lapse of time since the initial judgment.

William Kerney (Appellant) and Charles Gardner (Appellee) were involved in a legal case originating from a debt action tied to a promissory note. The events took place in Fulton County, Illinois, around August 8, 1851. Kerney had purchased a tract of land from Gardner, which was recorded in a written agreement. The promissory note, amounting to $276, was to be paid within one year as part of the agreement to purchase the land, with Gardner promising to convey the title upon payment. Kerney claimed that Gardner had not fulfilled his obligation to convey the title to the land, asserting that no deed had been offered, and thus the consideration for the note was invalid. The case proceeded through the court system, culminating in a trial where the court had to determine the legitimacy of the note and the related claims about title conveyance. The court ultimately ruled in favor of Gardner, affirming that the note had been given in exchange for the land and that the conditions of the agreement supported the note’s validity.	The plaintiff, Charles Gardner, claimed that William Kerney owed him $276 based on a promissory note tied to a land purchase. Gardner argued that the execution of the note and the agreement for the land established a mutual obligation, with Kerney having failed to uphold his part by making the payment for the property. Gardner sought to have the court enforce the payment stipulated in the promissory note.	In his defense, William Kerney argued that the promissory note lacked valid consideration because Gardner never conveyed the title of the land to him as initially agreed. Kerney contended that since Gardner had no right or title to the land at the time of the agreement, the contract was void, and thus he should not be held liable for the note. He requested that the court dismiss the case on the grounds that Gardner breached their agreement by failing to provide the promised conveyance of title.

In 1887, a legal action was initiated involving Wm. Bourton, Sr. and Wm. Bourton, Jr. against Rathbone, Sard & Company in Cook County, Illinois. The case originated in the Justice Court, where the defendant (Rathbone, Sard & Company) obtained a judgment against the plaintiffs (the Bourtons). Wm. Bourton, Sr. subsequently appealed the judgment to the Circuit Court, while Wm. Bourton, Jr. did not participate in the appeal. This omission meant that the proper legal procedures, such as issuing a summons for Wm. Bourton, Jr., were not followed. As the case moved to trial, Wm. Bourton, Jr. was absent from the proceedings, prompting Wm. Bourton, Sr. to request a continuance on the grounds that his co-defendant had not appeared. The Circuit Court rejected this motion and ruled against both Bourton plaintiffs. The Bourtons contested this decision, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction over Wm. Bourton, Jr. because he had not been summoned properly.	The plaintiffs, Wm. Bourton, Sr. and Wm. Bourton, Jr., claimed that the Circuit Court erred in proceeding with the trial without ensuring proper legal processes were followed, specifically regarding the presence and summoning of Wm. Bourton, Jr. They argued that the court's refusal to grant a motion for a continuance was a mistake and that a judgment against Wm. Bourton, Jr. was invalid due to the lack of jurisdiction.	The defense argued that a plea filed by Wm. Bourton, Jr. in Justice Court constituted an appearance in the Circuit Court, thus questioning the jurisdictional claims made by the plaintiffs. They contended that the plaintiffs failed to provide evidence of the corporate existence of Rathbone, Sard & Company, which was critical to their case. The defense maintained that the procedural irregularities cited by the plaintiffs did not negate the validity of the trial and judgment.

The case of "The Council of the Village of Glencoe v. The People ex rel. John A. Owen" took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. The conflict arose after John A. Owen, as relator for the People, filed a petition against the Village Council of Glencoe. The village was incorporated in 1869, governed by a council consisting of a president and five councilmen. Owen alleged that the council failed to act on a petition presented on July 16, 1874, by thirty voters requesting a vote on whether the village should reorganize under a newer incorporation act. The council postponed the election to April 1, 1875, circumventing its duty to hold it promptly and allegedly intending to defeat the will of the electors. Owen sought a writ of mandamus to compel the council to act according to their obligations as outlined in the law, arguing the postponement was unreasonable and unjust. The case revolved around questions of whether the council had a discretion in setting election dates and whether the conduct showed an abuse of that discretion.	John A. Owen, representing the public's interest, asserted that the council of Glencoe improperly postponed an election concerning the village's reorganization for an unreasonable period. He claimed this delay amounted to a violation of the voters' rights and sought a writ of mandamus to compel the council to fulfill its statutory duty by appointing judges and providing adequate notice for the election, as required by law.	The council, represented by the defense, argued that the decision regarding the timing of elections fell within their discretion, maintaining that they were not obligated to comply with the relator's petition. They contended that the granting of such a mandamus would infringe upon the council's legislative discretion and that the relator had no standing as a private citizen rather than a public prosecutor. The council essentially claimed their actions did not constitute an abuse of discretion.

In 1864, in Washington County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between John Seibert and others (plaintiffs) and Isadore Bach and others (defendants) regarding a contract for the sale of wool. The plaintiffs claimed they had entered into a contract to purchase three thousand pounds of wool at seventy-eight cents per pound. Upon demand, the defendants failed to deliver the specified quantity of wool. The plaintiffs brought an action of assumpsit against the defendants, seeking damages for their failure to fulfill the contract. The case was presided over by Judge Silas L. Bevan at the August term of the court. A key point in the proceedings was the testimony of a witness, which indicated that the defendants had not agreed to sell a specific quantity of wool but only what they could spare after meeting their own needs. As a result, the plaintiffs' claim regarding the sale was inconsistent with the actual agreement, leading to a variance between the proof and the declaration. Ultimately, the court's opinion highlighted the error in permitting the jury to decide on the basis of proof that simply established that wool was purchased, without confirming adherence to the contractual details laid out in the declaration.	The plaintiffs argued that they had a valid contract for the purchase of three thousand pounds of wool at seventy-eight cents per pound. They sought damages for the defendants’ failure to deliver the wool as per their contractual obligation, claiming that they were entitled to the difference between the contracted price and the value of the wool at the time it was demanded.	The defendants contended that there was a significant variance between the contract as presented by the plaintiffs and the terms established through evidence. They argued that they had not promised to deliver a specific quantity of wool but only a portion they could spare, which was not in line with the plaintiffs’ claims. The defendants sought a new trial based on this variance and contended that the instructions given to the jury were flawed as they did not require proof of a definite sale as declared.

In 1887, Samuel Berkowitz initiated legal action against John T. Lester and Charles Schwartz in Cook County, Illinois, seeking to recover penalties under section 132 of the Criminal Code, which relates to gaming. The case was brought before the Circuit Court of Cook County, but the defendants objected, leading to a dismissal of the suit. The circuit court ruled that it lacked jurisdiction over quasi-criminal actions under the state's constitution. This decision prompted Berkowitz to appeal the ruling. The Illinois Supreme Court heard the case, with arguments centered on the jurisdiction of the Cook County Circuit Court in criminal and quasi-criminal matters, as outlined in the constitutional provisions governing the state’s judicial system. The crux of the matter hinged on whether the Criminal Court of Cook County held exclusive jurisdiction over such cases, which would preclude the Circuit Court from exercising that jurisdiction. The Supreme Court examined various sections of the state constitution and concluded that the Circuit Court's jurisdiction was not diminished by the existence of the Criminal Court. Thus, the case was set to be reviewed and possibly reversed based on the findings regarding jurisdiction.	Berkowitz claimed that the Circuit Court had jurisdiction to hear his case regarding the penalties under the Criminal Code. He argued that the dismissal of his suit was incorrect, as all circuit courts in Illinois, including Cook County, should have the authority to handle quasi-criminal actions like the one he presented. He sought a reversal of the dismissal and the enforcement of the penalties he was owed.	The defendants contended that the Circuit Court of Cook County lacked jurisdiction over the case, arguing that the constitution grants exclusive jurisdiction over criminal and quasi-criminal matters to the Criminal Court of Cook County. Consequently, they supported the circuit court's dismissal of Berkowitz's suit, asserting that the legislature's delineation of jurisdiction effectively barred his claims in the Circuit Court.

In the spring of 1887, John R. Ziegler, an undertaker from Peoria, Illinois, entered into a written contract with Studebaker Brothers Manufacturing Company based in South Bend, Indiana. Ziegler ordered two coaches and a set of harness for a total of $2,200, agreeing to pay half upon receipt and the balance secured with notes within a year. Ziegler initially accepted the harness delivered but delayed the shipment of coaches due to unfavorable weather conditions. When the coaches were eventually delivered, Ziegler asserted that one coach was damaged and did not meet the agreement's specifications, leading him to refuse acceptance of that coach. Subsequently, after attempts to resolve the dispute failed, Ziegler returned the coaches and harness to the company. Studebaker Brothers claimed damages for the breach of contract, leading Ziegler to counterclaim for damages due to non-fulfillment of the contract. The case proceeded to the Circuit Court of Peoria County, where a jury ultimately found for Ziegler, leading to an appeal by Studebaker Brothers.	Ziegler claimed that Studebaker Brothers failed to deliver the coaches in accordance with the contract, asserting that the delivered product was defective and damaged, specifically regarding the styling and condition of the coaches. He sought damages for losses incurred due to the alleged non-fulfillment of the contract, including lost business opportunities and additional expenses during the period when he was unable to provide services due to the defective delivery.	Studebaker Brothers contended that they fulfilled the contract by delivering the coaches, as specified, and argued that Ziegler had accepted and used the harness, which was undisputed as being in good condition upon delivery. They claimed damages for Ziegler’s refusal to accept the second coach and sought compensation for expenses tied to cleaning and varnishing the coaches, re-selling the harness, and their agent's trip to Peoria for negotiations.

In 1865, Marshall P. Ayers and others filed a legal action against William J. Metcalf and others in the Morgan Circuit Court in Illinois. The case involved a dispute over unpaid debts totaling $11,695.46, which the appellants claimed were amounts they had advanced as bankers during various business transactions. The debts included a detailed bill of items, starting with a balance due on April 1, 1865, and including interest charges incurred up to July 8, 1865. During the legal proceedings, an attachment was sought and levied on the defendants' property. The jury ultimately found in favor of the defendants, awarding them $4,043.67. The plaintiffs appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, raising concerns about the jury instructions, the consideration of interest payments, the nature of admissions as evidence, and procedural irregularities regarding juror attendance.	The plaintiffs contended that they were owed money for various transactions, including overdrawn checks and accrued interest on these advances. They argued that the instructions given to the jury were erroneous, as they misdirected the jury by excluding considerations for interest and express charges. The plaintiffs sought to have the case retried, believing the jury was not properly instructed on critical financial agreements and the validity of their claims.	The defendants countered that the jury instructions were appropriate and that they had received more funds from the plaintiffs than owed. They argued that the trial court’s decisions were correct and that the plaintiffs had not substantiated their claims for interest adequately. The defendants urged the court to uphold the jury's verdict in their favor and supported the position that the trial process was properly conducted.

The case "John Kellerman v. Phœbe Arnold" took place in January 1874 in Coles County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Phœbe Arnold, brought an action against her husband’s liquor seller, John Kellerman, under the Liquor Law after her husband, a chronic drunkard and a poor provider, faced issues related to his drinking habits. Arnold claimed that Kellerman's sale of intoxicating liquors to her husband had caused her harm. During the jury trial, the court awarded her $1,500 in damages. However, Kellerman appealed the decision, arguing that the verdict was not supported by the law or evidence, that the damages awarded were excessive, and that punitive damages were mistakenly given without proof of actual damages. The court noted the particular circumstances of Arnold's husband, who had not significantly contributed to the family's support, as crucial to determining whether Arnold had a valid claim. The case highlighted the complexities of personal injury claims linked to the behaviors of individuals with substance abuse issues.	Phœbe Arnold claimed damages for the sale of intoxicating liquor to her husband, arguing that it caused her financial and emotional harm. She asserted that Kellerman should be held accountable for enabling her husband's chronic alcoholism, which adversely affected her means of support and caused damage to her property (a table that was broken during one of her husband's drunken episodes). Arnold requested a jury trial and compensation based on her claims of damage caused by Kellerman's liquor sales to her husband.	John Kellerman's defense rested on the argument that Arnold had failed to prove actual damages resulting from his sale of liquor to her husband. He contended that Arnold did not demonstrate any injury to her person, property, or means of support that would warrant the damages awarded. Kellerman also challenged the notion of exemplary damages, stating that they cannot be awarded without established actual damages suffered by the plaintiff. He claimed there were no aggravating circumstances that justified the punitive aspect of the damages.

Jacob Rosencrans v. Frederick Schnacke et al. is a legal case that took place in 1883 in La Salle County, Illinois. The case stems from a conflict regarding a mortgage transaction that occurred on November 8, 1871. The dispute began when appellees (plaintiffs) sought to redeem certain lands from a mortgage given by Frederick Schnacke and his wife to the appellant (defendant), Jacob Rosencrans, securing a loan amounting to $3,795.36. The notes associated with this mortgage drew ten percent interest, but the plaintiffs alleged that usurious practices were involved due to reserved usury in the form of side notes. Key individuals in the case include Frederick Schnacke, the appellant Jacob Rosencrans, and several witnesses who provided conflicting testimonies about the timing and amounts of payments made. The main issues revolved around disputed payments—specifically the amounts of $700, $400, and $1,500 made on various dates. The case was referred to a special master to determine the exact amount owed and issues of credited payments. Ultimately, significant discrepancies in evidence and testimony led to challenges regarding claims for payment, usury, and the legitimacy of the mortgage.	The plaintiffs, led by Frederick Schnacke, claimed that certain payments he made towards the mortgage were not properly credited, and they accused the defendant of usury. Schnacke sought to establish that payments of $700 in October 1873, $400 in October 1875, and a disputed payment of $1,500 were legitimate and should be acknowledged. The plaintiffs argued that these payments should reduce the overall debt. Furthermore, they contended that the usurious interest should not be applied against them, aiming to redeem their property from the mortgage encumbrance.	Jacob Rosencrans (the defendant) contended that the plaintiffs failed to provide credible evidence for their claims regarding payment dates and amounts. He maintained that the payments were not credited as claimed by Schnacke and argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiffs was unreliable. In addition, Rosencrans asserted that the usury defense raised by the plaintiffs did not apply, as the mortgage transaction was constructed validly under their agreement. He sought the court to uphold the original terms of the mortgage and to deny the existence of the alleged credits claimed by Schnacke.

John Ging filed a lawsuit against H. Robinson & Son in 1889 in Effingham County, Illinois. The case stemmed from an attachment action against C. Ambuehl, with the plaintiffs alleging that Ambuehl was about to fraudulently conceal or dispose of his property to evade creditors. The parties claimed that Ambuehl owed them $109.95 for goods sold and delivered. Ambuehl did not contest the debt but denied the allegation of fraudulent concealment. Ging, claiming ownership of the attached goods, filed an interpleader. A jury found that the property belonged to Ambuehl at the time of the attachment and not Ging. The court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, ordering Ambuehl to pay damages for nonperformance of promises amounting to $109.25 along with costs of the suit. Ging appealed the verdict on several grounds, including that the jury's verdict contradicted the law and evidence, and argued that improper jury instructions were provided. However, the appellate court concluded that Ging failed to preserve the claims of error in the bill of exceptions, thereby limiting their ability to review the case.	The plaintiffs, H. Robinson & Son, argued that C. Ambuehl was attempting to fraudulently conceal his assets to avoid paying debts owed to them for merchandise sold. They sought judgment for the owed amount of $109.95 and successfully obtained a court ruling that not only affirmed this debt but also assessed damages of $109.25 against Ambuehl for the nonperformance of contractual obligations.	The defendant, C. Ambuehl, contested the allegation of fraudulent concealment but did not dispute the claim regarding the outstanding debt. John Ging, representing himself, appealed the jury's verdict and the lower court's decisions, asserting that the jury had reached a verdict contrary to law and evidence, complained about the jury instructions given, and challenged the court's ruling on the motion for a new trial.

In January 1875, a legal dispute arose in Logan County, Illinois when William B. Broadwell obtained a judgment against the firm of Thomas Alsop & Son for $555.97. Following the judgment, on March 11, 1875, an execution was issued and was levied by the sheriff on sixty-seven sacks of flour owned by the firm. On May 15, 1875, Thomas Alsop, representing the firm, initiated a replevin suit against the sheriff, seeking recovery of the seized flour. The initial trial in front of a justice of the peace favored Alsop, who claimed that the flour was exempt from execution due to his and his son’s circumstances. However, the sheriff appealed to the circuit court, where the case was again ruled in favor of Alsop without a jury. The subsequent appeal reached the Illinois Supreme Court, raising questions about the validity of the exemption claims made by Alsop in light of his son not formally joining the replevin bond and their lack of evidence to substantiate their claim of exemption.	The plaintiff, Thomas Alsop, contended that the flour seized was exempt from levy and sale under legal statutes. He claimed an undivided half of the flour as exempt, based on his assertion that he and his son co-owned the property, and that his son had authorized him to make such claims of exemption.	The defendant, represented by the sheriff, countered that there was insufficient evidence to support Alsop's claims of exemption. They argued that Alsop's son did not formally join in the claim and there was no proof presented that he had any exempt property. Furthermore, it was asserted that Alsop was not the head of a family, as required to qualify for certain exemptions, thereby rendering their claims unfounded.

In 1886, Anton Martin initiated a legal action against Sigmund Hochstadter and others in Cook County, Illinois. The case started before a justice of the peace, where Martin filed an affidavit of claim, prompting a default judgment against Hochstadter for $150.80 and costs. The defendant appealed this judgment, and on June 29, 1886, filed an appeal bond. The Circuit Court became involved when the justice transmitted relevant documents on July 9, 1886, after both parties entered their appearances. However, on August 18, 1886, the court entered a default judgment against Hochstadter for failing to submit an affidavit of merits. Subsequently, Hochstadter sought to vacate the default judgment on October 1, 1886, but the court denied this motion. The case went on appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court, raising questions about the necessity and timing for filing an affidavit of merits in such appeals.	Anton Martin claimed that he was entitled to a default judgment due to Sigmund Hochstadter's failure to respond appropriately after the claimant submitted the required affidavit of claim. Martin argued that the appellate process should recognize the validity of his initial affidavit, as stipulated by statutory provisions.	Sigmund Hochstadter asserted that the judgment was erroneously issued due to a lack of an affidavit of merits filed in a timely manner. He contended that he should be permitted to present his defenses as the applicable law allowed for an oral plea and that any affidavit of merits should be filed only when the case was ready for trial.

The case "J. W. Butler Paper Company v. J. L. Regan Printing Company" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 24, 1889. The lawsuit originated in the Superior Court of Cook County and revolved around an attachment suit initiated by J. W. Butler Paper Company against J. L. Regan Printing Company. The primary issue stemmed from a debt that was not due at the time the lawsuit commenced. The defendant contested the initiation of the lawsuit by filing pleas, which were ultimately struck from the files without acceptance from the attorneys who had withdrawn from the case. Following this, a default judgment was entered in favor of the plaintiff. However, the defendant, represented by new counsel, moved to vacate the default judgment, asserting that the debt was not due when the suit was launched. This motion was granted, allowing the defendant to defend the action on its merits and resulted in the plaintiff failing to prosecute the case. The trial was held on March 18, 1889, but the court dismissed the suit at the defendant’s request due to the plaintiff’s inaction, leading to a judgment for costs against the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, J. W. Butler Paper Company, asserted that they were entitled to a default judgment based on the alleged debt owed by the defendant, J. L. Regan Printing Company. They sought to enforce the attachment based on the claim of a valid and matured debt, which, according to them, justified the initial suit.	The defendant, J. L. Regan Printing Company, argued that the lawsuit was improperly initiated as the debt was not due at the time the attachment suit was filed. They successfully moved to set aside the default judgment, contending that the plaintiff's claims lacked a solid foundation and that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate any attempt to support their allegations. They requested the court to allow them to plead and contest the merits of the case.

In 1888, the case of D. R. Klinger, Impleaded, etc., v. The People arose in Piatt County, Illinois. The State's attorney filed a quo warranto information against D. R. Klinger and others, accusing them of usurping the office of drainage commissioners for the town of Blue Ridge and falsely claims regarding the organization of drainage districts. The respondents, Klinger, Vandervort, and Wooding, allegedly undertook to create multiple drainage systems without proper authority, laying out plots and levying taxes. The respondents argued that the town, under township organization since 1883, had indeed formed a drainage district according to the legal statutes. However, the State maintained that the district was never legally organized as such, and the proposed drainage systems could not efficiently work together. The court evaluated the legislative framework regulating drainage systems and concluded that the claimed drainage district was improperly formed, including vast lands, with many sections not benefiting from the single drainage plan. Following the evaluation of the case, the court issued a judgment of ouster against Klinger and his co-defendants.	The plaintiffs, represented by the State’s attorney, claimed that Klinger and the other respondents usurped their positions as drainage commissioners by organizing drainage districts without proper authority. They asserted that the alleged petition to form a drainage district was invalid, as it attempted to merge multiple water sheds requiring separate systems into one, and contended that the organizational steps taken had no legal basis under the provisions of the irrigation acts of 1879 and 1885.	The defendants, primarily Klinger, contended that the drainage district had been legally established based on a petition from a majority of landowners in Blue Ridge, according to the laws governing drainage organization. They explained the necessity of separate drainage systems due to the varied geography of the land and claimed to have acted within the legal framework when organizing the district. Klinger’s plea detailed the procedures followed in creating the district and defended against the claims of usurpation of office.

The case involves The First National Bank of Springfield and J. F. Ryan, along with other appellees, concerning a promissory note dated August 30, 1884, worth $4,200. The note was executed to facilitate a transaction between the appellees for a property purchased from P. P. O’Donnell, who originally intended to have the note discounted at the bank. The reimbursement was supposed to benefit O’Donnell, but when presented to the bank, the cashier, Weber, required O’Donnell to guarantee the note, leading to an alteration in its form. The alteration made the note payable to O’Donnell rather than to the bank, with implications for the liability of the appellees. The court had to decide whether the alteration discharged the original signers' liability or whether their obligations to the bank remained intact despite the changes. The case was tried without a jury and involved interpretations of contract law related to guarantees and material alterations.	The plaintiff, The First National Bank of Springfield, claimed that despite the alteration of the promissory note, the appellees should still be held liable for the amount due. They argued that the substance of the transaction remained unchanged, as the note was still intended for the bank's benefit. The bank sought recovery of the debt based on the original consideration of the loan made to the appellees for O'Donnell's benefit, asserting that the liability of the signers remained valid despite the material alteration.	The defendants contended that the material alteration of the promissory note destroyed its identity and thus discharged their liability. They argued that because the change in the wording of the note meant it was not valid in its altered form, they should not be held responsible for its payment. They asserted that the original agreement was fundamentally altered without their knowledge or consent, and thus they sought dismissal of the case against them.

Elijah T. Essex v. James McPherson is a legal case that was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Rock Island County, presided over by Judge George W. Pleasants. The dispute arose from a civil matter wherein the plaintiff, Elijah T. Essex, sought a trial against the defendant, James McPherson. The central issue that emerged during the trial was the participation of one juror who had placed a wager—a bet involving a necktie—favoring the defendant's victory. This information was not disclosed to the plaintiff until after the trial had concluded. Essex argued that the juror's prior wager represented a conflict of interest that compromised the integrity of the trial, thus leading to his motion for a new trial. The court's deliberations focused on whether the juror's bias, implied by the wager, was the basis for a mismanaged trial process.	The plaintiff, Elijah T. Essex, claimed that the verdict rendered in favor of the defendant, James McPherson, was unjust on the grounds that one of the jurors had previously bet that McPherson would win. Essex asserted that this situation violated the principles of impartiality required in a jury setting and requested a new trial, citing that the juror’s prior engagement created an inherent bias that could have affected the verdict.	The defendant, James McPherson, contended that the juror in question had affirmatively stated that he bore no bias or prejudice towards either party, and thus, his participation should not invalidate the trial outcome. The defense argued against the plaintiff's claims of juror incompetence and maintained that the verdict in favor of McPherson should stand, as the wager did not demonstrate sufficient influence on the juror's decision-making process.

In September 1869, the case of Jonathan K. Cooper v. Willard M. Randall et al. was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Peoria County, Illinois, when the defendants, Willard M. Randall and others, erected and operated a flouring mill on a lot adjacent to the plaintiff's property. The plaintiff, Jonathan K. Cooper, alleged that the operation of the mill caused significant amounts of chaff, dust, smut, and dirt to be thrown into his house, rendering it uncomfortable for habitation. This case was an appeal, as a jury had initially sided with the defendants, prompting Cooper to contest their decision. The legal discussion primarily revolved around the interpretation of what constitutes a material injury to property, with the plaintiff arguing that even slight injuries should provide grounds for compensation.	Jonathan K. Cooper claimed that the operation of the flouring mill next to his home caused considerable discomfort due to the debris it produced. He contended that the presence of chaff, dust, smut, and dirt amounted to a nuisance that affected the reasonable enjoyment of his property. Cooper sought damages proportional to the degree of injury he asserted was caused by the mill, arguing that the mere existence of discomfort warranted legal recourse.	The defendants, led by attorneys Olivek C. Geat and W.W. O’Bbieh, argued that the mill was lawfully erected and operated with the appropriate diligence to minimize adverse effects. They maintained that liability should hinge upon whether the mill materially and substantially harmed Cooper's property, suggesting that minimal or merely fanciful inconveniences did not justify compensation. Their position was that Cooper's claims lacked sufficient evidence of significant injury.

Abner C. Harding v. The Town of Hale took place in 1871 in Hale Township, Warren County, Illinois. The legal dispute arose when the Town of Hale accused Harding of encroaching upon a public highway, specifically the Monmouth and Oquawka road. The case began in a justice’s court, where Harding was initially found not guilty. The Town then appealed to the Warren County Circuit Court, where a jury convicted Harding, resulting in a motion for a new trial which was denied. The case was subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, where errors were questioned, particularly focusing on jury instructions and the definition of the highway's boundaries.  Evidence presented included historical records from the county commissioners' court regarding the authorized width of the road, which was initially established at fifty feet. Harding had built a fence for a hedge near the road, which plaintiffs claimed encroached on the highway. Arguments centered on whether the road had been properly dedicated and the legal conditions under which a landowner could maintain a fence on the highway margins without obstruction penalties.  Plaintiff claims and instructions suggested that any obstruction on a public highway deserved penalties, while defendant's actions sought to clarify the legal boundaries and rights related to the highway.	The plaintiff, the Town of Hale, claimed that Harding built a fence obstructing the public highway, therefore violating regulations concerning public roadways. They argued that the fence was unlawfully placed in an area of the highway that had been traveled and maintained as such for over twenty years. The plaintiff requested damages for this alleged encroachment and sought the assertion that Harding was guilty based on the jury's interpretation of the evidence of his fence's obstruction.	Harding contended that the fence was constructed in accordance with the law allowing property owners to erect protective fences on the margins of public roads, as long as they did not occupy more than six feet of the highway. He argued that the historical establishment of the highway at fifty feet meant his actions were legitimate. Harding also highlighted that the jury received misleading instructions that excluded consideration of legal protections provided under the statute. His legal team sought reversal of the conviction, asserting that the court's instructions unjustly hindered his defense.

The case "William Hamilton et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois" originated from an incident that took place on September 1, 1883, on the farm belonging to Samuel Parks in Illinois. Samuel Parks and his son were investigating disturbances in their watermelon patch when they encountered William Hamilton, Hat Mitchell, and William Eaton. The assailants were attempting to steal melons, leading to a confrontation. Parks, armed with a shotgun, tried to deter them, but a physical altercation ensued. Mitchell struck Parks' son, and Hamilton physically assaulted Samuel Parks. Witnesses indicated that during the altercation, there was an exchange of blows, with Mitchell and Hamilton using weapons including a hoe and a pistol. Subsequently, in March 1884, Hamilton and Mitchell were convicted of assault with intent to murder, receiving a two-year prison sentence. They appealed their conviction on grounds that the evidence did not support the indictment. The case then moved to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, represented by the state, claimed that the defendants conspired to invade Samuel Parks' property with the intent to steal, which resulted in a violent confrontation leading to an assault. The state argued that the actions of Hamilton and Mitchell constituted a serious criminal endeavor, justifying their indictment for assault with intent to murder. They requested the affirmation of the lower court's decision based on the defendants' involvement in this unlawful enterprise.	The defendants argued that the evidence presented at trial was insufficient to sustain a conviction for assault with intent to murder. They claimed that there was no proof that the hoe and the pistol were deadly weapons and challenged the nature of the indictment as being vague and informal. They contended that their actions did not amount to the charges laid against them and sought a reversal of their conviction.

In 1852, in Whiteside County, Illinois, Edward Newhall and his partners initiated legal action against Gilbert Buckingham, the assignee of Hoyt and Hoskins, due to a claim for goods worth nearly one thousand dollars sold to Hoyt. After learning that Hoyt had absconded, Newhall sought an attachment on Hoyt's assets, seizing a small stock of goods owned by the partnership of Hoyt & Hoskins. Subsequently, Hoskins assigned his interest in the partnership to Buckingham, who notified the sheriff and claimed ownership of the seized goods. A trial was held to determine the rightful ownership of the goods, leading to a verdict in favor of Buckingham, prompting Newhall to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, Newhall & Co., contended that they had a rightful claim over the partnership’s goods, asserting that the assignment made by Hoskins to Buckingham was invalid. They argued that the court had erred in recognizing Buckingham's claim and maintaining the goods in his possession, insisting instead that the partnership assets were liable for their debts in accordance with legal statutes governing partnerships.	Buckingham, representing the assignee interests, maintained that he possessed the rights to the goods following Hoskins' assignment. He claimed that the court rightfully found in his favor and that the partnership goods could not be claimed by creditors without direct legal provisions allowing such an attachment. He also argued that the circuit court’s ruling upholding his assignment was valid, and he sought to retain possession of the goods.

The case "Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Emma J. Keen, Admx." was decided in June 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court, emerging from an incident that occurred on December 11, 1871. The accident took place a few miles south of Centraba, Illinois, where a brakeman, the intestate of the plaintiff, Emma J. Keen, was killed due to a boiler explosion on a train. The train was running between Centraba and Big Muddy, and the explosion also claimed the life of the train's engineer, Houck, who was deemed responsible for the negligence leading to the accident. Both men were considered fellow-servants working in the same branch of employment, which complicated the plaintiff's ability to recover damages for the death caused by the explosion.	The plaintiff, Emma J. Keen, as administratrix for the deceased brakeman, argued that the railroad company was negligent in ensuring the safety of its equipment and operations, which led to her intestate's death. She sought damages for the loss of her family member and held the company accountable for the unsafe working conditions contributing to the boiler explosion.	The defendant, the Illinois Central Railroad Company, contended that they were not liable for the accident since the deceased brakeman and the engineer were fellow-servants. Therefore, based on the legal principle that an employer is typically not liable for injuries sustained by one employee due to the negligence of another in the same employment sphere, the defendant requested the court to dismiss the case.

In the year 1844, in Randolph County, Illinois, the case involved a dispute over a sixty-two-acre tract of land owned by tenants in common, which included Joseph Louvalle, Felix Buatt, Therese La Chapelle, and others. The plaintiffs were the heirs of Antoine La Chapelle, who had previously erected a valuable dwelling house on the property, purportedly increasing its value. The defendants, including Pierre Menard and others, initiated partition proceedings under a statutory framework, which led to the appointment of commissioners to partition the land. The commissioners reported that the land could not be divided and conducted a sale of the property, which was sold for $877.52. Following the sale, the plaintiffs filed a bill in chancery seeking compensation for the increased value attributed to the dwelling house before the proceeds were distributed among the parties. They obtained an injunction to halt the distribution of the sale proceeds. The defendants acknowledged the existence of the improvement but disputed its impact on the sale price. The Circuit Court ultimately dismissed the plaintiffs' bill, leading the plaintiffs to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs claimed that the dwelling house built by their ancestor on the land significantly enhanced its value. They sought compensation for that increase before the distribution of the sale proceeds, arguing that the defendants should not share in the benefits of the improvement without contributing to its costs.	The defendants contended that if the plaintiffs were entitled to compensation for the improvement, they should have raised that claim in the original partition proceedings, which would bar them from asserting it now. The defendants admitted the improvement but denied that it materially increased the land's value and sought to dismiss the appeal based on the conclusions of the original partition proceedings.

This case, titled "F. F. Randolph et al. v. Samuel S. Chisholm," was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on September 21, 1888. The case arose from the Circuit Court of Coles County, with Judge C. B. Smith presiding. The parties involved include the plaintiffs, F. F. Randolph and others, and the defendant, Samuel S. Chisholm. At the heart of the dispute was a mechanic's lien for repairs made to a mill. The plaintiffs claimed an interest in the property in question, although the key point of contention was Randolph's title to the lot at the time he contracted for repairs. The evidence indicated that Randolph was in possession of the property and claimed title, which meant that whatever interest he had was subject to the lien. The case had previously been before the court, and after remand, a trial was conducted leading to a decree that was now being challenged.	The plaintiff, F. F. Randolph, argued that he had a valid interest in the property despite questions about his title at the time of the contract for mill repairs. Randolph claimed that being in possession of the property substantiated his right to contract for the repairs and thereby established his entitlement to a mechanic's lien. The plaintiff's legal requests centered on confirming this lien against the defendant, Chisholm.	The defendant, Samuel S. Chisholm, contended that the plaintiffs did not demonstrate valid title to the property at the time the repair contract was made, thereby undermining any claims for a mechanic's lien. Chisholm also raised the issue concerning the rendering of a decree against Randolph by default, implying that it was improper given that a demurrer was still pending. However, it was noted that this aspect of the appeal was irrelevant since Randolph himself was not a party to the appeal.

In the case of The Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company v. Mary Ann White, the incident occurred on December 19, 1883, in Illinois, near the 41st street crossing of the railroad’s tracks. John White, a carpenter employed by the railroad, was engaged in building a sidewalk and was on the tracks measuring his work with a tape line alongside another carpenter. On that cold morning, a switch engine from the railroad approached White’s position at a speed of eight to ten miles per hour. Although statutory signals were given, the engineer observed White on the track and made an attempt to stop the engine; however, the stop was impeded because the conductor’s position prevented effective use of the lever. A flagman, who usually monitored the crossing, was absent at the time of the accident. As a result of being struck by the engine, White sustained injuries that ultimately led to his death. This incident sparked a lawsuit wherein White’s estate sought damages for alleged negligence on the part of the railroad company.	The plaintiff, represented by Mary Ann White as administratrix of John White's estate, claimed that the railroad company was responsible for White's death due to the gross negligence of its employees. The plaintiff contended that the absence of the flagman and the failure of the crew to stop the engine despite being aware of White's presence amounted to a lack of reasonable care. The plaintiff sought damages, arguing that although White was on the tracks, his actions did not warrant a total absolution of the railroad's duty of care.	The defendant, the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company, argued that John White acted negligently by being on the tracks and failing to exercise ordinary care, thus contributing to the accident that led to his injuries and death. The defendant indicated that White should have been aware of the approaching train and had the ability to avoid the incident. The railroad company requested a jury instruction that emphasized the need for the jury to consider White's potential negligence and affirmed that if White's lack of care resulted in the accident, the plaintiff could not recover damages.

James B. Morris et al. v. Isabella Robey took place in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, commencing on April 30, 1869. The case involved a dispute over the sale of several lots in Chicago that were auctioned off by the sheriff due to a foreign attachment suit filed against Isabella Robey’s deceased husband, James Robey. The plaintiff, Samuel Delamater, obtained a default judgment of $168.85 against Robey, leading to the sale of properties that were valued at over $20,000. The lots in question included eight specific lots from various subdivisions in Chicago. The sheriff's sale, held on September 6, 1867, concluded with Morris purchasing the lots for only $217.06, an amount significantly less than their market value. Following Robey’s death in 1869, his estate, represented by Isabella Robey, challenged the sale, arguing that the sale process was improper as the lots were sold en masse without adequate efforts to sell them separately, leading to a shocking undervalue and an injustice against the estate.	The plaintiff, Isabella Robey, claimed that the sale of the properties was unfair and sought to set it aside based on significant inadequacy of price and irregularities in the sale process. She argued that the properties were erroneously sold together rather than individually or in smaller groups, which compromised their true market value. She requested that the court cancel the sheriff's deed and return the properties to her estate, advocating that the irregular sale violated her rights and caused irreparable harm.	The defendant, James B. Morris, contended that he was a bona fide purchaser and argued that the sale was conducted legally and should be upheld. He maintained that the plaintiff had not shown sufficient grounds for relief and claimed that the sale’s legitimacy was reinforced by the lawful actions of the sheriff and the absence of any defect in title. Morris argued that the court’s prior judgment allowing the sale reflected the procedural correctness. Additionally, he cited that any delay in the plaintiff's claims could be considered laches, suggesting that the claim for equitable relief should be barred due to the plaintiff's inaction.

In June 1887, Dennis Murto lent $225 to Robert McKnight through a promissory note and book account while McKnight was residing in Keithsburg, Illinois. Soon after, McKnight moved to Wichita, Kansas, sparking concerns regarding the payment of his debt. Murto spoke with Charles McKnight, Robert's son, who acknowledged the family's impending move and expressed his willingness to assist Murto with the debt. Charles assured Murto that he would take care of the obligation if Murto refrained from taking any legal action against Robert McKnight's properties as they prepared to relocate. However, despite subsequent conversations where Charles reiterated his father's debt responsibility, he eventually denied any agreement to pay and refused to acknowledge the alleged debt at a settlement meeting in December 1887. Murto ultimately filed suit against Charles McKnight on February 7, 1888, in Mercer County Circuit Court, aiming to recover the owed amount based on the verbal agreement with Charles. The case centered around the lack of written evidence for Charles' promise, which was critical given the Michigan statute of frauds stipulating that certain agreements, including promises to pay another's debt, must be in writing to be enforceable.	Dennis Murto claimed that Charles McKnight verbally promised to pay his father's debt to prevent him from taking legal actions against Robert's properties as they were being removed from Illinois. Murto sought a judgment that would require Charles to fulfill this promise, arguing that his reliance on Charles's assurance justified his forbearance in debt collection efforts from Robert and constituted a binding agreement for repayment.	Charles McKnight argued that his alleged promise to pay his father's debt was not valid under the statute of frauds, which mandates that agreements to pay the debts of another must be in writing. He maintained that no such written agreement existed and denied any intention or obligation to assume responsibility for Robert's debts. Furthermore, he contended that Robert McKnight's obligation remained unchanged, strengthening his position that the verbal contract was unenforceable.

Edward Wilson, serving as conservator for Sarah Littlejohn, initiated a legal case against Magdalena Scovel and others in 1888, in Fulton County, Illinois. The dispute centered around a promissory note on which Scovel claimed a judgment had been obtained. The main issue was whether Sarah Littlejohn was mentally competent at the time the note was allegedly assigned to Scovel. Wilson sought to prevent Scovel from collecting on the judgment by arguing that Sarah was not in a mental state to legally transfer the note, questioning the validity of the assignment and the goodwill of the transaction. The Circuit Court dismissed Wilson's bill, ruling in favor of Scovel, which led to an appeal by Wilson to the Illinois Appellate Court.	Edward Wilson, as conservator, claimed that the assignment of the promissory note to Magdalena Scovel was invalid due to Sarah Littlejohn's alleged mental incapacity. He requested the court to restrain Scovel from collecting a judgment based on the note, arguing that the assignment lacked legal validity and questioning the consideration and integrity of the transaction.	Magdalena Scovel defended against the claims by asserting that the assignment of the promissory note was valid and that the judgment obtained was rightful. Her main arguments rested on the assumption that Sarah Littlejohn was competent to assign the note at the time of the transaction. Scovel also stood to recover costs as per the dismissal of Wilson's bill.

In 1851, Samuel Steele engaged in a purchase agreement with William Hobbs for a mare at the price of $70. The agreement included a clause stating that if Steele sold the mare in the fall for less than the purchase price, Hobbs would refund the difference. Steele took possession of the mare, but shortly thereafter, it became afflicted with poll-evil, rendering it worthless. Despite Steele's efforts to care for the mare and sell it, he was unable to find a buyer due to the animal's condition. In 1853, after returning from California, Steele offered the mare back to Hobbs, requesting a refund of the purchase price. Hobbs refused to accept the mare or refund the money, leading Steele to file an action of assumpsit against Hobbs. The case was tried in the Hardin Circuit Court, where a jury ruled in favor of Hobbs. Steele's subsequent motions for a new trial were denied.	Steele argued that he had fulfilled his obligations under the purchase agreement by taking care of the mare and attempting to sell it. He claimed that the mare becoming worthless was not his fault, and he rightfully demanded the return of the $70 paid to Hobbs, as the consideration for the sale had entirely failed.	Hobbs contended that Steele was aware of the risks associated with purchasing the mare at the time of the agreement. He introduced testimony indicating that other buyers had previously inquired about purchasing the mare at higher prices. Hobbs asserted that he should not be responsible for the mare's depreciation in value, which occurred after the sale.

This case is titled "The People, etc., v. William Smith" and was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 4, 1885. It originated as a proceeding under the Bastardy Act initiated by Sarah Carroll against William Smith before a justice of the peace. The complaint was filed on April 13, 1883, and later appealed to the circuit court after the defendant entered a recognizance. The defendant moved to dismiss the case due to the death of the prosecuting witness, Sarah Carroll, and sought to suppress her deposition taken before her passing. The circuit court granted this motion, dismissing the proceedings based on the death of the prosecuting witness. The plaintiffs challenged this action through an appeal, asserting that the death of the prosecuting witness should not result in the dismissal of the case. Previous cases, including The People v. Nixon and Hauskins v. The People, were cited to argue that the public interest and the mother’s rights in the prosecution should prevail despite her death.	The plaintiff, The People, represented by the state, argued that the dismissal of the case based on the death of the prosecuting witness was erroneous. They contended that under the Bastardy Act, the state's interest in ensuring the father contributes to the support of the child remains intact even after the mother’s death. They requested the court to reverse the dismissal and remand the case for further proceedings, emphasizing the importance of the prosecution for public welfare.	The defendant, William Smith, through his counsel, argued that the death of the prosecuting witness warranted a dismissal of the proceedings. They maintained that the case lacked sufficient grounds to continue without the presence of the mother as the original complainant. The defense sought to suppress any evidence linked to the deceased and requested the case to be dismissed entirely based on this premise.

The case, "The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company v. The People, etc.," occurred in 1883 in Illinois. The incident arose from an indictment against the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company under Sections 221 and 222 of the Criminal Code, which address public nuisances and penalties for creating or continuing such nuisances. The indictment claimed that the railway company unlawfully maintained a railroad track on a street, which constituted an obstruction. However, the indictment failed to explicitly state that the track was indeed an obstruction, leading to questions about the nature of the nuisance. The court examined the evidence presented during the trial, which included testimonies about the effects of the track on the street, but ultimately concluded that the mere presence of the railroad track could not be classified as a public nuisance without more specific allegations supporting the claim.	The plaintiff, in this case, argued that the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company had created a public nuisance by unlawfully maintaining a railroad track on a public street. They contended that the continued presence of this track obstructed the street, therefore infringing upon the public's right to free access. The plaintiff sought a reversal of the lower court's decision regarding the indictment, emphasizing that the track constituted an obstruction under the criminal code, warranting appropriate legal penalties.	The defendant argued that the indictment was flawed and insufficient. They maintained that the mere presence of a railroad track in a street does not automatically denote a public nuisance and that the indictment failed to clearly establish that the track obstructed the street as required by law. The defense asserted that the prosecution did not provide enough evidence to prove that the railroad track materially obstructed the street, thus challenging the validity of the charges. They sought to have the indictment quashed based on these assertions.

In 1881, The Rock River Packing Company was established in Sterling, Illinois, with Joseph T. Miller as a director and shareholder, contributing significant capital. By 1885, the company was struggling financially and had borrowed $2,000 from Miller, documented by three unpaid judgment notes. On October 16, 1885, in an effort to settle his debts, the company sold surplus property—80,000 cans and some tin—to Miller for $1,877. Shortly after, Miller leased two storage rooms from the company. However, on October 31, 1885, Thomas S. Beach, the Sheriff, and George G. Keefer, his deputy, executed a seizure on the property to satisfy a judgment against the company from Blatchford & Company, despite Miller's prior notice of ownership. Miller brought a trespass action against Beach and Keefer for the unlawful seizure and sale of his property.	Miller claimed that as the rightful owner of the cans purchased from The Rock River Packing Company, the seizure of his property by Beach and Keefer constituted trespass. He argued that the sale was legitimate and without fraud, as it was made in payment of a bona fide debt. Miller sought damages for the illegal breaking and entering, seizing, taking, and selling of his property.	The defendants, Beach and Keefer, argued that the seizure was justified as it was executed under a legal judgment against the corporation. They contended that Miller, being both a director and a stockholder of the corporation, could not rightfully purchase its assets without violating corporate regulations, and they raised concerns about the financial state of the corporation at the time of the sale as potential evidence of fraud.

The case of Peter Gizler v. George Witzel took place in June 1876 in Madison County, Illinois. The incident at the center of the case involved an altercation between the plaintiff, Peter Gizler, and the defendant, George Witzel. The dispute arose when Witzel confronted Gizler in his vineyard, demanding he leave the premises. After Gizler crossed the fence and entered the street, Witzel followed him, brandishing a knife. Gizler picked up a club for defense, leading to a confrontation in which Witzel allegedly struck Gizler with the knife, resulting in injury. The trial was presided over by Judge William H. Snyder. The jury found in favor of Gizler, awarding him $100 in damages. Witzel appealed the decision, arguing that the verdict was not supported by the evidence presented.	The plaintiff, Peter Gizler, claimed that he was assaulted and injured by the defendant, George Witzel, who followed him into the street while wielding a knife. Gizler contended that Witzel's use of the knife was excessive and unprovoked, asserting that he had acted in defense only after Witzel's attack. Gizler's legal requests included compensation for damages resulting from the assault.	The defendant, George Witzel, argued that the verdict was contrary to the evidence, asserting he acted in self-defense. Witzel maintained that he did not initiate the confrontation and claimed that Gizler struck the first blow. He contended that the jury was improperly instructed and sought a reversal of the judgment based on these arguments.

In 1845, Alonzo Pate was indicted for forgery during the April term of the Adams Circuit Court in Illinois. The indictment contained three counts: forging a receipt for money claiming to be signed by George Randall, publishing the forged receipt as genuine, and forging a contract for land transfer from Randall to Pate. Each count alleged that the acts were intended to defraud Randall. Pate pleaded not guilty, but the jury found him guilty and sentenced him to nine years in the penitentiary. Pate's trial involved disagreements over evidence admissibility and jury conduct, leading to his motion for a new trial based on alleged errors. His petition was denied, leading to an appeal based on various alleged errors during the trial, including witness testimony issues and jury separation without Pate's consent.",	Pate, as the plaintiff in error, argued that the trial court made several errors: admitting the testimony of a specific witness (Phillips) while excluding another (Crawford), giving misleading jury instructions about reasonable doubt, allowing the jury to separate without his consent, and denying his motion for a new trial based on new evidence. He contended that these errors affected the fairness of his trial and warranted a reversal of the original judgment.",	The defense, representing the People of the State of Illinois, contended that all decisions made by the trial court were appropriate and within legal bounds. They argued that the witness testimony admitted was necessary to counter the defense's claims and that the jury instructions adhered to proper legal standards. Additionally, they maintained that the separation of the jury was presumptively consented to by Pate, and the court held no obligation to grant a new trial, as such decisions rested within the discretion of the Circuit Courts.",

In 1888, in Cook County, Illinois, Virginia B. Holmes filed a case against Henry V. Bemis concerning a judgment entered by confession related to a note issued by Holmes to Ira Holmes as an accommodation note. The background reveals that the note served as collateral for a larger $5,000 note for which Bemis was a guarantor. When Ira Holmes failed to pay, Bemis fulfilled the obligation, leading to the conflict over the judgment regarding the accommodation note. The Illinois Appellate Court reviewed the Superior Court's decision to deny Holmes' motion to vacate the judgment in favor of Bemis and decided on the validity of the confession. The court examined affidavits and determined that the evidence did not compel a trial on the merits or justify vacating the judgment.	Virginia B. Holmes contended that the judgment by confession entered against her was invalid because it did not strictly adhere to the terms laid out in the warrant of attorney. Holmes sought to open the judgment, claiming that it was an accommodation note and that Bemis should have had notice of this status. She requested a trial on the merits, arguing that the evidence presented created a conflict that necessitated jury consideration.	Henry V. Bemis argued that the judgment was valid as the note was delivered without any restrictions, and he had no notice that it was an accommodation note. Bemis maintained that, as he took the note before maturity and for value, he was entitled to affirm the judgment. He contended that the affidavits submitted by Holmes did not present sufficient evidence to warrant reopening the judgment or to show that any defense existed concerning his claim.

The case of Dugald A. McMillan v. Sebastian S. Lovejoy was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the final judgment delivered on January 25, 1886. The dispute originated in Stephenson County, Illinois, where McMillan was sued by Lovejoy based on a judgment rendered against him in Rock County, Wisconsin. The initial judgment awarded Lovejoy $1,555 in damages, along with $22.54 in costs, reflecting a total of $1,577.54. McMillan's legal team raised the defense of nul tiel record (no such record) and release, arguing against the validity of the Wisconsin judgment's certification. The case proceeded to trial, where a verdict was rendered in favor of Lovejoy, leading McMillan to appeal to the Appellate Court and subsequently to the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal question at hand was whether the transcript from the Wisconsin court, lacking specific formalities known as "placita," could be admitted as evidence.	Lovejoy claimed that a valid judgment had been issued in his favor by the Wisconsin circuit court and sought to recover the amount awarded in that judgment. His argument was that the properly certified transcript of the judgment should be sufficient evidence to enforce the debt against McMillan, regardless of the alleged formatting deficiencies.	McMillan's defense rested on the assertion that the judgment transcript lacked "placita," which they argued was a fatal defect. His legal team contended that without this formal requirement, the validity of the judgment could not be established, and therefore, the action upon which Lovejoy relied was legally unsound. They sought to dismiss the claim based on these grounds.

The case "The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy R. R. Co. v. Mary J. Lee, Admx." originated from an incident that occurred in 1872 at a railroad crossing in Illinois. Darius B. Lee, the deceased, was driving his team and wagon when he collided with a train operated by the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company. Following the accident, Mary J. Lee, as administratrix of Darius B. Lee's estate, filed a lawsuit against the railroad company, claiming negligence led to her husband’s death. A trial was conducted in November 1872, resulting in a jury verdict awarding $5,000 to the plaintiff. The case was subsequently appealed, focusing on the admissibility of testimony and the instructions given to the jury regarding comparative negligence.	The plaintiff, Mary J. Lee, argued that the railroad company was negligent in operating its train, specifically claiming that the train was traveling at an unsafe speed and that the company failed to sound the required signals (a bell or whistle) as it approached the crossing. She requested damages for the death of her husband, asserting that the company’s negligence directly contributed to the accident.	The defendant, the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company, contended that Lee's own negligence was a significant factor in the accident. They argued that he failed to exercise ordinary care for his safety, as he did not look for oncoming trains before approaching the crossing. They claimed that even if the train had not sounded its signals, this omission alone did not constitute negligence leading to liability, especially if the deceased was grossly negligent.

The case of Bernhard Hund v. Anton Geier took place in June 1874, in St. Clair County, Illinois. The central incident involved an accident where Anton Geier (the defendant) had obtained permission to haul earth across Bernhard Hund's (the plaintiff) property and alleyway. Geier sent his son with a team of horses to carry out this task. During this time, Hund's young son was kicked by one of the horses and suffered severe injuries, prompting Hund to seek medical attention. After the incident, Geier visited Hund to express regret and inquired about the physician treating his son. He suggested that Hund should hire a different doctor, claiming he would cover the medical expenses. However, after thirty-six visits by the physician, who billed Hund $100, Geier refused to pay, arguing that he did not agree to cover any costs related to the chosen physician. The dispute escalated to a legal trial, where the jury found in favor of Hund, leading Geier to appeal the decision. The appellate court reviewed the case, considering the nature of Geier's promise and the question of negligence involved.	Bernhard Hund's main arguments rested on the assertion that Anton Geier had made a clear promise to pay for his son's medical expenses following the horse-related injury. Hund contended that this promise, made in a moment of sympathy, should be upheld, as he had incurred costs by hiring a physician. He sought recovery of the full amount indicated in the medical bill, which Geier refused to settle, leading to the lawsuit initiated by Hund.	Anton Geier argued that his promise to pay for medical expenses was conditional and only applicable to reasonable charges for treatment by another doctor, not for the existing physician. He contended that there was no established consideration for the promise since Hund had already engaged the physician before Geier made his suggestion.
