Furthermore, Geier claimed that the existing physician's fees may have been exorbitant and not reflective of reasonable charges, thus arguing that he was not liable for the payment.

John Baxter, along with three others, was indicted for the murder of George Davenport during the October term of the Rock Island Circuit Court in 1845. They pleaded "not guilty" and requested a change of venue due to perceived prejudice against them, supported by an affidavit. The court approved a change to Carroll County, which was not the nearest county, prompting Baxter to object. Ultimately, despite moving for a change of venue several times, Baxter's motions were overruled. Meanwhile, his co-defendants were tried and executed. During the trial, the prosecution introduced the records of their convictions to the jury, which Baxter contested unsuccessfully. The jury found Baxter guilty, leading to a death sentence. Baxter subsequently sought a writ of error, raising multiple causes of error related to the change of venue and the introduction of evidence.	Baxter's main arguments included the assertion that the court erred by changing the venue to Carroll County instead of a closer county, claiming that this decision compromised his ability to receive a fair trial. He also contended that the introduction of his co-defendants' conviction records was improper and prejudicial against him.	The People of Illinois argued that Baxter had waived his objection to the venue change by moving to remand the case to Rock Island and claimed that the court's decision to allow the introduction of the conviction records was permissible, as the rules allowed the prosecution to establish guilt based on similar charges against co-defendants.

In January 1867, the case of Oliver C. Kelsey v. William S. Berry took place in Jacksonville, Illinois. The lawsuit was filed by Oliver C. Kelsey against William S. Berry, who owned the Mansion House hotel where Kelsey was a guest. Kelsey alleged that his valise was stolen while he was staying at the hotel. On the evening in question, Kelsey arrived by stagecoach around 6 PM, handing his valise to a hotel porter. Subsequently, a soldier at the hotel claimed the valise as his own and ordered the porter to take it inside. Kelsey left the hotel for the evening and returned the following morning. Evidence presented included testimony from the constable who served the summons and a clerk who noted that the soldier had taken the valise from behind the counter. The case revolved around whether Berry, as the innkeeper, was responsible for the valise's safekeeping, considering the actions of Kelsey and the soldier.	Kelsey argued that as a guest of the hotel and having handed his property to a hotel employee, the defendant (Berry) was responsible for the safe-keeping and return of his valise. He claimed that the hotel management failed to protect his belongings and was therefore liable for its loss. Kelsey sought damages for the value of the stolen valise based on the principle that innkeepers are liable for guests' belongings entrusted to them.	Berry contended that Kelsey had acted negligently by allowing another individual (the soldier) to claim the valise as his own without informing the hotel staff of its true ownership. Berry argued that this constituted a lack of proper care and responsibility on Kelsey's part, effectively releasing the hotel from liability for the loss. The defense claimed that Kelsey's failure to assert his ownership permitted the soldier to take the valise, asserting that the plaintiff's negligence was the true cause of the loss.

Solon Cumins et al. v. William Wood is a legal case that took place in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. The case arose when William Wood, the plaintiff, stored his household furniture with the defendant, William Wood, and alleged that certain articles were either broken or lost while in the defendants’ care. When Wood requested the return of his goods, some were returned damaged, and certain carpets were not returned at all. The case hinged on the question of who bore the burden of proof regarding negligence in the action brought by Wood against Cumins & King, the defendants. The court found that if a bailor demonstrates that the goods were in good condition when stored and were returned damaged or were not returned at all, the law presumes negligence on the bailee's part (the defendants) and requires them to prove they exercised proper care. The court concluded that the defendants were unable to adequately explain the loss of the carpets, which further strengthened the presumption of negligence against them.	The plaintiff, William Wood, claimed that the defendants were negligent in their handling of his stored goods, leading to the loss or damage of his household furniture. He requested compensation for the value of the missing and damaged items, asserting that they were stored in good condition and should have been returned undamaged. The basis of his claim rested on the traditional legal principle that places the burden of proof of negligence on the bailee when the goods are returned in a damaged state.	The defendants, Cumins & King, contended that they did not have the burden to prove negligence as there was no definitive evidence demonstrating that they had been negligent in the care of the furniture. They argued that the loss of the items, particularly the carpets, could have been attributed to accidents beyond their control, such as damage from a fire, which they claimed was the explanation for the condition of the goods when Wood retrieved them. The defendants requested the court to reverse the judgment of the lower court, arguing that the plaintiff had not met the necessary burden of proof regarding the alleged negligence.

Joseph King was involved in a legal case against Anson Haines and Jonathan Haines, where the action of assumpsit was instituted in January 1860 in Macon, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute concerning a partnership involving King and his co-partner Whitney. Anson and Jonathan Haines asserted claims against King as the surviving partner of Whitney & King. King denied the existence of the partnership and claimed there was no joint liability with Whitney, supporting his plea with an affidavit. The case went to trial, where the court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs (Haines), leading King to file a writ of error to reverse the judgment. Central to the case was the interpretation of the relevant statute concerning the verification of affidavits related to pleas in abatement and the necessary proof of partnership and liability when disputed by the defense.	The plaintiffs, Anson and Jonathan Haines, argued that Joseph King was jointly liable for the debts despite his denial of the partnership. They maintained that the execution of notes associated with the alleged partnership established King’s obligation to pay. They sought a judgment against King, relying on the notion that even if King contested the partnership, the notes themselves were sufficient evidence of his liability.	Joseph King countered by denying the existence of the partnership with Whitney and asserting that he should not be held jointly liable for any obligations tied to the partnership. His defense included the argument that the affidavit supporting the plea in abatement was insufficient and failed to positively attest to the truth of the claims. King contended that the plaintiffs were required to provide proof of partnership before the notes could be admitted as evidence against him.

The case of "The County of Peoria v. John Harvey" took place in Peoria County, Illinois, with the decision being rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1857. The dispute arose from an act passed on February 11, 1853, which authorized the establishment of a state road from Peoria to Rock Island. The commissioners appointed to oversee the road's layout assessed damages to various landowners, including John Harvey. However, Harvey's claim was that the damages assessed to him were inadequate, arguing that they would amount to at least $4,000. The County of Peoria objected to the assessments and sought to dismiss Harvey's appeal by claiming the county court lacked jurisdiction and that no damages had been properly awarded. Despite these objections, the court allowed the case to proceed, and a jury ultimately awarded Harvey $200 in damages. The County of Peoria's subsequent requests to overturn this decision through motions for a new trial were denied, leading to an appeal.	John Harvey, the plaintiff, argued that the damages assessed by the commissioners for the road cutting through his property were significantly too low, amounting to only a fraction of the actual loss he would incur. He sought a reassessment of the damages, asserting that the proper legal process for establishing the road was followed, despite the county's insistence on procedural defects.	The County of Peoria, as the defendant, presented multiple arguments to dismiss Harvey’s claims, asserting that there was no statutory basis for his appeal, as no damages were assessed to him initially, and that a jury was not properly constituted to evaluate such damages. They argued that the court lacked jurisdiction, objected to the introduction of evidence from Harvey, and contended that the evidence did not demonstrate that the road was legally established or that they had the authority to open it.

In June 1870, the case of Jay N. Faulk v. John W. Kellums originated in Effingham, Illinois, when John W. Kellums initiated a trespass action on the case against Faulk and Andrew M. Kirkpatrick concerning a promissory note. Both defendants were served with legal process; however, only Faulk entered a plea of "non-assumpsit," denying that he executed the note. The case was later moved to Clay County for trial, where a jury found in favor of Kellums, awarding him $4,493 in damages. Following this verdict, Faulk's defense team filed for a new trial and sought to prevent the judgment from being entered, but these motions were denied. Faulk continued to appeal after the jury's finding had been put in a legally valid form, but he raised various objections regarding the admissibility of testimony during the trial, highlighting the complexities involved with allegations of forgery and perjury.	The plaintiff, John W. Kellums, claimed that Jay N. Faulk and Andrew M. Kirkpatrick were liable for a promissory note they had presumably executed. He sought a legal remedy through the court to recover the amount of the note, alongside interest, totaling $4,493. Kellums argued that he was entitled to this sum based on the defendants' failure to fulfill the obligations of the note.	The defendants, represented by Faulk and Kirkpatrick, contended that the judgment entered against Faulk was improper since both defendants were served but only one had pleaded. They asserted that the court should have either dismissed the case regarding Kirkpatrick or included him in the judgment. Faulk's defense also challenged the judicial process, claiming there were errors in the admission of certain testimonies and in the overall handling of the trial.

In the case of Samuel Prevo, administrator of Rezin Beall, deceased, against Simon Lathrop, the legal proceedings began on April 21, 1835, in Clark County, Illinois. The crux of the dispute revolves around a verbal agreement made around 1823 or 1824 between Lathrop and Beall, wherein Beall intended to buy a tract of land for $400 to be paid in four equal annual installments. A note was later executed, but a disagreement arose over the applicable interest rate for the delayed payments. Beall believed he should only pay six percent interest, while Lathrop claimed twelve percent. As they could not reach a resolution at the time, they left the matter of interest open for future negotiation. Lathrop initiated a suit against Prevo, representing Beall's estate, seeking to recover the owed amounts. The Probate Court ruled against Prevo for $148, prompting an appeal to the Circuit Court, which further ruled in favor of Lathrop, increasing the judgment to $157. Prevo's defense hinged on two main points: that the claim for interest was barred by the statute of limitations and that the verbal agreement regarding interest was unenforceable under the statute of frauds. Ultimately, the Circuit Court upheld the original judgment.	The plaintiff, Simon Lathrop, argued that he had a valid claim for unpaid amounts resulting from the sale of land to Rezin Beall. Lathrop contended that a verbal agreement established a debt, and that the execution of a note should include the legal interest owed on it, which they had previously agreed to adjust in the future. Lathrop sought a ruling of $157 plus costs for the unpaid principal and interest.	Samuel Prevo, representing the estate of Beall, asserted that the claim for interest was barred by the statute of limitations, as the promise to adjust interest was made in 1832 and the suit arose after five years. Additionally, Prevo maintained that the verbal agreement concerning the interest rate was invalid under the statute of frauds, as no written memorandum existed for the land transaction.

In September 1867, the case Steele v. The People was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. This legal matter arose following a trial that involved discrepancies in the jury composition during the proceedings in a lower court. Specifically, counsel for the plaintiff claimed that the record indicated a trial by eleven jurors, while the transcript submitted to the Supreme Court showed that twelve jurors had participated. This inconsistency prompted the plaintiff to seek a writ of certiorari to correct the record discrepancies. Both parties had previously submitted the cause for decision to the court, and the motion for certiorari was brought forth later in the term of court. The court emphasized their standard practice to not entertain such applications after the term had concluded but stated that it may consider motions made during the term, contingent on a valid cause being shown.	The plaintiff, Steele, claimed that the record of the trial was inaccurate because it reflected that the trial was conducted by twelve jurors instead of eleven, which is how it transpired in the lower court. To address this, Steele sought a writ of certiorari to correct the transcript of the record to ensure it accurately reflected the jury's composition during the trial. The main argument emphasized the necessity of a correct and precise record to uphold the integrity of the judicial process.	The defendant, The People, contended that the motion for a writ of certiorari was invalid since it was made after the joinder in error and submission of the case. They argued that such conditions rendered the relief sought inconsistent and improper according to the procedural rules of the court. They maintained that the application for correcting the record needed to adhere to the established timelines and practices for appeals and motions.

In 1885, in Bloomington, Illinois, an ordinance was adopted by the city requiring burial permits to ensure public health and safety. Linus Graves, the appellant, was the general manager and chief stockholder of the Bloomington Cemetery Association. He sold a cemetery lot to a man named Falk and contracted to dig a grave for Falk's son. The grave was dug by an employee of Graves the day after, and Graves was present to direct the funeral procession but did not physically participate in the burial. Notably, no burial permit was obtained, which violated the city’s ordinance. The city pursued prosecution to recover the penalty for this violation. A trial without a jury resulted in a finding in favor of the city. The court examined the validity of the ordinance within the city charter's framework, asserting that the city had the authority to regulate burials to protect public health.	The city of Bloomington claimed that Linus Graves violated the burial permit ordinance when he conducted the burial of Falk's son without obtaining the necessary permit. The city sought to impose the penalties outlined in the ordinance against Graves, asserting that he, being part of the cemetery’s operations associated with the burial, was subject to the ordinance.	Linus Graves contended that the ordinance was invalid as it infringed upon the institution of the cemetery association, which was established prior to the ordinance's enactment. He also argued that he did not violate the ordinance since he was not directly involved in the burial, merely overseeing the proceedings. Furthermore, he claimed that the evidence presented did not sufficiently prove his engagement in the violation of the ordinance.

R. C. Bristol filed a case against the City of Chicago in 1859 in Illinois. The case arose from a legal dispute where Bristol sought to challenge something related to his rights or claims involving the City. Key individuals involved include R. C. Bristol as the plaintiff and representatives from the City of Chicago, with W. B. Scates acting as Bristol's attorney and E. Anthony representing the City. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court, indicating its significance and complexity. Nonetheless, the specific details surrounding the events leading to the case are not elaborated in the description.	R. C. Bristol's primary argument involved a motion to assign additional errors to the case after the argument had commenced. The plaintiff sought the court's permission to include these additional claims, suggesting that he believed there were further elements of the case that warranted consideration.	The City of Chicago, represented by E. Anthony, opposed Bristol's motion, emphasizing that additional errors could not be assigned without the defendant's consent. This defense highlighted procedural concerns regarding the timing and appropriateness of Bristol's request after the court sessions had begun.

In the case of Thomas Stout v. William McAdams, which took place in Bond County, Illinois, around October 1837, plaintiff Thomas Stout owned a mill located on Shoal Creek. The defendant, William McAdams, constructed a dam on the same creek below Stout's mill. Stout claimed that the dam caused flooding and significant damage to his mill's operations. The initial trial, presided over by Judge Sidney Breese, resulted in a ruling in favor of the defendant McAdams. The case was subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, which examined various legal concerns surrounding property rights, water usage, and the responsibilities of those who construct dams. The Supreme Court was tasked with reviewing the trial court's instructions to the jury, particularly concerning water flow rights and the responsibilities towards neighboring properties.	Stout claimed that McAdams’ dam unlawfully caused flooding that significantly damaged his mill. He argued that he had the right to use the water in a manner that did not injure his property, and he sought damages for the harm caused by the defendant's actions. The plaintiff contended that despite the defendant's general right to build the dam, he was liable for the consequences of flooding a neighboring property.	McAdams, through his general denial of the claims, argued that his construction was lawful and essential for his operation. He maintained that anyone who first occupies a property and establishes a mill has the right to use the water flowing through their land, even if it restricts others. He contended that the harm claimed by Stout was not a direct consequence of his dam's existence, implying that it was not his liability if the plaintiff could have adjusted his mill to prevent damage.

John Roach and Patrick Roach were indicted for the manslaughter of John Byron Dunlap at the November term of the McLean circuit court in 1874. The incident occurred on October 10, 1874, in McLean County, Illinois, stemming from a dispute over the use of a water well. The Roach brothers had previously improved the well's supply and claimed the right to use it for watering their stock. Dunlap and his associate, Wilcox, attempted to use the well for their stock, leading to a violent altercation that involved both parties wielding clubs. Evidence presented during the trial indicated that John Roach, believing he was in imminent danger after being assaulted, used a knife in self-defense. The jury found both defendants guilty, sentencing John to twenty years in prison and Patrick to one year. They subsequently sought a writ of error from the Illinois Supreme Court, raising issues regarding the instructions given to the jury.	The plaintiffs, representing the People of the State of Illinois, accused the Roach brothers of unlawfully killing Dunlap. They asserted that both defendants engaged in a mutual conflict and failed to exercise appropriate measures to avoid further confrontation. The prosecution contended that the Roaches used excessive force that resulted in Dunlap's death and that their behavior did not merit justification based on self-defense.	The Roach brothers argued that they acted in self-defense, citing a reasonable belief that their lives were in danger when the deceased and Wilcox attacked them. They claimed that the conflict began with provocation and maintained that, under the circumstances, their use of deadly force was justified. The defense objected to the trial court's jury instructions, which they believed unfairly assumed key disputed facts and misrepresented the principles of self-defense.

John Jimison filed a case against The County of Adams regarding the compensation of the county superintendent of schools. This legal dispute arose in 1889 in Adams County, Illinois. The contention centered on whether the county superintendent was a county officer whose compensation should be established by the county board according to the state constitution. The legal framework included various statutes and amendments related to the duties and compensation of the county superintendent. The county board had set the superintendent's salary at $800 per annum, which the plaintiff argued did not align with the per diem rate outlined in the amended statutory provisions. The case examined whether changes in the law affected superintendents already in office and clarified the authority of the county board in setting compensation. The ruling of the Circuit Court of Adams County, which had initially handled the matter, concluded that the plaintiff had no valid cause of action.	John Jimison argued that the county superintendent of schools was entitled to compensation based on the actual number of days worked, at a rate of $4 per day, as per the school law amendments that took effect on July 1, 1885. He contended that the county board’s designation of an annual salary was invalid and did not reflect the statutory requirements for compensation based on actual services rendered.	The County of Adams, represented by Almeron Wheat, contended that the statutes clearly distinguished the authority of the county board in determining the compensation for the county superintendent. They argued that the amendments to the law were specifically applicable to superintendents elected after July 1, 1885, and that the county board acted within its limits in setting the salary at $800 per year. They maintained that the previous structures should remain intact and that there was no valid cause for the claims made by Jimison.

The case "Mobile & Ohio Railroad Company v. William Moore" was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision issued on February 4, 1890. The dispute arose in Union County, Illinois, following the death of a mare owned by the plaintiff, William Moore, who claimed that the railroad company was negligent in failing to maintain proper fences and cattle guards at a public road crossing. Evidence indicated that the mare was struck and killed at the crossing where she had accessed the tracks. Documentation from Union County's June 1884 term confirmed that the county was not liable for damages incurred due to this road's condition, as it had agreed to cover all costs. The primary issue revolved around whether the absence of cattle guards affected liability in this incident, given that the mare was killed at the point where she entered the tracks. Ultimately, despite the initial verdict favoring the plaintiff with damages awarded, the evidence revealed that the mare's entry to the track was at the crossing, rendering the defendant's alleged negligence immaterial.	The plaintiff, William Moore, claimed damages from the Mobile & Ohio Railroad Company following the death of his mare, asserting that the railroad's negligence in not maintaining adequate fences and cattle guards at the crossing led to the accident. He sought recovery for his losses, arguing that the railroad's failure to prevent animals from entering the tracks was the primary cause of the incident.	The defendant, Mobile & Ohio Railroad Company, contended that the plaintiff was not entitled to recover damages, emphasizing that the mare entered the tracks at a public road crossing. They argued that the absence of cattle guards and fences was irrelevant to the incident since the horse's entry onto the track was not prevented by the railroad, thus negating any liability for negligence.

Matthew Henneberry brought a legal action against John M. Morse and others regarding a promissory note originally executed by the defendants to a third party, Lynch, in Galesburg, Knox County, Illinois. The dispute arose after Henneberry, as the assignee of Lynch, sought to enforce the note, which was tied to the purchase price of property previously occupied by A. Thorsalle. A trial resulted in a verdict favoring the defendants, indicating a failure of consideration that Henneberry allegedly did not adequately notice prior to acquiring the note. The case was presided over by Judge Arthur A. Smith in the Circuit Court of Knox County, and Henneberry appealed the decision, arguing substantive errors in the trial process.	Henneberry's main argument was that he lacked sufficient notice about the failure of consideration related to the promissory note before purchasing it. He contended that the note's clause should have informed him about the underlying issues. As the assignee of the original payee, Lynch, Henneberry sought a judgment mandating the defendants to honor the payment stipulated in the note.	The defendants contended that Henneberry had prior notice regarding the failure of consideration. They argued that the language of the note indirectly suggested there were issues that warranted scrutiny on Henneberry's part. Furthermore, they submitted that the jury's verdict, which found in their favor, was fully supported by the evidence, and they claimed the trial court did not err in its rulings or in the instructions provided to the jury.

In 1858, in Knox County, Illinois, John Brown (plaintiff) filed a replevin action against Lawrence Riley (defendant), seeking the return of two horses, a double wagon, and a harness that he claimed were unlawfully taken and detained by the defendant. The property, which originally belonged to Patrick Gibney, was sold to Brown by Gibney prior to the defendant's seizure. The sale occurred on February 24, 1858, with Brown paying Gibney a total of $275, including a debt to a loan holder, Thomas Moony. The defendant, who was a constable, claimed that he lawfully seized the property on March 8, 1858, under a valid execution issued against Gibney for a separate debt. Dispute arose regarding the timing of the sale and delivery of possession. Gibney was seen using the property shortly after the sale, leading to questions about the sale's validity. Throughout the trial, testimonies related to the method and timing of the sale and the execution were examined. The jury ultimately found in favor of the plaintiff.	John Brown claimed that the defendant unlawfully took and detained the property that he had purchased from Patrick Gibney. Brown argued that he had conducted the purchase in good faith and had taken possession of the items on the day of the sale. He requested the court to affirm his rightful ownership and return of the property, asserting that the sale was valid because it took place before any execution was levied against Gibney.	Lawrence Riley defended his actions by asserting that he acted lawfully as a constable executing a valid court order against Gibney. He presented evidence that the execution came to him after the sale to Brown, arguing that the property belonged to Gibney at the time of the seizure. His defense rested on the claim that the sale to Brown was fraudulent and intended to delay Gibney's creditors, requesting dismissal of the case against him based on lawful execution of office duties.

In 1887, a legal case arose in Coles County, Illinois, involving the Peoria, Decatur & Evansville Railway Company (appellant) and James N. Shelly (appellee). The case was brought forward after a colt belonging to Shelly was killed by the appellant's train. The incident occurred near the northwest corner of Pleasant Grove Township, where a public highway crosses the railroad. There were discrepancies over whether a fence was legally required at the collision site. While the appellant contended that the area was within the crossing of a public highway, the plaintiff argued that it was outside the designated crossing where fencing was mandated to prevent animals from wandering onto the tracks. Evidence suggested there was a considerable unfenced area that allowed animals to enter the railway tracks. The main legal question revolved around the necessity of the fence at that point and whether the lack of it contributed to the colt’s death.	James N. Shelly, the plaintiff, claimed damages for the loss of his colt killed by the railway's train. He argued that the railroad was legally required to have a fence in place at the location of the accident, as it was not on the public highway crossing but rather in an area that allowed animals to access the tracks. Shelly asserted that the negligence of the railway company in failing to construct the required fence led directly to the tragic incident involving his colt.	The Peoria, Decatur & Evansville Railway Company contended that the colt was hit within a public highway crossing where no fence was necessary, arguing that the law did not require fencing at that location. They maintained that the area surrounding the crossing was properly managed and that the presence of the colt was not their responsibility. The appellant sought the dismissal of the claims based on the assertion that no negligence had occurred.

The case, Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railroad Company v. Charles A. Koenigsam, took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered on November 20, 1883. The incident occurred on November 18, 1881, when the plaintiff, Charles A. Koenigsam, was a passenger on a train traveling from Havana to Springfield. The train, running about an hour late, attempted to cross a trestle bridge over Dry Creek when the bridge collapsed, plunging the passenger and baggage car approximately fourteen to sixteen feet into the creek below. Koenigsam sustained severe injuries, including head trauma and lacerations, requiring extensive medical care and rendering him unable to work for about four and a half months. He initially won a judgment for $2,000 in a lower court, which the railroad company appealed, arguing that the jury's decision was contrary to law and evidence and that the damage award was excessive.	Koenigsam claimed that the railroad company was negligent in the construction and maintenance of the bridge, asserting that it was inherently unsafe due to quicksand in the creek bed and improper maintenance leading to the accident. He contended that the railroad operated the train at a high speed over a known dangerous area, and sought damages for his injuries and suffering caused by the company's negligence.	The railroad company contended that it had constructed the bridge properly in 1873, maintained it well, and that it had been in good condition at the time of the accident. They argued that the bridge had been examined shortly before the accident and deemed safe. Furthermore, they claimed that the collapse was caused by unprecedented heavy rains that washed out the earth beneath the bridge, not any negligence on their part. The company sought to overturn the lower court's ruling, arguing that the evidence did not support a finding of negligence.

In September 1871, the case of James N. Wetherill v. William Ohlendorf et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from Cook County, Illinois, where Herman Gierke, a leaseholder, had contracted with Sullivan to construct a building at 343 South Halsted Street. William Ohlendorf and Louis Ohlendorf, along with Heeney & Campbell, provided materials for this construction. However, Sullivan abandoned the contract before completion, prompting Gierke to issue a written undertaking, certifying his responsibility for materials supplied by Heeney & Campbell post-contract abandonment. The dispute arose when Wetherill, having purchased the property following a judgment against Gierke, denied the validity of the liens imposed by Ohlendorf and Heeney & Campbell for the materials, arguing that no contract had been made between them and himself, the current property owner. The court was tasked with determining the legitimacy of the mechanic's liens claimed by the material suppliers.	The plaintiffs, including Ohlendorf and Heeney & Campbell, claimed that they were entitled to liens on the property for unpaid materials provided for the construction of the building. They argued that Gierke's written undertaking to pay for all materials furnished by Heeney & Campbell constituted a binding agreement that established their right to a lien against the premises. They sought to recover the amounts owed from Gierke and enforce the liens against the building and leasehold interest.	Wetherill, the defendant, contended that no valid liens were established against the property since the materials were delivered on the credit of the original contractor, Sullivan. He argued that the written undertaking by Gierke did not legally bind him to cover materials delivered before the agreement's date, as there was no consideration for the prior materials in the contract. Consequently, he requested the court to dismiss the claims of the plaintiffs, asserting that they had no basis for their liens.

In the case of Robert S. Brush v. Francis Seguin and James Byrns, which took place in Kankakee County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose surrounding a sorrel mare valued at $75. The actions originated when Brush filed an action of replevin against Seguin and Byrns, who were involved in executing a judgment against Brush for an earlier debt. This execution, dated April 22, 1858, was levied on May 20, 1858, by Seguin, acting as the sheriff, and Byrns, as his deputy. The initial trial began in January 1859 and resulted in a verdict favorable to the defendants. Brush subsequently motioned for a new trial, which was granted in April 1859, allowing the defendants to amend their pleadings and respond to Brush's second and third replications. After further hearings and motions, another trial occurred in January 1860, culminating in a verdict that again favored the defendants. Throughout this process, key issues included the validity of the bond received by the sheriff and the retained lien on the property despite the bond's existence. The case drew on specific legal regulations regarding executions and judgments in Illinois.	The plaintiff, Robert S. Brush, argued that he was the rightful owner of the mare and that the defendants had improperly levied execution against it. Brush contended that a forthcoming bond had been taken, which he believed released the property from the defendants' claim. He sought judgment to reclaim possession of the mare, asserting that the property was wrongfully detained.	The defendants, Francis Seguin and James Byrns, maintained that their actions as the sheriff and deputy sheriff were lawful and justified based on the existing executions. They asserted that the forthcoming bond did not release the property from the lien of the execution. The defendants countered that they were entitled to maintain possession of the mare, given that the initial execution proceedings were valid and that no sufficient evidence was presented to prove the plaintiff's claim.

The case titled "Benjamin Gibson, Plaintiff in Error, v. Uri Manly et al., Defendants in Error" was tried in the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision issued in December 1853. The background of the case stemmed from an action of ejectment initiated by Benjamin Gibson. A second trial was conducted on April 1, 1852, in the Menard Circuit Court, which resulted in a judgment favoring the defendant, Uri Manly. Following this judgment, Gibson sought to reinstate the case on the court's docket and vacate the original judgment, which led to the court granting a new trial. The central issue raised was whether the court had the authority to grant a new trial after a year had passed since the original judgment. The case eventually required interpretation of the statutory provisions governing the process of vacating judgments and granting new trials in ejectment cases.	Benjamin Gibson argued that the Menard Circuit Court had the right to vacate the prior judgment and grant a new trial based on statutory provisions that allow a party to request such actions within one year of a judgment being rendered. He contended that granting a new trial would promote justice and allow for a fair assessment of the case.	Uri Manly, the defendant, claimed that the circuit court did not possess the authority to grant a new trial after the expiration of one year from the time the judgment was entered. Manly argued that according to the law, once the year elapsed without a successful motion to vacate the judgment by the losing party, the judgment became conclusive, leaving no room for the court to act outside the statutory provisions.

James H. Orne v. Isaac Cook was a legal case that took place in Cook County, Illinois, and culminated in April 1863. The plaintiff, James H. Orne, was a dealer in carpets and associated with George Henkle, a furniture dealer. The defendant, Isaac Cook, owned the Young America Hotel in Chicago. In the fall of 1854, Cook leased the hotel to Hulme & White, who required credit to furnish the establishment. They sought Cook’s assistance to indorse their notes to secure purchases from Orne and Henkle. After negotiations, Cook agreed to indorse the notes and confirmed this in a letter that he signed. Based on Cook’s promise, Orne shipped goods worth approximately $2,560 to Hulme & White. However, Cook later refused to fulfill his promise to indorse the notes, leading to Hulme & White's insolvency. Consequently, Orne filed a lawsuit against Cook, claiming breach of agreement as Cook's assurances constituted an essential part of the transaction. The case revolved around whether Cook’s promise was valid under the statute of frauds and whether the court appropriately handled the plea related to it.	The plaintiff, James H. Orne, argued that he shipped goods based on defendant Isaac Cook’s verbal agreement to indorse the notes for Hulme & White. He contended that this agreement constituted an original undertaking and was thus not subject to the statute of frauds, which requires certain contracts to be in writing. Orne sought compensation for the goods he supplied, asserting that he acted in reliance on Cook's promise.	The defendant, Isaac Cook, raised the statute of frauds as his primary defense, claiming that the contract was not in writing as required and therefore unenforceable. He also asserted that the plaintiff's lawsuit was for the default of Hulme & White rather than for any direct claim against him. Cook's position was that the allegations against him were insufficient to establish an enforceable promise.

In the case of *Daniel Carroll et al. v. The People, use, etc.*, the action began as a debt suit initiated on May 15, 1882, concerning the bond of Dan Carroll, who held a license for a dram shop in Alexis, Warren County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Jane Lavis, sought damages after her husband, Samuel Lavis, became intoxicated from drinking beer sold by Carroll. On December 25, 1881, Samuel Lavis attempted to board a moving train while intoxicated, which led to a serious accident where he fell and sustained injuries that ultimately resulted in his death a few days later. The lawsuit aimed to recover the financial support lost by Mrs. Lavis due to her husband's death. Carroll’s bond, under the Dram Shop Act, was for compensation related to such incidents. During the trial, Mrs. Lavis was awarded a total of $3,900 ($3,000 from the bond and $900 in damages). Carroll contested the claims through several defenses, including a release he obtained from Mrs. Lavis after paying her $50, which he argued barred the suit.	Jane Lavis claimed she was entitled to recover damages for the loss of her husband's support due to the intoxication resulting from liquor sold by Carroll. She argued that the release she signed, which absolved Carroll from liability in exchange for $50, was obtained through undue influence and fraud from an intermediary, Swan Martin. Lavis sought to have the release deemed void and to recover the damages outlined under the Dram Shop Act.	Dan Carroll presented several defenses, including: asserting that the release signed by Lavis was valid and should bar the action; claiming that she was aware of the release's terms and the amount she settled for; and arguing that she could not repudiate the contract without first returning the $50 she received. Carroll maintained that the Dram Shop Act only held him liable for direct damages related to alcohol sales, not for care or attention rendered to the intoxicated husband.

The case 'Josiah Martin et al. v. Benjamin Brewster et al.' took place around September 1861, in Cook County, Illinois. The parties involved included the plaintiffs, Brewster, Templeton & Co., and the defendants, Josiah Martin & Hogue, who were residents of Warren County. The case arose from an action of assumpsit related to a financial dispute where Brewster, Templeton & Co. sought to recover debts due from Martin & Hogue. The plaintiffs asserted that they lent money for oats, which were to fulfill a contract with another company, Dean, Low & Co. The defendants were served with summons in Warren County, amid claims they should have been served in Cook County, where the suit was filed. The defendants filed a plea in abatement, arguing the court did not have jurisdiction as they resided outside the county and the cause of action did not accrue there. Testimony was provided by the plaintiffs' bookkeeper, demonstrating that transactions related to the debt occurred in Chicago. A verdict favored the plaintiffs, assessing damages at $637.07, leading to the defendants' appeal.",	The plaintiffs claimed that the debts and contracts asserted in the declarations were specifically made payable in Cook County and actually accrued in that county. They contended that since the agreements were made in Chicago at the request of the defendants, the jurisdiction was properly established, supporting their right to recover the owed amounts.",	The defendants contended that they were residents of Warren County and that the legal process should have been served there, which they argued negated the jurisdiction of the Cook County court. They maintained that the debts and contracts did not accrue in Cook County, nor were they specifically payable there, and emphasized this to support their plea in abatement.",

In the case of Mitchell, Lewis & Co. v. Upton Mfg. Co., which took place in Illinois, the action was filed on February 25, 1886. The dispute arose over a promissory note and the possession of certain property. The plaintiff, Mitchell, Lewis & Co., initiated a replevin action seeking to reclaim property that they claimed was wrongfully held by the defendant, Upton Mfg. Co. The trial, conducted by the court without a jury, focused on two critical issues: the authority of an individual named Burgess to assign the disputed promissory note on behalf of Upton Mfg. Co. and whether the plaintiffs had effectively established possession of the property through their agent. The court investigated these factual matters, leading to a finding of no liability against Upton Mfg. Co. for not allowing the property to be taken. The decision ultimately involved the awarding of costs to the defendant.	The plaintiff, Mitchell, Lewis & Co., claimed that they were entitled to replevin the disputed property, arguing that their agent had sufficient authority and a legitimate claim to possession of the property. They contended that a proper assignment of the promissory note in question was made and sought the court to rule in their favor and award the return of the property along with associated costs.	The defendant, Upton Mfg. Co., countered the plaintiff's claims by denying the validity of the assignment of the promissory note, asserting that Burgess did not have the authority to act on their behalf. They also argued that possession of the property was established legally and contested the plaintiff's claims of wrongful possession. Their primary request was for the court to dismiss the plaintiff's replevin action and award them the costs associated with the case.

In the case of John J. Phelan v. Mary Phelan, which took place in 1890 in Illinois, the plaintiff, John J. Phelan, filed for divorce from his wife, Mary Phelan, citing desertion as the grounds for his request. The couple was married in La Salle in 1877 and lived together until 1884 when John moved to Chicago. Despite his claims of having asked Mary to join him in Chicago, she consistently refused. John argued that he was entitled to a divorce based on the desertion. However, the court noted that John did not have a stable business or home in Chicago to provide for Mary, who had established a life in La Salle, with means of support and children from a previous marriage. The court concluded that Mary was under no obligation to leave her home to follow John without assurance of stability and support.	John J. Phelan's main argument was that his wife Mary had deserted him since her refusal to join him in Chicago constituted grounds for divorce. He asserted that he was entitled to a divorce under the precedent set in Kennedy v. Kennedy, asserting that desertion had occurred due to Mary's unwillingness to relocate. His legal request was for the court to grant him a divorce based on these claims of desertion.	Mary Phelan's defense centered on her right to remain in La Salle, where she had established her home and means of support. She argued that John had not demonstrated that he had a stable business or provided a home in Chicago. Therefore, her refusal to abandon her life and follow him did not constitute desertion. Since John had not met the necessary conditions to prove his case, she maintained that there were no grounds for the requested divorce.

In January 1867, the case of J. M. Hurd, Administrator of the estate of Matthew Darr, v. John W. and Wiley B. Slaten unfolded in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in the probate court of Jersey County when the Slatens filed a claim against Darr’s estate for $628.57. This claim was based on a judgment that Darr had against William Miller, which the Slatens believed was to be transferred to them. The controversy arose over a written assignment dated December 19, 1860, where Darr purportedly sold this judgment to the Slatens. At the time of this assignment, an execution was held by the sheriff based on the judgment. However, Darr's attorney indicated that the judgment was satisfied, leading to the execution being returned and denying the Slatens any benefit from the judgment, given that Miller was insolvent. The probate court initially allowed the Slatens' claim, which Hurd appealed. After the circuit court confirmed this allowance and overruled a motion for a new trial, the case reached the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, J. M. Hurd, claimed that the allowance of the Slatens' claim against the estate was incorrect. Hurd contended that the assignment of the judgment had not been properly executed until July 1862, after the execution in question had been satisfied. Hurd sought to have the circuit court's decision overturned, arguing for the dismissal of the claim based on the timing and execution of the assignment.	John W. and Wiley B. Slaten argued that they had paid for the judgment against William Miller and were supposed to benefit from it. They maintained that Darr’s estate was liable for the amount since they had lost their opportunity to collect from Miller due to the actions of Darr’s attorney, which deprived them of their rights to the judgment. The Slatens sought to uphold the claim allowed by the probate court.

On December 1, 1853, in Peoria, Illinois, plaintiffs William A. Gray, James Gray, and Bonus C. Reeves initiated an attachment against John MacLean. This legal action was aimed at seizing MacLean's property—specifically, the steamboat "Kentucky"—to satisfy a debt totaling $203.63. To release the steamboat from the attachment, MacLean and his surety, A. L. Merriman, executed a bond on December 3, 1853, promising to produce the steamboat to answer any judgment. However, the plaintiffs later declared that the steamboat was not forthcoming to satisfy the judgment after an execution was issued and returned with “no property.” The case proceeded to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the issues centered around whether the property was truly MacLean’s and if the executed bond could be challenged based on property ownership.	The plaintiffs claimed that MacLean had failed to produce the steamboat "Kentucky" as required by the bond issued during the attachment. They alleged a default on the bond and sought a judgment against the defendants for the outstanding debt. The plaintiffs asserted that despite the bond, MacLean and Merriman could not claim that the property was owned by a third party to evade their obligations.	The defendants, particularly Merriman, contended that the steamboat was not MacLean's property and therefore not subject to the attachment. Merriman pleaded non est factum, asserting that at the time the bond was made, the steamboat was the property of Hamilton and not MacLean. They requested dismissal of the plaintiffs' claims on the grounds of this ownership dispute.

In September 1872, in Illinois, John A. Mellendy and Hoah Green (the plaintiffs) were involved in a legal case against C. Dean Austin and Allan McClure, with Augustus Johnson being impleaded. The case arose when Johnson, a peddler, purchased goods worth $11,307.58 from Austin and issued notes for payment, with Mellendy and Green acting as sureties for these notes. It was agreed that Johnson would sell the goods and use the proceeds to pay off the notes. However, Johnson continued to buy more goods on credit and failed to properly apply the money he had sent Austin (around $1,800) towards the notes. After Johnson's failure to repay, Austin pursued a lawsuit against the plaintiffs, resulting in a judgment of $881.52 in September 1872. The plaintiffs believed their defense had been abandoned due to miscommunication regarding a payment made to their attorney. The lower court initially found in favor of Austin and dismissed the plaintiff's request for an injunction against the collection of the judgment.	The plaintiffs contended that Austin misapplied payments sent by Johnson, which should have been credited towards the notes. They argued that Austin had sufficient funds sent by Johnson to cover the debt, and sought a new trial along with an injunction to prevent Austin from collecting the judgment against them.	Austin defended against the claims by asserting that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that any money from the sale of the goods was sent to him, which would constitute a breach of agreement. He emphasized that the plaintiffs were negligent regarding the preparation of their defense, as they did not follow up on their correspondence with their attorney nor took timely action to defend against the judgment.

Charles H. Roosa filed a legal action against Peter M. Crist in the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1856. The case stemmed from a promissory note dated January 3, 1844, issued in Bethel, New York, for ninety dollars, payable to John Barlow or bearer. Roosa claimed that Barlow transferred the note to him before it matured, and the transfer occurred in New York where the law permitted the legal title to a note to pass by mere delivery. The plaintiff argued that the specific statutes in New York allowed for this transfer method and recounted the customary practices of merchants at that time regarding such notes. The defense raised multiple pleas, arguing general issues, payment to the original payee, and asserting that the note was not assigned or indorsed to Roosa properly, which they claimed made his claim invalid.	Roosa's main arguments centered on asserting his right to pursue a debt claim against Crist based on the transfer of the note from Barlow to him. He contended that the note was legally negotiable under New York law by simple delivery and sought a judgment to affirm his right to collect on it.	Crist's defense included several claims, such as the assertion that he had already satisfied the debt by repaying Roosa the amount he paid for the note, alongside interest. He also claimed that the note had not been properly assigned or indorsed to Roosa, thereby undermining the basis of Roosa's legal claim against him.

The case of Henry C. Wood et al. v. R. D. Johnson took place in the Circuit Court of Randolph County, Illinois, with the hearing concluding on October 10, 1883. The background involves the estate of J. V. Herring, who died intestate on March 19, 1881. Following his death, Henry C. Wood was appointed as the administrator of Herring's estate. The estate had total claims amounting to $337.05, while the personal property was valued at $228.17. To address debts, Wood was authorized to sell real estate, yielding $159.60 after expenses. Notably, Mary Ellen Herring, a minor, was allotted $543.10 as her dower in the personal property. The plaintiff, Johnson, contested an allowance made by appraisers, asserting that he had no prior knowledge of that decision and claiming insufficient assets remained to satisfy his claim. The case ultimately revolved around the validity of the allowances made and the proper handling of the estate’s claims against its limited assets.	The plaintiff, R. D. Johnson, argued that the allowance of $50 from the estate to Mary Ellen Herring should be set aside because he believed that J. V. Herring was neither a householder nor the head of a family at the time of his death. Johnson stated that he was unaware of the county court's approval of the appraisers' report and that there were no assets remaining to satisfy his claim if the allowance was upheld. His request was for the court to nullify the allowance so that his claim could be fully paid.	The defendants, represented by Henry C. Wood, acknowledged the administration of the estate and the existence of other claims against it. They countered Johnson’s assertions, maintaining that Herring was indeed a householder and that Johnson had full knowledge of the appraisers' report and its approval. They emphasized the absence of fraud or collusion in the actions of the administrator or the court. Additionally, they noted that the estate had multiple claimants and contended that all relevant parties should be included in the legal proceedings.

The case of William King v. John Dale arose in December 1838 in Illinois. The dispute was centered around a civil suit for criminal conversation (crim. con.) filed by John Dale against William King, relating to an alleged adulterous affair between King and Dale's wife, Cinthia Dale. During the trial, Dale successfully obtained a verdict and judgment against King, prompting King to appeal the decision. The appeals process raised several issues: the first was the inclusion of a juror who had previously expressed an opinion regarding the merits of a related criminal case involving Cinthia. The juror testified that he had formed an opinion based on the testimony against her but claimed he had no opinion about the civil case. The second issue concerned the authentication of a marriage certificate from Tennessee, which Dale presented as evidence. Lastly, there were objections to the admission of depositions from certain individuals. The Illinois Supreme Court, under Chief Justice Wilson, carefully reviewed these claims.	John Dale claimed that William King had engaged in an adulterous relationship with his wife, Cinthia Dale, thereby resulting in damages due to the loss of consortium. Dale sought financial compensation for the emotional and reputational harm caused by King's actions.	William King contended that the trial court erred in allowing a juror, who had formed an opinion regarding a related criminal case involving the plaintiff's wife, to serve. He also argued against the authenticity of the marriage certificate presented as evidence and objected to the admissibility of certain depositions that he believed were improperly introduced.

The case "Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company v. John Killenberg" took place in Illinois, culminating in a court decision issued in June 1876. The legal dispute arose from a judgment entered on March 17, 1875, against Thomas Gorman by a justice of the peace in East St. Louis for $41.10, which prompted a garnishee summons to the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company. Following the issuance of a summons, the railroad company failed to appear in court, resulting in a conditional judgment against it for $47.55. The company appealed this judgment, and during the subsequent trial in the St. Clair County Circuit Court in September 1875, it argued that it did not owe Gorman any money at the time the garnishee summons was served. The company’s cashier testified that the railroad had given Gorman certificates of indebtedness for work performed, which were settled before the garnishee process was initiated. The court was tasked with determining the company's liability based on this testimony.	John Killenberg, the plaintiff, claimed that the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company was liable as the garnishee for the judgment amount against Thomas Gorman. Killenberg sought to assert that Gorman was owed payment by the railroad company and that, despite its failure to appear at the initial summons, the company was responsible for settling the debt with him.	The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company, as the defendant, contended that it was not indebted to Thomas Gorman at the time the garnishee summons was served. The company's primary argument was supported by the testimony of its cashier, who stated that the company had previously settled its debts to Gorman with certificates of indebtedness. The railroad requested to be discharged as the garnishee, contending that Gorman sold the certificates before the garnishee summons was effective, thus absolving them of any obligation to pay.

The case of W. H. Tomlin et al. v. A. A. Blunt et al. was decided on February 21, 1889, in Mason County, Illinois, before the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose from a dispute involving the use of a church building that was funded by different Christian denominations, specifically through contributions from the Methodist and Baptist congregations. The plaintiffs, including W. H. Tomlin and a group of other individuals, were involved in a trust arrangement where the church edifice was meant to be accessible to all evangelical orders of Christians, with particular emphasis that it should be open when not in use by the Baptist denomination. The defendants, A. A. Blunt and others, were trustees of the church and had started to deny access to the building for congregations other than the Baptists. This exclusionality escalated as new locks were placed on the doors, preventing the Methodists and other denomination members from entering, even when the church was not being utilized by the Baptists. The plaintiffs sought an injunction to stop this behavior, claiming it violated the conditions stipulated in the property conveyance. The Circuit Court initially dismissed their claims, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that the trustees (defendants) were unlawfully excluding them from their rightful use of the church building, in violation of the conditions set forth in the original conveyance, which allowed access to all evangelical orders when the building was not in use by Baptists. They requested an injunction to restrain the defendants from continuing their exclusionary practices and sought general relief in this chancery case.	The defendants contended that the stipulation in the conveyance allowing use by other evangelical orders was void and repugnant to their rights as trustees of the Baptist church. They argued that the terms introduced an element of uncertainty regarding who could use the building, implying that their management of the church property was appropriate given their responsibilities as trustees. A demurrer was filed in response to the plaintiff's bill, leading to the dismissal by the Circuit Court.

Morris B. Derrick filed a claim against The Lamar Insurance Company to seek compensation for a property loss amounting to $4,865 due to a fire in Chicago in 1871. Derrick had purchased an insurance policy from the company for $3,500. The case revolves around a creditor's bill initiated on October 23, 1872, by Edwin Burnham and Edward R. Burnham, who had previously secured a judgment against Lamar Insurance Company. Following their judgement, a receiver was appointed on November 23, 1872, to manage the company's assets and liabilities. The court later ordered a process to validate claims against the company. Derrick presented his claim within the time stipulated, however, his claim was disallowed on June 11, 1874, due to an assignment of rights to John H. Wise before filing his claim. The court's decision was based on the assertion that Derrick had assigned his rights and thus didn't have a valid claim against the insurance company. This decision was contested, leading to the appeal that is being evaluated.	Derrick argues that the claim he filed against Lamar Insurance Company is valid despite the prior assignment to Wise, who he asserts was not a bona fide assignee. He believes that the assignment should be annulled due to misrepresentations made by the company's officers regarding its financial ability to pay claims. Derrick's appeal seeks to have the court reverse the previous ruling that disallowed his claim, allowing him to prove his claim in court.	The Lamar Insurance Company's defense rests on the assertion that Derrick's claim was invalidated due to the assignment of rights to John H. Wise prior to filing. The company contends that this assignment by Derrick precludes him from claiming any financial redress. Additionally, they argue that the claim is barred by the one-year limitation stated in the insurance policy, although this was countered with claims of fraudulent inducement on their part which allegedly led Derrick to not act within the stipulated timeframe.

In the case of Augustus E. Harmon v. Alonzo Campbell, which took place in Champaign, Illinois, in 1861, Augustus E. Harmon was the plaintiff, while Alonzo Campbell served as the defendant. The legal conflict arose from Campbell's efforts to foreclose on a mortgage that Harmon had allegedly executed to secure a loan for property. The foreclosure case was filed in the Champaign Circuit Court during the April term of 1861. Campbell petitioned the court for a default judgment against Harmon after Harmon failed to respond to the bill of complaint. As a result, a decree pro confesso was entered in favor of Campbell, which meant the allegations were accepted as true due to Harmon's non-appearance. The underlying issue included disagreements regarding the specifics of a note attached to the mortgage and the service of process purportedly being ambiguous.	Harmon claimed that the bill filed by Campbell for foreclosure was not consistent with the actual facts of his case, particularly regarding the date of the promissory note related to the mortgage. Harmon contended that the service of process was insufficiently detailed, leading to a lack of proper notice regarding the proceedings. He sought to contest the foreclosure decree based on these discrepancies.	Campbell argued that when a decree pro confesso is entered—due to the defendant’s absence—the allegations made in the bill of complaint automatically become accepted as true. He claimed that Harmon had defaulted by not appearing in court, thereby waiving his right to challenge the specifics of the claims made. Campbell asserted that the evidence and the allegations in the bill were sufficient to maintain the foreclosure action.

In December 1855, the case of George P. Doan et al. v. Sidney S. Duncan was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The context involved a disagreement regarding a purchase made by Charles Clarkson, who was presented as an agent for the defendant, Sidney S. Duncan. The plaintiffs, George P. Doan and others, alleged that they sold goods to Clarkson while he was acting as Duncan's agent. The trial was held at the Morgan Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Woodson, where the jury initially found in favor of the defendant, Duncan. The plaintiffs contended that they were owed payment for the goods supplied based on Clarkson's agency, while the defendant argued against the existence of such an agency. The case’s outcome hinged on whether Clarkson was indeed authorized to act on behalf of Duncan.	The plaintiffs claimed that Clarkson was publicly recognized as Duncan's agent for purchasing goods and that they should be compensated for the goods sold to Clarkson under that assumption. They contended that even if Duncan had private instructions that limited Clarkson's authority, these should not negate his liability for the purchases made on his behalf.	The defendant, Sidney S. Duncan, maintained that Clarkson had no actual authority to purchase goods from the plaintiffs on his behalf. He asserted that any implied agency was insufficient for holding him liable and that the plaintiffs were aware or should have been aware of this lack of authority. Therefore, he requested that the jury find in his favor, arguing that the plaintiffs did not prove Clarkson's authority to act as their agent.

In the year 1884, a legal case took place in Chicago involving the Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company and property owner John Jacobs. The case arose when the railroad company sought to condemn certain lots owned by Jacobs for railroad purposes. Jacobs owned lots 39 to 45 in sub-block 3 of block 12 in Sheffield’s addition, which he utilized for market gardening. The property included a residence where Jacobs lived, as well as a barn, shed, and out-houses situated on the lot. A jury trial in the county court resulted in Jacobs being awarded $8,900 as compensation for his property, but the railroad company disputed this decision, claiming the damages were excessive and that there were errors in evidence admission and jury instructions. The primary contention was around the value of the property, particularly its market value for various uses rather than limiting it to its value solely for building purposes.	Jacobs, the plaintiff, argued for fair compensation based on the market value of his property, asserting that it was particularly valuable for market gardening. His main legal request was for the county court’s judgment to stand, supporting the compensation awarded by the jury. He provided evidence, including the value of manure, to demonstrate that the land had a market value beyond its mere use for structures.	The Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company, the defendant, contended that the awarded damages were excessive and sought to challenge the jury's verdict. They argued that the trial court erred in admitting certain evidence regarding the property’s value and issued instructions to the jury that misled them regarding how to determine the property’s actual market value.

Samuel Songer filed a case against the County Court of Gallatin County regarding his rights to purchase swamp lands in connection with improvements he made on the property. On April 10, 1855, he applied to the County Court to establish a preemption for the west half of the northeast quarter and the east half of the northeast quarter of Section 11 of Township 85 North, Range 8 East. This was in accordance with an act approved on June 22, 1852, concerning the disposal of swamp lands. The County Court granted Songer the right to purchase only the southeast quarter of the northwest quarter of Section 11, which was the forty-acre area where his improvements were situated, and denied his request for the additional land. Unsatisfied with this ruling, Songer appealed to the Circuit Court, which, during its November 1855 term under Judge Baugh, affirmed the County Court's decision. Consequently, Songer sought further review by filing a writ of error to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Samuel Songer claimed that under the provisions of the act of June 22, 1852, he was entitled to purchase the entire quarter section of swamp land on which his improvements were located. He argued that the interpretation of the law allowed him to acquire more than just the forty acres that directly encompassed his improvements and sought a ruling to reverse the County Court's limitations.	The County Court, represented by defendant J. Olney, contended that the legislative intent of the 1852 act was to limit a preemption right strictly to the specific forty-acre tracts directly covered by the improvements. They maintained that Songer should only be allowed to purchase the land corresponding to his improvements and that his request for additional lands beyond this was not supported by the law.

This case, "Thomas K. Means et al. v. Isham Harrison, Exr," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 13, 1885. The dispute arose over a promissory note for $500 executed on January 25, 1872, by several defendants, including Thomas K. Means, to Barzilla Silkwood, the deceased. Isham Harrison, as executor of Silkwood's estate, brought the action against the defendants after the note became due. The case was initiated on October 15, 1884, and involved the legal complexities around the statute of limitations applicable to promissory notes. The defendants argued that the action was barred under the limitations law that had come into effect in 1872, which reduced the limitation period from sixteen years to ten years. However, the promissory note had been executed under the older law, which they claimed should apply. They also contended that the lodge, which was the beneficiary of the loan secured by the note, had made substantial payments towards it before Silkwood's death. The Circuit Court found in favor of Harrison, leading to an affirmation of the judgment by the Appellate Court.	The plaintiff, Isham Harrison, argued that the defendants were liable for the payment of the promissory note, as the note was valid and enforceable despite the defendants’ claims related to the statute of limitations and the payments made by the Masonic lodge. Harrison asserted that the explicit terms of the note required payment, and as executor, he had the authority to collect on the note in cash, not property. Consequently, he sought a judgment for the amount due on the note, totaling $896.67, which included interest accrued.	The defendants contested the action based on two main pleas. First, they claimed the statute of limitations barred the enforcement of the note since the cause of action did not accrue within ten years prior to the suit being filed. Second, they argued that the note had originally been issued for a loan to the Polar Star Lodge, which had made various payments towards the note’s balance. After Silkwood’s death, they alleged that Harrison improperly accepted property valued at $1400 from the lodge instead of cash, thus invalidating the plaintiff’s claims. They sought the dismissal of the suit based on these defenses.

The case "Cooper & Moss v. William R. Hamilton" originated in Peoria, Illinois, around September 1869. The appellants, Cooper & Moss, initiated an action against the appellee, William R. Hamilton, seeking to recover $50 for professional services rendered. The case began at the Peoria County justice of the peace court, where a jury ruled in favor of Hamilton. Following this, the case was appealed to the circuit court, leading to a similar judgment. The case stems from Hamilton’s request for legal assistance from McCoy, an attorney, to negotiate a settlement with his ex-wife, Mrs. Hamilton, who had contested the divorce obtained in Indiana. McCoy involved Cooper, Mrs. Hamilton's attorney, in the negotiations, which resulted in a written settlement agreement after numerous discussions. Once the terms were finalized, Hamilton insisted on a legally valid document, prompting Cooper to write and finalize the agreement. The appellants argued that Hamilton should pay for Cooper’s services while the defendant claimed Cooper acted solely for Mrs. Hamilton and thus should not be billed by Hamilton. The case revolves around the obligations of an attorney in preparing contracts and the expectations regarding payment for legal services rendered.	The plaintiffs, Cooper & Moss, contended that William R. Hamilton is obligated to pay them for the professional services they rendered in drafting the settlement agreement. They asserted that despite Cooper being Mrs. Hamilton's attorney, he also worked at Hamilton’s request to ensure the legal adequacy of the document, establishing an implied contract for payment. The plaintiffs claimed that there should be no expectation for Mrs. Hamilton to cover these legal expenses unless explicitly agreed upon.	The defendant, William R. Hamilton, argued that Cooper was exclusively representing Mrs. Hamilton's interests during the drafting of the settlement agreement, which meant that Hamilton had no obligation to pay for Cooper's services. He maintained that any professional services rendered by Cooper were done in representation of Mrs. Hamilton, and as such, he should not be liable for the fees incurred by her attorney in this context.

David Birks brought a lawsuit against John D. Gillett in 1883 in Logan County, Illinois, over a financial dispute related to the purchase of land. Birks was interested in a particular quarter section of land owned by Gillett, part of which was subject to a life estate held by Jemima Gillett, the widow of a former owner. Before proceeding with the purchase, Birks needed to acquire this life estate. Gillett encouraged Birks to negotiate with Jemima for her interest, promising to pay Birks $400 annually if he successfully acquired it. Birks approached Jemima, who demanded $500 per year, and eventually offered to cover the additional $100 out of his own funds to secure a life lease. Gillett subsequently executed a deed transferring the land to Birks, including covenants of warranty except for the portion affected by the life estate. The purchase price was agreed upon through two promissory notes, one of which was structured to not require payment until Jemima's death while also including interest terms. The dispute arose over Gillett's alleged promise to continue paying Birks $400 annually after Birks settled the debt, which Gillett denied, leading to the lawsuit.	Birks claimed that Gillett had agreed to pay him $400 per year for the dower interest as part of their agreement when the deed and notes were established. He argued that the special terms of the $4,000 note were structured to allow him to pay it off early and receive this annuity in lieu of a perfect title to the land. Birks sought a judgment for the alleged unpaid annual amounts, claiming that Gillett's actions amounted to a breach of their contract.	Gillett contended that the written documents, including the deed and notes, represented the complete agreement between the parties and excluded any subsequent verbal agreements about payments. He argued that since the terms clearly outlined the arrangements and payments related to the land sale, Birks had no legal basis for claiming additional funds. Gillett asserted that the court should dismiss the case based on the sufficiency of the written contracts and the absence of any evidence supporting Birks' claims.

This case, titled "Charles Kinsey, Plaintiff in Error, v. Isaac Nisley et al., Defendants in Error," was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court and decided in January 1860. The action was commenced by Charles Kinsey in the Circuit Court of Effingham County, where he sought to enforce a promissory note for $200 signed by Isaac Nisley and others. The note was related to money loaned at a specified interest rate. However, the defendants raised several defenses, including claims of non-assumpsit, usury in the contract, and usury regarding a land sale. The Circuit Court faced challenges with demurrers and pleas before ultimately deciding in favor of the plaintiff on one count but ruled that the entirety of the claim was forfeited due to usury, with penalties distributed between the county and the defendants. The case revolves around interpretations of Illinois interest laws from 1845 and 1849, particularly regarding allowed interest rates and the consequences of exceeding such rates.	The plaintiff, Charles Kinsey, claimed that he was owed $200 based on a promissory note executed by the defendants. He sought to recover this amount, asserting that the note was valid and enforceable. Kinsey argued that the defendants had not fulfilled their financial obligation under the agreement, which was made in accordance with the prevailing interest laws.	The defendants raised several defenses against Kinsey's claim. They included a non-assumpsit plea, asserting that they had not assumed any obligation. A key component of their defense was a claim of usury, arguing that the interest charged exceeded the legal limits defined by Illinois law. They contended that the note was subject to penalties for usury, which warranted a forfeiture of the plaintiff's claim rather than enforcement of the note.

In September 1875, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the case of John D. Easter et al. v. Joseph H. Boyd, which originated in the Circuit Court of Livingston County. The parties involved included plaintiff John D. Easter, who was represented by attorneys Mr. A.E. Harding and Mr. O. Chubbuck, and defendant Joseph H. Boyd, represented by Mr. Jason W. Strevell and Mr. Joseph F. Culver. The case centered on three promissory notes executed by Boyd, totaling $172.40, with specific provisions regarding attorney’s fees in case of non-payment. The notes stipulated that if they were sued, additional fees of $10 or $25 would be incurred depending on the court where the lawsuit was initiated.
