The plaintiff, John McElhanon, contended that he was the rightful assignee of James Hughes in bankruptcy and sought to enforce the debt on the bond he had executed during the prior injunction suit. He argued that the default of the defendants warranted a judgment awarding damages, which he asserted were assessed correctly.	The defense primarily argued that John McElhanon could not legally hold the positions of both plaintiff and defendant in this case, as this would contravene established legal principles highlighting the conflict of interest. They sought a dismissal of the case based on the insufficiency of the declaration due to this duality in roles.

William Tindall (the appellant) and Daniel Meeker (the appellee) were involved in a legal dispute that originated from two promissory notes. The case began before a justice of the peace, where Meeker sued Tindall for the amounts due on these notes, one accruing interest at 12% per annum and the other at 20% per annum. The justice ruled in favor of Meeker, awarding him a total judgment of $92.25, which included the principal and interest at the specified rates up to that point. Tindall appealed this judgment to the Madison Circuit Court, which affirmed the prior decision and further added $7.75 in interest, bringing the total judgment to $100. The case progressed over a lengthy period, spanning sixteen months from the justice's initial ruling to the trial in the circuit court, which occurred during the May term of 1834. The Circuit Court applied the rates specified in the promissory notes for calculating interest and maintained that the justice's original ruling was valid as he had jurisdiction when making the initial decision regarding the notes.	Daniel Meeker, as the plaintiff, argued that he was owed the amounts listed in the promissory notes along with the appropriate interest rates as specified. He contended that interest should be calculated from the dates of the notes, leading to a total exceeding $100. Meeker requested that the Circuit Court affirm the judgment made by the justice of the peace and enforce the collection of the full amount owed.	William Tindall's defense rested on two main arguments. He claimed that the Circuit Court erroneously allowed interest to be calculated at a rate greater than 6%, which he believed was the maximum allowable under the relevant statute. Additionally, he argued that if the higher interest rates were valid, the total amount due would exceed $100, thus placing the judgment beyond the authority of the Circuit Court. Tindall sought to reverse the judgment of the lower court on these grounds.

John W. Frieze filed a case against The People in April 1883 in Pope County, Illinois. The judgment was made in the Illinois Appellate Court, presided over by Judge Daniel M. Browning. The case revolved around procedural issues raised by Frieze regarding the trial court’s refusal to allow a motion for a continuance, the admission of testimony, and instructional errors given to the jury. Frieze argued that these procedural oversights impaired his ability to present his case effectively, claiming that the evidence supporting his motions should have been considered. A purported bill of exceptions was attached to the case record, but it was not certified by the clerk, which limited the court's ability to review most of the claims put forth by Frieze. The court focused on whether the trial court had made errors in the case proceedings and noted that many concerns regarding jury instructions and evidentiary issues cited by Frieze were not preserved correctly for appellate review.	John W. Frieze's main claims involved errors related to the trial court's handling of his case, specifically the denial of a continuance, the exclusion of crucial testimony, and issues with jury instructions. Frieze contended that the evidence he provided was sufficient to merit a continuance and insisted that the court mismanaged the admission of evidence and did not adequately respond to arguments about how various procedural violations affected the trial's outcome. He sought a reversal of the judgment based on these claims.	The defense, represented by Mr. James A. Rose, argued against the claims made by Frieze, emphasizing procedural deficiencies in how Frieze preserved his arguments for appeal. The defense maintained that the lack of a properly certified bill of exceptions barred consideration of most of the plaintiff's claims on appeal. The attorney illustrated that the trial court had properly applied legal standards and practices throughout the case, and therefore, no errors occurred that would warrant a reversal.

The legal case "The Board of Education of Normal School District v. The Trustees of the First Baptist Church of Normal" took place in 1872 in Normal, Illinois. The dispute arose when the Board of Education sought to recover the purchase money for a house and lot that had been sold by the church trustees. The original deed stipulated that the property should only be used for church purposes, and in the event it was used otherwise, the church's trustees were to pay the original grantor $200, thus granting them absolute title. The Board of Education argued that they had taken possession and used the property for educational purposes, thus necessitating payment for the property. The key individuals involved were the Board of Education, represented by their attorneys, and the church trustees, advised by their own counsel. The case centered on issues of deed construction, forfeiture for non-use, and the validity of the purchase contract based on a memorandum of agreement regarding the sale price.	The Board of Education claimed that they had fulfilled the conditions of the purchase agreement by taking possession and using the property for school purposes. They argued that good faith required them to pay the purchase money since they had been using the property, despite the church's claim regarding the intended use of the land. The plaintiff sought recovery of the purchase price due to the church trustees.	The trustees of the First Baptist Church defended against the Board of Education's claims by arguing that the property had been forfeited because it was no longer being used for its intended church purposes. They contended that the deed included a condition that allowed them to reclaim the property if it was not used accordingly, and they cited failure of title and the statute of frauds as part of their defense. The trustees requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims based on these legal principles.

On April 19, 1855, in Chicago, Illinois, a grand jury indicted John T. Gould for larceny. Gould secured a continuance on April 24, 1855, and on April 26, 1856, he and James Campbell entered into a recognizance in which Campbell acted as security for Gould. This agreement stipulated that they owed $1,000 to the People of the State of Illinois, contingent upon Gould appearing in court for the indictment. However, on June 13, 1855, Gould failed to appear in court, prompting the court to order the forfeiture of the recognizance and issue a scire facias against both Gould and Campbell to show cause for the forfeiture. The record, however, did not show that a scire facias had been issued. Subsequently, on March 22, 1856, a judgment was entered against Campbell. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court, where it was argued that due process had not been followed in issuing the scire facias that would support the judgment against Campbell.	The plaintiff, represented by James Campbell, claimed that the Recorder’s Court erred in rendering a judgment against him for the forfeiture of the recognizance without first issuing a scire facias. Campbell argued that there was no proper service of the scire facias against him, thereby rendering the judgment invalid. He requested the Supreme Court to reverse the judgment entered against him on these grounds.	The defendants, represented by the People of Illinois, maintained that the judgment against Campbell was valid due to his failure to ensure that Gould appeared in court as stipulated in the recognizance. They suggested that Campbell, as security, was liable for the forfeiture when Gould did not comply with the court's order. The State's Attorney implied negligence on Campbell’s part for not ensuring the proper documentation was presented.

The case, William A. Beaird v. Mary Foreman, administratrix of Joseph Foreman, deceased, was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1832. The events leading to this legal dispute occurred in St. Clair County, where Beaird, the plaintiff, had engaged the sheriff (foreman) to collect a debt of $155 from defendants Joseph Chance, John Bird, and William Kinney through a replevin bond. The sheriff collected the money but failed to remit it to Beaird upon request. Consequently, Beaird initiated a motion against the sheriff under the practice act, seeking a judgment for the collected amount and damages at a rate of twenty percent per annum due to the sheriff's failure to pay. The Circuit Court ruled in Beaird's favor in March 1828, awarding him the sum collected plus interest.	Beaird's main argument was that the sheriff had collected $155 on his behalf but refused to pay it over as required by law. He sought a judgment for the amount collected, as well as twenty percent damages accruing from the date of collection until paid. Beaird contended that the legal provision allowed him to pursue damages at this rate to discourage sheriffs from withholding money collected.	The defendant's defense was built around the premise that the interest awarded by the Circuit Court was erroneous, as it was framed as interest instead of damages. The defense argued that the judgment should only reflect damages, not the interpretation of those damages as interest. They claimed that the court's ruling misinterpreted the statutory language regarding the collection and payment of the withheld funds and mischaracterized the nature of what was due to the plaintiff.

John Wheeler sued Hezekiah McEldowney in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871. The case originated from a promissory note signed by "George Faulkner & Co." where the plaintiff claimed that Wheeler was a partner with Faulkner during the note's execution. The transaction involved a bond for a deed concerning mill property, recorded with knowledge and consent from Wheeler, which stated that Wheeler and Faulkner were partners under the firm name "George Faulkner & Co." Although Faulkner testified that Wheeler had no interest in the mill business, evidence suggested that Wheeler made most payments on the property. A jury trial was waived, and the court concluded that the recorded bond implied Wheeler's partnership, making him liable for the note despite his claims of non-partnership with Faulkner. The court found sufficient evidence to charge Wheeler based on public notice of their partnership through the bond and ruled against him.	The plaintiff, John Wheeler, contended that he was a partner with George Faulkner in the firm "George Faulkner & Co." and thus liable for the promissory note in question, which was executed for work carried out at a mill. Wheeler aimed to prove his partnership and sought to hold him accountable for the amounts owed on the note.	The defendant, John Wheeler, denied being a partner with Faulkner, asserting that he bore no joint liability on the promissory note. He claimed that his involvement was limited to real estate matters and maintained that Faulkner alone was responsible for the mill business. Wheeler argued that the evidence presented was insufficient to impose liability on him based on the note.

The case of **The City of Sterling v. Lucy A. Merrill** took place on **November 14, 1884**, in Sterling, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff, **Lucy A. Merrill**, and the defendant, **The City of Sterling**. Merrill claimed damages for a personal injury she sustained while walking on the east side of B Street in Sterling. Around **6 PM**, she stepped into a hole in the sidewalk, which caused her to fall and suffer injuries. After the trial, the court awarded Merrill **$2,000** in damages. The City of Sterling appealed the judgment to the **Illinois Supreme Court** after the Appellate Court affirmed the trial court's decision.	Merrill's main argument was that the City of Sterling was negligent in maintaining the sidewalks, which led to her injury. She claimed that the defect in the sidewalk existed long enough for the city to have discovered it with reasonable diligence, thus creating liability for her injuries. Merrill requested that the court uphold the damages awarded to her by the lower courts, emphasizing that she had a right to presume the sidewalk was safe.	The City of Sterling asserted that Merrill was contributorily negligent, claiming she could have avoided the hole if she had exercised ordinary care. The City argued against the necessity of actual notice of the defect, insisting that they had taken reasonable steps in maintaining the sidewalk prior to the accident. Additionally, they requested the trial court to provide specific jury instructions that, if Merrill had the opportunity to avoid the defect or if the sidewalk was briefly unsafe without actual notice, she could be barred from recovering damages.

The case "Chicago, Springfield & St. Louis Railroad Co. v. Henry H. Beach et al." took place in Litchfield, Illinois, with the final decision rendered by the Illinois Appellate Court on September 21, 1888. The appellant, the Chicago, Springfield & St. Louis Railroad Company, initiated an action for trespass against the appellees, Henry H. Beach and others, alleging unauthorized entry onto their railroad track on Adams Street. The appellees had removed railroad ties, rails, and other materials belonging to the appellant, which led to the claim of trespass. The path's ownership was complicated by prior contracts with the Empire Construction Company, which was tasked with constructing the railroad but had surrendered their contract amid financial difficulties. Notably, the railroad company had permission from the city ordinance to lay tracks, and although the appellant argued that it held rights as a successor company, the court focused on possession, impacting the outcome of the case. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of the appellees, asserting that the appellant failed to demonstrate actual possession of the property at the time of the alleged trespass, resulting in a judgment against the appellant for costs.	The Chicago, Springfield & St. Louis Railroad Company, as the plaintiff, claimed that the defendants trespassed by unlawfully entering their railroad property and removing essential materials like ties and rails without permission. They argued that as the general owner of the railroad track, they had the right to maintain the action even without actual possession at the time of the trespass. The plaintiff requested that the court recognize its ownership and grant damages for the unauthorized removal of its property.	The defendants, Henry H. Beach et al., contended that they did not trespass because the plaintiff was not in actual possession of the railroad track when the alleged trespass occurred. They justified their actions based on a chattel mortgage executed by the Empire Construction Company, which they argued provided color of right for their claim. The defendants requested dismissal of the case, asserting that the plaintiff had not proven its ownership or possession of the property in question.

The case "Fairbank Canning Company v. Elizabeth C. Innes" was decided on April 26, 1887, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case stemmed from the death of George Innes, who was employed by the Fairbank Canning Company to operate an elevator in their packing house. On February 3, 1885, shortly after beginning his shift, the elevator malfunctioned—specifically, the beams supporting it broke, causing the elevator cage to fall and fatally injure Innes. He had been an experienced elevator operator for many years and had prior conversations implying he would run the elevator at his own risk. However, there were critical safety deficiencies; a steam-brake that was previously on the elevator had been removed, and an air-brake—an essential safety feature—was not in place at all. Though the elevator appeared structurally sound externally, the absence of these brakes was significant in the context of the accident that led to Innes's death.	Elizabeth C. Innes, as the administratrix of her deceased husband’s estate, claimed that the Fairbank Canning Company was negligent in constructing and maintaining the elevator. She argued that the company failed to provide a safe working environment by not properly equipping the elevator with necessary safety features, specifically an air-brake, and by not informing her husband of the lack of safety mechanisms. In her legal action, she sought damages for the wrongful death of her husband, asserting that the company was liable for his death due to their negligence.	The Fairbank Canning Company contended that the evidence did not support a finding of negligence on their part. They argued that George Innes had assumed the risk of operating the elevator, especially given the superintendent’s warning that he would be running it at his own risk. Furthermore, they claimed there was no proof that the accident resulted from their negligent construction. Instead, they suggested the possibility of an intervening cause for the elevator's malfunction, invoking prior knowledge of the elevator's operational conditions as evidence that Innes was aware of the associated risks.

Henry C. Waterman initiated a replevin action against John S. Donalson in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1867. The case arose in Fayette County, Illinois, where Waterman sought the recovery of goods he purchased from David A. Waterman, who was his partner in a hardware business. On March 2, 1866, David sold his interest in the business to Henry in exchange for the assumption of debts (amounting to about $2,600) and the cancellation of loans between the two. Following the sale, creditors of the business filed writs of attachment against the goods, claiming that the sale was fraudulent, alleging that David intended to defraud creditors by making a sham sale to his uncle, Henry. During the trial, evidence indicated that Henry consistently refused to participate in any fraudulent activity and intended for the transaction to be genuine. The initial court ruled in favor of the defendant, Donalson, returning the goods to him.	Henry C. Waterman claimed that the sale of the goods from David A. Waterman was a bona fide transaction made to settle debts, arguing that the supposed fraudulent intent was unsubstantiated. He maintained that he paid a fair price for the business interest and stated his refusal to engage in any sham purchases or fraudulent actions. Waterman sought to recover the goods based on this premise, asserting that the evidence did not support the allegations of fraud.	John S. Donalson's defense rested on asserting that the sale from David to Henry was fraudulent, contending that David had previously expressed an intention to defraud his creditors. The defendant argued that Henry’s purchase was calculated to obstruct legitimate debt collection, implying that the consideration paid was inadequate and that Henry intended to support David in evading obligations to creditors. The defense sought to justify the seizure of goods under the writs of attachment based on those claims.

Patrick F. Dooley v. Sarah M. Dooley is a divorce case filed in the Will Circuit Court, Illinois, with its proceedings noted in the Illinois Appellate Court on April 5, 1886. The plaintiff, Sarah M. Dooley, accused her husband, Patrick F. Dooley, of habitual drunkenness that persisted for over two years. In her initial bill, she sought a divorce and later submitted supplemental bills outlining further threats from her husband and requesting injunctions. The court ruled for Patrick F. Dooley to provide $100 for alimony and $50 for solicitor's fees during the litigation. However, he failed to comply with the court's order. In June 1885, after a hearing, the court ordered Patrick to pay Sarah $250 for past maintenance and $50 monthly thereafter for the duration of the divorce proceedings. Patrick challenged the rulings, arguing the amounts were excessive and lacked supporting evidence. The case highlighted the rights of a wife to alimony under the Divorce Act, emphasizing the court's discretion in determining appropriate financial support for the wife and children while the divorce was pending.	Sarah M. Dooley claimed habitual drunkenness by her husband, Patrick, which she argued warranted her request for divorce. She sought $250 in alimony for past maintenance and $50 per month for ongoing support for herself and their eight children. Additionally, her claims included the need for protection from her husband’s threatened misconduct, as illustrated in her supplemental bills.	Patrick F. Dooley contested the ordered alimony and solicitor’s fees, asserting that the amounts were excessive and arguing that there was insufficient evidence to support the claims made by Sarah. He maintained that the circumstances did not justify such financial obligations and expressed that he had a right to appeal the court's decisions due to the alleged lack of proper factual findings in the documentation of the ruling.

In the case of Thomas McCormick et al. v. Horace H. Wilcox (1861), the events unfolded in Hancock County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a mortgage executed on June 16, 1856, by Thomas McCormick and his wife, Harriet, to secure two promissory notes originally owed to Daniel A. Burr. The notes, amounting to $400 and $500, were intended to be paid by 1857 and 1858, but only a partial payment of $257 was made by February 1857. On June 25, 1857, the notes were assigned to Horace H. Wilcox. In the subsequent chancery bill filed by Wilcox on January 23, 1859, he sought foreclosure on the mortgage, claiming that McCormick had failed to meet the payment obligations. The bill also indicated that the McCormicks had conveyed the mortgaged property to a third party, Francis M. Corby. The case involved additional claims by Benjamin Clark, who asserted some interest in the land, although the specifics of his title were unclear. The Hancock Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of Wilcox due to the absence of defenses from the McCormicks and others, leading to a foreclosure decree.	The plaintiff, Horace H. Wilcox, argued that the mortgage was valid and sought foreclosure on the grounds that Thomas McCormick and his wife had defaulted on the promissory notes. Wilcox contended that the property was not protected under homestead rights as claimed by the defendants, as these rights could not be retroactively applied. He requested a decree that would allow him to foreclose the mortgage and sell the property to recover the amount owed.	The defendants, including Thomas McCormick and Harriet McCormick, challenged the validity of the foreclosure decree on several grounds. They claimed that the mortgage encumbered their homestead rights, which were not sufficiently waived in the document. Additionally, they argued that the original mortgagee, Burr, had not been included as a party in the foreclosure action, questioning the legitimacy of the decree. They contended that Benjamin Clark's interests were unjustly foreclosed upon without proper cause, suggesting that the court should set aside the decree.

In December 1848, the case of James Love v. Arthur Fairfield was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following proceedings in the Madison Circuit Court. The essential dispute arose from a suit in attachment initiated by Fairfield on behalf of Alexander P. Field and David N. Hall against James Love. The plaintiff, Fairfield, sought to collect on a judgment involving Love, but the attachment bond executed by Field was challenged by Love on the grounds of its alleged insufficiency. Specifically, Love contended that the bond's condition did not adequately protect the rights of other interested parties as required by law, since it merely repeated the statutory language without modifications. Additionally, a motion was filed by Love to delay the proceedings, arguing that a copy of the assignment of the judgment from Fairfield to Field and Hall was not provided along with the declaration. However, both motions—one to quash the attachment and the other for continuance—were overruled by the court, and the case proceeded to trial. The court ultimately upheld the bond's validity, stating it conformed to statutory requirements, and found that the lack of the assignment had no bearing on the case, as the action was based on the recorded judgment rather than the assignment itself.	The plaintiff, Arthur Fairfield, asserted that the action of attachment was appropriately filed for the use of Field and Hall against Love. Fairfield maintained that the attachment bond satisfied statutory conditions and sought to collect costs and damages arising from the suit as per the terms set forth in the bond.	James Love, the defendant, claimed that the attachment bond was insufficient, arguing that it did not conform to statutory requirements concerning the protection of other parties interested in the proceedings. Love also sought a continuance on the argument that necessary documentation (the assignment of judgment) was missing, seeking to delay the trial on these grounds.

In May 1838, W.W. Babb and his wife, Nancy Babb, transferred certain lands to a third party, Butterworth. However, due to a suit filed by Babb's judgment creditors in July 1841, this conveyance was deemed fraudulent, leading to the lands being sold under a court decree to satisfy the creditors' judgments in October 1841. The lands were reconveyed to Babb by Butterworth in October 1843. After Babb's death in October 1849, Nancy filed a bill in chancery in February 1851, asserting her right to dower in the lands that had been sold and were now in the possession of Nicholas Summers, who had made improvements on the property. The Circuit Court ruled in September 1851, appointing commissioners to allocate her dower but prohibited her from benefiting from the improvements made by Summers. This led to Summers contesting the court’s decree.	Nancy Babb, as the plaintiff, claimed her right to a dower in the lands conveyed to Summers, arguing that despite her husband's prior conveyance of the land, the conveyance had been invalidated by the creditors. She sought to have her dower rights recognized and to ensure that her share included a fair valuation of the property.	Nicholas Summers contended that Nancy Babb should not be entitled to any benefit from the improvements he had made on the land after the conveyance and that her claim to dower should be limited to the value of the land at the time of its alienation, excluding any increase or enhancements in value due to his efforts.

John Hochlander filed for a divorce from Eva Hochlander in May 1872, in Cook County, Illinois. The summons for the divorce was issued on May 8, 1872, and was meant to be returnable to the third Monday of May of the following year. The defendant, Eva, did not appear, leading to her being defaulted and a decree of divorce along with an order for alimony was made by the court. The case was subsequently brought to the Illinois Supreme Court, where irregularities concerning the summons were raised. The court found that the process was flawed due to the way the summons was issued and served, specifically that it was returnable to a term more than a year later rather than the next term as required by law. This lack of adherence to procedural rules rendered the summons void, leading to questions about the court's jurisdiction over the defendant.	The plaintiff, John Hochlander, argued that he had successfully served the summons for the divorce to Eva Hochlander and sought a decree of divorce along with alimony. He contended that the service was valid despite subsequent arguments about the sufficiency of the summons' return.	The defense raised issues regarding the validity of the summons, claiming it was void due to being returnable beyond the statutory time frame. It contended that the court lacked jurisdiction to grant the divorce decree because the process did not comply with the required legal standards for summons issuance and service.

The case, "The County of McDonough v. Daniel Markham et al.," arose in December 1855 in McDonough County, Illinois. The County of McDonough initiated legal action against Daniel Markham and other defendants following the destruction of a bridge valued at fifty dollars, claiming damages of one hundred dollars for the destruction and removal of this public infrastructure. The case was first presented before a justice of the peace, who ruled in favor of the defendants, dismissing the suit and ordering the plaintiff to pay costs. The plaintiff then appealed to the Circuit Court of McDonough County. During the appeal, the defendants sought dismissal, arguing that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction, that the suit was not conforming to statutory requirements, and that there was no statute permitting the suit in its current form. The Circuit Court upheld the motion to dismiss, concluding that the county was not authorized to sue for the penalties under the specific provisions of the road law that were applicable to this case. The case was decided by Judge Walker, leading to a decision affirming the lower court's dismissal.	The County of McDonough contended that the defendants were liable under the road law of 1845 for the destruction of a public bridge, asserting their right to recover one hundred dollars as a penalty for this misconduct. The plaintiff argued that the case was valid and that the initial dismissal by the justice of the peace was erroneous, seeking the court to overturn this dismissal and allow their claim for damages.	The defendants, Markham and others, argued that the County of McDonough lacked standing to sue in this instance, as the suit was not brought under the correct statutory framework. They raised multiple points, including the justice's lack of jurisdiction, the improper manner and form of the suit, and the absence of a statute explicitly permitting such legal actions to be pursued by the county. Their requests included upholding the dismissal of the suit and maintaining the judgment for costs against the plaintiff.

On February 20, 1843, in Illinois, James Dunlap issued a note for $131,480.52 payable to the Bank of Illinois, which matured on April 20, 1843. The note was to be paid in state indebtedness. However, by April 10, 1845, the note remained unpaid. The bank, under a legislative act, assigned the note to John J. Hardin and Samuel Dunlap (now deceased). The plaintiffs, as assignees, sought judgment for the amount due. At the maturity of the note, the market value of the state’s indebtedness was significantly lower than the nominal value, which raised questions about the correct measure of damages. The Sangamon Circuit Court, during its proceedings in December 1850, ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $38,361.93.	The plaintiffs argued that Dunlap failed to pay the note by the due date and that they were entitled to a judgment based on the market value of the state indebtedness at that time. They claimed the note represented a debt that should be settled based on the actual market value of the Illinois state bonds, which had diminished since the initial agreement. They requested a judgment that reflected this reduced market value and sought legal recourse for the unpaid amount.	The defendant contended that the note was not a straightforward obligation to pay the face value but rather a conditional promise based on the value of state indebtedness. He argued that his liability was limited to the actual market value of the bonds at the time of payment and that the plaintiffs were attempting to recover more than what was due. The defense requested dismissal or reduction of the amount owed based on their interpretation of the contract's terms.

In August 1874, a legal dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, when Arno Voss initiated a suit against The German American Bank of Chicago regarding a promissory note dated October 4, 1873. The note, valued at $300, was originally made by Albert Michelson, with Voss acting as an endorser. The note stipulated that payment was due fifteen days after the date noted, plus interest at a rate of 10% per annum. Throughout the duration of the agreement, Michelson maintained funds exceeding the amount of the note in his account with the bank. During proceedings in a lower court, without a jury, Voss was awarded $246.10 on the note. The case hinged on whether the bank had the obligation to apply Michelson's funds to the note, discharging Voss as a surety. The court determined that the bank was not bound to do so under the circumstances presented and dismissed Voss's claims related to this matter.	Arno Voss claimed that he should be discharged from the obligation of the promissory note because The German American Bank failed to use funds that Albert Michelson had deposited in the bank to pay down the note before bringing the suit. He argued that since Michelson had sufficient funds to cover the note, the bank’s inaction in applying those funds to the payment should discharge him as a surety.	The German American Bank argued that they had no obligation to apply Michelson's deposited funds toward the payment of the note, as there was no binding agreement for the bank to do so. They contended that the case law cited by Voss did not apply in this situation and that there was insufficient evidence to support the claim that an extension of payment was granted to Michelson, which would have discharged Voss from his obligations.

The case "Daniel Hyde, Plaintiff in Error, v. Daniel F. Pryor, Defendant in Error" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1851. The dispute revolves around an estray horse that was initially in the possession of Pryor for over a year without being advertised as required by law. The horse escaped from Pryor and ended up on Hyde's property. Hyde, who was aware that the horse belonged to Pryor and had not been posted or advertised, refused to return the horse to Pryor when demanded. Hyde argued that since the horse was an estray, he should be entitled to keep it as it came into his possession. However, the facts indicated that Hyde had not complied with the legal obligation to notify the owner of the estray's presence in his possession. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Pryor, prompting Hyde to contest the judgment.	Daniel Hyde claimed that he rightfully possessed the horse as an estray and argued that since Pryor had failed to post and advertise the horse during his possession, he should be entitled to keep it. Hyde contended that he had adequately advertised the horse after it came under his control and sought a judgment reversing the Circuit Court's decision that favored Pryor.	Daniel F. Pryor's defense centered on the assertion that Hyde did not fulfill the legal obligations related to estrays, specifically the requirement to post and advertise the horse while in his possession. Pryor argued that his actions of taking up and correctly advertising the horse were in accordance with the law, and thus, he was justified in refusing to surrender the horse to Hyde when demanded.

The case of The City of Lacon v. Jesse Page took place in 1868 in Lacon, Illinois. Jesse Page was driving a lumber wagon when his horses ran away and one of the wagon's wheels fell into a hole in the street. This hole was approximately two feet long, one foot wide, and eight inches deep, resulting from the city’s neglect in maintaining a covered drain under the street. The absence of a sidewalk exacerbated the situation, as the street was heavily traveled, often causing vehicles to stray onto the area designated for the sidewalk. The hole’s defect was attributed to the city’s negligence in keeping its streets in good repair, leading to Page's injury when he was thrown from the wagon. Page subsequently brought a lawsuit against the city, which resulted in a judgment in his favor.	Jesse Page claimed that the City of Lacon was negligent in maintaining the street and its drains, leading to the dangerous condition that caused his injury. He argued that had the city properly repaired the street, the accident would not have occurred. Page sought damages for his injuries suffered due to the city’s failure to maintain its infrastructure, emphasizing his use of reasonable caution while driving.	The City of Lacon contended that the injury was partly due to the accident involving the runaway horses, asserting that they should not be held liable unless the injury solely resulted from their negligence. The city also argued that the hole was located in what was designated for a sidewalk and that liability should not extend to traffic-related injuries in this area.

The case titled "Samuel Clark, Administrator of Milton Shurtleff, deceased, plaintiff in error, v. John W. Clark, Administrator of Samuel Allen, deceased, defendant in error," was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1844. The dispute originated in the Circuit Court of Knox County, where John W. Clark sued Milton Shurtleff, claiming various forms of indebtedness: work and labor, goods sold and delivered, money lent, and money laid out and expended. The process began when the sheriff of Knox County could not locate Shurtleff, prompting the plaintiff to amend the declaration and assert that the cause of action accrued in Knox County. A summons was then issued in Tazewell County, successfully served to Shurtleff, resulting in a default judgment due to his previous absence. After the death of Shurtleff, the case was pursued against Samuel Allen, Shurtleff's administrator. A judgment in favor of the plaintiff was rendered in June 1843, but the defendant subsequently sought to reverse this decision, leading to the appeal to the higher court.	The plaintiff, John W. Clark, argued that the Circuit Court of Knox County had jurisdiction over the case, which involved claims for debts owed by the deceased Milton Shurtleff. He maintained that sufficient grounds existed for the claims, as the debts were accrued in Knox County where the contracts were made. The plaintiff sought to uphold the earlier judgment rendered in his favor for the claimed amounts.	The defendant, Samuel Allen, contended that the Circuit Court of Knox County lacked jurisdiction over Shurtleff, the deceased, at the time the claim was filed. The defendant argued that the plaintiff's declaration did not include a clear and distinct averment that would establish jurisdiction, specifically the requirement that the plaintiff resided in Knox County when the suit commenced or that Shurtleff promised to pay the debts in Knox County.

James M. Lowman filed a bill in chancery against George A. Lowman and others on August 18, 1884, in Stark County, Illinois, seeking to foreclose a mortgage dated April 1, 1873. The mortgage was recorded to secure a $400 note payable to Branson Bowman, who later endorsed it to James M. Lowman. George A. Lowman and William Bowman previously executed a separate mortgage for $5,000 on July 26, 1872, to secure their debt. In a transaction on September 10, 1874, George A. Lowman conveyed the mortgaged lots to Samuel Burge, which partially paid off the larger mortgage. The case revolved around whether the April 1, 1873, mortgage had been satisfied. The circuit court's decree dismissed the foreclosure request, and the Appellate Court affirmed this decision, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. Key individuals included the parties involved (James M. Lowman, George A. Lowman, Branson Lowman, and Samuel Burge) and the attorneys representing both sides.	James M. Lowman claimed he was the rightful owner of the $400 mortgage due to an assignment from his father, Branson Lowman, and argued that the mortgage had not been satisfied. He sought to foreclose on the mortgage to recover the debt owed. His case was based on the assertion that a mortgage should be upheld despite competing claims, primarily focusing on the validity of the mortgage in light of the past transactions involving the property.	The defendants contended that the mortgage sought to be foreclosed had been paid in full. George A. Lowman testified that he had transferred his interest in the notes and accounts of the business to his partner Branson Lowman, who agreed to release the mortgage before the property was deeded to Burge. They argued that the statute of limitations had run on the note and that enforcing the mortgage would be inequitable given the circumstances surrounding the other mortgage.

In 1869, a legal dispute arose in Kane County, Illinois, involving the Board of Supervisors of Kane County and Augustus M. Herrington and his heirs, stemming from the ownership of two lots (9 and 10) in block 52, Geneva. The case originated when the widow and heirs of James Herrington, deceased, filed a bill in the Kane Circuit Court seeking to prevent the sale of these lots and to compel their conveyance, arguing that the county held the property in trust for them. Historically, the lots had been utilized for county functions where a courthouse and jail were built. The ownership lineage traced back to a claim made by a settler, Haight, in 1835, who sold the claim to Herrington, who resided on the land until his death in 1839. Afterward, his family continued to reside on a portion of the land, with various transactions and claims impacting their right to the lots. The county purchased the land in 1841, relying on funds contributed by Herrington's heirs, thereby creating an implied trust in favor of the heirs. The case involved questions of arbitration, equitable interest, and the rights of the minor heirs, alongside disputes about the legitimacy of property transactions and the obligations of the county as a trustee.	The plaintiffs argued that the county had an implied trust to convey the lots in question to them, as they had contributed funds to the purchase of the land and had continuously resided there. They sought to enjoin the county from selling these lots and requested a legal conveyance of the property, claiming that various arrangements with the county had not extinguished their rights. They asserted that their interests were not barred by lack of notice or the statute of limitations, emphasizing their status as minors at the time of earlier transactions.	The defendants, representing the county, contended that the plaintiffs had no pre-emption right to claim the lots because of the prior legal transactions, including a lease agreement involving Augustus M. Herrington. They argued that the arbitration proceedings had been void as the county was not a party and had not recognized the plaintiffs' claims until later. The county asserted that it had conveyed different parcels of land to the heirs, acknowledging that the heirs had accepted these arrangements, thereby estopping them from claiming additional rights over the lots in controversy.

James H. Bowen, George S. Bowen, Chauncey J. Bowen, and George Whitman (plaintiffs) brought a replevin action against George L. Schuler (defendant) in the Lee Circuit Court of Illinois in June 1865. The case emerged from a dispute over a large stock of goods and merchandise that Lyman Culver had purchased from the plaintiffs for $1,500. After obtaining possession of the goods, Culver shipped them to Dixon and later sold them to Schuler. When the plaintiffs demanded the goods' return, Schuler refused. A jury trial concluded in favor of the defendant, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal the judgment, arguing several errors occurred during the trial, particularly regarding jury instructions and issues surrounding the rescission of the contract due to alleged fraud.	The plaintiffs contended that Culver had acquired the goods fraudulently, claiming he paid nothing for them. They argued that since there was no payment for the goods, they were entitled to rescind the sale and reclaim the merchandise. They requested a judgment reversing the lower court's decision and an order for the return of their property.	The defendant maintained that the plaintiffs could not maintain their action without first restoring or offering to restore the $1,500 payment made by Culver at the time of purchase. He argued that the plaintiffs failed to properly rescind the contract since they did not return the consideration received. The defendant also asserted claims of fraudulent intent were not adequately substantiated in the evidence presented.

Edward G. Bowzer filed a claim against the estate of Charles H. Crowell, who was deceased, in the Probate Court of Cook County, Illinois. The case was documented under docket number 17-2285 and opinions were filed on April 7, 1886. Bowzer initially sought a balance of $1,186.06 that he claimed was due from Crowell based on an account stated. After amendments to the claim, Bowzer asserted he advanced various sums totaling $1,426.25 to Crowell between August and November 1878, with the remainder owed being $1,186.06. The relationship between Bowzer and Crowell was one of business partners operating under the name C. H. Crowell & Co. However, the essential contention was that the partnership had ended, and Bowzer sought an accounting of the partnership’s finances. The jury ultimately found that there had been no such accounting or final settlement, and thus ruled in favor of the administratrix handling Crowell's estate. This verdict and judgment were subsequently upheld by the circuit court.	Bowzer's claims revolved around the assertion that he had advanced funds to Crowell while they were business partners and that an accounting had occurred showing Crowell owed him a balance of $1,186.06. Bowzer contended that the partnership was unresolved and sought a legal accounting of the partnership's financial dealings, arguing he should receive compensation based on these unsettled accounts.	The defense represented by the administratrix of Crowell's estate argued that Bowzer's claims were not supported by sufficient evidence of an actual partnership accounting or settlement. They contested that there was no established indebtedness and pointed out the weaknesses in Bowzer's evidence for his claims. The defense sought to uphold the decision made by the probate court to disallow Bowzer's claims.

The case 'The Tribune Company v. Hugh Bradshaw' took place in Chicago, Illinois, with a decision issued on June 16, 1886, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The primary individuals involved were Hugh Bradshaw, the plaintiff, and The Tribune Company, the defendant. The conflict arose from a breach of contract concerning advertising. In October 1883, the Tribune Company entered into a contract with Palmer to sell advertising space in the Chicago Daily Tribune. Palmer was responsible for filling this space with advertisements for a business index aimed at listing prominent local businesses. However, Hugh Bradshaw, who was solicited by a person named Crawford (who falsely claimed to be an agent of the Tribune Company), paid Crawford $6 to include his advertisement in this index. Despite the payment and the contract, Bradshaw's advertisement was not published, leading him to seek restitution from the Tribune Company. During a follow-up at the Tribune's office, when Bradshaw inquired about his advertisement, company cashier W. L. Ogden confirmed the advertisement was omitted and offered to refund the payment, which Bradshaw rejected. The jury ultimately favored Bradshaw, awarding him damages of $357, which he later remitted to $351.	Hugh Bradshaw claimed that The Tribune Company breached the contract by failing to publish his advertisement in the Business Index as promised. He argued that despite having paid the advertised amount, his ad was omitted from both the Tribune and the subsequent placards. Bradshaw sought compensation for the damages he incurred due to this breach, which he argued resulted in loss of potential business.	The Tribune Company asserted that Crawford, who solicited Bradshaw's payment, was not their agent and had no authority to act on their behalf, thereby absolving the company from liability under the contract. They contended that since there was no evidence of an agency relationship between Crawford and the Tribune, they could not be held responsible for the breach. The defendant also questioned the basis of Bradshaw's claimed damages, arguing that there was no proof that he could not obtain a similar advertisement through other means.

The case "James C. Stuart v. Ann S. Hamilton" took place in September 1872 in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose when James C. Stuart, the plaintiff, brought an action of debt against Ann S. Hamilton, the defendant, in the Superior Court. The plaintiff's claims were centered around two counts: the first count claimed double rent for a period of two and a half months during which the defendant purportedly held over the demised premises after her lease was forfeited, despite having received a notice to vacate. The second count sought compensation for use and occupation of the property during this time. The case proceeded to trial by consent without a jury, resulting in a court judgment favoring the plaintiff at the rate of double the yearly value of the premises. The defendant then appealed against this judgment, arguing that the court's decision was erroneous.	The plaintiff, James C. Stuart, argued that the defendant wilfully held over after her lease had been forfeited and that this entitled him to recover double rent for the time she occupied the property beyond her lease term. He contended that the law allowed for double rent in cases of wilful holding over after proper notice had been given, and thus sought a judgment that would compensate him accordingly for the alleged breach.	The defendant, Ann S. Hamilton, contended that the court erred in awarding double rent since the lease had been terminated by her landlord's action, rather than expiring naturally. She argued that, based on the statutory interpretation, she should only be required to pay a reasonable rent for the time she held over, asserting that the legal provisions for double rent apply solely in cases where the holding over occurs after the lease has expired due to the efflux of time.

In the case of David Rankin v. John Crow, the events took place in 1857 in Henderson County, Illinois. The action was initiated by David Rankin (the plaintiff) who claimed that John Crow (the defendant) had trespassed by cutting and hauling trees from his property. Rankin alleged two main instances of trespass: the first for cutting trees from a specified land parcel and the second for additional cuts from his premises. During the trial, Rankin presented a patent dated October 10, 1840, for the land issued to John Gibson and a subsequent deed from Gibson to himself dated January 2, 1856, which was acknowledged and recorded. The defendant's defense included claiming a lost deed from Gibson to a John H. Dunn, asserting that such a deed had existed that would invalidate Rankin's claim. The trial featured testimony regarding a purported deed and involved several witnesses who provided inconsistent accounts. Ultimately, the jury sided with Crow, and Rankin's motion for a new trial was overruled by the court.	David Rankin claimed that John Crow unlawfully cut and removed trees from his property, constituting trespass. He sought to establish his ownership through a patent and a deed from John Gibson, which he presented in court to support his claims of property right and entitlement.	John Crow defended himself by arguing that a deed existed which transferred the property in question from Gibson to Dunn, a fact that would negate Rankin's ownership. He introduced testimony regarding the loss of this deed and attempted to provide secondary evidence to support the transfer, though the evidence was challenged for being insufficient and unclear concerning the deed's actual terms and legality.

In April 1861, Henry Shute initiated legal action against The Chicago and Milwaukee Railroad Company concerning land condemnation proceedings in Lake County, Illinois. The railroad company sought to appoint commissioners to assess damages for Shute's land, which would be affected by the construction of its road. This request was made to the county judge on May 13, 1854. Shute contested the proceedings, but the county judge appointed commissioners despite Shute's objections. Subsequently, Shute pursued a writ of certiorari in the Circuit Court to review and challenge the county judge's decision. The Circuit Court upheld the appointment of commissioners and the actions taken by the county judge, asserting the legality of the proceedings.	Henry Shute claimed that the proceedings to condemn his land were improper. He argued that the application to the county judge should not have been allowed without proof of the circuit judge's absence, which he contended was a jurisdictional requirement. Furthermore, Shute argued against the act of incorporation of the railroad, asserting that it lacked provision for pre-condemnation compensation to landowners, thus violating the constitutional clause regarding compensation for property taken for public use.	The Chicago and Milwaukee Railroad Company contended that the proceedings followed the statutory requirements for land condemnation. They argued that the County Court effectively replaced the defunct county commissioners and thus had the authority to appoint commissioners. The railroad stated that the absence of the circuit judge did not need to be explicitly alleged in the petition for their actions to be valid. They asserted that the statute allowed for land to be condemned and subsequently compensated, emphasizing that compensation could be addressed post-condemnation without violating constitutional protections.

In the case of A. J. Hoagland v. The Great Western Telegraph Company, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the legal proceedings culminated in a judgment on March 13, 1889. The case revolves around a dispute concerning a stock subscription agreement between A. J. Hoagland (the plaintiff) and the Great Western Telegraph Company (the defendant). Hoagland had entered into a contract to subscribe for 100 shares of the company’s stock, valued at $250 each, but had only paid $1,000. The defendant's argument centered on the claim that by the time Hoagland subscribed, all the stock had already been taken by others, rendering his subscription void. The court had to consider instructions given to the jury on the relevant evidence and the validity of the stock subscription. The verdict relied on jury responses to special questions about the status of stock subscriptions at the time of Hoagland’s agreement. Throughout the case, procedural issues and the handling of evidence were also critically assessed.	A. J. Hoagland, the plaintiff, asserted that he had a valid contract for the subscription of 100 shares of stock and had made a partial payment of $1,000. He claimed that an additional amount of $1,500 was still owed, along with a sum of $8.75 due per share, as determined by a prior decree related to the company. Thus, he sought recovery of this amount based on the alleged failure of the defendant to honor the contract.	The defendant, Great Western Telegraph Company, contended that Hoagland's subscription was void because the stock had already been fully subscribed prior to his agreement. They argued that the jury received contradictory instructions, which they believed misled the jury regarding the validity of the stock subscription. Additionally, the defendant maintained that any failure to produce relevant court papers should not be held against them due to the absence of a court order to compel their production.

In the case of S. W. Henderson v. O. H. Palmer, which took place in 1874, the primary individuals involved were S. W. Henderson, the appellant and mother of H. B. Henderson, and O. H. Palmer, an agent of a telegraph company. H. B. Henderson, employed as a telegraph operator in Chattanooga, Tennessee, was facing criminal charges for allegedly embezzling $220 from the company before 1867. To halt the prosecution against her son, S. W. Henderson agreed to execute a note for $980 and a mortgage on her property—a house and lot that were solely hers, not jointly owned with her husband. This agreement was made under the premise that the company would dismiss the charges against her son. In 1869, facing foreclosure threats, she executed a new mortgage for the same amount, leading to eventual foreclosure proceedings by Palmer. S. W. Henderson sought to nullify the agreements and the foreclosure, claiming they were based on an illegal consideration that related to the compounding of a felony. The circuit court dismissed her claim, prompting her appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	S. W. Henderson, the plaintiff, argued that both the note and mortgage were invalid because they were executed under the threat of a felony prosecution related to her son. She contended that the only consideration for the note was the promise to dismiss the charges against her son, which constituted an illegal contract. Therefore, she requested the court to set aside and cancel the note, mortgage, and associated foreclosure proceedings as they represented a cloud on her property title.	O. H. Palmer, the defendant, denied any wrongdoing, asserting that the new mortgage was executed to correct an acknowledgment defect in the first mortgage and that the claim of illegal consideration was unfounded. Palmer requested the court to uphold the foreclosure, arguing that S. W. Henderson had not presented a valid defense in the scire facias proceedings due to the nature of that action being strictly limited to issues of payment or satisfaction.

A. P. Brown filed a petition for certiorari against Samuel R. Roberts and other Commissioners of Highways in Marion County, Illinois, regarding the Commissioners' decision to alter a highway by vacating and relocating parts of it. The case was decided on June 7, 1887. The core issue arose when Brown contested the legality of the Commissioners' actions. The lower Circuit Court upheld the Commissioners' order and Brown appealed the decision. During the proceedings, it was determined that the record returned by the Commissioners was the proper document for judicial review. The court focused on whether the Commissioners had jurisdiction and acted according to the law when they made their decision. The parties discussed whether a separate petition was required for altering one road and vacating another, as well as the adequacy of a damages agreement with the landowner affected by the changes. Ultimately, the court found the Commissioners acted legally, and the appeals raised by Brown were not valid according to the statutory definitions of "interested persons.	A. P. Brown claimed that the actions of the Commissioners of Highways in altering and vacating parts of the highway were illegal and sought to have their order quashed. He argued that the Commissioners did not have proper jurisdiction and that their procedures did not conform to statutory requirements regarding public input and property damages. He appealed for a reversal of the Circuit Court's affirmation of the Commissioners' order, demanding that the proposed highway alterations be annulled.	The Commissioners of Highways argued that they acted within their legal jurisdiction and that all procedures adhered to the law. They contended that the petition presented by Brown misinterpreted the nature of the order, and the necessary agreements concerning damages had been validly executed. They maintained that no valid appeal had been made against their decision and that the record they provided was the accurate account to be used in the court's review.

In 1875, the case of James M. Walker et al. v. Lorenzo Stevens was considered by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from the plaintiffs' claim against their attorneys, Lorenzo Stevens and his partners, for negligence in not diligently prosecuting a claim against the estate of Edwin Richards, who had died. The plaintiffs had initially hired the defendants to file a claim that was based on a circuit court judgment, which they presented for allowance in the county court on October 31, 1865. The defendants delegated the task to Mr. W. P. Smith, who, despite being a qualified attorney, failed to act properly, leading to the loss of the claim. The county court subsequently issued an order on August 15, 1866, distributing the estate assets, which exhausted the funds available, leaving nothing for the plaintiffs' claim. After an initial trial that resulted in a judgment for the defendants, the plaintiffs appealed, and the Illinois Supreme Court reversed that decision, remanding the case for a new trial, which produced a favorable verdict for the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs argued that their attorneys were negligent in handling their claim against the estate of Edwin Richards. They contended that due to this negligence, they were unable to secure a timely allowance for their claim, resulting in a loss when the estate's assets were redistributed. The plaintiffs sought damages amounting to $3,071.25, asserting that if their claim had been prosecuted with proper diligence, they would have been entitled to a share in the estate.	The defendants maintained that the failure to secure the allowance for the plaintiffs' claim was not due to their negligence but rather due to errors made by the county judge in distributing the estate's assets before the plaintiffs' claim was allowed. They sought to have the judgment for the plaintiffs reversed, arguing that the evidence did not support the verdict against them and that they were not liable for supposed negligence because they had delegated the case to a competent lawyer.

Richard Addizoat purchased three train tickets for himself, his wife, and children to travel from Chicago to Braidwood on the Joliet and Dwight accommodation train, departing at 5 PM on August 10, 1882. Upon arrival at Braidwood at 7:35 PM, the family travelled to the residence of John Miles, approximately 400 yards from the depot. They left their two trunks checked to the depot, which arrived on the same train. However, the trunks were left on the platform and transferred to the baggage room, where they were destroyed by fire the afternoon of August 11. The legal dispute primarily centered around whether Addizoat demanded his baggage immediately after arrival, as the jury had to determine what constituted a reasonable time for him to claim his belongings. It was established that four other trains arrived at Braidwood after Addizoat's train, and the trunks were not claimed or demanded throughout the following day.	Richard Addizoat claimed that the railroad company, Chicago & Alton R. R. Co., failed to deliver his baggage as expected. He argued that the company was liable as a common carrier until it was reasonable for him to claim his bags, stating that his failure to retrieve them on the evening of the incident should not absolve the company of its obligation to keep his belongings secure until he could collect them.	The defendant, Chicago & Alton R. R. Co., contended that they had fulfilled their duty as a common carrier by delivering the baggage to the depot. They argued that Addizoat did not demand his baggage in a timely manner; thus, their liability ceased after a reasonable time elapsed without a claim. They insisted that their responsibility transformed to that of a warehouseman once the baggage was placed in storage, which limited their liability, especially since the plaintiff did not provide sufficient identification or make inquiries following the incident with the baggage.

In the case of Ishmael Dazey v. George Orr and John H. Forbush, decided in December 1838 by the Illinois Supreme Court, the background involves a legal dispute following a judgment made in favor of the plaintiff, Ishmael Dazey, during the Spring term of 1837 at the Adams Circuit Court. Dazey had initially won a judgment against the defendants, Orr and Forbush, which led to a fieri facias (a type of execution of a judgment) issued for debt collection. The sheriff of Adams County, Earl Pierce, collected $30 from the defendants, but instead of returning the execution properly to the court, he merely endorsed the payment on it. Dazey's attorney, Robert R. Williams, managed to obtain the execution with the endorsement and subsequently returned it to the clerk's office, prompting an alias fieri facias to be issued. In July 1838, Orr and Forbush sought to quash this alias fieri facias in court without notifying Dazey, leading to the court granting their motion and imposing costs on Dazey. This appeal was brought forth by Dazey to challenge that ruling.	The main arguments presented by the plaintiff, Dazey, revolve around the failure of the defendants, Orr and Forbush, to provide notice before moving to quash the execution. Dazey contends that such notice is a necessary procedural step in order for the defendants to pursue their motion. He seeks to have the prior judgment of the Adams Circuit Court reversed and to recover the costs imposed against him.	The defendants, Orr and Forbush, argue that they followed appropriate legal procedures to quash the alias fieri facias that had been issued, as they claimed the execution was invalid. Their motions were executed without notifying the plaintiff, asserting that this procedural misstep did not invalidate their motion to quash. They seek to uphold the circuit court's decision that quashed the execution and affirmed the judgment against Dazey.

In 1887 in Green County, Illinois, John R. Calhoun & Co. filed a lawsuit against Stout & Smith after obtaining a judgment through a Justice of the Peace attachment for an alleged debt of $69. The case involved a commission dispute over the sale of two hay presses, with an agreed commission rate of 15%. The plaintiffs claimed to have retained $15 from the sales, leaving a balance of $78.75 owed as commission. The trial presented conflicting evidence regarding the origin of the sales; the defendants contended that their own traveling agent procured the sales, not the plaintiffs. They also claimed a contractual obligation for plaintiffs to endorse notes taken for sold machines, which plaintiffs denied. The jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding the amount claimed in commission despite the defendants' assertions and claims for a set-off.	The plaintiff, John R. Calhoun & Co., claimed payment of $78.75 as a commission on the sale of two hay presses, asserting that this amount was agreed upon based on a percentage of the sales. They argued that the commission was owed after deducting the cash retained from the sale and that the sales were duly executed, warranting the commission despite the defendants’ claims to the contrary.	The defendants, Stout & Smith, argued that they should not have to pay the commission, asserting that the sales were made by their own traveling agent. Additionally, they claimed that there was a contractual agreement necessitating the plaintiffs to endorse notes for the machines sold, which the plaintiffs failed to do, resulting in extra expenses for the defendants. They also sought to introduce a set-off for an amount charged to the plaintiffs, which was ultimately dismissed by the jury.

The case, "William Lawrence and John Donovon v. The People of the State of Illinois," emerged from an indictment for larceny against the defendants, Lawrence and Donovon, occurring during the May term of 1836 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included William Lawrence and John Donovon (the plaintiffs in error) and the representatives of the state, including James Grant (the State’s Attorney). The crux of the case stemmed from a jury verdict which found the defendants guilty of stealing several items — specifically, a blue coat valued at ten dollars, a cap worth two dollars, and seven pairs of pants valued at thirty-five dollars — belonging to John Holbrook. However, the verdict was problematic as it failed to establish the defendants' ages, which were relevant to the judgment. Consequently, the defendants withdrew their motion for a new trial and instead called for an arrest of judgment due to this perceived defect. The Circuit Court subsequently set aside the initial verdict, awarded a venire de novo, and conducted a new trial which confirmed their guilt but acknowledged their ages were under eighteen. Following this, the court continued to overrule motions for arrest of judgment, leading to the current appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that the Circuit Court improperly failed to uphold their motion for arrest of judgment based on the first jury's verdict being defective, as it did not include the ages of the defendants. They contended that this omission prevented a valid judgment from being issued. Additionally, they claimed that a new trial should not have been granted since no new trials are permitted in cases of felony or treason.	The defendants maintained that the Circuit Court was within its rights to set aside the initial verdict and award a new trial due to its defects. They argued that the verdict did not sufficiently ascertain necessary facts — specifically the ages of the defendants — which were crucial for determining the legal judgment. Therefore, they asserted that the Court's subsequent actions to rectify this were appropriate given the circumstances.

John Beyer et al. brought a legal case against William A. Tanner in April 1862, in the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a trespass issue in Kane County, Illinois. The dispute began on December 1, 1860, when the defendants, acting as highway commissioners, allegedly entered Tanner's property without permission, leading to the destruction of fences, grass, and crops on three different sections of land in the townships of Aurora, Sugar Grove, and Blackberry. Tanner claimed that the defendants had misidentified the correct line for the opening of a State road and had trespassed on his property while attempting to construct this road. The jury found the defendants guilty, awarding Tanner damages amounting to $95.42. The defendants subsequently moved for a new trial, which the court denied, and judgment was entered in favor of the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, William A. Tanner, asserted claims of trespass against the defendants for unlawfully entering his property and causing damage. He specifically accused them of destroying fences and crops such as wheat and grass across three parcels of land in Kane County. Tanner argued that the defendants, in their role as highway commissioners, had opened the wrong line for the State road, thus committing a trespass. He sought compensation for the damages incurred as a result of the defendants' actions.	The defendants, who were the highway commissioners, pleaded not guilty and argued that their actions were part of their duties in opening a State road. They contended that they might have been misled regarding the correct survey line for the road, resulting in their alleged trespass. Furthermore, they sought a new trial after the jury rendered a verdict against them, asserting that the judgment may have been flawed or erroneous.

E. Wesley Myatt v. Murphy Myatt was a legal case presented before the Illinois Supreme Court, with decision rendered in June 1867. The dispute arose in Bond County, Illinois, involving E. Wesley Myatt, the applicant seeking to revoke letters of administration granted to his mother, Murphy Myatt, and another individual, Williamson Plant, concerning the estate of Alexander Myatt, who had passed away. E. Wesley Myatt claimed that Murphy Myatt's marriage to Alexander was void due to her previous marital status with William Wilmarth, who was allegedly still alive at the time of her marriage with Alexander. Myatt's affidavit suggested that as a consequence, the rights of Alexander's children to the estate were being overlooked. Evidence presented indicated that Murphy and Wilmarth cohabitated and had children, but no official marriage license was found to substantiate that union. In 1832, Murphy had married Alexander Myatt under her maiden name after the alleged relationship with Wilmarth had ended. The courts evaluated whether Murphy’s marriage to Alexander was legitimate, balancing presumptions of marriage against the evidence of her prior relationship.	E. Wesley Myatt argued that Murphy Myatt’s previous relationship with William Wilmarth rendered her subsequent marriage to Alexander Myatt illegal and void. His claim was anchored on the assertion that any children from a void marriage would be illegitimate, thus he and his siblings had the right to administer Alexander’s estate. He sought the revocation of the letters of administration issued to Murphy Myatt, thereby asserting that she was not the lawful widow entitled to control the estate.	Murphy Myatt, representing herself, contended that she was indeed legally married to Alexander Myatt and that her prior relationship with Wilmarth was not recognized as a valid marriage due to lack of formal documentation and the admission from Wilmarth regarding his own marital status. The defense argued that E. Wesley Myatt did not have the standing to contest the administration of the estate as he allegedly was an illegitimate child, given that his mother was not married to Alexander if the past union with Wilmarth were deemed valid. The request was for the court to uphold the legitimacy of the letters of administration granted to Murphy.

Jacob Day v. The People of the State of Illinois is a legal case that took place in Champaign County, Illinois, around 1875. Jacob Day was indicted on multiple counts for allegedly selling intoxicating liquor to a person known to be in the habit of getting intoxicated. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, where it was revealed that the jury returned a verdict of guilty on ten counts but failed to specify which counts pertained to the defendant's guilt. This ambiguity in the jury's verdict led to procedural concerns about the correctness of the judgment rendered by the court. The case centered on ensuring that, in criminal indictments with multiple counts, the verdict must clearly state which specific counts resulted in a guilty finding for the defendant to avoid errors in judgment.	The plaintiff, represented by Jacob Day, maintained that the jury's verdict was flawed because it did not specify which counts the defendant was found guilty of. The principal argument stated that without this specification, it was impossible to determine the basis of the conviction, leading to an unfair judgment. The plaintiff requested a reversal of the judgment rendered against Jacob Day and sought a new trial where the verdict would conform to the legal requirements.	The defendant, represented by the state, did not present substantial arguments against the claim regarding the lack of specification in the jury's verdict. Their position ultimately relied on the validity of the guilty verdicts returned by the jury. The defense did not make explicit requests apart from upholding the original judgment, which was deemed problematic due to the issues surrounding the guilty count specifications.

In 1858, Lorenzo D. Hamilton and Jefferson L. Dugger were involved in a legal case against Ed. M. Dewey, stemming from a promissory note that was dated and payable in Atlanta, Logan County, Illinois. Hamilton, a resident of Cook County, initiated the case by having a summons issued to the sheriffs of both Cook and Logan counties. The summons served in Cook County resulted in Dugger being served, but Hamilton was not found at that time. Subsequently, Hamilton was served in Logan County on November 8, 1858, along with a copy of the declaration. Hamilton filed a plea in abatement, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction because the causes of action arose in Logan County, where both he and Dugger resided, and the process was improperly served from Cook County. The court sustained the plaintiff's demurrer to Hamilton's plea, compelling Hamilton to respond further, but he did not file another plea. Consequently, judgment was rendered against both defendants. Hamilton appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, which focused on whether the court could take cognizance of the action based on the jurisdictional facts stated.	The plaintiff, Ed. M. Dewey, claimed that Hamilton and Dugger failed to fulfill the obligations outlined in the promissory note. Dewey relied on the court's jurisdiction to hear the case initiated in Cook County, despite the fact that the alleged causes of action originated in Logan County and that Hamilton was served in Logan County.	The defendants, particularly Hamilton, asserted that the court should not have taken cognizance of the case because the actions leading to the suit occurred in Logan County, where the defendants resided. Hamilton contended that the court lacked jurisdiction, as he was served in Logan County by a process issued from Cook County, and he sought to have the judgment against him reversed.

In 1889, in Christian County, Illinois, the case of Frank P. Drennan v. R. C. Huskey et al. arose. The plaintiff, Frank P. Drennan, filed a bill in chancery to obtain a foreclosure decree on a trust deed associated with a $1,800 indebtedness evidenced by two bonds, which were signed by B. C. Huskey and his wife, Eva J. Huskey. These signed bonds were originally payable to Thomas J. Bunn but were linked to a larger loan provided by Loomis, an individual from Hartford, Connecticut. The bonds were tied to a commission agreement with Bunn and S. M. Moore, who charged an eight percent commission for securing the loan from Loomis. The interest on the loan was duly paid for several years until a default led to the advertisement of the property for sale. The death of Eva J. Huskey necessitated a chancery bill for foreclosure. Drennan, having purchased the bonds and their assignment, included R. C. Huskey, Alma Huskey (the sole heir), the trustee Powell, and tenant Fisher as defendants. The Huskeys’ defense claimed usury and asserted that they had already repaid an amount equivalent to the principal. The initial ruling favored the defendants, prompting Drennan to seek relief.	The plaintiff, Frank P. Drennan, argued that he was entitled to a decree of foreclosure on the trust deed due to the default on the bonds related to the loan processed via agents Bunn and Moore. Specifically, Drennan sought to enforce the mortgage given the outstanding indebtedness and maintained that the claims of usury raised by the defendants were baseless in light of no substantive evidence proving the existence of usury in the transaction.	The defendants, R. C. Huskey and Alma Huskey, contended that the loan transaction involved usury due to the commission deducted from the principal amount. They argued that not only was the business conducted through an agent who charged a commission, but they also claimed to have repaid an amount that equaled the principal sum of the loan.
