As a result, they requested the court to acknowledge this alleged usurious transaction and deny the enforcement of the foreclosure.

The case of Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Thomas Riley was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court and decided on December 9, 1887. The dispute arose in Will County, Illinois, involving Thomas Riley (the appellee) and the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company (the appellant). The core issue revolved around the railroad company's actions that led to the flooding of Riley's land. Specifically, the railroad had constructed a ditch along its right-of-way that diverted surface water from its natural channel, causing water to overflow onto Riley's property. The case was similar to a prior case involving the railroad, which had been determined in favor of the plaintiffs due to similar wrongful acts. The court examined whether the railroad was liable for damages resulting from the flooding and whether the Statute of Limitations applied.	Thomas Riley, the plaintiff, claimed that the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company was liable for flooding his land due to the diversion of surface water through a ditch created by the railroad. He argued that the railroad's actions constituted a continuing injury that had persisted for at least five years prior to the initiation of the lawsuit. Riley sought compensation for the damages incurred due to the flooding of his property.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, the defendant, contended that the claims were barred by the Statute of Limitations, suggesting that the plaintiff could not seek damages for acts that occurred more than five years prior to filing the lawsuit. The railroad argued that the specific damage claims had not been properly addressed in terms of their liability and presented instructions to the court which they believed were wrongly denied, asserting that they had been sufficiently instructed on their rights and liabilities.

In January 1863, the case of Samuel P. Hodgen v. Robert B. Latham was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in the Logan Circuit Court, where plaintiff Robert B. Latham accused defendant Samuel P. Hodgen of failing to pay for a large quantity of corn sold and delivered. The transaction included a complicated background involving a shared interest in the corn between Latham and John Wyatt. Witnesses testified that Hodgen agreed to purchase the corn for $1,128.10 but did not pay the amount on the agreed day, leading to claims of payment through a series of drafts that were ultimately not honored. The trial involved issues of the legitimacy of Latham's claim to sue alone, the ownership of the corn after several transactions, and whether debts involving drafts should have been accounted for in the jury's verdict. The court had to assess whether the drafts given by Hodgen as payment had legally constituted settlement or if they should have been retracted during the trial.	The plaintiff, Robert B. Latham, argued that he was entitled to the full amount for the corn sold, which was $1,128.10. He maintained that the sale was valid and that Hodgen failed to make the payment as agreed. Latham contended that there were no legal grounds for Hodgen's defenses, asserting that Hodgen should be liable for the total amount due without allowance for drafts that had not been honored.	Samuel P. Hodgen claimed that he had not only made arrangements for payment through drafts but argued that these drafts were valid legal instruments that settled his debt. He contended that the plaintiff had a duty to produce and cancel the drafts in question during the trial. Hodgen maintained that if the drafts were deemed legally outstanding, Latham should not be allowed to recover from him twice for the same debt. Additionally, he argued that Latham could not sue him alone, as there was joint ownership of the corn that should have included Wyatt as a party in the lawsuit.

Jacob Russell (appellant) was involved in a legal dispute with Edward H. Hadduck (appellee) regarding a bill of exchange. The case took place in Chicago, Illinois, during the February term of Court in 1846. A bill of exchange for $180.35 was drawn by Gracie in favor of John T. Smith & Co. in New York City, which was accepted by Russell. After Smith & Co. went bankrupt, the bill was transferred to Newberry & Burch in Chicago for collection. They then sold it to Hadduck in exchange for a check. Before the bill matured, Russell was notified by Gracie against paying it to Hadduck. The dispute centered on whether Hadduck was a bona fide purchaser for value, as Russell claimed that Hadduck was informed of prior interests in the bill, which could affect its validity. The trial court ruled in favor of Hadduck for the amount of the bill due, leading Russell to appeal the decision.	Russell claimed that Hadduck was not a bona fide purchaser of the bill of exchange because it was taken in payment of a precedent debt, which he argued is not a sufficient consideration to protect Hadduck's position against any claims from prior parties involved in the transaction. He maintained that Hadduck should have conducted further inquiries into the bill's legitimacy, suggesting that suspicions existed about its validity.	Hadduck contended that he acted in good faith, having no knowledge or suspicion that there might be a conflicting interest with Gracie. He argued that he provided a valuable consideration by paying for the bill with a check from his bank and that there were no suspicious circumstances that would have obligated him to inquire further into the bill's title. He maintained that, in the usual course of business, his transaction was legitimate and valid.

Frederick W. Michaelis filed a case against Sarah Wolf and others in Cook County, Illinois, which culminated in a decision on December 2, 1889. This case originally involved a mechanic's lien and related disputes over payments due to Michaelis, who was seeking certificates for amounts outlined in a contract. During a previous court session, the case was reviewed and then reversed before being remanded for further examination. Michaelis amended his bill to claim that the architect had fraudulently refused to issue the certificates needed for the fifth and sixth payments due, alleging that there was no valid reason for this refusal. The court examined the evidence presented by both sides before concluding that the claims of fraud were not substantiated by sufficient evidence, and affirmed the decision of the Circuit Court.	Michaelis argued that the architect had acted fraudulently by refusing to provide necessary certificates for the fifth and sixth installments of his contractual payments. He amended his complaint to present these allegations and sought the court’s intervention to support his claim of entitlement to the amounts due.	The defendants contended that the allegations of fraud presented by Michaelis were unsubstantiated. They provided evidence countering Michaelis’s claims and argued that the Circuit Court’s decision to dismiss the allegations of fraud was correct.

The case, "Kimball Favor et al. v. Isaac Marlett," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1844. It arose from a dispute in Kane County, Illinois. The core issue involved the alleged wrongful taking of unfinished furniture owned by Isaac Marlett, which had been assigned to him as a trustee by Franklin M. Grant to manage and sell. Marlett claimed that Kimball Favor and others, who owned the property where Grant had been a tenant, had unlawfully distrained and sold the furniture in question for unpaid rent that Grant owed them. The defendants claimed ownership of the furniture, arguing their right to sell it after distraining it for rent owed by Grant. During the trial, Marlett attempted to prove the value of the seized furniture with Grant as a witness, which the defendants objected to on grounds of Grant's potential interest in the case affecting his testimony. The trial court ruled in favor of Marlett, awarding him $92 in damages. This decision was appealed by the defendants, leading to a review of the appropriateness of Grant's testimony and the legal implications of the case.	Marlett claimed the furniture was his property as a trustee under Grant's assignment and sought damages for its unlawful taking by the defendants. He argued that the defendants had no legal right to distrain the furniture since it was entrusted to him and that his damages should reflect its rightful value. Marlett contended that the defendant's actions constituted a wrongful trespass and petitioned for legal recompense for the loss experienced due to the seizure and sale of the furniture.	The defendants, Kimball Favor and his associates, defended their actions by asserting their rights to the furniture due to Grant's indebtedness for rent. They argued that they lawfully seized the property to satisfy the debt owed to them, maintaining that Grant's tenancy and associated debts gave them the legal authority to act. The defendants contested the admission of Grant as a witness, claiming his interest in the case rendered him an incompetent witness and undermined the validity of the trial proceedings.

The case "Friedman, Sheirick & Co. v. Thomas L. Roderick et al." took place in December 1886 in Crawford County, Illinois. John S. Castle, a contractor and builder, constructed a dwelling for Thomas L. Roderick, who held a lien for the payment of the work. Upon completion, Roderick provided Castle with a note for $175, which stated the payment terms and explicitly mentioned that the note would not waive Castle's lien on the property. Castle, who owed money to Friedman, Sheirick & Co. for materials used in the construction, transferred this note to them as collateral security for his debt, without endorsing it. When the note matured and Castle's debt to Friedman, Sheirick & Co. remained unpaid, they filed a petition, seeking to enforce the lien and obtain an account of the amounts owed. However, Castle asserted that he did not authorize the lawsuit to be filed in his name and consented to its dismissal. The court ultimately dismissed the case against Roderick, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal.	The plaintiffs, Friedman, Sheirick & Co., argued that they were entitled to an equitable interest in the proceeds from the note given by Roderick to Castle. They sought a court order to maintain the petition in Castle's name as well as their own, requesting an account of the amount due, foreclosure of Castle's lien, and equitable distribution of the collected funds.	The defendant, Roderick, contended that the plaintiffs did not have the right to file the lawsuit in Castle’s name, as he did not authorize it. Following Castle’s affidavit confirming his lack of authorization, Roderick successfully moved to dismiss the case against him, arguing the illegitimacy of the plaintiffs' claims without Castle's consent.

In the case of John Endsley v. Joshua Johns, which took place in 1885 in Coles County, Illinois, the plaintiff, John Endsley, engaged in a transaction involving the sale of cattle to a man named John Kimlin, based on assurances given by the defendant, Joshua Johns. Endsley relied on Johns' representations that Kimlin's check for $1,041.74 was valid and would be honored by the bank. Reliant on this fraudulent advice, Endsley sold cattle to Kimlin, only to discover later that the check was worthless, resulting in a total loss. The case was brought forth as an action on the case, where Endsley asserted two counts of fraudulent misrepresentation against Johns. The jury ruled in favor of Endsley after a trial, prompting Johns to appeal the decision, claiming errors in jury instructions and misinterpretation of law regarding material misrepresentation and the necessity for the plaintiff to exercise ordinary care.	The plaintiff, John Endsley, claimed that the defendant, Joshua Johns, fraudulently misrepresented the validity of a check provided by John Kimlin. Endsley argued that he was assured the check was good and that this representation was made with the intent to deceive. As a result of this reliance, Endsley sold cattle for Kimlin's check, which ultimately bounced, causing him financial loss. The key requests of the plaintiff included compensation for the damages incurred due to the fraudulent misrepresentations.	The defendant, Joshua Johns, defended against Endsley's claims by arguing that the jury instructions regarding the materiality of misrepresentations were flawed, asserting that the jury was improperly allowed to determine what constituted material facts. Additionally, he contended that Endsley failed to exercise ordinary care in verifying the check's validity, and therefore should not recover damages. The defendant sought to have the original verdict overturned based on these alleged errors in jury instructions and the evaluation of evidence.

In May 1844, A.G. & W.N. Switzer filed a bill in chancery against Rachael Skiles and others in the Winnebago Circuit Court, Illinois. The case stems from a judgment recovered by the Switzer brothers against J.B. Miller on June 18, 1841, for $748.62, following which they obtained an execution that was levied on lots in Rockford. At the time, J.B. Miller claimed ownership of these lots and had secured them with several mortgages to the defendants, purportedly to evade the collection of the Switzers' judgment. In October 1841, the lots were sold to the Switzers for $790.89, but they claimed rightful ownership was thwarted by Miller’s fraudulent actions and the involvement of the defendants, who were to represent various claimants during a public land sale in 1843. A committee was to decide conflicting claims concerning the lots, but subsequent actions by Haight (an appointed trustee) and others undermined the Switzers’ rights. The Circuit Court sustained the defendants’ demurrer and dismissed the bill, prompting the Switzers to appeal.	The Switzers claimed that the mortgages filed by Miller were fraudulent and aimed at denying them their rightful judgment. They asserted they had purchased the lots in good faith after the judgment was made, and since Miller had no legitimate title at that point due to bankruptcy, they requested the court to annul the fraudulent transfers and reaffirm their ownership. The plaintiffs sought that the defendants, particularly Haight, be compelled to sell the lots and pay off their judgment from the proceeds.	The defendants claimed the mortgages were legitimate and argued that Miller did hold an interest in the lots that could be sold. They contended that since Haight's agreement was not documented in writing, it was void under the Statute of Frauds. They further asserted that the plaintiffs failed to substantiate their claims regarding fraud, and thus the court should dismiss the Switzers’ case due to lack of viable legal grounds.

In the case of Eugene Dougherty v. The People of the State of Illinois, the proceedings began with Dougherty's indictment for burglary during the September term of the Criminal Court of Cook County in 1882. After he was arrested and pleaded not guilty, the case experienced multiple continuances: it was continued by agreement at the November term, and then on the defendant's request at the December term. Subsequently, at the May term of 1883, the case was stricken from the docket, allowing it to be reinstated later on December 13, 1886. Following a denied motion by Dougherty to vacate the reinstatement order, he sought to be discharged and set at liberty during the December 23, 1886 term, but this request was continued and later overruled. Finally, Dougherty was tried, convicted, and sentenced to three years in prison at the January term of 1887, after significant delay in the legal process spanning over four terms.	The plaintiff, Eugene Dougherty, claimed that the trial court erred by not granting his motion to be set at liberty, arguing that the considerable delay of four terms without a trial entitled him to a discharge under section 18 of the Criminal Code. He contended that the delays were not due to his own actions, as required by the statute, and maintained that his right to a timely trial had been violated.	The defense, representing the State, argued that the delay in bringing Dougherty to trial was attributable to his own requests for continuance. They pointed out that the absence of a bill of exceptions left the presumption in favor of the trial court's decision to deny Dougherty’s discharge, as there was no sufficient evidence indicating the delays were not caused by the defendant himself.

On December 23, 1884, Robert D. Sheppard leased a property located in Chicago, specifically the first loft of the building at 197-201 Fifth Avenue, to George B. Cluett and others for a three-year term starting January 1, 1885. The lease stipulated a yearly rental of $2,000, payable monthly, and included a memorandum granting the tenant the privilege of storing a reasonable number of cases in the basement. Cluett and his co-tenants took possession of the premises in good order and occupied them until around January 1, 1886. Following this, Sheppard initiated legal action on January 6, 1887, seeking damages for unpaid rent, ultimately winning a judgment of $1,728.75 in the Superior Court, which was later upheld by the Appellate Court. The lease's provisions and the claimed eviction from the basement were central to the subsequent dispute.	The plaintiff, Robert D. Sheppard, argued that Cluett and his co-tenants were liable for unpaid rent during the lease period. He sought to enforce the terms of the lease, emphasizing that the tenants had accepted the premises and acknowledged their obligation to pay rent despite their claims regarding storage privileges in the basement. Sheppard maintained that the tenants had not been evicted as they had not effectively taken possession of the basement.	The defendants (Cluett et al.) contended that they had been effectively evicted from a significant portion of the leased premises before abandoning them. They claimed that their right to use the basement for storage was material to the lease and that the landlord’s actions deprived them of this right. The defendants argued that they were not liable for further rent after fulfilling their rental obligations for the time they occupied the premises.

The case, "The City of Chicago, Appellant, v. Christian Roth, Appellee," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1861. At the heart of the matter was an employment dispute involving Christian Roth, a carpenter commissioned to work on street crossings and streets in the West Division of Chicago during October and November 1859. Roth worked over a specified period under the direction of Peter Beygeh, the street commissioner, for a total of fifty-nine dollars and six cents ($59.06). Despite requests for payment to city officials, including the mayor and comptroller, Roth was repeatedly denied payment, even after performing necessary work including setting up protections for a polling place. The city had an allocated budget of twelve thousand dollars for street labor, which was nearing depletion. Complications arose when the city comptroller notified the street commissioner that no further payments would be made until taxes were raised, effectively making any work after that notice riskier for workers. This led to Roth seeking a resolution through the courts.	Christian Roth, the plaintiff, claimed that he was owed compensation for labor performed under the employment of the city of Chicago via its street commissioner. He argued that despite multiple requests and the work’s necessity, the city refused to pay for his services rendered, totaling $87.77. Roth sought a legal judgment to recover the unpaid wages based on the principle that as a laborer employed by a city official, he was still entitled to his wages regardless of the administrative shortcomings or instructions of the officials involved.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant, contended that Roth's recovery was precluded due to the fact that the street commissioner disobeyed lawful orders to suspend work, effectively making the payment a risk since the official had exhausted the appropriated funds. They argued that since they had provided notifications indicating that wages could not be authorized further, Roth was not entitled to payment for labor conducted after that point. The city's defense was fundamentally grounded on the assertion that any employment beyond the stated budgetary limits placed the responsibility, and thus the liability for payment, solely on the laborer.

In the case of The People, use, etc. v. Edward S. Gregory et al., which took place in Vermillion County, Illinois, the plaintiff brought a suit against Edward S. Gregory and his sureties on his official bond as the county sheriff. The proceedings stemmed from fees and emoluments that Gregory allegedly received during his term from November 1876, which he had not accounted for or paid to the county treasurer. The bond was executed to ensure Gregory would fairly account for and remit all funds received in his official capacity. The plaintiff identified thirteen breaches of the bond, though several were later withdrawn. A demurrer was raised by the defendants concerning the remaining breaches, which the trial court sustained, leading to a judgment in favor of the defendants. The plaintiff appealed, arguing that the court erred in sustaining the demurrer since even one well-pleaded breach ought to have resulted in a denial of the general demurrer. The case emphasized the constitutional obligation of county officials to account for all fees collected in excess of their officially sanctioned compensation.	The plaintiff claimed that Sheriff Gregory had failed to account for and pay over excess fees totaling $1,167.82 received during his official tenure, over and above the compensation fixed by the county board. The suit alleged multiple breaches of the bond that were supposed to ensure Gregory’s compliance with his obligations as sheriff, specifically under various statutes and constitutional mandates regarding county officer compensation and accountability. The plaintiff sought a judgment ordering the payment of those excess fees to the county treasury.	The defendant’s primary argument was rooted in the assertion that the allowances made by the county board for Gregory's compensation were for paying his deputies and thus were legitimate and within his rights. They contended that the plaintiff's claims lacked proper legal ground since the allowances should have covered all necessary expenses. The defendants maintained that the court's ruling to sustain their demurrer was justified, asserting that the breaches claimed by the plaintiff did not meet the legal standards necessary to pursue liability under the bond.

Oliver P. Canterberry v. Charles Miller is a legal case from January 1875, heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case took place in Sangamon County, Illinois. It revolved around a contract dispute regarding the sale of 100 head of hogs. On April 30, 1873, Canterberry and Miller entered into a written agreement where Canterberry sold the hogs to Miller for $4.50 per hundred pounds, with stipulations about delivery and weight. However, when the time for delivery arrived, Miller allegedly failed to accept and pay for the hogs according to the terms of the contract. The key issue presented in the case was whether the writings provided constituted a valid and enforceable contract between the parties. During the trial, the writings were excluded from evidence by the court, leading to a verdict in favor of Miller. The court examined the wording of the agreements and found that they essentially indicated each party was dealing with themselves, thus lacking the necessary mutual agreement required for a valid contract.	Canterberry, the plaintiff, argued that he had a valid written contract with Miller for the sale of 100 head of hogs. He claimed that Miller breached this contract by refusing to pay and accept the hogs as agreed. The plaintiff requested the court to recognize the contract and hold Miller accountable for the breach, seeking damages equivalent to the value of the hogs as stipulated in the agreement.	Miller, the defendant, contended that the documents presented by Canterberry did not constitute a valid contract as they essentially indicated that each party was both selling to and buying from themselves. He argued that there was no mutual agreement reflected in the writings, which led to the conclusion that no enforceable contract existed. Miller's defense focused on the lack of contractual clarity and the incorrect formation of the agreement.

The case "The Bogue-Badenoch Company v. Noel B. Boyden" was adjudicated on June 14, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court, following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County, where Judge Frank Baker presided. The dispute arose from a suit based on a replevin bond initiated by the late coroner of Cook County. The Bogue-Badenoch Company was the appellant seeking to reclaim property that had been in the sheriff's custody due to a judgment against them. The property in question was replevied by the appellants, and the merits of the original case were not tried, which left the issues open to examination in this appeal. The court was tasked with examining the record for potential errors, but concluded that no such errors were present, despite various objections raised by the appellants. A loose, unsigned paper that questioned the judgment was found, but it was deemed mere conjecture and not significant to the case’s outcome.	The Bogue-Badenoch Company (the plaintiff) claimed that the trial court made errors in the handling of the replevin suit. They sought to establish their rights over the replevied property and gain a favorable ruling in the appeal. They argued that the merits of their case had not been fully tried and should therefore be reconsidered by the appellate court.	Noel B. Boyden (the defendant) contended that the appeal should not proceed due to the lack of assigned errors as mandated by appellate rules. They maintained that the trial court's judgment was appropriate and should be affirmed, indicating that the procedural errors cited by the plaintiff were insufficient to warrant overturning the original decision.

In the legal case of Robert Burrows v. Ossian Guthrie et al., which took place in September 1871 in Cook County, Illinois, a partnership dispute arose between Robert Burrows and Ossian Guthrie. The partnership was formed in April 1869 to conduct business related to sidewalk construction. By September 30, 1869, an arbitration award was made to settle disputes regarding the division of profits, losses, and the disposition of partnership assets after disagreements about the dissolution of their partnership. Burrows objected to this award but later, in January 1871, withdrew his objections, leading the circuit court to enforce the award. The award included several provisions, notably that Guthrie would act as trustee to manage the partnership’s assets. Disputes continued, notably concerning the possession of a significant quantity of lumber belonging to the firm. Burrows, after the arbitration, allegedly took possession of this lumber by filing a replevin suit, which violated the award's stipulations. Eventually, Burrows was ordered to deliver this lumber to Guthrie under threat of contempt if he failed to comply.	Robert Burrows (the plaintiff) argued that he was entitled to ownership of certain assets from their partnership, specifically a large amount of lumber. His claim included the assertion that he had rightful possession of the lumber based on a replevin action he initiated against third parties and sought to have the court recognize this claim despite the prior arbitration award.	Ossian Guthrie and the other defendants contended that Burrows had accepted the arbitration award as binding, entrusting Guthrie with the management and disposition of partnership assets. They claimed Burrows acted in violation of the award by unlawfully taking possession of the lumber. The defendants requested the court to enforce compliance with the arbitration award, including the demand for the return of the lumber, payment of legal fees incurred from Burrows’ actions, and other specific obligations laid out in the award.

The legal case involves The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company against the People of the State of Illinois. It was decided on January 29, 1883, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated due to the railway company's charges for freight transportation from various points within Illinois to New York City. Specifically, the company was accused of imposing unjust discrimination by charging different rates for transporting goods over varying distances. This case was previously adjudicated, leading to the Illinois Supreme Court's reaffirmation of its stance regarding the regulation of interstate commerce and the prevention of unjust freight charges by the state. The court insisted that while Illinois has the right to regulate transportation charges within its jurisdiction, this does not extend to authority over charges applicable in other states. The chief judge emphasized the neglect of corporate powers that might harm public interest and the necessity for government control to prevent extortion and unjust discrimination.	The plaintiff, The People of the State of Illinois, argued that the Wabash Railway Company engaged in unjust discrimination in freight charges, violating the Illinois law prohibiting such practices. They contended that the company's pricing mechanism resulted in higher charges for shorter routes compared to longer ones, without justifiable reasons, thus unfairly disadvantaging local shippers. They sought enforcement of the law which mandated equitable freight rates reflecting the proportional distance traveled.	The defendant, Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company, argued that the charges set for freight transportation were legitimate and authorized under their interstate commerce operations. They claimed that the State of Illinois lacked constitutional authority to regulate rates associated with interstate commerce, which they argued was under the exclusive purview of Congress. The railway maintained that their pricing was consistent throughout its routes and denied any violation of state law concerning price discrimination.

Patrick Keefe brought a case against the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company after sustaining injuries while working as a laborer on a construction train. This incident took place in Sangamon County, Illinois, in the context of the railroad's operations. On the day of the accident, while unloading railroad iron from a platform car, Keefe was injured when the engineer of the train moved the train without giving the required preliminary signal, as mandated by railroad safety rules. The conductor had given the engineer the signal to reverse the train in order to switch tracks, but the engineer failed to follow protocol, resulting in Keefe being thrown from the platform car. A trial initially found in favor of Keefe, leading the railroad company to appeal the decision.	Keefe argued that the negligence of the engineer, who failed to provide the necessary signal before moving the train, was responsible for his injuries. He contended that this carelessness should make the railroad company liable for damages since he was working under the conductor's orders when the accident occurred. Keefe sought compensation for his injuries based on the premise that he had been placed at risk due to the engineer's failure to follow safety procedures.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company defended itself by asserting that Keefe, as a co-employee of the engineer, could not recover damages for his injuries because of the established common law principle that prevents one employee from suing another for injuries resulting from co-employee negligence, provided that the employer exercised due diligence in selecting its workers. They also argued that Keefe's role was not distinct enough from that of the engineer to warrant an exception to this rule, emphasizing that all employees on the train were part of the same general duty.

Josiah D. Dunning filed a trespass action against Ira H. Fitch in a case decided in September 1872 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The original incident took place in the town of Aurora, Illinois, where Fitch, acting as the tax collector, seized and sold personal property that Dunning claimed belonged to him. Dunning argued that Fitch's seizure was unlawful because part of the taxes assessed on the property belonged to a third party, Eeifsnider, and were improperly levied to pay bonds voted irregularly to aid a railroad company. The court's examination focused on whether Dunning owned or possessed the property at the time of the seizure. The evidence presented was contradictory, with a jury determining that Dunning was not the owner or in possession of the property in question.	Dunning claimed that the taxes utilized by Fitch to justify the seizure were illegal, asserting that $3.10 of those taxes were improperly levied to cover irregular bonds associated with the Chicago, Burlington, and Quincy Railroad. He sought damages for what he argued was an unlawful seizure of his personal property.	Fitch defended against the trespass claim by asserting that he legitimately acted as the tax collector for the town and that the property belonged to Eeifsnider, for which the taxes were duly levied. Fitch argued that Dunning's ownership or possession of the property at the time of the seizure was the key issue and maintained that legal questions about the assessment of the taxes were irrelevant to the case.

In December 1838, the case of Abel Gilbert and his wife against David Maggord was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a mortgage agreement executed by Gilbert and his wife, involving a foreclosure proceeding. At trial, the Circuit Court ruled in favor of Maggord after Gilbert confessed to one of the defenses presented by Maggord. Gilbert then introduced new evidence to counter the defenses. The case raised issues regarding the sufficiency of the scire facias writ and whether the wife of the defendant should have been made a party to the foreclosure process. The Circuit Court found that the wife was properly included as she was one of the mortgagors and her rights, including dower, needed to be addressed in the judgment. The court's judgment affirmed the inclusion of the wife as a co-defendant and ruled against the Gilbert couple's objections.	The plaintiffs, Abel Gilbert and his wife, argued that the scire facias writ used to initiate the foreclosure was legally insufficient and claimed that the Circuit Court erred in not recognizing this defect. They also objected to the wife being made a defendant, suggesting that her involvement was improper. Overall, their legal requests focused on challenging the validity of the foreclosure proceeding and seeking an overturn of the judgment against them.	David Maggord, the defendant, contended that the writ of scire facias was valid and properly executed and that the Gilberts had no basis to claim the wife should not be a defendant since she had signed the mortgage. He emphasized that including her was necessary to foreclose her rights regarding dower and equity of redemption. Maggord's requests included affirming the initial judgment rendered in his favor and the legitimacy of the foreclosure proceedings.

In the case of John D. Caton v. Andrew Bloom, decided on January 6, 1886, the incident took place while John D. Caton was employed as a laborer operating a stone-crushing drop hammer in Illinois. Caton suffered a severe injury resulting in the loss of his hand while operating the machinery. He alleged that the injury was due to the negligence of Andrew Bloom, his employer, for failing to provide and maintain safe machinery. The case was brought to the Illinois Appellate Court following a jury verdict in favor of Caton, who was awarded $4,000 by the lower court. The court found that there was conflicting evidence regarding whether Bloom exercised reasonable care in ensuring the safety of the machinery, and it was determined that this was primarily a factual issue for the jury to resolve. The jury was presumed better able to assess the evidence and make a judgment regarding negligence.	John D. Caton claims that Andrew Bloom's negligence in failing to provide and maintain safe machinery directly resulted in the loss of his hand. Caton argues that he was exercising ordinary care while operating the stone-crushing drop hammer when the accident occurred and seeks compensation for damages in the amount of $4,000.	Andrew Bloom contends that he was not negligent in providing and maintaining the machinery used by Caton. Bloom asserts that the evidence was conflicting regarding the safety of the equipment and requests that the court overturn the lower court's verdict in favor of Caton, claiming that the finding of negligence was incorrect.

In 1859, Richard H. Pease, a property owner in Chicago, contended with the city regarding a special assessment levied for improvements on West Lake Street. The assessment was confirmed by the Common Council on October 4, 1858, and was intended to collect $31,000 from property owners deemed benefited by the macadamization of the street. The city collector, Joseph N. Hendricks, filed a report in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas, detailing his efforts to collect unpaid taxes and assessments. Pease objected to the assessment, asserting that it was fraudulent and improperly calculated based on inflated property valuations. He claimed that part of the street improvement had already been completed by private parties prior to the city's assessment, which he argued rendered the tax illegal, as the Common Council had no authority to levy assessments for improvements not initiated by them. Several court proceedings ensued as Pease challenged the validity of the assessment and its execution.	Richard H. Pease claimed that the assessment on his lots was fraudulently inflated and that the City of Chicago lacked authority to levy an assessment for improvements that had been voluntarily completed by private property owners. He specifically challenged the value assigned to his lots and contended that the Common Council's processes leading to the assessment were improperly conducted, including claims that the assessment was not made in accordance with existing laws and that he had not received proper notice regarding the assessment procedures.	The City of Chicago, represented by its attorney, claimed that Pease's objections lacked merit and asserted that the assessment was legally sound as it complied with the city charter and the statutory authority granted to the Common Council. The city argued that it had followed the required procedures for levying the assessment, including public notices and obtaining necessary confirmations from the council, thus justifying the collection of taxes from property owners.

The legal case of N. B. Haynes v. Mary J. Mason took place in Cook County, Illinois, and was presided over by Judge Elliott Anthony. The events leading to the case began with the formation of a contract on March 26, 1885, wherein Mary J. Mason (plaintiff) was to be employed by N. B. Haynes (defendant) for a period of one year, commencing on March 30, 1885. The contract was not in writing and stipulated that Mason was to be compensated at a specified rate over the terms of her employment. Due to Haynes' business failure on November 7, 1885, he was unable to provide further employment, leaving Mason with an outstanding balance of $250 in salary for work performed up to that point. The case involved discussions about the validity of the contract under the statute of frauds, which pertains to contracts that are not to be performed within one year.	Mary J. Mason claimed that she was entitled to her unpaid salary for the period specified in her employment contract, maintaining that despite the contract being oral and not written, she fulfilled her obligations as per the agreement until Haynes' business failure. She sought judgment for the balance of the salary owed to her, which amounted to $250.	N. B. Haynes contended that the employment contract was void under the statute of frauds, as it was not capable of performance within one year from its creation unless in writing. Furthermore, Haynes argued that Mason should be held accountable for certain customer accounts, which he claimed she had agreed to guarantee, and he sought to have these accounts offset against any salary owed.

In September 1870, in Iroquois County, Illinois, a legal action was initiated by Henry H. Eastburn against the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company. The case arose when the railway company accidentally killed Eastburn's livestock while operating their trains. Following a trial held in the circuit court, the jury found in favor of Eastburn, awarding him $115 in damages. The railway company's appeal centered on the claim that the evidence presented did not support the jury's verdict. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case, focusing on whether the evidence was sufficient to uphold the jury's decision.	Henry H. Eastburn claimed that the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company was liable for the death of his livestock due to negligence in operating their railroad. He sought compensation for the loss, which resulted in a jury verdict in his favor for $115.	The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company contended that the evidence presented at trial did not justify the jury's finding of liability. They argued that the verdict was contrary to the evidence, essentially requesting the Supreme Court to reverse the decision and dismiss the trial court's judgment.

The case "Fayette T. Dimick, Admr. v. The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Co." took place in September 1875 in Illinois. Fayette T. Dimick represented the estate of Gilbert H. Dimick, who died in a fatal collision involving a train operated by the Chicago and Northwestern Railway. The plaintiff claimed that the railway company was negligent, leading to the death of Dimick. The allegations included faults in the management of the train, failure to clear obstructive vegetation on the railway's right of way, and the absence of the required audible warnings (bell ringing or whistle sounding) when approaching the crossing. During the trial, the jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding damages amounting to $3,500. However, the lower court later reversed this finding, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiff argued that the railroad company acted negligently by failing to manage its train safely, maintaining obstructions on its right of way that hindered visibility, and not providing adequate warnings (such as a ringing bell or sounding whistle) as Dimick approached the tracks. The plaintiff sought damages for loss of life due to this alleged negligence.	The defendant contended that the special findings by the jury regarding the decedent’s behavior indicated that he had acted negligently by not ensuring his safety when approaching the tracks. They maintained that he failed to hear a warning shout to stop before he was struck, implying that any negligence was on his part rather than the railroad's failure to provide signals.

In the case of Hannah Horner et al. v. Noel B. Boyden, the legal proceedings took place under the jurisdiction of the Illinois Appellate Court and were finalized on December 18, 1888. The core issue emerged from a replevin bond that was granted to the coroner (Boyden) in the context of a lawsuit involving Horner against Hanchett, a sheriff, and a party named Langbien. The appellants (Horner and others) claimed that goods had been wrongfully taken from them based on a replevin writ, which allowed certain items to be delivered to them by the sheriff. The plaintiffs sought to enforce the bond due to the alleged non-payment by Langbien for goods he had fraudulently procured. After a court trial without a jury, a judgment was rendered against the appellants for $474. They argued that the court erred in admitting the bond into evidence without proof of its execution. The trial included key elements such as the change of action from replevin to assumpsit, which asserted that the goods were fraudulently obtained, impacting the legal standing of the claims related to the replevin bond.	The plaintiffs, Hannah Horner et al., argued that they were entitled to damages of $474 due to the defendant’s alleged fraud in obtaining goods through deceit. They maintained that the bond underpinning their claims should be enforced despite not having attached a copy to their declaration, arguing that the findings of the court erroneously dismissed their position regarding proof of the bond’s execution. They sought legal relief for the damages incurred as a result of the defendant's actions, emphasizing that Langbien had obtained goods on credit with no intention to pay.	The defendant, represented by Boyden, contended that the court's allowance of the bond into evidence was justified, as the execution of the bond had not been formally denied through an affidavit. They argued that the plaintiffs had changed their action from replevin to assumpsit, which constituted an affirmance of the sale of all goods and negated their claim of fraud. Therefore, the defendant asserted that no defense could be made against the replevin bond based on claims of fraud related to the purchased goods.

In 1854, a legal dispute arose concerning the sale of real estate belonging to Abraham V. Knickerbocker, whose interests were represented by his guardian. The application for the sale was supposed to be made during the circuit court term on the fourth Monday of October, as indicated in the notice. However, the application was instead made at the November term, which followed. The October term never took place due to the absence of the judge, raising questions about the jurisdiction of the court. The records indicated that no petition was filed within the timeframe for the October term; hence, the jurisdiction was in question. The case emphasized that for the court to have jurisdiction, not only should a notice have been provided, but a petition must also be filed within the appropriate time. The court ruled that without these procedural steps, the application was rendered void.	The plaintiff, Abraham V. Knickerbocker, argued that the sale of his real estate was conducted improperly because the application was made at a different court term than the one specified in the notice, leading to a lack of jurisdiction. He sought the reversal of the decree that permitted the sale and claimed that procedural errors rendered the court's actions void.	The defendant, represented by Margaret Knickerbocker and others, contended that the statutory provisions concerning court continuance due to the judge's absence applied in this case. They argued that since the October term was improperly adjourned, the matter should have naturally carried over to the succeeding term, thus asserting that the court maintained jurisdiction to finalize the sale.

The case "The City of Chicago v. Bernard T. Brophy" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. It originated from an incident that occurred on December 20, 1872, when Bernard T. Brophy sustained serious injuries, including a broken leg, while driving his baker’s wagon on a public street in Chicago. The injury was caused by an obstruction—a ridge of dirt—left over a sewer that the city had recently constructed. This ridge, created during the installation of a branch sewer and a catch-basin, was not visible at the time of the accident due to snow covering the street. Testimonies indicated that this situation made the road unsafe for travel. The city had failed to remove the dirt or provide any warning about the danger, which led to Brophy's accident as he was unaware of the obstruction beneath the snow. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Brophy, awarding him $1,500 for his injuries.	Bernard T. Brophy claimed that the City of Chicago was negligent in failing to keep the streets safe, particularly regarding the unremoved obstruction that caused his accident. He argued that the dangerous conditions created by the city’s employees directly led to his injuries. Brophy sought compensation for the damages incurred due to this negligence, which he believed was sufficiently proven by evidence of the dangerous ridge that the city left without warning or caution.	The City of Chicago, represented by Mr. Egbert Jamieson, raised several defenses against Brophy’s claims. They contended that the verdict was contrary to the evidence presented and asserted that the jury instructions given to the plaintiff were erroneous. The city argued that there was insufficient proof of negligence on their part, claiming the damages awarded were excessive. They maintained that it was not established that the city employees were responsible for the dangerous condition or that any actual notice of such a condition existed prior to the incident.

In April 1865, in the Circuit Court of Stephenson County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving John W. Humphrey and others (plaintiffs) against Charles F. Taggart (defendant). The case was centered around a replevin bond, which is a legal document securing the return of property taken under legal authority. The plaintiffs, who had initially contested Taggart's claim, failed to prosecute their suit in a timely manner. Despite the plaintiffs' claims, the court found that they did not fulfill the requirements of the bond to pursue their suit without delay. The defendant sought legal recourse based on this failure, leading to a judgment against the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant had failed to uphold the terms of the replevin bond, arguing that they had kept the sheriff harmless and returned the replevied property. They contended that their plea adequately addressed the breaches outlined in the defendant's claims, which focused on the failure to prosecute the replevin action effectively and without delay.	The defendant countered that the plaintiffs did not comply with the specific condition of the replevin bond that required them to prosecute their suit to effect and without delay. The defendant argued that the plaintiffs' plea did not sufficiently address the breaches of the bond, particularly the independent obligation to pursue the legal action timely. As a result, the defendant requested that the court uphold the terms of the replevin bond, indicating that the plaintiffs were liable for their failure to act as required.

The case "Collins D. White v. Willard P. Alward" was decided on December 24, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose from a negotiable instrument—a promissory note—initially signed by Willard P. Alward, promising to pay $100 to C. A. Hamper. The issue revolved around whether Alward could be held liable, given that the instrument had been modified after its execution. Before maturity, the note was transferred to Collins D. White, who acquired it in good faith. However, it had certain blanks filled in by a prior holder, Smith, in a different handwriting and ink. Alward argued that these modifications constituted an illegal alteration of the note. The court needed to determine the implications of these changes on Alward's obligation to pay, particularly whether the unfilled blanks on the document granted the holder the authority to insert reasonable amounts in them.	Collins D. White, the appellant, contended that he acquired the note in good faith and was a bona fide holder. He argued that the addition of amounts to previously blank spaces did not constitute a material alteration and should not absolve Alward of his obligation to pay the agreed amount. He requested that the court enforce the note as it was validly executed and transferred.	Willard P. Alward, the appellee, contended that the alterations made to the note after its execution violated the terms of the original agreement and rendered the note invalid. He argued that the modifications should discharge him from his liability under the promissory note, maintaining that a holder cannot enforce a negotiable instrument that has been materially altered.

Jonathan J. Lyman v. Lucy Russell et al. is a legal case heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1867. The case stems from a dispute over a mortgage executed on January 20, 1858, by William Bandy and his wife in favor of O. L. Davis. The plaintiff, Jonathan J. Lyman, contended that prior to the mortgage, Bandy had sold the same land to Samuel Lyman on July 27, 1855. Samuel Lyman and his successors claimed to have been in open, notorious, and actual possession of the land since the time of the sale until Lyman's eventual purchase of it in 1863. This possession was evident to passersby along a public road, and Lyman had made improvements to the land prior to the mortgage. The plaintiff argued that the mortgage should be set aside because Davis, as a mortgagee, should have inquired about Lyman's possession and rights before taking the mortgage. A circuit court initially ruled against Lyman's claims, leading to his appeal. This case highlights the significance of actual possession as a form of notice to subsequent purchasers.	The plaintiff, Jonathan J. Lyman, claimed that the mortgage taken by O. L. Davis was invalid due to prior ownership and possession rights associated with the land, which was sold to Samuel Lyman by William Bandy in 1855. Lyman requested the court to set aside the mortgage and all proceedings related to it, asserting that Davis failed to investigate the status of the land and regarding the earlier unrecorded deed before executing the mortgage.	The defendants, Lucy Russell and her co-defendants, contested Lyman's claims, asserting ignorance of the deed from Bandy to Samuel Lyman and any interest the Lymans had in the land until after the mortgage was foreclosed. They argued that since they were unaware of the previous ownership, their rights to the mortgage should prevail.

The case "The Joliet Manufacturing Company v. Andrew F. Dice" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 28, 1883. It revolved around a dispute over the ownership of an invention related to a machine part known as "check rowers." The key individuals involved were the Joliet Manufacturing Company, located in Joliet, Illinois, and Andrew F. Dice, who resided in Aurelia, Iowa. The company hired Dice under a written agreement dated October 18, 1881, stipulating that he would work for them for five years, focusing on the manufacturing of various devices including shellers and powers. During his employment, Dice developed an improvement to the check rowers and was directed by the company to focus on this invention using company resources. The Joliet Manufacturing Company claimed that the invention should belong to them as a result of the nature of Dice's employment contract, which stated that any future improvements he made in the manufacturing process would belong to the company. After a series of appeals, the issue was whether the invention belonged to Dice or to the company, leading to significant legal consideration around the nature of employment contracts and intellectual property rights in the context of inventions.	The Joliet Manufacturing Company claimed that Andrew F. Dice should assign his rights to the invention of the improved check rowers to them, arguing that Dice's employment contract stated any future improvements he developed during his employment would belong to the company. The company sought court relief to compel Dice to assign the invention and additionally sought to prevent him from selling or assigning the invention to any other party.	Andrew F. Dice argued that he was the rightful owner of the invention, asserting that the contract only specified improvements related to “shelters and powers,” and did not encompass the check rowers. He maintained that there was no clear contract specifying that he was to invent the improved check rowers for the company, thus retaining the rights to his own invention. Dice contended that during his employment, he merely worked on the invention in good faith for the potential benefit of the company, without agreeing to assign ownership of the resulting invention to them.

In December 1831, a legal case took place in Madison County, Illinois, involving William P. and T. M. Bryan as the plaintiffs and Nathaniel Buckmaster as the defendant. The case originated when the plaintiffs sought to quash a fee-bill issued by the circuit court's clerk, which included improper charges for commissions related to two executions against the plaintiff's assets. The first execution's sheriff's return showed that no money had been made since there were no bidders for the property that was to be sold, yet the clerk charged a commission based on the full amount of the execution. The second execution resulted in some payment through a sale of real estate, but again, the clerk charged commissions incorrectly. The circuit court denied the plaintiffs' request to quash the fee-bill, prompting the plaintiffs to bring the case to the Illinois Supreme Court for a review of the charges and the authority of the clerk in such matters. The central legal questions revolved around the validity of the clerk's fee-bill and the statutory limitations on commissions for sheriffs.	The plaintiffs argued that the clerk had no authority to include charges for sheriff's commissions in the fee-bill when the sheriff's own returns did not include such charges. They contended that commissions should only be charged on the amounts actually collected by the sheriff rather than on the total amounts of the executions. The plaintiffs sought to have the fee-bill quashed on the grounds that it contained erroneous and incorrect charges that were contrary to established statutes governing sheriff fees.	The defendant maintained that the clerk acted within the scope of his authority by issuing the fee-bill, relying on language in the relevant laws. They argued that the sheriff was entitled to half commissions on the full amounts of both executions, despite the reality that the first execution produced no revenue. The defense asserted that the wording of the relevant legislation allowed for the clerk's actions and that the fees charged were therefore justified.

In the case of "Henry Fisher v. The State of Illinois," the incident leading to the legal claim occurred following the construction of a dam by the State of Illinois on the Illinois River. The dam, completed on October 21, 1877, caused damages to Fisher's property, specifically his lands located above the Copperas Creek dam. Fisher filed his claim on October 20, 1879, seeking compensation for the damages incurred, totaling $268. The claim was brought before the Illinois Court of Claims, and the Commission evaluated evidence and arguments presented by both parties. The case gained prominence during the August session of the Commission of Claims in 1889, leading to thorough consideration of the events that unfolded and the legal implications of the state’s action on Fisher's property rights.	The plaintiff, Henry Fisher, argued that the construction of the state dam had resulted in significant injury to his lands along the Illinois River. He claimed a total of $268 in damages, asserting that he filed the claim within the legally permissible timeframe of two years from the incident, thus not violating any statute of limitations. Fisher contended that the damage to his property was directly attributable to the state's actions in building the dam.	The State of Illinois, as the defendant, presumably argued against the claims of damage presented by Fisher. While specific defenses were not detailed in the available court opinion, typical defenses in similar cases might include contesting the amount claimed, demonstrating that the damages were not directly caused by state action, or asserting that the state was protected from such claims under specific statutory provisions related to public works.

The case of William Owens et al. v. John Weedman occurred in 1876 in DeWitt County, Illinois. The plaintiff, John Weedman, had a business agreement with Owens regarding the sale of hogs. Weedman had initially expressed interest in purchasing two carloads of hogs from Owens, stating he would only buy if Owens could provide the correct quantity. After giving Owens a $20 advance, they agreed for the hogs to be delivered on a specific Friday. However, on the delivery day, Weedman could not finalize payment on the hogs as he was unable to meet with Owens and ultimately instructed a bank clerk not to pay any further checks Owens attempted to process. Owens took possession of the hogs, which had been weighed and prepared for delivery, and later shipped them to Chicago with Drybread, who was involved in the transaction. The main issue in the case revolves around whether Weedman had the legal right to the hogs when converted by Owens and Drybread. A jury trial initially ruled in Weedman's favor, awarding him $550 in damages for the hogs he claimed were wrongfully taken.	Weedman's primary claims were based on his assertion that he was the rightful owner of the hogs that he had paid for and that Owens and Drybread wrongfully converted these hogs to their own use without his consent. He contended that he had engaged in a lawful contract with Owens for the sale of the hogs, which included payment that had already been partially made.	Owens and Drybread defended themselves by arguing that Weedman had not provided full payment at the time of the alleged conversion and therefore did not have a legal right to the immediate possession of the hogs. Their defense highlighted that the contract was for the delivery of two complete carloads of hogs, and since Weedman had failed to make the required payments, they were justified in taking possession and shipping the hogs.

On March 29, 1883, the Illinois Supreme Court decided the case of Anthony McNamara et al. v. Thomas Garrity. The case originated in Greene County, Illinois, where Thomas Garrity filed a bill in chancery against Anthony McNamara regarding the ownership of a ten-acre tract of land. The background of the dispute traces back to an agreement made on April 23, 1859, between Garrity and McNamara to purchase a forty-acre parcel from Davidson. According to the agreement, Garrity was responsible for one-fourth of the purchase price while McNamara would cover the remaining three-fourths. Garrity was to receive a ten-acre strip from the western side of the tract, while McNamara would keep the rest. Once the purchase price was settled, McNamara was to legally transfer the ten acres to Garrity. The necessary deed and mortgage were executed at the time. Garrity made his payment and took possession of the ten acres, improving the land which he cultivated for over twenty years. However, McNamara later denied Garrity’s rights to the land and refused to convey the property to him, prompting Garrity to seek relief through the courts.	Garrity's main argument revolved around his claim of a resulting trust in the ten acres of land due to his financial contributions and substantial improvements made over the years. He asserted that his payments and the exclusive possession of the land for over two decades established his rightful ownership, compelling McNamara to execute a deed for the property as per their original agreement. Garrity requested the court to enforce this deed, arguing that the Statute of Frauds did not apply because of his actions of payment and possession.	McNamara's defense centered on the assertion that the Statute of Frauds barred Garrity's claims since the agreement to convey the land was verbal and not supported by a written contract. Furthermore, he argued that any claim Garrity had was limited by the statute of limitations due to the time elapsed without written acknowledgment of the trust. McNamara contended that the evidence presented did not sufficiently prove Garrity's claims to the land or that a resulting trust existed.

In the case of William Guebert v. John Zick et al., filed in the Illinois Appellate Court on June 15, 1889, a dispute arose involving a series of property deeds. The key individuals included William Guebert (the appellant) and John Zick along with Helena and Rudolph J. Boekhoff (the appellees). The context centered around deeds executed by Helena and Rudolph Boekhoff to Guebert, which were alleged to be fraudulent. The plaintiffs claimed the deeds were intended to hinder, delay, or defraud Zick and other creditors. Two significant judgments, one in favor of Zick for $3,232.71 and another in favor of Theda Boekhoff for $2,092, were involved. It was claimed that Guebert was aware of the fraudulent intentions when purchasing the land. Additionally, an assignment related to Sophia Boekhoff, Helena and Rudolph's mother, to Guebert was also put into question, as it appeared to further the alleged fraudulent intent. The case involved complex relationships among four siblings entitled to properties, the conveyances executed, and the associated cash payments made. The court initially ruled to set aside the deeds and allowed the complainants to collect their judgments as if the deeds had never been executed.	The plaintiffs, represented by John Zick and others, sought to have the court set aside the deeds that Helena and Rudolph Boekhoff executed in favor of William Guebert. They argued that these properties were conveyed to Guebert with the intent to evade creditors. The plaintiffs claimed that Guebert had knowledge of this intent at the time of procurement of the deeds and that the conveyances should therefore be canceled to allow the collection of their outstanding judgments.	William Guebert contended that he had no knowledge of any fraudulent intent associated with the property conveyances at the time they happened. He argued that Helena approached him seeking a legitimate sale for financial reasons, specifically needing cash to settle her debts. Guebert maintained that there was insufficient evidence to support the claim of fraud regarding the deed he received from Helena and that any assertions made about Rudolph's deed should not invalidate his own actions entirely.

In February 1873, George F. Work executed a trust deed on a property in Chicago to secure payment for bonds totaling $10,000. Later, Work conveyed the property to Henry B. Jenks and then, on November 18, 1873, Jenks sold it to Algy Dean for $27,500. The deed from Jenks to Dean included an assumption clause regarding existing debts on the property. On November 4, 1874, Dean sold the property to Edwin Walker for $54,000, also incorporating an assumption clause in which Walker agreed to pay the existing debts. Sweet and Hutchinson, having acquired a portion of the bonds secured by the aforementioned deed of trust, subsequently brought a lawsuit against Walker for recovery of the bond amounts under Dean's assignment. Walker’s liability arose from his acceptance of the deed that contained the assumption of the mortgage obligations. The legal contention centered on whether Walker was bound to pay the mortgage despite not signing the deed. The court was tasked with resolving the obligations between the parties involved based on the assumption clauses in question.	The plaintiffs, represented by Algy Dean, asserted that Edwin Walker was liable for the mortgage debts on the property he purchased, based on the assumption clause in the deed that he agreed to pay. They argued that Walker’s acceptance of the deed, which contained the assumption, legally bound him to fulfill the mortgage obligation as he had acknowledged its validity and agreed to pay it. The plaintiffs sought to recover the amounts owed on the bonds secured by the trust deed.	Edwin Walker contended that he should not be held liable for the mortgage debts since the grantor (Jenks) was not personally liable for those debts at the time of conveyance. Walker argued that the assumption clause in his deed should be interpreted solely as an indemnity to Dean rather than imposing any obligation on him in relation to the mortgage payments. He maintained that the absence of a personal liability on the part of the original grantor invalidated any claims for indemnity against him, asserting that he should not bear the debt for a liability he did not assume originally.

In the year 1885, in Ford County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between two school districts, namely School Directors, District No. 4 and School Directors, District No. 2. District No. 4 was established from territory that was formerly part of District No. 2. The newly formed District No. 4 filed a bill in chancery alleging that, following the division of the districts, an appraisal of its property determined that the amount due to them was $162.60. Despite this amount being appraised, District No. 2 had not made any payments, and the township trustees were accused of failing to take action to recover the owed funds. The plaintiffs sought a court order compelling District No. 2 to pay the outstanding amount to the township treasurer for the benefit of District No. 4. Initially, a demurrer to this bill was overruled, and an answer was filed by District No. 2 contesting the claims and asserting that the debt was settled and barred by the five-year Statute of Limitations. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court for consideration of these arguments and subsequent rulings.	The plaintiffs, School Directors of District No. 4, contended that the amount of $162.60 owed to them following the division from District No. 2 was never paid. They requested the court to compel District No. 2 to remit this payment to the township treasurer to benefit the newly formed district. Their arguments emphasized that the creation of a trust fund from the appraisal mandated legal action to collect the owed amount.	The defendants, representing District No. 2, presented two main defenses against the claims made by District No. 4. First, they argued that the facts laid out by the plaintiffs did not provide a valid basis for relief in equity and should therefore lead to dismissal of the bill. Secondly, they asserted that the claims were barred by the Statute of Limitations since thirteen years had passed since the division occurred, categorizing the claim as stale.

In December 1843, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case of John Morrison v. John Hinton, for the use of Moses Silverburg, which originated from a promissory note dispute. The case began in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, where Hinton sued Morrison on a $100 note before a justice of the peace. After Morrison defended himself successfully, the case was dismissed at the district court level. Silverburg, the original creditor, appealed to the circuit court, where the jury found against Morrison, resulting in a judgment against him for $108.50. During the trial, Morrison attempted to introduce evidence of a judgment against him from a justice in Grant County, Wisconsin, which purportedly supported Hinton's claim. However, this evidence was rejected by the circuit court because it lacked a proper certification proving the justice’s official capacity at the time the judgment was rendered, leading to the eventual legal challenge before the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff's main arguments revolved around the validity and enforceability of the judgment from Wisconsin, suggesting it constituted admissible evidence in support of Hinton's claim against Morrison. The plaintiff contended that the defendant’s objections to the judgment's admissibility were unfounded and sought legal validation for the judgment rendered.	The defendant challenged the admissibility of the Wisconsin judgment, arguing that the certification provided was insufficient as it did not verify the official capacity of the justice at the time the judgment was issued. Morrison's defense highlighted that the clerk's certificate only established the justice's capacity as of the date of certification, failing to confirm his status at the time the original judgments were rendered. Instead of solely disputing the reasoning, the defendant urged that the evidence was fundamentally flawed and should be excluded based on a lack of proper authentication.

In November 1855, in Peoria, Illinois, Charles W. Zimmerman executed a promissory note in the amount of $700, promising to pay the order of William Kellogg at a designated office. The note was issued as part of a financial transaction, and later, Kellogg endorsed the note to Hezekiah M. Wead, the plaintiff, for the use of the Illinois Central Railroad Company. The case was initiated when Wead brought suit against Zimmerman, claiming that Zimmerman failed to pay the amount due by the specified timeframe. The legal action styled as an action of assumpsit prompted clarification on the validity of the declaration, which stated the nature of the note, its assignment, and the non-payment by Zimmerman. Questions arose regarding certain technical aspects of the declaration, but it was ultimately deemed sufficient for a clear understanding of the complaint against Zimmerman.	The plaintiff, Hezekiah M. Wead, argued that Zimmerman failed to fulfill his promise to pay the sum of $700 as stipulated in the promissory note, despite having received formal notice of the assignment of the note from Kellogg. Wead sought damages amounting to $1,000, asserting the failure to pay constituted a breach of contract. The plaintiff claimed the action was brought for the benefit of the Illinois Central Railroad Company, which was entitled to the proceeds of the note.	The defendant, Charles W. Zimmerman, challenged the sufficiency of the declaration on the grounds of technicalities in the pleading. He argued that the declaration improperly included reference to the benefit of the Illinois Central Railroad, which did not concern him, and claimed that the attorneys signed the declaration in a partnership name without their individual identification. However, the court ruled that these points did not detract from the assurance that Zimmerman was adequately informed of the claims against him.

The case of The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. v. The Jacksonville Depot Building Co. arises from a contract made in October 1866 in Jacksonville, Illinois. The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company entered into a lease agreement with the Jacksonville Depot Building Company, allowing the latter to construct a passenger depot and eating house on a portion of railway depot ground. The railway company agreed to occupy part of the building, pay 10% of the cost as rent, and ensure that passenger trains stopped for meals while the building company owned the structure. After the building was completed at a cost of about $28,000, the Railway Company occupied its part but moved to change the tenants of the eating house without the building company's consent, ultimately stopping the meals service for passengers. This led to a loss of tenants for the eating house, prompting the building company to seek damages for the alleged breach of contract from the Railway Company. The case was brought to court, resulting in a judgment in favor of the building company for $28,650.64, which included more than the original cost of the building. The Railway Company appealed the decision.	The Jacksonville Depot Building Company claimed that the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company's actions constituted a breach of the contract, specifically by failing to stop trains for meals as agreed upon, leading to damages due to ineffective occupancy of the building. The plaintiff sought to recover the full value of the building, arguing that the Railway Company's wrongful actions effectively rescinded their contract.	The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company defended itself by asserting that it could not be compelled to purchase the building, as no contract explicitly obligated it to do so. The defense argued that the plaintiff's claim should have been limited to recovering lost rent as damages rather than the entire value of the building, which they maintained was never transferred to the Railway Company. The defense contended that any breach did not warrant a rescission of the contract and thus should not result in a claim for the building's value.

Prentiss D. Cheney v. The City National Bank of Chicago is a legal case that originated in Jersey County, Illinois. The case was initiated on August 13, 1873, with a summons issued for Cheney to respond to a lawsuit filed by the City National Bank. The summons was initially returned "defendant not found," prompting the bank to issue a second summons on September 20, 1873, which was successfully served to Cheney. When the case was heard in court, Cheney moved to quash the second summons on procedural grounds, claiming it was issued less than ten days before the upcoming court term. However, the motion was deemed insufficient as it did not specify which summons it was addressing. The case further involved a promissory note given by Cheney for the purchase of land, which he claimed was encumbered by unpaid taxes amounting to $448.40—a fact known to the bank at the time of the note's issuance. The primary legal questions involved the validity of the second summons and the implication of land encumbrance on Cheney's obligation to pay the note.	The City National Bank of Chicago, as the plaintiff, argued that the promissory note issued by Cheney was valid and enforceable. The bank contended that despite Cheney's claims regarding the encumbrance on the land, he had not been disturbed in his possession, and thus he had no legitimate defense against the payment of the note. The bank requested the court to affirm its judgment in favor of the enforcement of the promissory note and issued a remittitur to correct any potential judgment excess.	Prentiss D. Cheney, the defendant, presented multiple defenses, primarily focusing on the procedural errors related to the summons and the claim that the land he purchased was encumbered. Cheney argued that the second summons was improperly issued as it was not returnable to the correct term, and he emphasized that the promissory note should not be enforceable due to the existing tax lien on the property. He asserted that under these circumstances, he should not be compelled to pay the note until any issues regarding the encumbrance were resolved or the lien paid.

The case "McAlpine, Polk & Co. v. Julia Zitzer et al." was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1887. It stems from a legal dispute concerning a mortgage on properties located in Olney, Illinois. The properties were mortgaged on May 7, 1880, by John Von Gunten and his wife to McAlpine, Polk & Co. as security for three promissory notes. In June 1880, a tax sale occurred due to unpaid property taxes for the year 1879, during which Charles Von Gunten—son of the mortgagor—purchased the properties, later obtaining a tax deed. McAlpine, Polk & Co. filed a bill of equity to foreclose the mortgage, alleging that the tax deed was procured through fraud and collusion between John and Charles Von Gunten. The circuit court ruled in favor of McAlpine, Polk & Co., declaring the tax deed void.
