However, upon appeal, the Appellate Court for the Fourth District dismissed the complaint against Julia Zitzer, who had acquired the properties via quitclaim deed from Charles Von Gunten, while affirming other parts of the decree. The Illinois Supreme Court later reviewed the case, focusing on the implications of the alleged collusion and the validity of the tax deed in relation to the mortgage.	McAlpine, Polk & Co. claimed that the tax deed obtained by Charles Von Gunten was fraudulent and should be set aside, as it was secured through collusion with his father, John Von Gunten, to circumvent the existing mortgage. They sought foreclosure of the mortgage on the property, asserting their rights as the mortgagees under the original agreement, and argued that the tax title acquired by Charles was not independent but rather in subordination to their mortgage.	Julia Zitzer and the other defendants contended that the tax deed was valid and should not be set aside, arguing that McAlpine, Polk & Co. had no standing to challenge the validity of the tax title. They maintained that procedural requirements surrounding the tax sale were met, countering claims of fraud and collusion. They also highlighted that different legal precedents supported the idea that third-party tax titles should not be adjudicated in a foreclosure proceeding unless they are directly linked to the mortgagor.

The case of "Merick A. Richardson v. Thomas Beldam" took place in Cook County, Illinois, originating from a judgment entered on October 5, 1885. The plaintiff, Thomas Beldam, had a judgment note from Richardson, promising to pay a debt of $13,522.66 with interest. Along with the note was a warrant of attorney allowing an attorney to confess judgment on behalf of the debtor. On the specific day of the judgment, the court opened by proclamation before the official adjournment time of 10:00 AM, at which point the judgment was recorded. Subsequently, Merick A. Richardson assigned his assets to creditors. On October 16, 1885, Roche, representing the creditors, filed a motion to set aside the judgment, arguing that it was entered before the officially appointed time of 10:00 AM, thereby alleging irregularity in the court's procedures. The court ruled the record was complete and deemed the motion insufficient, subsequently denying it.	The plaintiff, Thomas Beldam, claimed that the judgment obtained against Merick A. Richardson was valid, supported by a properly executed judgment note and warrant of attorney. He sought to uphold the judgment and execution that had been entered on October 5, 1885, contending that the court's actions were lawful as they followed the correct legal procedures despite the objections raised regarding timing.	The defendant, represented by Roche, argued that the judgment was entered prematurely, before the proclaimed time of 10:00 AM on October 5, 1885. The defense asserted that the court had not properly convened, claiming the judgment should be considered void or irregular due to this alleged procedural misstep. Roche sought to have the judgment set aside on the grounds of this claimed irregularity.

The case "The Chicago, Santa Fe and California Railway Company v. De Witt Phelps" was filed on June 16, 1888, in the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the County Court of Warren County. The plaintiff, Chicago, Santa Fe and California Railway Company, sought to condemn a strip of land for a right-of-way and additional land for depot facilities on July 19, 1887. The land in question belonged to De Witt Phelps. Following a presentation of the petition, a hearing occurred on August 3, where it was agreed that Phelps could file a cross-petition claiming damages for land not included in the original petition. However, the cross-petition was never officially filed, though its essence was understood during trial proceedings. The jury appraised the land taken at $955.52 and awarded additional damages of $1,658 for the land not taken, totaling $2,613.52. The railway company appealed the judgment, having failed to secure an order allowing them to enter the land pending the appeal, leading to further legal complexities regarding the rights associated with the payment of the award to Phelps and the implications for the appeal process.	The Chicago, Santa Fe and California Railway Company claimed they were entitled to take the specified land under the authority of eminent domain and requested that the court recognize their right to enter the property while the appeal was pending, following the provisions of the Eminent Domain Act. They sought to reverse the lower court's decision regarding compensation assigned for the land taken and the damages for the remaining property.	De Witt Phelps contested that the payment received for the land constituted a complete satisfaction of the judgment, arguing that this negated the railway company's ability to appeal. He maintained that the damages awarded were appropriate, and he had a right to assess damages to other land not directly taken, which he claimed was improperly handled in the lower court proceedings. Phelps asserted his understanding that accepting the deposited money would end further claims to the awarded compensation in the appeal.

The case "Lida K. Stelle et al., Administrators, use, etc., v. George T. Lovejoy" took place in Illinois, under the jurisdiction of the Illinois Appellate Court, with the final judgment delivered on July 27, 1887. The case stemmed from an appeal bond issued after a Justice's judgment was dismissed on November 21, 1876. The original judgment was made on June 10, 1875, and the suit regarding the appeal bond was initiated on June 7, 1884. The defendant, George T. Lovejoy, contended that the action was barred by the Statute of Limitations, which stipulates a five-year time frame for bringing legal action on judgments rendered by Justices of the Peace. The primary issue presented to the court was whether the statute of limitations barred the claim on the appeal bond, related to the earlier Justice’s judgment.	The plaintiffs, represented by Lida K. Stelle and other administrators, argued that the action on the appeal bond was valid and should not be subjected to the five-year statute of limitations governing the actions on Justice's judgments. They claimed that the appeal bond was a separate legal obligation, and thus they were entitled to pursue their claim within the ten-year period specified for actions on bonds.	The defendant, George T. Lovejoy, argued that the claims against the appeal bond were barred by the Statute of Limitations, contending that since actions on judgments from Justices of the Peace are limited to five years, it should similarly apply to the appeal bond. He maintained that the appeal bond served merely as security for the judgment and that any claims on it would also be subject to the same statute limitation.

In Rochelle, Illinois, on July 29, 1887, a collision occurred between a passenger train operated by the Chicago & Iowa Railroad Company and a wagon driven by Elliott Lane, a minor, who was hauling grain. The train was traveling east while the wagon approached the track from the north on Bartholomew Street. Significant obstructions near the crossing, including a coal chute, a tall hedge, and various structures, severely limited visibility for both the driver and other motorists. This resulted in Elliott Lane losing an arm in the accident. The plaintiff claimed that the railroad was negligent for permitting these obstructions and for operating the train at a dangerous speed without necessary warnings like bells or whistles. After a trial, the jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him $2,500 in damages, which led the defendant to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, represented by Gilbert Lane as next friend, argued that the railroad company acted negligently by allowing obstructive structures on its right of way, which hindered visibility at the crossing. The claims included that the train was operated at an excessive speed, failed to adhere to a local ordinance limiting speeds within city limits, and lacked adequate warning signals such as ringing a bell or blowing a whistle. The plaintiff requested damages for the injuries suffered due to this negligence.	The railroad company contested the claims by asserting that the evidence did not support the jury's verdict and that it complied with necessary safety regulations. The defense argued that the obstructions did not significantly hinder visibility if proper precautions were taken and that the train was traveling at a lawful speed. Additionally, they claimed that the plaintiff was not attentive enough to the train’s approach. The defendant sought a reversal of the judgment based on these arguments.

In December 1849, the case of Isaac G. Smith vs. Benjamin Whitaker for the use of Samuel Jonas was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The action stemmed from a debt claim involving an appeal bond executed by Smith before a justice of the peace in Hancock County, Illinois. The bond aimed to suspend the collection of a judgment while Smith appealed the decision. Whitaker, as the plaintiff, asserted that Smith had defaulted on this obligation after the Circuit Court affirmed the judgment. Smith initially contested the claim, offering several defenses against the bond's enforcement, arguing procedural issues with the recorded judgments. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court after Smith's appeals were unsuccessful in lower courts.	The plaintiff, Benjamin Whitaker, claimed that Smith had an obligation under the appeal bond, which was conditioned upon the payment of the judgment affirmed by the higher court. Whitaker contended that Smith was estopped from denying the existence of the judgment, as the bond clearly acknowledged it and fulfilled its legal purpose. Whitaker sought enforcement of the bond, which amounted to $250.	The defendant, Isaac G. Smith, presented various defenses, including a denial of the bond's existence (non est factum) and argued that there was no recorded judgment as recited in the bond’s condition. Smith insisted that the conditions for the bond had not been met and that procedural errors should invalidate the claim. However, these arguments were countered by the acknowledgment of the bond and its conditions in the declaration.

In December 1822, the case of S. Moore v. J. Watts, S. Crocker, and M. Wells was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in St. Clair County and involved the plaintiff, S. Moore, who claimed that he was subjected to assault and battery as well as false imprisonment. The defendants, J. Watts, S. Crocker, and M. Wells, included a justice of the peace, who issued a warrant for Moore's arrest based on an affidavit from Wells. The affidavit alleged that Moore had unlawfully entered Wells’ property and taken her grain. Moore argued that the defendants acted on their own accord without lawful justification. Evidence including the affidavit and the warrant were presented to the jury, and the court instructed them that these documents justified the defendants' actions. The case turned on the issue of whether the justice of the peace had jurisdiction, as the affidavit lacked clear language indicative of a felony. This led to questions regarding the legal foundation for the defendants' actions and the validity of the warrant that resulted in Moore's arrest.	The plaintiff, S. Moore, claimed that the defendants committed assault and battery and false imprisonment without lawful justification. Moore contended that the actions of the defendants were independent wrongdoings, asserting that the affidavit used to justify the warrant did not appropriately establish that he had committed a felony. He requested the court to reverse the lower court's judgment and sought damages for the wrongs he suffered.	The defendants argued that they acted in accordance with the law, based on the affidavit presented to the justice of the peace, which asserted that Moore committed a theft from Wells' property. They claimed that because the affidavit was filed and the warrant was issued, they were justified in arresting Moore. They maintained that the instructions given to the jury reflected the legal appropriateness of their actions and sought to have the court uphold the lower court's judgment.

In 1885, William J. Lemp entered into a contractual agreement with the Belleville Glass Company in St. Clair County, Illinois, in which he committed to purchasing 4,000 gross of bottles, with the option to take up to 8,000 gross at an agreed price. The contract allowed Lemp to retain 3% of the contract price as a guarantee for the glass company's performance. However, the glass company only fulfilled 4,700 gross before suspending operations, failing to deliver the remaining 1,300 gross. Consequently, Lemp was compelled to source these bottles elsewhere, facing a price increase that exceeded the remaining balance due of $506.15. The glass company sued Lemp for this balance, while Lemp counterclaimed for damages due to the glass company's failure to adhere to the contract. The jury's finding ultimately favored Lemp for the full amount, leading to his appeal.	The Belleville Glass Company, representing the Belleville Savings Bank, sought to recover $506.15 from William J. Lemp for bottles sold and delivered as part of their contractual agreement. The glass company contended that there was no obligation to provide more than 1,000 gross of bottles and argued that Lemp’s claims regarding the need for additional bottles and subsequent costs were unfounded.	William J. Lemp argued that he had a binding contractual agreement with the Belleville Glass Company to purchase a total of 6,000 gross of bottles, of which only 4,700 gross were delivered. He claimed that the company’s failure to provide the remaining bottles forced him to buy them from other suppliers at a higher price, effectively negating his obligation to pay the claimed balance of $506.15. Lemp's defense included a counterclaim for damages incurred due to the glass company's non-performance.

The case of John Brown v. Board of Education took place in Carlyle, Illinois, during the late 19th century. John Brown, a colored individual, was appointed as the janitor for the Carlyle public school on June 26, 1886, with a salary of $20 a month. However, on July 29, 1886, the board of education reconsidered this decision and opted to hire H.C. Franklin for the position at a higher salary of $22 a month. Although Brown was informed about the board's change of heart and protested the decision, he did not take action to assume his duties as janitor when the school opened in September. Testimony revealed that if he had offered his services at that time, they would have been refused. Subsequently, Brown filed a lawsuit for breach of contract against the Board of Education for not honoring the hiring agreement. The trial led to a jury verdict in favor of Brown, and he was awarded $50. The case was appealed by the Board of Education."  
	John Brown argued that the Board of Education breached their contractual agreement by failing to hire him as janitor, despite his acceptance and readiness to perform the duties. He sought damages amounting to the wages he would have earned under the agreement.	The Board of Education contended that they were justified in canceling Brown's appointment due to various reasons presented at trial. They argued that Brown had not made an effort to perform his contract duties when the school opened and claimed that he bore the burden of proving any potential earnings he could have received from other employment.

The case "Charles W. Carroll v. Thomas B. Holmes" was decided on December 9, 1887, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose from a promissory note for $1,434.60 made by defendant Thomas B. Holmes to plaintiff Charles W. Carroll on March 12, 1885, which was due four months after its date. This note became the focal point as Holmes claimed it was issued without consideration since the underlying transactions involved buying and selling grain and other produce with an understanding that no actual delivery would take place, but rather that they would settle based on market price differences. Holmes possessed a farm and small means and allegedly had no intention of fulfilling these contracts, leading to the argument that Carroll was aware of Holmes' intent, making the agreements gambling contracts under Illinois law. The jury found against Carroll, indicating that he knew these transactions were not legitimate business dealings.	Carroll argued that he was entitled to payment based on the promissory note he received from Holmes, which he claimed was valid and enforceable. He sought recovery of the amount owed on the note, asserting that the transactions leading to the note did not violate any statutory provisions and were legitimate contracts for the sale of commodities.	Holmes contended that the note was invalid due to lack of consideration, as the underlying contracts were established with mutual intent to engage in gambling rather than legitimate trading. He argued that both parties understood there would be no actual delivery of goods, thus rendering the note void under the Illinois Criminal Code, which prohibits gambling contracts. Holmes maintained that Carroll could not claim payment on the note because it was rooted in illegal agreements.

In 1872, in St. Clair County, Illinois, a case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court involving the plaintiff, Philip Schlattweiler, and the defendant, County of St. Clair. The legal dispute centered around the assessment of damages resulting from the establishment of a public highway that encroached upon Schlattweiler's land. The highway in question required the taking of approximately 0.44 acres of Schlattweiler's property, which was appraised at $100 per acre. The plaintiff claimed that the highway provided no benefit to him and imposed additional financial burdens, including a requirement to spend $140 or more on a new fence, along with the ongoing costs of maintenance. A jury in the circuit court assessed his damages at only $40, which Schlattweiler argued was insufficient and unjust given the circumstances and evidence presented. This led to Schlattweiler appealing the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court for a review of the jury's verdict and the denial of a new trial.	Philip Schlattweiler contended that the jury awarded him inadequate damages, claiming that the evidence overwhelmingly supported higher compensation for the land taken and the costs incurred due to the highway's establishment. He sought a new trial to reassess the damages in line with the evidence presented, which he argued demonstrated that the extent of his damages far exceeded the jury's verdict of $40.	The County of St. Clair contested Schlattweiler's appeal by arguing against the right to a writ of error in this case. They referenced previous cases asserting that such an appeal was unwarranted under the circumstances. However, they did not dispute the facts regarding the costs and judgments but instead focused on procedural grounds related to the appeal process.

The case "Ithiel C. Towner et al. v. Robert S. Tickner et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 22, 1885. The dispute arose in Elgin, Illinois, where plaintiffs Ithiel C. Towner and S. P. Richards sold a planing mill and certain machinery to defendants Robert S. Tickner and John L. Tickner. The written contract specified that as part of the sale, the defendants would assume a mortgage on the property and pay a specified amount, with full performance due on April 1, 1881. On that date, Towner and Richards tendered a warranty deed and bill of sale, but the defendants refused to complete the transaction, claiming various issues with the property, including the condition of a water wheel and disputes over additional machinery ownership. The tenant occupying the mill, Smith Hoag, was assured by the defendants he need not surrender the property, complicating matters further. Testimonies were conflicting regarding the condition of the assets and ownership, leading to significant challenges in determining the facts of the case. Despite these complications, Towner and Richards maintained their ownership of the property, while the defendants' refusal to perform led to the legal proceedings.	The plaintiffs, Towner and Richards, claimed that the defendants breached their contract by refusing to complete the purchase on the stipulated date. They asserted that they had fulfilled their obligations by tendering the deed and bill of sale for the real property and the machinery as specified in the written contract. The plaintiffs sought specific performance of the contract, arguing that the issues raised by the defendants, such as the condition of the machinery, were minor and could be rectified or compensated for, and thus should not excuse the defendants from fulfilling the contract.	The defendants, Tickner and Tickner, contended that they were justified in refusing to perform the contract due to alleged deficiencies in the property, particularly that the water wheel was not in the stated condition and that certain machinery claimed by a tenant (Hoag) did not belong to the plaintiffs as expected. They argued that these issues materially affected the value and usability of the mill, and claimed that they had informed the plaintiffs of their decision to not proceed with the purchase well before the performance date. Consequently, they requested that the court dismiss the plaintiffs' claim for specific performance.

John Muldoon initiated legal action against Mary Ann Adlard in the Superior Court of Chicago in September 1867 concerning a dispute over a building contract. Muldoon alleged that there was a balance owed for work performed on several cottages. The case revolved around the interpretation of this contract and whether the work was completed according to the agreed specifications. Testimonies from architects indicated that the cottages were not completed properly—there were omissions in finishing elements like newel posts, brackets, cornices, and the installation of gas pipes. Moreover, Muldoon argued that Adlard had not accepted the completed work, which was crucial to the case as it pertained to Muldoon’s entitlement to payment. The jury rendered a verdict in favor of Muldoon, awarding him $391.85, which Adlard later contested, leading to an appeal.	Muldoon claimed he was owed money for labor and materials provided under a building contract with Adlard. He argued that he had fulfilled his obligations under the contract and was entitled to the remaining balance. The basis of his claim rested on the assertion that the work was completed satisfactorily, pending any authorized changes that would affect the contract terms.	Adlard contended that Muldoon did not complete the construction as specified in the contract, claiming non-performance as the primary defense. She argued that since she never accepted the work due to its incompleteness, she should not be liable for further payments. Additionally, Adlard stated the contract authorized her to recoup damages from Muldoon for not adhering to the agreed specifications.

On January 19, 1854, in Aurora, Kane County, Illinois, James Thompson (the plaintiff) entrusted a box containing various personal items, including clothing and bank bills totaling $750, to The Chicago and Aurora Railroad Company (the defendant) for transport to Earlville, La Salle County. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant, as a common carrier of goods, failed to deliver the box safely. The plaintiff filed a lawsuit in November 1854, claiming the loss resulted from the defendant's carelessness, which included the box being broken open during transport. The case was tried in the Kane Circuit Court, which ruled in favor of Thompson, awarding him $730 in damages. The defendant appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, questioning the liability based on the nature of the contents of the box and whether they constituted goods legally transportable by the defendant under common carrier laws.	The plaintiff claimed that the defendant was a common carrier and failed to fulfill their obligation to transport and deliver the box containing his personal items safely. He argued that the loss of the box's contents, including cash, was due to the defendant's negligence, and he sought damages amounting to $2,000 for the loss incurred.	The defendant argued that they were not legally considered a common carrier of money or bank bills, putting the onus on the plaintiff to prove this claim. They contended that the plaintiff had failed to disclose the valuable contents, which constituted fraud, thereby releasing the defendant from liability. The defendant maintained that there was no express contract for the transport of bank bills, and argued that their practices in carrying freight did not normally include money.

In 1872, the partnership of F. Minzesheimer & Co., which included Ferdinand Minzesheimer, J.W. Schloss, and Regina Blumenthal, dissolved, leaving Schloss and Blumenthal to continue as J.W. Schloss & Co. Schloss and Blumenthal incurred debts totaling about $800 to Strauss & Co. Subsequently, on January 2, 1873, Minzesheimer claims to have purchased 10,700 cigars from Blumenthal for $428, although he had not physically seen the cigars at that time. The sale was made at a location far from where the cigars were actually stored. On January 4, Minzesheimer went with Blumenthal to the factory where the cigars were located and began the process of stamping them, which was required before they could be legally removed. However, while the stamping was in process, the cigars were seized by a deputy sheriff under a writ of attachment in favor of Strauss and Sawyer against J.W. Schloss & Co. Minzesheimer sought to recover the cigars in a suit for trespass against the appellants, claiming his rightful ownership based on the purchase agreement.	The plaintiff, Ferdinand Minzesheimer, argued that he had legally purchased the cigars from Regina Blumenthal and had taken all necessary steps to assume possession, including paying for the stamps and initiating the stamping process. He requested the court to recognize his ownership of the cigars and claimed damages for their wrongful seizure by the defendants.	The defendants, Strauss and Sawyer, contended that the sale of the cigars was fraudulent as it was intended to hinder their ability to collect debts from J.W. Schloss & Co. They argued that because the cigars had not been properly boxed and stamped at the time of the sale, the transfer of ownership was invalid, and thus, they were justified in seizing the cigars under the attachment.

The case "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Thomas McKee" took place in 1867 in Coles County, Illinois. It involved a legal dispute where Thomas McKee, the plaintiff, brought action against The Illinois Central Railroad Company, alleging that the company’s locomotive killed his horse. The incident occurred after the horse strayed onto the railroad tracks via a farm gate that was, according to McKee, negligently left open by the railroad. The Circuit Court instructed the jury to favor McKee if they found that the horse accessed the tracks through the open gate and that the railroad company had not acted to close the gate despite knowing it was left open. The court considered the responsibilities regarding the maintenance and operation of gates at farm crossings, as well as the duty of care owed by the railroad company to maintain fences and gates properly.	Thomas McKee claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent in allowing a gate at a farm crossing to be left open, which enabled his horse to enter the tracks and subsequently be killed by a train. He requested that the jury find for him based on this negligence and assess damages corresponding to the value of his horse.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company argued that the responsibility for keeping the gate closed fell upon the farm owner and not the railroad. They contended that since McKee did not allege in his declaration that the gate was negligently left open by the railroad, any evidence relating to that allegation should be excluded. They maintained that they were not liable for the horse's death due to the lack of such an allegation in the case brought against them.

Patrick Moran v. Caroline Pellifant is a legal case that took place in Lake County, Illinois, with the decision rendered on December 8, 1888. The case arose when Caroline Pellifant filed a bill against Patrick Moran and Peter Connolly, seeking to compel Moran to pay a note of $8400 plus accrued interest that he had agreed to pay. The matter dates back to July 12, 1869, when Pellifant executed a trust deed for her land to secure a note by Connolly. On September 14, 1875, she sold twenty-three acres of this land to Moran for $1,150, during which Moran assumed the debt to Connolly as part of the purchase deal. However, Moran failed to pay either the note or the interest, leading Pellifant to continue making payments to Connolly after the sale. The suit was initiated to recover these payments from Moran, leading to a hearing where Pellifant presented evidence supporting her claims, while Moran contended he was unaware of any obligation to pay.	Caroline Pellifant argued that Moran was legally obligated to pay the outstanding note and accrued interest to Peter Connolly as he had assumed this responsibility during the purchase of the land. She requested an accounting of the total amount due to Connolly and that Moran repay her for interest payments she had made on the note after selling the land. Pellifant sought a decree that would confirm Moran's liability and establish the sums owed as liens on the properties.	Patrick Moran acknowledged the purchase of the land but denied any knowledge of the conditions regarding the payment to Connolly, claiming he had fulfilled his financial obligations to Pellifant. He invoked the ten-year statute of limitations regarding the note, although he did not apply this defense to Pellifant's claims for the interest payments made on the note. He also contended that another party with an interest in the land had not been included in the lawsuit, arguing that this omission compromised the validity of the case.

In 1876 in Winnebago County, Illinois, James C. Mayberry filed a legal action against Charles Van Horn based on two promissory notes. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Circuit Court where Judge William Browrt presided. Mayberry claimed that Van Horn owed him money as per the promissory notes. According to the Illinois Practice Act, Mayberry filed an affidavit alongside his declaration, outlining the nature and amount of the debt after accounting for any allowable deductions. In response, Van Horn filed a general plea, asserting a set-off of $125 and an affidavit claiming to have a defense amounting to $65 against the suit. Mayberry admitted to the deduction of $65 from his claim and moved for judgment based on the remaining amount due on the notes.	James C. Mayberry's main argument centered on the promissory notes owed to him by Charles Van Horn. He provided the necessary affidavit under the Practice Act to clarify the demand and requested judgment for the amount remaining after accounting for Van Horn’s claimed deductions. Mayberry sought a legal ruling that affirmed his entitlement to the sum remaining after the admitted deduction of $65.	Charles Van Horn's key arguments were based on his assertion of a set-off against Mayberry’s claim, amounting to $125. He filed a general plea alongside an affidavit purporting to present a defense of $65, indicating he believed he had grounds to contest the suit on those merits. His defense was centered upon contesting the full amount owed while allowing for a portion of the claim due to this set-off.

The case of The Phœnix Mutual Life Insurance Company v. Henry S. Baker revolves around the insurance policy issued by Phœnix Mutual Life Insurance on October 7, 1870, assuring the life of Henry S. Baker for the benefit of his wife and children, with the policy amount set at $2500. The contract required annual premium payments to keep the policy in force, which Baker fulfilled for five years using a combination of cash and promissory notes. On October 5, 1874, Baker expressed a desire to surrender his policy in exchange for a "paid-up" policy, as outlined in the contract which stipulated that after three annual premiums, the policy could be surrendered to obtain a new one for the sum of premiums paid (subject to any existing debts). Despite Baker's requests and communications with insurance agents, the company failed to provide a paid-up policy, leading him to take legal action to reclaim the premiums he had paid. In 1876, Baker initiated the suit against the insurance company, seeking reimbursement, which resulted in a jury verdict awarding him $388.97. The case was then appealed by Phœnix Mutual Life Insurance.	Baker's main argument centers around the claim that the insurance company violated the terms of their contract by not issuing him a paid-up policy after he attempted to surrender his original policy as allowed by the agreement. He contends that he rightfully rescinded the contract and is entitled to recover all premiums paid under the assertion that the company did not fulfill its obligations.	The Phœnix Mutual Life Insurance Company argued that Baker had not properly surrendered the policy within the allowed timeframe and that the payments made were for an active life insurance policy that provided coverage for five years, rather than merely for a future paid-up policy. The defendant claimed that any request for a paid-up policy after the policy expired could not be honored, and they contended that the damages claimed by Baker were excessive and unwarranted.

The case of David McWilliams et al. v. Richard P. Morgan, Jr., decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1871, centers around a dispute regarding a piece of land in the newly laid out town of Dwight, Illinois. On August 6, 1853, Richard P. Morgan sold a right of way of 100 feet to the Chicago & Mississippi Railroad Company, with provisions for the maintenance of a depot if a town was established. By January 30, 1854, Morgan laid out the town, recording a plat that included a hexagonal piece of land designated for public use as a depot. This land was positioned between the railroad right of way and East Street. Over the years, this strip remained uninclosed and was used by the public for access to the depot without any objections from Morgan. However, in 1857, Morgan constructed a corn crib across the strip and subsequently claimed ownership over it, leading to concerns from the plaintiffs, who had purchased lots adjacent to this land, believing it was intended for public use. The plaintiffs argued that the marking of the land as "depot" implied public access, while Morgan contended that the land was reserved for private use related to the railroad.	The plaintiffs, David McWilliams and others, argued that the strip of land marked as "depot" on the town plat should remain open for public use. They claimed they purchased lots with the understanding that the land would be unencumbered and available for public enjoyment. The plaintiffs sought an injunction to prevent Morgan from building on the strip, asserting that such construction would violate their reasonable expectations based on the original plat and Morgan’s actions.	Richard P. Morgan contended that he did not intend to dedicate the piece of land for public use, emphasizing that the private ownership and his actions, including the construction of a corn crib, demonstrated his private claims over the land. He maintained that marking the land as "depot" did not necessarily indicate public access, as it was designated for private purposes associated with the railroad. Morgan sought to uphold his right to use the land as he wished without public interference.

On September 18, 1887, at approximately 5 PM in Hoopeston, Illinois, Catherine A. Eads filed a lawsuit against the City of Hoopeston for injuries sustained from stepping into a hole in a defective sidewalk. The hole measured six inches wide and more than a foot long, and was easily visible. Eads' daughter noticed the hole and was able to step around it, but Eads did not and subsequently fell and injured herself. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, stemming from a judgment against the City for $875 in damages based on the injuries. The key issues at trial revolved around whether Eads exercised ordinary care while walking and whether the city had notice of the sidewalk defect.	Eads argued that the City of Hoopeston failed to maintain its sidewalks in a reasonably safe condition, contributing to her injury. She asserted that the city was accountable for the defective sidewalk and claimed damages for the injury sustained. Eads maintained that the City did not adequately repair the sidewalk or warn pedestrians about its condition, demanding compensation for her injuries.	The City of Hoopeston contended that it had recently repaired the sidewalk and that the city officials routinely inspected the sidewalks, arguing that they had no notice of the defect that caused Eads' fall. The City claimed that the responsibility to notice and avoid the hazard fell upon Eads, as she had a duty to exercise ordinary care. The City sought to demonstrate that Eads was contributory negligent and urged for a reversal of the judgment against them.

Isaac M. Kirkpatrick and Joseph M. Whitman were involved in a promissory note related to a debt for $150 dated April 26, 1870, in Monmouth, Illinois. The note was executed with no payee's name filled in initially. Whitman, who was indebted to the First National Bank of Monmouth, attempted to borrow $150 to settle his account but was unable to secure a loan without Kirkpatrick's signature as a guarantor. Following the bank's refusal to accept Kirkpatrick's signature, Whitman ultimately filled out the note naming Richard A. Howk as the payee and provided it to Howk as security for a loan. When the situation was contested, Howk filed suit against Kirkpatrick after obtaining a judgment in a lower court, claiming the amount due under the note after Kirkpatrick failed to pay. Kirkpatrick appealed this judgment, asserting that the verdict did not align with the evidence disclosed during the trial.	Richard A. Howk, the plaintiff, claimed that Kirkpatrick owed him $150 based on the promissory note that Whitman provided, arguing that he took on risk by becoming party to the note and that he had been damaged when Kirkpatrick failed to fulfill his obligation.	Isaac M. Kirkpatrick, the defendant, contended that the evidence of the transaction did not support the amount claimed by Howk. He argued that because Howk had taken a colt from Whitman as collateral, the amount due should reflect that security and the judgment was excessive since it did not account for the value of the property taken.

The case of Samuel Claycomb v. Timothy Moshier took place in September 1871 in the Warren Circuit Court, Illinois. The dispute arose from a foreclosure of a mortgage executed on April 16, 1863, by William H. H. Claycomb and his wife to Andrew Claycomb, securing a sum of $5,665, which was later assigned to Timothy Moshier, the plaintiff. Samuel Claycomb, claiming an equitable interest in the property described in the mortgage as lot one in block ten in the city of Monmouth, contested the validity of the mortgage. Samuel alleged that a prior agreement among himself, William, and Andrew Claycomb rendered the mortgage void and that a subsequent mortgage for $3,750 executed in October 1863 should instead be recognized. The court proceedings involved evaluating the legitimacy of both mortgages, analyzing the understanding and intentions behind their execution, and examining various transactions between the parties throughout the years leading to the mortgage disputes.	The plaintiff, Timothy Moshier, contended that the mortgage he holds is valid and enforceable as it was recorded properly. He argued that the arrangement made between the parties regarding the payment of debts and the mortgage's intended security was clear, asserting that the larger mortgage amount included a mechanic's lien that had to be settled. Moshier requested the court to foreclose the mortgage and grant him the right to recover the owed sum, emphasizing the legitimacy of his claim to the property.	Samuel Claycomb, the defendant, claimed that the mortgage for $5,665 was null and void due to an agreement made during a settlement meeting with Andrew Claycomb and William. He argued that the smaller mortgage for $3,750 was the actual valid mortgage, and that the larger mortgage was fraudulently recorded by Andrew, thus requesting the court to acknowledge the smaller mortgage and dismiss the foreclosure action brought by Moshier.

In 1884, the legal case of "Robert McMillan et al. v. Mary F. McDill et al." was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over the validity of William McMillan's will, which bequeathed his property equally among seven devisees, including Mary McDill and Robert McMillan. Following his death, the contestants claimed the will was invalid due to the testator's alleged mental incapacity at the time it was created. The case involved multiple parties, including the named devisees, all contesting for their shares under the will. The trial court allowed statements made by some of the devisees to be admitted as evidence regarding the testator's mental state. However, these declarations were limited to those who made them and did not extend to their co-defendants. This led to a significant legal question about the admissibility of evidence when multiple parties have separate interests in the same matter, particularly regarding the validity of the will. The jury's decision was influenced by the contested evidence, which ultimately became a pivotal point in the case.	The plaintiffs contended that the will should be declared invalid on the grounds that William McMillan lacked the mental capacity to execute it. They argued that statements made by the devisees—indicating doubts about the testator's sanity—should be admissible as evidence to support their claims against the legitimacy of the will. They sought the court's ruling to declare the will void and prevent the distribution of property according to its terms.	The defendants, representing the interests of the other devisees, argued against the admissibility of declarations made by individual devisees pertaining to the testator's mental capacity. They maintained that the ruling allowed statements to affect the collective rights of all devisees, which was inherently unjust since it could defeat the will based on the admission of a single party. They requested that the court recognize the error in admitting such evidence and upheld the validity of the will, allowing for the proper distribution of the property according to its terms.

Patrick R. Morgan filed a legal action against Joseph T. Ryerson in April 1856 in Chicago, Illinois, after purchasing a horse from Ryerson for $225, which Morgan claimed was unsound at the time of sale. The case was an action of assumpsit, focused on a warranty provided upon the horse's sale. Morgan alleged that the horse became lame shortly after the purchase, with evidence suggesting that this lameness was present before the sale and rendered the horse unfit for use. In response, Ryerson argued that the horse was sound at the time of sale and contested the characterization of the horse as unsound. The legal proceedings included conflicting testimony from both parties. The jury eventually found in favor of Morgan, assessing damages at the total price paid for the horse.	Morgan argued that Ryerson had breached the warranty of soundness regarding the horse sold. He claimed that the horse was not sound and that he incurred considerable expenses while caring for the animal. Morgan sought to recover the full amount paid for the horse, asserting that it was unsound at the time of sale and thus rendered the purchase worthless.	Ryerson's primary defense was the assertion that the horse was sound both at the time of sale and when Morgan claimed it was unsound. He argued that any temporary injury the horse may have had did not constitute a breach of warranty. Ryerson requested the court to instruct the jury on the conditions of soundness and that the return of the horse must not imply a rescission of the sale without mutual agreement between the parties.

The case of George S. Hanna v. William R. Rayburn et al. took place in 1877 in McLean County, Illinois. The dispute arose over a transaction involving the exchange of land between the plaintiff, George S. Hanna, and the defendant, William R. Rayburn. On December 20, 1873, Hanna executed a deed transferring 380 acres of land, known as the Wrenn farm, to Rayburn in exchange for 320 acres of land in Franklin County, Kansas. Rayburn was to pay Hanna an additional sum secured by a mortgage on the Wrenn farm. Hanna alleged that Rayburn perpetrated fraud by falsely claiming to have received letters from a purported buyer, J.W. Potts, who was interested in purchasing the Kansas land at an inflated price. Hanna also claimed that there was a verbal agreement stipulating that the deed would not be recorded and would be cancelled if Potts did not arrive by March 15, 1874. The circuit court dismissed Hanna's lawsuit, leading him to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The court found the testimonies regarding the alleged verbal agreement inconsistent and noted a lack of evidence connecting Rayburn to the fictitious letters purportedly from Potts.	The plaintiff, George S. Hanna, claimed that the deed transferring the Wrenn farm to William R. Rayburn should be canceled due to fraud and a verbal agreement not to record it. He argued that Rayburn misled him by asserting that there were letters from a buyer, Potts, interested in purchasing the Kansas land at a price above its market value, which influenced the deal. Hanna sought to annul the transaction and reclaim his property, alleging that Rayburn's actions constituted fraud.	William R. Rayburn, the defendant, denied any wrongdoing, asserting that he was not involved in any fraudulent activities related to the fictitious letters. He contended that the deal was negotiated by Stipp, who actively sought the trade rather than Rayburn pushing the transaction. Rayburn claimed that there was no concrete evidence to support Hanna’s allegations of fraud or the supposed verbal agreement regarding the recording of the deed.

In this 1861 case from Illinois, George W. Brown appealed against the People after a series of legal proceedings resulting from an indictment against Levi Marquet for assault with intent to commit rape. The events stemmed from Marquet's failure to appear at the Warren Circuit Court for the April 1857 term after entering into a recognizance, a formal commitment accompanied by financial surety provided by Brown, valued at $800. The court later changed its schedule, moving the court date, but Marquet did not appear, leading to a conditional judgment against both him and his surety, Brown. Following the initial default, multiple scire facias (legal orders) were issued, compelling them to appear before the court. Despite Brown's claims of having Marquet in custody through various capias (arrest warrants) issued in Knox County, the court found no satisfactory excuse for his failure to surrender Marquet for the March term of court. Brown filed pleas to demonstrate his compliance with the recognizance, but the court maintained that as the surety, he had sufficient means to produce Marquet whenever required. Ultimately, the Circuit Court affirmed the conditional judgment against Brown after considering his pleas insufficient.	The plaintiff, the People, argued that George W. Brown, as the surety for Levi Marquet, failed to fulfill his contractual obligation by not ensuring Marquet's appearance in court after multiple notices and attempts to compel attendance. They maintained that the recognizance was forfeited due to Marquet's absence, leading to a conditional judgment against both parties. The plaintiff sought final judgment confirming the forfeiture, emphasizing Brown's obligation to secure Marquet's presence.	George W. Brown, the defendant, contended through several special pleas that he had effectively surrendered Levi Marquet to the sheriff of Knox County in compliance with the terms of the recognizance. He argued that Marquet had indeed been taken into custody before any scire facias was issued, thus nullifying his responsibility to produce Marquet as per the recognizance. Brown claimed that the Circuit Court erred in sustaining the plaintiff's demurrer to his pleas, maintaining that he had performed his duty under the recognizance.

The case "The Peoria and Pekin Union Railway Company et al. v. The Peoria and Farmington Railway Company" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 20, 1882. The dispute arose in Peoria County, Illinois, where the Peoria and Farmington Railway Company sought to obtain the right of way across the tracks of the Peoria and Pekin Union Railway Company. The case was consolidated and tried together with additional related matters. A jury awarded $1,800 in damages to the company seeking the right of way. The defendants subsequently appealed, arguing primarily that the court did not have jurisdiction and that the seeking company failed to prove its legal existence as a corporation. The trial's key issues included challenges to the petitioning company's formation, the nature of jurisdiction in eminent domain cases, and the admissibility of evidence regarding damages incurred due to compliance with statutory requirements.	The Peoria and Farmington Railway Company claimed the right of way across the tracks of the Peoria and Pekin Union Railway Company, arguing that they had complied with statutory requirements necessary to proceed with condemnation. They sought compensation for damages resulting from the imposition of their planned crossing and asserted that their right to condemn the land was supported by both their charter and evidence of their operational existence as a corporation.	The Peoria and Pekin Union Railway Company raised several defenses against the claims, insisting that the court lacked jurisdiction to hear the case, arguing that the petitioning company had failed to establish its status as a legally recognized corporation. They contended that the claims for damages due to delays caused by statutory requirements were too vague and speculative to warrant compensation, emphasizing that such issues could not be quantified as immediate damages.

Justus Ducommun and his co-plaintiff, Guinard, brought an action of debt against Barent and Henry Hysinger in the Greene Circuit Court, Illinois, in December 1852. The case stems from a judgment rendered in May 1849 by the Supreme Court of Albany, New York, in favor of the plaintiffs for $248.37 against the Hysingers. During the trial, the plaintiffs attempted to present the judgment as evidence, supported by official certification. However, the defendants challenged its authenticity by claiming a variance in the names mentioned in the judgment. The case was tried under the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court, which required the evidence to meet legal qualifications for authenticity.	The plaintiffs claimed they were owed $248.37 based on a prior judgment from the New York Supreme Court. They sought to introduce the judgment as evidence, asserting that it was properly authenticated per legal requirements.	The defendants argued that the presented judgment record was not properly authenticated according to the relevant legal standards. They pointed out a critical error in the case: the judgment referenced Barent Hysinger, while the plaintiffs' declaration was against Barnard Hysinger, indicating that different individuals were being referenced, which undermined the legal basis of the plaintiffs' claims.

The legal case "Cornwells & Elliott v. Krengel & Seiferd" took place in Chicago, Illinois, in 1864. The plaintiffs, Krengel & Seiferd, who were partners in a business, initiated an action of assumpsit against the defendants, Cornwells & Elliott, also business partners. The dispute arose from a series of letters exchanged between the parties regarding an order for paper. The defendants ordered paper, indicating that they wanted it to be sent quickly. However, the plaintiffs responded that they had no paper available but offered to make it. Following further correspondence, it became clear that the plaintiffs were unable to fulfill the order promptly due to operational constraints, which ultimately led to the defendants claiming a set-off based on an alleged contract formed through this correspondence. The Superior Court of Chicago, presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gary, ruled against the defendants, leading to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court regarding whether a binding contract existed.	The plaintiffs, Krengel & Seiferd, claimed that they had fulfilled their obligations in the exchange of correspondence and that there was no contract forming a basis for the defendants’ claim to payment. They argued that the letters did not constitute an acceptance of the order as required for a binding contract. Their legal request essentially sought the court to affirm the judgment disallowing the set-off claimed by the defendants and to recover the payment for the goods sold.	The defendants, Cornwells & Elliott, contended that the correspondence constituted a valid contract that committed the plaintiffs to fulfill the order for paper. They argued that the repeated references to the order in their letters implied acceptance of the agreement. They requested the court to recognize their claim of set-off based on the supposed contract formed through the letters, which would entitle them to deduct any debts owed against their payment for the goods.

The case of Frederick F. Rozier v. Julia Fagan et al. was decided in January 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from a dispute over land that had been sold by John Rice Jones, the administrator of the estate of Thomas Brady, without judicial confirmation of any debts owed by Brady. The land was sold under the authority of a legislative act passed on January 8, 1823, which allowed the administrator to sell estate properties to settle debts. The heirs of Thomas Brady (the plaintiffs) sought to recover the lands, arguing that the act which authorized the sale was unconstitutional, as it allowed the administrator to act without confirming the existence of debts through a court. The action was brought in the Circuit Court of St. Clair County, where the plaintiffs challenged the validity of the legislative act facilitating the sale and contested the administrator's authority. Ultimately, the issue revolved around whether the legislature had the power to bypass judicial procedures in determining debt obligations.	The plaintiffs, heirs of Thomas Brady, claimed that the act authorizing the administrator to sell land for debt payments was unconstitutional. They argued that the legislative body had no right to assume the existence of debts and authorize sales without judicial oversight. The plaintiffs sought recovery of the land sold by the administrator, stating that the proper legal and judicial processes had not been followed to ascertain the indebtedness of the deceased.	The defendants, represented by Mr. Gustavus Koerner, relied on the argument that the act of 1823 was valid in its authorization for the administrator to sell the estate's land. They contended that the legislature had the power to facilitate the payment of debts. The defense sought to uphold the validity of the sale made by the administrator, arguing that it was executed under lawful authority provided by the legislature.

The case "The Peoria and Pekin Union Railway Company v. Warren R. Buckley et al." was decided on June 13, 1885, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from Peoria County, Illinois, where Warren R. Buckley and Thomas J. Pursley, operating as Buckley, Pursley & Co., were grain dealers. They received two shipments of oats: one car on October 26, 1883, and another the following day. Following standard trading practices, these shipments were inspected, and tickets were issued denoting the ownership and where the grain should be delivered. The grain was sold to Patterson, a fellow board member, with the arrangement that the delivery would be made to a specified elevator. However, Patterson’s check for the purchase was dishonored due to insufficient funds. The core issue arose when Patterson directed the railway company to ship the oats elsewhere, which Buckley and Pursley contested, claiming they had not authorized such delivery. The case primarily revolved around the authority of the railway company to release the grain based on the provided tickets, which did not explicitly authorize delivery to Patterson, thus creating a contested situation regarding the rightful ownership and delivery of the oats.	The plaintiffs, Buckley and Pursley, claimed that the Peoria and Pekin Union Railway Company wrongfully delivered their oats to Patterson without proper authority. They argued that they had not given permission, either verbally or in writing, for the railway company to deliver the oats to Patterson, and thus, ownership of the oats remained with them until payment was made. They sought compensation for the value of the oats they could not retrieve after discovery of the dishonored check.	The defendant, the railway company, argued that it acted under the apparent authority bestowed by the delivery of inspection tickets which indicated the sale had occurred. They contended that if the plaintiffs allowed Patterson to appear as the owner and gave him evidence of ownership, the railway company should be protected for acting on his request. The company requested that the court recognize its delivery actions as legitimate based on the apparent ownership established by the actions of the plaintiffs during the time of the sale.

Madison Y. Johnson filed a trespass action against J. Russell Jones and several co-defendants, which took place in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, on August 28, 1862. The plaintiff alleged that the defendants, with force and violence, assaulted and arrested him, transporting him to Chicago, where he was unlawfully detained for two days. Subsequently, he was sent to Fort Lafayette in New York and later to Fort Delaware, where he was imprisoned for a total of five months without any charges or trial. The defendants argued that the arrest occurred during a rebellion and claimed they acted under orders to suppress unrest due to the plaintiff's involvement with a disloyal secret society, the "Knights of the Golden Circle." The court ultimately ruled on the legality of the arrest and the extent of executive power during wartime, particularly in regard to a citizen's rights and liberties.	The plaintiff argued that his arrest and subsequent imprisonment were unlawful and constituted a trespass since they occurred without any legal process or charges against him. He sought damages for the violation of his personal liberty, claiming that the defendants lacked the authority to arrest him without due process, particularly as there had been no general suspension of the writ of habeas corpus at the time of his arrest.	The defendants contended that the arrest of the plaintiff was justified due to the ongoing rebellion and his alleged membership in a subversive organization. They claimed that one of the defendants, who was the U.S. marshal for the Northern District of Illinois, was acting under orders from the President to detain the plaintiff and argued that the circumstances warranted such actions under martial law. They further maintained that the plaintiff should be treated as a belligerent due to his alleged disloyal ties, which justified the extraordinary measures taken against him.

The legal case "Richard Ball et al. v. John Benjamin" took place in September 1874 in Whiteside County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Richard Ball and others, had sold a double saw-bench to Daniel H. Call, who intended to use it in his planing mill business. Call provided the plaintiffs with a promissory note for the machine. Subsequently, John Benjamin purchased a half interest in Call's business without the saw-bench being listed in the inventory. After the saw-bench was delivered to the mill, Call sold his interest to Benjamin, who signed a bond obligating him to pay all debts related to their partnership. The plaintiffs claimed that this bond included their note for the saw-bench. The central issue was whether Benjamin assumed responsibility for the payment of the note when he took over Call's business. During the trial, evidence was presented regarding whether the saw-bench could be considered part of the "material" used in the construction of the mill, leading to a jury trial where their claims were ultimately rejected.	The plaintiffs argued that John Benjamin was liable for the debt concerning the double saw-bench based on a bond he signed when he acquired Call's interest in the business. They sought to recover the value of the saw-bench, contending that by purchasing the partnership, Benjamin had assumed responsibility for all debts related to that business, including their promissory note for the saw-bench.	In defense, John Benjamin argued that the saw-bench was not part of the construction materials for the mill as defined in the bond. He brought forth witnesses to testify that the saw-bench was stored in the basement and not used or attached to the mill. Benjamin maintained that the plaintiffs' right to recovery should be limited to the contract stipulated in the bond, and any promises made without consideration could not support an action against him.

In 1875, in Whiteside County, Illinois, a legal case was initiated concerning the foreclosure of a mortgage allegedly executed by Robert Newlin in favor of the county's drainage commissioner. The plaintiff, William C. Snyder, who was the assignee of the note and the successor to the drainage commissioner, filed the lawsuit against the unknown heirs of Robert Newlin, who had died after signing the mortgage. It was claimed that the names of his heirs were not known. The case moved through the circuit court, where a default judgment was entered against the unknown heirs, leading to a decree of sale of the mortgaged property. Walter Newlin and William Newlin later contested this decree, asserting that there was insufficient proof of Robert Newlin’s death and an absence of an affidavit confirming the existence of unknown heirs. They argued that the court improperly entered a default judgment against them because they were minors. However, the case's records showed no evidence supporting their claim of minority status at the time of the decree.	The plaintiff, William C. Snyder, claimed that a valid mortgage agreement existed, which entitled him to foreclose on the property owned by Robert Newlin in accordance with the terms of the note. He asserted that the default judgment and decree for sale were justified as they were appropriately executed based on the available evidence regarding the unknown heirs.	The defendants, claiming to be the heirs of Robert Newlin, contended that the court's decree was rendered without sufficient proof of Robert Newlin's death and without any affidavit confirming the identity or status of the heirs. They argued that as minors, they should have been protected from a default judgment. They sought to have the decree reversed based on these claims.

The case "Alfred Warner et al. v. John B. Helm et al." took place in the state of Illinois in December 1844. The key individuals involved were Alfred Warner and others as plaintiffs (appellants), and John B. Helm along with others as defendants (appellees). The case stemmed from a mortgage foreclosure initiated by Helm against B. F. Edwards concerning properties in Lower Alton. Edwards had borrowed $7,000 from Helm in May 1837 and subsequently executed a mortgage on the properties as security. In a lawsuit by Craig & Warner, Edwards was found liable for a judgment of over $7,600, leading to a sale of the mortgaged premises. However, Craig & Warner's attorneys purchased the properties without knowledge of the existing mortgage. The plaintiffs, unaware of Helm's mortgage, sought to have it set aside, claiming they had purchased the fee simple of the property. Helm, asserting his rights as the mortgage holder, defended by presenting that the property sold was only Edwards' equity of redemption. The case revolved around whether the foreclosure should proceed against the plaintiffs under these circumstances.	The plaintiffs, led by Warner, contended that they were unaware of the mortgage on the properties when they purchased them. They argued that Helm should either pay their debt before foreclosing on the properties or that the sale should be invalidated. They sought to have Helm barred from foreclosing or have their judgment against Edwards reinstated. Essentially, they demanded the recovery of their rights to the properties they believed were purchased outright, free of any mortgages.	Helm, as the defendant, maintained that his mortgage had priority and that the plaintiffs had only purchased Edwards' equity of redemption. He argued that the plaintiffs were negligent in not investigating the records before their purchase and had other unencumbered properties of Edwards available for levy to satisfy their debt. Helm requested the dismissal of the plaintiffs' cross bill and sought to enforce his mortgage foreclosure, citing that the delay had diminished the value of the properties.

On March 6, 1867, the General Assembly of Illinois passed a law aimed at assisting citizens in the American Bottom area of St. Clair County in building and repairing levees to protect against flooding from the Mississippi River. The law stipulated that the state taxes collected from specific townships would be appropriated over five years for these improvements. The St. Clair County clerk issued a certificate showing that the state taxes for 1866 totaled $12,946.11, which was presented to Sheriff Charles Becker, the acting tax collector. Becker collected about $8,000 from the taxes based on the certificate, but during a later settlement with Auditor Orlin H. Miner, the auditor refused to give Becker credit for the full amount claimed, arguing that the law was unconstitutional. Becker then pursued a mandamus to compel the auditor to allow the credit for the full amount stated in the certificate.	Charles Becker, on behalf of the People of the State of Illinois, contended that the auditor's refusal to allow credit for the full tax amount collected was unlawful. He sought a peremptory mandamus to ensure that the auditor credited the full amount as per the legislative act, arguing that the appropriate statutory provisions were indeed valid and binding.	Auditor Orlin H. Miner contested Becker's claims, asserting several defenses: first, that the legislative act of 1867 was unconstitutional; second, that such funds could not be diverted from the state treasury to a specific company for improvements; third, that existing appropriations for public schools would be violated; and fourth, that future tax amounts could not be appropriated before they had been collected and declared.

In 1859, Samuel Leach and William W. Leach filed equity bills against George D. Humphreys and associated parties in Hancock County, Illinois, seeking to compel Humphreys to reconvey lands that had been held as escrow but allegedly, wrongfully, due to a violation of contract. During court proceedings, a decree was issued in favor of the Leaches ordering Humphreys to convey the property back to them. By March 1860, Humphreys failed to comply, and the property was conveyed by a court-appointed master. Later transactions led to William W. Leach's transfer of property to Samuel Leach, who subsequently executed a trust deed to secure a debt to Eli M. Bruce. This trust deed was later transferred to The Southern Bank of St. Louis. In 1866, the defendants sought to reopen the case, which eventually led to the dismissal of the original bills, stating that there was no prior personal service to affect their rights and that the bank's lien was subordinate to pre-existing interests. The case culminated in a series of complex legal arguments regarding the interpretation of statutory provisions governing non-resident defendants and the finality of decrees in equity cases.	The Southern Bank of St. Louis claimed it acquired a valid lien on the property through a trust deed from Samuel Leach while the previous court decrees were in effect. The bank argued that its interest should prevail despite the reopening and subsequent dismissal of the earlier cases, as it acted in good faith and for value.	George D. Humphreys and other defendants contended that the bank operated under the assumption that the decrees were final when, in fact, they were interim and subject to change as the defendants, who had not received personal service, had the right to petition the court within a designated timeframe. They claimed that the bank's interest was subordinate to their prior lien rights arising from the initial trust deeds.

In 1878, Francis McCallum purchased lot 11 in block 21 of the Gifford addition to the city of Elgin, Illinois. After acquiring the property, he invested approximately $2,500 to grade the land and construct both a residence and a blacksmith shop. Before commencing these improvements, McCallum consulted the city engineer to obtain the correct grade for the street and sidewalk to ensure his buildings conformed accordingly. Following the engineer's guidance, McCallum completed his construction. However, in 1885, the city decided to raise the grade of the street and sidewalk in front of his property, prompting a notice to McCallum to raise his sidewalk by eighteen inches. Despite his protests about the inconvenience and damage that the change would cause, the city raised the sidewalk, which obstructed access to his property and required him to create an incline and decline to access his shop. This prompted McCallum to sue the city, claiming damages resulting from the changes imposed by the city.	McCallum claimed that the city's change of the street grade caused significant inconvenience and diminished access to his property, effectively hindering business operations at his blacksmith shop. He sought compensation for the damages incurred, which he believed amounted to between $400 to $600 based on testimonies from various witnesses who supported his stance that the property had been negatively impacted by the grade change.	The City of Elgin contested McCallum’s claims, arguing that the verdict was not supported by evidence and that the changes had actually benefitted the property rather than harmed it. The city contended that the jury should not have awarded damages based on the testimonies presented, emphasizing that their witnesses generally believed no significant harm had been done to McCallum’s property. They requested a reversal of the verdict on the grounds of these claims.

Jackson M. Johnson filed an action of ejectment against Charles Shinkle in the Circuit Court of Madison County, Illinois, which was later moved to the Montgomery County Circuit Court due to a change of venue. The case was presided over by Hon. Edward Y. Rice. The issue arose when Johnson sold and conveyed the land in controversy after the suit commenced. During the proceedings, the court found Shinkle guilty of unlawfully withholding possession of the premises and acknowledged that Johnson was entitled to the property in fee simple at the suit’s commencement. However, Johnson’s recent conveyance meant he was not entitled to physical possession at that time. The court ruled in favor of Johnson for the costs associated with the suit but ultimately refused to grant him a writ of possession for the land.	Johnson argued that despite having sold the land during the ongoing suit, he retained the right to recovery due to the principle that a conveyance by a plaintiff during an ejectment action does not defeat recovery rights, which would transfer to his grantee. He requested a writ of possession to reclaim the land from Shinkle based on the court’s acknowledgment of his earlier entitlement to it.	Shinkle's defense likely focused on the fact that Johnson had conveyed the land while the case was pending, contending that this act should nullify Johnson's claim for a writ of possession. Shinkle’s legal representatives argued against the issuance of the writ, maintaining that any ownership rights Johnson had were forfeited upon the conveyance during the litigation.

In 1875, in Joliet, Illinois, William Galligher executed a promissory note for $8,560 due in five years, payable to Robert Walsh. To secure the note, Galligher and his wife provided a mortgage on their property. Later that same year, Walsh sold the note and mortgage to John Van Horn, leading to a dispute about Walsh's liability—whether he was a guarantor or merely an indorser. In 1882, Van Horn filed a foreclosure suit in the Will County Circuit Court against both Galligher and Walsh, seeking not just foreclosure but a personal decree against Walsh for any remaining balance after the sale of the mortgaged property. After the court ruled against Walsh and imposed a personal decree for a deficiency of $589.06, Walsh appealed the ruling. The appellate court considered whether the personal decree against Walsh was permissible under the governing statutes and concluded that it was not.	The plaintiff, John Van Horn, argued that Robert Walsh, as an assignee of the note and mortgage, should be held liable for the deficiency resulting from the foreclosure sale. He contended that a proper legal framework existed for holding Walsh personally accountable despite his claims of being merely an indorser.	Robert Walsh argued that under Illinois law, a third party not involved in the foreclosure should not be held liable for deficiencies unless there was a statutory provision or equitable jurisdiction allowing such liability. Walsh contended that his role as an assignee did not equal assumption of a guarantor's responsibilities, and thus, he should not be compelled to pay the remaining balance after the foreclosure sale.

In January 1866, in Hancock County, Illinois, the case of Matthew McClaughry v. Andrew M. Cratzenberg arose when McClaughry, the plaintiff, filed an action of replevin against Cratzenberg, the defendant. McClaughry claimed ownership of a sorrel mare, a bay mare, and a male colt, collectively valued at three hundred dollars. He alleged that Cratzenberg had taken these animals from his possession and was wrongfully detaining them. McClaughry asserted that the property was not taken for any legal tax, assessment, or fine and, thus, sought restitution through the court. The case proceeded with McClaughry's affidavit leading to the issuance of a writ on June 27, 1865. However, during the October Term of 1865, Cratzenberg motioned to quash the writ, arguing that McClaughry's affidavit was insufficient as it failed to affirmatively state that the property was not taken for a tax, which was a requisite per the applicable statute. Although McClaughry attempted to amend his affidavit, the court denied his request and granted the motion to quash, ordering the return of the property to Cratzenberg.	McClaughry's primary claim was that the animals were taken from him without proper justification and were being wrongfully detained by Cratzenberg. He contended that the original affidavit sufficed to establish his ownership and that the property was not taken for any legal tax, thereby supporting his request for a writ of replevin to recover his animals.	Cratzenberg argued that McClaughry's affidavit was deficient because it did not explicitly state that the property was not taken for any tax, assessment, or fine as required by law. He emphasized that the affidavit's language implied that the property might have been taken under tax authority. Consequently, he sought the quashing of the writ and the dismissal of the case based on this procedural failure.

The case of "Dennis Meers v. William W. Stevens et al." took place in 1883 in Illinois. Dennis Meers, the appellant, was involved in a mortgage foreclosure dispute against William W. Stevens and others, arising from a $3,000 loan secured by a promissory note. The loan's terms included a four percent commission deducted at the loan's inception and ten percent interest payable at the end of one year. Upon the note's maturity, extensions were made twice, each requiring an additional $100, all of which Meers argued was usurious. The Appellate Court ruled these charges usurious, impacting the foreclosure proceedings. The court found evidence that the loan agreements were made through Meers' sons acting as his agents, leading to a conclusion that Meers should be accountable for the usurious transactions. The evidence highlighted a lack of clarity in the agent-principal relationships and suggested that these arrangements were structured to conceal illegal charges. The ruling upheld the Appellate Court's decision, affirming the crediting of usurious payments against the note after accounting for legitimate advertising expenses tied to the property sale under the trust deed.	The plaintiff, Dennis Meers, argued that the terms of the loan agreement were violated due to the imposition of usurious charges, including commissions taken by his agent (his son) and additional payments for loan extensions. He sought the court to recognize these charges as improper and to credit them against the mortgage amount owed, thus opposing the foreclosure initiated by Stevens.	The defendant, William W. Stevens, contended that the loan agreement, including the payment structures, was valid and that any claims of usurious practices were unfounded. Stevens maintained that he was not responsible for determining the legality of the charges, emphasizing that the agreements were acceptable under the terms presented by Meers through his sons.

In December 1830, in Gallatin County, Illinois, an appeal was brought by Timothy and Wm. Brinkley against Reuben Going. The case stemmed from a judgment rendered by a justice of the peace, who ruled in favor of Going for a debt action involving a joint and several note made by the Brinkleys to Going. The note featured an assignment to Thomas Hulett, which had been struck through by Going, indicating a dispute over the note's ownership. During the legal proceedings, the Brinkleys contended that Going could not pursue the action in his own name without proving either payment to Hulett or a retransference of the note back to him. However, despite this contention, the defense had acknowledged the validity of the note and indicated readiness to pay or accept judgment against them. The case moved from the justice of the peace to the circuit court, where the previous judgment was upheld.
