The Brinkleys argued that Reuben Going lacked the legal standing to maintain the action because he was not the rightful holder of the note. They asserted that the assignment to Hulett had not been properly accounted for or retransferred, and therefore any claim Going made as an assignee lacked merit, as the right of action was vested in Hulett.	Reuben Going defended his position by stating that the indorsement on the note was at his discretion and he could strike it out without affecting his rights to the note. He maintained that his possession of the note constituted evidence of being the bona fide holder, allowing him to advance the claim in his name, supported by the Brinkleys' acknowledgment that the note was valid.

Frances M. Doyle v. E. Sanford et al. took place in 1888, in Iroquois County, Illinois. The case involved Frances M. Doyle (the plaintiff), who sought to redeem real estate that was mortgaged. The original borrower of the mortgage was John T. Martin, who borrowed $300 from E. Sanford on July 10, 1875, with a 10% interest rate, secured by a mortgage on the property. Martin later sold the property to Hurlburt, who then conveyed it to Doyle on January 20, 1880. Throughout the proceedings, the main issues pertained to an alleged usury in the mortgage contract and the plaintiff's claim of tendering the required payment of principal and interest, which she maintained was rejected by the defendant. The case experienced multiple appeals, and originally, the court decided that the claim of usury was valid, allowing only 6% interest. Upon appeal, it was determined that the claims made by Doyle regarding both usury and tender were inconsistent, leading the court to uphold the findings from the prior appeal.	Frances M. Doyle argued that she had made a proper tender of the full payment due on the mortgage note, which was refused by the defendants, who demanded additional attorney's fees. Additionally, she claimed that there was usury in the original mortgage agreement and sought to apply only 6% interest rather than the contractual 10%. Doyle requested that the court formally recognize her tender and not impose the attorney's fees specified in the mortgage.	The defendants, E. Sanford et al., contended that Doyle could not claim the benefit of the tender due to her earlier assertions concerning usury. They asserted that her arguments of usury and tender were inconsistent and that the issue of usury had already been adjudicated in previous appeals. Furthermore, they appealed against the court's decision to allow only 6% interest rather than the agreed 10% as well as the denial of their claim to attorney’s fees as stipulated in the mortgage.

The legal case "The Village of Hyde Park v. The Washington Ice Company" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 15, 1886. The case emerged from judicial proceedings in Cook County, where the Village of Hyde Park sought to condemn a strip of land belonging to the Washington Ice Company as part of the proposed opening and extension of Onehundredth Street. The ice company's property, spanning approximately sixty-four acres, was vital for its operations in ice freezing and transportation. Since its establishment in 1878, significant investments were made in improving the site, which included creating an ice pond. The proposed street would bisect the ice pond, substantially impacting the company's operations by rendering part of the property useless. The ice company contended this would lead to depreciation in property value. The trial court's proceedings included assessing both the value of land taken and the potential damages to the land not taken during the condemnation process.	The Village of Hyde Park, as the appellant, argued that the court’s instructions regarding the assessment of damages to the property not taken were improper. The village sought the authority to condemn the land for public use, claiming that the proposed street would bring benefits to the area. However, they primarily contested the jury's findings regarding damage estimates to the property not taken by asserting that the evidence supporting these damages did not justify the amounts for which the ice company sought compensation.	The Washington Ice Company, as the appellee, defended against the condemnation by claiming that the proposed street would damage their property significantly. They contended that the instructions given to the jury were appropriate and demonstrated that the property's unique capacity for ice operations would be severely affected. The defense emphasized that the expected benefits from the new street access did not outweigh the damages incurred by the land's devaluation resulting from the construction, which would split their operational site and effectively make a portion of it non-usable.

The case "The Indianapolis and St. Louis Railway Company v. The People of the State of Illinois" was decided on October 31, 1889, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It stemmed from a proceeding in St. Clair County, where James D. Baker, the county collector, sought judgment for delinquent taxes on a parcel of real estate described as “total real estate other than track; schedule D; lot 5 a; survey 780; 18-acres.” The railway company argued that the property in question was part of its right of way and should therefore not be assessed by local assessors but rather by the State Board of Equalization. The company had submitted schedules for taxation which classified its various properties, but the disputed lot was not listed as part of the railroad track, leading to the issue of whether local assessors were authorized to tax this property. The circuit court ruled in favor of the collector, rejecting the railway’s claims and evidence regarding the use of the land for railroad purposes, asserting that the company was estopped from making those claims due to its own schedule omission.	The plaintiff, the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that the railway company was legally obligated to pay taxes on the parcel of land as assessed by the local assessor. The plaintiff argued that the company had failed to include the property in its returned schedules for taxation, and thus, the local assessor was entitled to assess the property as real estate other than railroad track. They maintained that the company’s schedule did not properly reflect all of its taxable properties, and the assessment made by the local authority was valid.	The defendant, The Indianapolis and St. Louis Railway Company, contended that the property being taxed was part of its railroad track and should therefore be assessed by the State Board of Equalization, not local authorities. The railway company's defense relied on the assertion that the omitted land was integral to its operational activities, used for side-tracks and terminal facilities. They argued that the local assessor did not have the authority to tax property they claimed was railroad track, and any tax assessment based on the local authority was unjust as it arose from a false return made by the company in good faith.

The case of Asahel Gage v. Charles B. Eggleston takes place in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision date of May 31, 1888. The principal individuals involved are Asahel Gage, the appellant (defendant), and Charles B. Eggleston, the appellee (plaintiff). The legal matter at hand revolves around a bill in chancery brought by Eggleston to remove a tax sale and the associated certificate, which he claimed were a cloud on the title of certain premises he owned. Gage, in response, denied all significant allegations made in Eggleston's bill. The case reached the appellate court following a decree that granted Eggleston the relief he sought. However, the defendant, Gage, appealed the decision, arguing that the decree lacked supporting evidence and did not specify any facts as found by the chancellor, which are essential under established rules of chancery practice in Illinois.	Charles B. Eggleston, the plaintiff, argued that the tax sale and certificate issued to Asahel Gage represented a cloud on his title to certain property. He sought a legal decree to remove this impediment, asserting that the tax sale was problematic and should not impact his ownership rights.	Asahel Gage, the defendant, contended that all material allegations made by Eggleston were untrue. He argued that the decree favoring Eggleston was not backed by any factual evidence, as there were no depositions or facts recited in the decree itself to support the relief granted to the plaintiff.

Lucius Stebbins and Luther L. Stebbins were involved in a legal case that took place in 1862 in Illinois. Lucius Stebbins had been indicted in Pike County. Following a petition from Stebbins, the Circuit Court of Pike County granted a change of venue to Adams County and took a recognizance from the plaintiffs in error for the defendant's appearance in the Circuit Court of Adams County. However, the Adams Circuit Court later entered a default and order of forfeiture on this recognizance, resulting in a judgment against Lucius Stebbins. Subsequently, a scire facias was issued against Luther L. Stebbins, leading to a judgment against both plaintiffs at the March term of the Circuit Court of Adams County with Judge Sibley presiding. The central issue revolved around whether the Circuit Court of Pike County had the authority to take such recognizance in a criminal case, a matter that was contested and ultimately led to an appellate review.	The plaintiffs contended that the Circuit Court of Pike County improperly handled the recognizance and related processes after the change of venue to Adams County. They argued that the judgment and subsequent forfeiture were executed wrongly and requested that the original proceedings be overturned due to these irregularities and the issuance of the scire facias against an incorrect party.	The defense maintained that the forfeiture of the recognizance was valid and appropriate. They argued that the powers possessed by the Circuit Court should include the ability to require recognizance from the defendant, even if not explicitly stated in statutes. They requested that the court uphold the forfeiture judgment despite the procedural challenges raised by the plaintiffs.

Andrew Wettig v. John B. Bowman is a legal case that took place in 1868 before the Illinois Supreme Court. The action began in the St. Clair Circuit Court, where John B. Bowman, the plaintiff, brought an ejectment action against Andrew Wettig, the defendant. The case revolved around a dispute over land ownership concerning a tax title claimed by Wettig under Illinois's seven years limitation act of 1839. The key individuals involved were Chief Justice Breese, who delivered the court's opinion, and attorneys Mr. Gustavus Koerner for Wettig (the appellant) and Mr. W. H. Underwood for Bowman (the appellee). The dispute arose from a sheriff's deed obtained by Wettig from a tax sale in 1852 and whether he met the statutory requirements to claim legal ownership of the land, including continuous possession, good faith claim, and payment of taxes for seven consecutive years. The case became contentious due to the exclusion of the sheriff's deed as color of title and accusations that the necessary taxes had not been paid.	The plaintiff, John B. Bowman, claimed rightful ownership of the land in question, arguing that Andrew Wettig failed to meet the requirements of the seven years limitation act. Specifically, Bowman contended that Wettig did not demonstrate continuous possession or the payment of all legally assessed taxes for the required duration of seven years, which are necessary to establish a valid claim under the statute. The plaintiff sought a judgment to enforce his ownership rights and remove Wettig’s claim on the property.	Andrew Wettig, the defendant, argued that he had acquired color of title through a valid sheriff's deed and had acted in good faith when claiming the property. He contended that the 1859 act for the relief of certain persons in the American Bottom relieved him from the obligation to pay the taxes for the year 1858, which he argued should enable him to fulfill the statute's requirements. However, he acknowledged not having paid the taxes for that year and attempted to assert that the legal basis for the taxes themselves was flawed, asserting his right to legal ownership despite these shortcomings.

In the case of Charles B. Eggleston v. Asahel Gage, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, in 1889, the appellant Eggleston sought to prevent Gage from obtaining a tax deed for a certain piece of real estate and requested the removal of specific documents from the county records that he claimed clouded the title of the property. The central issue involved the legitimacy of a tax sale certificate held by Gage, which Eggleston contended should be canceled due to a prior redemption of the property from a tax sale. The property in question had been sold to Gage for a special assessment on September 21, 1880, and subsequently sold to another party, John Carne, for delinquent taxes a day later. The land was owned by a certain Midiólas at the time of these sales. Midiólas redeemed the property from Carne's sale shortly thereafter, paying the required amounts and receiving a redemption certificate. Eggleston argued this constituted effective redemption under the state's revenue statute. However, he faced challenges due to precedent established by a prior Supreme Court ruling.	The plaintiff, Charles B. Eggleston, claimed that the redemption performed by Midiólas effectively canceled the tax sale to Asahel Gage. He argued that according to Section 211 of the Revenue Statute, since the property had been sold for special assessment and then re-sold for general taxes, Gage was not entitled to obtain a tax deed. Eggleston sought judicial intervention to enjoin Gage from taking out the deed and to remove documents representing a cloud on the property’s title.	Asahel Gage, the defendant, contended that the redemption process performed by Midiólas did not negate his rights as a purchaser from the tax sale. Gage argued that the statute's provisions regarding redemption apply to instances where the same entity is involved in various sales, rather than in situations where the properties are sold to different parties, as was the case here. He maintained that the prior ruling in Gage v. Parker established precedent binding in this case, which undermined Eggleston's claims regarding the applicability of the redemption statute.

In "Charles M. Linington v. George H. Strong et al.", the case originated from a contractual dispute involving a contract dated April 1, 1876, associated with George H. Strong and John Young granting Charles M. Linington the exclusive right to manufacture and sell certain improved pincers. The plaintiffs alleged that Linington was required to pay them a royalty of $1.44 per gross of pincers made and sold, with a minimum royalty on at least 2500 dozen per year. The first trial in the Superior Court of Cook County ruled in favor of the defendant (Linington), but this judgment was reversed by the Appellate Court, which remanded the case for a new trial. During the retrial, the plaintiffs argued Linington owed $1000 in royalties, as per the contract terms. Linington attempted to introduce evidence that he produced only 9135 pincers and ceased manufacturing after a certain time, but the court found this irrelevant due to the binding contract's terms. Moreover, the trial involved arguments regarding allegations of fraud related to the contract's representations and the responsibilities of the signing parties concerning contract awareness. Ultimately, the jury ruled that Linington was obligated to adhere to the terms of the contract based on the representations made.	The plaintiffs, Strong and Young, claimed that Linington failed to pay royalties as stipulated in their contract for the second and third years of the agreement. They sought the recovery of a total of $1,000, representing the unpaid royalties under the contract. They asserted that despite Linington's claims of having made only a fraction of the pincers required, he was legally obligated to pay royalties on the minimum annual amount specified in their agreement.	Linington contended that he had only produced a limited number of pincers and had ceased manufacturing, thus arguing that he should not have to pay royalties on the full amount stipulated in the contract. He further claimed that he had been induced to sign the contract based on fraudulent representations made by the plaintiffs regarding the contract's contents. Linington argued that he should be excused from the agreement due to these alleged misrepresentations and sought a finding in his favor to dismiss the plaintiffs' claims.

The case "The People ex rel. Christian Rosenberg v. John T. Angerer et al., County Commissioners" was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court, with a decision issued on June 7, 1887. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Monroe County, where Christian Rosenberg sought a writ of mandamus against John T. Angerer and the county commissioners. The petition was related to the abandonment and re-location of the old Bed Bud and Glasgow City road, which Rosenberg claimed was a legally established highway. The case involved various parties, including attorneys from both sides: Slate & Winkelmann for the appellant and W. H. Hobiíte Jr. and J. W. Eickebt for the appellees. During the proceedings, the Circuit Court refused to grant the writ of mandamus, leading to an appeal by Rosenberg. However, complications arose due to the loss of paperwork, resulting in a lack of proper records needed to support the appeal effectively.	Christian Rosenberg, the plaintiff, argued that the County Board unlawfully abandoned the old road that he claimed should legally serve as a highway between Bed Bud and Glasgow City. He sought a writ of mandamus to compel the county commissioners to recognize the road as the official highway and restore its status. Rosenberg's claims highlighted the importance of the road for the local community and the legal necessity of the county's adherence to established laws regarding its existence.	The defendants, including John T. Angerer and the county commissioners, contended that the appeal should be dismissed due to the plaintiff's failure to provide a sufficient abstract of the record as required by court rules. They argued that the absence of necessary documentation prevented the court from considering the merits of the case and that they complied with all legal requirements during the abandonment process. The defendants requested that the court affirm the original ruling due to the procedural deficiencies in Rosenberg's appeal.

The case of Francis B. Cooley et al. v. Reuben D. Jones et al. dates back to April 1861 in Illinois. The dispute arose over two drafts accepted by the plaintiffs, Sawyer, Mellen & Co., on October 29, 1857, drawn by A. N. Littig in favor of George W. Ashard. The drafts were related to a debt Littig owed to Cooley, Farwell & Co. After accepting the drafts, they were delivered to Ashard, who subsequently assigned them to R. D. Jones & Sons. The plaintiff, having been informed that Cooley, Farwell & Co. claimed the drafts, filed a suit in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas seeking to interplead, as they were unsure to whom they owed the payment. The plaintiffs aimed to settle the ownership rights over the drafts and requested the court to resolve their legal uncertainties regarding the payments owed to the competing claims by Cooley, Farwell & Co. and R. D. Jones & Sons. The case reflects the complexities surrounding the assignment of debts and the rights of parties involved when dealing with assigned securities.	The plaintiffs, Sawyer, Mellen & Co., claimed that they were willing to pay the amount due on the drafts but sought to determine who had rightful ownership between Cooley, Farwell & Co. and R. D. Jones & Sons. They requested the court to allow both defendants to interplead, settle their rights over the drafts, and enjoin R. D. Jones & Sons from continuing any actions against them. Additionally, they sought protection from Cooley, Farwell & Co. from initiating further legal actions related to these drafts while asserting that they would pay into the court any amount owed.	The defendants, Cooley, Farwell & Co., contended that they held rightful ownership of the drafts as they were drawn in connection to a prior claim assigned to them by Ashard. They asserted that Ashard had no authority to assign the drafts to R. D. Jones & Sons as he acted merely as their agent. They insisted that Jones & Sons were aware of this situation prior to accepting the drafts and argued that the assignment was fraudulent, thus conveying no legitimate title to Jones & Sons. On the other hand, R. D. Jones & Sons maintained that they received the drafts in good faith and without knowledge of any claims by Cooley, Farwell & Co., having made inquiries to ensure the transaction's legitimacy.

The case "William Bergan et al. v. Patrick Cahill et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1870. It originated from Peoria County, Illinois, concerning the will of Martin Morris, who had passed away. The will stipulated that all his real and personal property, including a cow, should be bequeathed to his wife, Johanna Morris, along with a power to sell property if necessary for her comfort. After the death of Johanna, the dispute arose regarding the true interpretation of the will concerning ownership of two lots. Martin Morris, the son, was to inherit the property upon his mother’s death, contingent on him paying his sister, Julia, a legacy of $100. However, Johanna passed away without exercising her power to sell the property, and William Bergan, as a grantee from Martin Morris Jr., claimed sole ownership of the lots. The heirs contested this claim, promoting the interpretation that Johanna was granted a fee simple estate, while Bergan argued it was a life estate that would pass to Martin Jr. upon Johanna's death. The circuit court determined to sell the property and distribute proceeds based on the heirs’ requests, prompting Bergan to appeal.	The plaintiffs, including the remaining heirs of Martin Morris, contended that the will granted their mother, Johanna, a full fee simple estate in the property, which would entitle them to contest Bergan's ownership claims after her death. They sought partition of the property, arguing that the provisions of the will intended for their mother to possess the property outright, not merely for her lifetime.	The defendant, William Bergan, asserted that he held valid title to the property through a conveyance from Martin Morris Jr., who received the property under the will. Bergan argued that the will created a life estate for the mother, which would pass to him as the grantee after her death. He maintained that the circuit court's decree for partition should be reversed, claiming full ownership based on the interpretation of the testator’s intentions in the will.

The case "Nelson Card et al. v. Hubert A. McCaleb et al." took place in September 1873 in Illinois, specifically concerning the Illinois and Michigan Canal. The key individuals involved were Nelson Card and Owen W. Huff, the plaintiffs, and Hubert A. McCaleb and Henry Holmes, the defendants. The plaintiffs asserted that they had an exclusive lease from the Board of Canal Commissioners, granting them the right to cut and remove ice from a designated portion of the canal. However, the defendants allegedly trespassed and removed ice from this area without permission. The case was consolidated for hearing as the issues at hand were similar. The plaintiffs sought to enforce their lease agreement, while the defendants contended that there was no lawful authority for the plaintiffs to claim exclusive rights to the ice.	The plaintiffs, Card and Huff, claimed that their lease from the Board of Canal Commissioners conferred upon them exclusive rights to cut and remove ice from a specified section of the Illinois and Michigan Canal. They argued that the defendants' actions in removing ice from this area constituted a trespass and requested that the court uphold their lease agreement to protect their rights against the defendants.	The defendants, McCaleb and Holmes, contended that the commissioners had no authority to lease the right to remove ice from the canal, as neither the statutes of 1871 nor 1872 explicitly granted such power. They further argued that the plaintiffs could not demonstrate exclusive rights because, under the law, all individuals residing along the canal had the free right to cut and remove ice. They requested the court to uphold the lower court's ruling dismissing the plaintiffs' claims.

The case, "The City of Elgin v. Robert Beckwith et al.," took place in Elgin, Illinois, and was decided on January 25, 1887, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The central issue of the dispute was a piece of land at the intersection of Chicago Street and the Fox River, which was claimed by Robert Beckwith and Harriet Dickenson (the plaintiffs) as a part of Lot 6, Block 20 in the original plat of Elgin created by James T. Gifford in 1843. The plaintiffs claimed ownership of the land that had accumulated as accretions along the river. The defendant, the City of Elgin, filed a special plea disclaiming interest in the land north of the north line of Chicago Street, as defined by the city’s assessment plat. In the first trial, the jury found in favor of the defendant, but the plaintiffs' motion for a new trial was granted. In the second trial, the jury found partially for the plaintiffs regarding some of the described land. The key contention remained over the definition of the true north line of Chicago Street in relation to the river bank which had been affected by natural changes over time. The court's instructions and the evidence admissibility became focal points of the legal arguments presented.	The plaintiffs argued that they owned the accretions to their property north of what they asserted was the true north line of Chicago Street. They maintained that the correct delineation of the street's boundaries took into account the historical river bank as plotted in Gifford's original layout, which had since been modified by natural accretions. The plaintiffs sought recovery of the disputed land as a rightful extension of their property.	The defendant, the City of Elgin, contended that the accretions belonged to them as extensions of Chicago Street's boundaries, which they argued remained defined by the original plat of Gifford. They sought to establish that the title to the land lay with the city by presenting evidence that the width of the street had effectively expanded due to the accretions south of the claimed line, which aligned with city property. They also challenged the admissibility of the plaintiffs' evidence regarding boundary lines and historical intent behind the original plat.

The case of Albert E. Goodrich et al. v. The City of Chicago took place in April 1858 in Illinois. The plaintiffs, Albert E. Goodrich and others, were steamboat owners operating on the Chicago River. They alleged that the City of Chicago failed to fulfill its legal responsibility to remove a sunken vessel wreck that obstructed the river at the mouth of the harbor. This obstruction resulted in significant damage to the plaintiffs' steamboat when it ran aground on the hidden wreck. According to the city charter, the City of Chicago had the authority to remove such obstructions, deepen, and widen the river. However, the plaintiffs contended that the City was legally bound to execute these actions, especially since it had enacted ordinances and levied taxes for such purposes. The case focused on whether the City had an absolute obligation to remove the wreck or if its responsibilities were discretionary. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court after the lower court upheld a demurrer filed by the City, which argued that plaintiffs could not claim damages for the City’s alleged failure to act.	The plaintiffs claimed that the City of Chicago was legally obligated to remove all obstructions from the Chicago River as per its charter. They asserted that the City had neglected this duty by allowing a wreck to remain submerged and unremoved, which directly caused damage to their steamboat. The plaintiffs demanded compensation for the damages incurred due to the City's failure to remove the wreck.	The City of Chicago defended itself by asserting that the charter granted it the authority to remove obstructions but did not impose an absolute duty to do so. The City argued that imposing such a blanket obligation would lead to unmanageable liability for damages. They contended that unless they exercised their authority and acted carelessly while doing so, they could not be held liable for damages resulting from unperformed duties.

In April 1860, the case "Georgiana Welch, Administratrix, and Abram Gale, Administrator, of the Estate of Benjamin C. Welch, deceased, Plaintiffs in Error, v. James T. Hoyt, Defendant in Error" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal matter arose from a promissory note for $112.50 connected to the sale of a buggy, purchased by Hoyt from the plaintiffs, who were the administrators of the estate of Benjamin C. Welch. The buggy was sold for $225, half of which Hoyt paid at the time of purchase, with the remaining balance recorded in the note. Hoyt contended that the plaintiffs had warranted the buggy to be of good quality; however, he claimed that it was made from poor materials and that the workmanship was deficient. After a trial in June 1859, where evidence supported Hoyt's claims regarding the buggy's condition, the court ruled in favor of the defendant. The plaintiffs' further attempts for a new trial were overruled.	The plaintiffs argued that Hoyt owed them the remaining balance of $112.50 for the buggy sold. They contended that the purchase agreement included a warranty of quality that justified the price paid, implying that Hoyt's claims of the buggy's poor condition were unfounded. The legal requests included the enforcement of the promissory note and the recovery of the outstanding balance.	Hoyt, the defendant, asserted that the buggy purchased was not of the warranted quality and was constructed from substandard materials. He presented evidence that the vehicle deteriorated quickly and incurred significant repair costs exceeding $100. Hoyt claimed that the buggy was unfit for use and sought to offset his damages against the plaintiffs' claim for the unpaid note, requesting a judgment for the difference due to the failure of consideration.

Barzillai Garretson and his wife, Christiana M. Garretson, were involved in a legal dispute with Jeremiah Strawn in the County Court of LaSalle County, Illinois, around September 1870. Strawn brought an action of assumpsit against the Garretsons and a third party, John Garretson, due to a promissory note executed by them. The case arose when process was served only on Barzillai and Christiana. In her defense, Christiana filed a plea of coverture, asserting her legal incapacity to be sued due to her marriage. However, upon Barzillai's failure to appear in court, a default judgment was entered against him for the amount owed on the note. The case centered around whether the court could render judgment against Barzillai despite Christiana's plea, leading to complications regarding the appropriate legal procedures and the enforcement of the written contract. The court eventually acknowledged that the statute invoked by Strawn did not apply to the situation, as Christiana's plea did not challenge the execution of the promissory note.	Jeremiah Strawn, the plaintiff, claimed that the Garretsons owed him money based on a promissory note executed to him. He argued that the note was supported by a written agreement to transfer a ten-acre woodland tract to the defendants upon payment, and that Christiana had benefited from cutting timber on that land prior to the legal proceedings. Strawn sought a judgment against Barzillai for the amount owed under the note after Barzillai failed to appear and defend against the charges.	Barzillai Garretson contended that the legal proceedings against him were flawed due to the coverture plea filed by his wife Christiana. This plea asserted that Christiana was not liable to be sued in her own right, which affected the case against Barzillai. His legal team argued that the trial court erred by allowing a judgment by default against Barzillai without resolving the matter concerning Christiana's plea. They sought to reverse the judgment against Barzillai on these grounds, claiming the default judgment was improper.

In the case of W. W. Ives v. Alice Hulce, which took place in 1885 in McLean County, Illinois, the plaintiff, Alice Hulce, initiated an action of replevin against W. W. Ives and Jos. Ator before a justice of the peace. The replevin action related to the unlawful detention of her personal property. The officer executing the writ reported that the defendants refused to return the property upon demand. Following the appeals process, the case was brought to the circuit court where a jury trial resulted in a verdict that found Ives guilty, assessing damages at $175, while Ator was found not guilty. After Ives's motion for a new trial was overruled, a judgment was entered stating that the plaintiff would recover only one cent in damages, instead of the jury-assessed amount. Subsequently, when the error regarding the judgment amount was discovered, a motion was made to amend the judgment to reflect the jury's award of $175. The court allowed this amendment, asserting that the initial judgment did not align with its intentions. This case dealt with complex issues surrounding the correction of clerical errors in judicial records and the understanding of jury verdicts in the context of replevin actions.	The plaintiff, Alice Hulce, argued that W. W. Ives unlawfully detained her property and sought to recover damages assessed by the jury amounting to $175 for this unlawful detention. Her legal request emphasized the need for the court to correct the judgment to reflect the true damages as determined by the jury.	W. W. Ives contended that the judgment entered by the circuit court for only one cent was correct, based on the nature of the proceedings. He sought a new trial, arguing against the damages awarded and emphasizing concerns about the procedural correctness of the judgment including how it reflected the court’s intentions versus clerical errors.

In December 1848, William B. Thorn filed a claim against the estate of James Ham, represented by Joel F. Watson, the estate's administrator. The claim was filed a little more than two years after administration letters were issued to Watson. Thorn initially presented his account to the Probate Justice, who acknowledged the validity of the claim but stated it could only be allowed if assets were found not inventoried by the administrator. When the case escalated to the Circuit Court, it was agreed upon by both parties to submit the matter without formal process. The Circuit Court ruled against Thorn, citing the Statute of Limitations, which barred claims not presented within two years of the administration letters unless new assets were discovered. The estate was determined to be solvent, with a potential surplus for distribution among Ham's children. Despite the decision made by the Probate Justice being found reasonable, Thorn's claim was deemed time-barred.	The plaintiff, William B. Thorn, argued that his claim against the estate of James Ham was valid and should be allowed despite being filed after the two-year limitation. Thorn contended that the estate was solvent and there would be surplus funds available. He sought a ruling from the court to ascertain the amount owed to him and allow for collection from any future discovered assets of the estate.	The defendant, Joel F. Watson, contended that Thorn's claim was barred by the Statute of Limitations, as it was filed more than two years after the issuance of letters of administration. Watson argued that Thorn's claim could only be satisfied if new assets, not inventoried or accounted for, were discovered. Additionally, Watson maintained a defense of set-off against Thorn's claim.

In the legal case of Village of Hyde Park v. Alonzo J. Snow, decided on October 23, 1883, the proceedings took place in Cook County, Illinois. The case was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court, with Judge Sidney Smith presiding. The principal question in this case was the same as that in a previous case, Village of Hyde Park v. George L. Thatcher, which was also decided in the same court term. Specific details about the incidents that led to the case are not available in this summary, but it is clear that the legal dispute involved the Village of Hyde Park and the defendant, Alonzo J. Snow. The nature of the allegations or claims made by either party is not fully detailed in the provided information.	The Village of Hyde Park, as the plaintiff, likely claimed that Alonzo J. Snow was in some manner accountable for an issue that had resulted in harm or legal violation against the Village. The court's judgment referenced a similar case (Thatcher), indicating that the Village sought to reverse a prior ruling that was unfavorable to them.	Alonzo J. Snow, the defendant, through his representation by Mr. William Law, would have argued against the claims brought by the Village of Hyde Park. The specific arguments or defenses he presented are not detailed in the provided information, but generally, a defendant in such cases seeks to demonstrate a lack of responsibility for the claims made against them or to emphasize flaws in the plaintiff's argument.

Lewis Andrews filed a case against The Board of Supervisors of Knox County in 1873, concerning the construction of a new jail in Galesburg, Illinois—the county seat. Andrews, a tax-payer and property owner in Knox County, contested the decision to build the jail, arguing that the existing jail in Knoxville, five miles away, was sufficient for the county's needs and that the expenditure was unnecessary. He claimed that a majority of the county residents opposed the relocation of the county seat from Knoxville to Galesburg. Andrews sought an injunction from the Knox circuit court to prevent the Board from proceeding with the contract to build the jail, following the approval of the county seat's relocation by the people in a previous election. After an ex parte temporary injunction was granted without notice to the Board, the Board moved to dissolve it. The case was transferred to the Peoria circuit court, where further legal maneuvers took place before the Board's motion to dissolve the injunction was considered. The court later ruled on the merits of the case.	The plaintiff, Lewis Andrews, argued that the Board of Supervisors was not authorized to build a new jail because the existing facility in Knoxville was adequate. He claimed that the decision to relocate the county seat to Galesburg faced opposition from a majority of residents, which would be confirmed by an upcoming election. Andrews requested an injunction to stop the Board from proceeding with construction contracts for the jail.	The Board of Supervisors contended that they were acting within their legal duties, as it was required by law to provide a sufficient jail and courthouse for the county. They argued that there had been no allegations of fraud or corruption to justify the claim against them. The Board maintained that their actions were necessary to fulfill their obligations to the public and opposed the injunction on the basis that they had not violated it and were awaiting its dissolution before proceeding with the project.

In April 1866, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the case of Sophia C. Newman et al. v. Wells Willetts concerning a legal dispute originating in Mercer County, Illinois. The case followed a judgment obtained by Wells Willetts against Sophia C. Newman for $814.85, due to an unpaid debt. On October 4, 1861, an execution was issued following this judgment. Over time, Willetts alleged that Sophia Newman owned land and had conveyed it to others without consideration in an attempt to obstruct the collection of his debt. Specifically, he contended that the property was originally owned by her late husband, Erasmus Newman, who had transferred it to her via a deed in 1857. However, due to marital law at that time, the court found that this deed was inoperative and consequently concluded that Sophia's rights were limited to a homestead right and an unassigned dower right, which were not subject to the execution. The Supreme Court's review ultimately focused on the question of Sophia's ownership interest in the disputed estate.	The plaintiff, Wells Willetts, claimed that he held a judgment against Sophia C. Newman and sought to enforce it by filing a bill in chancery. He asserted that Sophia owned the property in fee simple and that she had transferred this title to prevent him from collecting his debt, thus requesting the court to set aside the deeds in order to eliminate any impediment to selling the land to satisfy his judgment.	In her defense, Sophia C. Newman argued that she did not possess a fee simple interest in the land, as claimed by Willetts. She maintained that the conveyance from her husband to her was ineffective due to the legal restrictions of their marriage at the time. Furthermore, she stated that her only interests in the property were her rights of dower and homestead, both of which were protected from execution. Thus, she sought to have these rights recognized and preserved rather than having the deeds annulled.

In the case of James A. Monniea, use, etc., v. The German Insurance Company, decided on February 9, 1883, the legal proceedings took place in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included James A. Monniea, the plaintiff, and the German Insurance Company, the defendant. The dispute arose after Monniea had a judgment rendered against him, which he could not satisfy. As a result, the plaintiffs garnisheed the insurance company, which admitted it owed Monniea $700 under an insurance policy—$400 for a loss on his homestead and $300 for personal property. However, the insurance company claimed that Monniea's entire owed amount was exempt from garnishment due to his status as the head of a family and the applicable Illinois exemption laws, thus seeking to avoid the payment of the $300 claim. The key legal issues revolved around the interpretation of exemption laws regarding insurance money and whether it could be claimed as exempt property when it was not yet in Monniea's possession.	The plaintiff, Monniea, asserted that the $300 owed to him by the German Insurance Company was not exempt and should be available for garnishment. He argued that while the insurance company acknowledged the debt, the funds could be seized to satisfy his unsatisfied judgment. Essentially, Monniea sought a judgment in his favor against the remainder of the debt after excluding the exempt portion tied to his homestead.	The German Insurance Company contended that the $300 owed to Monniea was exempt from garnishment, citing Illinois exemption laws. They claimed that a schedule was presented to the garnishee officer, which outlined Monniea's exempt property and the argument that the insurance money represented a type of property that could not be seized under the law, as it was considered personal property owed to Monniea. The defendant's position relied on a legal interpretation that money due from the insurance policy could not be considered like other personal property that may be subject to execution.

In the case of Paul G. Schuh v. William D’Oench et al., which took place in June 1869 in Alexander County, Illinois, Paul G. Schuh filed a suit against William D’Oench and others. The proceedings began when a demurrer was filed by the defendants on April 7, 1869. However, on the same day, the court recorded a default judgment against the defendants. The plaintiff alleged that the defendants had failed to respond to the declaration appropriately. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court, where the significant issue debated was the procedural error regarding the timing of the demurrer and the default judgment. Justice Walker delivered the opinion, outlining the necessity for clear record-keeping in court procedures.	The plaintiff, Paul G. Schuh, claimed that the defendants did not adequately respond to the declaration. He argued that the default judgment was justified due to the defendants' failure to act in a timely manner and that the demurrer filed by the defendants did not negate the validity of the default.	The defendants argued that a demurrer had been filed prior to the entry of the default judgment and claimed that the court had made an error by not recognizing this. They contended that the default should have been set aside, as there was evidence to suggest that their demurrer was pending when the default was entered, which invalidated the judgment.

In June 1876, the case of John W. Patrick v. Robert Jack, Admr. took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. The main individuals involved were John W. Patrick, who was acting as the administrator of the estate, and Robert Jack, the administrator of the opposing party. The case arose from mutual accounts between Jack and Patrick’s deceased intestate, leading to a legal dispute over a judgment amount. Initially, in a trial before a justice of the peace, Patrick secured a judgment of $20 against Jack. However, Jack appealed this decision to the circuit court, resulting in a trial de novo. In this subsequent trial, the circuit court ruled in favor of Jack, granting him a judgment of $1.07 against Patrick, to be paid during the course of estate administration. The circuit court examined financial records from both parties, finding a small balance due to Jack, which shaped the court's conclusions about the accounts in question.	The plaintiff, John W. Patrick, claimed that he was owed a sum from the mutual accounts with the deceased and initially secured a favorable judgment in a lower court. He argued that the evidence provided in the trial supported his claims, emphasizing the legitimacy of the accounts in managing his intestate’s affairs.	The defendant, Robert Jack, contended that the accounts showed a balance in his favor rather than against him. He argued that the bookkeeping and evidence presented in trial sufficiently demonstrated that the plaintiff's claims were unfounded, leading to his successful appeal and the subsequent judgment against Patrick.

In the case of John R. Duffin v. The People of the State of Illinois, the events took place in Belleville, Illinois, culminating in a conviction on June 16, 1883. John R. Duffin, also known as Hamlet S. Felton, was indicted for forgery related to a promissory note dated April 12, 1880. The indictment included multiple counts accusing him of forging the names of Jacob Schmidt, Julius Winkles, and Wm. B. Padfield on a note that promised payment to the First National Bank of Belleville. Duffin’s defense argued the indictment was defective because it did not specify that Schmidt's name was signed in German, yet the court ruled otherwise. During the trial, Duffin claimed that he obtained the signatures under false pretenses, asserting he tricked the individuals into signing a different document than the note itself. Despite his claims of innocence, the evidence presented, including testimonies from the purported signers denying their involvement, ultimately led to his conviction.	The plaintiff, the State of Illinois, argued that John R. Duffin had forged a promissory note with the intent to defraud the First National Bank. They claimed he unlawfully obtained $4,000 by misrepresenting the nature of the documents to the individuals whose signatures were forged. The prosecution maintained that Duffin knowingly committed forgery to financially benefit himself at the expense of the bank.	John R. Duffin’s defense centered on the argument that the indictment was insufficient, as it failed to clearly indicate that the signature was in a foreign language. He claimed the signatures were genuine, though obtained through deception about the purpose of signing the documents. Duffin maintained that he did not intend to harm the bank, arguing that his actions did not constitute forgery as defined by law. He also highlighted issues related to the conduct of his counsel during the trial, contending that it compromised his defense.

In March 1819, in Madison County, Illinois, François Coleen and Abraham Claypole (the appellants) filed an appeal against Daniel Figgins (the appellee) regarding a legal dispute that arose from a writ issued by the Madison circuit court on March 31, 1819. This writ was intended to be returnable to a court term in May that year. However, the act establishing the circuit courts had just been approved on the same day, leading the court to determine that the writ was void because it could not take effect until April 1, 1819, which was after the writ had been issued. The court emphasized that an appearance by the defendant could not rectify a void writ, which is fundamentally different from a voidable process that can be cured by appearance. This ruling prompted the reversal of the lower court's judgment, making it apparent that the initial process lacked validity due to the timing of the court's establishment.	The plaintiffs, Coleen and Claypole, contended that the writ they received was improperly issued, as the court it was addressed to did not legally exist at the time of its issuance. They argued that this invalidates the proceedings. Their primary legal request was for the appellate court to recognize the void nature of the writ and reverse the previous court's judgment based on this procedural error.	The defendant, Figgins, did not contest the essential point regarding the issuance of the writ being void. His legal argument centered around the idea that the irregularities in the process could have been cured by an appearance in court. Figgins maintained that since he appeared, it should mitigate any defects related to how the process was served, arguing that procedural irregularities were not sufficient for a reversal of the case.

In the case of Samuel Marshall v. John C. Ender, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the dispute arose over ownership of a bond and trust deed originally issued by Carl M. Carlson, whose estate had an indebtedness of $2000. The case, adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 16, 1888, involved two claimants: Samuel Marshall and John C. Ender. Both claimed to be the rightful owner of the bond, which was secured on real estate. Marshall contended that he had purchased the bond from Nancy Swift, the last acknowledged holder, with the intention of investment. Ender, however, claimed he acquired the bond from Charles A. Schmidt, a loan broker, in a bona fide transaction. The complexities deepened because Schmidt had obtained a renewal agreement with Carlson's representatives before selling the bond to Ender, raising questions about ownership and the validity of both claims. A decree ordered both parties to present their claims, and ultimately, the trial court found in favor of Ender, leading to Marshall's appeal.	Samuel Marshall argued that he was the rightful owner of the bond, asserting that he had purchased it from Nancy Swift shortly before Schmidt obtained a renewal agreement with the representatives of Carlson's estate. Marshall maintained that although he left the bond in Schmidt’s care for investment purposes due to his work as a sailor, he had a superior claim over Ender based on his transaction with Swift.	John C. Ender contended that he purchased the bond from Schmidt after the renewal agreement was made, asserting that he had done so in good faith and for valuable consideration. Ender argued that the bond was over-due when both parties made their purchases, but the evidence supported his claim that he had rightful ownership due to his later, legitimate transaction with Schmidt and the fact that he retained possession of the bond.

Henry Kayser filed a legal case against William H. Hall, the Administrator of John G. Smith's estate, in the Illinois Supreme Court around June 1877. The case's origins lay in Madison County, where Kayser sought to enforce a claim based on a promissory note. The note, dated March 28, 1871, was for $5,000 and made payable to the maker, F. W. Smith, with an endorsement from John G. Smith. It was asserted that the debt was incurred when Kayser lent money to F. W. Smith, relying on the endorsement of his father, John G. Smith, who was deceased at the time of trial. A critical aspect of the case revolved around whether John G. Smith had assumed the role of a guarantor or a second indorser on the note. The Circuit Court of Madison County originally allowed Kayser's claim but later affirmed a judgment from the county court dismissing it. The Supreme Court's review centered on the nature of the endorsement and procedural irregularities surrounding the judgment set aside by the clerk without proper authority or notification.	Henry Kayser contended that he was owed $5,000 based on the promissory note endorsed by John G. Smith. He argued that the note was valid, asserting that the endorsements confirmed John G. Smith's liability as a guarantor. Kayser sought to reverse the Circuit Court's ruling, claiming that the evidence established Smith’s obligation to honor the debt according to the previously established agreements concerning the promissory note.	William H. Hall, as the Administrator of John G. Smith's estate, contended that John G. Smith's endorsement should be seen solely as that of a second indorser rather than a guarantor. The defense argued that for Kayser to hold John G. Smith liable, he needed to show that he had pursued the maker of the promissory note for payment or established the maker’s insolvency, which Kayser failed to do. The court's prior ruling in the county court was thus justified, as there was no substantial evidence to support Kayser’s claim against the estate.

In 1846, in Calhoun County, Illinois, William Frye was involved in a legal dispute with the Bank of Illinois and several insurance companies, including the Union and Missouri Insurance Companies. The case arose when the complainants filed a bill against Frye and John Shaw, alleging that various conveyances made by Frye, which claimed ownership of certain real estate mortgaged to the complainants by Shaw, were fraudulent. The complainants aimed to set aside these conveyances and subjected the properties to satisfy the mortgage debts owed by Shaw, claiming his insolvency. The court initially took the bill pro confesso against Frye, leading to an interlocutory decree that barred Frye from redeeming the mortgaged premises unless he paid the amounts owed by the next court term. Frye later sought to vacate this decree but was denied, resulting in a final decree that set aside the conveyances and ordered the mortgage properties sold to satisfy the debts if Shaw failed to pay within five days. Frye appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing numerous legal errors in the proceedings.	The plaintiffs, including the Bank of Illinois and the insurance companies, claimed that Frye had received fraudulent conveyances of real estate which they sought to annul. They asserted that Frye should be foreclosed from all equity of redemption on the mortgaged property unless he satisfied the debts owed to them by the first day of the next court term.	Frye's defense centered on the assertion that the plaintiffs, particularly the insurance companies, failed to allege that they were legally incorporated or had the authority to maintain the suit and enforce claims against him. He argued that the decree entered against him was erroneous because it required him to pay unspecified amounts without determining the underlying debt owed by Shaw, who had not been properly involved in the proceedings at the time.

Hezekiah Cunningham, the appellant, brought a case against William Fithian and others (appellees) regarding a dispute over a contract for the sale of land located in Milwaukee. The contract was established on April 4, 1836. Cunningham alleged that Fithian had engaged in fraudulent conduct related to this contract, though much of the fraud had been known to him soon after it occurred. Despite this knowledge, Cunningham did not file his bill to rescind the sale until June 12, 1841, five years after discovering the alleged fraud. During this interval, the property values significantly declined and Cunningham failed to pay taxes on the land for several years. His lack of diligence in seeking redress suggested negligence, further complicated by potential tax sales that might have impaired or uncertain title to the land. The case was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1845 after being dismissed by the Vermillion Circuit Court in October 1843.	Cunningham’s main arguments centered on the assertion that Fithian had committed fraud in the land sale contract thus warranting the rescission of the agreement. He sought equitable relief through the court, requesting to undo the contract based on the alleged fraudulent conduct. He claimed that the significant delay in filing for rescission was justified by the nature of the fraud, which he believed inhibited his ability to act sooner.	Fithian’s defense highlighted that Cunningham's delay in seeking a rescission of the contract, along with his failure to pay taxes and maintain the property, indicated a lack of diligence and responsibility. The defense argued that equity requires a party seeking to rescind a contract to act in a timely manner and also be in a position to restore the condition of the other party. By not being able to restore Fithian to his original position due to his negligence, Fithian contended that the court should deny Cunningham's claims.

On January 9, 1819, in Gallatin County, Illinois, a bond was executed by N. Buckmaster to William Grundy for the conveyance of a tract of land. This bond had a penalty amount of eight hundred dollars and was conditioned to become void upon the successful execution of a deed from Buckmaster to Grundy. Following the execution, the bond was assigned on the same day to Henry Eddy, who then brought the action in the circuit court against Buckmaster as the assignee of Grundy. During the proceedings, Buckmaster raised several exceptions; however, he ultimately suffered a judgment by default. He later moved to overturn this judgment on the basis that the bond was not assignable under common law and argued that the applicable statute of 1807 did not permit such an assignment either.	Henry Eddy, as the assignee of the bond executed by N. Buckmaster, claimed that the bond should be enforceable despite Buckmaster's defense against its assignability. Eddy argued that according to the statute of 1807, assignments of bonds and writings obligatory for the payment of money were valid, which would allow him to maintain an action in his own name.	N. Buckmaster contended that the bond, being for the conveyance of land, was not assignable under common law. He emphasized that the language of the statute of 1807 did not include bonds related to real estate in its provisions for assignability. As such, he sought to have the judgment against him reversed on these grounds.

In January 1870, in Sangamon County, Illinois, Joseph Seligman initiated legal action against John Laubheimer and others regarding the redemption of a mortgaged property. Seligman held a first mortgage on the property, which was executed alongside a second mortgage to another party, Saltgenstein, on the same day. Seligman's mortgage was recorded first. A foreclosure action ensued for Seligman’s mortgage, resulting in a decree that established him as the primary lien holder with an owed amount of $2,445.05, followed by Saltgenstein’s second lien, which owed $1,111.35. In January 1870, Seligman purchased the property at a foreclosure sale for $1,500, obtaining a certificate of purchase approved by the court. Saltgenstein later exercised his right to redeem the property before a year had elapsed. Following the redemption, Seligman filed a petition to ascertain the amount due, request a re-sale, and assert that his mortgage lien remained valid despite the redemption.	Seligman's central arguments centered around his entitlement to reclaim the property due to his first mortgage status and the nature of the redemption by the second mortgagee, Saltgenstein. He requested the court to affirm his mortgage lien as continuing and sought to determine the debt still owed to him, in addition to initiating a re-sale of the property.	The defendants, including Saltgenstein, argued that the statutory right to redeem the mortgaged property negated Seligman's mortgage lien after the sale. They contended that upon redeeming, Saltgenstein had restored the property’s status as if the foreclosure sale had not occurred, thereby challenging Seligman’s claims regarding the validity and continuity of his mortgage lien.

The case "The People ex rel. John D. Caton v. The Ottawa Hydraulic Company et al." took place in the city of Ottawa, Illinois, with notable legal proceedings initiated on November 28, 1884. John Dean Caton, representing the State of Illinois, filed an information in the nature of a quo warranto in the LaSalle County Circuit Court. The allegation was against the Ottawa Hydraulic Company, originally organized on November 15, 1851, by individuals including William H. W. Cushman and Lorenzo Leland. The state’s attorney claimed that the company had fraudulently misrepresented its purpose, which was supposedly to lease and operate water-power infrastructure for factories, while it was, in reality, engaged solely in speculation by sub-letting water-power and reaping significant profits. The claim also stated that the shareholders had failed to pay in any substantial capital stock, rendering the organization and its operations illegitimate. In response to Caton's allegations, the company contended it had operated legally for many years, with subsequent legislative recognition of its corporate existence and functions. The case eventually reached the Illinois Supreme Court on appeal after the Circuit Court sustained a demurrer against the State's charges and dismissed the case.	The plaintiff, John D. Caton, charged that the Ottawa Hydraulic Company operated fraudulently and without legal authority. He argued that the company had misrepresented its purpose by falsely stating its intent to build mills and factories while only engaging in speculative renting of water-power. The primary legal request was to declare the company's incorporation null and void and prevent its continued operation, thereby ousting those associated with the company from exercising any corporate powers.	The defendants, represented by Lorenzo Leland and Hiram T. Gilbert, contended that any grounds for declaring the company's incorporation invalid had been waived by the state through legislative recognition and amendments passed in 1853, which affirmed the company's legal status and expanded its operational powers. They argued that the act of 1853 essentially acted as a new charter, confirming the company’s rights and protecting its activities. The defense claimed that the allegations of misrepresentation did not invalidate their corporate existence and that the amendment eliminated any requirement for them to plead the public law.

Union Mutual Accident Association v. Lewis E. Miller is a legal case decided on November 18, 1887, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case revolves around an indemnity claim made by the appellee, Lewis E. Miller, against the appellant, Union Mutual Accident Association. Miller, a member of the association, claimed indemnity under a certificate of membership, which was governed by specific by-laws. A key issue arose concerning whether Miller received notices regarding assessments sent by the association. The by-laws stipulated that notices should be mailed to the member's last known address, and the mailing of such notices constituted legal notice, regardless of actual receipt. Evidence presented indicated that notices were indeed sent to Miller's provided address, but he claimed he did not receive them. The court had to address whether Miller’s lack of receipt could absolve him from the consequences of not meeting his assessment obligations.	The plaintiff, Lewis E. Miller, argued that he did not receive the assessment notices sent by Union Mutual Accident Association, which he claimed absolved him of any default on payments. He requested indemnity based on the certificate issued to him, asserting that the association had a duty to notify him of assessments directly and that their failure to do so should relieve him of any liabilities arising from non-payment.	The defendant, Union Mutual Accident Association, contended that the by-laws explicitly stated that sending notices via mail to the last known address constituted sufficient legal notification, regardless of actual receipt. They argued that Miller, being bound by the by-laws, was obligated to pay the assessments as the notices had been properly mailed. The defense requested that the court uphold the validity of their actions under the by-laws and that Miller should be held accountable for non-payment.

In the case of George L. Dunlap v. Perry H. Smith et al., the legal action arose in Cook County, Illinois, with the proceedings occurring in the Illinois Appellate Court on January 25, 1888. The lawsuit was prompted by a promissory note, with Dunlap as the appellant and Smith's estate as the appellee. The primary issue in contention was a claim for set-off amounting to $6,000 that Dunlap argued should be deducted from the amount owed on the promissory note. This claimed set-off stemmed from a significant loss of approximately $12,000 incurred in a joint wheat transaction conducted on the board of trade, involving both Dunlap and Smith. Dunlap contended that the loss was a joint liability and that Smith’s estate was responsible for half of it. Witnesses presented by Dunlap confirmed that both men had frequently engaged in business dealings as partners under the joint account designation of “Smith & Dunlap.” Despite testimonies supporting Dunlap's claim, the trial court had to weigh the evidence regarding the authorization of the wheat transaction as a joint venture.	The plaintiff, George L. Dunlap, claimed that he was entitled to set off $6,000 against the amount owed on a promissory note due to a loss incurred in a joint wheat transaction with Perry H. Smith. Dunlap argued that since the transaction was conducted on a joint account basis, Smith’s estate was liable for half of the $12,000 loss. He sought the court’s acknowledgment of this joint liability and requested a judgment reflecting the set-off.	The defendant, representing Perry H. Smith's estate, disputed Dunlap's claim for set-off, arguing that the transactions were not established as joint dealings. The defense maintained that the evidence presented by Dunlap did not unequivocally support the assertion that the wheat deal was a joint account. The defense sought to have Dunlap’s claimed set-off disallowed, enforcing the obligation under the promissory note without any deductions.

The case "First National Bank of Chicago v. The William Ruehl Brewing Company" took place in May 1889 in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, First National Bank of Chicago, brought an action to recover the amount of a check that had been drawn on them and subsequently endorsed to the defendant. The key individual involved is B. J. Ettelsohn, the drawer of the check, who stopped payment on it. Ettelsohn's appeal was made under the name of the bank. The defendant's claim revolved around the allegation that fraudulent representations were made regarding the value of saloon stock that induced Ettelsohn to issue the check as part of a loan. The trial was conducted without a jury, and the court ultimately found in favor of the plaintiff. Ettelsohn later filed motion for a new trial based on newly discovered evidence, which the court denied, asserting that the evidence presented was not sufficient to warrant a new trial.	The plaintiff, First National Bank of Chicago, argued primarily that the check issued by B. J. Ettelsohn was valid and that the court should enforce its payment. They sought recovery of the check's amount, asserting that Ettelsohn’s claims about fraud were unfounded and that the court had already made a just decision based on the evidence presented during the trial.	The defendant, William Ruehl Brewing Company, contended that fraudulent misrepresentations regarding the value of saloon stock were made to B. J. Ettelsohn, leading him to issue the check as part of a loan. They argued the evidence of fraud warranted a new trial due to newly discovered evidence that they believed would change the outcome of the case. The defense maintained that the initial court's ruling was incorrect.

In December 1835, in Illinois, Nancy Reavis and Isham Reavis were involved in a divorce proceeding initiated by Isham Reavis, which cited the grounds of desertion. The Circuit Court found in favor of Isham, confirming the desertion. Nancy admitted to the desertion but justified her actions by claiming extreme cruelty from Isham and his failure to protect her from insults. The jury supported the desertion claim, leading to the Circuit Court's decree dissolving their marriage, ordering alimony for Nancy, and deferring the precise amount to the next session. During the subsequent court term, despite evidence showing Isham's substantial assets, the court awarded Nancy only one cent in alimony and decreed that each party should pay their costs. Isham appealed this decision, contending that the nominal alimony was an error given his financial status and that evidence from the divorce proceedings should not have been considered again.	Nancy Reavis contended that she deserved a fair alimony amount for both herself and their child due to her husband's financial capability. She argued that the court's award of only one cent as alimony was grossly inadequate and not reflective of Isham's ability to provide proper financial support. She sought a reasonable yearly allowance to ensure her and her child's maintenance, arguing that the court had an obligation to consider Isham's estate when determining appropriate financial support.	Isham Reavis argued that the nominal alimony awarded was justifiable given that the court had admitted previously heard testimony, which he believed was irrelevant to the alimony determination. He contended that this admission affected the judgment regarding the alimony amount. Furthermore, he claimed the court was in error for deciding that Nancy should also pay costs associated with the hearing.

The legal case "William G. Miller v. James S. Craig" took place in April 1864 in Illinois, specifically in the Circuit Court of McLean County. The central figures in the case were William G. Miller, the defendant, and James S. Craig, the plaintiff. The case arose from a dispute over a deed wherein Craig had conveyed certain real estate to Miller. Craig filed a suit in chancery seeking to set aside the deed on allegations of misrepresentation by Miller and claims of mental incapacity that affected Craig's ability to enter into a valid contract. The Circuit Court initially ruled in Craig’s favor, rescinding the contract. Consequently, Miller appealed the decision, contesting the claims made against him and arguing that no fraud or undue influence occurred during the transaction.	James S. Craig, the plaintiff, argued that the deed conveying property to William G. Miller should be rescinded due to alleged misrepresentations and claims regarding his mental incapacity at the time of the transaction. He contended that these factors impeded his ability to comprehend the contract's implications and thus warranted the court’s intervention to set aside the executed deed.	William G. Miller, the defendant, contended that there was no fraudulent misrepresentation or deceit involved in the transaction. He asserted that Craig was fully capable of making informed decisions and had the opportunity to examine the property's condition prior to finalizing the deal. Miller argued that mere regrets over a perceived bad bargain do not justify the rescission of a contract and sought to have the Circuit Court's decree reversed.

The case "Ann Gould et al. v. David Garrison et al." took place in September 1868 in Illinois, where the plaintiff, Ann Gould, sought to enforce a mechanic's lien against the defendants, including David Garrison. The lawsuit was initiated due to property-related disputes, as claims for non-payment emerged. The proceedings involved questions regarding juristic authority, jurisdiction, and the legitimacy of service of process. The court addressed various procedural objections raised by the defendants, including claims about the sufficiency of notices and jurisdictional issues concerning the service of process. It was determined that personal service was not feasible, so notice by publication was deemed acceptable under Illinois law. By a final decree dated May 25, 1868, the court ruled to enforce the lien against Gould and determined amounts owed to the complainants.	The plaintiffs claimed they were owed a sum of $716 from the defendants concerning a contract made with Ann Gould. They argued that the court had jurisdiction over Gould due to proper notice by publication and that the decree issued complied with procedural requirements. The plaintiffs requested enforcement of the mechanic's lien and general execution against the defendants’ property.	The defendants, led by David Garrison, raised objections asserting that Ann Gould was not properly within the court's jurisdiction at the time of the judgment. They also contended that the decree regarding property advertisement methods was insufficient according to legal standards and that the decree wrongly stated the financial obligations were due from both defendants. The defendants sought to challenge the validity of the court's decision and requested that the objections to the decree be upheld.

Nathan Horner and Benjamin Hypes (the plaintiffs) filed a legal case against Mary C. Starkey, acting as the administratrix of the estate of the deceased William C. Starkey, in November 1861. The dispute originated in Monroe County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs sought to enforce two promissory notes dated November 14, 1838. These notes were made by William A. Strong and William C. Starkey, one for $51.17 and another for $12.68, both payable one day after the date specified. The plaintiffs initially filed their claim in the County Court, which refused to acknowledge the debts, asserting the statute of limitations as a defense. The plaintiffs appealed the decision to the Circuit Court, where Judge Omelveny presided over a non-jury trial. During the trial, testimonies were presented indicating that the debts were known to the defendant and that Starkey had previously stated he would repay the notes when able. However, the Circuit Court upheld the County Court's ruling, affirming the assertion of the statute of limitations and denying the plaintiffs' claim.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to payment on the two promissory notes, which had been formally signed and dated. They contended that a conversation between William Starkey and their collection agent indicated a promise to pay the debts in the future, which they believed nullified the statute of limitations. The plaintiffs requested the court to reverse the County Court's decision, allow their claims for payment, and grant a new trial.	The defendant's primary defense rested on the assertion of the statute of limitations, arguing that the promise to pay the debt was conditional and not binding, as it relied on the uncertain future ability of Starkey to make the payments. The defendant maintained that the language used by Starkey during his conversations did not constitute a firm commitment to pay and thus upheld the statute of limitations, validating the County Court's ruling.

The case "Eugene Russell et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois" arose in June 1867 in Effingham County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included Eugene Russell and others, who were indicted for murder. During the trial, the jurors were found to have separated without the court's authorization, which led to concerns about the potential influence on their verdict. Specifically, it was reported that one juror mingled in public, another returned home unattended, and others participated in conversations about the case outside the presence of an officer. This situation raised questions regarding the integrity of the jury's deliberation process and whether the separation resulted in prejudice against the accused. The plaintiffs initiated a motion for a new trial due to these irregularities.	The plaintiffs claimed that the unauthorized separation of the jury during the murder trial compromised their ability to deliver an unbiased verdict. They argued that the external influences the jurors were subjected to could have adversely affected their judgment. As a consequence, they requested a new trial, emphasizing that the separation was not approved by the court and asserting that the circumstances necessitated reconsideration of the verdict.	The defense did not provide specific arguments against the plaintiffs’ claims in the provided description; instead, they seemed to rely on the notion that the jurors believed they were not influenced while separated. The defense's position leaned on the understanding that the jury's actions could have been the result of misunderstanding rather than malice. However, they ultimately did not succeed in maintaining the original verdict.

The case "Louis J. Daegling v. The Illinois Vault Company" was decided on July 2, 1889, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute originated in Cook County, Illinois, where Louis J. Daegling, the plaintiff, was contracted to perform excavation and masonry work for the rebuilding of a structure that had been destroyed by fire. Daegling claimed that he was entitled to additional payment for extra excavation work and sought damages for delays he experienced during the project. The case hinged on the authority of architects, Burnham & Root, who were responsible for determining whether the extra work was covered under the original contract. Daegling contended that the architects had not adequately satisfied their obligations, leaving decisions to a superintendent who denied his claim for additional pay. The court had to evaluate the conflicting evidence presented regarding the claims and the obligations outlined in the contract.	Louis J. Daegling argued that he was entitled to payment for extra excavation work and damages for delays that occurred during the rebuilding project. He claimed that the architects had not fulfilled their role in evaluating his claims, which impacted his ability to receive due compensation.
