Nicholas Blocks, the plaintiff, argued that he fulfilled the contractual obligations by completing the house, albeit later than the deadline due to Simon's requested changes. He claimed that there was an outstanding balance of $547.50 from the contract price and an additional $111.50 for extra work. Blocks sought a mechanic's lien against Simon's property as security for the unpaid amounts, asserting the right to have the premises sold to recover the owed funds.	Simon Simon, the defendant, denied the allegations of performance by Blocks, contending that the construction was not completed as stipulated in the contract. He provided evidence of various non-performance issues and claimed damages resulting from these breaches. Simon also argued that the mechanic's lien should not be granted, as the delays and terms of payment exceeded the statutory requirements.

In 1883, Frederick M. Ker was indicted for embezzlement and related charges in Cook County, Illinois, involving personal goods belonging to a co-partnership firm called Preston, Kean & Co. Ker had been captured in Peru without legal authority and forcibly transported back to the United States. The indictment consisted of four counts: embezzlement as a bailee, embezzlement as a clerk, larceny, and receiving stolen property. The court sustained a demurrer to Ker's plea questioning the court's jurisdiction due to alleged illegal capture, thereby compelling him to plead not guilty. During the trial, Ker was found guilty of embezzlement and sentenced to ten years in prison. He appealed the judgment, claiming the court lacked jurisdiction due to the irregularity of his arrest.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Ker embezzled substantial funds and securities belonging to Preston, Kean & Co. They contended that despite the procedural issues surrounding Ker's arrest, the indictment was valid and supported by sufficient evidence demonstrating Ker's guilt in misappropriating the firm's property.	Ker's defense focused on the argument that the court lacked jurisdiction due to the illegality of his arrest in Peru and subsequent extradition. He asserted that the President's extradition warrant was not properly executed since no request was made to the Peruvian authorities for his surrender, and therefore, any prosecution in Illinois was invalid. Additionally, he argued technicalities regarding the ownership of the property he was accused of embezzling and the claim of variance in the indictment.

The case, "Theodorus Davis, Jr. v. Tristram P. Hoxey," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1837, and it stems from a legal dispute in Macoupin County, Illinois. The case centers around an action for trespass de bonis asportatis (wrongful taking of goods). The plaintiff, Theodorus Davis, claimed that the defendant, Tristram P. Hoxey, had killed two hogs that he believed belonged to him. During the trial, witnesses provided testimony, including one who saw the defendant with the hogs and another who testified that Hoxey offered to pay Davis $22 for killing the hogs. However, despite the evidence suggesting that the hogs belonged to Davis, the jury was instructed by the court to find in favor of the defendant, which led to an exception being taken by the plaintiff. This raised serious questions about the court's decision as the jury should have evaluated the evidence presented to them instead of being guided to a verdict for Hoxey.	The plaintiff, Theodorus Davis, claimed that the defendant, Tristram P. Hoxey, unlawfully killed hogs that belonged to him. He argued that there was enough evidence presented during the trial to support his claim of trespass. Davis sought a ruling from the court that would hold Hoxey accountable for his actions and reverse the jury's instruction that favored the defendant.	The defendant, Tristram P. Hoxey, contended that he was not liable for the claim of trespass. He asserted that there was insufficient proof that the hogs belonged to Davis. Hoxey's defense relied on the court's instruction to the jury, suggesting that they should find in his favor due to the lack of clear evidence tying him to the wrongful act, which he argued justified the jury's decision.

On January 15, 1855, the Illinois General Assembly passed an act to authorize the drainage of wet lands in certain townships of Cook County, creating a corporate entity known as "The Drainage Commissioners." This body was empowered to construct ditches, embankments, roads, and to levy assessments for the maintenance of such constructions. In the case, George Hessler found himself involved in a legal dispute after the county court of Cook County ruled in favor of The Drainage Commissioners regarding a judgment against his land due to non-payment of an assessment levied for the drainage works. Hessler challenged the legitimacy of this assessment, taking his case to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the act infringing upon individuals' rights to taxation by a private corporation was unconstitutional.	George Hessler contended that the assessment imposed upon his land for drainage was effectively a tax levied by a private corporation, which the Illinois General Assembly had no constitutional authority to authorize. He cited a precedent case, Harward et al. v. The St. Clair and Monroe Levee and Drainage Company, arguing that the act authorized an inappropriate use of taxation powers by a private entity that did not properly represent the interests of the taxpayers.	The Drainage Commissioners contended that the act provided them with the necessary powers to levy assessments for the drainage improvements, asserting that the assessments were necessary for the public good. They argued that the constitution did allow for certain levies under the right of eminent domain, distinguishing their situation from that in the Harward case. The defendants maintained that their assessment of benefits was justified because it did not impose an unfair burden on the affected landowners.

The case of **Pittsburg, Cincinnati & St. Louis Railway Company v. Henry R. Thompson** took place in September 1870 in Illinois. The plaintiff, Henry R. Thompson, filed a lawsuit against the Pittsburg, Cincinnati & St. Louis Railway Company after suffering personal injuries while a passenger on one of the defendant's trains. The accident allegedly occurred due to the negligence of the railway company, specifically citing poor road conditions. Thompson claimed that the road-bed was defective, leading to a derailment of the train cars, which resulted in his injuries. A trial was held in the Circuit Court of Cook County, where the jury found in favor of Thompson, awarding him $5,000 in damages. The railway company subsequently appealed the jury’s verdict and the judgment entered against them, arguing against the instructions provided to the jury and the qualifications of negligence liability.	Thompson's main argument centered on the negligence of the railway company in maintaining safe and adequate road conditions for passengers. He contended that the injury was a direct result of the railway's failure to ensure a safe travel environment, asserting that he had shown a prima facie case of negligence which the railway company failed to rebut. Thompson sought damages for the injuries sustained during the incident, claiming that the railway did not exercise reasonable care in its operations.	The railway company's defense argued that the accident might have been caused by an internal defect in the train's axle, rather than any negligence on their part regarding road conditions. They contested the jury instructions that imposed an unreasonable standard of care, arguing that they should not be expected to provide absolute safety to passengers at an impractical cost. The defendant claimed the damages awarded were excessive and sought to have the verdict overturned or reduced.

The case of "The Russell and Allison Drainage District v. A. J. Benson et al." took place in Lawrence County, Illinois, with the petition filed on July 23, 1883. The Russell and Allison Drainage District was established to protect certain lands from overflow by constructing a levee along the Wabash River, following the regulations set forth by the Act of May 29, 1879. After the proper proceedings were completed, including the confirmation of an assessment roll for the drainage district on June 4, 1884, the landowners involved, including A. J. Benson, sought relief in May 1886, claiming that their lands had been erroneously assessed for benefits, which were not subject to overflow. They petitioned the county court to amend the assessment roll and discharge certain lands from the assessments. The county court granted their requests, leading to the appeal by the drainage district. The key legal issue revolved around whether the amended state laws allowed for petitions to amend assessments even after the initial statutory timeframe had expired.	The plaintiff, the Russell and Allison Drainage District, argued that the defendants' petitions to amend the assessment rolls and discharge their lands from assessments were barred by the statutory deadline established in the Drainage Act of 1883, which required petitions to be filed within one year of the assessment confirmation. The plaintiff claimed that the amendments introduced by the 1885 Act did not apply retroactively to previously confirmed assessments and sought to have the lower court's order reversed.	The defendants contended that the Act of 1885 revived their right to petition for the discharge of their lands from the assessments, asserting that the legislature intended for the new provisions to apply broadly to all prior assessments, regardless of prior statutes. They argued that interpreting the 1885 Act to limit or extinguish their rights would unjustly affect them and undermine the legislative intent.

In the case of Andrew Huls v. James Buntin, dated June 1868, the legal proceedings took place in Crawford County, Illinois. The action involved a dispute over the northeast quarter of Section 29, Township 6 North, Range 10 West. The plaintiff, Andrew Huls, filed an ejectment action claiming ownership of the land based on titles derived from Samuel Shaw, through his heirs. During the trial in April 1867, the plaintiff attempted to present a book from the county clerk's office as evidence to prove Shaw's entry and purchase of the land. However, the court sustained the defendant's objection to this evidence, ruling that if the plaintiff's original patent was lost, they should have obtained a duplicate from the general land office. Both Huls and the defendant, James Buntin, claimed title from Shaw but through different legal channels. The trial included various legal arguments concerning the validity of the documents and the powers of an administratrix in executing land sales. Notably, the legitimacy of the chain of title and the application of the statute of limitations were central to the dispute, particularly in how the court viewed the claims of the heirs of Shaw and their minority status at Shaw's death.	Andrew Huls, the plaintiff, argued that he was the rightful owner of the land in question, supported by deeds from Shaw's heirs. He maintained that since both parties derived title from the same source, he was not required to trace title beyond that common source. Huls sought to rebut the defendant's claims by demonstrating that rights concerning property ownership should take into account the minority status of the heirs at the time of their father's death, hence negating any application of the statute of limitations against him.	James Buntin, the defendant, contended that the deed from Shaw's administratrix to him was valid, despite her marital status at the time of execution. He argued that even if the original court proceedings had potential irregularities, the decree had color of title and was binding. Buntin also asserted that he had acquired title through possession of the land for more than twenty years and had paid taxes on it, thus invoking the statute of limitations to support his defense against Huls's claims.

In 1884, the case "John Peyton v. John D. Shaw et al." was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court following an action of trespass initiated by John Peyton against highway commissioners John D. Shaw, Hughes, and Harris, among others. The plaintiff claimed that the defendants had unlawfully broken and entered his property, causing damage by tearing down fences, removing gates, and cutting down trees. The events leading to the lawsuit stemmed from a disputed public highway that the defendants asserted had existed on Peyton's land for over twenty years based on public use. Peyton had fenced the area since around 1865–1869, and he argued that the area used to be uncultivated land. The defendants, tasked with maintaining the highway, entered to remove Peyton's barriers, claiming a right to do so. The primary point of analysis was whether a prescriptive right to the road existed, contingent upon twenty years of uninterrupted public use without objection from the landowner.	John Peyton argued that the defendants trespassed on his property without legal justification, asserting that he had maintained the fences, gates, and trees on his land for many years, preventing any established public highway claim. He contended that no public highway existed where the alleged trespass occurred, and he sought damages for the unauthorized removal of his property.	The defendants maintained that they acted in their capacity as highway commissioners and claimed a legal right based on the existence of a public highway that had been established by public use for over twenty years. They argued that Peyton had unlawfully obstructed this highway with his fences and gates, justifying their entry and actions to clear the path without causing unnecessary harm.

Charles Ballance filed a bill in chancery in March 1844 at the Peoria Circuit Court, seeking an injunction against Isaac Underhill and others to prevent them from taking possession of a part of the Southeast fractional quarter of section nine in township eight north, range eight east, which they had threatened to obtain through actions of ejectment. Ballance argued that the defendants had fraudulently secured their title that violated his rights, claiming he should have had a preemption right to the land under an 1838 Act of Congress. Despite his efforts to obtain the land through the proper legal channels, his application was denied because the land was already purportedly entered by John L. Bogardus under an earlier pre-emption law. The court proceedings revealed that Ballance had been in possession of the land prior to the law's passage and asserted that Bogardus had not actually settled on the property, which was known to the defendants. The circuit court dismissed Ballance's claims after they sustained the defenses presented by the defendants.	Ballance claimed entitlement to the land based on a preemption right under the Act of Congress of June 22, 1838, asserting to have complied with all requisites for obtaining said preemption. He accused the defendants of obtaining title through fraud and false affidavits, arguing that Bogardus was not an actual settler and did not reside on the land at the critical time. The main relief sought was for an injunction to stop the defendants from ejecting him and to secure ownership of the land.	The defendants, Underhill and Bigelow, defended against Ballance's claims by asserting a plea of former recovery, highlighting previous court decisions that dismissed Ballance's rights to the land. They contended that the land was legally entered under Bogardus' name and that Ballance's claims did not justify granting the requested injunction. They filed a demurrer against Ballance's bill, leading the court to agree that Ballance could not legally claim a preemption right under the relevant law due to the land being located within the incorporated town limits.

In the legal case of Chicago, Burlington & Quincy R. R. Co. v. Jones, decided on February 25, 1886, the events took place in Illinois. The plaintiff, Jones, brought a claim against the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company (the defendant) related to the death of his livestock, specifically stock that was killed by a train. The case revolved around whether negligence occurred on the part of the railroad, specifically focusing on the failure to ring the bell or sound the whistle before the train approached. The incident led to litigation as Jones sought compensation for his losses. The court examined the evidence surrounding the accident, including the conduct of the train crew and the circumstances leading to the death of the stock.	The plaintiff, Jones, claimed that the railroad company's negligence resulted in the death of his livestock. He argued that the failure to ring the bell or sound the whistle constituted a breach of duty by the railroad. Jones asserted that this neglect directly caused the accident and sought damages for the loss of his stock.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy R. R. Co., contended that merely not ringing the bell or sounding the whistle was insufficient to establish liability. The railroad argued that the evidence presented did not convincingly demonstrate a causal link between their actions and the accident that resulted in the death of the stock. They requested the court to reverse the decision made in favor of the plaintiff based on the insufficiency of the evidence.

In October 1865, in Chicago, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between James D. Bruner and Catharine Dyball regarding the possession of a sewing machine. Bruner initiated the case by suing for replevin, which is a legal remedy to recover personal property allegedly wrongfully taken. On the trial date, Bruner falsely informed Dyball that the case was decided against her, leading to a dismissal of the suit and prompting him to pay costs. Dyball subsequently filed a new replevin action in the Superior Court, claiming the sewing machine. The jury found in Dyball's favor, awarding her $117.75 after determining that Bruner had wrongfully obtained the machine. The crux of the case revolved around whether Dyball needed to prove she made a demand for the property before filing suit and whether Bruner's actions constituted a conversion of the property.	Catharine Dyball claimed that James D. Bruner wrongfully assumed ownership of her sewing machine without proper demand. She pursued a writ of replevin and sought damages for the alleged conversion of her property. Dyball argued that Bruner had no rightful claim to the sewing machine and that his actions, including misleading her about the case's outcome, warranted legal restitution.	James D. Bruner contended that Dyball failed to prove a proper legal demand for the return of the sewing machine, which he claimed should preclude her recovery in replevin. He asserted that Dyball could only retain her right to the property through a bond executed under the replevin statute, implying that she had no viable legal claim once he dismissed the original suit. Bruner's position relied on technicalities related to the replevin process and the assertion of ownership.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois v. Alden Rhodes" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1853. It arose from a dispute related to property taxation in Greene County, Illinois. Alden Rhodes sold a tract of land to a buyer named Walker for $1,400, receiving a partial payment of $200 and promissory notes for the remaining balance to be paid in annual installments. Walker entered possession of the land and listed it for taxation for the year 1853. However, an assessment was made against Rhodes, the seller, for $1,000 based on the notes he received from Walker. Rhodes contested this assessment in the county court, arguing that the notes were not taxable, and the court agreed, setting aside the assessment. Subsequently, the county clerk, on behalf of the auditor, sought to reverse this decision through the Illinois Supreme Court, leading to this appeal. The case examined whether Rhodes could be assessed for the notes given that Walker had already listed the property for tax purposes, and it required interpretation of the state tax laws regarding property and credits.	The plaintiff, The People of the State of Illinois, claimed that Alden Rhodes was properly assessed for the notes he held against Walker, arguing that these notes constituted taxable credits. The state contended that according to the Illinois tax laws, all property, including financial credits, is subject to taxation, regardless of whether the property had been converted or is currently possessed. The appeal was based on the assertion that the lower court's ruling, which set aside the assessment, was in error.	Alden Rhodes, the defendant, argued that the notes he held were not subject to taxation because they represented a claim for payment that was not literally tangible property. He maintained that since the land had already been listed and taxed under Walker's name, he should not be assessed for the same property in the form of notes. Rhodes' request involved affirming the county court's decision to void the assessment against him.

In 1883, Horace P. Fletcher, a merchant in San Francisco, was dealing in Japanese goods under the business name Ichi Ban. He owed his brother, Isaac D. Fletcher, over $30,000, which was invested in the business. Eldred O. Williams from Boston entered the picture when he agreed to invest $20,000 in the Ichi Ban business on October 18, 1883, under conditions detailed in a formal agreement with Horace. This investment was to be managed by Horace Fletcher, who was to credit Williams with the earnings proportionally and allow him to withdraw a predefined amount quarterly. Williams later testified that he believed his investment had priority over Isaac's claims. The agreement of June 12, 1884, recognized Isaac's investments and established him as having priority for repayment over Williams regarding funds loaned to Horace. However, ambiguities existed about what Horace disclosed to Williams about his existing debts to Isaac. The case arose over who had the rightful claim to funds from the liquidation of a failed corporation, which involved both parties and ultimately led to the contest in court.	The plaintiffs, represented by Williams, argued that their investment in Horace Fletcher’s business entitled them to earn profits and that they should have priority over any debts Horace owed to Isaac Fletcher. They contended that the agreements made between the parties did not adequately protect Isaac's claims to the extent that it should deny Williams his rightful returns. They sought repayment and established claims based on their interpretation of the agreements.	The defendant, Isaac D. Fletcher, countered that under the agreements, he had priority over Williams concerning any funds related to the investments. He argued that Williams wasn't a partner in the business, and thus did not have a claim to the profits generated by it. Isaac maintained that any investments made by him to Horace predated Williams' entry into the business relationship, and thus the tripartite agreement granted him the right to repayment before Williams' claims could be addressed.

In the spring of 1874, William Johnson was elected as the collector for the township of Viola in Lee County, Illinois. Following his election, on December 18, 1874, the county clerk sent him a blank bond that he needed to execute along with sureties for approval. Johnson obtained surety signatures but when presented to the supervisor and town clerk for approval on December 30, 1874, they declined to approve the bond, citing issues with the sureties' qualifications and claiming it was presented late. On January 2, 1875, the county clerk notified Johnson of the tax amount he was supposed to collect, prompting him to prepare a new bond which he presented on January 5, 1875. However, by that time, the township board had already appointed another collector, asserting that Johnson’s application was submitted after the deadline for bond filing had expired. Johnson subsequently filed a petition for a mandamus to compel approval of his bond. The trial court found in his favor, granting the writ, leading to the appeal by the respondent.	The plaintiff, William Johnson, argued that the supervisor had a duty to approve his bond, as he had complied with the necessary requirements. He maintained that the board's refusal to approve his bond and subsequent appointment of another collector was improper. Johnson sought a mandamus to compel the approval of his bond, insisting that he had served within the statutory timeframe for bond submission, and noted that the sureties he provided were solvent and satisfactory.	The defendant, represented by the township board and supervisor, countered Johnson’s claims by asserting that he had failed to present a sufficient bond within the mandated timeframe and that two different bonds had been submitted for approval, creating ambiguity. They contended that the board acted within its rights in declining to approve Johnson's bonds due to procedural irregularities and the late submission of his second bond after another collector had been appointed.

Christian Linck filed a legal case against the City of Litchfield in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision rendered on January 21, 1889. The case stems from a previous suit where Linck had successfully recovered costs from the City, amounting to sixty-four dollars and fifty cents. Linck sought to recover the costs from this earlier judgment, claiming that not only should he receive the awarded amount, but also interest on that judgment. At the original trial in the Circuit Court of Montgomery County, presided over by Judge J. A. Creighton, the court denied Linck’s request for interest on the costs. This led Linck to appeal the decision on the grounds that a judgment for costs should indeed accrue interest under Illinois law, as stipulated in Section 3, Chapter 74 of the Revised Statutes.	Linck's primary argument centered on his entitlement to interest on the costs awarded to him in the previous case against the City of Litchfield. He contended that, according to Illinois law, any judgment, including one for costs, should draw interest at a rate of six percent per annum from the date of the judgment until it is satisfied. He filed the appeal after the Circuit Court ruled against him, claiming that the refusal to allow interest was erroneous.	The City of Litchfield, represented by attorneys Joseph E. Paden and George L. Zink, did not appear to provide a strong defense against the claim for interest, as the primary contention was based on statutory interpretation of whether a judgment for costs qualifies for interest under the relevant legal provisions. The defense largely relied on the Circuit Court's decision, which held that the judgment for costs did not accrue interest, arguing against Linck’s interpretation of the statute.

On May 10, 1861, in Chicago, Illinois, a riot occurred involving defendants Barbay Schramm, Louis Schramm, and Benedict Schramm, who were later charged with the offense after allegedly beating one Wolf Schaffer. Barbara Schramm (impleaded as Barbay Schramm) filed a plea of misnomer, claiming her legal name was Barbara Schramm, not Barbay, and that she had never been known by the latter name. The prosecution countered that she was equally known by both names. The trial proceeded with the same jury addressing both the plea of misnomer and the not guilty pleas of the other defendants. Ultimately, the jury found Barbara Schramm and Benedict Schramm guilty while acquitting Louis Schramm. Barbara Schramm contended that her plea of misnomer had not been resolved before her sentencing.	The plaintiff, Barbara Schramm, argued that she was improperly convicted as she was known solely by her true name, Barbara Schramm, and never by the name Barbay. She contended that since her plea of misnomer was pending and had not been resolved, she should not have been found guilty. Her legal request sought reversal of the guilty verdict and the judgment against her.	The defendants in response claimed that both the plea of misnomer and the not guilty plea could be tried by the same jury without the need for separate trials. They argued that the jury's overall guilty verdict covered both issues. The prosecution maintained that because Barbara was known by both names, the jury had the right to render a verdict without needing to address the plea of misnomer separately.

In February 1879, Emily H. Petty, the appellee, owned a house and lot in Chicago, which was encumbered with a $1500 debt. On February 12, she sold the property to John M. Secrist, who arranged for the deed to be made to his son, Oscar H. Secrist. In exchange, Petty received two promissory notes worth $200 each, paid $14 in cash, and agreed to pay $100 to Charles F. Swigart to have him surrender four promissory notes totaling $1900, which were secured by a mortgage on a different property in Indiana. Shortly after this transaction, Secrist exchanged the Chicago property with George W. Lackey for hotel furniture, with Lackey acting on behalf of his wife, Mary G. Lackey. On March 14, 1879, Petty filed a lawsuit against the Secrists, Swigart, and Lackey, claiming the notes and mortgage were worthless and asserting the transaction was the result of a fraudulent conspiracy by the defendants. An amendment later made Mary G. Lackey a party to the suit. Following a court hearing, the evidence indicated that the trial court found the allegations true and ruled in favor of Petty, prompting the current appeal to reverse that decree.	Emily H. Petty claimed that the promissory notes and mortgage she received for the house were worthless and asserted that the entire transaction was a result of a fraudulent conspiracy involving John M. Secrist, George W. Lackey, and others. She sought to have the court declare the transaction void and to regain her property.	The defendants, including John M. Secrist and Mary G. Lackey, contended that the trial court's ruling was erroneous, particularly the decision to strike a certificate of evidence from the files without formal proofs being presented. They argued that the judge's knowledge of his own official acts sufficed as evidence for the legal proceedings and that the evidence supporting the trial court’s findings was not preserved, thus challenging the legitimacy of the decree.

Josiah Mason, a widower residing in Greene County, Illinois, faced significant debt, amounting to approximately $7,000, while owning various parcels of land and personal property. In February 1879, he conveyed a 240-acre farm to his daughter, Eliza Osborne, and her husband, under a deed that stated a consideration of $7,000. However, the real considerations included payments for past services and an agreement for Eliza to care for Mason. Shortly after, the Osbornes sold the property to Rutherford M. Osborne, who was unaware of any insolvency issues. The crux of the case involved whether these transactions were fraudulent against Mason’s creditors since the properties were encumbered by debt. A lower court declared the deeds void, leading the Osbornes to appeal, arguing that the evidence did not support claims of fraud.	The plaintiffs were judgment creditors of Josiah Mason who sought to annul two deeds as fraudulent transfers meant to hinder their ability to collect debts. They argued that the conveyances to Eliza Osborne and subsequently to Rutherford M. Osborne were made while Mason was insolvent and that the transactions were structured to defraud creditors by disguising the true financial situation.	The defendants contended that they were bona fide purchasers who had no knowledge of Mason's financial difficulties or any fraudulent intent behind the transactions. They argued that the deeds were valid as between the parties involved, asserting that no credible evidence was presented to suggest that fraud had occurred. Furthermore, they stated that any rumor or suspicion about Mason's debts was too vague to impose a duty of inquiry on them as purchasers.

Nelson Morris filed a legal case against Lawrence Litchfield and others, which was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court. The case was decided on January 6, 1886, following a previous appeal that led to a reversal of an earlier judgment and an order for a new trial. The new trial included additional testimony presented by the plaintiffs, which was deemed potentially sufficient to support a favorable verdict for them. The credibility of the witnesses was emphasized as a critical aspect determined by the jury, and appellate courts generally refrain from interfering with the jury's verdict. The case underscores the importance of witness credibility and the jury's role in adjudicating such matters.	The plaintiff, Nelson Morris, asserted that due to new and further testimony introduced during the second trial, there was enough credible evidence to support a verdict in his favor. He sought legal recognition of his claims and the corresponding enforcement of the jury's decision based upon the evidence presented.	The defendants, led by Lawrence Litchfield, contended against the claims made by Morris, likely arguing the insufficiency or unreliability of the new evidence presented. Although specific defenses were not detailed in the description, they aimed to undermine the plaintiffs' case and sought to have the verdict overturned or the claims dismissed.

Isaac McClelland, the appellant, entered into a special contract with James Snider, the appellee, in which Snider was to quarry 700 yards of stone and deliver it to McClelland for the construction of certain buildings for the Illinois Central Railroad Company. The agreed remuneration was $1.10 per yard, with the stone intended to be measured in the walls of the buildings. However, the contract faced issues as Snider allegedly failed to deliver the full amount, providing only a portion of the stone, which was reportedly diverted for other uses such as wells and culverts. The case was set in Marion Circuit Court in May 1856, where the jury found against Snider's compliance with the terms of the contract, leading McClelland to claim damages as a result. The appeal arises from the trial court’s instructions to the jury that were challenged by the defendant.	McClelland argued that Snider breached the contract by not delivering the full 700 yards of stone as agreed. He claimed that he should be compensated for the reasonable value of the stone delivered, regardless of the contract price, and that Snider's failure to deliver as per the contract led to significant damages.	Snider defended against the claims by asserting that the instructions provided to the jury were erroneous. He contended that the manner of measuring the stone was not critical, and that any deviation in how the stone was used did not constitute a breach of the contract. Snider's defense emphasized that the compensation should adhere strictly to the contract terms, and thus he argued for a ruling against McClelland's claim for excessive compensation.

The case "Stephen D. Greer et al v. James Walker" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1866. The dispute originates from the estate of Moses Bedell, who died leaving a will that appointed his wife, Elizabeth Bedell, as executrix. His will stipulated that she should collect debts and distribute assets among heirs, which included giving her one-third of the real estate during her lifetime and the remainder to the children. A debtor named James Laws owed the estate $1,184, and through an arrangement, the executrix received an equivalent mortgage from James Mewhall to settle part of this debt. Mewhall transferred several parcels of real estate to Elizabeth as part of this agreement. Ms. Bedell then sold these properties to Joshua Bedell and subsequently conveyed them further, leading to the current dispute. The plaintiffs argue that the lands in question should be treated as a trust fund for the heirs, while the defendant claims rightful ownership due to established transactions. The case revolves around the legal authority of the executrix regarding the properties received as part of the estate's debt recovery and the extent to which these properties can be deemed to be held in trust for the heirs.	The plaintiffs argue that the properties purchased with funds due to the estate became a trust held by Elizabeth Bedell for the benefit of the heirs. They contend that the defendant, having purchased the land, either had notice of the trust arrangement or circumstances that would have led to such knowledge. They seek a judgment that recognizes their ownership rights to the land, maintaining that it should be utilized to satisfy the estate's debts or returned to the heirs.	The defendant contends that Elizabeth Bedell rightfully acquired the properties as a part of settling the debts owed to the estate. He argues that she acted within her legal authority as executrix to sell the land and that her actions were fair and uninfluenced by fraud. Furthermore, the defendant asserts that the plaintiffs have no legitimate claim to the properties since the fair value was exchanged in transactions and Ms. Bedell accounted for her actions appropriately in her dealings with the estate.

In January 1868, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed the case of Harmon Myer et al. v. William McDougal, involving a dispute over a piece of land previously owned by Robert Hayden, who passed away in November 1856. Upon his death, Robert Hayden had debts and had devised the land to his daughter, Elizabeth Hayden. She sold the land to Barney M. Hayden, who later became the administrator of Robert’s estate. Barney paid $218 to redeem the land from a prior execution sale, and issued promissory notes for the remaining balance secured by a mortgage on the property. However, the mortgage was improperly recorded as it failed to include the county details. Afterward, Barney filed a claim against Robert's estate, which was allowed, leading to a decree for the sale of the property to satisfy the estate's debts. The land was eventually sold at an administrator's sale to the plaintiffs, Myer and Bracken. They claimed to have acquired the title free of liens, while McDougal, the appellee, argued he held a superior lien due to the earlier mortgage.	The plaintiffs, Harmon Myer and Bracken, contended that they acquired paramount title to the property through a legitimate sale conducted by the estate's administrator. They denied any knowledge of the mortgage held by McDougal and asserted that the administrator's sale extinguished any claims to the property held by previous parties.	The defendant, William McDougal, maintained that his mortgage constituted a superior lien on the property, asserting that the prior claims against the estate were enforceable. He argued that the plaintiffs’ interests were subject to this lien, and claimed that the sale conducted by the administrator was executed improperly, as it did not consider the existence of his valid mortgage.

In January 1874, Mary A. Alexander filed a lawsuit against the President and Trustees of the Town of Mt. Sterling, Illinois, claiming negligence regarding the construction and maintenance of a sidewalk. The case arose after Alexander sustained injuries while walking on the defective sidewalk. The court proceedings revealed that the sidewalk, made of rough planks and laid on stringers, had been defectively constructed and remained in a hazardous condition for an extended period. During the trial, the jury found the municipal corporation not guilty, leading to a judgment against the plaintiff for costs. Alexander then sought to reverse this judgment, arguing that the jury was improperly instructed and that the evidence demonstrated the town's negligence.	Alexander claimed that the Town of Mt. Sterling was negligent in both the initial construction and ongoing maintenance of the sidewalk, which she argued resulted in her injuries. She insisted that the local authorities should have known about the unsafe condition of the sidewalk since they were responsible for its original construction and were required to ensure its safety. Alexander requested damages for the injuries sustained due to the town's negligence.	The Town of Mt. Sterling defended itself by arguing it had regularly inspected and maintained the sidewalk, asserting that it had neither knowledge nor reason to suspect any existing defects at the time of the accident. The defendant contended that the jury should find in their favor based on the claim that they had conducted necessary examinations and repairs shortly before the incident. They sought to demonstrate that they fulfilled their obligation to maintain the sidewalk safely.

Joseph McKee filed a slander case against Darius Ingalls in December 1842 in Illinois. The case revolved around allegations made by Ingalls, who reportedly stated that McKee was a “damned thief” and implied that if McKee had money, he must have stolen it. This exchange of words was the basis of McKee's slander claim, asserting that such statements were damaging to his reputation. The case was heard at the October term of the court before Judge Samuel D. Lockwood. The jury found in favor of Ingalls, leading McKee to file a motion for a new trial, arguing that the court misdirected the jury and that the verdict was against the law and evidence presented. The court ultimately ruled that the words spoken were not actionable if they were expressed without the intent to impute a felony or were spoken in “heat and passion.”	McKee's main argument centered on the claim that Ingalls' words were slanderous and damaging to his reputation. He contended that by calling him a thief without proper justification, Ingalls had committed slander, which presumptively implies malice. McKee sought damages for the harm done to his reputation and requested a new trial based on alleged misdirection by the court and improper jury instructions.	Ingalls defended against the allegations by arguing that his statements were not meant to impute felony; he claimed they were said in a moment of passion and did not constitute actionable slander. He asserted that the words used could be interpreted in a way that did not necessarily imply that McKee had committed theft. Therefore, he requested that the jury find in his favor, emphasizing that the lack of intent to cause harm negated any liability for slander.

In 1885, a tragic incident occurred at a barn located on Michigan Avenue in Chicago, owned by Aaron C. Goodman, who resided in Hartford, Connecticut. The barn was managed by real estate agents Lyman Baird and Francis Bradley, who were responsible for renting and maintaining the property during 1884 and 1885. The barn’s large carriage door was reportedly in a problematic state, and Baird and Bradley had verbally agreed to repair it when renting it out to Emma E. Wheeler. Despite this agreement, the necessary repairs were not made. On June 12, 1885, Joseph Garnett, an expressman, was delivering kindling when the unsecured door fell, severely injuring him; he died the following day. The case arose from the alleged negligence of Baird and Bradley in failing to maintain a safe environment in the barn. Evidence presented during the trial indicated that the agents had complete control of the property and thus bore responsibility for ensuring its safety. The previous leases stipulated that tenants were to maintain the property, but the agents’ failure to take action to repair the barn door played a critical role in the events leading to Garnett’s death.	The plaintiffs, represented by Joseph Garnett’s estate, claimed that the negligence of Lyman Baird and Francis Bradley led to Garnett’s death. They asserted that the agents failed to fulfill their responsibility to maintain the premises in a safe condition as agents of the property owner. The plaintiffs sought damages for the wrongful death of Garnett, arguing that the agents had knowledge of the dangers posed by the unstable barn door and disregarded their duty to repair it, thereby creating a hazardous environment.	The defendants, Baird and Bradley, contended that they were merely acting as agents for the property owner and were not liable for Garnett’s death. They argued that the tenants were responsible for maintaining the premises under the lease agreements and that any negligence attributed to them should not extend to third parties. Furthermore, they claimed that their actions did not constitute a breach of duty towards Garnett, as they were only obligated to fulfill their contract with Goodman, the property owner.

Jennie C. Vallette filed a legal case against John T. Perie and others in the Illinois Appellate Court in 1887. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, overseen by Judge John P. Altgeld. The proceedings took place following a previous judgment that the plaintiff contended was excessive. The appellate court was tasked with reviewing the circumstances surrounding the claims made by Vallette against Perie and the other defendants. Details regarding the specific event that led to the lawsuit are not provided in the description, but it can be inferred that it involved a financial judgment that the plaintiff sought to challenge.	The plaintiff, Jennie C. Vallette, argued that the original judgment rendered against her was excessive. She requested the appellate court to reconsider the amount and reduce the judgment to a more reasonable figure. Her claims were predicated on the notion that the previous ruling did not align with legal standards or the facts of the case.	The defendants, represented by attorneys H. C. Bennett and W. A. Phelps, contended that the original judgment should stand as issued. They likely argued that the amount was justified based on the circumstances leading to the case. Their request was for the court to uphold the initial decision made by the lower court without alteration.

John Bennett was indicted in December 1854 at the Menard Circuit Court for selling whiskey to John Duff in quantities less than one gallon without the required grocery license. The case stemmed from events that alleged sales made by Bennett over the preceding eighteen months, during which Duff testified that he bought whiskey from Bennett multiple times, but only received it in smaller amounts as he needed them. After the court refused Bennett’s motion to quash the indictment and he pleaded not guilty, the case went to jury trial. The jury found Bennett guilty based on the court's instructions that emphasized the importance of selling quantities less than one gallon without a license. Bennett later filed a motion disputing the judgment, which the court denied. Ultimately, it was held that the legislative changes made to the applicable laws before the indictment made such sales punishable, but procedural errors concerning the timeline of validity of the criminal code also emerged. Critical to the outcome was the definition of when the law was applicable concerning prior sales, leading to further resolution in the higher court regarding the legality of the indictment and proceedings.	The plaintiff, John Bennett, claimed that the indictment against him was invalid. He argued that the legal framework under which the prosecution was initiated had been incorrectly applied, as section 132 of the criminal code was not in effect for a significant period prior to the indictment. Thus, he contended that any sales he made before the legislative changes could not be used as a basis for conviction under the current law, and therefore, should not be penalized for those sales.	The defendants, represented by the People, maintained that the indictment was valid based on the laws revived in 1853, which allowed for penalties on sales of liquor less than one gallon without the necessary license. They contended that Bennett engaged in the sale of spirituous liquor in violation of these laws and sought to uphold the conviction and the imposed fine as appropriate under the then-applicable statutes.

Christian Hepp filed a case against Adam Jaenemann, which was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court. The last trial took place during the January term of 1887 in Monroe County, Illinois, presided over by Judge William Erd. This case had previously been tried in the Circuit Court on two separate occasions. During the latest trial, a jury rendered a verdict in favor of the defendant, Adam Jaenemann. Following this verdict, Christian Hepp's attorney filed a motion for a new trial, which was denied by the court. The case abstract submitted did not meet the court's requirements for reviewing the evidence or the jury's instructions, leading the court to refuse to take up these issues for consideration. As a result, the judgment from the previous trial was upheld.	The plaintiff, Christian Hepp, argued against the verdict in favor of the defendant, claiming there were errors in the trial process regarding jury instructions and the handling of evidence. He sought to overturn the verdict and requested a new trial based on these alleged mistakes.	Adam Jaenemann, the defendant, maintained that the jury's verdict was correct and that the trial had been conducted properly. His legal team argued against the plaintiff's claims of errors, asserting that there was no basis for a new trial and requested the court to affirm the original judgment.

In 1886, in the Village of Desplaines, Illinois, Benjamin Poyer was involved in a legal dispute concerning the rental of skiffs for hire on the Desplaines River. The village had established an ordinance requiring individuals to obtain a license to hire out boats, including skiffs, within its limits. Poyer, a resident of the village, admitted to renting a skiff without having obtained the necessary license from the village authorities. The ordinance had been passed on June 7, 1886, and stipulated that violators could face fines ranging from $15 to $25 for each offense. After being found guilty of breaching this ordinance in a trial held by a police magistrate and subsequently in the Criminal Court of Cook County, Poyer appealed the decision, resulting in the case being brought before the Illinois Appellate Court.	The Village of Desplaines, as the plaintiff, argued that Poyer breached the village's ordinance by renting skiffs without a license. They claimed the ordinance was legitimate and enforceable under their charter, emphasizing that its provisions were reasonable and authorized the village to require licenses for the operation of watercraft within its jurisdiction. The village sought to uphold the fine imposed on Poyer for his violation of the ordinance.	Poyer, the defendant, contended that the ordinance was invalid on the grounds that the village lacked the statutory power to pass it. He argued that the ordinance was unreasonable and questioned the village's authority to regulate the use of skiffs on the Desplaines River, which did not have a formal harbor. Poyer's defense included the assertion that the licensing requirements and associated fees were excessive and not justifiable.

The case of B. M. Shaffner v. P. B. S. Pinchback was adjudicated on March 13, 1889, in Cook County, Illinois. The parties involved were B. M. Shaffner, the appellant, and P. B. S. Pinchback, the appellee. B. M. Shaffner advanced $1,000 to P. B. S. Pinchback for the purpose of wagering on horse races. The specific events surrounding the case involved claims regarding the nature of the advance; whether it constituted a loan or was part of a joint account intended for betting. The legal implications of such advances in gambling scenarios were at the heart of the case. The Circuit Court of Cook County, led by Judge Julius S. Grinnell, had to determine the recoverability of the funds under Illinois law, particularly in a context involving gaming, which at the time had restrictions on the enforceability of contracts arising from gambling activities.	The plaintiff, B. M. Shaffner, claimed that he should be able to recover the $1,000 advanced to Pinchback for betting on horse races. Shaffner argued that regardless of the outcome of the bets, whether Pinchback won or lost, he should be repaid. Shaffner's legal team cited precedents that supported recovery of funds in such situations under Illinois statutes governing gaming transactions.	The defendant, P. B. S. Pinchback, admitted to receiving the $1,000 but contended that the nature of the transaction was rooted in illegal gaming. Pinchback argued that money advanced for wagering on horse races could not be recovered as it fell into the category of gambling. He maintained that any claims regarding the money should not be enforceable under the law, thus seeking dismissal of the case based on these premises.

Frank Mehlsack was injured while riding on the steps of a passenger train owned by the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company. The incident occurred in Cook County, Illinois, leading to a legal dispute that reached the Illinois Appellate Court. Mehlsack claimed that the railroad was liable for his injuries as he had intended to pay for his fare but had been unable to do so due to the crowded conditions on the train. The railroad company contended that Mehlsack had attempted to ride the train without paying, alleging that he did not establish the legal relation of passenger due to his actions. The case turned on the question of whether he was a passenger and if he exercised ordinary care for his safety while standing on the train's platform.	Mehlsack argued that he should be regarded as a passenger because he was willing to pay his fare. He contended that the overcrowding of the car forced him to stand on the steps, which contributed to his injuries. Mehlsack sought damages for the injuries sustained due to the negligence of the railroad company, claiming that the company had an obligation to ensure passenger safety, regardless of whether he had an opportunity to pay his fare.	The railroad company argued that Mehlsack was not a legitimate passenger because he jumped onto the train with the intent to steal a ride, indicating he did not intend to pay for his fare. They maintained that even if he was a passenger, his lack of ordinary care in standing on the steps led to his injuries. The company requested that the court reverse the jury's verdict, claiming that it was against the weight of the evidence presented and arguing procedural errors related to the plaintiff's counsel's role during the trial.

The case titled "Henry M. Shepard, Admr., etc. v. The National Bank of Lawrence County, Pa." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1873. The underlying dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving the estate of Charles W. Bicketson, who had passed away. After Bicketson's death, Henry M. Shepard was appointed as the administrator de bonis non of the estate, following the revocation of previous letters of administration granted to another individual, B. F. Quimby. A claim was filed against Bicketson's estate by the National Bank of Lawrence County, which was only presented after the statutory two-year period for such submissions had expired. The National Bank sought to recover $15,244.43 from the estate based on assets discovered after this two-year limit. The case went to the Circuit Court, which ruled in favor of the claimant, allowing for recovery from the subsequently discovered assets of the estate, resulting in an appeal by the administrator.	The National Bank of Lawrence County argued that despite the claim being filed after the two-year limit established by law, they were entitled to recover funds from the estate based on assets found after that period. They asserted that the statute allowed creditors to obtain satisfaction from any property belonging to the estate that had not been inventoried within the specified two years, regardless of whether the new property was discovered before or after the claim was filed.	Henry M. Shepard, the administrator, contended that the two-year statute of limitations barred the claim because it was not presented within the required timeframe. He maintained that the law should prevent the recovery of any claims filed after the two-year period unless specific conditions were met. Moreover, he argued that the court's earlier rulings should not apply to this case, emphasizing that the law concerning subsequently discovered assets was not unequivocally in favor of the plaintiff's interpretation.

Caroline Vogt v. C. L. Buschman et al. is a legal case that took place in June 1872 in Illinois. The case arose from a dispute over property that C. L. Buschman and others claimed after obtaining a judgment against Caroline Vogt's husband. Following this judgment, they issued an execution and levied on property that Vogt claimed as her separate property. The Circuit Court of Washington County ruled in favor of Vogt, granting her one-third of the levied property, while awarding the remaining two-thirds to the plaintiffs in the execution. Unsatisfied with this outcome, Vogt appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that she should retain full ownership of the property in question.	Caroline Vogt, as the plaintiff, contended that the property levied by C. L. Buschman and others was her separate property, not subject to the execution stemming from her husband's judgment. She sought a reversal of the Circuit Court's decision, which had allocated only one-third of the property to her and two-thirds to the defendants. Vogt's primary argument centered on asserting her rights to the full ownership of the property.	The defendants, C. L. Buschman et al., maintained that their legal claim to the property was valid due to the execution issued based on the judgment against Vogt's husband. They argued that the Circuit Court's ruling was justified and supported by the evidence presented. The defendants requested the Supreme Court to uphold the lower court's decision that divided the property ownership as it had been ruled.

The case, The President and Trustees of the Town of Mechanicsburg v. Rice R. Meredith, was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1870. The incident occurred when the plaintiff, Rice R. Meredith, sustained injuries due to a defective bridge located within the corporate limits of Mechanicsburg, Illinois. The case was heard in the Circuit Court of Sangamon County, presided over by Judge Benjamin S. Edwards. The plaintiff alleged that the town, through its corporate powers, had the responsibility to maintain the bridge and roads but failed to do so, leading to the accident. The plaintiff argued that the town had the power to levy taxes for repairs and to require labor from male inhabitants for road maintenance. The court was tasked with determining whether the town had neglected its duty to keep the bridge and surrounding areas safe for passage.	The plaintiff claimed that the town of Mechanicsburg had a legal obligation to keep the bridge in repair due to the powers conferred to them as a municipal corporation. He argued that the town had failed to fulfill this duty, leading to his injuries. The plaintiff requested damages for the injuries sustained as a direct result of the town's negligence in maintaining the bridge.	The town of Mechanicsburg, as the defendant, argued that the declaration filed by the plaintiff was insufficient as it did not adequately demonstrate that they had the duty or power to repair the bridge at the time of the accident. They claimed that the highway commissioners had performed repair duties leading up to the incident, suggesting that the town had effectively abandoned its responsibility. The defendant sought a dismissal of the case based on these grounds and the failure of the plaintiff to show that he exercised due caution when using the bridge.

The case "The Belleville and Illinoistown Railroad Company v. Richard A. Gregory and Wipe" took place in 1853 in St. Clair County, Illinois. The railroad company, established under a legislative charter to construct a railroad from Belleville to Illinoistown, sought to extend its operations. Plaintiffs Gregory and his wife accused the railroad company of trespassing on their land, allegedly entering and making embankments without their consent. The railroad company defended itself by citing the grant from the legislature, which allowed it to acquire land needed for the railroad by appointing commissioners to assess damages. Following court proceedings, the circuit court sustained the plaintiffs' demurrer, leading to a judgment against the railroad company for damages. The company subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, contesting the decision of the lower court.	The plaintiffs, Gregory and his wife, claimed that the railroad company unlawfully trespassed on their property by entering and making alterations without permission. They sought legal relief and damages for this unauthorized occupation of their land.	The railroad company contended that it had the legal right to enter the land based on a legislative grant that authorized the acquisition of necessary land for its railroad operations. They argued that commissioners were appointed under the law to determine the damages, and their attempt to enter the property was lawful following a tender of the assessed damages, which was ultimately rejected by the plaintiffs.

Abner Wheeler and Eliza Wheeler were married in 1839 in Illinois. They have seven children, ranging from one to fourteen years old. Abner abandoned Eliza and their children, moving to another state with another woman, with whom he was living in an adulterous relationship. He took most of his personal property and left behind certain lands in Illinois. Eliza filed a bill in equity seeking a divorce, alimony, and custody of their children. The case was heard in the Hamilton Circuit Court in October 1854, where the court found the case in favor of Eliza after hearing evidence, although the evidence was not preserved in the record. The court decreed the dissolution of the marriage, awarded custody of the children to Eliza, and granted her the lands mentioned in the bill for alimony. Abner did not appear to contest the claims.	Eliza Wheeler, the plaintiff, claimed that her husband Abner Wheeler had abandoned her and their children. She sought a divorce, requesting custody of their children and alimony in the form of specified lands that Abner owned. She argued for her rights under the grounds of abandonment and hoped for a ruling that would provide her with financial support for herself and her children.	Abner Wheeler, the defendant, argued against the decree issued by the circuit court on two grounds: first, he contended that the decree was rendered without sufficient evidence. Second, he claimed that the court erroneously decreed that his lands be granted to Eliza. However, his absence from court meant these defenses were not substantiated with arguments or evidence.

Nathaniel P. Wilder and Gurdon S. Hubbard were appellants in a legal case against The City of Chicago, which was decided in April 1861 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case revolved around a dispute involving a city collector and his sureties. The key issue in the case was whether the city had the authority to appoint additional collectors beyond the one elected by the populace. The court previously decided in a related case (Russell et al. v. The City of Chicago) that the Common Council of Chicago indeed had such power, allowing for the appointment of collectors who would have full rights and responsibilities in collecting dues. The specific context involved a collector attempting to withhold money owed to the city by claiming he was due commissions on special assessments he collected. The court ruled that regardless of the collector's claims, he was obligated to remit all collected funds to the city treasury without any retention. The judgment confirmed the responsibilities laid out in the previous ruling about the collector’s duties during his term.	The plaintiffs, Nathaniel P. Wilder and Gurdon S. Hubbard, contended that the city collector, Russell, had improperly withheld funds collected on behalf of the city. They argued that the collector was bound by ordinance to pay the collected amounts into the city treasury promptly and could not retain any fees or commissions for his personal use. The plaintiffs sought a judgment to collect the funds due to the city, asserting the city’s entitlement to the full amount collected by the collector.	The defendant, Russell, claimed a right to retain a portion of the collected funds, arguing that the city owed him commissions on the special assessments he collected and was therefore indebted to him in a larger sum. This argument was framed as a set-off against the city’s claims. However, the court deemed this defense untenable, emphasizing that the collector had no legal right to hold onto any collected funds due to the statutory obligation to pay them into the city treasury as they were collected.

The case, "The Merchants’ National Bank v. Augustus W. Ritzinger et al.," was adjudicated on November 13, 1886, in Illinois. It revolves around a financial dispute involving a banking instrument. The Merchants’ National Bank filed a case against Augustus W. Ritzinger and others concerning a check. The instrument in question was dated July 15, 1884, drawn by A. & J. C. S. Harrison, a banking house in Indianapolis, Indiana, for the payment of $2,000 to William Haerle, directed to the Merchants’ National Bank. The complexity arose from the description of the check containing the terms “original” and “(second unpaid),” leading to questions about whether it constituted a valid check or a foreign bill of exchange. The trial court and Appellate Court had initially upheld its classification as a check, prompting the defendants to challenge this ruling, primarily arguing that such wording rendered payment conditional.	The Merchants’ National Bank asserted that the instrument was a valid check, emphasizing that its essential characteristic is that it is instantly payable on demand. The bank argued against the assertion that the terms “original” and “(second unpaid)” rendered the check conditional, citing legal precedents demonstrating that multiple copies of a check or bill do not affect its decisiveness.	The defendants contended that the instrument in question should not be treated as a check due to the specific wording indicating conditional payment. They argued that since it was drawn by parties from Indiana on a bank in Illinois, it should be classified as a foreign bill of exchange, which requires acceptance before the drawer can be held liable.

The case "Young & Rowley v. August Schorling" took place in September 1871 in Illinois, specifically in Cook County. The key individuals involved were the plaintiffs, Young & Rowley, and the defendant, August Schorling. The case arose from a dispute where the plaintiffs sought to recover commissions based on the claim that they had been employed to sell Schorling's farm. The proceedings noted that there was no jury present, as both parties had waived their right to one, and the case was submitted directly to the court. The evidence presented was conflicting, as is typical when both parties testify. Ultimately, the court examined the credibility and weight of the testimonies to conclude the matter.	Young & Rowley claimed that they were entitled to commissions for services rendered in attempting to sell August Schorling's farm. They argued that they were acting under an employment agreement and requested the court to grant them compensation based on the assumed authority to sell the property.	August Schorling contended that the plaintiffs did not have the authority to sell his farm as they claimed. He maintained that the evidence did not support the plaintiffs' assertions of a valid employment arrangement and requested that the court dismiss the plaintiffs' claims due to insufficient evidence in favor of their position.

In February 1859, in McLean County, Illinois, a dispute arose between Henry Dickerson and John Sutton regarding a horse that Sutton allegedly purchased from a third party, which Dickerson claimed he had already bargained for. The situation escalated significantly when both individuals appeared in Justice of the Peace A. Moore's office, where they exchanged accusations and summoned an eyewitness to clarify the matter. Tensions led to an altercation involving Frank Dickerson (Henry's relative), resulting in the latter striking John Sutton. This incident led to Frank being charged and fined for assault. Sparking further complications, Henry Reams testified about a separate note for $112.50 made out to Dickerson for labor services, which later involved a horse as payment. During the proceedings, Sutton reportedly suggested that he would settle with Dickerson if he would either pay the fine assessed against Frank or retract his statement about Sutton’s dealings. With no substantial evidence of a new or unconditional promise to repay the debt, the case relied heavily on the statute of limitations, ultimately leading to legal challenges on those grounds.	John Sutton, the plaintiff, argued that Henry Dickerson owed him a debt stemming from a previous labor agreement. He contended that there was a new promise made by Dickerson to pay this debt, which was made within five years, thereby counteracting the statute of limitations defense. Sutton sought a verdict affirming the debt and leading to its collection.	Henry Dickerson, the defendant, presented a defense relying primarily on the statute of limitations, arguing that any alleged promise to repay the debt was conditional and insufficient to negate the limitations period. He asserted that there was no clear evidence of a new promise within the requisite timeframe to avoid the debt's enforcement limitations, aiming for dismissal of Sutton's claims based on these grounds.

In January 1875, in Illinois, Ephraim S. Hamilton and William Cessna filed a lawsuit against The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company. The case arose after a shipment of hogs, being transported from Rankin, Illinois, to Toledo, Ohio, suffered severe neglect by the railway company. The plaintiffs alleged that the railway company did not provide necessary water and care for the hogs during transit, leading to their death from dehydration. The jury found substantial evidence indicating that the company was responsible for the loss due to its negligence, specifically highlighting that there was a water supply available at Hoopeston, where the hogs were purportedly denied care. In defense, the railway company claimed it had no available water for the hogs' use during transportation, but did not successfully prove this claim as required. The plaintiffs argued that the company had a clear duty to care for the animals and provide water, which it failed to fulfill.	The plaintiffs, Hamilton and Cessna, argued that The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company was negligent in its duty to care for the hogs during transportation. They claimed the company failed to provide water that caused the hogs' deaths and requested compensation for the lost stock due to this negligence. They emphasized that it was the carrier's responsibility to ensure the animals were well cared for, particularly regarding their hydration.	The defendant, The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company, contended that they had no available water for the hogs along the route between Rankin and Toledo. They argued their actions did not constitute negligence, as they believed they were unable to meet the hydration needs of the hogs due to the supposed lack of water. Ultimately, the defendant failed to demonstrate that they were exempt from liability for this loss during transportation.

The case "The People, etc., v. Joseph L. Miller et al." took place in Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Appellate Court on April 15, 1886. The key individuals involved included Joseph L. Miller, identified as a defendant, and the People (the plaintiff), although specific details about the parties' roles were not fully described in the case overview. The dispute arose from a procedural issue regarding a default judgment against the defendants. The plaintiff alleged that the court had made an error in setting aside the default judgment, which warranted further examination. The affidavits supporting the defendants' motion to set aside the default were not included in the official record for review. However, the court considered those affidavits and indicated that, if permissible, they would find them sufficient to justify the lower court's decision to set aside the default upon payment of costs.	The plaintiff, represented by attorney D. W. Karraker, argued that the lower court had committed an error by setting aside a default judgment against the defendants. They contended that the affidavits submitted in support of the motion to set aside were not appropriately included in the record for appellate consideration, and thus the default should have been upheld.	The defendants, represented by attorney W. S. Day, maintained that the lower court acted correctly in setting aside the default judgment. They argued that the affidavits provided were sufficient grounds for the motion to set aside the default, and they requested that the appellate court uphold the lower court's decision.

In 1872, in St. Clair County, Illinois, Henry T. Blow filed a lawsuit against William E. Miller for breach of a lease agreement. The lease was for specific premises and outlined the terms of payment, indicating that Miller owed Blow $2,000 in rent payments that were due and unpaid. During the court proceedings, Miller's defense included claims of non est factum and a plea of nil debet, asserting he did not owe this amount. Blow’s declaration included two counts: the first detailing the original lease and the terms of payment, while the second count referenced a written lease without specifying detailed property descriptions. As the case progressed, procedural issues surrounding the demurrers and amendments to pleadings arose, leading to complex exchanges about the legal sufficiency and form of the documents filed. The case ultimately went up to the Illinois Supreme Court for appeal after the Circuit Court's rulings on these procedural matters.	The plaintiff, Henry T. Blow, claimed that William E. Miller failed to comply with the lease agreement by not paying the rent owed, which amounted to $2,000. He requested the court to enforce the lease terms and recover the unpaid debt along with additional damages incurred due to the breach.	William E. Miller contended that he did not owe the sum claimed by Blow, utilizing defenses such as "non est factum" (not my deed) and "nil debet" (he owes nothing). Miller also challenged the legal sufficiency of the plaintiff's claims by arguing that there were significant variances in the lease descriptions, and he pursued a $300 set-off against the claimed debt as part of his defense.

The case of William L. Coyne v. Phillip Dooley took place in Mercer County, Illinois, culminating in a final judgment issued on December 16, 1889. The central issue involved a promissory note that was claimed to have been altered after its execution. The note, originally drawn for $36.12 for the installation of lightning rods on Dooley's barn, was allegedly “raised” to $136.12 without Dooley's knowledge. Phillip Dooley, an unlettered man who could neither read nor write, had authorized his son to witness and sign the note on his behalf. Dooley’s position was that he had understood the note to reflect the correct amount when it was read to him before he signed. William L. Coyne was the holder of the note after it was assigned to him, and he claimed that he was not aware of any fraud when he purchased the note. The court’s task was to determine whether any negligence could be imputed to Dooley, given his inability to read and write and the circumstances under which he signed the note.	William L. Coyne, the plaintiff, argued that he was a bona fide holder of the note and should be able to collect the amount due, as he purchased the note in good faith and before maturity. He contended that the alterations made to the note after its execution rendered it invalid only if a lack of negligence could be proven on Dooley's part. His claim hinged on questioning whether Dooley was negligent in executing the note since it contained blanks that could be manipulated.	Phillip Dooley, the defendant, maintained that he did not consent to any changes made to the note after he signed it. He argued that as an illiterate person, he could not be held liable for negligence, given that he had required the note to be read to him before it was signed and that he had signed with the understanding of its original terms. Dooley's defense was based on the notion that any alterations made after his signature invalidated the note as it was effectively a fraud against him.

In 1860, a legal case titled *Erastus Hallack, Plaintiff in Error, v. Stephen March et al., Defendants in Error* was addressed by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over a promissory note dated November 19, 1856, in St. Charles, Illinois, where Stephen March agreed to pay Erastus Hallack $455.23. The case was filed in the Circuit Court of Kane County, and the defendants argued that Hallack should not be allowed to pursue the claim due to a prior arbitration agreement. Specifically, Hallack and March had mutually agreed to submit their disputes to arbitrators Eli Barber and J.S. Van Patten, with a third arbitrator, S.W. Durant, being chosen to resolve any disagreements. The plaintiffs contended that the arbitration was not binding due to insufficient assent from all partners involved, particularly questioning the authority of co-partner Bowman, who had not objected during the arbitration process. This case marked an important question regarding whether one partner can bind the firm in arbitration matters without full agreement from the others.	The plaintiff, Erastus Hallack, claimed that the defendants should not invoke the arbitration agreement as a defense, arguing that there was no mutual consent to submit to arbitration among all partners. He asserted that the arbitration process was invalid because co-partner Bowman did not have the authority to bind the partnership in that context. Hallack sought enforcement of the promissory note and the recovery of the owed amount.	The defendants, led by Stephen March, contended that Hallack was precluded from pursuing his claim because both parties had previously agreed to submit their dispute to arbitration, which reached an award indicating that the defendants owed Hallack only seventy cents. They argued that the presence of partner Bowman during the arbitration and his lack of objection demonstrated his assent to the submission, thus binding the partnership to the arbitration award.

Thomas M. Dunning initiated legal action against John Bird in 1887, seeking justice in Pope County, Illinois. The dispute arose after Bird killed Dunning's dog during one late night at Bird's property. Dunning's dog was part of a pack of eleven fox hounds, some belonging to Dunning and others to a neighbor.
