In 1885, in Lee County, Illinois, Plano Manufacturing Company entered into a written contract with A. M. Parmenter, who was acting as an agent to receive and sell their mowing machines. According to the agreement, Parmenter was to report the sales to the appellant (Plano Manufacturing) after the harvest and account for all received goods. After several transactions, an agent from Plano, Van Ness, met with Parmenter on October 24, 1885, to settle accounts. During this meeting, Parmenter provided a statement claiming he had received three machines, but he had actually ordered and received an additional machine that was not included in his account. Following an initial judgment in favor of Parmenter in a lower court, the case was appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court, where it was argued that the proper evidentiary standards and instructions were not followed, particularly regarding the burden of proof and the validity of the settlement sheet.	Plano Manufacturing Company claimed that A. M. Parmenter had failed to account for all mowing machines received under their contract. They argued that the account Parmenter submitted did not accurately reflect his transactions, as he admitted to ordering and receiving an additional machine that was unreported. The plaintiff requested that the court recognize this discrepancy and hold Parmenter accountable for the outstanding payment for the additional mowing machine.	A. M. Parmenter maintained that he had not received any machines beyond what he accounted for. He argued that the account he provided during the settlement meeting effectively closed the matter, and thus he should not be held liable for any discrepancies. The defense claimed that the burden of proof lay with the plaintiff to demonstrate fraud or a mistake in the settlement and that improper jury instructions had misled the proceedings.

In September 1874, the case of Thomas Knox et ux. v. Peter Brady was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute revolved around a deed executed by Thomas Knox and his wife, which contained a mistake in the description of the property intended to be conveyed. The court case emerged from the Circuit Court of Marshall County, presided over by Judge Samuel L. Richmond. The plaintiffs, Thomas Knox and his wife, sought to reform the deed to rectify the error in the property description. The historical context of the case involves legislation from 1869 that changed the legal capacities of married women in property transactions, establishing that deeds could potentially be reformed for mistakes. However, this legislation still prohibited married women from relinquishing their rights concerning their husband's property without following proper legal procedures.	The plaintiffs claimed that a mistake had been made in the description of property in a deed executed by them. They sought the court to reform the deed to include the property as originally intended, arguing that the mistake needed rectification to reflect the actual agreement made among all parties involved.	The defendant, Peter Brady, contended that any contract involving the rights of a married woman concerning her husband’s land was void due to her lack of legal capacity. He argued that the married woman's deed regarding her husband's property could not be validly altered or enforced without compliance with specific statutory requirements. The defendant maintained that the court did not have the authority to reform the deed as requested by the plaintiffs.

The case of William A. Lake vs. Simeon W. Morse and Benjamin Connelly arose in Kane County, Illinois, beginning on October 2, 1849, when Lake, the appellant, was summoned before a justice of the peace for a debt. The summons demanded that Lake respond to a complaint made by Morse and Connelly, acting for the use of William Fordham. After Lake failed to appear, the justice ruled in favor of the appellees, awarding them $90. Lake subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court, where a trial took place in March 1850. During the trial, the plaintiffs presented a note dated July 8, 1849, which was written and signed by Lake but named Morse and Connelly as payees, leading to objections from the defendant regarding the validity of the debt. The plaintiffs sought to amend the original summons to reflect their correct names and the court accepted the amendment, despite Lake's objections. The case was then tried without a jury, resulting in a judgment for the plaintiffs. Lake's application for appeal centered on the validity of the amendment changing the parties involved and the trial proceeding without a jury after this amendment.	The plaintiffs, Morse and Connelly, argued that they were owed payment based on a note signed by Lake. They requested the court to amend the original summons to reflect their correct names and sought judgment for the outstanding amount of $91.35, which was later remitted to $79.87 after adjustment.	Lake, the defendant, contended that the note presented as evidence did not establish any debt owed to the plaintiffs, as it was not directly payable to them. He objected to the amendment that changed the names in the summons and argued against the validity of trying the case without a jury after such an amendment. Lake's defense maintained that the process lacked proper authority to change the parties involved in the case.

On February 3, 1886, the Illinois Appellate Court heard the case of Charles R. Erwin and Emma A. Erwin against Althea L. Hall and others in Cook County, Illinois. The case revolves around a disputed real estate transaction involving the foreclosure of a mortgage originally signed by William Erwin in 1858. Following his death in 1862, the promissory note and mortgage were transferred to J.O. Glover, who was instructed to hold them in trust for William's widow, Althea L. Hall, and later for the benefiting complainants upon her marriage. In 1868, Hall was married, altering the trust’s conditions. By that time, Glover used the trust funds to facilitate the purchase of a one-third share in a Chicago lot. As the years passed, Hall faced financial difficulties and borrowed funds, securing debts against her interest in the property, while the complainants asserted their rights as beneficiaries. Following a series of transactions, including a foreclosure of the mortgage leading to the lot's sale, the complainants initiated legal action seeking to redeem their interest in the property. However, their initial efforts were dismissed, prompting them to file a new claim in 1882, which also faced challenges concerning the notice of their equitable rights and the conduct of the trustee during the sale process.	The plaintiffs, Charles R. Erwin and Emma A. Erwin, asserted that they held an equitable interest in an undivided one-third share of a lot in Chicago and sought to redeem the property following its foreclosure. They claimed that the trustee and the purchaser, Henry W. Harwood, had prior notice of their equitable rights at the time of the sale. Their bill requested the court to allow them to redeem the property and sought a cancellation of the deed of trust that had been executed in favor of McClaughry, claiming their ownership had been unjustly overridden.	The defendants, led by Althea L. Hall, contended that the sale had been conducted properly under the authority granted by the deed of trust. They argued that McClaughry had taken his security without notice of the complainants' rights, thereby acquiring the property clear of their claims. Additionally, it was asserted that the complainants had failed to demonstrate timely action or evidence to support redeeming the property, and the trustee was under no obligation to refuse the sale, even if there were claims of fraud.

Henry S. Ressler v. Frank F. Peats is a legal case heard in September 1877 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from actions taken by Frank F. Peats, Sheriff of Winnebago County, who unlawfully arrested Henry S. Ressler in Chicago, Cook County, based on a warrant issued for a larceny charge. The warrant had been granted by a justice of the peace in Winnebago County. Ressler claimed unlawful arrest and false imprisonment, resulting in a lawsuit against Peats. The initial action included two other defendants, but the suit was dismissed against them. The core of the dispute involved whether Peats was justified in executing the warrant outside his jurisdiction.	The plaintiff, Henry S. Ressler, argued that his arrest was unlawful as it occurred outside of the jurisdiction specified in the warrant. He claimed false imprisonment and contended that the warrant failed to adequately specify where the alleged offense had occurred, rendering it void and providing no protection to Peats as the arresting officer. Ressler requested relief for the unlawful actions taken against him.	The defendant, Frank F. Peats, maintained that the warrant was valid and that he had the right to arrest Ressler in Cook County, as Illinois law enabled an officer to pursue an individual across county lines when a warrant was issued. Peats argued that the warrant conformed to statutory requirements, providing him protection. He also contended that there was no abuse of authority in the duration of Ressler's detention and that the arrest was justified under the mentioned circumstances. Peats sought dismissal of the case based on these defenses.

The case of Maria L. Kinney et al. v. Jacob Knoebel et al. took place in St. Clair County, Illinois, where the appeal was filed in June 1868. The central individuals involved include the appellant Maria L. Kinney and her siblings, who are heirs of William C. Kinney, and the appellee Jacob Knoebel, the executor of their father William C. Kinney's estate. Following the death of William C. Kinney in 1858, a dispute arose over the sale of Section 12 of land, which was sold by the sheriff under questionable circumstances. The claim was that the executor, Knoebel, failed to properly sell the deceased's assets to cover debts due, particularly ignoring that part of the estate located beyond St. Clair County where the debts could be satisfied without needing to sell the more valuable Section 12. The appellants accused Knoebel of acknowledging a judgment's existence that had been satisfied before the land's sale and allowing the land to be sold en masse when it could have been divided. The property had significant value, approximately $60,000, while it sold for much less. The court was challenged to consider the legality of the sale and the claimed conspiracy between Knoebel, the sheriff Meyer, and the buyer Morrison to undercut bidding and improperly handle the estate's assets. Both parties presented their perspectives, leading to a drawn-out legal battle regarding the sale's legitimacy and the executor's authority under the will.",	The plaintiffs, represented as Maria L. Kinney et al., argued that the sale of Section 12 was improper and contested Knoebel's authority as executor since the will restricted him to sell properties outside St. Clair County for debt payments. They asserted that the substantial land sales conducted to pay minute judgments were against both the will's explicit provisions and statutory law, which limited property sales necessary for satisfying specific debts. Additionally, they contended that the sale was illegal due to a pre-existing satisfaction of one of the judgments prior to the land's sale, seeking redress to reclaim their interest in the estate and alleging conspiracy among the defendants to suppress the property's true value.",	The defendants, including Jacob Knoebel and Morrison, claimed that the executor acted within his rights in selling the property to settle debts of the estate and cited numerous legislative extensions allowing redeeming properties sold under earlier judgments. Morrison argued he was unaware of any alleged fraud and participated in what was believed to be a legitimate sale. The defense stressed the legitimacy of the sale prices and the necessity of liquidating the estate's assets given its insolvency, contending that the land was valued below the purchase cost. They highlighted that the judgments against the estate were formalized and validated their bought interests under execution, dismissing claims of conspiracy between the parties involved.",

William S. Proudfoot filed a legal case against John Wightman in September 1875 in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a transaction involving the sale of two five-acre lots within a larger tract of real estate. The contract for the sale of the land was purportedly executed on February 13, 1868, by Wightman, but executed through D.H. Horne, who acted as Wightman's agent. Proudfoot claimed that he made a partial payment of $10 towards a total price of $150 per acre for the property. However, Wightman contested the validity of the contract, stating Horne was not authorized to act as his agent concerning the sale of the land. Evidence presented in the court included conflicting testimonies regarding the authority granted to Horne by Wightman, as well as the actual market value of the property, which had significantly increased since the initial conversation. The case hinged on whether Proudfoot could prove that Horne had the necessary authority to sell the property.	Proudfoot argued that there was a valid contract for the sale of the land and sought to enforce the specific performance of that contract. He contended that he had made a partial payment and was entitled to a deed for the property based on the agreement he had with Horne, whom he believed was acting on Wightman's behalf.	Wightman denied having authorized Horne to sell the property, asserting that Horne lacked any written or clear parol authority to execute the sale. Wightman maintained that there was no preponderance of evidence to support Proudfoot’s claim, as the testimonies presented were conflicting and raised doubts about Horne's authority. Furthermore, Wightman argued that the transaction appeared unfair and was tainted by suspicions of fraud due to the significant increase in the property's value.

In the case of *William B. Barnes v. The People of the State of Illinois*, the events unfolded in the County Court of Greene County, Illinois, in 1887. The case was brought forth by William B. Barnes, the appellant, who was the nephew of the deceased, Hannah Chapman. Chapman, who was unmarried and had lived with Barnes for eleven years, fell ill with a contagious disease called phlegmonous erysipelas. Throughout her illness, Barnes cared for her, and before her death, she expressed gratitude by stating her desire to leave her possessions to him. During her illness, Chapman gave Barnes two promissory notes, one for $1,000 and the other for $300, instructing him to hold onto them. However, she later asked that these notes be returned to her trunk for safekeeping. Before her death, she directed her daughter to give the package containing the notes to Barnes if she died before his return from Kansas. After Chapman died, the notes were found and handed over to Barnes. The case concerned whether this transfer constituted a valid gift mortis causa, which hinges on the proper delivery and intentions associated with the gift.	The plaintiff, representing the estate of Hannah Chapman, claimed that the notes in question were assets of the estate and not the property of William B. Barnes. They argued that the delivery of the notes was not valid as a gift because it lacked the conditions required for a gift mortis causa, particularly regarding delivery and intent. The plaintiff sought the judgment of the court to affirm that the notes belonged to the estate of Hannah Chapman.	The defendant, William B. Barnes, contended that the circumstances surrounding the delivery of the notes constituted a valid gift mortis causa. He argued that Chapman expressed her intention to give the notes to him if she died before he returned and that the delivery to his daughter was appropriate under the circumstances. Barnes asserted that the notes were his property due to Chapman's intentions and the conditions under which the delivery was made, claiming the gift was complete upon Chapman's death.

The case titled "The Terre Haute and Alton Railroad Company, Plaintiff in Error, v. Daniel Earp, Defendant in Error" was heard in January 1859 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff, Terre Haute and Alton Railroad Company, aimed to recover $500 from Daniel Earp, who subscribed to ten shares of the railroad's capital stock. The conflict arose after the railroad company modified its operational plans by acquiring a significant stake in another company, the Belleville and Illinoistown Railroad Company, and constructing a new route extending to Illinoistown instead of solely to Alton. Earp contended that his subscription was for the original railroad's construction from Terre Haute, Indiana, to Alton, Illinois, and that the changes made were done without his consent. The Circuit Court of Shelby County initially ruled in favor of Earp by overruling a demurrer presented by the railroad company, leading to this appeal to the Supreme Court.	The Terre Haute and Alton Railroad Company argued that its purchase of a majority stake in another railroad and the subsequent construction of a new route were lawful actions authorized by amendments to its charter. They contended that these changes were in their interest to ensure a continuous route and sought to collect the subscription fee from Earp, claiming the changes did not absolve him from his financial commitments to the original charter.	Daniel Earp's defense centered on his argument that he agreed to his subscription specifically for the construction of the railroad to Alton, as stipulated in the original charter. He claimed that by altering the charter and constructing a route to Illinoistown, the company fundamentally changed the terms of their agreement, thus releasing him from his financial obligations. He maintained that such a significant modification to the charter was not authorized at the time of his subscription and was contrary to what he had consented to originally.

John O’Leary, the appellant, was involved in a legal case against the County of Cook, the appellee, in 1862. The crux of the matter revolved around an act of the Illinois legislature, approved on February 14, 1855, amending the charter of the North-Western University, which was located in Evanston, Cook County, Illinois. The contentious provision prohibited the sale of spirituous liquors within a four-mile radius of the university, imposing a penalty of $25 for violations that could be collected by the county. O’Leary was accused of selling liquor within two miles of the university, directly contravening the law. After an initial ruling in favor of the county by a justice of the peace, O’Leary appealed to the Circuit Court, where the judge ruled against him based on the constitutionality of the law. O’Leary's appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court questioned whether this law violated the Illinois Constitution's requirement that no local law should encompass more than one subject, expressed in its title.	The County of Cook's main argument was that O’Leary had violated the law by selling alcohol within the prohibited distance from the University, and thus, they sought to enforce the penalty laid out in the amendatory act. They maintained that the law's primary aim was to protect the university’s students from the temptations of alcohol, justifying the local liquor ban as a measure in alignment with the university's educational mission.	O’Leary contended that the act was unconstitutional, as it combined two separate subjects—one being the amendment of the university's corporate powers and the other the prohibition of liquor sales—within a single statute, thereby violating the state's constitutional provision. He argued that such a prohibition had no necessary connection to the university's goal of education and that the law was a public act, affecting community interests rather than local concerns specific to the university.

In the case of Mary J. Doolittle v. Roger Cook et al., taking place in Peoria, Illinois, in 1874, the events leading to the legal dispute began in 1864 when Henry I. Chase sold a quarter section of land to Roger Cook for $3,000. While Cook initially paid $100 in cash, he financed the remainder with notes due over a period of ten years at a 10% interest rate. Cook occupied the property both before and after the sale. In 1868, Chase executed a promissory note for $4,000 to Doolittle, securing it with a mortgage on the same quarter section of land, which was recorded shortly thereafter. However, Chase also executed a deed of trust to secure a separate debt to Woodward, leading to conflicting claims over the property. Doolittle sought to foreclose her mortgage on the property and subsequently filed a bill in chancery against multiple parties, including Cook and Woodward. The trial court ruled that Doolittle's mortgage on Cook's land was void due to prior occupancy and knowledge, ultimately finding in Cook's favor while establishing Doolittle’s rights over the two ten-acre lots.	Doolittle, the plaintiff, primarily claimed that her mortgage should be enforced against Cook's land, arguing that she had the right to foreclose on the property due to the outstanding debt represented by the promissory note. She sought a reversal of the decision that released Cook’s land from her mortgage obligations, insisting that despite Cook's prior occupancy, the mortgage should still bind the land in question.	Cook, the defendant, contended that the mortgage Doolittle sought to enforce was void concerning his land, arguing that as the occupant and holder of a bond to receive a deed, he had a superior claim. He maintained that the mortgage was merely a cloud on his title, and he sought to have it set aside. Woodward, another defendant, added that Doolittle's mortgage could not take precedence because he purchased the two ten-acre lots legitimately under a deed of trust, asserting equitable defenses regarding the mortgage's validity.

Mary Ann Schmidt v. Daniel Pierce arises from a legal dispute in 1885 in McLean County, Illinois. The case involves a bill to foreclose a mortgage that was allegedly made by Marshall Stailt, who served as the conservator of Mary Ann Schmidt. His appointment as conservator was based on a jury finding that Schmidt was non compos mentis; however, the jury was composed of only six men, leading the defense to question the validity of the conservator's appointment. The county court had the authority over the relevant subject matter and person, which was challenged by the defense. The argument from the defendant's side suggested that this invalidated the entire proceedings concerning the conservatorship. However, the majority opinion of the Illinois Appellate Court held that the county court had jurisdiction and that errors in proceedings do not negate that jurisdiction.	The plaintiffs, represented by Mr. George A. Hill, claimed that the foreclosing of the mortgage was valid due to the duly appointed conservator acting within his capacity. They argued that the county court had proper jurisdiction, and any objections related to the composition of the jury or the appointment of the conservator were not valid in this collateral proceeding. They sought to affirm the validity of the conservatorship and proceed with the mortgage foreclosure.	The defense team, led by Messrs. Blades & Heville, argued against the validity of the conservatorship, claiming that the appointment was unauthorized since the jury that declared Schmidt non compos mentis was not properly constituted with the required number of jurors. They asserted that this foundational flaw rendered the conservatorship invalid, leading to the conclusion that all related proceedings were void. Their request was to dismiss the foreclosure based on these claims.

In January 1868, the case of Richard H. Connor et ux. v. Joseph A. Berry et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from Sangamon County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs, Richard H. Connor and his wife, engaged in litigation against the defendant, Joseph A. Berry. The primary issue revolved around the husband’s liability for debts that his wife had incurred prior to their marriage. The marriage occurred after the enactment of the 1861 statute that provided protections for married women regarding their separate property. The debate centered on whether the husband was still accountable for his wife’s pre-marital debts in light of this new law. Ultimately, both parties presented arguments regarding the interpretation of the 1861 act and its implications on marital financial obligations.	The plaintiffs claimed that, under the 1861 act, which aimed to protect married women's separate property, the traditional common law principle of the husband being liable for his wife’s debts incurred before marriage should no longer apply. They argued that since the marriage took place after the passage of this law, the husband should not be held responsible for any of the wife's prior debts.	The defendant argued that despite the 1861 act, the husband remains liable for his wife's debts contracted before marriage. The defense emphasized that the common law principles regarding the husband’s control over his wife’s property and earnings continued to impose such liabilities, as the act did not fully abolish these legal incumbencies. They maintained that the obligations outlined by existing law still held true.

In October 1877, Mrs. Major, residing in Monmouth, Illinois, entrusted two boxes of goods to the C. B. & Q. R. R. Co. for transportation to Levi Morgan in Bridgeport, Ohio, and subsequently left the State. These boxes were, however, seized by a constable in Galesburg under a writ of attachment against Mrs. Major. A judgment was obtained based on constructive notice, leading to a sale of the goods to satisfy the debt, despite Mrs. Major's whereabouts being unknown to the constable, who made no effort to notify her. After the consigned goods were sold, Mrs. Major sought damages against the constable and his sureties through a justice of the peace in April 1881. The suit faced procedural issues, which resulted in a dismissal against one surety. Later, in circuit court, Mrs. Major managed to obtain a judgment against the remaining surety, requiring payment of $100 as damages. The circuit court found that the constable's failure to give notice was wrongful; however, various legal precedents suggest that notice may not be practical if the debtor is absent from the county.	Mrs. Major argued that the constable's seizure and sale of her goods were wrongful since he failed to provide her with actual notice of the execution due to her absence. She contended that the constable was obliged to attempt to notify her about the writ of execution, regardless of her current residence. Her legal request primarily sought damages for the levy and sale of her goods without proper notification.	The defendant contended that the absence of Mrs. Major from the county rendered it impractical for the constable to provide notice of the execution. They argued that the constable's actions complied with the law since he had no actual knowledge of her whereabouts and that Mrs. Major should have made a claim for exemptions instead of relying on the constable to notify her. They maintained that no notice was required due to her known absence from the state.

The case of "The City of Joliet v. William Harwood" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1877. The dispute originated in Joliet, Illinois, when William Harwood, the plaintiff, sought damages after a blast conducted by a contractor hired by the city resulted in a stone breaking a window in his store. The contractor, James O’Riley, was performing sewer construction work under the supervision of the city. The excavation required blasting, which went according to the specified plans. Despite O’Riley’s claims of using due care and employing skilled workers, a stone from the blast struck Harwood’s property, causing damage valued at $180. The case was initially heard before a justice of the peace and later escalated to the Circuit Court of Will County, where judgment was rendered against the city, prompting the city to appeal the decision.	Harwood claimed that the city was liable for the damages resulting from the blasting during the sewer construction work. He argued that the city effectively commissioned work that was intrinsically dangerous, therefore making them responsible for any resulting injuries to surrounding properties. Harwood sought compensation for the damage to his property, asserting that the blast, although performed with care by the contractor, directly led to the injury.	The City of Joliet contended that it was not liable for the damage caused by the contractor’s work. The city argued that the contractor, O’Riley, was a competent professional who performed the work according to the agreed-upon standards and that the city had merely contracted the work out to an independent party. The city claimed that the application of the doctrine of respondeat superior did not apply since the actions of the contractor were independent and not under the direct control of the city during the execution of the work.

The case "Town of Havana v. George A. Biggs" took place in January 1871 in Havana, Illinois. The plaintiff, the Town of Havana, initiated legal action against George A. Biggs, claiming that he unlawfully obstructed a public highway. During the trial in the Circuit Court, the jury was instructed that the burden of proof lay with the plaintiff to demonstrate that the road in question was a public highway at the time of the alleged obstruction and that Biggs unlawfully obstructed it. Several specific instructions were given to the jury regarding the nature of public highways, the requirements for proving dedication (the act of giving a right of way), and the evidence necessary to establish a public road. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Biggs, leading to a verdict and judgment for the defendant. The case was appealed, challenging the validity of various jury instructions during the trial.	The Town of Havana contended that George A. Biggs obstructed an established public highway, seeking a penalty for this obstruction. The plaintiff argued that evidence demonstrating the public's right of passage and the legal establishment of the road were sufficient for them to win the case. They claimed that the jury should have been allowed to consider multiple forms of evidence that could establish the highway's public status, including dedication by the landowner.	George A. Biggs's defense focused on contesting the plaintiff's claims regarding the existence and public status of the road. His arguments included asserting that the plaintiff had not met the burden of proof required to establish that the road was a public highway at the time of the alleged obstruction. Biggs maintained that simply because the public had traveled through the lane, it did not imply that he had intended to dedicate that lane for public use, which is a key requirement for establishing a public highway.

On August 16, 1887, M. Millard obtained a judgment for $5,000 against Richland County in the Marion Circuit Court. Millard's claim was for legal services rendered to the county, and he subsequently received this amount from James B. Lewis, the clerk of the court, on September 15, 1887. Prior to this, on December 18, 1880, Millard assigned all his claims against Richland County to George W. Dausch. Dausch later transferred these claims to The Workingmen’s Banking Company of East St. Louis. On October 30, 1886, Millard had also engaged Felix G. Cockrell, agreeing to pay him $1,000 for legal services related to the judgment against Richland County. This agreement indicated that Cockrell would have a claim to part of the judgment achieved. Following the judgment payment, a dispute arose over the $900 left with Lewis, as multiple parties—Cockrell, Millard, and Dausch—claimed rights to it. In January 1888, Cockrell sought a court order directing Lewis to pay the $900 to him, citing his agreement with Millard. However, Lewis contested this ruling, leading to the writ of error that brought this case before the Illinois Appellate Court.	James B. Lewis, the plaintiff, argued that he was not liable to pay the $900 to Cockrell as he did not hold the money in his official capacity as clerk, and that the court did not have the authority to compel the payment under a summary proceeding. He contended that the existence of multiple claims over the money necessitated a more formal legal proceeding to determine rightful ownership.	Felix G. Cockrell, the defendant, asserted that he was entitled to the $900 based on the agreement made with Millard. He argued that the clerk’s payment of the judgment to him was justified under the agreement and that he should be compensated accordingly. Cockrell maintained that his claim had been properly filed and recognized as legitimate, seeking the court to uphold the order for Lewis to pay him the disputed amount.

In 1888, in the city of Chicago, Charles J. Hustis and other plaintiffs were involved in a legal dispute against H. S. Pickands and other defendants concerning the alleged recovery of commissions for acting as brokers in the purchase of mining stocks. The plaintiffs argued that they were operating as brokers for the defendants at the time these transactions took place. However, the defendants contended that the plaintiffs had not obtained the necessary license to operate as brokers as mandated by an ordinance passed by the Chicago City Council. This ordinance prohibited individuals from exercising the business of a broker within the city limits without having the required license. Following the defendants' special plea that highlighted this lack of licensing, the plaintiffs demurred. The court ultimately overruled the demurrer and issued a final judgment against the plaintiffs, leading them to appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had earned commissions for brokerage services provided to the defendants in the purchase of mining stocks. They argued that the business of a stock broker was not explicitly included in the city ordinance requiring a license, therefore asserting that they were entitled to recover their commission regardless of the licensing issue. They contended that any licensing requirement should be a matter between themselves and the municipality, not affecting their contractual relationship with the defendants.	The defendants argued that the plaintiffs were engaging in brokerage activities without a license, which was a clear violation of the city ordinance. They maintained that, since the plaintiffs had not obtained the requisite license to conduct business as brokers, the plaintiffs could not legally claim any commissions for their services. The defendants insisted that the ordinance was valid, and thus the lack of a license rendered any brokerage agreements void. They sought a judgment dismissing the plaintiffs' claims based on this violation.

In 1856, a voluntary association named the Tonica and Petersburg Railroad Company was formed with the intent to construct a railroad from Tonica to Jacksonville, Illinois. The association aimed to apply for a legislative act of incorporation during the next session of the Illinois legislature. The key individuals involved included the members of the association and William McNeely, the administrator of an intestate who subscribed for two shares of stock in the railroad company. McNeely passed away shortly before the incorporation process was completed. The organization of the railroad company included the election of officers and obtaining stock subscriptions, valued at one hundred dollars each. The case was brought to trial after the company’s efforts to collect the owed stock subscription from the intestate's estate. During the trial, evidence was presented regarding the organization's structure, the calls for stock by directors, and notices to stockholders published in two newspapers. The court initially ruled in favor of the defendant, McNeely.	The Tonica and Petersburg Railroad Company argued that the subscription made by the intestate for two shares of stock was a valid contract, based on the anticipation of receiving an incorporation charter to build the railroad. The plaintiffs maintained that the contract was enforceable since it was founded on lawful objectives and was supported by good consideration, namely the mutual promises made in the subscription agreement.	The defendant, William McNeely, contended that the contract in question was void, labeling it as a "nudum pactum" (a bare covenant). McNeely argued that the subscription did not create legal obligations enforceable against the estate of the deceased since the company had not yet been formally incorporated when the intestate passed away.

John M. Webster and Jane Hill, acting as administrators of Curtis Hill’s estate, brought a case against Eli Vickers in Wayne County, Illinois. The dispute stemmed from an action of assumpsit regarding a promissory note for $12, issued on December 12, 1832, by Thomas Vickers in favor of Thomas Cottingham for a clock. Cottingham, while purportedly selling the clock, had promised certain warranties regarding its functionality, but it allegedly never kept time. After an initial ruling in favor of the plaintiffs by a justice of the peace, the case was appealed to the Circuit Court, where Judge Justin Harlan ruled in favor of the defendant, Eli Vickers, on the basis that there was a failure of consideration for the note. The case then progressed to the Illinois Supreme Court on appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that the trial court erred by allowing Cottingham, the payee of the note, to testify that he had no interest in the matter and that his testimonies contradicted the terms of the note. They contended that the evidence did not prove that the clock was not improperly used and claimed there was no breach of warranty, seeking to overturn the judgment of the Circuit Court and secure payment on the promissory note.	The defendant argued that the consideration for the note was insufficient since the clock sold was defective and did not operate as warranted. Eli Vickers contended that the evidence supported the conclusion that the note did not hold validity due to the failure of consideration, asserting that the testimony of Cottingham as an agent undermined the plaintiffs' claims.

The legal case of Samuel T. Bartlett v. John Cunningham took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered in January 1877. The case arose from a promissory note executed by L. P. Deatherage and Samuel T. Bartlett. John Cunningham was the plaintiff who initiated the action to enforce the note. Deatherage did not defend himself, resulting in a default judgment against him. Samuel T. Bartlett, the defendant, claimed that he signed the note as a surety and asserted that he had served a written notice to Cunningham on July 9, 1874, requesting immediate collection of the note. He argued that Cunningham failed to act on this notice in a timely manner, leading to his release from liability. During the trial, the jury found in favor of Cunningham, prompting Bartlett to appeal the verdict. The key issue at trial was whether Bartlett had validly served notice to Cunningham to initiate collection actions, with conflicting testimony surrounding the delivery and acknowledgment of the notice.	John Cunningham claimed that Samuel T. Bartlett and L. P. Deatherage were liable for the promissory note they executed. He sought a judgment against both parties for recovery on the note, contending that Bartlett failed to properly serve notice to discharge his obligations as a surety.	Samuel T. Bartlett contended that he was merely a surety on the promissory note and had served a proper written notice to Cunningham, asking for immediate collection on the note. He argued that, due to Cunningham's failure to act promptly on this notice, he should be released from liability. Bartlett also challenged the sufficiency of the evidence supporting the jury's verdict against him and raised objections to the court's jury instructions.

The case "Joseph Humphrey v. William N. Phillips et al." arose in September 1870 in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, Joseph Humphrey, initiated a suit in the Superior Court claiming that the defendant, William N. Phillips, was liable for breaches of contract related to a draft. The pleadings included three counts: one on a sight draft, a common count, and a count on an account stated. However, the defendant, Phillips, argued that he was a resident of McDonough County and claimed that the suit should not have been filed in Cook County. He contended that the service of process was improper as it was carried out in McDonough County instead of Cook. The dispute was fundamentally about the jurisdiction of the court, with the defendant asserting that the cause of action arose in McDonough County and that the contract was not made nor payable in Cook County. The crux of the matter rested upon whether the court had jurisdiction based on the nature of the service and the location of the alleged contractual agreement.	Joseph Humphrey, the plaintiff, claimed that the defendant breached a contract involving a draft. He presented three counts in his declaration, aiming to recover funds through a suit for assumpsit. Humphrey argued that despite the issues raised about jurisdiction, the court should hear his case because he believed he had a valid claim based on the draft, which he asserted was the sole cause of action.	The defendant, William N. Phillips, raised a plea in abatement, claiming that he was a resident of McDonough County at the time the suit was initiated and was improperly served in Cook County. He argued that the cause of action arose in McDonough County, and none of the contract terms were made concerning Cook County. His main request was for the court to dismiss the case due to lack of jurisdiction based on his residency and the venue of the contract.

The case of "The Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific R. R. Co. v. Frank A. Fisher" dates back to September 1872 and took place in Illinois. Frank A. Fisher, the plaintiff, purchased a ticket to travel from Ottawa to Marseilles on freight train No. 10, which was known to carry passengers. Upon boarding, Fisher was informed by the conductor that the train would not stop at Marseilles and was advised to take the last extra train instead. Despite his attempts to board the extra trains, he was denied passage. Fisher entered the caboose of train No. 10, fully aware of the regulations stating it was permissible to travel on that train. However, the conductor did not stop at Marseilles and instead continued to the next station, leading to Fisher being carried beyond his intended destination. Fisher then initiated legal action against the railway company, claiming that they failed their duty to transport him to Marseilles as per the stated rules, causing him inconvenience and loss.	The plaintiff, Frank A. Fisher, argued that he had a legal right to be carried to Marseilles on freight train No. 10, as he purchased a ticket for that destination. He claimed that the railway company had not revoked its policy of allowing passenger transportation on that train. Fisher contended that the conductor's refusal to stop at Marseilles was unjustified and that he should be compensated for the inconvenience caused.	The defendant, Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific R. R. Co., contended that their conductor had the authority to make operational decisions, including not stopping at Marseilles. They argued that they had informed Fisher prior to departure that the train No. 10 would not stop at his desired destination. The company maintained that it was within their rights under the circumstances to deny Fisher’s intended travel and therefore sought to have the judgment against them overturned.

The case "Chicago City Railway Company v. Mary A. Robinson, Adm’x" was decided on May 31, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The incident occurred in Chicago, where the Chicago City Railway Company operated a double-track streetcar line on State Street. The plaintiff, Mary A. Robinson, boarded the northbound streetcar with her son, who was just five and a half years old, and other relatives. They were traveling to a funeral. Upon reaching Twenty-fourth Street, the train stopped, and the passengers were instructed to alight from the east side of the rear platform. As the passengers disembarked, a nine-year-old boy ran westward across the west track, followed closely by the deceased child, who was subsequently struck and killed by the grip of a southbound train. The accident was marked by claims of negligence, as witnesses reported that no warning signals were sounded, and the train was moving quietly, contributing to the child’s inability to see it due to the standing train obscuring the view. The main legal issue was whether the deceased exercised reasonable care and whether the railway company was negligent in their operation.	The plaintiff, Mary A. Robinson, claimed damages for the wrongful death of her child, arguing that the railway company was negligent for operating the southbound train without appropriate signals or warnings, particularly given the presence of passengers disembarking from the opposite train. The plaintiff contended that the noise from the cable mechanism rendered the approach of the train almost silent, leading to a lack of awareness of the danger. The key argument was that the railway's operations created an unsafe environment, which contributed to the tragic accident.	The defendant, Chicago City Railway Company, defended against the claims by asserting that the evidence presented by the plaintiff failed to demonstrate due care on the part of the deceased child. They argued that it was negligent as a matter of law for individuals to cross a railroad track without stopping and looking for an approaching train. The defense insisted there was no evidence that their train was operating at an unlawful speed, and they contested the assertion that they were negligent in their actions.

John Bergen, the plaintiff in error, was involved in a divorce case against Sarah E. Bergen, the defendant in error, which took place in the Will Circuit Court, Illinois, in February 1855. The case arose from allegations of adultery committed by John Bergen with his own daughter, Phebe Bergen, from a previous marriage. The divorce proceedings commenced when Sarah E. Bergen filed a bill of chancery for divorce, stating that they had eight children together, of whom three were still living. She also detailed that John owned property valued at over $8,000 and requested an allowance for alimony, custody of the children, and the appointment of a receiver for the property. The court granted an injunction preventing John from selling or disposing of his assets, and after submitting the case, the court found the charges of adultery to be true based on evidence and admissions made by John. The court ultimately ruled in favor of Sarah regarding custody, alimony, and property division.	Sarah E. Bergen, the plaintiff, asserted that John Bergen had committed adultery by having a sexual relationship with their daughter, Phebe. She sought a divorce, the custody of their children, alimony, and the appointment of a receiver to manage John's property. Sarah claimed that she had no means to support herself or the children while the divorce proceedings were ongoing, and she requested financial help to continue her case.	John Bergen did not formally contest the allegations, as he allowed a default to be entered against him. He admitted the charges by not refuting them, and his lack of opposition suggested an acceptance of the facts. While John did not present a vigorous defense, his request included challenging the injunction against transferring his property.

In September 1868, a legal case titled "Daniel Sprague v. Darius Dodge et al." took place in DeKalb County, Illinois, under the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a leasing agreement where Sprague and his co-defendant, Booth, had leased a flouring mill from the plaintiff, Darius Dodge. The lease included a stipulation requiring the defendants to return the mill in as good condition as they received it, excluding damages from natural wear and tear or unavoidable accidents such as fire. However, the mill was destroyed by fire, leading Dodge to file a lawsuit against Sprague due to the alleged misconduct and negligence of Sprague that he claimed led to the fire. During the trial, evidence was presented that suggested Sprague may have set the fire deliberately. The legal proceedings included debates about the standards of proof required in civil cases when a criminal act is alleged. Sprague's legal team argued that the jury should find him not guilty unless the evidence was sufficient to convict him of arson beyond a reasonable doubt, a request that was ultimately denied by the court.	The plaintiff, Darius Dodge, claimed that the defendants failed to fulfill their obligation under the lease agreement by allowing the flouring mill to be destroyed by fire due to their negligence. Dodge sought damages based on the stipulation in the lease that required the defendants to return the property in good condition, holding them liable for the losses incurred from the fire.	Daniel Sprague's defense hinged on the argument that the plaintiff did not meet the burden of proof necessary to establish negligence or misconduct on his part leading to the fire. Sprague contended that the standard for the jury should be proof beyond a reasonable doubt due to the criminal implications of the allegations, and he requested the court to instruct the jury accordingly. The defense aimed to demonstrate that there was reasonable doubt regarding Sprague's culpability in the incident.

In 1886, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, the Freeport and Mississippi River Railway Company sought to condemn land owned by various individuals, including certain lots in Galena owned by Ann Eliza Johnson, for the purpose of building a railroad and depot. Madison Y. Johnson, the husband of Ann Eliza and a key figure in this case, was named as a defendant because of his relation to the landowner, though he was not personally identified as the owner of any interest. Johnson filed a cross-petition, asserting that the State of Illinois had previously secured rights over the same land for a different railroad project that had been abandoned, which he claimed vested the land as public property and could not be condemned again. The court dismissed his cross-petition, prompting his appeal on the grounds that it was a final order regarding his claim of ownership that was not addressed in the original petition.	The plaintiff, the Freeport and Mississippi River Railway Company, claimed the right to condemn the property for public railroad use, asserting their legal entitlement to proceed with the condemnation despite the presence of Madison Y. Johnson’s cross-petition. They maintained that Johnson's assertions regarding public ownership and previous rights were unfounded and irrelevant to their condemnation efforts.	Madison Y. Johnson’s main defense was that the right of way sought by the railway company was already public property due to previous state actions and, thus, could not be condemned again. He contended that the cross-petition set forth valid grounds for ownership claims that needed to be considered before moving forward with the condemnation. Johnson sought the dismissal of the original petition for lack of jurisdiction over the property in question.

In the case of William Shreeves v. John B. Allen, which took place in 1875 in Knox County, Illinois, the dispute arose from a promissory note and an alleged failure of consideration. William Shreeves, as the assignee of the note, brought the case against John B. Allen, the maker of the promissory note, following a verdict in favor of Allen in a preceding jury trial. The main issue in contention was whether Shreeves had taken on the assignment of the note in good faith before its maturity and without knowledge of any issues regarding consideration. The jury found for the defendant, prompting Shreeves to appeal the decision. Evidence showed conflicting views on Shreeves's awareness of the note's conditions and the business practices of Kenworthy, the payee. Ultimately, the court found errors in jury instructions regarding the validity of the note assignment and the obligations of an assignee regarding bad faith and negligence.	The plaintiff, William Shreeves, argued that he validly held the assignment of the promissory note before its maturity and claimed not to have acted in bad faith. He requested that the court reverse the jury's verdict in favor of the defendant, asserting that any failure of consideration raised as a defense should not apply to him as he had acted in good faith and for valuable consideration.	The defendant, John B. Allen, contended that Shreeves had not acquired the note in good faith, having lived in the same town as the payee and been privy to the payee's allegedly dishonorable business practices. Allen argued that Shreeves should have made further inquiries before purchasing the note and that his negligence would warrant the application of the defense of failure of consideration.

In September 1867, a legal dispute arose involving William Linton, acting for Benjamin F. Quimby, against the City of Chicago. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge E. S. Williams. The crux of the issue centered around the legality of garnishment against the city, a matter previously considered in a related case, Merwin v. The City of Chicago. The plaintiff, Linton, sought to establish the city's liability for garnishment in connection with debts owed by the city to Quimby. This legal challenge highlighted the complexities of municipal liability within the context of garnishment proceedings.	The plaintiff, William Linton, representing Benjamin F. Quimby, argued that the City of Chicago should be held liable to the process of garnishment regarding debts owed to Quimby. Linton sought a judgment that would enable Quimby to collect on these debts through garnishment, asserting that the city had a responsibility to comply with such legal processes.	The City of Chicago, represented by attorney S. A. Irwin, contested the plaintiff's claims by asserting that, based on previous judicial decisions, the city was not liable to the process of garnishment. They argued against the application of garnishment for debts owed by the city, which was supported by precedents established in similar cases.

Benjamin Lombard filed a case against The Chicago Sinai Congregation in the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a real estate transaction that began with an agreement on September 15, 1871, for the purchase of certain premises. The case evolved after the property was severely damaged by fire on October 9 or 10, 1871, before the completion of the sale. Lombard sought specific performance of the contract despite the fire damage. Initially, the court favored Lombard's claim, stipulating he was entitled to compensation for the destroyed property. While the Congregation remedied title defects by February 17, 1872, they were hesitant to finalize the sale due to disagreement over compensation. Lombard’s insistence on receiving compensation led to a prolonged legal dispute, punctuated by his filings for specific performance, which resulted in a series of appeals and court remands. The court ultimately assessed whether the compensation provided for the destroyed property was adequate and if Lombard was responsible for matured payments under the terms of the original contract.	The plaintiff, Benjamin Lombard, argued that he was entitled to specific performance of the purchase agreement despite the destruction of the property. Lombard sought compensation from The Chicago Sinai Congregation for the destroyed portions of the property, insisting that the sale should proceed with an equitable adjustment for the loss incurred.	The Chicago Sinai Congregation contended that while they remedied title issues, Lombard's request for compensation was unwarranted and insisted that all terms of the original purchase agreement, including payment deadlines, should be enforced as initially stipulated. They argued that he had conceded the title was good and highlighted that reparations for the property loss were adequately addressed during the proceedings.

The case "Louisville, New Albany & Chicago Railway Company v. Diamond State Iron Company" took place in 1888, and was presided over by the Illinois Appellate Court in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were representatives of the Louisville, New Albany & Chicago Railway Company, who acted as the plaintiff, and the Diamond State Iron Company, the defendant. The dispute arose from a contract in which the plaintiff agreed to sell 2,500 kegs of spikes to the defendant at a specified price, with the condition that the spikes would be delivered on board the cars at Wilmington, Delaware, within a specified timeframe, and that the defendant would provide shipping directions. The plaintiff shipped 500 kegs to Michigan City, Indiana, following shipping directions given by the defendant's agent, which were later paid for by the defendant. However, the plaintiff claimed to be ready and willing to deliver the remaining kegs but was prevented from doing so due to the defendant's failure to provide necessary shipping directions. The case was tried without a jury, and the court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding them $3,000 along with costs.	The plaintiff, Louisville, New Albany & Chicago Railway Company, claimed that they fulfilled their contractual obligations by delivering a portion of the spikes but were hindered from completing the delivery of the remaining spikes due to the defendant's failure to provide shipping directions. They sought damages for the non-delivery based on the breach of contract, asserting that they were ready and willing to deliver as stipulated.	The defendant, Diamond State Iron Company, argued that they could not be held liable for the non-delivery of the remaining spikes because they did not provide the necessary shipping directions as stipulated in the contract. They contended that the plaintiff's claims were unfounded since the plaintiff had not fulfilled all conditions for delivery. The defendant likely requested that the court dismiss the plaintiff's claims based on this defense.

In 1885, in Shawneetown, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between The Riverside Company and William A. Howell over the ownership of parts of lots 1143 and 1144. The case was an action of ejectment, which is a legal term for removing a person from real property. The defendant, Howell, contested the claim by establishing his title to the property through a tax deed. Previously, in 1875, lots 1143 and 1144 had been listed under Henry O. Doeker, but due to unpaid taxes, they were forfeited to the State. The Riverside Company was then listed with parts of the lots for unpaid city taxes from 1875 and 1876. However, it was argued that the taxes were invalid because the Shawneetown city council had failed to pass the required annual appropriation bill, which is essential for legally levying taxes. The court's role was to determine the validity of the tax deed and whether the taxes supporting the tax deed were legally assessed.	The Riverside Company claimed that the tax deed under which Howell based his ownership was void because it was founded on tax assessments deemed illegal. They argued that the city taxes were invalid due to the city council's failure to pass the necessary appropriation ordinance for the years in question. Consequently, they sought to reclaim their ownership of the property through the action of ejectment.	William A. Howell defended his title by asserting that the city taxes, despite being contested, were valid, and claimed that the judgment resulting from the tax sale should be deemed conclusive. He argued that the tax judgment could not be challenged in this collateral proceeding and maintained that any alleged failure by the city council to comply with procedural requirements did not impact the validity of the tax sale or the underlying taxes themselves.

In 1889, in Jefferson County, Illinois, a legal case arose between The Louisville, Evansville & St. Louis Railroad Company and plaintiff Sanford Hill. The incident occurred near Mt. Vernon, where Hill's cow was allegedly struck and killed by a train at a public road crossing. Hill claimed that the railroad company failed to perform its duty to signal the train's approach by either ringing a bell or blowing a whistle, which amounted to negligence. The case included an amendment to the original declaration, suggesting that the crossing was dangerous and that the train was operated recklessly and at a high speed. However, the railroad company filed a demurrer, arguing that the amended declaration improperly combined two distinct causes of action: one for statutory negligence (the failure to signal) and another for common law negligence (reckless operation). The trial court overruled the demurrer, leading to a judgment favoring Hill.	Hill's main argument was that the railroad company committed negligence by failing to adhere to statutory responsibilities to signal before crossing, which directly led to the death of his cow. He sought damages for the loss of his livestock due to the railroad’s failure to take necessary precautions at the crossing. He further reinforced his claims with an amendment that argued the crossing's inherent dangers and the reckless operation of the train.	The railroad company's defense centered on the assertion that the amendment had combined two separate legal claims in one count, which was procedurally improper. They contended that the original complaint lacked clarity and that the plaintiff should have separated the claims of statutory negligence from common law negligence into distinct counts. As such, the defendant requested that the court sustain their demurrer to the amended complaint on these grounds, arguing that the pleadings created confusion that hindered a fair trial.

In 1874, in Hancock County, Illinois, Daniel Otmer was indicted for the murder of Jacob Jingst, who was shot while passing along a public road on October 14, 1873. Following a trial, Otmer was found guilty by a jury and sentenced to thirty years in prison. He subsequently sought to reverse this judgment by presenting his case to the Illinois Supreme Court, claiming errors during the trial regarding jury instructions and the sufficiency of evidence. In challenging the jury's decision, Otmer argued that the evidence presented did not convincingly support his guilt, particularly highlighting alibi testimony that suggested he had been elsewhere when the murder occurred. His appeal rested on two main points: the appropriateness of specific jury instructions and whether the jury's verdict was upheld by adequate evidence.	The plaintiff, in this case, is represented by the state of Illinois, who charged Otmer with murder. The main claim was that Otmer deliberately shot Jingst as he passed along the road, which constituted a willful act of murder. The state sought to have the guilty verdict upheld, proclaiming that the evidence presented, although circumstantial, sufficiently proved Otmer's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.	Daniel Otmer's defense centered on two primary arguments: first, that significant errors were made in the jury instructions, which could have misled the jurors regarding their duty to find guilt based on reasonable doubt; and second, that the verdict was not sufficiently supported by evidence. Otmer's defense included testimony indicating that he was miles away from the shooting scene at the time of the murder, suggesting that he could not have committed the crime, which raised reasonable doubt concerning his guilt.

The case "The People ex rel. William D. Lindsey, Collector, v. Levin Y. Palmer" was decided on March 30, 1885, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Vermilion County, specifically related to the tax assessment of certain real estate owned by Levin Y. Palmer in the city of Danville. The premises in question spanned approximately five acres and were surrounded by public streets, making its location significant for the classification of the property. The property was used by Palmer as a residence, garden, and pasture for cattle. The primary concern was whether the property should be classified and taxed as city lots or lands. The county collector, representing the People, sought a judgment for unpaid taxes, contending that the property should be treated as city lots, which would warrant a lower tax assessment due to a three percent deduction recognized for such properties. Conversely, previous assessments classified the property as lands—assessed at $9,800—with additional percentages added by both county and state boards that increased the taxable value. The court reviewed agreed facts about the property’s characteristics, history, and its unique situation under Illinois revenue law.	The plaintiff, represented by the county collector, claimed that the property should be classified as city lots for the purposes of taxation. The argument rested on the assertion that the property, while not platted as traditional city lots, was nonetheless within the city limits, surrounded by city streets, and was functionally used as a residence. Thus, the collector sought judgment for taxes that reflected the classification of city lots, which meant a proper tax rate accounting for the three percent deduction.	The defendant, Levin Y. Palmer, defended against the taxation claims by arguing that the property should be classified as land rather than city lots. Palmer’s position was supported by the county clerk and local assessor who had treated the property as land in their assessments, applying higher percentages for taxation. Palmer asserted that since the property had never been platted into lots as required by state regulations, it should not be taxed as a city lot but rather as land, justifying the application of increased tax rates.

The case, "Town of Rice v. Chicago, Burlington & Northern Railway Company," took place in 1888 in the town of Rice, Illinois. The plaintiff, the Town of Rice, initiated a lawsuit against the defendant, a railroad company, claiming that the railroad unlawfully obstructed a public highway while constructing its railroad. The highway, which had been used by the public since 1842 and maintained for over 40 years, was fully occupied by the railroad’s tracks, embankments, and fences, effectively excluding public use. The case began in a justice of the peace court and was moved to the Circuit Court, where the court ruled in favor of the defendant. The Town of Rice then appealed the judgment to the Illinois Appellate Court, seeking to reverse the lower court's decision. The defendant contended that it had a legal right to occupy the highway due to a prior agreement with the town's highway commissioners, which was sanctioned by state law. However, the plaintiff argued that the agreement was void and sought to have the highway restored for public use. Key figures involved included the town officials and representatives of the railroad company.	The Town of Rice claimed that the defendant obstructed a public highway and sought the statutory penalty prescribed under Illinois law, which specified fines for such obstructions. The plaintiff argued that the railroad company acted unlawfully by taking control of the entire highway, violating the lawful expectations of the public’s right to use the road, which had been established through long-term use and repair. The plaintiff requested that the court recognize this unauthorized obstruction and impose the corresponding penalties.	The defendant, the railroad company, asserted that it had a legal agreement with the highway commissioners of the Town of Rice that allowed it to occupy the highway for the construction of its railroad. The company argued that under the Illinois statute governing railroads, it had the authority to take possession of public highways provided it restored them to usable condition. The defendant sought to uphold the initial judgment from the Circuit Court, claiming that the contract with the commissioners was valid and that the highway was being adequately addressed as a part of the railroad's operations.

John F. Boyer and Hattie C. Sherer were involved in a legal case concerning an alleged breach of a marriage contract. The events took place after Sherer, a married woman at the time, obtained a divorce in Terre Haute, Indiana, on December 11, 1882. Shortly thereafter, at Boyer's suggestion, she relocated to Edgar County, Kansas, where Boyer lived. They maintained a relationship marked by sexual intimacy from 1881 until just prior to Boyer's marriage in the fall of 1886. The case was initiated by Sherer on September 2, 1886. A significant aspect of the case was the conflicting accounts regarding whether a marriage contract had been made—Sherer claimed it was established before her divorce and reaffirmed later, while Boyer denied such a contract ever existed. The evidence Sherer presented included letters from Boyer during their relationship, which the court found to be inappropriate and indicative of merely a physical relationship rather than one committed to marriage. The trial court had ruled in favor of Sherer, awarding her $1,000, but Boyer appealed, asserting that the evidence did not support the verdict.	Hattie C. Sherer, as the plaintiff, claimed that John F. Boyer had breached a contract of marriage that was formed prior to her divorce and was renewed throughout their relationship. She sought damages, arguing that their intimate relationship created obligations akin to a marriage contract, intending to hold Boyer accountable for not marrying her as expected.	John F. Boyer contended that there was no marriage contract between him and Sherer, strongly denying her claims. He argued that the letters presented as evidence do not indicate a genuine commitment or intent to marry, but rather reflect a sordid relationship. He maintained that the jury's verdict was unsupported by the evidence and requested that the court reverse the decision in favor of Sherer.

The case "The People ex rel. Vosburgh v. John A. Jameson" occurred in September 1867 in Chicago, Illinois. The primary individuals involved were John S. Vosburgh, the plaintiff, and John A. Jameson, a judge of the Superior Court of Chicago. This legal matter arose from a trial where Vosburgh was the plaintiff against The Chicago and Great Eastern Railway Company, with Judge Jameson presiding. During the trial, Augustus Wallbaum testified, and the outcome was unfavorable for the defendant. Following the trial, Vosburgh prepared a bill of exceptions believing it did not accurately reflect Wallbaum's testimony. When Vosburgh submitted an amended bill to Judge Jameson for his signature, the judge refused, stating that he had already signed a different bill of exceptions that he believed to be correct. Vosburgh then sought a writ of mandamus from the Illinois Supreme Court, requesting the court to compel Judge Jameson to sign the amended bill of exceptions. The case illustrates the complexities of accounting for witness testimony and the power of judges to determine the accuracy of records pertaining to trials.	Vosburgh claimed that the original bill of exceptions failed to accurately represent the testimony of witness Wallbaum. He sought a writ of mandamus from the Illinois Supreme Court to compel Judge Jameson to sign an amended bill of exceptions that he had prepared. Vosburgh argued that the judge's refusal to sign the amended bill was unjust, as it did not reflect the complete and correct testimony from the trial.	Judge Jameson's defense centered on his assertion that he had already signed a bill of exceptions that he deemed to be accurate. He explained that he made this decision after thorough consideration, including consultation with a phonographic reporter who had been present during the trial. Jameson maintained that he could not sign the amended bill as it did not reflect what he believed to be the correct testimony presented during the trial. He argued that the responsibility for the correctness of the bill of exceptions rests solely with the judge, not with the relator.

Charles P. Mallett brought a case against Edward G. Butcher and Janies Corking in the Whiteside Circuit Court, Illinois, in 1866. The dispute arose from a judgment on a note that was based on money lost while gambling at a card game called “faro.” Mallett sought to set aside this judgment, arguing that it stemmed from a gambling contract that was void under Illinois law. The law prohibits any promises or agreements made in connection with gambling activities, rendering such agreements null and void. The defendants countered this by demurring to Mallett's bill, prompting the court to sustain their demurrer and dismiss the case. Mallett then pursued a writ of error to challenge this dismissal in the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the dismissal was in error and that he should have been granted relief based on the statute governing gaming contracts.	Mallett's main arguments centered around the Illinois statute that invalidates contracts related to gambling. He claimed that the judgment obtained by the defendants was based exclusively on a gambling contract, which is void. Mallett requested the court to set aside the judgment in favor of the defendants and argued that under the law, he was entitled to equitable relief despite not having raised the defense in the original legal action.	The defendants argued that Mallett should have asserted his defense in the initial action at law and that not doing so precluded any relief from a court of equity. They contended that since Mallett had knowledge of the alleged defense, he could not seek to vacate the judgment after the fact. They asserted that the previous ruling should stand and the case should be dismissed.

The case of Calvin M. Gibson v. Anderson Webster took place in June 1867 in Clay County, Illinois. The incident involved an unprovoked assault by Anderson Webster on Calvin M. Gibson, who was violently thrown to the ground. During the assault, Webster continued to strike Gibson after he was down, resulting in severe injuries, including the dislocation of Gibson’s ankle and a broken bone in his leg. As a consequence of the brutal attack, Gibson was confined to his home for four to six weeks and relied on crutches for several months, leading to a lifetime condition of a stiff and enlarged ankle. The jury's verdict awarded Gibson only twenty-five dollars in damages, which was criticized for being grossly inadequate given the severity of the injuries sustained.	Calvin M. Gibson claimed that he suffered significant physical injuries as a result of an unprovoked assault and battery committed by Anderson Webster. He argued that the assault was brutal and unjustified, resulting in both immediate harm and long-term consequences, and he sought appropriate damages to compensate for his pain, suffering, and inability to work.	Anderson Webster likely contended that there was insufficient evidence to support the claims of assault and that the jury instructions provided during the trial were misleading. Webster’s defense aimed to undermine the notion of unprovoked assault, possibly arguing that the events were misrepresented and did not warrant the claims made by Gibson for damages.

On January 18, 1856, Franklin C. Oliver sold twenty acres of land to James O. Walker for $1,300, with a $500 down payment. The remaining $890 was to be paid shortly after. Although the balance was settled before Walker's death on March 12, 1859, Oliver later conveyed the land to Nathan Simmons on February 8, 1865. In 1877, Caroline E. Cochran, as administratrix of James O. Walker's estate, initiated a lawsuit claiming that Walker's estate had lost the land due to Oliver's failure to fulfill the contract. The case involved various legal challenges regarding the plaintiff's standing as administratrix, including questions about jurisdiction and the statute of limitations. The trial, held without a jury, ultimately ruled in favor of Cochran.	The plaintiff, Caroline E. Cochran, argued that the land contract was valid, and since James O. Walker had paid the full purchase price prior to his death, Oliver was obligated to provide a deed to Walker or his estate. Cochran contended that the land had been wrongfully conveyed to Simmons, resulting in a loss to Walker's estate. As part of her legal request, she sought payment for the full amount of the contract, totaling $1,300.	Franklin C. Oliver's defense included several arguments: 1) The plaintiff was not the legal administratrix of Walker's estate, as he was a resident of Vermilion County at the time of death, not McLean County; 2) The lawsuit was barred by the statute of limitations; and 3) The plaintiff's claims were invalid as they had supposedly been previously adjudicated in a separate case regarding the same land. Oliver maintained that the contract should have been enforced by Walker's heirs rather than by Cochran.

The case of "The Town of Evans v. Beula C. Dickey, Exrx." arose in the Circuit Court of Marshall County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 12, 1886. It involved T. Lyle Dickey, an attorney who, after his death, was represented by Beula C. Dickey as the executor. The plaintiff, Dickey, sought to recover fees for professional legal services he provided to the Town of Evans in connection with lawsuits brought against the town in both the Circuit Court and the Supreme Court of the United States. During the trial, controversies arose regarding whether the town had formally employed Dickey for these legal services. The trial emphasized various evidentiary issues, particularly concerning the admissibility of Dickey's statements about his employment, which were deemed errors by the court. The evidence presented to the jury included contentions about the specifics of his employment and the role of another attorney, Mr. Jones, in the town's defense. Ultimately, the Illinois Supreme Court had to address the appropriateness of jury instructions and other errors before making a ruling.	The plaintiff, T. Lyle Dickey, claimed that he had been employed by the Town of Evans to provide legal representation in lawsuits against the town, specifically one filed by Sanborn. Dickey argued that he was owed payment for the professional services rendered during these legal proceedings. In his case, he sought compensation for his work as an attorney, asserting he had effectively represented the town's interests.	The Town of Evans countered the plaintiff's claims by arguing that the evidence presented did not conclusively establish Dickey's employment.
