They contended that the plaintiff's testimony regarding his employment was inadmissible and that he was improperly allowed to state his conclusions in court. Furthermore, they asserted that another attorney, Mr. Jones, had been the one employed by the town to handle the defense of the lawsuits, attempting to diminish the claim's validity by suggesting Dickey acted on Jones' behalf without a formal agreement.

In June 1867, in the Marion County Circuit Court of Illinois, a case titled "Charles M. Smith et al. v. John M. Rotan et al." was filed. The key individuals involved included the appellees (Charles M. Smith and others) and the appellants (John M. Rotan and others), who were the surviving sureties on a guardian bond of Willis Smith, a deceased guardian of the appellees. The case arose when the appellees sought to compel the administrators of the deceased obligors to account for the funds that were managed under the guardian bond. The central issue revolved around whether the heirs of the deceased obligors needed to be included as parties in this chancery case.	The plaintiffs, represented by B. B. Smith, argued that the administrators of the deceased obligors should account for the funds in question. They contended that including the heirs of the obligors was unnecessary due to the difficulties in ascertaining their residences, which aligned with established rules in equity law regarding necessary parties in such cases.	The defendants, represented by Messrs. O'Melvehy and Merritt, maintained that the heirs should also be made parties to the suit as their rights could be materially affected by the court's decree. They argued that all stakeholders with a substantial interest in the lawsuit must be included unless they are too numerous to ascertain their identities and locations.

In April 1855, Peter Schoonover (plaintiff) worked on Thomas Christy's (defendant) farm in La Salle County, Illinois. Their work relationship began when Schoonover commenced work on March 9, 1855, with an agreement that he would work until October 1, 1855, in exchange for a sorrel horse or mare and a red cow. On April 9, 1855, they entered into a written contract that stipulated Schoonover's responsibilities, including hauling straw and manure. After becoming ill and being unable to work for 27 days, Schoonover resumed work with Christy's permission. Upon recovery, he offered to make up the lost time, but Christy insisted that Schoonover complete the remaining work before he could compensate him for the missed days. Schoonover refused this condition, and both parties signed a new contract on April 17, 1855, which was intended to supersede the previous agreements. The contract indicated Christy was to provide Schoonover with specified animals for his labor. The case ensued after disagreements regarding the enforcement of their contracts and Schoonover's refusal to meet Christy’s conditions, leading to Schoonover pursuing the case before a justice of the peace and subsequently appealing to the La Salle County Court.	Schoonover argued that the final written agreement was the true contract governing their relationship, which entitled him to the promised horse and cow for his labor. He claimed that Christy's refusal to allow him to catch up on his work after his illness constituted a breach of contract, enabling him to sue for the value of his work. Schoonover requested damages based on the labor he performed, relying on the principal that he had fulfilled his obligations under the contract.	Christy contended that the agreement signed on April 1, 1855, superseded previous contracts and essentially required Schoonover to comply with new terms, including completing all work specified before receiving his compensation. Christy maintained that Schoonover had refused to fulfill his part of the agreement and thus forfeited any claims to the promised livestock. Furthermore, he sought a new trial after the jury found in favor of Schoonover, asserting that the directions given by the court were in error.

In the case of *David D. Lanterman et al., Administrators, v. George A. Abernathy et al.*, the legal proceedings took place in June 1868 in Illinois. The key individuals involved include George A. Abernathy, the complainant and heir of Martha Abernathy, and the administrators of James Lanterman, who was deceased. The case stemmed from a promissory note for $350 that George had executed in favor of Lanterman. This note was held by Lanterman at the time of his death, and Abernathy and other heirs sought to compel its surrender, alleging that it had been agreed previously that the note should benefit Lanterman’s wife’s children. Evidence presented included statements made by Lanterman indicating a belief that the Abernathy heirs would receive this money, but it was ultimately determined that this did not constitute a executed agreement for the trust of the note.	The plaintiff, George A. Abernathy, and the other heirs claimed that James Lanterman held the promissory note in trust for the benefit of his wife's children, including Abernathy. They sought the court's intervention to compel the administrators of Lanterman’s estate to surrender the note, arguing that there had been a mutual understanding that the note's benefits were intended for the heirs of Martha Abernathy.	The defendants, led by the administrators of James Lanterman, contended that there was insufficient evidence to support the plaintiff's claims about an express trust relating to the promissory note. They argued that the statements made by Lanterman prior to his death did not constitute a definitive agreement to hold the note for the Abernathy heirs, and thus no legal obligation existed for them to surrender the note.

In the case of **David E. McGinnis v. Thomas Fernandes**, decided on November 14, 1888, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute arose from a suit in ejectment filed by Thomas Fernandes against David E. McGinnis regarding a tract of land in Sangamon County. The land in question was initially owned by McGinnis, who executed a warranty deed to William W. McGinnis in April 1884. Under the arrangement, McGinnis received the consideration by having it applied to his debt with the Springfield Marine Bank. Subsequently, William W. McGinnis conveyed the land to Henry C. Latham, a trustee, who later sold it to Fernandes in October 1885. Despite the transfer, McGinnis retained possession of the land, continuing to farm it and making payments to Latham, which he claimed were not for rent but rather part of a verbal agreement to redeem the land. McGinnis sought to introduce evidence of this alleged oral arrangement suggesting the deed acted as a mortgage and provided for his right to redeem the land, but the court denied the admission of such testimony, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiff, Thomas Fernandes, argued that he was the rightful owner of the land following the purchase from Latham and sought to regain possession. He contended that McGinnis, despite his claims, did not hold any legal rights to the property since the deed, while appearing as an absolute sale, did not serve as a mortgage as McGinnis claimed. Fernandes requested the court to affirm his ownership through the ejectment action.	David E. McGinnis, the appellant, contended that the warranty deed executed to William W. McGinnis functioned more like a mortgage, granting him a right to redeem the land. He sought to prove an oral agreement that allowed him a specific timeframe to pay a set amount to reclaim ownership. McGinnis also claimed that the court erred by not allowing consideration of tenant rights since he had been paying rent and had not received a formal notice to quit. His defense hinged on the assertion that he had a legitimate claim to remain in possession of the land.

In 1859, in Chicago, Illinois, Frederick W. Myers, along with John Haslett and John Smith, was accused of stealing two mares belonging to John Mohr. The alleged theft occurred on June 10, 1859, as indicated in the indictment filed during the October term of the Recorder’s Court. Myers, concerned about prejudice from local authorities and community members, sought a change of venue, believing he could not receive a fair trial. However, his petition was denied by the court. The trial proceeded, and after witness testimonies—including that of David Carpenter, who implicated Myers in multiple larcenies—Myers was found guilty by a jury, which sentenced him to seven years in prison. His defense invoked several objections regarding the trial's conduct, including the admissibility of witness testimony and jurisdictional claims related to the alleged crime's location.	The plaintiff, Frederick W. Myers, argued that he was not guilty of the charges and requested a change of venue due to perceived bias in the Recorder's Court of Chicago. He asserted that the local populace and the judge were prejudiced against him, which would hinder his chance of receiving a fair trial. Throughout the trial, he contended that the evidence presented against him was improperly admitted and had no relevance to the specific charges.	The defense, representing the People, argued against the claims made by Myers, asserting that the court had jurisdiction as the stolen property was found within Chicago. They contended that the change of venue request did not meet the necessary legal standards. The prosecution also defended the admissibility of Carpenter's testimony and the introduction of evidence relating to other acts by Myers, which they argued was relevant in establishing his character and involvement in larcenies.

John Lynch (plaintiff) and Nehemiah A. Baldwin (defendant) were involved in a landlord-tenant dispute that took place in the city of Aurora, Illinois, culminating in a judgment delivered by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873. The plaintiff, as the landlord, issued a distress warrant against Baldwin for unpaid rent amounting to $350 for a house and lot that Baldwin was leasing. The property confiscated during the distress proceedings included groceries and fixtures related to Baldwin's business. During the trial in the Court of Common Pleas, Baldwin argued that Lynch's actions constituted an eviction which justified his non-payment of rent. Specifically, Baldwin claimed that Lynch had installed a water-pipe, pump, and sink without his consent in the upper room he rented, leading to water damage in his oyster saloon and eating house directly below. The jury ruled in favor of Baldwin, prompting Lynch's appeal, where he contested the trial court's instructions regarding the criteria for eviction.	Lynch claimed that Baldwin was liable for unpaid rent of $350. He argued that the defenses raised by Baldwin did not constitute legal justifications for non-payment. Specifically, Lynch asserted that the installation of plumbing equipment did not amount to an eviction and that Baldwin's failure to pay rent should be enforced, irrespective of any alleged interference with the leasehold.	Baldwin countered that Lynch's installation of plumbing caused damage to his business and effectively evicted him from the premises. He maintained that since the landlord interfered with the enjoyment of the leasehold through these actions, he should not be liable for paying rent. Baldwin claimed that the acts of the landlord amounted to a substantial injury, justifying a claim of eviction, and he sought to have the court rule that he did not owe rent during this interference.

Samuel Colcord v. Jediah F. Alexander is a legal case that took place in June 1873 in Bond County, Illinois, involving a dispute over land ownership. The primary individuals involved were Samuel Colcord, the appellant (defendant), and Jediah F. Alexander, the appellee (plaintiff). The contention arose over a parcel of land originally owned by Lansing & Ostrom, which was sold under a marshal's sale following a judgment against them in the United States Circuit Court for the Southern District of Illinois. Colcord claimed his title through this sale, while Alexander was seeking to enjoin Colcord from trespassing and to quiet his own title to the land. The case was presented as a bill in chancery by Alexander against Colcord, with Colcord asserting a cross-bill of his own. The circuit court ruled that the land description in the marshal's deed was too vague to be valid, thus making Alexander’s injunction against Colcord permanent and dismissing Colcord’s cross-bill.	Jediah F. Alexander, the plaintiff, argued that Samuel Colcord was trespassing on his land and sought an injunction to prevent such actions as well as to quiet title. He contended that the title claimed by Colcord, derived from a marshal's sale, was invalid due to the imprecise description of the property in the deed.	Samuel Colcord, the defendant, countered that he held a valid title to the land through a marshal's deed obtained from a sale executed under a judgment against Lansing & Ostrom. He argued that the description of the land, while potentially vague, was sufficient to identify the property and requested the court to dismiss Alexander's claims and uphold his title.

On October 12, 1885, in Adams County, Illinois, the Simmons Hardware Company filed an attachment lawsuit against Benjamin Bowen, a resident of Missouri, due to an outstanding debt. The sheriff could not locate Bowen to satisfy the attachment and served writs on Bowen's business partners, Thomas Pope, William R. Lockwood, and John W. Heitz. The garnisheed partners acknowledged owing Bowen $141.49 and admitted to having promissory notes totaling $336 in their possession, which belonged to Bowen but were located in Missouri at the time of the writ's service. Despite the service of the writ, Lockwood, acting on legal counsel, handed the notes back to Bowen but did not pay him the cash amount owed. The case was tried, resulting in a verdict in favor of the plaintiff for the cash sum, which was affirmed on appeal. The core issue was whether the garnishees could be held responsible for the promissory notes that were in another state during the garnishment process.	The plaintiff, Benjamin Bowen, argued that the garnisheed partners were indebted to him and should be required to pay the outstanding cash amount of $141.49. He contended that the service of the writ constituted an obligation for the garnishees to remit the owed sum despite the promissory notes being physically located out of state at the time the writ was served.	The defendants contended that they could not be charged as garnishees for promissory notes that belonged to Bowen and were located outside of Illinois at the time the writ was served. They maintained that under Illinois law, property outside the state could not be subject to garnishment and that their legal obligation to pay Bowen did not pertain to assets they could not legally enforce.

In 1871, in Grundy County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving Turpin H. Arnold and his wife against Edward E. Gifford. The case centers around a contentious transaction concerning an equity of redemption related to a parcel of land. The land, originally owned by Charles F. Washburn, was subject to a debt of approximately $900 to C. W. and E. E. Knoblocks. Washburn conveyed the land to the Knoblocks as security for the debt, with the understanding that it would be reconveyed upon repayment. Subsequently, Washburn became indebted to Turpin H. Arnold for $500. Through an arrangement involving Arnold, Washburn, and the Knoblocks, Arnold paid off the Knoblock debt, and the land was then conveyed to Mary J. Arnold (Turpin’s wife) as security for Arnold's debt. Arnold later persuaded Washburn to surrender a bond related to the property, supposedly to protect it from creditors. However, the defendant, Edward E. Gifford, challenged the validity of this transaction, claiming that there was no legitimate purchase and that the actions were fraudulent, aimed at hindering Arnold's creditors. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Gifford for redemption, which led to Arnold's appeal.	The plaintiffs, Turpin H. Arnold and Mary J. Arnold, contended that the transfer and arrangements regarding the land and the bond for deed were legitimate transactions entered into to protect the interest of Washburn and fulfill their financial obligations. They claimed that subsequent attempts to reclaim the land were fraudulent, and the actions of Gifford were in bad faith. They sought the court’s assistance to uphold the redemption of their interests against Gifford's claims of fraud.	Edward E. Gifford, the defendant, argued that the judgment associated with the equity of redemption was fraudulent and that no legitimate debt existed between Arnold and Washburn to support the arrangements made regarding the land transfer. Gifford asserted that the entire scheme was a coordinated effort to mislead creditors, and the lack of genuine consideration rendered the transaction void. He sought to have the court reverse the prior decree that favored the plaintiffs and uphold the perceived fraudulent nature of the plaintiffs' claims.

In January 1875, in Decatur, Illinois, William Vermillion brought an action against the City of Decatur. The essence of the case revolved around Vermillion's appointment as a pound-master, a role that ostensibly came with a fixed salary. As part of his duties, he was also appointed as a special policeman to enforce an ordinance preventing cattle and swine from running at large in the streets. Vermillion claimed he rendered services as a policeman and sought additional compensation for those services, despite having been informed at the time of his appointment that he would not be paid for acting in that role. The city contended that Vermillion was not entitled to any extra payment, as the powers conferred upon him as a special policeman were incidental and solely designed to assist him in executing his duties as a pound-master. The case highlighted issues of public service compensation, the understanding of the parties involved, and the legal obligations of public officials with fixed salaries.",	Vermillion claimed that he should receive compensation for his services as a special policeman in addition to his fixed salary as a pound-master. His main argument was based on the assertion that the extra duties justified additional pay, and he initially won compensation in a lower court. However, he had been informed at the time of his commissioning that he would not receive payment for services rendered as a policeman, which he claimed should not bar his recovery of fees.",	The City of Decatur argued that Vermillion was clearly informed that he would not receive compensation for his role as a special policeman. They maintained that his duties as a policeman were simply an extension of his responsibilities as pound-master and that an individual accepting public office with a set salary cannot later claim additional payment for duties they were informed would not be compensated. The city requested that Vermillion's claims be dismissed, as accepting the position implied acceptance of the terms that no additional pay would be provided for the auxiliary role.",

The case "The City of Lake View v. H. Tate" involves a dispute that arose in the City of Lake View, Illinois, during the late 19th century. The case was originally brought to a justice of the peace's court by the City of Lake View to recover a penalty for violating a municipal ordinance that regulated the speed of railway trains. The ordinance specified that passenger trains could not exceed a speed of ten miles per hour and freight trains six miles per hour. H. Tate, the defendant, was a locomotive engineer for the Chicago and Evanston Railway Company, accused of running a passenger train faster than the specified limit on February 21, 1889, in the East Railway District of Lake View. The initial ruling favored the city, awarding $200 in penalties. However, upon appealing to the Criminal Court of Cook County, the decision was overturned in favor of Tate. The Appellate Court affirmed this ruling, prompting the city to seek review from the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal context included municipal powers to regulate rail transport and questions surrounding the validity of ordinances perceived as discriminatory between competing railway lines.	The plaintiff, the City of Lake View, argued that H. Tate violated the municipal ordinance by running a passenger train at a speed greater than ten miles per hour. They maintained that the ordinance was within the city's authority to regulate train speed for public safety. The city sought to enforce the penalty specified in the ordinance for such violations.	The defendant, H. Tate, contended that the ordinance was invalid as it imposed unreasonable discrimination between the Chicago and Evanston Railway and the competing Chicago and Northwestern Railway. Tate argued that while his train was penalized, the other railway faced no speed limitations, creating an unfair competitive disadvantage. The defense asserted that the city did not justify the need for different regulations based on safety or the circumstances of the areas served by each railway.

On November 27, 1886, in a coal mine operated by The Consolidated Coal Company of St. Louis, a miner named Larcher was tragically killed when a significant amount of clod, dirt, slate, and other materials fell from the roof of the mine while he was loading coal into boxes. The plaintiff, Andrew Yung, administrator of Larcher's estate, alleged that this incident was due to the negligence of the coal company, which failed to furnish adequate props to support the roof, despite knowing the dangerous conditions that existed. Larcher left behind a widow and minor children, prompting the administrator to seek damages of $5,000. A jury trial in the Circuit Court of St. Clair County concluded with a judgment of $3,000 awarded to the plaintiff. The defendant then appealed the decision, arguing multiple points regarding the negligence claim and the proper party to bring the suit.	The plaintiff contended that the defendant, as the operator of the coal mine, had a duty to ensure the safety of the working conditions and specifically to provide proper supports to prevent debris from falling. He claimed that the failure to do so resulted in Larcher's death, asserting that this negligence warranted compensation for the damages incurred due to the loss of life, especially considering the dependents left behind.	The defendant argued that the plaintiff’s claims under the statute concerning miner safety were misplaced, asserting that the statute only required the provision of props and did not obligate them to install them. Moreover, they contended that the suit was improperly brought by the administrator instead of the deceased's widow, asserting that the declaration did not sufficiently demonstrate a legal basis for negligence under common law, particularly regarding the specific duty allegedly breached.

In the case of "William Sharp v. Emma A. Sharp," decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 27, 1886, Emma A. Sharp filed for divorce against her husband, William Sharp, in Cook County. The marriage took place in 1859 and was characterized by a series of incidents involving physical violence and emotional abuse by William. The plaintiff outlined acts of extreme and repeated cruelty, including incidents where William pushed Emma out of the house, slapped her, and kicked her on different occasions. Despite such incidents occurring years apart, the court considered the ongoing emotional abuse and neglect, along with the two violent acts, as contributing to extreme cruelty. The case progressed through the circuit court, where the divorce was initially dismissed due to a supposed lack of equity. This decision was later reversed by the Appellate Court, which ordered that a decree for divorce in favor of Emma be entered. William subsequently appealed the Appellate Court's ruling to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Emma Sharp claimed her husband committed extreme and repeated cruelty, alleging specific violent acts, neglect during her illness, and overall harsh treatment throughout their marriage. She sought a decree of divorce on these grounds. Emma argued that the cumulative effect of William's behavior constituted a compelling case of cruelty that justified the dissolution of their marriage, despite the time elapsed since the last violent incident.	William Sharp defended against Emma's claims by arguing that the incidents of physical violence were either exaggerated or benign and suggested that they occurred too long ago to constitute grounds for divorce. He contended that the couple's prolonged coexistence negated claims of extreme and repeated cruelty and questioned whether Emma had condoned past offenses by continuing to live with him after the incidents in question.

The case "City Cab Company v. Thomas W. Taylor" took place in Cook County, Illinois, and was decided on January 16, 1889. The City Cab Company was the appellant, and Thomas W. Taylor was the appellee. The case involved a legal dispute in which the details leading to the case are not clearly stated in the provided description. The appellate court noted that the record lacked a clear presentation of evidence and judicial findings from the lower court, stating that it is impossible to adequately review the circumstances of the case. The majority opinion emphasized that the findings of the judge presiding over the case were final, and without specific legal propositions detailed in the bill of exceptions, the court could not render a judgment based on conjecture. Ultimately, the court’s ruling was based on procedural issues related to the proper presentation of legal claims and defenses in the record.	The City Cab Company, as the plaintiff, likely sought relief from the court, but specific claims or requests are not detailed in the case description. The company’s arguments revolved around legal propositions that they believed warranted a different outcome, which were not properly incorporated into the record.	Thomas W. Taylor, the defendant, did not provide explicit defenses in the available case summary. However, it is indicated that the court could not overturn the judgment of the County Court based on conjectured propositions, which suggests that he maintained the legitimacy of the court's previous findings and the procedural handling of the case.

Anson Root v. George Curtis is a legal case that originated in 1852 in Kane County, Illinois. The case involves a dispute over property rights related to certain lands that were mortgaged following an exchange of goods. Ambrose, a key individual involved, had judgments against him, leading to the issuance of executions on his merchandise. To secure his release from these executions, Ambrose executed a delivery bond with Root as his security and later a chattel mortgage on the goods to indemnify Root against his liability. Ambrose exchanged these goods for land, and in turn, mortgaged the land to Root. The land was later sold under execution orders, and Curtis claimed title from that sale. As the case progressed through the Illinois Supreme Court, a pivotal question arose regarding the prioritization of the liens between the mortgage held by Root and the judgments against Ambrose. The court evaluated whether the mortgage or the judgment was the elder lien, weighing the nature and intent behind the creation of the mortgage.	Anson Root, the appellant, contended that his mortgage on the lands, executed by Ambrose, should have priority over the judgments against Ambrose. He argued that the mortgage was intended to secure the purchase money for the land acquired through Ambrose's deal, thereby establishing it as the elder lien. Root requested that the court recognize the mortgage as valid and enforceable against any claims arising from the judgments on Ambrose.	George Curtis, the appellee, maintained that the mortgage held by Root was not given as security for the purchase money of the land but merely as indemnity against Root's liability related to the delivery and appeal bonds. Curtis argued that this rendered the judgments against Ambrose the elder lien. He requested that the court affirm the lower court's ruling in his favor, asserting that the legitimacy of the mortgage was invalid on its face and did not confer priority.

In January 1876, the case of Gustus Sandburg v. Peter Papineau was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a series of financial transactions and judgments involving the parties. Gustus Sandburg, the appellant, had an execution placed with the sheriff based on a judgment he held against Peter Papineau, the appellee, for $182.50. Papineau was also involved in a separate legal matter where a judgment for $35 had been made against him by Kelso & Wiley, leading to a garnishee judgment. Papineau failed to answer at a return term, resulting in a conditional judgment against him in April 1875. After paying the garnishee judgment, Papineau attempted to satisfy Sandburg's execution by tendering the remaining amount owed, minus what he had paid on the garnishee judgment. However, the sheriff and Sandburg’s attorney refused to accept the payment. Subsequently, Papineau sought a stay of execution from the circuit judge, who allowed the stay until the next court term and ultimately credited Papineau’s payment against Sandburg’s judgment. Sandburg appealed this decision, claiming that the court's actions were erroneous.	Gustus Sandburg, the plaintiff, contended that the lower court acted improperly by crediting Papineau's judgment against his execution after the latter made a payment related to the garnishee judgment. Sandburg argued that this arrangement was unjust and sought to have the court reinstate full enforcement of the original execution amount against Papineau.	Peter Papineau, the defendant, maintained that he was legally bound to pay the judgment to Kelso & Wiley to satisfy the garnishee outcome, and thus deserved a credit against Sandburg's execution for the amount paid. He argued that the court acted within its authority to ensure equitable justice by crediting the garnishee payment against the judgment and preventing Sandburg from unjustly benefitting from an execution that sought a higher amount than owed after the adjustment.

William Lindley rented a farm from William T. M. Miller, where he and his family lived and worked. The lease expired on March 1, 1871, and an installment of rent was due on February 1 but was not paid. Following this, Miller issued a landlord’s warrant to distrain for the unpaid rent. The bailiff executed this warrant by seizing livestock, during which two additional animals, a horse and a cow, followed the seized stock. Although attempts were made to prevent this, they were unsuccessful. The bailiff informed Lindley of the situation and the location of his livestock. Before filing a suit to reclaim his property, Lindley requested all of his belongings but did not specify any claimed exemptions. In response, Miller claimed he had the right to distrain due to the overdue rent. Lindley contended there were breaches of contract on Miller’s part, including failing to provide necessary building materials and labor payments. When the trial concluded, the court ruled in favor of Miller.	Lindley’s main arguments revolved around the landlord's alleged breaches of the lease, which he claimed resulted in damages. He stated that Miller did not supply materials necessary for fencing, failed to provide hedge plants, and did not plaster the farmhouse, leading to his losses. Lindley sought to have his property returned and presented these claims as a defense against Miller's warrant of distress.	Miller's defense rested on the claim that Lindley owed rent for the leased property, justifying the distress and seizure of goods. He argued that unliquidated damages from the breaches of the lease could not offset the rent owed in this proceeding. Miller maintained that since Lindley had not properly established that his damages were equal to or exceeded the amount owed for rent, the distress was lawful, and no exemption had been timely claimed.

In the case of Lewis Keith v. William P. Buck, which took place in 1885 in Illinois, the background revolves around a promissory note issued by Buck to Keith and another individual, G. W. Robinson, for the sum of $500. The note was generated after Buck faced accusations from a 14-year-old unmarried woman, Tillie Lettow, claiming he was the father of her unborn child, alongside allegations of bastardy, attempted abortion, abduction, and seduction. Buck, fearful of criminal prosecution after hearing from Lettow's attorney, O. H. Wright, agreed to settle for $1,000 under duress. In a series of events leading to the note's issuance, Keith acted as a friend and assistive figure, encouraging Buck to settle to avoid potential imprisonment. After proceedings resulted in a judgment against Buck for paying damages to Lettow, Keith sought to recover the amount through legal action on the promissory note.	Lewis Keith claimed that he was owed repayment on the promissory note given by William P. Buck after assisting him in resolving criminal charges that originated from false accusations by Tillie Lettow. He argued that the agreement was valid despite Buck's assertion that it involved compounding a crime, as he maintained that the charges were groundless and legally baseless.	William P. Buck defended against the claim by asserting that the agreement related to the promissory note was illegal due to its roots in compounding criminal charges—abortion and abduction—that had no legitimate basis. He argued that because both he and Keith were implicated in a transaction that involved handling false accusations, they should not be allowed to pursue the agreement through legal channels and that Keith should be barred from recovery due to their joint pursuit of an illegal act.

In February 1860, James T. Raleigh and Abram Heartt, as copartners, executed a promissory note for $318.38 payable to Thomas Raleigh, due on May 1 of the same year. In January 1861, the partnership was dissolved, with Thomas Raleigh receiving the partnership's assets and agreeing to pay their debts. After the dissolution, Thomas Raleigh acknowledged the arrangement and treated James T. Raleigh as his sole debtor without making a claim against Heartt. It was alleged that at the time the note was issued, Thomas Raleigh owed James T. Raleigh for board and continued to accumulate this debt while boarding with him until January 1, 1863. There were promises made by Thomas Raleigh to settle this debt and the note, which were not fulfilled, as the note remained unpaid for over two years. The case involved a suit in equity to enforce an asserted equitable set-off between the parties, following a general demurrer that had resulted in the dismissal of the case in the Superior Court of Chicago, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, James T. Raleigh and Abram Heartt, argued that there was sufficient ground for an equitable set-off regarding the promissory note due to their mutual debts. They claimed that Thomas Raleigh had treated James T. Raleigh as the sole debtor after the dissolution, and there was an understanding that the debts incurred for board during the period were implicitly to be considered payments against the note. They sought to have the court recognize this understanding and enforce the set-off against Thomas Raleigh's demand.	The defendant, Thomas Raleigh, contended that the plaintiffs had failed to present an adequate legal basis for the equitable set-off they sought. His argument included the assertion that the mere existence of cross-demands did not warrant enforcement in equity and that there was no distinct agreement to apply the debts reciprocally. He also emphasized the legal requirements to establish mutual credit and relevant circumstances for an equitable defense, suggesting that no such basis had been convincingly demonstrated.

The case took place in 1850 in Randolph County, Illinois, where Charles N. Starbird initiated a legal action against the Trustees of Schools for Township six, in South range six West. Starbird secured a judgment against the trustees before a justice of the peace. One of the trustees sought to appeal the judgment to the Circuit Court. However, a motion was filed to dismiss the appeal, claiming the appeal bond was insufficient. The Circuit Court agreed to dismiss the appeal, leading the trustees to appeal this dismissal to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking a reversal of the decision. The proceedings highlighted issues regarding the validity and execution of the appeal bond, with references to prior case law influencing the court’s interpretation of obligations in appeal bonds.	Starbird argued that the appeal taken by the trustees was invalid due to the alleged deficiency in the appeal bond. He sought to have the court dismiss the trustees' appeal based on this lack of a sufficient bond, effectively upholding the judgment rendered in his favor by the justice of the peace.	The trustees contended that the Circuit Court's dismissal of their appeal was erroneous. They maintained that the bond had been accepted by the proper officer and that any deficiencies could be rectified. They requested the court to allow them to amend the bond to ensure it was compliant and sufficient for the appeal to be heard.

In 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Ferdinand Siegel and Seth F. Hanchett regarding a replevin bond. The case focused on the question of damages related to attorney's fees after a failed replevin suit. The original replevin suit was resolved on its merits after a second trial, but the plaintiffs sought to recover costs, including attorney's fees, associated with both trials. A jury was instructed to consider these fees in their assessment of damages. However, while evidence of the customary fees for the second trial was presented, there was no proof indicating that a retainer was paid or that any agreement existed for the attorney's compensation during that trial. The case referenced previous legal precedents regarding the implications of attorney's fees in similar contexts, specifically the liabilities incurred because of a bond's conditions. Ultimately, the court found that the attendance of the attorney raised a presumption of retainer and financial liability for the defendant.	The plaintiffs, Ferdinand Siegel et al., primarily argued that they were entitled to recover attorney's fees as part of the damages assessed in their action of debt on the replevin bond. They requested the court to instruct the jury to award these customary fees, asserting that such costs were included within the statutory condition of the bond, which required the payment of all costs and damages from wrongfully suing out the writ. They maintained that the evidence of fees incurred during the trials established their right to compensation for legal representation.	The defendant, Seth F. Hanchett, contended that the bond's condition did not cover attorney's fees for services rendered in defeating the replevin suit. They argued that absent proof of actual payment or a prior agreement to pay the attorney fees for the second trial, such allowances should not be granted. The defense maintained that liability for attorney's fees without evidence of payment was not warranted under the existing legal framework guiding damages and bond issues.

William H. Herron filed a legal case against Samuel L. Gill, the sheriff of Peoria County, regarding a dispute over the recovery of unpaid rent. The events leading to the case took place in Peoria, Illinois, with the originating circumstances unfolding around July 14, 1882. Herron had been the landlord of a tenant, Marvin A. Breed, who operated a general merchandise business with a stock of goods in Herron's rented store. At that time, Herron was owed $1,364.83 for rent. On July 14, 1882, Herron issued a distress warrant to Gill, instructing him to seize Breed's goods to satisfy his rent claim. However, prior to the issuance of this warrant, several judgments against Breed had been entered in the County Court of Peoria, resulting in execution warrants being issued to Gill on July 13, which had priority over the distress warrant. Consequently, when Gill acted on the distress warrant, the goods had already been claimed due to these earlier judgments. After legal proceedings, the Appellate Court affirmed the prior rulings, highlighting the complexities arising from the interconnection of landlord liens and existing creditor claims.	Herron argued that he had a lien on Breed's goods for the unpaid rent, based on the provisions for landlord liens in the statutes. He contended that since the goods had been in his tenant’s possession and were subject to the distress warrant he issued, he should be able to recover his owed rent from the proceeds of the sale of those goods. Herron sought a ruling that would compel Gill to pay him the amount owed from the assets of Breed that Gill had as sheriff.	In response, Gill maintained that he correctly acted upon the existing judgments against Breed which had already established liens on the assets before Herron's distress warrant was issued. He argued that according to Illinois law, specifically referencing the statutes regarding landlord liens, Herron had no legal priority over the goods already subjected to execution from those earlier judgments. Therefore, Gill contended that he could not satisfy Herron’s claim from the proceeds of the goods.

In 1835, Daniel Stringer initiated a legal action against John Smith and William Smith in the Sangamon Circuit Court, Illinois. The case involved an action of assumpsit and was overseen by Honorable Thomas Ford. After the Circuit Court trial, the court rendered a judgment in favor of the plaintiffs (Smiths) for a sum of $66.88. Stringer appealed this decision, seeking to reverse the judgment made by the Circuit Court without a jury's involvement. The appeal raised procedural questions regarding the legitimacy of the exceptions to the judgment by the defendants' counsel. The case drew comparisons to a previous decision in Swafford v. Dovenor, reinforcing legal precedents concerning trial procedures and the role of evidence in court judgments.	The plaintiffs, John Smith and William Smith, contended that the Circuit Court's ruling, awarding them $66.88, was justified based on the evidence presented regarding the assumpsit claim. They maintained that the court properly conducted the trial without a jury and upheld its judgment correctly despite the defendant's objections. Their primary legal request was for the judgment to be upheld on appeal.	The defendant, Daniel Stringer, argued that the exceptions taken against the Circuit Court's judgment were valid. His legal counsel claimed that the judgment on the facts proven and the law cited was improperly handled, warranting a reevaluation or a new trial. Stringer's defense was focused on procedural grounds, suggesting that a proper course of action had not been followed in challenging the Circuit Court’s decision.

The case "Julius Bauer et al. v. Joseph Bell" took place in September 1874 in Chicago, Illinois. The background of the case involves Joseph Bell, the plaintiff, who accused Julius and Herman Bauer, the defendants, of trespassing by breaking into his home. The incident involved the defendants forcibly opening the outer door of Bell’s house, breaking it, damaging furniture, and stealing a valuable piano. The case arose from a disagreement over the ownership of the piano, which the Bauers contended was rented while Bell maintained it had been sold to him and fully paid for. The jury, after evaluating conflicting testimonies regarding the sale or rental of the piano, affirmed that it was sold to Bell. The trial presented questions about the defendants' involvement in the trespass, with evidence suggesting that the Bauers directed the actions taken against Bell, despite their denial of involvement. The jury ultimately found the Bauers guilty, leading to a claim for damages.	Joseph Bell claimed that Julius and Herman Bauer committed trespass by illegally entering his home, damaging property, and stealing his piano. He argued that the piano was his property, having been sold to him and fully paid for prior to the incident. Bell sought compensation for the damages incurred from the unlawful entry and removal of his property.	Julius and Herman Bauer denied any wrongdoing, asserting that they were not involved in the trespass nor did they instruct anyone to take the piano. They contended that the instrument was rented, not sold, and contested the jury's finding, claiming that there was insufficient evidence to warrant the verdict against them. Their defense focused on the nature of the contract concerning the piano's ownership, insisting that the jury made an erroneous judgment regarding their involvement.

In 1867, in Tazewell County, Illinois, William J. Estep and others (plaintiffs) entered into a contract with William H. Fenton and others (defendants), who were trustees of a church organization, to construct a church edifice. The plaintiffs initiated an action of assumpsit to recover payment for their work after the church building was destroyed by fire shortly after its alleged completion. Though there was no formal acceptance of the building, evidence showed that trustees had allowed activities such as Sunday school and a funeral service to occur in it, which the plaintiffs argued indicated acceptance. Conversely, the defendants claimed the work was not completed per contract specifications, citing issues like structural faults and poor-quality materials. The case was initially tried in the Mason Circuit Court and later in the Tazewell County circuit court, where the jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding $1,003.60. The defendants appealed this decision, arguing that jury instructions regarding the acceptance and performance of the contract were misleading.	The plaintiffs argued that they had completed the church building as per the contractual agreement and that the presence of church activities indicated formal acceptance. They sought payment for their services based on the value of the work performed, asserting that the absence of explicit objections from the defendants regarding the quality of the work constituted acceptance.	The defendants contended there was no formal acceptance of the work and that the construction was not done according to the contract, citing numerous structural deficiencies. They claimed that the plaintiffs failed to deliver materials and workmanship of the quality agreed upon, and asserted that, while the building was used by the trustees, it did not exempt them from claiming damages for inadequate performance.

In the case of Christian Farni et al. v. Edward P. Tesson et al., which was decided in September 1869 by the Illinois Supreme Court, the events leading up to the case involved a judgment that Tesson and Danjin obtained against Boutcam and Carey. An execution was issued and levied on property, but the defendants obtained an injunction against the sheriff, resulting in the release of the personal property. The original injunction bond was found to be defective, leading to a motion from the defendants to dissolve the injunction in early 1858. The complainants filed a new bond later that month, but the record did not clearly show that the leave to file this bond was granted. The court heard a motion to dissolve the injunction in March of that year but ultimately did not allow it. It was not until the following October when the motion to dissolve was granted, leading the complainants to dismiss their bill. This case centers around the second bond filed by the complainants and whether it was valid since it was claimed that it was filed without proper authority. The court ultimately had to decide on the validity of bonds presented and the responsibility of the parties involved in this legal procedure.	The plaintiffs in this case argued that the second bond they filed was valid and necessary due to the defects in the first bond that led to the injunction being challenged. They contended that even though there was no formal order allowing the filing of the second bond, the court's refusal to dissolve the injunction suggested that it accepted this bond. The plaintiffs sought to maintain their suit and hold the defendants accountable for denying the validity of their own actions regarding the bond.	The defendants contended that the second bond was improperly filed and not authorized by the court. They maintained that since the bond was inadequate and that the plaintiffs filed it without the court's approval, they should not be allowed to claim its validity. The defendants argued that their right to have the injunction dissolved was supported by the original defects present in the bond.

In September 1872, in Hasi-iville, Illinois, Lewis M. Phillips initiated legal action against Morris Meyers regarding a promissory note. This note stipulated that if Morris Meyers were to become intoxicated, mistreat, or abuse his wife, Minnie Meyers, he would owe Phillips the sum of $600, intended for Minnie, plus interest. The backdrop of the case involves a tumultuous marriage characterized by Morris's habitual drunkenness and cruelty towards Minnie, leading her to file for divorce. As part of the ongoing divorce proceedings, an agreement was made where Minnie would dismiss her suit and return to live with Morris under the condition that he would cease his abusive behavior. In the lower court, the defense claimed the agreement lacked sufficient consideration due to its relation to an ongoing marital issue. The case subsequently grappled with whether the existence of this agreement and the promise to treat Minnie better constituted valid legal consideration.	Lewis M. Phillips argued that the promissory note was valid, asserting that it was based on sufficient consideration stemming from Morris Meyers’ agreement to stop mistreating his wife. Phillips contended that the consideration for the note was indeed present because Minnie dismissed her divorce suit and agreed to return to Morris, thereby forming a legitimate basis for the financial obligation outlined in the note.	Morris Meyers contended that the promissory note lacked legal enforceability due to insufficient consideration, claiming that the agreement was merely based on Minnie returning to live with him. The defense argued that any promise made by Minnie was not a valid basis for enforcing the financial obligation as it was tied to their marital arrangement, which traditionally isn't enforceable under law.

The case, titled "The City of Chicago v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. David L. DeGolyer et al.," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. The dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, concerning a contractual agreement between the City of Chicago and the contractor, David L. DeGolyer, for street improvement work. The contract was established on October 12, 1866, stipulating that payment would be made from the proceeds of special assessments levied at the time of the contract and any future assessments. The city failed to collect sufficient funds to pay the contractor because it did not obtain judgment on some part of the special assessments. At the time of the proceedings in December 1867, while the city was in the process of making additional assessments to cover any deficits, the contractor sought a writ of mandamus to compel the city to pay for the work completed. The main controversy stemmed from the city’s alleged failure to comply with payment obligations under the contract due to issues in collecting the special assessments.	The plaintiff, represented by David L. DeGolyer, claimed that the City of Chicago owed payment for street improvement work based on the agreed contractual terms, which specified that the contractor would be compensated from special assessments. The contractor argued that, despite some complications in collecting the assessments, the city was liable for payment as the funds were deemed collectible. The request included a peremptory writ of mandamus to compel the city to honor its financial obligations.	The City of Chicago defended itself by emphasizing adherence to the contractual stipulations, arguing that the contractor had agreed to seek payment only from the proceeds of special assessments. The city pointed out that it was actively working to collect these assessments, and the deficiencies in payment were acknowledged as part of the contract's terms. Furthermore, the city cited that it was proceeding in good faith with due diligence to rectify any shortfall and had plans to seek judgment on the necessary assessments, disputing any claims of negligence or bad faith.

The case of "William B. Smith v. Lewis W. Dauel," decided on November 30, 1888, took place in McLean County, Illinois. William B. Smith, the plaintiff, initiated an action of replevin against Lewis W. Dauel, a constable. The background of the case indicates that Dauel held two writs of execution against Smith. As the head of a family, Smith submitted a schedule of his personal property to Dauel, following legal procedures. However, when the appraisement was scheduled, Smith was absent from his home, having taken part of his property (horses, buggy, and harness) with him on a trip to Lexington, approximately eight miles away. The appraisers appointed by Dauel assessed the property's value without his presence and without adequately examining all the scheduled items. The appraisement was performed when a portion of the scheduled property was absent, and the valuation was found to exceed the actual worth of the items listed. Smith contended that he was unaware of the appraisement and that the whole procedure lacked the necessary legal compliance, prompting his demand for the return of his property.	Smith's principal argument was that the appraisement conducted in his absence, without proper notice, was invalid under the law. He asserted that the constable failed to comply with the requirement to summon appraisers without delay and to ensure that all scheduled property was present during the valuation. As a result of these failures, the plaintiff requested the return of his property, arguing that the incorrect appraisal did not provide lawful grounds for the subsequent levy on his assets.	Dauel, the defendant, argued that he followed the necessary procedures and obligations related to the execution. He claimed that the appraisers were summoned appropriately, and the plaintiff was sufficiently notified about the proceedings. The defense contended that Smith had not violated any legal duties, suggesting that the claimed irregularities did not undermine the validity of the appraisement. Dauel ultimately sought to uphold the actions taken under the execution as proper and lawful.

The case Sangamon Coal Mining Company, for use, etc., v. E. H. C. Richardson et al. was decided on June 14, 1889, by the Illinois Appellate Court. It emerged from the city of Chicago, Cook County, Illinois, involving the plaintiff, Sangamon Coal Mining Company, and defendants E. H. C. Richardson and others. The plaintiff was seeking to recover certain liabilities from the defendants, who were shareholders of the company, through a garnishment proceeding. The garnishment was initiated after a judgment had been rendered against the company in favor of creditors Charles W. Merriam, Isaac S. Collins, and George W. Dexter, whose execution was returned unsatisfied. The plaintiff claimed these shareholders owed unpaid sums on the shares of stock that they held in the company. However, the defendants admitted to being stockholders but contended that the full subscription price had been settled through the conveyance of property and business interests to the company, which was accepted in full payment. Disputes arose regarding the valuation of this property, with evidence indicating that it was potentially undervalued. The court's task was to ascertain whether garnishment could proceed given these claims and defenses.	The Sangamon Coal Mining Company claimed that the defendants, as stockholders, were liable for unpaid balances on their shares. The company argued that despite receiving property as full payment, the value of this property was inadequate and thus the defendants should still owe money. The plaintiff’s claim primarily revolved around the notion that the garnishees (defendants) could not claim that their subscription agreements absolved them of all financial responsibility to creditors.	The defendants countered that when they subscribed to the stock, they provided property of substantial value as payment, which the company accepted in good faith as full payment for their shares. They asserted that the company had no right to pursue them for additional payments since all obligations were satisfied at the time of the stock subscription. They argued that the garnishment could not legally be pursued until the original stock payment agreement was set aside, which had not occurred. The defendants emphasized the absence of any obligation to pay more unless an authorized demand for payment arose, which had not happened.

The case "City of Joliet v. Helena Gerber" took place in 1884 in Joliet, Illinois. The incident involved Helena Gerber, the plaintiff, who sustained injuries while walking on a sidewalk on the west side of Chicago Street. On June 25, 1884, Gerber fell after a plank on the sidewalk shifted and caused her to trip. She was accompanied by her husband and two children, who had previously walked over the same sidewalk without incident just two hours before the accident. While Gerber claimed the sidewalk was in a dangerous condition due to loose planks, not all witnesses agreed with her account. Some witnesses testified that they had not observed any loose planks on the sidewalk during their frequent use. The city's authorities denied having prior notice of a defect in the sidewalk's condition. The Circuit Court of Will County presided over the case, leading to a trial that resulted in a jury verdict awarding Gerber $8,500 for her injuries. The appeal challenged the evidence's sufficiency to prove the city had notice of the sidewalk’s dangerous condition.	Helena Gerber, the plaintiff, contended that the City of Joliet was liable for her injuries due to the dangerous condition of the sidewalk. Her claims included that the city allowed the sidewalk to become defective and that she fell while exercising ordinary care while walking. Gerber sought damages for her physical injuries and the mental anguish resulting from the fall, arguing that the city failed to maintain the sidewalk and was therefore responsible for her injuries.	The City of Joliet, the defendant, argued that there was no evidence demonstrating that the city had prior notice of any defects in the sidewalk that would warrant liability. The defense maintained that most witnesses had daily access to the sidewalk and failed to observe any dangerous conditions. They claimed that the city should not be held liable since it was not aware of any issues and that Gerber's fall occurred without any prior indications of danger. The defendant requested that the court reverse the judgment granted to Gerber.

In 1871, a legal dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving plaintiffs George Steele and others against defendant E. A. Buck. The case centered on a bond related to a charter-party agreement made in 1869 between Charles Vogell and William B. Crandall, who were designated as the principal parties, and Steele, who served as surety. The charter-party stipulated that Vogell and Crandall were to have exclusive use of the propeller named "Equator" for the 1869 navigation season, with the obligation to pay a designated fee and return the vessel in good condition at the end of the season. The plaintiffs alleged that Vogell and Crandall failed to fulfill their obligations by not returning the vessel as agreed. During the navigation season, the Equator was lost in a storm, with no negligence or fault attributed to the charterers, raising the question of whether they were excused from their obligation due to the destruction of the vessel by acts of God. The court's reject of evidence related to the storm and vessel's loss became pivotal in the trial.	The plaintiffs claimed that Vogell and Crandall breached the charter-party by failing to pay the stipulated sums for the vessel and by not returning the propeller at the end of the navigation season. They sought damages from Steele, the surety who promised to secure performance of the obligations of the charter-party. Their main argument hinged on the interpretation of the bond's covenant, insisting that the loss of the vessel did not absolve the defendants of their contractual responsibilities.	The defendants argued that the destruction of the vessel was due to an act of God, which, according to legal precedents, should excuse them from performance of the contract. They contended that the impossibility of returning the propeller, owing to its sinking in a storm without any fault on their part, negated their obligation under the bond. The defense maintained that justice and reason dictated that liability should rest with the party who agreed to bear the risk, and they claimed this should apply to their case.

In the case of Ferdinand B. Hubbard v. Solomon Hubbard et al., adjudicated in September 1871 by the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute traces back to a judgment amounting to sixteen hundred dollars that Renselaer M. Firman had secured against Ferdinand B. Hubbard in the Whiteside Circuit Court during the October term of 1861. This judgment was awarded based on an arbitration conducted by Solomon Hubbard, who was mutually chosen by the parties involved. The crux of the arbitration was to determine the amount owed by Hubbard to Firman concerning a land transaction. Hubbard contended that at the time of the submission, Solomon Hubbard had a vested interest in the outcome, which led him to keep this arrangement secret from him, amounting to fraud. After unsuccessful previous attempts to contest the award through legal pleas, Hubbard filed a bill in chancery to prevent the collection of Firman’s judgment, asserting that he was deprived of the testimony necessary to challenge the fraud until after his case had reached the higher court. The case sparked considerable contention regarding the supposed conflict of interest of the arbitrator and the legitimacy of the award against him.	Ferdinand B. Hubbard, the plaintiff, argued that Solomon Hubbard, acting as an arbitrator, did not provide notice to the involved parties about the hearing, which he claimed violated fairness protocols. He further alleged that Solomon had a hidden interest in the arbitration that influenced the outcome, thus rendering the judgment obtained through the award fraudulent. Hubbard sought to enjoin the collection of the judgment against him based on these claims.	In response, Solomon Hubbard and the other defendants maintained that Hubbard was aware of his interest in the matter submitted for arbitration when he selected him as the arbitrator. They argued that any claims regarding the lack of notice or other grievances could have been raised during the original trial about the award. The defendants asserted that the award was legitimate and not influenced by undue factors, emphasizing that Hubbard consented to Solomon's arbitration under circumstances he himself understood.

In December 1853, the case of William B. Warren v. The President and Trustees of the Town of Jacksonville was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered on a piece of land described as lying in the west half of the northeast quarter of Section 20 in Township 15, Range 10 West, near Jacksonville, Illinois. The land was initially owned by Joseph Duncan, who lost ownership following a judgment against him in June 1841, which led to the land being sold to Warren by the United States Marshal in October 1847. Historical agreements regarding the land indicated that a portion, known as Railroad Square, was to be kept open for public use and that streets running through it should remain unobstructed. The court was tasked with determining whether the land had been effectively dedicated as a public street through prior agreements and actions, as the community had used it for over seven years. Several critical legal instructions given to the jury were challenged, particularly concerning the concept of dedication by prior landowners, and the jurors ultimately found in favor of the defendants, the town trustees.	Warren claimed ownership of the contested land, arguing that it had not been dedicated for public use and that he had not consented to its conversion into a public street by the town of Jacksonville. He sought recognition of his property rights and argued that the land could not be taken for public use without due compensation.	The defendants, representing the Town of Jacksonville, contended that the land had effectively been dedicated as a public street through historical agreements and long-standing public use. They argued that the established public use of the land over many years demonstrated an implied dedication and that the prior owners had acquiesced to this use. They requested the court to affirm the jury's finding, thereby validating the public's right to use the land as a street.

James Q. Palmer filed a legal case against David M. Bethard and others in January 1873, in the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a partnership that was formed in 1864. The partnership lasted until a partial settlement in 1866, but no final settlement occurred. Palmer claimed he was misled during a subsequent settlement that indicated he owed money to Bethard. After he paid $2000, Bethard sued him for the remaining balance. Palmer lost both trials held in November 1871. He later sought to set aside the judgment against him, claiming he discovered new evidence showing errors in the earlier accounting. However, he was not present at the last trial and failed to act sooner despite having access to partnership documents. The court noted that Palmer's delay in addressing the issues and his lack of diligence over the four years between the dissolution of the partnership and the judgment were significant factors in the outcome of the case.	Palmer's main arguments were that the judgment against him was unjust due to the discovery of new evidence, which he claimed revealed mistakes in the partnership accounting that were not available during the trials. He also argued that he was misled by Bethard's attorney regarding the timing of the trial, which contributed to his inability to defend himself adequately.	Bethard and the other defendants contended that Palmer had ample time and opportunity to present his defense and that the failure to do so was a result of his own negligence. They emphasized that the alleged new evidence was not sufficient to warrant overturning the judgment, as Palmer had free access to the books and had four years to discover any errors prior to the trial.

In 1853, Patrick Halligan leased the United States Hotel and outhouses to Thomas J. Wade in Peru, Illinois, for a term of five years, agreeing on a rent of $650 per year for the first two years and $750 for the last three, payable quarterly in advance. In early 1852, Halligan sold a portion of the land to the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company, which subsequently entered the leased premises, affecting Wade's ability to operate the hotel. Wade, who occupied the premises from the winter of 1851-2, paid rent regularly until July 1, 1853. Upon his refusal to pay the quarter's rent due on that date, Halligan initiated legal proceedings against Wade to recover the amount. The case proceeded in the Circuit Court of LaSalle in February 1858, where evidence was presented regarding the condition of the leased property and the disturbances caused by surrounding businesses. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Wade, asserting that Halligan's actions had effectively evicted him from a portion of the premises, thus entitling Wade to damages and a reduction in rent.	Halligan claimed that despite any disturbances caused by other tenants in the building, Wade was obligated to pay the full rent for the hotel as he continued to occupy the premises when the quarter's rent was due. He argued that the lease agreement obligating Wade to pay rent remained valid regardless of any actions taken by Halligan or surrounding disturbances, and sought the total amount due along with interest.	Wade contended that Halligan’s sale of a substantial part of the leased premises to the railroad company constituted an eviction, which discharged him from any obligation to pay rent. He argued that Halligan’s subsequent actions and the disturbance caused by surrounding businesses adversely affected his ability to run the hotel, thus justifying his non-payment of the rent.

In 1852, in Stark County, Illinois, William W. Low purchased corn from Peter Forbes, with an agreement that Low would provide the sacks needed for sacking the corn, while Forbes would deliver the corn in those sacks. Low failed to furnish the sacks as agreed, leading to a dispute over whether Forbes was obliged to deliver the corn in bulk. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court on appeal from the Stark Circuit Court. The central issue was whether the seller, Forbes, could be excused from delivering the corn because the buyer, Low, did not provide the sacks. The court examined a precedent case, McKee v. Retter, to determine the obligations of both parties when the buyer fails to meet their part of the agreement.	The plaintiff, William W. Low, argued that even though he did not furnish the sacks, Peter Forbes still had an obligation to deliver the corn as per their contractual agreement. He claimed that the failure to provide the sacks did not exempt Forbes from delivering the corn and sought a reversal of the judgment that had not favored him in the lower court.	Peter Forbes, the defendant, contended that Low's failure to furnish the sacks excused him from delivering the corn. He argued that without the sacks, he was not required to provide the corn in any form, thus standing by the initial judgment made by the Stark Circuit Court. He sought to retain both the corn and the payments made by Low, asserting that the buyer's neglect absolved him of further obligations.

The case, "Robert Holloway et al. v. John Clark," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1861. The dispute originated from an ejectment action commenced by the plaintiffs, Robert Holloway and others, against John Clark to recover possession of land located in Warren County, Illinois, specifically the southwestern quarter of section 17, township 8 north, range 3 west. The legal proceedings began on May 28, 1857, when the plaintiffs claimed ownership based on a regular title originating from a government patent and a subsequent deed from James W. Perkins, who was the heir of a deceased title holder. The plaintiffs argued that they possessed a valid and uninterrupted chain of title dating back to October 6, 1847. The defendant, John Clark, sought to challenge this title by presenting various deeds, including tax sale deeds purporting to convey the title based on tax payments he claimed made from 1849 to 1856. The circuit court found in favor of the defendant, leading the plaintiffs to file for an appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed rightful ownership of the disputed land, asserting the validity of their title stemming from a government patent and subsequent conveyances. They presented evidence to demonstrate that their title was legally vested in their ancestor, James W. Perkins, who had the patent title prior to the tax sales claimed by the defendant. They contended that proper notice and legal processes associated with the tax sales were not followed and sought a judgment to confirm their possession and defend against any claims from the defendant.	The defendant, John Clark, maintained that he had valid claim and color of title through his possession of tax deeds and quit-claim deeds tracing back to tax sales conducted for unpaid taxes from the late 1830s and early 1840s. He argued that these deeds, alongside his record of tax payments, constituted sufficient legal grounds to claim ownership of the land. The defendant contended that the plaintiffs' prior claims were nullified by the redemption of taxes made by Perkins, which he argued had no effect on his title.

In 1835, a legal case known as "Cyrus Felt, plaintiff in error v. Wesley Williams, defendant in error" was held in Hancock County, Illinois. The case was tried in the Hancock Circuit Court before Judge Richard M. Young. The plaintiff, Wesley Williams, initiated an action of detinue against the defendant, Cyrus Felt, seeking the return of a cow described as "a large red cow with a white face." During the trial, Williams presented a witness who asserted that the cow did not match that description, stating instead that the animal was "a yellow or sorrel cow." This testimony raised questions about the accuracy of the description provided by Williams in his claim. The defendant, Felt, contended that there was a significant discrepancy between the description of the cow in the plaintiff's declaration and the evidence presented, leading him to request the court to instruct the jury to find in his favor. The trial court denied this request, which became a point of contention as the case progressed.	Wesley Williams, the plaintiff, argued that he had lawful rights to the specific cow in question, defined as a "large red cow with a white face." He sought to establish ownership of this cow based on his declaration but faced challenges regarding the accuracy of his description as demonstrated by witness testimony.	Cyrus Felt, the defendant, argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiff regarding the identity of the cow was insufficient due to a clear discrepancy between the description in the plaintiff's declaration and the witness's testimony. He contended that the court should have ruled in his favor because the testimony failed to support the claim for the specific cow demanded by the plaintiff.

The case "The United States Rolling Stock Company v. Conrad Wilder" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court and decided on January 25, 1886. The events leading to this case occurred in Cook County, Illinois, where Conrad Wilder, the plaintiff, claimed damages against the United States Rolling Stock Company. Wilder had suffered a significant injury, specifically the loss of his hand, during an incident in which he served as a switchman for the defendant's operations. He alleged that the injury resulted from the negligence of the company in retaining an incompetent engineer, Guernsey, who had been promoted from a lesser role despite being unfit for the responsibilities of operating the locomotive. The issues raised included whether the company knew—or should have known—of Guernsey's incompetence and whether such negligence directly contributed to Wilder's accident. A trial was held in the Superior Court of Cook County, resulting in a verdict favoring Wilder with an award of $5,000. The defendant appealed the decision, leading to a review by the Appellate Court, which affirmed the judgment, prompting the case to reach the Illinois Supreme Court.	Conrad Wilder, the plaintiff, asserted that the United States Rolling Stock Company was negligent in retaining an unqualified engineer in its employment. He claimed that the company's knowledge of the engineer's incompetence led to a hazardous working environment, culminating in his injury. Wilder sought damages for the loss of his hand, arguing that he had not contributed to his own negligence and that the circumstances of the accident were due solely to the company's failure to maintain a safe workplace.	The United States Rolling Stock Company contended that Wilder was partly responsible for his injury due to contributory negligence. They argued that Wilder should have been aware of the risks associated with working with the engineer and that he had not exercised reasonable care to ascertain the engineer's capabilities. The defendant requested the court to instruct the jury on the issue of contributory negligence, suggesting that Wilder might have been able to discover the engineer's incompetence with reasonable diligence.

The case revolves around the First National Bank of Shawneetown and its dispute with tax collectors Joel Cook and Elias Ulmsnider regarding tax assessments. Filed in 1875 in Gallatin County, Illinois, the bank sought to prevent the collection of taxes it believed were unlawfully assessed. The bank contended that the county assessor, A.K. McCabe, had raised the valuation of its stock from $40 to $100 without proper notice or consent, effectively increasing its tax burden. Initially, the shares of stock were assessed at a value accepted by their owners, but subsequent actions by the assessor and the county board led to an increased assessment against the bank. Moreover, a meeting of the county board that later corrected the assessment failed to occur in a legally prescribed timeframe, further complicating the situation. The bank argued that such actions constituted a fraud on the board's part and sought relief from the courts.	The First National Bank of Shawneetown claimed that its tax assessments were illegal because the county assessor had changed the values without proper notice to the bank or the owners of the shares. The bank sought an injunction to stop the collection of these taxes, arguing that they should only be required to pay taxes based on the initially accepted assessment of $40 per share, as revised by the State Board of Equalization.	Defendants Joel Cook and Elias Ulmsnider contended that the actions taken by the assessor and the county board to adjust tax assessments were lawful and that the bank was properly informed of the changes. They argued that the court lacked the authority to interfere with these tax assessments and maintained that the tax collection should proceed as calculated.

William Schilling filed a legal case against Emil Rosenheim in 1889 in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose from an agreement involving a tailor named Beckman, who was to make Schilling a suit of clothes using cloth provided by Schilling. Schilling asserted that he had no direct dealings with Rosenheim, as he believed Beckman was acting solely as a coat maker. Beckman and Rosenheim had an arrangement where Beckman sought prices from Rosenheim to fulfill Schilling's order. The essential testimony revolved around whether Rosenheim's cutter, who took Schilling's measurements, was acting on behalf of Beckman or whether Beckman had the authority to bind Schilling to a contract. The case presented issues of agency and authority, and the court initially instructed the jury to disregard certain evidence concerning conversations between Schilling and Beckman when Rosenheim was not present, which became a pivotal point in the court proceedings.
