The defendant, Illinois Central Railroad Company, argued that Othneile Cox was a fellow-servant working under their employment at the time of the accident and that any negligence resulting in his death was due to his own carelessness or that of other servants, for which the company could not be held liable. The defendant contended that they had employed competent personnel, and therefore, were not responsible for the acts of negligence committed by their employees during the course of their work.

The case of The Chicago and North Western Railway Company v. The Board of Supervisors of Lee County took place in April 1867 in Lee County, Illinois. The case involved the Chicago and North Western Railway Company (the plaintiff) appealing a judgment from the Circuit Court of Lee County that was in favor of the board of supervisors (the defendant). The central issue was related to the valuation of railroad property for taxation purposes. The plaintiff argued that under the revenue law of 1855, the real estate owned by the railroad should be valued only as land, disregarding any enhancements made to it for railway use, such as grading or laying tracks. However, the court found that the law required the railroad company's property, including the improvements, to be assessed at its full value. The case presented implications around property valuation and taxation for railroads in the context of Illinois law.	The Chicago and North Western Railway Company claimed that under the revenue law of 1855, their property should be assessed only as land, without considering any improvements made for railroad purposes. They sought a judgment that would require the property to be valued without regard to costs incurred for its preparation and use as a railroad right-of-way.	The Board of Supervisors of Lee County argued that the law mandates that the property occupied by the railroad, along with any improvements made upon it, should be valued fully for taxation. They contended that the statute specifically requires a detailed description of the property and its assessed value, which includes all enhancements made to it for railroad operations.

In 1885, the legal case "Elizabeth A. Bergen v. Henry Keiser" took place in Illinois. The dispute arose when Elizabeth Bergen's husband purchased a meal dryer and made improvements to a mill owned by Elizabeth using funds from his insolvent business, Bergen & Co. Elizabeth had traded her property in Jacksonville for three lots in Minier, where the mill was situated. Although there was no formal agreement regarding the mill's operations, it was generally understood that the family's livelihood would rely on the mill's earnings. The defendant, Henry Keiser, installed the meal dryer and conducted repairs at a cost of $649.82, which was to be paid upon completion. Elizabeth claimed she never authorized the purchase and was unaware of the contract terms, yet she was present during the installation and expressed satisfaction with the work. The issue was whether Elizabeth could be held liable for her husband's actions given her lack of formal consent and his financial insolvency.	Elizabeth Bergen, the plaintiff, argued that she did not authorize her husband to purchase the meal dryer and that she should not be held liable for the costs associated with the improvements made to the mill. She claimed that her husband acted beyond his authority in entering the contract with Keiser and that, therefore, the court should protect her from liability.	Henry Keiser, the defendant, contended that he acted in good faith believing that Elizabeth's husband was authorized to order the repairs and improvements to the mill. He argued that Elizabeth was aware of the work being done and did not object at any point, thereby implying her approval of her husband's actions. Keiser maintained that Elizabeth's silence amounted to consent, which made her liable for the debt incurred from the improvements.

Edward Hempstead filed a case against John W. Humphrey in 1865, after a judgment by confession was entered on a promissory note that was overdue by more than a year. The case took place in Stephenson County, Illinois, presided over by Judge Benjamin R. Sheldon. The judgment was made in vacation—without a full court session—and there was no evidence presented to confirm that the defendant, Humphrey, was alive or that the debt still existed. Following the judgment, a motion was filed to vacate and set aside the judgment due to the lack of proof regarding the defendant’s status and the debt. The court allowed the motion, relying on precedents from previous cases, notably Hinds v. Hopkins, which insisted on certain procedural requirements before a judgment could be made. However, during the proceedings, the court acknowledged that its earlier ruling in Hinds v. Hopkins was misapplied, particularly regarding the need for evidence of a meritorious defense.	The plaintiff, Edward Hempstead, argued that the judgment by confession against John W. Humphrey was improperly entered due to the lack of evidence that the defendant was alive and that the debt remained unpaid. Hempstead sought to have the judgment confirmed based on these procedural failings, claiming the judgment should not stand without proper verification of the defendant's status and the legitimacy of the debt owed.	John W. Humphrey, the defendant, contended that the judgment was not valid due to the absence of necessary evidence and procedures required for such a confession judgment. He requested that the judgment be vacated so that he could present a defense, asserting that there were significant legal implications surrounding the lack of an order from a judge for the confession judgment.

The case "Rock Island & Peoria Ry. Co. v. Reed" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on April 5, 1886. The dispute arose in Stark County, where the plaintiff, Reed, a local farmer, claimed that the Rock Island and Peoria Railway Company, the defendant, was negligent in its maintenance of its railway track. Reed alleged that his horse was killed when it wandered onto the railway tracks due to the absence of a proper fence separating his corn and livestock fields from the railway. The railway track was constructed through Reed's property, and the lack of a sufficient fence allowed the horse to access the tracks, leading to the unfortunate incident. The situation resulted in Reed seeking compensation for the loss of his horse, valued at $160, from the railway company. The case progressed to the Stark Circuit Court, where the jury was presented with the evidence, and the instructions were fully and fairly given. The court ultimately found in favor of Reed.	The plaintiff, Reed, claimed that the Rock Island and Peoria Railway Company was negligent for failing to construct and maintain a suitable and sufficient fence along its tracks that would prevent livestock from straying onto the railway. He sought compensation for the value of his horse, which he asserted had been killed as a direct result of this negligence.	The defendant, Rock Island and Peoria Railway Company, contended that they had fulfilled their obligations regarding safety and maintenance. They likely argued that the absence of a fence did not constitute negligence, suggesting that Reed bore some responsibility for not adequately protecting his livestock. The railway company sought to overturn the previous judgment and ultimately retain the claim of not being liable for the horse's death.

On March 23, 1859, in Illinois, Samuel Wood executed a mortgage to Denison K. Town to secure a payment of $2,856.47 related to a farm. Shortly after, Wood transferred the land to his sons, who subsequently sold it to Town for $12,525, with the mortgage considered paid as part of the sale. The mortgage consisted of several items, including a $621.50 balance on an old mortgage and a $600 amount that Town was to pay for Wood regarding certain executions owed to Constable Turner. Town claimed that he was released from the obligation to pay the $600 by a later agreement with Wood and also sought to release Wood from another debt. When Wood initiated a lawsuit against Town for not paying the $600, it led to a jury verdict against Town for $1,183 based on the claims of failure to pay and potential computation mistakes in the mortgage settlement.	Samuel Wood, the plaintiff, claims against Denison K. Town for failing to pay a sum owed under the mortgage, specifically the $600 that Town was supposed to pay for Wood's debts. Wood asserts that he is entitled to recover funds that were paid due to a mistake in accounting and argues that the conditions under which the mortgage was settled did not reflect accurate calculations. He seeks restitution for the amounts he has paid and contends that the circumstances justify his claims under both special and common counts of money had and received.	Denison K. Town, the defendant, argues that any claim for recovery can only pertain to the specific amount outlined in the special count, which is the $600, and that additional interest claimed by Wood was not warranted. Town maintains he had fulfilled his obligations under the mortgage agreement and contends that Wood's claims involve errors in accounting for prior agreements regarding interest rates and payments on the initial mortgage, and therefore disputes the jury's findings regarding the amounts owed.

In December 1838, in Edwards County, Illinois, the case of William Pickering v. Daniel Orange was argued before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case stemmed from an incident where the plaintiff, William Pickering, alleged that the defendant, Daniel Orange, kept dogs that had previously attacked and killed several of his sheep. The issue arose when Pickering claimed that Orange failed to control his dogs, known to have a ferocious disposition. During the trial at the Edwards Circuit Court, the jury ruled in favor of the defendant, determining not to hold Orange liable for the damages claimed by Pickering. However, the legal instructions given to the jury were questioned, particularly regarding the owner's responsibility for the actions of ferocious animals in their care.	William Pickering claimed that Daniel Orange was negligent in keeping his dogs, which had a known history of aggression, ultimately leading to the death of several of Pickering's sheep. He argued that the defendant should be held accountable for the damages caused by these dogs and sought monetary compensation for the loss of his property.	Daniel Orange contended that he was not liable for the damages caused by his dogs, arguing against the application of strict liability in this case. He asserted that the jury's instruction relating to the owner’s knowledge of the dogs' behavior and subsequent culpability was neither clear nor appropriately applied. Orange sought to maintain the verdict rendered by the lower court, which ruled in his favor.

In September 1869, in Chicago, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Charles B. Farwell and William H. Warren regarding a trespass incident. Farwell sought to purchase a lot to construct a warehouse and had engaged a real estate broker, Albert Crane, for assistance. Crane was in negotiations with Warren, who was occupying the premises, and it was agreed upon that Warren would vacate the property by the end of the month, allowing Farwell to take immediate possession. However, when Warren did not leave, Farwell's workers began removing Warren's household goods and ultimately demolished the house while Warren was away. Warren claimed his belongings were damaged during the removal and subsequently filed a lawsuit for trespass, resulting in a favorable judgment of $6,691.66 against Farwell, prompting Farwell to appeal the decision.	Warren claimed that Farwell unlawfully trespassed on his property by forcibly removing his personal belongings and destroying his home while he was absent. He argued that the defendants did not have the right to take possession of the property without following legal procedures, thus leading to significant damages for which he sought compensation.	Farwell contended that he was entitled to immediate possession of the property as per the terms agreed upon during negotiations, asserting that he acted under that premise. He challenged the admissibility of certain evidence during the trial and argued that his actions should be mitigated since he believed he had a right to enter the property based on Warren's statements about vacating.

In December 1855, John Clark attempted to purchase certain lands from the United States, situated in Livingston County, Illinois. These lands had been designated as swamp and overflowed lands under a federal act passed on September 28, 1850, which aimed to enable various states, including Illinois, to reclaim such lands. Clark claimed that the lands were not swampy or unfit for cultivation, thus not subject to the federal grant, and he contended that they still belonged to the public domain when he made his purchase offer. He tendered payment at the land office in Danville, Illinois, but his attempts were met with a demurrer to his bill, leading him to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The court ultimately concluded that it lacked jurisdiction to grant specific performance against the United States regarding the land sale.	John Clark argued that the lands he sought to purchase were not part of the swamp lands eligible under the federal grant and contended that they were fit for cultivation. He claimed that the lands remained public domain at the time of his purchase offer. Clark requested the court to enforce the contract for the sale of land, presuming that he had a right to buy these lands without any interference from the defendants.	The defendant, Livingston County, argued that the case fell outside the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court, as it involved the United States government, which cannot be compelled to perform in matters of state court. They contended that there was no legal foundation for Clark's claim, citing the federal acts that confirmed these lands to the states, and maintained that the circuit court's ruling to sustain the demurrer was correct.

James B. Campbell and Richard J. Hamilton, with John Tillson, Jr. as an impleaded party, filed their case against The President, Directors and Company of the State Bank of Illinois in December 1837. The dispute arose over the execution of a supersedeas bond. The bond in question was not signed directly by Campbell; instead, it was executed in his name by his attorney, Solomon Wills, without the requisite proof of authority. George Manierre was listed as a subscribing witness to the bond. The case originated in Fayette County, Illinois. The defendants argued that the bond was invalid because the attorney's authority to act on Campbell's behalf was not established, which they claimed invalidated the bond necessary for maintaining the appeal.	The plaintiffs contended that the bond should be considered valid, presuming that Campbell’s attorney had the authority to execute it on his behalf. They argued that unless the validity of the attorney's authority was explicitly challenged with an affidavit, the court should uphold the bond as executed correctly and presume the proper execution of duties by the clerk.	The defendants moved to quash the supersedeas, asserting that James B. Campbell did not personally enter into the bond and that the authority of his attorney, who had executed the bond, was questionable since no power of attorney was filed. They maintained that the lack of evidence of authority warranted the bond's invalidation, impacting the supersedeas appeal.

On November 1, 1885, John Wetenkamp and his associates decided to build a house in Chicago, Illinois, and entered into a contract with William Billigh and Henry Beck. Billigh was designated for masonry work while Beck was responsible for carpentry. The agreed price for the work was $7,450, structured in several payments contingent on progress milestones. Shortly thereafter, complications arose; Beck failed to complete his portion of the work, leading the appellants, Wetenkamp, to incur additional costs to finish the construction. Beck's sub-contractors, including Hlinka (working under Billigh) and the South Halsted Street Iron Works (working under Beck), filed for mechanic's liens on the property due to unpaid claims. The original contractors argued that their responsibilities had been implicitly redefined to separate contracts based on subsequent interactions and exchanges of documentation. A decree was made favoring Billigh and the lien claims from Hlinka and the Iron Works, prompting an appeal from Wetenkamp et al. over the validity and structure of contractor responsibilities and lien claims.	The plaintiffs, John Wetenkamp and others, claimed that the original contract was a joint agreement for a single project and that neither Billigh nor his subcontractor Hlinka were entitled to enforce mechanic's liens due to non-completion of the work. They contended that their liability was limited since they incurred more expenses than originally contracted, and they sought to dismiss the lien claims filed by the subcontractors.	The defendants, Billigh and Beck, contended that the original contract should be interpreted as separate agreements for masonry and carpentry work. They argued that subsequent conduct indicated a mutual understanding of their individual responsibilities. Billigh maintained that the plaintiffs had made payments to Beck that exceeded their contractual duties and asserted their rights to establish mechanic's liens as per the construction work completed.

Nathaniel Harmison initiated a trespass lawsuit against Reuben Clark, Jacob Clark Senior, Lucy Clark (Jacob's wife), and Jacob Clark Junior of Franklin County, Illinois, on March 11, 1832. The plaintiff alleged that the defendants unlawfully broke into his property, causing significant damage—setting fire to a mill-house, barn, two corn-cribs, a stable, and destroying 1,000 bushels of corn, among other items. The value of the lost property was estimated at $1,000. The case went through two trials. In the first trial, a default judgment was made against Jacob Clark Senior and Lucy Clark for their failure to respond to the suit, while the other defendants were acquitted. However, Jacob Clark Senior filed an affidavit claiming that he was unaware his wife was a party to the suit and requested a new trial. The court granted the request, leading to a new trial for all defendants. In the second trial, the jury ruled in favor of the defendants, and the case proceeded with further legal maneuvers regarding the judgments and exceptions taken by the plaintiff regarding the proceeding’s fairness.	Harmison's principal arguments included accusations of trespass and property destruction by the defendants, seeking compensation for damages amounting to $1,000. He contended that the defendants acted unlawfully by entering his property and setting fire to his possessions, which he believed warranted both a verdict in his favor and financial reparation.	The defendants argued against the claims made, asserting that the court’s prior decisions, including setting aside the default judgment against Lucy Clark and Jacob Clark Senior, were correct. They maintained that there were procedural issues in the plaintiff's exceptions and that the evidence against them was inadmissible. The defense emphasized that the initial rulings were appropriate and that any decisions made in the first trial should not impact their current claims.

Grant Newell, as the administrator of the estate of Patrick Terry, filed a petition in May 1889 within the Probate Court of Cook County, Illinois, seeking to sell real estate to pay off debts amounting to $1587.85. Patrick Terry passed away owning a specific lot in Ottawa, Illinois, which constituted his sole real estate asset. The initial petition included Terry's heirs and a party in possession of the land as defendants. Subsequently, it was amended to include Catharine Montgomery, the widow of Robert M. Montgomery, along with their children, as they claimed an interest in the property. The heirs argued that Robert M. Montgomery owned the lot and that after his death, they were engaged in litigation that led to a court decree establishing a lien against the property. They contended that Terry acted as a friend and advisor throughout the sale process, purchasing the property merely as a mechanism for aiding the heirs. After reviewing the evidence, the court found that Terry held the title in trust for Montgomery's heirs, dismissing the original petition for land sale.	Grant Newell claimed that the real estate owned by Patrick Terry should be sold to settle his debts. He maintained that since the personal estate was exhausted, the property could be used to satisfy the outstanding debts owed by the estate, believing he had the authority to sell the land to meet these financial obligations.	Catharine Montgomery and her heirs contested the sale, asserting that the land belonged to them based on a prior legal arrangement. They argued that Terry was merely an intermediary and had not conveyed the title to them due to inadvertence rather than fraud. They posited that they had been in possession of the property and were entitled to its ownership, contending that the property should not be sold to satisfy Terry's debts.

The case "The Adams Express Company v. Marvin Jones" took place in January 1870 in Illinois. The key individuals involved were Marvin Jones, the plaintiff, and the Adams Express Company, the defendant. The conflict arose when Jones sought to recover damages due to the non-delivery of a shipment consisting of a lot of trees that he had entrusted to the express company for transport. The trees were supposed to be transported from Shoals, Indiana, to Odin, Illinois. Initially, Jones won a judgment in a lower court, but the express company appealed the decision, arguing against the validity of the verdict. The Illinois Supreme Court primarily examined whether there was sufficient evidence to support the value of the trees at the time of shipment and concluded that the evidence did not substantiate Jones's claims.	Marvin Jones, the plaintiff, argued that the Adams Express Company was responsible for the non-delivery of the trees he shipped. He sought damages amounting to $126, claiming that he suffered losses as a result of the express company's failure to deliver the trees to the designated location.	The Adams Express Company contended that the plaintiff's claims were unfounded, asserting that the trees were dead and worthless by the time they arrived for transport. They argued that there was no evidence presented to establish the value of the trees, either as living specimens suitable for transplanting or based on their worth at the shipping location. Consequently, they requested a reversal of the lower court's judgment due to insufficient evidence supporting Jones's claims.

In February 1882, in Franklin, Morgan County, John Meredith organized an auction sale where Job Coates purchased two steers for $126. At that time, Meredith owed Coates $200 on a note, which Coates had left at home. They agreed that Meredith would sign a new note—serving as a memorandum for Coates until Meredith settled his prior debt. The note was placed at Jacksonville National Bank without endorsement. Meredith, involved in cattle trading, had John Harmon guarantee any overdrafts. The conflict arose when the note was not paid and Harmon took it to court in 1886, even after altering it to include himself as payee. This led to a series of trials, culminating in Coates' appeal after multiple jury verdicts favored Harmon.	The plaintiff, John Harmon, claimed as an indorsee of the promissory note signed by Job Coates and John Meredith. He argued that he was the legitimate holder of the note, placed it in action noting his rights of ownership, and sought payment for the amount due.	The defendant, Job Coates, contended that the note was intended only as a memorandum between Coates and Meredith and should not be treated as an enforceable instrument by third parties. He argued that Meredith's signature on the note was meant to signify a joint agreement and not a blank endorsement. Coates requested that the court recognize the intent behind the note's creation and awarded him a verdict that acknowledged this context.

The case of The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Co. v. Alfred Hale occurred in 1874, when Hale shipped a jack (an uncastrated male horse) from Burlington, Iowa, to Monmouth, Illinois, via the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad. The jack was in good condition at the time of shipment but arrived injured, specifically with a damaged leg. Hale, the plaintiff, claimed that due to the negligence of the railroad company (the defendant), he suffered damages amounting to $1,000 for the loss of the jack and an additional $400 for the expected income from the jack as a foal-getter during the breeding season. The jury ultimately assessed the damages at $200, prompting the railroad company to appeal the decision on the grounds that the jury should not have considered prospective profits, as the company had not been informed of the jack's purpose prior to shipping.	The plaintiff, Alfred Hale, argued that the railroad company was negligent in transporting the jack, which resulted in injuries that diminished its value. He contended that he was entitled to damages both for the jack's diminished worth and for the loss of income he could have earned by using the jack for breeding during the 1874 season. Hale essentially sought compensation for both the injury caused to the animal and the consequential financial loss.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad, contended that Hale failed to notify them of the specific purpose for transporting the jack. They argued that without that critical information, they should not be liable for any loss of profits related to the jack's intended breeding use. They maintained that the damages claimed by Hale were too speculative since there were no outstanding contracts proving potential profits had he not suffered the loss.

In September 1873, the case of David McWilliams et al. v. Richard P. Morgan was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Livingston County, overseen by Judge Charles H. Wood. The dispute arose over an injunction bond conditioned on the obligation of the obligors (David McWilliams and others) to pay Morgan any costs and damages awarded against them if the injunction was dissolved. The injunction was indeed dissolved, but no damages were assessed at the time, leading to a contention over whether the obligors could be held accountable for damages in a legal action. The court examined whether the required assessment of damages should have been made by the chancellor after the dissolution of the injunction, or if it could be determined in a subsequent trial. This case is reminiscent of a previous ruling where similar circumstances were present, emphasizing the necessity of having damages assessed to proceed with a recovery.	The plaintiffs, David McWilliams and others, asserted that they were not liable for damages stemming from the dissolution of the injunction because the required assessment of those damages had not taken place. They argued that without this assessment by the chancellor, they could not be held to account under the conditions outlined in the bond, and they sought to have the judgment of the lower court reversed.	Richard P. Morgan, the defendant, contended that according to the conditions set forth in the injunction bond, he was entitled to recover damages. He emphasized that the lack of an assessment by the chancellor after the dissolution of the injunction precluded the plaintiffs from contesting their liability. Morgan's request hinged on having the damages assessed as stipulated to establish the basis for recovery.

In December 1880, John Simpson, Sr. passed away intestate in Cook County, Illinois, leaving behind his widow and several children, including Amos P. Simpson, who had died two months earlier. The case arose from a dispute over whether the children of Amos P. Simpson—Asa H. Simpson, Ida M. Simpson, and Burnell Simpson—were entitled to inherit from their grandfather's estate. Before his death, Amos P. Simpson received a piece of property from his father and executed a release stating he relinquished any claims to his father's estate in favor of the other heirs. This release raised the central legal question of whether the children could inherit their grandfather's estate, given that their father had signed away any interest he might have had. The initial ruling deemed their father's release sufficient to bar their inheritance, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiffs, Asa H. Simpson and his siblings, argued that the release signed by their father, Amos P. Simpson, did not legally prevent them from inheriting their grandfather's estate. They contended that their father's release was ineffective because he died before he could inherit from his father, and thus had no real interest to assign, effectively allowing them a rightful claim to their grandfather's estate.	The defendants, including the other heirs of John Simpson, Sr., maintained that the release executed by Amos P. Simpson was binding and barred his children from claiming any interest in the estate. They argued that the release should be enforced as it represented a clear intention to relinquish any future inheritance rights stemming from their father’s estate.

The case "Walter S. Covill et al. v. Adam Phy" took place in April 1861 in Aurora, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Walter S. Covill and others, accused the defendant, Adam Phy, of trespassing to personal property, specifically for unlawfully taking and carrying away forty gallons of whisky valued at $500. The act was alleged to have occurred on August 23, 1859, and on multiple other occasions. The plaintiffs initiated the lawsuit in the Common Pleas Court of the city of Aurora, which holds concurrent jurisdiction with the Circuit Court, except in cases of treason and murder. However, the defendants challenged the court's jurisdiction by filing a plea in abatement, arguing that the alleged events occurred outside the city's jurisdiction (in the town of Montgomery), and that neither the plaintiffs nor the defendants resided within the city at the time the suit was filed. The court later sustained a general demurrer against this plea, leading to further proceedings, including trial and verdict. Ultimately, the jury awarded a minor amount of $2.75 to the plaintiffs against Covill, leading to further legal review by the Illinois Supreme Court regarding jurisdictional limitations.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants trespassed upon their property by unlawfully taking forty gallons of whisky. They argued that damages amounting to $500 were warranted for the alleged actions. They sought legal recourse from the Common Pleas Court of Aurora, asserting the court's authority over the matter despite the defendants' jurisdictional defense.	The defendants contended that the Common Pleas Court of Aurora lacked jurisdiction to hear the case as the events leading to the lawsuit occurred in the town of Montgomery, outside the city limits. They emphasized that both parties were not residents of Aurora at the time the suit was initiated and that the process served was unauthorized as it extended beyond the court's jurisdiction. Therefore, they requested the court to dismiss the claims based on jurisdictional grounds.

In the case of Louis Wilhelm v. The People of the State of Illinois, the events transpired in January 1874 in St. Clair County, Illinois. The case arose after Louis Wilhelm, the plaintiff in error, was convicted at the January term of the St. Clair Circuit Court for assaulting Xavier Schoenstein with intent to murder. Wilhelm was subsequently sentenced to four years of imprisonment. As part of his defense, he sought a continuance of his trial, claiming the absence of a key witness, Philip Grummel, who resided in Missouri. Wilhelm argued that Grummel could provide crucial testimony establishing his innocence, asserting he was at his own home at the time of the incident. However, his motion for continuance was denied by the court, which found his affidavit insufficient. Throughout the trial, several procedural issues were raised regarding jury selection and the handling of evidence, but the court rejected these claims, stating that no substantial harm was done to Wilhelm during the proceedings.	Wilhelm, the plaintiff in error, contended that he was wrongfully convicted of assault with intent to murder. He sought a continuance for his trial citing the absence of a material witness, asserting that Grummel's testimony would prove his innocence. Wilhelm argued that he was not near the scene of the alleged crime at the time it occurred and emphasized that his affidavit clearly stated his efforts to secure Grummel’s attendance at the trial.	The People of the State of Illinois defended against Wilhelm’s claims by arguing that the motion for continuance based on Grummel’s absence was unwarranted and the affidavit was inadequate. The court maintained that Wilhelm had not demonstrated that Grummel's testimony would be factually relevant to the case nor provided evidence that Grummel was an observer of the incident. The court also dismissed various procedural objections raised by Wilhelm, emphasizing that no substantial rights were compromised during the trial.

The case of "Harvey White v. John Jones et al." occurred in April 1865 in Illinois. Harvey White filed a replevin action to recover a stock of goods that had been seized by the sheriff under an execution against Waterman & Hall. On November 20, 1860, White had purchased the goods shortly before the sheriff's execution was issued. The controversy centered around the timing of the execution in relation to White's purchase and the subsequent arrangements made by Waterman & Hall regarding a note given to Jones for his judgment against Hall. A judgment was confessed on this note later that same day. The case hinged on whether the original execution created a valid lien on the goods and whether the note satisfied the previous judgment under which the goods were seized. Ultimately, the court found that the judgment against Waterman and Hall was void due to lack of jurisdiction because the legal authority to confess judgment had been unfulfilled.	Harvey White, the plaintiff, argued that his purchase of the goods was valid and protected from any liens, as the earlier execution against Waterman & Hall was void. He maintained that the note given to Jones satisfied the previous judgment against Hall. White requested the return of his goods, asserting that the sheriff's levy was wrongful since it was based on an invalid judgment.	The defendants, including John Jones, asserted that their claim on the goods was legitimate because the execution issued against Waterman and Hall was valid and held a legal lien on the goods. They contended that the first execution had not been satisfied by the later note issued by Waterman & Hall, and thus the levy on the goods was rightful. The defendants maintained that they acted within their legal rights to seize the goods under the execution.

James C. Moore filed a case against John A. Montelius, with the proceedings taking place in Ford County, Illinois. The events leading to the lawsuit began in March 1884, when B. F. Clark, then a tenant of Montelius, entered into a written agreement whereby Montelius purchased certain livestock from Clark. Following the agreement, Clark was responsible for managing the livestock and farm operations, receiving half of the proceeds from the sales. In December 1886, a constable acting under a legal execution against Clark seized twenty-one cattle from the premises. Montelius then initiated a replevin action to recover the cattle, claiming that the seizure was improper as the livestock did not belong to Clark at the time of the levy. The legal proceedings examined the nature of the sale and the retention of possession by Clark as it related to the legality of the transaction and the rights of the creditors involved.	The primary claim made by James C. Moore was that the cattle seized were not the property of B. F. Clark but rightfully belonged to him (Montelius). He argued that Clark had sold the cattle to him prior to the execution, making the seizure invalid. Moore contended that the understanding of the sale and possession did not constitute a fraudulent transfer regarding Clark's subsequent creditors, asserting his rightful ownership and demanding the returned possession of the livestock.	John A. Montelius' defense relied on the argument that the sale of cattle was legitimate and should not be deemed fraudulent since the execution creditor, James C. Moore, failed to prove that he held any claim on the property at the time of the sale. The defense claimed that the transaction was valid and that the creditor's execution could not challenge the sale made before any debts were incurred by Clark. Montelius requested the court affirm the ownership of the cattle based on the validity of the sale and the implications of exempt property in relation to the execution.

In 1846 in Du Page County, Illinois, Elihu Granger faced a legal challenge from Henry Warrington, who had previously accused Granger of malicious arrest and prosecution. The original case began in the Cook Circuit Court but was later transferred to Du Page County at Granger's request. Warrington claimed that Granger had wrongfully caused him to be arrested on a capias for an action of trespass without any reasonable cause and subsequently imprisoned for thirty days. During the trial, the jury found in favor of Warrington, awarding him $500. Granger contested the proceedings, arguing technical issues regarding the original papers being missing from the Du Page court and demanding their dismissal along with other procedural grievances during the trials that occurred over multiple terms.	Warrington's main arguments included the assertion that Granger had maliciously instigated his arrest without justification, leading to wrongful imprisonment. He sought damages for the malicious prosecution he endured, claiming that Granger had no reasonable cause for the arrest and that the subsequent legal actions taken against him were pursued in bad faith.	Granger defended against the claims by arguing that there was a reasonable and probable cause for his actions. He also raised procedural technicalities, such as the argument that the original court papers were not transferred correctly, which he believed should result in the dismissal of the case. Moreover, he contested the evidence presented by Warrington and argued against the admissibility of certain testimonies that he deemed irrelevant or improperly introduced.

In the case of James M. Sells v. The Sandwich Manufacturing Company, the dispute arose over a transaction involving a harvester and binder sold by the defendant to the plaintiff, James M. Sells. The events took place in 1886 in McLean County, Illinois. The case was initially presented before a Justice of the Peace, concerning the last of two notes given by Sells for the equipment. The purchased machine was meant to operate satisfactorily or be replaced by a new one. Sells brought the lawsuit after dissatisfaction with the machine's performance. During the trial, conflicting evidence emerged regarding whether the replacement machine functioned well. Despite this, a jury verdict favored Sells, awarding him $175.48 in damages. However, the judgment included an improper $10 attorney's fee, leading to a remittitur request, which the court accepted. The final judgment affirmed the modified amount of $165.48.	The plaintiff, James M. Sells, claimed that the harvested and binder failed to perform as promised, justifying his request for damages. He sought compensation for the poor performance of the equipment under the agreement that it would either work properly or be replaced with a new machine.	The Sandwich Manufacturing Company argued that the evidence did not support Sells' claims regarding the machine's performance. They contended that the jury could have been misled by inconsistent instructions, although they did not explicitly deny liability for the defective machine if proven. The defendant also sought to contest the inclusion of attorney fees in the judgment.

Josiah Mason et al. filed a suit against the Trustees of Schools in 1884 in Greene County, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute over two deeds that Mason executed, which the appellees, judgment creditors of Mason, alleged to be fraudulent. The plaintiffs sought to have these deeds set aside, claiming they were void as against them. The case had previously been presented at the May term of the Illinois Appellate Court, which found that the evidence did not sufficiently support the lower court's decision that the deeds were fraudulent. Following a remand for further proceedings, the Circuit Court of Morgan County tried the case again, considering the same evidence along with testimonies from three additional witnesses. Ultimately, the lower court ruled once more in favor of the appellees, leading to another appeal.	The plaintiffs, Josiah Mason et al., claimed that the two deeds executed by Mason were fraudulent and sought a court decree to declare these deeds void against their interests as judgment creditors. They argued that the initial findings by the lower court were justified and that the evidence presented supported their position that the deeds should be annulled.	The defendants, represented by Trustees of Schools, countered the allegations of fraud, arguing that the additional testimony provided in the retrial did not strengthen the plaintiffs' case. They maintained that the overall evidence failed to justify a decree against them, asserting that the initial court's reversal was warranted based on the insufficiency of the plaintiffs' proofs.

In September 1874, Adam Kolb filed a lawsuit against Anna J. O’Brien after he sustained an injury to his ankle while attempting to enter an omnibus that he claimed belonged to her. The incident occurred at the Adams street entrance of the Exposition Building in Chicago, where omnibuses were directed to wait in compliance with police regulations. On the night of the injury, Kolb, along with her friends, was hurrying toward the omnibus in a crowded area. As she stepped onto the vehicle's step, it allegedly backed up, causing her ankle to become trapped. A policeman intervened to assist her, and she was taken home by the same omnibus. Kolb suffered from significant pain and was unable to work for approximately twelve weeks, resulting in lost wages. Additionally, she incurred medical and caregiving expenses. The jury awarded her $2,200 in damages, but this amount was contested by the defendant as excessive.	Adam Kolb claimed that O’Brien was negligent in controlling the omnibus, which directly led to her injury. She argued that her suffering and the incapacitation she experienced warranted significant damages beyond her actual incurred expenses, which totaled approximately $175, including lost wages of $48 and medical expenses of about $50. Kolb sought compensation for both compensatory and potential punitive damages due to the alleged negligence.	Anna J. O’Brien contended that the damages awarded to Kolb were excessively high and not backed by substantial evidence of permanent injury or malice. She argued that the actual financial losses documented did not exceed $175, and therefore, the additional claims of suffering and future incapacity lacked sufficient basis. Furthermore, O’Brien highlighted the confusion surrounding which omnibus was involved, maintaining that it might not even belong to her. O’Brien requested the court to reverse the jury's decision and reduce the damage award.

The case, "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Theodore W. Thompson," was decided on January 25, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It stemmed from a dispute in Makanda, Illinois, where the Illinois Central Railroad Company was using a piece of land owned by Theodore W. Thompson to obtain water for its engines. The relationship between Thompson and the railroad company became contentious when Thompson claimed he had not been compensated for the use of his land. He notified representatives of the railroad about his expectation for payment, and despite this notification, the railroad continued to occupy the land without objection. This led Thompson to file a lawsuit seeking compensation for what he alleged was unauthorized use of his property, which resulted in a series of trials. The jury ruled in favor of Thompson on two occasions, confirming the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship due to the railroad's continued use of the land after being notified of the payment expectation. The Appellate Court upheld these decisions and forwarded the case to the Illinois Supreme Court due to its significant implications.	Theodore W. Thompson, the plaintiff, argued that the Illinois Central Railroad Company had occupied his land for an extended period without permission or compensation. He claimed that the railroad's representatives had been notified of his expectation for rent and continued to use the land without objection. Thompson sought a judgment for the amount of $300, reflecting the rental dues for the use of his property.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that the evidence was insufficient to establish a landlord-tenant relationship between them and Thompson. The company did not contest any trial court errors but argued that without proof of this relationship, Thompson was not entitled to recover any payment. They believed that the court should reverse the judgment based on this lack of evidence regarding liability.

On July 9, 1860, John Jacob Lindauer executed a warranty deed for a property in Chicago to Frederick N. Ehrenfels, who had previously loaned him money. Following Ehrenfels' death in December 1865, a dispute arose regarding the nature of the deed: whether it was an outright sale or a mortgage to secure Lindauer's debt. Lindauer alleged that the deed was meant to secure a loan of $3,000 and that Ehrenfels was to manage the property, using the rents to repay the debt. The property was located at Sherman and Van Buren Streets in Chicago, and contained two hotels at the time of the deed. Lindauer sought to redeem the property, claiming he could pay off his debt, while the defendants, including Ephraim H. Cummings as executor, contended that the deed was an absolute conveyance. The case was filed initially in the Superior Court of Chicago and subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1870.	John Jacob Lindauer claimed that the deed executed on July 9, 1860, was a mortgage intended to secure a debt of $3,000 owed to Ehrenfels. He argued that the arrangement included provisions for Ehrenfels to rent the property and apply the rent towards the debt repayment. Lindauer sought an accounting of the rents collected, offered to pay any outstanding balance, and requested the right to redeem the property from the alleged mortgage.	Ephraim H. Cummings, representing the estate of Ehrenfels, argued that the deed was intended as an absolute conveyance, not as a mortgage. The defendants admitted the existence of the original debts but contended that the notes had been surrendered as part of the consideration for the absolute deed. They denied any obligation to honor Lindauer's claims and asserted that the arrangements made post-deed were consistent with an outright sale of the property, asserting no equity existed for Lindauer to redeem.

Lyman Guinnip v. Henry M. Carter is a legal case that originated in January 1871 in Vermilion County, Illinois. The action was brought by Henry M. Carter, John G. Sample, and Jonas F. Parker, who were plaintiffs in a suit against Lyman Guinnip, the defendant. The case arose from a previous judgment recorded in the Court of Common Pleas of Tippecanoe County, Indiana, where the plaintiffs had recovered a sum of $1,171 along with costs. The suit was characterized as an action of debt, with the initial three counts presented in the traditional form of debt claims. A fourth count, however, was framed as a common count in assumpsit for interest. During the proceedings, Guinnip filed a demurrer against the declaration but later had it stricken from the files at the plaintiffs’ request. The Circuit Court delivered a judgment in favor of the plaintiffs for the total amount of $1,171 in debt, plus $28 in damages and costs. Subsequently, Guinnip sought to contest this judgment through a writ of error.	The plaintiffs argued that they were owed $1,171 based on a previous judgment and sought to enforce this judgment through their current action. They presented multiple counts in their declaration, including claims in debt as well as a common count in assumpsit regarding interest owed. The plaintiffs requested the court to uphold their claim and the associated damages as awarded in the initial ruling.	The defendant, Lyman Guinnip, contended that there was a misjoinder of counts within the plaintiffs' declaration—the presence of both counts in debt and a count in assumpsit in the same declaration. Guinnip maintained that the use of the word "promised" instead of "agreed" in the count for interest transformed it into a count in assumpsit, which was inappropriate when combined with counts in debt. As a result, he requested the court to reverse the judgment based on this alleged procedural error.

Mary Tobin brought a personal injury lawsuit against The Chicago City Railway Company in 1885, following an incident on one of the company's street cars in Chicago, Illinois. On the day in question, Tobin attempted to alight from the street car after signaling the conductor to stop. However, while she was in the process of exiting, the conductor suddenly started the car, causing her to fall and sustain injuries. Throughout the trial, evidence was presented to support Tobin's claim, including a testimony from her physician, Dr. Caldwell, who recounted what Tobin had said regarding the incident. However, the jury found for the defendant. Tobin subsequently appealed the verdict, focusing primarily on the rejection of some of her evidence that could have proved her claim.	Mary Tobin argued that the Chicago City Railway Company's negligence in controlling the street car led directly to her injuries when she attempted to disembark. She sought recovery for the personal injuries she sustained during the incident, asserting that she had acted with due care and had properly notified the conductor of her intention to exit.	The Chicago City Railway Company contended that Tobin's injuries resulted from her own negligence, asserting that she acted imprudently when exiting the moving vehicle. They pointed to the testimony provided by Dr. Caldwell, which indicated that Tobin did not wait for the car to stop properly before getting off. The company requested that the court uphold the jury's verdict in their favor.

In November 1866, The Board of Supervisors of Clay County was involved in a legal dispute with Levi M. Plaut before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from issues related to the support of a pauper who had become a charge to the county. The overseer of the poor, Phelps, had contracted with a woman named Mrs. Thompson to care for the pauper for a fee of $2 per week. However, as the pauper's health deteriorated, Mrs. Thompson found herself unable to adequately support him at that price. After Phelps, the overseer, was replaced by De Witt, who could not find someone else willing to care for the pauper at the agreed rate, De Witt ordered additional supplies for Mrs. Thompson. The contract for goods amounted to $73.92. When the county only credited this with a payment of $36, Plaut brought an action against the county for the balance. The Circuit Court of Clay County ruled in favor of Plaut, awarding him $37.92, which was then contested by the Board of Supervisors.	Levi M. Plaut claimed that the Board of Supervisors was liable for the cost of goods provided for the pauper's care. He argued that the actions of the overseer of the poor were legitimate and that the county was obligated to honor the expenses necessary for the adequate support of its paupers as per statutory requirements.	The Board of Supervisors contended that the county was not liable for the full amount claimed, arguing that the overseer's actions were outside of his authorized duties, and they sought to challenge the legality of the expenses incurred without a proper resolution or agreement. They maintained that they had only committed to a contract of $2 per week for care.

Richard S. Peale filed a case against Henry H. Hill in the Illinois Appellate Court after a contractual dispute arose from an agreement made on January 23, 1886. The contract required Hill to canvass La Salle County, Illinois, for sales of “Grant’s Memoirs” and to order a total of 850 sets by April 1, 1886, considering previously delivered copies in this count. Hill was to earn a commission of 40%, which would drop to 33.33% if he failed to meet the order requirement. Peale paid Hill the lower commission but did not pay the remaining balance, leading Hill to sue for the 6.67% owed. During the trial, Hill presented evidence that he had fulfilled the terms of the contract, ordering over 900 copies, while Peale attempted to introduce a previous contract dated June 22, 1885, claiming it was linked to Hill's obligations under the 1886 agreement. However, Peale faced challenges proving the existence and specifics of the previous contract. The trial was held without a jury, and the initial judgment was in favor of Hill.	Hill, the plaintiff, contended that he fulfilled his contractual obligations by ordering more than the required number of book sets for La Salle County, thus entitling him to the balance of his commission under the terms initially agreed upon. He requested the court to enforce the contract and award him the remaining 6.67% of the commission owed.	Peale, the defendant, argued that Hill had a prior contract from June 22, 1885, which stipulated additional obligations. He claimed that Hill did not perform under this prior contract and asserted that the contract from January 23, 1886, was only supplementary to it. Peale offered no substantial evidence proving this defense, particularly regarding the conditions outlined in the first contract and sought to have the court rule in his favor based on this argument.

In January 1888, the legal case of Conrad Seipp Brewing Company v. Patrick Doody took place in Cook County, Illinois. The incident at the center of the case involved an injury sustained by Patrick Doody, who was serving as a flagman at a railway crossing. The injury occurred when a beer wagon driven by one of the servants of the Conrad Seipp Brewing Company crossed the tracks. Doody claimed that the driver's carelessness led to his injury. A jury trial resulted in a verdict favoring Doody, awarding him $3,000. However, the court required that Doody enter a remittitur of $1,000, thereby adjusting the judgment to $2,000 in compensation for his injuries. The brewing company appealed the decision, contending that the jury's verdict was excessive and unsupported by evidence. The appeal raised questions about the nature of the evidence presented and the jury's assessment of damages.	Patrick Doody, the plaintiff, argued that he sustained significant injuries due to the negligence of the Conrad Seipp Brewing Company’s employee while on duty as a flagman at a railway crossing. He sought damages for his painful and permanent injuries, resulting in the jury awarding him $3,000, later adjusted to $2,000 after a remittitur. Doody's case was built on claims of reckless behavior by the brewing company’s servant which directly resulted in his injury.	The Conrad Seipp Brewing Company, the defendant, did not argue that legal errors occurred during the trial; instead, they claimed that the jury's verdict lacked support from the evidence presented. They suggested that the award was the result of passion and prejudice, implying that the jury misapprehended the facts. The defense argued that the conflicting testimonies around the incident should have led to a different verdict, one in favor of the defendant, as they believed the injury did not warrant the damages awarded.

In 1882, in Edgar County, Illinois, a legal proceeding was initiated by Paul Huston and others against Charles W. Clark and others for the establishment of the Sims Special Drainage District under the Drainage Act of May 29, 1879. The petition, signed by a majority of adult landowners with over a third of the lands in the proposed district, was filed on February 18, 1882. After a court hearing, a majority of the petition was confirmed, and the court appointed three commissioners to oversee the drainage operations. The commissioners assessed the costs and benefits of the proposed drainage work, concluding that the benefits would exceed costs and no lands would be negatively impacted. A jury was later summoned to assess the benefits and damages, resulting in a report showing no damages. The court allowed amendments to the assessment roll due to clerical errors in the land descriptions while upholding the proceedings and formalities of the assessments and reports.	The plaintiffs argued that the legislative act enabling the drainage district was unconstitutional and claimed that jurisdiction was improperly established due to an insufficient petition. They contended that the court erred in allowing a jury to assess benefits without properly identifying lands that would incur damages. The plaintiffs sought dismissal of the proceedings and asserted that the entire process violated their rights.	The defendants contended that the act was constitutional and valid under the specific provisions of the state constitution which allowed for the establishment of drainage districts. They argued that the commissioners’ report adequately substantiated that no lands would suffer injury and that the benefits justified the assessments. They maintained that the actions taken were within acceptable legal boundaries and requested that the court uphold the assessment and the establishment of the drainage district.

On May 29, 1854, Alfred G. Low initiated a legal process in the Cook Circuit Court, Illinois, by obtaining a writ of capias ad respondendum against Henry W. Burlingame and others, including John F. Stafford. The writ required bail of $588.32 and was executed by a sheriff who arrested Burlingame, leading to the execution of a bail bond worth $1,180 on June 7, 1854. Low later won a judgment against Burlingame for $641.85 in damages and $13.35 in costs on December 3, 1855. Subsequently, efforts to collect the judgment via execution were unsuccessful, leading Low to file an affidavit that resulted in a capias to detain Burlingame, who could not be found. This prompted Low to bring a debt action against the sureties, including Stafford. Stafford contended that the affidavit supporting the capias was legally insufficient because it did not demonstrate that the defendants had refused to surrender their estate or that they engaged in fraudulent behavior. The trial court found in favor of Low without addressing Stafford's claims, leading Stafford to appeal the decision.	Alfred G. Low, the plaintiff, argued that the defendants, including John F. Stafford, failed to satisfy a judgment against Burlingame and were liable under the bail bond for the debt incurred. Low sought to enforce the bond and recover $1,180 in debt, along with $703.09 in damages and costs, asserting that the legal processes followed were valid and appropriate.	John F. Stafford, as the defendant in error, argued that the affidavit that allowed the initial capias to be issued was insufficient according to both state constitution and statutory requirements. He claimed that the affidavit did not adequately show that the defendants had refused to surrender their estate or provided any basis for presuming fraud. Stafford contended these deficiencies rendered the bail bond void, and he urged the court to overturn the lower court’s decision, asserting that if his claim was true, it constituted a complete defense to the action.

The case, "The People ex rel. Ernst F. C. Klokke v. Levi P. Wright," took place in Chicago, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873. The dispute arose when Ernst F. C. Klokke filed a quo warranto proceeding against Levi P. Wright, claiming that Wright usurped the office of a commissioner of the board of police in Cook County. Klokke asserted that he had been duly elected to the position by the people and was unlawfully removed by Wright, who claimed his right to the position was based on an appointment by the mayor of Chicago. The case explored whether the board of police commissioners was a part of the executive city government and whether such positions could be filled by appointment rather than election. Ultimately, the court needed to determine the legality of Wright's appointment and Klokke's claim to the office, considering the statutory provisions around the board's creation and the constitutional implications involved.	Klokke's main argument was that he was the legally elected commissioner of the board of police and had been unjustly removed by Levi P. Wright. He contended that Wright's appointment by the mayor lacked legal standing. Klokke sought to reclaim his position and prevent further unlawful removal from office.	Wright defended his position by asserting that he was rightfully appointed by the mayor of Chicago and thus held the office legally. He argued that the statutory framework allowed the mayor to appoint commissioners, implying that Klokke's election was superseded by this authority.

The case "De Witt C. James et al v. Samuel T. Hambleton et al." was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1866. It originated from the Circuit Court of Pulaski County, where Samuel T. Hambleton, William Hambleton, and Allen Collier, acting as partners, filed a petition against De Witt C. James and others to enforce a mechanics' lien. The dispute arose from a contract in which the defendants had hired the plaintiffs to furnish materials for the construction of twelve brick buildings situated on lots in Mound City, constituting an entire block known as block one, tier one. The plaintiffs successfully obtained a default judgment due to the defendants’ failure to respond, leading to a master’s report that determined the amount owed to the plaintiffs as $3,103. The Circuit Court decreed that the amount be paid within twenty days and ordered the sale of the properties should the payment not be made. This decision was challenged in the supreme court by the writ of error on various grounds relating to the mechanics' lien law and the process followed in the initial court ruling.	The plaintiffs asserted that the defendants were contractually obligated to pay for the materials supplied for the construction of the specified buildings. They claimed that the mechanics' lien was valid against the entire block of buildings as they were constructed under one roof, and they sought enforcement of this lien against all properties in question. They argued against the necessity of apportioning the lien among the lots and contended that it was sufficient to treat the entire block as a single entity for the purpose of the lien.	The defendants contended that it was erroneous to enforce the sale of the buildings without allowing a redemption period longer than the typical execution lifetime. They also argued that the lien should have been apportioned according to the value of materials provided for each separate lot. Furthermore, they raised issues regarding procedural irregularities, including the lack of a court order for notice by publication and the absence of a rule requiring them to plead or answer before default was entered.

In September 1874, the case of William M. Zearing v. John Raber was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from Cook County, Illinois. The dispute involved a plot of land near Chicago owned by James, Springer, and Green, who had laid out a street called "Green Street" on their property while not officially acknowledging or recording the street's dedication. Walenta purchased part of this lot, including the street, and later, Zearing became the owner of the residual land except for the railroad right of way. Both parties were aware of the existing street when they made their respective purchases. However, Zearing later attempted to deny the existence of this street and obstruct its use, prompting Walenta to take legal action to prevent this obstruction.	The plaintiff, Walenta, argued that the existence of the street was implied in the description of the property sold to him and that Zearing was legally estopped from denying the street's existence or obstructing its use. Walenta requested that the court recognize his right to the street’s use and prevent Zearing from interfering with or obstructing access to it.	Zearing contended that the street's dedication was not officially recorded, and therefore, he should not be bound by its existence or any implied covenant stemming from the earlier sale. He requested the court to acknowledge his rights over the property, which included denying the street's existence.

In the case of W. Henry Moore v. Eugene Wayman et al., the legal proceedings took place in Washington County, Illinois, culminating on June 16, 1883. The case arose when W. Henry Moore filed a bill in equity to prevent the collector from executing a tax deed for two forty-acre tracts of land that had been sold for unpaid taxes. Moore's claim was based on alleged procedural errors in the collection process and the assertion that he did not receive proper notice regarding the tax sale. However, the evidence indicated that adequate notice had been given, and all necessary procedures were followed during the tax assessment and collection. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of Moore by enjoining the collector from making the deed. This decision was appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, which would ultimately determine the legitimacy of the tax deed and the associated claims made by Moore.	W. Henry Moore, the plaintiff, contended that the tax deed execution should be enjoined due to alleged technical errors in the tax collection process, including improper notice and failure to adhere to the legal requirements for tax sales. He sought equitable relief, arguing that the circumstances created an unjust situation regarding the ownership of the land and the tax liabilities associated with it.	Eugene Wayman, representing the collector and the interests of the tax deed holder, maintained that the taxes had been lawfully assessed and were due and unpaid. The defense argued that there were no valid grounds for enjoining the collection of taxes, as all procedural requirements had been met. The defense also pointed out that the plaintiff failed to offer any payment or remedy to the tax deed holder, which was necessary under established legal principles for seeking such equitable relief.

In January 1887, Hermann Niepert, operating from Bremen, Germany, filed a lawsuit against Henry Memory of Chicago, Illinois, in the Superior Court of Cook County. The suit arose from a contract dated September 20, 1879, wherein Memory allegedly sold 250 boxes of American bacon to Niepert's company at a price of 25 marks for 110 pounds, with specific shipping and payment terms. Memory's agent, Ferdinand Eggena, was claimed to have accepted the offer on behalf of Niepert. However, when the shipment was due, Memory failed to deliver the bacon, leading Niepert to purchase the bacon elsewhere at a higher market price. The core of the dispute lay in whether the contract was legally binding as a written agreement or merely an oral contract, affecting the statute of limitations for the claims. After a trial, the court found in favor of the plaintiff and assessed damages totaling $4,919.96. Memory appealed, leading the case to the Appellate Court for affirmation and eventually to the Illinois Supreme Court for further review.	The plaintiff, Hermann Niepert, argued that a valid contract existed for the sale of bacon that Memory failed to honor. He claimed damages due to financial losses incurred from purchasing the bacon in the market after the defendant's non-delivery. Niepert requested restitution for the loss incurred as a result of the non-delivery based on the contract terms.	The defendant, Henry Memory, contended that the contract in question was not a written agreement and thus did not qualify under the longer limitation period of ten years, asserting it fell under a five-year limitation for oral contracts. Memory also challenged the interpretation of the contract, claiming its terms were incomplete, which further invalidated his obligation to perform.

Cornelius O’Callaghan and Margaret O’Callaghan were involved in a legal dispute that culminated in an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, where O’Callaghan, the appellant, was taken to court for contempt due to his failure to comply with a court order requiring him to pay his ex-wife, Margaret, fifty dollars for her maintenance and support, as part of a divorce decree. The court had previously issued a decree for alimony that served as a lien on O’Callaghan's real estate in Chicago, valued at approximately $5,000. During the proceedings, O’Callaghan sought to modify the alimony payments, arguing that the amount was beyond his ability to pay. However, a decision on his petition was pending while negotiations were ongoing between both parties. The case was presided over by Judge William W. Farwell.	The plaintiff, Margaret O’Callaghan, claimed that Cornelius O’Callaghan was in contempt of court for failing to pay the mandated alimony. She argued that despite his ownership of valuable property that could cover the alimony payment, he chose not to comply with the court order. Margaret requested the court to enforce the decree by holding O’Callaghan in contempt and ordering him to make the required payments.	Cornelius O’Callaghan defended himself by arguing that the court should have enforced payment from his property rather than holding him personally in contempt. He stated that he had filed a petition to modify the alimony terms due to his financial inability to pay and that the court's action should not occur while his petition was under consideration. O’Callaghan also claimed that he had not been properly notified of the order to pay before the contempt proceeding was initiated.

The case "Nancy R. Thatcher v. Wesley Thatcher" took place in Illinois, with the legal proceedings occurring in the September term of 1854. Nancy R. Thatcher initiated a divorce action against her husband, Wesley Thatcher, alleging acts of extreme and repeated cruelty. A trial by jury ensued, which resulted in a verdict that upheld all allegations in the divorce petition, except the claim that Nancy was a dutiful wife. Despite the jury's findings supporting most of Nancy's claims, the trial court dismissed the divorce petition and ordered Nancy to bear the costs of the proceedings. The decision raised questions about the evidence requirements and the court's handling of the verdict and evidence, which ultimately led to an appeal.	Nancy R. Thatcher claimed that her husband, Wesley Thatcher, had committed extreme and repeated acts of cruelty against her, which justified her request for a divorce. She argued that the jury's verdict sustained her allegations and entitled her to a decree of divorce. Although the jury did not support her claim of being a dutiful wife, Nancy emphasized that the rest of her claims were verified, seeking a reversal of the trial court's dismissal of her petition and a proper decree for divorce.	Wesley Thatcher, the defendant, contest the claims made by his wife and argued against the jury's findings. Although the specific details of his defense are not provided in the summary, he appeared to challenge the validity of the allegations and sought to uphold the trial court's dismissal of the divorce petition. The defense likely requested that the court affirm the lower court's actions and decisions regarding the divorce and the associated costs.

In December 1856, the case of Margaret Collins v. Hugh Smith et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Adams Circuit Court in Quincy, Illinois. Margaret Collins, the plaintiff, initiated a suit in ejectment at the October term of 1853, aiming to recover a specific lot of land. This property had a complex title history that included multiple transactions, starting with an administrator's deed for the land sold to Thomas McClintock in 1841. Collins attempted to establish a resulting trust, claiming that the funds for the land purchase belonged to Joseph, William, and Samuel McClintock, and that Thomas McClintock acted as their agent. The trial commenced in 1855, and the jury ruled in favor of the defendants. Collins contested this outcome, arguing against the exclusion of critical testimony and evidence related to the equitable title of the property.	The plaintiff, Margaret Collins, argued that she had a rightful claim to the land based on a series of deeds tracing the ownership back to an administrator’s sale. She asserted that the funds used to purchase the property were provided by Joseph, William, and Samuel McClintock, which established a resulting trust. Collins sought to introduce testimony from Thomas McClintock to prove these claims, arguing that parol evidence was admissible to establish the trust and her ownership rights in the property.	The defendants, led by Hugh Smith, contended that the evidence presented by Collins regarding the resulting trust was inadmissible. They objected to the testimony from Thomas McClintock, arguing it could not substantiate the claim of ownership on behalf of the alleged beneficiaries. The defendants maintained that the court correctly excluded the evidence and instructed the jury to rule in their favor because the title as claimed by Collins was insufficient under the statute of limitations.

Rachel Ann Carpenter et al. v. Josephine Calvert is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1876. The case originates from Geneseo, Illinois, and revolves around the will of Lydia W. Mandain, who passed away on July 6, 1873, in Philadelphia. Mandain was a widow at the time of her death, having married twice and having had one illegitimate daughter, Josephine Hough, who became Mrs. Calvert. Mrs. Mandain's will bequeathed her estate primarily to her niece, Rachel Ann Carpenter, while leaving only modest sums to her daughter, Josephine Calvert, and relatives. Following the will's probate, Josephine Calvert contested its validity in circuit court, claiming her mother was not of sound mind during its execution and that undue influence was exerted by Rachel Ann Carpenter. A jury trial in October 1875 sided with Calvert, invalidating the will. The appellants, including Carpenter, appealed the decision, contesting the jury's verdict and the legal standards applied during the trial.	The main arguments presented by Josephine Calvert as the plaintiff were that her mother, Lydia W. Mandain, was partially insane and incapable of making decisions regarding her property at the time the will was executed. Calvert alleged that the will resulted from undue influence exerted by Rachel Ann Carpenter, who allegedly manipulated Mrs. Mandain through falsehoods and threats. Calvert sought to have the will set aside, claiming it was invalid due to her mother’s compromised mental state and the improper influence allegedly exerted over her.	Rachel Ann Carpenter's defense centered on denying the allegations of undue influence and asserting the validity of Mrs. Mandain's will. The defendants maintained that the proper execution of the will was duly performed, and evidence was presented to show that Mandain was competent to dispose of her estate at the time the will was created. They contended that the jury's findings were based on improper legal standards regarding testamentary capacity and the related testimony was misleading.

In 1871, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between James Welch (the plaintiff) and Peter Karstens (the defendant). The case originated in a justice of the peace court, where Welch sought recovery for an account. The justice ruled in his favor, awarding the full amount claimed. However, Karstens appealed to the Circuit Court, leading to a trial where the judgment against him was affirmed, including additional amounts for interest due to the delay in appeal and ten percent damages as a penalty for pursuing the appeal perceived as frivolous. The court found that Karstens had acknowledged the legitimacy of the account and had previously indicated he would pay. During the proceedings, the defendant raised a minor objection regarding the legibility of the summons, claiming it improperly listed the plaintiff's name, but this was not supported by a formal plea. The court upheld the prior judgment, deeming no errors in the process.	The plaintiff, James Welch, argued that he was entitled to recover the full amount of the account he claimed, which included interest accrued from the point the account was due. He requested not only the original amount but also additional damages for the delay caused by Karstens’ appeal, as permitted under Illinois law.	The defendant, Peter Karstens, contended that the total judgment awarded to Welch exceeded the amount endorsed on the summons, suggesting that this invalidated the judgment. He raised a technical objection regarding the legibility of the summons but failed to present a formal plea of misnomer either in the initial or appellate court.

The case "Thomas Lantry et al. v. Bernard M. Lantry" took place in the fall of 1859 when John Lantry, anticipating his imminent death, conveyed his eighty-acre farm to his brother, Thomas Lantry, through an absolute deed. John had a son, Bernard, born shortly after his divorce, who never lived with him. Thomas claimed that there was no monetary consideration for the property, and that John's intent was for him to care for the sick brother, stating that he could give his son something if he was worthy. Witnesses testified that John intended to deed the farm to benefit Bernard and approached others for assistance in creating a trust. The case revolved around the application of the statute of frauds and whether a parol trust could be enforced despite the lack of written evidence. The Illinois Supreme Court had to discern whether there were grounds to impose a trust based on allegations of fraud or misrepresentation, assessing Thomas's actions when John made the deed.	Bernard M. Lantry claimed that Thomas Lantry (the grantee) had verbally promised to hold the land in trust for him, citing the intention behind the original conveyance.
