Bernard sought enforcement of this alleged oral agreement as a parol trust, arguing that Thomas's receipt of land prevented him from properly executing a direct conveyance that would have benefited Bernard. He asserted that the circumstances surrounding the deed warranted an exception to the statute of frauds due to Thomas’s fraudulent conduct.	Thomas Lantry defended himself by asserting that the conveyance was an absolute transfer with no obligations attached, as he never sought to procure the deed and disputed the existence of any parol agreement to hold the property in trust for Bernard. He relied on the statute of frauds, stating that since there was no written evidence or proof of an agreement, the claim for a parol trust was unfounded. Thomas maintained that the intentions expressed prior to the conveyance did not translate into actionable legal claims and emphasized that there was a lack of fraud or misrepresentation in the execution of the deed.

The case of Frank C. Smith et al. v. Frank B. Stafford took place in Knox County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment issued on February 29, 1884. The plaintiffs, Frank C. Smith and others, entered a contract with the Peoria & Farmington Pailway Company to grade a section of road between Monmouth and Keithsburg. They subcontracted this work to the defendant, Frank B. Stafford, who began the grading work in June 1881. However, he left the project uncompleted by early September 1881, claiming it was due to the company's engineer failing to provide further work directions. After leaving the work unfinished, Stafford sought to recover a balance of $175 for the work he had claimed to have completed. A jury initially ruled in favor of Stafford, leading to an appeal by Smith and his associates challenging the ruling.	The plaintiff, Frank B. Stafford, contended that he had substantially completed the grading work according to the contract terms. He sought to recover the remaining balance owed to him under the contract, alleging he should not be held accountable for leaving the project incomplete as it was the company's engineer who delayed further work.	The defendants, Frank C. Smith and others, argued that they had already compensated Stafford for almost all the work through issued labor orders. They claimed Stafford abandoned the project without justification before the completion date outlined in the contract. The defense maintained that the engineer had complied with Stafford's requests for additional work, and the cessation of work came as a direct result of Stafford's refusal to continue.

On December 23, 1884, T. Lyle Dickey obtained a judgment for $2,000 against the Town of Bruce at the LaSalle Circuit Court. Following this, the Town of Bruce sought to appeal the decision, with a window of fifty days allowed for them to file a bill of exceptions. They requested extensions for this filing on February 12 and February 17, 1885, claiming that notice had been given to Dickey’s attorney regarding their intention to seek an extension. Dickey objected, arguing that no valid suit was pending at the time when those orders were made. On March 3, 1885, Dickey's motion to set aside the orders was denied, resulting in a judgment against him for costs. Dickey subsequently filed a writ to reverse the judgment. The case revolves around whether the Circuit Court retained jurisdiction to extend the time for filing the bill of exceptions, and whether proper notice was provided to the plaintiff prior to the extension requests. The conflict around the notice given to Dickey's attorney became a crucial point in the case.	T. Lyle Dickey claimed that the orders made by the Circuit Court extending the time for the Town of Bruce to file a bill of exceptions were void, asserting that they were made without jurisdiction as there had been no valid suit pending at that time. Dickey argued that he did not receive proper notification regarding the applications for extension and therefore sought to reverse the judgment against him for costs.	The Town of Bruce contended that notice of the extension application was indeed given to Dickey's attorney and argued that the court had jurisdiction to grant the extensions based on this notice. They maintained that the order for extension was valid and, consequently, the motion to set aside those extensions should be denied.

The case "Ichabod H. Miller et al., for the use, etc. v. Jeremiah Ballard" took place in January 1868 in Adams County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Ichabod H. Miller and others, were representing the Adams County Agricultural and Horticultural Association in a lawsuit against Jeremiah Ballard. The dispute arose from a subscription agreement dated December 24, 1866, in which Ballard pledged to contribute $100 towards securing the location of the State Fair in Quincy for two years. Following the subscription, the Adams County Agricultural Association was incorporated with a $100,000 capital to buy land and develop fairgrounds. The fair was successfully held in Quincy in 1867. The plaintiffs aimed to recover Ballard's subscription, asserting that various expenses had been incurred based on the promises made in the subscription paper, and that they were entitled to collect the amount pledged by Ballard. The Circuit Court initially ruled that it was necessary for plaintiffs to show that they had performed work or expended money to validate the subscription claim, which the plaintiffs contested as an error.	The plaintiffs contended that they were entitled to recover Jeremiah Ballard's $100 subscription based on his written promise to pay, which was intended to secure the State Fair's location in Quincy. They argued that it was immaterial whether they personally incurred expenses; rather, they emphasized that any party acting in reliance on the subscription letters could bring the claim. They maintained that the successful holding of the fair justified the collection of the subscription amount, irrespective of whether the fair association's expenditures exceeded the required amount for securing the event.	The defense, led by Jeremiah Ballard, argued that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that they had expended money or performed necessary services relying on the subscription. The defense contended that simply because the Adams County Agricultural Association was incorporated and expended funds did not establish a direct link to Ballard's commitment to pay. They insisted that without proof of specific reliance on his subscription by the plaintiffs regarding expenditures, the case could not hold. They also challenged the admissibility of certain evidence about a bond related to the fair's organization.

In the case of Patrick L. Touhy et al. v. Henry P. Daly, which took place in 1888, the dispute centers around the sale of a piece of real estate located in Rogers Park, Illinois. The key individuals involved are Patrick L. Touhy and his wife, Catharine O. Touhy (the appellants), and Henry P. Daly (the appellee). The sale was initiated in early 1886 when Mr. Daly’s son approached Mr. Touhy to inquire about the property’s availability. Following negotiations, a preliminary agreement for the sale was executed on June 6, 1886, by Mr. Touhy as the agent for his wife. The sale was ultimately consummated on July 20, 1886, during an office meeting where all parties, including the buyer, were present. The primary contention arises over whether Mr. Touhy acted with the authority to bind Mrs. Touhy in the agreement regarding commissions for the sale. The court needed to determine the joint liability of the couple concerning the commission due to the appellee for his role in the sale.	The plaintiffs, Patrick L. Touhy and Catharine O. Touhy, claim that they are not jointly liable for the payment of commissions to Henry P. Daly as no sufficient evidence establishes a mutual agreement or authorizing action by Mrs. Touhy. They argue that the contract for the sale was made solely by Mr. Touhy, and that any implied agency he might have held was expressly rejected by Mrs. Touhy when she became aware of the contract. Their legal request is for dismissal of the claims against them due to the lack of joint liability and the failure of the appellee to meet the burden of proof.	Henry P. Daly contends that he acted as the agent for both Patrick L. Touhy and Catharine O. Touhy in the sale of the property and is therefore owed commissions. His defense relies on the assertion that the evidence of the sale proceeding at a lawyer’s office, where both appellants were involved, supports the argument for joint liability. Daly sought to have the court instruct the jury that they must find joint liability to rule in favor of his claims, contending that the appellants' presented arguments about individual liability were insufficient.

In April 1839, Horace Landon obtained a judgment against John Evans for a sum of $691.28. An execution was issued for this judgment on January 29, 1841, which was levied on two lots, numbered 96 and 130, located in Carrollton, Illinois. Following the first execution, three appraisers attempted to assess the value of lot 130, but they could not agree on a consistent appraisal, leading the sheriff to return the execution. On July 7, 1841, a second execution was issued, again targeting the same property. Again, the appraisers could not reach an agreement on the value, and this execution was also returned without further action. In April 1843, the Circuit Court granted a motion by Landon to set aside the levy, allowing a new execution to be issued. This motion was supported by an affidavit stating that Evans had not been consulted during the initial levies, denying him the opportunity to choose different properties of Landon for the execution. Evans appealed this decision, questioning the validity of the circuit court's order.	John Evans contended that the initial executions on his properties were conducted without his knowledge or consent, which denied him the opportunity to choose alternative properties belonging to the defendant, Horace Landon, to levy against. He requested the court to uphold the validity of the executions and oppose the Circuit Court's decision that allowed Landon to set them aside.	Horace Landon argued that the Circuit Court's decision to set aside the levy was just, given that the appraisers had failed to reach a consensus on the value of the property in question. He maintained that the execution proceedings were mishandled, and emphasized that the statutory process was not followed correctly as the appraisers' disagreement invalidated the appraisement. Landon sought to affirm the Circuit Court's decision to set aside the previous levies and issue a new execution.

Catharine Durgon filed a case against Susannah McGuire, the administratrix of the estate of Bernard McGuire, on October 1, 1868, in the Illinois Circuit Court. The case stems from a legal dispute regarding the status of Durgon’s relationship with the deceased, Bernard McGuire, who was a cooper living in Chicago. Durgon and McGuire cohabited for approximately seven years, during which they believed themselves to be married despite not having a formal marriage ceremony or license. They worked together to build an estate but faced hardships after McGuire’s declining fortunes and health, with Durgon supporting the family through her own efforts and her previous marriage's son. After McGuire’s death, his daughter, Susannah, denied Durgon’s claims of being McGuire's wife, leading Durgon to seek recognition for her contributions and the marital status she believed she held. The heart of the case was determining whether a valid marriage existed based on their agreement and cohabitation rather than formalities.	Catharine Durgon claimed that she had a valid marriage with Bernard McGuire based on their mutual agreement to live as husband and wife. She requested recognition of this marriage to substantiate her claim for compensation for services rendered to McGuire during their cohabitation. Durgon argued that their long-term relationship and shared life constituted a valid marriage under common law, based on conduct, declarations, and reputation, rather than formal legal requirements.	Susannah McGuire, as defendant, denied that Durgon had a valid marriage with her father, arguing that there was no legal ceremony or marriage license, and therefore, Durgon could not claim rights as a wife. The defense cited various legal precedents indicating that formal marriage requirements must be met, and contended that any claims to a common-law marriage were unfounded without proper documentation or ceremonial formalities. They sought to dismiss Durgon’s claims based on these arguments.

The case of John B. Lovingston et al. v. The County of St. Clair arose in June 1872 in Illinois concerning land rights adjacent to the Mississippi River. The action of ejectment was initiated by the County of St. Clair on August 26, 1870, against John B. Lovingston and the Wiggins Ferry Company for a tract of land defined by various boundaries, including the river’s low water mark. The dispute centered on the legal rights to land accretions along the river, specifically if the plaintiffs had a rightful claim to alluvial formations due to their property being bounded by the river. The circuit court found in favor of the plaintiffs initially, leading to appeals and judicial analysis focused on matters of riparian rights and ownership of land created by natural deposits, known as alluvion. The judgment ultimately referenced historical legal principles and precedents regarding property rights along navigable waters.	The plaintiffs argued that they held title to the land based on an act of Congress granting swamp and overflowed lands. They asserted that as riparian proprietors, they were entitled to all accretions formed by the gradual deposition of soil along the Mississippi River, regardless of whether the river was navigable. Their claims detailed the legal definitions of alluvion and emphasized that accretions emerged naturally, irrespective of any provided artificial aids.	The defendants maintained that the land in question was not part of the plaintiffs' title, arguing that their grants did not extend to the river's center or include alluvial formations. They contended that the accretions resulted primarily from artificial structures and labor designed to manage the river's flow, and therefore should not be attributed to the plaintiffs. They also referenced previous grants and surveys as limiting the scope of the property rights claimed by the plaintiffs.

The legal case "William H. Kennicott v. Phillip Sherwood" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1859. The dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, where William H. Kennicott, the appellant, leased premises to Phillip Sherwood, the appellee, under a written lease agreement that included a covenant for Sherwood to return possession of the premises at the end of the lease term on May 1, 1856. Before the expiration of this lease, Kennicott executed a new lease to John Maynard for the same premises. As May 1 approached, Maynard instructed John Van Buskirk, an under-tenant of Sherwood, to hold over and refuse to surrender possession. This arrangement became problematic when Van Buskirk did not vacate the premises as required, leading Kennicott to demand possession, which was not fulfilled. After a jury trial, the jury found in favor of Sherwood, leading to Kennicott's motion for a new trial, which was overruled.	The plaintiff, William H. Kennicott, claimed that Phillip Sherwood breached the lease agreement by failing to surrender the premises at the end of the lease term. Kennicott sought damages for the loss incurred due to Sherwood's refusal to yield possession, arguing that the contract stipulations were clear and enforceable.	The defendant, Phillip Sherwood, contended that he was not responsible for the failure to surrender possession because the arrangement between Maynard and Van Buskirk gave them the authority to remain on the premises. Sherwood argued that he had fulfilled his covenant and could not be held liable for actions taken without his consent. He sought dismissal of the claims against him based on these reasons.

In September 1871, the case of Calvin W. West v. William Frederick took place in De Kalb County, Illinois. The central issue arose when William Frederick, the plaintiff, loaned a sum of money to Calvin W. West, the defendant. To secure this loan, Frederick received an absolute deed to West’s farm and issued a contract stipulating that upon repayment of the loan within one year, the property would be reconveyed to West. However, when the loan was not repaid by the maturity date, Frederick initiated a forcible detainer action to reclaim possession of the property. The litigation focused on whether this action was permissible under the relevant statute which extends forcible detainer to cases between vendor and vendee.	William Frederick argued that he was entitled to reclaim possession of the farm due to West's failure to repay the loan as per their agreement. He contended that the case fit within the statutory provisions that allow for forcible detainer actions by a vendor against a vendee who has failed to comply with the terms of a purchase contract.	Calvin W. West contended that the legal relationship established between the parties was not that of vendor and vendee, but rather one of a loan secured by a deed. He asserted that the possession of the land was not granted through a sale or contract with Frederick, thus invalidating the forcible detainer claim. West's defense indicated that the initial transaction was merely security for the loan and did not create a vendor-vendee relationship under the statute in question.

In the case "Peter Smith et al. v. Charles Wunderlich et al." decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873, the dispute arose from an alleged trespass case involving the unlawful ouster of the plaintiffs, Peter Smith and his partners, from premises located at No. 24 West Madison Street in Chicago. The plaintiffs had been operating a shoemaking business at this location and claimed they had a verbal lease until May 1, 1872. On December 11, 1871, the defendants, including Nicholas Dunne (the landlord) and Anson H. Buck, forcibly removed them from the premises. The plaintiffs contended that this ousting prevented them from conducting their business, leading to significant financial losses. The case was initiated on January 27, 1872, and trial commenced in November of the same year. During the proceedings, evidence was presented supporting the plaintiffs' claims regarding their lease and the resulting damages due to their ouster. However, the defense argued against the premises of the plaintiffs' lease validity and sought to refute the claims of damages.	The plaintiffs claimed they were wrongfully ousted from their leased premises by the defendants and sought damages for the trespass, which they argued included not only the difference between the actual rental value of the premises and their rent but also lost profits from their shoemaking business due to the ouster. They asserted that their lease was valid until May 1, 1872, and emphasized the significant financial impact caused by not being able to conduct their business from the ousted premises.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs did not have a legitimate claim to the premises beyond the period they alleged, arguing instead that the lease was month-to-month. They denied that any actual damages were incurred by the plaintiffs as a result of the ouster. Additionally, they argued that the plaintiffs had failed to take appropriate action to re-enter the premises before filing the lawsuit, which undermined their claims for damages related to lost profits.

The case of The Ætna Insurance Company v. The Alton City Bank began in the Alton City Court, Illinois, with the proceedings occurring around 1861. The core of the dispute revolves around a bill of exchange drawn on April 15, 1858, by William Young Brown, payable in the amount of $550. The sequence of endorsements led the bill to Ætna Insurance, which then deposited it with Alton City Bank for collection. As per standard banking procedures, the Alton City Bank forwarded the bill to responsible correspondents in St. Louis for handling. The correspondents presented the bill to the drawee for acceptance on April 29, 1858, but acceptance was refused. However, the bank failed to protest for non-acceptance. Subsequently, a demand for payment was made on May 12, 1858, which was also refused and properly protested afterward. The legal question arose over whether the Alton City Bank was liable for the negligence of its correspondents. The court’s focus was on whether a bank, upon forwarding a bill for collection to responsible agents, can absolve itself of liability for any resulting loss due to the agents' negligence.	The Ætna Insurance Company argued that the Alton City Bank failed to fulfill its obligations by not protesting the bill upon non-acceptance and by failing to notify the drawer and indorsers of the non-acceptance. As a result of these omissions, Ætna claimed to have suffered financial losses and sought redress through the court, asserting that the bank should be liable for the damages incurred due to their negligence in handling the bill.	The Alton City Bank contended that their actions adhered to the customary practices of banking. They argued that they properly forwarded the bill to competent and reliable correspondents in St. Louis and that they discharged their duty by doing so. The bank maintained that their obligations did not extend to liability for any negligence on the part of the correspondents, asserting that they had taken reasonable care in the selection of the agents and could not be held responsible for the loss incurred.

In April 1861, in Tazewell County, Illinois, an action of assumpsit was brought by Uri Winchester against Sabin D. Puterbaugh in the Tazewell Circuit Court, overseen by Judge Harriott. The case revolved around the sale of six mules by Puterbaugh to Winchester for the sum of $300, as documented in a bill and receipt. At the time of the sale, the mules had escaped into a pasture, and the agreement stipulated that Winchester would be responsible for recovering them. The court heard evidence indicating that one of the mules had been taken by a person named Weed, with no clear timeline established regarding when this occurred. Thus, the central issue was whether Puterbaugh, who sold the mules, had a legal obligation to deliver them to Winchester and whether he had an implied guaranty of ownership.	Uri Winchester, the plaintiff, argued that the sale implied that Puterbaugh had a valid title to the mules and was obligated to deliver them. Winchester's legal requests included seeking recovery for the value of the missing mule, asserting that the defense of Puterbaugh was invalid as he was supposed to facilitate the delivery.	Sabin D. Puterbaugh, the defendant, countered that the agreement did not bind him to retrieve or deliver the mules to Winchester, as this was part of Winchester's responsibility. He contended that since one mule was missing due to circumstances independent of his actions, he should not be liable for its value.

The case involves James B. Dunn as the plaintiff against the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, taking place in Knox County, Illinois, in September 1869. Dunn was involved in an incident while riding in a wagon pulled by mules when the defendant’s train sounded its whistle. The noise frightened the mules, causing them to turn abruptly, overturning the wagon, and throwing Dunn to the ground, resulting in a sprained ankle. Following the incident, Dunn claimed damages for the injury caused by the alleged negligence of the railroad company's employees. A jury ultimately awarded him $1,525 in damages, which prompted the defendant to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, James B. Dunn, argued that the employees of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company acted negligently by blowing the whistle of the train too close to the mules, leading to the accident. Dunn sought compensatory damages for his injury, which he asserted resulted from the railroad's employees' carelessness. He claimed that the accident was caused by their actions and sought reimbursement for the impact of the injury on his life, despite evidence suggesting a minimal impact on his recovery.	The defendant, represented by the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, contended that the whistle was blown in accordance with customary practices at the time and location. They argued that the damages awarded were excessive given the nature of the injury—a sprained ankle that would have healed within weeks had the plaintiff taken appropriate care. The defense claimed that the verdict for $1,525 was unreasonable and based on jury prejudice rather than the merits of the case. They requested that the judgment be overturned due to the excessive damages awarded to Dunn.

Sarah A. Simmons v. J. Perry Johnson et al. took place in 1868 in Randolph County, Illinois. The case involved Sarah A. Simmons, the widow of Luther Simmons, who sought to challenge the release of her dower rights in her deceased husband's estate. Following Luther's death, Sarah accepted the provisions of his will and executed a release in exchange for one dollar. This release relinquished her claim to both her dower rights and specific property or its value provided under state law. However, Sarah later contended that she did not comprehend that the release extended to her separate property or its value. During the trial, evidence was presented indicating that the document had been partially read to her prior to signing, and she acknowledged understanding its contents. A jury found in favor of the defendants, leading Sarah to file for a new trial, which was denied. She subsequently appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Sarah A. Simmons argued that the release she signed did not adequately inform her that it covered her entitlement to separate property or its value. She claimed a lack of understanding regarding the full implications of the release. After the jury ruled against her, she requested a reversal of the verdict, asserting that the evidence did not support the jury's decision, indicating fraud or misunderstandings in the execution of the release.	The defendants, administrators of Luther Simmons' estate, maintained that Sarah A. Simmons executed the release freely and with full knowledge of its content. They contended that there was no evidence of fraud or improper influence in the signing of the document. Their position was supported by the jury's finding, which indicated that the release was valid, and thus, they opposed Sarah's request for a new trial and the reversal of the judgment.

In 1886, in the city of Galesburg, Illinois, a legal case arose involving Frank Castle and several other defendants against Catherine Fogerty. The case stemmed from a tragic incident involving John Fogerty, Catherine's father, who became intoxicated after consuming liquor sold by A. A. Castle, one of the defendants. This sale, which occurred on two lots owned by the defendants, ultimately led to Fogerty's death. Catherine Fogerty filed a lawsuit seeking to enforce a $400 judgment against A. A. Castle for the damages related to her father’s death, asserting that the defendants, being the heirs of the deceased Rachel Castle, should have their reversionary interests in the lots subjected to the payment of this judgment. The court found that A. A. Castle had used the lots without permission from the other defendants and had self-claimed his rights, while the defendants had a history of allowing such business activities to occur without objection. The appeal highlighted the complexities surrounding the "Dram Shop Act," which addressed the liabilities of property owners concerning the sale of intoxicating liquors.	Catherine Fogerty's primary argument was that Frank Castle and the other defendants were liable for the $400 judgment owed to her due to their reversionary interests in the lots where intoxicating liquor was sold. She claimed that their knowledge and lack of objection to the illegal sale of alcohol by A. A. Castle on the premises made them jointly responsible for the damages incurred as a result of her father's intoxication and subsequent death.	The defendants contended that they should not be held liable under the "Dram Shop Act" because they only had reversionary interests in the property and were not actively controlling or permitting the sale of intoxicating liquors. They argued that the statute's provisions specifically targeted those with immediate landlord responsibilities, and therefore, their reversionary rights should not be subject to the damages claimed by the plaintiff.

In December 1840, the case of Thomas H. Cushing v. Abner Dill was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court following an appeal. The case originated from a trial in the Edgar Circuit Court, where Dill sued Cushing for cutting down trees on his property, under the “Act to prevent trespassing by cutting Timber.” Cushing, the appellant, was accused of directing workmen to cut timber on his own land but did not adequately delineate the boundaries to prevent them from mistakenly cutting on Dill's property. The testimony revealed that, although the trees were cut by Cushing's workers, there was no clear evidence that Cushing himself committed the act or that he expressly authorized the cutting of trees from Dill's land. The key individuals involved included Thomas H. Cushing, the appellant who operated a timber business, and Abner Dill, the appellee who owned the land where the trees were allegedly cut. The legal conundrum centered on whether Cushing’s negligence in properly notifying his workers of property lines made him culpable under the penal statute. The lower court had found in favor of Dill, awarding him $64 in damages; however, Cushing appealed the decision to the higher court.	Abner Dill, the plaintiff, claimed that Thomas H. Cushing was responsible for cutting down trees on his property without permission, thus violating the penal statute designed to protect landowners from timber trespassing. Dill argued that Cushing’s actions, whether direct or through his employees, constituted a wilful violation of the statute. He sought compensation for the damages incurred from the tree cutting.	Thomas H. Cushing, the defendant, contended that he was not personally liable for the cutting of the trees, as he had not physically cut them nor had he explicitly instructed his workers to do so on Dill's property. He argued that the penal statute requires proof of direct involvement or clear authorization, which was lacking in this case. Cushing also pointed out that the statute provides remedies in addition to common law, suggesting that Dill was not without another recourse for his injuries.

In 1850, Daniel McAvoy entered into a contract with William H. Long and other members of a committee responsible for digging a ditch near Meredosia, Illinois. The contract stipulated that McAvoy would be paid 12.5 cents for each cubic yard of earth excavated, with measurements to be conducted by David L. Hodges. The ditch was to be approximately two miles long, with specific dimensions outlined for its construction. The parties agreed that Hodges would determine the amount of excavation work, and they made payments to McAvoy as the work progressed. After completing the excavation, Hodges measured the work and determined it to be 3,003.25 cubic yards. However, McAvoy later sought to introduce an alternative measurement from engineer Napoleon Koscialowskie, which calculated the amount of excavation at 6,125 cubic yards. The defendants objected to this evidence, which the court sustained, leading to a circuit court ruling that bound the parties to Hodges' measurements. McAvoy then appealed the decision.	McAvoy's primary claim was that the measurement of the excavation work conducted by Hodges was incorrect, and he sought to challenge this by introducing expert testimony from Koscialowskie. He argued that he was entitled to payment based on the alternative measurement, which reflected a larger amount of work done. Ultimately, McAvoy sought to reverse the lower court's ruling which favored the defendants.	The defendants, represented by Brown & Yates, contended that Hodges' measurements were final and binding based on the terms of the contract. They argued that the contract explicitly appointed Hodges as the measuring authority whose decision could not be contested by expert witnesses. The defendants maintained that the rejection of Koscialowskie's testimony was correct, asserting that the court had the sole authority to interpret the contract without input from engineers, as it did not contain technical language that required such assistance.

In 1876, in LaSalle County, Illinois, Samuel Brunswick brought a lawsuit against Peter Birkenbeuel concerning four promissory notes that Birkenbeuel had issued to E. Brunswick & Co. and which had been endorsed over to Brunswick. The essential issue arose after Birkenbeuel argued that he had settled his debts by transferring two insurance policies to Brunswick as payment for the notes. The property covered by these insurance policies had been destroyed by fire, which, under the law, created a prima facie cause of action for the insured. The case went to trial, where differing testimonies from both parties emerged regarding whether the transfer of the policies constituted valid satisfaction of the notes. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of Birkenbeuel, concluding that there was an agreement recognizing the transfer of the insurance policies as a valid discharge of the debt.	Brunswick's primary argument was that he was owed payment on the promissory notes that Birkenbeuel issued. He claimed that the transfer of insurance policies did not constitute a proper settlement, thereby seeking the full amount due under the notes. Additionally, Brunswick contended that Birkenbeuel needed to demonstrate that the insurance policies were valid and that a complete cause of action existed in favor of Birkenbeuel against the insurance companies.	Birkenbeuel asserted that the transfer of the two insurance policies to Brunswick was indeed a valid payment that discharged the debt represented by the promissory notes. He argued that Brunswick accepted these policies in exchange for releasing the indebtedness, which involved a prima facie cause of action due to the loss of the insured property. Birkenbeuel maintained that he was not obligated to prove the validity of the insurance policies in the context of the defense against the notes, and he contended that terms of the instruction requested by Brunswick were inappropriate and misleading.

In the case of Lyman Plummer et al. v. The People, which took place in Bureau County, Illinois in 1855, Seymour Plummer was arrested and initially imprisoned based on a charge of larceny committed in Muscatine County, Iowa. Following his arrest, he was found guilty by a justice of the peace and required to post bail for his appearance in court. However, the mittimus (writ) issued for his imprisonment was deemed illegal after the sheriff discovered it was based on a charge from another state. Subsequently, a new mittimus was issued without any further hearing, which stated that the offense occurred in Bureau County. In an attempt to secure his release from this unlawful imprisonment, Seymour along with two sureties, Lyman and Edgar Plummer, executed a recognizance. The recognizance was later forfeited when the Plummers did not appear in court as required. The case revolved around the legality of the recognizance and the claims of duress made by both Seymour and his sureties regarding its execution.	The plaintiffs claimed that the recognizance was obtained under duress due to Seymour Plummer's unlawful imprisonment. They argued that the recognizance was not executed voluntarily but forced upon the sureties because Seymour was in an illegal detention. They sought to have the forfeiture of the recognizance dismissed based on these claims of duress.	The defendants (The People) argued against the claims of duress presented by the sureties. They maintained that the sureties could not plead the duress of their principal (Seymour Plummer) to escape their obligations under the recognizance, as legal principles prevent sureties from using this defense. The People contended that they had a valid record justifying the execution of the recognizance, and they requested the court to sustain the forfeiture.

On November 29, 1880, Ira N. Herrick executed two promissory notes for $17,040 each, secured by a deed of trust on six parcels of land in Cook County, Illinois. Following the default on the notes, the Cheltenham Improvement Company, which acquired the land, faced a foreclosure suit initiated by William H. Whitehead, the holder of the unpaid note. The trust deed stipulated that the grantor would pay all taxes on the lands, and if neglected, the trustee could pay those taxes and hold them against the property's sale proceeds. A considerable amount of taxes had been neglected, leading to legal actions. The case moved through the circuit court, where evidence was gathered, and requisite payments for taxes and solicitation fees were added to the amount owed. Whitehead claimed $1,000 for redeeming a tax title and $260 for an abstract of title, among other costs. The Cheltenham Improvement Company appealed after the circuit court ruled in favor of the plaintiff regarding these allowances.	The plaintiff, William H. Whitehead, alleged that the Cheltenham Improvement Company defaulted on the trust deed, and claimed a total of $15,161, which included the amount due on the promissory note, $1,000 for redeeming a tax title, $260 for obtaining an abstract of title, and $719 in solicitor's fees. He sought to have these amounts recognized and the foreclosure enacted to recover his debts through the sale of the mortgaged property.	The defendant, Cheltenham Improvement Company, argued that the $1,000 for the tax title and $260 for the abstract were improperly allowed. They contended that these items were not included in the original foreclosure bill or supported by the evidence presented. They also challenged the solicitation fee, asserting that it was only applicable if the foreclosure was filed in the name of the trustee, not the holder of the notes. The company requested that the appellate court reverse the decree of the circuit court regarding these allowances.

In the case of John G. Elliott v. James L. Rubel, Assignee, decided on January 21, 1890, by the Illinois Supreme Court, the central parties involved were John G. Elliott, a patent attorney, and James L. Rubel, the assignee of the W. O. Tyler Paper Company, which had made an assignment for the benefit of its creditors. The Paper Company was organized on July 1, 1885, and on August 8, 1887, it made the assignment. Elliott claimed to have provided legal services to the Paper Company for 247 days, from June 1885 to July 1887, under a contract for $50 per day, totaling $12,350. Following objections from Rubel regarding the claim, a hearing was held in the Cook County court on February 20, 1888, where the court ruled in favor of Elliott. However, upon appeal to the Appellate Court, this judgment was reversed, prompting a further appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Elliott's main argument was that he was entitled to payment for his legal services based on a contract with the Paper Company, which stipulated that he would be paid $50 per day in legal fees for his services while the company remained in litigation. Elliott claimed that the total amount owed to him exceeded the contractual limitation of $3,000, which he argued was invalid due to the circumstances surrounding his representation.	Rubel, as the assignee, contended that Elliott’s claim exceeded the maximum agreed payment of $3,000 as outlined in the contract. He argued that the attorney could not claim more than this amount for his fees and that the Paper Company had the right to cease prosecution of the case, thus limiting Elliott's potential fees to $3,000.

Job M. Hayes, a 22-year-old man, obtained a life insurance policy for $12,000 from Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Co. in February 1874, naming his nephews, Ellis W. Hayes and Daniel D. Hayes, as beneficiaries. At the time of his death on August 18, 1876, the policy was in his possession and was delivered by their mother, Maggie E. Hayes, to attorney James F. Hughes for collection. Hughes, as their guardian, informed the insurance company of the death and paid the semi-annual premium due, which the company accepted. After some negotiations, Hughes settled for $8,015, half of the policy's value, and dismissed the lawsuit he had filed. Years later, it was claimed by Maggie E. Hayes and Hughes that the settlement was void due to fraudulent representations made by the insurance company's agent during their negotiations. The case was brought to court in 1882, two years after Maggie was appointed administratrix of Job M. Hayes' estate, even though she never possessed the policy, which was held by Hughes. The court had to determine if Maggie, as administratrix, had the right to sue for the policy’s conversion.	The plaintiff, Maggie E. Hayes, as administratrix of Job M. Hayes, claimed that the insurance company unlawfully converted the life insurance policy, thereby seeking damages for the alleged wrongful conversion. She argued that the initial settlement made by Hughes on behalf of the minor beneficiaries was void due to fraudulent misrepresentations made by the company's agent.	The defendant, Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Co., argued that the administratrix did not have the right to sue for the conversion of the policy because, at the time of the alleged conversion, the policy was in the rightful possession of the guardian, James F. Hughes. They contended that Maggie lacked both possession and the right to immediate possession required to bring an action for conversion under Illinois law.

In 1868, in the city of Chicago, Illinois, Charles Botto filed a legal case against The Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company. The case focused on a policy of insurance held by Botto for $3,000. The central issue was whether the insurance company had validly canceled the policy before a fire occurred. The policy contained a clause allowing the company to cancel the insurance if the risk was increased or if additional insurance was taken out on the property. The defendant claimed that they had notified Botto of the cancellation and that it took effect on November 23, 1866. The court heard the case without a jury, and after examining the testimonies, it ruled in favor of Botto, stating that the cancellation was not valid since the company did not tender the unearned premium alongside the notice as required. The court ordered the company to pay Botto a total of $3,135, which included interest. The case was then appealed by the insurance company to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Charles Botto claimed that The Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company failed to properly cancel the insurance policy before the fire occurred. He argued that the company did not comply with the necessary legal requirements for cancellation, specifically by not returning the unearned premium. Botto sought the full amount of the insurance policy, plus interest, for his losses due to the fire.	The Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company contended that they had validly canceled the insurance policy before the fire, as they had sent a notice of cancellation to Botto. The company argued that the cancellation was final and that they were within their rights under the policy. They requested the court to dismiss Botto's claims and uphold the cancellation of the policy.

In October 1872, D. S. Vanpelt, a resident of Cincinnati, Ohio, was involved in a mortgage transaction in Olney, Illinois, with Bobinson and his wife to secure three promissory notes totaling $346.67. Despite a judgment of foreclosure in 1876, the property was never sold. In 1876, a mechanic's lien was filed against the property by Barlow, leading to a court decree in 1877 that established the lien and ordered the property sale. The property was sold to T. W. Hutchinson, an attorney for Barlow, after no redemption period was observed. McDonald acquired a tax title under a different sale. Following internal agreements, the parties became tenants in common of the property. In June 1883, Vanpelt filed a bill in Richland County against Hutchinson and others, claiming he was unaware of the mechanic's lien proceedings due to inadequate notice about his supposed non-residency, only being notified through a published notice in a local newspaper. He argued that Hutchinson failed to exercise due diligence in discovering his whereabouts, as previous records indicated his Cincinnati residency.	Vanpelt argued that the court's decree regarding the mechanic's lien was invalid because he was not properly notified of the proceedings due to alleged gross negligence by Hutchinson. He contended that Hutchinson had sufficient knowledge of his Cincinnati residence and failed to conduct a reasonable inquiry to ascertain his address. Vanpelt sought to have the court's previous decree reviewed and reversed.	Hutchinson contended that he acted reasonably under the circumstances, asserting that he made diligent inquiries to find Vanpelt's residence but was unable to do so. He stated that prior to the foreclosure proceedings, he had believed Vanpelt had moved within Ohio but could not determine his exact location. His defense relied on the sufficiency of the affidavit filed for notice publication, which stated that due inquiry was made.

John W. Taylor filed a legal action against Orange Smith on September 15, 1870, in Will County, Illinois. The case arose from a demand for $600, and on October 1, 1870, a justice of the peace ruled in favor of Taylor, awarding him $153.10 plus costs. This particular justice of the peace had been granted special jurisdiction by a legislative act on March 7, 1867, allowing him to adjudicate cases involving amounts up to $600. However, a new constitution was adopted on August 8, 1870, which posed the question of whether the justice could still exercise this extraordinary jurisdiction post-adoption. The Illinois Supreme Court had previously ruled in a related case (Phillips v. Quick) that any enlargement of jurisdiction beyond what was allowed under general law was unconstitutional, thereby creating a precedent for the current case. As such, the core issue revolved around the justice's authority to exercise jurisdiction beyond what was legally permitted under the new constitutional framework.	Taylor's main arguments were centered around the validity of the judgment rendered by the justice of the peace, asserting that the justice had jurisdiction under the special act at the time of the decision. He sought to maintain the judgment in his favor of $153.10 plus costs.	Smith's defense contested the jurisdiction of the justice of the peace, arguing that after the adoption of the new constitution, the justice could no longer exercise jurisdiction beyond the limits defined by general law. Smith claimed that the ruling was invalid due to this lack of jurisdiction, thus requesting a reversal of the judgment.

In 1859, Edward B. Chumasero, the appellant, found himself in a legal dispute with Horatio G. Gilbert, the appellee, in La Salle County, Illinois. The case involved actions of assumpsit (a legal term for a type of contract action) initiated by Gilbert against Chumasero, who had borrowed money formalized by promissory notes payable at the Broadway Bank in New York City. The notes included a standard promise to pay without any specifics regarding interest and exchange rates. Picture this as a situation where money was borrowed and needed to be repaid, but there was no explicit agreement on interest rates between the parties involved. At a trial presided over by Judge Ohamplin during the September term, the jury was waived by mutual consent, and judgments were eventually rendered against Chumasero. Gilbert sought to present evidence that, at the time of the notes' maturity, there was a 1.5% exchange rate applicable to the repayment, but Chumasero objected, arguing that there was no provision for such exchange in the notes. Despite the objection, the court allowed the testimony, leading to the court ruling in favor of Gilbert, with damages assessed at $711.89.	Gilbert claimed that Chumasero owed him money as evidenced by the promissory notes. He sought to recover the principal amount stated in the notes along with damages calculated based on the prevailing exchange rate at the time of maturity. Gilbert argued that the contract was clear and enforceable despite the absence of specific terms regarding interest and exchange.	Chumasero's primary defense was that the notes did not include any agreement for exchange payments, thus making it erroneous for the court to allow such damages. He contended that the legal framework should adhere to the lex fori—the local law governing interest rates on contracts—which did not support Gilbert's claims for an exchange. Furthermore, Chumasero maintained that since there was no specific averment about a higher interest rate due to the transaction's location, he was not liable for the additional claims.

The case "William J. Randolph v. The County Board of Pope County" was decided on July 10, 1886, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose when William J. Randolph, the county treasurer of Pope County, was removed from office by the County Board due to his failure to comply with statutory requirements to report financial information and settle accounts with the board. Randolph was to file a report, count the funds, and was also required to submit an additional bond. His removal was ordered after he neglected these duties despite multiple notifications and opportunities to comply. The County Board's actions were based on their established statutory authority to remove county officers for such failures. Randolph, sensing wrongful removal, petitioned the circuit court through a writ of certiorari to challenge the board's decision, asking for the record of proceedings leading to his removal to be reviewed.	Randolph claimed that the County Board acted beyond its jurisdiction in removing him from his position as treasurer. He argued that he was not properly notified of the board's orders, thus rendering the removal invalid. Randolph sought to have the earlier decisions of the County Board overturned and requested reinstatement to his position, asserting that any technical irregularities in the process warranted reversal of his removal.	The County Board contended that they acted within their statutory authority to remove Randolph due to his failure to comply with mandatory reporting and auditing requirements. They argued that the removal was properly backed by the evidence of his continued neglect of duty and that all necessary procedures were followed. The Board maintained that Randolph had received appropriate notice, and thus the removal was justified and valid, requesting the court to uphold their actions.

William Clark filed an action of ejectment against James W. Peckenpaugh in September 1867, in Illinois. The case revolved around the ownership of a piece of land. Clark presented evidence of a deed from the patentee to James Clark and another from James Clark to himself to claim his ownership. In contrast, Peckenpaugh established that he had color of title and had paid property taxes from 1855 to 1864. To counter Peckenpaugh’s assertions, Clark introduced a warranty deed from E. Muse, Jr., to Peckenpaugh, dated January 23, 1860. However, the court ruled in favor of Peckenpaugh, establishing that he had met the requirements of the limitation law of 1839, which stated that possession with color of title and payment of taxes for seven successive years constituted valid ownership rights. The court noted Clark's failure to connect his claim to the Muse title and deemed his arguments insufficient to negate Peckenpaugh's established defense.	William Clark argued that James W. Peckenpaugh could not establish his claim of ownership due to a lack of continuous payment of taxes under the same color of title since he had accepted a deed from Muse in 1860. Clark contended that this change in title negated Peckenpaugh's claim to the land, and he sought to have the court rule in his favor regarding the rightful ownership of the premises.	James W. Peckenpaugh's primary defense was that he possessed color of title and had consistently paid taxes on the property from 1855 to 1864, which satisfied the statutory requirements for ownership. He asserted that the subsequent acquisition of the Muse title did not negate his earlier claims. Peckenpaugh's position was that payments made after receiving the Muse deed did not need to be attributed strictly to that title, as he always maintained his claim of ownership.

Jonathan Ellis filed a legal action against Jacob Snider in 1830 in Union County, Illinois, originally before a justice of the peace. Ellis claimed an amount of ninety dollars. The case proceeded to the Union circuit court after Snider appealed the initial judgment. Prior to the trial in circuit court, upon Snider's request, Ellis submitted a written account listing charges totaling ninety-five dollars. However, evidence presented to the court indicated that Snider owed Ellis over one hundred dollars. The circuit court ruled that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction due to the amount owed exceeding one hundred dollars and subsequently reversed the initial judgment. Ellis then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court to review the circuit court's decision regarding jurisdiction.	Jonathan Ellis argued that the justice of the peace had jurisdiction to handle his claim as he was seeking less than one hundred dollars, despite evidence suggesting a larger debt was owed. Ellis contended that the court erred in ruling that jurisdiction was absent and sought to have the circuit court's decision reversed.	Jacob Snider's defense was based on the assertion that the amount Ellis was claiming was less than the sum proven to be owed, which suggested that the original claim exceeded the jurisdictional limit of the justice of the peace. Snider maintained that the circuit court correctly reversed the judgment based on this jurisdictional issue.

In 1853, in the Stephenson County, Illinois, Henry L. Niles filed a chancery bill against Caleb W. Brown, William Sills, and another individual named Jenks. Niles had previously obtained a judgment against Jenks for $990.50 in the Jo Daviess Circuit Court. Following the judgment, an execution was levied on certain lands owned by Jenks, and a related certificate of the levy was filed on April 5, 1853. The suit claimed that Jenks had fraudulently transferred ownership of these lands to Brown in 1847 to evade creditors. Brown then transferred the lands to Watson in 1849, without consideration, also suspect of fraudulent intent. Despite these transactions, Brown remained in possession of the lands until after the execution was levied. Upon trial, the court found that the deeds executed by Jenks to Brown and later to Watson were fraudulent and set them aside to satisfy Niles’ execution. Brown and Sills appealed the decision, asserting that the transactions were valid and claimed that Niles' judgment was fictitious.	Niles alleged that the deeds transferring land from Jenks to Brown and from Brown to Watson were executed to defraud creditors. He sought to invalidate these deeds so that the lands could be sold to satisfy the judgment he obtained against Jenks. Niles argued that the transactions were made without consideration and continued to keep the lands from his reach.	Brown and Sills defended by admitting the transactions but claimed they were valid, asserting that there was consideration involved and denying any fraudulent intent. They characterized Niles' judgment as fictitious and argued that their conveyances were made in good faith without any intention to hinder Niles' claims.

The case of "George Owen v. William Thomas" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1864. The dispute arose in Morgan County, Illinois, involving the parties George Owen and William Thomas. William Thomas initiated an action against George Owen, claiming damages for an alleged breach of a covenant of general warranty in a deed concerning a quarter section of land. Thomas asserted that Owen and his wife had conveyed a defective title and that the legal title was actually held by James Robertson and others, who had a paramount claim to the property. In defense, Owen contended that he held the fee simple title and had effectively conveyed this title to Thomas. The case hinged on the nature of the search conducted for a lost deed that is central to the claims. The evidence presented indicated that reasonable searches were made, but the original deed could not be located. Ultimately, the question revolved around whether oral testimony regarding the deed's contents was sufficient to establish its execution and enforceability.	The plaintiff, William Thomas, argued that George Owen breached a warranty covenant by failing to convey a valid title to a quarter section of land. Thomas claimed that Owen did not hold the true title, and he cited the inability to obtain possession due to claims held by James Robertson and others. Thomas sought damages based on this breach of covenant, asserting that he deserved compensation for the lapse in title security.	The defendant, George Owen, contended that the title was validly conveyed and that the legal title was with him and his wife at the time of the transaction. Owen claimed that he had provided the necessary proof of the title and any issues with the deed were due to the plaintiff's failure to conduct a more thorough search. He asserted that he had effectively conveyed the fee simple title, and thus he did not owe any damages to Thomas for the alleged breach of the warranty covenant.

Russell C. Mix filed a legal case against Charles M. Ross and others in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1870. The case originated in the city of Aurora, Illinois, where the city collector seized a span of Mix's horses to collect a special assessment of $119. This assessment was levied for a sidewalk construction that benefitted the lot owned by Mix. The local court dismissed Mix's injunction requesting to restrain the sale of his horses and also assessed damages against him for the injunction. The critical legal question was whether the city collector had the authority to levy personal property for the payment of this special assessment.	Mix argued that the collector did not have the legal authority to sell his personal property to satisfy the special assessment. He claimed that the statutory provisions only allowed for the collection of taxes and assessments against real estate and that the assessment in question did not qualify as a tax. Thus, he sought the court's protection against the seizure and sale of his horses.	The defendants contended that the city collector had the same authority to collect special assessments as state and county tax collectors. They argued that the relevant statutes permitted the seizure of personal property to satisfy any outstanding assessments. Their defense emphasized that special assessments create a lien on both real and personal estate, supporting their right to proceed with the sale of Mix's horses.

In 1871, in Vermilion County, Illinois, William Watson executed two promissory notes payable to Geo. W. Kenworthy and subsequently indorsed to J. F. Powers, who then transferred them to the plaintiffs, William G. Swannell and others. The plaintiffs initiated an action of assumpsit against Watson seeking enforcement of the notes. Watson's defense was based on claims of fraud and circumvention, asserting he was illiterate and had been misled about the nature of the notes by Kenworthy, the payee. The trial occurred before a jury, which ultimately returned a verdict in favor of Watson. The plaintiffs contended that Watson had acted negligently by not seeking assistance from nearby individuals who could have helped him read the notes, hence the court's focus was partially on Watson's failure to exercise due diligence. The appeal against the judgment asserted that the trial court had erred in admitting certain evidence and in its jury instructions regarding Watson's alleged ignorance and the validity of the notes.	The plaintiffs, William G. Swannell et al., argued that they were innocent purchasers of the promissory notes and deserved recovery despite Watson's claims. They maintained that Watson acted negligently by failing to read the notes or seek help to understand them before signing. They claimed that the alleged fraud by Kenworthy should not serve as a valid defense against a suit by an innocent assignee.	The defendant, William Watson, contended that the promissory notes were obtained through fraud and circumvention, as he was uneducated, could not read, and had relied on Kenworthy's misleading representation of the notes' contents. Watson argued that he had no reason to suspect deception and that he should not be held liable for the notes due to the fraudulent circumstances under which they were executed.

In August 1882, Harriet L. Gay filed a bill in chancery in the circuit court of Kankakee County, Illinois. The case involved a dispute over the ownership of real estate originally purchased by Harriet L. Gay in 1853 with proceeds from a property inherited from her father. At the time of purchase, she was married to Elkanah Gay, and they had two living children. The conflict arose when Elkanah Gay became indebted to A. T. Gay for a lumber purchase, leading to a promissory note that was subsequently transferred to Mace Gay. A judgment was obtained against Elkanah Gay in 1875, but no property was found during the initial execution. In 1882, an alias execution was issued, leading to a levy on the property owned by Harriet. A trust deed had been established in 1857 to protect the property from Elkanah's debts, but Mace Gay challenged its validity. The court initially ruled in favor of Harriet, but a cross-bill filed by Mace Gay sought to nullify the prior conveyances, resulting in a complex legal evaluation of debts, rights, and equitable interests.	Harriet L. Gay claimed that the execution against her property was invalid due to the trust deed established for protection against her husband Elkanah Gay's debts. She sought to enjoin further action on the levy and maintain her ownership of the land. Harriet argued that the trust deed was legitimate and should shield her property from her husband's creditors.	Mace Gay, the defendant, contended that the trust deed was a fraudulent conveyance made to evade creditors, thereby voiding Harriet's claims. He maintained that the indebtedness for the lumber preceded the creation of the trust deed, making the conveyance invalid concerning his judgment against Elkanah Gay. Mace sought to have the trust deed set aside and declared null and void in order to recover the debt owed.

In April 1863, the case of Daniel P. Vanmeter et al. v. Pleasant Durham et al., Administrators of Thomas W. Lyon, deceased, was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Kankakee County, presided over by Judge Charles E. Starr. The issue arose from an action of assumpsit initiated by the administrators of Thomas W. Lyon against Daniel P. Vanmeter and another defendant. The sheriff reported that Vanmeter had “waived reading, and accepted service” on March 29, 1862, but Vanmeter later contested that there was no valid service of process against him. A default judgment was entered against both defendants after a damages assessment, prompting them to file a writ of error arguing that the Circuit Court erred due to improper service of process.	The plaintiffs, as the administrators of Thomas W. Lyon, claimed that they were entitled to a judgment based on the actions against Vanmeter and the other defendant. They asserted that even with the sheriff's return of service indicating acceptance, the service was adequate to justify the jurisdiction of the court and the default judgment rendered.	The defendants contended that the service of process was insufficient because the service record did not meet legal standards, as established in previous rulings such as Maher v. Bull. They argued that the statement of "waived reading, and accepted service” did not constitute valid service, and therefore, the court had no jurisdiction to enter a default judgment against them. Their request was for the court to overturn the judgment.

Richard Eells was indicted in December 1843 in Adams County, Illinois, for harboring and secreting two slaves owned by Chauncy Durkee from Missouri. The indictment included several counts, alleging that Eells unlawfully harbored and prevented the rightful owner from reclaiming his property, which was in violation of the law regarding fugitive slaves. Eells was found guilty after a trial, where he objected to the indictment's form, particularly its failure to name the slaves and to allege his knowledge of their status as slaves. Eells sought to quash the indictment and later filed a motion to arrest the judgment after his conviction, both of which were denied. Ultimately, he was fined $400. The case was appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, which addressed the validity of the indictment and the constitutionality of state laws concerning fugitive slaves.	The plaintiff, Richard Eells, argued that the indictment was fatally defective because it did not specify the name of the slaves and failed to allege that he knew they were slaves. He contended that the law under which he was prosecuted was unconstitutional, as it conflicted with federal legislation and the constitutional protections granted to individuals. Eells claimed that the state law improperly penalized actions that federal law also addressed, leading to potential double jeopardy for the same offense.	The defendants, the People of the State of Illinois, argued that the indictment was sufficient and that the law under which Eells was charged was constitutional. They maintained that the indictment adequately detailed the offense without needing to include the slaves' names or Eells' knowledge of their status as slaves. The defendants contended that the state had the right to legislate on matters regarding fugitive slaves and that Eells' actions obstructed the legal rights of slave owners under state law.

In the case of Charles Gardner v. Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railway Company, which was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 16, 1885, the incident in question occurred at a railway crossing over a public highway. The plaintiff, Charles Gardner, sought to recover damages for the death of a span of horses and the destruction of a wagon, hayrack, and harnesses due to a collision with the defendant's train. The collision took place early in the evening under somewhat dark conditions. The plaintiff's servant, who managed the team, was killed in the incident, and the only other witness present was the driver of another team nearby at the time of the accident. The primary legal issue revolved around allegations of negligence against the railway concerning the failure to ring a bell or sound a whistle in advance of the crossing, along with the claim that the train was speeding. A trial resulted in a jury verdict and judgment for the defendant, prompting the plaintiff to appeal.	The plaintiff, Charles Gardner, claimed damages after his horses were killed and property destroyed due to a collision with a train. Gardner argued that the railway company failed to follow safety protocols by not sounding a bell or whistle prior to the crossing, which constituted negligence. He requested a reversal of the jury's verdict and sought damages for his losses resulting from the collision.	The defendant, Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railway Company, contended that the plaintiff had not presented sufficient evidence of negligence. They argued that the evidence presented at trial did not support the claim of negligence on the part of the railway company, asserting that the plaintiff's servant may not have exercised due care. Additionally, they highlighted that the plaintiff's request for instructions on comparative negligence was not warranted under the circumstances of the case.

In March 1846, Greenleaf M. Woodbury mortgaged real estate located in Schuyler and McDonough counties, Illinois, to David and Moses Manlove to secure payment of three promissory notes due in April 1847. By October 1851, the Manloves sought to foreclose the mortgage through the Schuyler Circuit Court by filing a scire facias. Woodbury presented several defenses, including claims of payment, failure of consideration, and issues surrounding the ownership of the properties. The court reviewed multiple pleas from Woodbury, including objections related to the recording of the mortgage and claims of unrecorded judgments against the property. Ultimately, the court found that Woodbury owed $513.88 on the mortgage and ruled in favor of the Manloves, allowing for a special execution against the mortgaged lands.	The plaintiffs, David and Moses Manlove, argued that Woodbury failed to fulfill his obligations under the mortgage agreement on the promissory notes. They contended that the mortgage was validly executed and had been recorded, thus providing grounds for foreclosure. The plaintiffs sought a judgment for the amount due and requested a special execution against the mortgaged property to satisfy the debt.	Woodbury presented several defenses, including claims that the mortgage lacked consideration and that there had been partial payments. He argued the mortgage should be invalidated due to the existence of prior judgments against the property and a failure of consideration regarding the conveyed premises. Additionally, he claimed the premises were incumbered, which diminished their value and sought to set off this value against the owed amount.

In January 1874, the case of The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. v. John McGinnis was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident took place in an incorporated town in Illinois, where John McGinnis, the plaintiff, owned a colt that was struck by a train operated by the defendant, The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. McGinnis claimed that the railroad company was negligent in its operation, leading to the death of his horse. The railway company contended that McGinnis should not recover damages because his horse was running at large in violation of local ordinances. The court examined the responsibilities of the railway operator, which included the obligation to exercise a high degree of caution in populated areas, especially considering the potential dangers that trains pose to both people and property. It was established that the train's speed, which was maintained at around seven to eight miles per hour, was excessive under the circumstances, particularly as it left a station, and that proper measures to control the train, such as applying the brakes, were not properly executed. The plaintiff's conduct was deemed only slightly negligent, while the railway company's negligence was classified as gross due to their failure to take adequate precautions.	John McGinnis, the plaintiff, argued that the railway company was grossly negligent in the operation of its train, as it failed to apply the brakes when approaching the colt on the track. He contended that even if he was partly at fault for allowing his horse to run at large, the railway's negligence was significantly greater, warranting him the right to recover damages for the loss of his horse. McGinnis claimed that the railway's operators did not exercise the necessary care appropriate for a train traveling through a populated area.	The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. defended itself by arguing that it had taken all reasonable precautions according to the law to prevent injury. They asserted that McGinnis' negligence in allowing his horse to roam freely contradicted local ordinances, thereby absolving the railroad from responsibility. The railway contended that since the horse was unlawfully at large, McGinnis should not be entitled to recover any damages for the incident.

The case "Union Mutual Accident Association v. Minna Frohard" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on May 29, 1889. The case arose from a tragic incident in which John Frohard, a member of Union Mutual Accident Association, was accepted as a member on September 1, 1885. A policy was issued to him that provided benefits to his wife, Minna Frohard, in the event of his death through external and accidental injuries. On January 28, 1887, while hunting, John Frohard accidentally shot himself and died. Following his death, Minna Frohard submitted proof of his passing and requested the association to levy a $2 assessment on its members to cover the amount stipulated in the policy. However, the association refused, arguing that hunting was a more hazardous occupation, limiting their liability to $500. Minna then brought suit in equity to compel the association to fulfill its obligations under the policy.	Minna Frohard claimed that her late husband’s accidental death while hunting should be covered under the insurance policy issued by Union Mutual Accident Association. She argued that the association was obligated to assess its members to raise the necessary funds, not just the $500 they had tendered. Her legal requests included compelling the association to levy the full assessment required to pay the policy amount and seeking general relief for the breach of contract.	The Union Mutual Accident Association defended itself by asserting that John Frohard’s actions of hunting fell under a category that was considered more hazardous than the occupation for which he was insured. Consequently, they contended that according to the association's by-laws, they were only liable for an amount not exceeding $500. The association sought to limit its liability and contended that any further obligation should be dismissed due to the classification of hunting as a more hazardous occupation.

On October 13, 1880, Henry H. Spencer leased a quarter-section of land to Andrew J. Dougherty under a written agreement. The lease stipulated that Dougherty would clear the land and prepare it for cultivation by specified dates, with Spencer agreeing to pay him for the cleared acreage over several years. Although Dougherty claimed to have cleared the land, he did so after the deadlines due to extraordinary high water affecting his work. Spencer, however, contended that Dougherty failed to meet the terms of the lease and did not execute the work as required. After a trial regarding a claim for work performed (indebitatus assumpsit), the court directed the jury to disregard a count related to a frame house as there was no evidence to support it. The jury ruled in favor of Dougherty for the work done, which led Spencer to appeal. The case went before the Illinois Appellate Court on June 7, 1887, with judges examining various legal interpretations regarding the nature of contracts and the notion of substantial performance.	Dougherty (plaintiff) argued that he had completed the work required by the lease, albeit after the contractual deadlines. He claimed that Spencer accepted the work and had benefited from it, thus he sought payment for the labor performed in clearing the land. Dougherty asserted that any delays were due to factors beyond his control and requested compensation based on the terms of their contract.	Spencer (defendant) contended that Dougherty did not perform the contract as stipulated; thus, he was not liable for payment. He argued that Dougherty had broken the lease terms by failing to complete the required work on time and therefore could not recover for the labor performed. Furthermore, Spencer claimed damages due to Dougherty's breach of contract and requested the court to uphold his rights arising from the non-performance.

In 1870, in Iroquois County, Illinois, the case "Hiram Phelps et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois" arose stemming from an indictment for the larceny of forty steers. The alleged incident took place on October 14, 1869. Hiram R. Phelps and his sons were accused of stealing the cattle, which, according to a written contract with Richard Amerman, partially belonged to Phelps. The contract stated that Phelps had purchased a half interest in Amerman's cattle and outlined responsibilities concerning care and costs related to the cattle. On the day of the alleged crime, while Amerman was away in Indiana, the cattle were driven to a pasture under the supervision of Phelps's son. Shortly after, Hiram R. Phelps and his sons were seen driving the cattle towards Ashkum, where Hiram shipped them under a different name, misrepresenting the situation to Amerman. During the trial, the defense argued that the jury should consider whether Phelps had a legitimate belief of ownership due to the contract. A critical point of contention was a jury instruction regarding the distinction between mere conversion of the cattle and larceny based on ownership claims.	The plaintiffs (the People of the State of Illinois) contended that Hiram R. Phelps and his sons committed larceny by unlawfully removing and converting the cattle for their own benefit without ownership rights, despite the contract. The prosecution emphasized that to convict on charges of larceny, the intent to steal was a necessary element, and that the actions of Phelps and his sons (driving and shipping the cattle) clearly exhibited an intent to commit the crime.	The defendants argued that Hiram R. Phelps acted under an honest belief that he was a co-owner of the cattle based on the agreement with Amerman. They maintained that the jury should be allowed to consider whether Phelps genuinely believed he had a right to the cattle. The defense further requested that a jury instruction regarding the definition of larceny and ownership be given without alteration, asserting that if Phelps held any belief in ownership, his actions could not constitute larceny.

The case of Charles Harward et al. v. The State of Illinois took place in January 1869 within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Madison County and was presided over by Judge Joseph Gillespie. Charles Harward and others brought the case against the State of Illinois concerning a taxation issue. The legal proceedings were based on an agreed state of facts which presented similar legal questions to those in a preceding case involving Harward and the St. Clair and Monroe Levee and Drainage Company. The court had to determine whether there should have been a judgment for the taxes in question.	The plaintiffs, Charles Harward and others, argued that the taxes in question should not have been imposed.
