The defendants, including the city officials and the bank, argued that the issue at hand did not fall under equitable jurisdiction and claimed that any relief should be sought by the city itself, not by the State’s Attorney or individual taxpayers. They contended that the laws did not provide a basis for the plaintiff's claims since there was no legal authority allowing the donation and emphasized that they did not improperly conduct the funds as alleged by the plaintiff.

On December 9, 1887, the case of *William H. Reynolds v. Timothy Moshier* was adjudicated in the Illinois Appellate Court. The conflict began with a lawsuit initiated before a Justice of the Peace, aiming to resolve issues related to a promissory note that was purportedly for $9, dated October 28, 1876. The note was allegedly owed to Timothy Moshier and signed by William H. Reynolds and J. A. Reynolds. During the proceedings, the appellant (William H. Reynolds) claimed that the note was improperly assigned to Elizabeth Reynolds and asserted that it was issued as part of a transaction involving personal property sold as an agent for Moshier at a chattel mortgage sale in January 1875. Evidence presented by the appellant indicated that Moshier had no interest in the note and did not authorize its issuance. Conversely, testimony from the appellee suggested that the note was valid because it was linked to property sold at the mortgage sale and that it had been in the possession of S. M. Reynolds, the husband of Elizabeth Reynolds. The jury ruled in favor of the appellee, awarding $18.05. However, the case was later appealed on grounds of improper jury instructions regarding the note's validity and its delivery.	The plaintiff, Timothy Moshier, claimed that he was the rightful holder of a promissory note for $9, asserting that it was given as security for property sold by William H. Reynolds at a chattel mortgage sale. He contended that the note had always been in possession of S. M. Reynolds and that it was never paid or delivered with Moshier's consent. The plaintiff sought a ruling that would affirm his right to collect the amount due on the note.	The defendant, William H. Reynolds, argued that the promissory note in question was invalid because it was issued without Moshier’s authority or knowledge. He contended that there was no proper delivery of the note to Moshier or any legal payee, which negated its enforceability. The defense maintained that the note was a construct of a private arrangement between him and Marion Reynolds to shield property from creditors, thus calling into question the legitimacy of any claims made by Moshier. Reynolds sought to have the judgment in favor of Moshier overturned.

The case "J. and M. Littleton, Appellants, v. Moses, a man of color, Appellee" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1831. It originated in the Union Circuit Court, where Moses, a man of color, brought an action against J. and M. Littleton for trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment. The specifics of the incident that led to the lawsuit are not detailed, but the trial resulted in a jury verdict in favor of Moses, awarding him forty dollars in damages. The defendants then appealed, claiming issues with jury instructions on the need for proof of actual restraint and arguing that the case did not involve questions of freedom or slavery. The court had to decide on the validity of the trial court’s instructions and the defendants' motion for a new trial, eventually affirming the initial judgment.	The plaintiff, Moses, claimed that he was subjected to trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment by the defendants. He sought damages for these wrongs, which culminated in a jury ruling that awarded him forty dollars. The core of his argument was based on the belief that he was unlawfully restrained and that this formed the basis for his legal claim against the Littletons.	The defendants, J. and M. Littleton, contended that the trial court erred in its instructions to the jury. They argued that there was no proof of actual restraint necessary to support the claims of false imprisonment and that the nature of the pleadings was consistent with a common action of assault and battery without involving issues of slavery. They also sought a new trial after the jury ruled against them, insisting that the verdict was not justified given the arguments made during the trial.

In May 1844, in Warren County, Illinois, James C. Gregory, along with Nelson Alley and William C. Gregory, entered into a recognizance before two justices of the peace. This recognizance required James C. Gregory to appear in court to answer charges of burglary and larceny; failure to do so would result in legal penalties. During a subsequent court session in June 1844, the court found that Gregory failed to appear and rendered a judgment against all recognizors by default, ordering the forfeiture of the recognizance for the penalty of $800. A writ of scire facias was issued against Nelson Alley and William C. Gregory, requiring them to appear in court and justify why execution should not issue. Despite the absence of an indictment against James C. Gregory, the scire facias process proceeded, and a judgment against the sureties was rendered by default, prompting an execution order. The case revolves around whether proper legal procedures were followed regarding the forfeiture of the recognizance and the issuance of the scire facias.	The plaintiffs in error argued that there was no valid cause of action against them because the record did not indicate that an indictment was ever found against James C. Gregory. They maintained that the judgment of forfeiture was improperly rendered without proper proceedings involving all parties, particularly the principal, Gregory. They requested that the judgment be reversed and that no execution should issue against them due to these alleged procedural errors.	The defendants, represented by the Attorney General, contended that the judgment was valid based on common law standards, arguing that the absence of an indictment did not negate the possibility of a forfeiture judgment when the principal was absent and the sureties defaulted. They argued that the procedural errors cited by the plaintiffs were not sufficient to invalidate the judgment, and thus the court should uphold the execution against the plaintiffs.

In December 1882, Jacob Wzieck applied for a fire insurance policy from Burlington Insurance Co. in Washington County, Illinois. The policy insured his dwelling and belongings for a term of five years, with a total coverage of $1,100. Wzieck paid for the policy by delivering two promissory notes, each for $12.25, maturing in October 1883 and 1884. A critical event occurred when Wzieck's property was destroyed by fire on July 25, 1884. At the time of the fire, the first note had not been paid, leading to a dispute over the validity of the insurance claim. Wzieck claimed that he had extended the payment of the first note with the insurance agent’s approval and had provided a new note in lieu of the old one, which was denied by the insurance company. The case initially resulted in a judgment against Burlington in a lower court, which was then appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court.	Wzieck asserted that he was entitled to recover damages under the fire insurance policy, despite the fact that one of the notes was overdue at the time of the fire. He claimed that an agreement had been made to extend the payment of that note, which should allow his insurance claim to be valid. Evidence was presented suggesting that the insurance agent, at least verbally, had recognized this extension.	Burlington Insurance Co. contended that the insurance policy was void due to the outstanding payment on the note, as the terms of the policy explicitly stated that any unpaid premium would invalidate the coverage. They rejected the plaintiff's claims regarding the extension of the note, arguing that such a change required written consent from the company's secretary. The insurance company maintained that the evidence did not support Wzieck’s assertions regarding the extension of payment.

In the case of Joseph Corcoran v. The People, the legal proceedings took place in La Salle County, Illinois, with the decision rendered on May 28, 1888. The appellant, Joseph Corcoran, was accused of being the father of an illegitimate child born to Bridget Cashman, an unmarried woman. Cashman testified that the incident occurred at a picnic on August 24, 1884. According to her, it was the only occurrence of illicit intercourse with Corcoran, and the child was born on May 17, 1885. Corcoran, however, completely denied ever having sexual relations with her. The case relied solely on Cashman's unsupported testimony, which was considered weak and lacking corroboration. During the trial, various errors were alleged regarding the admission of evidence; specifically, the plaintiff was allowed to present evidence about naming the child after Corcoran and her poverty, which the court later deemed irrelevant to the central issue of paternity. These factors potentially influenced the jury unduly against Corcoran. As a result of these errors, the appellate court decided to reverse the judgment and remand the case for further proceedings.	The plaintiff, Bridget Cashman, claimed that Joseph Corcoran was the father of her illegitimate child based on her testimony regarding a single act of illicit intercourse. She sought to establish his paternity and likely requested financial support or acknowledgment of paternity based on the legal implications of the bastardy claim.	The defendant, Joseph Corcoran, argued that he never had any sexual relations with Bridget Cashman, denying the allegations completely. He contended that the sole evidence provided by Cashman was insufficient and unsupported, suggesting that the trial's handling of certain evidence was erroneous and detrimental to his case.

The case of Frederick Korf v. Ann E. Lull took place in 1873 in Chicago, Illinois. It centers around a dispute regarding a contract for construction work on a brick building that Lull was having erected. Frederick Korf, the plaintiff, was a contractor engaged to perform various tasks including carpentry, plastering, plumbing, and painting under a written agreement. The case arose after Lull alleged that Korf did not complete the work according to the specified contract and failed to finish it within the agreed timeframe. Consequently, Lull claimed damages due to the inferior workmanship and delays in completing the project, and Korf sought to establish a mechanic's lien for work and materials he provided, including additional work beyond the original contract. A master was appointed to assess the case, and it was reported that Korf was owed $847.59 for the completed work and additional materials. However, Lull disputed this payment citing contract breaches, leading to a dismissal of Korf's petition, which he subsequently appealed.	The plaintiff, Frederick Korf, argued that he was entitled to payment for the labor and materials provided as per the construction contract, including extra work that was necessary. Korf maintained that Lull had accepted the work and could not waive claims regarding the quality after acceptance, particularly for latent defects. He sought to establish a mechanic's lien on the property for the unpaid amount.	The defendant, Ann E. Lull, contended that Korf's work was not completed according to the contract's specifications or within the stipulated timeframe. Lull claimed damages that exceeded the amount owed to Korf due to the poor quality of workmanship and delays in project completion. She argued that the responsibility for those defects and delays lay with Korf and sought the dismissal of Korf's claims based on these defenses.

William Mount v. William S. Hunter is a legal case that took place in January 1871 in Logan County, Illinois. The dispute arose when William S. Hunter filed a lawsuit against William Mount, claiming damages after Mount allowed his sheep, known to be affected with a contagious disease called "scab," to roam freely on open prairie land. As a result, Hunter's sheep became infected. The case was brought under a specific statute enacted on February 16, 1865, which states that any individual who allows sheep affected by a contagious disease to run at large—and thus potentially infect other sheep—can be held liable for damages. During the trial, a jury found in favor of Hunter and awarded him $388.75 in damages, which was later reduced by Mount's concession to $300. Mount appealed the decision, contending various legal technicalities including the nature of the action and the statute of limitations.	The plaintiff, William S. Hunter, argued that William Mount was responsible for the damage caused to his sheep due to Mount's negligence in allowing his infected sheep to roam freely. Hunter claimed damages based on the statute that holds individuals liable if they allow sick animals to infect others. His legal request was for compensation for the losses incurred due to the transmission of the "scab" disease to his sheep.	William Mount's primary defenses included claims that the lawsuit was improperly structured as it should have been filed as a penalty action rather than a case action. He also contended that the statute of limitations barred the action since it alleged harm within a timeframe that Mount believed did not meet the legal standards. Additionally, he argued that there was insufficient evidence to prove that the “scab” disease was contagious, challenging the evidence presented by Hunter about the condition of the sheep.

The case, "The People of the State of Illinois, for the use of Gregg et al. v. Smith M. Palmer et al.," was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1868. The dispute arose in Morgan County, Illinois, centering on the actions of Smith M. Palmer, the county sheriff, regarding an execution ordered in favor of Gregg and Hughes against William D. Powell and Samuel T. Crawley. The execution was issued on January 26, 1866, but Palmer failed to levy the execution within the required time frame. Instead, he waited until April 28, 1866, before returning the execution as "no property found," despite evidence that Crawley, a resident of Morgan County, had property that could satisfy the debt. The plaintiffs argued that the sheriff neglected his duty by not levying on Crawley’s real and personal property. These included two hundred and seven acres of land, which was encumbered but still had sufficient equity, as well as livestock. The court examined whether Palmer had a duty to act to enable the plaintiffs to secure their debt and questioned his argument regarding a lack of funds to record the levy.	The plaintiffs claimed that Sheriff Palmer failed in his duty to levy execution on Crawley's property, which was sufficient to satisfy the judgment. They argued that Palmer's neglect resulted in a loss of their ability to collect their debt. They sought damages for this neglect, asserting it was the sheriff's responsibility to act on behalf of the execution to secure their interests legally.	In his defense, Sheriff Palmer submitted several pleas, arguing the key issue was whether Crawley had property liable for levy and whether he was negligent. He contended that he had not been able to notify Crawley and that there was confusion regarding the ownership of the property. Palmer also claimed he could not levy on the property because the plaintiffs had not provided the necessary funds to pay fees related to the recording of the levy.

Between 1874 and 1877, a legal dispute arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving James E. Strawn, Mary F. Strawn, and their father, Augustus C. Prout. The case centered around the ownership and responsibilities related to a property located at lot 17 in block 3, University subdivision in Chicago. Prout agreed to perform plumbing and gas-fitting work on a building erected on this property for Mary F. Strawn's benefit, with the total cost contracted at $1,200. It was alleged that while Prout arranged the work, he was acting as an agent for James E. and Mary F. Strawn, thus making them responsible for paying for the work completed. However, both the Strawns and Prout contested this claim, asserting that Prout had acted independently without any agency relationship to Mary F. Strawn and that full payment had been made for the work done except for a remaining balance of $236. Following a review of evidence, the case, which involved multiple intervenors claiming liens on the property, was referred to a master to take proofs, leading to a lower court decree favoring the plaintiff, Patrick L. O’Hara.	Patrick L. O’Hara, the complainant, claimed that he entered into a contract with Prout to execute plumbing and gas-fitting work valued at $600 on lot 17 for which he was entitled to payment. O’Hara argued that Prout was acting as an agent for the Strawns, specifically Mary F. Strawn, and thus they were liable for the services rendered. O’Hara sought to enforce his lien against the property based on this connection.	The defendants, including Prout and the Strawns, denied O’Hara's claims, asserting that Prout acted solely on his own behalf and that they had fully paid for the contracted work. They argued that there was no agency relationship between Prout and Mary F. Strawn, stating that Prout had made the contract and payments independently. Moreover, they contended that any work done was under Prout’s initiative for his daughter and did not establish liability for Mary F. Strawn.

The case of Dawson Kerr et al. v. Willis M. Hitt took place in Cook County, Illinois, and was addressed by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The litigation arose due to the destruction of public land records, prompting Willis M. Hitt, as petitioner, to establish his title to a portion of land that had been owned by Mary J. Dennis, an executor of an estate previously claiming title through John S. Clark. The case involved a complex history, including a quit-claim deed given to Hitt by one of Dennis's executors. The principal parties included Hitt and several defendants, including Lombard Decham, who claimed an interest in the property. A critical aspect of the case was the contention over the boundary line between Hitt's and Decham's lands, which had been recognized and respected over many years, establishing a tacit agreement on the division. Ultimately, the court had to assess the validity of the legal processes followed and the historical ownership claims.	The plaintiff, Willis M. Hitt, sought to establish legal title to a parcel of land based on a quit-claim deed he received from one of Mary J. Dennis's executors. He argued that despite the destruction of records, the historical claims backed by an established boundary line required the court to affirm his title to the land. Hitt contended that he should be recognized as the rightful owner, and thus, he requested that the court grant a decree in his favor.	The defendant, Lombard Decham, filed a cross-bill arguing that there was a mistake in previous deeds concerning the land's boundaries. He claimed that the original conveyance from Clark to Dennis was meant to convey only a portion of the property rather than the entirety claimed by Hitt. Decham's defense also included the assertion of twenty years of adverse possession, asserting that his continuous and open ownership of the land barred Hitt's claims to establish title.

In January 1871, a legal case titled Asahel Gridley v. Samuel T. Bane was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in McLean County, Illinois, where the plaintiff, Asahel Gridley, pursued an action against the defendant, Samuel T. Bane, based on a promissory note. The note was supposed to have been jointly executed by Bane and two other individuals, J. C. Pierson and J. S. Pierson, for the benefit of J. H. Cheney. Bane was the only defendant in this case. The central issue revolved around whether Bane's plea—asserting that his signature was acquired through fraudulent misrepresentation by J. C. Pierson—was sufficient to defend against the enforcement of the note. Bane claimed he was deceived into signing the note under the belief that J. S. Pierson had already signed it, while in reality, the name was a forgery. The court had to consider if the lack of liability from J. C. Pierson affected Bane’s obligation to the payee or his assignee, Gridley.	The plaintiff, Asahel Gridley, argued that Samuel T. Bane was obligated to honor the promissory note despite claims of fraud. Gridley asserted that the note was valid and enforceable, having been indorsed to him by J. H. Cheney before maturity. The plaintiff sought to recover the owed amount based on the terms of the promissory note, focusing on the enforceability against Bane as one of the signers.	Samuel T. Bane contended that he should not be held liable for the promissory note, as his signature was obtained under false pretenses by J. C. Pierson, who falsely represented that J. S. Pierson’s signature was present on the note. Bane maintained that he was misled, believing in the existence of a second valid signature, and argued that the lack of this signature due to forgery invalidated the note’s enforceability against him. He requested that the court dismiss Gridley's claim based on these fraudulent misrepresentations.

In June 1852, the case of Charles Jacks v. Liberty Stimpson was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a trial in the Circuit Court of Rock Island. The incident leading to the case involved Jacks procuring a warrant for the arrest of Stimpson on charges of larceny, alleging that Stimpson had taken cattle from his property. The arrest was made under this warrant, but Stimpson was subsequently discharged after an examination before a justice of the peace. Stimpson claimed actual damages from the wrongful arrest and initiated a malicious prosecution suit against Jacks, resulting in a judgment against Jacks for $500 in damages. The case's foundation lay on proving that Jacks acted maliciously and without probable cause when he instigated the prosecution against Stimpson, which was a critical legal standard in malicious prosecution actions.	The plaintiff, Liberty Stimpson, argued that Charles Jacks maliciously initiated a false arrest and prosecution against him on a larceny charge without any probable cause. Stimpson claimed that Jacks’s actions resulted in actual damages due to the wrongful arrest. He sought compensatory damages for the suffering caused by the malicious prosecution.	The defendant, Charles Jacks, contended that he acted with an honest belief in Stimpson's guilt when he sought the prosecution, arguing he had sufficient cause to believe that a crime had been committed. Jacks asserted that his belief negated the claim of malice and that the existence of probable cause should protect him against the claim of malicious prosecution.

Michael Wallace was involved in a legal case against The People of the State of Illinois, which took place in 1871 in Perry County. The case stemmed from an indictment for larceny, where it was alleged that Wallace stole property belonging to the “American Merchants’ Union Express Company.” During the proceedings, Wallace's legal team filed a motion to quash the indictment, claiming that the ownership of the property was not properly stated. The circuit court ruled against this motion, leading to a trial where Wallace was found guilty of larceny. Subsequently, he attempted a motion in arrest of judgment, which was likewise overruled. This legal action raised the key issue that the indictment failed to specify whether the Express Company was a corporation, as the law requires property claimed by a company to be laid out as belonging to an incorporated body. The specifics of the indictment's ownership claims became the pivotal point of contention, ultimately resulting in appeals surrounding these rulings.	The plaintiff, represented by Michael Wallace, primarily argued that the indictment against him was flawed due to the failure to adequately state the ownership of the property alleged to have been stolen. Wallace contended that the American Merchants’ Union Express Company had not been established as a legal corporation in the indictment. Thus, he sought to have the indictment quashed on the grounds of this legal deficiency. He requested other judicial reliefs, including a reversal of the verdict reached in the previous trial.	The defense, representing The People of the State of Illinois, maintained that the indictment was properly issued and that the ownership of the stolen property was validly claimed. They argued that Wallace was rightfully found guilty based on the evidence presented during the trial. The state put forth that the court’s ruling on the motions entered by Wallace was correct and should be upheld, standing by the legal sufficiency of the indictment as it was.

In 1867, in Illinois, John Emery brought a legal action against R. C. Hoyt, who was the conservator for Samuel Reynolds. The case revolved around a promissory note for $1,000 executed by Reynolds on April 24, 1866. Emery claimed that the note was valid and sought its enforcement. The defense rested on the argument of insanity, asserting that Reynolds was not of sound mind at the time of signing the note. During the trial, evidence was presented regarding Reynolds' mental state, with testimonies from individuals who interacted with him around the date of the note’s execution. A jury found in favor of the defendant, Hoyt, meaning they accepted the argument that Reynolds was indeed insane during the execution of the promissory note. Emery's motion for a new trial was denied, and the case was appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court.	John Emery argued that Samuel Reynolds executed a valid promissory note while in a lucid state and therefore should be held liable for the debt. He sought a judgment for the amount owed under the note, contending that there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the defendant's claim of Reynolds' insanity at the time of signing.	R. C. Hoyt contended that Samuel Reynolds was insane when he executed the promissory note, thereby invalidating any contractual obligation. He maintained that the burden of proof lay with Emery to demonstrate that Reynolds had the capacity to contract at the time, asserting that insanity could preclude the enforceability of the note.

In January 1874, the case of Thomas H. Allen et al. v. James Hart was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from a transaction in DeWitt County, Illinois. The central figures were the plaintiffs Thomas H. Allen and Pasten, who sold a patent right called “Hathaway’s Magic Match Safe and Self-lighter,” along with exclusive territorial rights in Indiana, to the defendant, James Hart. Hart contended that he had been misled by fraudulent representations regarding the value and profitability of the territory associated with the patent before entering into the agreement. He claimed that he was induced to purchase the patent rights based on these deceptive assurances. Before initiating the lawsuit, Hart attempted to return the deed for the territory, seeking to rescind the contract based on the alleged fraud. The court had to determine if the vendors, Allen and Pasten, engaged in fraudulent misrepresentation that warranted Hart’s rescission of the contract and return of the paid consideration.	The plaintiffs, Thomas H. Allen and Pasten, contended that there was no fraud committed in their dealings with Hart. They argued that the defendant had the opportunity to inspect the subject of the contract and made a purchase at “arm’s length,” with any representations made being expressions of opinion rather than guarantees of value. They maintained that Hart’s dissatisfaction stemmed from his own folly, as the subject was available for examination and should have been assessed with due diligence.	James Hart's defense emphasized that he relied on false and fraudulent representations made by the plaintiffs, who assured him of the significant value and marketability of the patent territory. He argued that these misrepresentations were material to his decision to enter the contract and that he was misled about the profitability and success that other buyers had reportedly experienced. Hart maintained that the statements made by the vendors went beyond mere opinions and that he had a right to rely on them, leading to his claim for rescission and recovery of the consideration paid.

The case "Harrison Machine Works v. N. J. Miller” took place in Du Quoin, Illinois, involving a threshing machine sale in 1886. N. J. Miller, the plaintiff, expressed interest in buying a threshing machine from Harrison Machine Works. He initially contacted an intermediary, Bishop, to facilitate the purchase by sending a telegram to Harrison Machine Works. On June 3, 1886, Miller ordered the machine, contingent upon providing a mortgage to secure the purchase price. However, issues arose when Miller, who had promised to present a mortgage that would serve as a first lien on his property, delayed in providing the necessary security. Harrison Machine Works instructed Bishop not to deliver the threshing machine to Miller due to concerns about the adequacy of the collateral. Despite these instructions, Miller unlawfully took possession of the machine on June 19, 1886. The case arose from Harrison Machine Works’ attempt to reclaim the equipment through a legal replevin action after Miller's refusal to return it when requested by the company.	Harrison Machine Works claimed that they had not consummated the sale of the threshing machine because Miller failed to fulfill the agreed-upon condition of providing adequate security for the purchase price. They argued that Miller's unauthorized removal of the property constituted unlawful possession and that they were entitled to recover the machine as a result of Miller’s non-compliance with the terms.	N. J. Miller contended that he was entitled to the threshing machine as he believed he had a valid claim of ownership once he took possession. He argued against the plaintiff’s assertion that the sale was incomplete, insisting that Harrison Machine Works’ agents had acted beyond their authority, thus rendering their decision to prevent delivery ineffective. Miller claimed he should not be penalized for the issues surrounding the mortgage and that he had legitimately taken possession of the machine.

The case "Fail and Nabb v. Goodtitle, ex dem., Hay and Lagow" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1826. The action originated in the Lawrence Circuit Court, where it was tried as an ejectment case involving the right to possess certain land. The plaintiffs, Fail and Nabb, obtained a favorable verdict and judgment in their initial trial. Following this, the defendants, Goodtitle and his associates, appealed, claiming several errors had occurred during the trial, particularly regarding the admissibility of certain evidence, including a sheriff's deed. The court highlighted the inadequacies in the record regarding the defendants’ claims and pointed out that, unless properly presented, these points could not be addressed in appeal. The ruling emphasized that the acknowledgment of the sheriff’s deed before the Lawrence circuit court, rather than the Crawford circuit court, was appropriate and did not invalidate the deed under the applicable statute. It also noted the difficulties and expenses that would arise from requiring acknowledgments across county lines. Ultimately, the court affirmed the lower court's decision, indicating issues with evidence presented by the defendants that did not meet the required standards of proof regarding titles.	The plaintiffs, Fail and Nabb, asserted that their ownership rights were legitimate and upheld by a sheriff’s deed validly acknowledged in court. They sought to establish their title to the land in question, arguing that the objections raised by the defendants regarding the deed's legitimacy were invalid. Their primary claim hinged on the legal sufficiency of their evidence and the proper acknowledgment process of the sheriff’s deed under the law.	The defendants, Goodtitle, Hay, and Lagow, contended that the sheriff's deed presented by the plaintiffs was inadmissible as evidence because it had not been properly acknowledged before the Crawford circuit court, which they believed affected the validity of the deed. They aimed to reverse the verdict of the lower court by arguing that the errors in the trial significantly affected the outcome, maintaining that their objections regarding the admissibility of evidence were substantial.

On January 25, 1886, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Charles G. Barth et al. v. The Commercial National Bank in Ottawa, Illinois. The dispute arose from a series of judgments against B. G. Caulfield, specifically relating to properties in Cook County. On February 13, 1885, the Commercial National Bank filed a lawsuit alleging that it had a superior lien on certain lands due to an older judgment obtained against Caulfield in 1875. The bank had successfully pursued an execution sale after its executor returned the initial judgment unsatisfied. In contrast, Barth acquired a junior judgment against Caulfield and executed a sale on the property after Burley, another creditor to Caulfield, had also initiated a claim on the same properties. The case centers on the conflicting claims to the property based on the timing and seniority of the respective judgments and executions. The court needed to determine the precedence of these liens and the rightful ownership of the disputed properties.	The plaintiff, The Commercial National Bank, argues that it holds a superior lien due to a judgment from 1875, which was followed by an alias execution that established an execution lien on the properties in question. They assert that this lien remained valid and active until it was extinguished by their sale. Therefore, they request that Barth's subsequently acquired sheriff's deed be declared void and removed as a cloud on their title, affirming their ownership of the lands.	The defendant, Charles G. Barth, contends that the subsequent judgments and executions he acquired against Caulfield entitle him to the property. He argues that since his judgment was obtained while the prior judgment's lien had expired, it should take precedence. Barth claims that the prior judgment and execution did not extend sufficiently to protect the bank's interest once its time limits under the law were reached, thus positioning his claims as valid and deserving of recognition.

In June 1874, the case of Hiram Padfield v. Hiram Pierce was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centers around a piece of land that Hiram Padfield, the plaintiff, claims should rightfully belong to him. The land was previously associated with a judgment recovered by Daniel Pierce, who acted as Padfield's guardian. In 1850, upon turning 21, Padfield became entitled to make a decision regarding the land, which had been conveyed to his guardian in satisfaction of a $400 judgment against McKendree College. Despite being aware of his rights, Padfield chose to settle with his guardian by accepting the proceeds from the judgment instead of asserting his claim to the land at that time. Nearly 17 years later, Padfield attempted to claim the land after becoming unfriendly with the defendant, Hiram Pierce, suggesting that his motivations for filing were related to personal disputes rather than legitimate claims to the property. The court found that his long delay, coupled with the lack of any actionable claim, rendered his arguments moot.	Hiram Padfield claimed that the land conveyed to his guardian in satisfaction of a judgment rightfully belonged to him. He requested that the court enforce the conveyance of the legal title of the land to him, asserting that he had a valid claim since he was informed of his rights when he turned 21.	Hiram Pierce, as the defendant, argued that Padfield was estopped from asserting his claim to the land due to his decision to accept the proceeds of the judgment against his guardian, along with his significant delay in filing the claim—nearly 17 years. Pierce contended that Padfield's acceptance of settlement terms and the lack of any timely action constituted "gross laches," invalidating his claims.

In January 1867, a legal dispute arose in the Cumberland Circuit Court concerning the case of Michael C. McLain v. Westley Watkins. The case centered on a transaction related to the redemption of land sold under a judgment, specifically under the execution of a judgment favoring a person named Monroe. Once the redemption period expired, Watkins sought to redeem his land by paying the redemption money to the court's clerk, S. D. Tossey. Initially resistant, the clerk eventually agreed to accept the payment and forwarded it to McLain, a man who purportedly acted as Monroe's attorney. However, when McLain received the funds, he did not verify whether Monroe still had the right to receive them due to a prior transfer of the certificate of purchase to Joshua Miller. McLain instead paid Monroe, leading to a claim by Watkins that he was owed the redemption amount since it was not applied to the rightful party's redemption. The jury found McLain liable for the sum, leading to his appeal concerning the verdict.	Westley Watkins, the plaintiff, argued that Michael C. McLain was liable for the redemption money he had improperly handled. Watkins contended that McLain failed to verify the correct recipient for the funds and that as a result of McLain's actions, he lost the money meant for redeeming his land. He sought damages amounting to $153.40, which was the value of the redemption money.	Michael C. McLain, the defendant, claimed he was merely acting as an agent when he received the redemption money and that he acted according to the clerk's instructions. He contended that he was not liable since the responsibility for ensuring the proper payment rested with the clerk or the original parties involved. McLain asserted that by paying Monroe as directed, he was within his rights, arguing for a reversal of the jury's decision and seeking to have the judgment against him dismissed.

John D. Easter, impleaded with Chas. G. Scott, was the plaintiff in error, while Ira Minard was the defendant in error in this case, which took place in Kane County, Illinois, with the court session occurring during the May term of 1860. The legal dispute arose from a promissory note that Easter and Scott had signed, which Minard proceeded to enforce. Easter and Scott filed a plea of the general issue but also raised special pleas, claiming that the note had been secured through fraud and circumvention. Specifically, they argued that both the payee of the note (Minard) and the principal (Scott) falsely represented that a third person, Parks, would co-sign the note, indicating that without Parks' signature, the note would not be legitimately delivered. When the case was initially tried, the Circuit Court accepted Minard's argument, leading to a ruling in his favor despite the special pleas. However, the critical issues revolved around whether fraudulent misrepresentation occurred around the issuance of the note itself, rather than its consideration.	The plaintiff, John D. Easter, contended that the execution of the promissory note was procured through fraud. He asserted that there was a collusive agreement between Minard and Scott to mislead him by falsely indicating that the note would not be valid unless another party, Parks, co-signed it. Easter’s legal requests included the recognition of the fraud in the execution of the note, ultimately seeking to invalidate the enforceability of the note based on these claims.	The defendant, Ira Minard, argued against the plaintiff's claims, emphasizing that any representation made about Parks signing the note did not constitute fraud related to the nature of the note itself. Minard maintained that he was not aware of any fraudulent intentions and thus should not be held responsible for being a party to any fraud. His request aimed to uphold the validity of the promissory note and enforce its payment, countering the claims of fraud presented by Easter.

George F. Harding initiated legal action against John V. Le Moyne and others following the death of Charles W. Ricketson on October 4, 1866. Ricketson's will named his widow, Polly, and his daughter, Lizzie, as the sole devisees. Ricketson owned an undivided half of certain lands but was subject to a vendor's lien. An administrator was appointed to manage Ricketson's estate and sought court permission to sell the land to satisfy his debts. The widow and daughter later conveyed their interests in the property to Le Moyne. Several legal proceedings ensued, resulting in Harding purchasing parcels of the land at an administrator's sale in March 1884. After attempts to gain possession of the land from Le Moyne and his tenant, William Scully, Harding petitioned the court for that possession. Le Moyne argued that he owned a half-interest in the section and had leased his share to Scully. The court denied Harding's petition for possession, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Harding claimed that he legally purchased the land through the administrator's sale and sought to obtain possession from Le Moyne and Scully, who were in occupancy. He asserted that the defendants were unlawfully refusing to surrender possession of the properties he rightfully bought.	Le Moyne contended that he held a rightful title to an undivided half of the property and denied that the court had the jurisdiction to mandate their eviction. He argued that he and Scully were rightful occupants and challenged the validity of Harding's claim, stating that the sale did not confer upon Harding the right to possession due to existing conflicting claims and titles.

The case "Abraham F. Croskey et al. v. Francis E. Corey et al." originated in September 1868 in the Superior Court of Chicago, Illinois. The primary individuals involved were the plaintiffs, Abraham F. Croskey and his partner Shufeldt, and the defendants, Francis E. Corey and others. The case arose when the defendants sought to enforce a mechanic’s lien on property owned by Croskey. They alleged that Croskey purchased a quantity of lumber worth $2,099.49 intended for improvements on a specific lot in October 1866, and that they were owed $2,035.14 on January 11, 1867. Croskey and Shufeldt admitted ownership of the property and acknowledged some improvements but denied knowledge of the lumber quantity and its intended use. They argued that the improvements were for the benefit of their partnership, Croskey & Co., denying that any lumber purchased was specifically for the lot in question. The original court found in favor of the defendants, asserting a lien existed on the premises and ordering the sale of the property to pay the debt for the lumber.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants were attempting to enforce a mechanic's lien improperly. They argued that there was no evidence to support the claim that the lumber was purchased specifically for the property in question, thus invalidating the lien. Croskey and Shufeldt contended that their promissory note was accepted by the defendants in full satisfaction of their claim, which should have discharged any lien on the property. Their legal requests focused on overturning the decree that imposed the mechanic's lien on their property.	The defendants maintained that they sold lumber to the plaintiffs specifically for the purpose of improving the lot in question and were owed the amount stated in their claims. They argued that the plaintiffs' admissions of purchasing the lumber and making improvements supported their case for a lien. The defendants contended that the necessary evidence was presented to find that the improvements made on the lot were linked directly to the lumber provided.

The case, "William Richardson et al. v. George W. Ford et al.," took place in 1852, with proceedings culminating in June 1853 in La Salle County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included William Richardson and others as appellants, and George W. Ford and another as appellees. The dispute arose from a contract executed on July 9, 1852, wherein the appellees agreed to deliver two hundred good fat hogs to the appellants at Peru, between November 1st and November 8th. The appellants were to pay a total of $1,600, with an initial payment of $100 upon execution of the contract, followed by a subsequent payment of $400 due on or before September 1, 1853. The appellants claimed they paid the initial $100 but alleged they were ready and offered the additional $400 on September 1, which the appellees refused. The appellees subsequently failed to perform their part of the contract, leading the appellants to initiate legal action.	The plaintiffs, William Richardson et al., argued that the defendants breached the contract by refusing to deliver the hogs after the appellants offered the payment of $400, which they were prepared to pay on September 1. They sought recovery of the amount paid under the contract and asserted that they met the conditions of the contract; therefore, they were entitled to claim damages for the defendants' non-compliance.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs did not meet the necessary conditions precedent outlined in the contract. Specifically, they argued that the offer to make the $400 payment on September 1st was invalid as it came after the deadline had expired. The defendants maintained that since the plaintiffs failed to comply with the payment schedule, they were justified in treating the contract as rescinded and thus were not required to deliver the hogs.

In 1871, James E. Boyce purchased a through ticket in San Francisco for travel to Chicago, intending to use multiple railway services, including the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad. He checked a trunk but was told by the Central Pacific Railroad that his box of photographs was considered express matter and could not be checked. Upon arrival at Ogden, both his trunk and box were checked to Omaha. During his journey, Boyce fell ill and obtained a lay-over ticket, which allowed him to stop at Wilton, Iowa, before eventually reaching Chicago on October 11, 1871. When he arrived, he was unable to retrieve his baggage because it had been placed in a company warehouse upon arrival and was subsequently destroyed by fire on October 8, 1871, without any fault of the railroad company. The jury found the value of items in Boyce's trunk, but this included items not typically considered traveling baggage, raising questions about the company's liability.	Boyce claimed that the transportation company was responsible for the loss of his baggage, arguing that their obligation as a common carrier should extend until he could reasonably claim his luggage, which was delayed due to his health condition. He sought compensation for the lost items in his baggage.	The Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad contended that their liability as a common carrier ceased once Boyce's baggage was stored in a secure warehouse after arriving at its destination. They argued that the company was not at fault for the loss, as the destruction of the baggage was due to circumstances beyond their control and that Boyce’s illness and subsequent lay-over ticket should not extend the carrier's liability. Furthermore, they pointed out that the items demanded compensation for were not proper pieces of traveling baggage.

The case involves the City of Aurora and John C. Seidelman, the administrator for his deceased child, Louis Seidelman. On July 25, 1888, in Aurora, Illinois, a tragic incident occurred when six-year-old Louis fell into an open trench along Spencer Street, which had been created for laying water pipes. The trench was two and a half feet wide and six feet deep, and it had been left uncovered and unfilled for an unreasonable duration. On the day of the accident, water was intentionally poured into the ditch to expedite settlement, which softened the trench's banks, making them prone to caving in. Louis, while curiously observing a frog in the ditch, fell in when the ground beneath him gave way, resulting in him being trapped. He suffered severe injuries and died the following day. Louis's father, who worked long hours, argued that the city had a duty to maintain safety on public streets and was negligent for failing to secure the dangerous site. Following a jury trial, the city was found liable, and damages of $750 were awarded to the father.	The plaintiff, John C. Seidelman, claims that the City of Aurora was negligent in maintaining the safety of Spencer Street, specifically by failing to properly secure an open trench that ultimately led to the tragic death of his child. He argues that the city did not take sufficient care in guarding the trench or filling it in after its intended use. He requests damages for the loss of his child's life due to this negligence.	The City of Aurora contends that it acted with due care in the excavation and laying of the water pipe, arguing that it took appropriate measures to warn children to stay away from the site. The city also posits that the child's father was negligent for allowing Louis near the open trench, as he was aware of his child's tendencies to approach it. Additionally, the city sought to introduce claims that any negligence belonged with the parents rather than with the city.

On April 18, 1834, in Illinois, Stephen B. Munn made a written proposal to sell a tract of land to Samuel W. Lynn. Samuel communicated his father's acceptance of the offer in a letter dated June 26, 1834, signing it on behalf of David Lynn, his deceased father. Subsequently, Munn executed a covenant on July 19, 1834, to convey the property to Samuel. Payments for the land were made by Samuel, but sourced from his father's funds. David, however, resided with Samuel on the property and was thought to be the equitable owner. After David's death, issues arose regarding the true ownership of the land, with the plaintiffs, as David's heirs, arguing that the sale was intended for David. Samuel contended that the payments were loans from his father, asserting that he was the actual purchaser. The disputes culminated in a bill filed in the circuit court, where conflicting testimonies and intentions were presented regarding the true nature of the agreement and who benefitted from the land purchase.	The plaintiffs, heirs of David Lynn, claim that the land was intended to be purchased for David Lynn, not Samuel W. Lynn, and argue that Samuel only acted as an agent. They request that the court recognizes David's equitable ownership of the land, demands a partition among the heirs, and asserts that Samuel should account for the money he earned from the land and any improvements made.	Samuel W. Lynn argues that he purchased the land in his name with his father's funds acting as a loan and maintains that the sale was intended for him. He denies any mistake regarding the agreement and contends that the payments made for the land were meant as advancements from his father. Samuel seeks dismissal of the claims by the heirs and asserts his ownership rights to the property.

In January 1885, Olive Rhea filed a suit by attachment against George W. Powell in Cook County, Illinois. The core issue revolved around whether Powell had fraudulently disposed of property, specifically 210 shares of stock in a manufacturing corporation, to hinder Rhea, a creditor, from collecting her debt. Rhea claimed that Powell transferred ten shares of the stock to a third party, Kinsey, to secure a prior debt, thereby acting with fraudulent intent. The trial was conducted without a jury, and Powell's defense was based on a plea contesting the facts presented in the attachment affidavit. Ultimately, the court, presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gary, ruled in favor of the defendant, concluding that Rhea's assumption of a lien from the attachment was incorrect and that the evidence did not convincingly demonstrate that Powell transferred the shares after the attachment was levied.	Olive Rhea argued that George W. Powell fraudulently transferred ten shares of stock to Kinsey to evade Rhea's ability to collect her debt. She contended that this transfer was inherently fraudulent and done with the intention to hinder and delay her collection efforts, thus constituting grounds for the attachment action.	George W. Powell contended that the attachment levied on the stock was unauthorized under Illinois law since shares of stock in a corporation were not attachable. He argued that the evidence did not support Rhea's claim that the transfer of shares occurred after the attachment was filed, and that if the transfer was made, it was done in good faith for a legitimate purpose.

In January 1875, a legal case was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court involving Thomas Bates and Jane Davis. Jane Davis, the plaintiff, contended that her husband, Milton Davis, was a common drunkard who had been consuming alcohol for over thirty years. She claimed that the defendant, Thomas Bates, sold liquor to her husband, thereby injuring her means of support. During the trial in the Circuit Court of Vermilion County, evidence was provided indicating that Thomas Bates actively tried to prevent Milton Davis from purchasing liquor at his establishment, even instructing his employees to refuse service. The jury ruled in favor of Jane Davis, awarding her $300 in damages. However, the Illinois Supreme Court found significant flaws in the evidence presented, particularly the lack of demonstration on how the sale of liquor specifically affected Jane Davis's means of support. As such, the Court deemed the jury's verdict as improperly based on the concept of exemplary damages.	Jane Davis claimed damages against Thomas Bates for selling intoxicating liquors to her husband, Milton Davis, which she argued had adversely impacted her financial well-being. She asserted that these sales contributed to her husband's alcoholism and his inability to support the family. Her legal request was for compensation amounting to $300 for the alleged injury to her means of support, under the premise that the defendant's actions wrongfully harmed her financially.	Thomas Bates contended that he had made genuine efforts to prevent Milton Davis from obtaining liquor at his establishment, including refusing sales and instructing his staff to deny him service. Bates argued that there was no evidence to substantiate Jane Davis's claim that his sales of liquor had detrimental effects on her means of support. He maintained that exemplary damages were not warranted given the lack of proof of actual injury from the liquor sales.

Thomas C. McDowell, the Plaintiff in Error, entered a legal dispute against Richard P. Morgan, Jr., and others, Defendants in Error, regarding land rights in Livingston County, Illinois. This case arose from events beginning on January 4, 1858, when McDowell, through his agent Campbell, applied to enter certain tracts of land via the United States Land Office in Danville. The application was made according to regulations, but complications arose when it was revealed that Kersey H. Fell had previously applied to enter those lands but was not present to finalize his application. On January 25, 1853, Campbell completed the entry and received certificates for the lands, which McDowell later attempted to patent. However, in February 1856, McDowell discovered that Fell had been granted patents for those lands without notifying him. McDowell filed a bill in chancery to prevent ejectment suits initiated by Morgan, who was associated with Fell, claiming that they had improperly obtained legal title to the land. The case was tried in April 1861 but was dismissed for lack of equity.	McDowell argued that his entry of the land was valid and that he held an equitable title, which should not have been revoked without due process. He claimed that the land officers had acted improperly by allowing written applications for land during periods when offices were closed to private entry, effectively granting favoritism. McDowell sought an injunction to prevent Morgan from ejecting him from the land and requested that the court recognize his rights, enforcing the legal title originally obtained.	The defendants asserted that McDowell's entry was invalid because Fell had already established a right to the land through an earlier written application. They claimed that McDowell's agent had been aware of Fell's application and that the entry by Campbell was contingent on whether Fell decided to exercise his claim. Morgan contended that he acted legally and according to the protocols of the land office, maintaining that McDowell's bill lacked legal grounds and should be dismissed.

In the case "Franklin H. Whitney v. Truman Roberts," dated April 1859 and adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, the central dispute revolves around a fraudulent conveyance of land. The key individuals involved are Franklin H. Whitney, the plaintiff, and Truman Roberts, the defendant, as well as the Austins, who were the heirs of the land's original patentee. The incident began when Roberts misrepresented himself to the Austins, claiming to own the land and leading them to believe they were merely confirming an equitable title through a deed. He threatened legal action if they did not comply, while also fabricating support from their uncle, Reuben Scriptor, who testified he had never agreed to facilitate the conveyance. The Austins, unaware of their ownership of the land, were induced by Roberts' deceitful tactics to convey it, resulting in them accepting trivial sums in return for what turned out to be a total fraud. The factual context reveals that Roberts’ actions were based on concealment of critical facts, leading to the conclusion of a fraudulent transaction.	Franklin H. Whitney, as the plaintiff, contended that the conveyance of property to Roberts was obtained through fraud and deceit. He sought to reverse the dismissal of his complaint against Roberts, arguing that the evidence clearly demonstrated that the Austins were tricked into relinquishing their rights to the land. Whitney asserted that since the conveyances were void due to fraud, he should be recognized as the rightful owner and that the court should decree a return of the property to him based on the established fraudulent actions.	Truman Roberts, the defendant, argued against the reversal of the lower court’s dismissal, likely contending that he acted in good faith and did not commit fraud. His defense might include a claim that the transaction was valid, as he believed he held title to the land at the time of the conveyance. He could assert that the Austins willingly engaged in the transaction and that any misunderstanding regarding ownership was not the result of deceptive practices on his part.

In 1886, Dennis Glenney brought a case against the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company in the Illinois Supreme Court, located in Will County, Illinois. The dispute arose from the construction of a railroad that allegedly diverted water from its natural course, leading to flooding on Glenney's land. Glenney owned a tract of land in section 4, which was impacted by the increased water flow caused by a ditch the railroad company built 15 years prior to the lawsuit. This ditch was constructed to manage water flow along the railroad's right-of-way. Glenney claimed that the increased water volume caused by the ditch led to significant damage to approximately 45 acres of his land, which had previously been fertile meadow but was rendered nearly worthless. The railroad company asserted that the flooding was exacerbated by other parties who had installed drains into the railroad's ditch, claiming that it should not be held responsible for these additional water flows.	Dennis Glenney argued that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company's construction of a ditch to manage water diverted the natural flow, causing water to overflow onto his land and damage it significantly. He sought damages for the loss of value in his property, which had been fertile meadow land before the railroad's intervention.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company's defense rested on the claim that the flooding of Glenney's land was not solely due to their actions but was exacerbated by artificial drains constructed by other landowners without the railroad's knowledge or consent. They contended that they should not be liable for damages resulting from the actions of third parties who diverted water into the railroad's ditch.

T. Dwight Walker v. John Dement is a legal case heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1866. The case revolves around a series of promissory notes made by Collins and his wife to W. H. Godfrey, totaling $6,600, secured by a mortgage on certain property. After several transactions involving these notes, Heaton negotiated with Walker regarding the purchase of the notes. However, Heaton later transferred two of the notes to Walker without proper endorsement, which led to a dispute over the priority of liens on the mortgaged property. The core issue became whether Walker, who purchased the notes, had priority over the mortgage held by the appellee (Dement) who had retained a preferred lien on the property. In essence, the case examines the validity of the change in lien priority and the equitable interests created through the various transactions and assignments made between the involved parties.	The plaintiff, John Dement, argued that he had a valid equitably preferred lien on the mortgage property because he had an agreement that the notes he acquired from Heaton would take precedence over those held by Walker. Dement sought an injunction against Walker and others to prevent the sale of the mortgaged property to satisfy Walker's note. He requested that the court uphold his priority claim and foreclosure of the mortgage, allowing the proceeds to cover the notes he held.	Walker's defense centered on the argument that he purchased the notes before maturity and should hold a preferred claim against the mortgage since he had acquired the two notes first maturing. He contended that he was unaware of any agreements between Dement and Heaton. Walker sought to enforce the sale of the mortgaged property to satisfy his notes, insisting that he was entitled to the proceeds without regard to Dement's claims.

In the case of Hulda Purvis v. Isabelle Standifer, the legal proceedings took place in Moultrie County, Illinois, and were concluded on February 5, 1884. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court under the jurisdiction of Judge J. Meeker. The case involved two distinct lawsuits involving the same parties. Both cases raised errors related to the records and briefs submitted to the court. During the proceedings, the appellants' attorney sought to file additional records, but the court found that these records did not constitute part of the official record and subsequently struck them from the files. A motion was later made to continue the cases to amend the bill of exceptions, specifically to add the judge’s seal and to incorporate omitted matters. The court deemed these motions to be submitted too late and stated that the defects in the original record had been evident since prior submissions.	The plaintiff, Hulda Purvis, argued that the defects in the record required correction, and thus requested a continuation of the cases to allow for amendments to be made to the bill of exceptions. Purvis sought to have the court consider these amendments, emphasizing that they were crucial for ensuring completeness and accuracy in the legal proceedings.	The defendant, Isabelle Standifer, contended that the motions made by the plaintiff were untimely and should be denied. Standifer argued that the defects in the record had been apparent for a significant period and that the plaintiff’s counsel should have addressed these issues before the cause was submitted to the court. Therefore, Standifer insisted that the court should not grant the requested continuance or allow the amendments.

In December 1843, the case of James Dougherty et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from the legal interpretation concerning the definition of a riot under Illinois law. At the time, the legal standard relied on common law principles, which required an unlawful assemblage to constitute a riot. However, the Illinois criminal code had diverged from this requirement, allowing for a broader definition. Justice Catón delivered the court's opinion, highlighting that in the state, two or more persons could be guilty of a riot if they engaged in an unlawful act, with or without prior agreement. The discussion revolved around whether the indictment for a riot must include a claim of unlawful assemblage, with references to previous legal interpretations and the evolving nature of definitions in the Illinois criminal code. The ruling affirmed the lower court's decision, emphasizing the current statutory requirements for indictments.	The plaintiffs, James Dougherty and others, argued that the indictment against them was improperly constructed according to the requirements of the law at common law which necessitated an averment of unlawful assemblage. They contended that the definition of a riot should align with the common law standards, and sought to have the indictment dismissed based on this claim.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by the attorney general and state’s attorney, defended the necessity of broadening the definition of riot under the criminal code. They posited that under Illinois law, it was not required for an indictment to allege an unlawful assemblage for the offense of riot. Instead, they maintained that it was sufficient to show that two or more individuals perpetrated an unlawful act with force or violence, as outlined in the Illinois criminal statute.

The case "David N. Lowe v. The Town of Aroma" was adjudicated by the Illinois Appellate Court and decided on December 11, 1886. It originated from a complaint brought by David N. Lowe against The Town of Aroma to enforce a statutory penalty for obstruction of a highway. The venue for the case was Kankakee County, Illinois. The dispute arose after Lowe claimed that his right to use a public road had been obstructed by the Town of Aroma's actions. Initially, a Justice of the Peace ruled in favor of Lowe, and the decision was appealed to the Circuit Court, where a jury awarded a verdict favoring Lowe for damages related to the road's obstruction. The Town of Aroma contested the verdict, arguing that the evidence presented by Lowe did not sufficiently prove the existence of the road at the time of the obstruction.	The plaintiff, David N. Lowe, argued that the Town of Aroma had obstructed a legally established highway, thereby violating statutory regulations. He presented evidence including an order from the Commissioners of Highways that laid out the road in 1855, asserting that it had been used by the public for over twenty years before the obstruction occurred. Lowe sought a penalty for this obstruction and requested damages related to costs incurred as a result.	The Town of Aroma, as the defendant, countered the claims by stating that Lowe failed to demonstrate that the road was legally established at the time of the alleged obstruction since there was no record of assessment and payment of damages. They argued that the road had not been opened within five years of its layout, rendering the establishment void. The Town sought to have the verdict overturned, claiming it was against the weight of the evidence presented in court.

In December 1856, Thomas Wallace and Dudley McLaughlin entered into a sealed contract concerning a parcel of land in Will County, Illinois, specifying Wallace would pay McLaughlin $1,000 for an unencumbered title. Wallace made several payments and improvements to the land, totaling about $1,500, and maintained possession. However, the land was encumbered by two existing mortgages, which McLaughlin misrepresented as non-existent. After declaring a forfeiture in November 1861 due to Wallace's alleged non-payment, McLaughlin initiated an ejectment suit against Wallace, who had already made substantial payments and improvements. Subsequently, Wallace sought relief in equity to prevent McLaughlin from pursuing the ejectment, arguing that the existence of the encumbrances, along with McLaughlin’s prior assurances, entitled him to maintain his claim on the land.	Thomas Wallace claimed that McLaughlin's misrepresentation regarding the lack of encumbrances on the land invalidated McLaughlin’s right to declare a forfeiture of their contract. He requested a court injunction against McLaughlin's ejectment suit and sought an equitable resolution that would honor his payments and improvements made to the property, which would include a clear title.	Dudley McLaughlin contended that Wallace failed to make the agreed payments on time, which justified his declaration of forfeiture and subsequent ejectment suit. He argued that Wallace should forfeit all payments made, despite the existing encumbrances, and return the land, claiming that Wallace had no entitlement to relief based on the contract's terms.

Warren C. Winget and his wife, Sarah M. Winget, were involved in a legal case against the Quincy Building and Homestead Association, following their attempts to withdraw from the association after becoming dissatisfied with its operations. The case originated in Quincy, Illinois, where Winget aimed to secure loans through the association, requiring membership. He purchased 16 shares of stock in the association and later secured loans by bidding hefty premiums. Despite making significant payments on the loans, including installments and fines, he faced ongoing difficulties, ultimately leading to defaults and the association's intent to sell the property used as collateral. The Wingets argued that they had been misled by the association’s officers regarding the benefits of membership and the nature of the loans, claiming fraud based on alleged false representations. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court after various appeals and judicial decisions.	The Wingets claimed they were induced to join the association and take loans under false pretenses, arguing they were misled by the association's misleading representations about the financial benefits and operations of the organization. They sought to rescind the contracts related to their loans and stock purchase, asserting they were entitled to repayment of the sums paid to the association, given that the information provided by the association was inaccurate and deceptive.	The Quincy Building and Homestead Association defended itself by asserting that the Wingets had received the benefits of their contracts and could not contest the validity of the association's existence. They argued against the claims of misrepresentation, stating that the representations made were ambiguities rather than falsities. The association maintained that the loans were legal and not usurious, and therefore requested the court to uphold the contractual agreements and dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

In June 1867, in Clinton County, Illinois, John Koop was indicted for allegedly operating a tippling house on three different Sundays. The prosecution argued that Koop kept a boarding house with a grocery or saloon where he sold beer. Evidence indicated he sold beer on one of those Sundays, though witnesses could not specify which Sunday or verify if the saloon was open on others. The defense contended that the law required proof of sales on the specific Sundays alleged in the indictment, claiming that beer should not be classified as spirituous liquor under the statute. The court ruled that proof of operating a tippling house on any Sabbath day within eighteen months sufficed for the indictment, regardless of whether the specific Sundays were proved. Koop was convicted and fined $50.	The plaintiff, represented by the prosecution, claimed that John Koop violated the law by keeping his saloon open and selling beer on Sunday. They argued that the act of keeping a tippling house open, regardless of specific sales on the named Sundays in the indictment, constituted an offense under a statute against public morality.	The defendant, John Koop, contended that the prosecution failed to prove that he sold beer on the specific Sundays mentioned in the indictment. He also argued that beer should not be considered a spirituous liquor under the statute, and that because he ran a boarding house, the saloon could be deemed a sitting room for his boarders, which was not inherently illegal.

The case of "The Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railway Company v. Christian Schiller" centers on a legal dispute that arose in Jasper County, Illinois, around April 1883. The plaintiff, Christian Schiller, claimed that the Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railway Company had caused damage to his crops. The railway had constructed a line across Schiller's property and initially maintained cattle-guards at the crossing of a road that had been in common use for many years. In December 1881, several years after the railroad was completed, the railway company erected a barbed wire fence along the right of way and blocked the previously used road, believing it was not a public road. This action involved removing the cattle-guards and wing fences, which led to a situation where Schiller's hogs could access the railway right of way, subsequently entering his fields and damaging his crops. Schiller maintained that the railroad’s failure to properly fence and maintain barriers constituted negligence, resulting in the destruction of his crops.	Christian Schiller, the plaintiff, claimed that the removal of cattle-guards by the railway company, along with the erection of a barbed wire fence that obstructed the old road, directly led to his crops being damaged by his hogs entering the land. He argued that the railway company had a statutory duty to maintain adequate fencing to protect landowners from such occurrences. Schiller sought compensation for the damages to his crops, asserting that the railway's actions constituted a failure to comply with legal requirements to protect adjacent landowners from livestock encroachment.	The Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railway Company contended that the statute requiring fencing was aimed primarily at preventing stock from entering the railroad’s right of way and thereby ensuring the safety of passengers and employees. They argued that the fencing was not intended as a safeguard for adjoining landowners' crops and that their compliance with fencing laws should not incur liability for damages to crops from livestock. The defendant emphasized that any damages incurred were not due to negligence but rather a consequence of Schiller’s own livestock trespassing due to the removal of fences, disputing their liability.

In January 1875, a legal dispute unfolded in Tazewell County, Illinois, involving Robert G. Allen as the plaintiff against Louis Tobias and Philip Brown, as well as Peter Eichorn. Allen claimed that he was in the rightful possession of part of a lot in the town of Washington and accused the defendants of forcibly entering the premises, which included breaking down a fence he had erected to enclose the area. The initial complaint was filed before a justice of the peace but was dismissed due to the lack of a written demand for possession, leading Alan to appeal to the county court. Despite Allen's arguments that he had established actual possession of the property through the fence he constructed, the jury sided with the defendants, resulting in a judgment against him for costs. This decision was upheld on appeal to the circuit court, prompting Allen to take further action in hopes of overturning the judgment.	Robert G. Allen argued that he had rightful possession of the disputed portion of the lot due to the substantial fence he had constructed, which was adequate to indicate the premises were appropriated. He contended that the defendants had no right to forcibly enter the property and destroy his fence. Allen sought to reverse the judgment that had been made against him for costs and requested recognition of his legal possession.	The defendants, Louis Tobias, Philip Brown, and Peter Eichorn, contended that they were the rightful owners of the premises and claimed that their actions were justified. They argued that Allen failed to provide sufficient evidence of a prior demand for possession and maintained that his claim to the property did not meet legal standards. Their request aimed to uphold the judgment from the lower courts that favored their position and denied Allen's claims.

In February 1885, the City of Springfield adopted an ordinance for the paving and curbing of certain streets and alleys, specifying materials and construction methods. It demanded that costs for paving sections occupied by railway companies be borne by those companies while other street improvements would be funded through special taxes assessed on property owners. S. H. Wilbur and other plaintiffs, opposing the confirmation of these proceedings, brought the case before the Illinois Supreme Court after their objections were overruled by the county court. They contended that the ordinance was unconstitutional and invalid, arguing it contravened several legal principles regarding taxation and improvements. Specifically, they claimed the ordinance improperly treated multiple improvements as one and failed to accurately assess taxes on corner lots compared to interior lots.	The plaintiffs argued that the ordinance was unconstitutional because it violated principles of uniformity and equality in taxation. They claimed it improperly included multiple improvements into one ordinance rather than treating them separately, and they asserted that the tax assessment mechanisms were flawed, particularly as it did not reasonably differentiate between corner lots and interior lots. Their legal requests included reversing the county court's confirmation of the ordinance and declaring it void.	The defendant, the City of Springfield, contended that the ordinance complied with constitutional standards, pointing to precedent cases where similar ordinances were upheld. They maintained that the ordinance did not breach the uniformity requirement in taxation, even if it included multiple streets, as the improvements constituted a single common enterprise. The defendant also argued that any alleged deficiencies or omissions regarding specific lot assessments did not invalidate the entire ordinance, as the valid portions could be enforced independently.

William Becker filed a legal action against The German Mutual Fire Insurance Company of North Chicago in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873. The case primarily revolved around a premium note that Becker allegedly executed in favor of the insurance company. During the trial, the plaintiff's attorney attempted to introduce evidence of the note, which was signed as "Wilhelm Becker."
