The defendant contested the admission of this note, citing a variance in the name of the maker, arguing that Wilhem and William were not the same. The trial court overruled this objection and admitted the note, leading to the appeal by the defendant. The court's examination focused on the legal requirement that, for instruments in writing, any name disparity must be explained and proven in the declaration. The case underscored the importance of precise nomenclature in legal documents and the necessity for any variances to be appropriately supported by averments and evidence.	The plaintiff, William Becker, argued that the note he executed, although signed as "Wilhelm Becker," was valid and should be admissible as evidence in support of his claim against The German Mutual Fire Insurance Company. Becker sought to enforce the payment obligations stipulated in the note.	The German Mutual Fire Insurance Company contended that the note was inadmissible due to a variance in the name on the document. They argued that there was no averment in the declaration that reconciled the discrepancy between "William" and "Wilhelm." The defendant requested that the note be excluded from evidence on the grounds of this variance.

In 1871, in McHenry County, Illinois, an action of debt was initiated by Henry Willard (the appellee) against Volney B. Phillips (the appellant) to recover a penalty under a specific 1869 Illinois statute aimed at protecting butter and cheese manufactories. Willard owned and operated a cheese factory and purchased milk from local farmers, including Phillips. Phillips supplied milk but allegedly skimmed some cream before its delivery. The contract between Phillips and Willard was vague, although Phillips had advertised certain prices for milk. Willard claimed that the milk provided by Phillips was adulterated, leading to the lawsuit. The jury in the Kane County Circuit Court ruled in favor of Willard, awarding him $600, but Phillips appealed the decision, leading to this case being examined by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Henry Willard, contended that he was entitled to a penalty under the 1869 statute, which forbade the supplying of adulterated milk to cheese manufactories. He argued that Phillips had knowingly supplied diluted milk, which compromised the quality of the cheese produced. Willard sought the statutory penalty for this violation, claiming that the contamination of milk not only harmed his reputation but also his business.	Volney B. Phillips, the defendant, argued that the 1869 statute did not apply to him because he was selling milk for Willard’s personal manufacturing use rather than for a co-operative factory business model. He maintained that the law's language did not cover sales but rather intended to proscribe adulteration in collaborative contexts. Moreover, Phillips claimed any alleged skimming would not provide grounds for Willard to recover under the statute since the contract terms were not well-defined, and he should not be penalized for an act that was not in clear breach of contract.

The case "Douglass et al. v. McCord et al." was decided on January 6, 1886, by the Illinois Appellate Court. It involved a dispute over a construction contract in which Douglass and others (the plaintiffs) claimed that they were subcontractors with a lien for materials provided to a property. The case took place in Illinois and involved key individuals including the plaintiffs, represented by attorney S. R. Reed, and the defendants, represented by W. G. Cloyd along with Lodge & Huston. Initially, the court found that there was insufficient evidence to support the plaintiffs' claims about the lien due to a lack of due funds under the original contract. However, after remanding the case, the circuit court allowed the plaintiffs to amend their bill to assert that their contract was directly with the lot owners rather than the builder, as part of an agreement requiring the owners to pay for the materials. Upon reevaluation, the issues were found in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to a decree for the amount claimed.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had a valid lien as subcontractors for the materials used in the construction of a house and sought to amend the original bill to reflect a direct contract with the lot owners. They argued that the lot owners were responsible for paying for the materials under a prior agreement with the builder, which warranted their claims for compensation, totaling $393.77.	The defendants contested the validity of the plaintiffs' claims, originally asserting that there was not enough evidence to support the existence of a lien. Their defense hinged on the initial ruling that the full amount claimed by the plaintiffs could not stand because there was minimal payment due under the original contract. They sought to dismiss the case on grounds of insufficient justification for the plaintiffs' demands.

Daniel H. Tolman filed a lawsuit against Charles W. Requa in the Illinois Appellate Court, which culminated in a decision on January 6, 1886. The case arose from a contract of warranty associated with a promissory note executed by an individual named Allen, which was payable to Requa. The trial was conducted without a jury, and the judgment rendered was in favor of Requa. The legal dispute hinged on the validity of the guaranty written on the promissory note, along with allegations of fraud by the plaintiff regarding its execution. The court found that although there were conflicting facts presented, they aligned with the defendant’s defense and deemed it appropriate for the lower court to rule in favor of Requa.	The plaintiff, Daniel H. Tolman, argued that the defendant, Charles W. Requa, was liable under the terms of the warranty associated with the promissory note. Tolman sought to reverse the initial judgment that favored the defendant, claiming that the decision was unsupported by the evidence presented at trial. The plaintiff contended that the execution of the note and its guaranty involved fraudulent actions that invalidated the defenses raised by the defendant.	The defendant, Charles W. Requa, responded to the claims with a plea of non-assumpsit and two additional special pleas that suggested fraudulent circumstances surrounding the execution of the promissory note and guaranty. Requa argued that the pleas raised issues of fraud in consideration and lack of genuine consideration, which were sufficient to defend against the plaintiff's claims, even though the pleas were not distinctly articulated. The defendant’s arguments indicated that the claims of Tolman did not have merit, as the evidence presented during the trial supported the defenses.

In the case of Robert McDonald v. Lemuel Moore et al., which occurred in 1889 in Vermillion County, Illinois, the dispute arose over a building contract for the construction of a house. The contract was valued at $4,100, of which $3,500 had been paid by the plaintiff, Robert McDonald. He claimed that there was a remaining balance owed for labor and materials, with additional costs for extras already paid. The defendant, Lemuel Moore, contended that the work and materials provided did not adhere to the agreed specifications, leading to a jury allowance of $100 for defects. Despite acknowledging some issues during construction, McDonald occupied the house even before its completion and accepted it for use, albeit with dissatisfaction.	Robert McDonald, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to recover the remaining balance due for the construction of a house, based on the original contract. He stated that he had fulfilled his obligations and provided payments as agreed. McDonald sought a judgment for the amount he believed was owed, after having accounted for the payments made and any alleged extras.	The defendant, Lemuel Moore, defended against McDonald’s claims by asserting that the construction did not meet the contract specifications and that materials supplied were not up to par. Consequently, Moore highlighted that the work was substandard, justifying a reduction in the amount owed, which the jury considered by allowing a $100 deduction for alleged imperfections.

In February 1847, in St. Louis, Missouri, O. Hinton & Co., mail contractors, sold their property—consisting of stage horses and harness—to plaintiffs Aaron V. Burnell and others as creditors. Following the sale, Burnell and co. attempted to take possession of the property along the stage route between Peoria and Ottawa but were unable to do so before the defendant, Daniel M. Robertson, who was acting as an officer, seized the property on February 14, 1847, under various writs of attachment against Hinton & Co. The Circuit Court was tasked with determining the rightful ownership of the property after a jury found in favor of the defendant. The plaintiffs alleged that the attaching creditors had prior knowledge of the sale. However, it was concluded that actual possession was necessary to secure their claim against subsequent attaching creditors.	The plaintiffs contended that an effective transfer of ownership occurred through the bill of sale, which authorized them to take possession of the property. They argued that they had taken sufficient actions to gain possession and that the attaching creditors were aware of the transfer of the property, thereby claiming that the attachment was invalid. Their legal request sought to overturn the jury's verdict in favor of the defendant and to establish their ownership over the seized property.	The defendant maintained that since the property was seized before the plaintiffs could take possession, the attachment was valid. The central argument was that the absence of actual delivery of the property at the time of the sale meant that subsequent attaching creditors had a priority claim. The defendant contended that, based on established legal principles, a sale of personal property requires actual delivery to defeat the rights of subsequent attaching creditors.

The case of James Langabier v. The Fairbury, Pontiac and Northwestern R. R. Co. took place in September 1872 in Fairbury, Illinois. The plaintiff, James Langabier, a significant property owner on Walnut Street, filed a bill in chancery against the railway company, alleging they unlawfully took possession of the street at midnight on a Saturday to construct a railroad track. Langabier claimed this action was intended to circumvent legal injunctions and avoid compensating him for damages to his property, which he believed would lose half its value due to the railway's activities. He argued that the railway company did not attempt to assess or pay for the damage or take any court-approved processes. The court initially issued an injunction on a Sunday to halt the construction, but this was later quashed, and the bill was dismissed during the September term. Langabier contested this dismissal, asserting the urgency of his situation warranted legal intervention, particularly given the company's alleged insolvency and their intentions to continue construction without compensation.	The plaintiff claimed that the railway company wrongly seized Walnut Street on a Sunday with the intent of completing their railroad track to escape legal repercussions and financial accountability. He argued that their actions would cause irreparable harm to his property without adequate compensation, which he alleged the company had failed to assess or offer. Langabier sought an injunction to prevent the railway from carrying out construction and to protect his property rights.	The railway company's defense centered on the legality of the injunction issued on a Sunday, arguing that judicial acts could not be performed on that day according to common law principles. They maintained that the injunction issued by the master in chancery was void due to it occurring on a non-judicial day. The company argued that the plaintiff's claims were unfounded and that their actions did not constitute unlawful taking since they aimed to complete essential infrastructure work.

The case of Charles H. Briggs et al. v. Nick Roth, decided on December 8, 1888, arose in Iroquois County, Illinois. The central figures in this legal dispute were Charles H. Briggs and others (appellants) and Nick Roth (appellee), concerning a landlord-tenant relationship. The issue emerged when the appellee, Nick Roth, was hired by the appellants to work on a farm for $300 a year, including the provision of housing, pasture for livestock, and access to other farming essentials. Disputes regarding living arrangements and the boarding of the appellants' hired hands ensued, leading to a refusal by Roth to continue boarding the men. This refusal culminated in the appellants attempting to regain possession of the house through force, which included driving away Roth's livestock and locking him out. The situation escalated to an armed confrontation. Roth then sued the appellants for trespass, claiming damages for the invasion of his home and the loss of his livestock. The jury concluded that the appellants were at fault in their actions, assessing damages at $100 and ruling in favor of Roth.	Roth's primary claims included that the appellants had unlawfully attempted to break into his dwelling and drove away his cows and calves, which constituted a trespass. Roth sought damages for these actions and maintained that he was the rightful tenant entitled to the full enjoyment of the property. His assertion was that the appellants had violated his tenancy rights despite any alleged breach of contract on his part regarding the boarding of their hired men.	The appellants contended that Roth's refusal to board their workers was a breach of contract, which justified their actions in attempting to reclaim possession of the property. They argued that, under the circumstances, they were entitled to take necessary measures to eject Roth from the premises. The defense emphasized the notion that although some fault lay with both parties, the jury's verdict was unwarranted and that the damages awarded were excessive.

The case "First National Bank of Princeton v. Isaac Kurtz, Jr., and Isaac Kurtz, Sr." was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court, decided on January 10, 1887. The case originated in the Bureau Circuit Court on February 19, 1885, when the First National Bank of Princeton filed a suit against Isaac Kurtz, Jr. and his father, Isaac Kurtz, Sr., concerning two promissory notes for $800 and $1,500. Isaac Kurtz, Jr. was the principal on the notes, and his father was the surety. The defendants were served summons on February 27, 1885, alongside accusations that they had engaged in fraudulent conveyances of their assets to hinder creditors, leading to an attachment of property owned by Isaac Kurtz, Sr.  Isaac Kurtz, Sr. contested the attachment, claiming it was not fraudulent, while the court also unveiled intricate family property dynamics resulting from the death of Rachel Kurtz, Isaac Sr.'s wife, in 1869. Rachel had expressed desires regarding the distribution of her land to her children, which was contested after her death. Following a jury trial, the court ruled in favor of the bank for $2,480.80 against both defendants but simultaneously favored Isaac Kurtz, Sr. regarding the attachment, quashing it, thus leaving the bank obligated to pay costs.  Plaintiff claims stemmed from Isaac Kurtz, Jr.'s insolvency and accusations of fraud surrounding the land transaction. Evidence was presented regarding the intentions of Isaac Sr. to fulfill his deceased wife's wishes and to transfer land despite claims against them.  Plaintiff and defendant testimonies suggested various motivations and understandings, contributing to a complex discussion about legality and intent behind property conveyance amidst allegations of fraud.	The First National Bank contended that Isaac Kurtz, Sr. was guilty of both actual and constructive fraud when he executed a deed transferring property to his daughter and her husband shortly before the bank's claims arose. The bank argued that the transfers were made to delay and hinder the collection of debts. They asserted that regardless of the father's motives, the transfer represented a constructive fraud under the law as it appeared to disadvantage creditors.	Isaac Kurtz, Sr. contested the claims of fraud, asserting that he was unaware of his son's financial difficulties at the time of making the deed. He maintained that his actions were intended to fulfill his deceased wife's wishes regarding the property distribution and were not meant to deceive creditors. The defense emphasized that the transactions were for fairly valued consideration and intended to honor promises made to the heirs.

In December 1889, the Illinois Appellate Court addressed a legal dispute involving Dixon National Bank and Jacob Spielmann. The case originated from a set of promissory notes dated March 2, 1878, totaling $2,170, which were signed by Henry D. Dement under the firm name Spielmann, Dement & Pischel. The bank sought to recover the amount owed on these notes, which were intended to renew a prior debt from the now-dissolved firm. It was established that the firm of Spielmann, Dement & Pischel had been dissolved prior to the execution of the notes, and Dement had taken on the obligation to assume all the firm’s debts, providing protection to the remaining partners, Spielmann and Pischel. The crux of the case was whether the bank knew of the partnership's dissolution and Dement’s agreement to assume the debts at the time the notes were signed. The testimony presented by Dement indicated that he communicated the situation to the bank, while bank officers asserted they were unaware of the dissolution when they accepted the notes. Given the conflicting evidence, the jury's understanding was crucial to the case's outcome.	The plaintiff, Dixon National Bank, argued that the promissory notes were valid and enforceable as they were executed following the terms of a continuation agreement despite the dissolution of the firm. The bank claimed that its officers were unaware of the dissolution and had no reason to doubt Dement’s authority in signing the notes. Thus, they requested that the court uphold the validity of the notes and grant a judgment for the amount owed.	The defendant, Jacob Spielmann, contended that the notes should not be enforceable because the bank was aware or should have been aware of the dissolution of the firm and Dement’s assumption of its debts before the notes were signed. He argued that the bank’s acceptance of the notes constituted an unlawful renewal of a debt that was no longer valid due to the firm’s dissolution. Spielmann's request included a dismissal of the case against him, asserting that he should not be held liable.

Dyer v. Miller is a legal case that took place around June 8, 1886, in Illinois. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff, Dyer, and the defendant, Miller. The case arose from a dispute regarding an alleged agreement for renting a store. The agreement provided two options: one could either rent the store for six months at a rate of $50 per month or for a year at $40 per month. After Dyer began occupancy and paid some rent, the pivotal question emerged regarding whether a definitive choice had been made between the two options offered in the agreement. This determination was significant as it was argued that such a decision was a matter of fact, not law, and thus was meant to be resolved by a jury. However, in the lower court, this question was improperly taken from the jury's consideration. This led to the appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court, as the judgment made by the lower court was contested.	The plaintiff, Dyer, claimed that a valid rental agreement had been established, and his main argument centered around whether he had elected to fulfill the terms of either option presented in the original rental agreement. Dyer sought to have the court recognize his occupancy and associated payments as compliant with the terms he believed he had agreed to, and he requested that the jury be allowed to determine the factual question of his choice between the two rental options.	The defendant, Miller, likely contested the validity of the rental agreement as claimed by Dyer, arguing against the assertion that a decision between the two rental options had been made. Miller raised objections regarding the factual interpretations made by Dyer and asserted that the issue should not have been a jury matter, presumably advocating for a resolution in favor of his position, possibly seeking to affirm the lower court's judgment without sending the case to a jury for consideration.

The case "Michael Diversy v. Henry Will" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1862. The dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois, concerning a legal action of assumpsit filed by Henry Will against Michael Diversy, who was a surviving partner of the firm Johnson & Diversy. The first count of the complaint was based on a promissory note for $407.48 dated June 22, 1860, while subsequent counts were for goods purchased on different dates, totaling various amounts. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him $733.53 in damages. A key issue arose during the trial regarding the admissibility of witness Orrin J. Rose, whom Diversy wanted to call to testify about alleged overcharging and worthless goods related to the debt. The plaintiff objected on the grounds of Rose's interest in the outcome of the case, leading to the court excluding Rose from testifying. Diversy appealed the decision on the basis of the court's ruling to exclude the witness and the denial of a new trial.	The plaintiff, Henry Will, claimed that Diversy, as the surviving partner of Johnson & Diversy, was liable for debts owed for goods and services. Will argued that the witness Rose could provide testimony contradicting the alleged amount owed. He also presented evidence showing that Rose was interested in the outcome, thus disqualifying him as a witness.	The defendant, Michael Diversy, contended that the evidence provided by the plaintiff was inadmissible due to the disqualification of witness Orrin J. Rose based on his interest in the case. Diversy argued that the court's exclusion of Rose violated his rights to defend against the claims adequately. He sought to have the court overturn the judgment and grant a new trial, asserting that Rose’s testimony was critical to show the goods were overcharged and that some were worthless.

Edward Castle et al. were plaintiffs in error in a case heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1856, which originated in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas. The dispute arose from a promissory note issued by the plaintiffs, which was payable to their own order and endorsed to the defendants, William D. Judson et al. In response to the defendants' action based on this note, the plaintiffs filed pleas claiming a partial failure of consideration, arguing that not all goods promised in exchange for the note were delivered. An affidavit submitted by Edward Castle asserted that there was a justifiable defense amounting to $231.99, corresponding to the alleged goods not delivered. However, the court struck the pleas from the files due to the absence of a sufficient affidavit of merits. This ruling brought the case to the higher court for review, raising questions about the interpretation and constitutionality of the relevant statutes regulating practice in the Circuit and County Courts. These provisions aimed to expedite case processing and mitigate delays caused by frivolous defenses.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants failed to deliver goods associated with the promissory note, constituting a partial failure of consideration. They argued for the inclusion of a defense amounting to $231.99, which should be deducted from the total claim of the defendants. The plaintiffs sought to have their pleas considered valid and to challenge the judgment rendered in favor of the defendants.	The defendants contended that the pleas filed by the plaintiffs were struck from the record due to a lack of a proper affidavit of merits, which was necessary under the applicable statute for defenses involving contracts. They maintained that this procedural misstep justified the court's judgment and that the plaintiffs should be deemed to have defaulted.

Frederick C. Obermark was tried in 1887 in the County Court of Massac County, Illinois, on charges brought by the State’s Attorney on behalf of the people. The accusation involved unlawfully selling intoxicating liquors in quantities less than one gallon without a proper license to operate a dram shop. The case was prosecuted under proper procedural guidelines, as the information was signed by the State’s Attorney, though it was not sworn to. Following a trial, the jury found Obermark guilty, and the court imposed a fine of $50 along with additional costs. While there were complaints regarding the court's instructions and the denial of a new trial, the court noted that these arguments did not form part of the record since they were not included in a bill of exceptions. The court found that adequate evidence supported the verdict and chose to affirm the original judgment.	The plaintiff, represented by the State, claimed Frederick C. Obermark unlawfully sold intoxicating liquors without the requisite license, contravening Illinois law. The main argument was based on the illegality of his actions, which warranted a penalty. The plaintiff sought to impose a fine and hold Obermark accountable for costs incurred during the trial.	The defendant's key defenses included the claim that the information filed against him was defective due to the lack of a sworn affidavit and that the jury instructions were problematic. Obermark contended that the motion for a new trial was improperly rejected by the trial court. However, the defense failed to incorporate these arguments into a bill of exceptions, which limited their effectiveness in the appeal.

In 1853, in Morgan County, Illinois, Thomas Green and Ellery M. Merris filed a bill in chancery against Henry Oakes, seeking to prevent him from obstructing a public road that had been used continuously for over twenty years. The plaintiffs owned and occupied lands adjacent to this road, which they claimed was essential for their enjoyment and use of their property. Oakes intended to erect fences and gates at two points along the road, prompting the plaintiffs to seek an injunction. They argued that the road had been acknowledged as a public highway with the consent of the landowners. In response, Oakes contested the claim, denying that the road was a public highway and asserting he had properly been compensated for the right of way. After a series of legal maneuvers, the Circuit Court dismissed the bill in October 1855, leading the plaintiffs to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, John Green et al., argued that the road in question had been used as a public highway for over twenty years with the knowledge and consent of the landowners. They contended that its obstruction would irreparably harm their interests and requested an injunction to prevent Oakes from blocking the road. They claimed that the road's status as a public thoroughfare justified their demand for the court's intervention to safeguard their rights.	The defendant, Henry Oakes, argued that the court lacked jurisdiction over the matter and that the plaintiffs had available legal remedies, hence the case should be dismissed. He denied that the road had been legally established as a public highway for twenty years, asserting that he had previously been compensated for the right of way. Oakes contended the plaintiffs' claims were without merit and the bill should not have proceeded.

The case "Henry C. Kruse v. Otto Steffens et al." was adjudicated in January 1868 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from the estate of Diedrich Garloch, who passed away intestate around March 1, 1853, leaving behind a widow, Marie, and a minor daughter, Dorothy. After Diedrich's death, Marie maintained possession of the property until remarrying Otto Steffens in December 1853. Steffens became the administrator of Garloch's estate and arranged for the sale of the property to settle the estate's debts. In August 1855, the property was sold at auction, with the auctioneer, Frederick Schrieber, bidding on it and then immediately reconveying it back to Steffens without any payment or security, which raised suspicions of fraud. Dorothy married Henry C. Kruse in August 1863, and following her death in 1865, Kruse became the sole heir through their son. Kruse filed a suit in chancery in April 1866 to set aside the fraudulent sale and seek an accounting of rents and profits. However, the trial court dismissed his claim, prompting him to appeal.	Henry C. Kruse, as the plaintiff, argued that the sale and reconveyance of the property from Steffens to Schrieber and back to Steffens were fraudulent. He requested that these transactions be annulled and that he be granted an accounting of the rents and profits generated from the property, which were wrongfully received by Steffens.	The defendants, including Otto Steffens, contended that the sale was valid and there was no fraudulent intent involved. They likely argued both the legality of the transactions and possibly claimed procedural defenses regarding the timing and the nature of the claims made by Kruse.

In 1880, in La Salle County, Illinois, the case of Amzi F. Jackson et al. v. William Rickard arose from a partnership dispute involving the buying and selling of grain by Thomas Eyburn and Daniel E. Smith. After Eyburn's death, Smith continued the business until his own death in 1878. Following this, the heirs of Smith initiated a legal action against the heirs of Eyburn to settle the partnership's affairs. In the course of these proceedings, a contract was made for the sale of partnership properties, including the "Warehouse Property" and "Agricultural Works Property," to Amzi F. Jackson. Subsequently, William Rickard purchased the properties under a court-ordered sale. Rickard claimed that certain machinery belonging to the Agricultural Works property had been removed improperly and filed for an order requiring its return. The court issued an order for Jackson and the Marseilles Manufacturing Company to restore the machinery to its original position, asserting jurisdiction over the case. Jackson and others contested this order, arguing that the court lacked proper jurisdiction over them.	The plaintiffs, Amzi F. Jackson and others, contended that the court overstepped its authority by ordering them to restore the machinery taken from the Agricultural Works property after the purchase was made by William Rickard. They argued that the court's order was invalid as it failed to establish that the plaintiffs were parties to the suit and had received proper notice, consequently rendering the court's jurisdiction questionable.	William Rickard, the defendant, maintained that, as the buyer of the copartnership's property, he was entitled to all aspects of that property as they existed at the time of purchase. He argued that the agreement between Jackson and the heirs concerning the machinery was invalid as it infringed upon his rights. Rickard sought an order compelling Jackson and the Marseilles Manufacturing Company to return the machinery, framing the issue as a matter of restoring his purchase rights.

In December 1853, in Morgan County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Otho D. Critzer and Murray McConnel. The case revolved around a sum of three hundred dollars that was initially given to Critzer by Bonesteel. Bonesteel had received this money from McConnel with the intention that it would be used to purchase a specific judgment on McConnel's behalf. Bonesteel had agreed to either procure the judgment transfer or return the funds if the purchase was not completed within ten days. However, instead of following these instructions, Critzer misapplied the funds by using them to satisfy a judgment against himself rather than acquiring the judgment for McConnel as instructed. McConnel contended that Critzer was liable for the misapplication of the money, which was supposed to be used for a specific purpose. The case was heard at the March term of the Morgan Circuit Court, leading to McConnel winning the judgment, which Critzer subsequently appealed.	McConnel claimed that the three hundred dollars transferred to Critzer was his money, intended for the specific purpose of purchasing a judgment. He argued that Critzer misapplied these funds by using them to pay a judgment against himself rather than executing the purchase as directed. McConnel sought recovery of the misapplied funds, asserting his rightful ownership and Critzer's obligation to follow the instructions regarding the fund's use.	Critzer's defense focused on disputing McConnel's ownership claim and the nature of the transaction. He may have contended that any miscommunication or misdirection came from Bonesteel, who instructed him on what to do with the funds. Critzer likely argued that he was not solely responsible for the misapplication of funds and sought to alleviate his liability by shifting blame or questioning McConnel's claims.

The case "The City of Rock Island v. Bridget Cuinely" took place in the year 1888 in Rock Island, Illinois. The plaintiff, Bridget Cuinely, suffered personal injuries after falling on a defective sidewalk, which was alleged to be the responsibility of the City of Rock Island to maintain. The original judgment was issued in the Rock Island circuit court, awarding Cuinely $1,100 for her injuries. The city, contesting this ruling, appealed to the Appellate Court, which affirmed the lower court's decision. The case centered on whether the city was liable for negligence due to the sidewalk's poor condition—specifically its allegedly broken and loose planks. The court had to consider whether the allegations were sufficiently supported by the evidence and whether the city had been negligent in maintaining the sidewalk. Ultimately, various aspects of the case, such as the duty of the city to keep sidewalks in repair and the nature of the injuries sustained by Cuinely, were examined, leading to a focus on the city’s failure to address known sidewalk issues prior to the accident.	Bridget Cuinely claimed that the City of Rock Island was negligent for failing to maintain the sidewalk in a safe condition, causing her injury. She specifically alleged that the city allowed the sidewalk to remain in an unsafe state, with planks that were loose and unfastened. Cuinely requested compensation for her injuries, which included a dislocated and broken wrist due to the fall. Her arguments hinged on the city’s responsibility to keep public walkways in good repair and the argument that her injuries were a direct result of their negligence.	The City of Rock Island defended itself by arguing that there was a variance between Cuinely's allegations and the evidence presented, particularly regarding whether the sidewalk was actually broken or just poorly maintained. The city contended that the plaintiff had not proven that the planks were broken, a key point in establishing liability. Additionally, the city raised questions about its obligation to maintain the sidewalk, suggesting that there was insufficient evidence to demonstrate its negligence in this case.

George G. Wilcox filed an action of ejectment against Huntington W. Jackson and others in 1883, seeking to recover land in Cook County, Illinois. The basis of Wilcox's claim was that Julia Gamell (formerly Martin) had acquired the land from the government under an Act of Congress dated July 17, 1854, which provided for the survey of lands belonging to half-breeds or mixed bloods of the Dakotah or Sioux nation. Wilcox attempted to present evidence regarding a certificate from the general land office, which indicated that Gamell had located certain scrip on the disputed land. However, the trial court excluded the certificate, determining it necessary to attach a copy of the scrip to the record. Wilcox's legal representatives contended that the certificate sufficed to demonstrate title to the land, while opponents argued against the validity of the evidence presented.	The plaintiff, George G. Wilcox, asserted that he had rightful title to the land based on the certificate issued by the commissioner of the general land office, which documented the location of scrip allocated under federal statute. Wilcox argued that the trial court's exclusion of the certificate was erroneous as it adequately demonstrated the legitimate basis of his claim.	The defendants contended that Wilcox's evidence was incomplete since it lacked an attached copy of the scrip, rendering it inadmissible. They maintained that the record was insufficient to establish title and raised the possibility that the land was located within navigable waters, making it not subject to private entry or location.

William Bolun was put on trial in 1874 in Iroquois County, Illinois, for allegedly selling spirituous liquors in violation of state law. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court after Bolun was indicted and found guilty on six counts by a jury. The court imposed a fine of $120 and sentenced Bolun to serve 60 days in the county jail. Bolun challenged the judgment on the grounds of how the sentences were imposed, asserting that the court erred by not entering separate judgments for each of the six counts on which he was convicted. The relevant legal precedent cited in this case was The People ex rel. v. Whitson, which established that judgments on multiple counts should be separate and that imprisonment terms should begin successively.	The plaintiff, represented by the Illinois state, argued that William Bolun was guilty of selling spirituous liquors against state regulations. They maintained that the appropriate legal actions had been taken against Bolun, culminating in the jury's verdict of guilty on all counts.	Bolun's defense contended that the court had made an error in the sentencing process by failing to issue separate judgments for each count of the indictment. They requested that the judgment be reversed on these grounds, asserting that the proper legal procedure was not followed during sentencing.

In the case of "Robert Rankin v. Barcroft & Co. et al.," originating in Randolph County, Illinois, in 1885, the dispute revolves around a trust established by Robert Rankin for the benefit of Barcroft & Co. and other creditors. The case stems from an agreement made in 1871, where certain land was conveyed to Rankin upon trusts to pay off debts amounting to $16,000, including claims from Barcroft & Co. and John Swanwick, who were identified as the first lienholders. The plaintiff, Barcroft & Co., alleged that Rankin, who had previously accepted time drafts drawn by Joseph B. Holmes, refused to sell the land to satisfy these debts despite their claims being recognized as first charges against the property. Rankin's reluctance was compounded by his prior declaration of bankruptcy in 1873. The plaintiffs sought an accounting and a court order for Rankin to sell the property to satisfy the outstanding debts, as there were no other claims on the property. The circuit court initially found in favor of the claims made by the plaintiffs, acknowledging the debts Rankin was obligated to address under the agreement. Rankin contested this, claiming his rights to the property while denying the creditors' claims.	Barcroft & Co. claimed they were owed $12,960 along with other debts, asserting their primary position as creditors with first liens on the property. They requested that Rankin be ordered to sell the lands to pay these debts as outlined in the original trust agreement. They sought an accounting of the amounts due and insisted on enforcement of the trust provisions and contractual obligations to sell the land for debt settlement.	Robert Rankin, the defendant, contended that the claims made by Barcroft & Co. and Swanwick were not valid incumbrances or liens on the property as alleged, arguing that the plaintiff's claims did not meet the legal definitions necessary for enforcement. He emphasized his legal title to the land conveyed to him and challenged the findings of the circuit court while requesting a dismissal of the claims made against him.

In 1886, in Cook County, Illinois, Conrad C. Lenz and others (the plaintiffs) entered into contracts with the Chicago Lumber Company (the defendants) regarding the carriage of lumber from Muskegon, Michigan, to Chicago. The case stems from the defendants' failure to fulfill the terms of these contracts. One of the contracts was written, while the other was verbal; however, the court ruled that no damages could be claimed for the breach of the verbal agreement. During the trial, a significant number of witnesses testified, and numerous factual issues were raised. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to a judgment against the lumber company for breach of the written contract. The defendants appealed, citing various errors they believed warranted reversing the judgment.	The plaintiffs, Conrad C. Lenz et al., claimed that the Chicago Lumber Company breached a written contract for the transportation of lumber, causing them financial damages. They sought compensation for these damages as a result of the defendants' failure to perform the agreed-upon services.	The defendants, Chicago Lumber Company, argued that the trial court had erred in various respects during the proceedings, particularly in the admission and exclusion of evidence, and in the way jury instructions were handled. They contended that the evidence did not support the jury's verdict and requested that the judgment be overturned based on these alleged errors.

The case 'The Plume & Atwood Manufacturing Company et al. v. Frank C. Caldwell, Assignee, et al.' was reviewed by the Illinois Appellate Court on March 24, 1890. It originated from events involving the insolvent corporation George Bohner & Co., which was located in Cook County, Illinois. On January 26, 1889, the Commercial Rational Bank of Chicago obtained a judgment against George Bohner & Co. for $5,635.38. An execution was delivered to the sheriff later that day. Shortly thereafter, on January 28, 1889, the appellants (other creditors) filed for separate writs of attachment against the same debtor. On that same morning, the sheriff levied these executions and placed a custodian in charge of Bohner & Co.'s property. However, later that day, Bohner & Co. executed a deed of assignment for the benefit of creditors, which the assignee (Caldwell) promptly filed with the Court. The assignee then petitioned for an order for the sheriff to deliver the property, leading to a consent order for property delivery subject to all rights and liens from the various creditors. However, a dispute arose regarding the priorities among the bank and the attachment creditors, which was set for a hearing. Ultimately, the court found that the bank had the rightful preference due to its execution and levy while denying the attachment creditors any preference over other general creditors.	The plaintiffs, a group of creditors, argued that the bank had unlawfully received a preference by moving to execute its judgment just before the assignment was made, thus undermining their attachments. They claimed that the bank’s actions had deprived them of their rightful priority over the debtor's assets and requested that the court grant them higher priority in the distribution of the insolvent estate.	The defendant, represented by the Commercial Rational Bank, contended that their actions were proper and based on the bank’s diligence, executed in good faith when they acted swiftly after learning about the debtor’s insolvency. They argued that the plaintiffs had consented to surrender the property to the assignee, thus delegating control to the County Court, and did not produce sufficient evidence to show they had valid debts at the time they filed for attachments. The defense requested that the court affirm the bank's priority over the creditors.

Frederick Aholtz filed a case against James F. Durfee in an ejectment action. The case was heard in the Macon Circuit Court during its May term in 1881, where Durfee obtained a judgment in his favor for a lot located in Decatur, Illinois. Following this judgment, Aholtz requested a new trial, which was granted on the condition that he pay the associated costs within three months. However, Aholtz did not make the payment until December 2, 1882, which was more than a year after the original judgment was issued. In February 1883, Aholtz applied to the Circuit Court to vacate the 1881 judgment and seek a new trial, citing the delay in payment was due to the clerk not computing the costs because the case files were allegedly taken by an unknown person. The court denied this application, and Aholtz subsequently brought the case to the Illinois Appellate Court for review of the ruling.	Aholtz argued that the delay in paying the costs was not due to negligence on his part but was instead attributable to the clerk's inability to compute the amount owed because the case files were missing. He sought to vacate the previous judgment and obtain a new trial based on these circumstances.	Durfee contended that Aholtz's claims did not demonstrate sufficient diligence in pursuing the required payment and that the excuse for the delay was vague and insufficient. Durfee maintained that the Circuit Court was correct in denying Aholtz's motion for a new trial based on the delay in paying costs.

In April 1867, the case of Henry Mills et al. v. James McCabe took place in La Salle County, Illinois. James McCabe, a native of Ireland who claimed to have been naturalized according to U.S. laws, brought the action against election judges Henry Mills, Thomas Phillson, and Darius Fyffe for refusing his vote during a general election. The plaintiff asserted that he had undergone the necessary legal processes to become a U.S. citizen, which would grant him the right to vote. However, the defendants contended that McCabe had not been legally naturalized, as the Marine Court of New York—where he claimed naturalization—lacked proper jurisdiction as a court of record to perform such functions. The key issue in the case was whether the Marine Court was authorized to issue naturalization under the acts of Congress. The court examined statutory definitions and previous rulings to whether the Marine Court was classified as a legitimate court of record, ultimately determining it was not.	McCabe's primary argument was that he had been legally naturalized and was therefore a qualified elector entitled to vote. He claimed that the defendants wrongfully denied his vote, which violated his rights as a citizen. McCabe sought damages for the refusal of his ballot, which he maintained was unjust since he had met the legal requirements for citizenship.	The defendants argued that McCabe had not been properly naturalized, as the Marine Court had no jurisdiction to admit individuals to citizenship. They maintained that only individuals who had undergone naturalization through accredited courts of record could be regarded as qualified electors. Consequently, they contended that because McCabe was not a qualified elector, the refusal of his vote did not constitute a legal wrong.

The case "Christopher Ender vs. Philip Scott" took place in St. Clair County, Illinois, with notable events recorded in April 1849. The action arose from a dispute over the exchange of horses, where the plaintiff, Christopher Ender, claimed he was misled about the soundness of a horse he received from the defendant, Philip Scott. Ender alleged that Scott represented the horse as sound apart from a known illness, the distemper. Following the trial, the jury initially ruled in favor of Ender, awarding him $15 for damages due to the alleged breach of warranty. However, Scott, dissatisfied with the verdict, sought a writ of error, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case hinged on the legal definitions and requirements for establishing a warranty, particularly regarding the intent and clarity of the parties' assertions during the exchange.	The plaintiff, Christopher Ender, claimed that the defendant, Philip Scott, had provided a false warranty regarding the soundness of the horse exchanged. Ender argued that Scott's clear representation—stating the horse was sound except for the distemper—constituted a warranty. He contended that he relied on this assertion to complete the exchange, and therefore, sought damages for the breach of the warranty when the horse proved to be defective.	The defendant, Philip Scott, contended that there was no warranty regarding the horse’s condition that could hold him liable. His defense focused on the assertion that, even if he made statements about the horse's soundness, these did not sufficiently meet the criteria for establishing a warranty as defined by law. Scott argued that the statements made were not intended to provide a warranty and that the defect in the horse was evident and should have been recognized by the plaintiff, absolving him from any responsibility.

On March 16, 1871, Thomas S. Dobbins obtained a judgment against Henry T. Baldwin and others in the Peoria County Circuit Court, Illinois. An execution was issued and returned with no property found. A second execution was issued on April 8, 1872, and levied on the defendants' property on April 17, 1872. However, no further action was taken, and the execution was deemed unsatisfied by November 7, 1878. On January 16, 1879, the property was sold under a venditioni exponas to Gilbert G. Gibbons, who transferred the certificate of purchase to Mary C. Dobbins, ultimately receiving a deed on May 31, 1880. Meanwhile, Richard A. Cutter had recovered a judgment against Baldwin on March 2, 1878, which was later assigned to The First National Bank of Peoria. An execution was issued for Cutter's judgment in April 1878, also returned unsatisfied, followed by another in December 1880, which was levied on the same property in January 1881. The bank then filed suit to set aside the transfer of property to Mary C. Dobbins, claiming the deed should be annulled based on their superior judgment lien. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, where key legal arguments about the liens under the statutes of 1845 and 1872 were discussed.	Mary C. Dobbins claimed that her title to the property, acquired through the sheriff's deed from the venditioni exponas following her husband's judgment, was valid and should not be set aside. She sought to affirm her legal ownership of the property despite the intervening judgment obtained by the First National Bank of Peoria, arguing that her lien had priority over the bank's claims.	The First National Bank of Peoria argued that Dobbins' judgment lien had expired prior to the action taken under it, leaving their judgment lien effective and superior. They contended that their judgment, obtained after Dobbins', provided them with priority over the land in question, and therefore, the court should uphold their claim to the property while setting aside Dobbins' deed.

In May 1874, a judgment was rendered in favor of Clark W. Upton against Richard Gregg and Thomas S. Dobbins in the United States District Court. Frank M. Wilson and George Wilson purchased the property in question at an execution sale under this judgment, subsequently assigning their purchase rights to Van H. Higgins, who then acquired a deed for the property after the redemption period ended. Following this, Higgins conveyed the property to Henry G. Eeichwald. Meanwhile, on April 15, 1875, Thomas S. Dobbins transferred the property to his son, George Spurk Dobbins, who took possession. The transfer amount stated was $13,000, which was less than the debt owed by Thomas to George. Immediately after this transfer, the Upton judgment was still pending appeal, which was not resolved until April 1877. George Spurk Dobbins initiated legal action against Wilsons and Higgins to contest the ownership, seeking an injunction to prevent a formal deed transfer. His initial plea for an injunction was denied, and the court eventually dismissed his case, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	George Spurk Dobbins claimed that the property was wrongfully sold due to an existing lien held by the Upton judgment. He argued that Thomas S. Dobbins had sold the property to him in good faith for value, and he should be protected from the execution sale. He sought to have the sale set aside and the deed to the property declared invalid, claiming other unencumbered properties should have been pursued to satisfy the Upton judgment instead of his property.	The defendants, represented by Wilson and Higgins, contended that they held a legitimate title to the property obtained through the execution sale, asserting that the property remained liable for Thomas Dobbins' judgment regardless of the transfer to George. They argued that they were not bound by any alleged release of lien and that George Dobbins had failed to exercise his rights to challenge the sale in a timely manner. They insisted that the sale was meritorious and that any delay on George's part to seek remedy should bar his claims.

In the case of "Charles Besimer et al. v. The People," which took place in Bureau County, Illinois, the events unfolded during the March term of 1853 when Charles Besimer was arrested under a process linked to an indictment for adultery. Besimer, who was the principal of a recognizance executed for his appearance in court, did not appear, leading to a judgment against him and his surety, Albert Sherwin. The sheriff took the recognizance, and subsequent judgments were rendered based on Besimer's failure to appear. There were two writs of scire facias issued to compel his appearance, but both returned with "not found." The second writ was not under the court's seal, which rendered it void. The court's focus was on whether the indictment for adultery was valid under Illinois law, as a certain form of adultery could indeed be prosecutable, but the lack of proper service of process became a significant factor in the proceedings.	The plaintiffs argued that the recognizance was invalid due to improper legal procedures, specifically the failure to serve the cognizors personally and the issuance of a void writ of scire facias. They claimed that both attempts to compel their appearance were ineffective, and therefore, the judgment against them should not stand.	The defendants maintained that adultery could be an indictable offense under Illinois law and argued that the recognizance was designed for Besimer to respond to such an indictment. However, they faced challenges in proving the validity of the process used, particularly due to the lack of proper service which is necessary to enforce the judgment.

The case "The City of Jacksonville v. Lida E. Akers" dates to September 26, 1882, in Jacksonville, Illinois. The dispute arose from a contractual relationship between Lida E. Akers, a teacher, and the Board of Education for the City of Jacksonville. Akers had previously taught in the public schools and was appointed to teach in the fourth ward branch (colored) school in June 1875. She declined this position but was later appointed to the second grade of the fourth ward school (white), which she accepted. However, following a decision by the Board in August 1875, her appointment was revoked, and she was reassigned back to the colored school. Despite her assignment, Akers refused to teach in the colored school but appeared in the white school instead, challenging the Board's authority to assign her. The case ultimately sought to determine whether Akers acted in accordance with the rules governing her contract with the Board and if her refusal constituted a breach.	The plaintiff, the City of Jacksonville, claimed that Lida E. Akers breached her employment contract by refusing to teach in the colored school as required by the Board's regulations. They argued that the rules were binding and formed an integral part of the contract since her acceptance included the stipulation to adhere to these rules. The plaintiff sought enforcement of the contract and a judgment against Akers for her refusal to comply with the assignment.	The defendant, Lida E. Akers, contended that she was not obligated to teach in the colored school, arguing that she was initially hired for the white school. Akers claimed that the rules were not adequately communicated to her, and she perceived her appointment as contingent only on serving in the position she accepted. Her defense relied on the assertion that the Board's decision to revoke her white school assignment and reassign her to the colored school was unjustified and violated her contractual rights.

In June 1873, the case "Henry D. Kingsbury v. John Wall" was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from an accepted order drawn by Pluma McKnight on Henry D. Kingsbury, which requested Kingsbury to deliver $2,626.25 worth of clothing to William B. Jarvis or any assigned individual. The delivery of the clothing was contingent upon Jarvis providing a quit-claim deed from himself and his wife, transferring their interest in the St. Charles Hotel in Kinmuudy, Illinois. The critical issue arose regarding whether the agreement was assignable, allowing Jarvis to transfer his rights to Wall for the purpose of initiating a lawsuit. The court examined whether the payment's conditional nature rendered the order assignable under Illinois law. This case brought forth crucial questions about the assignability of contingent agreements and the legal framework surrounding bills of exchange and promissory notes.	The plaintiff, John Wall, argued that he was owed payment under the accepted order originally drawn on Kingsbury, which had been assigned to him by Wm. B. Jarvis. Wall claimed the right to maintain the suit based on the assignment and sought to recover the payment for the goods specified in the order.	Henry D. Kingsbury contended that the order was not assignable under Illinois law because it was contingent on certain conditions being met—that is, the delivery of the goods was dependent upon obtaining a deed from Jarvis's wife, who was a third party to the transaction. Kingsbury maintained that since the agreement involved a condition that might never occur, the lawsuit brought by Wall was improper.

John Doyle v. Philip Conlin is a legal case that originated in September 1876 in La Salle County, Illinois. The case began when Philip Conlin filed a lawsuit against John Doyle, claiming damages for the trespass of Doyle's cattle on Conlin's pasture land. The case was initially heard by a justice of the peace who ruled in favor of Conlin, awarding him damages. Doyle subsequently appealed this decision to the circuit court; however, by mutual agreement, the case was transferred to the city court of La Salle. In that court, a trial was conducted without a jury, resulting in a ruling that awarded Conlin $200 in damages for the proven trespass. Doyle contested the judgment, questioning the sufficiency of the evidence presented at trial. However, the court noted that while there were some conflicting testimonies, it found the evidence of trespass to be compelling and justified maintaining the original judgment.	Philip Conlin, the plaintiff, asserted that John Doyle's cattle trespassed on his pasture land, causing damages for which he sought compensation. Conlin's primary argument was that he had clearly proven the instance of trespass and was entitled to the damages awarded by the lower court.	John Doyle, the defendant, argued against the sufficiency of the evidence that supported the plaintiff's claims. Doyle’s defense focused on questioning whether the evidence presented met the necessary legal standards to uphold the judgment against him, and he sought to have the judgment reversed.

The case "The Peoria and Oquawka Rail Road Company, Appellant, v. Thomas Neill, Appellee" was heard in June 1855 at the Illinois Supreme Court, following a trial in Tazewell County, Illinois. Thomas Neill, the plaintiff, initiated a legal action against the Peoria and Oquawka Rail Road Company based on a bill of exchange that had been accepted by the company. The bill, drawn by Spenck and Hughes, instructed the company to pay Neill a sum of $300, due sixty days after March 14, 1854. Neill's claims were articulated in two special counts on the acceptance as well as traditional common counts. In response, the railroad company asserted a general issue and a special plea of set-off, stating that a third party, Etting, to whom Neill had assigned the bill, owed the company a significantly larger debt. Neill countered this by highlighting a previously resolved case against Etting, where the court had ruled against the railroad company on the same matter, arguing that this judgment barred the company's claim. The case proceeded to trial, and after evaluating the evidence, judgment was rendered in favor of Neill by the court. The company subsequently challenged the ruling, prompting an appeal.	Neill's primary argument was based on the acceptance of the bill of exchange by the Peoria and Oquawka Rail Road Company, which he presented as evidence during the trial. He requested payment for the accepted amount, asserting that the railroad's defenses were inadequate, particularly emphasizing a prior judgment against the company relating to the same debt owed by the third party, Etting. Neill contended that this prior ruling should bar any defenses raised by the company regarding his claim.	The Peoria and Oquawka Rail Road Company contended that their special plea for set-off should be upheld, arguing that Etting's debt to the company could offset Neill's claim. The company maintained that the bill of exchange was not a valid instrument due to alleged variances from the declared counts, and they objected to its admissibility as evidence. They also argued that without sworn proof of the signatures on the bill, Neill's claims were flawed. Essentially, they sought to block the enforcement of the acceptance by claiming the existence of a greater debt owed by a person not directly involved in the case.

In the case of Strong H. Earll for the use of Charles G. Patten against James Mitchell et al., the legal dispute arises from transactions over an extended period from January 12, 1854, to March 29, 1856, in Freeport, Stephenson County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Strong H. Earll, was engaged in the business of buying and forwarding produce and sought financial assistance from the defendants, who were brokers involved in loaning money and selling exchange. Throughout this timeframe, Earll drew about 260 bills of exchange totaling approximately $300,000 from the defendants, relying on these instruments as his means of financing. The crux of the legal action centers around whether these transactions constituted loans with usurious interest rates or legitimate purchases of bills of exchange. The plaintiff contended that the defendants charged more than the legal rate of interest, while the defendants claimed the transactions were legitimate purchases at fair market rates, justifying the deductions made. This case culminated in a jury trial at the Stephenson Circuit Court in December 1858, where the jury ultimately found in favor of the defendants' position regarding the nature of the transactions.	The plaintiff, Strong H. Earll, claimed that the amounts deducted by the defendants from the face value of the bills of exchange represented usurious interest rates exceeding the legal limit. He sought to recover the excess amounts taken by the defendants, arguing that the transactions were structured as loans rather than legitimate purchases, thus entitling him to restitution under the action for money had and received.	The defendants contended that the transactions in question were bona fide purchases of bills of exchange rather than loans. They argued that if the transactions were not deemed purchases, they had the right under trade customs to charge the excess over and above the legal interest rate as a commission. The defendants maintained that the deductions for discounting the drafts were within the customary and ordinary rates at the time of the transactions and were not indicative of usury.

H. Bailey et al. v. The Valley National Bank is a case that took place in Kankakee County, Illinois, with a decision issued by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1889. The case arose from a dispute over the execution of notes and issues surrounding an attachment proceeding connected with an assumpsit claim. Before the plaintiff (Valley National Bank) filed a formal declaration, the defendants (H. Bailey et al.) filed a notice of set-off, which was struck from the record by the court. The plaintiff subsequently filed an affidavit detailing the debt owed and two grounds for attachment, supported by an amended bond. The court ruled the attachment was valid since the defendant had been properly served in the original suit. Disputes arose regarding whether the plaintiff needed to prove corporate existence and whether the execution of the notes had been properly challenged by the defendant. Ultimately, the court had to determine the sufficiency of the defenses presented, particularly questioning the merit of the unverified plea and notices filed by the defendants.	The plaintiff argued that the court was correct in striking the notice of set-off from the record because it lacked a supporting plea to apply to. They contended that the attachment proceeding was valid since proper service of the summons had been made. The plaintiff also emphasized that the burden of proof regarding the execution of the notes rested on the defendant, who failed to properly challenge the plaintiff's claims under the applicable statutes.	The defendants contested the admissibility of the notes due to a lack of proof for their execution and questioned the corporate existence of the plaintiff bank. They argued that their notice should have been considered sufficient to shift the burden of proof regarding corporate existence to the plaintiff. The defendants claimed that the court erred by not allowing evidence related to the execution of the notes and the plaintiff's corporate status.

This case, John D. Gillett v. Robert Webb et al., was decided on December 4, 1885, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose after Gillett, the appellant, employed Webb and others (the appellees) to saw timber from Gillett's land into lumber. Initially, they agreed on a price of $10 per thousand feet for the sawing; however, this rate was later reduced to $8 for some of the wood. The appellees claimed that they had sawn a total of 362,315 feet of timber, primarily under the $10 agreement, and asserted that Gillett owed them $1,025.29. Gillett, through his defenses, acknowledged a debt of approximately $680, claiming that he tendered $685 but disputed the quality of some lumber, asserting that he should not have to pay for rotten lumber. The case was tried before a jury, and they found Gillett liable and awarded the appellees $900, after accounting for the disputed amount related to rotten lumber.	The appellees (plaintiffs) claimed that Gillett owed them a total of $1,025.29 for the lumber sawn under their contract. They argued that the original agreement, as well as subsequent agreements regarding the price per thousand feet, should be honored. They sought judgment for the full amount claimed, along with any costs associated with the suit.	The appellant (defendant), Gillett, contended that he acknowledged owing approximately $680 but had tendered $685 as payment. He argued that there was disagreement over the quality of the lumber, specifically regarding rotten wood, which should exempt him from paying for those portions. Gillett challenged several jury instructions, claiming they would mislead the jury and insisted that the court’s assistance regarding legal definitions related to "acceptance" of lumber was inappropriate.

The legal case of Harvey O’Neal et al. v. Benjamin O. Auten arose from events in Mason County, Illinois, involving a dispute over property ownership. On January 16, 1861, Benjamin O. Auten filed an original bill, claiming he purchased a parcel of land on March 12, 1858, from Jas. M. Buggies. Auten contended that Buggies had previously conveyed the land to C. P. Richardson, who in turn had agreed to convey it back to Buggies. Auten asserted that he possessed the land, made improvements valued at $5,000, and was seeking a formal conveyance of title from Richardson, who was refusing to do so, claiming ownership. The case involved conflicting accounts from Richardson and J.M. Ruggles, who also claimed to have a prior interest in the property, alleging that Richardson had failed to fulfill financial obligations related to their transaction. The complexity of the testimonies made it challenging to ascertain the definitive ownership and equities involved.	Auten, the plaintiff, argued that he rightfully purchased the land from Ruggles and had continuous possession and made substantial improvements on it. He sought a legal decree compelling Richardson to execute a deed transferring his interest in the property to Auten, as he claimed that Richardson was unjustly denying his ownership rights despite the settlement agreements made between Richardson and Ruggles that outlined the transfer of title responsibilities.	The defendant, C.P. Richardson, contended that he had legally acquired the property from Ruggles prior to Auten's purchase, asserting that he held full title and had made the necessary payments. He argued that the bond for a deed conditioned on payment of $900 had not been fulfilled by Ruggles, thus invalidating any claim Auten had to the property. Richardson denied any wrongdoing and claimed he had a legitimate interest in the land, seeking to maintain possession and claiming that there were unresolved financial obligations that complicated the title.

In April 1865, the case of Grosvenor et al. v. Magill & Latham took place in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Grosvenor & Co. (the plaintiffs) and Magill & Latham (the defendants). The dispute arose from a contract dated July 9, 1863, in which Grosvenor & Co. agreed to sell 2,500 barrels of fine salt to Magill & Latham for $3.40 per barrel, with a delivery date set for the first half of August 1863. During the trial, plaintiffs established they attempted to deliver the salt on August 16, but the defendants refused to accept it. The plaintiffs sought a ruling from the court stating that their delivery offer was compliant with the contract terms, as they claimed that the law does not specify a division of a day. The trial court denied this instruction, which led to an appeal by Grosvenor & Co. The court found that, for the specific terms of their contract, delivery by noon on August 16 constituted a valid performance.	The plaintiffs, Grosvenor & Co., argued that their offer to deliver the salt on August 16 was timely and complied with the contract terms. They sought a jury instruction clarifying that the law recognizes no division of a day and that their delivery attempt was valid. They believed that the refusal of the defendants to accept the salt was unjust, as they had offered it in accordance with the agreed-upon timeframe.	The defendants, Magill & Latham, contended that the delivery was not valid under the contract terms, emphasizing that the timeframe stipulated required delivery by noon on August 16 rather than later that day. They argued that the plaintiffs had not adequately proven their compliance with the contract and maintained that the plaintiffs' declaration of delivery was insufficiently specific, allowing the defendants to challenge the claim under general legal principles.

The case, "The City of Kankakee v. William Potter et al.", was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1887. The conflict arose over a special assessment imposed by the city of Kankakee to fund the reconstruction of a sewer extending through an alley in Block 24 of the original town of Kankakee City. The city sought to deepen and reconstruct this sewer, which was to be aligned with the existing public main sewer on Station Street. Certain lot owners, led by William Potter, objected to this special assessment, arguing that the ordinance authorizing it failed to sufficiently describe the nature and specifics of the proposed improvement, as mandated by the applicable statute. The County Court of Kankakee County sustained these objections, leading the city to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court to determine whether the ordinance met the statutory requirements for such local improvements.	The City of Kankakee, as the appellant, argued that the ordinance passed to implement the special assessment adequately outlined the nature and locality of the sewer reconstruction. They contended the ordinance included necessary details about the work being similar to the existing sewer and that the lot owners should have been aware of the prior sewer's condition. The City sought to enforce the special assessment based on this ordinance to fund the reconstruction work.	The defendants, represented by William Potter, contended that the ordinance was fundamentally flawed and did not meet the statutory requirements for special assessments. Their main argument was that the ordinance lacked a detailed description of the sewer project, including its dimensions, materials, and construction specifics. They asserted that without this essential information, the ordinance could not form a valid basis for the assessment, and therefore, the court should dismiss the assessment and uphold the objections.

In early 1862, the case Anthony S. Seely v. The People was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from Greene County, where Leick was appointed as a master in chancery and was required to file a bond for the faithful discharge of his duties. Seely, as one of the sureties for this bond, became embroiled in a legal dispute when it was discovered that the name of another surety, Samuel Heaton, was forged on the bond. The bond was meant to protect the interests of two wards, Jesse H. Neece and Pemnah Jane Neece, whose guardian, Alfred W. Neece, successfully obtained a judgment against Leick for misappropriating their funds. Seely argued that he should not be held liable under the bond because he was led to sign it under the false premise that Heaton had genuinely signed it, constituting a significant case of forgery. The trial was conducted without a jury, and the court initially ruled against Seely, prompting him to seek a new trial, asserting that the findings were contrary to law and evidence.	The plaintiff, representing the interests of the wards, claimed that Seely was liable as a surety on the bond, despite the forgery of Heaton's name. They maintained that the bond should be enforced to ensure the recovery of the misappropriated funds, as the bond was intended to provide a financial guarantee for the faithful performance of duties by the master in chancery.	Seely contended that he should not be held liable on the bond due to the fraud committed by Heaton, as the forgery of Heaton's name meant that he had been misled regarding the true nature of his liability. He argued that he signed the bond believing he was a co-surety with an actual party, which was fundamentally altered by the criminal act of forgery. Thus, he should be exonerated from any obligation under the bond, as he was deceived by a criminal act beyond his control and due diligence.

In early 1867, in Adams County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving Henry C. Craig as the defendant and Gersham B. Dimock along with Cyrus W. Hilborn as the plaintiffs. The case emerged from an action of replevin regarding a wagon and two horses that plaintiffs claimed were theirs, secured by a chattel mortgage executed on March 19, 1867, by a third party, Holden. The mortgage was originally recorded without the proper stamp but was later re-stamped and correctly recorded on June 21, 1867. Meanwhile, Samuel E. Chittenden had secured a judgment against Holden on June 20, 1867, and the execution was delivered to Craig, the sheriff, who subsequently levied on the same property. The dispute centered on the validity of the mortgage due to the timing of its stamping and recording. The legal question involved whether the unstamped mortgage was valid against the execution lien held by Chittenden.	The plaintiffs contended that the chattel mortgage constituted valid security for an existing debt and thus entitled them to reclaim possession of the wagon and horses. They argued that the failure to attach a stamp to the mortgage was due to inadvertence, not fraud, and maintained that the subsequent stamping cured any defect. They requested the court to recognize the mortgage as valid and rule in their favor to reclaim their property.	The defendant, Henry C. Craig, asserted that the unstamped mortgage was invalid under the act of Congress requiring such documents to be stamped for validity. He argued that since the mortgage was not properly stamped at the time the execution was delivered, he should be entitled to uphold Chittenden's execution lien on the property. Craig requested the court to dismiss the plaintiffs' claims based on the alleged invalidity of the mortgage.

The case "The Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railway Company v. The People ex rel. D. P. Smith" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1886. The case stems from an application brought by D.P. Smith, the county treasurer and collector, seeking judgment for delinquent taxes owed by the Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railway Company. The legal dispute occurred in Jasper County, Illinois, where it was established that the railway company had paid all taxes except for road and bridge taxes totaling $319 for 1884. The taxing issue involved three townships—Wade, Fox, and Crooked Creek—each having adopted a "labor system" for road and bridge tax purposes according to state law. The commissioners of highways in these townships had determined necessary funds to be raised and communicated this to the township supervisors, who in turn submitted it to the county board for action at a prior September meeting. However, the railway company contended, among other arguments, that the tax was levied without proper authority from the county board and thus was illegal and void. The county clerk had extended the tax without an affirmative order from the board, leading to the legal challenge regarding the legitimacy of the tax charge.	The plaintiff, represented by D.P. Smith, claimed that the Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railway Company owed delinquent taxes, specifically road and bridge taxes, as established for the townships by the highway commissioners according to state tax law. The plaintiff sought a judgment to enforce the collection of these unpaid taxes, asserting that the proper procedures had been followed in determining the tax amounts due for the year 1884.
