The defendant, the railway company, contested the validity of the road and bridge tax claim by arguing that the levy was made without any directive from the county board, making it unauthorized and thus void. They asserted that no action or order related to extending the tax was officially recorded by the board, and claimed that the certification of the tax was improper and lacked the required legal authority. The defendant maintained that all taxes owed were properly paid except the contested road and bridge tax, emphasizing the illegal nature of the tax charge as the basis for their objections.

In December 1861, George H. Rozet, the appellant, and Paul Queyrouse were involved in the Southern Shoe Manufacturing Company in New Orleans, where Rozet served as president. On December 5, 1861, William H. McClellan, the appellee, purchased fifty shares of stock from Rozet with a loan of $5,000. In exchange, McClellan drew a check, endorsed by Rozet, to receive the shares and Rozet's promissory note payable in four months. Rozet failed to meet the payment upon the note's maturity, leading to its renewal and the transfer of the fifty shares to McClellan as collateral security alongside authorization for McClellan to sell the shares if Rozet defaulted. When the note again matured, McClellan did not sell the stock, which subsequently decreased in value, and Rozet argued this was grounds for a claim against McClellan. The case revolves around whether McClellan was obligated to sell the stock upon Rozet's default and the implications of not doing so on liability for depreciation in stock value.",	Rozet claimed that McClellan was liable for failing to sell the stocks when the note was in default, thus contributing to the loss in value as the shares depreciated. Rozet argued that the agreement gave McClellan the authority to sell the stock, and by not exercising this power, McClellan failed to protect Rozet's interests in the pledged collateral. Rozet sought accountability for the loss resulting from McClellan's inaction.",	McClellan contended that he was not obligated to sell the pledged stock upon Rozet's default and would not be liable for any depreciation that followed. He referenced legal principles indicating that while a pledgee has the right to sell in case of default, there is no duty to act, and failure to sell does not incur liability for loss measured by decline in value. McClellan maintained that Rozet still held the general property in the shares and had the right to redeem them.",

In 1835, in Adams County, Illinois, an action of trespass de bonis asportatis was brought by Ebenezer Turner, Jr. against defendants James W. Whitney and George Taylor. The case was tried in the Circuit Court before Judge Richard M. Young, where the jury ultimately favored Turner, rendering a verdict against Whitney and Taylor for $22.12 plus costs. The plaintiffs, Whitney and Taylor, appealed the decision, arguing a legal point related to the nature of being complicit in the alleged trespass. Whitney contended that the jury should be instructed that they could not find him guilty unless he personally committed the alleged trespass rather than merely approving or commanding it. The trial court refused this instruction. This case revolves around principles of liability in trespass actions as articulated in Illinois law.	The plaintiff, Ebenezer Turner, asserted that Whitney and Taylor were guilty of trespass for taking his property. Turner sought monetary compensation for the value of the property unlawfully taken, in addition to coverage of legal costs incurred during the litigation process.	The defendants Whitney and Taylor contended that the trial court erred in refusing to instruct the jury that they could only be held liable for the trespass if they personally committed the act. Whitney claimed that the court should have differentiated between direct perpetrators and those merely giving command or approval, seeking a reversal of the lower court's judgment based on this legal interpretation.

Thomas G. S. Herod and Colvard initiated a replevin action against Milton Bartley, the administrator, in July 1853, at the Gallatin Circuit Court, Illinois. The case involved the recovery of a horse that the plaintiffs claimed ownership of. The plaintiffs presented evidence including a transcript from a justice of the peace indicating a judgment in favor of Hudson against Layton, which had been assigned to them and an execution of that judgment that had been satisfied by the sale of the horse to them. They alleged that the constable had levied the execution on the horse and allowed the previous owner to retain it until the sale day. However, the horse was not present during the sale nor was it in the possession of the witness. The defendant moved to exclude the judgment based on a jurisdictional issue, which the court accepted. Ultimately, the plaintiffs were deemed unable to substantiate their ownership claim, leading the court to rule in favor of the defendant.	The plaintiffs, Herod and Colvard, claimed that they had a legal right to the horse based on a judgment and an execution from a justice of the peace. They argued that the constable's proper levy of the execution on the horse prior to their purchase established their rightful ownership, and they requested that the court return possession of the horse to them.	The defendant, Milton Bartley, contended that the judgment the plaintiffs relied on should be excluded due to a lack of jurisdiction from the justice of the peace involved. Bartley argued that even if the judgment were admissible, the plaintiffs failed to prove their claim of title, as the sale of the horse conducted by the constable was illegal due to the horse's absence at the time of sale. The defendant requested that the court rule in his favor.

In the case of John W. Priest et al. v. Ruth Wheelock, the proceedings took place in Springfield, Illinois, and culminated in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1871. The case involved a mortgage executed by Henry Carrigan and his wife to Solomon B. Wheelock to secure a $1,000 note with a 10% interest rate, dated May 2, 1857, and due in one year. After Wheelock's death, a foreclosure bill was filed against the executrix of Carrigan's estate and John W. Priest, who had purchased the mortgaged property through a trust deed executed during Carrigan's lifetime. Several years had elapsed since a judgment from April 1859 against the mortgagor, leading to questions about whether the foreclosure was barred due to the statute of limitations. While Priest contended he was a bona fide purchaser and the property was free from the judgment lien after seven years, the court needed to determine if the mortgage's lien remained valid despite the judgment's expiration.	The plaintiffs aimed to foreclose the mortgage on the property, arguing that the mortgage lien remained in effect despite the lapse of seven years since the last judgment on the debt. They contended that the mortgage secured the debt and continued to bind the property until fully satisfied, regardless of the judgment's status. They asserted their right to enforce the mortgage as a means to satisfy the original debt, as the judgment merely transformed the form of the debt without extinguishing the mortgage.	The defendants, led by John W. Priest, claimed the foreclosure suit was barred due to the expiration of seven years since the judgment, arguing that he acquired the property free from any liens, thereby protecting bona fide purchasers. They maintained that because the original judgment was no longer a valid lien, the foreclosure couldn't proceed under the circumstances of the case, arguing that the mortgage's enforcement was similarly restricted due to the expiration of the judgment's lien.

In September 1868, a legal case took place in Kankakee County, Illinois, involving the plaintiff Ann Ellen Jackson and the defendant Sidney Dubois. The case revolved around a dispute over the ownership of a piano that Jackson claimed belonged to her before her marriage to William Jackson in England in 1865. Jointly immigrating to the United States, she alleged that her husband sold the piano to the defendant without her consent. The pivotal legal question was whether the piano, as property owned by Jackson prior to her marriage, remained her separate property after their marriage and subsequent move to the United States. The case was brought under an 1861 Illinois statute regarding married women's property rights, asserting that property owned prior to marriage remains the wife's separate property unless she authorized the husband to sell it.	Ann Ellen Jackson claimed ownership of the piano based on the argument that it was her property at the time of her marriage, and she neither authorized her husband to sell it nor ratified the sale. Citing the 1861 Illinois statute, she contended that her property rights were protected and that she could maintain the suit in her own name without her husband being joined as a party.	Sidney Dubois contended that the marriage had legally transferred ownership of the piano to William Jackson, which was consistent with the laws of England at the time of their marriage. He argued that the 1861 Act did not retroactively affect property rights acquired under English law prior to the act's passage and that any property owned by a wife before marriage became the husband's upon marriage.

In September 1867, the case of Charles K. W. Howard v. Angus McDonald et al. took place in the Illinois Supreme Court, arising from a dispute regarding a threshing machine. The action was an assumpsit brought by McDonald, Laughlin & Co. against Howard to recover the value of a threshing machine sold and delivered to him. The facts of the case revealed that the machine was allegedly not purchased on Howard's responsibility but rather by his son. The trial occurred during the March term of 1865 in the Circuit Court of DuPage County, presided over by Judge Isaac G. Wilson. The jury initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, assessing damages at $400. Following this, Howard appealed, claiming errors during the trial, particularly concerning jury instructions about testimony credibility.	The plaintiff, McDonald, Laughlin & Co., argued that Howard was liable for the payment of the threshing machine sold to him. They sought to recover the $400 assessed by the jury for the machine’s value, asserting that it had been delivered and that they had fulfilled their contractual obligations.	Howard contended that he should not be held accountable for the purchase of the machine, claiming it was bought by his son and not on his responsibility. He argued that the jury was misled by instructions regarding the witness' credibility and maintained that the evidence did not support the verdict against him.

The case, "The Heirs of Peter Critz v. Hiram L. Pierce," revolves around the will of Peter Critz, Sr., who passed away on June 26, 1881, in Logan County, Illinois, leaving behind an estate valued between $50,000 and $60,000. Hiram L. Pierce, named as the executor in the purported will, filed the document for probate shortly after Critz’s death. Initially, the county court refused to admit the will to probate, leading Pierce to appeal to the circuit court, which ultimately ruled to admit the will. The heirs of Critz contested this decision, arguing that the will was invalid due to the claimed unsoundness of mind of Critz at the time of its execution. Testifying witnesses confirmed proper execution of the will, but the heirs supplied evidence demonstrating Critz’s previous adjudication as a person of unsound mind and the appointment of Pierce as his conservator until his death. The main contention was whether the heirs could introduce evidence of Critz’s mental capacity or if it was confined to alleging fraud or improper conduct only.	The heirs of Peter Critz claimed that the will should not be admitted to probate because Critz lacked the mental capacity necessary to execute a will. They presented evidence of Critz's prior adjudication as unsound of mind and argued that the will was influenced by improper conduct and that the executor, Pierce, had a position of undue influence over Critz.	Hiram L. Pierce, the defendant and executor of the will, defended himself by asserting that the will was validly executed, fulfilling all statutory requirements for probate. He argued that, according to the law, evidence presented by the heirs regarding Critz’s mental capacity was inadmissible to contest the probate as it sought to establish a defense of unsoundness of mind, which he contended was beyond the scope of the appeal process.

In the case of Moses Rohrheimer v. James K. Eagle et al., decided on January 10, 1889, the legal proceedings took place in Kankakee County, Illinois. The appeal was brought forth by Moses Rohrheimer against James K. Eagle and others. The appeal was an examination of the prior judgment made by the Circuit Court, which was presided over by Judge H. J. Pillsuuby. A critical issue in this case involved the absence of a certificate from the judge concerning the bill of exceptions, which is typically necessary for the reviewing court to inspect the evidence presented in lower court trials. Due to this absence, the reviewing court could not evaluate the claims and evidence, leading to an assumption that the lower court's proceedings were regular and properly conducted.	The plaintiff, Moses Rohrheimer, sought to appeal the decision made by the Circuit Court. His main argument hinged on the contention that the original court's decision was incorrect, although the details of the specific claims made during the initial trial are not provided in the description. Without the certificate to the bill of exceptions, Rohrheimer's capacity to substantiate his claims based on the evidence was significantly hampered.	The defendants, represented in the case by James K. Eagle and others, effectively argued that the absence of the required certificate to the bill of exceptions meant that the appellate court could not reassess the evidence from the trial. They maintained that the presumption of regularity would favor the Circuit Court's judgment and, as such, there was no basis to overturn the original ruling.

In December 1888, a legal suit was initiated in Will County, Illinois, involving Philip Bischmann as the appellant and August Boehl as the appellee. The case arose from a claim by Bischmann that Boehl’s installation of a tile drain on his own property caused water from a large pond to flow onto Bischmann's land, resulting in consequential damages. The drain was placed some distance away from Bischmann’s property, leading to allegations that the drainage was improper and that the water flow altered the natural state of Bischmann's land. The case began in a justice of the peace court and was then appealed to the Circuit Court of Will County, where a jury found for Bischmann but awarded only nominal damages. Boehl appealed this decision, arguing that the ruling was unsupported by evidence and that the previous courts lacked jurisdiction given the nominal nature of the damages awarded.	Philip Bischmann, the plaintiff, argued that the tile drain laid by August Boehl improperly directed water from Boehl's pond onto Bischmann's land, causing damage that, while nominal in this instance, constituted a legal infringement on his property rights. He sought recognition of this invasion and claimed entitlement to damages, even if only nominal, due to the violation of his property rights.	August Boehl, the defendant, contended that the evidence did not substantiate Bischmann's claims of damages, asserting that the water, in its natural state, did not flow towards Bischmann's land but rather away from it. He argued that the courts did not have jurisdiction in this matter because the damages were nominal rather than actual, which he believed invalidated the claims for compensation. Boehl requested the appellate court to overturn the judgment of the lower courts.

Julie Ehrler v. Bartholomaeus Braun is a legal case that took place in Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment dated February 2, 1887. The dispute arose over two promissory notes that Braun claimed were forgeries and sought their cancellation through a bill in chancery. Braun had purchased real estate from Rudolph Becker on June 16, 1885, and secured $2,000 of the purchase price with the issuance of the two notes, each for $1,000, which were payable in one and two years. The notes were eventually sold to Frederick Freudenberg, who subsequently transferred them to Frederick Lipp, who held a forged duplicate of the deed of trust associated with the notes. Meanwhile, Ehrler possessed the purported genuine deed of trust and forged duplicates of the notes. Braun argued that the forgeries were committed by Freudenberg or an unknown party, asserting that he was willing to settle the matter by paying whatever was owed on the genuine note. The case involved pinned details about payments made on the genuine notes and disputed claims of acknowledgment concerning the notes' authenticity made by both Braun and Ehrler.	Braun, the plaintiff, claimed that the two promissory notes held by Ehrler were forgeries and sought their cancellation. He requested that the court order the removal of the forged notes and the forged deed of trust from legal records. Additionally, he expressed readiness to settle the outstanding balance on the genuine note, asserting he was innocent of any wrongdoing regarding the alleged forgeries.	Ehrler, the defendant, countered Braun’s claims by asserting the legitimacy of the notes she held and filed a cross-bill for the foreclosure of the deed of trust. She maintained that Braun had recognized the notes' legitimacy by requesting an extension of one, contradicting Braun's claims about their validity. Her defense relied on evidentiary testimonies from her agent supporting her position that Braun had acknowledged the notes.

In July 1866, John J. Schwartz contracted Charles Daegling to perform brickwork for a building located on State Street in Chicago, Illinois. The original plans called for a four-story structure, twenty-four feet wide by eighty feet long, featuring a pressed brick front. However, modifications were made, increasing the building's length to 120 feet and replacing the brick front with a stone front, which required an extension of four weeks. The construction was to be completed by mid-September, with the plastering finished by early October. On October 22, 1866, a severe storm caused the partially completed walls of the building to collapse. Prior to the collapse, the architect had instructed Daegling to brace the walls more securely, but he failed to do so. While some witnesses suggested that the inadequate bracing contributed to the building's downfall, others believed the storm's intensity was the primary cause. A jury trial ruled in favor of Daegling, leading to Schwartz's appeal.	Schwartz argued that Daegling was negligent in his construction work, specifically citing the failure to adequately brace the building's walls despite direction from the architect. He sought damages for the losses incurred due to the building's collapse, asserting that Daegling's actions were the reason for the construction delays and subsequent damages.	Daegling defended himself by claiming that his work on the building was performed securely and without negligence. He argued that the collapse was primarily due to the extraordinary severity of the storm, coupled with the delay caused by another contractor responsible for providing the necessary cut stone for the front of the building. Daegling contended that the measures he took were in line with reasonable construction practices and asserted that any additional bracing would not have prevented the collapse.

The case titled "The Northern Bank of Illinois v. Samuel Zepp" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1862. It involved the Northern Bank of Illinois, which was established under the general banking laws of Illinois, and its dealings with Samuel Zepp. The key issue arose after the bank filed a certificate on September 23, 1859, expressing its desire to withdraw its notes from circulation. The plaintiff brought an action of assumpsit related to banking transactions that took place after the bank had filed this certificate. The transactions in question involved deposits made with the bank in Waukegan on April 1, 1861. The defendant contended that, after filing the certificate, the bank was no longer able to engage in banking activities except for the purpose of winding up its business and handling pre-existing debts. The court needed to assess whether the bank retained liability for transactions occurring after the withdrawal of its notes from circulation and if the whereabouts of the certificate filing affected the claim.	The Northern Bank of Illinois, as the plaintiff, claimed that despite having filed a certificate to withdraw its notes from circulation, it was still liable for the deposits made by Samuel Zepp. The plaintiff argued that the law did not render all transactions void and that the bank could still be held accountable for obligations incurred after the filing, as long as the depositor had not been notified of the certificate filing. The plaintiff sought to recover the value of the deposits and damages from the transactions that took place after the certificate was filed.	Samuel Zepp, the defendant, contended that the Northern Bank of Illinois had legally ceased to conduct banking operations following the filing of the certificate on September 23, 1859. He argued that any transactions made after this date could not be enforceable as they did not fall within the bank’s allowable activities. Furthermore, the defendant claimed he was ready to pay the equivalent value in lawful currency, which he offered to the plaintiff before the suit was initiated, suggesting the plaintiff's refusal was unreasonable.

The case "James W. Primmer v. John Clabaugh" took place in June 1875 in Marion County, Illinois. The plaintiff, John Clabaugh, initiated a replevin action against James W. Primmer to recover a lot of mules, cattle, farming implements, and other personal property. Clabaugh claimed ownership based on two chattel mortgages executed by Emily H. Dolson, the wife of the deceased John J. Dolson. Primmer, the defendant, argued that the property belonged to the estate of John J. Dolson, for which he was the administrator. The case was referred to a referee for a report following the agreement of both parties. The referee reviewed the evidence and reached conclusions, which were contested by Primmer. However, the court upheld the referee's findings, ruling that the chattel mortgages were valid and that the property was not part of Dolson's estate but belonged to his widow, Emily.	The plaintiff claimed possession of the disputed property based on a chattel mortgage executed by Emily H. Dolson. He contended that the mortgage was valid and gave him the right to reclaim the property. Clabaugh argued that the funds used to acquire the property were Emily's separate property, affirming her rights to the assets even after her husband's death.	The defendant, James W. Primmer, contended that he held the property as the administrator of John J. Dolson’s estate. He raised objections regarding the competency of Mrs. Dolson as a witness based on the statutory provisions of the time, asserting that her testimony should not be considered. Primmer's primary argument focused on the claim that the property in question should rightly belong to the estate of Dolson rather than to his widow or her mortgagee.

In 1888, in Douglass County, Illinois, the case of John Dayton v. Thomas Rutherford et al. emerged regarding a dispute over drainage rights. The case arose when commissioners filed a complaint seeking to prevent John Dayton (the appellant) from cutting a ditch that would connect what was claimed to be a natural drain running through his property to a branch ditch within the established drainage district. This action was believed to potentially divert water from Dayton's land and other adjacent territories into the district's drainage system, which could disrupt the natural drainage patterns. The case involved conflicting evidence about whether the slough in question constituted a natural watercourse. The circuit court judge ruled that while Dayton could drain water from his land, the proposed ditching could harm the district drains, leading to the request for an injunction.	The plaintiffs, represented by the commissioners, argued that John Dayton's proposed ditch would improperly divert water into the district’s drainage system, which could damage existing drains. They sought an injunction to prevent him from cutting the ditch, asserting that the potential for ongoing harm justified the request for preventive relief.	John Dayton contended that he had the right to drain his own land without causing harm to others, as he was merely managing water from his property. He argued that the allegations of potential injury were speculative and that the evidence was insufficient to grant an injunction. Dayton maintained that the proposed ditch was necessary for proper land management and that the existing drainage system would not be adversely affected.

The case titled "The Peoria and Farmington Railway Company v. Orlando S. Barnum" was deliberated before the Illinois Supreme Court on June 16, 1883. It involved a petition filed by the Peoria and Farmington Railway Company, a corporation operating under Illinois law, to condemn lands owned by Orlando S. Barnum for the construction of a railway. The proceedings commenced in the county court of Warren County, where a jury was empaneled to assess the necessity for condemning the property. The jury viewed the premises before returning a verdict. Both parties agreed to submit the case for judgment without further evidence or argument, relying solely on the jury's observations and a series of legal instructions provided by the court. The court's decision, subsequently appealed by the railway company, was impacted by the fact that no evidence was recorded during the trial, leading the appellate court to presume the jury's verdict was correct based on what they had witnessed. The emphasis was placed on the jury's unique opportunity to assess the property first-hand, affecting the credibility of the legal arguments made by both sides.	The Peoria and Farmington Railway Company, as the plaintiff, claimed it required additional land for its railway operations and sought a legal ruling to condemn the specific land boundary owned by Barnum. The railway argued that the land was necessary for the overall construction and operation of its railway track, presenting their petition as sufficient to meet legal standards for land condemnation.	Orlando S. Barnum, the defendant, contended against the railway company's petition, arguing that the estimated damages and the manner in which the land would be taken were excessive and not justified. Without providing additional evidence or witnesses, Barnum's legal team focused on contesting the jury's assessment of damages and the instructions given to the jury during the deliberation process, suggesting they may have misinterpreted the law as it applied to their observations.

The case "Sarah Pollock et al. v. Peter Maison et al." revolves around an ejectment action initiated in the Circuit Court of Whitesides County, Illinois, during the October Term of 1861. The plaintiffs, Peter Maison and Augusta Maison, sought to reclaim certain lots (25 and 26 in block 2, and lots 1 and 2 in block 5) located in the town of Conie, Whitesides County, that were originally mortgaged by William Pollock, who had passed away prior to the lawsuit. The key individuals involved include Sarah Pollock, the widow of William Pollock, and Peter Pollock, their heir, who were in possession of the lots. During the trials held in 1862 and 1863, the plaintiffs introduced evidence, including a patent and a mortgage executed by William Pollock, while the defense argued that the mortgage debt was barred by the statute of limitations, thus negating the basis for recovering under the mortgage. The case highlights the legal intricacies surrounding ownership and mortgage rights following the death of an individual and the implications of statutory time limits on claims.	The plaintiffs, Peter and Augusta Maison, claimed rightful possession of the mortgaged property based on their ownership interests as assignees of the mortgage executed by William Pollock. They sought a court judgment to recover the disputed lots, contending that their legal title provided sufficient grounds for ejectment despite the defendants’ claims.	The defendants, Sarah Pollock and Peter Pollock, countered the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that the mortgage debt had been barred by the statute of limitations after nineteen years without any payments or acknowledgment of the debt. They argued that since the underlying debt was no longer enforceable, the plaintiffs could not maintain an action for ejectment based on the mortgage.

In 1882, John Totel filed a bill in the Circuit Court of La Salle County, Illinois, against Esaie Bonnefoy and another, seeking to prevent them from obstructing a ditch that drained surface water from his property into Buck Creek. This case arose from events dating back to 1861 when a ditch was constructed to drain water across the north-west quarter of a section of land then owned by King and occupied by tenant Michael Callahan, with the consent of King. Totel became the owner of part of the south-west quarter and argued he had an established prescriptive easement for the ditch's use. In 1877, a new ditch was dug jointly by Totel, Bonnefoy, and Douvia, which continued to serve the drainage needs until 1882 when it was blocked. The central issues were whether Totel had gained an easement through long usage and whether he had a natural right to the drainage of water. The Circuit Court ruled against Totel, and both the Circuit and Appellate Courts affirmed this decision.	Totel contended that he had a natural and prescriptive easement for the ditch used to drain water from his property. He asserted that the ditch had been used continuously for over twenty years and therefore claimed entitlement to maintain it as his drainage route. Totel sought a court order to prevent obstruction of the ditch, insisting that such use was a long-standing practice recognized under law.	The defendants, Bonnefoy and Douvia, countered Totel's claims by disputing the existence of a prescriptive easement, arguing that the ditch was not used uninterruptedly for the requisite twenty years. They maintained that the prior usage of the old ditch could not be combined with the new ditch's usage to establish a prescriptive right. They also argued that any natural drainage rights did not grant Totel the ability to obstruct their land for his personal drainage needs.

The case "Hector J. Humphrey et al. v. Henry C. Newhall" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court and decided in September 1868. The legal dispute originated in Henry County, involving key individuals Hector J. Humphrey (a non-resident), Henry C. Newhall (the plaintiff), and several other defendants, including Turner, Fandain, Allen, and Peterson. Newhall filed a suit in chancery to foreclose a mortgage that secured a note of $1,750 executed to him by Humphrey and Turner. Humphrey was served by publication due to his non-resident status, while the other defendants were served personally. The Circuit Court appointed Judge Ira O. Wilkinson, who ruled on the matter. When the defendants failed to respond to the complainant's bill, a pro confesso decree was rendered against them, meaning the court accepted the claims as true due to their inaction. Humphrey appealed, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction over him due to the alleged insufficiency of the affidavit supporting the service by publication.	The plaintiff, Henry C. Newhall, claimed that he was entitled to foreclose on the mortgage held against Hector J. Humphrey and other defendants due to their failure to respond to his complaint. Newhall’s legal request was for a decree affirming his right to foreclose the mortgage based on the defendants' default in pleading or answering.	Hector J. Humphrey, as the appellant, contended that the Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction to render a decree against him because the affidavit that supported his service by publication was insufficient. He argued that due to this jurisdictional issue, the decree should be reversed.

In 1846, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with a case involving George Crisman and others as plaintiffs against the People of the State of Illinois as defendants. The issue stemmed from a forfeited recognizance by Charles Crisman, who failed to appear at the Morgan Circuit Court for an indictment on larceny charges. The original recognizance, which included Charles Crisman as the principal and other individuals, including the plaintiffs, as sureties, was properly entered and acknowledged in open court. A writ of scire facias was issued to enforce the forfeited recognizance but was served only on three of the sureties in Scott County. These sureties appeared in court and moved to quash the writ, arguing that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction and that a judgment against them could not be rendered without serving all cognizors. Their motion was denied, leading to a default judgment against them, which prompted the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the circuit court acted improperly by issuing the writ of scire facias to a different county without adequate jurisdiction. They argued that the judgment could not be entered against them as not all cognizors were served with the process, requiring service on all parties for a valid judgment to exist.	The defendants, representing the People of the State of Illinois, contended that the circuit court had jurisdiction to issue the writ and that the scire facias acted as a valid legal process to obtain an execution against the recognizance. They argued that since the recognizance was joint and several, the process could be directed against each surety individually. Moreover, the court maintained that service could be made in any county where any of the defendants resided.

The case "The Niagara Fire Insurance Company v. Ariana E. Scammon, Adm’x" took place in April 1890 in Cook County, Illinois. The appeal concerns a fire insurance policy for $5,000, following the death of J. Young Scammon, who had been the plaintiff in earlier cases. The Circuit Court trial led by Judge Clifford involved a stipulation made in 1886, which stated that the outcomes of various cases involving Scammon should follow the results of his earlier case against the Commercial Union Assurance Company. The loss related to the insured property was reported to be $6,500, and there were issues regarding whether the insurance would still apply after various transactions and claims made against the policy. The court examined evidence regarding an alleged alienation of the property and previous actions under a mortgage connected to it. Ultimately, the court found no error in the Circuit Court's decision denying the appellant's motion for judgment based on the stipulation.	The plaintiff, represented by Ariana E. Scammon as administratrix of J. Young Scammon's estate, sought judgment based on a stipulation that tied the outcomes of multiple insurance claims together. The plaintiff's main argument centered around the assertion that the loss covered by the fire insurance policy in question was valid, despite the defendant's claim that a change in ownership (alienation) of the property voided the policy.	The defendant, The Niagara Fire Insurance Company, argued that the fire insurance policy was no longer in effect due to an alleged alienation of the property insured. They contended that the plaintiff was not entitled to recover on the policy, as ownership had transferred in a manner that breached the terms of the insurance agreement. The defendant requested that the court invalidate the claim based on this argument.

In the case of Jane E. Walton v. George W. Walton et al., filed in July 1872, in Cook County, Illinois, a petition for partition was brought forth by George W. Walton and Thos. H. O. Walton against Jane E. Walton. The case concerns an 80-acre tract of land in Cook County, which was originally owned by Thomas Walton, who passed away intestate in 1843, leaving behind a widow and nine children, including the petitioners and the defendant's husband, Eldridge G. Walton. It is claimed that George W. Walton owns an undivided 18/72, Thos. H. O. Walton 21/72, and Jane E. Walton 33/72 of the land. Eldridge G. Walton conveyed his interest to George W. Walton in 1856 but continued to benefit from the land until his death in 1869. After Eldridge’s death, Jane E. Walton claimed to inherit his interest. The primary dispute centers around whether Thos. H. O. Walton promised Eldridge G. Walton a gift of his share, upon which Eldridge made considerable improvements to the property. The matter was referred to a master, who substantiated the petitioners' claims regarding land ownership, leading to exceptions that were eventually overruled by the court.	The plaintiffs, George W. Walton and Thos. H. O. Walton, claimed that they rightfully own specific undivided interests in the property based on clear titles derived from their deceased father and other heirs. They requested a partition of the land, asserting that Jane E. Walton was improperly claiming an interest based on an unsubstantiated alleged gift.	The defendant, Jane E. Walton, argued that Thos. H. O. Walton had promised to give Eldridge G. Walton his one-ninth interest in the property. She contended that the improvements made by Eldridge were based on this promise, which should grant her an interest in the land. Her argument included that her sworn answer, which contained this claim, should be accepted as true unless disproven by two witnesses.

In September 1874, the case of "The City of Chicago v. Mary A. McCarthy" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident occurred on Sampson Street in Chicago, where Mary A. McCarthy suffered personal injuries due to a fall on a sidewalk that she claimed was defective. At the time of the accident, McCarthy was pregnant and alleged that her fall caused a premature birth of a deceased child. The jury in the Superior Court of Cook County found in favor of McCarthy, awarding her damages of one thousand dollars. The city of Chicago appealed this judgment, arguing that the court erred in refusing to grant a new trial and in denying certain jury instructions. The city contended that the sidewalk was newly constructed, laid only seven days prior, and that there was no evidence of any defect or knowledge of such by the city authorities. The court reviewed the evidence and maintained that the injury was due to McCarthy's lack of ordinary care while walking.	Mary A. McCarthy claimed that her injuries resulted from the negligence of the City of Chicago for allowing a defective sidewalk that caused her to fall. She sought damages for the physical and emotional harm suffered due to this incident, emphasizing the severity of her situation as she was pregnant at the time.	The City of Chicago contended that the sidewalk in question was newly constructed and had been in place for only seven days before the incident, thus no negligence or defective condition could be attributed to the city. They argued that the evidence did not support the jury's verdict since there was no knowledge of a defect and that the fall was primarily due to McCarthy's own negligence. The city requested a reversal of the judgment and a new trial based on these points.

Julia Graham, involved in the management of Graham's Distillery in Rockford, Illinois, entered a contractual agreement with John Eiszner, a cooper based in Chicago, for the supply of barrels suitable for sour mash whisky. This agreement, established on October 24, 1885, was documented in a proposition outlining the terms and prices for the delivery of barrels, half barrels, and kegs for the distillery. Byron Graham, Julia's son, accepted the proposition on behalf of the distillery. The barrels were delivered and accepted, but when payment was not made for twelve promissory notes that were issued corresponding to the contract, Eiszner initiated legal proceedings to recover the amounts due. During the trial, evidence suggested that the barrels leaked, which Julia Graham claimed resulted in significant financial loss of nearly one thousand gallons of whisky. The defense included claims of failure of consideration related to the quality of the barrels. Ultimately, a jury found in favor of Julia Graham for $1,604.23, prompting Eiszner to appeal due to perceived errors in the trial process and pleadings.	Julia Graham argued that she was entitled to recover the amounts due under the twelve promissory notes executed as part of their agreement with Eiszner. She claimed the barrels provided were of poor quality, leading to substantial leakage and financial losses. The plaintiff sought enforcement of the contract and payment for the amounts specified in the notes.	John Eiszner contended that there was a failure of consideration regarding the notes due to the barrels leaking, which he claimed was due to poor workmanship and unseasoned materials. Eiszner sought to introduce evidence concerning an express warranty regarding the barrels, asserting that the written contract did not cover warranties and that parol evidence should clarify this. His defense was that he should not be liable for the losses Graham claimed due to the barrels.

The case "Town of Middleport v. Ætna Life Insurance Company et al." was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1876. The background involves the Town of Middleport, Illinois, which, following a voter-approved proposition on June 8, 1867, voted to appropriate $15,000 as a donation to the Chicago, Danville, and Vincennes Railroad Company to assist in the construction of its railroad within the town's limits. However, actual construction did not commence until spring 1871, and the town officials realized they could not fulfill the donation from the town's funds. Subsequently, in February 1871, they attempted to issue bonds totaling $15,000 plus additional costs to fund this obligation. These bonds were produced, but later surrendered and replaced with different bonds bearing interest. The legality of these bond issuances came into question, principally whether the town officials had the authority to issue such bonds without explicit voter consent or legislative authorization, as well as the compliance of the actions with existing laws and the constitution. The controversy revolved around whether the town officers had the authority to go beyond the method stipulated initially for repaying the appropriation, leading to the legal proceedings initiated by the holders of the bonds against the town.	The plaintiffs, in this case, argued that the bonds issued by the Town of Middleport were valid financial instruments as they were authorized by a vote of the electors and thus should be honored. They contended that since the town had approved the funds in support of the railroad, the issuance of bonds was a legitimate means of fulfilling this commitment. They sought the court to enforce the validity of the bonds and requested that the town be compelled to pay the debt represented by those bonds.	The defendants, representing the Town of Middleport, contended that the bonds were void as they were issued without any legal authority. They argued that the legislature's act only allowed the town to raise the funds through taxation, not through the issuance of bonds. The town officials had exceeded their powers, and since the bonds did not receive valid authorization from the electorate or conform to newly adopted constitutional provisions, the defendants requested the court to declare the bonds invalid and relieve the municipality from any obligations associated with them.

The case "The Village of Hyde Park v. The Oakwoods Cemetery Association" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 14, 1886. The conflict originated in Cook County, Illinois, where the Village of Hyde Park sought to condemn certain lands owned by the Oakwoods Cemetery Association for the purpose of constructing a public street. The cemetery association was incorporated under Illinois law, specifically an act approved on February 12, 1853, that permitted it to own and manage up to 500 acres of land for cemetery purposes, subject to taxation exemptions. Moreover, an amendment in 1867 explicitly stated that no road could be established on cemetery grounds without the consent of its directors. Despite the cemetery lands being generally unused for burial, the Village moved to condemn portions of this land, believing that they had the authority under a 1872 law allowing municipalities to lay out streets. The cemetery association opposed this action, asserting that their lands were protected from such condemnation based on the provisions established at their incorporation. The case remained dormant for several years, with significant action occurring only in December 1885, when a motion was made to dismiss the Village's petition based on an agreed statement of facts.	The Village of Hyde Park argued that it had the legal authority, under applicable statutes, to condemn the cemetery lands for public street purposes and sought to extend its municipal control to the areas desired for development. The Village maintained that the absence of graves or special improvements along the proposed street did not violate the exemption claimed by the cemetery association.	The Oakwoods Cemetery Association contended that the cemetery lands were explicitly exempt from condemnation for any public purpose without their consent, as established in the original charter and subsequent amendments. They relied on the language of the law, asserting that the Village's actions directly conflicted with the protective measures provided by the legislature to preserve the integrity and use of the cemetery grounds.

On February 27, 1886, Stephen Monroe sold a property for $90,000 through real estate brokers Edgar M. Snow and his associates. The case, "Stephen Monroe v. Edgar M. Snow et al.," was brought to the Illinois Appellate Court, with the trial occurring in Cook County. The plaintiff, Monroe, had previously authorized the brokers to sell the property at that price but later contested the commission due to a supposed price change on February 13, 1886, when he allegedly raised the selling price to $100,000. The key individuals involved included the plaintiff Monroe and the brokers Snow, who claimed to have acted under the seller's verbal authority. The central dispute revolved around whether Monroe had indeed authorized the brokers for the $90,000 price and if the price change had occurred.	Monroe, the plaintiff, claimed that he had not agreed to the commission for the sale of his property as he alleged there was a price change made without his consent. He argued that the brokers were not entitled to a commission since they did not have his authority to make a sale at the original price of $90,000 after he purportedly raised it to $100,000.	The defendants, Snow and his associates, contended that they had indeed received Monroe's verbal authorization to sell the property for $90,000 at the meeting on October 31, 1885. They maintained that Monroe's statements and actions corroborated their claim, particularly a letter he sent acknowledging the sale. The defendants argued that there was no error in the trial's proceedings and that sufficient evidence supported their claim to the commission based on their legitimate brokerage agreement.

The legal case 'The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. John C. Stickney, v. John Marshall et al.' was decided in December 1844 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Sangamon County, Illinois, during the July term of 1841. John C. Stickney, acting as a relator for the People of Illinois, brought the case against John Marshall and 21 others, who were associated with the Bank of Illinois at Shawneetown, alleging that they were unlawfully exercising banking franchises not authorized by the state Constitution and laws. The relator sought an order to oust the defendants from performing these banking functions, claiming they had usurped their authority contrary to law. The defendants countered with a plea asserting that their banking activities were authorized by multiple legislative acts, including prior charters confirmed over two decades by the territorial and state legislatures. A demurrer to the defendants' plea was overruled by the circuit court, leading to a judgment in favor of the defendants, which prompted Stickney to appeal, arguing that the legislative acts permitting the bank's operations were unconstitutional. The case raised significant questions concerning the validity of bank charters granted before the Illinois Constitution was adopted and the powers of the legislature concerning existing banks.",	The plaintiff, John C. Stickney, claimed that the defendants were exercising banking franchises illegally. He argued that their authority to operate the Bank of Illinois was not granted by the Constitution or the laws of Illinois. He sought a judgment to oust the defendants from exercising these banking franchises, thereby asserting that their operations were unconstitutional and thus null and void.",	The defendants contended that their operations were legally founded on several acts passed by the Illinois Territory and the State of Illinois that incorporated the Bank of Illinois. They argued that these acts, particularly the 1835 act that extended the bank's charter, were valid and constitutional. They maintained that the legislature had the authority to continue the existence of the bank and to grant modifications, including capital increases, thus asserting their rights under existing laws.",

In the case of "The People, for use of Tirza A. Johnston v. James J. Borders et al.", the legal proceedings stem from events that occurred in St. Clair County, Illinois, during the late 19th century. George W. Guthrie was appointed as guardian to Tirza A. Johnston and her three sisters in 1874. He provided a surety bond in the amount of $40,000 with two sureties, including James J. Borders. Upon Tirza reaching the age of majority on September 23, 1881, Guthrie submitted a final accounting to the County Court, indicating that he owed Tirza $4,298.80. This amount was acknowledged in a receipt signed by Tirza. However, after Guthrie passed away in early 1888, litigation arose against his sureties to recover the owed amount, leading to various defenses presented by the defendants, focusing on claims that the guardian had fulfilled his obligations and had an agreement with Tirza to manage her funds. The case highlighted complex issues of agency, estoppel, and the integrity of the receipt signed under potential misrepresentation.	The plaintiff, representing Tirza A. Johnston, argues that despite the receipt acknowledging payment, no actual funds were transferred from Guthrie to Tirza at the time the receipt was signed. They claim that the guardian procured this receipt under fraudulent pretenses, misinforming Tirza that her signature was necessary for a legal settlement. The plaintiff requests recovery of the funds due from the guardian’s estate, asserting that the sureties should fulfill their obligation as guaranteed by the bond.	The defendants contest the plaintiff's claims by asserting that the receipt signed by Tirza effectively discharged the guardian and the sureties from liability, positing that Tirza had made an agreement with Guthrie to manage her funds. They argue that both the receipt and the court's approval of the final settlement constituted an estoppel, preventing Tirza from later asserting claims of payment owed, as no demand was made for payment during Guthrie's life, nor was there notice given to the sureties after his death.

In 1887, Benson Wood, as the administrator of an estate, brought a case against the Illinois Central Railroad Company in the Illinois Appellate Court. The incident occurred in Effingham County, where Wood's intestate had died due to an explosion of a lamp allegedly caused by the negligence of the railroad company. The plaintiff argued that the railroad failed to provide a safe lamp for its employee to use while performing work that involved removing old paint from railroad cars. During the trial, evidence was presented indicating that the lamp provided was defective and had been improperly repaired, which resulted in an explosion. Testimony from various witnesses, including employees of the railroad, aimed to demonstrate the unsafe condition of the lamp. However, the court instructed the jury to find in favor of the defendant, claiming there was insufficient evidence to support the plaintiff’s claims.	The plaintiff, Benson Wood, claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company acted negligently by providing a lamp that was defective. He sought damages under statute for the death of his intestate, asserting that the explosion resulted from the railroad company's failure to supply a safe workplace environment and equipment for its employees. Wood maintained that the explosion, which led to his intestate's death, was due to the railroad's negligent practices in maintaining their tools and equipment.	The defendant, Illinois Central Railroad Company, argued that there was no evidence to substantiate the claims of negligence. They contended that the explosion was an unavoidable accident and that there were no defects in the lamp at the time of its use. The railroad claimed that the employee handling the lamp was responsible for its condition and usage, and that there was no knowledge of any defect from the railroad's side. The defendant ultimately sought to have the case dismissed, asserting that the evidence presented did not warrant a judgment against them.

C. D. Cook et al. v. Adolphus Miller is a legal case decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on January 6, 1890. The case originated in Jefferson County, Illinois, involving key individuals C. D. Cook, the plaintiff, and Adolphus Miller, the defendant. The dispute arose from a tax sale held on June 8, 1883, where Cook purchased a lot belonging to D. O. Warren for $228, following the issuance of a tax judgment for unpaid taxes. Miller claimed a mortgage interest in the same property, having previously lent money to Warren, and argued that the tax judgment was illegal because it included paid taxes and an unconstitutional tax. He filed a bill to prevent Cook from taking out a tax deed, asserting that this action would significantly harm his mortgage security. After the case was remanded and further proceedings occurred, the case revolved around the validity of the tax judgment and the conflicting rights between Cook and Miller over the property.	The plaintiffs, represented by C. D. Cook, argued that the tax judgment under which they purchased the lot was valid, despite the defendant's claims. They maintained that they bought the property in good faith and sought the enforcement of their tax title. Cook requested that the court validate their tax deed and dismiss Miller's claims, asserting that Miller had not redeemed the property within the necessary time and therefore lost his rights over the lot.	The defendant, Adolphus Miller, asserted that the tax sale was invalid and based on an inaccurate judgment including paid taxes and unconstitutional fees. He claimed that the tax deed Cook sought to obtain would nullify his mortgage rights on the property, resulting in irreparable harm, as Cook's title would serve as a cloud on his mortgage security. Miller requested that the court declare the tax judgment void as it pertained to his mortgage interest and maintain an injunction against Cook from obtaining the tax deed.

In December 1857, an appeal case titled "Lewis B. Chenowith, Appellant, v. James Lockard, Administrator, etc., Appellee" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from the County Court in Coles County, where probate matters were transacted. Lewis B. Chenowith challenged a judgment that had been rendered in this County Court, which was subsequently under review by the Circuit Court. The appeal was based on the proceedings that occurred in the lower courts, with no bill of exceptions taken to indicate the grounds upon which the Circuit Court made its decisions. As a result, the evidence considered during the earlier proceedings was largely the focus, but the absence of specific records limited the basis for the Supreme Court's evaluation of any potential errors made by the lower court. The Chief Justice, Catón, noted the lack of the necessary documentation to contest the findings reached in the lower courts.	The plaintiff, Lewis B. Chenowith, appealed the decision made by the County Court, seeking to overturn the judgment rendered. His claim involved challenging the outcome of probate matters handled by the lower court, although specific details regarding his arguments or legal requests were not provided directly in the summary.	The defendant, James Lockard, who represented the interests of the estate as the Administrator, maintained that the findings of the County Court and Circuit Court should be upheld. Although specific defenses were not detailed, the fact that the appeal did not include a bill of exceptions meant that the Supreme Court could not determine if any errors had occurred in the prior rulings.

The case of John Thomlinson et al. v. Emanuel Earnshaw et al. dates back to 1884 and took place in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Emanuel Earnshaw and others, initiated an action of assumpsit against the defendants, John Thomlinson and others, over an account for stone provided by the plaintiffs from their quarry. The stone was to be used in constructing a courthouse in Washington, Indiana, as per an oral contract. From April 27, 1877, to November 9, 1877, the plaintiffs delivered stone, with a total owed amounting to $7,974.75. The defendants had made partial payments totaling $7,216.39, leaving an unpaid balance of $768.36. At trial, the jury found in favor of the plaintiffs regarding the defendants' plea of set-off, which claimed damages due to the inferior quality of the stone. The jury awarded the plaintiffs a verdict that included interest, resulting in a total of $1,009.27. However, the court later determined that the evidence did not support the allowance of interest due to the lack of a formal liquidation of the account.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were owed a balance of $768.36 for the stone provided under the oral contract. They argued that despite the defendants' claims of receiving inferior quality stone, they were entitled to be paid the remaining amount, as the jury had found against the defendants' set-off plea. The plaintiff's legal requests included a judgment for the unpaid balance and interest due on that amount.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs should not be entitled to the full amount claimed due to the inferior quality of the stone delivered. They asserted a set-off pleading that the quality of the materials led to damages. They requested a dismissal of the plaintiffs’ claims, arguing that the plaintiffs were not entitled to recover the principal amount claimed, nor the alleged interest.

In the case of Orient Insurance Company v. Albert M. Weaver, the events unfolded in Peoria, Illinois. The dispute arose from a fire that occurred on January 31, 1884, which destroyed a stock of merchandise insured under a policy issued by Orient Insurance Company to Weaver. The merchandise, primarily furniture, had been valued at $15,000 despite claims that it was worth significantly less. The key individuals involved included Albert M. Weaver, the insured party, and Aaron Bamberger, who was alleged to be the actual owner of the goods. The circumstances leading to the fire prompted suspicion of fraud, with assertions that Bamberger had set the fire while managing the store predominantly in Weaver's name. Testimonies indicated Bamberger was seen near the premises just before the fire. The trial revealed complications surrounding ownership and authenticity of the claims submitted by Weaver, leading to the insurance company's opposition on grounds of alleged fraud.	The plaintiff, Orient Insurance Company, claimed that Albert M. Weaver had made numerous false representations regarding the insurance policy, including overvaluing the goods and misrepresenting their ownership, location, and the cause of the fire. The insurer alleged that these misrepresentations were fraudulent and made with the intent to defraud the insurance company. They sought to deny the claim based on these fraudulent actions and requested the court to recognize the fraud in Weaver's statements.	Albert M. Weaver defended against the claims by asserting that he was the lawful owner of the goods and that he had not committed fraud. He suggested that any allegations of wrongdoing were unfounded and claimed a right to indemnity under the insurance policy. Weaver argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiff did not establish fraud with the required level of certainty and sought to uphold the original jury verdict in his favor.

Horace Clark was involved in a tragic accident while working as a laborer, hauling wheat from a railroad car using a two-horse wagon in 1873. This incident took place on the tracks of the Chicago and Northwestern Railway in Whiteside County, Illinois. Clark’s team of horses became frightened by an engine that was switching out a train and subsequently backed the wagon, leading to Clark falling and having his arm run over by the engine, which ultimately resulted in his death a couple of days later. Prior to the accident, employees of the railway had cautioned Clark about the dangers of operating his wagon in that area. The situation was further complicated by conflicting testimonies regarding whether Clark had signaled the engineer of the danger. A jury rendered a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, Catharine E. Clark, administering a judgment of $4,408 against the railway company. The case was subsequently appealed, leading to discussions of negligence on both sides.	The plaintiff, Catharine E. Clark, brought the case against the Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company to recover damages for the wrongful death of her husband due to alleged negligence on part of the railway. The plaintiff's main argument centered on the claim that the railway company failed to ensure the safety of the area where the accident occurred. She requested that the jury find the railway company liable despite any minor negligence attributed to Horace Clark, asserting that the railway's negligence significantly exceeded that of her husband and was the immediate cause of his death.	The defendant, the Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company, contended that there was no negligence on their part, arguing that Horace Clark had been warned of the dangers and that he had acted negligently in managing his team. The railway company maintained that any negligence on their part was minimal or non-existent and sought to have the jury instructed on the principle of comparative negligence, asserting that Clark's actions contributed to the accident.

In the case of Matthew Kiely et al. v. J. Clemsen McFarland et al., a legal dispute arose from a judgment issued by the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, on January 16, 1880. The court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, Matthew Kiely and others, against the defendants, J. Clemsen McFarland and others. Following this, an execution was issued on November 29, 1882, based on that judgment. However, during the February term of 1883, the defendants sought to quash the execution and obtained a court order that recalled the execution and stayed further proceedings. This order was controversial and led to an appeal, which was considered timely, as it occurred before a pivotal Supreme Court decision in a related case. The court examining the appeal determined that the lower court's decision was in conflict with established rulings from prior cases, prompting the reversal of the order and subsequent remanding of the case for further action.	The plaintiffs, Kiely et al., argued that the execution issued from the previous judgment should stand as it was legally obtained and in line with related case laws. They contended that the defendants’ action to quash the execution was unfounded and sought to have the execution reinstated, enabling them to pursue the judgment owed to them.	The defendants, McFarland et al., maintained that the order to quash the execution was justified, citing issues related to the judgment being treated as a wholly separate debt not affirmable in bankruptcy proceedings. They likely argued that this separation warranted the recall and stay of execution, thereby seeking the court's validation of their position and the ability to halt proceedings initiated based on the original judgment.

In January 1868, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Matthew McClurken v. Eloise P. McClurken, arising from an action of ejectment in Randolph County, Illinois. The key players involved were Matthew McClurken (the plaintiff), who was seeking to recover possession of a tract of land previously owned by his brother, Thomas McClurken, and Eloise P. McClurken (the appellee), the widow of Thomas. The case revolved around the legality of the ownership and rights to the property. The plaintiff introduced a series of documents establishing his legal title to the land, including a patent from the government and several deeds. Conversely, the defendant claimed possession of the property as a homestead and sought dower rights as Thomas McClurken's widow. The evidence presented included testimonies about the deceased’s use of the land and relevant court documents regarding the estate.	Matthew McClurken argued that he held a legal title to the property, having established this through a chain of title from the government. He contended that the appellee's claims of homestead and dower could not override his superior legal title. The plaintiff requested that the court grant him possession of the land, reversing the previous judgment against him and recognizing his rightful ownership.	Eloise P. McClurken maintained that she had the right to occupy the property under homestead laws and as the widow entitled to dower rights. She presented evidence that her late husband had resided on the property and claimed legal ownership. The defense contended that the plaintiff’s title was flawed and that his acknowledgment of some interest by Thomas McClurken constituted an admission against interest that should prevent him from claiming the property.

In the case of George W. Miller v. Victor K. Glass, the events unfolded in Cook County, Illinois. The situation arises from a legal proceeding that took place on February 12, 1884. The plaintiff, George W. Miller, appealed a judgment by default entered against him in favor of the defendant, Victor K. Glass, on February 23, 1883, which amounted to $1,431 plus costs. The record reveals significant procedural shortcomings; the judgment was made despite the absence of a declaration or any indication of proper service or notice to the defendants in the case. When Miller sought to challenge the judgment, he argued that the court lacked jurisdiction due to the failure to provide notice and proper documentation that outlined a valid cause of action. The appellate court noted that the records did not demonstrate any steps taken by the superior court to re-instate the case or hear it properly following a remanding order from a higher court dated November 23, 1882. Thus, the court examined the procedural integrity that was minimally required to validate the judgment rendered.	George W. Miller claimed that the superior court's judgment against him should be overturned because it was rendered without due process. He argued that the court failed to provide sufficient notice of the judgment and did not establish a proper record of jurisdiction. Specifically, he pointed out the lack of a summons, declaration, or any proof of notice, thereby contesting the legitimacy of the judgment entered against him.	Victor K. Glass defended the judgment by asserting that procedural rules were followed, and he emphasized that a good record was present to support the initial judgment. Glass contended that Miller had not sufficiently challenged the adequacy of the record and implied that Miller's claims were ultimately without merit.

In the case of William H. Broadwell v. David Sanderson, which was decided on November 23, 1888, the legal matter originated in the Circuit Court of Morgan County, Illinois. The case concerned a promissory note that was made payable to the plaintiff, David Sanderson, and was originally signed by W. B. Broadwell, who was the son of the appellant, W. H. Broadwell. The note was executed in California shortly before the dispute arose. The appellant, W. H. Broadwell, was sued alone despite having signed the note. His primary argument revolved around the assertion that there was no consideration for his signature on the note, claiming he signed it only at the request of Sanderson after the money had been disbursed to his son. The trial presented a jury with conflicting evidence regarding whether it was understood at the time of signing that the appellant’s signature would be required as security for the loan made to his son. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him $82,102.66, after the plaintiff remitted $1,000 in response to a motion for a new trial.	The plaintiff, David Sanderson, claimed that W. H. Broadwell was liable under the promissory note for the amount owed, as he had signed it to provide security for his son’s loan. Sanderson argued that the money advanced was intended to be used to settle a debt that W. B. Broadwell owed to his father. The essence of Sanderson's claim was the validity of the promissory note and the obligation of both signatories, asserting that the defendant had indeed agreed to secure the loan through his signature.	W. H. Broadwell, the defendant, mounted a defense based on the assertion of a lack of consideration for his signature on the promissory note. He contended that he signed the note only after the money had already been paid to his son and that there was no initial agreement for him to act as a surety. Broadwell claimed that his signature was not part of the original transaction and thus, should not hold any legal obligation without further consideration.

The case of Joseph Mabley v. Charles D. Irwin et al. took place in 1885, specifically in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Joseph Mabley, the plaintiff, and Charles D. Irwin along with his partners, the defendants. Mabley filed a lawsuit against the defendants, accusing them of misconduct related to their employment as commission men. He alleged that he employed them to act on his behalf in buying and selling grain and that he placed money in their hands for this purpose. However, Mabley claimed that as a result of the defendants' disobedience to his instructions, he suffered financial losses. During the trial, issues arose centered around the admissibility of evidence, particularly concerning the inquiry into whether Mabley had placed money in the defendants' hands. Mabley's attempt to demonstrate the defendants' agency through circumstances and related testimony was met with objections from the defendants, which led to crucial evidence being excluded. Ultimately, the trial court ruled in favor of the defendants, prompting Mabley to appeal for a new trial.	Joseph Mabley contended that he had employed the defendants as commission men to manage his transactions of buying and selling grain. He asserted that he placed money in their control and claimed that their failure to follow his instructions resulted in financial losses. Mabley sought to prove that the defendants were acting as his agents and requested the court to hold them accountable for the lost funds, urging for a judgment in his favor based on their misconduct.	The defendants, Charles D. Irwin et al., maintained that they had not acted improperly and denied any liability for the losses claimed by Mabley. They contested the plaintiff's ability to provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate that he had placed money in their hands or that they had failed to account for it. The defendants requested the court to uphold the original verdict in their favor and argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiff was insufficient and wrongly excluded in the earlier trial.

The case "Louis Bibel v. The People, for use of the City of Bloomington" took place in 1873 in Bloomington, Illinois. The appellant, Louis Bibel, contested a special assessment levied by the city council for paving Center Street with Nicholson pavement. The city council had passed an ordinance under which this special assessment was applied, designating that the expenses might be levied on the properties deemed benefited. However, the procedure was challenged as the ordinance allowed the mayor to select a jury of six freeholders to assess damages rather than the required twelve, and it did not ensure the assessment would reflect the proportional benefits to those properties. Bibel argued that the assessment was illegally conducted and sought to contest its validity in multiple courts, ultimately leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court after the lower courts ruled against him.	The plaintiff, Louis Bibel, argued that the special assessment was void due to several reasons: the assessment process did not comply with the statutory requirement to proportion benefits fairly, the jury that assessed the benefits was improperly constituted by being reduced from the legal number of twelve to six, and the delegation of authority to the mayor for selecting the jury was unauthorized. Bibel requested that the assessment be declared illegal, asserting that due process and proper jurisdiction had not been observed.	The defendant, representing the city, contended that the special assessment had been lawfully conducted under the city charter. They argued that the ordinance was in line with the authority given to the city council to levy such assessments and that the jury process was valid, even if not strictly adhering to the typical jury composition. The defense maintained that there was no legal basis for overturning the assessment and sought to uphold the ruling of the lower courts that favored the city.

John Whittaker v. James Coombs took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, culminating on April 18, 1884. Whittaker, the plaintiff, was employed by Coombs as a common laborer and was tasked with various duties, including unloading cars and filling an ice house. At some point during his employment, the superintendent directed Whittaker to couple cars that were being pushed together by other workers. Despite being inexperienced in this task, Whittaker did not inform the superintendent of his lack of skill. Unfortunately, while attempting to couple the cars, Whittaker's right hand was caught, resulting in the loss of two fingers. Following the injury, he incurred medical expenses totaling $250. The core issue for the court was whether Whittaker’s claim about the carelessness involved and the superintendent's awareness of his inexperience could be substantiated by evidence.	Whittaker claimed that Coombs was negligent by directing him to couple cars despite knowing he was unskilled and inexperienced. He argued that this led to his injury and demanded compensation for medical costs amounting to $250. His legal request centered on the assertion that the injury resulted from the inadequate safety measures imposed by his employer.	Coombs contended that there was insufficient evidence to show that Whittaker was unskilled or that the cars were negligently pushed together. They argued that Whittaker did not inform the superintendent of his inexperience and that he chose to couple the cars from a dangerous position, which was a negligent decision on his part. Coombs maintained that the responsibility for the injury rested with Whittaker due to his failure to disclose his lack of experience and his choice of method in coupling the cars.

In September 1874, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of The City of Chicago v. Mary McGraw, arising from a dispute in Cook County, Illinois. The case centered on a trespass claim brought by Mary McGraw against the City of Chicago for damages to her property caused by the city’s actions related to the Illinois & Michigan canal. The plaintiff's title to the property originated through a series of transactions involving her husband, John McGraw, and their son, Peter J. McGraw. In 1859, John and Mary conveyed the property to Peter, who later reconveyed it back to Mary in 1863. At the time of the alleged injuries and the trial, John McGraw was alive and living with Mary. The defense argued that John was a necessary party to the suit since he originally held the title, questioning the legitimacy of Mary’s claim under the act concerning the separate property of married women. The court examined the nature of the property title and whether the city had a lawful authority in the actions that led to Mary's claim.	Mary McGraw contended that she was the rightful owner of the property, having acquired it in good faith from her son, independent of her husband. She argued that the damages inflicted by the city constituted a trespass against her sole and separate property. Mary highlighted that she had controlled and managed the property exclusively and could pursue the action independently, citing legal precedents that allowed married women to sue for property damages in their name without including their husbands.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant, claimed that the actions leading to the property damage were executed under legitimate authority and therefore should not result in liability. The city stressed that the ordinance and contract relevant to the canal’s modification were not adequately presented in court, undermining Mary McGraw's assertion that the city was responsible. The defense maintained that any project conducted by the city required clear evidence of municipal authorization for liability to apply and argued that such evidence was lacking.

In the case of Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Albert Adler, the incident took place on December 8, 1888, in Joliet, Illinois. The case arose from a tragic event where William Beuck, while driving a horse and buggy westward on Fourth Avenue, was fatally struck by a locomotive of the Denver passenger train operated by the Chicago and Alton Railroad. The crossing of Fourth Avenue and Eastern Avenue, where the accident occurred, faced significant public use, especially due to a nearby exhibition by Barnum's show that attracted many pedestrians.
