The plaintiff, William F. Lynch, argued that he had a rightful claim to the horse purchased from Wickliffe, which was taken by an official under the pretense of being government property. He sought to uphold the initial judgment made by the lower court and maintain the verdict that favored him, representing that Wickliffe was liable for the return of the price of the horse.	The defendant, John B. Wickliffe, contended that the instruction given to the jury regarding the exclusion of evidence from a witness due to his alleged interest was erroneous. Wickliffe argued that the jury should not have the power to disregard testimony deemed competent by the court solely based on the witness's perceived interest in the outcome of the case. He sought a reversal of the lower court's judgment and a new trial to ensure that all evidence was properly considered.

This case, Uri Manly et al. v. Benjamin N. Gibson, was an action of ejectment that took place in December 1851 in Petersburg, Illinois. It involved the trustees of the State Bank of Illinois (the plaintiffs) seeking to recover possession of two specific lots (lots 1 and 2 in Block 66) from Benjamin N. Gibson (the defendant), who had possession of the premises at the time the suit was initiated. The plaintiffs presented various pieces of evidence, including a certificate from the county surveyor asserting that the disputed lots were part of a twenty-acre tract surveyed from the property previously entered by a man named James Estep. The plaintiffs attempted to introduce deeds and a survey to support their claim, but the trial court rejected this evidence due to a failure to present the original plat of the addition in question. This led to a jury verdict in favor of the defendant, Gibson. This decision was later appealed, with the plaintiffs arguing that the exclusion of the evidence was erroneous.	The plaintiffs asserted that they had valid legal claims to the two lots in question based on prior deeds and survey evidence. They argued that the trial court erred in excluding their evidence and contended that the plat of the addition was not a necessary record for establishing the title to the town lots. The plaintiffs requested possession of the lots based on the demonstrated historical evidence of their ownership.	The defendant, Gibson, contended that the plaintiffs failed to present the necessary evidence to support their claim as required by law, specifically challenging the absence of the plat of Taylor’s Addition. Gibson maintained that the evidence presented by the plaintiffs was insufficient and lacked the requisite legal weight, arguing that the jury's verdict in his favor was justified due to the plaintiffs' failure to adequately establish their title.

Henry Allphin filed a legal action against Adam M. Working in 1889, concerning a dispute over unpaid labor for construction work done in Leoti, Kansas. The case arose from Allphin's claim for compensation for various buildings constructed under contracted arrangements with Working. The dispute included complex accounting related to the work performed and payments issued between the two parties. The legal proceedings were held in the Circuit Court of Hancock County, presided over by Judge C. J. Scofield. Both parties were represented by attorneys, with Mack & Son representing the appellant, Working, and O’Hara & Scofield along with W. H. Mead representing the appellee, Allphin. The evidence and accounting records presented in court were extensive, leading to significant labor in investigating the claims, yet the court found a remittitur of $400 to have corrected any prior verdict errors. The court's role was to evaluate the fairness and legality of the disputed amounts based on the agreements made.	Allphin claimed that he was owed payment for labor performed in the construction of several buildings. His primary argument rested on the claim that Working failed to fulfill the financial obligations outlined in their contracts and arrangements. Allphin sought recovery of the unpaid wages totaling $1,062.39.	Working contested the claims, suggesting that there were errors in the verdict amount and accounting associated with the labor performed. His defense involved a remittitur of $400, aimed at reducing the originally claimed amount as inappropriate. Working’s request focused on challenging the judgment made by the lower court while maintaining that the overall verdict was excessive or unjust.

In the case of John M. Stevens v. John E. Hurlburt, which was decided on June 14, 1887, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the conflict arose in Sangamon County, Illinois. The plaintiff, John E. Hurlburt, initiated an action of replevin against the defendant, John M. Stevens, concerning a chattel mortgage. The background reveals that Hurlburt was indebted to one McGuire and sought the suretyship of V. P. Manchester for a $250 note. To secure Manchester, Hurlburt executed a note and a chattel mortgage for the same amount on property in question, dated February 28, 1885. Shortly thereafter, Manchester sold the note and mortgage to Stevens for $160. On December 29 or 30, 1885, Stevens, through a constable, took possession of the mortgaged property. On January 2, 1886, Hurlburt filed the replevin action to recover the property. The case's legal complexities arose from the ability of Manchester's assignee (Stevens) to enforce the mortgage given that Manchester had not paid the debt himself and therefore had no claim. The court had to consider the rights of the original parties under the terms of the mortgage and the assignment.	Hurlburt claimed that Stevens could not maintain the action for replevin due to the fact that his predecessor, Manchester, had not fulfilled the conditions required to enforce the mortgage since he had not paid off the debt for which he was a surety. Accordingly, Hurlburt sought the return of his property, arguing that the mortgage was invalid against him as he had not been damaged and that Stevens, as an assignee, could not claim the property.	Stevens argued that he should be allowed to enforce the mortgage since he had acquired it through a legitimate assignment, and he contended that Hurlburt was estopped from making defenses against the mortgage due to prior conversations implying the transaction was valid. Stevens maintained that the timing of the property’s seizure was not pertinent, asserting his right as an assignee to recover the property and demonstrate that the mortgage was enforceable despite the original mortgage’s context.

The case "Kingman & Company v. Stephen Martin et al." was decided on December 9, 1887, in the Illinois Appellate Court, specifically regarding a contract dispute over the exclusive sale of Strowbridge broadcast seeders. Kingman & Company (the appellant) entered into a written agreement with Stephen Martin and others (the appellees) on October 31, 1885, to sell 400 seeders manufactured by Stephen Freeman & Sons. The total contract price was $1,459.59, of which $125 was acknowledged as paid, leaving a balance due of $1,334.59. The contract included a warranty that guaranteed the exclusive sale of these seeders within a specified territory in Illinois. However, the appellees claimed a breach of this warranty, asserting that a different version of the seeder, manufactured by a third party, was sold in the territory. The lower court allowed the jury to hear evidence regarding this alleged breach, ultimately leading to the jury granting the appellees a set-off of $690 for damages incurred. The appellant contended that allowing such evidence was incorrect as the warranty only applied to the specific machines sold under the contract, and no other Strowbridge seeders were sold within the territorial limits at that time.	The plaintiff, Kingman & Company, argued that the exclusive sales warranty in the contract was breached because different seeders were sold in the agreed territory by the defendants, which led to financial damages. They claimed entitlement to the remaining balance due under the contract and sought damages that were directly related to the breach, as envisioned at the time of contract creation.	The defendants, Stephen Martin et al., contended that the warranty was violated by the sale of inferior seeders made by a different manufacturer within the exclusive territory. They argued that the sales of these alternative machines undercut the exclusive nature of their contract, leading to their claimed damages as a valid set-off against the sums owed. They requested that the jury's decision affirm the damages awarded for the breach.

The case involves Charles Gretzner as the plaintiff against the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company in 1867, in Chicago, Illinois. Gretzner was injured in a collision between a train operated by the railroad company and his wagon at a street crossing. The plaintiff's allegations were centered around the negligence of the railroad, claiming that the train was operating at an excessive speed and that a flagman was not stationed at the crossing to warn of the train’s approach. Initially, a jury ruled in favor of Gretzner, awarding him $7,500 in damages. However, the defendant contended that their actions were not negligent and presented evidence that the bell was rung continuously prior to the collision and that a flagman was present, contradicting the plaintiff's claims.	The plaintiff, Charles Gretzner, contended that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was negligent in the operation of their train, leading to the collision that caused his serious injuries. His claims included the failure to have a flagman present at the crossing and the operation of the train at an unsafe speed. He sought damages for the injuries sustained from the accident.	The defendant, Chicago and Alton Railroad Company, argued that they were not negligent, as they had followed appropriate safety protocols including ringing the bell continuously and having the flagman present at the crossing. They asserted that the evidence strongly favored their defense, emphasizing that the conduct of the plaintiff contributed significantly to the incident due to his lack of caution while approaching the crossing.

In the case of Jackson Johnson et al. v. Elisha Lawson, heard by the Illinois Appellate Court on September 21, 1888, the conflict arises from a promissory note for $570.40 executed by the plaintiffs, Jackson Johnson and William Johnson, to the defendant, Elisha Lawson, on March 20, 1886. The dispute centers on an earlier transaction involving John Johnson, the brother of Jackson Johnson, who purchased 40 acres of land from a party named Dawson. John Johnson had given a note for $1,067.66, supported by Jackson and Isaac Johnson as sureties. The agreement purportedly included the provision that John Johnson would secure these sureties with a mortgage on the land. The plaintiffs allege that Lawson falsely claimed not to hold a mortgage on the property, misleading Jackson Johnson and preventing him from investigating the land records. This alleged deception led to the execution of the note in question. The plaintiffs argued that Lawson's fraudulent statements constituted grounds for defense against the note. The circuit court heard the case, but the plaintiffs’ ability to present evidence regarding Lawson’s misrepresentation was restricted, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiffs, Jackson Johnson and William Johnson, claim that the execution of the note was secured through Lawson's fraudulent representations regarding the absence of a mortgage on the land in question. They argue that these false statements misled them into signing the note, as they relied on Lawson's assurance that there were no liens on the property, contrary to the reality. Their main legal request is to have the court recognize this fraud as a defense against their obligation under the promissory note.	Elisha Lawson, the defendant, counters the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that they willingly executed the note without reliance on any misrepresentations. Lawson argues that the note was given in exchange for a legal compromise regarding the earlier note issued to Dawson and that any potential misstatement should not void the obligation if the plaintiffs held a broader understanding of the circumstances. His request is essentially to uphold the validity of the promissory note and dismiss the fraud claims.

Irwin Z. Smith initiated a legal action against The Chicago, Alton and St. Louis Railroad Company in Madison County, Illinois, in early January 1873, seeking recovery of a tract of land situated in the American bottom, near St. Louis. This land was allegedly occupied by the defendant as part of their railroad track. The case experienced several trials: the initial trial concluded with a verdict favoring Smith, but subsequent trials resulted in decisions favoring the defendants. Each verdict led to appeals and motions for retrials, primarily examining the lawfulness of the defendants’ possession of the land, which Smith argued had never been legally condemned or lawfully obtained. The railroad company claimed possession through prior condemnation proceedings initiated by another railroad entity, which were later found invalid due to improper notification about ownership during the condemnation process. Ultimately, the court deliberated on whether ejectment, a legal action for dispossession, could be pursued given the circumstances surrounding the condemnation and possession.	Smith claimed he was the rightful owner of the land in question through valid conveyances from the United States, asserting that the railroad company’s possession was unlawful as it had failed to execute proper condemnation proceedings. He sought to recover possession of the property through ejectment, arguing that he had a legal entitlement to reclaim his land due to the defendants' continuous wrongful occupation.	The defendant, represented by the railroad company, argued that their possession of the land could not be legally contested via ejectment, citing their occupation under the belief that they had a right to do so through previous condemnation proceedings. They contended that the plaintiff had no grounds to reclaim the land as they were utilizing it for public use, which should afford them immunity from ejectment claims. They maintained that the proper remedy for disputes over condemnation should be through mandamus, compelling the company to establish legal possession rather than an ejectment action.

In September 1876, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed a dispute between John P. Lewis and others, collectively known as the plaintiffs, and Alonzo Rose, the defendant, concerning the possession of a specific property—lot 8 in block 2, situated in the city of Dunleith, Illinois. The case stemmed from an action of ejectment, where the plaintiffs sought to recover possession of the property they claimed title to via mesne conveyances from Simon E. Lewis. The defendant, Alonzo Rose, asserted his claim through a judgment rendered in a previous mechanic’s lien case in 1858 involving the same property, linking his claim to a debt incurred by Taylor S. Graham, the defendant in the prior case. The initial verdict favored Rose, establishing that if the findings on the legality of the previous judgment and sale of the land were sound, then the plaintiffs could not establish their title. The legal proceedings involved complex interactions regarding the rightful ownership and obligations stemming from the mechanic's lien laws, wherein Graham had been determined to have a questionable title barring significant equitable rights. The Circuit Court's decision, which had been previously ruled on, surfaced again as the basis of whether Lewis and Rose could assert their claimed interests over the disputed property.	The plaintiffs, led by John P. Lewis, argued that they held rightful title to the property based on their deed from Simon E. Lewis. They requested the court to recognize their title and grant them possession of the property. Their claims rested on the assertion that the prior judgment against Graham did not sufficiently divest Lewis of his title, thus maintaining the legitimacy of their claim for ejectment.	The defendant, Alonzo Rose, contended that he held title to the property through a legitimate judicial sale following a mechanic’s lien ruling against Graham. He argued that the court's previous findings established that Lewis had no actual or equitable claim to the property, thus invalidating the plaintiffs' claim. Rose maintained that the prior judgment and sheriff's sale effectively transferred any interest Lewis may have had, and requested the court to uphold the Circuit Court’s ruling in his favor.

The legal case titled "The South Park Commissioners v. Samuel E. Todd" took place in 1884 in Cook County, Illinois. The background of the case involves Mary E. Pierce, who, on October 17, 1870, mortgaged two lots and a third lot in her subdivision to secure a loan. The mortgage was handled by Harvey B. Hurd, who was acting as both the attorney for Todd, the mortgagee, and the agent attempting to sell the lots on behalf of Pierce. The South Park Commissioners initiated condemnation proceedings against the lots for park purposes without notifying Hurd or Pierce, who were unaware until after the commissioners had issued their report. During this time, a claim for compensation was made by Edward L. Baker, representing an unrelated party, which was ultimately allowed by the commissioners. Todd contested this claim, asserting that the money should have been paid to him due to his secured interest in the property from the mortgage. The case raised questions about the lawfulness of the commissioners' authority in distributing condemnation money in situations where the rightful owner is non-resident or unknown.	The plaintiff, Samuel E. Todd, argued that the South Park Commissioners unlawfully paid condemnation compensation to Edward L. Baker without recognizing his rights as the mortgagee. He claimed that under Illinois law, when the owner of the property is a non-resident, as both he and Pierce were, the compensation should have been paid into the county treasury for the rightful owner. Todd sought reimbursement of the $1,670 that he claimed was wrongly paid to Baker as it undermined his legal rights concerning the mortgage.	The South Park Commissioners defended their actions by arguing that Todd had not proven his interest in the property sufficiently, particularly concerning the specific lot involved, which had been incorrectly described in the documentation. They contended that they were justified in the payment to Baker based on their understanding at the time. Additionally, they argued that the legal title was not adequately established in court, which complicated ownership claims.

The case "Merritt L. Joslyn v. Frederick Collinson" dates back to April 1861 and takes place in Woodstock, McHenry County, Illinois. The key individuals involved are Merritt L. Joslyn, the plaintiff, and Frederick Collinson, the defendant. The case arises from a dispute over a promissory note that was issued by W. W. Paine on September 20, 1857. This note promised to pay $130 to L. W. Baldwin nine months later, with interest. Baldwin subsequently indorsed the note to Joslyn, the plaintiff. Collinson provided a guarantee for the payment on the back of the note, stating he would pay the amount due. When a legal action was initiated by Joslyn against Collinson to enforce this guarantee, the court initially ruled in favor of Joslyn after rejecting Collinson's general demurrer. However, the case hinged on the nature of the guarantee as either part of the original transaction or a subsequent independent commitment, which necessitated new consideration. Ultimately, the case raised important questions about the validity of guarantees and the necessary legal principles underpinning them.	The plaintiff's primary contention was centered around the enforceability of Collinson's guarantee on the promissory note. Joslyn claimed that Collinson had guaranteed the payment of the note, making him liable for the amount due when Paine defaulted. The plaintiff argued that the court should uphold the enforceable agreement and allow recovery of the amount stated in the note, plus interest. Joslyn sought the court’s affirmation of this guarantee as a valid binding obligation.	The defendant, Collinson, argued that the guarantee he provided was entered into after the original promissory note had already been executed and negotiated. He contended that because the guarantee was a subsequent agreement, it lacked the new consideration necessary for its validity. Collinson maintained that the threshold legal requirements to support such a guarantee had not been met, and thus, Joslyn's action was invalid. He requested that the court dismiss the judgment favoring the plaintiff.

In February 1886, the case of Fisher v. Phillips was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute originated over a rental agreement involving the late Albert T. Phillips and the appellant, Fisher. After Phillips’ death, his widow and nephew, now holding the title to the property, pursued the case against Fisher for unpaid rent. Fisher claimed that a release of the rent obligation had been agreed upon, asserting that this release was part of a settlement related to alleged slanderous statements made by Phillips regarding Fisher. The plaintiffs countered that the release was invalid due to lack of consideration and was instead connected to an agreement that prevented Fisher from prosecuting Phillips for criminal charges regarding property tax listing. Phillips had left Illinois for Kansas due to fears of criminal prosecution, and the arrangement was made by his wife, who paid Fisher $100 to relieve the rent obligation and avoid prosecution. The case was heard by a jury which delivered a verdict in favor of the plaintiffs, determining that the release lacked valid consideration.	The plaintiffs asserted that the alleged release of rent by Fisher was void due to a lack of consideration. They argued that the arrangement was not about settling a slander claim but was made in exchange for Fisher's agreement not to prosecute Phillips for failing to list his property for taxation. They maintained that the rent was still owed and that the defendant’s claims were without legal foundation.	The defendant, Fisher, contended that a valid release had been agreed upon, which discharged him from the obligation to pay rent. He argued that this release was part of a settlement regarding slanderous remarks made by Phillips. Fisher emphasized that the payment of $100, made by Phillips's wife, constituted valid consideration for the release of the rent.

In 1864, in Hancock County, Illinois, William Bostick was indicted for assault with a deadly weapon. He was initially recognized by a justice of the peace to appear in court with his sureties, including Samuel R. Combs. Bostick failed to appear at the next court term, leading to the issuance of another recognizance in which Combs was the sole surety for Bostick's appearance at the May 1865 term. Once again, Bostick did not fulfill his obligations, resulting in the court declaring his recognizance forfeited, but Combs' recognizance remained intact. On June 12, 1865, a scire facias was issued against both Bostick and Combs to explain why the forfeiture should not be made absolute. Combs challenged the validity of his recognizance, claiming it was void; however, the court rejected this motion and awarded execution against Combs. The case subsequently went to appeal, questioning the validity of the recognizance entered into by Combs alone, and the appropriateness of the resulting judgment against him.	The plaintiff, representing the People of the State of Illinois, argued that Combs, as the surety, was liable for the amount of the recognizance due to Bostick's failure to appear in court. They maintained that the execution against Combs was justified since he had entered into a second recognizance to ensure Bostick's appearance.	Combs contended that the second recognizance was void because it was entered into solely by him without Bostick's participation. He argued that since he had not been defaulted and there was no forfeiture against his original recognizance, the court lacked the authority to enter judgment and award execution against him. Combs maintained that his actions were intended to prevent the forfeiture of the initial bond related to Bostick.

In 1887, Minnie Lowentrout and her husband, along with partner Shansten, were subcontractors for the Lake Erie & Western Railroad in Bloomington, Illinois. Facing financial difficulties, they abandoned their unprofitable contract, with chief contractor Eager stepping in to finish the work. By July 1887, most workers quit due to unpaid wages for June and July, and a separate claim was made by Harber & Co. for equipment provided. In June 1887, Lowentrout transferred ownership of several lots, including one purchased for $3,000 in 1880 from Miller and previously deeded to his wife, to her for a nominal price of one dollar. Creditors of Lowentrout & Shansten, who had secured judgments for unpaid debts, filed a chancery suit to set aside this transfer, alleging it was fraudulent. The court's examination revealed that regardless of who originally financed the property, it was formally titled in the husband's name for the purpose of enhancing his creditworthiness, ultimately determining that the transfer was made with a fraudulent intent.	The plaintiffs, creditors of Lowentrout & Shansten, claimed that the conveyance of property from Lowentrout to his wife was fraudulent and aimed to evade obligations to settle debts. They sought judicial intervention to set aside the transfer, asserting that it should be deemed void to protect their interests as creditors.	The defendants argued that the property conveyed to Mrs. Lowentrout rightfully belonged to her and contested the assertion of fraudulent intent behind the transfer. They maintained that the transfer was legitimate, denying any intent to defraud existing creditors, and sought to validate the conveyance based on the original ownership and financial contributions of Mrs. Lowentrout.

ASAHEL GAGE v. JOHN H. NICHOLS is a legal case decided on September 27, 1884, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The background of the case revolves around a tax sale that occurred on September 18, 1873, concerning several lots in Cook County, Illinois. The complainant initially, George Rose, sought to set aside the tax sale of these lots, arguing that the assessor did not return his assessment book by the legal deadline of July 1, 1872. This late filing, along with alleged irregularities in the levy and certification processes of the taxes, underpinned the complaint. Despite the tax sale being challenged on these grounds, it was noted that the complainant did not raise issues of substantial justice regarding the taxes owed. Instead, the focus was on procedural errors. The court ultimately ruled in favor of setting aside the sale, but this decision was contested by the appellant, Asahel Gage, who argued that the relief was improperly granted without requiring the complainant to reimburse the amount he paid for the property plus six percent interest. The legal principle, "he that seeks equity must do equity," was central to the case, leading to significant discussion on the fairness of the judgment based on the refund of taxes paid.	The plaintiff, John H. Nichols, claimed that the tax sale should be set aside as it was a cloud on his title. He argued that the assessors had failed to comply with legal requirements regarding the assessment and levy of taxes, including not returning the assessment book on time and irregularities in tax certification. He sought to nullify the tax title and prevent the appellant from obtaining a tax deed for the lots, asserting that these procedural missteps were sufficient grounds for the court to intervene.	The defendant, Asahel Gage, contended that the court erred by granting the relief to the plaintiff without requiring him to reimburse the purchase price of the property, along with interest. Gage maintained that while there might have been procedural irregularities, they did not affect the substantive merits of the tax itself. He argued that the court's decision to set aside the tax sale unconditionally was a violation of established legal principles requiring equity to be granted equitably.

In the case of Hester A. Tewes et al. v. A. E. Harmon, heard by the Illinois Appellate Court, the legal dispute arose from costs related to witness fees in a case that was tried twice in the Circuit Court of Champaign County, Illinois, presided over by Judge C. B. Smith. During these trials, several witnesses were subpoenaed and present but were not called to testify. Following the trials, the defendant in error (A. E. Harmon) filed a motion to retax the costs, arguing that they should not be responsible for the fees of witnesses that were brought to court but ultimately not used. An affidavit was submitted as evidence to support this motion. The court initially allowed the motion to retax costs based on the argument that the plaintiff had unnecessary witnesses. The key legal issue revolved around whether the court had the authority to limit witness fees after the clerk had prepared the fee bill. This situation prompted the appellate review to clarify the application of statutory provisions regarding witness fees and costs.	The plaintiff's main arguments rested on the assertion that the defendant should bear the costs of all witnesses summoned to court. They contended that the presence of the witnesses was crucial, even if they were not ultimately called to testify, and that denying costs for those witnesses would undermine the legal process. The plaintiffs sought to reverse the prior ruling that favored the defendant's request to retax the costs.	The defendant's key argument was grounded in the claim that the costs associated with several witnesses who were not called to testify should not be charged against him, as these were unnecessary expenses. He asserted that the court had improperly allowed costs for witnesses who were present merely for potential testimony that was later deemed unnecessary. The defendant requested the appellate court’s affirmation of the trial court's decision to retax the costs and thus relieve him from paying for the unused witnesses.

Thomas Coates was involved in a criminal case with the People of the State of Illinois, culminating in a judgment by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1874. The incident took place in Cook County, Illinois, where Coates and two other individuals were indicted for murder. The specific contention was regarding the ambiguity of the indictment, which asserted that all three individuals inflicted a mortal wound using a stick of wood, each holding it with their right hand. A motion to quash the indictment was overruled, and Coates subsequently entered a plea of guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter. The court sentenced him to ten years in the penitentiary.  During the proceedings, the main argument raised by the defense relied on the premise that the indictment was physically impossible. However, the court rejected this view, stating that it is not implausible for multiple individuals to hold the same stick simultaneously while inflicting harm. As per Illinois statute, all accessories to a crime are charged as principals, establishing the legal framework supporting the indictment’s validity. Furthermore, the court addressed potential jurisdictional issues regarding the length of the sentencing for manslaughter and confirmed the court’s authority to impose a sentence of greater length than traditionally expected.	The plaintiff, represented by Mr. Vah Buren Denslow, contended that the indictment for murder was void due to its ambiguity. Coates claimed that the suggestion of multiple individuals being implicated in the act of murder with a single stick was physically improbable and should negate the charges against them. The legal requests primarily revolved around quashing the indictment based on these arguments and subsequently seeking a lighter sentencing upon pleading guilty to manslaughter.	The defense, articulated by Mr. James K. Edsall, countered that the indictment correctly held all accused parties as principals. They argued that the act described in the indictment was not physically impossible, as it is conceivable for three individuals to strike with a stick held together. Additionally, they asserted that the court had the jurisdictional authority to impose a sentence up to ten years for manslaughter, as confirmed by prior legal precedents and statutes, establishing the validity of their actions in sentencing.

The case of "The People ex rel. Frederick Ropiequet v. Owners of Lands" took place in Illinois, specifically in St. Clair County, with the court decision filed on January 22, 1884. The case arose when the collector of taxes in St. Clair County sought a court order to sell lands and town lots due to delinquent taxes from 1881 and prior years. During a hearing regarding the tax assessments, no objections were filed against the notice of sale; instead, the defendants claimed that only state and county taxes could be levied. The court learned that the parties were present through their attorneys, and the tax collector provided evidence of publication and a corrected list of delinquent properties. Ultimately, it was found that due to the parties' consent, the court could only render judgment concerning the state and county taxes, as the objections regarding other tax amounts were sustained by agreement. This precluded any appeal or reversal of the judgment made by consent.	The plaintiff, represented by Frederick Ropiequet, sought to enforce the collection of delinquent state and county taxes owed on certain lands and lots. The primary argument was that the taxes were due and that the court should order the sale of the properties to satisfy these debts. The plaintiff contended that the objections raised concerning other types of taxes were valid and should be upheld.	The defendants contested the authority to levy taxes beyond state and county taxes, indicating a limitation on the tax collector's ability to claim additional amounts. They relied on the collective agreement during the proceedings to assert that their objections regarding non-state and county taxes were valid and should be recognized, thereby contending that the court should limit any judgment to only the amounts claimed for state and county taxes.

In 1888, E. Emrich, located in Fairfield, Illinois, shipped a box of clothing marked for Freehold, New Jersey, consigned to his brother. The Ohio & Mississippi Railroad Company, the appellant in this case, was responsible for transporting the goods. Upon shipment, Emrich received a receipt with the stipulation that the railroad's responsibility would end once the goods were delivered to the next carrier. The box was ultimately lost, and Emrich sought $100 in damages. The primary dispute was whether Emrich, as the shipper, had the standing to sue despite the implied presumption of ownership lying with the consignee. The court concluded that the relationship established between Emrich and the railroad permitted him to pursue the claim, even absent formal ownership proof. The trial revealed evidence indicating that the box never reached its intended destination, prompting Emrich's inquiry into its whereabouts, which confirmed the loss. The appellants attempted to show that they had delivered the goods to a connecting line, but evidence supporting this claim was deemed insufficient.	The plaintiff, E. Emrich, argued that he was entitled to recover damages for the loss of the goods during their transportation by the Ohio & Mississippi Railroad Company. Emrich maintained that the contract for shipping was with him as the consignor, allowing him to sue for breach of contract and seek compensation for the loss of his goods. He asserted that there was enough evidence to establish his ownership and prove the railroad's liability for failing to deliver the box to its destination.	The defendant, Ohio & Mississippi Railroad Company, contended that Emrich could not maintain this action as he was merely the shipper and needed to prove ownership of the goods. They argued that, based on the terms outlined in the receipt, their responsibility only extended to delivering the goods to a connection in Cincinnati, Ohio, not to the final destination in New Jersey. The railroad claimed that the loss of the box did not establish liability without clear evidence of failure to deliver to the next carrier.

In 1884, Artemas D. Watson and Eda Watson entered into a deed in Chicago, transferring property inherited by Artemas from his father to his mother, Catharine Watson. Eda, who was recently married to Artemas, claimed that she was misled into signing the deed, believing it was paperwork for her husband's father's estate, without understanding its actual content. Evidence presented during the case suggested tension between Eda and her mother-in-law and a potential intent by Artemas and Catharine to induce an abortion, which Eda asserted affected her state of mind. However, this information was deemed irrelevant to the case's core issue. The deed was formally executed and acknowledged before a notary public, who verified that Eda had signed it voluntarily. The central question in the case was whether Eda could dispute the deed’s validity based solely on her testimony, which was contradicted by Artemas.	Eda Watson sought to have the deed set aside, arguing that she had been a victim of fraud and misrepresentation by her husband, Artemas. She claimed that she had not read the deed or had it read to her and that she was led to believe it was simply a document to settle her husband's father’s estate. Eda requested the court to nullify the deed based on these allegations of deceit.	Artemas Watson defended against Eda's claims by asserting that she was indeed informed about the deed and its implications before signing. He testified that he had asked her multiple times to sign the deed and clarified its purpose. He contended that Eda was an intelligent individual capable of understanding the document, and therefore her claims of ignorance should be dismissed. He sought to uphold the deed's validity and claimed that Eda's testimony alone was insufficient to negate the acknowledged deed.

In December 1853, the case of Charles W. Hunter v. George H. Silvers was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from an action of wilful detainer where Hunter sought to reclaim possession of a property located at the corner of Second and Walnut streets in Alton, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Charles W. Hunter, the plaintiff, and George H. Silvers, the defendant. The matter stems from an initial lease agreement executed between Hunter and Silvers in April 1852, which granted Silvers occupancy of the property for one year. After the lease expired, Hunter requested Silvers to vacate the premises, supported by a written notice delivered in April 1853. Despite this, Silvers remained in possession, leading to a series of court proceedings wherein both the local justice and the Madison Circuit Court ruled in favor of Silvers. The case evaluation hinged on the interpretation of a bond related to the lease agreements, which included conditions about renewal and purchase rights but left ambiguities regarding an actual lease’s enforceability beyond the original year.	Hunter argued that Silvers had a legal obligation to vacate the property at the end of the one-year lease as stipulated in the lease agreements. He sought legal possession of the property, claiming that Silvers, despite being given proper notice, refused to surrender possession. Hunter emphasized that nothing in the bond or lease allowed Silvers to remain past the lease term without a valid renewal.	Silvers contended that the bond signed by Hunter granted him privileges that effectively extended his lease beyond the initial term. He asserted that the bond included a provision for renewal for up to five additional years and a right to purchase the property, which should be considered as legal grounds for his continued possession. Silvers maintained he had complied with payment obligations and sought recognition of the bond's terms that prevented Hunter from reclaiming possession unilaterally.

The case "Letcher v. Morrison" arose from events in Madison County, Illinois, involving a dispute over property deeds and fraudulent conveyances related to a judgment obtained by Edward Norton against James Duncan in April 1842. Duncan, allegedly with the intent to defraud Norton, conveyed land to Isaac A. Letcher in December 1841 for $3,225, a transaction which the plaintiffs claimed lacked genuine consideration. Following Duncan's death in 1846, Letcher further conveyed a portion of this land to John Duncan, James's brother, also as part of a supposed conspiracy to hide assets from Norton. The plaintiffs contended that these transactions were fraudulent and aimed to obstruct the collection of the judgment owed to Norton. Over time, the case escalated, leading to a series of legal actions and sales of the disputed properties. Norton eventually sought legal redress to void the fraudulent transfers and to claim the properties in question.	The plaintiffs, Isaac A. Letcher and William Hadley, asserted that the conveyances from James Duncan to Letcher and subsequently to John Duncan were fraudulent and intended to defraud the judgment creditor, Edward Norton. They maintained that true ownership of the land should remain with Norton and that no valid consideration was transferred in the transactions. They requested a court ruling to annul the fraudulent deeds and restore title of the land to themselves, as well as the recovery of legal costs.	The defendant, James L. D. Morrison, countered that the conveyances were genuine and lawful, asserting that Letcher had paid adequate consideration for the property. Morrison claimed that he had no knowledge of any fraudulent intent behind the conveyances and considered himself a bona fide purchaser of the land with legitimate dealings. He requested that the court uphold the validity of the transactions and dismiss the complaints of fraud against him.

In December 1855, at Bement station in Piatt County, Illinois, Griffin M. Bruffett and others (the plaintiffs) entered into a contract with the Great Western Railroad Company to transport 2,000 hogs from Bement to Chicago. The railroad company failed to fulfill this contract, leading the plaintiffs to suffer damages amounting to $2,000. The case escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court following the trial court's decision in favor of the defendant, the Great Western Railroad Company of 1859. The plaintiffs contended that the defendant was liable due to its claim of reincorporation, asserting that a legislative act from January 22, 1859, which created the "Great Western Railroad Company of 1859," was merely a change of name rather than a separate entity. The core concern revolved around whether the new corporation was the same entity as the original railroad company responsible for the contract.	The plaintiffs argued that the recent legislative act was a mere reincorporation of the earlier Great Western Railroad Company and that it retained liability for contracts made by the previous incarnation. They contended that the turnover of rights and properties to a different company did not absolve the Great Western Railroad Company from its obligations under the contract to transport their hogs. They sought a judgment for the $2,000 in damages due to the defendant's breach of contract.	The defendant maintained that the act of the 22nd of January, 1859, effectively established a new corporate entity that did not inherit liabilities from the previous Great Western Railroad Company. They argued that no judicial forfeiture occurred, and that any obligations incurred by the old company could not be transferred or assumed by the new one without explicit legal authorization. The defendant requested that the court affirm the lower court's judgment in their favor.

Randolph Updike, the appellant, filed a legal action against George W. Henry, the appellee, in the Kane Circuit Court of Illinois during the November term of 1852. The case revolved around a contract in which Henry agreed to manufacture three lumber wagons for Updike within a specified timeframe. However, a dispute arose regarding the ownership of the wagons upon their completion. Updike claimed that he had rights to the wagons; yet, Henry had not delivered or designated them for Updike's use at the time of the dispute. As a result, Updike initiated a replevin action, which is a legal recovery of property. The trial concluded with the circuit court ruling in favor of Henry, leading Updike to appeal the decision.	Updike argued that the completion of the three lumber wagons should vest ownership in him, thereby warranting a replevin action to reclaim the property. He contended that he had paid for the wagons in advance and claimed the right to retrieve them based on the contractual agreement.	Henry contended that no title to the wagons transferred to Updike upon their completion, as the wagons had never been delivered or specifically designated for him. He asserted that Updike's remedy lay in seeking damages for breach of contract rather than pursuing a replevin action. Henry also argued that the absence of a witness to support Updike's claims warranted the refusal of a continuance.

John V. Farwell & Co. brought a replevin action against Seth F. Hanchett and others to reclaim certain dry goods alleged to have been fraudulently purchased by Simon Heller. The events unfolded in Chicago, Illinois, where Simon Heller, claiming to be financially sound, misled Farwell & Co. regarding his financial status to obtain credit, despite being insolvent at the time of his purchases. Heller had signed a statement in April 1882 detailing his purported financial circumstances to gain credit for future goods. However, by December 1884, he accrued debts exceeding four thousand dollars to Farwell & Co. and executed a note for $550 regarding this debt. During the trial, there were disputes over the ownership of the goods and the validity of Heller's earlier financial claims. The defendants contended that the plaintiffs did not adequately demand the goods, which were under the sheriff's possession at that time due to an execution against Heller.	The plaintiffs claimed that the dry goods in question were purchased through Simon Heller’s false financial representations, alleging fraudulent behavior and asserting the right to reclaim the goods through replevin. They requested that the court recognize their ownership and entitlement to the goods since the sale was based on deceit.	The defendants, including Hanchett, countered the claims by arguing that the plaintiffs did not prove ownership of the goods since the items were in the possession of the sheriff via an execution against Simon Heller. They also contended that the plaintiffs failed to make a formal demand for the goods before initiating the lawsuit, which is essential in such cases unless the contract is rescinded.

The case "James H. Gaff v. Alfred E. Harding" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1872. It originated in the Livingston Circuit Court and involved a dispute over a chattel mortgage and a replevin action. The key individuals involved included the plaintiff Alfred E. Harding, who held a chattel mortgage on certain property to secure a bona fide debt, and the defendant, sheriff James H. Gaff, who was in possession of the property at the time it was levied upon due to an execution against the mortgagor, Dodwell. When Dodwell failed to settle the execution debt, Harding communicated with Gaff to clarify his rights concerning the property. They reached an agreement that Gaff would consider the property under his actual possession for the purposes of the replevin suit. When Harding demanded the property, Gaff refused to relinquish it, leading Harding to file the replevin suit to recover the property.	Alfred E. Harding claimed that he had a legitimate chattel mortgage on the property and that he had the right to replevy it under the circumstances when he notified the sheriff of his intention. Harding argued that Gaff was estopped from denying possession of the property since Gaff had agreed to treat the property as being in his control for the purpose of the lawsuit. Consequently, Harding sought to have the court rule in his favor and return the property to him.	Sheriff James H. Gaff contended that the property was not in the actual possession of Harding at the time of the demand. Gaff’s key argument was that the agreement with Harding did not grant Harding the legal standing to reclaim the property through a replevin action since the property was still under his custody due to the execution levy. Gaff's position was based on his interpretation of the situation leading up to the replevin suit.

The case "The Town of Talkington v. Robert Bullard" took place in May 1888 in Sangamon County, Illinois. The case was initiated when the Town of Talkington filed a suit against Robert Bullard, seeking a penalty for allegedly obstructing what the town claimed to be a public highway. The dispute revolved around whether there had been a dedication and acceptance of the area in question as a public highway. The evidence presented in court was conflicting, leading to two separate juries ultimately ruling in favor of Bullard. The Town of Talkington contended that the obstruction warranted a penalty, but the outcome was challenged based on the jury's findings and the instructions provided by the court to the juries.	The Town of Talkington claimed that Robert Bullard had obstructed a public highway, which warranted the imposition of a penalty for the alleged infraction. The town argued that an official dedication and subsequent acceptance of the roadway as a public highway had occurred, thus making Bullard liable for any obstructions he caused.	Robert Bullard defended against the claims by asserting that there had been no formal dedication or acceptance of the roadway as a public highway. He argued that the evidence did not support the Town's claims, leading to two juries finding in his favor. Bullard contended that the court’s instructions regarding the case were appropriate and did not contain any significant errors that would warrant overturning the jury's verdicts.

In the case of C. & A. R. R. Co. v. Schweitzer, the events unfolded on December 17, 1883, when a fire allegedly caused by the C. & A. Railroad Company led to damages claimed by the plaintiff, Schweitzer. The legal proceedings took place in Illinois, with the case being filed in the Illinois Appellate Court, and the decision was delivered on June 8, 1886. The key individuals involved included the plaintiff, Schweitzer, who claimed damages due to the fire, and representatives from the C. & A. Railroad Company as defendants. The main contention revolved around the declaration filed by the plaintiff, which was challenged by the defendant on the grounds of a purported defect in the legal documentation and the assertion that the damages sought were excessive.	The plaintiff, Schweitzer, claimed that the C. & A. Railroad Company was responsible for a fire that caused significant damages to his property. His legal arguments centered on the assertion of negligence on the part of the railroad company, leading to the request for compensation for the damages incurred due to the alleged fire.	The primary defenses presented by the C. & A. Railroad Company included objections to the declaration, specifically arguing that it was defective due to the omission of the specific date of the fire. Additionally, the defendant contended that the damages awarded were excessive. They asserted that these points were critical grounds to overturn the jury's decision, requesting the court to dismiss the claims based on these arguments.

In the case of Joseph Kitchell v. Samuel Bratton, the legal proceedings took place in December 1836 in Illinois. The case arose from a dispute over certain personal property that had been levied as the property of J. and P. Higgins under an execution favoring Bratton, the appellee. The appellant, Joseph Kitchell, claimed ownership of the property based on a mortgage deed he held from the Higgins. This deed indicated that the mortgage was created as security for a debt that the Higgins owed to Kitchell. During the trial held at the Crawford Circuit Court in March 1836, questions arose regarding the interpretation of the mortgage and whether Kitchell had maintained possession of the property as stipulated in the deed. The Circuit Court initially ruled against Kitchell, leading him to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing errors in jury instructions related to the validity of the mortgage under statutory provisions governing conveyances and creditors’ rights.	Joseph Kitchell asserted that he possessed a valid mortgage deed for the property in question, which exempted him from the requirements of recording it, given that valuable consideration had been provided. He argued that the mortgage was legally sound and that the failure of the lower court to correctly instruct the jury diluted his rightful claims to the property.	Samuel Bratton contended that Kitchell's claims were invalid due to his failure to prove continuous possession of the mortgaged property as was required under the relevant statutory framework. Bratton's defense emphasized that, without proper possession by Kitchell, the mortgage could be deemed fraudulent under the statute of frauds which governs conveyances not recorded and lacking necessary conditions.

In June 1870, in Clay County, Illinois, the case of James C. Gill v. Levi Skelton was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case centered around a slander action initiated by James C. Gill against Levi Skelton. The dispute arose from statements made by Skelton that Gill claimed were defamatory. Gill succeeded in the lower court, receiving a jury verdict and judgment in the amount of $400. The evidence presented in court confirmed that the statements were indeed actionable slander as laid out in Gill's declaration. The case record indicated that no rulings regarding the admission or exclusion of evidence were questioned, and the instructions provided to Gill were based on well-established legal principles. Skelton's legal team expressed dissatisfaction with certain instructions that were not granted, but a supplemental record confirmed that the essence of their requested instructions was covered in those that were given. Chief Justice Lawrence delivered the opinion of the Court, emphasizing procedural requirements for preserving error assignments related to jury instructions.	James C. Gill, the plaintiff, argued that Levi Skelton's words constituted slander. He claimed that the statements made were defamatory and damaging to his reputation, leading him to seek compensation for the harm inflicted. Gill requested a financial judgment of $400, asserting that the words spoken were actionable under the law as presented in his declaration.	Levi Skelton, the defendant, contended that the court erred by refusing several of his proposed jury instructions, which he believed were crucial for his defense. His legal representatives argued that error assignments on the jury instructions should be respected. However, they faced the challenge that there was no record of the specific instructions granted to counter those rejected, which hindered their appeal process.

In 1874, in Livingston County, Illinois, John Hayward filed a replevin action against John Ramsey to recover personal property he claimed was rightfully his. A trial took place on January 12, 1874, resulting in a judgment favoring Ramsey. Following this, Hayward appealed to the circuit court, filing an appeal bond with the justice of the peace on January 14. The circuit court, in session for eight days, called for Hayward to present his case on February 6, but he failed to appear, leading to the dismissal of his appeal. The court affirmed the initial judgment and awarded a procedendo. An issue arose regarding whether the timing of the appeal, which was perfected less than ten days before the court's term, impacted the court's jurisdiction for trial. The statutory provision indicated a ten-day requirement before a trial could occur in such a situation.	The plaintiff, John Hayward, argued that his appeal from the justice of the peace was valid, and his failure to appear should not have resulted in the dismissal of his case. He contended that the appeal was perfected according to statutory guidelines, and the trial was improperly conducted without respecting the mandated ten-day preparation period before the term of the court.	John Ramsey, the defendant, argued that the appeal was dismissed correctly based on procedural grounds. He contended that the circuit court had authority to manage cases according to the statute, and the dismissal was in line with the procedural rules related to the timing of perfecting an appeal.

Job Toles, the plaintiff in error, initiated a legal action against Miles Cole, the defendant in error, in 1850. The case took place in Kane County, Illinois, and was primarily centered on a bond related to a debt claim. Toles claimed that Cole was responsible for the payment of the judgment that could be recovered in a specified prior lawsuit, which formed the basis of the bond agreement in question. The case was initially heard before Judge Hugh T. Dickey at a special term of the Kane Circuit Court, where a jury ultimately ruled in favor of Toles, awarding him $281.81 along with costs. Following this verdict, Cole sought to challenge the decision by filing a writ of error.	The primary claim made by Job Toles was based on a bond requiring Miles Cole to pay any judgment that might be rendered in a related suit. Toles sought to recover the specified amount stated in the bond, which the jury initially found to be $281.81, in addition to legal costs incurred.	Miles Cole's defense relied on the plea of "non est factum," which contends that the defendant was not bound by the alleged obligation as specified in the bond. He disputed the judgment rendered by the jury and sought to have it overturned, arguing that the jury's findings and the subsequent judgment were incorrect.

In 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, Herman and Bruno Weber, nephews of Amalia Christen, filed an action of ejectment against her concerning ownership of certain parcels of land that had belonged to her deceased husband, Ludwig Christen. The plaintiffs claimed that two deeds executed by Christen and his wife conveyed the property to them. Although the deeds were acknowledged and recorded, they were taken back by Mrs. Christen shortly after recording and kept until her husband's death in 1885. The plaintiffs, unaware of the deeds until afterward, later expressed approval upon learning of the transaction. However, evidence suggested that the original intention of Christen was to shield the property from his creditors rather than make a legitimate transfer of ownership. The case hinged on the crucial legal question of whether the execution and recording of the deeds constituted a delivery that would effectuate the transfer of property title.	The plaintiffs claimed that the execution and recording of the deeds by Ludwig Christen successfully transferred property ownership to them, arguing that their subsequent approval constituted acceptance. They sought recovery of the property based on this premise.	The defendant, Amalia Christen, contended that the deeds never constituted a valid transfer of ownership due to a lack of actual delivery, arguing that the original intent of her deceased husband was to retain control over the property and shield it from creditors. She claimed that the deeds were executed without the knowledge or consent of the grantees, and thus did not take effect.

In June 1871, the legal case of Joshua E. Sandifer v. Thomas H. Hoard was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from a promissory note issue that took place in Bond County, Illinois. The dispute involved Joshua E. Sandifer (the appellee), who was the assignee of a promissory note originally made by Thomas H. Hoard (the appellant) to G. J. Sandifer for the payment of $250. The appellant contended that he had already paid the note to the original payee while it was still held by him and that the assignment to the appellee occurred after the note had matured. During trial, Hoard's legal team sought to introduce evidence pertaining to admissions made by the payee regarding the payment. However, this evidence was excluded by the court despite its relevance to the defense of payment. The jury ruled in favor of Sandifer, awarding the total sum of the note, which prompted Hoard to move for a new trial on the grounds of the erroneous exclusion of evidence, a motion that was denied.	Joshua E. Sandifer, as the assignee of the promissory note, claimed that Thomas H. Hoard owed him the full amount due under the note, which had been assigned after its maturity. He pursued a verdict on the grounds that the note was legally binding despite the defenses presented by Hoard. Sandifer argued that even if the note had been claimed to be paid, the evidence proving this was improperly excluded from the trial.	Thomas H. Hoard contended that he had already settled the debt with the original payee of the note before it was assigned to Sandifer, asserting that he had made payment while the note was still in the payee's possession. He further argued that the assignment of the note occurred after its maturity, which should invalidate the appellee's claim to enforce the note against him. Hoard's defense hinged on the belief that evidence concerning the payee's admissions regarding payment was crucial but was wrongfully disallowed in court.

Josephus Scott filed a lawsuit against Samuel P. Sharp and J. H. Rice in Edgar County, Illinois, with the case reaching the court on August 26, 1886. The suit originated in a Justice of the Peace court to recover the value of mole ditches that were constructed by the defendants for the plaintiff. The preliminary judgment made at the Circuit Court level resulted in a decision against Scott, who contested a sum of $104.80. The case involved conflicting evidence that led to the appeal, with Scott arguing that the jury's verdict was not supported by the evidential weight presented during the trial. The Illinois Appellate Court reviewed the contradictory evidence and framed the issue as one appropriate for jury determination, deciding that the jury's finding should not be disturbed.	The plaintiff, Josephus Scott, argued that the jury's verdict was contrary to the evidence presented during the trial. He sought to reverse the decision of the Circuit Court, which had ruled against him regarding the valuation of the mole ditches made by the defendants. Scott contended that the jury had made an error in weighing the evidence and thus requested a reconsideration of the judgment against him.	The defendants, Samuel P. Sharp and J. H. Rice, maintained that the evidence against Scott was sufficient to support the jury's verdict. They argued that the matter of conflicting evidence was appropriately placed in the hands of the jury, and asserted that the judgment by the lower court should be upheld. The defendants requested that the appellate court affirm the ruling made by the Circuit Court, supporting the verdict in their favor.

In 1838, Emanuel Orr and Evin Shelby executed a joint and several promissory note to Joseph Thompson for $14.50, which was due in twelve months. Following the note's expiration and after Thompson's death, a legal action was initiated on November 13, 1845, before a justice of the peace for the sum owed on the note using the name “Joseph Thompson, for the use of William Curtis.” Shelby appeared and confessed judgment for $19.50, which was granted by the justice. On April 27, 1846, process was issued against Orr requiring him to show cause for not rendering judgment against him as well. Orr claimed in his defense that Thompson had died before the commencement of the initial suit, a plea that was overruled by the justice. This led to a separate judgment against Orr for $20.25. Orr appealed to the Circuit Court but sustained the initial ruling. The appeal debated the validity of the judgment against Orr, focusing on the implications of Thompson's death and the necessity for proper parties in the action.	The plaintiff, Joseph Thompson (suing for the use of William Curtis), contended that Orr was liable for the debt owed under the promissory note despite Thompson's death. The claim asserted that the action brought against Orr was appropriate under joint liability principles inherent in the note, and that the prior judgment against Shelby did not negate Orr's obligation.	Emanuel Orr argued that the action against him was invalid because the nominal plaintiff, Joseph Thompson, had died before the suit's initiation. He maintained that this should have qualified as a defense abatement, asserting that the suit should have been filed in the name of Thompson's legal representative and not as an independent action. Orr requested a re-evaluation of the pleas and a reversal of the judgment rendered against him.

In the case of Richard P. Travers et al. v. Grover S. Wormer et al., the dispute originated in Cook County, Illinois, during the year 1883. The plaintiffs, Grover S. Wormer and others, filed a suit against the defendants, Richard P. Travers and others, to recover the value of a steam boiler that had been sold and delivered to the defendants. The case was brought under the legal doctrine of assumpsit, which deals with the recovery of damages arising from the failure to fulfill a contractual obligation. The defendants responded by pleading the general issue along with several special pleas. By mutual agreement in open court, the parties chose to have the case tried without a jury. The trial concluded with an initial ruling in favor of the defendants, which was entered of record by the court. However, after the defendants' findings were recorded, the plaintiffs requested a new trial. In a subsequent ruling, the court set aside the earlier finding in favor of the defendants and instead ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them damages of $300. This caused the defendants to object and file their motion for a new trial.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to recover the sum of $300, representing the value of the steam boiler sold and delivered to the defendants. They sought a legal remedy based on the defendant's failure to compensate them for the boiler after its delivery, asserting that the court's initial ruling in favor of the defendants was erroneous and that they were wrongfully denied the value of the asset sold.	The defendants contested the plaintiffs' claims on the grounds of general issues and specific pleas that challenged the validity of the plaintiffs' assertion regarding the boiler sale. They argued that the initial finding of the court in their favor should stand and maintained that the court erred in its later decision to vacate that finding and rule in favor of the plaintiffs without conducting a proper retrial.

In the year 1873, in Alton, Illinois, the case Western Screw and Manufacturing Company v. James Cousley arose when Cousley sought compensation for services he claimed to have rendered to what was intended to be the Western Screw and Manufacturing Company. The situation originated from one Ingalls, a patentee who attempted to set up a company to manufacture patent screws. He purchased property and sought to form a corporation with a capital stock of $100,000. Cousley subscribed for $500 of this stock under the agreement that his payment would be made through labor. However, due to inadequate stock subscriptions, the organization was never completed. The stockholders then created a new company, with a reduced capital stock of $50,000, which ultimately succeeded in purchasing the property. The crux of the case involved whether Cousley could be compensated for work done before the first company was fully organized, as he had worked under Ingalls from March to May 1873, prior to the new corporation's establishment in July 1873.	Cousley, as the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to compensation for services rendered as a superintendent for the initial attempts at forming the Western Screw and Manufacturing Company. He claimed that despite the company not being fully organized, he had performed work that justified his expectation of payment, effectively arguing for the recognition of a valid contract based on the services provided.	The defendant, represented by the new Western Screw and Manufacturing Company, contended that it bore no legal responsibility for debts incurred prior to its formation. They maintained that any contract made for services before the company was fully organized would not be binding upon the later formed company. Thus, the defense asserted that Cousley should seek payment from the party that directly employed him, namely Ingalls, rather than from the newly established corporation.

The case of William Hill et al. v. Joseph Hill et al. was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1887. The dispute arose following the death of Green B. Hill, who passed away on February 27, 1885, at the age of eighty. The heirs and widow of Green B. Hill filed a bill for partition and assignment of dower in lands which they claimed he had owned. On August 1, 1881, Green B. Hill allegedly executed two deeds intended to convey certain lands to his sons, Preston and Joseph Hill. However, these deeds were not delivered but remained in Green B. Hill's possession until his death. After his passing, Preston and Joseph were found to have taken the deeds from Green B. Hill's locked trunk and recorded them. The plaintiffs contended that the deeds were invalid as they were never delivered. The circuit court originally dismissed the claims of all the complainants except for the widow, granting her dower rights in the lands. The matter subsequently moved to appeal by the heirs.	The plaintiffs argue that Green B. Hill intended to convey the land to them, but the deeds were never delivered, which invalidates them. They seek to have the deeds set aside as clouds on the title to the property. The plaintiffs maintain that since the deeds were not properly delivered and the circumstances surrounding their recording were questionable, the lands should rightfully belong to the heirs as stipulated by Green B. Hill's wishes.	The defendants, Preston and Joseph Hill, contend that the execution of the deeds constituted a valid and effective transfer of property rights from Green B. Hill to them, emphasizing their father's intent to deliver the deeds to them. They argue that the evidence supports the conclusion that the deeds were placed in the trunk by Green B. Hill, thus solidifying the delivery and validity of the deeds. The defendants request that the court affirm the validity of the deeds as evidence shows their father expressed a wish for the sons to inherit the property after his death.

In 1868, a legal case took place in Kane County, Illinois, involving B. F. Parks and others (the plaintiffs) against William H. Miller, the Treasurer of Kane County (the defendant). This case arose from an application by Miller for judgment against certain delinquent lands for unpaid taxes from the year 1865. The county court initially entered a judgment in Miller's favor. Subsequently, the case was appealed to the circuit court of Kane County, where the judgment was upheld. The plaintiffs contested the legality of the county court proceedings, claiming that there was no jurisdiction because the court was convened without the required presence of associate justices or proper notice. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the situation and discussed the legislative authority governing county court operations within counties that adopted township organization and whether there were appropriate terms of court for county business.	The plaintiffs contended that the county court lacked jurisdiction to enter judgment due to the absence of associate justices and claimed that the collector's notice of application for judgment was void as it did not specify the first day of the term. They argued that these procedural defects invalidated the judgment against the delinquent lands. They requested that the court overturn the judgment that had been entered against them.	The defendant, William H. Miller, maintained that the county court was legally constituted to handle county business and enter judgments for taxes without the necessity of two justices of the peace present. Miller asserted that the township organization act provided the authority for the county judge to act alone in such cases. He argued that the collector had the discretion to designate the term of court for the tax judgments and that the notice given was sufficient to confer jurisdiction.

In September 1877, the case of May Hubbard v. Marcus C. Stearns was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The controversy revolved around a disputed boundary line between two lots located in the canal trustees’ subdivision of a fractional section in Cook County, Illinois. The lots in question were originally owned by the canal trustees and were divided by an old fence erected before 1848. May Hubbard owned lot 14, which she inherited from her father, Henry G. Hubbard, who purchased it in September 1848. Marcus C. Stearns owned lot 13, which was purchased by his predecessor, Davis, also in September 1848. As the dispute escalated, Stearns claimed part of Hubbard's lot, asserting that the old fence marked the proper dividing line and that he had occupied the land for over twenty years, thereby establishing ownership through adverse possession. Hubbard sought to have the original boundary line recognized and to remove the alleged claim made by Stearns as it served as a cloud on her title, preventing her from selling the property. The Superior Court of Cook County initially ruled in favor of Stearns.	May Hubbard claimed that the boundary line dividing her lot from Marcus C. Stearns' lot was not where Stearns had built a fence, but rather along the original line established by the canal trustees. She argued that Stearns' claim over her property was invalid and constituted a cloud on her title, hindering her ability to sell the unsold portion of her lot. Hubbard requested the court to establish the original boundary line to resolve the dispute and clear the title of any encumbrances.	Marcus C. Stearns defended his position by asserting that the fence he constructed had been the recognized boundary line for more than twenty years and that he and his grantees had continuously occupied the disputed land under a claim of ownership. He argued that under the Limitation Act of 1827, this long period of adverse possession barred Hubbard from recovering any rights to the land in question. Stearns maintained that whether the fence was the true dividing line was immaterial since the occupation had been acknowledged for over two decades.

Jacob Spangler brought a case against the Indiana and Illinois Central Railway Company in January 1859 before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute revolved around Spangler's subscription to stock in the railway company, for which he was to pay $50 for each share based on assessments made by the board of directors. Spangler claimed he was improperly required to pay the full amount of his subscription without the proper assessments being called and without receiving notice, a contention related to the company's charter stipulations. The case took place in Macon County, Illinois, and involved a procedural issue concerning the sufficiency of the legal declaration filed by Spangler. The court targeted the legal obligations regarding the payment of stock subscriptions based on the board's periodic assessments and the notification process, balancing corporate obligations against shareholder rights.	The plaintiff, Jacob Spangler, argued that the defendant had required him to pay the total subscription amount for stock without proper notices regarding periodic assessments, as specified by the company's governing rules. He contended that the defendant's actions were not justified under the original contract, as it was not reasonable to expect payment of the full subscription amount in one lump sum without proper notification of prior calls for payment.	The defendant, Indiana and Illinois Central Railway Company, contended that the declaration filed by Spangler was insufficient because it did not adequately address whether the board of directors had made the required assessments nor provided details on the placement of such assessments. The defendant argued that without these details, Spangler could not claim a legal obligation to make the payments in question and that assessments were necessary before any legal action could be initiated.

James E. Greenleaf, the appellant, brought a case against Nelson C. Roe, the appellee, in the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1856, following earlier proceedings in the Cook County Court of Common Pleas. This case was an action of assumpsit, indicating a claim for recovery in a contract dispute. The plaintiff had initially filed a declaration, to which the defendant responded with a demurrer that was subsequently overruled. After the defendant was granted additional time to plead, the plaintiff filed a general issue plea but failed to include an affidavit of merits, resulting in the plea being stricken from the record. A default judgment was entered against the plaintiff after hearing proofs presented in court. Subsequently, the plaintiff motioned to set aside the default, indicating his inability to procure an affidavit of merits in time due to his residence in Boston, Massachusetts. This motion, accompanied by pleadings for a special set-off claim, was denied multiple times by the court. The proceedings emphasized the sound discretion of the court concerning default settings, and the court concluded that the plaintiff had not demonstrated significant grounds for interference.	The plaintiff, James E. Greenleaf, claimed that the default judgment rendered against him was unjust, primarily because he was unable to file an affidavit of merits due to his residence in another state, which hindered his ability to respond adequately to the pleadings. He sought to set aside the default judgment to allow for the pleading of a set-off he purportedly was entitled to, which would require a reopening of his case and a consideration of the merits.	Nelson C. Roe, the defendant, contended that the plaintiff's repeated motions to set aside the default were without merit and that the court had acted within its discretion. The defendant argued that the plaintiff failed to show grounds sufficient to warrant intervention by the appellate court, as he chose not to request additional time to submit the necessary affidavit of merits.
