The defendant maintained that the judgment should remain in place, affirming the court's decision to enter a default due to the plaintiff's failure to comply with procedural requirements.

The case, "The People ex rel. A. H. Bell v. Charles S. Zane," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 29, 1883. The underlying criminal case involved Lewis Biggs, who was indicted for murder by the grand jury of Macoupin County. Concerns arose about the prejudicial atmosphere against Biggs in Macoupin, leading him to petition for a change of venue. The venue was initially moved to Christian County but subsequently changed to Sangamon County by the Macoupin circuit court. Biggs, while still in custody in Macoupin County, was transferred to Sangamon. Upon reaching Sangamon County, the State's Attorney motioned to remand the case back to Macoupin, claiming Sangamon lacked jurisdiction. The Sangamon circuit court refused to try Biggs, despite his waiver of any jurisdictional objections. This led A.H. Bell, representing the People, to seek a writ of mandamus from the Illinois Supreme Court to compel Circuit Judge Zane of Sangamon County to take jurisdiction and proceed with the trial.	The plaintiff, represented by A.H. Bell, claimed that the Sangamon County circuit court had a duty to take cognizance of the indictment against Lewis Biggs and to try the case, as all relevant records were already transferred and Biggs had waived his jurisdiction objections. The relator sought a writ of mandamus to compel Judge Zane to proceed with the trial and argued that the change of venue, while irregular, did not affect the court's obligation to try the case if the defendant waived objections.	The defendant, Circuit Judge Zane, contended that the Sangamon County circuit court lacked jurisdiction to try the case after the venue change was violated. They argued that jurisdiction was fully vested in Christian County following the initial order and that the proceedings in Sangamon could not commence without the proper transfer of jurisdictional authority. The defense sought to maintain that the circuit court should not be compelled to act outside its jurisdiction.

The case "Robert Green, Appellant, v. Richard Lewis, Appellee" originated in the McHenry Circuit Court, Illinois, in 1851 and was eventually decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1852. The key individuals involved were Robert Green, the defendant, and Richard Lewis, the plaintiff. Lewis had performed labor on a farm jointly operated by Robert Green and his brother Joseph Green from July 1846 to 1848. The services provided by Lewis were the subject of the dispute, with Lewis asserting that he was entitled to compensation from Robert Green alone. During the trial, evidence was presented concerning the nature of the employment relationship between Lewis and the Greens, including witness testimonies about the arrangement and financial handling of labor on the farm. The jury ultimately ruled against Robert Green, resulting in a verdict and judgment requiring him to pay Lewis $270, which Green contested in his appeal.	Richard Lewis claimed that he worked on Robert Green's farm and was entitled to compensation for his labor. He argued that he had been employed by Robert Green individually, despite the farm being worked jointly by both Green brothers. Lewis requested payment for his services, asserting there was a clear understanding that he worked directly for Robert Green.	Robert Green contended that the lawsuit should have included both him and his brother Joseph Green, asserting that the services Lewis provided were part of a joint liability. Green's defense relied on the argument that the labor was performed for the benefit of both brothers, not just for him individually, and therefore, he should not be held solely responsible for payment.

The case of R. P. Roberts et al. v. Darius Clelland took place in 1876 in Cook County, Illinois. The initial proceedings involved a mechanic's lien case where a lien was established against Darius Clelland's property due to a default in payment owed to the Frear Stone Manufacturing Company. The property was ordered to be sold, and during the sale, it was offered in separate parcels but received no bids. Consequently, it was sold en masse to A. D. Carter, the solicitor for the petitioner, for the agreed amount and costs. Carter subsequently assigned the certificate of purchase to several parties, including R. P. Roberts, G. 0. Griffith, and Daniel L. Sibley. A motion was later filed by Cornell, who sought to set aside the sale, claiming irregularities. Although Carter appeared in defense, no notice was given to the assignees regarding this motion. The court allowed the assignees to join as parties but upheld the order to set aside the sale. The case was then appealed, focusing on whether the assignees could contest the motion to set aside the sale without prior notice.	The plaintiffs, R. P. Roberts and others, argued that they were not given notice of the motion to set aside the sale, even though they were the rightful assignees of the certificate of purchase. They claimed that the original proceedings that led to the setting aside of the sale were flawed and requested to reverse the court's last order that affected their rights regarding the purchase.	The defendant, Darius Clelland, contended that the original purchaser and their assignees were chargeable with notice of any irregularities in the sale. He argued that while the purchasers needed notice of motions to set aside sales, such notice was not necessary for assignees. Clelland requested that the motion to set aside the sale be upheld, denying any claim made by the assignees to contest this motion without having been duly notified.

In 1870, the Kankakee and Illinois River Railroad Company petitioned for the condemnation of a right of way over land owned by H. C. Todd, Trustee, in Kankakee County, Illinois. This action was taken under the right of way law established in 1852. Commissioners were appointed to assess compensation for the land, ultimately determining that Todd was entitled to just one dollar for the land taken and a mere penny for damages. Todd's appeals in the circuit court resulted in a similar jury verdict, which led him to elevate the case to the Illinois Supreme Court. Evidence presented during the trial indicated that the railroad would traverse valuable blocks in the town of Momenee, with values estimated between $1,000 and $4,000 each, along with farm land worth $75 to $100 per acre. Todd contended that the lower courts erred in denying specific jury instructions regarding compensation calculations, particularly regarding how benefits should not offset damages when assessing the compensation for the taken land.	H. C. Todd claimed that the jury had not been properly instructed about assessing the value of the land taken for the railroad. He argued that compensation should be based solely on the land's value without deductions for any anticipated benefits from the railroad. Todd sought a ruling that would ensure full compensation for the distinct parcels of land—specifically the blocks and streets in the town—through which the railroad would run, asserting that benefits acquired elsewhere should not mitigate damages incurred from the construction.	The Kankakee and Illinois River Railroad contended that the jury verdict was appropriate, as it reflected the commissioners' report regarding compensation for the right of way. The railroad emphasized that benefits from the railroad's construction could justifiably offset damages related to the land taken, thereby supporting the jury's findings and the lower court's judgment without requiring further instructions.

In December 1829, the case of James M. Duncan v. Clement B. Fletcher arose in Fayette County, Illinois. The dispute was submitted to arbitration by mutual consent of the parties involved. The plaintiffs and defendants agreed that their case would be referred to James Black, who would adjudicate the matter based solely on the books of C. B. Fletcher as evidence of the account's accuracy. The agreement established that the arbitration would take place on September 29 of that year, regardless of the parties' presence. Following the arbitration, Duncan challenged the final judgment, citing two primary errors: the absence of an indication that the arbitrator had been sworn and a lack of a specific date on which the award was given. The legal intricacies involve the statutory requirements related to arbitration and whether the absence of certain formalities invalidated the award.	The plaintiff, James M. Duncan, argued that the judgment from the circuit court should be reversed due to two key issues: (1) the award did not affirmatively state that the arbitrator took an oath as required by law, and (2) the exact date on which the award was made was not specified. Duncan contended that these omissions could invalidate the arbitration process and sought a ruling from the higher court to address these alleged errors.	The defendant, Clement B. Fletcher, maintained that the objections raised by Duncan were technical in nature and that the courts should presume compliance with the swearing of the referee and the requirements of the arbitration process since no fraud or injustice had been alleged. Fletcher argued that because he did not raise these objections in the original court, he should not be permitted to introduce them at a later stage. His position was that the judgment should stand as it was rendered.

On February 21, 1870, John G. Roberts was appointed as the guardian for his two nephews, William E. Pease (born September 9, 1855) and Henry L. Pease (born December 9, 1857), by the County Court of Sangamon County, Illinois. He received a bond and funds totaling $5,371.83 from the previous guardian. On July 25, 1870, Roberts was petitioned by sureties to provide a new bond or counter security, which he failed to do. As a result, the court revoked his guardianship on August 3, 1870. Subsequently, without disclosing his prior appointment, Roberts applied for guardianship in Tazewell County, where he misled the court about his previous status. He secured a bond and letters of guardianship under false pretenses, as neither he nor his sureties could provide adequate security. After a series of actions that included presenting fraudulent documents, the Tazewell County Court eventually found that his letters of guardianship had been procured through fraud. The Pease brothers, having promoted their case against Roberts, initiated legal action to annul his appointing as guardian. Their case was complicated by the absence of any due diligence on Roberts’ part, and after several legal challenges, the circuit court restored Roberts' guardianship before they sought a review in appellate court, leading to the case at hand.	The plaintiffs, William E. Pease and Henry L. Pease, allege that John G. Roberts obtained his letters of guardianship through fraudulent means, including concealing material facts about his prior appointment and the validity of his bond. They seek the cancellation of the Tazewell County Court's letters and a judicial declaration that all related proceedings are void due to this fraud.	John G. Roberts asserts that he did not conceal any material facts that he was legally obliged to disclose when he applied for guardianship in Tazewell County. He argues that it was not his responsibility to inform the Tazewell County Court about the previous proceedings in Sangamon County. Roberts maintains that his actions were legitimate and that any purported fraud was fabricated by his wards.

In the case of **Thomas Knobloch v. Solomon Mueller**, which took place in the circuit court of St. Clair County, Illinois, the events trace back to the death of **George Christian Mueller** on March 27, 1870. Initially, a will dated March 14, 1870, was probated but later set aside by the court, declaring his estate to descend intially as intestate. His heirs, **George** and **Solomon Mueller**, alongside their sisters **Catharine Rebhan** and **Margarite Reinhardt**, believed they owned the estate equally. In 1979, Catharine filed for partition of the property, believing the estate had been divided properly. The court ruled in her favor, permitting her to sell her interest to **Thomas Knobloch** for $5050. However, in **April 1883**, a previously undiscovered will from **1855**, which bequeathed the estate to George and Solomon, was found and probated. Subsequently, Solomon brought a bill against Knobloch to remove his deed as a cloud on his title, contending that Knobloch’s deed should be invalidated due to the new evidence of the will. The court had to navigate through claims of mutual mistake and whether Knobloch, as a bona fide purchaser, was entitled to his claim against Solomon's assertion.	**Solomon Mueller**, as the plaintiff, claimed that the newly discovered will of 1855 should validate his title to the estate, which had originally been awarded under a misapprehension. He sought to have Knobloch's title deed set aside, asserting that it was a cloud on his legitimate title derived from the will, and requested an injunction against Knobloch and others to halt any ongoing legal actions regarding the estate.	**Thomas Knobloch**, the defendant, argued that he purchased the land in good faith, without any notice of adverse claims, relying on the earlier partition decree. He contended that Solomon should be estopped from claiming a title contrary to the earlier court decision that had established Catharine's interest. Knobloch maintained that he had the rights of a bona fide purchaser, entitled to protections under equity law, and that Solomon's claims were inherently flawed due to the consented nature of previous court rulings.

In September 1870, the case of Talmadge E. Spaids v. Oliver W. Barrett et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. Talmadge E. Spaids, a dealer in oysters, claimed that Barrett and others intentionally defrauded him by falsely swearing that he owed them $2,996.30 for transportation and that he was fraudulently hiding his assets to evade creditors. This affidavit led to the issuance of a writ of attachment against Spaids' property, specifically $5,000 worth of oysters, preventing him from accessing his goods. Spaids asserted that the affidavit forged by Barrett was knowingly false and that the defendants maliciously aimed to cause him financial harm by demanding more than the actual amount owed. As a direct consequence of the attachment, Spaids paid the inflated sum under duress to save his perishable goods, which had been neglected and were losing value due to the defendants’ actions. The case raised significant legal questions regarding the validity of the release Spaids executed and the lack of probable cause for the wrongful attachment.	Spaids claimed that Barrett and the other defendants maliciously attempted to ruin his business by filing a fraudulent affidavit that resulted in the wrongful attachment of his goods. He sought damages for the financial loss and destruction of his oysters and argued that he was wrongfully compelled to pay an inflated debt due to duress. His primary legal requests included the reversal of the prior judgments and the acknowledgment of his right to recover damages for the wrongful actions taken against him.	The defendants contended that the statements made in the affidavit were protected by legal privilege, as they pertained to a legal proceeding. They argued that Spaids had sufficient means to contest the affidavit and that he was only entitled to seek remedy through the attachment bond. The defendants maintained that there was no malicious intent or falsification involved in their claims against Spaids, essentially denying any wrongdoing.

In 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, Augusta Wilmers filed a legal case against Charles Volksdorf under the Bastardy Act, seeking financial support for her illegitimate child, which she alleged Volksdorf fathered. The complaint arose after Volksdorf had previously contributed to the child's support voluntarily for about eighteen months but stopped after Wilmers married another man. The initial trial in the Criminal Court of Cook County resulted in a guilty verdict against Volksdorf, requiring him to pay $493.50. However, the Appellate Court subsequently reversed this judgment, ruling that Wilmers could not proceed with her case since she was married at the time of the complaint, which they argued contradicted the provisions of the Bastardy Act. Wilmers then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the complaint was valid as she was unmarried at the time of her child's birth.	Augusta Wilmers claimed that she was entitled to bring the complaint against Charles Volksdorf as he was the father of her illegitimate child. She contended that the provisions of the Bastardy Act allowed her to initiate legal action for child support since she was unmarried when the child was born, despite her later marriage. She sought a reversal of the Appellate Court's decision that barred her from prosecution under the Act.	Charles Volksdorf maintained that Wilmers could not initiate the complaint due to her marriage at the time she filed it, asserting that the statute required the mother to be unmarried both at the time of making the complaint and at the time of child support request. He argued that her marriage invalidated her claim under the Bastardy Act, thereby defending against the charges and seeking affirmation of the Appellate Court's ruling.

John R. Allen v. Chauncey M. Payne took place in September 1867 in Kankakee City, Illinois. The case arose after Allen sold the furniture of a hotel, which he had occupied, to Payne, along with the remainder of his lease. Payne claimed he did not receive all the furniture that he purchased. Conversely, Allen argued he delivered all the furniture and that Payne owed him for services provided by himself and his family after Payne took possession, as well as for money received at a county fair that was meant to be shared between them. The jury ultimately sided with Payne, leading Allen to appeal the decision, claiming the verdict was not supported by the evidence. The case involved contradictory testimonies from both parties and was presided over by Judge Charles H. Wood in the Circuit Court of Kankakee County.	Payne's primary argument was that he did not receive all the furniture included in his purchase from Allen. He sought a verdict affirming that he was entitled to the full value of the furniture he had originally agreed to buy and was due compensation for the incomplete delivery.	Allen contended that he delivered all the furniture sold to Payne and submitted a counterclaim for money owed to him for services rendered by his family and himself after the sale, as well as a portion of profits from the county fair. His defense relied on establishing that he met his obligations under the agreement made with Payne.

In 1883, in Illinois, the legal case "Samuel J. Baird et al. v. Trustees of Schools" arose concerning a promissory note made by defendants Daniel McIntyre, Samuel J. Baird, and Benjamin Beed to the trustees of schools. The trustees were seeking repayment due to a deficit left by McIntyre as the township's school treasurer. The trial took place in the Circuit Court of Whiteside County, presided over by Judge Joseph M. Bailey, where the jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, affirming that Baird and Beed, despite their claims of being merely sureties, were liable on the note as part of their relationship to the defaulting treasurer. The case was appealed to the Appellate Court, which upheld the trial court's judgment. Key individuals involved included Justice Scott, who delivered the court's opinion, and the attorneys representing both sides, namely Mr. J. E. McPherran and Messrs. Bennett & Green for the appellants, and Messrs. J. & J. Dinsmoor for the appellees.	The plaintiffs, the Trustees of Schools, claimed that the promissory notes signed by Baird and Beed, as sureties for McIntyre, were valid and enforceable. They argued that the notes were given to cover a deficit McIntyre owed to the school fund due to his defaulting behavior as treasurer. The plaintiffs sought to hold Baird and Beed liable for the amount stated in the notes since they signed them as sureties.	The defendants, Baird and Beed, contended that they were only acting as sureties on McIntyre's official bond and argued that there was no consideration for the notes as they were executed under a misunderstanding of their legal liabilities as sureties. They further claimed the notes exceeded the actual sum due from McIntyre to the school fund. They requested that the court dismiss the judgment of the lower courts, asserting their lack of liability.

John H. Daniels and Frederick Aholtz were involved in a legal dispute in 1874 regarding adjoining arable lands enclosed by a common fence in Hacon County, Illinois. At that time, both men had cultivated corn on their respective sides of the field. After one occupant, Prather, harvested his corn, he sold the remaining corn stalks from the entire enclosure to Daniels for $60, permitting him to turn his cattle into the field to feed on those stalks. Unbeknownst to Daniels, Aholtz still had corn unmatured on his side of the field, and he was unaware of any claims from Prather. When Daniels released his cattle, they strayed into Aholtz’s section and damaged his corn. Subsequently, Aholtz filed a lawsuit against both Prather and Daniels for trespass and won a judgment. Daniels appealed, arguing he was not liable for trespass since he acted under Prather’s license. The court addressed the issue of whether Prather had the authority to grant such a license and affirmed the original judgment against Daniels.	Aholtz, the plaintiff, argued that Daniels had trespassed onto his property by allowing his cattle to graze on the corn stalks without permission. Aholtz claimed damages for the destruction caused to his corn crop, pointing out that Daniels had acted on Prather's false representation that he owned the entire field. Aholtz requested the court to hold both Daniels and Prather liable for the damages incurred due to the trespass.	Daniels contended that he could not be held liable for trespassing since he had received permission from Prather, who he believed was the sole owner of the corn stalks at that time. He argued that Prather's license should protect him from liability, claiming he had taken reasonable steps to avoid harm to Aholtz’s crops. Daniels sought to overturn the trespass judgment, asserting that the responsibility rested on Prather for misrepresenting ownership of the property.

On January 1, 1876, in Illinois, a legal case titled "William P. Corbin v. James W. Pearce" involved two key individuals: William P. Corbin, the plaintiff, and James W. Pearce, the defendant. The background of the case traces back to July 16, 1875, when McAuley, Toe & Co. obtained a judgment against a third party, Cox, in the amount of $154.50. Subsequently, an execution based on this judgment was issued against Cox for $104.50 and handed to constable Pearce on July 19, 1875. On August 23, 1875, Cox assigned his personal property to Corbin for the benefit of his creditors, at which point Corbin took possession of the goods, which included a stock of clothing. However, on August 26, 1875, Pearce levied upon a portion of these goods, prompting Corbin to file an action of replevin to retrieve the seized property. The case eventually ascended to the circuit court after unsuccessful attempts at resolution in the lower court. The trial in the circuit court relied solely on a written statement of the facts provided by both parties, with no additional evidence presented.	Corbin's primary argument was that the execution Pearce relied upon was invalid due to discrepancies in the amounts between the judgment and the execution itself. Additionally, he asserted that any amendment to the execution after the levy on September 1, 1875, rendered it void. Corbin requested the court to overturn the circuit court's decision, grant a new trial, and ultimately return the seized goods to him.	Pearce contended that the execution was valid despite the alleged variances because the execution had been issued based on a legitimate judgment. He argued that the title to the goods seized was vested in him legally due to the lawful levy made under the execution. Pearce maintained that any actions taken by the justice that amended the execution did not affect his rightful possession of the property and requested the court to affirm the circuit court's ruling in his favor.

In December 1846, the case of Mastin B. Shelburne, Executor of David Robinson, deceased, vs. Richard Robinson took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. The background of the case involves David Robinson, who passed away in November 1833, leaving a will that bequeathed one sixteenth of his estate to Richard Robinson as one of the legatees. The plaintiff, Mastin B. Shelburne, was appointed as an executor alongside another individual, and after taking the necessary oaths, they proceeded with the probate of the will in Kentucky. In January 1836, Shelburne paid Richard Robinson $250 in cash and $46.87 in merchandise under the assumption that this represented an accurate distribution of his legacy. Five years later, during a final account settlement in 1842, an amount of $3377.89 was reported as being in the hands of the executors for distribution, but the earlier payment to Robinson was not included. Nearly ten years after the initial payment, Shelburne requested that Robinson return the alleged overpayment, which Robinson refused. This prompted Shelburne to file suit for recovery, claiming an overpayment had been made. The related legal issues focused on whether his claim was barred by the Statute of Limitations.	The plaintiff, Mastin B. Shelburne, claimed that he had overpaid Richard Robinson as a legatee of David Robinson's estate. Shelburne sought to recover the excess amount that he believed was mistakenly paid, arguing that he was entitled to the return of the funds. His legal request was for a judgment to recover the amount he had overpaid.	The defendant, Richard Robinson, presented several defenses, including a plea of non-assumpsit, asserting that there was no agreement to pay back the overage. He also argued that the claim was barred by the Statute of Limitations, indicating that the overpayment issue had not been raised in a timely manner, given that more than ten years had elapsed since the payments were made. He contended that Shelburne’s claim lacked merit due to this delay.

In 1876, in McLean County, Illinois, a legal case titled "Hillary Ball et al. v. Fanny Palmer et al." was initiated concerning a petition for partition of certain lands after the death of Catharine Ball, who died intestate in 1849. Fanny Palmer claims to be the half-sister and sole heir of David Ball, Jr., the deceased only child of David Ball, Sr.—also one of Catharine Ball's children. The appellants, Mary and Elizabeth Ball, assert exclusive ownership of the land, arguing it was gifted to them by their mother and that they have possessed it for over twenty years while paying taxes. They also contend that a payment of $200 made by Catharine to David Ball, Sr. should be considered an advancement that should be factored into the inheritance distribution (hotchpot). Fanny Palmer's petition against Mary and Elizabeth Ball challenges their exclusive claim, invoking the Statute of Frauds and asserting her entitlement to a share of the estate. The Illinois Supreme Court was tasked with evaluating whether the appellants had established an adverse possession of the property and the validity of their claims.	Fanny Palmer, as the appellee, argued that the appellants did not hold a valid claim to the exclusive ownership of the land since Catharine Ball died intestate, without any deed transferring ownership. She maintained that the possession claimed by Mary and Elizabeth was not adverse as it aligned with the rights of other heirs. Palmer requested a partition of the property and the inclusion of the $200 given to David Ball, Sr. in the estate distribution, stating that the appellants failed to prove an independent title or adverse possession based on the necessary legal standards.	Mary and Elizabeth Ball contended that the land rightfully belongs to them, alleging it was a gift from their mother, Catharine Ball. They maintained their claim of adverse possession based on their long-term residence and payment of taxes. They argued that even if they lacked a clear title by gift or prescription, the $200 received from their mother by David Ball, Sr. should be recognized as an advancement, necessitating its inclusion in the estate's hotchpot for distribution among heirs. The appellants aimed for a dismissal of Palmer's claims and a decree affirming their exclusive ownership.

In April 1861, in Iroquois County, Illinois, the case of Francis M. Wilson v. The People was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case was a bastardy trial, where Wilson was accused of fathering a child with the complainant, who was the child's mother. The jury found Wilson guilty, leading to a judgment that required him to pay fifty dollars annually for seven years as well as to post a bond of $800, ensuring payment of the judgment. The relationship between Wilson and the mother of the child was alleged to have occurred in the dining room of the house where they lived. Following the verdict, Wilson sought a new trial, alleging that he had newly discovered evidence that could provide an alibi, specifically stating that his mother could testify that the alleged conception could not have happened at the time the complainant claimed it did. The case revolved around the credibility of the complaining witness and whether the previous verdict should be overturned based on the introduced evidence.	The plaintiff, in this case, argues that the jury's finding of guilt against Wilson was justified based on the credible testimony provided by the complaining witness, who testified about the circumstances surrounding the conception of the child. The plaintiff seeks the enforcement of the judgment that requires Wilson to pay child support and bond to secure payment.	The defendant, Wilson, contends that he was taken by surprise by the testimony of the complaining witness regarding the location and circumstances of the alleged conception. He argues that he has newly discovered evidence through his mother's potential testimony that could prove an alibi and insists that the Circuit Court should grant a new trial to allow this evidence to be presented. However, he acknowledges the discretion of the court in deciding whether or not to grant such a request.

In 1888, a legal dispute arose in Bloomington, Illinois, involving Linus Graves, who was in charge of the cemetery grounds adjacent to Lincoln Street. The city claimed that Graves had illegally excavated and obstructed the public street by digging post holes to construct a fence without obtaining the necessary permission, leading to a complaint lodged with the police magistrate. Graves was fined for his actions, but he appealed the decision. During the appeal in the County Court, the verdict favored Graves in two separate trials, prompting the city to challenge the ruling. The city argued that their actual possession of the street extended up to the old fence, claiming that the post holes were dug in a gutter created during street grading. In contrast, Graves contended that the excavation was conducted north of the gutter, which marked the city’s actual possession boundary. Witnesses provided conflicting statements about the city’s activity in maintaining the area, with the court considering both oral testimony and maps to determine the limits of the city’s claim.	The City of Bloomington, as the plaintiff, argued that Linus Graves unlawfully excavated and obstructed a public street, asserting their right to maintain and regulate that part of Lincoln Street adjoining the cemetery. They sought enforcement of the municipal ordinance against Graves, as they believed he had violated the city’s rights regarding the proper use of the public street.	Linus Graves, the defendant, contended that he was not trespassing or obstructing a public street, as the post holes were dug north of the designated gutter which marked the extent of the city’s possession. He argued that the city had failed to maintain this part of the street and that his use of the land did not constitute a violation of any ordinance. Additionally, he maintained that the city’s claims regarding their possession were unsubstantiated.

The case "James H. Karr, and Michael B. White, Appellants, v. Hiram E. Barstow, Appellee" took place in Iroquois County, Illinois, beginning on April 2, 1858. The dispute arose from an action of trespass where the plaintiff, Hiram E. Barstow, alleged that the defendants (Karr and White) took and carried away certain goods belonging to him. Prior to this case, Barstow had brought an action of replevin against Karr, recovering the same goods along with a nominal amount for damages. The defendants raised several defenses, including claims that Barstow's earlier action of replevin barred his current trespass action. The trial included multiple motions and demurrers regarding the pleas filed by the defendants. A jury ultimately found in favor of Barstow, assessing damages at $600. The defendants filed an appeal, arguing various procedural and substantive points regarding the sustaining of demurrers and the instructions given to the jury during the trial.	Barstow's main argument was that he had a valid claim resulting from the alleged trespass, as he had already successfully recovered the goods in a prior replevin action. He requested damages for the wrongful taking of his property, emphasizing that the defendants could not subsequently claim that his recovery in the replevin negated his right to sue for trespass.	The defendants contended that Barstow's prior recovery of the goods in the replevin action precluded him from bringing a separate trespass action for the same incident. They argued that since he accepted the goods as a full satisfaction for the trespass, he could not collect additional damages for the same loss. The defendants requested dismissals of the actions based on these legal principles and the purported errors in judgment by the lower courts.

In the case titled "John Hughes, Plaintiff in Error, v. Samuel S. Streeter, Defendant in Error," the events took place in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, leading up to a court decision issued by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1860. The case arose after John Hughes attempted to quash an execution issued against him based on a judgment obtained by Samuel S. Streeter. The judgment in question dated back to August 16, 1859, where Streeter successfully claimed $618.92. The dispute intensified following a sale of property that supposedly satisfied this judgment; however, Hughes contended that the execution should be invalidated because the sale had already fulfilled the obligation of the judgment. Hughes' plea, backed by affidavit evidence, emphasized that once a judgment has been satisfied through the sale of property, no further execution could be issued until the satisfaction of that judgment was officially vacated by a competent court. The court's initial ruling allowed the continuation of the execution against Hughes, leading to his request for review in order to overturn the decision that had set aside the sale and returned the satisfaction of the judgment.	The plaintiff, John Hughes, claimed that the execution issued on August 16, 1859, was invalid because the judgment had already been satisfied through a prior sale of property. He argued that, according to established legal principles, no additional execution could occur unless the prior satisfaction was formally vacated by a court. Consequently, Hughes requested the court to quash the second execution based on his argument that the previous transaction fulfilled the judgment obligation.	The defendant, Samuel S. Streeter, countered by requesting that the court set aside the sale of the property made under the initial execution due to a defective description of the land, which failed to properly identify the specific parcel sold. He pointed out that lack of a clear and definite description meant no legal title passed from the sale, justifying the need to vacate the previous judgment satisfaction and to correct the execution process to properly reflect any rights acquired and enforce the judgment he sought.

In January 1869, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed the case of The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company v. Thomas Payne, Administrator of Albert Payne, deceased. The incident occurred in Adams County, Illinois, when Albert T. Payne was driving a covered buggy on a highway and was struck by a train operated by the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company at a railway crossing. Payne was killed instantly. The plaintiff, Thomas Payne, the administrator of Albert's estate, initiated the lawsuit under an act from 1853, claiming that the railroad company's negligence caused the death. He alleged failure to provide warning signals at the crossing, such as a warning board, bell ringing, or train whistle, and claimed that the train's engineer was intoxicated at the time of the accident. The case involved significant legal discussions about negligence, liability, and the responsibilities of both parties in the event of an accident at a railroad crossing.	The plaintiff claimed that the defendant's negligence directly caused the death of Albert Payne. He argued that the railroad company failed to provide adequate warnings at the railway crossing, which included not sounding a whistle or ringing a bell as mandated by law. He contended that the company was grossly negligent, asserting that even if Albert Payne exhibited some negligence in approaching the crossing, it should not absolve the company of liability if their negligence was greater.	The defendant contested the claims of negligence, asserting that Albert Payne himself failed to exercise ordinary care as he approached the railroad crossing. The railroad company denied that they were negligent and argued that any potential negligence on their part did not exceed that of the deceased. They emphasized that the plaintiff must demonstrate that their negligence was grossly greater than that of Payne for them to be liable.

In 1886, in the city of Chicago, Mary E. Campbell and Andrew Campbell were married. Shortly after their marriage, Mary alleged that Andrew began a pattern of extreme cruelty, which included numerous threats and physical abuse. On May 9, 1886, she claimed that Andrew violently assaulted her by choking, beating, and bruising her. Furthermore, on that same day, he allegedly threatened her life and forcibly took a gold watch that belonged to her. Mary filed for divorce based on these claims of extreme and repeated cruelty. The case initially went to the Circuit Court of Cook County, where the court sustained Andrew's demurrer, dismissing Mary's bill on the grounds that her allegations did not sufficiently state a cause for divorce. Mary appealed this decision, leading the case to be reviewed by the Illinois Appellate Court.	Mary E. Campbell, the plaintiff, argued that her husband Andrew had committed extreme and repeated cruelty, which included various acts of physical violence and threats against her life. She requested a divorce, asserting that the allegations made were sufficient under Illinois law to substantiate her claim of cruelty and that at least two distinct acts of personal violence were adequately detailed.	Andrew Campbell, the defendant, claimed that the plaintiff's allegations did not sufficiently establish the grounds for divorce. He demurred to the bill, maintaining that the evidence presented did not support the claims of extreme and repeated cruelty. His request was for the court to dismiss Mary’s bill for divorce entirely.

In January 1873, the case of Henry Heberer v. Margaret Heberer et al. was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in St. Clair County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included Henry Heberer, the appellant, and Margaret Heberer, the widow of the deceased George H. Heberer, along with his children: Henry, Adam, Peter, and Charles Heberer. The case revolved around a dispute for the partition of a parcel of land after George H. Heberer's death. The partition was complicated as the commissioners reported that a division could not be made without significant prejudice to the parties involved. The land was appraised at $3720, but during the sale, it was sold for $3500 due to a lack of bids, and the widow was allowed to occupy part of the residence as her homestead. Subsequently, exceptions were raised against the sale, claiming inadequate pricing and lack of competition. The court determined that no fraud occurred, but the sale was contested on grounds of inadequacy of price, prompting a motion for a re-sale.	Henry Heberer claimed that the land was sold for a price that was significantly below its actual value, arguing that there was inadequate competition during the sale. He requested the court to set aside the sale and order a re-sale of the property, asserting that the original appraisal value was not adequately represented by the sale price and highlighted possible buyer interest that could increase the sale amount.	The defendants, including Margaret Heberer and the minor heirs, argued that the sale had been properly conducted with adequate advertising and bidding. They maintained that while there was a claim of inadequate price, there was no proof of fraud or misrepresentation during the sale process. They requested the court to uphold the original sale and dismiss the motion to set it aside, as they believed the transaction was valid and above board.

In the case of John Maloney et al. v. Edward Dewey et al., the events unfolded in Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1889. Edward Dewey, as the complainant, obtained a decree in the Circuit Court of the United States for the foreclosure of a deed of trust on land owned by Mary Maloney, who was deceased. The defendants in the foreclosure case included John Maloney, William Maloney, John Maloney Jr., Catherine Maloney, and others who claimed some interest in the property as heirs of Mary Maloney. Following the court's decree, the property was sold, and Dewey became the purchaser. Subsequently, John Maloney et al. filed a bill in the Superior Court, asserting that the United States courts' decree was void against John Maloney Jr. and William Maloney, citing reasons including their mental incapacities and the illegality of the guardian ad litem. Ultimately, the court's jurisdiction and the validity of the original decree were contested by the plaintiffs, hoping to regain their ability to redeem the property based on a lack of due process.	The plaintiffs, including John Maloney Jr. and William Maloney, argued that the foreclosure decree was void due to several issues: John Maloney Jr. was a minor at the time of the decree, and the guardian ad litem was a clerk of the court, violating conflict of interest rules. Additionally, they claimed William Maloney was insane during the process, and thus, inadequate protections were provided for his rights. They contended that no grounds existed for the legality of the sale and sought to have the decree annulled so they could redeem the property based on these claims of improper jurisdiction and procedural violations.	The defendants, including Dewey, countered the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that the preceding court had proper jurisdiction over the matter. They argued that the plaintiffs did not demonstrate sufficient grounds for invalidating the decree, claiming that most objections were not adequately presented in the initial bill. Furthermore, they maintained that any alleged fraud or error in the original proceedings did not nullify the decree’s authority because the questions at hand were not sufficient to challenge jurisdiction. The defendants also highlighted their status as bona fide purchasers, asserting that their rights should remain protected and the original decree affirmed.

In 1884, the case of Board of Supervisors v. H. S. Magoon took place in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The conflict arose when H. S. Magoon, the appellee, sought to alter a road that crossed his land. He initially petitioned the road commissioners of Scoles Mound township for the alteration, but they denied his request. Magoon then appealed the commissioners’ decision to three supervisors, who conducted a lengthy trial to evaluate the merits of the case. After the trial, the supervisors affirmed the decision of the road commissioners. Dissatisfied with this outcome, Magoon filed a common law writ of certiorari to court, seeking to quash the proceedings of the supervisors and commissioners on the grounds that the necessary legal protocols were not followed during the hearings about the road's alteration. The circuit court quashed the writ, leading to an appeal to the Appellate Court for the Second District, which upheld the circuit court's judgment. Subsequently, the case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court.	H. S. Magoon, the plaintiff, claimed that the road commissioners did not properly notify him about the hearings regarding his petition to alter the road and that the proceedings were invalid as a result. He argued that due process was violated in the decision-making process of the commissioners and supervisors, which caused him a legal disadvantage. Thus, he sought to have the court quash the proceedings and declare the decisions made by the supervisors and commissioners void.	The Board of Supervisors contended that Magoon had participated actively in the proceedings and, therefore, was estopped from challenging their legality afterward. They pointed out that he had received adequate notice of the hearings and continued to seek the alteration throughout the process, indicating his acknowledgment of the proceedings' legitimacy. The supervisors asserted that proper procedure had been followed, and they asked the court to uphold their decision and affirm the validity of the original hearings.

In September 1870, the case of Hannah Strother v. Robert Law was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, involving parties from Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, Hannah Strother, filed the case as the widow of Bolton F. Strother, who had passed away. The case arose from a mortgage executed by her and her late husband to Van H. Higgins on certain premises. Following a default in payment, the mortgage deed contained an irrevocable power of sale allowing for the premises' sale without court intervention. The sale occurred post-mortem of the mortgagor, raising questions regarding the legality of such a sale after the death of Bolton F. Strother. The court examined the nature of powers in a mortgage, particularly a power coupled with an interest, which allows such actions even after the grantor's death. Various objections to the sale's regularity were presented, including challenges to the sale's execution and the adequacy of notice publication. Ultimately, the court concluded that the objections were unfounded, affirming the legitimacy of the power exercised and the sale made.	Hannah Strother, as the plaintiff, claimed the right to redeem the mortgaged premises and sought dower rights in the property sold under the mortgage. Her primary argument hinged on the assertion that the sale, conducted post her husband's death, was illegitimate because the power of sale under the mortgage should not have extended beyond his life, thereby preserving her interest in the property.	The defendant, Robert Law, maintained that the sale was valid and legally executed under the irrevocable power granted in the mortgage. He argued that the power was coupled with an interest, allowing the sale to proceed despite Bolton F. Strother’s death. Moreover, he contended that the objections regarding the sale's process and notice were without merit and that the deed duly transferred absolute title to the property in question.

The case "George F. Harding v. Frederick C. Gibbs" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court on May 9, 1888. It centers around a lease agreement and an option to purchase real estate located in Illinois. On March 25, 1885, Frederick C. Gibbs leased the premises from Uzziel P. Smith, which included an agreement allowing Gibbs to purchase the property within the first year for $9,500. The terms stipulated that Gibbs had the right to be notified of any outside offers, which he could match within ten days. If he chose not to, Smith could sell to another party. On May 9, 1885, Smith informed Gibbs of an external offer of $9,500, but Gibbs did not respond within the designated timeframe. Subsequently, George F. Harding purchased the property outright from Smith, who had conveyed ownership before Gibbs was notified. Gibbs later attempted to exercise his purchase option by tendering payment and demanding a deed, leading to this lawsuit for specific performance against Smith and Harding after Harding refused to sell.	The plaintiff, Frederick C. Gibbs, argued that he should be granted specific performance of the purchase option included in the original lease with Uzziel P. Smith. He maintained that Smith's communication or lack thereof regarding the sale did not negate his rights under the agreement to purchase the property. Gibbs claimed that he acted in good faith and should be granted the ability to complete the purchase as outlined within the terms of the lease.	The defendants, George F. Harding and Uzziel P. Smith, contended that Gibbs failed to comply with the terms of the option agreement, which required him to respond to its conditions promptly. They argued that since Gibbs did not elect to purchase within the required ten days after notice of an outside offer, his option to purchase lapsed. The defendants emphasized that Harding's acquisition of the property was valid, and Gibbs was not entitled to specific performance due to his negligence in exercising his rights timely.

In 1888, in Adams County, Illinois, George W. Montgomery and others filed a legal action against William L. Black, Samuel N. Black, and Charles C. Connor. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants were partners under the firm name W. L. Black & Co. and were responsible for a promissory note of $100 and a bank overdraft of $1,038.02. The case arose due to the plaintiffs' assertion that the defendants, as partners, had incurred debts that they were liable to repay. Two of the defendants, Samuel N. Black and Connor, denied their joint liability. The trial was held without a jury, and the court ultimately found in favor of the defendants, leading to an appeal by the plaintiffs. The Appellate Court affirmed the initial decision, supporting the finding that the defendants were not liable for the debts attributed to W. L. Black & Co.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants were partners in the firm W. L. Black & Co. and were therefore jointly liable for the outstanding debts represented by the promissory note and overdraft in question. They requested the court to hold the defendants liable for the debts incurred under the firm name.	The defendants contended that they were not partners under the name W. L. Black & Co. and denied any joint liability for the debts claimed by the plaintiffs. They argued that the representations of W. L. Black about the firm did not bind them, and thus they should not be held responsible for the debts incurred in his dealings.

John W. Norris filed a legal case against the Merchants National Bank of Deadwood, Dakota, on August 18, 1887, in the Superior Court to obtain an attachment against the defendants. Shortly after filing, a writ of attachment was issued and served on garnishees. The defendants responded on August 31, 1887, entering a special appearance to move to dismiss the suit for lack of jurisdiction. Following some procedural exchanges, the defendants filed a general issue on September 21 and moved to dismiss the case on November 7, 1887. The court delayed its decision until April 7, 1888, when it denied the motion to dismiss. However, on April 21, the court agreed to set aside its earlier order, allowing the defendants to withdraw their plea and ultimately dismissed the suit. The court refused to set aside this dismissal order on April 28, 1888. The plaintiff appealed, citing error in the dismissals and the jurisdictional issues surrounding national banks due to separate congressional legislation.	The plaintiff, John W. Norris, argued that the defendants' attempts to dismiss the suit for want of jurisdiction were unfounded, especially since they had waived any objection to jurisdiction by entering a general plea. He contended that the dismissal was erroneous and sought to have the court reverse the dismissal so that the case could proceed on its merits.	The Merchants National Bank contended that the jurisdiction issue was valid and that federal law precluded state courts from issuing attachments against national banks. They maintained that by their actions, they had not waived their right to challenge jurisdiction and formally requested that the court dismiss the case against them.

The case of **Joshua W. Cabeen v. James T. Breckenridge** took place in September 1868 in Mercer County, Illinois. The dispute centered around a tract of land that both parties claimed to own. Joshua W. Cabeen, the plaintiff, sought to recover the land via an ejectment action in the circuit court after he secured a deed (dated December 7, 1863) that transferred the property to him from James Smith, who had received it from Joseph Watson, and Watson had previously obtained it from the original patentee, Daniel Dougherty. The crux of the case lay in the fact that the defendant, James T. Breckenridge, was already in possession of the premises under a lease from Daniel Pauline, who had a longstanding claim that predated Cabeen's ownership. Both Cabeen and Breckenridge derived title from the same source, with Breckenridge’s lease agreement established prior to the recording of Cabeen's deed. The circuit court listened to evidence from both sides to determine who held the legal title to the land.	Joshua W. Cabeen contended that he had a valid claim to the property based on his recorded deed from James Smith, which established his legal title. Cabeen argued that the defendant's possession of the property was unlawful since he was claiming through a lease that originated after Cabeen's title was recorded. He requested that the court uphold his ownership of the land and rule in his favor, allowing him to eject Breckenridge from the property.	James T. Breckenridge defended his position by arguing that he held superior title due to his prior possession and lease arrangements with Daniel Pauline, which predated the recording of Cabeen's deed. He claimed that the principle of possession serves as notice, which protected his rights to the land despite Cabeen's subsequent deed. Breckenridge requested that the court dismiss Cabeen's claims and uphold his right to possession, asserting that he had the better title based on his occupying the premises openly and visibly.

In 1876, the case of Frederick Trude, Administrator vs. John Meyer took place in Cook County, Illinois. The case arose after the death of John Trude, whose estate was represented by Frederick Trude, the administrator. The dispute centered around a promissory note for six hundred dollars that John Meyer, the defendant, allegedly issued to John Trude during his lifetime. Both individuals were of German descent and were known to be closely acquainted. The plaintiff presented evidence in the form of a written instrument in German, which was translated to acknowledge the receipt of six hundred dollars from Johann Trude. However, the defendant contended that the note had already been paid prior to Trude's death. He maintained that he made the payment in cash, except for one hundred sixty dollars, for which he issued another note found among the deceased’s effects. A jury trial resulted in a verdict favoring the defendant, leading Frederick Trude to appeal the decision.	Frederick Trude claimed that John Meyer owed the estate six hundred dollars based on a promissory note. He argued that the note had not been paid and sought the outstanding amount. The plaintiff believed that the circumstances surrounding the note's possession and payment were suspicious, particularly alleging that it may have been taken from a sick John Trude without proper authority. During the trial, the plaintiff sought to introduce evidence confirming the amount owed but failed to properly assert a claim for one hundred sixty dollars, which he now suggests should be considered.	John Meyer contended that he had fully satisfied the debt represented by the promissory note. He claimed that he paid six hundred dollars in cash to John Trude shortly before his death, along with providing a written note for the remaining one hundred sixty dollars. Meyer’s defense was based on the premise that the payment had occurred, and therefore, no debt remained. He argued that the plaintiff failed to state any claim for the outstanding one hundred sixty dollars in the original pleadings, making them ineligible for recovery.

On February 16, 1881, Patrick McGinnis sold seven thousand bushels of corn to Herbert S. Gilbert & Co. at a price of thirty-nine cents per bushel, with delivery scheduled for August and September of that year. As part of their agreement, Gilbert & Co. was to provide financial advances to McGinnis as needed throughout the contract. Shortly after the agreement, when McGinnis sought an advance, he refused to sign a note, asserting that he could get funds from the bank instead. Gilbert & Co. insisted on a note for the advance and consequently, McGinnis denied the delivery of corn. On October 3, 1881, Gilbert & Co. filed a lawsuit against McGinnis in La Salle County Circuit Court for breach of contract due to the non-delivery of corn. The trial court ruled in favor of McGinnis, and this decision was upheld by the Appellate Court, leading Gilbert & Co. to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The key issue in the case was whether evidence regarding a customary practice of requiring notes for advances could be introduced in court.	Herbert S. Gilbert & Co. contended that McGinnis failed to deliver the corn as per their agreement, which entitled them to damages. They argued that a customary practice among grain merchants involved taking notes for advances made under such contracts, and they sought to introduce evidence of this practice to support their case and explain the ambiguity surrounding the contract terms.	Patrick McGinnis maintained that he fulfilled his obligations under the contract and that Gilbert & Co. had no right to enforce the agreement without the stipulated terms being met, namely the requirement of a note for any advances. His defense focused on the assertion that the custom Gilbert & Co. referred to was inconsistent with their express agreement, and thus, evidence of this custom should not be admissible in court.

In 1881, John Davidson and Richard Reardon, serving as Highway Commissioners of Du Page Township in Illinois, undertook the construction of a tile drain aimed at improving drainage for a roadway. This project was predicated on an agreement with their co-defendant, Thomas T. Sprague, who claimed he would manage the resulting water flow. However, Sprague later extended the drain toward the property of Thomas T. Sprague, directing water onto Sprague's land, which led to flooding and damage. Sprague initiated a trespass case against Davidson and Reardon, alleging that their actions in constructing the drain caused significant adverse effects on his land, rendering it less suitable for use. The case was adjudicated in the Circuit Court of Will County, where it was determined by a judge, given that a jury was waived. The court found Davidson and Reardon responsible for the damages incurred by Sprague and determined the compensation owed for the flooding incident.	The plaintiff, Thomas T. Sprague, argued that the actions of Davidson and Reardon in constructing a tile drain resulted in significant flooding on his land. He claimed that they acted with negligence and carelessness, directly leading to the overflow of surface water that damaged his property. The plaintiff sought damages assessed at $50 for the losses he incurred due to the drainage system put in place by the defendants.	The defendants, Davidson and Reardon, contended that they were not responsible for the flooding of Sprague's land as the damage resulted from the actions of their co-defendant, Lord. They claimed that they acted within their rights as highway commissioners to manage water flow, and that any adverse effects on Sprague’s property were due to Lord’s unauthorized extension of the drain, not their actions. They requested the court to reverse the initial judgment against them and asserted that the plaintiff failed to prove that their actions directly caused the damages.

In April 1866, the case 'Town of Vinegar Hill v. John Busson' took place in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The Town of Vinegar Hill initiated legal action against John Busson for allegedly obstructing a public highway. This roadway had reportedly been in public use for over twenty years, and the Town claimed to have a survey confirming its status as a public road. The case was brought first to a justice of the peace, then appealed to the Circuit Court, where a jury trial ultimately favored Busson. Unsatisfied with the ruling, the Town appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court for further review. The Supreme Court's discourse centered around jury instructions regarding public road status and the sufficiency of evidence presented regarding the use of the highway in question.	The Town of Vinegar Hill claimed that there was a long-standing public use of the road obstructed by Busson, which amounted to the right of the road being established by prescription. They sought legal recognition of the road as a public highway and requested damages for the obstruction caused by Busson.	John Busson defended against the claims by arguing that the plaintiff had not sufficiently demonstrated the road's legal status as a public highway at the time the lawsuit commenced. He contended that the jury was properly instructed regarding the legal requirements to ascertain whether the road in question was indeed a public highway. His request was to uphold the decision of the Circuit Court, which favored him and ruled against the Town's claims.

This case, "Doan, King & Company v. Sidney S. Duncan," took place in December 1856 before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in July 1854 when one Clarkson, who was employed as a clerk by defendant Sidney S. Duncan in Waverly, Illinois, purchased goods from the plaintiffs, wholesale merchants based in St. Louis, Missouri. Clarkson bought a bill of goods worth $305.62 on behalf of Duncan but appropriated the goods for his own use. The plaintiffs argued that Clarkson was authorized by Duncan to make the purchase. The court had to determine whether Clarkson, employed as a store clerk, had the authority to buy goods on credit in a foreign market for his employer. The evidence suggested Clarkson had acted on behalf of Duncan in previous transactions, but the court found the evidence inconclusive regarding his authority for this specific purchase. The outcome hinged on whether a clerk, by virtue of employment, had the implied authority to make significant purchases on credit.	The plaintiffs, Doan, King & Company, claimed that they were owed $305.62 for goods sold and delivered to Clarkson, whom they maintained was authorized by Duncan to make the purchase. They sought to hold Duncan liable on the grounds that Clarkson acted within his employment authority.	The defendant, Sidney S. Duncan, contended he was not liable because Clarkson, as a clerk, did not possess the authority to purchase goods on credit for him. Duncan argued that a clerk’s role inherently does not include the power to make such purchases, thereby exempting him from responsibility for the transaction. He maintained that the evidence did not sufficiently establish any prior authorization or subsequent ratification of Clarkson's actions.

In 1882, Henry M. Green initiated a legal case following the failure of William L. Pitts, the supervisor of Cerro Gordo township, to fulfill the duties associated with his position. Pitts, who was elected as supervisor, was responsible for managing funds collected from dog licenses but allegedly neglected to handle them according to statutory requirements. The case was filed in the Illinois Appellate Court where the plaintiff, on behalf of the people of Cerro Gordo, argued against Pitts' sureties, including Jonathan Quinn and the plaintiff himself, for breach of an official bond. Pitts had died on September 15, 1882, and the suit claimed that he failed to disburse the dog license funds as mandated. The court primarily examined the sufficiency of the declaration against the sureties and the legal requirements for establishing their liability. It was concluded that the declaration did not adequately demonstrate a breach of the bond's conditions, as there was insufficient evidence that Pitts had not fulfilled his obligations or that the sureties were liable for the funds he managed. The case was presided over by the Circuit Court of Piatt County, Judge C. B. Smith, before being appealed.	The plaintiff contended that Pitts failed to fulfill his duties as supervisor, specifically regarding the management of a license fund collected before his re-election. The suit sought damages for the alleged breach of the sureties' bond, asserting that the money remained unaccounted for and was necessary for the town's use. The plaintiff argued that the bond held by the sureties made them responsible for any losses incurred by the town due to Pitts' failure to disburse the funds appropriately.	The defendants, acting as sureties for Pitts, argued that the plaintiff did not sufficiently establish a cause of action against them. They contended that without a positive assertion that the money was still in Pitts' possession at the end of his term or that they were required to respond until a formal demand was made, there was no legal basis for liability. Furthermore, they asserted that merely dying without having paid disbursed the funds did not constitute a breach of the bond’s conditions.

The case "Henry Weaver, Admr. v. Peter Fries" took place in St. Clair County, Illinois, in June 1877. At the heart of the case was a promissory note executed on May 6, 1867, by Peter Fries in favor of Frederick Weaver, the father of Fries' wife. The note promised to pay $400 with interest of ten percent per annum. The plaintiff, Henry Weaver, acting as the administrator of Frederick Weaver’s estate, brought forth the case against Peter Fries to collect on the note. The defendant, Fries, claimed that the note was meant solely as a record of an advancement of $100 from Frederick to him and his wife, implying that there was a mutual understanding that he would not be required to repay it. The alleged agreement included conversations wherein Frederick Weaver supposedly disclaimed any intention to hold Fries liable for the note. The primary legal issues arose from the defendant's pleas, which contended the note was not a legally enforceable obligation.	The plaintiff argued that Fries was legally obligated to repay the $400 stated in the promissory note. The plaintiff maintained that the execution of the promissory note was valid and that it was supported by adequate consideration. They sought a judgment to recover the amount owed under the terms of the note, including interest.	The defendant contended that the promissory note was executed as a mere memorandum of a $100 advancement intended for him and his wife, and that there was an explicit understanding that he would not be liable for repayment. Fries argued that the note was invalid as a binding contract due to the verbal agreement that should supersede the written obligation. He claimed that any conversation where Frederick indicated he would not demand payment supported his case, asserting that there was no legal basis for enforcing the note due to its supposed lack of consideration.

The case of "William Carr v. James Barnett" took place in Vermilion County, Illinois, with a judgment issued on August 26, 1886. The dispute arose over a horse that the defendant, James Barnett, had taken up as an estray about ten years prior to the suit. Barnett had appraised the horse and subsequently purchased it during an irregular sale without fully complying with the estray laws. Since then, he claimed ownership and used the horse as his own. The plaintiff, William Carr, was unaware of Barnett's claim until shortly before initiating the lawsuit. Carr sought to recover possession of the horse through a replevin action. The case presented issues regarding the rightful ownership and the compliance with estray law, as well as the timing of the legal action concerning the Statute of Limitations on property claims.	William Carr argued that he was the rightful owner of the horse and sought its return through a replevin action. He contended that the defendant had unlawfully converted the horse to his own use and that his possession was not legitimate due to non-compliance with estray laws. Carr maintained that he should be entitled to recover the horse despite the time that had passed since Barnett's initial claim, asserting that the unlawful appropriation granted him a valid cause of action.	James Barnett defended against Carr's claims by arguing that the Statute of Limitations of five years applied to the case, as the cause of action accrued when he first took possession of the horse ten years prior. He asserted that since the legal claim fell outside this time frame, Carr's action was barred. Barnett also noted that he had not concealed his possession and claim of the horse, emphasizing that the statute provided him a complete defense to the replevin suit.

In January 1869, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case "Joseph Peyton et al. v. Martha Jeffries," originating from the Circuit Court of Coles County. The case involved Martha Jeffries, the widow of John P. Jeffries, who sought the assignment of her dower in part of lot 53 in Charleston, Illinois, where a three-story brick building had been leased by her husband before his death on November 2, 1859. Following John Jeffries' death, the estate's administrators sold the property to Joseph Peyton on April 3, 1862, to pay debts, prompting Martha to file a suit in October 1865 for her dower rights. The defendants, including Peyton, argued against her entitlement to dower in the purchased property, citing various legal statutes that differentiate between dower and homestead rights. The case dealt with the allocation of Martha's dower and her claims regarding rents from the property, which had been destroyed by fire in 1861. The background includes complex interactions regarding the sale of the property, debts of the late John Jeffries, and competing claims from both the widow and the purchasers.	Martha Jeffries claimed she was entitled to dower rights in one-third of the rental value of part of lot 53 from 1862 onwards, including interest. She requested fair compensation for her dower rights and sought to establish that her dower should not be limited to only properties she occupied as a homestead. Furthermore, she demanded that her dower interest be honored and assigned on the lot despite the sale.	The defendants argued that the assignment of dower should be restricted solely to the homestead where Martha lived. They contended that the court improperly calculated the amount payable to Martha and exempted her from her share of necessary repairs and taxes on the lot. Additionally, the defendants claimed that the decree could not hold them jointly liable for the dower payment since their interests were distinct and separate. They sought to reverse the decree that allowed Martha too large a portion of the rental income and incorrectly directed the sale of the property with inadequate redemption terms.

Edward B. Lycan was indicted for embezzlement in 1883, following a controversial transaction involving Ellen Wilkes, his employer. The case unfolded in Peoria County, Illinois, where Lycan was accused of unlawfully converting significant funds belonging to Wilkes, specifically $600, which he was entrusted with. This embezzlement case arose after Wilkes had given a mortgage on her possessions to Newton Matthews to prevent creditors from seizing her property. She claimed that Lycan, whom she trusted to manage the sale of her assets, ultimately failed to turn over the full proceeds. Despite a defense claiming that Lycan had legitimately purchased the property and paid Wilkes, the jury found him guilty and he was sentenced to three years in prison. However, the trial's integrity was questioned due to judicial remarks suggesting the judge's dissatisfaction with the testimony, which may have biased the jury against the defendant.	The plaintiff, Ellen Wilkes, argued that Edward B. Lycan, as her agent, had unlawfully embezzled $600 of her money with the intent to convert it for personal use. She maintained that the defendant was obligated to turn over the proceeds from the sale of her properties, which he failed to do, effectively stealing from her under the guise of managing her assets.	Edward B. Lycan contended that he acted in good faith and had purchased the property from Wilkes. He maintained that he paid her for the assets as agreed and claimed that the sale proceeds were not as high as asserted by Wilkes. His defense also pointed out that the court's comments during the trial could have influenced the jury's perception of his testimony, arguing that these remarks were prejudicial and unprofessional.

In the case of George Miller et al. v. William H. Bruns et al., heard in April 1866, the legal proceedings occurred in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, William H. Bruns and Charles Wachsmuth, initiated an action of assumpsit, a type of contract law claim, against the defendants George Miller and Robert Stafford, regarding the purchase of high wines. The case was tried in the Circuit Court, and after a jury verdict favored the plaintiffs, a motion for a new trial by the defendants was denied. The dispute centered on whether the defendants had implicitly admitted the correctness of an account for high wines, the details of which were communicated to them in November 1864. The plaintiffs presented a detailed account indicating a balance owed of $915.14. The case raised significant questions about business practices and the treatment of unobjected accounts among merchants.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had sent an account to the defendants detailing the purchases of high wines along with the amounts owed, including interest and credits. They argued that since the defendants did not object to the correctness of this account within a reasonable time, it should be regarded as an admission of its correctness. The plaintiffs sought the payment of the alleged balance due based on this account.	The defendants contended that the court erred in its instructions to the jury about the implications of the unobjected account. They argued for a new trial on the basis that the jury was not properly instructed to consider the lack of objections as an automatic admission of the account's correctness, rather than just a circumstance to evaluate. The defendants requested that the judgment be overturned and that they receive a new trial.

The case "Louis Houck v. Joshua L. Yates" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1876. It originated from a suit in ejectment brought by plaintiff Joshua L. Yates against Louis Houck over an undivided half of 300 acres of land on Dickey’s Island, located in the Mississippi River, specifically on the Illinois side in Alexander County. The parties agreed to a set of facts to limit expenses, noting that the land in question had emerged about 20 to 25 years prior, and had increased in size over time to roughly 600 acres. They acknowledged that the island's legal boundaries were defined based on established government surveys, specifically regarding fractional sections of land near the Mississippi River. The court examined arguments about the navigability of the river and its implications for land ownership, particularly the rights of riparian owners. The dispute included the definition of boundaries as they pertained to meandered lines established for surveying purposes.	Yates claimed a valid title in fee simple to the disputed land, arguing that the boundary of his property extended to the center of the Mississippi River due to his status as a riparian owner. He sought legal recognition of this claim and an injunction against Houck's encroachment on what he asserted was his rightful property.	Houck contended that the Mississippi River was not navigable according to common law definitions, which limited the reach of Yates's property claim. He argued that the meandered line run by the government surveyors should define the southern boundary of Yates's land, thereby excluding the disputed strip of land from Yates's ownership. He requested that the court uphold this interpretation, thereby denying Yates's claims to the land.

The case of Mary E. Butz, Administratrix, v. Jacob Schwartz arose from a promissory note dispute and was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on November 23, 1889. The case took place in Adams County, Illinois. The original plaintiff (the payee of the note) died after the suit was initiated, and Mary E. Butz was appointed as the administratrix of the deceased plaintiff's estate, stepping in as the new plaintiff. The case involved multiple trials; two previous trials resulted in verdicts for the defendant, Jacob Schwartz, while one jury was unable to reach a verdict. The primary contention was whether Schwartz had signed the promissory note, and if so, whether his signature was secured through fraud. Key individuals in the case included the defendant Jacob Schwartz, the deceased original plaintiff, and agents of the payees David W. Jennings and Marion Hughes, who testified about the circumstances of the note's execution.	The plaintiff contended that the defendant fraudulently obtained his signature on a promissory note. Specifically, they argued that the defendants’ agents misrepresented the purpose of the note, which was purportedly meant to facilitate a business arrangement involving lightning rods. The plaintiff sought to prove that these fraudulent actions invalidated the defendant's obligation under the note.	The defendant, Jacob Schwartz, claimed he validly signed the promissory note and denied any allegations of fraud. He argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiff was insufficient to establish fraud, maintaining that the note was executed legally as part of a legitimate transaction concerning lightning rods.
