He requested the court to admit his testimonies regarding conversations with the agents involved.

In the case of John J. McLean v. The County of Montgomery, which took place in Montgomery County, Illinois, during the late 19th century, the legal dispute arose due to payments made to McLean while he served as the circuit clerk from December 1880 to December 1888. After collecting various fees associated with his responsibilities, it was acknowledged that McLean received payments from the county treasury to compensate for a deficiency in his salary and other office expenses that had not been fully covered. The trial revealed that McLean's office earnings during his first term amounted to over $15,500, and during his second term, he collected nearly $13,400; however, he claimed that certain necessary expenses and deputy hires exceeded the fees collected. The case was tried without a jury, focusing on the legality of the payments made to McLean for fees in criminal cases that he argued were necessary due to unpaid salary.	The plaintiff, the County of Montgomery, claimed that McLean received unauthorized payments for criminal case fees because he had already collected sufficient fees to cover his salary. They argued that these fees should not have been reimbursed from the county treasury under Section 15 of Chapter 53, which restricts such payments when the fees collected equal or exceed the clerk's salary. The plaintiff sought restitution of $1,507.72 that had been improperly paid.	McLean contended that his collected fees were used to pay for necessary office expenses and deputy salaries, leading to a shortfall in his own salary. He argued that since the county board had approved his expenses in prior audits, they were bound by their own actions and could not recover the payments, citing an estoppel. He maintained that the funds he received were justified given the operations of his office.

The case "The Quincy, Missouri and Pacific Railroad Co. v. Isaac N. Morris" originated in Quincy, Illinois, in 1877. The key individuals involved were Isaac N. Morris, a resident property owner and taxpayer, and the Quincy, Missouri and Pacific Railroad Company. The conflict centered around a proposed municipal subscription for railroad stock, amounting to $500,000, which had been voted on by the citizens of Quincy in 1869. The election was held under an ordinance by the city council, but at the time, no law existed authorizing such a subscription. After the adoption of a new state constitution in 1870, which prohibited municipalities from subscribing to private corporations unless authorized by law, Morris sought to prevent the city from issuing bonds to the railroad company for the previously approved stock subscription. He argued that the election and resulting subscription were invalid as they lacked the necessary legal authorization. The city council had made a subscription and authorized the issuing of bonds following a state law passed in 1871, declaring such actions valid despite their initial illegality. The core issue of the case rested on the legality of the bond issuance based on the prior citizen vote and subsequent constitutional provisions.	Isaac N. Morris claimed that the city of Quincy was unlawfully attempting to issue bonds to the Quincy, Missouri and Pacific Railroad Company based on a subscription of stock that was not valid due to the lack of proper legal authorization during the election. He argued that the subscription violated the new constitutional prohibition against municipal aid to private entities and was thus seeking a court order to prevent the bond issuance and validate the city’s actions.	The Quincy, Missouri and Pacific Railroad Company contended that the subscription had been legally established following appropriate legislative actions. They argued that the bond issuance was legitimate because the city’s voters had expressed their support for the subscription before the constitutionally imposed restrictions took effect. The defense maintained that the subscription served a corporate purpose by enhancing local trade and commerce, thus justifying the city's engagement with the railroad company.

In the case of George H. Amos et al. v. John C. Burrus, which took place in Greene County, Illinois, the events stem from a legal judgment rendered on December 22, 1881. The plaintiff, George H. Amos, had successfully sued Greene County for damages amounting to four hundred dollars, plus costs of twenty-six dollars and thirty-five cents, in an action of assumpsit. Following this judgment, Amos demanded that the Greene County board of supervisors direct their clerk to issue an order for payment from the county treasurer to cover the judgment and the associated costs. However, the county board refused to comply. Subsequently, Amos filed a petition for a writ of mandamus, requesting the court to compel the county board to pay the ordered amount. In February 1882, the circuit court defaulted on the county board's response, granting the mandamus writ. The board appealed this decision, claiming the request lacked sufficient grounds, as it had not established that funds were available in the treasury to fulfill the payment at that time. The appellate court examined the legal provisions regarding the conditions under which a county may settle judgments and the criteria necessary for the issuance of a mandamus.	The plaintiffs, led by George H. Amos, argued that the county board had a legal obligation to draw an order for the payment of the judgment against Greene County, which included damages and costs awarded to him. They asserted that following the judgment, a request for payment was properly made to the county board, which was legally required to fulfill this request by issuing payment through the county treasurer.	The defendant, represented by the Greene County board, contended that the writ of mandamus should not have been granted because the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that there were sufficient funds in the county treasury to cover the amount due. They argued that under the law, the county board was prohibited from issuing payment orders without available funds and that the plaintiffs did not adequately prove such funds existed.

In June 1870, Henry F. Eames and the Germania Turn Verein entered into a written agreement for the sale of real estate in Chicago, with Eames as the vendor. The contract stipulated a payment of $33,000, divided into installments with the first payment of $500 serving as a deposit, which was to be forfeited if the buyers did not fulfill their payment obligations but refunded if the title was not good. Despite initial approval of the title by Eames’ attorney, concerns arose within the Germania Turn Verein regarding an existing lien of over $51,000 on the property due to a decree against a previous owner, Gage. After learning about this lien, Eames affirmed his willingness to convey a good title if payments were made, but the Germania Turn Verein declared the contract ended, leading Eames to sue for the recovery of the payments made (totaling $2,500). The lower court initially ruled in favor of the Germania Turn Verein, prompting Eames to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The Germania Turn Verein claimed that the property title was not good due to the existing lien from a court decree against a former owner, which they argued justified the cancellation of the contract. They sought to recover the money they had paid towards the purchase of the property.	Eames contended that the lien from the court decree was no longer valid at the time of sale, as it was more than a year old without execution being issued. Thus, he argued, the Germania Turn Verein had no grounds to refuse the fulfillment of the agreement. Eames sought to affirm the contract and recover the payments made.

In September 1873, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Ferdinand Stumps against The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company. The incident occurred on Brown Street, between Luke and Walsh streets, in a street railway context where a branch track led to the lumber district. Seven-year-old Stumps was injured while attempting to climb onto a moving train's ladder. The railway company maintained that Stumps was not near a detached car, and testimony from five unimpeached witnesses supported their claim. The first trial's verdict was reversed, as the court found the jury's decision was against the weight of evidence. During the second trial, additional testimony was presented about the presence of a detached car and Stumps' actions at the time of the accident. The court concluded that there was no evidence of negligence on the railway's part, as the train was operated with great care and was under control, moving slowly and with all crew members present and vigilant.	Ferdinand Stumps, through his next friend A. M. Pence, claimed that The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company was negligent in the operation of their train, leading to his injury. The primary argument was that a detached car was left on the tracks, which contributed to the accident. The plaintiff contended that the company's failure to maintain safety standards directly caused the injury, and therefore sought damages for the personal injuries sustained.	The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company's defense focused on the argument that there was no negligence involved in the operation of the train. They asserted that the train was moving at a lawful and careful speed, and all crew members were performing their duties properly. The defense maintained that if there was a detached car, it did not contribute to Stumps’ injuries since he was found to have been trying to climb onto a moving train, which absolved them of liability.

The case of James Wilhite et al. v. Zadock Pearce et al. originated in the Crawford Circuit Court, Illinois, in June 1868. The parties involved included Zadock A. Pearce and his wife Louisa Jane, as plaintiffs, and James S., Hilton H., William O. Wilhite, Aura Wilhite, Aula Wilhite, I. P. Murphy, and Mary Murphy as defendants, who were heirs-at-law of the deceased Enoch Wilhite. The plaintiffs initiated proceedings in chancery seeking the partition of certain real estate alleged to have belonged to Enoch Wilhite at the time of his death. Proper process was served on all defendants except I. P. Murphy, who was served by reading. Some defendants, being minors, had a guardian ad litem appointed. The adult defendants failed to respond, resulting in a default judgment against them and a decree that the property be sold to settle any liens, distributing the remaining balance among the entitled parties. The defendants subsequently appealed, arguing that critical errors occurred, such as the absence of evidence in the record upon which the decree was based and the improper service of process.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to a partition of the real estate left by Enoch Wilhite. They argued that the defendants, particularly the minors, should be subject to the decree regardless of the lack of evidence presented against them. The plaintiffs requested the court uphold the decree that authorized the sale of the property to satisfy any liens, with the remaining proceeds allocated to the rightful parties.	The defendants contended that the decree was erroneous due to several factors, including the lack of preserved evidence and improper service of process on I. P. Murphy. They asserted that the court failed to establish proof of the alleged lien on the property and did not sufficiently address the claims against the minor defendants. Moreover, they argued that the involvement of a solicitor who acted as the master in the case created a conflict of interest.

In September 1876, the case of John S. Henry v. The Meriam & Morgan Paraffine Company was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a promissory note executed by an individual named Big-don, which was payable to Armstrong & Co. for the amount of $380 and later assigned to John S. Henry, the plaintiff in this case. Henry filed an affidavit alongside his declaration stating that he was owed $380 plus 10% interest from October 16, 1875, as well as $40 in costs incurred while attempting to collect the note. The defendant, The Meriam & Morgan Paraffine Company, responded by pleading a general issue and raising a claim of "nul tiel corporation," arguing that the corporation did not legally exist. Following the pleadings, Henry requested a judgment for the amount claimed, minus the $40 that the defendant acknowledged as a valid offset. The court ruled in favor of Henry, despite the defendant's objections, citing that their claims did not provide a sufficient defense against the outstanding amount owed.	John S. Henry, the plaintiff, claimed he was owed a total of $380 from the defendant as per the assigned promissory note, along with 10% interest since October 16, 1875, and an additional $40 for costs incurred in collection efforts. Henry provided an affidavit demonstrating the amount due and requested a judgment for the outstanding balance, acknowledging the $40 defense raised by the defendant.	The defendant, The Meriam & Morgan Paraffine Company, argued two main points: first, they pleaded a general issue contesting the entirety of the plaintiff’s claims, and second, they claimed "nul tiel corporation," asserting that they did not legally exist as a corporation. The defendant acknowledged a partial defense concerning the $40 but insisted that the court could not issue a judgment as the plea of nul tiel corporation had not been resolved.

The legal case "Mary Parrott v. Austin J. Goss" took place in Cook County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on October 29, 1885. The case arose from an action of covenant initiated by the plaintiff, Austin J. Goss, against the defendant, Mary Parrott. Goss sought to recover damages for an alleged breach of a covenant of warranty against incumbrances in a deed that Parrott had executed. Following the filing of a plea of non esse factum by Parrott, the court entered a default judgment against her for $758.21 and associated costs, without addressing her plea. This raised legal issues regarding the court's authority to enter a default judgment after a plea had been filed, as established by precedent where such an action required the plea to be either struck from the record or otherwise resolved. Consequently, a motion to set aside the default judgment was presented, but procedural limitations prevented the details from being addressed on record, leading to the conclusion that the judgment was issued in error.	The plaintiff, Austin J. Goss, claimed that Mary Parrott had breached a covenant of warranty concerning a deed. He sought damages amounting to $758.21 as compensation for the breach, contending that the default judgment should be upheld as proper legal redress for the violation of the covenant.	Mary Parrott, the defendant, filed a plea of non esse factum, arguing that the deed in question should not be enforced against her. Her primary defense was that the court erred in entering a default judgment while her plea was still on record, indicating that due legal process had not been followed. She sought to have the default judgment vacated based on these procedural issues.

The case "Sullivan vs. Dollins" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1849. The appeal originated from Franklin County, Illinois. The key individuals involved in the case include the appellant, presumably Sullivan, and the appellee, Dollins. The case revolves around a motion to dismiss an appeal based on the authority of the attorney who executed the appeal bond in Sullivan's name. The question arose whether the attorney, II. B. Montgomery, had the appropriate authority to sign on behalf of Sullivan. The court noted that there is a presumption that the clerk of the Circuit Court was satisfied with the attorney’s right to act on behalf of the appellant at the time the appeal bond was accepted. The crux of the legal proceedings involves whether or not additional proof of the attorney’s authority is necessary unless questioned by affidavit.	The plaintiff, Sullivan, claims that the appeal bond executed by his attorney, II. B. Montgomery, should be accepted as valid. Sullivan argues against the motion to dismiss the appeal, relying on the presumption that the clerk ensured the attorney's authority was legitimate when accepting the bond.	The defendant, Dollins, argues that the appeal should be dismissed due to questions regarding the authority of Sullivan's attorney to execute the appeal bond. Dollins contends that the appeal lacks validity unless proper evidence is presented to substantiate the attorney's right to act on behalf of Sullivan.

The case "The City of Chicago v. Washington Hesing, Admr. etc." was decided in September 1876 in Illinois. The case revolved around the tragic drowning of Max Werner, a four-year-old boy who fell into a deep ditch filled with water located in front of his parents' home. The accident occurred while his mother was engaged in her usual domestic duties, allowing the child to leave the house unsupervised. The child fell into the ditch, which was unguarded and considered dangerous, and was not rescued until it was too late, resulting in his death. The child's parents, who were laborers, could not be held liable for negligence, as it was determined that they had taken reasonable care for their child's safety given their working situation. The city was found to have gross negligence in allowing such a hazardous ditch to exist in a public area without any protective measures.	The plaintiff, Washington Hesing, as the administrator of Max Werner's estate, claimed that the city of Chicago was negligent in their duties to maintain safe public spaces, specifically by allowing a deep water-filled ditch to exist without proper safeguards. The plaintiff sought damages for the loss of the child, asserting that the city’s negligence directly contributed to the tragic drowning of the minor.	The city of Chicago, as the defendant, argued against the claims of negligence, suggesting that the mother may have been negligent in not rescuing her child sooner after discovering him in the water. However, the city’s defenses were primarily centered around the assertion that the parents had a duty to supervise their child constantly, a claim which the court rejected due to the parents' working-class status and the child's young age. The city sought to deny liability based on these points.

In September 1876, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the case of The People ex rel. John H. Hungate v. Almond B. Cole, an attorney accused of failing to pay over money collected in a legal judgment. The case originated from a judgment obtained by an attorney firm in March 1870, representing Robert B. Bussell against George W. Calvert, for a total amount of $314.40. The defendant, Almond B. Cole, acknowledged collecting $280 from Calvert, but failed to pay over the full amount owed to Bussell during his lifetime or to Hungate, acting on behalf of Bussell's estate. Upon Bussell's death in December 1872, Cole retained $80 of the judgment amount, which he refrained from paying, citing the lack of an authorized party to receive the payment. The court examined these claims and determined that Cole had willfully withheld funds that were meant to be held in trust for his client, violating his professional obligations as an attorney.	Hungate, representing the estate of Robert B. Bussell, claimed that Almond B. Cole, as their attorney, had unlawfully retained funds collected on behalf of Bussell. The plaintiff argued that Cole failed to pay the collected money to Bussell before his death and subsequently to Hungate after being appointed as the administrator of the estate. The legal request was to have Cole's name removed from the roll of attorneys due to his breach of professional conduct by withholding funds owed to the estate.	Almond B. Cole defended himself by claiming that the appointment of the administrator of Bussell's estate was somehow illegal, which he argued justified his refusal to pay the withheld funds. He contended that there was no authorized party to give a valid receipt for the funds collected. However, the court found that such excuses were insufficient to absolve him from his professional responsibilities and obligations to his client and his client's estate.

In April 1852, Meredith Hawkins entered into an agreement with Thomas Hunt for the exchange of lands in Jefferson County, Illinois. Hawkins had claims against Hunt, which he agreed to satisfy, in addition to paying Hunt $71 through a note due at Christmas 1852. Hunt verbally promised to convey a tract of land, currently rented to a tenant, to Hawkins at the next term of the Jefferson circuit court and authorized Hawkins to take possession and receive rents. After Hawkins fulfilled his obligations—including notifying the tenants and settling his claims—Hunt refused to honor their agreement and allegedly conspired with Conner, the other party involved, to destroy their contract. Seeking relief, Hawkins filed a bill for specific performance of the verbal contract, requesting that Conner and Hunt be compelled to deed the land to him. However, the defendants filed demurrers to dismiss Hawkins' suit, which the circuit court upheld. Hawkins appealed, contesting the dismissals as erroneous.	Hawkins claims that he reached a verbal agreement with Hunt for the exchange of lands, which he acted upon by settling debts and attempting to take possession of the property. He argues for the specific performance of the contract, asserting that Hunt has failed to comply and is attempting to transfer his promissory note to an assignee, which necessitates legal intervention to protect his interests in the property.	The defendants, including Hunt, Conner, and Conger (the tenant), argue that Hawkins' allegations are insufficient to enforce the specific performance of a verbal contract for land, which requires clear evidence of part performance. They claim that Hawkins did not fully pay the purchase price or take actual possession of the land, as it was occupied by Conger without complying with any rental agreements to Hawkins. The demurrers filed by the defendants were initially sustained by the circuit court, dismissing Hawkins' bill against them.

The case of Frank Marquis v. City of Chicago was decided on September 18, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. It arose from an appeal against a $100 fine imposed on Frank Marquis by the Criminal Court of Cook County. The fine was for an alleged violation of Section 1307 of the Revised Ordinances of the City of Chicago, which prohibited the maintenance of gaming devices such as keno or faro tables. The prosecution's argument relied on the broader interpretation of the ordinance, which included devices used for purposes of gaming. However, there was no evidence proving that Marquis maintained specific prohibited devices; instead, the evidence indicated he operated what was labeled a lottery or policy shop. The court had to interpret the ordinance concerning the specifics of penal statutes, leaning on established legal interpretations regarding the strict construction of such laws.	The City of Chicago, as the plaintiff, contended that Frank Marquis was guilty of violating the ordinance prohibiting the maintenance of gaming devices. The City argued that the ordinance's inclusion of general terms covered other forms of gaming activity beyond those explicitly listed, implying that Marquis maintained a lottery operation as part of this violation.	Frank Marquis, the defendant, argued that the evidence presented did not support the claim that he kept or maintained the specific gaming instruments mentioned in the ordinance. His defense hinged on the legal principle that general words in penal statutes should apply only to cases of the same kind as those specifically mentioned, arguing that the ordinance was being improperly construed to include activities that were not clearly encompassed by its language.

The case "Edward W. Walker v. George W. Brown" was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the final opinion filed on February 17, 1886. The case number is No. 133-2247, and it was documented in volume 18 of the Illinois Appellate Court Reports, page 643. The specific details of the events leading to the lawsuit are not provided, but it is noted that the evidence presented was deemed sufficient to support the findings of the lower court. Key individuals involved include the plaintiff Edward W. Walker and the defendant George W. Brown, with representation from attorneys Wilson & Zook for the appellant and Joseph H. Barker and F. C. Hale for the appellee. The presiding judge was Kirk Hawes, although the summary did not detail the nature of the dispute or the claims made by either party.	The plaintiff, Edward W. Walker, argued against the defendant, seeking a resolution in favor of his claims. While specific details of the legal requests and main arguments are not outlined in the provided case description, it can be inferred that Walker aimed to obtain a favorable judgment based on the strength of the evidence presented.	The defendant, George W. Brown, likely contested the claims made by Walker, although the precise nature of his defenses is not detailed in the case description. Brown's counsel, Barker and Hale, would have presented arguments against the plaintiff’s claims, potentially seeking dismissal or a judgment in favor of the defendant.

Eugene L. Brown filed a lawsuit against the City of Aurora following an incident that occurred in Kane County, Illinois, in which he sustained injuries from a fall on a sidewalk. The case was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 20, 1883. Initially, Brown was awarded $6,000 in damages by the Kane Circuit Court based on claims of negligence against the city for failing to maintain the sidewalk in a safe condition. However, the City of Aurora appealed the decision to the Appellate Court for the Second District, which found that the evidence did not support the jury's verdict and consequently reversed the judgment. The Appellate Court determined that the sidewalk was relatively safe, that Brown was aware of its slippery condition, and that he did not exercise the ordinary care expected of a reasonably prudent person. The Appellate Court also concluded that the city had acted with ordinary care in maintaining the sidewalk, leading to Brown's current petition for review by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Eugene L. Brown, argued that the City of Aurora was negligent in maintaining the sidewalk where he fell, leading to his injuries. He sought to prove that such negligence warranted the damages awarded by the Kane Circuit Court, claiming the city failed to uphold its duty to ensure safe public walkways.	The City of Aurora contended that the sidewalk was in a reasonably safe condition at the time of the incident, maintaining that Brown was aware of its defects and did not exercise proper care while walking on it. The city asserted that it had fulfilled its obligations in constructing and maintaining the sidewalk, thereby reversing the initial judgment against it.

In 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the case of Indianapolis, Decatur & Springfield Railroad Company v. Davis & Finney was brought forward. The dispute arose when the plaintiffs, Davis & Finney, alleged that the general freight agent of the railroad company promised them a rebate on freight charges for their shipments. The plaintiffs contended that this agreement was valid and enforceable. However, the railroad company attempted to defend against the claims by arguing that the promise from the freight agent was made without proper authority and constituted illegal discrimination against other shippers, violating statutory regulations. The court would later sustain a demurrer to the company’s special plea, thus denying their arguments. The case was linked to a previous companion case against the same railroad company, indicating a potentially broader issue with the company’s practices regarding freight charges and rebates.	The plaintiffs' main argument was that the railroad company, through its general freight agent, made a valid promise to provide a rebate on freight charges for shipments. They sought enforcement of this promise and claimed damages amounting to $1,540.49 as owed to them based on this alleged agreement.	The defendant's key arguments included claims that the promise made by the general freight agent was without authority and thus void. They also contended that the agreement constituted discrimination in violation of the statute against such practices, which should render the promise unenforceable. The railroad company maintained that they were not obligated to fulfill the rebate due to these legal grounds.

The case "Harvey McNair et al. for the use of Chauncey H. White, v. Nancy Platt" arose in September 1867 and was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individuals involved include Harvey McNair and Charles H. Acres, who were business partners, and Nancy Platt, a defendant. McNair and Acres operated a partnership that sold goods. Before the partnership, McNair was already indebted to Platt. An arrangement was made wherein Platt would buy goods from McNair, and the value of those goods would be credited toward her existing debt with him. Despite the partnership's formation, Platt continued purchasing goods, which were charged to her account. When the partnership failed, and an assignment was made for the benefit of creditors, Chauncey H. White, representing the plaintiffs, sought to recover the value of the goods purchased by Platt from the firm. The jury found in favor of Platt, and after a motion for a new trial was denied, the case advanced to the Supreme Court on appeal.	The plaintiffs, represented by White, claimed that Nancy Platt owed for goods purchased from the partnership of McNair and Acres. They argued that the sales should not have been credited against Platt’s debt to McNair, as there was no formal agreement allowing such offsets post-partnership formation and that any previous arrangements did not hold without consent from both partners.	Nancy Platt contended that the goods purchased were agreed to be credited against her debt to McNair, as per their prior arrangement. She argued that McNair had established this understanding and that her purchases were intended to offset her claims against him. Platt's defense hinged on demonstrating that the partner Acres was aware of this arrangement and that the purchases legitimately applied toward her outstanding notes against McNair.

Luke Fant v. The People of the State of Illinois is a legal case that took place in Will County, Illinois, in February 1867. The case emerged when Luke Fant was indicted by the grand jury for keeping open a "tippling house" (a bar or saloon) on the Sabbath, which was against the law as outlined in the 127th section of the Criminal Code. The jury found Fant guilty based on testimonies from two witnesses who claimed to have been in his establishment on a Sunday, consuming alcoholic beverages. However, it was noted that the saloon was quiet, with no signs of disorder. Fant's defense argued that the city of Joliet had its own ordinance prohibiting such activities on Sundays and that the city was responsible for enforcing this law, which should negate the state’s charges. The trial court did not accept this defense, leading to Fant being fined $100 and seeking a new trial, which was denied.	The prosecution claimed that Luke Fant was guilty of keeping a tippling house open on a Sunday, thereby breaking the state law designed to maintain public order on the Sabbath. They argued that the activity encouraged idleness and other forms of misbehavior, which the law sought to prevent.	Luke Fant’s defense contended that the city of Joliet had the jurisdiction to regulate and prohibit the operation of tippling houses through its own ordinances. They argued that since the city had its own legal framework and was active in enforcing it, the state should not pursue an additional prosecution against him for the same act. Furthermore, they asserted that the prosecution did not prove the essential charge that the house was kept open to encourage immoral behavior.

The case of The Union Steamboat Company v. Doha Knapp took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered in September 1874. The plaintiff, Doha Knapp, had shipped goods from Maucli Chunck, Pennsylvania, to Chicago on September 8, 1871, using the Union Steamboat Company as the carrier. Upon arrival at the Chicago dock on September 20, the goods were not promptly communicated to the consignee, John Knapp. Instead, the company sent a notice of the goods' arrival, which was vague and not directed to the specific address of the consignee. Consequently, the goods were destroyed by fire on October 9, 1871, before the consignee was informed. Evidence presented indicated that Knapp had made multiple inquiries at the depot regarding the arrival of the goods but was told they had not yet arrived. The jury found in favor of Knapp, awarding damages for the loss of the goods. This case raised critical questions about the duty of carriers to notify consignees of the arrival of goods, especially when specific delivery details were provided.	Doha Knapp claimed that the Union Steamboat Company was negligent in not providing proper notice of the arrival of her goods. She argued that the company failed to send a notice directed to her husband at their specific address, which constituted a breach of duty as a carrier. As a result, the plaintiff sought damages for the lost goods and was awarded $353.18, later remitting part of the amount and receiving a final judgment of $192.50.	The Union Steamboat Company defended itself by arguing that they had notified the consignee of the arrival of the goods, albeit not by the correct address. They asserted that their actions met the legal requirements for notification. Additionally, they claimed that because the notice sent after the goods were destroyed had been returned undelivered, they should not be held liable for the loss.

In 1872, the case of Robert Kinder v. Joseph Gillespie was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Circuit Court of Madison County. The key individuals involved were Robert Kinder, the plaintiff, and Joseph Gillespie, the defendant. The case arose when Kinder's horses escaped from his property and were subsequently seized by the town constable of Edwardsville for allegedly running at large, a violation of a local ordinance. Kinder asserted that he did not permit the horses to roam freely; they escaped against his will, and he actively searched for them. Despite his efforts, the horses were impounded before Kinder could reclaim them. The central issue hinged on whether the seizures of Kinder's horses were lawful given his claims of innocence and diligence in trying to recover them.	Robert Kinder, the plaintiff, argued that his horses were not running at large as they escaped from his enclosure without his consent or knowledge. He contended that he made diligent efforts to locate and reclaim them. Kinder's legal request was for the return of his impounded horses and to have the actions of the town officials deemed unlawful since he did not willfully neglect the ordinance governing the control of animals in the town.	Joseph Gillespie, the defendant, based his defense on the assertion that Kinder's horses were indeed running at large, violating the town ordinance. He indicated that the constable acted lawfully in impounding the horses as per the ordinance's provisions. Gillespie's defense was that the fees and charges imposed by the ordinance were valid and that Kinder had not paid or tendered them before attempting to reclaim his horses.

The case "The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company v. William Hawk" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on June 17, 1887. The incident occurred on April 14, 1882, near Forrest, Livingston County, Illinois. William Hawk, the plaintiff, was injured while assisting in removing a wreck from the railroad track belonging to the defendant, Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company. At the time, a freight train had derailed, leading to the formation of a wrecking crew, including Hawk, overseen by a foreman named Button. During the removal efforts, the crew was ordered to lift the floor of a wrecked car by hand and prop it up with wooden sticks. While they were following Button's orders, the prop slipped, causing the car floor to fall and fracture Hawk's ankle. Hawk claimed that the defendant had failed to provide adequate machinery and had negligently ordered unsafe lifting methods, leading to his injury. The case progressed through lower courts, where Hawk won judgments in the circuit court and Appellate Court, prompting the defendant to appeal.	William Hawk, the plaintiff, argued that the defendant, represented by foreman Button, acted negligently by failing to use proper machinery for lifting the wreck and instead ordering workers to lift it manually. He claimed that this negligence caused him to sustain a serious injury when the prop failed, resulting in a fractured ankle. Hawk sought damages for his injuries, asserting that the commands given by Button were those of the railway company and that the company should be held liable for the negligence of its representative.	The defendant, Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company, contended that Hawk and Button were fellow-servants within the same line of employment, thereby limiting the company's liability for the negligence of Button, whom they considered as an equal in the hierarchy. The defense asserted that the injuries resulted from Hawk's participation in the lifting operation, and they argued that the court’s instructions regarding liability were erroneous, claiming there was no ground for the judgment made against them.

In September 1874, the case of Charles Boettcher v. Henry Bock et al. was decided in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case stems from a civil dispute involving a judgment rendered by a justice of the peace in Cook County. On November 15, 1873, the case was initially called before Justice R. C. Hammill after a change of venue from Justice Francis Rolle. After continuations, a trial with witnesses occurred on November 17 and 18, where the parties consulted and Henry Bock (the defendant) agreed to a judgment amount of $163.94 in favor of Charles Boettcher (the plaintiff). The plaintiff accepted this judgment, and a formal ruling was made in his favor after mutual consent. This agreement led to a question about whether the defendant could appeal the judgment, given that it was considered a confession of judgment. The case ultimately considered the definitions of judgment confession and its implications on the ability to appeal.	The plaintiff, Charles Boettcher, claimed that the defendant, Henry Bock, had agreed to a judgment in his favor for $163.94. Boettcher argued that because the judgment was voluntarily accepted by both parties after negotiation, it constituted a confession of judgment, thus barring the defendant from appealing the decision. The plaintiff sought to uphold the judgment rendered by the justice of the peace and eliminate any objections on procedural grounds.	The defendant, Henry Bock, argued that the nature of the judgment was not correctly represented and that he should be allowed to appeal. He contended that the transcript of the proceedings did not adequately reflect the nature of the plaintiff’s demands, suggesting the judgment should not be construed as a confession of judgment. Bock aimed to dispute the ruling on procedural grounds and retain the ability to present a defense against the plaintiff’s claims.

Nehemiah Faucher v. Thomas Tutewiller et al. is a legal case that took place in Cumberland County, Illinois, with a decision rendered in January 1875. The dispute emerged over boundary lines between adjacent tracts of land owned by the parties involved. Thomas Tutewiller and others (the petitioners) owned lands in sections 32 and 33, while Nehemiah Faucher, Henry Faucher, and Walter N. Ruffner (the defendants) owned the adjacent lands. The boundary lines were reportedly lost or destroyed, prompting the petitioners to seek the appointment of a commission of surveyors to delineate these boundaries officially. The circuit court agreed, found the boundary to be in dispute, and appointed surveyors to establish the line based on government surveys. After the surveyors produced a report regarding the boundary, Nehemiah Faucher filed exceptions to this report, leading to a court hearing where the report was ultimately approved and confirmed.	The plaintiffs argued that there was a clear and disputed boundary between their lands and those owned by Nehemiah and Henry Faucher, prompting their request for the appointment of surveyors to re-establish these boundaries. They sought a judicial order directing the surveyors to determine and permanently establish the lost or disputed boundary lines, emphasizing the importance of using government-established survey markers as a basis for the adjudication.	The defendants contended that the court’s order may have allowed the surveyors to arbitrarily establish a line instead of simply re-establishing the original government lines. Nehemiah Faucher specifically objected to the usage of the term "establish" as suggesting that surveyors could create a new boundary without regard to official surveys. They also argued that the court had improperly included them as defendants, stating that one of the named parties was not interested in the outcome of the dispute.

In 1857, in the city of Peru, Illinois, Richard Pendergast brought a legal action against The City of Peru regarding the violation of a local ordinance. The case arose after Pendergast, who operated a liquor business, was found to be selling alcohol without a proper license. The matter was initially heard by a police magistrate in Peru and was later appealed to the La Salle County Circuit Court. During the trial, it was revealed that the defendant had previously sold liquor before the lawsuit commenced, and he admitted to violating the city ordinance by pleading guilty in the police court. Evidence was presented, including a certified copy of the city ordinance, which stated that any person needed a valid license to sell alcoholic beverages, and outlined penalties for violations. The court found sufficient evidence to support the claim that Pendergast had sold liquor without a license and rendered judgment accordingly.	Richard Pendergast claimed that The City of Peru had wrongfully charged him for penalties associated with selling liquor without a license. He appealed the decision from the police court, seeking to recover damages from the city based on the violation of local ordinances that mandated the requirement of a license for selling alcoholic beverages.	The City of Peru defended itself by asserting that Pendergast admitted to selling liquor without a license and had pleaded guilty to violating the city's ordinances. The city argued that there was no error in the original ruling and that the evidence, including the certified copy of the ordinance and Pendergast's admissions, clearly established the violation.

In the case of Alexander E. Guild, Jr. v. The City of Chicago, the legal proceedings took place in September 1876 in Cook County, Illinois. The case stemmed from a special assessment conducted for the public improvement of Dearborn Street, intended to extend from Jackson Street to Fourteenth Street. The city of Chicago adopted provisions of a state act that allowed local improvements through special assessment under certain guidelines. Guild, whose property was affected by this assessment, argued that various aspects of the assessment process were unconstitutional and violated established legal procedures. Specifically, he contended that the ordinance for the assessment was invalid due to legal misinterpretations regarding property assessment limits and procedural deficiencies.	The plaintiff, Alexander E. Guild, Jr., argued that the city of Chicago's ordinance to adopt the assessment was unconstitutional, claiming it violated provisions regarding the title of acts relating to city incorporation, as well as the delegation of legislative powers. He asserted that the city had improperly assessed his property based on non-contiguous properties and failed to follow necessary procedures in the assessment process, including the lack of a required map and a report from the board of public works. Guild sought a judgment to invalidate the assessment and any related charges against his property.	The City of Chicago, represented by the defendant, argued that the assessment was valid under the law, asserting that the provisions allowing for special assessments applied broadly to any property that benefited from the improvement, regardless of contiguity. The city contended that the procedural objections raised by Guild were unfounded since the applicable laws had been amended since the assessment was adopted. They also maintained that the omission of certain procedural documents did not invalidate the legitimacy of the assessment process, and thus the assessment should stand as lawful and appropriate.

In 1885, James Wilderman and William Pitts entered into a contract in St. Clair County, Illinois, regarding the drilling of a well. Wilderman was to complete a well that would yield eight barrels of water daily for two days, with Pitts assisting in testing the well. However, Wilderman did not finish the well, leaving it in a condition where sand clogged it, preventing water flow. After withdrawing his tools in September 1885, he never returned to complete the work or make further tests despite claims that no time was fixed for completion. In March 1886, when Wilderman sought access to test the well, the defendants refused him, citing the expiration of his time. The case proceeded to trial, where a jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him $250, despite arguments over the well’s unfinished state and capacity.	The plaintiff, Wilderman, claimed he was entitled to the $250 as stipulated in their contract for completing the well. He argued that the defendants had failed to facilitate the test of the well, which was a prerequisite to payment. Wilderman maintained that since there was no specific timeframe for the contract completion, he was still entitled to recover the payment despite not meeting the well's capacity requirements.	The defendants argued that Wilderman did not fulfill his contractual obligation to complete the well, which was necessary before he could demand payment. They contended that the well was left unfinished and unusable, as evidenced by the only test showing it could not produce the promised water capacity. They asserted that Wilderman had made no effort to finish the work within a reasonable time, and therefore, he was not entitled to recover under the terms of the contract.

In 1868, in East St. Louis, Illinois, the City of East St. Louis sought to condemn a piece of property owned by Louisiana St. John in order to construct a city prison. The city claimed authority to appropriate the property based on a provision from its city charter established in February 1865, which allowed the acquisition and use of property for public purposes. The charter mandated that compensation be provided when taking private property for public use and stipulated that, if necessary, compensation should be determined by a jury of disinterested freeholders. However, the Illinois constitution also required legislative approval for taking private property for public use, emphasizing that such actions must be for public purposes explicitly stated in law. The core of the dispute revolved around whether the stated purpose of constructing a city prison fell within the permissible uses outlined in the charter, as the specific designation for such use was not included in the city's authority.	The City of East St. Louis, as the plaintiff, argued that it had the legal right to condemn the property owned by Louisiana St. John for the construction of a city prison, asserting that the city charter provided explicit authority to acquire property for public uses such as streets and public grounds. They sought the court's affirmation of this power, contending that the construction of a city prison served a public purpose under the charter.	Louisiana St. John, the defendant, contended that the city did not possess the authority to condemn his property for the purpose of constructing a prison, as this specific use was neither explicitly mentioned in the city charter nor aligned with the public purposes authorized by law. The defendant argued that the city could only take property for purposes directly related to public streets and grounds and that the proposed use of his property violated constitutional protections against the appropriation of private property without proper justification.

In June 1852, the case of John D. Jennings v. Ichabod Gage et al. was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in New York, where merchants Gage, Dater, and Massey sold goods to Henry Van Valin. Payment for these goods was to be settled through notes secured by a mortgage on real estate in Wisconsin, with the condition that the goods would not be delivered to Van Valin until he provided an acceptable indorser. The goods were sent to Chicago, with the condition that they would not be delivered without direction from J. H. Burch, an authorized figure in the transaction. Van Valin, however, managed to obtain possession of the goods after paying the shipping charges but without giving the required indorser. He subsequently sold the goods to Jennings. Gage and his partners demanded the goods back from Jennings, who refused, leading the plaintiffs to file a lawsuit for trover to recover the value of the goods, amounting to $1,339.74. Following this, the court had to consider specific jury instructions related to the contract and possession of the goods.	The plaintiffs argued that they retained ownership of the goods as Van Valin never provided the necessary security (the indorser) as per their agreement. They contended that Van Valin had obtained possession of the goods wrongfully and, therefore, they were entitled to recover the value of the goods from Jennings.	Jennings, the defendant, contended that he purchased the goods in good faith from Van Valin, who had actual possession at the time of the sale. He argued that since the plaintiffs had allowed Van Valin to have possession, they should bear the loss and could not recover the goods from him without first cancelling the contract and the corresponding mortgage.

In December 1847, in Pike County, Illinois, Theodore Digby and Sunderland G. Sears, who owned a considerable amount of real and personal property and operated a merchandising business as Digby & Sears, faced mounting debts totaling approximately $4,000 to $5,000. As creditors began to press for payment, Digby and Sears conveyed their property to James Digby, Theodore's brother, for a nominal price of one dollar, claiming this sale was part of a legitimate transaction while actually intending to shield their assets from creditors. The conveyances, which included notes amounting to over $6,200 for future payments over several years, effectively left Digby and Sears without any means to satisfy their existing debts. Creditors of Digby and Sears, including Josiah Nesbitt and Joseph Charless, sought to challenge the legitimacy of this transaction, alleging it was fraudulent and designed to defraud creditors by making the assets unreachable. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after initial dismissals and denials in lower courts.	The plaintiffs, Josiah Nesbitt and Joseph Charless, claimed that the conveyance of property from Theodore Digby and Sunderland Sears to James Digby was fraudulent. They argued that the transaction was designed to evade creditors and sought a declaration that the conveyances should be considered void. The plaintiffs requested the court to set aside the fraudulent transfers and allow for the sale of the conveyed property to satisfy their judgments after accounting for any legitimate mortgages.	The defendants, Theodore and James Digby, along with Sears, acknowledged the outstanding debts but asserted that the conveyances conducted to James Digby were legitimate transactions meant to resolve the debts via promissory notes. They claimed the property was encumbered with mortgage obligations that James Digby had agreed to assume and argued that the claims of fraud were unwarranted, insisting that the conveyance did not intend to defraud creditors but to manage outstanding debts.

In 1885, the case of Levi S. Hodge v. Charles O. Boynton arose in DeKalb County, Illinois, before the Illinois Appellate Court. The plaintiff, Levi S. Hodge, brought an action of assumpsit against the defendant, Charles O. Boynton, claiming a debt that amounted to $5,646.33. The defendant filed pleas of general issue and set-off. The jury eventually rendered a verdict in favor of Hodge for $800, from which he remitted $152.10 due to an error where the jury failed to account for two percent per month on two notes relevant to the defendant's set-off plea. Following the verdict, Boynton appealed, arguing that the verdict was contrary to the evidence and asserting that the trial court erred in modifying jury instructions related to a prior settlement between the parties.	The plaintiff, Levi S. Hodge, claimed that he was owed a substantial sum of money from Charles O. Boynton, specifically $5,646.33. He sought a verdict from the jury to recover this amount, presenting evidence to support his claim while arguing against Boynton's defenses.	The defendant, Charles O. Boynton, contended that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence presented during the trial and claimed that the court mistakenly modified jury instructions concerning a prior settlement that allegedly resolved all business matters between them. Boynton sought to challenge the verdict and sought relief from the judgment issued in favor of Hodge.

In 1873, in Lake County, Illinois, the case "The People of the State of Illinois v. Aristus Brown et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The individuals involved included the People of the State of Illinois as the plaintiff, represented by Attorney General Mr. J. K. Edsall, and the defendants, Aristus Brown, Clark W. Upton, Moses Evans, and Lorenzo Hinkston, who served as sureties for Walter W. Hastings, the sheriff of Lake County. The case arose from a defalcation by Hastings in handling the State revenue he collected. The parties waived formal pleadings and agreed on the facts to present a specific legal question: whether a mistake made by the Auditor of Public Accounts, which misrepresented the sheriff's account and impeded the defendants from obtaining indemnity, could be used as a defense. The Court had to determine the validity of this defense based on the principles of estoppel.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants could not claim estoppel based on the Auditor's mistake, as there needed to be an element of fraud for estoppel to apply. The Attorney General maintained that the defendants’ prejudice from receiving erroneous information did not mitigate their responsibility, asserting that the law does not permit individuals to escape liability on the basis of mistakes made by government officials.	The defendants argued that the mistaken information provided by the Auditor should serve as a defense, preventing the State from recovering the funds. They contended that they were misled by the Auditor's erroneous statement regarding the sheriff’s account, which hindered their ability to claim indemnity. However, they failed to provide substantial arguments to support this defense.

The case "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Gustave Demars" took place in Kankakee County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. The conflict arose when Gustave Demars hired the Illinois Central Railroad Company to provide six passenger cars for an excursion. On August 28, 1856, a letter from W.P. Johnson, the general passenger agent of the railroad, indicated that Demars could arrange for the cars with three days' notice. Demars notified the railroad on September 22, 1856, about his requirement for four cars for an excursion scheduled for September 25, but the cars were not provided. This resulted in Demars selling 243 tickets and subsequently having to refund the money to those who purchased tickets. The jury ruled in favor of Demars, awarding him $376, leading to the railroad's appeal based on alleged errors during the trial regarding evidence and breach of contract terms.	The plaintiff, Gustave Demars, claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company's failure to provide the agreed-upon cars constituted a breach of contract, leading to economic damages from the sale of tickets for his excursion. He sought damages based on the expected revenue from ticket sales minus the cost for the car rentals, asserting that he should have been compensated for the lost opportunity and the related expenses incurred.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that there was no breach of contract, arguing that Demars only requested four cars, whereas the contract stipulated six. They maintained that since Demars did not formally demand the full number of cars, the company was under no obligation to fulfill a modified request. Additionally, they claimed that the damages awarded to Demars were excessive and not substantiated by the evidence presented at trial.

In February 1883, William W. Charles v. W. L. Lasher arose when W. L. Lasher visited the Chicago Piano Storage Company to secure a mortgage on a piano being sold to Mrs. M. E. Potter. Lasher witnessed the sale and was informed that the piano would be delivered to Potter's residence at 38 E. Harrison Street. Lasher provided a loan for the purchase, secured by a chattel mortgage and notes. On May 22, 1883, Mr. D. H. Tolman, a money lender, received a warehouse receipt for the piano as collateral from the storage company's manager, G. C. Wheeler, who subsequently sold it to Charles. After the storage company failed on May 25, 1883, Mrs. Potter defaulted on her mortgage payments. Charles took possession of the piano and Lasher sought its return through a replevin action against him, leading to a dispute over the ownership of the piano between Charles and Lasher based on the claims of delivery and legal title.	The plaintiff, William W. Charles, argued that he held a valid chattel mortgage from Mrs. Potter, which granted him ownership rights over the piano. He asserted that the piano was rightfully delivered to him after he took possession via a warehouse receipt. Charles requested that he be awarded possession of the piano, claiming that Lasher had refused to return it after its proper retrieval.	The defendant, W. L. Lasher, contended that the mortgage he held against the piano was valid and that he had a legitimate claim to ownership due to the nature of the delivery process. He argued that there was insufficient evidence to prove that the piano was effectively delivered to Potter, which would invalidate her ownership and, consequently, Charles's claim. Lasher requested that the court recognize his ownership rights and deny Charles possession of the piano.

In December 1838, in the Municipal Court of the City of Chicago, the case of Hiram Pearsons and Richard J. Hamilton (appellants) v. Amos Bailey (appellee) was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from an action of assumpsit initiated by Amos Bailey, a county surveyor, against Pearsons and Hamilton for a total of $532.00. This amount included $112.00 for services rendered by chainmen employed to aid in surveying the town of Canal Port and $420.00 for Bailey's fees in surveying and laying out town lots at a statutory rate of $0.25 per lot. The defendants argued that Bailey could only recover what was prescribed by statute, which only included the surveying fee and not additional charges for chainmen. Furthermore, Bailey provided evidence that he was the county surveyor and presented the account to Pearsons, who refused payment, while Hamilton acknowledged a portion but insisted on a release before paying. The jury returned a verdict favoring Bailey, leading the defendants to appeal the judgment.	Amos Bailey, the plaintiff, claimed he was owed a total of $532.00 for his services as a county surveyor and for money expended on chainmen. He contended that the defendants were responsible for payment based on the services rendered, which included the statutory fee for surveying and costs incurred for hiring chainmen who were essential to his work.	Hiram Pearsons and Richard J. Hamilton, the defendants, argued that under the statute governing county surveyors, Bailey was limited to charging only the prescribed fee of $0.25 per lot. They contended that he could not recover additional costs for chainmen since their employment was the surveyor's responsibility, and they requested the court to instruct the jury accordingly. The defendants insisted that any implied promise for reimbursement for chainmen costs was incorrect, as it did not apply to surveys of town plats.

In 1874, M. A. Hayes was a tenant of property owned by Prout, which had been purchased by Kimmell. Kimmell subsequently leased the property to Hayes, establishing a rental agreement through a written lease prepared by Kimmell’s agent, Cole. Hayes consistently paid rent under this lease agreement until February 1874, when Kimmell agreed to sell the property to A. M. Lawver, effective March 1, 1874. Following the sale, Lawver, both personally and through his agent, Cole, approached Hayes to collect back rent and inform her of the change in ownership. Despite numerous reminders from Lawver, Hayes failed to pay the rent, although she expressed a willingness to do so. Hayes later contested the legality of the lease's delivery and claimed that Lawver had not validly claimed rent from her due to lack of attornment. The case was presented as an appeal from a lower court ruling in favor of Lawver, and the Illinois Supreme Court ultimately evaluated the validity of Hayes's claims against Lawver regarding the lease and rental payments.	M. A. Hayes claimed that the lease from Kimmell, which she signed, had not been properly delivered to her, disputing the validity of her obligation to pay rent to Lawver. She argued that there was no formal attornment to Lawver, asserting that necessary legal procedures, including demand for rent and notice to quit, were not followed. Hayes sought to challenge the judgment made by the lower court that favored Lawver in the forcible detainer action.	A. M. Lawver contended that under the signed lease, Hayes had accepted her role as a tenant, making the issue of delivery irrelevant for the purposes of enforcing the lease. Lawver also argued that Hayes demonstrated attornment by promising to pay rent to him after receiving notice of the property transfer. He maintained that a written notice and demand for rent was provided to Hayes, which adequately fulfilled legal requirements, and he asserted that the findings from the original judgment were consistent with law and supported by evidence.

In February 1873, in Mercer County, Illinois, George A. Moore initiated a legal dispute against John Mauck involving two attachment suits. The conflict arose when Mauck claimed Moore wrongfully took possession of certain goods and real estate belonging to him. Moore was away in California during the proceedings, leaving his wife, Mary A. Moore, to manage their property. Mauck accused Mary of wrongfully taking the property, asserting that it was his because Moore hadn’t paid rent for the premises. Mauck's actions led him to seize Moore's goods through legal attachment processes, resulting in a trial that addressed whether these actions were justified. The court found that a jury correctly affirmed Mauck's stance, ruling in favor of the defendant after deliberating on the validity of the attachment process and the rightful ownership of the premises.	George A. Moore claimed that John Mauck unlawfully took his goods and forcibly removed his family from their home. Moore contended that Mauck's actions, facilitated through attachment suits, were without proper justification and violated his rights as a property owner. He requested the court to recognize his ownership of the goods and premises and to restore possession to him.	John Mauck defended his actions by stating that he had properly instituted attachment suits against Moore for unpaid debts. He asserted that the goods were legally seized under the writs of attachment, and claimed that the premises in question were his property, which Moore had occupied as a tenant. Mauck argued that Mary A. Moore had acted improperly in claiming the property as exempt. He requested the court to uphold the validity of his actions and confirmed the jury’s verdict favoring him.

Mary J. Illingsworth v. Enos Slosson is a legal case decided on June 16, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in Cook County, Illinois, where the plaintiff, Mary J. Illingsworth, entered into a written contract with the defendant, Enos Slosson. According to this contract, Slosson, acting as a broker, was to procure a $10,000 loan for Illingsworth for a term of five years at an interest rate of 6%. He was to receive a commission of 2.5% for this service. However, Slosson failed to secure a loan under the agreed terms, only managing to connect Illingsworth with a lender named Mayo who offered a lower amount ($9,000) at a higher interest rate (7%) than initially specified. Consequently, the jury awarded Illingsworth $125, but Slosson contended that he could not recover compensation for his efforts due to his failure to fulfill the contract as explicitly written, leading to the appeal of the verdict.	The plaintiff, Mary J. Illingsworth, argued that she was entitled to compensation for the services rendered by the defendant, Enos Slosson, despite his failure to procure the specified loan under the contract's terms. She contended that Slosson had expended effort and time in an attempt to fulfill the agreement and that the jury's verdict should reflect some remuneration for these efforts.	The defendant, Enos Slosson, contended that he could not recover any compensation, as he did not secure the loan on the terms specified in the contract. He argued that the written agreement was clear and that no services rendered could merit payment without fulfilling the conditions of the contract. Slosson maintained that the conditions established an explicit contract which did not allow for recovery based on implied obligations or quantum meruit since he failed to perform the contract as required.

The case "Arthur W. Windett v. James Hamilton" took place in September 1869, in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Arthur W. Windett, an attorney, filed a lawsuit against the defendant, James Hamilton, seeking to recover $1,000 for legal services rendered. During the September term of court, default judgment was granted in favor of Windett. However, Hamilton sought to vacate this judgment, leading to a motion entered at the same term, which was postponed to the October term for a hearing. At the October term, the Circuit Court allowed Hamilton’s motion to set aside the default and vacate the judgment due to procedural issues related to the service of summons. Specifically, the plaintiff's original summons lacked a proper return, and there was a discrepancy between the amount claimed in the summons and the amended declaration. Consequently, Hamilton argued to quash the alias summons and dismiss the suit, which the court granted, resulting in Windett being ordered to pay court costs.	The plaintiff, Arthur W. Windett, claimed that the court erred in setting aside the default judgment at a subsequent term and in refusing to permit the sheriff to enter a "not found" return for the original summons. He contended that the default had been entered correctly and that the dismissal based on the quashing of the alias summons was improper, asserting that he should have had the opportunity to amend his declaration to avoid the dismissal.	The defendant, James Hamilton, argued that the court had the authority to vacate the prior judgment at the October term since the default was taken during the September term. He maintained that the original summons was not properly addressed, specifically highlighting a variance in the amounts claimed between the alias summons and amended declaration. Hamilton's motions aimed to quash the alias summons due to procedural defects and to dismiss the suit altogether, which the court ultimately granted.

In 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, Lewis Umlauf filed for divorce against his wife, Victoria Umlauf, citing her desertion as the reason. The Superior Court granted the divorce on April 22, 1887, but awarded custody of their two sons, Arthur, nine years old, and Oscar, six years old, to their mother, Victoria. The court mandated Lewis to pay $40 monthly for child support. He did not appeal the custody decision and complied with the monthly payments until November 1887. Lewis later petitioned for custody of the children, but this request was dismissed by the court. The court considered the welfare of the children, stating that despite the circumstances, it was determined to be in their best interest to remain with their mother due to their tender ages and delicate health. The appellants maintained that both parents were fit, but the court emphasized prioritizing the children’s welfare over the parents' desires.	Lewis Umlauf, the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to custody of his sons after being granted a divorce based on his wife's desertion. He argued that both parents were fit to care for the children, but that the court should prioritize the best interests of the children, which he believed would be better served in his custody. Lewis sought a modification of the earlier court decree to grant him custody of his older son, Arthur, without compromising the welfare of the younger son, Oscar.	Victoria Umlauf, the defendant, defended her custody of both children, asserting that the circumstances surrounding their ages and health justified her retaining custody. She emphasized her commitment to their well-being and argued that the emotional and physical conditions of the boys required their mother’s presence and care. Victoria also contended that the father’s past actions and the current well-being of the children did not warrant a change in custody.

In 1852, James Garner and two other plaintiffs initiated an ejectment action against Levi Willett in Mercer County, Illinois. The dispute centers around the ownership of lot number 5, block 6, in the town of Rew Boston. Plaintiffs claimed title to the entire lot based on patents from the United States dated January 20, 1853, while the defendant owned a patent for the same land, dated November 1, 1839. The plaintiffs adjusted their claim during the proceedings to assert that two of them, Benjamin C. Taliaferro and John O. Pepper, held two-thirds of the property, a claim unopposed by the defendant. The case was tried without a jury in 1855, wherein evidence showed that the defendant was in possession of the lot during the suit's initiation, and held title via regular conveyances from the original patentee, John W. Deniston. The legal principles discussed reference the precedence of older patents and the validity of the government-issued patents pertaining to land ownership claims, as well as the right to preempt claims based on earlier filings. The court focused on whether the title was legitimately transferred and the appropriateness of the patents.	The plaintiffs argued that they derived their title from legitimate U.S. patents and sought to reclaim possession of the lot from the defendant. They contended that the patents issued to them were valid and that the defendant’s claim was inferior due to their later patent, asserting that the older patent should not be deemed valid given their established rights.	The defendant rebutted the plaintiffs' claims by asserting his established legal title to the subject property, derived from the earlier patent issued in 1839. He argued that the plaintiffs had failed to demonstrate any fraud in obtaining their patent and that the land office properly confirmed his title under previous acts of Congress. Additionally, he presented evidence that the entry and application for his patent were timely and compliant with legal requirements.

In September 1872, the case of Thomas Ward et al. v. Harvey Brown was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a trespass incident. The core issue arose when Harvey Brown's cattle, which were being pastured by a third party named Conners, escaped through a poorly maintained fence from Conners' adjacent field into the premises of Thomas Ward, where they caused damage. The original suit was filed by Ward against Brown before a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment favoring Ward for $24 in damages and costs. After an appeal, the case was moved to the Circuit Court of LaSalle County, where the judgment was upheld. Brown, represented by attorney E.F. Bull, appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging the liability for the trespass committed by the cattle while they were in the possession of Conners.	The plaintiff, Thomas Ward, argued that specific damages were incurred due to the trespass of the defendant's cattle on his property. Ward sought compensation for the damages caused by Brown's cattle, asserting that Brown should be liable for their actions regardless of their bailment status with Conners.	The defendant, Harvey Brown, contended that he should not be held liable for the trespass since the cattle's actions occurred without his knowledge or consent while under the control of Conners, the bailee. Brown’s defense emphasized that their arrangement with Conners removed his direct responsibility over the cattle, arguing that the negligence of Conners or the insufficient fence separating the properties was the root cause of the incident.

In December 1843, the case of Thomas Stokes et al. v. Charles Kane was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following a previous judgment by the Winnebago circuit court. The circuit court trial occurred during the April term of 1841 and concluded with a verdict in favor of the plaintiffs, Stokes and others, awarding them $93. The defendants, led by Charles Kane, appealed the decision, arguing against the admissibility of a deposition presented by the plaintiffs. Central to the case was a witness named Whitcomb, who the defendants contended had an interest in the case's outcome. The circuit court had ruled against excluding the deposition based on this interest, which led to the appeal. The legal point being contested was whether a witness can be deemed incompetent simply because of their interest in the event of the suit. The plaintiffs maintained that the interest was either balanced or adverse, thereby rendering the witness competent to testify.	The plaintiffs, Thomas Stokes and others, claimed that the testimony of the witness Whitcomb was valid and should not have been excluded despite the defendants' assertions of his interest in the case. They argued that the nature of the witness's interest was not adequately demonstrated by the defendants and contended that the circuit court was correct in allowing the deposition to be read as evidence. The plaintiffs sought to uphold the original judgment in their favor and the awarded damages of $93.	The defendants, represented by Charles Kane, contended that the court erred in allowing the deposition from the witness Whitcomb, asserting that his interest in the outcome of the case disqualified him from testifying. They claimed that the circuit court should have excluded the deposition based on this supposed incompetency of the witness. The defendants requested that the appeal result in the reversal of the original verdict and judgment in favor of the plaintiffs.

On February 16, 1865, in Cumberland County, Illinois, Arthur Teader, alongside his bail, Edwin S. Norfolk and Benjamin G. Glenn, entered into a recognizance for his appearance at the March term of the Circuit Court charged with larceny. This recognizance was approved and filed properly. However, the March term did not occur, and a Special Term held in July did not address Teader's case. When the regular September term commenced, Teader failed to appear, prompting the court to call upon Norfolk and Glenn to produce their principal, which they could not do. Consequently, a default judgment was rendered against Teader and his sureties for the specified amount of two hundred and fifty dollars each. A writ of scire facias was then issued, which Norfolk received while Teader and Glenn could not be found. Upon their failure to plead, the court rendered a judgment against Norfolk and Glenn, leading them to file a writ of error to challenge this judgment.	The plaintiffs, Edwin S. Norfolk and Benjamin G. Glenn, contended that the judgment against them for the forfeiture of the recognizance was erroneous because a court term had not been held as required when the recognizance was due. They argued that under statute, matters pending during a non-sitting of the court should be continued to the next term and sought reversal of the judgment against them based on this claim.	The defendant, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, argued that the forfeiture was valid and correctly taken during the next regular term. They maintained that the law did not require a forfeiture to be declared at the first term if the court did not sit, and that the plaintiffs failed to prove that no regular term was held. Furthermore, they insisted that the plaintiffs had the option to surrender their principal at any time to release themselves from liability, suggesting their inaction was a surrender of liability.

The legal case "Daniel J. M. Walker v. Osee Welch et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1853. The proceedings originated from a lawsuit initiated by the appellees (Osee Welch and others) against the appellant (Daniel J. M. Walker) concerning a book account. The trial took place during the May Term of 1852 at the Jo Daviess Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Sheldon. During the jury trial, the court rendered a verdict unfavorable to Walker, leading to a judgment against him. Walker subsequently filed an appeal, arguing against the decision made in the lower court regarding the motion to discharge the defendant on common bail and the handling of a set-off during the trial.	The plaintiffs, represented by attorneys Higgins and Strother, brought a claim against Walker for an assumpsit related to a book account. They argued that the verdict returned by the jury was sufficient to support the judgment rendered against Walker and contended that procedural decisions made by the lower court were appropriate and valid.
