Walker's defense team, consisting of Glover and Cook along with J. P. Stevens, contended that there were errors in the trial process related to the motion to discharge the defendant on common bail. They argued that the discretion exercised by the court in this matter was erroneous and that it was improper to allow the set-off to be withdrawn after the evidence had been presented and the jury had reached a decision.

The case, "The City of Springfield v. Horace Hickox et al." took place in 1845 in Springfield, Illinois. The City of Springfield initiated this lawsuit against the defendants, Horace Hickox and others, to recover a penalty of twelve dollars for violating municipal ordinances requiring merchants to obtain annual operating licenses. The ordinance stipulated that failure to obtain a license would render the violator liable for a penalty that would be enforced by action before the Mayor. A summons was issued on August 22, 1844, and upon hearing, the Mayor ruled in favor of Springfield. The defendants appealed the judgment. During the proceedings, the defendants introduced a city order as evidence for a set-off against the city's claim. This order, from the mayor, indicated a debt of $50, payable from unappropriated city funds but was refused payment due to the absence of funds in the treasury at the time. Despite defendants admitting to operating without a license, they argued the order should offset Springfield's demand. The Circuit Court heard the case without a jury and ultimately ruled in favor of the defendants, awarding them $38 and costs, prompting Springfield's further appeal, focusing on the admissibility of the city order and the exclusion of their evidence.	The City of Springfield argued that the defendants were legally responsible for the twelve-dollar penalty due to their failure to secure the mandated licenses under the municipal ordinance. They contended that the defendants did not meet the requirements set out in the ordinances and claimed the right to recover the penalty in a suit before the Mayor. Furthermore, the city challenged the validity of the defendants' set-off argument based on the nature of the city order presented as evidence.	The defendants countered by claiming that the city order, drawn on the city's treasurer, constituted a legitimate and valid set-off against the city's claims. They argued that the order represented evidence of indebtedness and that a prior demand on the treasurer was unnecessary for the action to proceed. They asserted their right to offset the penalty owed to the city with the amount stated in the city order, asserting that they were legally entitled to the funds owed to them by the city.

Thomas D. McKee filed a writ of error concerning a tax judgment rendered against him by the Board of Supervisors of Champaign County in January 1870. The case took place in the Illinois Supreme Court, where the key individuals included McKee as the plaintiff and the Board of Supervisors as the defendants. The legal dispute arose when the Board of Supervisors decided to increase the valuation of improved properties by one hundred percent and the valuation of unimproved properties by twenty-five percent within the township. McKee challenged this decision, arguing that the Board's action did not conform with the established legal standards for equalizing property assessments among different townships in the county, as determined in a prior case.	McKee contended that the Board of Supervisors' method of increasing land valuations was unlawful. He argued that the Board must apply a uniform percentage increase or decrease to all real estate within a township when equalizing assessments. Additionally, he claimed that the absence of proper notification from the tax collector regarding the intended application for judgment rendered the tax judgment against him invalid and contestable.	The Board of Supervisors defended their actions by asserting their authority to equalize assessments as per statutory requirements. They likely claimed that their decisions were made in accordance with the powers granted to them, and therefore, the adjustments to property valuations were legitimate. They sought to uphold the tax judgment against McKee, arguing that the procedures followed met the necessary legal standards.

In the legal case of B. M. Rowland v. Springfield Fire and Marine Insurance Co., the events unfolded in Richland County, Illinois around March 1885. The plaintiff, B. M. Rowland, sought to recover the value of property that was destroyed by fire on March 12 or 13, 1885. Rowland applied for fire insurance on March 7, 1885, through L. W. Mitchell, a sub-agent of the defendant company. Rowland paid a premium of five dollars and signed an application for insurance on his property worth $200, with the understanding that the insurance was subject to approval by the company's general agent. However, the application was later rejected, and the premium was returned before the fire occurred. After the destruction of his property, Rowland, despite knowing of the rejection, insisted that he was entitled to the insurance payout and initiated legal action against the insurance company to recover the value of the lost property. The case was tried, but the court ruled that no valid contract was made between Rowland and the insurance company due to the rejection of his application and the conditions laid out in the receipt he received.	The plaintiff, B. M. Rowland, claimed that he entered into a binding insurance contract with Springfield Fire and Marine Insurance Co. through its agent, L. W. Mitchell. Rowland argued that the agent's promise to insure his property, along with the premium payment, constituted a valid agreement for insurance coverage. He sought damages for the full value of the property destroyed by the fire, arguing that he was misled into believing that his property was insured until officially notified otherwise. Rowland asserted that he had fulfilled all conditions necessary for securing insurance and expressed that the denial of his claim constituted a breach of contract.	The defendant, Springfield Fire and Marine Insurance Co., contended that no valid insurance contract was ever formed between the parties because the application submitted by Rowland was explicitly subject to the approval of the company’s general agent, which was not granted. They argued that Mitchell, as a soliciting agent, lacked authority to bind the company to an insurance contract. The defendant emphasized that the application was promptly rejected, and the premium was returned, negating any claim for insurance coverage. The defendant requested the court to dismiss Rowland's claims, asserting the absence of a contractual obligation to pay for the alleged loss.

In 1846, the case of Levi D. Boone v. Caleb Stone et al. took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. This legal matter arose from a scire facias issued to revive a prior judgment rendered in favor of Caleb Stone, Manning, and Glover against Levi D. Boone in August 1837. The scire facias indicated that the judgment had been assigned to a third party, Elias B. Paine, who sought to have the judgment revived. Levi D. Boone countered with several pleas, arguing that the assignment was not made as claimed, that the original plaintiffs had declared bankruptcy and were discharged before the assignment, and that there was no record for the claim against him. The lower court sustained a demurrer against Boone’s first two pleas and ruled against him, prompting Boone to appeal the decision. The case was brought in the Madison Circuit Court and involved legal arguments around the implications of bankruptcy on the enforcement of judgments.	The plaintiff, represented by Elias B. Paine in the capacity of an assignee, claimed that the judgment should be revived despite Boone's defenses. The plaintiffs contended that the current action was legitimate as Boone was still liable for the original judgment, regardless of the bankruptcy status or assignment issues raised by him.	Levi D. Boone raised three main defenses: firstly, that the assignment of the judgment mentioned in the scire facias was invalid; secondly, that the original judgment's plaintiffs had declared bankruptcy and were discharged before the judgment was assigned to Paine, thus nullifying their right to collect; and thirdly, that there was no valid record of the judgment against him, seeking to have the case dismissed.

On October 18, 1884, Edward C. Huling, Henry S. Farwell, and Stephen Laskey formed a partnership in Chicago, Illinois, to manufacture and sell men’s furnishing goods with a total capital of $60,000. Farwell contributed $40,000 and Huling $20,000, sharing profits with Farwell and Huling each receiving 45% and Laskey 10%. The partnership lasted less than nine months, dissolving by mutual consent on July 29, 1885. Huling sold his interest to Farwell, but the price was to be determined by arbitration. After an unsatisfactory award, Huling initiated legal proceedings on August 12, 1885, seeking to set aside the arbitration award, demanding an accounting and settlement of the partnership's financials. The court appointed a master to examine the accounts, resulting in a report that valued Huling’s interest in the firm’s assets (excluding goodwill) at a deficit of $3,403.30 but attributed $5,000 in goodwill, creating a balance of $1,596.70 in favor of Huling. Both parties filed exceptions to the master's report in the circuit court, leading to varying conclusions and appeal processes involving the Appellate Court. Ultimately, the circuit court’s decisions faced several challenges regarding the appropriateness and sufficiency of the master's findings related to goodwill valuation.	Huling argued that the master undervalued his interest in the goodwill, asserting it should be $25,000 instead of $5,000. He contended that the master relied on flawed testimony and made errors in assessing the business's performance, as he believed there was a profit on the date of dissolution rather than a loss. Huling sought a judicial determination that would recognize his rightful share in the profits and a reassessment of the partnership accounts in his favor.	Farwell and Laskey contended that the master's report, which credited Huling with a $5,000 goodwill value, was erroneous as they asserted that the goodwill had no value at the dissolution time. They maintained that Huling was in fact indebted to the firm and sought the court's validation of their claims against Huling, arguing the master's findings were not supported by competent evidence and that Huling had failed to demonstrate the actual worth of any goodwill.

In the case of Jacob Sholty v. Commissioners of Highways of Dale Township, which took place in Illinois in January 1872, the central issue revolved around the legality of the commissioners' actions in opening a road. Initially, the commissioners made an order to open a certain road, which was subsequently appealed to three supervisors. These supervisors upheld the commissioner's order, leading to a writ of certiorari being filed in the circuit court. The circuit court, upon reviewing the proceedings, found the commissioners' order to be illegal and set it aside. Following this ruling, the commissioners initiated new proceedings to establish the road again, which led Sholty to file a bill against them. He argued that the application to reopen the road was made within a year of the supervisors' decision, claiming that the statutory provision should prohibit new proceedings in such a timeframe. Ultimately, this case examined the interpretation of the statute regarding the establishment and alteration of highways in relation to the timeline of appeals and decisions made by supervisors.	The plaintiff, Jacob Sholty, claimed that the commissioners did not have the authority to open the road since their order was made within one year of the supervisors' previous decision. He argued that the ongoing legal procedures violated the legislative intent aimed at making the supervisors’ decisions final for one year. He requested that the new application to open the road be declared invalid based on these grounds.	The defendants, the Commissioners of Highways, contended that the previous order established by the supervisors had been rendered a nullity by the circuit court's ruling. They maintained that since the ordinance was declared void, a new application could be rightfully initiated. The defendants requested the court to affirm the new proceedings and allow the road to be opened as per their order.

In January 1886, Wilson Ames initiated a legal action against Robert Moir & Company, claiming on a contract dated June 9, 1870, for the sale of one hundred barrels of high-wines at $1.07 per proof gallon. The contract stipulated conditions regarding delivery, with the buyer allowed to call for the goods between July 1 and July 20 of the same year, and if not called for by the latter date, the seller could deliver them until the end of July with three days' notice. The dispute arose primarily around whether the contract qualified as a written agreement under statutes concerning the statute of limitations. Ames contended that it should be governed by the sixteen-year limit for debts, while the defendant claimed it fell under the five-year limit due to an absence of a formal written contract. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, which reviewed the lower court's decision that upheld Ames' claim.	Wilson Ames argued that the instrument in question constituted a valid written contract. He maintained that it included all essential elements, such as the names of both parties, a description of the goods, the price, and delivery terms, supporting his position that the obligations implied by the agreement warranted legal recognition for the duration of sixteen years, as opposed to the five-year limit claimed by the defendant.	Robert Moir & Company contended that the document did not satisfy the requirements of a written contract or evidential proof of debt, therefore subjecting the claim to a five-year statute of limitations. They argued that essential contract elements were lacking and that the court should dismiss Ames' claims based on this legal foundation.

The case "The Paris and Decatur Railroad Co. v. Thomas J. Mullins" arose in January 1873 and took place in Edgar County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Thomas J. Mullins, had initiated the action against the Paris and Decatur Railroad Company, seeking compensation for a colt that was killed by a train belonging to the railroad. This legal proceeding initially commenced before a Justice of the Peace, where Mullins secured a judgment in his favor. The case was subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court, which upheld the initial ruling, resulting in a second judgment for Mullins. A key aspect of the case was whether the railroad company acted negligently in operating the train. Evidence presented in court was conflicting; the railroad argued that the colt had suddenly dashed onto the tracks from the side, making it impossible for them to stop. Conversely, evidence in support of Mullins indicated that the colt had been on the track for a considerable distance before being struck, suggesting that the train operator had sufficient time to react and avoid the incident.	The plaintiff, Thomas J. Mullins, claimed that the Paris and Decatur Railroad Company was negligent in its operations, specifically in failing to slow down the train when the colt was on the track. He sought compensation for the value of the colt, asserting that the train's operator could have detected the animal in time to prevent the accident through reasonable diligence.	The defendant, Paris and Decatur Railroad Company, contended that the colt had suddenly entered the tracks, and thus the train operator was unable to stop in time to avoid the accident. The railroad argued that evidence indicated the colt was not visible in advance, thereby absolving them of negligence.

John Totel filed a complaint in the Illinois Appellate Court against Esaie Bonnefoy and others regarding the filling of a ditch that had allowed surface water drainage from his property for over twenty years. The case took place in La Salle County, Illinois, and was heard on May 27, 1887. Totel claimed that the ditch was the natural drainage course for the surface water from his land and had been agreed upon by previous landowners, including Bonnefoy. The defendants contended that the natural drainage direction was different than what Totel asserted and argued that the ditch had been constructed fraudulently in 1877 to benefit Totel's land while adversely affecting theirs. The defendants filled in the ditch, prompting Totel to seek an injunction to prevent any further obstruction. The court dissolved the temporary injunction that had initially been granted to Totel and dismissed the bill against the defendants.	Totel claimed that the surface water from his property naturally drained through a ditch that crossed the land of the defendants. He requested an injunction to prevent the defendants from filling in the ditch again, asserting that he had the right to use it for drainage based on long-standing usage and mutual agreements among previous landowners.	The defendants argued that the natural drainage course was not as Totel claimed but instead directed southeast. They denied the existence of a legally enforceable right for Totel to use the ditch based on mutual consent, maintaining that the development of any drainage system was instigated by Totel for his benefit. They asserted that the alleged historical usage lacked a proper legal basis since it was by a verbal parol license, which is revocable.

In the case of Henry J. Chase v. George Debolt, the legal proceedings originated in Peoria County, Illinois, with the initial complaint filed by Debolt against Chase in 1845. Debolt sought to recover $75.93 for work performed at Jubilee College, which Chase managed as an agent for Bishop Chase. During the trial, Debolt called Chase as a witness; this led to controversy when the Circuit Court permitted the justice of the peace to testify about what Chase testified to in the lower trial. The core issue was whether Chase, acting as an agent for Bishop Chase, could be held liable for the payments due for Debolt’s labor. It was established that Debolt was aware that he was working for Bishop Chase, not Chase himself, based on testimony from other witnesses who confirmed that payments were made from the Bishop's funds. Amidst assignments of error, including objections to hearsay and the refusal of a new trial, the appeal hinged on whether Chase should be held personally liable for the work performed by Debolt.	The plaintiff, George Debolt, claimed that Henry J. Chase owed him $75.93 for labor performed at Jubilee College. Debolt argued that Chase, as the agent of Bishop Chase, was responsible for ensuring payment for the work rendered. During the trials, Debolt's position relied on the testimony that he had been employed by Chase without knowledge of Chase's agent status, implying that Debolt was led to believe that Chase was acting as a principal in the employment agreement.	The defendant, Henry J. Chase, contended that he should not be personally liable for the amount claimed by Debolt because the work was performed under the employment of Bishop Chase, of which Debolt was aware. Chase asserted that since he was acting as an agent and not as a principal, and since Debolt had received payments from the Bishop directly, he had no obligation to Debolt. Chase objected to the introduction of hearsay evidence and claimed that Debolt had been informed of his agency status prior to engaging in work at the College.

The case "Eva Lawrence, Guardian, etc. v. The City of Chicago" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. It originated in the Superior Court of Chicago, presided over by Chief Justice Joseph E. Gaby. The primary individuals involved include Eva Lawrence, who served as the guardian in this case, and the City of Chicago as the defendant. The details of the specific events that led to the legal action are not provided, but the case is noted to be identical in its legal context to a previous case, Wright v. The City of Chicago, suggesting that it may involve similar legal principles or circumstances related to municipal liability or responsibility.	The plaintiff, Eva Lawrence, as guardian, likely asserted claims against the City of Chicago related to an alleged harm or wrongdoing attributable to the city's actions or negligence. Although specific arguments were not detailed, the appeal indicates that the plaintiff sought some form of redress or compensation, paralleling the claims made in the previous Wright case.	The City of Chicago, represented by attorney S. A. Irvin, presumably presented defenses against the claims made by Lawrence. The nature of these defenses is not explicitly outlined, but they would typically encompass arguments that challenge the plaintiff's assertions or seek to demonstrate a lack of liability, possibly citing legal precedents or statutes that protect the city from certain claims.

The case "Paschal P. Mathews et al. v. George Cowan et al." stems from events that occurred in Cook County, Illinois on December 3, 1870. The plaintiffs, Paschal P. Mathews and others, delivered three hundred barrels of flour to the defendants, George Cowan and a partner, as part of a cash sale agreement. The plaintiffs had previously sold a total of five hundred barrels to the defendants, two hundred of which had already been delivered and paid for. On the delivery date, the defendants provided a check for $1,473, which was meant to cover the cost of the flour. However, the check was dishonored when presented, and it was revealed that the defendants were insolvent, leading to claims of fraud. The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants had no intention to pay for the flour upon its delivery, claiming they were intentionally misled by the defendants who presented the check knowing it would not clear. The case went to trial, where issues regarding the validity of the contract and the defendants' intentions were contested, ultimately leading to an appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants fraudulently induced them to deliver the flour by using a check they knew was worthless, intending to deceive the plaintiffs out of their property. They contended that this amounted to a conversion of their property and sought damages for the loss of the flour, asserting that the actions of the defendants were both wrongful and fraudulent.	The defendants argued that the contract for the sale of flour was valid at the time of purchase and asserted that any potential fraud was not present during the purchase agreement but may have occurred at the point of delivery. They contended that Haven, one of the defendants, was an infant and therefore not liable for the contract, seeking to have the claims dismissed based on this defense of minority and lack of intent to defraud during the original sale.

The case "Nancy Terry et al. v. The Trustees of Eureka College" originated in September 1873 in Woodford County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Nancy Terry and her husband N. B. Terry, were involved in a legal dispute concerning a deed of trust related to a mortgage. The Trustees of Eureka College filed a bill in chancery to foreclose this deed, claiming that the Terrys had defaulted on their payment obligations, particularly the interest on the secured notes. The sheriff confirmed that the summons was duly served upon the defendants. After the master conducted a sale of the premises as per the decree, the defendants objected to the sale, challenging the timing of the complaint's filing and the admissibility of the deed due to its acknowledgement status. The court dealt with these objections, stating that the entire debt could be foreclosed as per the terms of the deed, which allowed for that action upon default of interest payments. The court also ruled that the deed's acknowledgment issues were not a valid defense under the law as it stood at the time.	The plaintiffs, the Trustees of Eureka College, claimed that the defendants had defaulted on their obligation to pay interest on the notes secured by the deed of trust. They argued that according to the deed's terms, the entire debt became due upon this default, justifying the foreclosure of the property. They sought a decree to have the property sold to recover the debt in full, maintaining that the defendants' objections were unfounded.	The defendants, Nancy Terry and N. B. Terry, presented several arguments against the foreclosure. They contended that the bill of complaint was prematurely filed, as the notes were not due at the time of the filing. Additionally, they argued that the deed should not be admissible in evidence since it was not acknowledged properly by the married woman, one of the grantors. The defendants requested that the court dismiss the actions of the plaintiffs based on these defenses.

In the late 1850s, the Illinois River Railroad Company was organized and began construction of its railway. The County of Morgan subscribed $50,000 in bonds to support this project, intending for these funds to be used solely for work conducted within the county. In 1859, the railroad's president ordered two bonds worth $2000 each to pay contractors Allen & McGrady for work on the project. However, when contractor Allen & McGrady attempted to redeem these bonds, they were informed by the bankers, Brown & Elliott, that the bonds were only to be delivered for work done in Morgan County, a stipulation the county later asserted. This led to litigation involving various claimants, including William Thomas, who had received the order for the bonds from Allen & McGrady. The County Court ruled that the bonds could only be used for work done in Morgan County, but since no such work had been completed, the claims for the bonds were dismissed. Subsequent actions involved other creditors attempting to collect debts from the railroad, leading to a series of complicated legal proceedings regarding the bonds and the railroad's status culminating in multiple claims for ownership and payments related to the bonds.	William Thomas claimed he was entitled to $4000 worth of the bonds issued by the County of Morgan, arguing that since work had now been completed on the road within Morgan County by the successors of the original railroad company, he should be granted access to these funds. He contended that the previous court ruling only applied to the situation as it stood at that time and did not preclude him from claiming the bonds based upon the newly fulfilled conditions.	The County of Morgan maintained that no delivery of bonds was warranted since the conditions stipulated — work being done in Morgan County by the original railroad company — had not been satisfied at the time Thomas acquired the orders. They insisted that since the order was issued before any work was performed in Morgan County by the successor company, Thomas's claim for the bonds was invalid, and further asserted that he lacked standing to seek an equitable remedy since the appropriate legal remedies had not been exhausted.

In April 1867, a legal dispute arose between Frederick Beckman and others (the plaintiffs) and John P. Kreamer and others (the defendants) in Kankakee County, Illinois. The plaintiffs owned land that included a small lake, which had an outlet to the Kankakee River and was rich with fish. The defendants unlawfully entered the plaintiffs' property with boats and fishing equipment, intending to fish in the lake without the plaintiffs' permission. This action led the plaintiffs to file a trespass suit against the defendants, asserting their exclusive rights to the land and fishery. Initially, the plaintiffs won a modest sum of $25 in a lower court, but this amount was later reduced to $5 on appeal to the Circuit Court. The court decided on apportioning costs between the parties, which the defendants contested. The case raised significant questions regarding the common law rights to fish in non-navigable waters and the powers of the courts regarding cost apportionment in trespass actions.	The plaintiffs claimed ownership of the land surrounding the lake, asserting a legal or equitable title and actual possession of the adjacent lands. They asserted that the defendants' actions constituted a clear trespass on their exclusive fishing rights, for which they sought damages due to the unauthorized entrance onto their property. The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to recover costs associated with the case, asserting that the Circuit Court's cost apportionment was unfair and not in accordance with the statutes.	The defendants argued against the plaintiffs' claims by contesting the Circuit Court's apportionment of costs from the initial trial. They asserted that the court had incorrectly applied the law regarding cost apportionment, which they believed should be divided according to the actual judgment rendered, rather than according to the discretion perceived by the court. They maintained that their entry onto the lake did not constitute a significant trespass and sought to appeal the cost distribution that unfairly charged them based on the circumstances of the case.

This case, Edwin S. Humphrey v. Thomas Clement, was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867. The dispute arose from a contract involving the sale and conveyance of a tract of land. Edwin S. Humphrey had executed the contract in favor of Zopher P. Humphrey, who subsequently assigned it to Thomas Clement. The case was presented in the Circuit Court of Bureau County, presided over by Judge Madison E. Hollister. The defendant, Edwin S. Humphrey, admitted to making the contract and acknowledged the tender of payment in legal tender notes when due. However, he contended that Zopher P. Humphrey had originally agreed to pay the purchase price in gold and alleged a similar agreement with Clement upon the assignment. The crux of the issue was that while a deed of general warranty was tendered, the plaintiff, Clement, refused to accept it because Humphrey's wife had not released her dower rights. The court's role was to enforce the contract's specific performance, while also addressing the implications of the wife's contingent dower rights.	Thomas Clement, the plaintiff, claimed that he was entitled to the specific performance of the contract for the land sale. He argued that he had tendered the necessary payment in legal tender notes, which the law recognizes as valid for such transactions. Clement insisted that the court should enforce the contract as written, compelling Edwin S. Humphrey to convey the land to him irrespective of the wife's dower rights, given that the property would have a perfect title if the payment was properly made.	Edwin S. Humphrey, the defendant, argued that the contract stipulated payment in gold, which had not been respected in the context of the agreement. He claimed that the refusal to accept the deed was justified due to the lack of a waiver of dower rights from his wife, asserting that no equitable title could be conveyed without her consent. He contended that any judicial decision should consider this dower interest, and thus he sought to retain a portion of the purchase money until the dower issue was resolved.

The case of **Adam Smith et al. v. James Dinsmore** took place in **1885** in **Whiteside County, Illinois**. The primary individuals involved were **Adam Smith**, **Henry Smith**, **James Dinsmore**, and **Peter Bressler**. The dispute centers around a series of mortgages executed by Bressler in favor of the **Etna Life Insurance Company** in **1881**, totaling **$8,200**, **$6,500**, and **$6,000** on 1,080 acres of land, with 410 acres covered by the largest mortgage. Following these transactions, Dinsmore bought **220 acres** from Bressler on **March 26, 1883**, for **$7,700**, with an arrangement to pay off the existing mortgage to clear the land title. Dinsmore later acquired a release from the Etna Life Insurance Company for the mortgage on that land by settling the debts owed under the mortgages. Afterward, a third party, **John Martin**, obtained a judgment lien against Bressler and foreclosed on the land Dinsmore had purchased. The court initially ruled in favor of Dinsmore, decreeing that Martin and the Smiths pay him for the amount he had spent to clear the mortgage, leading to their appeal based on Dinsmore's right to subrogation.	The plaintiffs, Adam Smith and Henry Smith, contest Dinsmore's right to subrogation by arguing that he should not be entitled to collect the amounts awarded by the court as he did not pay all the debts on behalf of the mortgages. They claim unjust enrichment and assert that Dinsmore has improperly increased the amount of his mortgage claim beyond what he rightfully paid. They seek a reversal of the judgment favoring Dinsmore.	James Dinsmore argues that he has the right to be subrogated to the position of the original mortgagee (the Etna Life Insurance Company) after paying off the mortgages to clear the title to his land. He contends that his payments were necessary to protect his investment and that the subrogation doctrine entitles him to recover amounts either through payments made or the sale of the property. He dismisses claims of unjust enrichment, asserting that he merely stepped into the shoes of the mortgagee to maintain his rights as a result of legitimate financial transactions.

The case "William Patton et al. v. George W. Campbell" emerged from a transaction conducted on October 20, 1870, involving Patton & Co. from New York and Durham & Wood from Chicago. Patton & Co. sold goods worth $1,600 on a four-month credit to the latter. However, by early November of the same year, Durham & Wood failed financially, prompting Patton & Co. to file a replevin action to reclaim their goods. In the course of this legal action, a replevin bond of $1,000 was executed, and $800 to $900 worth of goods were replevied. Unfortunately, key documents related to the case were destroyed in a fire on October 8-9, 1871, leading to the dismissal of the action. Subsequently, George W. Campbell, as the assignee in bankruptcy for Durham & Wood, filed a chancery bill against Patton & Co. seeking to recover the value of the goods. The court ruled in favor of Campbell for $850, prompting Patton & Co. to appeal. The defense argued that the court of chancery lacked jurisdiction and that the goods were fraudulently purchased. However, upon review, the court found that Campbell had a valid claim, and the replevin action was justified.	The plaintiff, George W. Campbell, as the assignee in bankruptcy for Durham & Wood, contended that the goods sold by Patton & Co. had been replevied during a legal dispute and sought to recover their value. He maintained that the court had jurisdiction to address the matter, specifically citing the accidental destruction of the replevin documents which warranted equitable relief. The plaintiff asserted that their claim was valid and requested the recovery of $850.	The defendants, William Patton et al., contended that the court of chancery lacked jurisdiction over the case, asserting that legal remedies were adequate for the plaintiff’s claims. They also argued that the sale was fraudulent on the grounds that Durham & Wood misrepresented their financial situation and intentions. Consequently, they requested the court to reverse the prior decree, claiming the right to rescind the sale due to alleged fraudulent conduct.

In the case of Chicago City Railway Co. v. Patrick Hennessy, the incident took place in Chicago, Illinois, in 1885. The plaintiff, Patrick Hennessy, as the administrator of the estate of James Hennessy, a deceased eight-year-old boy, filed a lawsuit against the Chicago City Railway Company. The boy died while playing on a conveyor apparatus, which was part of a construction project for an endless cable railway contracted to C. B. Holmes. The conveyor was using a revolving screw powered by steam to move materials for the construction. During its operation, the boy climbed onto the conveyor and was tragically drawn into the machine, resulting in his death. The lawsuit was initiated to recover damages for the deceased’s next of kin, raising questions about who was liable: the railway company or the independent contractor, Holmes.	The plaintiff claimed that the railway company was liable for the injuries leading to the death of the child because it had a duty to ensure safety during the construction activities for the railway project. Hennessy argued that the fatal accident occurred due to negligence associated with the operation of the machinery involved in the construction.	The defendant, the Chicago City Railway Company, contended that it was not liable for the boy’s death because it had hired an independent contractor, C. B. Holmes, to complete the construction without retaining any control over the work or the machinery used. The company maintained that any negligence was solely that of the contractor and denied any responsibility for the actions taken by Holmes or the workmen involved in the construction.

Darius H. Denton filed a lawsuit against Amos C. Jackson in 1883, concerning a financial transaction involving the purchase of pork and lard on the Chicago Board of Trade. Denton began dealing in these commodities in the spring of 1881 and employed Jackson as a commission merchant to facilitate his trades. By December 12, 1881, Denton had $3,275.69 in margins with Jackson, but Jackson claimed that Denton’s margins were insufficient and sold the commodities at a loss of $1,927.50 without confirming Denton's authorization to do so. Denton argued that he still had sufficient margins and denied authorizing the sale, while Jackson countered that he acted under Denton’s authority. The case spanned multiple court levels, ultimately reaching the Illinois Supreme Court after appeals, where the jury initially sided with Denton.	Denton claimed that Jackson wrongfully sold his pork and lard without proper authorization, despite having sufficient margins on deposit. He argued that the transaction was authorized neither by him nor by the customs of the Board of Trade, which requires notice before any sale under such circumstances. Denton sought recovery for the amount he deposited in margins.	Jackson contended that he was acting under the authority granted by Denton when he sold the commodities. He claimed that the margins were nearly exhausted, thus justifying the sale. Jackson also argued that he had credit from Denton, which he appropriated to cover losses incurred by another of his clients, J.K. Plank, without proper consent from Denton.

In the case of Levi H. Strong et al. v. Patrick Shea et al., decided in September 1876, the Illinois Supreme Court examined a dispute involving property ownership in Cook County, Illinois. The central figure in this case is Patrick Shea, who originally owned a parcel of land but faced financial difficulties. He secured a loan from Eisendrath, representing this obligation through a promissory note. To satisfy this debt, Shea conveyed his property to a trustee, who later sold it to Eisendrath. Subsequently, the land changed hands through various quitclaim transactions. In 1869, the property was transferred to Levi H. Strong and others, who claimed rightful ownership. However, Shea had remained in actual possession of the property throughout these dealings and continued to make improvements, pay taxes, and utilize its resources, which he argued demonstrated his ownership. Despite the destruction of some records in a fire, Shea sought to reaffirm his title to the land through legal means, leading to the appeal after the Circuit Court dismissed his claims.	The plaintiffs, Levi H. Strong and others, asserted their legal rights to the land, which they believed was confirmed through a series of conveyances beginning with Eisendrath and culminating in their acquisition. They aimed to restore records lost in a fire and validate their ownership claim against Shea. They contended that the chain of title had been legally established, arguing for the restoration of their rights under the perspective that Shea's claims were invalid due to their legitimate ownership stemming from the property's lawful transactions.	The defendant, Patrick Shea, presented several defenses. He argued that he had continually claimed and exercised ownership of the property, evidenced by his possession and significant improvements made over the years. He contended that his agreement with Boyer, who acquired the title from Eisendrath, had been a secure transaction reflecting Shea’s true ownership interests, as Boyer acted merely as a trustee. Shea claimed that he had appropriated the property, paid taxes, and sold timber, affirming his rightful claim. Moreover, he emphasized that he was unaware of the subsequent transactions involving the title, asserting that the quitclaim actions did not signify a waiver of his ownership rights.

The case "The Western Union Telegraph Company v. The Chicago and Paducah Railroad Company et al." originated in LaSalle County, Illinois, around the winter and spring of 1874. During this period, the Chicago and Paducah Railroad Company was nearing the completion of its railroad from Streator to Altamont. Negotiations commenced with the Western Union Telegraph Company regarding a contract for placing telegraph poles along the railroad line. The key individuals involved were Ralph Plumb, the vice-president and general manager of the railroad company, and Anson Stager, the general superintendent of the telegraph company. A contract was drafted, which included the provision that the railroad would furnish poles and labor for the telegraph line, while the telegraph company would supply materials. Although the formal execution of the contract by the railroad company was never completed, Plumb's acceptance via letter indicated a mutual understanding. Subsequently, both companies operated under the agreement for over a year, but tensions arose when the railroad company permitted another telegraph company to use the same poles, prompting the Western Union to seek an injunction to prevent this. The matter led to a dismissal of the complaint, resulting in an appeal by the Western Union Telegraph Company.	The Western Union Telegraph Company claimed that a binding contract existed despite the lack of formal signature by the railroad company. They argued that the railroad's actions and Plumb’s letter constituted acceptance of the contract terms, thus obligating the railroad to refrain from allowing other telegraph companies to use the poles. The plaintiff sought an injunction to prevent the Atlantic and Pacific Telegraph Company from stringing its wires on the poles already used by the Western Union, emphasizing that such unauthorized use would infringe upon their rights established under the contract.	The Chicago and Paducah Railroad Company contended that the contract was never formally executed and was not binding. They invoked the statute of frauds and argued that the agreement should not be enforced due to issues related to public policy and the potential creation of a monopoly. They maintained that Plumb lacked authority to bind the company to the contract and claimed that no binding agreement existed without a formal signing.

Samuel Kitson filed a petition in the County Court in Cook County, Illinois, seeking release from imprisonment based on a capias ad satisfaciendum issued due to a prior judgment against him for $85,882.54, in favor of Johh V. Farwell and others (appellees). The case arose from a previous action where malice was determined to be the essence of the claim leading to the judgment against Kitson. The County Court denied his petition, asserting that malice was indeed the gist of the original action and subsequently dismissed the petition. Upon appeal to the Circuit Court, the court tried the case before a jury but directed a verdict against Kitson, affirming the County Court's judgment and ordering his remand to the sheriff's custody. Kitson appealed this decision, claiming errors in the exclusion of evidence and the introduction of the original case records by the defendants without proper identification. Ultimately, the court evaluated the procedural decisions made during the trials and confirmed the finality of the original judgment regarding malice.	The plaintiff, Samuel Kitson, argued that his imprisonment was unjust and requested to be released based on his claims of not having engaged in fraudulent practices related to the debt that led to the judgment. He contended that he had acted in good faith and that the original debt was not incurred through any deceitful means.	The defendants, represented by Johh V. Farwell, maintained that the original judgment was valid and that malice was central to the claims against Kitson. They successfully argued that introducing the records of the earlier case was appropriate, thus reinforcing the judgment's finality and asserting that Kitson's attempts to introduce contradictory evidence were untimely and irrelevant due to the principles of res judicata.

On May 9, 1851, in Macoupin County, Illinois, Elijah Mitchell issued a promissory note for $450 to the deceased individual, which accrued interest at a rate of ten percent per annum for borrowed money. Following the death of the debtor, Samuel T. Mayo, as the administrator of the estate, issued a notice under the provisions of the Statute of Wills, calling for claims against the estate to be presented in the county court. Mitchell appeared at the hearing, where his claim and note were formally acknowledged and allowed by the court. The legal question submitted to the Illinois Supreme Court was whether the allowance of the note changed the interest rate from ten percent to six percent, as required by law for judgments against an estate.	The plaintiff, Elijah Mitchell, argued that he was entitled to interest at the rate specified in his original note (ten percent) following the legal allowance of the claim against the estate. He sought judicial confirmation that the interest rate should remain at ten percent, despite the court’s ruling that might influence the judgement in the context of the estate.	The defendant, Samuel T. Mayo, contended that upon the county court's allowance of Mitchell’s claim, the original note was extinguished, thereby limiting the interest to six percent according to the statutory guidelines for debts from estates. Mayo argued that the ruling of the county court rendered a conclusive judgment, which was subject to the statutory interest reduction irrespective of the original agreement.

The case "Chicago, Pekin and Southwestern Railroad Company et al. v. The Town of Marseilles" originated in La Salle County, Illinois, with a trial held on November 10, 1881, presided over by Judge George W. Stipp. The plaintiffs, which included the Chicago, Pekin and Southwestern Railroad Company, initiated an action of debt upon an appeal bond. The defendants were the Town of Marseilles. The only issue presented in the trial was non est factum, which means the defendants disputed the validity of the bond. The jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, leading to a judgment against the defendants. Later, during the same term but with Judge McEoberts presiding in the absence of Judge Stipp, the defendants filed a motion for a new trial, which was overruled. The defendants then appealed this decision. They argued that it was improper for Judge McEoberts to hear the motion since it had been tried by Judge Stipp. The appellate process ultimately led to the Illinois Supreme Court being involved, assessing whether Judge McEoberts had the authority to rule on the new trial motion.	The plaintiffs argued that the trial concluded with a valid verdict and judgment against the defendants. They maintained that all procedures were properly followed and that the appeals that the defendants made were without sufficient grounds for overturning the ruling of the lower courts. They contended that any failure to secure a new trial was due to the actions or inactions of the defendants.	The defendants contended that their motion for a new trial should have been heard by Judge Stipp, the judge who presided over the initial trial. They asserted that Judge McEoberts lacked the authority to deny their motion since he was not the presiding judge during the trial. The defense argued that this situation denied them the opportunity to have a fair review of the evidence supporting the verdict, which should invalidate the judgment against them.

The case "South Chicago Railroad Company v. Morgan Dix et al." took place in 1883 in Hyde Park, Illinois. It involved a petition by the South Chicago Railroad Company, which sought to condemn a 30-foot wide strip of land extending from Seventy-first street to the village's water-works, across three blocks, for the purpose of constructing a side-track necessary for their railroad operations. The railroad company was incorporated under Illinois laws governing railroads and had permission per a village ordinance to lay its main line through Hyde Park. The controversy arose over whether the proposed track constituted a necessary side-track or an independent branch road. The opponents argued that the track served a private interest rather than the overall operation of the railroad, while the railroad company contended that it was essential for the efficient operation of their services and the delivery of coal to the water-works. The lower court dismissed the petition initially, leading the railroad company to appeal this decision.	The South Chicago Railroad Company claimed that the strip of land was essential for the construction of a side-track required for the successful operation of their railroad. They emphasized that the proposed side-track would facilitate the convenient delivery of freight and the operational aspects of their main line, which ran through public streets under specific restrictions. They argued that even if the side-track also served private interests, it was still necessary for the overall operational needs of the railroad.	The defendants, led by Morgan Dix, argued that the proposed track was not a side-track but rather an independent branch road meant solely for private use, primarily serving coal delivery to the water-works. They contended that since the track was designed only for this purpose and not for public freight or passenger traffic, the railroad company had no right to condemn the land for this use under eminent domain. The motion filed sought to dismiss the petition based on these grounds.

In September 1867, Lewis Russell initiated a chancery suit against David W. Paine in the Whiteside Circuit Court, Illinois, seeking to foreclose a mortgage on certain lands. The case arose when Russell claimed that Paine had defaulted on a note associated with the mortgage. Paine, however, denied ever executing the note and contended that Russell had no legitimate claim to seek a decree of foreclosure. The Circuit Court examined the arguments and evidence presented by both parties but ultimately dismissed Russell's case, placing the costs on him. This dismissal prompted Russell to appeal the decision, hoping for a reversal in the higher court.	Lewis Russell argued that he had a valid mortgage against David W. Paine's property and sought to foreclose it due to Paine's alleged default on the associated note. Russell insisted that he was entitled to a court decree to enforce the mortgage and recover his losses.	David W. Paine countered Russell's claims by asserting that he never signed or executed the note that Russell referenced. He maintained that, as a result, Russell had no legal grounds to pursue foreclosure proceedings and requested the court to uphold the dismissal of the case.

Patrick Walsh initiated a lawsuit against Matthew J. Brennan and Thomas Walsh in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1869. The case revolved around a lot of land that Patrick had conveyed to Thomas Walsh in 1859. This conveyance, although absolute in form, was allegedly tied to a trust that aimed to secure debts owed by Patrick. In 1862, Thomas Walsh sold the property to Brennan, a transaction Patrick claimed was unauthorized and conducted without his consent. He argued that Brennan had knowledge of the trust when he purchased the property. Testimonies presented were conflicting, especially regarding whether Brennan was aware of an alleged agreement between Patrick and Thomas Walsh regarding the sale. The court was tasked with reviewing the evidence of this transaction and deciding on Patrick’s right to redeem the property.	Patrick Walsh claimed that the property in question was held in trust by Thomas Walsh for debts owed to him, and that Brennan, in purchasing the property, had notice of this trust. He sought to reclaim the property by arguing that the sale was unauthorized and contrary to his interests. Walsh requested a reconveyance of the property upon payment of the secured amount, less costs related to rent and profits.	Matthew J. Brennan contended that he purchased the property in good faith, without knowledge of any trust or claims held by Patrick Walsh. Testimony from Brennan’s associates suggested the sale was conducted transparently and with Walsh's approval. They argued that the plaintiff's claims of an unauthorized sale lacked foundation, as there was evidence of a valid transaction at the full market value of the property, and that significant time had lapsed without any complaint from Walsh.

Emma Stevens and Cornelia Canup filed a bill in equity against John Wait and others regarding a tract of land in Coles County, Illinois, containing approximately 34 acres. The case emerged from a family dispute over the ownership of the land, originally conveyed by Stephen Wait to his five children in a deed dated June 17, 1857. The plaintiffs claimed joint ownership of the land with equal parts, while a fifth party, Samuel M. Bussell, owned a smaller portion. The plaintiffs contended that the description of the land in the deed was sufficient to identify the premises despite some ambiguities. The main question revolved around whether the deed effectively conveyed the land the plaintiffs claimed, as one of the critical defenses cited was the opponents’ long-term possession of the property, which they argued created ownership rights over time. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of the defendants.	The plaintiffs, Emma Stevens and Cornelia Canup, argued that they, along with the other family members, were rightful owners of the land based on the 1857 deed issued by Stephen Wait. They contended that the description of the land provided in the deed was sufficient for identification, despite its ambiguities, and that any possessory claims by the defendants were invalid due to the shared ownership as tenants in common. They sought a partition of the land in order to establish their rights and ownership officially.	The defendants, led by John Wait, argued that the deed did not effectively describe the land claimed by the plaintiffs, making their claims invalid. They also invoked the Statute of Limitations, asserting that the cause of action was barred due to the lengthy possession of the land without adverse claims from the plaintiffs, essentially arguing that their continuous possession constituted a form of ownership. To counter the plaintiffs’ assertions, they pointed to previous conveyances and the nature of their possession as tenants in common.

The case "The People ex rel. Josiah Little, Collector, v. Owen L. Clayton et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court and concerns events that unfolded in Lee County, Illinois, in 1885. The issue arose from an application by Josiah Little, the county collector, who sought a judgment against certain properties for unpaid drainage taxes and special assessments. The appellant filed for judgment after a drainage assessment was confirmed on March 9, 1885. Although a notice was published on March 14, 1885, informing property owners that the assessment must be paid by June 6, 1885, the delinquent list was reportedly submitted to the county collector on March 10, 1885. The defendants raised objections, arguing that the summons for judgment was premature and lacked necessary formalities under the law since the delinquency should not have been recorded until after the deadline outlined in the notice. The case was appealed after the county court ruled in favor of the objections, prompting the current review.	The plaintiff, Josiah Little, claimed that the drainage assessment became payable immediately upon its confirmation by the court on March 9, 1885. He asserted that the delinquent list was validly returned to the county collector in compliance with legal requirements. The plaintiff argued that any irregularities in the timing of the notice publication did not substantively affect the ability of property owners to pay, thereby upholding the validity of the assessments as a lien on the properties.	The defendants contended that the proper procedural notice regarding the payment of the drainage assessments was not provided in a timely manner, which rendered the delinquent list invalid and the resulting judgment premature. They argued the collector could not file for judgment until after the notice deadline of June 6, 1885, passed and thus insisted that no delinquency should have been recorded prior to that date.

In 1874, the case of William Rietzell v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in St. Clair County, Illinois. The legal proceeding was initiated as a scire facias, which is a writ requiring a party to show cause why a certain action should not be taken. Rietzell, the plaintiff in error, was a surety for a defendant named William Hartman, who was charged with larceny. Hartman failed to appear in court, leading to a default judgment against both him and Rietzell. The court proceedings addressed the legitimacy of the recognizance taken and the application of the law governing such situations at the time. The main issue was whether the court was justified in defaulting Rietzell based on Hartman’s absence. The court ultimately examined relevant statutes regarding recognizances and the procedures for defaults and affirmations based on the statutes at that time.	Rietzell argued that the judgment entered against him was erroneous as he was not properly notified or served process, and that the court should reverse the default judgment against him. He contended that there was an insufficiency in the scire facias pertaining to the recognizance's proper taking and certification. His legal request was for the court to vacate the default judgment due to these alleged deficiencies.	The People of the State of Illinois maintained that the default judgment against Rietzell was valid based on the legal statutes governing recognizances. They argued that the scire facias was appropriately issued and contained all necessary requirements. The defense contended that Rietzell, as the surety, was aware of the provisions of the law applicable at the time and had the responsibility to ensure the principal's appearance in court. They urged the court to uphold the default judgment based on the lack of appearance by Hartman.

In the case of William Giffert et al. v. Charles B. Wilson, decided on January 6, 1886, the events took place in West Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved include the plaintiff, Charles B. Wilson, and the appellant, William Giffert, along with Hanchett, the sheriff. The case originated from a replevin action where Wilson sought to reclaim various household goods and furniture from Giffert and Hanchett, who had seized the goods under a writ of attachment. The core issue was whether the goods were subject to this writ, which Giffert obtained against the estate of Rachel Wice. Wilson claimed ownership of the goods based on a chattel mortgage from Wice dated March 18, 1884, which secured an $1,800 loan. Although the mortgage was not recorded, Wilson contended that he had taken possession of the goods by acquiring the key to the storeroom, locking it with a new padlock, and informing the landlord of his intent to pay rent. Giffert argued that without proper recording of the mortgage, the goods were subject to his attachment, as they were still in Wice's possession when the sheriff seized them on March 26, 1884. The jury ultimately found in favor of Wilson, affirming his ownership of the goods.	The plaintiff, Charles B. Wilson, claimed ownership of the household goods through a chattel mortgage executed by Rachel Wice, which was intended to secure a loan of $1,800. Wilson argued that he took possession of the goods prior to any attachment issued against Wice's estate. He asserted that the delivery of the key to the storeroom and his act of locking it with a new padlock constituted a change of possession, despite the mortgage being unrecorded. Wilson requested the court to affirm his ownership and to return the goods unlawfully taken by the sheriff.	The defendant, William Giffert, contended that the unrecorded chattel mortgage and the fact that the debt had not matured meant the goods were subject to his writ of attachment. Giffert maintained that since the mortgage was not properly recorded and the possession did not change hands in a legally recognized way, he was justified in seizing the goods from Wice's estate. Giffert sought to have the attachment upheld, asserting that his claims took precedent over Wilson's unrecorded mortgage.

Levi Shipley filed an action of assumpsit in September 1867 in the Livingston Circuit Court against Harrison Carroll and Elizabeth Carroll over a promissory note signed by Elizabeth before her marriage to Harrison. The note was initially made payable to Philip Foley, who subsequently indorsed it to Shipley. In response, the defendants filed seven pleas, with one being a significant point of contention—Elizabeth claimed that the note was signed merely for amusement and was never intended for delivery, and that Foley had stolen it from her. Issue arose regarding the validity of the note, particularly in the context of how fraud affects its enforceability. The court originally ruled against Shipley, leading him to file a writ of error to challenge the verdict.	Levi Shipley’s primary claim was based on the enforcement of the promissory note made by Elizabeth Carroll. He argued that he was a bona fide holder for value, as he had received the note through lawful indorsement from Foley before maturity. Shipley sought to have the court acknowledge the validity of the note and to reverse the lower court’s judgment that barred his claim.	The defendants, particularly Elizabeth Carroll, contended that the note was void due to the alleged circumstances under which it was signed. They claimed that it was intended only for amusement and that it was stolen thereafter by Foley, who did not have legitimate ownership or the right to transfer it. Elizabeth asserted that the fraud purportedly involved in the note's procurement negated any validity in Shipley's claim to recover under it.

The case of The International Bank v. George S. Poppers began around the year 1878, in Cook County, Illinois. The situation involved a dispute in which The International Bank filed a forcible entry and detainer action against Catharine Walsh to recover possession of premises they claimed were wrongfully detained. The bank succeeded at the justice of the peace level, leading Walsh to appeal to the circuit court, where she was required to file multiple appeal bonds, ultimately settling on a $2000 bond with an approved surety after a series of rulings by the court. Following the proceedings and the bank winning its claims at different court levels, the bank brought a suit on the second bond. George S. Poppers, the defendant, entered several pleas arguing that the execution of the second bond had discharged the earlier ones. A jury trial resulted in a verdict for the bank, awarding it $1200 in debt and $1000 in damages. However, this judgment was reversed by the Appellate Court, which prompted the bank to appeal further, reaching the Illinois Supreme Court.	The International Bank claimed that they were entitled to recover possession of the property, establishing that the execution and approval of the $2000 appeal bond should release any liability associated with the previous bonds. They sought a judgment affirming their right to the debt owed under the second bond and reimbursement for damages, ultimately arguing that no recovery could be made on the initial bond due to the issuance of the new one.	George S. Poppers contended that the execution and approval of the $2000 bond served as a satisfaction and discharge of the prior bond. His arguments were centered around the notion that under applicable statute, the new bond effectively released him from any prior obligations, and as the surety on that bond, he should not be held liable under the previous arrangements.

Jacob M. Douglass v. David T. Littler took place in the Logan circuit court in Illinois, with the initial filing on January 6, 1868. The case stems from a deed executed on July 16, 1864, in which Douglass transferred ownership of three half sections of land to Littler, who allegedly did so through fraudulent means. Douglass claimed he owned the land outright and that Littler deceived him by falsely asserting an interest in the land. Littler had written letters to Douglass in July 1864, misrepresenting that he owned the land and claiming Douglass’ title was worthless due to tax sales. On the ground of fraud, Douglass sought to have the deed set aside, arguing that he had been manipulated into the transfer. Littler, having purchased a questionable tax title to the land, deceived Douglass into believing his title was void. He then visited Douglass, presenting false claims about the legitimacy of Douglass's title. Despite Douglass's reluctance to accept payment for the deed, Littler gifted him $25. The legal issue revolved around whether Littler’s representations constituted fraud and if Douglass relied on them when executing the deed.	Douglass argued that Littler had committed fraud by misrepresenting the status of the land title. He contended that Littler falsely stated he owned the land and that Douglass's rights had been extinguished due to tax sales. As a result, Douglass sought to rescind the deed on the grounds of fraud, demanding that the court recognize his original ownership of the land and nullify the transfer to Littler.	Littler denied committing fraud, asserting that any statements he made about the land were merely opinions based on his understanding of the tax title, which he believed to be valid. He claimed Douglass willingly transferred the land, having abandoned any interest in it for years. Littler requested the court uphold the deed, relying on the limitation statutes and denying that he had falsely represented the status of the land title.

In January 1866, the case of "The St. Louis, Alton & Terre Haute Railroad Company v. Elisha Linder et al." was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Coles County, Illinois, where the plaintiffs, Elisha Linder and Daniel W. Linder, brought suit against the railroad company for the wrongful death of their livestock. The livestock had strayed onto the railroad tracks and were subsequently killed by one of the company’s trains. Central to the case was whether the railroad company was liable for failing to properly fence its tracks as required by law. The plaintiffs asserted that the cattle were killed in areas where the company was obligated to have proper fencing in place. The court had to decide on the admissibility of certain jury instructions regarding liability, negligence, and the ownership of the livestock involved.	The plaintiffs claimed damages amounting to $365.50 for their livestock that had been killed by the defendant's train. They argued that the railroad company was liable for failing to fence its tracks adequately and that their livestock had been killed in a location where the company was legally required to maintain a fence. The plaintiffs contended that the wrongful death of their livestock was a direct result of the defendant's negligence in failing to provide sufficient fencing on the railroad.	The defendant, St. Louis, Alton & Terre Haute Railroad Company, claimed that the livestock may have entered the tracks at a point where the company was not required to maintain a fence. They argued that liability only arose from gross negligence if animals wandered onto the tracks from areas not under the company’s fencing jurisdiction. The defendant sought to prove that either the plaintiffs did not have proper ownership of all the livestock that were killed or that various conditions limited their liability, emphasizing that the company should not be held responsible under the presented circumstances.

The case of Malvina Harriman et al. v. Carlos Sampson, Jane B. Way et al. was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, resulting in a judgment on May 27, 1887. The primary location of the events was Clay County, Kansas, where Sarah B. Watts, the deceased, lived with her daughter Jane B. Way. Watts died on August 14, 1884, after being bedridden for months, during which she stayed at Way’s residence. Harriman, along with other heirs, filed a bill to prevent Robert Farwell, the estate’s administrator, from distributing funds allegedly owed to Watts to Way. The plaintiffs argue that the money, derived from promissory notes owed to Watts, rightfully belongs to her estate. Jane B. Way claimed these funds were given to her as part of an alleged agreement with her mother, wherein she would care for her mother in exchange for the funds. The court considered various testimonies regarding the nature of this supposed contract and the claims made by both parties.	The plaintiffs, Malvina Harriman et al., claimed to be the legal heirs of Sarah B. Watts, asserting their entitlement to the funds being collected by the estate administrator. They sought a decree from the court confirming that the money collected on two promissory notes, which were included in Watts’ estate, should be distributed amongst her rightful heirs rather than being given to Jane B. Way.	Jane B. Way, the defendant, countered the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that her mother, Sarah B. Watts, entered into an oral contract with her, wherein Watts agreed to transfer the money and promissory notes in exchange for care during her final years. Way claimed that this agreement was fulfilled and that the funds should thus rightfully belong to her as her separate property.

In 1888, a legal case was brought in the Illinois Appellate Court involving John Alling and other creditors against William T. Wenzell and other stockholders of the Papillon Manufacturing Company. This case arose due to the company's failure to meet its financial obligations, leading creditors to seek enforcement of individual liabilities from stockholders under specific provisions of corporate law. The Papillon Manufacturing Company had a capital of $600,000 divided into 6,000 shares. A significant issue in the case was the legitimacy of 2,000 shares issued to the company's former president, Clark, and its secretary, Lotz, for material of questionable intrinsic value. The plaintiffs argued that these shares, treated as fully paid, unfairly increased the burden on other stockholders. The dispute hinged on whether this arrangement could be considered valid, as it implicated the equitable treatment of all stockholders regarding liabilities owed to creditors.	The plaintiffs claimed that the issuance of 2,000 shares to Clark and Lotz, for material deemed practically worthless, was unfair to other stockholders and creditors. They contended that this arrangement constituted a breach of their rights and sought to hold all stockholders accountable for the company's debts equally. Their legal requests included reversing the treatment of these shares as fully paid and affirming that all stockholders should share the liabilities equitably, thereby safeguarding creditors' interests.	The defendants contended that the shares in question should be considered fully paid and that the arrangement between Clark and Lotz and the company was valid. They argued that the plaintiffs, as subsequent stockholders, had no grounds to contest this arrangement, as they had subscribed to their stocks without knowledge of the transaction. The defendants requested the court to dismiss the claims against them, asserting that the plaintiffs did not meet the burden of proving their case and that the transactions were valid under corporate law.

In November 1854, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Leander Jay S. Turney v. Cornelius L. Organ. The dispute arose from an action of assumpsit brought by Organ against Turney, based on a promissory note. The sheriff initially returned the summons by stating that it had been served by reading it to Turney. At the return term, a default judgment was entered against Turney for the amount specified in the note. Following this, Turney appeared before the court and filed a motion to arrest the judgment, contending the improper service of the summons. Simultaneously, Organ filed a cross-motion, requesting the court to permit the sheriff to amend the return of service to reflect proper notice. The court granted Organ's motion, allowing the sheriff to amend his return to show that Turney had been duly served. Consequently, the motion to arrest the judgment was denied by the court, affirming the regularity of the proceedings against Turney.	The plaintiff, Cornelius L. Organ, claimed entitlement to the amount due under a promissory note and sought enforcement of the judgment by default that had already been entered against Turney due to his failure to appear. Organ argued that the original return of service was defective, but upon allowing the sheriff to amend it, it demonstrated that Turney had indeed been properly served with the summons.	The defendant, Leander Jay S. Turney, contended that the service of the summons was insufficient due to the sheriff's initial return stating that it was served merely by reading it to him. Turney filed a motion to arrest the judgment, seeking to overturn the default judgment on the grounds of improper service, arguing that the legal requirements for service had not been adequately met.

The case "The Fourth National Bank of Chicago v. The City National Bank of Grand Rapids" arose in September 1871 after a check transaction between two banks. The Fourth National Bank of Chicago (the appellant) and the City National Bank of Grand Rapids (the appellee) were involved in a dispute over a check drawn by a man named Latourette. Latourette had borrowed $5,000 from the Fourth National Bank and, on October 6, 1871, he issued a check for $1,000 to the City National Bank. The check was presented for payment on October 17, 1871, but by then, the Fourth National Bank was unable to process transactions due to a fire that devastated Chicago the day after the check was written. The Fourth National Bank contested the claim to the funds, asserting that Latourette had filed for bankruptcy shortly after the check was issued, and attempted to assert liens on his deposits despite the payment already being made for the check. The controversy centered on the rights of the check-holder and the bank's ability to withhold funds in light of Latourette's insolvency. Ultimately, the case sought to clarify and determine the legal standing of the banks in relation to the payments and the obligations owed by Latourette.	The City National Bank of Grand Rapids claimed that it was entitled to the $1,000 drawn on the check since it had paid value for it and the funds were available in Latourette's account at the time the check was presented. They sought to enforce their right to the funds from the Fourth National Bank.	The Fourth National Bank of Chicago argued that they had a superior claim to Latourette's deposits due to a lien on his funds to secure outstanding debts, even if those debts were not yet due. They contended that the bankruptcy of Latourette altered the legal landscape and that they had rights to an equitable set-off against the amount claimed by the City National Bank.

The case of Henry Holston v. Thomas B. Needles took place in the Circuit Court of Washington County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment dated January 25, 1886. The dispute revolves around property ownership and the rightful possession of a strip of land measuring 1 foot in width, located on the west side of a larger parcel of land originally comprising two lots (6 and 9) in block 5 in the city of Nashville. The plaintiff, Henry Holston, sought to recover possession of this strip, which had become an issue after a partition wall was constructed between his property and that of his neighbor, Thomas B. Needles (the defendant). The plaintiff presented three deeds to prove his claim of ownership, tracing the chain of title to the lots back to a common owner, A. B. Johnson, and demonstrating that the bounds of the property had been correctly identified despite claims of uncertainty made by the defendant. Throughout the trial, it was established that the appellant (Needles) had made erroneous statements regarding property size, which led to an incorrect survey performed by a hired surveyor. The outcome of the case hinged on the interpretation of these deeds and the legitimacy of the defendant's possession of the contested property strip.	The plaintiff, Henry Holston, claimed ownership of a strip of land 1 foot wide on the west side of lots 6 and 9 based on three legal deeds. He argued that these deeds provided clear and sufficient evidence of his title to the property. Holston contended that the construction of a partition wall had encroached upon his property due to the defendant’s misrepresentation of land ownership, asserting that he was entitled to recover the unlawfully possessed land.	The defendant, Thomas B. Needles, contended that his possession of the disputed land was lawful and that no proper demand for possession had been made prior to the ejectment action. He claimed that Holston's entrance into the property was wrongful and that the improper survey, which allocated more property to Needles than entitled by his deeds, led to the dispute. Needles maintained that he had been acting in good faith, relying on his understanding of the property boundaries, and argued against Holston's interpretation of the deed descriptions.

In June 1877, the Illinois Central Railroad Company was involved in a legal case against Joseph Hammer. The incident occurred in Effingham County, Illinois, where Hammer was struck by a moving car while standing on a railroad track. At the time, Hammer was trying to avoid an oncoming engine that was passing on the main track and stepped onto the side track. Unbeknownst to him, a detached car had been switched onto the side track and was coming towards him at speed. Although railroad employees noticed Hammer standing on the side track prior to the collision, they failed to take action that could have prevented the injury.
