Evidence presented indicated that the employees believed Hammer would move off the track but did not act in time to avert the accident. The jury received instructions from the court that suggested the possibility of Hammer recovering damages even if his negligence was slight. This was contested as improper in connection with the rules of contributory negligence.	Joseph Hammer claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company's negligence led to his injury. He argued that despite his position on the side track, the railroad employees saw him and could have stopped the car before it struck him. His legal request included recovery of damages for the personal injury he sustained due to the company's failure to exercise a reasonable degree of care in preventing the accident.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company defended itself by asserting that Hammer was partially negligent for standing on the tracks. They argued that despite any shortcomings in their employees’ actions, Hammer's own negligence contributed to the incident. The defense contended that the jury should not have been instructed to allow recovery based on slight negligence from Hammer if the company’s employees had simply fallen short of a high standard of care.

Jacob Peterson Klepper v. Charles J. Borchsenius took place in La Salle County, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Appellate Court on July 27, 1883. The case arose from a promissory note dated February 10, 1875, for $500, involving multiple parties: Peter G. Peterson as the principal debtor and co-sureties Charles J. Borchsenius and Jacob Peterson, Sen. The conflict centered on whether Borchsenius was liable as a co-surety for contributions toward the payment of this note. During the trial, it was revealed that Borchsenius had initially stated that he would only be liable for $100 of the note when he signed it, which was indicated by the figures '100' written next to his name. The appellee, Klepper, claimed he had paid more than his proportional share of the note, thus seeking a contribution from Borchsenius. The court's pivotal actions included excluding evidence that could have supported Borchsenius’s claim regarding the limitation of his liability and subsequently ruled in favor of Klepper.	The plaintiff (Klepper) claimed that he was entitled to contribution from the defendant (Borchsenius) as a co-surety on the promissory note. He argued that the defendant had paid less than his proportional share of the debt and that the payments Klepper made exceeded what was due from him. Klepper sought a judgment requiring Borchsenius to contribute to the amounts he had already covered, based on the principle of equity among co-sureties.	The defendant (Borchsenius) contended that he limited his liability to $100 when signing the note and was not a true co-surety because of his prior verbal agreement with both the principal debtor and the payee regarding his limited responsibility. He argued that the note itself did not conclusively establish his obligation as a co-surety and that extrinsic evidence should have been allowed to prove the limitation of his liability, which was improper for the court to dismiss.

In December 1842, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of The President, Directors, and Company of the Bank of Illinois v. John C. Stickney et al. in Gallatin, Illinois. The case arose when Stickney & Co., who were indebted to the Bank of Illinois for $10,959.09 on two promissory notes, gave the bank a mortgage on their stock of goods and two lots of land to secure the debt. The notes, dated October 24, 1839, bore interest at 8% annually. When the bank decided to take possession of the goods to recover its debt, Stickney & Co. agreed to sell the goods, stipulating that the sale should occur on credit for twelve months. Both parties executed written agreements for the sale to be conducted under these terms. Following the sale, the bank provided Stickney & Co. an accounting that included interest calculations, which Stickney & Co. received without immediate objection. However, a year later, they sought a refund of the interest paid, which the bank refused, leading to this lawsuit. Stickney & Co. initially won a verdict for $700 at trial, prompting the bank to appeal, arguing that they were entitled to the interest calculated according to the terms of the mortgage and sale agreement.	Stickney & Co. claimed the Bank of Illinois wrongfully charged them interest on their promissory notes after the sale of the goods, seeking a refund. They argued that the terms of their agreement with the bank did not support continued interest charges due after the sale of their property on credit when the goods had been sold.	The Bank of Illinois defended by asserting their entitlement to interest until the maturity of the sale notes, as per the original mortgage agreement which allowed them to charge interest until the proceeds from the sale were received. The bank contended that the terms of the agreement were adhered to and that Stickney & Co. had accepted the accounting without objection at the time.

Nathan Disbrow filed a lawsuit against The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company in September 1873, following a series of events primarily centered around his eating house located near the railway track in Harvard, Illinois. Disbrow alleged that the railway company deliberately stationed freight cars on its tracks to obstruct access to his eating house whenever passenger trains stopped for meals at the station. The company had multiple tracks where trains stopped and where cars were often switched, resulting in passengers facing dangers when attempting to cross the tracks. Disbrow’s eating house was situated directly across from the railway’s own eating house. Evidence also indicated that Disbrow engaged in soliciting passengers boarding trains for his business, which was viewed as a nuisance by the railway company. Following a series of legal proceedings that included a verdict against Disbrow in the lower court, he appealed the decision.	The plaintiff, Nathan Disbrow, claimed the railway company intentionally obstructed access to his eating house by positioning freight cars in front of it. He argued that this action was harmful to his business, as it negatively impacted his ability to serve customers during peak times when passenger trains were at the station for meals. Disbrow sought damages for the loss of income and the inconvenience caused by the blockade of access to his establishment.	The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company defended itself by asserting that its actions were lawful and necessary for operational safety. It argued that the stationing of freight cars was part of the regular operation of its business at the Harvard station. The company stated that it was not obligated to maintain an unobstructed path across its tracks for the benefit of a private business. It emphasized that any obstruction was justified as a means to ensure the safety of its passengers, thereby protecting itself from potential liability.

In September 1867, in Peoria County, Illinois, an action of assault and battery was initiated by George Pageter against Nelson Clark. The case was tried in the circuit court, where the jury found in favor of Pageter and awarded him damages amounting to $125. Following the trial, Clark's motion for a new trial was rejected, leading to the subsequent appeal, seeking to reverse the judgment based on various alleged errors. The key individuals involved in the case were George Pageter, the plaintiff, and Nelson Clark, the defendant. Chief Justice Breese presided over the court's opinion, which addressed the procedural aspects of the trial and the jury’s verdict.	The plaintiff, George Pageter, claimed that Nelson Clark engaged in assault and battery against him. His legal requests included a trial by jury and the awarding of damages for the injuries suffered as a result of Clark's actions. Pageter maintained that his evidence supported a clear case of assault, where he responded to Clark's actions with the plea of "de injuria.	The defendant, Nelson Clark, contested the claims against him by arguing 'not guilty' and citing the defense of "son assault demesne" (justifiable use of force). In his appeal, Clark argued that the jury may have been misled by the instructions they received during the trial. He requested a new trial, asserting that the initial verdict was unjust and not sufficiently justified by the evidence presented.

In the Fall of 1847, John C. Woodworth, facing a debt of $93 to Tarbox, secured the payment through a deed of the south-west quarter of a land property while receiving a bond for reconveyance upon settling the debt by the following spring. To redeem this land, Woodworth sought a loan of $100 from John Coates, who agreed to lend the money under the condition that he would receive payment of $135. To facilitate this transaction without additional costs, the deed was assigned directly to Coates rather than Woodworth. In the event of Woodworth's default on the repayment, the agreement entailed Coates selling the property and using the proceeds to settle his debt, withholding any remaining balance for Woodworth. However, after Coates sold the land for $300, he refused to remit any surplus remaining after covering his loan. Woodworth then filed a bill in chancery against Coates to recover these funds. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1852.	Woodworth’s bill asserts that he was never the true owner of the land; he contends that Coates acted as a trustee, having loaned him the money to redeem the property, and should therefore pay him the surplus from the sale. He argues that the transaction constituted a resulting trust, where Coates was to sell the land only to recover his loan and return any excess proceeds to him.	Coates denies having entered into a loan agreement, claiming instead that he purchased the land outright from Tarbox using his own funds. He states that he acted in his own interest rather than as a trustee for Woodworth, suggesting that Woodworth had no rightful claim to any surplus from the sale of the property.

The case "Chicago and Northwestern Railway Co. v. John R. Bensley et al." took place in September 1873 in Illinois, specifically concerning a shipment of oats that was supposed to be delivered to John R. Bensley and his associates. The oats were shipped from a location in Iowa to Chicago on October 5, 1871. However, the oats were never delivered due to their destruction in the Great Chicago Fire, which occurred on October 9, 1871. The core of the dispute revolved around whether the oats had been unloaded from the freight car before the fire. The case involved testimony about the timing of the delivery, particularly whether the oats were unloaded at the Galena depot on October 7, 1871, and if the handling of the delivery was conducted properly by the railway company. The jury's decision to award damages was appealed by the railway company on the grounds that the verdict went against the evidence and that an instruction crucial to their defense was denied. The court argued that the railway's liability as a common carrier does not end until goods are unloaded from the car.	The plaintiffs, John R. Bensley, David W. Bensley, and Reuben Wagner, claimed damages for the non-delivery of their carload of oats, which they argued was due to the negligence of the Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company. They contended that the railway company was liable for the destruction of the oats, which occurred while in the carrier's custody at their freight depot, thus demanding compensation for their loss.	The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company, represented by Mr. B. C. Cook, asserted that they should not be held liable for the oats as they claimed the goods were safely unloaded and stored in a secure depot prior to the fire. They sought to challenge the jury's verdict by stating it contradicted the testimony presented and objected to the refusal of a jury instruction that would absolve them of liability if the jury found the oats arrived securely and were stored properly.

In September 1867, Daniel R. Brandt initiated a legal action against William Y. Daniels in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case involved a dispute over certain chattels that were subject to a mortgage executed by Yan Osten to Daniels. Osten, with Daniels's knowledge and consent, sold these chattels to Harpel, who subsequently mortgaged the property again to Daniels. Gallagher & Hunter then entered the picture, intending to purchase from Harpel. They were informed of Daniels's original mortgage but proceeded with the sale, relying on an agreement with Daniels to pay the mortgage debt within 90 days. Transferring possession of the property without acquiring a new mortgage from Gallagher & Hunter, Daniels's consent implied a waiver of his mortgage rights. Gallagher & Hunter sued for credit from Brandt, assuring him the property was unencumbered, leading Brandt to eventually foreclose on the mortgage after non-payment. This resulted in Daniels demanding the property back, which prompted Brandt to invoke an action of trover against him.	Brandt claimed that he was the rightful owner of the chattels by virtue of the foreclosure process on the mortgage he held. He contended that he had no knowledge of any incumbrance on the property and had entered into the transaction in good faith, relying on the assurances provided by Gallagher & Hunter. He sought a legal declaration affirming his right to the property and ultimately secured a judgment in the lower court for $250 against Daniels.	Daniels argued that his initial mortgage on the chattels remained valid despite the sale and subsequent transactions involving Harpel and Gallagher & Hunter. He maintained that Brandt should have recognized his mortgage rights as a previous lienholder and that he was entitled to claim the chattels from Brandt following the foreclosure. Daniels contended that he had not waived his rights to the property due to the circumstances surrounding the sale and insisted on the validity of his mortgage against Brandt’s claim.

In the case of George Scroggs v. Joseph O. Cunningham, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1876, the dispute originated in Champaign County, Illinois, following the dissolution of a partnership between Scroggs and Cunningham. The partnership had been established with specific agreements regarding profit-sharing and accounting, requiring an annual settlement of accounts. The articles of dissolution stipulated that an account must be taken, focusing on moneys drawn by the partners since July 1, 1871, and any excess amounts drawn would be owed back to the partnership. However, the parties interpreted this clause differently; Scroggs argued that it should include all financial transactions and individual accounts, while Cunningham contended it was strictly limited to moneys drawn. As the scheduled account verification date approached on July 1, 1872, Cunningham failed to provide access to the partnership books or render any account, prompting Scroggs to seek legal recourse to enforce their agreement and settle the partnership’s financial standing.	The plaintiff, George Scroggs, claimed that Joseph O. Cunningham had violated their partnership agreement by refusing to take the necessary accounting of their financial dealings upon the dissolution of the partnership. Scroggs argued that the articles of dissolution required a comprehensive accounting of all moneys, requiring determination of net profits and settlement of accounts. He requested the court compel Cunningham to render a proper account, pay any amounts owed to him based on the accounting, and include interest from the date the account should have been taken.	The defendant, Joseph O. Cunningham, contested the interpretation of the articles of dissolution, arguing that the account to be rendered should only pertain to moneys drawn since July 1, 1871, and did not encompass an extensive review of all individual accounts or debts. Cunningham maintained that he was not obligated to provide an accounting beyond what he believed the terms stipulated. He requested the dismissal of Scroggs' claims on the premise that they were exceeding what was agreed upon in the partnership contract.

In the case of Joseph Schwarzendahl et al. v. George W. Beck, which took place in Illinois and culminated with a court decision on February 23, 1886, the central issue revolved around a promissory note for a principal amount of $1,320, which had been reduced to approximately $340 following certain payments. The plaintiffs, Joseph Schwarzendahl and others, found themselves in a position where a judgment against them was entered in favor of the defendant, George W. Beck. This judgment occurred by confession under a warrant of attorney appended to the note, which included an additional $50 in attorney's fees. The plaintiffs asserted that there was nothing due on the note, contradicting the defendant's claims. Following this, the plaintiffs filed a motion to vacate the judgment and argued they had a valid defense. However, their motion was initially denied by the court below, leading them to appeal the decision. Upon reviewing the affidavits submitted by the plaintiffs, the appellate court formed the opinion that the motion to vacate should have been granted.	The plaintiffs argued that the judgment against them, which favored the defendant, was unjustified as they claimed there was nothing owed on the promissory note. They contended that their affidavits demonstrated a valid defense against the debt, and sought to vacate the judgment, enabling them to present their defense in court.	The defendant maintained that the judgment was appropriately entered based on the promissory note in question and the warrant of attorney that permitted such a judgment. He likely asserted that the amounts claimed were valid and that the plaintiffs' motion to vacate lacked merit.

In June 1874, the Illinois Central Railroad Company faced legal action from Nannie A. Goddard, the administratrix of James M. Goddard's estate. The incident occurred at a public road crossing in Jackson County, Illinois, where Goddard was struck and killed by a train. The plaintiff claimed that the railroad company was negligent for failing to ring a bell or sound a whistle as their train approached the crossing. This failure to provide adequate warning was cited as a significant factor contributing to the incident that resulted in Goddard’s death. The case revolved around whether Goddard exhibited any contributory negligence and the degree of negligence exhibited by the railroad.	The plaintiff argued that the railroad's negligence directly caused the death of James M. Goddard, asserting that the railroad failed to provide appropriate warnings at the crossing, thus breaching its duty of care. The legal request was for damages amounting to $5,000 for the wrongful death of Goddard, emphasizing that even if Goddard displayed some negligence, it should not bar recovery unless his negligence was slight compared to the defendant's.	The defendant, Illinois Central Railroad Company, contended that Goddard’s own negligence in not adequately looking for oncoming trains contributed to the accident. They asserted that the court erred by allowing the jury to consider recovery based on the defendant's negligence being greater than that of the deceased. They also requested jury instructions stating that Goddard had a responsibility to look for approaching trains at the crossing, arguing that his failure to do so negated his right to recover damages.

The case of Canfield S. Hamilton v. The President and Trustees of Carthage occurred in January 1860 in Hancock County, Illinois. The action was brought by the appellees, the President and Trustees of Carthage, against the appellant, Canfield S. Hamilton. The plaintiffs sought recovery of a penalty for Hamilton's alleged sale of spirituous liquor without a proper license, in violation of a local ordinance. Initially, the case was heard by a justice of the peace, who ruled against Hamilton, ordering him to pay a penalty of $140 plus costs. Hamilton appealed this decision to the Circuit Court, where the trial was conducted without a jury. The court found Hamilton guilty and imposed a $20 penalty. Hamilton subsequently appealed the Circuit Court's ruling to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that Hamilton violated a municipal ordinance prohibiting the sale of spirituous liquor without a license. They asserted that the justice of the peace had the jurisdiction to impose penalties for such violations and that the evidence of their legal incorporation as a municipal corporation was sufficient to support their claims.	Hamilton contended that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate their legal incorporation as a town. He argued that without proper evidence of their corporate status, they could not lawfully impose fines or penalties. He also questioned the jurisdiction of the justice of the peace in adjudicating matters related to penalties exceeding five dollars.

The case "Strawn et al. v. Taylor" was decided on February 25, 1886, by the Illinois Appellate Court. It involved a dispute over the foreclosure of a mortgage executed by Preston A. Berry and his wife to Taylor. The key individuals involved were James G.L. Strawn, who was made a defendant in the case due to his claimed interest in the mortgaged premises—either as a purchaser, mortgagor, or judgment creditor, but subject to the mortgage's terms. The case originated when a bill in chancery was filed seeking foreclosure. All defendants were served with legal process, but they failed to respond, resulting in a decree issued on June 24, 1884, that demanded payment of $81,136.25 for principal and interest due on the notes and an additional $850 as attorney’s fees. The case was marked by the lack of any substantial defenses against the foreclosure decree, described by the court as 'frivolous.'	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to foreclosure of the mortgage due to the non-payment of the amounts owed, specifically the principal and interest totaling $81,136.25. They also sought to recover $850 in attorney's fees as part of the costs associated with the foreclosure proceedings. The plaintiffs maintained that the defendants had been duly served and failed to contest the claims effectively.	The defendants, including Strawn, raised objections to the foreclosure decree; however, all their arguments were deemed frivolous by the court. They failed to provide any meritorious defense against the plaintiffs' claims, which undermined their position in contesting the foreclosure and the amounts due under the mortgage.

On January 12, 1864, Fritz Maxe purchased a bill of iron from Topping Brothers & Company in Stanton, Illinois. Shortly thereafter, Maxe received an order from J. H. Stephenson for additional iron, which he settled with Stephenson. Maxe drew a second order on Stephenson for $585.04 on March 4, 1864, but this order was not presented until ten days later, when payment was refused. A witness informed Maxe about the non-payment, to which he responded that he had “nothing to do with it.” The case arose when Topping Brothers sought payment through legal action, claiming that Maxe had an obligation to settle for the iron purchased. The case moved from the Alton city court to the Madison Circuit Court, where the jury found in favor of Maxe. The appellants appealed the decision, questioning the evidence's support for the jury's verdict.	Topping Brothers & Company claimed that Fritz Maxe was liable to pay for the $585.04 order drawn on J. H. Stephenson & Company for iron sold to him. They argued that Maxe had been informed of the non-payment and that he had made a promise to pay or provide a note in the future. The plaintiffs sought payment for the iron, asserting that the order was valid and enforceable, despite Maxe's claims to the contrary.	Fritz Maxe contended that he was not liable for the payment as he had settled with Stephenson for a previous order that was void due to not being stamped. Maxe argued that the new order should not incur liability as there were unresolved questions regarding his prior transaction and that he had indicated he would take action the next time he visited the store. His defense rested on the premise that insufficient evidence supported the claim against him.

Martin Ryan and others initiated a legal case against James L. Anderson in January 1861, located in Schuyler County, Illinois. The case involved a motion to dismiss an appeal resulting from a lower court's judgment that awarded costs only. The parties appealed this decision, with an agreement stating that the appeal could occur under the bond of three township directors—William McMurphy, R. M. Worthington, and George Metz—without needing further security. The court highlighted that they had jurisdiction over the subject matter and that the agreement among the parties allowed for the appeal, even though the proper procedural approach would have been through error. The key individuals in this case included the plaintiff parties acting in their official capacities and the defendant, Anderson.	The plaintiffs argued that the court should uphold their right to appeal based on the agreement made among the directors of the township. They contended that despite the original judgment being for costs only and not related to a franchise or freehold, the appeal should still proceed as there was mutual consent to contest the decision.	The defendant, through their attorney O. G. Skinner, sought to dismiss the appeal by arguing that the lower court's judgment was not appealable due to its nature, primarily because it only pertained to costs and did not involve a franchise or freehold. They also pointed out that the appealing parties did not sign the appeal bond, which should invalidate the motion to appeal.

Charles W. Clayton filed a case against The City of Chicago in 1867, focusing on an application for judgment concerning real estate tax assessments. The core issue arose from the addition of a forty percent increase to property valuations in the city’s south division. This increase was a subject of legal scrutiny, as the ordinance imposing the tax included stipulations such as one mill on the dollar for permanent improvements. The Superior Court of Chicago was tasked with addressing whether this tax was valid, particularly concerning the specificity of its purpose per the city’s charter. The court found that it is impossible to foresee all necessary permanent improvements for a rapidly developing city, thus ruling that the ordinance's wording was legally sufficient. Other issues raised included concerns over notice compliance regarding the collection of taxes and procedural informality in passing the ordinance, which were found to have no substantial impact on the validity of the tax imposition. Ultimately, the court's major concern in this appeal was whether there was a legal basis for the penalty addition, leading to a judgment reversal.	The plaintiff, Charles W. Clayton, contended that the tax assessment included an improperly specified purpose in the ordinance and raised objections regarding procedural compliance in the tax collection process. He requested that the court overturn the tax judgment due to these alleged formalities and inadequate specification of tax purpose under the city charter, specifically challenging the legal basis for the forty percent increase in property valuation.	The City of Chicago defended the tax assessment, arguing that the specification of the tax purpose as "one mill on the dollar for permanent improvements" was indeed sufficient under the charter's provisions. The city also maintained that the procedural shortcomings claimed by the plaintiff did not invalidate the tax, asserting that all necessary actions for the imposition of the tax had been completed according to law. Moreover, they contended that the notice provided for tax collection sufficed and that any related procedural objections were immaterial to the matter of the land tax judgment itself.

The case of "Nelson Mason, Assignee, etc., v. Catharine E. Tiffany, Admx., etc., et al." took place in September 1867 in Lake County, Illinois. The main individuals involved were Nelson Mason, the assignee of the business Mason, McArthur & Co., and Catharine E. Tiffany, who was the administratrix of George B. Tiffany's estate. The case arose after Nelson Mason sought to enforce a claim against the estate of George B. Tiffany following the insolvency of the surviving partners of his firm, George B. Tiffany & Co. The controversy centered around a contract in which Tiffany & Co. ordered the manufacture of boilers from Mason, McArthur & Co. Before the delivery of the boilers, George B. Tiffany passed away. The surviving partners continued operations under his name and issued notes for the boilers' price. However, after the death of Tiffany and subsequent to a general assignment for the benefit of creditors by the surviving partners, several judgments against them remained unsatisfied. The plaintiff claimed that the estate was responsible for the debt arising from the boilers ordered by the partnership, while the defendants challenged the legitimacy of the claim based on various grounds.	The plaintiff argued that as the assignee of Mason, McArthur & Co., he had the right to collect the promissory notes executed by the surviving partners in the name of George B. Tiffany & Co. He contended that the debt was equitable and still owed to him, despite the defendants' assertion that the claim was barred by the statute of limitations. The plaintiff requested the court to enforce the payment of the amount owed from the estate of George B. Tiffany.	The defendants presented several defenses, primarily arguing that the boilers were not delivered under the contract made by George B. Tiffany since he had died before their delivery. They claimed the firm of Tiffany & Co. was not insolvent and that the assigned assets could cover the debts. Additionally, the defendants contended that the plaintiff's claim was invalid as it had not been presented to the estate within two years, thus barring it under relevant statutes. They asserted that since the estate was not liable for the claim and had rightfully refused to honor the demand for payment, the plaintiff should not be able to pursue the case.

In 1876, James H. Roseman filed a legal case against Henry L. Miller in the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a sheriff's sale of land that Roseman owned. The situation began in June 1869 when a judgment was made against Roseman for $1,735.45, resulting in a sheriff's sale of two independent tracts of land in Grundy County on February 19, 1870. The lands were sold in a group for a nominal amount of $10, despite their true value being estimated between $6,000 to over $8,000 at the time. The sheriff granted a deed to Roseman in May 1871. Afterwards, Roseman transferred half of the land to another defendant, Beach. The tracts were distinct and had their own structures but were sold as a single unit, which raised concerns of potential injustice due to the inadequate bid. Roseman claimed he believed the sale would be canceled upon full payment of the owed judgment, stating he paid part of the judgment amount and that the sheriff indicated the sale was informal. The sale was later questioned because it lacked a court seal, which could render it invalid.	The plaintiff, James H. Roseman, argued that the sheriff's sale was invalid due to the gross inadequacy of the bid and the lack of a court seal. He contended that he was misled by the sheriff into believing the sale could be canceled upon payment, which he did. Roseman requested the court to redeem his lands, set aside the sheriff's sale, and enjoin any further actions regarding the property.	The defendants, Henry L. Miller and Beach, contended that they were rightful purchasers of the property. Beach claimed to have bought the land without notice of any prior equities or misunderstandings. They asserted that Roseman had not provided proof of payment regarding the purchase and argued that the sale was legitimate despite the nominal bid. The defense relied on the idea that the transaction was valid and that any claims of informal notice to Roseman did not undermine their position.

In the case of Harriet K. King v. Eugene B. Mix et al., decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875, the events unfolded in Kane County, Illinois. Harriet K. King, the plaintiff, sought legal redress against Eugene B. Mix and other defendants regarding a dispute over property rights. The case involved appeals related to homestead rights, where King claimed she was entitled to a homestead in the premises in question. After extensive court proceedings, the court found that the property was not susceptible to division. Following the court's directions from a previous appeal, it was determined that King should be awarded a total of $1,720, representing $1,000 plus 6% interest for the period since she was expelled from the premises, as this was deemed a fair adjustment of the equities between the parties. The defendants paid this sum to King's solicitors, concluding the financial aspects of the dispute. However, King later sought to have the decree set aside based on claims of misrepresentation and lack of authority given to her solicitors. Despite her efforts, the court ultimately upheld the original decree.	Harriet K. King asserted that she was entitled to a homestead in the property, valued at $1,000, and was seeking an accounting of rents and profits, insisting that her share would exceed the amount determined by the court. She contested the legitimacy of the previous decree, arguing that her solicitors lacked the authority to agree to the terms on her behalf and that she had not received adequate compensation for her interest in the property.	The defendants, Eugene B. Mix and others, defended against King's claims by asserting that the evidence indicated the property could not be partitioned as a homestead. They contended that the court's decision to award a sum of $1,000 with interest was appropriate and within the discretion granted to the court. Moreover, they argued that the decree had been agreed upon by King’s solicitors and, regardless of authority issues, upheld the validity of the settlement reached.

Mary L. Lambert and others v. Frances Hyers involves a foreclosure case that originated on February 24, 1885, in Cook County, Illinois. Frances Hyers was the complainant while the Lamberts were the defendants. An order for foreclosure was granted, and despite the defendants appealing, they did not finalize the appeal process. A master’s sale occurred on June 10, 1885, with John C. Ender being the highest bidder, resulting in a sale certificate later assigned to Frances Livingston. The Lamberts attempted to regain control through a writ of error but lost their case at a later appeal. In February 1888, a writ of assistance was ordered to give Frances Livingston possession of the property, prompting the Lamberts to appeal this issuance. The critical legal question was whether the reversal of the original foreclosure decree nullified the basis for the writ. The court noted that the principles of law allow strangers to the decree to bid at judicial sales without risk of reversals affecting their title, affirming the Circuit Court's issuance of the writ.	The plaintiffs, Mary L. Lambert and others, argue that the title acquired by the master’s deed was invalidated by the reversal of the foreclosure decree. They claim that the issuance of the writ of assistance lacked legal grounding since the title had been purportedly divested.	The defendant, Frances Hyers, contends that the writ of assistance was issued correctly, as the reversal was based on an error that did not affect the title acquired by the property purchaser at the master’s sale. She maintains that the Lamberts neglected to contest the sale at the time and thus cannot challenge it later.

The legal case "The Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Company v. George W. F. Smith" took place in 1875 in Illinois. The plaintiff, George W. F. Smith, was involved in a dispute with the Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Company over the death of his mule, which was struck and killed by a locomotive at a public road crossing. The incident occurred when the mule had just escaped its owner’s enclosure and was crossing the track when it was hit by the train. The track curved at that location, and the railroad company had allowed weeds to grow, obstructing the view of the railway by the train's crew, which contributed to the accident. The plaintiff's claims were rooted in the negligence of the railroad company for failing to maintain a clear right of way, which could have prevented the visibility issue that led to the collision. Disputed evidence also suggested that the train's crew may not have sounded the whistle or rung the bell as required before approaching the crossing. Ultimately, a jury found in favor of the plaintiff after considering conflicting testimonies about the company's negligence, leading to a judgment against the railroad.	The plaintiff, George W. F. Smith, argued that the railroad company was negligent in two primary respects: firstly, for failing to ring a bell or sound a whistle within the required distance before approaching the crossing; and secondly, for allowing excessive weeds to grow on its right of way, obstructing visibility for both the train crew and the general public. Smith sought damages for the value of his mule that was killed as a result of the accident, asserting that the company’s lack of maintenance directly contributed to the incident.	The defendant, the Indianapolis and St. Louis Railroad Company, denied the claims of negligence, asserting that they had not violated any laws regarding sound signals. They contended that they had fulfilled their legal obligations and that any negligence was not on their part. The company also argued that the circumstances surrounding the injury were not entirely their responsibility and may have resulted from the mule's own actions. The defendant's request was essentially to have the case dismissed in light of their defense.

In the case of *The Attorney General v. The Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company*, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the dispute arose in the context of corporate and municipal law following the construction and operation of a railroad. The Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company was incorporated in 1861 for the purpose of building a railroad from Chicago to Evanston. However, the incorporation faced challenges primarily due to its failure to commence operations within ten days after the Illinois Constitution of 1870 went into effect, which stipulated that any charter not actively in operation would no longer be valid. The Attorney General, representing the People of Illinois, filed a petition for a quo warranto, seeking to challenge and restrain the railroad company's claims and activities related to steam-powered operations within the city after claiming that the company lacked the authority to do so. The proceedings progressed, leading to a crucial decree concerning the legitimacy of the railroad's claims to operate. After hearings and considerations of various ordinances and statutes applicable at the time, the court ultimately engaged both parties in significant discussions surrounding their rights and validations of the company's corporate existence.	The Attorney General claimed that the Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company was operating unlawfully because it had not been in operation within the statutory timeframe required by the state's constitution. The plaintiff sought an information in the nature of a quo warranto, demanding that the railroad company prove the legitimacy of its claimed rights and privileges to construct and operate a railroad powered by steam within the jurisdiction of Chicago. Furthermore, the plaintiff requested the court to prevent the railroad from initiating any construction or operations related to the disputed routes and facilities.	The Chicago and Evanston Railroad Company asserted that it was a validly incorporated entity that had fulfilled its organizational requirements before the constitution took effect. The company denied the claims of invalidity, stating that it had established its charter and had been in operation since before the constitutional deadlines. It highlighted prior judicial decrees that upheld its authority to operate within the city and argued that the Attorney General's claims were barred by previous adjudications. Furthermore, the defendant countered that the City Council had conferred valid permissions to undertake the contested rail operations under existing laws.

Alanson G. Freeman and others initiated a legal case against The Ottawa Building, Homestead and Savings Association, which was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court on May 15, 1885. The central issue revolved around the interpretation of loan agreements made by stockholders in a building and loan association. The case was a continuation of previous rulings, particularly referencing Holmes et al. v. Smythe. Freeman had obtained a loan while being a stockholder and was bound by the terms of interest and installment payments on his stock shares. The dispute involved whether the transactions constituted usury and the legalities surrounding stock forfeiture for non-payment of loans. The court emphasized that the dealings were consistent with established legal precedents concerning such financial transactions, asserting Freeman’s obligations were valid under the applicable statutes.	The plaintiffs argued that the statute authorizing the creation of the loan association was unconstitutional, claiming that the loan made to Freeman was usurious. They sought legal relief based on these assertions, wanting the court to invalidate the obligations imposed upon them as a result of the loan.	The defendant contended that the transactions were lawful and that the plaintiffs, particularly Freeman, were correctly held liable under the non-payment provisions of the loan agreement. The defense emphasized that forfeiture of stock due to willful neglect of payments was legitimate under the association's charter and that no additional notices were required in such cases.

In April 1857, an ejectment action was initiated by Asbury F. Johnson against Andrew J. Bletch in Iroquois County, Illinois. The case stemmed from a dispute over possession of certain premises. Johnson served a notice to Bletch at his dwelling, reportedly giving a copy of the declaration and notice to Bletch's wife. However, Bletch did not comply with a rule requiring him to plead within twenty days, leading to a default judgment in October 1857 that awarded possession to Johnson. The case was appealed on the grounds that the notice served failed to meet statutory requirements, specifically that it didn’t confirm proper service of notice according to the law. The appeal raised concerns over the sufficiency of the service return, including whether the notice was left at the defendant's dwelling house and whether the date of service was recorded, both of which are essential for establishing jurisdiction in ejectment cases.	The plaintiff, Asbury F. Johnson, claimed that he properly served Andrew J. Bletch with a notice of the ejectment action and sought to recover possession of the premises. He argued that Bletch's failure to appear and plead within the stipulated time justified his default judgment in the lower court.	The defendant, Andrew J. Bletch, contended that the service of notice was insufficient as it did not comply with the statutory requirements. He argued that the return did not confirm that the notice was left at his dwelling, nor did it provide a specific date of service, which he asserted was necessary for the court to have jurisdiction over him. Bletch sought to have the default judgment reversed on these grounds.

In 1836, a contractual agreement was made between Joseph Davis (the defendant) and Thomas Wiley (the plaintiff) for the performance of 800 rods of ditching at a rate of 62.5 cents per rod, with a total payment of $500 structured in two installments: $300 due on December 1 and $200 due twelve months later. The contract stipulated that Wiley would start and continue the work unless prevented by health issues, in which case Davis would accept the work completed up to that point and wait for the remainder. When Wiley claimed to have completed his obligations but did not receive the final payment of $200 from Davis, he brought the case to court. Initially, the court ruled in favor of Wiley, but Davis appealed, arguing that Wiley had not fully performed his obligations by neglecting to complete 400 rods of work. The issue was whether the covenants were independent or dependent, which significantly affected what needed to be established in court regarding performance.	Thomas Wiley contended that he had diligently fulfilled his responsibilities under the contract, as he had completed the work or was unable to finish due to health constraints. He claimed entitlement to the final payment of $200 based on his assertion that Davis had breached the contract by failing to pay this amount despite Wiley's performance.	Joseph Davis argued that Wiley had not satisfactorily completed the 800 rods of ditching as required by the contract, as evidenced by the absence of 400 rods. He contended that Wiley's obligations were a condition precedent to any payment, asserting that without the completion of the work, he was not required to pay the final installment.

On February 12, 1845, Thomas Mulligan filed a bill in Chancery against James Riggin and Andrew Miller in Madison County, Illinois. The core of the dispute concerned a piece of land, namely the southwest quarter of Section 16, Township 3 North, Range 9 West, which Mulligan claimed to have obtained through a warranty deed from Jacob Swiggart on September 10, 1836. Mulligan asserted he had possessed the land without any knowledge of competing claims until January 1845. Riggin, prior to Mulligan’s acquisition of the property, had secured a judgment against Robert Whiteside for a debt amounting to $77.85, which gave him what he believed was a lien on Whiteside's property. After several enforcement actions—including a levy on the land in 1834—Riggin attempted to sell the land more than eleven years after his original judgment. Mulligan sought an injunction to prevent Riggin from proceeding with the sale, asserting his ownership rights. The case examined the duration of a judgment lien as well as the necessary parties involved in the dispute.	The plaintiff, James Riggin, argued that the prior judgment against Robert Whiteside entitled him to collect the debt through a lien on the disputed land. He contended that his execution and subsequent actions were valid and that Mulligan's claim was subordinate due to the late filing and enforcement of the judgment. Riggin sought the court's permission to proceed with the sale of the land in an effort to satisfy his judgment.	The defendant, Thomas Mulligan, contended that Riggin's lien had lapsed due to inactivity over the statutory period of seven years, as stipulated by Illinois law. Mulligan argued that since he purchased the property bona fide within that timeframe, he should retain clear title without the encumbrance of Riggin's stale judgment. Mulligan further claimed that Riggin had not included necessary parties, specifically the heirs or legal representatives of Whiteside, in the bill filed with the court. As a result, Mulligan requested the court uphold the injunction that prevented the sale of the property.

On December 6, 1883, Nathaniel G. Slack and Albert L. Garitt, partners in the firm Slack & Garitt, were indebted to the First National Bank of Rushville in a significant amount. To secure this debt, they executed a bill of sale, transferring a large quantity of personal property and assigning multiple accounts receivable to the bank. Among these was an account worth $2,701.53 owed by Joseph Horne & Co. On June 10, 1881, Horne & Co. sent a draft for $580.90 to Slack & Garitt as part of payment for their debt. Nathaniel G. Slack received this draft and consulted his attorney, E.J. Pemberton, on how to proceed. Following the attorney's advice, Slack went to another town to cash the draft, subsequently pocketing the funds instead of applying them to the assigned debt, which he was obligated to do. The bank later requested repayment, but Slack refused, leading to the bank’s lawsuit against him. The jury ruled in favor of Slack, but the bank appealed, claiming the trial court erred by not granting a new trial.	The First National Bank of Rushville contended that Nathaniel G. Slack wrongfully cashed a draft that was intended to settle an account that he had previously assigned to the bank. The bank argued that Slack had no legitimate claim to the funds after the assignment and that he had willfully and maliciously defrauded them by pocketing the money instead of using it to pay the owed amount. The bank sought a reversal of the initial jury verdict that favored Slack.	Nathaniel G. Slack maintained that he acted upon the advice of his attorney regarding the draft and believed he was permitted to cash it. His defense rested on the assertion that he was not aware he was violating any obligations to the bank at the time of the action. Slack argued that the advice he received constituted good faith action and that any potential wrongdoing should not negate his reliance on legal counsel.

In June 1870, a legal case took place in the Wabash Circuit Court, Illinois, involving a partnership dispute. The parties included Abraham Mauck, the surviving partner, and the heirs of his deceased partner, John Mauck. The partnership, established verbally in August 1857 under the name A. & J. Mauck, focused on real estate transactions, pork trading, and flour milling. After John Mauck's death on June 13, 1861, the partnership ended without a settlement of its affairs. At that time, the partnership owed $77,845.30 and had assets totaling $63,833. Abraham Mauck had withdrawn $514.35, while John Mauck's withdrawal was $616.15. Following the dissolution, debts remained, and Abraham Mauck, as the sole surviving partner, had managed to pay most debts except for $33,700.82. He sought a court order to collect outstanding debts and sell the firm's real estate to settle the remaining liabilities. The court determined the firm was insolvent by $14,022.30 and authorized Mauck to proceed with these actions, ensuring a structured sale process. The case raised issues concerning the authority of a court in managing partnership assets and ensuring fairness in the process.	The plaintiffs, representing the heirs of John Mauck, claimed that Abraham Mauck improperly managed the partnership assets and sought a fair accounting and settlement of the partnership affairs. They contended that not all debts and asset distributions were transparently handled and that the court should oversee the dissolution process to protect their interests.	The defendant, Abraham Mauck, argued that he acted within his rights as the surviving partner by paying off the firm's debts and managing the assets. He justified the private sale of real estate for more than its assessed value, emphasizing that the sale was necessary to address the partnership's insolvency. He contended that no fraud or improper conduct was involved in the process and that the court had the equitable authority to authorize his actions.

The case "The Metropolitan Bank, Appellant, v. Benjamin Godfrey, and Thomas W. Wason, Appellees" arose from a contractual dispute in 1851 regarding the construction of the Alton and Sangamon Railroad in Illinois. Key players included Benjamin Godfrey, the contractor, and Henry Dwight, Jr., who acted as a financial agent for Godfrey. Godfrey conveyed land, bonds, stocks, and personal property to Dwight as security under their agreement. Dwight, however, kept profits from the project and failed to account for them to Godfrey, leading to a dispute over the lands not used in construction. In October 1851, Godfrey signed a complex contract with Dwight without fully understanding its terms, which led to disagreements about its execution and the return of lands. The Metropolitan Bank became involved after Dwight conveyed the land to them in 1854, claiming they had the right to hold it as a security for debts owed by Dwight. The case highlights issues of contract interpretation, financial obligations, and the rights of parties in a contractual arrangement.	Benjamin Godfrey, as a plaintiff, asserted that the lands he conveyed to Henry Dwight should be re-conveyed to him, arguing that the contract he signed did not properly reflect their agreed-upon terms. He claimed he was led to sign under duress and without understanding the implications of the contract clauses; that Dwight committed fraud by failing to account for the profits from the railroad construction; and that the Metropolitan Bank, having acquired the lands, did so without rightful ownership. Godfrey sought reformation of the contract and the return of his property due to the complex and unclear terms that did not align with their original agreement.	The Metropolitan Bank contended that it properly acquired the lands from Dwight through a legitimate transaction that satisfied its financial obligations. They argued that Dwight was indebted to them and thus had the right to convey the land. The Bank claimed it had no knowledge of Godfrey's equities or any fraudulent dealings, asserting they were bona fide purchasers for value. They maintained that the contracts were valid and enforceable, and that they acted within their rights under New York banking laws.

Abraham M. Johnson (the defendant/appellant) was involved in a legal dispute with Hiram Bright (the plaintiff/appellee) in 1853, in Stephenson County, Illinois. Johnson had entered into a sealed covenant with Amos F. Culver and Bright, agreeing to compensate them with either half of the recovered property or its monetary equivalent for their legal services in lawsuits aimed at recovering real estate. However, Culver left the country before the lawsuits were initiated. Bright continued the legal proceedings, which Johnson later compromised by settling with the adverse claimants, effectively discontinuing the lawsuits. As a result, Bright sought payment for the legal services rendered under the original agreement. The case proceeded with various legal motions and the court's decisions regarding the parties' roles and responsibilities as outlined in the original agreement.	Bright claimed that Johnson had breached the covenant by settling with the defendants without allowing him and Culver to complete their legal services. He argued that despite Culver's absence, he (Bright) had provided the necessary services to justify payment as stipulated in the original agreement. Bright sought compensation for his efforts in facilitating the legal recovery of the property, which included receiving part of the settlement that Johnson had reached.	Johnson contended that he was not liable for payment because the services stipulated in the covenant were not fully performed, given Culver's departure from the case. He argued that he was entitled to the joint services of both attorneys, implying that the lack of Culver's participation should absolve him from the obligation to compensate Bright. Johnson also filed several procedural motions challenging the court’s decisions regarding the handling of the case and the admission of evidence relating to the covenant.

The case "The People ex rel. Jacob Chritzman et al. v. George W. Crossley et al." took place in September 1873, in Illinois. The plaintiffs, represented by Jacob Chritzman, Stephen G. Paddock, Charles Baldwin, and Jacob L. Sweet, sought to challenge the election of George W. Crossley, Hiram W. Hubbard, Entiben B. Foster, and Levi R. Jerome as directors of the Illinois Masons’ Benevolent Society. The core issue was whether members of the society had the right to vote by proxy during the election held on April 2, 1873. The society was established to provide financial support to members' families upon death. Its organizational laws permitted amendments that allowed proxy voting. The plaintiffs contended that the election was invalid due to alleged improper proxy voting, while the defense maintained that the society's by-laws expressly permitted this method of voting. The Illinois Supreme Court ultimately recognized the validity of the proxy voting authorization in the by-laws based on prevailing legal precedents.	The plaintiffs asserted that the election of the defendants to the board of directors was invalid due to alleged violations concerning the execution and legitimacy of the proxy votes cast. They requested the court to strike down the election results and invalidate the defendants' claims to the director positions, arguing that without valid voting by the members, the election could not stand.	The defendants argued that the election was valid and that the by-laws of the Illinois Masons’ Benevolent Society allowed for proxy voting. They contended that no objections were raised regarding the execution of the proxy forms at the time of the election. They sought to affirm their election results and maintain their positions as duly elected directors, asserting that the allegations did not undermine the legitimacy of the proxy votes received.

Stephen Monroe v. Edgar M. Snow et al. is a legal case that took place in Chicago, Illinois, with the court's decision rendered on January 21, 1890. The plaintiffs, Edgar M. Snow and Theodore G. Dickinson, are real estate brokers. In December 1884, the defendant, Stephen Monroe, approached the plaintiffs seeking assistance in selling his property located at 190 and 192 Fifth Avenue, Chicago. Monroe initially authorized the brokers to sell the property for $100,000 but indicated a minimum acceptable price of $95,000. Over the next year, after failing to sell the property, Monroe allegedly directed Snow to lower the selling price to $90,000 in October or November 1885. Despite the brokers finding a buyer willing to purchase the property for $90,000, Monroe later refused to complete the sale and insisted that he would only sell for $100,000. This led the brokers to file a lawsuit for commissions on the proposed sale. The case revolved around the arguments surrounding the authorization to sell at different price points and the admissibility of various pieces of evidence related to these transactions.	The plaintiffs claim that they were authorized by the defendant to sell the property at a price of $90,000 and that they successfully found a willing buyer. They argue that they are entitled to a commission of 2.5% on the $90,000 sale based on this verbal agreement, despite the defendant's refusal to finalize the sale. They contend that the negotiations and various communications, including written evidence, corroborate their position that they were acting within their authority.	The defendant argues that he never authorized the plaintiffs to sell the property for $90,000 and instead maintained that the exclusive selling price was $100,000. He claims that the brokers cannot collect a commission for a sale that was not completed due to his refusal to consent to it. Furthermore, he contests the admissibility of certain evidence presented by the plaintiffs, asserting that the brokers lacked written authority to sell the property as required by the statute of frauds.

Elizabeth D. Andrews et al. v. William A. Black et al. is a legal case that took place in January 1867 in Illinois, specifically dealing with a probate issue concerning the will of Andrew Black. The case came about after the probate court of Madison County had admitted Andrew Black's will to probate following a thorough examination and proper evidential support. One of the devisees under this will, who was also a child and heir-at-law of Andrew Black, contested the decision by appealing to the Circuit Court. After hearing the appeal, the Circuit Court upheld the original probate court's decision, leading to the present case being brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The main legal questions considered were whether an appeal can be made from an order admitting a will to probate and whether any evidence aside from that provided by subscribing witnesses can be presented regarding the sanity of the testator.	The plaintiffs, represented by counsel, argued that the appeal from the probate court's decision to admit the will to probate was valid and should be allowed under the statute of wills. They claimed that a broader range of evidence, specifically regarding the testator's sanity, should be admissible in the appellate court besides just the testimony of the subscribing witnesses.	The defendants contended that the appeal from the probate court was not valid and that the statute explicitly limits the evidence on the testator’s sanity to that of the subscribing witnesses when the probate had been granted. They maintained that any other evidence presented should not hold weight in the decision-making process regarding the sanity of the testator.

William McKinney was jointly indicted for the murder of Edmund A. Philleo in 1843, along with co-defendants George Blaylock and Isaac McKinney, in the Rock Island Circuit Court, Illinois. The indictment, described as “a true bill,” initiated a protracted legal battle over several court terms. Initially, a jury was empaneled but could not reach a verdict, leading to multiple continuances and trials. By May 1845, McKinney faced trial alone and ultimately received a guilty verdict after the jury deliberated on the evidence presented. Following the verdict, he filed motions to arrest judgment and for a new trial on various grounds, which were all denied by the Court. The judge pronounced the death sentence upon him. McKinney's case included claims of procedural errors, such as issues related to the jury's administration of oaths and objections to the indictment's integrity, culminating in an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court for review of these matters and the resultant judgment from the lower court.	William McKinney, as the plaintiff in error, claimed that the indictment against him was defective, and the oaths administered to jurors and witnesses were not in compliance with legal requirements. He asserted improper judicial procedures in the handling of his trial, including alleged lack of proper orders for jury conduct during trial recesses and failure to adequately furnish necessary legal documents prior to arraignment. He requested a reversal of the conviction and a new trial based on these alleged legal breaches.	The defendants, representing the People of the State of Illinois, argued against McKinney's claims, stating that proper judicial procedures were followed. They contended that any alleged irregularities mentioned by McKinney did not constitute grounds for a reversal of the conviction. They maintained it was the defendant's responsibility to object at the time of the trial regarding any perceived discrepancies. Furthermore, they supported that all necessary legal documents were made available to McKinney prior to his arraignment, thus upholding the conviction and the sentence imposed.

In February 1889, the case of David S. Dempsey v. Jesse Whiteside was decided in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose in Armington, Tazewell County, Illinois, where the plaintiff, Dempsey, asserted that he had left a sum of money with the defendant, Whiteside, intended to cover two promissory notes totaling $545. Dempsey claimed that payments of $472 were made to Whiteside in June 1884 and June 1886 through his son, James, who served as the principal witness. Receipts purportedly signed by Whiteside indicated that the funds were received for this purpose. However, Whiteside contested the authenticity of these receipts, arguing they may have been modified or originally intended for a different purpose. The trial was conducted without a jury, leading to a judgment favoring Dempsey after a finding that the evidence, although conflicting, supported his claims.	Dempsey claimed that he had deposited money with Whiteside for the explicit purpose of paying off two promissory notes. He contended that the money was received by Whiteside, and therefore, he was entitled to its return, amounting to $572.50. The principal evidence consisted of receipts allegedly signed by Whiteside acknowledging the transaction, and Dempsey sought compensation for the claimed amounts due to what he argued was Whiteside's failure to apply the funds correctly.	Whiteside denied the validity of the receipts and the claim that the money had been properly allocated towards the promissory notes. He suggested that the receipts were either forged or misrepresented and argued that any payments made by James Whiteside were not intended for the debts in question. Furthermore, he contended that evidence pertaining to James Whiteside's financial state was irrelevant and would not have impacted the case. Whiteside sought to have the judgment reversed, citing errors in the trial court's handling of evidence and witness testimonies.

In January 1873, in Mason City, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between John G. Adams, the plaintiff, and four defendants: William Brannan, Dabney Hall, Frank Bryant, and Danville F. Bryant, all of whom were saloon-keepers. The case involved a claim that the defendants sold intoxicating liquor to Samuel Mitchell, leading to his intoxication. As a result of this intoxication, Mitchell fell and broke his leg. Adams, having taken charge of Mitchell during his incapacitation, cared for him until he healed. He filed a lawsuit to recover a total of $2,000 from the defendants, demanding compensation for the caregiving services rendered (which included $1,600 for the time provided care and a statutory penalty of $400 for the days Mitchell was kept). The jury initially ruled in favor of Adams, awarding him $248; however, the defendants appealed, arguing against the validity of the claims and the judgment amount. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for a decision.	The plaintiff, John G. Adams, argued that the defendants were liable for causing the intoxication of Samuel Mitchell through the sale of liquor, which resulted in an injury wherein Mitchell broke his leg. Adams requested compensation under the Illinois statute, seeking a reasonable sum for taking care of Mitchell while he was incapacitated due to intoxication, along with an additional penalty of $2 per day for the duration of care required post-intoxication.	The defendants contended that they were not liable because Mitchell had not consumed alcohol from their establishment after the morning of the incident. They argued that the injury (the leg fracture) was too remote from any potential liability, as it was unclear whether Mitchell was still intoxicated at the time of the accident. The defense insisted upon the need to show a direct connection between the intoxication caused by their liquor and the injury sustained by Mitchell, challenging the admissibility of certain evidence presented against them in court.

In 1854, in Peoria, Illinois, William Senior entered into a verbal contract to furnish materials and erect a building. Following the completion of the work, Senior sought to enforce a mechanics' lien against Alexander Brebnor and others involved, claiming he was owed compensation per the agreement. The case was brought before the Peoria Circuit Court, where Senior's petition for a mechanics' lien was denied, ruling that the contract lacked a specific provision requiring the completion of the work within three years. A jury trial found for the defendants, leading Senior to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the court erred in its judgment regarding the validity of the mechanics' lien.	William Senior claimed that the defendants owed him money for the materials and labor used in the construction project based on their verbal contract. He sought to enforce a mechanics' lien, asserting that he had fulfilled his obligations and was entitled to compensation. Senior argued that despite the absence of a written agreement with a specific timeline, the terms of performance and his actions should have sufficed to secure his lien under the law.	The defendants, represented by Manning & Merriman and J. K. Cooper, argued that the mechanics' lien could not be legally sustained because the contract did not include a provision stating that the work would be completed within three years, as required by statute. They maintained that the statute must be adhered to strictly since it creates special privileges and should not be extended beyond its specified cases. Their position was that due to this omission, the lien did not attach, and thus, the plaintiff's claims were meritless.

In the case of William Winkelmann v. Drainage District, the dispute arose in 1887 in Monroe County, Illinois. The plaintiff, William Winkelmann, claimed damages of $300 for land that was taken by the Drainage District for the construction of a levee, a public utility project intended to benefit properties in the area. The claim was made under the provisions of the Drainage Act of 1879, which allowed landowners to seek compensation for land taken for such projects. The jury impaneled by the court determined that while damages of $300 were owed to Winkelmann, there were also benefits assessed to his land amounting to $536. The defendant, the Drainage District, argued that the benefits should offset the damages. Winkelmann contested this, claiming that the jury had no authority to offset benefits against damages for land taken, asserting his right to full compensation under constitutional provisions prohibiting the taking of private property without just compensation. The court’s judgment in the lower court was in favor of the Drainage District, prompting Winkelmann to appeal.	Winkelmann's main arguments centered around the assertion that his rights were violated as the jury had improperly offset benefits against the damages he was owed for his land taken by the Drainage District. He maintained that under the Illinois Constitution, he was entitled to just compensation without deduction for benefits received from the levee project. Winkelmann requested that the appellate court reverse the lower court's judgment and order the full payment of $300 without considering the alleged benefits to his property.	The Drainage District defended its position by arguing that the jury was correct in offsetting the assessed benefits against the damages to Winkelmann's property. The defendant cited statutory provisions that permit the offset of benefits against damages within the context of drainage projects. They contended that Winkelmann was not entitled to recover the full extent of the damages due to the advantages conferred by the drainage improvements.

In the case of Frank R. Baker v. Robert Strahorn and Juliette Strahorn, the proceedings took place on April 17, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case involves Frank R. Baker, appealing against Robert Strahorn and Juliette Strahorn, who are his daughter's parents seeking to adopt his daughter Edna, a seven-year-old girl. The plaintiffs, Robert and Juliette Strahorn, are the grandparents of Edna, whose mother is the daughter of the petitioners. The background reveals that Edna's parents were separated due to a divorce decree granted to the mother on grounds of the father's cruelty. Following the divorce, the father failed to provide any support for his wife or daughter, leaving them destitute. The court had originally granted custody of Edna to her mother. Given the mother's delicate health and her consent to adoption, the Strahorns filed a petition for Edna's adoption. The court required evidence of non-support from the father and analyzed the welfare of the child as paramount in their ruling.	The plaintiffs, Robert and Juliette Strahorn, argued for the adoption of their granddaughter Edna, emphasizing that her welfare is of utmost importance. They highlighted that the child's mother, who had custody following the divorce, was in favor of the adoption. The plaintiffs sought legal recognition of their right to adopt Edna, given the absence of support and care from the child's father since the divorce and the challenging circumstances faced by the mother.	Frank R. Baker, Edna’s father, contended against the adoption based on his parental rights and natural authority as a father. He highlighted that despite the turbulent family dynamics, he should maintain some rights over his child. Baker argued that the divorce decree should not automatically transfer the right to consent for adoption solely to the mother without his involvement or consideration.

In January 1871, the case of Thomas Purser v. John C. Short was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal dispute stemmed from a property matter involving land originally patented to Joseph Patterson. This land was conveyed to Isaac H. Alexander and Hezekiah Cunningham. In 1837, Alexander passed away, leaving behind a wife and two minor children who died later that same year. Alexander's will was validated, allowing his executors to sell the estate's real estate to satisfy various obligations. The will granted the widow a life estate in the land. In 1839, the executors sought court approval to sell her interest, a decision to which she consented. The sale was concluded with William P. Bryant as the purchaser. Years later, the widow married Dr. Fithian, and they transferred their interest to Purser for a nominal amount. However, since the life estate ended with her death, the question arose regarding the validity of the initial sale to Bryant and its implications on property ownership, ultimately involving the right to partition the land.	The plaintiff, Thomas Purser, argued that the initial sale and subsequent transfer of property implicated rights to land that should allow him to claim a full ownership interest. He sought to prove that the sale conducted under the court decree was invalid and that his conveyance from the widow should entitle him to assert a larger claim on the property.	The defendant, John C. Short, maintained that the original sale to Bryant, executed by the widow's executors, was lawful and binding despite any alleged irregularities. He defended the validity of Bryant's ownership following the completion of the sale, asserting that the subsequent life estate of the widow did not affect the ownership rights that passed through the executors. The defendant aimed to uphold the chain of title that identified his right to the property and sought affirmation of the already established ownership status.

The legal case "John G. Fellers et al. v. William Rainey, Jr. et al." was initiated in the equity side of the St. Clair County Circuit Court, Illinois, during February in 1873. The case involves two sets of heirs of Isaac Rainey, deceased since February 26, 1871, who died intestate with real and personal estate. William Rainey, Jr., the complainant in the initial proceedings, sought a decree to compel other heirs to account for advancements received from Isaac Rainey, arguing they had withheld information. The adult defendants failed to answer to a rule taken against them, leading to a decree favoring William Rainey, Jr. and his brother, Jefferson Rainey, Jr. The Fellers sought to set aside this decree, alleging fraud by William Rainey, Jr. based on letters he wrote, which they believed were misleading. The case was then transferred to the Jefferson County Circuit Court, which dismissed the Fellers' complaint on the grounds of a general demurrer. They brought the matter to the Illinois Supreme Court to reverse this dismissal.	The plaintiffs, Emeline and John G. Fellers, claimed that the decree favoring William Rainey, Jr. was obtained through fraud. They asserted that William Rainey, Jr. had misled them and other defendants into waiving their rights to contest the original suit, assuring them that their rights would not be harmed in the process. They requested the court set aside the prior decree based on these alleged fraudulent actions.	The defendants, William Rainey, Jr. and others, contended that there was no fraud in the issuance of the original decree. They argued that the plaintiffs, particularly Emeline Fellers, had a full opportunity to contest the claims made against them but chose not to. They maintained that the decrees were valid and could not be vacated merely because the plaintiffs now sought to challenge the findings based on their interpretation of the facts.

In 1866, J. R. Askew and J. T. Springer entered into a partnership to purchase and sell a 44-acre parcel of land near Jacksonville, Illinois, for $13,375. They agreed to split the profits and losses from the sales of city lots created from this land, with the partner making sales receiving a commission of five percent. However, a dispute arose over the commission structure when Springer made most of the sales while Askew contributed no sales effort. Following the first sale, the partners disagreed on how commissions should be calculated, leading to tensions in their partnership. Eventually, a settlement was reached in 1878 concerning the partition of unsold property but did not address the commissions. Subsequent to this, Askew sought an accounting of partnership profits, which revealed that he was due $304.37 from Springer. The trial court ruled on the matter, ordering Springer to pay Askew $245.37, dissolve the partnership, and cover two-thirds of the costs associated with the case. Springer appealed the decision, arguing about the correctness of the accounting and the imposition of costs.	Askew, the plaintiff, claimed he was entitled to the commissions from sales made under the partnership agreement. He argued that the contract stipulated that the partner making the sale should receive a commission from the total proceeds, which needed to be compensated adequately for the labor and effort he had put into selling the property. He requested a formal accounting of the partnership's finances and a partition of remaining partnership assets.	Springer, the defendant, contended that the partnership agreement was misinterpreted regarding the commission structure. He argued that the commission should be calculated based on the gross proceeds and claimed that he had notified Askew to terminate the agreement. Springer further asserted that any delay in claiming commissions should be barred by the Statute of Limitations due to the long period without a settlement of this specific issue.

The case "Board of Directors for Leveeing Wabash River v. Chambers Houston" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1874. The case arose in Wabash County, Illinois, concerning a levee construction project along the Wabash River. The Illinois legislature, through an act from 1865, appointed a board of directors responsible for locating and supervising the levee's construction within designated townships.
