The board was empowered to assess benefits on real estate for improvements made and had the authority to enforce tax assessments via a summons against delinquent property owners. Chambers Houston, the defendant, faced legal action for failing to pay the assessments levied on his land as part of this initiative. The case revolved around the constitutionality of the assessment process under the Illinois Constitution of 1848, specifically whether the act created a valid public corporation authorized to impose taxes.	The plaintiff, the Board of Directors for Leveeing Wabash River, claimed that the assessments made against Chambers Houston's property were legitimate under the authority granted by the Illinois legislature. They argued that the board was a public corporation established to serve public interests, thus justifying the taxation levied on homeowners within the region to fund the levee project.	Chambers Houston, the defendant, contended that the assessments were unconstitutional and invalid due to the nature of the corporation created by the legislature. He argued that the board was essentially a private corporation without the authority to impose taxes, as it did not represent a local government or receive consent from the property owners it taxed. Houston's defense was supported by legal precedents indicating that taxation powers could only be granted to duly constituted public corporations rather than private entities.

In the case of Samuel B. Raymond v. George M. Vaughan, the events trace back to September 15, 1874, when Samuel B. Raymond and George M. Vaughan formed a partnership in Chicago, Illinois, to operate as brokers in the wholesale sugar market. They agreed to manage separate agency businesses under their individual names, dividing profits with Vaughan receiving one-third and Raymond two-thirds. This arrangement lasted until January 20, 1876, when Vaughan was adjudicated as temporarily insane and committed to an asylum. During this period, Raymond continued the business without formally terminating their partnership, acting as conservator of Vaughan's estate. After Vaughan's release from the asylum in May 1879, a settlement was discussed, but the business transactions from Vaughan's time of insanity were not addressed. Vaughan filed a bill for an accounting against Raymond on October 11, 1880, asserting his entitlement to profits generated during his incapacitation. The Illinois Appellate Court ultimately had to address whether the partnership still existed and if Raymond had a legal obligation to account for the partnership’s earnings while Vaughan was mentally unfit.	Vaughan claimed that the partnership between him and Raymond continued despite his insanity. He sought a judicial accounting to recover his share of profits earned while he was incapacitated. Vaughan argued that Raymond had a fiduciary duty to manage the partnership's earnings appropriately for their mutual benefit, especially during Vaughan's period in the asylum, which was not formally recognized or resolved at the time of Vaughan’s release.	Raymond contended that the partnership was dissolved when Vaughan was found insane, asserting that insanity leads to an automatic dissolution of partnership. He argued that as a conservator appointed by the court, he was not obligated to account for the partnership earnings as they were not declared during his final accounting in the county court. Raymond maintained that the prior decision regarding his conservatorship should bar Vaughan's claims based on the doctrine of res judicata.

The case "William Linton v. Mary Ann Porter" was decided in April 1863 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arises from a promissory note made by the appellant, William Linton, to the appellee, Mary Ann Porter. In the background of the case, Porter's husband passed away, leaving behind an iron pile hammer, which Porter subsequently sold to Linton. In exchange for the hammer, Porter received a promissory note as payment. The hammer is currently in Linton's possession. The case initially began before a justice of the peace, where Porter won the judgment, and this judgment was later upheld by the Superior Court of Chicago. The main contention in the appeal was the defense's claim of "want of consideration," arguing that the note should be void due to a lack of proper legal grounds for its execution.	Mary Ann Porter claims that the promissory note given to her by William Linton is valid as it was issued in exchange for the sale of the iron pile hammer. She argues that the sale and delivery of this personal property constitute good consideration for the note. Porter contends that an implied warranty of title accompanies the sale, thereby asserting her right to enforce the note despite Linton's defense based on the alleged lack of consideration.	William Linton, the defendant, argues that the promissory note is invalid due to want of consideration, claiming that he should not have to pay for the hammer since, according to him, the sale lacks substantial legal basis. He seeks to repudiate the note while retaining possession of the hammer, asserting that the note should not be enforced against him given the circumstances surrounding the sale.

The case, "The People of the State of Illinois, on the relation of William Davenport v. Welcome B. Brown," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1850. The dispute arose in Woodford County, Illinois, where a petition was filed by William Davenport and others seeking a peremptory mandamus. They wanted the county judge and his associates to provide an abstract of votes regarding the adoption of a township organization, as well as to designate a suitable time and place for electing town officials in accordance with this organization. The context for this case lies in a law passed by the Illinois Legislature on February 12, 1849, which allowed counties to organize themselves into townships, contingent upon a majority vote from all eligible voters in the county. However, upon investigation, it was revealed that only 153 out of more than 600 legal votes were cast in favor of the township organization in Woodford County. This led to the question of whether the township organization had been legally adopted as per the requirements laid out in the state constitution.	The plaintiffs argued that a majority of all legal voters in Woodford County had favored the adoption of the township organization and requested the court to issue a mandamus compelling county officials to take necessary actions to proceed with this organization. They contended that the election results demonstrated a clear mandate from the voters.	The defendants, which included the county judge and justices, countered the plaintiffs' claims by stating that a mere 153 votes in favor of the organizational change out of over 600 total votes did not satisfy the constitutional requirement for a majority of all legal voters in the county. They asserted that the township organization could not be considered valid because it did not achieve the requisite votes as mandated by the constitution.

In 1849, in Marshall County, Illinois, Daniel M. Robertson, a constable, faced a legal action regarding his failure to return an execution on time. The case was initially brought by the County Commissioners of Marshall County for the benefit of Cochran & Perry. The action was commenced in the Probate Court of Marshall County and concerned the official bond of Robertson. After a judgment against Robertson and his sureties for $1,000 was rendered, they appealed to the Circuit Court. During the trial, the defendants (Robertson and his sureties) contested the ruling on several grounds, including lack of jurisdiction and failure to provide security for costs as required by statute. The Circuit Court upheld the probate ruling, leading to further exploration of the bond's liability and the measure of damages due to Robertson's actions. Notably, the defendants aimed to introduce evidence of the insolvency of the party involved in the original execution, which the court excluded. Ultimately, they were ruled against for the total penalty amount of the bond and a quarter of the original judgment as costs.	The plaintiffs, comprising the County Commissioners of Marshall County, claimed that Robertson, as constable, neglected his duty by failing to return an execution within the designated time frame. They sought the full amount due from his official bond, noting that the statute clearly outlined the damages to be awarded in such cases, which amounted to the execution's value plus interest.	The defendants contended that the Circuit Court erred in not dismissing the case due to a lack of security for costs and argued that the Probate Justice lacked jurisdiction. They attempted to demonstrate that Cochran & Perry had not suffered actual damages due to Robertson's failure but were prohibited from introducing evidence of the insolvency of the party that the execution had been against. They insisted that under the law, they should only be liable for nominal damages, and sought to overturn the judgment entirely.

In September 1854, Mark Ayers executed a mortgage to Timothy B. Mason on certain real estate in Iroquois County, Illinois, to secure a debt of $10,447.97. Subsequently, on February 9, 1855, Ayers executed a second mortgage to Mason encompassing both new and previously mortgaged lands. However, this second mortgage was junior and subject to an earlier mortgage held by Charles Sherman. After a foreclosure decree obtained by Sherman in 1855, which did not include Mason as a party, Sherman took possession, later selling the property to William Cesna and then to Stephen Cesna, both of whom paid taxes and maintained possession. In 1869, Mason's representatives sought to foreclose the second mortgage in an amended bill but faced defenses from Sherman and Stephen Cesna, who cited the Statute of Limitations based on their long possession and tax payments. The Circuit Court dismissed the claim regarding lands held by Cesna while allowing foreclosure on other lands, prompting an appeal.	The plaintiffs, led by Abigail H. Mason, contended that the second mortgage held by Mason should be foreclosed on the lands in question. They argued that the previous foreclosure involving Sherman was improper as it did not include Mason as a party, thereby allowing them to pursue their claim against the lands.	The defendants, including Sherman and Stephen Cesna, asserted that the Statute of Limitations barred the foreclosure of Mason's junior mortgage due to their continuous possession of the property for over seven years coupled with the payment of taxes. They argued that Sherman's possession established color of title, and therefore, Mason had no grounds to foreclose on the lands since they were effectively held free of the junior mortgage.

The case of Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Jacob Frazier took place in Marion County, Illinois, in the latter part of September 1871. The key individuals involved were Jacob Frazier, the plaintiff, and the Illinois Central Railroad Company, the defendant. The incident at the center of the case involved a fire that escaped from the railroad's engine. The fire ignited a significant amount of dry grass and weeds situated along the railroad's right of way, which subsequently spread to the plaintiff's meadow and grounds, resulting in the destruction of his hay, rails, and hedge. Frazier argued that the railroad company had been negligent in allowing combustible materials to accumulate on its property, thereby causing the fire that damaged his property.	Jacob Frazier claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent for failing to clear dry grass and weeds from its right of way, which contributed to the fire that caused damage to his property. He sought compensation for the losses incurred due to the destruction of his hay, rails, and hedge as a result of the fire.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company argued that it had employed proper mechanical appliances to prevent the escape of fire from its engines. They contended that the presence of dry grass and weeds on their property, while acknowledged, did not constitute negligence as there were circumstances that might mitigate their liability. The company asserted that the plaintiff also bore some responsibility for the condition of his own land, suggesting that the fire's spread was at least partly due to Frazier's negligence regarding his property.

Henry Bradford, the Plaintiff in Error, filed a lawsuit against the City of Chicago, the Defendant in Error, in May 1860. The case stemmed from a payment of eighty-two dollars and eighty cents made by Bradford under a city assessment related to the proposed opening and extension of South LaSalle Street from Madison Street to Jackson Street. The ambivalence around the assessment arose from its invalidity, characterized by a lack of necessary marks signifying the amounts assessed. The Circuit Court had initially ruled in favor of the city on the ground that the assessment was not sufficiently clear to warrant a refund. Bradford argued that the street had not been opened and that the city was thus liable for the repayment. The litigation focused on whether the assessment was void and what constituted adequate reasons for Bradford to recover his payment.	The plaintiff claimed that the assessment was void due to a lack of clarity in its figures and that the city had failed to proceed with the street improvement resulting in an inability to collect the benefits outlined in the assessment. Bradford sought to recover the amount paid, asserting that the payment was compulsory due to the threat of legal actions against his property for non-payment.	The defendant city argued that the assessment, although flawed, still stood, and that the plaintiff had not provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the city had abandoned the project or that the assessment was completely invalid. The city contended that there was no legal basis for refunding the money because improvements had not been officially abandoned. Moreover, they stated that the assessment served as a trustee fund for potential benefits to property owners involved.

Thomas Leachman v. Michael Dougherty took place in the town of Ursa, Adams County, Illinois, in the year 1874. Thomas Leachman served as the town clerk and also held the position of town collector. On September 1, 1874, the town's commissioners of highways prepared a written statement indicating that a total of $1,200 was needed for road and bridge purposes for the upcoming year. However, Leachman failed to present this statement to the town supervisor or to the board of supervisors during their September meeting. Consequently, no tax was levied for the proposed amount. On October 30, 1874, Leachman, as town clerk, certified that the commissioners had assessed the $1,200 tax and filed this certificate with the county clerk. Relying on this certification, the county clerk improperly extended the tax against the property in the town, which then led Leachman to distrain the property of Michael Dougherty, the appellee, for the unpaid tax. The core of the dispute centered on the legality of the tax levy and collection as the board of supervisors did not take the required action to authorize the tax.	Leachman, as the plaintiff, argued that the taxes collected from Dougherty were based on an illegal extension of a tax that lacked valid authorization from the board of supervisors. He claimed that the tax was improperly imposed since the necessary statutory procedures were not followed. Leachman's legal requests included the reversal of the tax collection and the assertion that the county clerk did not have the authority to extend the tax without the required board action.	Dougherty, the defendant, contended that Leachman's conduct as the collector was unlawful since he executed a tax collection based on a warrant that lacked valid jurisdictional backing. He argued that the tax was extended unlawfully, and hence, Leachman should not be protected by the collector's warrant even if it appeared regular on its face. Dougherty requested that the court recognize the illegal collection and affirm that he was not liable for the wrongful tax imposition.

The case "The State National Bank v. James Reilly" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 9, 1888. It involved a dispute between James Reilly, the plaintiff, and the State National Bank, the defendant. The case arose from the presentation of a check for $221.17 that was drawn by the clerk of the United States District Court for the Southern District of Illinois, signed by a judge, and issued to Reilly for a dividend from a bankrupt estate. The funds involved were deposited by the court's clerks into the defendant bank, which had been designated as the depository for these funds. The conflict stemmed from the bank's refusal to honor the check, arguing that it had already paid out all funds related to the bankruptcy estate referenced in the check. The court's examination focused on the bank's compliance with relevant laws and its obligations regarding trust funds deposited by the court, ultimately concluding that the bank did not misappropriate the funds and was not liable for any deficit.	The plaintiff, James Reilly, argued that the State National Bank was obliged to pay him the amount of the check, as it represented a legal order from the court for a dividend due from a bankrupt estate. He contended that the bank had knowledge of the nature of the funds and thus was responsible for ensuring payment according to the instructions provided in the check, which detailed the relevant case.	The defendant, State National Bank, claimed that it had properly handled the deposits as per the relevant act of Congress and rules of bankruptcy, maintaining the account as a unit for the court. The bank argued that it had already disbursed all available funds by paying checks that had been properly drawn. Thus, it contended that it was not liable to pay the check presented by the plaintiff, as the funds attributed to that specific bankruptcy case were already exhausted.

This case, "Butler & McCracken v. Ella Gain," was decided on April 5, 1889, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in East St. Louis, Illinois, involving the lumber merchants Butler & McCracken as plaintiffs against Ella Gain, the property owner, and Benjamin Summers, the original contractor. In August 1887, Summers contracted to build a house for Gain for $685, which was to be completed within 45 days. By October 11, 1887, the house was completed, and Gain had already paid Summers $500 without obtaining a sworn statement from him detailing any subcontractors or materials provided, as required by law. Summers had subcontracted Butler & McCracken for lumber worth $286.42, of which only $85 had been paid, leaving a balance of $201.42 owed to them. Butler & McCracken filed a mechanic's lien notice against Gain's property on November 2, 1887, within four months after the last payment to Summers. However, Gain appealed after the initial decree to enforce the mechanic's lien was reversed by the Appellate Court for lack of equity, leading to the present case.	Butler & McCracken's main argument centered around their entitlement to a mechanic's lien for the unpaid balance of $201.42 for materials furnished to Summers for the construction of Gain's house. They contended that Gain had violated the statutory requirements by paying Summers without retaining sufficient funds to satisfy their lien, as they had properly notified Gain of their claim within the necessary timeframe after the work was completed.	Ella Gain defended herself by asserting that she had no prior notice of Butler & McCracken's claim to the lien. The court found that Gain was justified in not demanding a sworn statement from Summers, as she had not been made aware of any subcontractors or materialmen entitled to payments. Gain argued that since the required notice under the applicable statutes had not been served within the specified 40 days, she was free to pay the contractor without liability to the claimants.

The case "John A. Owen et al. v. The City of Chicago" took place in September 1869, in Chicago, Illinois. The case stemmed from a special assessment for the opening or extending of West Adams Street. The assessment involved notices issued concerning the proposed extension of the street from its then western terminus, which the public and the parties understood to be at Leavitt Street. Evidence indicated that at the time of the proceedings, West Adams Street was already an open and traveled street as far west as Leavitt Street, with sidewalks built and properties sold adjacent to it. However, the assessment included claims for damages for land associated with Adams Street located east of this point. The plaintiffs argued that the actions taken by the city in opening the street east of Leavitt Street were not authorized by the notice given, which only addressed extensions westward. It was noted that the assessment was also deemed to be inequitable and grossly unequal.	The plaintiffs, John A. Owen et al., claimed that the notices regarding the special assessment for the street extension were misleading and did not authorize the city’s actions to open or extend Adams Street beyond the actual western terminus at Leavitt Street. They contended that the assessment included damages for property east of that terminus, which was outside the scope of the notification, leading to an inequitable distribution of costs.	The City of Chicago, represented by its counsel, maintained that the assessment was valid and proper within the legal framework governing street openings and extensions. They argued that regardless of the terminus's understanding, the law allowed them to assess damages incurred as a part of the opening process. They contended that there was a legal right to extend the street based on the ongoing public usage and prior actions regarding the street.

The case of Matthew McElheny v. Sarah E. Musick; Same v. James Musick was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1872. The dispute arose in Logan County, Illinois, involving the children of James Musick, who were represented by their guardian, Matthew McElheny. The children sought to compel McElheny to account for the rental income of a 160-acre farm inherited from their deceased father, who passed away in 1853. The guardian had leased the farm to John Thomas, initially for nine years in 1856, at a rate that the plaintiffs believed was below the market value. The farm's management began with the first guardian, Henry Musick, who secured a lease with Thomas that lacked provisions for tenant repairs. After Henry Musick ceased being the guardian, McElheny took over and entered into a new lease agreement with Thomas, intending to maintain the property for the children's future benefit. During the proceeding, testimony revealed conflicting opinions on the appropriate rental rate, with evidence showing that the guardian acted in good faith and followed proper procedures, including court approvals. Despite acknowledging that a higher rental price may have been possible, the guardian prioritized the long-term health and preservation of the estate.	The plaintiffs, representing the children of James Musick, claimed that their guardian, Matthew McElheny, failed to secure the maximum rental value for their inherited farm. They contended that the leasing terms negotiated with John Thomas were insufficient and that the guardian should account for the difference in potential rental income, arguing that McElheny’s decisions constituted mismanagement of the estate.	The defendant, Matthew McElheny, defended his actions by asserting that he acted in good faith and prioritized the welfare of the children over immediate financial gain. He argued that the rentals he secured were reasonable considering the long-term upkeep and preservation of the farm's condition. McElheny highlighted that he had obtained approval from the probate court for the lease and emphasized the importance of securing a reliable tenant for a longer term, despite the potential for higher rents in the short term with less responsible tenants.

Franklin Hadaway initiated a legal case against Zepheniah Kelly, which took place in September 1875 in Whiteside County, Illinois. During the proceedings in the circuit court, both parties agreed to resolve their disputes through arbitration. The chosen arbitrators conducted a hearing where evidence was presented, and subsequently issued a written award. Hadaway, the appellant, sought to have this award overturned, claiming it was obtained through improper means and alleging misconduct by the arbitrators as well as by Kelly, the appellee. However, the circuit court rejected his motion to set aside the award and ruled in favor of Kelly, upholding the arbitrators' decision. The court's judgment was based on the failure to find any evidence that undue means were used or that there was any misbehavior by the arbitrators during the arbitration process.	Franklin Hadaway contended that the arbitration award in favor of Zepheniah Kelly should be annulled. He argued that the award was procured through undue means and that the arbitrators acted improperly. Hadaway maintained that certain items in his account, which he believed were clearly established in his favor, were unjustly excluded by the arbitrators. His legal requests revolved around the motion to set aside the award and to have the court consider the merits of those excluded claims.	Zepheniah Kelly, the appellee, defended the arbitration award by asserting that there was no evidence of undue means or any wrongful actions by the arbitrators. Kelly contended that the law presumes arbitrators consider all evidence presented and that their decisions must be respected unless proven fraudulent. The defense maintained that the arbitrators’ findings were conclusive and that Hadaway’s objections did not provide just cause for the award to be overturned.

In the year 1875, in Saline County, Illinois, Hezekiah G. Mason and Willard Mason filed a lawsuit against the City of Shawneetown and its officers. The case stemmed from the city's issuance of levee bonds to fund the construction of a levee intended to protect the city from flooding caused by the Ohio and Wabash rivers. The plaintiffs sought to prevent the city from imposing taxes to pay the interest and principal of these bonds, claiming that the city had exceeded its legal debt limit when issuing them. The case was initially heard in the circuit court of Gallatin County but was moved to Saline County. After evaluating the evidence, the lower court dismissed the plaintiffs' complaint and ruled in favor of the city, leading the plaintiffs to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the City of Shawneetown had violated the constitutional debt limit by issuing levee bonds that exceeded the permissible amount. They argued that the total indebtedness of the city, including these bonds, should not exceed 5% of the value of its taxable property. They requested that the court enjoin the city and its officers from levying any taxes for the payment of interest on or principal of the bonds.	The defendant, the City of Shawneetown, contended that its issuance of the levee bonds was lawful and in accordance with the municipal charter, which allowed it to issue such bonds without requiring a prior vote from the citizens. The city argued that the ordinance under which the bonds were issued was valid and reflected the will of the people, as an election had already taken place with a majority voting in favor of the bond issuance. The city sought to affirm its authority to collect taxes for the payment of the bonds and claimed damages incurred from the wrongful injunction.

Charles D. Hauk, involved in the gas business and serving as secretary of the Bloomington Gas Company, initiated negotiations around September 13, 1883, with Wm. J. Brownell and John E. Pollock, among others, to establish gas works in Springfield, Illinois, using the Lowe Patent Gas Process. Hauk indicated it was necessary to purchase a license for manufacturing gas under the patent, claiming he could procure it for $7,000. After securing the interest of Brownell and Pollock, Hauk represented that he had purchased the license and paid for it in full. They bought a one-fifth interest in the patent from him for $1,400. However, Hauk's representation was false; he acquired the license for both Springfield and Peoria for only $2,500 in cash and $7,500 in stock, far less than the amount he claimed. The gas company was never formed, leading Brownell and Pollock to sue Hauk for the amount they paid. The circuit court awarded them $1,542.10, which included the principal amount and interest.	The plaintiffs, Wm. J. Brownell and John E. Pollock, argued that Hauk fraudulently misrepresented the price he paid for the license to manufacture gas. They asserted that this deceit induced them to invest $1,400 into an enterprise that ultimately failed and sought the return of their money based on the fraudulent misrepresentation and the fiduciary nature of their relationship with Hauk.	Hauk contested the claim by suggesting that even if his representations were misleading regarding the license price, it did not provide a basis for recovery since it was merely a misstatement about the selling price. He further claimed that the plaintiffs should not recover without returning any purchased interest in the license, as they could not rescind the contract unilaterally without reconveying any rights attained.

The case titled "The Chicago and Northwestern Railway Co. v. John Button et ux." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873. The incident occurred while John and Elizabeth Button were traveling on the Chicago and Northwestern Railway from Chicago to Sterling, Illinois. During the alighting process at their destination, the train suddenly started moving, resulting in Elizabeth Button being violently thrown and sustaining significant injuries to her spine. The couple brought the case against the railway company to recover damages for the personal injuries Elizabeth suffered. They claimed that the railway company had a duty to allow them a reasonable time to disembark safely, which it failed to do. The lower court ruled in favor of the Buttons, awarding them $325 and costs, prompting the railway company to file a writ of error challenging the judgment.	The plaintiffs, John and Elizabeth Button, claimed that the Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company was negligent in its duty to safely transport them, particularly during the disembarking process. They argued that the sudden movement of the train while they were attempting to exit led to Elizabeth Button’s severe physical injuries. Their legal request was for compensation for the personal injury sustained, resulting in the lower court jury awarding them a judgment of $325 against the airline.	The defendant, Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company, contended that the lawsuit was improperly initiated because the husband, John Button, was included as a party when, under Illinois law, personal injury claims for a wife's injuries should be brought solely by the wife. The railway company's defense involved questioning the admissibility and credibility of certain verbal admissions as evidence, arguing that they should be treated with caution due to their inherent uncertainties.

On September 30, 1858, in Ogle County, Illinois, A. B. Fuller was incarcerated under an indictment for passing counterfeit money. On September 13, 1858, Fuller and Henry A. Mix appeared before Judge J. Y. Eustice of the 22nd Circuit and executed a recognizance, acknowledging a debt of $500 to the People of the State of Illinois. This recognizance required Fuller to appear in court on the first day of the next term to respond to his indictment. After being called to court on October 4, 1858, Fuller defaulted, leading to the forfeiture of the recognizance. The case involved various pleas regarding the validity and circumstances of the recognizance, including claims that Fuller was unlawfully imprisoned and that he was not present in the correct jurisdiction at the time of the recognizance signing. Ultimately, the trial jury found against Mix, ruling in favor of the People for the amount due on the recognizance, which led to the appeal by Mix challenging the court’s procedural decisions.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, argued that the recognizance executed by Mix was valid and enforceable, as Fuller had failed to appear in court as required, thus justifying the forfeiture of the recognizance and the claim for the $500. The People contended that the court had jurisdiction over Mix and that the conditions of the recognizance had been breached on Fuller's part.	Henry A. Mix, the appellant, raised several defenses, including claims that the recognizance should be quashed since there was no judgment of forfeiture against Fuller. He asserted that at the time of the recognizance, Fuller was unlawfully imprisoned in another county without legal authority. Mix also argued that the court erred in sustaining certain demurrers and that the circumstances of Fuller's imprisonment made it impossible for him to comply with the recognizance's terms.

The case, "The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Alexander H. Irvin," was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1874. The dispute arose in Alexander County, Illinois, where the Illinois Central Railroad Company (the plaintiff) sought to prevent the collection of taxes on two boats—namely, a wharf boat and a steamboat—which it claimed as its property. The steamboat was utilized primarily for transporting passengers and freight between Cairo, Illinois, and Columbus, Kentucky, thereby connecting the railroad with other transport systems. The wharf boat was used to transfer freight linked to the railroad. The Circuit Court had previously ruled that the injunction against the tax collection would be made permanent for the wharf boat but dissolved for the steamboat. This ruling led the plaintiff to appeal the decision regarding the steamboat, contesting its taxation status under the provisions of its charter.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company argued that the steamboat should be exempt from taxation based on the 22nd section of its charter, which provides that the company would only be liable for state taxes assessed on its property related to railroad operations. The plaintiff maintained that the steamboat was necessary for its business connectivity and should thus fall under the same exemption as its railroad property.	Alexander H. Irvin, the tax collector (the defendant), contended that the steamboat did not qualify as railroad property under the statute, as it facilitated water transport rather than railroad operations. The defense argued that the charter did not grant authority for the railroad company to engage in waterborne transportation, suggesting that the exemption applied only to property essential for completing and operating the railroad.

The case "Joseph Lighthall v. John Colwell et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1870, arising from a dispute in La Salle County, Illinois. Joseph Lighthall, the plaintiff, entered into a contract with John Colwell, the defendant, to build a house, with a contract price of $620. It was stipulated that a portion of the payment had already been made, amounting to $500, leaving a balance of $120. Lighthall claimed that he fulfilled the contract's terms, providing all necessary materials and completing the house as specified. In response, Colwell contested this assertion, alleging that the construction deviated from the agreement. He asserted multiple defenses, including lack of compliance with the contract norms, the plaintiffs not using specified materials, and issues related to boarding carpenters while building the house. The case was tried before a jury, which ruled in favor of Lighthall. Colwell subsequently appealed, prompting a review by the Illinois Supreme Court, which scrutinized the admissibility of evidence and the interpretations of the agreement.	Joseph Lighthall argued that he adhered to the terms of the contract and completed the construction of the house as agreed upon. He sought to recover the remaining $120 from John Colwell, asserting that he had already provided the materials and labor necessary to fulfill the contractual obligations.	John Colwell defended against the claims by alleging that Lighthall did not complete the house in accordance with the agreed conditions. He raised several defenses, including that the plaintiffs failed to comply with the contract terms, did not use clear siding as specified, and he was entitled to compensation for additional boarding costs for carpenters, which were wrongly excluded from the agreement.

In September 1872, the Illinois Supreme Court considered the case of Juliette E. Hubbard v. Grace J. Rogers, which arose from an unfortunate rental arrangement in Cook County, Illinois. Mrs. Rogers rented a house from Mrs. Hubbard to operate as a boarding house, agreeing to pay an annual rent of $2,000, due monthly on the fifth. To furnish the house, Mrs. Rogers borrowed $400 from Mrs. Hubbard, with the understanding that this would be added to her rental obligations, raising her monthly commitments to $200. The lease began on May 1, 1869, but soon problems arose. Although the first month's rent was paid and the $200 initially paid was considered part of the $400 loan, subsequent rent payments were not made. After missing the June rent and experiencing additional financial difficulties, a compromise occurred where Mrs. Hubbard remitted part of the rent in exchange for a chattel mortgage on the house's furniture for the remaining owed rent. However, Mrs. Rogers failed to pay the installment due in October, leading Mrs. Hubbard to issue a distress warrant, which was successfully replevied by Mrs. Rogers. On November 2 or 3, Mrs. Hubbard sought to seize the furniture on the grounds that rent for November was due, even though the lease specified that no rent was owed until the fifth of the month. Moreover, by that time, Mrs. Hubbard had decided to terminate the tenancy. The court ultimately had to deliberate on the legality of her actions against the background of the lease agreement, financial transactions, and the prior settlement.	The plaintiff, Juliette E. Hubbard, claimed that Mrs. Rogers had defaulted on rental payments, seeking damages for the illegal seizure of her property. She contended that the distress warrant issued for the November rent was unjustified as no rent was due at the time of the seizure, arguing that Mrs. Rogers had also previously secured a chattel mortgage on the furniture for outstanding debts. Mrs. Hubbard sought compensation for the value of the furniture taken without proper justification, emphasizing that her rental rules had clearly outlined the payment structure, and that the tenancy had been terminated prior to the seizure.	The defendant, Grace J. Rogers, contended that the rent for October had not been properly paid and that part of the $400 borrowed at lease execution remained unpaid. She attempted to recoup this amount against the damages incurred from the plaintiff's actions, arguing that the legality of the seizure was questioned since the tenancy had effectively ended and no November rent was due. Mrs. Rogers defended her actions by asserting that the plaintiff's claims were unfounded and were based on incorrect assumptions regarding the lease and the financial dealings between them.

In April 1866, the case of Henry L. Swartwout v. Joseph Evans was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, following previous proceedings at the April Terms in 1864 and 1865. The conflict arose over an alleged conversion of a mowing and reaping machine claimed by the plaintiff, Joseph Evans, as his sole property. The initial trial ruled in favor of the plaintiff, but this judgment was reversed in 1865 on appeal, prompting a retrial. During the retrial, testimony was presented by Joseph Evans, Jr., who recounted a demand made by his father to the defendant, Swartwout, regarding the machine. The demand's specifics—whether it was for the entire machine or just for Evans' share—became a pivotal point of contention between the parties. The court allowed questioning about the nature of the demand despite the defendant’s objection, ultimately focusing on whether the jury's decision was supported by the evidence presented.	The plaintiff, Joseph Evans, asserted that the defendant, Henry L. Swartwout, converted a mowing and reaping machine that belonged to him. Evans claimed that he made a rightful demand for the machine, and contended that Swartwout refused to return it, asserting ownership over the machine. Therefore, Evans sought to recover the machine or damages for its conversion.	The defendant, Henry L. Swartwout, contended that he had purchased the machine and was the rightful owner, having made a claim on it based on a purchase agreement with Evans’ brother. Swartwout objected to the characterization of the demand made by the plaintiff, arguing that it was misleading and improperly led the witness, potentially skewing the jury's understanding of the ownership dispute. His defense focused on discrediting the plaintiff's claim to ownership and the validity of the demand for the machine.

The case "William Whitaker v. James Robinson" took place in LaSalle County, Illinois, with the final judgment delivered in September 1872. The dispute arose from a real estate transaction beginning in 1855 when the land was sold through a contract that required installment payments. The contract allowed the vendor, Robinson, to declare a forfeiture if payments were not made on time. Whitaker became involved in the case through assignments by previous holders of the contract—David Tullís assigned his interest to Julian and Radcliffe, who further assigned it to Whitaker. By 1858, the last payment was due, but it wasn’t paid, prompting Robinson to send a representative to demand payment and tender a deed. However, both Julian and Radcliffe had left the country, and thus the deed could not be tendered as required. Afterwards, Robinson sold the land to Evans, who made improvements before the lawsuit was filed. Whitaker sought specific performance of the original contract or the return of the purchase money, asserting ownership over the land due to his interest in the contract.	Whitaker claimed that he was entitled to specific performance of the original land sale contract. He argued that despite the vendor's attempts to declare a forfeiture due to non-payment, he should have received a deed, and further contended that his delays were justified given the circumstances. In the alternative, he requested the return of the purchase money he had previously paid on the contract if specific performance was denied.	Robinson (the vendor) defended against Whitaker's claims by citing the significant delay of eight years without adequate justification from Whitaker after the last payment was due, which indicated a lack of action on his part. He maintained that he had the right to declare a forfeiture of the contract upon failing to receive payment, and argued that he had done everything within his power to tender the deed, having attempted to locate the original purchasers. Furthermore, Robinson's position emphasized that the statute of limitations could bar any claim for recovery of the purchase money.

The case took place in 1860 in Ottawa, Illinois, involving the City of Ottawa and the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company, represented by George H. Walker. The dispute arose from a sewer construction project ordered by the Ottawa city council, which involved a monetary assessment of $4,200 on certain properties deemed benefited by the improvement. The city council appointed commissioners to assess this amount on the relevant real estate. Notices were published in the local newspaper, informing all interested parties of the assessment process. However, the railroad company claimed that the notice was insufficient for them to address their objections timely. The company did not appeal the assessment initially but later sought an injunction against the city collector to prevent the collection of the assessment by filing a bill in chancery. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendants, sustaining the injunction against the city and making it perpetual, leading the plaintiffs to seek a writ of error to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, The City of Ottawa and George H. Walker, argued that the proceedings for the sewer assessment followed proper legal protocols, and that the defendants had ample opportunity to voice objections concerning the assessment before the city council. They contended that the final decree of the Circuit Court, which perpetuated the injunction against the enforcement of the assessment, was erroneous and sought to have the injunction dissolved so that they could proceed with the collection of the assessment.	The defendant, Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company, asserted that the notice provided regarding the assessment was in accordance with the city's ordinance and contested the validity of the assessment process. They claimed that the plaintiffs failed to file any timely objections to the assessment and denied any wrongdoing. Their defense emphasized that appropriate legal remedies were available for challenging the assessment, negating the need for the issuance of an injunction.

In June 1867, in Marion County, Illinois, Samuel Lester and his wife Ann Lester filed a bill in chancery against William White to compel him to convey a one-fifth interest in a specific tract of land. The dispute arose after White acquired the land from the heirs of John Morgan, who initially filed a claim under the pre-emption clause of the Illinois Central Railroad Act. After White's death, the case proceeded against his heirs. The original circuit court dismissed the bill citing that the testimony of two witnesses for the defendants was valid, despite the plaintiffs’ objections. The plaintiffs contended that these witnesses, who had previously conveyed a deed for the land to White, should not have been competent to testify. The underlying issue was whether the pre-emption right was merely a chattel interest or an interest requiring a written transfer. The court at the circuit level ruled it as a chattel interest, leading to the dismissal of the bill.	The plaintiffs, Samuel and Ann Lester, argued that they were entitled to a conveyance of Ann's one-fifth interest in the disputed land. They claimed that William White had no rightful title to the land because he did not secure a deed from Ann, one of the heirs. They also criticized the admission of certain witness testimonies that supported White's claim, asserting that these witnesses were incompetent due to their vested interests.	The defendant, represented by William White's estate, argued that he had lawful ownership of the land based on the agreement with the other heirs of Morgan and a deed executed by a commissioner under court order. The defense contended that the pre-emption right was a chattel interest that could be transferred without a written agreement. They asserted that the court’s previous decision to dismiss the case was justified based on their interpretations of property rights related to the pre-emption law.

In the case of Elizabeth Hamilton, et al. v. Winthrop C. Gilman, et al., decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1850, the legal proceedings took place in Sangamon County, Illinois. The case involved Elizabeth Hamilton and others as plaintiffs, opposing Winthrop C. Gilman and others as defendants. The plaintiffs filed a bill against the defendants, which included parties some of whom were described as infants. During the proceedings, it was noted that no evidence was presented to support the claims made in the bill. This lack of evidence was a significant aspect of the case, as it directly impacted the court's ability to enter a decree.	The plaintiffs argued for a decree against the defendants, alleging that the actions or conditions necessitated legal intervention. Their case was based on a bill which sought relief, but it was clear that they intended to establish a legal basis for their claims against the defendants, including the minor parties involved.	The defendants contended that no decree could be issued against infant parties without sufficient proof to support the claims made by the plaintiffs. They emphasized the lack of evidence presented in court, which was critical in their defense against the allegations.

The case "Peter V. Lowe v. Henry Ravens" took place in Illinois, with the final judgment rendered on December 11, 1886. The dispute arose from a contractual agreement wherein Peter V. Lowe, the plaintiff, was to furnish materials and construct a house and barn for the defendant, Henry Ravens, for a total payment of $3,000. Lowe claimed that extra materials and work were required beyond the original contract's scope, which he argued entitled him to an additional payment. Ravens, in response, filed several defenses, including a claim that Lowe breached the contract by providing substandard materials and workmanship. He maintained that no additional work or materials were provided beyond those stipulated in the contract. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court after being initially litigated in the Circuit Court of Kankakee County, where Judge Alfred Sample presided.	Peter V. Lowe argued that he was owed payment for extra materials and work he provided under the contract to build a house and barn for Henry Ravens. He sought to recover the outstanding balance that he claimed was due to him, totaling $3,000. Lowe maintained that the quality of the work and materials provided met acceptable standards and that Ravens' defenses lacked merit.	Henry Ravens countered Lowe's claims by asserting a breach of contract on Lowe's part, arguing that he provided poor quality materials and workmanship. Ravens denied that any extra materials or services were given beyond the initial agreement, contending that Lowe was not entitled to additional compensation. Thus, Ravens maintained that he owed nothing further to Lowe under the terms of their contract.

The case, titled "The Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company v. Warren W. Whipple," originated when Warren W. Whipple filed a lawsuit against the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company in November 1853 in La Salle County, Illinois. The claim was for $71.20, regarding cattle that Whipple alleged were killed by the railroad, which he claimed was responsible due to trespass. Whipple's claim was resolved in his favor by Justice of the Peace N. Duncan, who ruled on the matter without the company's representatives appearing at the trial. The railroad company argued that they weren't in operation at the time of the incident and that the road was being managed by contractors. A writ of certiorari was filed by the railroad company in December 1856 to review this judgment after they claimed they were improperly served in the original suit, citing that the process was not legally executed. The case was ultimately transferred to Peoria County for proceedings.	The plaintiff, Warren W. Whipple, claimed that the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company was responsible for the death of his cattle, alleging that the company had trespassed on his property. Whipple contended that the railroad company should be held liable despite any operational claims they made regarding contractors managing the railroad. He filed a petition for a writ of certiorari to review the justice's judgment in his favor, arguing that the judgment rendered by the lower court was justified and sought confirmation of this decision.	The defendant, Chicago and Rock Island Railroad Company, contended that they were not responsible for the alleged injuries as they were not operating the railroad at the time; the construction and management were conducted by independent contractors. They argued that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction over the case and that there was insufficient evidence of proper service of process. Furthermore, they sought to quash the writ of certiorari, asserting that the initial judgment was correct, and that the evidence needed to appeal based on jurisdictional errors was improperly excluded by the court.

In January 1875, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with a foreclosure case involving a mortgage on a quarter section of land in Livingston County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were William Sheer, Philip H. Tompkins, Ártemus O. Sheer (the plaintiffs), Timothy Hall, Francis M. Hall, C. E. Hall, and Laura Templeton (the defendants). The land originally belonged to Martha Wilson, who sold it to Laura Templeton in 1867 with her husband’s consent, although he did not sign the deed. Templeton then mortgaged the property to secure payment for the land, and eventually sold it to Timothy Hall, who assumed responsibility for the mortgage. The controversy arose when Timothy Hall contested the validity of the original conveyance, arguing that the deed from Wilson conveyed no valid title after her later marriage. The case was complicated further by a second mortgage held by Templeton, leading to a dispute between the parties over rightful ownership and obligations under the mortgages. The evidence showed that although the property value was significant, lapses in title documentation created legal issues regarding the respective claims.	The plaintiffs, led by Sheer and Tompkins, sought to foreclose the mortgage held against the property, arguing that valid mortgages were executed and assigned properly. They claimed that the original conveyance from Martha Wilson to Laura Templeton, despite the lack of her husband’s signature, was legally sufficient for the transfer of interest, and that the subsequent dealings of Timothy Hall did not invalidate the mortgage obligations. They requested the court to enforce the foreclosure and allow the sale of the property to satisfy the mortgage debts.	The defendants, particularly Timothy Hall, contended that the original deed from Martha Wilson was invalid and did not legally transfer title to Laura Templeton. Hall based his defense on the assertion that the lack of his wife’s husband's signature rendered the deed ineffective, and therefore, he had no legal obligation to pay the mortgages. He also sought to establish that the legal title passed to him through a subsequent quitclaim deed from Wilson, asserting that this conveyed ownership and negated the earlier mortgage claims.

In 1867, in Cook County, Illinois, Daniel Bunker, Jr. initiated a legal action against Joseph H. Green, following the sale of a stock in trade by B. F. Green and Thomas M. Ackerly to Joseph H. Green. Bunker claimed that the sale was executed with the intent to hinder, delay, and defraud creditors, as Green and Ackerly owed him money. A writ of attachment was placed on the goods sold to Joseph H. Green, leading to a trial where the jury ruled in favor of Bunker, awarding him $828 in damages. The case was subsequently appealed on several grounds, including procedural objections regarding the absence of replications to the pleas of justification and issues surrounding the judgment entered after the plaintiff's death, which occurred during the pendency of the new trial motion.	Daniel Bunker, Jr. contended that the sale of goods to Joseph H. Green by Green & Ackerly was fraudulent and intended to evade creditor claims. He sought compensation for damages resulting from the wrongful attachment and argued that the trial should have considered the relevant procedural merits during the trial phase, asserting his rights as a creditor.	Joseph H. Green and his co-defendants argued that the trial proceeded without necessary legal issues being joined, thereby waiving any procedural errors they later claimed. They also claimed that the entry of judgment after Bunker’s death and prior to the jury verdict date was improper. Additionally, they maintained that certain evidence should have been admitted to support their defense regarding the sale.

The case "Charles S. French v. Julius Willer" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 15, 1888. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, where Charles S. French (the appellant) filed a forcible detainer suit against Julius Willer (the appellee). French claimed entitlement to possession of certain premises in Cook County that Willer was unlawfully occupying after the expiration of a lease from the Connecticut Mutual Life Insurance Company. The lease contained provisions requiring Willer to surrender possession upon its expiration and included a warrant of attorney permitting immediate judgment for possession if Willer defaulted. After French's complaint and supporting affidavit were filed, the court granted a judgment for possession in favor of French and issued a writ of restitution. Willer subsequently motioned to quash the writ and vacate the judgment, which was denied. Upon appeal, the Appellate Court reversed the judgment and recognized the case as significant enough for review by the Supreme Court of Illinois.	Charles S. French, the plaintiff, argued that he was the rightful possessor of the property and that Julius Willer unlawfully withheld possession after the lease had expired. French relied on the terms of the lease that mandated Willer to surrender possession and included a warrant of attorney that allowed for a confession of judgment for possession without the need for service of process.	Julius Willer contended that the court had no jurisdiction over him because the entry of judgment was based on a warrant of attorney in a forcible detainer action, which he argued was not permitted under the common law. Willer asserted that the procedural requirements prescribed by the statute were not followed, making any judgment entered against him invalid and void.

Caroline Lenfers and her husband, Henry Lenfers, filed a case against Anna C. Henke in September 1874 in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The dispute arose over the assignment of dower rights in mineral lands where both parties had ownership interests. Caroline Lenfers owned one-third of the land, while Anna Henke held the remaining two-thirds. The situation was complicated by an agreement made between Caroline and her daughter, Mary Louisa Camphouse (Henke's mother), that the mineral rents from the land would be divided equally. After the discovery of valuable lead mines on the property, which were opened after the husband’s death, complications arose when the rents were not divided as agreed. The defendants, which included Anna Henke and her guardian, contested the claim, leading to legal action. The court was tasked with determining whether the agreement constituted a valid assignment of dower and whether Caroline Lenfers had the right to receive a portion of the mineral rents.	The plaintiffs, Caroline Lenfers and her husband, argued that the agreement between Caroline and her deceased daughter's husband constituted a valid assignment of dower rights to the mineral rents generated by the opened mines. They asserted that regardless of the agreement's written form, its validity should be recognized, and they sought the court's declaration that the terms of the agreement still applied after the husband's death. If the court found the agreement void, the plaintiffs requested that dower be assigned to Caroline based on her rightful share of the mineral rents.	The defendants, Anna C. Henke and her guardian, denied that the plaintiffs had any rightful claim to dower over the opened mines, asserting that the agreement was null and void, likely due to lack of formalization in writing. They contended that at common law, dower rights could not be claimed from mines that had not been worked during the husband’s lifetime, and thus, the claims of the plaintiffs regarding the division of mineral rents were unfounded.

In November 1860, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the case of James M. Warren versus John McCarthy et al., administrators of the deceased Payton White. The case arose from a previous decree by the Mason Circuit Court in Kentucky, which found Warren indebted to Payton White for the sum of $1,503.96, awarded on October 26, 1853. The plaintiff, Warren, claimed that the defendants were responsible for enforcing this decree. However, Warren contended that the court lacked jurisdiction to issue the second decree, as he argued he was not properly served with notice or process and had not entered an appearance in the proceedings. This legal contention stemmed from events that began in 1846 when a decree was made in favor of Payton White against Warren for $1,182.96. After the subsequent decree in 1853, Warren, who had been residing in Illinois since 1846, sought to contest the validity of the later decree on the grounds that it was based on a lack of jurisdiction.	James M. Warren claimed that the second decree from the Mason Circuit Court was void due to lack of jurisdiction, as he had not been served with process or given notice of the proceedings. He argued that the initial decree from 1846 was final and conclusive, and that no new jurisdiction was established for the 1853 decree. Warren sought to recover the amount due under that decree, asserting that the second decree could not be legally enforced against him.	The defendants contended that the subsequent decree in 1853 was valid and binding, and that it was issued after proper proceedings had taken place. They argued that the 1846 decree was merely interlocutory and did not prevent the issuance of the later decree. The defendants maintained that they were entitled to enforce the second decree and sought to overrule Warren’s claim based on the supposed nullity of the earlier decree.

In 1876, in West Chicago, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving Martin Andrews and The People ex rel. Julian S. Rumsey (the county treasurer). The case centered on a circuit court judgment ordering the sale of Andrews's lands due to delinquent special assessments levied for park purposes and unpaid state and county taxes. The judgment stemmed from previous rulings made by the county court. A key issue was whether the special assessment for the parks and boulevards exceeded the legal limits established by the statute. Andrews argued that the cost of the improvements included an inflated measure of damages, as he contended the net damages should've been assessed instead. He also claimed the supplemental act concerning the park assessments was void because it lacked a public vote. The court was urged to dismiss the assessment due to alleged issues of fairness and legality, including a lack of benefit to the property and inadequate notice procedures regarding the assessment.	Andrews claimed that the special assessments imposed for the park improvements were illegal because the total costs exceeded the statutory limit. He argued that the net damages should be used as the basis for assessment and asserted that the park tax improperly overlapped with an assessment meant for another town. Additionally, he contended that the supplemental act governing the assessments was void, as it was not ratified by a public vote, and disputed the judgment by claiming the assessment did not reflect the actual benefit to his property.	The defense, represented by Julian S. Rumsey, contended that the special assessments were valid and had been appropriately confirmed by prior judgments. They argued that the reassessment disputes presented by Andrews could not be raised in this proceeding, as those judgments were final. The defense maintained that the park improvements were legally justified and that the notice provided for the assessment complied with the statutory requirements. They asserted that previous court decisions had ruled in favor of similar positions, rendering Andrews's complaints unfounded.

In December 1841, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between William Troy and Owen Reilley. Reilley initiated an action of assumpsit against Troy, claiming he had sold goods to Troy and sought recovery for the owed amount. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Reilley, leading Troy to file for a new trial on the grounds of newly discovered evidence, specifically citing lost affidavits that he believed supported his case. The Circuit Court denied this motion, prompting Troy to appeal. During the appeal, it was noted that the affidavit on which Troy's motion was based was not included in the record, and the court clerk certified it as lost. Troy attempted to remedy this by submitting a new affidavit detailing the lost document's contents and requesting permission to file it nunc pro tunc, but this request was also denied. Multiple errors were assigned by Troy regarding the denial of his motions and the absence of the original affidavit.	The plaintiff, Owen Reilley, claimed that William Troy owed him payment for goods that had been sold and delivered. Reilley successfully secured a judgment in the lower court. Troy's subsequent claims for a new trial relied on an assertion of newly discovered evidence, specifically the lost affidavits, and argued that the denial of his motions constituted a significant error that warranted a reevaluation of the case.	William Troy, as the defendant, contended that the Circuit Court erred in denying his motions for a new trial based on newly discovered evidence, specifically the loss of his original affidavit. He argued that without the affidavit, the Supreme Court could not ascertain whether a new trial was justified. Additionally, Troy asserted that the court should have allowed him to file the newly reconstructed affidavits, claiming that both the loss of the original and the submission of copies needed to be recognized as valid reasons for his appeal.

In 1871, in Mason County, Illinois, a legal proceeding was initiated involving Hattie Williams and other petitioners against Daniel Martz and several others. The petitioners sought to permanently establish the corners and boundaries of certain lands due to disputes and claims of lost or destroyed markers. The circuit court, led by Judge Charles Turner, appointed a group of commissioners, including John R. Faulkner, Francis P. Powell, and James Boggs, to survey the lands and resolve the boundary issues. The commissioners submitted a report with a new survey plat. Appellants (Martz and others) filed objections to the report, asserting that it was erroneous and did not adhere to the original government survey specifications. The circuit court approved the report and established the disputed boundaries, which prompted the appellants to appeal the decision, arguing that the commissioners exceeded their powers.	The plaintiffs, led by Hattie Williams, claimed that the commissioners successfully re-established the lost corners and boundaries in accordance with the law. They sought court approval of the commissioners' report and the establishment of lines that would reflect the true and original government survey of the land.	The defendants, represented by Daniel Martz and others, argued that the commissioners did not properly follow the legal requirements established in the 1869 act for re-establishing the original corners and boundaries. They contended that the survey made by the commissioners was flawed and overstepped their authority by attempting to create new corner markers instead of restoring the original ones.

The case of James H. Gudgell v. Elias Pettigrew et al. took place in Illinois during the early 1860s after a partnership dispute arose among Gudgell and Pettigrew. The partnership, established on March 24, 1856, was structured so that both parties shared profits and losses equally, with Gudgell initially contributing $900, while Pettigrew invested $1,482.96. Over time, additional partners joined, and complications regarding debts and asset collections emerged. When Gudgell exited the partnership, he left significant debts owed to Pettigrew’s businesses. The relationship soured as Gudgell allegedly withheld financial records and did not account for the firm’s debts, prompting Pettigrew to seek court intervention. The matter escalated to arbitration, where decisions about outstanding debts, collections, and financial responsibilities were made. The arbitrators determined the amounts Gudgell owed Pettigrew and initiated the appointments of a receiver to manage collections and distributions related to the partnership’s finances.	The plaintiffs, led by Pettigrew, alleged that Gudgell misappropriated funds and failed to account for significant collections made on behalf of the partnership. They sought the appointment of a receiver to manage the partnership's assets, payment of outstanding debts, and a decree for financial restitution for what Gudgell owed. The plaintiffs argued for clarity in the distribution of collected assets and a cancellation of any improper transactions made during the partnership, ultimately requesting a formal accounting to ensure fair resolutions for the debts.	Gudgell, the defendant, contended that the arbitrators exceeded their authority and that the award they issued was neither clear nor final. He argued that the financial responsibilities and judgments against him were assumed under unclear circumstances. Gudgell maintained that the requests for payment were unjustified and that the distributions mandated by the court did not accurately reflect the partnerships' financial arrangements. He further asserted that the award should not have been confirmed by the court, underscoring that he had not consented to the specifics determined by the arbitrators and that his financial obligations were not properly accounted for.

In the case of Thomas W. Purcell v. Alfred Parks, heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1876, the dispute stemmed from Purcell's role as county clerk of Marion County. He was elected during the November 1873 election, commencing his term on the first Monday of December 1873. At that time, the county board did not set his compensation. A new law had been enacted on March 29, 1872, which required a fixed compensation subject to certain limits, as outlined in the state constitution adopted in 1870. It was not until March 1874 that the county board established a salary of $1,000 per year for Purcell, retroactive to the start of his term, despite his objections. The county treasurer subsequently filed a suit on behalf of the county to recover a balance of $1,060.61, arguing that Purcell had received fees exceeding the salary set by the board without proper authority, given that his compensation had not been fixed prior to his term start. The case focused on whether the county clerk could collect and keep fees until a compensation was duly established by the county board.	The plaintiff, Alfred Parks, claimed that Purcell, the defendant and county clerk, had wrongfully appropriated fees exceeding his established salary of $1,000 as set by the county board after his term had commenced. Parks requested a recovery of the exceeding fees, totaling $1,060.61, asserting that Purcell had no legal claim to those additional fees in the absence of a predetermined compensation prior to the start of his term.	Purcell contended that as the county clerk, he was entitled to collect and retain all fees from his office until the county board formally fixed his compensation. He argued that since the board had failed to act before his election, he was within his rights to keep the fees he received as compensation for his services. He claimed that the board's action to set compensation after his term began constituted an illegal retroactive change in compensation.

In December 1850, the case of Thomas Hollowbush et al. v. Murray McConnel was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in the Morgan Circuit Court concerning the ownership and redemption of mortgaged premises, which included a ferry. The case had previously been remanded to ascertain the value of rents and profits related to the property. The plaintiff, McConnel, sought to redeem the mortgaged premises after a prior decree had been reversed, which initially allowed the property to be sold. Hollowbush, claiming possession since 1845, contended that the ferry was not part of the mortgaged premises and that McConnel had no right to claim rents and profits during their possession. The matter had been contested in earlier courts, and by 1850 the Circuit Court ruled in favor of McConnel's right to redeem, leading to an appeal from Hollowbush to the Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Murray McConnel, argued that he had the right to redeem the mortgaged premises before the predetermined sale date. McConnel contended that he should be credited the value of rents and profits accrued from the Naples ferry while Hollowbush held possession after purchasing the mortgage. He requested the court to affirm his rights based on facts that emerged after the previous decree and highlighted that he was entitled to an accounting of these rents and profits based on prior court decisions.	The defendants, Thomas Hollowbush et al., claimed that the Circuit Court erred in allowing McConnel to redeem the premises and in charging them for the rents and profits from the Naples ferry. They argued that the ferry should not be considered part of the mortgaged premises and that McConnel's entitlements were unfounded and should not have been permitted. They requested the court to reconsider their charges and maintain the original decision that favored them.

In September 1868, the case of John O’Brien v. Henry Palmer was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from an action of assumpsit initiated by Henry Palmer against John O’Brien concerning the purchase price of a property known as "Palmer’s Great Western Circus," which Palmer had sold to O’Brien. The case was tried in the Superior Court of the City of Chicago, where the jury found in favor of Palmer. O’Brien appealed the judgment, citing errors related to jury instructions and the rejection of a motion for a new trial, arguing that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence. A significant point of contention was whether O’Brien was required to return five promissory notes that Palmer had previously executed in favor of O’Brien as part of a prior transaction involving the circus property. The jury assessed Palmer’s damages at $4,396.65 and stated that he was entitled to possession of the five notes. However, the court ultimately rejected the latter component of the jury's verdict as surplusage, choosing to only enter judgment for the monetary award.	The plaintiff, Henry Palmer, argued that he was owed a sum of $4,396.65 for the sale of the circus property to the defendant, John O’Brien, and that the defendant had failed to fulfill the terms of their agreement. Palmer claimed that despite having previously sold the circus to O’Brien and receiving promissory notes in return, O’Brien's refusal to return the notes constituted a breach of contract. Palmer sought the verdict to be upheld and the damages awarded.	John O’Brien, the defendant, contended that the jury’s verdict should be set aside on several grounds, notably that the jury had received misleading instructions and that the verdict contradicted substantial evidence presented during the trial. O’Brien claimed that he had already fulfilled the payment obligations outlined in the contract and that the notes he retained were part of the consideration in their transactions. He sought to have the jury's decision overturned and for a new trial to be granted.

On April 7, 1875, at approximately 10 A.M., a collision occurred at a railroad crossing between a passenger train of the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company and a team with a wagon driven by Robert Damerell, an acquaintance of the area. The incident took place at a crossing of a public highway located one and a half miles south of West Point, Illinois. The train was traveling south and, due to the higher elevation of the tracks, the crossing was nearly level with the public roadway. There were obstacles such as a hedge that might have obstructed visibility at the crossing. As Damerell approached the crossing, he did turn towards it but failed to notice the train until the last moment, despite knowing the train's schedule. Witnesses provided conflicting accounts regarding whether the train's bell was rung prior to the crossing, but ultimately, it was found that the train operators took reasonable precautions. Unfortunately, the horses and the wagon were struck, resulting in the death of two horses and damage to the wagon.	The plaintiffs, Emanuel and Robert Damerell, sought damages for the losses incurred from the collision, claiming that the railroad company had failed to properly warn them of the oncoming train, specifically arguing that the train's bell was not rung, nor was the whistle blown in time to avoid the accident.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company, argued that they had taken the necessary precautions by ringing the bell continuously from a distance of one and a half miles prior to the crossing, satisfying their legal obligation. They contended that the negligence lay with Damerell, who, despite being aware of the train's schedule and the conditions at the crossing, failed to look both ways before heading onto the tracks.

The case titled "City of Bunker Hill v. Benjamin Johnson" was decided on January 16, 1883, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose in Macoupin County, Illinois, involving the City of Bunker Hill as the plaintiff and Benjamin Johnson as the defendant. The central issue in the case was the exclusion of a printed book that was claimed to be the charter and ordinances of the City of Bunker Hill, which had been published by the authority of the city council. Johnson's legal team challenged the lower court's decision to exclude this evidence from the jury. Their appeal contended that this exclusion compromised the fairness of the trial. However, a significant procedural issue arose regarding the legitimacy of the bill of exceptions presented by Johnson's side; it lacked the seal of the judge who presided over the initial trial, rendering it void. The appellate court examined this procedural flaw and determined that it precluded the consideration of the appeal on its merits.	The plaintiff, City of Bunker Hill, aimed to uphold the decision made in the lower court, which had excluded the printed book as evidence. They argued that the exclusion was appropriate and that any appeals regarding the evidentiary rulings were not valid due to the procedural defects in Johnson's appeal, specifically the absence of the judge’s seal on the bill of exceptions. Essentially, the City contended that the appeal lacked proper grounds for consideration.	Benjamin Johnson, as the defendant, sought to challenge the trial court's decision to exclude the printed book that he claimed was crucial to his case. His legal representation argued that the exclusion denied him a fair opportunity to present evidence supporting his claims.
