The plaintiffs, who were the owners of a lot with a four-story brick building situated 75 feet north of Harrison Street, contended that the construction of the viaduct obstructed access by raising the street grade and closing the public alley at the rear of their property. The property was leased at the time to Eastman & Wilkins for a five-year term ending in October 1883, and the plaintiffs sought damages for the injury to their reversionary interest due to the construction work. Initially, the Superior Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $10,000 in damages, a decision that was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court after the city appealed, arguing that the plaintiffs' claims were flawed since they were only reversioners of the property, not absolute owners.	The plaintiffs argued that the city's construction of the Harrison Street viaduct permanently damaged their property by hindering access due to the elevated roadway and the closure of the rear alley. They claimed the city was responsible for converting a stone sidewalk in front of their property to its own use. The plaintiffs requested damages, contending that the improvement negatively affected the property's market value and caused permanent damage to their reversionary interest.	The city of Chicago, as the defendant, contended that the plaintiffs had not adequately established their ownership status and argued that the damages claimed were for the possession of the property rather than the reversion. They maintained that the evidence and declarations made by the plaintiffs were improper as they did not specifically assert that the damages were solely to the reversionary interest. The city requested a dismissal of the plaintiffs' claims based on these legal technicalities.

In January 1868, the case of The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. Coleman Gaines. v. John M. Garner et al. reached the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from Logan County, which faced a dispute over the adoption of township organization following two elections held in 1859 and 1865. In the 1859 election, 973 out of 1426 votes cast favored township organization, but the order for submission to vote was not recorded. The December term thereafter recognized the election positively even without formal entry. A subsequent election in 1865 saw 1612 out of 3054 votes cast in favor, and the county court again decided to implement township organization, appointing commissioners to divide the county into townships. However, six taxpayers appealed the county court's decision, seeking an injunction that was initially granted but later dismissed. After the commissioners divided the county, the supervisors were elected, with John M. Garner becoming the chair. The central issue revolved around whether the township organization was legally adopted despite procedural discrepancies regarding the recording of election orders.	The plaintiff, Coleman Gaines, claimed that the adoption of township organization was invalid due to the lack of recorded orders in both elections and disputes over the voter counts. The plaintiff sought to overturn the county court's decisions that recognized the township organization based on purported procedural failures and the appeal filed by the taxpayers.	The defendants, including John M. Garner, argued that both elections were valid and represented the will of the voters, as the county court had acted as per the law by conducting elections and appointing commissioners. They contended that the failure of the clerk to record the order was a minor technicality that did not undermine the legitimacy of the elections or the subsequent actions taken under the township organization law.

On March 31, 1886, the Commissioners of Highways for the township of Edwardsville, Madison County, Illinois, petitioned the county's Board of Supervisors for funds to construct two bridges over Cahokia Creek. The estimated cost for each bridge was $1,750, totaling $3,500. They argued that this cost exceeded twenty cents on the one hundred dollars of the latest property tax assessment and that significant funds from their road and bridge tax were necessary for ordinary repairs. The Board of Supervisors denied this petition on September 14, 1886, prompting the Commissioners to seek a writ of mandamus from the Illinois Supreme Court to compel the Board to appropriate the necessary funds. The case raised questions about whether the cost of the proposed bridges honored statutory limits, whether tax funds were allocated correctly, and if part of the bridge was within city boundaries.	The Commissioners of Highways claimed that their petition for funding was justified on the grounds that the construction of the bridges was necessary, exceeded the legal threshold for funding (twenty cents per one hundred dollars), and that the road and bridge tax levied was intended for repairs. They sought a writ of mandamus from the court compelling the Board of Supervisors to allocate $1,750 for the funding of one of the bridges as stipulated in their petition.	The Board of Supervisors countered the petition by claiming that the road and bridge tax levied was not at the full lawful amount and that the major portion of tax funds was not necessary for road repairs when the petition was presented. They argued that the proposed bridge project was flawed since part of it was located within the corporate limits of the city of Edwardsville, violating stipulations regarding funding for bridges.

In 1848, in Montgomery County, Illinois, the case involves Daniel Rogers and Aquilla C. Wiley. Levi A. Rogers, who owned certain lands, executed a mortgage to Wiley on March 23, 1848, to secure a debt due later that year. The mortgage was recorded. Daniel Rogers contested the legitimacy of the mortgage, claiming that he had purchased the land from Levi on January 25, 1847, and that Levi had no right to mortgage the property because he was indebted to Daniel. Daniel asserted that Wiley had prior notice of his ownership of the land before the mortgage was executed. After a decree of foreclosure was entered against Levi Rogers in the Circuit Court, Daniel Rogers filed a writ of error, challenging the validity of the foreclosure and Wiley's knowledge of the prior unrecorded deed.	Daniel Rogers, as the plaintiff, claimed that he was the rightful owner of the property due to his prior purchase from Levi Rogers. He argued that Levi had no legal right to mortgage the land, as it belonged to him. Daniel contended that Wiley was aware of this transfer when he arranged the mortgage with Levi, and he requested the court to annul the foreclosure decree in favor of Wiley.	Aquilla C. Wiley, as the defendant, argued that the mortgage was valid and properly executed, contending that he had no knowledge of any prior unrecorded deed to Daniel Rogers at the time the mortgage was taken. He maintained that the evidence presented did not conclusively prove that he was aware of Daniel's ownership. Wiley requested the court to enforce the foreclosure since the recorded mortgage was legitimate.

William T. Spencer and William E. McMasters were involved in a slander case heard in the Stephenson Circuit Court in Illinois, in November 1854. McMasters and his wife sued Spencer for allegedly making defamatory statements about McMasters’ wife. Spencer entered a general plea, along with a special plea of justification claiming the truth of the slanderous words he allegedly spoke. The plaintiffs replied with a claim of injury, establishing the legal issue for the jury. During the proceedings, Spencer sought a continuance to prove his plea but later moved to withdraw it, which the court denied. The jury found in favor of McMasters, awarding $400 in damages. Spencer's motions for a new trial were overruled as the court found no errors in the proceedings or excessive damages. The court addressed various legal principles related to slander, particularly regarding the sufficiency of the evidence and issues related to the plea of justification.	The plaintiffs, William and Martha McMasters, claimed that Spencer made slanderous statements about Martha, directly damaging her reputation. They sought monetary damages for the emotional and reputational harm caused by these statements, asserting that the words spoken imputed adultery to Martha, which was clearly actionable under the law.	Spencer's primary defense rested on his plea of justification, claiming that the statements he made were true. He argued that he expected to prove this justification but was impeded by the court's refusal to allow him to withdraw his plea. Spencer contended that the jury's verdict was influenced by prejudice and sought a new trial on the grounds of excessive damages and the court's errors in refusing his requested instructions.

In September 1869, the case of Joseph R. Jones v. James McGuirk arose from an incident involving the steam tug "Ada Allen" in Chicago. The key individuals were Joseph R. Jones, the United States Marshal for the Northern District of Illinois, and James McGuirk, the owner of the tug. The events leading to the case began on November 22, 1866, when Jones, in his capacity as marshal, seized the tug as part of a legal process in an admiralty case involving a libellant named John Eigg. Jones retained possession of the vessel until it was bonded out of his custody. However, during Jones's custody, the tug leaked water and eventually sank in the Chicago River due to what was perceived as negligence on his part. McGuirk accused Jones of failing to exercise due diligence in safeguarding the tug, resulting in damage and the loss of potential profits from its use. The matter was brought before the Superior Court of Chicago, where a jury found in favor of McGuirk and awarded him damages amounting to $1,375.	The plaintiff, James McGuirk, argued that Joseph R. Jones, as the United States Marshal, had a legal duty to exercise care in the safe-keeping of the tug while it was under his custody. McGuirk claimed that Jones's negligence led to the sinking of the tug, causing significant damage and financial loss due to its unavailability for two months. He requested compensation for the repairs needed and for the loss of income during the period the tug was out of commission.	In response, Joseph R. Jones claimed that the liability for any harm done to the tug did not rest with him but rather with the custodian he had appointed to oversee it. He also argued that McGuirk should have been present to ensure the protection of his property and that he was not sufficiently responsible for any damage incurred. Jones contended that if he bore any responsibility, it was only towards the libellant in the admiralty case, not the tug's owner.

The legal case, 'The Union Stock Yards National Bank v. George W. Dumond,' was decided on May 8, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, involving key individuals, namely the Union Stock Yards National Bank and George W. Dumond. The dispute centered on the bank's handling of Dumond's deposit. Dumond had provided funds to the Stock Yards Bank with specific instructions for handling those funds. However, the bank failed to follow these instructions properly by depositing Dumond's money with the Merchants National Bank and subsequently losing track of the funds’ identity. The court considered a previous case, Drovers National Bank v. O’Hare, as critical precedent, highlighting the bank's responsibility to adhere to the depositor's directives. As a result, the trial court ruled in favor of Dumond.	The plaintiff, George W. Dumond, argued that the Union Stock Yards National Bank failed to adhere to his explicit instructions regarding the deposit of his funds. He claimed that the bank's negligence in preserving the identity of his deposit, by delivering it to a third party without notice, constituted a breach of duty. Dumond sought compensation for the loss incurred due to this improper handling of his deposit.	The defendant, Union Stock Yards National Bank, contended that it acted according to the banking practices of the time and disputed any responsibility for the mismanagement of Dumond's deposit. The bank’s defense rested on the argument that the handling of such transactions was consistent with typical banking operations, and hence, it should not be held liable for the loss of the funds. The bank sought to have the judgment against it overturned and exonerated from any financial liability.

In September 1873, the case of Harvey Oil v. Richard Rowley was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated when Richard Rowley, the defendant, took possession of cattle belonging to Harvey Oil, the plaintiff, claiming that the animals were running at large in violation of state laws. Rowley argued that as a householder, he had the right to impound the cattle and provide for their care until the owner paid the required fees. The defendant presented three justifications: first, that the cattle were unlawfully at large; second, that they were similar to species recognized by law for impounding; and third, that a township ordinance prohibited cattle from running at large during the night. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of Rowley, who argued his claims based on the lack of payment for the care of the cattle and the conditions under which they were impounded. However, the court sustained a demurrer against each of Rowley’s pleas, leading to an appeal by Rowley based on his assertion that the cattle fell within the legal definitions allowing for their impounding.	The plaintiff, Harvey Oil, argued that the defendant's claims lacked legal standing under the Illinois law of 1869, which specifically defined the scope of animals allowed to be impounded. They contended that the law did not encompass the cattle in question—cows, heifers, and steers—and that Rowley had no lawful basis to retain possession or charge fees since he had not provided lawful justifications for impounding them. The plaintiff requested the return of their animals as well as any associated damages.	Richard Rowley, the defendant, claimed that he acted within his legal rights when he impounded the cattle, citing the statute concerning domestic animals and a township ordinance governing their confinement. He asserted that the animals had been found at large, allowing him to take them up safely, and that he had provided care, thus forming a lien for the unpaid fees. Rowley maintained that the statutory definitions did include cattle of the species he was referring to and that the ordinance justified his actions, therefore denying the plaintiff's claims.

In 1876, the case of Carlton Drake v. Isaac R. Drake originated in the De Kalb Circuit Court, Illinois. Carlton Drake (the plaintiff) filed a lawsuit against Isaac R. Drake (the defendant) seeking repayment of a debt. The defendant, Isaac R. Drake, was served with an alias summons in Cook County where he resided. He then filed a plea asserting that he could not be sued in De Kalb County, as he was not a resident there and was improperly served. The court sustained a demurrer to the defendant's plea, and when Isaac R. Drake requested to amend his plea, that request was denied. Consequently, the case proceeded without a jury to a court trial, where the court ruled in favor of Carlton Drake, awarding him $2,722.50. The appeal raised questions about the court’s decision to sustain the demurrer and deny the amendment to the plea.	The plaintiff, Carlton Drake, argued that the defendant owed him a debt and was improperly asserting that he could not be sued in De Kalb County. His legal request was for a judgment in his favor to recover the specified amount owed, asserting that the defendant's claims regarding venue were invalid.	The defendant, Isaac R. Drake, contended that he was a resident of Cook County and that the lawsuit was improperly brought in De Kalb County, which violated his statutory rights to be sued in his home county. He sought a judgment quashing the writ and declaration against him and argued against the validity of the court's proceedings based on jurisdictional issues.

In the case of Charles S. Hempstead et al. v. William Dickson, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1858, the dispute centers on a property located in Galena, Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The case originated after the death of Lawrence Ryan, who passed away on February 25, 1851, leaving behind a will that outlined the distribution of his property among his heirs. The will entrusted a specific lot to his wife and two other individuals, until the youngest child of Lawrence reached a certain age. Francis Ryan, one of Lawrence’s children, had conveyed his interest in the property to the plaintiffs, Hempstead et al. However, prior to reaching legal age, Francis faced judgments against him, leading to the sale of his interest in the lot. The defendants, led by William Dickson, claimed ownership of three-fourths of the lot, having acquired it through a series of deeds that originated from the sale of Francis's interest. The case was submitted to the court, where the issue was whether Francis's minority at the time of judgment had a bearing on the legitimacy of the sale.	The plaintiffs, Charles S. Hempstead et al., claimed that they were entitled to an undivided fourth of the disputed lot based on the deed executed by Francis Ryan. They argued that the judgments against Francis were invalid due to his status as an infant at the time they were rendered, asserting that this should render the subsequent sale of his interest improper.	The defendant, William Dickson, contended that the judgments against Francis Ryan were valid and binding despite his minority, arguing that they followed the proper legal protocols. Dickson maintained that the estate acquired through these judgments was legitimate and that the property in question rightfully belonged to him based on the series of transfers stemming from the sheriff's sale.

In the case of Winston Meeks v. William H. Sims et al., the events took place in Ford County, Illinois, related to a construction project. On April 23, 1874, Winston Meeks hired Carney & Sons to build a structure on his property. To facilitate this construction, Carney & Sons sourced lumber and other materials from the appellees, who were the suppliers. The materials were delivered between April and September 1, 1874. On September 14, 1874, the appellees notified Meeks that they were owed $786.78 for the materials supplied and declared their intention to place a lien on the building and Meeks' property for this unpaid amount. Subsequently, on June 12, 1875, the appellees filed a petition to enforce their lien as materialmen. The court later ruled in favor of the appellees, affirming that they were owed $767 and ordering Meeks to pay within thirty days or risk having the premises sold. Meeks appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court for a reversal of this judgment.	The plaintiff, William H. Sims et al., claimed that they provided lumber and materials to Carney & Sons, who used them in the construction of Meeks' building. Upon not receiving payment, they asserted their legal right to enforce a mechanic's lien on the property to secure payment for the materials supplied, amounting to $767. They filed their petition within the statutory period, arguing that they had met all legal requirements for such a lien.	Winston Meeks, the appellant, offered several defenses against the enforcement of the lien. He argued that the appellees did not file their petition within the required statutory timeframe. Additionally, Meeks claimed that the lien was extinguished by accepting an order for payment drawn by Carney & Sons. He also contended that appellees had other claims against Carney & Sons that should have been consolidated with this case, and that he was not properly credited for all payments owed.

On May 22, 1874, in Will County, Illinois, Charles Bearss borrowed $1,200 from Thomas P. Ford, securing the loan with a deed of trust on his homestead property. Subsequently, on December 28, 1874, Bearss and his wife borrowed an additional $290.36 from Ford, again securing the loan with a deed of trust on the same property. Both loans had interest rates of 10% per annum and matured on May 22, 1879. In April 1878, facing foreclosure due to overdue interest and taxes, Bearss negotiated with Ford. They agreed that Bearss would deed the property to Ford with the condition that he could reclaim it by paying the debts before July 1, 1879. Ford would also lease the property to Bearss for the interim period, with monthly rent to be treated as interest towards the debts. However, after Bearss failed to make the required payment by July 1, 1878, Ford received the deed and lease but found that the deed lacked a release of the homestead. When Bearss refused to correct this, Ford sought to foreclose on the trust deeds. The case was brought to the circuit court and subsequently to the Illinois Supreme Court for review.	The plaintiff, Thomas P. Ford, argued that the deed executed by Bearss was effectively a mortgage and not an outright sale. He claimed that since Bearss failed to fulfill the payment condition of the deed, Ford was entitled to foreclose on the property to satisfy the outstanding debts based on the original trust deeds.	Charles Bearss contended that the deed constituted an absolute sale of the property with a right of repurchase, rather than merely securing the existing debts. He insisted that since his obligations were effectively extinguished upon the transfer, he should retain ownership of the property despite not making the payment by the stipulated date.

William Deniston et al. v. George Hoagland, Guardian, etc., took place in Illinois, with the final decision rendered in January 1873. The case arose from a legal dispute over a parcel of land originally owned by John Deniston, who passed away intestate, leaving behind several heirs, including William Deniston and Samuel Deniston. Samuel had taken possession of the land and improved it until his death in March 1870. It was alleged that about six years prior to the lawsuit, William had sold his interest in the land to Samuel for $250, for which payment was completed. However, this transaction was flawed as William later sold the same property to Aaron Pollard for $500, without a proper acknowledgment from his wife. The plaintiffs, represented by George Hoagland as guardian for John and Aaron Deniston, sought to have the sale to Pollard set aside, claiming it was fraudulent concerning their equitable rights as heirs. The trial court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs and decreed specific performance, prompting the defendants to appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed that William Deniston fraudulently conveyed property that rightfully belonged to Samuel Deniston, their father, after he had already completed a prior sale to him. They requested that the court set aside the deed from William to Pollard and compel William to convey the property to them, arguing that the transaction with Pollard was made with full knowledge of Samuel's prior ownership.	The defendants contended that the sale to Pollard was valid and had been completed in good faith. They argued issues related to evidence and the competency of witnesses, claiming that the decision should be reversed based on procedural errors and improper exclusion of testimony. Furthermore, the defendants asserted that the statutory defenses, including the Statute of Frauds, were overlooked in the lower court's judgment.

The case "George I. Brown v. Joseph Walker" was heard by the Illinois Appellate Court on November 23, 1889, concerning a dispute over the ownership of six pigs. This case originated in the Circuit Court of Clark County, Illinois, and was appealed by George I. Brown (the plaintiff) following a verdict in his favor by a jury. The trial examined the identity of the pigs in question, with over twenty witnesses providing testimony on either side. Brown asserted that the pigs he claimed were marked with distinctive characteristics, while Walker, the defendant, contended that his pigs had their ears frozen off, which led to discrepancies in markings. The trial revealed a broader issue of witness credibility since both parties confidently disputed the ownership based on conflicting testimonies about what was observed. During the trial, various procedural aspects and testimonies were challenged, including the judge's exclusion of certain evidence and the instructions given to the jury regarding witness credibility. Ultimately, the question of identity was central to the verdict, which was upheld by the appellate court.	George I. Brown's primary claim was that the six pigs in question were his property, identifiable by specific marks such as a swallow fork in their ears. He presented evidence intending to prove his ownership, contending that any alterations to the pigs’ ears, such as recent cuts, were not an indication of ownership but rather an issue of misidentification. Brown sought the legal remedy of replevin to reclaim his pigs from Walker’s possession.	Joseph Walker defended against the claims by asserting that the pigs were not owned by Brown but were his and had been frozen during cold weather if their ear markings were altered. Walker introduced expert testimony regarding the state of the pigs' ears and sought to discredit the plaintiff's asserting of ownership by highlighting inconsistencies in Brown's claims and supporting evidence that indirectly reinforced his own position.

In April 1840, during a session of the Cook Circuit Court in Illinois, John Stone was indicted for the murder of Lucretia Thompson. The grand jury that issued the indictment had been summoned after the regular grand jury was discharged. The court allowed a special application for the summoning of a new grand jury, which subsequently indicted Stone on May 1, 1840. Following this, Stone was tried and convicted of murder. The trial proceeded with significant procedural disputes, including the withdrawal of a juror who was later revealed to be an alien, which was a legal ground for disqualification. Stone's defense counsel objected to several aspects of the trial process, including the manner of jury summoning and the legitimacy of the jurors empaneled. Ultimately, the circuit court overruled Stone's motions for a new trial and sentenced him to death.	John Stone, the plaintiff in error, claimed that the Circuit Court lacked the authority to summon a new grand jury or petit jury after the regular juries had been discharged. He argued that both juries were summoned illegally, which undermined his constitutional rights. Additionally, he contended that the court erred in allowing a juror to be withdrawn mid-trial without discharging the entire jury and in refusing to grant a new trial based on these grounds. Each point raised a series of legal challenges to the integrity and legality of his trial.	The People of the State of Illinois, as the defendants in error, maintained that the Circuit Court acted within its common law authority to summon a new jury when regular jurors were unavailable. They argued that the trial was conducted fairly and that any procedural issues, such as the alien juror, were properly handled by the court. They asserted that Stone's challenges to the jury's legitimacy and the trial's conduct were not valid, particularly since the remedy sought by Stone would not rectify the alleged errors. They upheld that the overall process was in compliance with state law.

E. W. Farnham v. William F. Monroe is a legal case that emerged from a dispute involving a lease and a guaranty executed in May 1887, in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were E. W. Farnham, the plaintiff, who acted as a guarantor for a leasing agreement, and William F. Monroe, the defendant, who was the lessor. The case centers around FD. Farnham’s guaranty written on the back of the lease which stipulated that the lessees, initially Bell & Co., could not assign the lease without the lessor's consent. Consent for assignment was granted by Monroe under the condition of obtaining a responsible surety, which Farnham provided. However, once Bell & Co. assigned the lease to another party, Bobbins, and subsequently vacated the premises by the end of December 1887, Monroe demanded the unpaid rent for January 1888 from Farnham under the terms of the guaranty. Farnham appealed after the Circuit Court ruled in favor of Monroe, leading to this legal dispute over the interpretation of the guaranty and the implications of the lease assignments.	The plaintiff, E. W. Farnham, claimed that his guaranty was only valid while Bell & Co. occupied the premises. He argued that since they had assigned the lease to another party, their obligation to pay rent should also terminate, thereby releasing him from his guaranty obligations. Farnham sought to avoid the January 1888 rent payment, believing that the assignment of the lease discharged his liability.	The defendant, William F. Monroe, contended that Farnham’s guaranty clearly obligated him to ensure payment of rent regardless of subsequent lease assignments. Monroe asserted that the guaranty covered the obligations of the lessees as stipulated in the lease agreement, and that the mere assignment of the lease did not absolve Farnham from responsibility. He maintained that the contractual terms of the written guaranty must stand as they are, independent of any negotiations or changes thereafter.

In December 1860, Ephraim Potter executed a will, which he left un-finished. He passed away in January 1861, and both his heirs and the legatees named in the will included relatives, notably the plaintiffs (James M. Potter et al.) and defendants (John Potter et al.). The plaintiffs challenged the will, asserting that it was not dictated or written by Ephraim, but rather by several relatives who conspired to deprive the complainants of their inheritance. They alleged that the will was made under undue influence by Abram, Elizabeth, and Marian Potter, and claimed that Ephraim did not properly sign or acknowledge the will. The defendants countered that the will was validly executed, properly witnessed, and that it expressed the true intent of the deceased. The case was brought to the Woodford Circuit Court and was heard by a jury, which found in favor of the defendants, affirming the validity of the will.	The plaintiffs argued that the will was improperly created through conspiracy, alleging that the defendants exerted undue influence over Ephraim to dictate and execute the will without his true consent. They claimed that the will was not written or attested as required by law and requested the court to set aside and cancel the will, thereby restoring the rightful property to the complainants.	The defendants contended that the will was legally and properly executed according to statutory requirements. They denied any allegations of conspiracy, fraud, or undue influence, asserting that Ephraim Potter willingly participated in the will's creation. They provided evidence that the will was properly signed and witnessed as per legal requirements and argued that the plaintiffs failed to meet their burden of proof in contesting the will's validity.

Henry A. Mix, the appellant, was involved in a legal case against Moses Nettleton, the appellee, in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1862. The case originated in Ogle County but was later moved to Winnebago County for trial. Nettleton brought a suit in debt against Mix, based on an obligation promising payment of $1,050 in county orders, as well as interest, for value received. The trial concluded with a verdict favoring Nettleton, awarding him $955.50 in debt and $614.44 in damages, although he later remitted part of the awarded amounts, resulting in a final judgment of $520.17 in debt and $292.15 in damages. Mix appealed the decision, challenging the nature of the obligation and the court's rulings regarding motions for a new trial and in arrest of judgment.	The plaintiff, Moses Nettleton, claimed that Henry A. Mix was liable under a note stating he owed $1,050 for value received, payable in country orders provided by Mix. Nettleton sought monetary damages stemming from this obligation due to Mix's failure to comply with the terms.	The defendant, Henry A. Mix, contended that the action of debt did not apply to the obligation as it was formulated, arguing that it did not represent a specific sum of money but rather the delivery of things (county orders) of unspecified size and denomination. Mix's defense highlighted legal precedents indicating that actions in debt require a sum specifically certain, contesting the validity of the plaintiff's claims.

In 1849, Thomas R. Green was involved in selling and locating land warrants in Chicago, with Henry A. Mix acting as his agent in Ogle County. Asa Talmadge sought to purchase land warrants for 360 acres from Mix for $432.25, secured by two bonds for warranty deeds contingent upon payment. After Talmadge made part payment, Green passed away, leaving his heirs, including John S. Green, as the estate's beneficiaries. Subsequent transactions involved the heirs quitclaiming interests in the lands, with Talmadge's payment issues leading to foreclosure actions against him. Talmadge attempted to redeem the lands in 1858, but his offers were rejected, resulting in the lands being sold at execution. Francis Burnap later redeemed the lands and sought judicial relief to enforce his rights. The case centered on whether the original transaction was a sale or a mortgage, leading to disputes over the nature of the agreements formed and the right to redeem the land.	The plaintiff, Jambs S. Dwen, acting as executor, claimed the right to redeem the lands based on his status as the purchaser of Talmadge's title, asserting that the original transaction constituted a mortgage rather than a sale. Dwen sought to pay the principal and interest on the notes and requested the court to grant him relief by allowing the redemption of the property.	The defendant, represented by John S. Green, denied that the original transaction involved a loan or that Talmadge had any rights to the property as claimed by the plaintiff. Green argued that Thomas Green had not sold the warrants but had entered the lands for his own benefit. He claimed Talmadge had forfeited his rights due to non-payment and that the legal title resided with the heirs. Green insisted there was no obligation to redeem as the contract had been treated as abandoned.

The case "John M. Long v. Thomas Linn" was decided in September 1873 by the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose from an ejectment action brought by Thomas Linn, represented by his guardian, against John M. Long for the recovery of a specific lot of ground located in Chicago. A trial was conducted with a jury, and the jury reached a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, indicating that Thomas Linn was entitled to possess the estate in question. Following the verdict, the defendant filed a motion for a new trial, which the court denied, subsequently ruling in favor of Linn with a judgment granting him recovery in fee simple ownership of the property. However, an error was discovered regarding the discrepancy between the jury's verdict as recorded by the clerk and the version noted in the bill of exceptions. The verdict failed to explicitly specify the estate that was awarded to the plaintiff, which, according to the law, is essential for the judgment to be valid. This led to the appeal to the Supreme Court of Illinois.	The plaintiff, Thomas Linn, claimed ownership of a lot in Chicago and asserted that he was entitled to recover possession via ejectment. His legal request was aimed at obtaining a judgment that recognized his estate in fee simple regarding the property, confirming his right to the land in question.	John M. Long, the defendant, contended that the jury's verdict was insufficient for the court to render judgment in favor of the plaintiff. He argued that the verdict did not specify the type of estate awarded to Linn, which is a critical requirement under the Ejectment Act. Long maintained that without this specification, no valid judgment could be issued, and, therefore, he requested the court to reverse the decision or remand the case for a new trial.

The case "The Presbyterian Church of New Boston v. James M. Emerson" took place in 1872 in New Boston, Illinois. The plaintiff, the Presbyterian Church of New Boston, filed a lawsuit against James M. Emerson, the defendant, seeking to recover the price of lumber that was purportedly sold to Emerson and used in the construction of a church building. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court after an appeal from a lower court judgment. During the trial, the plaintiff presented evidence of their account books, which included original handwritten entries documenting the sale of lumber in 1869 and 1870. The testimony revealed that the lumber was sold to the trustees of the church, with a portion of the amount owed carrying an interest agreement of ten percent if payment was not made by the agreed date. Despite conflicting testimonies regarding the accuracy of the account entries, the lower court affirmed the plaintiff's claim, stating that there was sufficient evidence of sale and delivery of materials used in the church's construction.	The plaintiff claimed that they had sold lumber to the defendant for the purpose of constructing a church building. They argued that all transactions were documented correctly in their account books, and sought a verdict that would allow them to recover the full value of the materials provided along with interest at a rate of ten percent from the date of delivery of the lumber, per their agreement with the defendant.	The defendant, James M. Emerson, contested the plaintiff's claims on several grounds, which included arguing that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence. He challenged the admissibility of the plaintiff’s account books and contended that the instructions given to the jury were erroneous. Emerson asserted that the plaintiff's testimony could not be considered credible due to the contradictions from multiple witnesses and insinuated that the plaintiff failed to adhere to necessary legal standards in documenting the account.

In 1884, the legal case of James S. Perry et al. v. George W. Burton et al. arose in Cook County, Illinois, concerning a tract of eighty acres of land. The land had a complex ownership history traced back to Isaac Cook, who entered the property in 1835 and subsequently conveyed portions of it to Asa M. Chambers and Sheldon Benedict. Over the years, various transactions occurred, culminating in Perry and John N. Henderson obtaining an interest in the property from Chambers in 1871. Disputes arose over the legitimacy of a conveyance from Benedict to Chambers due to the loss of the original deed, which led to oral testimony being presented as evidence. The opposing party (Burton and others) claimed their title originated from a series of transactions, including a tax sale and a court-ordered sale by an estate administrator. The core issue became whether the appellees could substantiate color of title through evidence of tax payments for the land and how those taxes pertained to the competing claims. Ultimately, the Illinois Supreme Court had to evaluate the sufficiency of the evidence presented, particularly in relation to the lost deed and tax payment claims.	The plaintiffs, James S. Perry and John N. Henderson, argued that they held a rightful claim to the disputed land based on their chain of title stemming from the conveyance by Chambers. They asserted that the lost deed from Benedict to Chambers was sufficiently validated through oral testimony. They requested the court to partition the land and quiet title against any claims made by the defendants, emphasizing the legitimacy of their ownership despite the complications surrounding the lost documentation.	The defendants, represented by Burton, contended that their title to the property was superior, primarily through claims of prior ownership and tax deeds. They argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiffs regarding the lost deed and subsequent title claims was inadequate. The defendants sought to disprove the plaintiffs’ claims by demonstrating issues in the continuity and regularity of the title associated with the plaintiffs, particularly challenging the sufficiency of the oral evidence provided regarding the lost deed.

In the case of North British and Mercantile Insurance Co. v. Charles F. Steiger, filed on September 28, 1883, the background involves a fire insurance policy concerning a hominy mill owned by the appellee, Charles F. Steiger. The insurance contract stipulated that the policy would become void if the risk associated with the property increased without written consent from the insurer. Initially, a steam dryer was used for drying corn, but shortly before the building was destroyed by fire, Steiger replaced it with a fire dryer that operated directly from a fire. The court had to deliberate whether this change significantly increased the risk and whether the policy was valid. The policy also included a condition prohibiting additional insurance on the same property without consent. Evidence revealed that Steiger had obtained other insurance which violated this provision. The majority of the appellate court ultimately concluded that questions regarding the increase of risk from the modified equipment and the breach pertaining to additional insurance were appropriate for a jury's decision.	The plaintiff, North British and Mercantile Insurance Co., argued that the insurance policy was void due to two breaches: first, the installation of a new fire dryer which allegedly increased the risk of loss, and second, the acquisition of additional insurance on the same property without the company's consent. The plaintiff sought to deny coverage for the losses incurred due to the fire based on these grounds.	The defendant, Charles F. Steiger, contended that there had been no actual increase in risk due to the installation of the fire dryer, asserting it was within the jury's purview to determine this matter. He also argued that any violations of the insurance policy's conditions had been waived by the insurer since the insurer's agent had some prior knowledge of the additional insurance. Steiger sought to have the court affirm the jury's decision in his favor.

John Hogan, acting for the use of Samuel Wilson, brought a legal action against William H. Shutler and Robert Wood in 1867 in Cairo, Illinois. The case arose from a bond issued on September 20, 1866, when the steamboat Cumberland was seized under a writ. The bond's condition stipulated that if the steamboat or double the amount for which it was seized was made available to satisfy a court judgment, then the bond obligation would be void. Hogan's case was based on a judgment rendered in January 1867, in favor of Wilson for unpaid supplies provided to the steamboat. The plaintiff claimed that neither the boat nor the required sum was forthcoming to satisfy the judgment, thus alleging a breach of the bond's condition. Throughout the proceedings, the defendants maintained that the boat was eventually seized and sold to satisfy the judgment. The case ultimately reached the Illinois Supreme Court following the overruling of a demurrer to the defendants' plea.	The plaintiff, John Hogan, alleged that the defendants failed to provide the steamboat Cumberland or the equivalent monetary amount required under the bond's terms. Hogan sought to enforce the forthcoming bond due to this claimed breach, asserting that the defendants were liable for the original judgment amount plus costs, which totaled $487.69.	The defendants, Shutler and Wood, contended that they complied with the bond requirements as the steamboat was seized and sold as part of a special execution following the initial judgment. They argued that the condition of the bond was met since the boat was forthcoming to satisfy the judgment, thus invalidating Hogan's claims. The defendants requested the court to affirm their plea and dismiss the case against them.

In 1861, in Chicago, Illinois, Isaac H. Burch extended a draft to Gurdon S. Hubbard for $13,000, which Hubbard accepted as payment involving a quantity of pork as collateral. Over time, $6,500 was paid against the draft, but Hubbard, fearing financial ruin due to a business failure, sought to negotiate his release from liability by arranging for a warehouse receipt for the pork to be delivered to Burch as security. Charles P. Hunt was tasked to communicate this arrangement to Burch. The receipt was delivered, and it was intended that by doing so, Hubbard would be released from liability on the draft. A dispute arose regarding whether the delivery of the receipt constituted a legal discharge of Hubbard’s obligations under the acceptance. Burch, following subsequent financial difficulties, assigned his assets, including the draft, to creditors. Hubbard did not initially contest the payment but later claimed that the conditions of the agreement provided a discharge. The case went to trial, where conflicting testimonies about the understanding of the agreement and the value of the collateral property were presented.	Burch claimed that Hubbard was liable for the remaining amount on the draft despite the delivery of the warehouse receipt. He argued that the receipt did not legally discharge Hubbard from his obligations as the original acceptor of the bill of exchange. Burch sought to recover the remaining balance owed following the transactions and to affirm his rights under the agreement without being bound by the collateral arrangement.	Hubbard argued that the delivery of the warehouse receipt was intended as a complete discharge of his obligation under the draft. He maintained that the receipt constituted sufficient consideration for the agreement to release him from liability, regardless of the subsequent decline in the value of the pork. Hubbard claimed that the legal framework supported his position, stating that the delivery of property as collateral was meant to indemnify him against loss and constituted a release of his role as an acceptor.

Frederick A. Willoughby v. John Hurley is a case that originated in a school district dispute in Knox County, Illinois, where two rival parties were contesting the position of school director. The litigation arose between John Hurley and his adversary, McTeirney, who both claimed to be lawfully elected as school directors and appointed their own teachers, leading to a situation where both teachers attempted to teach in the same school. Legal actions included attempts at injunctions, which were refused against Hurley while one against McTeirney was granted. Subsequently, a quo warranto proceeding was initiated against Hurley to remove him from office based on complaints from McTeirney. Willoughby was one of five attorneys representing Hurley, and despite their efforts, Hurley lost both cases. Hurley initially thought he could cover attorney fees from school funds but later paid the fees personally: $50 to two of the attorneys and $40 to Willoughby. The crux of the dispute arose over whether the payment to Willoughby was for both cases or just the chancery case. The jury found in favor of Hurley, and Willoughby appealed, arguing that the evidence did not support the jury's verdict.	Willoughby, representing himself, claimed he was owed additional attorney fees beyond the $40 paid to him by Hurley, arguing that this payment only covered fees for the chancery case and not the separate quo warranto proceedings. He sought a reversal of the lower court's judgment which favored Hurley, asserting that the evidence favored his position.	John Hurley, represented by attorney Lawrence, contended that the $40 payment to Willoughby was understood to be a complete settlement for all services rendered, due to the disastrous outcome of the litigation. Hurley maintained that he was not obligated to pay additional fees since the verdict was supported by the evidence presented.

In February 1884, John B. Jeffery incorporated the John B. Jeffery Printing Company in Illinois with a nominal capital of $150,000. The company faced financial challenges and disputes arose over claims made by multiple stakeholders, including creditors and stockholders. D. K. Tenney, acting as an attorney for Jeffery's wife, managed claims against the company, which included judgment notes and other debts amounting to over $75,000. After entering judgments and obtaining a receiver for the company, Tenney facilitated a sale of the company’s assets, which raised allegations of conspiracy to defraud creditors and mismanage company funds. A lawsuit was subsequently filed by the J. W. Butler Paper Company claiming wrongful conversion of assets. The case was ultimately appealed from the Superior Court of Cook County, leading to scrutiny over Tenney's actions and overall intentions concerning the debts and asset sales.	The plaintiffs, including The J. W. Butler Paper Company, contended that there was a conspiracy by Tenney and Robbins to defraud the company and its creditors. They claimed that through this conspiracy, the assets of the company were misappropriated and sold to benefit Tenney and Robbins at the expense of other creditors. They sought to have the assets returned to the company or a monetary equivalent to compensate for the loss.	The defendants, Tenney and Robbins, argued that they acted within their rights as individuals pursuing lawful claims against the company on behalf of their client, Mrs. Jeffery. They maintained that they had no knowledge of any fraudulent intentions from Jeffery and that their actions were simply aimed at securing owed payments on legitimate debts. They requested dismissal of the claims against them, asserting that they were not liable for any alleged conspiracy or misappropriation.

The case "The People, for use of Macon County, v. William W. Foster et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 18, 1890. The dispute centers around the financial dealings of William W. Foster, who served as the sheriff of Macon County. The plaintiff, representing the county, claimed that Foster mismanaged county funds by wrongfully receiving payments that he was not entitled to during his term. The key individuals involved were William W. Foster, the sheriff, and the county board that authorized payments to him. The core of the case revolved around whether the funds in question came into Foster's possession during his term and whether the sureties on his bond could be held accountable for these issues. The court examined multiple alleged breaches of Foster’s bond and the legality of the payments made by the county board based on reports foster submitted during and after his term in office.	The plaintiff claimed that Foster collected and retained several sums of money that belonged to the county. It argued that the sheriff made illegal demands for payments based on his reports, which inaccurately reflected a deficit in his compensation. The plaintiff sought recovery of these amounts, asserting that they were paid under a mistake of law and that the county was entitled to recover these funds based on Foster's breach of his duties as sheriff.	The defendant contended that the payments were made voluntarily by the county board and that the board acted under a mistake of law, believing they were obliged to fulfill Foster's claims. The defendant argued that the sureties on his bond were not liable for payments made post his term and did not come from funds earned by him while in office. Additionally, the argument emphasized that the sheriff's reports were not false representations and that the board was responsible for any mistakes regarding the payments made based on their audit.

In 1882, a legal dispute arose in Kankakee County, Illinois, involving Helen M. Mix and others against The People of the State of Illinois. The case was concerned with a bill in chancery aimed at foreclosing a lien on certain lands and town lots due to unpaid taxes for 1878, 1879, and 1880. The plaintiffs alleged that these properties had been fraudulently assessed at inflated values compared to other similar properties, leading to inflated tax liabilities. The bill filed in March 1882 initiated the foreclosure proceedings, claiming that the total amount due—including penalties and interests for back taxes—was $3687.40. James Mix, who was assessed for the properties, became a defendant in the case. The legal arguments presented included claims of lack of proper authority of the complainants' counsel and accusations of unlawful assessment and levying processes. The case was eventually brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, where various procedural issues and the validity of the assessments and collection methods were scrutinized.	The plaintiffs, representing the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that properties owned by Helen M. Mix were subject to a tax lien due to unpaid taxes, penalties, and interest. They requested foreclosure of this lien as allowed under Illinois law, asserting that the total outstanding amount was $3687.40, which included taxes from the years 1878, 1879, and 1880.	The defendants, including James Mix, argued that the tax assessments were fraudulent and illegally executed, contending that the property was assessed significantly higher than its actual value. They contended that the county court lacked jurisdiction to impose such taxes and maintained that the county's attempts to compromise the tax amounts were unauthorized. They also asserted that the plaintiffs did not have the legal authority to bring the suit, as the State's attorney did not prosecute the action, and that other parties with an interest in the property were not made defendants in the case.

The case of John W. Chickering et al. v. Thomas H. Failes et al. arose in April 1862 in Illinois, specifically in Cook County Circuit Court. The dispute centered around land ownership following the death of David Lee, whose estate was managed by executors Thomas H. Failes and Caleb O. Halsted. The plaintiffs, led by Chickering, initially sought to redeem a mortgage on certain lands, arguing that they had rights to the property based on a prior Supreme Court ruling which had partially reversed a lower court's decision concerning the same lands. The case had seen prior proceedings, and a significant aspect of the trial was the attempt by the defendants to amend their answers to assert that the title to the contested lands rested with them as executors under Lee's will, due to the payment of taxes for over seven years. This legal battle also involved questions surrounding the admissibility of new evidence and amendments after a previous ruling. The core issue revolved around the rightful ownership of the property and whether the lower court's actions conformed to the appellate court's directive.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had the right to redeem the mortgaged premises based on a previous Supreme Court decision that favored their position. They argued that the lower court had overstepped its authority by allowing the defendants to amend their pleadings and introduce new evidence, which they claimed contradicted settled legal principles. Additionally, the plaintiffs maintained that the defendants had no legitimate claim to the title to the land in question due to the prior ruling and subsequent judicial principles establishing their entitlement.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs' claims were not valid due to the legal title being vested in the executors of David Lee's estate. They argued that the amendments to their answers and additional evidence were necessary to assert their rightful ownership and were allowed under the court's discretion following the remand from the Supreme Court. The defense asserted that the payment of taxes over the required period created a statutory bar, protecting their claim to the property. Thus, they requested that the court uphold the new pleadings and evidence, which they claimed demonstrated the validity of their title.

H. Leroy Thayer filed a case against Ferdinand W. Peck involving a financial transaction that took place in Joliet, Illinois, on July 27, 1875. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1876, following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Will County, where Hon. Joslah McBoberts presided as judge. The evidence considered during the trial focused on a bill of exchange worth $5,250, which Thayer had endorsed and instructed to be paid to the First National Bank of Joliet. However, during the trial, the plaintiff failed to provide evidence that the bill was presented for payment to the drawee bank, which is a necessary step to hold the drawer—Thayer—legally responsible for payment. Due to the lack of evidence regarding presentment or an excuse for not presenting the bill, the initial judgment rendered against Thayer was deemed erroneous.	The plaintiff, H. Leroy Thayer, claimed that he was owed $5,250 under an inland bill of exchange that he had endorsed. He argued that the defendant, Ferdinand W. Peck, should pay the amount due on the bill. Thayer's legal request was for the court to enforce the payment of the endorsed bill by holding the drawer (himself) liable.	Ferdinand W. Peck, the defendant, argued that there was insufficient evidence to support the plaintiff's claim. His key contention was that the plaintiff failed to present the bill to the drawee bank or provide any justification for the lack of presentment. This omission was critical, as it did not meet the legal requirement necessary for pursuing a claim against the drawer of the bill.

In September 1868, in Chicago, Illinois, J. T. D. Elliott was involved in a legal case concerning the assessment of certain lots for improvements on Michigan Avenue. The city collector, A. H. Heald, filed for judgment against the properties assessed under Elliott's name. Elliott challenged the validity of this assessment, claiming that the city had not provided the required legal notice regarding the judgment application. He argued that the city commissioners intentionally failed to assess other properties that were benefited by the improvements. Additionally, Elliott asserted that essential procedures of the city charter related to the improvement ordinance and the duties of city officials were not properly followed. There were also claims that notification for meetings and assessment roll filings was not given as mandated by law. Despite Elliott's objections and his presentation of witnesses to support his claims, the objections were overruled, and the court entered judgment for the assessed amount, along with orders to sell part of the assessed property to satisfy the judgment. Elliott then appealed the ruling to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Elliott, the plaintiff, claimed that the city failed to provide proper legal notifications as required for the assessment process. He alleged that the city commissioners did not assess all properties that benefitted from the improvements and contended that the city's actions violated various material requirements of the city charter. Elliott sought to nullify the judgment against his property based on these procedural failings and the argument that the assessments were unjust and misleading.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant, countered Elliott's claims by arguing that the assessments were conducted lawfully and that the commissioners exercised their judgment appropriately in determining which properties benefitted from the improvement. They maintained that the decisions made by the Board of Public Works were conclusive in the absence of any demonstrated fraud. The city highlighted that all necessary procedures had been substantially complied with under the law, thereby supporting the initial judgment made against Elliott’s properties.

On January 27, 1862, in Fulton County, Illinois, Stephen Lindsey, Sr., at the age of eighty-seven, conveyed a farm of 270 acres and a bill of sale for livestock and farming equipment to his youngest son, Hezekiah Lindsey. In return, Hezekiah issued seven notes for $150 each, secured by a mortgage on the farm, along with a bond for $1,000 to support his father for life. Stephen Sr. died on September 2, 1864. Some of Stephen Sr.'s other children filed a legal claim seeking to nullify the deed and bill of sale, arguing that Stephen Sr. lacked the mental capacity to engage in such contracts and that Hezekiah had exerted undue influence over him. The defendant, Hezekiah, denied these allegations. The case was heard in the circuit court, which ultimately dismissed the plaintiffs' claims.	The plaintiffs, Stephen Lindsey, Jr., and others, contended that their father, Stephen Lindsey, Sr., was mentally incompetent at the time of the property transfer to Hezekiah Lindsey. They asserted that he had been subjected to undue influence, rendering the deed and sale invalid. They sought to have the court nullify the transaction based on these claims.	Hezekiah Lindsey denied the allegations of undue influence and mental incompetence, arguing that Stephen Sr. was fully aware and capable of understanding the transaction when it occurred. Hezekiah maintained that his father's decision to convey the property was voluntary and consistent with prior arrangements made before their transfer. He requested that the court uphold the validity of the deed and dismiss the claims brought against him.

The case "C. M. Murch v. Samuel W. Wright" took place in January 1868, in Moultrie County, Illinois. The central issue involved a dispute over a piano forte. C. M. Murch, the plaintiff, initiated an action of replevin against Samuel W. Wright, the defendant, in the Circuit Court of Moultrie County during the October term of 1867. Murch claimed that the piano was his property, as per a conditional sale agreement, although it had been mischaracterized as a lease. Under the terms of the agreement, the price for the piano was set at $700, with Wright having made an initial payment of $50, which was described as the first month's rent, followed by monthly payments of $50 over the course of thirteen months. Upon consultation, the courts found that the arrangement resembled a conditional sale rather than a true lease, subject to the risk of Wright losing possession to creditors due to unpaid debts. The court's decision ultimately reaffirmed the validity of the conditional sale but also acknowledged the complications arising from the creditor's claims on the same property.	C. M. Murch contended that the agreement between him and Samuel W. Wright constituted a conditional sale of the piano, rather than a lease. He argued that the payments made were part of a purchase agreement that would transfer ownership upon full payment. Murch's legal request was for the return of the piano, which he believed was rightfully his property under the terms of the contract.	Samuel W. Wright defended himself by asserting that the arrangement was a legitimate lease rather than a sale, suggesting that he had paid rent for the use of the piano. He argued that Murch's lien on the piano was rendered ineffective because the piano had been seized by creditors during its possession. Wright's legal request ultimately resulted in a judgment in his favor, seeking a return of the piano.

On January 6, 1887, in Cook County, Illinois, The Chromotype Company was indebted to George E. Lloyd, George F. Harding, and Van Schaack & Sons. Lloyd and Harding had their claims secured by chattel mortgages, while Van Schaack & Sons had no such security. To defraud its creditors, the company assigned certain open accounts to Lloyd, which he accepted, and subsequently collected $101 from them. Later, on January 20, 1887, the same accounts were assigned to Harding for $1,000. On January 29, 1887, Lloyd transferred his chattel mortgage and notes against the company to Grant. Van Schaack & Sons obtained a judgment of $152.15 against the company, but the execution was returned unsatisfied. They initiated garnishment proceedings against Lloyd, which led to Harding and Grant interpleading in the matter. The interpleader was dismissed, and a judgment of $101.31 was rendered in favor of the company for the use of Van Schaack & Sons against Lloyd. Both Harding and Grant appealed the judgment.	The plaintiffs, represented by Harding and Grant, argued that the assignment of accounts to Lloyd was fraudulent and sought to set aside the fraudulent conveyance. They claimed entitlement to the moneys collected by Lloyd from those accounts, asserting that they had a valid legal interest in the accounts as creditors. The plaintiffs requested that the court recognize their rights over the proceeds of the assigned accounts.	The Chromotype Company, through its defense, contended that the assignment to Lloyd was binding even if fraudulent, as he collected and united legal and equitable title to the accounts. They argued that Harding had no rights to the funds collected because he was not a legitimate creditor, and that Lloyd’s promise to use the collections as credits against his notes was unenforceable. The defendant requested the court to affirm the judgment against Lloyd, asserting that the assignment had divested the company of any rights over the accounts.

In 1874, the case "Trustees of Schools Town 16 N., R. 11 W., in Morgan County, et al. v. Peter Braner" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in Morgan County, where the defendant, Peter Braner, filed a bill in the circuit court to set aside a conveyance of land to the trustees of the local school and the school directors. The conveyance was stated to be for school purposes and was reflected in the deeds associated with the property. However, since March 1872, the school directors had removed the schoolhouse from the site and had plans to sell the land for purposes other than educational. The plaintiffs argued that such a sale would violate the intended use of the property as stipulated in the original conveyance. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiff, leading the defendants to appeal on the grounds that the school directors, who were necessary parties due to their interest in the property, were not included in the case.	The plaintiffs claimed that the land in question was conveyed for school purposes and should continue to be used as such. They contended that the sale of the land to anyone for purposes outside education would constitute a violation of the deed's terms. The plaintiffs sought to prevent the sale through an injunction and requested that the land be reconveyed back to them.	The defendants argued that the conveyance did not restrict the use of the land solely to the operation of a school and that the trustees were still legally able to use the property for any legitimate school-related purposes. They contended that the bill filed by the plaintiffs was defective for not including necessary parties (the school directors) and asserted that the plaintiffs were not entitled to the relief they sought.

On July 17, 1868, in Cook County, Illinois, Eugene B. Myers, a bookseller, entered into a written agreement with Eugene L. Gross and his associated publishing company to sell a compilation of the statutes of Illinois. According to the contract, Myers was to advertise and sell the entire edition of books at $8 per copy (later raised to $10), receiving a commission of 20% of the gross receipts and remitting 80% back to the publishers. The contract allowed the publishers to sell a few copies directly, without commission due to Myers. The total edition comprised approximately 1,000 copies, although the exact number became a point of contention. Disputes arose when the publishers sold 294 copies to the State, which Myers claimed entitled him to additional commissions. The case escalated as Myers sought restitution for unpaid commissions based on the terms of their agreement, leading to trial without a jury in the Superior Court, where the court found in favor of Myers and awarded him damages.	Myers, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to commissions on the copies sold by the publishers beyond the few allowed under their agreement. He claimed the publishers had violated the contract by selling more copies than permitted and failing to account for commissions on sales made, including a significant sale to the State. Myers requested a judgment requiring the defendants to pay him the owed commissions and damages, totaling $1,169.36.	The defendants, Gross and his publishing company, contended that Myers had no right to commissions for sales they made beyond a small exception in the contract. They argued that their sales complied with the terms, and also maintained that Myers had forfeited his claims due to his own defaults in handling the commission accounting. They requested the court to uphold their interpretation of the contract and contest Myers' entitlement to the claimed commissions.

The case "The Board of Trustees of Schools, etc. v. The People ex rel. The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company" arose in January 1872 in Macoupin County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included the Board of Trustees of Schools, representing the educational authority, and the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company, which sought assistance in constructing a railroad. The background of the case centers around a subscription made by voters in the township authorizing the issuance of bonds to support the railroad construction in exchange for the railroad's passage through the township. Following the affirmative vote from the electorate, the trustees of the school district were petitioned to issue these bonds, but they refused. The railway company, having complied with all conditions of the subscription, sought a legal remedy through a writ of mandamus to compel the trustees to fulfill their obligation. The conflict centered on the legality of the action taken by the school trustees and whether they had the authority to engage in such a financial arrangement.	The plaintiff, the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company, claimed that the Board of Trustees of Schools had a legal obligation to issue the bonds as voted upon by the electorate, in accordance with the provisions set forth in the charter regulations. The plaintiff argued that the trustees' refusal to issue the bonds constituted a failure to comply with the voters’ decision, which aimed to financially support the construction of the railway, deemed essential for township development.	The defendants, represented by the Board of Trustees of Schools, contended that they did not possess the power to issue bonds for the railway project as it fell outside the scope of their authority. They argued that the Illinois Constitution limited such powers to recognized corporate authorities and stated that school trustees were not entitled to levy taxes or engage in activities unrelated to the educational purpose of school districts. Hence, the act enabling the trustees to issue bonds for the railway was unconstitutional, leading to their refusal to comply with the petition.

On October 12, 1874, Joseph Luke executed a promissory note for $1,950, payable to Bernard Jansen within ten years. To secure the note, Luke, with his wife, mortgaged 200 acres of land in Effingham County, Illinois. By April 8, 1881, interest on the note had accrued, and because Luke failed to pay this interest or the taxes on the mortgaged property, Jansen sought foreclosure on the property to recover his losses. Jansen claimed that he had to pay taxes that had been accrued on the land. He filed a bill to foreclose the mortgage, naming several defendants, including Henry B. Kepley, who claimed ownership of a portion of the mortgaged land through a sheriff's sale. The circuit court ruled in favor of Jansen by allowing the foreclosure of the mortgage, leading to an appeal by Kepley to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Jansen, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to foreclosure on the mortgage due to unpaid interest and taxes on the mortgaged land. He sought a decree that required repayment of the missed interest payments and the taxes that he personally paid to preserve the mortgage security. Jansen contended that these payments were necessary to protect his rights under the mortgage agreement, even before the principal debt was due.	Kepley, as the defendant, claimed that he held paramount title over the mortgaged lands due to a sheriff’s sale conducted on judgments rendered for taxes where he asserted that the liens from taxes took precedence over the mortgage. He argued that the lands had been sold under a judgment for taxes due on other properties, making Jansen's claims regarding foreclosure and tax reimbursement invalid. Kepley also maintained that he was not a necessary party to the foreclosure suit since his title was adverse to that of the mortgagor.

The legal case "The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company v. William A. Kennedy" was decided in the Illinois Appellate Court on January 22, 1887. It arose in Knox County, Illinois, where two horses owned by the plaintiff, William A. Kennedy, were killed after straying onto a section of the defendant's railroad track. The horses escaped from a nearby stable during a severe snowstorm. The plaintiff sought damages for the loss of his horses, claiming that the railroad company failed to keep the cattle guard clear of snow, thereby allowing the animals to access the tracks. Initially, a judgment by a Justice of the Peace favored the railroad company; however, upon appeal to the Circuit Court, the jury ruled in favor of Kennedy, awarding him $150 in damages and $25 in attorney's fees. The case hinged on the laws regarding the maintenance of cattle guards by railroad companies, particularly during inclement weather.	The plaintiff, William A. Kennedy, argued that the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company was negligent in failing to clear the cattle guard of snow, leading to the deaths of his horses. He alleged that the railroad failed to uphold its statutory duty to maintain the cattle guards adequately, which resulted in his animals having access to the tracks. Kennedy sought compensation for the value of the horses and related legal fees due to this negligence.	The defendant, the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, contended that the severe weather conditions created an extraordinary situation that made it unreasonable to expect them to clear the cattle guard of snow in a timely manner. They claimed that they were engaged in clearing the tracks of snow and ensuring passenger safety during the ongoing storm, which made it impractical to address every cattle guard along the lengthy railroad. The railroad company argued that the plaintiff had not proven negligence or the necessity of immediate maintenance given the unusual circumstances.

William Kennedy and his associates (appellants), operating as Kennedy & Sons, were involved in a legal case against George Gibbs and his company (appellees), Gibbs & Co. The case originated in Chicago, Illinois, with proceedings beginning in September 1852. The plaintiffs, Gibbs & Co., were forwarding and commission merchants who had received a consignment of goods from the defendants. They incurred freight charges amounting to $182.10 while handling those goods. Additionally, they charged the defendants $5.79 for receiving and checking the goods and $4.70 for the commissions on the prepaid freight. The plaintiffs argued those charges were customary and reasonable within the industry. The case progressed to the jury, where the court instructed that the plaintiffs should be awarded interest on the freight amount. However, this point became contested as the defendants disagreed over the classification of the transaction, specifically questioning if it constituted a loan. The central focus of the legal argument pivots around whether the charges were simply business expenses or a loan arrangement.	The plaintiffs, Gibbs & Co., claimed they were entitled to recover freight charges and associated fees (totaling $192.59) from the defendants for services rendered as forwarding and commission merchants. They argued that the charges were customary and reasonable, and thus they sought both the recovery of the claimed amounts and interest on the freight charges.	The defendants contended that the transaction should not be considered a loan of money, as defined under Illinois law, because the money was advanced in the ordinary course of business rather than as part of a loan agreement. They asserted that the plaintiffs could not be entitled to interest as a matter of course unless it was demonstrated that there had been an unreasonable and vexatious delay in payment. Moreover, they maintained that the inclusion of the commission charges would make the transaction appear usurious if interpreted as a loan.

Harriet Steele filed a petition for dower in 1868 in Illinois, involving a dispute over property rights. The involved parties included Harriet Steele as the petitioner and Haines H. Magie as the defendant. The background of the case revolves around a series of property transactions initiated by a man named Wright who purchased land from the State in 1833. Wright sold the property before fully paying for it or obtaining the patent, subsequently entering a contract for the deed with Coles. In July 1835, Coles conveyed the property to Steele, Harriet's husband, through a general warranty deed. However, it was determined that Steele never held legal or equitable title to the property since the rights were not fully executed or transferred to him. The court highlighted that Steele merely had an incomplete equity which did not establish a right of dower for Harriet, as legal requirements for such a claim were not fulfilled. The court's ruling leaned on precedents that outlined the criteria necessary for a wife to claim dower rights based on her husband's property interests.	Harriet Steele argued that she was entitled to dower rights in the property owned by her husband, claiming that the legal title should transfer to her upon the conveyance from Coles. She maintained that her husband had a sufficient property interest that should vest her with the right of dower, under the assertion that ownership transferred automatically through exempted contractual paths.	Haines H. Magie, representing the defendant, asserted that Steele never acquired the requisite legal or equitable title to the property necessary for Harriet to claim dower rights. The defense argued that because Wright did not complete his transaction with the State before selling and because Steele's conveyance did not alter the nature of the title, Harriet's claim for dower lacked legal grounding. The defense referenced earlier court decisions affirming that incomplete equities did not confer dower rights.

In 1841, in Tazewell County, Illinois, David Bailey, the appellant, was involved in a legal dispute against the administrators of Nathan Cromwell, deceased, namely William Cromwell and others. The case arose from the actions of the administrators who brought a lawsuit against Bailey based on a promissory note made by Nathan Cromwell prior to his death.
