In 1868, in Chicago, Illinois, Mary Fennell brought a lawsuit against The Provident Life Insurance Company concerning a life insurance policy issued on the life of her deceased husband. The case arose after her husband was killed while performing his duties. The plaintiff argued that she was entitled to the insurance payout and had previously received a favorable verdict and judgment in the lower court, leading to an appeal by the insurance company. The key individuals in this case included Mary Fennell as the plaintiff and representatives from The Provident Life Insurance Company as the defendant.	Mary Fennell claimed that she was owed a death benefit under the life insurance policy, which was meant to cover her husband's death by accidents. She argued that the insurance policy did not restrict coverage based on the specific occupation of her husband and that he was entitled to the payout regardless of the circumstances of his death while working.	The Provident Life Insurance Company contended that the court erred in not allowing them to present evidence that the deceased's occupation as a switchman at the time of insurance and that he was killed while performing duties as a brakesman. They argued this information was material to the case and believed the plaintiff was not entitled to claim benefits without demonstrating that the circumstances of his death fell within the policy coverage. The defendant also attempted to challenge the acknowledgment of premium payment in the policy, claiming it had not been fully paid.

Charles Ballance filed an ejectment action against Michael Flood in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1869. The case originated from a dispute over property involving a tract of land that was claimed by Ballance under a patent issued to Augustus Langworthy in 1840. After Langworthy's death, his heirs were added as parties to the suit. The trial involved conflicting evidence about possession of the land. Ballance claimed prior possession to establish his right of recovery, but the defendant, Flood, argued using the twenty-year statute of limitations and provided evidence of prior possession by the Bartons, his predecessors in title. The jury found for the defendant, leading Ballance to appeal the decision.	Ballance's primary argument was that he was the rightful owner of the land due to prior possession and connection to the title under Langworthy. He contended that the court erred in refusing certain jury instructions that would have supported his claims. Specifically, he argued that his possession of adjoining property should legally include the newly purchased tract and that, if he had established prior possession, he was entitled to recover the property.	Flood countered Ballance's claims by citing the twenty-year statute of limitations and asserting evidence of prior possession through the Bartons, from whom he held the title. He claimed that Ballance failed to establish a sufficient connection to the patent title or demonstrate exclusive possession for the required period. Flood argued that the jury instructions provided regarding ownership and possession were appropriate and supported the verdict in his favor.

The case, John T. Hadfield et al. v. Cyrus L. Berry, arose in 1888 and was heard in the Circuit Court of Peoria County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, manufacturers and dealers in fireworks from Middletown, Connecticut, and New York City, supplied a quantity of "Standard Fireworks" to the Koch Brothers, retail dealers in Peoria, under a specific arrangement. The essence of the dispute was whether the fireworks belonged to the plaintiffs (Hadfield et al.) or to the Koch Brothers, who had been levied upon by the Peoria County sheriff, the defendant Berry, in satisfaction of a judgment debt. The court had to determine if the arrangement constituted a bailment or a sale of the goods. The trial found in favor of the defendant, concluding that the goods were property of the Koch Brothers liable for seizure. The plaintiffs contested the trial court’s findings, arguing they retained ownership of the goods until payment or return. The judgment against the plaintiffs led to their appeal, which ultimately centered around the nature of the relationship and contract details between the parties involved.	The plaintiffs contended that the Koch Brothers were merely bailees of the fireworks and that legal ownership remained with them. They argued that as the true owners, the fireworks could not be considered the property of the Koch Brothers, thus should not have been levied upon. They sought recovery of their property and enforcement of their claim to rightful ownership according to the conditions established in their contractual agreement with the Koch Brothers.	The defendant, Cyrus L. Berry, maintained that the goods had been sold to the Koch Brothers and were thus correctly seized as the property of the judgment debtors. The defense argued that the arrangement qualified as a sale, granting the Koch Brothers absolute rights to sell or keep the goods. The court found that the plaintiffs had not presented adequate evidence to counter the claim of the Koch Brothers as the lawful owners of the fireworks at the time of the levy.

John B. Legnard filed a petition against Cecelia J. Armstrong in 1886 regarding a mechanics' lien for materials supplied to a double brick building located at 306 and 308 West Monroe Street in Chicago, Illinois. The property was owned by Cecelia, and her husband, John M. Armstrong, acted as her agent overseeing the construction and contracting processes. Legnard had a subcontract with the contractor, Edward Hayden, to supply brick for the building. A notice of intention to establish a lien was served to John M. Armstrong, addressing him directly and indicating that Legnard sought to hold the building and its ground liable for the amount of $800 for the bricks supplied. However, the court found that the notice was insufficient, as it was addressed to the husband, who had no ownership interest in the property, thus failing to comply with legal requirements necessary to establish a lien.	Legnard claimed that he had provided $800 worth of brick for the construction of the building under a subcontract with the primary contractor. He asserted that he properly notified the building's owner of his intention to hold the property liable for the outstanding amount due, seeking the establishment of a mechanics' lien against the property.	Cecelia J. Armstrong contended that the notice of lien served to her husband did not meet the requirements laid out in the mechanic’s lien statute, as it was not addressed to her directly. The defense argued that proper notice must be directed to the actual owner of the property to establish a lien, and thus the notice was inadequate to affect Mrs. Armstrong's estate in the building or the ground upon which it was situated.

In 1880, W. E. Richmond and Charles K. Moore entered into a contract in Cook County, Illinois, where Richmond was to sail the vessel “Scotia” for Moore for a sum of $1,000. However, Moore prevented Richmond from fulfilling the contract, leading to Richmond sustaining financial losses. Richmond filed an action of assumpsit (a legal claim for breach of contract) in the Superior Court of Cook County, which included both special and common counts related to the contract. The trial was held without a jury, and the court found in favor of Richmond, awarding him $566 in damages. Moore defended himself by arguing that the contract was void since it was made on a Sunday, which he claimed violated statutory regulations. The case was subsequently appealed to the Appellate Court, which affirmed the original judgment, prompting Moore to take the matter to the Illinois Supreme Court.	W. E. Richmond claimed that Charles K. Moore had breached their contract by preventing him from sailing the vessel “Scotia,” resulting in financial damages. Richmond sought to enforce the contract and recover the amount he was owed for the non-fulfillment, arguing that the contract made on a Sunday was still valid under Illinois law.	Charles K. Moore contended that the contract was void because it was made on a Sunday, in violation of the Illinois statute prohibiting labor and other business activities on that day. He maintained that the absence of a written memorandum of the contract further supported the claim that it should not be enforced as it did not comply with statutory requirements. Moore argued that Richmond's representations that he was competent for the position were false, leading to his discharge for just cause.

On July 12, 1886, a contract was established between William P. Nelson (the appellant) and The Pickwick Associated Company (the appellees) concerning painting and glazing a building in Cook County, Illinois. The contract stipulated that the work was to be completed by February 15, 1887, and specified that $25 per day would be deducted from the contract price for any delays beyond this date. Additionally, it required the contractor to coordinate with other contractors to avoid any delays. The work was to be supervised by architects, and their approval was necessary for any payments. Nelson experienced delays in completing his work due to the failure of other contractors to finish their tasks, which, coupled with rising wages, led him to incur additional costs amounting to $473.20. Nelson claimed these costs were due to the obstruction caused by the delays of other contractors. He alleged that a general agent of the appellees had verbally promised him that the company would cover any additional expenses that arose from these delays. The central issue was whether Nelson was entitled to recover this extra cost when the contract seemed to outline that additional time could be granted by the architects without covering these extra charges.	Nelson's main arguments centered on the delays caused by other contractors, which he contended prevented him from completing his work on time, causing him financial losses amounting to $473.20. He requested damages for these delays, asserting that the promise made by the company's general agent implied that he would be reimbursed for additional costs incurred due to such delays. He argued that it was the legal duty of The Pickwick Associated Company to ensure that the work was sufficiently prepared to avoid delays impacting his contract performance.	The Pickwick Associated Company's key argument was that the contract contained provisions stating that delays caused by other contractors would allow for additional time but did not entitle Nelson to recover extra damages. They contended that any promises of additional payments made by their general agent were not binding as they lacked sufficient legal consideration, based on the terms of the original contract. The company also emphasized that the responsibility for managing and mitigating such delays was part of the contract's obligations and that they could not be held responsible for the financial impact of those delays.

In October 1870, James Frisby sold a tract of land in McLean County, Illinois, to Bobert L. Scott for a total of $3,100, secured by five annual promissory notes and a mortgage on the land. After Scott defaulted on the first note, Frisby initiated foreclosure proceedings. A decree required Scott to pay approximately $1,528.80; if he failed to do so, the property was to be sold. Frisby became the purchaser when the land was sold after Scott's payment default. After the statutory redemption period, plaintiffs Hughes & McCart, who were judgment creditors of Scott, redeemed the property and obtained a deed. Frisby, after the redemption, sought to foreclose two more of Scott's remaining notes. The trial court granted relief to Frisby, allowing additional foreclosure of the land. Hughes & McCart appealed this decision, claiming the mortgage lien had been waived in the foreclosure process.	Hughes & McCart argued that the foreclosure sale of the property did not include the unpaid notes' mortgage lien, as the master did not specify in the sale and purchase documents that the sale was subject to this lien. They contended that this omission released them from the mortgage obligations, affording them clear title to the property upon redemption.	Frisby contended that the sale was indeed subject to the mortgage lien for the unpaid notes, evidenced by statements made during the sale process. He maintained that the failure to include this detail in the master’s report or related documents should not compromise the decree's terms, asserting that his intentions regarding the lien were clear and that any evidence reflecting this should be admissible in court.

In the case of The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. The City of Bloomington, the events took place in Bloomington, Illinois, during the late 19th century, specifically in 1875. The Illinois Central Railroad was constructed through the corporate limits of Bloomington in 1852. At the time of construction, Chestnut Street did not extend to the railroad. However, due to city expansions and subsequent ordinances, Chestnut Street was later planned to cross the railroad. Landowners Flagg and Davis initially granted the railroad company the right of way through their properties, which were being used for farming. When the city authorized the opening of Chestnut Street, it also required the railroad company to create a proper crossing. The railroad company refused to fulfill this obligation, prompting the city to complete the necessary grading and construction of the crossing at a cost of $634.25. The city subsequently sued the railroad company to recover these expenses, leading to a court trial where the only disputed issue was whether the railroad company was obliged to construct the crossing.	The City of Bloomington, as the plaintiff, argued that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was legally obligated to construct a safe crossing for Chestnut Street over the railroad track, as mandated by the city ordinance. The city sought to recover $634.25, the full cost incurred in grading and constructing the crossing, asserting that the railroad company should bear this financial responsibility due to its refusal to comply.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company, as the defendant, contended that there was no statutory obligation in its charter that required it to construct or maintain crossings for roads established after the railroad was built. It argued that imposing this burden on the railroad company without compensation violated constitutional principles regarding equal treatment under the law. The company maintained that it should not be subjected to a duty beyond what would be expected of a private individual under similar circumstances.

In January 1872, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case involving Chalton C. Buckles and others against The Northern Bank of Kentucky. The dispute originated from a promissory note given by Buckles and John Buckles (as surety) for an outstanding balance on a land sale which took place in October 1868. The land, measuring 926.5 acres in Logan County, was purchased from Clay & Bedford for $40 per acre, with an initial payment of $30,000. The note was issued for the remaining purchase price. A significant part of the land (106.5 acres) was believed to be improperly sold as Clay & Bedford lacked title to it. A judgment was passed against the defendants for $8,586.14, including costs; however, the judgment had been in error as it failed to deduct taxes paid on the land. Furthermore, Buckles asserted that there was a partial failure of consideration since part of the land sold was not rightfully owned by the sellers. The court also noted the procedural issue of a remittitur being filed after the judgment had already been rendered.	The plaintiffs, Chalton C. Buckles and others, claimed that the defendants (Clay & Bedford) sold them land for which they had no rightful title, affecting the value of the property. They argued that they were entitled to a judgment that properly considered the tax payments made on the property and that the court had erred in not allowing for a deduction for partial failure of consideration.	The defendants argued that the plaintiffs had no basis for claiming a failure of consideration as they acquired good title through a judicial sale. They asserted that any misstatements regarding the title did not invalidate the sale, and they contended that judicial notice should be taken concerning the circuit court's terms, which affected the timing of the remittitur filed.

In early February 1869, in Springfield, Illinois, Alfred A. North and his wife, America North, were involved in a legal dispute with plaintiff James Phillips. Phillips had previously obtained a judgment against North for $5,422.58, of which $4,000 had been paid, leaving a remaining amount due of $1,753. Following the judgment, Phillips attempted to collect on the debt by filing a creditor's bill, asserting that North had fraudulently conveyed certain lots to his wife to evade creditors. The facts revealed that on February 2, 1869, North transferred ownership of the lots to Allen, who in turn conveyed them back to Mrs. North, leading Phillips to seek the sale of a different lot in a subsequent transaction. Both Alfred and America North contended that these transactions were legitimate exchanges of property and did not intend to hinder Phillips’s ability to collect on the debt.	James Phillips claimed that Alfred North engaged in fraudulent conveyance of properties intended to evade his creditors. He argued that the transfers made from North to Allen and then back to North's wife were designed to protect North's assets from being subject to Phillips's judgment. Phillips sought a court order to have the lot in dispute sold to satisfy his judgment against North.	Alfred North and America North defended against Phillips's claims by asserting that the transactions were made in good faith and were legitimate exchanges involving property that America North owned. They maintained that there was no intent to defraud Phillips and that any property given in exchange was fairly owned by America North. The defendants emphasized that since there was no proven fraud, the transactions should not be viewed as fraudulent in law concerning Phillips's creditor claims.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. v. Charles E. Lippincott, Auditor, etc." was decided in September 1872 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The primary individuals involved were Norman L. Freeman, the petitioner and Reporter of the Decisions of the court, and Charles E. Lippincott, the State Auditor. The dispute arose when Freeman, having delivered ten volumes of the court reports to the Secretary of State, demanded to receive payment for them. Lippincott refused to issue a warrant for payment, claiming that the law authorizing such payments had been repealed by section 18 of article 4 of the Illinois Constitution. The case revolves around whether this constitutional provision nullified previous laws regarding appropriations for the payment of court report volumes.	The plaintiff, represented by Norman L. Freeman, contended that under existing laws, he was entitled to receive payment for the ten volumes of court reports he had delivered. Freeman argued that the relevant statutes that required the auditor to compensate him were still in effect and had not been repealed by the constitutional provision cited by Lippincott. He sought a writ of mandamus from the court to compel the auditor to issue the payment warrant amounting to sixty dollars.	The defendant, Charles E. Lippincott, claimed that the law under which Freeman expected payment was invalidated by the 18th section of article 4 of the state constitution, which outlined the end of all appropriations requiring state treasury funds. Lippincott argued that all financial obligations related to previous appropriations ceased at the end of the first fiscal quarter after the adjournment of the last general assembly, implying that Freeman's claim for payment could not be honored.

The case of The Peoria and Rock Island Railroad Company v. Sylvia L. Lane, Admx. etc. originated from an incident in which Oliver N. Lane was killed due to an accident involving a baggage car on a train operated by the Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Company. The accident occurred while the train was using a section of track owned by The Peoria and Rock Island Railroad Company, which had a financial agreement with the operator of the train. Sylvia L. Lane, as the administratrix of Oliver's estate, filed a lawsuit in Rock Island County, which was later moved to Warren County. The trial concluded with a jury awarding $4,708.33 in damages to Lane, claiming the railroad company was negligent in its duties of ensuring safety, allowing improper use of the track and failing to secure switches properly. The judgment was incidentally linked to complex issues surrounding responsibility for negligence when multiple companies are involved in train operations.	The plaintiff, Sylvia L. Lane, claims that The Peoria and Rock Island Railroad Company was negligent in permitting the Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Company to use their tracks without adequate safety measures. She argues that the accident, resulting in her husband's death, was caused by the negligence of the railroad company in maintaining the tracks and the switches, and that the company should be held responsible for damages due to this negligence.	The defendant, The Peoria and Rock Island Railroad Company, contends that they are not liable for the negligence of the Rockford, Rock Island and St. Louis Railroad Company, the operator of the train involved in the accident. They argue that any negligence occurred was solely within the responsibility of the other company, as they were merely allowing the other company to operate on their tracks. Additionally, the company asserts that the deceased displayed a high degree of negligence by leaving a safe area (the passenger car) for a more dangerous one (the baggage car), thus absolving them from liability unless gross misconduct could be proven on their part.

The case "Solon Cummings et al. v. David B. McKinney" arose in December 1842 in the Illinois Supreme Court, involving a legal dispute between the plaintiffs, Solon Cummings and others, and the defendant, David B. McKinney, who served as a constable. The background of the case dates back to January 4, 1840, when the plaintiffs obtained a judgment against John Sims from a justice of the peace in Lee County for a sum of $50.16. Following this, on January 25, 1840, an execution was issued against Sims, which McKinney seized. However, it was alleged that McKinney falsely reported the seizure, stating "no property found," despite there being sufficient goods to satisfy the debt. The action brought forth claims of a false return to an execution from the plaintiffs. During the trial, it was shown that the plaintiffs had provided a purported indemnifying bond to McKinney, but the court determined that their notices to produce this bond were insufficient. As a result, the jury was instructed not to consider evidence regarding the bond. The case went to trial in May 1842 in the Lee Circuit Court, and a verdict was found for McKinney. Following this, the plaintiffs appealed the decision.	The plaintiffs, Solon Cummings and others, argued that McKinney, in his capacity as a constable, had failed to properly execute the court judgment against John Sims, thereby wrongfully returning the execution with a claim of "no property found." They sought compensation for this alleged neglect of duty, asserting that McKinney had sufficient property available to satisfy their judgment. Additionally, they contended that the court's rulings on the notices concerning the indemnifying bond were erroneous.	The defendant, David B. McKinney, maintained that he had acted appropriately in executing his duties as a constable and that the plaintiffs' notices regarding the indemnifying bond were insufficient. McKinney claimed that they had failed to present evidence supporting their assertions regarding the bond and that nothing required him to guarantee indemnity prior to making the levy. He requested that the court uphold the jury's verdict in his favor, indicating there was no neglect on his part.

In 1882, Albert M. Forbes issued a promissory note to Charles Schmidt for $400, which was to be paid six months later. Clemens J. Pausinsky, as assignee of the note, brought action against Forbes for its payment. Forbes' defense was based on a special plea of failure of consideration, arguing that the note was obtained through fraudulent representation regarding shares of stock of the Germania Mining and Smelting Company. Forbes contended that he had agreed to buy 500 shares of fully paid, non-assessable stock, but it was later discovered that the stock was not as represented. The lack of proper consideration for the note was supported by evidence demonstrating that only a fraction had been paid on the shares, which both Schmidt and Pausinsky were aware of at the time of the transaction. The first instance in court resulted in a judgment for Pausinsky, which Forbes appealed, leading to further examination of the validity of the note under contract law principles involving failure of consideration.	Pausinsky claimed that the promissory note was valid and enforceable, seeking the full amount owed. He contended that, as the assignee of the note, he was entitled to recover the funds specified, asserting that Forbes' defenses regarding the stock's fraudulent sale did not apply to his right to payment.	Forbes maintained that the note was void due to a failure of consideration, asserting that the stock he purchased was misrepresented as fully paid and non-assessable, when in fact it was not. He argued that both Schmidt and Pausinsky had knowledge of this defect before the note was transferred and that he had offered to return the worthless stock in exchange for the note, which was refused.

Knox College filed a suit in chancery in April 1863 against Timothy Moshier and William B. Patterson for the foreclosure of a mortgage executed on January 1, 1856, for the purchase of land in Knox County, Illinois. The mortgage was duly recorded on April 24, 1857, and was granted as security for a loan of $750. The appellant, Moshier, claimed that he had a legitimate interest in the property through a deed executed by Patterson, which he believed was not subject to the complainant's mortgage. The court proceedings involved a battle over the validity of Moshier’s claim regarding notice of the mortgage and the subsequent amendment of the complaint to include allegations of that notice. The case involved several hearings and testimonies, ultimately leading to a decree of foreclosure and sale of the mortgaged premises, with Moshier appealing this decision on multiple grounds, including the admissibility of testimony and the court's approval of amendments to the complaint.	The plaintiff, Knox College, argued that the mortgage it held on the property was valid and enforceable, and sought a decree for foreclosure and sale of the property to satisfy unpaid debts. Knox College contended that Moshier was aware of the mortgage and did not make any payments towards it, thus his claim of an interest in the property was secondary and subject to their lien.	Timothy Moshier contended that he had a valid interest in the property through a deed from Patterson, executed on March 5, 1857, prior to the recording of the mortgage. He denied having knowledge of the mortgage at the time of acquiring the deed and argued that he was a bona fide purchaser. Moshier claimed that the evidence against him was not sufficient and that he should not have been punished through the foreclosure decree.

In 1867, in Saline County, Illinois, Andrew J. Webber purchased land from Bales for $1,500. Webber received the deed, which was recorded later that day. On the same day, George B. Groves, who had a pending legal action against Bales in Franklin County, executed an attachment that was delivered to the sheriff. This attachment was levied on the same land after Webber received his deed, although the certificate of the levy was not filed until several days later. Groves pursued the case against Bales in court, resulting in a special execution against the same property. Webber filed a bill in equity to prevent the sale, arguing it would cloud his title. The case was heard in Perry County, where a decree favored Webber, enjoining the sale. Groves and others subsequently appealed the decision. The main contention revolved around whether there was equitable jurisdiction since the defendant claimed he had an adequate legal remedy.	Groves and his co-plaintiffs claimed that their attachment and subsequent execution process should take precedence over Webber's purchase. They argued that their legal action was valid and that Webber was not a bona fide purchaser, thus their rights to the property via the attachment should be upheld.	Webber countered that he was a bona fide purchaser, having paid for the land and received the deed prior to the attachment being issued. He claimed there was no complicity in any fraudulent activity related to his purchase and that the court had jurisdiction to prevent a sale that would create a cloud on his title, as he had a legitimate legal interest in the property.

On April 28, 1882, the Davis Sewing Machine Company (lessors) leased certain commercial premises in Cook County, Illinois, to Walter Scates and John M. Greist for five years, ending on April 30, 1887. During their lease term, Scates and Greist operated a business under the name “Chicago Attachment Company” alongside their own. In February 1883, Greist sold his interest in the company to Thomas S. Ridgway. Later that March, Scates leased a part of the premises, signing both his name and Ridgway’s. By July 1883, Scates and Ridgway incorporated, establishing the Chicago Attachment Company, which recorded that it would receive properties from the two men as full payment for shares. They executed a bill of sale for the joint property, anticipated to include everything necessary for their business, excluding the lease. Although the lease mentioned restrictions on assignment without lessor consent, disputes arose over the appellants' responsibilities after they abandoned the premises on July 1, 1884. This led to claims for unpaid rent, with the lessors asserting that the appellants were liable as assignees of the lease.	The plaintiff, Davis Sewing Machine Company, claimed that the Chicago Attachment Company was liable for unpaid rent following the abandonment of the leased premises. They argued that the assignment of the lease had not been executed properly and that the appellants should be responsible for honoring the lease terms, as they accepted the benefits of the lease.	The defendants, Chicago Attachment Company, contended that the rental agreement was invalid due to the lease's assignment conditions not being met (lack of lessor consent) and the alleged improper application of the statute of frauds. They argued that because the assignment was made without written consent, they should not be held responsible for the rent owed.

The case "John Culver v. Alonzo Elwell" was heard in September 1874 in Cook County, Illinois, before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case centered around a construction contract in which John Culver engaged William E. Lockman to build five buildings on different lots within Culver's addition to Evanston. Alonzo Elwell, claiming to be a subcontractor, petitioned for his claims, alleging that other parties, specifically Philo Marsh and Benjamin Peoney, provided labor and materials for the construction. Marsh and Peoney filed separate answers, asserting similar claims and requesting that their contributions be adjudicated, alongside seeking a mechanic’s lien on the properties. A jury trial concluded with a verdict for Elwell, Marsh, and Peoney to recover a total of $1,113.47 from Culver. Following a motion for a new trial that was denied, the court ruled that the amount would be divided among the parties involved, with specific amounts designated for each. Culver appealed the decision citing various errors in the trial process, particularly regarding the lack of a formal issue for jury trial and procedural missteps related to the adjudication of claims.	The plaintiffs, Elwell, Marsh, and Peoney, argued that they were entitled to recover amounts for labor and materials provided during the construction of the five buildings under the subcontractor agreement. They sought to establish mechanic's liens on the properties as security for their claims and requested the court to adjudicate the respective amounts owed to each party.	Culver, the defendant, contended that there were no properly joined issues for the jury to decide and objected to the trial proceeding without his opportunity to respond to the claims set forth by Marsh and Peoney. He argued that the court erred by failing to give him sufficient time to prepare his defense and maintain that the judgment against him was inappropriate because it did not include a verdict against the original contractor, Lockman. Culver asserted that the verdict and decree were not consistent with statutory requirements for mechanic's liens and claimed errors in how the liens were addressed concerning the distinct buildings involved.

Bartholomew Cunningham and James O'Donnell, co-partners, initiated a legal action against William L. Wright before Justice of the Peace Peter Foote in Cook County, Illinois, on March 30, 1887. The summons for the case was scheduled for April 11, 1887, but neither party appeared at the time of the continuance, leading to a rescheduling of the case. When the case was called again on April 18, 1887, only the defendant, Wright, attended. The justice rendered a judgment in favor of the defendant for $69 and costs after hearing Wright's testimony. An execution was issued on May 10, 1887, which was returned unsatisfied by July 19, 1887. The defendant subsequently filed a transcript of the judgment with the Circuit Court, leading to an execution being levied on Cunningham's goods on December 20, 1887. Cunningham then motioned the Circuit Court to set aside the judgment and quash the execution, which was denied.	The plaintiff, Bartholomew Cunningham, claimed that the judgment rendered against him by the justice lacked jurisdiction because he was not present at the trial and argued that the statute requires dismissal of the suit in the event of the plaintiff's absence without consent for a continuance. Cunningham sought to have the judgment set aside, quash the execution, and release the levy on his property.	William L. Wright, the defendant, argued that the absence of the plaintiff during the proceedings allowed the justice to rightly grant him a judgment. He maintained that the existence of his cross-claims or setoffs against Cunningham did not alter the automatic dismissal rule regarding the plaintiff's absence and opposed Cunningham's motion to quash the execution. Wright's position was that the proceedings followed the statutory requirements for judgment given the circumstances.

John W. Laimbeer v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. William Swineburn is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1868. The dispute arose from the results of the November 1866 election for the position of constable in Cicero, Cook County, Illinois. John W. Laimbeer was elected to the office, but William Swineburn, who had competed against him, filed a legal challenge (an information in the nature of a quo warranto) claiming that Laimbeer was not eligible for the position. Swineburn alleged that Laimbeer had not been a resident of the town of Cicero for the required one year prior to the election, as stipulated in the township organization law of 1861. Upon examination, the court found that Laimbeer had not been a resident of Cicero for the requisite time, having lived in several different locations, including Chicago, Missouri, and returning to Cicero only a few months before the election. The court upheld that Laimbeer held the office without legal authority due to his ineligibility.	The plaintiff, William Swineburn, claims that John W. Laimbeer was not eligible to serve as constable as he did not meet the residency requirement of being a resident of Cicero for one year prior to the election. Swineburn sought to have Laimbeer ousted from office by arguing that the election was invalid due to this lack of residency.	Laimbeer, represented by Messrs. Hurd, Booth & Kreamer, likely asserted that he met the residency requirement and perhaps disputed the interpretation or application of the residency law. However, the verdict from the jury found otherwise, leading to the affirmation of the judgment against him.

On March 17, 1857, Alexander Beard, elected as a marshal in Beardstown, Illinois, executed a bond in the amount of $1,000 to the County Court of Cass County, with the appellants John B. Shaw, Joseph H. Shaw, and Henry Menke serving as his sureties. The bond stipulated that Beard must properly account for and pay all moneys collected through his duties. In February 1858, summons was issued against Beard and his sureties for failing to return an execution within the required timeframe. The first bond for costs was filed on June 3, 1858, but was deemed improper. The court allowed a cross-motion to amend the bond after denying the appellants' request to dismiss the case due to lack of a proper bond. The Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Harriott, ruled against the appellants for $1,000 in damages and allowed an execution to issue for $63.61. The appellants disputed the court's decisions through an appeal process.	The plaintiffs, represented by C. H. C. Havekluft and justices of the County Court of Cass, argued that the appellants, as sureties on Beard's bond, were liable for his failure to fulfill his duties as constable. They maintained that the bond was valid and that the subsequent bond amendments were acceptable for ensuring the recovery of funds owed due to Beard's alleged negligence.	The defendants (the appellants) contended that the court erred by not allowing their motion to dismiss the suit based on the improper bond for costs. They claimed that there was no legitimate bond filed at the initiation of the suit and that the court exceeded its authority by ruling against them without sufficient legal basis. They sought to have the case dismissed on these grounds.

Henry Utley v. Fanny B. Burns is a legal case that took place in June 1873 in Whiteside County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Fanny B. Burns, sued the defendant, Henry Utley, a physician and surgeon, alleging that he provided unskillful treatment for her fractured arm. After a trial, the jury ruled in favor of Burns, resulting in a judgment awarding her damages amounting to $800. The defendant subsequently sought to reverse the judgment through a writ of error, claiming the court erred by denying his motion for a change of venue and by giving specific jury instructions. The case highlights issues of medical malpractice and the standards of care expected from surgeons.	The plaintiff, Fanny B. Burns, claimed that Henry Utley, the defendant, failed to provide the necessary skill and care in treating her fractured arm, resulting in damages. She requested compensation for the alleged unskillful treatment that caused her injury, arguing that the level of care a surgeon must provide must correspond to the injury's severity.	The defendant, Henry Utley, argued that the court erred in its rulings, particularly by not allowing a change of venue, which he claimed was warranted. He contended that the jury instructions regarding the standard of care were incorrect, asserting that a surgeon should be held to a reasonable standard of care, not one proportionate to the severity of the injury. He requested a reversal of the judgment based on these claims.

In December 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, a judgment promissory note for $775 was executed by Casterline in favor of the appellee, Charles H. Mullikin, to secure a debt of $776. As collateral, Casterline provided a chattel mortgage on a stock of monuments that he was manufacturing in Chicago. Casterline was permitted to retain possession of the goods until he defaulted on the payment. By July 1884, after Casterline failed to repay the debt, William T. Hixon obtained a judgment against him for $237.92 and executed a writ of execution, which led to the sheriff seizing Casterline's goods. Mullikin then replevied the goods, asserting his rights under the chattel mortgage. The jury ruled in favor of Mullikin, but Hixon appealed, leading to an examination of whether Mullikin’s mortgage retained validity despite Casterline's continued possession and the timing of actions taken post-default.	Hixon claimed that Mullikin’s chattel mortgage should have been invalidated due to Mullikin's failure to take possession of the goods promptly after the debt's maturity. Hixon argued that Mullikin's delayed action constituted a fraudulent design to protect the goods from other creditors. Hixon sought the court to affirm his rights to the seized property under the execution of his judgment against Casterline.	Mullikin's defense rested on the legality of his chattel mortgage and the understanding that it allowed Casterline to retain possession until default. Mullikin contended that he had a legitimate claim over the property based on the mortgage's terms. He asserted that any actions taken concerning the goods were within the bounds of a valid mortgage arrangement, and thus he requested that the court uphold the jury's verdict in his favor regarding the ownership of the goods.

In 1848, James H. Rees brought an ejectment action against the City of Chicago concerning a thirty-one-foot parcel of land at the south end of lot five in block two of the original town of Chicago. The city had previously commenced condemnation proceedings to transform this land into part of a public street known as North Water Street. Initial ownership of the property belonged to W. G. and G. W. Ewing, who had leased the land. In January 1849, the City Council passed an order to establish North Water Street, leading to the condemnation of the land. The Ewings did not contest the condemnation and accepted the compensation awarded. Although a subsequent court ruling in 1851 reversed the judgment affecting parties appealing the assessments, the Ewings continued to acknowledge and act in favor of the street being established. Rees ultimately acquired the remaining interest in 1856 through a deed following a partition sale in which they relinquished their interests.	Rees, as the plaintiff in error, argued that he had a legitimate title to the land following the partition sale and contended that the land had neither been legally condemned nor dedicated for public use by the Ewings. He asserted that any actions taken by the city regarding the street were invalid since they did not follow proper legal protocols and challenged any claims of estoppel by the city due to the previous court ruling that had affirmed his title.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant in error, maintained that the land had been validly condemned for public use, and thus, they possessed rightful ownership. They provided evidence showing that the Ewings had accepted compensation for the land and had acted in a manner indicating their intent to dedicate the property for public use. The city argued that the prior condemnation proceedings legally divided the title, and since the Ewings acquiesced to the public use of the property as a street, the plaintiff was estopped from claiming ownership.

In 1881, Robert C. Martin was indicted in the Circuit Court of Perry County, Illinois, for assault with intent to inflict bodily injury. He was required to post a $500 bail, and the plaintiffs acted as his sureties. Following the indictment, the proceedings were certified to the county court for trial. A capias was issued for Martin's arrest and served, leading to the sureties entering into a recognizance for Martin's appearance in the county court. However, during the February term of 1882, the circuit court judge, previously involved as Martin's attorney, ordered the case transferred back to the Circuit Court of Perry County for trial. At the May 1882 term, Martin failed to appear, resulting in a default judgment and a forfeiture of the recognizance issued against him and his sureties. After a series of pleadings by the sureties, which included a general demurrer and a plea of nul tiel record, the court ultimately ruled against them for the penalty and court costs, prompting an appeal on the grounds of jurisdiction over the case and the validity of the transfer.	The plaintiffs claimed that the sureties should be held liable for the forfeited recognizance, as the defendant Martin failed to appear in the circuit court. They argued that the transfer from the county court to the circuit court was valid and binding under the recognizance agreement.	The defendant’s main argument focused on the assertion that the Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction over the case, as the transfer from the county court was invalid due to the county judge's earlier involvement as an attorney. They contended that the recognizance was strictly for Martin's appearance in the county court, and hence they could not be held liable for failing to appear in the circuit court, as that venue change was unauthorized.

In 1884, in Knox County, Illinois, Andrew J. Combs was involved in a legal dispute initiated by Mary Lanfear, who filed an affidavit for a writ of attachment claiming that Combs owed her $400 for services rendered. The Sheriff, John A. Stuckey, executed the writ, seizing Combs' property. On January 19, 1884, a bond was executed by Combs, with Stuckey as the surety, facilitating the release of the seized property. However, Lanfear later amended her affidavit to include additional debts not originally stated. The attachment proceedings culminated in a judgment for Lanfear against Combs for $125.60 and the costs associated with the case. The case subsequently led to an appeal regarding the validity of the bond and whether Stuckey, as the surety, was liable for the judgment resulting from the amended affidavit.	The plaintiff, representing Mary Lanfear, argued that the Surety Bond signed by John A. Stuckey made him liable for the judgment rendered against Andrew J. Combs in the attachment suit, regardless of the amendments made to the original affidavit. They contended that the amendment to the affidavit was valid and that Stuckey should bear responsibility for any judgment resulting from that suit, given his role as a surety on the bond.	John A. Stuckey, the defendant, contended that his liability on the bond was limited to the original cause of action outlined in the initial affidavit, which did not include the additional items of indebtedness added later. He argued that the judgment rendered was not based on the same cause of action as the original attachment suit, thus questioning his obligation under the bond in light of these amendments.

In the case of William Sharp et al. v. H. A. Smith et al., which was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on February 14, 1890, the dispute arose between the school directors of District No. 2 in Moultrie County, Illinois, and the contractors who were to build a brick schoolhouse for the district. The contract, signed on August 11, 1888, stated that Hugh A. Smith and Riley W. Creech would construct the schoolhouse in exchange for $924.60. Prior to the contract, the legal voters of the district had approved funding of $700 for the construction. After the schoolhouse was completed, the directors issued an order for the remaining balance, but payment was blocked by a legal injunction from some taxpayers. The central legal question revolved around whether the directors, particularly Sharp and Coplin, were personally liable under the contract or if the liability lay solely with the school district.	The plaintiffs, William Sharp, Joshua Coplin, and Christopher Monroe, claimed that despite having completed the construction of the schoolhouse, they were left unpaid for part of the contract due to the injunction issued by the taxpayers. They argued that the directors should be held individually liable for the full amount of the contract because their names appeared directly on the contract, indicating they were acting as individuals, rather than solely in their capacity as directors of the school district.	The defendants, H. A. Smith and Riley W. Creech, contended that they entered into the contract with the school district as a whole and not with the individual directors. They argued that the contract did not explicitly bind the directors in their personal capacity, and thus, any claims against them should be dismissed since they were acting on behalf of the district.

In the case of Schaub v. Risser, decided on February 20, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the plaintiff, Mary E. Schaub, sued R. G. Risser and Charles E. Dashiell over two promissory notes. The notes were signed with the firm name Risser & Dashiell, one for $400 due thirty days after its date of July 25, 1881, and the other for $500 due one day after its date of September 13, 1881. Both were made payable to Upton Schaub, Mary’s husband, who assigned them to her on November 25, 1881. Dashiell was not served in the case. Risser denied joint liability and pled the general issue. During the trial, the main issue was whether Upton Schaub was aware that the money loaned was not intended for the firm’s business but rather for Dashiell's personal use in purchasing goods. There was conflicting testimony, with Risser and Dashiell’s accounts suggesting non-liability and the Schaub’s account implying otherwise. The court ultimately found in favor of Risser, ruling that the evidence supported his denial of liability.	The plaintiff, Mary E. Schaub, claimed that R. G. Risser and Charles E. Dashiell were jointly responsible for repaying the two promissory notes made out for $400 and $500. She argued that the notes were valid and sought to enforce their repayment under the terms stipulated. Her main contention was that Upton Schaub, at the time he secured the notes, intended for the funds to benefit the firm rather than for personal use, thereby implicating Risser in the liability.	The defendant, R. G. Risser, provided the primary argument that he should not be held jointly liable for the promissory notes signed by the firm. He approached the case by denying joint liability under oath and contended that the funds were not used for the firm’s business. Risser's defense hinged on the assertion that Upton Schaub was aware that the money was to be used solely for Dashiell's personal expenses, thus absolving him of any obligation to repay the loans.

Daniel O’Hara filed a replevin action against Judson M. W. Jones in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a dispute over goods claimed by Jones under a distress warrant for unpaid rent. The incident took place in Chicago in April 1867, involving a commercial lease for a store at 122 Lake Street, which James H. Lynch rented from Jones. The lease, dated July 20, 1866, granted Jones a lien on Lynch’s property as security for rental payments, which were set at $5,000 total and due monthly. By March 1, 1867, Lynch had accumulated four months of unpaid rent, totaling $1,666.67. Following a general assignment of his property to O'Hara for the benefit of creditors on March 9, Lynch transferred control of the store and its contents to the plaintiff. Jones subsequently exercised his right to levy upon the goods while O'Hara continued selling them until the distress notice. The Cook Circuit Court ruled in favor of Jones after a jury was waived, which led O'Hara to motion for a new trial, ultimately seeking judgment for the return of the goods.	The plaintiff, Daniel O’Hara, argued that the goods taken by Jones were rightfully in his possession following their assignment from Lynch. O'Hara contended that the landlord's lien claimed by Jones did not supersede his rights as an assignee of Lynch’s estate. The plaintiff sought the return of the goods and payment for losses incurred due to their unlawful detention.	Judson M. W. Jones defended his actions by asserting that under the lease agreement, he retained a valid lien on all of Lynch's property for unpaid rent. Jones argued that the assignment of goods to O'Hara did not extinguish his lien rights, as O'Hara, as an assignee, took the goods subject to the existing debts and liens. He requested the court to uphold the validity of his distress warrant and affirm his right to retain possession of the goods.

John McGanahan v. The East St. Louis and Carondelet Railway Co. is a legal case that took place in March 1873 when McGanahan was employed as a brakeman by the East St. Louis and Carondelet Railway Company. While performing his duties of coupling freight cars, he sustained injuries when one of the cars he was working with came together violently, resulting in his right hand getting caught between them. McGanahan claimed that the defendant failed to provide safe equipment, specifically citing that the car used to transport railroad iron was shorter than necessary, causing the iron to project over the ends, which contributed to his injury. The incident occurred on the defendant's tracks, where McGanahan was engaged in his job duties, while the train was backing up to couple with the box car. Subsequently, he filed a lawsuit seeking damages for the injuries suffered, alleging negligence on the part of the defendant.	McGanahan's primary argument is that the East St. Louis and Carondelet Railway Company exhibited negligence by providing unsafe coupling equipment that inadequately accommodated the size of the railroad iron being transported. He contends that the railway company had a duty to furnish safe and suitable cars and appliances, which they failed to do, leading to his injury. McGanahan seeks damages for the injuries sustained due to the company's negligence while he was performing his job.	The defendant, East St. Louis and Carondelet Railway Co., argued that McGanahan's declaration did not adequately demonstrate that their alleged negligence directly caused his injury. They contended that the injury was not due to the iron projecting over the end of the car but rather was a result of McGanahan’s actions while coupling the cars. Therefore, the defendant asserted that the claim did not provide sufficient grounds for recovery as it failed to link their negligence directly to McGanahan’s injury.

In November 1882, Erastus H. Ferris, a captain of a schooner, lost his vessel on the Great Lakes and sought payment from his insurance company, the Marine Insurance Company of Buffalo. He received two drafts for $511.33 and $1980 from E. K. Bruce, the insurance company’s agent in Chicago. Unsure of how to handle the collection of these drafts due to his unfamiliarity with local banks, Bruce introduced Ferris to Schweisthal, the cashier at the International Bank of Chicago on December 26, 1882. After endorsing the drafts, Ferris directed that the smaller draft be turned over to Bruce, and the bank agreed to collect the larger draft, for which it charged a $15 fee. Disputes arose regarding the instructions given to the bank about the disposition of the collected amount. While Ferris claimed that the cash should be held until he called for it, the bank contended that they were instructed to hold the money until either Ferris or Bruce provided further directions. The bank collected $1980 but credited it to Bruce's overdrawn account without clear indication that Ferris had directed this payment to Bruce. Ferris filed a legal action against the bank for the amount collected, leading to a jury trial and an eventual appeal.	Ferris argued that he instructed the International Bank to collect the larger draft and hold the proceeds until he called for them. He maintained that the bank acted in violation of these instructions by paying the money to Bruce instead of holding it for him, thus making the bank liable for the amount collected. Ferris sought a judgment for the balance due after accounting for the smaller draft.	The International Bank defended itself by asserting that Ferris either directly or through Bruce authorized the bank to collect the money and hold it subject to the order of either party. The bank claimed that it followed proper instructions when crediting Bruce’s account, especially since Bruce's directive was provided in Ferris’s presence. The bank argued it was not liable to Ferris if it was acting upon valid instructions regarding the disposition of the funds.

In 1889, a legal case titled "Daniel J. Campau v. Henry V. Bemis" took place in Cook County, Illinois. The case involved a dispute over three oil paintings that portrayed famous horses, namely “St. Julien,” “Bunesotter,” and “Little Brown Jug.” Daniel J. Campau, the plaintiff, claimed ownership of these paintings, which he had previously displayed in the office of "The Horseman" newspaper company, where he was president. After selling his stock in the company to Henry V. Bemis, the defendant, the paintings remained in the office. Discrepancies arose over their ownership when Bemis claimed they belonged to the corporation rather than to Campau. Campau requested the paintings be sent to him, but Bemis instructed an employee not to send them, arguing they were corporate property. The jury found in favor of Campau, determining the artwork was rightfully his, leading to a verdict of $1,500 against Bemis. Bemis appealed the decision, contesting the evidence of conversion and Campau's ownership.	The plaintiff, Daniel J. Campau, asserted his rightful ownership of the three oil paintings. He argued that the paintings were never sold to the Chicago Horseman Newspaper Company, despite their display in its office. Campau requested the court to recognize him as the legal owner of the paintings and sought damages for their wrongful retention by the defendant, Henry V. Bemis, totaling $1,500.	The defendant, Henry V. Bemis, contended that the paintings were the property of the Chicago Horseman Newspaper Company, of which he claimed ownership following his acquisition of Campau's stock. He argued that there had been no formal demand for the paintings nor proof of actual conversion. Bemis asserted that his instructions to the employee were in line with protecting the company's assets, and he requested the court to dismiss the action based on a lack of evidence supporting Campau's claims.

In September 1874, the case of Alonzo Gage et al. v. John Schroder was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court concerning an action of ejectment for two tracts of land. The plaintiffs, Alonzo Gage, Allen Mulleins, and Samantha J. Mulleins, claimed to be the children and only heirs of Stephen I. Gage, who had passed away. The defendant, John Schroder, held a deed derived from a sale ordered by the county court of Lake County in May of 1863, executed by Leonard Loomis, the administrator of Stephen I. Gage's estate, to pay off debts. A significant issue arose during the trial regarding the proof of the original petition and other court documents which were lost. The court permitted the use of parol evidence to establish the contents of these lost records, leading to a judgment in favor of the defendant, underscoring the complexities of jurisdiction and evidence in cases involving the heirs of deceased individuals.	The plaintiffs asserted that they held rightful title to the disputed land as heirs of Stephen I. Gage. They challenged the validity of the defendant's claim to the property, arguing that the court proceedings which led to the transfer of the title were flawed due to the absence of a guardian ad litem appointed for the infant defendants during the sale process. Their legal request was to recover the two tracts of land based on their asserted ownership rights.	The defendant, John Schroder, contended that the sale of the property had been legally conducted as per the decree of the county court, which had acquired jurisdiction through the filing of a petition and proper service of notice. He argued that the process was valid even in the absence of a guardian ad litem, pointing out that the failure to appoint one did not negate the court's jurisdiction, thus enabling the sale and the title transfer to remain lawful. His request was for the court to uphold the validity of the previous court's judgment and affirm the sale of the property.

In the case of Joseph Gartside et al. v. John J. Outley et al., dated January 1871, the dispute arose over certain coal lands in Illinois, primarily concerning the rights to these lands stemming from historical leases and mortgages. The Belleville & Illinoistown Railroad Company executed a lease to John A. Twiss on May 9, 1856, granting him rights to mine coal for an indefinite period, which was subject to forfeiture for non-compliance. In March 1853 and May 1855, the railroad company also executed deeds of trust to secure mortgage bonds, effectively asserting prior rights over the property in question. After several legal and operational changes, including a consolidation of railroad companies and the foreclosure of the deeds of trust in 1862, the St. Louis, Alton & Terre Haute Railroad Company eventually acquired the property. However, by the time this ownership was established, Twiss and his assignees were not in possession of the lands. There were controversies over the lease's forfeiture and the subsequent rights of the parties involved, particularly whether Twiss’s surrender of rights was lawful or aimed at fraudulent ends.	The plaintiffs, Joseph Gartside et al., claimed to be the legal successors to the rights established under the original lease with Twiss. They argued for possession of the coal lands based on the validity of the lease and contended that even after the various transfers and encumbrances, their rights as assignees were unjustly ignored, particularly during the sale of the property that involved the foreclosures of the railroad's debts.	The defendants, John J. Outley et al., maintained that the plaintiffs had no legal claim to the coal lands because the original lease had been forfeited prior to their acquisition of the property. They argued that when the mortgagee took possession due to default, all rights under the lease were terminated. The defendants further argued that any acceptance of rent by the mortgagee did not equate to a valid lease extension beyond a year-to-year tenancy, and they contested the legitimacy of the plaintiffs' claims regarding the sale and the lease instrument itself.

The case "The Safety Deposit Life Insurance Company v. Samuel C. Smith" took place in Illinois, with the final decision being rendered in September 1872. Samuel C. Smith, the appellee, was employed as a bookkeeper by one of the corporators of the Safety Deposit Life Insurance Company before the company was officially organized. His employment began around January 1870 and continued until the company was established in March or April of that year. Upon the company's formation, Smith did not inform the stockholders of the services he had rendered or that he expected compensation for them. Additionally, there was no evidence that the company used Smith's labor or acknowledged his service for payment. The case presented questions similar to a prior case, Rockford, Rock Island & St. Louis R. R. Co. v. Sage, which had been decided on similar grounds. Ultimately, the court determined that there was no basis for recovery for Smith's claims.	Samuel C. Smith, the plaintiff, claims that he is entitled to payment for the bookkeeping services he rendered to the company prior to its official organization. He argues that his services were beneficial to the company and that he expected to be compensated for his work, despite not having claimed this before the stockholders when the company was established.	The defendant, Safety Deposit Life Insurance Company, contends that there is no liability for the services performed by Smith prior to the company's organization. The defense argues that at the time of formation, neither Smith nor anyone else informed the stockholders of his services or of any expectation to receive payment. Furthermore, they assert that there is no evidence of the company appropriating his labor or agreeing to pay him for these services.

In December 1882, F. M. Willard mortgaged two horses to George W. McMahill to secure a note for $2.50 due one year later. Before the note's due date, Willard attempted to sell the horses to McMahill, delivering the note and mortgage papers but retaining possession of the horses. In December 1883, just after this arrangement, Willard re-mortgaged the same horses to Martin Humes to secure a new debt of $190. Early in January 1884, McMahill replevied the horses from Willard and subsequently, Humes took action to replevy them from McMahill, claiming his rights under the new mortgage. The central issue in the trial was whether the attempted sale and delivery to McMahill was valid and completed as per legal requirements, particularly whether there was actual delivery of possession that would protect McMahill's claim against Humes as a subsequent purchaser. The evidence presented included testimonies from both Willard and McMahill regarding the arrangements made during the attempted sale and the context of their possession and control of the horses.	The plaintiff, Martin Humes, argued that he was an innocent purchaser of the horses with a valid mortgage. He claimed that McMahill never retained actual possession of the horses necessary to establish ownership against Humes. Humes requested the court to recognize his rights under the mortgage against McMahill, emphasizing that no proper delivery had taken place that would validate McMahill’s claim.	The defendant, George W. McMahill, asserted that he had a legitimate claim to ownership based on the initial mortgage agreement and the attempted sale. He contended that he took possession of the horses, albeit briefly, and that any subsequent arrangements to loan the horses did not invalidate his ownership. McMahill's defense relied on case law to argue that he did not defraud Humes and that the court should affirm his ownership based on the evidence of the initial transaction.

The case "Harry M. Ryan v. Edward Kirchberg" took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the judgment entered on November 4, 1885. The dispute arose from a forcible detainer action, where the plaintiff, Harry M. Ryan, sought possession of leased property previously held by the defendant, Edward Kirchberg. The original lease was executed on May 31, 1884, by James B. Waller, who later assigned the lease to Ryan. The lease permitted Waller, or his assigns, to terminate the lease with a 60-day written notice. On May 1, 1885, Ryan entered judgment against Kirchberg based on a warrant of attorney in the lease. Kirchberg claimed that he had accepted a termination of the original lease and had entered into a verbal lease with Ryan for one year beginning October 1, 1884. When Ryan refused to receive the rental payment for April 1885, Kirchberg filed a motion to vacate the judgment, asserting that he had a valid defense under the alleged new verbal lease. However, the court initially overruled his motion, prompting Kirchberg to appeal, thus raising the question of whether he had a legal defense against the forcible detainer action.	The plaintiff, Harry M. Ryan, claimed that Edward Kirchberg was unlawfully occupying the leased property after the termination of the original lease. Ryan sought a judgment for forcible detainer under the warrant of attorney included in the lease agreement, alleging that Kirchberg was guilty of unlawfully remaining on the premises and requested that a judgment be entered in his favor to regain possession of the property along with costs associated with the action.	The defendant, Edward Kirchberg, argued that he had entered into a new verbal lease with Ryan, effectively surrendering the original lease. He claimed that this new lease permitted him to remain in possession of the property and that Ryan's refusal to accept the rent constituted an improper denial. Kirchberg sought to vacate the initial judgment, asserting that the evidence he presented in his affidavit stated a valid legal defense against the forcible detainer claim and required the court to give him an opportunity to present that defense.

Joseph French, the appellant, was involved in a legal case concerning slander brought against him by John R. Creath, an infant under the age of twenty-one, represented by his father, George Creath, as next friend. The case originated in the circuit court of Jackson County, Illinois, and was later moved to Randolph County due to a change of venue. The conflict arose when Creath alleged that French had made slanderous statements that accused him of a crime committed in 1815. During the trial, a verdict was reached in favor of the plaintiff. French then filed a motion for a new trial and an arrest of judgment, arguing procedural errors, namely the lack of a formal order appointing Creath's next friend and the contention that the slanderous words were not actionable because the statute for the alleged offense had been repealed. The case was eventually appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court for review.	The plaintiff claimed that Joseph French made slanderous statements that falsely accused him of committing a crime. He sought legal recognition of the harm caused by these allegations and a verdict that affirmed the action for slander despite the repeal of the statute that originally created the offense in question.	Joseph French's defense rested on two main arguments: firstly, that there was no court order appointing the next friend for the infant plaintiff, and secondly, that the allegations were not actionable since the statute under which the offense was defined had been repealed. French argued that such words could not lead to a successful slander claim due to the expiration of the relevant legal framework.

In 1885, at Grand Trunk Junction in Cook County, Illinois, John Touhy, a switchman for the Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railway Company, received severe personal injuries while attempting to couple freight cars. The switch crew, consisting of Touhy and others including Griggs, the foreman, was responsible for moving cars in the switch yard. On the day of the incident, Touhy signaled for the switch engine to back up and couple to a set of freight cars. However, as he attempted to make the coupling, his left hand was caught between the draw-bars of the cars, resulting in the amputation of two fingers and permanent damage to another. The main issue at trial was whether the railway company was legally liable for Touhy's injuries, considering the roles and responsibilities of the switch crew. It was disputed whether Touhy acted with negligence by failing to adequately signal the engineer and fulfill his duties before attempting to couple the cars.	John Touhy claimed that he was injured due to the negligence of the railway company and its employees, particularly pointing to Griggs, the foreman, for signaling the train to back up without ensuring that Touhy was clear of the cars. Touhy argued that Griggs' negligence in issuing the signal amounted to a breach of duty that caused his injury, leading him to seek $1,500 in damages for personal injuries sustained while performing his role as a switchman.	The Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railway Company contended that Touhy was himself guilty of contributory negligence. They argued that he failed to follow proper safety protocols by not signaling the engineer appropriately after making a coupling attempt and remaining between the cars, which led to his injuries. The defense claimed that the engineer acted under a legitimate signal from Griggs and that any negligence on Griggs' part did not render the company liable, as both Touhy and the engineer were fellow servants who shared the responsibilities and risks inherent in their work.

The case of The Sangamon and Morgan Railroad Co. v. Jesse Henry arose in December 1850 when Henry, the appellee, entrusted a shipment of hogs to the Sangamon and Morgan Railroad Co., the appellants, for transport from Jacksonville to Naples, Illinois. The hogs were to be delivered on the same day, as Henry intended to sell them at the St. Louis market. However, due to various delays including equipment failure and overloading, the hogs did not reach Naples until the following day. This delay resulted in significant hardship for Henry, as a steamboat he intended to use was waiting at Naples but departed without the hogs due to their late arrival. As a result, Henry incurred additional costs for feeding and caring for the hogs and ultimately had to sell them at a lower price than he could have achieved had they been delivered on time. The legal proceeding involved a jury trial where it was concluded that the railroad was liable for the damages caused by the delay.	The plaintiff, Jesse Henry, claimed that the railroad company failed to deliver his hogs on the agreed date, causing him financial loss. His main arguments revolved around the contractual obligation of the railroad to deliver the hogs on time, which they failed to fulfill. He sought damages for the decrease in value of the hogs due to the delay, the costs incurred for their care while they were late, and the loss from having to sell the hogs at a lower price than what could have been obtained in St. Louis.	The defendants, Sangamon and Morgan Railroad Co., argued that the plaintiff should only recover for any decrease in the value of the hogs due to their delayed delivery and for expenses directly related to their confinement during transit. They maintained that their liability was limited to the delivery point of Naples and contended that any future sale in St. Louis was beyond their responsibility. The defendants sought to limit the damages awarded to the plaintiff by claiming that Henry's expectations concerning the St. Louis market were immaterial to their obligations in Naples.

David L. Hough filed a chancery bill in the La Salle Circuit Court, later transferred to the Lee County Circuit Court, against Michael Coughlan and others. The case centered around a contract to convey a tract of land, which originated from a bond made by Michael Goughian to Timothy Horgan on October 2, 1849. David L. Hough was assigned this bond on January 25, 1862, over twelve years after its execution and shortly afterwards filed a legal action for specific performance regarding the land. The defendants claimed that the bond was never delivered, the consideration was not paid, and they had continuously possessed, cultivated, and improved the land since 1851, thus staking a strong claim to ownership. The Circuit Court ultimately dismissed Hough's complaint, leading him to appeal the decision.	Hough argued that he was entitled to specific performance of the contract to convey the land based on the bond assigned to him. Hough contended that his rights under the contract had been unjustly denied and that he deserved to secure the property on the basis of the legal contract that existed, seeking a reversal of the dismissal order from the lower court.	The defendants contended that the bond was never delivered to Hough and that he had no legitimate interest in the property as they had occupied it openly and made significant improvements for many years. They further argued that Hough's delay in asserting his rights constituted laches, and thus, the court should deny his request for specific performance. They highlighted that the presence of another party's claim and the public nature of their improvements should preclude Hough from succeeding in his claim.

On February 12, 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, Lewis Umlauf filed for divorce against Victoria Umlauf, citing desertion as the grounds. The initial hearing in the Superior Court took place on October 22, 1883, where a decree was issued in favor of Lewis. This decree was subsequently affirmed by the Illinois Appellate Court but reversed by the Supreme Court, leading to the case being remanded to the Superior Court for a re-hearing. While the divorce proceedings were ongoing, Victoria filed a petition on December 20, 1886, requesting alimony pendente lite for her and her two children, along with legal fees. The court ordered Lewis to pay her a total of $20 by December 25, 1886, and $10 weekly thereafter, in addition to $100 for her attorneys. Lewis appealed this order, contesting the necessity and amount of the alimony, asserting that he had limited financial means, while Victoria maintained she had no resources of her own.	Lewis claimed that Victoria was not entitled to the requested alimony because he believed she was well-off, living in a furnished home and possibly backed by financial support from another individual. He argued that his own financial situation was limited and that the court's order for alimony was unwarranted and excessive.	Victoria argued that she had no means of supporting herself or her children and needed the alimony to maintain her household and to afford legal representation in the divorce proceedings. She emphasized her financial need versus Lewis’s admitted means and argued that the amount of alimony awarded was justifiable given the circumstances of the case, including the support of their two children.

John B. Hunter, as the administrator of the estate of Samuel W. Hunter, deceased, filed a case in January 1863 against Wesley A. Bilyeu and Finis Bilyeu concerning a note executed by them dated March 30, 1850, which was due March 30, 1855. The case arose in Bond County, Illinois, where the Bilyeus claimed there were omissions and errors in a title bond related to certain lands they believed they had purchased from the intestate. They had been placed in possession of the property and made improvements but later discovered that specific tracts they believed they had bought were not included in the title bond prepared by S.W. Hunter, who had also sold some of these tracts to Joseph Smith. Despite notification of their rights, the complainants did not defend against previous proceedings filed by the administrator, thinking it was unnecessary since their rights were not in question. The Bilyeus sought to have the court order the defendants to convey the lands they believed they were owed and to cancel the actions taken on the note due from them.	The plaintiffs argue that they were wrongfully denied a title to certain tracts of land that were to be conveyed to them by Samuel W. Hunter. They seek an injunction against the collection of the note tied to these lands, request a reformation of the title bond to properly reflect the lands they were contracted to receive, and ask the court to compel the defendants to convey the proper tracts to them. They assert that errors in the bond, which omitted certain properties, should be corrected to meet the original agreement.	The defendants contest the claims, arguing that the bond accurately reflected the agreement made and that all payments were made accordingly except for the last note.
