They assert that the plaintiffs had previously failed to appear in court to protect their claims regarding the omitted lands, and stress that there’s insufficient evidence to prove any mistakes were made in the bond regarding parcel ownership. They invoke the statute of frauds to support their defenses and assert that the previous court decrees should be upheld.

In 1887, the case of Michael Mann v. City of Elgin arose in Elgin, Illinois, where Michael Mann, the appellant, was prosecuted for obstructing North Division Street, which was part of a platted addition in the city. The land originally belonged to P. J. Kimball, Jr., who created a subdivision and dedicated the street for public use. Mann claimed a parcel of this land based on his deed, which described his lot but did not explicitly include the street that his fence encroached upon. He moved his fence north into the street by 36-37 links, this action prompting the suit against him initiated by the City of Elgin. The city relied on evidence that the public had occupied and used the street for travel and that all parties involved, including Mann, had acknowledged the street’s existence for over seventeen years. The case was tried before a jury in the Circuit Court, resulting in Mann being fined $100 for violating the city ordinance related to the obstruction of streets.	The City of Elgin claimed that Michael Mann unlawfully obstructed North Division Street by moving his fence into the public right-of-way. They argued that the street had been dedicated for public use, confirmed by over seventeen years of public usage. The city maintained that Mann's actions were a clear violation of the ordinance governing the use of streets and that he was estopped from claiming ownership of the land since the street occupied part of the lot described in his deed.	Michael Mann contended that he had the right to move his fence based on his interpretation of the property deed, arguing that the platting of the subdivision was flawed as it did not properly delineate the street boundaries. He also asserted that the city's mapping and dedication of the street were not legally binding due to alleged irregularities in the platting process. Mann claimed he was merely correcting a long-standing surveying error and that his actions were not an obstruction but a rightful claim to his property.

Thomas C. Hoag filed a lawsuit against Charles Carpenter in 1886 in Cook County, Illinois, seeking to recover taxes amounting to $56.42 for the year 1882 on certain premises that Hoag had leased to Carpenter. The lease had specified that Carpenter was responsible for paying all ordinary taxes during the term. This lease started on February 1, 1872, and was later extended for another five years. At trial, Hoag presented the lease as evidence, demonstrating that he had paid the 1882 taxes while Carpenter admitted he had not. Carpenter countered with a previous lease from 1868, claiming that an oral agreement exempted him from 1882 taxes due to tax payments made for the year 1867. Evidence was presented about the original lease being destroyed in the 1871 Great Fire, and Hoag sought to create a new lease. The court found that accepting the new lease effectively surrendered any rights Carpenters may have had under the old lease, leading to a conclusion that Carpenter was responsible for the taxes.	Thomas C. Hoag claimed that under the lease agreement, Charles Carpenter was required to pay the taxes for 1882. He produced evidence of the lease and the taxes paid, arguing that Carpenter did not fulfill his contractual obligation regarding tax payments. Hoag requested a judgment for the recovery of the unpaid taxes.	Charles Carpenter argued that due to an oral agreement made at the time of the 1868 lease, he paid the prior year's taxes (for 1867) under the condition he would be exempt from paying taxes for the final year in the subsequent lease. He asserted that evidence of this agreement should release him from the obligation to pay the 1882 taxes, claiming a right based on that agreement.

Anna Bartell filed a case against John F. Bauman, the administrator of her late husband Theodore Bartell's estate, in the Illinois Appellate Court. This legal matter arose after Anna Bartell renounced her husband’s will and opted to take her share under Illinois statutory law. Following the administrator's final report, which disclosed a balance of $508.91 for distribution to heirs, Anna's creditors, Panins and Grott, sought to garnish her share of the estate, citing a prior judgment against her. The county court initially approved the administrator’s report and ordered the funds to be paid to the heirs. However, during the garnishment hearing, the court discharged the garnishee, leading to the appeal in question. The nature of the case revolves around whether the funds were in the hands of the administrator as part of his legal obligation or if Anna Bartell had a personal claim to them that could be garnished.	The plaintiff, Anna Bartell, claims that the funds in the hands of the administrator should be subject to garnishment to satisfy her creditors. She argues that, as a widow entitled to her statutory share of her deceased husband’s estate, she has a right to demand her portion from the administrator. Anna contended that given the order of distribution, she should be able to enforce her entitlement to the money in a manner similar to other debtors.	The defendant, John F. Bauman, maintains that the funds in question are in custodia legis (in the custody of the law) and that as the administrator, he is not subject to garnishment proceedings. He argues that the garnishment process does not apply since the money he holds is intended for distribution as per legal obligation, and thus, he should not be held liable to pay debts against Anna Bartell until legal requirements are met, such as an official demand for payment.

In January 1868, the case of Samuel Lindley v. Hannah Smith was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a property dispute over certain tracts of land in Clark County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Hannah Smith (formerly Hannah Hollenbeck), sought to recover an undivided half of the land inherited from her deceased father, Lawrence Hollenbeck, who died around 1851. The legal troubles stemmed from a deed executed on January 14, 1859, in which Hannah and her husband Joseph Hollenbeck conveyed the land to Thomas J. Sturr and Charles M. Taylor, with additional complexities arising from a deed of trust. During the trial, it was established that Hannah had not relinquished her interest correctly according to legal protocols required for married women to transfer real property. The court took the case without a jury, ultimately ruling in favor of Hannah Smith, after determining that the acknowledgment of her deed was insufficient to legally transfer her title.	The plaintiff, Hannah Smith, asserted that as one of the heirs of Lawrence Hollenbeck, she had rightful ownership of the land in question. She argued that the deed executed in 1859 did not effectively transfer her title due to deficiencies in the acknowledgment clause regarding her identity, thus maintaining her claim to an undivided half of the property. Hannah requested that the court affirm her title to the land and grant her recovery of the said premises.	The defendant, Samuel Lindley, contended that the acknowledgment of the deed was sufficient to validate the transfer of the property, arguing that the certification of the deed was mostly compliant with statutory requirements. He sought to present evidence contradicting the plaintiff's claims about the validity of the prior deed, asserting that Hannah's prior conveyance constituted a legally binding transfer of her interest in the land. Lindley also claimed that the action was barred by the statute of limitations, expecting the court to dismiss Smith’s claims based on this argument.

Edward N. Cooper filed a suit against Jonathan E. I. G. Cooper in Clark County, Illinois. The case was brought to the Illinois Appellate Court and decided on November 30, 1888. The dispute arose from a claimed amount due to Edward N. Cooper for wages and the purchase price of a tract of land, which was to be settled with mules and other chattel property. During the trial, a jury found in favor of Edward N. Cooper, awarding him $100. The court examined the evidence, determining that it supported the jury's verdict. A significant element of the case involved the contention over the size and value of the mules that were part of the land trade, affecting the recovery basis. Jonathan E. I. G. Cooper argued that the plaintiff's evidence regarding the value of the mules was irrelevant, but the court found it necessary to ascertain the terms of their original agreement. The court also addressed concerns about the admission of certain evidence, particularly regarding a mortgage record, concluding that general objections raised were insufficient for reversal.	Edward N. Cooper claimed that he was owed wages and the purchase price for land sold to Jonathan E. I. G. Cooper. He asserted that his payment for the land was to be made through the transfer of mules and other personal property, and sought to prove the value and existence of these items as part of the original agreement. Cooper requested compensation based on the jury's finding that he had worked for Jonathan and that he had not been paid for his labor or the property exchanged.	Jonathan E. I. G. Cooper contended that he had fulfilled his payment obligations and argued against the relevance of the evidence regarding the mules' value. He maintained that Edward N. Cooper's claims failed to show that he had not received the agreed items under the original contract. Additionally, he raised procedural objections regarding the admission of mortgage evidence, arguing that the plaintiff's claims did not meet legal standards for documentation and proof of payment.

Robert McCart filed a legal action against Cyrinius Wakefield, the administrator of an estate, in McLean County, Illinois, in January 1874. The case centered around a bond that McCart claimed was lost. This action for debt required that McCart prove to the court that the bond had indeed been lost in a clear and satisfactory manner. During the proceedings, it was noted that the bond had last been seen in McCart’s office, but there was no indication that a thorough search had been conducted for it there. Additionally, the bond had been part of the case papers during a trial, further complicating the issue of its loss. The court pointed out that while instructions had been given to a clerk to search for the bond, the specifics of how that search was executed were unclear, raising doubts about whether the claim was substantiated.	McCart’s primary argument hinged on the assertion that a bond, relevant to his case, was lost. He sought debt recovery based on this alleged loss. He requested the court to accept the claim of the lost bond as valid and allow for recovery of the amount due under the bond, asserting that a satisfactory proof of the loss had been provided.	The defense, represented by Cyrinius Wakefield, argued that McCart failed to provide clear and satisfactory evidence of the bond's loss. They contended that there was insufficient proof that a proper search had been executed both at the time the bond was reported lost and afterward, particularly in McCart’s office. The defense highlighted the lack of detail regarding the steps taken by the clerk when asked to search for the bond and challenged the adequacy of the evidence regarding the bond’s contents and execution.

In January 1871, the legal case of George W. Price v. School Directors took place in McLean County, Illinois. The case involved George W. Price, who, along with two others, offered land for a schoolhouse site in a local school district. An election was held, and a majority of legal voters in the district chose the site offered by Price. On the day the deed for the land was created, a school director informed Price about commencing construction on the site and requested him to prepare the deed to be recorded. Price complied and left the deed with the recorder. However, weeks later, the school directors discovered that the deed contained a condition restricting its use for "the benefit of white people only," with a reversion clause if the land ceased to be used for school purposes. The directors were dissatisfied with this condition and asked Price to amend it, but he refused. They filed a bill to correct the deed's objectionable condition, as it was not part of their original agreement, and Price had acted in bad faith by adding it without their knowledge.	The plaintiff, George W. Price, claimed that the condition attached to the deed was never part of the original agreement and was inserted without the knowledge or consent of the school directors. He sought the court's intervention to reform the deed to eliminate the restrictive clause, arguing that as this was a charitable donation for educational purposes, equity would allow for correcting any defects in the conveyance.	The defendants, the school directors, contended that Price acted in bad faith by unnoticedly adding a discriminatory condition to the deed. They argued that the condition restricted the benefits of the school and was not agreed upon, thereby violating good faith. They also maintained that any expectation of the deed's contents could not solely rely on their own oversight but rather on Price’s obligation to notify them about the deed's terms.

In the case of David T. Littler v. The City of Lincoln, litigation arose from a dispute regarding the obstruction of streets in a platted addition to the city of Lincoln, Illinois. The events leading to this dispute began with Littler's petition to the city council on November 18, 1878, in which he sought to vacate parts of the town plat, claiming ownership of the lots in question, except for two owned by the estate of Bell. The city council responded with an ordinance on February 3, 1879, vacating the streets and allowances for Littler's statements, contingent upon him conveying additional land to the city for street purposes. Subsequently, a conflict arose regarding the construction of a fence by Littler that obstructed what the city claimed were public streets. The city of Lincoln initiated legal action against Littler based on these obstructions. The case was first heard before a justice in Logan County, who ruled in favor of Littler. This judgment was appealed by the city to the Circuit Court, which subsequently ruled against Littler, imposing a penalty. Littler then appealed this decision to the Appellate Court, which upheld the prior ruling. The case was then brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for a final decision on March 29, 1883.	The City of Lincoln, as the plaintiff, claimed that Littler was obstructing public streets within the city limits, violating municipal ordinances against such obstructions. The city presented evidence of Littler's previous petition and the ordinance that vacated streets in response to Littler's representations, asserting that public rights had been infringed upon by Littler's actions.	Littler, the defendant, argued that he was the sole owner of the lots involved, as evidenced by a deed of vacation he executed on April 29, 1879. He contended that the statute allowed him to vacate the plat without the city's concurrence and that the areas in question had never been used or accepted by the public as streets. Littler maintained that no legal rights were detrimentally affected by the vacation of the plat and that there was a lack of evidence supporting the city's claims regarding public rights.

The case "Adaline Darling et al. v. Peter McDonald" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1875. It originated in the Richland Circuit Court, where appellee Peter McDonald sued the estates of Andrew Darling and his heirs for payment regarding services rendered during Darling's prolonged illness, specifically for nursing and caring for him. Over a two-year period leading to Darling's death, McDonald accompanied him on multiple trips for medical treatment in New York City and St. Louis and provided daily care that included dressing wounds and attending to his medical needs, which were exacerbated by a severe throat cancer. Witnesses noted that McDonald's caregiving was exceptional and invaluable, to the point where the pastor of Darling's church remarked on the significant nature of the services provided. While Darling allegedly made promises of financial compensation for McDonald's assistance and expressed intentions to help him with a business transition, the services were performed without a formal agreement for payment. After a jury awarded McDonald $1,420.60, the defendants appealed the verdict, arguing the amount was excessive given the lack of a defined contract regarding compensation.	McDonald claimed that he was entitled to payment for his invaluable nursing services rendered to Andrew Darling during his illness. He argued that, despite the absence of a formal contract, there was a mutual understanding based on Darling's promises to compensate him, which were supported by witness testimonies regarding the nature and importance of the services provided.	The defendants contended that the jury's verdict was based on excessive damages without sufficient evidence to support such a high amount. They argued that there was no binding contract concerning payment for services, asserting that Darling’s intentions to provide financial support were conditional and primarily aimed at aiding McDonald’s transition to a different business rather than as compensation for caregiving.

The case of Norman C. Thompson et al. v. Mansfield Elliott was decided in September 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a promissory note worth $70 executed by Mansfield Elliott, dated July 24, 1860, and payable to Thompson & Co. at the office of G. E. Boucher & Co. on or before November 1, 1865. The conflict arose when Elliott provided a receipt, indicating that he had made a payment of $135 to E. G. Boucher & Co. for two notes held by Thompson & Co. The plaintiffs, Norman C. Thompson & Co., claimed that E. G. Boucher & Co. did not have the authority to receipt payment on their behalf, stating that the agency was limited to specific purposes rather than collections. The judge in the initial proceedings sided with Elliott, leading to Thompson & Co. appealing the decision. The case was heard in Kankakee County and grappled with issues surrounding the authority of agents in contract negotiations.	The plaintiffs argued that E. G. Boucher & Co. were not authorized to collect payments on notes due to them. They maintained that the written contract with Boucher & Co. did not grant them such authority and therefore the receipt issued to Elliott was invalid. The plaintiffs sought to overturn the lower court's decisions, asserting that they were entitled to receive payment on the promissory note executed by Elliott, which had not been legally satisfied.	The defense argued that E. G. Boucher & Co. had the authority to receive payment on behalf of Thompson & Co. They provided testimony indicating that the receipt issued by Boucher & Co. was valid, and that Elliott had correctly paid the amount owed. The defendant claimed that there was a known business practice that allowed for such authority, reinforcing their position that the receipt effectively canceled the debt obligation, justifying the lower court's decision in their favor.

The case of City of Champaign v. Sarah E. Jones occurred on March 2, 1888, in the city of Champaign, Illinois. The incident involved Sarah E. Jones, who was driving a two-wheeled cart pulled by an old horse along the main street, which had been recently paved with brick. The city had undertaken street cleaning but negligently left mud and dirt scraped into a ridge down the middle of the street, which subsequently froze overnight. On the day of the incident, as Jones attempted to pass between a hitched team of horses and the mudrow, the team unexpectedly backed up, causing her horse to swerve and strike the frozen mud. This resulted in Jones being thrown from the cart and sustaining severe, permanent injuries. She was awarded a judgment of $2,000 for these injuries by the lower court. The city argued that the condition of the street was apparent to Jones and that her own carelessness was to blame for the accident.	Sarah E. Jones claimed that the City of Champaign was negligent in its maintenance of the street, specifically in leaving a hazardous mudrow that led to her accident. She argued that the city's actions directly contributed to her injuries and sought compensation for the damages resulting from the incident. Jones presented evidence that the city's negligence in leaving the mud unaddressed was a significant factor in causing her injury.	The City of Champaign contended that Jones should have been aware of the dangerous condition of the street and argued that her actions, particularly her attempt to pass the hitched team at a trot in a narrow space, constituted contributory negligence. They maintained that the city's conditions were patent, meaning they were obvious to her, and that any injury sustained was primarily due to her own carelessness rather than any fault of the city.

In the case of Edward K. Rogers v. Milton O. Higgins et al., dated September 1868 and adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, the legal matter arose in Chicago, Illinois. The principal parties involved were Edward K. Rogers, the plaintiff, and Milton O. Higgins, the defendant. The issue centered around a piece of property that was originally purchased by Ann Wright in June 1842 and sold, later on, to Elizabeth Rogers (the mother of the plaintiff) in October 1845. Although Elizabeth Rogers occupied the land and paid for it, the 1845 deed was held in escrow until 1847, which became crucial due to the legal context surrounding married women's rights to convey property. The crux of the case lay in whether the deed executed by Mrs. Wright was valid. The court learned that Mrs. Wright was a married woman and that at the time of the sale, Illinois law did not allow her to convey real estate without her husband's consent. In December 1863, Mrs. Wright transferred the property to Higgins, who was allegedly aware of Rogers' rights to the land. However, Rogers filed a suit in equity to prevent Higgins from claiming the property, arguing that the deed to Higgins was void and that he had a rightful claim to it. The initial ruling dismissed Rogers’ bill, compelling him to cover legal costs.	Edward K. Rogers claimed that the conveyance of the property from Ann Wright to himself via his mother, Elizabeth Rogers, was valid, arguing that he had paid for and possessed the land for years. He contended that the later deed transferring the property to Higgins was flawed due to the incapacity of Mrs. Wright to convey her property as a married woman under Illinois law at the time. He requested the court to enjoin Higgins from continuing an ejectment action aimed at recovering the property, seeking legal recognition of his rights and an affirmation of his title.	Milton O. Higgins defended his claim by asserting that he legitimately purchased the property from Ann Wright, who conveyed her title appropriately, despite the earlier claims by Rogers. He argued that the deed he received was valid, claiming he had made the purchase with full notice of Rogers’ previous possession and claims. Higgins contended that Rogers should be deemed to have acted at his own risk and cannot now seek to enforce rights that are unsupported by a valid deed. Moreover, he requested the court to allow him to proceed with the ejectment suit against the tenant occupying the property.

Edgar M. Reading v. Joseph H. Mead et al. was a legal case decided on April 8, 1885, in the County Court of Cook County, Illinois. The case revolved around a financial dispute where the Meads (plaintiffs) brought an assumpsit action against Reading (defendant) for a claim amounting to one thousand dollars. The court conducted a trial without a jury, which was waived by the involved parties. The presiding Judge was Mason B. Loomis. During the proceedings, the court found in favor of the plaintiffs, determining that the amount owed was actually eleven hundred and forty-five dollars and fifty cents. However, this amount exceeded the court's jurisdictional cap of one thousand dollars. The plaintiffs subsequently remitted the excess amount of one hundred and forty-five dollars and fifty cents, leading to a judgment of one thousand dollars. Reading sought to appeal the judgment, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction due to the original claim exceeding its limits.	The plaintiff, Joseph H. Mead, claimed that Edgar M. Reading owed him a debt of one thousand dollars and sought recovery of this amount through an assumpsit action. Mead argued that the court had jurisdiction to hear the case, despite the original claim exceeding the jurisdictional limit. Following the court's findings, the plaintiff stipulated to reduce the claim to the permissible amount of one thousand dollars.	The defendant, Edgar M. Reading, contended that the initial claim exceeded the jurisdictional threshold of the court, thereby questioning the legal authority of the court to decide on such a claim. He argued that the plaintiff failed to disclaim any right to recover more than the jurisdiction limit before submitting the case, which rendered the court's finding null. Reading's position was that despite the remittitur made after the verdict, it could not confer jurisdiction retrospectively.

The case "St. Louis and Cairo Railroad Company v. Maggie A. Carroll" originated in October 1882 during the St. Louis fair when Dr. Channig, along with Maggie A. Carroll and his daughter, attempted to travel from Barksville Station to East St. Louis. They sought round trip tickets but were informed by a railroad agent that tickets were unavailable. Upon boarding the train, they were initially allowed to travel for half fare based on verbal assurances from the conductor. However, on their return trip from East St. Louis, the conductor insisted that Carroll pay the full fare. Carroll only paid half fare and believed Miss Channig had also covered her fare. The conductor demanded additional payment, asserting that if full fare was not paid, one passenger would have to leave the train at Cahokia Station. Ultimately, Carroll was forced to leave the train at Cahokia Station, and after borrowing money, she continued her journey home later that evening. The conductor's actions were based on the company’s regulations, which warranted payment of the regular fare without a proper ticket. The incident raised questions about adherence to company policy and passenger responsibilities.	The plaintiff, Maggie A. Carroll, claimed she was wrongfully ejected from the train after being denied a return ticket despite having followed all procedures. She argued that the railroad company's failure to provide round trip tickets amounted to a breach of contract and sought damages for the wrongful expulsion, which she believed was unjust, given the circumstances of her travel.	The defendant, St. Louis and Cairo Railroad Company, argued that the regulations requiring a ticket or full fare were reasonable and essential for their operation as a common carrier. They claimed that Carroll’s failure to inform the conductor of her previous journey and circumstances resulted in her misunderstanding of the fare requirements. The defendant maintained that Carroll was rightfully ejected from the train for not paying the required fare and requested the court to overturn the previous ruling in favor of Carroll.

In the case of Alexander Watt v. Bryant T. Scofield, which took place in early 1871 in Hancock County, Illinois, the plaintiff, Bryant T. Scofield, brought an action of trover against the defendant, Alexander Watt. The case arose from disputes related to a quantity of corn that had been cultivated by a tenant, Kenny, on Scofield's farm under a lease agreement. Kenny had rented the farm from Scofield and was indebted to him for unpaid rent. In November 1870, Watt, a merchant, purchased 350 bushels of corn from Kenny, fully aware that Kenny was a tenant of Scofield and that the corn was grown on Scofield's property. Scofield demanded the return of the corn after learning of the sale, citing his statutory lien on the crops for the unpaid rent. The court trial involved determining whether Watt's purchase of the corn was valid given Scofield's lien rights as a landlord.	Scofield claimed that he had a statutory lien on the corn growing on his farm for the rent that Kenny owed him. He argued that as the landlord, he had the right to enforce this lien against any purchaser, including Watt, who was aware of the tenant's status and the lien. Scofield sought the return of the corn and damages for its alleged conversion by Watt.	Watt contended that he was a bona fide purchaser of the corn and should not be held liable for the landlord's lien. He argued that the demand for the corn by Scofield was invalid because the rent had not yet become due at the time of the demand. Watt claimed that he had no knowledge that the rent was unpaid, asserting his right to retain the corn he purchased.

Frank Hahn, the appellant, entered into a business arrangement where he furnished stone to a contractor named Hayes for usage in building projects overseen by the appellees, James Maxwell and others, in Cook County, Illinois. After delivering the last batch of stone, Hahn presented his bill to the appellees. They assured him they would pay him if he waited for a month. However, after this period, the appellees declined to pay. This situation arose after the agreement for the buildings changed hands, transferring the contract from Hayes to the appellees. Notably, Hahn missed the opportunity to secure a lien on the buildings, which would have legally protected his right to payment for the stone, because he trusted the appellees' verbal promise to pay. The lack of a written promise and consideration for it rendered his claims weak. The Circuit Court ruled appropriately, affirming that Hahn had no valid cause to hold the appellees financially responsible for Hayes' debt, despite his reliance on their initial assurances.	Frank Hahn claimed that he was owed payment for the stone supplied, having believed the defendants (James Maxwell et al.) would fulfill this obligation following their verbal promise to pay. He argued that he did not file a lien notice based on this promise and sought legal recourse to recover the debt from the appellees, who he believed had taken over the financial responsibility.	The appellees contended that they were not liable for Hahn's debt, as it was originally a debt owed by Hayes. They argued that Hahn's decision to delay serving a lien notice was a voluntary act that lacked legal grounding, particularly since the promise made was not supported by written documentation or consideration. The defendants asserted that the Circuit Court correctly found no cause of action against them.

On April 22, 1884, in Illinois, a contract was established between Esterly & Son (the plaintiffs) and Dickerson & Nichols (the defendants), who were appointed as special sales agents for Esterly & Son to sell twine binders for the season ending September 1, 1884. The contract stipulated that the parties were expected to use their best efforts to complete and ship all ordered machines. As part of this agreement, a blank order for machines was filled out to include one Esterly Twine-binding Harvester, and the defendants were required to insure the machines against fire loss. During the contract period, three machines were provided to Dickerson & Nichols, of which one was sold and settled while the second was also sold. The third machine was destroyed in a fire on July 10, 1884, at their place of business. This lawsuit was initiated by Esterly & Son to recover the value of the burned machine after being ruled against in the circuit court where the judgment favored the defendants for costs, prompting an appeal from the plaintiffs.	The plaintiff, Esterly & Son, argued that Dickerson & Nichols failed to fulfill their contractual obligation to insure the third machine that was subsequently lost to fire. They sought recovery of the machine's value, asserting that since the defendants were responsible for insuring the equipment, they should bear the loss resulting from the fire incident.	The defendants, Dickerson & Nichols, contended that they held the machines under the terms of the agency contract and were not responsible for the loss as they believed they were not liable for the fire damage. They maintained that their obligations under the contract had been fulfilled, and thus they did not owe any damages to the plaintiffs.

The case "The People ex rel. Philiskey F. Stanley v. Michael W. Ryan" was decided on January 25, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arises from a petition for mandamus filed by the plaintiff, Philiskey F. Stanley, to compel Michael W. Ryan, the county clerk of Cook County, to issue a tax deed for certain lots in Garland's addition to the town of Winnetka. These lots had been sold for taxes on September 27, 1880, for the amount of $10.65, which represented the tax for the year 1879. The purchaser of these lots paid the taxes for 1880, totaling $31.50, on February 8, 1881. Following the statutory required notice, the redemption period expired without the lots being redeemed. However, when Stanley presented the necessary affidavits and certificate of purchase to Ryan, he refused to issue the deed. Ryan contended that the certificates of purchase had become null and void because the lots had been redeemed on April 1, 1881, by a person named S.H. Ingraham for $60.98, which was the sum deposited with the clerk. The court faced the issue of whether Ryan's plea was sufficient to deny the mandamus request.	The plaintiff, Philiskey F. Stanley, claimed that all necessary statutory requirements for redemption had been met and that he was entitled to a tax deed for the lots. He presented evidence showing that the redemption period had expired and asserted that the county clerk was obligated to issue the deed according to the law.	The defendant, Michael W. Ryan, argued that the certificates for the lots were void because they had been redeemed by S.H. Ingraham before Stanley's request. Ryan asserted that the requirement to properly redeem the lots included payment of the bid amount along with all subsequent taxes, and he was prepared to verify that the redemption was valid and the deed should not be issued.

Ferdinard W. Peck initiated legal action against Timothy Cooper in November 1884, following an incident in Chicago where Peck, a colored person, was forcibly ejected from a company-operated omnibus. At the time, the People’s Omnibus and Baggage Line, a corporation established in 1871, controlled the service in which the incident occurred. Cooper served as the president of the corporation and was sued individually for the alleged wrongful act. This case went through multiple trials in the Superior and Appellate Courts, culminating in a jury finding Cooper liable for the damages sustained by Peck, with the court awarding Peck $2,600. The primary legal issue centered on whether Cooper had directed the drivers to exclude colored individuals from riding in the omnibuses, which was established as unlawful and made him liable despite the corporate shield typically protecting corporate officers.	The plaintiff, Ferdinand W. Peck, argued that he was unlawfully ejected from an omnibus operated by the defendant’s company solely due to his race, which constituted a violation of his right to travel. Peck sought damages for the injuries he sustained as a result of this unjust ejection, claiming that Cooper, in his capacity as president, ordered this discriminatory exclusion of colored persons.	Timothy Cooper contended that he was not personally liable for the actions of the omnibus driver, as he acted within the framework of his duties as president of a corporation. He argued that the corporation should bear the primary responsibility for the alleged wrongful act and that any orders he may have given were not illegal in nature. Cooper also expressed that certain pieces of evidence presented during the trial, including his stockholding status, were irrelevant and prejudicial against him.

In June 1870, in Madison County, Illinois, a legal case was brought against Hiram Sippy by the School Directors in their corporate capacity. The case involved a promissory note that the directors had executed. The court proceedings were initiated after the directors faced a demurrer to the declaration, which was ultimately overruled. The relevant law from 1865 permitted school directors to borrow money for certain purposes but specifically required them to issue bonds for such debts, indicating that they did not have the legal authority to execute promissory notes. Chief Justice Lawrence stated that the directors' ability to contract debts must be derived solely from legislative authority and emphasized the need for prudence in managing school funds. The court determined that, without evidence showing compliance with the statutory requirements, the promissory note was not binding on the school district. Consequently, the judgment for the amount indicated on the note was reversed, and the case was remanded for further legal proceedings.	The plaintiffs, the School Directors, argued that the promissory note they executed constituted a valid obligation. They sought a judgment for the amount due as indicated on the note, contending that the defendants owed them this sum based on the document's face value.	The defendant, Hiram Sippy, contended that the School Directors did not possess the legal authority to execute a promissory note based on the statutes governing their powers. He argued that the law only allowed them to issue bonds upon a vote by the public and did not grant them the power to create binding promissory notes. Consequently, the defendant requested the court to dismiss the action based on the lack of legal authority for the note.

In September 1876, in Stephenson County, Illinois, a legal action for trespass was initiated by the plaintiff, George Hamm, against the defendant, Mary E. Culvey. The case arose from a personal assault that occurred between the two parties. Justice Soholeield of the Illinois Supreme Court delivered the opinion on the matter after examining the appeals made by the defendant regarding a jury's verdict which found her guilty of the assault. The jury determined the damages to be $75. The defendant filed special pleas justifying her actions but was ultimately found guilty by the jury. The court considered the nature of the verdict and stated that formal objections against the wording of the verdict were not sufficient grounds for reversal, citing legal precedents and amendments that uphold the finality of the jury's determination.	George Hamm, the plaintiff, claimed that Mary E. Culvey committed a personal assault against him, thus seeking justice for the trespass committed. His main arguments rested upon proving the guilt of the defendant in the act of assault as well as claiming damages, which the jury quantified to be $75.	Mary E. Culvey, the defendant, mounted her defense based on two special pleas that aimed to justify her actions during the incident. She contended that the jury’s verdict and subsequent judgment were not responsive to the issues presented in the case. Her requests included overturning the verdict and seeking a new trial based on claims that the verdict lacked technical nicety and was formally objectionable.

The case "City of East St. Louis v. Philip H. Wehrung" was decided in January 1868 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The events took place in East St. Louis, Illinois. The dispute arose when Philip H. Wehrung was prosecuted for operating a dram shop and selling intoxicating liquors without the required municipal license. The city alleged that his business was conducted in violation of local ordinances. Wehrung contended that the city’s licensing ordinance was unconstitutional because it imposed different fees based on the street location of the dram shop, which he argued violated the requirement for uniformity in taxation. However, the court stated that a license does not constitute a tax in the constitutional sense, thus allowing municipalities to implement differential license fees based on location advantages, provided that all individuals have equal opportunities to apply for the same license.	The City of East St. Louis claimed that Philip H. Wehrung operated a dram shop without the necessary license as mandated by municipal ordinance. The city requested the enforcement of this ordinance, asserting that the differential licensing approach based on locality was valid and legal under Illinois law, emphasizing that the ordinance aimed to regulate the liquor trade effectively within its jurisdiction.	Philip H. Wehrung defended himself by arguing that the municipal ordinance imposing different license fees based on the location of the dram shop was unconstitutional and void. He claimed that the ordinance's differential treatment amounted to an illegal tax that violated the principle of uniform taxation mandated by the constitution. Wehrung also contended that he offered the required license fee in the form of police commissioners' certificates, which should be accepted according to the law, but the city rejected this payment.

The case "The People ex rel. Peter Greenwood et al., Commissioners of Highways, v. The Board of Supervisors" took place in Madison County, Illinois, with a decision rendered on June 7, 1887. The plaintiffs, represented by the Highway Commissioners, sought to compel the Board of Supervisors to allocate additional funds for the construction of a bridge over Wood River. The plaintiffs had previously petitioned the County Board for a total of $2,500, asserting that the town's needs warranted such funding. However, the Board had only appropriated $1,000, claiming that the town had not demonstrated that it could cover half of the bridge's costs according to statutory requirements. The primary contention revolved around whether the Commissioners had properly recorded their proceedings and findings, which would necessitate aid from the County Board. The plaintiffs argued they met all conditions for the aid, asserting the necessity of the bridge and the burden placed on the town. The case involved complex statutory interpretations concerning required record-keeping by municipal corporations and the admissibility of oral testimony regarding official actions.	The plaintiffs claimed that the County Board had not provided the mandated financial assistance necessary for bridge construction, despite their assertion of having fulfilled the statutory requirements. They argued that they had officially determined the bridge's necessity, assessed the financial burden on the township, and levied a tax to cover half the estimated construction costs. This assertion was bolstered by the claim that their petition, submitted in good faith, adequately reflected statutory compliance for a mandamus writ to compel the Board to allocate the necessary funds.	The defendants countered the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that the legal requirements had not been satisfied. They argued that the plaintiffs failed to provide evidence of the necessary determination regarding the existence of conditions that would justify County aid. The Board indicated that the plaintiffs had not provided half of the necessary funds for the bridge, which was a prerequisite according to the statute, thereby justifying their refusal to grant further financial support. Furthermore, they contended that their decision to award $1,000 should be considered a complete settlement of any claims regarding the bridge construction.

Daniel McLaughlin filed a slander lawsuit against Frank R. Fisher in the Illinois Supreme Court in 1890, after Fisher allegedly made false statements about McLaughlin's conduct as president of the Illinois Miners’ Protective Association. McLaughlin claimed that Fisher publicly asserted he was being paid by a coal company to foment discord among miners, thereby harming his reputation and the interests of those he represented. The case took place in Sangamon County, specifically in the Circuit Court, led by Judge James A. Creighton. This incident occurred on January 1, 1888, when Fisher allegedly made these defamatory remarks, intending to damage McLaughlin’s reputation and standing within the miners’ community. The essential duties of McLaughlin as president involved promoting the welfare of miners and fostering harmony among them. Fisher's remarks were considered vindictive as they aimed to portray McLaughlin as corrupt, which led to the legal dispute over whether those remarks were actionable slander.	The plaintiff, Daniel McLaughlin, argued that Frank R. Fisher maliciously made false and defamatory statements about him. McLaughlin contended that these statements impaired his ability to serve as president of the Illinois Miners’ Protective Association and damaged his personal reputation and standing within the miners' community. He sought damages for slander, claiming that the false accusations caused him significant emotional distress and potential loss of his posHtion within the association.	The defendant, Frank R. Fisher, defended against the claims by arguing that the words he spoke were not slanderous per se and were not actionable without evidence depicting how they were harmful or damaging. Fisher asserted that McLaughlin’s allegations lacked the necessary contextual foundation and specific extrinsic facts to support their slanderous characterization. Therefore, he requested that the court sustain his demurrer and dismiss the charges against him.

In 1886, in Chicago, Archibald Haas was employed as a registered pharmacist at a drug store owned by Merz Brothers. During Haas’s absence, a boy named Goddard, who had been instructed by both Haas and August Merz not to sell poisons but otherwise to sell items in the store, sold poisons to a customer. This action violated the Illinois Pharmacy Act, which stipulates that only registered pharmacists may dispense such items and outlines penalties for violations. After a justice of the peace penalized Haas with a $50 fine for permitting the unlawful sale, the Criminal Court of Cook County upheld the judgment, prompting Haas to appeal, arguing that he shouldn’t be held liable as a mere employee of the store.	Archibald Haas, the plaintiff, argued that he should not be penalized under the Pharmacy Act for the actions of the boy, as the store belonged to Merz Brothers, and he was only an employee. He contended that if liability were imposed on him for the boy's actions, it would undermine the law’s intent and efficacy, enabling owners to escape responsibility by hiring a qualified person to lead the operations.	The People of the State of Illinois, the defendant, maintained that Haas, as the registered pharmacist in charge of the store, bore personal responsibility for any illegal sales conducted in his establishment, including by unlicensed helpers. The state argued that Haas's instructions to the boy were insufficient for compliance with the statute and that knowledge of what constituted poisons was essential for operating the drug store legally.

The case of Benjamin F. Ayer et al. v. The Town of Lake took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the final decision rendered on October 26, 1882. The plaintiffs, Benjamin F. Ayer and others, contested a second assessment levied under an ordinance intended to cover the costs associated with the laying of a water pipe along Fifty-first Street, from Halsted Street to Ashland Avenue. A petition was submitted requesting the appointment of commissioners to carry out this second assessment due to the deficiency from the first assessment which had not yielded enough funds for the improvement project. The first assessment had been confirmed by default, as the plaintiffs did not appear in court. However, the ordinance did not specify how much of the first assessment had been collected or the amount of deficiency. It also failed to indicate whether the plaintiffs' property was delinquent. The court ultimately found that these omissions were critical and jurisdictional, without which the court lacked authority to confirm the second assessment.	The plaintiffs argued that the second assessment for the unpaid costs of the water pipe installation was invalid due to insufficient documentation regarding the delinquency of their properties, the amount collected from the first assessment, and the deficiency that justified the second assessment. They contended that the ordinance had not adhered to the statutory requirements, which stipulate that such facts must be clearly established for the court to have jurisdiction. They sought the reversal of the County Court's judgment that confirmed the second assessment.	The Town of Lake's defense hinged on the assertion that, although the required jurisdictional facts were not present in the record, a presumption should arise that the County Court had considered necessary evidence not shown due to the absence of a bill of exceptions by the plaintiffs. The defense argued that it was the plaintiffs' responsibility to provide evidence against the confirmation of the second assessment if they wanted to challenge it. They sought to uphold the judgment confirming the second assessment based on this presumption of jurisdiction.

The case of Cary S. Vise et al. v. The County of Hamilton took place in Hamilton County, Illinois, with the judgment delivered by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1857. Cary S. Vise and others, who were attorneys appointed by the Circuit Court of Hamilton County, were tasked with defending an individual who had been indicted for forgery and was unable to hire counsel. After providing their legal services, the attorneys sought compensation from the county, claiming that their services were worth a total of twenty dollars each. This claim was brought before the County Court of Hamilton County, which refused to allow payment. The case was then agreed upon and sent to the Circuit Court to determine the county's liability for the fees that the appellants sought for their services rendered on behalf of the accused. Ultimately, the Circuit Court ruled that the county held no obligation to compensate the appointed attorneys for their defense of the accused individual.	The plaintiffs, Cary S. Vise and the other attorneys, claimed that they were entitled to compensation from the County of Hamilton for providing legal defense services to an indigent accused individual. They argued that the county should be liable to pay them for the services rendered, which they valued at twenty dollars each, as their appointment by the court constituted a formal obligation to represent the defendant.	The County of Hamilton, represented by its counsel, argued that it was not liable for the legal fees claimed by the plaintiffs. They maintained that the county had no part in the prosecution of the defendant and did not engage the plaintiffs for their services. The defense emphasized that the prosecution was conducted in the name of the People of the State of Illinois, asserting that the county was under no obligation to provide counsel for the accused and that attorneys appointed by the court could not recover fees from the county.

Emil Johnson, a seven-year-old boy, was involved in an accident on July 15, 1883, in Chicago, Illinois. He was walking with an adult relative, Miss Kowackson, near the Clark Street swing bridge, which was in the process of closing after having been swung open to allow a vessel to pass. Despite being aware that the bridge was not fully closed, Johnson pushed past his guardian and ran onto the bridge, where his foot became caught between the bridge and its south approach, resulting in severe injury that required amputation. The case was brought to trial on August 4, 1883, with claims that the city had failed to maintain the bridge safely, neglecting proper lighting and guardrails. However, the trial judge ruled in favor of the City of Chicago, leading Johnson to appeal the decision.	The plaintiff, represented by his next friend, asserted that the City of Chicago failed to fulfill its duty to maintain the Clark Street swing bridge in a safe condition. Claims included that the bridge and its approaches were in an unsafe state, lacking sufficient lighting and necessary safety guards, contributing to the accident that caused personal injury to Johnson. The plaintiff sought damages for the injuries sustained due to what was claimed to be negligent and unsafe conditions under the city's control.	The City of Chicago contested the claims by arguing that the evidence did not establish a defect in the bridge or its approaches. The defendant indicated that the area was getting dark, and some gas lamps had not been lit, but maintained that these factors did not amount to negligence. They emphasized that Johnson, despite being warned, acted recklessly by running onto the bridge while it was closing, which was a substantial factor in the accident. Consequently, the City requested the court to affirm the trial's judgment in their favor.

John McAuley initiated this case against the Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company on June 10, 1881, seeking damages due to the construction and operation of a railroad in proximity to his property located in Carpenter’s addition to Chicago. The railroad's operation, which began in 1872, resulted in vibrations and the presence of dust, smoke, and ashes affecting McAuley's home, thereby depreciating its value. The railroad, originally constructed by a different corporation, came under the control of the Chicago and Eastern Illinois Railroad Company after a series of ownership changes and is at the heart of this dispute. On trial, McAuley was awarded $3,000 in damages by the court, a decision he appealed after being affirmed by the Appellate Court. The primary legal questions involved the appropriateness of the five-year Statute of Limitations as it applied to his claim and the inherent distinction between permanent versus transient nuisances.	McAuley claimed that the railroad's close proximity to his property led to significant damages, including physical vibrations and the accumulation of harmful substances. He asserted that these conditions constituted a taking of value from his property without just compensation. His legal requests included recovering damages for the alleged trespass and nuisance caused by the railroad's operations.	The railroad company argued primarily that McAuley's claims were barred by the five-year Statute of Limitations since the railroad had been operational since 1872, and McAuley did not file the lawsuit until 1881. The defense contended that the nuisance was permanent, meaning damages should have been sought within the prescribed time period, and emphasized that no new damages to McAuley’s property occurred after the transfer of management of the railroad.

In the case of E. M. Bradley v. Daniel C. Linn et al., the events took place around December 18, 1883, involving a partnership engaged in manufacturing pottery under the name "Frederick Stoneware Company." The key individuals involved included E. M. Bradley, Daniel C. Linn, Louis E. Ellet, and Farnell. Ellet was tasked with managing the business and represented the firm in commercial matters. However, without the knowledge of the other partners, Ellet executed a partnership note for $110.45 on December 18, 1883, to Farnell for advances made to the firm. This note was later assigned to plaintiff Bradley after its maturity. The legal proceedings began when Bradley filed a suit to recover the amount specified in the note against Linn, Jacoba, and Ellet. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court after a lower court judgment against Bradley for costs. The dispute hinged on Ellet's authority to execute the note and whether the other partners were bound by it.	The plaintiff, E. M. Bradley, argued that he should be entitled to recover the amount of the partnership note executed by Ellet, which was assigned to him after its maturity. Bradley contended that the execution of the note was valid and sought to hold the other partners, Linn and Jacoba, liable for the debt incurred by Ellet in his capacity as a partner.	The defendants, Daniel C. Linn and Jacoba, contended that they neither executed the note nor authorized Ellet to do so. They argued that under partnership law, Ellet did not have the authority to bind the partnership to the note, as it did not pertain to the usual business operations. Furthermore, they asserted that Bradley took the note after its maturity and thus could not claim it against them.

Joseph Frazier, the appellant, and Frederick Miller, the appellee, were involved in a legal dispute regarding a contract and property conveyance. The case originated in Wabash, Illinois, around February 15, 1850, when Miller transferred approximately seventy-three acres of land and personal property valued at one thousand dollars to Frazier. The contract stipulated that Frazier was to provide support and maintenance for Miller and his wife for the rest of their lives. However, Frazier failed to fulfill this obligation, neglecting to provide adequate food, clothing, and shelter, and treating Miller and his wife with harshness, including physical abuse. In response, Miller filed a bill in equity seeking rescission of the contract, cancellation of the deed, and recovery of the personal property. The Illinois Supreme Court ultimately heard the case, which raised complex issues about jurisdiction, effective remedies, and the handling of the bond Frazier had executed.	Miller's main arguments were that Frazier breached their agreement by failing to provide the necessary support, thus justifying the rescission of the contract and cancellation of the deed. Miller sought the return of the land and personal property, asserting that damages alone would not adequately remedy the harm caused by Frazier's neglect and mistreatment.	Frazier contended that Miller had a legal remedy available through the bond for damages due to breaches, arguing that equity should not intervene in this case. He also raised technical objections concerning the absence of an affidavit regarding the loss of the bond that he had withheld from Miller, claiming that this deficiency entitled him to dismissal of the bill.

In 1883, the case of Z. Dowden et al. v. Jesse F. Wilson began in Ford County, Illinois, where Dowden and other plaintiffs sought to foreclose a mortgage on a tract of land. This mortgage was given to secure three promissory notes totaling $1,000 related to the purchase of a patent for a wagon brake. The case followed a previous suit on the same issue, which had been appealed and reversed due to procedural issues, resulting in a failure to act within two years, causing the prior case to be discontinued. During the trial, the records from the previous case were reportedly destroyed in a fire, leading to disputes over evidence. The defendants sought to introduce secondary evidence in the form of certified copies of depositions from the prior case, which the plaintiffs objected to. The court ultimately ruled on the merits of the case and the validity of the mortgage. Despite the defense's claims regarding the worthlessness of the patent, the court found a lack of sufficient evidence to support this claim, particularly since the defendants did not produce evidence of practical testing of the brake or prove any fraud.	The plaintiffs argued for the enforcement of the mortgage securing promissory notes issued for the purchase of a patent for a wagon brake. Their main position was that regardless of the defendants' assertions regarding the brake's worthlessness, they had not proven that the patent was invalid or that fraud had occurred during the purchase. The plaintiffs requested a decree foreclosing the mortgage due to the defendants' failure to satisfy the promissory notes.	The defendants contended that the patent was worthless, claiming that they were misled during the sale. They asserted that the invention lacked novelty and should not have constituted a valid consideration for the promissory notes. The defendants argued that the original contract for the patent could be rescinded due to alleged fraudulent misrepresentations. They sought to have the mortgage set aside and a re-trial granted, claiming procedural errors in the original court's handling of the case.

In December 1840, the legal dispute arose in Fayette County, Illinois, involving plaintiffs Ormsby Van Winkle and Enoch Wakefield against defendant Paul Beck, Sen. The case originated before a justice of the peace, Mark E. Jones, who oversaw a suit initiated by the plaintiffs. The parties mutually consented to submit their case to arbitrators, who ultimately awarded the plaintiffs thirty-eight cents, leading the justice to render a judgment in their favor. Dissatisfied with the outcome, the plaintiffs appealed the decision to the Circuit Court of Fayette County in October 1839, where the appeal was dismissed upon the defendant's motion presided by Judge Sidney Breese. The dismissal prompted the plaintiffs to seek a reversal from the Illinois Supreme Court through a writ of error, leading to the current proceedings.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to appeal the decision made by the justice of the peace after the arbitrators’ award. They contended that the judgment rendered in their favor, albeit for a small amount, warranted a review and reversal. Their legal request aimed to seek reconsideration of the appeal and challenge the dismissal by the Circuit Court.	The defendant contended that the parties had voluntarily chosen to submit their dispute to arbitration, and as such, they must be bound by the arbitrators' decision. The defendant moved for dismissal of the appeal, asserting that no appeal should lie in cases where parties have agreed to arbitration. The defense reinforced that the judgment by the justice based on the arbitrators' award was final.

The case "The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company v. William Eaves" took place in 1866 in St. Clair County, Illinois. The plaintiff, William Eaves, was driving approximately twenty cattle along a highway when a passenger train frightened the cattle, scattering them. After gathering them again, Eaves and his son heard a possible approach of another train. Despite his son's warning, Eaves decided to rush the cattle across the tracks. Unfortunately, a coal train arrived, killing three of the cattle. The law mandates that railway companies must give signals, such as ringing a bell or sounding a whistle, at least eighty rods before reaching a crossing. In this incident, witnesses stated that the train's warning was only given just before the collision, suggesting a failure by the railway company to adhere to these requirements. Eaves filed a lawsuit for damages, and the jury found in his favor, awarding him $300. However, the case was subsequently appealed, raising questions about the negligence of both parties involved.	William Eaves claimed that the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company acted negligently by failing to ring a bell or sound a whistle as required by law, which resulted in the death of his cattle worth $600. He argued that the company’s negligence directly caused the damages and sought compensation for his losses.	The defendant, Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company, contended that Eaves was also negligent for rushing the cattle across the tracks without proper vigilance despite a warning from his son about an approaching train. They maintained that both parties were at fault (in pari delicto) and requested the finding of the jury to be overturned due to this mutual negligence.

In 1873, in Cook County, Illinois, John F. Eberhart was involved in a legal dispute with the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway Company concerning the condemnation of certain lots he owned. Eberhart owned a total of 73 lots in Eberhart & Wedge’s addition to Chicago, of which the railway company sought to condemn lots 11, 12, and 17 in block 4 and lots 3, 4, and 5 in block 3, as they would be structurally impacted by the construction of a diagonal railroad through the property. The railway company compensated Eberhart $6,000 for the lots taken, but Eberhart claimed additional damages for the value depreciation of other adjacent lots not condemned. The case raised the legal question of how damages should be assessed for property not physically taken but affected by the construction of the railway. The jury found no damages for the other lots, leading Eberhart to appeal the decision.	John F. Eberhart, the plaintiff, argued that the construction of the railroad negatively impacted the market value of his adjacent lots, resulting in damages that should be compensated. He requested that the court award damages based on the depreciation of the market value of the lots not taken, asserting that the jury should have considered the losses incurred due to the railway's presence.	The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway Company, the defendant, contended that the only compensation owed was for the specific lots taken and that no damages should be awarded for the remaining adjacent lots, as they were not physically taken. They argued against the inclusion of opinions regarding the value depreciation of these other lots and supported the jury's finding of no damages in that regard.

In September 1872, in Whiteside County, Illinois, Henry P. Price and others filed a case against Clarence E. Bailey, among others. The case stemmed from an incident in which a minor, alleged to have damaged a merchant's showcase, was arrested by Bispham, who falsely claimed to be a constable, at the behest of the merchant Culver. The minor was taken to a location where Price was present, who pretended to be a justice of the peace. A sham trial was conducted, resulting in a judgment against the boy without proper legal proceedings or the opportunity to consult an attorney. The boy was coerced into finding sureties for his release under the threat of imprisonment, despite having been wrongfully arrested for a minor offense and not causing any intentional damage. The court ultimately heard an appeal from the defendants, contesting the jury's verdict which favored the plaintiff.	The plaintiffs argued that they were wrongfully subjected to assault, battery, and false imprisonment as a result of the defendants’ actions. They contended that the boy was falsely arrested and treated as a criminal without due process or proper legal authority. They claimed damages for the wrongful acts committed against him, specifically citing emotional distress and unlawful detention.	The defendants maintained that the verdict was contrary to the law and the evidence presented. They did not provide a substantial defense and Bispham acknowledged guilt by not contesting the charges. Their argument centered on the legality of the arrest and the authority invoked by Price, which they claimed was legitimate, despite it being shown that there was no basis for their claims of legal authority.

In November 1853, the case of John H. Cummins v. John D. Cummins was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal dispute arose between John H. Cummins, the plaintiff (referred to as Plaintiff in Error), and John D. Cummins, the defendant (Defendant in Error), concerning a guardianship issue. John H. Cummins, the ward, filed a bill against his testamentary guardian, John D. Cummins, seeking an account of lands and moneys that had been received by the guardian. It was established that the guardian had acquired certain lands following an execution based on a judgment against the estate executor. The guardian acknowledged that the total value of the assets related to this land was $427.12. However, he also claimed to have incured expenses for maintenance and education that exceeded the assets. The court initially dismissed the bill, ruling against the plaintiff. The case progressed with both parties presenting their claims through bill, answer, replication, and exhibits, but without further proofs being submitted at that point.	The plaintiff, John H. Cummins, argued that as the ward, he had the right to an accounting from his guardian regarding the assets that came into the guardian's possession. He claimed that the guardian failed to properly demonstrate the expenditures of the estate income in support of the ward's education and maintenance, and was entitled to a decree for an account.	The defendant, John D. Cummins, responded by admitting to the receipt of certain assets but asserted that he had incurred expenses for the ward's maintenance and education that exceeded those assets. He argued that the expenditures were necessary and should be taken into account, seeking dismissal of the plaintiff's bill based on the grounds that he had already expended funds responsibly.

In the case of The Illinois Mutual Insurance Company v. Sellers Hoffman, the proceedings originated from a fire insurance policy dispute involving a cotton mill known as the "Kelleyville Works" located in Delaware County, Pennsylvania. The incident occurred on August 24, 1888. The Illinois Mutual Insurance Company, based in Alton, Illinois, had issued a policy on December 6, 1887, which insured the property for a total of $3,000, amidst a total valuation of $90,000 for various items, including buildings and machinery. The litigation began in the Circuit Court of Madison County, with the trial taking place before a judge without a jury, as agreed upon by both parties. Following the court's judgment in favor of the plaintiff, which was subsequently upheld by the Appellate Court, the key issue arose from the interpretation of the insurance policy's clauses regarding the company's liability in the event of a loss. The case hinged on understanding the differentiation in coverage and the proportion of losses that the insurance company would be responsible for following the fire.	The plaintiff, Sellers Hoffman, argued that the Illinois Mutual Insurance Company owed a payment for damage sustained by the cotton mill as per the fire insurance policy. Hoffman contended that given the total loss from the fire was $51,000, the company should be liable for the proportionate amount of $2,550, as calculated based on the policy terms. The plaintiff sought this amount as compensation for the losses incurred and requested the court to affirm the previous judgments in favor of the insured's claim.	The defendant, Illinois Mutual Insurance Company, maintained that its liability was limited to only one-thirtieth of the total fire loss, which they calculated to be $1,700 due to the existence of other insurance policies covering the same property. The company argued that according to the policy's specific provisions, it was not obligated to cover more than this partial amount. They sought a dismissal of the higher claim amount suggested by the plaintiff and contended that their interpretation of the policy provisions was correct.

In April 1860, in Chicago, Illinois, John B. Smith, Charles H. Schwab, and Mary C. Allen were indicted for conspiracy to seduce a minor, Lizzie M. Engles, aged fifteen. The indictment contained two counts: the first alleged that they conspired to procure Lizzie to have illicit relations with Schwab through deceitful means. The second count accused them of conspiring to cause Lizzie, a minor, to engage in such acts. Lizzie testified against the defendants, recounting how Mrs. Allen lured her into Schwab and Smith's store under false pretenses, offering drinks and enticing gifts. She described being coaked and eventually confined against her will, where Schwab attempted to seduce her. The trial included testimonies from several witnesses for the defense, who attested to the good character of the defendants. Ultimately, the court instructed the jury on the elements of conspiracy and what constituted unlawful acts, leading to a guilty verdict against all defendants.	The plaintiffs, representing the People, argued that the defendants engaged in a conspiracy to seduce a minor, Lizzie M. Engles, using deceitful and fraudulent means. They contended that the actions of the defendants constituted an indictable offense under both common law and state law, positing that conspiracies to commit such unlawful acts warrant punitive measures regardless of whether the means employed were strictly criminal.	The defendants maintained their innocence, claiming that the prosecution failed to prove their guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. They argued that to convict for conspiracy, the prosecution needed to demonstrate an agreement to commit an unlawful act, emphasizing that no evidence established they had conspired prior to Engles arriving at their store. Furthermore, they contended that their actions did not involve criminality as defined under the law, and thus, they should not be punished.

In June 1877, in Washington County, Illinois, J. F. Finley initiated a legal action against Hugh P. Green regarding a promissory note made by David W. Halbert and Joseph A. Halbert, which was payable to Green. The note was endorsed to Finley, who sought to collect on it. Initially, a justice of the peace ruled in favor of Green, obliging Finley to pay costs. Finley then appealed to the circuit court, where he waived a jury trial, and the case was tried by the court. The main contention revolved around the nature of Green's liability concerning the note. Finley argued that Green was effectively the maker of the note, thus holding absolute liability. In contrast, Green's counsel maintained that his liability was that of an indorser only, contingent upon the Halberts’ failure to pay. The court ultimately found that Green’s role was indeed that of an indorser, as he could not simultaneously be the maker and payee, and thus could only be held liable under that capacity.	The plaintiff, J. F. Finley, claimed that Hugh P. Green was liable as the maker of the promissory note, arguing that his obligation to pay was absolute and unqualified. Finley sought a judgment that would enforce the payment of the note, positing that Green's endorsements implied full responsibility.	Hugh P. Green's defense contended that his liability was not absolute as a maker but rather that of an indorser. Green argued that his endorsement of the note was conditional, asserting no liability unless the original makers, the Halberts, failed to pay. Further, he pointed out that the Halberts were capable of paying, and appropriate legal steps had not been taken to demand payment from them, which absolved him of responsibility.

In the case of Chicago and Alton Railroad Co. v. Abraham Bock, which took place in Logan County, Illinois, on October 22, 1882, the plaintiff Abraham Bock owned a pasture adjacent to the railroad tracks of the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company. During the night, several of Bock's horses escaped from the pasture and ended up on the tracks. Some of these horses were struck by trains, resulting in significant injuries that rendered them worthless. Bock subsequently brought a lawsuit against the railroad company seeking damages for the injuries sustained by his horses. The case proceeded to trial by jury, during which the jury found in favor of the plaintiff. The railroad company appealed the decision, arguing that the evidence did not support the jury's verdict. A key issue in the case was whether the railroad had exercised ordinary care in the management of its trains to avoid the injured animals, particularly given that it was stipulated both parties were not at fault for the horses being on the track.	The plaintiff, Abraham Bock, argued that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was negligent in the operation of its trains, which led to the injuries of his horses. He asserted that the railroad had a duty to exercise ordinary care and vigilance to avoid harming animals that may be on the track, which the plaintiff claimed was not upheld by the company's employees. The primary legal request was for recovery of damages due to the lost value of the horses injured by the trains.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company defended itself by arguing that it had exercised due diligence and care in the operation of its trains during the incident. The railroad's employees testified that they took the necessary precautions, and those operating trains on the night in question stated they did not see any horses on the track. The railroad company maintained that since no one witnessed the specific incident of the horses being struck, the evidence presented by the plaintiff was insufficient to establish negligence on their part.

John B. Miller v. Thomas L. Price is a legal case that began in Clinton County, Illinois, in the year 1866. The conflict arose over the possession of certain lands claimed by both parties, who traced their titles back to Elisha Duncan. On July 7, 1859, Duncan executed a deed of trust to Nathaniel Holmes which was duly recorded. Following some irregularities, Duncan executed another deed of trust for the same property on July 11, 1859. A deed of release was subsequently executed by Holmes on July 14, 1859, referencing a supposed defect in the earlier deed of trust and releasing any claims associated with it. However, the plaintiff's argument hinged on which deed of trust the release applied to, as both deeds were recorded around the same time but with inconsistencies. Eventually, after a series of transfers, the defendant's claims were purportedly derived from an unencumbered deed of trust dated July 11, which had not been released. The primary legal question was about the intended operation of Holmes' release and whether the record of deeds had been altered.	The plaintiff, John B. Miller, contended that he held a valid title to the property derived from Elisha Duncan. He argued that Holmes' deed of release was meant to operate on the earlier deed of trust dated July 7, thus effectively clearing any claims on the land that were connected to that deed. Miller sought to recover possession of the lands from Thomas L. Price, claiming rightful ownership based upon a legitimate conveyance from Duncan.	The defendant, Thomas L. Price, argued that the deed of release executed by Holmes on July 14 specifically referred to the second deed of trust dated July 11, rather than the one dated July 7. He maintained that since the original deeds were not presented in court and the records suggested a fraudulent alteration regarding the dates, the legal title to the property rightfully belonged to him based on a chain of ownership derived from the unaddressed deed of trust.

In the case of Michael Smith v. Josiah Forth, which took place in 1887, the controversy arose over a saloon bill involving a dispute between the plaintiff, Michael Smith, and the defendant, Josiah Forth. The case originated in the circuit court of White County, Illinois, where Smith sued Forth before a Justice of the Peace.
