After a trial, the court ruled in favor of Smith, awarding him a judgment of $816.85. Forth then appealed this judgment to the Illinois Appellate Court. The primary evidence against Forth was an account book maintained by Forth’s bartender, which detailed the items sold to Smith. During the trial, Forth's defense claimed that he had an arrangement with the saloon owner to receive drinks without charge, a claim denied by the bartender. The appeal centered on whether the account book was admissible evidence and the adequacy of any objections raised by Forth during his original trial.	Michael Smith, the plaintiff, argued that he was owed payment for drinks obtained from Josiah Forth's saloon, asserting that the bartender's account book supported his claim that Forth had not paid the $816.85 in question. Smith maintained that the itemization of the sales in the account book confirmed the legitimacy of the debt and sought to uphold the original judgment rendered in his favor.	Josiah Forth, the defendant, contended that he had an arrangement with the saloon allowing him to receive drinks without charge, asserting that his total bill should not exceed $3.00. He challenged the admissibility of the bartender's account book and claimed that there was inadequate foundation laid for its introduction as evidence at trial. Forth also argued that the objections to the admission of the book should not have been raised for the first time during the appeal, as no objections were filed during the original trial.

In the case of *Elloa A. Marsh et al. v. James Scott*, decided on May 9, 1888, by the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute originated from a transaction involving a patent for an improvement on steam-engine valve gear. The plaintiff, Elloa A. Marsh, and his business partner Minard Lafever, had been assigned a patent by the United States on December 28, 1880, but the patent was not signed by the Secretary of the Interior. Without realizing the omission, they engaged in negotiations with the defendant, James Scott, to sell him a one-third interest in the patent for $5,300, part of which was paid in cash ($500) and the rest through real estate, including two lots. The plaintiffs later conveyed ownership of the lots to Scott but faced challenges when it was revealed that the patent was not validly issued. The Superior Court of Cook County ultimately set aside the conveyance on the grounds of fraud and lack of consideration, ordering the property to be returned to Scott along with a refund of the cash payment.	The plaintiffs, Marsh and Lafever, argued that the defendant, James Scott, falsely represented the validity and value of the patent during the transaction. They sought the rescission of the contract on the basis of fraudulent misrepresentations and requested the return of the two lots they had conveyed to Scott, along with the reimbursement of the cash payment made as part of the transaction.	The defendant, James Scott, contended that the contract was valid despite the absence of the Secretary of the Interior's signature on the patent. According to Scott, even though this misrepresentation was revealed after the transaction, it did not nullify the contract since Marsh had subsequently corrected the signature issue. Scott maintained that the plaintiffs were accountable for the fraudulent claims regarding the patent's validity.

William R. Miller, Appellant, and Gabriel Marckle, Appellee, were involved in a legal dispute that took place in January 1859 in the state of Illinois. The case stemmed from the October term of the Morgan Circuit Court in 1858, where Marckle sought foreclosure of two mortgages executed by Miller on the same tract of land. Miller contested the validity of one mortgage, claiming it was executed without any consideration and solely to shield his property from creditors. He argued that the mortgage was fraudulent and thus unenforceable. The Circuit Court, however, ruled in favor of Marckle, ordering the foreclosure of both mortgages. The legal question at hand was whether Miller could defend against the foreclosure based on claims of his own fraudulent actions. This question was subsequently brought before the Illinois Supreme Court for review.	The plaintiff, Gabriel Marckle, claimed the right to foreclose on two mortgages held against Miller's property. He maintained that the mortgages were valid agreements and that Miller could not defend himself against foreclosure due to his claims of fraud. Marckle asserted that the mortgages were executed lawfully and sought the court's assistance in enforcing them, regardless of the alleged fraudulent intent behind their execution.	William R. Miller's defense was anchored on the argument that one of the mortgages was executed solely to defraud his creditors and that no real consideration was provided for it. He contended that due to the fraudulent nature of the transaction, he should be allowed to contest the foreclosure. Miller requested the court dismiss Marckle's foreclosure action, highlighting that courts should not assist parties involved in fraudulent agreements.

In September 1872, the case of The Board of Supervisors of Peoria County v. James Roche was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The events stemmed from an order issued by the Peoria Circuit Court during its September 1869 term, directing the clerk of the court to provide appropriate storage for court papers to protect them from dust and moisture. George A. Wilson, the clerk, and his deputy, James Roche, were tasked with organizing these old court papers, some dating back to 1826. Roche performed the work at night, believing he would be compensated by the county, as directed by his supervisor. The clerk's findings indicated a lack of proper maintenance for the records prior to their involvement. Roche submitted a bill for his services amounting to $230, which was reviewed by the county's judiciary committee. However, while payment was eventually offered, the central question was whether the county was legally obligated to compensate Roche for the work performed, given that it was ultimately the clerk's duty to maintain the records in good order.	The plaintiff, James Roche, claimed compensation for his work organizing the court papers under an order from the judge. He argued that the nature of the work was necessary for the preservation of court records and that he had been instructed by the clerk that he would be paid for his services by the county. Roche's legal request sought recovery of the $230 for the labor he performed, asserting the county’s obligation to pay for work ordered by the court and necessary for the proper functioning of the court system.	The defendant, The Board of Supervisors of Peoria County, contended that they were not legally obligated to pay for Roche's services. They argued that the duty to maintain the court records rested solely with the clerk of the court and that Roche, as the deputy, had no direct contract with the county for his work. The Board maintained that no formal agreement existed to justify payment, and any allowance provided was merely an act of discretion, not an acknowledgment of legal liability.

On January 31, 1885, Mrs. Josephine Ryhiner passed away intestate in Madison County, Illinois, leaving behind her only heirs, Frederick C. Ryhiner (one of the plaintiffs) and Mrs. Louisa Thedinga. At the time of her death, she had no debts and held a bank deposit of $17,727.68 at F. Ryhiner & Company. On May 4, 1885, the company made an assignment for the benefit of its creditors and appointed the plaintiffs as assignees. They published a notice in two local newspapers on May 15, inviting creditors to present their claims within three months. However, no direct notice was sent to Mrs. Ryhiner or her representatives. Subsequently, on September 21, 1885, Charles H. Seybt was appointed as the administrator for Mrs. Ryhiner and filed a claim against the assignees. The assignees objected, claiming the administrator's claim was not timely filed as it was submitted after the three-month period. Initially, the County Court sustained the assignees' first exception but allowed the claim, postponing it to all other claims presented in the timeframe. The administrator appealed, and the Circuit Court allowed the claim in full. The assignees objected, arguing that allowing the claim would violate the provisions of the statute regulating creditor claims.	The plaintiffs contended that the claim filed by the defendant was barred because it was not presented within the three-month timeframe stipulated by law following the public notice. They argued that the relevant statute mandates that claims not filed within the specified time should not participate in the distribution of the debtor's estate. They sought to have the Circuit Court's decision reversed, reaffirming the County Court's ruling that the claim was untimely and should not be entitled to participate in the distribution of assets.	The defendant argued that the failure to notify the heirs of Mrs. Ryhiner by mail rendered the three-month limitation inapplicable. The defense maintained that because no notice was sent directly to Mrs. Ryhiner or her heirs, their claim should not be considered late. They asserted that this lack of mailed notice created grounds for the claim to be allowed, arguing that the law concerning notice should be interpreted in a manner that protects the rights of creditors who were not adequately notified.

In 1883, the case Joseph Dinet v. Alexander Eilert was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute originated in Cook County, Illinois, regarding the ownership of a property that included a building with a boiler and engine on land claimed to belong to the defendant, Joseph Dinet. The plaintiff, Alexander Eilert, derived his title from a sale of the property from a previous owner, Louth, to Smith. A critical point of contention was whether Dinet induced Smith to believe that Louth had the right to sell the property through a conversation during which Dinet allegedly provided consent for the sale while concealing relevant information. The trial court instructed the jury on the aspects of estoppel, but there was significant conflict in testimonies regarding the specifics of Dinet's representations and the circumstances of the sale. The appellate court ultimately found that the jury instruction was misleading regarding the elements necessary to establish estoppel by conduct, thereby affecting the validity of the trial's outcome.	The plaintiff, Alexander Eilert, claimed that Joseph Dinet was estopped from denying Smith's title to the property, which he acquired from Louth. Eilert contended that Dinet's actions and words led Smith to believe that Louth had the authority to sell the property and that Dinet implicitly consented to the sale, which caused Smith to act on that belief.	The defendant, Joseph Dinet, argued against the application of estoppel, stating that the jury instructions were flawed and did not accurately reflect the necessary elements of estoppel by conduct. Dinet contended that the plaintiff failed to establish that Dinet made any representations or concealed information regarding his knowledge of the property sale that would have induced Smith to act.

The case, "The Lake Erie and Western Railway Company v. John Zoffinger," took place in Bloomington, Illinois, with the final judgment rendered on June 14, 1883, by the Illinois Supreme Court. John Zoffinger, the plaintiff, filed a lawsuit against the Lake Erie and Western Railway Company, claiming personal injuries resulting from a train incident. Zoffinger alleged that he was struck by a train that the railway company was operating over the tracks. During the initial trial, Zoffinger was awarded $3,500 by the circuit court, which was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court upon the defendant's appeal. The court findings indicated a conflict in testimony regarding the event, but the jury sided with Zoffinger, leading to a clear case for recovery. Evidence presented during the trial suggested that the train was moving at an unusual speed, failed to sound any warning signals, and that the train lacked adequate lighting. Zoffinger maintained that he was exercising due care for his safety at the time of the incident.	John Zoffinger claimed that the Lake Erie and Western Railway Company's negligence led to his injuries. He argued that the train was operated carelessly, as it was moving too quickly, lacked a warning bell or whistle, and there were no lights on the car that struck him. Zoffinger asserted that he was observing due care for his safety when the incident occurred and sought to recover damages for his injuries sustained during the accident.	The Lake Erie and Western Railway Company defended itself by arguing that Zoffinger was intoxicated at the time of the accident, which contributed to his injuries. The defendant attempted to present evidence of Zoffinger's behavior in a saloon shortly before the incident, but the court excluded this testimony as inadmissible. The railway company maintained that Zoffinger's alleged lack of due care should preclude any recovery for the injuries he claimed to have sustained.

In 1885, the case of Mary E. Stoltz et al. v. Henry Doering was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court concerning the inheritance of a tract of land located in DeKalb County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Henry Doering, was attempting to reclaim land originally owned by his brother, John Doering, who had died intestate in 1860. The defendants, Mary Elizabeth Stoltz and her husband, Jacob Stoltz, claimed ownership of the land, asserting that Mary was the legitimate daughter of John Doering, despite being born out of wedlock. John Doering had acknowledged Mary as his daughter after he moved to the United States, and she had lived in the possession of the property while paying taxes since his death. The key issue revolved around whether a child born out of wedlock could inherit under Illinois law, given that Illinois statutes excluded illegitimate children from inheriting property from their fathers unless the father had married the mother and acknowledged the child.	The plaintiff, Henry Doering, argued that as the brother of John Doering, he was the rightful heir to the property since Mary Elizabeth Stoltz, being an illegitimate child, had no legal claim to inherit under both common law and Illinois statutes. He contended that under the law, a bastard does not have the right to inherit from a father and sought a judgment to reclaim the property.	The defendants claimed Mary Elizabeth Stoltz was entitled to inherit from her father due to his public acknowledgment of her as his daughter and the belief that, under German law where she was born, she had rightful claim to inheritance. They also presented arguments based on the statutes of limitations, asserting their long-term possession and payment of taxes on the land. However, they struggled to demonstrate a connected title to the property as required by Illinois law.

In 1889, in Wayne County, Illinois, the case Louisville, Evansville & St. Louis Railway Co. v. George Lewis was presented before the Illinois Appellate Court. The plaintiff, George Lewis, sought damages from the Louisville, Evansville & St. Louis Railway Company following the death of his horse, allegedly caused by the negligence of the railroad company. The case was heard under the jurisdiction of Judge C. S. Conger in the Circuit Court. Key individuals involved included George Lewis as the plaintiff and representatives from the railway company, specifically Mr. J. R. Creighton as their attorney. The core issue revolved around whether the jury properly weighed conflicting evidence and if their decision was influenced by any bias or prejudice. The jury had found in favor of Lewis, leading to the appeal by the railway company.	George Lewis claimed that the railway company was responsible for the death of his horse due to negligence. He sought monetary damages as compensation for the loss incurred from the incident, arguing that the evidence presented clearly supported his claims against the defendant.	The Louisville, Evansville & St. Louis Railway Company contended that the evidence did not robustly support the verdict in favor of Lewis. Their defense maintained that the jury's findings might not have been justified and argued for the case to be overturned, requesting that the court dismiss the trial's verdict.

In November 1853, Elisha Linder owned land in what is now Mattoon, Illinois, and wished to promote the area's growth by having the Terre Haute & Alton Railway cross at a point on his property. He executed a bond to an individual named Messer, agreeing to convey twenty acres of land for $50, contingent upon the railway crossing the Illinois Central Road at or near the center of his land. Messer, alongside other railway officials, acted in a manner suggesting he was holding the land for their joint benefit. Following the establishment of the railway line, Linder conveyed land to several parties, but later reconveyed it to himself to facilitate the layout of the town. Then, in October 1865, Linder filed a lawsuit against David Carpenter, claiming that the contract and conveyance were obtained by fraud. The circuit court dismissed Linder's claims, which subsequently led to this appeal before the Illinois Supreme Court, as Linder sought to have the court order Carpenter to account for the proceeds from the sold lots and reconvey unsold lots back to him.",	Elisha Linder claimed that his initial contract with the railway officials was obtained through fraudulent representations about their ability to influence the railway's location. He argued that they misrepresented their control over the line and threatened displacement unless he conveyed the land. Linder sought to rescind the deed that conveyed the land, requesting that Carpenter account for the proceeds and return any unsold lots, asserting that he was misled into the agreement.",	David Carpenter contended that the allegations of fraud were unproven and characterized Linder as having full knowledge of the situation, given his status as a stockholder in the railway company. Carpenter argued that Linder had ratified the contract through subsequent dealings and had also waited an excessive amount of time before claiming fraud. Therefore, Carpenter requested the court to uphold the circuit court's dismissal of Linder's claims.",

The case of Joseph G. English, Conservator, v. Ann N. Porter took place in Illinois and was decided on March 26, 1884, by the Illinois Supreme Court. Joseph G. English filed a bill in equity as the conservator of Robert L. Porter, with the intent to annul certain conveyances of real estate that Robert had made to Ann N. Porter. The basis for the lawsuit was the claim that Robert was insane at the time the conveyances occurred and that Ann had exerted undue influence over him. Evidence presented indicated that the contested deeds were executed on April 7 and 15, 1881. Robert was declared insane on May 12, 1881. Numerous witnesses were called to testify regarding Robert’s mental capacity at the time of the conveyances, with opinions divided over whether he was competent to handle his affairs. Some witnesses described a gradual mental decline, while others maintained he was capable of transacting business. The court examined the nature of Robert's mental state, ultimately deciding he was capable of making the conveyances despite evidence of some cognitive impairment.	The plaintiff, Joseph G. English, argued that the conveyances made by Robert L. Porter to Ann N. Porter were invalid due to Robert's insanity and that Ann had exercised undue influence over him. He requested the court to set aside these property transfers, claiming they were made without the mental capacity necessary to understand the nature and consequences of the transactions.	Ann N. Porter contested the claims by asserting that Robert was mentally competent and capable of managing his affairs at the time the conveyances were executed. She presented testimony from multiple witnesses, including professionals and acquaintances, who attested to Robert’s competency. Additionally, she argued that the conveyances were made as payments on debts owed to her, thereby negating claims of undue influence.

The legal case "The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company v. Herman Kichler et al." took place in September 1868 in Tazewell County, Illinois. It involved an accident on the railway operated by the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company that allegedly resulted in the destruction of thirty barrels of whiskey and twenty barrels of pork. The plaintiffs, Kichler and others, sought damages from the railway company for these losses, with a jury trial waived and a judgment rendered in favor of the plaintiffs for $3,243. The primary issue during the trial revolved around whether tax had been paid on the whiskey in question, which was pertinent to determining its value, as tax status could affect the worth of the lost goods. The defense attempted to introduce evidence of a lack of payment for the whiskey's tax, but the trial court excluded this evidence, leading to a significant point of contention.	The plaintiffs claimed compensation for the loss of their whiskey and pork that were destroyed in a railway accident. They argued that the railroad company was responsible for the property they had undertaken to deliver, and sought to recover the calculated value of the destroyed items, set at $3,243. Their position was that the value computation should consider whether taxes had been incurred on the whiskey, as it influenced its worth in the market.	The defendants contended that the trial court erred by not allowing them to present evidence that the whiskey had been shipped without tax payment, which would lower its value. They argued that the plaintiffs had a duty to prove the worth of the whiskey correctly, taking into account the lack of tax paid per the revenue laws. The defense claimed that failing to admit this evidence violated their rights and misrepresented the true value of the goods lost in the railway accident.

In September 1868, the Illinois Supreme Court considered the case of Jonathan Jackson et al. v. Jacob Berner, stemming from a dispute over property in Chicago's school section addition. Jacob Berner filed an ejectment action against Jonathan Jackson and others, heirs of Gideon M. Jackson, deceased, to regain possession of part of lot eighteen in block one hundred and thirty-one. Gideon M. Jackson had purchased adjacent lots in 1845 and constructed a hotel, unknowingly encroaching on lot eighteen. After Jackson’s death in 1850, his heirs continued to occupy the premises. The court considered the legitimacy of Berner’s title and the claim of adverse possession by Jackson's heirs, who had maintained occupancy of the property for over twenty years. A critical aspect of the case involved the admissibility of a duplicate patent related to the property, which was challenged on technical grounds. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of Berner, leading to the appeal by the defendants.	Berner contended that he held valid title to lot eighteen through mesne conveyances from the State and sought to eject Jackson’s heirs from the property. He argued that the Jackson family’s claim to adverse possession was invalid as they had never occupied the property in a manner that was hostile or exclusive.	The defendants claimed that they had held possession of the property for more than twenty years, asserting that this long-term occupancy constituted adverse possession, which should bar Berner's claims. They disputed the plaintiff's title and pointed to technical objections regarding the admissibility of the property patent that Berner sought to present in court.

The case of William W. Low et al. v. William Martin was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1857, following a dispute originating in November 1853 during a circuit court session in La Salle, Illinois. The plaintiffs, William W. Low and others, were in a legal battle against William Martin, who was accused of fraudulent activities as a warehouseman. The crux of the case revolved around thirteen counts of fraud, wherein the defendant had allegedly issued receipts for grain that he never received or stored for the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs claimed that these receipts were issued with the intent to defraud them, as they resulted in monetary loss based on the receipts' fraudulent claims. The statute in question penalizes warehousemen who falsely represent that they have goods belonging to others in storage, allowing any aggrieved party to seek damages. The case raised important legal questions about the issuance of warehouse receipts and the protections afforded under both common law and the statute regarding fraudulent practices.	The plaintiffs argued that they had been wrongfully defrauded by the defendant, who issued receipts for grain that he did not possess. They maintained that the defendant's actions caused them to suffer financial losses because they acted upon the faith of those fraudulent receipts. The plaintiffs sought damages based on the value of the grain that was purportedly in store but never delivered.	The defendant contended that the plaintiffs had not adequately demonstrated that they suffered any damages from the issuance of the receipts. He argued that the first and second counts of the complaint were flawed due to a lack of evidence showing that the plaintiffs were harmed by his actions. The defendant sought to dismiss these initial counts, asserting that the claims did not establish a valid cause of action.

The case of Mary J. Eads v. Calvin R. Thompson et al. took place in Illinois, culminating in a ruling by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 23, 1884. The legal proceedings originated from a creditor's bill filed by Mary J. Eads against several defendants, including Harvey Garrett, Eleanor Garrett, and Calvin B. Thompson. The underlying issue revolved around Eads seeking to subject certain real properties to satisfy a judgment she obtained against Harvey Garrett.  The case highlights a complicated family estate matter following the death of Coleman Garrett in 1878, which left his estate divided among his nine heirs, including Harvey Garrett. Harvey sold his share of the estate to Calvin B. Thompson in 1879—before Eads's judgment against him was obtained. This sale was claimed by Eads to be fraudulent, intended to obstruct her ability to collect her debt. Similarly, Eleanor Garrett was accused of acquiring land that should rightfully belong to Harvey, purportedly to hinder Eads's claims.  In the circuit court, the complaint was dismissed for most defendants, and Eads appealed this decision, seeking to hold the remaining defendants accountable for the property that should satisfy her judgment.	Mary J. Eads argued that the property transactions between Harvey Garrett and the other defendants were fraudulent, executed with the intent to hinder her collection of a previously awarded judgment. She sought to set aside the sale of real estate, asserting that the properties in question should be subject to her claim as payment for the judgment against Harvey Garrett.	The defendants, particularly Calvin B. Thompson and Eleanor Garrett, contended that the property transactions were legitimate and in good faith. They argued that the sale from Harvey Garrett to Thompson was made when there was no existing judgment against him, hence it could not be considered fraudulent. Additionally, they presented evidence to support that Eleanor acquired certain lands using her own funds, negating claims that their ownership was meant to obstruct the plaintiff.

In 1859, the case of "The Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company, Appellant, v. Epperson W. Brown, Appellee" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The incident occurred on June 21, 1857, when three mares, one mule, and one colt belonging to Epperson W. Brown were killed by a locomotive operated by the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company. Brown claimed that the railroad company, which had its track open for use since February 14, 1855, failed to erect necessary fences as mandated by statute, which led his animals to stray onto the railroad track. The case was filed in the Circuit Court of Marion County, where Brown sought $850 in damages. The jury ruled in favor of Brown, awarding him $730. The Railroad Company appealed the decision, arguing that the evidence did not support the verdict due to several unmet statutory requirements for liability.	Epperson W. Brown argued that the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company was liable for the death of his animals due to its failure to provide proper fencing along the railroad track, as required by statute. He contended that the track was in use without adequate safety measures, resulting in his cattle being unlawfully allowed to wander onto the train tracks. Brown's claims focused on the breach of statutory obligations by the railroad, asserting that he was entitled to compensation for the damages suffered, amounting to $850.	The Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company’s defense relied on the assertion that the evidence presented did not meet the necessary statutory requirements to hold them liable. They argued that the jury's verdict was not supported by proof that the road had been operational for the required six months or that the injury occurred at a place where the company was mandated to fence. Moreover, the defendant claimed that no negligence was proven, which was necessary for liability under the statute, and that the declaration lacked required averments.

In the case of *Thomas J. Robinson et al. v. William H. Appleton et al.*, dated February 1, 1887, the dispute arises from a real estate transaction involving a mortgage foreclosure. The events date back to November 1, 1866, when James E. Cooley executed a bond to David B. Sears for real estate located in Rock Island County, Illinois. The bond stipulated that Cooley would convey all his rights and interests in the property for a total consideration of $30,000, to be paid in several installments, out of which all were paid except for the last two notes. Following Cooley's death, his executors initiated foreclosure proceedings in 1883 to recover the outstanding amount. The Circuit Court found that $17,248.40 was due and ordered the property sold if payment was not made. The appellants, who claimed under Sears, contested this by raising several legal points regarding the executors' authority and the nature of the vendor's lien. The case involved complex issues surrounding vendor's liens, the legality of quit-claim deeds, and the rights of parties holding title through after-acquired interests.	The plaintiffs, representing the executors of James E. Cooley, claimed that they were rightfully seeking to enforce a vendor's lien due to unpaid purchase money following Cooley's death. They argued that the lien survived Cooley's death and that they had the legal authority to foreclose on the mortgage. The plaintiffs requested the court to uphold the Circuit Court's decree, which required the sale of the property unless the outstanding debts were paid.	The defendants, who asserted claims under David B. Sears, contended that the appellees lacked standing to bring the foreclosure action since they were not the original vendors. They argued that the lien could not be enforced as Cooley’s obligation was void due to non-payment and the nature of the quit-claim deed. Furthermore, they raised the Statute of Limitations as a defense, claiming that the right to bring the suit had lapsed over time.

John A. Metcalf filed an action of assumpsit in January 1861 against Moses S. Edmiston and Kramer in Edgar, Illinois. The plaintiff sought to recover approximately $2,500 for hogs that he had sold and delivered to the defendants. The case did not involve a jury; instead, it was tried directly by the court, which ultimately ruled in favor of the defendants, ordering Metcalf to pay costs. Following the judgment, Metcalf moved for a new trial, asserting several errors in the trial court's proceedings and evidence admission, leading to his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The key issues included the admissibility of railroad company records as evidence and the interpretation of partnerships related to the sales.	The plaintiff, John A. Metcalf, argued that the trial court's judgment was erroneous based on several points. He claimed the judgment violated law and evidence principles, contended that the court improperly admitted railroad books and the deposition of a witness (Me Whinny). Metcalf also argued that the court wrongly concluded that the arrangement with Kramer did not constitute a partnership and that he could not recover costs under the common counts.	The defendants, represented by John P. Usher, contended that the court properly admitted the evidence presented and upheld the original judgment. They maintained that Metcalf had not provided sufficient evidence to support his claims against them. The defendants sought to affirm the trial court's decision to dismiss Metcalf's claims and retain the costs incurred.

In 1873, a legal conflict arose in Saline County, Illinois, involving the Cairo and Vincennes Railroad Company and George Joiner, acting as a guardian. The case began when Joiner sought to bring the railroad company to court. However, the manner of serving the process was contested. The defendant claimed that the service was not properly executed as required by the Illinois Practice Act in force since July 1, 1872. The officer responsible for serving the summons attempted to serve it by reading it to a station agent instead of delivering a physical copy to an appropriate individual, such as the company's president. The case was subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court due to the alleged improper service of process.	The plaintiff, George Joiner, asserted that the Cairo and Vincennes Railroad Company was liable and sought a legal judgment against them. However, the central issue in the case was not the merits of Joiner's claims but rather the procedural validity of how the railroad company was summoned to court.	The defendant, represented by the Cairo and Vincennes Railroad Company, contended that the lower court erred by issuing a judgment by default without proper service of process. They argued that the service was defective since it did not comply with the requirement to serve the president of the company, as no evidence was provided indicating that he could not be found within the county.

The case "William Strawn et al. v. Phebe G. Strawn" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1870, following a legal dispute over the special dower of Phebe G. Strawn, the widow of Jacob Strawn, who passed away on August 23, 1865. Jacob Strawn left behind an estate valued at approximately $500,000 and eight children—three from a previous marriage and five with Phebe. After his death, Phebe and four of her children, who were adults, lived in a substantial homestead. The estate appraisal provided Phebe with certain items: beds, bedding, household furniture, and a year's worth of provisions. The three stepchildren contested the appraisal, arguing that the provisions allowed were excessive and that the term "family" under the statute should only refer to minor children, not adults or household helpers. This contention led to an appeal to the circuit court and subsequently to the Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, William Strawn and others, claimed that the circuit court's allowance to Phebe Strawn for her special dower was excessive. They argued that the term "family" in the relevant statute should only encompass the widow and any minor children, suggesting that, with no minor children left, Phebe was entitled to allowances sufficient only for herself. They contended that the court had improperly interpreted the law regarding what constituted necessary goods and provisions.	Phebe G. Strawn, the defendant, argued that the allowance made by the appraisers was reasonable given the circumstances, asserting that the law's intent was to support not just the widow but her entire household, including adult children living at home, while maintaining her standard of living. She defended the appraisers’ decision to include items necessary for her family composition, which included household help and adult children, contending that the interpretation of "family" in the statute should encompass these individuals.

In April 1857, the case of Samuel T. Stillson et al. v. Warren Hill was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in LaSalle County during the December 1855 term of the county court. Warren Hill initiated a lawsuit against Samuel T. Stillson and Hallock under the legal premise of assumpsit, claiming a debt arising from a partnership. Stillson challenged this by filing a plea in abatement to deny the existence of the alleged partnership, as well as a plea of non-assumpsit, which contests the obligation to fulfill the debt. The county court ruled in favor of Warren Hill, awarding him $371.34 plus costs. Stillson appealed the ruling, arguing that the plea in abatement had not been waived despite submitting the plea of non-assumpsit. The primary legal question considered by the Supreme Court was whether submitting a plea of non-assumpsit negated the earlier plea in abatement concerning the partnership's existence.	Warren Hill, the plaintiff, claimed that Stillson and Hallock were partners and therefore jointly liable for the debts owed. He sought to validate his claims through the statute governing partnerships, asserting that the defendants' denial of partnership should not exempt them from liability in this joint action. Hill's legal request was primarily to enforce the judgment that held the defendants accountable for the debt claimed.	The defendants, primarily represented by Stillson, argued against the partnership assertion raised by Hill. Stillson contended that his plea in abatement, which denied the existence of a partnership, should remain valid and not be considered waived by the simultaneous plea of non-assumpsit. He sought to have the court recognize this distinction in pleading, asserting that both pleas should be addressed together, potentially undermining Hill's claims.

In 1863, in Aurora, Illinois, the case of Orvis C. Hinds et al. v. John Ingham was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal proceedings concerned a promissory note dated September 19, 1854, wherein the defendants, O.C. Hinds, J.A. Hinds, and A.H. Hinds, jointly promised to pay the plaintiff, John Ingham, $300, with interest. Over the years, several indorsements were made on the back of the note, including payments of interest and a partial payment of $30 made by A.H. Hinds on January 13, 1859. Disputes arose over whether an agreement to extend the time for payment had discharged A.H. Hinds from his obligations as a surety. The trial court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, and the defendants appealed, challenging the decision based on the alleged release of the surety’s liability.	The plaintiff, John Ingham, claimed the defendants were liable for the outstanding balance of the promissory note. He argued that the testimony and evidence, particularly the indorsements on the note and the payments made, demonstrated that A.H. Hinds had waived any claims for release from liability as a surety. The plaintiff requested the court affirm the trial court's judgment.	The defendants asserted that A.H. Hinds was discharged from liability due to an extension of the time for payment that occurred without his agreement or knowledge. They argued that the legal principle stipulates that such an extension, if made with the principal maker and the payee without the surety's consent, releases the surety from further obligations. They requested the court to overturn the judgment and rule in favor of the defendants.

George W. French, the appellant in this case, was involved in a legal dispute with Calvin Carr, the appellee, concerning improvements made on government-owned land sold to French. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Kane County, Illinois, where Carr sued French in 1844 for the value of improvements he had made to the land, which he claimed were worth between $550 and $600. In a previous agreement, Carr had sold his claim to the land improvements to French, who later sought to revisit the terms after discovering issues with the property's boundaries. In July 1842, Carr took back the land improvements in exchange for a house and lots in Elgin. Following Carr’s bankruptcy petition in August 1842, French moved onto the land but continued to dispute the payment owed to Carr, claiming apprehension about Carr's creditors. Ultimately, the Court had to determine whether Carr retained any rightful claim to the improvements after being declared bankrupt and the implications of this status on the sale agreement between Carr and French.	Carr claimed that he was entitled to $550 for the improvements made on the government land before his bankruptcy declaration. He argued that the prior agreements with French were valid and sought to enforce the payment despite the bankruptcy, asserting that his claim constituted a property right under Illinois law.	French's defense centered on the assertion that Carr's bankruptcy effectively nullified any ownership rights he had in the improvements at the time of the alleged sale. He contended that the bankruptcy law stripped Carr of his rights to dispose of the improvements, making the agreement without consideration, thus he should not be liable for the payment.

In December 1848, the legal case of Ezekiel Walters v. James Short arose in Brown County, Illinois, following a dispute concerning a written instrument dated April 1, 1847. James Short filed a lawsuit against Ezekiel Walters, claiming that Walters had promised to deliver $50 worth of cattle to his residence by July 10 of that year. The original case was brought before a justice of the peace, where Walters was initially favored. Short then appealed to the Circuit Court, where the trial was conducted without a jury. During the proceedings, Walters denied executing the instrument but later admitted the signature's authenticity. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Short, awarding him $80 and costs. Walters subsequently sought a new trial, which was denied, leading to further legal examination of the case's merits regarding the instrument's validity and the nature of its alterations.	James Short argued that the written instrument constituted a binding agreement for Walters to deliver a specified quantity of cattle. Short maintained that he was entitled to payment based on the terms of this document, which he claimed was a valid contract despite Walters' denials. He sought enforcement of this agreement through the court, requiring Walters to fulfill his cattle delivery obligation as stipulated.	Ezekiel Walters contended that the instrument in question was not a valid promissory note because it lacked specific details, such as a named payee and the implied consideration for the agreement. Walters claimed that the interlineation of the document indicated an alteration that should render it void. He argued that Short failed to provide sufficient evidence to support the claim that the modified instrument was properly executed and that the obligation to pay was valid.

The case of "The Michigan Central Railroad Company v. William J. Carrow" took place in September 1874 in Illinois. The plaintiff, William J. Carrow, a traveler, checked a trunk containing valuable merchandise, specifically jewelry valued at $30,000, with the defendant, the Michigan Central Railroad Company, as ordinary baggage. When the baggage car caught fire, the contents were destroyed. Carrow sought to recover damages for his loss, claiming that the railroad company, as a common carrier, was liable for the destruction of his property. The main individuals involved were Carrow, representing the interests of travelers, and the railroad company as the carrier of goods. The case was significant in addressing the liability of carriers for personal luggage, particularly when hidden valuable merchandise was involved.	Carrow argued that the Michigan Central Railroad Company, as a common carrier, was liable for the loss of his jewelry due to their failure to protect his checked baggage. He claimed that the company had a duty to ensure the safety of all luggage checked in as baggage, and his claim for damages amounted to $30,789.78, reflecting the value of the destroyed items.	The Michigan Central Railroad Company contended that they were not liable for the loss since Carrow failed to disclose the contents of the trunk, which he represented as ordinary baggage. They argued that he had engaged in a form of legal fraud by not informing them about the valuable merchandise. Furthermore, the company asserted that they had no knowledge of the trunk's contents and had not breached any duty of care, maintaining that their contract only covered the transport of personal luggage.

In September 1875, the case of Elias Wenger v. Marshall Calder took place in Kankakee County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff, Elias Wenger, and the defendant, Marshall Calder, a physician and surgeon. The case arose when Wenger filed suit against Calder, alleging malpractice during the treatment of a dislocated elbow. The treatment given by Calder allegedly resulted in further pain and suffering for Wenger, prompting him to seek damages. Initially, the jury ruled in favor of Wenger, awarding him $1,500 in damages. However, the court identified several errors in the jury instructions provided during the trial, particularly concerning the measure of damages for pain and suffering and the absence of evidence supporting claims of willful negligence on Calder's part. The court concluded that the jury was misled and that the damages awarded could not account for the original injury caused by Calder's faultless action.	The plaintiff, Elias Wenger, claimed that Marshall Calder had failed to use reasonable care and skill in treating his dislocated elbow, resulting in additional pain and suffering beyond what was originally caused by the injury. Wenger sought damages for both this additional suffering and any permanent injuries sustained due to Calder's alleged malpractice. He requested that the jury consider the extent of pain and added suffering when determining the financial compensation due to him.	The defendant, Marshall Calder, contended that there was no evidence to support claims of willful negligence or malpractice in his treatment of Wenger's elbow. He argued that any pain or suffering experienced by Wenger was not attributable to his actions and requested the court to reverse the damages awarded by the jury, as the jury instructions were erroneous and misleading, not based on credible evidence of malpractice.

William Hauskins v. The People of the State of Illinois took place in Madison County, Illinois, with the decision issued by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1876. The case arose under the Bastardy Act, after a complaint was filed against Hauskins, alleging he was the father of a child born to a woman in Madison County. The child was born on February 20, 1874, and died on January 9, 1876. The legal proceedings began on September 11, 1875, after which the county court dismissed the case, leading to an appeal by the prosecuting witness to the circuit court. The central issue was whether Hauskins could be held liable for child support after the child's death. The Illinois Supreme Court had to determine jurisdiction and the validity of the lower court's proceedings given the death of the child.	The plaintiff, represented by the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that Hauskins was the father of the illegitimate child and sought to enforce his financial responsibility for the support of the child under the provisions of the Bastardy Act. They argued that despite the child's death prior to the judgment, Hauskins should still be liable for the child support payments accrued during the child's life.	Hauskins contended that the legal proceedings should abate due to the child's death, arguing that the prosecution could not continue once the child died. He also raised concerns regarding the sufficiency of jurisdiction and evidence that established the parentage of the child.

Lucy N. Wight and others (plaintiffs) were involved in a legal dispute with "The People" (defendants) concerning the alleged usurpation of ferry franchises in Galena, Illinois. The case was brought as a quo warranto proceeding, asserting that the plaintiffs unlawfully claimed certain rights to operate ferries. The legal proceedings began with a demurrer filed by the defendants, which was something akin to a formal objection to the legal sufficiency of the plaintiffs' claims. This demurrer was overruled by the circuit court, which led to the defendants failing to provide any further response. Consequently, during the March term of 1850, Judge Sheldon ruled that the franchises claimed by the plaintiffs lacked sufficient legal support, thus forfeiting them to the people of Illinois. In response to this unfavorable ruling, the defendants, now plaintiffs in error, appealed the decision, leading to the case being brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1854 for review.	The plaintiffs claimed that the ruling from the circuit court was erroneous, arguing that the quo warranto information was improperly filed. They contended that the legal action was presented not in the name of the people of Illinois, as required by constitutional law, but in the name of the State’s attorney. The plaintiffs sought to reverse the circuit court’s judgment and reinstate their claimed franchises.	The defendants (originally the plaintiffs in error) maintained that the quo warranto information was not validly filed according to constitutional provisions. They argued that the failure to present the case "in the name and by the authority of the people of the State of Illinois" rendered the information defective and insufficient to sustain the judgment made by the lower court. They requested the Supreme Court to uphold the circuit court's ruling.

In September 1874, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, a legal proceeding unfolded between Richard Bowden (plaintiff) and William Bowden (defendant). This case involved the defendant being arrested on a capias ad satisfaciendum (ca. sa.) due to allegations that he refused to surrender his property to satisfy a judgment owed to the plaintiff. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant had fraudulently disposed of his property to evade an execution on the debt. The defendant requested a jury trial in the county court, which resulted in a guilty verdict against him, leading to his remand to custody. Following this, an appeal process began in the circuit court. The circuit court denied a motion to dismiss the appeal, whereupon another jury found the defendant not guilty of fraud. The plaintiff contended that the circuit court erred in various aspects, including the dismissal of his appeal and insufficient bond approval for the defendant’s release. The case highlighted issues related to the statute governing insolvent debtors and the rights of creditors and debtors regarding fraudulent intent in property disposition.	Richard Bowden, the plaintiff, alleged that William Bowden refused to surrender his estate to satisfy a pre-existing judgment and fraudulently disposed of his property to obstruct the execution of the judgment. The plaintiff argued that the county court's remand was an improper procedure and insisted that the circuit court should have dismissed the appeal against the remand order. He contended that the jury's verdict, finding the defendant not guilty of fraud, should not have been considered valid and sought a judgment in his favor along with the recovery of costs.	William Bowden, the defendant, countered that the remand order from the county court was a judicial act, and therefore, allowed for an appeal. He maintained that the evidence did not sufficiently establish fraudulent intent in the sale of his property. The defendant argued that it was his legal right to sell property to pay debts, provided there was no deceptive motive. Additionally, he contended that the circuit court correctly denied the motion for a new trial and upheld the jury's verdict that found him not guilty of fraud, hence he requested that judgment be rendered in his favor.

In 1883, Edward Cody entered a legal dispute with The Commercial Fire Insurance Company regarding a fire insurance policy covering his two-story brick building located at 3725 South Halsted Street, Chicago. The building experienced a partial loss due to a fire, resulting in damages amounting to $540. Cody's claim against the insurance company was based on the policy's provisions. The plaintiff filed a declaration that included special counts as well as common counts, asserting his right to recover damages from the insurer. The defendant, represented by Hynes, English & Dunne, contended that Cody had forfeited his insurance policy by allowing a smokehouse to remain on the property, which they argued caused the fire. The jury trial concluded with an inconsistent verdict: while the jury ruled in favor of Cody, they awarded him only one cent in damages. Following the trial, Cody's motion for a new trial was denied, leading him to appeal the decision.	Edward Cody argued that he was entitled to recover the full amount of $540 in damages for the loss sustained by the fire, as the insurance policy should have covered the losses incurred. He maintained that the jury's award of just one cent was unreasonable and inconsistent with the evidence presented during the trial. His legal requests included seeking a new trial and a judgment that accurately reflected the actual damages incurred.	The Commercial Fire Insurance Company claimed that Edward Cody forfeited his insurance policy by allowing a smokehouse to remain on the insured premises, thus increasing the risk of fire as forbidden by the terms of the policy. They contended that if the risk was indeed increased by conditions under Cody's control, he was not entitled to recover any damages. The defendant's aim was to uphold the jury's original verdict, claiming it should have reflected a victory for them given the circumstances surrounding the fire.

The case of Strong et al. v. Allen took place in April 1867 in Illinois and was presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose when a writ of error was filed in connection with a previous case involving the plaintiffs, Strong and others, and the defendant, Allen. During the court proceedings, it was noted that the transcript of the record had not been filed within the mandated time frame of the first two days of the term. The defendant's counsel argued that this omission should result in the dismissal of the case. However, the court clarified that there is no specific law requiring the record to be filed by that time, and referred to Rule 75 which governs such cases. The case involved procedural elements concerning the maintenance of a writ of error and the responsibilities of the court clerk.	The plaintiffs argued that the failure to file the transcript of the record within the specified time did not justify dismissing the writ of error they had filed. They sought to continue their case without being penalized for the clerical oversight regarding record submission.	The defendant's key argument focused on the procedural requirement that the transcript should have been filed on time, insisting that this failure warranted dismissal of the writ of error. They requested the court to dismiss the case on the grounds of the plaintiffs' neglect to comply with filing procedures.

The case of Joshua J. Moore v. Norman H. Purple took place in December 1846 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Peoria County, where Purple filed an action of assumpsit against Moore. The declaration involved two counts: one concerning a promissory note and another regarding money had and received, as well as work and labor provided. During the October term of 1845, Moore failed to plead, leading to a default judgment against him. Consequently, a jury was summoned to assess damages, determining the amount to be $148.96. An appeal was made by Moore to the Supreme Court, challenging the judgment on several grounds, chiefly concerning the validity of the damage assessment process, including claims of insufficient notice and the legality of the writ of inquiry issued by the sheriff. The case was revisited in May 1846, during which the Circuit Court allowed the sheriff to amend his record, prompting further examination of the previous proceedings in the Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Norman H. Purple, asserted that he was entitled to damages based on a breach of contract, represented by the promissory note and his claims for money received and work performed. Purple contended that the damages were duly assessed by a jury as per the court's instructions and requested the court to uphold the lower court's judgment of $148.96 in his favor.	Joshua J. Moore contested the judgment by claiming that the assessment of damages was flawed due to a lack of proper notice regarding the execution of the writ of inquiry and the proceedings not taking place in open court. Moore argued that the writ did not comply with legal standards required for such assessments. He sought to reverse the judgment on these bases, insisting that the court's actions were improper and that he had not been legally informed of the proceedings against him.

In the case of Lucinda Eyster v. John Eyster, decided in June 1853, the legal dispute arose from a divorce proceeding initiated by John Eyster against Lucinda Eyster. The case took place in Ogle County, Illinois, and was heard at the May term of the Ogle Circuit Court in the year 1849. The Circuit Court had rendered a decree granting John Eyster a divorce from Lucinda Eyster. There was a contention raised regarding the service of summons, specifically whether it was served properly. The sheriff's return indicated that the summons had been served by reading, but the parties agreed to allow the presentation of affidavits to clarify the manner of service. The sheriff later confirmed that he had delivered a copy of the summons and expressed willingness to amend his return to reflect such service, which was a crucial aspect of the court's review. The Illinois Supreme Court was tasked with reviewing the Circuit Court's decree and the validity of the service.	Lucinda Eyster, the plaintiff in error, contested the divorce granted to John Eyster, asserting that the manner of service of the summons was improper as initially stated by the sheriff's return. The main legal request was for the court to recognize that the service of process should be deemed incomplete or inadequate based on the stipulation of the parties regarding the amendment of the return.	John Eyster, the defendant in error, defended the divorce decree by arguing that the sheriff had indeed delivered a copy of the summons and was willing to amend the return to reflect the proper service. He contended that since the stipulation allowed for such an amendment, the return should be accepted as corrected, thereby affirming the validity of the service and the divorce granted by the Circuit Court.

In 1886, the case of Frank G. Jaques v. John B. Lester was filed in the Circuit Court of Champaign County, Illinois. The dispute arose over the title to certain lands originally conveyed by P. S. Loughborough. The plaintiff, John B. Lester, claimed to be the rightful owner of the lands in question through an unrecorded deed from Loughborough to William J. Graves, dated May 24, 1845. Lester argued that despite the 1855 deed from Loughborough's devisee, Elizabeth Loughborough, to James F. Gamble and others, which became recorded in June 1855, his actual possession of the land constituted a superior claim. The defendant, Frank G. Jaques, claimed title through the 1855 deed and asserted that Lester had no legal standing, as he did not possess a recorded title at that time. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Lester, but Jaques appealed, leading to a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, John B. Lester, sought to have the deed from Elizabeth Loughborough declared invalid, asserting that the title he derived from the original grantor, P. S. Loughborough, was superior. He claimed continuous possession of the land since 1845 and argued that the deed transferring title to Jaques was recorded after his original deed, thereby creating a "cloud" on his title that needed to be removed.	The defendant, Frank G. Jaques, denied Lester's claims to the land. He argued that he held a valid title under the deed from Elizabeth Loughborough, recorded in 1855, and contended that Lester's unrecorded deed did not confer valid ownership. Jaques maintained that Lester's continued possession of the land did not equate to legal ownership and thus sought to uphold his recorded title.

William H. Stoelker filed a case against The Chicago Building Supply Company in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision rendered on July 13, 1887. The case arose from a dispute concerning certain building materials that were to be delivered for a construction project managed by Stoelker. The events unfolded in Cook County, Illinois, where Stoelker, the owner, had contracted carpenters to erect a house. The Chicago Building Supply Company had initially refused to deliver materials directly to the carpenters. Subsequently, a meeting was convened involving all parties, leading to a revised agreement: The defendant was to supply the materials if Stoelker agreed to withhold enough payment from the contractor to cover the costs. The materials were supplied under this arrangement, and Stoelker retained the necessary funds as promised. The Chicago Building Supply Company raised the issue that this arrangement might constitute an agreement to pay someone else's debt, potentially invoking the Statute of Frauds, which requires certain agreements to be in writing. The court had previously instructed the jury on this legal principle, and the plaintiff maintained that the instructions were appropriate and did not mislead the jury.	Stoelker claimed that The Chicago Building Supply Company had a contractual obligation to deliver the building materials, which he fulfilled by withholding funds from the contractor to pay for the materials. Stoelker sought to recover the amount due based on this agreement, contesting that his arrangement was valid and that the refusal of delivery by the defendant was improper.	The defendant contended that the agreement between Stoelker and the carpenters was, in essence, a guarantee for the debt of another party (the contractors), thus placing it under the provisions of the Statute of Frauds. The defense argued that such a collateral agreement must be in writing to be enforceable and that the jury instructions regarding this matter should not have been misleading.

Cornelius Desmond was employed as a switchman by the Terre Haute, Alton and St. Louis Railroad Company in 1858, working for four months at a salary of $35 per month. On January 20, 1859, he was partially paid by the company—receiving half of his due wages in cash and the other half in the form of fourteen promissory notes, each valued at five dollars, which were payable at the company's office in St. Louis starting October 20, 1859. These notes were intended to be redeemable for transportation services and included an interest rate of 6% until paid. After the notes became due, Desmond attempted to present them for payment but was refused, leading him to hold onto them. He subsequently filed a lawsuit against the railroad company in the East St. Louis city court, where he initially won a judgment for the amount owed. However, the company appealed, and the case was transferred to the circuit court of St. Clair County. The circuit court found in favor of the defendant, leading Desmond to appeal further, arguing that the notes had never been paid.	Desmond's main argument centered around the claim that he was owed payment for the promissory notes he received as a part of his wages for labor performed for the railroad company. He contested that the notes had not been paid back, and sought a reversal of the circuit court's judgment which found against him, maintaining that the evidence of his claim—specifically the promissory notes—should have been admissible in court to support his case.	The railroad company's defense rested on the argument that the notes presented by Desmond were issued by a different entity, the Terre Haute, Alton and St. Louis Railroad Company, and there was no evidence provided to establish that they were the same company or that the company being sued was liable for the debts of that entity. Moreover, they asserted that the legal requirements for showing liability under the act of 1861 for debts assumed upon purchase of the railroad had not been met, as there was no proof demonstrating that the defendant railroad had purchased the road or was bound by the debts of its predecessor.

In the case of **Anson Rising et ux. v. James H. Carr**, which took place in **September 1873** and was adjudicated in the **Illinois Supreme Court**, the dispute arose from prior litigation between the same parties regarding a property deed. Anson Rising and his wife (the plaintiffs) contended that the deed conveyed to James H. Carr (the defendant) should be interpreted as a mortgage rather than an outright sale, thereby allowing them the right to redeem the property. The prior decision had determined the deed was absolute in form, not a mortgage, but the plaintiffs sought further action by presenting an amended bill in the circuit court. The core of the case revolves around whether the deed constituted security in the nature of a mortgage or was merely an absolute transfer of ownership. The circuit court eventually ruled, based on the Supreme Court's previous findings, leading to further disputes over the interpretation and implications of the decrees issued.	The plaintiffs, Anson Rising et ux., primarily argue that the property deed held by James H. Carr constitutes a mortgage, which grants them the right to redeem the property. They seek an accounting of the amounts owed and assert that the deed was intended as security for a loan rather than an outright sale, contrary to prior court findings.	James H. Carr, representing himself, contends that the matter is **res adjudicata**, meaning it has already been conclusively determined by a previous court decision. He argues that the property was purchased outright with no intent of creating a mortgage, thereby denying the claim that the deed should be treated as security. Carr maintains that the plaintiffs have not provided new evidence that would warrant a reconsideration of the case.

In November 1868, Julius Wangelin and his associates forcibly took possession of a mill in Lebanon, St. Clair County, Illinois, owned by Henry S. Goe. Goe, who had purchased the mill for $14,000 and had improved its operations, was out for lunch when Wangelin and others broke into the mill with weapons and expelled him from the property. Since then, they have maintained control over the mill with armed guards, depriving Goe of the ability to operate the mill and causing him significant financial harm. Goe alleged he was entitled to relief as there was no adequate remedy at law, given that the defendants had no property subject to execution. This led to Goe seeking an injunction to prevent Wangelin and others from interfering with his possession of the mill.	The plaintiff, Henry S. Goe, claimed that he legally owned the Wangelin Mill tract and that he was violently ejected from the property by Wangelin and others. He argued that he had made substantial improvements and was operating the mill profitably. Goe sought an injunction to restrain the defendants from further interfering with his possession and operation of the mill, claiming that he had suffered irreparable harm for which he had no adequate remedy at law.	The defendants, Wangelin and Houer, contended that the court lacked jurisdiction to grant the requested injunction since Goe had an adequate legal remedy for trespass. They argued that the allegations in Goe's complaint disclosed no basis for equity jurisdiction because the alleged acts were completed, and an injunction could not undoes past actions. The defendants asserted that under current legal standards, the remedy lay in law rather than equity, and thus, the motion to dissolve the injunction should have been granted.

Centralia and Chester Railroad Company v. Elihu H. Henry et al. arose from a legal dispute originating in 1886 in Washington County, Illinois. The Centralia & Chester Railroad Company sought to condemn a right of way over lands owned by Elihu H. Henry and others. After a jury assessed compensation for this right of way at $650, the landowners were dissatisfied and appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court. While the appeal was pending, the railroad company executed a statutory bond allowing it to take possession of the right of way. In March 1887, the railroad took possession, cutting timber and plowing the land. The Supreme Court later affirmed the lower court's judgment, resulting in a suit against the railroad company on the bond as they retained possession of the right of way when the suit was initiated. The railroad company and its sureties contested the claim by arguing they were not in possession at the time of the lawsuit. The Circuit Court ruled against the railroad company, requiring them to pay the full amount assessed by the jury.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Centralia & Chester Railroad Company had taken possession of their property without adequate compensation as outlined in the condemnation proceedings. They sought to enforce the bond executed by the railroad, arguing that the company was liable for the full amount determined by the jury, which included the assessed damages.	The defendants, including the railroad company and its sureties, argued that they had not maintained possession of the right of way as alleged by the plaintiffs and that the entry was authorized by the bond, which eliminated any trespass claims. They contended that there was no evidence to support the claim of ongoing possession at the time the suit was initiated. Additionally, they claimed the damages assessed were excessive, but this point was not raised properly in the Circuit Court motions.

On July 27, 1876, Malcolm McDowell subscribed to 50 shares of the Chicago Steel Works' stock, signing a stock note to pay $5,000 upon demand by the company's directors. The company demanded payment in December 1879, but McDowell did not comply and instead sought legal recourse, filing a bill in the Superior Court of Cook County on December 17, 1879, to prevent the sale of his stock. The company agreed not to sell at that time but reserved the right for future actions. When the company reaffirmed its demand for payment in April 1880 and McDowell failed to pay, his stock was sold on May 22, 1880, at a public auction for $5,000, with proper notice given in a daily newspaper. McDowell filed a bill against the company and the Buckinghams, claiming conspiracy against him and seeking an injunction, accounting, and for the stock issuance. His subsequent legal challenges regarding the sale’s validity were met with denials from the defendants, and the original bill did not contest the sale until years later. In November 1884, McDowell raised issues about the lack of notice regarding the sale, claiming it was fraudulent.	McDowell argued that the sale of his stock was invalid due to the absence of notice and claimed that the circumstances surrounding his stock subscription had changed. He alleged a conspiracy by the Buckinghams to force him out of the corporation and sought an accounting of the profits, issuance of his stock or its recovery, and an injunction against any future transfers of the stock.	The Chicago Steel Works and the Buckinghams maintained that the sale of McDowell's stock was valid since they had followed the conditions laid out in the stock note, which authorized them to sell upon his default without the need for personal notice. They contested McDowell’s claims of conspiracy and fraud, emphasizing that his lengthy delay in challenging the sale and his acceptance of funds post-sale operated as an estoppel against his claims.

Moses Thorpe, the Plaintiff in Error, was involved in a legal case against Samuel S. Starr, who was acting as the Administrator of the estate of Aaron Starr, the Defendant in Error. The case took place in December 1855 in Illinois. Aaron Starr initiated the lawsuit against Moses Thorpe for debt (in the form of assumpsit); however, before the completion of the case, Aaron Starr passed away on November 24, 1853. Following his death, the cause was referred to arbitrators by court order, who ultimately ruled in favor of Aaron Starr. Upon the suggestion of Aaron's death, an order was made to substitute Samuel Starr as administrator of the estate in the case. However, there was a procedural issue because the plaintiff was deceased, and the court's judgment was entered in favor of Aaron Starr without formally recognizing Samuel Starr as party plaintiff.	The plaintiff's main arguments centered around the validity and enforcement of the arbitrators' award against Moses Thorpe for a debt. The claim asserted that the award, which favored Aaron Starr, should be approved as a judgment by the court despite the fact that Aaron had died prior to the award being entered.	Moses Thorpe's defense highlighted three main issues: first, that there was a fundamental inconsistency between the writ issued and the declaration made in court; second, that the judgment was erroneously entered in favor of Aaron Starr, who was deceased at the time; and third, that the court's judgment was informal and inadequate, as it failed to properly account for legal requirements concerning the substitution of the administrator as the party plaintiff.

Henry Hellman v. August Schiffer and Lorenz Reitz, Sheriff, is a legal case decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on December 11, 1886. The dispute arose after Hellman recovered a judgment against Schiffer for $7,203 on May 25, 1885, during the regular May term of the Will County Circuit Court. Following this, Hellman sought a rule on the Sheriff to issue a certificate of purchase for a tract of land he had purchased for $1,965 under execution of that judgment. The property involved was 26.32 acres located in Will County, Illinois. However, the Sheriff refused to apply the sale proceeds to Hellman's judgment, claiming other liens were on the real estate. During this period, another creditor, Herman Badenhoop, obtained a judgment against Schiffer for $1,458.52, and several other attachment judgments were also filed against Schiffer. When the real estate was sold, the court had to determine how to distribute the proceeds among the various competing claims.	Hellman contended that he should receive the full proceeds from the sale of the real estate since he held the principal judgment against Schiffer. He argued that the entire amount should apply to his execution and that any other claims for pro rata shares were unfounded. Hellman requested the court to ignore the presence of other liens affecting his entitlement to the total sale amount.	The Sheriff and Badenhoop contended that the law required proceeds from the sale of the property to be divided among all judgments issued at the same term. They argued that Hellman should not automatically receive priority over other claims, insisting that the distribution of sale proceeds must occur on a pro rata basis according to their respective amounts due. They maintained that the law treats competing liens equally under the statutes governing such circumstances.

In 1887, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of William H. Grubey v. Ira M. White arose when the plaintiff, Grubey, obtained a judgment by default against the defendant, White, amounting to $355 plus costs of the lawsuit. Grubey's judgment seemed to stem from a dispute related to a gambling debt, specifically involving transactions on the open board of trade, characterized by "puts" and "calls." The defendant, Ira M. White, subsequently moved the court to set aside the default judgment. However, he failed to demonstrate any due diligence or justification for not defending himself initially, claiming that the basis of the judgment was a gambling-related debt. The Illinois Appellate Court, presided over by Judge Bollin S. Williamson, evaluated the motion based on Section 135 of Chapter 38 of the Revised Statutes, which permits vacating judgments relating to gambling contracts. The court noted that such provisions did not extend to adversary judgments, leading to a judicial interpretation that upheld the validity of the original judgment.	The plaintiff, William H. Grubey, claimed that he was entitled to a judgment amounting to $355 due to a default by the defendant, Ira M. White. Grubey sought to affirm the judgment which had been entered without a defense interjected by White. He maintained that the court had rightfully awarded him compensation for the gambling debt originating from the open board of trade transactions.	Ira M. White contended that the judgment should be set aside on the grounds that it was based on a gambling debt, which under Illinois law could be vacated. He argued that according to Section 135 of the Criminal Code, such judgments could be contested. White's motion to have the judgment vacated was unsuccessful as he could not provide justification for not presenting a defense during the original proceedings, nor show any collusion or consent to the judgment.

J. W. Middleton Company v. George W. Roycroft is a legal case stemming from a tragic incident that occurred on February 17, 1887, at a printing and binding establishment operated by J. W. Middleton Company in Cook County, Illinois. The case involves George W. Roycroft, the administrator of Joseph J. Roycroft, a minor who was employed by the appellant company. Joseph Roycroft was only fifteen years old and had been working there for a mere ten days. During his employment, he tragically fell approximately sixty feet down an unguarded elevator shaft, resulting in his death. Evidence presented in court indicated that there was no one in charge of the elevator, which had a dark shaft and doors that could be opened from the outside without proper notification. On the day of the accident, Joseph was instructed by a superior to use the elevator for a task. When he returned to the elevator after delivering a load, he mistakenly stepped into the dark shaft when the elevator was no longer there, having been moved without the required signal or warning. Previous complaints about the dim lighting and lack of guards had reportedly been made to the company by an elevator inspector, emphasizing the hazardous work environment leading to this accident.
