The plaintiff, George W. Roycroft, claims that the death of his minor son was the result of the negligence of his employers, the J. W. Middleton Company. He argues that the company failed to provide proper safety measures for the elevator, including adequate lighting and guarding, and that they did not follow regulations regarding the proper signaling before moving the elevator. He seeks compensation for the wrongful death of his son, asserting that the negligence and unsafe working conditions were deliberate and directly led to the fatal accident.	The defendant, J. W. Middleton Company, contends that they took reasonable safety precautions and had rules in place regarding the use of the elevator. They argue that Joseph Roycroft had been instructed on how to use the elevator and that his actions were reckless given his prior knowledge of using it. The company seeks to refute the claims of negligence by emphasizing the absence of oversight from their employees regarding the elevator operation and refers to possible shared responsibility for the accident due to the minor’s actions.

The case of Lake Erie & Western R. R. Co. v. Max Rosenberg took place in 1889 in Bloomington, Illinois. The lawsuit arose when plaintiff Max Rosenberg shipped a carload of horses from Paxton to Bloomington via the Lake Erie & Western Railroad Co. On the evening of October 20th, Rosenberg's agent, Allen, inquired about shipping the horses and was assured by the railroad agent Abbott that the horses could be unloaded promptly upon arrival. However, when the horses arrived in Bloomington at 12:45 a.m., they were not promptly unloaded, leading to a delay until 7 a.m. The horses suffered from the conditions of confinement, becoming overheated and subsequently shivering and coughing. This led to some horses falling ill, with two later dying as a result. The jury found substantial evidence suggesting that the railroad caused the damages due to the delay.	The plaintiff, Max Rosenberg, claimed damages against the Lake Erie & Western Railroad Co. for the delayed unloading of his horses. He argued that the railroad's agent assured him that there would be no delay, which led to the condition of the horses upon arrival. He sought compensation for the sickness and death of the horses resulting from the railroad's failure to unload them promptly as promised.	The defendant, Lake Erie & Western Railroad Co., denied responsibility for the horses' condition, arguing that any injury sustained was due to the inherent vitality of the animals, rather than negligence on their part. They contended that there was no obligation for the railroad to be ready to unload animals at night since the conditions leading to their overheating were beyond their control. Additionally, they objected to the admission of certain evidence regarding the condition of the horses at unloading.

In 1886, Elizabeth Richards filed for divorce from her husband, William Richards, in La Salle County, Illinois. The case stemmed from allegations of habitual drunkenness, adultery, and extreme cruelty, with Elizabeth claiming that William had been habitually drunk for over two years prior to the filing. The trial included testimony from numerous witnesses, some of whom had never seen William intoxicated, but Elizabeth's and her witnesses' accounts were deemed credible. The court considered the context of William's drinking habits, emphasizing that negative testimonies did not necessarily refute the claims of habitual drunkenness. The judge pointed out that evidence of extreme cruelty was also relevant to the case. The jury was instructed that habitual drunkenness could be established even if William was not intoxicated at all times, which was a point of contention during trial. After reviewing the substantial and conflicting evidence, the court ultimately upheld the jury's verdict supporting Elizabeth's claims.	Elizabeth Richards claimed that her husband, William, was guilty of habitual drunkenness, extreme cruelty, and adultery. She sought a divorce on these grounds, asserting that William's drinking had severely affected the marriage and rendered him unfit for the responsibilities of husbandry and fatherhood. Elizabeth provided extensive testimony along with evidence supporting her accusations, which led to a jury verdict in her favor regarding habitual drunkenness.	William Richards defended against Elizabeth's allegations by presenting testimonies from several witnesses who stated they had not seen him intoxicated. His defense argued that the evidence presented did not meet the burden of proof necessary to establish habitual drunkenness. William requested that the jury be instructed on the requirement of a preponderance of evidence, insisting that mere instances of drinking were insufficient to demonstrate a habitual state that impaired his duties.

In 1888, George Ball (plaintiff) entered into a legal dispute with Henry Ballenseifen (defendant) in Illinois. The case revolved around a promissory note for $300 that was issued in connection with the purchase of land by Ballenseifen, who acquired the property from Michael Louis. The transaction was completed with the execution of deeds, notes, and a mortgage involving both Ballenseifen and an attorney named Perley. At the time of the transaction, there was an unpaid judgment against Michael Louis, which became a valid lien on the land and ultimately led to the land being sold due to execution, resulting in Ballenseifen losing his title to the property. George Ball claimed he was owed the amount on the promissory note but was countered by Ballenseifen's pleas of failure of consideration, which maintained that the note was issued without the proper underlying asset due to the invalid title caused by the judgment. The trial concluded in favor of Ballenseifen, prompting George Ball to appeal the decision, asserting that the verdict was not supported by the evidence.	George Ball's main arguments centered on his position as the payee of the promissory note made by Ballenseifen, asserting that he was entitled to recover the outstanding balance due to the note. He contended that he had complied with all necessary legal formalities and that the defenses raised by Ballenseifen did not validly negate his claims. Ball requested the court to overturn the lower court's judgment and enforce the payment of the amount due on the note.	Henry Ballenseifen's key defenses hinged on the assertion of "failure of consideration" for the promissory note. He argued that the purchase of the land was invalid due to a pre-existing lien (an unpaid judgment against Michael Louis) that rendered the property title defective. Consequently, Ballenseifen claimed that since the consideration for the note (the land) failed, he should not be held liable for payment. He requested the court to affirm the lower court's judgment in his favor, maintaining that he was justified in his defenses.

The case involves John Doe, ex dem. Noblet Herbert, Thomas Janney, and John D. Brown (plaintiffs) against John C. Herbert and Charles Louviere, the tenant (defendants). The events trace back to 1810 when Ninian Edwards possessed the land in question until he sold it to Thomas F. Herbert via a deed executed and recorded on September 7, 1818. Thomas F. Herbert took possession of the land and maintained it until his death in 1821. Following his death, Charles Slade, as the administrator of Thomas F. Herbert, executed a deed in 1823 transferring the land to the plaintiffs, supported by Illinois law authorizing such sales. The plaintiffs presented evidence of their title and existing possession by tenant Louviere. The defendants sought to counter this by introducing a deed from Thomas F. Herbert to John C. Herbert, dating back to September 29, 1818, that lacked a subscribing witness and had not been delivered or accepted by John C. Herbert prior to the grantor's death, which became a pivotal issue in deciding property ownership. The court had to resolve whether the plaintiffs had met the burden of proof regarding title and possession, which they did as established by prior possession laws and the accepted practice of property conveyance.	The plaintiffs argued that they held valid title to the property based on the deed executed by Charles Slade, the administrator of Thomas F. Herbert, which was executed in accordance with Illinois law permitting administrators to sell property of deceased persons. They presented evidence demonstrating prior possession of the property dating back to 1810, showing a continuous claim of ownership through peaceful possession by their predecessor. The plaintiffs requested the court to uphold their title and grant them possession of the land, asserting that the defendants' claim was insufficient to negate their title.	The defendants argued that the plaintiffs had not established a valid title to the property, primarily contesting the validity of the deed from Charles Slade to the plaintiffs. They contended that the deed purportedly executed by Thomas F. Herbert to John C. Herbert was valid and should be upheld, especially since the deed was formally recorded despite lacking a subscribing witness. The defendants claimed that there was no delivery or acceptance of the deed from Thomas F. Herbert to John C. Herbert, thus disputing the legitimacy of the plaintiffs’ claims.

The case titled "Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Kate Murphy, Administratrix, etc." took place in January 1870 in McLean County, Illinois, involving the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company (defendant) and Kate Murphy, the administratrix of the estate of James Murphy (plaintiff). James Murphy was an employee working under the foreman, Hill, tasked with inspecting and repairing freight train cars. On the day of the incident, after completing repairs, Murphy was walking between the rails of the main track when he was struck by a switch engine operated on the station grounds. The switch engine was under the control of the yard master but had roles in switching cars for Murphy's repair crew. Murphy sustained injuries from the collision that led to his death shortly afterward. The case revolves around the issue of whether the railroad company could be held liable for Murphy's death, considering he and the engineer of the switch engine were regarded as fellow servants under the common master doctrine.	The plaintiff, Kate Murphy, argued that the railroad company was liable for the wrongful death of James Murphy due to the negligence of the engineer operating the switch engine. She sought damages on the basis that the railroad company failed to ensure the safety of its employees, particularly by allowing an unsafe working environment where one employee's actions could endanger another.	The defendant contended that James Murphy and the switch engine's engineer were fellow servants under the same employer, and as such, the common master rule exempted the railroad company from liability for injuries sustained by one employee due to the negligence of another. The defense cited that any carelessness by the engineer was inherent in the working relationship, and thus, the risks of such negligence were accepted by Murphy when he took the job.

The case "The Covenant Mutual Benefit Association v. Lauba Hoffman et al." was decided on September 27, 1884, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from a certificate of membership in the Covenant Mutual Benefit Association issued to Peter Hoffman for a sum of ten dollars, which provided a $5,000 benefit upon his death, payable to his wife, Laura Hoffman, and their children. Following Peter Hoffman's death on August 2, 1881, the benefits were claimed by his widow and their five children. However, after the suit commenced, one child, Peter Hoffman, Jr., died in May 1882, leading to legal proceedings primarily concerning the rightful beneficiaries of the insurance payout. The trial court ruled in favor of Laura and the four surviving children, awarding them the full amount. The defendants argued that the benefits should have been distributed differently due to the total number of surviving beneficiaries at the time of the suit, asserting it was erroneous to grant the full value of the policy without including the deceased child's name.	The plaintiff, represented by Laura Hoffman and her surviving four children, claimed the entire $5,000 benefit as stipulated in the policy, upon demonstrating that they met all stipulated conditions following Peter Hoffman's death. They argued that, per the certificate's terms, even with one child's prior death, the remaining heirs were entitled to the full compensation, as the certificate included provisions for heirs if some beneficiaries had predeceased the holder.	The defense contended that the trial court erred by allowing judgment in favor of only the widow and the four children, as the certificate explicitly noted equal benefits for all five children. They argued that the incorrect exclusion of the deceased child's name from the suit compromised the claim. Additionally, they challenged the acceptance of death proofs, which they believed were insufficient for substantiating claims against the association due to Peter Hoffman Jr.'s earlier death after the lawsuit began.

Nathaniel Norton brought a lawsuit against John A. Colby on September 1, 1866, in the Illinois Supreme Court regarding two promissory notes dated February 19, 1835, which were supposed to mature two and three years later. The defendant Colby raised multiple defenses, including the general issue, and claimed that he had not promised to pay within the required legal timeframe—specifically, within sixteen years or even five years before the suit was initiated. The jury found in favor of Norton, leading Colby to appeal the decision. Norton's claim centered on a supposed new promise made by Colby, which would purportedly override the statute of limitations. The evidence presented by Norton comprised conversations that he had with Colby, where the latter denied the existence of the notes and suggested that if any were found against him, he would pay them. The Illinois Supreme Court deliberated on whether these discussions constituted a new promise sufficient to bypass the statute of limitations.	The plaintiff, Nathaniel Norton, argued that John A. Colby had made a new promise that would revive the claims on the old promissory notes. Norton sought to show that conversations between him and Colby indicated an acknowledgment of the debts. He maintained that as Colby's statements suggested he would pay any notes produced against him, this constituted a recognition of the notes in question, thereby circumventing the statutory time limits for initiating the lawsuit.	John A. Colby, the defendant, contended that the lawsuit was barred by the statute of limitations, asserting that no valid promise had been made within the relevant timeframes. He maintained that his statements during discussions with Norton did not constitute an acknowledgment of the specific debts, but instead denied the existence of any outstanding notes. Colby requested the court to overturn the lower court's decision based on this defense, emphasizing the lack of a binding new promise regarding the debts in question.

In 1876, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose in the case of Eli G. Runals v. George F. Harding et al. The key individuals involved included Eli G. Runals, the plaintiff, and George F. Harding, an executor of Alonzo Campbell's estate, representing the defendants. The case originated from a creditor's bill brought against Runals by Harding, who had acquired a judgment against Runals from the executors of Alonzo Campbell. The debt in question, approximately $15,000, was based on notes and acceptances Runals had issued for the benefit of E.M. Whipple. In Spring 1867, collateral securities worth $48,000 were entrusted to Campbell to secure Runals' indebtedness, under the agreement that Campbell would pursue these securities first before holding Runals liable. Over time, Campbell directed Runals to deliver the securities to Josiah Lombard, who would convert them into cash and secure an agreement to settle the debt owed to Campbell. Campbell, however, passed away, leading to disputes over the negotiations and agreements regarding the handling of the debt. Runals contended that the executors never pursued Lombard effectively, leading to losses on the securities.	The plaintiff, Eli G. Runals, claimed that the judgment rendered against him was improper because the executors of Alonzo Campbell had been negligent in pursuing the collateral securities and had failed to enforce the debt against Lombard as agreed. He maintained that he was led to believe that the executors would first seek repayment from Lombard before proceeding against him. Runals sought to have the judgment dismissed based on these claims of mismanagement of the debt collection process.	The defendants, led by George F. Harding as executor, asserted that Runals's claims were unfounded, arguing that they had acted appropriately in bringing the judgment against him. They contended that Runals had not adequately fulfilled his obligations and had agreed to the judgment without contest after it was determined that they would initiate collection proceedings against Lombard thereafter. The defendants claimed that there was no requirement for them to pursue Lombard first and sought to have the court uphold the judgment against Runals on the basis of his contractual obligations.

Frederick Rearick filed a libel case against Daniel Wilcox, the publisher of the Quincy Whig newspaper, regarding an article published on April 15, 1875. At that time, Rearick was a candidate for police magistrate in Quincy, Illinois. The article accused Rearick of dishonesty, corruption, and the potential misuse of the office he was campaigning for, claiming he had a history of fraudulent behavior as mayor and would exploit the office for personal gain. The case was heard in the Circuit Court of Adams County and resulted in a jury's verdict of $25 in favor of Rearick. However, Rearick appealed this decision, citing errors in jury instructions related to the assessment of damages and the understanding of malice in defamation actions.	Rearick claimed that the article published by Wilcox constituted libel, as it contained false statements about his character and fitness for office. He argued that these defamatory statements harmed his reputation and sought compensatory damages for the injury he sustained from the publication, insisting that malice could be presumed from the libelous nature of the article.	Wilcox defended himself by pleading the general issue and argued that the publication was made with the belief that it served the public good. He requested that any potential damages awarded to Rearick be mitigated by the fact that the article was published during an electoral campaign and without malice toward Rearick. Wilcox contended that the circumstances surrounding the publication should lessen the liability regarding damages.

In July 1838, George Thompson delivered two promissory notes to Elisha S. and J. Wadsworth, pledging a set of goods as collateral for the notes. Thompson initially provided a variety of goods to fulfill what he believed would amount to $1,000 in value and was given a receipt indicating these goods would be forfeited if the notes were not paid when due. As the due date approached, Thompson informed J. Wadsworth that he would not be able to pay and requested an extension, which was granted for three weeks. Prior to the end of this extended period, Thompson’s attorney attempted to settle the amount owed, but Wadsworth stated that a part of the collateral had already been sold at auction. On October 31, 1838, the Wadsworths issued a sale notice for the remaining goods set for November 10 unless payment was made. In 1845, Thompson filed an action against the Wadsworths in the Cook Circuit Court, where he was ultimately awarded damages for trover and conversion, amounting to $1,001.32. The Wadsworths appealed the decision, claiming errors in the court's findings.	George Thompson, the plaintiff, argued that the Wadsworths had wrongfully converted and sold his goods without proper notification or adherence to the agreed-upon terms regarding the collateral. He claimed damages for the value of the goods, which were assessed by the court, and rightfully sought restitution for what he believed was his property misappropriated by the defendants.	The Wadsworths defended their actions by asserting that they had the right to sell the collateral due to Thompson's failure to pay the notes at maturity, contending that the contract signed implied a mortgage rather than a pledge. They also argued against the judgment amount, stating that it should have reflected a deduction for the amounts owed on the original notes. They claimed the court's ruling was incorrect and requested a new trial, maintaining that they acted within their legal rights.

In 1883, in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving several lot owners and the city of Chicago. The case was initiated by the People ex rel. William F. Carroll, who filed a petition for a writ of mandamus to compel the court clerk to file objections raised by the lot owners against an assessment related to the opening of a street. Sixteen property holders objected to the confirmation of the benefit assessments against their lots, presenting their objections collectively. Despite a request to file these objections accompanied by a tendered fee of one dollar and fifty cents, the clerk refused to file them unless each objector paid the fee individually. This situation prompted the court to interpret section 33, chapter 53 of the Revised Statutes of 1874 concerning fees and legal proceedings. The court's ruling hinged on whether the assessments constituted a singular suit, regardless of the number of defendants, emphasizing that a single fee should suffice for all objectors to participate.	The plaintiff, William F. Carroll, argued that the objections to the assessment filed by multiple lot owners should be treated as a singular action, thus requiring only one dollar and fifty cents as a fee for filing, rather than demanding that each owner pay individually. Carroll maintained that the statutory provisions should allow for the filing of the objections collectively, as they constituted one indivisible suit.	The defendant, represented by the clerk of the court, contended that the law required each property owner involved in the case to pay the filing fee individually due to the numerous defendants. The defense argued that the legal interpretation of the statute allowed for separate fees based on the number of defendants involved in the proceeding, thus justifying the clerk's refusal to file without strict adherence to this requirement.

In September 1870, Amanda F. Coleman, a married woman, sold two lots in Springfield, Illinois, to the Springfield and Illinois S. E. R. R. Co. for $9,000. Coleman and her husband executed a deed for the property, but it was not delivered immediately. On October 3, 1870, two certificates of deposit were issued by the First National Bank of Springfield, totaling $9,000, to her. A few days later, Amanda's husband, A. W. Coleman, drew $4,500 from the deposit using his wife's name and signed as her agent. He applied a substantial part of this to satisfy two mortgages and withdrew the rest in cash. Subsequently, he drew from the second certificate until all $9,000 was depleted by November 21, 1871. In April 1879, Amanda initiated a legal suit against the bank to recover the withdrawn money, claiming her husband's authority to act on her behalf was questionable. Following nearly nine years of silence from the bank regarding the withdrawal, the case centered on whether A. W. Coleman had the authority to withdraw the funds or whether Amanda ratified his actions post facto. The jury found in favor of Amanda, leading to a final judgment of $6,889.65 in her favor after deductions for mortgages.	Amanda F. Coleman's primary argument in her claims was that she did not grant her husband the authority to draw the funds from the bank on her behalf. She sought recovery of the full amount deposited, asserting that the bank should have demanded verification of her husband's authority before processing the withdrawals. Amanda claimed she was entitled to the full value of the certificates plus interest, challenging the bank's assumption that her husband could act as her agent without any explicit authorization.	The First National Bank of Springfield contended that they acted within their rights in honoring the withdrawals made by Amanda's husband. They argued that at no point did they obstruct Amanda's ability to reclaim her funds and that any delay in her claims was not due to their actions. The bank asserted that they had adequately fulfilled their obligations as a depository and requested that the judgment be reversed because they believed they should not be liable for interest on the deposits, given that they never received a formal demand for payment from Amanda throughout the duration of the dispute.

In the case of "Martha J. Ruffin, Admx. etc. v. William R. Farmer, Admr. etc.", which took place in June 1874 in Illinois, the plaintiff Martha J. Ruffin, acting as administrator of John F. Plasters' estate, sought to recover a legacy of $200. This legacy was part of the last will of Jane Bicharts, who passed away in September 1860. Jane Bicharts' will was probated in December 1860, and it explicitly stated that John F. Plasters was to receive $200 upon reaching the age of twenty-one. John F. Plasters was born in 1846 and died intestate on March 24, 1863, prior to turning 21. Following Plasters' death, Ruffin was appointed as administrator of his estate on December 16, 1870. The claim for the legacy was initially allowed by the county court in Jackson County and subsequently upheld in the circuit court during a jury trial. The case was then appealed by William R. Farmer, the administrator of Jane Bicharts' estate, to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Martha J. Ruffin, argued that as the administrator of John F. Plasters' estate, she was entitled to the legacy of $200 that was bequeathed to Plasters by Jane Bicharts' will. She claimed that since Plasters died before reaching the age of 21, his administrator was entitled to claim the legacy on his behalf once the time he would have attained that age arrived.	The defendant, William R. Farmer, contended that there were errors in how the will was construed and challenged the jurisdiction of the court regarding the administration of the estate. He argued against the admission of certain evidence and maintained that the instructions refused to him by the trial court were appropriate for the jury to consider.

William H. Cary et al. v. Otto Norton was a legal case adjudicated by the Illinois Appellate Court on February 12, 1890. The case originated from an employment dispute between the appellee, Otto Norton, and the appellants, William H. Cary and others, concerning a balance of salary allegedly owed to Norton for the year 1887. Norton claimed he was wrongfully discharged from his employment before receiving all payment due under his contract. The trial was held in the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Richard S. Tuthill. The crux of the case revolved around whether the employment contract was enforceable under the statute of frauds, with Norton maintaining he was entitled to wages for the entirety of the period he worked, while the defendants contended the contract did not require performance beyond one year. The jury ultimately sided with Norton, leading to the appeal from Cary and the other appellants who sought to challenge the verdict.	The plaintiff, Otto Norton, asserted that he was entitled to a balance of salary for the year 1887, claiming he was wrongfully discharged from his employment. He argued that his employment contract entitled him to wages for the entire duration of service and that the specific terms of the contract fell within the statute of frauds. Norton sought a ruling to enforce this claim and recover the salary he believed was due.	The defendants, William H. Cary et al., contended that the employment contract in question did not envisage a performance extending beyond one year, and thus Norton was entitled only to wages for the period he was actively employed. They argued that the contract's enforceability under the statute of frauds was in dispute and that the evidence presented did not warrant the trial's outcome. The defendants requested the court to overturn the jury's verdict and judgment in favor of Norton.

In July 1882, in Peoria County, Illinois, Peter Schertz was involved in a legal case against the People, represented by Isaac Taylor, the county collector. The case arose when a judgment and order for the sale of certain city lots owned by Schertz was sought, following a special assessment for the improvement of Adams Street. Schertz contested the judgment, arguing that the city council did not pass any ordinance for the improvement, that the court failed to appoint commissioners for the assessment, and that the prior judgment was void due to lack of jurisdiction and proper notification regarding the assessment. The court struck Schertz's objections, leading him to appeal the decision. His key contentions included claims of a procedural deficiencies in how the assessments were handled and unjust favoritism towards the Central City Horse Railroad Company concerning the improvement assessments.	Schertz contended that the ordinance for the Adams Street improvement was never passed, the court never appointed commissioners to assess costs, and that the judgment confirming the assessment was void. He argued that he was not properly notified of the proceedings, which discriminated against him, as the adjacent horse railroad company was allowed to improve its own right of way without corresponding assessments.	The People, represented by Taylor, argued that the court had jurisdiction to confirm the special assessment judgment and that Schertz was barred from questioning previous proceedings due to the confirmation judgment's conclusive nature. They maintained that the objection raised by Schertz needed to have been addressed during the initial confirmation process and that the validity of the confirmation was based on the adherence to statutory requirements.

The case of Jonathan Welden et al. v. Thompson W. Francis took place in December 1850 at Michigan City, Indiana, concerning a dispute over two promissory notes made by the defendants, Jonathan Welden and Betsy Welden, for the sale of two donkeys (a jack-ass and a she-ass) sold by the plaintiff, Thompson W. Francis. The plaintiffs accused the defendants of failing to fulfill their payment obligations under the promissory notes, alleging that the animals were warranted to be sound. Witnesses were presented by both sides to testify about the condition of the jack-ass at the time of the sale and performance thereafter, with mixed opinions regarding whether the animal was sound. The jack-ass allegedly became unsound and valueless, leading to its death in December 1848. This case was tried before the Illinois Supreme Court, which reviewed the testimonies and the evidence presented, ultimately affirming the judgment made at the lower court.	The plaintiff, Thompson W. Francis, argued that he sold the two animals under a warranty that they were sound in every way and sought to collect on the full amount of the promissory notes issued by the defendants. The plaintiff maintained that there was no breach of warranty, as the evidence did not sufficiently prove that the animals were unsound at the time of sale.	The defendants claimed that the sale included a warranty that the animals were sound, but the jack-ass was unsound and became valueless, leading to its death. They argued that the plaintiff should only be entitled to the payment of the notes minus damages representing the value lost due to the unsoundness of the jack-ass. They cited testimony to support their position, asserting that the condition of the animal was known to be poor at the time of sale.

J. H. Wade filed a suit against the Town of La Moille in Bureau County, Illinois, regarding ten municipal bonds issued by the town. These bonds, issued on December 1, 1870, were tied to a vote held on August 6, 1870, to provide financial aid to an Illinois Grand Trunk railway. The plaintiff contended that the bonds and their interest coupons were valid and sought to recover the amounts due. However, the bonds were issued after the adoption of a constitutional provision in Illinois that prohibited municipal aid to private corporations, including railroads, effectively voiding such bonds. The legal proceedings commenced in the Circuit Court under Judge Francis Goodspeed and progressed through the Appellate Court, ultimately reaching the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, J. H. Wade, argued that the Town of La Moille was obligated to honor the bonds and interest coupons issued for the railroad project. Wade maintained that despite the constitutional provisions enacted subsequent to the issuance of the bonds, they should still be considered valid, and thus he requested the court to enforce their payment and recover the owed amounts.	The Town of La Moille contended that the bonds issued for the railway project were invalid due to the constitutional prohibition against municipal aid to private corporations established on July 2, 1870. The defendant argued that this served as a legal basis to deny any liability on the bonds, asserting that there was a complete lack of authority for the municipality to issue such aid and, therefore, no recovery could be granted even to innocent holders. Their key defense was grounded in previously established legal precedents, which reinforced the invalidity of bonds issued without proper authority.

The case of Arthur M. Rugg et al. v. John M. Davis took place in Peoria, Illinois, with the judgment delivered by the Illinois Appellate Court on January 16, 1885. The dispute arose from a contractual agreement related to the purchase of grain. The plaintiffs, grain dealers in Peoria, sent a letter to the defendant, J. M. Davis, a dealer in Blandinsville, offering to purchase specific grades of grain under certain conditions. The letter stipulated that the acceptance of the offer must reach them by a specified time and included terms such as Peoria weights and inspection. In response, Davis sent a telegram accepting the offer but indicating a desire to deliver different varieties of grain than those originally offered. The appellants, however, contended that the acceptance did not match their offer exactly and refused to honor the contract, leading Davis to sue for damages for the alleged breach of contract. The central issue revolved around whether a binding contract existed based on the exchange of communications between the parties.	The plaintiff, J. M. Davis, claimed that the defendants were liable for damages for failing to accept and pay for the grain he alleged had been purchased from him. Davis contended that his acceptance of the defendants' offer was valid, asserting that he was ready and willing to deliver the grain as per the terms discussed in the correspondence, and therefore sought legal remedy for the breach of what he believed to be a binding contract.	The defendants, represented by Arthur M. Rugg and others, argued that no contract existed due to the material differences between their offer and Davis's acceptance. They claimed that Davis's acceptance involved a new proposition, which did not correspond to the original terms of the offer. The defendants asserted that since their acceptance required precise adherence to the offered terms and Davis’s response deviated from those, they were under no obligation to take the grain, thereby denying any liability for damages.

The case of "The St. Louis, Alton and Terre Haute R. R. Co. v. Benjamin L. Dorsey" took place in June 1873 in Illinois. The plaintiff, Benjamin L. Dorsey, brought an action of covenant against the St. Louis, Alton and Terre Haute Railroad Company. Dorsey successfully obtained a judgment against the railroad company amounting to $1900, along with costs of the suit. The case was initially heard in the Alton City Court, presided over by Judge Henry S. Baker, where the jury ruled in favor of Dorsey. The railroad company appealed the decision, leading to the Supreme Court of Illinois reviewing the case on grounds of various alleged errors, including how the lower court handled motions for a new trial.	The plaintiff, Benjamin L. Dorsey, asserted that he was wrongfully denied the benefits from the covenant made with the St. Louis, Alton and Terre Haute Railroad Company and sought judgment for what he was owed, which resulted in the jury awarding him $1900 along with legal costs.	The defendant, St. Louis, Alton and Terre Haute Railroad Company, contended that the verdict was contrary to law and challenged the handling of motions for a new trial by the lower court, claiming errors in not properly assessing the evidence and in the judgment favoring the plaintiff. They argued that the necessary exceptions regarding the overruled motion for a new trial were not appropriately preserved in the record.

John Waggeman v. Daniel J. Bracken is a legal case that was decided in September 1869 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a dispute over a contract related to the construction of a house. Bracken, the plaintiff, claimed that Waggeman, the defendant, owed him money for the building services provided. The primary contention was whether there was a formal contract between the parties. Bracken prepared a written agreement outlining the terms of the construction, which Waggeman took, made significant alterations, but did not sign. Despite Bracken commencing construction based on the original agreement, Waggeman expressed dissatisfaction during the process, ultimately asserting that the terms of the project should be governed by the estimates and plans instead of the unexecuted agreement. The case was heard in Peoria County, Illinois, under Judge S. D. Puterbaugh.	Bracken argued that he should be compensated for the work performed on the house based on a "quantum meruit" principle, asserting that despite the lack of a signed contract, he had provided services with the expectation of being paid. He claimed that the estimates, plans, and his labor should establish a basis for his recovery, emphasizing that the work was done under an implied agreement despite Waggeman’s alterations to the initial written contract.	Waggeman contended that there was no binding contract as the written agreement was never executed by him. He maintained that any modifications he made were not accepted by Bracken, and that the assertions made about an agreement were invalid since mutuality was absent. Waggeman argued that there was no formal acceptance of Bracken's terms which led to the completion of the project under a quantum meruit basis, rather than a contractual obligation to pay.

The case "Joel B. Fordyce et al. v. Solomon H. Shriver et al." arose from a partnership dispute in the context of a mercantile business formed around September 1, 1873, in Cornell, Livingston County, Illinois. The partnership included Joel B. Fordyce, John G. Fordyce, A. J. Santee, I. B. Santee, Solomon H. Shriver, and J. L. and M. J. Garrison, with each party contributing equal capital and sharing profits and losses. I. B. Santee managed the day-to-day operations, as other partners resided outside Illinois.  By May 1877, the plaintiffs sought legal intervention, accusing I. B. Santee of mismanagement that led to significant financial losses. They claimed that his reckless management resulted in total debts of about $24,235.47 against assets of only $9,140.16, inferring a loss of around $12,039.46. The plaintiffs requested a dissolution of the partnership, appointment of a receiver, and a thorough accounting of losses sustained. The Circuit Court found that the partnership had expired and appointed a master to state the account and report on the partnership’s financial issues.	The plaintiffs, primarily Joel B. Fordyce and John G. Fordyce, contended that their partner I. B. Santee recklessly mismanaged the business, leading to substantial financial losses. They contested an overvaluation of stock that contributed to losses. The plaintiffs sought the appointment of a receiver, the dissolution of the partnership, and an accounting of all business affairs to recover losses incurred due to mismanagement.	The defendants, particularly Shriver and A. J. Santee, argued that they were not liable for the losses attributed to I. B. Santee. They claimed he managed the business effectively and that the losses were not the result of negligence on their part. They also contended that the allegations of mismanagement lacked sufficient evidence and were general in nature without specific claims established within the partnership agreement.

The case "The City of Chicago v. John Martin et ux." arose in September 1868 in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the City of Chicago as the appellant (defendant) and John Martin and Bridget Martin as the appellees (plaintiffs). The case originated from a personal injury claim brought by Bridget Martin, who alleged injuries sustained due to a defect in a public street maintained by the city. The trial court found in favor of the Martins and awarded them $1,000 in damages, stating that the city was liable for its failure to adequately repair the street where the injury occurred. The city appealed this decision, arguing that the street was not a significant thoroughfare and that any negligence on its part did not amount to gross or willful negligence, which would justify the punitive damages awarded to the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs, John and Bridget Martin, claimed that the City of Chicago was negligent in maintaining the street where Bridget Martin was injured, contending that the city failed to repair a known defect in a timely manner. They sought damages for personal injuries, specifically requesting punitive damages on top of compensatory damages, based on the assertion that the city’s negligence rose to the level of gross or willful misconduct.	The City of Chicago argued that it should not be held liable for the injuries claimed by the Martins. The city contended that the street in question was not heavily trafficked or located in a business area, and therefore, the level of care it was required to exercise was lower. The city maintained that any negligence was not gross or willful and requested that the awarded damages be reversed because punitive damages are inappropriate when mere negligence is shown without evidence of malice or reckless disregard for safety.

In May 1846, Robert Pierson initiated a legal action against Michael and James Connelly in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The case pertained to a promissory note dated June 2, 1829, which was due six months later. The defendants pleaded that the cause of action was barred by the Statute of Limitations because more than sixteen years had passed since the note's maturity. The plaintiff countered that the statute was inapplicable, citing a partial payment of ten dollars acknowledged through an indorsement on the note, which occurred on June 17, 1833. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him the amount of the note plus interest. The Connellys then appealed the decision, contesting the sufficiency of the evidence regarding the payment and its implications under the Statute of Limitations.	Robert Pierson's main arguments centered around the claim that the partial payment acknowledged on the promissory note within sixteen years of the suit's initiation removed the claim from the Statute of Limitations. He argued that the indorsement proving payment was valid and warranted a judgment favoring his claim for the amount owed.	The Connellys contended that the claim was barred by the Statute of Limitations due to the significant lapse of time since the note's maturity. They argued that the indorsement acknowledging partial payment was insufficient evidence to establish that the action could proceed, asserting that such evidence could not be used to counteract the statute's limitations.

In 1889, the case of Postal Telegraph-Cable Company v. Charles D. Lathrop and Luther C. Marley took place, centering around damages arising from errors in the transmission of telegraph dispatches. The plaintiffs, Charles D. Lathrop and Luther C. Marley, operated in Chicago and instructed their agents in New York via telegraph to engage in coffee trading transactions. The orders were specific to the purchase or sale of coffee for future delivery and executed in the agents' names without informing the parties involved of the plaintiffs' interest. The case involved a series of problematic dispatches, leading to miscommunications that impacted their trading activities. The defendants, the Postal Telegraph-Cable Company, argued that the business dealings were akin to gambling and asserted that any issues arising from the dispatches should not constitute a cause of action. Ultimately, the case hinged on standard practices in telegraphy and responsibilities regarding errors in message transmission.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Postal Telegraph-Cable Company was liable for damages incurred due to errors in the transmission of their telegraphic messages related to the buying and selling of coffee. Lathrop and Marley argued that these mistakes resulted in financial losses and requested compensation for those damages, asserting that the company failed to exercise ordinary care in the transmission process.	The Postal Telegraph-Cable Company contested the claims, arguing that the plaintiffs and their agents had a pre-existing understanding of the nature of their business, which consisted of trading operations that could be interpreted as gambling. The defendants maintained that they should not be held responsible for the losses, emphasizing that the errors may have resulted from external factors beyond their control. They also sought to limit their liability to merely refunding the transmission fees.

In 1885, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Central Illinois Coal Co. v. Marshall Field et al. arose when Marshall Field and others initiated an action of assumpsit against Central Illinois Coal Company. They sought recovery for an open account concerning merchandise that had been sold and delivered. The plaintiffs filed a declaration and an accompanying affidavit detailing the amount due from the defendant, after allowing for all just credits and deductions as per the relevant legal provisions. The defendant was served process in Cook County and subsequently submitted pleas in bar but did not file an affidavit of defense concerning the plaintiffs’ claims. Following a motion from the plaintiffs, the court struck the defendant's pleas and entered a default judgment against them. During the assessment of damages, the court allowed the plaintiffs to present the affidavit as evidence to the jury, who then assessed damages based solely on this affidavit, awarding the plaintiffs the full amount claimed along with costs. The core legal question centered on the admissibility of the affidavit as prima facie evidence in the context of jury assessments.	The plaintiffs asserted their right to recover amounts due from the defendant based on an open account for merchandise sold and delivered. They supported their demand with an affidavit that detailed the amount owed after due considerations of credits and deductions. Their primary legal request was for the jury to assess damages based on this affidavit, despite the defendant's objections.	The defense argued that the court erred in allowing the affidavit to be read into evidence during the jury assessment of damages. They contended that the affidavit should not be admissible in cases where the defendant has appeared and a jury is involved, suggesting that its application should be limited to exparte assessments. They did not provide evidence to contradict or corroborate the affidavit.

In the case of Mary Bozarth v. W. D. Landers et al., the legal proceedings took place in 1885 and were filed in Mt. Vernon, Illinois. The case centers around a mortgage foreclosure dispute involving Martin E. Bozarth and his wife, Mary Bozarth. Martin Bozarth had incurred a debt to the complainants and secured it with a mortgage on certain lands, with Mary joining the execution of the mortgage. Upon default, the complainants filed a lawsuit to foreclose the mortgage. In their responses, Martin admitted to the debt but claimed the interest was usurious and that he had settled the legitimate dues. Mary, on the other hand, argued that she had acquired a tax title to the mortgaged premises independently and claimed to have no interest in the property except for her dower rights. The initial court decreed a foreclosure against both the mortgagor and his wife, barring Mary from asserting her title rights. This decree was appealed to the Appellate Court, which affirmed the original decision. Subsequently, Mary Bozarth sought further appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, asserting the validity of her tax title.	The plaintiffs, who are the complainants in the mortgage foreclosure case, argued that the mortgage executed by Martin E. Bozarth and Mary Bozarth should be enforced because they were owed a debt secured by the mortgage. They asserted that their claim to foreclose was valid, as the mortgagor had defaulted on the mortgage obligations, and they sought a judgment that would allow them to take possession of the mortgaged property without interference from Mary Bozarth, whom they claimed had no rights due to her husband’s mortgage.	The defendants, particularly Mary Bozarth, contended that she did not owe any payments related to the mortgage and claimed ownership over the mortgaged premises through a tax title acquired independently. She argued that her interests were not adequately considered in the foreclosure proceedings, and she maintained that she should not be barred from asserting her title rights. Both Mary and Martin expressed their intention to contest the legality of the mortgage and its terms, asserting that the transaction was usurious.

In 1874, George W. Reed initiated a legal case against Daniel Horne in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose regarding the procedural handling of a plea that Reed had filed. The Superior Court struck the plea from the record due to the absence of an affidavit of merits, which the court believed was required by an earlier statute from 1853 concerning civil actions in Cook County. There was no record of exceptions filed that could clarify the grounds on which the plea was removed. Additionally, neither party requested a jury to assess damages, which led the court to determine damages directly based on authorized statutory provisions. The case was effectively a question of procedural correctness and the implications of court practices in assessing damages without a jury. The Illinois Supreme Court was called upon to decide the legality of the actions taken by the Superior Court.	The plaintiff, George W. Reed, claimed that the Superior Court erred in striking his plea from the record. He asserted that the requirement for an affidavit of merits was not in effect and maintained that the removal of his plea was unjust. Reed requested the Supreme Court to review the decision of the lower court and sought to have the original plea reinstated.	The defendant, Daniel Horne, contended that the Superior Court's actions were justified based on existing court practices. He argued that without a bill of exceptions to document the motions and objections regarding the striking of the plea, the plaintiff could not demonstrate any reversible error. The defense supported the court's authority to assess damages without a jury, given that neither party had requested such an assessment.

In the case of Leonard Miller v. W. W. Gray, which transpired in Carmi, Illinois in 1888, Leonard Miller, acting as a surety for Martin C. Beck, provided a notice to the payee W. W. Gray, stating his intention to relinquish his role as a surety on a promissory note. This notice was served on February 10, 1888, and was acknowledged by Gray on February 13. However, a suit was brought against Miller and other parties on March 20, 1888, resulting in a judgment before a justice of the peace. This judgment was subsequently appealed to the County Court and then the Circuit Court due to a conflict of interest involving the presiding judge. The case ultimately revolved around whether Miller's notice to Gray was sufficient to release him as a surety, considering the financial status of the principal debtor, Martin C. Beck, who was deeply insolvent and had significant debts. The court examined the timeliness of the suit following the notice and reviewed the related circumstances surrounding the obligations of the parties involved.	The plaintiff, W. W. Gray, argued that the notice provided by Leonard Miller was insufficient for releasing him from his obligations as a surety on the promissory note. Gray contended that Miller failed to clearly demand legal action be taken against the principal debtor promptly, thereby justifying the delayed suit.	Leonard Miller’s defense centered on the claim that he had appropriately notified Gray to take action on the note, thereby discharging his obligations as a surety. Miller asserted that a suit initiated thirty-six days post-notice was not conducted within a reasonable timeframe and demonstrated a lack of diligence on Gray's part. He claimed that the insolvency of the principal created an environment where the suit would have been ineffective even if it had been filed immediately.

The case "The Chicago City Railway Company v. Frank Brady" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on March 10, 1890. The incident took place in Chicago, Illinois, where Frank Brady was driving a loaded wagon on State Street. While attempting to maneuver his wagon onto a scale located on the east side of the street just south of 33rd Street, he inadvertently drove too far, causing the fore-wheels of the wagon to go off the scale. Unable to back the wagon onto the scale due to the load, Brady instead drove north in order to return to the scale from the north. As he crossed the east track of the street railway, a cable car traveling from the north struck the wagon. This collision resulted in Brady falling off the wagon, leading to severe personal injuries that rendered him totally disabled for life. The core dispute centered around the question of negligence, with conflicting evidence presented that led to a jury finding in favor of Brady.	The plaintiff, Frank Brady, claimed that the Chicago City Railway Company was negligent, which directly resulted in his personal injuries from the collision with the cable car. He argued that the railway company failed to operate its trains safely and that this negligence led to his accident. In his request, Brady sought compensation for the injuries sustained and the lifetime disability he faced as a result.	The defendant, the Chicago City Railway Company, contended that Brady was also negligent in his actions, which contributed to the accident. They maintained that the responsibility for the collision should not solely lie with the railway company, given that Brady had moved his wagon onto the tracks during a maneuver that could be deemed hazardous. The defendant sought to challenge the jury's findings and requested that the verdict be overturned in their favor.

On May 19, 1884, John J. Roberson and others (appellants) employed Laura Troutt (appellee) to teach a five-month school term starting September 1, 1884, with a monthly payment of $30. She taught until December 15, 1884, when the appellants discharged her for alleged negligence, cruelty, and refusal to enforce school rules. Troutt was compensated for the time she taught but claimed wrongful dismissal and sought payment for the remainder of her contract. Following judgments in her favor at both the justice and circuit court levels, the appellants appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court. The central legal question revolved around whether Troutt's discharge was justifiable based on the claims made against her, as she denied the charges and argued that the rules were unreasonable.	Laura Troutt contended that her discharge was wrongful and pursued wages for the unexpired term of her employment. Her main arguments included a denial of the allegations of negligence and cruelty, and she asserted that the rules imposed by the appellants were unreasonable, thereby absolving her from the obligation to comply with them.	John J. Roberson and the other appellants asserted that Troutt was negligent, cruel, and failed to adhere to the school regulations established by the board of directors. They claimed that these violations justified her dismissal, thus requesting that the court uphold the agreement to terminate her employment without further payment due, based on their accusations.

In 1871, John Griffin entered a legal dispute with Abraham J. Knisely regarding the rental of a dock on Halsted Street, located in Chicago, Illinois. Initially, Griffin shared the dock premises with A. E. Chamberlain & Co. from May 1, 1870, to May 1, 1871. In March 1871, Griffin sought to extend the rental agreement for another year but was unable to finalize a new lease. While Knisely prepared a written lease in accordance with their agreement, Griffin hesitated to sign, wanting additional negotiations, which led to Knisely ultimately withdrawing the rental offer on April 27, 1871. Griffin occupied the premises despite Knisely's subsequent notification of new terms, which significantly increased the rental costs. This led to a legal claim for rent due from May 1, 1871, to May 1, 1872, as Griffin continued to occupy the premises without a formal lease in place.	Knisely, the plaintiff, claimed that Griffin owed him rent for the dock from May 1, 1871, to May 1, 1872, amounting to $1,200, based on a new rental rate of $12 per foot front for the entire dock. He argued that Griffin's continued possession of the property after being informed of the terms constituted acceptance of those terms, even though Griffin contested the amount owed, claiming he should only be responsible for the previously agreed rent for a portion of the dock.	Griffin, the defendant, contended that he was not liable for the increased rental rate because the prior rental agreement had not been formally completed. He argued that Knisely's withdrawal of the offer prior to the new lease's effective date meant that he could only be charged based on the previously agreed terms, which were lower than the new terms presented by Knisely. He asserted he should only owe $326.98, which he had already paid into the court as partial rent.

John Becker and Thomas Williams were involved in a legal dispute that dates back to 1868 in Illinois. The case arose when Williams had a claim against Martin Gibbs, who had conveyed a tract of land to Becker with the stipulation that Becker could sell the land and use the sale proceeds to pay Williams and other creditors of Gibbs. Becker sold the land but failed to pay Williams the debt owed. Williams then initiated legal action against Becker to recover the debt he claimed was due from Gibbs. Initially, Williams' claim was successful before a justice of the peace, and he was awarded a judgment. The matter was subsequently appealed to the circuit court, which upheld the original judgment. Becker then brought the case before the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking to reverse the decision.	The plaintiff, Thomas Williams, argued that John Becker was liable for the debt owed to him because he failed to apply the proceeds from the sale of the land as stipulated in the agreement with Gibbs. Williams requested that the court enforce the judgment against Becker to recover the amount due to him.	The defendant, John Becker, contended that he was not legally obligated to pay Williams' debt, as there was no explicit agreement that he would pay Williams as a preferred creditor upon receiving the land. Becker asserted that his only duty was to apply the proceeds of the land sale to pay Gibbs' debts, which he had done. He requested the court to reverse the judgment rendered against him, arguing that the case should have been examined with regard to his lack of absolute liability for the debt.

In April 1861, in Illinois, the case of George Smith v. William Moore was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from an executory contract regarding the purchase of land. George Smith, the appellant, had previously been involved in a ruling related to the same facts, where it was established that a purchaser of land, upon being granted possession, could remove any improvements made to the property after the purchase, as long as those improvements were not permanent fixtures. The court examined the implications of this ruling in light of the mechanics' lien law, which grants rights to those providing labor or materials on a property. Smith's position was that improvements made on the land, even if later sold for profit, could not be removed by Moore, the appellee, who contended that his rights as a vendor were affected by the mechanic's lien law, which might give him precedence over Smith's claim.	The plaintiff, George Smith, argued that as the purchaser of the land under an executory contract, he had the right to remove any improvements that were installed after the acquisition of the property. He asserted that these improvements were made in contemplation of their permanence with the land and that any actions by the defendant, William Moore, should not override this right. Additionally, Smith requested the court to affirm his claim to the proceeds from any removal and sale of those improvements.	The defendant, William Moore, contended that as the vendor in a contract, he was entitled to claim the improvements made to the property, arguing that they should be viewed as permanent fixtures that could not be removed by the buyer. Moore claimed that the relationship between him and Smith resembled that of a mortgagor to a mortgagee, which would limit Smith's rights to remove anything from the property. He sought to establish that his rights under the mechanics' lien law superseded those of the plaintiff, potentially granting him priority over any claims to the improvements or the proceeds from their sale.

In 1867, Joseph Stout initiated a legal action against Warren Hill in the La Salle Circuit Court, Illinois, concerning a financial instrument related to a mortgage. The dispute arose over a promissory note that specified an amount of $464 plus interest at ten percent, with payment contingent upon the foreclosure of a mortgage from 1856 involving a property owned by William Cantlin and Michael Boach. The note indicated that payment would be made once Hill had time to complete the foreclosure process and subsequently sell the land. The plaintiff, Stout, received the note from Daniel Condon, who endorsed it without recourse. The case hinged on the interpretation of the note, particularly regarding the payment timeline, which was complicated by the presence of a homestead right attached to the mortgaged land. This right hindered the foreclosure process, and the court acknowledged that the payment was not due at the time of the lawsuit, deeming the claim premature. The Circuit Court's decision was that the time for payment had not yet arrived due to the existence of the homestead right.	Joseph Stout contended that Warren Hill was obligated to pay him the amount specified in the promissory note, asserting that Hill's failure to fulfill this obligation constituted a breach of contract. Stout claimed that the note should be enforceable despite any delays related to the foreclosure of the mortgage, and he sought to recover the amount due along with accrued interest.	Warren Hill argued that the lawsuit was premature, as the promissory note stipulated that payment was contingent upon the foreclosure of the mortgage and the sale of the property, which had not yet occurred due to the homestead right. Hill maintained that the payment was not due because the conditions outlined in the note had not been satisfied, and he requested the court to dismiss the claims against him based on this premise.

Norman Hall filed a lawsuit against The Rose Hill and Evanston Road Company in September 1873, in Cook County, Illinois. Hall claimed to be the owner of five shares of stock in the company and sought a dividend payment of $10 per share. The defendant, The Rose Hill and Evanston Road Company, contested his ownership, asserting that the shares were spurious and issued without the proper authority of its board of directors. The case was tried before a jury, which concluded in favor of the company, leading Hall to appeal the decision. During the proceedings, evidence was presented, including witness testimonies regarding the legitimacy of the stock issuance. Hall’s primary witness had credibility issues and provided inconsistent accounts, while other credible witnesses affirmed that no official meeting of the board had authorized the issuance of the disputed shares. The jury ultimately found that the shares Hall claimed to own were indeed invalid due to improper issuance.	The plaintiff, Norman Hall, claimed that he was entitled to dividends on five shares of stock he owned in The Rose Hill and Evanston Road Company. He argued that the company owed him a payment of $50, based on the $10 dividend per share, and sought to recover this amount through the lawsuit.	The defendant, The Rose Hill and Evanston Road Company, contended that Hall's shares were not valid as they were issued fraudulently and without the authorization of the board of directors. The company presented evidence contradicting Hall's claims, including witness testimony that supported the invalidity of the shares. The defense maintained that Hall failed to prove the legitimacy of his stock ownership and requested the court to dismiss his claims.

Daniel F. Buckley filed lawsuits against Joel Eaton, Jr. and against E. L. H. and Charles S. Gardiner in 1871. The cases originated from the Superior Court of Chicago, presided over by Judge William A. Porter. The legal disputes involved multiple parties and the specific events leading to the lawsuits are not detailed in the provided description. However, it is noted that the appellant (Buckley) failed to adhere to the procedural rules required by the court, specifically regarding the assignment of errors and the filing of an abstract of the record. This disregard for procedural norms would play a significant role in the court's handling of the case.	The primary argument from the plaintiff, Daniel F. Buckley, revolved around his grievances against the defendants, Joel Eaton, Jr., E. L. H., and Charles S. Gardiner. Buckley sought to appeal the judgments from the lower court and presumably aimed for a remedy or compensation for his claims, although specific legal requests were not detailed in the text.	The defendants, represented by attorneys from SawiN & Wells and Mr. S. M. Davis, focused on procedural objections regarding Buckley’s appeal. They highlighted the appellant’s failure to comply with court rules, particularly the lack of an assignment of errors and the absence of a proper abstract of the record needed for the appeal process. This lack of procedural adherence was central to their defense.

Edward Shepard and Hartman Markoe purchased land known as the south-east quarter of section 27, township 38, range 4 in Cook County, Illinois, as tenants in common from the United States. On September 8, 1836, Shepard sold the east half of this land to Maurice Wakeman, which was recorded in the county records. Later, Shepard, acting as Markoe's attorney, facilitated the sale of the west half to Edward Reid, with the transaction concluding in November 1836. Markoe's warranty deed for the west half was recorded in May 1839. Over the years, both Shepard and Markoe seem to have accepted this distribution of the land without any formal partition agreement. The defendant, Nunna Rinks, occupied the west half based on the title derived from Reid. In May 1874, Shepard initiated an ejectment action against Rinks, aiming to reclaim an undivided half of the west half, asserting that no partition had occurred to transfer the legal title. The lower court ruled in favor of the defendant, prompting Shepard to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1875.	Edward Shepard claims that he is entitled to recover possession of the undivided one-half of the west half of the south-east quarter of section 27, arguing that no formal partition of the land took place between him and Markoe. He contends that he maintains rights to the land in question because the legal title was not transferred to the defendant.	Nunna Rinks defends against Shepard's claims by asserting that there was an informal or parol partition between Shepard and Markoe, where each party took possession of their respective shares. Rinks claims that her possession of the west half was lawful, supported by a warranty deed from Markoe and the acknowledgment of Shepard's actions, which indicated cooperation and consent to the possession arrangements made.

In February 1868, the Adams House in Chicago was owned by Elisha C. Sprague. Schuyler S. Benjamin and John J. Pearce had a lease for the property set to expire on April 30, 1868. As a condition for renewing the lease for an additional three years, the lessees requested necessary repairs. A new lease was established on February 21, 1868, allowing Pearce & Benjamin the right to make repairs up to $8,000, with costs verifiable by an architect’s certificate. The plaintiffs, Heeney and Campbell, undertook repairs exceeding this amount, claiming they did so at the request of the defendants. The lessees, Benjamin and Pearce, argued that the additional repairs were contracted by Sprague and thus he alone was liable. The case was tried without a jury, resulting in a judgment for the plaintiffs, with damages assessed at $1,047.03. The defendants appealed, contesting the court's finding and the conclusion drawn from the evidence.	The plaintiffs, Heeney and Campbell, claimed they were owed payment for repairs made on the Adams House that surpassed the agreed amount in the lease. They asserted that the extra work was conducted at the request of the defendants, who agreed to the payment for such repairs regardless of the exceeded limit stipulated in the lease. They sought to recover the additional costs incurred for the excess repairs.	The defendant, Schuyler S. Benjamin, maintained that the extra repairs were commissioned by Sprague, the property owner, who should be solely liable for those costs. Benjamin argued that the plaintiffs were not entitled to payment for the work performed beyond the original contract amount, thus challenging the court's finding and asserting that it was against the weight of the evidence.

George Kizer and Daniel Kizer initiated this legal case against Michael Kennedy in the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1850. The dispute originated from an incident on March 15, 1847, when the defendant allegedly took and carried away goods valued at one thousand dollars, believed to be the property of the plaintiffs. The action was categorized as trespass de bonis asportatis, where the plaintiffs sought to recover damages for the unlawful taking of their property. During the proceedings in the Bureau-Circuit Court, the defendant pleaded not guilty and presented a special plea justifying the action taken. The trial judge, T.L. Dickey, ruled against the plaintiffs' demurrer to this special plea, leading the plaintiffs to appeal this decision to the Supreme Court, arguing that the lower court's ruling was in error.	The plaintiffs, George Kizer and Daniel Kizer, claimed that Michael Kennedy wrongfully took their property without permission, constituting a trespass. They maintained that the value of the goods taken amounted to one thousand dollars and requested restitution for their losses, arguing against the validity of the defendant's special plea that sought to justify the action as lawful.	Michael Kennedy defended the case by asserting a special plea, indicating that he entered the premises to distrain property for overdue rent that had been accrued three months prior to the taking. He claimed that his actions were justified as they occurred on the last day of the tenancy agreement and that the seizure was legally permissible under the circumstances. The defendant requested that the Court affirm the ruling of the Bureau-Circuit Court, contending that the plea was valid and the plaintiffs' claims should be dismissed.

In April 1865, the case of *James H. Eames and William Fordham v. Lansing Morgan, Gilbert Morgan and Edward L. Furniss* was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a transaction involving a piece of land in Chicago, where the plaintiffs (Eames and Fordham) were induced by the defendants (Morgan and Furniss) to deliver one thousand cords of wood in exchange for a lot of land. The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants falsely represented that the lot was clear of any encumbrances and that they had good title to the property. Eames executed a bond to convey the property once the wood was delivered, retaining possession of the lot until then. The plaintiffs contended that they were deceived into this transaction due to the defendants' fraudulent assertions about the property's title. The case proceeded to trial in the Cook Circuit Court, where the jury found in favor of the defendants, leading the plaintiffs to appeal on several grounds, including issues of the sufficiency of the declaration and claims of error in jury instructions.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were defrauded by the defendants' misrepresentations regarding the title and encumbrances on the lot they were purchasing with the wood. They argued that their delivery of the wood was induced by these fraudulent statements, for which they sought compensation amounting to $2,484, asserting that they never received any payment or deed for the lot due to the deceitful actions of the defendants.	The defendants relied on several arguments, including that the plaintiffs did not adequately prove the existence of fraud and that they should have exercised ordinary care to verify the accuracy of the defendants' claims about the title. The defendants argued that any false representations made did not equate to fraud if the plaintiffs could have discovered the truth through reasonable diligence. They also contended that the plaintiffs' failure to perform their part of the contract absolved them of liability, and they requested that the court overturn the judgment to favor them.

Cassius B. Dewey, a 26-year-old grave-stone cutter from Mendota, Illinois, was involved in a tragic accident at the Princeton depot of the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company around 12:35 A.M. on a night in 1861. Dewey had just returned from business in Princeton and was attempting to board a passenger train behind a stationary freight train. The freight train had just pulled into the first switch track, stopping between the ticket office and the passenger train, which was preparing to accept passengers. As the passenger train arrived, the freight train began to move forward after taking on water. In a hazardous move to cross through the gaps in the freight train while it started moving, Dewey became caught between the bumpers of the train cars and suffered severe injuries, leading to his death within an hour. His widow, Nancy M. Dewey, later filed a suit against the railroad company, claiming negligence caused her husband’s death. The incident reflects both the serious risks associated with train operations at night and the importance of safety measures at busy depots.	Nancy M. Dewey, as administratrix of her husband's estate, claimed that the railroad company acted negligently by stopping their freight train in a dangerous position, obstructing safe passage for passengers. The plaintiff argued that due to the positioning of the freight train, Dewey was placed in hazardous circumstances that led to his fatal accident. She sought damages of $5,000 for the wrongful death of her husband, highlighting the financial and emotional impact on her family.	The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company claimed that Cassius B. Dewey was guilty of gross negligence for attempting to cross between moving train cars. They argued that Dewey, as an adult, was expected to exercise reasonable caution and should have known it was dangerous to pass through the freight train. The defendant also contended that while there may have been negligence on the part of the railroad, Dewey's actions contributed significantly to the accident, and thus the company should not be held liable. They requested the court to reverse the lower court's verdict in favor of the plaintiff.

In 1852, in the State of Illinois, the case involved The People of the State of Illinois as the plaintiffs against Philip Thurber as the defendant. The central issue arose from Thurber acting as an agent for a foreign insurance company without complying with the statutory requirements as laid out in the Revised Statutes, specifically the 22nd and 23rd sections of Chapter 64, which pertained to licensing. The Illinois Supreme Court discussed the constitutionality of the law enforcing these licensing provisions, highlighting that the law did not violate the state's constitutional requirement for uniform taxation. The plaintiffs contended that Thurber's non-compliance constituted a violation of the law, while Thurber's demurrer (objection) to the plaintiffs' declaration was sustained by the Circuit Court, resulting in a judgment in favor of him. Consequently, the plaintiffs brought the case to the Supreme Court to challenge the lower court's decision on the grounds of error in sustaining the demurrer.	The plaintiffs, representing the State of Illinois, claimed that Thurber had violated the licensing laws by acting without the necessary compliance measures. They argued that the statutory provisions did not infringe any constitutional mandates regarding taxation and commerce, emphasizing that the law, in itself, creates a license upon compliance. The plaintiffs sought to reverse the lower court's judgment and hold Thurber accountable for his violations.	Thurber's primary defense rested on the assertion that the licensing law in question was unconstitutional, arguing that it violated the state and federal constitutions regarding taxation and commerce. He contended that the law's requirements could not legally impose a burden on him as an agent of a foreign insurance company. His demurrer led to the Circuit Court’s ruling in his favor, upholding the argument that the law was misapplied or did not apply to his circumstances.

On June 4, 1856, Joseph Tatnall and others sold a parcel of land to John Gatewood for $6,400, with part of the payment secured by a mortgage.
