The mortgage was recorded on January 19, 1859, after a judgment was issued against Gatewood, with Hays acquiring the property at a court-ordered sale on March 3, 1860. Subsequently, Williams, who had obtained a judgment against Gatewood on December 29, 1859, redeemed the property from Hays' sale on March 5, 1861, and later purchased it outright on May 7, 1861. The case revolved around the validity of the mortgage and whether Hays and Williams had notice of it, determining their respective rights to the property. The Illinois Supreme Court was asked to resolve the dispute between the complainants (Tatnall) and the defendants (Hays and Williams) regarding their claims on the land after these transactions.	The plaintiffs claimed that Hays had notice of the mortgage prior to his judgment lien and that Williams, having redeemed the property from Hays, was not a bona fide purchaser. They sought a decree of foreclosure on the mortgage and demanded payment for the unpaid notes secured by the mortgage, claiming that all interests of Hays and Williams in the property should be barred except for the equity of redemption.	The defendants contended they were not aware of the mortgage at the time of their respective judgments and asserted that any notice was constructive and insufficient to affect their rights. Hays denied having any personal knowledge of the mortgage and argued he acted as a bona fide purchaser. Williams maintained that he lawfully acquired the property through redemption and subsequent sale, and that he should not be bound by Hays' prior notice of the mortgage.

In June 1867, the case of Samuel Lester et al. v. The Heirs of William White was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Marion County, Illinois, involving Samuel Lester and his wife Ann Lester, who sought to compel William White to convey a one-fifth interest in a specific tract of land, following White's acquisition of the property under controversial circumstances. The property had originally been claimed by John Morgan, who had a pre-emption right; however, errors in land conveyance led to a dispute about rightful ownership. During the course of litigation, White died intestate, leading to the case continuing against his heirs. The initial Circuit Court ruling dismissed the Lesters' bill, prompting them to appeal. Key issues in the case revolved around the legitimacy of evidence presented by witnesses who had covenanted with White regarding the land's title.	The plaintiffs, Samuel and Ann Lester, claimed that they were entitled to a one-fifth interest in the contested property and demanded a deed from the defendant, William White, for Ann’s share. They contended that the earlier dismissal of their bill was erroneous, particularly arguing against the inclusion of certain testimony that undermined their claim. They sought to reverse the lower court's decision and obtain the conveyance of Ann's rightful interest in the land upon payment of her share of the purchase money.	The defendant, William White, asserted that he had legally acquired the property through a deed from Morgan’s heirs and claimed that Abraham Wimberly was the rightful owner of the pre-emption, with whom White had transacted. White argued that he was advised by counsel to secure a deed from Morgan's heirs and that the pre-emption interest was validly transferred to him. His requests included affirming that the lower court's dismissal of the Lesters' bill was justified.

Robert Fergus et al. v. Edward I. Tinkham is a legal case that reached the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1865. The initial proceedings began when Edward I. Tinkham filed a bill in chancery against Robert Fergus and others, seeking to foreclose a mortgage on a note for $13,000 dated December 13, 1859. The mortgage specified that upon default in interest payments, the full principal became due. The case arose from alleged defaults in interest payments from January 1860 to July 1861. Fergus and his co-defendants, including Margaret Fergus, John T. White, Richard M. Casler, and Mary Brown, were served with process, except for White, who was a non-resident and was notified through publications in the Daily Post from May 24 to June 24, 1861. The lower court found that the primary sum owed had become due due to non-payment of interest. On December 4, 1861, the court decreed Fergus to pay $15,267.50 or risk the sale of the mortgaged premises. This finding led to the defendants seeking a writ of error based on several objections regarding notice and the validity of the claims presented.	The plaintiff, Edward I. Tinkham, claimed that the defendants failed to pay the interest on the note secured by the mortgage, which entitled him to foreclose. He argued that the non-payment of an interest installment resulted in the principal sum becoming due, based on the terms of the mortgage. He sought to have the court enforce the repayment of the amount owed, which he calculated at $15,267.50, or allow the property to be sold in satisfaction of the mortgage.	The defendants, led by Robert Fergus, contended that the notice provided to the non-resident party (John T. White) was insufficient, as it did not meet the statutory requirements. They also argued that the court had no proof of the mortgage execution being necessary since they admitted to it in their pleadings. Lastly, they challenged the decree on the grounds that Tinkham had recovered an amount greater than what was specified in his bill, specifically for interest he had not claimed, classifying the court's decree as erroneous.

The case "H. W. McFadden et al. v. D. C. White et al." took place in Mason County, Illinois, with the ruling issued by the Illinois Appellate Court on January 21, 1889. The plaintiffs, H. W. McFadden and others, were landowners within a designated special drainage district. They filed a chancery bill to prevent the drainage commissioners from allocating funds from the district's general funds for the purpose of constructing and repairing what are described as subordinate ditches, which are deemed unnecessary for the overall drainage of the district. The plaintiffs argued that these subordinate ditches were intended solely for specific areas and should not be financed by the general fund. They sought not only to restrain future appropriations but also to require current and previous commissioners to account for and return misused funds. The Circuit Court had sustained a demurrer to the bill, which brought the issue before the appellate court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the drainage commissioners were unlawfully appropriating funds from the general treasury for subordinate ditches, which they contended were unnecessary for the district's comprehensive drainage needs. They requested the court to restrain the commissioners from making further appropriations for such projects and demanded a return of previously misappropriated funds to the district treasury.	The defendants, represented by the drainage commissioners, maintained that the allegations made by the plaintiffs were insufficient to warrant the court's intervention. They argued that there was a lack of specific evidence demonstrating misappropriation and that the commissioners were presumed to act within the bounds of the law. The defendants contended that the bill was fundamentally flawed and should be dismissed as it was properly held bad by the lower court.

James J. Ryan filed a writ of error against Abner Eads in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1827. The case originated from the Washington Circuit Court, where judgment had been entered by default against Ryan. A critical issue arose regarding the service of the writ; the return was made by an individual identifying himself only as "Deputy Sheriff," rather than using the sheriff's name. The court highlighted that deputies must operate in the name of their principal and that such an insufficient return renders the judgment erroneous. The proceedings were challenged based on this irregularity, which exposed a flaw in how the legal process was carried out. The implications of this irregularity needed to be addressed, despite the case's ongoing matters related to a mortgage.	Ryan argued that the judgment entered against him was invalid due to the erroneous nature of the return of service by the deputy sheriff. He claimed that the deputy lacked authority in issuing the return without the sheriff's name, resulting in a lack of proper notification and due process. He requested the court to reverse the judgment due to these procedural errors.	Eads defended the judgment by arguing that the procedural errors cited by Ryan did not substantially affect the case's merits. He likely contended that the lower court’s judgment should stand despite the alleged irregularity in the service return, possibly emphasizing that Ryan was not prejudiced by the deputy's actions.

In the case of Francis Hurlbut v. William B. Bradford, which took place in 1884 in Knox County, Illinois, the legal dispute arose over a portion of land described as the north-west quarter of section 8, town 11 north, range 4 east. The case was brought by the plaintiff, Francis Hurlbut, against the appellant, William B. Bradford, seeking recovery of the land through an action of ejectment. The trial was conducted without a jury, with both parties submitting evidence regarding the title to the property. Hurlbut presented a clear chain of title dating back to the United States government, while Bradford countered with a tax deed and his own chain of title that included tax receipts from 1839 to 1846. The court focused on whether the payments of taxes made by Bradford or his predecessors were sufficient under the law, particularly regarding the requirements of coinciding claims and tax payments to establish ownership. Ultimately, the court concluded that Bradford did not sufficiently prove his claims, leading to the ruling in favor of Hurlbut.	The plaintiff, Francis Hurlbut, argued that he held a valid chain of title to the parcel of land in question, tracing his ownership back to the United States government. Hurlbut's legal request was for the court to affirm his rightful ownership and grant a writ of restitution, allowing him to reclaim the land from Bradford.	The defendant, William B. Bradford, contended that his ownership was established through a tax deed and associated tax payments made over several years. He argued that these payments should protect his claim to the land and that the period of tax payments fulfilled the legal statute of limitations allowing him to maintain his title against Hurlbut's claim.

In June 1875, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company v. Charles T. Stratton, concerning an incident that occurred in 1863. The plaintiff, Charles T. Stratton, was a ten-year-old boy who had traveled from St. Louis with his father. They intended to take an evening express train to Salem, which was believed to stop at that station. Upon arrival, as they attempted to disembark, Stratton fell or was thrown under the moving train, resulting in the amputation of both of his legs. The case revolved around claims of negligence by the railway company, particularly whether the train had stopped adequately or started moving again too quickly, endangering the passengers as they alighted. The jury initially found in favor of plaintiff Stratton, awarding him $6,000 in damages.	The plaintiff argued that the railway company was negligent in failing to stop the train for a reasonable amount of time to allow him to disembark safely. He contended that the company did not exercise due care, resulting in his violent fall under the train as it started moving suddenly while he was in the act of stepping off. The plaintiff’s legal requests centered around compensatory damages for the severe injuries sustained due to this negligence.	The defendant, Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company, asserted that the train had indeed stopped for a reasonable duration, allowing other passengers, including women and children, to deboard safely. They contended that any failure to safely disembark was due to the actions of the plaintiff and his father, who neglected to exercise adequate care and chose to attempt to exit the train prematurely. The defendant argued that any liability for the accident rested with the father for not adhering to safety protocols.

In September 1874, the case of Jonathan Y. Scammon et al. v. Sarah A. Campbell was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County, where Sarah A. Campbell, the widow of James B. Campbell, filed a petition for dower following her husband's death intestate. The defendants in the case included J. Y. Scammon, John D. Jennings, and John L. Clark, who claimed ownership of certain sub-lots in Chicago that were originally owned by James B. Campbell. The court proceedings began with Scammon failing to respond to the petition, leading the court to consider his consent. Jennings and Clark, on the other hand, denied the dower claim but admitted that the title was once in James B. Campbell’s name, questioning only his identity. The court appointed a master in chancery to take evidence, which ultimately confirmed the petitioner’s claim as the valid widow. Upon review, the court found that Campbell was seized of the lots during his marriage and determined that Sarah had the right to a dower, or a share of the property, during her lifetime. The court quantified the dower’s annual value and other compensatory damages through a jury verdict, leading to a decree for the defendants to pay her set amounts annually.	Sarah A. Campbell claimed her right to dower on the grounds that she was the widow of James B. Campbell, who owned the property in question. She argued that as such, she was entitled to one-third of the yearly rental value of the unimproved lots despite the improvements made by the defendants. She sought her share of the property and compensation for damages resulting from the defendants' failure to comply with the assumptions of her dower rights. Her legal request included determining the yearly value of her dower and receiving the respective payments from the defendants.	The defendants, Jennings and Clark, contended that they owned undivided interests in the property and denied the plaintiff's claim of dower by questioning the identity of James B. Campbell, asserting that it had not been proven that he was the same person to whom the plaintiff was married. They argued that the rental value calculated for the dower was inappropriate and claimed that the assessment was influenced by improper testimony. Furthermore, the defendants disputed the court's decree for joint and several liabilities, arguing that each should only be accountable for their proportional interests.

In April 1867, in Chicago, Illinois, the legal case "Henry C. Pitney et al. v. William H. Brown" involved a dispute over the will of Aaron Pitney, who had passed away. The will directed that after his debts and funeral expenses were paid, the remaining fund should be equally divided between the children of his late brother, Mahlon Pitney, and his brother-in-law, William H. Brown. The main issue arose regarding whether the distribution of the residue should be per stirpes (by branch) or per capita (equally among individuals). The Circuit Court initially ruled that Brown would receive half of the residue, with the remaining half going to the three children of Mahlon Pitney. This decision was appealed by the complainants (the children), who argued for a per capita distribution. The appeal sought judicial clarification on the interpretation of "equally divided" as stated in the will.	The plaintiffs, Henry C. Pitney, Phoebe T. Watkins, and Mary E. Brayton, sought a judicial construction of Aaron Pitney's will, specifically the fourth clause concerning the equal distribution of the residuary fund. They argued that under this clause, the legatees should take their shares equally per capita rather than per stirpes, meaning each individual should receive an equal portion of the estate rather than dividing it based on family branches.	William H. Brown, the defendant, argued that the language of the will indicated an intention to distribute the residue equally between him and the children of Mahlon Pitney, leading to a per stirpes division. He contended that the clause indicating a portion of the property came from his father was relevant and suggested a different intent than that proposed by the plaintiffs.

On December 1855, a legal dispute arose in Mount Sterling, Illinois involving James Givens as the defendant and the President and Trustees of Mount Sterling as the plaintiffs. The case stemmed from the town's attempt to extend certain streets through lands owned by Givens. The town aimed to exercise its authority to condemn private property for public use, as provided by Illinois law. During a trial, it was determined that the plaintiffs did not adequately prove ownership of the lands in dispute. A jury assessed the damages Givens would incur from the street extensions, ultimately determining he was owed $290 in damages. This ruling prompted the plaintiffs to bring the case to the Illinois Supreme Court, questioning the jury’s decision and the validity of their claims regarding land ownership and damages.	The plaintiffs argued that they had the legal authority to extend streets over the property owned by James Givens and that their proceedings should suffice to claim the land. They contended that the jury wrongly assessed damages without clear proof of Givens’ ownership, thus challenging the validity of the compensation awarded to him.	Givens' defense centered on the acknowledgment of his ownership by the town during the condemnation process. He asserted that the town had valued his land and assessed appropriate damages, thereby establishing his right to compensation. Givens argued that the town did not have grounds to dismiss his claims based on the absence of formal title proof since their proceedings implied acknowledgment of his ownership.

Sarah J. Everett et al. v. Isaac S. Boardman is a legal case from January 1871, taking place in Macon County, Illinois. The case began when Isaac S. Boardman filed a suit in chancery against Sarah J. Everett and the heirs of James E. Everett, who had recently passed away. The dispute centered around a mortgage executed by James E. Everett and his wife, which Boardman sought to foreclose. The mortgage in question described a property as "lot No. six," but included a metes and bounds description that actually referred to "lot two." The underlying issue arose because the property intended for the foreclosure was not accurately described in the mortgage document. The circuit court had previously granted a foreclosure based on the understanding that the mortgage applied to lot two, where the mortgagors had ownership. The defendants, claiming that the description in the mortgage did not accurately reflect the property, sought a reversal of the circuit court's decision through this writ of error.	The plaintiff, Isaac S. Boardman, argued that the mortgage executed by James E. Everett and his wife was valid and should be foreclosed upon despite the errors in the description. Boardman contended that the recitals and references within the mortgage adequately identified the property as lot two, which should be treated as the actual mortgaged property. Boardman sought to ensure that his rights under the mortgage were upheld and that the foreclosure proceeded without a reformation of the deed's description.	The defendants, led by Sarah J. Everett, claimed that the mortgage incorrectly specified "lot No. six," which they asserted was not owned by the mortgagors. They contended that the intended property was lot two, which they did own. Furthermore, they argued that a reformation of the deed would not legally transfer the widow's dower rights in lot two to satisfy the mortgage. Their appeal aimed to contest the foreclosure based on these claimed inaccuracies in the property's description.

Cornelius Powell, a 73-year-old resident of Peoria, Illinois, made his last will and testament on March 7, 1883, shortly before his death on March 12, 1883. The will granted his daughter, Mary A. McGough, only five dollars, while leaving his wife, Catharine Powell, five hundred dollars, and the residual estate to his stepdaughter, Julia Burley. Powell had been married twice; his first wife had passed away, and he had a distant relationship with his daughter, McGough, who had lived in New York for two decades. During his final illness, Powell’s care was largely provided by Burley, who also tended to his disabled wife. The core of the dispute arose when McGough contested the validity of Powell's will, claiming he lacked the mental capacity to draft it. A jury trial was held to evaluate the circumstances surrounding the will's creation.	Mary A. McGough, the plaintiff, contended that Cornelius Powell was not of sufficient mental capacity to make a will due to his advanced age and deteriorating health. She presented evidence from a physician who had examined Powell on multiple occasions prior to his death, asserting that he exhibited symptoms consistent with being unable to handle business matters or understand his actions sufficiently to execute a valid will.	Julia Burley, the defendant, argued that Powell was mentally competent at the time of drafting his will. She presented evidence demonstrating Powell's ability to walk, engage in conversations, and manage his daily needs in the days leading up to his death. Additional testimonies from neighbors and a county judge who helped draft the will supported the assertion that Powell understood the contents and implications of his will, bolstering claims of his mental capacity.

In the case of Joseph D. Webster v. John M. Cobb, the legal proceedings took place in Illinois, culminating in a judgment rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1856. The case revolves around a promissory note executed by Henry Fowler, owed to Thomas A. Stewart for $1,083, dated October 10, 1852. This note was guaranteed in writing by the defendant, J.D. Webster, before its delivery to Stewart. Subsequently, Stewart assigned the note to the plaintiff, Cobb, before it matured. Webster contested the validity of the assignment and claimed that he had already paid the note before the assignment took place. The court had to determine if the plaintiff could enforce the guaranty against Webster and whether the assignment was made in good faith. The trial concluded with the court ruling in favor of Cobb, contrary to the claims made by Webster.	The plaintiff, John M. Cobb, argued that he was entitled to recover the amount of the promissory note, as it had been properly assigned to him by Thomas A. Stewart. He maintained that Webster had written a guaranty on the back of the note, affirming his obligation to pay. Cobb requested that the court recognize his right to enforce the guaranty and sought judgment for the sum of $1,295, alleging that Webster was liable for the amount as the guarantor of the note.	The defendant, Joseph D. Webster, presented several arguments, including that the note had been paid to the payee, Stewart, prior to the assignment to Cobb. He contended that the assignment was merely a colorable transaction designed to evade repayment. Webster also claimed that Cobb had prior knowledge of the payment and satisfaction of the note when it was assigned, arguing that this knowledge invalidated Cobb's claim. Additionally, Webster filed a general denial and special pleas arguing that the assignment lacked sufficient consideration.

The case "Fletcher Stevens, Plaintiff in Error, v. Frederick Faucet et al., Defendants in Error" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1860. The dispute arose from an agreement between two parties: Stevens & Co. (comprised of W.H. and F. Stevens) and Faucet & Co. (which included Frederick Faucet). The agreement, dated August 7, 1855, outlined the terms under which Faucet & Co. would supply hides to Stevens & Co. for tanning and the subsequent sale of leather. During the course of their business relationship, the plaintiffs claimed that the defendants wrongfully converted hides and leather, specifically stating they were entitled to the profits from the leather manufactured under their agreement. The trial began with the plaintiffs proving that Stevens & Co. had received 18,815 hides but only returned 8,248. They asserted the defendant, Fletcher Stevens, had sold a large portion of the hides, leading to the current legal issue. The key individuals involved include Fletcher Stevens and Frederick Faucet, among others, and the case focuses on the interpretation of their contractual agreement to establish the nature of their partnership or lack thereof.	The plaintiffs, represented by Fletcher Stevens, claimed that they were joint owners of the hides and leather produced under the contract. They argued that the actions of the defendant constituted conversion of property entrusted to their partnership, seeking compensation for the value of the hides not returned and for the profits from the sale of leather.	The defendant, Fletcher Stevens, contended that no partnership existed regarding the ownership of the hides and leather. He argued that the agreement established their roles distinctly, with the ownership of the hides and leather remaining with Faucet & Co. He asserted that any profits or losses were to be divided only after the completion of transactions involving the leather, which did not equate to actual ownership of the hides.

In January 1875, the case of Alexander R. Chestnut v. Emily Chestnut arose in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a divorce proceeding initiated by Alexander R. Chestnut against his wife, Emily Chestnut, in the Morgan County Circuit Court. The court had ordered temporary alimony for Emily at the rate of $1,600 per year from the date of service of process until the case's conclusion. The payment was stipulated to be $400 within twenty days and quarterly thereafter. However, just one day after the order was made, Alexander dismissed his divorce action. This dismissal led to a dispute regarding the temporary alimony payments that were allegedly due to Emily, amounting to $639.88 when the current proceeding commenced. The defendant's key argument was that the order for temporary alimony was made after the dismissal of the divorce case, thus claiming the court had no jurisdiction. As a result, a scire facias proceeding was initiated by Emily to enforce the payment of this alimony.	Emily Chestnut, the plaintiff, claimed that Alexander R. Chestnut owed her $639.88 under the temporary alimony order previously set by the court. She sought to enforce this order through a scire facias writ. Emily argued that the record of the alimony ruling should be upheld, allowing her a rightful claim for the payments due.	Alexander R. Chestnut contended that the alimony order was invalid because it was issued after he had already dismissed his divorce case, thus nullifying the court's jurisdiction over the matter. He argued that the dismissal of the bill effectively revoked the right to temporary alimony, maintaining that a married woman could not sue her husband for alimony in a legal action.

The case of John Gibbons v. The German Insurance and Savings Institution took place in Quincy, Illinois, culminating in a court decision on February 13, 1889. The dispute arose when John Gibbons filed a claim against his insurance provider, the German Insurance and Savings Institution, alleging that his furniture and library were damaged as a result of steam escaping from a heating apparatus installed in his premises. Gibbons argued that the escaping steam generated excessive heat, which charred his belongings, thus constituting a loss. The legality of whether this damage could be considered under the terms of the fire insurance policy was the crux of the matter. The case revolved around the interpretation of "fire" in the context of insurance coverage and whether damage caused by excessive heat, resulting from steam rather than actual ignition, could be classified as a fire-related loss. As it was established that the damage was caused by steam and not a conventional fire, the court needed to determine if the insurance policy should cover such incidents.	John Gibbons contended that the damages to his property were indeed caused by fire, asserting that the hot steam escaped from its designated path and burned his belongings. He argued that, despite the absence of actual ignition, the heat produced was sufficient to inflict damage, and thus should be interpreted as a loss covered by a standard fire insurance policy. Gibbons sought recovery of damages based on the premise that the steam, by its properties, functioned as fire, and requested the court to recognize the loss as qualifying under the terms of his insurance coverage.	The German Insurance and Savings Institution countered that their policy did not cover damages resulting from steam or heat that had not led to ignition. They argued that the terminology in the insurance policy distinctly defined fire, and since the damage occurred due to steam escaping from the heating apparatus rather than an actual fire, the claim fell outside the scope of the policy. The defendant maintained that damages caused by excessive heat do not equate to fire damage as per the understanding of terminology under the insurance terms.

In December 1825, the legal case of James C. Wright v. The People took place in Illinois, involving a dispute over the interpretation of a bond obligation. The case arose when the bond's conditions were allegedly separated from its penalty, causing a dispute about the legitimacy of the obligation. James C. Wright was the plaintiff challenging the decision of the lower court that had found him liable for committing a fraud that would require criminal charges. The key legal principles investigated revolved around whether the act of separating the condition from the penalty constituted an indictable fraud that would affect the public, as opposed to being a mere private injury that could have been guarded against with common prudence. The opinion of the court, led by Justice Smith, examined past precedents set in similar cases to establish whether such actions warranted criminal indictment under common law.	The plaintiff, James C. Wright, argued that his actions were being wrongly interpreted as fraud that impacted the public. Wright's main claim was that the separation of the condition from the penalty on the bond was a private injury rather than a public offense. He maintained that the alleged fraud did not meet the criteria necessary for indictment, claiming that it was something common prudence could have prevented.	The People, representing the state, contended that Wright's actions constituted a form of fraud that was indictable under the law. They argued that any attempt to separate the obligation's conditions from the bond's penalty could mislead individuals and undermine public trust in legal agreements. Therefore, they requested that the court uphold the previous judgment and affirm that Wright's behavior warranted legal scrutiny and punishment.

In September 1874, the case of Peter Keller v. Ernst Fournier et al. was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Superior Court of Cook County where Judge Joseph E. Gary presided. The case revolved around an action of assumpsit relating to a promissory note. The underlying issue came to the court's attention due to a procedural error claimed by the appellant, Peter Keller, regarding the execution of the trial out of its scheduled order on the docket as established by the general practice act. The bill of exceptions submitted did not demonstrate that Keller raised an objection to the case being advanced and tried out of turn, which became a crucial factor in assessing the appeal.	The plaintiff, Ernst Fournier and others, asserted that the appellant, Peter Keller, was liable on a promissory note. Their main argument was centered around the legal enforceability of the note itself, following standard procedures and rules governing such financial instruments. They sought to affirm the judgment originally made against Keller in the lower court and claimed he was responsible for the alleged debts stemming from the promissory note.	The defendant, Peter Keller, contended that the case was improperly advanced on the docket and tried out of its designated order, which, according to the general practice act, constituted a procedural error. Keller argued that this procedural misstep invalidated the proceedings and the resulting judgment against him. He requested that the court find this error significant enough to reconsider the case's outcome and dismiss the claims against him as a result.

Ignatius R. Sims was the appellant in a legal case against John Hugsby, the appellee, concerning a debt action that took place in December 1831 in the Morgan circuit court, Illinois. Hugsby initiated the action, claiming that Sims owed him $450 based on a writing obligatory. Sims was the only defendant served and failed to appear in court, resulting in a default judgment. The clerk assessed the damages and reported a judgment amount of $287.37 as due. Sims later appealed this judgment, arguing that it exceeded the amount he owed based on the original writing and that there was no jury to assess damages. He contended that the clerk had made an error by assessing more than the debt owed and that the judgment should only reflect the actual debt without additional damages.	Hugsby, the plaintiff, claimed that Sims owed him $450 based on a contractual obligation. He sought to recover this amount through his action of debt. Hugsby argued that, despite Sims's default, the judgment rendered was valid and deserved to be affirmed.	Sims, the defendant, contended that the judgment against him was in error as it amounted to more than what was actually owed. He claimed that there was no jury present to assess damages and maintained that the court should have only issued a judgment for the debt without extra damages. Sims argued that the clerk's assessment of damages was incorrect, and therefore, he appealed for reversal of the judgment.

The case "James M. Pottle, for the use of Christopher S. Luce, Plaintiff in Error, v. Solomon McWorter" took place in December 1851 in Illinois. The dispute arose over a promissory note that was related to a partnership between the plaintiff and the defendant. When issues emerged during the settlement of their partnership accounts, the matter was referred to arbitrators. The arbitrators initially awarded the plaintiff $392.91, stipulating that the defendant should execute three promissory notes, payable in installments over nine months. However, the defendant later discovered a computational error in the award, resulting in a higher amount than intended. An agreement was reached with the arbitrators to examine this mistake, contingent on the defendant executing the notes. Nevertheless, the arbitrators failed to correct the error, which led the defendant to claim that the consideration for the notes had entirely failed. The case was first tried in the Pike Circuit Court, which rendered a verdict in favor of the defendant. The plaintiff sought a new trial, which was denied, leading to this writ of error to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff claimed that the defendant owed him $392.91 based on the arbitrators' award. He argued that the promissory note represented a legitimate debt incurred under the terms of their partnership settlement. The plaintiff contested the defendant's claims regarding computational errors and maintained that the agreement made with the arbitrators was valid, asserting that the notes were executed with the intent to honor the arbitrated settlement.	The defendant raised several defenses, including the argument of non-assumpsit, asserting that no debt was actually owed. He claimed that the arbitrators had made an error in calculating the partnership accounts and that the amount stated was inflated due to this miscalculation. The defendant contended that reliance on the arbitrators' original award was misplaced and that the promissory note was given without any valid consideration, effectively nullifying any obligation to pay.

In the case of William B. Packard et al. v. William Van Schoick, filed in January 1871, the proceedings took place in Bloomington, Illinois. The plaintiff, William B. Packard, and his associates claimed that they had entered into a contract to furnish materials and construct brick and stone work for a schoolhouse. According to the contract, they were to be compensated at the rate of fourteen dollars per thousand for the brick work. A central issue was the interpretation of the term "wall measure," which the plaintiff argued was a recognized local practice for measurement, including openings like windows and doors. The defendants contested this interpretation and argued that the term had been interlined after the contract's draft was completed, asserting they had not agreed to include openings in the measurement. The Circuit Court in McLean County, presided over by Judge John M. Scott, was tasked with interpreting the contract and the associated evidence.	The plaintiff, William B. Packard, contended that he had completed the work as per the contract and sought payment based on a certificate provided by the supervising architect, George W. Buetieg. He argued that the certificate confirmed the completion of the brick work and warranted the payment he requested. Packard claimed that since the work was satisfactorily completed, the defendants were obliged to pay him the due amount.	The defendants, led by William Van Schoick, maintained that the plaintiff had failed to establish a valid cause of action. They argued that under the contract's terms, payment was conditional upon obtaining an estimate and certificate from the superintendent of work, which the plaintiff had not secured prior to filing the lawsuit. Additionally, they disputed the interpretation of "wall measure," insisting it did not encompass openings, and contended that the certificate provided by the plaintiff was insufficient and issued after the lawsuit had commenced, thus failing to comply with contract terms.

John Whalen, an employee of the Illinois and St. Louis Railroad & Coal Company, was involved in a tragic accident on December 19, 1882, while working as a switchman in the company’s East St. Louis yard. On that day, while fulfilling his duties, he was fatally struck and crushed by railroad cars after being knocked from the engine, which was a regular switch engine. The circumstances leading to his death involved a dangerously positioned scale shed that had been maintained by the company too close to the track—only seven inches away. Despite being warned about a bent coupling pin on the engine, Whalen moved to the side step of the engine to perform his duties, intending to turn switches ahead, and was subsequently killed by the train. At trial, the plaintiff, representing Whalen’s estate, alleged that the railroad company acted with culpable negligence by allowing the scale shed to be dangerously positioned and sought damages for the loss sustained by the family. The initial trial concluded without the railroad company presenting any evidence in its defense.	The plaintiff, William Whalen, as administrator of the deceased's estate, claimed that the Illinois and St. Louis Railroad & Coal Company was negligent in maintaining the scale shed too close to the track, constituting a safety hazard. The plaintiff argued that Whalen had the right to assume that the employer had provided a safe working environment and requested compensation for the pecuniary loss suffered by the next of kin due to Whalen’s wrongful death.	The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad & Coal Company did not present any evidence during the trial to defend against the claims of negligence. The company argued that the jury should find in their favor, suggesting that Whalen must have had some knowledge of the danger, despite the lack of concrete evidence to prove this assumption. Their defense relied primarily on a general assertion rather than specific rebuttals to the claims made by the plaintiff regarding the unsafe conditions of the work environment.

Bronson Murray and Samuel Schlosser entered into a contract on March 1, 1860, for the sale of a tract of land on credit. According to the contract, Schlosser was to pay for the property in installments, and failure to make timely payments would allow Murray to rescind the contract and assert his rights as a landlord. Schlosser took possession of the land but failed to make the required payments. In March 1865, while Schlosser was serving in the military and absent from home, a notice of forfeiture was served to his wife, declaring that the contract was rescinded and demanding rent payment. Schlosser never paid rent and, in June 1866, Murray demanded possession of the property. Murray subsequently initiated a forcible entry and detainer action against Schlosser. The court initially instructed the jury that personal notice to Schlosser was necessary for rescission to be valid, which led to a misunderstanding of the contract terms.	The main argument of the plaintiff, Bronson Murray, is grounded in his assertion that Schlosser defaulted on the payment terms outlined in their contract. Murray argues that due to Schlosser's failure to make payments, he rightfully rescinded the contract and should be entitled to possession of the property as well as rent payments. Murray believes that the service of notice on Schlosser's wife was sufficient, despite Schlosser's absence due to military service.	The defendant, Samuel Schlosser, contends that the notice of rescission served to his wife while he was away on military duty was inadequate for ending the contract. He argues that personal notice was required for a valid rescission to occur, and since he did not receive such notice, he should not be held liable for rent or eviction. Schlosser's defense hinges on the interpretation of contract terms regarding the requirement for notice.

The case "James W. Burke et al. v. William Weaver et al." took place in 1874 in the Macon County Circuit Court in Illinois. The key individuals involved were the plaintiffs, James W. Burke and others, and the defendants, William Weaver and others. The dispute arose over a sale of real estate that had been ordered by a decree of the court. The plaintiffs challenged the validity of the sale, alleging that a conveyance of the property was fraudulent and that the lands were equitably subject to their judgments. The court's initial ruling directed that a master in chancery was to sell the property unless the defendants satisfied the judgments within 90 days. Following the sale, the master submitted a report, which was met with exceptions filed by the defendants regarding the adequacy of notice given and the execution of the deed. The circuit court upheld the defendants’ exceptions, thus setting aside the sale of the lands.	The plaintiffs asserted that the conveyance of the property was fraudulent and argued that the lands were equitably subject to their judgments. They contended that the sale conducted by the master in chancery was not valid, due to his failure to follow legal procedures regarding notification and the execution of a deed. They requested the court to declare the sale invalid and to protect their judgments through the enforcement of the sale of the property.	The defendants claimed that the master in chancery's report was inadequate because it failed to specify the notice given for the sale and incorrectly stated that a deed was executed rather than a certificate of purchase, as required by law. They requested the court to uphold their exceptions, arguing that the master exceeded his authority and that the report did not comply with statutory requirements, thus leading to an erroneous decree.

In the case of William B. White v. Thomas Mackin, filed in the Illinois Appellate Court on January 6, 1886, the dispute centers around a mechanic's lien related to construction work done on a building. The plaintiff, William B. White, claimed that he was owed $1,166.67 for work performed under a written contract that detailed specific plans and specifications, which had been agreed upon by both parties. The contract stipulated that the completion of the work must meet the satisfaction of an architect, selected as part of the agreement. The contention arose over certain tinning work; the architect asserted that it was included in the specifications, while White contended that it was not and therefore refused to execute this task. Subsequently, Mackin, the defendant, hired another mechanic to perform the tinning, for which he compensated accordingly. The architect adjusted the payment certificate, deducting the cost of the tinning from the total amount due to White. After reviewing the pleadings and evidence, the court found that White was entitled to $672.24, a sum determined by the architect's certification.	The plaintiff, William B. White, argued that he was entitled to $1,166.67 for the work completed on the building as per the contract. He asserted that the refusal to perform the tinning was justified, as he believed it was not part of the original contract specifications. White sought enforcement of the mechanic's lien for the claimed amount.	The defendant, Thomas Mackin, contended that the architect correctly interpreted the contract, including the tinning work as part of the specifications. Mackin argued that he acted reasonably by hiring a different mechanic to complete the tinning after White's refusal. He supported the architect's deduction from the final payment to White, leading to the reduced amount certified as due.

The case "George Baren v. John Cain" took place in 1883 in Adams County, Illinois. The primary individuals involved are George Baren, the plaintiff and horse owner, and John Cain, the defendant and a sewing machine agent. Baren loaned a young horse to Cain for hauling sewing machines, with the understanding that he would not receive compensation for the use of the horse. The agreement stipulated that the horse was to be returned to Baren before plowing season. However, shortly after borrowing the horse, Cain tied it to a gate at his premises, resulting in the horse injuring itself severely and ultimately dying. Baren filed a suit for $150 before a justice of the peace due to the horse's death, alleging negligence on Cain's part. The justice of the peace ruled in favor of Baren, but Cain appealed to the circuit court, which dismissed the case on jurisdictional grounds and ruled against Baren for court costs. Baren then appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court, arguing that the initial court had jurisdiction.	George Baren claimed that John Cain, as the bailee of the horse, was negligent in his care, leading to the horse's injury and death. Baren sought compensation for the damages incurred through the horse's loss, presenting his case based on an implied contract of gratuitous bailment due to the lack of financial compensation for the horse's use.	John Cain contended that the initial court did not have jurisdiction to hear the case. During the appeal, he maintained that the suit should have been dismissed on those grounds. Cain's legal counsel pushed for a dismissal without further proceedings, citing jurisdictional issues as the reason for the circuit court's previous ruling against Baren.

The case "Nat. Bank of Lawrence Co. et al. v. John V. Le Moyne et al." originated in the probate court of Cook County, Illinois, concerning the estate of Charles W. Becketson, who had passed away. The proceedings involved certain creditors asserting their claims against the estate's administrator, H. M. Shepard, seeking to collect debts owed to them. Initially, the probate court ruled in favor of the creditors, which led to further appeals. The case was subsequently heard in the circuit court of Cook County, where the probate court's decision was affirmed. Dissatisfied with the ruling, the appellants (creditors) took their case to the Appellate Court for the First District, which also affirmed the lower court's judgments. The appeals were consolidated and brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, where they presented two main legal questions regarding the entitlement of John V. Le Moyne to a judgment based on the Tiernan contract and the determination for dividends from the proceeds of land sales ordered by the circuit court in June 1870. The proceedings have a long history of legal scrutiny involving issues related to court procedures and the sufficiency of the original record presented in the appellate reviews.	The plaintiffs, comprising various creditors, argue that they were entitled to recover debts owed from the estate of deceased Charles W. Becketson, specifically seeking validation of John V. Le Moyne's claims related to the Tiernan contract. They request the court to affirm their right to collect dividends from the proceeds generated from the sale of the estate's lands.	The defendant, H. M. Shepard as the estate administrator, contends that the appellate court's decisions are sound and that the creditors have failed to adequately present their claims during prior proceedings. The defense emphasizes that substantial procedural objections, including issues with the bill of exceptions not being comprehensive, render the appeals void. They seek to uphold the circuit court's judgment against the creditors' claims.

In the case of O. P. Loomis v. Hannah Downs, which took place in Champaign County, Illinois, the dispute arose from an action of assumpsit concerning a promissory note of $490 that was claimed to be lost. The incident occurred in the late 19th century, specifically leading up to the court's decision on November 18, 1887. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff, O. P. Loomis, and the defendant, Hannah Downs. Loomis alleged that the note was lost, as he could not produce it during the trial. He testified that he had never transferred or endorsed the note to anyone, and the last time he had possession of it was when he received a payment of $100 from Downs at her store. Downs contended that she had paid the entirety of the note to a man named Miller, who claimed to be Loomis's former partner and said he had transferred the note. She asserted that Loomis's name was indorsed on the note under the statement “Received pay in full.” The core issue was whether Downs had indeed paid the note or if it had inadvertently been left in her possession. The jury ultimately sided with Downs, finding sufficient evidence to support her claim of payment.	O. P. Loomis claimed that the promissory note for $490 was lost and argued that he had not sold, transferred, or endorsed the note to anyone else. He further asserted that he maintained possession up until the last payment he made to Downs. Loomis's legal request was for the court to recognize the loss of the note and hold Downs responsible for the full amount due, as he argued that the payment claim made by the defendant was invalid.	Hannah Downs defended herself by stating that she had paid the remaining amount of the note to a third party, identified as Miller, who claimed to be Loomis's partner. Downs asserted that Miller presented the note with Loomis’s endorsement that indicated it was paid in full. Her key argument was that she acted on a valid payment claim presented to her and that her actions were justified, as she believed she was paying a legitimate holder of the note.

H. H. Harris was indicted for forgery by a grand jury during the September term of the Circuit Court of Macon County in 1887. He pleaded not guilty at his arraignment in January 1888. The trial took place over three days in October 1888, where a jury found him guilty and recommended a six-year imprisonment sentence. Harris was present in court during the trial, but when it came time for sentencing on October 25, 1888, the record did not confirm his presence. His defense counsel filed a motion for a new trial shortly after the verdict, but the court overruled it without any evidence that Harris was present during that hearing. The case raised significant legal questions regarding the necessity of the defendant's personal presence during sentencing for felony charges.	Harris contended that the court erred in sentencing him without being personally present at the time the sentence was pronounced. He claimed that this violated established legal principles that require a defendant to be present during any felony sentencing. He sought to reverse the judgment based on this alleged procedural error.	The defense argued that there was no error in the jury's verdict and that Harris had been present during the trial and the verdict. However, they acknowledged the absence of a bill of exceptions showing Harris's presence at the hearing of the new trial motion. The defense's key argument hinged on the interpretation of the law regarding the necessity of the defendant's presence at sentencing, claiming that the record should have clearly demonstrated Harris's attendance.

In June 1874, the case "Wiggins Ferry Company v. Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company" was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in St. Clair County, Illinois, involving two corporate entities: Wiggins Ferry Company and Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company. The dispute revolved around a written contract stipulating the terms of transportation services. The Wiggins Ferry Company claimed that the railway company was obligated to use its ferry services for transporting passengers and freight across the Mississippi River at St. Louis. The railway company allegedly breached the contract by transporting goods via a rival ferry service at Venice without the ferry company's consent. The court was tasked with determining if the railway company violated its contractual obligations based on the language and limitations explicitly stated in the contract.	The Wiggins Ferry Company argued that the Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company breached their contract by employing a rival ferry service instead of their ferry for transporting people and freight. They contended that the contract expressly required the railway company to utilize their services for all transport activities to or from Bloody Island and St. Louis. The plaintiff sought recovery for damages caused by these breaches and urged the court to strictly interpret the contractual agreement in their favor.	The Ohio and Mississippi Railway Company contended that they were not in violation of the contract because the obligation to use the Wiggins Ferry Company was limited to transportation "to or from Bloody Island" and "to or from St. Louis." They argued that since the railway company had the right to extend its track and employ another ferry for transport from other points, the breaches claimed by the plaintiff did not constitute a violation of the agreement. The defendant requested the court to dismiss the case based on the interpretation of the contract's terms.

In the case of John Stenzel v. William Sims decided on March 28, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the events originated when John Stenzel appealed a judgment made against him in a lower court, specifically a Justice of the Peace. The case was moved to the Cook County Circuit Court, where it was placed on the trial calendar. However, when the trial commenced, neither Stenzel nor his counsel was present. Consequently, William Sims, the appellee, requested the dismissal of the appeal, which was granted along with monetary damages against Stenzel. Following this dismissal, Stenzel filed a motion to set aside the judgment, supported by an affidavit suggesting that he had employed a different attorney who failed to manage the appeal adequately. Despite this claim, the court determined that Stenzel's attorney's negligence was imputed to him, and he exhibited a complete lack of diligence regarding the appeal process. The appellate ruling highlighted that the trial court's dismissal was in accordance with established procedures, and because there was no abuse of discretion, the case could not be reversed.	The plaintiff, William Sims, claimed that John Stenzel failed to appear for trial, which justified the dismissal of the appeal he had filed. Sims argued that the dismissal was proper and invoked statutory damages against Stenzel due to his absence and the negligence of his attorney, which detailed an inadequacy in Stenzel's diligence towards the case.	John Stenzel contended that the Circuit Court erred by dismissing his appeal without proceeding with the trial, asserting that the case should have been heard de novo in line with statutory provisions. He argued that the trial court's actions were unauthorized and relied on the court's established authority regarding appeals. Stenzel sought to set aside the dismissal by highlighting procedural mismanagement attributed to his newly retained attorney’s negligence.

The case of Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company v. William L. Eastburn took place in September 1870 in Iroquois County, Illinois. The legal dispute arose when William L. Eastburn filed a lawsuit against the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company for damages related to the injury and death of his horses and cattle, allegedly caused by the railway's trains and engines. Eastburn claimed that part of his livestock was killed by a train traveling east and another part by a train traveling west. The case was brought before the Iroquois Circuit Court, where a jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding him damages totaling $300. The railway company appealed the decision, arguing that the evidence did not adequately connect them to the injuries inflicted on the livestock. The court examined the evidence, which included testimonies indicating that the railway was the only one operating in the relevant area, leading the jury to reasonably infer the railway's responsibility for the deaths of the animals.	The plaintiff, William L. Eastburn, argued that the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company was responsible for the deaths of his horses and cattle due to negligence in the operation of their trains. He sought damages to compensate for the loss of his livestock, claiming that the railway's engines were directly linked to the incidents that caused the deaths of his animals.	The defendant, Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, contended that there was insufficient evidence connecting them to the injuries suffered by the plaintiff's livestock. They argued that, according to previous cases, proof of connection must be established beyond a reasonable doubt. In their appeal, they sought to have the judgment rendered against them overturned, asserting that the evidence presented did not meet the required legal standards for confirming liability.

In January 1875, a legal dispute arose in Cumberland County, Illinois, between the School Directors of District No. 3, T. 9 N. R. 8, and Anderson Fogleman. The case stemmed from an assumpsit action initiated by Fogleman, acting for the use of Reuben Bloomfield. At the heart of the matter were three financial orders drawn by previous school directors, amounting to $75 and two amounts of $50 each, intended as partial payment for constructing a schoolhouse in the district. The directors issued these orders without obtaining the required approval from the voting populace of the district, as mandated by the Illinois school law of 1865. When the circuit court tried the case without a jury, it ruled in favor of Fogleman, awarding him $230.40. The directors appealed the court's decision, questioning both the legality of the orders and the authority of their predecessors in issuing them.	The plaintiff, Anderson Fogleman, claimed that he was owed payment according to the financial orders issued by the school directors for services related to the construction of the schoolhouse. He contended that the orders were valid contractual obligations despite the lack of voter approval for the schoolhouse construction.	The defendants, the current school directors, contended that the financial orders were invalid because they were issued without the necessary voter authorization for constructing the schoolhouse. They argued that under section 48 of the school law of 1865, any contract for a schoolhouse without community consent was null and void. They pleaded general issue, a special plea regarding the lack of voter approval, and cited a failure of consideration as a basis for their defense.

John T. Major and John Collins were involved in a legal dispute that culminated on November 26, 1882, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, where Major, the property owner, had entered into a contract with Collins, a builder, on August 21, 1880. Collins was to construct five houses on five separate lots for a total payment of $2,950. Each lot was valued at approximately $250, and the houses were deemed to be worth around $800 each. Major failed to pay the full amount due after only contributing $100. Collins, asserting his rights under the mechanic's lien law, filed a petition claiming he completed the houses as per the agreement, and he sought a lien on the property to recover the outstanding balance. Major contested the claim, asserting that nothing was owed after reaching a settlement with Collins, a claim that also implicated Hartwell, who Collins had assigned the rights to the contract. The court was tasked with determining the validity of Collins’ claim, the nature of the payments, and the implications of the assignment to Hartwell.	Collins claimed that he had fulfilled the contract to build five houses for Major and sought to enforce a mechanic’s lien against Major’s properties to recover the $3,085 still owed to him. He also asserted that he assigned the contract rights to Hartwell, who was entitled to the proceeds of the contract. Collins argued that the court should grant a lien against the properties to secure payment, as the work and materials provided warranted such security.	Major maintained that he did not owe any further money to Collins, claiming that they had reached a mutual settlement regarding the work done. He further argued that the assignment of rights to Hartwell was not valid as he contended that he was unaware of such an assignment at the time. Additionally, Major brought forward evidence of existing incumbrances on the property that should be considered in the court's decision.

The case "The Illinois Educational Association v. Peter Strauder" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1875. The dispute arose over a contractual agreement dated October 9, 1873, where Peter Strauder was hired by the Illinois Educational Association to lay bricks and set stones in a building called the "Howe Literary Institute." The terms stipulated that Strauder would be compensated at a rate of $3.75 per thousand bricks laid, with the materials provided by the Association. However, due to economic difficulties, the Association halted the work, prompting Strauder to seek damages and enforce a mechanic's lien for unpaid work. Subsequently, an agreement was reached where the Association would pay Strauder $500 and he would continue his work for a reasonable compensation, disregarding the original contract rate. Upon completion, a disagreement arose regarding the measurement of the work performed, specifically how openings in the walls should be accounted for during the measurement of the brickwork. The case was escalated to court to determine a fair resolution.	The plaintiff, Peter Strauder, claims that he is entitled to reasonable compensation for the work he performed under the modified agreement, asserting that the total compensation should reflect the complexities involved in laying brickwork for the third story of the building. He argues that the jury's decision on the compensation was justified based on the evidence presented, which indicated a higher value of labor for the more intricate work on the third story compared to the previous work.	The defendant, Illinois Educational Association, contends that the measurement of the brickwork should exclude the openings, thereby reducing the amount payable to Strauder. They argue that the arrangement made after the work stoppage did not guarantee any specific price for the completed work and that the jury's assessment of reasonable compensation was excessive and unsupported by evidence.

In 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal conflict arose involving William G. Hibbard and others (appellants) and William J. Holloway (appellee). The dispute began with a suit filed by Holloway to recover amounts owed on cartage tickets that had been issued to Fitzgerald, a teaming service provider, by Hibbard and his partners. The tickets, which indicated a debt of 50 cents, were bought by Holloway from Fitzgerald. Initially, the justice of the peace rendered a judgment against Bartlett (who was served) for the amount owed, which he subsequently appealed. However, the judgment extended beyond Bartlett to include Hibbard and Spencer, who had neither been served nor had made an appearance in court. They argued that they were not properly brought into the case, asserting a lack of jurisdiction. The case escalated to the Illinois Appellate Court, which examined the validity of the debt represented by the tickets, questioning their function as negotiable instruments or mere acknowledgments of service.	Holloway's primary argument was to assert that he was entitled to recover on the cartage tickets as if they were promissory notes, affirming a debt owed to him. He contended that the tickets represented a legitimate claim against Hibbard, Spencer, and Bartlett, asserting that the nature of the tickets justified his legal claim.	Hibbard and Spencer countered that they were unjustly subjected to the judgment as they had never been served, nor did they appear in the superior court proceedings. They claimed that being copartners with Bartlett did not equate to jurisdiction over them. Furthermore, they argued that the tickets in question did not constitute a negotiable promissory note, lacking necessary language to imply a promise to pay.

In 1877, in La Salle County, Illinois, Cassius M. Clay faced charges of libel for publishing defamatory statements about Amanda Masters and Etta Masters in the Streator Pioneer newspaper. The indictment claimed that Clay intended to vilify the two women through false and scandalous allegations, including an account of their alleged maltreatment of their mother, which misrepresented their actions and led to public disgrace. Upon his conviction in the La Salle Circuit Court, Clay was fined $300 and committed until paid. He appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking reversal of the conviction on several grounds, including the sufficiency and certainty of the libel described in the indictment and assertions that he did not author or publish the contested article.	The plaintiff's main arguments revolved around the assertion that the indictment did not accurately detail the libel intended to justify the charges against Clay. They contended that the language used in the indictment was sufficiently clear to convey the nature of the libel and that the information presented correctly identified the individual responsible for the defamatory statements made about the Masters sisters.	Clay's defense emphasized several key points: firstly, that the libelous content was not set forth with adequate precision in the indictment. He argued that the published article varied from the indictment, which he claimed should have warranted quashing the indictment. Furthermore, he insisted that he did not write or consent to the publication of the article. Clay sought to establish that the evidence against him was too weak to justify the verdict and maintained that he should not be held solely accountable for the article's publication.

The case "City of Mason City v. Morgan Barngrover" originated on November 15, 1886, when the city of Mason City, located in Illinois, initiated legal proceedings against Morgan Barngrover for allegedly violating a city ordinance. The ordinance, enacted on November 23, 1885, declared that any fence constructed of barbed wire within the city limits was considered a nuisance, permitting fines between $5 and $25 for violations. Mason City, a small city with a population nearing 2,000, allows cattle to roam freely within city limits. Barngrover owned several lots in the city that were enclosed by a barbed wire fence, which had been erected a year or two prior to the ordinance's passage. The dispute focused solely on the validity of the ordinance itself. The case affirmed that the ordinance was unreasonable in its application to Barngrover and his property, leading to the court ruling in favor of the defendant, thereby upholding Barngrover's right to maintain the barbed wire fence in its existing condition.	The City of Mason City contended that Morgan Barngrover had violated a city ordinance that prohibited the maintenance of barbed wire fences within municipal limits. The plaintiff sought to impose a fine on Barngrover for failing to remove the barbed wire fence, arguing that it constituted a public nuisance according to the city's governance and police powers.	Morgan Barngrover argued against the validity of the city's ordinance, asserting that it was unreasonable and exceeded the municipal authority. He maintained that the ordinance wrongly declared his barbed wire fence a nuisance without sufficient justification or evidence of any actual obstruction or threat posed by the fence. Ultimately, Barngrover sought to have the charges dismissed and to affirm his right to retain the fence.

In 1875, in Stephenson County, Illinois, Joseph Kroer was indicted for keeping a tippling house open on the Sabbath, specifically on March 10, 1874. This case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following Kroer's conviction on two counts of the indictment: one for keeping the saloon open during the day and another for keeping it open at night on the Sabbath. Kroer's defense raised several issues, including objections to the legality of the indictment, the qualifications of a juror who displayed bias against saloon keepers, and the alleged errors in jury instructions given by the trial court. The court addressed concerns regarding the interpretation of “Sabbath night” and concluded that the offense could occur between the preceding midnight and the dawn of the Sabbath morning. The court also upheld the juror's competence despite their expressed bias against the business of saloon keeping. Ultimately, the court affirmed the trial court's decisions and highlighted the distinction between keeping a saloon open for tippling purposes versus simply opening the door.	The plaintiff (the State of Illinois) claimed that Kroer was guilty of violating section 127 of the Criminal Code by keeping his tippling house open on the Sabbath. The prosecution contended that evidence showed multiple patrons accessed the saloon during the Sabbath, engaging in the consumption of intoxicating liquor. The plaintiff argued that the counts of the indictment were valid, and the court's jury instructions accurately reflected the conditions under which the offense could be established.	Kroer defended himself by challenging the counts of the indictment on the basis that the language concerning “Sabbath night” was ambiguous and did not constitute a violation. Additionally, he raised concerns about jury bias, arguing that the juror's admitted prejudice against saloon keeping should disqualify him. Kroer also contested the court’s instructions that allowed for the conviction based on the house being "kept open" under conditions he claimed were overly broad and misapplied the statutory definition of the offense.

In the case of "The People ex rel. Fuller v. The Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railroad Company," the proceedings took place in Coles County, Illinois, with the appeal being decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 27, 1886. The case originated from a tax judgment application made during the May term of the county court in 1885 by the county collector for the collection of delinquent taxes on lands and properties for the year 1884. The defendant, the Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railroad Company, contested the judgment regarding corporate taxes levied by the City of Mattoon. The county court initially ruled in favor of the Railroad Company by rejecting the tax assessment submitted against its property. The appeal arose as the People (representing the state) argued that proper procedures for tax levies were not adhered to in the ordinance process, raising questions about the legality of the tax levy made by the City of Mattoon.	The plaintiff, represented by the county collector, claimed the Railroad Company owed taxes assessed by the City of Mattoon as stipulated in the relevant ordinances. They argued that the ordinance for assessing the tax was valid and legally compliant, seeking to overturn the county court's ruling that denied the tax judgment. They contended that the necessary legal formalities for passing the tax levy ordinance had been adhered to and that the Railroad Company was liable for the delinquent taxes.	The defendant countered by asserting that the city council failed to follow proper legislative procedures in imposing the tax. Specifically, they argued that no separate appropriation ordinance was passed before the tax levy ordinance, and that the ordinance enacted included discrepancies in the amounts. They maintained that the tax assessment against their property was invalid and thus sought to uphold the county court's dismissal of the tax judgment against them.

Henry Curtis initiated a legal action for ejectment in Washington County, Illinois, in December 1825, seeking to recover an undivided interest in a tract of land. The crux of the case centered on the legitimacy of a sheriff’s deed that purportedly transferred ownership of the property to Curtis. The concerns revolved around whether the deed adequately demonstrated compliance with relevant statutory procedures, particularly whether the land had been appraised and sold for at least two-thirds of its valuation as prescribed by Illinois law. The statutes mandated that real estate must be valued by three disinterested freeholders before a sale under execution. Curtis argued that the deed failed to show such appraisal was conducted, a point crucial for establishing the legality of his claim to the property.	The plaintiff, Henry Curtis, maintained that the sheriff’s deed presented as evidence to support his claim of ownership was insufficient. His principal argument revolved around the assertion that the deed did not prove that the land was appraised as required by the applicable statutes, which would render the deed invalid and inadequate for recovering the property in question.	The defendant, John Doe, represented by Daniel Swearingen, contended that the sheriff acted within the bounds of his authority and that the sale was valid under applicable law. The defense argued against the necessity of demonstrating that the appraisal occurred, asserting that proper procedure was followed and the sale should be recognized despite the lack of a verifiable appraisal indicated in the deed.

The case "James E. Tyler et al. v. Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 20, 1883. The dispute arose from a series of transactions involving deeds of trust executed by B. E. Guyton and his wife. Initially, they executed three deeds of trust on different tracts of land to secure notes totaling $27,500, which were due on July 1, 1880, to the Massachusetts Life Insurance Company. After failing to make timely interest payments, the trustee Bappleye conducted a sale of the property under the power granted by the deeds of trust, selling it to A. J. Smith for the insurance company on January 30, 1878. Tyler, as the holder of a subsequent set of promissory notes, along with Warren, sought to challenge the validity of the sale, alleging irregularities and requesting the court to permit redemption from the initial trust deeds. The Cook circuit court dismissed their complaint, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiffs, Tyler and Warren, claimed that the sale conducted by the trustee was irregular and, therefore, void. Their primary arguments included that the trustee improperly consolidated notice for the sale instead of providing separate notices for each deed of trust and that the trustee’s deed was defective for failing to explicitly convey the interest of the assignors. They sought to have the sale set aside, claiming it barred their right to redeem the land.	The defendants, the Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company, argued against the plaintiffs' claims by stating that the single notice provided for the sale was adequate and legally sufficient. They contended that the notice recounted the information necessary for stakeholders and that the sale was executed following proper procedures. Furthermore, they asserted that any alleged usury did not invalidate the sale because the plaintiffs acquiesced to the sale by not contesting it in a timely manner, thus precluding them from later raising usury as a defense.

The case of Miller C. Baldwin et al. v. Timothy M. Bradley took place in 1873 in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Miller C. Baldwin, H. Pomeroy Baldwin, and Albert A. Alexander, were partners who had lent money to a firm called Kiernan & Son. They made two loans of $900 each, one on March 29, 1872, and another on April 18, 1872, secured by two separate pledges of whisky—22 barrels for the first loan and 20 barrels for the second. When Timothy M. Bradley, the Cook County sheriff, seized the whisky under legal writs of attachment directed against Kiernan & Son, Baldwin and his partners sought recovery through an action of replevin for the whisky. While 20 barrels were returned, 22 barrels remained unaccounted for, prompting the plaintiffs to also file a count in trover for those barrels. A trial yielded a verdict favoring the plaintiffs for $308, but they sought a new trial to claim the full amount due on their pledges, which led to this appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that they had a legitimate claim over the 22 barrels of whisky, which were pledged as security for a loan. They contended that they were entitled to recover the full value of the barrels that had been converted, amounting to $962.85, as the pledges were independent and each secured its respective loan. They requested a new trial to achieve this recovery after receiving only a partial judgment in their favor.	The defendant, Timothy M. Bradley, contended that he acted lawfully as sheriff, having seized the whisky under legal attachment writs against Kiernan & Son, asserting that the whisky was their property. Bradley argued that the plaintiffs' recovery should be limited to the amount still due from Kiernan for the total pledges and proposed that the seized 20 barrels should be considered as a payment towards the debt, thus affecting the overall claim of the plaintiffs.
