The church maintained that any income generated from renting parts of their building was strictly applied to cover a mortgage and support their religious activities, rather than being used for personal or profit-driven purposes.	The City of Chicago defended the tax assessment by arguing that any property rented out for non-religious purposes should be subject to taxation, regardless of the church's claim that the generated income was utilized for religious purposes. They pointed out that the law mandated that buildings erected for religious worship must be used directly for sacred purposes rather than for commercial profit, thus establishing that the portions of the property used for retail and office spaces were liable for taxation.

The case "Jacob A. Dickason v. J. P. Dawson" took place in Quincy, Illinois, with the judgment delivered by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1877. Jacob A. Dickason (the appellant) sought to reclaim a tract of land previously owned by Geo. W. Foss, who had defaulted on a mortgage to Mary Grey. After Foss gave a second mortgage to the National Insurance Company, they obtained a judgment for unpaid debts, resulting in the sheriff's sale of the property. Dickason purchased the property at this sale and received a sheriff's deed. However, prior to this, Foss had leased the property to Mary Grey, allowing her to take possession. At the time of the suit, Grey had sublet the property to J. P. Dawson (the appellee), who was living there. The court considered various legal aspects surrounding possession and mortgage rights related to the transactions involving Foss, Grey, and the sheriff's sale.	Dickason’s main argument was based on his right to recover possession of the land as a purchaser under the sheriff’s sale following a judgment against Foss. He contended that he should be granted immediate possession since he held a legal title to the property after the sheriff's deed.	Dawson's defense rested on the fact that he was a tenant under Mary Grey, the prior mortgagee. The defense argued that Dickason's failure to make a written demand for possession before filing the suit was grounds for dismissal. Furthermore, they claimed that Grey's priority as a mortgagee provided her the right to  retain possession against any subsequent purchasers until her mortgage debt was satisfied.

Henry Bernhard filed a case against James W. Brown in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the decision date being June 15, 1889. The case originated in Effingham County, Illinois, presided over by Judge William C. Jones. The dispute arose over a due bill regarding the sale of flour, but the court noted that the record presented was not properly certified by the circuit clerk, lacking necessary documentation to substantiate the claims made in the appeal. This included the absence of due bills and receipts that were pivotal for the judgment claim. The court, consequently, indicated that they must affirm the initial judgment made by the trial court without evaluating the merits of the case, due to these record deficiencies.	The plaintiff, Henry Bernhard, claimed that James W. Brown owed him a certain quantity of flour as per a due bill. The plaintiff requested that the court uphold the judgment from the trial court, despite not providing the proper record and exceptions that would typically support such an appeal.	The defendant, James W. Brown, argued that the appeal should not proceed due to the inadequacies in the case record, which included a lack of exceptions to the circuit court's judgment and failure to file a motion for a new trial. Brown's legal team sought to dismiss the appeal based on these procedural issues, asserting that the court could not consider the merits of the case.

On February 18, 1857, the State of Illinois established a normal university, forming the Board of Education of the State of Illinois as a corporate body. Edwin W. Bakewell and Julia A. Bakewell conveyed 40 acres of land to this Board on February 25, 1858, with a condition that the university remains in its original location. A subsequent deed on February 9, 1860, aimed to annul this condition, granting an absolute title to the Board. The university continues to operate in its initial location. In 1883, the General Assembly passed a joint resolution directing the Board to convey this land back to Julia A. Bakewell, claiming the original deed's conditions had not been fulfilled. The Board refused this directive. Following further legislative action in 1885 declaring the land title vested in Julia A. Bakewell, she filed for a writ of mandamus in McLean County Circuit Court to compel the Board to execute the conveyance. The court issued the writ, leading the Board to appeal the decision.	Julia A. Bakewell argued that the original deed contained a conditional conveyance, which was not honored as the university remained in its initial location. She asserted her rights to the land based on legislative declarations made by the General Assembly, which stated that the Board had not fulfilled the conditions tied to the property. Therefore, she requested that the court compel the Board to convey the land title to her through a writ of mandamus.	The Board of Education contended that it was a private eleemosynary corporation, whose property could not be transferred without due process of law. It argued that the legislative acts attempting to transfer property to Julia A. Bakewell lacked constitutional grounds and amounted to an arbitrary seizure. Furthermore, the Board maintained that accepting state appropriations did not change its status to a public institution and did not constitute a relinquishment of its private rights over the property.

The case "Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company v. Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company" was decided on January 16, 1889, in Cook County, Illinois. It involved a dispute between two railroad companies regarding the right to construct a new track. The Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company (plaintiff) sought an injunction to prevent the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company (defendant) from interfering with the construction of a railway track across the defendant's existing tracks. The legal background stemmed from a contract established on November 2, 1882, which conveyed a right of way to the appellant for laying tracks across a designated area. This contract included specific reservations, allowing the appellees to maintain and operate their railroad tracks without hindrance from the appellants. However, the appellants had fears that the proposed construction by the appellees would obstruct their ability to operate their existing tracks. The situation became critical as the appellees aimed to establish a freight yard and connect it with tracks that would potentially cross the appellants' tracks. The court had to address whether the appellees had the legal right to construct the new track based on the contract.	The plaintiff, Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company, argued that they had the right to construct a new railway track based on their ownership of the property and the reservations in the 1882 contract. They claimed that any interference from the defendant would result in uncertain damages that were unjustifiable. The plaintiff requested an injunction to restrain the defendant from preventing the construction of their track across the defendant’s tracks.	The defendant, Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company, countered that the proposed construction would hinder their current operations and violate previously established rights. They contended that the plaintiff was attempting to enforce their claims through an injunction that would disrupt the existing status quo of the tracks. The defendant argued that they had been in exclusive possession of their tracks and that any interference was necessary for their business operations.

On October 14, 1881, Clark Hollenback filed a lawsuit in attachment against Davidson Todd and Thomas J. Terrell in Kendall County, Illinois. The suit originated due to the attachment of 8,000 to 9,000 bushels of corn stored in a warehouse owned by Jacob S. Budd. This corn was claimed to belong to Todd and Terrell, who had been conducting business by buying and storing grain. After Todd and Terrell’s failure to settle debts by September 1, 1881, Jacob Budd took possession of the warehouse and acquired contracts for grain previously assigned to Todd & Terrell. Following the attachment of the corn, Jacob S. Budd filed a plea of interpleader asserting ownership. A jury trial ruled in favor of Budd, which was later affirmed by the Appellate Court. Hollenback appealed the decision, challenging various evidentiary rulings of the trial court regarding the ownership and the alleged fraudulent transfer of property.	Hollenback, the plaintiff, argued that the transaction involving the transfer of ownership of the corn was fraudulent and aimed to defraud creditors. He claimed that the corn was still the property of Todd and Terrell and sought to establish that the attachment should be valid as the property was not legitimately transferred to Budd.	The defendants, represented by Jacob S. Budd, contended that he legitimately purchased the corn and possessed it within the warehouse. They cited possession as prima facie evidence of ownership and argued that the plaintiff failed to prove any fraudulent intent in the transfer of contracts and property. Thus, they requested that the attachment be lifted, affirming Budd's ownership of the corn.

The case of Caroline W. Benneson et al. v. William T. Savage et al. took place in Illinois, culminating in a decision by the Illinois Supreme Court on October 31, 1889. The dispute revolved around a mortgage agreement executed on March 29, 1873, by Charles A. Savage to secure a debt of $6,000 owed to the banking firm of L. & C. H. Bull. This mortgage was in the form of a trust deed, executed by Charles and co-defendants Elvey W. Savage and Anna Wells. As the principal debtor, Charles later extended credit agreement deadlines and attached additional interest coupons to the original promissory note. After several delays and a judgment by the circuit court for $8,652.78 against Charles, the plaintiffs, claiming rights to foreclose on the mortgage, argued that the property was tied to their interests as sureties. The case highlighted multiple parties and issues surrounding the extension of the mortgage and validity of claims on the mortgaged property.	The plaintiffs contended that the trust deed secured a debt owed to them, and that the transactions regarding the extension of payment and additional interest coupons were consistent with the original agreement. They requested foreclosure on the mortgage based on the unpaid debts, taxes, and insurance expenses incurred while holding the mortgage. They maintained that the due processes of foreclosure should proceed despite the defendants’ objections surrounding the legitimacy and current standing of the trust deed.	The defendants argued primarily that the original debt contract differed significantly from the one secured by the trust deed, claiming it invalidated their responsibilities under the trust deed. They contended that extensions of payment were made without their consent, effectively releasing the property from the mortgage lien. Furthermore, they asserted that the plaintiffs had neglected to apply assets from Charles A. Savage towards the debt, thus failing to uphold their obligations as creditors. The overarching claim involved accusations of bad faith and fraudulent transfer of assets to remove defenses against the debt.

The case of Phœnix Insurance Company of Brooklyn v. A. H. Carlock took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered on November 23, 1889. A. H. Carlock had obtained an insurance policy from the Phœnix Insurance Company on September 16, 1884, covering his dwelling with a value of $2,000. The policy contained a clause stating that if the premium note was not paid on time, the policy would become null and void until the payment was received. Carlock issued a premium note for $62.50, payable on October 1, 1885. When the note was not paid, Carlock requested an extension, which was granted. Carlock further communicated with the insurance company regarding payments but failed to settle the outstanding balance. After a fire on June 13, 1888, that resulted in damages estimated at $1,600 to the house and $175 in personal property, Carlock sought to recover the loss from the insurance company. The circuit court proceedings involved various communications and extensions relating to the premium payment, culminating in a jury verdict favoring Carlock.	A. H. Carlock, the plaintiff, claimed that the extensions provided by the defendant regarding the payment of the premium effectively waived the requirement for prompt payment as stipulated in the insurance policy. Carlock sought recovery for the losses incurred in the fire based on the insurance policy, arguing that the company's actions indicated an intention to continue coverage despite the late premium payment.	The Phœnix Insurance Company defended against Carlock's claims by contending that the extensions granted for payment did not legally constitute a waiver of the policy's conditions regarding prompt payment. The insurance company argued that it had not relinquished its right to enforce the contract terms, and they sought to uphold the policy's validity based on its initial conditions.

The case of Henry J. East v. Oliver W. Crow was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1873, following a trial in the Grundy County Circuit Court. The dispute originated from a verbal lease agreement where Henry J. East rented a farm to Oliver W. Crow from March 1, 1870, to March 1, 1871. Issues arose regarding the terms of this lease and subsequent financial accounts between the landlord and tenant, culminating in East suing Crow for $175 in December 1870. Crow responded with a plea of general issue and set-off. During the November 1872 trial, the jury found in favor of Crow, awarding him $86.73 instead. East appealed the verdict contesting the jury instructions and the overall verdict, claiming it was not supported by the evidence.	Henry J. East argued that the trial court made errors by giving incorrect jury instructions favoring the defendant and by refusing to provide crucial instructions that would have clarified the standards for evaluating Crow's counterclaims. East contended that the jury returned a verdict that was against the weight of the evidence presented during the trial.	Oliver W. Crow contended that the instructions properly clarified the burden of proof and that he had sufficiently demonstrated valid claims for set-off against East. Crow argued that East failed to prove his account and that the evidence presented justified the jury's verdict in favor of Crow. He maintained that the elements of set-off he provided were valid and applicable to the claims at issue.

In the case of The East St. Louis Connecting Railway Company v. The People ex rel. M. T. Stookey, Collector, the events unfolded in St. Clair County, Illinois, culminating in a court decision issued on January 25, 1887. The case began when the treasurer of St. Clair County sought judgment for delinquent taxes owed by the East St. Louis Connecting Railway Company. The railway company contested the application on the grounds that the assessed property values used for taxation were excessively inflated—specifically, they claimed the valuation was fraudulently excessive by six-tenths on its main track and five-tenths on its side-track. The railway provided evidence of partial tax payments but sought to prove that the assessments were grossly excessive and oppressive, a claim that was ultimately dismissed by the court. The county court maintained it lacked jurisdiction to review the property assessments made by the State Board of Equalization, which is responsible for setting valuations for taxation. The court’s refusal to allow evidence of fraudulent assessment led to the rejection of the railway company's objections and the affirmation of the tax judgment.	The plaintiff, represented by Collector M. T. Stookey, argued for the enforcement of tax payments against the East St. Louis Connecting Railway Company, seeking judgment for the delinquent taxes owed. The focus of their claims emphasized that the assessments made by the State Board of Equalization were valid and that the county court had the authority to collect the unpaid taxes without reviewing the assessment values.	The East St. Louis Connecting Railway Company contended that the assessments imposed on their properties were fraudulently high and should not be enforced. They argued that the county court should have the jurisdiction to review and potentially reduce these excessive valuations. Their defense was centered on showing that the assessment figures did not reflect the true value of the property and were unfairly inflated, infringing on their rights as taxpayers.

In 1853, in Fulton County, Illinois, Matthew H. Mitchell, as the administrator of a deceased estate, contested a claim presented by Reuben Jacobs and others against the estate. The County Court ruled against Jacobs' claim, leading him to appeal to the Circuit Court. Jacobs' appeal bond was only signed by Henry Emery and a security, which raised questions about its legitimacy. The appeal process faced various procedural issues, including summons not being issued against all parties. Ultimately, the Circuit Court continued the case, and objections concerning the appeal bond’s validity were raised. The case hinged on the interpretation of legal procedures regarding the appeal and whether the defendants waived their objections by participating in the proceedings. The court examined related rulings from previous cases to determine the implications of procedural irregularities. A key issue also revolved around the admissibility of secondary evidence due to the absence of an important lease document, which had been removed from the court by the opposing party’s counsel.	The plaintiff, Matthew H. Mitchell, argued that the appeal to the Circuit Court was invalid due to procedural errors—including the appeal bond not being properly executed or approved. He contended that there was no legitimate appeal pending because of these failures and requested that the court dismiss the appeal based on these claims.	The defendants, represented by Reuben Jacobs and representing their own interests, countered that the appeal bond issue had been addressed improperly. They contended that the irregularities should be waived because they had already appeared in court and consented to continuances. Furthermore, they posited that the secondary evidence regarding the absent lease should be admissible given the circumstances of its removal, which was beyond their control.

Martin Clayburgh, the appellant, brought a case against the City of Chicago, the appellee, in April 1861. The action arose in Chicago, Illinois, where the city council failed to collect an assessment levied to compensate Clayburgh for damages incurred due to the city opening a street over his property. The situation unfolded from a scenario where the city had appropriated private property for municipal use, specifically for street widening or extension. Clayburgh claimed that while the assessments for benefits resulting from the improvement had been conducted, the city neglected its duty to collect these assessments and compensate him for the damages sustained. The city responded to the plaintiff's declaration with a demurrer, which the lower court sustained, leading to a judgment against Clayburgh. This prompted him to file a writ of error, seeking to reverse the court's decision.	The plaintiff, Martin Clayburgh, argued that the City of Chicago had a legal obligation to assess and collect compensation for damages when appropriating private property for public use. He claimed that although the city had assessed the benefits resulting from the street improvement, it failed to collect the owed assessments, effectively neglecting its legal duty. Clayburgh contended that he was entitled to damages due to this willful refusal and sought to recover them through an action on the case for negligence, asserting that the city’s actions directly resulted in his financial loss.	The City of Chicago, as the defendant, maintained that the proper remedy for the plaintiff's grievances was through a mandamus to compel city authorities to fulfill their duties, rather than through a direct action for damages. The city argued that the law permitted individuals to sue corporations for breaches of duty, but in this scenario, they contended that the appropriate legal recourse should involve mandamus actions. The city also referenced precedent cases to support its position that an action on the case would not be appropriate given the circumstances.

Paul Stephens et al. v. Samuel Sweeney is a legal case that took place in December 1845 in Illinois, specifically in Jo Daviess County. The case originated from a debt claim on an appeal bond for $200 filed by Samuel Sweeney against defendants Paul Stephens and William C. E. Thomas. The appeal was addressed in the Jo Daviess Circuit Court during the March term of 1845, overseen by Judge Thomas C. Browne. Sweeney's claim was based on a prior judgment in his favor during a trial concerning the same bond, amounting to $96.72 plus costs, which he alleged had not been paid. The breach cited by Sweeney was the non-payment of this judgment and he sought damages of $50. It is noted that only Thomas entered an appearance in court and responded to the declaration, while Stephens had not been served with process. Despite this, a jury ruled in favor of Sweeney, leading to a jury verdict of $116.03 against the defendants. The legal principles regarding the limits of damages linked to the declared ad damnum (amount claimed) were questioned in subsequent appeals, as well as the legitimacy of the judgment rendered against Stephens.	The plaintiff, Samuel Sweeney, argued that he was owed payment as stipulated in the appeal bond, following a prior ruling that had favored him. He sought recovery not only of the initial judgment amount of $96.72 but also damages amounting to $50, leading to a total claim of $200 against the defendants. The suit contended that the bond condition required payment of whatever judgment might arise from the appeal or dismissal thereof, which had not been fulfilled by the defendants.	The defendants, represented mainly by William C. E. Thomas, contended that Paul Stephens had not been served with the legal process and therefore could not be included in the judgment. Thomas himself attempted to argue against the claimed damages, emphasizing procedural inaccuracies. He maintained that the assessed damages exceeded what was established in the initial declaration, questioning the validity of the verdict that favored Sweeney based on the improperly defined limits of recovery.

In September 1873, the case "Leonard J. Nichols v. Charles Mitchell" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Whiteside County, Illinois, concerning the title to a piece of real estate claimed by both parties. Leonard J. Nichols, representing his minor brother Charles C. Nichols, argued that both he and Charles were heirs to their deceased father, Norton J. Nichols, who had left behind three children—Leonard, Charles, and their deceased sister, Ameret. Leonard claimed to have quitclaim deeds from the other heirs, establishing his title, which could only be challenged if prior court proceedings regarding the estate were invalid. The main contention was whether the court that handled the partition proceedings had acquired proper jurisdiction over Leonard and Charles’ interests. Leonard argued that the service of process was irregular since it was directed to their guardians rather than to them directly, and therefore, the partition was invalid. The defense, however, was that the service to the guardians and the proceedings conducted were valid under Illinois law, even if minor irregularities occurred.	Leonard J. Nichols claimed that the partitions made during the prior proceedings were invalid due to improper service. He argued that the court lacked jurisdiction over him and his brother since they were not directly served with process, and that the property in question should rightfully belong to him as an heir of their father. Leonard sought a judgment for the recovery of the real estate held by Charles Mitchell, asserting that the previous partition and sale of the property were null and void.	Charles Mitchell, as the appellee, contended that he held a valid title to the property through a purchase made under court-sanctioned sale as part of the partition proceedings. He argued that even if there were irregularities, the service performed upon the guardians met the statutory requirements, thereby giving the court jurisdiction. Mitchell maintained that all interests were justly represented in the partition, and as such, he sought to uphold the court's previous decisions affirming his ownership of the property.

On November 29, 1879, Seth T. Sawyer and Robinson S. Sawyer acquired a lot in Alton, Illinois, at a sheriff's sale, following a judgment against George T. Brown for $160. The lot had previously been encumbered by a deed of trust executed by Brown to Metcalfe & Bradshaw to secure a note for $3,000, which was purportedly larger than Brown's actual debt of around $1,500-$1,600. Metcalfe & Bradshaw later sold the lot at a trustee's sale for one dollar, after having paid $381 to redeem it from a prior execution sale. In 1885, the Sawyers filed a chancery bill in the Madison County Circuit Court seeking to annul the deed of trust and subsequent transactions, claiming they were fraudulent against creditors. The circuit court ruled that the deed of trust was fraudulent and that Bradshaw should compensate the Sawyers for the lot's value. However, the Appellate Court later reversed this decision, leading to a writ of error by the Sawyers for review.	The plaintiffs, the Sawyers, argued that the deed of trust and subsequent sales involving the lot were fraudulent and void against creditors, seeking to have these transactions set aside. They contended that the deed's purpose was to mislead and hinder creditors by misrepresenting the amount owed on the underlying note, demanding either the annulment of the transactions or compensation for the value of the lot, which they claimed was approximately $800.	The defendant, Bradshaw, contended that the transaction was not fraudulent, asserting that the deed of trust was valid as it was intended to secure a legitimate portion of the debt for future advances. Bradshaw claimed that the apparent discrepancy in the debt amount did not constitute fraud and that there was no evidence of intent to mislead creditors. He requested the court to affirm the Appellate Court's decision, which had overturned the ruling of the lower court.

Joseph Kelly was tried for burglary during the January term of 1884 in the Criminal Court of Cook County, Illinois. The prosecution included a count for a former conviction of robbery from July 1882. Kelly was found guilty and sentenced to fourteen years of imprisonment. The legal issues arose from an act approved on June 23, 1883, allowing increased punishment for repeat offenses. Kelly's defense raised several constitutional objections, asserting that the act violated the proportionality of penalties and put him in jeopardy multiple times for the same offense. Furthermore, he claimed that his previous conviction for robbery was not valid due to procedural irregularities, questioning the legitimacy of using this conviction as a basis for enhanced punishment during his current trial.	Joseph Kelly, the plaintiff, argued that the increased punishment statute was unconstitutional since it imposed penalties disproportionate to the offenses committed. He claimed it violated his rights by putting him in jeopardy for the same crime twice. Additionally, he contended that his prior conviction for robbery was invalid because he had waived his right to a jury trial, which he believed rendered the conviction null and void.	The defendant, represented by the State of Illinois, contended that the statute was constitutional, allowing for stiffer penalties for repeat offenders. They argued that the previous conviction served as a legal basis for the enhanced punishment as it was within the jurisdiction of the court, despite any irregularities in the process. They asserted that the nature of the offenses justified the increased sentences stipulated by the act.

In the case of James Cochran v. John R. Fogler, Admr., which took place during the September term of 1882 in the Circuit Court of Fayette County, the situation arises from a foreclosure of a mortgage. Samuel Fogler, the deceased, provided a mortgage on property owned by James Cochran and his wife. Upon Fogler's death, John R. Fogler, acting as the administrator of the estate, initiated foreclosure proceedings. The court decreed that Cochran owed $2567.55, and it directed the sale of the property if payment was not made. The property was sold to Fogler for $2786.42, and a deed was issued on February 21, 1884. Cochran and his wife, who had continued to reside on the property, later refused to vacate when Fogler demanded possession. Fogler’s initial attempt to evict Cochran via a forcible detainer suit resulted in a judgment where Cochran was found not guilty of wrongful possession. Despite this ruling, Fogler sought a writ of assistance to obtain possession based on the foreclosure decree. Cochran resisted, citing the earlier judgment against Fogler. The Circuit Judge ruled in favor of Fogler, which led to an appeal to the Appellate Court, which affirmed the lower court's order.	John R. Fogler, as the plaintiff, asserted that he had legal rights to the property following the foreclosure decree and sought a writ of assistance to take possession. He contended that the prior judgment from the forcible detainer suit did not bar his claim since he had not yet presented the master’s deed and court order required by the decree, and thus his right to possession had not been fully realized.	James Cochran, the defendant, argued that the judgment in the forcible detainer suit served as a bar to Fogler's application for a writ of assistance. Cochran maintained that since the court had ruled in his favor regarding the possession, he should not be compelled to surrender the property without Fogler meeting the foreclosure decree's requirements.

The case of The City of Rockford v. Tompkins Tripp took place in Illinois, with the events leading to the lawsuit occurring in the fall of 1872, and the final decision rendered in September 1876. The incident involved a personal injury to the plaintiff, Tompkins Tripp, caused by a runaway team of horses. Tripp was standing or moving slowly in the street when he was run over by the team. The horses had been tied to a hitching post that had been erected by the City of Rockford. On February 1, 1873, a single horse tied to a cutter bolted after becoming frightened, which caused the team tied to the hitching post to react and run away, ultimately leading to Tripp’s injury. The city was accused of negligence regarding the hitching post, which was claimed to be defective. Witnesses testified that the hitching post was cross-grained and brash, suggesting it was not adequately constructed. However, the evidence regarding the post's construction and the absence of any apparent defects at the time it was set were brought into question.	Tompkins Tripp claimed that the injuries he sustained were due to the negligence of the City of Rockford in providing a defective hitching post. He argued that the city failed to ensure that the hitching post was safe and adequately maintained, which directly led to the incident. Tripp sought monetary compensation for his injuries, ultimately recovering a verdict of $80 in his favor at trial.	The City of Rockford, represented by Mr. C. M. Brazes, contended that they were not liable for Tripp's injuries. The defense argued that there was no evident negligence on their part, as they had used "selected sawed oak posts" of appropriate size and quality when installing the hitching posts. Additionally, they asserted that the injuries were too remote and not a direct consequence of any alleged defect in the hitching post, thus claiming that the city had met its duty of care concerning public safety.

William Wilder initiated a replevin action against Robert L. Greenlee and others in September 1868, in Chicago, Illinois. The case centers on a portable steam engine that Wilder claimed was fraudulently removed from the possession of his bailee. The defendants contended that the engine rightfully belonged to James Baxter, claiming that it had been sold to him by Wilder under misleading pretenses. The trial was held without a jury, and the court ultimately favored the defendants, concluding that the engine did indeed belong to Baxter. Following this decision, Wilder sought a new trial based on the argument that the initial verdict was contradictory to the evidence and presented newly discovered evidence that he believed warranted further examination. His motion was denied, prompting him to appeal the ruling to the Illinois Supreme Court.	William Wilder's primary argument was that the steam engine in dispute had been unlawfully taken from his bailee through deceitful means. He maintained that the court's original finding favored the defendants despite evidence suggesting the engine belonged to him. Wilder requested a new trial based on the newly discovered evidence that he believed strengthened his claim and could potentially prove that the engine was fraudulently obtained.	The defendants, led by Robert L. Greenlee, argued that the steam engine was the lawful property of James Baxter due to a legitimate purchase from Wilder. They contended that the evidence presented did not support Wilder’s claim and that the original court's decision was correct in favoring them. The defendants requested that the court affirm the initial judgment and deny the motion for a new trial, asserting that the case should remain concluded in their favor.

In the case of Ezra C. Read et al. v. John L. Wilson, which was decided in April 1859, the dispute arose in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiffs, Ezra C. Read and others, claimed ownership of a set of watches (twenty gold and twelve silver), valued at $2,500, that were allegedly taken by the defendant, John L. Wilson, a sheriff for Cook County. The controversy emerged after Wilson executed a levy on the watches as part of debt collection against R. W. Roath and W. Tyler Roath. The plaintiffs held a chattel mortgage on the watches, originally secured by the Roaths to cover a promissory note for $8,000. The mortgage allowed the mortgagors to retain possession of the items unless the plaintiffs deemed them at risk. Evidence presented showed that the plaintiffs had sent an agent to take possession of the watches prior to Wilson's levy. The trial was held by the court without a jury, and the judge ultimately ruled in favor of the defendant, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiffs contended that they rightfully owned the watches due to a chattel mortgage executed and recorded before the defendant's execution was delivered to him. They argued that the defendant wrongfully seized the property that belonged to them and contested the sheriff's claim of ownership based on the execution that targeted the Roaths. Specifically, they maintained that the sheriff lacked the authority to take the watches since they were under the plaintiffs' ownership by virtue of the recorded mortgage.	The defendant's primary defense was based on claiming ownership of the watches by virtue of an execution against the Roaths, which he asserted gave him the legal right to seize the property. Wilson argued that the mortgage held by the plaintiffs did not sufficiently protect their interest, as the terms allowed the mortgagors to retain possession, which he contended was a violation of statutory provisions for chattel mortgages. Moreover, the defendant asserted that the plaintiffs' evidence did not demonstrate proper transfer of possession or ownership at the time the judgment creditor's rights intervened.

The case of Leonard Hodges v. Eldora Percival took place in Chicago, Illinois. The incident leading to the legal action occurred on December 17, 1886, when Leonard Hodges and three others were in an elevator owned by Eldora Percival, who also rented out apartments in a five-story brick building where the accident occurred. During their ascent to the fifth floor, the elevator became uncontrollable, ascended past its intended stop, and then fell to the ground floor, causing injuries to Hodges and the other passengers. The injuries were significant enough to warrant a lawsuit, which commenced on February 12, 1887, in the Superior Court of Cook County. Following the trial, a jury ruled in favor of Hodges, awarding him $1500 in damages. After the Appellate Court upheld this decision, the case reached the Illinois Supreme Court, where various legal arguments around negligence and the admissibility of evidence concerning safety measures taken after the accident were debated.	Leonard Hodges, the plaintiff, claimed damages for the injuries he sustained as a result of the elevator accident. His principal argument was that Eldora Percival, the defendant, was negligent in maintaining the safety of the elevator, specifically alleging that the elevator was out of repair and lacked proper safety devices, such as an air-cushion, which were known to be effective in preventing injuries from falls. He sought compensation for his injuries due to this negligence.	Eldora Percival, the defendant, argued against the claims of negligence and maintained that he had provided reasonable care for the elevator's maintenance. His key defenses included the assertion that the elevator was not subject to the same safety requirements as newer models and contested the admissibility of evidence regarding an air-cushion that was installed after the accident, asserting that this should not be interpreted as an admission of prior negligence.

In the case of David McFall v. Alice D. Smith, which took place in February 1890, the plaintiff, Alice D. Smith, engaged the services of David McFall, a practicing physician, for assistance during childbirth. The plaintiff alleged that McFall acted negligently during the delivery, leading to severe injuries and prolonged suffering. The delivery resulted in significant tearing and lacerations, which left the plaintiff a "hopeless invalid" and inflicted ongoing pain. Despite Smith's multiple requests for proper care and attention, McFall allegedly provided inadequate treatment, including the careless administration of anesthetics, ultimately leading to her injuries. The jury returned a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, awarding her $900 for damages incurred, stating that the negligence of the defendant significantly contributed to her condition.	The plaintiff's main claims against the defendant included allegations of negligent and unskillful medical practice. She presented eight counts that highlighted various instances of negligence, including inappropriate administration of anesthetics, a lack of care during the childbirth process, and failure to stitch or treat her injuries properly. The plaintiff sought damages for the pain, anguish, and additional medical expenses resulting from the defendant's actions.	The defendant, David McFall, contested the plaintiff's claims by arguing that his medical care was appropriate and consistent with standard practices. He denied causing any significant injury, asserting that any lacerations were not substantial enough to require stitching and that they would heal naturally. The defendant contended that the administration of morphine and his absence during childbirth did not contribute to the plaintiff's injuries, emphasizing the testimonies of several medical professionals who supported his treatment decisions.

In 1883, in Randolph County, Illinois, Aaron Stout (the appellant) entered a legal dispute with Mattie C. Ellison (the appellee) concerning a stock of drugs, medicines, and various household items. At the center of the case was the ownership of property originally owned by E. Ellison, Mattie's husband. The conflict arose when Mattie, after experiencing alleged mistreatment from her husband, temporarily left him. Shortly after, E. Ellison offered her half ownership of the store if she returned, which she accepted. Despite this offer, no formal written transfer of ownership was executed as required by law. In October 1883, E. Ellison sold the goods to Stout without notifying him of Mattie's claim on them. Mattie later attempted to reclaim the goods, leading to this trial. Initially, the jury found in her favor, awarding her $251, but she remitted $150, resulting in a judgment of $101 against Stout. The case raised significant questions about property rights between spouses and how transfers must adhere to statutory requirements.	Mattie C. Ellison claimed that she had a legitimate ownership interest in the property sold to Aaron Stout, contending that E. Ellison had offered her half of the store. She argued that the lack of a formal written transfer invalidated Stout's ownership. Mattie sought the return of the drugs, household items, and preserved goods, asserting that she had a right to these possessions due to her connection to the property and the inadequate legal formalities observed in its transfer.	Aaron Stout's primary defense was that he purchased the goods from E. Ellison without any knowledge of Mattie's claims to the property, arguing that the alleged transfer was invalid due to its lack of written documentation required by law. He contended that Mattie's presence during the inventory and her assertion that she only wanted her clothing indicated she had relinquished any claims to the other items. Therefore, Stout sought to maintain his ownership and avoid any liability for return of the property.

In 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Benjamin H. Warder et al. v. John P. White arose when plaintiff John P. White, a real estate agent and broker, sought to recover $750 in commissions from defendants Benjamin H. Warder, Bushnell, and Glessner. The dispute centered around a property purchase that the defendants had intended to make through Shields, who had been contracted by them to act as a broker. Initially, the defendants had no prior acquaintance or knowledge of White, only dealing with Shields. During the trial, it was revealed that Shields worked as a clerk in White's office, establishing a link between White and the defendants' contract. Despite the defendants arguing a lack of privity of contract with White due to a personal trust placed in Shields, evidence suggested that once the defendants learned of White's role, they had an obligation to recognize him as the principal. The court focused on the legal principles of agency and found no substantial errors in the proceedings leading to the verdict.	The plaintiff, John P. White, claimed he was entitled to the commissions for the real estate transaction facilitated by Shields, asserting that the defendants had a contractual obligation to him once they discovered he was Shields’ principal. White requested the court to enforce their obligation to pay him directly for the commissions rather than Shields, emphasizing that the defendants recognized those commissions as due from them.	The defendants contended that there was no legal contract between themselves and White since they had engaged Shields directly, whose employment involved personal trust and confidence, thereby prohibiting any delegation of authority. They argued that any contract with Shields could not benefit White due to a lack of privity and expressed their request for the court to dismiss the claim based on these grounds.

In September 1872, the Illinois Supreme Court adjudicated a case involving two railroad corporations: The Peoria, Pekin and Jacksonville R. R. Co. (appellees) and The Peoria and Springfield R. R. Co. (appellants). The case arose in the Peoria county court, where the appellees sought to condemn certain lands owned by the appellants for their railway purposes. Initially, the appellees had acquired land for their railroad, but needed access over land that was leased to the appellants after the appellees already owned it. The appellants contested this, arguing that lands appropriated by a railroad could not be interfered with by a competing railroad. They asserted that their land, which had been leased, was exempt from the condemnation under eminent domain as they were not using it for railroad purposes. The court ultimately had to consider whether a railroad's land could be subjected to condemnation and whether one railroad could legally block another's access to necessary land.	The appellees claimed that they required access to certain lands for the operation of their railroad, which were essential for their franchise. They argued that the land in question was not being used by the appellants for any necessary railroad operations and that the law allows for eminent domain to condemn such lands regardless of prior ownership or leasing by another railroad.	The appellants contended that once land is appropriated by a railroad, it should not be subject to interference by another railroad using eminent domain powers. They claimed their lease of the land was a legal safeguard against any condemnation that would obstruct their business and argued that legislative authority should exempt their land from reappropriation unless necessary for their railroad operations.

The case of Washington Corrington v. Hiram Pierce took place in Peoria County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment on December 8, 1888. The dispute involved Corrington, who owned 85 acres of land, and Pierce, who owned several lots adjacent to Corrington's land. The contention began when Joseph Cody, another landowner abutting Corrington's property, placed a fence on what Corrington claimed was his land. Corrington sued Cody in a forcible entry and detainer action. During this time, an agreement was made among Corrington, Pierce, and Cody to resolve the boundary dispute through a survey. However, after the survey was completed and the boundary line was established, Cody refused to comply with the agreement. Pierce, who attended the trial and was aware of Cody's repudiation, did not object to it at that time. Subsequently, while Pierce attempted to build a fence along the new boundary, Corrington tore it down, leading to the trespass claim brought by Pierce against Corrington. The case raised questions about the validity of the boundary agreement and whether Pierce was bound by Cody's repudiation.	Hiram Pierce, the plaintiff, claimed that Corrington committed trespass by unlawfully tearing down the fence that Pierce built according to the boundary line established by surveyors. Pierce argued that despite Cody's refusal to honor the agreed-upon boundary line, he (Pierce) was still entitled to enforce the agreement and seek damages for the trespass. Pierce requested judgment against Corrington for the damages incurred, which were assessed at $25 in prior jurisdictions.	Washington Corrington, the defendant, contended that since Cody repudiated the boundary agreement in the presence of Pierce, Pierce was also released from obligations under that contract. He argued that the subsequent actions and declarations from Cody affected the contractual obligations among all parties and that Pierce’s silence and lack of dissent indicated his agreement to abandon the survey. Thus, Corrington sought to dismiss the claims made by Pierce, asserting that Pierce was estopped from claiming rights under the survey agreement due to his lack of action in response to Cody’s refusal.

Adde Aden v. Julia Ann Cruse was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court in 1887, following an incident that occurred on election day in November 1884 in Mill Creek, Illinois. The case involved the plaintiff, Adde Aden, seeking damages for the wrongful death of her husband, Julia Ann Cruse. Cruse had become intoxicated after consuming liquor provided by the appellant, Aden, which led to him falling off his horse and sustaining fatal injuries. On the day in question, Aden invited Cruse and another person to drink apple brandy with him after Cruse had already consumed liquor earlier that morning. Following several rounds of drinking, Cruse, in a state of intoxication, attempted to ride home, resulting in an accident that led to his death eight days later. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding her $800 in damages. Despite the appellant's belief that he was not liable under the Dram Shop Act, the court had to determine if Aden's actions fell under the provisions of the statute regarding giving intoxicating liquor.	The plaintiff, Adde Aden, claimed that her husband's death was a direct result of the intoxication caused by the liquor given to him by the defendant, Julia Ann Cruse. She argued that, according to Section 9 of the Dram Shop Act, she had the right to recover damages due to the loss of support, as Cruse's intoxication was the immediate cause of the fatal accident. The plaintiff contended that the defendant was liable for providing intoxicating drinks that contributed to Cruse's intoxication.	The defendant, Julia Ann Cruse, contended that the Dram Shop Act, which regulates the sale and distribution of intoxicating liquors, applied only to those directly engaged in the liquor trade, and not to private individuals who offer liquor as a gesture of hospitality. The defense argued that Aden's actions did not constitute the unlawful sale or giving away of liquor in violation of the statute, as he was neither a dram-shop keeper nor in the business of selling intoxicating beverages. They maintained that the act of treating a friend was not an act of negligence that would incur liability under the law.

In 1873, in Yates City, Knox County, Illinois, William H. Robinson, a member in good standing of the Yates City Lodge No. 448, A. F. & A. Masons, was charged with unmasonic conduct. He was notified of a trial scheduled for June 19, 1873, but informed the lodge's master that he could not attend due to his duties as the county surveyor. Despite his absence, the lodge conducted the trial and found him guilty, resulting in his expulsion. Robinson then sought to recover initiation fees he had paid upon joining the Lodge. The initial claim was filed before a police magistrate, and after an appeal, the case went to the circuit court of Knox County, where the judgment sided with the lodge.	William H. Robinson argued that he should recover the initiation fees he had paid upon his expulsion from the Masonic lodge. He contended that the lodge's actions were improperly conducted, as he was not allowed to present his defense during the trial for the charges against him. Robinson sought a legal remedy to reclaim the fees, asserting that his expulsion invalidated the contract related to those payments.	The Yates City Lodge defended itself by asserting that Robinson voluntarily paid the initiation fees without any fraud or coercion. The lodge maintained that the by-laws permitted them to expel members for unmasonic conduct, and that Robinson's absence from the trial did not affect the lodge's jurisdiction. They argued that since the fees were paid voluntarily and were not contingent upon his membership status, no grounds existed for his claim.

In the year 1885, the highway commissioners of Kankakee levied a road and bridge tax on all property within the town, specifically to fund the construction of a bridge within the city limits of Kankakee. Thomas Kerr, a taxpayer, later contested this tax payment of $4.12, which he claimed was collected improperly as a permanent injunction was granted by the Circuit Court to prevent the construction of the bridge. A lawsuit initiated by Pleasant Durham had asserted that the funds collected were insufficient for the bridge and claimed that the highway commissioners had no legal right to impose such a tax within city boundaries according to the city's charter. Kerr, along with other residents, sought to restrain the tax collection citing the failure of the bridge project. The Supreme Court affirmed the Circuit Court's decision that the levy was invalid, leading Kerr to demand the return of his tax payment as the intended purpose for which the tax was collected had failed. The officials, however, argued that the payment was voluntary, thus not eligible for reimbursement.	Thomas Kerr claimed that the tax he paid for the failed bridge project should be returned because it was essentially a bailment for a special purpose that could not be fulfilled. He argued that since the project had been abandoned, he was entitled to recover the funds as the situation rendered the collection of the tax invalid.	The highway commissioners contended that the tax payment was made voluntarily and not under compulsion. Consequently, they argued that since the payment was not made under duress, Kerr was not entitled to a refund. They referenced legal precedents which upheld that taxes collected for general purposes cannot be reclaimed unless paid under duress.

The case "The People ex rel. W. H. Stickney v. John M. Palmer" was filed in June 1872 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The key individual involved is W. H. Stickney, the relator, who sought a writ of mandamus against John M. Palmer, the Governor of Illinois. The background of the case stems from an election held on November 7, 1871, in Chicago, where Stickney received a majority of the votes for the position of police magistrate. Following his election, the common council of Chicago canvassed the votes on November 20, 1871, and declared Stickney duly elected, issuing a certificate of election. However, when he applied to the Governor for his commission, Palmer refused, arguing that the 1870 constitution abolished the office of police magistrate in Chicago. The case revolves around the constitutionality of the office's existence and whether Stickney's election should entitle him to a commission.	Stickney's main argument is that he was duly elected as a police magistrate in Chicago and is entitled to receive his commission. He asserts that the election was valid and that the refusal by Governor Palmer to issue the commission is unwarranted, as the office had not been legally abolished for the context of his election.	Governor Palmer's defense rests on the assertion that the new 1870 constitution abolished the office of police magistrate in Chicago. He contends that the system established by the constitution, which requires the appointment of justices of the peace and police magistrates, implicitly prohibits any future elections for that office. Palmer’s request to the court is for a ruling that affirms his view that the office is indeed abolished, thereby justifying his refusal to issue the commission.

The case of George Curtis v. Anson Root took place in April 1862 in Illinois. George Curtis is the appellant, while Anson Root is the appellee. The dispute originated from an action of ejectment initiated by Root against Curtis in the Circuit Court of Kane County, Illinois. The case was eventually relocated to the Kendall Circuit Court and later to the Court of Common Pleas of Elgin. Initially, a jury trial ruled in favor of Curtis, but after a series of motions for new trials from both parties, the case was tried again, resulting in a verdict for Root. Curtis appealed the decision. The case involved a complex history of transactions related to a mortgage made by Ruel Ambrose to Anson Root and the subsequent purchase and foreclosure of the land in question. This involved various judgments, including a significant judgment against Ambrose from Weed, Masters & Weed, which was a lien on the land despite the land title being acquired post-judgment. Key elements of the dispute centered around the proper execution and timing of the mortgage documents and whether the records reflected the true nature of the transactions.	The plaintiff, Anson Root, claimed that a mortgage issued by Ruel Ambrose should secure him against liabilities stemming from a bond he signed on behalf of Ambrose. Root contended that the mortgage created a lien on the property in question, asserting that the mortgage was executed simultaneously with the deed from Morgan to Ambrose and was intended to secure the purchase money for the property. Root sought to maintain his claimed priority over the judgment obtained by Weed, Masters & Weed.	George Curtis, the defendant, argued that the mortgage was not intended to secure the purchase money but was executed for entirely different considerations. He contended that the information visible on the mortgage did not suggest it created a priority lien and that the purchaser should have relied solely on the public records. Curtis emphasized that without clear evidence of Root's knowledge regarding the mortgage's true nature, Root should not be favored in the legal judgment.

In October 1835, John Evans entered into a transaction with the School Commissioner of Greene County, during which he purchased a portion of land from the sixteenth section, providing notes as consideration for the purchase. However, before Evans initiated legal action for the balance owed, the State of Illinois conveyed the title of the land to third parties, Greene Weaver and J. W. Dunnahay, thus raising concerns regarding the validity of Evans's claim. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, where the defendant (the School Commissioner) contended that the consideration for the notes had failed due to this earlier conveyance. In their ruling, the court evaluated the defendant's plea and found it inadequate as it did not sufficiently demonstrate how the consideration failed. The court underscored that the defendant was required to show not only that the State had granted title to others but also that no patent had been issued to him prior to these transactions and that this patent was not intended to assert his rights. Ultimately, the court maintained that the School Commissioner had fulfilled his duty regarding the sale, and the title assurance depended on the law governing the office, which further complicated the plea presented by the defendant.	John Evans, as the appellant, asserted that he had legally entered into a contract with the School Commissioner for the purchase of the land and provided necessary notes as payment. He claimed that regardless of the subsequent conveyance of the land by the State to other parties, he was entitled to recover the amount due under the notes. Evans contended that the failure of consideration was inadequately demonstrated and maintained that he had valid claims based on his purchase agreement.	The School Commissioner of Greene County argued that the consideration for Evans's notes had failed due to the State’s prior conveyance of the title to additional parties, which, according to the defendant, invalidated Evans's claim. The defendant’s plea contended that because the State issued patents to others, the School Commissioner could not fulfill the obligation represented by the notes. The defense focused on establishing that the public officer's actions did not meet legal requirements, thus relieving the defendant from liability for the payment.

Stephen Merritt (plaintiff) and Nathan Merritt (defendant) are brothers engaged in a legal dispute in the Illinois Supreme Court that culminated in a decision in April 1858. The case originated from a debt collection on a promissory note worth $900, signed by Nathan in favor of Stephen in October 1841, for a quit-claim deed to their father's estate. Stephen argued that Nathan had not repaid the note despite repeated requests. Conversely, Nathan claimed a set-off against this note based on another note issued by Stephen to their brother Daniel Merritt in 1836, which Nathan argued was endorsed to him through Daniel by his father's estate after Daniel sold his interest in their father's estate to Nathan. Key events include the death of their father, Elisha Merritt, in 1841, and subsequent legal and financial arrangements between the brothers concerning the estate. The complexity arose from issues surrounding the statute of limitations and the ownership and transfer of notes relative to their father's will, which dictated that any debts owed to him by his sons were to be deducted from their inheritances.	Stephen Merritt contended that Nathan Merritt owed him $900, as promised in the promissory note executed in 1841. He claimed that Nathan failed to make payment despite several requests. Stephen asserted that the note Nathan sought to set off against this debt was invalid due to various legal reasons, including the statute of limitations and a previous arbitration award that he argued effectively canceled that debt.	Nathan Merritt defended against Stephen's claims by asserting that the debt owed to Stephen was countered by a valid set-off involving a note given by Stephen to Daniel Merritt for $967, which he claimed was duly assigned to him. He argued that the note had not been paid and that there was an agreement by Stephen to settle the debt within sixteen years before the case began. Nathan maintained that as an executor of their father's estate, he was entitled to satisfy Stephen's claim through this set-off.

Charles S. Wynn and Henry A. Longley were involved in a legal dispute stemming from the sale of wool. The transaction took place on October 8, 1886, in Chicago, Illinois. Wynn, the vendor, sold a quantity of wool to Longley, who later claimed that Wynn had knowingly misrepresented the quality of the wool. Longley asserted that the wool was worth significantly less than the price he paid, as it was not the kind of wool Wynn had represented it to be. The case was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court, where it was tried without a jury. The trial court initially found in favor of Longley, awarding him damages amounting to $81,000. However, the appellate court noted that there was no evidence presented during the trial to establish the actual value of the wool at the time of sale, or the value it would have had if it had indeed been the quality Wynn claimed. The court underlined that this absence of evidence was critical to the judgment.	Longley claimed that Wynn deceived him by misrepresenting the wool's quality. He argued that the wool delivered was worth significantly less than what he paid and less than what it would have been worth had it been as represented. Longley sought damages to compensate for the difference in value, amounting to $88,000.	Wynn's defense focused on challenging Longley's claims of deceit, arguing that the measure of damages should be accurately established through evidence reflecting the wool's actual value versus its represented value. The defense contended that no sufficient evidence was presented to support Longley's claims regarding the wool's worth, which they claimed made the original judgment flawed.

In the case of Lewis E. Montgomery v. Samuel T. Brush et al., the events unfolded in the summer of 1885 when plaintiffs Edward McGuire and Samuel T. Brush, who resided in Jackson County, Illinois, contracted the services of Milligan & Mcllvane for the pasturing and selling of 218 head of their cattle. After the cattle were transported to the Tanner farm for pasturing, a legal dispute arose. Montgomery, who had prior contracts with Milligan & Mcllvane, was involved when they placed 131 of the plaintiffs' cattle into his pasture. Montgomery claimed he had no knowledge that these cattle belonged to McGuire and Brush and assumed they were being pastured for him in line with an agreement with Milligan & Mcllvane. McGuire and Brush later sought legal recourse, alleging that Montgomery converted their cattle when he sold them without their consent. The case progressed through the Circuit Court of Sangamon County, where a judgment of $1500 was rendered against Montgomery, which he appealed. The case was eventually heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, culminating in a final judgment in September 1887.	The plaintiffs claimed that Lewis E. Montgomery wrongfully converted their 131 head of cattle that were pastured under an agreement with the agents Milligan & Mcllvane. They asserted that at the time of the alleged conversion, Montgomery had either actual or constructive notice of their ownership. Consequently, they sought damages for the value of the cattle, which led to the initial judgment of $1500 in their favor.	The defendant, Lewis E. Montgomery, argued that he received the cattle believing they were to replace another lot he had previously consented to be removed under an existing arrangement with Milligan & Mcllvane. He maintained that he had no notice or awareness of the ownership of the cattle belonging to McGuire and Brush and requested the court to dismiss the claims against him, asserting that the plaintiffs lacked both the property and possession rights necessary to support their case.

In September 1868, Charles B. Farwell sought to purchase a lot in Chicago, intending to construct a warehouse. He instructed real estate agent Fowler to find an immediate possession property. The lot was owned by Crane, who had a verbal agreement with tenant William H. Warren, stating Warren could leave at any time. Crane confirmed with Warren that immediate possession was possible, leading Farwell to consummate the purchase. Before taking possession, Farwell asked Fowler to negotiate with Warren. Fowler's visit established that Warren would vacate shortly, having assured that he would not hinder construction. After initial work commenced, Warren unexpectedly retracted his consent to vacate and demanded compensation to leave. This led to Curran, who was supervising Farwell's construction, to remove Warren's belongings and demolish his house without Farwell's direction. Warren subsequently filed a lawsuit for trespassing, resulting in a jury verdict finding Farwell liable for $8,000, later remitted to $5,000, prompting Farwell's appeal.	William H. Warren claimed damages for trespass against Charles B. Farwell and Dennis Curran, asserting that they unlawfully entered his property, removed his belongings, and demolished his house without consent. Warren contended that despite prior promises made by him to vacate, the circumstances of removal were unjustified and led to significant loss.	Charles B. Farwell defended against the trespass claim by arguing that Warren's initial agreement to vacate gave him implied permission to enter the property and proceed with construction. He contended that Warren’s subsequent attempt to revoke that permission and demand compensation for vacating was unjust. Farwell emphasized the principle that Warren’s own actions should estop him from claiming damages, as his conduct had invited the defendants to commit the acts for which he sought compensation.

In December 1842, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case of Joshua T. Bradley, the appellant, against Zophar Case, the Commissioner of School Lands for Clinton County, the appellee. This case involved a promissory note related to the sale of land from a sixteenth section designated for school purposes, authorized by Illinois state legislation. The dispute arose in Clinton County, where the land was sold under a law enabling such sales if certain conditions were met, including consent from a significant portion of local inhabitants. Bradley contended that the legislature lacked the authority to order the sale of the land, thereby arguing that any purchase made was invalid and that the promissory note was without consideration. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Bradley, awarding him the amount due on the note along with significant interest. The case escalated to the Supreme Court as Bradley sought to reverse this ruling.	The plaintiff, Joshua T. Bradley, argued that the sale of the sixteenth section of land was unconstitutional and that the state legislature did not possess the authority to authorize such sales without federal consent. He claimed that as a result, he acquired no title to the land, rendering the promissory note he signed void due to lack of consideration. Bradley requested the court to uphold the initial ruling that favored him, which declared the note invalid and awarded him the judgment amount with interest.	The defendant, Zophar Case, contended that the Illinois legislature had the necessary authority to authorize the sale of school lands as they were entitled to determine the manner in which state-owned lands could be utilized. He argued that the notes signed for the purchase were valid contracts grounded in a legal framework established by previous acts of legislation. The defendant further sought to reverse the Circuit Court’s judgment and uphold the legality of the sale and the validity of the promissory note.

The case "Richard Mason v. William Dousay" was adjudicated in April 1864 by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from an action of assumpsit initiated by William Dousay in the Superior Court of Chicago. The dispute revolved around a bill of exchange dated May 14, 1861, for the sum of $128.05, drawn by Nathan D. Inman in favor of Dousay and directing payment by Richard Mason, the defendant, who resided in Chicago. The plaintiff alleged that the bill was duly presented and accepted, but payment was later refused by Mason. The key facts reveal that while the bill was drawn in Michigan, it was made payable in Chicago, where Mason had his business. The court considered various legal principles regarding the acceptance of bills of exchange and the required adherence to local laws. The trial was conducted without a jury, leading to a judgment against Mason after a ruling that neither Michigan's laws about written acceptance nor the defense assertions could negate the validity of the claim.	The plaintiff, William Dousay, claimed that Richard Mason accepted the bill of exchange and thus owed him the amount owed under the agreement. Dousay argued that Mason's oral acceptance of the draft, conveyed when Mason indicated he would pay "in the course of thirty or sixty days," constituted valid acceptance. He sought the judgement for damages sustained due to Mason's refusal to pay after acceptance.	The defendant, Richard Mason, contended that the bill of exchange was governed by Michigan law, requiring acceptance to be in writing. He argued that since the bill was drawn in Michigan by a resident of that state, the lack of a written acceptance invalidated the obligation. Mason claimed that the plaintiff could not prove a valid acceptance under the law of Michigan, and therefore sought dismissal of the claims against him.

In December 1830, the case of Alexis Phelps v. Robert R. Young was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, following an appeal from the Adams circuit court. The central issue revolved around a debt claim where Alexis Phelps, the appellant, sought to collect from Robert R. Young, the appellee, who was a non-resident debtor. Phelps asserted that Young was indebted to him for a sum of fourteen hundred dollars based on a written instrument signed by Young. The proceedings involved specific legal requirements for an attachment action under Illinois law, particularly concerning the adequacy of the affidavit that initiated the attachment. The court needed to determine whether Phelps's affidavit sufficiently stated the nature and amount of the indebtedness as mandated by the statute. Additionally, there were concerns about an alleged irregularity in the taking of depositions since the original magistrate had passed away before the depositions could be taken.	Phelps claimed that Young was indebted to him in the amount of fourteen hundred dollars, supported by a signed written instrument. He sought the enforcement of his claim through an attachment, arguing that he complied with statutory requirements by stating the nature and amount of the indebtedness in his affidavit.	Young challenged Phelps's claim based on the sufficiency of the affidavit, arguing it did not adequately specify the nature of the indebtedness as required by law. He also raised objections regarding the procedure for taking depositions, particularly regarding the transfer of magistrate duties after the original magistrate's death and the lack of specified time and place for the depositions.

The case "Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railway Company v. The People ex rel. A. E. D. Scott, Collector" arose in 1883 in Moultrie County, Illinois, when the Peoria, Decatur and Evansville Railway Company contested a tax assessment levied against it. The county board imposed a tax to address existing county debt, primarily to repay railroad aid bonds that were legally binding. The total tax for the year was assessed at $1.38 per $100 of taxable property valuation. The railway company agreed to pay $1.00 but objected to the remaining $0.38, amounting to an excess of $450.28. The critical question was whether the county court had the authority to levy a tax exceeding one dollar per hundred dollars' valuation under Illinois law. The appellate court reviewed the jurisdiction and the applicable statutes, focusing on the legislative provisions and the authority of the county board to levy such taxes for pre-existing debts.	The plaintiff, represented by the railway company, argued that the county board exceeded its authority in levying a tax greater than one dollar per hundred dollars of taxable property. They contended that under both statutory provisions and constitutional constraints, the tax assessed should not exceed the permissible limit without a vote from the county's electorate. The railway company claimed the disputed excess tax was invalid and sought to have it overturned.	The defendant, represented by the State's attorney, maintained that the county board had the implicit authority to levy the tax in question per the railroad charters under which bonds were issued. They argued that the charters required the county to collect sufficient taxes to cover both interest and principal on these contracts, thereby justifying the tax assessment even if it exceeded the general limit. The defense contended that the evidence supporting the legality of the excess tax was valid, asserting that it was necessary for fulfilling obligations tied to legal contracts.

In January 1874, the case of Emily Beseler v. Jacob Stephani was addressed in the Illinois Supreme Court. This case originated from an incident involving Emily Beseler, the plaintiff, who alleged that Jacob Stephani, the defendant, had assaulted her multiple times. The first count detailed an incident where Stephani forcibly dragged Beseler against her will from one room to another and attempted to engage in non-consensual sexual acts, causing her significant physical and emotional distress. The second count portrayed a similar event on April 13, 1871, where Beseler claimed she was held against her will by Stephani while being ill. The third count described the most severe incident on April 16, 1872, where Stephani allegedly dragged a pregnant Beseler out of his house to an isolated area, leaving her alone to suffer. The fourth count detailed general abuse and mistreatment by Stephani towards Beseler. In his defense, Stephani countered with pleas of not guilty and claims of accord and satisfaction, arguing that a written release had been obtained. However, Beseler contended that this release was procured through fraudulent means. The jury eventually ruled in favor of the defendant, leading to an appeal by the plaintiff regarding the jury instructions given during the trial.	Emily Beseler, the plaintiff, argued that she suffered multiple assaults by Jacob Stephani, which included being dragged, held against her will, and attempts at sexual violence. She claimed that these actions resulted in significant physical and emotional injuries. Beseler's primary legal request was for damages related to the breaches of her personal safety and dignity, asserting that these assaults had lasting effects on her health.	Jacob Stephani, the defendant, denied the allegations of assault and claimed that any sexual relations were consensual. His defense included arguments of accord and satisfaction, stating that a written release absolved him of liability. He contended that the plaintiff could not recover damages because any sexual contact was consensual and that the instruction given to the jury regarding the law of consent was appropriate.

In January 1875, in Union County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Andrew J. Kuykendall, the plaintiff, and Alexander J. Nimmo, the defendant. Kuykendall was the sheriff who levied certain goods belonging to Philip Mead, who had outstanding judgments against him. Prior to these judgments on January 9, 1875, Philip Mead executed a deed of assignment to Kuykendall to benefit his creditors, which became central to the case. The primary legal question at issue was the fairness and legality of this deed of assignment, especially concerning allegations that it was intended to hinder, delay, or defraud Mead's creditors. The case was decided in the Union Circuit Court, which was tasked with determining the fairness of this assignment without a jury, given that the evidence may be insufficient in the bill of exceptions. The court ultimately deemed the transaction to be conducted in good faith for the benefit of all creditors involved, ruling that the assignment passed the title of the property to Kuykendall.	The plaintiff, Andrew J. Kuykendall, claimed ownership of the levied goods based on the deed of assignment from Philip Mead, which stated that the property was assigned for the benefit of Mead's creditors without any preferences. Kuykendall argued that the assignment was valid and sought to establish his right to maintain a replevin action against the sheriff responsible for executing the levy.	The defendant, Alexander J. Nimmo, contended that the assignment was fraudulent and thus void against the executions that had been issued against Mead on the prevailing judgments. Nimmo asserted that the intention behind the assignment was to hinder and delay creditors from collecting debts. He challenged the fairness of the transaction, implying that it should not be upheld due to suspicions of fraud.

In December 1845, the case of Sarah Bonham et al. v. Abraham Badgley et al. was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a bill filed by the defendants, who sought a partition or sale of real estate that they claimed was owned by Joseph Bonham, the late husband of Sarah Bonham. Joseph Bonham had reportedly married Sarah Beer, a daughter of his sister, which raised questions about the legality of the marriage due to consanguinity. Joseph died shortly after, leaving no legitimate children, and his mother, Sophia Bonham, was the only remaining direct heir, following which she also passed away in 1834 without leaving a husband or children. After Joseph's death, Susannah Beer, Sarah's mother, occupied the land until her death in 1843, at which point Sarah took possession.
