The defendants, claiming as descendants of Sophia Bonham, asserted that the title was never in Sarah and sought a judicial partition of the land. The Illinois Supreme Court primarily debated the nature of the marriage and whether Sarah could inherit through it.	The plaintiffs, led by Sarah Bonham, argued that she was the rightful heir to the property based on the descent from her mother, Susannah Beer. They contended that the alleged marriage between Sarah and Joseph Bonham, while admittedly within the prohibited degrees of kinship, was not void but voidable, thus legitimizing Sarah’s claims to the estate for civil purposes. They asserted that the estate descended to her through her mother and that she had been in continuous possession of the property, thereby entitling her to the benefits associated with it.	The defendants' key arguments included the assertion that Joseph Bonham had not died seized of the land in question since it was unclear whether he conveyed the property before his death. They contended that Sophia Bonham was the rightful heir, and since she died without the heirs being seized of the land, it did not automatically pass to Sarah. They also claimed that Sarah's claim was based on a marriage that was void ab initio, thus making her and her descendants ineligible to inherit. Furthermore, they argued that the adverse possession of the land by Susannah Beer tolled the right of entry for Joseph Bonham's heirs.

The case "The National Bank of Illinois v. Mary S. Baker" took place on May 16, 1889, presided over by the Illinois Supreme Court. It stemmed from events that began on December 14, 1885, when William Baker and his wife, Mary S. Baker, executed a promissory note for $600 with W. H. Kretsinger, offering collateral in the form of stock and a life insurance policy for the loan. This included a certificate for 100 shares of the "Journal of Commerce Company" and a $5000 life policy on William Baker, payable to Mary S. Baker. In January 1886, Kretsinger received payment for this note from an agent of the National Bank of Illinois, which William was heavily indebted to, and subsequently transferred the note and collateral to the bank. William was gravely ill and died shortly thereafter, and Mary S. Baker attempted to redeem the pledge by tendering the amount due on the note, which the bank refused to accept. The legal question concerned whether the transfer of collateral to the bank effectively passed full ownership of the insurance policy and stock to the bank or if it remained as security against the promissory note. The courts concluded that the security only served to back the note rather than transferring full ownership.	The National Bank of Illinois contended that the transfer of collateral to them by Kretsinger gave them full entitlement to both the insurance policy and the stock certificate pledged against the promissory note. They argued that following the death of William Baker, they had a right to the proceeds without needing to allow for redemption by Mary S. Baker.	Mary S. Baker argued that the collateral transferred was essentially worthless, given that the stock was counterfeit and had no genuine market value. She claimed that the security only served as collateral against the promissory note. Therefore, upon tendering the due amount on the promissory note, she maintained she had the right to recover any remaining funds from the insurance policy. She asserted that the bank did not legally possess the right to sell the collateral without first giving her notice to redeem the property.

John Bryner served as the sheriff of Peoria County in the mid-19th century. In 1860, he initiated a legal action against the Board of Supervisors of Peoria County, seeking payment for official services he rendered, which included mileage for summoning jurors and serving subpoenas. The case was decided without a jury by Judge Powell, based on an agreed set of facts. The defendant acknowledged the services provided but disputed the county's obligation to pay for these expenses. The total amount Bryner claimed included $163.30 for mileage, $50.80 for serving subpoenas, and $32 for printing costs, totaling $246.10. Despite the agreement on the services rendered, the Board of Supervisors denied liability for compensation, resulting in the court's evaluation of the validity of this claim.	Bryner argued that as the sheriff, he was entitled to compensation for services performed while executing official duties, which he stated were necessary for the administration of justice. He claimed a total amount based on mileage for summoning jurors, serving subpoenas, and printing related materials, asserting that these services were integral to his responsibilities as sheriff and deserved remuneration.	The Board of Supervisors contended that there was no legal or moral obligation for the county to compensate the sheriff for the charges he presented. They maintained that the office of sheriff is taken “cum onere,” meaning that the sheriff assumes the burdens of the office as part of the role, including the financial aspects of the services rendered. The county acknowledged the correctness of the services but denied any liability for payment.

In December 1843, in Illinois, Frederick A. Carpenter was involved in a legal case against the People of the State of Illinois. The case arose from an indictment against Carpenter consisting of two counts: one for assault on Washington F. Adams with intent to commit murder, and another for assault with intent to commit mayhem. Carpenter pleaded not guilty. The jury ultimately found him guilty of a lesser offense, specifically an assault with intent to commit bodily injury. Carpenter was sentenced to thirty days in prison and fined thirty dollars. The main legal question debated was whether the jury had appropriately convicted Carpenter of a lesser offense not explicitly mentioned in the indictment. This led to a discussion on legal precedents regarding the nature of indictments and the ability of juries to convict for lesser included offenses when not specifically charged.	The plaintiff argued that the jury could not find the defendant guilty of a different offense than what was laid out in the indictment. They claimed that the indictment for assault with intent to commit murder should not allow for a conviction of a lesser charge, as the jury must find all necessary facts constituting that lesser offense. They maintained that assaults of this nature are not indictable offenses in themselves, falling under the jurisdiction of justices of the peace instead of circuit courts.	The defendant, represented by attorneys J. Gillespie and Nathaniel Niles, contended that the jury's conviction of an assault with intent to inflict bodily injury was improper given the indictment was solely for greater offenses. They argued that the assault with intent to cause bodily injury required specific findings that were not present in the jury’s verdict. Furthermore, they pointed out that the legal framework does not allow for conviction of a lesser offense not charged in the indictment itself and emphasized that such cases should be reserved for lower courts.

The case "John C. Edwards et al. v. Michael Hushing et al." was decided on February 21, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. It involved a legal dispute over two omnibuses and two horses that were seized under a chattel mortgage. The plaintiffs, John C. Edwards and others, claimed that the mortgage was fraudulently procured by Robert McWilliams, the husband of the defendant Mary McWilliams. They alleged that he misrepresented the contents of the mortgage, causing them to sign an agreement that included an omnibus they did not intend to include. Testimonies were presented from various witnesses, supporting the plaintiffs' allegation of fraud, while the defense countered this with contrasting testimony. During the trial, the court ruled that there was insufficient evidence to submit the question of the mortgage's execution and alleged fraud to the jury, which raised significant controversy regarding procedural fairness.	The plaintiffs argued that the execution of the chattel mortgage was procured through fraud. They contended that Robert McWilliams misrepresented the terms of the mortgage, leading them to sign it under false pretenses. They sought to reclaim the omnibuses and horses taken under the mortgage, asserting they had made a tender of the amount due but were refused by the defendants.	The defendants argued that the mortgage was valid and that the property was rightfully seized to satisfy the debt owed on the promissory note and unpaid rent. They maintained that the plaintiffs had acknowledged the mortgage's execution and thus were not entitled to reclaim the seized property.

In the case of Seth F. Hanchett v. Amelia Rice, dated April 26, 1887, the dispute originates from a replevin action concerning household furniture taken by a Sheriff on behalf of creditors of Isaac A. Rice, Amelia Rice’s husband. The case took place in the Illinois Appellate Court after an appeal from the Superior Court of Cook County. Amelia claimed the furniture was her separate property, purchased with her own funds she received from her parents and earnings from her past work. The couple married in Baltimore, Maryland, in 1854, and lived in multiple locations, including Richmond, Virginia, and Chicago, Illinois. Throughout their marriage, Amelia maintained control of a significant amount of money, initially given to her at marriage, which she asserted was used to acquire the furniture in question. The court's investigation delved into the implications of marital property laws prior to and post the Married Women's Acts of 1861 and 1869, determining that the legal framework at the time largely favored the husband's ownership of the wife's property unless otherwise documented.	Amelia Rice contended that she rightfully owned the household furniture, asserting it was purchased with her own money, including funds given to her by her parents and money earned for services provided while her husband was in military service. She sought recovery of the furniture, maintaining it was her separate property regardless of her husband’s financial liabilities.	Seth F. Hanchett, representing the creditors of Isaac A. Rice, argued that the furniture was legally owned by the husband, as the common law presumed that property acquired during marriage belonged to the husband unless a valid transfer had taken place. He highlighted that Amelia did not provide adequate evidence under the law to prove the furniture was her separate property, as it was purchased with funds that, under existing legal principles, belonged to her husband.

In the case of Kiles et al. v. Watkins, which took place in Illinois and culminated in a judgment filed on February 25, 1886, the conflict arose over a promissory note for $1,000 executed by William Watkins and his son, Elijah, to the plaintiffs, Kiles et al. The plaintiffs, represented by attorneys Ketcham & Gridley, initiated legal action against the defendants, alleging that the defendants defaulted on the note. The defendants contended that William Watkins had signed the note as surety for his son, operating under the understanding that the loan was intended to be temporary. They claimed that the execution of the note was contingent on the arrangement that once Elijah secured funds from another source, specifically from an individual named Taylor, the note would be canceled, and William would be released from his obligation. The situation became complicated when it was asserted that, although a second note was signed under these conditions, it was not applied to settle the original debt as agreed but was instead used to address Elijah's other debts with the plaintiffs without William's consent. The jury ultimately found the defendants' account credible amidst conflicting testimonies.	The plaintiffs claimed that the note executed by William and Elijah Watkins represented a valid and enforceable debt of $1,000, which had not been repaid. They sought to collect the amount owed under the promissory note, asserting their right to enforce the obligation despite the defendants' defenses regarding the nature of the agreement and the use of a subsequent note.	The defendants argued that William Watkins signed the promissory note solely as a surety for his son and that the signing was based on the understanding that the loan would be temporary. They maintained that once Elijah could borrow money from Taylor, the obligation to pay the original note would be canceled, which did not happen. Instead, they alleged that the new note signed by Elijah was improperly applied to his individual debts rather than satisfying the original promissory note, which they claimed was done without William's consent.

In the case of William W. Kirkland v. Sarah L. Conway et al., a dispute arose regarding the interpretation of a will after the death of William Kearney, who passed away in January 1877 in Piatt County, Illinois. The will, dated January 11, 1877, was admitted to probate shortly after his death. In the will, Kearney bequeathed various tracts of land to his heirs, including specific allocations to his daughter Sidney Dubson, grandson William Ward Kirkland, and the heirs of his deceased daughter Sarah Elizabeth Conklin. The main contention was over the designation and location of a 50-acre parcel of land given to Dubson and how the remaining land was to be divided among the other heirs. The circuit court initially determined that the 50 acres should be situated in the southeast corner of section 7. Subsequent questions arose regarding the distribution of the land allotted to Kirkland and the Conkle heirs after accounting for the 50 acres reserved for Dubson. The case involved intricate details about the layout of the land in question and the specific allocations described in the will.	William W. Kirkland (the plaintiff) argued that the will's provisions should be interpreted to ensure that he receives the 314 acres designated to him and sought clarity on the division of the remaining land among the heirs of his deceased aunt, Sarah Elizabeth Conklin. He requested the court to confirm his claim to the specified acreage and to ensure that the distribution aligns with the language used in the will.	Sarah L. Conway and other defendants (including those representing Sidney Dubson) contended that the initial ruling by the circuit court regarding the 50 acres was correct and that Kirkland's claims regarding the land distribution did not align with the testator's intentions. They argued for a clear definition of the heirs' portions, asserting that Kirkland's desired allocations exceed what was intended by the language in the will, particularly suggesting that the distribution of land to the Conkle heirs was improperly calculated.

In 1883, the case of Benn Philips Reynolds v. Maria E. De Geer took place in Cook County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Benn Philips Reynolds, owned certain goods and chattels which were seized by a writ of attachment initiated by the defendant, Maria E. De Geer. The defendant falsely claimed that the plaintiff was a non-resident of Illinois, leading to the wrongful seizure of the plaintiff's property. After the attachment was quashed, the justice of the peace presiding over the matter ruled against the defendant on the attachment but also ended up ruling that the plaintiff owed the defendant $71. An immediate execution to collect this debt was granted, and while the goods were held by the constable, the defendant took possession of them without the plaintiff's consent. The plaintiff attempted to reclaim the goods after appealing the justice's decision, but contended that the defendant's actions prevented him from recovering his property. The case progressed through the courts due to issues surrounding the legality of the attachment and the subsequent seizure of goods.	The plaintiff claimed that the defendant maliciously and without probable cause initiated a wrongful writ of attachment to seize his goods, causing him harm. He asserted that the attachment was dissolved in his favor and sought damages for the conversion of his property, alleging that the defendant took possession of it improperly and refused to return it despite his demands.	The defendant argued that the attachment was lawful and based on probable cause, citing that the plaintiff had an outstanding debt. The defendant maintained that the plaintiff could not successfully pursue claims for malicious prosecution or trover due to the pendency of the appeal concerning the original attachment decisions and asserted that the execution was valid under existing legal judgments.

Anna Schmidt initiated a legal case against Michael Bauer and others, with the case being recorded in the Illinois Appellate Court on May 8, 1889. The proceedings took place in Cook County, Illinois, and were handled by Judge Joseph E. Gary. The dispute centered around a judgment entered by confession based on a warrant of attorney. Schmidt's appeal contended that the warrant was joint and improperly authorized a judgment against her alone. The case record included a note allegedly related to the dispute, but there was no bill of exceptions provided to clarify evidentiary matters. Consequently, the court relied on the presumption that the judgment entered was valid on its face, despite the lack of evidence included in the record.	Anna Schmidt's main arguments focused on the assertion that the warrant of attorney was joint, meaning it did not give sufficient authority for a judgment to be confessed against her individually. She contested the validity of the note presented in court, claiming it was not the same as the one originally referenced in the case. Schmidt sought to have the judgment vacated, asserting procedural and evidentiary errors in the entry of the judgment.	The defendants, represented by attorney Francis Lackner, argued that the judgment was valid as entered. They contended that the court was justified in presuming the evidence presented supported the judgment since no bill of exceptions was available to dispute this presumption. The defendants maintained that the entry of judgment, conducted in term time, complied with the applicable legal requirements and that the absence of additional evidence did not undermine the validity of the judgment.

In the case of Harry E. Holmes v. The City of Mattoon, the events unfolded in the year 1884, specifically on September 27, when the Illinois Supreme Court rendered its decision. The case originated from a legal dispute involving the city of Mattoon, located in Illinois. The appeal was brought forth by the city to the Appellate Court for the Third District, following a previous judgment from the County Court of Coles County, presided over by Judge Charles Bennett. The contention arose over the legality of an act from 1879 that permitted municipal corporations, like the city of Mattoon, to appeal court decisions without the requirement of posting a bond, a standard procedure in most civil cases. The plaintiff, Harry E. Holmes, challenged this act, arguing that it was unconstitutional as it supposedly constituted local and special legislation. However, the defense argued that municipal corporations act as agents of the State and should therefore be exempt from such requirements when they pursue legal action for the public good. The court evaluated these claims, emphasizing the sovereign powers of the State in legal proceedings and the constitutional validity of the act in question.	The plaintiff, Harry E. Holmes, claimed that the act of 1879 allowing municipal corporations to appeal without providing a bond was unconstitutional. He argued that it violated the provisions against local and special legislation outlined in the state constitution. Holmes contended that requiring municipalities to follow standard legal procedures, including bond requirements, was essential for maintaining the integrity and fairness of the judicial process.	The City of Mattoon, represented by Mr. T. L. McGrath, defended against the plaintiff's claims by asserting that the act of 1879 was constitutionally valid. The city argued that it was acting in the public interest, not for private gain, and that municipal corporations, as instruments of the State, should have the same exemptions granted to the State itself. They posited that the act did not contravene any constitutional provisions regarding local or special legislation.

The case involves Blanche Latimer, a six-year-old girl, against The Illinois Central Railroad Company for trespass. The incident occurred on June 14, 1887, in DeWitt County, Illinois, when the child was riding as a passenger on a train operated by the defendant. The conductor forcibly removed her from the train at a location that was not a regular station, approximately half a mile from the designated depot. Latimer's uncle had placed her on the train, intending for her to be taken home to Clinton, which was four and a half miles away. After she was ejected, the child ran back towards the depot crying and was allegedly traumatized, leading to functional heart issues according to medical testimony presented during the trial. The Circuit Court's initial judgment favored Latimer, and the Appellate Court upheld this decision, prompting the railroad company to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Latimer claimed that the railroad company committed trespass by improperly and forcibly ejecting her from the train at an incorrect location that was not a regular station. She argued this act caused her significant distress and medical issues. The plaintiff sought damages for the wrongful act, emphasizing that railroad companies are not permitted to remove passengers at "out-of-the-way places" within the corporate limits of a station from which they are entitled to travel.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that they had the lawful right to remove any passenger who failed to pay the fare from the train, arguing that the removal was appropriate because it was within the corporate limits of the depot. They also asserted that the definitions of "regular station" were misapplied during the trial. The defendant sought to have the suit dismissed on procedural grounds, arguing that the lawsuit was initiated without the proper authority to represent Latimer as a minor.

In the case of **Lechner v. Surrells**, which took place in June 1886 in Illinois, the appellant couple, Lechner (husband and wife), faced a legal judgment against them that had been rendered by a justice of the peace. The couple appealed this judgment to the county court. On the first day of the June term of the court, the appeal was dismissed, and a procedendo was awarded shortly thereafter. The Lechners then filed a motion to set aside the default judgment against them, arguing that the husband was unable to attend court due to illness. Supporting their motion, the couple submitted affidavits stating that prior to the court's session, the husband had sent a letter to the plaintiff's attorney, explaining his inability to attend and requesting a continuance. However, due to a lack of communication from the plaintiff's attorney, the letter was not conveyed to their chosen legal representatives, leading to the default judgment. Despite their claims, the affidavits did not sufficiently present a meritorious defense, prompting the court to deny the motion.	The plaintiff, Surrells, claimed that the judgment obtained against the Lechners should stand as the couple failed to appear in court and did not provide adequate justification for their absence. The plaintiff contested the validity of the arguments made by the Lechners in their motion to set aside the default judgment.	The Lechners defended against the default judgment by claiming their husband’s severe illness prevented attendance at court, as demonstrated by a letter sent to the plaintiff's attorney requesting a continuance. They argued that their legal representatives were not properly notified due to the plaintiff's attorney's negligence, and they believed their absence was justified. However, they were ultimately unable to present a convincing meritorious defense in their appeal.

William H. Austin et al. v. Daniel N. Bainter took place in Hancock County, Illinois, with the Illinois Supreme Court involved in the proceedings. The case emerged from a mortgage foreclosure action where the plaintiff, Daniel N. Bainter, claimed against the defendants, William H. Austin and Albers, who executed a mortgage to secure the payment of two promissory notes originally made to one Ooulson. The notes, each for $2,833.33, had a six percent interest rate and were due in 1858 and 1859. After several legal developments, including an agreement in June 1860 between Bainter and the makers of the notes, a decree was issued showing that a sum of $1,948.36 was due, leading to a scheduled sale of the mortgaged premises. The defendants subsequently challenged this determination, resulting in the case being brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after a verdict had originally been found in favor of the defendant in error.	The plaintiff, Daniel N. Bainter, aimed to enforce the mortgage and seek a decree for the amount due on the promissory notes, which he argued had accrued interest as per their agreement. He contended that the agreement allowed for a ten percent interest rate on the unpaid balance and sought to validate the foreclosure of the mortgage based on the unpaid debt.	The defendants, represented by Austin and Albers, contended that the jury's finding was incorrect and that the evidence did not support the plaintiff's claim for the amounts stated in the decree. They argued that the decree was calculated improperly and that the interest charged exceeded what was contractually agreed upon, seeking to have the decree revised or overturned based on those grounds.

Patrick Murray, a bachelor, owned a lot in Springfield, Illinois, and died intestate in Texas on August 10, 1860, leaving no personal estate, debts, or property aside from the lot, valued at $700. His only surviving blood relative was a sister, who had married Matthew Glancy, who later obtained letters of administration for Murray's estate on September 25, 1867. Glancy filed an inventory showing no personal property and sought to create debts against Murray's estate to justify a sale of the lot, spending $30 on legal and administrative fees. Glancy published a notice for creditors and, after presenting a petition to the county court to sell the lot for these artificially created debts, faced opposition from Johanna Fitzgerald, an heir. The county court granted the sale, prompting Fitzgerald to seek to reverse the order through a writ of error to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Johanna Fitzgerald, the plaintiff, argued that the county court's order to sell Patrick Murray’s lot was unjust, as there were no legitimate debts at the time of his death. She contended that the administrator, Matthew Glancy, improperly created debts for personal expenses, and that the sale of the real estate for such fabricated claims was contrary to the law, which prohibits selling a decedent's estate to cover debts that were not present at the time of their death.	Matthew Glancy, the defendant, maintained that the county court's approval of the order to sell the estate was valid, arguing that as an administrator, he was entitled to recoup administrative expenses incurred during the process. He also contended that the absence of personal property warranted the sale of real estate to satisfy any claims that arose during the administration of the estate, including the expenditures he claimed were necessary for managing the estate.

In the case of Merchants’ Navigation Company v. Maria Amsden, which took place on June 10, 1885, in Chicago, Illinois, the plaintiff, Maria Amsden, suffered personal injuries following a collision involving the propeller vessel "William J." and the bridge over the Chicago River at State Street. During the incident, Amsden was crossing the bridge on a streetcar. The trial led to a verdict in favor of Amsden, and she was awarded $2,000. The Merchants’ Navigation Company contested this decision by appealing for a writ of error. Amsden's legal team presented evidence to establish the defendant's ownership of the vessel at the time of the incident, including a copy of the vessel's enrollment record and a bill of sale from the previous owner, the Detroit Dry Dock Company. The admissibility of these documents was confirmed in court, asserting that they sufficiently indicated that the defendant was the owner of the vessel, thus liable for the accident. The court also ruled that complaints regarding the evidence’s exclusion related to mitigation of damages were unfounded, as the case was strictly compensatory in nature.	Maria Amsden's primary argument was that she suffered personal injuries due to the negligence of the Merchants’ Navigation Company, whose vessel collided with the bridge while she was on a streetcar. She claimed she was entitled to damages as compensation for her injuries, which were corroborated by evidence that established the defendant’s ownership of the propeller at the time of the accident. Amsden sought a total of $2,000 in compensatory damages.	The Merchants’ Navigation Company contended that the damages awarded were excessive, arguing that the severity and permanence of Amsden's injuries were overstated. They challenged the admissibility of certain evidence intended to mitigate damages, asserting that the vessel's crew misinterpreted a newly introduced signaling code, which they believed contributed to the accident. The defendant claimed that this information was crucial and should have altered the outcome regarding their liability.

In the case of Frederick F. White v. Catharine Russell et al., decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875, the dispute centers around the estate of J. V. B. Bossman, who was in partnership with the plaintiff, Frederick F. White. The case arises from allegations that Bossman, while insolvent, purchased a property in Chicago using funds from the partnership and transferred the title to his wife, intending to shield the asset from creditors. After Bossman's death, his estate proved to be insolvent, and White sought to recover debts owed to the partnership. The estate's assets were significantly less than the debts, prompting White to present claims both against the partnership and Bossman's individual debts. Catharine Russell, Bossman’s widow, was involved as she inherited the property in question, which White argued was fraudulently conveyed to avoid creditor claims. The Circuit Court dismissed White's bill after the defendants filed a demurrer, leading White to appeal the decision.	Frederick F. White claimed that the conveyance of the property to Bossman's wife was fraudulent, designed to hinder and delay creditors. He sought relief to have the property subjected to the payment of the debts owed by the estate and the partnership, arguing that the fraudulent nature of the conveyance warranted equitable intervention.	Catharine Russell, on behalf of the estate, contended that the claim had been allowed against the probate estate and that only the administrator had the authority to pursue the property to satisfy debts. They argued that there was no need for White to file the suit, as proper legal procedures were not followed and there was a general rule that limited creditors from taking action without the administrator.

Robert R. Clark initiated an action of debt against Adolph Fick in 1889 in Cook County, Illinois, to recover rent on certain lands, which Clark claimed Fick occupied under a lease. Fick denied both the existence of a lease and his occupancy of the land during the period for which rent was sought. The case presented a notable conflict of evidence, leading to a contentious trial. The jury ultimately found in favor of Fick, which raised further scrutiny regarding whether that verdict was backed by evidence. Clark argued that the jury's decision was unfounded due to the overwhelming evidence supporting his claims, but the appellate court maintained that the jury's verdict would remain conclusive in cases of evenly balanced evidence. Legal representation for Clark was handled by Mr. Wm. A. Montgomery, while Fick was represented by Mr. J. P. W. Brown.	Robert R. Clark's main argument centered around his assertion that Adolph Fick was legally bound by a lease agreement for the land in question and owed rent for the period claimed. He contended that the evidence presented clearly supported his position, and therefore, he requested the court to overturn the jury's verdict in favor of Fick and grant him the owed rent.	Adolph Fick's primary defense was the outright denial of having entered into a lease agreement with Clark and asserting that he did not occupy the said land during the period in question. Fick argued that the evidence presented did not support Clark's claims and that the verdict reached by the jury reasonably reflected the conflict of evidence, effectively appealing to affirm the jury's decision.

The case "Benjamin F. Sanborn et al. v. James A. Benedict" involves a dispute between a farmer, James A. Benedict, and grain dealers, Benjamin F. and George W. Sanborn, along with Thomas Mahaffey. The events leading to the litigation took place near Pecatonica, Winnebago County, Illinois, in June 1872. Benedict and Benjamin Sanborn discussed a contract for the sale of 2,000 bushels of corn at fifty cents per bushel, with terms for delivery contingent upon Sanborn providing ten days' notice. Although Sanborn initially accepted the terms and made a $10 payment to Benedict, a dispute arose when Benedict, ready to deliver the corn, was met with refusal from the defendants to accept or pay for the corn. Consequently, Benedict filed an action for breach of contract, claiming damages after repeated refusals from the defendants. The jury trial confirmed the validity of the contract, leading to the plaintiff’s claims of breach due to the defendants' failure to notify Benedict regarding the delivery.	The plaintiff, James A. Benedict, claimed that the defendants breached their contract for the sale of corn by failing to accept delivery after he made it clear he was ready to deliver the corn within a reasonable time. Benedict argued that a valid contract existed for the sale of corn, and due to the defendants' refusal, he sought damages amounting to $1,000. He presented multiple counts highlighting his readiness to deliver the corn, the agreement terms, and the defendants’ continuous refusal to receive the corn.	The defendants, Benjamin F. and George W. Sanborn, contended that the contract constituted an absolute sale and argued that the contract itself was invalidated due to a lack of actual possession of the corn at the time of the contract. They claimed that Benedict could not recover damages as he failed to tender the corn appropriately and argued for a new trial based on the instructions given to the jury, asserting that no obligation to pay arose until they made a demand for delivery.

In January 1873, in Edgar County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving Charles Bodine and Jacob Mason as defendants against Henry M. Swisher, acting on behalf of William C. Walker, as the plaintiff. The case was a debt action on a replevin bond, wherein Swisher sought to recover damages that a jury had assessed at $850 plus interest stemming from a prior bond agreement, leading to a total of $994.50. During the trial, the jury delivered a verdict that specified damages but did not clearly stipulate a total debt amount. Consequently, based on this verdict, a judgment was made to recover a total of $2,000 in debt and $994.50 in damages, in addition to court costs. The defendants challenged the verdict, asserting that the jury had not adequately articulated both debt and damages. Following this, the judge attempted to amend the record to reflect both amounts, leading to further dispute regarding the legitimacy of this amendment without the consent of the jury or the defendants’ counsel. Ultimately, the court needed to review whether the procedures followed conformed to correct legal practices.	The plaintiff, Henry M. Swisher, claimed that the jury had awarded him damages in a replevin bond case, amounting to $850 with an additional interest that brought the total to $994.50. He sought to recover these amounts through legal action as per the jury's verdict, which concluded in his favor without addressing the full amount of the debt, which necessitated a total judgment that included the asserted debt plus damages.	The defendants, Charles Bodine and Jacob Mason, contended that the judgment was flawed because the jury's verdict only included an assessment of damages without specifying the total debt amount. They argued that the trial court's decision to later amend the verdict to include the debt was improper and lacked the necessary consent from either the jury or their counsel, rendering the judgment invalid according to correct legal protocol.

The case "National School Furnishing Company v. William O. Cole et al." took place in Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a court decision on February 13, 1889. The key individuals involved included the National School Furnishing Company (the appellant) and William O. Cole along with other parties (the appellees). The issue arose from a transaction involving a sale of Dakota school bonds that were later discovered to be forged. The plaintiff claimed that they paid $631.50 through an express company for these bonds, after inspecting the documentation provided. The appellant's role consisted mainly of facilitating the transaction by notifying the appellees of the bond availability and collecting fees. The dispute centered on whether the appellant was liable as a vendor for the authenticity of the bonds and if they should be held accountable for the forged documents presented during the sale.	The plaintiff claimed that they made a payment to the express company for school bonds procured through the National School Furnishing Company, believing those bonds to be authentic based on accompanying documents. They argued that since the appellant was involved in the transaction, they should be held responsible for the authenticity and genuineness of the bonds.	The defendant contended that they were not the actual vendor of the bonds and that the sale was completed between the appellees and the entities that forwarded the bonds. They argued that the plaintiffs had independently inspected and accepted the bonds, thus assuming full responsibility for their validity. The defendant maintained that the evidence did not support the finding that they guaranteed the genuineness of the bonds.

Eliza Jane Masters, as administratrix of the estate of Thomas Masters, filed a legal action against William Masters concerning a promissory note that William had executed in favor of Thomas during his lifetime. The case was initiated in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, and the trial took place with a jury. Following the jury's verdict, the court ruled in favor of William Masters, resulting in a personal judgment against Eliza Jane for the costs of the lawsuit. Eliza then appealed this decision to the Illinois Appellate Court, raising various errors, especially questioning the admission of evidence and the ruling on her motion for a new trial. A significant concern was that the judgment against Eliza was in her personal capacity, which she contested as improper since she had represented herself as an administratrix.	Eliza Jane Masters, as the plaintiff, argued that the court had made several errors in its rulings throughout the trial, particularly regarding evidence admission and the overruling of her motion for a new trial. She asserted her claim based on the promissory note and sought a reversal of the judgment that held her personally liable for the costs, insisting that such a judgment should instead reflect her role as administratrix of her deceased husband's estate.	William Masters, the defendant, contended that the judgments and rulings made by the Superior Court were appropriate and justified. His key argument was based on the jury’s verdict, which favored him, and he sought to uphold the court's decision that Eliza Jane was personally liable for the costs associated with the suit, as it was not evident from the record that she had acted only in a representative capacity.

On March 31, 1886, the Illinois Appellate Court reviewed a divorce case filed by Carrie L. Brown against her husband, William H. A. Brown, in Cook County, Illinois. The case concerned allegations that William was already married to another woman at the time of his marriage to Carrie, rendering their union invalid due to bigamy. The legal proceedings followed after Carrie filed a bill for divorce, asserting that she had a valid claim based on the existing marriage of William. During the full hearing of the case, the court examined affidavits from both parties. The chancellor ruled in Carrie's favor, ordering William to pay her $100 in solicitor’s fees, indicating grounds for the divorce complaint. Following the court's examination of the law regarding divorce and the definitions of marriage, the court affirmed its authority to grant temporary alimony and legal fees, emphasizing the legislature’s intention behind the Divorce Act.	Carrie L. Brown, the plaintiff, argued that she was entitled to a divorce from William H. A. Brown due to his existing marriage at the time of their marriage, thereby rendering their union invalid. She sought financial relief through the court, specifically requesting temporary alimony and coverage of her solicitor's fees, asserting that the circumstances of her marriage justified her claims under Section 15 of the Divorce Act.	William H. A. Brown, the defendant, contended that since his marriage to Carrie was void due to his prior existing spouse, the court lacked the authority to grant temporary alimony or legal fees under the Divorce Act. He argued that the legal definitions of "husband" and "wife" did not apply to their case, as no lawful marital relationship existed at the time of their union.

In September 1868, the case of Charles J. Wheeler v. John D. Randall was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in the city of Aurora, Illinois, where the plaintiff, John D. Randall, accused the defendant, Charles J. Wheeler, of deceit related to a transaction involving a flock of sheep. Randall claimed that Wheeler made false and fraudulent representations regarding the condition of the sheep he sold, specifically that the sheep were diseased with scab, an infectious disease affecting sheep. The case was presided over by Judge Richard Gr. Montony in the Court of Common Pleas before it was appealed. The plaintiff initially secured a verdict and judgment in his favor, prompting Wheeler to appeal the decision on the grounds that the necessary elements of fraud were not sufficiently established, particularly the requirement that Wheeler knew the representations he made were false.	The plaintiff, John D. Randall, argued that the defendant, Charles J. Wheeler, engaged in deceit by selling a flock of sheep while making false representations about their health. Randall sought damages for the fraudulent sale, claiming that the sheep were infected with scab, which was a contagious disease. He contended that Wheeler should be held accountable for the harm caused by such fraudulent misrepresentation and requested both actual damages and vindictive damages as a punishment for Wheeler's actions.	The defendant, Charles J. Wheeler, countered the claims by asserting that liability for deceit requires proof of knowledge that the statements made were false. Wheeler argued that while the representations could be deemed false, the plaintiff did not establish that he knew of their falsity at the time of the sale. He contended that incorrect jury instructions contributed to an erroneous verdict, particularly the allowance of vindictive damages for the alleged spreading of disease, which he argued was not illegal in itself. Wheeler requested the court to overturn the judgment on these grounds.

Samuel G. Smith and his wife, Mary A. Smith, were involved in a legal dispute with Nicholas Marc regarding the ownership of certain lots in the Ninawa Addition to the city of Peru, Illinois. The case was initiated during the February 1861 term, under the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. It centered around a mortgage that Samuel G. Smith had executed on March 2, 1853, to secure a loan from Alexander Cruikshank, granting him the power to sell the properties described if Smith defaulted on the loan. In December 1859, Cruikshank, through his attorney William Chumasero, sold the properties to Nicholas Marc when Smith defaulted. Smith's arguments hinged on his rights under the Illinois Homestead Act, claiming the properties were exempt from such sales. The case involved significant discussions about the legislative intent of the Homestead Act and whether the mortgage and subsequent sale were valid.	Nicholas Marc, the appellee, claimed ownership of the disputed properties based on a mortgage sale following a default by Samuel G. Smith. He argued that the sale conducted by Cruikshank was valid and that all necessary procedures were followed, making him the rightful owner. Marc sought to affirm the court’s recognition of his ownership and the legitimacy of the sale despite Smith’s claims regarding homestead protections.	Samuel G. Smith, the appellant, contended that the properties were protected under the Homestead Act, asserting that the sale was invalid as it did not meet the requirements for alienating a homestead. He argued that there was no formal release or waiver of the homestead rights established by the act and that the properties should be exempt from forced sales, requesting that the court recognize his rights to the properties as a homestead.

In the case of George Mentzer v. John L. Robinson, which took place in Cerro Gordo, Illinois, between July 1885 and May 1888, the two parties were equal partners in a tile and brick manufacturing business. George Mentzer primarily handled manufacturing, while John L. Robinson managed sales and bookkeeping, although his bookkeeping methods were reportedly disorganized. Tensions arose regarding the partnership's finances, leading to discussions about dissolving the partnership. They agreed on the settlement terms except for the outstanding debts and credits of the partnership. To clarify the accounts, a clerk was hired to organize the financial records. On May 7, 1888, they met to settle the accounts. Mentzer learned that many debts had been settled before the dissolution, which led him to refuse payment of the amount stated in the agreement, prompting Robinson to file suit for the unpaid balance. The court ruled on this case in February 1889, ultimately finding for the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, John L. Robinson, claimed that George Mentzer owed him $2,154.30 per their dissolution agreement, which included payment for Robinson's interest in the business and the outstanding book accounts. Robinson asserted that despite the claims of settled accounts, the amount due remained valid, and he sought judgment for the unpaid balance.	The defendant, George Mentzer, contended that the consideration he paid was based on the understanding of the book accounts showing approximately $1,975 due. He argued that since many accounts had been previously satisfied, he should not be liable for the full amount. Mentzer's defense hinged on the claim of partial failure of consideration, asserting that due to the inadequacies in the partnership's bookkeeping, he should receive a deduction from the amount owed.

In 1858, Edward L. Henrickson and Harry Reinback were partners in trade under the firm names Henrickson & Reinback and Reinback & Van Winkle. They faced various disputes regarding their partnership accounts and decided to submit these matters to arbitration. To formalize this agreement, they executed an arbitration bond valued at $5,000 with securities. However, the bond was lost, and during the arbitration process, the arbitrators awarded that Harry Reinback should pay $1,296.90 to the two partnership firms and also determined that the partners were entitled to equal shares of all uncollected assets. Subsequently, Henrickson filed a suit against Reinback for failing to comply with the arbitration award, claiming he hadn't received the awarded sum or his share of the outstanding assets. The case escalated to the Circuit Court, which ultimately ruled that the award's terms were too uncertain and dismissed Henrickson's claims, leading to Henrickson appealing the decision.	The plaintiff, Edward L. Henrickson, claimed that Harry Reinback failed to comply with the arbitration award. He alleged multiple breaches, including the non-payment of $1,296.90 and the failure to account for his share of uncollected assets and arbitration costs. Henrickson asserted he was ready to perform his obligations according to the award but faced Reinback's refusal. Additionally, Henrickson sought damages amounting to $2,000 due to Reinback's violations of the award.	The defendant, Harry Reinback, contended that the award was void due to uncertainty. He argued that the plaintiff did not adequately specify legal certainty regarding his interest in the award and that the amount claimed was ambiguous. Reinback's legal representatives filed a demurrer challenging the sufficiency of the allegations presented by Henrickson, asserting that the claims were not sufficiently grounded in the law and that the Circuit Court properly sustained their objections.

This case, titled "Cyrus P. Bradley, Appellant, v. Michael Geiselman, Appellee," arose in the mid-19th century, specifically June 1856, in Illinois. The legal dispute originated from an alleged trespass involving certain personal property. Michael Geiselman, the plaintiff, claimed ownership of the property based on a sale made to him by Elisha W. King and Henry A. Layton, who operated under the firm name H. A. Layton & Co. The defendant, Cyrus P. Bradley, contested the claim and pled the general issue. The case was initially brought to the Cook County Court of Common Pleas but was moved to Kane County for trial. During the trial presided over by Judge I. G. Wilson at the May term in 1855, significant procedural questions arose regarding the admissibility of a deposition of a witness, which was a critical part of the defendant's defense. The trial's pivotal issue involved whether the presence of the witness barred the defendant from using the deposition in evidence. Ultimately, the legal question was centered around evidentiary rights during the trial.	The plaintiff, Michael Geiselman, contended that he was the rightful owner of the personal property in question, based on a legitimate sale conducted by the firm H. A. Layton & Co. He sought to establish his claim against Cyrus P. Bradley, alleging that the latter had unlawfully seized his property. Geiselman aimed to demonstrate the legitimacy of his ownership as part of his legal argument.	The defendant, Cyrus P. Bradley, argued that he had a right to rely on his deposited evidence during the trial despite the presence of the witness. He maintained that the legal procedures allowed him to read the deposition in evidence, which was vital for his defense. Bradley contended that compelling him to abandon his deposition and rely on the witness called by the plaintiff would undermine the fairness of the trial and could lead to tampering and surprise advantages in litigation.

In the case of Uri S. Prout et al. v. Elmer Grout, the legal dispute originated in June 1874 in Lawrence County, Illinois. The action was initiated by Hath an R. Grout against Elmer Grout, leading to the issuance of a writ of attachment served on TJri S. Prout and George W. Prout, who were named as garnishees. The plaintiffs claimed that they, having issued a promissory note for $700 to Charles Lamott on August 30, 1867, made payments reducing the amount owed to $240 before the note was due on August 30, 1870. Elmer Grout claimed this note after it was assigned to him prior to the service of the summons. However, TJri S. Prout contended through an amended answer that the note had been levied and sold by a constable before it became due and that the purchaser, Wilkinson, held legal title. The circuit court ruled against the garnishees, stating they failed to provide sufficient defense against the attachment process, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiffs, represented by Hathan R. Grout, argued that the promissory note in question was valid and the garnishees, TJri S. Prout and George W. Prout, owed the remaining balance on the note at the time of the attachment. They contended that the garnishees had not disclosed accurate information regarding their indebtedness, leading to the initial judgment against them. Therefore, they requested enforcement of the attached debt and associated costs.	The defendants, TJri S. Prout and George W. Prout, argued that the court misapplied the law regarding the attachment of the promissory note since it should not have been levied upon under a writ of attachment but rather reached through garnishee process. They claimed that the note had already been sold before the attachment process, rendering the attachment invalid. Their defense hinged on the assertion that the court erred in allowing the attachment as well as in imposing costs against them without basis.

In 1864, Samuel McCarthy obtained a permit from the Board of Public Works in Chicago to occupy part of Clark Street for up to four months, allowing him to store building materials while constructing a building on a nearby lot. His bond conditioned that he would restore the street and sidewalk to good condition after use and indemnify the city against any damages incurred due to his activities. However, during this time, McCarthy excavated a large pit in the sidewalk, which became a hazard. In November 1864, a passerby named Edwin R. Beckley fell into this pit and sustained injuries, leading him to sue the City of Chicago. The city paid $6,000 in damages to Beckley following a successful judgment against it. McCarthy and his associates were accused of breaching the indemnity bond by failing to protect the city from the resultant lawsuit and its financial liabilities.	The City of Chicago, as the plaintiff, claimed that McCarthy breached the indemnity bond by not covering the damages they had to pay following Beckley’s accident. They argued that McCarthy's excavation was the primary cause of the hazard that led to Beckley's injuries and subsequent lawsuit. The city sought to hold McCarthy accountable for all related legal costs and damages due to his failure to maintain the sidewalk and public safety.	McCarthy contested the validity of the bond and asserted that the Board of Public Works acted without authority in requiring the bond with specific conditions. He also challenged the allegations regarding the variance between the original claims made and the proof presented during the trial, arguing that the city’s additional failure to maintain safety measures (like lighting) contributed to the incident and that he should not bear full liability.

In September 1873, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed the case of Lydia Sturman v. Jacob Streamer et al., stemming from events that occurred in Livingston County, Illinois, with the initial filing in May 1871. The case involved a dispute over a mortgage on a piece of land owned by Lydia Sturman and her husband. To secure a debt, they executed a mortgage to Jonathan Duff, who later sold it to Eichard Evans. Lydia's husband had sold livestock for $752.81, but issues arose when he assigned the collection of a related note to attorney Alfred E. Harding. The legal complications involved contrasting claims about the intended application of collected funds for paying off the mortgage. Lydia claimed that the proceeds from the judgment collected should have gone towards their mortgage, whereas Streamer asserted that the arrangement was to pay different debts he had against the Sturman family. The court had to evaluate conflicting testimonies and evidence, ultimately relying heavily on the procedural aspects of the law and the presentation of ownership.	Lydia Sturman claimed that the proceeds from the judgment collected by her husband's attorney were misappropriated and should have been applied to the mortgage. She alleged that the agreement with Streamer was that the debt recovery would be used to satisfy their mortgage obligations, which Streamer failed to honor.	Jacob Streamer contended that the note assigned to Harding was meant to be sued in his name and that any collections were intended for debts that he held against the Sturman family. Streamer insisted that he acted legally in his capacity as the holder of the mortgage and the judgment, maintaining that his arrangements with the Sturmans were different from what Lydia claimed.

In September 1876, the legal case Rock Valley Paper Company v. Morris H. Nixon etc. was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a promissory note issued by the Rock Valley Paper Company and was presided over by the Hon. Henry Booth in the Circuit Court of Cook County. The plaintiff, Rock Valley Paper Company, claimed that Morris H. Nixon and others owed them a debt related to the note. The service of process was executed by delivering a copy of the summons to the president of the company, Albert Felsenthal. The case primarily revolved around whether the service was sufficient and if the evidence presented by the plaintiff was valid, especially concerning the execution of the promissory note, which was signed by both the company and its president. Various objections were made regarding procedural matters and the sufficiency of evidence, but the court found these objections without merit.	The Rock Valley Paper Company argued that the service of process was properly executed as the summons was delivered to its president, Albert Felsenthal. The plaintiff contended that the promissory note was a valid instrument and that the absence of opposing evidence warranted a judgment in their favor. They claimed a total of $556.22 was due, and sought enforcement of the debt represented by the note.	The defendants argued that the delivery of the writ was not executed properly, as the return should have explicitly stated that a copy was "left" with the president. They also claimed a variance existed because the declaration described the note as being executed solely by the defendant, while it was signed by both the company and Felsenthal. Furthermore, they objected to the admission of an affidavit included in the evidence, stating that it was unnecessary and irrelevant to the case.

In January 1862, a legal dispute arose between David Marckle and Samuel F. Haskins, taking place in Morgan County, Illinois. The case initially began when Haskins sued Marckle before a justice of the peace regarding a sale involving a horse. The justice ruled in favor of Marckle; however, Haskins appealed to the Circuit Court, which ultimately ruled in Haskins' favor, awarding him seventy-five dollars. Disagreement existed regarding the nature of the sale, specifically whether Marckle was aware that Haskins was acting as an agent for his brother during the transaction. The key points of contention involved the warranty of the horse's soundness and whether Marckle knew he was dealing with an agent. Testimonies from various witnesses conflicted on these issues but mainly suggested that Marckle believed he was negotiating directly with Haskins and the horse's soundness was called into question.	Haskins, as the plaintiff, claimed that Marckle had made an agreement to purchase a horse that was represented to be sound at the time of sale. Haskins argued that as the agent of his brother, he had the authority to sell the horse and that any warranty related to the horse’s soundness should extend to him despite being an agent. He sought enforcement of the warranty and payment for the horse.	Marckle, the defendant, contended that he was unaware that Haskins was acting as an agent for his brother at the time of the bargain. He argued that since he believed he was contracting with Haskins personally, any warranty for the horse's condition could not be imposed on him as the agent was not liable. Furthermore, Marckle sought to affirm the initial judgment from the justice of the peace, claiming that there was no clear evidence that the horse was unsound at the time of sale.

The case "St. Louis, Jacksonville and Chicago Railroad Co. v. James H. Lurton et al." took place in Illinois, with the legal action initiated in 1870 surrounding a breach of contract dispute. The plaintiffs, James H. Lurton and his co-plaintiffs, arranged with the Jacksonville, Alton and St. Louis Railroad Company in 1858 for the construction of a bridge over their property as part of an agreement where the plaintiffs would not contest the railroad’s right of way. However, the railroad company failed to build the bridge or grade an alternative crossing by the time the railroad was completed in January 1866, resulting in the plaintiffs suffering financial losses when they later sold the property for less than it was worth had the railroad fulfilled its contractual obligations. The railroad company was subsequently consolidated into the St. Louis, Jacksonville and Chicago Railroad Company, which inherited the agreement's liabilities. The plaintiffs claimed damages due to the failure to perform the contract, while the defendant argued there was no unreasonable delay in completing the railroad and that the plaintiffs' sale of the lots hindered the fulfillment of the contract.	The plaintiffs claimed that the railroad company failed to construct a bridge or passway as stipulated in their contract. They argued that because of this failure, they sold their lots for $2,500 less than their value would have been had the railroad fulfilled its obligations. They requested damages to compensate for the financial loss incurred due to the non-construction of the bridge.	The railroad company argued that it did not unreasonably delay the completion of the project and claimed that the plaintiffs had sold the lots before the deadline for bridge construction, which eliminated the company's responsibility under the contract. The defense focused on the assertion that the plaintiffs could not recover damages for delaying the road's completion as it was never stipulated in the contract.

The case "The Trustees of Schools v. John S. Wright et al." was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court and revolves around a transaction that occurred in May 1835 in La Salle County, Illinois. The trustees of schools in the township filed a bill in chancery in 1845 against John T. Temple and several others, including John S. Wright, regarding a sale of school land. During the initial sale, Temple purchased 520 acres of land for $3,104.40 with promissory notes as payment, guaranteed by sureties. The transaction saw various individuals involved, including a school commissioner and the county commissioners' court. The trustees alleged that the purchase money remained unpaid and sought to charge the lots with this debt and have them sold to satisfy the amount due. Over the years, the title for the land was transferred multiple times, eventually being conveyed to John S. Wright, who claimed to have made full payment and was unaware of any outstanding debts related to the purchase. The case became complicated as the claims involved various defenses regarding the knowledge of the unpaid purchase money.	The plaintiffs, the Trustees of Schools, claimed that John S. Wright and his grantees owed unpaid purchase money for the land purchased from the school commissioner, alleging that the lots should be sold to satisfy this debt. They argued that although the purchase money notes had been given, no mortgage was executed to secure the payment of those notes, thus creating a lien on the land.	John S. Wright and his co-defendants insisted they were bona fide purchasers for value, claiming they had purchased the lots in good faith and without knowledge of any unpaid purchase money. They maintained that they paid the full purchase price, and thus, no further claims could be made against them in connection with the original seller's obligations.

The case "Mary Ann White et al., Administrators, etc., v. The County of Bond" took place in 1871, in Bond County, Illinois. The plaintiffs, who were the administrators of the estate of Stephen D. White, brought the case against the County of Bond, following the death of the deceased due to alleged negligence in maintaining a bridge over the east fork of Shoal Creek. The claim asserted that the county failed to keep the bridge in good repair, which directly contributed to White's fatal accident. The case was initially heard in the Bond Circuit Court, where a general demurrer by the defendant (the County of Bond) was upheld, resulting in a judgment against the plaintiffs for costs. Dissatisfied with this outcome, the plaintiffs appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs contended that the County of Bond was liable for wrongful neglect in maintaining a bridge, which led to the death of Stephen D. White. They argued that this neglect constituted a failure of duty on the part of the county's officers, warranting compensation for the damages suffered as a result of this negligence.	The County of Bond defended itself by asserting that it could not be held liable for negligence in this instance, according to precedents set by previous cases. They argued that unless there is a statute specifically allowing such a private action against a county for neglecting corporate duties, they are not liable for injuries resulting from defective highways or bridges. The defense drew parallels to past rulings, emphasizing the distinction between municipal and quasi-corporations and maintained that counties are not subject to the same levels of liability.

In the case of Michael Moritz v. Francis A. Hoffman et al., which took place in Du Page County, Illinois, around 1864, the legal dispute arose when Michael Moritz, the plaintiff, filed a bill in chancery against Francis A. Hoffman, his wife, and Alexander Siller, to subject certain real estate to the payment of a judgment that Moritz had obtained against Hoffman. The core issue revolved around alleged fraudulent conveyances made by Hoffman to his wife, which Moritz claimed were intended to evade his debts. The case was heard in November 1863 at the Circuit Court of Du Page County, where the court ruled against Moritz, dismissing his claims. Moritz subsequently appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, asserting various errors in the lower court's handling of the case, particularly concerning the nature of the conveyances and the legitimacy of his claims as a creditor.	Michael Moritz, the plaintiff, argued that the conveyances made by Francis A. Hoffman to Theodore Hoffman and Bertha Siller were fraudulent and void against his judgment, as he claimed to be a creditor at the time of these transactions. Moritz sought to have the court decree that these conveyances should be subject to his judgment and execution, asserting that he was entitled to relief for debts owed to him.	The defendants, Francis A. Hoffman and his associates, contended that the conveyances were legitimate, voluntary transfers made while Hoffman was solvent and without fraudulent intent. They argued that Moritz was not a bona fide creditor at the time of the transactions in question, asserting that he had no right to attack the validity of the conveyances since they were made to secure a home for Hoffman's family, and the transactions did not impair Moritz's rights as a creditor.

In the case of Mart A. Marmon v. Thomas F. Harwood et al., which took place in McLean County, Illinois, the case arises from a creditor’s bill filed by Thomas F. and Willis S. Harwood against Maria Paist and others, including Mary A. Marmon, in March 1888. The plaintiffs aimed to set aside certain deeds executed by Maria Paist that conveyed real estate to Mary A. Marmon and Mary L. Cheney. The plaintiffs had previously obtained a judgment against Maria Paist concerning a promissory note she had signed with her son, O. L. Cheney. After the plaintiffs sought to enforce their judgment through an execution, no property could be found to satisfy the debt, prompting the lawsuit. The central allegation was that the conveyances were fraudulent as they occurred while Maria Paist was indebted to the plaintiffs, therefore hindering the collection of their judgment. Evidence suggested that Paist had conveyed properties worth significantly more than her debts without receiving any consideration in return. The case was initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs at the circuit court level, leading to an appeal by Mary A. Marmon.	The plaintiffs, Thomas F. and Willis S. Harwood, argued that the conveyances made by Maria Paist to her daughter and daughter-in-law were fraudulent. They claimed these transactions served to hinder their ability to collect on a judgment against Paist, as the conveyed properties were not accompanied by any consideration and exceeded the value of Paist's debts. The plaintiffs sought to have the deeds set aside to allow their judgment to be collected from the properties in question.	Mary A. Marmon, representing the defense, asserted that the conveyances from Maria Paist were not fraudulent against pre-existing creditors, as Paist had retained sufficient property to cover her debts at the time of the transfer. Marmon maintained that she had no knowledge of any alleged fraud and contended that the transaction was legitimate. She sought to have the initial ruling on the fraud reversed, arguing that the court's decision was based on an erroneous interpretation of the circumstances surrounding the conveyance.

The case of *The Chicago West Division Railway Company v. William A. Becker, Admr.* took place in Chicago, Illinois, with the final judgment issued on May 16, 1889. The case emerged following the tragic incident that occurred on the evening of November 28, 1885, when Henry J. Becker, an eight or nine-year-old boy, was fatally injured by a streetcar operated by the Chicago West Division Railway Company. Witnesses testified that the boy was pushed from the car by the conductor, which resulted in him being run over by the streetcar. The incident transpired on Blue Island Avenue near its intersection with Henry Street. The plaintiff, William A. Becker, the boy's administrator, claimed damages for the wrongful death of his son. There were no eyewitnesses to the accident, and the testimony relied on hearsay evidence from two boys who communicated the child’s statements about the incident after he was injured. The trial began in the Superior Court of Cook County, where a verdict favored the plaintiff. The case was subsequently appealed to the Appellate Court and then to the Illinois Supreme Court, questioning the admissibility of the deceased's remarks after the accident.	The plaintiff's main argument was that the streetcar conductor had negligently pushed Henry J. Becker off the car, leading to the boy’s fatal injuries. The plaintiff sought damages on behalf of the deceased child, contending that the railway company was liable for the wrongful death due to the alleged actions of its employee. The evidence presented hinged on the statements made by the child after the accident regarding the conductor’s actions.	The defendant, the Chicago West Division Railway Company, defended itself by challenging the admissibility of the statements made by the deceased child, asserting that they were not part of the res gestae and thus should not be considered as valid evidence. The railway company contended that the evidence presented did not sufficiently establish that the conductor was at fault and sought to have the judgment of the lower courts reversed, arguing that the trial court erred in admitting hearsay statements made by the deceased after the incident.

David Puterbaugh filed a case against Charles B. Smith and others in the Illinois Supreme Court regarding the constitutionality of the amendatory act of 1879, which permitted circuit judges to impose summary punishments for refusing to obey subpoenas issued by notaries public in depositions related to cases in other states. The events transpired in Stephenson County, Illinois, where Puterbaugh had been subpoenaed to give a deposition in Kansas. Subsequently, he was imprisoned by order of the circuit court without a jury trial. The case raised significant questions about the rights guaranteed under the Illinois state constitution, particularly the right to a jury trial in criminal prosecutions, and whether the summary punishment without a trial undermined those rights.	The plaintiff, Puterbaugh, argued that the portion of the 1879 statute allowing for summary punishment for disobeying notary subpoenas violated his constitutional right to a trial by jury. He contended that the summary punishment system effectively denied individuals due process and circumvented established legal protections.	The defendants maintained that the enforcement of court authority during trials was legitimate and necessary for the administration of justice. They argued that the legislature had the power to provide for contempt proceedings and asserted that the statute’s intended purpose was to uphold the court's authority.

In 1834, David L. W. Jones died intestate, owning seventy-seven acres of land near Chicago, Illinois. He left a widow, Frances, and a young daughter, Margaret. A man named Whitlock became the estate's administrator in 1835. In December 1836, the Illinois Legislature passed an act allowing the administrator to sell the deceased's property to pay debts, with proceeds intended to support the widow and daughter. In April 1837, Seth Paine was appointed as the new administrator. He sold the land in July 1837 to Harrison Hewhall at a sale price of $10 per acre, with proceeds purportedly meant to fund Margaret's education. Margaret, who was two years old at the time of the sale, later married Timothy E. Young. In October 1853, the Youngs initiated an ejectment action for the recovery of the land, willing to repay Hewhall for his expenses. However, it was determined in a previous Supreme Court case that the original sale was void since debts weren't properly established, invalidating the administrator's authority. After this decision, Orlando Davidson, who had a claim related to the property, filed a bill seeking to bar the Youngs from asserting legal claims to the land, arguing that Margaret was equitably estopped from claiming it.	The plaintiff, Orlando Davidson, argued that even though the sale by the administrator was void due to lack of authority and improper debt assessment, Margaret Young should be equitably estopped from contesting the title to the land. Davidson contended that Margaret's prior consent to the sale, her knowledge of the sale's purpose for her education, and her actions following the sale created an equitable estoppel. He sought a decree to restrain the Youngs from claiming ownership or possession of the property.	The defendants, Timothy Young and Margaret Young, contended that the original sale conducted by the administrator was void and without legal standing, hence, the plaintiff's claim to assert title over the land should also fail. They argued that no equitable estoppel should apply because Margaret, as an infant, made no fraudulent misrepresentation. The defense also pointed out that any actions taken by Margaret after reaching the age of majority did not amount to a ratification of the prior sale.

In January 1868, four individuals—William Wallace, William O. Carpenter, Augustus A. Carpenter, and Hall—entered into an agreement to purchase an 80-acre tract of land located near Chicago for $90 per acre. Each party agreed to share equally in the financial responsibilities of the purchase, with the understanding that the title would be held in the name of William O. Carpenter for convenience. As the process unfolded, $250 was paid as earnest money by Carpenter, who also agreed to advance funds on behalf of the others. Wallace, residing in Ohio, was responsible for his share of the first payment but returned home to arrange his finances. Meanwhile, the group sold their interest in the property for a $4,800 profit to Ford and Heisler, with a portion of this amount retained as a deposit. After the sale was agreed upon, Carpenter notified Wallace of purported title defects, misleading him into thinking the contract had fallen through. Unbeknownst to Wallace, the sale proceeded without his knowledge, and the proceeds were divided among the Carpenters and Hall. Wallace remained unaware until 1870 when he discovered the fraud. He subsequently sought legal relief, alleging misrepresentation and claiming his rightful share of the profits.	Wallace contended that he was entitled to one-quarter of the profits from the land sale as the contract was made on his behalf. He argued that the actions of Carpenter and Hall in misleading him constituted fraud, and he claimed that he had never been in default in his obligations regarding the financial arrangements. Wallace requested the court to grant him relief and an accounting of the profits generated from the land sale.	The Carpenters argued that the agreement between the parties was void under the Statute of Frauds, claiming it lacked requisite written documentation. They maintained that because the contract was unenforceable, Wallace was not entitled to any profits. They resisted Wallace’s claims by asserting that he had no legitimate entitlement to the money advanced as it was merely formalized under an invalid agreement.

In September 1876, the case of Jacob Darst v. Jacob Gale et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court concerning a legal dispute over real estate in Peoria. Jacob Darst, the plaintiff, filed a bill against defendants Jacob Gale, Sidney Pulsifer, and Erastus D. Hardin. The dispute centered around a deed of trust executed on October 1, 1859, by the Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company, intended to secure payment on ten bonds valued at $1,000 each. Darst aimed to halt the sale of the real estate by the defendants under this deed, claiming it as a cloud on his title. The defendants answered with a cross-bill, seeking to prevent Darst from taking possession, correct a description mistake in the trust document, and appoint a receiver. After hearings on the original and cross-bills, the court dismissed Darst's bill and granted relief requested by the defendants. Following this decision, Darst appealed.	Jacob Darst, the plaintiff, argued that the deed of trust was void due to the Peoria Marine and Fire Insurance Company's improper execution of authority. He sought to enjoin the defendants from selling the property and requested that the court declare the deed void to clear the title to the real estate he claimed.
