The defendants contended that the deed of trust was valid and enforceable, asserting that despite any questionable authority, the corporation's directors had knowledge of and acquiesced to the pledge of the bonds as security for the loan. They sought to enjoin Darst from taking possession of the property and to correct the property description in the deed.

On September 1, 1873, in Whiteside County, Illinois, Jacob Bryson (plaintiff) brought a case against David M. Crawford (defendant) concerning a contract for the sale of land. According to the agreement, Bryson was to pay a total of $1,188.33 in installments, with specific payments scheduled: $300 on November 1, 1870; $250 on June 1, 1871; and $638.33 on November 1, 1871. In exchange for these payments, Crawford would execute a deed for the land after the second installment was paid, with Bryson securing the remaining balance with a mortgage. The contract emphasized that timely payment was essential. On June 1, 1871, Crawford sent Bryson a notice that the $250 payment was due and warned that failure to pay within ten days would result in forfeiture of the contract. After the ten days, Crawford declared the contract forfeited for non-payment and demanded that Bryson vacate the property, despite Bryson not having paid the due amount. Bryson remained on the property but eventually rented it from Crawford, acknowledging him as the landlord. The case was tried before a jury, which ruled in favor of Crawford.	Bryson argued that Crawford was in default for not tendering a deed before declaring the contract forfeited. Bryson contended that mutual abandonment had occurred, and he sought to recover the money paid under the contract, asserting that Crawford's failure to provide the deed invalidated the forfeiture.	Crawford maintained that Bryson was the one in default for failing to make the required payment of $250 on time. He asserted that he was not obligated to provide the deed until the payment was made. Crawford argued that Bryson's acknowledgment of tenancy further validated the forfeiture because Bryson continued to stay on the property and rented it from him, which implicitly accepted the contract's termination.

The case "Joseph H. Reynolds v. James F. McCormick" was adjudicated in January 1872 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Adams County, Illinois, between two key individuals: Joseph H. Reynolds (the plaintiff) and James F. McCormick (the defendant). The primary issue was whether Reynolds was the sole owner of certain property that had been replevied (recovered) or if McCormick had a claim to the property as well. Both men were former partners practicing medicine together and claimed differing rights to the property. The court examined testimonies from both parties, which were contradictory, thus complicating the determination of ownership. The lower court's instructions to the jury were challenged by Reynolds, who contended that his claim of ownership should prevail, particularly if the only basis for McCormick's claim was a purchase. Ultimately, the case turned on the question of whether the property was jointly owned as partnership property.	Joseph H. Reynolds claimed that he was the sole owner of the property and requested its immediate return. He argued that the defendant's only claim was based on a purchase from him, which he disputed. Reynolds maintained that the evidence showed he had the rightful ownership and possession of the property, asserting that McCormick could not claim ownership without a solid basis beyond just his assertion.	James F. McCormick responded by asserting that he was entitled to the property because he had purchased a half interest from Reynolds while they were partners. He argued that both he and Reynolds had shared ownership of the property as partners. McCormick contended that the evidence favored his claim of purchase and that the jury should find in his favor based on the established facts.

The case of James P. Craig v. The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. Harvey Nevill took place in Randolph County, Illinois, with the final judgment issued in June 1868. The core issue arose from the operations of the Randolph County Plank Road Company, which was incorporated in 1853 to construct a plank road from Chester to Sparta, utilizing existing public highways for its construction. By 1859, the company faced difficulties in maintaining the road, largely due to the neglect of the adjacent public highway, which had fallen into disuse as travelers diverted to the plank road. In January 1868, the company announced its intention to cease toll collection due to financial struggles and indicated that the road would be closed if it was not acquired by the public. This led to the county's attorney filing a lawsuit, duly verified by Harvey Nevill, to prevent the company from closing the road and to ensure it remained accessible to the public. The case escalated through the court system, raising questions about the company's rights and responsibilities toward the public's use of the plank road, particularly in light of its public status and the company's duty to maintain it.	The plaintiff, represented by Harvey Nevill, argued that the Randolph County Plank Road Company could not obstruct or abandon its franchise without legislative authority and that doing so would create a public nuisance. The plaintiff requested a court order to prevent the company from enclosing the road and obstructing public access, arguing that the road had become essential for community travel and that the company's published notice indicated an intent to abandon the road, thus infringing on public rights.	The defendants (the plank road company) contended that they had constructed the road over mostly private property and that they were legally justified in ceasing operations without public obligation. They claimed that the public highway had not been officially vacated and that any neglect was due to public authorities' failure, not their own. Furthermore, they denied that their actions constituted a nuisance, asserting the legality of their ownership and use.

The case "Thomas Madden v. Abram Cooper" arose in 1868 in Jersey County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Thomas Madden, contested a judgment from the Circuit Court that sanctioned the sale of the real estate owned by Elisha Madden, the deceased, to settle outstanding debts. Elisha Madden had passed away, leaving behind 160 acres of land and personal property valued at approximately $310.87, while his debts totaled around $703.30. The court was petitioned by the administrator, John M. Davis, to facilitate the sale. The case principally examined whether proper notice of the sale had been given according to statutory requirements and whether the court had jurisdiction over the matter. The objections raised by the plaintiff primarily concerned the adequacy of notice regarding the court's proceedings. The court found that the notice was sufficient under the applicable law as it had been published appropriately, and the procedural irregularities cited did not adversely affect the outcome.	The plaintiff, Thomas Madden, claimed that the Circuit Court had no jurisdiction to authorize the sale of Elisha Madden's real estate due to alleged deficiencies in the notice provided for the sale. He argued that the notice did not comply with the statutory requirements, specifically regarding the timeframe for publishing the notice before the court proceedings. He requested the reversal of the Circuit Court's judgment and the prevention of the real estate sale on the grounds of these jurisdictional issues.	The defendant, Abram Cooper, defended against the plaintiff's claims by contending that the Circuit Court had jurisdiction and correctly adhered to statutory requirements for notice publication. The defendant's position was bolstered by the argument that despite the plaintiff's objections, the notice was published in accordance with the law and sufficiently informed the public of the proceedings. The defense requested the court to uphold the judgment of the Circuit Court and affirm the legal sale of the real estate to satisfy debts.

The case "Jonathan H. Baker et al. v. The Bishop Hill Colony" was adjudicated in September 1867 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a bill in chancery filed by the Bishop Hill Colony against Jonathan H. Baker and several other parties regarding the foreclosure of a mortgage. The facts reveal that John I. Hall, a defendant, entered into possession of the mortgaged premises around 1855 or 1856, later acquiring a tax title from Baker & Co. in 1856. Hall executed a mortgage deed to the complainants in 1858, pledging the property to secure two promissory notes. However, the mortgage was executed based on Hall’s apparent title, with the complainant unaware of any prior unrecorded arrangement between Hall and Baker & Co. In June 1860, Baker & Co. and Hall finalized an agreement where Hall delivered possession back to Baker & Co., leading to further disputes over rights and claims. The case involves issues of mortgage rights, titles, and foreclosures, requiring an examination of multiple parties' claims and the handling of the unsold property.	The plaintiffs, represented by the Bishop Hill Colony, argued that they held a valid mortgage from Hall that secured their interests in the property. They sought foreclosure of the mortgage and sale of the mortgaged premises due to Hall's failure to pay the amount due. The plaintiffs contended that Baker & Co.'s arrangement with Hall was made without their knowledge and consent, therefore infringing upon their rights.	The defendants, including Baker & Co. and Hall, claimed that the ownership and rights to the property were transferred through a bond for a deed. They argued that Baker had no right to enforce the mortgage since he had not conveyed the proper title at the time of the agreement. They also maintained that they had been in lawful possession of the property and that the plaintiffs were not legitimate parties to the foreclosure action, as their claims were inferior to the others involved in the case.

The case "Elijah Carter v. David Barnes and Wife" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1861. The legal dispute originated from a mortgage agreement executed by David Barnes and his wife, which was intended to secure a loan of three thousand dollars to Elijah Carter on November 17, 1856. The mortgage described a parcel of land located in Rock Island County, Illinois, but the legal description failed to provide clear locational details. As a result, the description in the mortgage was ambiguous, making it impossible to identify the land in question. The court faced a demurrer, challenging the validity of Carter's claim based on the unclear land description. Ultimately, the trial court dismissed Carter's bill, leading him to pursue a writ of error for a reversal of that decision.	Elijah Carter, the plaintiff, argued that the mortgage he held on the property should be enforceable and sought a foreclosure of that mortgage. He contended that the trial court erred in sustaining the demurrer filed by the defendants, which led to the dismissal of his bill. Carter's main legal request was to have the court reverse the previous decision and allow for a foreclosure on the mortgage, claiming that an identifiable tract of land was supposedly secured by the mortgage.	David Barnes and his wife, the defendants, contended that the mortgage's land description was fundamentally flawed, thus rendering it void. They argued that the description was so vague that it prevented identification of the property, asserting that a valid foreclosure could not proceed on such shaky grounds. The defendants requested the court to affirm the previous ruling that sustained their demurrer and dismissed Carter's bill, indicating that the trial court had made the correct decision based on the unclear legal description.

In 1864, a legal case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court involving Alfred S. Curtis as the plaintiff and Horace L. Sage as the defendant. The case originated from a dispute over a parol agreement made during the sale of real estate. Curtis, having sold land to Sage, claimed that Sage had promised to pay off certain existing incumbrances on the property. However, Sage failed to fulfill this promise, resulting in Curtis being compelled to pay the debts himself. The Circuit Court found in favor of Curtis after he was permitted to amend his declaration to include specific details about a deed which was referenced in the original declaration but not fully detailed. The case attracted legal scrutiny regarding the amendment's allowance during trial and whether the claims fell under the statute of frauds, particularly concerning agreements not to be performed within a year.	The plaintiff, Alfred S. Curtis, claimed that the defendant, Horace L. Sage, breached a parol agreement to pay off certain incumbrances on a property sold to Sage. Curtis argued that he had endured financial harm when Sage failed to uphold his promise, leading him to pay off the debts himself. Curtis requested a ruling from the court that would hold Sage accountable for the non-payment of the promised obligations.	Horace L. Sage, the defendant, contended that the plaintiff's claims were unenforceable due to the statute of frauds, asserting that the parol agreement was not to be performed within a year. Sage argued that the contract did not obligate him to pay off the debts until the debts themselves became due, which would exceed a one-year period, thus rendering the agreement void.

In 1873, in Cook County, Illinois, James Stinson, the appellant, was involved in a legal dispute with John S. Gould and others (appellees) over the ownership and payment of eight iron lamp posts and fixtures. The controversy arose from a previous transaction in the summer of 1872, where Stinson purchased a fountain from Crawford, Chamberlain & Co. and later decided to return it. An agreement was made for a credit towards the purchase of vases or other goods instead. However, during the course of events, Crawford, Chamberlain & Co. sold their stock to Brown, who then sold the items to Gould and others without any reservations. Stinson later ordered lamp posts through Crawford. The issues went to trial without a jury, with the judge ruling in favor of the appellees for $494 in the initial resolution, since Stinson's request for a set-off of $350 against the value of the goods was denied. Stinson argued that he should be entitled to this credit based on his dealings with Crawford, but the court ultimately found that he was aware the goods rightfully belonged to the appellees.	The plaintiffs, John S. Gould et al., claimed that they rightfully owned the lamp posts and fixtures and sought to recover their value from James Stinson, who had received the goods. They maintained that Stinson could not set off his claim against Crawford as the appellees were the legitimate owners of the goods, and therefore, he owed them payment for the full amount.	James Stinson, the defendant, contended that he was entitled to a set-off of $350 for a fountain previously purchased from Crawford, Chamberlain & Co. He argued that, due to the transactions involving Crawford, he should be able to offset his obligations regarding the lamp posts. Stinson claimed that Crawford acted in such a way that misled him regarding the ownership of the posts, thus allowing him grounds for the set-off.

In the case of Ellis Kaufman v. Edgar Loomis, dated May 19, 1884, the legal dispute arose over the matter of securities related to debts originally guaranteed by Loomis. The events took place primarily in Cook County, Illinois, involving key individuals such as Ellis Kaufman, Edgar Loomis, and representatives from the International Bank. The case's foundation was built upon Loomis's guaranty of several debts totaling approximately $7,500 related to Babcock & Ten Broeke and S. D. Cozzens. An extension of these debts was negotiated, requiring Cozzens to transfer rights associated with a patent, specifically the Tanner car-brake patent, into a trust managed by Loomis's attorney, Mr. Bisbee. Loomis engaged in a failed attempt to sell the patent rights for $11,000 due to the refusal of the bank's president, Lcewenthal, to consent to the deal. Subsequently, the U.S. Supreme Court rendered a decision that invalidated the patent rights, resulting in the securities being deemed worthless. Kaufman, who received the rights over these debts from the bank solely for collection purposes, pursued Loomis to fulfill his guaranty on the $3,000 note for Babcock & Ten Broeke. The case underwent several judicial reviews, with the Appellate Court ultimately siding with Loomis.	The plaintiff, Ellis Kaufman, claimed that Edgar Loomis should be held liable on his guaranty for a $3,000 note arising from loans made by the International Bank. Kaufman requested a judgment that would enforce Loomis's obligations under his guaranty, asserting that the validity of the patent rights and the related securities did not constitute a legal defense against Loomis's responsibility to pay.	The defendant, Edgar Loomis, contended that he could not be held liable on the guaranty due to the actions of the bank and its representative, Lcewenthal, who refused to consent to a sale of the securities at an offered price of $11,000 and thus caused their eventual loss in value. Loomis argued that the bank's refusal to act in his interest as a guarantor invalidated his obligations, as it resulted in significant financial detriment due to the securities becoming worthless.

In 1877, in Aurora, Illinois, the case of Charles Blasey et al. v. William Delius arose concerning the foreclosure of a mortgage on real estate valued at $3,400. The dispute began when a notary public prepared a mortgage with a power of sale clause. Charles Blasey objected to this clause during the execution, leading to the notary drafting a new mortgage without it, which was then executed and recorded. Evidence showed that a certified copy of the original mortgage included a homestead rights release. The Blaseys contested the legitimacy of the mortgage, claiming it had been altered post-execution to include the release clause, but the court found this assertion unsubstantiated. There was no credible evidence to support claims of forgery or alteration, and testimonies indicated that the mortgage was executed as per the record. The court examined the totality of evidence and found no fault with the execution or terms of the mortgage, which led to the subsequent court proceedings seeking foreclosure.	The plaintiff, William Delius, sought to foreclose on the mortgage, arguing that a legally executed mortgage document existed, which included a release of homestead rights. Delius contended that the mortgage was valid based on the certified copy and that the defendants had failed to provide credible evidence to prove any alterations or fraud in its execution.	The defendants, Charles and Margaret Blasey, argued that the mortgage had been altered after execution, specifically claiming that it did not originally contain a release of their homestead rights. They asserted that the variations led to potential unfairness in the foreclosure action. The Blaseys contended that they were not informed of the contents of the mortgage, which misled them during its execution and resulted in the alleged alteration.

In January 1872, a legal dispute arose in Lee County, Illinois, between George W. Acres (the plaintiff) and David George (the defendant). The case centers around an incident involving cattle owned by Acres that found their way into the field of George. The key individuals involved are Acres, the owner of the cattle, and George, the owner of the field where the cattle were found. The situation escalated when the cattle entered George's property through a breach in the partition fence, which had been created by George's own cattle. The issue at hand relates to the responsibilities surrounding the maintenance of the fence and the rights regarding the handling of the cattle.	The plaintiff, George W. Acres, argues that his cattle were on the defendant's land with George's consent, and that they only accessed the land due to a breach in the fence caused by George's cattle. Acres contends that under these circumstances, the defendant had a duty to repair the fence and, therefore, cannot justifiably detain his cattle based on the "Domestic animals" act of 1867. Acres requests that the court recognize his rights and the liabilities of the defendant in this situation.	The defendant, David George, likely argued that since the cattle were on his property, he had the right to take custody of them under the prevailing laws regarding domestic animals. George may have contended that regardless of the circumstances surrounding the breach, once the cattle were found on his property, he could exercise his rights to detain them. He seeks to maintain custody of the cattle and to have the court rule in favor of his interpretation of the law concerning livestock on private property.

In December 1836, the case of Samuel Swafford v. The People of the State of Illinois was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The proceedings stemmed from an earlier verdict rendered by a justice of the peace in Franklin County, where Swafford was found liable for an assault and battery, resulting in a judgment against him for fifty dollars and court costs. Dissatisfied with this verdict, Swafford sought to appeal to the Circuit Court of Franklin County. However, the appeal was dismissed due to an informality in the bond he provided, which was required under the statute that governs such appeals. The bond was improperly executed in favor of Eve Reynolds, the victim, rather than the People of the State of Illinois as mandated by the statute. Swafford challenged this dismissal by bringing the case before the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Samuel Swafford, claimed that the judgment rendered against him by the justice of the peace was unjust and sought to appeal it. He argued that the bond he executed was adequate for the appeal process and contended that the dismissal by the Circuit Court was improper due to the informality of the bond.	The defendant, represented by the Attorney General, contended that the appeal was correctly dismissed because the bond was not executed in accordance with the state statute, which strictly required the bond to be given to the People of the State of Illinois. They argued that the legislative statute does not allow for amendments to appeal bonds in criminal cases, and thus the Circuit Court's dismissal of the appeal was justified.

John Hossack and Lester Underwood were involved in a legal dispute that took place in LaSalle County, Illinois, with the court decision occurring in September 1870. The conflict centered around a scire facias, which is a writ used to revive a judgment. Hossack, the plaintiff, had previously won a judgment against Underwood. However, it was claimed that Hossack had transferred the judgment to various parties to secure debts owed to them. The transfers included John F. Nash and Richard Thorne before reaching the estate of William C. Richardson. Underwood's defense argued that these assignments rendered the original judgment invalid for Hossack's claims. The case presented complex questions of legal title and assignment of judgments, particularly regarding whether Hossack retained rights over the judgment after the transfers.	Hossack argued that the judgments assigned to Nash and Thorne were intended solely for securing debts rather than relinquishing his rights to pursue the balance owed on the original judgment. He contended that Underwood had acted fraudulently in procuring the assignments to prevent him from collecting the excess owed. Hossack sought the revival of the judgment, specifically for the portion that exceeded the amounts for which it had been pledged.	Underwood's defenses were built on the argument that the transfers of the judgment to Nash, Thorne, and subsequently to Eames and Richardson extinguished Hossack's ability to claim further amounts. He contended that since the underlying debts owed by Hossack were paid off, the legal title to the judgment could not be revived in Hossack’s favor, as the interests had legally transferred to others. Underwood sought dismissal of Hossack's attempt to revive the judgment.

The case "The Insurance Company of North America v. Jacob Hofing" took place in Menard County, Illinois, with the final judgment rendered on September 21, 1888. The plaintiff, Jacob Hofing, had obtained a fire insurance policy from the defendant, The Insurance Company of North America, insuring his frame barn and various personal property items, collectively valued at $1,350. Following a fire that resulted in damage to these properties, Hofing made a claim under the policy. The defendant raised concerns regarding a misrepresentation in the application and claims process, specifically the ownership of the barn which was jointly owned with his wife. Although the insurance company alleged that this misrepresentation constituted fraud, the evidence presented did not substantiate the claim of intent to defraud. The jury found in favor of Hofing, leading to a verdict of $189.20 in damages, despite the defendant's arguments regarding ownership and claim validity.	The plaintiff claimed that the fire insurance policy provided coverage for the loss of his barn and personal property after a fire incident. He argued that despite a misrepresentation regarding the ownership, he did not intend to defraud the insurance company and was entitled to compensation for his losses. Hofing sought recovery for the amount based on the insured values as stated in the policy.	The defendant contended that the plaintiff’s claim should be barred due to misrepresentations regarding property ownership, asserting that Hofing falsely claimed sole ownership of the barn in the proof of loss. The defendant also argued that the insurance policy was indivisible, claiming that any breach regarding the barn ownership affected the entire policy, thereby voiding any recovery on the personal property. They sought to have the judgment reversed based on these defenses.

The case of George F. Harding, impleaded with H. M. Wead, v. Mary Larkin et al. revolves around a dispute over a real estate transaction and subsequent eviction. The events leading to the case began on December 26, 1855, when defendants Harding and Wead sold a quarter section of land to Curtis and Albert Warden, including a covenant to warrant and defend the title. After a series of property transactions, the Warden heirs—Mary, William, Joshua, Sarah, Eveline, James, John, Berzilla, and Lydia Larkin—became the owners following their father's death on October 25, 1859. Trouble arose when Thomas Cross, claiming a paramount patent title through a series of patent grants from the U.S. government, ejected the Wardens from the land. The plaintiffs claimed they were forced to incur significant legal costs—totaling approximately $400—while defending against this eviction in various court actions. They argued the defendants had breached their covenant by failing to defend the title as promised. The court case was brought in the Cook Circuit Court before being escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1866.	The plaintiffs argue that the defendants breached the covenant of warranty by failing to defend their title against the eviction by Thomas Cross, which stemmed from a paramount patent title. They seek recovery for the costs associated with defending the eviction, including legal fees and expenses incurred in their attempts to recover the title, totaling around $400. The plaintiffs contend that they are entitled to this reimbursement due to the defendants’ failure to fulfill their covenant.	The defendants, Harding and Wead, presented several defenses, including a plea of performance, claiming they had fulfilled their obligations under the covenant, and a plea of non est factum, suggesting the defendants did not have any claim in the matter. They also raised a set-off for a debt owed by the deceased Samuel Larkin for legal services rendered in the past. They contested the plaintiffs' right to recover costs incurred in defending against the eviction.

The case "Kirk Hawes, Judge, v. The People ex rel. Emilie Pulver" took place in Illinois, culminating in a decision on June 15, 1889. The key individuals involved include Kirk Hawes, the judge of the Superior Court of Cook County, and Emilie Pulver, the plaintiff, who had brought a suit against the Rochester German Insurance Company for damages related to a fire that destroyed her insured personal property. The original suit commenced on March 22, 1887, and was concluded on March 29, 1887, with a verdict against Pulver. On April 9, 1887, after her motion for a new trial was denied, Pulver was granted an appeal with a requirement to file a bill of exceptions within sixty days. An extension was agreed upon by both parties, extending the deadline to July 9, 1887. However, when Pulver presented her completed bill of exceptions to Judge Hawes on June 22, 1887, he failed to sign it, citing doubts about his authority due to the timing of the presentation. The subsequent legal proceedings involved a petition for a writ of mandamus to compel Judge Hawes to sign and seal the bill of exceptions, which was considered necessary for the appellate court’s review of the case.	Emilie Pulver claimed that Judge Hawes had an obligation to sign and seal the bill of exceptions, as she had adhered to the procedural requirements by presenting it within the stipulated timeframe. She argued that despite the judge's refusal to sign the document on account of timing and authority doubts, the law mandated him to do so once the bill was settled. Her legal request was for a writ of mandamus to compel Judge Hawes to fulfill this duty so that her appeal could be properly reviewed by the appellate court.	Judge Hawes contended that he lacked the authority to sign the bill of exceptions, given that the court term had closed according to legal theory, leading to the belief that the record could no longer be altered. He argued that while the extension for the bill was agreed upon, he doubted the legality of signing it after the term had technically ended and thus refused to sign it. His defense rested on the interpretation of jurisdiction and the proper conduct of judicial duties outside the court term.

Charles T. Harvey and John R. Parsons entered into a contract on July 15, 1861, in Chicago, where Parsons sold Harvey a Fairbanks & Wilmarth sawing machine for $975. The payment terms included a $150 cash deposit and the remainder to be paid in Lake Superior pig iron delivered in Chicago during the navigation season at a price of $26 per ton. If the payment was not made in that season, the amount owed would accrue interest from December 1 until the iron was delivered the following spring. The legal dispute arose when Parsons sought to recover the contract price in January 1862, claiming Harvey failed to deliver the iron. However, the court concluded that Parsons did not make a demand for the iron in the fall, allowing Harvey until spring 1862 to fulfill his obligation. This means that the lawsuit was initiated too early, before a cause of action had arisen.	The plaintiff, Charles T. Harvey, claimed that he was not liable for the suit brought by Parsons for the value of the pig iron, as he was entitled to wait until spring 1862 for delivery, based on the contract's terms. He requested the judgment from the lower court be reversed, asserting that the action was premature since he had not yet defaulted on the payment due to Parsons's failure to demand the iron in the fall.	John R. Parsons, the defendant, argued that Harvey was obligated to pay for the sawing machine as per the agreed terms of the contract and that he was entitled to bring action to recover the price. Parsons contended that he had the option to demand the payment or delivery of the pig iron during the navigation season, and since Harvey did not fulfill this obligation, he sought the court's judgment favoring his claim for damages.

William D. Noble was indicted for forgery and found guilty in the St. Clair Circuit Court. Seeking to reverse this judgment, Noble appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1822. The main controversy revolved around four assigned errors related to the trial. Firstly, a juror, Moses Short, had formed an opinion about the case but had not expressed it publicly, raising concerns about jury impartiality. Secondly, David Rankin, the individual allegedly harmed by the forgery and who would receive a portion of the judgment, was allowed to testify against Noble. The third point concerned Rankin's religious beliefs, particularly his lack of belief in punishment after death, which raised questions regarding his credibility as a witness. Finally, Noble contested the admission of a civil suit record as evidence to establish the amount he allegedly intended to defraud Rankin. In examining these points, Justice John Eeynolds delivered the opinion that the judgments and practices during the trial adhered to legal standards, affirming the ruling.	The plaintiff, William D. Noble, argued that several errors occurred during his trial, including the disqualification of a juror who had formed an opinion, the admission of an interested party as a witness, the credibility of that witness due to religious beliefs, and the improper introduction of evidence from a civil suit to prove the amount he intended to defraud.	The defense contended that the juror's unexpressed opinion did not disqualify him, emphasizing that slight impressions in a juror's mind do not prevent impartiality. They also argued that allowing Rankin to testify was necessary for justice, given that forgeries must be prosecuted, and that his interest in the outcome did not disqualify him as a credible witness. Lastly, they maintained that the civil suit record was legitimate evidence of Noble's intent to defraud.

The case of John B. Smalley et al. v. Alfred W. Ellet originated in Macoupin County, Illinois, during the May term of 1852. The dispute arose from a promissory note dated January 18, 1851, for $254.11, executed by William C. Smalley to Alfred W. Ellet. To secure the debt, William C. Smalley mortgaged half of a portable steam saw mill to Ellet, with the mortgage recorded shortly after. John B. Smalley owned the other half of the mill. On April 7, 1851, both Smalleys sold the entire mill to Ira O. Haven and Franklin Morrison, who in turn executed a chattel mortgage to John B. Smalley for $100. The debt from the sale became due on February 7, 1852, but John B. Smalley claimed possession of the mill and sold it, asserting he had not known of Ellet's mortgage rights. Ellet sought an injunction against Smalley, arguing that it was unfair for Smalley to sell the mill while knowing of Ellet's claim. After various court actions, which included the hearing and reporting of testimony, a decree was rendered against John B. Smalley, culminating in this case reaching the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Alfred W. Ellet, claimed that he held a valid mortgage on half of the steam saw mill owned by William C. Smalley. Ellet argued that John B. Smalley had notice of his rights when taking a mortgage, and that due to this, his claims should take priority. He requested a court order to enjoin the sale of the mill by John B. Smalley and sought payment of his debt or confirmation of the sale to settle the debt owed by William C. Smalley.	John B. Smalley, the defendant, denied having notice of Ellet's rights regarding the mortgage at the time he executed his own mortgage and sold the mill. He contended that Ellet had lost his rights under the mortgage due to inaction and also argued against the competence of W. C. Smalley as a witness, claiming his involvement in the case disqualified him from providing testimony favorable to Ellet. Smalley’s requests included the dismissal of Ellet’s complaint and a ruling that Ellet did not have a valid claim.

Samuel T. Lindsay served as the sheriff of Crawford County, Illinois, from December 1878 to December 1880. During his term, the Board of Supervisors set his annual salary at $1,200, with total compensation for his services to be paid from the fees generated by his office. Lindsay reported collecting a total of $2,440.01 in fees over his two-year tenure but also incurred expenses for deputy hire and other miscellaneous costs, which he claimed amounted to $1,000 in total. He argued that he was owed additional amounts for fees earned in criminal cases where defendants were acquitted or discharged without costs. The county board's approval of Lindsay's reports caused contention regarding the obligation to pay these additional fees, particularly since Lindsay's total fees collected exceeded his set salary.	Lindsay's main arguments centered around his claim for unpaid salary and fees earned in criminal cases, which he asserted amounted to $761.20. He contended that, according to Illinois statutes, he was entitled to be reimbursed from the county treasury for fees in cases where defendants were acquitted, especially since the provisions stipulated that such fees would be paid only if his collected fees were less than his salary.	The County of Crawford countered that Lindsay had exceeded his salary through collected fees and was not entitled to payment from the county treasury for criminal case fees. They argued that since the total fees collected surpassed the $2,400 salary for his term, he was ineligible for additional compensation. The county maintained that the law expressly limits the payment of such fees to instances where the collected fees are insufficient to cover salary, which was not the case here.

The case "John Gohn et al. v. Joseph Dœrle" took place in 1877 in St. Clair County, Illinois, involving the plaintiff, Joseph Dœrle, who was about 15 years old at the time of the incident. Dœrle was employed by the defendants, John Gohn, Ferdinand Heim, and Michael Heim, to perform specific tasks in their manufacturing establishment, which was focused on creating an ice box called the "Triumph Refrigerator." The circumstances of the case stem from an injury Dœrle sustained while allegedly oiling a part of a planing machine, an act purportedly directed by one of the defendants. Initially, a jury found in favor of Dœrle, awarding him $700 in damages, but this verdict was overturned, leading to a retrial. In the second trial, the jury awarded Dœrle $3000, yet the defendants contested the outcome and subsequently appealed the judgment to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Joseph Dœrle, claims that he suffered personal injuries due to the negligence of his employers while he was employed in their planing mill. He argued that he was specifically instructed by one of the defendants to oil the machinery despite his designated work being limited to moving planks and wood. Dœrle sought recovery for his injuries, which he attributed to the alleged wrongful act of being directed to perform a task beyond his assigned duties.	The defendants contended that they did not instruct Dœrle to oil the machinery, asserting that the evidence regarding this claim was conflicting. They argued that Dœrle had a choice in his actions and had been cautioned to avoid the machinery. The defendants emphasized that there was no conclusive evidence proving they were guilty of gross negligence, asserting that the jury instructions given during the trial were misleading and improperly assumed negligence on their part.

In September 1873, in LaSalle County, Illinois, the case Zimri F. Ames v. Cornelius Snider arose from a dispute following a civil lawsuit related to work and labor done by Snider for Ames. Snider had originally brought a suit against Ames for $275, but due to an oversight, Ames did not respond, leading to a default judgment. After being surprised by the judgment, Ames sought legal counsel and subsequently accused Snider of perjury in the initial civil proceedings, which resulted in Snider's arrest. Snider claimed that this prosecution was malicious as there lacked sufficient cause for the charges against him. The jury initially found Ames liable for malicious prosecution, leading to a damages award of $350 in favor of Snider.	Cornelius Snider, the plaintiff, claimed malicious prosecution against Zimri F. Ames for having caused his wrongful arrest on a perjury charge. He contended that Ames acted without probable cause and sought damages for the reputational and emotional harm he suffered due to the arrest and subsequent legal proceedings.	Zimri F. Ames, the defendant, argued that he had probable cause to initiate the prosecution against Snider based on advice from legal counsel. He maintained that his actions were taken in good faith and that any potential malice could not be inferred unless there was an absence of probable cause. Ames requested the court to recognize that consultation with competent counsel provided him legal protection against claims of malicious prosecution.

The case "The Trustees of the First Congregational Church v. Robert Stewart" took place in January 1867, in Bond County, Illinois. The trustees of the First Congregational Church, who are responsible for managing the church's property, filed a suit against Robert Stewart. They alleged that Stewart had repeatedly intruded upon their rightful control of the church by officiating as the pastor without consent. The plaintiffs argued that Stewart was neither a member of the congregation nor legally appointed to perform such duties, and they sought an injunction to prevent him from further interfering with their worship services. Initially, a temporary injunction was issued against Stewart, but the lower court later sustained a demurrer filed by Stewart, effectively dismissing the Church's suit. This dismissal led the plaintiffs to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that they, as the trustees of the church, were the rightful legal owners of the church property and had the authority to determine who could officiate and conduct religious services. They argued that Stewart had no legal right to act as the minister and intended to continue his actions unless forcibly prevented. They requested an injunction to restrain Stewart from further officiating as the pastor and from entering the church against their will.	Stewart contended that, while he may have unlawfully officiated, the matter should be resolved within legal rather than equitable jurisdiction, asserting that the trustees could seek damages through legal means rather than an injunction. He claimed that any violations he committed could be remedied through law, and therefore did not warrant the intervention of equity courts to restrict his actions.

James Van Inwagen v. The City of Chicago is a legal case that took place in September 1871 within the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court. The city of Chicago brought this action against James Van Inwagen, an agent of the Astor Insurance Company of New York, to recover a fee of two percent on the insurance premiums he had collected. The legal basis for the claim was rooted in an act from February 13, 1863, which mandated that certain insurance companies not incorporated in Illinois pay a specified tax on premiums to the city. The legal dispute arose when Van Inwagen contended that the taxation statute had been repealed by a later act from March 10, 1869, which regulated taxes and licenses for insurance businesses in Illinois. The Superior Court of Chicago originally ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding the city a total of $237.08 based on the premiums reported between January 1, 1868, and January 1, 1869. The defendant appealed, arguing that the statute under which the city claimed the funds was no longer in effect at the time the action was initiated.	The city of Chicago claimed that under the act of February 13, 1863, it was entitled to collect two percent of the premiums received by James Van Inwagen for the insurance business conducted by the Astor Insurance Company in Chicago. The city requested a judgment for the amount claimed, as it asserted that this obligation was still valid at the time of the lawsuit despite the defendant's contentions about the repeal of the relevant statute.	James Van Inwagen's primary defense was that the section of the law requiring him to pay the two percent fee was repealed by the subsequent act passed in 1869. He argued that this repeal abolished the city's right to collect the fees, as the new law provided a different tax structure and was inconsistent with the prior statute regarding insurance agencies. His position was that the right to claim such funds was lost due to the repeal and did not represent a vested right that could be enforced post-repeal.

In 1884, the case of Highway Commissioners, etc., v. John M. Hamilton et al. arose in Champaign County, Illinois, concerning the power of highway commissioners to incur municipal debts. The appellant, Highway Commissioners, sought to address a claim initially litigated in the case of Town of Harwood v. Hamilton, where it was determined that the commissioners lacked the authority to create a debt beyond what could be financed through taxes levied for that particular year. The appellants attempted to bring forth a lawsuit against the commissioners to access funds earmarked for road and bridge repair for that year. The underlying issue revolved around whether the commissioners could be held liable for the payment of the claim without established authority to contract that debt. The court referenced previous decisions to support its position and emphasized that the commissioners could not create liabilities for which there was no legal means of payment.	The plaintiffs argued that the highway commissioners improperly incurred a debt by attempting to access funds for road and bridge maintenance that were not under their lawful purview. They sought recovery against the commissioners, claiming that their actions constituted an unjustifiable financial obligation that should be honored directly from the funds set aside for repair.	The defendants, represented by the highway commissioners, contended that the claim was invalid as the commissioners were not authorized to create such a debt beyond the taxation limits imposed by law. They maintained that all funds necessary for their obligations had to come from legally levied taxes, and any liability incurred outside of this framework could not be enforceable. As a result, they requested the court to dismiss the claim.

The case "Samuel H. House v. Canfield S. Hamilton" was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1867. The dispute arose in Hancock County, Illinois, where Canfield S. Hamilton, as the plaintiff, initiated an attachment suit against the defendant, Samuel H. House. Hamilton had obtained a writ of attachment, which commanded the sheriff to seize House’s property. The sheriff traveled to Knox County, where he levied upon property belonging to House, which had been there for several days. House subsequently filed a motion to quash the levy, asserting that he was not in the act of removing his property and that it had been in Knox County for over a week before the writ was issued. Both parties presented evidence regarding House's activities and intentions relating to the property. The core issue was whether the sheriff had the authority to levy the attachment in Knox County, given that the property had been moved there prior to the issuing of the writ.	The plaintiff, Hamilton, argued that the seizure of the property was justified based on evidence suggesting that House had intentions to engage in business in Missouri, thereby implying a risk of removing assets to avoid creditor claims. Hamilton sought to maintain the levy on House's property, asserting that the actions taken by the sheriff were permissible under the attachment statute.	The defendant, House, contended that the property had not been in the act of removal at the time of the levy, as it had been in Knox County for at least twelve days before the writ was issued. He supported his motion to quash with affidavits stating he had no intention of fleeing or removing his property. House argued that the court lacked jurisdiction since there was no service or levy in Hancock County, where the writ originated.

The case of John Steinmetz et al. v. Anna Barbara Lang et al. arose in 1874, when a bill in chancery was filed to foreclose a trust deed executed by Anna Barbara Lang and the now-deceased Michael Lang in 1864. The trust deed was established to secure the payment of a promissory note for $250, due two years after its issuance, with a ten percent annual interest rate. The case proceeded through the legal system after the original payee, Peter H. Fischer, passed away in 1874, and estate representatives, Steinmetz and Zernitz, sought to enforce the debt. A key issue in the case was an indorsement on the back of the note, which was canceled. Testimony indicated that the canceled statement suggested a release of the trust deed, but without corroborating evidence. The executors of Fischer asserted that the note still represented a valid debt, whereas the defense contended that the cancellation signified payment or release of the obligation. Ultimately, the plaintiffs appealed after the lower court dismissed their bill.	The plaintiffs, executors of Peter H. Fischer's estate, claimed that despite the canceled indorsement on the note which purportedly indicated a release of the trust deed, the evidence surrounding the note and trust deed suggested that the debt remained outstanding and enforceable. They requested the court to allow the foreclosure of the trust deed to secure the payment of the debt.	The defendants, Anna Barbara Lang and Charles Lang, argued that the canceled indorsement on the back of the note was indicative of a release of the trust deed, thereby nullifying any obligation to pay. They contended that the plaintiffs failed to provide satisfactory evidence that the note had not been satisfied and that the enforcement of the trust deed was unwarranted under these circumstances.

The case, John Johnston v. The Ewing Female University, took place in Knox County, Illinois, with the action initiated on August 29, 1863. The dispute arose from Johnston's refusal to honor a subscription made for the construction of a university building prior to the institution's incorporation. Johnston had agreed to contribute $400 in real estate provided that a building worth at least $10,000 was erected within eighteen months. The court proceedings began in the Knox Circuit Court, where the plaintiff sought to recover the subscription amount. Several special pleas were filed by Johnston, contesting the validity of the subscription based on alleged non-compliance with the conditions outlined in the subscription document and questioning the university's corporate status at the time. Ultimately, the case involved detailed examination of evidence, including the incorporation certificates and the status of the building's construction at the relevant time.	The plaintiff, Ewing Female University, claimed that Johnston was legally obligated to fulfill his subscription contract for the university’s construction. They argued that the university was legally incorporated, and the building's erection had complied with the subscription's terms, as the structure was commenced before the eighteen-month deadline and was valued above $10,000 according to the evidence presented. The university requested the court to enforce the subscription and recover the subscribed amount.	The defendant, Johnston, contended that the subscription was not enforceable since the condition that the building be completed within eighteen months was not met. He raised several special pleas, including questioning the university's corporate status when he made the subscription and arguing that the only cause of action was based on the specific terms of the subscription paper, which he claimed had not been fulfilled. Johnston sought to have the court dismiss the plaintiff’s claims based on these defenses.

In April 1858, the Illinois Supreme Court heard a case originating from Cook County Court of Common Pleas involving Richard K. Swift and James S. Johnson, who were impleaded with Lyman P. Swift, as appellants, versus James B. Whitney and George B. Marsh as appellees. The matter concerned a set of claims related to financial instruments involving currency transactions. The plaintiffs challenged a default judgment against them that was subsequently assessed in damages concerning various financial instruments considered promissory notes. The key legal question was whether those instruments could be admitted as evidence under the common counts without the execution being proved. The court ruled on admissibility and addressed issues regarding the nature of currency within the established legal framework, drawing upon precedents to support their conclusions about the evidence, the disposition of damages, and the overall legal handling of these financial instruments.	The plaintiffs argued that the financial instruments in question were valid promissory notes and should be admissible as evidence under the common counts for their claims. They asserted that the common counts did not require the execution of such instruments to be proven, and they contended that the court had the authority to assess damages based on the evidence presented. Essentially, the plaintiffs sought the affirmation of the default judgment that had been entered against the defendants.	The defendants contested the admissibility of the financial instruments as evidence, claiming that their execution needed to be proven for the common counts to apply. They argued that the plaintiffs had not specified the objections correctly and that certain key evidentiary standards had not been met, which should preclude the court's judgment from being affirmed. The defendants requested the court to dismiss the claims based on these procedural grounds and the nature of the evidence presented.

Isaac Miner was indicted during the April term of 1869 at the Bond County Circuit Court in Illinois for allegedly engaging in an open state of adultery with Eliza Jones, who was also accused of having a lawful husband. The indictment included two counts: the first claimed that Miner and Jones lived together in an open state of adultery while both had lawful spouses, and the second charged them with living together in a state of fornication. The jury found Miner guilty on the first count, leading to a $20 fine and judgment for costs against him. Upon appeal, significant questions arose regarding the adequacy of the evidence to support the conviction, particularly concerning the definitions of adultery and the proof required for such a charge in Illinois law. The legal standards highlighted that mere familiarity or a presumption of illicit conduct does not fulfill the requirement for an open state of adultery. The court scrutinized the competency of witnesses, especially in cases involving marital relations and the rules governing testimony.	The plaintiff, representing the State of Illinois, asserted that Isaac Miner and Eliza Jones were involved in an open and illicit relationship while still married to other individuals. The plaintiff aimed to prove that their cohabitation constituted a legal offense under the statutory definition of adultery, requiring evidence of habitual illicit intercourse and an actual marriage relationship which amounted to an "open state of adultery.	Isaac Miner, through his attorney, argued that the conviction for adultery could not be sustained as the evidence presented did not meet the burden of proving an "open state of adultery." Only rumors and presumptions of marriage were provided, which were legally inadequate to establish guilt. Additionally, he contended that the testimony of Eliza Jones's alleged husband should be deemed incompetent as it violated the rules concerning witness testimony involving spouses in criminal cases. Miner requested the court to reverse the judgment of the lower court and grant a new trial.

The case, *The Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Co. v. John Logan*, took place in Henderson County, Illinois, with key events occurring in March 1873. The plaintiff, John Logan, initiated the lawsuit against the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company to recover damages for the death of three hogs and the injury of a mare belonging to him. The initial hearing was conducted before a justice of the peace, but the case was escalated to the circuit court presided over by Judge Arthur A. Smith. In this court, Logan's claim was successful, resulting in a judgment of $30.25 in his favor. The railway company then appealed the decision, leading to further proceedings in the Illinois Supreme Court. This case highlights the legal obligations of railway companies regarding the fencing of their tracks to prevent livestock from being injured or killed by trains, as outlined in the act of 1855.	John Logan claimed that the Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company was responsible for the damages incurred due to their negligence in failing to properly fence their railroad. He argued that as the owner of the livestock that suffered harm, he had the right to recover damages without the need to prove actual negligence in the operation of the trains.	The Toledo, Peoria and Warsaw Railway Company contended that the circuit court erred by not allowing a jury instruction that would require proof of negligence on their part before the jury could find for the plaintiff. They aimed to demonstrate that the lack of evidence of negligence should preclude any liability for the damages claimed by Logan.

In 1887, in Fulton County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving Morrison & Whitlock as the plaintiffs and James M. Stewart as the defendant. The plaintiffs initially initiated a replevin action against the defendant to reclaim property that they believed was rightfully theirs. During the return term of the court, it was recorded that the plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed their case, with an order reflecting that the plaintiffs would bear the costs, and the court ordered the return of the property along with one cent in damages awarded to the plaintiffs. However, a subsequent motion was filed to amend the judgment to accurately reflect that the property return and costs were actually awarded to the defendant, not the plaintiffs. The Circuit Court agreed to amend the judgment after reviewing the record and hearing testimony that affirmed the original order contained an inadvertent clerical error.	The plaintiffs, Morrison & Whitlock, claimed that they were entitled to the return of property and sought damages in a replevin action against the defendant, James M. Stewart. They presented their case to the court, which initially recorded a judgment in their favor for the return of the property and a minimal amount of damages.	The defendant, James M. Stewart, contended that the judgment had been incorrectly entered in favor of the plaintiffs. He successfully argued that the original ruling contained a clerical error and filed a motion to amend the judgment to reflect that the returned property and costs were awarded to him, rather than the plaintiffs.

This case, "Loring Delano et al. v. Levi H. Rood," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1844, stemming from actions that originated in La Salle County in November 1839. The key individuals involved were Loring Delano, Charles Hayward, and Levi H. Rood. The dispute revolved around a covenant action initiated by Rood against Delano and Hayward over a bond executed on May 11, 1837. The bond stipulated that if Rood tendered a deed for a specific town lot in Ottawa, Delano and Hayward were to pay Rood $1,000. The case arose after Rood tendered the deed but the defendants failed to pay the agreed amount. The defense claimed that the bond was executed for an usurious consideration. After a trial in which a jury ruled in favor of Rood with a verdict of $1,149, the defendants sought a new trial, which was denied. This led to an appeal based on claims related to the nature of the contract and allegations of usury.	The plaintiff, Levi H. Rood, argued that the bond executed by Loring Delano and Charles Hayward entitled him to payment of $1,000 upon tendering a deed for the property. He maintained that he fulfilled his obligations under the bond by tendering the deed and claimed damages for the defendants' failure to perform their part of the contract.	The defendants, Delano and Hayward, contended that the bond was invalid due to being executed for an usurious consideration. They argued that the terms of the agreement effectively constituted a loan with an interest rate exceeding the legal limit of 12% per annum, suggesting that the arrangement was a disguised loan rather than a genuine sale.

Two brothers from Massachusetts, Abijah Edmonds (later Charles Johnston) and Charles Edmonds, became separated, with Charles Edmonds remaining in contact to support their aged parents. The elder brother changed his name and became a successful physician. Over the years, he assisted his younger brother briefly with small remittances. At one point, with the intent of acknowledging his debt for their parents' support, Charles Johnston agreed to a note for $3,129.59 in favor of Charles Edmonds. In a complicated family arrangement involving mutual support and trust, Johnston confessed a judgment rather than pay the note outright, influenced by his financial struggles. This judgment was executed in 1862 and linked to ongoing communication of familial affection and obligations. After Charles Johnston's death, Charles Edmonds filed a claim against Johnston's estate based on the judgment, which led to legal proceedings contesting its validity and claims of it being satisfied by Johnston's executors.	The plaintiff, Charles Edmonds, argued that he was owed a legitimate debt from his brother Charles Johnston’s estate, stemming from their family support arrangement. He claimed that the judgment was valid and should be honored, seeking a total of $7,105.88 (the original judgment plus interest) from the estate during its administration.	The defendants, Ellis Howell and other executors of Charles Johnston's estate, contended that the judgment was illegal, had been satisfied, and questioned its admissibility in court without prior presentation of supporting documents. They also claimed that the judgment was intended to defraud other creditors, suggesting it should be dismissed.

In 1854, in Peoria County, Illinois, James Jackson initiated an ejectment lawsuit against William Cummings concerning ownership of a specific piece of property—lot one, block ten in Brimfield. Jackson asserted his title to the property derived from a grant by the United States. In response, Cummings presented evidence of a legal sale of the property to him through a series of tax judgments and a sheriff’s deed, claiming rightful possession. Jackson challenged the legitimacy of Cummings' title by raising multiple objections against the documents and proceedings that led to the tax sale, including the validity of the judgment, the precept, and the sheriff's deed. He contended that these documents contained legal defects and lacked proper execution under Illinois law. The case was heard during a March term before Judge Peters.	Jackson's primary argument revolved around the illegality and informalities of the documents presented by Cummings, claiming that they did not conform to legal requirements. He highlighted irregularities in the judgment and related proceedings, questioning the authenticity of the tax sale and asserting that proper procedures were not followed to protect his property rights.	Cummings defended his position by asserting that the objections raised by Jackson were without merit. He argued that strict adherence to technical compliance was unnecessary when the substance of the proceedings indicated lawful execution. Cummings maintained that the court must prioritize the rights of the State to collect taxes through legitimate sales. He contended that the tax sale was valid and that Jackson’s challenges did not demonstrate any real harm or confusion about ownership.

The case "Supreme Lodge of Ancient Order of United Workmen et al. v. Florentina Zuhlke" originated in 1885 and was tried in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois. The case involved the plaintiff, Florentina Zuhlke, who was the wife of Edward Zuhlke, and the defendants, which included various branches of the Ancient Order of United Workmen. The legal conflict arose following the death of Edward Zuhlke on October 15, 1881, after which Florentina sought to claim a $2000 benefit stipulated on a membership certificate issued in January 1881. The lawsuit asserted that the certificate guaranteed benefits to her as his beneficiary. During the trial, it was established that there was a plea of general issue filed by the defendants, who contended they were not jointly liable for the certificate. The case underwent scrutiny regarding the validity of Edward Zuhlke's expulsion from the Grand Lodge in 1884, a decision the defendants claimed barred the claim due to improper actions taken amid his alleged insanity. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, which was later affirmed by the Appellate Court, resulting in an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, Florentina Zuhlke, claimed entitlement to the $2000 life insurance benefit stated in her husband’s membership certificate with the Ancient Order of United Workmen. She argued that her husband's expulsion from the Grand Lodge prior to his death should not prevent her recovery of the benefit, especially given that the expulsion proceedings occurred while he was insane. She sought a judgment confirming her right to the amount stipulated in the policy upon her husband's death.	The defendants contended that they were not jointly liable for the insurance benefit, suggesting that only the Grand Lodge was liable. They claimed that the expulsion of Edward Zuhlke effectively terminated any benefits due to him or his beneficiaries, asserting that he had made false statements regarding his health when he joined, which justified the expulsion. Furthermore, they argued that if Zuhlke's expulsion was valid and that he was sane during the proceedings, this would bar his wife from making a claim.

Thomas B. Shaw v. Azilda Shaw was a legal case filed on November 14, 1885, in the Circuit Court of Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The case was presided over by Judge William Brown and involved Thomas B. Shaw as the defendant and Azilda Shaw as the plaintiff. Azilda brought a bill for divorce against Thomas, alleging extreme and repeated cruelty as well as habitual drunkenness over a period exceeding two years. The legal proceedings saw the defendant denying all material charges while accusing Azilda of neglect and improper conduct, alleging that she had condoned any previous grievances. During the court proceedings, Thomas's attorney filed an answer to the divorce petition, but in the absence of both Thomas and his attorney, the court took testimony from a deputy sheriff, who stated that Thomas had instructed him to let the case go uncontested. Ultimately, a letter from Thomas directed his attorney to let the case go by default, which led the court to strike the answer from the files, leading to a default judgment against Thomas. This decision was contested in higher court due to improper handling of the defendant's answer.	Azilda Shaw, the plaintiff, claimed that her husband, Thomas B. Shaw, had subjected her to extreme cruelty and habitual drunkenness for over two years, which justified her request for a divorce. She sought alimony and other equitable relief in light of these circumstances.	Thomas B. Shaw, the defendant, denied all allegations made by Azilda and countered her claims by accusing her of neglecting her marital duties and asserting that she had condoned his actions. He argued that the court's decision to strike his answer from the records was erroneous, and he requested that the decree determining alimony and property division be reversed.

In May 1855, an action of replevin was initiated in the Circuit Court of Menard County, Illinois, where R.A. Mock (the defendant) sought to recover possession of 141 head of cattle from Jacob Armstrong (the plaintiff). The case revolved around claims and various pleas filed by Mock concerning the alleged taking and detention of the cattle. While Mock asserted several defenses, including that he did not take or detain the cattle, Armstrong’s claims were ultimately presented to a jury, which found in favor of Armstrong. This ruling was challenged by Mock, who filed a motion for a new trial, asserting issues with how the trial was conducted and the court's refusal to provide certain jury instructions. However, the court subsequently overruled this motion, and the matter was advanced to the Illinois Supreme Court for further review.	Jacob Armstrong, as the plaintiff, argued that R.A. Mock unlawfully took and detained his cattle. He sought a judgment affirming his ownership of the cattle and possession thereof, contending that the jury adequately demonstrated the merits of his claim despite the lack of a formal ruling on all issues raised during the trial.	R.A. Mock, the defendant, contended that he did not take the cattle or engage in any unlawful detainment. Mock's defense included multiple pleas aimed at dismissing the accusations against him. He requested a new trial, disputing the jury's verdict and the trial's procedural integrity, particularly concerning the instructions provided to the jury.

In September 1876, the case of Andrew J. Wright et al. v. John Smith was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over a chattel mortgage and involved key individuals, namely the plaintiffs Andrew J. Wright and others, and the defendant John Smith. Wright claimed ownership of property through a purchase from Samuel Cully, whereas Smith contested this claim based on a chattel mortgage that Cully had previously granted to him. During the trial, it was revealed that evidence concerning the mortgage's execution was necessary but had to be provided through secondary evidence due to a fire in October 1871, which resulted in the destruction of all relevant records in Cook County. The lower court excluded testimony relating to the chattel mortgage on the grounds that the plaintiffs' motion was granted without specific objections being raised regarding the mortgage's acknowledgement. This led to an appeal by Wright, who contended that the exclusion was erroneous.	The plaintiffs, represented by Hr. I. D. Adair, argued that they had legally purchased the property from Samuel Cully and sought to reclaim it through replevin. They contended that the lower court's decision to exclude evidence concerning the chattel mortgage was incorrect and that the evidence was sufficient to establish the existence and validity of the mortgage, despite the absence of a specific acknowledgment by the correct justice of the peace.	The defendant, represented by Hr. James Ennis, maintained that he had a rightful claim to the property based on the chattel mortgage from Cully. He argued that the exclusion of testimony regarding the mortgage was justified and pointed out that any objection to its validity should have been specifically raised during the initial trial. The defendant's position was that the court had ruled correctly in excluding the testimony since no specific objection to the mortgage's acknowledgment was made at that time.

Charles B. Phillips initiated a legal action against William P. Kerr on June 19, 1858, in Chicago, Illinois. The case revolved around an affidavit filed by Phillips to hold Kerr to bail, alleging that Kerr was indebted to him in the amount of $5,921.86 for money had and received in August 1857. Subsequently, a capias ad respondendum was issued, which is a writ requiring the defendant to appear in court. Kerr responded by filing a motion to quash the writ, citing irregularities in the affidavit, including improper party identification and insufficient positive allegations of fraud. Despite this motion pending, the court scheduled proceedings on December 17, 1858, where Kerr failed to appear after being called three times. Phillips was granted a default judgment, and the court assessed damages at $6,410.78. The appeal focused on procedural issues concerning the default judgment being entered while the motion to quash was unresolved.	Phillips claimed that Kerr owed him a debt for money had and received. He sought to recover the amount of $5,921.86 plus interest, asserting that Kerr's failure to appear in court warranted a default judgment. Phillips contended that the legal procedures followed in entering the judgment were legitimate and according to the provisions set by the court for handling damages.	Kerr's defense was centered around the claim that the affidavit for the writ of capias was improperly executed and contained several irregularities, including incorrect party identification and a lack of definitive allegations regarding fraud. He requested that the court quash the writ and discharge the bail, arguing that the unresolved motion should halt any further proceedings against him, and contended that there were procedural errors in the subsequent default judgment process.

In November 1844, a legal proceeding occurred in Hancock County, Illinois, where a claim was allowed by the Probate Justice on behalf of David Wallace against the estate of Moses J. Wallace, who was deceased. The claim was for $194.50. James Welch, serving as the administrator of Moses J. Wallace's estate, appealed this decision to the Circuit Court. During the trial held in May 1846, a jury ruled in favor of Wallace, awarding him $255. The Circuit Court subsequently issued a judgment stating that Wallace was to recover this amount from Welch, along with court costs, and allowed execution against the assets in Welch's hands as the administrator. Welch appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, challenging the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court as no required bill of exceptions had been filed and contesting the cost judgment as erroneous.	James Welch claimed that the Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction since no bill of exceptions was taken in accordance with legal requirements. He argued that this omission should prevent the enforcement of the judgment against the estate. Additionally, Welch contended that the costs awarded against the estate were improper, asserting that he had not designated a specific term for settling claims against the estate, thus the estate should not be responsible for costs related to claims filed outside of that term.	David Wallace, the appellee, maintained that Welch's failure to file a bill of exceptions meant he could not contest the Circuit Court's jurisdiction. He asserted that the judgment for costs was appropriate because it was presumed that claims were filed timely, thus the estate was liable for costs associated with establishing Wallace’s claim. Wallace rightly anticipated a judgment in his favor as the law favored creditors who followed the necessary procedures for filing claims against an estate.

William Scully v. George Hamilton took place in Sangamon County, Illinois, where the owners of a large tract of land, namely George Hamilton and James C. Hamilton, entered into a written agreement on April 17, 1877, for the sale of 4,161.34 acres of land to William Scully. The agreement specified a price of $50 per acre for 3,807.42 acres and $45 per acre for 353.92 acres, totaling an additional $10,000 for certain conditions. Scully paid $15,000 in cash at the time of the agreement and agreed to pay the remaining balance through notes and mortgages. Essential conditions included a survey of the land to verify the acres, with adjustments made depending on actual measurements compared to government records. Following the agreement's execution, all parties satisfactorily completed their obligations by April 1, 1878. However, in early 1885, Scully was notified that a survey requested by the vendors revealed an excess of 68 acres for which they demanded additional payment. When Scully refused, the present suit was initiated, leading to a trial without a jury, where the court favored the plaintiff's claim for the additional payment. An appeal was subsequently made to the Illinois Appellate Court regarding the construction of the contract.	The plaintiff, William Scully, argued that the contract allowed for reimbursement concerning any discrepancies in the land measurements—specifically, that any excess land identified by a survey conducted by the vendors warranted additional payment. He claimed a right to the adjustment based on this survey and sought a judgment for the amount demanded due to the alleged excess land.	The defendant, George Hamilton, contended that the demand for additional payment was inappropriate as the survey was conducted nearly seven years after the completion of the contract. He argued that Scully's right to request adjustments under the contract's provisions was time-barred and that no reasonable period had been adhered to for the survey's execution. The defense maintained that the statutory limitations applied to the case could not be sidestepped simply because the excess land was only identified years after the contract terms had been satisfied.

In 1886, in Chicago, Illinois, John P. Altgeld deposited $1,000 as a first payment for the purchase of certain lots, receiving a receipt from the agents Aaron B. Mead and Albert L. Coe, which stated that the money would be refunded if the title was proven to be unsatisfactory. After consulting with his attorney, Altgeld determined that the title for the property, held by the seller Julia M. Ray, was not good and refused to proceed with the purchase unless a marketable title was provided. Despite Altgeld's requests and lack of actions to perfect the title from the agents or Ray, they retained the deposit. Altgeld subsequently initiated a lawsuit against Mead and Coe to recover the deposited amount, leading to a trial without a jury where the court ruled in favor of Altgeld.	The plaintiff, John P. Altgeld, argued that the agents, Mead and Coe, personally guaranteed in the receipt that the $1,000 would be refunded if the title was found defective. He claimed the title was indeed not marketable based on legal counsel's opinion, thus entitling him to the return of his deposit. He sought a judgment ordering the return of the $1,000.	The defendants, Mead and Coe, contended that they were acting merely as agents for Julia M. Ray and should not be personally liable since the relationship was primarily between Altgeld and Ray. They asserted that their receipt implied no personal liability on their part and that the court should have considered the opinions of legal experts regarding the title's validity. They argued that the title's legal sufficiency was a question of law that contradicted Altgeld's claims.
