The town maintained that since the funds were allocated elsewhere prior to Elrod providing his services, he was not entitled to recover his claimed amounts, asserting the action was improperly filed as it sought compensation from an already depleted special fund.

In November 1866, the case of The Illinois Central Railroad Company v. George Whalen took place in Marion County, Illinois. George Whalen, the plaintiff, brought an action against the Illinois Central Railroad Company, claiming damages for the alleged killing of a black mare and a white mule, as well as injuries sustained by a sorrel mule, all of which were his property. The incident was believed to have occurred on October 20, 1866, when a train from the railroad was moving south. The animals were subsequently found along the railroad, "badly smashed up." Although there was no conclusive evidence that the train struck the animals, the circumstances led the jury to infer that the railroad's operations were responsible for the injuries. A significant aspect of the defense relied on the assertion that the railroad had constructed a sufficient fence at the location of the incident, which was claimed to be in disrepair only after the accident, on October 22. The court highlighted the lack of proof that the fence was defective on the date of the incident, thus questioning the validity of the defense's argument.	George Whalen claimed that the railroad's negligence led to the death and injury of his livestock. He argued that the railroad company failed to properly signal their approaching train by not ringing the bell or blowing the whistle. Whalen sought damages for his losses, insisting that the jury should find in his favor based on this negligence and on the assertion that the animals were struck due to insufficient fencing.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company's defense centered on two main arguments. Firstly, they contended that they had maintained a proper and sufficient fence along their railroad, and thus should not bear liability for the incident. Secondly, they claimed that there was no sufficient evidence to establish negligence, particularly regarding the accusation of failing to ring the bell or blow the whistle, as the sole witness could not definitively testify on this matter. The defendant requested that the verdict be overturned based on these points.

Margaret Bez filed a bill against the Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railway Company in Joliet, Will County, Illinois, challenging an ordinance passed by the City Council that allowed the railway companies to lay connecting tracks on Michigan Street. The ordinance was enacted on October 17, 1885, without a petition from property owners representing more than half of the street's frontage, as required by law. Bez claimed to be a property owner whose lot directly faced Michigan Street, asserting that the railway tracks would make the street essentially worthless, thereby damaging her property and business. The defendant railway companies, as well as the city, contended that they had the authority to lay the tracks, and that any damages Bez might experience were merely consequential in nature. After an initial temporary restraining order was granted, the circuit court eventually sustained the defendants' demurrer, dismissed the bill, and awarded the railway companies $50 for damages. Bez appealed the decision, citing a lack of legal authority for the ordinance.	The plaintiff, Margaret Bez, argued that the ordinance allowing the railway to lay tracks on Michigan Street was void due to the absence of a necessary petition from owners of more than half the street's frontage. Bez contended that the construction of the tracks would severely limit access to her property and diminish its value, thus she requested an injunction to prevent the railway companies from laying the tracks.	The defendants claimed that the construction of the tracks was authorized by the city ordinance and that Bez lacked grounds to seek an injunction since the fee of the street was owned by the city. They argued that the remedy for any damages incurred by Bez was exclusive to legal proceedings, citing judicial precedent that defined such damages as consequential rather than actionable through equity. The defendants requested that the court uphold the validity of the ordinance and dismiss Bez's claims.

The case "The Miami Powder Co. v. Zenas N. Hotchkiss et al." was decided on December 4, 1885, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The plaintiff, The Miami Powder Company, organized under Ohio law, engaged in the manufacture of gunpowder and was represented by Messrs. Wilson & Raum, and Messrs. Puterbaugh & Puterbaugh. The defendant, Zenas N. Hotchkiss, a hardware merchant based in Peoria, Illinois, was a long-time agent for the company, often purchasing gunpowder on credit, secured by promissory notes. The disputes arose from three suits in attachment initiated by the plaintiff against Hotchkiss for $6,000 worth of goods attached as Hotchkiss's property. Hotchkiss claimed the goods belonged to him as his son asserted ownership through a purchase from him. The court restricted evidence from the plaintiff, citing a plea of "nul tiel corporation" by Hotchkiss, challenging the existence of the Miami Powder Company. The jurisdictional issue was whether the plaintiff could prove corporate existence. The court ultimately excluded the plaintiff's evidence, directing a verdict for the defendant.	The Miami Powder Company argued that it was a recognized corporation and sought to establish its corporate identity de facto. It presented promissory notes and account statements provided by Hotchkiss, asserting that these transactions indicated he recognized the company as a legitimate corporate entity. The plaintiff contended that the evidence demonstrated Hotchkiss was estopped from denying the company's existence due to his dealings with it, and subsequently sought recovery on the attached goods.	Zenas N. Hotchkiss's defense centered on the claim that The Miami Powder Company was not a legally constituted corporation, referencing the "nul tiel corporation" plea. He challenged the validity of the evidence presented by the plaintiff, arguing that the company failed to prove its lawful incorporation and corporate status. Furthermore, he contended that as he had given notes to the company, this did not equate to an acknowledgment of its legal standing if it was not formed according to law.

In the case of Samuel S. Gardner et al. v. Samuel I. Russell, which took place in September 1875 in Cook County, Illinois, the appellee, Samuel I. Russell, initiated an action of assumpsit against the appellants, Samuel S. Gardner and others. The basis of the lawsuit revolved around two promissory notes, each valued at $500, dated November 10, 1873, with payment due dates of June 10, 1874, and August 10, 1874, respectively. The defendants responded by pleading the general issue along with special pleas that included breach of warranty and failure of consideration, and submitted an affidavit of merits. Various legal proceedings followed, including filed replications and a demurrer to the special pleas which was subsequently overruled by the court. The defendants' requests to rejoin were denied, leading to arguments concerning potential procedural errors, including the timing of the trial and the order of the docket. However, the court indicated that no substantial errors were found in the proceedings.	The plaintiff, Samuel I. Russell, claimed that the defendants, Samuel S. Gardner et al., defaulted on the two promissory notes totaling $1,000. He argued for an enforcement of the contracts represented by the notes and sought a judgment in his favor for the amounts due. Russell asserted that the defendants provided insufficient grounds for their breaches and that their defenses should not invalidate the claims based on the promissory notes.	The defendants contended that the plaintiff, Samuel I. Russell, breached warranties related to the agreement underlying the promissory notes, claiming a failure of consideration that warranted dismissal of the claims. They argued procedural issues, such as the timing of the trial and the admissibility of certain replications. By filing a demurrer to the plaintiff's replications, they sought to establish that the replications were flawed and insufficient for a legal response to their pleas.

The case "The Board of Supervisors of Cumberland County v. Gordon Webster et al." was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1870. The conflict arose in Cumberland County, where the Board of Supervisors intended to levy a tax of twenty cents on every $100 of taxable property for the construction of a bridge across the Embarrass River. This action was taken during their June 1867 session, where seven of the eight supervisors were present, and the proposal was passed with a vote of four to three. However, it was argued that the order was void as it did not meet the requirement of a majority of the entire board, which is stipulated by the township organization laws of Illinois. The law mandates that a majority of all supervisors must approve any fund appropriation, including for infrastructure projects like bridges. The plaintiffs sought to enjoin (prevent) the tax collection, asserting that the Board acted outside its legal authority. The key individuals involved were the supervisors of Cumberland County and the plaintiffs, Gordon Webster and others, who took legal action against the board's tax levy.	The plaintiffs claimed that the tax levy imposed by the Board of Supervisors was unauthorized and void due to the lack of a majority vote from the entire board. They argued that according to Illinois law, specifically the township organization laws, a majority of all supervisors must concur for such a levy to be valid. The plaintiffs requested that the court issue an injunction to prevent the collection of the tax, claiming that it was imposed without legal authority.	The defendants, representing the Board of Supervisors of Cumberland County, contended that the special act allowing them to levy a tax did not specify the required number of votes. They argued that as long as a quorum was present, the levy could be enacted. They attempted to differentiate between the levy of the tax and its appropriation, asserting that a majority could levy the tax even if a majority of the whole board did not support its use for bridge construction.

In 1887, in the city of Havana, Illinois, a resolution was adopted by the city council to purchase a 60-acre tract of land from Reuben A. Henninger for cemetery purposes, involving the issuance of bonds totaling $2,000. The transaction sparked legal action when John M. Dehm filed a bill in chancery alleging that the purchase was invalid as it did not meet municipal regulations requiring a direct annual tax to pay for incurred debts. He sought an injunction to prevent bond payments and cancel the purchase. A temporary injunction was granted, halting any payments or land improvements. Despite recognizing the illegality of the original resolutions, the city passed another resolution later that included provisions for proper tax assessments. Dehm continued to file supplemental bills to challenge subsequent transactions and payments related to the cemetery land. The Circuit Court ultimately upheld the legality of the bonds issued under the new ordinance while making the original bonds perpetually enjoined as they were deemed invalid.	John M. Dehm claimed that the city failed to comply with statutory requirements when purchasing cemetery land and issuing bonds without an established tax for repayment. He sought to enjoin the payment of the bonds issued under both the initial invalid resolution and the subsequent resolutions, along with requesting the cancellation of the land purchase.	The City of Havana contended that the actions taken in passing the ordinance and issuing new bonds complied with statutory requirements. The defendant argued that, despite the initial purchase being flawed, the appropriation for the cemetery bonds and subsequent ordinances adequately addressed any legal deficiencies, warranting validation of the bonds and payment for associated services rendered.

Tristram P. Hoxey, a clerk of the County Commissioners’ Court of Macoupin County, was involved in a legal action during the September term of 1838. The case took place in Macoupin County, Illinois. Hoxey, along with his sureties John Wilson and Charles Storer, was sued by the County of Macoupin for debt related to a bond. A writ was issued against all three defendants, confirmed executed by the sheriff. However, Hoxey was the only defendant who pleaded to the charges. The Circuit Court ultimately rendered a judgment solely against Hoxey. Following this, the case was brought up for review, where it was deemed that the initial judgment was erroneous, as all defendants should have been jointly liable in the action of debt.	The County of Macoupin claimed that Tristram P. Hoxey, along with his sureties, failed to fulfill their obligations under the bond. They brought an action of debt against all three defendants, asserting that judgment should be rendered against each of them as they were all served with the process.	Hoxey, as the primary defendant, pleaded to the declaration, challenging the action taken against him alone. His defense rested on the premise that all defendants should be liable jointly in the action of debt, and thus he contended that the judgment against him without considering the other defendants was incorrect.

The case, "Augustus D. Butterfield, adm’r etc. et al. v. Terris Johnson," was adjudicated in September 1867 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It involved a legal dispute concerning a bill in chancery filed by Terris Johnson against several defendants, including Augustus D. Butterfield. The central issue was an error in a note where the word "dollars" was omitted, leading to a contention about the correct spelling of Butterfield's Christian name. The summons initially named Sylvanus H. Butterfield but was returned served to S. H. Butterfield. The sheriff's return indicated he served "S. H. Butterfield," raising questions about whether the defendant named Sylvanus or a different individual, Sylvius, had been correctly identified. The court had to evaluate whether service of process was properly executed. Ultimately, this case was situated within LaSalle County, Illinois, and raised procedural questions regarding service of process and interpretation of summons.	The plaintiff, Terris Johnson, asserted that the initial summons and accompanying documents contained errors regarding the naming of the defendant Butterfield, which warranted correction through the court process. Johnson's request was to amend the service to reflect the accurate name and allow the case to proceed properly.	The defense, led by attorneys Crawford & Beck for Butterfield, argued that the service of the summons was correctly executed according to the name specified in the original writ. They contended that the sheriff could only act based on the writ in his possession and that his return indicated he considered S. H. Butterfield to be the correct defendant, hence the legal procedures had been followed appropriately.

On February 12, 1849, the Illinois General Assembly approved an act to establish a ferry on the Mississippi River in St. Clair County, granting certain individuals, including Paul Mehlgarten and his associates, the rights to operate the ferry for a term of fifteen years. The act required them to construct roads, bridges, and maintain the ferry. On November 16, 1852, the plaintiffs, Edward Haven and others, acquired an undivided half of the ferry and land. After Mehlgarten's death, his heirs, who resided in Europe, automatically inherited his half but had not actively managed the ferry operation. The plaintiffs continued to operate the ferry, incurring costs for repairs and maintenance amounting to $4,872.36, which the defendants had not reimbursed despite their co-ownership. The case arose when the plaintiffs sought to recover these expenses from the defendants, asserting that the defendants were liable for their share of the costs necessary to meet the ferry’s operational obligations.	The plaintiffs claimed they and the deceased co-tenant had complied with the legislative requirements for maintaining the ferry and its infrastructure. They asserted that following Mehlgarten’s death, as co-tenants with the defendants, they expended considerable funds for operation and repair of the ferry and connected structures. The plaintiffs sought reimbursement for one-half of these costs, totaling $4,872.36, asserting the defendants had become indebted for their share.	The defendants argued that there was no express request or agreement for the plaintiffs to incur the expenses on their behalf, as they had not managed the property since Mehlgarten's death. They contended that because the plaintiffs could not prove an express or implied promise from them to pay for the expenses incurred, they were not liable for the costs of operation. The heirs maintained that as co-tenants, without a formal agreement for additional expenditure, they could not be held accountable.

The case "Francis Regnier v. Eliza S. Cabot" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1845 and stems from an action of slander originally brought by Cabot against Regnier in the Menard Circuit Court. The court ruled in favor of Cabot, awarding her $1,600 for damages related to statements made by Regnier, which alleged that she committed fornication. These allegations were made public prior to Cabot's marriage, damaging her reputation. Regnier contended that Cabot was seen in compromising situations with Elijah Taylor, attempting to justify his statements and mitigate damages. However, multiple efforts to introduce evidence that would support his claims were denied by the court. The proceedings involved several trials and a venue change to Morgan County, where the case was ultimately resolved. The primary legal issues concerned the admissibility of evidence regarding the plaintiff's character and the validity of the defendant's arguments.	The main claims made by Eliza S. Cabot included that Francis Regnier made slanderous statements about her character, specifically accusing her of fornication, which were false and damaging. She sought compensation for the resulting harm to her reputation as well as damages that reflected the impact of the false allegations on her personal and social standing.	Francis Regnier's defense primarily relied on the general issue of non-justification and the claim that he had evidence suggesting Cabot’s questionable character. Regnier sought to present evidence to mitigate damages by implying suspicions about Cabot’s chastity based on her associations with Elijah Taylor. However, the court rejected his attempts to introduce specific evidence that would imply the truth of his statements.

In 1860, Vernon Sanford and his wife conveyed a lot in Sanfordville, Illinois, to their son-in-law, Gilbert Finkle, who claimed he purchased the lot for two dollars. The Sanfords argued that the land was a gift. Finkle took possession and improved the property without recording the deed. In early 1864, while Finkle was away in Idaho, the Sanfords obtained the unrecorded deed, destroyed it, and subsequently executed a new deed for the property in favor of their daughter, Nancy Finkle. In 1881, Finkle returned and filed a bill to cancel the deed to his wife and requested a new deed in his name, claiming that the Sanfords acted without his consent. The Sanfords denied these claims, asserting that Finkle voluntarily surrendered the deed, which resulted in his wife becoming the legal owner. The circuit court initially ruled in favor of Finkle.	The plaintiffs, Vernon Sanford and his wife, claimed that Gilbert Finkle surrendered the original deed, thereby allowing them to convey the property to their daughter, Nancy. They argued that the conveyance was valid and had been acted upon for many years without Finkle's objection, contesting his request to cancel the deed to his wife and restore his name on the property.	Gilbert Finkle contended that he had never relinquished his claim to the property, as he was unaware that the deed had been destroyed by the Sanfords. He claimed that the Sanfords had acted deceitfully to change the ownership of the land without his consent while he was away and sought relief from the court to reclaim the property and have his wife's deed canceled as a cloud on his title.

In 1873, Caesar A. Roberts and his wife, Sarah G. Roberts, executed a deed of trust for their residence property in Pekin, Illinois, to secure a mortgage bond for $2,500 in favor of Dana D. Dickinson, with William H. Robinson named as the trustee. After both Robinson's and Roberts's deaths—Robinson in 1880 and Roberts in October 1883—a bill was filed on December 15, 1883, to foreclose the deed, claiming an unpaid principal sum and interest. The court case involved the widow and heirs of Roberts contesting the legal foreclosure by asserting defenses related to usury and payment, arguing that the principal amount had already been paid back, and that no additional funds were advanced at the time of the agreement. The legal proceedings also included factual discussions about the flow of funds, the role of loan brokers, and the legitimacy of charges. Ultimately, the circuit court ruled to dismiss the bill for foreclosure, which led to an appeal being filed.	The plaintiffs (Elliott Callender and others) claimed that they were owed the full principal sum of $2,500 plus interest, as well as additional fees for insurance and attorney's services under the deed. They sought to enforce the mortgage agreement by foreclosure on the property since they asserted that the amount was due and unpaid following the execution of the deed.	The defendants (Sarah G. Roberts and heirs) defended against the foreclosure by arguing several points, including claims of usury, asserting that the lender did not actually loan the entire principal at the time of the deed execution. They contended that the money received had been significantly less than claimed and alleged that the entire principal had been repaid. Furthermore, they disputed the legitimacy of charges by the broker, Robinson, arguing that he took excessive fees without authorization or knowledge of the lender, Dickinson.

In September 1870, in Chicago, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Mark Skinner and others (the plaintiffs) and The Lake View Avenue Company (the defendant). The Lake View Avenue Company, organized under the law for constructing roadways, sought to condemn land owned by Newberry, deceased, for which the plaintiffs served as trustees. The company filed a petition to the judges of the Superior Court of Chicago for this condemnation, resulting in the appointment of appraisers. However, the appraisers' report condemned the land without awarding compensation, leading to the court's approval of this report. The plaintiffs contested this decision through an appeal, arguing that the procedure followed was irregular and that their rights were not properly considered. The central issue arose around whether the approval of the appraisers’ report constituted a final judgment and whether an appeal could be made against it.	The plaintiffs argue that the condemnation of the land was improperly undertaken, citing irregularities in the proceedings, such as the lack of notice regarding the meeting of the appraisers to assess damages. They maintain that the judgment approved by the court failed to comply with legal requirements, specifically the procedural necessities outlined in the statute governing such condemnations. The plaintiffs request that the court reverse the lower court’s decision and remand the case for proper consideration of the condemnation process.	The defendant contends that the action of the superior court in confirming the appraisers' report is final and that no appeal should lie, according to the statutes governing the corporation's actions. They argue that all procedural aspects were met and that the filing of the petition by their attorney provided sufficient jurisdiction, which the plaintiffs erroneously contest. The defendant requests the court to uphold the lower court's judgment as lawful and binding.

In September 1870, the case Augustus Tower et al. v. Peter Pitstick was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a legal action initiated by Augustus Tower against Peter Pitstick regarding alleged trespasses on Tower's property in Troy Grove, Illinois. The conflict arose when the highway commissioners of the town ordered the removal of fences that Tower had installed, claiming the area was a public highway. Despite an initial refusal from the commissioners to establish the highway, a subsequent appeal by petitioners resulted in the supervisors laying out a highway across Tower's property. Tower was notified to remove his fences but did not comply. Consequently, Pitstick, acting under the orders of the highway commissioners, removed the fences, leading to Tower filing a trespass claim seeking damages. During the trial, the court ruled in favor of Tower, awarding him $500, which prompted Pitstick to appeal the decision on the grounds of improper proceedings regarding the highway's establishment.	The plaintiff, Augustus Tower, claims that the removal of his fences constituted unlawful trespass on his property. He argues that the actions taken by the defendants, Peter Pitstick and the highway commissioners, were not properly authorized as the process to establish a public highway was flawed. Tower seeks compensation for damages amounting to $500 resulting from the trespass.	The defendant, Peter Pitstick, argues that the area in question was legally established as a public highway by the supervisors, and that he acted in accordance with the highway commissioners’ orders to remove the fences which were illegally obstructing this public path. Pitstick contended that the defenses raised were valid and upheld the proper process, requesting the court to overturn the initial judgment in favor of Tower on these grounds.

Solomon Rothschild and Julius Stern, partners, filed a lawsuit against The Michigan Central Railroad Company in 1873 after a shipment of 10,000 cigars was destroyed in a fire. The goods were being transported from Detroit to Chicago. Upon arrival in Chicago, the cigars were reportedly deposited in the defendant's warehouse. However, the warehouse was consumed by a destructive fire in October 1871. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court after the jury ruled in favor of the Railroad Company. Their verdict led to a subsequent motion for a new trial by the plaintiffs, which was denied, prompting the appeal. The case centers around the debate of whether the Railway Company fulfilled its duties as a common carrier and the particulars of their liability in this instance.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Michigan Central Railroad Company failed in its duty as a common carrier. They argued that the evidence did not adequately show the cigars were correctly unloaded into the warehouse or that they were destroyed there. Furthermore, they contended that the goods being unloaded on a Sunday did not absolve the defendant of liability, claiming damages for the value of their lost cigars and requesting the court to reverse the previous verdict.	The defendant maintained that they safely delivered the cigars to their warehouse in Chicago, where they were subsequently destroyed by a fire without any fault on the part of the Railroad Company. They argued that their obligations as common carriers ceased once the goods were stored and that they should be regarded as warehousemen thereafter. Consequently, the defendant requested the court to uphold the jury's verdict and dismiss the plaintiffs' claims for lack of evidence supporting their assertions.

Peter Dolan filed a legal case against John Farrell in the Circuit Court of Jersey County, Illinois, which culminated in a decision on November 23, 1889. The case revolved around a mortgage foreclosure concerning a note for $125 executed by Dolan to Martin B. Miner on August 27, 1869. Dolan alleged he had made payments towards this note, including cash, specific articles, and work performed by his wife, which he claimed should be credited to the amount due. Both Dolan and Farrell were illiterate, complicating the proceedings. The case primarily hinged on conflicting testimonies regarding the payments and credits claimed by Dolan, raising questions of the credibility of the witnesses. A master, appointed to oversee the evidence, eventually determined that $153 remained unpaid, leading to a decree in favor of the plaintiff.	Peter Dolan contended that he had fulfilled his obligation by making payments on the note secured by the mortgage. His primary arguments were that his payments included cash and value for work done by his wife for John Farrell, which should be credited towards the outstanding balance. Dolan sought to have the mortgage foreclosed in light of these claims, requesting the court to recognize these credits and determine the accurate amount due.	John Farrell's defense centered around the assertion that Dolan had indeed made the payments he claimed. However, the defense provided evidence aimed at disputing the credibility of Dolan and his wife regarding the transactions in question. Farrell contested the completeness of the payments and sought to refute the claim that the outstanding balance was $153. Ultimately, he sought dismissal of the foreclosure based on his arguments about payment and the credibility of Dolan's evidence.

In 1873, the city of Chicago undertook the construction of a tunnel stretching nearly six miles from Lake Michigan to a location near the intersection of Twenty-second Street and Ashland Avenue. This tunnel, which was nine feet high and nine feet wide, was built approximately sixty feet below the surface and extended through the property owned by Harriet Allcock, the plaintiff in this case. Following the tunnel's construction, significant subsidence occurred on Allcock's property, resulting in a depression of about four to five feet at its center, which expanded roughly thirty to forty feet in all directions. As a result of this subsidence, the buildings and fences on her property sustained considerable damage. Consequently, Allcock filed a lawsuit to recover the damages incurred, and during a jury trial, she was awarded $2,170. The city of Chicago later sought to overturn this judgment by filing a writ of error, arguing that the damages awarded were excessive and that the court had erred by instructing the jury to allow interest on the damages from the time they were incurred.	Harriet Allcock claimed damages due to the construction of the tunnel that caused severe structural damage to her property. She sought compensatory damages for this harm, arguing that the city should be held liable for the injuries caused by the lawful exercise of its rights in constructing the tunnel through her land.	The city of Chicago defended against the claims by arguing that the damages awarded by the jury were excessive and that there was an error in the court's instructions regarding the calculation of interest on the damages. The city maintained that according to Illinois law, interest could not be awarded in cases of property damage unless specifically authorized by statute.

In the case of *Ida Irene Law et al. v. The People ex rel. Louis C. Huck, Collector*, which was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1877, the central issue revolved around the levy of taxes by the city of Chicago. The case arose from actions taken by the city council to raise funds through various taxes, including interest on temporary loans that exceeded the constitutional limit on municipal indebtedness. The city had been in a state of financial distress since the devastating Great Chicago Fire of 1871, which destroyed a significant portion of its infrastructure and reduced its tax base. By August 1875, the city was already heavily indebted, having reached this limit under the state's constitution. The plaintiff, a group of taxpayers, contested the legality of tax levies set to pay for the interest on these temporary loans, arguing that they violated constitutional restrictions on city indebtedness. The case involved intricate deliberations over municipal powers, the validity of loans against anticipated revenues, and the overall constitutionality of the city's financial practices. The court thoroughly examined whether the levies for payments on temporary loans constituted illegal debts and the authority of the city to engage in such financial dealings under its charter.	The plaintiffs argued that the city of Chicago had exceeded its constitutional limit of indebtedness when it levied taxes to pay interest on temporary loans. They contended that the temporary loans created a debt contrary to the limits set forth in both the state constitution and the city's charter, making both the loans and the tax levies to pay them void. They sought a judicial declaration that the tax levies were illegal and unenforceable, asserting that no lawful basis existed for the city to incur these debts.	The defendant, represented by the city officials, asserted that the temporary loans were necessary to meet current expenses, and that they were lawful as they were intended to cover projected revenues for the fiscal year. They argued that the city had the authority to anticipate tax revenues and to make appropriations for necessary expenses from such levies, maintaining that these actions did not constitute an illegal increase in debt. They claimed the loans were executed in good faith and under the assumption they would be paid from future tax collections, which they believed remained within the confines of the law.

The case titled "The Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company, Appellant, v. James McCutchin, Appellee" took place in Illinois, with the circuit court proceedings occurring during the 1860s. The dispute arose from a judgment rendered against the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company by a justice of the peace in Clay County on April 16, 1869. The railroad company appealed this decision, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction because the summons was served on a person, Charles Weir, who was not authorized to accept service on behalf of the company. Throughout various sessions of the Circuit Court, motions to dismiss the case on the basis of jurisdiction were discussed. The plaintiff and defendant eventually agreed on the facts: Weir was never the agent for the railroad company, and no service had been properly conducted upon the company itself. The case was thus tried based upon this agreement of facts, leading to a judgment for the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, James McCutchin, argued that the judgment made by the justice of the peace should be upheld despite the lack of proper service to the railroad company. He contended that an appeal from a judgment can confer jurisdiction to the Circuit Court even if the appellant (in this case, the railroad company) was not served with process before the justice of the peace, allowing for a trial on the merits.	The defendant, the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad Company, claimed that the Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction due to improper service of process. They filed motion to dismiss the cause based on a plea in abatement, asserting that because Charles Weir was not an authorized agent, the service on him did not confer jurisdiction. The defendant requested that the court dismiss the case because the justice of the peace did not acquire jurisdiction over the subject matter.

In the case of Lewis D. Leach v. The People ex rel. O. P. Patterson, decided on June 20, 1887, by the Illinois Supreme Court, the central issue revolved around delinquent taxes levied on real estate owned by Lewis D. Leach in Wayne County, Illinois. The taxes in question were associated with bonds purportedly issued by the county in 1869 to fund a donation and subscription for the Illinois Southeastern Railroad Company. Leach contested the validity of the bonds, arguing that they were issued under an unconstitutional statute, which established a new board of supervisors for the county without proper legislative authority. This act was perceived as a special legislation violating the Illinois Constitution, which mandated a general law for township organization. The historical context included the county’s transition to a township organization in 1860, which established a board of fifteen supervisors, and a subsequent act in 1867 that sought to reduce this board to five members, creating a conflict regarding the lawful management of the county's financial affairs.	The plaintiff, Lewis D. Leach, claimed that the bonds issued for the Illinois Southeastern Railroad Company were invalid because the board of supervisors that authorized them was constituted under an unconstitutional act. He argued that this statute failed to meet the requirements of the state constitution regarding the governance of township organizations, thus rendering the bonds void.	The defendant, represented by the People ex rel. O. P. Patterson, contended that despite any constitutional issues surrounding the board's creation, the actions of the de facto board of supervisors had been recognized and operated effectively for years, thereby validating their financial decisions and the bonds issued. They argued that the acts of de facto officers should be upheld for the public good, as they had acted under a color of authority.

E. S. Fowler filed a suit against August Peterson in 1887 in Sangamon County, Illinois, claiming unpaid wages for services rendered as a servant or laborer. The case was initially heard in front of a Justice of the Peace and later appealed to the County Court, where Fowler was awarded a judgment of $132, after having $5 remitted from an initial verdict. Both parties served as the only witnesses, with their testimonies contradicting each other regarding the agreed rates of pay for different periods worked. Despite discrepancies in Peterson's memorandum book, the jury appeared to place greater weight on Fowler's testimony during deliberation. This led to the jury siding with the plaintiff, as the record did not reveal the rationale behind their decision. The instructions provided to the jury were described as few, brief, but clear and sufficient for the case at hand.	E. S. Fowler claimed that he was owed wages for his service, asserting that a specific rate had been agreed upon for different periods of work. He sought a total balance of $137, which was later adjusted to $132 after remittal. Fowler's primary argument rested on his testimony regarding the agreed pay rate and that he was entitled to the wages owed as a laborer.	August Peterson contested Fowler's claims by challenging the agreed-upon rates for the service provided and supported his position with entries made in his memorandum book. Peterson argued that the jury should not have found in favor of Fowler based on the contradictory testimonies, suggesting that Fowler's case lacked substantive support. Additionally, Peterson aimed to have the verdict overturned on the grounds of insufficient evidence to substantiate the claimed wages.

The case of **James M. Anderson & Co. v. William H. Dezonia** originated in **St. Louis, Missouri**, where the plaintiff worked as a traveling salesman for the defendants, a wholesale grocery company. The events took place in **1887**, with the lawsuit stemming from the plaintiff's assertion that a special contract was made for a salary via a letter from Carter, an employee of the company. This letter, which the plaintiff later destroyed, allegedly outlined terms for employment that included a salary ranging from **$100 to $125 per month** and geographical considerations for relocating his family. After an initial introduction to the company, the plaintiff was encouraged to take a trial trip without a formal contract but with a verbal understanding that he would be compensated for his services. Despite two trips, the plaintiff reported no positive sales results, leading to a refusal from the defendants to pay the claimed salary, as they contended that no formal contract existed. Consequently, the plaintiff filed a suit for his claimed salary based on the alleged contract.	The plaintiff, William H. Dezonia, claimed that he had entered into a special contract for his employment as a traveling salesman, as communicated through a letter from the defendants' employee, Carter. He sought to recover a salary of no less than **$100 per month** in addition to his travel expenses, asserting that the letter constituted a valid binding contract upon acceptance. The plaintiff contended that he relied on the terms proposed in the letter when he accepted the position.	The defendants, James M. Anderson & Co., argued that no valid contract existed for a specific salary, as the letter from Carter was merely an inquiry relating to a potential position and not a definitive offer. They maintained that the plaintiff’s preference for a trial trip rather than signing a written contract meant that any employment arrangement lacked clear terms. The defendants proposed that the plaintiff worked under a commission basis of **4% on sales** and was responsible for his own expenses, thereby contesting the salary claim.

In December 1830, in Gallatin County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between plaintiff Hampton Pankey and defendant Stephen Mitchell. The case originated when Mitchell successfully sued Pankey before a justice of the peace for a debt of $37, resulting in a judgment in favor of Mitchell. Pankey later appealed to the circuit court, where the original judgment was affirmed. During the proceedings, Pankey claimed to have a note signed by both himself and another individual, Stephen Roach, for the same amount, which was allegedly lost. However, evidence from a witness revealed that after a series of events, the note had been altered by Pankey without Mitchell's consent, changing the amount to $44.50. This alteration rendered the note void, raising questions about its legality and Pankey's authority to modify it. Pankey attempted to introduce a plea of non est factum, denying the validity of the altered note, but the court did not permit this plea to be heard. The circumstances surrounding the case led to a significant examination of contractual integrity and the legal implications of modifications to financial instruments.	Hampton Pankey argued that he had a valid claim based on a lost note initially valued at $37. He contended that the debt was owed to him and sought to recover the amount despite the alterations made to the note in question. Pankey aimed to show that the original agreement still held merit and that the alteration did not impact his right to collect the debt from Mitchell.	Stephen Mitchell's defense centered around the assertion that Pankey had unlawfully altered the note from $37 to $44.50 without his or Roach's consent, which invalidated the note. Mitchell claimed this material alteration rendered the instrument void, insisting that the evidence presented allowed him to plead non est factum to deny the altered note's legitimacy. He objected to the affirmation of the previous judgment by the circuit court, citing procedural errors in not allowing his defense to be heard.

The case is titled "James H. Smith et al. v. John D. McLean et al." and was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 11, 1887. It arose from a lease agreement concerning premises located at 83 and 85 Wabash Avenue, Chicago, Illinois, negotiated on February 18, 1884. James H. Smith and Thomas W. Pattison (the plaintiffs) leased a portion of a building from John D. McLean and Jacob Retterer (the defendants) for a specified period, which included conditions regarding rent payments and responsibilities after fire damage. A fire destroyed the leased premises on April 14, 1885, leading to disputes on whether the defendants were liable to pay rent despite the destruction. The core of the case revolved around the interpretation of the lease terms, especially concerning damages, tenant obligations, and landlord responsibilities. The Superior Court's initial rulings and subsequent appeals culminated in the Supreme Court's review of the issues involved.	The plaintiffs contended that the defendants were not relieved from their obligation to pay rent due to the fire that damaged the premises, as the lease stipulated that rent would cease only if the premises were unfit for occupancy. They argued that the premises were repaired and restored to a condition suitable for occupancy within a reasonable timeframe, thereby invoking their right to collect the agreed-upon rent from the defendants.	The defendants asserted that the lease was terminated automatically due to the destruction of the premises by fire, which occurred without their fault. They argued that this fire led to their ousting from the property and asserted that the destruction excused them from their covenant to pay rent. They contended their position based on the premise that a satisfaction of conditions regarding fire damage warranted release from rental obligations.

In 1871, the case of William Broughton v. Electa Smart took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute centered around a series of claims made by Electa Smart (the plaintiff) against William Broughton (the defendant), who was her sister's husband. Electa alleged that William had promised to marry her and failed to fulfill this promise, which led to her emotional distress and seduction. The context revealed that Electa had lived with the defendant's family for over a decade, during which she claimed to have engaged in illicit relations with him. Although the case began as an action of assumpsit, with Electa seeking damages for services rendered, it evolved to include allegations of seduction and abandonment. The jury initially ruled in favor of Electa, awarding her $10,000 in damages. However, the courtroom proceedings were contentious, with conflicting testimonies concerning the alleged promise to marry, leading the court to eventually seek further evaluation of the case.	Electa Smart claimed that William Broughton made several promises, including a promise to marry her upon request and within a reasonable time. She also sought damages for seduction and abandonment, alleging that their long-term relationship involved expectations of marriage that William failed to honor. She amended her declaration to include these additional claims, emphasizing the emotional and financial harm she suffered due to William's actions.	William Broughton denied the allegations, asserting that he never promised to marry Electa. He presented testimonies supporting his position, including statements from family members that contradicted Electa's claims. Broughton argued that Electa’s testimony lacked credibility and that she had willingly engaged in their relationship without any expectation of marriage. Furthermore, he contended that the true nature of their relationship was one of an informal living arrangement rather than one based on an expectation of marriage.

In 1866, the case of Daniel T. Elston et al. v. The City of Chicago was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from actions taken by the city regarding an assessment to deepen and widen the Chicago River. The plaintiffs, including Robert R. Clark and Blanche Elston, argued that the city did not have the authority to impose the assessment and sought to recover money that they had voluntarily paid. In 1857, property owners along the river had collectively agreed to advance funds for these improvements if the city levied an assessment on them. The city council subsequently ordered a special assessment and appointed commissioners to oversee it. After the work on the river was completed in 1858, payments were made by the plaintiffs for the assessed improvements. However, in 1859, the city collector sought additional judgment against the same property for the balance due. The plaintiffs claimed their payment was involuntary because of the circumstances surrounding it; however, the defendant maintained that the payments were made voluntarily. The trial began without a jury in the Superior Court of Chicago, which sided with the city, and the plaintiffs then appealed to the Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the city had no authority to impose the assessment for deepening the river, and therefore, the actions taken in that regard were void. They argued that their payment was made under compulsion and requested the recovery of the money they had paid. They also contested the validity of the assessment, citing that the stipulation made by Coventry, an attorney for the Elston estate, lacked proper authority, making any judgments against the property non-binding.	The defendant, the City of Chicago, argued that the city had the power to widen the river, and thus the assessment acted within its jurisdiction. The city contended the payments made by the plaintiffs were voluntary, as there was no formal judgment enforcing the payment at the time of their transaction. The city maintained that the plaintiffs had willingly participated in the improvement agreement and had full knowledge of the facts, negating any claims of compulsion. The city sought affirmation of the lower court's decision, requesting the dismissal of the appeal.

The case "William B. Ogden et al. v. Abner Kirby" took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the decision delivered by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. The dispute arose when William B. Ogden and others (the plaintiffs) sought to recover $2,000 from Abner Kirby (the defendant). This amount was pledged by Kirby to support the construction of a railroad extending from Fort Howard, Wisconsin, to Menominee, Michigan. According to the terms of the subscription, the payment was contingent upon the railroad being completed and operational by July 1, 1872. The plaintiffs filed the action of assumpsit after the jury in the Superior Court ruled in favor of Kirby. The plaintiffs contested various aspects of the trial’s jury instructions, particularly the interpretation of the contract and whether the railroad met the operational requirements stipulated by the agreement.	The plaintiffs argued that Kirby was liable for the $2,000 subscription due to the completion of the railroad to Menominee by the specified date. They claimed that the trial court misinterpreted the contract concerning what constituted "completion" and "operation" of the railroad. The plaintiffs also pointed out errors in the jury instructions provided by the court, which they believed led to an unfavorable verdict. The key legal requests were to reverse the trial court's judgment and to recognize the subscription as valid due to the railroad being completed and in operation as per the contract's terms.	Kirby defended against the claims by asserting that the railroad was not completed and operational as required by the contract by the deadline of July 1, 1872. He contended that the jury had been correctly instructed that it wasn't sufficient for the railroad merely to reach Menominee; it had to provide reasonable facilities for handling freight and passengers. The defendant sought to reinforce this interpretation with his instructions to the jury, arguing that mere completion of the line did not fulfill the contractual obligations due to the lack of proper operational infrastructure.

In June 1874, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed a case involving James Garvin and William Gæbe, the administrator of Louisa Schmalsede's estate, in Washington County, Illinois. The dispute arose over property that had been levied upon by Garvin, who was an officer acting under two executions against the goods of Christ Schmalsede, the husband of the deceased Louisa Schmalsede. Louisa had acquired the majority of the property through her late father William Schmalsede's will, raising questions about its ownership following her husband’s financial difficulties. The court reviewed evidence demonstrating that Louisa had independently grown wheat on land she rented, using her own teams and employing labor for which she compensated. The dispute hinged on whether the property belonged to Louisa, as the administrator sought to recover it for her estate.	The plaintiff, William Gæbe, claimed that the property, including the wheat produced on rented land, belonged to Louisa Schmalsede and should not be subject to the debts of her husband. He argued that all property acquired through her own efforts and resources was legally hers, reinforcing that any involvement from her husband in the cultivation did not diminish her ownership rights.	The defendant, James Garvin, contended that the property should be subject to the execution since it pertained to the debts of Christ Schmalsede. He implied that the appropriated property did not qualify as belonging solely to Louisa, and thus, he sought to uphold the levies made against it.

In the case of Elizabeth Epling et al. v. George W. Hutton et al., decided on September 27, 1887, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute involved the heirs-at-law of Seth Mason, who were contesting the validity of his will. The key individuals involved were Elizabeth Epling and others as the appellants (heirs) and George W. Hutton as one of the appellees (devisees under the will). The contested will had been executed on April 10, 1885, during Mason’s illness, which included severe pain and mental challenges due to his condition. The appellants claimed that Mason was not of sound mind when he made the will, that Hutton, his nephew, improperly dictated its terms, and that it lacked proper execution and witness attestations. The trial confirmed the will's validity after a jury found it was indeed the last will and testament of Seth Mason, leading to the dismissal of the plaintiffs' claim.	The plaintiffs argued that Seth Mason was not of sound mind when he executed the will, claiming undue influence exerted by George W. Hutton. They contended that the will was dictated by Hutton, was not signed by Mason or anyone in his presence, and lacked the required witnesses. They sought to have the will set aside, asserting that it did not meet the legal requirements for a valid testament.	The defendant, George W. Hutton, defended by asserting the validity of the will, arguing that it was duly executed while Mason was of sound mind. He stated that no undue influence was proven and emphasized that all legal formalities had been complied with during the will's signing. The defense focused on demonstrating that Mason had the requisite mental capacity to make a testamentary disposition of his estate.

Green H. Jones was involved in a legal case against The People of the State of Illinois, which was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1870. The case originated in Alexander County, where a prosecution for bastardy was brought against Jones. The primary issue arose when Jones's defense attempted to quash the affidavit that led to the warrant for his arrest, arguing that the complaint was made by someone other than the mother of the child in question, which they claimed was not permissible under the law. The circuit court rejected this motion, and a trial subsequently concluded with a verdict against Jones. Following the unfavorable judgment, he sought a writ of error to contest the ruling.	The plaintiff, representing the State of Illinois, maintained that the complaint made against Jones was valid and that he was legally liable for bastardy. The plaintiff's primary argument revolved around the assertion that the mother, or an appropriate complainant, brought forth valid allegations against Jones, necessitating his accountability for the financial support of the alleged illegitimate child.	The defendant, Green H. Jones, contended that the affidavit and warrant should have been quashed because the complaint was presented by someone other than the mother of the child, violating the statutory provisions governing such cases. He also argued that the trial court erred in not allowing a new trial based on the weight of the evidence, asserting that the evidence presented overwhelmingly supported his claim of non-paternity. He sought to have the judgment overturned.

In June 1870, the case of David W. Wise, Administrator of Bond v. William H. Twiss, Administrator of M. N. Twiss was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Clinton County, presided over by Judge Silas L. Bryan. At the center of the dispute was a bill in chancery filed by Twiss against Parmenas Bond, the surviving partner of the firm of Parmenas and Richard S. Bond, seeking to enjoin the collection of a judgment that was allegedly satisfied through a property conveyance. The plaintiff claimed that an agreement existed between Twiss and Richard S. Bond for the satisfaction of the judgment through the conveyance of a specific lot in Trenton. However, the evidence presented included an unrecorded deed that conveyed a different lot than what was claimed to satisfy the judgment, leading to a conflict over whether the terms of the agreement were fulfilled. The court found that the plaintiff failed to provide sufficient evidence to support his claims.	The plaintiff, David W. Wise, argued that the judgment against him had been satisfied by an agreement involving the conveyance of a specific lot in Trenton. He sought to enjoin the collection of the judgment based on this alleged satisfaction, presenting witness depositions that testified to a verbal agreement between Twiss and Richard S. Bond regarding the property transaction.	The defendant, William H. Twiss, contended that the evidence presented did not support the plaintiff's claims of a satisfied judgment. He argued that the deed submitted by the plaintiff conveyed a different lot than described in the bill and did not constitute valid evidence of a satisfaction of the judgment, leading to the conclusion that the complaint should be dismissed.

In 1882, in St. Charles, Illinois, a parol agreement was allegedly made between Hannah R. Dodge and her mother, Sarah Gorham, wherein Hannah agreed to live with and care for her mother for her lifetime in exchange for the transfer of property. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after the death of Sarah Gorham and disputes arose among her heirs regarding the validity of the alleged agreement. The other defendants, including William J. Gorham, contended that there was no enforceable contract due to the lack of a written agreement and asserted defenses under the Statute of Frauds, claiming that the verbal agreement did not meet legal requirements. The evidence presented to the court included testimony from a granddaughter who summarized discussions about the arrangement; however, it was noted that Hannah did not take possession of the property nor perform her obligations, particularly during her mother’s last days, ultimately leading to the questioning of her entitlement to the property. Moreover, it was revealed that Sarah had executed a last will and testament that specifically bequeathed certain assets, including a legacy to Hannah, reinforcing the complicated nature of the claims upon the estate.	Hannah R. Dodge, the plaintiff, claimed that there was a binding parol agreement with her mother, Sarah Gorham, entitling her to ownership of the property in question for her life-long commitment to care for her mother. She requested the court to enforce the alleged agreement for specific performance, despite the absence of a written document, arguing that her actions and dedication to care for her mother fulfilled the terms of the agreement, thus exempting it from the Statute of Frauds.	The defendants, heirs of Sarah Gorham, denied the existence of any binding contract, invoking the Statute of Frauds. They argued that since no written agreement existed, and no actions indicating ownership or possession were taken by Hannah, the claims should not be recognized in court. Additionally, they emphasized the legal effect of Sarah's will that bequeathed a legacy to Hannah and specified the property to another heir, asserting that Hannah's acceptance of the legacy estopped her from pursuing further claims related to the property's ownership.

In November 1854, a legal dispute arose in Illinois involving John Roach et al. as the plaintiffs and Lewis L. Perry, the executor of Jacob Roach's estate, as the defendant. The key individuals in the case included John Roach, Jacob Roach (the deceased whose estate was being handled), and Lewis L. Perry. The case centered around whether a partnership existed regarding a farm that Jacob Roach and the defendants owned in common. The plaintiffs argued that they had made financial advances concerning the property and sought an accounting as partners. The defendants contended that a partnership existed and that they had been managing the farm collectively. The circuit court found proof of the partnership, which was essential in establishing the plaintiffs' claims for reimbursement of their advances. The legal proceedings also included complexities regarding the calculation of interests and financial contributions among the partners.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had made significant financial advances for the farm owned in common with the other defendants and sought an accounting to determine their share of the partnership after alleging that a partnership existed. They contended that the circuit court should grant them the appropriate financial reimbursement based on their contributions, asserting that the defendants were liable for not adequately accounting for these advances.	The defendant argued that a partnership was indeed established between the parties involved, thereby justifying their collective management of the farm. They asserted that there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the claim for compensation for labor and contributions unless a special agreement existed to warrant such a charge. They sought to have the court affirm the circuit court's ruling that recognized the partnership and its equitable treatment in accounting for financial interests.

In September 1877, in Illinois, Joshua L. Smallman, the captain of a steamboat chartered for an excursion by the Young Men's Christian Association, encountered Mary J. Whilter, who was selling goods (peanuts, popcorn, watermelons) for profit on the trip from Chicago to Highland Park. Though Whilter paid $33.75 for her goods, Smallman denied her permission to sell them on the boat, placing her items in the baggage room instead. Unable to retrieve her goods in time to sell them at the picnic site after disembarking due to the crowd's congestion, Whilter claimed damages. Initially, she won a judgment of $36.75 against Smallman in the lower court, leading to his appeal.	Whilter contended that Smallman wrongfully prevented her from selling her goods on the chartered boat, thus causing her financial loss. She argued that she should be compensated for the lost opportunity to sell her items during the excursion, leading to her initial victory in the lower court.	Smallman argued that Whilter had no legal right to sell her goods on the boat without prior permission from him or the Young Men’s Christian Association. He maintained that by placing her goods in the baggage room and handling them appropriately under crowded conditions, he acted within his authority, and therefore, chose not to be held liable for any claimed damages.

The case of Jarret Garner v. M. C. Willis took place in Gallatin, Illinois, in December 1830. The dispute arose from a succession of judgments against John Huston, with Willis acting as the constable responsible for executing these judgments. There were two prior judgments on a justice’s docket: one in favor of William Wight and the other in favor of Garner. Following Wight’s judgment, he obtained an execution that was not levied. Subsequently, Garner secured an execution on his judgment, which Willis levied on Huston’s horse. Afterward, Wight initiated a second execution on his original judgment, which Willis also levied on the same horse and sold to Garner. However, Garner took possession of the horse without Willis's consent or command. The case hinges on whether Garner’s execution had been satisfied in law before Wight’s, thus determining who had rightful ownership over the horse. The lower court sided with Wight, leading Garner to file a writ of error to overturn this judgment.	Garner argued that his execution should have precedence and that he was wrongly deemed to have committed trespass by taking possession of the horse sold to him at auction. He contended that the timing of the executions and the manner in which the proceeds should be applied warranted a ruling in his favor. Garner sought to reverse the judgment of the lower court and recover damages.	Willis defended against Garner's allegations by citing that the oldest execution had created a lien on Huston's property, which extended to subsequent executions made under the same judgment. He maintained that Garner's unilateral possession of the horse was unauthorized and constituted trespass. The defense rested on the assertion that Garner’s execution did not negate Wight's prior claims to the property in question.

Isaac C. Choate was indicted in Pulaski County and subsequently arrested in Massac County under a capias directed to the sheriff of Massac. He was released after entering into a recognizance to appear for the indictment, with individuals from Massac County serving as his sureties. However, Choate failed to appear, leading to the forfeiture of the recognizance. Afterward, a scire facias (a legal order) and an alias scire facias were issued against the sureties, but both were returned nihil, indicating that the sureties could not be found. Consequently, the court issued a judgment of execution against the sureties. The plaintiffs, who were Choate's sureties, asserted that they had not been notified about the proceeding concerning the recognizance and argued that the court lacked jurisdiction over them. They claimed that the judgment was void and sought to enjoin it. The case was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court, which reviewed the arguments and evidence surrounding the jurisdiction and the subsequent actions taken by the court.	The plaintiffs argued that the judgment against them was void due to a lack of jurisdiction since they resided in Massac County and had not received notice of the proceedings related to the recognizance. They contended that the court had no authority to render judgment without proper jurisdiction over the individuals involved and sought to have the judgment enjoined.	The defendants maintained that the sheriff of Massac County had the authority to take the recognizance, therefore binding the sureties to their obligations. They argued that the court had valid jurisdiction based on the returns of nihil for the scire facias, which established the court's authority to proceed with the case. The defendants contended that the plaintiffs had recourse through a writ of error to challenge any errors in the record that did not pertain to the court’s jurisdiction.

The case of Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company v. John Riddle took place in September 1871 in Illinois. The central issue arose when John Riddle, the plaintiff, sought damages from the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company after their train killed his hog. The case was heard in the Circuit Court of Mercer County, presided over by Judge Arthur A. Smith. The key individuals involved included Mr. B. C. Cook and Mr. H. Bigelow, representing the railroad company, and Messrs. Bassett & Connell, representing Riddle. The core of the dispute revolved around the admissibility of statements made by the locomotive driver, Lampson, regarding the incident after it had occurred.	The plaintiff, John Riddle, claimed that the railroad company was responsible for the death of his hog due to negligence. He sought damages for the loss, contending that the railroad company should be held accountable for the actions of its employees, particularly the engine driver, whose admissions were believed to support his case.	The defendant, Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Company, argued that the statements made by the engine driver, Lampson, after the accident were inadmissible as evidence. They contended that such declarations could not bind the principal (the railroad company) since they were not made during the transaction in question. The defense sought to have the claims dismissed based on this argument.

In September 1877, the case "James Mix et al. v. The People" was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from Kankakee County, where James Mix and others (the appellants) had executed a bond while appealing a judgment related to delinquent taxes against real estate. The appeal necessitated a bond that had specific conditions. The court's examination focused on breaches of this bond, which were specially assigned in the declaration. The appellants raised several defenses, but the court found many of them insufficient. Key issues included whether the bond complied with statutory requirements and whether the appellants could be compelled to respond to the bond's obligations before all remedies against the property (land) were exhausted.	The plaintiff, The People, asserted that the appellants breached the terms of the bond executed in relation to their appeal. They argued that the bond was a valid obligation under common law and that the conditions outlined within it were binding. The People's claims hinged on the assertion that the appellants did not fulfill their obligations regarding the appeal.	The defendants (appellants) put forth several defenses: they claimed that the bond was invalid because the judgment they appealed from was against the land itself and not personally against them. They also argued that their obligations under the bond should not take effect until all remedies against the property were exhausted. Furthermore, they included a plea alleging that the judgment they were appealing did not exist, which was rejected by the court.

In December 1857, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed a case involving Jules P. Baulos as the Plaintiff in Error and George W. Ash as the Defendant in Error. The events leading to this case began in 1856 at the Sangamon Circuit Court, where a decree was rendered in favor of George W. Ash regarding a mortgage executed in May 1852 by Ira C. Ash and Amanda V. Ash, with Horace E. Ash as her trustee. The mortgage was said to have been financed by the Defendant, George W. Ash, for the purchase of the land. The primary issue revolved around whether Amanda V. Ash had only a life estate in the property or an estate in fee simple, which would affect her heirs. The court of first instance determined that Amanda had a fee simple estate, ordering Baulos and others to pay the owed amount or face the sale of the mortgaged premises. The Plaintiff Baulos, claiming to be one of the heirs of Amanda V. Ash, contested this decree, asserting that Amanda had only a life estate.	The plaintiff, Jules P. Baulos, argued that the lower court erred in not dismissing the complaint and in decreeing that he and others must pay the mortgage debt and allow the sale of the premises. He contended that Amanda V. Ash only held a life estate in the property and that the title to the property should pass to her heirs upon her death, rather than owing any debt related to the mortgage.	George W. Ash, the defendant, maintained that Amanda V. Ash held an estate in fee simple at the time of the mortgage execution and that the court correctly ordered the payment of the mortgage debt by Baulos and others. The defendant's argument was rooted in the interpretation of the deed, asserting that the wording clearly assigned Amanda V. Ash full ownership rights without limitation to a life estate.

In 1889, in the city of Danville, Illinois, a legal case arose involving the City of Danville and plaintiff Margaret Makemson. The incident occurred on Williams Street, a public thoroughfare where the city had constructed a fourteen-foot high embankment that was thirty feet wide at the top. The street included a streetcar track with iron rails, which projected three inches above the surface, and lacked any guard or railing along the embankment edges. While driving into the city with her husband in a two-horse wagon, one of the horses became startled by a child's carriage on the sidewalk. This caused the wagon to overturn, throwing Makemson to the foot of the embankment and resulting in serious injuries. The plaintiff alleged that the city was negligent for not providing safety measures, such as guardrails, to protect users of the street, particularly given the dangerous construction of the embankment. The case was tried before a jury which found for the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, Margaret Makemson, claimed that the City of Danville was negligent for failing to provide adequate safety measures, such as guardrails, along the embankment of Williams Street. She argued that the city's actions created a dangerous condition that resulted in her being seriously injured when the wagon overturned. Makemson requested damages for her injuries, which were heard and ultimately awarded by the jury.	The City of Danville defended itself by asserting that the evidence did not support the jury's verdict, claiming that the injury was not a result of the city's negligence but rather an accident that could not have been foreseen or prevented. They argued that the plaintiff had other safe streets available to her, suggesting she could have used an alternative route to avoid the hazardous situation. The city contended that the plaintiff's team management was also at fault due to the presence of a young and inexperienced horse.

George W. Rearden v. John B. Smith is a legal case that took place in November 1864 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a covenant action initiated by John B. Smith against George W. Rearden, following a transaction in which Rearden sold certain lands to Smith. In the sale agreement, Rearden guaranteed that the lands were not classified as "graduated lands" under federal law and agreed to pay $1,200 if they were found to be so. After several procedural steps including a default by Rearden, the court allowed a jury to assess damages, which led to a verdict in Smith's favor for the full amount guaranteed. However, Rearden challenged the judgment, specifically questioning the sufficiency of the record regarding the jury's involvement and verdict. Despite these claims, the court ultimately found that any potential record deficiencies were remedied by the applicable statutes that protect against procedural errors, maintaining fairness in legal proceedings.	The plaintiff, John B. Smith, argued that George W. Rearden had entered into a binding covenant concerning the sale of lands and had failed to uphold his guarantee. Smith asserted that the lands in question were indeed graduated lands and that he was entitled to the sum of $1,200 as stipulated in their agreement. He requested the court to uphold the lower court's judgment, which ruled in his favor, and to enforce the payment of the damages awarded.	The defendant, George W. Rearden, contended that there were significant deficiencies in the court records, specifically regarding the impaneling of the jury and the return of the verdict. He claimed that the entry in the record did not adequately demonstrate that a jury was properly called or that a verdict was duly rendered. Rearden sought to have the judgment reversed on these grounds, arguing that the lack of formal record violated procedural norms.

In the case of The Pennsylvania Co. v. Chandler S. Redfield et al., which took place in Englewood, Illinois, the plaintiff, The Pennsylvania Company, initiated an action against the defendants, who were sureties on a bond for an individual named Broomhall. Broomhall was acting as an agent for The Pennsylvania Company when he failed to pay a sum of three thousand dollars that he had received while performing his duties. The plaintiff claimed that Broomhall's inability to account for the funds constituted a breach of the bond agreement, prompting them to seek redress from the sureties. The trial occurred without a jury, and the court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, determining that the damages owed amounted to fifteen hundred and nineteen dollars. Following the initial ruling, the plaintiff appealed, arguing that the damages awarded were insufficient and that the court should have recognized a more significant amount based on the evidence presented during the trial.	The Pennsylvania Company, the plaintiff, asserted that the defendants, as sureties, were liable for the breach of bond by Broomhall, who failed to remit the three thousand dollars he collected during his tenure as an agent. The plaintiff requested that the court find for them on the grounds of this breach and sought monetary damages to compensate for the loss. They contended that the evidence warranted a larger amount than what was awarded by the trial court.	The defendants contended that the evidence presented by the plaintiff was insufficient to support the claim of a larger damage amount. They argued that the trial court was justified in its findings and that the conclusions reached were sound and based on the evidence reviewed. The defendants requested the appellate court to uphold the original ruling and dismiss the plaintiff's appeal regarding the damage amount.

In January 1859, a legal dispute arose in Marshall County, Illinois, involving Stephen Merritt and several other plaintiffs against John G. Farris and other defendants, who were acting as school directors for School District No. 10. The plaintiffs, residents and taxpayers of the district, sought to enjoin the collection of a school tax that they claimed was improperly levied. The plaintiffs argued that the notice for the election allowing the tax was insufficiently specific and lacked conformity to legal requirements, particularly in describing the election's purposes. They raised concerns over the tax amount, which they felt was excessive, and argued that the directors had no power to levy a tax for the construction of a schoolhouse without a vote from the district residents. Moreover, they contended that property owners within the district were improperly excluded from tax assessments, violating the State constitution's requirement for uniformity in taxation. The court initially granted an injunction, but the defendants countered with evidence to dissolve it, leading to the court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' bill. The plaintiffs then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the school tax levied by the directors was invalid due to insufficient notice of the election and various legal irregularities. They argued that the directors exceeded their authority in levying the tax without a vote from the residents.
