Furthermore, they asserted that several district property owners were not assessed, creating an inequitable tax burden. They requested that the court issue a permanent injunction preventing the tax from being collected.	The defendants, acting as school directors, maintained that they had the legal authority to levy the tax for the schoolhouse construction and to fund educational services, as permitted by state law. They defended the sufficiency of the election notice and asserted that a site for the schoolhouse was indeed selected with the voters' consent. The defendants acknowledged that some property owners were omitted from the tax but argued that such omissions did not invalidate the entire tax levy. They requested that the court dismiss the plaintiffs’ claims and uphold the tax.

John D. Cleghorn filed a legal case against Thomas H. Postlewaite et al. in 1867, stemming from disputes over tax assessments in the town of Lodi, Iroquois County, Illinois. Cleghorn had moved to Lodi in December 1863 and was asked by Postlewaite, who was then the assessor, to provide a list of his taxable property in June 1864. Cleghorn completed the blank statement left by Postlewaite, declaring two horses worth $100, a watch valued at $6, and about $25,000 in credits, while his debts amounted to approximately $30,000. He certified the list as complete and delivered it to the assessor, who accepted it without objections. However, in December 1864, Cleghorn was informed that his taxable property had been assessed at $10,000, leading to a tax demand of $405. He claimed that this assessment was erroneous and unjust, stating he was unaware of any changes to the amount until the tax collector approached him. Cleghorn feared property distress due to the potential for tax collection actions, prompting him to seek an injunction against the collection of this tax in the Circuit Court of Iroquois County.	Cleghorn argued that the tax assessment of $10,000 was incorrect and requested the court to enjoin the collection of this tax. He claimed he had completed and submitted a full list of his taxable property, which the assessor accepted without objection. He contended that he had no knowledge of any reevaluation of his tax liability, which was done arbitrarily by the assessor without proper notice, and therefore sought to have the assessment declared null and void.	The defendant, Postlewaite, contended that Cleghorn had legal remedies available to contest the re-assessment but failed to act in time because he was unaware of it until much later, in December. The defense maintained that since the property tax assessment process had lawful procedures, any changes complied with statutory requirements, implying that the assessment could stand.

In 1861, a legal dispute arose in Iroquois County, Illinois, involving Henry Bacon as the defendant and Daniel Lawrence as the plaintiff. The case originated from an action on a note in which Lawrence had won a judgment against Bacon for $48.16, along with court costs, at a local justice of the peace. Following the judgment, Lawrence appealed his own decision on the same day it was rendered. Subsequently, on January 16, 1861, a summons was issued from the Circuit Court to Bacon, who was duly served. Lawrence then moved to dismiss his appeal in the Circuit Court, while Bacon sought to join in the appeal. The court, however, permitted Lawrence to dismiss his appeal. Bacon objected, claiming he wished to secure a review of the case, asserting there was a good defense on the merits of the case, and he perceived that he also had the right to appeal. The court ultimately ruled against Bacon, dismissing his appeal, which prompted him to formally except to the judgment.	The plaintiff, Daniel Lawrence, argued that he should be allowed to dismiss his appeal regarding the initial judgment rendered in his favor at the justice of the peace. He maintained that if Bacon was dissatisfied with the judgment, he should have initiated his own appeal, thus acquiescing to the original ruling. Lawrence sought to uphold his original judgment by dismissing his own appeal.	Henry Bacon, the defendant, contended that he had a good defense and would have appealed the decision if Lawrence had not already done so. He requested permission to join in the appeal process, arguing that he was unjustly denied the ability to secure a trial in the Circuit Court. Bacon claimed that allowing Lawrence's dismissal without considering his position was contrary to law and equity.

The case, titled "The People, use, etc., v. The Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company," was decided on January 16, 1883, by the Illinois Appellate Court. It originated in the Circuit Court of Piatt County, Illinois. The case involved the State's Attorney of Piatt County suing the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company for alleged violations of a statute prohibiting railroad corporations from obstructing public highways by stopping trains or leaving cars or locomotives on the tracks at highway crossings. The statute stipulated penalties for such violations, which the State's Attorney sought to claim on behalf of the state. The suit claimed thirty separate violations of the law, each carrying a potential penalty. The key individual in the case was the State's Attorney, who was prosecuting the action for his own financial gain. The court had to address whether it was appropriate for him to conduct this suit in his official capacity while having a personal interest in its outcome.	The plaintiff, represented by the State's Attorney of Piatt County, argued that the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company was liable for thirty penalties due to violations of the statute against obstructing public highways. The claims were grounded in a public policy context, stating that the railroad's actions not only violated the law but also warranted penalties that should be enforced by a public official on behalf of the state's interests.	The defendant contended that allowing the State's Attorney to prosecute this case for personal gain contradicted public policy and the principles of impartiality in legal proceedings. The defense argued that the prosecution should be free from any pecuniary interest to ensure a fair trial for the defendant. They highlighted that legal proceedings must not be used for the benefit of court officers or public officials beyond their official duties.

The case of Elias Richardson et al. v. Hiram D. Olmstead took place in La Salle County, Illinois, with the final judgment delivered in September 1874. The key individuals involved were Hiram D. Olmstead, the plaintiff, and Elias and William H. Richardson, the defendants. The case stemmed from a contractual agreement made on May 27, 1870, wherein Olmstead delivered his corn to the Richardson's warehouse in Ottawa for sale. Under the terms, he would be paid the market price whenever he requested payment. The corn, however, was mixed with other grain in a common bin, complicating the ownership status after delivery. By August 25, 1870, Olmstead had delivered 931 bushels of corn, which became the center of contention after a fire destroyed Richardson's warehouse in April 1871. The case centered around whether the agreement constituted a sale or a bailment, as Olmstead asserted it was a sale, while the Richardsons claimed otherwise.	Olmstead claimed that the agreement was a sale of the corn he delivered, asserting that he was entitled to receive payment at the market price, which he had not yet collected due to the destruction of the warehouse. He argued that at the point of grain delivery, he transferred ownership to the Richardsons and that they were therefore liable for its value.	The Richardsons argued that the arrangement constituted bailment rather than a sale, claiming that Olmstead wanted to store his corn until spring and that no clear return of the original grain was required. They contended that since the corn was mixed with other deliveries, they were not obligated to pay for the specific corn delivered, only to return corn of equivalent value.

In September 1866, Robert Strahorn and his company, based in Chicago, authorized M. Y. Butler to draw $500 from them when he acquired stock for shipment by railroad. Butler presented this to the First National Bank, and a system was established whereby he could use drafts for purchasing hogs, later drawing against Strahorn for advances. However, on February 3, 1867, Strahorn informed the bank they would no longer accept any drafts from Butler. On February 4, a carload of hogs intended for Strahorn was shipped but the ownership was then transferred to W. H. Hubbard, who paid Butler for them and directed the hogs to Conger & Co. The hogs arrived in Chicago and were held by the Union Stock Yard, but Strahorn was denied delivery. This prompted Strahorn to sue for conversion, claiming a right to the hogs as they were meant to settle Butler's debt to them. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court and hinged on whether Strahorn had a lien over the hogs due to their prior arrangements and debts with Butler.	Strahorn & Co. argued that because Butler was indebted to them and shipped the hogs to them, they had a rightful lien on the hogs. They claimed that this lien prevented Butler from legally selling the hogs to the bank or any other party. They sought recovery of the hogs or compensation for their value, asserting that the conversion of the property by the bank and Hubbard was unjustified.	The Union Stock Yard & Transit Company contended that Butler had the right to change the destination of the hogs while they were in transit. They stated that since Strahorn had not taken possession of the hogs or established a claim over them before Butler's instructions to sell, they had no legal basis for their lien. Furthermore, they argued that Butler's actions complied with his right to manage his assets, and thus they were not liable for the transaction.

In the case of **Martha A. Walker v. John W. Doane**, heard before the Illinois Supreme Court on November 20, 1883, the dispute arose over the possession of property located on Ellis Avenue in Cook County. Martha A. Walker, the plaintiff, claimed a right to the property based on her status as the widow of the deceased owner. Following her husband's death, an administrator sold the property, which was subject to a dower decree granting Walker annual dower payments of $350. Despite this, John W. Doane, the defendant, purchased the property at an administrator's sale but subsequently withheld possession from Walker. The case was initially examined during the March term of 1882, and after a remand, the Superior Court found most of Walker's claims substantiated. The court recognized her right to the property and instructed Doane to surrender possession, also accounting for the rental value, taxes, and waste due to his negligence. The core issue was Walker's claim against Doane for rightful possession of the premises and compensation for damages incurred during his occupancy.	Martha A. Walker's primary argument was that she was entitled to possession of the Ellis Avenue property as decreed by the dower award. She claimed Doane unlawfully withheld possession since his purchase, causing her damages through taxation liabilities and waste. She requested an accounting for the rental value of the property since the administrator's deed, as well as full possession of the premises. Walker sought a decree that would ensure she received her rightful equity in the property against Doane.	John W. Doane contended that he had acquired the property through a lawful purchase at an administrator's sale and that Walker's claims were invalidated by the dower arrangement. He argued that the dower decree did not confer rights allowing her to occupy the property. Doane requested dismissal of Walker's claims, asserting that he had no obligation to compensate her for the property while he was the registered owner.

The case, "The Germania Fire Insurance Company of New York v. Emil Klewer," was decided on December 18, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The key individuals involved were Emil Klewer, the plaintiff, and the Germania Fire Insurance Company, the defendant. The background of the case dates back to August 20, 1882, when Klewer procured a three-year insurance policy for his house in Norwood Park, Illinois, from the Agricultural Insurance Company. A clause in this policy prohibited additional insurance. In May 1883, he also obtained a policy from the Hartford Fire Insurance Company, which similarly stated that it would be void in case of other insurance or if the house was vacant for over ten days. Importantly, Klewer remained unaware that the Hartford policy was issued under his name until after his house burnt down. By August 22, 1885, Klewer had vacated the house, which remained unoccupied until its destruction by fire on November 15, 1885. He subsequently secured another policy from Germania Fire Insurance Company on October 16, 1885. However, the defendant raised defenses citing other existing insurance policies and the house's vacancy, along with accusations that Klewer had intentionally burned the building. The trial concluded with a verdict for Klewer, leading to the appeal by the Germania Insurance Company.	The plaintiff, Emil Klewer, argued that the Germania Fire Insurance Company was liable for the fire damage incurred on his property. He asserted that, at the time of the policy issuance, the company's agent was fully aware that the house was vacant and had not objected to this condition, effectively waiving any rights to claim forfeiture based on vacancy. Klewer maintained that the policy was valid and that he had not burned the building, hence entitled to recovery for the loss.	The Germania Fire Insurance Company's main defenses included claims of other existing insurance coverage and the assertion that the house had been vacant, violating the policy's terms. They also contended that Klewer had intentionally set fire to his own property, seeking to avoid liability. The defendant requested the court to overturn the prior judgment, asserting that these factors justified denying Klewer's claim.

The legal case "The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company et al. v. Isaac McDougal et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 14, 1885. The case arose in Menard County, Illinois, involving a dispute over a strip of land, fifty feet wide on each side of the railway track belonging to the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company. The land in question was identified as swamp land that had been granted to the State of Illinois by the United States government and subsequently to Menard County. Appellees (the plaintiffs) sought to recover this land, arguing that the county court had the authority to sell it and that they had acquired valid title through that sale. The defendants (the railway company and others) contested the plaintiff's claims asserting that Menard County lacked proper title and that the sale process had been flawed, claiming that the necessary procedural steps were not observed when the land was sold.	The plaintiffs contended that they were rightful owners of the disputed land as it was part of swamp land granted by Congress to the State of Illinois and subsequently conveyed to Menard County. They argued that the county court had the authority to sell and convey such land, and that the deed executed was valid under the prevailing statutes. Their request was for the court to affirm their title to the parcel in question.	The defendants, on the other hand, argued that there was no adequate proof of title in Menard County regarding the land as the relevant congressional act did not explicitly identify these lands. They suggested that the county court was not authorized to sell the land without proper identification and processes being followed before the sale. The defendants sought to dismiss the plaintiffs' claims and maintain their position on the disputed land.

Thomas J. Buntain, the plaintiff in error, was involved in a legal case against Rufus Dutton, the defendant in error, which was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1859. The dispute arose from a promissory note issued by Dutton to Buntain in the amount of $165, which was due eight months after its issuance on June 27, 1856. The note was executed in consideration of a reaping and mowing machine sold by Buntain to Dutton via his agent, Fergus M. Blair. Dutton claimed that the machine was defective and did not operate as warranted, arguing that the consideration for the note had failed. As such, Buntain presented the note for recovery while Dutton contended that the machine’s inability to function effectively invalidated the debt. The case was heard in Edgar County in Illinois.	Buntain claimed that Dutton owed the amount specified in the promissory note despite any claims regarding the condition of the reaping machine. He argued that the promise made by his agent to repair the machine was not binding and did not constitute a new contract that would negate Dutton’s obligation to pay the note. Buntain requested the court to affirm the validity of the note and grant a judgment for the amount owed.	Dutton maintained that the note was a result of the sale of a reaping and mowing machine that was sold under the assumption it would perform well, as warranted by Buntain's agent. He asserted that the machine was, in fact, worthless and did not operate as promised, leading to the failure of consideration for the note. Dutton requested the court to dismiss the case based on these grounds, arguing that he should not be held liable for a note tied to a defective product.

William Runnamaker brought a legal action against Henry Cordray in June 1870 in the Jasper Circuit Court, Illinois. The case arose after Cordray moved to Jasper County, where a judgment from an Ohio justice of the peace against him was discovered. Runnamaker claimed that Cordray verbally promised to pay the Ohio judgment amount but later asserted it was unjust. During the trial, Runnamaker attempted to introduce evidence of the Ohio judgment, which was denied by the court. The trial was held without a jury, and the judge ruled in favor of Cordray, ultimately deciding against Runnamaker's claims. Runnamaker sought to reverse this decision by filing a motion for a new trial, which was denied, leading him to escalate the case to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Runnamaker argued that Cordray had made a verbal promise to pay the judgment against him. He contended that the promise indicated Cordray's acknowledgment of the debt and that he had not fulfilled the obligation. Runnamaker sought a recovery based on this purported promise, along with a court judgment in his favor to collect the amount owed.	Cordray's defense relied on the assertion that the verbal promise was not legally binding due to a lack of consideration. He argued that the obligation to pay was already dictated by the original judgment, and the promise did not alter or increase his liability. Furthermore, Cordray contended that the judgment itself could not be used as evidence for a new claim, asserting that Runnamaker should have declared the case differently to have a valid claim.

In January 1877, William J. Brownell purchased the stock of boots and shoes belonging to O. Bugg at a sheriff's sale, intending to provide employment for John P. McLean, who had worked as a salesman for Bugg for sixteen years. Elisha B. Steere, a long-time friend of Brownell, arranged to be an equal partner by contributing half the price. However, their partnership lacked written agreements regarding operations and financial arrangements. They established the business under the name W.J. Brownell & Company, with Brownell managing day-to-day operations while McLean was responsible for purchasing and sales. Disputes arose when Brownell directed McLean to account for his draws from the business, leading to conflicts about payments and the division of assets after their agreement to dissolve the partnership in 1882. After the dissolution, they agreed to an arbitration process to settle accounts, during which they sold their remaining stock. An award from the arbitrators found Brownell owed money to Steere, but Steere subsequently filed to set aside the award, leading to further legal complications and an eventual split in the financial balance between them.	Steere claimed that the arbitrators' award was unjust and sought to set it aside. He argued that Brownell had insufficiently compensated him for the partnership’s earnings and sought a thorough account of their partnership dealings, alleging that Brownell owed him additional funds beyond the arbitrators' decision.	Brownell defended against Steere’s claims by arguing that he had been unfairly held accountable for McLean’s salary and for the costs ensuing from the lawsuit initiated by McLean against both partners. He insisted that the arbitration process was fairly conducted and that the assets had been appropriately accounted for during the partnership’s dissolution. Furthermore, he maintained that the sale process did not necessitate any additional compensation for McLean that should fall to him.

On September 30, 1872, in Atlanta, Illinois, a tragic incident occurred involving a six-year-old boy named Frederick Becker, who was killed by a freight train operated by the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company. At the time of the accident, Frederick was crossing the railroad tracks at a street-crossing while exercising due care. The case arose several years later when David Becker, as the administrator of Frederick's estate, filed a lawsuit in the Logan Circuit Court against the railroad company. He claimed that the train approached without ringing its bell or sounding the whistle, violating legal requirements, and was traveling above the permitted speed limit. The jury ruled in favor of Becker, awarding damages of $2,500. The railroad company appealed the verdict, arguing the evidence was insufficient for the jury's decision, and that the trial court committed errors regarding jury instructions and the assessment of damages.	The plaintiff, David Becker, argued that the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company was liable for Frederick's death due to negligence. Becker claimed that the train had not made the necessary auditory warnings (ringing the bell or sounding the whistle) as it approached the crossing, and it was traveling at an excessive speed, violating ordinances. He sought compensation for the pecuniary injuries suffered by the deceased's next of kin as prescribed by the relevant statute.	The defendant, Chicago and Alton Railroad Company, asserted that there was insufficient evidence to support the verdict and contended that the jury instructions were erroneous. They maintained that the whistle was blown and the bell rang while the train approached the crossing. The defendant also argued that Frederick had acted negligently by attempting to cross the tracks when he could see the train approaching, claiming that he had stumbled onto the tracks and that the train's speed was not in violation of any ordinances.

In 1870, David E. Day lent $200 to A. G. Humphrey to settle a promissory note owed to the First National Bank of Gales-burg, which was signed by Humphrey as principal and W. S. Hinckley as surety. The transaction involved Humphrey borrowing the amount from Day to pay off the existing note. During this process, Day provided a check to the bank, while Humphrey covered the remaining interest. Initially, they did not discuss any security from Humphrey, but after the note was surrendered, the bank endorsed it to Day without recourse. The note was treated as paid by the bank at the time of this transaction. However, there were conflicting accounts regarding whether Hinckley, the surety, was present during the arrangement, which raised concerns about the validity of the payment as it pertained to him. The dispute arose when, after several years, Day sought payment from Hinckley alone since Humphrey had become insolvent by that time.	The plaintiff, David E. Day, claimed that he was entitled to payment on the promissory note after lending money intended to settle the note at the bank. He argued that the arrangement made between him and Humphrey constituted a proper settlement of the debt owed, and sought a judgment requiring Hinckley to fulfill the financial obligation as the surety.	The defendant, W. S. Hinckley, contended that he was not present or involved in the agreement between Day and Humphrey regarding the note. He argued that since he did not consent to the transaction, the payment did not legally bind him, especially since the arrangement took place without his knowledge. Therefore, he requested that the court affirm his position, and he maintained that the evidence did not sufficiently support Day's claims against him.

Nathaniel Norton brought a legal action against The Merchants’ Loan and Trust Company in 1862, which took place in the Superior Court of Chicago, Illinois. The case arose from a dispute concerning a promissory note that was guaranteed by the defendant. Norton claimed that the interest charged on the note was usurious, meaning it was set at an illegally high rate. During the proceedings, Norton pleaded the general issue along with five special pleas, which included a request for permission to file additional pleas. However, the court denied his request to present the usury argument. Following a trial, a verdict was reached in favor of the defendant, leading to a judgment against Norton.	Nathaniel Norton contended that the rate of interest charged on his promissory note was usurious. He argued that the amount of interest calculated was excessive and requested the court to allow him to file additional pleas that would substantiate his claim of illegal interest. Norton sought to overturn the previous judgment made by the lower court asserting that the interest was improperly computed and consequently, unfairly charged against him.	The Merchants’ Loan and Trust Company replied that there was no usurious agreement made and that the calculation of interest, which was done by an employee, was merely a clerical error. They maintained that because there was no malicious intent or corrupt pact, the claim of usury was invalid. The defendant also argued that the court acted within its discretion in refusing to allow additional pleas from Norton, asserting that the original judgment should stand as lawful.

In the case of Stephen F. Hanford v. Isaac Blessing, the dispute arose from a real estate transaction involving a warehouse in Manteno, Illinois, in November 1864. Isaac Blessing owned the warehouse and held a lease from the Illinois Central Railroad Company. He transferred both the warehouse and the lease to Stephen F. Hanford — the central issue in the case was whether this transfer constituted an absolute conveyance or a mortgage. Hanford claimed he advanced money at Blessing’s request and sought to recover funds from a co-partnership and to prohibit the enforcement of a judgment that Blessing had obtained against him for a promissory note. The key individuals involved were Stephen F. Hanford and Isaac Blessing, with Hanford acting as the appellant who challenged the prior court's decision in favor of Blessing (the appellee). The case culminated in a thorough examination of the property transfer, the associated agreements, and the intentions of both parties regarding the nature of the transaction.	Hanford contended that the transaction was intended as a mortgage rather than a sale, and he sought an accounting for funds he claimed to have advanced for Blessing. He requested to prevent the enforcement of a judgment obtained by Blessing for a promissory note, arguing that the transfer of the warehouse was conditional upon repaying certain amounts and did not constitute a full ownership transfer.	Blessing argued that the transfer was an absolute sale, supported by the documentation at the time. He claimed that Hanford had full ownership and had acted as the owner by renting out the property, thereby negating any argument that he was merely a mortgagee. Blessing challenged the validity of Hanford's claims about advancing money and the partnership, asserting that Hanford provided no sufficient evidence to support his demands for recovery.

On April 5, 1870, in Will County, Illinois, an action of assumpsit was initiated by partners Samuel H. Sweet, Wesley Dempster, and Charles Hutchinson against Samuel C. Stearns (the principal) and his sureties: Herman D. Stearns, Frank Bush, and Edward Aiken. The case revolved around five promissory notes executed by the Stearnses to the plaintiffs, which were set to be payable at different intervals over the following twelve months. The notes did not specify interest payments. Samuel C. Stearns was not available for the trial, prompting the court to proceed with the sureties only. The main issue was whether the payment of interest on the notes, made without the sureties' knowledge, constituted an extension of payment obligations that could affect the sureties' liabilities. The trial concluded with a judgment favoring the plaintiffs for $1,000.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants were liable for the promissory notes despite the payments of interest made by the principal without the sureties' consent. They contended that this payment did not constitute a valid agreement to extend the payment terms of the notes. Therefore, they sought enforcement of the notes against the sureties, leading to the resolution in favor of the plaintiffs for the amounts due.	The defendants claimed they were merely sureties for the principal, asserting that they were not informed of the interest payments made by the principal and that such payments should not constitute an extension of the contracts without their knowledge. They argued that the mere act of paying interest did not create a legally binding agreement to extend the payment due date and requested dismissal of the claims against them.

In September 1872, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case originating from Mercer County, Illinois, involving William O. Dungan as the plaintiff and Levi Hall as the defendant. The case arose from a trespass claim wherein Dungan asserted that Hall, acting as the county sheriff, unlawfully levied upon and sold goods he claimed were exempt from execution. Hall had received an execution in favor of a third party, Willits, and appointed a special deputy, B.W. Kile, to execute the writ. Kile conducted the initial levy, but Hall later intervened to manage the execution personally before the sale of the goods. A key point of contention revolved around whether Dungan had voluntarily surrendered the property for levy and if any of the goods had been released due to an agreement prior to the sale. During the trial, conflicting evidence was presented regarding Dungan’s demand for the return of the exempt goods. The legal question of the sheriff's authority to appoint a special deputy also emerged as a matter of significant deliberation.	The plaintiff, William O. Dungan, claimed that his goods were exempt from execution and sought to recover three times their value due to the unlawful levying and sale by Levi Hall, the sheriff. Dungan asserted that he had made a valid demand for the return of specific exempt items before the sale occurred and argued that Hall had no legal authority to appoint Kile as a deputy to carry out the levy.	The defendant, Levi Hall, contended that the levy executed by his appointed deputy, R. W. Kile, was valid under common law, which permits sheriffs to appoint special deputies for specific writs. Hall's defense focused on the legality of the levy and the argument that Dungan voluntarily allowed the deputy to take possession of the goods, thus negating his right to claim the items as exempt.

In 1881, Edward E. Ayer was the owner of two vessels, the "Milwaukee Belle" and the "Jessie Hoyt," which were registered in South Chicago, Illinois. Ayer, who resided in North Chicago, sought to enjoin the assessment of taxes on his vessels by the town of North Chicago. He argued that the assessment was improper, as both vessels were duly registered in South Chicago, which is recognized as a port of registry under United States law. Ayer had already paid the taxes assessed in South Chicago without complaint but contested the taxes levied by North Chicago. The case came before the Illinois Supreme Court after the defendants, William Vogt and William T. Johnson, treasurer of the county, filed a demurrer against Ayer's bill. The Supreme Court ultimately ruled that North Chicago lacked the authority to tax Ayer’s vessels, as they were required by statute to be listed in the place where they were registered.	Edward E. Ayer claimed that the taxes assessed on his vessels by the town of North Chicago were unlawful. He argued that the vessels were registered in South Chicago, where the situs for taxation should legally lie, based on Illinois state statutes governing the assessment of watercraft. Ayer requested the court to enjoin the collection of the taxes imposed by North Chicago on his vessels.	The defendants, William Vogt and William T. Johnson, did not provide substantial defenses against Ayer's claims, as they filed a demurrer to the bill. They contended that the tax assessment was valid and sought to uphold the demurrer, indicating they believed the case did not warrant legal remedy or intervention by the court.

In February 1874, Sarah A. Campbell filed a petition in the Illinois court system seeking the assignment of dower on behalf of her deceased husband, James B. Campbell. The case was initially ruled in her favor, but the decision was appealed and subsequently reversed by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. This reversal prompted the case to be remanded for further proceedings. Tragically, before these proceedings could take place, Sarah A. Campbell died intestate on March 12, 1875. Willis M. Hitt was appointed as her administrator and sought to revive the lawsuit in order to claim damages and mesne profits concerning the dower rights of his intestate. However, the lower court dismissed the petition, leading to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, wherein the prior rulings and legal principles were debated. The Supreme Court ultimately ruled that the ability to assess damages was extinguished with the death of Campbell and reaffirmed the dismissal.	The plaintiff, Willis M. Hitt, as the administrator of Sarah A. Campbell's estate, claimed that he was entitled to recover damages and mesne profits related to Sarah's claim for dower. Hitt argued that, despite the reversal, the interests of the deceased widow could still be protected and sought the revival of the suit in order to pursue these claims on her behalf.	The defendants, represented by Jonathan Y. Scammon and others, contended that the claim for dower could not be pursued following the widow's death. They argued that because Sarah A. Campbell did not establish her right to dower during her lifetime, her administrator could not validly continue the suit. The court’s precedent established that without a decree for dower assignment at the time of her death, there was no basis for the administrator to seek damages, leading to the dismissal of Hitt's claims.

In the case of Simon Deimel et al. v. Willard S. Brown et al., the events occurred in the context of a creditors' bill initially presented to the Illinois Superior Court, which later led to the appeal resolved on January 29, 1890. The primary individuals involved were Simon Deimel and his affiliates as appellants and Willard S. Brown along with other judgment creditors as appellees. The case centered around whether the appellants had paid for goods worth $14,700 purchased from Jacob Biersdorf in February 1884. The appellants claimed they had settled their account with Biersdorf, reflecting a mutual relationship where Biersdorf also owed them for lumber and merchandise, leading to a complicated web of transactions and allegations of payment or offsets. The court inquired into the adequacy of evidence presented, especially in light of significant doubts raised about the integrity of the books of account maintained by the appellants.	The plaintiffs (appellees) argued that the appellants owed them the value of goods they purchased from Biersdorf, supporting their claims with judgments and potential recoveries from Biersdorf's estate. They sought confirmation that the appellants had not sufficiently proven their defense of having settled the account, implying entitlements to recover funds from the appellants as they traced property and transactions back to the original sale.	The defendants (appellants) contended that they had indeed settled payments with Biersdorf through mutual accounts and adjustments. They asserted that their accounting was legitimate and denied owing further amounts by stating that all transactions were settled in September 1884. They maintained that the discrepancies in the books were a result of the destruction caused by fires, although the court noted that witnesses contradicted this assertion, establishing doubts about the credibility of their defense.

Mary A. Snyder, the administratrix of John H. Snyder's estate, brought a legal action against the Chicago and Northwestern Railway Company and the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railroad Company following the death of her husband in a train collision. The incident occurred on October 7, 1882, at a railroad crossing near Western Avenue in Chicago. John H. Snyder was a conductor for the Chicago and Northwestern Railway and was operating a train when, due to a signal error at the crossing managed by H. E. Torrence, a joint agent for both railroads, his train collided with another train of the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul. The plaintiff alleged that both railway companies were negligent in managing the signals at the crossing and sought damages for the fatal accident. The Superior Court of Cook County ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding $5,000 in damages, a decision that was upheld by the Appellate Court.	The plaintiff claimed that both railway companies were negligent in maintaining proper signal protocols at the crossing, leading to the collision that resulted in John H. Snyder's death. The main arguments included that Snyder was exercising due care and that the change in signals by the joint agent, Torrence, was performed negligently, causing the fatal accident. The plaintiff requested compensation for the pecuniary injury inflicted upon Snyder's widow as a result of his untimely death.	The defendants contended that the court erroneously instructed the jury and argued that Snyder himself was negligent by not stopping the train at least 200 feet before the crossing, as required by law. They claimed that if Snyder had complied with this statute and the semaphore signals, the collision could have been avoided. The defendants also maintained that any negligence on the part of the joint agent did not absolve Snyder of responsibility for the actions of his coworkers under his command, which could have contributed to the incident.

In December 1820, in Illinois, John Thornton and others, acting as appellants, brought a case against George Smiley and John Bradshaw, the appellees. The dispute arose from a promissory note executed by Smiley and Bradshaw to Hezekiah West, who was acting as the administrator of the estate of the deceased Weaver. The appellants joined West in their action for the recovery of money, despite West alone having loaned the estate's funds to the defendants. The defendants objected to the plaintiffs' joint action, claiming improper joinder as the note was made solely to West, an argument the court found valid. The court ruled in favor of the defendants, leading to the appeal by Thornton and others to reverse this decision.	The plaintiffs, John Thornton and others, argued that they were entitled to recover the money lent by West on behalf of the estate of Weaver. They contended that the defendants’ obligations to repay the note executed to West, in his role as administrator, should not hinge on the joinder of other administrators in the action. They sought to overturn the lower court’s ruling that favored the defendants based on the claims of improper party joining.	The defendants, Smiley and Bradshaw, contended that the lawsuit was improperly brought since the note was executed only to West, who acted independently in his capacity as administrator. They argued that any action to recover the loaned money should have been initiated solely by West, asserting that the joinder of his co-administrators was inappropriate. They maintained that the plaintiff's claim had no foundation as it rested on improper legal grounds.

In 1868, in Kane County, Illinois, the defendants, Adsit and Abbey, were indicted for allegedly obtaining a farm through false pretenses. Following their indictment, a capias was issued, leading to their arrest by the local sheriff. Without a court order allowing for bail, the defendants were incarcerated in Geneva. In response, they filed a writ of habeas corpus in the Cook County Circuit Court, seeking to be released on bail due to the illness and unavailability of the judge in the Kane County circuit. The case was presided over by Judge Erastus S. Williams. The opposing argument was presented by Judge J. G. Wilson, who claimed that the Cook County court lacked the authority to grant bail since the indictment was pending in another circuit, referring to legal statutes and historical precedents regarding bail authority. The hearings highlighted the hardship faced by the defendants and raised important legal questions regarding jurisdiction and the power of courts within their respective circuits.	The plaintiff, representing the People of Illinois, contended that the Cook County Circuit Court had no jurisdiction to grant bail to the defendants, as they were indicted and held in another circuit of jurisdiction. They emphasized the importance of following legislative guidance regarding bail procedures, asserting that the local circuit court must maintain its authority and respect the jurisdictional limits set by law.	The defendants, Adsit and Abbey, argued for their right to be granted bail due to the unusual circumstances surrounding their case, particularly the illness of the presiding judge in the Kane circuit. Their counsel highlighted the potential hardships faced by the defendants and urged the court to allow bail under the prevailing legal standards despite the jurisdictional challenges presented by the opposing counsel.

The case "The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Co. v. Louis Fehringer" took place in St. Clair County, Illinois, culminating in a judgment delivered in June 1876. The central issue arose when Louis Fehringer, the plaintiff, claimed that he owned certain lands affected by water flow. He alleged that the Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Company, the defendant, constructed an earthen dam on their adjacent property in 1871, obstructing the natural flow of water from Fehringer's land. This obstruction resulted in the flooding of Fehringer's land, leading to damage and loss of crops. During the trial, Fehringer presented evidence showing that prior to 1871, the defendant had previously installed a culvert on their railroad embankment, allowing water to escape. However, in 1871, they closed this culvert, causing water to back up on Fehringer’s land. The defendant argued that the proof presented was inconsistent with the allegations in the complaint, claiming it did not support the assertion of a dam being constructed. The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Fehringer, leading to a judgment of $465 in damages for the plaintiff.	Louis Fehringer, the plaintiff, argued that the defendant's construction of an earthen dam on their property obstructed the natural flow of water from his land. He contended that this obstruction caused his land to overflow, resulting in the loss and destruction of his crops. Fehringer sought compensation for damages incurred due to the defendant's actions, asserting that the railroad's closure of the culvert had effectively turned their embankment into a dam, which was a direct cause of the flooding.	The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Company argued primarily that the evidence presented by the plaintiff deviated from the specifics of the legal allegations. They maintained that proof of closing the culvert did not equate to the construction of a dam as stated by the plaintiff. The defendant further claimed that these inconsistencies warranted a dismissal of the claims made against them. Additionally, they argued that the jury's verdict was against the weight of the evidence presented during the trial.

The case "The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad Company v. William McClintock" took place in 1873 in Illinois, specifically in St. Clair County. The key individuals involved were the appellant, The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad Company, and the appellee, William McClintock. The background of the case revolves around the principles of eminent domain; McClintock appealed a decision from commissioners who had assessed damages to his property after it was taken for the railroad company’s use. The circuit court awarded McClintock $5,000 in damages, and the railroad appealed this judgment, questioning whether it would bear interest since they had taken possession of the property. The case centered on the legal interpretation of whether judgments in such condemnation proceedings accrue interest when possession is taken and retained.	The plaintiff, William McClintock, argued that the judgment rendered by the circuit court regarding the damages for his property should accrue interest. He claimed that, according to the spirit of Illinois statutes, judgments related to eminent domain cases should include interest due to the applicant retaining possession of the property. McClintock sought to recover an additional amount of $266.65 in interest corresponding to the time the railroad company held the property without compensation.	The defendant, The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad Company, contended that the judgment awarded by the circuit court should not bear interest. They argued against the inclusion of interest, seeking to overturn the circuit court's ruling. The railroad company acknowledged the awarded damages of $5,000 but did not believe they should be liable for additional interest charges, thus appealing the decision made by the circuit court.

In 1876, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between William Fitzgerald and Josiah E. Kimball. The case originated when Kimball was summoned by a justice of the peace, Justice Pollok, on April 20, 1876, with the summons being made returnable on April 25, 1876. The constable returned the summons on April 21, 1876, with an endorsement indicating that he had served it by reading it to Kimball. However, Kimball later claimed that there was no actual service, prompting Fitzgerald to take the matter to the circuit court. Fitzgerald's motion led the circuit court to quash the writ of certiorari and dismiss the appeal against Kimball. Kimball subsequently appealed this decision, questioning whether the circuit court had acted correctly.	Fitzgerald claimed that the circuit court's decision to quash the writ of certiorari and dismiss the appeal was incorrect. He argued that the service of the summons had not been properly established, thus warranting review. He sought appellate relief on these grounds, asserting that there were errors in the initial judgment by the justice of the peace.	Kimball, represented in the appeal, argued that the return from the constable, which stated that the summons was served to him, was conclusive and could not be contradicted. He maintained that Fitzgerald was negligent for not making a defense before the justice of the peace and that his claims of ignorance regarding the judgment were unfounded. Kimball asserted that the judgment of the circuit court should be affirmed, as Fitzgerald had all the means to know about the judgment due to the official return.

In 1855, in Fulton County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose after the death of W. C. Walters, with his widow, Marville C. Walters, acting as administratrix of his estate. The case began when creditor Nathan Beadles petitioned the county court, stating that the personal estate was depleted and requesting the sale of real estate to pay outstanding debts. Walters owned a homestead of 72.5 acres and a separate tract of 72 acres of timberland used primarily for supplying fuel. The issue centered on whether the timberland could be considered part of the homestead under Illinois law. During proceedings, it was revealed that Marville Walters had temporarily left the homestead for a year due to health issues related to her confinement, during which time she rented out the homestead. After reviewing evidence, the court initially ruled that her absence constituted a loss of homestead rights, leading to an appeal by Walters to the circuit court.	Marville C. Walters claimed that the 72.5 acres constituted a legal homestead she occupied with her child. She argued that her absence during her illness did not indicate an intention to abandon the homestead and that the timberland, though not adjoining, was crucial for the enjoyment of the homestead. Her legal requests included maintaining her rights to the homestead and preventing the sale of both properties to satisfy debts.	The defendant contended that Marville Walters had abandoned her homestead rights by renting out the premises while residing elsewhere for her health. They argued her absence was not temporary and that her return was primarily to avoid the sale of the property to pay estate debts. Additionally, they argued that the 72 acres of timberland could not qualify as part of the homestead under the law, emphasizing its distance from the homestead.

The case "The Golden Rule v. The People ex rel. Charles P. Swigert" was decided on November 13, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It involves a corporation known as the Golden Rule, which was organized under Illinois's general Incorporation law of 1872. The proceeding was brought forward by way of "quo warranto," alleging that the Golden Rule and its directors were usurping powers not conferred by law. The plaintiffs claim that the corporation had engaged in unauthorized life insurance activities, providing benefits from a relief fund set up for members upon their death.  The Golden Rule aimed to provide aid to its members and establish a relief fund through voluntary contributions. However, the lawsuit claimed that the organization operated as an insurance company without proper authorization under state law. The case hinged on the nature of the fund and whether it served as a proper benefit for members or effectively functioned as illegal insurance. The lawsuit progressed through lower courts, ultimately resulting in an appeal from the corporation after a demurrer to its defenses was upheld, asserting that the corporation’s activities were illegitimate.	The plaintiffs, on behalf of the People, assert that the Golden Rule has unlawfully engaged in activities constituting a life insurance business, which is not permissible under the provisions of its incorporation. They argue that this activity represents a usurpation of powers that are not authorized by state law, specifically citing violations related to the management of the relief fund and the distribution of its benefits. The plaintiffs seek a judgment of ouster against the Golden Rule and its directors to halt these unlawful practices.	The Golden Rule and its directors contend that their operations are legal and compliant with the terms established under the incorporation law. They claim that the contributions to the relief fund come solely from voluntary donations, and that their structure is designed to provide mutual aid among members without elements of a formal insurance policy. The defendants appeal the lower court's ruling that maintained the plaintiffs’ demurrer, arguing for a reversal and a dismissal of the action against them based on their lawful activities.

On October 2, 1871, the Merchants’ Despatch Transportation Company received two packages of boots in Worcester, Massachusetts, to be transported to the plaintiffs, Moses Kahn, Mark Kahn, and Felix Kahn, in Mattoon, Illinois. After transiting to Chicago, the goods were reportedly destroyed in a fire on October 9, 1871, while stored in a warehouse awaiting further shipment. The plaintiffs initially filed a suit before a justice of the peace, where they won a judgment, leading the defendant to appeal to the circuit court. The circuit court upheld the previous ruling, concluding the transportation company remained liable under common carrier obligations despite the destruction by fire. The Supreme Court of Illinois reviewed the case to determine if the transportation company's duty had been fulfilled according to standard protocols for common carriers.	The plaintiffs claimed that the Merchants’ Despatch Transportation Company failed in their duties as common carriers by not using the most direct and safe route to transport the goods, which would have prevented the loss. They argued that the destruction of the goods in the fire did not exempt the company from liability and sought damages amounting to $116 for the loss incurred due to the fire.	The defendant contended that the destruction of the goods due to the fire was an inevitable accident, which should excuse them from liability as common carriers. They argued that they were not required to take the goods through Chicago and that doing so was not the only option available for transporting the goods to their destination.

In June 1881, the Chicago Mining Company was established as a corporation under Michigan law. On June 23, 1881, William Sturges, as trustee, issued six certificates for one thousand shares each. Shortly after, three of these certificates were surrendered, and one new certificate for three thousand shares was issued in the name of John V. Farwell, the appellant in this case. The stock was delivered to Farwell as collateral security for a debt of $17,500. The appellees, who are judgment creditors of the Chicago Mining Company, claimed that Farwell owned unpaid shares, and they filed a bill to compel him to pay the unpaid amount to satisfy their judgment against the corporation. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the appellees, asserting that Farwell was liable for the unpaid stock subscriptions based on the Michigan corporate statute. However, the legal analysis revolves around the interpretation of Michigan law regarding stockholder liability, which asserts that liability can only be enforced under specific conditions. At the time of the appeal, sufficient evidence was lacking to show that Farwell had a personal liability to pay for the shares, prompting an examination of the corporate statutes and legal precedents.	The plaintiffs, represented by the appellees, contended that John V. Farwell was personally liable for unpaid subscriptions of stock he held in the Chicago Mining Company. They argued that, as judgment creditors of the corporation, they were entitled to compel Farwell to pay an amount sufficient to satisfy their owed judgment, claiming he owned shares that had not been fully paid. They sought a court order requiring Farwell to pay the unpaid amount from the shares to satisfy their claims.	The defendant, John V. Farwell, argued that under Michigan law, there was no personal liability for unpaid stock subscriptions unless specific conditions had been met, such as an assessment call from the corporation or an order from a competent court defining stockholder liability. He maintained that the law governed by Michigan statutes did not impose such liabilities on stockholders, and the attempt to enforce this judgment was flawed. Farwell requested the court to reverse the lower court's decision and dismiss the claims against him.

The case of Kuhl v. Illinois Staats Zeitung Co. took place in Illinois, with the court's final decision rendered on July 28, 1886, by the Illinois Appellate Court. At the trial level, Judge Rollin S. Williamson presided over the case. The action involved a dispute regarding an appeal bond, in which Kuhl, the plaintiff, sought to recover debts owed under the bond. During the trial, the jury found in favor of the plaintiff. The defendant contested certain pre-trial motions, including the denial of a continuance and the successful supply of a lost declaration by the plaintiff. The defendant also attempted to suppress the deposition of a witness, claiming procedural irregularities. However, these objections were made too late in the proceedings, and the court exercised its discretion appropriately without any abuse.	The plaintiff, Kuhl, argued that the defendant, Illinois Staats Zeitung Co., was obligated to honor the appeal bond, which had not been fulfilled. Kuhl sought a judgment against the defendant for the debt believed to be owed. The claims rested on the assertion that due process was followed in the trial, and the jury’s decision to side with Kuhl indicated the validity of the bond and the resulting debt.	The defendant argued primarily procedural defenses, objecting to the court’s discretion in denying requests for a continuance and the allowance of the plaintiff to supply a lost declaration. Furthermore, the defendant contested the use of a witness deposition on the grounds that it had not been properly introduced, claiming that the title of the case was incorrectly stated. The defendant sought to have the judgment against them overturned based on these procedural objections.

In April 1862, the case "John James, Plaintiff in Error, v. Washington Bushnell et al., Defendants in Error" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose over a plot of land located in the northwest quarter of the southeast quarter of Section 18 in Township 33, Range 5, which was claimed by the complainants as tenants in common. John James, the plaintiff, was accused of trespassing on this land without consent from the owners, having allegedly mined 200 tons of coal and cut timber from the land, which he was using for his own benefit. The defendants included Washington Bushnell and others who were associated with the ownership claims of the land. The case hinged on issues of property rights, the legitimacy of ownership claims, and whether James's actions constituted an irreparable injury to the landowners’ interests. The defendants, including James, denied the allegations and asserted they had either no title or a lawful claim to the land in question. The case that emerged had significant nuances regarding the necessary evidence and parties involved, setting the stage for the court's ruling.	The plaintiffs claimed to own a one-third interest in a valuable piece of land covered with timber and containing a coal mine. They argued that John James was trespassing, extracting coal and cutting timber without their consent, thus causing irreparable harm. They requested that the court enjoin James from further interference, seek an account of the resources taken, and award general relief for the damages incurred.	The defendants, including John James, contested the plaintiffs' ownership claims, arguing that the plaintiffs had not proven their title to the land and asserted that they possessed a remedy at law. James also maintained that he had not removed timber or coal from the plaintiffs' land. He claimed legitimate possession and legal interests based on previous transactions involving the coal rights, asserting that the plaintiffs' allegations lacked support and were improperly brought before the court.

The case of George Thomas et al. v. William H. Caldwell et al. took place in Mason County, Illinois, and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1869. The dispute arose from a contract between the plaintiffs, George Thomas and others, and the defendants, William H. Caldwell and others, for the construction of a church. The contract stipulated that the church was to be a frame structure measuring 30x40 feet with a height of 14 feet, to be completed by August 1867. The plaintiffs were responsible for providing materials and labor while the defendants agreed to pay a total of $1,611, half due shortly after the contract was signed, and the remaining balance upon completion. The plaintiffs claimed to have completed the building by early September 1867, but it was destroyed by fire shortly after. Although the plaintiffs received a payment of $811, they lacked a copy of the contract for their legal claims and sought its production from the defendants. The defendants, however, denied the existence of a valid contract, particularly disputing the liability of one co-defendant. They argued that the plaintiffs bore the risk of loss until formal acceptance of the building was made and urged that the courts lacked equitable jurisdiction in this matter since a legal remedy was available.	The plaintiffs claimed they fulfilled their contractual obligations by completing the church building, which the defendants accepted and occupied until its destruction. They sought relief by requesting the production of the contract, which they could not access, arguing that this limited their legal options. Ultimately, they requested a decree from the court to ascertain the amount due for their work and to mandate payment from the defendants.	The defendants asserted that they did not enter into a binding contract, particularly emphasizing that one of the defendants, Short, had not signed the contract and thus bore no liability. They maintained that the church construction was incomplete and not accepted, pointing out that the financial contributions from subscribers depended on the completion of the project. They contended that the plaintiffs had an adequate legal remedy available and that the court should not interfere under chancery jurisdiction.

In October 1869, the case of James Pratt vs. Russell Grimes was brought before the Illinois Circuit Court. The dispute arose from a previous decree in equity that favored the defendant, Russell Grimes. The Illinois Supreme Court reversed this decree, citing insufficient proof of settlement between the parties, and remanded the case back to the lower court without providing any specific directions for further proceedings. The core issue at this stage involved a motion filed by Pratt, seeking permission to introduce further evidence which had not been part of the previous record. The court considered various precedents, debating whether the reversal and remand allowed the introduction of new evidence. Some cited cases suggested that a lower court could allow additional testimony when an appeal resulted in a reversal without directions, while the defense argued that one of the depositions crucial to the case was lost and not included in the record. This indicated a need for further proceedings to ensure a fair review. Ultimately, the motion to introduce further evidence was allowed.	James Pratt, the plaintiff, argued that the previous decree by the lower court had been based on insufficient evidence of settlement. Following the Supreme Court's reversal, Pratt sought to introduce new evidence to strengthen his case, thereby requesting a fair hearing and a new trial to consider this evidence.	Russell Grimes, the defendant, contended that the Supreme Court's remand did not preclude him from presenting further testimony that could influence the case's outcome. He claimed there was a missing deposition that was integral to establishing the facts, which he believed could change the situation if it had been part of the record.

In September 1877, in LaSalle County, Illinois, Frederick Minke filed a lawsuit against his neighbor William E. Hopeman, a butcher by trade. Minke owned a 240-acre farm with a dwelling house and several out-buildings that he valued greatly, as it was home to his family. Hopeman had purchased the adjacent farm and operated a slaughterhouse, where he slaughtered various animals and rendered animal fats. This business generated an unbearable stench, particularly during hot weather, which infiltrated Minke's home. The unpleasant odors caused sickness among Minke's family, leading to discomfort during meals, and they occasionally had to leave the table to vomit. Minke claimed that the slaughterhouse created a nuisance, diminishing the value of his property and making the environment unhealthy. He sought a court injunction to prevent Hopeman from conducting his business in a manner that produced these offensive odors.	Minke's primary claims centered on the assertion that Hopeman's slaughterhouse operations created a substantial nuisance due to the offensive smell that affected his family's health and enjoyment of their home. He sought an injunction to compel Hopeman to stop the slaughtering of animals or rendering of fats within a specific distance from his dwelling, thereby protecting his family's well-being and preserving the value of his property.	Hopeman defended against the claims by arguing that the court should not intervene through injunction until it had been established that a nuisance existed through a jury trial. He also contended that he had previously been acquitted of any wrongdoing related to the operations of his slaughterhouse. Furthermore, he maintained that he should retain the right to conduct his business as long as it is done without necessarily violating neighborly rights.

The case "The Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company v. Minnie Kaste" took place in the city of Chicago, Illinois, culminating in a court decision on October 26, 1882. Minnie Kaste, the plaintiff, sued the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company following an accident at a railway crossing on Church Street, where she sustained injuries due to the alleged negligence of the defendant. The incident reportedly involved Kaste being struck by a tender attached to a locomotive, which occurred at a crossing that required the presence of a flagman and the maintenance of a bell tower according to a city ordinance. The crossing was under the ownership of the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, which complicated the jurisdiction of the case. Initially, Kaste filed multiple counts of negligence against both railway companies but later dismissed her claims against the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, proceeding with her case solely against the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company. The court proceedings revealed that the defendant had only a temporary license to operate on the tracks owned by the Chicago & Alton Railroad, raising questions about the responsibilities outlined in the ordinance.	Minnie Kaste claimed that the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company failed to adhere to the city ordinance requiring the placement of a flagman and the erection of a bell tower at the railroad crossing. She argued that these failures contributed to her injuries when she was struck by the defendant's locomotive tender. Kaste sought damages, claiming negligence also resulted from the obstructing of Church Street by the defendant’s cars, which obscured her view of oncoming trains. She asserted that the defendant's negligence directly caused her injuries and requested compensation for her damages.	The Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway Company argued that they could not be held liable under the city ordinance, as they did not own or possess control over the tracks where the accident occurred. They contended that they only had a temporary right to run their trains on the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company's tracks under its regulations. The defendant asserted they had no power or responsibility to station a flagman or erect a bell tower, nor to move the cars left by the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, which they claimed were the actual cause of any negligence regarding the accident.

The case "Harvey S. Clark et al. v. Imlay Moore et al." took place in 1870 in Mendota, Illinois, when George Wells constructed an oil mill. The appellees (Moore and others) provided $10,000 worth of machinery for the oil mill, while the appellants (Clark, Davis, and Dawson) supplied materials for the construction and held mortgages on the property. Clark and Davis initiated a petition against Wells to enforce a mechanic's lien, to which Dawson later became a party by filing a bill of interpleader. The LaSalle County Circuit Court ruled in favor of the appellants in a February 1870 decree, selling the property after establishing the rights of the parties involved. However, the appellees claimed they were not included in the original proceedings and had no knowledge of them, thus alleging the appellants defrauded the court. In January 1871, the appellees filed a petition claiming their superiority as lien holders and requesting a recalibration of the decree and a re-sale of the property. The circuit court later found in favor of the appellees by setting aside the prior sale and establishing their lien.	The plaintiffs, represented by Moore, contended that their lien as material providers was superior to those of the appellants. They claimed they were unjustly excluded from the initial proceedings and sought to have the original court's decree set aside. They requested the court to recognize their lien, establish the true amount owed to the appellants, and allow for the re-sale of the property, asserting their right to participate in any proceeds from the prior sale.	The defendants, represented by Clark and others, argued that the circuit court lacked the jurisdiction to set aside the previous decree since it involved parties not originally included in the proceedings. They maintained that the original sale should be upheld, contesting the assertion that the appellees’ claims should be prioritized. They requested that the court reject the appellees' claims and confirm the validity of the earlier decree regarding their lienholder status.

In 1872, the case "Marshall M. Pool et al. v. George H. Potter et al." arose in Gallatin County, Illinois, following the death of Orville Pool, who left behind a significant estate and was survived by his widow Madaline Pool and four children: Marshall M. Pool, Augusta M. Townshend, Ellen Peeples, and Mary Docker. To manage the estate, the heirs entered into a complex written agreement to appoint a trustee for its proper division without conventional legal proceedings. They required the chosen trustee, George H. Potter, to provide a "good and sufficient bond," which was to be approved by a circuit court judge. However, the bond provided by Potter was deemed insufficient because it did not fulfill the terms of the agreement, specifically omitting one party, Madaline Pool, and not being enforceable as required. Disputes arose when Marshall M. Pool and others sought to prevent Potter from acting as trustee, leading them to file a complaint in court after a temporary injunction was issued. The circuit court ultimately dismissed their bill, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal.	The plaintiffs, led by Marshall M. Pool, argued that the appointment of George H. Potter as trustee was invalid because he did not provide a good and sufficient bond as stipulated in their mutual agreement. They sought to restrain Potter from acting as trustee based on the claims that his bond was insufficient and inadequate for his role.	George H. Potter and the other defendants contended that since Potter was appointed by the circuit judge, he was a de facto trustee, and his appointment should not be challenged. They argued that the plaintiffs had an adequate legal remedy available by requesting the judge to require Potter to provide a sufficient bond, implying that the court should not interfere in this matter.

The case "Bolton v. McKinley" originated in the Circuit Court of Illinois and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1858. The dispute arose from a prior judgment that had been rendered based on a cognovit, which is an agreement in which a debtor acknowledges the debt and consents to a judgment against them without a trial. Initially, the jury favored setting aside the original judgment, leading to the Circuit Court's decision to do so. The plaintiff, Bolton, who had originally secured the judgment, sought an appeal after the judgment was overturned. However, the appeal was initially dismissed on the grounds that the appropriate legal procedure to bring the case to the Supreme Court was through a writ of error rather than an appeal. Subsequently, Bolton moved to reinstate the appeal, arguing that the dismissal was premature since errors had been joined prior to the dismissal. The key individuals involved were Bolton, the plaintiff, and McKinley, presumably the defendant, along with the jury and judges from the Circuit Court and Illinois Supreme Court who handled the proceedings.	The primary claim made by Bolton, the plaintiff, was to reinstate the appeal that had been dismissed by the Circuit Court. Bolton argued that the dismissal was inappropriate because errors had been properly joined prior to the dismissal. He contended that, despite the procedural issue concerning the use of an appeal as opposed to a writ of error, the involvement of both parties in the judicial process should allow for the appeal to be considered by the Illinois Supreme Court.	McKinley, the defendant, did not provide explicit defenses within the major opinion; rather, the initial dismissal of Bolton's appeal was based on the procedural grounds related to the choice of legal action (i.e., appeal versus writ of error). The argument implied by the circumstances was that McKinley was contesting the appropriateness of Bolton's appeal process, maintaining that the proper legal protocol had not been followed to bring the matter before the Supreme Court.

The case, "The City of Chicago v. The Phoenix Insurance Company," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on November 15, 1888. The central issue arose when the city of Chicago filed a lawsuit against the Phoenix Insurance Company, which was a foreign insurance entity. The city aimed to recover a two percent fee on the gross receipts from the company's agency operations in Chicago, as stipulated by an ordinance passed by the city council on July 15, 1886. The ordinance mandated that corporations not incorporated under Illinois state laws must obtain a license to conduct fire insurance business in Chicago, along with associated fees. The dispute focused on whether the city had the legal authority to enact such an ordinance, especially considering the relevant provisions of the Insurance Law enacted by the state legislature in 1879, which allowed for taxation of foreign insurance companies. The court had to evaluate the provisions of the ordinance in light of state law and the implied powers of municipal corporations to impose fees for the purpose of revenue generation.	The City of Chicago contended that the ordinance it passed was valid under its charter to oversee business operations and secure revenue through licensing foreign insurance companies. The city sought to enforce the ordinance to compel the Phoenix Insurance Company to pay the required license fee based on its gross receipts from the preceding half year.	The Phoenix Insurance Company argued that the ordinance was unauthorized because the city lacked the power to impose a licensing requirement for foreign insurance entities based on the provisions of the 1879 Insurance Law. The defendant maintained that the state specifically repealed any municipal licensing powers conflicting with this legislation. The company asserted that the ordinance was merely an attempt to raise revenue rather than an exercise of legitimate police power, which should not be permitted.

The case of Truesdale v. Ford occurred in Illinois and reached the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1865. During the first call of the docket, the plaintiff's counsel, Mr. Cooper, indicated readiness to proceed with the argument. The case's central issue involved a motion made by the plaintiff's counsel requesting the reversal of a prior judgment due to a non-joinder in error—a procedural issue where a party fails to join all necessary defendants in an appeal. In this instance, the argument presented by the plaintiff was that the defendant's failure to comply with a specific legal rule regarding joinder justified an appeal. The proceedings began with both parties having filed briefs, suggesting that the case had been prepared for argument over previous hearings.	The plaintiff argued that the defendant should not be allowed to contest a judgment due to non-joinder in error, claiming that the right to insist on reversal had been waived by the defendant's actions of filing briefs. The legal request was to reverse the earlier judgment based on this non-compliance, asserting that procedural rules were not adequately followed by the defendant.	The defendant's main argument revolved around the assertion that the plaintiff could not seek a reversal solely based on the non-joinder in error. By filing briefs, the defendant claimed that they effectively waived any objections related to non-joinder, and thereby preserved their arguments against the plaintiff's motion.

The legal case of Elizabeth Bowers v. Samuel S. Block et al. was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision rendered on June 15, 1889. The case originated from the county court proceedings in Cook County concerning a parcel of land owned by Maria McMurtry, who had passed away. Elizabeth Bowers, the defendant, was served summons on June 3, 1882, in a case where the administrator, William E. McMurtry, petitioned to sell the property to settle the deceased’s debts. The court records indicated the proceedings were regular, and various documents related to the estate were presented during the case. Bowers claimed to have had occupancy and a potential title to the land through her children as heirs of her deceased husband. However, she did not assert this during the earlier sale proceedings, which left her estopped from later claiming ownership against the purchaser at the administrator’s sale. The complexity of ownership and estoppel plays a significant role in determining Bowers' rights to the property in question.	The plaintiffs (appellees) argued that Elizabeth Bowers was estopped from claiming ownership of the property after she was properly served and failed to assert her title in prior proceedings. They maintained that the administrator's sale was valid and that they had acquired rightful possession through it. The plaintiffs relied on the statute requiring occupancy claimants be made parties to such sales, thus reinforcing the regularity and correctness of the judicial processes leading to the sale of the property.	Elizabeth Bowers asserted that she and her children claimed a possessory title from their deceased father, having occupied the land since 1863 and believed their claim had matured under adverse possession laws. She contended that the court had erred by excluding evidence of her children’s title, which she argued established their right to ownership. Bowers implied that the claim of ownership was evident due to long-standing possession, which she hoped would invalidate the earlier proceedings and the administrator’s sale.
