Koch had employed an agent named Friday to purchase corn on his behalf for shipment to St. Louis. Friday, while acting as Koch's agent, purchased corn, including from Willi, without disclosing his agency and subsequently sold some of it. On October 24, Willi sought to recover a debt by buying the corn from Friday. After this exchange, Koch's attachments were levied on the corn, but no sale occurred. Eventually, Willi took possession of the corn in December, leading Koch to file an action for its value. The case was argued in the Illinois Supreme Court, as Koch sought to reverse the judgment made in the lower court in favor of Willi.	August Koch claimed that he was the rightful owner of the corn and asserted that Willi had no legal grounds to purchase it from Friday since the agency relationship was not disclosed. Koch argued that his attachments on the corn should have satisfied his claim to the property and requested recovery of the corn's value.	Jacob Willi contended that he purchased the corn in good faith to secure his debt from Friday, who he believed had the right to sell it, despite the undisclosed agency. Willi argued that he acted under the impression that the transaction was legitimate and that there had been no formal sale of the corn under the attachments. His request was for the court to uphold the judgment in his favor.

The case "Woman’s Union Missionary Society of America v. George O. Mead" was decided on January 18, 1890, by the Illinois Supreme Court. It involves the will of Phebe L. Smith, who died on December 24, 1885, leaving behind a complex estate. At the time of her death, her only heirs were her uncles, James Ogden and Benjamin Franklin Smith. After Ogden's death, George O. Mead became the executor of his will. Smith’s will, executed in New York City, contained several bequests, including one to her sister, Eliza S. Turner, and instructions regarding the distribution of her residuary estate among various charitable organizations after Turner's death. The will also set forth detailed conditions pertaining to specific bequests, particularly regarding the Hahnemann Hospital in Chicago. After specific legacies were satisfied, disputes arose over the identification of certain charitable organizations mentioned in the will, leading to the present legal action for clarification and distribution of the estate.	The plaintiffs, representing the various charitable organizations, argue that Phebe L. Smith intended to bequeath her residuary estate to them, despite any misnaming or misdescription in the will. They assert that the organizations, including the Chicago Training School for Nurses and the Woman's Union Missionary Society, have sufficiently proven their identities and eligibility to receive the bequests. They seek a court ruling confirming their rightful claims to the estate's distribution.	The defendants, including the heirs of Phebe L. Smith, contest the validity of the claims made by the charitable organizations. They contend that the misnaming or uncertainty in the will's references to the organizations renders the bequests void. Moreover, the defendants argue that additional property acquired by Smith after making her will did not pass under it and that the intended charitable organizations are not explicitly named or clearly defined. They seek to have the court rule that these organizations should not receive any part of the residuary estate due to the alleged ambiguities and deficiencies in the will.

The case of John A. Burke v. Monroe County took place in 1875 involving a dispute over the responsibility for supporting a pauper residing in the town of Waterloo, located in Monroe County, Illinois. John A. Burke, the plaintiff, claimed reimbursement for expenses incurred for the care of a pauper. He presented his claim to the Monroe County Board; however, the board denied the request, maintaining that the pauper was not a county charge but rather a responsibility of the town of Waterloo. This denial led Burke to appeal the decision to the Circuit Court, where the judge ruled against him, ordering Burke to pay the costs. Burke subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the crux of the case revolved around the interpretation of a 1872 legislative act regarding the responsibilities of incorporated towns and cities in relation to their paupers.	Burke argued that the town of Waterloo was improperly asserting that it was solely responsible for the care of the pauper. He contended that the 1872 legislative act required uniform taxation and repealed any previous local laws that mandated incorporated towns to support their paupers. Burke sought a reversal of the Circuit Court's decision and a ruling that would hold Monroe County accountable for the expenses incurred for the pauper.	The defendant, Monroe County, maintained that the act of 1872 did not repeal the provisions in the town's incorporation grant that required it to care for its paupers. The county presented two key defenses: first, they argued that the 1872 act was unconstitutional as it embraced more than one subject, which was not clearly expressed in its title. Second, they asserted that the terminating clause of the act applied only to cities, not to incorporated towns, thereby leaving the responsibility intact for Waterloo.

In 1881, William A. Porter sold a horse worth $85 to Frank Park at the request of Frank P. Drennan, who promised to guarantee payment of a promissory note for $61.30 owed by Charles F. Goodrich. This note, which was past due at the time of the agreement, was related to Drennan's promise to Porter. Porter sold the horse under the reliance that Drennan would fulfill his obligation, but the promise was not honored as the note wasn’t paid, and Drennan ultimately refused to accept liability. Porter subsequently filed suit against Drennan in the Illinois Appellate Court after a demurrer to his declaration—a formal objection—was sustained in the Circuit Court of Christian County, resulting in judgment against him for costs. The case, which raised questions about the nature of guarantees and the sufficiency of legal claims, was ultimately a contest over contractual obligations and the enforceability of promises not formally documented in writing.	William A. Porter claimed that Frank P. Drennan guaranteed the payment of a promissory note as part of the transaction involving the sale of the horse. Porter asserted that Drennan’s failure to ensure the payment of the note, which he argued was worthless at the time, made him liable to repay the amount owed under the contract of guaranty. Porter sought to affirm this guaranty and recover the amount specified in the note.	Frank P. Drennan contended that the claim against him was unfounded due to the lack of written documentation regarding the guaranty. He argued that without a proper indorsement of the note, as required by law, he could not be held liable. Drennan claimed that his actions did not constitute a formal contract and as such, he should not be compelled to pay the amount Porter's claims.

The case of Clovis Soucy v. The People ex rel. Nicholas McCracken took place in the village of Cahokia, Illinois, on March 3, 1884, during a village supervisor election. Two candidates, Clovis Soucy and Nicholas McCracken, were vying for the position. The election turned contentious, with interference reported by supporters of McCracken against voters supporting Soucy. Ultimately, the election judges certified that Soucy received 30 votes, while McCracken received 29, thereby declaring Soucy the winner. However, three ballots submitted at the back door of the polling place were contested as they were not cast in the ballot box due to voter intimidation at the front. McCracken filed a quo warranto lawsuit against Soucy, alleging he had wrongfully usurped the supervisor's office. Soucy defended his position by asserting that he had been legally elected to the office in 1882 and had the right to hold it until a duly elected successor qualified. The case raised significant issues regarding electoral fraud and the integrity of the voting process.	Nicholas McCracken, the relator, argued that the three votes cast at the back door should not be counted since they did not go through the proper voting process. He claimed these ballots were invalid and, upon their exclusion, he would be the rightful holder of the office with a majority of valid votes. McCracken sought a judgment of ouster against Soucy, aiming to reclaim the supervisor position based on his interpretation of the election law.	Clovis Soucy contended that he was validly elected and qualified to hold the office of supervisor based on the certificate provided by election judges. He further claimed that McCracken's election was tainted by fraud and violence, as evidenced by the interference that obstructed legal voters from casting their votes. Soucy maintained that judicial support should not be extended to McCracken, who attempted to profit from an election characterized by wrongdoing.

In 1843, in St. Clair County, Illinois, the case of Isaac Letcher v. Edward Norton arose from a dispute over property ownership following a mortgage. Isaac Letcher, the appellant, claimed rights to certain goods that had been levied as part of a court execution against James Duncan, the mortgagor. A sheriff's execution was directed against Duncan, leading to a trial to establish the rightful ownership of the property. Letcher claimed property possession based on a mortgage executed by Duncan on April 4, 1842, which was intended to secure repayment of a promissory note. During the proceedings, Letcher attempted to introduce evidence that Duncan was permitted to remain in possession of the mortgaged property until a default occurred, but this was rejected by the trial court. Additionally, Letcher sought to prove that a valid consideration was exchanged during the mortgage's execution, but this, too, was excluded by the court. Letcher appealed the adverse ruling from the circuit court, challenging the rejection of key testimonies and the interpretation of the mortgage terms.	Letcher argued that the mortgage agreement explicitly allowed Duncan to retain possession of the property until default and that the exclusion of key evidence concerning the validity of the mortgage and its consideration was erroneous. He sought to demonstrate that there was no fraudulent intent regarding the mortgaged property and requested a verdict in his favor based on the claims of legal ownership and proper execution of the mortgage.	Edward Norton, representing the appellee, contended that the execution against Duncan was valid and that Letcher's claims of ownership were unfounded. Norton argued that the terms of the mortgage did not allow Duncan to maintain possession after the mortgage's execution without creating a fraudulent situation regarding creditors. Thus, the security and possession provisions were framed as inherently questionable due to the failure to abandon possession after mortgage execution, with Norton requesting the court to uphold the judgment in favor of the defendant.

In 1850, in Kane County, Illinois, Harrison Graves and others were implicated in a legal matter concerning a recognizance that had been established for the appearance of William H. Graves at a court term. The recognizance was signed by William H. Graves, and an indictment for larceny was found against Harrison Graves in December 1848. At that same term of court, a default judgment was entered against Harrison Graves and others for failing to appear. A scire facias was filed against William H. Graves for the forfeiture of the recognizance. However, the case raised a significant question regarding the identity of the individuals involved, as the recognizance pertained to William H. Graves, while the indictment was against Harrison Graves. The matter escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court after the lower court upheld the scire facias despite Harrison's defense showing that he and William were not the same person. E. S. Leland and B. F. Fridley represented the plaintiffs, while B. C. Cook acted as the district attorney for the People.	The plaintiffs contended that the scire facias, which sought to enforce the recognizance against William H. Graves due to an indictment against Harrison Graves, was invalid. They argued that the breach of obligation claimed in the forfeiture did not apply, as there was no evidence demonstrating that Harrison Graves was indeed the same person as William H. Graves who entered the recognizance. They sought reversal of the judgment made by the lower court.	The defendant, represented by the district attorney, maintained that although there were distinctions between William H. and Harrison Graves, the forfeiture of the recognizance should stand because it was based on Harrison’s non-appearance following the indictment for larceny. The contention was that the legal obligations of the recognizance extended beyond individual identity aspects.

In 1869, the case of David J. Noble v. Matilda McFarland was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Mercer County, Illinois, regarding ownership of land located in the north-west quarter of section 22, town 14 north, range 5 west of the 4th p.m. Matilda McFarland, the plaintiff, claimed rights to the property as one of the heirs of James Toucey, who had died intestate in Virginia in 1838, leaving behind a widow and four children. Matilda, married to George McFarland, had eight children but had to file the case following her husband’s death in 1864. She initiated the ejectment action in 1867. The defendant, David J. Noble, claimed possession through a series of conveyances and asserted that he had been in possession and had paid taxes on the property since 1851. The trial was based on an agreed statement of facts, which laid out the family lineage and the history of claims to the property, leading to the court proceedings.	Matilda McFarland, as the plaintiff, claimed ownership of an undivided one-fourth interest in the disputed land based on her inheritance from her father, James Toucey. She argued that she was not barred by the statute of limitations because she filed the lawsuit within three years following her husband's death, and her rights were preserved despite her coverture. The plaintiff contested the claims of the defendant, who denied her interest in the property.	David J. Noble, the defendant, contended that the statutes governing married women's property did not divest him of the claim he had established through earlier conveyances and his long-term possession of the property. He further argued that the plaintiff needed to prove actual ouster since he held the property under color of title and had exclusive possession, claiming that her action was barred by the statute of limitations due to her delay in filing suit. His request was to reverse the lower court's judgment.

On December 23, 1869, in Bridgeport, Connecticut, Eliza Wood delivered three Cook County bonds, each valued at $1000, to her brother Warren W. Selleck while visiting him. In exchange, Selleck provided a written acknowledgment promising to return the bonds “whenever called for.” The arrangement indicated an intention to retain the right to demand the bonds back, contradicting any notion of an absolute gift. Over the following years, Mrs. Wood communicated her expectations regarding the management and security of the bonds, emphasizing that her financial support aimed to benefit her brother and sister-in-law, rather than provide them with a gift. Selleck later used one bond for payments related to a house and sold the other two for personal gain. Following Mrs. Wood's death on September 1, 1878, her heirs, including Selleck and his sisters Polly Selleck and Sarah Chatfield, sought to clarify the ownership and distribution of her estate, including the bonds. The probate court found Selleck indebted to Mrs. Wood's estate for the value of the bonds, leading to his appeals through the Circuit Court and Appellate Court, where the case's merits regarding gift versus loan were argued.	The plaintiff, representing Selleck, argued that the bonds were given to him as a gift and not as a loan, hence he should not be held responsible for returning their value in the estate's distribution. He maintained that the use of the bonds was permissible and that no debt existed, as he interpreted the relationship facilitated through Mrs. Wood as a non-enforceable arrangement.	The defendants, the sisters of Mrs. Wood, contended that the transaction was a loan rather than a gift, emphasizing that Mrs. Wood's written agreement for Selleck to return the bonds upon request established a legal obligation. They asserted that Selleck's use of the bonds did not eliminate his debt to the estate and requested that he be held accountable for the value of the bonds in the estate distribution, as ordered by the probate and lower courts.

Abner Eason et al. were involved in a legal case against Daniel Chapman in November 1858, in the Illinois Supreme Court, regarding allegations related to the killing of a horse owned by Chapman. The case originally took place in the Williamson Circuit Court but was transferred to the Franklin Circuit Court where it was tried before Judge Parrish during the September term of 1857, culminating in a judgment awarding Chapman $500. The defense argued the case by calling witnesses to impeach the character of one of Chapman’s key witnesses, Caroline Riddle. They sought to establish that Riddle's general character for truthfulness was poor, using witness Charles Starix to testify about her bad reputation, but faced objections from Eason’s counsel concerning the admissibility of such opinions. The court sustained the objection, preventing Starix from answering whether he would believe Riddle if she were sworn in, leading to the assertion that this decision constituted an error of law on the part of the trial court.	The plaintiffs, Eason and others, claimed that the trial court's refusal to permit the defensive witness to answer whether he would believe Riddle based on her character for truthfulness constituted an error. They argued this undermined the fairness of the trial and sought a reversal of the judgment, implying that the jury did not receive all pertinent information needed to assess the credibility of the witnesses.	The defense contended that the trial court had correctly ruled on the admissibility of the testimony regarding Riddle’s character. They emphasized that the legal standard permits the introduction of witness opinions only under specific circumstances and that the character of a witness should remain a matter of fact for the jury's consideration. They sought to uphold the jury's verdict of $500 in favor of Chapman based on the evidence presented at trial.

In June 1887, in Franklin County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Edmund Wilcox and Harvey B. Parker concerning the accounts of a conservatorship. Harvey B. Parker had been adjudged insane in May 1887 and was committed to the asylum. Subsequently, his son, John R. Parker, assumed responsibility for the family, including younger siblings, and incurred debts after their father’s adjudication. Edmund Wilcox was appointed as the conservator to manage Harvey's estate and submitted annual financial reports that were approved by the County Court. However, upon filing a final report in February 1885, it was revealed that Wilcox had paid out more than he had received, prompting a challenge from Parker, who contested the accuracy of Wilcox's final accounting. This case transitioned to the Circuit Court under Judge David J. Baker, where the court found that Wilcox had not completely accounted for the estate and was ordered to repay certain amounts.	Edmund Wilcox, as the plaintiff and conservator, argued that the debts he sought to be credited were incurred by his ward’s eldest son while he had assumed the responsibilities of the family. He claimed that these debts were necessary for the care of Harvey's children and sought credit for various payments made during his conservatorship, including expenses related to their care.	Harvey B. Parker, through his contestation, maintained that Wilcox's claims for credits on the debts incurred after his adjudication were unwarranted. Parker contended that these debts should not be charged against his estate because they were not legitimate obligations of his ward, and thus the conservator should not be entitled to recover the claimed amounts.

In the case of John B. Frink v. Pratt & Co., the events unfolded in Decatur, Illinois. John B. Frink, who was the plaintiff, was a landlord who had leased his farm to Daniel Wampler for three years beginning on March 11, 1884, with a rental fee of $500 per annum payable each January 1. During Wampler's tenancy, he raised corn on the property in 1884 and 1885. By January 1, 1886, Wampler had failed to pay the rent for the year 1885 and had approximately $149 still owed for the 1884 rent. On December 11, 1885, Wampler sold a total of 2,498 bushels of corn to Twaddell, an agent for the defendants, Pratt & Co., for shipment. The sale was completed with the shipment of the corn from Lake City to Decatur. Following the sale, Frink filed a legal action in trover against Pratt & Co., alleging wrongful conversion of his corn and asserting a lien on the crops for the unpaid rent. The case was tried without a jury and the issues were ruled in favor of the defendants. The Appellate Court upheld this judgment, leading Frink to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, John B. Frink, claimed that Pratt & Co. wrongly converted corn that was raised by his tenant, Daniel Wampler, arguing that he had a statutory lien on the crops for unpaid rent. He asserted that the defendants either knew of his lien or should have been aware of it, making them liable for the conversion of the crops. Frink sought damages to recover losses attributed to the alleged wrongful conversion of the corn.	In defense, Pratt & Co. contended that they were bona fide purchasers of the corn from Wampler and had no knowledge of Frink's lien. They argued that Frink lacked legal grounds for the trover action because, under the law, a landlord with a mere lien does not possess the title or right to immediate possession of the crops. Therefore, they requested dismissal of Frink's claims, asserting that he had no right of recovery over the corn.

In 1868, the city council of Sparta, Illinois, held an election to decide on a proposed subscription of $70,000 worth of stock in the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company, contingent upon the railroad constructing and operating its line within the city limits. The voters approved the proposition on December 21, 1868. Based on this approval, the railroad company began construction, which led to the railroad's operational line extending through Sparta. However, after the company tendered a request for $75,000 in city bonds in exchange for stock, the city authorities refused to issue the bonds, leading the railroad company to seek a writ of mandamus to compel their issuance. The lower court sustained a demurrer against the petition, ruling that the bonds could not be issued due to a conflict with the statute that limited the bond term to ten years, while the voted term was for twenty years. The case was appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Company argued that the city of Sparta was obligated to issue the bonds in accordance with the election results, which approved funding contingent on the railroad's construction. They contended that the refusal to issue the bonds constituted a breach of the city's obligations under the approved subscription agreement and requested a writ of mandamus to compel the city to fulfill its promise.	The City of Sparta defended its refusal by asserting that the election to approve the subscription was not legally binding because the terms approved (twenty years and eight percent interest) exceeded the statutory limits set by the legislation authorizing such a subscription (which stipulated a maximum of ten years and ten percent interest). The city argued that, hence, they were under no obligation to issue the bonds and that the proceedings leading to the election were without proper authority.

In September 1876, the legal case of George I. Stow v. Harriet Steele took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. Harriet Steele was in possession of the east 60 feet of lot 2 in block 44 of the original town of Chicago, claiming a life estate as her assigned dower in the whole lot owned by George I. Stow. The legal conflict arose when Therese La Framboise, as the widow of a former owner, filed a petition against Stow and Steele for her dower rights in the same 60 feet. The Superior Court of Cook County granted La Framboise her claim, ejecting Steele and placing La Framboise in possession of the property. The case escalated to the Supreme Court, where La Framboise passed away, leading the court to appoint her administrator as a party. The Supreme Court initially reversed the lower court's decree, remanding the case back. Eventually, a decree ordered that Steele's possession be restored, an order for writ of restitution was issued, fulfilling Steele's claim while the case was still pending against Stow.	Harriet Steele, as the plaintiff, contended that she had rightful possession of the 60 feet in question as her assigned dower. She sought the restoration of her possession after it was transferred to Therese La Framboise by the Superior Court's ruling, which had failed to consider her existing rights.	George I. Stow, the defendant, did not present a substantive claim regarding the ownership of the 60 feet. Instead, he appealed the decree affecting Steele, arguing that he had not been adversely affected by the earlier judgment and sought to dissolve the lower court's decision without claiming any right to the property.

In April 1857, John Kingsley initiated a lawsuit against George O. Kingsley and David D. Irons in the Circuit Court of Tazewell County, Illinois, claiming that he had been wronged by a judgment obtained in a prior suit. The controversy arose from a 1852 case where George O. Kingsley, alongside Francis P. Kingsley, sued John Kingsley for a promissory note that John alleged had no proper consideration and was not genuine. Following judgments and an execution issued against John Kingsley in 1856, he contested the legitimacy of the release provided by George O. Kingsley, which was meant to settle the judgment. The case proceeded through various legal arguments regarding the validity of the release and the conditions under which it was executed. The pivotal issue was whether the release was binding despite the failure to have Francis P. Kingsley sign as security for debt repayment, amidst claims of fraud and lack of genuine consideration.	John Kingsley (the plaintiff) argued that the release of the judgment obtained against him was void because it was contingent upon having Francis P. Kingsley sign as security, which did not occur. He contended that George O. Kingsley failed to fulfill his part of the agreement, and thus the release should not be considered valid, allowing John to challenge the judgment made against him. He sought the court to cancel the release and declared that the judgment should still stand.	George O. Kingsley (the defendant) asserted that the release was valid because it was executed properly and there was no evidence of fraud in its formulation. He claimed the judgment was obtained fairly and the notes merely acted as a condition for the release, which did not affect its legality after being signed and delivered. He requested the court to uphold the validity of the release, stating that John Kingsley's failure to have Francis P. Kingsley sign as security did not invalidate the release contract.

In the case of French, Potter & Wilson v. S. Wolf, filed on May 18, 1887, in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, the plaintiffs – French, Potter & Wilson – initiated legal proceedings through an attachment. The key individuals involved included the plaintiffs and the defendant, S. Wolf. The plaintiffs claimed that they were owed a debt and sought to attach S. Wolf's property to secure the debt's payment. During the trial, after the plaintiffs presented their evidence, the defendant challenged the attachment, arguing there was no evidence supporting it. The Circuit Court withdrew the plaintiffs' evidence from the jury and directed them to return a verdict for the defendant regarding the attachment claim, while finding in favor of the plaintiffs on the issue of the debt, awarding damages of $65.83. The plaintiffs contended that the oral instruction to the jury was improper and sought to reverse the judgment on these grounds.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to recover a debt from the defendant, S. Wolf, and sought to enforce this claim through an attachment of the defendant’s property. They argued that the jury’s verdict should not have been directed by the court in an oral instruction, contending that this procedural error warranted a reversal of the judgment.	The defendant, S. Wolf, contended that the plaintiffs had not provided any evidence to support the attachment, asserting that the evidence presented erroneously referred to the husband of S. Wolf rather than S. Wolf herself. The defendant requested the court to quash the attachment based on the lack of supporting evidence, which led to the jury's directed verdict in favor of the defendant on the attachment issue.

Josiah D. Bodley filed a case against James M. Higgins in the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision rendered in September 1874. The case arose from a conflict surrounding a set of promissory notes that were executed to be delivered to Higgins as part of a compromise with Bodley's debtor, A. R. Bodley. The dispute centered on whether these notes were properly accepted by Higgins' agent, Jones, due to objections regarding their form. During negotiations, A. R. Bodley had agreed to relinquish part of his claim in exchange for these notes. However, conflicting testimonies emerged about the acceptance of the notes by Jones, the agent representing Higgins. The notes were retained by Driscoll, A. R. Bodley's attorney, creating further complications regarding their intended delivery to Higgins. Testimonies suggested that despite objections about the notes' form, there was a mutual understanding that the notes would still be valid for settling the debt owed to Higgins. The jury was tasked with evaluating the evidence and determining the legitimacy of the notes and the circumstances of their delivery.	The plaintiff, James M. Higgins, claimed that the promissory notes were valid and should be enforced to satisfy a debt owed by A. R. Bodley. He argued that the notes constituted a legitimate compromise of his previous claim and that any objections to their form were irrelevant since the notes were intended for his benefit. Higgins sought a judgment that reaffirmed his entitlement to the amount specified in the notes.	Josiah D. Bodley, the defendant, argued against the validity of the promissory notes, claiming that their delivery was not properly executed due to objections regarding their form. He maintained that the notes were left with his attorney, Driscoll, and were not intended to be accepted without alteration. Bodley contended that, because the original chattel mortgage and other instruments were not simultaneously surrendered, the notes could not be considered validly delivered, thus he requested the court to dismiss the claim.

In 1869, a legal case arose in the Illinois Supreme Court involving Margaret O'Connor, acting as the administratrix for her deceased husband Martin O'Connor, and Catharine O'Connor, who presented a claim against Martin's estate. The claim was for services believed to have been rendered by Catharine's son while serving as an unpaid helper for his uncle, Martin, who died childless and without a will. The claim was presented more than three years after Martin's death and raised concerns about its legitimacy. The case was initially brought to the probate court of LaSalle County but was later moved to Grundy County due to a change of venue. During the trial, the administratrix sought jury instructions to consider the delay in presenting the claim and the circumstances surrounding it. However, the court modified the instruction, which likely reduced the jury’s focus on the significant delay and other relevant factors when evaluating the claim's fairness.	Catharine O'Connor claimed that her son had provided services to his uncle, Martin O'Connor, thus entitling her to a payment from the estate for these services. She argued that despite the lengthy delay in presenting the claim—over three years following Martin’s death—the services were rendered and deserved compensation from the deceased's estate.	The defense contended that the lengthy delay in asserting the claim raised questions about its validity. They argued that no claim was made during Martin O'Connor's lifetime, which should influence the jury’s perception of the request as suspicious. The defense maintained that the jury should be informed of this delay during deliberations and that it warranted skepticism regarding the legitimacy of the claim.

The case, Merchants’ Dispatch Transportation Company v. Edward Hallock, stems from an incident that occurred in October 1871 in New York and Chicago. Merchants’ Dispatch Transportation Company, a freight carrier, received a shipment of household goods, classified as "old furniture," at their office in New York. The goods were transported via the Michigan Central Railroad and arrived at the company’s depot in Chicago on October 7, 1871. The next morning, the goods were stored in the company’s warehouse after being unloaded from the freight cars. However, on October 8th and 9th, a disastrous fire swept through Chicago, resulting in the destruction of the stored goods. Both parties agreed that the fire was responsible for the loss, and that it happened without fault or negligence on the part of the Transportation Company. The crux of the case revolved around the terms of the bill of lading and whether the company, having stored the goods in a suitable warehouse, was still liable for their loss after failing to provide notice to the consignee regarding the goods' arrival.	Edward Hallock, the plaintiff, claimed damages for the loss of his household goods, arguing that the Merchants’ Dispatch Transportation Company, as a common carrier, had a duty to notify him of the arrival of his goods. He contended that since they did not provide such notice, they should remain liable for the loss incurred due to the fire.	The Merchants’ Dispatch Transportation Company contended that their liability as a common carrier had terminated upon the safe delivery of the goods to their warehouse. They argued that there was no agreement to notify Hallock of the goods' arrival and that their practices conformed to standard operating procedures for freight transportation, thus absolving them of further responsibility once the goods were safely stored.

The case "John R. Moore et ux. v. Madison Neil et al." was decided in January 1866 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from a bill filed in chancery by the plaintiffs, John R. Moore and his wife, seeking to nullify a sale of real estate conducted by an administrator under a court decree dated back to May 1842. This sale was intended to satisfy debts owed by the estate of John B. Smith, deceased. The Shelby Circuit Court, which had initially heard the case, dismissed the plaintiffs' bill. The plaintiffs claimed that the administrator’s notice for the sale was insufficient because it did not specify the county or state where the court was located, leading to doubts about the jurisdiction of the court that authorized the sale. The notice was published in a local newspaper, which was argued to sufficiently identify the location. This case evolved from challenges regarding the adequacy of legal notice and procedural sufficiency in administrator sales, drawing on principles established in prior cases regarding jurisdiction and the protection of bona fide purchasers.	The plaintiffs contended that the sale of the real estate was invalid due to defects in the jurisdiction of the court, mainly focusing on the alleged inadequacy of the administrator's notice. They argued that the notice lacked necessary details, such as the specific county and state, which should have been included to ensure proper legal notification of the proceedings. Thus, they sought to set aside the sale and restore the title of the property to themselves.	The defendants, who purchased the property at the administrator's sale, argued that the notice provided was sufficient and that any defects in the proceedings were not severe enough to nullify the sale. They pointed out that the notice had been published in a local newspaper, specifying the Shelby Circuit Court, which indicated to any reasonable reader where the court was located. They maintained that the jurisdiction of the court was established and that procedural errors did not invalidate the sale.

The case, titled "The People, for the use of John Beaird et al. v The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Company," was filed on November 8, 1887, in the Illinois Supreme Court, having originated in the Circuit Court of St. Clair County. Key individuals involved included plaintiffs John Beaird and Charles Schroeter, who were partners, and the defendant, the Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Company. The suit arose from the railroad company's alleged failure to furnish cars and transport coal, which the plaintiffs claimed was part of the company's legal duty. The case initially progressed in the Circuit Court where an amended declaration was filed, asserting claims for treble damages under relevant statutes due to the railway’s negligence. The Circuit Court sustained the plaintiffs' claim, leading to a judgment in their favor. However, this judgment was later reversed by the Appellate Court for the Fourth District, which ruled against the plaintiffs citing a failure to meet the Statute of Limitations and other procedural issues, thus imposing costs on the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs, John Beaird and Charles Schroeter, claimed that the Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Company failed to fulfill its duty to provide transportation for coal the plaintiffs intended to ship. They sought treble damages under the applicable statute, arguing that the railroad’s negligence entitled them to this higher compensation due to the company's failure to perform its legal obligations.	The defendant, the Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Company, contended primarily that the plaintiffs did not have coal ready for transportation when the cars were to be provided and that the Statute of Limitations barred the claims made in the amended declaration. The railroad argued that the Appellate Court's decision to reverse the Circuit Court's judgment was appropriate due to these procedural and factual shortcomings.

Manda Myers, as the administratrix of Logan K. Myers' estate, brought a case against the Indianapolis and St. Louis Railway Company following her husband's death on February 13, 1883. The incident occurred while Logan, a section hand for the railway company, was working on the tracks. A freight train, after leaving Ashmore station, experienced a separation of cars, with two cars and a caboose detaching from the main train. Logan, having stepped off the track to let the train pass, returned to the track without checking for any approaching hazards and was struck and killed by the detached cars that were trailing the first section of the train. The trial involved discussions about the instructions given to the jury, focusing on Logan's negligence and whether the railway had acted with due care. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court after the Appellate Court had issued a ruling against Manda Myers, who claimed the jury instructions were erroneous and prejudicial to her case.	The plaintiff, Manda Myers, contended that her husband’s death was caused by the negligence of the Indianapolis and St. Louis Railway Company. She argued that the instructions provided to the jury did not adequately represent the facts of the case, particularly regarding her husband's ability to ascertain danger before stepping onto the track. The plaintiff sought damages for her husband's wrongful death, claiming that the railway's negligence directly led to this tragic accident.	The railway company defended against the claims by emphasizing that the separation of the train was accidental and not detectable by the crew in time to prevent the accident. They argued that Logan Myers was negligent himself for not taking precautions before returning to the track, as he could have observed the danger if he had looked. The defendant's legal team maintained that the company exercised due care and requested that the jury find in their favor based on the evidence presented.

In 1864, in Chicago, Illinois, Joseph E. Young brought an assumpsit action against Thomas Rock and others in the Superior Court. The case revolved around the recovery of a balance of an account for labor performed in grading a segment of the Chicago & Great Eastern Railroad near Crown Point, Indiana. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant owed them a sum exceeding $2,400. During the trial, the jury heard testimonies from two witnesses who attested that during a conversation on July 26, 1864, the defendant admitted to owing the plaintiffs the specified amount, although the defendant contended that the total due was less than what was claimed by the plaintiffs. The trial concluded with a jury rendering a verdict in favor of the plaintiffs for $2,005 after the court denied the defendant's motion for a new trial. The case was subsequently appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the majority opinion affirmed the lower court's judgment based on the evidence presented during the trial.	The plaintiffs, Joseph E. Young and associates, claimed that they were owed a substantial amount for labor performed on a railroad grading project. They asserted that the defendant, Thomas Rock, admitted to owing them a minimum of $2,400 during a conversation. The plaintiffs sought to recover this balance through the legal action.	The defendant, Thomas Rock, contested the claims, arguing that the total amount due for the work performed did not exceed $3,995.40. Rock also referenced payments he claimed were made, totaling around seven-eighths of the amount due, thus disputing the remaining balance. His defense hinged on the assertion that the plaintiffs' claim was inflated and that the jury's verdict was not justified.

The legal case titled "The Town of Ottawa and Philo Lindley, Plaintiffs in Error, v. George E. Walker et al., Defendants in Error" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1859. This case arose when the town of Ottawa passed a tax levied for the purpose of building a bridge within the city limits. Plaintiffs Philo Lindley and the Town of Ottawa sought to challenge the legitimacy of this tax. They argued that the city of Ottawa had exclusive authority over the streets, bridges, and roads within its corporate limits, based on its charter established on February 10, 1853. On the other hand, the defendants claimed that the town also had concurrent jurisdiction over the same matters due to prior legislation. The case involved the interpretation of legislative acts to determine whether the town could lawfully impose taxes for building a bridge within the jurisdiction of the city. As a result, relief was sought through an injunction to prevent the tax's collection.	The plaintiffs contended that the tax levied by the town of Ottawa was unauthorized, as the city council held exclusive rights to manage and maintain infrastructure within the city limits, including roads and bridges. They sought an injunction to prevent the extension of the tax on the town's collector's book, claiming that the town meeting that voted on the tax did not have the legitimate authority to do so and that the levy was thus void.	The defendants argued that the town had the right to levy the tax based on the precedents set by earlier legislative acts that conferred township authorities with powers related to roads and bridges. They claimed that the tax was relevant and necessary for the construction of the bridge and sought to defend the validity of the tax and the authority of the town's actions.

John Henderson was indicted for perjury by the People of the State of Illinois in 1886. The indictment stemmed from Henderson's testimony during the murder trial of Henry Lightfoot for the alleged murder of Benjamin W. Moore. It was alleged that during the trial, Henderson had falsely claimed that Moore offered him $250 to kill Lightfoot on November 18, 1885, in Makanda, Illinois. This claim was critical to the defense in the murder case. The prosecution argued that Henderson's testimony was fabricated, aiming to exonerate Lightfoot. Henderson moved to quash the indictment, claiming the indictment was insufficient; his requests were denied. The jury found him guilty of perjury after conflicting testimonies emerged about whether Henderson was in Makanda on the specified date. Witness testimonies cast doubt on the authenticity of his claim that Moore made such an offer. The court's opinion emphasized that the material aspects of Henderson's testimony were crucial to the perjury charge, and the evidence presented confirmed the jury's verdict.	The plaintiff, representing the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that John Henderson committed perjury by providing false testimony during the murder trial of Henry Lightfoot. They argued that Henderson's statement about Moore offering him money to commit murder was a deliberate lie aimed at influencing the outcome of the trial. The prosecution sought a conviction for perjury, asserting that Henderson's false testimony undermined the integrity of the judicial process.	In his defense, John Henderson contended that the indictment was flawed, arguing that the details specified in the indictment regarding time, place, and amount were immaterial to the charge of perjury. He claimed to have witnesses who could corroborate his account of the alleged offer made by Moore. Henderson also argued that there was insufficient evidence to support the conviction and maintained that he was not present during the claimed conversation, asserting that the allegations made against him were untrue.

John L. Brown filed a lawsuit in 1865 against The Illinois Central Mutual Insurance Company in the Alexander Circuit Court, claiming debt resulting from a contract. The case was initiated after the defendant's agent in Alexander County was served with the process. The defendant contested the jurisdiction, arguing it resided in Sangamon County and that neither the debt nor the contract was associated with Alexander County. The plaintiff countered, asserting that the contract was indeed made in Alexander County, where the cause of action arose. The case underwent several legal proceedings, including a demurrer from the defendant, which was ultimately not resolved before a trial was agreed upon without a jury. During subsequent court sessions, various motions and amendments were made concerning the entry of the case record and the eventual ruling on the jurisdictional issue, which was decided in favor of the plaintiff, finding the issues aligned with the plaintiff's claims. However, confusion arose regarding the final judgment submissions and the assessment of damages.	The plaintiff, John L. Brown, argued that the contract was made in Alexander County, where the cause of action accrued and was thus appropriately presented in that jurisdiction. He sought a judgment in favor of the debt mentioned in his declaration and requested the court to enforce the recovery of the owed amount, asserting that the issues were found favorably for him during the trial.	The Illinois Central Mutual Insurance Company contended that it was a resident of Sangamon County, and therefore the Alexander Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction over the case. They maintained that the contract in question did not accrue in Alexander County and filed various motions, including a demurrer to oppose the plaintiff's claims. Their requests ultimately included seeking to be absolved from the allegations and costs.

The case "Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. Mary Garvy, Adm’x" took place in January 1871 in Bloomington, Illinois. The incident involved the tragic death of an individual, who was attempting to cross a railroad track at a public street crossing. On a dark night, the deceased, along with two companions, encountered a northbound train, which they paused to let pass. Immediately after the front train passed, they stepped onto the track and were struck by detached freight cars moving at slow speed, which were not under the control of any operator. The accident resulted in one fatality. Evidence presented during the trial indicated that there were no warning signals or lights on the cars, no brakeman present to alert pedestrians, and crucially, that the freight cars were being operated without a locomotive. The jury was instructed that these circumstances constituted negligence on the part of the railroad company, leading to their finding in favor of the deceased’s estate.	The plaintiff, represented by Mary Garvy as administratrix, claimed that the railroad company was negligent in causing the wrongful death of the deceased. The central arguments included the railroad's lack of safety measures, such as the absence of lights and signals on the freight cars, and the fact that there was no human operator to manage the train's speed or alert pedestrians to its approach. The plaintiff sought damages for the death, arguing that the railroad company's negligence directly led to the accident.	The defendant, Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, contended that the deceased may have been negligent due to alleged impairments, such as being deaf, and argued that the deceased’s recklessness contributed to the accident. They claimed that the error lay not with their company but with the actions of the deceased and companions as they attempted to cross the tracks. The defense sought dismissal of the claims or a reduction in damages based on these factors.

Joseph McPherson brought a case against Rufus C. Hall in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1867, concerning a dispute over a sale of oats. The transaction occurred around February 25, 1865, when Hall, via his agent Stiles, agreed to buy 5,000 bushels of oats from McPherson, who was represented by his agent Parks, at a price of 614 cents per bushel. The oats were to be delivered during the month of March 1865, but Hall did not demand the oats throughout that month. On March 31, McPherson attempted to deliver warehouse receipts for the oats to Hall, but Stiles, Hall's agent, was absent, preventing the tender of the receipts. The plaintiff claimed damages for the defendant's failure to receive and pay for the oats.	McPherson asserted that he fulfilled his obligation by attempting to deliver the warehouse receipts for the oats, which he claims were genuine and ready for transfer. He argued that Hall's non-response and failure to demand the oats resulted in damages, warranting compensation.	Hall contended that the tender of the warehouse receipts was insufficient without proof that the receipts genuinely represented the oats and that the oats were not subject to any warehouse charges. The defense argued that the plaintiff's actions did not constitute an adequate tender since Hall was not present to accept the delivery, which undermined the validity of the receipts.

In the case of Frank F. Cole v. John T. Cosgrove, the events unfolded in Illinois, leading up to the legal decision filed on January 6, 1886. Frank F. Cole, the defendant, had been entrusted with a stock of boots and shoes as a pledge by John T. Cosgrove, the plaintiff. Cosgrove initiated a legal action known as trover against Cole, seeking damages for what he claimed as the wrongful conversion of the pledged goods. During the proceedings, evidence revealed that Cole, while in possession of the goods, committed fraudulent acts that were inconsistent with his responsibilities as a pledgee. These actions were deemed sufficient to terminate the bailment agreement and subsequently made Cole liable for the loss of the items in question. The jury ultimately awarded Cosgrove damages amounting to $7,842.55, which prompted Cole to bring the case before the Illinois Appellate Court, challenging the verdict. After reviewing the evidence, the court acknowledged that while errors in jury instructions may have been present, they were not significant enough to impact the overall judgment regarding damages.	The plaintiff, John T. Cosgrove, argued that Frank F. Cole wrongfully converted the pledged stock of boots and shoes, leading to significant financial loss. Cosgrove maintained that he was entitled to a judgment for damages caused by Cole's fraudulent actions while in possession of the goods. He sought damages totaling $7,842.55 based on the jury's verdict, asserting that Cole's conduct was unlawful and breached the terms of the bailment agreement.	The defendant, Frank F. Cole, contended that any errors related to jury instructions should negate the verdict in Cosgrove's favor. He argued that the claims of wrongful conversion were unfounded, asserting that the actions taken while in possession of the goods did not constitute a breach of the duty owed as a pledgee. Cole aimed to have the court reverse or modify the judgment against him and sought relief from the substantial damages awarded.

The case "The Board of Trade of the City of Chicago v. J. Buckingham et al." originated from events following the devastating fire in Chicago on October 8 and 9, 1871, which destroyed a significant amount of stored grain in several elevators. The elevators involved included Galena, Hiram Wheeler, Munger and Armour, Nation and Central A, totaling over a million bushels of grain. After the fire, the unburned grain was still at risk from the ongoing blaze as well as the elements. The Board of Trade of Chicago, acting on behalf of the unknown owners of the grain and with the consent of the warehouse owners, took possession to salvage and sell the grain. They successfully sold it at auction for approximately $60,000 to $70,000 after hiring labor to preserve it. Prior to the sale, the warehouse owners had agreed in writing to allow the Board of Trade to sell the grain, with the understanding that they would receive two cents per bushel for storage. The case escalated when the Board of Trade filed a bill in chancery seeking approval of the sale and distribution of the proceeds among claimants, including warehousemen who sought a lien for additional storage charges beyond the agreed amount. The situation turned intricate as the warehouse owners contested the distribution, asserting their rights to a greater claim due to their lien on the fund generated from the sale.	The Board of Trade contended that they had acted to preserve the grain for the benefit of the unknown owners and sought the court’s approval to distribute the proceeds from the sale. They argued that the warehousemen had lost their lien over the grain once they permitted the sale to occur and that their actions indicated an understanding that only the agreed two cents per bushel would be their claim.	The warehousemen, represented by J. Buckingham and others, argued that they maintained a valid lien for the full amount of storage charges incurred while the grain was in their possession. They claimed that their agreement with the Board of Trade did not constitute a release of their lien beyond the stipulated amount for storage and that they were entitled to a share of the proceeds from the sale of the grain.

John McCully and others (the appellants) brought a trover action against Charles M. Hardy (the appellee) regarding an office safe originally owned by the appellants. The case took place in Cook County, Illinois, and the incident stems from events around 1879 when the appellants lent the safe to a man named Bishop. Bishop used the safe in his Chicago office for approximately two and a half years. Subsequently, the safe was seized under an execution against Bishop and sold to a plaintiff in the execution, who later transferred it to Hardy. After Hardy acquired the safe, the appellants demanded its return, but Hardy refused. The key legal question was whether the appellants were estopped from claiming the safe due to Bishop's actions while possessing it. The court noted no awareness on the part of the appellee regarding the appellants' ownership rights at the time of his purchase. After careful examination of the evidence, the court found the appellants retained ownership of the safe at the time of the levy and sale, negating any valid title claim by Hardy.	The plaintiffs, McCully et al., argued that they are the rightful owners of the safe that was wrongfully taken from them when executed against Bishop. They asserted that Hardy's possession of the safe was without legitimate title, and they sought its return along with associated legal costs.	The defendant, Charles M. Hardy, contended that the appellants had allowed Bishop to act in ways that suggested he was the owner of the safe, arguing that this should estop the appellants from claiming ownership. However, he asserted that the sale to him, made through judicial proceedings, had been legitimate and that he had no knowledge of any competing ownership claims at the time of purchase.

The case "City of Springfield v. Benjamin M. Griffith" took place in Springfield, Illinois, with a decision issued by the Illinois Appellate Court on May 25, 1886. The key individuals involved were Benjamin M. Griffith, the plaintiff, and the City of Springfield, the defendant. The dispute arose over alleged damages to Griffith's property resulting from the city raising the grade of Sixth Street in front of his residence. Griffith claimed that the raised street grade (approximately eleven inches) led to various negative effects, including diminished access to his property, the need to raise his lots to conform to the new grade, and the accumulation of water that flooded his property. Griffith argued that the raised grade required him to incur expenses totaling $280 to make adjustments to his property to counteract the impacts of the street alteration. He also suggested that this alteration diminished his property value by as much as $3,000. Witnesses supported Griffith’s claims regarding these damages. The city’s actions ultimately led to a legal examination of whether Griffith's damages were justifiably caused by the city’s changes to the street.	Benjamin M. Griffith contended that the City of Springfield’s raising of Sixth Street's grade resulted in significant damage to his property. He argued that this action destroyed the ease of access to his home, necessitated costly adjustments to his lot to align with the new street level, and led to water accumulation on his property, damaging his dwelling. Griffith sought damages for these expenses and claimed that the overall value of his property was negatively affected due to the city's actions.	The City of Springfield defended against Griffith's claims by asserting that the damages he alleged were not legally recoverable. They argued that the raised grade did not warrant the expenses incurred by Griffith and that any effect on property value due to appearance alone was not compensable. The city maintained that any inconvenience or expense associated with adjusting the property to the new street grade was a risk that property owners assume when purchasing property next to municipal roads, and because the declaration's claims did not align with the evidence presented, there should be no recovery for the alleged damages.

In June 1867, the case of Henry Love v. Hugh Moore was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following an incident in Marion County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Henry Love, was a school teacher whose teaching certificate was revoked by the defendant, Hugh Moore, who served as the superintendent of schools. Love claimed that Moore's revocation of his certificate was illegal and sought damages for the wrongful act. During the trial, the court instructed the jury that Moore could only be found liable if it was proven that he had acted willfully and maliciously. Love sought to clarify that malice could be inferred from Moore's actions, even without evidence of personal hatred. However, the court denied this instruction, which led to the appeal. The case raised questions about the standard of proof required to demonstrate malice in such actions.	Henry Love argued that the revocation of his teaching certificate by Hugh Moore was unlawful and sought damages as a result. He contended that the jury should be allowed to infer malice from Moore's rash and wrongful conduct, without needing to prove personal hatred or ill-will. Love requested that the court instruct the jury accordingly, as he believed that Moore's actions met the criteria for malice based on the evidence of his behavior.	Hugh Moore defended against Love's claims by asserting that he could only be found liable if his actions were proven to be willfully and maliciously wrong. Moore contended that he acted within his authority and denied any intent to harm Love personally. His defense was centered on the argument that the standards for demonstrating malice were not sufficiently met, as defined by the court's instructions.

In January 1867, the case of William Coultas, impleaded, v. Lynn L. Green was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, stemming from the Mason Circuit Court. The litigation arose when Lynn Green sought to set aside a sheriff's sale of certain lands purchased by Coultas. A stipulation was filed between Coultas and Green which stipulated the amounts owed by both parties and the desire to annul the sheriff's sale. Specifically, Coultas was owed $4,947.50 on notes assigned to him, while Green was owed $2,035 on a note assigned to him. The stipulation also sought a court decree setting aside the sale, mandating Theodore L. Cooper to pay these amounts, failing which the real estate would be sold to satisfy the debts. The stipulation's terms required a decree to be rendered at the term of court during which the agreement was made. However, Green later attempted to dismiss his bill, which Coultas contested, leading to an appeal.	The plaintiff, Lynn L. Green, argued that the sheriff's sale of the real estate to William Coultas should be annulled due to a mutual stipulation made by the parties. Green asserted that the court should follow through on the stipulation, which laid out the mutual obligations related to debts owed to both parties. He requested that the court render a decree to set aside the sale and compel Theodore Cooper to settle the debts stipulated.	William Coultas, the defendant, contended that the mutual stipulation entered between the parties bound them to follow through on its terms and that the court should have rendered a decree as specified in the stipulation. Coultas objected to Green's motion for dismissal, arguing that the stipulation prevented either party from taking further steps in the case without compliance and that the court should be compelled to enforce the agreement that had been made.

The case "The Chicago and Iowa Railroad Company et al. v. Daniel J. Pinckney et al." was adjudicated in September 1874 in Illinois. The primary individuals involved were the plaintiffs, Daniel J. Pinckney and others, and the defendant, the Chicago and Iowa Railroad Company along with the town of Mount Morris. The legal action arose when Pinckney and his associates filed a bill in the Circuit Court of Ogle County, seeking to prevent the town from issuing bonds worth $75,000 to the railroad company. The election for the bond issue had taken place on June 30, 1870, before the adoption of the 1870 Illinois Constitution, which prohibited municipalities from gifting or subscribing money to railroad companies. The plaintiffs contended that the election was void due to defects in the notice and claimed that the new constitutional mandate made the proposed donation illegal. The court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, but the defendants appealed, asserting the legality of the election and the bond issuance.	The plaintiffs, led by Daniel J. Pinckney, argued that the issuance of bonds by the town to the Chicago and Iowa Railroad Company should be prevented based on two main points: first, that the constitution adopted in July 1870 prohibited municipalities from making donations to railroad corporations; and second, that the election vote, which favored the donation, was invalid due to defects in the notice provided to voters. They sought an injunction to stop the bond issuance, asserting that the legal framework did not allow for such financial aid from the town to a private corporation.	The defendant, the Chicago and Iowa Railroad Company and the town of Mount Morris, countered the plaintiff's claims by asserting that the election and subsequent bond donation were valid. They maintained that the constitutional provision protecting subscriptions made prior to its adoption encompassed donations as well, thus making the bond issue permissible. They argued that any deficiencies in the election notice were inconsequential since the required information had been provided through the filed petition, which was accessible to voters. Thus, they sought to reverse the lower court's decree and to confirm the legality of the bond issuance.

On August 14, 1868, Benjamin Whisler borrowed $2,500 from the Ætna Life Insurance Company, securing the loan with a note and a deed of trust on 193 acres of land, which included a forty-acre tract later involved in this case. Whisler sold this property to N. Watson on December 26, 1872, and Watson subsequently sold it to Charles Aulger on July 1, 1873. Aulger later sold the forty-acre tract to John Clay for $1,000 on January 11, 1877. Clay paid $500 upfront, with the balance due by January 1, 1878. Aulger agreed to convey the deed upon full payment, emphasizing that time was of the essence. The Ætna Life Insurance Company demanded payment to release the property from the mortgage. On the due date, Clay attempted to tender the remaining payment to Aulger, but he left without completing the transaction. Attempts to formalize the transaction went unresolved until Clay's death on April 30, 1879. The initial legal action sought to halt the sale of the land by the insurance company and was later amended to seek specific performance of the contract for the conveyance of the property. The lower court ruled in favor of executing the contract and decreed that Aulger was to convey the land to Clay's heirs with conditions that they pay the principal and accrued taxes.	The plaintiff, represented by the heirs of John Clay, claimed that they were entitled to specific performance of the contract regarding the sale of the forty-acre tract. They argued that Clay had made a valid tender of the payment at the time of the note's maturity and sought to compel Aulger to convey the property.	Aulger, the defendant, contended that Clay's tender was insufficient as it was not kept good, meaning that the funds tendered were not available for immediate payment when required. He argued that this lack of readiness prevented the cessation of interest accrual on the outstanding payment. Aulger also claimed that the court had made an error in conveying the title in fee to Clay's heirs, as only dower and homestead rights should have been granted.

Richard Tone purchased land from Berry Wilson on January 9, 1868, for $3,000, paying $1,000 upfront and issuing three promissory notes for the remainder, secured by a mortgage on the property. Tone relied on Wilson's representation that he owned the title to the entire property, but it later emerged that Wilson only had title to four-sevenths of one tract and three-sevenths of another. After failing to pay one of the notes, Wilson initiated foreclosure proceedings. Tone sought legal advice but was incorrectly informed that he could not defend against the foreclosure unless he proved Wilson’s insolvency, which he couldn't do. Tone's lawsuit sought to rescind the conveyance, recover the purchase money, or secure specific performance, but his claims were dismissed in lower court, prompting him to appeal.	Tone contended that Wilson misrepresented ownership of the land, which he later discovered was only partial. He claimed this misrepresentation amounted to fraud and sought relief by asking the court to set aside the deed, refund the money paid, prevent the sale of the property under the foreclosure decree, or enforce specific performance of the contract.	Wilson argued that Tone was precluded from raising his initial defense regarding the failure of title due to his inaction in the foreclosure proceedings. Wilson maintained that he acted in good faith and did not knowingly make any false representation regarding the land ownership. He also asserted that the plaintiff’s inability to pay the mortgage did not absolve him from the debt, emphasizing that any hardship experienced by Tone was self-created.

Leverett S. Chittenden filed a case against John Evans regarding the recovery of a colt. The initial trial took place before a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment that favored Evans. Chittenden appealed the decision, and the case was moved to the Circuit Court of Kendall County. The venue was subsequently changed to DuPage County, where the trial was conducted before a court and jury and resulted in the same outcome. Chittenden sought a reversal of the judgment on several grounds, arguing procedural errors and issues with the jury's verdict.	Chittenden argued that the court erred in changing the jury's verdict, which he believed should have been upheld as it was substantively valid. He also contended that the trial court improperly refused to give some of his requested jury instructions, claiming that these instructions were necessary to inform the jury of the applicable law. Finally, Chittenden asserted that the evidence did not support the jury's finding against him.	Evans maintained that the jury's verdict was indeed appropriate and that the court had correctly handled the amendment of the jury's verdict before entering judgment. He argued that the jury instructions given were appropriate and provided a fair representation of the case. Furthermore, Evans countered that the evidence presented was sufficient to support the jury's findings and emphasized the consistency in the verdicts rendered by three different juries throughout the case.

In 1866, in Henry County, Illinois, the legal case of Elias H. Morse v. George W. Iman arose from a dispute concerning trespass and property rights. The conflict originated when Elias H. Morse (the plaintiff) accused George W. Iman (the defendant) of unlawfully removing three loads of hay from land that Morse claimed to be his property. However, the situation was complicated by the fact that neither party owned the land in question; both were actually in possession through an informal agreement with a third party, Larson, who owned the land. Morse had cut grass from the land with Larson's permission, while Iman claimed he had an understanding with Larson to access the north half of the field where he removed the hay. As such, the case eventually escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court after an initial trial in a justice of the peace court and a subsequent appeal to the Circuit Court, where the trial had ruled in favor of Morse.	The plaintiff, Elias H. Morse, claimed that the hay taken by George W. Iman constituted a trespass since he believed the grass was rightfully his based on his use of the land and Larson's permission. Morse argued that his possession of the land allowed him to recover damages for the removal of the hay. He requested that the court uphold the lower court’s judgment in his favor.	The defendant, George W. Iman, defended against the trespass claim by asserting that he had been in actual possession of the portion of land from which the hay was cut. He contended that, as a lawful user of the land by agreement with Larson, he had legally appropriated the hay in question. Iman argued that since Morse did not own the land, he had no rightful claim to the grass cut there.

In December 1858, Jahalon Tyler filed a petition in the Mercer Circuit Court of Illinois to enforce a mechanics’ lien against property owned by James D. Coburn. The case arose from a contract made on November 1, 1858, in which Coburn agreed to buy bricks to construct a cellar wall for his dwelling. The contract specified payment at nine dollars per thousand for bricks delivered on the property or eight dollars per thousand if delivered from the kiln. Tyler claimed to have supplied 8,000 bricks initially and, after a settlement on November 30, 1857, received a note for payment from Coburn. However, Tyler later provided an additional 2,500 bricks, of which 1,500 were delivered to the cellar at the higher price, with all bricks being consumed in construction. Tyler alleged that Coburn had not paid for these materials and sought to establish a lien on the property while requesting payment and potential sale of the premises if the debt was not settled. Coburn responded with a demurrer to the petition, which was ultimately overruled, leading to a decree favoring Tyler’s claims.	Tyler claimed that Coburn failed to pay for bricks delivered under a contract to furnish materials for a construction project. He requested that a mechanics' lien be established on Coburn's property, seeking a legal decree for the payment owed and the possibility of selling the premises if Coburn defaulted on this payment.	Coburn argued that the original contract was deficient as it did not specify a concrete timeline for when the bricks were to be delivered, which he claimed was necessary to establish a lien under the law of 1845 regarding mechanics' liens. He contended that an agreement to deliver within a "reasonable time" was insufficient to create a binding obligation, and therefore, the petition should be dismissed.

Oliver F. Fuller v. Mary Ledden is a legal case that took place in September 1877 in Illinois. The case stems from an action of debt initiated by Mary Ledden in the Superior Court of Cook County against Oliver F. Fuller, a stockholder in the Bank of Chicago. The dispute arose over the recovery of $488.62, which was owed to the plaintiff for money previously deposited in the bank. The action was based on the provision in the bank's charter that made stockholders liable for debts to creditors up to double the amount of stock held. Ledden claimed that Fuller was liable for the bank's debts incurred while he was still a stockholder. Fuller, on the other hand, argued that he had sold his shares on January 24, 1874, prior to the debt's incurrence, and that, according to the charter, the right to action against him was limited to three months following the notification of stock transfer. The case was initially filed on July 25, 1874, and the court had to determine if a creditor's action against a stockholder was limited by time frames established in the bank's charter.	Mary Ledden, the plaintiff, asserted that Oliver F. Fuller, as a stockholder in the Bank of Chicago, was liable to her for debts incurred by the bank while he was a member. She sought to recover the sum of $488.62, arguing that payrolls for the stocks assigned to Fuller gave rise to statutory liability which he could not escape merely by transferring his stocks.	Oliver F. Fuller contended that he had sold his stock before the money was deposited and thus was not liable for the debts incurred by the bank after that date. He argued that according to the terms of the bank's charter, any legal action against him should have occurred within three months following the notification of his stock transfer, which he contended had not been complied with.

Isaac S. Tower initiated a legal action against Timothy M. Bradley and Anna Hilton in 1872, in Cook County, Illinois. The case involved a replevin action, which is a type of lawsuit for the recovery of personal property that has been wrongfully taken or detained. Tower claimed that Bradley and Hilton had wrongfully taken his property and kept it without his permission. The trial was conducted before a jury, which resulted in a verdict and judgment in favor of the defendants, Bradley and Hilton. Following the trial, Tower sought to have the verdict reviewed, presenting his case to a higher court through a writ of error.	Tower's main arguments centered around the assertion that the lower court had improperly directed the jury regarding the verdict, claiming this altered the substance of the case. He argued that the defendants were not entitled to keep the property, emphasizing his ownership and right to a return of the property taken. Additionally, he contended that the jury instructions provided to the defendants were incorrect.	The defendants, represented by counsel, maintained that Tower's claims were unfounded and that they rightfully had the property in question. They argued against the points raised by Tower, particularly regarding the alleged wrongfulness of the taking and the validity of the jury's verdict. The defendants argued there was no legitimate error in the instructions given and contended that the trial's outcome should be upheld, as Tower failed to present adequate grounds for appeal.

In 1883, in the Illinois Appellate Court, William E. Baird brought a legal action against Wesley Best, following a transaction involving three promissory notes of $233.33 each. These notes were given by Best to Isaac Chapman as part of a purchase agreement for land. Baird, as the assignee of Chapman, sought to recover the last unpaid note. The case arose after Baird claimed that Chapman endorsed the note to him. Best contested the claim by filing a general issue and several special pleas, including allegations of failure of consideration and a dispute over the assignment of the note by Chapman. The court initially ruled in favor of Baird for the amount of $430, but it was contested by Best, leading to an appeal. The legal proceedings highlighted issues surrounding the validity of the pleas and the evidence required to challenge the assignment of the note.	Baird's primary argument was that he was entitled to recover the unpaid amount from the promissory notes endorsed to him by Isaac Chapman. He claimed that the assignment was valid and that Best was legally obligated to fulfill the payment. Baird sought to execute the last unpaid note, emphasizing the rightful transfer of the note as per the agreement made during the land purchase.	Best's defenses were centered around two main arguments: firstly, that there was a failure of consideration for the notes, meaning he believed that the reason for issuing the notes was no longer valid. Secondly, he contended that the assignment of the note from Chapman to Baird was not properly executed, implying that Baird did not hold a legitimate claim.
