Best's requests included the dismissal of the complaint based on these defenses.

In January 1875, a legal action was initiated in the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a dispute over a tract of land located in St. Clair County, Illinois. The case was brought by William Meacham against Thomas Winstanly, where Meacham sought to recover an undivided interest in the property. During the trial in the St. Clair Circuit Court, Meacham claimed to trace ownership of the land back to the United States. Winstanly, however, contested this claim by presenting evidence of having established color of title and paying taxes on the property for seven consecutive years while it was vacant. Winstanly also demonstrated possession and actual occupancy backed by the color of title. The circuit court sided with Winstanly, leading Meacham to appeal the decision, arguing that Winstanly failed to legally substantiate his claims regarding the tax payments on the land for the required seven years.	William Meacham’s primary argument was that Thomas Winstanly did not adequately prove the payment of all legally assessed taxes on the property for a continuous period of seven years under a valid color of title. He contended that the taxes from the year 1852, when the color of title was allegedly acquired, should not be counted toward the seven-year requirement. Meacham requested the court to reverse the circuit court’s judgment in favor of Winstanly and recognize his claim to the land.	Thomas Winstanly's defense centered on demonstrating that he had indeed paid all legally assessed taxes on the land for seven successive years while having a valid color of title. He argued that the statute did not mandate that the taxes for the first year be assessed after acquiring the color of title. Winstanly maintained that he provided proof of payment for the years in question and established possession under the color of title, which amounted to a complete bar against Meacham’s ejectment action. He urged the court to uphold the lower court's judgment in his favor.

In September 1871, the case of John H. Daniels v. Charles D. Wilber took place, primarily in Chicago, Illinois. The case revolved around a dispute regarding compensation for labor and services rendered by Wilber to Daniels in relation to the negotiation of a sale of certain real estate owned by Daniels. Wilber claimed that he traveled from Wilmington, Illinois, to Chicago to negotiate with a treasurer of a coal company interested in purchasing Daniels’ coal lands. Although Wilber asserted he provided valuable services, the evidence of any formal employment agreement between him and Daniels was insufficient. Furthermore, there was no clear contract delineating the amount of compensation expected for his services. About six months after the successful sale of the land by Daniels, Wilber presented a bill for $1,000 to cover his services, but the actual compensation recovered was disputed and considered by the court to be excessive. The Illinois Supreme Court later addressed the issue of damages and the reasonable value of Wilber’s services.	Wilber, the plaintiff, claimed compensation of $1,000 for his services in facilitating the sale of coal lands owned by Daniels. He argued that his efforts in negotiating with the treasurer of the coal company were instrumental in the successful sale that Daniels made thereafter. Therefore, he requested recovery of damages reflecting the value he assigned to his services.	Daniels, the defendant, contended that there was no satisfactory proof of employment or agreement regarding payment for Wilber’s services. He argued that the amount claimed by Wilber was excessive, particularly given that the amount Wilber himself presented in his bill reflected the maximum value of the service provided under the circumstances. Daniels sought to have the court dismiss the claims for being disproportionately inflated.

In 1887, in Champaign County, Illinois, Julia C. Shimp initiated a legal action against Cedar Rapids Insurance Company regarding a fire insurance policy. Following a fire loss, the plaintiff sought to recover funds under her insurance agreement. The defense claimed Shimp failed to provide proof of the loss within the stipulated time frame set by the policy, an obligation which the plaintiff argued had been waived. The case was a retrial after an earlier judgment in favor of Shimp was reversed by the Illinois Appellate Court. Upon the later trial, Shimp introduced new witnesses who attested that the company's adjuster had allegedly declared intentions to deny the claim regardless of the evidence she might provide. However, the adjuster denied making such statements, and the court highlighted that the evidence was conflicting. Additionally, it was mentioned that Shimp’s application contained material misrepresentations regarding the use of the insured property, which further complicated her claim. Ultimately, the issue of whether the insurer had been adequately informed of the property's true nature and the timing of the proof of loss submission were central to the proceedings.	Julia C. Shimp argued that Cedar Rapids Insurance Company had waived its requirement for timely proof of loss after the fire incident. She sought recovery based on her claim that the adjuster had indicated intentions to deny her claim regardless of proof presented. Shimp contended that the acceptance of a premium note post the required proof submission should constitute a waiver of that requirement.	Cedar Rapids Insurance Company maintained that Shimp failed to submit proof of loss within the timeline specified by the insurance policy, which was a critical obligation. The defense argued that the acceptance of the premium note did not waive this necessary condition. They also asserted that the evidence provided by Shimp regarding the adjuster's intent was unconvincing and was contradicted by the adjuster's reports, which did not suggest an intention to deny the claim.

In the case of **Henrietta Blanchard v. Augustus J. Burbank et al.**, which took place in **Chicago, Illinois** in **December 1882**, the plaintiff, Henrietta Blanchard, alleged that the defendants—Augustus J. Burbank, Joshua W. Carr, Anna Ewart, and the Washingtonian Home—committed acts of false imprisonment against her. Blanchard, who had been suffering from health issues and was in a delirious state, was taken against her will from her home by Burbank and Carr under the pretense of visiting a friend in the country. Instead, she was conveyed to the **Martha Washington Home**, an asylum for troubled individuals. The plaintiff accused the defendants of detaining her there forcibly for **fifty-seven days** without a court order and claimed that they confiscated **$800** from her, returning only **$326**. Following the trial, the jury found Burbank and Carr guilty, assessing damages to Blanchard at **$500** while exonerating Ewart and the Washingtonian Home. Both parties subsequently filed for a new trial, which was denied.	The plaintiff, Henrietta Blanchard, argued that the defendants unlawfully restrained her and kidnapped her from her residence without her consent or a court order. She claimed the defendants falsely represented their intentions, which led her to comply with their demands. Blanchard sought damages for false imprisonment and the misappropriation of her money, asserting her rights had been grossly violated while she was detained at the Martha Washington Home.	The defendants contended that Blanchard was in a state of insanity and unable to care for herself, making her admission into the Washingtonian Home justified. They maintained that the plaintiff consented to go to the Home after receiving advice from a doctor. Additionally, they denied the amount of money claimed by the plaintiff, asserting that only **$326** was taken and subsequently returned after accounting for her stay in the Home. They argued that their actions were lawful under the circumstances.

On October 28, 1874, in White County, Illinois, Louisa Goodman filed a complaint against Charles Lewis, claiming he was the father of her illegitimate child. The case began before a justice of the peace, who required Lewis to appear at the subsequent county court term. Initially, Lewis was found not guilty at the county court level, but Goodman appealed the decision to the circuit court. At the circuit court trial, a jury found Lewis guilty of being the father, prompting the court to render judgment in accordance with the law. Lewis then sought to challenge the judgment in the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction to hear the appeal from the county court, and further contesting the legitimacy of the second jury instruction given at trial.	Louisa Goodman, the plaintiff, claimed that Charles Lewis was the father of her child and sought legal acknowledgment of paternity. She appealed the initial not guilty verdict in the county court, leading to the circuit court trial where she aimed to establish paternity based on the evidence presented during the proceedings.	Charles Lewis, the defendant, contended that the circuit court did not have jurisdiction to hear the appeal from the county court regarding the paternity case. He argued that a lack of statutory authority for such an appeal rendered the circuit court's judgment invalid. Additionally, he challenged the jury instruction concerning the burden of proof required for a verdict, asserting that the verdict wasn't supported by sufficient evidence.

The case "John R. True, Treasurer, v. George R. Davis, Treasurer" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on October 29, 1889. It arose in Cook County, where John R. True, the treasurer of the newly incorporated city of Lake View, sought to mandate George R. Davis, the Cook County treasurer and collector, to pay over taxes and assessments collected for Lake View. The background centers on a municipal election on April 5, 1887, where voters decided to incorporate Lake View as a city. True was elected treasurer on April 2, 1889, and took office, expecting to receive funds collected by Davis. However, following a contentious election on June 29, 1889, for the annexation of Lake View to Chicago, Davis refused to pay True, claiming Lake View had ceased to exist as an independent municipality. True contested the validity of the annexation, arguing it violated constitutional provisions regarding municipal debt limits and was not supported by a true majority of voters in Lake View. He stated that the supposed annexation was declared valid despite failing to meet the required majority. The case essentially examined the legitimacy of municipal annexation and financial obligations resulting from it.	John R. True, as the plaintiff, contended that the annexation of Lake View to Chicago was invalid and unconstitutional since it did not receive majority approval from Lake View voters. He requested a writ of mandamus compelling George R. Davis to pay over taxes and special assessments collected for Lake View, arguing that due to the faulty annexation, he remained the legitimate treasurer entitled to the funds.	George R. Davis, as the defendant, maintained that he could not legally pay True due to the annexation of Lake View to Chicago, which he claimed had rendered Lake View no longer a separate municipal entity. Davis argued that the election results indicated the majority decision of citizens favored annexation, legitimizing his refusal to recognize True as treasurer.

In April 1866, the legal case of Joseph McPherson v. Robert H. Parks was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Superior Court of Chicago, presided over by Judge John A. Jameson. The case involved a dispute concerning the sale of 10,000 bushels of oats, paralleling another case with similar circumstances. The key individuals involved were Joseph McPherson, the appellant (plaintiff), and Robert H. Parks, the appellee (defendant). The legal proceedings addressed the validity and rights related to the sale, leading to a question of whether the original instruction given to the plaintiff was erroneous.	The plaintiff, Joseph McPherson, argued that the instructions provided during the trial were in error, which affected the outcome of the sale agreement concerning the oats. He sought to have the judgment in the lower court overturned, emphasizing that the legal basis of his claims was similar to those in a previously adjudicated case.	The defendant, Robert H. Parks, contended that the claims made by the plaintiff were unfounded, and he intended to uphold the original ruling of the lower court. His defense sought to establish that the trial's instructions were adequate and that the sale transaction was executed within lawful bounds.

The case "John G. Fortman et al. v. James M. Ruggles et al." was adjudicated in January 1871 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from a request made by Mason County's treasurer to the county court for a judgment against several individuals for unpaid special drainage taxes and state and county taxes on their lands. A judgment was rendered in June 1866 against these lands for all taxes except the special drainage tax. The plaintiffs, Buggies and Thompson, appealed to the circuit court, which ruled in June 1867 in favor of collecting the special drainage tax as well. During this process, the parties involved did not appear in the court below. Subsequently, two plaintiffs sought to vacate the judgments against their lands, but their motions were overruled. The case was appealed on the grounds of improper jurisdiction due to the lack of statutory notice to the defendants regarding the application for judgment against their properties.	The plaintiffs, represented by J. B. Wright, argued that the circuit court had improperly entertained jurisdiction to render judgment because the collector failed to provide the required notice to the defendants about the impending application for judgment due to delinquent taxes. They contended that the lack of notice prevented the court from lawfully adjudicating the case, and they sought the reversal of the judgments against their lands.	The defendants did not file briefs, but their primary defense rested on the argument that the initial judgments lacked jurisdiction due to the failure of the collector to provide statutory notice. It was asserted that without such notice, the judgments rendered were void and unenforceable. The defendants argued for the dismissal of the prior judgments on these grounds.

In 1871, the case of Angeline Long, Administratrix, v. Elmer B. Thompson, Guardian, et al., was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, following earlier proceedings in the Circuit Court of DuPage County. The case involved Angeline Long, who was the administratrix for her deceased husband, Abram Long, who died intestate. Following an order from the county court authorizing the sale of her husband’s real estate to pay debts, a surplus of $942.53 remained after fulfilling these obligations. On September 5, 1866, without notice to the heirs, the court ordered a distribution of this surplus, allocating one-third to the administratrix and the remainder to the heirs. However, the administratrix failed to execute the distribution order. Subsequently, the heirs expressed their intention to vacate this order due to the lack of notice and procedural irregularities. The probate court eventually set aside the distribution order, a decision that the administratrix appealed in hopes of reversing it. The court had to determine whether notice was required for the order’s validity, and whether the probate court could vacate its own orders at a later date.	Angeline Long, as the administratrix, claimed that notice to the heirs was unnecessary for the distribution order, arguing that the statute had no explicit requirement for it. She also contended that since the probate court’s judgments are records, they cannot be vacated at subsequent terms without extraordinary circumstances. Long sought to have the order of the probate court that vacated the distribution restored on appeal.	The defendants argued that the distribution order was void because the heirs were not given notice, which violates principles of fairness and due process in judicial proceedings. They maintained that all parties whose rights are affected must be notified, and since the distribution had not been finalized, the probate court retained the authority to set aside its previous order.

The case "Daniel B. Waterman v. Chicago & Iowa Railroad Company" arises from a legal suit commenced in the Circuit Court of Kane County, Illinois, on December 16, 1889. The plaintiff, Daniel B. Waterman, claimed an amount due to him for his role as president of the Chicago & Iowa Railroad Company, specifically for the salary owed to him from March 4, 1880, to March 15, 1882, which he asserted had been set at $5,000 per year by a purported board of directors at a meeting on May 28, 1880. Waterman argued that he fulfilled his duties as president until a successor was elected. However, the legality of the board's actions was contested by the defendant, who claimed the board’s composition and decisions were invalid. The core issue centered around whether Waterman was a legally recognized (de jure) president or merely an acting president (de facto). The defendant contended that the election of the board on March 3, 1880, was illegal, rendering any salary resolution void, and referred to a prior court ruling that ousted Waterman and other directors involved. They maintained that his claim to the salary could not be validly asserted without establishing his legal right to the position.	The plaintiff, Daniel B. Waterman, claims he is entitled to recover his salary as president of the Chicago & Iowa Railroad Company for the period of March 4, 1880, to March 15, 1882. He asserts that a board of directors had legally appointed him and fixed his annual salary at $5,000, a resolution that he claims is valid for compensation due for duties carried out until his successor was appointed.	The defendant, Chicago & Iowa Railroad Company, argues that Waterman was not a de jure president due to the illegality of the board that appointed him, as their election resulted from improper procedure. They assert that any resolutions adopted, including Waterman's salary, are void. The defendant emphasizes that a judgment of ouster from a preceding court decision invalidated Waterman's claims and posits that without a valid title to the office, Waterman cannot recover salary on the basis that his appointment was rendered null.

Henry C. Sailors v. The Nixon-Jones Printing Co. took place in the spring of 1884, focusing on a business relationship involving a commercial reporting and rating system in St. Louis, Missouri. The case involved Henry C. Sailors, who initially owned a third of the business, and his partners, Jules T. Guibout and Tryon J. Woodward. Sailors sold a one-third interest in the business to a man named Black and later to Nixon. In January 1885, Sailors, Guibout, and Woodward executed a written agreement stipulating that Sailors would not be actively involved in managing the business for two years while Guibout and Woodward were declared the sole responsible managers. The business faced financial difficulties, leading to a debt that was incurred on the order of Guibout while Sailors was not involved in management. The contentious issue hinged on whether Sailors could be held liable for debts incurred during this period, as Guibout and Woodward identified Sailors as a partner in their dealings, a claim that Sailors disputed. The case culminated in a trial where the jury's verdict favored the plaintiff (the Nixon-Jones Printing Co.), prompting Sailors to appeal the decision based on multiple legal grounds.	The plaintiff, The Nixon-Jones Printing Co., argued that Henry C. Sailors was a partner in the business operations, and thus jointly liable for the debts incurred during the time of his involvement. They presented depositions from Guibout and Woodward that indicated Sailors agreed to share in the financial obligations, despite the written contract claiming otherwise. The plaintiff contested that Sailors had held himself out as a partner without formally authorizing such representation.	Henry C. Sailors contended that he was not a partner under the legal definition, as per the contract with Guibout and Woodward. He maintained that the contract expressly limited his role to a joint owner with no liability for debts contracted before he began his active partnership after two years. Additionally, Sailors sought to exclude the deposition testimony presented by the plaintiff as it was deemed incompetent and misleading, arguing that such testimony did not demonstrate any authorized partnership.

In 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal case arose between Nicholas Dyk and Jitche De Young, a married woman who was pregnant at the time of the incident. The altercation began when Dyk attempted to retrieve a receipt from De Young, which related to a payment her husband owed him. During this process, the receipt was torn, and De Young alleged that Dyk struck her in the abdomen, resulting in permanent harm to her health. The situation was rife with conflicting testimonies regarding whether Dyk actually struck De Young or caused her any injury. Ultimately, the legal proceedings highlighted the controversies over the extent of De Young's injuries and Dyk’s use of force. The case emphasized the jury's role in determining the facts and the evidence presented, with the court maintaining that there was sufficient evidence to support the jury's verdict.	Jitche De Young claimed that Nicholas Dyk committed an assault and battery against her, resulting in physical harm during a confrontation over a receipt. She argued that the injuries she sustained had permanently damaged her health. De Young sought damages for the harm inflicted upon her, asserting that Dyk’s actions during this encounter constituted a legal wrong that warranted compensation.	Nicholas Dyk contended that he did not strike De Young and that any injuries claimed were either non-existent or exaggerated. He disputed the assertion that he committed assault and battery, arguing that his actions were defensive based on the context they were in. Dyk requested that the court dismiss the claims against him, asserting that the plaintiff had failed to provide sufficient evidence that he had harmed her.

On June 24, 1835, in Rock Island, Illinois, James May purchased two tracts of land from Robert and Thomas Symms for $300, with the intention that the Symms would secure the legal title for May. The transaction included a deed conveying the land, which was government land that the Symms had improved, granting them a pre-emption right for purchase. The deed specifically referred to the "fractional piece" and detailed the payment terms, including $150 paid upfront and additional amounts upon securing the patent from the government. After the purchase, Thomas Symms successfully obtained the title for the land and represented to May that he needed help covering the costs incurred in securing the title. May subsequently paid $29.37 for these expenses. Despite the agreement, Thomas Symms fraudulently conveyed parts of the land to a third party, James Symms, who had notice of May's rights. May filed a bill seeking an injunction against further sales of the property and a decree for the rights to the land, alleging that the Symms held the land in trust for him. The Rock Island Circuit Court dismissed his bill on demurrer, leading May to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	James May's primary arguments centered around the claim that the Symms had fraudulently conveyed the land despite their agreement to convey it to him. He asserted that he had fully paid for the land and that the Symms, as tenants of May, were obligated to honor the original deed and his rights to the property. May sought an injunction to prevent further sales and requested that the court compel the Symms to convey their rights in the land back to him, emphasizing that he was a bona fide purchaser and had adhered to all agreements.	The defendants, Robert and Thomas Symms, argued that the court should reject May’s bill based on a demurrer, asserting that no legal basis existed for the claims made against them. They contended that May had no valid claims for the injunction or for the conveyance of land since the deed descriptions lacked specific details and that they were free to transfer the land as they had done. They maintained that their actions complied with relevant land laws at the time.

H. Leroy Thayer filed a lawsuit against John Allison in the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking to recover $7,500 allegedly owed under a contract for the sale of 320 acres of land in Grundy County. The contract, executed on December 15, 1881, specified a total purchase price of $16,000, with initial payments of $500 cash, $7,500 due on March 1, 1882, and two subsequent payments. A key provision allowed Allison to rescind the contract before the second payment was due by returning the contract to Thayer, who would retain the $500 already paid. During the legal proceedings, Allison claimed he had rescinded the contract citing this provision. The trial was held without a jury, resulting in a judgment against Thayer, which was affirmed by the Appellate Court. The case hinged on whether the deadline for rescinding the contract was extended and whether Allison exercised this right in a timely manner.	Thayer's primary argument revolved around the assertion that Allison had not properly exercised his right to rescind the contract within the specified timeframe. Thayer contended that the deadline to rescind was March 1, 1882, and that any extension of the deadline for the second payment did not equate to extending the rescission right. Additionally, he sought to maintain his claim for the second installment of $7,500, arguing that the letters exchanged did not constitute a valid extension of time for rescission.	Allison's defense was built upon his claim that Thayer had agreed to extend the time for the rescission option until April 1, 1882, allowing him to rescind the contract before that date. He provided evidence of correspondence that suggested a mutual understanding to extend the deadline. Allison contended that his actions in returning the contract on March 29, 1882, constituted a valid rescission, and he argued that there was no requirement for him to endorse a release on the contract in order to effectuate this rescission.

The case "Ichabod H. Miller et al. v. Jeremiah Ballard" originated in Adams County, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1868. The plaintiffs, led by Ichabod H. Miller, represented the Adams County Agricultural and Horticultural Association. They sought to recover a subscription of $100 made by the defendant, Jeremiah Ballard, to finance the location of the State Fair in Quincy for two years, starting in 1867. A subscription paper was circulated, and various individuals pledged amounts to support this endeavor. Subsequently, the Agricultural Association was incorporated and began developing a fairground after securing a commitment from the State Agricultural Society, which resolved to hold the Fair in Quincy contingent upon satisfactory bonds. The main legal contention arose concerning the necessity of proving that the plaintiffs had directly expended money or services based on Ballard's subscription, which the court addressed as an error. The case highlighted the legality of subscription promises and the responsibilities of parties involved in the fundraising efforts.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to recover the subscription amount from Ballard based on the subscription paper, which stipulated that funds were to be used to secure the Fair's location in Quincy. They maintained that it was unnecessary for the plaintiffs themselves to have expended money or services as long as third parties acted upon the faith of the subscription. They sought a judgment in their favor to collect the amount pledged by Ballard for the use of the Agricultural Association.	The defendant, Jeremiah Ballard, contended that for the plaintiffs to recover the pledged amount, they needed to demonstrate that the funds were expended or services performed directly related to the Fair, which they failed to substantiate. Moreover, he argued against the sufficiency of the evidence provided linking his subscription to any necessary expenditures by the Association. He sought a dismissal of the claims made by the plaintiffs.

In April 1866, in Wheaton, Illinois, Leonard Pratt, a student at Wheaton College, was suspended from the institution for joining a secret society known as the Good Templars, in violation of the college's rules. The college's faculty suspended him until he expressed a willingness to conform to their regulations. In response, Pratt's father sought a writ of mandamus to compel the college to reinstate his son as a student. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, which examined the college's authority to create and enforce such rules. The court acknowledged the importance of college discipline and the discretion afforded to college authorities in regulating student conduct to ensure proper governance and management of the institution.	The plaintiff, represented by Leonard Pratt's father, argued that the suspension of his son violated his rights as a student and sought a legal demand for the reinstatement of Leonard as a student at Wheaton College. The plaintiff maintained that joining the Good Templars, a society focused on promoting temperance, should not have led to disciplinary action as it did not conflict with moral or legal standards.	Wheaton College, represented by its faculty and trustees, defended its decision by asserting that the rules prohibiting students from joining secret societies were reasonable and necessary for maintaining discipline within the college. The college argued that these regulations were within their power as an incorporated institution, and any rights associated with being a citizen were surrendered upon enrollment. The college emphasized the importance of adhering to its rules for the successful management and governance of the institution.

The case of **Henry C. Craig v. Gersham B. Dimock et al.** originated in **Adams County, Illinois**, during the **October term of 1867**, with a final judgment rendered in **January 1868**. The plaintiffs, **Gersham B. Dimock and Cyrus W. Hilborn**, brought an action of **replevin** against the defendant, **Henry C. Craig**, concerning a **wagon and two horses** that were claimed under a **chattel mortgage** executed by a third party, **Holden**, on **March 19, 1867**. The plaintiffs alleged they were rightful owners of the property secured by the mortgage, which had been improperly recorded due to a lack of a stamp until June 21, 1867. Compounding the issue, **Samuel E. Chittenden** had obtained a judgment against Holden, which led to Craig (then the county sheriff) executing a levy on the property before the mortgage was duly stamped and recorded. The case revolved around the validity of the mortgage due to the omission of the stamp, with the defense arguing that its lack rendered the mortgage void against innocent third-party creditors.	The plaintiffs claimed ownership of the wagon and horses based on a chattel mortgage executed by Holden. They maintained that the mortgage, though initially unstamped due to inadvertence, was subsequently stamped and recorded correctly. Thus, they argued that it should be considered valid and enforceable against claims from the defendant (Craig).	The defendant argued that the chattel mortgage was invalid because it lacked the appropriate stamp at the time it was recorded, in accordance with the **Stamp Act of June 30, 1864**. He contended that this omission made the mortgage ineffective as evidence in court, thereby protecting his interests as a judgment creditor who had levied the properties prior to the mortgage's stamp being affixed.

In 1849, Adam Eidman passed away, leaving behind a widow and four minor children: Michael, Louisa, William, and Margaret Eidman. Following Adam's death, the widow remarried William Althoff and relocated to Minnesota. She died in August 1865. A lawsuit was initiated in 1855 by their stepfather for the partition of Adam's 43.5 acres of land in St. Clair County, Illinois, resulting in a court decree establishing that the children held an undivided five-sixths interest in the property. The land was sold, generating net proceeds of $624.86, which were owed to the children, then represented through their guardian, John Scheel. Scheel, however, did not file any reports or settlements related to these funds. After Scheel's death, an account was filed in 1870 against his estate for the due amount. In 1874, the St. Clair Circuit Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, the children of Adam Eidman, but the defendants, the executors of Scheel's estate, appealed the decision, questioning the legitimacy of the claimed debt, procedural errors in naming, and the applicability of the statute of limitations regarding guardianship claims.	The plaintiffs, heirs of Adam Eidman, argued that they were owed the proceeds from the sale of their father’s land, amounting to $624.86, plus compound interest. They contended that a mutual agreement established the amount owed following testimony at the probate court, leading to a favorable ruling and judgment against Scheel's estate. Their legal request was for the court to affirm the previous judgment against the deceased guardian’s estate in order to recover the funds due to them.	The defense, representing the estate of John Scheel, contended that the plaintiffs lacked standing due to naming irregularities in legal filings, specifically regarding one plaintiff's name and claims made by a deceased individual. Additionally, they argued insufficient proof that Scheel ever received the funds mentioned, along with claims that the statute of limitations barred the suit. They requested the court to reverse the previous judgment, claiming these alleged errors rendered the decision invalid.

The case, "City of Chicago v. William Kenney," took place on December 2, 1889, in Cook County, Illinois. It arose when the defendant, William Kenney, was arrested by police officer James Kelly for disorderly conduct, specifically for violating a city ordinance. The arrest occurred while Kenney was in the midst of committing the offense. After being charged, he was tried in a police court, where he pleaded not guilty. The justice of the peace found Kenney guilty and imposed a fine of $20, also ordering that he be committed to the house of correction if he failed to pay the fine. Kenney subsequently appealed the verdict to the Criminal Court, claiming that the record of his original trial did not include a written complaint, which he argued meant the justice lacked jurisdiction. The case highlighted issues surrounding the legal requirements for commencing suits under municipal ordinances and the jurisdiction of justices of the peace.	The City of Chicago, as the plaintiff, argued that the arrest and subsequent trial of Kenney were lawful and that the justice of the peace had jurisdiction to impose the penalty for his violation of city ordinances. They asserted that the absence of a written complaint did not invalidate the justice’s ability to hear the case, as the arrest had been conducted in view of the offense. The City sought to uphold the fine and the decision made in the police court.	William Kenney, the defendant, contended that the justice of the peace lacked jurisdiction to hear the case because there was no written complaint filed prior to the trial. He argued that the failure to meet this procedural requirement rendered the proceedings invalid, thus challenging the legitimacy of the fine imposed against him. Kenney maintained that without proper jurisdiction, the court should dismiss the case against him.

In 1861 and 1862, Eliza Nixon (defendant) employed John Halley (plaintiff) to perform labor and provide goods for a mill property in Iowa, which she claimed to own. The legal dispute arose when Halley sued Nixon for payment, leading to a trial in the Circuit Court of DeKalb County, Illinois. The court found in favor of Halley, prompting Nixon to appeal, arguing that she was not the actual owner of the property and thus should not be liable for the debt. Nixon was the wife of Daniel H. Ball, who had previously owned the property. Halley was initially hired by Daniel H. Ball to work at the mill, but after the arrival of Nixon, she assumed control, discharged other workers, and continued to acknowledge the debt owed to Halley. The case ultimately hinged on whether Nixon could deny her ownership and obligation to pay for the work performed under her direction.	John Halley asserted that he performed labor and provided materials for Eliza Nixon's mill property at her request and that she had acknowledged her obligation to pay him for these services. Halley argued that the employment agreement was valid under Iowa law, where a married woman could enter into contracts regarding her property, irrespective of sole ownership. He requested full compensation for the outstanding debts incurred from his labor.	Eliza Nixon contended that she could not be held accountable for the debt because she was not the legal owner of the mill property. She presented the argument that under the instructions she requested, if she did not hold title to the property, Halley could not recover payment for his services. Nixon maintained that her husband was the true owner and that any obligation to pay Halley should fall on him, not her.

The case of Nathan Barbero v. Joel Thurman, Administrator concerns a claim made against the estate of the deceased William Darnell. The claim was filed as a promissory note on March 16, 1863, at the Knox County Court, which was the designated date set by the administrator for adjusting claims. However, the case was continued multiple times over the years without any adjudication. In September 1866, the case was finally docketed again and continued by agreement until it was tried at the subsequent term, where the claim was allowed. An appeal was then filed to the circuit court, which ultimately disallowed the claim. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court to review the decision of the circuit court, focusing on whether the claim was barred by the statute of limitations due to its delayed adjudication after being dropped from the docket for over three years.	The plaintiff, Nathan Barbero, argued that his claim was validly filed within two years of the appointment of the administrator for estate claims. He contended that the claim was "exhibited" as per the statutory requirements by filing it on the designated date. Barbero maintained that the failure of the court clerk to keep the claim on the docket did not negate his compliance with the law, and that the administrator was adequately notified of the claim despite its delay in adjudication.	The defendant, represented by Joel Thurman, contended that Barbero's claim was barred by the two-year statute of limitations for presenting claims against estates. The argument emphasized that the claim was not adequately pursued over the course of its extended delay, as it was not maintained or adjudicated for over three years following its initial filing, and thus should not be allowed to proceed.

In April 1866, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the case of James H. Carr v. Simeon K. Miner, originating from the Jo Daviess Circuit Court where it was initiated at the August Term of 1863. The case involved Carr, who accused Miner of not properly handling funds amounting to $1,800 that were owed to him from a transaction involving Tisdal and Meyers. This dispute arose after a letter from Miner purportedly confirmed the receipt of the funds on Carr's behalf. The defendant, Miner, countered with several defenses, including a plea of set-off for services rendered and a previous judgment against Carr for $532.57. Following a jury trial, the court found in favor of Carr and awarded him $752.79. After a motion for a new trial was filed, the defendant agreed to a judgment increase to $996.75, which was ultimately upheld when Carr appealed the decision based on errors he believed were made during the trial process, particularly regarding the admission of evidence.	Carr claimed that Miner collected $1,800 on his behalf but failed to account properly for the total amount received, which he alleged included $1,100 in cash and a note for $700. He asserted that the defendant should be held liable for the full amount as a receipt-like confirmation in letter form indicated. Carr sought the recovery of these funds, asserting that Miner acted improperly, particularly in light of a previous judgment against him.	Miner contended that he had the right to set-off from the amount owed to Carr based on services he provided and a judgment he had secured against Carr. He maintained that the funds were either paid out or were being accounted for by him. Miner also argued that Carr had not sufficiently proven that the judgment he obtained was fraudulent and claimed that the admission of certain evidence was improper.

John McManus filed a petition in 1883 in Marshall County, Illinois, regarding a dispute with the commissioners of highways, led by Robert McDonough, concerning the establishment of a public highway through his property. The commissioners assessed damages to McManus for locating part of the road over his land. However, McManus sought to quash this decision, arguing that the commissioners failed to publicly announce their decision during the hearing as required by the Road and Bridge law. The case went through various court levels, with the Circuit Court affirming the commission's actions. McManus's appeal was subsequently taken to the Illinois Supreme Court, focusing on the procedural validity of the commissioners' actions and the jurisdiction of other involved officials, including a justice of the peace involved in assessing damages.	McManus claimed that the entire process involving the establishment of the highway was void because the commissioners did not publicly announce their decision at the hearing. He argued that this oversight violated the provisions of the Road and Bridge law, which aimed to ensure timely decisions to allow interested parties to appeal. McManus sought the court's intervention to quash the proceedings established by the highway commissioners, asserting that jurisdiction had not been validly established.	The defendants, represented by the highway commissioners and their legal counsel, contended that the written memorandum provided by the commissioners, which bore the date of the hearing, was sufficient to establish that they had publicly announced their decision. They argued that any procedural issues were merely technical and did not undermine the validity of the decision made. The defense also maintained that the justice of the peace had acquired jurisdiction effectively through McManus's appearance in court, waiving any potential defects in the summons.

In 1844, in Adams County, Illinois, George Frazier, the School Commissioner, was sued by the County Commissioners of Adams County for breaches of an official bond worth $12,000. The bond was conditioned on Frazier's faithful discharge of his duties. The breaches alleged included Frazier’s failure to ensure that two purchasers, Taylor and Kemp, paid for school land they bought at auction. The complainants contended that Frazier neglected to sue these purchasers for the difference when he later sold the land for a lower price. Additionally, Frazier allegedly failed to remit certain funds to the township treasurer. The matter was initially tried in the Adams Circuit Court, resulting in a jury verdict favoring the plaintiffs, assessing damages at $575.72. Upon the defendants' motion for a new trial based on various errors including the form of the jury's verdict and evidentiary issues, the court denied this motion and upheld the damages awarded.	The plaintiffs argued that Frazier breached his official bond by failing to ensure payment for school land that had been sold. Specifically, they claimed he sold the same land to another party at a reduced price and did not take legal action against the initial purchasers for the lost difference. They also asserted that Frazier failed to pay over certain funds that he held, which were owed to the township treasurer.	The defendants presented several defenses, including claims that Frazier had paid over the owed moneys, that the township treasurer had not executed a proper bond, and that there was an overall performance of duties by Frazier. They challenged the admissibility of evidence related to the bond and the jury’s ability to assess damages without explicitly defining a debt owed. They also sought to strike testimony from a co-defendant.

The case "Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Co. v. Francis H. Cobb" took place in March 1872, with subsequent actions extending to 1873 and culminating in a court decision in June 1876 at the Illinois Supreme Court. The primary individuals involved were Francis H. Cobb, the plaintiff, and The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Company, the defendant. In the initial action, Cobb sued the Railroad for trespassing on his property, where they laid down a railway track and removed soil, resulting in a judgment of $600 in favor of Cobb. Following this, a second action was filed on March 6, 1873, to recover damages for continued trespass after high waters had affected the land, leading Cobb to re-enter and repair his fence. The Railroad persisted in its trespass by breaking down Cobb's fence and using the land again, prompting Cobb to file a third trespass action in August 1873, which was consolidated with the second action. The trial in February 1875 resulted in a jury award of $5,000 to Cobb. The disputes revolved around property possession and the nature of legal rights connected to prior occupancy, as both parties lacked formal paper titles to the land.	Francis H. Cobb claimed that The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Company trespassed on his property both by laying down a railway track and by removing soil and sand. He sought to recover damages for these actions across multiple lawsuits, arguing that he had peaceably possessed the land since at least 1867. His legal request included compensation for damages incurred from the railroad's continued trespasses after he had re-entered the land to assert his ownership and maintain his property.	The Illinois and St. Louis Railroad and Coal Company argued that their possession of the land predating Cobb's claims should invalidate his right to recover damages. They contended that Cobb's re-entries onto the property were illegal and should be treated as forcible, therefore questioning the legality of his claims. The company sought a dismissal of Cobb's claims and argued that previous judgments favoring Cobb were based on incorrect interpretations of possession law.

The case "The Teutonia Life Insurance Co. of Chicago v. Anna Beck" was decided in September 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a life insurance policy dated October 1869, applied for by Jacob Beck, intended to provide benefits to his wife, Anna Beck, in the event of his death. The crux of the case centered on a clause stating that the policy would be null and void if any statements in the application were found to be untrue. The assertion at issue was whether Jacob Beck had accurately disclosed his health history, particularly regarding a past illness characterized as delirium tremens. Testimony revealed a conflict of evidence: while a company physician asserted that Jacob had suffered from the condition prior to obtaining the policy, Anna Beck argued, supported by multiple witnesses, that her husband did not drink heavily and had not been seriously ill. The trial court, upon observing the witnesses and assessing credibility, found in favor of Anna Beck.	Anna Beck, the plaintiff, claimed that the Teutonia Life Insurance Company wrongfully denied the benefits due under her late husband’s life insurance policy. She argued that the company had no evidence to suggest that Jacob Beck's application was false, particularly regarding his health statements. She maintained that her husband had not experienced serious illnesses that would invalidate the policy and sought the full amount of the policy, totaling $1,123.48, along with interest.	The primary defense presented by the Teutonia Life Insurance Company revolved around the assertion that Jacob Beck had provided false information in his insurance application, specifically concerning his health history. The company claimed he had previously suffered from delirium tremens, asserting that this omission rendered the policy null and void under the terms of the contract. Their request was for the court to uphold the denial of the insurance claim based on this alleged misrepresentation.

In January 1866, The St. Louis, Alton and Terre Haute Railroad Company was involved in a legal dispute with James Montgomery. The case was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court after Montgomery, the plaintiff, sought damages for hay that was burned while in the custody of the railroad. The hay had been placed on platform cars on a Friday. On Saturday morning, when the railroad was prepared to transport the hay, Montgomery requested that it not be taken until he had spoken with Mr. Ketchum, the buyer. The next day, sparks from a passing locomotive ignited the hay, resulting in significant damage. Montgomery argued the railroad was at fault for the loss. The court's analysis focused on whether the railroad's actions constituted negligence, particularly since the hay was left exposed at the plaintiff’s request, which led to the decision to appeal.	The plaintiff, James Montgomery, claimed that The St. Louis, Alton and Terre Haute Railroad Company was negligent for allowing his hay to remain on the platform cars where it was exposed to sparks from a passing train, leading to its destruction. He sought compensation for the value of the hay consumed in the fire and argued that the railroad company failed to exercise the required care to prevent the fire.	The railroad company contended that they were not negligent as their duty as a common carrier did not apply once Montgomery requested that the delivery be stalled. They argued that their liability at that point was akin to that of a warehouseman, meaning they were required only to exercise reasonable care, which they maintained by taking steps to prevent fire escapes. The railroad asserted that Montgomery's request to delay transport of the hay had put it in a vulnerable position, and they had complied with his wishes without additional negligence.

Sarah C. Newman filed for divorce from her husband, Augustus Newman, on December 17, 1870, in Cook County, Illinois. She alleged that he had willfully deserted her and had been absent for two years. The defendant, Augustus, denied these claims and countered with a cross-bill, asserting that it was Sarah who had deserted him. Initially, the court ordered Augustus to pay alimony of $25 per month and $50 in solicitors' fees to Sarah's attorneys. The case went to trial on April 3, 1872, and the jury ruled in favor of Augustus on both the divorce claims and his cross-bill. Following the trial, the court granted Augustus a divorce and dismissed Sarah's bill. Additionally, it later ordered Augustus to pay $150 to Sarah's solicitors for their services, a decision which prompted the appeal from Augustus. The court reviewed established legal principles concerning alimony and solicitor's fees during divorce proceedings, particularly regarding responsibilities when the wife is without means and the effects after a defeat in court.	Sarah C. Newman claimed that Augustus had willfully deserted her for two years, which provided grounds for her request for a divorce. She sought alimony during the proceedings and payment of her solicitors' fees to support her case.	Augustus Newman refuted Sarah's allegations by asserting that she was the one who deserted him. He counterclaimed for a divorce based on her alleged desertion. He argued that, since the jury found in his favor, ordering him to pay Sarah’s solicitors’ fees was unwarranted and against established legal precedent.

In the case of Agnes Walters et al. v. The Town of Lake, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the claim arose from a special assessment for the improvement of Winter Street, specifically from 43rd Street to 47th Street. The Illinois Supreme Court dealt with the matter in a decision dated May 16, 1889. The assessment was initiated following a publication notice by commissioners appointed by the county court, which was published five successive days, starting from August 30, 1888. However, the appellants, represented by H. T. & L. Helm, argued that the published notice was defective because it stated that the assessment roll had been returned to the court before it actually was, thus questioning the legal adequacy of the notice. Nonetheless, the appellants appeared before the County Court on September 11, 1888, where they raised objections to the confirmation of the assessment roll, effectively waiving any defects in the notice. The jury was tasked with determining whether the assessed property values were equivalent to the benefits received, amid conflicting testimonies about the assessments' fairness. Ultimately, the court examined multiple objections, including the validity of assessments against the Town of Lake and the reasoning behind the apportionments made by the assessment commissioners.	The plaintiffs contended that the notice regarding the special assessment was fundamentally flawed, which they argued should invalidate the assessment process. They claimed that the absence of personal appearances by the affected parties and the timing of the publication violated established statutory requirements. The plaintiffs sought to have the assessment roll overturned due to these purported defects and requested reconsideration of the assessment's fairness regarding the benefits received from the property improvements.	The Town of Lake, represented by Burke, Hollett & Tinsman, defended the validity of the assessment and the adequacy of the notice, asserting that the appellants waived their rights to challenge any defects in the notice by participating in the hearing and filing objections in the County Court. They maintained that the assessment roll constituted competent evidence and that the jury's instructions appropriately focused the inquiry on whether the assessments matched the benefits provided to the property owners. The defense argued that the commissioners' findings and actions regarding public and property benefits were conclusive and that the appellants failed to prove their properties were over-assessed relative to their benefits.

In September 1871, the case of Henry Truitt v. George O. Griffin was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from the Peoria circuit court. The dispute arose when Henry Truitt, as a garnishee, was served a writ of attachment concerning a debt owed by Cincinnatus Bradley. The sheriff served the writ on Truitt and other parties, indicating that they might hold assets belonging to Bradley. Truitt denied liability but acknowledged holding U.S. government bonds in trust for Bradley and his family. He had previously received property from Bradley in a trust intended to cover legal expenses related to criminal charges Bradley faced in Indiana. Amid various legal arguments, including a defense of the statute of frauds and perjuries, a trial was held where the court found in favor of the plaintiff, resulting in a judgment against Truitt for $648.89. The case raised issues about the sufficiency of service of the writ and the validity of the garnishee's defense.	The plaintiff, George O. Griffin, claimed that Truitt, as a garnishee, was liable for the debt of Bradley, expressly relying on the statute of frauds to challenge Truitt’s assertions regarding the trust. The plaintiff argued that Truitt's defenses regarding the trust and equitable interests were invalid and that he was obligated to satisfy the debt owed, given that the garnishee had funds derived from property that should rightfully be applied to cover the debt.	Truitt countered by asserting that he was not liable as a garnishee, referencing that he held the funds in a valid trust for Bradley primarily to cover legal defense costs. He argued that the act of creating this trust was legitimate and made in good faith before any liens were attached. Truitt maintained that the service by the sheriff was insufficient to confer jurisdiction over garnishees, arguing that no property was levied to satisfy the writ at the time.

In May 1849, Samuel Gaty, William Me Cune, and Robert Glasby filed a bill to enforce a mechanics’ lien against Thomas J. Casey and others in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from a transaction on July 24, 1848, in which Gaty and his associates sold two large steam-boilers and gauge cocks to Casey for $978.05, intended for repairing machinery at a mill owned by Casey in Adams County, Illinois. However, prior to the sale, the mill property had been encumbered by substantial deeds of trust. After a fire in January 1850 destroyed the mill, the salvaged boilers were sold by Kennedy & Foster for $625, with a portion retained to await the outcome of this lawsuit. The complainants argued that they were entitled to a lien on the boilers as they were used in the mill. The defendants contended that previous encumbrances on the property took precedence over the plaintiffs' claims, leading to ongoing disputes over the rightful ownership and money from the sale of the damaged materials.	The plaintiffs claimed entitlement to a mechanics' lien on the two steam-boilers and gauge cocks they sold to Casey. They argued that the lien was valid since the materials were affixed to the mill, despite the property being encumbered by prior deeds of trust. They sought a decree that the proceeds from the sale of the salvaged materials be paid to them, asserting that their lien should take priority over the deeds of trust, given that these incumbrances did not apply to the materials furnished for the mill's repair.	The defendants, led by Bushnell and Kennedy & Foster, contended that the prior deeds of trust retained paramount importance and that their claims exceeded the value of the property, including the boilers. They insisted that because the contract for sale was enacted outside Illinois, the lien could not apply, reinforcing their assertion that the previous encumbrances took precedence over any lien claimed by the plaintiffs.

The case, "The People ex rel. James T. Ely et al. v. Julian S. Rumsey," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1872. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, where James T. Ely and other relators were appointed as official stenographic reporters under an act from March 6, 1867. This act allowed for the appointment of reporters in the courts of Cook County. However, the services rendered by these reporters occurred after the adoption of the 1870 Illinois Constitution. The crux of the case centered on whether the act that appointed the reporters was abrogated by the new constitution. The relators argued that they were entitled to compensation for their work, while the defendant, Julian S. Rumsey, Cook County's treasurer, contended that the appointment had ceased due to the constitutional changes, which sought to ensure uniformity in the courts across the state. The court had to examine the constitutional provisions and their implications on the previously established appointive authority under the act.	The plaintiffs, represented by James T. Ely and others, claimed that they were entitled to be compensated for their services as official reporters despite the changes introduced by the 1870 Illinois Constitution. They argued that section six of the schedule permitted them to continue their duties until removed according to the law under which they were appointed. The relators contended that the constitutional provisions did not retroactively invalidate their appointment, and they sought a writ of mandamus to compel the treasurer to issue payment for their rendered services.	The defendant, Julian S. Rumsey, countered the claims by asserting that the act under which the relators were appointed was a special local law and was therefore abrogated by the 1870 Constitution, which aimed to eliminate such acts in favor of uniform laws governing courts. Rumsey argued that the constitutional provisions regarding uniformity in court operations rendered the relators' appointments invalid. Thus, he contested the validity of their claims for compensation and sought to avoid any obligation to pay for services rendered beyond the scope of law.

In 1872, in Livingston County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Lewis T. Larned and James Carpenter. Carpenter, who was a non-resident, had previously obtained a judgment for $146.25 against Lighty & Graybill in 1862, but this amount had remained unpaid. Graybill, one of the defendants, acted as a surety on the note that led to Carpenter's judgment. Esty, acting as Carpenter’s agent, facilitated the recovery of this judgment. In 1865, Lighty sold land and received a $1,000 note, which he turned over to Larned after being indebted to him for $400 to $500. The agreement allowed Larned to keep part of the proceeds for his payment, with the balance to be held for Lighty's use. Subsequently, Graybill proposed to Esty that if Carpenter would accept $80 towards the judgment, it could be satisfied, to which Esty and Carpenter agreed. Esty advanced the $80 to Carpenter out of his own funds and, upon Larned's promise to reimburse him, obtained a discharge of the judgment, which Carpenter sent to Esty. However, Larned later refused to pay, claiming that Esty owed him for goods sold. The case was brought at the Livingston County Court in Carpenter’s name for Esty’s use, leading Larned to appeal owing to the alleged misnaming of parties in the suit.	The plaintiff, James Carpenter (for the use of Esty), claimed that Larned had a legal obligation to pay the $80 that had been promised to Esty as part of the agreement to satisfy Carpenter's judgment. Esty maintained that he had advanced the money relying solely on Larned's commitment to repay this amount.	The defense posited that the suit was improperly brought in Carpenter’s name, arguing that the legal interest in the contract belonged to Esty rather than Carpenter. The defendant contended that the action was flawed due to this misnaming and thus could not be sustained under the law.

In 1885, in Williamson County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose involving property rights between the plaintiff, Smart, the wife of William Smart, and the defendant, Coke. The case originally began when a constable, T.E. Cagle, executed a levy on various items, including a tramway engine, a tramway lumber car, and a heading and shingle mill, which were claimed to be the property of William Smart, as part of a debt owed to the defendant, David Coke. Following the levy, Smart, contesting the ownership of the property seized, submitted a written notice asserting her claim. This dispute over ownership was initially heard by a justice of the peace, but Smart was unsuccessful and subsequently appealed the judgment to the Circuit Court. The appeal ultimately led to the Illinois Appellate Court, which found errors in the instruction provided during the trial that resulted in a verdict that was contrary to the evidence presented by Smart regarding her ownership of the property.	Smart contended that she was the rightful owner of the property seized, specifically the tramway lumber car and the heading and shingle mill. Her primary argument was that the evidence clearly supported her ownership claims, and she sought to overturn the previous judgments against her, thereby reclaiming her property that was wrongfully levied.	Coke, as the defendant, maintained that the property in question belonged to William Smart and was thus subject to seizure to satisfy his debt. Their position relied on the legality of the levy executed by the constable as part of the execution process, arguing for the upholding of the previous judgments which favored the enforcement of the debt collection.

The case "The People ex rel. Julius S. Grinnell, State's Attorney, v. Francis A. Hoffman et al." originated from Cook County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on March 27, 1886. The central figures were Julius S. Grinnell, the State's Attorney, and defendants Francis A. Hoffman Jr., Samuel B. Raymond, and Daniel Corkery. The situation arose when these individuals claimed to have usurped the role of election commissioners in Chicago and the town of Lake by asserting they were operating under a new Election law that had been adopted via a local vote. Grinnell contended that this law was unconstitutional as it purportedly imposed a local or special law for the management of elections contrary to the Illinois constitution, which prohibits such laws. The defendants had already begun preparing for upcoming elections, organizing precincts, and conducting registrations based on this law. The court was tasked with determining the legitimacy of this newly adopted law and whether the defendants had the authority to act as election commissioners under it.	The plaintiff, represented by State's Attorney Julius S. Grinnell, argued that the Election law of 1885 was unconstitutional because it was a local or special law, thus violating section 22 of article 4 of the Illinois Constitution. Grinnell asserted that this law allowed for different rules in different localities, undermining the general principle that laws governing elections should be uniform across the state. He sought to oust the defendants from their claimed positions as election commissioners and prevent them from conducting elections based on this purportedly invalid law.	The defendants, including Hoffman, Raymond, and Corkery, contended that they were validly appointed under the Election law of 1885, which had been approved by the voters in Chicago and the town of Lake. They asserted that the law was constitutional because it was a general law that could be adopted by localities and that the appointment and role of election commissioners were appropriately vested in the county court. Furthermore, they claimed that their actions were lawful and necessary for the proper conduct of elections in the affected areas.

Jonathan Depuy v. Daniel J. Schuyler is a legal case that originated in 1867 in Lee County, Illinois. The case involves Jonathan Depuy (the plaintiff) who filed an action in assumpsit against Daniel J. Schuyler (the defendant) concerning a negotiable promissory note originally made payable to the Union Dispatch company and subsequently endorsed to Depuy. The case began in front of a justice of the peace, where judgment favored Schuyler. However, Depuy appealed the decision to the Circuit Court of Lee County, where a jury trial led to a verdict in favor of Depuy. Schuyler then escalated the matter to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking to overturn the Circuit Court's ruling. The case centered around the validity of the endorsement of the note and the legal presumptions regarding negotiable instruments in the absence of evidence to the contrary.	The plaintiff, Jonathan Depuy, argued that as the indorsee of the promissory note, he was presumed to have acquired it in good faith, for value, and before maturity. He claimed that Schuyler failed to provide any substantial evidence showing that the note was fraudulent or that it was executed without consideration. Depuy requested the court to affirm the judgment of the Circuit Court, which ruled in his favor.	The defendant, Daniel J. Schuyler, contended that the endorsement of the note was made under circumstances that were fraudulent, thus questioning the fairness of the transaction. He argued that there was a lack of consideration for the note and that the conditions under which it was executed should nullify the presumptions in favor of its validity. Schuyler sought to overturn the Circuit Court's ruling by demonstrating that Depuy's claims had no merit.

Bradley Rust filed an action in debt against Frothingham and Fort following a judgment obtained in New York. This suit was initiated in the Monroe Circuit Court. The case was built upon a prior legal ruling, and the defendant, Rust, contested the allegations by demurring to the declaration. The circuit court overruled his demurrer, leading to further legal proceedings where Rust contested the validity of the service of process and the legitimacy of an attorney's appearance on his behalf in New York, claiming he did not receive due process. While the issues of nul tiel record and a plea of payment were debated, the circuit court ultimately found for Frothingham and Fort, awarding them the amount claimed, plus damages. Rust appealed, claiming various errors in the circuit court's decisions regarding the demurrer, validity of the pleas, and assessment of damages without jury intervention.	The plaintiff, Frothingham and Fort, claimed that a valid judgment had been rendered in New York against Bradley Rust, which he was obliged to pay. They argued that their declaration was sufficient to establish their case and that the demurrer by Rust should have been overruled. They sought to confirm the validity of the New York judgment and recover the debt amounting to $254.60 along with damages of $100, asserting that the processes followed were legal and appropriate.	Bradley Rust contended that the trial court erred in ruling against his demurrer and in sustaining the plea of nul tiel record, arguing that he was never served with process in New York and that the attorney's appearance was unauthorized. He also claimed a variance existed between the debt stated in the declaration and in the writ, and criticized the court's judgment for assessing damages without a jury trial, asserting that the damages could not be calculated without additional evidence.

Bernhard Smyth, Felix E. O’Rourke, and William A. Herring, plaintiffs residing in New York, engaged attorneys Andrew Harvie and Murray F. Tuley, who were partners in law practice in Chicago, to collect a debt from Charles McDonnell. They successfully obtained a judgment and, through a levy on McDonnell's real estate, purchased it for $400, for which a certificate of purchase was issued in the plaintiffs’ names. McDonnell later redeemed the property, paying $440 to the sheriff. Defendant Harvie collected this redemption money, issuing a receipt in the firm's name; however, he did not pay the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs subsequently sought to recover this amount, along with an additional sum of $128.54 which had also been collected without being remitted to them. The defense raised by Tuley was based on the dissolution of the partnership before the collection of the redemption money, arguing that he was not responsible for funds collected after the dissolution. The superior court ruled in favor of the defendants for part of the claim, which led the plaintiffs to appeal.	The plaintiffs asserted that the attorneys failed to remit the funds they collected on their behalf, claiming a total of $568.54. They contended that the retainer was a joint and continuing contract, and that both attorneys were responsible for the collected funds, regardless of the partnership dissolution. They argued that the attorneys were obligated to ensure the money collected after the judgment was paid to them.	The defendants, particularly Tuley, claimed that he was not liable for the redemption funds collected by Harvie because the partnership was dissolved prior to that collection. Tuley maintained that any obligations from the partnership ceased with the dissolution, and thus he should not be held accountable for the actions of Harvie post-dissolution. They requested the court's ruling to affirm that Tuley was not liable for the funds in question.

The case of "The City of Elgin v. Francis McCallum" took place in 1885 in Elgin, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Francis McCallum, the plaintiff, who owned a dwelling and blacksmith's shop on Grove Avenue, and the City of Elgin, the defendant. The issue arose when the City of Elgin raised the grade of the sidewalk in front of McCallum's property, elevating it approximately eighteen inches above the old grade. This alteration significantly interfered with McCallum’s ability to access his premises, as it resulted in the sidewalk reaching half the height of his picket fence. Consequently, McCallum was compelled to remove his gate and construct new steps to access his property. He claimed that the changes required him to build inclines for easy access to both the sidewalk and his shop. McCallum sought $600 in damages, asserting that the raising of the sidewalk necessitated expensive adjustments to his property. Witnesses for McCallum supported his claims, whereas the City’s witnesses argued that the property benefited from the sidewalk elevation, estimating its value increase to be around $2,000. The court was tasked with assessing whether McCallum was entitled to recover damages after considering the special benefits conferred by the city’s improvement.	The plaintiff, Francis McCallum, argued that the City of Elgin's action in raising the sidewalk grade caused significant damage to his property. He requested $600 in damages to cover the costs of modifying his dwelling and shop to accommodate the new sidewalk height, as well as compensation for loss of time and other inconveniences. His claim rested on the assertion that the alterations profoundly impacted his ingress and egress, negatively affecting both residential and operational access to his property.	The City of Elgin defended itself by arguing that the elevation of the sidewalk provided special benefits to McCallum's property that should offset any alleged damages. The City’s witnesses contended that the overall value of McCallum's property had actually increased due to the sidewalk improvements. The City asserted that the legal framework required that such benefits be considered when evaluating claims for damages arising from changes in municipal infrastructure.

The case 'Greenup Wilson et al., executors of Thomas Wilson, deceased, plaintiffs in error, v. Hiram Van Winkle, defendant in error' was initiated in June 1842 in Edgar County, Illinois. Hiram Van Winkle filed a claim against the executors of the deceased Thomas Wilson for $1,000, representing a promissory note made by George Eller to Wilson, which was later assigned to Van Winkle. A jury initially ruled in favor of Van Winkle, awarding him $873.45. The executors appealed this decision to the Circuit Court, where the judgment was increased to $1,015.15 due to interest accrued. Subsequent legal proceedings revealed that Van Winkle had tried numerous times to collect the amount owed after the note was invalidated by a chancery court decision due to Wilson's lack of title to the corresponding land involved in the original contract. The executors argued against the judgment based on the absence of the note and the statute of limitations, but their defenses were ultimately dismissed, leading to a writ of error that brought the case to the Supreme Court of Illinois.	Hiram Van Winkle, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to recover the money he had paid for the assignment of the promissory note after the previous owner, Thomas Wilson, failed to uphold his end of the contract. He sought recovery of the amounts due, including interest, maintaining that the executors of Wilson's estate should refund the paid amount with appropriate legal interest due to the long delays caused by the estate's legal challenges.	The executors of Thomas Wilson asserted that the court erred in rendering judgment against them, particularly due to the absence of the actual promissory note during the trial, arguing that without this primary evidence, the claim could not be substantiated. They also contended that the claim was barred by the statute of limitations, an argument that they did not raise earlier in the lower court proceedings.

Marshall Field et al. v. Lavina A. Herrick et al. is a case that arose in Chicago, Illinois, where the plaintiff, Lavina A. Herrick, entered into a lease agreement with the defendants, Marshall Field and Leiter, on February 2, 1878. This agreement allowed the defendants to rent a store located on Wabash Avenue for a term of two years, starting on March 1, 1878, with a rent of $6,500 to be paid in monthly installments. However, at the beginning of their lease, the defendants were unable to take possession of the premises due to the prior tenant, John Cox, still occupying the space. Cox's previous agreement with the plaintiffs had extended his tenancy beyond the original expiration date, and he remained in possession without any notice of termination. The defendants claimed that because they were kept out of possession by the previous tenant, they should not be liable for rent. The court case eventually involved questions regarding the obligations of landlords to ensure possession and how these obligations affect rent agreements.	The plaintiffs’ main argument revolved around the enforcement of the lease agreement and their right to collect rent from the defendants. They asserted that the defendants had a contractual obligation to pay rent despite being unable to access the property initially. The plaintiffs sought damages totaling $3,236.68, arguing that the defendants were liable for rent under the terms of their lease, regardless of Cox's occupation of the premises.	In response, the defendants claimed that they were wrongfully prevented from taking possession of the leased premises by the previous tenant, Cox. They argued that since they were kept out of possession due to the plaintiffs' failure to ensure a lawful eviction of the prior tenant, this constituted a breach of the lease agreement, thereby absolving them of their obligation to pay rent. Their defense included several special pleas emphasizing that the ability to take possession was a condition precedent for any claim of rent.

In June 1868, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of George B. Morrison et al. v. John W. Norman et al., which originated from a circuit court decision in Clinton County, Illinois. The case was an action of ejectment where the plaintiffs, George B. Morrison and others, contested their right to the title of a property against the defendants, John W. Norman and others. The plaintiffs argued that they proved a title under the patentee, while the defendants claimed their position based on color of title and payment of taxes over a period of seven years. The circuit court initially favored the defendants' claims except against certain plaintiffs who were within the saving clause due to their coverture (marital status). The court ruling was primarily based on the validity of a tax deed the defendants presented as color of title.
