The case references various precedents regarding the validity of tax deeds and the obligation to provide notice of tax sales, concluding that the deed was regular on its face and presumed to convey good faith until proven otherwise.	The plaintiffs contended that the defendants failed to establish good faith in their claim of color of title because they did not provide evidence proving that required notices of the tax sale were given. They argued that the defendants' reliance on a tax deed was invalid since it lacked the necessary notifications mandated by the constitution before the deed could confer any title.	The defendants argued that the tax deed they presented sufficed as color of title, claiming that it was regularly executed and presumed to convey title in good faith. They maintained that the objections raised regarding the notice of the tax sale did not apply, as the deed was submitted merely to support their claim of color of title, not as a paramount title. The defendants further contended that even if there were flaws, they were not legally obligated to indicate proof of notice since the deed was not being presented as paramount title.

The case of The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company v. Hannah Olson took place in Galesburg, Illinois, with the incident occurring on February 19, 1881. The plaintiff, Hannah Olson, brought the case on behalf of her deceased husband, Neis Olson, who had died due to injuries sustained while working in the railroad yard. Neis was employed at the railroad and was tasked with removing ashes and cinders from the roundhouses. During his final moments at work, he was struck and killed by a tender (part of a locomotive) that was backing down the track after the whistle blew for the end of the shift. Evidence showed that the railroad had cleared the track but had left the surrounding areas filled with snow. Neis Olson attempted to leave by walking on the track, which was known for frequent engine movement. The situation was complicated by both the train's lack of warning (no bell was rung) and Olson's decision to walk along a dangerous route without adequate caution. Despite the presence of other workers, including one who passed by him shortly before the incident, Olson's decision led to his tragic death.	The plaintiff claimed that the railroad company acted negligently by not clearing the snow between the roundhouse and the machine shop, which forced her husband to walk on the track, the only passable route. She charged that while he was walking on the track lawfully, the defendant's engineer drove the locomotive recklessly, failing to provide warnings, which caused the accident that led to his death. The plaintiff sought damages amounting to $3,000 for the wrongful death of her husband due to the alleged negligence of the railroad.	The railroad company denied the allegations, claiming that they took reasonable steps to clear the snow and that their engineer was experienced and acted prudently. They argued that the plaintiff's husband was also negligent for walking on the railroad track, a known hazard for workers, and that his actions significantly contributed to the incident. The defense pointed out that other employees were able to navigate the area without incident, thus arguing that the railroad had complied with safety standards, and sought to have the court overturn the jury's verdict favoring the plaintiff.

In the case of John Karnes v. Mahlon B. Lloyd et al., which took place in Illinois around September 1869, the dispute arose from issues regarding property redemption and a confession of judgment. The parties involved included John Karnes as the appellant and Mahlon B. Lloyd, along with Davenport, as appellees. The core of the case hinged on a prior judgment which allowed Lloyd to redeem property from Karnes. After a previous ruling in an earlier case, Lloyd and Davenport allegedly filed for a judgment that enabled Lloyd to redeem the property, which Karnes claimed to have previously purchased. Karnes accused them of committing fraud concerning the validity of the judgment under which the redemption was claimed. Following an examination of the circumstances and a motion by Karnes to file an amended bill alleging fraud, the Circuit Court allowed further inquiry into the redemption process. However, it was concluded that there was no evidence of fraud, and therefore, the redemption was upheld as valid.	John Karnes, the plaintiff, asserted that the judgment confessing fraud by Davenport to enable Lloyd to redeem his land was fraudulent. He argued that the redemption was invalid due to alleged dishonesty and irregularities in the judgment process, including a claim that the total sum paid for redemption was insufficient. He sought the court to reverse the previous decree, claiming that he had rightful ownership of the property which was being unjustly claimed by Lloyd.	Mahlon B. Lloyd and Davenport, the defendants, denied the allegations of fraud, asserting that the confession of judgment was made in good faith and supported by a valid consideration. They argued that Lloyd's right to redeem the property was lawful and that Karnes's claims regarding the redemption amount were raised too late, as he had accepted the payment tendered to him. Their position was that the redemption was regular and valid, and they sought affirmation of their right to the property.

In 1882, Andrew J. Mann and O. M. Edwards formed a partnership owning mill property in Marion, Illinois, with Edwards holding two-thirds and Mann one-third of the interest. After C. M. Edwards, the husband of Judah E. Edwards, passed away, Mann sold his interest in the mill to Judah E. Edwards, with payment to come from several debts owed by their partnership. A dispute arose over a debt not originally included in the contract, and it was unclear if Judah E. Edwards had agreed to its inclusion. Mann subsequently sued Judah E. Edwards based on the contract signed between them, which was also signed by John D. Edwards. Judah E. Edwards, however, claimed that the contract was not valid (plea of non est factum) and that a prior judgment against both Edwards had resolved the same issue, precluding this lawsuit based on the principle of former recovery. This case escalated to the Illinois Appellate Court after Mann sought a reevaluation of the lower court’s ruling in favor of the defendants.	Andrew J. Mann, the plaintiff, contended that Judah E. Edwards was liable for the payment due under the contract pertaining to the mill property. Mann sought to enforce the contract despite the conflicting interpretations regarding the debt inclusion, aiming to recover the amount owed based on the terms agreed upon with Judah E. Edwards and John D. Edwards.	Judah E. Edwards, the defendant, argued that he should not be held liable under the contract due to the plea of non est factum, asserting that the contract was invalid. Furthermore, he claimed that a previous judgment against both him and John D. Edwards on the same matter served as a legal bar to Mann's current claims, thereby precluding him from seeking recovery based on the same subject matter.

In the case of John Schroeder v. Thomas Walsh, taking place in Grundy County, Illinois, the events stem from a series of transactions involving the plaintiff, John Schroeder, who was the sheriff, and the goods owned by Ward & Pierce. On September 26, 1878, a writ of attachment was issued by Wm. Young & Co. against Ward & Pierce, leading to the levying of goods valued at approximately $2,200. The defendant, Thomas Walsh, claimed ownership of these goods through a sale made by Ward & Pierce on September 17, 1878, asserting that the transaction was legitimate. The core issue revolved around the legitimacy of this sale, with the plaintiff contending that it was fraudulent and designed to hinder and delay creditors. The trial jury eventually ruled in favor of the defendant, affirming the sale as legitimate and bona fide, leading to an appeal from the plaintiff concerning perceived legal errors in the trial court's guidance to the jury.	The plaintiff, John Schroeder, argued that the sale of goods from Ward & Pierce to Thomas Walsh was fraudulent and intended to obstruct creditors. He requested that the court reverse the findings of the initial trial and rule that the sale was invalid, asserting that the evidence demonstrated that the goods should properly be subject to his attachment as sheriff acting on behalf of Wm. Young & Co.	The defendant, Thomas Walsh, contended that the sale was legitimate, bona fide, and conducted in good faith for valuable consideration. He asserted that the transfer of goods occurred prior to the attachment and that the delivery of the goods was valid. He maintained that the plaintiff failed to deliver sufficient evidence of fraud, and requested that the court uphold the jury's verdict that found in his favor, thus confirming the validity of his ownership of the goods.

On December 1, 1863, William J. Murphy purchased a tract of land from Moore for $134.40, paying part in cash and agreeing to pay the remainder via seven promissory notes, with the last note maturing in 1870. Less than four months later, on March 26, 1864, Murphy sold the land to Daniel G. Staley, for a higher price and with similar payment terms. An important aspect of both contracts was that they allowed for forfeiture due to non-payment after specified periods. Staley took possession of the land, made improvements, paid taxes, and met the payment due in December 1864. However, he failed to pay the December 1865 installment on time but attempted to pay in January 1866. Murphy refused the payment, claiming that the contract was forfeited due to Staley's late payment. Consequently, Murphy initiated an ejectment action to reclaim the land, while Staley filed a complaint to prevent the eviction, wishing to make good on his payment and obtain a deed. The circuit court ruled in Murphy's favor regarding the ejectment action, while also dismissing Staley's suit.	Staley’s claims centered on challenging Murphy's right to cancel the contract without first returning the purchase money and the unpaid notes. Staley argued that Murphy’s act of bringing an action of ejectment was invalid because he had failed to fulfill the necessary legal requirements to rescind the contract. Specifically, Staley contended that, according to customary legal rules, the vendor (Murphy) must return the purchase price and any unpaid notes before pursuing rescission. He sought to maintain possession of the property and requested a decree that would secure his interest in the land.	Murphy's main defenses were grounded in the assertion that the contract allowed him to declare forfeiture upon late payment, which Staley failed to meet. He argued that he was legally entitled to reclaim the land through ejectment given Staley's default. Murphy pointed out that the contractual agreements did contain forfeiture clauses and that, as per the agreements, he was not required to return the already paid purchase money before initiating ejectment proceedings.

Uri Osgood v. Delos W. McConnell is a legal case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1863. The case originated in Joliet, Illinois, and centers around a monetary transaction that took place on May 8, 1861. Delos W. McConnell deposited $388 in current bank notes with Uri Osgood’s exchange collection office, with the agreement to pay back this same amount with a 10% interest three months later. A jury trial ensued, wherein the jury found in favor of McConnell, awarding him $450. Osgood appealed the decision, questioning whether he had the right to present extraneous evidence to demonstrate that the "current bank bills" mentioned in their agreement were not equivalent to coin value. Ultimately, the court had to examine the definitions and interpretations of "current bank bills" and the nature of the agreement made between the parties to determine the rightful outcome of the case.	The plaintiff, Delos W. McConnell, argued that he was entitled to payment based on the agreement made with Osgood to return the deposited amount of $388 in "current bank notes" with 10% interest after three months. McConnell maintained that the payment should be made in the same form of currency as received and that there should not be any alteration in the terms of their agreement based on external interpretations of the value of currency.	The defendant, Uri Osgood, contended that the trial lacked legal authority because the mode of trial was not agreed upon when the issues were formed during a vacation term. Osgood argued that the jury's verdict was improperly altered by the court from its original form and asserted that the term "current bank bills" referred specifically to depreciated bills and should not equate to coin value. He maintained that the court erred in permitting the trial to proceed without an agreed method between the parties.

In 1855, a legal dispute arose in Washington County, Illinois, involving James L. McClurken and Harvey B. Lucas as plaintiffs in error, and James Logan as the defendant in error. The case originated from a petition for a mechanics’ lien filed by Logan against McClurken, who had contracted Logan to perform labor on a woolen factory in exchange for payment of $1.50 per day and board. Logan claimed to have worked approximately thirty-two and a half days, totaling a debt of $60.35, minus an advance payment of $5.35, leaving a balance of $55 due. Lucas, despite not being the primary contractor, claimed legal title to the property in question. Initially, Lucas attempted to respond to the petition without a sworn affidavit and filed a demurrer, which the court overruled. This ruling led to Logan obtaining a reference to a master for testimony and compensation, further complicating the matter. Ultimately, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the case to address a critical error regarding the enforcement of the mechanics’ lien statute, emphasizing that no lien could exist without evidence of a timely contractual agreement between the parties.	Logan, the plaintiff in the original action, claimed that he had entered into a contract with McClurken to provide labor for the construction of a woolen factory. He argued that he was owed $55 after partial payment and requested that the property be sold to satisfy this debt due to the mechanics’ lien he filed. The claim centered around the existence of a valid contract and the corresponding rights under Illinois law to enforce a lien for unpaid labor.	Lucas, as one of the defendants, asserted that he had a legal title to the premises and denied knowledge of the accounts between Logan and McClurken. His defense revolved around the claim of title possession prior to obtaining formal title and an assertion that the petition did not meet statutory requirements necessary for enforcing a mechanics’ lien, including the lack of a timely executed contract to support the lien.

In the case of Samuel L. Boyd et al. v. Blair Strahan et al., the dispute arose over the estate of John Strahan, who died in 1859, leaving a will that detailed the distribution of his assets. The will included two significant clauses: the eighth, which granted his wife, Mary Y. Strahan, $1,200 and household furniture "to her and to her heirs and assigns forever," and the ninth, which bequeathed the remaining personal property to her for her "own proper use and benefit during her natural life." Mary Y. Strahan passed away in March 1860, leaving her own will that bequeathed her residual personal effects to her brother, Samuel L. Boyd, and sister, Rebecca. Boyd and Rebecca, as appellants, claimed $1,855.55 as legatees from Mary Y. Strahan's estate. However, the appellees, the heirs of John Strahan, claimed rights to the property based on their status as heirs. The case was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court after the Circuit Court of Randolph County ruled in favor of the appellees in a bill to determine the title to the disputed personal property.	The plaintiffs, Samuel L. Boyd and Rebecca, argued that the terms of John Strahan's will granted Mary Y. Strahan an absolute title to the personal property mentioned, particularly as the will conferred her rights to dispose of the estate as she saw fit during her lifetime. They contended that since Mary Y. Strahan had a vested interest in the property, it passed on to them as residuary legatees upon her death.	The defendants, heirs of John Strahan, contended that the language of John Strahan's will granted Mary Y. Strahan only a life estate in the residuary personal property, as concluded from the clauses outlined. They argued she could not pass an absolute title to her heirs or devisees because her right was limited to her "use and benefit during her natural life." Thus, they claimed the undisposed property should revert to the next of kin of John Strahan.

Elisha Lewis and others brought a replevin action against Monroe Swift in September 1870 in Kankakee County, Illinois. Swift, a constable, had seized a mowing machine and horse rake under a writ of attachment against Faber, the alleged owner, in favor of James Campbell. This seizure occurred shortly after Faber left the state. The appellants, Lewis et al., claimed that they had previously sold the equipment to Faber on credit and had subsequently purchased it back shortly before Faber absconded. Beebe, one of the appellants, testified that he had attempted to reclaim the machines and considered that he had taken possession by sight. However, he did not physically move or touch the items, which remained on Faber's property. The defense argued that the appellants had not established rightful ownership or possession, as they failed to take the property into their custody or retain any formal possession prior to the attachment. The jury was instructed to consider whether the appellants had established adequate possession to challenge the attachment of the property.	The plaintiffs, Elisha Lewis et al., claimed that they had rightful ownership of the mowing machine and horse rake after purchasing them back from Faber shortly before his departure. They argued that Beebe had established possession of the property by sight and that their ownership should be recognized, despite Faber's subsequent financial issues and the attachment placed on the property.	The defendant, Monroe Swift, contended that the plaintiffs did not properly establish ownership because they failed to take actual possession of the property before the attachment. Swift argued that the legal standard required the plaintiffs to physically possess the property to claim rights against attaching creditors. The defense highlighted inconsistencies in Beebe's actions and statements concerning the ownership of the equipment.

In January 1862, in St. Louis, Missouri, John Anstedt (the appellant) was involved in a legal dispute against Michael Sutter (the appellee) concerning the sale of wine. The case arose when Sutter, a licensed dram-shop keeper, sold Anstedt 25 bottles of Rhein wine for $25.00. Anstedt consumed the wine with others and, despite being partially intoxicated, left without paying. Sutter claimed the unpaid amount, and a local justice found in favor of Sutter, awarding him $22. Anstedt appealed the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that Sutter's claim was unfounded because sales of intoxicating liquors on credit were void under Missouri law. The case revolved around whether the wine was sold on credit, as Sutter never requested payment immediately and told Anstedt to go home instead of settling the bill at that moment.	Sutter's primary argument was that he sold the wine to Anstedt on credit, which meant he expected future payment rather than immediate cash. This perspective aligned with the reality of how the transaction unfolded; the lack of immediate payment and Sutter’s suggestion for Anstedt to return home signified a credit sale. Consequently, Sutter sought to enforce the debt owed by Anstedt for the wine.	Anstedt contested that the sale was not on credit, asserting that all sales are presumed to be for cash unless specifically proven otherwise. He argued that Sutter had the option to demand payment immediately and noted that Sutter's statement telling him to go home did not indicate it was a credit sale. Anstedt maintained that the sale was void under Missouri law, which stated that any sale of intoxicating liquors on credit and any debt incurred from such sales were not recoverable by law.

In the case of The Governor of Illinois, for the use of William Thomas, Trustee, v. Joseph G. Bowman, the legal proceedings took place in June 1867 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from an action of debt brought by the plaintiff, William Thomas, as the Governor of Illinois, against Joseph G. Bowman, who was one of the sureties on a bond related to the financial misconduct of Ebenezer Z. Ryan. Ryan had been appointed as an assignee of the Bank of Illinois and was responsible for managing certain assets. A decree from the Circuit Court of the United States for the northern district of Illinois mandated Ryan to pay $45,467.27 to William Thomas, but he failed to fulfill this obligation. This failure prompted Thomas to seek recovery from Bowman based on his suretyship, as Ryan had not properly accounted for funds or submitted required reports. The higher court had previously ruled on similar points in The Governor, for the use of Thomas, v. Lagow, reaffirming that sureties are liable for breaches that occurred prior to the statute enacted in 1849, which did not suspend the right to action on such bonds.	The plaintiff, William Thomas, claimed that Joseph G. Bowman, as a surety on the bond, was liable for the debt resulting from Ebenezer Z. Ryan's failure to meet the requirements set out in the U.S. Circuit Court decree. Thomas argued that because the first breach—Ryan's failure to burn and cancel notes and report the funds—occurred prior to the 1849 act, Bowman was responsible for the damages. The plaintiff sought a judgment to recover the total amount owed, as well as compensation for the damages resulting from the lack of compliance.	The defendant, Joseph G. Bowman, argued against the liability for damages caused by breaches occurring after the enactment of the 1849 law, suggesting that the changes in legislation should limit his responsibility. Additionally, he contended that not all breaches noted by the plaintiff were adequately addressed in the pleadings, claiming that the case should be dismissed based on these defenses and seeking judgment on the initial demurrer that prevented the case from proceeding.

The case "Chicago & Iowa Railroad Company v. William Duggan" took place in September 1871, in Kendall County, Illinois. The dispute arose after the Chicago & Iowa Railroad Company sought to construct a railroad, which required the appropriation of land owned by William Duggan. The commissioners appointed by the circuit court of Kane County evaluated the situation and reported on the compensation that Duggan should receive for the land taken and the damages incurred due to the railroad's construction and operation. Dissatisfied with the commissioners' decision, Duggan appealed, leading to a trial by jury in the Circuit Court of Kendall County. The jury ultimately determined that Duggan was entitled to $107.80 in compensation for the land taken and $150 for damages. This verdict prompted the railroad company to file an appeal against the judgment rendered by the Kendall County court.	William Duggan, the plaintiff, claimed compensation for land taken by the Chicago & Iowa Railroad Company for its right of way through his farm. He appealed the decision from the commissioners regarding the amount of compensation and damages, seeking a fair assessment reflective of the impact the railroad’s construction and operation had on his property.	The Chicago & Iowa Railroad Company, as the defendant, argued against the trial court's allowance of new witness testimony to determine damages after they had closed their evidence. They contended that this violated procedural rules, although ultimately, they did not demonstrate any substantial harm stemming from the additional testimony, as it was cumulative and did not catch them by surprise.

Daniel Francisco purchased a tract of land from Levi Wright, which was encumbered by a mortgage held by the State Bank. After the mortgage was foreclosed, and without being a party to the foreclosure proceeding, Francisco paid off the amount owed under the decree made by the court. He claimed that Wright had promised to pay off the mortgage and therefore sought reimbursement. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1845, where it was established that Wright had not requested Francisco to pay the amount of the mortgage nor had ever promised to reimburse him for doing so.	Francisco's primary claim was that he was entitled to recover the amount he paid to satisfy the mortgage based on the assumption that Wright had promised to pay off the mortgage after the sale of the property. He argued that since Wright had agreed to satisfy the mortgage, he should be liable to reimburse him for the payment he made to the bank.	Wright contended that he was not liable to reimburse Francisco because there was no express or implied promise for him to do so. He emphasized that Francisco had paid the mortgage voluntarily and without any request or consent from Wright. Wright also argued that any potential claims were merged within the deed made during the sale of the property, which contained a warranty against incumbrances.

In June 1874, the case of St. Louis and Southeastern Railway Co. v. Isham Wheelis was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from an incident involving the railway company and Isham Wheelis, a landowner whose property was allegedly impacted by the railway’s operations. Wheelis claimed that the railway failed to properly fence its tracks, which resulted in the loss of personal property, including livestock and materials, when they escaped onto the railway's unprotected tracks and were injured or killed. The location of the incident was identified as Wheelis's farm, situated about a mile from the town of Ashley, within an area that was not part of a village or town. The case involved legal discussions regarding the responsibilities of the railway company to maintain its infrastructure as required by law and the duty to protect adjacent property from potential damages caused by its operations.	The plaintiff, Isham Wheelis, claimed that the St. Louis and Southeastern Railway Co. was negligent in failing to fence their tracks, which allowed his livestock to escape onto the tracks, leading to injuries or death. Additionally, he accused the railway of causing damage to his property, specifically hay and rails, which were destroyed by fire from the railway’s engines. Wheelis sought compensation for these losses, asserting that the railway company's actions directly resulted in his damages.	The St. Louis and Southeastern Railway Co. contended that the jury's decision was erroneous and argued against the circumstances surrounding the challenge of the juror array. They maintained that the evidence did not support Wheelis's claims of negligence, asserting that the damages were not a direct result of their operations. The railway company requested the court to overturn the jury's findings and findings of damage compensation, arguing procedural flaws in the jury selection and the plaintiff's lack of sufficient evidence.

In October 1856, Caspar Pfeiffer borrowed $1,850 from banker F. H. Benson in Chicago, leaving an $800 deposit intended to pay a debt secured by a deed of trust. The note for $800 was initially payable to George T. De Roe, with John Y. Le Moyne as the trustee. When De Roe visited Chicago in June 1857, he was made aware of the deposit but did not have the note to surrender. He subsequently engaged in another transaction with Benson, which involved a separate note. Confusion arose regarding whether the $800 had been paid to satisfy the debt, leading to a legal dispute. The original plaintiffs, the owners of the property, sought a decree to relieve their property of this encumbrance, while Nathaniel Douglas, acting as executor for the deceased Stephen De Roe, submitted a cross-bill asserting that the trustee should be ordered to sell the property due to alleged payment of the note. This case traversed to the Illinois Supreme Court, where the critical question was whether the $800 note had indeed been paid.	The plaintiffs claimed that the debt secured by the deed of trust had been satisfied and sought a court decree to remove the encumbrance from their property. They argued that the original deposit of $800, left by Pfeiffer, amounted to a valid payment of the debt, thus establishing their rightful ownership without the burden of the trust deed.	The defendants countered with a cross-bill asserting that the $800 note had not been paid. They contended that the evidence did not substantiate the claim of payment, as the debt was still listed in Benson's accounts. The burden of proof to show repayment rested on them, and they argued that the plaintiffs did not furnish sufficient evidence that the note had been satisfied.

In 1861, the Marine Company of Chicago was engaged in a financial transaction with a partnership firm known as Carver & Co. Benjamin F. Carver, a member of that firm, was indebted to the Marine Company. On June 26, 1861, Carver drew a check in favor of the Marine Company using the firm’s name, which was then misappropriated to settle his individual debt. This check was credited to Carver's individual account rather than the partnership's accounts. In July 1861, another member of Carver & Co. attempted to draw a check against the balance believed to be owned by the firm but found that it had already been settled due to Carver's actions. Despite having knowledge of this misappropriation, Carver & Co. did not repudiate the check until they filed suit against the Marine Company on June 26, 1865. The court found that by retaining the check and not promptly repudiating the actions of Carver, the other members of Carver & Co. effectively ratified his unauthorized transaction, thus having implications for their right to recover the funds owed to them.	The Marine Company of Chicago, as the plaintiff, claimed it was owed a balance of $638.89, which it alleged was misapplied by Carver for personal debt repayment, thus violating the duties of partnership. The plaintiff sought recovery of the misapplied funds, arguing that Carver's actions should not benefit him due to the improper appropriation of partnership money for personal use.	Carver & Co. (defendants) contended that the Marine Company failed to promptly repudiate Carver's actions upon learning of the misapplication of funds. They argued that the acceptance and retention of the check amounted to a ratification of Carver's actions, ultimately undermining any claim of wrongful appropriation. The defense maintained that at the time of the suit, Carver was still indebted to the Marine Company, indicating that there was no harm to the Marine Company effectively invalidating the claims.

Sarah D. Winchester filed a legal case against Mary E. Grosvenor in 1868, with the proceedings occurring in Chicago, Illinois. The case had previously been reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court during its April term in 1867. Initially, the court had reversed a lower court's decision and permitted Grosvenor to remit part of the judgment amounting to three hundred dollars. However, following a petition for rehearing from Winchester, further scrutiny of the evidence and the affidavit that led to the writ of attachment revealed previous errors in judgment by the court. Thus, the justices determined they inadvertently allowed Grosvenor to enter a remittitur instead of remanding the case for a new trial. This led to the conclusion that the evidence was not clear enough to warrant a specific judgment, necessitating a retrial by a new jury. Ultimately, the court modified its earlier reversal, which resulted in the case being remanded for further proceedings.	Sarah D. Winchester argued that the previous ruling allowed for a remittitur when the evidence presented did not support such an outcome. She contended that the proper course of action should have been to remand the case for a new trial rather than allowing the defendant to receive judgment based on an incomplete assessment of the evidence.	Mary E. Grosvenor maintained that the initial judgment in her favor should stand, claiming compliance with the court's instructions. She asserted that she followed appropriate procedures after the court's original decision, arguing for the validity of the judgment rendered by the lower court after her remittitur was entered.

Robert Fisher filed a legal case against A. J. Ham in the Illinois Appellate Court, with the judgment issued on February 17, 1887. The case stemmed from an appeal regarding a promissory note that Fisher claimed Ham had executed. The dispute was focused on whether adequate evidence supported the existence and execution of the note. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Champaign County and was presided over by Judge James F. Hughes. Plaintiff Fisher was represented by attorneys J. S. Wolf and M. W. Mathews, while defendant Ham was represented by attorneys J. L. Ray and F. M. Wright. The primary issue was centered on the execution of the note and whether it had been paid or settled.	The plaintiff, Robert Fisher, asserted that A. J. Ham executed the promissory note in question. Fisher maintained that the evidence presented in the trial supported his claim and requested that the judgment favor him based on the validity of the note. He contended that the jury’s verdict was warranted by the evidence demonstrating the note’s execution.	The defendant, A. J. Ham, contended that the evidence did not sufficiently support the jury’s verdict regarding the execution of the promissory note. Ham's defense also included objections to the refusal of certain jury instructions that he believed were pertinent to the case. He sought to have the court reverse the prior judgment based on these claims.

The case of Silas W. Robbins v. Thomas Laswell originated in Illinois in 1866, following the abrupt termination of a partnership between the two men. Robbins and Laswell had been business partners, and when their partnership ended, Laswell drove off with and converted partnership stock that had been paid for by Robbins, valued at $547. The case has previously appeared in court, leading to a partial restatement of accounts. The court, presided over by Chief Justice Laavrence, determined that while the master had initially understated Robbins' due balance, the amount of discrepancy was less than previously assumed. Key events include the valuation of stock driven off by Laswell and the miscalculation of both sales and expenses by the master in the accounting. The court scrutinized the financial dealings between Robbins and Laswell, ultimately revealing the profits generated during their partnership and the resulting balance owed to Robbins, which was calculated to be $1,685.15.	Robbins argued that he was entitled to a proper accounting of the partnership profits, including compensation for stock that Laswell improperly converted for personal use. He claimed that the master’s statement failed to accurately reflect the profits and did not include certain expenses he had advanced in the course of their business. Robbins requested a decree confirming the balance due to him, including interest from the date of the partnership's termination.	Laswell contested the claims of Robbins, arguing against the inclusion of certain sums in the accounting and disputing the calculation of profits attributed to the partnership. His defense centered on the assertion that the master's report had inaccuracies regarding sales figures and expenses, and he did not acknowledge the full extent of Robbins' claims for reimbursement. Laswell's primary request was for the court to uphold the master’s initial accounting findings.

Nathan Dyke, the plaintiff, was granted a warrant for eighty acres of land under the "Act granting bounty land to certain officers and soldiers" on September 28, 1850. He subsequently located the land in the Palestine land district and received a certificate of entry. On December 20, 1851, Dyke executed a bond with James McVey for the conveyance of forty acres of the land, conditioned on McVey paying $50 within five years. Dyke died shortly after, leaving his widow Jane Dyke and son N. V. Dyke as heirs. The widow and son later sold twenty acres of the land to Thomas Nettleton. On September 8, 1853, McVey filed a bill in chancery against Jane Dyke, N. V. Dyke, and Nettleton, seeking a conveyance of the forty acres he was promised. Despite having offered payment, N. V. Dyke contended the sale to McVey was void under the congressional act. The court examined the legal standing of the contract involving the sale of the land and its implications based on the act's provisions.	The plaintiffs, represented by N. V. Dyke as the administrator of Nathan Dyke's estate, argued that the land sale to McVey was void and claimed that the provisions of the congressional act rendered any contract affecting the land prior to certain conditions void. They maintained that McVey's claim was invalid since the sale was not legally enforceable under the act of Congress.	James McVey, the defendant, contended that the sale agreement with Nathan Dyke was valid since it occurred after the issuance of the land warrant. He argued the act did not nullify contracts made after the warrant's issuance, thus he was entitled to enforce the bond for the sale of forty acres. McVey had also tendered the agreed payment, seeking a court order for the conveyance of the land.

John Reynolds, the Governor of Illinois, initiated a legal action against James Hall, the State Treasurer, and his sureties following Hall's official bond, which he had executed for the faithful performance of his duties. Hall was elected Treasurer on December 28, 1828, and his bond, dated January 16, 1829, was approved by Reynolds on January 22, 1829. The bond stipulated that if Hall fulfilled his duties, the obligation would be void. The defendants contended that Hall had properly accounted for all funds and included a set-off for certain amounts the state owed Hall. However, during the trial, a report concerning the State Bank of Illinois, which was signed by Hall, was excluded as evidence, a decision that was challenged by Reynolds. The main issue debated was whether Hall's sureties could be held liable for his performance as Cashier of the State Bank, a role added by subsequent legislation after the bond's execution. The Supreme Court ultimately examined the nature of Hall's office and the responsibilities that had been placed upon him, emphasizing that the terms of the bond were based on laws in effect at that time.	The plaintiff, John Reynolds, argued that the sureties should be held liable for any misapplication of funds by Hall, asserting that he had not faithfully performed his duties under the bond. Reynolds sought to enforce the obligation outlined in the bond, claiming damages for the amount Hall allegedly mismanaged.	The defendants, including Hall and his sureties, contended that they had fulfilled the bond's conditions. They argued that Hall had accounted for all received funds and that any new responsibilities imposed on Hall, particularly those as Cashier of the State Bank, were not covered by the original bond. The defendants maintained that the sureties could not be held liable for Hall's actions in a capacity that was not explicitly included in their bond agreement.

Connor Carmody filed a legal case against The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company and others in the Illinois Supreme Court on September 27, 1884. The case originated from a dispute over a strip of land measuring 250 feet wide by 1,221 feet long, situated along the half-section line in Section 23. Initially, Carmody sought to recover the entire strip of land, but later narrowed his claim to the portion located east of the half-section line after dismissing part of his case against other defendants. Carmody asserted that he claimed title to the land through a common source, a deceased individual named William E. Davis. The railroad company defended itself by citing a deed of release from Davis to another railroad company in 1857, along with its long-term possession of the land, claiming adverse possession for over twenty years. The court had to consider whether Carmody had proper title to the land and examine the implications of the historical ownership and partition proceedings related to the estate of William E. Davis.	Connor Carmody argued that he held valid title to the disputed land through a deed obtained from Luella Y. Davis, one of William E. Davis's heirs. He claimed that no proper partition had been made concerning the land in question, thereby entitling him to claim the full extent of the property that had not been legally excluded. Carmody sought a judgment that would affirm his title to the land, allowing him to recover possession.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company contended that Carmody lacked valid title to the land due to the existence of a deed of release from William E. Davis, which effectively transferred possession to the Jacksonville and Carrollton Railroad Company over twenty years prior to the case. They argued that this, combined with their long-term possession, constituted a bar to Carmody's claim. Furthermore, the railroad maintained that the deed allowed for more than the specified one hundred-foot strip, as it pertained to it acquiring land for depot grounds and other railroad-related uses.

The case "The Northwestern Distilling Company v. Daniel R. Brant" took place in September 1873 in Chicago, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Daniel R. Brant, the plaintiff, and Edward F. Lawrence, the president of the Northwestern Distilling Company, the defendant. The dispute arose from a lease agreement dated April 17, 1869, where Brant leased premises to the distilling company. The central issue was Brant's claim that the company failed to restore the leased property to its original condition at the end of the lease term, which he argued constituted a breach of the covenant in the lease agreement. Although the lower court ruled in Brant's favor, upholding his claim, the Northwestern Distilling Company appealed the decision, ultimately contesting whether they could be held liable under the lease based on the manner in which the lease was executed.	The plaintiff, Daniel R. Brant, argued that the Northwestern Distilling Company breached the covenant to restore the leased premises to the condition they were in when they were received. He sought recovery based on the terms laid out in the lease, which explicitly required the company to return the property in good condition upon the expiration of the lease term.	The defendant, Northwestern Distilling Company, contended that a legal action for covenant could not be successfully brought against them due to the manner in which the lease was executed. They claimed that the covenant was made by Edward F. Lawrence as an individual, not on behalf of the company, and therefore the company was not liable. The defense argued that proof of the company's intention to be bound by the covenant required reform of the contract through equity, which was not established.

Fred Peters v. Henry Sennett is a legal case from 1886 in McHenry County, Illinois, where Fred Peters (the plaintiff) accused Henry Sennett (the defendant) of trespassing by constructing a drainage system across Peters' land. The proceedings began when Sennett, who owned adjacent land with a pond, sought to drain water for agricultural purposes across Peters' property. Under Illinois legislation enacted on June 23, 1883, Sennett filed a plat showing the intended drain path and obtained a summons served to Peters. A justice of the peace held a trial, ruling in favor of Sennett, allowing him to construct the drain, which led Peters to file a writ of error challenging the sufficiency of Sennett's defense under the drainage act, focusing particularly on the nature of the materials used in the drain's construction.	Fred Peters claimed that Henry Sennett's actions constituted trespass by constructing a drain on his land without proper justification. Peters argued that Sennett failed to meet the legal requirements set out in the drainage act, including the need for adequate materials and proper filing procedures. He requested the court to uphold the wrongful entry of Sennett onto his property.	Henry Sennett defended his actions by asserting that he followed the procedure permitted by the Illinois drainage act, which allowed landowners to construct drains across others' properties for agricultural use. He maintained that his filings were sufficient and that the justice of the peace ruled in his favor after a proper trial. Sennett contended that the construction was justified since he complied with statutory requirements, including filing a bond and obtaining necessary permissions.

In January 1872, the legal case of Marcus A. Lettick v. George H. Honnold was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court after being replanted to Sangamon County District Court from Christian County. The dispute involved Marcus Lettick (the appellee), who sued George Honnold (the appellant) on two promissory notes for rent. The notes were originally signed by Wm. J. Hiskett, with Honnold acting as surety. The motor of the case revolved around claims of eviction. Hiskett was the main tenant who alleged he was evicted before his lease termination, leading to the argument that the consideration for the notes failed. However, when examined, Hiskett’s testimony did not support claims of eviction; instead, it indicated he voluntarily surrendered part of the property to another party. The jury found in favor of Lettick, leading Honnold to appeal the judgment. Throughout the trial, issues related to the rejection of evidence on lease duration were raised, but the court determined that the evidence concerning eviction was conclusive enough that it would not have affected the outcome.	Marcus Lettick, as the plaintiff, argued that the promissory notes were valid and binding, despite George Honnold's claim of eviction by Hiskett. Lettick's main contention was that there was no eviction as Hiskett had given consent for others to take possession of the property. Thus, he sought enforcement of the notes for rent due, asserting that the defendant (Honnold) could not avoid liability based on the alleged failure of consideration due to eviction, which was not proven.	George Honnold, the defendant, contended that the promissory notes were invalid because Hiskett, the principal debtor, had not been served with process and was evicted before the lease's end. He asserted that this constituted a failure of consideration for the rents that were to be paid. He maintained that the trial court erred by not allowing him to fully utilize his special plea regarding the duration of the lease in front of the jury, arguing this undermined his ability to present his complete defense.

John Traynor v. Potter Palmer was a legal case presented before the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1877. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Cook County, where a trial was held presided over by Judge Henry Booth. The case involved a dispute regarding a covenant made by a grantor in a deed. The plaintiff, Potter Palmer, initiated the action against the defendant, John Traynor, based on a warranty against incumbrances following a property sale for taxes. The facts of the case reference a prior ruling in Rufner v. McConnel that established significant precedent regarding the limitations of recovery against a grantor when such covenants charge the estate to the legal representatives only, not the grantor personally.	The plaintiff, Potter Palmer, argued that the defendant, John Traynor, breached a covenant regarding the warranty of the property. Palmer contended that he should be compensated for the encumbrances on the property related to tax sales, which he had to discharge. He sought legal redress based on the terms outlined in the covenant included in the deed.	The defendant, John Traynor, countered the plaintiff's claims by asserting that the covenant was intended to only bind his estate and not him personally. Traynor maintained that he could not be held liable for the alleged breach of covenant as it was limited to his heirs and legal representatives, thus invoking a legal precedent that restricts recovery against a grantor in such cases.

In November 1853, the case of Garrison Wilderman et al. v. Andrew Sandusky was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court. The action originated in Franklin County, where Sandusky filed a trespass lawsuit against four individuals with the surname Wilderman, accusing them of wounding cattle. Initially, the case was heard by a justice of the peace and then escalated to the Circuit Court. During the trial, the jury found three of the defendants—Nancy Wilderman, Simon Wilderman, and Garrison Wilderman—guilty and assessed damages at thirty-five dollars. Following the verdict, the Wilderman defendants sought to appeal the decision, asserting that the court had erred in its judgment and the verdict's validity. However, they had no new trial granted, leading to their continued pursuit of the appeal process.	Andrew Sandusky, the plaintiff, claimed that the Wilderman defendants committed trespass by wounding his cattle. He sought damages for these actions, which resulted in a jury verdict finding three of the Wilderman defendants guilty. Sandusky pressed for the court's decision to be upheld, emphasizing the jury's confirmation of wrongdoing on the part of the appellants.	The Wilderman defendants argued that the jury's verdict was defective and that the court should not have rendered judgment based upon it. They contended that their treatment during the trial was unfair and sought a reversal of the judgment, alongside a new trial. However, they faced challenges as the court maintained that their verdict constituted a sufficient finding of guilt for the three defendants, with the fourth defendant effectively acquitted.

In April 1866, the case titled "The Town of Winfield v. William H. Moffatt et al." was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. It stemmed from a dispute in Du Page County regarding an appeal to lay out a public road, which was initially denied by the commissioners of highways. A group of citizens, including petitioners Jordan and Gary, sought to appeal this decision. They submitted an appeal to the supervisors of towns after their request for the road was refused, executing an appeal bond approved by the town clerk. The supervisors reversed the commissioners' initial decision and allowed the road to be laid out. However, a further petition for a writ of certiorari was filed, claiming this action was illegal due to alleged defects in the appeal bond and questioning the legitimacy of the petitioners' status as landowners or agents. The Circuit Court dismissed the writ and ruled in favor of the defendants, prompting the town of Winfield to bring the case before the Illinois Supreme Court.	The Town of Winfield contested the legality of the action taken by the supervisors to lay out the road, arguing that the appeal bond was insufficient and did not properly reflect the order of the commissioners of highways. They also contended that the petitioners did not demonstrate ownership or agency regarding any land along the proposed route, which they claimed should disqualify them from appealing the commissioners' decision.	The defendants argued that any objections regarding the appeal bond's validity or the petitioners' qualifications to appeal should have been raised before the supervisors during the initial hearing. They maintained that the acceptance of the bond by the town clerk verified jurisdiction and that no prejudice should arise from the alleged defects. Furthermore, they asserted that the details of ownership or agency were not required to be presented in a specific manner at the time of appeal, suggesting the need for the opportunity to remedy any deficiencies.

The legal case "The President and Board of Trustees of the Town of Ashton v. Freeman Ellsworth" took place in September 1868 in Ashton, Illinois. The case arose when the President and Board of Trustees of Ashton filed a prosecution against Freeman Ellsworth for selling liquor in town without a proper license. This action was based on a specific section of an act from March 5, 1867, which amended the town's charter, initially named Ogle Station, to Ashton. The contentious section prohibited the trafficking of intoxicating beverages and stated that no person was allowed to bring in or sell such drinks without a license. Violators faced a fine, which underscored the prohibition’s intent. The circuit court, however, ruled that the prohibition could not be enforced without a specific ordinance. The case was influenced by a previous ruling in Strauss v. The Town of Pontiac, which had a similar charter provision that was deemed enforceable independently of a supplementary ordinance. The legal questions centered around the necessity of additional ordinances for enforcing the charter’s prohibitions.	The plaintiff, represented by the President and Board of Trustees of Ashton, argued that according to the town's charter and the provisions laid out in the legislative act, Ellsworth's actions constituted a direct violation of the law against trafficking in intoxicating beverages. The plaintiffs sought to enforce the prohibition on liquor sales within the town and requested that the court recognize the charter’s section as self-executing without needing further ordinances for enforcement. The plaintiffs asserted that the circuit court's ruling, which favored Ellsworth, was incorrect and that a reversal was necessary to uphold the law.	Freeman Ellsworth, the defendant, contended that the charter’s prohibition against selling liquor could only be enacted through a specific town ordinance and therefore could not sustain a legal action on its own. The defense maintained that the circuit court's judgment was valid, emphasizing that the prohibition did not provide a sufficient legal basis for prosecution without an ordinance outlining its enforcement. The defendant argued that the legislative intent required a formal ordinance to be in place before any enforcement actions could be taken.

In December 1885, the case of I. Lauferty v. Roan Johnson was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court, concerning a promissory note executed in Rock Run Township, Stephenson County, Illinois, on May 19, 1884. The note involved a promise to pay $257.75, with a provision for attorney’s fees, payable to E.G. Webster or order, due sixty days after issuance at the Second National Bank, Freeport. The debtor, Roan Johnson, had no defenses or offsets against this note. When the case was brought to court, the plaintiff, Lauferty, included this note in his declaration, supported by two special counts and general common counts. However, the defendant's counsel raised an objection to the admission of the note, leading to its exclusion from evidence by the court. The trial concluded with the court favoring Johnson, resulting in summary judgment against Lauferty for costs. After trying to overturn this ruling with a motion for a new trial, the appeal was made to the Appellate Court, focused on whether the inclusion of attorney's fees in the note compromised its negotiability.	The plaintiff, I. Lauferty, contended that the promissory note, which included a clause for attorney's fees, remained negotiable despite the additional language. Lauferty argued that the attorney's fees referenced would only become applicable after the note’s maturity, thereby not affecting the core amount due. He requested the court to recognize the note's validity and to consider it a legitimate enforceable claim.	The defendant, Roan Johnson, maintained the position that the inclusion of the phrase regarding attorney's fees rendered the note non-negotiable and that the court was correct in excluding it as evidence. Johnson's counsel contended that the terms made the amount due uncertain until after default, which should nullify its enforceability at maturity.

In September 1872, the case "Benjamin N. Smith, County Judge, etc. v. The People ex rel. S. K. Bartholomew" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the circuit court of McHenry County, Illinois. The central issue was whether the expenses associated with the care and support of an insane individual, Winifred Dougherty, should be borne by the town of Coral, where the individual resided, or by the county. Benjamin N. Smith, as the County Judge, sought a writ of mandamus to compel the county treasurer to pay a claim submitted by S. K. Bartholomew, who was the supervisor and overseer of the poor in Coral. The claim arose from an account detailing costs incurred for Dougherty's maintenance. The legal basis revolved around the interpretation of statutes pertaining to the support of paupers and the responsibilities of town versus county authorities. The case acknowledged prior legislative acts from February 1853 and April 1869, which lay the groundwork for determining how these costs should be allocated.	The plaintiff, Benjamin N. Smith, argued that the county treasurer was obligated to pay the expenses incurred for Winifred Dougherty's care under the statute concerning paupers. He contended that the special act of February 10, 1853, which established that paupers should be a township charge, was repealed by more recent legislation, thus making the county responsible for the costs.	The defendant, represented by S. K. Bartholomew, contended that the statute of 1869 did not repeal the earlier act regarding township responsibilities. The defendant maintained that the 1853 act remained in effect, requiring the town of Coral to cover the costs associated with Dougherty's care. He argued that any interpretation of the newer statute that would impose county liability without due process was unconstitutional.

On September 1, 1845, a tax title to a piece of land was conveyed by FTevins and Alstine to Lucius Kingman. The purchase funds were supplied by John Tillson, who intended for Kingman to act as trustee, responsible for paying taxes and selling the land while accounting to Tillson for the proceeds. In 1856, Kingman conveyed the property to Hinchman & Loomis, who subsequently transferred the title to Sanderson Lyon, one of the plaintiffs. The defendants, William Kain and others, argued that Kingman’s seven years of tax payments on the land (from 1846 to 1853) created a legal claim under the statute of limitations. However, the court found insufficient evidence to establish Kingman’s tax payments met the legal requirements to protect Kain's title. The case illustrates a dispute over the rightful ownership of the property and the validity of tax payments made under a trust agreement.	The plaintiffs, Sanderson and John W. Lyon, asserted their ownership of the land through a series of legal conveyances originating from the patentee. They maintained that the defendants' claim to the property was merely colorable and that the defendants had not met the statutory requirements to establish a bar against their claim through the payment of taxes.	The defendant, William Kain, contended that he held a valid title based on the tax payments made by Lucius Kingman for seven consecutive years while he held the color of title. Kain argued that, according to the statutory limitations, these payments should protect his claim to the property despite the plaintiffs’ assertions.

In the case of Pollard Kirkland v. Lott and Dailey, which was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1839, the background involves a legal dispute stemming from a promissory note executed by the defendant, Lott, to the plaintiffs, Kirkland, for the amount of $188. The events took place in Jerseyville, Illinois, where the defendant claimed to have entered into a contract with the plaintiffs for the purchase of three lots of land. The plaintiffs allegedly pointed out the location of these lots, which were by number on a plat of the town. However, the defendant argued that the lots he purchased were not in the location the plaintiffs had represented, and that they had fraudulently concealed this fact. The case originally went to trial in the Greene Circuit Court, where the plaintiffs won a judgment of $189.88, prompting the defendant's appeal.	The plaintiffs, Kirkland, contended that the defendant owed them payment for the promissory note issued for the purchase of the lots. They maintained that the allegations made by the defendant regarding failure of consideration were unfounded and that the agreement was valid. They sought to uphold the judgment initially rendered by the Greene Circuit Court for the amount due on the note.	The defendant, Lott, presented several defenses, including claims of failure of consideration and fraud. He asserted that the lots sold were not as represented by the plaintiffs and that the plaintiffs knowingly withheld the true location of the lots, thus deceiving him into making the purchase. The defendant requested that the court recognize his claims of fraud and failure of consideration as valid defenses against the enforcement of the promissory note.

In the case of David Haddix v. Frederick Einstman, which took place in Morgan County, Illinois, in 1881, David Haddix (the appellant) entered into a contract with Warner, a representative of Frederick Einstman (the appellee), for the sale and storage of his wheat. The plaintiff offered his wheat at one dollar per bushel, but Warner only offered ninety cents. A storage agreement was reached where Haddix's wheat would be stored for a month free of charge, after which a fee of one cent per bushel per month would be charged. However, instead of storing all the grain as agreed, Warner shipped a substantial portion of Haddix’s wheat mixed with Einstman’s grain to Toledo, Ohio, while the rest was sent to Batty Brothers at Waverly. Haddix claimed that Einstman wrongfully converted his wheat for his own use, as there was no intention to transfer ownership of the grain. The case was brought to the Illinois Appellate Court seeking relief for this alleged conversion.	The plaintiff, David Haddix, argued that his wheat was wrongfully converted by Frederick Einstman’s agent, Warner, who mixed it with other grain and shipped it away without authorization. Haddix contended that he had no intention of relinquishing ownership of his wheat and that a contract of simple bailment existed. He claimed that the conversion was unlawful and sought the value of the grain from Einstman, as he did not authorize its sale or conversion.	The defendant, Frederick Einstman, contended that he was not liable for the actions of his agent, Warner, asserting that Warner had the authority to manage the grain business. Einstman maintained that unless Warner had explicit authority to store the wheat or if any conversion actions were ratified post-factum, he could not be held responsible. The defense focused on the contention that the plaintiff was not entitled to relief since the wrongful acts, if any, were beyond the declared authority of the agent.

In the case of Benjamin L. T. Bourland v. George L. Gibson et al., decided on November 18, 1887, the dispute arose in DeWitt County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were plaintiff Benjamin L. T. Bourland and defendant George L. Gibson along with others. The case stemmed from Bourland's action on a promissory note which he claimed was due. Earlier proceedings had been conducted in May 1886, and upon remand, Bourland filed an additional replication asserting he had not refused to deliver the deed associated with the note. However, the court sustained a demurrer to this replication, as it did not adequately challenge the defendant's plea, which claimed the note was given in consideration of a deed that had not been delivered. The matter proceeded to jury trial, where the jury found in favor of the defendant, leading to the affirmation of the verdict.	The plaintiff, Benjamin L. T. Bourland, argued that he was entitled to enforce the promissory note. He contended that he had not refused to deliver the deed related to the note, and he sought a judgment in his favor for the amount due under the note. His legal requests were predicated on the assertion that there was a failure on the defendant's part to fulfill the terms of the agreement linked to the note and the deed.	The defendant, George L. Gibson, contended that the promissory note in question was given in exchange for a deed that had not been delivered. He maintained that the allegations made by the plaintiff were insufficient to overcome his defense, which was confirmed by the jury’s decision. The defendant sought dismissal of the plaintiff's claims and argued that evidence presented during the trial supported the verdict in his favor.

In the case of Samantha Warren v. Ira P. Warren, et al., Samantha Warren, the plaintiff, is the daughter of Hiram Warren who settled on a farm in Will County, Illinois, in 1833. After the death of her mother in 1841, her father requested that Samantha, who was then over eighteen, stay and care for him and the family's youngest child. Despite never being legally compensated, she dedicated over thirty-eight years of her life to managing the household and assisting in the farm’s operations while also raising her siblings. Throughout her father's life, he repeatedly acknowledged that the farm would belong to her and promised to convey the property to her. After her father's death in August 1879, he left no will, and his other children contested the verbal agreement that their father had with Samantha. The case revolves around whether this verbal promise constituted a binding contract for the land's transfer, particularly in light of the Statute of Frauds, which typically requires written contracts for the sale of land.	Samantha Warren claims that her lifetime of unpaid services to her father were equivalent in value to the property he intended to convey to her. She argues that her father's repeated promises and acknowledgments constituted a binding agreement for specific performance to transfer the land to her. Samantha seeks to enforce this agreement despite the absence of a written contract, claiming that her long-term caretaking duties served as sufficient consideration for the land.	The defendants, representing Hiram Warren's other children, argue that there was no binding contract for the property transfer and claim that any such agreement was verbal and thus void under the Statute of Frauds. They contend that Samantha's actions could be interpreted as familial duty rather than contractual services and insist that the law does not obligate their father to compensate her for her care since she acted out of love and obligation.

In June 1874, the case of Mary S. Bond et al. v. Rufus N. Ramsey et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict centered around a promissory note dated May 5, 1869, in which John P. Blackwell and R. H. Ramsey promised to pay Mary S. Bond and Joshua S. Bond (the plaintiffs, acting as executors of Leah P. Webster's will) $510 with six percent interest after twelve months. The defendants argued that the note was part of a transaction involving a deed for several lots in Carlyle, asserting that the plaintiffs lacked ownership of the property and therefore could not transfer valid title. During trial proceedings, the defense claimed a failure of consideration based on the lack of title in the grantor. A jury verdict and judgment favored the defendants, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal, asserting that the verdict was contrary to the evidence presented during the trial.	The plaintiffs claimed that they executed a deed conveying the identified lots to Blackwell, satisfying the terms of the promissory note. They argued that their role as executors allowed them to act on behalf of Leah P. Webster's estate and that any defects in the deed did not negate Blackwell’s obligation to pay the note. They requested that the court overturn the lower court's judgment in favor of the defendants, thereby enforcing their rights to collect the debt.	The defendants contended that the promissory note was invalid due to the plaintiffs' lack of ownership of the lots at the time the note was executed. They asserted that the plaintiffs had no rightful power to convey the property because Leah P. Webster’s estate did not have a clear title to the lots, thus arguing a failure of consideration for the note. They requested the court to maintain the original judgment in their favor due to these claims.

In 1853, in Kane County, Illinois, the Galena and Chicago Union Railroad Company sought the right of way over lands owned by the heirs of Comfort Bennett, who had passed away. Plaintiffs Amelia Pound (Bennett's widow) and her children claimed ownership of the land that was being used for the construction of the railroad. The plaintiffs alleged that the Railroad Company had committed trespass by constructing its railroad through their property without proper compensation. At trial, the jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $650 for damages. The Railroad Company appealed the decision, leading to a review by the Illinois Supreme Court, which considered the relevant evidence, including notices served on property owners and previous court proceedings regarding land condemnation.	The plaintiffs contended that the Galena and Chicago Union Railroad Company trespassed on their property by constructing a railroad through their land without the proper legal authority or compensation. They sought damages amounting to $2,000 for the loss suffered due to the alleged trespass. The plaintiffs emphasized that they were rightful owners and had not consented to the use of their property.	The defendants argued that they had followed the necessary legal processes to obtain the right of way through the property, including appointing appraisers to assess damages and providing notices to the relevant landowners. They sought to introduce evidence to support their claim of having obtained condemnation rights lawfully. The defendants insisted that the plaintiffs' objections to the admission of evidence related to this process were improper and maintained that all necessary legal requirements had been satisfied.

On June 5, 1883, Julius Rosenthal, the public administrator for Cook County, applied for letters of administration for the estate of Dorothea Grumme, a non-resident who died intestate in June 1882. Three days later, Eugene E. Prussing, a creditor of the estate residing in Cook County, filed a similar application for the same estate. Both men claimed that Dorothea left a personal estate valued at $1,000.82 and had no immediate heirs in Illinois, as her next of kin lived in Hanover, Germany. The probate court found the facts corroborated by both petitions but dismissed Rosenthal's request, favoring Prussing. This decision was upheld by the circuit and Appellate Courts, leading Rosenthal to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal question to be evaluated was whether a public administrator is entitled to administer the estate of a non-resident when a creditor resides in the state.	Julius Rosenthal argued that, by virtue of his position as public administrator, he should be granted letters of administration for the estate of the non-resident intestate, Dorothea Grumme. He contended that, according to the relevant statutes, the public administrator has the right to administer the estates of non-residents, especially when there are no local heirs or next of kin. His primary legal request was to reverse the probate court's decision that favored Prussing.	Eugene E. Prussing claimed that as a creditor of the estate residing in Illinois, he had the legal right to precedence over the public administrator in the application for letters of administration. He argued that the statutory provisions favoring local creditors supersede the claims of the public administrator, asserting that the law clearly provides for this preference regardless of the deceased being a non-resident.

In late November 1885, Nathan Davis, the appellant, consented to Norman T. Gassette, the appellee, to sell property located on Archer Avenue, owned by Davis's wife. Gassette undertook significant advertising efforts but failed to sell the property. In April 1886, a potential buyer, E. Pardridge, expressed disinterest in the property after inspecting it, stating it was in a bad neighborhood. In May 1887, another broker, Pflaum, initiated negotiations for a trade between Pardridge and Davis. After some time, a deal was made to exchange properties involving the South Park Avenue property. Although Davis denied giving Gassette exclusive agency for the sale, Gassette claimed to have assisted in the transaction, arguing that he deserved a commission for bringing Pardridge's attention to the property and subsequently advising Davis on the deal. The case was presided over by Judge Richard W. Clifford in the Illinois Appellate Court, and it hinged on the validity of Gassette's commission entitlements based on his earlier communication with Pardridge.	Gassette, the plaintiff, claimed that he had an exclusive agency to sell Davis's property and that his previous discussions with Pardridge directly contributed to the eventual trade between Davis and Pardridge. He asserted that he was entitled to commissions for his services rendered in facilitating the connection, despite the fact that the actual transaction was negotiated through another broker.	Davis, the defendant, argued that he never granted Gassette exclusive agency and that Gassette's past attempts to sell the property did not culminate in a successful transaction. He contended that the negotiations leading to the eventual trade were initiated by Pflaum, and thus Gassette's prior efforts and claims were insufficient to warrant any commission.

In November 1823, a legal case arose in Gallatin, Illinois, involving the parties Forester and Funkhouser as appellants against Guard, Siddell & Co. as appellees. The case revolved around a verdict that had been issued by a lower court which the appellants contended was erroneous. The primary issue raised was the propriety of granting a new trial based on several reasons that questioned the jury's decision-making process. Among those reasons were allegations that the verdict contradicted the law and evidence presented, the emergence of new testimony without substantial details, the influence of jurors' statements made during deliberations, and the improper separation of a juror while the jury was deliberating. The appellant's arguments brought to light concerns about the integrity of the jury's deliberation and the necessity of a fair re-evaluation of the case given the claims made regarding the handling of the verdict.	The plaintiffs, Forester and Funkhouser, argued that the lower court erred in granting a new trial based on a series of reasons. They maintained that the jury's verdict was contrary to the law and the evidence presented. They also indicated that the claim of new testimony was insufficient as it lacked details about the witness and the facts to be proven. Additionally, they highlighted that jurors’ statements made after the verdict should not be considered as grounds to challenge its validity, and they asserted that the separation of a juror during deliberation was improper.	The defendants, Guard, Siddell & Co., contended that the lower court acted appropriately by granting a new trial due to multiple legitimate concerns regarding the jury's verdict. They asserted that new material testimony had indeed surfaced, which warranted a re-evaluation of the case. Their position emphasized that the verdict had been unduly influenced by juror discussions that occurred post-deliberation, and they argued for the necessity of addressing these procedural irregularities to ensure a fair trial.

In January 1865, the case of George Erlinger et al. v. The People of the State of Illinois was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The action originated from a debt claim involving a bastardy bond that George Erlinger entered into as the principal, with Joseph Erlinger as security, before a justice of the peace. This bond was intended to guarantee George's appearance at the Circuit Court to answer charges of bastardy. The case was initiated during the June term of 1863, and the plaintiffs, representing the People of the State of Illinois, sought enforcement of the bond. The appellants demurred against the declaration, but their objection was overruled, leading to a final judgment ordering payment of the bond’s penalty. The key issues revolved around the validity of certain conditions of the bond and whether they could be severed if deemed invalid.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendants were liable under the terms of a valid bastardy bond, which George Erlinger had entered into, to ensure his appearance in court regarding accusations of bastardy. They contended that the bond’s conditions, while some may be invalid, still included valid terms that warranted enforcement. The plaintiffs requested enforcement of the bond and sought payment for damages and costs amounting to $500, which was ordered by the court.	The defendants contended that the bond was involuntary and contained unauthorized conditions that rendered it void. They argued that the bond did not conform to statutory requirements, claiming that this invalidated the instrument in its entirety. They further asserted that the suit should be initiated for the benefit of the county judge for the child’s use, rather than for the mother’s benefit.

The case "Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Co. v. Henry Holbrook" emerged from events that unfolded during the October term of the St. Clair Circuit Court in 1872. The plaintiff, Henry Holbrook, initiated an assumpsit action against the Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Co. The summons was served, and the declaration containing common counts for work, labor, and money found due was filed in a timely manner. Default was entered against the railroad company on the third Thursday of the term due to their failure to respond, prompting a writ of inquiry to assess damages. Evidence presented in court subsequently led to a damages judgment of $9,500 in favor of Holbrook. The defendant’s attorneys later moved to amend the record to reflect that the damages assessment hearing had been improperly held prior to the scheduled date. Citing the court minutes, they argued that the damages should have been assessed on the seventh Tuesday of the term instead of the fifth. The court's refusal to amend the record led to an appeal concerning whether this decision was erroneous.	The plaintiff, Henry Holbrook, argued that the defendant railroad company failed to respond adequately in court, leading to his victory by default. He emphasized that the damages assessed at $9,500 were justifiable, based on the evidence presented.
