Holbrook sought to uphold this judgment and argued against the defendant's motion to amend the record, asserting the initial proceedings were valid.	The Cairo and St. Louis Railroad Co. contended that there was an error in the handling of court records, specifically concerning the timing of the damages assessment. They argued that the damages should not have been assessed until the seventh Tuesday of the term, as that was the date set by the court. The defendant’s attorneys sought to amend the record to reflect this purported scheduling error, which they believed to be essential in contesting the awarded damages.

The case of "The Town of Waltham v. Jacob Kemper" originated in September 1870 in LaSalle County, Illinois. Jacob Kemper, the plaintiff, filed a lawsuit against the Town of Waltham. Kemper claimed that the town failed to keep a public highway in proper repair, which resulted in his wagon and team getting mired in mud. Despite exercising due care, he was unable to extricate himself without suffering injuries that left him wet, chilled, and ultimately sick for an extended period. This incident hindered his ability to attend to his normal business. The case was presented before a jury, which found in favor of Kemper. The Town of Waltham appealed the decision, and the central issue to be resolved involved the town's liability in this matter. Previous case law was discussed to analyze whether the town had a legal obligation to maintain the highway and be held liable for failure to do so.	The plaintiff, Jacob Kemper, argued that the Town of Waltham had a statutory duty to keep public highways in repair. He claimed that due to the town's negligence, he suffered damages as a result of his team and wagon becoming mired. He sought compensation for the hardships he experienced, including medical issues stemming from the incident, loss of property, and the inability to conduct his usual activities.	The Town of Waltham contended that it was not liable for the claims made by Kemper. They asserted that under both common law and state statutes, towns established as civil divisions of a county are generally not liable to private actions for damages resulting from the neglect of public duties. The defense referred to legal precedents which support the notion that towns do not have the same liability as other municipal corporations, such as cities, for injuries incurred from neglecting to maintain public highways.

The case titled "The People ex rel. Henry B. Miller, Collector, etc. v. P. L. Sherman et al." took place in the village of Hyde Park, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1876. The key individuals involved included Henry B. Miller, the county collector representing the plaintiffs, and P. L. Sherman, representing the defendants. The case arose from a special assessment applied to certain lots and real estate in Hyde Park for the purpose of installing cast-iron water supply pipes as part of a local improvement project. The county court initially refused to grant the assessment judgment, concluding that the ordinance enabling the assessment was invalid. The plaintiffs contended that the ordinance was enacted in accordance with constitutional provisions, asserting their legal authority to levy special assessments for municipal improvements.	The plaintiff, represented by Henry B. Miller, argued that the General Assembly had conferred authority to the corporate authorities of localities to impose special assessments for public works like water supply systems. The plaintiff asserted that the ordinance allowing the assessment was valid since it was in compliance with the constitution and general laws governing local improvements. They requested the court to reverse the lower court's decision and uphold the validity of the assessment for the water supply pipes.	The defendants contended that the ordinance was void for several reasons, including that it incorporated multiple distinct local improvements, which they asserted could not be grouped under a single assessment. They argued that the ordinance lacked essential provisions on how the pipes would be laid and did not allocate any of the costs to the village itself, claiming that these deficiencies rendered it unconstitutional. They maintained that notice regarding the special assessment was irregular or insufficient, which should invalidate the application for judgment.

The case "George S. Wright et al. v. Achsah Dunning" was decided in September 1867 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It involves Achsah Dunning, the widow of Eben Dunning, who is seeking recovery of her homestead rights in certain lands owned by her late husband. The land in question was occupied by Eben Dunning as a home until his death, and Achsah was made a party to a previous litigation concerning the partition of this property. The court in that proceeding adjudicated her entitlement to dower but not to homestead rights. Consequently, a decree awarded her a yearly allowance in lieu of dower, to be paid during her lifetime. Following the sale of the land, Achsah removed from the premises and did not assert any homestead claims until after her husband's estate was settled. The core of the conflict resides in whether Achsah can claim homestead rights post-sale, despite earlier court proceedings which did not recognize such rights.	Achsah Dunning, the plaintiff, argues that she has homestead rights to the property despite previous proceedings where her dower rights were established. She seeks the recovery and assignment of her homestead, claiming the right to reside in the land her husband owned as a homestead at the time of his death.	The defendants, George S. Wright et al., argue that Achsah is barred from claiming homestead rights due to her participation in a prior court decree that granted her dower rights and remitted her to a yearly allowance. They assert that she abandoned her claims to homestead, having vacated the property and indicated a lack of intention to return. Thus, they contend she cannot assert rights that were not claimed in previous proceedings.

Edward Humphreys (the appellant) filed a legal case against Collier and Powell (the appellees) in December 1829. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a promissory note that was made in Missouri on April 3, 1822, and was payable five months later. The plaintiff claimed that the note had been assigned to him on June 1, 1825. Humphreys attempted to prove that pursuing the maker of the note (who had become insolvent) would have been futile under Missouri law. During the trial, he sought to introduce a witness's deposition detailing the maker's insolvency, which the defendant objected to. The court allowed this evidence to be presented to the jury, despite the defendant's argument that it was improper. The case revolved around the legal principles regarding evidence, assignments, and the necessity of pursuing debtors. The court ultimately found that the judge's actions regarding evidence and jury instructions were irregular.	The plaintiff, Edward Humphreys, sought to recover on a promissory note he claimed was assigned to him. He argued that it was unnecessary to pursue the maker of the note, as prosecution would not yield any results due to the maker's insolvency. He aimed to prove this point through witness testimony regarding the maker's financial status and previous discharge under Missouri's insolvent laws.	The defendant, Collier and Powell, contended that the evidence of the note's assignment and the witness's testimony about the maker's insolvency should not have been admitted in court. They argued that the plaintiff failed to prove the due diligence required to pursue the maker before assigning the note. Additionally, the defendant claimed that the testimony provided did not support the plaintiff's claim and pointed out that the assignment of the note included terms that negated the plaintiff's argument of being a valid debtor.

The case "Mary J. Hall et al. v. William H. Davis" took place in the jurisdiction of the Illinois Supreme Court, with the decision rendered in June 1867. The legal dispute revolves around a petition for partition regarding approximately 700 acres of land initially filed by William H. Davis against defendants Mary J. Hall and James H. Hall. The case originated on July 10, 1856, when a summons was issued to Mary J. Hall, while James H. Hall was not found. A notice of the lawsuit was published in a local newspaper for four weeks, and the court defaulted the defendants in September 1856, subsequently granting a judgment for partition. The court established that the lands were inherited from Samuel B. Hall and accordingly distributed the ownership interests. Mary and Harriet Hall later sought to vacate previous proceedings, claiming they were not properly notified and that their interests had not been represented. They argued that Mary J. was a minor at the time and Harriet B. was never made a party to the earlier proceedings. The court denied their motion, prompting Mary J. Hall to challenge this decision, asserting that her rights were not protected under the decree.	The plaintiffs, Mary J. Hall and Harriet B. Hall, contended that they were not properly notified of the partition proceedings, and that their interests in the inherited land were not taken into account. They claimed that Mary J. Hall was a minor at the time of the original proceedings, and that Harriet B. Hall was not included as a party in the case. They requested relief for the assignment of dower rights, partition of the property according to their rightful shares, and reversal of the earlier decree which did not recognize their roles as rightful heirs.	William H. Davis, the defendant, maintained that the previous proceedings were correct and legally sound. He argued that the summons served to Mary J. Hall provided sufficient jurisdiction, as it clearly directed the sheriff to summon the defendants to appear in court. Davis contended that since neither Hall had appeared in the original case, the court's decree was valid and should not be overturned simply based on their subsequent claims. His defense relied on established legal precedents regarding the sufficiency of court process and notifications.

In December 1841, in Springfield, Illinois, the case of Edmund D. Taylor et al. v. Jonas Whitney arose. The involvement centered around Jonas Whitney who filed a bill in chancery against Taylor and others, who were agents and contractors for the fund commissioner of the state. Whitney sought to prevent the construction of any turnout or depot for the Northern Cross railroad at any location other than designated lots in his addition to Springfield. This injunction was based on a legislative act that authorized the mutual conveyance of certain lots between the auditor of public accounts and Whitney, under which the state was expected to respect the specific lots where the railroad facilities were to be located. The court initially granted the injunction and denied motions from the defendants to dissolve it. Eventually, the parties agreed to make the injunction perpetual, leading to an appeal by the defendants, which contested the lower court's consistent refusals to dissolve the injunction and the final decree establishing it as permanent.	The plaintiff, Jonas Whitney, claimed his legal rights to control the placement of the railroad turnout and depot locations based on a state act that authorized him to dictate where these constructions should occur. Whitney argued that the state was obligated to adhere to the original agreement regarding the designated lots, as he had donated these lots to the state for that specific purpose. He sought to enjoin the defendants from constructing the turnaround or depot at any location outside the specified lots.	The defendants, led by E.D. Taylor, argued against the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that the state had full discretion over the location of the railroad facilities as per legislative acts, and thus, they were not bound to comply with the specific lot donations made by Whitney. They maintained that the legislative provisions allowed for alternative constructions for the purpose of public benefit, and the state was not legally required to follow Whitney’s stipulations regarding the placement of the depot and turnouts. The defendants sought to have the injunction dissolved.

In 1869, in St. Clair County, Illinois, Andrew Stolberg initiated a legal action against Fredericke Ohnmacht regarding a claim of forcible entry and detainer. The case arose when Stolberg sought to regain possession of a property he alleged Ohnmacht had unlawfully entered. Initially, a summons was issued by a justice without the necessary affidavit being filed beforehand. When Ohnmacht appeared and moved to dismiss the suit due to this jurisdictional issue, the justice overruled this motion and allowed Stolberg to file the affidavit on the day of the trial. The justice subsequently ruled in favor of Stolberg. However, Ohnmacht appealed the decision to the circuit court, which ultimately granted the motion to dismiss the case, as the justice lacked jurisdiction due to the improper issuance of the summons.	Stolberg's main argument was that the justice's initial ruling was valid despite the lack of a filed affidavit prior to the summons. He contended that the affidavit should not be a strict requirement and that verbal complaints made under oath were sufficient to establish jurisdiction. Stolberg sought to overturn the circuit court’s dismissal of his case, arguing that the proceedings had been incorrectly handled.	Ohnmacht's defense centered around the assertion that without the affidavit being filed before the issuance of the summons, the justice had no jurisdiction to hear the case. Ohnmacht moved to dismiss the action based on this jurisdictional flaw and argued that filing an affidavit on the day of the trial could not retrospectively remedy the lack of jurisdiction. Ohnmacht contended that the justice could not compel a defense in light of the procedural missteps.

In the case of "Lewis W. Green v. Joseph Buckingham," which took place in 1887 in Vermillion County, Illinois, the conflict arose from an incident involving a trespass. The plaintiff, Lewis W. Green, accused Joseph Buckingham of breaking into what he claimed to be his property and unlawfully cutting down willow trees. In this case, the legal background involved complex property rights; particularly whether Buckingham was entitled to the willows that were on the disputed land. Buckingham, who owned the loom used in conjunction with the property, had previously granted Green permission to enclose the area to improve his fence, but he retained the right to the willows. The situation culminated in Green's filing of a trespass action against Buckingham.	The plaintiff, Lewis W. Green, claimed that the defendant, Joseph Buckingham, had unlawfully entered his property and cut down willow trees without his consent. Green sought compensation for the damages incurred due to this alleged trespass and argued that Buckingham had not been granted the right to remove or damage the trees.	The defendant, Joseph Buckingham, contended that he had received permission from Green to enclose the land in question, which included the willows. He filed pleas of not guilty, liberum tenementum (asserting rightful possession), and the statute of limitations. Buckingham maintained that any errors in the trial's proceedings had not negatively impacted the trial's outcome, claiming the verdict was justified based on the evidence presented.

John Shepherd filed a claim against the State of Illinois regarding a property dispute linked to the construction of a dam on the Illinois River near Copperas Creek. The claim was initiated on May 1, 1880, and concerns a specific parcel of land owned by Shepherd, which is described as the northwest quarter of the southeast quarter of section 30, township 8, north, range 8 east of the 4th P.M., comprising 40 acres. Shepherd argued that the construction of the dam had raised the water level in the river, causing significant damage to his property, quantified at $600. The incident leading to the claim occurred when the dam was closed in October 1877, which established the timeline for the complaint.	The primary argument put forth by John Shepherd was that the flooding caused by the newly constructed dam led to the depreciation of his property, resulting in damages of $600. He sought compensation for the loss incurred due to the actions of the State of Illinois, asserting his ownership of the affected land and the resultant financial impact of the dam's construction on his property value.	The State of Illinois contended that Shepherd's claim was barred by the statute of limitations, arguing that the petition was not filed within the required two years after the cause of action had accrued. They pointed out that the dam was closed in October 1877, and hence, the clock for the limitations period started at that time. Due to the failure to comply with the statute, the state called for the rejection of the claim.

In 1873, in Illinois, the case Ptolemy E. Hosmer v. Livesay Carter et al. arose from a dispute regarding a deed involving a tract of land. The key individuals involved were Livesay Carter, Mary E. Boyd, her husband Albert G. Boyd, and Ptolemy E. Hosmer. The original bill was filed by Livesay Carter against the Boyds and Hosmer, seeking to annul a deed that Carter had previously executed, conveying the land to his daughter Mary. The contention centered around an alteration made to the deed—specifically, the removal of the term “body” in the phrase “body heirs” from the deed, which Carter claimed occurred without his consent. Mrs. Boyd, believing she had the consent of her father, made the alteration. The circuit court ruled in favor of Carter, reinstating the word "body" and thereby limiting the estate to Mary's heirs. Following this, the Boyds executed a mortgage on the property to secure a debt owed to Hosmer, prompting him to file a cross-bill to foreclose the mortgage. The central issue in court was whether Mrs. Boyd had sufficient interest in the property to convey through a mortgage. The court initially dismissed Hosmer's cross-bill, which was challenged as an error.	The plaintiff, Livesay Carter, claimed that the deed to his daughter, Mary E. Boyd, had been improperly altered post-delivery without his consent, thus seeking to restore the original terms of the deed. He argued that the removal of the term “body” modified the intended limitation of the property to Mary's heirs, thus affecting the validity of subsequent actions taken by the Boyds involving the mortgage.	The defendants, represented by Ptolemy E. Hosmer, contended that they were not responsible for the alteration of the deed and argued that Mrs. Boyd had the legal right to mortgage her interest in the property despite the omission of the word "body". Hosmer maintained that the mortgage was valid and sought to foreclose, emphasizing that the original debt was bona fide and that Mrs. Boyd, having a life estate, could still convey her interest.

Lewis Steward v. Annie H. Miller is a case adjudicated by the Illinois Appellate Court, resulting in a decision on December 4, 1885. The case originated in May 1883 when Annie H. Miller, the plaintiff, initiated legal action against Lewis Steward, the defendant. The controversy arose over a promissory note executed by Steward in favor of Miller, which amounted to $2,968.33. Throughout the proceedings, the defendant sought to challenge the validity of the note by claiming a lack of consideration. The trial court ultimately ruled against Steward’s defenses, asserting that his claims about the absence of consideration were appropriately dismissed. The court further noted that the absence of the witnesses mentioned in Steward's motion for trial postponement did not justify a continuance since Steward had knowledge of their whereabouts and could have secured their attendance earlier. The court also highlighted that the note constituted Steward's individual obligation, emphasizing that it should be pursued solely by Miller, who held the rights to the claim regardless of any potential beneficiary interests involved with a deceased individual.	Annie H. Miller, the plaintiff, claimed that Lewis Steward had failed to honor a promissory note he executed, which obligated him to pay her the amount of $2,968.33. Miller’s argument focused on the legitimacy of her rights to recover on the note, contending that Steward's defenses regarding consideration were unfounded and lacked merit. She sought a judgment in her favor based on the validity of the note.	Lewis Steward, the defendant, sought to challenge the plaintiff's claims by arguing that the promissory note was executed without good or valuable consideration, thus rendering it unenforceable. He also requested a continuance of the trial based on the absence of certain witnesses who could potentially support his position. However, the court found insufficient grounds for his motions and ultimately dismissed the defenses.

Patrick Flynn, the appellant, brought a legal action against the Board of Supervisors of Winnebago County in September 1872, in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a previous case ruled in the Winnebago Circuit Court. Flynn, having served as the sheriff of Winnebago County, sought recovery for fees and compensation for services he and his deputies rendered to the county. The dispute primarily revolved around whether specific statutory provisions allowing a higher rate of fees for certain officers (enacted in 1865 and continued in 1867) remained valid following the adoption of the Illinois Constitution in 1870. The court needed to determine if these earlier special laws were repealed because of the new constitutional framework.	The plaintiff, Patrick Flynn, claimed that he was entitled to certain fees and compensation for his services as sheriff, citing the special acts that were in effect prior to the constitutional changes. He sought to recover the additional fees that he believed were owed to him based on these acts.	The Board of Supervisors of Winnebago County contended that the constitutional amendments enacted in 1870 had repealed the earlier special acts concerning fees and compensation for officers. They argued that Flynn could only claim fees under the general fee legislation in place at the time and that his claims under the special law could not be upheld.

In December 1843, the case "Erastus Higby v. The People, ex rel. Abraham S. Fishbourne" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from Marshall County, where pivotal individuals included Erastus Higby, the defendant, and Abraham S. Fishbourne, the informer and plaintiff acting on behalf of the state. The legal matter arose from an action of debt initiated by Fishbourne to recover a penalty of fifty dollars for violating the state law regulating licenses for clock peddlers. This law mandated that sellers obtain a license before attempting to sell clocks. The initial case was brought before a justice of the peace and later appealed to the circuit court, where it was heard without a jury. The circuit court found in favor of Fishbourne, imposing a judgment of fifty dollars against Higby, allocating half of the sum to Fishbourne and the other half to the county. Higby appealed, challenging the propriety of the dismissal request, arguing that the case was improperly initiated.	The plaintiff, Abraham S. Fishbourne, claimed that Erastus Higby violated the Illinois statute regulating clock peddlers by selling clocks without a required license. Fishbourne sought recovery of a fifty-dollar penalty stipulated in the law, asserting that the suit was appropriately brought in the name of the state for the benefit of both Fishbourne, as the informer, and the county.	The defendant, Erastus Higby, contended that the lawsuit was improperly filed in the name of the people. He argued that the action should have been brought either in the name of the county or, more appropriately, in the name of the informer, since the law specifically stipulated that penalties were to benefit the informer and the county, not the state.

James McKinney and Isaac Finch were involved in a legal dispute that reached the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1834. The case originated in a justice court in Morgan County, where Finch sued McKinney over a sealed promissory note. After Finch won a judgment against McKinney, the case was appealed to the Circuit Court. During the Circuit Court trial, Finch presented the sealed note as evidence. McKinney countered by revealing that on the same day, another suit had been dismissed involving a non-sealed note against him, which was initiated by Finch as well. The dismissal occurred because Finch failed to sufficiently demonstrate the agency of John A. McKinney, who signed the note on McKinney's behalf. Both notes in question had a combined value of less than $100, meaning they could have been consolidated into a single action. McKinney attempted to argue that the 16th section of the “Act concerning Justices of the Peace and Constables” should bar Finch's claim. However, the Circuit Court ruled against McKinney on this defense and awarded judgment to Finch for the sealed note.	Finch's primary argument was based on the validity of the sealed promissory note, which he presented as evidence in the Circuit Court. He sought a judgment against McKinney for the amount owed under this note, asserting that he had a rightful claim for recovery based on the legal binding nature of the document.	McKinney contended that Finch's lawsuit should be barred under the 16th section of the “Act concerning Justices of the Peace and Constables,” which states that parties must consolidate all related demands in suits with a total value under $100. He argued that because Finch did not consolidate his two claims against him, Finch should be prevented from recovering on the sealed note.

In 1867, in Chicago, Illinois, the case of E. W. Dutcher v. Charles H. Beckwith arose from a dispute regarding the collection of a debt for groceries. Charles H. Beckwith (the plaintiff) initiated legal action against Elisha W. Dutcher (the defendant) to recover $149.40, the amount due for groceries delivered to him. The transaction involved F. W. Dutcher, Elisha's brother, who acted as an agent. He visited Beckwith's store accompanied by Aaron W. Pitts, who acted as the guarantor for the payment. After the purchase, the bill was sent to Pitts for collection. Pitts later handed the bill to Elisha, indicating it was sent to him for collection, and Elisha made the payment to Pitts. The court found that Beckwith had not conferred sufficient authority on Pitts to collect the debt, as merely sending the bill did not constitute an agency for collection. The trial was conducted without a jury, and the court ruled in favor of Beckwith, leading to an appeal by Dutcher to the Supreme Court of Illinois seeking to reverse the judgment.	The plaintiff, Charles H. Beckwith, claimed he was owed $149.40 for groceries provided to the defendant. He alleged that the payment made by the defendant to Pitts should be considered valid since Pitts had guaranteed the payment and was therefore an agent in this context. Beckwith requested the court acknowledge the legitimacy of his claim and uphold the judgment against the defendant for the amount owed.	The defendant, Elisha W. Dutcher, argued that the payment made to Pitts was invalid because Pitts was not authorized to collect the debt on Beckwith's behalf. Dutcher contended that simply sending the bill through the mail to Pitts did not grant him any agency to collect funds, and as such, the payment was made at his own risk. The defense sought to have the judgment in favor of Beckwith overturned and was looking to be relieved of the financial obligation.

In the case of Virginia Wolf and Abram D. Wolf v. George W. Campbell, the legal proceedings took place in 1887, specifically on June 7th, in Jefferson County, Illinois. The case originated as an action of forcible detainer, wherein the plaintiffs, Virginia Wolf and Abram D. Wolf, sought to regain possession of certain premises under statutory provisions. The trial was conducted without a jury, and all factual and legal issues were submitted to Judge Carroll C. Boggs. Following the finding that was in favor of the plaintiffs, a judgment was entered, prompting the defendant, George W. Campbell, to appeal the court’s decision. The defendant’s main contention was that the evidence presented did not substantiate the plaintiffs' right to possession. However, the court ruled there were no substantial objections to the complaint or the notice served to the defendant to deliver possession. The record presented to the appellate court raised questions about whether the defendant properly preserved the issue of evidence sufficiency in their motion for a new trial. The court ultimately concluded that the preservation of evidence sufficiency issues was not successfully demonstrated, leading to the upholding of the original judgment.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to possession of the premises in question under the clause of the statute regarding forcible entry and detainer. They argued that the evidence presented supported their claim, and there were no substantial objections to the court’s original findings or rulings. The plaintiffs sought to affirm the trial court's judgment that awarded them possession of the premises.	The defendant contended that the evidence presented did not demonstrate a right of possession for the plaintiffs. He argued that the issues regarding the sufficiency of evidence were not properly preserved for appellate review due to a lack of a formal motion for a new trial being incorporated into the bill of exceptions. The defendant requested the appellate court to overturn the judgment of the lower court based on these grounds.

In the case of John R. Bassett, Adm’r pro tem., v. Emily J. Noble, the events date back to 1848 when the appellee, Emily Noble, at age four, lost her mother and was subsequently bound to her grandfather, William Crapnell. Following her grandfather's death in 1859, Emily, her younger brother, and her widowed mother continued to live on a farm managed by Crapnell’s son, who is also the intestate. Over the years, Emily contributed to household chores and farm work, even attending school with the financial support of her uncle, who expressed intentions to reward her for her hard work with land inheritance. After her uncle's death in 1881, Emily filed a claim against his estate for wages, money allegedly loaned to him, and compensation for various services rendered during his last illness. A county court upheld her claims, awarding her $2,500, which was later reduced to $2,000 in an appeal to the circuit court. The case eventually escalated to the Illinois Appellate Court for further deliberation on the legitimacy of her claims and the application of the Statute of Limitations.	Emily Noble, as the plaintiff, asserted claims against the estate of her deceased uncle for wages accrued over fifteen years, monetary amounts she claimed to have loaned him, and compensation for care provided during his last illness. She sought acknowledgment of her contributions and financial reimbursement for her services, arguing that such amounts were due to her as he had implied he intended to reward her involvement with land.	The defendant, represented by John R. Bassett, argued that Noble's services were rendered as a member of the family rather than as an employee expecting remuneration. They contended there was no express or implied contract for wages. Furthermore, they highlighted that the claims for loans were barred under the Statute of Limitations, and the declarations of intent made by the deceased were mere expressions of gratitude, lacking legal recognition of debt.

In November 1863, the case of Edward Merkle v. Peter Wehrheim took place in Centralia, Illinois. The dispute arose over a real estate transaction involving a half lot of land measuring twenty feet in width. The plaintiff, Edward Merkle, sold this property to the defendant, Peter Wehrheim, for $1,200. At the agreement's signing, Wehrheim made an initial payment of $50 and pledged to pay an additional $450 upon delivery of the deed, with the remaining balance to be paid in three annual installments plus interest. However, Merkle did not hold the title to the property at the time; instead, he had a prior agreement to obtain it from a third party, Zick. Although Wehrheim attempted multiple times to pay the required amounts and obtain the deed, Merkle offered only a deed for nineteen feet instead of the promised twenty feet, citing complications regarding the overhanging eaves of his house. The situation escalated as Wehrheim insisted on receiving the entire twenty feet as per the original contract, leading to a legal confrontation over the specific performance of the contract.	The plaintiff, Edward Merkle, argued that he was unable to fulfill the terms of the contract due to issues with the title and the refusal of Zick to convey the full twenty feet of land. He maintained that the modifications to the agreement—providing a deed for nineteen feet instead—were valid and sought to defend against Wehrheim's claims for specific performance based on the alleged unwritten secondary agreement.	The defendant, Peter Wehrheim, contended that he had fulfilled his contractual obligations by making timely offers to pay the outstanding amounts and demanded specific performance based on the original contract's terms. Wehrheim asserted that Merkle's offer of a deed for only nineteen feet was unacceptable and claimed his right to receive the full twenty feet as outlined in their agreement, thus rejecting any modifications to the contract.

In the case of Andrew Killpatrick, Administrator, v. Thomas Helston, which took place in Hillsboro, Illinois, the events arose following the death of Joseph Helston in February 1885, who died intestate. Joseph's father, the defendant Thomas Helston, filed a claim against his son’s estate in May 1885, seeking compensation for ten and a half years of work he performed as a clerk at a previously agreed upon rate of $25 per month plus board. The County Court initially allowed a claim of $2,000. Subsequently, Thomas amended his claim in the Circuit Court to propose a new rate of $35 per month. The trial led to a judgment of $1,800 in his favor. The evidence presented supported that Thomas performed essential clerical duties for Joseph's hardware business and was regarded as a diligent worker. Despite the familial relationship, the court noted that there was an implied agreement for compensation due to the mutual understanding of the arrangement between Thomas and Joseph. The court concluded that these circumstances established a presumption of liability for Joseph's estate to compensate Thomas for his services rendered.	The plaintiff, Andrew Killpatrick (acting as administrator of Joseph Helston's estate), claimed that the services provided by Thomas were compensated adequately by non-monetary means such as board and clothing during his employment. The plaintiff argued that the lack of a formal agreement negated Thomas's claim for additional wages and maintained that the relationship between them was typically that of parent and child, not employer and employee.	Thomas Helston contended that his long service as a clerk was entitled to fair compensation, suggesting that the originally agreed-upon amount of $25 per month was an underestimation. He argued that he was invited to serve by his son and had an understanding that would allow for his compensation in light of the work he performed, which he believed was worth more than the previously stated rate. Thomas sought to increase his claim to reflect this value, leading to the amended account presented in court.

In 1886, in Muncie, Vermilion County, Illinois, Lydia A. Hoobler, aged approximately 71 and in ill health, became embroiled in a legal dispute following the death of her husband, John Hoobler. The couple had married around 1872 and lived on a thirteen-acre homestead worth $1,500 until separating in 1885. John Hoobler died on April 17, 1886, leaving behind personal property mainly consisting of promissory notes valued at $4,000. Lydia was unaware of his death until nearly 60 days later and subsequently sought letters of administration for her husband’s estate. Shortly after, Andrew J. Hoobler, John’s heir, visited Lydia, persuading her to sign a quit-claim deed and an assignment that relinquished her interests in her husband's estate for $100 and payment of her attorney's fees. Lydia alleged that she was mentally and physically incapacitated at the time of signing and claimed she was misled about the estate's value and her rights. This led her to file a suit in chancery seeking to cancel the documents she signed.	Lydia A. Hoobler claimed that the quit-claim deed and assignment executed in favor of Andrew J. Hoobler were obtained through fraud, as she was mentally incapacitated and unaware of the true value of her husband’s estate during the time of signing. She sought the cancellation of these documents, the recovery of her dower and homestead rights in the estate, and maintenance of her widow’s award, alleging that Andrew had misrepresented the financial status and value of the estate.	Andrew J. Hoobler contended that the deeds were executed with Lydia’s full comprehension and consent. He argued that he presented the situation of the estate accurately, suggesting that Lydia was aware of her rights and the alleged agreement between her and John regarding their estate. The defense maintained that Lydia's claims were unfounded and that the transaction was legitimate, emphasizing that no undue influence or misrepresentation took place during the signing of the documents.

In 1872, in Chicago, Illinois, the Fourth National Bank of Chicago initiated a legal action against William N. Sturges involving a bill of exchange worth $1611.13. The case arose after Sturges, who was procuring grain through an agent named E. Blair in Iowa, agreed to pay for drafts drawn by Blair that were to be cashed at the First National Bank in Washington, Iowa. After these drafts were cashed, the bank sought payment from Sturges, who contended that he had not formally accepted the drafts and alleged a prior settlement on the matter. The dispute was primarily centered on whether Sturges had accepted the drafts, a situation complicated by differing testimonies regarding the existence of any settlement. The trial took place in the Superior Court of Cook County, with evidence provided by representatives from both the bank and Sturges.	The Fourth National Bank contended that Sturges had both verbally agreed to accept the drafts before they were drawn and reaffirmed his obligation to pay after the drafts were issued. They argued that evidence of Sturges' acceptance of the drafts sufficed to validate their claim, and they maintained that the shipping receipt accompanying the draft provided sufficient authority for them to cash it.	Sturges claimed that the proof presented did not support the special count against him and argued that he had merely agreed to accept the drafts but did not do so formally. He asserted that a settlement of the balance due had been reached prior to the lawsuit, although this was contested by bank officials. Sturges maintained that the grain received was in short supply and that a different matter involving his agent Blair was a valid reason for not honoring the payment.

The case, "N. K. Fairbanks, Executor, v. The Merchants National Bank of Chicago," was decided on January 16, 1889, in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved include N. K. Fairbanks, the executor of the estate of Sarah T. Peck, and The Merchants National Bank of Chicago, which acted as the pledgee for shares of stock. The case arose from a dispute regarding the ownership of dividends and additional shares from stock in the Chicago City Railway Company. Originally, Sarah T. Peck had given one hundred shares of stock to her husband, John T. Peck, which he pledged to the bank to secure his individual debts. While the stock remained in pledge, Sarah continued to receive dividends until June 19, 1883. The rail company later allowed stockholders to subscribe for additional shares at a discounted rate, which Sarah Peck did. The bank claimed the dividends collected by Sarah and the new shares issued were rightfully theirs, as they were secured by the pledged shares. The court below found in favor of the bank, and Fairbanks subsequently appealed, challenging the decree and asserting the original stock remained Sarah's property, with no proper transfer made to the bank.	N. K. Fairbanks, as executor, contended that the stock and the associated dividends belonged to Sarah T. Peck, asserting that her intention was to maintain ownership despite the pledge. Fairbanks argued that the stock was merely secured as collateral for John T. Peck's debt. He claimed the renewal of loans by the bank released the security on the stock, leading to the conclusion that Sarah retained the rights to the dividends and the new shares that accumulated as a result of her original stock ownership.	The Merchants National Bank defended its position by claiming rightful ownership of the dividends and the new shares due to the pledge arrangement. The bank asserted that the renewals of the loan did not constitute a release of the security since the original indebtedness remained intact. It emphasized that a pledgee is entitled to the dividends on pledged stock and that there was no evidence the bank acquiesced to the collection of dividends by Sarah Peck. The bank also maintained that the renewal of notes did not alter or release their claim to the collateralized stock.

Charles F. Keener, as the executor of the estate of John Peniger, deceased, appealed a case in December 1857 to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Scott County, Illinois, and involved the plaintiff's wife, Sarah Crull, who had worked for Peniger from 1833 to 1838 while she was single. She claimed that Peniger had agreed to pay her $200 per year for her services but had failed to do so before his death. After Peniger's passing, Keener, as executor, sought to recover the debt for Sarah's services. During the proceedings, it was established that the debt had become barred by the statute of limitations, and the case hinged on whether a conversation in 1850 between George Longwith and Peniger constituted a new promise that could revive the debt. The court ultimately examined conflicting legal interpretations regarding such statutes and whether mere acknowledgment of the debt could take the case out of the statutory limits.	The plaintiff, Charles F. Keener, claimed that as the executor of John Peniger, he should be entitled to collect on the debt owed to Sarah Crull for her services. He argued that the admission made by Peniger to George Longwith about the unpaid debt was sufficient to constitute a new promise and therefore revive the claim, allowing them to overcome the statute of limitations.	The defendants, George and Sarah Crull, contended that the statute of limitations barred the plaintiff's claim for the debt. They argued that the conversation between Peniger and Longwith did not sufficiently establish a new promise, as it was made to a third party rather than to Sarah or her authorized representative. They insisted that the acknowledgment of the debt was not unequivocal and did not satisfy the requirements necessary to remove the debt from the statute of limitations.

William H. W. Cushman, the appellant, engaged in a legal dispute against Joseph O. Glover and Burton C. Cook, the appellees, in the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1850. The case originated from an action of trover regarding a promissory note for $75 executed by J. V. A. Hoes, payable to the appellees, with a due date of February 27, 1850. The case was initially brought before a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment in favor of the appellees. Cushman, dissatisfied with this outcome, appealed to the Circuit Court, where the judgment was again in favor of the appellees. The case revolved around two powers of attorney granted by Isaac H. Fredenburgh, which authorized Cushman and John Fredenburgh to act on behalf of Fredenburgh regarding claims owed to him. Tensions arose over the ownership of the promissory note, particularly as it was claimed that the appellees had acquired it as part of their service representing Fredenburgh in a ferry-related claim.	The plaintiff, Joseph O. Glover and Burton C. Cook, asserted that they were entitled to recover the amount specified in the promissory note, which they had appropriately secured from the note's maker. They argued that they had legally acted as attorneys and that their claim to the note was justified under their powers of attorney in relation to Isaac H. Fredenburgh's interests. They sought a judgment in their favor for the full value of the note plus associated costs.	William H. W. Cushman contended that the power of attorney he received from Isaac H. Fredenburgh gave him the legal right to act on the principal's behalf, potentially including the disposition of the note. He argued that his authority was equal to that of John Fredenburgh and aimed to assert that the second power of attorney did not eliminate his rights to the note. Cushman requested that the court overturn the earlier judgments, claiming he retained rights over the promissory note.

In 1860, the case of William F. Keeler et al. v. George C. Campbell took place in La Salle County, Illinois. William F. Keeler and others (plaintiffs) initiated an action of assumpsit based on an assigned promissory note against George C. Campbell (defendant). The plaintiffs included a special count as well as common counts in their declaration. The defendant responded by filing a demurrer against the special count and pleaded the general issue to the common counts, essentially contesting the validity of the plaintiffs' claim. The lower court overruled the demurrer and issued a judgment for the plaintiffs without addressing the common counts. The defendant appealed this judgment, arguing that the assignment of the promissory note was improperly documented and that the damages should not have been assessed while the issues regarding the common counts remained undetermined.	The plaintiffs argued that the defendant was liable under the terms of the assigned note and that the lower court's ruling in their favor on the special count was justified. They maintained that the action of the court to issue a judgment while leaving the common counts unresolved was appropriate, presenting their claim for damages based on the alleged breach of the promissory note.	The defendant contended that the special count did not adequately comply with legal requirements necessary for the assignment of a promissory note and that it lacked an averment of indorsement on the note itself. The defendant further claimed it was erroneous for the court to assess damages without resolving the issues surrounding the common counts, asserting that this practice contradicts established legal norms and could lead to improper multiple judgments.

In the case of James Lindsay v. Sarah Stout decided in September 1871, the legal proceedings took place in Edgar County, Illinois. The case involved James Lindsay (the plaintiff) filing a lawsuit against Sarah Stout (the defendant) regarding two promissory notes. The initial complication arose from the defendant's plea in abatement, claiming that Lindsay was a married woman at the time the suit commenced and that her husband was still alive. This assertion suggested that Lindsay may not have had the legal standing to sue. Lindsay responded by demurring, then withdrew the demurrer and claimed that the promissory notes were her sole and separate property. Following this exchange, the defendant filed a general issue and special plea alleging that the notes had been obtained through fraud. As the case progressed, the defendant later withdrew the general issue, leaving the trial to proceed based solely on the plea of fraud. Ultimately, a jury found in favor of Lindsay, awarding her $265.33, but the court found errors in the process that required further examination of the unanswered plea regarding fraud.	James Lindsay asserted that the promissory notes were her separate property and contended that the issue of her legal standing to sue could not apply to her case. She sought enforcement of the promissory notes, requesting the court to adjudicate in her favor and award damages resulting from the defendant's actions.	Sarah Stout defended against the claims by raising a plea in abatement, arguing that Lindsay was a married woman and thus could not maintain this suit independently. Furthermore, she claimed that the promissory notes were obtained through fraudulent means, which she sought to prove at trial. Stout ultimately aimed to have the court dismiss Lindsay's claims based on these defenses.

This case, Thomas H. Fowler et al. v. Joseph W. Arnold, was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1861. The dispute originated in Sangamon County, Illinois, where Joseph W. Arnold filed an action of assumpsit (a legal term for a type of lawsuit concerning a breach of contract) against Thomas H. Fowler, Rufus S. Lord, and Edwin S. Fowler. The defendants challenged the writ by filing a plea in abatement, which is a procedural motion intended to halt the proceedings. However, the plaintiff, Arnold, successfully moved to strike this plea from the court's files. The court's decision to strike down the plea was the primary focus of the appeal, as it was determined to be improperly entitled, with omissions of the names of two defendants in both the margin and the body of the plea. This raised concerns about the proper identification of parties involved in legal proceedings, particularly in dilatory pleas where technical accuracy is crucial.	The plaintiff, Joseph W. Arnold, claimed that the defendants improperly filed a plea in abatement, which he argued was not correctly entitled and therefore should be dismissed. Arnold's legal request was for the court to strike this plea from consideration, as it failed to meet the necessary technical requirements for legal documents within the jurisdiction.	The defendants—Thomas H. Fowler, Rufus S. Lord, and Edwin S. Fowler—sought to challenge the action through a plea in abatement. However, their defense was primarily based on technicalities of the legal process, arguing against the validity of Arnold's claim without disputing the justice of the demand. They contended that their plea should be allowed to proceed in spite of the procedural shortcomings identified by the plaintiff.

In the case of William L. Rush v. Joseph Fister and Peter Arb, which was decided on June 7, 1887, in Alton, Illinois, the dispute revolves around a promissory note signed by the defendants and made payable to W. W. Green, who was the administrator for De Witt Helen. The note, amounting to $282, was supposed to be paid for the rent of three and three-quarters acres of wheat land for the period from August 1, 1883, to August 1, 1884. The case was brought by William L. Rush, acting as the assignee of Annie Carter, who previously held the note. The only defense raised by the defendants was a non-assumpsit plea. During the trial, the court instructed the jury that if they found Annie Carter was a married woman residing in Missouri at the time she assigned the note, and if it was not proven that Missouri law had changed to allow such an assignment, they had to find for the defendants. This instruction was contested since all parties admitted to Annie Carter's marital status and residence but did not address the validity of the assignment itself. The case ultimately focused on whether the assignment of the note was valid and raised questions about instructions provided to the jury that could prejudice the plaintiff’s case.	The plaintiff, William L. Rush, claimed that he had valid title to the promissory note through the assignment from Annie Carter. He argued that the common law accepted the assignment as valid because it was supported by the consent of Carter’s husband. Rush sought to enforce the note, asserting that the defendants improperly denied their obligation to pay, thus demanding payment based on the validity of the assigned note.	The defendants, Joseph Fister and Peter Arb, contended that the assignment of the promissory note was invalid because it was made by a married woman without proper evidence showing that Missouri law permitted such an assignment. They claimed that since Annie Carter resided in Missouri, the presumption was that the common law applied, which prevented a married woman from assigning the note. They also argued that they had already settled the debt with a third party, Buckman, who they claimed had legitimate ownership of the note, thus stating that they should not be liable to Rush.

Henry D. Cogswell filed a bill of interpleader in January 1875 against William Armstrong and several other parties in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case centers on a land purchase made by Cogswell from Armstrong on August 18, 1869, where Cogswell paid with three promissory notes secured by a mortgage on the property. After some payments were made on these notes, Armstrong transferred the two remaining notes to S. M. Murphy & Co. to secure his own debt. Disputes arose when Armstrong, while indebted to other parties, instructed Cogswell to pay the remaining balance to him, despite these conflicting claims from the other creditors. A default was entered against Armstrong when he did not appear in court. Ultimately, the case focused on determining to whom Cogswell should pay the remaining balance on the notes, alongside considerations of a prior judgment he held against Armstrong.	Cogswell argued that both S. M. Murphy & Co. and the other parties were claiming interest in the notes he originally provided to Armstrong. His claims sought a legal determination of who was entitled to the remaining balance due on the notes after accounting for previous payments. Cogswell requested the court to allow him to deduct the judgment of $72 he obtained against Armstrong from the balance owed.	S. M. Murphy & Co. contended that they were entitled to the amount claimed through the garnishee judgment against Armstrong, asserting that Cogswell had no right to dispute their claim to the funds. They argued that Cogswell, having initiated the interpleader, could not seek a portion of the funds for himself.

In 1880, in Galena, Illinois, Edward C. Simmons, a 28-year-old laborer, was killed while working for the Chicago and Tomah Railroad Company. He was part of a team engaged in excavating a hill, which involved dangerous practices of undermining a bank of clay. Despite warnings from both the railroad's superintendent and his foreman regarding the hazardous nature of the work, Simmons continued working at a particularly risky spot of the excavation. During this unsafe operation, a significant mass of earth fell and fatally injured him. Following his death, his administrator, Mary Ann Simmons, pursued legal action against the railroad company, claiming negligence, after a previous trial ruled in her favor but was reversed upon appeal. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court after the lower courts directed a verdict for the defendant, citing the lack of sufficient evidence for the plaintiff’s claims.	The plaintiff, represented by Mary Ann Simmons, alleged negligence on the part of the defendant, asserting that the railroad company failed to provide a safe working environment. The suit claimed that the company neglected its duty to ensure the work was conducted safely and that they did not employ competent supervision necessary to protect workers, leading to the fatal accident. The plaintiff sought damages for the death of Edward Simmons, arguing that the defendant's improper management directly caused the incident.	The defendant, the Chicago and Tomah Railroad Company, argued that the evidence presented was insufficient to establish negligence on their part. They maintained that Simmons voluntarily engaged in a known risky activity, having been cautioned about the dangers and being aware of the hazardous conditions. The defendant contended that the plaintiff's claims centered on the theory of negligence must be dismissed because Simmons assumed the risk that came with his work, and that there was no breach of duty or negligence involved in how the work was managed.

In the year 1842, in Knox County, Illinois, the case of Henry S. Cooper v. Gilbert Buckingham emerged. Buckingham initiated an action of assumpsit against Cooper, which included two counts – one on a promissory note and the other in indebitatum assumpsit (a type of claim for the recovery of debt). Cooper, as the defendant, entered a non assumpsit plea to the declaration and submitted four special pleas regarding the first count. Following this, Buckingham filed replications, resulting in various factual issues being raised. Despite being permitted to amend his declaration, it appears no amendments were made. At the next court term, Buckingham motioned to strike Cooper's pleas from the records, leading the court to rule in favor of Buckingham and issue a default judgment against Cooper for $162.05. This procedure became the subject of appeal due to alleged irregularities in how the case had been handled in the previous court.	Buckingham's primary arguments were based on the claim that Cooper owed him money as stipulated in the promissory note and in the indebitatum assumpsit. He sought to hold Cooper accountable for the claimed debt through the legal action initiated against him, ultimately seeking a judgment in his favor for the amount owed.	Cooper's defenses revolved around disputing the claims presented by Buckingham. He asserted a non assumpsit plea, indicating that he did not owe the amount alleged. Cooper also filed several special defenses pertaining to the promissory note in question, seeking to demonstrate that the court did not have sufficient grounds to rule against him, especially in light of the summary judgment that was issued without proper jury review.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois v. Kirk Hawes, a Judge of the Superior Court" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on February 1, 1888. The dispute involved a petition for a writ of mandamus aimed at compelling Judge Kirk Hawes to sign and seal a bill of exceptions in a case previously heard in his court. The original case was initiated by Emilie Pul ver against the Bochester German Insurance Company regarding damages from a fire affecting her insured personal property. After a jury verdict favored the insurance company, Pul ver's request for a new trial was denied, leading her to seek an appeal. She completed a draft of the bill of exceptions by June 22, 1887, which was not signed by Judge Hawes due to his concerns over his authority to do so after the closure of the term. Despite a written stipulation to extend the deadline for the filing of the bill of exceptions, the judge refrained from signing it. The legal question raised was whether the stipulation authorized the judge to act after the term had officially ended.	The plaintiff, Emilie Pul ver, claimed that the judge had the legal authority to sign the bill of exceptions even after the term had ended, especially since the parties involved had an agreement to extend the deadline. Pul ver's main legal request was the issuance of a writ of mandamus to compel Judge Hawes to fulfill his duty of signing the settled bill of exceptions for the appeal.	Judge Kirk Hawes defended his refusal to sign the bill by arguing that the judicial record was closed at the end of the term, and he had no power to act upon the bill afterward. He maintained that the authority to extend the filing time for the bill could not be exercised in vacation and that he had acted within his lawful discretion by choosing not to sign the bill of exceptions.

Lucas R. Williams was indicted in Cook County, Illinois, for allegedly practicing medicine without the proper certification, in violation of the "Act to regulate the practice of medicine in the State of Illinois," approved on May 29, 1877. Williams, a graduate of Rush Medical College, received his diploma on February 16, 1875, before the enactment of the law. He presented his diploma to the State Board of Health on November 22, 1877, which confirmed its authenticity and issued him a certificate of qualification. However, on February 6, 1880, the board revoked this certificate, claiming authority to do so under the act. Williams was subsequently convicted and fined fifty dollars for practicing medicine after the revocation of his certificate. The case was then brought to the Illinois Appellate Court for review.	The plaintiff, the People, argued that Williams was practicing medicine without the required certification after his revocation. They contended that the State Board of Health had the authority to revoke his certificate due to alleged unprofessional conduct, and thus Williams should be penalized for violating the medical practice act.	Williams's defense was based on the assertion that he had complied with all necessary requirements to practice medicine as per the law prior to the revocation of his certificate. They argued that the statute did not explicitly state that a revocation would nullify his right to practice medicine retroactively. Since he had initially received a certificate confirming his qualifications, the defense claimed that there was no legal basis for his conviction.

In September 1845, Caleb Jones and his wife were involved in a legal dispute with Marshall Smith stemming from the sale of property following two judgments against Jones. Smith, who acted as surety for Jones, purchased the property after executions were levied on the judgments. There were allegations of mistakes regarding the execution dates and claims that Jones fraudulently conveyed property to their daughter. The case progressed with various filings, including Jones's cross-bill that aimed to challenge the original judgment claims. The Illinois Supreme Court focused on procedural aspects, particularly the striking of Jones's cross-bill, which sought to establish that the judgments had been satisfied through an agreement with the creditors. The cross-bill included claims against the original judgment creditors who were not parties in the initial suit but had a vested interest given the allegations made. The court found error in not allowing the cross-bill to be prosecuted and considered its implications on Jones’s rights.	The plaintiffs, represented by Caleb Jones, claim that he had already made satisfactory arrangements regarding the judgments against him and that the issuance of executions against his property was improper. They argue that the agreements made with the judgment creditors included the acceptance of notes and mortgages in full satisfaction of the judgments, which should have been recorded. Jones seeks to have the previous sales set aside and the judgments satisfied on record.	Marshall Smith, the defendant, argues that he acquired valid rights through his purchase at the sheriff's sale and denies the claims made by Jones regarding the satisfaction of the judgments. Smith contends that the mistakes and allegations of fraud do not negate the legal standing of the judgments nor his claim to the property purchased. He asserts that he was justified in pursuing the original suit to confirm his rights derived from the executions.

The case, "The Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railway Company et al. v. John Eininger," was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court and decided on May 15, 1885. The incident occurred around 4 p.m. in Chicago when the plaintiff, John Eininger, a minor, was allegedly injured by a freight train operated by the defendants while he was walking along Twenty-fourth Street at a railroad crossing. The injury reportedly happened when the plaintiff was either attempting to climb onto the moving train or walking on the railway track, which the defendants claimed was illegal. Evidence showed that the injury occurred after the plaintiff had walked from a distance north of the crossing, crossing onto the private right of way of the railway company. The case revolved around whether the plaintiff exercised appropriate care and whether he could be held negligent given his age and the circumstances surrounding the incident. The defendants contended the plaintiff’s actions led to his injury, while the plaintiff argued against the lack of safety measures at the crossing, such as the absence of a flagman, in their claims.	The plaintiff asserted that he sustained injuries while rightfully crossing the railroad track at Twenty-fourth Street, suggesting negligence on the part of the railroad companies for failing to provide safety measures such as a flagman, which was required by city ordinance. His legal request included damages for the injuries sustained due to what he claimed was the defendants’ negligence.	The defendants claimed that the plaintiff was not a lawful traveler and was attempting to climb onto the moving train when he was injured, thereby attributing the injury to the plaintiff's own negligence. They sought to demonstrate that the plaintiff was outside of the protections afforded to lawful crossings and that they were not liable for his actions, which they argued violated state law.

In 1873, the Illinois Supreme Court addressed a legal dispute stemming from the will of Osborne Ridgeway, who passed away in 1841. The case involved parties including plaintiffs Robert Underwood, Benjamin F. Burns, and James McGee, who purchased interests from some of Ridgeway's seven children. The will specified that Ridgeway’s wife, Jane, would receive support from the family farm during her lifetime, after which the farm would be sold, and proceeds divided among the seven youngest children, with provisions for cases of death among those children. Alexander and George Ridgeway contested the validity of the assignments made by their siblings, asserting that such interests were not directly assignable until certain conditions specified in the will were met. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, facilitating the sale of the land and distribution of proceeds, prompting the Ridgeway brothers to appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed they had purchased the equitable interests of almost all of the seven children specified in the will, thus entitled to the proceeds of the property once sold. They sought a court decree for the property’s sale and distribution of proceeds based on their claims of ownership and assignment validity, challenging only the rights of the remaining, unpurchased children.	The defendants, specifically Alexander and George Ridgeway, contended that their siblings' assignments were invalid and denied that any valid legal interests were transferred. They argued that the question of when the interests vested was unclear and that the conveyances made before the widow's death were not enforceable. They maintained that their expected shares were being diminished without their rightful consent.

Frank J. Hoffman initiated a garnishee proceeding against Fitzwilliam & Sons in McLean County, Illinois, resulting in a court case decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1876. The action arose from wages owed to Hoffman, who was employed by Fitzwilliam & Sons. The garnishment was based on a writ served against the employer, seeking to secure payment of wages that had become due. Prior to the service of the writ, Hoffman had earned $500 in wages but had received these payments in weekly installments, not exceeding $25. After the writ was served, it was discovered that the wages he was entitled to receive did not exceed the statutory exemption, allowing for payment to him without legal hindrance. The court was concerned with the applicable statutes regarding wage garnishment and whether Hoffman could collect his earnings after the service of the writ.	The plaintiff argued that Fitzwilliam & Sons were obligated to pay Hoffman's wages that had accrued after the service of the garnishment writ, even though the judgment debtor had previously been working under an employment contract. The plaintiff's main contention was that the wages should be safeguarded from garnishment because they were below the statutory exempted amount of $25 and that Hoffman's status as the head of a family entitled him to receive his earnings.	Fitzwilliam & Sons contended that, according to existing statutes, they had the legal right to pay Hoffman his wages that had accrued post-writ, as those amounts were less than the legal exemption limit. The defense argued that it did not matter whether Hoffman terminated his previous employment contract upon the service of the writ, as the subsequent payment arrangement remained within the statutory exemption provisions preventing garnishment.

In January 1871, in Pecatonica, Illinois, Serdatius Kitzinger entered into a contract with George W. Sanborn and others for the sale and delivery of twelve fat hogs. The agreement stipulated that the hogs were to be delivered on January 14, 1871, but the delivery was contingent upon favorable weather conditions. Sanborn and his associates sought to enforce the contract when Kitzinger failed to deliver the hogs, resulting in a legal dispute. Initially, the case was heard in a justice court, where Kitzinger was favored, but upon appeal to the circuit court, a jury ruled in Sanborn's favor, awarding him nine dollars in damages. Kitzinger contended that the delivery was conditional based on weather, asserting that the stormy conditions on the delivery date prevented performance. The jury found that the conditions regarding the weather were not part of their agreement, leading Kitzinger to appeal the judgment.	Sanborn argued that Kitzinger had unconditionally agreed to deliver the hogs on the specified date and that the failure to do so, regardless of the weather, entitled him to damages. He sought compensation for the difference between the contract price and the market value of the hogs at the time they should have been delivered.	Kitzinger's defense rested on the claim that the contract was conditional upon good weather. He maintained that the inclement weather on the delivery day constituted a valid excuse for his inability to fulfill the contract. He also argued that the plaintiffs had failed to demonstrate they were ready and willing to pay for the hogs at the time of delivery.

James Mason, the appellant, engaged in legal action against Robert Wash, the appellee, who was suing on behalf of the City Bank of New York, concerning a promissory note issued by S. S. and C. Porter in New York. The note, executed six months prior to its due date, was assigned to Mason by its creators, and upon maturity, payment was refused. This event prompted Mason to present the note at New York for payment, which was subsequently declined, and he duly notified of non-payment. Following this, a legal dispute arose regarding Mason's liability as the assignor of the note. The defendant, Wash, demurred to the declaration claiming Mason's obligations, which the court overruled. Washing then pleaded his discharge under New York's bankruptcy laws, which led to further legal maneuvers including a demurrer from Mason. After a series of motions and judgments, including a motion to arrest judgment that was overruled, the case advanced to an appeal with several errors assigned for consideration, including the proper application of state laws and bankruptcy regulations.	Mason claimed that as the assignor of the promissory note, he was entitled to recover the amount owed due to non-payment by the makers. He argued that the proper legal procedures regarding the assignment and collection of the note had been followed, thereby establishing his right to seek enforcement of the debt.	Wash contended that Mason's liability as the assignor was contingent upon having pursued due diligence in collecting payment from the makers of the note. He further claimed that he was protected from liability under the provisions of the New York bankrupt laws, which discharged him from debts incurred prior to his bankruptcy proceedings.

John B. Jolly and G. P. Calvin, acting as administrators, filed a case against Stephen Fitzgerald and his family in the Illinois Appellate Court, with a decision made on June 7, 1887. The dispute centered on a tract of land in White County, Illinois, which was allegedly conveyed fraudulently to hinder Fitzgerald's creditors. This conveyance involved Solomon Charles transferring the land to John W. Stum, who was Stephen's brother-in-law, and subsequently to Fanny Fitzgerald, Stephen’s wife. The plaintiffs, representing Fitzgerald's creditors, claimed that the conveyances were mere fronts to delay and defraud the creditors, as it was suggested that Stum was holding the title in secret for Stephen. Emergency procedures had been followed over several years, including a bankruptcy adjudication for Stephen in 1873, followed by evidence hearings which led to previous court dismissals against Stum and the Fitzgeralds. In light of this, the court determined that the plaintiffs were barred from pursuing their claims because the legal principles of "res adjudicata" applied, precluding them from contesting matters that had already been settled in previous legal proceedings.	The plaintiffs argued that the conveyances of the land were fraudulent and made to hinder and delay Stephen Fitzgerald's creditors. They sought a decree to recognize the land as the property of the bankrupt estate and requested that the land be sold to satisfy their judgments against Fitzgerald. They asserted that the conveyances should be reversed based on the alleged collusion and fraudulent intent.	The defendants, including Stum and the Fitzgerald family, denied the allegations of fraud. They contended that the plaintiffs were barred from seeking remedies since prior decisions had already adjudicated similar claims. They argued that the plaintiffs could not maintain a bill against Fitzgerald under the Bankrupt Act without involving the assignee, and they emphasized the finality of the previous court decrees.

In September 1868, the case of James Keating v. Bridget Keating was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The legal dispute originated from a divorce suit initiated by Bridget Keating against her husband, James Keating, in the Recorder’s Court of Chicago, presided over by Judge Evart Yan Burén. The court initially ruled in favor of Bridget, granting her a decree that included the fee to a property located at 205 Third Avenue, owned by James, along with a monetary award as alimony. The controversial aspect of the ruling centered on the extent and nature of the alimony awarded, which James claimed was excessive and improperly granted. After addressing the case, the court of review found that the justification for granting the fee title based on Bridget’s alleged financial contribution was unfounded. The case cited previous rulings emphasizing that, in divorce proceedings, the preferred method for awarding alimony is through annual allowances under court control, rather than outright ownership of property.	Bridget Keating's main arguments include that the alimony awarded to her was justified based on her financial contributions, which the court initially recognized by granting her ownership of the property. She sought to establish her entitlement to a significant share of James Keating's assets through both property ownership and monetary compensation, asserting that such an arrangement was necessary for her support post-divorce.	James Keating's key arguments revolved around the claim that the award of the property as alimony was unjustified since the property was not purchased with Bridget's money, contrary to the court’s findings. He contended that the better practice for determining alimony should involve periodic monetary allowances rather than transferring property ownership. James sought a modification of the decree, requesting instead a life estate or annuity for Bridget but not the outright fee in the property.

In December 1857, in Macoupin, Illinois, Charles P. French (the appellant) was involved in a legal dispute with Henry Lowry (the appellee). Lowry initiated the case before a justice of the peace, claiming $44 for carpenter work and materials he had provided. The justice ruled in favor of Lowry, prompting French to appeal the judgment to the Circuit Court. During the trial, Lowry presented witnesses who testified to the account of work done and materials supplied. One witness mentioned that in March 1855, he presented an account to French, who acknowledged part of it but indicated that some payments wouldn’t be due until the following Christmas. French attempted to counter the claim by pointing to a previous lawsuit he had filed against Lowry for a different amount, but this was deemed unrelated. After reviewing the evidence, the Circuit Court upheld the original judgment in favor of Lowry.	Lowry's primary claim was that he was owed $44 for work done and materials provided to French. He supported his claim with testimonies indicating that he had completed the work and presented his account properly to the defendant, who did not dispute its accuracy at the time but raised concerns over the payment timeline.	French argued that the amount claimed by Lowry should not be due until a later date, referencing a conversation he had where Lowry confirmed that part of the payment would not be owed until Christmas. He also attempted to invalidate the claim by citing a prior judgment on a separate, unrelated account, suggesting that it involved the same subject matter, which was not relevant to this case.

In the case titled "The Kankakee Stone and Lime Company v. The City of Kankakee," the proceedings took place in Kankakee, Illinois, culminating in a judgment on April 3, 1889. The core issue revolves around a local ordinance mandating the construction of a sidewalk on the east side of Fifth Avenue and Bourbonais Grove road, with special assessments to be levied against adjacent properties benefiting from this construction. The Kankakee Stone and Lime Company (the appellant) did not fulfill its obligation to construct the required sidewalk and consequently, the city council initiated a petition to the county court for a special assessment against the company's property.   The court appointed commissioners who determined the assessment amount. The appellant contested this assessment, asserting that the ordinance was improperly passed without mayoral certification and that the jury’s instructions were misleading regarding the valuation of their property. Issues arose concerning whether current property usage could be considered in determining market value for the assessment. The jury ultimately returned a verdict that influenced the modification of the assessment roll by the court, which upheld the modified roll.
