The case represents a conflict between municipal improvement mandates and property owners' rights concerning assessments and perceived benefits.	The Kankakee Stone and Lime Company claimed that the sidewalk ordinance was not properly enacted because it had not been certified or approved by the mayor. They argued that this procedural flaw should invalidate the special assessment against their property. Furthermore, they contended that the jury was incorrectly instructed to exclude the current use of their property from consideration in determining its market value, which they asserted led to an incorrectly high assessment that did not properly reflect the benefits of the sidewalk.	The City of Kankakee defended the ordinance’s validity and the assessment process, asserting that the ordinance had been read without objection and that any procedural objections made by the appellant were raised too late and thus not admissible. The city maintained that the assessment adequately reflected the benefits derived from the improvement, and that the instructions given to the jury correctly guided them to evaluate the potential increase in property market values resulting from the sidewalk, irrespective of current uses.

In September 1868, the case of Thomas Fortin et al. v. The United States Wind Engine and Pump Company was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated from a dispute in Kankakee County, Illinois, involving two brothers, Thomas Fortin and his brother, who farmed and raised stock together. They had a history of purchasing goods jointly, with payments being made interchangeably between them. The conflict arose when the brother purchased a pump intended for joint use on their farm, but it was placed on his portion of the land. The United States Wind Engine and Pump Company contested the purchase's labeling as a joint account, prompting the court to examine evidence regarding their business practices. The court had to decide whether the jury's conclusion that the brothers were jointly liable for the purchase was supported by adequate evidence.	The plaintiffs, Thomas Fortin and his brother, argued that the pump purchased from the defendant company was meant for their joint farming and stock-raising endeavors. They contended that their established practice of purchasing goods together justified the conclusion that the pump was acquired on a joint account, despite being placed on one brother's land. The plaintiffs sought a judgment affirming their joint liability for the purchase.	The defendant, The United States Wind Engine and Pump Company, contended that the pump purchase could not be deemed a joint account because only one brother was present at the time of the transaction. They argued that as it was positioned solely on the land of the brother who made the purchase, the liability should not extend jointly. The defense requested that the findings of the jury, which suggested joint liability, be overturned as they viewed the evidence as insufficient to support such a conclusion.

Thomas F. Harwood et al. v. Emma C. Cox is a legal case that took place in McLean County, Illinois, culminating in a decision on November 18, 1887. The dispute arose from foreclosure proceedings wherein a decree had been rendered against Emma C. Cox and her husband, concerning three mortgages they had executed. Following this decree, the court allowed for a sale by a master, from which Thomas F. Harwood purchased the property in question. However, after the sale, significant irregularities were noted: the master did not file a duplicate of the certificate of purchase, failed to report the sale to the court, and costs associated with the sale were not paid. Fifteen months post-sale, Harwood, through his attorney, received a deed for the property from the successor of the master, but whether he had fully acquired the certificate remains unclear. The case escalated when Cox filed a motion to set aside the sale, arguing that it was not in accordance with the original decree and violated necessary legal protocols. The court ultimately determined that the sale should be vacated due to these procedural failures.	The plaintiff, Emma C. Cox, contended that the sale of the property to Thomas F. Harwood was invalid due to multiple irregularities, including the absence of a filed duplicate of the purchase certificate, lack of payment of necessary costs, and the failure of the master to report the sale to the court. She argued that these factors nullified the sale and thus requested the court to set aside the sale and the deed issued to Harwood.	Thomas F. Harwood, the defendant, affirmed that he legally purchased the property and claimed that the sale was valid despite the irregularities. He argued based on precedent that the court should not be able to unilaterally set aside the sale after the expiration of the time for redemption and that the lack of a reported sale should not invalidate his rights, especially since a third party (Whitbeck) bought the property from him on the assumption of its validity.

Elmer Nichols was indicted for larceny in the Court of Common Pleas of Aurora, Kane County, Illinois. The indictment stated that Nichols, in possession of goods belonging to Joel Jenks, stole items valued at $210, including a horse, a buggy, and a harness. Following the trial, Nichols was found guilty and sentenced to one year in the penitentiary. He filed a motion for a new trial, claiming there were errors in the indictment and trial process, but this was overruled. The jury determined that the property was taken with felonious intent based on the evidence presented, and no error in the judgment was identified by the court.	The plaintiff, represented by Mr. C. J. Metzner, claimed that the indictment had deficiencies, particularly regarding the venue, and argued that these issues warranted a new trial. They contended that the jury's decision lacked justifications due to these supposed errors.	The defendant, represented by Mr. C. Blanchard, asserted that there were no errors in the trial process or the jury's decision. They argued that the lack of venue in the indictment could not be challenged after the verdict had been given, as there had been no motion to quash the indictment prior to the verdict, and maintained that the evidence supported the jury's findings of felonious intent.

In June 1837, the case of Francis Arenz v. William Reihle and Joseph Bains was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court. The initial proceedings took place in the Morgan Circuit Court in 1835, where two attachments had been issued against Samuel P. Judson, with Arenz summoned as a garnishee in both cases. The parties agreed to consolidate the cases and have them tried by the court without a jury. The trial involved the question of ownership of goods that had been attached and claimed by Reihle and Bains. Arenz contended that the goods, which had been delivered to him by Judson, did not belong to Judson but to David Sheldon, who had initially claimed them prior to the attachments. Throughout the trial, Arenz contested the introduction of certain evidentiary records and the decisions made by the court regarding additional interrogatories and judgments. The court ultimately ruled in favor of Reihle and Bains for one of the attachments and against Arenz for another, leading to his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, William Reihle and Joseph Bains, claimed that Francis Arenz was improperly holding goods that rightfully belonged to Samuel P. Judson and were subject to their attachments. They sought to recover $1,782.18, arguing through the evidence presented that the goods delivered to Arenz and claimed by him were indeed Judson’s property, thus liable to the plaintiffs' claims.	Francis Arenz, the appellant, argued that the goods he held were legitimate and not subject to the attachments. He contended that errors had occurred during the trial, including the court permitting the introduction of certain records and interrogatories that should have been excluded. He also argued that the judgments against him were erroneous and did not reflect a fair analysis of the ownership of the goods in question.

In September 1876, the case of Dick Richardson et al. v. Moses W. Lester et al. was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a garnishment action involving Richardson & Robinson, who were debtors against whom the defendants were executing a chattel mortgage. The location of the case was Coolc County, Illinois, where the Superior Court initially presided over the matter. The defendants were summoned as garnishees by judgment creditors of Richardson & Robinson, claiming no property or rights belonging to the debtors were in their possession. The evidence presented showed that although only one partner executed the mortgage, the other partner witnessed it and knew it pertained to partnership property and debts. This complicated the matter as the relationship between the partners and their obligations was scrutinized. The court needed to determine if the defendants were correctly denying the creditors a claim against the property involved.	The plaintiffs, representing the judgment creditors of Richardson & Robinson, argued that the defendants wrongfully failed to account for property secured under the chattel mortgage. They claimed that the property was seized should rightfully serve to satisfy the debts owed by Richardson & Robinson, insisting that the defendants held possession of assets that should be accessible to cover those obligations.	The defendants contended that they did not possess any moneys, rights, credits, or effects owed to either Richardson or Robinson. They further claimed legitimacy in their ownership and right to the property derived from the chattel mortgage, emphasizing that the mortgage was valid despite only one partner executing it. They argued that the witnessing of the mortgage execution by Robinson estopped him from denying its validity, particularly since he did not object when the property was sold.

The case "George Sickmon v. Joshua Wood" took place in September 1873 in Warren County, Illinois. The legal dispute arose from a mortgage foreclosure action initiated by Joshua Wood against Harlan P. Garish and George Sickmon. The mortgage in question contained a mistaken description regarding the land, where it was stated to refer to the "south-west quarter of section 12, in township 8 north, range 2 west of the third principal meridian," when it should have referred to the fourth principal meridian. While Sickmon was served with the foreclosure notice, Garish, the mortgagor, was not brought into the court proceedings. Sickmon filed a demurrer, claiming a defect in the bill due to the lack of notice of the alleged mistake in the mortgage description. Consequently, the court entered a decree of foreclosure against Sickmon, prompting him to appeal this decision. The case examines the validity of the enforcement of a mortgage when errors in the land's description are present, particularly against bona fide purchasers who may not have been aware of the error.	The plaintiff, Joshua Wood, claimed that George Sickmon, as a purchaser of the equity of redemption, was subject to the foreclosure of the mortgage executed by Harlan P. Garish. Wood contended that the mortgage's description, while imperfect due to a typographical error regarding the principal meridian, was still valid enough to proceed with the foreclosure. He argued that Sickmon was obligated to comply with the foreclosure process despite the claim of mistake.	The defendant, George Sickmon, asserted that the foreclosure action was flawed due to a lack of necessary legal notice regarding the alleged mistake in the mortgage description. Sickmon argued that the bill was defective because it did not establish that he had purchased the property with notice of any mistakes. He claimed that, as a bona fide purchaser, he was entitled to protection from claims based on defects he was unaware of, calling into question the court's ability to enforce the foreclosure decree without a complete and accurate description of the property.

In 1870, in DeWitt County, Illinois, a case arose between William H. Cottingham and his associates (the appellants) and Riley V. Owens and his associates (the appellees). The dispute stemmed from a contract concerning the sale of 100 hogs, which Owens and his partners, including Barber and Peck, claimed they had paid $400 for but which Cottingham and Lake, the defendants, refused to fulfill. The plaintiffs' position was that they had paid for the hogs as stipulated in their agreement, but the defendants argued that the hogs they offered for delivery did not meet the weight and quality conditions specified in the contract. The plaintiffs contended they were ready and willing to pay for the hogs, offering a check rather than cash, which had been their standard practice. After a jury trial, the plaintiffs won a judgment of $481.14, leading the defendants to appeal on grounds including misjoinder of plaintiffs and the alleged misrepresentation of the hogs' quality.	The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to recover $400, which they had paid under a contract for the purchase of hogs that the defendants failed to deliver as agreed. They argued the case for money had and received, emphasizing their readiness to perform their part of the contract by offering a check for payment. They maintained that the jury's verdict and subsequent award were justified based on the evidence presented.	The defendants claimed that the plaintiffs had improperly joined their lawsuit, arguing the suit should have been in the names of Strain and Owens alone. They contended that the hogs they had tendered were of the required weight and quality, asserting that the plaintiffs did not show sufficient readiness to pay on the agreed date. Additionally, they invoked set-off claims related to money loaned and expenses incurred for feeding the hogs, suggesting these should reduce the amount owed to the plaintiffs.

In October 1865, Samuel J. Walker owned real estate in Chicago, which he conveyed to Henry H. Honoré. Honoré simultaneously executed a mortgage back to Walker for two promissory notes totaling $36,000, secured by the property, due in one and two years at an interest of 8%. The mortgage was recorded on December 30, 1865. Walker later sold one note to Wilshire & Co. and pledged the remaining note as collateral. Following several transactions and Walker’s accumulation of debt, Wilshire & Co. initiated foreclosure proceedings against Honoré in 1877, leading to a judgment. Afterward, Walker attempted to block the sale of the mortgaged premises through various proceedings. The case revolved around whether the conveyance from Honoré to Walker extinguished the mortgage assigned to Wilshire & Co., which was contested due to the existing debts Walker owed and the mortgage's secured status through record notice.	The plaintiffs, represented by Wilshire & Co., asserted that the mortgage and notes they held were assigned as security for debts owed by Walker, and thus should remain in force. They claimed that Honoré's conveyance did not extinguish their rights as mortgagees and that any transaction between Walker and Honoré without their consent should not affect their security interests.	The defendants, including Walker and associated parties, contended that the conveyance from Honoré to Walker constituted a merger that extinguished the mortgage on the property. They argued that since Walker had acquired the equity of redemption, it invalidated the prior mortgage rights claimed by Wilshire & Co., asserting that the mortgage could no longer be enforced against the property.

The legal case of Lelia P. Roby v. Louisa Murphy originated in Cook County, Illinois, with the action being filed during the September Term of 1886. The defendant, Lelia P. Roby, was alleged to have made false and defamatory statements about the plaintiff, Louisa Murphy. Specifically, Roby accused Murphy of theft and promiscuity, stating in public that Murphy was a thief who stole various items, including jewelry and clothing. Furthermore, Roby allegedly made slanderous remarks, calling Murphy names such as “dirty bitch,” “dirty slut,” and claimed that Murphy had engaged in immoral behavior while Roby was away. The case was presided over by Judge Johet P. Altgeld, and it escalated to the Illinois Appellate Court. During the trial, the jury ruled in favor of Murphy, awarding her $2,500 in damages. However, the court later required a remittance of $1,000, leading to a final judgment against Roby for $1,500 after Murphy complied.	Louisa Murphy claimed that Lelia P. Roby maliciously made false and defamatory statements about her that injured her reputation. She argued that Roby's words implied that she was a thief and engaged in promiscuous behavior, which brought her public disgrace and scandal. Murphy sought damages amounting to $15,000 for the defamation suffered due to Roby's remarks. Her legal requests were based on the assertion that the statements were slanderous and actionable.	Lelia P. Roby defended herself by arguing that the statements made were not slanderous or actionable in the eyes of the law. She contended that the terms used did not necessarily imply criminal behavior or immoral conduct. Roby also focused on the legality of the jury instructions given during the trial, claiming they misled the jury regarding the definition and determination of slanderous words. She requested that the appellate court find in her favor due to alleged errors in the instructions and reverse the judgment rendered against her.

On May 12, 1888, in Cook County, Illinois, Ruth M. Bemis filed a bill against Isaac C. Ogden, John Carne, Jr., and Hiram Coombs in the Superior Court. Bemis claimed ownership of specific real estate, asserting that the defendants held invalid tax deeds that purported to establish a title to the same property. The deeds, originating from tax sales conducted in 1877 and 1879, were deemed illegal due to deficiencies in proper legal process, specifically a missing certificate from the county clerk, which is required for the validity of tax sales. The court initially found in favor of Bemis, ordering the tax deeds to be set aside due to their status as a "cloud" on her title. The key issue revolved around the legality of the tax sales, where it was established that valid process must accompany any tax deed for it to transfer ownership.	Ruth M. Bemis claimed that the defendants' tax deeds were void and without legal standing. She sought a judicial decree to remove these deeds as a cloud on her title to the property in question. Her primary argument hinged on the assertion that the tax sales from which these deeds arose violated statutory requirements, primarily due to the absence of the required certificate from the county clerk, which confirmed the legitimacy of the tax sale process.	The defendants, represented by Isaac C. Ogden, John Carne, Jr., and Hiram Coombs, argued that the tax deeds in question were valid. They contended that even if there were minor discrepancies, such as differences in names, the ownership and process were sufficient under the law. Furthermore, they attempted to prove that the necessary certificates were present, albeit perhaps not recorded, thereby asserting that the sales were valid despite Bemis's claims to the contrary.

The case "The Callender Insulating and Waterproofing Company v. Sheridan S. Badger" was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on March 13, 1889. The parties involved were the Callender Insulating and Waterproofing Company, a manufacturer of wire, and Sheridan S. Badger, the buyer who purchased a substantial quantity of this wire intended for electrical use. The dispute arose when Badger claimed that the wire sold was defective and would not serve its intended purpose, arguing that this failure was either due to an express or implied warranty from the manufacturer. The situation was complicated by the question of whether the wire had been laid properly without any mechanical damage, which both parties debated vigorously. The case was characterized by evidence from letters and witness testimonies regarding the interactions and agreements between the parties. The jury was presented with conflicting evidence concerning the installation and functionality of the wire, leading to a lengthy trial.	The Callender Insulating and Waterproofing Company, as the plaintiff, claimed that they were entitled to recover the price for the wire sold to Badger. The plaintiff asserted that the wire was properly manufactured and guaranteed to perform adequately if laid correctly. They contended that any failure of the wire to function was not due to defects in manufacturing but rather a result of how it was installed by the defendant.	Sheridan S. Badger, the defendant, argued that the wire was inherently defective and did not serve the purpose for which it was sold. He claimed that the plaintiff's warranty on the wire's quality was either unfulfilled or void due to the wire's ineffectiveness. Badger sought to recover damages based on the premise that he was not bound to pay for a product that did not work as warranted.

In January 1863, in Edgar County, Illinois, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a case involving four plaintiffs, William B. French, John E. Wynne, George H. Christian, and Gower Wynne, against the defendant, Sheriff William M. Snyder. The plaintiffs had originally obtained a judgment against John Mills and Orson Q. Herrick for a total of $199.70 in damages, plus costs. In February 1860, they issued a pluries execution to Snyder to collect this debt. The plaintiffs alleged that Snyder, as sheriff, failed to levy sufficient property from Herrick, who was known to possess valuable horses at the time the execution was issued. Despite being aware that Herrick owned and kept these horses, Snyder did not make an appropriate levy, allowing Herrick to transport the horses out of state shortly after. This failure led to the plaintiffs being unable to recover the debt owed to them. At the trial held in October 1862, the jury ultimately returned a verdict in favor of Snyder, which prompted the plaintiffs to appeal, challenging various aspects of the trial, including the jury instructions and the handling of evidence.	The plaintiffs claimed that Snyder did not fulfill his duty as sheriff by failing to levy sufficient property to meet the execution amount. They argued that he had knowledge of valuable assets belonging to Herrick and that his negligence resulted in their financial loss. They requested the court to hold Snyder responsible for his failure to execute the levy properly and sought a new trial based on erroneous jury instructions and the admission of improper evidence during the trial.	Snyder contended that he believed the property he levied upon was adequate to satisfy the execution. He argued that the jury was correctly instructed on the standards of diligence required of a sheriff in such cases. Snyder also presented evidence that supported his actions and claimed that the plaintiffs had not established that they suffered a total loss of the judgment amount, as the debt could still have been paid by the original judgment debtors. He asserted that his decisions regarding the levy met the requisite standards of care expected from a sheriff.

In the year 1845, in Pike County, Illinois, James Dunlap initiated a lawsuit against Horatio N. Davis and others regarding a bill of exchange. The case began when Dunlap filed an affidavit for an attachment on September 12, 1844, followed by filing a declaration on April 16, 1845. The plaintiff's attorney, David A. Smith, argued for a continuance because he was unable to access the bill of exchange necessary for the trial due to another pending lawsuit in St. Louis, Missouri. He stated that repeated attempts were made to procure the instrument but were unsuccessful, and he requested a postponement to the next term to prepare adequately for the trial. The court, however, presided by Judge Samuel D. Lockwood, denied the motion for a continuance, ruling that Dunlap failed to show adequate diligence in preparing for trial and lacked a valid reason for not producing the necessary evidence. Consequently, Dunlap submitted to a nonsuit, and the court awarded costs to the defendants.	James Dunlap claimed that he could not proceed with the trial due to his inability to obtain the bill of exchange, which was held by an attorney in St. Louis. He argued that the court should grant a continuance to allow time for him to retrieve the bill and prepare his case, asserting that he had made reasonable efforts to secure the document and would be prepared for trial in the upcoming term.	Horatio N. Davis and the other defendants contended that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate sufficient diligence in preparing for the trial. They argued that Dunlap had voluntarily placed the bill of exchange out of his control, which was the reason for his inability to present it in court. The defendants maintained that since the case was ready for trial, the plaintiff should not be granted a continuance based on his own neglect.

In April 1862, in Marseilles, Illinois, the appellate case "Abner Strawn et al. v. William Cogswell et al." arose from a dispute over a mechanics' lien petition. The case involved appellants Abner Strawn and others, who owned a grist mill, and appellee William Cogswell, along with Cushman, who claimed they provided materials and labor for improvements to the mill. The petition by Cogswell alleged that he had performed work outside the initial contract, which was not compensated. The trial uncovered objections to juror eligibility, the nature of work performed, the quality of materials, and issues related to the timeliness of work completion. After a trial, the jury found in favor of Cogswell, awarding him $1,000, and a decree was issued that secured a lien on the mill for the owed amount, directing the property’s sale within twenty days.	The plaintiffs contended that Cogswell had completed the work on the mill in a workmanlike manner and should be compensated for the unpaid balance of the contract, along with interest. They argued that any delays were either caused by the defendants' actions or were accepted by them, thus waiving their right to damages for late completion. Furthermore, they highlighted that the defendants had accepted the work as sufficient, suggesting entitlement to recover under the contract.	The defendants denied the claims asserting that the work performed was not completed in accordance with the contract terms and that the materials used were defective and not as specified. Additionally, they maintained that any delays were not their fault, and they sought to argue against Cogswell’s claims for a lien, contending improper jury instructions were provided and that the variation from the contract had not been justified.

In June 1874, the case of William B. Wescott v. Chauncey E. Wicks et al. was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated from a mortgage that Wescott held, assigned to him from Pease, which was executed by Chauncey E. Wicks and A. W. Wicks. This mortgage was related to land purchased by the Wicks brothers from Pease. After A. W. Wicks's death, a partition action commenced, but Wescott was not included in the proceedings. Eventually, a commissioner was appointed to sell the land, leading to a purchase by O. E. Wicks, who secured the sale with a new mortgage. Geiger, acting for O. E. Wicks, sought to have Wescott release the original mortgage but failed to disclose that O. E. Wicks had previously mortgaged the land. Wescott then filed a bill in chancery to revive and foreclose the Pease mortgage. The initial court proceedings faced a general demurrer, which was sustained, ruling that there was no equity in Wescott's position. Wescott appealed this judgment, asserting that despite the case's complexities and the way it was presented, there was equity in his claims.	Wescott's main argument was that his original Pease mortgage should be restored and foreclosed. He sought to address the shortcomings in the earlier ruling by indicating that the partition proceedings were flawed since they did not include him as a party. He believed that his rights were not adequately considered due to the lack of transparency in the dealings that followed A. W. Wicks's death, particularly regarding the subsequent mortgage and property sale.	The defense, led by Chauncey E. Wicks, contended that the case against them was improperly presented, lacking the necessary factual clarity required for equitable relief. They maintained that Wescott's bill was defectively stated, thus justifying the demurrer which claimed there were no grounds for equity in his claims. The defendants sought a dismissal of the case based on these procedural grounds.

Thomas Snell and other appellants filed a bill in chancery against James De Land, the appellee, for partition and accounting of two farms they owned as tenants in common. The management of one farm was under the appellants, while the management of the other farm rested with the appellee. A long and complex accounting was required to address the financial transactions between the parties. The case was referred to a special master who gathered evidence and made findings that were subsequently reported to the court. After an appeal by the appellants regarding this report, the court reviewed the evidence and the objections but ultimately overruled them. The Circuit Court entered a decree requiring the appellants to pay the appellee the sum of $1,320. The decision was made on November 23, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court, with Judge C. Epler presiding in the Circuit Court of DeWitt County.	The plaintiffs, Thomas Snell and others, argued for a fair accounting between the co-owners of the farms to resolve the financial discrepancies stemming from their respective managements. They sought a partitioning of the farms to ensure an equitable distribution of assets and fairness in financial obligations, challenging the findings of the special master that led to the required payment to the defendant.	James De Land, the defendant, maintained that the special master's report was accurate and that the financial management of the properties justified the accounting presented. He argued that the amount owed to him was correct and that the appellants' objections lacked sufficient merit. The defense aimed to uphold the master’s report and the subsequent decree of the Circuit Court.

In 1889, in Logan County, Illinois, an action was brought against George W. Taylor and others by James N. Longan and others related to the bond of a school township treasurer. Longan, who was the treasurer, had made certain entries into his books and submitted a report to trustees detailing the state of his financial accounts on his last day in office. The report indicated that he was indebted for a particular amount which was being claimed in the debt action. Although Longan testified that he had paid out all funds received post-bond execution for the benefit of the school districts, the evidence presented showed that he had only a small amount left, which he also claimed to have paid out. The trial was conducted without a jury, leading to a judgment against both Longan and his sureties for $1,201.07. The defendants sought to challenge the validity of the entries Longan had made in his book and the report presented, arguing they should not be held accountable given the entries’ alleged untruths.	The plaintiffs argued that the entries made by Longan in his official capacity as treasurer and the final report he submitted were binding and conclusive evidence of the amount owed. They contended that these official documents should prevent Longan and his sureties from disputing the accuracy of the information contained therein. Their legal request sought recovery of the claimed amount based on this evidence.	The defendants contested the validity of the entries and the report, asserting that they were not estopped from proving that those entries were false and that the reported amounts were incorrect. They argued that the reports made by Longan should not operate as definitive evidence against them, allowing them to present evidence of different financial realities that contradicted Longan’s documentation.

The case "John Mee et al. v. John C. Paddock et al." was decided in September 1876 by the Illinois Supreme Court. It originated in Whiteside County, where the plaintiffs, John Mee and others, filed a bill in chancery against the town collector regarding a tax levied by the town of Hume for the year 1874. The tax in question was for the making and repairing of bridges, as well as road-related expenses. The plaintiffs argued that the tax amount exceeded the legally allowable rate of forty cents per hundred dollars without proper authorization from the legal voters of the township. They sought an injunction to prevent the collection of the tax, which the court ultimately issued in favor of the plaintiffs.	The plaintiffs contended that the tax levied by the commissioners of highways for the year 1874 was unauthorized and exceeded the limit of forty cents per hundred dollars of assessed property. They argued that no election took place to approve the higher tax rate, and thus, demanded the court to enjoin the collection of any tax that exceeded this limit.	The defendants, represented by the town collector, acknowledged the facts of the complaint but argued that the statutory provisions allowed for the tax to be extended beyond the forty-cent limit if authorized by a vote of the legal voters. They maintained that previous provisions did not impose the same restrictions on the tax for building bridges and that the tax was necessary for the maintenance of local infrastructure.

The case of Edward Prince v. The City of Quincy originated in 1889 in Adams County, Illinois. Edward Prince, the appellant, entered into a contract with the City of Quincy to construct and operate a waterworks system within the city's corporate limits. The contract stipulated that Prince would be compensated at a rate of $2,600 per year, plus $200 for each of the first one hundred hydrants, for a term of thirty years. Prince fully performed the stipulated services, providing water through seventy-seven hydrants during the fiscal year beginning March 31, 1880. Despite the city’s receipt of water and sufficient revenue to cover Prince's claim, the city council neglected to allocate funds for his payment, leading to Prince's loss. Following a general and special demurrer in the trial court, the case was appealed to the Appellate Court, which upheld the lower court's decision, stating that the contract was void due to the city's existing indebtedness exceeding the constitutional limit.	Edward Prince claimed that the City of Quincy breached their contract by failing to allocate the necessary funds from the city’s revenue to pay him for water provided through seventy-seven hydrants during the fiscal year. He argued that his services were rendered in accordance with the contract terms and that the city had sufficient revenue to cover his payments. Prince sought recovery of the amounts due for the water supplied, asserting that the city's refusal to pay constituted a wrongful act.	The City of Quincy asserted that the contract with Prince was void as it contravened the constitutional provision limiting municipal indebtedness. The city contended that it could not incur additional debt beyond the established limit and thus was not liable to pay for the water supplied under the terms of the contract. The city argued that the refusal to pay was not a tort, as the council's actions were within its legislative powers, and therefore no valid claim for recovery existed against the city.

In 1857, the case of Abner C. Harding v. Samuel Butts was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a dispute over land title in Warren County, Illinois. The case arose from an action of ejectment filed by the plaintiff, Harding, who claimed ownership of a half-section of land based on a series of deeds originating from the estate of John Fleming, who had died in 1837. Harding asserted that he paid taxes on the land for several years and relied on documentation that included a deed from the auditor conveying the land, a will of John Fleming, and tax receipts showing ongoing payments by the executors of Fleming's estate. The defendant, Butts, admitted possession of the land and claimed title through a conveyance from another party. The court, after hearing evidence from both the plaintiff and the defendant, ruled in favor of Butts, leading Harding to seek further legal remedy. Another related case against Rufus Ford addressed a similar land ownership claim based on the same statutes; both cases hinged on the interpretation of a revised statute concerning color of title and tax payment.	Harding contended that he was the legal owner of the disputed land as he held color of title made in good faith, supported by the payment of all legally assessed taxes for seven successive years, as per the provisions in the Illinois Revised Statutes. He argued that under the relevant statute, this entitled him to claim ownership of the vacant and unoccupied land, and he requested the court to recognize his legal right to the property.	The defendant, Samuel Butts, contended that the statutory provision allowing for the transfer of property upon the payment of taxes was unconstitutional, arguing that it effectively transferred ownership without due process or notification to the original owner. Butts demonstrated that he was in possession and claimed rightful title through a series of transactions linked to William Daugherty, asserting the legitimacy of his claim over the land in question.

Worcester A. Dickerman and other appellants filed a case against William T. Burgess and other appellees in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1858, stemming from a judgment and subsequent property sale that Dickerman contested. The case originated with Alden Thomas, who had engaged in business dealings with H. O. Stone. In March 1850, Stone secured a judgment against Thomas for $45. Burgess, representing Stone, claimed additional attorney fees from Thomas, resulting in a trial where Burgess's testimony led to a judgment that exceeded what Stone originally claimed. After Thomas paid $31 towards the judgment, Burgess took steps to have the remaining balance collected through a sheriff's sale without proper notification or public bidding, ultimately leading to the sale of Thomas's property, worth approximately $5,000, for just $38.33. Thomas remained unaware of the sale until 1855, when he learned that his property had been sold. Burgess and his associates allegedly orchestrated the sale to benefit themselves, further obscuring their actions and violating legal requirements for public sales. As the dispute progressed, Dickerman, representing the heirs of Alden Thomas after his death, sought to contest the legitimacy of the sale and its fraudulent basis.	The plaintiffs, as legal representatives of Alden Thomas, claimed that the sale of property was fraudulent due to a lack of notification and public bidding, violating statutory requirements. They alleged that Burgess had knowingly exploited misunderstandings regarding the debt and orchestrated the sale without proper process to profit illegally at their expense. They requested that the court set aside the sheriff's sale, declare the conveyances to Burgess's associates fraudulent, and restore the property to them in its original condition along with other legal remedies.	The defendants contended that the proceedings were conducted properly and denied any wrongdoing, claiming that the sale adhered to legal processes. W. T. Burgess argued there was a misunderstanding about the amount owed and that he handled the execution and sale lawfully. He claimed that the plaintiffs were guilty of laches, having delayed their claims for several years, which should prevent their relief. H. O. Stone and Samuel P. Burgess supported this argument, stating the plaintiffs were aware of the sale and did not act promptly to protect their interests.

In April 1867, a legal case entitled "Clapp et al. v. Reid et al." was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Illinois and involved key individuals named Clapp as the plaintiffs and Reid as the defendant. The focus of the case was on procedural matters related to a plea proposed by the defendant. The defendant's attorney, Mr. Tuley, sought permission to withdraw a previously filed joinder in error and to submit a plea of release of errors. The court was deliberating on the merits of this plea, particularly on the propriety of objections raised against it. It was noted that such objections could only be challenged at the demurrer stage of the plea. The outcome hinged on whether the plea would be upheld or overruled by the court, potentially leading to a judgment reversal.	The plaintiffs argued against the defendant's request to withdraw the joinder in error and to file a plea of release of errors, contending that the facts presented did not adequately support this plea. They maintained that the objections to the plea should be evaluated solely through a demurrer process and believed that the defendant's legal grounds for appeal lacked sufficient merit.	The defendant's key argument was aimed at securing permission to withdraw the joinder in error and to file a plea of release of errors. Through Mr. Tuley, the defense asserted that the objections regarding the merits of the plea could only be assessed through proper demurrer. They requested that, should their plea be deemed unsatisfactory upon review, a judgment of reversal should follow.

The case of Robert J. Haines v. The People centers on a legal dispute regarding the maintenance of a bridge on Main Street in St. Charles, Illinois. The events leading up to the petition for a writ of mandamus began in the early 19th century when a public highway was established that included a bridge over the Fox River. By 1812, the proprietors of a mill-dam created a race-way for their private use, which necessitated crossing over the public highway with a bridge. Although the original parties kept the bridge in good repair for many years, by 1885, the current owners of the race-way no longer maintained the bridge, leading to safety concerns for public travel. The city council deemed the bridge unsafe and required the current owners, Bohert J. Haines, Oliver H. Butler, and the S. L. Bignoll Hardware Company, to repair it, which they failed to do. As a result, a petition was filed seeking a mandamus to compel these parties to repair the necessary infrastructure. This case came before the Illinois Appellate Court in 1886 following a failure to comply with earlier court directives.	The plaintiff, represented by the city authorities, argues that the defendants (the owners of the race-way) are legally obligated to maintain and repair the bridge that crosses their race-way on Main Street. They assert that this obligation arises from the original construction of the race-way for private use, which should not interfere with public rights. The plaintiff seeks a writ of mandamus to compel the defendants to repair the bridge to ensure public safety.	The defendants contend that they should not be held responsible for maintaining the bridge, citing the original contractual obligations were not binding upon them. They argue that previous agreements regarding the maintenance costs should absolve them of this duty, and that mandamus is not an appropriate remedy for enforcing such obligations, as they do not hold an official duty to act in this context.

The case "Morris Barbe et al. v. Herman Glick et al." took place in December 1886 in the context of a legal dispute between Morris Barbe and others (the plaintiffs) and Herman Glick and others (the defendants). The plaintiffs initiated an action in assumpsit in the Illinois Appellate Court after filing a suit in the United States Circuit Court for the District of Colorado regarding the same matter. The Colorado suit had already progressed to the point where an attachment was issued against the defendants' property in that jurisdiction. The plaintiffs contended that the attachment provided a means of securing the debt owed to them while the case was still pending. The defendants, however, filed a plea in abatement to halt the Illinois suit on the grounds that the case in Colorado was still active and should take precedence. The court examined various precedents and statutory provisions related to the interaction between attachment actions and subsequent suits. Ultimately, the court determined that the mere existence of a pending attachment action in another state should not bar subsequent legal actions in Illinois concerning the same issue.	The plaintiffs argued that they had initiated the current action in Illinois despite the simultaneous proceedings in Colorado because they sought a remedy for the same cause of action. They contested the defendants' plea in abatement, asserting that the previous attachment in Colorado did not provide a complete resolution of their claims, and thus a suit could still be validly filed in Illinois to seek the owed debt.	The defendants contended that the Illinois action should be abated due to the active attachment proceedings in Colorado. They argued that since the Colorado suit had been filed first and involved the same parties and the same cause of action, it warranted dismissal or suspension of the Illinois action. The defendants believed that they were afforded sufficient protection under Colorado law through the attachment that had already been executed.

In June 1867, in Illinois, David Nichols sold eighteen fat hogs to William Mercer. While transporting the hogs to the town of Arlington, three of them died from heat. This incident led to a dispute regarding the terms of the sale contract, specifically whether the risk of transporting the hogs fell on Nichols or Mercer. A jury ruled in favor of Mercer, awarding him the value of the deceased hogs, which prompted Nichols to appeal the decision. The central issue in the appeal was related to the correctness of jury instructions concerning the original intent and understanding of the sale contract between the parties, including where the hogs were to be delivered and the associated risks of transporting them.	David Nichols argued that according to the contract, the risk of loss during transportation of the hogs should have been borne by William Mercer. He claimed misunderstandings regarding contract terms and requested that the court overturn the jury's decision, asserting that the instructions given to the jury were misleading and that the context of the agreement indicated Mercer should be responsible for the risk involved in the transport of the hogs.	William Mercer contended that the terms of the sale explicitly stated that the hogs were to be delivered at his risk. He requested affirmance of the jury's verdict, arguing that the instructions provided to the jury were appropriate and that any inaccuracies in the plaintiff's instructions did not mislead the jury regarding the essential terms of the contract. Mercer maintained that any misunderstanding about the delivery terms was irrelevant since clear evidence indicated a mutual agreement regarding delivery at Arlington.

On April 24, 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, Abram Netter found himself embroiled in a legal dispute initiated by James C. King and Bernard Curtis. They brought an assumpsit suit against Netter to recover an indebtedness totaling $4,553.27. Following their judgment against him, King and Curtis pursued a writ of attachment, targeting the Board of Trade of the City of Chicago and the Chicago Provision, Grain and Stock Board as garnishees, hoping to recover the owed funds. In response, both boards denied owing any debt to Netter or possessing any of his property. However, they confirmed Netter held membership certificates in both organizations. Despite their response, the plaintiffs aimed to have a receiver appointed to manage and sell Netter's interests in these certificates. The case revolved around the statutory process of garnishment and whether the garnishees had failed to disclose any significant property or effects belonging to Netter. The court analyzed relevant provisions of the law, particularly concerning the garnishment process and the necessity for the garnishees to possess actual property of the debtor.	The plaintiffs, King and Curtis, sought to enforce a judgment against Abram Netter by pursuing garnishment actions against the Board of Trade and the Chicago Provision, Grain and Stock Board. They claimed that these boards had property or assets belonging to Netter and requested the appointment of a receiver to manage and sell his membership certificates in both organizations, thus enabling the recovery of the owed amount.	The defendants, represented by the Board of Trade and the Chicago Provision, Grain and Stock Board, argued that they were not indebted to Netter and did not possess any of his property. They demonstrated that the membership certificates associated with Netter were in his possession and clarified that they were not liable for disclosing additional items of value. Consequently, they requested to be discharged from the garnishment process, asserting that the plaintiffs failed to establish any grounds for their claims.

The case "Ab. N. Van Alstine v. James K. Lemons" took place in December 1857 in Illinois. Key individuals involved include Ab. N. Van Alstine, the appellant, and James K. Lemons, the appellee who is the administrator of Harvey St. John. The dispute arose from a claim that the appellant presented to the Circuit Court, which was on appeal from the County Court. The appellant attempted to support his claim with a decree from the Surrogate Court of New York, but the court sustained an objection from the defendant’s counsel, preventing the introduction of this evidence. The appellant did manage to submit judgments from the Circuit Court of Montgomery County, New York, and a deposition, which were admitted as evidence. However, it was established that neither the appellant nor the deceased individuals involved resided in Illinois. The appellee invoked the statute of limitations as a defense, leading the court to rule against the appellant for costs. The appeal for a new trial was denied, and the appellant contended that the court made errors in its judgment.	The plaintiff, Ab. N. Van Alstine, argued that the decrees and judgments he presented were valid and should support his claim. He sought to challenge the circuit court's ruling that excluded his New York Surrogate Court decree as admissible evidence. He also contended that the court misapplied the statute of limitations and unjustly ruled in favor of the defendant.	The defendant, James K. Lemons, argued that the statute of limitations from 1849 barred the claims made by the plaintiff because the judgments related to a case in another state. The defendant's counsel successfully contested the evidence of the New York Surrogate Court decree and asserted that the absence of letters of administration in Illinois further invalidated the plaintiff's claims, leading to a judgment against the appellant.

The case "Great Western Railroad Company of 1859 v. The City of Decatur" was decided in January 1864 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Decatur, Illinois, concerning an ordinance prohibiting railroad companies from obstructing traveled railroad crossings. The plaintiff, the City of Decatur, represented by Henry Churchman, claimed that the Great Western Railroad Company violated this ordinance by leaving cars stationary across Morgan Street, a public crossing, which impeded the movement of teams and vehicles. On October 9, 1863, Churchman encountered cars obstructing the street when he attempted to cross it for dinner. He stated there was limited space (only ten to twelve feet) for others to pass safely between the cars. Another witness corroborated the claim that the cars remained in position for several hours, presenting a hazard for team traffic. Initially, the case was brought before a justice of the peace and later appealed to the Circuit Court, where the court sided with the City and ruled against the railroad company.	The City of Decatur's primary argument was that the Great Western Railroad Company had breached an ordinance designed to keep railroad crossings free from obstruction. The City asserted that the railroad's cars standing on Morgan Street created a hazardous situation for teams and vehicles that needed to traverse the area, impeding public traffic and violating the ordinance. They sought a penalty of twenty-five dollars for each instance of obstruction.	The Great Western Railroad Company contested that Morgan Street was improperly defined as a "traveled railroad crossing," arguing there had not been sufficient proof to establish the public character of the street during the trial. They challenged the court's decision, claiming that the jury should not have found the company liable under the circumstances and highlighted the lack of objections during the initial trial regarding the status of the street.

In 1889, the legal dispute arose in St. Clair County, Illinois, involving Mary Price as the plaintiff and James M. Hay and others as defendants. The case focused on a lawsuit brought by Price against Hay and his associates, claiming compensation for professional legal services that were purportedly rendered during the contestation of her father's will. Price argued that these legal representatives were initially employed by her, while Hay contended that they were contracted through Mr. Kase under a written agreement which stipulated that Kase would receive $10,000 if the will was set aside. Following a jury trial, the verdict favored Price, awarding her $81,000. The defendants appealed, arguing that the jury was misled by erroneous jury instructions and that their damages were excessive. The court noted that the case involved complex interactions surrounding the employment of the attorneys, the legitimacy of contracts, and the responsibilities owed by the involved parties, culminating in questions about what constituted acceptable grounds for recovery.	Mary Price, the plaintiff, claimed that the defendant attorneys were directly employed by her for legal services related to contesting her father’s will. She sought compensation for these services, asserting that they were rendered with the expectation of remuneration. The plaintiff argued against the assertions made by the defendants regarding their employment by Kase, emphasizing that the work performed was beneficial to her and should be compensated accordingly.	The defendants contended that they were not employed directly by Mary Price but rather by Mr. Kase, who had a written contract entitling him to a significant fee upon successfully challenging the will. They argued that any services rendered were under the auspices of Kase’s agreement, and thus, they claimed no direct liability to Price. Furthermore, the defendants challenged the adequacy of the damages awarded, asserting that the jury instructions were erroneous and led to an inflated compensation claim.

In June 1877, the case of The Town of Grayville v. William F. Whitaker was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from an incident where William F. Whitaker was injured after falling off a bridge maintained by the Town of Grayville. The bridge, located in a less frequented area of the village, lacked railings on both sides, and Whitaker was traversing it at night when visibility was poor. He was well aware of the condition of the bridge. Whitaker claimed that the Town's negligence in failing to install safety railings led to his fall and subsequent injuries. The case was initially heard in the Circuit Court of White County, presided over by Judge Tazewell B. Tanner. The trial centered around whether the Town had a legal duty to ensure the bridge was safe for public use and whether it had exercised reasonable care in its maintenance.	The plaintiff, William F. Whitaker, argued that the Town of Grayville was negligent in its duty to maintain the bridge safely, specifically by failing to install necessary railings. He asserted that the Town’s negligence directly led to his injuries when he fell from the unguarded bridge. Whitaker sought damages for his injuries, claiming he had exercised reasonable care while attempting to cross the bridge.	The Town of Grayville contended that it did not act with gross negligence, claiming that the standard of care required for municipal corporations is one of ordinary prudence rather than absolute safety. The Town argued that the jury should determine whether it failed to exercise ordinary care in maintaining the bridge. Furthermore, the Town asserted that if it was found to be negligent, Whitaker himself might have contributed to the injuries due to his own lack of care while crossing the bridge.

The case, "William H. Cogshall v. John M. Beesley, Guardian, etc.", arose in January 1875, in Mason County, Illinois. It involved plaintiff William H. Cogshall, who initiated an action of assumpsit against defendants John M. Beesley, acting as guardian, and Francis S. Cogshall. The circuit court conducted a jury trial which resulted in a verdict favoring Cogshall, awarding him $398.50. Following the verdict, a motion was made by the defense for a new trial. During this process, the plaintiff requested to amend his declaration by dismissing his claims against Francis S. Cogshall, a request that the court approved. As a consequence, the court rendered a judgment in favor of Francis S. Cogshall for his costs associated with the case. The judge presiding over the trial was Hon. Lyman Lacey. The court later overruled the motion for a new trial and affirmed the verdict against the remaining defendant, John M. Beesley. The court emphasized that the appellate review was hindered due to the incomplete presentation of all evidence in the bill of exceptions, reinforcing the validity of the jury's verdict.	The plaintiff, William H. Cogshall, claimed that he was entitled to a monetary judgment based on the debt or obligation owed to him. He sought to amend his declaration to remove one of the defendants, Francis S. Cogshall, which the court allowed, and it was decided that he would not pursue claims against that particular defendant further.	The defendant, John M. Beesley, contended that the verdict was inconsistent with the evidence presented during the trial. He requested a new trial based on this assertion. Additionally, he raised an issue regarding the amendment of the declaration, arguing that the alteration after the verdict was inappropriate.

In January 1889, a legal case took place in Jackson County, Illinois, known as Rockford Insurance Company v. Andrew Seyferth. The case arose when Andrew Seyferth, the plaintiff, sought to recover the value of property he had insured with Rockford Insurance Company after it was destroyed by fire. The jury found in favor of Seyferth, assessing his damages at $1,000. The insurance policy required proof of loss to be submitted to the company for claims. Seyferth claimed to have fulfilled this requirement; however, the insurance company argued that he had misrepresented himself as the sole owner of the property in his application for insurance, alleging a breach of warranty regarding the title that could void the policy. The case highlighted complexities involving the obligation of the insured to submit proof of loss, the reliance on an agent’s knowledge in filling out insurance applications, and the legal implications of misstatements made during the application process.	Andrew Seyferth, the plaintiff, argued that he had a legitimate insurable interest in the property and that the loss was rightly assessed at $1,000 by the jury. He maintained that he submitted proof of loss as required under the insurance policy, seeking compensation for the damages sustained due to the fire.	Rockford Insurance Company, the defendant, contended that Seyferth breached the warranty of the insurance policy by claiming to be the sole owner of the property without disclosing any other interests. They argued that this misrepresentation nullified the policy, thereby avoiding their obligation to pay the claim. Furthermore, they asserted that Seyferth failed to provide the necessary proof of loss as mandated by the terms of the insurance policy.

On October 6, 1871, in New York City, the wholesale jewelers Henry Oppenheimer & Co. delivered a box weighing 25 pounds to a driver from the United States Express Company for transportation to their business in Chicago, Illinois. The box contained watches and jewelry valued at $3,800. At the time of the delivery, May & Stern, the consignors, filled out a bill of lading which restricted the Express Company's liability to $50 unless the true value of the package was disclosed. Despite having a long-standing business relationship with the company and being familiar with the receipt's conditions, they did not disclose the value or properly fill out the receipt. The box was shipped, but it was lost in a fire on October 8, 1871, without any negligence on the part of the Express Company. After a trial, the court rendered a judgment for the plaintiffs for $50, following which they appealed.	The plaintiffs claimed they were entitled to the full value of the lost merchandise, arguing that they had not agreed to the terms restricting liability stated in the receipt. They contended that the Express Company should be responsible for the loss that occurred during transit since they were unaware of the limitations outlined in the receipt.	The defendant, the United States Express Company, argued that the plaintiffs were aware of the liability limitations as they had a long-standing relationship with the company and frequently used its services. They maintained that the plaintiffs' failure to disclose the true value of the goods constituted bad faith, which warranted enforcement of the $50 liability cap explicitly stated in the receipt.

In 1869, in Kane County, Illinois, Samuel Fletcher and his wife, Ledicia, were indicted for the false imprisonment of their son, Samuel Fletcher, Jr., who was described as blind and helpless. The case emerged from allegations that the couple cruelly imprisoned the boy in a cold and damp cellar for several days during mid-winter, leaving him without heat and living in severe conditions. The boy eventually escaped and was subsequently taken care of by town authorities. It was reported that Samuel Fletcher justified his actions by stating that he was treating the boy's condition, claiming that he was infested with vermin and applying kerosene to his body. The court found the treatment of the child to be inhumane, recognizing the importance of parental discretion while condemning any form of wanton cruelty towards children. The principal focus of the case involved the definition of reasonable parental authority and its limits concerning child welfare.	The plaintiff, representing the State of Illinois, asserted that Samuel Fletcher's actions constituted false imprisonment and extreme cruelty against his son, Samuel Fletcher, Jr. They argued that the imprisonment was without reasonable cause and highlighted the shocking inhumanity of keeping a blind and helpless child in a damp cellar. The claims emphasized that parents must exercise their authority within the bounds of reason and humanity, and invoked prior legal instances where parents had been held accountable for exceeding these bounds through cruelty.	The defendants contended that under the law, parents have been given considerable discretion regarding their authority over their children, and that the treatment of their son fell within their parental rights. They attempted to justify their actions as efforts to address the child's alleged infestation and maintain order, arguing that they were not acting with malice or intent to harm. The defense requested dismissal of the charges against Ledicia Fletcher, asserting there was no evidence linking her to any wrongdoing in the case.

In the fall of 1879, William Miller (appellee) rented a farm from Kiser for two years, agreeing to give one fourth of the crops and make specific improvements. Miller began to implement some improvements but in May 1880, Bernhard Ticker (appellant) purchased the farm from Kiser and was to fulfill the landlord's interest in the growing crops, settling with Miller. A new arrangement was established where Miller was released from certain obligations and the rent was adjusted to one third of the crops instead. Ticker received his share of the crops for 1880 and 1881, but Miller did not complete the remaining work outlined in their original contract. Ticker previously sued Miller in 1881 for a small amount, which included the same claims that are now part of this case. The justice refused Miller's claims at that time and did not allow them to be presented further. The court ultimately found no evidence that Ticker had an express or implied obligation to pay Miller for the unperformed work, resulting in a judgment against Miller.	William Miller claimed compensation for the work and improvements he made to the farm while under contract with Kiser. His main argument hinged on the assertion that Ticker, as the new owner, should be liable for these improvements based on the previous agreements. Miller contended that his contributions entitled him to some form of remuneration from the continued operations of the farm under Ticker’s ownership.	Bernhard Ticker defended against Miller's claims by asserting that the prior judgment rendered by a justice of the peace barred Miller from pursuing this action, as Miller had presented his claims within that previous suit but was denied relief. Ticker maintained that there was no agreement, either express or implied, obligating him to pay Miller for his work, and that the adjustment of the rental agreement reflected a compromise that released Miller from further obligations regarding the work he had initially agreed to undertake.

In 1873, Letitia S. Baldwin and her husband, Thomas Baldwin, sold a 200-acre tract of land in Peoria County, Illinois, to Mahala Thurston for $7,000. Thurston paid $2,000 initially and provided promissory notes for the remaining balance, receiving a bond for a deed that allowed her possession of the land while payments were made. After the sale, Thurston granted Alexander Pool the right to build a dam and create a mill-race on the property. In September the same year, she sold her purchase contract to William Baldwin while he was aware of the previous agreement with Pool. Pool began construction in June 1873, but Baldwin and his wife filed a lawsuit to enjoin Pool from continuing his work, asserting ownership of the land and objecting to Pool's activities. The Circuit Court initially sided with Pool, dissolving the injunction and dismissing Baldwin's claims, leading the Baldwins to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Letitia S. Baldwin and Thomas Baldwin, argued that they were the rightful owners of the property and that Alexander Pool did not have the right to build a dam or create a mill-race on their land. They sought to prevent Pool from continuing any work that would affect their ownership and the integrity of the property.	Alexander Pool contended that Mahala Thurston, the prior purchaser, had legally granted him the right to work on the land. He argued that the Baldwins had sold the land and given possession to Thurston, who was not in default under the purchase contract at the time. Thus, Pool claimed he had legitimate rights to carry out his construction as there was no breach affecting the security of the Baldwins' interest in the property.

In 1853, William Montgomery brought a legal action against Harley Wayne and others in McHenry County, Illinois. The dispute arose from the alleged illegal levy of an execution on Montgomery's oxen. Montgomery contended that the execution had already been satisfied through a prior levy on a wagon of greater value. The case began in a justice of the peace court and was subsequently appealed to the circuit court, where it was tried without a jury. Key individuals involved included the plaintiff William Montgomery, the defendant Harley Wayne, and a constable named Cram, who executed the levy. During the proceedings, evidence was presented regarding the legitimacy of the prior levy, specifically the constable's claim of having levied the wagon, which was not present at the time of sale. Montgomery contended that the transaction invalidated the authority to levy on the oxen, leading to his claim against the defendants.	Montgomery's primary argument was that the levy of execution on his oxen was invalid because the execution had already been satisfied through a prior levy on his wagon, which had a greater value than the amount owed. He asserted that the constable did not have proper possession of the wagon at the time of sale, and therefore, the levy was incomplete and should not be regarded as a legitimate satisfaction of the execution.	The defendants argued that the previous levy was valid and constituted a legal satisfaction of the execution. They maintained that even if there were defects in the levy process, it did not preclude the levy on the oxen. The defendants contended that Montgomery should not be allowed to argue the illegitimacy of the prior levy after having benefited from the sale of the wagon and recovering its value.

In 1873, a legal case was presented before the Illinois Supreme Court involving Charles F. Happel and Frederic Happel as the defendants against George W. Brethauer, the plaintiff. The dispute originated from a suit brought against the Happel brothers by Brethauer in a justice of the peace court, with the initial demand listed at $200. After evidence was presented, it was determined that the amount owed to the plaintiff was $164; however, the defendants provided evidence of offsets, reducing the claim to $87.50. Following this, Brethauer appealed to the circuit court after the justice of the peace rendered a judgment of $87.50, which the defendants contested, claiming a lack of jurisdiction. The circuit court upheld the initial ruling. The underlying issue revolved around whether the justice of the peace had the proper jurisdiction under the law, specifically in regards to the constitutionality of the act increasing the jurisdiction of justices and police magistrates. The case was presided over by Judge John G. Rogers in Cook County.	The plaintiff, George W. Brethauer, argued that the initial judgment rendered by the justice of the peace, which concluded that he was owed $87.50, was appropriate based on the evidence presented. Brethauer maintained that the Circuit Court had proper jurisdiction to hear his appeal and requested that the court affirm the justice's ruling.	The defendants, Charles F. Happel and Frederic Happel, contested the jurisdiction of the justice of the peace, asserting that the case should be dismissed due to the jurisdictional limitations outlined in the statute. They contended that the initial procedural issues and the amount claimed exceeded the jurisdictional threshold and that the justice's summoning process did not comply with the proper legal standards.

In the case of Henry C. Cunningham v. The N. O. Nelson Manufacturing Co., which was decided on December 4, 1885, in the Illinois Appellate Court, the events trace back to May 19, 1883. On this date, Henry Powell executed a chattel mortgage to The N. O. Nelson Manufacturing Co. to secure a series of notes, the last of which was due on November 13, 1883. While the first two notes were paid, the last two remained unpaid. Subsequently, on September 19, 1883, Powell executed a second mortgage on the same property to Cunningham to secure a note due September 19, 1884, which included a usual insecurity clause. Both mortgages were duly recorded. On June 23, 1884, more than seven months after the last payment became due, the manufacturing company took possession of the property. The next day, Cunningham, claiming under the second mortgage, replevied the property after making a demand. A trial in the circuit court resulted in a judgment favoring the manufacturing company, which was awarded a return of the property. The central issue was whether the manufacturing company lost its lien against the second mortgage by delaying possession after its debt matured.	Henry C. Cunningham, the plaintiff, argued that by taking a second mortgage on the property, he had the right to secure his interests despite the prior mortgage held by The N. O. Nelson Manufacturing Co. He contended that the manufacturing company's delay in taking possession of the mortgaged property after the debt's maturity resulted in his second mortgage becoming a superior claim. He sought a return of the property based on this reasoning.	The N. O. Nelson Manufacturing Co., the defendant, maintained that their first mortgage took precedence over the second one held by Cunningham. They argued that the delay in taking possession did not affect the validity of their mortgage and that Cunningham, as a second mortgagee, had full knowledge of the first mortgage at the time of securing his own. Therefore, any claim of superior rights by Cunningham due to the delay was unfounded, and they requested the court to uphold their right to possession and enforced their original mortgage interest.

Cornelius Thurman v. Benjamin Burt took place in December 1867 in Champaign County, Illinois. Cornelius Thurman, the plaintiff, had previously been sued by Benjamin Burt for the sum of $1,259.95. In an effort to avoid lengthy litigation, the parties agreed on a settlement, which included a judgement in favor of Burt but provided Thurman with a stay of execution on the payment for three years. Despite this agreement, Burt issued an execution against Thurman in November 1868, threatening to seize Thurman's business property. Under duress from these threats, Thurman paid Burt $400 and executed promissory notes totalling $929. The plaintiff alleged that he acted under coercion and that the notes were unjustly obtained without legal consideration. He sought relief from the court to cancel these notes and enforce the original agreement's terms. The case was dismissed by the circuit court, prompting Thurman to appeal, claiming that he deserved protection from Burt’s coercive actions.	Thurman claimed that the promissory notes were extorted from him under duress, stating that he was threatened with a levy on his property and closure of his business if he did not pay Burt immediately. He argued that no payments were due at the time of the execution, and he was willing and able to comply with the original judgment agreement. Thurman requested the court to cancel the notes, prevent Burt from selling them, and to affirm the original agreement, maintaining the stay of execution.	Burt admitted to the execution but denied that he had threatened Thurman or acted with coercion. He argued that the arrangement for the payment and notes was amicable and denied any allegations of duress. Burt maintained that his actions were in accordance with the court's judgment and that the payments made by Thurman were willingly accepted.

In March 1866, in Morgan County, Illinois, Steven Sutton, acting as the administrator of Jacob Emerick's estate, secured a default judgment against Christopher Shaffer for $1,100. This amount was claimed to be received by Shaffer from the estate. Following the judgment, an execution was issued and levied on Shaffer's property by sheriff James Dick. Shaffer contested the judgment by filing a bill to enjoin the execution, claiming he was unaware of the legal proceedings because he believed the process served to him was merely a subpoena to testify as a witness. He asserted he did not owe anything to Emerick’s estate. In contrast, Sutton’s answer indicated that Shaffer, as Emerick’s son-in-law, had indeed received the estate's money before dividing it among the heirs, all of which was backed by evidence, including testimonies from Sutton's witnesses. The circuit court eventually dissolved the injunction and dismissed Shaffer’s complaint.	Shaffer claimed that he had no notice of the lawsuit against him in Morgan County and that the process he received was simply a subpoena for him to appear as a witness, which he could not attend due to illness. He alleged that he had no financial obligation to Emerick's estate, contesting the default judgment against him.	Sutton countered that the process was properly served, and the foundation of his claim was substantiated; Shaffer had received funds from Henderson on behalf of the estate shortly after Emerick’s death. Sutton argued that Shaffer's denial of any indebtedness was false, emphasizing that adequate notice was given, and the nature of the received funds clearly established Shaffer's financial liability.

Joseph M. Street, the plaintiff, was involved in a legal dispute with the County Commissioners of Gallatin County. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1822. Street was previously serving as the clerk of the county commissioners’ court, but he was removed from this position by the commissioners. The case centers around whether the commissioners had the authority to remove Street. The court received evidence, including the records from the county commissioners’ court, which indicated that there was no stated cause for Street's removal according to the statutory requirements of the state. The fundamental question revolved around the legality of the removal and the authority of the county commissioners in this context.	The plaintiff, Joseph M. Street, claimed that his removal from the position of clerk was unlawful because the county commissioners failed to provide a valid cause for his removal as mandated by state law. He argued for the issuance of a mandamus to restore him to his position, asserting his right to hold office unless appropriately removed according to legal procedures.	The County Commissioners of Gallatin County did not formally respond to the writ served to them, which could be construed as a tacit admission of the lack of legal standing for the removal. Their defense did not present any stated reasons for Street's removal, effectively undermining their position and authority in the matter.

In 1871, in Chicago, Charles V. Dyer, who owned offices in the city, entered into an arrangement with attorneys Thomas J. Jones and Thomas J. Sutherland, who were partners operating a law practice. The attorneys were allowed to use Dyer’s offices without paying rent, provided they handled his ordinary legal business. However, on May 17, 1871, Dyer requested Sutherland to bid on a public house, which he did for a maximum price of $45,000. After the sale, Sutherland also assisted Dyer in leasing the property. Jones and Sutherland later charged Dyer for these services, believing they fell outside their contractual obligation.
