In March 1872, Sutherland initiated a lawsuit against Dyer for the recovery of these charges, but after a month of proceedings, Jones dismissed the case and issued Dyer a release from that claim. Subsequently, Sutherland attempted to sue Dyer again for the same services, this time in his own name, leading to the trial and preliminary judgment.	The plaintiff, Thomas J. Sutherland, claimed reimbursement for services rendered to Dyer in bidding for and leasing a public house, amounting to a total of $1,681.25 after a jury verdict. Sutherland sought compensation based on customary attorney commissions for these services, alleging that he was entitled to payment despite the original arrangement that did not specify commissions.	The defendant, Charles V. Dyer, contended that there was no valid implied contract for payment of commissions since the services were rendered within the scope of a general agreement for legal services without charge. He argued that the services performed by Sutherland as an attorney did not warrant claiming commissions like those customarily expected from real estate brokers. Dyer also asserted that Sutherland could not pursue a claim after dismissing the original lawsuit and issuing a release.

In January 1883, in Williamson County, Illinois, John A. Dunaway engaged in a conversation outside a store with individuals, including Hartwell Hendrickson, an attorney representing Dunaway's wife in divorce proceedings. After this discussion, Dunaway entered the store, drew a revolver, and shot at Hartwell, but instead, accidentally shot Hendrickson, inflicting a serious wound. Dunaway was reportedly under the influence of alcohol at the time of the incident. The case was tried in November 1883, where he was found guilty of assault with intent to commit murder and subsequently sentenced to six years in prison. The court found that Dunaway’s actions showed intention to kill someone, regardless of whether that person was Hartwell or Hendrickson, and determined there was no accidental discharge of the firearm.	The plaintiff, the People of the State of Illinois, claimed that Dunaway intentionally shot Hendrickson with the intent to commit murder. They argued that there was sufficient evidence to prove that Dunaway acted with malice and intent to harm when he fired the weapon indiscriminately into a crowd, and thus he deserved to be convicted of assault with intent to murder.	Dunaway's defense contended that he did not intend to shoot Hendrickson and that his intentions were directed solely toward Hartwell. They claimed that because he shot in the direction of Hartwell, he could not be guilty of attempting to murder Hendrickson. The defense argued for a dismissal based on lack of specific intent to harm Hendrickson, maintaining that any act of shooting should not be misinterpreted to imply intent to murder someone other than the specific target.

In January 1868, the case of Illinois Central Railroad Company v. Dennis Baker took place in Ford County, Illinois. The dispute arose after a colt belonging to Dennis Baker was killed by a train operated by the Illinois Central Railroad Company while it was traversing a section of the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railroad. The incident occurred as the train approached the town of New Benton; witnesses testified that the train was moving slowly down a slight grade and chased the colt and two other horses towards a culvert which had deep ditches filled with water on either side. The plaintiff, Baker, claimed the railroad company was negligent for not stopping the train, despite having sufficient time to do so, resulting in the death of his horse, valued at $100. After a jury trial at the circuit court, Baker was awarded damages, prompting the railroad company to appeal the verdict based on claims of insufficient evidence for the jury's decision.	Dennis Baker argued that the Illinois Central Railroad Company was negligent in its duty to prevent the killing of his colt by failing to stop the train in a timely manner. He sought compensation for the value of the colt, claiming that the train operators had enough time to stop before reaching the animal.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that the jury's verdict was contrary to the evidence presented, indicating that Baker failed to prove where the colt had entered the tracks. They requested the court to set aside the jury's verdict and argued that the evidence did not substantiate that the train operators acted with gross or willful negligence in the incident.

In September 1876, The People ex rel. Louis C. Huck, County Treasurer, appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a dispute over special assessments levied for the improvement and enlargement of Lincoln Park, located in Cook County, Illinois. The key individuals involved included Louis C. Huck, representing the county, and Henry H. Gage, among others as defendants. The matter arose when the assessments were made by the supervisor and assessor of the town of North Chicago for the purpose of acquiring land wholly within its corporate limits to add to Lincoln Park. The case also involved a small portion of the park located in the town of Lake View. The dispute was centered on the authority to levy such assessments and whether the proper procedures were followed. The court had to evaluate if the assessments could be deemed as made by the appropriate corporate authorities of the town, referencing prior rulings to support the authority of local officials in these matters.	The plaintiff, Louis C. Huck, claimed that the special assessments made for the improvement of Lincoln Park were valid and should be enforced. Huck argued that the supervisor and assessor of North Chicago were indeed the corporate authorities eligible to levy these assessments as per the Illinois Constitution. The request was for the court to reverse the county court’s judgment that had previously refused to uphold the new assessments and to direct the county court to enter judgment for the outstanding amount against the delinquent parties.	The defendants, including Henry H. Gage, contended that the assessments were improperly levied and challenged the authority of the local officials to impose such taxes for the park improvement. They argued that there was a lack of statutory support for the assessments and sought to have the county court’s ruling upheld, which denied the enforcement of the assessments.

J. Edwin Martine filed a legal case against Thomas Nelson in September 1869 in Illinois. The case arose from a dispute over the payment for painting work performed on Nelson’s house. Martine, a house painter, claimed that he had performed work valued significantly higher than the $350 he was initially offered but was only paid a portion of this amount. The disagreement centered around whether there was a valid special contract in place for the work. Nelson asserted that the work was conducted under a special contract while Martine contended that the actual job turned out to be more extensive than represented by Nelson, leading to his financial loss. The court proceedings included testimony from both parties, with a jury ultimately determining that no special contract existed and awarding Martine a verdict for the unpaid balance, amounting to $727, after deducting the $150 already paid by Nelson.	The plaintiff, J. Edwin Martine, argued that he had completed painting work on Thomas Nelson’s house without a proper contract. Martine claimed that he relied on Nelson’s misrepresentations regarding the extent of work needed, which led him to agree to a price that was far lower than the actual costs incurred. Martine sought recovery for the unpaid portion of his fee based on the fair value of his work, insisting that the statutory mechanics' lien law should protect him as a house painter.	Thomas Nelson, the defendant, contended that the work was done under a special contract for a set price of $350. He maintained that Martine had agreed to this price based on the plans provided, asserting that the understanding was that it covered all expected work without any misrepresentation on his part. Nelson argued that Martine should have performed due diligence to clarify the work scope prior to starting and sought to dismiss Martine's claim based on the alleged contractual agreement.

In January 1868, Robert W. McClaughry, the county clerk of Hancock County, Illinois, brought a case against the Board of Supervisors of Hancock County. The dispute stemmed from McClaughry's claim for payment of $41.81 for necessary stationery and supplies that he had provided for the operations of his office. The board had appointed a special agent responsible for purchasing stationery, but McClaughry contended that the agent had failed to adequately supply his office, forcing him to make purchases himself. The case was tried in the Circuit Court of Hancock County, where a jury trial was waived, and the court ruled in favor of McClaughry, awarding him $15. The board appealed the decision, leading to this case being heard by the Illinois Supreme Court.	McClaughry argued that he was entitled to reimbursement for the reasonable expenses incurred in purchasing stationery, due to the failure of the appointed agent to supply the necessary materials for his office. He maintained that under section 32 of chapter 41 of the Revised Statutes, clerks have the right to procure necessary supplies when they are not provided by the special agent, and thus the county must pay for the legitimate expenses.	The Board of Supervisors contended that since they had appointed an agent to handle the procurement of stationery, McClaughry should not have made purchases independently or sought reimbursement. They argued that the legal framework did not support McClaughry's claims for payment since an agent was designated for that purpose.

The case, "John Fuller v. J. Victor Dauphin," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on May 9, 1888. The dispute arose over a five-acre island in Plum River Slough near the town of Savanna in Carroll County, Illinois. The plaintiff, J. Victor Dauphin, claimed that John Fuller had unlawfully cut timber on his property, leading to a demand for $100 in damages. The controversy centered around the ownership of the island, with Dauphin asserting his title under the swamp lands acts and the conveyance of the land by Carroll County in 1854. In contrast, Fuller claimed title based on a patent from the United States awarded to Luther Bowen in 1845. The central question revolved around the boundary description and whether the land in dispute was included within the terms of the patent. Expert testimonies indicated that meander lines, used for surveying land near water bodies, do not establish official boundary lines. Ultimately, the court found no compelling evidence to establish Fuller's claimed title based on possession or taxation metrics, leading to a reversal of the previous judgment.	The plaintiff, J. Victor Dauphin, claimed ownership of the island based on swamp land legislation and a conveyance from Carroll County in 1854. Dauphin sought damages for timber cut from his property by John Fuller and argued that the land fell under his legal title. He maintained that the description of the island in his claim was valid and supported by legislative frameworks.	John Fuller, the defendant, contended that his patent from the United States conferred ownership rights to the land in question, arguing that it included the island as it bordered the navigable Plum River Slough. Fuller claimed that the meandered lines used in surveys did not constitute official boundaries and that he had made property tax payments based on a legitimate color of title. Furthermore, he asserted that Dauphin failed to demonstrate requisite possession under statutory limitation laws.

Walter Kimball v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. H. W. Jones was a legal case adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1867. The dispute arose in Chicago, where H. W. Jones, a physician, was appointed as a sanitary inspector by the board of health, which had been organized under an act passed in March 1867. Jones was responsible for overseeing health measures within his district, focusing on preventing pestilence. After providing his services from April 5 to May 27, 1867, Jones submitted a bill for $30, which was approved by the board of health. However, Walter Kimball, the city comptroller, refused to pay the bill despite having the necessary funds allocated for such expenses. This led Jones to seek a writ of mandamus against Kimball to compel him to fulfill the payment obligation.	Jones, the relator, argued that his appointment as a sanitary inspector by the board of health was legitimate and necessary for the public health objectives outlined in the act of 1867. He claimed that Kimball had a duty to authorize the payment of his salary, which had already been certified by the board, and sought a peremptory writ of mandamus to compel Kimball to pay the owed amount.	Kimball contended that the board of health did not possess the authority to appoint Jones as an agent for sanitary affairs. He relied on the assertion that the law did not explicitly grant the board powers to divide the city into sanitary districts or appoint inspectors. Consequently, he requested the court to overturn the initial order for a writ of mandamus, arguing that he was not obligated to pay Jones.

In 1836, in Morgan County, Illinois, George T. Purkett sold parcels of land and associated dividends from the Illinois Land Association to John Gregory and others. The transaction was formalized through a promissory note that the defendants executed as part of their agreement to receive these lands and dividends. By 1838, a dispute arose, leading to Purkett initiating action for debt against Gregory (the defendant) after Gregory claimed that Purkett failed to fulfill his obligation to pay the association the amounts owed for the lands bid on. The case was tried at the March term in 1838 before Hon. Jesse B. Thomas, where the primary issue centered around whether the consideration for the promissory note failed due to Purkett's alleged failure to make the required payments, which would have entitled Gregory and the other defendants to their share of the dividends.	The plaintiffs, George T. Purkett and William H. Graves, argued that the defendants were obligated to honor the promissory note despite Gregory's claims of non-payment by Purkett. They contended that the defendants' assertion of a failure in consideration was unfounded and sought to collect the amount due under the note.	John Gregory contended that there was a failure of consideration for part of the debt mentioned in the note, specifically $163. He claimed that due to Purkett's failure to pay the amount owed for the choice of lands as agreed, the defendants were deprived of receiving the corresponding dividends, which constituted their right under the agreement. Gregory argued that the note was therefore invalid to that extent, asserting a partial failure of consideration.

In the case of Johanna Uhre et al. v. Anton Melum, originating in the Cook County Circuit Court, the dispute centers around a creditor's bill filed by the appellee against the appellants. The events leading to this case began with a judgment recovered by the complainants, Johanna Uhre and another, against Anders Uhre and Knud K. Forrast in May 1882 for $130 and associated costs. An execution was issued later that year, which was returned without any property found or satisfaction of the judgment. The key individuals involved include Johanna Uhre, the wife of Anders B. Uhre, and the defendant Anton Melum. The crux of the issue lies in allegations that Anders Uhre transferred property to his wife Johanna without consideration while being heavily indebted. The complainants argue this conveyance was made to defraud and hinder Anders' creditors. The case became complicated when defendants claimed that Anders did not own the properties and denied any fraudulent intent in the conveyance. The court ultimately needed to determine whether the creditor's claims were valid based on the evidence and allegations presented.	The plaintiffs argue that as creditors of Anders Uhre, they are entitled to relief against a property conveyance made to his wife, Johanna, claiming that it was done without consideration and with the intent to defraud creditors. They allege that at the time of the property transfer, Anders was heavily indebted and deemed insolvent, claiming that the conveyance was a fraudulent attempt to shield assets from creditors. They seek to have the property conveyance set aside, asserting that their judgment should serve as a lien on the properties in question.	The defendants, Anders and Johanna Uhre, assert that Anders lacks ownership of the properties and claim that the conveyance to Johanna was legitimate and not intended to defraud creditors. They strongly deny that Anders was collecting rents from the properties and argue that the plaintiffs have not adequately proven their claims of debt or insolvency at the time of the property transfer. Their defense hinges on the assertion that the creditor's complaint is fatally defective due to the lack of evidence showing that the plaintiffs were creditors at the time of the conveyance.

In 1871, in Cook County, Illinois, Moses C. Wright, a commission merchant, was indicted for unlawfully converting the proceeds from the sale of peaches that had been consigned to him by Abijah Birdsey. The incident took place on November 1, 1870, when Birdsey claimed that Wright failed to deliver $61 in proceeds after the sale, contrary to the instructions provided. The case was brought under the statute enacted on March 4, 1869, aimed at protecting consignors in such transactions. During the trial in February 1871, the jury found Wright guilty, and he was fined $100. Wright appealed the judgment to the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing that the demand made by Birdsey was insufficient for a conviction, as it did not clearly apprise him of the potential penalties he faced under the law.	The plaintiff, Abijah Birdsey, claimed that Moses C. Wright unlawfully converted the proceeds from the sale of peaches he consigned to Wright and failed to deliver the proceeds after Birdsey made a demand for them. Birdsey sought to hold Wright accountable under the statute designed for the protection of consignors, asserting that Wright's actions constituted a misdemeanor.	The defendant, Moses C. Wright, argued that the evidence presented against him was insufficient to sustain the guilty verdict. He claimed that the demand made by Birdsey did not meet the legal requirements stipulated by the statute, as it lacked the necessary clarity and formality to inform him of the potential consequences of failing to comply. Wright requested a reversal of the judgment based on these grounds.

In 1867, the case of Isaac Cook v. Jehiel F. Norton et al. took place in Chicago, Illinois. Isaac Cook initiated an ejectment action against Jehiel E. Norton, his wife Emily M. Horton, Grace J. Clarke, and Julia Wilkie, seeking to recover two-thirds of a lot in Chicago. The ownership of the lot traced back to James Byan, who purchased it from the State on September 15, 1845. Byan had sold one-third of the property to Cook earlier that year and executed a contract for its conveyance. Byan was later subjected to a judgment lien by one Ballingall, leading to a series of property transfers as Byan's interest was sold under execution to Ballingall in April 1846. Subsequently, Cook conveyed his interest to Smith, who ultimately sold the entire lot to Lewis W. Clark. After Clark's death, his heirs, including Emily and Grace, entered the lawsuit. Cook claimed title rights through a sheriff's deed stemming from Ballingall's purchase. However, the court found that Clark's heirs were in possession of the lot and had paid taxes for several years, establishing claim and color of title. Ultimately, the court found in favor of the defendants, leading to Cook's appeal.	Isaac Cook argued that he held a valid title to two-thirds of the lot due to a sheriff's deed he obtained after Ballingall's purchase and subsequent execution of the lien. Cook maintained that he had bona fide ownership based on prior agreements and valid transactions. He sought recovery of the property based on his legal claim of ownership and the historical transactions validating his rights.	The defendants contended that they held rightful possession of the property through their ancestor, Lewis W. Clark, who had occupied and paid taxes on the lot for seven successive years, qualifying under claim and color of title principles. They asserted that the evidence presented did not sufficiently establish Cook's claims over their rights to the property, emphasizing that Cook failed to show relevant tax payments concurrent with possession.

In September 1875, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between John M. Reynolds and Joseph M. Greenbaum concerning a forcible detainer action. The plaintiff, Greenbaum, sought the recovery of premises leased to Reynolds, claiming that Reynolds had forfeited the lease due to non-payment of rent. The lease in question was acknowledged to have been executed by both parties. It was left with the scrivener who prepared it for both their benefits and, as per legal requirements, this constituted a sufficient delivery of the lease. The crux of the case was whether Reynolds was occupying the premises as a tenant under the lease or as a vendee based on an alleged verbal purchase agreement made after the lease was executed. The trial jury found in favor of Greenbaum, asserting that Reynolds was indeed a tenant under the lease.	The plaintiff, Joseph M. Greenbaum, claimed that he was entitled to recover possession of the demised premises from John M. Reynolds due to non-payment of rent, which constituted a forfeiture of the lease agreement. Greenbaum argued that the lease was valid and enforceable, and that Reynolds had not fulfilled his obligations under this contract.	The defendant, John M. Reynolds, contended that he was not merely a tenant but claimed ownership through a verbal contract of purchase made after the lease was signed. He argued that this purchase agreement should exclude him from the claims of forcible detainer under the lease. Reynolds asserted that the jury should have considered this verbal agreement in determining his right to the premises.

George Baker was involved in a legal case with the People of the State of Illinois, culminating in a court decision in September 1868. This case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court following an indictment in the Kane Circuit Court for an assault with a gun against William Warner, where Baker allegedly intended to inflict bodily injury. The indictment included two counts. Initially, a motion by the defendant to quash (invalidate) the indictment was made. However, the jury ultimately found Baker guilty on the second count. Subsequently, a motion to arrest the judgment was denied, resulting in a judgment imposed on Baker, which included a fine of $25 and associated costs. The legal dispute hinged on procedural and substantive issues related to the indictment's compliance with the Criminal Code in Illinois, as the court found defects in how the assault charge was structured.	The plaintiff's primary claim revolved around the indictment for assault with a deadly weapon, asserting that Baker intended to inflict bodily harm on the victim, William Warner. The prosecution maintained that the indictment adhered to the appropriate legal standards and sought to uphold the jury's conviction, arguing that Baker's actions and intent met the statutory requirements for the charge as defined in the Criminal Code.	The defense, led by George Baker, argued that the indictment was defective because it did not specify that no considerable provocation appeared or detail circumstances that demonstrated an "abandoned and malignant heart," both of which are essential elements to substantiate the charge of assault with a deadly weapon. The defense requested the court to quash the indictment, indicating that the failure to include these critical elements rendered the findings against Baker legally insufficient.

Wilson D. Darlington et al. v. Thomas W. Chamberlain is a legal case decided on December 16, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in Cook County, Illinois, where the appellants (Darlington et al.) acted as commission brokers for the Holderman Brothers, who purchased livestock in the vicinity of Pontiac and Rantoul, Illinois, for sale at the Chicago market. For years, appellants advanced money to Holderman Bros. for purchasing feed and livestock. In the summer of 1883, the appellants advanced $6,000 to Holderman Bros., intending the money for buying and feeding stock. Subsequently, Holderman Bros. arranged for loans from the appellee, Thomas W. Chamberlain, a banker, to finance their purchases, with an agreement that the proceeds from sold stock would be credited to Chamberlain. In June 1885, after some time agreeing to allocate the proceeds from sales to Chamberlain’s credit, the appellants failed to honor this arrangement and instead credit the proceeds to themselves to satisfy debts owed to them by Holderman Bros. This led to Chamberlain suing the appellants to recover proceeds from the sale of cattle and hogs, ultimately resulting in a jury finding against the appellants.	The plaintiff, Thomas W. Chamberlain, claimed that he was owed the proceeds from the sale of cattle and hogs that were sold by the appellants as commission brokers. He argued that an agreement existed mandating that the proceeds from the sales were to be credited to his account, stemming from the loans he provided to Holderman Bros. for the stock purchases. Chamberlain contended that the appellants wrongfully converted these proceeds and sought a judgment for the amount owed, which was evidenced by the jury's verdict against the appellants.	The defendants, Wilson D. Darlington et al., argued that they possessed a general lien on the proceeds from the stock sales to recover debts owed to them by Holderman Bros. They maintained that their established relationship entitled them to claim the proceeds as security against the advances made. However, they acknowledged that this right could be waived based on the dealings and agreements between the parties. They ultimately contended that the lien was not waived, and they had the right to appropriate the funds to satisfy the judgment notes they held against Holderman Bros.

The case "Henry W. Farrar v. Eugene B. Payne et al." was adjudicated in September 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute involved a tract of land in Cook County, Illinois, originally sold by Gibbons (one of the defendants) under a trust deed to secure a promissory note made by John W. Sharp for $654. Both the plaintiff, Henry W. Farrar, and the defendant, Eugene B. Payne, claimed title to the land through Sharp. Farrar's title was established via an attachment proceeding against Sharp, with documents including a levy, a certificate of sale, and a sheriff's deed. Conversely, Payne claimed through the trust deed executed from Sharp to Gibbons, which was legally recorded. The original bill was filed by Farrar to redeem the land, while Payne countered with a cross-bill seeking to set aside deeds held by Farrar as clouds on his title. After reviewing the facts, the court found that the sale under the trust deed had been properly executed, and it ultimately ruled in favor of Payne.	The plaintiff, Henry W. Farrar, argued that he held a valid title to the land derived from attachment proceedings against Sharp. He claimed the right to redeem the land based on the legal instruments recorded in support of his ownership and contended that procedural deficiencies—specifically insufficient notice regarding the sale under the trust deed—should void the sale conducted by the trustee, Gibbons.	The defendant, Eugene B. Payne, defended his claim to the title by arguing that the sale under the trust deed was valid and that proper notice had been given. He asserted that the actions taken by the trustee in advertising and conducting the sale were in compliance with the trust deed's requirements and claimed Farrar had no standing to contest his title since he had only an equity interest, not a legal claim, due to the prior lawful sale under the trust deed.

In June 1873, in Madison County, Illinois, Thomas M. Hope filed a lawsuit against the City of Alton regarding property damage caused by a defect in the city’s street gutter system. Hope owned two lots, which housed a brick store and a frame dwelling. The city had previously graded and macadamized Fourth Street, where the inadequately maintained gutters failed to effectively drain water. This negligence resulted in water flooding onto Hope's property. Witnesses testified that the gutter was narrow and deep, with significant breaks that allowed water to flow directly onto Hope's lots, damaging his buildings. The case was tried in the Circuit Court of Madison County, where it culminated in a jury verdict awarding Hope $200 in damages.	The plaintiff, Thomas M. Hope, claimed that the City of Alton was negligent in maintaining the gutters on Fourth Street, which led to flooding and subsequent damage to his properties. He argued that the city had a legal obligation to keep these public improvements in proper repair, which it failed to do. Hope sought damages for the injuries caused by this negligence, specifically related to the flooding of his properties.	The City of Alton contended that the trial court made an error by refusing to give a jury instruction that would limit Hope's ability to claim damages for specific injuries, namely to the brick wall of his building. The city maintained that, according to the pleadings, the plaintiff was not entitled to recover for damages related to the brick wall. They argued that any potential error did not prejudice their case sufficiently to overturn the judgment.

The case "David L. Phillips et al., Administrators, v. The City of Springfield" was adjudicated in 1866 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in Springfield, Illinois, stemming from an action brought against Francis Clinton for assaulting Lucinda Emmons, the wife of Elias Emmons. The incident occurred on November 14, 1864, when Clinton, having rented out property that he owned (previously the home of the Emmons), found Lucinda in the house after a change of tenants. Mrs. Emmons, having moved in under questionable circumstances, was asked firmly but peacefully by Clinton to leave the property. She alleges that Clinton used excessive force, including pushing her out of the house and placing her belongings outside. Although Clinton was initially found guilty and fined, he appealed to the Circuit Court, which upheld the fine. After his death, his administrators continued the appeal, arguing that the verdict was against the evidence, and that the court erred in denying their motions for a new trial and to arrest judgment.	The plaintiffs, represented by David L. Phillips and Anna Clinton, contended that the verdict from the lower court was unjust, claiming it was unsupported by the evidence presented. They requested the reversal of the judgment against Clinton, arguing that he acted within his rights to remove an intruder from his lawful possession without breaching the local ordinance concerning misdemeanors.	The defense asserted that Clinton’s actions were justified as he was removing an intruder, Mrs. Emmons, from property that was rightfully his and that he acted without unnecessary force. They highlighted the ordinance's focus on public disorder, arguing that Clinton's conduct did not violate any law or the spirit of the ordinance, as he was merely protecting his property and rights against an unauthorized occupant.

On December 6, 1887, in Warren County, Illinois, David R. Shelton purchased a 65-acre stalk field from William O’Riley for $40, intending to use it for cattle pasturage. The stalk field was adjacent to the right of way for the Chicago, California, and Santa Fe Railway Company, which was not fenced at that time. Both parties expected that the railway company would build a fence along its right of way, as it was legally required to do. The plaintiff, Shelton, argued that O’Riley had an obligation to build the fence within weeks of the purchase to allow him to effectively pasture his cattle; without this fencing, the land would hold no value for him. Shelton's claims were supported by his testimony and that of three other witnesses. Conversely, O’Riley refuted this claim, supported by his own testimony and witnesses. The jury sided with Shelton's version of the facts, leading to a trial court judgment that O’Riley was obligated to provide the fencing.	David R. Shelton contended that William O’Riley had a contractual obligation to build a fence along the right of way to make the purchased stalk field suitable for cattle pasturage. He argued that without this fencing, the land would be worthless to him. Shelton sought the court's enforcement of this obligation based on the understanding he and O’Riley had at the time of purchase, alongside testimony supporting his claim.	William O’Riley denied that he was obligated to build the fence following Shelton's purchase of the stalk field. He presented evidence and witness testimony to contradict Shelton's assertions about the fencing obligation, asserting that it was the railway company's responsibility to build the fence, and not O’Riley's. O’Riley requested that the court dismiss Shelton’s claims based on this defense.

The case, "The Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company v. The People of the State of Illinois, ex rel.," was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on January 10, 1889. The lawsuit arose in Clinton County, Illinois, initiated by George Locey against the Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company. Locey, a resident of Carlyle, Illinois, sought damages after the railway company's train, which he believed to be a regular passenger train, failed to stop at Carlyle, where he intended to disembark. On January 21, 1887, Locey had received an urgent message to return home, prompting him to travel from Sumner to Carlyle. He flagged down train No. 3, which he was assured by the railway's agent would stop at Carlyle. However, when the train reached Shattuck, it did not stop, leading Locey to miss his destination and incurring extra travel costs. The case hinged on whether train No. 3 was indeed a regular passenger train under the Illinois statute requiring such trains to stop at advertised stations.	The plaintiff, George Locey, claimed that the Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company violated the statute mandating regular passenger trains to stop at advertised stations. Locey argued that he was aggrieved due to the company's failure to stop at Carlyle, which caused him both distress and additional travel expenses. His legal request sought the statutory penalty for this violation and damages for the incurred costs.	The defendant, Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company, contended that train No. 3 was not a regular passenger train as defined by the relevant statute, arguing that it was merely a section of another train that did not always stop at Carlyle. The company's defense relied on interpretations that suggested Locey was not a person aggrieved by the alleged omission of duty since the train schedule and stops were not under their violation. They requested the court to dismiss the charges against them based on this reasoning.

The case "Rees v. City of Chicago" was decided in April 1865 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The situation arose in the city of Chicago and involved a legal action in ejectment initiated in the Superior Court of Chicago. The case was notable for its procedural dynamics, namely a writ of error filed by the plaintiff, Rees, against a judgment that was made in the lower court. While the writ of error was pending, the judgment in the Superior Court was vacated at the instigation of Rees, who requested a new trial under the applicable statutes. This led to the defendant, the City of Chicago, motioning to dismiss the writ of error, arguing that without an active judgment to review, the writ was no longer applicable. The court had to determine whether the existence of the new trial affected the continuing validity of the writ of error.	The plaintiff, Rees, claimed that the judgment in ejectment should be vacated to allow for a new trial, bending the proceedings in line with statutory provisions. By pursuing the writ of error, Rees aimed to challenge the initial ruling even as a new trial was granted in the lower court. The intent was to safeguard his rights and retain the opportunity for judicial review regarding the initial judgment's validity.	The defendant, City of Chicago, contended that the winding of the new trial effectively nullified the prior judgment, rendering the writ of error moot. Their primary argument was that without an existing judgment, the appellate court should dismiss the writ since there was no decision to review. The defendant sought to conclude the litigation by asserting that the actions of the plaintiff negated the grounds for the ongoing appellate review.

In 1883, in Cook County, Illinois, Leonard Roehr and Daniel Duggan, contractors, submitted the lowest bid of $6,250 to build a school house for the Board of Education of District 1, Township 37, Range 15. The Board awarded them the contract and required them to prepare a bond and schedule their property for a subsequent meeting. However, on the same day, an injunction was filed against the Board, preventing further action regarding the construction. The plaintiffs were informed of this injunction at their next meeting but were advised to hold themselves ready for the project. As weeks passed without the injunction being lifted, the Board ultimately decided to abandon the project. The plaintiffs claimed they suffered significant losses after purchasing materials, hiring laborers, and dedicating their time to the undertaking while under the belief that the contract was valid. A jury found in favor of the plaintiffs, awarding them $902 in damages.	The plaintiffs argued that the Board of Education had breached their contract by preventing them from proceeding with the school house construction. They contended that they relied on the Board's assurances and incurred losses from materials and labor due to the failure to execute the work as planned. They sought damages for these losses and argued that their contract should be honored.	The defendant, the Board of Education, contended that the contract was void as it did not have the necessary petition from a majority of the district's voters to authorize the construction of a school house, as required by Illinois law. They argued that the plaintiffs were aware of this legal limitation and thus should not be entitled to damages for what they termed a null contract.

John Briley, the plaintiff in error, initiated legal action against Alfred Copeland, the defendant in error, concerning a case of non-feasance in office as a constable. This case occurred around June 1851 in Massac County, Illinois, where a justice of the peace handled the initial case. Briley sought damages amounting to $50. The trial at the justice level concluded with a judgment favoring Copeland. Subsequently, Briley appealed to the circuit court, but the court dismissed the suit, claiming that the justice lacked jurisdiction over the matter. However, according to the relevant statute, justices of the peace do have jurisdiction in cases involving constables for amounts not exceeding one hundred dollars. The Illinois Supreme Court, upon reviewing the case, determined that the justice indeed had jurisdiction and that the circuit court erred in dismissing the matter. Consequently, the judgment from the circuit court was reversed, and the case was sent back for further proceedings.	Briley's main arguments revolved around the claim that Copeland, as a constable, failed to fulfill his duties (non-feasance), warranting compensation for damages. He requested that the court reverse the circuit court's dismissal of his case and uphold the justice's jurisdiction to hear the original claim.	Copeland's defense relied on the assertion that the justice of the peace did not have the jurisdiction to hear the case, leading to the circuit court's dismissal. The defense maintained that the legal standards interpreting the jurisdictional limits were correctly applied, and therefore contended that the decision made by the circuit court should be upheld.

In 1883, in Peoria County, Illinois, the case of William J. Dobbins, Admr. v. Sarah J. Cruger, Admx. et al. unfolded. The plaintiff, William J. Dobbins, acting as the administrator of an estate, sought to recover a judgment against William H. Cruger. This judgment had been awarded prior to the conveyance of real estate from Thomas S. Dobbins to Mary J. Cruger, William's wife, via a warranty deed. Dobbins argued the property should be liable for the debts owed by William H. Cruger, as it was conveyed to his wife with knowledge of her husband's financial obligations. The case highlighted complex questions regarding the assignability of judgments and whether the transaction between the grantor and grantee could be seen as fraudulent. The court deliberated on these matters, considering previous legal precedents regarding the assignability of judgments and the rights of creditors. The outcome hinged on whether Dobbins had grounds to challenge the conveyance as fraudulent, given that his claims could be contradicted by established principles of property law.	The plaintiff, William J. Dobbins, claimed that the property transferred to Mary J. Cruger should be subjected to his prior judgment against her husband, William H. Cruger. He argued that the transaction was part of a scheme to hinder creditors, thus he sought to enforce his judgment against the property conveyed via the warranty deed.	Sarah J. Cruger, as the representative of her deceased husband, defended the case by asserting that the conveyance was legal and that Dobbins had no standing to question it. The defendants contended that the property was rightfully conveyed without any fraudulent intent, and that Dobbins could not challenge the title established by the warranty deed, citing legal principles that protect such titles against later claims by grantors with full covenants.

On September 8, 1888, Albert W. Morse was involved in an incident while driving a laundry delivery wagon on Wabash Avenue in Chicago. During the late afternoon, the horse he trusted for the past thirteen or fourteen years inadvertently pulled the wagon into a hole in the asphalt pavement, created due to ongoing repairs. The wagon overturned, resulting in Morse breaking his leg. He subsequently filed a lawsuit against the City of Chicago, seeking compensation for his injury, alleging negligence on the city's part in maintaining safe streets.	The plaintiff, Albert W. Morse, argued that the City of Chicago failed to ensure the safety and proper maintenance of its streets, leading to his accident and subsequent injury. He requested compensation for the damages incurred as a result of the city's negligence.	The City of Chicago contended that the instructions given to the jury—specifically, those suggesting that travelers could presume streets were safe—were erroneous. The city argued that the jury must consider evidence of due diligence and care, and that the instruction may have misled the jury about the necessity of exercising caution when using the streets. Consequently, the city sought to have the judgment reconsidered and overturned based on these flawed instructions.

The legal case of "The Belleville Savings Bank v. Susana Reis et al." took place in Illinois with a decision rendered on March 1, 1889. The dispute arose from a bill filed by the Belleville Savings Bank to foreclose a mortgage. Susana Reis and others, the defendants, responded to the foreclosure attempt stating that the mortgage had already been satisfied. In the process, the defendants filed a cross-bill requesting the cancellation of the mortgage and the surrender of the corresponding note. A decree was entered by default at the February term of the Circuit Court in 1886, affirming the defendants' claim. The bank attempted to vacate this decree at subsequent court terms but was unsuccessful. At the September term of 1886, the bank sought a hearing on the original foreclosure bill but was denied the opportunity to present evidence, as the prior order confirming the satisfaction of the mortgage still stood. The court's denial of the appellant's motions and requests became the subject of the appeal.	The plaintiff, Belleville Savings Bank, argued that the mortgage should not have been declared satisfied and disputed the entry of a decree that favored the defendants. They sought to vacate the decree, reassert their claim on the mortgage, and present evidence that contradicted the defendants' assertions. The bank maintained that it was denied a fair hearing on its original foreclosure claim and sought to challenge the validity of the earlier decree entered against them in response to the cross-bill.	The defendants, led by Susana Reis, contended that the mortgage in question had indeed been satisfied and thus, the foreclosure action was unwarranted. They filed a cross-bill to cancel the mortgage, which was initially upheld through a decree by default. They argued that the plaintiff's attempts to vacate this decree were without merit, as they had not provided sufficient justification or evidence to support the motion. Additionally, the defendants stated that the initial ruling and subsequent practices adhered to procedural guidelines and were rightful under the circumstances.

In April 1860, the Illinois Supreme Court dealt with a case involving the School Trustees against Mary Ann Kirwin, the executrix of Francis M. Kirwin's estate, along with administrators of Rolla French's estate. The events date back to 1858 when Rolla French was appointed township treasurer and was responsible for managing approximately $3,000 belonging to the school funds. French, who had no personal wealth other than a modest salary, deposited these funds into Kirwin's bank under his name, with Kirwin being aware of this arrangement. After both French and Kirwin died, the school trustees sought to recover the funds, claiming that the school money had been commingled with the bank’s general funds in a way that made it difficult to trace. The case revolved around whether the school trustees could claim the remaining funds from Kirwin's estate, despite the mixing of money and lack of clear identity for the school funds held by Kirwin's bank.	The school trustees argued that Kirwin knowingly accepted deposits of school funds from French and that as a trustee of these funds, he had a duty to preserve them. They sought a decree to recover the entire amount deposited by French in Kirwin's bank, asserting that Kirwin’s acceptance of these funds created a trust obligation to return them to the school trustees.	Kirwin's estate, represented by Mary Ann Kirwin, contended that the money deposited by French was mixed with bank funds, compromising the identity of the school money as a distinct fund. Therefore, they argued, the trustees were not entitled to pursue the funds beyond the specific amount of money that could be separately identified and was already acknowledged to belong to the school fund.

In September 1875, the case of Amon S. Gilbert v. Wallace G. Bone was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from Warren County, Illinois, where Gilbert, the plaintiff, accused Bone, the county clerk, of issuing a marriage license to Gilbert's minor daughter without obtaining the necessary consent from her parent or guardian. Initially, the case was reviewed in 1872 but was sent back for further proceedings following a ruling that there was an error in overruling Bone's demurrer. Upon remand, Bone amended his pleas, and the jury ultimately ruled in favor of Bone. Gilbert then moved for a new trial, arguing that the verdict was unsupported by evidence. However, the court examined the record and ruled that the evidence presented did not warrant a new trial, stating that it is not enough for the court to simply disagree with the jury's conclusion without clear evidence against it. The crux of the trial centered on the testimony provided by Bone, who claimed he relied on the sworn statements given by the parties involved regarding their ages at the time of the marriage license issuance.	Amon S. Gilbert argued that Wallace G. Bone had acted unlawfully by issuing a marriage license for his minor daughter without obtaining the requisite parental consent. Gilbert sought to hold Bone liable under the relevant penal statute, asserting that the license was issued in violation of legal requirements regarding the age of consent and parental rights.	Wallace G. Bone defended against Gilbert's claims by stating that he had no prior knowledge of the age of Gilbert's daughter at the time of issuing the marriage license. Bone testified that he had conducted a personal examination of the applicant under oath, who claimed to be of legal age. Bone contended that he had satisfied the legal obligations required of him, asserting his innocence in issuing the license based on the evidence he gathered at the time.

In January 1872, in Illinois, Marcus Belden purchased approximately 900 bushels of corn from John R. Innis, which was stored in a warehouse owned by a railroad company. The terms of the sale required Belden to pay the market price on a day specified by Innis during the subsequent summer season. In June, when the market price of corn was 35 cents per bushel, Innis demanded payment. However, in February 1872, the warehouse and its contents, including the corn, were destroyed in a fire, leading to disputes over the obligations of both parties. Innis filed a lawsuit against Belden, seeking payment for the corn. The case was initially decided in favor of Innis, but Belden appealed the decision, claiming that his trial court did not adequately evaluate the evidence.	John R. Innis, the plaintiff, claimed that he had a valid sale agreement with Marcus Belden for the sale of 900 bushels of corn stored in a railroad warehouse. Innis sought payment based on the market price of corn on a specific date in June, arguing that Belden owed him for the corn that had been destroyed under circumstances that should not negate the sale.	Marcus Belden, the defendant, contended that there was insufficient evidence to support the claim that a sale had occurred. He argued that Innis's testimony was inconsistent and not credible, which was further contradicted by the testimony of four other witnesses. Belden's defense focused on the assertion that the circuit court erred by not granting a new trial based on the overwhelming doubt cast on Innis's claims by the evidence presented.

In 1861, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of Sylvester Stevens et al. v. Alvah Wheeler et al. Sylvester Stevens and other heirs of Zadock Stevens, who died in July 1838, claimed ownership of land that had once belonged to their father. The land in question, located in Hancock County, Illinois, was primarily valuable for its timber. The complainants argued that Alvah Wheeler, a personal associate of Zadock Stevens, unlawfully removed $6,000 worth of timber from the property without accounting for it. The background indicated that, following Zadock Stevens' death, several heirs conveyed their interests in the land to Wheeler, claiming that he had secretly purchased it on their behalf. Wheeler maintained that he purchased the land from Russell Hoyt and made lasting improvements on it. The court examined the claims involving the original purchase agreement and subsequent possessions. Key individuals involved included Sylvester Stevens, Alvah Wheeler, and other heirs related to Zadock Stevens. The case progressed through the Hancock Circuit Court before reaching the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs argued that they, as heirs of Zadock Stevens, were rightful owners of the property. They claimed that Wheeler had cut down timber valued at $6,000 without proper accounting and sought to either partition the land or sell it, dividing the proceeds among the heirs. They also requested that the court require Wheeler to account for the timber cut and removed from the land and sought further equity relief.	Alvah Wheeler refuted the plaintiffs' claims by asserting that he held the equitable title to the land. He stated that he had a verbal agreement with Zadock Stevens to purchase the land and provided evidence that he had taken possession of the land, improved it, and had not faced challenges to his ownership for nearly twenty years. Wheeler requested a decree to perfect his title and compel the plaintiffs to convey all their rights to him, claiming that their claims were against the statute of frauds and perjuries.

The case of K. K. Jones v. H. A. Albee took place in September 1873 in Cook County, Illinois. The suit was initiated by H. A. Albee, who brought an action of assumpsit against K. K. Jones in the Superior Court of Cook County. The case centered around a written guaranty on a promissory note dated September 21, 1870, for $2,326.31, which H. A. Albee claimed Jones had guaranteed. During the trial, a jury rendered a verdict in favor of Albee for $2,984.96. Jones appealed the judgment, seeking a reversal. The defendant challenged the trial court's refusal to accept an additional plea that alleged he was induced into the agreement through fraud and misrepresentation by the plaintiff. The court held that the allegations of fraud were not sufficiently detailed and that a plea seeking to alter the written contract with parol evidence was not legally viable. The case also raised questions about the authority of Judge Josiah McRoberts, who presided over the trial. Ultimately, the court's opinion clarified that judges from different circuits could preside in the Superior Court if requested.	H. A. Albee, the plaintiff, claimed that K. K. Jones guaranteed a promissory note and sought enforcement of this written agreement. Albee alleged that he incurred damages as a result of Jones's failure to honor that guaranty and thus requested compensation based on the amount owed under the promissory note.	K. K. Jones, the defendant, defended against Albee's claims by asserting that he was misled into signing the guaranty due to fraud and misrepresentation by Albee. He contended that the amount quoted by Albee for a manufacturing business and patent rights was inflated, and he claimed a parol agreement limited his liability on the indorsement. He also challenged the validity of Judge McRoberts's authority to preside over the trial.

The case, titled "The Farmers & Merchants’ Insurance Company v. John A. Chesnut et al.," was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1869. The dispute arose following a fire that occurred in February 1867 at a property insured by David Wigle. After the fire, the Farmers & Merchants’ Insurance Company dispatched an agent to estimate the loss, which was determined to be $1,852.51. Wigle initially disagreed with the assessment but later negotiated and accepted the amount. Following this, a written acknowledgment detailing that the payment would be made within 90 days was provided to Wigle. However, when the company failed to pay, the assignees in bankruptcy for Wigle’s estate filed suit to recover the agreed sum. The case involved several legal arguments relating to the validity of the promise made by the company and whether certain policy provisions had been breached.	The plaintiffs, representing Wigle's bankruptcy estate, argued that the insurance company had promised to pay the agreed-upon amount following the fire and that this settlement was binding. They cited the written acknowledgment provided by the company as evidence of acceptance of the proof of loss and asserted that the company had waived its right to contest the claim by engaging in negotiations with Wigle.	The Farmers & Merchants’ Insurance Company contended that Wigle's insurance policy was void due to his failure to disclose a nearby wooden building in the application. They also argued that the suit was not filed within the one-year period required by the policy and claimed that the document presented was merely an adjustment of loss and not a promise to pay, which they deemed binding. Furthermore, the company asserted that the officers who made the settlement lacked the authority to bind the company.

In 1863, William Schirmer was indicted for murder in the Randolph County Circuit Court, Illinois. The trial took place in Chester, Illinois, with Judge Silas L. Bryan presiding. The grand jury, appointed by the court and led by Foreman Jonathan Ohesnutwood, returned a "true bill" for murder on September 15, 1863. The trial commenced shortly after, during which Schirmer pleaded not guilty. After hearing the evidence, the jury rendered their verdict on September 18, 1863, finding Schirmer guilty of manslaughter instead of murder. Subsequently, he was sentenced to life imprisonment at hard labor, with one day of solitary confinement. Following the conviction, Schirmer's counsel filed a writ of error to challenge the trial's legality, claiming that essential records related to the indictment and trial were missing or improperly certified.	The plaintiff, William Schirmer, argued that the record of his trial was incomplete. He contended that the initial record did not demonstrate that the indictment was properly returned into open court by the grand jury, nor did it confirm that the indictment was endorsed as a "true bill." Schirmer's claims included the assertion that the jury was not legally impaneled, that he was not present during essential trial moments, and that the proceedings failed to adhere to legal requirements of a fair trial. He requested a review based on these alleged inconsistencies.	The defendants, representing the People of the State of Illinois, maintained that the records submitted to the court were complete and legally sufficient. They argued that although the initial record had deficiencies, the amended record provided by the clerk of the Circuit Court was certified and accurate, thereby affirming the legality of the trial and the jury's verdict. The defendants requested that the court uphold the original judgment and sentence, contending that there were no grounds to dispute the validity of the trial proceedings.

In the case titled "The Village of Hyde Park v. Nathan Corwith," the legal dispute was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision rendered on May 12, 1887. The key individuals involved were Nathan Corwith, the plaintiff, and the Village of Hyde Park, the defendant. This case arose from prior condemnation judgments related to land that the Village had forfeited for public use. The plaintiff claimed that these judgments, which were based on an earlier ordinance asserting that costs for public improvements would be covered by special assessments, warranted payment from the Village. The plaintiff sought to recover owed compensation as the Village’s actions were perceived as having deprived them of property rights without due payment. The proceedings unfolded in the context of a complex dual case scenario—one involving an appeal from the Appellate Court and another leading back to the Superior Court of Cook County, indicating a multifaceted legal landscape with previous rulings relevant to the current action.	The plaintiff argued that the Village of Hyde Park was obliged to pay for the condemnation judgments, citing that the Village had taken possession of the land. They contended that, irrespective of the debt being structured as an obligation under an earlier ordinance, the Village was legally bound to honor the judgments. Furthermore, the plaintiff's claim asserted that the enabling ordinance for special assessments was inapplicable since it had been "repealed," thus holding the Village responsible for compensating damages directly.	The defendant, represented by the Village of Hyde Park, contended that the action sought by the plaintiff was seeking a remedy that had previously been ruled out in a separate but related case. The Village maintained that existing ordinances specified payments from special assessments and excluded alternative payment avenues such as general taxation. They argued that it was legally impermissible for the plaintiff to demand payment through direct judgment action, as the established mode of payment was fixed by the legislative authority of the Village, emphasizing that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate any negligence or failure on their part in levying special assessments.

John Phillips was indicted on January 11, 1869, in the circuit court of Rock Island County, Illinois, for an assault on Jasper H. Hampton with a loaded revolver. The incident occurred on October 30, 1868. After filing a plea in abatement to challenge the court's jurisdiction—which was rejected—Phillips pleaded not guilty and went to trial. The jury found him guilty of assault with a deadly weapon with intent to inflict bodily injury, resulting in a $250 fine. Phillips sought to withdraw his not guilty plea to file a special plea claiming he had already been convicted of the same offense in Iowa. This request was denied, and the evidence from the Iowa case was also excluded from the trial. The majority opinion stated that the lower court did not abuse its discretion in these matters, and highlighted insufficient reason for the special plea which lacked legal foundation. The court emphasized that the Iowa conviction did not bar further legal action in Illinois because the crime was alleged to have been committed under the jurisdiction of both states.	John Phillips argued that the prior conviction in Iowa should bar further prosecution in Illinois, claiming the crime was the same, as it occurred on the Mississippi River, which serves as a boundary between the states. He requested to withdraw his not guilty plea and present the records of his Iowa conviction as evidence to demonstrate that the exclusive jurisdiction resided with that court.	The People of the State of Illinois contended that the offenses were not the same in legal terms, given the distinct jurisdictional boundaries of the states. They maintained that the court had properly excluded Phillips' plea and evidence connected to his Iowa conviction. The prosecution argued the nature of the crime and its jurisdictional implications did not allow for a double jeopardy claim or for the records to be admissible in the Illinois court.

The case of Ransom Bullock v. William P. Geomble took place in September 1867 in Illinois, specifically in Livingston County. Ransom Bullock, the plaintiff, owned a herd of cattle that he grazed in the area and had employed Patrick Kearney to care for the herd while he was away. During Bullock's absence, seventeen of his cattle escaped and were later found by Kearney in the local pound, where they had been taken by Geomble, who claimed to be the pound-master. Without consulting Bullock, Kearney arranged with Geomble to retrieve sixteen of the cattle, leaving one steer as security for outstanding fees. When Bullock returned, he rejected this arrangement and demanded the return of his steer, which Geomble refused. Bullock subsequently filed a replevin action to recover the steer. The case was first heard in front of a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment for the defendant, which was upheld in an appeal to the Circuit Court. This appeal to the Supreme Court followed, bringing various grounds of error and a request for reversal.	Ransom Bullock argued that he was the rightful owner of the steer and that Geomble had no legal right to impound it. Bullock claimed he had tendered sufficient payment to cover all required pound fees, and he contended that Geomble’s refusal to return the steer was unjustified. He also raised issues concerning the validity of the town’s ordinance that allowed the impounding and assessed damages without providing the opportunity for a trial by jury, which Bullock stated violated his constitutional rights.	William P. Geomble defended against Bullock's claims by asserting that he was acting according to the town ordinance, which allowed for the impounding of cattle that caused damages. Geomble argued that the ordinance required Bullock to pay for damages caused by his cattle before recovering his property. He maintained that his fees for keeping the cattle were justified and that the arrangements made by Kearney were legally binding.

The case of Nicholas Schoonhoven v. James B. Gott was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1858. The origins of the case trace back to the Kane County Circuit Court, where an action of assumpsit was initiated by the plaintiff, James B. Gott, against the defendant, Nicholas Schoonhoven, during the April term of 1856. A summons was issued that named the plaintiff correctly but inaccurately referred to the defendant as Nicholas Schoonhoven, while all other documentation (precipe, bond for costs, declaration) identified him as Nicholas Schoonover. The defendant sought to have the case dismissed due to this claimed variance between the name on the summons and that on the declaration. The motion to dismiss was ultimately overruled by the court, which subsequently rendered judgment against Schoonhoven, prompting him to appeal the decision. The primary issue for consideration was whether the variance between the names constituted a material error sufficient to warrant dismissal.	The plaintiff, James B. Gott, argued that the court's ruling was justified despite the variance in names. He implicitly relied on the notion that the subsequent proceedings were valid, and that any discrepancies in the case documents should not negate the legitimacy of the judgment rendered against Schoonhoven. The plaintiff sought to uphold the judgment of the lower court, rejecting the defendant's request for dismissal based on this procedural issue.	The defendant, Nicholas Schoonhoven, presented a principal argument that the variance between the names on the summons and declaration was significant and material, warranting dismissal of the case. He claimed that the discrepancy hindered the identification of the proper parties in the legal proceeding, thus infringing upon the rules of pleading. Schoonhoven maintained that the court should have recognized this variance and acted to dismiss the case, asserting that it constituted adequate grounds for reversing the prior judgment.

Thomas Connor v. Israel T. Nichols is a case adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1863, focusing on an action of ejectment concerning a property in Chicago. The plaintiff, Israel T. Nichols, sought to reclaim possession of premises historically occupied by the defendant, Thomas Connor, who had resided there since at least 1852 with his family. The case arose after Connor executed a deed of trust in 1858 to secure a debt, while stipulations confirmed his family’s continuous residency and indicated that the debt was not for purchasing or improving the property in question. The crux of the case centered on whether Connor’s homestead right was valid despite the trust deed, as no express release of this right appeared in the deed. The court was tasked with determining if the trust deed legally transferred Connor's homestead rights, considering several relevant precedents regarding homestead laws.	Israel T. Nichols claimed ownership of the property based on a deed of trust executed by Thomas Connor and his wife. He argued that the deed granted him the right to possess the premises in Chicago, despite the defendant's assertion of homestead rights. Nichols requested that the court uphold his claim and grant him the possession of the property, reinforcing that Connor's rights had been waived by the execution of the trust deed.	Thomas Connor defended his claim to the premises by asserting his homestead rights, which protect a family's residence from being claimed without proper release. He argued that the trust deed executed by him and his wife lacked any mention of a waiver of these rights and, therefore, could not strip him of his entitlement to the property. Connor's position emphasized that the court should recognize the validity of his homestead claim and reverse the initial judgment in favor of Nichols.

In March 1868, in the town of Odell, Adolph Schroeder and his wife, Hattie, became involved in a legal incident that led to a false imprisonment claim against the town's authorities. Mrs. Schroeder was charged with assault and battery, resulting in a trial before a justice of the peace. After being fined $15, she was immediately imprisoned in the town prison without proper legal authority, as no warrant or mittimus had been issued. The prison lacked basic amenities—no fire, bedding, or furniture—rendering it particularly uncomfortable during cold weather. Following her release the next evening, Hattie Schroeder claimed that the improper imprisonment caused her significant and lasting health issues. The lawsuit was ultimately filed in the McLean circuit court, where the jurors awarded her $900 in damages for the false imprisonment.	The plaintiffs, Adolph and Hattie Schroeder, argued that Mrs. Schroeder was unlawfully imprisoned by the town's officer, as he acted without a proper warrant or legal authority. They requested damages for the false imprisonment and the health injuries suffered by Mrs. Schroeder due to her confinement under inappropriate conditions.	The defendants, representing the town of Odell, contended that they were not liable for Mrs. Schroeder's imprisonment as it was conducted by the constable outside the bounds of authorized action. They argued that the trustees did not order the act of imprisonment and that the town's responsibilities were limited to upholding ordinances, exempting them from liability for the wrongful and illegal actions of individual officers acting beyond their powers.

In 1856, in Pulaski County, Illinois, a legal case arose involving William McBean as the defendant and William W. Ritchie as the plaintiff. Ritchie initiated this action claiming malicious prosecution against McBean for accusing him of perjury. The case was moved from Massac County to Pulaski upon a change of venue. During the trial, Ritchie claimed that he was prosecuted without probable cause and maliciously by McBean. Ultimately, the jury found in favor of Ritchie, awarding him $650 in damages. A motion for a new trial was later overruled, prompting McBean to seek a review from the Illinois Supreme Court due to perceived errors in jury instruction regarding the legal standards for establishing malice and probable cause in a malicious prosecution claim.	Ritchie contended that McBean prosecuted him for perjury maliciously and without probable cause. He argued that his acquittal from the charge was sufficient to demonstrate the lack of probable cause for the prosecution, and thus he was entitled to damages for the injury to his reputation and wrongful prosecution.	McBean contended that the prosecution was justified and that there was a basis for the original perjury accusation. He argued that Ritchie had not met the burden of proving both malice and the absence of probable cause necessary to succeed in a malicious prosecution claim. McBean asserted that the jury was incorrectly instructed to presume malice from the mere fact of Ritchie’s acquittal.

On December 18, 1867, Ezekiel B. Phillips was injured by the explosion of a steam boiler at the Union depot in Chicago, involving the Illinois Central Railroad Company. The case was initially brought to court in 1868, which was reversed and remanded before a second trial culminated in a judgment against the railroad company for $16,000. The plaintiff claimed the engine was old, worn, and poorly maintained, leading to the explosion. However, testimonies revealed that the boiler, although 13-14 years old, underwent significant repairs in 1866 and was deemed safe prior to the explosion. Expert witnesses testified that the boiler was made of high-quality materials, thoroughly checked, and showed no indications of defects or mismanagement at the time of the incident. The court heard arguments regarding the presumption of negligence due to the explosion and evaluating the burden of proof regarding the railroad's duty of care to Phillips as a lawful visitor to the depot.	The plaintiff claimed that the Illinois Central Railroad Company failed to ensure the safety of the boiler, which was old and unsuitable for use. He argued that the company's negligence in management and maintenance led to the explosion, resulting in his injuries. The plaintiff sought damages of $16,000, asserting that the railroad had a responsibility to maintain safe practices to prevent such incidents.	The defendant argued that the boiler had been recently repaired and maintained properly, claiming that it was safe at the time of the explosion. They contended that the injuries sustained by Phillips were not the result of any negligence on the part of the railroad company, as they had adhered to standard operating procedures and had performed necessary tests on the boiler. The defense asserted that any claim of negligence was rebuttable and that the burden of proof lay with the plaintiff to show actual negligence.

George W. Cothran filed an action of assumpsit against J. Alder Ellis and others in the Cook County Superior Court, Illinois, concerning transactions related to the purchase and sale of grain. The case originates from actions taken between December 1881 and January 1882 when Ellis, acting as a commission merchant, purchased wheat for Cothran, who later directed Ellis to sell the wheat at specified prices. Disputes arose regarding Ellis's refusal to obey Cothran's orders, leading to financial losses. The initial ruling found in favor of Cothran, leading to an appeal by Ellis. The core issue revolved around whether Ellis, as Cothran's agent, had an obligation to follow Cothran's instructions and whether Cothran bore any responsibility for losses resulting from Ellis's actions. The Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the legal propositions presented during the trial and proceeded to rule on the interpretation of agency law in relation to the commission merchant's duties.	Cothran argued that Ellis, as his commission agent, was obligated to follow his directions regarding the sale of wheat. He claimed that by refusing to sell when instructed, Ellis caused significant financial losses. Cothran sought recovery of damages amounting to the difference between the purchase price of the wheat and the price that could have been obtained had Ellis followed his directions, less any applicable commissions.	Ellis contended that he acted within his rights as a commission merchant and that any losses incurred were Cothran's responsibility due to his own failure to comply with margin requests or directions. Ellis argued that he was not liable for losses resulting from his refusal to sell because Cothran had not established a clear agency agreement that mandated Ellis to execute sales under the alleged conditions. He emphasized that the nature of the transactions called for a distinct handling of sales and purchases, which Cothran failed to understand.

M. M. Wheeler filed a legal action against The County of Wayne in April 1880, in the Circuit Court of Wayne County, Illinois. The case revolved around the plaintiff's purchase of swamp lands from the county, which were conveyed through multiple deeds dated between 1860 and 1866. These deeds were claimed to be warranty deeds, implying certain obligations regarding the title. However, after Wheeler took possession, the lands were sold at a master’s sale due to a foreclosure of a trust deed that the county had executed as security for certain railroad bonds. Wheeler was not made a party to the foreclosure, which he argued violated his rights to the property he had purchased. He claimed that the county had a responsibility to assist in canceling the trust deed and the foreclosure sale and to cover the legal costs he incurred in the process, which amounted to significant expenses. The county's position was challenged, and the legal argument centered on whether the deeds contained covenants of title, as well as the validity of the county's obligations in relation to the actions taken on the land following the sale.	The plaintiff, M. M. Wheeler, argued that the county was liable for the costs he incurred in legal actions to clear a cloud on his title due to a foreclosure that affected the swamp lands he had purchased. He asserted that the county had agreed to cover these expenses in return for his actions to cancel the trust deed and defend against a reforeclosure suit. He sought compensation for various legal fees and expenses, amounting to approximately $4,000, alleging that the county breached its agreement to assist and cover these costs.	The County of Wayne contended that the deeds issued to Wheeler were effectively quitclaim deeds without any express covenants of warranty regarding the title. The county argued that it could not be held liable to cover costs associated with the cancellation of the trust deed since it had not made any binding agreement beyond the conveyance itself. They maintained that even if there had been a promise to assist in legal matters, it lacked consideration and thus was void. The defendant emphasized that no authority permitted the county to execute warranty deeds for its swamp lands and asserted that the claims against it were invalid.

The case titled "George N. Titus et al., Trustees, etc. v. James Mabee et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1861. The case arose from a bill filed by the trustees of bondholders of the St. Louis, Alton and Chicago Railroad. The key individuals involved included the appellants, George N. Titus and his fellow trustees, and the appellees, James Mabee, Samuel Pitts, and sheriff Brown. The dispute centered around the foreclosure of certain property—specifically a freight car, an iron safe, and an iron planing machine—levied upon by sheriff Brown to satisfy judgments in favor of Mabee and Pitts. The trustees claimed that the property was vital for the railroad's operation and was included under a prior mortgage agreement intended to protect the interests of bondholders. The lower court had initially dissolved a temporary injunction that had been put in place to prevent the sale of this property, which led the trustees to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, as trustees for the bondholders, asserted that the property levied upon (a freight car, an iron safe, and an iron planing machine) was essential for the railroad's operations and should be protected under a mortgage executed prior to the levies. They argued that the levied property was necessary for the railroad's business and was either in the railroad's possession prior to the mortgage or was later acquired to be funded by the railroad's earnings.
