The plaintiffs sought the court's intervention to reinstate the injunction to prevent the sale of this property.	The defendants contended that the properties in question had become personal property and were not covered under the original mortgage. They argued that the iron safe and planing machine were not permanently attached to the railroad property, thus making them susceptible to being sold to satisfy the judgments. The defendants maintained that the law allowed for the seizure of such properties to execute judgment debts, and they sought to have the injunction lifted entirely.

On April 8, 1874, Oliver H. Lee obtained a judgment in the Superior Court of Cook County against Samuel J. Walker and Joseph Young for $5,168.12, excluding interest and costs. On November 16, 1874, William P. Rend (appellees) purchased this judgment, which was assigned to them by Lee. Subsequently, in May 1876, Henry F. Eames (appellant) negotiated to acquire control of the judgment to secure a title to real estate in Chicago that belonged to Walker. Eames successfully had the judgment assigned to him by the appellees. In November 1876, after issuing an alias execution on the judgment and filing a bill in chancery, Eames had the applicable real estate sold by sheriff's auction to Allen Jordan for $5,768.05. Eames later received a deed for the property after the redemption period expired. The case arose from Eames's claim to recover the proceeds from the sale of this real estate after the sheriff's execution, minus $1,000 for collection costs. The Superior Court ruled in favor of the appellees, and this judgment was affirmed upon Eames's appeal to the Appellate Court.	The plaintiff, Henry F. Eames, claimed he was entitled to recover the amount realized from the execution sale of real estate, having arranged for the assignment of the original judgment for the purpose of securing his title to said property. He contended that his agreement with the appellees only required him to pay Young by crediting whatever amount he realized from the judgment, thus asserting that he should be compensated for the proceeds.	The defendants, William P. Rend et al., argued that the assignment of the judgment to Eames implied a debt owed by him for the full amount realized from the judgment’s execution, less the $1,000 collection fee. They contended that by agreeing to the assignment, Eames assumed responsibility for the proceeds from the sale to the appellees. Therefore, they opposed Eames's claim to recover any additional amounts beyond the stipulated terms.

The case "Conrad L. Niehoff et al. v. Charles H. Dudley et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1866. The dispute originated in the Cook Circuit Court, where Charles H. Dudley and Samuel Gummer (the plaintiffs) filed an action against Peter J. Cass, William H. Eanstead, Conrad S. Miehoff, and Gustavus Troost (the defendants). The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants owed money based on five promissory notes executed by Cass & Co. Each note specified payments for providing substitutes for military service and stated payment was due upon the volunteer being received into service. Miehoff and Troost argued that they were not partners in the business nor authorized Cass & Eanstead to enter such contracts. A trial resulted in a verdict in favor of the plaintiffs for $475.25. Miehoff and Troost appealed the decision, asserting that they were not liable.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants were jointly liable for the unpaid amounts on the promissory notes related to the provision of military substitutes. They contended that the notes specifically stipulated that payment was due once the named individuals were called into service, and that all proper procedures had been followed giving rise to the indebtedness. The plaintiffs sought to enforce the payment of $475.25 through the court's judgment.	The defendants, specifically Miehoff and Troost, contended that they were not partners with Cass & Eanstead during the time the relevant notes were executed and did not authorize them to act on their behalf. They maintained that their involvement with Cass & Co. did not constitute a partnership, and thus, they could not be held liable for the promissory notes in question. They argued that the agreement made it clear that no liability for the business dealings of Cass & Co. extended to them.

On November 18, 1873, in McLean County, Illinois, Joseph Hartfield sold two horses, named Billy and Mack, to Heman Allen for a total price of $275, with an initial payment of $20. A written bill of sale stipulated that the remaining balance was due on November 21, 1873. After paying the initial amount, Hartfield placed the horses in Allen's care. In December, Hartfield went to collect the remaining payment but found Allen offering him three notes in lieu of cash, which Hartfield refused to accept. Tensions escalated, leading Hartfield to demand either the horses or the money, to which Allen responded that he would not provide either. The horses were subsequently sent to the Mann brothers, who were acting under Allen's instructions. Hartfield ultimately brought a trover action against Allen and the Manns for the return of his horses.	Joseph Hartfield claimed that he owned the two horses and sought their return after Heman Allen violated their sale agreement by refusing to pay the remaining balance in cash and instead offering worthless notes. Hartfield argued that the actual sale required payment before possession should be transferred, emphasizing that Allen's acquisition of the horses was fraudulent since there was never any agreement to accept notes as payment. Hartfield requested damages for the wrongful possession and the return of his property.	Heman Allen and the Mann brothers contended that there was no fraudulent intent on their part and that they believed the transaction was valid. They argued that Allen’s offer of notes could be regarded as a legitimate form of payment, despite Hartfield’s refusal to accept them. Furthermore, they claimed that the Manns had no involvement in any wrongdoing and should not be held liable if there was no conspiracy to defraud Hartfield. The defendants sought the reversal of the lower court's decision.

The case, titled "The Western Union Telegraph Company v. The Pacific and Atlantic Telegraph Company," originated from an appeal filed in September 1868 at the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Chicago, where both telegraph companies operated. The primary issue was about the right to attach telegraph wires to utility poles along a railway route extending from Chicago towards La Crosse, Indiana. The Western Union Telegraph Company (appellant) sought an injunction to prevent the Pacific and Atlantic Telegraph Company (appellee) from attaching their wires to the same poles already used by Western Union. The Superior Court of Chicago had refused this injunction and dismissed Western Union's cross bill, prompting Western Union to appeal. The Illinois Supreme Court granted a temporary injunction while the case was being reviewed, indicating that the cross bill presented valid legal grounds for consideration.	The plaintiff, Western Union, claimed that the lower court erred by denying their request for an injunction and dismissing their cross bill. Their arguments focused on the need to protect their telegraph infrastructure from potential interference by the defendant's operations, asserting that they had a legitimate right to the poles and the space necessary for their wires.	The defendant, Pacific and Atlantic Telegraph Company, contended that the lower court acted appropriately by dismissing the cross bill and denying the injunction. They argued that the plaintiff's case lacked sufficient grounds for equity to be exercised in their favor and emphasized procedural issues, such as the necessity for the defendant to have been given a chance to respond formally to the allegations laid out in the cross bill before any final decision was rendered.

In September 1868, in Chicago, Illinois, Robert Wilson initiated a civil action against Charles A. Reno and Patrick Quinn, alleging trespass for false imprisonment and assault and battery. The case arose after Wilson accused Reno of orchestrating his arrest under a false charge of stealing a load of coal. Reno was the only defendant properly served; he entered a plea of not guilty and submitted a special plea, which the court deemed inappropriate. After a trial, the jury ruled in favor of Wilson, awarding him $1,700 in damages. Reno appealed this decision, claiming the damages awarded were excessive and arguing that the court failed to provide certain jury instructions that he believed were essential for his defense. The court found no justification for Reno’s accusation and highlighted the severe humiliation Wilson faced during his arrest, emphasizing that the damages were warranted under the circumstances, albeit Reno's claim about the excessive nature of those damages.	The plaintiff, Robert Wilson, asserted that he was wrongfully arrested and imprisoned by Charles A. Reno and Patrick Quinn on a baseless charge of larceny. He contended that there was no probable cause for the accusation, and his arrest subjected him to degrading and humiliating treatment. Wilson’s claims focused on the emotional and reputational harm caused by the false imprisonment and sought compensatory damages for his suffering, which the jury ultimately assessed at $1,700.	The defendants, particularly Reno, contested the judgment by claiming that the damages awarded to Wilson were excessive. They argued that the jury was not properly instructed regarding the role of the defendants in the arrest and that Reno's actions did not warrant liability under the specified circumstances. Reno requested jury instructions that would remove his responsibility from the affirmative decision for arrest if the jury determined he did not specifically charge Wilson with larceny, positing that witnesses' assertions of Wilson's supposed wrongdoing during the arrest should absolve him of liability.

In the case of Lewis W. Thompson v. William McLaughlin, which took place in September 1872, the legal proceedings were held in the Illinois Supreme Court following an action of ejectment initiated by Lewis W. Thompson against William McLaughlin. The dispute arose over a piece of land, with Thompson seeking to recover title through two main claims: one based on a tax title and the other under the limitation law of 1839, which allows for title acquisition through seven years of actual possession and tax payment. In a previous decision (McLaughlin v. Thompson, 55 Ill. 249), the court had initially ruled the tax title void, claiming the judgment for tax sale improperly included a county tax levied at the wrong time, a misapprehension rectified during this trial upon discovering that the law was in effect. The court had to revisit the requirements for establishing a valid tax title, including whether proper documentation was filed in accordance with legal requirements. Thompson’s testimony focused on his claim of occupying and paying taxes on the land for seven consecutive years, from 1855 to 1861, although the court found his evidence insufficient to prove continuous possession during that time lapse. Additional complexities arose with the introduction of various tenants and agreements that were challenged based on their relevancy to the title dispute.	The plaintiff, Lewis W. Thompson, argued that he held a valid claim to the land based on a tax title and also sought to recover ownership under the first section of the limitation law of 1839. He asserted that he had paid taxes on the property for seven consecutive years and had exercised control over it by placing a house on the land for a time. Thompson requested the court uphold his claims and grant him rightful ownership of the property.	The defendant, William McLaughlin, contended that the claim to the tax title was invalid because Thompson failed to provide a copy of the advertisement and a certificate of publication as required by law at the time of the tax sale. McLaughlin also argued that his own claims of occupancy and title were sufficient to question Thompson’s title. He maintained that the evidence presented by Thompson did not adequately demonstrate continuous possession for the required seven years, thus failing to establish his claims under the limitation law.

In 1887, the case "Algernon S. Osgood v. W. H. Pacey & Son" was brought before the Illinois Appellate Court, concerning a mechanic's lien claimed by W. H. Pacey & Son against Algernon S. Osgood. The events unfolded in Joliet, Illinois, where Osgood owned a house and lot. Osgood, a resident of Chicago, had an agreement with his mother, Mrs. Hri Osgood, who lived in Joliet, that enabled her to receive the rents from his property for her support. The conflict arose when Pacey & Son were hired to improve the interior of the property, with the work to be paid from the rental income. However, Osgood did not engage Pacey & Son directly nor was he informed about the contractual agreement for repairs made with his mother. The court initially sided with Pacey & Son, granting them a decree for a mechanic's lien for the work done, but this led to the appeal by Osgood.	Algernon S. Osgood, the plaintiff, contended that he was not liable for the mechanic's lien claimed by W. H. Pacey & Son as he had not authorized the work done on his property. He argued that the contract for the repairs was made with his mother, who acted not as his agent but in her own capacity as a beneficiary of the rental income. Osgood maintained that the mechanics' lien could only be valid if it was established through a contract directly with the owner of the property.	The defendant, W. H. Pacey & Son, asserted their right to claim the mechanic's lien based on the work done to improve Osgood's property, contending that they entered into a lawful contract through Mrs. Osgood. They argued that Osgood had acknowledged that any unpaid rent from a previous tenant could cover the costs, exhibiting a form of implied consent. Pacey & Son's primary defense hinged on the assertion that the agency existed between Osgood and his mother, allowing the claim for the lien.

In the case of George W. Miller v. Abram M. Pence et al., the legal dispute arose from a series of property judgments and sales dating back to the late 1870s in Cook County, Illinois. George W. Miller, the plaintiff, originally owned the land in question. On December 5, 1877, a judgment was issued against Miller and a co-defendant, Brahmstadt, for $963, which initiated execution proceedings on the property. The sheriff subsequently sold the land to Abram M. Pence on January 7, 1878. Pence acquired legal possession, improved the property, and established a tenant. Meanwhile, another judgment was rendered against Miller on September 26, 1877, which led to a separate sale to Aughinbaugh, further complicating ownership claims. Pence sought to clear a cloud on his title by filing a bill against Aughinbaugh to set aside the sale connected to the latter judgment, which was granted and later upheld on appeal. Miller contested Pence's ownership through a writ of error, arguing Pence was improperly involved in the process that led to the sale and had knowledge of the invalidity of the judgments. Ultimately, despite Miller's claims, the court weighed the evidence and procedural history, which favored Pence as the rightful owner of the property.	George W. Miller claimed that Pence, as the attorney for Brahmstadt, had a conflict of interest in acquiring the property through the execution sale and had knowledge of defects in the underlying judgment record. Miller sought possession of the land, arguing that Pence’s purchase was invalid due to these alleged issues. He emphasized that Pence should be charged with notice of these defects, asserting that the titles were intertwined and that Pence’s actions constituted a legal wrong against him.	Abram M. Pence defended against Miller's claims by asserting that he had no involvement as an attorney in the initial lawsuit that led to the judgments against Miller. Pence maintained that he acted independently in acquiring the property through legal means and that the court properly upheld his ownership during the chancery proceedings against Aughinbaugh. He contended that Miller did not redeem any rights or seek to overturn the judgments in question, emphasizing the finality of the prior court decisions and the legitimacy of his title to the property.

The case "Trustees of Schools of Township 27, N. R. 10 East, in Winnebago County v. William Bibb" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1853. The dispute originated in the Winnebago Circuit Court, where the Trustees of Schools initiated a lawsuit against William Bibb to recover interest on a note related to the school fund. The plaintiffs claimed that Bibb defaulted on payments due under the terms of the note, which stipulated different interest rates based on timely payments. The original act governing the school fund was enacted on February 12, 1835, establishing penalties for default in interest payments, while a revised act from February 12, 1849, adjusted the interest rates and penalties. The circuit court had rendered a judgment in favor of the defendant, which prompted the plaintiffs to appeal, arguing that the court misapplied the law regarding the interest owed.	The Trustees of Schools contended that the circuit court erred in finding that William Bibb was not liable for the interest due. They argued that per the statute, they were entitled to receive twelve percent per annum on the unpaid interest and principal from the day of default. The plaintiffs requested the court to rectify the judgment, asserting that their interpretation of the law was accurate and should have resulted in a judgment in their favor for the owed amounts.	William Bibb defended against the claims by asserting that the circuit court’s ruling was correct and in accordance with the law. He implied that the penalties imposed on borrowers who defaulted on payments were not meant to be excessively punitive and maintained that he had met the obligations under the law. The defendant's arguments supported the notion that the correct interpretation of the law, as applied in the circuit court, necessitated the judgment in his favor.

In 1884, the case of Andrew Katz v. Catharine Moessinger, Admx. took place in Cook County, Illinois, involving key individuals Andrew Katz and Catharine Moessinger. The underlying issue revolved around a transaction involving two promissory notes for which Moessinger had signed as a surety for Katz. After a judgment was rendered against both, Moessinger paid it off. Katz later declared bankruptcy and raised defenses against Moessinger's claims, arguing that he was no longer liable due to the bankruptcy discharge, and also cited the Statute of Limitations. Following the death of Moessinger, his administratrix was appointed as the plaintiff. The case involved complex legal questions regarding the implications of bankruptcy on the repayment of debts and the validity of promises made post-discharge. A jury trial concluded with a judgment in favor of the plaintiff, which was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court, leading to contention over the legal nuances of the promises made by Katz during and after bankruptcy.	The plaintiff, through the administratrix of Moessinger's estate, claimed that Katz owed repayment for the judgment amount following his bankruptcy. They contended that Katz made an unconditional promise to pay the debt after his bankruptcy discharge, which should not be exempted by the discharge. The plaintiff sought to recover the amount paid under the judgment and argued that the defenses presented by Katz were legally invalid in light of the new promise.	Andrew Katz contended that his debts had been discharged through bankruptcy and therefore should not be liable to repay any claims against him. He also cited the Statute of Limitations, asserting that the claims were not valid due to the passage of time. Katz argued that any promise made after his bankruptcy should be considered conditional, thus invalidating the plaintiff's claim.

The case "The Monticello Female Seminary v. The People of the State of Illinois" took place in Madison County, Illinois. It involved the Monticello Female Seminary, an institution of learning located near Alton, Illinois, which was established by a legislative charter in 1843. The seminary originally occupied eight acres of land and later acquired additional tracts, totaling four land parcels: 40 acres, 20 acres, 14.75 acres, and an unspecified block 17. The seminary utilized these lands for a variety of purposes directly related to its educational mission, such as gardening, raising livestock, and providing food for approximately 175 residents, including scholars and teachers. In 1881, the county collector sought judgment against these tracts for unpaid property taxes. The key issue at hand was whether the seminary's lands should be exempt from taxation, as stipulated in Section 3 of Article 9 of the 1870 Illinois Constitution, which allows for tax exemptions for properties used exclusively for educational, religious, or charitable purposes.	The Monticello Female Seminary claimed that all four tracts of land were exempt from taxation because they were used exclusively for the educational purposes of the institution. The seminary argued that the lands provided necessary supplies and services for its operation and did not generate income or profit from any activities conducted on them.	The People of the State of Illinois, represented by the county collector, contended that the tracts of land had been properly assessed for taxation and that the seminary's use of the land for agricultural purposes was tantamount to using it with a view to profit, which does not qualify for tax exemption under state law. The defense stressed that the property must be used exclusively for educational purposes to qualify for tax exemption and pointed out that some of the lands were being utilized for farming and pasturage.

In the case of Terrence Burns v. Christopher C. Miller et al., filed on June 13, 1884, in the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute centers around the inheritance and ownership of certain lands located in Johnson County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Terrence Burns, is one of the heirs of Frederick Miller, who passed away in April 1868. The defendants claim title to the land based on a court decree from a previous partition suit that involved Frederick Miller's widow, Lavina Miller, and other heirs to assign dower and divide the real estate. The land in question includes various parcels primarily described in section 1. During the trial, it was established that the land had initially been ordered sold as part of the earlier proceedings. The main contention arises over whether the disputed lands were assigned through the decree as dower to the widow or sold in the partition suit. The complexities in the legal descriptions of the properties involved led to arguments about the legitimacy of the defendants' claims to the land, particularly as Frederick Miller reportedly had no ownership rights over some parcels listed in the decree.	The plaintiff's claims assert that as the legal heirs of Frederick Miller, they are entitled to recover the lands in question since the previous decrees had established their ownership rights. The plaintiff contends that the legal descriptions in the previous decree were incorrectly interpreted by the defendants and that the land, being part of Frederick Miller's estate, rightfully belongs to his heirs. The plaintiff requests formal recognition of their claims to the properties and seeks restitution and recovery of possession of the lands they believe belonged to their deceased ancestor.	The defendants, in their defense, argue that they hold rightful possession of the land based on a decree rendered in a partition suit that ordered the sale of certain properties, purportedly including the ones claimed by the plaintiff. They assert that the court had properly defined the land involved and that the final report regarding dower rights was valid, suggesting that the plaintiff's claims are undermined by the prior legal proceedings that confirmed their ownership. They seek to uphold the results of the earlier decree and maintain their current possession of the lands in question.

The case "George A. Robbins et al. v. Juliette A. Kinzie" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1867. The plaintiff, Juliette Kinzie, was married to John H. Kinzie, who passed away on June 21, 1865. During their marriage, John acquired an estate in the properties in question. Juliette sought recovery of her dower rights, claiming she had never relinquished these rights despite a deed executed on June 30, 1834, in which she joined her husband in conveying the property to Mark Benlien. Subsequent transfers of the title occurred, leading to its ownership eventually being in the hands of George A. Robbins. The case revolved around whether Juliette’s earlier acknowledgment in the deed constituted a waiver of her dower rights. The key individuals involved included Juliette Kinzie as the widow and George A. Robbins as the defendant claiming ownership of the property.	Juliette Kinzie contended that she was entitled to her dower rights from her deceased husband’s estate, asserting that she had never formally relinquished these rights. She claimed that the earlier deed, which involved her acknowledgment, did not effectively eliminate her dower claim, seeking a court order to have her dower rights recognized and allotted to her.	The defendants, led by George A. Robbins, argued that Juliette had relinquished her dower rights through her acknowledgment in the 1834 deed. They maintained that following this conveyance, she had no claim to dower because the property had been transferred to various parties, ultimately to them, thus asserting that her subsequent attempts to release dower rights were void.

Edward P. Morgan and Ralph R. Root initiated an action against Erastus Peet in 1866 in Peoria County, Illinois, concerning a promissory note previously executed by Burdick and Peet. Erastus Peet had endorsed this note, which was subsequently assigned to Earl and then to the plaintiffs. The case arose when the note's holder failed to file a lawsuit against the makers within the appropriate time frame, which led to Peet's liability being discharged. Peet became involved due to the familial connection as he was the father of one of the makers of the note. During the proceedings, the plaintiffs argued that Peet made a new promise to pay the note after the discharge had occurred. However, the defendant asserted he was unaware of his legal discharge and had only been aware of the facts surrounding the failure to bring suit. The case emphasized the need for a new promise to be made with an understanding of the discharge circumstances.	The plaintiffs argued that despite the initial discharge of Peet's liability due to the holder's failure to bring suit in a timely manner, he made a new promise to pay after this discharge. They contended that this promise should be binding and asked the court to enforce it, insisting that the true knowledge of the circumstances surrounding the original discharge was acknowledged by Peet.	The defendant, Erastus Peet, countered the claims by asserting that he was not liable since his obligation had been discharged due to the holder's inaction. Peet argued that he did not have the requisite knowledge regarding the legal implications of the holder's failure to sue, which he believed precluded any binding promise on his part to pay the note.

In 1885, the City of Springfield, Illinois, initiated legal action against the City of London Insurance Company, a foreign fire insurance entity that was not incorporated under Illinois law. At the time, the City of Springfield had maintained an organized fire department and sought to recover a tax of two percent on the gross receipts from insurance premiums collected by the company in the city for that year. The city argued that an ordinance mandated such payments, which were intended to support the fire department. However, the defense claimed that the ordinance was no longer valid due to a legislative change in 1879, which repealed previous laws allowing municipalities to levy such taxes unless expressly permitted by their charters. The case was presided over by the Honorable James A. Creighton in the Circuit Court of Sangamon County.	The City of Springfield claimed that under its ordinance, the City of London Insurance Company was required to pay a tax of two dollars for every hundred dollars of gross receipts obtained from insurance premiums during the year 1885. The city sought to recover these funds to support its fire department, citing both historical practice and an assertion that the ordinance remained in effect.	The City of London Insurance Company contended that the city lacked the authority to impose such a tax due to a legislative act enacted in 1879, which repealed previous provisions allowing municipalities to levy such taxes. The defendant argued that the changes made it clear that only cities with specific charters could impose taxes on insurance premiums, and that Springfield’s ordinance did not meet this requirement.

In the case of Karl Keppler v. August Elser, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, the incident leading to the dispute occurred around May 1883. The plaintiff, August Elser, testified against the defendant, Karl Keppler, claiming that Keppler had engaged in an affair with his wife while Elser was away hunting. Elser stated that he had observed Keppler coming to his home late at night, ultimately leading to a confrontation on the night of May 12, 1883. Elser claimed he caught Keppler leaving his wife’s bedroom when he returned home unexpectedly. After this incident, Elser accused Keppler of ruining his marriage and family, which Elser stated led to his divorce. The trial court initially rendered a judgment in favor of Elser, awarding him $1,500 for damages in a criminal conversation action. However, this judgment was called into question due to the need for proof of an actual marriage in criminal conversation cases, a standard that Elser failed to meet.	The plaintiff, August Elser, claimed that the defendant, Karl Keppler, had an adulterous relationship with his wife, which constituted criminal conversation. Elser contended that he had evidence of Keppler's intrusion into his home and relationship, asserting that this led to significant harm, including the disintegration of his marriage. Elser sought damages for the emotional and reputational distress caused by Keppler's actions.	The defendant, Karl Keppler, argued that there was insufficient evidence to prove that Elser and his wife were legally married at the time of the alleged acts. The defense maintained that the law required proof of an actual and valid marriage in order to sustain an action for criminal conversation, and that Elser's testimony did not meet this requirement. Since Elser could only offer testimony that referred to the relationship as “my wife,” the defendant contended that this was inadequate for legal recognition of a marriage.

In the case of William Drury v. Charles C. P. Holden, which took place in Chicago, Illinois, the events leading to the legal battle began when Charles C. P. Holden executed a series of trust deeds to secure debts. On April 23, 1869, he created a deed of trust for several lots to secure a higher debt owed to the Jonathan Bevor estate. Later, in 1871, he executed another trust deed to secure a separate debt of $6,500 owed to Edward A. Kelly. After a sequence of transactions involving multiple parties, Holden conveyed lots to William H. Holden, who ultimately sold the property to Drury in 1876, which was subject to existing encumbrances (the debts). Disputes arose when Drury attempted to assert ownership over the "barn lot," which was sold at a trustee's sale in 1879 under the belief that the debts securing it had been extinguished. The lower court found that the sale was invalid as the debts remained intact, leading to an appeal by Drury.	William Drury, the plaintiff, contended that the decree should affirm the validity of the sale and his ownership of the properties. He argued that the lower court's ruling contravened the general legal principle requiring that mortgaged lands be sold to satisfy debts in a specific order. Furthermore, he asserted that he had no obligation to pay the encumbrances since his purchase was made subject to them.	Charles C. P. Holden, the defendant, claimed that the sale to Drury was void because the underlying debts had not been extinguished. He argued that Drury, having purchased the lots with knowledge of the existing encumbrances, held the properties as the primary fund to settle those debts. Holden maintained that the lower court's decision was correct, stating that Drury's assertions disregarded the established rules regarding the liability of properties purchased subject to debts.

In 1890, the case of Louis Hutt et al. v. The City of Chicago was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose from an ordinance passed by the Chicago City Council on March 15, 1886, which called for the extension of South Canal Street from Lumber Street to Archer Avenue, necessitating the condemnation of land for this purpose. Notably, the ordinance did not specify how the street would cross the Chicago River, which posed a significant issue since all assessments of benefits to property owners along the proposed route were based on the expectation that a bridge would be constructed. Various assessments were made, and property owners whose land was affected filed objections to the confirmed assessments, reasoning that benefits should not be ascribed to a future bridge that had never been ordered. The case ultimately centered on the appropriateness of assessing property benefits based on a speculative bridge that might be constructed at a later date.	The plaintiffs, represented by various property owners, argued that the benefit assessments made by the city were improper as they relied on the assumption that a bridge would be built across the river. They contended that the ordinance itself made no provisions for a bridge and thus should not permit speculative assessments based on potential future improvements. They sought to have the court confirm that property assessments should only consider existing improvements, not future contingencies like the construction of a bridge.	The city of Chicago, as the defendant, maintained that it was within its rights to assess benefits based on the probable future enhancement that a bridge across the river would bring. They argued that it was a standard practice to consider the natural and probable consequences of proposed improvements when estimating benefits. The city sought to uphold the validity of the assessments and the confirmation made by the court on behalf of the city budget.

In 1883, in Chicago, Catharine McNichols and her husband James MeNichols entered into a contract with Jacob Kettner for the construction of a cottage on a lot owned by Catharine. James signed the contract, but Catharine claimed she was not part of the agreement. Catharine expressed financial constraints during discussions about payments but eventually assumed responsibility for paying Kettner using funds from her son, Henry. Throughout the construction process, Catharine was aware of the contract and the ongoing work, yet contended that she did not authorize her husband's actions. The case revolved around the validity of the mechanic's lien Kettner placed on the property for unpaid services, and whether Catharine was bound by her husband's actions as an agent in this matter.	Catharine McNichols filed a claim asserting that she should not be held responsible for the payments under the contract signed solely by her husband. She argued that her husband acted without her authorization and that the mechanic’s lien placed by Kettner was therefore invalid. Catharine sought to have the lien declared void and to be absolved of any financial obligation for the construction of the cottage.	Jacob Kettner defended his position by arguing that Catharine was aware of the contract and its terms, as well as the work being conducted on her property. He emphasized that she made all payments associated with the contract, which demonstrated her consent to the agreement. Kettner argued that Catharine allowed her husband to act as her agent in this transaction and was therefore estopped from denying the validity of the contract and the resulting lien.

Bernard Fowler filed a case against James Redican in September 1869 concerning a dispute over the sale of several lots in Chicago. The events leading to the litigation began in June 1868 when Redican, claiming ownership of lots 14 and 16 in block 15 and lots 12 and 13 in block 16 of Stinston's subdivision in Chicago, engaged Thomas A. Hill & Co. as his agents to sell the lots. Hill & Co. offered the lots to Fowler for $1,170.33, and Fowler paid $100 as a deposit. Since the deal was agreed upon, Fowler relied on it, took possession of the lots, and began substantial improvements, including erecting two houses worth $500. However, when Fowler attempted to pay the remaining balance on July 1, 1868, Redican refused to accept the payment and execute a warranty deed. Fowler sought specific performance of the sale contract in court, asserting that sufficient agreement existed to compel Redican to complete the sale. Redican denied that a sale occurred and claimed that the statute of frauds applied, asserting that no valid contract existed due to the lack of a complete written agreement.	Fowler claimed that he entered a binding agreement to purchase the lots after paying a deposit and taking possession. He stated he made substantial improvements to the property based on the contract and thus requested the court compel Redican to execute a deed for the lots while allowing him to pay the remaining balance of $1,070.33.	Redican argues that he did not own the lots at the time of the sale and had not authorized Hill & Co. to act as his agents. He further contended that he never received the deposit and that no valid contract existed because the memorandum was insufficient under the statute of frauds. Redican requested the court dismiss Fowler's claims, asserting that the alleged agreement lacked necessary details and was unenforceable.

In 1876, Harry Herrick began operating a hat store at 115 Madison Street, Chicago, and was later joined by his brother, Charles K. Herrick, in 1880. The landlord, Edward W. Morrison, executed a series of annual leases, the last dated April 8, 1884, which ended on April 30, 1885. In the summer of 1884, Morrison allegedly made an oral agreement with the Herricks for a five-year lease starting May 1, 1885, contingent on their promise to make valuable improvements to the store. The Herricks, relying on this agreement and acknowledging Morrison's consent, invested several thousand dollars in permanent improvements. However, no written lease was provided for the new term. On July 8, 1885, Morrison executed a lease to a different party, Miner and others, for the same premises, thereby leading to a dispute over possession and the oral agreement's enforceability. The case revolves around whether the improvements made by the Herricks should exempt the oral agreement from the statute of frauds.	The plaintiffs, Harry Herrick and Charles K. Herrick, sought specific performance of the oral lease agreement made with Edward W. Morrison for the premises at 115 Madison Street. They argued that through the significant and valuable improvements made with Morrison's knowledge and consent, they should be entitled to the benefits of the lease despite the lack of a written agreement. They contended that Morrison's actions constituted a fraudulent denial of the promise made to them.	Edward W. Morrison, the defendant, denied the existence of the oral agreement and claimed that the statute of frauds precluded the enforcement of any lease not documented in writing. He sought to dismiss the Herricks' claims, asserting that their improvements did not legally establish the existence of a binding agreement, and pointed out that a lease had been granted to Miner and others, thereby transferring the rights to the property.

The case of Chicago & Alton Railroad Co. v. James E. Sebring took place in February 1886, in McLean County, Illinois. The key individuals involved were the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, represented by its legal counsel, and James E. Sebring, an employee of the company. The conflict arose after Sebring claimed a reward of $500 for providing information leading to the arrest and conviction of a person who threw a stone at a train. The court's previous decision established that Sebring, as an employee, was entitled to claim this reward. However, the critical issue in this case was the applicability of the reward offer regarding the specific circumstances that led to the incident. The court had to determine whether the assault was linked to a personal conflict Sebring had with a stranger or if it fell under the terms of the reward, which was intended to cover cases where individuals acted with malice against the railroad. The court ultimately ruled that the incident stemmed from a personal quarrel, which excluded it from the reward's intended purpose.	James E. Sebring, the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to the $500 reward offered by the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company for his role in reporting the wrongful act against the train. He claimed that the stone-throwing incident was an attack that warranted the reward, despite his status as an employee of the railroad.	The defendant, Chicago & Alton Railroad Company, contended that the reward was not applicable to Sebring's case. They argued that the incident arose from a personal dispute between Sebring and a stranger, making it a matter outside the scope of the reward, which was to deter malicious acts against the company rather than personal conflicts.

George Chandler filed a case against John P. White and others in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1877. The dispute stemmed from a series of transactions involving a piece of land purchased by Warren E. Esty from James H. Allen. Esty secured the payment of the remaining balance with a deed of trust to White. However, Esty attempted to defraud multiple parties by executing a series of forged documents, including a forged release of the deed of trust, to secure a loan from a bank using the purported ownership of the land. The bank was misled by the fraudulent paperwork and lent money to an individual claiming to be Henry Porter, who did not exist. A public sale of the land was later conducted by White, as trustee, to repay the secured note—a sale contested by Chandler, who claimed the sale should be void due to the fraudulent release and lack of proper notification. Ultimately, Chandler's amended bill sought to set aside the sale to Milton L. Grube and to declare the deed of trust void. The court examined the actions of the involved parties, particularly focusing on the implications of the forgery and whether they could be estopped from asserting the validity of the forged release.	Chandler's principal argument was that the sale conducted by White was invalid due to a forged release of the deed of trust. He contended that White, by not providing notice about the forgery, was estopped from denying its validity. Chandler sought to have Grube's title set aside and requested that the deed of trust be declared satisfied so that the bank could redeem its interest in the property.	The defendant, John P. White, contended that he was not negligent regarding the release's validity and had no prior knowledge about the forgery. White argued that any alleged estoppel due to his actions was invalid as there was no fraudulent purpose on his part. He maintained that the sale of the land was conducted in accordance with the deed of trust, and the notice provided for the sale was sufficient under the circumstances despite the destruction of the courthouse where the sale was to take place.

The case "Wallahan et al. v. The People" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court during the September Term of 1867. It centers around a legal dispute involving the appellants, represented by attorneys R. E. Williams and T. M. Shaw, who sought to have an additional transcript filed at the current term stricken from the record. This additional transcript contained an amended bill of exceptions, which had been amended two years and four months after the original trial. The appellants argued that allowing such an amendment after such a long period could threaten the rights of parties, as the evidence was primarily based on memory rather than documented notes. The Supreme Court was required to consider whether the amendment was proper and whether there was sufficient information to justify it.	The plaintiffs, represented by Wallahan et al., claimed that the additional transcript, which included amendments to the bill of exceptions, was not legally part of the case record. They argued that such amendments should only be made when there is proper documentation or information to support them, as allowing changes after significant time could undermine the integrity of the proceedings.	The defendants, in this case referred to as "The People," argued that the amendments made to the bill of exceptions were justified. They contended that the presumption existed that the court below had acted based on sufficient memoranda. They further maintained that the absence of exceptions regarding the source of information indicated that there were indeed valid grounds for amending the bill.

In September 1877, in DuPage County, Illinois, the case of Frederick Weiger and John W. Gates against George W. Gould arose from a dispute over a sale of oats. Gould, the plaintiff, claimed that he had sold 682 bushels of oats to the defendants for 40 cents per bushel. However, the defendants disputed this claim, insisting that no such agreement was reached. After delivering six wagon loads of oats, a disagreement emerged about the price the defendants were willing to pay. The defendants offered to pay 28 cents per bushel for the oats, and after deliberation, the parties reached an agreement on this adjusted price. Gould received the payment without protest at that time but later claimed that the agreement had been made under duress. The central issue revolves around the quality of the oats delivered, which Gould admitted were not merchantable, being wet and dirty. The case escalated to a jury verdict in favor of Gould for $35.39, which the defendants subsequently appealed.	The plaintiff, George W. Gould, contended that he had an agreement with the defendants to sell his oats for 40 cents per bushel, which he claimed was the market price for good white oats. He asserted that the defendants took the oats and later sought to pay him a lesser price (28 cents per bushel). Gould's main argument was that he was owed compensation based on the original price he claimed had been agreed upon, and he sought to reverse the defendants’ decision to pay a lower price after the delivery.	The defendants, Frederick Weiger and John W. Gates, maintained that no contract for the sale at 40 cents per bushel existed. They argued that the oats delivered were of poor quality and not merchantable. Furthermore, they contended that the issues were settled when they agreed to pay Gould 28 cents per bushel and that Gould accepted this payment without objection at the time. The defendants requested that the court reverse the initial judgment in favor of Gould, emphasizing that Gould should not profit from a claim based on an alleged agreement that did not meet the agreed terms.

In 1869, in Woodford County, Illinois, the case "Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Co. v. John Darst" arose when John Darst, the plaintiff, brought an action against the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, claiming damages for the alleged killing of his horse by one of the company’s trains. Darst argued that the railway company had failed to maintain proper fencing along the sides of their railroad, leading to the incident. He stated that the accident occurred at a location where fences were necessary to prevent animals from accessing the tracks and highlighted that this area had been open for more than six months. The company, however, did not have sufficient fencing to keep Darst's horse from getting onto the railroad tracks. This case appears to revolve around responsibilities of railway companies in preventing livestock from getting onto train tracks, particularly focusing on the adequacy of protective measures like fencing.	John Darst, the plaintiff, asserted that the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company was negligent in failing to erect and maintain adequate fences alongside their railroad. He claimed that the horse was killed because the company did not provide sufficient barriers to prevent animals from getting onto the tracks. Darst requested compensation for the loss of his horse, amounting to two hundred dollars, on the grounds that this negligence led to his financial damages.	The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, as the defendant, contended that the declaration presented by Darst was insufficient, particularly claiming it did not directly assert that the injury resulted from their failure to fence the tracks. They argued that the way the plaintiff framed his arguments did not meet the necessary legal standards to support his claim, thus requesting the court to arrest the judgment based on these perceived deficiencies in the declaration.

John Warner et al. filed a case against John Campbell in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1861. The dispute centers around a promissory note made on June 26, 1857, where Lemuel Andrews was the principal and Warner and B.J. Cobb were sureties, promising to pay $5,000 to Campbell, payable at the Windham County Bank in Brattleboro, Vermont. The note was due twelve months later, but by the time of the suit, it was overdue. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants defaulted on the note. The defendants contended that an agreement existed which allowed for the postponement of payment without their consent, thus absolving them of their obligations as sureties. After a trial by jury in the Circuit Court, the jury found in favor of the plaintiff, awarding damages of $5,598. The defendants appealed, arguing the court had erred in excluding certain evidence and that the jury's verdict was not supported by law or evidence.	The plaintiff, John Warner et al., argued that the defendants, including the deceased Lemuel Andrews as the principal obligor, were obligated to pay the overdue promissory note. They maintained that the defendants' agreement to defer the payment, made without the consent of the sureties, did not release the sureties from their obligations. The plaintiffs sought the amount due on the note and presented evidence supporting their claim during the trial.	The defendant, John Campbell, claimed that there was an agreement to extend the payment of the promissory note, which was made without the knowledge or consent of the sureties, thus releasing them from any liability. They asserted that the acceptance of interest paid in advance constituted a valid agreement extending the payment term. The defense requested a new trial, arguing that the court had improperly excluded relevant evidence and failed to provide proper jury instructions that reflected this understanding.

The case of John J. Mayers et al. v. Maria Smith took place in Illinois, with the judgment being delivered on September 27, 1887, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated after the death of David Smith, Maria Smith's husband, which Maria attributed to intoxication resulting from alcohol purchased or gifted to him by the defendants, John J. Mayers and Harry H. Miller. Maria filed a lawsuit seeking damages for the loss of her means of support due to her husband's death. The initial ruling was in favor of Maria in the circuit court, and this decision was subsequently upheld by the Appellate Court for the Third District. The case primarily revolved around legal issues related to jury selections and the admissibility of certain evidence, particularly regarding the questioning of jurors and the evidence of Maria's means of support. Defendants contended that they were denied their right to challenge jurors even before they were sworn in. The controversy prompted a review of statutory provisions regarding juror challenges and the proper procedures to follow when selecting a jury in civil cases.	Maria Smith, the plaintiff, argued that her husband's death was directly linked to alcohol supplied by the defendants, which led to a substantial loss of her means of support. She sought damages for this loss, emphasizing her dependence on her husband's earnings and establishing that his death had left her with no other financial resources. Maria's claims were based on the Dram-shop Act, which allows for the recovery of damages in cases where intoxication caused by a seller's liquor leads to injury or death.	The defendants, John J. Mayers and Harry H. Miller, contended that they were improperly denied their right to peremptorily challenge jurors who had been previously accepted but not sworn. They argued that this denial infringed upon their statutory rights regarding jury selection, which should allow challenges to jurors at any point before they are sworn. They also attempted to introduce evidence showing that they had instructed their staff not to serve alcohol to David Smith, suggesting that they should not be held liable for his intoxication and subsequent death.

The case "City of Ottawa v. The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. John D. Caton et al." took place in September 1868, involving the City of Ottawa, located in LaSalle County, Illinois. The conflict began when the Illinois General Assembly passed an act on March 7, 1867, that authorized the City of Ottawa to construct two pivot bridges over the Illinois & Michigan Canal, appointing local commissioners to oversee the construction. The bridges were planned on Columbus Street and Walnut Street, with funding to be raised through taxation. After completing the bridges, the commissioners informed the city authorities of their responsibility to maintain and operate them; however, the city failed to open the bridges for boat passage and did not keep them in repair, raising concerns for local businesses and the community about increased dangers in navigating the canal. The city council initially attempted to challenge the validity of the tax for bridge construction but later withdrew the challenge to support local development, particularly related to new businesses. In response to the city's neglect, interested parties sought a writ of mandamus from the Circuit Court, compelling the city to assume responsibility for the bridges.	The plaintiffs, representing local citizens and property holders, argued that the City of Ottawa had a legal obligation to maintain and manage the newly constructed bridges as mandated by the legislative act. They requested a peremptory writ of mandamus to compel the city to take charge of the bridges and ensure they were opened for boat traffic and maintained properly. They asserted that the city's inaction posed safety risks and impaired local economic potentials, as new businesses depended on the functionality of the bridges.	The City of Ottawa, represented by its attorney, contested the issuance of the writ, arguing several points: they claimed that the legislative act was unconstitutional because it improperly appointed commissioners and empowered the Board of Supervisors to levy taxes. They also contended that the act comprised multiple subjects, violating statutory requirements. The city argued the council had the discretion not to maintain the bridges and that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing, claiming they had alternative legal remedies available.

The case "John Wolf, Exr. v. Jacob Beaird et al. Exrs." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 20, 1888. It involves a legal dispute stemming from the estate of Edward J. French, who passed away testate on March 3, 1880. John Wolf was appointed as the executor of French's estate on March 8, 1880, after French’s will was probated. Wolf allowed two claims against the estate in favor of John B. Gharst, with payments made in good faith under the belief that the estate was solvent. Gharst received full payment for his claims on October 15, 1880. However, later claims filed against the estate made it insolvent, revealing that Gharst had been overpaid. After Gharst's death in 1881, Wolf pursued a claim against Gharst's estate to recover the excess amount paid, resulting in legal proceedings through multiple courts, including a county court, circuit court, and the Appellate Court. The case focused on the principles of mutual mistake and equitable recovery of funds paid under such circumstances.	Plaintiff John Wolf claimed that he overpaid John B. Gharst due to a mutual mistake regarding the solvency of French's estate. He sought recovery of the excess payment made to Gharst, arguing that he should be compensated for the amount that exceeded Gharst's proper share after the realization of the estate’s insolvency.	The defendants, Jacob Beaird et al., executors of Gharst’s estate, contended that Wolf could not recover the excess payment as he only had the right to sue either in his individual capacity or as executor after paying out his own funds. They argued that the claim for recovery was not valid until Wolf had individually compensated the estate for the overpayment.

In the case of In re John Mullin et al., the legal matters arose from an earlier judgment in which Charles Spangenberg had been awarded $5,000 against defendants John Mullin and Peter McHugh for trespass due to assault and battery. This original judgment was upheld by the Illinois Appellate Court and the Supreme Court of Illinois. Following the judgment, Mullin and McHugh were taken into custody under a writ of capias ad satisfaciendum issued to enforce the judgment. They subsequently filed a petition in the county court seeking to be released from imprisonment by handing over their property. Their petition was denied in the county court, which they then appealed to the circuit court. The key legal questions considered at the hearing included whether malice was a fundamental aspect of the original action, as defined by legal statute, and whether that determination relied solely on the record of the prior case. Both questions were answered affirmatively, affirming the lower courts' decisions. The matter was decided on July 28, 1886, with all proceedings occurring in Cook County, Illinois.	The plaintiff, Charles Spangenberg, argued that the original judgment for $5,000 was valid and that the defendants' subsequent attempts to escape imprisonment by offering their property were without merit. He maintained that the judgment for assault and battery correctly reflected the malice involved in the case. Spangenberg requested the court to uphold the previous rulings and affirm his right to collect the judgment.	The defendants, John Mullin and Peter McHugh, contended that their imprisonment was unjust and sought relief from the county court, arguing that they should be released by turning over their property. They questioned whether the element of malice was necessary in the original assault and battery judgment and sought a determination on this issue to support their claim for release from custody. Their appeal to the higher court sought to reverse the lower courts' decisions denying their petition.

In the case of Charles F. Kendall v. Charles F. Young, which was decided on August 8, 1888, the legal dispute arose over a contract for the sale of a stock of goods and fixtures in a store located in Topeka, Kansas, between the two parties. The contract, dated November 15, 1885, stipulated that the goods were to be invoiced at cost, with an initial estimate for certain items totaling $747.09. A conflict occurred during invoicing when Young queried the cost of cotton bats, which had no identifying marks. Kendall claimed the cost to be 13½ cents per pound, but Young insisted on seeing the original invoices as verification. After Kendall refused to produce the requested documents, claiming it would be too burdensome, Young halted the invoicing process and expressed that he would not proceed without the original bills. Subsequently, Kendall testified that he had destroyed his bills and had only a previous invoice to offer. The case was appealed after a verdict favored Young, leading to a legal examination of the contract's terms and responsibilities of each party regarding proof of costs.	The plaintiff, Charles F. Young, claimed that he was entitled to a refund of $1,000 he had paid under the contract, asserting that the defendant, Charles F. Kendall, failed to provide adequate evidence of the cost of the goods as required by their agreement. Young argued that the inability of Kendall to supply original invoices constituted a breach of contract, which justified his refusal to continue with the transaction.	The defendant, Charles F. Kendall, contended that the contract did not require him to produce the original invoices and that upon Young's refusal to accept the cost he identified, he had no obligation to continue the sale. Kendall claimed that demanding specific proof was not warranted by the contract terms, and he argued that the court's instructions to the jury regarding the evidence of cost were erroneous.

Addie Rothschild filed a legal action against Charles J. Bruschke and others in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in the Circuit Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge John P. Altgeld, and the decision was rendered on June 14, 1889. The basis of the lawsuit was a promissory note that had been executed by the defendants to Rothschild's order. Initially, the suit was brought by S. Kuhn & Sons, who were the legal owners of the note at the time the action was filed. Rothschild later acquired the title to the note after the suit had started, prompting a legal amendment to substitute her name as the plaintiff. Despite this amendment, the court determined that Rothschild could not maintain the action as the legal ownership of the note resided with S. Kuhn & Sons when the suit commenced, and her later involvement did not confer the right to sue independently.	Rothschild's primary argument was based on her ownership of the promissory note, which she contended entitled her to pursue a claim against Bruschke and the other defendants. She requested the court to recognize her as the lawful holder of the note and grant her a judgment in her favor based on that ownership.	The defendants argued that Rothschild could not maintain the suit as she was not the original legal owner at the time the lawsuit was filed. They insisted that the legal title to the note was held by S. Kuhn & Sons at the initiation of the case, making their initial filing in their name proper. Thus, they requested the court to recognize that any subsequent amendment to add Rothschild as a plaintiff did not change the legitimacy of the case as it started with the true legal owners.

In January 1871, Walter Falls filed a case against The City of Cairo in the Illinois Supreme Court following a special assessment on his properties within the city. The assessment was imposed in 1868 to cover the costs of grading and filling Washington Avenue and Poplar Street after a decision made by the city council. Falls owned multiple lots that were assessed for these improvements. He paid a total of $1,602.56 for these assessments, although the city later abandoned the collection of such payments and resorted to issuing bonds for the remaining expenses. Seeking to recover the amount he paid, Falls argued that the assessments were illegal and unconstitutional due to their failure to comply with city charter provisions and that his payment was forced upon him. The case was reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court, focusing on whether Falls could reclaim his payment after the abandonment of the assessment.	Walter Falls contended that the assessments had been illegal, unconstitutional, and void. He argued that payment was made under duress, which was compulsory, and claimed that the city’s abandonment of the assessments justified his request for recovery. Falls also asserted that the basis for the payment, the public improvement, had failed, and therefore retaining the payment would violate equity and good conscience.	The City of Cairo defended against Falls’ claims by arguing that the assessments, although possibly illegal, were paid voluntarily. The city contended that since the improvements had been completed, the value of Falls' property had increased, meaning he received the benefit of the payment. The city also highlighted that its abandonment of the collection of other assessments did not alter Falls’ obligation, as those who had paid were not entitled to recovery simply due to the non-payment by others.

The case of "Martin O. Walker et al. v. Chauncey Tucker et al." was decided in September 1873 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a contractual agreement made on July 15, 1865, involving the leasing of land for coal mining. The parties were divided into plaintiffs, Martin O. Walker and others, representing the Carbon Hill Coal Company from Chicago, Illinois, and the defendants, Chauncey Tucker and Henry Tucker, attorneys for the firm Tucker, Brown & Co., based in Buffalo, New York. The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to the possession and use of farming lands in addition to mining rights under this lease agreement. However, the defendants argued that they were wrongfully denied access to the farming lands, which led to several breaches of covenant claims. The court examined the lease terms and the intention behind them to determine the rights and obligations of each party.	The plaintiffs contend that the lease agreement entitles them not only to mine coal but also to possess and use the farming lands specified in the contract. They argue that the defendants' refusal to grant access to these lands constitutes a breach of the agreement, leading to their claims for damages for the claimed breaches of covenant regarding the possession and utilization of the farmland in conjunction with the mining rights.	The defendants, in response, assert that the plaintiffs unlawfully withheld possession of the farming lands from them after the lease was established. They claim that this wrongful exclusion amounted to eviction, which prevents them from fulfilling their obligations under the contract. Additionally, they argue that the contract does not imply a separate rental obligation for the farming lands since the contract language is clear and unambiguous regarding the rights associated with mining and agricultural use.

Benjamin Lombard initiated a legal case against Silas W. Cheever and others in the Marshall Circuit Court of Illinois in October 1846. Lombard's case revolved around a replevin action regarding watercraft on the Illinois River. He alleged that he owned and had possession of the watercraft, which were unlawfully detained by the defendants. Following the exclusion of certain evidence he presented, Lombard voluntarily consented to a non-suit, allowing for an opportunity to set it aside and seek a new trial. However, his motion to set the non-suit aside was subsequently overruled by the Circuit Court. Central to the case were issues relating to the ownership and legal right to operate ferries, with Lombard asserting that he had a legitimate claim to the watercraft based on a license. The proceedings highlighted complex questions of law regarding the sufficiency and admissibility of evidence regarding the licenses Lombard sought to introduce.	Lombard claimed ownership of certain watercraft on the Illinois River, asserting that the defendants unlawfully detained them. His argument relied on references to licenses issued to him to operate a ferry, which he maintained justified his claim. He requested that the court recognize his ownership and entitlement to reclaim the property from the defendants, thus seeking a reversal of the lower court's ruling which upheld the exclusion of his evidence.	The defendants, led by Cheever, denied Lombard's claims, arguing against his ownership and asserting that they legally possessed the watercraft in question. They contended that Lombard had failed to provide sufficient evidence to support his allegations regarding the licenses and his rights to operate a ferry, thereby undermining his claim for restitution of the watercraft.

William H. Wachter initiated a legal case against Harriet Albee, the administratrix of the estate of the deceased Cyrus P. Albee, in March 1874. The case took place in Illinois, and the primary issue at hand was a claim for $2,000 that Wachter alleged he had loaned to Albee during his lifetime. Wachter's claim was brought forth as an action of assumpsit, which is a legal term used for a type of lawsuit for recovering the value of a benefit (or debt) owed. Albee's estate contested the claim based on the Statute of Limitations, arguing that enough time had passed since the alleged loan for the claim to be no longer legally enforceable. A trial was conducted without a jury, leading to a judgment against Wachter, which prompted him to appeal the decision. The crux of the case revolved around whether the evidence presented by Wachter was sufficient to counteract the legal bar imposed by the Statute of Limitations.	Wachter claimed that he lent Albee $2,000 in 1865 and sought to recover this amount. His arguments hinged on alleged admissions made by Albee in 1869 and 1870, in which Albee acknowledged that he had not paid back the loan and had plans to settle the matter. Wachter argued that these admissions constituted a new promise to pay, which would remove the barrier created by the Statute of Limitations and allow him to recover the debt.	The defendant, represented by Albee's estate, contended that the plaintiff had failed to provide sufficient evidence to establish a new promise to pay that would invalidate the Statute of Limitations. The defense argued that Albee's statements only indicated that he acknowledged receiving the money but did not constitute a commitment to repay the loan. Furthermore, it was asserted that promises or admissions made to individuals other than the creditor did not hold legal weight to overcome the statute.

In April 1861, a legal dispute arose in Peoria County, Illinois, involving key individuals Samuel Silsbury, Samuel Smith, John C. Smith (the plaintiffs in error), and Peter Blumb (the defendant in error). The case centered around a contractual agreement for the construction of cattle pens at Blumb's distillery. Frye, Smith & Co. was contracted by Blumb to build the pens and was to be compensated for the costs out of the price for distillery slops provided by Blumb. However, there were modifications made to the original plan without adequate agreement on the cost implications, which led to disputes over payments. After a jury trial in the Circuit Court, a judgment was rendered against Silsbury and Smith for $126.08, prompting Silsbury to appeal the decision, claiming errors in the admission of evidence, particularly regarding witness testimony and the exclusion of certain written contracts. The case presents issues of contractual interpretation, liability for work, and the admissibility of witness accounts.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant owed them for the unpaid balance of services rendered, specifically an account for hardware totaling $176.32. They requested the court to enforce the payment based on their understanding of the contractual obligations related to the construction of the cattle pens and the costs incurred in the process.	The defendant, Peter Blumb, argued that he had not entered into a contract with the plaintiffs directly and maintained that any liability rested with Frye, Smith & Co. He insisted that the plaintiffs were incorrectly seeking compensation under the assumption of an agreement that did not bind him. Moreover, he requested the court to exclude Carroll's testimony, arguing it was pertinent to demonstrate that any cause of action should be directed towards Frye, Smith & Co. rather than himself.

The case "The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company v. James McLaughlin" took place in January 1868 in Springfield, Illinois. The plaintiff, James McLaughlin, a boy, sustained serious injuries when he was playing near a freight car on a public street where the railway track was laid down. During the incident, the yard-master of the railway company climbed onto the freight car to loosen its brakes. At that moment, McLaughlin was reported to be playing with other boys and had initially climbed onto the stirrup of the car but had let go as the yard-master approached, standing on the ground. The car, which was initially standing still, began to move unexpectedly, resulting in McLaughlin's foot being run over by the car wheel. The key individuals in this case included the plaintiff, McLaughlin, and the defendant's employee, the yard-master. The court determined that there was no negligence on the part of the railroad or its employee, as there was no indication McLaughlin was still climbing on the car when the brakes were loosened.	James McLaughlin claimed that the injuries he sustained were a result of the negligence of the railway company's employee. He argued that the yard-master failed to provide a warning before the car began to move, and that the railroad company had a duty to ensure the safety of children playing near its tracks and to guard against such incidents.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad Company defended itself by asserting that there was no negligence involved in the actions of its yard-master. They argued that the yard-master had no way of knowing that McLaughlin was in a position of danger when the brakes were loosened. The defense maintained that it was unreasonable to expect the yard-master to give a signal as the car was merely standing on its track, and the railroad company was not responsible for guarding its cars from children playing nearby.

The case titled "United States Express Company et al. v. Byron L. Smith, Receiver" was decided on December 2, 1889, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The background of the case involves the insolvency of Traders Bank of Chicago, which led to the filing of a bill by Tallman for the appointment of a receiver on October 2, 1888. The court appointed a receiver, who was empowered to manage the bank's assets and institute lawsuits to recover any money owed to the bank. At the time of the receivership, the Traders Bank had deposits in various New York banks. Several creditors, including the United States Express Company and Merchants National Bank, had filed attachment suits against these funds to secure their claims. The receiver sought to halt these attachment proceedings and demanded the release of these funds, arguing that they should be under his control as the appointed receiver. The core contention revolved around the issue of jurisdiction and recognition of the receiver's authority over the funds located in New York banks, particularly in light of prior judgments made in those courts.	The plaintiffs, including the United States Express Company and Merchants National Bank, argued against the receiver's claims, asserting that they had legal rights to the attached funds as creditors of the Traders Bank. They requested that the receiver's petition to enjoin them from continuing their attachment proceedings be dismissed and maintained their right to recover the debts owed to them directly from the funds held in the New York banks.	The defendant, Byron L. Smith as the receiver, contended that the plaintiffs' attachment suits were impermissible due to the receivership. He argued that those proceedings should cease, that the attached funds belonged to the insolvent Traders Bank, and therefore, should be released to him as the appointed receiver. He asserted that since he had taken appropriate legal steps to secure the release of the funds, the plaintiffs were precluded from claiming any rights to them.

In 1850, Elisha Hunt, the appellant, allowed the father of Asa Morton, the appellee, to take possession of a piece of land in Pike County, Illinois, without a specific rent agreement, simply permitting him to occupy the land until spring. The father cultivated the land and raised crops in 1851. By winter 1851-52, the father left, and Asa Morton continued to possess and cultivate the land. Hunt contended that the tenancy had expired, and in February 1853, he initiated a forcible detainer action against Morton. Subsequent proceedings led to a jury verdict in Hunt's favor, but Morton appealed. The case continued through various court sessions, during which evidence supporting Hunt's claim was excluded. At a trial in 1855, the court instructed the jury to rule in favor of Morton, leading to a verdict against Hunt. Hunt's motions for a new trial were denied.	Elisha Hunt claimed that Asa Morton was unlawfully occupying his land after the period of tenancy had expired. He sought to recover possession of the property through forcible detainer proceedings, asserting that Morton had received notice to vacate but failed to do so after the tenancy ended.	Asa Morton argued that his possession of the land was legitimate and that he continued the tenancy established by his father, which implicitly transformed into a tenancy from year to year. Morton contended that Hunt had not given the legally required notice to terminate the tenancy, thus maintaining that the forcible detainer action was unfounded.

The case "Chicago Electric Light Renting Company v. William S. Hutchinson" took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the decision rendered on March 28, 1888. The parties involved were William S. Hutchinson, the plaintiff, and the Chicago Electric Light Renting Company along with its manager, John H. Hapgood, the defendants. The case stemmed from a promissory note issued on September 8, 1885, wherein the Chicago Electric Light Renting Company, signed by Hapgood, promised to pay Hutchinson $125.00 for a smoke consumer purchased for the company's use. After both defendants were duly served, a default judgment was initially entered against them for $126.20 and costs. Subsequently, a stipulation allowed the Chicago Electric Light Renting Company to plead without prejudice to its rights against Hapgood. The defense included pleas of non-assumpsit and denial of joint liability. During the trial, it was found that Hutchinson failed to present the note as evidence, affecting the viability of his claim. The court ultimately determined that Hutchinson's case could not succeed due to insufficient evidence.	The plaintiff, William S.
