Hutchinson, claimed that the Chicago Electric Light Renting Company was liable for $125.00 based on a promissory note signed by the company's manager, John H. Hapgood. He sought the enforcement of this note through court judgment, which was initially granted in default against both defendants. Hutchinson argued that he was entitled to recover the amount stated in the note for the smoke consumer purchased.	The defendants, represented by the Chicago Electric Light Renting Company and Hapgood, contended there was no joint liability as claimed by Hutchinson. They asserted a defense of non-assumpsit, arguing that the promissory note was not properly executed, as there was no evidence demonstrating that Hapgood had the authority to bind the company in such a manner. They also maintained that Hutchinson's failure to introduce the note as evidence meant his claims could not be substantiated, undermining his case.

The case of Edward S. Wilson v. Alex. L. Byers and others took place in Jasper County, Illinois, with a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1875. The events revolve around a dispute over land title stemming from transactions dating back to April 1820 when David Rawlings applied to the Shawneetown land office to purchase a quarter section of land, specifically the southeast quarter of section 34, township 4 north, range 10 east. Rawlings was unable to complete the payment and relinquished part of the land, assigning his entry certificate to James Elliott. Elliott completed payment for the west half of the quarter section, receiving a patent that incorrectly described the land in township 4 south instead of the intended 4 north. This error continued to create confusion over the true ownership of the land. In the ensuing years, Thomas W. Lilley acquired the land and eventually conveyed lots to the complainants, who filed a bill to correct the erroneous patent issued to Wilson, who had obtained patents for the land in question. The court had to determine the correct tract intended for purchase by Rawlings and recognized the equitable claims of the complainants against Wilson’s patent.	The plaintiffs argue that they are the rightful owners of the land based on their possession and subsequent conveyances from Lilley. They contend that the patent obtained by Wilson constitutes a cloud on their title and should be corrected to reflect their equitable rights. The plaintiffs request the court to compel Wilson to convey the legal title to them, asserting that the initial transaction contained mutual mistakes which warrant correction.	The defendant, Edward S. Wilson, claims rightful title to the land based on the patent he obtained from the United States. He argues that the plaintiffs failed to establish their claim due to laches and that they do not possess rightful ownership credentials. Wilson's defense hinges on the assertion that there was no mutual mistake regarding the land description at the time of patent issuance, and he requests the court to affirm his legal title.

In December 1830, the case "Thomas Allison and others, Appellants, v. Thomas P. Clark, Appellee" was adjudicated by the Illinois Supreme Court. The background of the case involves a dispute over a tract of land in Morgan County, Illinois. On February 16, 1826, the Allisons entered into a contract with Clark, agreeing to convey land upon receipt of $207, which was to be paid by the end of February 1827. Clark claimed he was prepared to pay on that date but faced a refusal from the Allisons, who subsequently sold the property to a third party with knowledge of Clark's claim. The Allisons countered that Clark did not pay the agreed amount, presenting a new note as evidence of a different contractual agreement. The lower circuit court ruled in favor of Clark, prompting the Allisons to appeal the decision, which ultimately raised questions about the specific requirements for the payment and conveyance of the land.	The plaintiff, Thomas P. Clark, alleged that he was ready to fulfill his contractual obligation to pay for the land by the stipulated deadline and subsequently did so in May 1827, yet the Allisons refused to convey the property. Clark sought specific performance of the contract, requesting a court order to compel the Allisons to convey the land as originally agreed.	The defendants, the Allisons, denied the claim of payment and asserted that Clark had entered into a new contract, represented by a note issued after the original agreement. They contended that this new contract had not been fulfilled, which constituted a valid defense against Clark's request for specific performance, maintaining that they were under no obligation to convey the land until all appropriate payments were satisfactorily completed.

John C. Smith v. John B. Hoag was a legal proceeding that took place in September 1867 in Mercer County, Illinois. The case originated as an action of forcible entry and detainer initiated by John B. Hoag against John C. Smith. Hoag claimed that Smith forcibly entered his property without permission. The case was originally presented before a justice of the peace and subsequently appealed to the Circuit Court of Mercer County, where a verdict was rendered against Smith. The key individuals involved were John C. Smith (the appellant) and John B. Hoag (the appellee), with representations from attorneys Messrs. Glover, Cook & Campbell for Smith and Messrs. Goudy & Chandler for Hoag. The Circuit Court ruled against Smith after concluding that there was sufficient evidence to support Hoag's claim of prior possession and that Smith's entry was indeed forcible. Following a denied motion for a new trial, the case proceeded to the Illinois Supreme Court for appeal.	The plaintiff, John B. Hoag, maintained that he had prior possession of the property in question, which was forcibly invaded by the defendant, John C. Smith. His legal arguments revolved around the assertion that Smith did not possess valid rights to enter the property and that any claim to ownership by Smith was irrelevant to the issue of forcible entry. Hoag sought legal recognition of his possession and a ruling affirming the initial judgment against Smith for the forcible entry.	John C. Smith, the defendant, contended that the entry was not forcible because Scott, the landlord associated with the property, had ownership rights that allowed him to enter. Smith's defense rested on the argument that he was either the rightful owner or had a claim to possession that justified his actions. He also asserted that there was a question of whether the previous possession had been abandoned, potentially altering the nature of the alleged forcible entry. Smith sought to have the prior judgment overturned, arguing that the court had erred in its instructions to the jury.

In 1867, the case "Charles M. Smith et al. v. John M. Rotan et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiffs, Charles M. Smith and others, initiated a bill in chancery against John M. Rotan and others, who were surviving sureties of Willis Smith, a deceased guardian. The case emerged from a dispute regarding the accounting for funds associated with a guardian's bond held by the deceased. The plaintiffs sought to compel the administrators of the deceased obligors to provide an accounting for the funds due to the plaintiffs, who were minors at the time and thus entitled to receive an accurate accounting of their entitlements. A central issue of the case was whether the heirs of the deceased obligors needed to be included as parties to the lawsuit in order for a judgment to be valid. The court noted the general rule in equity that all parties with substantial interests in the litigation should be made parties to the action, but recognized that exceptions can be made if determining the residence of numerous parties is impractical.	The plaintiffs argued that the surviving sureties of the deceased guardian should be compelled to account for the funds owed to them as minors under the guardian’s bond. They maintained that the inclusion of the deceased's heirs as defendants was unnecessary because the administrators could fulfill the required accounting and were representative of the estates involved.	The defendants contended that the heirs of the deceased obligors were necessary parties to the accounting proceedings, as they had an interest in the matter. However, they also argued that since the heirs were numerous and scattered, and their residences could not be easily determined, the court should proceed without including them as parties in the case.

On March 23, 1872, in Bond County, Illinois, Darius C. Warren entered into a written contract with Andrew Daniels to exchange a forty-acre tract of land owned by Warren for two town lots located in Greenville, including a house and well. The contract detailed that the lots were encumbered by a deed of trust for $227, with stipulations regarding rent proceeds intended to pay for repairs and the deed of trust. After the agreement, Daniels took possession of the land and made improvements. However, upon inspecting the lots, Warren informed Daniels that he would not uphold the contract. Daniels subsequently provided a good deed for the lots and requested a deed from Warren in return, which Warren refused. This led Daniels to file a bill in chancery for specific performance of the contract. The court hearing involved extensive evidence and testimonies, ultimately siding with Daniels despite Warren's claims that the lots were not in Greenville and that the deed of trust amount was misrepresented.	Andrew Daniels, the plaintiff, contended that he fulfilled his part of the contract by providing a valid deed for the Greenville lots and demanded specific performance of the agreement. He argued that the properties were as represented in the contract, and that Warren's refusal to provide a deed for the forty-acre land was unjustified.	Darius C. Warren, the defendant, argued against the enforcement of the contract, claiming that the Greenville lots were not correctly located and that the associated deed of trust exceeded the agreed amount of $227. His main contention was that the representations made prior to the contract were misleading, particularly regarding the value and location of the properties, asserting that these factors should invalidate the exchange.

Elijah Smith, who sued for the benefit of William Johnson, brought this case against William Bridges. The legal proceedings occurred in December 1819 before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Madison County, Illinois, where Smith claimed that the writing he held, purported to be a promissory note, lacked the essential features required by law to constitute a valid note. Specifically, it did not indicate an obligation from Bridges to pay any person, violating the principles governing promissory notes, which must include the name of the payee or otherwise guarantee payment to a specified person. The court examined the nature of promissory notes and the requirements for an instrument to be actionable.	The plaintiff, Elijah Smith, argued that the document in question did not meet the necessary legal criteria to be considered a valid promissory note. He contended that it did not specify a payee or demonstrate an obligation for Bridges to make any payment. As a result, Smith sought to have the court recognize the invalidity of the notes and the inability to maintain action on these instruments.	William Bridges, the defendant, likely contended that the writing lacked the essential characteristics of a promissory note and thus should not be enforceable. Bridges may have argued that since the document did not specify to whom payments were to be made, it could not be construed as a binding financial obligation. This defense implies a request for dismissal of the claims brought by the plaintiff due to the insufficiency of the document.

James B. Fletcher v. Matthew Patton took place in Sangamon County, Illinois, culminating in a court decision on August 26, 1886. The case centered around a contract dispute involving the sale of 103 head of beef cattle. Fletcher, the plaintiff, claimed that on May 23, 1884, he entered into a contract with Patton, the defendant, to purchase the cattle at a price of $5.75 per hundred gross. The agreement stipulated that Fletcher could demand delivery anytime between June 25 and July 15. Fletcher asserted that he requested the cattle on July 3, but Patton repudiated the contract and instead sold the cattle to other buyers on July 7. As a result, Fletcher sought damages based on the price increase of the cattle after his demand. The case was characterized by conflicting evidence regarding the nature of the contract—whether it was absolute or conditional—leading to a legal dispute over damages.	The plaintiff, James B. Fletcher, argued that he had a binding contract with the defendant for the purchase of cattle, asserting that he had lawfully demanded delivery. Fletcher claimed that the defendant's refusal to deliver the cattle constituted a breach of contract, and he sought damages corresponding to the difference between the contracted price and the market rate after July 3, when the demand was made.	The defendant, Matthew Patton, contended that the contract was conditional and not final until he received market reports, which he had not seen at the time of the demand. Patton argued that the transaction was contingent upon price stability and claimed that Fletcher had agreed to retrieve his mail, which he did not do. This defense highlighted the contention regarding the nature of the agreement and sought to justify the defendant's actions.

John H. H. Bennett v. Jennie McLaughlin is a case decided on June 27, 1883, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute stems from a contract made on August 20, 1880, in Jacksonville, Illinois, where McLaughlin hired a White sewing machine from Bennett for $50. The agreement stipulated a payment plan starting with a $10 upfront payment and subsequent monthly installments. McLaughlin paid a total of $16, including the old machine given in exchange for the initial payment. By March 1882, she refused to continue payments or return the sewing machine. The defendant's (McLaughlin's) argument was centered around her status as a minor at the time of the contract and the claimed equivalency in value of the old machine to the new one. The trial court ruled against Bennett, leading him to appeal, claiming errors in the instructions given to the jury regarding the contract's enforceability.	Bennett's main argument was that McLaughlin should return the sewing machine since she had failed to fulfill the payment obligations after initially making a partial payment. Bennett contended that his rights to reclaim the machine were valid, despite McLaughlin's defense of being a minor at the contract's signing. He sought possession of the sewing machine based on the contractual agreement and claimed that McLaughlin's refusal to pay violated the terms.	McLaughlin’s defense was predicated on her claiming to be a minor when signing the contract, which allowed her to void it legally. She maintained that the old machine provided as part of the payment was equitably equivalent in value to the new sewing machine, thus contesting Bennett’s claim. McLaughlin argued that she should not be compelled to forfeit the sewing machine or make further payments, as the partial payment had satisfied her side of the contract.

In 1846, Aaron Corey, the appellant, faced legal action in the Madison Circuit Court, Illinois. During the May term of that year, he sought to quash two executions that had been issued in favor of William Russell, the appellee, against him. The Honorable John D. Catón presided over the hearing of these motions. However, the court denied Corey's application to quash the executions. The case progressed to the Illinois Supreme Court due to this denial, where the decision of the lower court was reviewed. Notably, the testimony that informed the Circuit Court's decision was not included in the record available for review, as Corey did not file a bill of exceptions to introduce the evidence. This lack of evidence rendered the Supreme Court unable to assess the propriety of the Circuit Court's ruling.	The plaintiff, Aaron Corey, argued that the executions issued against him were unjust and requested the court to quash them. He claimed that the Circuit Court's denial of his application was erroneous, seeking a reversal of that decision on appeal.	The defendant, William Russell, maintained that the executions were valid and justifiable. Russell's key argument revolved around the procedural shortcomings from the appellant, specifically noting that Corey failed to submit a bill of exceptions to present the evidence needed for a proper appellate review. He requested the affirmation of the lower court's decision.

On March 3, 1865, in Chicago, Illinois, Edward W. Mitchell entered into a contract with N. P. Lassen for the sale of 10,000 bushels of number one oats at a price of 61 cents per bushel. The terms of the contract specified that the oats were to be delivered during March, as requested by Lassen, with payment due upon delivery. After the contract was made, Mitchell claimed he was ready to deliver the oats throughout March; however, Lassen did not request or accept the delivery on any day that month. The case was tried in the Superior Court of Chicago, where a jury found in favor of Mitchell, awarding him $2,000 in damages. Lassen subsequently sought a reversal of this decision, arguing that the evidence did not support the verdict and that Mitchell did not fulfill his contractual obligations.	Edward W. Mitchell, the plaintiff, claimed that N. P. Lassen breached their contract by failing to request the delivery of oats or make payment for them as agreed. Mitchell maintained that he was ready and willing to deliver the oats at any time during March 1865 and sought damages of $2,000 for Lassen's failure to perform under the contract.	N. P. Lassen, the defendant, contended that there was insufficient evidence demonstrating that Mitchell was ready and able to deliver the oats on the specified date. He argued that Mitchell's attempts to sell the oats at a lower price after a decline indicated a rescission of their contract and that Mitchell was not entitled to damages for a breach that was attributable to his own actions. Lassen requested the reversal of the trial court's judgment based on these assertions.

In the case of James Day v. Cushman, Eaton & Co., the legal proceedings took place in December 1838 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from a judgment rendered in September 1837 in the La Salle Circuit Court under the presiding judge, Hon. Jesse B. Thomas. The plaintiff, James Day, was facing a default judgment against him related to the foreclosure of a mortgage through a scire facias, which is a legal procedure to compel someone to appear in court. The cash judgment against Day amounted to $1,219.17 plus costs. The primary issues in question revolved around the necessary details that must be included in a scire facias, specifically that it should name individuals in the partnership of Cushman, Eaton & Co. and provide that the last installment of the mortgage payment had become due, which were deemed essential for the validity of the foreclosure action.	The plaintiff, James Day, claimed that the scire facias was fatally flawed due to the omission of the Christian names of the individuals forming the partnership "Cushman, Eaton & Co." Furthermore, he argued that the document failed to state that the last installment of the mortgage payment had come due, as required by statute. As a remedy, Day sought to have the default judgment reversed based on these procedural errors.	Cushman, Eaton & Co. did not provide a detailed defense in the summary. However, it can be inferred that their position rested on the validity of the foreclosure process as executed in the lower court. The defense likely argued against the claims made by Day without addressing the specific procedural omissions mentioned.

In April 1867, the legal case of James McKindley et al. v. Maria Buck et al. was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the Superior Court of Chicago, where Judge Joseph E. Gary presided. The dispute arose after a judgment was made against Maria Buck, one of the defendants, leading her to seek to set aside the default judgment. The plaintiff, James McKindley, had successfully obtained this judgment. The court highlighted that once a term of the Circuit Court had expired, there was no authority left to set aside a judgment, though minor amendments could be made with notice to the opposing party. Maria Buck's attempt to use a writ of error coram nobis was deemed inappropriate, as such a remedy had fallen out of use. The Supreme Court noted that proper procedures must be followed to avoid unnecessary complications in litigation. Ultimately, the attempts to rectify the previous ruling by alternative means were found to be without merit.	The plaintiffs, James McKindley et al., argued that the previous judgment against Maria Buck was valid and should remain in effect. They contended that the Superior Court erred in allowing actions to contradict the judgment after the term had concluded, thereby extending litigation beyond permissible bounds. The plaintiffs sought to uphold the original judgment against Buck.	The defendant, Maria Buck, claimed that she had valid reasons for failing to present her defense during the original proceedings and sought to have the default judgment set aside. She attempted to introduce affidavits to support her motion but was informed that these needed to be appropriately documented in a bill of exceptions. The defense contended that errors had occurred, and thus the judgment should be revisited, asserting that her past actions were justified.

The case, "The Maywood Company et al. v. The Village of Maywood et al.", took place in Cook County, Illinois, with a decision rendered on May 15, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from claims made by the Village of Maywood and its residents against the Maywood Company regarding a 16-acre area in what is known as Block 58, which both parties claimed should be designated as a public park. The Maywood Company, incorporated in April 1869, had purchased over five hundred acres in the area and promoted Block 58 as a public park equipped with various attractions. Residents and lot owners acted under the assumption that they had the right to use this land as a public park, based on promotional materials distributed by the company over the years. However, the company's refusal to transfer control of the park to the newly incorporated Village of Maywood in 1881 led to the legal action to enforce what residents felt was their right to the park.	The Village of Maywood and its residents claimed that the Maywood Company had dedicated Block 58 as a public park through its actions and representations over the years. They sought to have the court declare the area a public park, to surrender control to the village trustees, and to set aside a trust deed created by the company that secured certain bonds. Their primary arguments rested on the notion that the public had been allowed to use the land as a park for many years, which constituted an acceptance of its dedication.	The Maywood Company contended that they had not formally dedicated the land to the public, arguing that their representations and the plat recorded did not create a binding legal obligation. They also claimed that the trust deed provided necessary legal protection against any immediate interference with the property. The company maintained that the use of the land as a park was not officially recognized and thus should remain under its ownership and control.

In April 1862, in Illinois, Louis Heintz, the appellant, faced legal action from Aaron Cahn and others, appellees, concerning a promissory note for $219.98. The note was signed by William Muller and F. Kusowsky as makers and was guaranteed by Heintz. The action was one of assumpsit against Heintz, who had been alleged to be a guarantor for the note. The trial was held without a jury, presided over by Judge Manniere. During the trial, Heintz admitted that his signature appeared on the note but denied having made a binding guaranty or receiving any consideration for it. The court evaluated evidence regarding the partnership of the payees, the existence of a guaranty, and the application of payments made after the note's issue, concluding that Heintz had sufficient obligation under the guaranty despite his claims. The lower court found for Cahn & Co., awarding them a judgment for $230.50. Heintz subsequently appealed the decision, arguing various points regarding the clarity and terms of the guaranty, the evidence of the partnership, and the handling of payments related to the note.	The plaintiffs, Cahn & Co., maintained that Heintz was liable as a guarantor of the promissory note. They argued that the evidence showed that Heintz’s name appeared on the note at its execution and contended that there was sufficient consideration to support the guaranty. They also claimed that the partnership’s identity as payees did not need to be proven rigorously given the circumstances, and that any payments made after the note's execution did not absolve Heintz of his liability.	Heintz contended that the plea of general issue did not put the partnership of Cahn & Co. at issue, thus undermining the plaintiffs' case. He also argued that there was no valid consideration for his purported guaranty and that the endorsement was made without his explicit consent as it was written in blank. Heintz asserted that he did not intend to be primarily liable mainly due to the terms of the agreement and that the court's acknowledgment of the guarantees without a clear consideration was erroneous.

In 1884, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute emerged involving Andrew Portones and Joseph Badenoch, Jr. et al. The issue arose over a mechanic's lien filed by the firm Holmes & Sprool for work done as plasterers on two houses owned by Portones and his partner, Albert White. Other parties, including Badenoch & Co. and a plumber named William Johnston, also filed petitions to enforce liens for materials and plumbing work related to the same properties. Portones appealed a decree from the Superior Court of Cook County that awarded liens to Holmes & Sprool, Badenoch & Co., and William Johnston. The Appellate Court upheld the Superior Court’s decree, and Portones specifically contested only the lien awarded to Badenoch & Co. The court concluded that Badenoch & Co. had a right to enforce their lien based on an implied contract for materials furnished and maintained accurate records separating the materials used for the relevant properties. The court also addressed procedural concerns about not including a previous note holder in the case, concluding that their interests were not prejudiced.	The plaintiff, Joseph Badenoch, Jr. and J.J. Badenoch, asserted that they were entitled to a mechanic’s lien for the lumber they provided for the construction of buildings owned by Portones. They argued that they had an implied contract and that the materials were furnished at the request of the property owners within the stipulated time frame set by the Lien law. Their claim included a request for enforcement of this lien against the properties in question.	Andrew Portones, the defendant, contended that the lien should not have been granted as the holder of a prior trust deed was not made a party to the proceedings. He argued that this omission could potentially affect the validity of the lien. Portones maintained that the failure to incorporate this necessary party constituted an error which prejudiced his rights, although the court found that the trustee's presence was not crucial in this case since the sale would be subject to existing encumbrances.

James W. Tufts filed a case against Susan Johnson in 1888 in Sangamon County, Illinois. The dispute arose from a replevin action concerning a soda-water apparatus and founts that Tufts sold conditionally to Fleury Medicine Company, retaining ownership until a series of notes were fully paid. Tufts alleged that certain notes had become due and unpaid, granting him the right to reclaim the property. However, Johnson allegedly colluded with Fleury and Company to obtain possession of the apparatus without a legitimate basis, knowing Tufts retained rights to it. This situation led to Tufts's claim for the return of the property following the non-payment of notes. The lower court sustained a demurrer to some counts of Tufts’s declaration, prompting the appeal.	Tufts claimed that he had the right to reclaim the soda apparatus due to Johnson's unjust retention after the non-payment of notes that were part of the conditional sale. He argued that Johnson was aware of his ownership rights but still received a bill of sale from Fleury and Company in a scheme to defraud him. Tufts sought the return of the property and asserted that the demurrer to his declaration was improperly sustained.	Johnson contended that the demurrer to Tufts's claims was justified, arguing that the facts alleged did not sufficiently demonstrate that Tufts still held the right to reclaim at the time the suit commenced. She likely suggested that any non-payment issues were either resolved or not applicable when the action was initiated. Johnson’s defense centered on challenging the validity of Tufts's claims based on procedural technicalities regarding the rights to the property.

The case of Samuel Glickauf v. Gottlieb Kaufmann et al. took place in September 1874 in Illinois. The dispute arose over two promissory notes executed by a third party, Leopold Rothchild, and payable to the order of the appellees, which included Kaufmann. Glickauf, the appellant, was implicated as a guarantor of these notes. The appellant claimed he did not undertake the guarantee as alleged nor did he execute a written guaranty on the notes. The key individuals involved were Samuel Glickauf and Gottlieb Kaufmann. The case centered on the interpretation of Glickauf's role regarding the notes and whether his indorsement constituted a guarantee or merely an indorsement at common law. The court examined the evidence including a tripartite agreement signed by the creditors and Glickauf, clarifying his obligations related to the notes.	The plaintiffs, represented by Kaufmann and other creditors, argued that Glickauf acted as a guarantor when he endorsed the promissory notes. They requested the court to recognize his obligation as primary, rather than secondary or as a mere indorser, based on the agreement made by Glickauf to assume responsibility for a percentage of Rothchild's debts.	Glickauf contended that he did not undertake to guarantee the notes as alleged and posited that his endorsement was not intended to create a guarantee. He filed three pleas claiming he had not guaranteed the notes in writing nor any form, maintaining he was merely an indorser. He requested the court to dismiss the claims against him on these grounds.

The case of George Freeland and Samuel Wheeler against The Board of Supervisors of Jasper County was decided in January 1862 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from an action on a bond for the penal sum of $600 that was conditioned for the payment of a debt owed by one Burnett to Jasper County. The bond was executed by the appellants, Freeland and Wheeler, and a third party, Isaac Clery. During the proceedings, only Wheeler was served with process, while Freeland could not be found, and Clery's status was not clear. A trial ensued, resulting in a judgment against both Freeland and Wheeler for the total debt amount of $600, along with additional damages of $462.24. The appellants contended that the judgment was erroneous as it did not stipulate that satisfaction could occur upon the payment of damages alone, thereby allowing for a double recovery. The complexities in procedural aspects arose due to the involvement of multiple defendants and the failure of the clerk to properly document the case, including a demurrer filed and subsequently withdrew by the defendants.	The plaintiffs, represented by the Board of Supervisors of Jasper County, argued for the enforcement of the bond that required Freeland and Wheeler to pay the specified sum of $600 in debt and $462.24 in damages. They maintained that the judgment should stand as it was, despite the issues raised by the appellants, asserting that proper procedure and recovery were followed.	Freeland and Wheeler contested the judgment, arguing that it was incorrect as it failed to state that full payment would settle the debt, citing precedents that have established that damages assessed on such bonds should suffice for satisfaction. They raised procedural issues regarding the demurrer and the assessment of damage against defendants not participating in the trial, emphasizing the clerical errors in recording procedures and the calculation of judgment among multiple defendants.

The case "Nixon, Ellison & Co. v. The Southwestern Insurance Company, of Cairo, Illinois" was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1868. The dispute arose from a legal action initiated by Nixon, Ellison & Co., a partnership consisting of Richard G. Nixon, William Ellison, and Thomas Block, against The Southwestern Insurance Company, located in Cairo, Illinois. The action was based on a policy of insurance, and the legal proceedings began at the April term of the Alexander Circuit Court. The defendant, The Southwestern Insurance Company, filed a plea in abatement, asserting that the proper name of the company was simply "The Southwestern Insurance Company," as established by an act of the General Assembly of Illinois. They contended that the plaintiffs incorrectly referred to them as "Southwestern Insurance Company, of Cairo, Illinois." In response, Nixon, Ellison & Co. registered a demurrer against the plea, but the court overruled this demurrer. Ultimately, the court quashed the writ, leading to a judgment against the plaintiffs for costs, prompting Nixon, Ellison & Co. to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Nixon, Ellison & Co. argued that the plea in abatement filed by The Southwestern Insurance Company was technically defective, as it did not comply with legal requirements regarding how a corporation must present such a plea. They contended that the plea should have been filed by an attorney appointed under the company's common seal, rather than by the company's president and secretary. The plaintiffs sought to reverse the lower court's ruling that upheld the defendant's plea and quashed their writ.	The Southwestern Insurance Company maintained that the plaintiffs had improperly named them in the lawsuit, claiming that their official name was simply "The Southwestern Insurance Company." They insisted that any reference to "of Cairo, Illinois" was erroneous. The defense requested that the court quash the writ and assert that the proper procedure had not been followed by the plaintiffs, ultimately seeking a dismissal of the case against them.

Albert G. Sloo v. The President, Directors, and Company of the State Bank of Illinois is a legal dispute originating in May 1837 in the St. Clair Circuit Court, located in Illinois. The case revolves around a significant judgment entered against Sloo and his partner, Horatio G. McClintoc, for $125,000 due to a confession of judgment made by McClintoc, who acted without Sloo's authorization. The judgment was based on a power of attorney executed solely by McClintoc, allowing them to confess the judgment on behalf of the partnership, A.G. Sloo & Co., while Sloo was absent from the state. Upon discovering the judgment, Sloo moved to set it aside, asserting that he never consented to the power of attorney or authorized McClintoc to act on his behalf. The Circuit Court denied Sloo's motion, leading to the appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The key issues at stake included the validity of the judgment against Sloo based on the lack of his consent and whether the confession by one partner could bind the other.	Sloo argued that the Circuit Court wrongfully entered a judgment against him without proper authorization. He maintained that there was no evidence of indebtedness or bond filed to support the confessed judgment. Sloo argued that since he was not present nor had he authorized McClintoc to confess judgment on his behalf, the court should set aside the judgment. Thus, he sought either for the judgment to be vacated or for the execution against his property to be restrained.	The State Bank of Illinois contended that McClintoc, as a partner, had the authority to confess judgment on behalf of the partnership under the executed power of attorney. Their defense relied on the argument that Sloo's subsequent actions and conversations implied his assent to the judgment. The Bank maintained that the judgment entered was valid and that Sloo's claims were untenable given McClintoc’s purported authority within the context of their partnership.

The case "Andrew Wilkinson v. Hannah E. Deming" took place in Illinois, with the final decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. The central individuals involved were Andrew Wilkinson, the plaintiff, and Hannah E. Deming, the defendant. The background of the case lies in the divorce proceedings that occurred in January 1871, when the mother of the child, Sarah A., obtained a decree of divorce against Andrew Wilkinson for cruel treatment and was granted custody of their daughter. Following the mother's death on December 2, 1873, she appointed Hannah E. Deming as the testamentary guardian of the child through her will. Wilkinson sought to revoke Deming's guardianship, arguing for his right to regain custody of his daughter. The case was examined by the Circuit Court of Whiteside County, which had to determine the implications of the prior divorce decree and the subsequent actions concerning guardianship.	Andrew Wilkinson argued that the divorce decree rendered him incapable of holding custody rights over his daughter anymore. He claimed that since he was the father, he had the right to contest the guardianship appointed by the mother’s will, considering his daughter’s best interests. Specifically, he sought to revoke the letters of guardianship granted to Deming and to regain custody of Sarah A., contending he was fit to provide for and care for her.	Hannah E. Deming's defense was based on the argument that the divorce decree had permanently severed Wilkinson's custody rights due to his fault in the marriage. She maintained that the mother, as granted custody, had the authority to appoint a guardian through her will, and since she was now the appointed guardian and the child expressed a desire to stay with her, there was no basis for Wilkinson's claims. Deming stressed that there was no evidence suggesting she was an unfit guardian for the child.

The case of Robert R. Williams v. John Doe, ex dem. George Claytor, Mason C. Fitch, Harvey Scribner, and Henry Renckin took place in December 1838 in Quincy, Illinois. The action was initiated as an ejectment suit to recover the South half of Lot No. 3, in Block No. 5 of Quincy. Robert R. Williams was the appellant, who claimed ownership through a series of deeds that traced back to a patent from the United States to the county of Adams. The plaintiff's side presented evidence, including a patent and deeds that supported his claim of possession and ownership over the lot. The defendant offered a decree from a previous chancery suit that voided the deeds leading to Williams' claim, asserting that they were fraudulent. The Circuit Court initially accepted the plaintiff's evidence but excluded the defendant's decree and certain other documents. After the jury rendered a verdict against the defendant with only nominal damages awarded to the plaintiff, the defendant appealed the decision, citing multiple errors in the trial court's handling of evidence and the exclusion of documents that supported his claims.	The plaintiff, Robert R. Williams, contended that he had rightful ownership of the property based on a clear chain of title established through several deeds, including a patent from the United States. He argued that the deeds demonstrating his claim were valid and that he had possession of the premises at the commencement of the lawsuit. Williams sought to affirm the Circuit Court's ruling in favor of his claim and to confirm his ownership of the disputed lot.	The defendants claimed that the deeds relied upon by the plaintiff were fraudulent and void due to a prior decree from a chancery court that had annulled these deeds. The defendants contended that the Circuit Court erred by excluding the decree and other related evidence that would demonstrate the invalidity of the plaintiff's claims. They requested the court to reverse the lower court's ruling based on these alleged evidentiary errors.

In 1848, Robert Dawson and Garrett W. Robbins were involved in a legal dispute in the Brown Circuit Court of Illinois. The case centered around Robbins suing Dawson for payment for work done on a steam mill's machinery. Robbins' claim was based on the assumption that there was an agreement for remuneration for his services. Dawson contested the claim, asserting that the work was done under a special contract, which allegedly specified a set payment amount. The jury ultimately found in favor of Robbins, awarding him $55.09. Dawson's subsequent motion for a new trial was overruled, leading to the case being escalated to the Illinois Supreme Court. The court's review centered on whether the Circuit Court had erred in denying a new trial, hinging on the existence of the alleged special contract and its terms, including a potential set-off claim by Dawson which Robbins seemingly admitted during the trial.	Robbins, the plaintiff, claimed compensation for services rendered in the construction of the steam mill's machinery. His lawsuit was framed as an assumpsit, pursuing recovery for work performed. Robbins maintained that he was entitled to payment, despite Dawson's defenses and contentions regarding the nature of their agreement.	Dawson, the defendant, contested Robbins' claims on multiple grounds. He argued nonassumpsit, asserting that no valid contract existed and that he should not be held liable for the payment. Additionally, he claimed a set-off, stating that the work performed was part of a special agreement that did not obligate him to pay the full amount claimed by Robbins. Dawson asserted that any supposed contract was ambiguous and potentially rescinded due to Robbins' misrepresentations regarding the work required.

In December 1845, the case of John R. Smoot v. Benjamin Lafferty was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court. The plaintiff, John R. Smoot, alleged that the defendant, Benjamin Lafferty, who was the sheriff of Gallatin County, unlawfully leveraged and sold Smoot's ferry boat. This action was conducted under certain execution and fee bills without adhering to the statutory requirement for property appraisal by three disinterested householders, as outlined in the Act of January 6, 1843. The case originated in Gallatin Circuit Court, where Smoot claimed damages and sought redress for what he described as the unlawful levy and sale of his property. The court initially ruled in favor of Smoot, awarding him $131 in damages, prompting Lafferty to appeal the decision. The subsequent legal arguments centered around the constitutionality of the applicable valuation law, leading to the Supreme Court's eventual involvement to resolve the matter.	The plaintiff, John R. Smoot, argued that his ferry boat was unlawfully seized and sold by the defendant without proper appraisal as mandated by the relevant state law. Smoot contended that this violation constituted trespass, and he sought damages amounting to $131 for the direct financial losses incurred as a result of the alleged illegal action by Lafferty, the sheriff.	The defendant, Benjamin Lafferty, maintained that the actions performed during the levy and sale of the ferry boat were conducted in accordance with his duties as sheriff. Lafferty filed a demurrer, disputing the sufficiency of Smoot’s claims and the validity of the law under which the auction was conducted. His defense ultimately hinged on the argument that the appraisal requirement was unconstitutional, as substantiated by previous rulings from the Supreme Court of the United States.

In September 1858, Gabriel Marckle filed a bill for the foreclosure of two mortgages on land in Morgan County, Illinois, executed by Wm. R. Miller. The first mortgage was on January 17, 1857, for notes totaling $325 and $272.50, and the second was on October 2, 1857, for $1,000. Wm. R. Miller admitted to the execution of these documents but claimed that the third note was intended to defraud creditors. After Miller's death in August 1860, his widow, Louisa Miller, became involved in the case. She argued that the property was a homestead and that her husband had not released his homestead rights. Following a court decree, Marckle became the legal owner, and Louisa sought to overturn the foreclosure to retain her rights to the homestead for herself and their minor children. The court handled multiple affidavits from both parties, which presented conflicting views about the validity of the mortgages and execution of the homestead exemption. The case reached the Illinois Supreme Court, which ultimately addressed the legal rights stemming from the Homestead Act and prior agreements.	Louisa Miller and her co-plaintiffs claimed that the foreclosure should be vacated because Wm. R. Miller's rights as a homeowner under the Homestead Act were never formally released. They asserted that since Louisa was not part of the original foreclosure suit and had not relinquished her homestead exemption, the decree of foreclosure and subsequent sale should not stand. They requested that the court undo the decree and confirm their right to retain possession of the homestead.	Gabriel Marckle contended that Wm. R. Miller did not assert his homestead rights at the time of foreclosure. He submitted evidence to suggest that the mortgages were valid, including affidavits implying that the first mortgage was related to the purchase money for the property, thus exempting it from homestead protection. Marckle sought a writ of possession for the property, arguing that the foreclosure was legitimate and should not be reversed.

The case "Cyrus H. McCormick v. Wheeler, Mellick & Co." was heard in April 1864 by the Illinois Supreme Court, originating from a dispute in the Circuit Court of Rock Island County. The primary issue was an action of ejectment regarding a west one hundred acres of the northeast quarter of Section seven, Township nineteen north, Range three east of the fourth principal meridian. The dispute stemmed from the priority of various judgment liens against William Marshall, Jr. Multiple judgments were rendered against him from December 1857 to January 1861, with significant sums owed to various parties. The crucial judgment favoring Wheeler, Mellick & Co. for $6,472.42 was issued in January 1861, but a judgment favoring McCarn & Scott was also significant since it involved a subsequent transaction. The legal arguments hinged on the validity of various sales, satisfactions, and potential amendments to the records concerning these judgments. The case revealed complications arising from inadequate notice in sheriff's sales and the implications of setting aside those sales without preserving third-party rights.	The plaintiff, Wheeler, Mellick & Co., argued that their judgment lien had priority over the defendant's claims. They sought possession of the property based on their title derived from an execution process following their judgment. The plaintiffs contended that all procedural necessities were met during their acquisition, making their claims valid and enforceable.	The defendant, Cyrus H. McCormick, contended that the sales under the previous judgment liens were improperly conducted and that the satisfaction of the Lee judgment retroactively voided any subsequent claims. McCormick argued that the procedural failures in the execution processes and documentation meant that he held a superior title that should protect him from the plaintiffs' claims.

In January 1874, Joseph Spangler filed a lawsuit against The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. in the Illinois Supreme Court, following an incident where his livestock was injured on the railway track. The event occurred at a location known as Sangamon Switch or Sangamon Station, which had distinct features including a station house, warehouse, store, blacksmith shop, post office, and several residences. The railway track was alleged to be improperly maintained as it lacked fencing and suitable cattle-guards at a nearby highway crossing. The defendants argued that the incident occurred within the limits of a village, thus exempting them from the requirement to maintain such safety features. The case rested on whether the railway company had a legal obligation to provide protections at that specific location, as dictated by local law and precedent.	Joseph Spangler claimed that the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. neglected to properly fence its railway and install suitable cattle-guards at the highway crossing where the incident occurred. He sought compensation for the injuries incurred by his livestock due to this alleged negligence, arguing that the lack of safety measures led to the animals getting onto the track and ultimately being injured.	The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. contended that they were not legally required to provide fencing or cattle-guards at the location of the incident, as it was situated within village limits. They maintained that the absence of these features was permissible under the law, pointing out that the definition of a village includes various types of dwellings and businesses, and that the site met these criteria. Their key argument was that they were not negligent because the situation fell under exemptions established by previous court decisions.

In the case of Mrs. M. Cudahy v. Alice Powell, which was decided on December 2, 1889, in Cook County, Illinois, Mrs. M. Cudahy alleged that Alice Powell was involved in the malicious prosecution against her following the loss of a valuable shawl. Cudahy had lost the shawl and, after six months of searching for it, she learned from her sister that a woman had been seen wearing it. This led Cudahy and a friend to approach the police regarding the situation. The police subsequently brought Powell to the station while holding the shawl, which Cudahy identified. Powell was detained for a couple of days as a result of this arrest. The circumstances of the arrest were questioned, particularly regarding whether it had the authority of Cudahy. As the trial proceeded, conflicting testimonies emerged, but the jury ultimately sided with Powell, finding insufficient evidence in Cudahy's favor. The case raised issues of malicious prosecution and the justification of an arrest made without formal process.	Mrs. Cudahy claimed that Alice Powell was responsible for her malicious prosecution. She sought damages for the wrongful arrest, arguing that the arrest was made without proper authority and without probable cause. Cudahy contended that her identification of the shawl and the subsequent actions taken by the police were unjustified, effectively claiming that Powell had orchestrated a false accusation against her.	Alice Powell argued that the police acted independently and did not require Cudahy’s instructions for her arrest. Powell contended that there was no malice or lack of probable cause on her part. She maintained that the jury's finding was just, and emphasized that there was enough conflict in the evidence to warrant a ruling in her favor, as the burden of proof for malicious prosecution had not been met by Cudahy.

In the case of Patrick Moran et al. v. John Hope Gordon et al., the legal proceeding was initiated regarding a financial disagreement stemming from an 1880 shipment of fifty tubs of butterine from Chicago to Fraser, Gordon & Co. in Glasgow, Scotland. The plaintiffs, who were surviving members of Fraser, Gordon & Co., filed the suit to recover a balance they claimed was due for advances, freight charges, and other expenses related to this shipment. The dispute arose from differing interpretations of the transaction: the plaintiffs argued that the goods were consigned to them, while the defendants believed they had sold the goods. Following a waiver of jury trial, the case was presented to the court directly, which also examined various correspondences between the parties that highlighted misunderstandings about the nature of the transaction leading to a dispute about its final valuation. Eventually, a sale was recorded on November 19, 1881, and the plaintiffs sent an account sales to the defendants, indicating a balance owed. Notably, the defendants did not respond until over three months later, during which the court established silence as a potential admission of the account's accuracy. The trial culminated with a judgment favoring the plaintiffs, leading to the defendant's appeal.	The plaintiffs contended that they were owed a balance for advances made on the butterine shipment and that the transaction constituted a consignment rather than a sale. They argued that the defendants had effectively admitted the correctness of the account by their prolonged silence and failure to object to the account sales provided. They sought a judgment to recover the stated amount due for the advances and related charges.	The defendants maintained that the butterine was sold rather than consigned, as asserted by the plaintiffs. They argued against the interpretation that their silence constituted an agreement to the account sales and insisted that the plaintiffs' claims were exaggerated. The defendants sought to have the decision reversed, disputing the findings of the court regarding the nature of the transaction and the implications of their lack of response to the account.

The case "The American Central Insurance Company v. Louis B. Rothchild" took place in June 1876 before the Illinois Supreme Court. The action arose from a fire that destroyed Rothchild's property, for which he sought recovery under a fire insurance policy issued by the American Central Insurance Company. One condition of the policy required Rothchild to produce a certificate confirming the circumstances of the loss, signed by a notary or magistrate nearest to the location of the fire. During the litigation, Rothchild secured a certificate from a relevant official, arguing that the requirements of the policy were met. The case highlighted various facts and instructions surrounding evidentiary standards and the interpretation of policy language.	Rothchild argued that he satisfied all conditions of the insurance policy, including producing the necessary certificate of loss. He maintained that the evidence substantiated his claims for recovery, as the policy covered not only the initial stock but also any replacements made subsequently. Rothchild sought to establish that he did not intentionally cause the fire and therefore was entitled to recovery for the damages incurred.	The American Central Insurance Company contended that Rothchild may have set the fire intentionally to benefit from the insurance payout, thereby violating the terms of the policy. They argued that the certificate provided did not meet the specific conditions outlined in the policy, claiming inconsistencies that should invalidate Rothchild's claim. The defendant requested that the jury consider these special defenses and rule against the plaintiff based on the alleged misconduct and procedural noncompliance.

In 1839, an action of debt was initiated by William Ewbanks against Daniel Ellis and Adair in the Adams Circuit Court, Illinois. The summons for this case was issued on August 20, 1839. However, the summons mistakenly bore a date indicating the year as "one thousand eight hundred and thirty" instead of "one thousand eight hundred and thirty-nine." The summons was served on August 28, 1839, and returned on September 4, 1839. After a judgment was rendered against the defendants by default for a debt of $101.50 plus $21.31 in damages and court costs, the defendants sought a writ of error from the Illinois Supreme Court in May 1840 to overturn this judgment, claiming clerical error regarding the summons date. A supersedeas was granted while the case was under review. During the December term of 1841, Ewbanks’ attorney submitted an affidavit clarifying that the omission was indeed a mistake by the clerk, which had not been discovered until November 1841. Subsequently, the Circuit Court allowed the summons to be amended to reflect the correct date. Upon review, the Supreme Court was presented with the amended record. In December 1842, McDougall, representing the plaintiffs in error, moved for a judgment for costs against the defendant, but this motion was ultimately overruled.	The plaintiff, William Ewbanks, argued that the default judgment against Ellis and Adair was valid despite the clerical error associated with the summons date. He maintained that the case should proceed according to the amended record, which reflected corrections regarding the issuance of the summons.	The defendants, Ellis and Adair, contested the validity of the original judgment by highlighting the clerical error that led to confusion over the summons' date. They sought to reverse the default judgment, claiming that they were subjected to an unjust ruling based on a mistake that affected their ability to respond to the charges properly.

In the case of *Helen S. Brown v. Peter P. Keller*, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1865, the dispute centers around a debt claim regarding rent in Chicago, Illinois. The plaintiff, Peter P. Keller, initiated an action of debt against the defendant, Helen S. Brown. The trial involved three counts: two for unpaid rent and one for use and occupation of premises. The jury reached a verdict finding the amount of rent due to be $222.40. However, the defendant, Brown, challenged the judgment, asserting that the verdict was improperly framed, claiming that it presented an action for assumpsit instead of debt. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court on a writ of error, wherein it was argued that the judgment was erroneous due to this alleged misclassification of the nature of the action taken.	The plaintiff, Peter P. Keller, contended that significantly overdue rent was owed by the defendant, Helen S. Brown, due to her occupation of the premises. He sought a judgment for the amount found due by the jury, totaling $222.40, along with associated costs. Keller maintained that despite the informal phrasing of the verdict, it effectively responded to the issue of debt presented in the case.	The defendant, Helen S. Brown, claimed that the verdict delivered by the jury and the corresponding judgment issued by the lower court were incorrectly characterized as pertaining to debt when they were in fact in assumpsit. She argued that this mischaracterization rendered both the verdict and the judgment erroneous, as they failed to adhere to the required legal definitions and forms for actions related to debt. Brown insisted that this procedural flaw warranted a reversal of the judgment.

Timothy Wright filed a case against The City of Chicago in September 1871, after a special assessment warrant was issued for improvements on a section of West Randolph Street. The assessment was levied based on an ordinance that required the street to be curbed and improved under the supervision of the board of public works. This ordinance mandated curbing where it was not already built and where conditions were unsatisfactory. Wright, as the property owner affected by this assessment, contested the validity of the ordinance, arguing that it improperly vested discretionary powers in the board of public works which should have resided solely with the common council. The case was appealed from the Superior Court of Cook County, presided over by Judge Joseph E. Gaey.	Wright claimed that the ordinance under which the assessment was imposed was void since it improperly conferred decision-making authority to the board of public works rather than the common council. He argued that the ordinance failed to follow proper legal procedures, which adversely affected his property rights, leading him to seek a judgment against the assessment.	The City of Chicago, represented by Corporation Counsel M.F. Tuley, defended the validity of the ordinance stating that it was a lawful exercise of municipal authority to improve public streets. They contended that the decision regarding necessary improvements fell within the rights of the city government under existing laws and that the special assessment was justified as a means to fund imperative municipal improvements.

The case "The People of the State of Illinois v. William F. Tompkins et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874. The plaintiffs, representing the state, initiated this action against William F. Tompkins, who served as the chief grain inspector for the city of Chicago, along with his sureties, for failing to remit funds he had collected in his official capacity. Tompkins was appointed to his position in July 1871 and executed a bond for $50,000, ensuring he would faithfully perform his duties. Upon his removal from office in April 1873, Tompkins retained $1,666.98, which the state argued he was obligated to hand over to his successor, William H. Harper. The issues at the heart of the case revolved around the duties expected from Tompkins as chief inspector and the implications for the sureties related to his bondsman duties at the time the bond was executed.	The plaintiffs contended that Tompkins had failed to deliver the funds collected for grain inspection to his successor, contravening the obligations of his official bond. They argued that the bond's condition imposed liability for any damages stemming from his failure to comply with state regulations regarding the inspection of grain. The plaintiffs sought recovery of the $1,666.98 he failed to pay over, asserting a right to enforce the bond against Tompkins and his sureties for this amount.	The defendants, including Tompkins and his sureties, argued that the bond did not explicitly impose the duty of collecting and custody of the funds on Tompkins at the time it was executed. They maintained that since the legal framework establishing such duties was adopted after the bond was signed, the sureties could not be held responsible for Tompkins' actions regarding the funds he had collected, as these duties were not known to them at the time of the bond's execution.

The case "Chicago Forge and Bolt Company v. Alfred Major" took place in Illinois, with the decision rendered on February 13, 1889. The conflict arose between the Chicago Forge and Bolt Company (the defendant) and Alfred Major (the plaintiff) regarding damages allegedly caused to Major's property due to the operation of the company's bridge works. The American Bridge Company originally established a works site in 1871, which included two steam trip hammers, situated on a tract of land near Chicago. Major purchased the property in 1881, where he later constructed a dwelling. The hammer shop was moved closer to Major's residence in 1885, and six steam trip hammers began operation in November 1886. Major claimed that emissions from the works, including gas, smoke, and vibrations from the operation of the machinery, caused significant damage to his property and health, producing discontent and discomfort. Major filed the lawsuit claiming damages on multiple counts relating to personal health effects and diminished property values due to the operations of the defendant's facility.	Alfred Major, the plaintiff, claimed that the Chicago Forge and Bolt Company's operations produced harmful emissions affecting his health and damaging his property. He sought compensation for the physical injury and annoyance experienced due to noxious substances, vibrations, and disruptions resulting from the operation of the trip hammers. His lawsuit included claims for reduced rental and selling values of his property, asserting that these operational nuisances hindered the enjoyment and benefit he could derive from his premises.	The Chicago Forge and Bolt Company contended that any claims regarding damages were barred by the statute of limitations as they related to past operations. The defendant also argued that Major had not proven actual damages to his property, asserting that the operation of the machinery did not diminish the market value of the premises. The defendant requested jury instructions that emphasized the requirement for evidence of depreciation in property value linked to the company's works, maintaining that any increase in value should negate claims for damages.

The case, "The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. v. Board of Education," originated in the late 19th century in Collinsville, Illinois. The proceedings began on January 4, 1888, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The plaintiff, Frank B. Lemen, sought a mandamus to compel the Board of Education to enroll his two children in the Webster School rather than the Clay School located in their designated sub-district. The sequence of events unfolded as follows: In March 1885, the Board established sub-districts, including one in which Lemen resided. By October 1885, the Board had a suitable school building ready at the Clay School for the children to attend. However, Lemen chose to send his children to the Webster School while staying with relatives in Collinsville. On the first day of the school term in September 1886, the children were placed at the Webster School without the Board's knowledge. The Board soon learned of this and ordered the principal to remove the children from Webster and assign them to the Clay School, based on sub-district regulations and overcrowding in Webster. Lemen sought to challenge this order, claiming the route to the Clay School was unsafe and arguing that his children had a right to attend the Webster School due to their brief enrollment there and his prior arrangements. However, the Board maintained that its decision was reasonable and necessary. The case hinged on issues of jurisdiction, the reasonableness of the Board's regulations, and Lemen's claims about the dangers associated with the route to the Clay School.	Frank B. Lemen, the plaintiff, claimed that his two children should be allowed to attend the Webster School instead of the Clay School. He argued that the route to the Clay School was hazardous and detrimental to his children's health. Additionally, he contended that because he had arranged for the children to stay in Collinsville and had briefly enrolled them at the Webster School, they had acquired a right to continue attending that school.	The Board of Education defended its decision by asserting its authority to define sub-districts and assign students accordingly. They contended that the designated school in the Clay sub-district was well-equipped to accommodate the children and that the claimed dangers of the route to the Clay School were exaggerated. The Board argued that its regulations were reasonable given the circumstances, including overcrowding at the Webster School.

The case, "The Commissioners of Highways of the Town of Ross, in Vermilion County, v. The Supervisors of the Towns of Newell, Blount and Grant," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1870, following an appeal from the Circuit Court of Vermilion County. The case arose when the town of Ross's highway commissioners ordered the opening of a road, which prompted an appeal to the supervisors of neighboring towns. A.J. Miller appealed the commissioners' decision, claiming that insufficient damages had been awarded for the opening of the road. The supervisors were initially brought into the matter to review the appeal submitted by Miller, but their jurisdiction was contested due to alleged deficiencies in the appeal's documentation. Specifically, it was argued that the appeal was not formally addressed to the town clerk as required by the relevant statutes. Despite these objections, the court concluded that the initial appeal, although somewhat informal, met the essential criteria set out in the law. Therefore, the circuit court dismissed the writ of certiorari, and the commissioners subsequently appealed this dismissal.	The plaintiffs, The Commissioners of Highways of the Town of Ross, claimed that the appeal filed by A.J. Miller was invalid due to its informal nature and alleged failure to meet the statutory requirements for appeals from highway commissioners. They argued that no proper appeal was taken, thus the supervisors had no jurisdiction over the matter. The plaintiffs sought to uphold the original decision of the highway commissioners and argued for the dismissal of Miller's appeal.	The defendants, The Supervisors of the Towns of Newell, Blount, and Grant, contended that they had the jurisdiction to review Miller's appeal despite the claimed informalities in the documentation. They argued that the appeal complied with the essential requirements under the township organization law, and that any deficiencies did not affect their jurisdiction. The supervisors maintained that once the appeal was filed, they acquired the authority to assess the matter, regardless of the formal details of how the appeal was articulated.

The case "Robert J. Cassell v. Elisha Williams" took place in Woodford County, Illinois, and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1851. The background of the case involves a trespass action initiated by Elisha Williams against Robert J. Cassell, who was acting as a constable. The dispute arose after Cassell seized a mare from Williams in connection with an execution against him. The seizure occurred on March 11, 1850, following an execution issued on January 24, 1850. Williams had previously notified Cassell that he claimed the mare as exempt from execution. Before the trial over the right of property, Williams disclaimed any ownership of the mare, stating that it belonged to a third party, George Kingston, from whom he had taken it under a forfeited mortgage. Despite this, Cassell proceeded to sell the mare. In the subsequent trial, Williams argued that the sale was wrongful since he had limited property worth less than $25, thus claiming the mare was exempt from execution under the law. The Circuit Court ruled against Cassell, requiring him to pay Williams three-times the value of the mare, which was appraised at $33. However, subsequent legal proceedings questioned the legitimacy of Williams' ownership claim.	Elisha Williams, the plaintiff, argued that his mare was wrongfully seized and sold by Cassell, who was acting in his capacity as a constable. Williams contended that he had claimed the mare as exempt from execution, asserting he had very limited property beyond household necessities. He sought to recover three times the value of the mare, alleging that his property was wrongfully taken as it was exempt under execution laws.	Robert J. Cassell, the defendant, maintained that Williams did not have ownership rights to the mare at the time of the seizure, as he had previously disclaimed ownership during the trial of right of property. Cassell argued that the judgment regarding the property’s status did not automatically confer ownership to Williams, and emphasized that the legal process should reflect that specter. Cassell sought to have the judgment against him overturned, asserting that he should not be liable for claims when the understanding of ownership was not consistent with the established legal framework.

Frank S. Weigley filed a case against Canute R. Matson and others in the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision rendered on May 9, 1888. The case arose after Weigley obtained a judgment against a debtor named Sea and subsequently levied execution against Sea's property. Weigley sought to annul prior judgments and executions granted to other creditors of Sea, aiming to prioritize his claim. The contested judgments had been entered by confession, with no allegations of fraud or collusion against them. Weigley argued that the underlying judgments had been irregularly entered, asserting that the court was not in session at the time the judgments were supposedly entered. This case involved substantial legal intricacies around the validity of court judgments and the rights of creditors.	Weigley contended that the prior judgments against his debtor, Sea, were improperly entered because they were supposedly done outside of court sessions and without proper procedures. He sought relief by asking the court to vacate these prior judgments to give priority to his execution against Sea's property.	The defendants argued that the record of the contested judgments, which indicated they had been entered in open court, was conclusive evidence of their validity and could not be contradicted by oral evidence. They maintained that the alleged irregularities did not undermine the legitimacy of the judgments, emphasizing that execution can be valid even if the record has not been formally written up at the time of issuance.

On February 5, 1872, in Coles County, Illinois, a trespass lawsuit was brought by Hannah Haskins against Lowry Haskins and William M. Herron. Hannah, a married woman with two small children and in the late stages of pregnancy, was residing peacefully in her home when she was forcibly evicted by a group led by a constable named Curry. This group, comprising nine men, entered her home under the pretext of removing her belongings, despite adverse weather conditions and her health issues. The situation escalated to the point where Hannah was subjected to a non-consensual physical examination, and her possessions were carelessly removed, resulting in damage to her property. The next day, she was taken from her bed and transported three miles to her father’s house in severe cold. The actions of the defendants were alleged to have caused her significant mental and physical harm, and she sought damages for this unlawful eviction.	Hannah Haskins claimed she was unlawfully evicted from her home without consent or legal justification, while being in peaceful possession. She argued that the defendants, Haskins and Herron, acted in collusion to violate her rights and that their actions constituted trespass and assault. She requested damages for the mental and physical suffering caused by the eviction, resulting in a judgment of $1,000.	The defendants argued that their actions were justified under a writ of restitution stemming from a judgment against Hannah's husband in a prior forcible detainer action. They contended that they were acting under this judgment and that any eviction, albeit forceful, was lawful under the circumstances. They also cited procedural errors during the trial and contested the sufficiency of the plaintiff's evidence to support her claims.

In October 1870, George Baugh obtained a judgment against Alexander D. Hay in the Marion Circuit Court. An execution was issued that resulted in the sheriff seizing real estate in the town of Centralia, specifically two lots: lot 2 in block 27 and lot 4 in block 50. Due to a lack of bids, both lots were ultimately sold together for $627.99 to Baugh on February 25, 1871. Hay claimed that lot 2 was part of his homestead, thereby exempt from sale, as he lived with his family on lot 1, which was valued significantly higher than $1000. In July 1871, Hay sold lot 2 to William S. Hay (the plaintiff). However, Baugh conveyed the same lot to John Merklebach on February 1, 1873, after receiving the sheriff's deed. Hay argued that the amalgamation of the properties during the sale was improper and that he had other real estate which could have been sold first. Ultimately, the court held that lots 1 and 2 were separate legal entities, and since Hay did not demonstrate that the sale was illegal or that he had other properties available for sale, his claims would not stand.	William S. Hay, as the plaintiff, sought to set aside the sheriff's sale of lot 2, claiming it was part of his homestead and thus exempt from levy and sale. He argued the illegality of a combined sale of two distinct parcels and requested injunction relief to cancel the sheriff's deed and secure his rights to the property.	The defendants, represented by Baugh and Merklebach, contended that the sale was valid as lot 2 was not part of Hay's legal homestead and therefore not exempt from execution. They maintained that Hay had ample opportunity to contest the sale before the redemption period expired but failed to do so. Therefore, they argued he could not retroactively seek to annul the sale without demonstrating fraud or significant injustice.

The case, "William F. Weld et al. v. James H. Rees," was filed in April 1867 in the Superior Court of Chicago, Illinois. The dispute revolves around a property located in Chicago that was sold under a mortgage and deed of trust. The defendant, James H. Rees, had originally obtained a mortgage from Richard L. Swift in December 1854, securing a debt of $5,000 with the property as collateral. Subsequently, in March 1862, the trustees sold the property to William H. Brooks, acting as an agent for Weld, for $4,000 at a public auction. The sale was executed following notice published in a local newspaper. The defendant struggled to pay his debts and later attempted to redeem the property by paying the owed amount, leading to the present legal action. The court previously determined that Rees, the defendant, had the right of redemption and ruled that the quit-claim deed to Bronson was void, a decision which was subsequently appealed by Weld and associates to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs, Weld and others, argued that the notice of sale was insufficient, as it did not meet the terms specified in the deed of trust regarding the publication period. They claimed that the sale was made at too low a price and sought to have the sale set aside. Additionally, they contested the defendant's right to redeem the property, asserting that he was estopped from asserting a claim to it because he executed a quit-claim deed to Bronson.	The defendant, Rees, contended that the requirements for notice were satisfactorily met and that the sale price was not so inadequate as to constitute fraud. He argued that the terms of the sale were legally binding and that his previous quit-claim deed had effectively transferred his interest in the property. He sought confirmation that the sale was valid and that he was barred from redeeming the property due to the prior agreement.

William S. Maus, acting as the treasurer of Tazewell County, engaged in a legal dispute with the Logansport, Peoria and Burlington Railroad and its co-owners—Charles L.
