Frost, Edward Weston, and Henry G. Marquand—over unpaid taxes. This case unfolded in Tazewell County, Illinois, starting with the filing of a bill in chancery on August 17, 1861. The conflict centered upon Maus's authority to remove the railway's iron rails from the track due to taxes amounting to $2,157.67, which had not been paid for multiple years. The railroad, a vital transportation line for freight and mail, claimed that Maus's actions were illegal, lacked authority, and would harm operations. The Circuit Court agreed upon a statement of facts, detailing the railroad's established operations and the refusal of its representatives to pay the taxes owed. The court was tasked with deciding whether Maus had the legal right to take the rails under Illinois law, especially given that the railroad had no personal property to seize for tax collection. The case posed significant implications regarding taxation law and the rights of railroad companies in the state, particularly after amendments that altered the definition of railroad property in terms of taxation.	The plaintiff, William S. Maus, asserted that he had the authority as treasurer and ex-officio collector of Tazewell County to collect unpaid taxes by removing the railroad's iron rails. He argued that the railroad was liable for taxes assessed on its fixed and stationary personal property and that his actions were within legal bounds. He sought an injunction against the railroad's claims, which he alleged were improperly hindering his ability to collect debts owed to the county.	The defendants contended that the removal of the rails by Maus was illegal and without proper authority under state law, which grants certain protections to property that serves public functions, such as railroads. They argued that the taxes on the railroad's fixed and stationary property should allow for collection through different means rather than disassembling crucial public infrastructure. They sought to have the injunction against Maus's actions made permanent.

Charles M. Chadwick (plaintiff) and John Parker (defendant) were involved in a legal dispute over the possession of a house in Chicago stemming from a lease agreement dated March 7, 1865. The lease was for five years, commencing July 5, 1865, with a monthly rent of $541.66. Chadwick defaulted on several rent payments, and in March 1866, Parker notified him that the lease was terminated due to these defaults and instructed him to vacate the premises within ten days. The case began in a justice of the peace court in Cook County and was subsequently appealed to the Superior Court of Chicago. At the trial, Chadwick's attempts to present evidence of his readiness to pay the overdue rent were rejected, and the jury found in favor of Parker, leading to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Chadwick argued that he never received a proper demand for the overdue rent on the specified day and claimed his readiness to pay should negate the forfeiture of the lease. He sought to contest the legality of Parker’s termination of the lease and regain possession of the property.	Parker maintained that the lease allowed him to terminate it due to Chadwick's failure to pay rent on time. He argued that the legal requirements for terminating the lease had been met, including proper notice of termination and that Chadwick failed to pay the overdue rent within the ten-day notice period.

George W. Carter and Benjamin C. Bradley entered into a partnership to carry out farming operations on a tract of land located in Champaign County, Illinois. Disputes arose between the partners regarding their respective claims and interests in the property, which led to the filing of a lawsuit by Carter against Bradley. Carter's lawsuit aimed to compel Bradley to execute a deed for a specific quarter section of land that was part of their partnership agreement. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1871, which noted that the partnership's accounts had never been fully adjusted, resulting in unresolved claims of significant amounts. The court determined that the earlier ruling that favored Bradley, which mandated a deed transfer upon payment to Carter for the land, was erroneous because it neglected the necessary adjustment of all partnership matters and claimed equities before determining the rightful ownership of the land.	The plaintiff, George W. Carter, argued that he was entitled to a deed for the quarter section of land based on the partnership agreement he had with Benjamin C. Bradley. He sought to enforce the execution of this deed and claimed that he was entitled to be reimbursed for the purchase price of the land along with additional costs incurred for improvements made on the property. Carter asserted that due to the unresolved partnership disputes and the complexity of their financial relations, the court should properly investigate all equities before ruling on the land's ownership.	Benjamin C. Bradley, the defendant, contended that the court's decree mandating him to execute a deed was inappropriate and that the obligations concerning the partnership accounts required adjustment first. He argued that the court had erred by not addressing the financial disputes and claims arising from their partnership prior to determining rights to the land. Bradley maintained that all aspects of their partnership and its financial implications needed to be thoroughly evaluated before any conveyance of property could be confirmed.

On January 16, 1862, in Quincy, Illinois, Thomas Jasper filed a chancery bill to foreclose a mortgage executed by the Quincy English and German Seminary on a parcel of land. The mortgage was originally executed on July 11, 1861, as security for notes held by James F. Jaquess, who later transferred them to Jasper. Harrison Dills, who also held a mortgage on the same property, was named as a defendant, along with others involved in a cross-bill filed by Dills. By October 1862, the court decreed the mortgage foreclosed, allowing the master in chancery to sell the property if payment was not received within seventy days. A sale was conducted on August 15, 1863, where the master accepted a bid of $22,000 from Jaquess, who subsequently failed to comply. The master then resold the property to Porter Smith for $15,600. The president and trustees of the seminary sought damages from Jaquess for his failure to honor his bid, arguing that this left them at a disadvantage compared to the second sale price. The case raised significant issues regarding the rights and liabilities of bidders in masters' sales and their responsibilities following defaults.	The plaintiffs, represented by the Quincy English and German Seminary and Dills, argued that Jaquess should be held liable for the difference between his initial bid of $22,000 and the sale price of $15,600 after the resale. They contended that Jaquess's failure to fulfill his purchase obligation caused a significant financial loss. They requested a decree from the court to ensure Jaquess compensated them for the loss, considering his refusal to pay and lack of assets to cover the damages.	The defendant, Jaquess, asserted that his bid was not valid as the sale was not confirmed by the court, thereby discharging him from any obligations. He argued that the subsequent resale effectively negated his bid and any liability to the plaintiffs. Additionally, it was contended that the plaintiffs sustained no damage since they had the option to redeem their property by paying the remaining mortgage debt. The defense emphasized procedural issues surrounding the initial sale and the lack of formal confirmation from the court.

In September 1875, the legal case "Henry Muller et al. v. John B. Inderreiden et al." took place in the Illinois Supreme Court, which stemmed from a prior judgment made in December 1873 in the Superior Court of Cook County. The key individuals involved were plaintiffs John B. and August Inderreiden, and defendants Henry Muller and Caroline Muller. The plaintiffs had previously won a judgment against Henry Muller for $540.70 in damages, which he failed to pay. Following this, an execution was issued for the collection of the debt, but the sheriff could not find property to satisfy the judgment. The only property identified was a lot in Chicago, which was claimed by Caroline Muller as her sole and separate property. The plaintiffs alleged that this conveyance was a fraudulent attempt to hide assets from creditors and that the property should rightly belong to Henry Muller since it was paid for with his funds. The court had to determine the ownership and whether the property could be sold to satisfy the plaintiffs' claims, ultimately finding that the property was subject to the plaintiffs' judgment.	The plaintiffs claimed that the property in question, a lot and buildings in Chicago, should be considered the property of Henry Muller as it was purchased with his funds despite being titled in the name of his wife, Caroline. They argued that the transfer of the property to her was fraudulent, aiming to place it beyond the reach of Henry's creditors. They requested that the court decree the lot as property subject to their execution order for the satisfaction of their judgment.	The defendants did not actively contest the charges as they filed a default. However, it was implied in their defense that Caroline Muller had a legitimate claim to the property, asserting her right as it was titled in her name. They maintained that the property was their homestead and that it should be protected from execution based on homestead rights under the law, which they claimed was not addressed appropriately by the plaintiffs' accusations.

The case "Walter S. Hurd v. Ed. Ascherman et al." was decided on March 27, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Knox County, where the plaintiffs, Ed. Ascherman and Herman Signitz, who were judgment creditors of Leander B. Beynolds, sought to challenge conveyances made by Beynolds before he faced financial difficulties. They claimed these conveyances were fraudulent and intended to hinder the ability of Beynolds' creditors to recover their debts. The plaintiffs included Hurd due to his interest in land conveyed by Beynolds. Initially, the Circuit Court dismissed the plaintiffs' bill regarding two tracts of land and granted Hurd relief on a cross-bill regarding the property conveyed to him. On appeal, questions related to the validity of these conveyances became center stage. The plaintiffs alleged that a chattel mortgage from Beynolds to Hurd was fraudulent since it was made while Beynolds was nearly insolvent. The court determined that Hurd’s judgment against Beynolds was fraudulent towards the creditors, and hence the assets and sums realized under that judgment were held in trust for the complainants.	The plaintiffs claimed that several transactions, including a chattel mortgage from Beynolds to Hurd and a judgment favoring Hurd, were fraudulent and aimed at defrauding creditors. They maintained that the judgment and mortgage were executed without adequate consideration and were part of a scheme to conceal assets from creditors. As such, they sought to have these transactions set aside and declared void, demanding equitable relief that would consider their claims against Beynolds' assets.	Hurd defended against the plaintiffs’ claims by asserting that the judgment he obtained was legitimate and based on legitimate debts owed to him by Beynolds. He denied any fraudulent intent or collusion in the conveyance of the property and the chattel mortgage. Hurd contended that the mortgage was valid and not merely a cover-up, arguing that he had acted lawfully in his dealings with Beynolds.

In 1881, The People of the State of Illinois initiated legal action against The Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company. The case arose from allegations related to unjust freight charges. The railway operated a line running from Peoria, Illinois, to New York City, New York, with a segment passing through Gilman, Illinois. It was claimed that the railway company charged different rates for transporting the same type of freight over differing distances. Specifically, the railway charged $39 for transporting corn from Peoria to New York (a longer route), while charging $65 for a shorter distance from Gilman to New York for similar freight. The plaintiffs argued that this constituted an unjust discrimination in violation of state law. The case was brought to the Illinois Supreme Court, where a key issue was whether state law governed rates for freight that also involved interstate transportation. The lower court had sustained a demurrer regarding these claims, prompting the appeal.	The plaintiffs argued that the Wabash railway made unjust discriminations in its freight rates, charging a lower rate for a longer distance (Peoria to New York) while imposing a higher rate for a shorter distance (Gilman to New York) for the same class of freight. They sought to have the court recognize this discrimination as a violation of Illinois law and demanded compensation of $5,000 for the unfair practices, arguing that the rates were contrary to state statutes concerning fair transportation practices.	The defendant contended that the state law could not apply to transportation charges for freight that involved movement out of Illinois, asserting that such regulation would conflict with federal power to regulate interstate commerce. They argued that the differentiation in charges was permissible under the law and that the case should be dismissed as the statute purportedly did not govern transactions involving inter-state shipping, thus protecting the railway's pricing practices.

The case "The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company v. Mahan and Hunt" took place in April 1866 in Illinois. The plaintiffs, Mahan and Hunt, initiated an action against the Chicago and Alton Railroad Company for the destruction of goods caused by fire that spread from one of the railway company’s locomotives. A central issue during the trial was whether the goods belonged to both Mahan and Hunt collectively or solely to Hunt. To prove their joint ownership, the plaintiffs were allowed to present declarations confirming their partnership. However, the defendants sought to introduce evidence of an earlier lawsuit by Hunt against the railroad company regarding the same goods, which represented an assertion by Hunt of individual ownership. The trial court did not permit this evidence, and the case hinged on whether this was a procedural error.	Mahan and Hunt claimed that they were partners and therefore collectively owned the goods destroyed by the fire. They sought to recover the total value of these goods from the railroad company, claiming that the company was responsible for the destruction due to negligence.	The Chicago and Alton Railroad Company argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiffs regarding their partnership was insufficient. They insisted that Hunt's prior lawsuit claiming ownership of the goods individually should have been admissible evidence, as it contradicted the partnership claims made by the plaintiffs. The defendants maintained that this evidence proved that there was no partnership regarding the ownership of the goods.

George Wright initiated a legal case against Carlos Lattin and others in the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1865. The case revolves around a property dispute in De Kalb County, stemming from a contract entered into on August 17, 1858, between Clark Wright and the De Kalb County Agricultural Society. The Society had leased premises for conducting annual fairs and exhibitions for a term of ten years and two months, including provisions for maintaining structures and fences. After Joseph Wright adopted this lease agreement in 1861, he and his agents allegedly damaged the Society's property by tearing down fences, damaging buildings, and using the land for livestock, which rendered it unfit for its intended use. The defendants claimed their actions were lawful and necessary due to the actions of Joseph Wright, who, they argued, effectively evicted the Society and voided their leasehold rights. The case exhibits complex issues of landlord-tenant relations, particularly concerning the definition of eviction and tenant rights under a lease.	The plaintiff, George Wright, claimed that the defendants broke and entered his property, removing fences and buildings unlawfully. He argued that the defendants had acted without legal authority, infringing upon his rights as the owner of the premises. Wright sought damages for the removal of property and injury to the estate, asserting that the defendants were responsible for restoring the premises to their original condition.	The defendants, led by Carlos Lattin, countered the plaintiff’s claims by asserting a special plea that the actions taken were lawful. They argued that they were acting under the lease agreement established by the De Kalb County Agricultural Society, stipulating their rights to manage and ultimately remove improvements from the property after the lease term. They contended that the actions of Joseph Wright, who previously claimed ownership, amounted to an eviction of the tenant (the Society) and justified their removal of the structures, thereby nullifying the plaintiff's claims.

McHenry Brooks brought a replevin action against James H. Record in January 1868. The case originated in Coles County, Illinois, where Brooks claimed ownership of a mare that Record had taken. Brooks purchased the mare from the true owner, Asa Lanick, on December 1, 1866, with the price set by Jesse Cooper, who was aware of a mortgage on the mare but did not disclose it during the sale. After the sale, the mare was intended to be delivered to Brooks but was instead taken by Record, who acted on behalf of Huffman, to whom Cooper had assigned the mortgage. There were multiple attempts to retrieve the mare, and on December 5, 1866, Record forcibly took possession from Brooks’ agent, Husely. The court was then tasked with determining the rightful ownership of the mare.	Brooks asserted that he rightfully owned the mare as he purchased it from Lanick with the presence of the mortgagee, Cooper, who failed to disclose the mortgage at the time of the sale. He argued that he had made a complete and lawful purchase with proper delivery, thus claiming the mare legally.	Record, representing Huffman, claimed that as the assignee of the mortgage, he had the right to the mare despite Brooks' claims. He argued that since the mortgage was not disclosed during the transaction, and because he acted to reclaim it, Brooks had no legal standing to maintain possession of the mare.

In the case of William McFarlane v. John Pierson, adjudicated in December 1886 by the Illinois Appellate Court, the dispute arises from a landlord-tenant relationship concerning a farm in Jackson Township, Will County, Illinois. McFarlane (the appellee) had entered a written lease agreement on March 3, 1885, granting him rights to parts of the property, including use of a house room, kitchen, orchard, and a specified share of the produce. The lease required McFarlane to maintain certain responsibilities, including some repairs and shared labor on the farm. McFarlane moved onto the premises on March 5, 1885, alongside his wife and other workers. However, dissatisfaction grew, and after completing two months of work, McFarlane abandoned the property. He argued that he was effectively evicted, claiming wrongful acts by Pierson (the appellant) as cause for his abandonment. Pierson contended that McFarlane left without legal excuse and was not entitled to recovery for his labor, leading to the case being appealed after varying verdict results in lower courts.	McFarlane claimed that he was wrongfully evicted by Pierson's actions, which he argued justified abandoning the lease. He sought to recover compensation for the work and labor he performed during his tenancy, asserting that his abandonment was a result of Pierson's failure to fulfill certain obligations under the lease, which amounted to an unlawful eviction.	Pierson maintained that McFarlane had no legal justification for abandoning the premises, asserting that he left voluntarily without meeting his contractual obligations. He argued that any dissatisfaction or claims of eviction were unfounded and that McFarlane was not entitled to damages for the labor performed under the lease, as there was no wrongful eviction.

The case of Terre Haute and Indiana Railroad Co. v. Jacob Jenuine centers around an incident that occurred in the village of Greenup, Illinois, in the late 19th century. The incident involved the death of a cow after it was struck by a train operated by the Terre Haute and Indiana Railroad Co. The accident took place at a crossing on the main public highway leading into the village. Due to the configuration of the railway, there was a deep cut in the highway and a curve in the tracks that obscured the train's approach, making it difficult for both the cow and the train crew to see each other until the moment of collision. The cow was unable to see the train coming, and the engineer did not spot the cow until too late. The legal questions revolved around whether the railroad company was negligent in operating the train at a high speed and failing to give proper warning through statutory signals, and whether those actions contributed to the cow's death.	Jacob Jenuine, the plaintiff, claimed that the Terre Haute and Indiana Railroad Co. was negligent, arguing that the train was running at a dangerous speed and failed to sound the required signals, like ringing the bell or sounding the whistle, as mandated by law. He contended that these actions directly led to the death of the cow, and he sought compensation for the loss sustained due to the alleged negligence of the railroad company.	The defendant, Terre Haute and Indiana Railroad Co., argued that there was no negligence on their part. They contended that the engineer could not have seen the cow before the collision due to the obstructed view created by the train's construction and the terrain. Furthermore, they asserted that even if the train had been going faster or slower, the cow's behavior and the circumstances of the accident would not have changed, indicating no negligence regarding speed or failure to give signals. The defendant requested that the court dismiss the claims made by the plaintiff based on the lack of evidence supporting negligence.

On July 24, 1888, in Mason County, Illinois, the Chicago & Alton Railroad Company was operating a northbound passenger train between Greenview and Mason City. The railroad track was properly fenced as per legal requirements. Early that morning, due to a negligence incident, an open gate left by an unknown person caused 12 to 20 horses belonging to Alfred Legg to stray onto the track. As a result, the train struck and injured 11 horses, including a pony, a mare, and a colt owned by Legg. The plaintiff, Alfred Legg, argued that the train's engineer and fireman should have seen the horses and taken action to prevent the collision, while the railroad company contended that the horses appeared suddenly on the track and that all possible measures were taken to avoid the accident. The plaintiff was awarded $205 in damages in the lower court, prompting an appeal from the railroad company.	Alfred Legg claimed that the train crew was negligent in failing to observe the horses on the track and take proper action to avoid the collision. He argued that the right of way was clear and that the train's crew should have exercised ordinary care while operating the train. Legg requested compensation for the damages incurred resulting from the death and injury of his horses, asserting liability on the part of the Chicago & Alton Railroad.	The Chicago & Alton Railroad contended that they had acted responsibly, claiming that the horses unexpectedly came onto the track. They argued that the train engineer was unable to see the horses in time due to the conditions of the landscape, which obscured the view. The railroad asserted that the engineer took all possible actions to prevent the accident once the horses were spotted. The defense also challenged the admissibility of certain evidence presented by the plaintiff and argued that they did not act negligently.

The Burlington Insurance Company, represented by appointed special agents S. M. and W. F. Johnston, engaged in a legal dispute stemming from a contract for agency services, which was originally established on November 14, 1883, and set to operate through 1884. The contract stipulated that the Johnstons would manage the insurance company's interests in Illinois, except Cook County, in return for reimbursement of specified expenses and commissions based on net premiums. Following the performance of their duties, the Johnstons requested advances from the company to pay agents and cover expenses, which they agreed to repay upon demand. However, the Johnstons accumulated more funds than permitted by the contract limits, totaling $3,000. When the company sought repayment of this balance, the Johnstons failed to comply, prompting the lawsuit. The legal proceedings centered on whether their bond to the Insurance Company also covered personal debts incurred by the Johnstons in their agency role. On November 20, 1886, the Illinois Appellate Court found that the bond only secured the Johnstons' performance of their duties and did not extend to personal debts beyond the scope of the agency contract.	The Burlington Insurance Company argued that the Johnstons were deeply indebted for funds advanced to them for expenses, which exceeded stipulated limits in their contract. They maintained that through various transactions, the Johnstons accrued a debt to the company exceeding $3,000. The company sought to recover these amounts, asserting that the contractual agreement obligated the Johnstons to repay the advances upon request, which they subsequently failed to do.	The Johnstons contested the plaintiff’s claims by asserting that the bond they executed was specifically for the performance of their duties as agents and did not cover their personal debts or loans made by the company. They contended that the expenses in question were incurred independently and thus argued that their individual obligations were not included under the bond’s terms.

Lizzie M. Chase filed a legal case against Calvin De Wolf in September 1873 in Illinois. The case originated when Chase sought a writ of replevin to regain possession of certain personal property from another individual, which had been decided upon by H. B. Boyden, a justice of the peace. The venue of the trial was later transferred to Calvin De Wolf, who ruled in favor of Chase, awarding her the property and nominal damages of one cent. However, complications arose when the constable involved made demands for illegitimate fees amounting to $85 for delivering the goods, which Chase contested as illegal. After the justice of the peace issued an execution to collect these fees, he later recalled it due to its questionable legality. Chase then petitioned the circuit court of Cook County for a writ of mandamus to compel De Wolf to issue a new execution for the costs, but the justice claimed he had no legal authority to do so. The case involved extensive legal considerations around the validity of the charges and the obligations of justices of the peace regarding legal costs.	Lizzie M. Chase contended that the justice of the peace, Calvin De Wolf, had a legal duty to issue an execution for the recovery of costs from the judgment she won in her prior case. She argued that the execution for the costs should include the fees charged by the constable, which she believed were legal, despite them being questioned by De Wolf. Chase sought a mandamus order from the court to compel De Wolf to issue the execution.	Calvin De Wolf maintained that the charges made by the constable were neither legal nor justified. He argued that the law did not authorize him to issue an execution for fees that were considered illegal and oppressive. De Wolf asserted that, as these charges were not authorized under statutory law, he was right to recall the execution and was not obliged to enforce such unjust claims.

The case "Thomas G. Allen v. John Breusing" took place in November 1863 in Illinois, specifically involving the Circuit Court of Randolph County. The key individuals involved were Thomas G. Allen, the plaintiff acting as a sutler for the 80th Regiment of Illinois Volunteer Infantry, and John Breusing, the defendant and colonel of the same regiment. The background of the case pertains to Allen issuing checks to the soldiers in exchange for goods, resulting in a debt of $500. Allen requested Breusing to guarantee these payments in exchange for an extension on a $300 due bill between them. Subsequently, Breusing had to pay $350 of Allen's debt to the soldiers, which Allen failed to repay. Allen's complaint included a special count upon the due bill and common counts for goods sold and money lent. The court below sustained a demurrer against Breusing's special plea, which aimed to claim a defense based on payment, leading to this appeal.	The plaintiff, Thomas G. Allen, contended that the defendant's special plea did not adequately address the entire declaration as it only responded to the first count regarding the due bill. Essentially, Allen argued that Breusing's plea of payment was insufficient and raised specific objections, including the lack of a clear timeline for the extension of the due bill and its categorization as neither a set-off nor accord and satisfaction.	The defendant, John Breusing, presented a special plea claiming that he guaranteed Allen's payment to the soldiers in exchange for an extension on the due bill. He argued that his payment of $350 was a direct consequence of his guaranty, making it a substantial plea of payment that should affect the judgment. Breusing contended that the lower court erred in sustaining the demurrer and that his plea properly addressed part of Allen's claims regarding the due bill debt.

The case involves D. Theodore Merritt as the appellant against Philander G. Merritt and others as appellees, taking place in Cook County, Illinois. The background involves a foreclosure suit that had been pending for almost five years and was called for trial on June 24, 1887. On that day, the appellant's solicitor was not present, leading to the court's dismissal of the suit due to lack of prosecution. The solicitor for the appellees did not inform the appellant's solicitor about the dismissal immediately, which contributed to a delay in the appellant's awareness of the case's status. The dismissal occurred, and when the appellant's solicitor later sought reinstatement of the case, the mortgage note was barred by the statute of limitations. The appellant subsequently filed a new bill to either reinstate the foreclosure suit or proceed with the mortgage foreclosure, which the court dismissed for lack of equity.	D. Theodore Merritt, the plaintiff, argued for the reinstatement of the dismissed foreclosure suit. He claimed that because the dismissal occurred during a term when the court had the authority to reverse its decisions, the original dismissal should not be considered final until the end of that term. The plaintiff sought to foreclose the mortgage and contended that he had the right to file a new suit within one year of the non-suit, as the statute’s expiration occurred while the case was still pending.	The defendants, led by Philander G. Merritt, contended that the court appropriately dismissed the foreclosure suit due to lack of prosecution and that the dismissal was indeed final once the term passed. They argued that there were no extraordinary circumstances warranting reinstatement, and that the statute of limitations barred any new efforts to foreclose the mortgage. Thus, they requested the court to uphold the dismissal and deny any requests for reinstatement.

In 1879, Daniel Welker, an employee of the Metropolitan Police Commissioners of East St. Louis, obtained a personal judgment of $25 against the commissioners for services rendered. Although an appeal was filed, it was later dismissed, and a procedendo awarded. Subsequently, an execution was placed in the hands of a constable to collect the judgment. In response, the commissioners filed a bill in chancery against Welker and the constable to prevent enforcement of the judgment. The plaintiffs claimed the Metropolitan Police Act was unconstitutional, arguing they could not be held personally liable as agents of the city for contracts made under that act. During the January term of 1885, the court made a decree that perpetuated the injunction and required costs to be paid by Welker and the constable. The court grappled with whether equitable relief could be granted in this situation, given that personal liability should have been addressed in the earlier suit.	The plaintiffs, the Metropolitan Police Commissioners, contended that they should not be held personally liable for the judgment because the act under which they operated was declared unconstitutional. They sought relief from what they considered an unjust judgment by asserting they had no authority as agents to bind the city, thus arguing that the court of equity had jurisdiction to reverse the prior decision.	The defendants, Welker and the constable, argued that the plaintiffs had a fair opportunity to present their case regarding personal liability during the previous court proceedings. They maintained that the matter had been adequately adjudicated and that the plaintiffs were responsible for claiming exemptions in garnishment proceedings, which they failed to do, resulting in the loss that they should bear.

The case "The City of Chicago v. James McGinn" occurred in September 1869 in Chicago, Illinois. At the center of the dispute was an ordinance passed by the City of Chicago's common council on April 22, 1867, which regulated the passage of vessels through the city's swing bridges over the Chicago River. The ordinance imposed requirements for vessel signals, stated prohibitions against passing bridges when signals were displayed, and stipulated that bridge tenders should allow sufficient time for vehicular passage before closing the bridge to vessels. The City of Chicago brought this action against James McGinn in the police court for a penalty alleged for violating this ordinance. The police court ruled in favor of the city, imposing a penalty under the ordinance's provisions. McGinn appealed this judgment to the superior court, where a jury found in favor of McGinn, concluding that the city's actions in closing the bridge constituted an unlawful obstruction of navigation. The case then reached the Illinois Supreme Court, where it scrutinized both the authority of the common council to create such an ordinance and the validity of the claims raised by McGinn regarding the ordinance's unconstitutionality and the potential obstruction it posed to navigation.	The City of Chicago claimed that James McGinn violated the ordinance regulating vessel passage through city bridges, specifically citing that McGinn attempted to pass a bridge while the required signals were in display. The city sought to impose penalties as specified in the ordinance, arguing that it was within their rights to regulate the navigation of vessels in accordance with the city's charter, which allowed for such ordinances to ensure orderly traffic between land and river.	James McGinn argued that the ordinance was void because the common council lacked the authority to impose such regulations. He contended that, even if the council had such authority, the ordinance constituted an unconstitutional obstruction of navigation rights. McGinn maintained that the city's ordinance improperly hindered the passage of vessels by unlawfully closing the bridges, thus making the penalties sought by the city unjustified.

The case "Alexander R. Chesnut v. Thomas J. Chesnut, Ex’r etc." was decided on October 3, 1884, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The litigation centers around a dispute between Alexander R. Chesnut, the appellant, and Thomas J. Chesnut, the executor of the estate of the deceased Alexander K. Chesnut, Sr. The case arises from financial transactions involving Alexander E. Chesnut, Sr., who had funds deposited with M. P. Ayers & Co., a banking firm. On May 31, 1880, a power of attorney was executed by the elder Chesnut, granting his son authority to manage financial transactions on his behalf. The executor is attempting to recover two specific amounts: one from a check for $659.33 made out to A. E. Chesnut, which was cashed without evidence of the appellant's involvement, and $1,612.73 from another check drawn by the testator to the appellant. The court found in favor of the executor initially, leading to the appeal from the appellant who argued the judgments were unfounded.	The plaintiff, Thomas J. Chesnut, claims that the appellant, Alexander R. Chesnut, wrongfully received sums of money intended for the estate of Alexander K. Chesnut, Sr. The executor seeks to recover a total of $2,768.66, which includes the amounts of two checks. The first check of $659.33 from Wiegand & Widmayer was claimed to have been received by the defendant, and the second check for $1,612.73 was drawn by the testator and paid to the appellant.	The defendant, Alexander R. Chesnut, argues that the trial court erred in its finding, claiming insufficient evidence supports the plaintiff's claims. He contests the legitimacy of the judgment regarding the first check, asserting that it was not proven he had possession or knowledge of it. As for the second check, the appellant contends there is no evidence that it was a loan or that the money was received for the testator's benefit, thus negating the executor's claims.

The case of John Higgins v. Bridget Halligan took place in LaSalle County, Illinois, with a decision rendered in September 1867. The plaintiff, Bridget Halligan, was the executrix of the estate of Patrick Halligan, deceased, and sued John Higgins for the use and occupation of certain premises in the city of LaSalle. Bridget claimed that John had been her tenant for several years at an annual rent of $500, which was payable quarterly. On July 11, 1866, she notified him that the tenancy would end on September 10, 1866. Furthermore, on July 17, she offered to re-let the premises at a higher rent of $700 per annum, but John failed to execute a new lease and continued to occupy the premises beyond the termination date without her consent. Halligan sued for back rent, claiming that Higgins owed her $250 for the period following the termination of the original lease. The case went through various legal challenges, including a demurrer to Higgins' defenses and ultimately ended in court with a finding that favored Halligan.	The plaintiff, Bridget Halligan, claimed that John Higgins had unlawfully retained possession of the leased premises after the termination of their tenancy on September 10, 1866. She argued that Higgins was obliged to pay rent at a new rate of $1,000 per annum due to his failure to sign a new lease after she expressed her willingness to re-let the property. Halligan sought payment for the outstanding rent, amounting to $250, along with potentially higher sums based on the renewed lease terms.	John Higgins defended himself by arguing non-assumpsit, claiming he had paid the rent due and that his obligation to pay was fulfilled with a tender of $125 prior to the lawsuit. He contended that the plaintiff's notices were inadequate to legally terminate the tenancy. Higgins also claimed that the landlord-tenant relationship had changed due to his holding over past the original lease period, implying he should not be liable for the increased rent that Halligan was claiming.

In September 1868, the case of Josiah H. Reed et al. v. Aspasia C. Noxon was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from an attachment proceeding initiated by Reed against Noxon in Marshall County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Josiah H. Reed, alleged that the defendant, Aspasia C. Noxon, had fraudulently conveyed her property with the intent to hinder and delay her creditors, as per the provisions of the act of February 13, 1865, regarding attachments in Circuit Courts. During the trial, the plaintiff's affidavit was contested by the defendant, who denied the allegations and subsequently won on the merits, with the jury returning a verdict and judgment in favor of Noxon. The case's legal specifics included discussions on the necessity of proving intent in fraudulent conveyance and the admissibility of evidence regarding claims of fraud.	The plaintiff, Josiah H. Reed, claimed that Aspasia C. Noxon had made a fraudulent conveyance of her property intended to obstruct her creditors. Reed requested the court to find in his favor by confirming the fraudulent nature of the mortgage and seeking restitution. He aimed to demonstrate that Noxon's intent was solely to hinder or delay her creditors.	The defendant, Aspasia C. Noxon, contended that the mortgage in question was not made solely with the intent to defraud creditors and argued that fraud must be proven with direct evidence rather than inferred from circumstantial evidence. Noxon maintained that the jury should not presume fraud without explicit proof and pointed out that certain evidence presented by the plaintiff was inadmissible based on procedural grounds.

The case, Benjamin F. Smith, impl'd etc., et al. v. A. C. Vanderburg, took place in 1867 in Chicago, Illinois. Abram C. Vanderburg filed an action of assumpsit against Benjamin F. Smith and other partners of the Morrell Electro Magnetic Fluid Company in the Recorder’s Court of Chicago. The action involved a promissory note dated April 19, 1866, purportedly executed by Smith and others, which was payable sixty days after issuance. The plaintiff claimed it was due to a partnership agreement and additional services provided to the company. Smith disputed that he was a partner at the time the note was executed and contended that his liability was not established. The case was eventually moved to the Circuit Court, where the plaintiff won a verdict. Following unsuccessful motions for a new trial, Smith appealed the ruling.	The plaintiff, Vanderburg, contended that Smith and the other defendants were liable under a promissory note, asserting that they had formed a partnership responsible for debts incurred by the Morrell Electro Magnetic Fluid Company. Vanderburg's claims included recovering the amount due on the note alongside common money counts for goods sold and for labor provided at the defendants' request.	Smith, the defendant, argued that he was never a partner in the firm at the time the note was executed. He maintained that the agreement did not constitute a partnership and pointed out that the partnership was effectively dissolved when the capital was withdrawn prior to the note's issuance. Smith asserted he could not be held liable, as he had not authorized the borrowing or execution of the note and that any debts incurred post-withdrawal of capital should not hold him responsible.

In 1849, in Illinois, the legal case of Adam Swartz against Thomas L. Barnes arose when Swartz, the plaintiff, sought to reverse a judgment regarding a garnishee of J. Rapplye. The case began at a justice of the peace court, and Barnes, appearing as the garnishee, answered the claims against him. A subsequent appeal led the issue to the Circuit Court, presided over by Judge Min-shall in September of the same year. During the proceedings, the parties agreed to forgo a jury trial and submitted the case to the Court instead. After considering the evidence and counsel's arguments, the Circuit Court ruled in favor of the defendant, Barnes, resulting in a judgment for costs against Swartz. Following this, Swartz filed a motion for a new trial, which was denied. Court records indicated confusion regarding the waiver of the jury trial, with affidavits suggesting Swartz believed he had not relinquished his right to a jury trial.	Adam Swartz, the plaintiff, argued that the Circuit Court incorrectly proceeded without a jury trial, which he claims he did not waive. His main legal request included a reversal of the judgment and a new trial, asserting that the court erred by discharging the garnishee without due process.	The defendant, Thomas L. Barnes, contended that both parties had waived the right to a jury trial, as indicated in the record. He maintained that the Circuit Court's proceedings were valid, asserting that the case had been properly submitted to the Court for trial and that any affidavits presented by the plaintiff could not alter the existing record.

On October 31, 1889, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed the ejectment case of Charles E. Bradish et al. v. Alexander Yocum originating from Sangamon County, Illinois. The central issue in this case involved a disputed 60-acre parcel of land located near Mud Lake, initially owned by Yocum and later sold to Ella G. Bradish through an agreement made on December 17, 1880. Yocum conveyed various portions of his land to different parties, including a deed dated November 2, 1883, through which he claimed to have transferred ownership of the 60 acres to Yocum. The court found itself interpreting competing claims regarding the meaning of the words “sold” and “conveyed” in the different deeds associated with this property. Evidence presented included testimonies about land ownership and transactions, including prior dealings and ambiguous agreements. The circuit court had ruled in favor of Yocum, leading to an appeal by the Bradishes.	The plaintiffs, Charles E. Bradish and Ella G. Bradish, claimed that the 60 acres in question were not effectively conveyed in the deed from them to Yocum. They argued that the deed should be interpreted in light of the preceding written agreement of December 17, 1880, which they contended specified what land was sold to them by Yocum. Additionally, they maintained that the wording of the deed contained latent ambiguities that justified their position, requiring the court to acknowledge those distinctions in ownership.	The defendant, Alexander Yocum, argued that the wording of the deed clearly encompassed the 60 acres as part of the conveyance. He contended that the term "sold" in the context of real estate should be considered synonymous with “conveyed,” thereby strengthening his claim. Furthermore, Yocum stated that since the plaintiffs did not present written propositions during the trial to clarify these terms, they should be precluded from arguing about the construction of the deed in the appellate court.

The case titled "Ebenezer Z. Ryan, Surviving Assignee of the Bank of Illinois, Plaintiff in Error, v. James Dunlap et al., Defendants in Error" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in November 1855. The case originated in Shawneetown, Illinois, and involved a dispute over mortgage liens. On February 19, 1840, John C. Stickney mortgaged two lots to the Bank of Illinois to secure a debt of up to $12,000, with the mortgage recorded on March 10, 1840. Stickney later conveyed the lots to E. H. Gatewood on December 29, 1840, who subsequently mortgaged the same properties for a separate obligation in 1842. Following a series of transactions, including compromised bail bonds and the assignment of mortgages, Gatewood executed a note to the bank in 1843, which was claimed to have satisfied Stickney’s original debt. However, this satisfaction lacked proper formalities. The conflict arose when Dunlap and others pursued foreclosure actions, while Ryan, as the bank's assignee, claimed priority due to the original mortgage. The validity of the mortgage release and the authority of the bank's officers, particularly the cashier, were central to the legal questions at stake.	The plaintiff, Ebenezer Z. Ryan, argued that he, as the surviving assignee of the Bank of Illinois, held a legitimate priority claim regarding the original mortgage, which they contended had not been properly discharged. Ryan contended that the actions taken by the bank's cashier and officers did not adequately follow legal protocols required for releasing a mortgage and therefore maintained that the original mortgage should still be valid.	The defendants, led by James Dunlap, contended that the original mortgage had indeed been paid off and discharged through the actions of the bank's agents. They argued that the bank’s officers had the authority to release the mortgage and that the transaction followed customary banking practices. The defendants maintained that no fraud had occurred and that the bank's management had acted within the bounds of their prescribed powers.

The case "The People ex rel. Bernard Wernsing v. Samuel Winter et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on January 25, 1886. The central issue arose over tax liabilities dating from 1870 to 1878 regarding a homestead owned by Samuel Winter in Effingham County, Illinois. Winter contested the collection of these taxes after a complex series of legal proceedings, which began when the county collector sought a judgment for the unpaid taxes. A personal judgment against Winter had previously been adjudicated in favor of the People in 1879, resulting in the sale of the property to the county due to tax delinquency. However, this sale was ultimately reversed when Ella Douthett, who had purchased the certificate of purchase, discovered she could not obtain clear title due to the property being a homestead. Following this, Douthett sought to be subrogated to the county’s rights to collect the taxes. However, by the time the collector reentered the delinquent taxes on the books in 1884, the court found that these taxes had already been paid through the earlier sale and that no further payment was due.	The plaintiff, representing the People of Illinois through Bernard Wernsing, claimed that Winter still owed the back taxes from 1870 to 1878 despite prior payments. They contended that the earlier judgment against Winter should allow them to collect the taxes again through the legal mechanism of a judgment order, essentially seeking to enforce the collection of these taxes once more based on the record of the earlier proceedings.	The defendant Samuel Winter countered the claims on several grounds: first, he argued that the taxes had already been paid and should no longer be pursued. Secondly, he indicated that there had been a prior personal judgment which had satisfied the tax obligation, and that the earlier sale of the property invalidated the tax claims brought forward. Furthermore, Winter claimed that the collection proceedings were improperly aligned with the interests of private parties, specifically Douthett, and thus lacked merit for actions in rem against his homestead.

In 1887, at Savoy station, a tragic accident occurred involving the Illinois Central Railroad Company. James A. Beer, a locomotive engineer, died after colliding with a train that was standing on the track. The collision happened while both trains were traveling in the same direction, with the forward train being notably late by approximately four hours. The case was brought to court by Sally Neer, the administratrix of Beer’s estate, seeking damages resulting from his death. The central issue revolved around whether Beer had exercised due care, as he did not become aware of the preceding train until it was too late. The railroad company argued that Beer was familiar with established safety rules requiring engineers to approach stations with vigilance, regardless of whether they were informed about the lateness of other trains. On the day of the incident, the weather conditions were inclement—rainy and foggy—potentially impairing his visibility.	The plaintiff's claims centered on alleging negligence by the Illinois Central Railroad Company, asserting that it failed to inform Beer of the lateness of the preceding train, which contributed to the accident. The plaintiff maintained that Beer was using due care in operating his train and expected safety measures to protect him against such unforeseen dangers. The lawsuit sought $5,000 in damages for Beer’s untimely death.	The defendant, Illinois Central Railroad Company, posited that they had no obligation to notify Beer about the preceding train's lateness, as per their established rules. They argued that Beer was adequately trained and knowledgeable about these safety procedures, which mandated engineers to approach stations with extreme caution at all times. It was maintained that the collision was primarily a result of Beer’s negligence for not adhering to those rules, especially under adverse weather conditions. The company's defense asserted that Beer willingly accepted the risks associated with his employment.

In June 1875, David J. Thomas, owner of a factory in Colby, Wisconsin, engaged T. M. Taylor, a general insurance agent, to procure insurance for his factory. Taylor, representing the Fame Insurance Company among others, helped Thomas complete an application for $2000 insurance on the factory, which was primarily manufacturing clothes-pins and broom-handles, with an undisclosed shingle-making operation. The application was filled out with some of its details provided by Thomas and others by Taylor. The application lacked an accurate representation of the factory, particularly regarding the shingle manufacturing department, and a necessary diagram was not prepared prior to Thomas signing the application. Following the application, the policy was issued, and after Thomas paid the premium, the factory was destroyed by fire in May 1876. The loss was initially handled by the insurance companies, but the Fame Insurance Company later declined to pay, leading Thomas to commence a lawsuit in September 1876. The case saw multiple trials and reversals in the Appellate Court, with the eventual restoration of Thomas as the plaintiff in November 1881.	Thomas claimed that the Fame Insurance Company was obliged to pay for the loss following the fire under the terms of the insurance policy. He argued that the details surrounding the application process were misrepresented by Taylor, an agent of the company, and that he himself had acted in good faith concerning the information provided about the factory.	The Fame Insurance Company contended that the policy was void due to misrepresentation and concealment of material facts regarding the risk, specifically the existence of the shingle manufacturing operation. The company also argued that the substitution of plaintiff after the one-year limitation period for filing a claim invalidated the lawsuit due to failure to meet the policy time limits for claim initiation.

In 1837, a legal dispute arose between Elias Freer and Gurdon S. Hubbard along with Henry G. Hubbard in Chicago, Illinois. The case was initially brought before a justice of the peace, where judgment was rendered against the defendants, the Hubbards. Following this, the Hubbards appealed to the Municipal Court of the City of Chicago. The appeal process required an appeal bond to be executed, which was filed in the name of the firm "Hubbard and Co." However, this bond was executed with only one seal, leading Freer to file a motion to dismiss the appeal on the basis that the bond was defective. The Hubbards attempted to counter this motion by requesting permission to amend or file a new bond, but their request was denied, and the motion to dismiss was granted.	Elias Freer, the plaintiff, claimed that the appeal bond submitted by the Hubbards was insufficient due to the absence of proper execution (only one seal being affixed rather than the required dual seals). He motioned for the dismissal of their appeal based on this defect, arguing that the law stipulates the necessity of a "good and sufficient bond" in the appeal process.	The Hubbards argued that the appeal bond was amendable and requested the court to allow them to correct the bond's execution. They maintained that the motion to dismiss should not have been granted, as the statute mandates that a party should be allowed to file a sufficient bond if their initial submission is deemed insufficient.

Nelson Perin v. Augustus A. Parker was a legal case decided on March 28, 1888, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The case originated in Cook County, Illinois. Augustus A. Parker, a commission merchant based in Chicago, engaged in a transaction on the Chicago Board of Trade on December 30, 1882, to sell 50,000 bushels of corn for Perin, who was a resident of Cincinnati, Ohio. The agreement involved the delivery of 25,000 bushels in January and another 25,000 bushels in May. After making sales, Parker requested Perin to provide margins due to rising corn prices but was repeatedly refused. When Parker sought to secure the corn in January, Perin declined to send the necessary funds. Despite multiple demands for margins, Perin's refusal persisted, leading Parker to buy in the corn to mitigate losses, which culminated in a lawsuit by Parker to recover the money he advanced along with commissions. After a jury trial, Parker received a judgment of $6,114.28, prompting Perin to appeal based on various claims of error.	The plaintiff, Augustus A. Parker, claimed that Perin had employed him as a commission merchant to sell corn and was obliged to provide funds for margin calls as dictated by the rules of the Chicago Board of Trade. Parker argued that Perin’s refusal to supply margins led to financial loss and that he should recover the amounts advanced under the common money counts, along with accrued interest.	Nelson Perin, the defendant, contended that Parker failed to establish a valid cause of action for the money he demanded, arguing that the amounts claimed were not legally due and that the advances made were not requested in a lawful manner. Perin maintained that he was not obligated to pay for margin calls, claiming that Parker had violated his duties as a commission merchant and that the demand for older margin payments was unreasonable. He requested reversal of the judgment based on these points.

Solomon Vehon v. Benjamin Lindauer et al. is a legal case that took place in Chicago, Illinois, with a decision rendered on August 3, 1887. The case arises from issues related to garnishments, where Vehon, the plaintiff, was pursuing claims against Lindauer and others. The case was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court, with Judge John P. Altgeld presiding over the matter in the Superior Court of Cook County prior to the appeal. The primary events that transpired involved a legal challenge regarding the attachment of property or funds, prompting examination and verdicts against the garnishees involved in the case. Key individuals include the plaintiff Solomon Vehon and defendant Benjamin Lindauer, with legal representation provided by the law firms of Hofheimer & Rosenberg for the appellant and Tenney, Bashpord & Tenney for the appellees.	Solomon Vehon, as the plaintiff, argued that the garnishees owed him debts that were subject to his claims due to prior agreements or obligations. He asserted that the evidence supported his position, and he sought a legal victory that would affirm the verdict against the garnishees, compelling them to satisfy the debt owed to him.	The defendants, including Benjamin Lindauer, contended that the garnishment claims presented by Vehon were not substantiated by sufficient evidence. They argued that the verdicts against the garnishees should not be upheld, as the appropriate legal standards were not met, and they requested the dismissal of the plaintiff's claims.

Alice P. Prescott filed a case against William Maxwell in 1868 in Cook County, Illinois. The case revolves around a mechanic's lien under the 1863 act. The original contractors, Clancy & Walsh, were engaged to complete a building for $3,100. They received full payment before completing the work. On October 26, 1864, Maxwell took over the plumbing work for $239. When Prescott refused to pay for this plumbing work, Maxwell filed for a mechanic's lien. The jury awarded Maxwell $286, but Prescott appealed, arguing that there should not have been interest included beyond the claimed amount and that their instructions were flawed. The case presented complex issues regarding contract completion, payment, and jurisdictional rules about mechanic's liens.	The plaintiff claimed that Maxwell performed plumbing work on her property and was entitled to payment under the mechanic’s lien statute. Prescott sought to enforce the lien despite claiming that the original contractors had been paid in full, which should prevent further claims for work done after that payment.	The defendant, William Maxwell, argued that he was entitled to the amount claimed (and additional interest) due to the nature of his work and the original contract terms. He maintained that Prescott's refusal to pay was unjust, given that he relied on the contract with Clancy & Walsh, and that Prescott had improperly modified the jury's instructions, leading to an incorrect verdict and excess judgment against him.

In the year 1834, Edward Keys owned a lot in block fifteen of Peru, La Salle County, Illinois. He died intestate, leaving a widow and children. In 1837, George W. Howe became the administrator of Keys' estate. Howe obtained a mortgage on the property from Spaulding to secure a debt of $530. After foreclosing on the mortgage, the property was sold at a sheriff’s sale in May 1840 to Jesse Williams. Williams later transferred his purchase to Crosier, who then deeded the lot to Frederick S. Day and Isaac C. Day in 1842. In 1851, a third party named Willis, having purchased the lot from Keys’ heirs through Walbridge, pursued an ejectment action against the Days and succeeded in reclaiming the property. Following this, Willis sold the lot to the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad for $1,600. Later on, the Days filed a chancery suit against Walbridge in September 1855, alleging that Walbridge’s purchase from the heirs of Keys and subsequent conveyance to Willis was fraudulent.	The plaintiffs, Frederick S. Day and Isaac C. Day, claimed that Walbridge engaged in an unconscionable act by purchasing the lot from the heirs of Keys, aware of the Days' claim to the property. They argued Walbridge's actions defeated their rights and constituted fraud, entitling them to reimbursements for their losses, specifically seeking the amount they paid for the property in the original sheriff's sale and taxes subsequently paid.	Walbridge contended that he acted within his rights in purchasing the land from the heirs, emphasizing that the administrator could not affect the title of the heirs. He argued that the title remained with the heirs despite the foreclosure and that any alleged fraud was not his responsibility. Walbridge maintained that if fraud occurred, it was against the previous purchasers, not the defendants, and sought reversal of the lower court's ruling that had found him liable to the Days for their losses.

On January 5, 1884, the Institute of the Immaculate Conception in Belleville, Illinois, was entirely consumed by a fire, resulting in the tragic loss of twenty-four inmates who perished in the blaze. Two additional individuals died from injuries sustained while attempting to escape the burning building. A coroner's jury was convened to investigate the incident, which lasted for six days and resulted in multiple verdicts concerning the cause of the fire and the identification of the victims. The jury was not sworn individually for each body but was instead sworn in groups based on classifications of the victims—identified, unidentified, and those who died by jumping. This led to a total of twenty-seven verdicts being returned. The central legal issue arose from a dispute regarding the compensation of the jury member, Jacob Bollman, for his service at the inquest. Bollman sought compensation of $156 for his six days of service, asserting he was owed payment based on the number of victims, whereas the county argued for a flat rate of $1 per day under the Fees and Salaries Act.	The plaintiff, Jacob Bollman, claimed that he was entitled to compensation at the rate of $1 per day for each of the six days he served during the coroner's inquest into the twenty-six burn victims. He contended that the language of the Fees and Salaries Act implied he should receive payment based on the individual bodies investigated, not a singular inquest. Bollman sought a total of $156, which reflected his interpretation that his compensation should be multiplied by the number of victims.	The defendant, County of St. Clair, contended that Bollman's compensation should be limited to $1 per day for the six days of jury service, irrespective of the number of bodies involved in the inquest. The county argued that the Fees and Salaries Act specifically stipulated payment for attendance at an inquest, not per body examined. They asserted that allowing Bollman's interpretation would lead to excessive and unjust financial demands on the county, potentially resulting in untenable costs in similar future cases.

In 1874, in Waverly, Morgan County, Illinois, a dispute arose involving Cleveland J. Salter (the appellant) and James Sample (the appellee). The case centers on a property transaction where Singleton purchased a lot from Salter for $150 on credit. Singleton built a small frame house on the lot, contributed partly by Salter, but later sold the house to Ranz before the purchase money became due. Ranz then sold the house to Dennis, who moved it to his own lot and made modifications to it. Salter discovered the house had been relocated and demanded its return from Sample, who had purchased it from Dennis. Salter initiated a writ of replevin to reclaim the house, asserting his ownership of the original lot. The primary legal question involved whether the house, once established on a new lot, was classified as real estate or personal property, and whether Salter could successfully reclaim it through replevin.	Salter claimed that the house was his property, as it had been constructed on his lot and subsequently removed without his consent. He argued that since there was a verbal contract for the sale of the lot, the house was permanent property affixed to his land, and thus, he was entitled to reclaim it through a writ of replevin.	Sample contended that the house had effectively become real property attached to Dennis' lot once it was moved and properly affixed there. Therefore, he argued that replevin could not be asserted for property classified as real estate. He maintained that Salter could not reclaim the building as personal property after it had been permanently fixed to another's land.

In 1871, in Belleville, Illinois, the case of Anthony S. Badgley et al. v. August Votrain involved complex familial dynamics following the death of Etienne Deshayes, who died intestate, leaving behind nine grandchildren, including August Votrain. The case arose when Votrain sought to enforce an instrument executed by Deshayes, which allegedly assigned him $12,000 worth of property (comprising $9,800 in mortgages and $2,200 in promissory notes) and gave him a share in Deshayes' estate after his death. Despite the completion of this instrument, it was established that no actual delivery of the assigned property took place, which is crucial for legally binding transfers. The case's legal implications centered on the notions of trust, assignment, and consideration, as Votrain's claim stemmed from voluntary familial relations without the transfer being executed per statutory requirements. The defendants included the other grandchildren and the administrator of the late Deshayes' estate.	August Votrain, as the plaintiff, argued that he was entitled to the $12,000 of property assigned to him by his grandfather, Etienne Deshayes, as stipulated in a written instrument. He sought a court decree for the administrator of Deshayes' estate to fulfill the transfer of this amount and to receive one-third of the remaining estate. His claims were based on the assertion that the document constituted a valid gift and trust, despite lacking formal execution according to statutory requirements.	The defendants contended that the documented assignment lacked legal enforceability due to several essential elements being incomplete. They argued that there was no actual delivery of the notes or mortgages and that the assignment was made without any valuable consideration, being purely a familial act. This inconsistency with the legal requirements for transferring promissory notes and the informal nature of the arrangement reinforced their position against the enforcement of Votrain's claims.

Louis Nichols, a landowner in St. Clair County, Illinois, executed a deed on November 17, 1885, conveying approximately 178 acres of land to his wife, Mary W. Nichols, for a purported consideration of $9,000. This case arose in the context of subsequent legal actions initiated by John Wallace and H. Seiter & Company, who were judgment creditors of Nichols. They sought to set aside the deed, alleging that it was a fraudulent conveyance aimed at hindering and delaying their ability to collect debts owed by Nichols. The plaintiffs claimed the conveyance lacked genuine consideration and was made in bad faith, asserting that the land was held in a secret trust for Nichols' benefit. The case was consolidated and tried in the Circuit Court of St. Clair County, presided over by Judge William H. Snyder. During the proceedings, it was determined that Nichols did not owe his creditors at the time of the conveyance and possessed sufficient assets to cover his debts, thus making the deed valid.	The plaintiffs, as judgment creditors, argued that Nichols' conveyance of land to his wife was fraudulent. They claimed that the deed was a sham, lacking real consideration, and designed to protect the property from being levied for the satisfaction of their judgments. The plaintiffs requested the court to set aside the deed and allow them to proceed with executing their judgments against the land, asserting that the property was effectively owned by Nichols and should be subject to their claims.	The defendants, Louis and Mary W. Nichols, contended that the conveyance was legitimate and made in good faith to establish a separate estate for Mary’s benefit. They argued that at the time of the conveyance, Nichols retained enough assets to satisfy his debts, thereby protecting the interests of his creditors. The defendants maintained that there was no fraudulent intent in the transaction and that the deed should not be set aside as it complied with legal standards regarding property conveyances between spouses.

William Bryan filed a bill for an injunction against the City of East St. Louis and its Mayor, Maurice Joyce, regarding property located in lot 79 of block 36 in Illinois City, which Bryan had owned since 1871. The case took place in 1883, and concerned Bryan's right to possess the land after the abandonment of the Collinsville Plank Road Company, which had occupied a portion of his property since 1850. Although the company had constructed a plank road diagonally across lot 79, Bryan contended that once the Plank Road Company abandoned the lot in 1879 and its charter expired in 1880, the city had no right to claim it as a public street. Bryan claimed that since March 12, 1881, city officials had removed his fences and obstructed his attempts to rebuild them, asserting a public sidewalk was planned along the site of the abandoned road. The defendants, however, argued that a public highway existed over this lot, used continuously for more than forty years, which justified their actions.	Bryan’s main argument was that he rightfully owned lot 79 and had maintained peaceful possession of it. He contended that the previous occupation by the Collinsville Plank Road Company had ended and that the City of East St. Louis had no authority to interfere with his property rights or construct a public sidewalk without proper legal condemnation. Bryan requested a permanent injunction to prevent the city from making any construction on his property.	The defendants acknowledged tearing down Bryan's fence and intended to construct a sidewalk, but claimed that lot 79 was a public highway due to long-standing usage. They argued that there existed a legal prescriptive right to maintain a public road over the lot, thus justifying their interference with Bryan's possession. They asserted that the court lacked jurisdiction to restrain their actions because there was a complete legal remedy available to Bryan.

Thomas Richter filed a legal case against William Schroeder and certain insurance companies concerning a dispute over insurance payments due under a mortgage made by Schroeder. This case was situated in Illinois and was heard by the Illinois Supreme Court, with a decision rendered on May 19, 1884. The dispute arose from an agreement whereby a receiver was appointed to manage the insurance claims related to the mortgaged property, and H.H. Anderson was employed as the receiver’s attorney to initiate lawsuits against the insurance companies. Following significant litigation, Anderson presented a petition to the court requesting compensation for his legal services and expenses incurred, amounting to $1,007.10. The court, upon reviewing the testimony and a report from a master regarding Anderson's services, ultimately ordered the payment of this sum, which was then affirmed on appeal. However, Richter appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court over the amount awarded. The Supreme Court's opinion focused on the proper management of funds held in court and addressed the question of payment to Anderson concerning his claimed fees and expenses.	Thomas Richter's primary argument was centered around enforcement of his claim to insurance moneys under the mortgage agreement with Schroeder. He contested the amount awarded to H.H. Anderson for legal services, arguing that the court should not approve payments exceeding what Anderson himself requested. Richter suggested that the recipient of court-administered funds should be carefully monitored to prevent overpayment.	H.H. Anderson, acting pro se, defended the court's initial decision to grant him $1,007.10 for his legal services, asserting that he provided significant assistance in navigating the complex litigation surrounding insurance claims. He also stated that he had accrued $150 in expenses and was entitled to compensation that reflected the value of his work. The arguments included claims that much of the litigation stemmed from Richter's own neglect, questioning whether Anderson should be compensated at all.

In January 1868, the case "Louisa Plaster v. Jeptha Plaster" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The initial events trace back to November 1854, when a divorce was granted to Louisa due to Jeptha's desertion. At that time, they had a three-year-old child, for whom Louisa was awarded custody and a portion of Jeptha's assets as alimony. In March 1866, Louisa sought further relief regarding child support and alimony by re-docketing the case and filing a supplemental petition. This led to a legal battle wherein the lower court sustained a demurrer to her petition, effectively dismissing her claims. The case was then appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court, which ultimately reviewed the merits of Louisa's claims for support and education for their child, as well as additional alimony.	Louisa claimed that Jeptha should provide compensation for the past support and education of their child since the divorce decree. She also sought a decree for future support and alimony, arguing that as a father, Jeptha still bore the financial responsibility for their child's upkeep, despite the court granting her custody. She insisted that the court was mistaken in its previous rulings that relieved Jeptha of this obligation.	Jeptha contended that the custody arrangement absolved him of the responsibility to provide additional support for the child, asserting that he was no longer obligated to contribute after the custody was granted to Louisa. He argued that the payment of alimony in gross satisfied any future claims Louisa might have, as their divorce severed all marital rights and duties, including support obligations.

The case of John H. Garnhart v. Daniel Rentchler et al. took place in St. Clair County, Illinois, with the decision rendered in June 1874 by the Illinois Supreme Court. John H. Garnhart, the appellant (plaintiff), had entered into a contract with Daniel Rentchler and others (the appellees/defendants), wherein the appellees agreed to sell machines for Garnhart and were entitled to a commission based on the sales. The contract stipulated that the appellees would receive 20 percent on cash sales and 12 percent on sales made on credit. Additionally, the defendants were responsible for setting up the machines and addressing any complaints. However, issues arose when Garnhart failed to provide machines that met the contractual specifications, leading to the return of 31 machines that were sold by the defendants. As the machines did not conform to the agreement, the defendants could not complete the sales and thus were unable to collect their commissions. The central dispute revolved around whether the defendants were entitled to recover commissions, and the court ultimately evaluated the fulfillment of the contract terms by both parties.	The plaintiff claimed that the defendants were entitled to recover commissions for the effort made in selling the machines, arguing that their inability to complete the sales was due to Garnhart's failure to deliver conforming machines. The plaintiff contended that the contract specified the plaintiffs were to be compensated based on sales completed, and he sought to hold the defendant accountable for the commissions owed for these perceived sales.	The defendants argued that they were entitled to commissions only for actual sales of machines that had been received and set up according to the contract. Since all 31 machines were returned due to non-conformance with the contract, they maintained that no valid commissions were due. They emphasized that the contract did not provide for payments based on preliminary contracts or orders and that the plaintiff was absolved from liability for failing to fulfill orders.

The case "South Park Commissioners v. Trustees of Schools" took place in Cook County, Illinois, with the proceedings initiated in March 1881. The South Park Commissioners petitioned to condemn a parcel of land in Hyde Park, which was owned by the Trustees of Schools of the respective township. The aim was to acquire the land for park purposes, as authorized by the enabling act for the South Park Commissioners. The land in question had specific measurements, totaling approximately three-quarters of an acre, and the jury was tasked with determining just compensation for its taking. After examining the property and hearing testimonies from both parties, the jury set the compensation amount at $29,440. Subsequently, the Commissioners sought to overturn this judgment, asserting that the compensation was excessive.
