A central issue remained regarding the procedural right to open and close the case during the trial, which became a focal point of appeal after the circuit court permitted the landowner to have that privilege.	The South Park Commissioners contended that the judgment awarding $29,440 for the condemned land was excessive. They argued that in determining compensation, the court had erred by allowing the defendant to open and close the evidence presentation during the trial, which they claimed infringed on their procedural rights as the petitioners.	The Trustees of Schools argued that the judgment should stand, asserting that the procedure followed by the circuit court was correct. They maintained that they were entitled to present their case first in determining compensation due to the nature of the proceedings, which they believed justified their right to open and close the arguments.

In 1884, the case "Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Ry. Co. v. Noah Pratt" took place in Illinois, where Noah Pratt, the plaintiff, filed a lawsuit against the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railway Company (defendant) in the Illinois Appellate Court. The issue arose when Pratt shipped a cargo of 72 hogs weighing a total of 15,840 pounds from Gatlin, Illinois, to Indianapolis. The hogs, needing water and care during transit, became overheated, resulting in the death of nine hogs and significant injury to others. Upon arrival, Pratt notified the railway agents that the hogs required water; however, his requests were ignored, and the hogs were not watered until after being transferred to another railway company. A key point in the dispute was a written shipping contract, which stipulated that Pratt would accompany and care for the hogs at his own risk, contingent upon the railway company providing facilities to do so. The case examined the obligations of the railway company to ensure the welfare of the livestock during transit.	Pratt argued that the railway company failed in its duty as a common carrier by not providing water for the hogs during transit, which directly led to their suffering and death. He sought damages for the loss and injury to his livestock, contending that the absence of water at critical points in the journey constituted negligence on the part of the railway.	The railway company contended that Pratt, due to his contractual agreement, bore the responsibility for caring for the hogs, including watering them. The company asserted that Pratt's claim for damages should be invalidated, citing a provision that required written notice of the claim to be submitted within five days of unloading. Additionally, they argued that Pratt may have overloaded the car with hogs, contributing to their condition.

In 1877, in LaSalle County, Illinois, William Harvey and others initiated legal proceedings against their guardian, Joel Harvey, to compel him to provide an accounting of funds he managed on their behalf. After the guardian submitted an account that the court rejected, it was determined that he owed a certain sum to the wards. The county court ordered the guardian to pay this amount within a specified time. Joel Harvey subsequently appealed the decision to the circuit court. Before the appeal was resolved, he passed away, leading to his executrix, Rachel Harvey, being substituted as the defendant in the case. Upon her appearance, she sought to have the action abated against her, and the court granted this request, thereby imposing all costs on the wards. The wards then appealed this judgment, seeking to reverse the court’s decision that held them liable for costs.	The plaintiffs, William Harvey and others, contended that they were entitled to an accounting from their guardian, Joel Harvey, who they alleged failed to properly manage and account for their funds. After his death, they argued that the executrix, Rachel Harvey, should be held responsible for providing an accounting. They sought a reversal of the circuit court’s judgment that dismissed their action and imposed costs on them.	The defendant, Rachel Harvey, maintained that the action should abate due to the death of her predecessor, Joel Harvey. She argued that under Illinois statute, the summary proceeding against a guardian does not survive against a representative after the guardian’s death, thus contesting the validity of the plaintiffs' claims against her. She also contended that a judgment for costs against the plaintiffs was not warranted as the proceeding was improperly evaluated.

The case of George Morton v. William Tenny took place in April 1855 in Tazewell County, Illinois. The action was tried without a jury in the Tazewell Circuit Court, where George Morton (the plaintiff) sought to enforce a promissory note against William Tenny (the defendant). The core issue of the case revolved around a dispute regarding the terms of the promissory note. The declaration described the note as being payable “on or before” January 1st, while the note presented in evidence was characterized as payable “on” January 1st. The plaintiff initially won the case in the lower court, leading the defendant to appeal the judgment, asserting that a legal variance existed between the declaration and the proof due to the differing phrasing regarding the payment date.	The plaintiff, George Morton, argued that the promissory note was correctly described in the declaration and that the differences in phrasing did not constitute a legal variance. He asserted his right to enforce the note as per its terms and requested the court to affirm the judgment in his favor.	The defendant, William Tenny, contended that the description of the promissory note in the declaration as payable “on or before” a specified date created a variance when the evidence presented indicated it was payable “on” that date. He argued that this difference should invalidate the enforceability of the note and requested the court to overturn the lower court's judgment in favor of Morton.

The case "Joseph Lane et al. v. William T. Adams" took place in 1857 in the Clark Circuit Court, Illinois. The key individuals involved included the appellants Joseph Lane, James McCabe, Lewis Bradley, William Calvert, and the appellee, William T. Adams. The case arose from a legal action of assumpsit initiated by Adams against Lane and the other defendants, concerning a promissory note executed by the defendants. The plaintiff's claim was based on the assertion that the defendants owed him payment for real estate sold. During the trial, the court rejected the introduction of the note as it did not match the description in the special count. Subsequently, the plaintiff provided evidence proving the execution of the note, which the court allowed under the common counts, leading to a ruling in favor of the plaintiff. The court determined that the terms of the promissory note were fulfilled on the plaintiff's part, necessitating the defendants' payment.	The plaintiff, William T. Adams, claimed that the defendants owed him $376.80 based on a promissory note related to a payment for real estate sold. Adams argued that since the note was executed by the defendants, he was entitled to recover the total sum due under the legal action of assumpsit, supported by claims under common money counts for money had and received, and for money due on account stated.	The defendants, led by Joseph Lane et al., pleaded the general issue and argued against the admission of the promissory note into evidence, claiming it varied from the description in the initial special count. They sought to non-suit the plaintiff, contending that the case should be dismissed without a judgment in favor of Adams due to the noted discrepancies and objections related to the evidence presented.

In 1869, Elias Ray, a minor, entered into a contract with George W. Haines to work for nine months. This contract was made in Woodford County, Illinois. However, after working only six weeks, Ray decided to leave the job. The key individuals involved included Elias Ray, the plaintiff, and George W. Haines, the defendant. The case revolved around the legality of the contract between a minor and an adult, specifically whether the minor was obligated to fulfill the terms of the contract or could recover for the services rendered prior to leaving the job.	Elias Ray claimed that since he was a minor, he was not legally bound by the contract to work for nine months. He requested compensation for the services he rendered during the six weeks he worked for Haines, arguing that he should be entitled to recover the value of those services, as the contract was not enforceable against him due to his age.	George W. Haines defended against Ray's claims by arguing that the contract was valid at its inception and that Ray should be held accountable for his agreement to work for nine months. However, during the proceedings, Haines acknowledged the amount that was due to Ray when he left, which implied some recognition of the plaintiff's work.

Lawrence Looby was involved in a legal case that took place in Illinois, culminating in a decision on December 4, 1885. The case originated when Looby was prosecuted before a justice of the peace for carrying concealed weapons. He faced a fine of $25 as a result of this initial judgment. Subsequently, Looby appealed the decision to the circuit court, where the fine was significantly increased to $150. Throughout the process, Looby was represented by attorney E. Lynch, while S. H. Blane represented the People (the appellee). The Illinois Appellate Court ultimately reviewed the case to determine whether there were any errors in the circuit court's ruling.	The plaintiff, Lawrence Looby, contended that the imposition of a fine for carrying concealed weapons was unjust and excessive. He appealed the circuit court’s decision, seeking to overturn the increased fine and arguing that the original penalty of $25 was sufficient and more appropriate for the alleged offense.	The defendant, representing the People, maintained that the circuit court's judgment was correct and justified. They argued that the increased fine of $150 was appropriate given the nature of the offense of carrying concealed weapons, and they requested the appellate court to affirm the circuit court's decision without finding any error.

This case, Collins D. White v. Thomas J. Primm, was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1865. The dispute arose from a judgment that was originally rendered by a justice of the peace in St. Louis, Missouri, in favor of the plaintiff, Collins D. White. The case focused on the jurisdiction of the Missouri justice and the validity of the process served during the original case. The defendant, Thomas J. Primm, who resided in Menard County, Illinois, argued that he was not properly served with process in Missouri. Witness testimonies were presented by both parties regarding the defendant's whereabouts in early March 1856 to establish whether he was in St. Louis during the time of service. The court had to consider if the method of service used—leaving a copy of the summons with a member of the defendant's family at what was claimed to be his "usual place of abode"—was valid under Missouri law, as the service was questionable and fundamentally impacted the jurisdiction issue at hand.	The plaintiff, Collins D. White, primarily claimed that the judgment against the defendant rendered by the Missouri justice was valid, and that proper jurisdiction and service had been established. He aimed to recover the amount of the foreign judgment and argued that the return of service by the constable was sufficient to confirm the jurisdiction of the justice.	The defendant, Thomas J. Primm, asserted that the service by the constable was invalid because it did not conform with the requirements of Missouri law. He contended that a hotel or boarding house where a guest may temporarily stay should not qualify as a "usual place of abode," challenging the effectiveness of the service and arguing that no proper personal notice of the suit had been received.

In the case of Angelina Sommers v. Henry W. Sommers, which took place in 1885, the dispute arises from a divorce proceeding initiated by Angelina Sommers in the Circuit Court of Will County, Illinois. The couple, married in Germantown, Pennsylvania, in 1872, allegedly lived together until May 1875, when Henry deserted Angelina in Chicago. Angelina claims Henry left without cause and has not returned since, denying her the ability to live together as husband and wife. They have one son, who has been in Angelina's custody. Henry, while admitting the marriage, disputes the claims of desertion, maintaining that they lived together until May 1875 and emphasizes the visits he made to Angelina at her father's home in Germantown over the years. During the court proceedings, the defendant raised questions regarding the jurisdiction of the court, asserting that Angelina was not a resident of Will County at the time the divorce was filed, which is a violation of statutory requirements. The court was tasked with determining the validity of these arguments, leading to the examination of residence, jurisdiction, and evidence surrounding their relationship.	Angelina Sommers, the plaintiff, claims that her husband, Henry, willfully deserted her in May 1875 without cause. She asserts that this abandonment justifies her request for a divorce. She emphasizes her residence in Will County at the time of filing the divorce bill and argues that the court has jurisdiction over the case. Angelina seeks not only a divorce but also claims custody of their son, whom she maintains has been under her care.	Henry Sommers, the defendant, contends that he did not abandon Angelina but left her with a promise to return after a visit to her father. He asserts that they lived together until May 1875 and that he continued to visit her frequently, cohabiting during these visits until February 1884. Additionally, Henry challenges the court's jurisdiction, arguing that Angelina was not a resident of Will County when she filed for divorce, asserting that the case should be dismissed on these grounds.

In the legal case of William Buck v. Cyrus L. Buck, decided on November 13, 1886, by the Illinois Supreme Court, the dispute centers around the partition of real estate located in Warren County, Illinois. The key individuals involved are William Buck, the plaintiff, and Cyrus L. Buck, the defendant, both of whom have claims to the estate of Murray Buck, who died intestate. The plaintiff William Buck filed a bill for partition, asserting his right as an heir to a share of the real estate allegedly owned by Murray Buck at the time of his death. The defendant, Cyrus L. Buck, claimed that he held the entire property based on a will that had been admitted to probate in Knox County, Illinois. William Buck contended that a Vermont probate court had refused to recognize the will, treating this refusal as a conclusive adjudication against the validity of the will. The case had previously been heard, and upon a remand from the Supreme Court, the circuit court dismissed the bill based on the conclusion that the will was valid and the defendant was the rightful owner.	The plaintiff, William Buck, argues that he is entitled to a share of the real estate of Murray Buck based on his status as an heir, following the latter's intestate death. He claims that the will purportedly devised the entire property to the defendant, Cyrus L. Buck, but points to a previous refusal of probate by a court in Vermont as proof that the will is invalid. He seeks a partition of the estate and challenges the legitimacy of the will under which the defendant claims sole ownership.	The defendant, Cyrus L. Buck, maintains that he holds rightful ownership of the real estate under a valid will that was admitted to probate in Knox County, Illinois. He argues that this probate stands unreversed and should be viewed as conclusive evidence of his title. Additionally, he contends that the dismissive action by the circuit court was appropriate, as the previous decision of the Supreme Court found no equity in the plaintiff's claims. He requests confirmation of his ownership and dismissal of the plaintiff’s bill.

Charles W. Weston et al. v. The People ex rel. Henry B. Miller is a legal case that took place in Cook County, Illinois, in 1876. The case involved Henry B. Miller, the County Collector of Cook County, who sought judgment against certain lands and lots for unpaid taxes and special assessments. The collector submitted an affidavit claiming that he could not collect the taxes due, listing delinquent properties for which the taxes and associated fees remained unpaid. The affidavit was sworn before a county clerk and dated June 3, 1875. Various objections were raised by the plaintiffs against the validity of the judgment, arguing that the necessary governmental procedures for tax collection had not been followed as mandated by law. However, the County Court, presided over by Judge Martin H. M. Wallace, dismissed these objections and rendered judgment in favor of the collector.	The plaintiffs, represented by Messrs. Hoyes & White, contended that the certificate and oaths required for the collection of taxes and assessments were not made correctly, asserting that the affidavit submitted by the collector did not comply with legal standards. They requested that the judgment against the delinquent lands be overturned based on these procedural deficiencies.	The defendant, represented by Mr. John M. Rountree, argued that the collector's affidavit was in substantial compliance with the legal requirements. They maintained that the collector had taken the required oath and that previous legal precedents supporting the validity of such affidavits had been modified. Thus, the defendant requested that the original judgment be upheld, affirming the authority of the collector in this matter.

In the case of Madison Y. Johnson v. John H. Von Kettler, which was decided in September 1872, the events unfolded in Jo Daviess County, Illinois. The dispute arose when Madison Y. Johnson (the appellee) and his wife, an administratrix of an estate, were imprisoned for contempt by an order of the county court. This order mandated the administratrix to pay a claim made by Julius K. Graves against the estate, which they allegedly failed to comply with. Johnson was accused of being involved in facilitating the arrest. The key issues revolved around whether the county court had the jurisdiction to issue such an order against Johnson, who claimed that his actions were lawful. The jury ultimately found against Johnson, awarding him damages for false imprisonment, which were later reduced. The case was previously reviewed, leading to a remand where defective pleas were amended and the merits were retried. The trial court faced criticism regarding its procedures, particularly the change of venue and the handling of evidence.	The plaintiff, Madison Y. Johnson, claimed damages for false imprisonment. He argued that he was arrested unlawfully based on an order from the county court that lacked jurisdiction, as he was not a party to the order requiring the payment of the claim. Johnson sought compensation for the distress and damages he incurred as a result of this wrongful act.	The defendant, John H. Von Kettler, contended that the arrest was justified under the county court's order, asserting that the court had jurisdiction to issue the order even if the process was irregular. He maintained that he acted in good faith and that any damages claimed by Johnson were excessive and not warranted by the circumstances. The defendant requested that the court dismiss the appeal or reduce the damages awarded to Johnson.

Solomon F. Lewis v. John J. McGraw, Adm’r, etc. is a legal case that was decided on February 25, 1886, in the Illinois Appellate Court. The case revolves around the estate of Isaac Loucks, deceased, who had left a will executed in 1874 that devised his homestead property to his widow. Loucks died in 1879, and his will was probated in 1882; however, letters executory were not issued until after the widow's subsequent actions concerning the property. In 1883, the widow transferred the property to another party, Basback, who later conveyed it to Solomon F. Lewis. Following the widow's death in 1884, McGraw was appointed as the administrator of Loucks' estate to pay off debts, including a claim from a creditor named Sweeney. The administrator filed a petition to sell the homestead property to settle these debts, which Lewis and others contested. Key legal issues involved whether the necessary parties were included in the petition and the extent of creditor rights regarding homesteads.	The plaintiff, John J. McGraw, the administrator of the Loucks estate, claimed that he needed to sell the real estate to pay off debts owed by the deceased at the time of his death. He argued that the statutory requirements were met by including the necessary parties in the lawsuit, despite contentions from Lewis and others regarding the claims and the inclusion of additional representatives. Given the widow's death and the nature of the property, the plaintiff maintained that proceeding with the sale was legal and necessary.	Solomon F. Lewis, one of the defendants, contended that the petition to sell the property was flawed because it failed to properly address the debts claimed and argued against the validity of the creditor's claim as well as the legal necessity of including the widow’s representatives as parties to the case. He argued that the homestead exemption should protect the property from being sold to satisfy the debts, claiming that it was exempt due to its value being below the statutory threshold.

The case "John B. Smalley, Appellant, v. Richard A. Edey, Appellee" was decided in December 1853 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The roots of the case stemmed from an action of assumpsit brought by Richard A. Edey against John B. Smalley. The conflict originated from a written agreement dated April 22, 1850, where Smalley promised to pay Edey $148.27, contingent upon Edey not settling the amount with a third party, Richard Hoover. Edey claimed he was compelled to pay Hoover that sum and alleged that Smalley failed to fulfill his promise to pay him or Hoover. During the trial, Edey presented the written instrument; however, he did not present any evidence proving that he had made the requisite payment to Hoover, which was a critical condition of his claim. The court initially ruled in favor of Edey, prompting Smalley to appeal the decision.	Edey's primary argument was based on the written agreement where Smalley promised to pay him $148.27 if Edey was forced to pay that amount to Hoover. Edey claimed Smalley failed to fulfill this obligation after he had already settled with Hoover. His legal request was for the court to enforce the agreement and compel Smalley to pay the amount.	Smalley’s defense centered on the argument that Edey failed to meet the necessary condition precedent of paying Hoover before he could demand payment. Smalley contended that the instrument did not constitute a promissory note because the payment was contingent upon an uncertain event—the payment by Edey to Hoover. Smalley requested the court to dismiss Edey’s claims based on these arguments.

The case "George W. Cornwell v. Arminda J. Broom, Adm’x, etc." pertains to a legal dispute that originated on January 30, 1889, in Effingham County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Arminda J. Broom, acted as the administratrix of the estate of her deceased husband, John Broom. The focus of the lawsuit was to recover the principal and interest from a promissory note originally given to John Broom by the defendant, George W. Cornwell, on August 11, 1865. The note was for $300, due one day after the date issued, with a stipulated interest of ten percent annually. The case involved Cornwell and William Gillmore, who was dismissed from the proceedings. The trial, which was decided without a jury, concluded with a judgment in favor of the plaintiff for $913.33, covering both the principal and interest due, as well as court costs. Cornwell subsequently appealed the judgment, asserting that a potential defense existed concerning the statute of limitations on the owed amount.	The plaintiff, Arminda J. Broom, claimed that George W. Cornwell owed her the amount due on a promissory note given to her late husband, John Broom. The plaintiff's legal argument included the validity of the note and claimed that a payment had been made to the note on April 22, 1876, which kept the suit within the statute of limitations. She sought recovery of the full amount owed, which included both the principal of the note and accrued interest.	The defendant, George W. Cornwell, argued primarily on the basis of the statute of limitations, contending that the claims did not accrue within the preceding ten years before the suit was filed. He also attempted to refute the claim concerning the April 1876 payment, which he asserted was made by him alone without the consent or knowledge of Gillmore, who acted merely as a security for the note. Cornwell sought to have the court dismiss the claims based on these defenses.

In December 1835, the case of Abraham Marshall v. Abraham Maury was heard before the Illinois Supreme Court, following initial proceedings in the Schuyler Circuit Court. The case concerned a scire facias action brought by Abraham Maury against Abraham Marshall to foreclose on a mortgage executed by Marshall to Maury. The Circuit Court, presided over by Hon. Stephen T. Logan, denied Marshall's motion to quash the scire facias, which claimed that the document did not properly reference the note linked to the mortgage or outline any breaches. The court subsequently ruled in favor of Maury for the amount due on the mortgage and allowed for a special execution according to statutory provisions. Marshall appealed, seeking to contest the Circuit Court's decision on multiple grounds regarding procedural errors and the judgment rendered.	The plaintiff, Abraham Maury, argued that the scire facias was properly filed to foreclose the mortgage and that the Circuit Court should grant the judgment for the outstanding amount due. Maury requested the court affirm the lower court's decision, as he believed the procedural objections raised by Marshall were without merit.	Abraham Marshall, the defendant, claimed that the scire facias was invalid because it failed to adequately reference the corresponding note and did not specify any breach of the mortgage or note. Marshall contended that the judgment rendered was improper since it lacked a rule to plead and rendered a general judgment rather than a specific one. He requested that the Supreme Court reverse the lower court's decision due to these alleged errors.

In 1851, in the Ogle County Circuit Court (later moved to Lee County, Illinois), a legal dispute arose involving Milo Kelly and Harvey Colburn, the owners of a tract of land, and Daniel Chapman, who was seeking to enforce a mechanic's lien for work performed on a flouring mill. Chapman alleged that he had a verbal contract to work for the defendants for 208 days and claimed the labor was reasonably worth $520, with a remaining balance of $397.76 due after a settlement. At the trial, Moses Nettleton was added as a defendant due to his interest as a mortgagee. Kelly denied any agreement with Chapman and asserted no interest existed until after work began, while Nettleton claimed two prior mortgages on the property. The case was presented to a jury, which ultimately found in favor of Chapman, leading to a decree for a special execution for the sale of the property to satisfy the amount owed plus costs. Nettleton was also ordered to pay costs and dismissed from the case.	The plaintiffs, represented by Daniel Chapman, argued that he had a valid mechanic's lien due to a verbal contract with Kelly and Colburn. He sought recognition of this lien and requested a special execution for the sale of the property to recover the amount owed for labor performed, which he claimed was $520, with $397.76 remaining after payment.	The defendants, Kelly and Nettleton, contested the claims. Kelly denied having entered into any contract with Chapman and claimed no interest in the property until after the work began. Nettleton asserted his rights as a mortgagee, outlining that he held two mortgages on the property predating the mechanic's lien. They sought to dismiss the claims based on these defenses.

In September 1869, the case "City of Chicago v. Robert M. Hobson et al." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court, concerning a local ordinance in Chicago mandating the inspection of fresh water fish before sale. The defendants, including Robert M. Hobson, sold multiple packages of fish that did not bear the fish inspector’s brand, although these packages had been derived from larger barrels, which had undergone inspection. The ordinances stipulated that fish in certain packaging categories must be inspected before sale, and violations could result in penalties. The defendants contended they complied with the law by having the initial barrels inspected, which were subsequently repackaged into smaller units of fifteen pounds each for their retail customers. The fish inspector, however, refused to inspect the smaller packages because they did not meet the minimum weight of twenty-five pounds required for inspection. The case arose from a disputed fine imposed for selling the fish without proper inspection branding on the repackaged items.	The City of Chicago, as the plaintiff, argued that the defendants violated the local ordinance requiring all fresh water fish to be inspected and branded by the fish inspector before being sold. They asserted that the lack of an inspection brand on the smaller fifteen-pound packages constituted a breach of the ordinance, thereby justifying a penalty of up to twenty-five dollars per uninspected package.	The defendants contended that they had followed the ordinance by having their initial fish packages inspected and branded. They argued that breaking down the inspected larger packages into smaller ones did not constitute a new violation of the ordinance since the law was fulfilled at the time of the original inspection. They sought to avoid the imposition of any penalties, claiming no legal transgression had occurred when they sold the repackaged fish.

In the case of Merchants and Mechanics Insurance Company v. William Schroeder, which took place in Cook County, Illinois, a fire insurance dispute arose following the total destruction of the plaintiff's insured property on December 17, 1878. The policy, under which the Merchants and Mechanics Insurance Company provided coverage, secured a total of $1,000 against damages for various property items, including a planing mill, machinery, and stock. The plaintiff, William Schroeder, estimated his total loss at $5,900 and successfully sued for a partial recovery of $1,010.37 after trial proceedings that began on July 10, 1885. The insurance company, challenging the judgment, argued that the policy was void due to alleged over-statements in the insured values stated in Schroeder’s application. Key players included the plaintiff, who testified the values were conservative, and the defense, which insisted misrepresentations invalidated the claim. The case was presided over by Judge Lorin C. Collins.	The plaintiff, William Schroeder, claimed that he had complied with all the requirements outlined in the insurance policy and sought damages for the property lost in the fire that was covered by the policy. He argued that the insurance amount and valuations presented in the application were merely estimates reflecting his opinion and did not constitute false representations that could void the policy.	The defendant, Merchants and Mechanics Insurance Company, asserted that the policy was void due to inaccurate representations regarding the values of the insured property made in the application. They maintained that such misrepresentations constituted a breach of warranty, which should bar any claim for recovery. The defense also argued for a reduction in damages based on the presence of other insurance on the property, which they believed should limit Schroeder's recoverable amount.

The case "Daniel Durham v. Benjamin Goodwin" took place in Kankakee County, Illinois, during the November term of 1869. The dispute arose when Daniel Durham (the plaintiff) accused Benjamin Goodwin (the defendant) of letting his (Goodwin's) horses and mules breach Durham's farm fence, resulting in damage to Durham's corn, wheat, and oats. The plaintiff contended that Goodwin's stock broke into his fields, allowing other animals to enter and cause further damage. The case was initially decided in the circuit court, but the defendant appealed, leading to a review by the Illinois Supreme Court. The main issue centered around the adequacy of jury instructions provided during the trial. The Supreme Court found that the instructions given were erroneous, particularly those that assumed certain facts. Consequently, the court decided to reverse the lower court's judgment and remand for a new trial.	Daniel Durham argued that Benjamin Goodwin was responsible for the trespass committed by his breachy stock, which damaged his crops. He claimed that Goodwin's animals not only entered his properly fenced farm but also permitted other animals to do the same. Durham sought compensation for the damages incurred due to this breach of property.	Benjamin Goodwin contended that the jury instructions provided in the initial trial were inappropriate. He asserted that Durham could not hold him liable for damages caused by animals that were not under his control. Goodwin argued that the trial court had erred in the way it framed the jury instructions, which misrepresented the nature of liability in trespass actions.

The case "Terre Haute & Indianapolis R. R. Co. v. Martin V. Elam" took place in Illinois, with the judgment issued by the Illinois Appellate Court on November 24, 1886. At the center of the dispute was a fatal incident involving the plaintiff's hogs, which were killed by a locomotive belonging to the defendant, Terre Haute & Indianapolis Railroad Company. The primary issue at hand was whether the location where the animals were killed qualified as a public road crossing under Illinois law, specifically Section 62 of Chapter 114 of the Revised Statutes. The railroad had a right of way over land owned by an individual named Heninger, who initially designated a crossing point. Over time, modifications to the road and crossing configurations were made, leading to ambiguity about the road's legal status as a public crossing. Witnesses in the case included Heninger, who did not intend for the passway to be a public road and Brown, the landowner who had a road leading from his farmhouse but had not established it as a public thoroughfare. Ultimately, the court found that the location in question was neither a public road nor appropriately fenced by the railroad, leading to the conclusion that the railroad was liable for the incident.	The plaintiff, Martin V. Elam, claimed compensation for the value of his hogs that were killed by a locomotive owned by the Terre Haute & Indianapolis Railroad Company. He argued that the railroad failed to comply with its statutory duty to maintain appropriate fencing at road crossings, thereby making the railroad liable for the deaths of his livestock.	The defendant, Terre Haute & Indianapolis Railroad Company, contended that the location of the incident did not constitute a public road crossing as envisaged by the statute. They maintained that the area was not treated as a public road by the community and thus did not require fencing. The railroad argued that any fencing obligations were negated by their contractual arrangements with Heninger, the landowner.

In 1876, in Washington County, Illinois, a legal case titled "Hugh C. Adams et al. v. The State of Illinois, for use, etc." was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case involved school directors who allegedly exceeded their statutory authority by borrowing money and allegedly mismanaging funds. The directors were supposed to follow specific guidelines set forth in the 47th section of the School Law of 1874, which limited their borrowing power to certain amounts and required that any money they borrowed be paid to the district's treasurer. The case centered on whether the directors acted within their legal powers and if they would be liable for any financial losses incurred by the district as a result of their actions. The court examined the responsibilities and limitations placed on school directors and the consequences of failing to adhere to their statutory duties.	The plaintiffs, represented by Hugh C. Adams and others, claimed that the school directors had violated the statutory limitations on their authority by improperly managing funds and borrowing money. They argued that the directors' actions were in direct violation of the established laws governing school finances, and as a result, the directors should be held accountable for any financial losses that ensued from their unauthorized actions.	The defendants contended that they acted within the scope of their authority and followed the necessary legal procedures when borrowing funds. They argued that the statutory provisions were open to interpretation and that their actions did not constitute a violation of the law as interpreted. They requested the case be dismissed, claiming that the plaintiffs' assertions were unfounded and that the school directors should not be held liable for financial losses.

Charles Eckley and his sureties were defendants in a legal case brought by the heirs of Patrick Clark in August 1876. This case arose from a dispute regarding the final accounting of Clark's estate, which Eckley administered after Clark’s death. The heirs contested the accuracy of the final account filed on November 21, 1872, claiming that certain items had not been accounted for and that errors had been made during the settlement. The initial ruling by a lower court favored the heirs, requiring Eckley to pay them $894.84. Following the lower court's decision, both parties raised exceptions regarding the master's account, leading to further evaluation by the Illinois Appellate Court. The court found faults in how the previous court handled procedural matters, particularly concerning the burden of proof regarding the final account's correctness and deductions made from it.	The plaintiffs, heirs of Patrick Clark, argued that Charles Eckley, the estate administrator, failed to accurately account for various financial transactions and erroneously charged items to the estate. They sought to impeach the final account, demanding a thorough review and corrections reflecting the true financial state of the estate. Ultimately, they claimed $894.84 - a combination of principal and interest - should have been awarded to them as part of the estate settlement.	Charles Eckley contended that the final account he filed was prima facie correct and that the burden of proof rested with the plaintiffs to demonstrate its inaccuracies. He argued successfully that several claims made by the heirs lacked sufficient evidence to support their assertions. Eckley requested the appellate court to reverse the lower court's decree, claiming that findings were based on unfounded assertions rather than solid proof of wrongdoing in his handling of the estate's finances.

In 1890, in Jacksonville, Illinois, an ejectment action was initiated by Frank H. Clark against Susie Kirkpatrick regarding ownership of lot 27 in Tilton & Cassell’s addition. Clark claimed title through Matthew Ashelby, a common source of title with Kirkpatrick, and presented a duly recorded warranty deed as evidence. During the trial, Kirkpatrick testified about her long acquaintance with Clark and attempted to introduce evidence suggesting the deed was made to deceive her husband and creditors. This evidence, which included discussions about Clark's supposed lack of interest in the property and the arrangement made to defraud creditors, was excluded from the trial based on objections regarding its competency and relevance. The court ruled that the defendant's attempts to show equitable title or prove fraud were inadmissible in an ejectment proceeding, as the legal title must prevail. The trial concluded with a judgment in favor of the plaintiff, prompting Kirkpatrick's appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Frank H. Clark argued that he was the rightful owner of lot 27 due to a valid deed from Matthew Ashelby, asserting that the trial court's decisions during the trial were correct and that he should be granted possession of the property based on his legal title.	Susie Kirkpatrick contended that the deed transferring ownership to Clark was fraudulent, aimed at hindering her husband's rights and defrauding her creditors. She sought to introduce evidence to demonstrate that she was the actual purchaser of the lot and that the arrangement to title the property in Clark's name was a scheme to protect the property from creditors.

In 1855, in Massac County, Illinois, Joel Vaughan initiated a legal case against John Thompson. Vaughan, a poor farmer and head of a family, owned minimal personal property, including a mule worth around $30 to $35, several hogs worth about $15, and a couple of cows valued at approximately $10 each. Thompson, serving as a constable, sold Vaughan's mule while attempting to enforce a debt owed by Vaughan. Vaughan claimed the mule was exempt from execution, as it was below the legal threshold of property meant to satisfy debts, and he had notified Thompson of this exemption during the execution. Vaughan had secured a debt obligation for a wagon purchased from a man named Smith, establishing a lien agreement, which allowed Smith to obtain the wagon should Vaughan default. The case was tried at the Massac Circuit Court, where the jury ruled in favor of Thompson, prompting Vaughan to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Vaughan argued that the mule was his property and exempt from seizure under the law due to his overall lack of valuable assets, claiming that the total of his possessions only amounted to what was legally protected from creditors. He asserted his rights to keep the mule, as he was not required to surrender any of the exempted property to satisfy his debt, seeking to have the sale of his mule deemed unlawful.	Thompson defended his actions by asserting that Vaughan had fraudulently sold the mule to Smith to avoid paying his debts. However, he failed to prove that the sale was legitimate or that the property was not exempt, claiming he had the right to act without proper confirmation of Vaughan's exemption rights. Thompson maintained that Vaughan was not the rightful owner, since he had transferred the mule as collateral to Smith.

The case, "Thomas Bell et al. v. Henry Sheldon et al.," was heard in June 1851 in the Illinois Supreme Court. This legal action arose from a prior decision made in the McHenry Circuit Court concerning an action of assumpsit. The plaintiffs, Thomas Bell and others, were in conflict with the defendants, Henry Sheldon and others, over a financial matter amounting to $530.42. Several special pleas were filed by the defendants in addition to the general issue, but the court sustained demurrers against these special pleas. Following this, without addressing a crucial plea of non-assumpsit (a plea denying that a contract exists), the court rendered a judgment in favor of the plaintiffs. The presiding judge for this matter was Judge Henderson during the April term of 1851. This procedural oversight, where a final judgment was issued without resolving the key plea, resulted in the case being appealed to the Supreme Court.	The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants were liable for the sum of $530.42 based on the action of assumpsit. They sought final judgment against the defendants after the court had sustained their demurrers to several special pleas filed by the defendants, which indicated a lack of defense against the plaintiffs' claims.	The defendants contended through their special pleas that the plaintiffs were not entitled to the judgment rendered against them. They filed a plea of non-assumpsit, which was not adequately addressed by the lower court before the judgment was issued. The defense argued that the issue raised by this plea needed to be tried and resolved prior to any judgment being entered in favor of the plaintiffs.

The legal case of The Enterprise Distilling Co. v. R. D. Bradley took place in 1885 in Tazewell County, Illinois. The case originated when The Enterprise Distilling Co., along with two other defendants, Edward Spellman and James Dolieny, were sued for compensation related to services rendered by a physician. The action was initially heard in front of a justice of the peace, where a judgment for $45.50 was made against all defendants. Subsequently, all defendants appealed the judgment to the circuit court. During the trial, the court rendered a verdict against only R. D. Bradley, while the other defendants were not dismissed from the case. This led R. D. Bradley to appeal the decision, arguing that under common law principles, judgments in contract actions against multiple defendants must involve all parties; a judgment cannot be rendered against one while dismissing others without a personal defense being applicable.	The Enterprise Distilling Co. claimed that R. D. Bradley, along with his co-defendants, had employed the plaintiff physician's services and thus was liable for the payment of $45.50 for these services. They contended that since the defendants jointly employed the physician, all should be held accountable collectively for the debt incurred, as stipulated under the contract.	R. D. Bradley's defense centered on the argument that the judgment rendered against him alone was erroneous. He contended that under the common law principle governing contract cases with multiple defendants, a judgment must be issued against all defendants or none. He asserted that the trial should not have allowed for a verdict against him without addressing the involvement and liability of the other co-defendants, leading to an unfair legal outcome.

On April 9, 1859, in New Boston, Illinois, Hiram Mills and his wife, Martha A. Mills, executed a mortgage on their homestead property to secure a debt of $685.45 owed to Gideon Ives and Elmore Dennison. The property was the Mills' residence at the time. In the fall of 1859, the Mills sold the property to Russ Scudder as part of a trade for land in Nebraska, but the Nebraska title turned out to be defective, leading to the rescission of the contract in August or September 1861. The Mills family returned to the property after reclaiming it from Scudder. Ives and Dennison initiated foreclosure proceedings against the Mills, arguing that the defendants could not claim homestead protections due to the previous sale, even though the sale had been rescinded. The case was presented to the Illinois Supreme Court after the lower court ruled in favor of the Mills.	The plaintiffs, Gideon Ives and Elmore Dennison, asserted that the defendants, Hiram and Martha A. Mills, could not invoke homestead protections because they had previously sold the property, even if that transaction was later rescinded. They argued that the mortgage should be enforced to recover the debt as the homestead rights were compromised due to the sale.	The defendants contended that the mortgaged property was their homestead and that they had never waived their rights under the homestead act. They argued that the mortgage did not affect their homestead rights, and despite the sale to Scudder, the homestead status was reclaimed upon rescinding the sale. They maintained that the mortgagee had not acquired any rights through the sale that would allow them to foreclose on the homestead.

In 1886, the case of Darius C. Warren v. C. D. Cook was filed in the Circuit Court of Jefferson County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Darius C. Warren, sought to prevent defendant C. D. Cook from obtaining a tax deed for a town lot in Mt. Vernon that Cook had bought at a tax sale in June 1883. Warren claimed that he had already paid the taxes associated with that property for the years 1875 to 1882 in May 1883, before the judgment that led to the sale. His lawsuit included accusations that the county tax rate was unconstitutional and that the tax judgment was altered inappropriately without his knowledge after it was signed. The case was heard in the circuit court, which ultimately dismissed Warren’s bill, prompting him to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court, seeking a reversal of the lower court's decision.	Darius C. Warren argued that the tax deed should not be issued to Cook because he had already paid the taxes before the judgment leading to the sale. He asserted that the tax rate was illegal, violating state law, and claimed that there were unauthorized alterations to the tax judgment after it was signed. Warren's main legal request was to enjoin the issuance of a tax deed for the property.	C. D. Cook contended that Warren had appeared through his attorney in the county court and had withdrawn his objections to the tax judgment. Cook argued that the judgment against Warren's property was valid and binding due to his attorney's general authority to represent him. Additionally, Cook maintained that Warren had a chance to contest the tax judgment but failed to do so. Ultimately, Cook requested that the dismissal of Warren’s claims be upheld.

In 1881, Andrew Langdon and other appellants filed a legal action against Minot J. Wilcox and other appellees in Cook County, Illinois, under the Water Craft Act, seeking to enforce a lien against two steam dredges owned by the defendants. The plaintiffs claimed that they were owed $456.20 for supplies purchased for the dredges. After the initial filing of the petition and bond, the defendants released the dredges from attachment by posting a bond as permitted by the Act. Subsequently, confusion arose in the pleadings due to the inclusion of common law declarations that were deemed irregular and irrelevant to the statutory proceeding. The plaintiffs sought to have their case tried on these common law pleadings, which the court denied. The defendants requested the removal of these common law pleadings, a motion which the court permitted. This procedural contest led to an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court regarding the handling of the pleadings and the validity of the statutory proceedings.	The plaintiffs argued that they were entitled to a lien on the defendants' dredges for unpaid supplies valued at $456.20. They sought to have the court allow their common law pleadings to be used for their case, claiming that the attachment of the dredges should not be quashed simply because the bond was filed to release them. They asserted that the trial should proceed under common law rules rather than those specific to the Water Craft Act.	The defendants contended that the plaintiffs' inclusion of common law pleadings was inappropriate and constituted a misunderstanding of the legal process required under the Water Craft Act. They insisted that the statutory procedure was correctly followed and that the bond releasing the dredges had nullified any claim to the lien. The defendants requested the court to strike the common law pleadings as they had no place in this statutory action.

The case of The Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Co. v. Jesse H. Thompson took place in January 1874 in Illinois. The core of the case revolves around an incident involving the transportation of live hogs from Mt. Pulaski, Logan County, Illinois, to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The plaintiff, Jesse H. Thompson, filed a lawsuit against the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company, claiming that the company’s negligence resulted in the death of several hogs during transit. The hogs were subjected to excessively warm conditions during their journey, leading to overheating. Thompson alleged that the railway agents failed to provide necessary water to the hogs at appropriate times, contributing to their deaths. The defense argued that the plaintiff's agent neglected his duty to care for the hogs and that the company was not solely responsible for the unfortunate outcome. The complexity of the case included discussions on the responsibilities of the railway regarding the care of live stock, the duty to provide water, and the definition of negligence in this context.	The plaintiff, Jesse H. Thompson, claimed that the Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company demonstrated gross negligence by failing to provide water to the hogs, which were in danger of dying from overheating. Thompson argued that the railway's agents did not act appropriately despite requests to move the train from a location where the air could not properly circulate and to water the hogs. He sought damages for the loss of the hogs due to the company's negligence during transportation.	The defendant, Toledo, Wabash and Western Railway Company, contended that the plaintiff’s agent was also negligent in failing to care for the hogs adequately during transit. They argued that the hogs were already in poor condition before boarding the train and claimed that there was no direct causation established between the railway's actions and the deaths of the hogs. The defendant asserted that the company's responsibility to supply water was contingent upon the agent's communication of needs.

In April 1867, in Will County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between James Steele and The First National Bank of Joliet. The bank filed a bill in chancery against Steele to recover a sum of money that it claimed was owed to it from a judgment against three men: Pope, Morgan, and Longworth. The bank alleged that these men were partners who owned 150 cattle valued at $8,000 and arranged for the cattle to be sold by Steele in Chicago. The sale yielded over $4,000, which Steele was said to have held in trust for the defendants to satisfy the bank's judgment. The bank accused Steele and the defendants of conspiring to defraud it by hiding this money. Steele denied these allegations, claiming he had no knowledge of the judgment and stating that he sold the cattle under a different agreement, paying off existing debts rather than holding the money for the bank. The court noted that Steele had payments to make for the mortgage on the cattle and that he paid the remaining amount to two of the partners, which they later alleged did not include consent for payment to the bank. The dispute culminated in the Illinois Supreme Court hearing the case, which involved testimonies regarding the payment agreements and the legality of Steele's actions concerning the partners.	The First National Bank of Joliet claimed that Steele held $2,530.70 in trust for the defendants from the sale of cattle and should have applied this amount toward the judgment owed by those defendants. The bank argued that Steele conspired with the defendants to defraud it of its rightful payment and that he should be held liable as he had acquired funds that belonged to the judgment debtors.	Steele's primary defense was that he did not owe any money to the judgment defendants nor held any of their property at the time the bank filed its bill. He contended that the cattle were not his but were under a mortgage, and that all proceeds from their sale were paid to the relevant creditors, including paying off the mortgage. He maintained that any agreements concerning the funds were not valid because they lacked the necessary written consent from all partners, thus denying any fraudulent intent.

The case, "The Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Co. v. Henry Pindar et al.", took place around October 1, 1867, in Fairbury, Illinois. A train operated by the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company passed through the town and inadvertently ignited multiple fires, one of which spread to a building owned by Henry Pindar and Robert Pindar. Despite efforts to extinguish the fire, their store was consumed, along with $3,600 to $3,700 in treasury and bank notes and various goods. The plaintiffs, Henry and Robert Pindar, filed a lawsuit to recover damages amounting to $14,000. At the trial, a jury ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, leading the railway company to appeal, arguing that the fire's cause was due to their employees' negligence, citing that sparks from the engine spread the fire and that proper precautions were not observed. The case raised questions about the standard of care expected from the railway company and the responsibilities of property owners to mitigate their losses.	The plaintiffs claimed that the fire, which spread from the railway company's burning building to their store, was a direct result of negligence on the part of the railway company. They argued the company failed to maintain suitable machinery to prevent sparks from escaping and that the high wind conditions exacerbated the danger. Their primary request was for compensation for the full extent of their losses, amounting to $14,000.	The defendant, the Toledo, Peoria & Warsaw Railway Company, contended that they exercised reasonable care in maintaining their machinery and that any sparks that escaped did not result from gross negligence. Furthermore, they argued the plaintiffs failed to take adequate measures to safeguard their property, as the money they lost in the fire was easily accessible and could have been saved with minimal effort. Hence, they requested the court to reverse the previous judgment favoring the plaintiffs.

The case, "The Board of Supervisors of Jefferson County v. David C. Jones et al. Executors, etc.," originated in the Circuit Court of Jefferson County, Illinois, under the presiding Judge James M. Pollock. The background involves a dispute over the fees owed to a deceased county clerk, William Dodds, who had filed a suit against the Jefferson County board before his death. The suit sought to recover fees for services rendered by Dodds as the county clerk, based on a law enacted in 1865 that specified certain fees for clerks in fifty-one counties, including Jefferson. After Dodds's death, his executors were substituted as plaintiffs. The trial was held without a jury, and the Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of Dodds's estate, granting the fees based on the 1865 Act. This judgment prompted the appeal by the Board of Supervisors, as the legality of the fees being awarded under the special law was questioned.	The plaintiffs, represented by the executors of William Dodds's estate, argued that the fees for the county clerk's services should be granted according to the Act of 1865. They contended that this Act, although labeled as a special law, was valid and should be upheld, thus entitling Dodds's estate to receive the greater fees specified under this statute.	The defendants, the Board of Supervisors, contended that the Act of 1865 was unconstitutional as it constituted a special law that violated Section 11 of Article 10 of the Illinois Constitution, which mandates that fees for county officers must be uniform. They argued that the law was invalid, and since the Illinois Constitution abrogated prior special statutes on fees, the parties should revert to the general law, which did not provide for the higher fees awarded by the circuit court.

In the legal case "Ira K. Mansfield v. J. B. Allison," the dispute took place in 1885 in Winnebago County, Illinois. The case went before the Illinois Appellate Court and was presided over by Hon. William Brown. Ira K. Mansfield is the appellant in this matter, while J. B. Allison serves as the appellee. The court's proceedings revolve around an appeal filed by Mansfield; however, it became evident that he had failed to assign any errors upon the record as required by court rules. The absence of assigned errors meant that there were no issues available for the court's review. Consequently, the court was limited in its ability to evaluate the case further, which led to the significant decision regarding the appeal.	Ira K. Mansfield, as the plaintiff, likely sought to challenge a previous decision made by the Circuit Court of Winnebago County. Mansfield's claim would have included requests for the court to overturn the lower court's decision, though specifics are not provided in the case description. His arguments presumably aimed to demonstrate that errors existed in the previous ruling that warranted a reversal.	J. B. Allison, as the defendant, argued that the appeal should be dismissed based on Mansfield's failure to comply with procedural requirements—specifically, that he did not assign errors upon the record. This lack of compliance was presented as a critical reason for affirming the lower court's judgment, indicating that they believed the case lacked merit for further trial or review.

In March 1838, in Jo Daviess County, Illinois, Moses Whitesides, along with John C. Smith, was involved in a legal action initiated by John Lee, Jesse G. Lindell, and Elliot Lee. The case arose from a promissory note that was made payable to Lee & Co., allegedly executed by Smith on behalf of the partnership of Smith & Whitesides. The plaintiffs claimed damages amounting to $3,805.34. During the trial held in May 1839, Whitesides attempted to contest the validity of the note by arguing that there was no existing partnership at the time the note was executed, citing a notice of dissolution published in the Galena Gazette. Whitesides' requests to admit this evidence, as well as a plea of non est factum to deny the execution of the note, were denied by the court. After the Circuit Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, Whitesides appealed the decision, contending that crucial evidence that could prove his case was wrongly excluded from the trial.	The plaintiffs, John Lee, Jesse G. Lindell, and Elliot Lee, claimed that Moses Whitesides and John C. Smith were liable for a promissory note due to their status as co-partners. They contended that the defendants executed the note in their partnership capacity, which justified their legal action to recover the owed amount along with damages.	The defendant, Moses Whitesides, contended that he was not part of a partnership with John C. Smith at the time the promissory note was executed. He attempted to present evidence of a published notice of the partnership's dissolution, which was allegedly known to the plaintiffs. Additionally, he sought to file a plea of non est factum to deny the execution of the note. Whitesides requested the court to admit this evidence, arguing it was critical for establishing that he was not liable for the note; however, these requests were denied.

The case "John V. Farwell et al. v. L. E. Crandall" was decided on January 25, 1887, by the Illinois Supreme Court. The case arose in Cook County, Illinois, following a voluntary assignment made by A. H. Norton for the benefit of his creditors. Upon Norton's assignment, L. E. Crandall was appointed as the assignee. On February 3, 1886, John Y. Farwell & Co. obtained a judgment against Norton for $4,361.34, but when they sought to execute it, the sheriff returned it as nulla bona, meaning no assets were found for collection. Farwell & Co. then initiated a garnishment proceeding against Crandall, asserting that the assignment made by Norton was intended to defraud creditors. Crandall responded by petitioning the county court to restrain the garnishment proceedings, claiming that he held no property aside from what was assigned to him. The county court decided to enjoin further garnishment actions against Crandall, thereby reserving the right for Farwell & Co. to contest the assignment's validity in that court. This decision was subsequently upheld by the circuit and Appellate Courts.	The plaintiffs, John Y. Farwell & Co., argued that Norton's assignment was fraudulent and intended to hinder and delay creditors. They sought to continue their garnishment proceedings against Crandall to recover the amount owed under their judgment against Norton. They claimed that the assignment should be set aside because it was made with fraudulent intent.	Crandall, the defendant and assignee, contended that the county court had exclusive jurisdiction over the administration of Norton's estate and that any contest of the validity of the assignment should occur within that court. He argued that the garnishment proceedings interfered with the proper handling of the assignment and the distribution of assets among all creditors, as prescribed by law. Consequently, Crandall requested that the garnishment action be restrained and enjoined.

Henry H. Gage v. Josiah H. Bissell et al. is a legal case from 1887 in Cook County, Illinois. The case revolves around a dispute over two lots (6 and 7, block 22, Bavenswood) that were claimed by Henry H. Gage through tax deeds dated April 4, 1873, and January 24, 1876. The appellee, Hambright, initiated the case, stating that he and co-defendant Bissell were the rightful owners of the lots as tenants in common. They argued that Gage's tax deeds were unlawful and did not convey any valid title to him. The original bill filed sought to partition the property between Hambright and Bissell, assert that Gage could only claim back taxes paid, and request that Gage's tax deeds be canceled as they posed a cloud on their title. Defendant Bissell admitted to the allegations, whereas Gage disputed the claims, asserting his ownership of the property. The court proceedings included the introduction of various evidences, concluding with the court's order for partition and ruling that Gage's tax title was illegal and void.	The plaintiff, Hambright, claimed that he and Bissell were the rightful owners of the disputed lots and that Gage's tax deeds were invalid due to lack of proper notification as required by law. He requested the court for partition of the lots, to ascertain the amount owed to Gage for taxes and to annul Gage's tax deeds as they were seen as clouds on the title of the rightful owners.	Gage defended his position by asserting his legal ownership based on the tax deeds. He argued that the court was obliged to determine his rights under the deed dated April 4, 1873, which the plaintiff had acknowledged in his bill. Gage contended that until the validity of his title was successfully challenged, he possessed the legal right to the property.

The case of Charles D. Hauk v. William J. Brownell took place in Springfield, Illinois, culminating in a judgment delivered on March 23, 1887. The dispute arose when Hauk (the plaintiff) sold a one-fifth interest in a gas license to Brownell and his associates (the defendants) for $1,400. The plaintiffs alleged that Hauk had made fraudulent misrepresentations regarding the cost of obtaining the license for the "Low Patent Gas Process." Hauk had claimed that the license was purchased for $7,000, when in fact, he had paid considerably less by using depreciated stock of the Citizens’ Gas Company, valued at only 75 cents on the dollar. Throughout the proceedings, Hauk's relationship with the defendants was characterized as a joint venture, and they had engaged in numerous negotiations before the agreement. The trial court found in favor of the defendants, concluding that Hauk's misrepresentation, attributable to their fiduciary relationship, warranted legal recourse.	The plaintiffs claimed that Hauk committed fraud by misrepresenting the price he paid for the gas license. They asserted that he indicated they were paying for the license at one-fifth of its actual cost, which was falsely represented as being $7,000. The plaintiffs sought to recover the $1,400 they had paid for the interest in the license, arguing that the misrepresentation entitled them to rescind the contract and receive a refund due to Hauk’s deceit.	Hauk defended against the claims by arguing that the representations regarding the cost of the license were not fraudulent because the parties did not share a fiduciary relationship and were instead dealing at arm’s length. He contended that potential misstatements about the license's cost were merely opinions regarding value and did not constitute grounds for rescission. Hauk also claimed that the circuit court provided erroneous jury instructions, which could mislead jurors concerning the nature of their business relationship and the legitimacy of the claims.

In 1876, in Chicago, Illinois, Frank B. Orr and others (the appellants) supplied hardware and building materials to Solomon Snow for the construction of a block of five dwelling houses. The homes were located on separate sub-lots but were under a single roof. The contract allowed Snow to acquire materials as needed without specifying the total amount or a concrete completion deadline, although it was generally understood that the construction would be finished by January 1, 1877. The materials were delivered between October 18 and November 24, 1876. When the appellants sought to enforce a lien on the properties for the materials supplied, the Northwestern Mutual Life Insurance Company and Kieffer, who had an interest in the property, contested the claim. The case progressed through the judicial system, ultimately reaching the Illinois Supreme Court, where the initial ruling was that the appellants were entitled to a lien based on the evidence of their contract and the understanding of the construction timeline.	The plaintiffs, led by Frank B. Orr, claimed a right to enforce a lien on the property based on a contract to supply materials to Snow for the construction of the houses. They argued that despite the ambiguity in the contract regarding the quantity of materials and completion timeline, they had fulfilled their obligations by delivering materials as requested. They sought the court's recognition of their lien against the entire block of buildings.	The defendants, including the Northwestern Mutual Life Insurance Company, argued that the lien should not be enforceable. They claimed that the original petition failed to specify a timeframe for the delivery of materials, and each house should be treated separately regarding the lien. They contended that the findings of the master in chancery were inconsistent with the law and the evidence presented.

This case, titled "The City of Chicago v. L. D. Ward et al.," was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in April 1864. The dispute centers around the city’s efforts to extend Fourteenth Street from State Street to Indiana Avenue. The city assessed taxes on certain real estate to fund this extension, but a portion of this assessment was not collected due to objections from property owners. The city's collector filed for judgment against the delinquent property based on an assessment roll. The property owners contested the process, arguing that the original assessment was void due to lack of proper notice and the common council's insufficient authority to confirm it. The case reflects the tensions between municipal powers, property rights, and procedural requirements in tax assessments pertaining to urban development.	The City of Chicago claims that the assessment for extending Fourteenth Street was valid and was confirmed according to the municipal charter. The city seeks a judgment against the delinquent property for the uncollected assessments. The city argues that a subsequent reassessment was carried out properly in accordance with the law, despite objections. The city requests the court to reverse the prior decision that refused the judgment against the property owners.	The defendants argue that there was never a legally valid assessment for the extension of Fourteenth Street. They claim the original assessment lacked the proper confirmation by the common council, as required by law. Further, the defendants contend that the notices provided were insufficient and did not fulfill legal requirements, rendering the assessment void. They assert that the court’s prior judgment, which refused the city’s application for judgment against the property, remains valid and should bar any new assessments based on the same issues.

The case "Orrin L. Mann et al. v. John H. McKiernan" was adjudicated on May 19, 1884, in the Illinois Supreme Court. The parties involved included the plaintiff, John H. McKiernan, and defendants Orrin L. Mann, George W. Sheldon, and John G. Wilson. The case originated in the Superior Court of Cook County and related to a dispute over the possession of goods that were seized by sheriff Orrin L. Mann under an execution issued from the court. The plaintiff claimed to have purchased the goods from Samuel Kirchoffer, the execution debtor. During the trial, it was established that McKiernan was in actual possession of the goods when they were taken. The main issue was whether this sale was made in good faith or with the intent to hinder Kirchoffer's creditors. A verdict was reached against all defendants for the value of the seized goods, which was subsequently affirmed by the Appellate Court. The case came to the Supreme Court after the defendants appealed the decision.	The plaintiff, John H. McKiernan, argued that he had legitimately purchased the disputed goods from Samuel Kirchoffer, who was the execution debtor. He claimed to have been in actual and open possession of the goods at the time they were seized by the sheriff. McKiernan contended that the sale was valid and not intended to defraud creditors. Thus, he sought compensation for the value of the goods taken.	The defendants, particularly Orrin L. Mann, asserted that the seizure of the goods was justified under an execution issued from the court following a judgment against Kirchoffer. They contended that any sale of the goods to McKiernan was fraudulent and aimed at preventing creditors from collecting debts owed by Kirchoffer. The defense focused on the claim that the sale lacked good faith and sought to have the judgment in favor of the plaintiff overturned.

The case titled "John C. McCord v. The Mechanics’ National Bank of Chicago" was decided in September 1876 in Illinois. It involved John C. McCord, the defendant, and The Mechanics’ National Bank, the plaintiff. The dispute arose from a promissory note executed by Bobbins on October 1, 1872, which promised to pay McCord $1,000 plus interest by January 1, 1874. McCord sold this note to the bank and provided a guaranty of its payment, which was stated to take effect on June 9, 1874. The crux of the case was whether this guaranty was valid since McCord claimed it was executed later, in December 1873. The bank contended that the guaranty was part of the transaction from the outset. The case was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court after the Circuit Court sustained a special demurrer against McCord's plea regarding the timing of the guaranty’s execution.	The Mechanics’ National Bank claimed that McCord was liable under the terms of the promissory note and the guaranty he executed. They argued that the execution of the note and the guaranty were interconnected and valid as presented. They sought enforcement of the payment from McCord, emphasizing the sufficiency of the note's execution and the legal binding nature of the agreement.	McCord's defense centered on the timing of the guaranty’s execution and claimed that it was not made at the same time as the note. He submitted a special plea asserting this point, which was later challenged by the bank via a special demurrer. McCord contended that the plea raised a legitimate defense, but the court found it insufficient as it effectively amounted to a general issue. He also questioned the adequacy of proof concerning the assessment of damages.

In the case of Pierson W. McNail v. Andrew Welch, the legal proceedings began on March 24, 1886, in Washington County, Illinois, to foreclose a mortgage executed by McNail in favor of Welch on May 10, 1882. The mortgage was intended to secure a note for $1,250, which was due in three years with an interest rate of 8% annually, and an additional 2% penalty for late payment. McNail admitted the execution of the mortgage and note but claimed that he was not indebted to Welch because he had made a payment of $1,010 on a previous debt to Welch, of which he was unaware of the payment at the time of the mortgage execution. The legal discussion revolved around whether the late payment clause in the note constituted usury, as McNail alleged that the clause was added after the note's execution without his consent. After a series of court hearings, it was determined in the Circuit Court that evidence of the alleged payment and alterations to the note was contradictory, and McNail’s claims were further weakened by his conduct and lack of inquiries about the payment after its supposed occurrence.	The plaintiff, Andrew Welch, claimed that McNail was liable for the full amount of the mortgage note, asserting that the clause allowing for a 2% penalty for late payment was valid. Welch maintained that McNail had executed the note with full knowledge and accord of its terms, and refuted any claims of previous payments made by McNail, arguing that such payments were not substantiated or recorded.	Pierson W. McNail's defense centered on several points: he claimed that he had already paid $1,010 toward the old note, thereby nullifying the current debt. Additionally, McNail argued that the clause relating to penalties for non-payment constituted usury, rendering the entire note invalid. He asserted that the clause had been added without his consent after the note was signed, fundamentally altering the agreed terms.

Ninian Edwards filed a chancery case against William A. Beaird, the sheriff of St. Clair County, in Illinois in November 1823. The case arose because Edwards, a non-resident property owner, contested a tax levied on his town lots by the county court. He argued that as he was not a resident of St. Clair County, he should not be subject to the tax assessment. The case was heard in the circuit court of St. Clair County, where Edwards sought relief from the tax and requested an injunction against Beaird to prevent him from collecting the assessed tax. Beaird responded by filing a motion to dismiss the case, which was granted by the court, prompting Edwards to seek a writ of error to challenge the dismissal.	The plaintiff, Ninian Edwards, argued that the tax levied on his town lots by the St. Clair County court was improper because he was not a resident of the county. He sought relief from this tax assessment and requested that Beaird, as sheriff, be enjoined from collecting it, claiming that the law creating the tax did not differentiate between residents and non-residents.	The defendant, William A. Beaird, contended that the circuit court appropriately dismissed Edwards's bill and that the act of 1819, which imposed the tax, did not distinguish between property owners based on their residency. Beaird argued that the lien for the tax attaches to the property itself and not the individual owner, thereby supporting the dismissal of the case due to a lack of equity in Edwards's claims.

In 1877, the Illinois Supreme Court adjudicated the case of Charles N. Holden et al. v. The Board of Commissioners of Cook County.
