Hunter, defended himself by asserting that he signed the note as a surety and claimed that the note had been altered after his signature was obtained, which would render it invalid. He argued that the alterations changed the contract terms without his consent, and therefore he should not be liable. Hunter also contended that during the proceedings, the court improperly allowed the filing of pleas without an affidavit of merits, which should have invalidated Truesdell's claims.

In the case of Daniel Wann et al. v. John McNulty, the legal proceedings took place in the Jo Daviess Circuit Court, Illinois, in 1845. The plaintiffs, Daniel Wann and others, were members of a firm known as the "East Fork Furnace Company," involved in smelting lead ore. The defendant, John McNulty, initiated an action of assumpsit for $2,749.70, alleging that he was owed money for lead supplied to the company. Two defendants pleaded non assumpsit, while the remaining two were defaulted. The court proceedings included motions to introduce evidence of a prior judgment against one of the defendants, Robert Shaw, for the same cause of action, but the court denied these motions. The case revolved around whether the previous recovery constituted a bar to the current action. The trial culminated in a verdict for McNulty.	The plaintiffs, led by McNulty, asserted that they were owed payment for lead loaned to the East Fork Furnace Company. They relied on a special count based on an order for payment from Wann to McNulty and included common money counts. Their main arguments were centered on the assertion that the company was indebted to them for the lead provided.	The defense argued that there was a previous judgment against Robert Shaw, a member of their firm, for the same debt. They sought to introduce this prior judgment as evidence to bar McNulty's current claim, asserting that a recovery against one partner should preclude claims against the other partners.

Nelson, a mulatto, was arrested in Hancock County, Illinois, on December 25, 1862, under the act of February 12, 1853, which prohibited the immigration of negroes and mulattoes into the state. The arrest followed a complaint stating that he had entered the state with the intention of residing there. He was not confirmed as either a free person or a slave at the time of the complaint. After being declared guilty by a justice of the peace, Nelson was fined $50 and placed in the sheriff's custody until the fine was paid or he was "otherwise disposed of according to law." He appealed this decision, which was moved to the Circuit Court of Adams County, where he was again found guilty, leading to a writ of error to the Illinois Supreme Court. The case revolves around the constitutionality of the 1853 act in relation to both the Illinois Constitution and the United States Constitution, particularly focusing on issues of involuntary servitude and the rights of free persons of color.	Nelson argued that the act under which he was convicted violated the Illinois State Constitution and the U.S. Constitution by imposing penalties that equated to involuntary servitude. He claimed that the legislation was unconstitutional, as it did not properly define the nature of the offense involving free persons of color and that the procedure followed by the justice of the peace was improper. He sought to have the conviction voided based on these allegations.	The state defended the law by asserting that the act was constitutional, as it fell within the authority of the legislature to define crimes and their corresponding punishments. They argued that punishing the act of immigration of free persons of color did not equate to slavery as defined by the constitution, and that the law provided necessary police powers for the state. The state maintained that even if portions of the act were problematic, the valid parts could still be enforced, and therefore requested the court to uphold the lower court's judgment against Nelson.

The case "Herman Heckenkemper et al. v. John E. Dingwehrs" took place in November 1863 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose from a debt action initiated by John E. Dingwehrs against Herman Heckenkemper and two co-defendants regarding a sealed note executed on April 29, 1861. The note was due twelve months post-execution and represented a financial obligation linked to the guardianship of the heirs of John Hordhouse, deceased. The defendants contended that they had an agreement with Dingwehrs in May 1861, where Heckenkemper was to establish a claim in the Clinton County Court related to his role as the guardian to the heirs. Upon successfully establishing a claim of $335—which the County Court approved—Dingwehrs was supposed to credit this amount against the note. However, when the case went to trial, the court sustained a demurrer to the defendants' special plea that sought to set off the established claim against the obligation on the note. The trial ultimately resulted in a favorable judgment for Dingwehrs for the full amount of the note, further leading to the appellate scrutiny of whether the special plea was valid.	The main argument put forth by the plaintiff, John E. Dingwehrs, emphasized that the special plea by the defendants, which asked to credit their individual claim against the joint debt, was inherently invalid. Dingwehrs maintained that under statutory law, individual claims could not be set off against joint obligations in a joint action. He requested the court uphold the initial judgment that favored him, thereby enforcing the full amount of the note, which included principal and interest.	The defendants, represented by Heckenkemper, argued that there existed a valid agreement wherein their claim against the heirs of John Hordhouse—which had been legally acknowledged by the County Court—should be credited against Dingwehrs’ claim on the note. They asserted that this understanding was binding and requested the court to allow the credit for the established amount to be applied to reduce their debt obligation. They insisted that the plea should not be entirely dismissed and that the facts presented were sufficient to merit their request.

George W. Myers and his wife entered into a mortgage agreement with Wm. C. and H. A. Manny in Brown County, Illinois, during the late 1860s to early 1870s. The plaintiffs, Myers, failed to pay off the mortgage, leading the defendants, Manny, to file a bill to foreclose the mortgage in January 1872. In response, Myers filed a cross bill, claiming a mistake had been made in including more land in the mortgage than intended. The court initially decreed the sale of the mortgaged premises to recover the unpaid debt. During the proceedings, the plaintiffs submitted a stipulation that allowed the defendant in possession to retain the property until sold, while also stating that should the property not sell for enough to cover the lien, the defendant would pay rent at a specified rate. However, the issue arose over a portion of the decree that granted immediate possession of the property to the purchaser upon sale, a matter central to the appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed that the mortgage included more land than intended and sought to rectify this by filing a cross bill. They argued against the immediate possession order given to the purchaser upon sale, emphasizing that such possession should only occur after the deed was delivered, aligning with statutory law governing real estate sale processes.	The defendants argued that the mortgage was valid and that the debt had not been paid, thereby justifying the foreclosure action. They maintained that under existing law, the purchaser of the foreclosed property should not have immediate possession before receiving the deed, countering any claims for altered possession rights in the decree.

In 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between David C. Geary, the plaintiff, and Patrick O’Neil, the defendant. The case centered around a transaction involving the sale of liquors that Geary claimed to have sold and delivered to O’Neil. During the trial, the defendant contended that while the goods were charged to him, it was understood that he would not be held responsible for payment, as the liquors were intended to be purchased by his brother, James Geary. Conversely, the plaintiff argued that it was understood prior to the delivery that O’Neil would be responsible for the goods. The jury ultimately found in favor of the plaintiff, and following the trial court's denial of O’Neil’s motion for a new trial, the defendant appealed the judgment.	The plaintiff, David C. Geary, claimed that he had sold and delivered a quantity of liquors to Patrick O’Neil and sought recovery of the payment for these goods. He argued that there was an agreement that O’Neil would be responsible for the payment, despite the defendant's claims suggesting otherwise. Geary requested that the court uphold the jury's verdict in his favor, asserting that the evidence supported his position regarding the sale and responsibility for the payment.	Patrick O’Neil, the defendant, argued that he did not promise to pay for the liquors, stating they were intended for his brother, James Geary. O’Neil maintained that he should not be held responsible for the payment, as the credit for the goods was given to James rather than to him. Furthermore, he contested the trial court's jury instructions and alleged errors in admitting certain evidence, asserting that the ruling should be reversed based on these claims.

Jonathan L. Bingham, the appellant, engaged in a legal dispute with John A. Maxcy, the appellee, culminating in an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1853. Bingham owned an undivided half of two tracts of land inherited from his mother; however, the local records did not indicate his title to this property. One tract was adjacent to his residence and within the same enclosure, while the other was an unoccupied woodland. Following a judgment against him, Maxcy initiated an execution to recover the debt. When the sheriff attempted to levy this execution, Bingham expressed a desire to offer land as part of the settlement but did not adequately provide this information. The sheriff proceeded to levy on Bingham's personal property instead, for which Bingham executed a delivery bond. Subsequently, Bingham sought to have the levy set aside in circuit court, but the motion was denied, leading to his appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Bingham argued that he had a right to prevent the levy on his personal property and insisted that the sheriff should have first satisfied the execution using his real estate, which was exempt under state law until personal property was exhausted. He claimed he would have furnished details of his real estate had he been properly notified by the sheriff prior to the levy, thus seeking to overturn the levy imposed on his personal property.	Maxcy contended that the sheriff correctly levied the execution after giving the requisite notice to Bingham. Furthermore, Bingham failed to assert his rights under the statute that protects the property of defendants, as he did not provide a list of his other accessible property. The argument was that since Bingham did not inform the sheriff of his property rights until post-levy, he waived any protections he might have had under the law.

The case of W. Irving Culver v. Charles Phelps took place in 1889, in Cook County, Illinois. The dispute arose over the ownership of a piece of property described as lot 10, block 10, in the "Ironworkers' Addition to South Chicago." The plaintiff, W. Irving Culver, sought to set aside several deeds that he claimed clouded his title to the property, namely a sheriff's deed to the Mechanics’ National Bank, a deed from the bank to Francis R. Butler, and a deed from Butler to Culver. The ownership lineage traced back to William H. Colehour, the original owner of the property. The troubles began after a judgment rendered in 1875 against the Colehours in favor of the Mechanics' National Bank, which led to the execution sale of the property. The central issue was whether the Superior Court had proper jurisdiction over William H. Colehour to issue the 1875 judgment, as there were allegations regarding the validity of the summons served at that time. A petition was filed to restore lost records relating to the case, where the court found that the only summons served before judgment rendered was void. Despite challenges, the case progressed through the court system, ultimately reaching the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, W. Irving Culver, argued that the deeds in question created a cloud on his title to the property he claimed ownership of. He contended that the original judgment against the Colehours was void due to lack of jurisdiction, as the summons was improperly returnable. Culver requested the court to set aside the deeds executed under that judgment and to restore his rightful title to the property based on his claim of ownership from the original deed he possessed.	Charles Phelps, the defendant, maintained that the 1875 judgment was valid and that proper notice was given before the judgment was rendered. He contested the plaintiff's claims by asserting that multiple summons had been issued and that Culver's evidence did not accurately reflect the service of the summons. The defendants sought to have the court affirm the validity of the uncontested judgment and uphold the chain of title stemming from that judgment, which had resulted in the deeds in question.

In December 1882, E. W. Valentine, a traveling salesman for a tobacco and cigar company based in Chicago, engaged in discussions with P. M. Schwartz, a cigar manufacturer from Pontiac, Illinois, about potential employment. Valentine expressed interest in transitioning from his current position, indicating that he would consider working for Schwartz. They had preliminary conversations but did not finalize any contract right away. On December 21, 1882, Valentine sent Schwartz a letter detailing his interest in the position and proposing a salary of $1,300 for the first year. Schwartz telegraphed Valentine three days later to arrange further discussions about employment. However, due to delays in communication, Valentine did not receive Schwartz's response until January 1, 1883, by which time he had already accepted a different job with another company. Valentine argued that he would have secured the position with Schwartz had the telegraph company successfully delivered the message on time. Thus, he filed a lawsuit against the Western Union Telegraph Company claiming damages for their failure to deliver the telegram promptly.	Valentine claimed that the delay in the delivery of Schwartz’s telegram resulted in lost salary opportunities. He argued that had the telegram been delivered on time, he would have finalized the employment contract with Schwartz, thus entitling him to damages equivalent to the difference between his prospective salary from Schwartz and what he ultimately earned from the job he accepted. Valentine sought compensation for these lost earnings due to the telegraph company's alleged negligence in delivering the message.	The Western Union Telegraph Company defended itself by arguing that it was not liable for the delay in delivering the telegram. They contended that they had fulfilled their obligations by transmitting the dispatch from their office to the central office and that delays were not the company's fault. They might also have claimed that Valentine did not properly address the telegram or failed to take reasonable steps to ensure prompt communication, which could have mitigated the delay.

In the case of John Alsop v. Ohio & Mississippi Railway Co., the incident occurred in Shelby County, Illinois, leading to a legal dispute filed in 1886. The plaintiff, John Alsop, sought damages for his cow that was injured by an engine belonging to the defendant, Ohio & Mississippi Railway Company. The cow allegedly was on the railway's track due to a deficiency in the required fencing, which allowed the animal to stray onto the right of way. After an initial ruling in the favor of the defendant at the Circuit Court level, Alsop appealed the decision. The court considered whether sufficient evidence existed to uphold the verdict against Alsop's claims of liability on the part of the railway.	The plaintiff, John Alsop, argued that the railway company was liable for the injuries sustained by his cow due to their failure to maintain adequate fencing along the railway's right of way, as required by law. He contended that the cow entered the railway property because the fence was insufficient, leading to the injury caused by the train. Alsop claimed damages based on the statutory duty of the railroad to prevent livestock from accessing the tracks, implying no negligence needed to be established on his part regarding the cow's presence on the track.	The defendant, Ohio & Mississippi Railway Co., claimed that the injury to the cow occurred at a point where no fencing was required by law, arguing that they should not be held liable without evidence of negligence in the operation of the train. They suggested that Alsop's cow had strayed onto the tracks unlawfully and maintained that the railway was not liable since the injury took place outside the corporate limits where fencing was mandated. The company sought to uphold the Circuit Court's decision that ruled in their favor.

In the case of Robert Doyle v. Frank Douglas Machinery Company, heard by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1874, Robert Doyle, representing himself, filed a lawsuit against Frank Douglas Machinery Company. The proceedings took place in the Cook County Superior Court, presided over by Judge John Burns. The case was tried without a jury, as the parties consented to a bench trial. Doyle, as the plaintiff, presented his claims and evidence to the court. The central issue revolved around the sufficiency of the evidence supporting his claims, particularly concerning a note introduced in the court without objection, despite a claimed variance. Additionally, there were questions raised about the existence of the corporation, which Doyle argued was adequately supported by parol evidence indicating it was duly organized and had elected officers.	The plaintiff, Robert Doyle, argued that the evidence presented during the trial was sufficient to support his claims against the defendant. He highlighted that a note, which was material to his case, had been introduced without any objections and contended that any variances were inconsequential. Doyle sought judgment against the defendant for a sum of $3027.62, asserting that the details of the presented evidence substantiated his legal requests for relief.	The defense, represented by Messrs. Carter, Becker & Dale, contended primarily that the judgment against them was unsupported by sufficient evidence. They pointed out that the existence of the corporation was not adequately proven and argued that the variance between the note and the declaration should have invalidated the evidence presented. However, they faced a challenge in asserting these objections, as the evidence in question had already been introduced without objection during trial.

The case of Russell Hinckley v. Albert Kersting took place in Illinois and was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1859. The case arises from a financial dispute involving the sale of bank bills. Russell Hinckley, the plaintiff, is a banker who purchased a ten-dollar bill, which later turned out to be worthless, from Albert Kersting, a German butcher with limited English proficiency. The transaction occurred after an agent of Kersting brought the bills to Hinckley's bank for exchange. This initial exchange included a review of the bills, during which a five-dollar bill was identified as bad and rejected. Ultimately, Hinckley received gold for the other bills after a discount. Shortly thereafter, Hinckley discovered that the ten-dollar bill was also worthless and sought to return it to Kersting, who refused to take it back. The case was initially brought before a justice of the peace, then appealed to the Circuit Court of St. Clair County, where Judge Snypeb oversaw the proceedings. The jury ruled in favor of Kersting, prompting Hinckley to appeal the court's decision regarding jury instructions and his motion for a new trial.	Hinckley claimed that Kersting was liable for the value of the worthless ten-dollar bill, asserting that the defendant's agent had transferred the bill with the assumption it had value. The plaintiff sought a judgment to recover the money he paid for the bill, arguing that he had acted reasonably in inspecting the bills and believed he was making a lawful transaction. He requested that the court instruct the jury to view the contract for the bill as distinct from the others, emphasizing that he was entitled to recompense due to the nature of the sale and the supposed worth of the bills.	Kersting argued that the risk associated with the transaction, due to the nature of bank bills as items of commerce, fell on Hinckley, the buyer. He asserted that there was no express warranty of value on the bill and that Hinckley had ample opportunity to examine the bills and should have been aware of their worth. The defendant's position relied on the principle of "caveat emptor," indicating that buyers must beware when purchasing items of fluctuating value and that, as a seasoned banker, Hinckley should bear the responsibility for his decision to buy the worthless bill.

Charles M. Tibballs and William H. Whitehead, as the surviving partners of David Shirk, filed a legal case against Washington Libby in 1877 in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated from financial dealings involving the Great Western Insurance Company of Chicago, which was incorporated under Illinois law. Tibballs and Whitehead accused Libby, who was a trustee and stockholder of the insurance company, of being liable for a debt of $5,000 that the company owed them. This debt arose from an insurance policy that covered their property, which was destroyed in a fire on October 9, 1871. The plaintiffs' case included claims based on Libby's subscription to the company's stock and alleged that he had not fulfilled his financial obligations as a stockholder. Throughout the proceedings, the court evaluated the structure of the insurance company, its capitalization, and the extent of Libby’s liabilities as a stockholder. Ultimately, the plaintiffs sought to hold Libby financially accountable for the debts of the insurance company, opposing his claims of non-liability. The trial court's initial judgment favored Libby, prompting the plaintiffs to appeal.	The plaintiffs claimed that Washington Libby was liable for the debts of the Great Western Insurance Company due to his position as a stockholder who had not fully paid for his shares. They argued that since the company had an outstanding debt of $5,000 to them, Libby, having subscribed to $10,000 worth of stock, must cover this liability. They contended that Libby was a trustee and a director of the company, responsible for fulfilling the company's financial obligations to its creditors, including the plaintiffs.	Washington Libby denied the claims brought against him, asserting that he was never a subscriber of the stock or a director of the insurance corporation. He highlighted that based on his assertions, he should not be held liable for the company's debt. Libby's argument was focused on disputing the plaintiffs' characterization of his role in the company and the nature of his financial obligations as stockholder and trustee.

William Treutler filed a legal case against Christopher Halligan in Cook County, Illinois, during the year 1877. The trial was presided over by Judge W. K. McAllister. During the court proceedings, neither Halligan nor his attorney appeared when the case was called for trial. Consequently, the case was submitted to a jury, which returned a verdict in favor of Treutler. Following the verdict, Halligan attempted to vacate the judgment and sought permission to present a defense. However, this motion was denied by the court. The court noted that there was no indication of abuse of discretion in denying the motion and that Halligan's absence was attributed to his own negligence or that of his attorney. The details provided in affidavits suggested Halligan had not taken an active role in defending himself against the lawsuit. As a result, the court affirmed the judgment against Halligan.	William Treutler's primary arguments centered around the allegation that Christopher Halligan had defaulted by failing to appear at the trial. Treutler sought a judgment in his favor based on the absence of the defendant and the resulting jury verdict. He requested the court to uphold the judgment that had been rendered against Halligan due to his negligence.	Christopher Halligan's key arguments included a motion to vacate the judgment on the grounds that he had not been given the opportunity to defend himself in court. He asserted that both he and his attorney neglected to appear, and he sought leave to present his defense post-verdict. However, the court found no justification that warranted relief, emphasizing that any lack of defense was due to Halligan's own negligence.

In June 1850, the legal case of Neill Donnelly, appellant, against The People of the State of Illinois, ex relatione Derrick C. Bush, appellee, took place in the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in the McHenry Circuit Court, where it was alleged that Neill Donnelly had unlawfully usurped the office of sheriff of McHenry County. The complaint against him included claims that he failed to take the anti-duelling oath mandated by the Illinois Constitution when assuming office. The proceedings were initiated by Derrick C. Bush, who acted on behalf of the people of the State of Illinois, represented by state attorney Alonzo Platt. The case involved arguments regarding the constitutional requirements for prosecutorial information in quo warranto proceedings.	The plaintiff, represented by Derrick C. Bush, claimed that Neill Donnelly had illegitimately taken the position of sheriff and enjoyed the privileges associated with that office despite not fulfilling the constitutional requirement of taking the anti-duelling oath. The primary legal request was to have Donnelly ousted from the office based on this alleged usurpation of authority.	The defendant, Neill Donnelly, likely argued against the validity of the claims made by Bush, potentially contending that the process followed was improper or legally flawed. His defense was likely based on an assertion that the information filed was defective, as the required formalities and constitutional language were not adhered to in the prosecution, although the specifics of his arguments are not detailed in the provided information.

The case titled "The People of the State of Illinois ex rel. Lorenzo Bull v. Orlin H. Miner, Auditor" was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1868. The case arose in Quincy, Illinois, where Lorenzo Bull, acting on behalf of the Merchants and Banners’ National Bank, sought a writ of mandamus against Orlin H. Miner, the Auditor of Public Accounts. The bank aimed to compel the Auditor to issue a warrant for the refund of certain taxes that shareholders had paid in 1865 under protest. These taxes were levied by the state on the shareholders' shares. The relator asserted that, while taxes were due, the assessment method was illegal, referencing previous court decisions. The court noted that despite the relator's claims, the taxes were legally applicable, and the payments made were in adherence to their contractual agreement concerning tax obligations. The court ultimately regarded the application to refund the taxes as lacking grounds for equitable relief, siding with the legality of the initial tax assessments.	The plaintiff, represented by Lorenzo Bull, argued that the taxes levied on shareholders of the bank for 1865 were illegally assessed and consequently demanded a refund. The plaintiff acknowledged that taxes were due but insisted that the method of assessment violated legal standards, based on precedent from a Supreme Court of the United States case. The plaintiff's main legal request was for a writ of mandamus to force the Auditor to refund the disputed taxes paid under protest.	The defendant, Orlin H. Miner, represented by the Attorney General Robert G. Ingersoll, contended that the taxes were legally assessed and that the banks had voluntarily paid them knowing they were due. The defense argued that even if there were technical issues regarding the assessment method, it did not alter the fact that the property was taxable. They maintained that the state could not be compelled to refund taxes that were paid voluntarily, regardless of the alleged illegalities in their assessment, as the obligations arose from a recognized contract between the state and the banks.

The case titled "The United States Life Insurance Company v. William Vocke, Admr." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court on October 31, 1889. It revolved around the insurance policy of Otto Wilhelm Kielgast, who died by a self-inflicted gunshot on January 17, 1885, shortly after taking out a life insurance policy on July 22, 1884. The plaintiff, Elizabeth Kielgast, as the administratrix of his estate, sued the United States Life Insurance Company to recover the insurance amount. The defendant claimed the policy was void because it contained a clause stating that if the insured died by self-destruction within three years, the policy would not pay out. During the trial, crucial evidence from a coroner’s inquest, which indicated that Kielgast was in a state of temporary insanity at the time of death, was excluded by the lower court. The jury found his death to be accidental; however, the key point of contention was the admissibility of the coroner’s inquest evidence, which the defendant argued should establish the fact of suicide.	The plaintiff argued that the life insurance policy was valid and that the conditions for voiding the policy had not been met since Kielgast was suffering from temporary insanity at the time of his death. Therefore, she sought the full insurance payout from the defendant.	The defendant's main defense was based on the claim that the insurance policy explicitly stated it would become void if the insured died by self-destruction within a specified period. They argued that the coroner's inquest, which found that Kielgast died by his own hand, was relevant evidence that should have been allowed in court to support their claim of policy voidance.

The case "The City of Lacon v. Jesse Page" took place in September 1868 in Lacon, Illinois. The key individuals involved were Jesse Page, the plaintiff, and the City of Lacon, the defendant. The incident occurred when Jesse Page was driving his horse-drawn lumber wagon along a street in Lacon. The city had previously constructed a covered drain under the street, which fell into disrepair, creating a significant hole near the edge of the street where no sidewalk had been installed. As Page's horses ran away, one of the wagon's wheels went into the hole, causing the wagon to bounce and Page to be thrown violently to the ground, resulting in injuries. Following this incident, Page filed a lawsuit against the city, arguing that the city was negligent by failing to properly maintain the streets, which directly led to his injuries.	Jesse Page's primary argument was that the City of Lacon was negligent in maintaining the streets and allowing a hazardous condition to exist. He contended that the hole in the street, which caused his accident, was a result of the city's failure to keep the infrastructure in good repair. Page sought compensation for the injuries he sustained due to this negligence, asserting that under Illinois law, the city should be held liable for the dangerous conditions of its streets.	The City of Lacon contended that Page's injuries were not solely attributable to the city's negligence but were also partly due to the fact that Page's horses ran away, which was an accident. The city argued that liability should not be established unless it could be proven that the injury resulted entirely from the city's own negligence and carelessness. They maintained that the injury was partly caused by the incident with the runaway horses and not solely by the defect in the street.

The case of Jacob Darst v. Joseph Collier took place in Peoria County, Illinois, culminating in a decision in September 1877. Jacob Darst and Joseph Collier entered into a partnership on November 2, 1874, for coal mining, where Darst owned the mine, and Collier contributed his labor and management skills without charge. The partnership was intended to operate as long as both parties agreed. Expenses and profits were to be shared equally, with Darst receiving a small royalty. However, the partnership ended within a year, leading to disputes over the shared profits and improvements made. The parties agreed to submit their differences to arbitration, which included a comprehensive submission of all matters related to the partnership. In September 1875, the arbitrators awarded Collier $2,360.50, plus costs, which led Darst to challenge this award in court, arguing that the arbitrators exceeded their authority in their findings.	The plaintiff, Joseph Collier, claimed that the arbitrators’ award of $2,360.50 was valid and should be enforced by the court. He argued that the arbitration was a binding resolution of the disputes arising from the partnership, which included the valuation of joint improvements and costs incurred. Collier sought the court's affirmance of the award and a judgment for the total amount determined by the arbitrators, including any applicable interest.	The defendant, Jacob Darst, contended that the arbitrators did not adhere to the specific terms of the partnership agreement in determining the value of improvements. He maintained that the only question for arbitrators to consider was the value of joint improvements at the time of dissolution, and he requested the court to set aside the award on these grounds, asserting that the arbitrators had exceeded their authority by awarding additional sums beyond what he believed was permissible.

In 1888, in Champaign County, Illinois, a legal case arose involving the Illinois Central Railroad Company and plaintiff Michael Sheehan. The dispute began when Sheehan entered a railroad car, intending to travel from Champaign to Ludlow. He entered the car in a somewhat aggressive manner, which led to a confrontation with a brakeman. Following this, Sheehan was forcibly ejected from the car, alongside his friends. Although they were allowed to return and complete their journey, Sheehan contended that the railroad employees had assaulted him. The case revolved around issues of whether Sheehan's violent entry, combined with his intoxication, justified the conduct of the railroad's staff. The jury ultimately found that while Sheehan's behavior was inappropriate, the railroad company had a responsibility to protect him against the actions of its employees during his time in the waiting car.	Sheehan claimed he was unlawfully ejected from the railroad car and was assaulted by the company’s employees. He argued that his ejection was not justified, as he had entered the car with the intention to pay for a ticket and become a passenger. Sheehan sought damages, asserting that the railroad company was liable for the actions of its employees, regardless of his intoxication or the manner of his entry.	The Illinois Central Railroad Company contended that Sheehan's level of intoxication was sufficient to warrant his removal from the car, arguing that he was not a lawful passenger. They maintained that the actions taken by their employees were necessary to manage an unruly individual and claimed that Sheehan’s behavior justified their response, including the use of force. The defense requested dismissal of the case based on these arguments.

In April 1865, William T. Stewart purchased a stock of goods in Horris, financed by his father, George W. Stewart. The business, however, proved unsuccessful, leading William to sell his stock to his father on June 30, 1865. Just prior to this sale, William ordered goods from Beardslee & Bros in Chicago, and after the sale, his father took possession of the goods that arrived a few days later. On September 7, 1865, Beardslee & Bros filed an attachment against William T. Stewart, prompting the sheriff to levy against George W. Stewart's stock of goods, which included items purchased after the transfer. George W. Stewart then sued the sheriff for trespass, claiming the levy was improper. The court found against the sheriff, awarding George W. damages for the seized goods. It concluded that the sale from William to George was fraudulent regarding Beardslee & Bros, as both parties knew of William's insolvency at the time of the sale. The court held that the sheriff was not liable for levying on the goods as George failed to point out which items were not part of William’s original stock.	George W. Stewart, the plaintiff, argued that the sheriff incorrectly levied against his stock of goods that were not part of William T. Stewart's original inventory. He claimed that the seizure of goods was unlawful, leading to the award of damages amounting to $364.77 for goods specifically found not to be part of the original stock sold by William. He asserted that the subsequent incorporation of newly ordered goods into his stock was legitimate and should not have been subject to attachment.	The defendant, the sheriff, contended that he acted within his duty when levying the attachment based on the information available at the time. He argued that the levy was appropriate as George W. Stewart did not adequately distinguish between the goods that belonged to William and those acquired afterward. The sheriff maintained that he should not be held liable for the goods taken during the levy since George intentionally mixed the goods and failed to identify which items should be exempt.

On September 1, 1832, Esther E. Robinson leased the Commercial Hotel in Galesburg, Illinois, to James Boyd and his wife, Mary Boyd, for three years at an annual rent of $2,700, payable in monthly installments. The lease included an option for a two-year extension. On May 1, 1883, Boyd and Robinson entered into a supplemental agreement allowing them to operate a saloon on the premises for an additional $100 per year in rent. On March 28, 1834, Fraternity Hall Association bought the hotel from Robinson and the Boyds began paying rent to them. Between May 1, 1833, and May 1, 1834, James Boyd operated a saloon in the hotel, initially as a sole proprietor and then later as a silent partner with Dominick Morley. Their partnership required Morley to supply capital and manage the business, while Boyd provided the space. Disputes arose over the lease conditions, specifically regarding the covenant that restricted underletting without the landlord's consent. The Fraternity Hall Association sought to evict the Boyds, claiming a forfeiture of the lease due to alleged violations of this covenant.	The plaintiff, Fraternity Hall Association, claimed that the Boyds violated the lease’s covenant against underletting by allowing Morley to join him in running the saloon without the association's written consent. They argued that this constituted grounds for forfeiture of the lease and sought a forcible detainer to recover possession of the Commercial Hotel.	The defendants, James and Mary Boyd, argued that their arrangement did not breach the covenant against underletting since the original lease was held jointly, and they only modified their operation by entering into a partnership for business purposes rather than renting the space to Morley. They contended that their actions were consistent with the lease’s intent, as they sought to avoid vacancy rather than circumvent the lease terms, thereby claiming that they maintained legal rights to the premises.

William Dayton filed an action of replevin against William Fry in Greene County, Illinois, in early January 1863. The dispute arose from an incident that occurred on August 13, 1862, when Dayton and Matthew J. Dayton entered into a delivery bond related to property seized under an execution order by the sheriff. The property in question was claimed to belong to Dayton despite the bond asserting it was associated with Matthew J. Dayton. The Circuit Court ruled in favor of Fry, prompting Dayton to appeal the decision, arguing the legal basis of the bond and the execution. The case was subsequently reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court.	Dayton contended that the lower court wrongly overruled his demurrer against Fry's plea, which claimed that Dayton could not assert ownership of the property due to the delivery bond. He argued that Fry's justification for the seizure was defective as it failed to establish that the execution was unsatisfied and in full force at the time the property was seized. Dayton sought to have the lower court's judgment reversed.	Fry argued that Dayton should be estopped from claiming ownership of the property due to the existence of the delivery bond, which identified the property as belonging to Matthew J. Dayton and was approved by him. Fry maintained that the legal basis for the seizure was valid under the bond and that the court's ruling to award the return of the property was correct because the legal requirements for a replevin action were not satisfied by Dayton.

The case "Elias S. Gibson et al. v. Asenath Gibson et al." took place in June 1876 in Marion County, Illinois. The case revolved around the estate of John Gibson, who had passed away, leaving behind debts. Creditors of the deceased filed a bill in the equity side of the Marion circuit court seeking to sell the deceased's land to pay off the debts. The plaintiffs claimed that the deceased had fraudulently conveyed the land to his son, Elias Gibson, shortly before his death, to avoid paying outstanding debts. The defendants, including Elias Gibson, denied these allegations. They contended that as John's only heir, Elias inherited the legal title to the land and that the claims against the deceased did not constitute a lien on the property. The validity of the claims made against the deceased estate was questioned, especially since there was no proof that the debts had been allowed by a court of competent jurisdiction. After examining the evidence and hearing the arguments, the court initially sided with the plaintiffs, prompting the defendants to appeal the decision. The heart of the case centered on the legal rights of heirs regarding claims against an estate and the legitimacy of the creditors' claims, leading to a complex legal examination of property and inheritance rights.	The plaintiffs, comprising creditors including Asenath Gibson (the deceased's widow), argued that the debts owed by John Gibson at the time of his death should be settled by selling the land he had transferred to his son, Elias. They claimed this transfer was fraudulent and aimed to deceive them as creditors. They sought to subject the land to their claims, asserting that the debts were valid and had been allowed by the administrator of the estate.	The defendants, particularly Elias Gibson, contended that he was the legal heir to the property following his father's death. They argued that the judgments against the administrator of the estate did not constitute a lien on the land, and as the heir, he had the right to contest the creditors' claims. The defense emphasized that there was insufficient proof of the debts or their validity, which should be demonstrated before any action could be taken against the inherited property.

In December 1845, the case of Chester Hitchcock et al. v. Daniel S. Haight was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute originated in Winnebago County, Illinois, involving Chester Hitchcock and his co-plaintiffs as the plaintiffs in error against Daniel S. Haight as the defendant in error. The primary issue arose when the plaintiffs requested a rule for the defendant to join in error regarding a scire facias that had been served. However, this service occurred two days after the return day, leading to a critical question about the validity of the writ. The court had to determine whether the defendant was properly before them given that the scire facias's vitality was in question due to the timing of its service.	The plaintiffs claimed that the service of the scire facias on the defendant was valid and sought a court order compelling the defendant to join in error. Their main argument hinged on the procedural aspects of the service and the implications for the judiciary's ability to adjudicate the matter effectively.	The defendant's main argument was that the service of the scire facias was invalid as it was executed two days after the return day, which rendered the writ ineffective. As a result, the defendant contended that he was not properly before the court and challenged the plaintiffs' claims as lacking legal standing.

In 1886, William Hall and Simeon F. Hall, operating as commission merchants in Emporia, Kansas, entered into an arrangement with the cattle buying firm of Greer & May. They agreed to sell cattle shipped to the Chicago market for Greer & May on a commission basis. As the shipping date approached, Greer & May requested that Hall and Sons pay the draft for cattle purchases. On August 13, 1886, Hall and Sons sent a telegram to the First National Bank of Emporia, stating they would honor Greer & May's draft for the cattle they bought. Despite having honored several drafts from Greer & May in the past, Hall and Sons later refused to pay on a specific draft, claiming that this draft was only authorized for one shipment and that the intended cattle never actually reached them. Instead, they received different cattle, leading to a dispute that ultimately went to trial. The jury found against Hall and Sons, indicating they were obligated to pay the draft despite the complications arising from the consignment.	The First National Bank of Emporia, as the plaintiff, claimed that Hall and Sons had made a binding promise to honor drafts for cattle sold to them by Greer & May. The bank argued that it had advanced funds based on this promise and that the plaintiffs were liable for payment despite the confusion regarding the consignment and delivery of the cattle. The bank sought the fulfillment of the draft payment as per the agreement that Hall and Sons had entered into.	Hall and Sons asserted that the telegram sent to the bank only authorized the payment of one specific draft and that the use of the singular "draft" was intentional. They contended that because the cattle drawn against the draft were not the intended cattle but rather an inferior substitution, they were not liable for payment. They claimed that the diversion of the cattle during transit had caused them significant detriment, thus contesting the legitimacy of the draft payment obligation.

John S. Wallace and Thomas W. Holmes filed a legal action against Dexter Curtiss in the Illinois Supreme Court, with the case being decided in April 1864. The dispute centers around a covenant for the sale of lumber, specifically outlining the terms for inspection and delivery. According to the agreement dated April 10, 1861, the plaintiffs were to deliver whitewood lumber to the defendant’s lumber yard in Chicago by July 1, 1861. An inspector, agreed upon by both parties, was to measure and assess the lumber's quality. The plaintiffs delivered an initial cargo of lumber which was inspected and accepted. However, when they attempted to deliver a second cargo, the defendant refused to receive it, citing failure to meet contract obligations. The plaintiffs claimed breach of contract due to the refusal to accept the second shipment and failure to pay for the first. The defendants raised several defenses including "non est factum," payment claims, and set-off, leading to a jury trial where the plaintiffs succeeded.	The plaintiffs argued that they fulfilled their obligations under the contract by delivering an accepted first cargo of lumber and offering a second delivery, which the defendant wrongly refused to accept. They claimed damages for breach of covenant, emphasizing that the inspection process was agreed upon and executed properly. They requested the court to enforce the contract and award compensation for the unpaid balance for the lumber delivered.	The defendant contended that the second cargo was not properly inspected as required by the contract, arguing that no competent inspector was chosen for subsequent deliveries. They asserted invalidity of the plaintiffs’ claim due to alleged non-compliance with the contractual terms and raised a defense based on their special pleas, which argued various discrepancies in the plaintiffs' delivery and inspection processes.

On September 1874, in Joliet, Will County, Illinois, Harbard Senichka filed a legal action against Hervey Lowe to recover two lots he claimed were sold for delinquent taxes from 1865. The case was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court following a trial without a jury in the Circuit Court of Will County. During the proceedings, evidence revealed that the only documentation regarding the publication of the tax notice was a certificate from the publisher, which lacked sufficient form to establish the court's jurisdiction. The court historically required a separate certificate indicating proper notice to confer jurisdiction. The case referenced past rulings where insufficient notice led to a lack of jurisdiction for tax-related judgments, emphasizing strict adherence to legal requirements in tax cases.	Senichka argued that he had valid title to the two lots based on their sale due to unpaid taxes from 1865. His central claim was the assertion that the statutory requirements for notifying property owners about tax judgments were not met, leading to an improper judgment against his property.	Lowe's defense claimed that the findings in the county court's judgment established sufficient basis for the court's jurisdiction. He contended that the evidence, although challenged, warranted upholding the previous judgment, emphasizing that the law's procedural requirements might have been adequately satisfied by the findings of the lower court.

In the case of John P. Bedden v. John M. Clark, decided in January 1875, the legal dispute took place in Vermilion County, Illinois. The case involved John P. Bedden (the plaintiff) and John M. Clark (the defendant), arising from an incident in 1872. Bedden accused Clark of trespass for herding cattle on his privately owned, uninclosed land without permission. At the trial, the court allowed the admission of a local stock ordinance passed in 1871 as evidence, although Clark objected to it. The jury found in favor of Bedden, confirming that he had possession of the land and had the right to prevent others from using it unlawfully. The evidence presented established that Bedden had made improvements to the land and had exercised dominion over it, therefore lawfully warning Clark to stop herding his stock on the property. The instruction given to the jury emphasized that herding stock on someone else's land without consent constitutes trespass, which supports Bedden's claims for damages.	The plaintiff, John P. Bedden, claimed that the defendant, John M. Clark, committed trespass by herding his stock on Bedden's uninclosed land without permission. Bedden sought damages for the trespass, asserting his legal right to control access to his property, which he had been maintaining and improving. He argued that Clark's actions were unauthorized and that he was entitled to compensation for any damages incurred.	The defendant, John M. Clark, argued that he had the right to herd his stock on the land, claiming that he did so with Bedden's permission. Clark's defense relied on the assertion that there were local ordinances allowing livestock to run at large in the area, implying that he did not believe he was violating any laws. He contended that his actions did not constitute trespass as they were done with Bedden's tacit consent.

The case "Northern Line Packet Company v. Alfred A. Binninger" arose from an incident that occurred on November 19, 1869, when the plaintiff, Alfred A. Binninger, was a passenger on a steamboat operated by the Northern Line Packet Company. The boat was en route from Davenport, Iowa, to Gordon's Landing, Illinois. Upon arrival, it was dark and there was difficulty in landing due to ice conditions. The captain instructed Binninger to jump from the boat, which he did, landing on a concealed stone that caused severe injuries; both bones in his lower right leg were broken. He initially objected to jumping due to safety concerns, but the captain's insistence and the lack of alternative means to disembark led him to attempt the jump. Binninger filed suit against the company, claiming negligence in properly securing a safe landing.	Binninger argued that the Northern Line Packet Company was negligent in facilitating a safe landing due to poor conditions and inadequate instruction. He contended that the captain improperly ordered him to jump into dangerous conditions without a safe method of disembarking. Binninger sought damages for the injuries sustained, which he argued were directly caused by the negligence of the company's crew, leading to significant personal suffering and impairment.	The Northern Line Packet Company contended that Binninger’s injuries were a result of his own negligence in jumping from the boat without assessing the safety of the landing. They argued that the landing was made in the usual manner and that any concealed hazards were not under their control or known to them. The company maintained that the plaintiff's actions contributed to his injuries, and thus they should not be held liable for damages.

John B. Hunter v. Urban B. Harris, Administrator, took place in Illinois, with the case being decided on October 3, 1888, by the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose over a promissory note for $10,000 that Hunter was alleged to have executed in favor of William S. Smith on March 6, 1880, with a maturity of five years and six percent interest. Following Smith's death in 1883, the suit was brought by Harris, his administrator. Hunter denied having signed the note, leading to a trial focused solely on the authenticity of the signature. Both parties presented testimony from numerous witnesses regarding the handwriting analysis. The plaintiff's side included twenty-five individuals asserting that the signature was genuine, while the defendant's side had an equal number of witnesses stating the opposite. The court had to consider the credibility and quality of this conflicting evidence. Additionally, issues arose concerning the admissibility of certain evidence related to the note’s existence prior to Smith’s death and procedural instructions given to the jury during the trial.	The plaintiff, Urban B. Harris, claimed that the promissory note was valid, having been in the possession of the deceased William S. Smith prior to his death. Harris’s evidence primarily consisted of witness testimonies asserting the authenticity of Hunter’s signature. Harris sought to recover the $10,000 stated in the promissory note, along with interest, arguing that substantial evidence confirmed the note's execution.	John B. Hunter contested the existence of the promissory note, arguing that he did not sign it. His defense relied on witness testimonies that contradicted the authenticity of the signature. Hunter contended that the circumstances around the note's purported execution were suspicious and raised doubts about its validity. He requested a new trial, asserting that the evidence did not support the jury's verdict and that the court had erred in its instructions regarding the evidence and its admissibility.

In September 1875, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case "Asahel Eurigh v. The People ex rel. Henry B. Miller." The case arose from an appeal made by Asahel Eurigh, challenging the assessment of taxable property in Hyde Park and South Chicago. The legal dispute centered around the assessors' failure to submit their assessment rolls by the statutory deadline of July 1, 1874, as mandated by section 90 of the Revenue Law. Eurigh contended that this failure rendered the assessment invalid. The key individuals involved included Asahel Eurigh (the appellant), representing himself in the appeal, and Henry B. Miller, representing the People (appellees). The case was presided over by the Honorable M. R. M. Wallace at the County Court of Cook County.	The plaintiff, Asahel Eurigh, argued that the assessors' failure to return their assessment rolls by the legally required deadline invalidated the tax assessment. He contended that such procedural lapses directly affected his rights and invoked the principle that no individual should lose property without due process of law. Eurigh sought to have the court declare the tax assessment void and prevent any implications arising from it.	The defendant, represented by Henry B. Miller, argued that subsequent sections of the Revenue Law (sections 191 and 280) nullified the impact of the failure to meet the July 1 deadline. They maintained that the law explicitly stated that an assessor's late return does not invalidate the assessment and that the taxing power held by the General Assembly allows for such legislative flexibility without violating constitutional rights. Thus, they requested that the court affirm the validity of the assessment as it stood.

Milton Jerome filed a case against The City of Chicago in September 1871, regarding a special assessment for improvements on West Monroe Street in Chicago. The legal proceedings began at the March term of 1870 when Jerome applied to the Superior Court of Chicago for a judgment based on the city collector’s report related to the special assessment warrant for curbing and curb walls. A key point of contention was the exclusion of evidence that Jerome argued proved no notice had been given regarding the confirmation of the assessment by the common council. The court determined that there was no filed objection related to this claim, leading to the proper exclusion of the evidence. Additionally, there was a dispute regarding whether the court erred in not allowing Jerome to file an objection at the hearing. The opinion stated that the decision to allow or deny the filing of the objection was at the court's discretion, and since no affidavit supported Jerome's application, the higher court could not affirm that this discretion was abused. Ultimately, the case hinged on a technical interpretation of procedural requirements related to special assessments.	Milton Jerome claimed that the special assessment for the street improvements was not valid due to a lack of proper notice for confirmation by the common council, which should have been given in accordance with the city charter. He contended that this procedural oversight was a violation of his rights and sought to have the court recognize this error and reverse any judgment about the assessment.	The City of Chicago, represented by M. F. Tuley, argued that there was no valid objection filed by Jerome regarding the lack of notice, and therefore the exclusion of evidence related to this claim was appropriate. The defendant also maintained that the determination to permit or deny Jerome's objection was at the discretion of the court and that since no supporting affidavit was provided, the court did not err in its judgment.

In 1882, Edward Jaggerman, the plaintiff, shipped a load of 165 barrels of apples from Staunton, Macoupin County, Illinois, to G. A. Benton in St. Louis, Missouri, via the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Company (the defendant). The apples were documented under a bill of lading indicating their intended destination as East St. Louis. Upon arrival in East St. Louis on September 29, the apples were transferred to a connecting carrier but not delivered to the consignee until October 3 or 4, at which point they were found to be in poor condition. Jaggerman initiated legal action to recover $140.25 in damages that resulted from the delayed delivery, alleging that the defendant failed to deliver the apples as per the agreed contract. The case was first heard by a justice of the peace, resulting in a judgment for the plaintiff. The defendant, however, appealed to the circuit court, where the original judgment was upheld, leading to another appeal by the defendant to the Appellate Court for the Fourth District, ultimately resulting in the Supreme Court's review in 1886.	The plaintiff contended that the defendant was liable for damages due to improper delivery and delays in transporting the apples. They argued that the apples, which were shipped in good condition, did not arrive at their intended destination as required by the bill of lading. Consequently, due to the delay, the consignee suffered losses because the apples were sold at a reduced price.	The defendant argued that once the apples arrived at East St. Louis, they fulfilled their contractual obligation by transferring the shipment to a connecting carrier for further transportation to St. Louis. They claimed no unreasonable delay occurred on their part regarding the transport to East St. Louis and thus requested the jury to find in favor of the defendant based on these grounds.

The case "Stephen P. Smith et al. v. George Sheldon" was adjudicated in September 1872 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Warren County, Illinois, involving the plaintiffs Stephen P. Smith and others against the defendant George Sheldon. The central issue stemmed from the enforcement of an alleged trust and a claim of fraudulent acquisition of property. The plaintiffs contended that they had purchased a tax title and made significant improvements to the property under the belief that they were the legitimate owners. As it turned out, the legal title was still held by the government. In previous court proceedings, specific relief sought by the plaintiffs was declined, but the court noted their equity seemed strong and suggested that they could seek further relief upon payment of the agreed amount for the property. Upon filing for specific performance of the contract, the circuit court granted relief. However, the defendant, Sheldon, argued that the plaintiffs had unreasonably delayed their response to the contract performance and were guilty of "laches," claiming this as a defense against their request for performance.	The plaintiffs claimed that they had an equitable right to the property based on their belief that they were the rightful owners and had complied with the terms of a prior agreement. They sought specific performance of the contract, asserting that they were not bound by delays in fulfilling the contract because no unreasonable time had passed since the previous judgment. They argued that they had made payments necessary for the property and had approached the court to enforce their rights based on the court's previous acknowledgment of their strong equities.	The defendant, George Sheldon, countered that the plaintiffs were guilty of unreasonable delay in complying with the contract and therefore should not be granted the equitable relief they sought. His defense centered on the principle of laches, suggesting that because the plaintiffs did not act promptly, they should not receive assistance from the court. Sheldon emphasized that the prior legal title was effectively held by a trustee, and the plaintiffs had not established a clear right without addressing their delays.

In the case of **David Marston, appellant v. John R. Wilcox, appellee**, the legal proceedings took place in Illinois, culminating in a decision rendered by the Illinois Supreme Court in December 1836. The dispute arose over Wilcox's claim to be a creditor of the late Morrill Marston, who passed away on March 9, 1831. Wilcox initially received letters of administration on June 7, 1831, based on his assertion of being a creditor. However, Marston's next of kin, David Marston, contested this claim, leading to the revocation of Wilcox's letters of administration by the Probate Court on September 26, 1831, due to the determination that Wilcox's claims were fraudulent. Wilcox appealed to the Circuit Court, which reversed the Probate Court's decision, citing lack of authority to review its original judgment. This decision was also appealed to the Supreme Court, which then reversed the Circuit Court's ruling and directed further proceedings based on the evidence. Key pieces of evidence included various notes allegedly signed by the intestate and receipts from Wilcox, but the legitimacy of Wilcox’s claims was brought into question through the presentation of a receipt from Wilcox which indicated payment in full of all debts.	David Marston contended that Wilcox was not a legitimate creditor of Morrill Marston's estate and had received letters of administration through fraudulent claims of indebtedness. He argued that a receipt Wilcox provided on February 3, 1831, served as prima facie evidence that all debts had been settled, thus nullifying Wilcox's claims. Marston sought to have the Probate Court's ruling maintained that revoked Wilcox's letters of administration and asserted his rights as the next of kin to administer the estate.	John R. Wilcox argued that the notes he held, including one for $200 dated October 21, 1823, and another for $453.10 from August 9, 1815, proved his status as a creditor. He contested the validity of the receipt presented by Marston, claiming it did not extinguish the alleged debts owed by the intestate. Wilcox asserted that the Circuit Court was correct in reversing the Probate Court's decision, thereby reinstating his standing as the administrator of the estate.

In December 1851, the legal case "The People of the State of Illinois, on the relation of Harrison P. McClintock, v. Onias C. Skinner" was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The initial dispute arose when Harrison P. McClintock sued a defendant named Smith in a justice of the peace court and was awarded a judgment for $62.52. Smith appealed, and a jury awarded McClintock a larger amount of $130.62. Subsequently, McClintock decided to remit $30.62, effectively lowering his claim to $100. However, Smith then moved to arrest the judgment, a motion that the court initially overruled. The circuit court, acting on its own accord, set aside the jury's verdict and continued the case, prompting McClintock to seek a peremptory mandamus to compel the circuit judge to enter a judgment of $100 based on the jury’s verdict. The case revolved around jurisdictional issues, specifically whether the justice court had the authority to hear a case exceeding $100, and whether the circuit court could dismiss the appeal based on jurisdiction from the justice court.	The main argument of Harrison P. McClintock, the plaintiff, was that after winning the jury verdict awarding him $130.62, which he later reduced to $100 through a remittitur, he was entitled to a judgment based on that verdict. He sought a mandamus order to compel the circuit court to follow through with entering the judgment since, in his view, the jury verdict validated the amount he was eligible to recover.	The defendant, Onias C. Skinner, the judge of the Adams Circuit Court, argued that the jurisdiction of the circuit court was no greater than that of the justice of the peace. Consequently, since the verdict exceeded the maximum jurisdictional limit of the justice's court (i.e., $100), the circuit court should have dismissed the case. Moreover, Skinner noted that McClintock could not confer jurisdiction to the circuit court by remitting part of the verdict and that the court had no authority to enter judgment on a verdict that was already void due to jurisdictional limits.

The case of Lyman Trumbull et al v. Union Trust Company et al. revolves around the insolvency of the firm T. W. Hall & Co., which consisted of three partners: Thomas W. Hall, Charles Hall, and William P. Hall. Their business involved the merchant trade and factoring of wool, with their offices located in Chicago at 46 to 52 Dearborn Avenue. Facing financial difficulties, the firm made a voluntary assignment of their assets for the benefit of creditors on July 19, 1888. This occurred after the firm had incurred significant debt, including a substantial amount owed to the Union Trust Company stemming from advances made for wool that had been consigned to them. Complications arose when the Union Trust Company claimed a first lien on a specific quantity of wool as collateral for these advances. However, the remaining creditors, including various individuals and banks, contested this claim. The case proceeded in the County Court of Cook County, Illinois, culminating in a dispute over the appropriate distribution of the wool's proceeds, which amounted to $51,739.93 following its sale by the assignee, John Kinsey. Key issues included the authority for the assignment made by two of the three partners, the validity of the lien claimed by the Union Trust Company, and the rights of other creditors to the remaining assets stored by the National Storage Company.	The plaintiffs, including the Union Trust Company and various creditors, claimed that the Union Trust Company had a valid first lien on the wool and its proceeds based on prior agreements for advances made against the wool consigned by Ayers & Fell. They contended that Hall & Co. had created a security interest in the wool as collateral for the debts owed. The plaintiffs sought the enforcement of this lien to recover part of the unpaid advances, asserting that the company's claims should take precedence over other creditors.	The defendants, led by the assignee of Hall & Co., contended that the Union Trust Company failed to establish a valid lien on the wool because the advances were commingled with other debts and not properly identified. They argued that the assignment executed by only two partners was invalid until later ratified by the third partner, making any claims based on it ineffective during that interim. Additionally, the defendants asserted that the lien claimed by the Union Trust Company was not enforceable due to the lack of specific proof linking the debts to particular wool.

In August 1850, Charlotte A. Woodbury filed a lawsuit against John Frink in Peoria, Illinois. The case arose from an action of assumpsit concerning a trunk containing wearing apparel valued at $100 that Woodbury had entrusted to Frink, a common carrier. Woodbury alleged that the trunk was to be transported by stage from Peoria to Springfield but was never delivered. Evidence presented in court indicated that Frink had received the trunk in September 1847, and an agreement was made regarding compensation for its transport. However, the court instructed that the burden of proof was on Woodbury to establish the non-delivery of the trunk, indicating that she needed to provide evidence of its non-arrival at the designated location. The trial concluded with a judgment favoring Frink, indicating that the burden of proof was not met by Woodbury, as she failed to provide sufficient evidence to prove that the trunk was not delivered.	Woodbury argued that Frink, as a common carrier, failed to deliver her trunk containing valuables after agreeing to transport it from Peoria to Springfield. She claimed non-delivery of the trunk constituted a breach of contract and sought damages for the lost items valued at $100.	Frink contended that Woodbury did not meet her burden of proof regarding the non-delivery claim. His defense was grounded in the assertion that unless Woodbury provided substantial evidence of the trunk's non-delivery, he was not obliged to demonstrate its delivery. Frink argued that the absence of such evidence absolved him of liability for the alleged loss.

Ezra S. Baldwin was a druggist based in Warren, Jo Daviess County, Illinois. On December 17, 1874, Jesse Wells filed a sworn complaint alleging Baldwin had violated a local ordinance prohibiting the sale or distribution of intoxicating liquors. In response, the police magistrate issued a capias for Baldwin, which was executed by the town constable by reading the warrant to him rather than arresting him. Baldwin subsequently appeared before the magistrate, confessed guilt to the charges, and was fined $100 plus costs. Later, Baldwin filed a bill seeking to enjoin the collection of this judgment, contending that the magistrate lacked jurisdiction, and that he had confessed under duress due to threats from the town attorney. The magistrate’s court dismissed Baldwin's request after a hearing, leading Baldwin to appeal the decision citing multiple errors in the court's judgment.	Baldwin claimed that the judgment against him was void due to the magistrate's lack of jurisdiction and that he had not given his voluntary consent to the judgment, alleging he was under duress. He argued that the process by which he was brought to court was flawed, being based on a warrant that he did not genuinely consent to, as well as claiming that the town's ordinance under which he was charged was not valid.	The defendants, represented by the town, asserted that Baldwin appeared before the magistrate voluntarily and confessed guilt without coercion. They denied any illegal arrest or duress, stating that Baldwin was informed of his rights and chose to accept the terms offered by the magistrate. Additionally, they contended that the ordinance was valid and that the penalties imposed were within the jurisdiction of the municipality.

William Baker v. Philip R. Palmer is a legal case that took place in September 1876 in Illinois. The court involved was the Illinois Supreme Court, with Mr. Justice Walker delivering the opinion. The case arose from a debt action brought by Philip R. Palmer against William Baker based on a judgment previously rendered by the county court of Hastings County in the Dominion of Canada. The context of the case included Baker claiming he had been discharged from liability due to an insolvency ruling by the Canadian court. This insolvency ruling occurred in November 1868, and Baker argued that his discharge negated the claims Palmer had against him. The court reviewed procedural objections about the filings and focused on the implications of the foreign judgment in its decision-making process.	Palmer claimed that he was owed a debt based on a valid judgment from a Canadian court. He argued that Baker's claim of discharge under Canadian insolvency law was insufficient because the plea did not clearly demonstrate that the discharge released him from the specific debts for which Palmer was suing. Palmer maintained that the foreign judgment should be recognized and enforced as evidence of Baker's indebtedness, as the foreign court had jurisdiction over the matter.	Baker contended that he was discharged from the debts owed to Palmer under the Insolvent Act of 1864 from Canada, citing a complete and unconditional discharge granted by a Canadian court before the lawsuit was filed. His defense relied on the assertion that since the Canadian court's ruling was valid, it should absolve him of the debt claimed by Palmer. Baker further argued that the Canadian judgment should not be enforced in Illinois because it lacked necessary evidence showing its applicability to the particular debts being claimed.

On April 10, 1870, Isaac N. Bassett purchased a tract of land in Mercer County, Illinois, at a master in chancery sale for $1,600, as part of a partition process where the land was found not divisible. On July 2, 1870, an administrator’s sale was held for half of the property to settle the debts of the deceased Robert Lockard, wherein Bassett bought this half for $818. Bassett claimed that Robert Lockard transferred the land to his five minor sons to defraud creditors. Bassett then filed a supplemental bill in court to seek credit for the amount he paid at the administrator’s sale against the notes from his master’s sale purchase or to receive payment directly from the master. A demurrer to his bill was sustained, resulting in the dismissal of his case. The court found no basis to grant the relief sought by Bassett due to the absence of warranty at the judicial sale and the principle of "caveat emptor," which holds that buyers assume the risks of their purchases.	Bassett’s main argument centered on his contention that he was entitled to a credit for his $818 payment made during the administrator's sale against the notes from the master’s sale, or alternatively, he sought direct payment of that amount from the master. Bassett's claim was fundamentally about ensuring fairness after he had placed substantial financial commitment into land that became subject to debts resulting from previous ownership.	The defendant, represented by Messrs. Pepper & Wilson, argued that Bassett purchased the land at a judicial sale, where the principle of "caveat emptor" applies, meaning he purchased the property with all its risks, including any existing liens or debts. They maintained that as there was no warranty of title involved, Bassett could not claim relief based on a failure of title due to debts that were not cleared by the preceding transaction.

The case of Andrew Pederson v. George T. Cline took place in 1888 in the village of Winnetka, Illinois. The dispute arose when Andrew Pederson, the plaintiff, claimed he had been in possession of a five-acre property with a house for nearly ten years. He alleged that the defendant, George T. Cline, forcibly entered the premises by breaking a window while the house was temporarily vacant and securely locked. Prior to filing the suit, the plaintiff claimed to have made a proper demand for possession of the property. The initial suit was filed in a justice's court, and upon appeal, the case was tried without a jury in the Circuit Court of Cook County. The court admitted evidence from the defendant indicating that he had a tax title to the property through an individual named Stanley and that he was put in possession by Stanley’s lessee. The defendant's counsel argued that if the evidence showed that the defendant's entry was made without real force under an adverse claim, the plaintiff could not recover in this case. The court rejected this proposition, stating that the inquiry into title was not competent in an action for forcible entry and detainer.	The plaintiff, Andrew Pederson, argued that he had maintained possession of the property for nearly ten years before the defendant forcibly entered it. He asserted that his entry constituted a forcible detainer for which he sought legal reclamation of his possession. Pederson claimed that he made a proper demand for the property before initiating the lawsuit, seeking judgment for restitution of possession.	The defendant, George T. Cline, maintained that he had a valid tax title to the property through an individual named Stanley.
