Additionally, he asserted that the defendant did not substantiate the authority of the attorney who confessed the judgment and that the court lacked proper authorization for the collective entry of the judgment.	The defendant, Chicago Marine and Fire Insurance Company, argued that the confession of judgment was valid as it was confessed in open court, which presumes the regularity of the proceedings. They maintained that it was sufficient that proof of the execution of the warrants of attorney was presumed, rather than explicitly presented in the record. The defendant also contended that the consolidation of the different actions was appropriate since they involved similar matters, and thus the judgment on the dual notes was justified. They insisted that the court was aware of its officers, negating the need to show that the attorney who confessed was formally recognized as such.

In 1861, in Hennepin township, Illinois, Edward F. Pulsifer (the defendant) was approached by the local assessor to provide a list of personal property for taxation, including personal property belonging to his deceased father's estate, for which he was an executor. Pulsifer submitted a valuation of $11,608 for his property and $2,700 for the estate. Unsatisfied with these values, the assessor increased them dramatically to $25,000 and $27,000 respectively and then imposed penalties by doubling these amounts, alongside doubling the valuation of Pulsifer's real estate. When notified and summoned to a meeting to correct the lists, Pulsifer refused to make the required affidavit confirming the accuracy of his property's valuation. Following the refusal, Pulsifer filed for an injunction to prevent the tax collection, and while the Circuit Court relieved him of penalties and taxes on certain legacies, it denied relief regarding the increased valuation. This led the collector to appeal the decision to the Illinois Supreme Court.	Pulsifer, the plaintiff, argued that the increased valuations assigned to his properties were excessive and unjustified, claiming that he acted in good faith and provided accurate lists of his property. He sought to have the court restrain the tax collector from collecting what he deemed wrongful taxes and the penalties imposed due to the inflated assessments made by the assessor.	The tax collector argued that Pulsifer had failed to provide accurate valuations when assessed and had given a false return, which justified the penalties imposed by the assessor. The defendant maintained that the assessor acted within his statutory authority and that Pulsifer’s refusal to comply with legal requirements, including making the necessary affidavit, negated his claims for relief from the inflated assessments.

The legal case "The Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company v. John O’Neile" took place in November 1851, in Randolph County, Illinois. The involved parties included John O’Neile, the defendant, who had obtained an insurance policy from the Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company for $1,900 on his stock of goods in his store. The policy was issued on May 15, 1848, for six years. On April 13, 1850, O'Neile's store was destroyed by fire, resulting in a loss of approximately $2,000 worth of goods. At the time of the fire, O’Neile had approximately $9,922 worth of stock on hand and had purchased goods worth about $12,000 leading up to the incident. He reported the loss to the insurance company as required and had consistently paid his premium assessments. The insurance company contended that O’Neile had taken out another insurance policy on the same goods with a different company without notifying them, claiming this violated their charter, which could void the insurance coverage unless prior consent was given. The case was tried before Judge Underwood and a jury during the March term of 1851, with the jury ultimately favoring O’Neile.	The Illinois Mutual Fire Insurance Company claimed that John O’Neile's additional insurance policy on his stock of goods, obtained from another company without their knowledge or consent, voided their insurance policy according to the company's charter. They argued that the charter's provisions on double insurance applied in this situation, asserting that O’Neile violated their terms by not notifying them about the other policy. The plaintiff sought to overturn the jury's verdict in favor of O’Neile and requested a new trial based on this argument.	John O’Neile defended against the plaintiffs’ claims by asserting that the charter's provisions regarding double insurance did not apply to insurance on goods, only to buildings. He maintained that he gave adequate notice to the insurance company of his loss and had adhered to the policy's requirements. His defense included emphasizing the exclusion of usage evidence that the insurance company attempted to present, stating that written contracts could not be modified or controlled by external usages or prior agreements.

In January 1873, the case of Charles Anderson v. Anna C. Jacobson was brought before the Illinois Supreme Court. The case originated in Ford County, Illinois, where Charles Anderson (the plaintiff) initiated an action against Anna C. Jacobson (the defendant) involving a promissory note and an account. Anna C. Jacobson, the defendant, responded with several defenses including a general denial, set-off claims, and a plea of coverture (the legal status of a married woman). The jury ultimately ruled in favor of Jacobson, leading to a trial where Anderson’s arguments and evidence were challenged. The case raised several legal issues including the validity of secondary evidence (a copy of a lease) and whether claims of fraud regarding the note could be introduced without being formally pleaded.	Charles Anderson's main arguments centered around the validity of the promissory note and the associated account. He claimed that the note was enforceable, asserting that Anna C. Jacobson was liable for the amount due. He sought a judgment that would compel Jacobson to pay the owed sums, contesting the defenses raised by the defendant.	Anna C. Jacobson defended herself by arguing the general issue and presenting a set-off claim, which asserted that she had legitimate reasons to counter Anderson's claims. She also raised a plea of coverture, indicating that her legal status affected her liability. Additionally, Jacobson argued against the admissibility of evidence presented by Anderson, stating that it did not adhere to required legal standards.

Ole M. Tomle v. Leah J. Hampton is a legal case that took place in Batavia, Illinois, culminating in a judgment on December 8, 1888. The incident involved Leah J. Hampton, a minor, who was injured due to an alleged negligence on the part of Ole M. Tomle, the owner of a commercial building where the incident occurred. For ten years, Tomle had owned the business property, which included a glass show window and an uncovered opening in the sidewalk. This opening, which measured ten inches wide by five feet long, led to a vault or cellar below, extending to a depth of ten feet. On the night of October 10, 1883, Leah was sent by her parents to the drug store located in the building. While peering into the show window, she accidentally stepped into the opening and fell into the cellar. The injury she sustained was serious, leading to long-term health issues and requiring her to use crutches. The case was initially tried in the circuit court, where a jury awarded Leah $2,000 for her injuries, which prompted Tomle to appeal the decision. Key facts included concerns over Tomle's responsibility regarding the maintenance of the property, the conditions of the sidewalk, and previous warnings about its dangerous condition.	The plaintiff, Leah J. Hampton, claimed that Ole M. Tomle was negligent in maintaining the storefront and the adjacent sidewalk, resulting in an unprotected opening that constituted a public nuisance. She argued that the openings created a hazardous condition that directly caused her injury, emphasizing that she was exercising due care at the time of the incident. Leah requested damages for the pain and suffering endured due to her injuries, leading to significant medical complications and loss of normal functioning.	Ole M. Tomle defended himself by claiming that he was not liable for Leah's injuries since he was not in possession of the building at the time and had rented it to tenants who were responsible for maintaining the premises. He argued that there was no written agreement requiring him to keep the property in repair, and maintained that the tenants should be the ones liable for any safety issues. Furthermore, Tomle contended that the opening was not a nuisance per se and disputed the severity and permanence of Leah's injuries, suggesting that her claims were exaggerated, or "shamming," aimed at extorting a large sum of money from him.

John De Koven and E. W. Blatchford, acting as trustees for the estate of I. H. Burch, deceased, appeared in the County Court of Cook County, Illinois, to contest a special assessment related to the construction of a sewer on Sheffield Avenue and Lawrence Avenue in the City of Lake View. The assessment was undertaken by the city to fund the sewer installation. The trustees raised objections to the assessment, arguing that it was illegal for several reasons. They claimed the assessment improperly included the streets that intersected their property and contended that the land should have been assessed in separate parcels rather than as a whole. Additionally, they argued that the property already had sufficient sewer capacity and therefore did not benefit from the new sewer being proposed. The county court dismissed their objections, leading the trustees to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, John De Koven and E. W. Blatchford, claimed that the special assessment for the sewer was illegal because it did not account for the streets intersecting their land. They argued that the assessment should have been done in parcels instead of as a single tract and that their property already had sufficient drainage due to an existing sewer, negating any benefit from the new sewer.	The defendant, the City of Lake View, maintained that the assessment was valid. They asserted that it was reasonable to presume that the city commissioners deducted the streets from the total area when determining the benefits of the property. The city argued that the law does not require separate assessments for tracts of land owned by the same person, even if divided by roads, and contended that the existing sewer's condition did not preclude the potential benefits from the new sewer installation.

The case known as "The People, on the relation of Gustavus Koerner et al. v. Nicholas Ridgley et al." was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in January 1859. It involved a legal dispute in Springfield, Illinois, regarding the management of the State Bank of Illinois. The complainants, including Gustavus Koerner, George T. Brown, and Richard Yates, alleged that the defendants—trustees Nicholas Ridgley, Uri Manly, and John Calhoun—were unlawfully continuing to manage the bank's assets despite being removed from their positions by the Governor of Illinois. The court proceedings stemmed from a quo warranto information filed by the complainants, asserting that the defendants were acting unlawfully by holding onto the bank's books and assets. The defendants claimed their appointment as trustees was valid and that they had lawfully taken control of the bank's assets to wind up its affairs.	The plaintiffs contended that the defendants were unlawfully holding and executing the duties of their trusteeship after being removed by the Governor. They argued that the actions of the defendants contradicted the peace and dignity of the people of Illinois, warranting an ouster under the quo warranto statute. The plaintiffs sought a judgment determining that the defendants no longer had the right to manage the bank's assets and were thus acting against the public interest.	The defendants countered that their trusteeship was not an office or franchise under the law, asserting they had been validly appointed and were operating pursuant to a deed that granted them the bank's assets. They argued that the plaintiffs failed to establish that the defendants held any public office or franchise as defined by law, meaning the quo warranto action was improperly applied. The defendants maintained they were legally in possession of the bank's assets and had the right to continue managing them.

Silas W. Robbins and Thomas Laswell entered into a partnership agreement on March 1, 1853, in Illinois, whereby Robbins advanced $254 to Laswell for the purchase and management of cattle, with an agreement that profits would be shared and that Robbins would receive a minimum of 20% annual return on his investment. Over time, Robbins claimed to have advanced more than $5,000 for cattle, hogs, and horses purchased under this partnership. However, Robbins alleged that Laswell had not managed the stock properly, failed to provide full reports, and wrongfully kept profits for himself. Disputes led Robbins to file a case in the Sangamon Circuit Court, seeking an accounting and to recover the amounts Laswell was supposed to remit. Laswell admitted the existence of the agreement but denied liability, claiming it was an attempt to cover an usurious transaction. The case progressed through various hearings, and a master in chancery was appointed to review and report on the accounts between the parties.	Robbins claimed that he was entitled to reimbursement for the money he advanced for stock purchases and sought half of the profits from the sales, according to the partnership agreement. He asserted that Laswell had misappropriated funds, failed to manage the stock adequately, and refused to provide an accurate account of their transactions. Robbins requested a full accounting and the appointment of a receiver to manage the remaining stock.	Laswell contended that the partnership agreement was intended to disguise an usurious transaction and argued that he was not obligated to account for the profits or the stock he had in possession. He denied wrongdoing and refused to comply with the requests for full disclosure regarding their financial dealings, asserting that Robbins had no valid claim to the profits or assets in question. Laswell claimed that any financial reports provided were the result of a misunderstanding and that sufficient evidence existed to suggest that the agreements had been settled previously.

The case, "John B. Kreitz v. Charles F. A. Behrensmeyer," was a contested election proceeding regarding the office of county treasurer of Adams County, Illinois. The election took place on November 2, 1886, with John B. Kreitz as the Democratic candidate, Charles F. A. Behrensmeyer as the Republican candidate, and B. L. Dickerman representing the Prohibition party. After the election, the judges of the respective voting precincts counted the votes. Kreitz was declared the winner with 4,618 votes against Behrensmeyer's 4,604 votes and Dickerman's 272 votes. Behrensmeyer, claiming various irregularities in the vote counting, sought to contest the election results, alleging that many legal votes for him were incorrectly counted for Kreitz. The county court was approached to determine the validity of the election results and whether a recount was necessary. Major concerns raised by Behrensmeyer included illegal voters, miscounts, and other procedural issues in counting votes across several precincts.	Charles F. A. Behrensmeyer, the plaintiff, contended that he received more legal votes than reported and that the election judges failed to count many valid votes for him while mistakenly counting illegal votes for Kreitz. He sought a recount of the ballots, citing specific precincts where he believed that the judges made errors in counting and certifying the votes.	John B. Kreitz, the defendant, contended that the election was conducted properly and that all votes were correctly counted. He denied Behrensmeyer's allegations of miscounts and illegal voting, asserting that he was legitimately elected by a majority of legal votes. Kreitz requested the court to dismiss the case based on the assertion that the election results were valid and properly certified without any evidence of misconduct by the election officials.

In June 1874, Francis F. Cole initiated a lawsuit against The Joliet Opera House Company in the Will County Circuit Court, located in Illinois, to recover a balance owed on a subscription for capital stock in the company. The case arose after the defendant, The Joliet Opera House Company, challenged the validity of the subscription, claiming that Cole's signature was obtained through fraud and misrepresentation. The defendant filed a plea of fraud, which the plaintiff subsequently demurred. The court sustained the demurrer, leading to a trial by jury that resulted in a verdict favoring the plaintiff for $1,477. The defendant's motion for a new trial was denied, prompting an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The court found errors in the handling of the fraud plea and the required evidence of notice concerning payment calls for the subscription, ultimately leading them to reverse the initial judgment.	The plaintiff, Francis F. Cole, claimed that he was owed a balance on his subscription to the capital stock of The Joliet Opera House Company, stipulating that the calls for payments were made appropriately according to the subscription agreements. He sought to recover $1,477, asserting that he had fulfilled his obligations under the terms of the subscription.	The defendant contended that Cole's signature was obtained through fraudulent means and that he should not be bound by the subscription agreement. They argued that the evidence presented by the plaintiff failed to demonstrate that proper notice of the payment calls was given at least twenty days before the suit was initiated, asserting that without this notice, the plaintiff had no cause of action.

In the case of George S. Poppers v. Mary J. Meager, the events unfolded in Cook County, Illinois, with the judgment filed on April 17, 1889. The dispute revolved around a lease agreement between George S. Poppers, the appellant (defendant), and Mary J. Meager, the appellee (plaintiff). Ms. Meager filed for a judgment by confession seeking recovery for unpaid rent owed by Mr. Poppers under a lease. The motion for the judgment was initiated on June 25, 1888, and subsequently, Mr. Poppers attempted to set aside the judgment on June 27, 1888. The main points of contention involved whether the warrant of attorney was valid, the applicability of unliquidated damages as a set-off against the rent owed, and the procedural correctness of issuing an execution on the judgment before the record was officially completed. The legal principles discussed included the roles of the attorney mentioned in the warrant and the separation between the claims for rent and the unliquidated damages. Ultimately, the court examined these elements during the appeal process about the judgment's validity.	Mary J. Meager claimed that George S. Poppers was in arrears for rent as per the lease agreement between them. She argued that the warrant of attorney for confession of judgment was valid and did not require naming a specific attorney, as it was customary practice. Furthermore, she contended that the claim for unliquidated damages proposed by Poppers was not related to the demand for unpaid rent and thus should not be considered as a set-off in the proceedings.	George S. Poppers defended against the judgment by asserting that the warrant of attorney was defective because it did not name a specific attorney and only partially executed its intended purpose. He raised objections concerning the claims for unliquidated damages, arguing they were relevant to the rent dispute and thus warranted consideration. Additionally, he pointed out that execution on the judgment should not have occurred prior to the judgment being officially recorded, questioning the procedure followed in this case.

The case "The Consolidated Coal Company of St. Louis v. Amelia Maehl" pertains to a workplace accident that occurred on December 13, 1887, at the Anchor coal mine in Macoupin County, Illinois. John Maehl, the husband of the defendant Amelia Maehl, was employed in the mine and, along with four fellow workers, exited the mine when tragedy struck. After throwing their tools onto the cage that would hoist them to safety, the cage reached the top, where three of the men disembarked. Maehl called for a light to gather his tools, but the engineer misinterpreted this signal and left the engine unattended. As a result, the engine unexpectedly activated, causing the cage to ascend suddenly, which threw Maehl off and down the mine shaft, resulting in his death. Following the incident, his widow initiated a lawsuit under mine safety statutes, securing a $5,000 verdict against the coal company.	The plaintiff, Amelia Maehl, claimed that the defendant failed to ensure a safe working environment as mandated by mining safety laws. Her arguments included wilful neglect in providing adequate lighting at the top and bottom of the shaft, failing to station competent individuals at these locations to manage hoisting signals, and lacking maintenance on essential machinery such as the hoisting engine, which malfunctioned. She sought recovery for her husband's death, citing the coal company's negligence in correctly managing the safety protocols required for operating the mine.	The defendant, The Consolidated Coal Company, argued that Maehl's death was not attributable to their negligence. They contended that Maehl was partially responsible for his own death by bringing tools onto the cage, violating safety protocols. The company also claimed that proper procedures and maintenance were in place, suggesting that the accident's timing—prior to the regular hoisting operations—further diminished their liability. They requested the court to overturn the jury's verdict based on these defenses.

On November 4, 1857, Timothy Mosier entered into a mortgage agreement with David Norton and his wife, to secure a note of $6,000, which was to be paid two years later with an annual interest of ten percent. This case, Timothy Mosier v. David Norton et al., originated in the Circuit Court of Henry County, Illinois, and was presided over by Judge Geo. W. Pleasants. In 1860, Mosier paid $2,782.50 to redeem the mortgaged land from a prior foreclosure, after which he filed his bill to foreclose the mortgage on September 6, 1866. The defendants acknowledged the execution of the mortgage and the payment of the redemption money but alleged usury in the original contract, arguing that the mortgage was a facade to conceal an illegal interest rate. During the proceedings, both parties presented conflicting testimonies regarding the valuation of the properties and currency involved in the transaction. The court scrutinized the allegations of usury and determined the necessity of an equitable resolution to the conflicting claims and evidence presented by both parties.	Timothy Mosier asserted that he had the right to foreclose the mortgage due to the original agreement’s terms, and sought to include the $2,782.50 he paid for redemption, along with ten percent interest on that amount from the time of the redemption. He aimed to recover the full amount due under the mortgage, rejecting the defendants' claims of usury.	The defendants, led by David Norton, contended that the mortgage was usurious, claiming that the agreement was executed to circumvent Illinois laws restricting interest rates. They argued the actual value of the loan was distorted by including fictitious valuations of collateral properties, which they claimed were overvalued to disguise unlawful interest. They requested the dismissal of Mosier's bill and sought an accounting of rents and profits for the property they claimed Mosier had received since taking possession.

In June 1877, the case of George Briscoe v. Johnson A. Power was heard in the Illinois Supreme Court, following a proceeding in the equity side of the circuit court in Marion County. The core issue involved a dispute over payment responsibilities related to a deed of trust on land jointly owned by both parties. Johnson A. Power, the complainant, claimed that he had to pay off a part of a debt secured against their respective properties, which were conveyed to him and Briscoe in previous transactions. Specifically, Power sought to compel Briscoe to pay his share of a mortgage debt that had been secured on the entire tract of land they owned. The historical context presented that the land transactions and the debt relationships date back to 1861, with the original obligors being Samuel Gaity and Catharine Van Hear. Power contended that after satisfying the mortgage payment, he was entitled to recover Briscoe’s proportional share. Briscoe’s defense centered around a previous suit he filed, which he argued made Power’s current claims invalid, asserting that Power failed to pursue his equities in that suit. Ultimately, the circuit court found in favor of Power, leading to Briscoe's appeal.	Johnson A. Power argued that he had paid a significant portion of the mortgage debt secured on the land they both owned and sought contribution from George Briscoe for his share. He claimed that the legal obligation to pay had been clearly established through earlier negotiations and decrees. Power requested the court to decree that Briscoe contribute accordingly and to impose a lien on Briscoe's remaining property to secure this payment.	George Briscoe’s defense focused on the claim that Power's lawsuit was barred due to the previous foreclosure case, where Power did not file a cross-bill to present his equities. He maintained that since the earlier suit dealt with a different parcel of land and the claims were ultimately resolved, Power had no right to initiate the current suit. Briscoe disputed the claim for contribution, arguing he had fulfilled his own financial obligations related to prior agreements.

The case of Petefish, Skiles & Co. v. William Watkins took place in 1888 in Springfield, Illinois. The dispute arose from a promissory note of $1,000, signed by Elijah Watkins, with William Watkins acting as surety. The note dated April 19, 1884, was given to the banking firm of Petefish, Skiles & Co. as a temporary financial solution while Elijah sought other financing. The plaintiffs alleged that William Watkins had defaulted on the payment of the note. The defendant argued that the plaintiffs had agreed to accept a new note from Robert Taylor to retire the original note but later misapplied the loan proceeds to Elijah's individual debts instead. The Cass County Circuit Court initially ruled in favor of William Watkins, which was later affirmed by the Appellate Court leading to the present appeal.	The plaintiffs, Petefish, Skiles & Co., contended that they were entitled to payment on the promissory note. They argued that there was no valid agreement that the proceeds from the Taylor note were meant to satisfy the debt represented by the original note. They sought to enforce their right to collect the debt owed by William Watkins.	William Watkins, the defendant, claimed that he signed the note as surety under the understanding that it was a temporary financial arrangement. He asserted that the plaintiffs had agreed to apply the proceeds of the Taylor note against the original debt. Watkins maintained that he fulfilled his obligations by arranging for the new loan and that the bank misapplied the funds to other debts related to Elijah Watkins, invalidating his liability.

The case "Jesse J. Yoakum et al. v. William Yoakum et al." was decided in January 1875 by the Illinois Supreme Court. The dispute arose in Sangamon County involving William Yoakum, an elderly and infirm man over eighty years old, and his adult sons, who were defendants in the case. William, who was illiterate and unable to understand legal matters, conveyed real estate to his sons with the belief that he would retain a life estate allowing him to live on the property during his lifetime. His sons, Jesse and others, persuaded him to execute these deeds with the understanding that he would receive proper support and a lease for life, which was not explicitly stated in the deeds. After realizing that the life lease was not secured, William sought legal recourse to set aside the deeds based on claims of undue influence and misrepresentation concerning the transaction.	The plaintiffs, William and Letitia Yoakum, claimed that the deeds conveying their property to William's sons were executed under undue influence and that they were misled about the terms of the conveyance. They argued that the intention was to reserve a life estate for William, which was not fulfilled in the deed's wording. They sought to have the court set aside the deeds and restore possession of the property to William along with legal provisions for their support.	The defendants admitted to the execution of the deeds but argued that it was a voluntary act on the part of the complainants. They maintained that the contents of the deeds were fully explained to William and that he understood the transaction. The defense also claimed they had paid the agreed amount as consideration and were willing to provide for their father’s support. Moreover, they asserted that the modifications made in the deeds accurately represented William's wishes.

In December 1876, Harrison Dills, the plaintiff and owner of two business lots in Quincy, Illinois, entered into a written agreement with Alexander F. Pool, the defendant, to sell these properties for $20,000. As part of the deal, Pool assumed two encumbrances totaling $12,177 on the properties. Dills was to retain ownership until February 1, 1877, as Pool would need to get consent from the trustee of the encumbrances before substituting debts. The agreement also included Pool executing warranty deeds for 800 acres of land in Missouri to Dills as part payment. Dills claimed that Pool failed to pay off the encumbrances as agreed, leading to significant amounts still owed. Pool contended he had paid off the debts. Evidence revealed complexities regarding the payments and ownership of the Missouri land tied to the debts. The original trial did not allow specific testimony that could clarify these matters, which led Dills to appeal the decision of the lower court in favor of Pool.	Dills argued that Pool breached their contract by failing to pay off the two encumbrances on the Quincy property as agreed. He sought damages for this breach, asserting that significant amounts were still owed on the debts, including $819.10 to Wheat and Marcy and $8,985.59 to the Grand Lodge of Masons. Dills challenged Pool's claims of having discharged these debts through the conveyance of land.	Pool contended that he had satisfied his obligations by paying the debt to the Grand Lodge of Masons and asserted that the note held by them was returned to Dills upon this payment. He maintained that the 800 acres provided by him were sufficient to cover the amount due. Pool argued that the evidence supported his claim and that Dills received the agreed value for the property.

In 1889, the case "Aaron W. Burnside v. P. L. O’Hara et al." was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court. The dispute arose from a mechanic's lien issue related to plumbing, gas fitting, and sewer construction at Burnside's residence. P. L. O'Hara, who was involved in this matter, claimed a lien for $215.88 against Burnside after acting on a contract with an unlicensed contractor named Cook, who had initially started the work. To enable Cook to carry out the project, O'Hara allowed Cook to use his plumbing license for purchasing the necessary materials, for which Cook agreed to pay O'Hara 10% on the cost of materials. However, when Cook abandoned or was discharged from the job, O'Hara claimed he had a new agreement with Burnside to complete the work, seeking $175.88 for its completion. The case highlights the complexities of contractor licensing laws and the requirements for asserting mechanic's liens in accordance with statutory provisions.	Burnside, as the plaintiff, argued that O'Hara's claim for a mechanic's lien should be invalidated due to non-compliance with necessary statutory requirements. Burnside maintained that O'Hara did not fulfill the conditions precedent to attaching a lien, specifically the requirement of delivering a sworn statement detailing subcontractors, laborers, and materials. Without this statutory compliance, Burnside asserted that O'Hara's lien claim was baseless and requested that the lien be discharged.	O'Hara, the defendant, contended that he had a valid claim to a mechanic's lien because he completed the work under the new contract with Burnside. He argued that the court should recognize his rightful claim for compensation for services rendered and sought to uphold the lien against Burnside. O'Hara insisted that he should not be penalized for the licensing issues surrounding Cook and that his agreement with Burnside warranted the enforcement of the lien.

The case "The City of East St. Louis v. Ernst W. Wider" took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, in January 1868. The conflict arose when Ernst W. Wider, a merchant, sought to renew his license, which had expired on September 1, 1867. On September 5, 1867, Wider attempted to pay for the renewal of his merchant's license by tendering certificates of indebtedness issued by the police commissioners to the city treasurer. The treasurer refused to accept these certificates, insisting that only United States currency or city orders were valid forms of payment per the city's ordinances. Despite this refusal, Wider continued to sell goods without a valid license, leading to his prosecution for violating city ordinances. The case was appealed from the city court to the Illinois Supreme Court, which was tasked with determining the validity of Wider's tender and the implications of continuing to operate without a license after the tender was refused.	The City of East St. Louis, as the appellant, argued that Ernest W. Wider was liable to penalties for engaging in business without a valid merchant's license. The city contended that Wider's attempt to tender certificates of indebtedness was not a legitimate payment method as per the city ordinances, which expressly required payment in United States currency or city orders for obtaining a license.	Ernst W. Wider, as the appellee, claimed that his tender should have been accepted and that he was still entitled to a license upon payment. He argued that the treasurer's refusal constituted a wrongful denial of the license, which prevented him from complying with the regulations. Wider could have pursued further legal actions, such as a mandamus, to compel the issuance of the license had the city treasurer acted improperly.

On January 25, 1887, the Illinois Supreme Court heard the case of George Bartelott v. The International Bank, originating from the Superior Court of Cook County. The legal dispute dates back to October 17, 1881, when George Bartelott initiated an action of assumpsit against the bank and Berthold Lowenthal, seeking legal redress over a property transaction. Bartelott claimed he purchased a property from Samuel J. Walker in 1870, believing it to be free of any liens. However, he later discovered a trust deed encumbering the property for two promissory notes of $15,000 each, which were linked to other debts Walker owed to the bank. Bartelott asserted that Walker had paid a sum of $20,000 to the bank in September 1873 to satisfy these debts and believed this would also clear the collateral notes. After paying the bank $15,000 in April 1874 to secure the release of the property, Bartelott claimed that the bank fraudulently concealed the fact that the earlier notes were paid off. Bartelott's claims involved misleading statements by the bank regarding the status of his property's mortgage. The case underwent several trials and appeals, with initial judgments being overturned, leading to a complex legal battle.	Bartelott argued that he was misled by the bank regarding the status of the two promissory notes linked to the trust deed on his property. He claimed that the bank, aware that Walker had paid the debts, falsely represented that the notes were still owed when he inquired about them. Bartelott requested compensation for damages arising from his reliance on these representations and sought restitution for the $15,000 he paid to the bank based on the incorrect assumption that he needed to settle the outstanding debts to protect his property.	The International Bank contended that there was no evidence of a specific agreement that the payment of the $20,000 by Walker would result in the cancellation of the two $15,000 notes. They maintained that the collateral notes remained valid because of a contract allowing them to retain such securities for outstanding debts. The bank further argued that Bartelott had not established his claims to recover the funds and highlighted procedural issues with his pleadings during the trials, asserting that the defenses were adequate under the law.

In August 1873, in LaSalle County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Ann Morrissey and John W. Stephenson regarding possession of a house. The conflict began when a deputy sheriff executed a writ of possession issued from a prior ejectment judgment against William Morrissey, Ann's husband, evicting both William and Ann from the residence. While Ann's husband was not present during the eviction, she attempted to re-enter the house after the eviction, claiming it was their family home. Ann managed to break in through a window and stayed there with her children. Shortly after, Stephenson, accompanied by Hough (the plaintiff in the earlier judgment), entered the property intending to rent it. Ann forcibly removed them from the premises when she returned. This series of events led Stephenson to file a forcible entry and detainer suit against Ann Morrissey. The court had to consider whether Ann’s rights to the property were valid, given her claim of a homestead.	Ann Morrissey's opposing party, John W. Stephenson, claimed that he was legitimate in occupying the previously mentioned premises due to the valid ejectment judgment against William Morrissey. According to Stephenson, since Ann was living with her husband at the time of the original judgment, she was equally bound by the outcome. He sought legal retribution for her alleged unlawful re-entry and the assault she purportedly conducted to remove him from the house.	Ann Morrissey contended that she had a valid homestead right to the property based on her prior ownership and occupancy with her first husband, who had died many years prior. She posited that the judgment against her second husband, William, should not apply to her or her children, as they had their own claim to the property independent of him. Ann sought to introduce evidence supporting her position regarding her homestead rights, which was ultimately rejected by the court during the trial.

Louisa McCall et al. v. Henry R. Lee took place in the state of Illinois, with the claim filed on April 11, 1881, in the county court of Fulton County. The case involved Thomas McKee, who acted as the administrator for the estate of Kate H. Lee, seeking a claim against the estate of Catherine Dwire, who had passed away on April 24, 1879. Dwire's estate had already been subject to her will, and letters testamentary were issued to her executors on May 10, 1879. The claim was put on hold pending the outcome of another related case that was decided in March 1883, allowing for its eventual reinstatement. The county court dismissed the claim initially, but when appealed to the circuit court, the judgment was reversed and found in favor of the claimant. The appellate court affirmed this ruling, leading to the case being reviewed by the Illinois Supreme Court for the legality of the re-instatement of the claim and arguments surrounding the substitution of parties.	The plaintiff, Henry R. Lee, argued that he had a rightful claim to certain property and assets that were originally transferred to his mother-in-law, Catherine Dwire, as part of a family agreement, which stipulated that the property would revert back to him upon her death. Lee contended that the property in question was rightfully his as it was part of his deceased wife's estate, and he sought payment from the Dwire estate proportional to his claim.	The defendants, the executors of Catherine Dwire's estate, primarily contested the re-instated claim on procedural grounds, arguing that the claim should not have been re-instated after the clerk's failure to keep it on the docket. They asserted that allowing an amendment to substitute Lee's name as the claimant was improper because it introduced a new cause of action that exceeded the time limit for filing claims. Furthermore, they argued that the classification of claims was not determined by the circuit court, which they claimed was an error impacting the legitimacy of the ruling.

Maria Conway filed a lawsuit against the City of Joliet following an incident that occurred on a defective sidewalk in Joliet, Illinois. The case was presented before the Illinois Appellate Court, with the opinion filed on December 4, 1885. Conway sustained personal injuries from a fall on the sidewalk, which was acknowledged as defective, and the city authorities had prior notice of its condition. The incident took place in a location where the sidewalk was frequently used by the public, and prior court precedents indicated that even if a sidewalk is known to be in disrepair, individuals could still pursue recovery for injuries if ordinary care is exercised. The testimony presented did not indicate any lack of reasonable care on Conway's part or suggest that she was contributorily negligent.	Maria Conway's primary argument was that the City of Joliet was negligent in maintaining the sidewalk, which led to her injury. She sought a judgment for damages, claiming that the fall caused severe injuries, including a miscarriage, and resulted in long-lasting pain and other sex-specific ailments that impaired her ability to work.	The City of Joliet contended that Conway could have known the sidewalk was defective and should have exercised more caution while using it. They suggested that, had she taken reasonable care, she might have avoided the injury. Additionally, the defendant argued that the damages awarded were excessive, questioning the amount based on the assessment of her injuries.

John Prindeville was indicted for rape in the Recorder’s Court of Chicago, Illinois, in 1866. During the trial, he pleaded not guilty; however, he was found guilty of assault with intent to commit rape. The jury sentenced him to one year in the penitentiary. Following the verdict, a motion for a new trial was denied, prompting Prindeville to seek a writ of error to reverse the judgment. The central argument in his appeal was that he could not be convicted of assault with intent to commit rape if he had only been indicted for rape, asserting that these are distinct crimes. He contended that a proper indictment was necessary to support a conviction for the lesser charge, emphasizing that the elements of the crimes were not interchangeable. The case showcased the legal principles surrounding the relationship between higher and lesser offenses within criminal law, including the idea that a conviction for a lesser offense could be maintained under an indictment for a greater one under specific circumstances.	The plaintiff, John Prindeville, argued that being indicted for rape did not allow for a conviction of a lesser offense, such as assault with intent to commit rape, unless he had been properly indicted for that specific crime. He claimed that he should either be acquitted of the charge of rape or tried on the appropriate lesser charge. His request was primarily for the reversal of the judgment against him, suggesting that his due process rights were violated by being convicted of a crime for which he had not been indicted.	The defendants, representing the State of Illinois, maintained that the conviction for assault with intent to commit rape was legally permissible under the indictment for rape. They argued that the elements of both offenses were inherently connected, and therefore, the jury could lawfully convict for the lesser offense if the evidence supported it. The defense further asserted that the procedural rules of the court regarding the necessary timing of jury instructions were followed, and no error was found in how the trial was conducted.

The case of Andreas J. Petterson v. Allen S. Sweet took place in Peoria, Illinois and was decided on July 27, 1883. The legal dispute arose from a forcible detainer action by plaintiff Andreas J. Petterson against defendant Allen S. Sweet over possession of a portion of a house. Initially, Sweet had occupied the premises under an agreement to pay rent to Petterson, who claimed to be the landlord after the death of the prior landlord, Charles Etting. Sweet paid rent for five months but subsequently refused payment upon receiving notice from a third party, Henry Mansfield, who claimed ownership. Sweet contended that he had a lease arrangement with Etting prior to his death. Petterson proved the presence of a parol agreement but the trial excluded evidence Sweet offered that would support his claim to the title, including leases and tax payments made by Mansfield. The court found for the plaintiff despite arguments regarding the rightful landlord-tenant relationship, leading to Sweet's appeal.	Petterson claimed that he had a valid landlord-tenant agreement with Sweet, which required Sweet to pay $7 in rent per month. He argued that Sweet’s refusal to continue payments constituted unlawful detainer, and he sought recovery of possession of the premises from Sweet.	Sweet's defense was based on the assertion that he entered into occupancy under a lease with Charles Etting, who was the previous landlord. Sweet argued that he was entitled to continue his tenancy under the belief that Petterson was claiming a right to the property fraudulently and without just cause. He requested the admission of evidence to show his legitimate occupancy and landlord relationship through Etting and Mansfield.

In November 1883, Anna Viskocil purchased notes from Charles Drabek, a loan agent in Chicago, on behalf of Jan and Katerina Wacha. The notes, initially a $500 loan, were secured by a trust deed to Josef Matousek as trustee. Although Drabek handled the transaction, Viskocil took possession of the notes and received interest payments directly from him. The principal note was due in November 1885 and was extended for two years, during which time Viskocil and the Wachas had no direct communication. By April 1887, the Wachas discovered that Viskocil held crucial notes and subsequently filed a lawsuit seeking to have the trust deed declared a cloud on their title, along with a request for the trust deed and related notes to be delivered for cancellation. The Superior Court's initial ruling favored the Wachas, which prompted Viskocil to appeal the decision.	The plaintiffs, Jan and Katerina Wacha, argue that they made payments to Drabek as their loan agent and wish to have the trust deed executed in favor of Matousek and the notes it secured canceled as they believe Drabek's handling of the transaction improperly impacted their relationship with Viskocil.	Anna Viskocil contends that Drabek was not her agent for collecting the notes, asserting that any payments made to him were done so at the risk of those making the payment. She emphasizes that fraudulent representations made by Drabek cannot be imposed on her as she was not privy to them and that customary practices in the industry do not bind her to the actions taken by Drabek without her authorization.

In September 1874, in Cook County, Illinois, A. C. Warriner, a commission merchant operating in Chicago, faced charges regarding the handling of goods he received on commission from Hafford & Company, based in Mattoon. The prosecution accused Warriner of failing to account for and pay over the proceeds from these goods, which he had sold but then misappropriated the proceeds for his own use. The jury found Warriner guilty of the charges, leading to a judgment that included a fine of four hundred dollars. Warriner sought to overturn the verdict, arguing that the evidence was insufficient and that improper evidence was admitted against him while excluding pertinent evidence in his favor.	The plaintiff, Hafford & Company, asserted that Warriner converted the proceeds from the sale of their goods for his personal use, which violated the terms of their commission agreement. They argued that although Warriner attempted to compensate them with checks, these checks were dishonored, evidencing that he had not fulfilled his obligation to account for the sales properly. Consequently, they sought restitution for the amount due, specifically $197.90, plus the imposition of relevant penalties.	Warriner contended that he followed the agreed-upon method of sending checks to Hafford & Company for the proceeds of the sales. He claimed that the mere issuance of checks satisfied his obligation and that any failure to keep the checks good did not constitute a legal offense. Furthermore, he suggested that there were extenuating circumstances regarding the unavailability of funds to honor the checks, arguing that the prosecution did not sufficiently demonstrate his wrongdoing beyond a reasonable doubt.

Asa B. Searls was involved in a legal case in 1852 in Illinois, where he was indicted alongside Amanda Hedley for living together in an open state of fornication. During the trial, which took place at the March term in the Lee Circuit Court, the presiding judge was Wilkinson. Searls was tried alone for the charges. The State's attorney requested jury instructions that suggested the offense could be established through mere circumstances raising presumption of cohabitation and unlawful intimacy. The court's instructions implied that a single act of sexual intercourse could support a conviction, regardless of whether Searls and Hedley actually lived together. The court found this instruction to be erroneous as it did not require sufficient proof of cohabitation nor uphold the standards of the statute meant to prevent public scandal and disgrace arising from open illicit intimacy. The outcome indicated a flaw in the jury's instruction regarding the necessary proof for such a conviction.	The plaintiff, Asa B. Searls, contended that the jury was misled by the trial court's instructions, which allowed for a conviction based on minimal evidence of unlawful intimacy and did not adequately require proof of persistent cohabitation. Searls sought to reverse the judgment based on these erroneous instructions that failed to uphold the legal standards for establishing the crime of fornication.	The defense, representing the People, argued that the evidence presented met the legal threshold for proving the offense of fornication. They maintained that the jury instructions, as requested by the State's attorney, were appropriate and sufficient in establishing the presumption of unlawful intimacy, concluding that a conviction could be sustained based on the circumstances indicated by the evidence.

The case of Thomas G. Riley v. John Du Bois took place in February 1884 in Livingston County, Illinois. The plaintiff, Thomas G. Riley, sold a cow to the defendant, John Du Bois, for four cents per pound based on the cow's live weight. The cow was selected from among others in Riley's pasture and was meant to be weighed on his scales before payment. On the day after the cow was selected, Du Bois's agents attempted to catch her, but she broke loose and ran onto a neighboring farm. After some pursuit, Riley caught the cow and tied her to some willows. Riley and Du Bois's agents agreed that Du Bois would return to kill the cow. However, they didn't come back until Sunday morning, and by then, the cow was found dead. The case centered around whether Riley had delivered the cow and whether the loss incurred from the death of the cow was Riley’s or Du Bois's responsibility based on the terms of their agreement.	The plaintiff, Riley, argued that a valid agreement was made regarding the sale of the cow, and that the cow should be considered delivered when tied at the willows. He maintained that any claim for payment was waived due to the agreement to kill the cow at that location. Riley contended that the death of the cow was not his responsibility, as he had fulfilled his part of the sale by delivering and securing the cow, regardless of the payment being made at that time.	The defendant, Du Bois, claimed that since the cow was never officially delivered to him before her death, he should not be held responsible for payment. He argued that there was no formal acceptance of the cow when she was tied to the willows, and therefore the risk of loss remained with Riley until the cow was killed and processed as agreed. Du Bois maintained that any agreements made after the cow's death were irrelevant to their original contract.

In the case of Thomas Padfield v. William R. Padfield, decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in June 1873, the events unfolded around April 26, 1869, when Thomas Padfield transferred a substantial amount of promissory notes, totaling $42,800 in principal and $16,000 in accrued interest, to his son, William B. Padfield. This transfer was made for the purpose of collection, with the understanding that William would pay Thomas $2,000 annually for his support during his lifetime. The transaction had additional stipulations regarding the distribution of proceeds after Thomas's death, intending to benefit two of Thomas’s children. However, William allegedly collected sums from these notes and refused to account for them. The case arose when Thomas sought a legal account of the collected funds and a return of uncollected notes. The Circuit Court dismissed Thomas's bill in favor of his son, leading to this appeal.	Thomas Padfield, the plaintiff, claimed that his son, William, collected funds from a large sum of promissory notes entrusted to him for collection but failed to account for the amounts received. Thomas requested an accounting of the collected funds and sought the return of any uncollected notes, asserting that the notes were meant to be managed and collected by William on his behalf.	William B. Padfield, the defendant, denied the allegations and argued that the notes were assigned to him as part of a contractual agreement. He claimed that one-third of the notes were transferred outright to him, while the other two-thirds were to be held in trust to ensure Thomas's support and to eventually be distributed according to the latter's will. William maintained that the contractual terms clearly established his ownership and responsibilities regarding the notes.

In September 1873, in Stephenson County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Paul B. Adams (the plaintiff) and John B. Ozburn, Thomas Ozburn, David W. Ozburn, and William Ozburn (the defendants), regarding damage caused to Adams' crops by the defendants' livestock. The incident occurred on adjoining farms that were separated by a division fence. Adams owned and maintained one-half of the fence, while the defendants owned and were responsible for the other half. It was established that the defendants' portion of the fence was inadequate to prevent their animals from escaping and destroying Adams' crops. Initially, Adams won a judgment of $23 in a justice of the peace court, which the defendants appealed. Upon further trial in the circuit court, a jury awarded Adams $75, concluding that the insufficient fence on the defendants' side allowed their livestock to cause damage. Both sides acknowledged that the animals were owned separately but were kept in a common herd by the defendants, who exercised joint control over them.	Paul B. Adams claimed that the inadequacy of the defendants' portion of the division fence caused his crops to be destroyed by their livestock. He sought compensation for the damages, arguing that the defendants were fully responsible due to their failure to maintain a proper fence.	The defendants contested the judgment on two main arguments. First, they claimed that Adams’ portion of the fence was also defective, suggesting that the damage might have been caused by the stock crossing over his fence rather than theirs. Second, they argued that since the livestock belonged to them in severalty and not jointly, a single action against all defendants should not be maintainable.

The case "Commissioners of Highways v. David E. Newby, by his Next Friend" originated in the Circuit Court of Clay County, Illinois, on June 15, 1889. The dispute began when David E. Newby, a minor and non-resident owner of 40 acres in Clay County, contested the establishment of a road over his property by the Commissioners of Highways. Newby claimed that the order to open the road was issued through irregular and illegal proceedings, which he argued rendered the order void. His legal representative filed a petition seeking a common law writ of certiorari to examine the records and proceedings of the highway commissioners, asserting they violated proper legal and constitutional protocols. Upon review, the Circuit Court quashed the road's establishment order and required the defendants to pay court costs. This ruling prompted the Commissioners of Highways to appeal, asserting various errors in the Circuit Court's decision regarding the striking of amended records, demurrer to their responses, and the quashing of the established road order.	Newby contended that the proceedings undertaken by the Commissioners to establish the road were flawed. He argued that there was no lawful agreement on compensation for the use of his property and that necessary procedural steps were not followed, particularly concerning the assessment of damages by a jury as mandated by statute. He claimed that the absence of these prerequisites rendered the establishment of the road void and thus sought a writ of certiorari to authenticate this claim and have the order quashed.	The Commissioners of Highways maintained that the Circuit Court made several errors, including improperly striking their amended records and failing to recognize that the questioned proceedings complied with legal standards. They also argued that the writ of certiorari was barred by the petitioner’s delay and inaction (laches). They asserted that the order to open the road should not have been quashed, as they believed their actions were within their legal jurisdiction and followed statutory requirements.

In February 1850, in Belvidere, Boone County, Illinois, Arasmus D. Bishop needed a $400 loan before traveling to California. He contracted with Joseph R. Williams, who agreed to provide the loan under the condition that Bishop would convey certain real estate to him. Bishop conveyed the property through a deed and, in return, Williams executed a bond to reconvey the property back to Bishop within two years for an amount of $800. The plaintiffs, comprising Bishop's heirs, argued that the transaction was, in reality, a loan secured by a mortgage on the property, not an absolute sale. After Bishop's death, a legal dispute arose when Williams refused to reconvey the property despite monetary offers from Bishop's heirs. The case eventually required a jury to determine the true nature of the transaction, leading to a significant court ruling.	The plaintiffs contended that the deed transfer to Williams was merely a security for the loan of $400 and that the agreement constituted usurious interest, making the transaction effectively a mortgage. They sought to redeem the property, claiming that Williams refused to execute a reconveyance despite multiple attempts to pay the loan amount. They requested an account of the funds due and sought recovery of the property.	The defendant, Williams, argued that the transaction was an outright sale of the property and that the bond for reconveyance was a separate agreement. He maintained that there was neither a loan circumstance nor any understanding that the deed was a mortgage. Williams asserted that he had legitimate ownership of the property and had remained in possession since the sale.

The case "Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company v. George Trayes" took place on the evening of November 25, 1883, in Chicago. The incident occurred during dark and stormy weather, with rain and sleet affecting visibility. George Trayes was crossing Kinzie Street at Bobey Street when he was struck by a locomotive and tender that the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company was backing across the intersection. Trayes was hit on his right shoulder and suffered significant injuries, resulting in a substantial loss of use of his right arm. Testimony revealed that the locomotive did not comply with a city ordinance requiring a "brilliant and conspicuous light" at the front; only a red lantern was affixed to the corner of the tender. Noise from a passing freight train may have also masked the sound of the locomotive's bell. The jury was tasked with determining the facts, including whether the railway company had been negligent in failing to provide adequate warnings of their approach.	George Trayes, the plaintiff, claimed that the Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company acted negligently by failing to adequately signal the approach of their locomotive and tender, contributing to his injury. He referenced the violation of a city ordinance requiring a bright light on the locomotive and contended that the minimal warning provided (a single red lantern) was insufficient on a dark night, especially considering the presence of a competing noise from a freight train. Trayes sought damages for the personal injuries he sustained as a result of this negligence.	The Chicago & Northwestern Railway Company, the defendant, argued that they had followed legal protocols in their signaling and operations. They claimed the presence of the locomotive and the ringing of the bell were adequate warnings, and they contested the assertion that the red lantern did not comply with regulations. The railway company maintained that any fault for Trayes’s injuries could not be attributed to them, suggesting that the circumstances around the incident did not constitute negligence.

Urban B. Harris filed a replevin action in 1888 against Martha M. McCasland to recover a piano. The case originated in Bond County, Illinois, after John McOasland, Cora McOasland's father, promised his wife to buy Cora a piano as consideration for her signing a deed to convey their farm. John bought the piano, which remained under Cora's exclusive custody until she turned 21 in February 1887. John later incurred debts, which led him to execute a note to Harris and to transfer ownership of the piano to him through an informal bill of sale. However, Cora claimed ownership, asserting her rights in a letter to Harris. When Harris attempted to take possession of the piano, Martha, as Cora’s mother, defended the claim, stating that the piano belonged to Cora or was part of the consideration for her dower’s release. The jury trial at the Circuit Court (presided by B. H. Canby) resulted in the instruction that a demand for the piano was required before replevin could be maintained, which was central to the case.	The plaintiff, Urban B. Harris, argued that the piano had been conveyed to him by John McOasland as security for a debt, and he sought possession through replevin. Harris claimed the right of ownership based on the bill of sale executed by John, asserting that such transfer ignored Cora’s ownership claim.	The defendant, Martha M. McCasland, contended that the piano belonged to her daughter, Cora, as part of an agreement made between John McOasland and herself regarding the farm and the piano. She argued that since the piano was given to Cora as a gift, it could not be taken back, especially without a formal demand and refusal. Martha maintained that Cora's possession was rightful, and as such, Harris could not claim it through replevin.

The case of Milford D. Buchanan v. The International Bank was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court in September 1875. It arose from a series of financial transactions involving Alpheus C. Badger and the International Bank. On January 19, 1871, Badger executed two trust deeds securing two promissory notes, each for $6,666.66, in favor of Samuel J. Walker. These debts formed the basis for the conflict, as Walker later borrowed $9,500 from the bank and used the notes as collateral. The complexity increased when Walker had substantial other debts (over $2 million), leading to disputes over the proper application of collateral to various debts. Buchanan, as the cashier for a commercial loan company, purchased the notes without knowledge of prior liens, claiming they were free of encumbrance. Yet, the court found that the trust deeds had been recorded before the transactions with Kinney (where Buchanan acquired his interest), and therefore Buchanan's purchase was subject to these prior claims. The case raised issues regarding the validity of the trust deeds, the contractual obligations related to collateral, and the extent of the bank's security rights.	Milford D. Buchanan's primary argument centered on his claim to the premises that were secured by the trust deeds. He sought to cancel the trust deeds executed by Badger, asserting that he was a bona fide purchaser of the property. He contended that he had no actual notice of the prior liens and relied on the representations made by Walker regarding the clear title to the premises. Buchanan requested that the court recognize his rights in the property free from the International Bank's claims.	The International Bank, in its defense, argued that the trust deeds held priority since they were recorded before Buchanan's purchase. The bank maintained that the trust deeds were valid security for not only the specific debts they were tied to but also for any and all other debts Walker incurred, as per a prior agreement. The bank requested the court to enforce the trust deeds, allowing the sale of the secured property, with the proceeds applied to settle the debts owed to them by Walker.

On December 22, 1868, an election was held in the town of Lacón, Marshall County, Illinois, where a majority voted in favor of a $60,000 subscription to the capital stock of the Hamilton, Lacón and Eastern Railroad Company. However, at the time, no law empowered the town to hold such an election or to become a stockholder in the railroad. Subsequently, on March 5, 1869, the Illinois legislature passed an act aimed at legalizing this election and its results, allowing the town to bind itself to the railroad company. The town’s supervisor subscribed to the stock, issuing sixty bonds of $1,000 each which provided for annual interest. George O. Barnes purchased one of these bonds and initiated a lawsuit against the town to recover the payment due. The legal contention revolved around whether the town’s vote and subsequent subscription were valid, given the lack of legal authority at the time of the election.	The plaintiff, George O. Barnes, argued that he was entitled to payment on the bond he purchased, as he claimed to be an innocent purchaser for value. He contended that the subsequent legislative act legitimizing the town's election and subscription should protect the validity of his bond. Barnes sought recovery of the amount due under the bond, asserting that the actions taken by the town's supervisor were lawful due to the legislative endorsement.	The Town of Lacon contended that the election held in 1868 was void as there was no legal authority for it, making any subsequent actions based on that election (including the bond issuance) also invalid. The town asserted that the curator act passed by the legislature could not retroactively confer authority that was not present at the time of the election. Thus, they argued, the bonds were absolutely void, leaving Barnes with no legal claim to enforce them.

Isaac G. Israel initiated a legal action against William T. Reynolds and others in St. Louis, Illinois, around December 1849. The case revolved around an agreement made in May 1848, where Reynolds & Co. promised to pay for a boiler that Israel had purchased for his sawmill, with a cost not exceeding $350. Israel filed a declaration comprising five counts against the defendants, alleging breach of the agreement. The defendants responded with a general demurrer to the first four special counts and the fifth common count. The Circuit Court initially sustained the demurrer for the first five counts, leading to a jury trial that resulted in a verdict for the defendants. Israel subsequently sought a new trial, which was denied. The case highlights intricate legal arguments regarding the nature of the written agreement, considerations in declarations, and issues around the specificity and validity of claims made by the plaintiff.	The plaintiff, Isaac G. Israel, claimed that the defendants, as co-partners, entered into a written agreement to pay him for a boiler purchased for his sawmill. He argued that the defendants breached their promise and requested payment of the specified amount based on the terms of the written agreement. The plaintiff maintained that he had suffered damages due to the defendants’ failure to fulfill their obligations.	The defendants argued that the first four counts of Israel's declaration were invalid as the written agreement did not meet statutory requirements for enforceability. They contended that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate a sufficient consideration for the agreement and that he had not adequately proved damages. Additionally, they claimed that the general issue plea to the common count had no merit, thereby supporting their motion against the plaintiff's claims.

In September 1872, in Woodford County, Illinois, a legal dispute arose between Anthony Hazelbaker and Mary Ann Goodfellow regarding the ownership of approximately five hundred bushels of corn and a mule. The case was initiated by Mary Ann Goodfellow (the plaintiff), who claimed these items as her sole property. The corn had been cultivated by her and their children after Hazelbaker deserted the family about three years prior, stating he would support himself and that they must do the same. During the marriage, Goodfellow had rented the land and paid for its cultivation herself. The husband made no claim to the corn, having only provided minimal labor for which he was compensated by Goodfellow. The mule was associated with a mare obtained from a horse bought with Goodfellow's earnings before the enactment of a significant statute in 1869, which established that a married woman could retain her own earnings free from her husband's debts. The main contention revolved around whether the crops and mule were subject to the husband's debts, especially after he abandoned the family, underlining the implications of the 1869 law that sought to protect a wife's property in cases of abandonment.	Mary Ann Goodfellow argued that under the Illinois statute enacted in 1869, her earnings and those of her children were protected from her husband's debts because he had deserted the family. She claimed ownership of the corn and the mule, asserting that both the cultivation and transaction regarding the mule were under her control and funding post-abandonment, thus making them exempt from her husband’s creditors.	Anthony Hazelbaker contended that the corn and mule rightfully belonged to him as they were accrued or purchased with his resources prior to the enactment of the 1869 statute. He argued that the corn was cultivated during their marriage, and since the horse (which was traded for the mare from which the mule came) was bought with money from him, the mule also belonged to him and should be liable for repayment of his debts.

In December 1847, the Illinois Supreme Court heard a case titled "Daniel O. Dickinson, appellant, v. Eli Whitney, appellee," which originated in the Lake Circuit Court. The dispute involved Eli Whitney, who had stored 726 bushels of wheat with Daniel O. Dickinson. Whitney contended that Dickinson had sold his wheat without authorization and had not paid him the money owed for it. Evidence was presented in court, including a receipt and testimonies from multiple witnesses. Dickinson had informed others that he sold the wheat at a price of one dollar per bushel and claimed to have contracted the wheat to the captain of the steamboat Empire. However, as the situation developed, it became apparent that Dickinson might have mixed Whitney’s wheat with others in his warehouse, and during the trial, he was pressed on whether he had sold the wheat as per Whitney's instructions. Ultimately, the jury had to determine if Dickinson had indeed sold the wheat and thus owed the amount stated by Whitney.	Eli Whitney, the plaintiff, argued that Daniel O. Dickinson had wrongfully sold his wheat and had received payment for it, constituting a breach of his duty to deliver the proceeds. Whitney sought compensation for the loss, claiming he was entitled to the money that Dickinson had received from the sale of the wheat. He asserted that Dickinson was liable for money had and received.	Daniel O. Dickinson, the defendant, contended that he had either contracted to sell Whitney's wheat at the agreed price and was simply preparing to deliver it or that he was not bound to deliver the same wheat but rather a quantity of equal quality. He also argued that the loss of wheat in his possession could be attributed to wastage and that he should not be held accountable for amounts that exceeded what was stored. Additionally, he claimed that he should be exonerated unless the jury found he had failed to follow instructions concerning the sale.

In 1872, in Enfield, Illinois, Jonah Morlan delivered a quantity of oats to the firm of William A. Howell, James W. Millspaugh, and Charles Carroll, partners acting as wharfingers. The oats were intended for shipment to John T. Moore & Co. in New Orleans. However, the plaintiffs (Morlan) alleged that the defendants failed to follow shipping instructions and instead forwarded the oats to another party, C. C. Twitchell, leading to a loss when Twitchell's business failed. The case was initially tried in 1873 in the Circuit Court of Gallatin County, where the jury ruled in favor of Morlan, granting him $433.23. Yet, a formal judgment was not entered, prompting an appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. The venue then shifted to White County, where a new judgment was entered "nunc pro tunc" by the court, restoring the initial verdict. The case revolved around whether the defendants had indeed been notified of the shipment change and their liability for the lost oats.	The plaintiff, Jonah Morlan, claimed the defendants failed to comply with his shipping instructions regarding oats, resulting in a financial loss when the oats were shipped to the wrong party. Morlan sought recovery of the oats' value amounting to $433.23, asserting that he provided clear instructions that were ignored by the defendants, who did not act with due diligence in following the changes.	The defendants, represented by Howell, Millspaugh, and Carroll, contended that they did not receive the request to change the shipment destination of the oats and argued that the jury's decision was not supported by sufficient evidence. They claimed that since only one of them testified to not receiving the letter instructing the change, there was insufficient evidence to establish that notification occurred, positing that the judgment should be overturned.

On February 11, 1869, Henry H. Walker executed a deed of trust in favor of Abraham S. Prather, which was recorded in Cook County, Illinois, on July 12, 1869. Prather sold the property to John T. Matthews on June 25, 1874, but the deed was not recorded until November 11, 1874. On March 6, 1875, Matthews sold part of the land to Albert Cooper. In the interim, on November 2, 1871, Walker had transferred a portion of the property to Samuel J. Walker, whose subsequent sale of it to Henry E. Pickett led to a deed of trust being executed to John G. Rogers to secure promissory notes held by Samuel J. Walker. O. B. Heaton purchased these notes without knowledge of Prather's deed of trust and later acquired the property through a sale conducted by Rogers on September 23, 1874. Heaton argued that he had no actual or constructive notice of Prather’s deed during his purchase. However, the case also noted that a fire had destroyed records in Cook County on October 9, 1871. The court was tasked with addressing whether Heaton could redeem the property from the deed of trust given the circumstances of the property’s title history.	Edgar S. Heaton, as the appellant, sought to redeem property that he claimed he rightfully acquired. He contended he was entitled to treat the appellees as holding the title as Prather did prior to his sale and argued that he had no actual or constructive notice of Prather's deed of trust when he made his purchase based on an attorney's opinion stating that the title was clear.	The appellees, led by Prather, argued that Heaton was bound by constructive notice of the deed of trust because it had been recorded, and previous legal precedents affirmed that buyers are responsible for being aware of such records. They maintained that Heaton could not ignore the prior mortgaging of the property and that they were purchasers in good faith who had acquired an absolute title.

George H. Hess brought a case against The People ex rel. H. B. Miller concerning an application for judgment against delinquent lands for state and county taxes at the Cook County court during the June term of 1875. On June 14, the county court established a deadline for objections to the judgment, requiring them to be filed by 10 AM on June 21. Hess did not submit objections by that deadline. After the deadline passed, he appeared in court to challenge the judgment against his land as delinquent, but the court denied his request, declaring him in default. On July 1, 1875, Hess attempted again to submit objections and requested that the default be set aside, which the court refused. The court continued examining the delinquent tax list and eventually entered a formal final judgment against Hess’s lands for unpaid taxes. Hess sought an appeal to the circuit court but was denied, leading him to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court.	The plaintiff, George H. Hess, contended that he had the right to file objections to the judgment against his property even after the designated deadline set by the county court. He argued that the statute allowed for objections to be made at any time before final judgment, and he insisted that the county court erred by affirming the default against him and not permitting an appeal to the circuit court.	The defendant, The People ex rel. H. B. Miller, maintained that the county court acted within its lawful authority by enforcing a rule that limited the time for filing objections.
