During the proceedings, a summons was issued to Fulton, but only McCoy was served, leading to complications when McCormick was defaulted due to his withdrawal from the case. The Circuit Court dismissed the appeal and rendered a judgment including damages and costs. McCormick contested this dismissal, raising issues regarding the proper service of the nominal plaintiff, Fulton, highlighting that Fulton's absence jeopardized his right to defend against any claims. The case, therefore, revolved around the procedural requirement that all necessary parties must be properly represented in court before a judgment can be made.	The plaintiff, represented by Fulton for McCoy, argued that McCormick owed the amount specified in the promissory note and sought damages and costs following the default judgment. The claims were based on the lack of service on Fulton, which the Circuit Court failed to address, leading to the improper dismissal of McCormick's appeal.	McCormick's primary defense centered on the procedural errors that occurred prior to the judgment, emphasizing that Fulton, as the nominal plaintiff, had not been served properly. He contended that without Fulton's appearance in court, the default judgment against him was invalid, and he had the right to a fair trial with all essential parties present.

The case, "The Great Western Telegraph Company, for use of Elias R. Bowen, Receiver, v. F. D. Gray," was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on May 27, 1887. The core issue arose from a contract between the Great Western Telegraph Company and F. D. Gray, who was a subscriber to the company's capital stock. The company had appointed Elias R. Bowen as a receiver due to its financial difficulties, with debts exceeding $400,000. The plaintiff sought to recover $875 from Gray, representing 35% of the par value of 100 shares of stock, which were not fully paid. Prior to this case, the company had undergone a chancery suit in which it was determined that not all stockholders could be made parties to it, thus prompting an assessment on unpaid stock subscriptions. The key participants included Elias R. Bowen (receiver), F. D. Gray (defendant), and the board of directors of the Great Western Telegraph Company. The circuit court sustained a demurrer to the plaintiff's declaration, leading to the current appeal.	The plaintiff argued that Gray, as a stockholder of the Great Western Telegraph Company, was liable for the unpaid assessment under the terms of the subscription agreement. The plaintiff maintained that a previous court ruling had established the necessity for the collection of this assessment to satisfy the company's debts, and the receiver had the authority to initiate this action against Gray.	The defendant, F. D. Gray, contended that he was not a party to the original suit in which the receiver was appointed, nor was he involved in the proceedings that resulted in the assessment order. He argued that the declaration did not adequately demonstrate that he was legally bound by those proceedings, thereby invalidating the claim against him for the assessment amount.

In 1883, in Ford County, Illinois, James Mix appealed to the Illinois Supreme Court regarding a judgment rendered by the county court on delinquent taxes and special assessments against certain lands and town lots he claimed to own. Mix filed written objections against the judgment, but the county court overruled his objections. The case was initially submitted for decision in January 1879, leading to a reversal of the county court's judgment due to insufficient proof regarding the necessary advertisement for judgment against the delinquent properties. However, upon rehearing in January 1880, the court considered Mix's defense on the merits, which effectively waived his objections to any defects in notice or advertisement. The court engaged with various legal principles regarding tax notice and jurisdiction, ruling that as long as the property owner's appearance was made and a defense was filed regarding the merits of the taxes, the defect in advertisement did not negate the court's jurisdiction. Additionally, it was found that the ordinances regarding tax levies by the city of Paxton were valid even without proof of publication, as prior appropriations were necessary before such levies could be made.	James Mix, the plaintiff, argued that the judgment against his properties was invalid due to procedural issues involving the advertisement for judgment against delinquent taxes. He asserted that the notices were not proven as statute required, which he claimed deprived the court of jurisdiction to render judgment against his properties. Mix sought reversal of the county court's judgment and relief from the tax assessments and special charges on his land.	The defendant, The People ex rel. John B. Shaw, contended that Mix had waived his objections by entering an appearance and defending against the tax liabilities on the merits. The defense argued that the advertisement of delinquent lands acted as a summons and that any procedural defects were irrelevant, as Mix engaged in the case substantively. They highlighted that all required information was present in the delinquent list filed and that any discrepancies claimed by Mix were not raised properly during the original proceedings.

The case "James R. Williams v. The People ex rel. Samuel J. Wilson, Collector" took place in White County, Illinois, with a decision handed down by the Illinois Supreme Court on April 22, 1890. James R. Williams, a taxpayer, contested a judgment against his lands for taxes owed in relation to $99,500 in bonds issued by White County in 1872 to the Cairo and Vincennes Railroad Company. The bonds were authorized based on an election held on October 1, 1867, which Williams argued was invalid due to the lack of proper notice required by law. The election notice was supposed to provide at least 30 days' notice, but the order to hold the election was issued only 27 days prior, rendering the election and subsequent bond issuance illegal. The court had to determine the validity of the bonds issued and whether the subscription to the stock of the railroad company could be legitimized under existing law.	Williams claimed that the bonds were invalid due to the failure to provide required notice for the election held to authorize them. He argued that without a legally conducted election and valid approval from the voters, the county lacked the authority to issue the bonds. Therefore, he requested that the judgment against his property, meant to cover taxes for the interest of these bonds, be overturned.	Samuel J. Wilson, as the collector, defended the validity of the bonds by asserting that the election had indeed taken place and that subsequent legislative acts could validate prior defects in the election process. He contended that the 1869 act, which declared prior elections valid, should apply in this instance. Wilson's argument rested on the premise that any procedural issues could be cured by subsequent legislative actions, maintaining the necessity of the bonds for financing the railroad project.

On January 10, 1889, the case of Matthew Conner et al. v. Charles A. Akin, Administrator, etc., was heard in the Illinois Appellate Court. This case stemmed from a citation issued by the County Court of Franklin County, which ordered the appellants, Matthew Conner and Julia Conner, to appear and answer to allegations made by Charles A. Akin, the administrator of the estate of Sarah Hammons, who had died intestate on April 6, 1878. The citation was initiated by Joseph Hammons, who claimed that the Conners had either concealed or embezzled assets belonging to the deceased's estate. The case moved through the County Court and then to the Circuit Court, where it was decided against the appellants, prompting their appeal to the Appellate Court. The core of the evidence revolved around claims that a sum of $1,600 from the deceased's estate had been received by the Conners. However, upon review, the court found no sufficient evidence to substantiate these claims against both Conners, especially concerning Mathew Conner's involvement, leading to significant legal questions about the findings of the lower court.	The plaintiff, represented by Charles A. Akin, contended that Mathew Conner and Julia Conner had concealed and embezzled funds belonging to the estate of Sarah Hammons. The plaintiff's primary argument rested on claims that the Conners had $1,600 in their possession at the time of Hammons's death, which belonged to her estate. The plaintiff sought to compel the Conners to return these alleged funds to the estate through legal proceedings instigated by the citation.	The defendants, Matthew Conner and Julia Conner, rejected the allegations of embezzlement and concealment, arguing that there was insufficient evidence to support the claims made against them, particularly as it pertained to Mathew Conner. The defense maintained that even if Julia Conner had received funds, the evidence did not legally justify holding Mathew accountable for the alleged joint possession, thus contesting the Circuit Court's order requiring them to jointly return the amount.

George W. Lawrence filed a divorce suit against Julia S. Lawrence on August 27, 1872, in the Superior Court of Cook County, Illinois, following the procedures applicable to non-resident defendants, which included notifying Julia through a publication. By default, since Julia did not appear in court, the divorce was granted, and a decree was entered in favor of George. However, at a later date in May 1873, Julia filed a petition stating she had not received proper notice of the divorce other than through publication. This petition was allowed, and she subsequently denied the allegations in George's original divorce bill, except for the marriage. A jury ultimately heard the case, resulting in a verdict favoring Julia, which led to the previous divorce decree being set aside and the dismissal of George's complaint. The case underscores the issues surrounding divorce proceedings, non-resident notifications, and the rights of those involved in divorce decrees.	George W. Lawrence (the plaintiff) argued that the divorce decree should stand, asserting that his ex-wife's entry into the case was improper and that any claims she had regarding lack of notice or the ability to contest the divorce should not apply, particularly since he remarried during the process.	Julia S. Lawrence (the defendant) contended that the divorce decree was not valid because she had not been properly notified outside of publication in a newspaper. She invoked the provisions of the Chancery Practice Act, asserting her right to contest the original ruling due to inadequate notice, and sought to have the divorce decree annulled.

In 1851, in Macoupin County, Illinois, a case arose between William Weir and David C. Stephenson involving a trespass claim regarding shooting a yoke of steers. The incident led to a lawsuit initiated by Stephenson against Weir before a justice of the peace, demanding fifty dollars in compensation for the damages. During the trial, a jury found that Weir should pay fifty dollars for the steers and awarded five dollars in damages and costs. Following this verdict, Weir admitted to shooting the steers and agreed to have their value assessed, resulting in the jury determining their worth as fifty dollars. After the trial, Weir took possession of the steers and sold them, which later became a point of contention. In the circuit court, Weir's appeal was initially dismissed, but the court ultimately ruled that the original action of trespass was transformed into a new suit for the steers' value. The proffered agreement between the parties did not prevent Weir from appealing, as the nature of the lawsuit significantly changed, thus warranting a new assessment in the circuit court.	David Stephenson claimed that William Weir unlawfully shot his steers, arguing that as a result, he was entitled to monetary damages. Stephenson sought compensation based on the jury's finding of the steers' value and additional damages incurred during the process of the trial.	William Weir acknowledged the trespass but argued that the original agreement allowed him to determine the steers' value through the jury's verdict. He contended that the informal nature of the original verdict did not preclude him from appealing the case. Weir maintained that the nature of the suit changed due to the mutual consent of both parties, thus challenging any limitations previously imposed by the initial claim amount listed on the summons.

In 1860, a legal dispute arose in Ogle County, Illinois, involving Frederick G. Petrie, the sheriff at the time, who acted on behalf of John Reed against John Fisher and others. A replevin action commenced on October 30, 1860, led to the execution of a replevin bond, which was meant to protect Fisher from unlawful property seizure. Petrie, however, left office without executing the writ. His successor issued an alias writ on December 13, 1860, which was executed. The replevin action was tried on June 23, 1862, resulting in a judgment for Fisher and a return of the property not being fulfilled. Petrie subsequently brought this action on the replevin bond to seek a remedy for Fisher's alleged failure to meet the bond's conditions.	The plaintiff, Petrie, argued that the replevin bond was valid and enforceable despite his successor executing the writ, claiming that the bond was intended to indemnify the defendant if the plaintiff failed to maintain the replevin suit effectively. Thus, he sought damages based on the conditions of the bond that were allegedly breached since the property had not been returned as ordered by the court.	The defendants, led by Fisher, contended that the bond could not be enforced as it was executed in favor of Petrie, who did not execute the writ himself. They maintained that since the bond was nominally payable to Petrie, they should not be held responsible after his term ended and his successor executed the writ without obtaining a new bond. They asserted that this procedural defect barred any claims against them.

The case of *Moline Wagon Company v. Preston & Company* took place in 1890 in Cook County, Illinois. It involved two corporate parties: the Moline Wagon Company (the appellant) and Preston & Company (the appellee). The core issue was whether certain negotiable papers, which the Moline Wagon Company had purchased from Preston & Company, could be returned. During the trial, Mr. Whittle, the business manager of Preston & Company, testified that there was no agreement allowing the return of the papers. The Moline Wagon Company attempted to cross-examine Whittle regarding a significant debt he owed to Preston & Company, aiming to demonstrate a potential bias in his testimony. However, the trial court sustained an objection against this line of questioning. Following this, the Moline Wagon Company presented witnesses who claimed that there was indeed an agreement allowing for the return of the papers, in direct contradiction to Whittle's testimony. The jury ultimately sided with Whittle, leading to a judgment in favor of Preston & Company. The Moline Wagon Company then appealed the ruling on the grounds that the trial court erred in excluding evidence that could have affected the jury's decision.	The Moline Wagon Company argued that the evidentiary ruling by the trial court was erroneous, specifically regarding the exclusion of cross-examination questions aimed at impeaching Mr. Whittle's credibility. They contended that such questioning was relevant to demonstrating Whittle's potential bias due to his debt to Preston & Company. The plaintiff sought to overturn the verdict and secure a judgment that recognized their right to return the negotiable paper.	Preston & Company defended against the plaintiff's claims by asserting that no agreement to return the negotiable papers existed. They aimed to establish the validity of Whittle's testimony, which denied any such agreement. Furthermore, they maintained that the trial court acted correctly in sustaining the objection to the cross-examination, arguing that the cross-examination attempted by the Moline Wagon Company was not relevant to the matter at hand.

The case "The Ohio, Indiana & Western Railway Co. v. Thomas J. Johnson, Administrator" originates from an incident on February 29, 1888, involving the railway company and the accidental death of George L. Johnson, a 17-year-old who worked part-time as a brakeman. Johnson had recently applied for a job, misrepresenting his age as 21. His father, Thomas J. Johnson, informed the conductor, Green, that his son was too young for such work, which Green denied. On the day of the incident, Johnson was on a train traveling from Peoria to Bloomington when he was believed to have been struck by a projecting water spout that had been left unsecured by the railway company. Witnesses testified that Johnson appeared to have been knocked off the train as it descended a grade. He was later found unconscious and succumbed to his injuries days later. The court examined questions of negligence related to the railway's maintenance of the water spout and the conditions surrounding the accident, with evidence suggesting that the apparatus was indeed left in a dangerous state.	The plaintiff, Thomas J. Johnson, claimed damages for the wrongful death of his son, arguing that the railway company was negligent in leaving the water spout in a hazardous condition, which resulted in his son's fatal injuries. He requested compensation that appropriately reflected the pecuniary loss incurred due to the death of his son, considering his son’s potential to contribute to the family financially.	The defendant, Ohio, Indiana & Western Railway Co., contended that they were not liable for the accident, arguing that the evidence did not clearly prove negligence or that Johnson was struck by the water spout while working. They sought to dismiss the claims based on a lack of definitive proof establishing their responsibility for the incident and questioned the framework used to determine damages.

On May 5, 1886, in Will County, Illinois, E. J. Ogden, through his agent and attorney, entered a judgment against Ann Daly and Michael Daly for $89.95, including $25 for attorney's fees. This judgment was issued during a vacation of the court and without the Dalys’ knowledge or consent. The Dalys claimed that they had not executed the related note and warrant of attorney and that it was a forgery. Subsequently, an execution based on this judgment was issued, and the sheriff was set to levy the Dalys' property in North Joliet. In response, the Dalys filed a bill in chancery to vacate the judgment, seeking an injunction to prevent the sale of their property and a cancellation of the judgment. The case was heard in the Circuit Court, where Ogden and Reitz denied the allegations and contended the judgment was valid. The case went to an appellate court following a decree against the Dalys' claims.	The plaintiffs, Ann and Michael Daly, argued that the judgment against them was invalid as it was entered without their authority, knowledge, or consent. They claimed that the note and warrant of attorney associated with the judgment were forgeries and that they were not indebted to E. J. Ogden. Therefore, they sought a permanent injunction against the execution on their property and requested the cancellation of the fraudulent judgment.	The defendants, E. J. Ogden and Lorenz Reitz, denied all allegations made by the plaintiffs, asserting that the note and warrant of attorney were not forgeries and that the judgment was obtained lawfully. They argued that the plaintiffs were indeed indebted to E. J. Ogden for medical services and maintained that the evidence clearly supported the validity of the judgment. They requested the dismissal of the plaintiffs' bill to vacate the judgment.

Between October 17, 1885, in Jefferson City, Illinois, Joshua D. Gardiner was assaulted and robbed, being struck on the head, rendering him unconscious. W. H. Gardiner, acting on behalf of the injured Gardiner, accused Levi G. Mays of the assault. Mays, who had recently been living five miles away, was seen in the vicinity of the assault on the evening in question. Statements from witnesses—including a woman named Marion Hill—suggested suspicious behavior by Mays; however, Mays denied making any threats and maintained he was not at the Gardiner residence that night. After being bound over for trial and unable to post bail, Mays was acquitted of the charges against him in a subsequent trial. The case escalated to a claim of malicious prosecution against Gardiner based on the assertion of lacking probable cause for his accusations.	The plaintiff, Levi G. Mays, claimed malicious prosecution by W. H. Gardiner, arguing that Gardiner initiated charges against him without reasonable or probable cause. He sought damages from Gardiner, asserting that the prosecution caused him harm, despite his eventual acquittal of the assault charges.	The defendant, W. H. Gardiner, contended that he acted based on information he believed to be credible at the time of prosecution. He argued that there were sufficient grounds for suspicion of Mays' involvement in the crime, asserting that the evidence supported his actions and that he was justified in seeking legal recourse based on reasonable prudence and the advice of counsel.

The case "The City of Chicago v. W. W. Crosby" took place in 1884 in Chicago, Illinois. It stemmed from an ordinance that required property owners to maintain the sidewalks in front of their premises. The city of Chicago initiated legal action against W. W. Crosby, the owner of a property located at 27 Kingsbury Street, to recover a penalty for failing to repair a sidewalk that had become dangerously broken. Initially, the justice of the peace ruled in favor of Crosby, leading the city to appeal to the Criminal Court of Cook County. The trial confirmed that while Crosby was notified to repair the sidewalk, he denied any legal obligation to do so, stating that the damage was not caused by his actions. Meanwhile, the city argued that the ordinance imposed an obligation on him to maintain the sidewalk. This dispute over responsibility for repairing the sidewalk culminated in a series of court judgments that affirmed Crosby's position.	The plaintiff, the City of Chicago, claimed that W. W. Crosby violated a city ordinance requiring the maintenance of the sidewalk in front of his property. They sought a penalty against Crosby for his failure to repair the sidewalk, arguing that the ordinance necessitated property owners to ensure their sidewalks were safe and free from obstruction.	The defendant, W. W. Crosby, argued that he was not responsible for repairing the sidewalk as the damage had occurred naturally over time and was not caused by any actions of his own. He contended that the city had failed to fulfill its responsibilities to maintain the public street and that imposing such penalties on property owners was not permissible under the laws governing the jurisdiction.

The case "Lyon v. Blakney et al." was decided by the Illinois Appellate Court on February 25, 1886. The key individuals involved were the plaintiff, Lyon, and the defendants, Blakney and others. The legal dispute centered around the validity of an assignment of certain notes. The court below examined the circumstances surrounding the assignment, particularly focusing on the mental capacity of the party who assigned the notes. The judge handling the case, O. L. Davis, found that the individual was mentally incapacitated at the time of the assignment, which was a pivotal point in the case. Lyon challenged this finding, leading to the appeal.	The plaintiff, Lyon, argued that the assignment of the notes in question was valid and should be enforced. Lyon claimed that the evidence did not support the conclusion that the assigning party was mentally incapacitated. He sought to reverse the lower court's decision affirming the assignment's invalidity based on alleged mental incapacity.	The defendants, led by Blakney, argued that the lower court's finding of mental incapacity at the time of the assignment was correct. They contended that the evidence demonstrated that the assigning party lacked the mental capacity necessary to complete the assignment legally. The defendants requested that the appellate court uphold the lower court's decision affirming the assignment's invalidity.

In December 1854, in Greene County, Illinois, the Illinois Supreme Court reviewed a legal dispute initiated by David C. McAdams against Henry Boyd and Ellis. The case arose from an action of replevin, which occurs when someone seeks to recover goods claimed to be wrongfully taken or detained. McAdams claimed ownership of a buggy allegedly possessed by the defendants, Boyd and Ellis, who, despite requests, refused to return it. The defendants responded by pleading separately, with Boyd claiming he did not detain the buggy and Ellis asserting that the buggy belonged to him, not McAdams. The court found merit in the defendants' pleas and subsequently reversed the decision of the lower court.	The plaintiff, David C. McAdams, asserted that he was the rightful owner of the buggy and sought its recovery from the defendants. He claimed that they wrongfully detained the buggy and requested a court ruling to have it returned to him.	The defendants, Boyd and Ellis, contended that they did not unlawfully detain the buggy from McAdams. Boyd argued against the detention, while Ellis claimed ownership of the buggy, contending that McAdams had no right to maintain the action. They sought to have the court dismiss the case, asserting that the allegations against them did not warrant a judgment.

The case of John W. Seymour et al. v. Duncan Mackay et al. arose in Carroll County, Illinois, and was adjudicated by the Illinois Appellate Court, with the final decision issued on December 11, 1886. The litigation involved a dispute over a loan arranged in 1867, where John W. Seymour loaned David Belding $3,700 at ten percent interest, secured by a trust deed on certain lands. The trust deed was recorded in 1871 in the name of Seymour's wife, Helen M. Seymour, to protect their interests, especially due to Seymour's hazardous occupation on the railroad. In 1871, Helen was persuaded by her father, Belding, and Duncan Mackay to release the trust deed under the belief that it was necessary to secure additional funds for Belding. Consequently, Belding transferred the land to Mackay, who claimed to have paid off other debts. Seymour claimed that Mackay's involvement was fraudulent and that he had not consented to the release of the trust deed, leading to a cross-bill being filed to restore the trust deed, declare that the securities were still valid, and seek an accounting of the liens involved.	The plaintiffs, primarily through Seymour's cross-bill, argued that the release of the trust deed was procured through fraud and sought to have the cancellation declared void. They asserted that Mackay's actions misled them into relinquishing their rights over the property. Consequently, they requested the court to restore the trust deed, determine priorities among the liens held, cancel competing mortgages, and ultimately facilitate a sale of the land to satisfy the debt associated with the promissory note.	The defendant, Mackay, denied any wrongdoing or knowledge of the Helen M. Seymour trust deed's existence until the cross-bill was filed. He asserted that he did not hinder Belding from obtaining loans and refuted claims regarding misleading information about the land's value. Mackay argued that the release of the trust deed was conducted with full knowledge by Seymour and that any subsequent agreements or new notes accepted by Seymour constituted a ratification of the trust deed's release. He sought the dismissal of the claims against him related to the trust deed.

In September 1871, in Cook County, Illinois, the case of Samuel S. Hayes v. Johanna Moynihan was adjudicated in the Illinois Supreme Court. The conflict arose when Hayes sought to excavate his land adjacent to Moynihan's property to construct a brick building. He requested permission to extend his foundation beneath her wall and agreed to cover any damages that might occur to her building due to this construction. Following his construction activities, damages were claimed against Hayes for injuries sustained by Moynihan's brick building. The case had previously been tried, resulting in a reversal due to excessive damages being awarded. This trial concluded with a jury verdict that awarded damages $10 less than the prior amount. The testimony presented reflected conflicting estimates, with witnesses arguing for significantly different damage amounts, leading the court to evaluate the veracity of these claims.	Johanna Moynihan, the plaintiff, contended that as a result of Hayes's excavation and the subsequent construction of his building, significant damages were inflicted upon her property. Moynihan claimed that Hayes's promise to cover these damages constituted a valid agreement, and she sought recompense for the costs associated with the repairs required for her building.	Samuel S. Hayes, the defendant, argued that the damages were excessive and challenged the sufficiency of the evidence supporting the awarded amount. He contended that the agreement was not in writing and thus void under the statute of frauds. Hayes further asserted that the claim was inappropriate since no formal estimate of damages was requested before the lawsuit was initiated. He also sought the exclusion of certain cost items, like "risk," from the damage calculations.

Anson Collins and John Waggoner were involved in a legal dispute that escalated in December 1826 in Illinois. The case began when Waggoner sued Collins in replevin for the return of a cow. After a trial, the court found in favor of Waggoner, issuing a verdict and judgment that awarded him the cow. Collins had previously obtained a judgment against Waggoner that allowed him to execute against Waggoner's property, leading to the cow being seized and sold by a constable, wherein Collins became the purchaser. Waggoner contended that his original cause of action arose before May 1821 and highlighted that he had offered to pay the judgment with state bank notes or replevy the cow for three years, but Collins refused to allow it. The case turned on whether trespass could be claimed if there was an abuse of process, wherein it was determined that actions taken under an execution that had expired were unlawful, rendering both Collins and the constable liable for the tortious taking of the cow. The Illinois Supreme Court examined these details under Chief Justice Wilson's majority opinion.	Collins, the appellant, argued that the execution he obtained was legitimate and that his actions in having the cow seized were lawful. He claimed that Waggoner's defense lacked merit since he had already exhausted his legal remedies, and thus, the court should affirm the original judgment in his favor.	Waggoner, the appellee, contended that Collins had abused the execution process by continuing to enforce it after its expiration. He maintained that he had offered acceptable forms of payment and that Collins's refusal constituted an unlawful seizure, making Collins and the constable liable for trespass, which should prevail over Collins's claims.

In 1872, in Randolph County, Illinois, Robert J. Richmond brought a legal action against Mary Caldwell and Jane Nimmock regarding a debt dispute. The case arose from a penal bond written on February 1, 1867, in which the defendants agreed to sell multiple lots in the town of Eden for $800, secured by a promissory note due by February 1, 1870. Richmond claimed he had paid $760 towards the note, as Mary Caldwell had assured him the title to the lots was clear. However, after the payment, he learned Caldwell could not convey a perfect title to at least one of the lots—specifically, Lot No. 1—and argued this significant defect rendered the other lots mostly valueless. When the note became due, Richmond demanded a warranty deed and an abstract of title but did not pay the remaining amount due to the title issues. The court first ruled in favor of Richmond for $740 but did not specify the breakdown between debt and damages, prompting an appeal.	Robert J. Richmond's primary arguments were based on the assertion that Mary Caldwell misrepresented the state of the title to the properties, leading him to incur damages. He claimed Caldwell's failure to provide a warranty deed and her admission that she could not convey a clear title were in breach of the covenant under the penal bond. Richmond requested payment of his damages totaling $2,000 resulting from this breach and the inability to gain clear ownership of the property.	Mary Caldwell and Jane Nimmock defended against the claims by indicating that Richmond's pleadings were defective because they failed to demonstrate readiness to perform on his part. They raised the "nil debet" plea, arguing that Richmond’s claims regarding the title's defects were unfounded. Their position highlighted that this plea created a technical barrier to Richmond's claim, and they sought to dismiss the case or at least challenge the judgment awarding him damages.

Chalon Guard and others (the appellants) initiated a legal action in July 1851, in the Circuit Court of Hardin County, Illinois, concerning a debt related to an injunction bond. The case involved an agreement made on April 10, 1851, where the appellants consented to forbear from suing the appellee, James A. Whiteside, until December 25, 1851, in exchange for a horse valued at $75, which was delivered as part of the agreement. The lower court ruled on a plea filed by the defendants that claimed this agreement constituted a bar to the action, essentially arguing that the appellants had relinquished their right to take legal action until the specified date had passed. However, the agreement was contested via a demurrer that was sustained by the presiding Judge Denning, leading to a judgment against the appellants for damages amounting to $594.34.	The appellants claimed that the agreement to delay the lawsuit, which included the exchange of a horse, should not preclude their ability to pursue the debt recovery on the bond they were owed. They argued that the court's acceptance of the defendant's plea and demurrer was erroneous and that they should be allowed to proceed with their case.	The appellee, James A. Whiteside, contended that the agreement constituted an absolute release of the debt claims for the time specified, effectively preventing the appellants from bringing the lawsuit until after December 25, 1851. He claimed that the covenant not to sue within a limited timeframe should bar the action instituted by the appellants before that date had elapsed.
